Q. 104. (2, 2, 2

Contrary to his custom, Grotius has approached this epistle without a preface. We shall not depart from the received custom. Timothy, to whom the epistle was written, had Lystra as his homeland, Acts 16:1, which was a city of Lycaonia, Acts 13:6. Born of a Greek father and a Jewish mother, ch. 16:1, who is named Eunice, daughter of Lois, 2 Tim. 1:5; both the grandmother and the mother are commended there for their sincere faith, from which Timothy was instructed in the sacred scriptures from infancy, 2 Tim. 3:15. Grotius, in his preface to 2 Thessalonians, affirmed that his ancestors lived in Thessalonica and made Jason his relative, but both are without foundation. Origen, in his commentary on Romans 16, called Timothy a kinsman of Paul, but without a witness. It seems to be gathered that he was present with the Apostle not at Antioch in Syria, where the name of Christians arose, Acts 11, but at Antioch in Pisidia in Asia Minor, at Iconium, and at Lystra. 2 Tim. 3:10, although the afflictions endured there could have been known to him from the report of Paul, even though he was not yet present with him then, Acts 13 and 14. This is certain, that Paul took him as a companion of his travels at Lystra when he came there for the second time, and that testimony had been borne to Timothy of his integrity and virtue by the brothers who dwelt at Lystra and Iconium, Acts 16, which happened some years after those afflictions. Hence, not a few say that he was appointed the same as Bishop of Ephesus, which the Papists understand as a dignity and office superior to the order of presbyters; but what difference in the time of Paul or Timothy will ever be taught to have been in use? Cornelius à Lapide says he was created Archbishop, which was a proud title then clearly unknown to the Church, just as the notion of a Metropolitan Church among the Ephesians and of a Primate in Asia Minor was unknown at that time. Jerome, in 'On Illustrious Men', makes Polycarp the Bishop of the Smyrneans a leader in all of Asia. He would not have attributed this name to him if Timothy had been Primate there. It is also uncertain to Salmeron whether Timothy was a Bishop. He is certainly never called so in Scripture. He was sent by Paul to the Thessalonians, 1 Thess. 3. He was also sent again with Erastus into Macedonia, Acts 19:22. Furthermore, he was sent to the Corinthians, 1 Cor. 4, and to the Philippians, Phil. 2. It is evident from 1 Tim. 2 that he was left at Ephesus by the Apostle when he was heading into Macedonia. But that he was appointed Bishop in the Ephesian Church is not evident from Scripture. Indeed, since he was sent so often by Paul and was frequently present with him outside of those missions, even when he was a prisoner at Rome, how could he have performed the duties of the Ephesian Episcopate? Walo Messalinus, in 'On Bishops and Presbyters', p. 64, says: Paul, he says, sent Timothy to Ephesus and ordered him to remain there for a short time. He also directed the same man to Thessalonica. But he also sent him to the Corinthians, as is evident from 1 Corinthians chapter 4. He later recalled him to Rome. Timothy, therefore, was traveling through the churches. Which is properly a task and an Apostolic office. Certainly, he never undertook the administration of one church—

PRæter morem suum ἄνευ προοιμίου hanc aggressus est Grotius epistolam. Nos receptum morem non migrabimus. Timotheus, ad quem perscripta est epistola, patriam habuit Lystram, Act. XVI. 1. quæ civitas Lycaoniæ erat, Act. XIII. 6. Patre natus Græco, matre Judæa, c. XVI. 1. quæ Eunice nominatur, filia Loidis, 2. Tim. I. 5. utraque tum avia, tum mater à fide ἀνυποκρίτῳ ibi comendatur, unde ἀπὸ βρέφους Timotheus informatus fuit in sacris literis, 2. Tim. III. 15. Majores ejus Thessalonicæ habitasse, Grotius præloquio ad 2. ad Thessal. affirmavit, Jasonemq; fecit ejus propinquum, sed utrumque citra fundamentum. Cognatum Paulo Timotheum dixit Origenes in cominent. ad Rom. XVI. sed sine teste. Apostolo adfuisse Antiochiæ, non Syriæ, ubi Christianorum nomen ortum, Act. XI. sed Pisidiæ in Asia minori, Iconii, Lystræ colligi videtur 2. Tim. III. 10. quanquam poterint afflictiones ibi exantlatæ ipsi è relatione Pauli notæ esse, tametsi eidem tum nondum adfuerit Act. XIII. & XIV. Id certum est, quod socium itinerum Lystræ Paulus assumpserit, quum secundo eò venisset, ac Timotheo testimonium perhibitum fuisset probitatis ac virtutis à fratribus, qui Lystris atque Iconii morabantur, Act. XVI. quod aliquot annis demum post illas af- flictiones contigit. Dehinc Episcopum Ephesinum eundem constitutum non pauci dicunt, quod Papistæ de dignitate ac munere superiori presbyterorum ordine intelligunt; quale vero discrimen Pauli vel Timothei tempore in usu fuisse nunquam docebitur? Cornelius à Lapide Archiepiscopum creatum dicit, qui superbus titulus Ecclesiæ tum plane ignotus fuit, æque ac ignota illo tempore notio Metropolitanæ Ecclesiæ penes Ephesios, ac Primatis in Minori Asia. Hieronymus de viris illustribus Polycarpum Smyrnensium Episcopum Principem in tota Asia facit. Quod nomen ipsi non tribuisset, si Timotheus Primas ibi fuisset. Penes Salmeronem incertum etiam est, anne Timotheus Episcopus fuerit. Nunquam certe ita vocatur in scriptura. Missus est à Paulo ad Thessalonicenses, 1. Thess. 3. Missus etiam cum Erasto iterum in Macedoniam, Act. XIX. 22. Missus porro ad Corinthios, 1. Cor. IV. ad Philippenses, Phil. II. Ephesi relictum ab Apostolo, cum is in Macedoniam tenderet, constat è 1. Tim. II. Sed constitutum Episcopum in Ecclesia Ephesina, è scriptura non constat: Imo quum toties missus à Paulo, eique extra illas ablegationes frequenter adfuerit, etiam cum Romæ captivus esset, quomodo Episcopatu Ephesino fungi potuit. ## 1:1 Introduction: Notes by J. On the First Epistle to Timothy. Prolegomena
NOTES BY J. ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY. PROLEGOMENA.

he undertook. For in this way he would have been Bishop of several churches: Corinth, Thessalonica, Philippi, Ephesus, and also Rome. Eusebius reports that Timothy is written as the first Bishop of the Ephesian parish, Ecclesiastical History, book 3, ch. 4. But he does not add the authors. Metaphrastes, on the contrary, says that he succeeded John in the Episcopate, which Justinian does not prove. This cannot be true. For he presided over the Church while John was still alive. But what John would have returned from Patmos and settled there if Timothy had been appointed to the Episcopate there? Cornelius à Lapide wishes for Timothy to be designated by the Angel in Rev. 2. But Ribera and others deny this, lest it be thought that he had cast off his first love, which is objected against the Angel. Baronius teaches that the Apocalypse of John was written in the seventeenth year of Domitian, in the year of Christ 97, at which time it is not certain that Timothy was still alive, whose martyrdom Metaphrastes refers to the age of Domitian. Eusebius, however, in book 3, ch. 20, proves from Irenaeus that the Church of the Ephesians was indeed founded by Paul, but corroborated by John, who remained with it until the times of Trajan. Those who say that Paul left Timothy as Bishop at Ephesus when he was departing for Macedonia, Acts 20, are refuted by those four passages of Scripture. B. Chytraeus warned in his Onomasticon: First, he says, in Acts 19 it is expressly written that Timothy and Erastus were sent ahead into Macedonia by Paul before he departed from Ephesus: Then, when Paul had come into Macedonia after the tumult at Ephesus had been settled, Acts 20, Timothy writes the second epistle to the Corinthians together with Paul (2 Cor. 1), sent from Philippi, a city of Macedonia, through Titus and Luke, 2 Cor. 13. Thirdly, when Paul was sending the epistle to the Romans from Corinth a little later that same year, he ascribes greetings to the Romans in the name of Timothy, his fellow worker, Rom. 16. Fourthly, when Paul was returning from Greece through Macedonia into Asia, Timothy is also counted among the other companions, Acts 20. Although Scripture does not constitute Timothy as a Bishop in the Ephesian Church, superior to the presbyters in power of order and jurisdiction, he is not, however, to be relegated to the order of the laity with the Donatist Petilianus in Augustine, book 3, against the letters of Petilianus, ch. 106. For both epistles given to him sufficiently teach that Timothy was established in the sacred ministry: Having scrutinized the entire epistle, Theophylact writes in the prologue, I noticed that the Apostle does not admonish Timothy in the same manner as he does the other disciples: But he instructs him in the way that befits those who perform the duty of teaching, not the office of listening. Which Chrysostom had also observed in the prologue. Theodoret, even if he does not make him a bishop (superior to the presbyters, as the Papists wish); yet he says that the care of souls was entrusted to him in the argument of the epistle, indeed he says that the divine Paul committed the care of Asia to him. For he was a fellow worker of Paul, Rom. 16:21, sent to the Corinthians to recall to their memory the ways of the Apostle, how he taught everywhere in the Church, 1 Cor. 4:17, who worked the work of the Lord just as also Paul, 1 Cor. 10:10, and he preached Jesus Christ together with Paul and Silvanus, 2 Cor. 1:19, who served with him and in him in the Gospel, Phil. 2:22, whom Paul and Silvanus call their brother in 1 Thess. 3:2, and a διάκονον, a minister of God, and their συνεργὸν, fellow-worker, in the Gospel of Christ to confirm the Thessalonians; whom the Apostle, along with Silvanus, joined to himself in his epistles and epistolary admonitions to various churches: to the Corinthian, 2 Cor. 1:1; to the Philippians, ch. 1:1; to the Colossians, ch. 1:1; to the Thessalonians, 1 Thess. 1:1, 2 Thess. 1:1; as also to Philemon, v. 1. Whence it is clear that he was a distinguished teacher of the Church, held in great value and honor by the Apostle; that he was a bishop among the Ephesians does not appear at all, so much so that the contrary shines forth not obscurely from this conjunction with Paul in various places and his συνεργείᾳ (cooperation) in the sacred ministry. That he indeed informed various churches, whom, as we observed before, he was sent here and there by Paul like an Apostle: thus we judge that he can not incorrectly be reckoned among the second order of Apostles. The Apostle attributes distinguished praises to him, both elsewhere and especially in Phil. 2:20: 'For I have no one,' he says in his commendation of the same person there, 'ἰσόψυχον (like-minded), who will genuinely care for your concerns'; and v. 22: 'But you know his proof, that as a child with a father he served with me for the Gospel.' He calls him brother, and deems him worthy of equal honor with Silvanus, who is called a prophet, Acts 15:32. Theophylact asks in the prologue why Paul wrote an epistle to neither Silas, nor Clement himself, nor Luke, nor any other of those who were with him—of whom it is certain there were many—except only to Timothy and Titus; and he says that one can answer, following Chrysostom, that Paul took them around with him, but entrusted the churches to be cared for to Timothy and Titus: whence it was also necessary that he should declare by letter what ought to be done through them. Crocius prefers that this was done because the state of the Church, in which he had left them, required it. This we admit so far, provided that Timothy is not tied to a fixed see: indeed, he also had to be admonished about those things which would be of use to him not only at Ephesus, but also here and there elsewhere.

who were speaking beyond the correct doctrine, and that he should rebuke them. For the Apostle himself had already delivered Hymenaeus and Alexander, who had suffered shipwreck regarding the faith, to Satan, that they might learn not to blaspheme. Concerning which Theodoret also says on this passage: 'Those who had believed from among the Jews, because of their knowledge of the Old Testament, were proposing certain questions to those who had believed from among the Gentiles, attempting to refute them as ignorant of the divine utterances, contending that they should observe the legal institution of life, and trying to persuade them.' Chrysostom, Homily I: 'There were,' he says, 'in that city (Ephesus) certain false apostles from among the Jews, who were trying to draw the faithful back to the law, which he objects to them as a crime in almost all his epistles.' They did this, however, not as if compelled by conscience, but led by vain glory, because they wanted to have disciples from this, and were contending against Paul and were led by envy and malice; and this is what he calls ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν, to teach otherwise. Theophylact repeats most of these things according to his custom. Secondly, an occasion was also given to Paul by certain curious men who were babbling about frivolous little questions, neglecting the primary doctrine necessary for edification, which Flacius here observes that the Apostle had predicted to them in Acts 20: which cause (ἀφορμὴ), however, can also be referred to these same false teachers. Thirdly, it seems that Timothy, as a neophyte, just like the Ephesian Church itself, had need of further information, which the holy Apostle provides to him through this epistle. Chrysostom and Theophylact ask here why he did not inform him sufficiently before, before, that is, he entrusted the Church to him to be governed? And Chrysostom answers: that he had need of doctrine, not that by which disciples were instructed, but that which was appropriate for a Master. Theophylact adds that no one has yet reached such perfection that he does not need information; and therefore, even if someone is appointed to instruct others, it would certainly still be necessary that he be led and cultivated by those who appear to be more perfect in the faith and to have progressed the most. Furthermore, since the Church was recently established, it was by no means easy for Paul alone to have everything in his care and to form it in the faith. We add: That there was an absolute need for Apostolic authority for Timothy, not only because of adversaries, but also because of the faithful; and furthermore, that the Apostle wished to serve not only that Church, but others also to which Timothy was to arrive, indeed the universal Church of Christ, for whose use the Holy Spirit consecrated this epistle, so that it might both prescribe rules of office to bishops and teachers, and define the form of ecclesiastical polity regarding the different orders in the Church through certain canons. Which, therefore, along with the propagation of orthodoxy and the deposit of faith, is the proper scope of this epistle.

When Paul took him as a companion of his journey, he circumcised him because of the Jews: concerning which Chrysostom says: 'Wonderful that he takes him because of the Jews who were in those places.' This is the reason for circumcising. 'For they could not bear to hear the word from an uncircumcised person.' And why? See the work. He circumcises, so that he may abolish circumcision. Ignatius, in his epistle to the Philadelphians, testifies that Timothy remained celibate. Baronius says he was crowned with martyrdom under Trajan in the year of Christ 109. But we warned a little earlier that Metaphrastes thinks this happened already under Domitian, the brother and successor of Titus. In the fasti, his death is drawn back to the times of Nero, under whom, on the 24th of January, which is dedicated to him for this reason, when he had vehemently rebuked the idolatrous cults at the festival of Diana, he is said to have been stoned to death. Dorotheus, however, making no mention of martyrdom, says in his Synopsis that he died at Ephesus and was honorably buried there, whose bones are said to have been translated to Constantinople by Constantine the Great. Jerome reports in epistle 53 against Vigilantius, and Nicephorus in book 10, ch. 14.

The occasion for the epistle was not single. For Athanasius in his Synopsis observes that the cause was first given by the Pseudo-Apostles: certain men at Ephesus were infected with Judaism, introducing a foreign doctrine and seducing the simpler folk under the pretext of the law. When the Apostle had understood this, he admonished Timothy to remain there, so that he might correct them. Moreover, he writes this epistle to him, and first reminds him of the faith in Christ, which he knew, and teaches concerning the law, so that he might restrain them.

As to the time this epistle was written, authors disagree. Chrysostom seems doubtful whether he wrote it after the Epistle to the Ephesians or not. Since that one makes mention of chains, Eph. VI. 20, it is considered to have been written from chains at Rome. For on chapter I, homily I, at the words: 'As I besought thee to abide still at Ephesus, when I went into Macedonia,' he has this: 'What, I pray, does this mean? Was the epistle of Paul, which he had written to the Ephesians, not sufficient? Had they perhaps despised the letter? Or did he indeed entrust these things to his disciple before that letter? For he himself had been for a very long time in this city, in which was the temple of Diana: here indeed he endured those great and well-known struggles: where, after the theater was dismissed, having called and admonished the disciples, only then did he depart from there, and afterwards came to them again. Most, however, determine that the first to Timothy was written not long after the second to the Thessalonians, before Paul had come to Ephesus for the second time, Acts 19:1, since he promises his arrival, 1 Tim. 3:14. For it is said that he departed from Ephesus intending to go to Jerusalem, Acts 18:21. At which time some think he left Timothy at Ephesus; and while he was traveling through Galatia and Phrygia, v. 23, he wrote this first epistle to Timothy from Laodicea, a town of Phrygia. So also Bunting in his Itinerary, p. 227, who refers this to the year of Christ 53, noting that in the following year, 54, Paul came again to Ephesus from Laodicea, a city of Phrygia, at an interval of 57 miles, and there taught for two years in the school of Tyrannus, from Acts 19. In the final journey into Macedonia described in Acts 20, this command about remaining at Ephesus was not given to Timothy. Flacius gathers from this, that because he was captured not long after, he could not have given him hope of a return there, and in his final journey he protested to the Ephesian elders in his farewell address that they would never see him again. Before the final farewell, therefore, described in Acts 20, it seems entirely probable to Flacius that this epistle was written, although he does not disguise that it seems strange to him why in that farewell he warned them only about future matters, and not about these very seducers who were already present at that time. It might perhaps be said here, however, that he mentioned only future things because, after the epistle to Timothy was written, peace had already been secured for the Ephesians from those earlier seducers by the prudence of Timothy: but that he foresaw in the Spirit that after his own death others would arise from the Ephesians themselves, who would create greater dangers. Although Flacius, along with some others, also thinks that not all of Paul's journeys and acts were recorded by Luke, and that therefore many things are uninvestigable. Cf. B. Chytraeus in his Onomasticon and B. Balduinus on 1 Tim. 1:3. Although he had Timothy with him on his third journey into Macedonia, Acts 20:4, he could nevertheless have returned to Paul from Ephesus. For he did not have a permanent seat at Ephesus, but frequently undertook travels. This opinion is approved by our B. Gerhard, who holds that this exhortation was given by Paul to Timothy on the third journey into Macedonia, Acts 20:1, that he should remain at Ephesus. Concerning which see Beza on ch. 1:3. Grotius thinks that in 1 Tim. 1:3 that journey is designated which is indicated in Acts 20:3, so that Timothy came from Ephesus to Troas for the sake of seeing Paul, and soon returned to Ephesus. But that journey is later. Furthermore, if Timothy came from Ephesus to Troas to visit Paul, it is necessary that he had been left at Ephesus by Paul, which does not fit Luke's narrative. For in ch. 19, v. 22, while Paul was persisting in Asia, Timothy was sent by the Apostle with Erastus into Macedonia. Therefore he was not present at Ephesus with Paul when the riot was stirred up by Demetrius, or when, the riot having been settled, he said farewell to the disciples at Ephesus, Acts 20:1, setting out for Macedonia, where Timothy had already been sent ahead. Which happened according to Bunting in the year of our Lord 56. From there, having departed from Ephesus, by the same author, Paul came to Troas at an interval of fifty-three miles, where, when he did not find Titus, he was troubled in his spirit, 2. Cor. 2:13, and from Troas, as is said there, he sailed into Macedonia, and came to Philippi, 58 miles distant from Troas, from where he wrote the second epistle to the Corinthians, and sent it to them by Titus and Luke, as is held in its final subscription. From Philippi, also observing Bunting, at an interval of 120 miles through Greece, in which he stayed for three months, Acts 20:2, he came to Corinth, and there wrote the epistle to the Romans, which he sent to them by Phoebe. In the year 57 after the birth of Christ, when Paul had wintered at Corinth, 1 Cor. 16:28, with spring now approaching, he did not sail directly from Corinth to Syria, but to avoid the plots of the Jews, he returned to Philippi at an interval of 73 miles, where he celebrated the feast of the Passover, Acts 20:3, shortly after the Passover. feast, he came from Philippi by sailing 58 miles to Troas, where he found Timothy, Acts 20:5, there with others who were accompanying Paul into Asia, awaiting Paul, when he had preceded him there with his companions. It does not appear, therefore, how Timothy could have come from Ephesus to Troas as if left there by Paul, for the sake of seeing Paul: since, departing from him at Ephesus, he had gone into Macedonia.

The place from which this epistle was written has already been indicated, namely Laodicea, which is the metropolis of Phrygia Pacatiana, distinguished by this name from the Laodicea placed on the Lycus river near Colossae, Col. 4:16. Athanasius, however, thinks it was written from Macedonia; which also seems to be the opinion of Baronius, as well as Beza, who says it was written from Philippi or from another city of Macedonia, but without a probable reason. We see no sufficient cause, however, which might move us from the received final subscription.

The argument is, to express it in three words, THE TYPE OF AN ECCLESIASTICAL TEACHER. For he admonishes Timothy concerning care regarding doctrine, so that they may be recalled from the mixture of the false doctrine of the Judaizers and useless questions to the sincere Christian faith: The sum of which, as far as the law and its use and the Gospel concerning Christ are concerned, is presented in ch. 1, as also regarding prayers, which he orders to be made for all, especially magistrates, exhorting men and women alike how they ought to pray, and instructing these women so that they may neither publicly teach nor affect to dominate, ch. 2. Then he sets forth the requirements of a good Teacher or Bishop, as well as of Deacons, primarily concerning their life, so that they may know how one ought to behave in the Church, which is the house of GOD: yet he presents the main chapters of Evangelical doctrine at the same time, ch. 3. Thirdly, he orders them to persevere in true doctrine and the constant exercise of piety, against the predicted apostasy of the Anti-Christ, ch. 4. Fourthly, he gravely admonishes how men of different age, different sex, and order, especially widows, both the older and the younger, ought to be instructed and conduct themselves; and in what honor presbyters are to be held, with certain private admonitions also inserted, ch. V. What, moreover, is the duty of servants, he teaches at the beginning of ch. VI. Finally, in place of a colophon, he commands them to avoid those not persisting in sound doctrine, and their avarice, as a plague to which the heterodox were addicted, but to pursue righteousness with the most serious obligation to keep the admonitions, and he instructs what to prescribe to the rich of this world, and how the deposit of faith ought to be guarded, and he seals the epistle with a prayer for grace, in the remainder of chapter VI.

The five parts of the epistle, therefore, can be conveniently established in that manner, which it is also permitted to distribute into the epigraph, the treatment itself, and the postscript, as they call it, or the conclusion; so that the treatment itself is tripartite, as it concerns both the principal sacred duties, regarding faith and prayers, in the two prior chapters; and the requirements of those who are to be set over the ecclesiastical office, whether they are to be Bishop, Deacon, or Presbyter, ch. III; and the rules and direction of those who are in the sacred ministry, regarding their own person, ch. IV, and regarding others, and ecclesiastical polity, by which men of different age, order, and sex, ch. V and VI, v. 16. In place of a conclusion, he gives some advice concerning the rich. The economy of the treatise can also be arranged by dichotomy, if anyone should prefer that: so that the first part is general, both concerning sacred offices in ch. I & II, and concerning Ecclesiastical persons and their requirements, who are to be set over an Ecclesiastical office in ch. III, and who are already set over the same: And the second part be special, by which persons of different order in ch. V & VI. The whole epistle is

Exhortatory; concerning which Flacius says excellently: He warns, he says, especially about the zeal for retaining the sound doctrine of the Gospel: of which he has inserted other illustrious passages from time to time, like gems or most bright stars, because the first care in the Church must always be had for this highest treasure and as it were the fountain of every good, but at the same time he also warns about avoiding false doctrine, and repressing false and curious Teachers alike. He also instructs him how he ought to conduct prayers and rites in the temple, and to appoint useful ministers, and altogether to treat and judge Ecclesiastical matters, and finally how he ought to privately fashion the morals of individual orders. Furthermore, the order of the sentences, according to Flacius, is here primarily and in general: Because the first and highest care and duty of a sincere Bishop is to propose sound and salutary doctrine to his hearers, and to repel the false: Therefore the Apostle in the first chapter warns Timothy, that having rejected all novelties, fables, and curious doctrines, he should teach only those things which make for promoting faith and charity; and at the same time he exhibits the true and salutary sum of the doctrine of justification by mere grace in himself, as in a certain living example, to be proposed to all: just as he is accustomed to propose himself not only as an example of morals, but also of justification, Gal. II, Phil. III. Or (that we may speak more briefly) he proposes the doctrine concerning the Law or contrition, the Gospel or faith, justification, and new obedience, and that in a certain living and conspicuous practice. The second care of the Bishop is of public prayers and rites, and the form of the Church: and therefore in the second chapter he gives precepts concerning that matter. For very much depends on this, that all things be directed and instituted piously and prudently for edification. Thirdly, because very much also depends on the life and whole conduct of a sincere Teacher, and from that the hearers are accustomed to seek every example of both piety and honesty, as well as probity: therefore in the third chapter the Apostle teaches both what kind of Teachers are to be appointed, and how they ought to conduct themselves with their whole family, whether they be pastors or deacons. For he wishes all of them, together with their family, to be blameless. In the fourth place, since false doctrine for the most part infests a rightly formed and constituted Church, the enemy over-sowing tares: therefore in ch. IV he predicts that seeds or doctrines of Demons are to come: so that, warned and made more vigilant by this prophecy, they may maturely resist both those foretold and all other errors and seducers; or rather that from this prophecy and most certain signs they may learn to recognize the abominations of the Anti-Christ. Furthermore, because a pious Teacher must also privately correct and form the lives and morals of his hearers, as a shepherd his individual sheep: Therefore he teaches him how he ought to warn individual ages and orders, and move them to true piety. In the last chapter he treats primarily of that harmful plague of avarice, which he not undeservedly calls the root of all evils and especially of vices: which without doubt raged vehemently there, as in a mercantile city; and which in the last times under the Anti-Christ, who is to turn the house of the Lord into a den of thieves, is to rage, with not so much Simony reigning, as horrible, infinite, and most shameful sacrileges.

PART I. OF THE GENERAL EPISTLE.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

After the inscription and the vow, the Apostle warns Timothy to denounce that they should not teach otherwise, nor attend to fables and useless genealogies, having proposed the sum and use of the Law, as well as of the Gospel, so that he may fight the good fight in them, and retain faith and a good conscience, from which some have fallen, and among them Hymenaeus and Alexander.

There are two parts, the inscription with the vow having been premised: I. The denunciation concerning heterodoxy, and concerning the sound doctrine of the Law and the Gospel, to verse 17. II. The exhortation concerning keeping faith and a good conscience, verses 18, 19.

PART I. Denunciation concerning heterodoxy, and concerning the sound doctrine of the Law and the Gospel.

vers. 1. Paul an Apostle of Jesus Christ) Paul always uses this beginning, so that his words may have greater authority.

Not on account of Timothy, for whom even the name of Paul alone sufficed against the magnificent titles of countless seducers; but on account of those to whom these things were to be proclaimed by Timothy, whom he desired to be thus fortified by divine authority in those things which were to be proclaimed not in the name of Paul, but of Jesus Christ, whose Apostle he was.

By the commandment of God the Father) So also Rom. XVI. 26. and Tit. I. v. 3. He begins from the highest cause.

If Christ is excluded from this notion, Grotius Arianizes. The Father is the one and same highest cause, and the Son, as also the Holy Spirit. Just as there cannot be three Gods, so neither can there be three causes, without prejudice to the Athanasian Creed, without prejudice to the Christian faith.

And our Saviour Jesus Christ) In the Manuscript and very many codices it is: God the Father our Saviour, and Jesus Christ. Rightly. For so also to Titus: By the commandment of our Saviour God. They changed it who remembered that the name Saviour is attributed to Christ in most places. But they did not remember that it is also attributed to God the Father, who sent Christ to accomplish salvation for us, Luke I. 47. below here IV. 10. Tit. II. 10. III. 4. Jude v. 25. In the Old Testament that title is frequently given to God, Deut. XXXII. 15. 1 Sam. X. 19. Ps. XXIV. 5. XXV. 5. and elsewhere often in the Psalms, Is. XII. 2. XVII. 10. XLV. 15. 21. Jer. XVI. 8. Mic. VII. 7. Hab. III. 17.

Blessed Luther followed that manuscript, or rather those twin codices. And thus also almost all the codices of Beza had it. Only one, the Claromontanus, had the reading which Grotius exhibits in the text: And another certain one reads simply: The commandment of God our Father, and of the Lord Jesus Christ. And since Beza, Casaubon, and others in various editions, with the Vulgate also not differing, read it thus, as the manuscript of Grotius, I do not see what reason he had to insert the other reading of the Claromontanus codex into the text.

Of our hope) That is, who Christ is the cause of our hope. See 1 Thess. I. 3. A similar expression Ps. LXXI. 7.

Christ is not only the cause of hope, but also the sole foundation of hope, and the object in which we hope, as we are taught in Psalm II. v. last, and elsewhere passim. Rightly therefore Theodoret notes: That these things are not to be taken distinctively; since both God is the object and cause of hope, and Christ is our Saviour: but he called God salvation, and Christ hope, he says. Not dividing the names, nor indeed attributing this to that, and that to this, but understanding both in each person. For blessed David placed both in one person: Hear us O God our Saviour, the hope of all the ends of the earth, Ps. 64. Moreover, it is opportune, as Theophylact teaches after Chrysostom, that he called the Savior also hope, because for one who is teaching and preaching, since he struggles with many difficulties and dangers, as one against whom all war is waged, salvation is to be hoped for, and if he falls, those who fight under him fall more easily saying: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. Therefore, we must not fall, since we have a Savior, not simply some man, but God Himself and the Father, who most quickly delivers us from any danger. But if we are not immediately rescued from dangers, better things are nevertheless to be hoped for by us: for Christ is our hope, of whom we can be ashamed of nothing. Therefore, for these two reasons, every danger must be endured, either because we are to be saved most quickly through Christ, or because we are to be cherished by good hope. Blessed Gerhard advises that the Apostle is looking toward the Judaizers, who placed the hope of their salvation in the law and ceremonies, whereas Christ alone is and ought to be our hope, through whose merit alone we can hope for and obtain remission and eternal life.

v. 2. To Timothy, my genuine child in the faith) Timothy had been commended to Paul from an early age by his mother, so that he might be instructed by his examples, 2 Tim. 3:10, where it is clear that he was with Paul before Paul came to Lystra, although Luke mentions Timothy there for the first time in Acts 16:1, because at that time, with the testimonies of the churches preceding, he was assumed into the office of an evangelist, when he had previously been a follower of Paul. Paul calls him a son in the faith, however, because through faith we receive a certain new nature, and are as it were born again, 1 Cor. 4:13, 15, 17; 2 Cor. 6:13; Eph. 5:1; Phil. 2:22; 1 Thess. 2:7; 2 Tim. 1:2; 2:1; Philem. v. 10; 3 John v. 4. Add Gal. 4:19. He adds genuine, as in Phil. 4:3; Tit. 1:4, because he was a son of Paul who was not in the least degenerate.

I do not read that Timothy was commended to Paul from an early age by his mother, 2 Tim. 3:10, nor even that he was with Paul before he came to Lystra and took him on, Acts 16:2, nor was he known to Paul before that time, because only then was he commended to him by the testimonies of the brethren of Lystra and Iconium. By whom he was converted to the faith of Christ is not added there, but that he was found there by Paul as a disciple, by which name those converted to Christ were called. There is no doubt, however, that he had a Christian mother and learned the sacred scriptures from infancy, being imbued with the rudiments of Christianity in his infant years; perhaps also, since he had not been circumcised, he was initiated by the sacrament of baptism: although I would not rashly assert this, since examples do not easily occur of those who were first baptized and subsequently circumcised in the Christian Church. But that Timothy was a follower of Paul before he was taken on by Paul at Lystra is a Grotius fable; if he calls him a follower in the Papist sense, regarding the final degree of holy orders, it is a wonder that a polyhistor would be ignorant that those orders were unknown to the Apostolic age, unless he is to be judged to have concealed this for the sake of the Papists rather than to have been ignorant of it. Paul calls him a son not because of regeneration, since he had already been reborn from the word of truth, Jas. 1:18, or through baptism, but because of instruction and imitation. For he was already endowed with faith, as he was numbered among the faithful disciples, Acts 16:1. For as Augustine in his book against Adimantus, ch. 5, advises that the name of son is accepted in the scriptures in three ways: according to nature, doctrine, and imitation, where the third way ought to be referred to regeneration, or rather this fourth way should be added, since he is also called a son by reason of age: which sense Erasmus establishes here. But Blessed Hunnius is more correct: he calls Timothy his son, not only in the way that old men call their juniors sons (for that Timothy was at that time still a young man appears from this epistle, ch. 4), but he calls him a son in the faith, in that Paul, although he was already a disciple of Christ, taught and confirmed him more fully in the faith of the Gospel. He adds the epithet, however, when he greets him as a genuine son (γνήσιον), (as Blessed Hunnius continues) because of his sincerity and constancy, because, following in the footsteps of the Apostle, he was handing down the doctrine of the Gospel with great praise for his pious fidelity and perseverance, and was most constantly defending it against the enemies of the cross, not without danger to his life.

Grace, mercy, peace from God our Father and Christ Jesus our Lord) So also 2 Tim. 1:2; Tit. 1:4; 2 John v. 3; peace and mercy, Gal. 6:16; Jude v. 2; grace and peace, 1 Cor. 1:3; 2 Cor. 1:2; and often elsewhere. The doubling of the meaning has something of a pathetic quality. Cf. Num. 6:24 ff.

Regarding the word mercy, Theophylact judges with Chrysostom that it is added in the prayer out of a certain vehemence of charity, or because the Devil is armed more vehemently against a shepherd or others: which Hugo Cardinalis also understands as the power of giving the Holy Spirit: but here the ministering gifts, whether ordinary or extraordinary, are not in view; therefore, neither is mercy here, which is the ornament of a Bishop, as Rupert of Deutz wishes, but the most benign will of God, which favors without any merit and rejoices to do good, is designated by the word grace, which is the source and origin of all good things, which for the sake of greater emphasis is expressed through mercy, looking upon our misery graciously and with a feeling of compassion. For mercy, according to Phavorinus, is sympathy for calamity, so that by these words it is hinted that we owe everything in the cause of salvation to the mere grace of God. On which Haymo says on this passage: Peace is conferred upon us through mercy, not through our merit. R. Moses Maimonides distinguishes these attributes of GOD in More Nebuchim, chapter LIV, as follows: Just as we are accustomed to call grace Chaninah when we bestow something upon one to whom we owe nothing (Job XIX. 21; Gen. XXXV. v. 5, 11), so because God creates, preserves, and governs those to whom He is not yet obligated by any right, He is therefore called Chaninon, gracious. He is called merciful, not as if He were subject to passion, but because something similar proceeds from God to His saints as from an earthly father toward a son, who is moved to clemency, compassion, and mercy toward him. This grace and mercy of God shines forth most especially in the gift of peace obtained through Christ and conferred upon us through faith.

v. 3. As I besought thee to abide still at Ephesus, when I was going into Macedonia) I agree with those who think that this indicates that journey, mentioned in Acts XX. 3, whereby Timothy came from Ephesus to Troas for the sake of seeing Paul, and soon returned to Ephesus, where he is believed to have spent the remainder of his life.

Regarding this opinion of Grotius, it has already been spoken of in the Prolegomena. That Timothy spent the remainder of his life in Ephesus after he was with Paul in Troas does not accord with the truth. For he was a prisoner in Italy, and he is said to have been freed from that captivity in Heb. XIII. 23. He was with Paul in Rome, and wrote letters with him to the Philippians, to the Colossians, and to Philemon, as the inscriptions testify. Beza on the word προσμεῖναι: Therefore, Timothy was previously traveling through the churches with Paul; then, as necessity dictated, Paul wished him to remain at Ephesus, not that he was added to that church as a bishop, but so that the established church might oppose the false apostles; from whence he was also later recalled to Rome by the Apostle himself. For the Apostle had also taught at Ephesus for two years, yet he is not called the Ephesian bishop on that account; nor is it certain whether Timothy later returned to Ephesus from Rome, as one who was an evangelist.

Ἵνα παραγγείλῃς τισὶ) Here that ἵνα παραγγείλῃς is used for παραγγεῖλαι, which is a locution like Eph. V. 33. Since for that reason you were left there, do what I commanded: Charge certain ones, namely those who have need of such a charge.

Μὴ ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν) That they teach no other thing than what we have taught. See below VI. 3.

Some refer the word ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν as much to the hearers as to the teachers, such as Haymo, Hugo Cardinalis, and Lombard: But it is more correctly restricted by Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, Primasius, and Ambrose to the teachers, which is evident from v. 7, and therefore it should not be rendered with Erasmus, lest they follow a different doctrine, but with the Vulgate, lest they teach otherwise, which, as Calvin observes, is broader than if you render it, they teach another thing; since the latter refers to the subject matter, the former also to new forms of teaching, who nevertheless warns that not only that which conflicts with the pure doctrine of the Gospel is called another doctrine, but whatever corrupts the pure Gospel either with new and extraneous figments or obscures it with profane speculations. Crocius has this to say about them: They teach otherwise who teach things which are not found in Scripture, or even which manifestly conflict with Scripture. They teach otherwise who indeed propose things that are read in Scripture, but neither sincerely nor integrally, but either add from their own, or take away, or interpolate, studiously mixing vain and useless things with true and useful ones, and curiously sought-out unnecessary things with necessary ones. To the former pertains the fact that some were handing down fables. To the latter, that they were teaching the law in such a way and perverting its use. These are the words of Crocius, not doubting that the Apostle prohibits both. Nor do we doubt that all these things are prohibited by this word ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν: even if we do not consider it necessary that the same word be explained simultaneously by both 'to teach another thing' and 'to teach otherwise.' For those who are handed down neither sincerely nor integrally, or with human addition, are not only taught otherwise, but also exhibit another thing than what Scripture teaches. For nothing is to be added to it, nor taken away. If it is added, it is something other than Scripture. If it is taken away, or not handed down sincerely, it is also different from the Word of God: which must be left integral and sincere, just as it proceeded from God, and is μηδεμιᾶς προσθέσεως ἢ ἀφαιρέσεως ἐπιδεχόμενον, as Varinus defines it as a rule or norm. To teach otherwise, says Theophylact, is to introduce certain other disciplines, and decrees alien to the true ones. For there were many from the Jews who, while they lied that they were Apostles, and out of a desire for glory wished to be called teachers, were inducing disciples to the observation of the old law. Beza notes: that a different doctrine is spoken of, not only that which is entirely other, but also that which adulterates the true doctrine, that is, which mixes even the slightest bit of human speculation with the Word of God, so that this prohibition of Paul embraces the very form of teaching itself. Ἕτερος is taken in this way in Acts II. v. 4, 1 Cor. XIV. 21. In vain, however, does Estius say that another doctrine is understood, which excludes the former, and therefore infers that this place cannot be opposed to traditions. For not only is nothing against the Gospel to be taught in the Church, but also nothing besides the Gospel, Gal. I. 8, 9. And the Pseudo-Apostles, who are noted here as heterodox, did not deny justification through faith in Christ, but were adding works to faith in justification. Concerning which one should read above all B. Luther, Von der Haupt-Summa Gottes Gebotes, Tom. II. Jen. fol. 475, Altenb. Tom. II. fol. 827. 'These certain ones, whom the Apostle means here, have certainly not been simple people, but [disciples] of the high Apostles Peter and the others, who have so often seen their miracles, and heard many a beautiful sermon and teaching, and in addition the judgment decided at Jerusalem by the Apostles, Acts XV, yet they have not attained the right understanding.' Fol. 828. 'Yet those disciples fell for it, and hung an addition onto it, let the teaching and the judgment of mere grace go, and seized the works which the Apostles were doing, and pressed them upon the conscience, saying: You must do this and that, or not do it. Thus the false teachers broke in, and dampened the faith, struck down grace, drove out Christ. For whoever arrives at the point that he wants to help the conscience with works and reconcile God, has already lost grace with Christ and every treasure.' That, therefore, is ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν according to B. Luther.

v. 4. Μηδὲ προσέχειν μύθοις) He deals here with those who had come from Judaism to Christianity, and were mixing Jewish fables with Christianity. The following things show this, and Tit. I. v. 14. Add also below IV. 7, 2 Tim. IV. 4. Such were among certain Jews the fables about those things which God did before this world was founded, about man made first as an androgynous being, about his intercourse with beasts, and with Lilith, about the demons born from that: About Behemoth and Leviathan, about the existence of souls before the body, about angels distributed into stars and regions, and many similar things. Tertullian on Valentinus: He introduced many fables.

Valentinus's fables are too recent for the Ephesians to have been warned about them at that time, nor can it be taught that those little fables of the Jews, which are brought forward here, are of that antiquity; even if Augustine also brings forward such things. Nor is it likely that those trifles were handed down by any Christian teacher, even if only whitewashed in name, or admitted by a hearer. Concerning modern Jews, given over to a reprobate sense, it is no wonder that they do not deny faith even to these most inept trifles. Beza understands it as curious and vain speculations, Calvin as trifles and ineptitudes. But Crocius acknowledges that fables are taken here generally for all things alien to Scripture and useless. Fables, says Theophylact with Chrysostom, he does not call the law, but certain observations and fabricated dogmas. For the Manichaeans, who rejected the Old Testament, were taking it concerning the law. Theodoret: He called, he says, not the doctrine of the Law, but the Jewish interpretation, which is called by them δευτέρωσις, fables. The Holy Apostle seems to explain this, ch. VI. 3, with the words: 'if anyone does not consent to the wholesome words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness,' and v. 20, through 'profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called.' That there is, however, a special regard for 'profane and old wives' fables,' is evident from ch. IV. 7, just as, conversely, a parallel passage confirms the general sense, 2 Tim. IV. 7, where 'fables' and 'the truth' are opposed to each other, so that it is certain that whatever is alien to the truth is reckoned among fables. The verb προσέχειν is suitable not only for hearers, but also for teachers: because προσέχειν is to apply oneself to some matter, as προσέχειν τοῖς ναυτικοῖς in Thucydides.

And endless genealogies) He calls them genealogies, which the Jews [call] ספרות, for the reason that it was imagined that one of these emanated from another, and was as it were begotten, in this way: Crown. בינה ἔννοια intelligence, חכמה ἀκμὴσοφ wisdom, פחד or גבורה fear or power, גדולה or חסד magnificence or mercy. תפארת GOD, הוד majesty, נצח victory, יסוד foundation, which is also כל all, מלכה kingdom, which is also שכינה the presence of GOD. Tertullian teaches us in his Prescription that these were taken from the Platonists: which is true, but with some names retained and some changed. But Plutarch teaches us in his Isis that such genealogies existed long ago among the Persian magi. The Platonists, who wrote περὶ ἀρχῶν, also remember them. Porphyry, however, says that he discovered that those things which were circulated under the name of Zoroaster were made by the Gnostics, whom Paul notes here, and that he had shown this. And I think he speaks the truth: you have mention of Βυθὸν, σιγῆν, ἐννοίας in Proclus on the Timaeus, and in Damascius and others. But Paul truly said ἀπεράντοις here. For many added other many properties to these with equal right, like those Gnostics from whom the Valentinians and Basilidians drew their origin, who also used the name of αἰώνων for ספירות, and made their συζυγίας and γενεαλογίας. For they also used this name, as can be seen in Irenaeus at the beginning of book I, Tertullian, and Epiphanius. The writer of the Constitutions under the name of Clement called them Αἰῶνας ἀπέρας. Moreover, they referred the γενεαλογίας of the Gods, which existed in Hesiod and Orpheus, through certain ἀλληγορίας to those αἰῶνας of theirs, that is, to the ספירות. And because of these things they wanted to appear more learned than the rest, and they despised other Christians as being more unrefined: And hence it is that they made the name of γνωστικῶν for themselves. See what we said in the preface to the Gospel of John. When Proclus had discussed the genealogies which are in Plato's Timaeus: Ἀλλὰ τούτων ᾅδων ὀυδὲν ἀυγὲι τῶν πραγμάτων φροντίζοντι ὅπως ἂν ἔχοι.

The things which are brought forward here from the Rabbis are foreign: For they do not concern those genealogies, even if they are greatly recalled to γενεὰς or generations: For αἱ γενεαὶ and αἱ γενεαλογίαι are entirely different: although they are not even called generations by the Rabbis, but עשר ספירות, ten enumerations, as Buxtorf explained, by whose authority those are not ten genealogies or generations, but ten primary and mystical positions concerning divine properties, notions, or attributes, and they are generally the foundations upon which the whole Cabalistic Theology is built, through the correct knowledge of which its students penetrate to the inner parts of Cabalistic Theology, who furthermore observes these things about them under the word ספירות: Thus indeed they commonly render ספירות here as enumerations: but the Author of the preface to the book Schare ora wishes them to be so called from clarity and splendor: For he writes thus: The Cabalists handed down and arranged in order for us the divine properties and called them על שם הזכות והבהירות ספירות כספיר מלשון .Sephiroth from clarity, from the meaning of the work of the Sapphire stone, Exodus XXIV. 10. Just as, indeed, forms are seen in a clear object: So the Sephiroth are the type and form of all beings, and just as things are seen in a clear object without any addition: So all things are seen in those Sephiroth without addition, etc. Reuchlin, book III de Cabala, has this to say about the same things in Galatinus, p. 734. Many of us treat the ten enumerations called by the Cabalists עשר ספירות in many ways, some in the manner of a tree, others in the form of a man, so that mention is often made of the root, trunk, branches, and bark. But often also of the head, shoulders, legs, feet, right side and left. These are the ten divine names which we mortals conceive of God, whether essential, or personal, or notional, or common, and they are named thus: כתר, that is, crown, חכמה, that is, wisdom, בינה, i.e., prudence or intelligence, חסד, i.e., clemency or goodness, גבורה, i.e., gravity or severity, תפארת, that is, ornament, נצח, that is, triumph, הוד, that is, confession of praise, יסוד, that is, foundation, מלכות, i.e., kingdom. Above the crown, however, is placed אין סוף, i.e., infinity, and it is the abyss. Those ten Sephiroth are certainly not without their use, since the divine properties are contained in them. But who would call them useless and vain? They exhibit the perfection of God, who, even if He is most simple in Himself, yet because of our mode of conceiving, His essence is declared by diverse attributes. It is by no means to be believed that these are the genealogies reprobated here by Paul. Concerning them, R. Moses in his commentaries on chapter I, book Jetsim: Abraham our Father called the Sephiroth, as if Sapphires, to signify that just as the Sapphire receives all colors: So all forms, blessings, and emanations are attributed to God, yet in such a way that all these things proclaim the highest unity of the blessed God.

The things which are deduced Cabalistically from these ten properties are without doubt more recent than this Pauline epistle.

But I do not find in Tertullian's De Praescriptione against Valentinus that those Sephiroth were taken from the Platonists. At least he applies the aeons here in chapter XXXIII. But also when Valentinus names indeterminate genealogies, it is recognized, in whom that I-know-not-what aeon of new and not one name generates sense and truth from his charity, and these in turn beget word and life: Then also these beget man and the Church; from which first ogdoad thence ten other aeons, and the remaining twelve aeons arise with wondrous names into the mere fable of thirty aeons. What, I ask, do those inventions have in common with the Rabbinic Sephiroth? Moreover, it is evident from Chronology that the Valentinians and Gnostics are later in time than this Pauline epistle. Although Irenaeus uses the names of generation and emission when recounting the portents of the aeons, I do not see him calling them genealogies in the cited place, nor could a place in Tertullian or Epiphanius be brought forward for that matter.

Furthermore, if you listen to most all the Interpreters, the Apostle is not dealing here with divine emanations, but with human genealogies, about which the Jews moved infinite questions, which the Judaizing Christians also strove to foist upon the Church. They commemorated grandfathers and great-grandfathers, says Theophylact, so that they might claim glory from history. But he called them endless genealogies, either because they traced their genealogies too far back, or because they had brought no utility in the end, nor had they obtained any useful and compendious result, but brought things which could both be recalled with difficulty and were altogether perplexed. Theophylact indeed adds that they may be understood concerning the fables of the Gentiles and the generations of the gods, which they commemorate: But since the Apostle openly designates the Jews, naming them νομοδιδασκάλους, others prefer the former sense: for whom the investigation of genealogies was held in high regard, and indeed they were even published by the Prophets in the books of Chronicles: inasmuch as by them the distinction of tribes and families was formerly shown to be necessary, both for the sake of not confusing tribes and families, and for the sake of claiming inheritances, and for the sake of distinguishing the firstborn from others with their descendants, and for the sake of deciding disputes arising from the pretension of rights and possessions, and especially for the sake of more correctly recognizing the genealogy and lineage of Christ: The study of which, however, after Christ was exhibited, and the form of the Jewish polity and the distinction of tribes and families was removed, is useless, and finds neither origin nor end in most cases, therefore the Apostle called them ἀπεράντοις. Which is by no means to be extended to the genealogy of Christ, inasmuch as it is defined in the scriptures, and therefore is not ἀπέραντον or interminable. For the investigation of it is necessary on account of the mind of scripture: whereas on the contrary that of others is neither necessary, nor possible, and is bounded by no limits, and is implicated in uncertain narratives, just as even in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah the genealogies could not be indicated, Neh. VII. 62.

Αἵ τινες ζητήσεις παρέχουσι μᾶλλον) Many questions were born from thence, since some ordered those classes and names differently, each according to his own judgment. Thus the Basilidians otherwise, the Valentinians otherwise. See Irenaeus book 5, 6, 7, and following. Add Lactantius book 5, Tertullian. When Valentinus had fashioned only thirty Aeons, they added many others, for they aggregated first four, then another four. For ζητήσεις in the Manuscript is ἐκζητήσεις. Thus οἱ ἐκζητηταὶ φρονήσεως, Baruch III. 14. The Rabbis call such questions מבעיות.

Η᾿ οἰκονομίαν Θεῦ τὴν ἐν πίστει) These indeed seem to tend toward explaining the dispensation of God concerning our salvation: But in reality it is simple through faith in Christ: nor does it need so many circumlocutions. Concerning the word οἰκονομίας see Eph. I. 10. Some books have οἰκοδομήν. But the former is more correct.

Although not a few codices read oikonomian, and Theodoret, Chrysostom, and Theophylact explain it in that sense as the dispensation of salvation; yet most codices have oikodomian, edification, as the Syriac also, the Vulgate, Ambrose, Beza, and B. Luther have rendered it. And that the word oikodomia is not unusual is evident from Thucydides, Book I, and Plutarch, De sollertia animalium. Moreover, it is called the edification of God, both because it is from God, and because it is founded in God, and because it tends to the glory of God. The edification of God is, says Haymo, when someone speaks those things which have some utility, through which they prepare and build up the temple of God in the hearts of the hearers. But that edification is brought about not through fables, or endless genealogies, and useless questions, but through faith or doctrine divinely delivered, which is called faith, which is believed, for the sake of explaining which the Apostle digresses to the sum of the Law and the Gospel.

v. 5. But the end of the commandment is love) Our doctrine tends toward love; theirs produces dissensions. Parangelia is said of the Gospel, and below in verse 18, and in the plural number parangeliai, 1 Thess. 4:2. Telos, see Ecclesiastes 12:13.

After the Apostle has rejected the heterodoxies, he now exhibits the sum of orthodoxy, partly in general, partly in particular, both as regards the Law, whose genuine use he asserts; and as regards the Gospel, whose salutary practice he teaches by his own example. He calls the end of the commandment in general charity, but not of the Gospel, as Grotius perverts it. For the Law is directed both to the love of God and of neighbor as its internal end, and both tables are summed up in the love of God and neighbor; the former table prescribing to us the love of God, the latter the love of neighbor. In the Gospel, the love of God toward us is set forth, but the love of man toward God is not commanded. The confusion of Law and Gospel is frequent and easy for Grotius, in the Socinian and Arminian manner. We do not deny, however, that the commandment here also embraces the Gospel.

From a pure heart and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned) Paul gives us also a brief genealogy, but a very useful one. From faith, the unfeigned emeth emunah, mention of which is in 2 Tim. 1:5, is born a good conscience, that is, abstinence from sins, Acts 23:1, below 19, 3:9, 2 Tim. 1:3, Heb. 9:14, 10:22, 13:18, 1 Pet. 3:16, 21. Hence purity of heart, that is, interior, Acts 15:9. Hence furthermore love, which is also peace, 2 Tim. 2:22.

There is no genealogy here. From faith there is not only the purification of the heart, which consists in the cleansing from sins through the blood of Christ, 1 John 1:7, but also a good conscience is born, when indeed sanctification follows faith, which is also a consequence of that purification. For through faith the conscience is purged from dead works by the blood of Christ, that immaculate lamb, that we may serve the living God, Heb. 9:14, and faith is effective through charity, Gal. 5.

v. 6. But a good conscience, which is born from faith, is not itself abstinence from sins, but the tranquility of the heart on account of the remission of sins or justification, Rom. 5:1, which is followed by the pursuit of holiness and abstinence from sins, lest the tranquility of the conscience be disturbed. Those three are the adjuncts of love, which follows justification: First, because it redounds from the pure heart of a justified man, as one whose heart has been cleansed through the blood of Christ, both in the sacrament of baptism, which is received for the remission of sins, Acts 2:38, by which we are washed from sins, ch. 22:16, and are freed from an evil conscience; and through the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, which is done by the proclamation of the Word, 1 Pet. 1:2, 22. The Law demands both that the heart be pure from all sin, and that it be sincere, not deceitful. As regards the former, no one can say of himself: My heart is pure, Prov. 20:9; therefore there is need of faith, by which sins are not imputed, Rom. 4:6. But the latter follows from that non-imputation, and is connected with the same, Ps. 32:1, 2. Therefore it is required of the justified that they have a sincere heart, not a hypocritical one. Then love arises from a good conscience, so that, certain of the remission of sins and the purification of the conscience, we may strive to love God and neighbor, as is right, with a prompt and sincere mind, and indeed to love God with all our heart, and our neighbor as ourselves. Thirdly, from unfeigned faith: as it is the cause of both the purity of the heart and the goodness and tranquility of the conscience. For he who has believed in God with an upright mind will by no means allow himself to be separated from true charity, which is accustomed to embrace everyone in the same way, as Theophylact says here. Faith unfeigned also produces charity unfeigned. As is the mother, so is the offspring. Faith is feigned, says Haymo, which confesses with the mouth, but is not held in the heart nor adorned with works. Faith therefore (if it be sincere), with Chrysostom as author on this passage, indicates what is true, and from sincere faith charity is born. For he who truly believes in God will never be able to desist from it. But what that faith unfeigned is, B. Luther teaches in his Summa des Christlichen Lebens, Vol. VI, Altenb., fol. 39: That faith must come, and such faith that is not hypocrisy, and mixed with confidence in one's own holiness. For where that is not, there the heart does not become pure before God, nor does the conscience stand when the sharp judgment and reckoning shall begin.

v. 6. From which some having missed the mark) Wandering, below VI. v. 21. 2 Tim. II. 18. They turned aside to vain talking) They turned aside, as below V. 15. 2 Tim. IV. 4. התפכו vain talking, an unfruitful dissertation. Those who use such things are vain talkers, Tit. I. 10.

Those who have wandered from faith and love have turned aside to vain talk. That which wanders from faith and love is vain, however much it may be adorned with a pomp of words. There is a metaphor in the word ἀστοχήσαντες, wandering from the mark, taken from bad archers, as noted by Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius. As archers have their mark set before them, from which, if any, while wishing to be considered skilled, wander, they are mocked by all, especially in public games. Thus he says that certain ones have most shamefully, and not without ignominy, wandered from love and its inseparable companion and guide, unfeigned faith, as if from a mark. The Vulgate explained ἐξετράπησαν as 'they were converted.' It is more correctly translated 'they turned aside.' Εἰς ματαιολογίαν to vain talk, to studies, doctrines, and empty discourses, namely myths and genealogies. Here Erasmus notes the Scholastics, whom Estius excuses in vain, since he must necessarily admit that sin was sometimes committed by some either through excessive curiosity or superfluity. See B. Meisner in Academic Schools concerning the vicious method of disputing of the Scholastics.

v. 7. Desiring to be teachers of the law) Tertullian on Cerinthus: He also proposes the law, namely to exclude the Gospel and to vindicate Judaism. There had always been many Jews in Ephesus: Some of these, having embraced Christianity in appearance, retained much of Judaism: Among the Jewish fables was also the conversation of the law with God before the world was founded: And they wanted the world to have been founded for the sake of the law. See Rabbi Israel on the soul. Teachers of the law חפשי תורה, Luke V. 17. Acts V. 34. Not understanding either what they say, nor about what they confidently affirm) They do not see what they are saying. They say the law is necessary to be observed, and they do not observe it. They affirm many things which they have from no certain sense or revelation. To affirm confidently is to affirm for certain, Tit. III. 8. מכל.

While the Apostle explains who such wanderers are, he simultaneously involves the causes of the aberration, namely both pride and presumption, because they wish to be considered interpreters of the law above others, such as were the lawyers in the time of Christ, who did not fear to prove Christ himself from the law and those concerning whom the Apostle [writes] Rom. II. 19. Whence Theophylact: Through ambition they were authors of ignorance and error to themselves, as well as ignorance of the scripture, whence they are ignorant, whether of the things they assert, such as the δευτερώσεις concerning the necessity and use of the law, and various traditions, as regards the conclusions to which Chrysostom and Theophylact refer, which taught otherwise concerning the scope and duration of the law. Hyperius and others [say] that they did not rightly hand down the doctrine of justification, [and] confused the law with the Gospel: Or those concerning whom they assert things which seem to be referred to the principles of the conclusions, whence the βεβαίωσις of the assertions was sought, as Haymo, Danaeus, and B. Gerhard understand. For he who, regarding the law, understands neither the things he asserts, nor the things by which he wishes to give assurance to his assertions, and thus has no true knowledge and understanding in either the conclusions or the proofs, however much he may advertise himself as a lawyer and Doctor, wanders from the scope of the law and the truth, and consequently deflects into vain talk. Therefore, for the sake of honor, he now explains the use of the law.

v. 8. But we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully) The law has always had this use, and now also has it, to show that crimes and wicked deeds are displeasing to GOD. See Rom. VII. 12. כמשפט Lawfully.

But we, says the Apostle, know, opposing the knowledge of himself and other true Doctors to the ignorance of the false teachers. He admits, however, by way of anticipation, forestalling the objection, as if by Apostolic doctrine the law itself were argued as not good, because the law does nothing toward obtaining justification and salvation. We know entirely, for there is no need that we first learn from these teachers of the law that the law is good, both because it proceeded from a good God, and because it informs us about the good, what must be done and how evil must be fled, and because it leads us to the good, if it is performed, Rom. VII.

v. 12. But it is good, if one uses it lawfully: It is always good in itself, nor is it rendered not good intrinsically by abuse, but in order that it may be good for us and result in good, its legitimate use is required, which

God intends. Thus, therefore, the Apostle touches upon the end of the law, which is threefold: first, that it may convince us of sin and its guilt, and thus be a schoolmaster to us unto Christ, through whom we are freed from sin; then, that it may direct those freed from sin in charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned, lest we fall away from the grace exhibited. Finally, that it may press upon the unfaithful for punishment, and restrain the wicked. The first use is wont to be called Pedagogical; the second, Paedeutic; the third, Political, which we would rather call forensic, so that both the divine and human forum may be regarded. Legitimately, says Theophylact, he uses the law who is led through the law to Christ. For the law, which lacks the power of justifying, sends back to Christ, and the law itself demands this, that one use it legitimately, that is, just as the law itself commands, which sets Christ before itself. But the Adversaries were not using the law lawfully, neglecting in great part the use of the law intended by God. For they neither rightly estimated sins from the law, being occupied by Pharisaic corruptions, and thus erecting their own righteousness, they did not receive Christ, who is the end of the law, as was fitting: nor could they be occupied in the paedeutic or directive use of the law lawfully, being occupied more with empty traditions and ceremonies than with moral matters: And because they fell away from true faith through the mixture of law and Gospel, and the denial of mere grace, the law struck them with a curse, as being destitute of true righteousness, which is in Christ alone. He discourses especially about the third use, because the second is already comprised in the summary compendium of Christian doctrine under the name of charity, which is the fulfilling of the law Rom. XIII. 8, 9, 10, and now in v. 5. But he shows the first by his own example in practice, when he confesses himself the primary sinner, and attributes his salvation solely to divine grace and the redemption of the Savior Christ.

Eidos touto, hoti dikaio nomos ou keitai) eidos for oida יֹדֵעַ. For it is frequent for the Hebrews to place a participle for a present verb, which they lack. The Latin reads eidotes. The sense is: If the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had been such as those ancestors of theirs had been, there would have been no need for the law of Moses. The Egyptian sojourn and the contagions born thence made it necessary. That law of God given through Moses has in great part effects common with other civil laws of peoples. Philo on the allegories: 'He commands this, but not to him who has been made according to the image and the idea. For that one has virtue even without exhortation, automatically.' Then: 'To him who is perfect and made according to the image, no one needs to command or forbid. For the perfect one needs nothing.' Laertius reports the saying of Xenocrates about Philosophers: 'To do voluntarily alone what the rest do involuntarily through the law.' That is Servius on that VII. Aeneid: Holding himself of his own accord and after the manner of the ancient God, he thus spoke out: Xenocrates, who when he had first opened a school of Philosophy (whereas before philosophers used to treat of matters in porticoes) and had been asked what he could provide for his disciples, replied: that they might do of their own will what others are compelled to do by law: Tacitus, Annals III. The most ancient of mortals, as yet without any evil desire, lived without reward, without crime, and therefore without punishment or constraints: nor was there need of rewards, since honorable things were sought for their own sake, and where they desired nothing against custom, nothing was forbidden through fear. The same in [his work on] Germany: And good customs have more power there than good laws elsewhere. Clement, Stromata IV, as Socrates cites: For the sake of the good, law would not exist. The same, Stromata V: For the perfect, righteousness is not in civil contracts, nor in the prohibition of law, but from self-governance and love toward God. Plato, on Laws IX. It is a shameful thing in a way to legislate everything that we are now about to do in such a city, which we say will be inhabited well and with all correctness for the practice of virtue, where there are also other things on this matter. Aristotle's saying is also praised: That this very thing has resulted from philosophy, to do without being commanded what some do through fear of the laws. Cornelia in Propertius: My nature gave me laws derived from my blood, so that I could not be better through fear of a judge. Dio Chrysostom, dissertation LXXVI: For if all were good, clearly there would be no need for written (laws) for us, where there are also more things pertaining to this. Epicurus does not depart far from this: The laws are established for the sake of the wise, not so that they may not commit injustice, but so that they may not be treated unjustly.

No one could have attained that meaning of Grotius by guessing. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had entirely the same law which Moses later, by divine command, consigned to two tablets. For the Decalogue exhibits the law inscribed by nature upon the Protoplasts: which, although it was obscured by the fall, was not, however, entirely erased. Regarding the forensic and ceremonial law, the reason is different; the former was given for the Jewish polity, the latter was sanctioned in great part for the prefiguring of the Messiah. Neither properly concerned other peoples than the Jewish. But these are not the subject at present. The reason for the moral law is explained: That it does not lie upon the just man. The just man was such by nature before the fall of Adam. By grace, after the fall, are those who, with Adam, believe in the Messiah. In that part, the descendants of the Patriarchs do not differ from the Patriarchs. For all who believe in Christ are justified and saved equally, Acts 15:11. And thus Ambrose understands the just man, who, having received remission, has been justified. Therefore, the law does not press upon them, it does not lie upon them, neither by reason of a curse, nor by reason of compulsion, rigor, or even the necessity of observance for salvation. He does not deny that it is necessary for the reborn by way of rule and direction, and custom, which would be contrary to the Word: Nor does he say 'is not placed', but 'is not laid down', by which is signified primarily the burden of the curse, which lies upon the despisers of the law and others, recounted at length. Bernard: It is not said, he says, that it ceases for the just, that they do not have the law or that the just are without law; but for the just the law is not laid down: But it is given liberally to the voluntary, in that it is sweetly inspired. Fren.

says Theophylactus, to a wanton and unruly horse, they are not imposed by an easy guidance. Rightly, therefore, B. Hunnius: The Apostolic pronouncement, he says, is not to be taken simply, but in a qualified sense: For it is certain that even to the righteous Adam a law was given before the fall, Gen. II. It is certain that for the pious and regenerate the law was given for this reason, that looking into it as a mirror they might more clearly behold and more deeply acknowledge the deformity of their nature: and that in the state of new obedience they might follow the guidance of the law as a prescribed form and norm, according to which they offer and perform their duties to God: And thus far indeed the law is given even to the righteous. But by reason of the third end (which is to coerce the refractory in their duty, and to preserve external discipline among men) the law is not given to the righteous.

v. 10. Ἀνόμοις δὲ καὶ ἀνυποτάκτοις) There is here a πλοκὴ in νόμος and νόμοις. For νόμος is the law of Moses: Ἄνομοι are those who set no law for themselves, namely from the use of reason: who are not a law unto themselves, Rom. II. 14. The same are ἀνυπότακτοι, בני בליעל, men without a yoke, unbridled.

Ἀσεβέσι) פֹּשְׁעִים, such as are blasphemers, against whom is the law Num. XV. 30.

Καὶ ἁμαρτωλοῖς) This is a sufficiently general name: But here it seems to be understood especially of the seditious, in the way those are called in Num. XVI. 31, XXXII. 14. Moreover, there is a law against such in Exod. XXII. 28.

Ἀνοσίοις) who commit foul deeds, זִמָּה, Ezech. XXII. 9. ἀνοσιουργοὶ to Plato.

Καὶ βεβήλοις) that is, the sacrilegious, against whom is the law Deut. (VII. 26.

Πατραλῴαις κᾀ μητραλῴαις) against whom the law is by an argument from the lesser to the greater Lev. XX. 19, Deut. XXI. 18.

Ἀνδροφόνοις) Against whom the law is, Exod. XXI. v. 12, 14, Lev. XXIV. 17, Deut. XIX. 11, 12, 13.

Πόρνοις) Against violent ravishers the law is Deut. XXII. 25. Against seducers Exod. XXII. 6, 17. Furthermore, the law forbids Hebrew girls to prostitute themselves, Levit. XIX. 29, Deut. XXIII. 17.

Ἀρσενοκοίταις) Against whom is the law Levit. XVIII. v. 22, XX. 13.

Ἀνδραποδισταῖς) To kidnappers, against whom is the law Exod. XXI. 16, Deut. XXIV. 7. It is the greatest kind of theft, to steal a free man.

Ψεύσταις) Such as those who break faith in contracts. Against them is the law Lev. VI. 1, and following.

For perjurers) Against whom is the law Exod. XX. 7. Lev. XIX. 12. Deut. V. 11.

He enumerates those for whose restraint the law was given, and whom it oppresses with the burden of a curse. The Vulgate, B. Luther, and Piscator rendered Ἀνόμους as unjust. Beza as despisers of the law, others as lawless. Ἀσεβεῖς are to others the impious, who sin against the first table of the law. The name ἁμαρτωλοὶ occurs not only for the seditious, but also for other notable sinners, Luke III. v. 31. XV. 1. Gen. XIII. 13. 1 Sam. XV. 13. Βέβηλοι are those who sin publicly and without any shame. However, we judge the distinction of B. Hunnius to be preferable to that of Grotius; who observes that those things are placed first which encompass the whole genus of wicked men, whom he names unjust, disobedient, impious, and sinners, not in the degree and manner in which we all are by nature, but clearly κατ' ἐξοχὴν (by way of eminence), when effort is given to such gross and external sins, which both strike the eyes and are condemned by the judgment of reason.
