And therefore those sins which are enumerated in particular, as being in conflict with the law of God, are not (in this place at least) to be understood as concerning the internal prevarication of the law or sins confined within the hiding places of the heart, but as concerning manifest ones, which no one, unless bereft of his senses, denies to be sins. But those transgressors are distributed according to the series of the commandments of the second table. For in the first place he puts those who break the barriers of the fourth and fifth commandments, such as πατραλοῖαι, parricides, and μητραλοῖαι, matricides, who take away the light from those by whose benefit it was granted to them to behold this light, namely their progenitors and parents. And there they sin in the highest degree against the fourth commandment: Honor thy father and thy mother, and similarly against the fifth commandment: Thou shalt not kill. What punishment they are worthy of is clear from the fact that the law commands those who merely curse their parents, or only strike them, but do not even kill them, to be punished with death, Exod. XXI. Lev. XX. Next to these are further reckoned those who simply violate the fifth commandment, murderers, whom the law likewise commanded to be taken from the midst, Gen. IX. & Exod. XXI. Subjoined to these are those who contaminate themselves with illicit and nefarious lusts against the sixth commandment: such as fornicators, who have relations with unmarried persons; then those who lie with males, who practice unspeakable lust with males, a crime against nature, which is called Sodomitic. And the law of God commands these also to be exterminated, as being utterly unworthy of the use of light, Levit. XX. From these the Apostle makes a transition to the sins of the seventh commandment, from the heap of which he touches upon that which is primary and most atrocious, namely man-stealing, when someone abducts and snatches away from another not bronze, not gold, not iron, not garments, not cattle, not houses or fields, but human beings, and thus that which among human affairs has the most value of all, a wife or children, whether by force or by deceit. To whom the Mosaic law likewise dictates the extreme sentence of death, Exod. XXI. Finally, he also refers to this dark and ill-omened catalog those who sin by the violation of the eighth commandment. Such are liars, who, in order to harm their neighbor, or to sow dissension among those who were living peacefully, by means of devised lies and false testimonies forbidden by the eighth commandment, strive to disturb their concord and to set them against one another in hostile contentions, or even in duels. Partners in the nefarious violation of the eighth commandment are perjurers, who do not shudder to violate a given pledge by the crime of perjury.

v. 11. And if there is anything else that is contrary to sound doctrine, according to the gospel of the glory of the blessed God) It is a synecdoche, for the law does not restrain everything that the Gospel disapproves, but the graver things. See what we have said in the Annotations to book I, chapter IV, of the Law of War and Peace. The doctrine of the Philosophers and Rabbis is partly sound, partly morbid, which in the Gospel is entirely sound, below VI. 3. 2 Tim. I. 13. IV. 3. Tit. I. 9. II. 1. It is אָמְנָה שְׁלֵמָה as the Hebrews say. The Gospel is called of the glory of God from the effect, because God obtains the greatest glory from it, 2 Cor. IV. 6. 15. Eph. I. 6. 12. 14. Philipp. I. 11. But God is called here and below VI. 15 blessed (μακάριος), so that the Hebrew יָשִׁיר may be expressed; God was sufficient to Himself for blessedness, He did not need us. Therefore He did whatever He did for our sake. The Syrian here placed מברכא (blessed). The Greeks also say of their gods that they are blessed (μάκαρες), but falsely.

That double error of Grotius recurs, that the law does not restrain all sins, but the graver ones, and that it is also the function of the Gospel to restrain sins. By the former, the perfection of the law is derogated; by the latter, the nature of the Gospel is overturned, which is a proclamation of grace, not of wrath, just as conversely the law works wrath, Rom. IV. 15. By sound doctrine, heavenly doctrine is understood generally, and not the Gospel: which is so called either by metaphor, because it does not suffer from the diseases of errors; or by metonymy, because it brings true health to the soul: whereas the Gospel is called specifically that sound doctrine which heals consciences wounded by the terrors of the law, by showing them Christ the Savior and Physician, as B. Gerhard does here.

Crocius does not answer the Antinomians badly here: The sense is, he says, that the law is opposed to all things that fight against the pure doctrine of salvation. The Antinomians twisted this word of the Apostle against the law, concluding that sins are argued by the Gospel, and therefore there is no use for the law today. They truly twist it: For it does not follow that crimes, whether named then or unnamed otherwise, are opposed to the Gospel. Therefore the Gospel argues them directly. They are opposed, because the Gospel does not abolish the law but establishes it: crimes are repugnant to the fruits of faith, which the Gospel delivers. While it offers medicine, it indirectly convinces us of sickness. But the recognition of the disease is directly from the law. Therefore its use is necessary. The response of B. Hunnius is fuller: But they are opposed to the Gospel the enumerated crimes, not because it is the duty of the Gospel, specifically so called, to argue and condemn sins: But first because by these enormous sins of impious men Christ is crucified anew, who is the heart and head of the whole Evangelical preaching: Then because by these sins, which the Apostle recounts in his catalogue, the conscience is so laid waste that there can be no place for faith (which we know pertains to the doctrine of the Gospel and is born from it). Thirdly because by these same atrocious offenses the fruits of Evangelical faith and justice are hindered, so that a man walks worthily neither before God nor the Gospel, but is reprobate to every good work. Finally because they cause man to wander from the end of the revealed Gospel, which is that, being freed from sins, we may serve God in holiness and justice, Luke 1, and be a peculiar people, zealous of good works, Tit. 2. Furthermore, Grotius changes the received distinction here. For these words xατὰ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον τῆς δόξης τῦ μακαρίε Θεῦ look to v. 11, where the Vulgate prefixed those words to supply the sense: WHICH IS according to the Gospel. Concerning which Theophylactus says: Construct this context of the discourse thus: Of sound doctrine, which consists according to the Gospel. He says according to the Gospel, not according to the law, to show that he neither abolishes the law nor teaches things contrary to it, but rather that there is a sweet agreement between the law and the Gospel, since the law is opposed to all things that fight against the Gospel. Moreover, it is called the Gospel of glory, not only because it reveals the glory of God and serves to celebrate the same, but also because it is the means of obtaining the glory of God, so that we may enjoy the same eternally, because it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, Rom. 1, 16.

Ὅ ἐπισεύθην ἐγὼ) A Greek manner of speaking, such as Rom. 3, 2. 1 Cor. 9, 17. Tit. 1, 3.

Vers. 12.

Καὶ χάριν ἔχω τῷ ἐνδυναμώσαντί με Χρισῷ τῷ Κυρίῳ) I cannot perform so great a thing without his extraordinary help. Ἐνδυναμῶντί με is מעזני 2 Sam. 22, 33. or הזק Psalm 19, 2. see Act. 9, 22. 1 Tim. 4, 17. Heb. 11, 34.

Ὅτι πισόν με ἡγήσατο) In order to obtain great help from God, it is not enough to be called by God, but it is necessary that we show faith in that to which we have been called: As Paul did 1 Cor. 4, 2. c. 7. 25.

Θέμενος εἰς διακονίαν) After he had applied me to the ministry. For θέμενος here is of more than perfect signification. Διακονία by excellence is the Apostleship Act. 1, 17. 25. Rom. 11, 13. 2 Cor. 4, 1. c. 5. 8.

These things are rightly understood concerning ministering gifts, not sanctifying ones, concerning assistance and comfort in the parts of the office, in which CHRIST found the Apostle faithful. For πισὸν here and in 1 Corinth. 4, 12 does not imply justifying faith, but the faithfulness of the office. Where indeed Estius rightly says: Now what he says, because he deemed me faithful, is not to be taken as if GOD found Paul faithful, but did not make him so (which Chrysostom and his followers might seem to have thought to a little-attentive reader), but by saying less he wished more to be understood. For men indeed entrust the dispensation of their affairs to those whom they deem faithful, even if they do not make them so. But GOD judges no one faithful whom He does not make so. And that the Apostle wished to signify this is proved by the thanksgiving itself. For no thanks are owed to God because He judges a man who is faithful as such (for this judgment is necessary in God) but because He makes him such.

Vers. 13.

Τὸν πρότερον ὄντα βλάσφημον καὶ διώκτην, καὶ ὑβρισὴν He shows the magnitude of the benefit from his former state. He had been such a blasphemer that he even compelled others to blaspheme Act. 26, 11. He was also a persecutor, as appears Act. 9, 4. 5. c. 22, 4. c. 26, 11. 1 Cor. 15, 9. and injurious, as appears Act. 8, 3. c. 9, 2. Concerning the word ὑβρίζον see Matth. 22, 6.

Ἀλλ’ ἠλεήθην, ὅτι ἀγνοῶν ἐποίησα ἐν ἀπιστίᾳ) He does not bring forward the cause why he had to be forgiven, but why God forgave him rather than others. There are שְׁגָגוֹת, ignorances, sins, but in the class of sins less grave than those which are done בְּיָד רָמָה, as is Num. 15, 30. See Luke 12, 40. ἐν ἀπιστίᾳ designates the time, when I was still an unbeliever, he says. Ἠλεήθην is said in that form in which ἠπιστεύθην is, רֻחַמְתִּי in Pual, see Act. 23, 1.

Thus Grotius seems to be sailing with the wind for the Papists, when he says that a reason is given why God pardoned Paul rather than others, just as Becanus gathers from this passage a venial sin, which he calls 'ex causa' [from a cause], because it is in some way worthy of pardon, because it was committed not out of malice, but out of ignorance: And Bellarmine argues in book I de grat. & statu pecc. ch. 3 & 11 that in such a venial sin there is something that diminishes the sin. On the contrary, Salmero, as also Thomas and the ordinary gloss, judges that these do not diminish but exaggerate the sin, as if he were saying, God saw me blinded by unbelief, so that I did not recognize my evils, therefore by His mere mercy He anticipated me. Comparing the passage Gen. 8, 21. But Estius says best: It seems to be said that having done it through ignorance with respect to mercy and pardon to be obtained from God is in the aforementioned sentences neither alleged properly for the exaggeration of the sin, nor for its extenuation, especially since it is in some way common to all sins that they are done through ignorance, as is taught in 2. sent. d. 22. but it is brought forward as the reason for the most suitable object, concerning which God might exercise His mercy. For the object or matter of mercy is misery. Whence the greater the misery, the more it is born to move mercy. What therefore the Apostle says is such: Therefore I obtained mercy, because my misery was great, namely this, that I did such evils through ignorance and unbelief, like a sick man who in his insanity strikes the physician, as Augustine beautifully explains in Sermon VIII de verb. Apost.

Ver. 14.

Ὑπερεπλεόνασε δὲ ἡ χάρις τῦ Κυρίυ ἡμῶν) The grace of our Lord grew much in me, that is, spiritual gifts. Ὑπερεπλεόνασε בְּמְאֹד מְאֹד פָּרַץ. Thus that ὑπερπερίσσευσεν ἡ χάρις, Rom. 5, 20. For Paul loves such words, as we have already noted elsewhere.

Μετὰ πίστεως κὰ ἀγάπης τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησῦ) How much, he says, faith and love, both of God and of neighbor, grew in me on account of Christ. Cyprian to Donatus: Let our breast only thirst and lie open: as much faith as we bring there, so much of the inundating grace we draw. The ancients note here that free will is joined with grace, but in such a way that the parts of grace are not only prior but also superior.

These things about free will do not agree with the text. For there is nothing about free will. The Apostle attributes everything to grace. And indeed to superabundant grace, which exerted itself in an admirable way in the remission of sins and the calling of the Apostle. It superabounded, says Chrysostom, that is, mercy exceeded the measure; for these things are not of one showing mercy, but of one loving, and desiring, and affected by an excessive force of love. It is added therefore, μετὰ πίστεως κὶ ἀγάπης, not that grace abounded through the merit or work of faith and love; for grace is not grace in any way, unless it is gratuitous in every way, as Augustine's rule from Rom. 11, 6 holds. But that grace together with faith and love, which is in Christ Jesus, superabounded, this is, that not only the grace of the remission of sins, but also of the donation or operation of faith and love in the Apostle, which is excited in us by the Holy Spirit, exerted itself superabundantly, or if you prefer to render PER: that through that very gracious donation of faith and love in him, who was an adversary of the faith, and not a lover of the faithful, but a notable persecutor, grace

Divine [grace] has superabundantly exhibited and demonstrated itself in Christ Jesus, that is, which Christ has acquired, who is for me his mediator, not the law.

Verse 15.

Πιστὸς ὁ λόγος, καὶ πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιος) You have the same words below in ch. 4, 9. Πιστὸς ὁ λόγος also below in ch. 3, 1. & 2. Tim. 2, 11. & Tit. 3, 8. The Hebrews say אמת הדבר. This statement, which I am about to make, is not only true, but also worthy of being highly valued. Thus Diodorus Siculus said ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιον. Dionysius of Halicarnassus in his Rhetorics [used] Ἀποδοχῆς ἀξιῶσαι. In a similar sense we shall have ἀποδεκτὸς below in ch. 2, 3.

From the example of the Lord's grace shown to himself, transferring the hypothesis to the thesis, he proceeds to the general proclamation of the grace of CHRIST, or rather to the sum of the Evangelical sermon of grace, so that all sinners may draw faith and comfort from it. Crocius in the school of Calvin does not deny this end: It is not enough, he says, for the Apostle to transfer to the increase of faith in the ministry that which rivals were objecting against the authority of the office. He further transfers it to the solid utility of all the greatest sinners who repent, by the example of Christ's coming and the Divine mercy declared toward himself, so that they may understand that what the adversaries themselves were casting as a reproach, is useful to the Church. For while CHRIST made a Shepherd out of a monstrous beast, He published a manifest specimen of grace, from which all the greatest sinners may conceive certain confidence: For the way to salvation is closed to no one, however grave their sins. But if this is intended by Paul, it is necessary that the saving grace of God be not particular, but universal. The Apostle here exhibits 1. The eulogy and certainty of the Gospel, that the word is not uncertain or doubtful, but πιστὸς, faithful, that is, most true and most certain, to which faith may be safely applied, and πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιος, worthy to be accepted with all reception, and which all, by faithful apprehension, may deservedly make their own and apply to themselves. Πάσης, he says, ἀποδοχῆς, so that it may be implied that the Word of the Gospel is to be received in all ways, venerated with all religion, and is in every part worthy of all faith. Some seem to have read χρηστὸς, human, like Ambrosiaster, but all the codices with the Syriac and Vulgate have πιστός. Which also other Greeks and Latins have retained. In Hebrew they say it corresponds to נאמן אדני, the word of the Lord, as also Blessed Gerhard says. But that he attributes this eulogy to this statement is not to be taken with the mind as if other things in the scriptures were less certain: But because he here proposes the sum of the Gospel, and the most principal article of faith, and one which concerns all who ought either to conceive saving faith or, once conceived, to cherish it against any temptations whatsoever, by which method it is also taught that for faith, which responds relatively to this Word, since the Word and faith are relatives, there is required ἀποδοχὴ or reception of the Word and of Christ, who is exhibited through the Word of the Gospel to be looked upon by faith, John 1, 12, as the proper object of the Gospel. Chrysostom also adds this cause for that eulogy, that that word seems incredible to our reason, and therefore is defined as worthy of all reception of faith. It seemed incredible, he says: Since a man who had spent his whole previous life vainly and emptily, and had led it through evil works, was afterwards said to be saved by faith alone. Finally, it is thus opposed to the fables and vain talk of the heterodox, which had nothing certain, nothing worthy of acceptance. The Jews boasted of tradition and cabala, which they equated to the written law. But this is the true and heavenly cabala received from God through the word of the Prophets and Apostles, superior to all acceptance, most worthy of all acceptance. Paul Fagius observes that the Apostle looks to this: The word, he says, קבל does not simply mean to look to, but to receive something as certain and indubitable, to acquiesce and to have faith. Hence is derived the word Cabala, by which the Hebrews understand whatever is authentic, certain, and indubitable. From this, however, Cabala was born, because formerly the sacred mysteries, especially those concerning the kingdom of Christ, were handed down by the Fathers from mouth to mouth by succession, which one received from another, whence it was called Cabala from receiving, etc. The Apostle alluded to that Cabalistic method in 1 Tim. 1, where he also used the word Cabala. For he writes thus: A faithful word, and worthy of all acceptance or Cabala, because Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, as if he were to say: If anyone desires to hear a cabala, I will indicate a certain, true, and indubitable one. And that is, that Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners. This is a true Cabalistic dogma, about which there is absolutely nothing to be doubted. Those things certainly cohere: A faithful word and worthy of all acceptance. For because it is faithful, it is also worthy of acceptance; but this latter is added peculiarly, so that the nature of faith, as we have said, may be explained.

That Christ Jesus came into the world) that is, he appeared to men as a gift of God, John 1:9, ch. 3:2, ch. 6:14, ch. 9:39, ch. 11:27, ch. 12:46, ch. 18:37.

To save sinners) Matt. 9:13, Mark 2:17, Luke 5:32, Rom. 5:8.

The Apostle now adds, in the second place, a summary of the Gospel, which consists in the truth of the advent or incarnation of Christ, and the end of the same, the salvation of sinners. He says that Jesus Christ came, to intimate that the promised Messiah, that is, that anointed one of the Lord, who is Christ to the Greeks, has been exhibited: And that the same is no other than JESUS, who obtained this name at his circumcision, Luke 2:21. Just as St. John has thus comprised the sum of faith in these two words: These are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ the Son of God, and 1 John 5:1. He who believes that JESUS is the CHRIST, is born of GOD. But since JESUS CHRIST is the Son of GOD, he designates here the advent of the Son of GOD into this world; who, although he was always in the world, because the world was made by him, is nevertheless said to have come into the world when he willed to be in the world in the assumed human nature, and to be manifested in the flesh, 1. Tim. 3:16, when the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, John 1:14, when the eternal Son of GOD was made a partaker of our flesh and blood, and took on him the seed of Abraham, Heb. 2:14 and 16. For he came forth from the Father, and came into the world by being born, just as in turn he left the world and went to the Father by dying and ascending into heaven, John 16:28. The end of the incarnation is that he might save sinners. Whom? Not angels, but men; not the righteous, for he finds no righteous ones, not even one, Psalm 14:3, but those subject to sin, and guilty of death and eternal damnation. For all had turned aside, together they had become unprofitable, Romans 3:12. The whole world was ὑπόδικος (guilty) before GOD, verse 19. All were concluded under unbelief, ch. 11:32, under sin, Gal. 3:22, that he might save ἁμαρτωλὺς (sinners), who, by the corrupt habit of nature, by internal thoughts, words, and deeds, were resisting GOD. Not some, but indefinitely, all, with no one excepted, with no one excluded. For God willed to have mercy on all, Rom. 11, 32; He gave His only-begotten Son to the whole world, John 3, 16; the Savior of the world, 1 John 4, 16. He did not come to destroy, but to save sinners. For GOD did not send His Son to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through Him, John 3, 17. Not only to deliver and absolve sinners from sin and the penalty of sin, death, and eternal condemnation, but to procure and bestow upon them salvation and life, and eternal salvation. To save, namely by taking away evil and conferring good, taking away through satisfaction, conferring through merit, both of which He intends to perform through the calling to the communion of the salvation procured, through justification, by which sins are remitted and His righteousness is imputed to us through faith: as well as through glorification, by which, being fully freed from sin and its penalty, we are advanced to salvation and eternal life. He does not say, that He might begin to save, and that they might furthermore save themselves, but that He might save, namely, plainly and perfectly. Not that He might save the soul, but that He might save sinful men, and thus body and soul. He does not say, that He might save for a time, but absolutely, that He might save, namely, unto eternity.

Ὧν πρῶτός εἰμι ἐγώ) This is not of the sentence, but added to it incidentally. It is, however, a statement spoken hyperbolically out of the highest modesty, such as also 1 Corinthians 15, verse 9.

He applies this universal redemption of Christ to himself individually, and by his own example teaches that everyone ought to apply it to himself and apprehend it by true faith. Therefore, just as he had transferred the hypothesis to the thesis: so now he returns from the thesis to the hypothesis and his own example. This is not, therefore, added incidentally, but by design, so that we may conclude that CHRIST likewise wishes to save us, not destroy us, by his example, even if we are the greatest of sinners. For He did not come to save only a certain kind of sinner, but to save any sinners whatsoever, liable to any sins whatsoever. The Apostle acknowledged himself as the first, not by reason of time, as a certain heretic dreamed in Thomas on this passage, as if the soul of Adam, the first sinner, migrated into Paul; but by reason of transgression: Concerning which Augustine in Psalm 70. Were there not sinners before him? What then is 'I am the first'? Preceding all, not in time, but in wickedness. Which are not spoken by hyperbole or out of modesty, but out of true humility and contrition of soul and the sense that sin so confronted his mind, so tormented him, as if he were the greatest among all sinners. Indeed, says Danaeus, he speaks out of a serious and intimate sense of the soul, and such as all infidelity, and especially the most obstinate, ought to be apprehended by us with fear and horror of conscience. By which confession he abrogates for himself all merit, dignity, preparation, and disposition toward grace, and teaches us that, however burdened we may be with sins, we should not despair, but apprehend by true faith this Savior of sinners and His salvation procured for all. If anyone should say, says Chrysostom, that a King wishes to forgive everyone their faults, faith will not be given to the words as it would be if they saw him who had offended more and more grievously than all others, having been granted pardon. For no ambiguity can now remain, since the King is thought to wish to forgive everyone, who has absolved him who was notable above other sinners; this also Paul says: When, he says, God wished to make men more certain that He had forgiven them all their sins, He chose him who had offended more than all, to whom He might forgive all crimes. For when I have obtained pardon, no one is now permitted to doubt concerning himself, just as the custom of speaking also holds: If God has forgiven this man, He will punish no one, so that by this it is shown that he himself was indeed not worthy of pardon, but that he had merited it for the salvation of others. Let no one therefore doubt, he says, let no one despair of himself, since I myself have been saved.

Verse 16.

Ἀλλὰ διὰ τοῦτο ἠλεήθην, ἵνα ἐν ἐμοὶ πρώτῳ ἐνδείξηται Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς τὴν πᾶσαν μακροθυμίαν) Christ is the image of God. When God forgives, He is also accustomed to have prokatarktikas (preliminary) causes, such as that one of which we spoke above at 13, and besides these, telikas (final) causes, that is, some use which He proposes to Himself. See what we said on Luke 7, 47. Thus the Midrash on Psalm 51 says that David was permitted to fall so that he might be able to comfort others. But here 'first' (prōtos) is placed for 'before' (proteron), as in John 1, 15; in me Christ, before others who were to be converted by me, shows His highest leniency. Some codices have here 'in me the first' (en emoi prōtō) with the same meaning. I interpret 'all' (pasan) here as 'the highest', as just now 'of all acceptance' (pāsēs apodochēs). Thus in Herodotus 'all hope' (elpis pāsa) means 'the greatest hope'. This leniency, 'long-suffering' (makrothymian), Peter also calls it in 2 Peter 3, 15.

The Apostle does not compare himself with those to be converted later, but with the greatest sinners, and just as he professed himself the most notable among them out of serious contrition of heart: so he proclaims that mercy was exhibited to him in particular, and the highest long-suffering was demonstrated to him by Jesus, whom he had persecuted (Acts 9, 5), above others, so that others also might have reason to expect the same. Which Theodoret declared thus: Just as, he says, a physician, when many are sick at the same time in one house, and all despair of their health, if he takes one who is most severely affected, and by giving him medicines leads him to the most perfect health, he makes it so that all the others are of good cheer and conceive confidence: So the Lord Christ, the physician of souls, when He had become man for the salvation of sinners, not only freed me, who was most wicked and the most criminal of all, from my former stains, but also overwhelmed me with the greatest gifts, showing through me to all men His highest patience and clemency. So that no one of those who have committed the greatest crimes, looking at me, should despair of salvation. There is no need, therefore, to make a comparative out of a superlative, and from an indefinite, which corresponds to a universal, a particular restricted to the times following the Pauline conversion, let alone to those who were to be converted through Paul. JESUS CHRIST yesterday, today, the same and forever, Heb. 13, 8. The emphasis was also rightly observed by Chrysostom in the word ALL: He did not say, he says, that he might show patience in me, but all patience, as if he were saying more openly: There is no one in whom greater patience ought to be had, nor can a sinner easily be found who needs such an abundance of compassion. All, he says, he showed in me patience, not a part, as in the case of those who have sinned moderately.

Πρὸς ὑποτύπωσιν τῶν μελλόντων πιστεύειν ἐπ' αὐτῷ εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον) ὑποτύπωσις as also τύπος are the first outlines of pictures or works. Preformation is taken here for an example. For by the example of Paul, who after such cruel deeds had obtained the gifts of the Spirit, and consequently also a right to eternal life (for those gifts were a pledge of eternal life), even those from the Gentiles who had lived wickedly dared to hope for eternal life, after they had received the same life which Paul professed.

Others understand by ὑποτύπωσις not the first outlines, but an illustrious and living demonstration of a thing. The example of Paul also provides such a demonstration. Hypotyposis, says Flacius, is a Greek word signifying not just any example, but an illustrious example, and as it were a living prefiguration or adumbration set before the eyes.

But not only to those who were from the nations, much less only to those who were to believe through Paul, but to all who believe. For both Jews and others from the nations had to hope for grace through this illustrious example of Paul, provided they were going to believe. Οἱ μέλλοντες πιστεύειν are not those to whom God is going to grant faith by an absolute good pleasure, but those who are going to have faith through the Word of the Gospel, which is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, which God wills to deny to no one, provided we do not place an obstacle in the way of Him who intends conversion, 1 Tim. 2:4, 2 Pet. 3:9, Acts 7:51, which [is granted] not immediately but through the hearing of the Word, not through an irresistible grace, but one which, while indeed effective in itself in the first act for conversion, does not however work in an irresistible manner, nor exert its efficacy in the second act in those who are resisting by actual malice, or who are hindering the operation of the Holy Spirit.

Verse 17.

To the King of all ages: עתיק יומי Dan. 9:17. Incorruptible: see Rom. 1:23 and what is said there: and Wisdom 12:1. Invisible: Heb. 11:27. That is proper to God. For He dwells in unapproachable light, below ch. 6:16. God in Himself is not seen. But He is seen in His works, Rom. 1:20, and most openly in the Son, 2 Cor. 4, Heb. 1:3. To the only wise God: So also Rom. 16:27, not that this title is not attributed to others in some sense, but because whatever this is, it comes from God. So also Jude v. 25. The same expression is below ch. 6:6. But in the Manuscript it is wise, so that that 'only' refers to 'invisible.' And thus indeed the Latins read. Honor, glory: Our writers use [them] asyndetically even in two words. To the ages of ages: So also Gal. 1:5, and Phil. 2:20, and 2 Tim. 4:18, Heb. 13:21, 1 Pet. 4:11, ch. 5, v. 11, Rev. 1:6, ch. 5:13, ch. 7:12.

From the commemoration of superabundant Divine grace, the Apostle turns himself to thanksgiving for all Divine patience and long-suffering: That [thanksgiving] indeed is directed, according to Theodoret, to the most holy Trinity; according to Chrysostom, to God the Father: yet without excluding the Son and the Holy Spirit, [and] according to others, to CHRIST JESUS Himself; which opinion seems most agreeable. For he had proclaimed the superabundant grace of Christ, he had attributed to Him the gift of faith and charity, verse 14, he had designated the advent of CHRIST into the world to save sinners, verse 15, he had taught that all long-suffering had been shown to him by CHRIST, and he had proposed himself as an example to those believing in CHRIST, that grace would likewise be shown to them by Christ, v. 16. Since all these benefits are here peculiarly assigned to CHRIST, there is no doubt that the doxology for the same is also directed to CHRIST: who is also the King of the ages, as being the King of Kings, Rev. 17:14, ch. 19:29. Through whom the ages were created, Heb. 1:3. Blessed Gerhard interprets 'King of the ages' as King of the whole universe, because under the name of ages is comprehended whatever is measured by ages or times, that is, every creature. Incorruptible, the eternal and unchangeable Jehovah, Ps. 102:28, Isa. 45:23, Jer. 23:6, Rev. 1:8. He is called Life itself, John 14:6, 1 John 5:20. Invisible, Exod. 34:20. Only wise, because He is the hypostatic wisdom itself, Prov. 8:23, Luke 11:49. The only wise God our Savior, Jude v. 26, to whom is due glory and honor, John 5:23 (Isa. 45:23), Rom. 14:11, Rev. 5:12, who is God over all blessed for ever. Amen! Rom. 9:5.

Latin:

IN. J. NOTATA AD EPISTOLAM PRIOREM AD TIMOTHEUM. PROLEGOMENA.

nem suscepit. Hoc enim modo plurium Ecclesiarum fuiffet Episcopus, Corinthi, Thessalonica, Philipporũ, Ephesi atq; etiam Roma. Eusebius refert Timotheũ primum Ephesinæ Parœciæ Episcopum scribi l. III. histor. Eccles. c. IV. Sed non addit autores. Meta- phrastes contra dicit, eum Johanni successisse in Episcopatu, quod non probat Justinianus. Hoc verum esse non potest. Præerat n. Ecclesiæ Johan- ne superstite. Ast qui Johannes ex Pathmo rediis- set, ibiq; consedisset, si Timotheus illic in Episco- patu constitutus fuisset. Cornelius à Lapide vult Timotheum per Angelum Apoc. II. designari. Sed id negant Ribera & alii, ne putetur charitatem pri- mam abjecisse, quod Angelo objicitur. Baronius Apocal. Johann. An. Christi 97. Domitiani deci- mo septimo scriptam docet, quo tempore adhuc superstitem Timotheum fuisse haud constat, cujus martyrium ad Domitiani ætatem refert Metaphra- stes. Eusebius vero l. III. c. XX. ex Iren. probat, E- phesiorum Ecclesiam à Paulo quidem fundatam, à Johanne vero, qui apud eam ad Trajani tempora usque permanserit, corroboratam fuisse. Qui Pau- lo Epheso discedentem in Macedoniam, Act. XX. Timotheum Ephesi reliquisse Episcopum dicunt, illis quatuor scripturæ loca refragari. B. Chytraus monuit in Onomastico: Primo, inquit, Act. XIX. expreffe scribitur, Timotheum & Erastum præmissos esse in Macedoniam à Paulo, priusquam Epheso disce- deret: Deinde cum post sedatum Ephesi tumultũ Pau- lus in Macedoniam venisset, Act. XX. Timotheus unà cum Paulo scribit secundam epistolam ad Corinthios (2. Cor. I.) missam ex Philippis urbe Macedoniæ per Titum & Lucam, 2. Cor. 13. Tertio cum Paulus paulo post eodem anno epistolam ad Romanos Corintho mit- teret, Timothei synergi sui nomine salutem Romanis adscribit, Rom. XVI. Quarto cum Paulus ex Græcia per Macedoniam rediret in Asiam, inter cæteros co- mites Timotheus quoq; recensetur Act. XX. Quanquã vero Episcopum non constituat scriptura Timo- theum in Ecclesia Ephesina, presbyteris ordinis ac jurisdictionis potestate superiorem, non tamen in Laicorum ordinem redigendus cum Petiliano Do- natista apud August. l. III. contra lit. Petil. c. 106. Nam in sacro ministerio constitutum fuisse Timo- theum, utraque ad ipsum data epistola satis docet: Universam scrutatus epistolam, scribit de præsenti Theophylactus in prologo, adverti, non eundem in modum Apostolum commonenfacere Timotheum, quo & discipulos reliquos: Sed ita instruere, ut eos decet, qui docendi munere, non audiendi officio funguntur. Quod etiam in prologo observarat Chrys. Theodo- ret9, etsi episcopum (presbyteris, ut Papistæ volunt, superiorem) eundem non faciat; Ei tamen curam animarum creditam dicit in argumento epistolæ, imo curam Asiæ ipsi divinum Paulum commisisse ait. Fuit n. Pauli συνεργὸς, Rom. 16, 21. missus ad Corin- thios, ut in memoriam revocaret illis vias Aposto- li, quomodo ubique in Ecclesia doceret, 1. Cor. IV. v. 17. qui opus Domini operatus est pariter, ut & Paulus, 1. Cor. X. 10. & juxta cum Paulo & Silvano Jesum Christum prædicavit, 2. Cor. I. 19. qui ipsi & cum ipso fervivit in Evangelio, Phil. II. 22. quem 1. Thess. III. 2. fratrem suum vocant Paulus & Sil- vanus, & διάκονον ministrum Dei, & συνεργὸν suum in Evangelio Christi ad confirmandos Thessalo- nicenses, quem Apostolus, cum Silvano adjunxit sibi in epistolis & commonitionibus Epistolicis ad diversas Ecclesias, ad Corinthiacam, 2. Cor. I. 1. ad Philippenses, c. I. 1. ad Colossenses c. I. 1. ad Thef- salonicenses, 1. Thess. I. 1. 2. Thess. I. 1. ut & ad Phile- monem, v. 1. Unde Doctorem insignem Ecclesiæ ipsum fuisse, in magno pretio ac honore ab Apo- stolo habitum patet; apud Ephesios Episcopum fuisse adeo non apparet, ut contrarium potiꝙ haud obscure ex ista in diversis locis cum Paulo conjun- ctione ac συνεργείᾳ in sacro ministerio eluceat. Eundem nempe diversas Ecclesias informasse, quē uti antea instar Apostoli à Paulo huc illuc missum fuisse observavimus: Ita secundo Apostolorum ordi- ni non inrecte accenseri posse arbitramur. Tri- buit ei Apostolus elogia insignia tum alibi, tum imprimis Phil. II. 20. Οὐδένα γὰρ, inquit in præco- nio ejusdem ibidem, ἔχω ἰσόψυχον, ὅςις γνησίως τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν μεριμνήσει; & v. 22. Τὴν δὲ δοκιμὴν αὐ- τẽ γινώσκετε, ὅτι ὡς πατρὶ τέκνον σὺν ἐμοὶ ἐδύλευσεν εἰς τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον. Fratrem nuncupat, & æquali cum Silvano, qui Prophetæ dicitur, Act. XV. 32. ho- nore dignatur. Quærit Theophylactus in prologo, cur Paulus nec Silæ, nec Clementi ipsi, nec Lucæ, nec eorum alteri cuiquam, qui apud ipsum versa- rentur, quos fane constat, multos fuisse, epistolam scripserit, nisi Timotheo duntaxat & Tito; atque ita respondere posse, præeunte Chrysostomo ait, quod illos secum circumduxerit Paulus, Timotheo ve- ro & Tito curandas demandarit Ecclesias: Unde & necessarium fuerit, ut per literas denuntiaret, quæper hos agi oporteret. Crocius mavult, id fa- ctum esse, quod status Ecclesiæ id requireret, in quâ eos reliquerat. Quod hactenus admittimus, ut Ti- motheus tamen non ad certam sedem alligetur: Imo de iis etiam monendus fuerit, quæ non Ephesi modo, sed & alibi passim ipsi ex usu essent.

qui præter rectam doctrinam loquebantur, illosque increpet. Nam & ipse Apostolus Hymenæum & Ale- xandrum naufragium circa fidem passos Satanæ jam tradiderat, ut discerent non blasphemare. Quo de etiam Theodoretes ad hunc locum: Qui ex Judæis crediderant propter Veteris Testamenti cognitionem sibi placentes, iis, qui ex gentibus crediderant, quas- dam quæstiones proponebant, eos quidem ut divinorū eloquiorum ignaros redarguere conantes, ut scilicet legalem vitæ institutionem servarent, contendentes eis persuadere. Chrysostomus homilia I. Erant, in- quit, in ea civitate (Epheso) ex Judæis quidam falsi Apostoli, qui fideles rursus ad legem conabantur re- trahere, quod fere in omnibus epistolis pro crimine ipsis objicit. Faciebant autem hoc non quasi conscien- tia compulsi, sed inani gloria inducti, quod vellent hinc habere discipulos, atque adversus Paulum con- tenderent teloque ac livore ducerentur, & hoc est, quod vocat ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν aliter docere. Quæ pro more suo pleraque repetit Theophylactus. Secundo data etiam est Paulo occasio à curiosis quibusdam hominibus, qui de frivolis quæstiunculis garrie- bant neglecta primaria & ad ædificationem ne- cessaria doctrina, quod eis futurum, Apostolum Act. XX. prædixisse hic observat Flacius: Quæ ta- men ἀφορμὴ ad eosdem quoque falsos Doctores referri potest. Tertio videtur Timotheus ceu Neo- phytus, æque uti & ipsa Ecclesia Ephesina infor- matione ulteriori opus habuisse, quam per hanc epistolam eidem exhibet S. Apostolus. Quærit autem Chrysostomus & Theophylactus hic, cur non antea ipsum satis informarir, priusquam scilicet ipsi Ecclesiam gubernandam committeret? ac re- spondet Chrysost. Doctrina illi opus fuisse, non qua discipuli instruebantur, verum quæ Magistro con- grueret. Theophylactus addit, perfectionem nemi- nem adhuc attigisse eam, ut non indigeat informa- tione; ideoque etsi ad alios instruendos constitu- tus sit quispiam, necesse profecto adhuc fore, ut ab iis deducatur excolaturque, qui perfectiores in fi- de, ac plurimum profecisse videbuntur. Adhæc cū recens esset Ecclesia instituta, haudquaquam facile fuisse, ut solus Paulus omnia curæ haberet, & ad fi- dem formaret. Addimus nos: Autoritate Aposto- lica opus omnino fuisse Timotheo, non propter adversarios tantum, sed etiam propter fideles, & præterea inservire voluisse Apostolum non solum illi Ecclesiæ, sed aliis quoque, ad quas Timotheus perventurus erat, imo universæ Christi Ecclesiæ, in cujus usum hanc epistolam consecravit Spiritus S. ut tum Episcopis & Doctoribus regulas in officio præscriberet, tum formam politiæ Ecclesiasticæ quoad diversos in Ecclesia ordines per certos ca- nones definiret. Qui proinde juxta cum propaga- tione orthodoxias & depositi fidei, scopus pro- prius est hujus epistolæ.

Cum itineris socium affumeret Paulus, ob Ju- dæos, eundem circumcidit: Quo de Chrysostomus: Mirabile quod illum affumit propter Judæos, qui in illis locis erant. Haccaufa circumcidendi. Non enim ferebant audiri verbum ab incircumciso. Et cur? Vide opus. Circumcidit, ut circumcisionem tollat. Cælibem mansisse Timotheum Ignatius epist. ad Philadelph. testatur. Martyrio coronatum sub Trajano an. Christi 109. Baronius ait. Sed id jam sub Domitiano Titi fratre ac successore factum Metaphrasten putare paulo ante monuimus. In fa- stis retrahitur mors ejus ad Neronis tempora, sub quo 24. Januarii, qui ob id ei dicatus est, quum in festo Dianæ cultus idolatricos vehementer re- prehenderit, lapidibus obrutus dicitur. Doro- theus vero nulla martyrii mentione facta Ephesi mortuum dicit, in Synopsi, ibique honorifice se- pultum, cujus ossa Constantinopolin translata esse à Constantino M. refert Hieronymus epist. LIII. contr. Vigilant. & Nicephorus l. X. c. 14.

Occasio epistolæ non una fuit. Primum enim à Pseudo-Apostolis causam datam esse observat A- thanasius in Synopsi: Ephesi quidam Judaïsmo inse- cticonabantur alienam inferre doctrinam, & simpli- ciores prætextu legis seducere. Hoc cum intellexisset Apostolus, admonuit Timotheum, ut illic bæreret, quo eos corrigerēt. Scribit autem illi epistolam hanc, & primum commonefacit eum fidei, quam sciebat, in Christum, & docet de lege, ut cohibeat eos,

Quod ad tempus exaratæ hujus epistolæ, discre- pant autores. Chrysostomus videtur dubius, an post Epistolam ad Ephesios scripserit, nec ne? Quæ quum vinculorum mentionem faciat, Eph. VI. 20. Romæ è vinculis scripta censetur. Nam ad caput I. hom. I. ad verba: Quemadmodum oravite, ut remaneres Ephesi, quum irem in Macedoniam; ita habet: Quid hoc quæso sibi vult? Ita non sufficie- bat Pauli epistola, quam Ephesiis scripserat? Num- quid literas forte contempserat? An vero ante illas literas discipulo ista mandavit? Nempe & ipse in civitate hac plurimum temporis fuerat, in qua Diana erat templum: Hic nempe magna illa notaque certamina perpessus est: Ubi postquam solutum est theatrum, convocatis admonitisque discipulis ita de- mum inde profectus est, & rursus ad eos postmodum venit. Plerique vero priorem ad Timotheum non multo post alteram ad Thessalonicenses exaratam sta- tuunt, antequam altera vice Paulus Ephesum ve- nisset, Act. XIX. 1. siquidem adventum promittat, 1.Tim.III.14. Dicitur enim Epheso discessisse Hie- rosolymam profecturus, Act. XIIX. 21. Quo tem- pore putant nonnulli eum Ephesi reliquisse Timo- theum; & quum peragraret Galatiam & Phrygiam v. 23. e Phrygiae oppido Laodicea scripsisse primam hanc epistolam ad Timotheum. Ita etiam Buntin- gius in itinerario p. 227. qui id refert ad ann. Chri- sti LIII. quod proximo anno LIV. Paulum a Lao- dicea Phrygiae civitate 57. milliarium interstitio Ephesum iterum venisse, ibique per biennium in schola Tyranni docuisse ex Act. XIX. cap. monet. In ultima in Macedoniam profectione Actor. XX. descripta non esse hoc mandatum de manendo E- phesi datum Timoth. Flacius ex eo colligit, quod non multo post captus sit, ut ei non potuerit spem reditus illuc facere ac in profectione ultima Ephe- sinis Presbyteris in concione valedictoria pro- testatus sit, eos se nunquam amplius visuros. Ante ultimam ergo valedictionem, Act. XX. de- scriptam, hanc epistolam exaratam esse omnino probabile videtur Flacio, licet non dissimulet, mi- rum sibi videri, cur in ea valedictione tantum de futuris, ac non de hisce ipsis & jam tum praesentibus seductoribus eos admonuerit. Dici autem hic fortassis poterit, ideo futurorum tantum meminis- se, quod post scriptam ad Timotheum epistolam prudentia Timothei a seductoribus illis prioribus quies jam Ephesinis conciliata fuerit : Post suum autem obitum ex ipsismet Ephesinis surrecturos in Spiritu praevideret, qui majora pericula creaturi sint. Quanquam & ita censeat Flacius cum aliis nonnullis, a Luca non omnia itinera & acta Pauli conscripta esse, atque inde multa esse impervesti- gabilia. Conf. B. Chytraeus in Onomastico & B. Balduinus in 1.Tim. I.3. Licet autem in tertia pro- fectione in Macedoniam Act. XX. 4. Timotheum secum habuerit: Potuit tamen ille Epheso rediisse ad Paulum. Sedem enim non habuit Ephesi ordi- nariam, sed frequenter instituit peregrinationes. B. Gerhardo nostro probatur ea sententia, quae in tertia profectione in Macedoniam a Paulo Timo- theo hanc exhortationem datam vult Act. XX.1. ut maneret Ephesi. De qua vid. Beza ad c. I. 3. Gro- tius putat, 1. Tim. I.3. illud iter designari, quod Act. XX. 3. indicatur, ut ex Epheso Timotheus Troada venerit, Pauli videndi causa, redieritq; mox Ephe- sum. Sed iter illud posterius est. Porro si Epheso Troada venit Timotheus ad visendum Paulum, necessum est, ut Ephesi relictus fuerit a Paulo, quod narrationi Lucae non congruit. Nam c. XIX. v. 22. persistente Paulo in Asia, Timotheus cum Erasto missus ab Apostolo est in Macedoniam. Non ergo adfuit Ephesi Paulo, cum tumultus a Demetrio excitaretur, aut cum sedato tumultu di- scipulis Ephesi valediceret, Act. XX. 1. proficiscens in Macedoniam, quo praemissus jam erat Timo- theus. Quod factum juxta Buntingium anno Do- mini quinquagesimo sexto. Exinde Epheso digres- sus, autore eodem, quinquaginta trium milliarium intercapedine Troadem venit Paulus, ubi cum no inveniret Titum, contristatus est in spiritu suo, 2. Cor. II. 13. ac Troade, ut ibid. dicitur, navigavit in Macedoniam, ac Philippos venit, 58. milliaribus a Troade distantes, unde epistolam secundam ad Corinthios scripsit, iisdemq; per Titum & Lucam misit, ut in subscriptione ejus finali habetur. A Phi- lippis, observante itidem Buntingio, intervallo 120. milliarium per Graeciam, in qua per tres d menses substitit, Act. XX. 2. Corinthum venit, ibiq; epistolam ad Romanos scripsit, qua illis per Phoe- bem misit. Anno post Christi nativitatem 57. cum Paulus Corinthi hybernasset, 1. Cor. XVI. 28. in- stante jam Vere non recta via ex Corintho in Syria solvit, sed ut insidias Judaeorum vitaret, 73. millia- rium intercapedine Philippos remeavit, ubi pa- schatis festum celebravit, Act. XX. 3. Paulo post pa- schat. festum Philippis per 58. milliaria navigando Troada venit, ubi invenit Timotheum, Act. XX. 5. illic cum aliis, qui Paulum comitabantur in Asiam expectantem Paulum, quum eo ipsum cum sociis praecesserit, Non ergo apparet, quomodo Ephe- so ceu ibi relictus a Paulo, Troada venire potue- rit Timotheus, videndi Pauli causa: quum Ephe- so ab eo discedens in Macedoniam iverit.

Locus unde scripta est haec epistola jam indica- tus est, Laodicea nempe, quae metropolis est Phry- giae Pacatianae distinctae hoc nomine a Laodicea Lyco amni imposita vicina Colossis, Col. IV. 16. Athanasius tamen ex Macedonia scriptam putat; quod etiam videtur Baronio, ut & Bezae, qui Philip- pis vel ex alia urbe Macedoniae, sed sine probabili ratione, scriptam dicit. Nullam a. videmus causam sufficientem, quae nos a recepta subscriptione fi- nali dimoveat.

Argumentum est, ut tribus verbis id exprimam, TYPUS DOCTORIS ECCLESIASTICI. Monet enim Timoth. de cura quoad doctrinam, ut a mixtura falsa doctrina Judaizantium & quae- stionum inutilium ad sinceram fidem Christianam revocentur: Cujus summa quantum ad legem, ejus- que usum & ad Evangelium de Christo exhibetur c. I. ut & quoad preces, quas pro omnibus, impri- mis magistratibus, fieri jubet, adhortans viros & mulieres simul, quomodo orare debeant, hasque instruens, ut nec publice docere, nec dominari af- fectent, c. II. Deinde requisita boni Doctoris vel Episcopi, ut & Diaconorum sistit, imprimis vitam concernentia, ut quomodo in Ecclesia, quae DEI domus, versandum sit, sciant: Doctrinae tamen Ev- angelicae praecipua capita simul exhibet, c. III. Ter- tio praedicta apostasia Anti-Christi in doctrina ve- ra & jugi pietatis exercitio perseverare jubet, c. IV. Quarto quomodo diversae aetatis, diversi sexus, & ordinis homines, imprimis vidua tum seniores, tum juvenculae instrui, ac sese gerere debeant; quove in honore habendi sint presbyteri graviter commo- nefacit, insertis etiam privatis quibusdam monitis, c. V. quod praeterea servorum sit debitum, sub ini- tium c. VI. docet. Denique colophonis loco vi- tare non persistentes in sana doctrina, & avaritiam eorum, ceu pestem, cui dediti heterodoxi erant, justitiam vero sectari cum gravissima obligatione ad servanda monita jubet, ac quae divitibus seculi praescribere, quomodo fidei depositum custodire debeat, informat, votoque gratiae epistolam obsi- gnat, cap. VI. reliquo.

Partes itaque quinque epistolae ea ratione con- stitui commode possunt, quam etiam liceat distri- buere in epigraphen, tractationem ipsam, & post- scriptum, ut vocant, vel coronidem; ut tractatio ipsa sit trimembris, utpote tum de praecipuis officiis sa- cris, qua fidem ac preces, duobus prioribus capiti- bus; tum de requisitis eorum, qui muneri Ecclesia- stico, sive Episcopi, sive Diaconi, sive Presbyteri futuri sint, praefici debent, cap. III. tum de regulis & directione eorum, qui in ministerio sacro sunt, quoad personam propriam, c. IV. & quoad alios, ac politiam Ecclesiasticam, qua diversae aetatis, ordinis, & sexus homines c. V. & VI. v. 16. Coronidis loco de divitib. nonnulla commoneat. Oeconomia tra- ctationis etiam per διχοτομίαν, si quis ea potius delectetur, institui potest: Ut pars prima sit gene- ralis tum de sacris officiis cap. I. & II. tum de perso- nis Ecclesiasticis, earumque requisitis, quæ præficien- dæ sunt muneri Ecclesiastico c. III. & quæ eidem jam præfectæ sunt: Et pars altera sit specialis, qua diversi ordinis personas c. V. & VI. Tota epist. est

Parænetica; de quo eximie Flacius: Monet, inquit, imprimis de studio retinendæ sanæ Evangelii doctri- næ: cujus subinde alia illustria loca, tanquam gem- mas aut lucidissimas stellas inserferit, quia hujs sum- mi thesauri ac veluti fontis omnis boni semper prima cura in Ecclesia habenda est, simul vero etiam monet de vitanda falsa doctrina, ac reprimendis falsis pari- ter & curiosis Doctoribus. Instruit quoque eum, quomodo tum in templo preces ac ritus obire, tum utiles ministros constituere, ac omnino Ecclesiastica tractare & judicare, tum denique singulorum ordi- num mores privatim fingere debeat. Ordo porro sen- tentiarum, Flacio docente, hic potissimum ac in ge- nere est: Quia prima summaque cura officiumque sinceri Episcopi est sanam salutaremque doctrinam suis auditoribus proponere, & falsam repellere: Ideo Apostolus primo capite monet Timotheum, ut rejectis omnibus novitatibus, fabulis & curiosis doctrinis, ea tantum doceat, quæ ad promovendam fidem & cha- ritatem faciant; simulque veram ac salutarem sum- mam doctrinæ justificationis ex mera gratia in se, tanquam in vivo quodam exemplari omnibus pro- ponendam exhibet: sicut solet ille sese non solum pro exemplo morum, sed etiam justificationis proponere Gal. II. Phil. III. Seu (ut brevius dicamus) proponit doctrinam de Lege aut contritione, Evangelio aut fi- de, justificatione, & nova obedientia, idque in viva quadam conspicuaque praxi. Secunda cura Episcopi est publicarum precum & rituum, formag, Ecclesiæ: ideoque in secundo capite de ea re præcipit. Plurimum enim & in eo situm est, ut sint omnia ad ædificationem pie prudenterque directa & instituta. Tertio quia etiam plurimum situm est in vita & toto regimine sinceri Doctoris, indeq, omne exemplum tam pietatis ac honestatis, tum & probitatis petere auditores so- lent: ideo in tertio capite Apostolus docet, tum quales Doctores constituendi sint, tum quomodo illi sese cum tota familia sua gerere debeant, sive sint pastores, si- ve diaconi. Omnes enim vult una cum familia sua inculpatos esse. Quarto loco quoniam plerumque recte formatam constitutamque Ecclesiam falsa doctrina infestat, superseminante inimico zizania: ideo c. IV. prædicit ventura esse semina aut doctrinas Dæmoniorum: quò hac prophetia præmoniti vigi- lantioresque effecti, tum illis præindicatis, tum & aliis omnibus erroribus ac seductoribus mature resi- stant; vel potius ut ex hac prophetia notisque certis- simis abominationes Anti-Christi agnoscere discant. Porro quia pio Doctori etiam privatim auditorum suorum vitæ moresque, ceu pastori singulæ oves, cor- rigendi & formandi sunt: Ideo docet eum, quomodo singulas ætates ac ordines monere, & ad veram pie- tatem permovere debeat. Postremo capite agit po- tissimum de noxia illa peste avaritiæ, quam non im- merito radicem omnium malorum præsertimque vi- tiorum vocat: quæ procul dubio illic, ut in mercatoria civitate, vehementer grassata est; quæque postremis temporibus sub Anti-Christo, domum Domini in speluncam latronum conversuro, grassatura, re- gnante non tam Simonia, quam horribilibus infini- tisque ac propudiosissimis sacrilegiis.

PARS I. EPISTOLÆ GENERALIS.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Post inscriptionem, & votum monet Timo- theum Apostolus, ut denunciet, ne secus do- ceant, fabulisve ac genealogiis inutilibus at- tendant, proposita summa & usu Legis, nec non Evangelii, ut in illis bonam militiam mi- litet, ac fidem & bonam conscientiam reti- neat, qua exciderint nonnulli, & inter eos Hymenaeus, & Alexander.

Partes duæ sunt, præmissa tamen inscriptio- ne cum voto: I. Denunciatio de heterodoxia, & de sana Legis & Evangelii doctrina, ad vers. 17. II. Adhortatio de servanda fide & conscientia bo- na, vers. 18. 19.

PARS I. Denunciatio de heterodoxia, deque sana Legis & Evangelii doctrina.

vers. 1. Παῦλος Ἀπόστολος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) Hoc initio sem- per Paulus utitur, quo major sit dictis ejus autoritas.

Non ob Timotheum, cui vel solum nomen Pauli adversus innumerorum seductorum magnificos titulos sufficiebat; sed ob eos, quibus hæc denun- cianda erant à Timotheo, quem ita divina autori- tate munitum cupiebat, in iis, quæ non Pauli, sed Jesu Christi nomine, cujus ille Apostolus erat, denuncianda.

Κατ' ἐπιταγὴν Θεοῦ Πατρὸς) Sic & Rom. XVI. 26. & Tit. I. v. 3. Incipit à causa summa.

Si excludatur ab hac notione Christus, Ariani- zat Grotius. Unica est causa eademque summa Pater, & Filius ut & Spiritus Sanctus. Ut non tres Dii, sic neque tres causæ dici possunt, salvo Atha- nasii Symbolo, salva fide Christiana.

Καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) In Manuscripto & codi- cibus plurimis est: Θεοῦ πατρὸς Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν, καὶ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Recte. Nam sic & ad Titum: Κατ' ἐπιταγὴν τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεοῦ. Mutarunt qui meminerunt Σωτῆρος nomen ple- risque in locis tribui Christo. At non meminerant etiam Deo Patri ejus tribui, qui Christum ad salutem nobis con- ficiendam misit, Luc. I. 47. infra hic IV. 10. Tit. II. 10. III. 4. Judæ v. 25. In Veteri Testamento frequenter Deo is titulus datur, Deut. XXXII. 15. 1. Sam. X. 19. Ps. XXIV. 5. XXV. 5. & alibi in Psalmis sæpe Es. XII. 2. XVII. 10. XLV. 15. 21. Jerem. XVI. 8. Mich. VII. 7. Abac. III. 17.

Manuscriptum illud, vel codices potius istos ge- minos sequutus est B. Lutherus. Atque ita etiam habuerunt omnes fere codices Bezæ. Unus Clara- montanus tantum eam, quam in textu exhibet Gro- tius, habuit lectionem: Et alius quidam simplici- ter legit: Ἐπιταγὴν τοῦ Πατρὸς ἡμῶν Θεοῦ, καὶ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Et quum Beza, Casaubonus, aliique in diversis editionibus Vulgato etiam non discrepan- te sic legant, ut Manuscriptum Grotii, non video, quid causæ habuerit, alteram Claræmontani codi- cis lectionem textui inserere.

Τῆς ἐλπίδος ἡμῶν) Id est, qui Christus causa est spei no- stræ. Vide 1. Thess. I. 3. Similis loquutio Ps. LXXI. 7.

Christus non tantum causa est spei, sed etiam fundamentum spei unicum, & objectum, in quod speramus, ut Psalm. II. v. ult. & alibi passim doce- mur. Recte ergo notat Theodoretus: Hæc non esse διακριτικῶς accipienda; siquidem & Deus sit objectum ac causa spei, & Christus sit σωτὴρ ἡμῶν: Deum autem, inquit, salutem, & Christum spem vocavit. Non nomina dividens, nec hoc quidem illi, illud vero huic tribuens, sed utraque persona intelli- gens. Etenim B. David utrumque posuit in una persona: Exaudi nos Deus Servator noster, spes omnium finium terræ, Pf.LXIV. Opportune autem, docente post Chrysoflomum Theophylacto, Salva- torem dixit & spem, quia docenti & prædicanti, quandoquidem multis difficultatibus & periculis col- luctatur, ut in quem omne bellum infertur, speran- da est salus, & quo cadente, & simul, qui sub se militant, facilius cadant necesse sit: Ut illud: Per- cutiam pastorem, & dispergentur oves. Non itaque cadendum est, quando Salvatorem habemus, non hominem quendam simpliciter, sed Deum ipsum & Patrem, qui nos celerrime à quovis discrimine exi- met. Quod si à periculis haudquaquam mox erua- mur, nobis tamen speranda sunt potiora : quippe quorum spes Christus, cujus pudere nil possumus. His itaque duabus de causis discrimen omne ferendum est, vel quia celerrime sumus per Christum salvandi, vel quia spe bona fovendi. B. Gerhardus monet, respicere Apostolum ad Judaizantes, qui in lege & ceremoniis spem salutis suæ collocabant, cum solus Christus sit & esse debeat spes nostra, per cujus solius meritum remissionem & vitam æternam sperare ac consequi possumus.

v. 2. Τιμοθέῳ γνησίῳ τέκνῳ ἐν πίςει) Timotheus à prima ætate commendatus Paulo fuerat à matre, ut ejus exemplis instrueretur, 2. Tim. 3, 10. ubi apertum sit, eum Paulo ad- fuisse, antequam Paulus Lystram veniret, quanquam ibi pri- mum Timothei meminit Lucas XVI. 1. quia eo tempore testimoniis Ecclesiarum præcedentibus, in munus Evange- listæ assumptus est, cum antea fuisset Pauli ἀκόλουθος. Vocat autem Paulus eum filium in fide, quia per fidem novam quandam naturam accipimus, & velut iterum gignimur, 1. Cor. IV. 13. 15. 17. 2. Cor. VI. 13. Eph.V. 1. Philipp. II. 22. 1. Thess II. 7. 2. Tim. I. 2. II. 1. Philem. v. 10. 3. Joh. v. 4. Adde Gal. IV. 19. Addit γνησίῳ, ut Phil, IV. 3. Tit. I. v. 4. quia filius erat Pauli minime degener.

Timotheum Paulo à prima ætate commenda- tum fuisse à matre 2. Tim. III. 10. non lego, ac ne id quidem, quod Paulo adfuerit, antequam Ly- stram veniens eum assumeret, Act. XVI. 2. nec ante illud tempus Paulo notus fuit, quia tum demum commendatus eidem testimoniis Lystrensium & Iconiorum fratrum. A quonam ad fidem Christi conversus sit, ibi non additur, sed quod ibi à Paulo ceu μαθητὴς, quo nomine ad Christum conversi di- cebantur, inventus sit. Dubium tame non est, quin matrem Christianam habuit, & sacras literas ab infantia didicit, in ætate infantili Christianismi rudimentis imbutum; forte etiam, quum circum- cisus non fuerit, sacramento baptismi initiatus fuit: quanquam hoc non temere asseruerim, quum exempla haud facile occurrant eorum, qui prius baptizati, postmodum circumcisi fuerint in Eccle- sia Christiana. Antequam autem Timotheus Ly- stræ à Paulo assumptus, ipsum Pauli ἀκόλουθον fuis- se, fabula Grotiana est; quæ si Papistico sensu ἀκό- λουθον dicat, de ultimo gradu sacrorum ordinum, mirum, quod Polyhistor eos ordines ætati Aposto- licæ ignotos fuisse ignorarit, nisi in gratiam Pa- pistarum id potius dissimulasse censendus sit, quàm ignorasse. Filium eundem vocat Paulus non ob regenerationem, quum ex verbo veritatis, Jac. I. v. 18. aut per baptismum jam renatus fuerit, sed ob informationem atque imitationem. Fide enim jam præditus fuit, utpote discipulis fidelibus an- numeratus, Act. XVI. 1. Nam ut Augustinus libr. contr. Adimantum cap. 5. monet, tribus modis no- men filii accipitur in scripturis secundum naturam, doctrinam, & imitationem, ubi tertium modum ad regenerationem oportet referri, vel addendus po- tius hic quartus modus, quum ætatis ratione etiam filius dicatur : quem sensum hic constituit Erasm. Sed rectius B. Hunnius : Timotheum nominat fi- lium suum, non eo tantum modo, quo senes vocant juniores suos filios, (fuisse enim Timotheum eo tem- pore adhuc juvenem, apparet ex hac epistola c. IV.) sed filium illum vocat in fide, eò quod Paulus eum, licet prius etiam esset discipulus Christi, in fide Evan- gelii plenius edocuit & confirmavit. Epitheton au- tem addit, dum germanum filium (γνήσιον) salutat, (uti pergit B. Hunnius) ob sinceritatem & constan- tiam, quod Apostoli vestigia terens magna cum laude pie fidelitatis ac perseverantiæ doctrinam Evangelii tradebat, & non sine periculo vitæ adversus hostes esus constantissime propugnabat.

Χάρις, ἔλεος, εἰρήνη ἀπὸ Θεῦ Πατρὸς ἡμῶν κᾺ Χριςῦ Ἰησῦ. τῦ Κυρίυ ἡμῶν) Sic & 2. Tim. I. 2. Tit. I. 4. 2. Joh. v. 3. εἰρήνη κᾺ ἔλεος, Gal. VI. 16. Judæ v. 2. χάρις κᾺ εἰρήνη, 1. Cor. I. 3. 2. Cor. I. 2. & alibi sæpe. Geminatio autem significatus similis habet aliquid περιπαθὲς. Conf. Num. VI. 24. seqq.

De voce ἔλεος judicat cum Chrysostomo Theo- phylactus, eam ex charitatis vehementia quadam in voto additam, vel quia Diabolus vehementius in pastorem armatur vel alios: Quam Hugo Car- dinalis etiam de potestate dandi Spiritum Sanctum intelligit: Sed hic non spectantur dona ministran- tia, sive ordinaria, sive extraordinaria; proinde nec misericordia hic, quæ decus Episcopi est, ut Rupertus Tuitiensis vult, sed benignissima Dei vo- luntas, quæ sine omni merito favet & benefacere gaudet, voce χάρις ἀπὸ τῦ χαίρειν designatur, gra- tia quæ fons & origo omnium bonorum, quæ ma- joris emphaseos causa per misericordiam expri- mitur, miseriam nostram gratiose, & cum com- miserationis affectu respicientem. Nam ἔλεος se- cundum Phavorinum est συμπάθεια συμφορᾶς, ut ita hisce vocibus: omnia in causa salutis meræ Dei gratiæ nos debere, innuatur. Quo de Haymo in hunc locum: Pax per misericordiam nobis confer- tur, non per meritum nostrum. R. Moses Maimo- nides hæc attributa DEI in More Nebuchim cap. LIV. sic distinguit: Quemadmodum nos gratiam Chaninah vocare solemus, cum quippiam largimur ei, cui nihil debemus, (Job. XIX. 21. Genes. XXXV. v. 5. 11.) Ita quia Deus creat, conservat & gubernat eos, quibus nullo jure est adhuc obligatus, ideo voca- tur Chaninon gratiosus. Misericors dicitur, non quasi passioni esset obnoxius, sed quia simile quid à Deo ad sanctos ejus provenit, quod à Patre ter- reno super filium, qui ad clementiam, compassio- nem, & misericordiam erga ipsum commovetur. Quæ gratia & misericordia Dei maxime in pace per Christum partæ per fidem nobis collatæ dono effulget.

v. 3. Καθὼς παρεκάλεσά σε προσμεῖναι ἐν Ἐφέσῳ, πορευόμε- νος εἰς Μακεδονίαν) Assentior putantibus indicari iter illud, quod Act. XX. 3. ut ex Epheso Timotheus Troada venerit Pauli videndi causa, redieritque mox Ephesum, ubi creditur reliquum vitæ egisse.

De hac Grotii opinione dictum jam in Prole- gomenis. Ephesi reliquum vitæ egisse Timo- theum, postquam in Troada Paulo adfuit, veri- tati non consonat. Fuit enim in Italia captivus, & liberatus ex captivitate illa dicitur Ebr. XIII. 23. Adfuit Romæ Paulo, & cum eodem epistolas scri- psit ad Philippenses, ad Colossenses, & ad Phile- monem, ut testantur inscriptiones. Beza ad ver- bum προσμεῖναι: Antea igitur Timotheus cum Pau- lo Ecclesias peragrabat: tunc ita ferente necessita- te, voluit eum Paulus Ephesi subsistere, non ut illi Ecclesiæ tanquam Episcopus additus esset: Sed ut Ecclesia constituta Pseudo-Apostolis occurreret: unde etiam postea revocatus est Romam ab ipso A- postolo. Nam Ephesi quoque per biennium docue- rat Apostolus, qui tamen Ephesinus Episcopus pro- pterea non dicitur: neque constat, an Timotheus postea sit Ephesum Roma reversus, ut qui fuerit Evangelista.

Ἵνα παραγγείλῃς τισὶ) Hic illud ἵνα παραγγείλῃς est po- situm pro παραγγεῖλαι, qualis loquutio est Eph. V. 33. Quan- doquidem ea de caussa ibi relictus es, fac quod mandavi: De- nuntia quibusdam, nempe qui tali denuntiatione ops habent.

Μὴ ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν) Ne aliud doceant, quam nos do- cuimus. Vide infra VI. 3.

Verbum ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν nonnulli tam ad au- ditores, quam Doctores referunt, utpote Haymo, Hugo Cardinalis & Lombardus: Sed id rectius à Chrysostomo, Theodoreto, Theophylacto, Primasio, & Ambrosio restringitur ad Doctores, quod è v. 7. constat, ideoque non cum Erasmo reddendum, ne diversam sequantur doctrinam, sed cum Vulgato, ne aliter doceant, quod Calvino observante latius patet, quam si reddas, aliud doceant; quum hoc ad materiam referatur, illud etiam ad novas docendi formas, qui tamen monet, non vocari aliam do- ctrinam tantum, quæ cum pura Evangelii doctri- na pugnat, sed quæcunque purum Evangelium vel corrumpit novis & adventitiis figmentis vel pro- fanis speculationibus obscurat. Crocius ita de his habet: Aliud docent, qui docent, quæ in scriptura non inveniuntur, aut etiam cum scriptura manifeste pugnant. Docent aliter, qui proponunt quidem, quæ in scriptura leguntur, at nec sincere, nec in- tegre, sed vel addunt de suo, vel demunt, vel in- terpolant, studiose miscentes veris & utilibus vana & inutilia, necessariis non necessaria curiose conqui- sita. Ad prius pertinet, quod fabulas aliqui trade- rent. Ad posterius, quod legem sic docerent, & usum perverterent. Hæc Crocius, non dubitans, quin Apostolus utrumque prohibeat. Neque nos dubitamus, hæc omnia prohiberi hac voce ἑτερο- διδασκαλεῖν: etsi opus non censeamus, ut eadem vox & per aliud & per aliter docere simul explice- tur. Nam qui nec sincere nec integre, vel cum additamento humano traduntur, non tantum ali- ter docentur, sed etiam aliud exhibent, quam scri- ptura docet. Huic enim nec addendum quid est, nec demendum. Si addatur, est aliud à scriptura. Si dematur, aut non sincere tradatur, etiam diver- sum est à Verbo Dei: quod integrum & sincerum relinquendum, prout à Deo prodiit, estque μηδε- μιᾶς προσθέσεως ἢ ἀφαιρέσεως ἐπιδεχόμενον, uti regulam vel normam definit Varinus. Docere ali- ter, inquit Theophylactus, est alias quasdam disci- plinas inducere, & decreta à veris aliena. Erant namque ex Judæis plerique, qui cum se Apostolos mentirentur, & gloriæ cupiditate dici se præceptores optarent, ad legis veteris observationem inducebant discipulos. Beza notat: diversam doctrinam dici, non eam modo, quæ penitus alia est, sed etiam quæ veram doctrinam adulterat, id est, cum Verbo Dei vel tantillum humanarum speculationum admiscet, adeo ut ipsam quoque docendi formam complectatur hoc Pauli interdictum. Ἕτερος ita accipitur Act. II. v. 4. 1. Cor. XIV. 21. Frustra tamen Estius aliam do- ctrinam intelligi dicit, quæ priorem excludat, ad- eoque non posse hunc locum traditionibus oppo- ni infert. Nam non solum nihil contra Evangelium, sed etiam nihil præter Evangelium docendum est in Ecclesia, Gal. I. 8. 9. Et Pseudo-Apostoli, qui hic ut heterodoxi notantur, non negabant justifi- cationem per fidem in Christum, sed fidei in justi- ficatione addebant opera. Quo de legendus im- primis B. Lutherus Von der Haupt-Summa Got- tes Gebotes Tom. II. Jen. fol. 475. Altenb. Tom. II. fol. 827. Diese etliche/so der Apostel hie meynet/ sind gewißlich nicht schlechte Leute gewesen/ sondern der hohen Aposteln Petri/ und der andern Jün- ger/ die so offt ihre Wunderwerck gesehen haben/ und manche schöne Predigt und Lehre gehöret/ darzu das Urtheil zu Jerusalem durch die Apostel beschlossen/ Actor. XV. noch haben sie den rechten Verstand nicht erlanget. Fol. 828. Noch fielen jene Jünger darauff/ und hiengen einen Zusatz dar- an/ liessen die Lehre und das Urtheil von der blossen Gnade fahren/ und ergriffen die Werck/ so die Apo- stel thäten/ und drungen dieselbe auffs Gewissen/ sagten: So und so must du thun/ oder nicht thun. Also rissen die falsche Lehrer ein/ und dämpffeten den Glauben/ schlugen die Gnade nieder/ trieben Chri- stuma us. Dann wer dahin geräth/ daß er mit Wercken dem Gewissen helffen/ und GOtt versüh- nen will/ hat schon die Gnade mit Christo und allen Schatz verlohren. Illud ergo est ἑτεροδιδασκα- λεῖν juxta B. Lutherum.

v. 4. Μηδὲ προσέχειν μύθοις) Agit hic de iis, qui ex Judai- smo ad Christianismum venerant, & Judaicas fabulas admi- scebant Christianismo. Ostendunt id sequentia, & Tit. I. v. 14. Adde & infra IV. 7. 2. Tim. IV. 4. Tales erant apud Judæos quosdam fabulæ de eis, quæ Deus fecit ante mun- dum hunc conditum, de homine facto primum ἀνδρογύνῳ, de ejus concubitu cum bestiis, & cum Lilith, de Dæmonibus inde natis: De Behemotho & Leviathane, de animarum ὑπάρξει ante corpus, de Angelis in sidera & regiones distri- butis, multaque similia. Tertullianus de Valentino: Mul- tas introduxit fabulas.

Valentini fabulæ recentiores sunt, quam ut de iis monendi tum fuerint Ephesini, nec ej¹ antiqui- tatis esse illas fabellas Judæorum, quæ hic adducū- tur, doceri potest; etsi tales etiam adducat Augu- stinus. Nec verisimile est, illas affanias ab ullo sive Doctore Christiano, etsi nomine dealbato tantum, traditas, sive auditore admissas. De Judæis moder- nis, in sensum reprobum traditis, non mirum, quod etiam nugis istis ineptissimis fidem non derogent. Beza de curiosis & vanis speculationibus, Calvinus de nugis & ineptiis intelligunt. Sed agnoscit Cro- cius, fabulas generaliter hic accipi de omnibus à scriptura alienis & inutilibus. Fabulas, inquit Theo- phylactus cum Chrysostomo, non legem dicit, sed observationes nonnullas, & commentitia dogma- ta. De lege enim accipiebant Manichæi, qui vetus Testamentum abjiciebant. Theodoretus: Fabulas, inquit, vocavit non legis doctrinam, sed Judaicam interpretationem, quæ vocatur ab eis δευτέρωσις. S. Apost. explicare videtur, c. VI. 3. verbis: μὴ προσέρχεται ὑγιαίνοσι λόγοις τοῖς τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ χρισῦ, ὸ τῇ κατ’ εὐσέβειαν διδασκαλίᾳ, & v. 20. per τὰς βεβήλες κενοφωνίας ὸ ἀντιθέσεις τῆ ψευδω- νύμε γνώσεως. Haberi tamen specialem respectum ad μύθυς βεβήλυς ὸ γραώδεις, fabulas profanas & aniles, è c. IV. 7. patet, quemadmodum vicissim generalem sensum confirmat locus parallelus, 2. Tim. IV. 7. ubi οἱ μύθοι & ἡ ἀλήθεια sibi opponun- tur, ut constet fabulis accenseri, quicquid à verita- te alienum est. Verbum προσέχειν non tantum auditoribus, sed etiam Doctoribus convenit: quia προσέχειν est incumbere in aliquam rem, ut προσ- έχειν τοῖς ναυτικοῖς apud Thucydidem.

Καὶ γενεαλογίας ἀπεράντοις) γενεαλογίας vocat, quas Judæi ספרות, ideo quod fingebatur harum alia ex alia emanare, & quasi gigni, hoc modo: Corona. בינה ἔννοια intelligentia, חכמה ἀκμὴσοφ sapientia, פחד vel גבורה גדולה vel חסד magnifi- Timor vel potentia, centia sive misericordia. תפארת DEUS, הוד Majestas, נצח victoria, יסוד fundamentum, quod & כל omnia, מלכה regnum, quod & שכינה præsentia DEI. A Platonicis hæc desumpta docet nos Tertullianus in Præscriptione: quod verum est, sed quibusdam nominibus retentis, quibusdam mutatis. Sed jam olim apud Persarum magos tales fuisse γενεαλογίας docet nos Plutarchus in Iside. Et meminere eorum Platonici, qui περὶ ἀρχῶν scripsere. Zo- roastris tamen nomine, quæ circumferebantur, ea à Gnosti- cis, quos hic notat Paulus, esse facta deprehendit, & osten- disse se ait Porphyrius. Et puto, eum verum dicere : Βυθὸν, σι- γῆν, ἐννοίας mentionem habes apud Proclum ad Timæum, apud Damascium & alios. Vere autem hic Paulus dixit ἀπε- ράντοις. Nam multi ad has proprietates alias multas pari ju- re adjecere, ut Gnosticorum illi, ex quibus originem traxere Valentiniani & Basilidiani, qui & pro ספירות usurparunt nomen αἰώνων, eorumq; fecere συζυγίας & γενεαλογίας. Nam & hoc nomine utebantur, ut videre est apud Irenæum initio l.I. Tertullianum, Epiphanium. Αἰῶνας ἀπέρας dixit scriptor Constitutionum sub Clementis nomine. Γενεαλογίας autem Deorum, quæ exstabant apud Hesiodum & Orphea per ἀλ- ληγορίας quasdam ad illos suos αἰῶνας, id est, ספירות referebant. Et propter ista videri volebant eruditiores cæteris, sperne- bantque alios Christianos, ut rudiores: Et hinc est, quod γνωστικῶν nomen ipsi sibi fecere. Vide, quæ diximus in ante. loquio ad Evangelium Johannis. Proclus cum de genealo- giis, quæ sunt in Platonis Timæo, disputasset: Ἀλλὰ τούτων ᾅδων ὀυδὲν ἀυγὲι τῶν πραγμάτων φροντίζοντι ὅπως ἂν ἔχοι.

Aliena sunt, quæ hic è Rabbinis adducuntur: Non enim illa γενεαλογίας concernunt, etsi maxi- me ad γενεὰς vel generationes revocentur: Prorsus enim diversæ sunt αἱ γενεαὶ, & αἱ γενεαλογίαι: quan- quam nec generationes dicuntur Rabbinis, sed עשר ספירות decem numerationes, exposuit Buxtorffius, quo autore illæ non decem sive genealogiæ sive generationes sunt, sed decem positiones primæ & my- sticæ de proprietatibus, notionibus sive attributis di- vinis, suntque generatim fundamenta, super quæ tota Cabalistica Theologia ædificata est, per quorū rectam cognitionem ad intima Theologiæ Cabali- sticæ ejus studiosi penetrant, qui porro hæc de illis observat in voce ספירות: Sic quidem hic communi- ter reddunt ספירות numerationes: sed Autor præ- fationis in librum Schare ora vult eas sic dici à luci- ditate & splendore: Sic enim scribit: Cabalistæ tradi- derunt & ordine disposuerunt nobis divinas proprie- tates vocaruntque eas על שם הזכות והבהירות ספירות כספיר מלשון .Sephiroth à claritate, ex si- gnificatione opus lapidis Sapphirini Exod. XXIV. 10. Quemadmodum n. in re lucida conspiciuntur formæ: Sic Sephiroth sunt typus & forma omnium entium, & quemadmodum res conspiciuntur in re lucida sine ulla additione: Sic conspiciuntur omnia in istis Sephi- roth sine additione &c. Reuchlinus l. III. de Cabala ita de iisdem habet apud Galatin. p. 734. Decem nu- merationes à Cabalistis עשר ספירות appellatas mul- ti ex nobis multifariam tractant, quidam in arboris modum, alii ad formam hominis, ut sæpe mentio fiat de radice, trunco, ramis, & corticibus. Sæpe vero et- iam de capite, humeris, cruribus, pedibus, latere dex- tero & sinistro. Eæ sunt decem divina nomina, quæ nos mortales de Deo concipimus, vel essentialia, vel personalia, vel notionalia, vel communia, & nomi- nantur sic כתר, id est, corona, חכמה, id est, sapien- tia, בינה, i. e. prudentia sive intelligentia, חסד, i.e. clementia seu bonitas, גבורה, i. e. gravitas vel seve- ritas, תפארת, id est, ornatus, נצח, id est, triumphus, הוד, id est, confessio laudis, יסוד, id est, fundamen- tum, מלכות, i. e. regnum. Supra coronam vero po- nitur אין סוף, i. e. infinitudo, & est abyssus. Illæ sane decem Sephiroth suo usu non destituuntur, quum proprietates divinæ illis contineantur. Quas vero quis inutiles & vanas dicat? Perfectionem Dei ex- hibent, qui etsi simplicissimus in se sit, ob nostrum tamē concipiendi modum attributis diversis ejus- dē declaratur essentia. Hæc enim esse γενεαλογίας hic reprobatas à Paulo, minime credendum. De illis R. Moses in commentariis suis ad c. I. l. Jetsim: Abraham Pater noster vocavit Sephiroth, quasi Sap- phiros, ad significandum, quemadmodum Sapphirus omnes colores recipit: Sic Deo omnes formas, benedi- ctiones, emanationesque tribui, ita tamen, ut hæc omnia summam Dei benedicti unitatem prædicent.

Quæ ex istis decem proprietatibus Cabalisticè de- ducuntur, sine dubio recentiora sunt hac Paulina epistola.

A Platonicis autem desumptas esse illas Sephi- roth non invenio in Tertulliano de præscripto ad Valentin. Saltim æonas huc applicat cap. XXXIII. Sed & cum genealogias indeterminatas nominat Va- lentinus agnoscitur, apud quem Æon ille nescio qui novi & non unius nominis generat è sua charite sen- sum & veritatem, & hi aque procreant sermonem & vitam : Dehinc & isti generant hominem & Eccle- siam; de qua prima ogdoade exinde decem alii æones, & duodecim reliqui æones miris nominibus oriuntur in meram fabulam triginta æonum. Quid illis com- mentis, obsecro, commercii cum Sephiroth Rab- binicis? Valentinianos autem atque Gnosticos tem- pore posteriores esse hac epistola Paulina è Chro- nologia constat. Irenæus etsi generationis & emis- sionis nomina de æonum portentis recensendis adhibeat genealogias, tamen eum vocare loco ci- tato haud video, necque Tertulliano aut Epipha- nio locus eam in rem adduci potuit.

Porro si plerosque omnes Interpretes audias, non de emanationibus divinis hic Apostolus agit, sed de genealogiis humanis, de quib9 infinitas quæ- stiones movebant Judæi, quas Judaizantes etiam Ecclesiæ obtrudere sategebant. Avos & proavos, inquit Theophylactus, commemorabant, ut gloriam ex historia vendicarent. Interminatis autem dixit genealogiis, vel quia altius illi genealogias repeterent, vel quia nullam demum attulissent utilitatem, nec u- tilem aliquem & compendiosum essent eventum sor- titi,sed ea afferrent, quæ & difficulter memoria repeti possent, & admodum essent perplexa. Subjungit qui- dem Theophylactus, quod de fabulis gentilium & generationibus Deorum, quas commemorant, intel- ligi possint:Sed quum Apostolus Judæos aperte de- signet,nominans νομοδιδασκάλυς,priorem sensum præferunt alii:quibus genealogiarum indagatio in pretio erat, quin etiam à Prophetis editæ fuerint in libris Chronicorum: utpote quibus distinctio tribuum & familiarum olim necessaria ostendeba- tur, tum ob non confusionem tribuum & familia- rum, tum ob hæreditates adserendas, tum ob pri- mogenitos ab aliis cum descendentibus dignoscē- dos, tum ob lites ex prætensione jurium & posses- fionum oriundas decidendas, tum imprimis ob genealogiam & prosapiam Christi rectius agno- scendam: Quarum vero studium post exhibitum Christum, & sublatam politiæ Judaicæ formam, tribuumque ac familiarum distinctionem, inutile est, nec ortum, aut exitum in plerisq; invenit, ideo ἀπεράντοις dixit Apostol9. Quod minime ad γενεα­ λογίαν Christi, utpote in scripturis definitam, ad- eoq; nec ἀπέραντον vel interminabilem extenden- dum est. Ejus enim indagatio propter scripturæ mentem necessaria est: quum ex adverso aliarum nec necessaria sit, nec possibilis, nullisque finibus terminata, & incertis narrationib9 implicita, quē- admodum jam Esdræ & Nehemiæ tempore indi- cari non poterant genealogiæ, Neh. VII. 62.

Αἵ τινες ζητήσεις παρέχουσι μᾶλλον) Multæ inde nascebantur quæstiones, cum alii aliter classes illas & nomina ordinarent suo quisque arbitratu. Sic aliter Basilidiani, aliter Valenti- niani. Vide Irenæum l. 5 6. 7. & sequentibus. Adde Lactan- tium l. 5. Tertull. Cum Valentinianus Ænos tantum triginta finxisset, isti addiderunt alios complures, quatuor enim primū, deinde alios quatuor aggregaberunt. Pro ζητήσεις in Manu- scripto est ἐκζητήσεις. Sic οἱ ἐκζητηταὶ ᾿ φρονήσεως, Baruch. III. 14. Rabbini quæstiones tales vocant מבעיות.

Η᾿ οἰκονομίαν Θεῦ τὴν ἐν πίστει) Videntur quidem hæc eo tendere, ut explicent dispensationem Dei circa salutem no- stram: Sed revera ea simplex est per fidem in Christum: nec tot ambagibus indiget. De voce οἰκονομίας vide Eph. I. 10. Quidam libri habent οἰκοδομήν. Sed illud rectius.

Quanquam oikonomian Codices non pauci legant, eaque ratione explicet Theodoretus, Chrysostom. & Theophylactus de dispensatione salutis; pleriq; ta- men Codices habent oikodomian, ædificationem, uti Syrus etiam, Vulgatus, Ambrosius, Beza, B. Luther. reddidere. Nec inusitatam esse oikodomias vocem e Thucydide l. I. & Plutarch. de solert. animal. pa- tet. Dicitur autem oikodomia theou, tum quod a Deo, tum quod in Deo fundata sit, tum quod ad gloriam Dei tendat. Ædificatio Dei est, inquit Haymo, quan- do quis ea loquitur, quæ aliquid utilitatis habent, per quam præparant & ædificant Dei templum in cordi- bus auditorum. Fit autem ea ædificatio non per fa- bulas, aut genealogias interminabiles, & quæstio- nes inutiles, sed per fidem vel doctrinam divinitus traditam, quæ fides dicitur, quæ creditur, cujus ex- plicandæ gratia ad summam legis & Evangelii di- greditur Apostolus.

v. 5. To de telos tēs parangelias estin agapē) Nostra doctri- na ad dilectionem tendit, Illorum parit dissidia. Parangelia de Evangelio dicitur & infra 18. & multitudinis numero parangeliai, 1. Thess. IV. 2. Telos soph Ecclesiastæ XII. 13.
