Quid autem pro istis petis, nisi ut relictis erroribus suis convertantur ad Deum, accipiant fidem, accipiant charitatem, & de ignorantiæ tenebris liberati in agnitionem veniant veritatis. Quod quia ipsi præstare sibi ne- queunt, male consuetudinis pondere oppressi & Diaboli vincu- lis illigati neq; deceptiones suas evincere valent, quibus tam per- tinaciter inhæserunt, ut quantum amanda est veritas, tantum & ligant falsitatem, misericors & justus Dominus pro omnibus sibi vult hominibus supplicari, ut cum videmus de tam profun- dis malis innumeros erui, non ambigamꝫ Deum præstititsse, quod ut præstaret, oratus est : Et gratias agentes pro his qui salvi facti sunt, speremus etiam eos qui nondum illuminati sunt, eodem Divinæ gratiæ opere eximendos de potestate tenebrarum, ut in regnum Dei, priusquam ex hac vita exeant, transferantur. Philo de Judæorum Pontifice maximo : Οὐ μόνον ὑπὲρ ἁπάντων ἀνθρώπων γένους, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑπὲρ τῶν τῆς Φύσεως με- ρῶν, γῆς, ὕδατος, ἀέρος, καὶ πυρὸς, τάς τε εὐχὰς καὶ τὰς ἐυ- χαριςίας ποιεῖται. Sunt quædam preces pro omnibus : Sunt & aliæ pro fidelibus tantum, ut Joh. 17, 9.

## 2:2
Vers. 2.

Ὑπὲρ βασιλέων) The Greeks called the Roman Emperors βασιλέας, not looking to the Latin word, but to the thing itself. For they were in fact ἀνυπεύθυνοι. Tertullian: Looking up thither (that is, to heaven), we Christians, with hands outstretched, because we are harmless, with head bare, because we do not blush, finally without a prompter, because from the heart, we pray for all Emperors, [asking] for them a long life, a secure empire, a safe home, brave armies, a faithful senate, an honest people, a quiet world, and whatever are the wishes of a man and a Caesar. Dionysius in Eusebius: Καὶ τούτῳ διηνεκῶς ὑπὲρ τῆς βασιλείας αὐτῶν, ὅπως ἀσάλευτος διαμείνῃ, προσευχόμεθα. This excellent custom, like many praiseworthy things, comes from the Jews, Psalm 20. Ezra 6, 16. Josephus 12, 17. Ἀπαιτήσαντες τῶν ἱερέων τίνες & πρεσβυτέρων ἠσπάζοντο, καὶ τὰς θυσίας ἐπεδείκνυον, ἃς ὑ- πὲρ τοῦ Βασιλέως ἔλεγον προσφέρειν τῷ Θεῷ. He mentions this custom also in 7, 17. & elsewhere often: And there exists a precept concerning that matter in Pirke Avoth.

And of all those who are in authority) Christians prayed not only for Emperors, but also for the Governors of the provinces in which they lived, who are ἡγεμόνες 1 Pet. 2:14. See also what is said in Matt. 27:2. The writer of the second book of Maccabees, chapter 3:15, calls Hyrcanus a man placed in authority, בִּגְדֻלּה. Even if they are infidels, according to the interpretation of Theophylact, Kings, it is nevertheless necessary to pray for them. For the rulers of the empire and kingdoms at that time were strangers to the Christian faith. He also adds the fruit of these prayers, which are made for all: But two things, he says, when we pray for all, we obtain, which are the best. For even hatreds, if we have any against others, are dissolved, since no one can be of an unjust mind toward him for whom he prays. And kings, their wickedness changed into probity by prayers, are rendered better, and no longer rage fiercely against them. For how wonderful must that seem, to hear persecutors and executioners asking those whom they afflict with punishments to pray for them. Concerning thanksgivings for others similarly: He who gives thanks because he sees his neighbor filled with good things, it follows certainly that he should pursue the same with benevolence. Whence it happens that when we ourselves are affected with good things, we ought to show far greater gratitude toward God. But that Grotius says prayer for the King and magistrate is merely an excellent custom of the Jews, and derives such intercession not from the sacred scriptures of the Old Testament, but from Pirke Avoth, that does not agree with the commands of Jer. 29:7, Baruch 1:11, nor with the love which subjects are bound to show to Magistrates, as children to fathers.

That we may lead a quiet and peaceable life) Safe from the invasion of barbarians and from robbers. Seneca, Epistle LXXIV: They seem to me to err who think that those who are faithfully devoted to philosophy are stubborn and refractory and contemners of magistrates and Kings, or of those through whom public affairs are administered. For on the contrary, no one is more grateful toward them; and not undeservedly; for they provide more for no one than for those to whom it is permitted to enjoy tranquil leisure. Therefore, those to whom public security provides access to the purpose of living well, it is necessary that they honor the author of this good as a parent. Afterward: He loves those through whom it is permitted to him to do this safely. Again: Under whose protection he is placed, he practices good arts. Then: Thus the benefit of this peace pertains to all, it reaches more deeply to those who use it well. Likewise: He will therefore confess that he owes much to him by whose administration and providence it happens that he has abundant leisure and the control of his own time: Lactantius at the end of his Institutions to the Emperor: It was fitting that in strengthening the state of the human race, the divinity should use you as author and minister: To whom we supplicate with daily prayers, that he may guard you first, whom he willed to be a true guardian, then inspire in you a will which may always persevere in the love of the Divine Being, which is salutary to all, for your happiness, and for the rest for peace.

In all godliness and gravity) He added this incidentally, so that he might admonish Christians of their duty. We do not, he says, desire public tranquility and security for this reason, that we may use it for carousing and lusts: But for sacred assemblies, for upright and modest manners, בְּהַדְרֵי קֹדֶשׁ Psalm 110:3. What gravity (σεμνότης) is, see Phil. 4:8. Aristotle interprets it as a dignified seriousness.

This was not added merely incidentally. The object and the end of prayer for the Magistrate is noted. For we seek this, that the Magistrate may not only be able to provide security and tranquility for subjects, and does provide it by Divine grace, but that he may also be a protection for piety and honesty, to which God can also bend their hearts through the prayers of subjects, who are ignorant of the true God and serve idols. Chrysostom and Theophylact refer piety to doctrine itself, and rightly. For without true faith there is no true worship of God, and thus no godliness. In all piety, he says, that is, not only that which is in dogmas, but also that which is in the manner of life. The Vulgate translates gravity as chastity, the Syriac as purity, others say it notes honesty and gravity of manners more correctly, which according to Theophylact ought to be seen not only in abstinence from lust, but in every virtue, which we admit concerning every virtue according to the second table. Therefore the Apostle alleges three ends, as blessed Hunnius warns, which emerge from the office of the Magistrate: First, a placid and quiet life, while the fatherland is defended from external enemies, and barriers and chains are thrown upon the disturbers of tranquility, lest they dare to run riot against others at their pleasure, and violate the common peace and leisure. The second end is piety, which is in exile where, with the regime of political government shaken, everything is permitted to everyone with impunity. And finally honesty, of which even the sounder Heathens had care, much greater regard for it must be had by Christians, lest flagitious acts and crimes, like a broken embankment, pour themselves out and prevail.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Ὑπὲρ βασιλέων) Græci Imperatores Romanos voca- bant βασιλέας, non vocem Latinam respicientes, sed rem ipsam. Erant enim re ipsa ἀνυπεύθυνοι. Tertullianus : Illuc, (id est, in cœlum) suspicientes Christiani, manibus expansis, quia innocui, capite nudo, quia non erubescimus, de- nique sine monitore, quia de pectore, oramus pro omnibus Im- perantibus, vitam illis prolixam, imperium securum, domum tutam, exercitus fortes, senatum fidelem, populum probum, or- bem quietum, & quæcunque hominis & Cæsaris vota sunt. Dio- nysius apud Eusebium : Καὶ τούτῳ διηνεκῶς ὑπὲρ τῆς βασιλείας αὐτῶν, ὅπως ἀσάλευτος διαμείνῃ, προσευχόμεθα. Mos hic egregius, ut multa laudabilia venit ab Judæis, Psal. 20. Esdr. 6, 16. Josephus 12, 17. Ἀπαιτήσαντες τῶν ἱερέων τίνες & πρεσβυτέρων ἠσπάζοντο, καὶ τὰς θυσίας ἐπεδείκνυον, ἃς ὑ- πὲρ τοῦ Βασιλέως ἔλεγον προσφέρειν τῷ Θεῷ. Meminit hu- jus moris & 7, 17. & alibi sæpe : Et extat ea de re præce- ptum in Pirke Avoth.

Καὶ πάντων τῶν ἐν ὑπεροχῇ ὄντων) Non tantum pro Imperatoribus orabant Christiani, sed & pro earum in quibus vivebant provinciarum Præsidibus, qui ἡγεμό- νες 1. Petr. 2, 14. Vide & quæ dicta Matth. 27, 2. Scriptor Maccabaici secundi cap. 3, 15. Hyrcanum vocat ἄνδρα ἐν ὑπεροχῇ κείμενον, בִּגְדֻלּה. Etfi infideles sunt, interprete Theophylacto, Reges, est tamen pro his deprecandum. Erant enim fidei Christianæ expertes tunc temporis imperii & regno- rum moderatores. Addit etiam fructum harum pre- cationum, quæ pro omnibus fiunt: Duo autem, in- quit, cum pro universis à nobis oratur, quæ optima sunt, consequimur. Nam & odia, si quæ nobis in alios sunt, dissolvuntur, cum nemo queat in eum, pro quo de- precetur, iniquo animo esse. Et reges, precibus immu- tatæ in probitatem nequitiæ, meliores redduntur, nec ultra in eos efferati desæviunt. Nam quam debet illud mirum videri, persecutores & carnifices audire ab his deposcentes pro se orare, quos afflicient suppliciis. De gratiarum actionibus pro aliis similiter: Qui pro- pterea gratias agit, quia proximum videt bonis exple- ri, sequitur certe, ut eundem benevolentia prosequa- tur. Quo fit, ut cum & ipsi bonis afficimur, majorem longe erga Deum præferre gratitudinem debeamus. Quod vero Grotius precationem pro Rege & ma- gistratu morem tantum egregium Judæorum dicit, nec è sacris literis Veteris Testamenti, sed è Pirke Avoth præceptum intercessionum ejusmodi de- ducit, id nec mandatis Jerem. 29, 7. Baruch. 1, 11. nec amori quem subditi Magistratibus, ceu filii Patri- bus, exhibere tenentur, convenit.

Ἵνα ἤρεμον καὶ ἡσύχιον βίον διάγωμεν) Tuti à barbarorum invasione & à latronibus. Seneca epist. LXXIV. Errare mihi videntur, qui existimant, philosophiæ fideliter deditos con- tumaces esse ac refractarios & contemptores magistratuum ac Regum, eorumve per quos publica administrantur. E contrario enim nulli adversus illos gratiores sunt: nec immerito; nullis enim plus præstant, quam quibus frui tranquillo otio licet. Itaq; hi quibus ad propositum bene vivendi aditum confert securitas publica, necesse est autorem hujus boni ut parentem colant. Postea: Diligit eos per quos hoc facere ei tuto licet. Rursus: Sub quorum tutela positus exercet artes bonas. Deinde: Sic hujus pacis beneficium ad omnes pertinensis, altius ad eos perve- nit, qui illa bene utuntur. Item: Confitebitur ergo multum se debere ei, cujus administratione ac providentia contigit illi pingue otium, & arbitrium sui temporis: Lactantius fine Institutionum ad Imperatorem: Erat congruens ut in fir- mando humani generis statu, te autore ac ministro divinitas uteretur: Cui nos quotidianis precibus supplicamus, ut te im- primis, quem verum custodem voluit esse, custodiat, deinde in- spiret tibi voluntatem, quæ semper in amore Divini Numinis perseveret, quod est omnibus salutare, tibi ad felicitatem, & cæ- teris ad quietem.

Ἐν πάσῃ ἐυσεβείᾳ καὶ σεμνότητι) Hoc obiter addidit, ut officij sui Christianos admoneret. Non ideo, inquit, nos tranquillitatem & securitatem publicam optamus, ut ea utamur ad comessationes & libidines: Sed ad sacros cœtus, ad probos pudicosque mores, בְּהַדְרֵי קֹדֶשׁ Psal. 110, 3. Quid sit σεμνότης vide Phil. 4, 8. Aristoteles interpretatur βαρύτητα εὐσχήμονα.

Non id tantum obiter additum. Objectum notatur & finis orationis pro Magistratu. Id enim expetimus, ut Magistratus non tantum securitatem ac tranquillitatem præstare subditis possit, ac præ- stet Divina gratia, sed ut pietati & honestati etiam præsidio sit, quo Deus eorum quoque corda flecte- re potest per subditorum preces, qui Deum verum ignorant, & idolis serviunt. Pietatem refert Chrysostomus & Theophylactus ad ipsam etiam do- ctrinam, & recte. Nam sine vera fide nullus est verus Dei cultus, & ita nulla ἐυσέβεια. In omni pie- tate, inquit, id est, non ea solum, quæ est in dogmati- bus, verum ea etiam, quæ est in vitæ ratione. Σεμνότη- τα Vulgata vertit castitatem, Syrus puritatem, alii honestatem & morum gravitatem notare rectius ajunt, quæ secundum Theophylactum non solum in abstinentia à libidine, sed in omni virtute cerni de- bet, quod de omni virtute secundum tabulam se- cundam admittimus. Tres itaque fines allegat Apo- stolus, monente B. Hunnio, qui ex officio Magistra- tus emergunt: Primo placida & quieta vita, dum & ab externis hostibus patria defenditur, & tranquilli- tatis turbatoribus repagula injiciuntur & vincula, ne pro libitu in alios grassari, & communem pacem atque otium violare audeant. Secundus finis est pie- tas, quæ exulat, ubi labefactato politica gubernationis regimine, cuique quodlibet impune licet. Et denique honestas, cujus curam etiam saniores Ethnici habue- runt, multo majus ejus ratio Christianis habenda est, ne flagitia atque scelera, velut aggere rupto se effun- dant & invalescant.

## 2:3
Verse 3.

For this) Namely this, that we should pray for the rulers of the Republic. And what? We pray that kings and rulers may be found having, along with royal power, a sober mind, says Justin Martyr. This prayer had its outcome in some part in Hadrian, Severus, and Antoninus, who were quite fair to Christians: but more perfectly in Constantine and the Roman Princes after him: then also in the Kings of other peoples.

Good and acceptable) Beautiful and pleasing. See above ch. 1:15 and below ch. 5:4.

Before our Savior God) Regarding that ἐνώπιον τῦ Θεῦ see Luke 1:6, Acts 8:21, 2 Cor 7:12, ch. 8:21. Regarding the title σωτῆρος see above ch. 1:1.

It is called good, which is beautiful, which is becoming, which is honorable, which is illustrious, and also which is useful. Others express it with the Vulgate as that which is good, or right, and legitimate, by which word good, useful, and pleasant are simultaneously comprehended with honorable. It is derived from καλέω, because it calls us to the love of itself, and by calling, as it were, draws us. Ἀποδεκτὸν, acceptable, not to men, but to God himself; God receives these, He commands these, says Chrysostom.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Τῦτο γὰρ) Hoc nempe, ut oremus pro Reipublicæ re- ctoribus. Et quid? Εὐχόμεθα τὲς βασιλεῖς κὶ ἄρχοντας μετὰ ἦ βασιλικῆς δυνάμεως κὶ σώφρονα τὸν λογισμὸν ἔχοντας εὑρεθῆναι, ait Justinus Martyr. Hæc precatio eventum suum habuit aliqua ex parte in Adriano, Severo, Anto- nino, qui Christianis æqui admodum fuere: perfectius vero in Constantino & post eum Principibus Romanis: deinde & aliorum populorum Regibus.

Καλὸν καὶ ἀποδεκτὸν) Pulchrum & gratum. Vide su- pra c. 1, 15. & infra c. 5, 4.

Ἐνώπιον τῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεῦ) De illo ἐνώπιον τῦ Θεῦ vide Luc. 1, 6. Act. 8, 21. 2. Cor. 7, 12. c. 8, 21. De titulo σωτῆρος supra c. 1, 1.

Καλὸν dicitur, quod pulchrum, quod decorum, quod honestum, quod præclarum, etiam quod utile. Alii exprimunt cum Vulgatæ quod bonum, vel re- ctum, & legitimum, qua voce simul bonum, utile, & suave cum honesto comprehenditur. Dicitur à καλέω, quod ad sui amorem nos vocet, ac vocando quasi trahat. Ἀποδεκτὸν acceptum non hominibus, sed ipsimet Deo, hos suscipit Deus, hos jubet, ait Chrysostomus.

## 2:4
Verse 4.

Who desires all men to be saved) God, as Arnobius speaks in II Against the Nations, uniformly grants the power of coming to Him to the high, the low, slaves, women, and children. The fountain of life is open to all, and no one is prohibited or driven away from the right of drinking. But it appears clearly that this statement must be taken universally from the equally negative statement in Peter ch. 2 and 3:2, μὴ βελόμενός τινας ἀπολέσθαι [not willing that any should perish]. This is the antecedent will. Add John 3:16.

The opinion of Grotius is entirely to be approved, that the Apostle's sentiment is to be understood concerning kinds of individuals, and not indeed concerning individuals of kinds, as Calvin and Beza contend. Crocius adds his vote to this in his argument, that one ought to pray for all and individual men: Not only, he says, for some of all stations, but prayers ought to be made for individual men of all stations. The Confession of Beza at the Acts of the Colloquy of Montbéliard, p. II, p. 195, acknowledges this, as does Tossanus in his commentary on this passage: But it will not be a good argument, 'one must pray for individuals, because God wills some to be saved.' One must pray for individual Kings who will exist in every age, because God wills some Kings to be saved. The most distinguished theologian Daniel Chamier noted this in his own time, Panstrat. tom. III, book VII, on predestination, ch. 6, no. 9. Certainly if the word 'all men' is not a genus containing many species under itself, but the lowest species signifies the individuals of the kinds, then it will be permitted for us to say: God chose all men, God reprobated all men, and will damn them with the devils. But no one will prove that these are affirmed correctly. Whoever would affirm this would affirm it without the consensus and example of the canonical writers. For we read nothing of that in the scriptures. And further: This explanation, he says, agrees best with the scope of the speaker, and responds to other texts, and is proven by the work itself. It agrees best with the scope of the speaker: for the Apostle exhorted that for all, not for some only, they should pray. He proves this, because God wishes well to the whole human race; if He did not wish well to individuals of the races, if He did not desire salvation for all in some way, how would the faithful pray for all? He answers with other texts, Peter says: He does not wish any to perish, 2 Pet. 3, 9. Ezekiel thus expresses the will of God: I do not delight in the death of the sinner. He delights, therefore, in life. It is proven by the work: God promised the Messiah not only to some, but to the whole human race. He sent the same not to a few, but to the whole human race. And Christ did not give Himself for a few, but for the whole human race.

Chamier in the cited place has it thus: Paul's design departs separately: For he commands to pray not for kinds of individuals, but for individuals of kinds. The proof is Kings & πάντες οἱ ἐν ὑπεροχῇ, for whom the Church prays individually for various times & places, for example, for Nero at the time when the Apostle was writing these things. But it is not a good argument: Pray for Nero, because God wishes some Kings to be made safe or to be saved.

We add here Bullinger in the Decades, written in the year 1549: Our God is the God of all men and nations, who according to the Apostle's saying wishes all men to be saved, & to come to the knowledge of the truth. And therefore for the sake, life, & salvation of all men He revealed His Word, so that it might be a rule and a certain way of leading men through the path of justice into eternal life.

Wolfgang Musculus, whom Crocius calls a most vigorous interpreter, in his exposition of John ch. 3, 16, has it thus: For although the whole world is not saved through Christ; yet such a will of God is proposed and commended to us in these words, which is not to destroy, but to save ALL. Thus Paul 1 Tim. 2. God wishes all men to be saved &c. And in the Prophets: I do not want the death &c. This love, will, and this counsel of God is to be embraced by us without any rashness of curious investigation, nor is it to be disputed rashly, as the impious are accustomed to do.

Benedictus Aretius on this passage: He adds, he says, because God wishes all men to be saved: Therefore we ought to pray for the salvation & conversion of all. For why will you not pray for him, whom God wishes to be saved? And I take all men not only from the whole species, that is, that He wishes some from all nations to be saved, but of all individuals.

As for that hypothetical explanation, in which Crocius professes to willingly acquiesce with Bullinger, Musculus, Aretius, Chamier, and Pareus, until a better one is shown. He wishes all to be saved, if all believe; this was treated most extensively on John 3, 16, and also in the 'im gründlichen Beweiß' of the Theological Faculty of Wittenberg, part II, ch. I, p. 217 seqq. But we have demonstrated immediately from the confession of the Reformers of great name, Spanheim, Maresius, and others, how illusory that hypothesis is.

We add here only the testimonies of the ancients: Arnobius on Psalm 90. It is certain, he says, that God wishes all men to be saved: But each one becomes wicked by his own will.

Chrysostom on this passage: Imitate your GOD: If He wishes all to be saved, it is right to pray for all. If He wishes all to be saved, then you also, if you wish it, pray for them.

Primasius on this passage: GOD wishes all men to be saved. It is certain that GOD wishes all good things, but men are precipitated into evil by their own fault. Likewise: The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is the God of all men, and therefore He desires all whom He has made to be saved.

But as for the fact that Augustine is cited for that opinion of Calvin, we have spoken of it expressly in the Syncretistic Calixtine tract, special postul. II, page 240. And Philip Melanchthon observed this long ago, not only regarding Luther but also regarding Augustine (whom Crocius, however, was not afraid to allege as a trio for Calvin) in his response to the Bavarian articles, 22, whose words it is helpful to cite, approved by Hermann Hildebrand in the orthodox declaration of the three articles, page 174, and by all who added their vote to that declaration in the school of Calvin: I know, he says, that other more horrible disputes are stirred up by some, of which there certainly ought to be some limit. I propose to those who are in the assembly of the called, and who are in sorrows, the UNIVERSAL PROMISE, nor do I posit contradictory wills in God, and I often think of the struggle of a certain holy man, who repeatedly uttered this voice before death: Thy word is a lamp to my feet. We saw Luther himself in a certain struggle of his, I and others, often repeating this saying: He has concluded all under sin, that He might have mercy on all. I remember a holy matron in her struggle, by these words often repeated, showing that she was uplifted by true consolation: Come to me all, etc. And antiquity is known to me by the benefit of God. This opinion, in which I acquiesce with the sounder writers of pious antiquity, agrees. And those who interpret Augustine more harshly do him an injury. Regarding Augustine, Hildebrand also observed this on page 148. Likewise when in epistle 107 to Vitalis, in the Enchiridion to Laurentius chapters 102 and 103, in the book on predestination of the saints chapter VIII, book 4 against Julian chapter VIII, in the book on corruption and grace chapters 14 and 15, concerning the saying in 1 Timothy 2 (God wishes all men to be saved) he had brought forward three expositions, which can be understood concerning the absolute and consequent will: Finally, he also explains it similarly concerning the antecedent and conditional will: just as a judge by his antecedent will wishes every man to live, that is, insofar as he considers the man before the sin: But by his consequent will he wishes this one or that one to be punished with death, insofar as he regards him as an adulterer or a murderer. For thus in the book on the Spirit and the Letter to Marcellus chapter XXXIII, where a question of this kind is proposed: If we believe by will, it is asked concerning this, whence is it to us? If by nature, why not to all, since the same GOD is the Creator of all? If by the gift of GOD, why not this also to all, since He wishes all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth? To this question he answers: GOD wishes all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth: yet not in such a way that He takes away from them free will, by which, using it either well or ill, they may be most justly judged. Since this is so, the infidels indeed act against the will of GOD when they do not believe His Gospel: yet they do not therefore overcome it, but rather defraud themselves of a great and supreme good, and entangle themselves in penal evils, about to experience in punishments the power of Him whose mercy they despised in His gifts. Thus the will of God is always invincible: but it would be overcome if He did not find what to do concerning the despisers, or if they could in any way escape what He has determined concerning such people. Dr. Johannes Bergius in German Annotations on this passage: The will of God concerning the salvation of all men. chapter IV, praises the opinion of Augustine in this way: But in the answer to the false statements of the Pelagians against Augustine, it is best explained.

With this distinction removed, which Divine knowledge contains within the secret of His justice, it must be most sincerely believed and professed that GOD wishes that all men be saved. Since indeed

The Apostle solicitously commands, which is most piously observed in all Churches, that supplication be made to God for all. Augustine, or Prosper in his name, clearly teaches, just as we ought not to pray for all kinds of things, but for all people: that thus also God wills that all people be saved, so far, namely, as is consistent with His justice. See also the book On the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 33. In which we also, alongside many other theologians of the Reformed Churches, whose words shall be cited hereafter, remain so much the more and more securely, because it is confirmed irrefutably by other concordant sayings of Scripture. Prosper of Aquitaine, the genuine disciple of Augustine, in his Sentences on the Chapters of the Gauls, sentence 8, has it thus: He who says that God does not will all men to be saved, but a certain number, speaks more harshly than one ought to speak concerning the height of the inscrutable grace of God, who both wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and fulfills the purpose of His will in those whom He predestined as foreknown. John Damascene, around the year of Christ 732, in book II of On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 29: It is necessary to know that God antecedently wills all to be saved and to possess His kingdom. For He did not create us for punishment, but that, as good, He might make us partakers of His goodness: but He wills that those who sin be punished, as He is just. Therefore, the first is called the preceding will and good pleasure, existing from Him. But the second is the consequent will and permission, having its cause from us. Oecumenius, around the year 1069, in this place. If God wills all to come to the knowledge of the truth, why does that which He wills not happen? It does not happen because they do not will it. For God does nothing in us by necessity. These are the words of Theophylact: If it pleases God that the whole human race should attain salvation, imitate Him yourself. If you wish to be equal to Him in will, you must surely pray for the rest. The Scholastics, Thomas, Scotus, and others could also be brought forward for this opinion, but we pass them over by design.

However, the Synod of Mainz, convened in the year 848 by order of the Emperor Louis, over which presided Rabanus Maurus, Archbishop of Mainz, Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt, and the other Bishops of Germany, must not be passed over here, in which this opinion of the monk Gottschalk, a Belgian priest, was rejected and condemned, that God does not will all men to be saved, but only those who are saved. Hildebrand, praised in Calvin's school, cited and approved this on page 156. Nor, indeed, with Dr. Bergius, l. c. cap. 7, is the Apostle's statement to be restricted to all those to whom the Gospel was preached in the time of the New Testament, so that it is not understood to apply to the Gentiles in the time of the Old Testament, nor to those who in the time of the New Testament heard nothing of Christ. For the Apostle speaks universally, without restriction to a certain time, about all men, and God has already testified in the Old Testament that He does not will the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live, Ezek. 18 and 33, and the Apostle teaches that the saving grace of God has appeared universally to all men, Tit. 2:14. Indeed, St. Peter professes that God does not will that ANY should perish, but that ALL should turn to repentance, 2 Epist. III, 9. Nor does Christ pertain only to the times of the New Testament, but Jesus Christ, says the Apostle, Heb. 13:8, is the same yesterday, today, and forever. And the Lamb was slain from the foundation of the world, Rev. 13:8. We have already shown that some Reformed also acknowledge this: And this opinion of Dr. Bergius is clearly singular here, and not easily heard in the Church before him. Crocius, certainly, arguing here against the, as he calls him, Learned Man, his companion in faith, thus sufficiently refuted the objection of Bergius, his colleague in the Prussian conversation: If God wills individual men to be saved, therefore He reveals the mystery of redemption to individual men. But God does not reveal the mystery of redemption to individual men, but only to some. Acts 14:6, Eph. 2:12. He replies again, if the discussion is about direct, ordinary revelation, which is through the preaching of the Evangelical Word, the major premise is not simply true. For first, God does not reveal the mystery of redemption to infants and the deaf through the external preaching of the Word, and yet there is no doubt that He wills them to be saved. Secondly, it can happen for a reason that He does not reveal it to some, although in some way He wills to save them, namely, because either the adults rejected the word with Cyclopean contempt and abandoned impiety, and their descendants imitate their impiety, or because they suppress the legal revelation in their mind, which was always universal, Acts 17:27, or because they neglect the indirect revelation, which is the fame of the Church, by which all ought to be excited to join themselves to it. God at certain times reveals the business of redemption to the whole world. The greatest part extinguished the light that was kindled by their own fault. Thirdly, the Apostle says that God allowed all nations to walk in their own ways, and that the Ephesians were strangers to the covenants of the promise. But he does not say that this was done by a decree of God preceding all causes. The alienation of the Ephesians, as also of the other nations, from the covenants of the promise was spontaneous, not by the fault of GOD absolutely denying salvation, but of themselves withdrawing. God allowed all nations to walk in their own ways by their own fault. Otherwise, He created the whole human race that they might seek GOD, if perhaps by feeling after Him they might find Him, Acts 17:27. To seek is not merely to discover that God exists, but to flee to faith in Him and to seek His grace. God therefore shows by all the works of His providence, if they repent and trust in Him, that He wishes to open the bosom of His mercy to them. As for the word σωθῆναι, although Blessed Luther in his earlier writings, namely Tom. II, explained this generally of every help and salvation, even temporal: Jenensi Germ. fol. 485, he explained it: In his later writings, however, from which his mind is to be judged, he interprets it of eternal salvation, as in the Haus-Postill for the Feast of the Purification of Mary: Simeon says: GOD has prepared such a Savior, that all nations may enjoy Him and be saved through Him. Therefore it must properly be GOD'S will and intention, as St. Paul also says in 1 Timothy 2, that all men should be helped through Christ the Savior, not temporally, but against sin and death.

Καὶ εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας ἐλθεῖν) And that they may be saved, He wills them to come to the knowledge of the truth, namely the Evangelical. Since this is so, we ought both to devote effort that the truth may become known to all, and to join prayers for all to that labor. For it is God's to give the increase to what is planted and watered.

The Neostadt Admonition, and Crocius from it, explains these things thus: That GOD wills the conversion of all seriously, as far as His approval and joy are concerned; but that He does not will all, but only those whom He has chosen, to be converted and saved, as far as His affection for conversion and salvation is concerned. Aretius here invents a condition: He wills that all men be saved in reality, but on this condition, that they perform penance and convert themselves to Christ, the Son of GOD. Neither pleases: Not the former: The Apostle does not say: GOD approves the conversion of men: no: God rejoices in the conversion of men: But God wills that all should arrive at the knowledge of the truth. And in reality that is only a hypothetical will according to the mind of Crocius. For he does not will that God approves the conversion of all men, or rejoices in the conversion of all men, but that He approves the conversion of those who are converted, that is to say, to will salvation if they are saved, to will conversion if they are converted, to rejoice if they are converted. But the Apostle expressly says that GOD wills that all men should arrive at the knowledge of the truth, and consequently be converted. But he who seriously wills an end, it is necessary that he also will the means leading to the end. Not the latter. For the Apostle does not say, God wills all men to be saved, if they arrive at the knowledge of the truth, in a hypothetical sense. But there are two absolute propositions, no hypothetical one: namely, that God wills both that all men be saved, and that all should come to the knowledge of the truth, or be converted. For the knowledge of the truth is not to be understood as simple information, but is to be taken as the faithful reception of the truth, just as in Isaiah 53:11, John 17:3, and elsewhere, faith is described through knowledge. But then in reality that condition is impossible, while the absolute decree of predestination stands. For how can those be converted who, by an absolute decree, have been reprobated and excluded from efficacious grace, without which there is no conversion? If GOD wills conditionally, says Spanheim in his disputation on universal grace, page 6, He either wills to effect the condition necessary for salvation in all, or only to demand it. If only to demand it, He does not will the conversion and salvation of such, by demanding from them an act which He knows they can no more perform than an Ethiopian can shed his blackness, a leopard his spots, or Lazarus rise from the sepulcher.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Ὃς πάντας ἀνθρώπως θέλει σωθῆναι) Deus, ut Arnobius II. contra nationes loquitur, sublimibus, infimis, servis, fœ- minis pueris, uniformiter potestatem ad se veniendi facit. Patet omnibus fons vitæ, neque ab jure potandi quisquam prohibetur aut pellitur. Plane autem universim sumendum hoc di- ctum apparet ex æque negativa apud Petrum c. 2. & 3, 2. μὴ βελόμενός τινας ἀπολέσθαι. Hoc est θέλημα προηγέμενον. Adde Joh. 3, 16.

Probanda omnino sententia Grotii, quod de singulis generibus, non vero de generibus singulo- rum, ut Calvinus & Beza contendunt, intelligenda sit Apostoli sententia. Cui calculum adjicit Cro- cius in argumento, quod pro omnibus & singulis ho- minibus orandum sit: Non tantum, inquit, pro ali- quibus omnium statuum, sed pro singulis omnium sta- tuum hominibus orationes debent fieri. Agnoscit Confessio Beza ad Act. Colleg. Mompelg. p. II. p. 195. & Tos- sanus in Comment. hujus loci: Non autem bonum erit argumentum, pro singulis orandum est, quia Deus aliquos vult servari. Orandum est pro singu- lis Regibus omni seculo futuris, quia Deus aliquos Reges vult salvos fieri. Notabat hoc suo tempore insignissimus Theologus Daniel Chamierus tom. III. Panstrat. libr. VII. de prædestinatione cap. 6. num. 9. Certe si vox omnis hominis, non est genus plures species sub se continens, sed infima species genera sin- gulorum significat, tum dicere nobis licebit: Deus omnes homines elegit, Deus omnes homines reproba- vit, & damnabit cum Diabolis. At nemo proba- bit, hæc bene affirmari. Qui affirmaret, is citra ca- nonicorum scriptorum consensum & exemplum af- firmaret. Nihil enim ejus in scriptum legimus. Et porro: Hæc, inquit, explicatio optime scopo di- centis convenit, & respondet aliis textibus, & opere ipso comprobatur. Scopo dicentis convenit optime: Apostolus enim hortatus est, ut pro omnibus, non pro aliquibus tantum orent. Id probat, quia toti huma- no generi Deus bene vult, si non singulis generum bene vellet, si non cunctis desideraret salutem aliquo modo, quomodo pro cunctis orarent fideles? Respondet aliis textibus, Petrus ait: Non vult, ullos perire, 2. Pet. 3, 9. Ezechiel sic Dei voluntatem exprimit: Non delectror morte peccatoris. Delectatur igitur vita. Opere comprobatur: Deus Messiam promisit non tantum aliquibus, sed toti humano generi. Misit eundem non paucis, sed toti humano generi. Et Christus se non dedit pro paucis, sed pro toto humano genere.

Chamierus loco citato ita habet: Pauli institutum seorsim abit: Jubet enim orari non pro singulorum generibus, sed pro singulis generum. Ar- gumento sunt Reges & πάντες οἱ ἐν ὑπεροχῇ, pro quibus sigillatim Ecclesia orat pro variis temporibus & locis, exempli gratia, pro Nerone tum, cum Aposto- lus hæc scriberet. Non est vero bona ratio: Orate pro Nerone, quia Deus vult aliquos Reges salvos fie- ri vel salvari.

Addimus hic Bullingerum in De- cadibus serm. ann. 1549. conscriptis: Deus noster omnium hominum gentiumque Deus est, qui juxta A- postoli dictum vult omnes homines salvos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis venire. Ideoque in omnium hominum gratiam, vitam, & salutem Verbum suum revelavit, ut scilicet regula & via quædam sit ducen- di homines per viam justitiæ in vitam sempiternam.

Wolffgangus Musculus, quem Crocius Interpretem nervosissimum vocat, in exposit. Johannis cap. 3, 16. ita habet: Quanquam enim non salvatur mundus universus per Christum; talis tamen voluntas Dei nobis his verbis proponitur & commendatur, quæ sit non ad perdendum, sed ad salvandum UNIVER- SOS. Sic Paulus 1. Tim. 2. Deus vult omnes ho- mines salvos &c. Et in Prophetis: Nolo mor- tem &c. Ista nobis dilectio, voluntas & hoc consi- lium Dei absque ulla curiosa pervestigationis temeri tate amplexanda, nec temere, ut impii solent, dispu- tandum est.

Benedictus Aretius ad hunc locum: Addit, inquit, quia Deus omnes homines vult sal- vos fieri: Ergo nos pro omnium salute & conversio- ne orare debemus. Cur enim non orabis pro eo, quem Deus velit salvari? Et omnes homines non solum de tota specie accipio, hoc est, ut ex omnibus nationibus aliquos velit salvari, sed de individuis omnibus.

Quod ad hypotheticam illam explicationem, in qua Crocius se cum Bullingero, Musculo, Aretio, Chamiero, Pareo lubens acquiescere profitetur, donec melior monstretur. Vult omnes servari, si omnes credant; de ea ad Johann. 3, 16. fusissi- me actum, nec non im gründlichen Beweiß Facult. Theol. Witteberg. part. II. cap. I. pag. 217. seqq. Quam vero illusoriam esse hypothesin, il- lico ex propria Reformatorum magni nominis Spanhemii, Maresii aliorumque confessione de- monstravimus.

Addimus hic tantum suffragia veterum: Arnobius in Psal. 90. Constat, inquit, Deum velle omnes homines salvos fieri: Unus quisque autem proprio fit iniquus arbitrio.

Chrysostomus in hunc locum: Imitare DEUM tuum: Si o- mnes ille vult salvos fieri, merito pro omnibus o- portet orare. Si omnes ille vult salvos fieri, vel is & tu, si & tu vis, ora pro eis.

Primasius in hunc locum: DEUS omnes homines vult salvos fieri. Constat DEUM omnia bona velle, sed ho- mines suo vitio præcipitantur in malum. Item: Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus omnium hominum Deus est, & ideo cupit salvari omnes, quos fecit.

Quod vero Augustinus illi Calvini sententiæ præ- tenditur, de eo ex professo diximus in Syncre- tissimo Calixtino tract. special postul. II. pag. 240. Et observavit id jam pridem Philippus Melanch- thon non tantum de Luthero, sed etiam de Augu- stino (quam tamen trigam pro Calvino non est veritus allegare Crocius) in respons. ad Bavar. ar- tic. 22. cujus verba adducere juvat, approbata Hermanno Hildebrando in orthod. declar. trium articulorum pag. 174. & omnibus, qui illi declara- tioni in schola Calvini calculum suum adjecere: Scio, inquit, alias disputationes horridiores moveri a quibusdam, quarum certe modum aliquem esse opor- tet. Ego his, qui sunt in cœtu vocatorum, & sunt in doloribus, propono UNIVERSALEM PRO- MISSIONEM, nec pono contradictorias in Deo voluntates, & sæpe cogito agonem cujusdam sancti viri, qui subinde repetebat hanc vocem ante mor- tem : Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum. Vidi- mus ipsum Lutherum in suo quodam agone ego & alii sæpe repetentem hoc dictum : Conclusit omnes sub peccatum, ut omnium misereretur. Memini sanctam matronam his verbis sæpe repetitis in ago- ne ostendere, se vera consolatione erectam esse : Ve- nite ad me omnes &c. Et nota mihi est Dei bene- ficio antiquitas. Congruit hæc sententia, in qua ac- quiesco cum sanioribus scriptoribus piæ vetustatis. Et qui Augustinum durius interpretantur, inju- riam ei faciunt. De Augustino & hæc observa- vit Hildebrandus pag. 148. Item cum in epistola 107. ad Vitalem in Enchiridio ad Laurentium cap. 102. & 103. libr. de prædest. sanctorum cap. VIII. libr. 4. contra Julianum cap. VIII. libr. de corruptione & gratia cap. 14. & 15. de dicto 1. Timoth. 2. (Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri) tres expositiones attulisset, quæ de voluntate absoluta & consequente intelligi possunt: Tandem etiam de voluntate an- tecedente & conditionata similiter explicat : quo- modo judex voluntate antecedente vult hominem o- mnem vivere, hoc est, quatenus hominem conside- rat ante peccatum : Sed voluntate consequente vult hunc vel illum morte mulctari, quatenus nem- pe spectat ut adulterum aut homicidam. Sic e- nim libro de Spiritu & litera ad Marcellam cap. XXXIII. ubi hujusmodi quæstio proponitur: Si vo- luntate credimus, de hac quæritur, unde sit nobis? Si natura, cur non omnibus, cum sit idem DEUS omnium Creator ? Si dono DEI, etiam hoc quare non omnibus, cum omnes homines velit salvos fieri, & in agnitionem veritatis pervenire ? Ad hanc quæstionem respondet : Vult DEUS omnes homi- nes salvos fieri & in agnitionem veritatis venire : non sic tamen, ut eis adimat liberum arbitrium, quo vel bene vel male utentes justissime judicentur. Quod cum sit, infideles quidem contra voluntatem DEI faciunt, cum ejus Evangelio non credunt : nec ideo tamen eam vincunt, verum seipsos frau- dant magno & summo bono, malisque pœnalibus implicant, experturi in suppliciis potestatem ejus, cujus in donis misericordiam contempserunt. Ita voluntas Dei semper invicta est : vinceretur autem, si non inveniret, quid de contemptoribus faceret, aut ullo modo posset evadere, quod de talibus ille consti- tuit. D. Johannes Bergius in Annot. Germ. ad h. l. Der Wille Gottes von aller Menschen Seligkeit. cap. IV. laudat Augustini sententiam hoc modo: Aber in der Antwort auf die falsche Aussagen der Pelagianer wider Augustinum wird es am besten erkläret.

Remota hac discretione, quam Divina scien- tia inter secretum justitiæ suæ continet, sinceris- sime credendum est atque profitendum, DEUM velle, ut omnes homines salvi fiant. Siquidem

Apostolus solicite præcepit, quod in omnibus Ec- clesiis piissime custoditur, ut Deo pro omnibus supplicetur. Da Augustinus, oder in seinem Na- men Prosper klärlich lehret / gleichwie wir nicht für allerley/ sondern für alle Menschen beten sol- len: daß also auch GOtt wolle/ daß alle Menschen selig werden / so weit nemlich / als seiner Gerech- tigkeit gemäß ist. Vid. & libr. de Spiritu & lite- ra cap. 33. Worben wir auch nebens vielen an- dern der Reformirten Kirchen Theologen / deren Wort hernach sollen angeführet werden / so viel mehr und sicherer verbleiben / weil es mit andern gleichlautenden Sprüchen der Schrifft unwider- sprechlich bestätiget wird. Prosper Aquitanicus, γνήσιος Augustini discipulus, in sententiis ad ca- pitula Gallorum sententia super octavum ita ha- bet : Qui dicit, quod non omnes homines velit DEUS salvos fieri, sed certum numerum, durius lo- quitur, quam loquendum est de altitudine inscruta- bilis gratiæ Dei, qui & omnes vult salvos fieri, & in agnitionem veritatis venire, & voluntatis suæ pro- positum in eis implet, quos præscitos prædestinavit. Johan. Damascenus circa annum Christi 732. libr. II. de orthod. fide cap. 29. scire vero oportet, Deum antecedenter velle omnes servari, & ejus regno poti- ri. Neque enim ad pœnam nos condidit, sed ut bo- nus bonitatis suæ participes nos reddat : Peccantes autem puniri vult, ut justus. Dicitur igitur pri- mæ præcedens voluntas, & beneplacitum ex ipso ex- istens. Secunda vero voluntas sequens & permissio ex nobis causam habens. Oecumenius circa ann. 1069. in h. l. Si DEUS omnes vult in cognitio- nem veritatis venire, cur non fit, quod vult ? Non fit, quia illi nolunt. Nihil enim ex necessitate facit in nobis DEUS. Theophylacti hæc sunt: Si Deo id libet, ut universum hominum genus assequatur sa- lutem, imitare hunc ipse. Cui si voluntate par esse volueris, erit profecto tibi pro cæteris deprecandum. Possent etiam Scholastici, Thomas, Scotus, aliique in hanc sententiam adduci, sed illos consulto præ- terimus.

Non tacenda autem hic Synodus Moguntina, Anno 848. coacta jussu Imperatoris Ludovici, cui præfuere Rabanus Maurus, Archi-Episcopus Mo- guntinus, Haymo Episcopus Halberstadiensis, reliqui- que Germaniæ Episcopi, in qua Godefralci monachi, Belgæ, Presbyteri hæc sententia rejecta & conde- mnata fuerit, quod Deus non velit omnes homines sal- vos fieri, sed eos solum, qui salvantur. Hanc addu- xit & approbavit in Calvini schola laudatus Hilde- brandus pag. 156. Nec vero cum D. Bergio l. c. cap. 7. restringenda Apostoli sententia ad illos omnes, quibus tempore Novi Testamenti prædicatum est Evangelium, ita ut nec de gentibus tempore Veteris Testamenti, nec de iis, qui tempore Novi Testamenti nihil de CHRISTO audivere, acci- piatur. Nam loquitur Apostolus universaliter citra restrictionem ad certum tempus de omnibus hominibus, ac testatus jam est Deus in Veteri Te- stamento, se nolle mortem peccatoris, sed ut con- vertatur & vivat, Ezech. 18. & 33. ac universaliter omnibus hominibus apparuisse gratiam DEI σωτήριον docet Apostolus, Tit. 2, 14. Imo S. Pe- trus profitetur, DEUM non velle, ut ULLUS pereat, sed ut OMNES ad pœnitentiam conver- tantur, 2. Epist. III, 9. Neque pertinet Christus tantum ad tempora Novi Testamenti, sed JESUS CHRISTUS, inquit Apostolus, Ebr. 13, 8. heri, hodie, idem & in secula. Et agnus occisus est ab ori- gine mundi, Apoc. 13, 8. Id agnoscere etiam Re- formatos nonnullos jam oftendimus: Et singula- ris hic plane est D. Bergii sententia, nec facile ante ipsum audita in Ecclesia. Crocius certe hic con- tra Virum, ut vocat, Eruditum, suae fidei socium, disputans, objectionem Bergii, collegae sui in con- versatione Prutenica sic satis profligavit: Si Deus vult singulos homines salvari, ergo mysterium redem- ptionis singulis hominibus patefacit. At DEUS mysterium redemptionis non patefacit singulis homi- nibus, sed tantum aliquibus. Actor. 14, 6. Eph. 2, 12. Resp. rursum, si de directa, ordinaria patefactione, quae sit per Verbi Evangelici praedicationem, sit ser- mo, major non est simpliciter vera. Nam primo infantibus & surdis DEUS non patefacit myste- rium redemptionis per externam Verbi praedicatio- nem, & tamen dubium non est, quin eos velit salvos fieri. Secundo potest ex causa fieri, ut aliquibus non patefaciat, quamvis aliqua ratione eos salvos fa- cere velit, nempe quod vel majores cyclopico contem- ptu & projecta impietate verbum repulerunt, & eorum impietatem posteri imitantur, vel quod pate- factionem legalem opprimunt in animo, quae sem- per universalis fuit Actor. 17, 27. vel quod patefa- ctionem indirectam negligunt, quae sit fama Ecclesiae, quae omnes debebant excitari, ut illi se adjunge- rent. Deus certis temporibus toti mundo redem- ptionis negotium patefacit. Maxima pars sua culpa extinxit lucem accensam. Tertio Apostolus dicit, quod Deus siverit omnes gentes suis ipsarum viis incedere, & Ephesii fuerint alieni a pactis pro- missionis. Non autem dicit, quod id factum sit de- creto Dei omnes causas antecedente. Ephesiorum ut & caeterarum gentium alienatio a pactis promis- sionis fuit spontanea, non culpa DEI salutem abso- lute negantis, sed ipsorum se subducentium. Deus sivit omnes gentes suis viis incedere ex propria ipsa- rum culpa. Alioqui condidit totum genus huma- num, ut quaererent DEUM, si forte palpando eum invenirent, Actor. 17, 27. Quaerere non est nude de- prehendere, quod Deus sit, sed ad ejus fidem confu- gere, & ejus gratiam expetere. Ostendit igitur Deus omnibus operibus sua providentia, si resipi- scant, & ipsi confidant, se misericordiae sinum eis aperire velle. Quod ad verbum σωθῆναι etsi hoc generaliter de omni auxilio ac salute, etiam tem- porali, B. Lutherus in prioribus scriptis, utpote Tom. II. Jenensi Germ. fol. 485. exposuerit: In posterioribus tamen scriptis, e quibus mens ejus aestimanda, interpretatur id de salute aeterna, ut- pote in der Haus-Postill Festo Purificat. Mariae: Simeon sagt: GOTT habe solchen Heyland bereitet/ daß alle Völcker sein geniessen/ und durch ihn selig werden sollen. Darumb muß es eigentlich GOTTES Will und Meynung seyn/ wie S. Paulus 1. Timoth. 2. auch saget/ daß allen Menschen durch Christum den Heyland soll geholffen werden/ nicht zeitlich/ sondern wider die Sünde und den Tod.

Καὶ εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας ἐλθεῖν) Et ut serventur, vult eos venire ad cognitionem veritatis, Evangelicae scilicet. Hoc quum ita sit, debemus & dare operam, ut omnibus innotescat veritas, & ei labori preces pro omnibus adjungere. Dei enim est, incrementum dare plantatis & rigatis.

Admonitio Neostadiensis, & ex ea Crocius haec ita explicat: Velle DEUM serio conversionem omnium, quantum ad approbationem & laetitiam suam; non autem velle omnes, sed tantum, quos ele- git, converti & servari, quod ad suam affectio- nem attinet conversionis & salutis. Aretius hic conditionem fingit: Vult omnes homines salvos fieri revera, sed hac conditione, ut pœnitentiam agant, & se convertant ad Christum, Filium DEI. Neutrum placet: Non prius: Non dicit Aposto- lus: DEUS approbat conversionem hominum: non: Deus lætatur in hominum conversione: Sed Deus vult, ut ad agnitionem veritatis omnes perve- niant. Et revera illa tantum est hypothetica vo- luntas ex mente Crocii. Non enim vult, Deum approbare conversionem omnium hominum, lætari conversione omnium hominum, sed approbare eo- rum conversionem, qui convertuntur, hoc est, velle salutem, si salventur, velle conversionem, si convertantur, lætari, si convertantur. At Apo- stolus diserte ait, DEUM velle, ut omnes homi- nes ad cognitionem veritatis perveniant, adeoque convertantur. Qui autem serio vult finem, media etiam velit ad finem perducentia necesse est. Non posterius. Non enim dicit Aposto- lus, Deus vult omnes homines servari, si ad a- gnitionem veritatis perveniant, sensu hypothetico. Sed duæ sunt propositiones absolutæ, nulla hy- pothetica: Deum nempe velle, & ut serventur omnes homines, & ut ad veritatis cognitionem veniant, seu convertantur omnes. Agnitio enim veritatis non de simplici notitia intelligenda, sed de fiduciali veritatis susceptione accipienda, quem- admodum Esa. 53, 11. Johan. 17, 3. & alibi, fides per cognitionem describitur. Tum vero reve- ra impossibilis est illa conditio, stante absoluto prædestinationis decreto. Quomodo enim con- verti possunt illi, qui per absolutum decretum à gratia efficaci, sine qua nulla est conversio, reprobati sunt & exclusi. Si conditionate vult DEUS, inquit Spanhemius disput. de grat. uni- versali pag. 6. vel conditionem ad salutem necessa- riam in omnibus vult efficere, vel exigere tantum. Si exigere tantum, talium conversionem & salutem non vult, exigendo ab iis actum, quem novit, non magis eos præstare posse, quam Æthiopem ni- grorem, Pardum maculas exuere, Lazarum surge- re ex sepulchro.

## 2:5
Verse 5.

For there is one God) It is no wonder that GOD wills well to all, since He Himself is the one Lord of all men, by right of creation. You have a similar sentiment in Rom. 3:30, Gal. 3:20.

These things can be referred not only to the immediately preceding matters concerning the universal gracious will of GOD, but also to the higher matters concerning prayers to be poured out to GOD for all. It is rightly said that one must pray to GOD for all, because GOD is the one God of all: And that GOD wills the salvation of all men, as He who is not only the GOD of all men by right of creation, but also by the love and affection with which He embraces all men: both because He created all in His own image, and because He has mercy on those who have fallen into sins. Here Crocius, with Bullinger and his Calvin, acknowledges that even if by the word GOD the most holy Trinity is understood, as Lombard interpreted, yet the Apostle here does not refer it so much to unity and substance as to man, or that there are not many Gods, but that one true God is now the God of all, so that there is a silent comparison of one God with the WHOLE WORLD and diverse nations, from which arises a mutual respect, which Calvin well noted. While this stands, neither Calvin's gloss concerning the kinds of individuals in the preceding verse has a place, nor Berg's concerning the men of the New Testament. For that respect concerns the whole world or all men of all times. The Jews, says Crocius, imagined that GOD, who manifested Himself to Abraham, was only the God of Israel, not of the Gentiles. Hence they could reason: Each nation has its own God. What is the salvation of other infidels to the God of Israel? Would He then will all men to be saved, who has professed Himself the GOD of Israel for so many centuries? Would the salvation of infidels be a care to Him? They were mistaken. For Moses had not said: Jehovah is only our God: But Jehovah is our God, Jehovah is one. There are no other true Gods besides Him, which, since the Jews would not understand, the Apostle presses them, writing to the Romans: Is He the God of the Jews only? Certainly also of the Gentiles, Rom. 3:29. Similarly here he urges that GOD wills all to be saved, and therefore one must pray for all, because He is the one God of all. For He is not the effector of the faithful and another of the infidels, but He is one Creator and maker, says Theodoret. The sense therefore is, GOD wills all men to be saved, because He Himself is the one God of all men, says Musculus. We have defended this statement against the Socinians in the Anti-Crellius, which should be compared here.

And one Mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus) What Philo said of the high priest of the Hebrews, that he was a boundary between both, so that through some mediator men might propitiate God, and God might dispense graces to men, using some instrument and dispenser, who also calls the high priest a mediator in his book on special laws: that fits Jesus perfectly. For He first obtained this, that God would not preclude the ways of penance nor forgiveness for men who had fallen into grave sins and were not performing penance, which is that first reconciliation pertaining to men universally, of which it is treated in Rom. 5:10 and 2 Cor. 5:19; then that God would give to the Apostles the gifts of tongues and other gifts, instructed by which men might be more easily led to the knowledge of the truth, concerning which benefit it is treated in Eph. 4:8. This benefit is indeed general for the good of the whole human race. This office of mediator was prefigured in Job 42:8. Tertullian translates mediator as sequestrator.

This argument teaches again that God wills the salvation of all and each; because to all and each human being He gave one Mediator, Jesus Christ, who is described by His human nature, not because He is Mediator according to His human nature alone, which was the error of Stancarus, and is defended by the Papists even today. For Jehovah Himself is our righteousness, Jerem. 23, 8. And what need would there have been for the incarnation of the Son of God, if the duties of the Mediator could have been performed by His human nature? But because by the name of CHRIST JESUS it was sufficiently established that not a ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον, but a θεάνθρωπον, or a man, who is GOD blessed forever over all, Rom. 9, 6, was designated, and by the mention of human nature the mystery of the Divine incarnation of the οἰκονομία was at the same time insinuated, after the Apostle had hinted at the mystery of the most holy Trinity, as if he were saying, as there is one God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit for all: So also for all there is one Mediator, the Son of God, made man for the sake of the salvation of all; both the common fellowship of all men; because Christ the Mediator is a partaker of human nature, which He has in common, not with some, but with all men, so that He may take care of all and promote their salvation; and the universal duty of prayers, that one ought to pray for all men, on account of that one man in grace, Rom. 5, 15, who is the Mediator between all men and God, as the brother of all: So also the propitiator of all, and intercessor for all before God. Since he could say, says Crocius, Crocius, God Jesus Christ, preferred to say, the man Jesus Christ, first to note the bond, which Calvin well observes, of our conjunction with God. Then, to persuade the faithful all the more of the will of God toward all men, whose nature He assumed, Conf. Ebr. 2,17. Which is also the reason why he does not say, Son of David, lest the Jews, on the occasion of the title, draw Him more to themselves and not grant Him to the Gentiles. He says the man Christ Jesus, lest anyone at any time restrict the work of mediation to one nature: but that we should attribute it to both natures or to the whole person, not only as He is God, nor only as He is man, but insofar as He is God-man. Thus the Apostle excellently demonstrates that God wills all men to be saved, because He is the one Mediator of God and men: therefore, that prayers ought to be made for all without reluctance. Crocius acknowledges that all men are to be understood: He names, he says, the Mediator of men, and indeed not of some, whether few or many. For he does not say, Mediator of God and of some men, nor does he say, of just men, nor does he say, of all the unjust, but of men, namely of all. For just as in the preceding verse he said, who wills all men to be saved, and in the following says: He gave Himself for all: So here the syncategorematic particle of all is to be understood.

But the Arians oppose the name of Mediator to the Deity in vain. For these things do not conflict, that He is Mediator by office and God by nature; indeed, He would not even be a Mediator between God and men unless He were God. Concerning which Theophylact says here: When he had said that God wills the salvation of all, he continues to confirm that very thing thus. Therefore God sent His Son as Mediator to us, that He might reconcile Himself to men. Someone will say, why then have not all attained salvation? Because they have by no means admitted this reconciliation. That the Son is God is clear from the fact that He is both a reconciler and has been made Mediator. For he who is a Mediator of two interposes himself as a middle between those who are at variance with each other, and ought to show himself common to both sides. Since therefore the Son of God and Mediator of men is a participant of both, namely of Divinity and humanity, being God and man, the same therefore embraces both natures, namely human and Divine. The pious Ancients warned about this:

Augustine in Enchirid. to Laurent. ch. 108. For we would not be liberated even through Him, the one Mediator of God and men, the man Jesus Christ, unless He were also God. And long before Augustine, Irenaeus book 3, ch. 20. It was necessary for the Mediator of God and men, through His own affinity to both, to bring both into concord, and to cause that God should assume man, and man should give himself to God. Even some among the Papists add their vote to the truth here: Dionysius the Carthusian in this place. He is the Mediator of God and men, speaking properly, not as GOD, nor as man, but as God-man, but as God incarnate. For thus it befits Him both to satisfy or reconcile, and to have the fitness or efficacy of reconciling, the first of which befits Him by reason of the assumed human nature, but the second by reason of the united Deity, from which the works and sufferings of Christ the man obtain an infinite dignity and efficacy in a certain way. Among the more recent, although most contend that Christ is Mediator only according to the Human nature; yet Claudius Espensaeus in this place, tract. on Christ the Mediator, to say nothing of others for this time; We have wondered, he says, that some maintain that CHRIST is, and is called, Mediator according to the Human nature only, and that those who think otherwise are openly accused of Arianism and heresies of that kind. Some urge the Apostolic passage 1 Tim. 2. But I ask in turn, why do the Fathers, expounding this place, elicit from the same place and word that Christ is God, and urge it, if the Apostle here understood CHRIST to be Mediator only insofar as He is man? But the word only, which is introduced, the Apostle did not add. Let those who add it fear the plagues denounced against this evil (Rev. 22), and not only did he not add it, but he even added the contrary, CHRIST JESUS, he says. Of which the former name is not of a mere man, but of one anointed by God, and assumed into the union of the person (Heb. 1, Acts 4, Ps. 44), the latter name is also of the God-man, as the Angel teaches in Matt. 1. We have from the Greeks and Latins by great consensus, concerning the necessary concurrence of both natures to the name of Mediator, as it were a most weighty and UNANIMOUS decree of the Senate, where Espensaeus cites Chrysostom, Theodoret, Cyril, Damascene, as also Augustine lib. IX. de Civit. Dei ch. 15. At the end of the digressions, page 276, that Sorbonic Doctor has it thus: The Scholastics ascribe merit, satisfaction, redemption, mediation indeed to the Human nature, but insofar as it is such, that is, insofar as it is of such efficiency, dignity, sufficiency, and, if I may say so, supersufficiency, they attribute it to the Divine nature or to the personal union with the same. To merit, to mediate, to satisfy belongs to the assumed nature, says Cajetan. But that they are of such efficacy in satisfying, they have from the Divinity. And Gabriel Biel observes from that: Through Christ our Lord. Through, he says, the preposition signifies mediation; Christ the Lord [signifies] both natures. The gloss of Anselm has the same. The sum of all is: Just as God could not pray for our salvation unless He were made man, so man could not prevail in prayer unless He existed as God at the same time. We do not contemplate the tears, prayers, and remaining executions of mediation simply, but as redeeming, expiating, propitiating, prevailing, satisfying, and as such, not proceeding more from man only, than from God only, but from the God-man. And furthermore: And this mediation is altogether salutary and life-giving, and its action, execution, efficacy, efficiency, and as the Greeks say ἐνέργεια, insofar as it is such, is neither merely Divine, since it is not of God naked, but incarnate, or of man made: nor merely human, since it is no more of man naked, but deified, but θεανδρικὴ, God-manly, or God-virile, that is to say, as existing simultaneously of God and man, as Damascene deduces at length in book III of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 19. This is Espencaeus, whom Vasquez, therefore, in part III, disp. 85, chapter 2, did not fear to number among the heretics. Who establish that the very office and duty of Mediator belongs to that suppositum by reason of both natures, as the eliciting principle. But Gilbert Genebrard and Scaevola Sammarthanus in the eulogies prefixed to the work call the same man Admirable.

As for the duties of the mediator, Grotius designated two: 1. the reconciliation of God and men, 2. the acquisition of Divine grace, from which God gave to the Apostles the gift of tongues and other gifts, by which men, once instructed, might be more easily led to the knowledge of the truth. But just as there is no doubt about the former; so as to the latter, it is indeed certain that all gifts and goods which are granted to us, not only to the Doctors of the Word, but to any men whatsoever, not only ministering, but also sanctifying, not only spiritual, but also corporal, ought to be attributed to the Mediatorial office of Christ; yet who will admit that the discourse here is about such ministering gifts proper to the Apostles, or that the office of Mediator is fully described by those two duties, or that they are opposed to each other ἀντιδιῃρημένως? Far more correctly are two offices of the Mediator commonly designated: 1. obedience rendered for us, both active through the fulfillment of the law, and passive through satisfaction for our sins, 2. intercession, by which He pleads for us, by virtue of the satisfaction and merit of His obedience, 1 John 2:2, Heb. 9:15. It is the office of the Mediator to reconcile dissenting parties, and to restore to the party that offended the grace of the one who was offended, and to repair the former friendship. Sin had alienated men from God: and therefore, in order that men might be reconciled to God, sin had to be expiated, which was done through the blood and death of CHRIST, when He gave Himself as a ransom (ἀντίλυτρον) for us. But once sin was expiated, justice was also needed so that we might enjoy the grace of GOD. For what communion has injustice with justice? 2 Cor. 6:16. CHRIST therefore was made for us by God righteousness, 1 Cor. 1:29, so that He might render us friends to GOD. But in order that the friendship may be constant, so that we do not fall from the covenant of grace, there is an absolute need for His constant intercession for us, as Mediator. And therefore He also intercedes for us at the right hand of God, Rom. 8:34.

Moreover, while he says, 'there is one Mediator,' he excludes others, just as he excludes many gods when he says there is one God. Therefore, the saints are not our Mediators. Nor does he make any distinction here with the Papists, as if there were only one Mediator of redemption, but many of intercession. He teaches that there is no one but one and the only Mediator between God and men. And he declares with a resonant voice that there is no Mediator of men except the one who gave Himself as a ransom (ἀντίλυτρον) for men, the man JESUS CHRIST. The intercession of the Mediator cannot be torn away from redemption. For by the power of redemption and merit, he who undertakes the parts of the Mediator for men before God must intercede, 1 John 2:2.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ἐὶς γὰρ Θεὸς) Non mirum est, DEUM omnibus be- ne velle, cum ipse unus sit omnium hominum Domi- nus, opificii jure. Similem sententiam habes Rom. 3. 30. Gal. 3, 20.

Non tantum ad immediatè præcedentia de uni- versali DEI voluntate gratiosa, sed etiam ad su- periora de precibus ad DEUM pro omnibus fundendis hæc referri possunt. Merito pro omni- bus orandum esse DEUM, quia DEUS est unus omnium: Et DEUM velle omnium hominum salutem, utpote qui non solum omnium hominum DEUS est opificii jure, sed etiam amore, ac dile- ctione, qua omnes homines complectitur: tum quia omnes ad imaginem suam condidit, tum quia prolapsorum in peccata miseretur. Agnoscit hic Crocius cum Bullingero, & Calvino suo, etsi vo- ce DEUS sacrosancta Trinitas intelligatur, ut Lombardus interpretatus est, non tamen hic A- postolum id tam ad unitatem & substantiam, quam ad hominem referre, seu quod non sint plures Dii, sed unus verus Deus jam sit omnium Deus, ut tacita sit comparatio unius Dei cum TOTO MUNDO, diversisque nationibus, ex qua nascitur mutuus respectus, quod bene annotavit Calvinus. Hoc stante, nec Calvini glossa, de generibus singulorum in præcedenti commate lo- cum habet, nec Bergii de hominibus Novi Te- stamenti. Nam respectus ille totum mundum vel omnes homines omnium temporum concer- nit. Judæi, inquit Crocius, fingebant DEUM, qui se Abrahamo manifestavit, esse tantum Deum Israelis, non gentium. Hinc poterant ratiocina- ri: Habet unaquæque gens suum Deum. Quid ad Deum Israelis salus aliorum infidelium? Lucne vellet omnes homines salvos fieri, qui se DEUM Israelis professus est tot seculis? Num infidelium salus illi esset curæ? Errabant. Moses enim non dixerat: Jehovah tantum Deus noster est: Sed Jehovah Deus noster, Jehovah unus est. Non sunt præter illum alii veri Dii, quod cum Judæi nol- lent intelligere, Apostolus eos premit ad Romanos scribens: An Judæorum Deus solum? Certe & gentium, Rom. 3, 29. Similiter hic urget, DEUM velle omnes salvos fieri, proinde pro omnibus oran- dum, quia omnium unus Deus sit. Non enim a- lius fidelium est effector, alius infidelium, sed unus est Creator & opifex, inquit Theodoreius. Sensus igitur est, DEUS vult omnes homines salvos fieri, quia ipse est unus omnium hominum Deus, inquit Musculus. Dictum hoc adversus Socinianos vindicavimus in Anti-Crellio, qui hic con- feratur.

Εἷς κὴ Μεσίτης Θεῦ κὴ ἀνθρώπων, ἄνθρωπος Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς) Quod de summo Ebræorum Sacerdote dixit Philo, fu- isse eum μεθόριον ἀμφοῖν, ἵνα διὰ μέσε τινὸς ἄνθρωποι μὲν ἱλάσκωνται Θεὸν, Θεὸς δὲ τὰς χάριτας ἀνθρώποις ὑποδιακόνῃ τινὶ χρώμεν@ ὀργάνῳ καὶ χορηγῷ, qui summum Sacerdotem etiam μεσίτην vocat libro de legibus specia- libus: id in Jesum optime congruit. Is enim primum id obtinuit, ut Deus hominibus in gravia peccata lapsis neque vias pœnitentiæ neque pœnitentiam agentibus ve- niam præcluderet, quæ est prima illa conciliatio ad ho- mines universim pertinens, de qua agitur Rom. 5, 10. & 2. Corinth. 5, 19. deinde ut Deus Apostolis daret lin- guarum & alia dona, quibus instructi homines ad veri cognitionem facilius deducerent, de quo beneficio agitur Ephes. 4. vers. 8. Est vero hoc beneficium generale ad totius humani generis bonum. Præfiguratum hoc μεσί- τy munus in Jobo 42. vers. 8. Tertullianus μεσίτην ver- tit sequestrem.

Argumentum hoc iterum docet, Deum velle omnium & singulorum salutem; quia omnibus & singulis hominibus unum dedit Mediatorem Jesum Christum, qui ab humana natura describitur, non quod secundum humanam naturam solum Mediator sit, qui Stancari error fuit, & à Pontifi- ciis hodieque propugnatur. Nam Jehovah ipse est justitia nostra, Jerem. 23, 8. Et quid opus fuis- set Filii Dei incarnatione, si ab Humana natura Mediatoris partes expediri potuissent? Sed quia nomine CHRISTI JESU satis constabat, non ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον, sed θεάνθρωπον, vel ἄνθρωπον, qui est DEUS benedictus in secula super omnia, Rom. 9, 6. designari, & mentione humana naturæ tum οἰκονομίας Divinæ incarnationis mysterium si- mul insinuatum, postquam sacrosanctæ Trinitatis mysterium innuisset Apostolus, quasi dicat, ut unus omnium est Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus: Ita omnibus etiam unus est Mediator Filius Dei, homo factus salutis omnium causa; tum commune omnium hominum consortium; quia Christus Me- diator humanæ naturæ consors est, quam commu- nem habet, non cum quibusdam, sed cum omni- bus hominibus, ut omnium curam gerat, ac salu- tem provehat; tum universale precum debitum, quod orandum sit pro omnibus hominibus, ob unum hominem illum in gratia, Rom. 5, 15. qui Media- tor est inter omnes homines & Deum, ut omnium frater: Ita & omnium propitiator, & intercessor pro omnibus apud Deum. Cum posset dicere, inquit Crocius, Crocius, Deus Jesus Christus, maluit dicere, homo Jesus Christus, primo ut vinculum notaret, quod bene observat Calvinus, nostrae cum Deo conjunctionis. Deinde, ut tanto magis persuaderet fidelibus de volun- tate Dei erga omnes homines, quorum naturam ad- sumpsit, Conf. Ebr. 2,17. Quae etiam causa est, quod non ait, Filius Davidis, ne tituli occasione Judaei ad se magis trahant, gentibus non concedant. Dicit ho- mo Christus Jesus, ne quisquam ullo tempore media- tionis opus ad unam naturam restringeret: sed utrique naturae vel toti personae omnes tribueremus, nec tan- tum qua Deus, nec tantum qua homo, sed quatenus est Deus-homo. Ita egregie demonstrat Apostolus, Deum velle omnes homines servari, quia est unus Mediator Dei & hominum: proinde pro omnibus preces fieri debere haud gravatim. Omnes homi- nes intelligi agnoscit Crocius : Hominum, inquit, Mediatorem nominat, & quidem non aliquorum, si- ve paucorum, sive multorum. Non enim ait, Me- diator Dei & hominum aliquorum, nec ait, hominum justorum, nec ait, omnium injustorum, sed hominum, scilicet omnium. Ut enim versu praecedente dixit, qui vult omnes homines servari, & sequenti dicit: Semetipsum dedit pro omnibus: Ita hic subintelligen- da est particula syncategorematica omnium.

Nequicquam autem Ariani Mediatoris nomen opponunt Deitati. Non enim pugnant haec Mediatorem esse officio, & natura Deum; imo ne esset quidem Mediator inter Deum & homines, nisi Deus esset. Quo de Theophylactus hic: Cum vel- le Deum dixisset cunctorum salutem, idipsum confir- mando ita prosequitur. Propterea Deus Filium suum Mediatorem ad nos legavit, ut se hominibus conciliaret. Dicet aliquis cur ergo non omnes sunt assecuti salutem? Quia nequaquam conciliationem hanc admisere. Quod autem Deus sit Filius liquet ex eo, quia & conciliator sit, & Mediator effectus. Qui enim est Mediator duorum se medium interpo- nit ad invicem dissidentium, & alterutris commu- nem se debet exhibere. Cum itaque Dei Filius & ho- minum Mediator utriusque est particeps, Divinitatis videlicet & humanitatis, Deus existens & homo, u- tramque ergo idem naturam complectitur, humanam scilicet & Divinam. Monuere de eo pii Veteres:

Augustinus in Enchirid. ad Laurent. cap. 108. Nam neque per ipsum liberaremur unum Mediatorem Dei & hominum, hominem Jesum Christum, nisi esset & Deus. Et longe ante Augustinum Irenaeus libr. 3. cap. 20. Oportuit Mediatorem Dei & hominum per suam ad utrosque οἰκείωσιν in concordiam utrosque reducere, & facere, ut Deus assumeret hominem, & homo se daret Deo. Etiam è Pontificiis hic calcu- lum addunt veritati nonnulli: Dionysius Carthusi- anus in h. l. Est Mediator Dei & hominum proprie loquendo nec ut DEUS, nec ut homo, sed ut Deus- homo, sed ut Deus incarnatus. Sic quippe competit ei, & fatisfacere seu reconciliare, & idoneitas vel efficacia reconciliandi, quorum primum competit ei ratione assumptae humanae naturae, secundum vero ratione Deitatis unitae, ex qua opera & poenae Christi hominis infinitam quodammodo dignitatem & efficaciam sortiuntur. E recentioribus etsi plerique Christum tantum secundum Humanam naturam Mediatorem esse contendant; Claudius tamen Espensaeus in h. l. tract. de Christo Mediat. ut alios hac vice taceam; Mirati sumus, inquit, aliquos tueri, CHRISTUM secundum Humanam naturam tantum esse, dicique Mediatorem, & secus sentientes aperte Arianismi, & id genus haeresium insimulari. Quidam urgent locum Aposto- licum 1. Tim. 2. Sed quaero ego vicissim, cur Patres hunc locum enarrantes ex eodem loco & vocabulo Christum esse Deum eliciunt, & urgent si Apostolus hic CHRISTUM Mediatorem esse tantum, quate- nus hominem intellexerit? Atqui vocabulum tan- tum, quod introducitur, Apostolus non apposuit. Quod qui addunt, timeant plagas huic malo denun- ciatas (Apoc. XXII.) nec modo non apposuit, verum etiam contrarium adjecit, CHRISTUS JESUS, in- quit. Quorum illud nomen est non meri hominis, sed à Deo uncti, & in unionem personæ assumpti (Ebr. 1. Act. 4. Psal. 44.) posterius etiam nomen est Dei hominis, ut Angelus docet Matth. 1. Habemus ex Græcis & Latinis magno consensu de utriusque na- turæ ad Mediatoris nomen concursu necessario velut gravissimum & UNANIME Senatusconsultum, ubi adducit Espensæus Chrysostomum, Theodoretum, Cyrillum, Damascenum, ut & Augustinum lib. IX. de Civit. Dei cap. 15. In fine digressionum pag. 276. ita habet Doctor ille Sorbonicus: Scholastici meritum, satisfactionem, redemptionem, mediatio- nem naturæ quidem Humanæ adscribunt, sed quate- nus talem, hoc est, quatenus est tantæ efficientiæ, digni- tatis, suffiienttiæ, &, ut ita dicam, supersufficientiæ, naturæ Divinæ seu personali cum eadem unioni tri- buunt. Mereri, mediare, satisfacere naturæ assum- ptæ est, inquit Cajetanus. Ut autem ea tantæ in sa- tisfaciendo efficaciæ sint, ex Divinitate habent. Et Gabriel Biel observat ex illo: Per Christum Domi- num nostrum. Per, inquit, præpositio mediationem significat; Christus Dominus utramque naturam. Idem habet glossa Anshelmi. Summa omnium est: Sicut pro salute nostra orare Deus, nisi homo factus, ita exorare homo, nisi Deus simul existens, non poterat. Lacrymas, preces, reliquasque mediationis executiones non simpliciter contemplamur, sed ut redemptrices, expiatrices, propitiatrices, exoratrices, satisfactrices, & ut tales, non magis ab homine tantum, quam à Deo tantum, sed ab homine Deo profectas. Et porro: Et omnino salutaris hæc & vivifica mediatio, ejusque quatenus talis actio, executio, efficacia, efficientia, & ut Græci loquuntur ἐνέργεια neque Divina tantum est, cum non sit Dei nudi, sed humanati, seu hominis fa- cti: neque humana tantum, cum nihilo magis sit homi- nis nudi, sed Deificati, sed θεανδρικὴ, Deivira, seu Dei virilis, nimirum ut Dei simul existentis & homi- nis, ut ample deducit Damascenus libr. III; orthod. fid. cap. 19. Hæc Espensæus, quem ideo Vasquez in parte III. disp. 85. cap. 2. inter hæreticos nume- rare non veritus est. Qui ipsum munus & officium Mediatoris illi supposito ratione utriusque natu- ræ, tanquam principio elicientis convenire statu- unt. Sed Gilbertus Genebrardus & Scævola Sam- marthanus in elogiis operi præfixis vocant eun- dem Admirabilem.

Quod ad mediatoris munia, duo designavit Gro- tius, 1. reconciliationem Dei & hominum, 2. Gratiæ Divinæ, ex qua Deus Apostolis dedit linguarum & alia dona, quibus instructi homines ad veri cogni- tionem facilius deducantur, acquisitionem. Sed uti de priori dubium nullum est; Ita quantum ad poste- rius, id quidem certum, quod omnia dona & bo- na, quæ nobis conceduntur, non tantum Docto- ribus Verbi, sed quibusvis hominibus, non tan- tum ministrantia, sed etiam sanctificantia, non tan- tum spiritualia, sed etiam corporalia Mediatorio Christi officio accepta ferri debeant, hic tamen de donis ejusmodi ministrantibus Apostolorum pro- priis sermonem esse, vel per illa duo munia Media- toris officium plene describi, aut eadem sibi ἀντι- διῃρημένως opponi, ecquis admittet? Longe re- ctius communiter duo munia Mediatoris desi- gnantur 1. obedientia pro nobis præstita tum activa per legis impletionem, tum passiva per satisfactio- nem pro peccatis nostris, 2. intercessio, qua pro no- bis interpellat, virtute satisfactionis & meriti obe- dientiæ suæ, 1. Joh. 2, 2. Ebr. 9, 15. Mediatoris est, partes dissidentes conciliare, & parti, quæ of- fendit, gratiam penes eam, quæ offensa fuit, resti- tuere, atque amicitiam pristinam resarcire.
