Pec- catum alienaverat homines à Deo : ideoque ut ho- mines Deo reconcilientur , peccatum expian- dum erat, quod factum est per sanguinem & mortem CHRISTI, cum dedit semetipsum ἀντί- λυτρον pro nobis. Sed expiato peccato justitia opus etiam erat, ut gratia DEI frueremur. Quæ enim communio injustitiæ cum justitia? 2. Corinth. 6, 16. CHRISTUS ergo nobis factus est à Deo justitia, 1. Corinth. 1, 29. ut amicos nos redderet DEO. Quo vero constans sit amicitia, ne exci- damus fœdere gratiæ, opus omnino est jugi ejus, ceu Mediatoris, pro nobis intercessione. Id- eoque etiam ad dextram Dei interpellat pro nobis, Rom. 8,34.

Cæterum dum ait, unus est Mediator, alios ex- cludit, æque uti plures excludit Deos, cum unum Deum dicit. Non ergo sancti Mediatores no- stri sunt. Neque vero ullam hic distinctionem facit cum Pontificiis, quasi Mediator unus tan- tum sit redemptionis: Plures autem intercessionis. Non nisi unum & unicum Mediatorem esse docet, inter Deum & homines. Nec hominum Me- diatorem esse, nisi qui se dedit pro hominibus ἀντίλυτρον hominem JESUM CHRISTUM, sonora voce perhibet. Intercessio Mediatoris non potest divelli à redemptione. Nam vi redem- ptionis & meriti oportet intercedat, qui Mediato- ris partes subit pro hominibus apud Deum 1. Joh. 2. verf. 2.

## 2:6
Verse 6.

He who gave Himself as a ransom (ἀντίλυτρον) for all) Christ obtained those great benefits for us not only by prayers, but by immense obedience even unto death, and indeed the death of the cross. Ἀντίλυτρον (ransom) כפר. See what was said at Matt. 20:28. Ἀντίλυτρον is a word signifying a price, as is also ἀντίψυχον, which Josephus and Ignatius use several times.

Crocius presents the connection thus: The argument is invincible: those for whom the Mediator gave Himself as the price of redemption, He wills to be saved. But He gave Himself as the price of redemption for all. This I would wish to be observed against Calvin and Berg. All, Crocius continues, were lost by sin, all in the power of death and Satan. They were not to be redeemed without a price: they could not redeem themselves, nor was there any other outside of CHRIST who would suffice. For they were too tightly bound, sold under sin, destitute, dead in sins; therefore CHRIST gave Himself as a ransom (ἀντίλυτρον). He adds the observation of Aretius, and Crocius approves it: Aretius observes that he does not say λύτρον (ransom), but ἀντίλυτρον (ransom in exchange), when another pays what the guilty party could not, as when in war head is given for head, and the life of one is redeemed by the death of another. CHRIST, however, uses the simple word λύτρον with the preposition ἀντὶ in Matt. 20:28, Mark 10:45. He understands this, however, not improperly but properly spoken. Just as redemption is properly spoken; Rom. 3:24, Col. 1:14, Gal. 3:13. Nor does he incorrectly explain the particle ὑπὲρ: the particle 'for' often signifies the end and utility, sometimes the place and stead. It is taken in the former way when CHRIST is said to have given Himself for our sins, Gal.

1:4, having suffered for sins 1 Pet. 3:18, and Paul to fill up the sufferings of CHRIST in his flesh for the Church, Col. 1:24, and likewise when we are commanded to lay down our life for the brethren, 1 John 3:16. It is taken in the latter way here and elsewhere, where Christ is said to have suffered for the unjust, 1 Pet. 3:18, ch. 4:1, died for us Rom. 5:8, delivered for us Rom. 8:32, to have tasted death for us Heb. 2:9. I do not doubt that it is to be taken this way here also: for He gave Himself as the price of redemption, while He paid the punishment, which we ought to have paid, having taken it upon Himself. Yet the former meaning is not excluded, since the latter always includes it, even if the former does not always include the latter. These things, being properly observed, slay the opinion not only of other Calvinists, but of Crocius himself. For if CHRIST gave Himself as the price of redemption in the place of all, while He paid the punishment which we ought to have paid, having taken it upon Himself, not only was some common benefit procured for the ungodly, but the remission of sin and eternal salvation were acquired. For whose sins He paid, for them He satisfied. For whom CHRIST satisfied, for them He acquired the remission of sins. But where there is remission of sins, there is salvation and eternal life. Now the Apostle does not say (these are the words of Crocius) 'for some,' as if He had given Himself as a ransom (ἀντίλυτρον) for some in that way. Elsewhere he says that He exposed Himself for the Church. Why we should restrict the particle 'for all' (ὑπὲρ πάντων) here to the Church or to the kinds of individuals, no suitable reason occurs in the text. And further: Nor is it the Apostle's purpose to commend only the dignity and sufficiency of the ransom (ἀντίλυτρον), but also the affection and counsel of the Mediator and of God the Father who sends Him. For he does not say, 'who is the price of redemption, which would suffice for all, if He Himself willed.' Thus He would not attribute more to those men who were, are, and are to be, than to those who are never to be. For it would suffice for many worlds to be actually redeemed, if GOD willed. Yet he would not truly say that CHRIST gave Himself for a thousand worlds as to sufficiency to be actually redeemed. For neither the Apostle, nor anyone else in Scripture says, 'He gave Himself for a thousand worlds.' Mention is made of one world, not many. These things are not undeservedly opposed to others in the school of Calvin. He adds: For what end He gave Himself for all, is clear from the words themselves: He gave Himself as the price of redemption. Therefore for those to be redeemed from sin and the punishment of sin. It seems to stand in the way that not all are saved. Aretius anticipates this well when he writes on this passage: He died for all, as the Apostle speaks here, nor does it hinder this that not all embrace the benefit of his death. Because by their own evil and vice they spurn the grace offered to their nature, not by any fault of God. Hence it was already clear to Timothy and all the faithful that God wishes all to be saved, and that they ought to pray for all, even the most lost scoundrels and tyrants, although they are rendered no better by our prayers, since CHRIST gave himself as a price of redemption for all. For would the faithful neglect the salvation of any mortal, when GOD has neglected the salvation of no one? These are the twins of our orthodoxy. Therefore, they are not undeservedly opposed again by most Reformed. Yet there still underlies ὕπουλόν τι: Since Crocius thus writes in his epistle on Titus II, page 357: The grace of redemption is IN SOME WAY truly universal: just as his brother Ludovicus Crocius says in his dissert. Apolog. th. 108: that CHRIST in some way died for all men, who in the Synod of Dort in Judic. ext. p. 117. rejected that opinion, that God gave all and individual men to be redeemed. Which was done in favor of the Synod of Dort and the absolute decree of election, which is called there the heart and palladium of the Reformed Church. But how can they be brought into agreement with us in this difficult and fundamental controversy, if, indeed, leaving behind the Canons of Dort, their public confessions, and older catechisms—such as the Unaltered Augsburg Confession, the Saxon Repetition, the Württemberg, the Bohemian, the Body of Doctrine, the Confession of Frederick III the Elector Palatine, the Anhalt Confession published at Neustadt in the year 1581, the Greater Zurich, Bernese, Basel, and Schaffhausen Catechisms—they would sincerely adhere to them, as has been expressly shown in the thorough proof published in the name of the Theological Faculty of Wittenberg, Part II, Chapter II, Question XII, et seqq.

Τὸ μαρτύριον καιροῖς ἰδίοις) It is a πρόθεσις (preposition/purpose) related to the whole matter that preceded. For in that He gave Himself to death for all, by that very fact He bore witness to the truth of His doctrine, and that at the time which the Prophets had predicted. See Gal. 4:4, Eph. 1:10, καιροῖς ἰδίοις בּעִתּוֹ. But in that manuscript, τὸ μαρτύριον is missing.

Christ did not deliver Himself to death as a testimony to the truth of His doctrine: nor was His death a μαρτύριον, but an ἀντίλυτρον (ransom); therefore, others understand the testimony as that of the love of God and of the Mediator Christ. But if you refer this to the delivery of Christ, the Apostle had already said more when he had named the delivery of Christ to death as the price of redemption. Therefore, there was no need for him to designate the passion by the word μαρτυρία, as Theodoret, Chrysostom, and Theophylact understand it regarding the passion which He sustained in His own times. Rather, the Apostle proceeds to the proclamation of this divine grace and the redemption of Christ, which he celebrated. For these follow one another: the grace of God, the merit of Christ, and the preaching of the Gospel. And that universal grace of God and redemption of Christ had to be announced through the ministry of the Word, so that all might be able to enjoy it. Therefore, he adds τὸ μαρτύριον, the testimony. For what else is the proclamation of the Gospel than the testimony of the Holy Spirit, or of the Most Holy Trinity concerning Jesus, which resounds in the Church through the ministry of the Word? John 15:27, 1 John 5:7-8, John 20: last verse, 2 Tim. 3:15. Therefore, the delivery of Christ to death is not properly the μαρτύριον itself, and it is only a confirmation of the truth of Christ's doctrine: but it is the object of the testimony. For that which Christ delivered Himself as a ransom for all, and that God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, is τὸ μαρτύριον or that testimony of which all the Prophets testified (Acts 10:43), of which all the Apostles and Teachers of the Word also had to testify (John 15:27, Rom. 10:8 et seqq., 1 John 1:2, ch. 5:9 et seqq.). Wherefore the blessed Luther rendered the sense excellently: 'Daß solches zu seiner Zeit geprediget werde' (That such things be preached in His time): whether it be rendered simply as 'testimony in its own times,' and an ellipsis of the preposition εἰς be posited, in this way: Εἰς τὸ μαρτύριον καιροῖς ἰδίοις, or whether it be supplied with Camerarius, who has it here thus: Τὸ μαρτύριον he names περὶ τῦ Μεσίτε κὰὶ ἀντιλύτρε προς σωτηρίαν ἁπάντων (concerning the Mediator and the ransom for the salvation of all). There is, however, an ellipsis in these, so that it may be a new beginning, τὸ μαρτύριον ἐγενήθη or ἐβεβαιώθη, that is, τᾶυτα ἐμαρτυρήθη καιροῖς ἰδίοις, κὰὶ εἰσήγεν πρὸς τῦτο τὸ μαρτύριον ἐγὼ κήρυξ ἐτέθην. He observes that interpreters have mixed this explanation with the words of the Apostle. Whence, as far as the sense is concerned, the Vulgate version also returns to this: 'Cujus testimonium suis temporibus confirmatum est' (Whose testimony was confirmed in its own times), from which, however, according to the Roman, Greek, and Syriac codices, the 'cujus' (whose) and 'confirmatum est' (was confirmed) ought to be removed, as Cornelius à Lapide acknowledges. For the same sense also emerges if you translate it simply: 'Testimony in its own times.' Or also 'This testimony (is) in its own times.' Or with Erasmus: 'That it might be a testimony in its own times,' which Calvin and Bullinger also approve: or as Beza, 'Which is that testimony destined for its own times.' All of which can be reduced to the same sense. There is another version of Beza: 'Christ, I say, that testimony destined for its own times.' For Christ, as Crocius himself admits, is not said to be a testimony in this name quite conveniently, because all the Prophets testified of Him. Beza would prefer that μυστήριον (mystery) be read (instead of μαρτύριον), which he found in only one ancient codex: but one codex cannot prejudice all others. Nor is Christ Himself, as Crocius again acknowledges, called a mystery elsewhere, but that which was done concerning Christ. However, we do not deny that the times of the New Testament are looked to in those καιροῖς ἰδίοις: yet, in turn, it must not be denied that this was also preached in the Old Testament, as far as the substance of the Gospel is concerned. Wherefore, this is proper to the New Testament only as far as the circumstance is concerned, namely, that the Apostles and their successors had to testify in their own times concerning that which Christ had already delivered Himself for us as a price of redemption, which the Prophets in the Old Testament testified that He was about to deliver Himself. For He died for our sins κατὰ τὰς γραφὰς (according to the scriptures), 1 Cor. 15:3. Cf. Luke 24:26, 27; Acts 10:43.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ὁ δὺς ἑαυτὸν ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων) Magna illa beneficia Christus non solis precibus nobis impetravit, sed ingenti obedientia ad mortem usque & quidem cru- cis. Ἀντίλυτρον כפר. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. 20, 28. Ἀντιλύτρον vox significans admodum, ut & ἀντίψυχον, qua utitur Josephus & Ignatius aliquoties.

Nexum ita exhibet Crocius: Argumentum est invictum, pro quibus Mediator se dedit redemptio- nis pretium, eos vult servari. Atqui dedit se re- demptionis pretium pro omnibus. Quod contra Calvinum & Bergium observari velim. Omnes, pergit deinceps Crocius, erant perditi peccato, o- mnes in potestate mortis & Satanæ. Citra pre- tium redimi non debebant: Ipsi redimere se non poterant, nec alius extra CHRISTUM erat, qui sufficeret. Nimis enim arctē vincti, sub peccatum venditi, inopes, in peccatis mortui; Dedit igitur CHRISTUS semetipsum ἀντίλυτρον. Addit Aretii observationem, eamque probat Crocius: Aretius observat, quod non dicat λύτρον, sed ἀντί- λυτρον, cum alius solvit, quod reus non poterat, ut cum in bello caput capite, vita unius alterius mor- te redimitur. CHRISTUS tamen utitur simplici voce λύτρον, cum præpositione ἀντὶ Matth. 20, v. 28. Marc. 10, 45. Intelligit autem hic non improprie sed proprie dictum. Sicut redemptio proprie dicta; Rom. 3. 24. Coloss. 1, 14. Galat. 3, 13. Nec inrecte particulam ὑπὲρ explicat: Particula pro sæpe signi- ficat finem & utilitatem, interdum vicem & lo- cum. Priori modo capitur, cum CHRISTUS dicitur semetipsum dedisse pro peccatis nostris Galat.

1, 4. passus pro peccatis 1. Petr. 3, 18. & Paulus ad- implere passiones CHRISTI in carne sua pro Eccle- sia, Col. 1, 24. itemque cum jubemur animam ponere pro fratribus, 1. Johan. 3, 16. Posteriori modo capi- tur hic & alibi, ubi Christus dicitur passus pro inju- stis, 1. Petr. 3, 18. cap. 4, 1. mortuus pro nobis Roman. 5, 8. traditus pro nobis Rom. 8, 32. gustasse mortem pro nobis Ebr. 2, 9. Ita hic quoque accipi non dubito: Seipsum enim dedit pretium redemptionis, dum pœ- nam, quam nos luere debebamus, in se susceptam luit, Non tamen excluditur prior significatio, quippe quam posterior semper includit, etsi ipsa posteriorem non semper includat. Quæ probe observata jugulant non aliorum tantum Calvinianorum, sed ipsius- met etiam Crocii sententiam. Si enim loco o- mnium dedit seipsum CHRISTUS pretium re- demptionis, dum pœnam, quam nos luere debe- bamus in se susceptam luit, non tantum commune quoddam beneficium impiis comparatum est, sed acquisita peccati remissio & salus æterna. Quo- rum enim peccata luit, pro iis satisfecit. Pro qui- bus satisfecit CHRISTUS, illis acquisivit remis- sionem peccatorum. Ubi autem peccatorum est remissio, ibi salus est, & vita æterna. Jam non ait Apostolus (verba sunt Crocii) pro aliquibus, quasi pro aliquibus ita se ἀντίλυτρον dederit. Alibi di- cit, quod se exposuerit pro Ecclesia. Cur ad Eccle- siam vel genera singulorum particulam ὑπὲρ πάντων hic restringamus, causa idonea in textu non occurrit. Et porro: Neque tamen Apostolo est propositum so- lam dignitatem & sufficientiam ἀντιλύτρου com- mendare, sed etiam affectum atque consilium Me- diatoris & Dei Patris eum mittentis. Non enim ait, qui est pretium redemptionis, quod sufficeret pro omnibus, si ipse vellet. Ita non plus iis homi- nibus tribueret, qui fuerunt, sunt, & extituri sunt, quam iis, qui nunquam sunt extituri. Suf- ficeret enim pro pluribus mundis actu redimendis, si DEUS vellet. Neque tamen vere diceret, dedisse CHRISTUM se pro mille mundis quoad suffici- entiam actu redimendis. Nec enim Apostolus, nec alius quisquam in scriptura dicit, dedit semet- ipsum pro mille mundis. Unius mundi non pluri- um fit mentio. Quæ aliis in schola Calvini non immerito opponuntur. Addit: Quo fine pro o- mnibus se dederit, ab ipsis verbis clarum: Dedit se redemptionis pretium. Ergo pro redimendis à pec- cato & peccati pœna. Videtur obstare, quod non omnes servantur. Hoc bene Aretius præoccupat, cum in hunc locum scribit: Mortuus est pro omni- bus, ut hic loquitur Apostolus, nec impedit hoc, quod non omnes mortis beneficium amplectuntur. Quia suo malo & vitio natura suæ oblatam gra- tiam aspernantur, non aliqua Dei culpa. Hinc jam patebat Timotheo & omnibus fidelibus, quod Deus velit omnes servari, & quod debeant pro omnibus orare, etiam perditissimis nebulonibus & tyrannis, quamvis nihilo reddantur meliores no- stris precibus, cum CHRISTUS se dederit pro omnibus redemptionis pretium. Num enim fide- les ullius mortalis salutem negligant, cum DEUS nullius salutem neglexerit. Quæ orthodoxiæ no- stræ gemella sunt. Ideo plerisque Reformatis iterum non immerito opponuntur. Subest ta- men adhuc ὕπουλόν τι: Quum ita Crocius in e- pist. ad Titum II. pag. 357. scribit: Gratia re- demptionis ALIQUO MODO vere universa- lis est: prorsus ut frater ejus Ludovicus Crocius dissert. Apolog. th. 108. ait: CHRISTUM aliquo modo pro omnibus hominibus mortuum esse, qui in Synodo Dordrac.in Judic. ext. p. 117. repro- bavit illam sententiam, Deum omnes & singulos homines dedisse redimendos. Quod in gratiam synodi Dordracenæ & absoluti electionis decreti, quæ ibi cor & palladium dicta Ecclesiæ Re- formatæ, factum. Quomodo autem in hac ardua & fundamentali controversia in concor- diam nobiscum redigi possunt, si nempe relictis canonibus Dordracensibus, confessionibus suis pu- blicis, & catechesibus antiquioribus, utpote Con- fessioni Augustanæ invariatæ, repetitioni Saxonicæ, Würtenbergicæ, Bohemicæ, corpori doctrinæ, con- fessioni Friderici III. Palatini, confessioni Anhalti- næ Anno 1581. Neostadii editæ, Catechismo ma- jori Tigurino, Bernensi, Basiliensi, Schaffhusino, sincere adhærescerent, ut ex professo ostensum im gründlichen Beweiß Facultatis Theol. Witte- bergens. nomine edito part. II. cap. II. quæst. XII. seqq.

Τὸ μαρτύριον καιροῖς ἰδίοις) Est πρόθεσις relata ad rem totam, quæ præcessit. Quod enim se pro omnibus dedit ad mortem, eo ipso testimonium præbuit veritati doctrinæ suæ, idque eo tempore, quod Prophetæ prædixerant. Vide Gal. 4, 4. Eph. 1, 10. καιροῖς ἰδίοις בּעִתּוֹ. At in Manuscri- pto illo deest τὸ μαρτύριον.

Non in testimonium veritatis doctrinæ suæ sese tradidit in mortem Christus: neque μαρτύριον mors fuit, sed ἀντίλυτρον; Ideo testimonium alii dilectionis Dei & Mediatoris Christi intelligunt. Sed si hoc ad traditionem Christi referas, plus jam dixerat Apostolus, cum pretium redemptionis tra- ditionem Christi in mortem nominarat. Idcirco non opus erat, ut jam passionem voce μαρτυρία de- signaret, quemadmodum Theodores. Chrysostomus, Theophylactus de passione, quam suis temporibus sustinuerit, intelligunt. Progreditur potius Apo- stolus ad gratiæ hujus divinæ, & redemptionis Christi, quam celebravit, præconium. Hæc enim se con- sequuntur, gratia Dei, meritum Christi & prædica- tio Evangelii. Atque illa universalis Dei gratia, & redemptio Christi annuntianda erat per ministe- rium Verbi, ut omnes eadem frui possent. Ideo addit τὸ μαρτύριον testimonium. Quid enim aliud est præconium Evangelii? quam testimonium Spiritus sancti, vel Sacrosanctæ Trinitatis de Jesu, quod in Ecclesia per ministerium Verbi re- sonat, Joh. 15, 27. 1. Joh. 5, 7-8. Joh. 20. v. ult. 2. Tim. 3, 15. Non ergo traditio Christi in mortem proprie est ipsummet μαρτύριον, & confirmatio solum est veritatis doctrinæ Christi: Sed objectum τῶ μαρτυ- ρίᾳ. Nam id, quod Christus semetipsum tradiderit εἰς ἀντίλυτρον pro omnibus, & quod Deus omnes homines salvari velit, & ad agnitionem veritatis pervenire, est τὸ μαρτύριον vel testimonium illud, de quo testati sunt omnes Prophetæ, Act. 10, 43. de quo testari etiam debuere Apostoli & Doctores Ver- bi universi, Joh. 15, 27. Rom. 10, 8. seqq. 1. Joh. 1, 2. cap. 5, 9. seqq. Quapropter optime sensum reddi- dit B. Lutherus: Daß solches zu seiner Zeit gepredi- get werde: sive simpliciter reddatur testimonium temporibus suis, & ellipsis statuatur præpositio- nis εἰς, hoc modo: Εἰς τὸ μαρτύριον καιροῖς ἰδίοις, sive cum Camerario ea suppleatur, qui hic ita ha- bet: Τὸ μαρτύριον nominat περὶ τῦ Μεσίτε κὰὶ ἀν- τιλύτρε προς σωτηρίαν ἁπάντων. Est autem ellipsis in his, ut sit de novo exordio, τὸ μαρτύριον ἐγενήθη sive ἐβεβαιώθη, id est, τᾶυτα ἐμαρτυρήθη καιροῖς ἰδίοις, κὰὶ εἰσήγεν πρὸς τῦτο τὸ μαρτύριον ἐγὼ κήρυξ ἐτέθην. Quam explicationem cum verbis Apostoli commiscuisse Interpretes obser- vat. Unde eo, quantum ad sensum, redit etiam Vulgata versio: Cujus testimonium suis tempo- ribus confirmatum est, cujus, scilicet rei, à qua ta- men juxta Codices Romanos, Græcos, & Syrum tollendum esse, cujus & confirmatum est, agnoscit Cornelius à Lapide. Nam & ita sensus idem e- mergit, si simpliciter vertas: Testimonium temporibus suis. Aut etiam hoc testimonium (est) suis temporibus. Vel cum Erasmo: Ut esset testimonium suis temporibus, quod Calvinus & Bullingerus quoque approbant: vel ut Beza, quod est testimonium illud suis temporibus destinatum. Quæ omnia ad eundem sensum reduci possunt. Aliorior est altera Bezæ versio, Christus, inquam, testimonium illud suis temporibus destinatum. Christus enim, fatente ipsomet Crocio, non satis commode testimonium dicitur hoc nomine, quod de eo testati sint omnes Prophetæ. Mallet Beza legi μυστήριον (pro μαρτύριον) quod in uno veteri codice tantum invenit: Sed unus codex o- mnibus aliis præjudicare non potest. Nec Christus ipse, quod agnoscit iterum Crocius, dicitur alibi mysterium, sed id, quod circa Christum factum. Illis autem καιροῖς ἰδίοις respici tempora Novi Te- stamenti, uti non negamus: Ita tamen vicissim haud etiam negandum est in Veteri Testamento id quoque prædicatum, quantum ad substantiam Evangelii. Quapropter Novo Testamento hoc proprium est quoad circumstantiam tantum, quod nempe testificari temporibus suis Apostoli & successores eorum debuerint de eo, quod sese jam tradiderit Christus pro nobis in pretium re- demptionis, quam in Veteri Testamento Prophe- tæ testificati sint, quod se traditurus sit. Nam mortuus est pro peccatis nostris κατὰ τὰς γραφὰς, 1. Corinth. 15, 3. Conf. Luc. 24, 26. 27. Actorum 10, 43.

## 2:7
Vers. 7. εἰς ὃ ἐτέθην ἐγὼ κήρυξ καὶ ἀπόστολος) For the publishing of which martyrdom of Christ I have been appointed an Apostle by God. For in this sense we have the same words in 2 Tim. 2:4, ἐτέθην נשומיתי. Thus we have τιθέναι in Rom. 4:17, 1 Cor. 7:28, above ch. 1:2. In the manuscript: ὃ ἐπιστεύθην ἐγὼ, as above ch. 1:11. καὶ διδάσκαλος ἐθνῶν) He is destined especially for the teaching of the Gentiles, Acts 9:15, Rom. 11:13, Gal. 2:7, 9, 2 Tim. 1:11. ἐν πίστει καὶ ἀληθείᾳ) Concealing nothing true, admitting nothing false.

It is more to be an Apostle than a herald. For a herald is also one who preaches the Word in one place. An Apostle, however, can preach it throughout the whole world by virtue of his office. Such also was the office of Paul, therefore he preached both to Jews and Gentiles: yet he was peculiarly destined as the Teacher of the Gentiles. He inserted indeed the asseveration: Ἀλήθειαν λέγω ἐν χριστῷ, ὀὐ ψεύδομαι, which refer themselves not only to the preceding matters concerning the heraldship and Apostleship, but also to the following matters concerning the Teacher of the Gentiles, and especially to those words ἐν πίστει καὶ ἀληθείᾳ. For his own conscience bore witness to him concerning those things, to which he could appeal with a cheerful mind, 2 Cor. 1:12. Theophylact applies these to the preceding matters concerning prayers. If therefore the Son of God suffered death for these Gentiles, and I myself am their Teacher, I would wish that you neglect nothing in praying for them. Those words 'in faith and truth' can be expounded as 'faithfully and truthfully', or 'faithful and truthful': not that he commends himself, but that he may give assurance of his office and his heraldship under oath or with Christ as witness (Compare Rom. 9:1, although the Greek Interpreters and the Syriac omit 'in Christ' along with a few Codices) inasmuch as it concerned him greatly. For in the office of a steward nothing more is required than that he be found πιστὸς, 1 Cor. 4:2, and it is necessary that the heraldship of the Word be true and sincere, of which the Apostle could boast in his office, 2 Cor. 2:17, chap. 1:12. Thus also explain Calvin, Piscator, Crocius, as well as Cardinal Hugo, Theophylact, and Oecumenius, who oppose faith to syllogisms and rhetorical ornaments, and truth to fallacy or imposture.

PART II. Instruction for both sexes concerning prayers and holy assemblies.

Latin:

Vers. 7. εἰς ὃ ἐτέθην ἐγὼ κήρυξ καὶ ἀπόστολος) Ad quod Christi martyrium publicandum ego à Deo constitutus sum Apostolus. Hoc enim sensu eadem verba habemus 2. Tim. 2, 4. ἐτέθην נשומיתי. Sic τιθέναι habemus Rom. 4, 17. 1. Cor. 7, 28. supra c. 1, 2. In manuscripto: ὃ ἐπι- στεύθην ἐγὼ, ut supra c. 1, 11. καὶ διδάσκαλος ἐθνῶν) Præcipue gentibus destinatur do- cendis Actorum 9, 15. Rom. 11, 13. Galat. 2, 7. 9. 2. Timoth. 1, 11. ἐν πίστει καὶ ἀληθείᾳ) Nihil veri subticens, nihil falsi ad- miscens.

Plus est, esse Apostolum, quam præconem. Nam præco est etiam, qui uno in loco prædicat Ver- bum. Apostolus autem prædicare id per totum orbem potest vi muneris sui. Quale erat etiam Pauli officium, ideo & Judæis & gentibus prædica- vit: Peculiariter tamen destinatus gentium Do- ctor. Inserferit vero asseverationem: Ἀλήθειαν λέγω ἐν χριστῷ, ὀὐ ψεύδομαι, quæ sese non tantum ad præcedentia de præconio & Apostolatu, sed etiam ad sequentia de Doctore gentium, & maxi- me ad illa ἐν πίστει καὶ ἀληθείᾳ referunt. Nam de illis testimonium ipsi reddebat propria conscien- tia, ad quam hilari animo provocare poterat, 2. Cor. 1, 12. Theophylactus hæc applicat ad supe- riora de precibus. Si itaque Dei Filius pro gen- tibus hisce perpessus est mortem, & earundem ipse sum Doctor, nihil ipse negligas velim pro his deprecari. Illa in fide & veritate possunt expo- ni fideliter & veraciter, vel fidus & verax: non quod seipsum commendet, sed ut officio & præ- conio suo fidem faciat sub juramento vel teste Christo (Conf. Rom. 9, 1. etsi Græci Interpretes & Syrus illa per Christum cum paucis quibusdam Codicibus omittant) utpote cujus plurimum in- tererat. In officio enim œconomi nihil amplius requiritur, quam ut πιστὸς inveniatur, 1. Cor. 4, 2. & præconium Verbi verum ac sincerum sit opor- tet, quo de gloriari poterat in munere suo Apo- stolus, 2. Corinth. 2, 17. cap. 1, 12. Sic expli- cant etiam Calvinus, Piscator, Crocius, ut & Hugo Cardinalis, Theophylactus, & Oecumenius, fi- dem syllogismis & luminibus Rhetoricis, verita- tem fallaciæ seu imposturæ opponunt.

PARS II. Informatio utriusque sexus circa preces & sa- cros conventus.

## 2:8
Ver. 8. βούλομαι ὖν) He returns to that which he had begun above in ver. 1. חפצתי, this I wish, this I desire. See below ch. 5, 14. Tit. 3, 8. The Apostle does not so much return to prayers as he pursues that subject, because the things which were introduced, even though didactic, exhibiting chief doctrines, pertain to the exhortation concerning prayers and contain its arguments. Now, therefore, he subjoins instruction concerning the requirements or adjuncts of prayers or of those praying, and indeed distinctly regarding men and women, the reason for which is evident from ver. 10. Nor is the illative particle ὖν added rashly. For from the most benign will of God and His public satisfaction, it is deduced that in EVERY place hands are to be lifted up.

προσεύχεσθαι τὲς ἄνδρας ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ) ממקומו. Zephaniah 2, 11. That is, wherever assemblies were held. For he is dealing with public prayers. Prayers to God are today no less pleasing in any church whatsoever than in the Jerusalem temple, John 4, 24.

We admit that it is chiefly about public prayers because of ver. 10: It is not, however, about those alone. For the exhortation in ver. 1 was general, which it is clear is continued here, and holy hands are no less required for private prayers than for public ones. Nor do Theodoret, Chrysostom, Theophylact, or Oecumenius restrict these to public prayers. Nor did Christians at that time have public oratories. Grotius wished here to gratify the Papists, who wish public prayers, which are made in the celebration of masses, to be designated. But in the Apostle's time, masses were unknown, nor is it evident by any argument that the Apostle looked only to public prayers.

ἐπαίροντας ὁσίους χεῖρας) With hands expanded to heaven, as we have heard Tertullian saying. This custom is from the Hebrews, as appears in Ps. 141, 2, and among the Rabbis, who call it נשׂאיות כפים. There is no need here to repeat what was said on Luke 18, 12 and Matt. 27, 24. One may add the passage in Isa. 1, 15, Lam. 3, 41, and that of Apollonius: Πολλὰ μάλ’ ἀθανάτοισιν ἐς αἰθέρα χεῖρας ἄειρον Εὐχόμενος - ὁσίυς χεῖρας ἐπαίρειν, to lift up pure hands, in Seneca's Oedipus; pure, that is, contaminated by no crime. Philo on the Essenes: κἀι τάς τε ὄψεις καὶ τὰς χεῖρας εἰς ὀυρανὸν ἀνατείναντες, τὰς μὲν ἐπειδὴ τὰ θεᾶς ἄξια καθορᾷν ἐπαιδεύθησαν, τὰς δὲ ὅτι καθαραὶ λημμάτων ἐισὶν, ὑπὸ ὐδεμιᾶς προφάσεως τῶν ἐἰς πο- ρισμὸν μιανόμεναι. This was signified by the washing of hands used by the Jews before prayers, Ps. 26, 6.

Papists also drag these things to an external washing, which might be done in public prayer, as can be seen in Cornelius à Lapide. But just as it is not established that the Jews prayed only with washed hands, whether in the Old or New Testament, so neither was any law concerning it handed down to Christians by the Apostles, nor can it be taught that that custom prevailed in the time of the Apostles. Ps. 26, 6 does not deal with an external or bodily washing of hands, but with a spiritual one, by which hands are washed with innocence, not with water. Hands are sufficiently clean, says Tertullian on prayer, ch. II, which we have washed once with the whole body in Christ. And Chrysostom says: Pure hands, that is, clean, not washed with water, but clean from greed, rapine, and slaughter. That washing is indicated in Isa. 1, 16. This general requirement of prayers is therefore twofold, while a mind devoted to God by the lifting of hands, and pure, purified by the blood of Christ and by faith, and free from the impure filth of crimes, is demanded by the mention of pure hands. Now two special things are subjoined, namely, that prayers be made without wrath and without doubting.

χωρὶς ὀργῆς καὶ διαλογισμοῦ) Not only hands, that is, external actions, ought to be pure, but hearts as well. There are, however, two things that most render prayers unpleasing to God: Hatred against a brother, which he here called wrath, because hatred is inveterate wrath; and doubting concerning God's promises. Regarding the former, see Matt. 5, 24 and Maimonides in the rules of praying, where he says, if anyone feels his mind agitated and his heart swelling, let him not pray, but be quiet until his mind is sedate. For a like reason, priests, when they were about to perform their duty in the temple, abstained from wine. Regarding the latter, see Matt. 14, 31. Add that of Clement to the Corinthians: οἱ δίψυχοι καὶ δισάζοντες περὶ τῆς τῦ Θεῦ δυνάμεως εἰς κρῖμα, κὰι εἰς σημείωσιν πάσαις ταῖς γενεαῖς γίνονται. For διαλογισμὸς in this place is a disputation within the mind against faith.

Regarding the former, Chrysostom says: By the name of wrath he wished to signify the profane memory of injuries. Let the intention of the one praying, he says, be clean from the plague of such a memory, let it approach Him free from every vice and perturbation: Let no one be so bold as to proceed to pray to God while exercising enmities. Regarding the latter requirement, that prayer ought to be made without διαλογισμῷ, most people also easily agree that hesitation is excluded, such as Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius, Lombard, Valla, B. Luther, Hyperius, Aretinus. Disputation, says Theophylact, he calls hesitation and ambiguity, that is, do not approach prayer as doubtful and hesitating, but imbued with a more certain faith, and doubting nothing, whether you are about to receive what you ask or not. Cornelius wrongly drags this to a disputation of the mind, which follows wrath. Calvin [drags it] to an external disputation, whether prayers conceived for the unfaithful and impious are approved by God, as Crocius explains. He had already warned before concerning the Gentiles, that prayers ought to be made for them, and had taught that this was acceptable to God, ver. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 8. βούλομαι ὖν) Redit ad id, quod supra inchoave- rat v. 1. חפצתי, hoc opto, hoc desidero. Vide infra c. 5, 14. Tit. 3, 8. Non tam redit ad preces, quam materiam illam persequitur Apostolus, quia quæ injecta fue- re, etsi didactica, doctrinas præcipuas exhiben- tia, ad parænesin de precibus pertinent, ejusque argumenta continent. Jam ergo de requisitis vel adjunctis precum vel precantium & quidem di- stincte quoad viros & mulieres, cujus causa è v. 10. patet, informationem subjungit. Nec te- mere additur particula illativa ὖν. Nam ex be- nignissima Dei voluntate, ejusque publica satisfa- ctione deducitur, quod in OMNI loco manus at- tollendæ.

προσεύχεσθαι τὲς ἄνδρας ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ) ממקומו. Sopho- niæ, 2, 11. id est, ubicunque conventus habebantur. Agit enim de publicis precibus. Preces Deo hodie non minus gratæ in quavis Ecclesia, quam in templo Hierosolymitano, Joh. 4, 24.

Præcipue de publicis precibus agi ob v. 10. ad- mittimus: Non tamen de iis solis agitur. Nam generalis erat adhortatio v. 1. quam hic continua- ri liquet, nec minus sanctæ manus ad privatas pre- ces requiruntur, quam ad publicas. Nec restrin- gunt hæc ad publicas preces Theodoretus, Chryso- stomus, Theophylactus aut Oecumenius. Nec tum habebant eo tempore Christiani publica oratoria. Gratificari hic voluit Grotius Papistis, qui preces publicas, quæ fiunt in missarum celebratione, de- signari volunt. At Apostoli tempore ignotæ e- rant missæ, nec ullo argumento patet, publicas tantum preces spectasse Apostolum.

ἐπαίροντας ὁσίους χεῖρας) Ad cœlum expansis manibus, ut Tertullianum dicentem audivimus. Is mos ab Ebræis, ut apparet Psal. 141, 2. & apud Rabbinos, qui id vocant נשׂאיות כפים. Nihil opus hic repetere, quæ dicta ad Lucam 18, 12. & Matth. 27, 24. Addi potest locus Esa. 1, 15. Lam. 3, 41. & illud Apollonii: Πολλὰ μάλ’ ἀθανάτοισιν ἐς αἰθέρα χεῖρας ἄειρον Εὐχόμενος - ὁσίυς χεῖρας ἐπαίρειν tollere puras manus Senecæ in Oedi- pode, puras, id est, nullo contaminatas facinore. Philo de Essenis : κἀι τάς τε ὄψεις καὶ τὰς χεῖρας εἰς ὀυρανὸν ἀνατείναντες, τὰς μὲν ἐπειδὴ τὰ θεᾶς ἄξια καθορᾷν ἐπαιδεύθησαν, τὰς δὲ ὅτι καθαραὶ λημμάτων ἐισὶν, ὑπὸ ὐδεμιᾶς προφάσεως τῶν ἐἰς πο- ρισμὸν μιανόμεναι. Hoc significabat manuum lotio ante preces Judæis usurpata, Psal. 26, 6.

Papistæ hæc etiam ad externam lotionem tra- hunt, quæ fiat in oratione publica, ut apud Corne- lium à Lapide videre est. Ast uti Judæos non nisi lotis manibus sive in Veteri sive in Novo Te- stamento precatos esse haud constat, ita nec ulla de eo Christianis lex tradita ab Apostolis, nec do- ceri potest, morem illum Apostolorum tempore obtinuisse. Psal. 26, 6. non de externa vel corpo- rali manuum lotione agitur, sed de spirituali, qua innocentia, non vero aqua lavantur manus. Sa- tis mundæ sunt manus, inquit Tertullianus de o- ratione cap. II. quas cum toto corpore in Christo semel lavimus. Et Chrysostomus : Puras, in- quit, manus, id est, mundas, non aqua lotas, ve- rum cupiditate, rapina, cædibus mundas. Lo- tio ea indigitatur Esa. 1, 16. Hoc ergo requi- situm precum generale geminum est, dum animus devotus ad Deum sublatione manuum, & purus, fanguine Christi ac fide purificatus, & ab impuris criminum sordibus liber, manuum purarum men- tione postulatur. Jam subjunguntur duo specia- lia, ut nempe sine ira & sine dubitatione preces fiant.

χωρὶς ὀργῆς καὶ διαλογισμοῦ) Non manus tantum, id est actiones externas oportet esse puras, sed & corda. Duo autem sunt, quæ maxime preces ingratas Deo reddunt: Odium adversus fratrem, quod hic iram dixit, quia odium est ira inveterata: & dubitationem de Dei pro- missis. De illo priori vide Matth. 5, 24. & Maimonidem in regulis orandi, ubi ait, si quis senserit animum sibi com- motum, & cor turgens, ne oret, sed quiescat, dum mens sit sedata. Pari de causa Sacerdotes, quum in templo mu- nere suo functuri essent, à vino abstinebant. De altero vide Matth. 14, 31. Adde illud Clementis ad Corinthios: οἱ δίψυχοι καὶ δισάζοντες περὶ τῆς τῦ Θεῦ δυνάμεως εἰς κρῖμα, κὰι εἰς σημείωσιν πάσαις ταῖς γενεαῖς γίνονται. Nam δια- λογισμὸς hoc loco intra animum disputatio contra fidem.

De priori Chrysostomus: Iræ nomine profa- nam injuriarum memoriam significare voluit. Munda, inquit, sit orantis intentio bujusmodi memoriæ peste, vitio omni atque perturbatione li- bera accedat ad eum: Nullus adeo audax sit, ut ini- micitias exercens ad Deum pergat orandum. De posteriori requisito, quod absque διαλογισμῷ fieri debeat oratio, plerique facile etiam consen- tiunt, quod hæsitatio excludatur, utpote Chry- sostomus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius, Lombar- dus, Valla, B. Lutherus, Hyperius, Aretins. Disceptationem, inquit Theophylactus, hesitatio- nem & ambiguitatem dicit, hoc est, ne subdubius & hæsitans ad orationem accedas, sed fide certiori imbutus, & nihil ambigens, utrum quod postulas sis, necne, accepturus? Cornelius id perperam ad disceptationem animi, quæ iram sequitur, trahit. Calvinus ad disceptationem exteriorem, an Deo probentur preces pro infidelibus & impiis con- ceptæ, ut explicat Crocius. De gentibus jam ante monuerat, quod pro illis preces fieri debeant, idque Deo acceptum esse docuerat vers. 3.

## 2:9
Vers. 9. Likewise also the women) Namely, I wish them to pray. In this respect they are equal in right: God hears the prayers of both sexes. For both Christ has died, Galat. 3, 28. ὡσάυτως, that is, in the same way with pure hands, without anger, without dissension. Besides these common precepts, he now adds also special ones for the sex that is by itself fierce.

ἐν καταστολῇ κοσμίῳ) καταστολὴ is the same as στολή. As can be seen in Isa. 28, 17 and chap. 61, 3. Where in the Hebrew it is עטה and מעטה. κόσμιον is 'decorous' in the Glossary. He wishes the attire to be clean, not luxurious. The Rabbis also give beautiful precepts concerning this matter.

μετὰ αἰδῦς κὰι σωφροσύνης κοσμεῖν ἑαυτάς) Supply 'I wish'. Shamefastness and modesty are the true ornaments of the feminine sex. With these and what follows, that saying of Melissa to Clareta agrees well: 'modesty and temperance instead of gold and emerald', where there is more on this matter. Laberius: 'To what purpose, emerald, precious glass, do you fit the Chalcedonian stone-fires? Unless to sparkle? Integrity is the carbuncle.'

Crates: 'An ornament is that which adorns; but that which makes a woman more modest adorns; and neither gold, nor emerald, nor scarlet makes her such, but whatever puts on an appearance of dignity, good order, and shamefastness.' Aristotle in the Oeconomics: 'To use expense and private means and other equipment even less than the laws of the city allow, considering that neither the brightness of garments, nor outstanding beauty, nor the size of gold contributes so much to the constitution of a woman as the good order of affairs and the dignity and seemliness of life. Since all such ornament of the soul is more lovable and by far more stable, so that until old age she may procure for herself and her children true adornment.' Plutarch has similar things in his Conjugal Precepts. There is also an old maxim: 'For a woman, character is the ornament, not gold.' not elaborate. For he considers that indecorous and ungraceful. The Greeks more significantly call the habit καταστολήν, that is, a certain stole and garment, which covers a person on all sides. He wishes, therefore, that women pray with veiled bodies, and not shamelessly uncover any parts of the body. Whence he says, adorning themselves with modesty and sobriety. He requires an honest habit, but does not define specifically which one is suitable. The circumstances of time, place, and persons teach this. Concerning which Basil in Regulae Breviores, q. 210: that use is honest for its own purpose which is suitable to the time, place, person, and necessity. The Apostle commends modesty and chastity, as the word σωφροσύνης is understood by Cyprian in the book on the habit of women, and by Erasmus; and declared by others as modesty, as the directors of the external habit, with which he wishes the inner man to be adorned. Cf. 1 Pet. 3:4. Therefore, it is not to be maintained with Pelagius, according to Jerome in Book I against Pelagius, that the glory of garments and ornament is contrary to God, provided that an adorned and modest habit is permitted.

καὶ ἐν πλέγμασι) πλέγματα, 1 Peter ch. 3:3. ἐμπλοκὴν τριχῶν. The Latin interpreter there says 'capillaturam' (hair-dressing), here 'tortos crines' (twisted hair). Well. Thus Juvenal called it 'flexum capillum': the same, 'annulos in orbe comarum': Clement of Alexandria, περιπλοκὰς τῶν τριχῶν ταῖς ἑταιρικαῖς, in Pædagogus III. 11. Naumachius: Μηδὲ κόμας περίαλλὰ πολυσχιδέας πλέκε σειράς. This is what Isaiah 3:24 called מעשה מקשה, the work of the curling iron, where the Latin calls the curling hair 'calamistratam comam'; Cicero in Pro Sextio, by the Rabbis they are called πλέγματα, משבשות. The Syriac renders it the implication by which hairs are twisted into curls. Jerome to Demetrias: Some women curl their hair with art, some twist it back, knot it, and arrange it into curls, some separate them into curls and horns with curling irons, some even attach foreign and fictitious hair to themselves, some let hair down from the forehead. Tertullian on the apparel of women, ch. VII. What does such great burden of adorning the head provide for salvation? Why is it not permitted for your hair to rest, now bound, now relaxed, now raised, now let down? Some are eager to restrain it in curls, others to let it escape as wandering and fleeting, not with good simplicity. You attach, moreover, I know not what enormities of futile and textile hairpieces, now in the manner of a cap, as a sheath for the head and a cover for the crown, now raised back onto the neck. It is a wonder that one contends against the precepts of the Lord. It has been pronounced that no one can add to his stature, Matt. 6. You clearly add to the weight certain 'collyridae' (coils), by attaching the hubs of shields to your necks. If you are not ashamed of the enormity, be ashamed of the defilement: lest you place the spoils of another's head, perhaps unclean, perhaps guilty and destined for hell, upon a holy and Christian head. Rather, drive this slavery of ornament from a free head. You labor in vain to appear adorned, you labor in vain to employ the most skilled builders of hair-dressing. God commands you to be veiled. Gregory Nazianzen in a poem against women adorning themselves maliciously: Beware, he says, women, lest you fortify your head with false and adulterous hair as if with certain towers, delicately show your soft necks from your shoulders, or anoint the forms of God with foul colors, so that you wear not faces but masks.

Αργυρίῳ ἢ χρυσῷ) For there is much ornament of women from both. See the Digest under the title 'de auro, argento, mundo', and what we have just brought from Melissa. Phintys the Pythagorean, giving precepts to married women, says: χρυσὸν δὲ καὶ σμάραγδον ἁπλῶς μὴ περιτίθεσθαι, καὶ γὰρ πολυχρήματοι, καὶ περιφανίαν ἐμφαῖνοι ποχτὰς δαμοτικάς. Concerning this whole matter, see Clement, Pædagogus II. 10.

ἢ μαργαρίταις) Women call the pearl 'unionem' in public. Pliny IX. 35, where there is much on this luxury of women. For there were patrimonies hanging from their ears. The Rabbis call strings of pearls חרוזים.

H ἱματίῳ πολυτελεῖ) Propertius: 'The matron walks dressed in the census of her grandsons.' Repeat here what we just brought from Aristotle: These are the μαλακὰ ἱμάτια, Matt. 11:8. Justin has among the precepts of Pythagoras in History Book XX: The ornaments of matrons are modesty, not clothes.

Gregory Nazianzen, Orat. II, on his sister Gregoria: Not gold, he says, adorned her, not hair yellow by nature, not knots of hair and the imposture of those making a stage with great infamy for the precious head, not the magnificence of flowing and transparent clothing, not the splendors of stones, coloring the nearby air, not the arts and deceits of painters, etc. One blush pleased her, which modesty brings, one whiteness, which abstinence produces. But the Apostle reproves especially luxury in public, where one gathers for the sake of prayer. For the sake of prayer, says Theophylact, not for the sake of dancing, should one approach. Why then does the head care for these things for itself, and dress the hair, interweaving it with pearls, when at one time it hangs it from the crown, at another places it around, at another lets it down to the feet, which certainly results in disgrace and ignominy rather than ornament, especially when things of such value have been purchased by the tears of the poor, widows, and orphans. For it is of the highest simplicity, not to say madness, and of a mind having no concern, that you have come to pray, to seek pardon for a sinner, just as if you were going to come forth to a wedding, that you are groomed and adorned.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ὡσάυτως κὰι τὰς γυναῖκας) Nempe precari volo. Hac in parte juris pares sunt: Utriusque sexus preces Deus exaudit. Pro utroque Christus est mortuus, Galat. 3, 28. ὡσάυτως, i sest, itidem puris manibus, sine ira, sine dissiden- tia. Præter hæc communia præcepta addit jam & specialia sexui per se feroci.

ἐν καταστολῇ κοσμίῳ) καταστολὴ idem quod στολή. Ut vi- dere est Esa. 28, 17. & cap. 61, 3. Ubi in Ebræo עטה & מעטה. κόσμιον decorum in Glossario. Habitum vult esse mundum, non luxuriantem. Etiam de hac re pulchra præcipiunt Rabbini.

μετὰ αἰδῦς κὰι σωφροσύνης κοσμεῖν ἑαυτάς) Supple βύλο- μαι. Pudor & modestia vera ornamenta sexus fœminini. Cum his & quæ sequuntur, bene convenit illud Melissæ ad Claretam: κοσμιότητα κὰι σωφροσύνην ἀντὶ χρυσῦ κὰι σμα- ράγδω, ubi plura ad hanc rem. Laberius: Smaragdus ad quam rem viridem, pretiosum vi- trum, Quo Calchedonios aptas ignes lapideos. Nisi ut scintillent? Probitas est carbunculus.

Crates: κόσμος τὸ κοσμῦν κοσμεῖ δὲ τὸ κοσμιωτέραν γυναῖ- κα ποιεῖν ποιεῖ δὲ τοιάυτην ὔτε χρυσὸς, ὔτε σμάραγδος, ὔτε κόκκος, ἀλλ’ ὅσα σεμνότητος, εὐταξίας, αἰδῦς ἔμφασιν περι- τίθησιν. Aristoteles in Oeconomicis: δαπανῇ τε κὰι ἰδιώτῃ, κὰι τῇ ἄλλῃ κατασκευῇ χρήσασθαι, καὶ ἐλάττονι ἢ κατὰ τὰς τῆς πόλεως νόμους ἐνθυμυμένην, ὅτι μήτε τὸ τῶν ἐνδυμάτων λαμπρὸν, μήτε τὸ κάλλος τὸ ἔξοχον, μήτε χρυσίον μέγεθος ὕτω συντελεῖ εἰς σύσασιν γυναικὸς, ὡς ἡ τῶν πραγμάτων εὐταξία κὰι τὸ τῦ βίε σεμνότης κὰι ἐυπρεπία. ὡς ἅπας μὲν τοιῦτος ὁ τῆς ψυχῆς κόσμος ἐπέραστος μᾶλλον, κὰι βεβαιότερος πολλῷ, ὥστε μέχρι γήρας ἑαυτῇ τε κὰι τοῖς παισὶ τὸν ἀληθῆ καλλωπισμὸν προσπο- ρίζεσθαι. Paria habet Plutarchus in præceptis conjugali- bus. Est & sententia vetus: Γυναικὶ κόσμος ὁ τρόπος, ὐ χρυσία. non exquisitis. Id enim ducit pro indecoro & in- venusto. Habitum significantius Græci καταστο- λὴν dicunt, id est, stolam quandam & ami- ctum, quæ undequaque hominem contegat. Vult itaque velato corpore mulieres precari, nec ullas corporis partes impudenter retegere. Unde cum verecundia inquit, & sobrietate ornantes. Ho- nestum requirit habitum, non definit autem spe- cialiter, quis conveniat. Id temporis, & loci, & personarum περιστάσεις docent. Quo de Basi- lius in Regul. Breviar. q. 210. usus ille ad pro- prium scopum honestus conveniens tempori, loco, personæ ac necessitati. Commendat au- tem Apostolus verecundiam & pudicitiam, ut σωφροσύνης vox Cypriano intellecta libr. de habi- tu mulier. & Erasmo: aliis per modestiam de- clarata, tanquam rectores externi habitus, qui bus interiorem hominem ornari vult. Conf. 1. Petr. 3, 4. Non ergo cum Pelagio apud Hiero- nymum libr. I. adversus Pelag. statuendum, glo- riam vestium & ornamentum Deo esse contra- rium, siquidem habitus ornatus & modestus per- mittatur.

καὶ ἐν πλέγμασι) πλέγματα Petrus 1. Epist. cap. 3, 3. ἐμ- πλοκὴν τριχῶν. Latinus Interpres ibi capillaturam, hic tortos crines. Bene. Sic flexum capillum dixit Juvena- lis: Idem in orbe comarum annulos: Clemens Alexan- drinus, περιπλοκὰς τῶν τριχῶν ταῖς ἑταιρικαῖς, Pædagogi III. 11. Naumachius: Μηδὲ κόμας περίαλλὰ πολυσχιδέας πλέκε σειράς. Hoc est quod Es. 3, 24. dixit מעשה מקשה opus calami- stri, ubi crispantem crinem Latinus: Calamistratam co- mam Cicero pro Sextio, Rabbinis πλέγματα dicuntur משבשות. Syrus reddit implicationem, qua crines tor- quentur in cincinnos. Hieronymus ad Deme- trium: Quædam fœminæ capillos arte crispant, quædam eos retorquent, innodant, & in cincinnos componunt, quædam in cinnos & cornua calami- stris eos discriminant, quædam etiam alienos & fictitios crines sibi apponunt, quædam à fronte crines demittunt. Tertullianus de cultu fœmi- narum cap. VII. Quid tanta ornandi capitis one- rositas salutem subministrat? Quid crinibus vestris quiescere non licet, modo substrictis, modo relaxatis, modo suscitatis, modo elisis? Aliæ gestiunt in cin- cinnis coërcere, aliæ ut vagi & volucres elabantur non bona simplicitate. Affigitis præterea nescio quas enormitates futilium atque textilium capilla- mentorum, nunc in galeri modum, quasi vaginam capitis & operculum verticis, nunc in cervicem retro suggestum. Mirum quod contra Domini præcepta contenditur. Ad mensuram sibi neminem adjicere posse pronunciatum est, Matth. 6. Vos plane adjicitis ad pondus collyridas quasdam, scu- torum umbilices cervicibus adstruendo. Si non pudet enormitatis, pudeat inquinamenti: Ne exu- vias alieni capitis forsan immundi, forsitan nocen- tis & gehennæ destinati sancto & Christiano capiti suppares. Imo hanc ornatus servitutem à libero capite propellite. Frustra laboratis ornatæ videri, frustra peritissimos quosque structores capillaturæ adhibetis. Deus vos velari jubet. Gregor. Nazian zenus in carmine contra mulieres malitiosius se ornantes: Cavete, inquit, mulieres, ne caput vestrum nothis & adulterinis crinibus tanquam turribus quibusdam muniatis, mollia colla è sca- pulis delicate ostentetis, seu Dei formas fœdis coloribus inungatis, sic ut jam non facies sed lar- vas gestetis.

Αργυρίῳ ἢ χρυσῷ) Multus enim ex utroque ornatus mulierum. Vide digesta titulo de auro, argento, mun- do, & quæ ex Melissa modo attulimus. Phintys Pythago- rica dans præcepta fœminis nuptis ait: χρυσὸν δὲ καὶ σμά- ραγδον ἁπλῶς μὴ περιτίθεσθαι, καὶ γὰρ πολυχρήματοι, καὶ πε- ριφανίαν ἐμφαῖνοι ποχτὰς δαμοτικάς. De tota hac re vide Cle- mentem Pædagogi II. 10.

ἢ μαργαρίταις) Ludorum in publico fæminæ unionem di- cant. Plinius IX. 35. ubi multa de hoc fœminarum luxu. Erant enim patrimonia de auribus pendentia. Lineas mar- garitarum חרוזים vocant Rabbini.

H ἱματίῳ πολυτελεῖ) Propertius: Matrona incedit census induta nepotum. Repete hic, quæ ex Aristotele modo attulimus: Hæc sunt μαλακὰ ἱμάτια Matth. 11, 8. Inter Pythagoræ monita habet Justinus historiæ libr. XX. Ornamenta matronarum pudici- tiam, non vestes esse.

Gregorius Nazianzenus Orat. II. de Gregoria sorore: Non illam, inquit, aurum ornavit, non natu- flava come, non crinum nodi & impostura pre- tiosum caput summa cum infamia scenam efficièn- tium, non circumflua & pellucida vestis magnifi- centia, non lapidum splendores, propinquum aë- rem colorantes, non pictorum artes & præsti- giæ &c. Unus illi rubor placebat, quem pudor affert, unus candor, quem parit abstinentia. Re- probat autem Apostolus imprimis luxum in pu- blico, quo orandi causa convenitur. Orandi, inquit Theophylactus, non tripudiandi causa ac- cedat. Cur ergo caput hæc sibi curat, & crines co- mit, margaritis hos interplectens, cum alias è ver- tice suspendit, alias circumponit, alias pedibus de- mittit, quod sane probro cedit & ignominiæ potius, quam ornamento, præsertim cum tanti res pretii per pauperum sint & viduarum & orphanorum lacry- mas comparata. Est enim summæ simplicitatis, ne dicam vesaniæ, & animi nihil pensi habentis, ad o- randum te concessisse, peccantis veniam petituram, perinde tanquam ad nuptias prodituram, te com- ptam esse & ornatam.

## 2:10
Vers. 10. But which is becoming to women professing godliness through good works) The Syrian expressed the sense well: But through good works, (namely if they adorn from the preceding) as it becomes women having professed (Christian, that is) piety. Ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι here and below in ch. 6, 21 is to profess: And thus Ambrose translates it here. So Lucian: Τίνα τὴν ἄσκησιν ἐπαγγέλλεται; what art does he profess? He says this: See, woman, what you professed in baptism, you wished to be called a Christian. This name demands a life exceptionally pure and holy.

The Vulgate has 'promising', which pleases Beza, Musculus, and Grotius, although Piscator explains it as 'professing', and Crocius admits it is taken that way below in chapter 6, 21. B. Luther also rendered it in chapter 6, 21 as 'fürgeben'. But here, 'die Gottseligkeit beweisen'. For he joins it with the following words: 'durch gute Wercke': that a modest habit of body, not an excessive cultivation of external adornment, becomes women who are spiritually adorned with piety. Thus there is no need for either Crocius's parenthesis or Grotius's transposition. The true adornment of Christians, says St. Augustine in Epistle 73 to Possidius, and of Christian women, is not only no lying paint, but not even the pomp of gold and clothing, but good morals. Thus no crack is left for the gloss of the Papists concerning the profession of deaconesses and nuns. Nor is there any need, as with Crocius, to go off to the baptismal vow, which seems foreign here.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ἀλλ' ὃ πρέπει γυναιξὶν ἐπαγγελλομέναις θεοσέ- βειαν δι' ἔργων ἀγαθῶν) Bene sensum expressit Syrus: Sed per opera bona, (nempe si ornent ex præcedentibus) ut decet fœminas pietatem (Christianam scilicet) professas. Ἐπαγγέλ- λεσθαι hic & infra c. 6, 21. est profiteri: Atque ita vertit hic Ambrosius. Sic Lucianus: Τίνα τὴν ἄσκησιν ἐπαγγέλλεται; quam artem profitetur? Hoc dicit: Vide mulier, quid in baptismo sis professa, Christiana dici voluisti. Nomen hoc vitam exigit eximie puram atque sanctam.

Vulgata habet promittentes, quod Bezæ, Mu- sculo, & Grotio placet, utut Piscator explicet profitentes, atque ita infra cap. 6, 21. accipi fa- teatur Crocius. B. Lutherus reddidit etiam cap. 6, 21. fürgeben. Sed hic, die Gottseligkeit bewei- sen. Nam conjungit cum verbis sequentibus: durch gute Wercke: quod bene spirituali or- natu pietatis mulieres deceat corporis habitus modestus, non nimius externi ornatus cultus. Ita nulla vel parenthesi Crocii vel trajectione Grotii opus. Verus ornatus maxime Christia- norum, inquit S. Augustinus epist. LXXIII. ad Possid. & Christianarum non tantum nullus fu- cus mendax, verum ne auri quidem vestisque pompa, sed boni mores sunt. Ita nulla relin- quitur Papistarum de professione Diaconissarum & monialium glossa rima. Nec opus est, ut cum Crocio ad baptismi sponsionem abeamus, quæ hic videtur aliena.

## 2:11
Vers. 11. Let a woman learn in silence) Without chattering, from which that tender sex often does not abstain even in church, as Chrysostom noted here. And this precept is from the Synagogue, where women have a place secluded from the sight of men, and listen in silence to what is read or said:

Nay, not from the Synagogue, but from divine inspiration. It is divine, not human. Not only, says Theophylact as interpreter, should a woman be adorned in gesture and habit, but also in voice. For I would not have her speak, nor discourse even about spiritual things themselves, but only in such a way that she may learn. We learn by reading, we also learn by asking. This he does not grant them, as is clear from 1 Cor. 14. For they ought to ask, not publicly, but at home from their husband. Therefore they ought to learn by listening. Nay, he commands silence, he restrains the liberty of asking questions. In which they differed from the men. It was permitted to these to interrogate. It was permitted to these to judge the Prophets, as Crocius rightly observed here.

ἐν πάσῃ ὑποταγῇ) With total obedience, namely to preserve the order established by the presbytery. πάσῃ here is total, as above in chapter 1, 15.

The woman is divinely subjected to the man. Which subjection she ought to testify to, both always and especially also in the public assembly of the Church. She does not testify to it while she does not listen in silence.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Γυνὴ ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ μανθανέτω) Sine garritu, à quo tenellum illud genus sæpe nec in Ecclesia abstinet, ut hic notavit Chrysostomus. Et hoc præceptum ex Syna- goga est, ubi mulieres seclusum à virorum aspectu locum habent, & cum silentio, quæ præleguntur aut dicuntur, auscultant:

Imo non ex Synagoga, sed à θεοπνευστίᾳ. Di- vinum, non humanum. Non solum inquit, Theophylacto interprete, gestu & habitu ornata sit mulier, verum & voce. Non enim velim loqua- tur, neque de spiritualibus ipsis edisserat, sed id mo- do ut discat. Discimus legendo, etiam quærendo discimus. Hoc illis non concedit, ut patet ex 1. Cor. 14. Quærere enim debent, non publice, sed domi à viro. Ergo discere debent audiendo. Imo silen- tium imperat, quærendi licentiam cohibet. Quo differebant à viris. His licebat interrogare. His licebat censere Prophetas, ut hic recte observavit Crocius.

ἐν πάσῃ ὑποταγῇ) Cum summa obedientia, nempe ad servandum ordinem à presbyterio constitutum. πάσῃ hic est summa ut supra c. 1, 15.

Mulier divinitus subjecta est viro. Quam subjectionem tum semper, tum imprimis etiam in publico Ecclesiæ conventu testari debet. Non testatur, dum non auscultat cum silen- tio.

## 2:12
Vers. 12. γυναικὶ δὲ διδάσκειν ὀυκ ἐπιτρέπω) It was the duty of the president to teach; but he sometimes entrusted his office in this regard to Presbyters, and sometimes also to others. The Apostle does not wish this to be permitted to women: namely, unless they have a Prophetic inspiration, and while they have it. See what we have said on 1 Corinthians 11, 5 and chapter 14, 35. Prophecy is outside of positive laws: Maimonides forbids women even to open a school. Tertullian on the veiling of virgins: A woman is not permitted to speak in the Church, nor to teach, nor to baptize, nor to offer, nor to claim for herself any share of a masculine duty, much less of a priestly office.

That the President or Prelate or Bishop, as they are distinguished from Presbyters by the Papists, was a distinct office in the Apostle's time, but that he entrusted this same duty to presbyters, and sometimes also to others, is a vain and false assertion, consistent with no document or testimony of scripture or of the antiquity of the Church: nay, it is entirely contrary to scripture. For neither are Bishops found to be superior to Presbyters in the scriptures or the ecclesiastical history of the primitive Church, nor is the duty of teaching enjoined any less upon Presbyters than upon Bishops. Nay, they are said to be constituted Bishops by the Holy Spirit to feed the flock acquired by the blood of God, Acts 20, 28. And Bishops are called heralds of the Word among the Philippians, chapter 1, v. 1. Nor does the Apostle use the word Ἐπισκόπε otherwise than for a herald of the Word, 1 Tim. 3, 2; Tit. 1, 7, or the name τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς otherwise than for the ministry of the divine Word, 1 Tim. 3, 1. Finally, presbyters are called ἐπισκοπῶντες, 1 Peter 5, 2. But if it is the property of Bishops to teach, by what right do they bear the title of Bishop in the Papacy who do not teach, just as Johannes Keiserbergius, when Wilhelm von Honstein was elected Bishop of Strasbourg, said in a sermon: In a hundred years it has been neither seen nor heard that any of the Bishops have exercised spiritual duties. They have visited not souls, but purses, and this indeed every year.

ὀὐδὲ ἀυθεντεῖν ἀνδρὸς) See what we have said on Ephesians 5, 22, 24; Colossians 3, 18. Phrynichus says the word ἀυθέντε began to be used in his own time in the meaning of δεσπότε. Hence ἀυθεντεῖν is ἐξουσιάζειν ישלט. Iamblichus: ἐκᾶι κἂι περὶ τὸ ἄρχειν μὲν τὸν ἄῤῥενα, ἄρχεσθαι δὲ τὴν θήλειαν ὁμογνωμονήσωσιν. Euripides: Τῶν δὲ ἡγεμονίαν τῶν ὅλων τὸν ἄνδρ᾽ ἔχειν. See Esther 1, 17. You have similar precepts in the Hebrew book Musar.

Ἀλλ’ εἶναι ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ) That is, to keep silence, as much as possible. Euripides: Γυναικὶ γὰρ σιγήτε καὶ τὸ σωφρονεῖν Κάλλισον ἄσω δὲ ἥσυχον μένειν δόμων. ἡσυχία שקט. See 2 Thessalonians 3, 12. However, 'I command' is understood here.

These things follow very well from the preceding. If it were permitted for a woman to speak and teach in the Church, the power of commanding or ordering men would be permitted to her. For those who teach publicly command and order in the name of God. When he had enjoined silence upon women, says Theophylact, lest by chance the woman might have found some more just cause for speaking, he says, let her not teach. For that is to have authority over the man himself. But rather he enjoined that she be subject to the man. For he says, your turning shall be to your husband; let it be so, therefore, that she must be silent. For when she is silent, she shows her subjection. You should understand, however, that the Apostle did not enjoin silence upon the woman everywhere, or forbid her the ability to instruct others in any place, but only in the Church. For she has the power to teach others separately. Since Priscilla also instructed that Apollo, and a faithful woman reminds her husband. Things to be noted against the Anabaptist and Quaker confusion: In whose assemblies the parts of teaching are promiscuously granted to women and men. But since the Apostle takes away the power of teaching in a public assembly from women, he also abrogates authority and rule over the man from the wife, which rests upon the command of the Lord, Gen. 3:16, and orders her to be in silence not only in the Church, as Crocius wishes, concerning which the Apostle had already warned before, but also in the house: lest, namely, she speak against her husband, as being more eminent and the Lord, just as he deduced this ἐξοχὴν, where that precept is built upon, immediately from the history of creation and the primordial seduction.

Latin:

Vers. 12. γυναικὶ δὲ διδάσκειν ὀυκ ἐπιτρέπω) Præsidis erat docere; sed is interdum Presbyteris, interdum & aliis suum hac in parte munus mandabat. Mulieribus id Apo- stolus permitti non vult: nempe nisi habeant afflatum Pro- pheticum, & dum eum habent. Vide quæ diximus ad 1. Corinth. 11, 5. & cap. 14,35. Prophetia extra leges est po- sitivas: Maimonides fœminis etiam ludum literarium vetat aperire. Tertullianus de virginibus velandis: Non per- mittitur mulier in Ecclesia loqui, sed nec docere, nec tingere, nec offerre, nec ullius virilis muneris, nedum sacerdotalis officii sor- tem sibi vindicare.

Præsidis vel Præsulis aut Episcopi quà à Presby- teris distinguuntur à Papistis, hoc proprium fuisse Apostoli tempore docere, sed eundem hoc munus presbyteris, interdum & aliis demandas- se, vana sit & falsa assertio, nullo scripturæ, nullo antiquitatis Ecclesiæ documento vel testi- monio constans: imo scripturæ prorsus adver- sa. Nam nec Presbyteris superiores Episcopi reperiuntur in scripturis aut historia Ecclesiasti- ca primitivæ Ecclesiæ, nec minus injunctum est Presbyteris docendi munus quam Episcopis. Imo illi constituti dicuntur Episcopi à Spiritu san- cto ad pascendum Verbo Dei gregem sanguine Dei acquisitum, Actor. 20, 28. Et Episcopi vocan- tur præcones Verbi apud Philippenses cap. 1. v. 1. Nec aliter vel Ἐπισκόπε voce quam de Verbi præ- cone utitur Apostolus, 1. Tim. 3, 2. Tit. 1, 7. vel τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς nomine, quam de ministerio Ver- bi divini 1. Tim. 3, 1. Denique ἐπισκοπῶντες di- cuntur presbyteri, 1. Petr. 5, 2. Si autem Episco- porum proprium est docere, quo jure titulum Episcopi gerunt in Papatu, qui non docent, quemadmodum Johannes Keiserbergius, Wilhel- mo ab Honstein in Episcopum Argentinensem Electo, pro concione dixit: In centum annis neque visum neque auditum esse, quod aliquis Episcoporum spiritualia exercuerit. Non animas, sed bursas visitaverunt, & hoc quidem omni anno.

ὀὐδὲ ἀυθεντεῖν ἀνδρὸς) Vide quæ diximus Ephes. 5, 22. 24. Coloss. 3, 18. Vocem ἀυθέντε dicit Phrynichus jam suo tempore usurpari cœpisse in significatu δεσπότε. Hinc ἀυ- θεντεῖν est ἐξουσιάζειν ישלט. Jamblichus: ἐκᾶι κἂι περὶ τὸ ἄρχειν μὲν τὸν ἄῤῥενα, ἄρχεσθαι δὲ τὴν θήλειαν ὁμογνωμονήσωσιν. Euripides: Τῶν δὲ ἡγεμονίαν τῶν ὅλων τὸν ἄνδρ᾽ ἔχειν. Vide Esther 1, 17. Similia præcepta habes in libro Ebræo Musar.

Ἀλλ’ εἶναι ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ) Id est silentium servare, quantum fieri potest. Euripides: Γυναικὶ γὰρ σιγήτε καὶ τὸ σωφρονεῖν Κάλλισον ἄσω δὲ ἥσυχον μένειν δόμων. ἡσυχία שקט. Vide 2. Thess. 3, 12. subauditur autem hic jubeo.

Hæc optime consequuntur ad superiora. Si loqui ac docere permitteretur mulieri in Eccle- sia, permitteretur ei in viros imperandi vel mandandi potestas. Nam nomine Dei præci- piunt atque imperant, qui publice docent. Cum taciturnitatem, inquit Theophylactus, fœminis indixisset, ne causam forte justiorem aliquam ad loquendum fuerit nacta mulier, ne doceat inquit. Id namque est habere in virum ipsum imperium. Quin potius subjectam esse hanc viro injunxit. In- quit enim, ad virum sit conversio tua, sit itaque, ut illi silendum sit. Cum enim silet, ejus præfert subjectionem. Intelligas autem, non ubique Apo- stolum mulieri injunxisse silentium, vel alios in- struendi quovis in loco facultatem interdixisse, sed in Ecclesia duntaxat. Quippe quæ seorsum ha- beat alios docendi potestatem. Siquidem & Pri- scilla Apollo illum instruxit, & fidelis mulier vi- rum commonefacit. Quæ contra confusionem Anabaptisticam & Quacquerorum notanda: In quorum cœtibus promiscue mulieribus & viris docendi partes conceduntur. Quum autem do- cendi potestatem in publico cœtu adimat mu- lieribus Apostolus, autoritatem etiam atque imperium in virum abrogat uxori, quod nititur mandato Domini, Gen. 3, 16. ac jubet eam esse in silentio non tantum in Ecclesia, ut Crocius vult, quo de prius jam monuerat Apostolus, sed etiam in domo: ne scilicet obloquatur ma- rito, ceu eminentiori & Domino, quemadmo- dum hanc ἐξοχὴν, ubi præceptum illud superstrui- tur, è creationis & primævæ seductionis historia actutum deduxit.

## 2:13
Vers. 13. For Adam was first formed, then Eve) Which is a sign of more eminent dignity in the man, 1 Cor. 11:8. Eve for חַוָה also 2 Cor. 11:3. And thus Origen cites it from the Greek Interpreters. But now in the LXX it is read ζωὴ, with the sense, not the sound of the word, rendered.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ἀδὰμ γὰρ πρῶτος ἐπλάσθη, εἶτα Εὔα) Quod signum eminentioris in viro dignitatis, 1. Corinth. 11, 8. Εὔα pro חַוָה etiam 2. Cor. 11, 3. Et sic ex Græcis Inter- pretibus citat Origenes. Nunc autem in LXX. legitur ζωὴ, sensu, non sono vocis reddito.

## 2:14
Vers. 14. And Adam was not deceived) Another argument from the weakness of the sex, a huge proof of which was given from the very beginning. He was not deceived, namely by the serpent. For the serpent did not attack the man, but the woman as being weaker, 2 Cor. 11:3. And therefore in Gen. 3:13, the woman says: The serpent deceived me. But it is just that that which is weaker should obey the stronger. Democritus: By nature, to rule is proper to the stronger. He says therefore, according to Theophylact, because the woman once taught the man, and perverted everything, therefore I would not have her have the power of teaching henceforth. Note however (Theophylact continues), how he did not say that Eve was deceived, but the woman, as if he were discoursing about the female gender itself. For just as all human nature was lost in Adam: so also through Eve, levity slipped into the whole female gender, by which the transgression itself first invaded Eve.

But the woman being deceived was in the transgression) Deceived by the serpent, as we have said. She was in the transgression, she was in fault. The same expression is in the Hebrew, 1 Kings 14:34. יִהְיֶה מַחְטָא. Tertullian on the apparel of women: The woman draws from Eve the ignominy of the first sin, and the odium of human perdition.

Crocius acknowledges that more is signified against Calvin himself, who rendered it, she was guilty of transgression, namely that she was the cause of transgression to Adam, and that this is well expressed by Luther translating it, and has introduced the transgression, he notes. So that ἐν παραβάσει is the same as εἰς παράβασιν.

Latin:

Vers. 14. καὶ Ἀδὰμ οὐκ ἠπατήθη) Alterum argum:en- tum ab imbecillitate sexus, cujus documentum ingens jam ab initio datum. Non deceptus est, nempe à serpente. Non enim virum serpens aggressus est, sed fœminam ut im- becilliorem, 2. Cor. 11, 3. Ideoque in Gen. 3, 13. fœmina di- cit: ὁ ὄφις ἠπάτησέ με. Æquum autem est, id, quod est imbecillius, parere valentiori. Democritus: Φύσει τὸ ἄρχειν οἰκήϊον τῷ κρείσσονι. Ait igitur, juxta Theophylactum, quia semel mulier virum edocuit, & cuncta pervertit, id- circo nequaquam hæc habeat velim de cætero docendi potestatem. Adverte autem (pergit Theophylactus,) quemadmodum non Evam dixe- rit deceptam esse, sed mulierem, tanquam de ipso muliebri genere disseruisset. Nam quemadmodum natura omnis humana in Adam perdita est: Sic & per Evam in omne fœmineum genus dilapsa est levitas, qua & prævaricatio ipsa primum Evam invasit.

ἡ δὲ γυνὴ ἀπατηθεῖσα ἐν παραβάσει γέγονε) Decepta à ser- pente, ut diximus. Ἐν παραβάσει γέγονε in culpa fuit. Eadem loquutio in Ebræo, 1. Reg. 14, 34. יִהְיֶה מַחֲטָא. Tertullianus de habitu mulieris: Mulier de Eva trahit ignominiam primi delicti, & invidiam perditionis huma- næ.

Plus significari adversus Calvinum ipsum, qui reddidit, transgressionis rea fuit, agnoscit Crocius, nempe quod Adamo fuerit causa transgressionis, idque bene exprimi à Luthero vertente, und hat die Ubertretung eingeführet/ notat. Ut ἐν παρα- βάσει idem sit, quod εἰς παράβασιν.

## 2:15
Vers. 15. She shall be saved through childbearing) That is, if she keeps the other things which I have said, the fact that she devotes effort to seeking children will not hinder her salvation. This was not said in vain. For there were to be, in those very places, those who would teach the contrary. Below ch. 4. A similar expression is almost that of Cicero: To arrive at honors through play and negligence.

Theophylact explains it thus, that the Apostle has also conferred a cause of salvation upon women, namely the procreation of children, that is, that he has entrusted children to them to be educated and imbued with the best morals. But that is not what is being treated here. For he does not teach how they themselves might also instruct others unto salvation and thereby save them, but that they themselves might attain salvation: nor concerning the institution, but he teaches concerning the generation of children. And therefore, neither is Augustine’s metaphorical interpretation concerning the production of good works to be understood, which he handed down in book 12 of De Trinitate, chapter 17: because one must not depart from the literal meaning of the word τεκνογονίας. Nor, however, with Cornelius à Lapide, is the merit of the labors which a woman suffers in childbirth and the education of children to be carved out from this, or the suffrages and merits of children to be feigned here with Justinianus. Merits are entirely excluded in the matter of salvation by the Apostle in Ephesians 2:8, Titus 3:5, Romans 11:6. How, therefore, could he ascribe merits to the generation of children? Rightly, therefore, Grotius departs from these, explaining that τεκνογονία will not hinder salvation. Vatablus rendered it: She shall be saved, being subject to the generation of children, so that it is a Grecism, διὰ τῆς τεκνογονίας, that is, τεκνογονῆσα, generating children. Thus Romans 4:11, δι᾽ ἀκροβυσίας for ἐν ἀκροβυσίᾳ. Thus also Bellarmine explains in his book on matrimony, chapter 2, that the phrase 'through the generation of children' is put for 'in the generation of children,' and that such a phrase is most frequent in the scriptures; and Cornelius à Lapide on Romans 2:27, at the words 'through the letter and circumcision art a transgressor of the law': Note, he says, the Grecism 'through the letter,' that is, 'having the letter.' For thus διὰ is taken by the Greeks. Similar is 1 Timothy 2:15, 'She shall be saved through the generation of children,' that is, 'she shall be saved, generating children, if she shall have remained in faith.' Similarly Vasquez and others. Whence the argument, which Bellarmine also infers in book 4 of De Justificatione, chapter 7, § 'according to the testimony' from this passage for merits, by the confession of Cornelius and Bellarmine himself, falls into the sponge. Nor less also what the Papists seek from this passage for the sacrament of matrimony, that a promise is added to marriage: as if the spouses receive sanctifying grace THROUGH marriage itself: which Vasquez himself confessed to have little strength. Compare concerning that use of the preposition διὰ in Acts 14:22, 2 Corinthians 6:8, Galatians 4:13, 1 Peter 3:20.

If they remain in faith, and love and sanctification with sobriety) He had begun in the singular, he ends in the plural: because where it is a matter of some whole genus, these are equivalent. A similar change is in 1 Kings 18:26. The name of love is sometimes accustomed to be taken in such breadth that it comprehends all duties following faith. But here it is taken more strictly; and by ἁγιασμὸν (sanctification) seems to be understood conjugal chastity, as 1 Thessalonians 4:4. By σωφροσύνην (sobriety), however, modesty, as above in chapter 9 and Titus 2:5. In the Glossary, σωφροσύνη is modesty.

There is therefore no cause, because of the plural, to refer this to children with Chrysostom and Theophylact, since the discourse is about a woman, if indeed the plural has regard to the sense, the name of woman being taken for every woman procreating children, to all of whom this comfort is rendered: therefore it is not to be disapproved that the blessed Luther retains the plural number with the Greek codices and the Syriac, which was also done by Erasmus, the Tigurines, and Piscator, even though the singular pleased Castalio, Beza, and the Belgians more here. However, the condition of salvation is not expressed here, but the condition of the subject to be saved, which ought to remain in faith and love and sanctification, by which Theophylact also understood chastity, and sobriety, as the Vulgate has it, which Theophylact interprets as honesty, or continence. Claudius Espencaeus understands by these two the sanctification of the mind and the purity of the body. Justinianus says it embraces holiness, worship, and religious ceremonies, but that the names of sobriety comprehend all that pertains to breaking and thoroughly subduing wicked desires. It is possible, if love is explained as charity toward one's neighbor, that by sanctification the worship of God may be understood: which, as they befit both sexes, so for the sake of women, chastity is to be considered added, which the blessed Luther explains, 'sammt der Zucht' (together with discipline), because this is especially to be inculcated in women. Thus the blessed Hunnius also interpreted it, rendering this paraphrase of the sentence: The woman was indeed made subject to the seduction of Satan. But it is well. She has not therefore fallen from all hope of salvation. For Christ obtained this for her, that in her feminine state and work of τεκνογονίας (childbearing), however much it may not be free from every stain of sin, she can nevertheless be saved, if indeed she has remained in faith, and in those virtues from which faith cannot be torn away, namely, love of neighbor, sanctification, and chastity. Who also rightly vindicated against the abuse of the Papists, as if the salvation of women is not ascribed to faith alone, but also to the virtues joined with it: that a fallacy of composition and division is committed in the Papistic argument, and indeed of many questions. For if one asks about the cause of the blessedness and salvation of women, it is not attributed to charity, not to sanctification, and not to chastity, but to faith in Christ. The other virtues joined to it do not obtain the status of a cause, but are referred to the description of the person to be saved, and indicate by what marks and properties those faithful and blessed women can be recognized, namely, from the study of charity, the works of sanctification, and the testimony of preserved chastity.

Latin:

Vers. 15. σωθήσεται διὰ τῆς τεκνογονίας) Id est, si cætera, quæ dixi, servat, quod operam dat quærendis liberis, non impediet ejus salutem. Dictum hoc non frustra. Nam futuri erant, iis ipsis in locis, qui contra docerent. Infra c. 4. Similis ferme loquutio Ciceronis: Per ludum & negligen- tiam ad honores pervenire.

Theophylactus id sic explicat, quod causam sa- lutis etiam mulieribus contulerit Apostolus, fi- liorum nempe procreationem, hoc est, quod li- beros ipsis educandos & optimis moribus imbuen- dos commiserit. Sed id hic non agitur. Non enim quomodo ipsæ etiam alios ad salutem in- formare adeoque salvare possint, sed quod ipsæ salutem consequantur, docet: Necde institutione, sed de generatione liberorum docet. Ideoque nec Augustini interpretatio Metaphorica de produ- ctione bonorum operum intelligenda, quam libr. XII. de Trin. cap. 17. tradidit: quia a proprietate vocis τεκνογονίας discedendum non est. Nec ta- men cum Cornelio à Lapide hinc exsculpendum meritum laborum, quos patitur mulier in partu & educatione liberorum, aut suffragia & meri- ta liberorum cum Justiniano hic fingenda. Me- rita prorsus excluduntur in salutis negotio ab Apostolo Ephes. 2, 8. Tit. 3, 5. Rom. 11, 6. Quo- modo ergo generationi liberorum merita adscri- beret? Merito ergo ab his discedit Grotius, ex- plicans, quod non impeditura sit τεκνογονία sa- lutem. Vatablus reddidit: Servabitur subjecta generationi filiorum, ut sit Graecismus, διὰ τῆς τεκνογονίας, id est, τεκνογονῆσα, liberos generans. Sic Roman. 4, 11. δι᾽ ἀκροβυσίας pro ἐν ἀκροβυσίᾳ. Sic etiam explicat Bellarminus libr. de matrim. cap. 2. illud per generationem filiorum positum esse pro eo in filiorum generatione, eamque phra- sin in scripturis esse frequentissimam, & Cor- nelius à Lapide in Rom. 2, 27. ad verba per lite- ram & circumcisionem es prævaricator legis: No- ta, inquit, Graecismum per literam, id est, ha- bens literam. Sic enim sumitur à Graecis διὰ. Simile est 1. Timoth. 2, 15. Salvabitur per filio- rum generationem, id est, salvabitur filios gene- rans, si permanserit in fide. Similiter Vasquez & alii. Unde argumentum, quod etiam Bel- larminus libr. IV. de justif. cap. 7. §. secundum testimonium ex hoc loco pro meritis infert ipsius Cornelii & Bellarmini confessione, in spongiam incumbit.
