Nec minus etiam quod pro sacra- mento matrimonii ex hoc loco petunt Papistæ, quod conjugio promissio sit addita: quasi PER ipsum matrimonium gratiam sanctificantem ac- cipiant conjuges: quod parum roboris habere fassus est ipse Vasquez. Conf. de usu illo præ- positionis διὰ Actor. 14, 22. 2. Cor. 6, 8. Galat. 4, 13, 1. Petr. 3, 20.

Ἐὰν μείνωσιν ἐν πίστει, καὶ ἀγάπῃ καὶ ἁγιασμῷ μετὰ σωφρο- σύνης) Inceperat in singulari, definit in plurali: quia ubi de toto aliquo genere agitur, hæc idem valent. Similis διαπλαγὴ 1. Reg. 18, 26. Solet interdum dilectionis no- men in ea amplitudine sumi, ut omnia officia fidem subse- quentia comprehendat. Sed hic strictius sumitur; & per ἁγιασμὸν videtur intelligenda pudicitia conjugalis, ut 1. Thessal 4. v. 4. Per σωφροσύνην vero modestia, ut su- pra cap. 9. & Tit. 2. v. 5. In Glossario σωφροσύνη mode- stia.

Non ergo causa est ob pluralem hæc ad libe- ros cum Chrysostomo & Theophylacto referendi, quum sermo sit de muliere, siquidem ad sensum respectum habeat plurale, mulieris nomen de omni muliere liberos procreante accipiatur, qui- bus omnibus solatium hoc redditur: ideo non improbandum, quod pluralem numerum cum Græcis codicibus & Syro retineat B. Lutherus, quod etiam ab Erasmo, Tigurinis & Piscatore factum, etsi Castalioni, Bezæ, & Belgis singularis hic po- tius placuerit. Non autem hic exprimitur con- ditio salutis, sed conditio subjecti salvandi, quod manere debet in fide ac dilectione ac sanctifica- tione, per quam etiam Theophylactus intellexit pudicitiam, & sobrietate, ut Vulgata habet, quam de honestate interpretatur Theophylactus, vel continentia. Claudius Espensæus sanctificatio- nem mentis & corporis puritatem per hæc duo intelligit. Justinianus sanctimoniam, cultum, & religiosas ceremonias complecti ait, sobrietatis ve- ro nomina id omnia comprehendere, quod ad frangendas penitusque edomandas pravas cupi- ditates pertinet. Potest, si dilectio de charitate proximi explicetur, per sanctificationem cultus Dei intelligi: quæ uti sexui utrique conveniunt: Ita ob mulieres addita censenda pudicitia, quod B. Lutherus explicat, sammt der Zucht, quia mu- lieribus hæc imprimis inculcanda. Sic B. Hun- nius etiam interpretatus est, hanc reddens senten- tiæ paraphrasin: Mulier facta quidem est obnoxia seductioni Satanæ. Sed bene habet. Non ideo spe omni salutis excidit. Hoc enim ei Christus impetra- vit, ut in suo muliebri statu & opere τεκνογονίας, quantumvis id non sit ab omni labe peccati liberum, salvari tamen possit, si videlicet manserit in fide, & à quibus fides divelli nequit virtutibus, dilectione videlicet proximi, sanctificatione & castitate. Qui etiam probe vindicavit ab abusu Pontificiorum, quasi salus mulierum, non soli fidei adscribatur, sed conjunctis etiam virtutibus: Committi in argu- mento Papistico fallaciam compositionis & divisionis, quin & plurium interrogatium. Etenim si de causa quæratur beatitudinis ac salutis fœminarum, ea non charitati, non sanctificationi, castitative tribui- tur, sed fidei in Christum. Cæteræ virtutes ad- junctæ non causæ rationem obtinent, sed ad de- scriptionem salvandæ personæ referuntur, & indi- cant, quibus notis ac proprietatibus agnosci queant fideles illæ beatæque mulieres, nimirum ex studio charitatis, operibus sanctificationis, & servatæ ca- stitatis testimonio.

## 3:1 Argument
SECTION II. OF PART I. OF THE EPISTLE CONCERNING ECCLESIASTICAL PERSONS. CHAPTER III. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

As the Apostle teaches that the desire for the Episcopal office is praiseworthy: So he sets forth the requirements of Bishops, both in general and in particular regarding virtues and testimony from those outside, and at the same time exhibits the things pertaining to Deacons and their wives: So that Timothy may know how one ought to behave in the Church as the house of God, as in that which guards the truth of the divine mysteries and especially the great mystery of godliness concerning the incarnation of God.

There are two parts: I. Information concerning Bishops and Deacons and Deaconesses, to verse 13. II. The end of the information made to Timothy, by which the conversation in the house of the Lord, and the preservation of the truth of the mysteries of faith, to verse 16.

PART I. Information concerning Bishops and Deacons.

Vers. 1. Πιστὸς ὁ λόγος) Chrysostom refers this to what had preceded: but it is more true that it is a preface for commending the sentiment which follows: such as that above, beginning with the same words in chap. 1, 15. It is most true, he says, what I am now about to say: Some codices have here ἀνθρώπινος λόγος. But Jerome noted that it was so also in some codices in the previous passage, chap. 1, 15. Doubtless this error was born from abbreviations of writing not dissimilar, πς & ᾱς.

If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a good work. 'Επισκοπὴ, פקדה, signifies inspection of any kind, as in Num. 4:16, Ps. 109:8. The inspectors or prefects of the Church are the presbyters of Acts 20:28, who in the Synagogue are זקנים or קשישין, also פרנסין. The chief of these later began to be called by way of eminence ὁ ἐπίσκοπος, as in the canons which are called Apostolic, and in the letters which are called Ignatius's, and in Tertullian and others. This is in the Apocalypse ὁ Ἄγγελος, elsewhere in Paul ὁ προεςὼς ἐν λόγῳ κοπιῶν, and similarly in Justin ὁ προεςώς. In the same way, in the Synagogue, he who was the chief was called ὁ ἀρχισυνάγωγος, or ἄρχων τῆς συναγωγῆς, ὁ πρόεδρος to Philo, the Hebrew ראש הקהל, in Syriac ריש כנושתא, as we said on Matt. 9:18. But here, as we said, ἐπισκοπὴ is the honor of the presbyter, קשישותא, here Syr. Both ὀρέγεται and ἐπιθυμεῖ here mean אהב, he desires, he seeks. Nor was that at that time a matter of ambition, but of the greatest fortitude, because the office of Presbyter was joined not only with the most grievous labors but also with the highest dangers, for the reason that these men, as teachers of others, were especially dragged off to punishment. Ἔργον, מעשה, in this place is the function itself, the ministry itself, as below in 2 Tim. 4:5. Truly, this function is beautiful and honorable. And therefore, there are required for it not only the virtues common to all true Christians, but also certain more excellent ones: to the extent that the Presbyters themselves stand above the common people.

After the Apostle has dealt with sacred offices, he now deals with Ecclesiastical persons, both those who are still to be set over the sacred office, chapter 3, and those who are already set over it, chapter 4. Among these, he brings forward Bishops in the first place, and briefly teaches that it is not illicit to desire that office: but he explains at greater length what kind of person a Bishop ought to be. Although the name of Bishop is used generally of any inspectors of an army, Num. 31:14, of the people, 1 Macc. 1:53, of a city, Judg. 9:28, it occurs regarding inspectors of the Church, both of the High Priest, Num. 4:16, and of other Priests, 2 Kings 11:18, of inspectors of the Levites, Neh. 11:22, and even of the Levites, 2 Chron. 32:12. Grotius acknowledges that in the books of the New Testament this is used of Presbyters, and thus this name was already attributed to the Prince of the Presbyters in the Apostolic age. The Canon law supports this, C. Cleros dist. 21, C. nullus, dist. 60, C. Legimus, dist. 93, etc. Otherwise than Bellarmine contends in his book on clerics, chapter 14, that by divine right the Bishop is greater than the Presbyter, both in the power of order and also in jurisdiction. The Apostolic Canons do not reach the Apostolic age, nor are they of Apostolic authority, even by the judgment of the Papists themselves. Bellarmine himself observes that Ignatius is inconsistent here in his book on clerics, chapter 15, response to the 11th objection. Sometimes he says the Bishop holds the place of God, the Presbyters the place of Christ, the Deacon the place of the Apostles, as in the Epistle to the Trallians; sometimes he gives the Bishop the place of Christ, the Presbyters the place of the Apostles, the Deacons the place of the LXX disciples, as in the Epistle to the Smyrneans. How, therefore, is the Bishop superior to the Presbyters by divine right, when their authority is so uncertain? Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa says in his book II, De Concordantia Catholica, chapter 13, that Presbyters are distinguished from Bishops not by power, but by the execution of power, and that by ecclesiastical law alone. Regarding the desire for the Episcopate, the opinion of Gregory the Great in book VI on 1 Kings 1 pleases me: 'It is the right order that men should be sought for the Episcopate, not that men should seek the Episcopate.' However, 'to seek' must be understood as ambition. For a modest offering of oneself to undertake the burden of the presbyterate is not illicit. For how is it to be judged simply illicit to seek a good work? To those who are to be promoted and who seek the Episcopate, we leave the warning of Augustine to be piously weighed, which is found in Epistle CXLVIII. Above all, I ask that your religious prudence consider that there is nothing in this life, and especially at this time, easier, and broader, and more acceptable to men than the office of Bishop, or Presbyter, or Deacon, if the matter is handled perfunctorily and flatteringly, but nothing more miserable and damnable before God; likewise, that there is nothing in this life, and especially at this time, more difficult, more laborious, more dangerous than the office of Bishop, Presbyter, or Deacon, but before God nothing more blessed, if one serves in the way that our Commander orders.

Latin:

SECTIO II. PARTIS I. EPISTOLÆ DE PERSONIS ECCLESIA- STICIS. CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Ut Episcopalis muneris desiderium laudabile docet esse Apostolus: Ita Episcoporum requi- sita tum in genere, tum in specie quoad vir- tutes & testimonium ab exteris sistit, si- mulque Diaconorum, & uxorum ipsorum προσκείμενα exhibet: Ut nempe sciat Timo- theus, quomodo versandum in Ecclesia ceu domo Dei, ut in qua custoditur veritas my- steriorum divinorum & imprimis ma- gni pietatis de incarnatione Dei myste- rii.

Partes duæ sunt: I. Informatio de Episcopis & Diaconis ac Diaconissis, ad v. 13. II. Finis in- formationis ad Timotheum factæ, qua conversa- tionem in domo Domini, & asservationem veri- tatis mysteriorum fidei ad v. 16.

PARS I. Informatio de Episcopis & Diaconis.

Vers. 1. Πιστὸς ὁ λόγος) Trahit Chrysostomus ad ea, quæ præcesserant: Sed verius est esse præfationem com- mendandæ ei, quæ sequitur, sententiæ: qualis supra illa iis- dem verbis incipiens cap. 1, 15. Verissimum est, inquit, quod jam dicturus sum: Quidam codices hic habent ἀν- θρώπινος λόγος. At sic etiam in quibusdam codicibus fuisse loco superiore cap. 1,15. notavit Hieronymus. Nimi- rum natus hic error ex scribendi compendiis non dissimili- bus πς & ᾱς.

Εἴ τις ἐπισκοπῆς ὀρέγεται, καλῦ ἔργυ ἐπιθυμεῖ) Ἐπισκο- πὴ פקדה inspectionem qualemcunque significat, ut Num. 4, 16. Psal. 109, 8. Ecclesiæ inspectores sive præ- fecti sunt presbyteri Actorum 20, 28. qui in Synagoga זקנים vel קשישין item פרנסין. Horum princeps postea κατ' ἐξοχὴν dici cœpit ὁ ἐπίσκοπος, ut in canoni- bus, qui Apostolici dicuntur, & in literis, quæ dicun- tur Ignatii, & in Tertulliano aliisque. Hic est in Apo- calypsi ὁ Ἄγγελος, Paulo alibi ὁ προεςὼς ἐν λόγῳ κοπιῶν, Justino similiter ὁ προεςώς. Pari modo in Synagoga qui princeps erat, dicebatur ὁ ἀρχισυνάγωγος, aut ἄρχων τῆς συναγωγῆς, ὁ πρόεδρος Philoni Ebræum ראש הקהל Syriace ריש כנושתא, ut diximus ad Matth. 9, 18. Sed hic ut diximus ἐπισκοπὴ honor presbyteri קשישותא hic Syr. Tam ὀρέγεται quam ἐπιθυμεῖ hic valet אהב optat, quærit. Neque id tunc ambitionis erat, sed maxi- mæ fortitudinis, eo quod Presbyteri munus non tantum cum gravissimis laboribus, sed & cum summis periculis es- set conjunctum, ideo quod hi maxime, ut aliorum Magi- stri, ad pœnas raperentur. Ἔργον מעשה hoc loco est ipsa functio, ipsum ministerium, ut infra 2. Tim. 4, 5. Pulchra sane & honorifica est hæc functio. Et propterea requiruntur ad eam non tantum communes omnibus vere Christianis virtutes, sed & quædam excellentiora: quanto ipsi Presbyteri supra plebem eminent.

Postquam de officiis sacris egit Apostolus, jam de personis Ecclesiasticis, tum qui muneri sacro praficiendi adhuc sunt cap. 3. tum qui jam præ- fecti, cap. 4. agit. Inter illas primo loco Epi- scopos adducit, quod officium desiderare non es- se illicitum breviter docet: Sed qualis esse de- beat Episcopus prolixius exponit. Episcopi autem nomen etsi generaliter adhibeatur de qui- busvis inspectoribus exercitus, Numer. 31, 14. populi, 1. Maccab. 1, 53. civitatis, Jud. 9, 28. oc- currit de Ecclesiæ inspectoribus, tum de sum- mo Sacerdote Num. 4, 16. tum de Sacerdotibus aliis, 2. Reg. 11, 18. de inspectoribus Levitarum Nehem. 11, 22. etiam de Levitis, 2. Paral. 32, 12. In libris Novi Testamenti de Presbyteris id usur- pari, sicque Presbyterorum Principi hoc nomen jam Apostolico tempore tributum esse, agno- scit Grotius. Cui suffragatur jus Canonicum C. Cleros dist. 21. C. nullus, dist. 60. C. Legimus, dist. 93. &c. Secus atque Bellarminus contendit l. de cleric. cap. 14. Jure divino majorem esse Episco- pum Presbytero, tum ordinis potestate, tum etiam jurisdictione. Canones Apostolici non capiunt ætatem Apostolicam, nec Apostolicæ autoritatis sunt, vel ipsis Papistis arbitris. Igna- tium varium hic esse Bellarminus ipse observat l. de cleric. cap. 15. resp. ad XI. object. Aliquan- do dicit Episcopum tenere locum Dei, Presbyteros locum Christi, Diaconum locum Apostolorum, utpote in Epist. ad Trall. aliquando Episcopis dat lo- cum Christi, Presbyteris locum Apostolorum, Diaconis locum LXX. discipulorum, utpote in Epist. ad Smyrnenses. Quomodo ergo jure di- vino superior est Episcopus Presbyteris, ubi tam incerta est eorum autoritas? Non potesta- te, sed executione potestatis distingui Presbyteros ab Episcopis, idque solo jure Ecclesiastico ait Nic. Cusanus Cardinal. lib. II. de Concord. Ca- thol. cap. 13. De desiderio Episcopatus placet Gregorii M. sententia libr. VI. in 1. Reg. 1. Re- ctus est ordo, ut homines quærantur ad Episcopa- tum, non ut quærant homines Episcopatum. In- telligendum autem est τὸ quærere ambitionis. Nam modesta oblationis ad subeundum onus pres- byterii, non illicitum est. Bonum enim opus quærere, quomodo simpliciter illicitum censen- dum? Illis, qui promovendi sunt, & quærunt Episcopatum, Augustini monitum pie expen- dendum relinquimus, quod habetur Epist. CXLVIII. Ante omnia peto, ut cogitet religiosa prudentia sua, nihil esse in hac vita, & maxi- me hoc tempore, facilius, & latius, & homini- bus acceptabilius Episcopi, aut Presbyteri, aut Diaconi officio, si perfunctorie atque adulatorie res agatur, sed nihil apud Deum miserabilius & damnabilius, item nihil esse in hac vita, & ma- xime hoc tempore, difficilius, laboriosius, pericu- losius Episcopi, Presbyteri aut Diaconi officio, sed apud Deum nihil beatius, si eo modo militetur, quo noster Imperator jubet.

## 3:2
Verse 2. 'It is necessary, therefore, for the Bishop to be blameless.' He is to be taken from those who have never fallen after baptism. Thus is mystically fulfilled the law of Lev. 21:17, by which one is forbidden to perform the priesthood: 'If there is a blemish in him.' Hence the writer of the first book of Maccabees, ch. 4:41, calls them 'blameless priests.' Philo, in his work On Monarchy, says these things about that matter: 'These are the laws of the sacred rites: it is commanded that the priest be perfect and whole, having no defect in his body, neither lacking any part through deficiency or mutilation, nor having any excess from birth, or one that has grown on later from disease, nor having his skin changed into leprosy, or whiteness, or wild sores, or warts, or any other eruptions that have broken out, all of which seem to me to be symbols of perfection regarding the soul.' Cicero on the Senate: 'That order is free from vice.'

In general, the Apostle first requires that a Bishop or Presbyter be blameless: which does not mean never having fallen after baptism. For thus no one would easily be admitted to the pastorate or the presbyterate. For in many things we all stumble, James 3:2. 'Επιλαμβάνεσθαι means to rebuke. 'Ανεπίληπτος, according to Thucydides, is one who is not liable to rebuke because of some crime committed. 'Επίληπτοι are called those who suffer from the falling sickness, by which they are seized in such a way that they can move no limb: whence this appellation is not to be snatched at to apply to all who have fallen after baptism. The same are called by Paul 'unreprovable' (ἀνέγκλητοι), Tit. 1:16, against whom no crime can be justly brought. Τὰ ἐγκεκλημένα are those things which are publicly brought forward in trials as crimes and reproaches; they explain this regarding more serious crimes, and those not hidden but public: because according to Rabanus to Heribaldus, it is a scandal to the people of GOD to have such persons placed over them, who are known to be vicious beyond measure. The Apostle does not say, says Augustine in Tractate XLI on John, if anyone is without sin. For if he said this, every man would be rejected, and no one would be ordained, but he says, is without crime, such as homicide, adultery, or any uncleanness of fornication, theft, fraud, sacrilege, and other things of this kind. For a crime is a grave sin worthy of accusation and condemnation. Bellarmine also acknowledges in Book I de Clericis, chapter 24, that by this name a grave crime and lethal sin is excluded, praising the interpretation of Augustine in the cited place, and in Book I against the two epistles of the Pelagians, chapter XIV. Therefore Gregory the Great, in Gerhard page 295, says: These, who are still subject to the war of vices, ought by no means to preside over the teaching of others through the exercise of preaching. And they also except penance, which Jerome proves by the example of David in chapter 3 of Micah, who even after the most grave crimes of adultery and homicide, having performed penance in Psalm 51, professes: I will teach the wicked thy ways. And Gregory the Great, by the example of Peter in Book VII, Epistle LIII (whose words are repeated in Canon Law, dist. 50): What is found to be more grave, or to deny the Son of God with an oath, in which we know Peter himself to have fallen: But after the denial, penance followed, and after penance, mercy was given, because he did not expel from the Apostleship him whom he had previously predicted would deny him. In which things, indeed, especially of the circumstances, both in admitting to sacred office and in tolerating or restoring, account must be taken, and what is not permitted according to strict justice is sometimes prudently dispensed according to equity: just as God himself dispensed in the case of Aaron after the worship of the calf, of Jonah after his most grave disobedience, and in others.

The husband of one wife) Thus below, concerning her who was being enrolled into the order of senior women, it is commanded that she be the wife of one husband, having experienced one husband. So here in a presbyter it is required that he has experienced only one woman. In the Constitutions of Clement: 'Such must the bishop be, the husband of one wife, having been a monogamist.' Clement of Alexandria, Stromata IV: 'And if the Apostle, on account of incontinence and burning, grants a second marriage by way of indulgence, since he does not sin according to the covenant, for he is not forbidden by the law, yet he does not fulfill the perfection of the life according to the Gospel in its intensity. But he secures for himself a heavenly glory by remaining with himself, and keeping the union dissolved by death undefiled, and obeying the economy becomingly, according to which he has become undistracted from the ministry of the Lord.' Add other things which are said in Luke 2:36. Plutarch in his Roman Questions: 'The first marriage is to be envied, but the second is to be avoided.' Among all nations, second marriages are less honored: in some places they are even restrained by certain penalties: See the title of the Code 'concerning second marriages.' See Servius on that line of Virgil: 'Perhaps I could have succumbed to this one fault.' See Chrysostom in his sermon on Virginity c. 37, and in his other book to the Widow, and Jerome to Furia. Nor indeed ought Christians to have yielded in that part of praise to the Gentiles, among many of whom none were admitted to female priesthoods unless they were women of one husband, as Tertullian teaches us in his work 'On Monogamy,' and in his first book 'To His Wife,' and in his 'Exhortation to Chastity': and Jerome to Gerontius: Nor would presbyters have honestly despised in themselves that rule which they observed in choosing women. Hence it came about that those who were being chosen into the priestly order were required to be of one marriage: and if any became digamists, they were cast down from their position, as Tertullian testifies in that 'Exhortation to Chastity': and, looking back to this very passage, in his first book 'To His Wife': 'How much second marriages detract from faith, how much they clamor against holiness, the discipline of the Church and the prescription of the Apostle declares, when it does not allow digamists to preside, when it does not grant that a widow be enrolled into the order unless she has been a woman of one husband.' The same author in that book 'On Monogamy' says that those who are in the clergy are bound by the Apostle to the yoke of monogamy. In the Apostolic Canons, which seem to have been collected at the end of the second century, we have this Canon: 'He who has been entangled in two marriages after baptism, or has acquired a concubine, cannot be a bishop, or a presbyter, or a deacon, or at all of the priestly list.' Where that addition 'after baptism' is from the custom of certain Churches, which did not want marriages contracted before baptism to come into the reckoning. And so Jerome also teaches us that such men, who had become widowers before baptism and had contracted marriages afterwards, were sometimes admitted to the clergy. In the following Canon, he who has taken a widow is excluded from the clergy, because, of course, it is the same thing to do something or to give cause to another to do it. And so he who has made a woman a digamist is equated to digamists. See Basil's Canon X to Amphilochius, and Justinian's Novella 23 and 37. However, these words do not require that a presbyter have a wife, or have had one, but it permits it, provided he has not had more than one.

As regards the special requirements of a Bishop: (1) Let him be the husband of one wife: Which is not to be understood positively, as if he must necessarily be chosen having a wife, but negatively, so that he who is set over or who presides over the Church may not have more wives than one: so that in this way digamists or polygamists are excluded; which is the first thing 'laid down' (proskeimenon), so that he may be 'without reproach' (anepileptos). In this way the Blessed Luther explains it in his propositions on digamy, taking the words of the Apostle not positively, but negatively, so that the Bishop is not bound to have one, but is bound not to have more women than his wife. Vigilantius indeed, with some others, as Jerome testifies, taught that no one should be promoted to the episcopate who was released from marriage as a widower, nor were persons to be ordained unless they had first taken wives. But our people never made that opinion their own. The Papists, in order to defend the celibacy which the Roman Pontiff prescribed for the Clergy, as a mark of the Anti-Christ (concerning which see chapter IV, v. 1), or with Ambrose in his book 'On the Dignity of the Priesthood' chapter IV, explain these things concerning the spiritual marriage of the Bishop with the Church, just as Pope Calixtus (Tom. I, Conc. 7, Epist. II) interprets 'wife' as the Church, so that it is understood that the Bishop is prohibited from ruling more than one Church. But this gloss is inept, since the discussion here is about such a wife from whom the Bishop and Presbyter receives children, and for that reason it is prescribed to him how they are to be governed: or they want it to be required, which Grotius strives to defend here with the Papists, that he has experienced only one woman, just as Bellarmine contends is required by the Apostle, that Bishops do not have or have not had, namely before ordination, more wives than one. But that interpretation is forced. For first, the Apostle does not speak in the past tense, admitting to the presbyterate only him who has NOT HAD more than one wife. But he requires that the Bishop be nothing but the husband of one wife. Since it is in the present tense, therefore, the discussion is about the Bishop as he ought to be, not about the past, as he was. Which, furthermore, is most manifest from the other requirements: for who would say that those are to be taken in the past tense? That a Bishop ought to have been previously vigilant, sober, well-ordered, hospitable, not a drunkard, not a striker, not greedy for filthy lucre; but not in the present, that he ought to be such, since he is now established in the episcopate? Indeed, the requirements of him who is to be chosen and set over the presbyterate are designated, but not in an exclusive sense, as if it were only a matter of the requirements of one to be chosen, and not of the requirements of one established in office. For such he ought to be, no less when he presides than when he is first appointed to the Episcopate. He must be appointed ἀνεπίληπτος; he must also remain in the Episcopate ἀνεπίληπτος. Thus, a man of many wives is not to be appointed, nor should he be a man of many in the Episcopate. Thirdly, for τὸ esse ἀνεπίληπτον it is required specifically to be μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα. Nor should he be a man of more than one wife. Which is certainly not to be understood only as that he has not had more than one, but that he does not have more than one, and thus if he has more, it is implied that he would not be ἀνεπίληπτος. Therefore, fourthly, simultaneous polygamy is excluded here, not successive. For the latter can well consist with τῷ esse ἀνεπίληπτον. Nor does the Apostle say δεῖ εἶναι μονόγαμον, but μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα; he requires the singularity not of marriages, but of a wife. Nor is there any reason for the objection of Bellarmine and Cornelius à Lapide that 'irreproachable' is to be understood not only as lacking crime, but also those things which have the mark of incontinence and the suspicion of a propensity toward lust. For ἀνεπίληπτος is not said for that reason, so that every species of vice, infirmity, and imperfection is excluded, as Cornelius wishes, or so that not even a suspicion of incontinence remains, which Bellarmine contends, since a remedy for lust is provided if anyone does not contain himself, namely marriage, 1 Cor. ch. VII, v. 2, 9. Continence is either abstinence from any intercourse, or from illicit intercourse. A command for the former continence is given to no one; therefore sin has no place here. The latter is indeed required of all, but it can well consist with matrimony. Nor is a transition to second vows immediately a certain sign of vicious incontinence, since other causes for the same may also exist: Nor is the gift of continence for all, or at least for all Presbyters: For not all receive this word

Matt. ch. XIX. Second marriages, as they are by no means a vice, except according to the Cataphrygians, so they can vitiate no state, and not even the priestly one. They accord with divine institution: because it is not good for man to be alone, Gen. II. Nor are they prohibited to priests anywhere, but rather approved by God, 1 Cor. VII. 39, 1 Tim. V. 14, and enjoined by Paul upon all who are not endowed with the gift of continence, 1 Cor. VII. 9, and v. 2, because of fornication let every man have his own wife. I pass over the fact that the Apostle himself seems to number himself among the widowers, 1 Cor. VII. 8, whom Ignatius in his Epistle to the Philadelphians and Clement of Alexandria in Stromata book III assert to have been a widower. And yet he did not doubt that he had the power to lead about a wife, as Cephas and the rest of the Apostles, 1 Cor. IX. 15. How then could successive digamy have been held as a crime or an illicit thing? Fifthly, it is permitted here to a Bishop to be the husband of one wife, whether he is to be appointed or has been appointed to the Episcopate; therefore those who live in marriage cannot be excluded, nor those who have successively had several wives. For he who takes another after the death of his spouse is just as much a man of one wife as he who is still joined to his former marriage. For he ceased to be the husband of the dead spouse, the law of marriage having been dissolved by death, Rom. VII. 2. 3. Sixthly, Theodoret gives the reason for this permission and precept from his own opinion and that of others: 'But that "husband of one wife," some seem to me to have said correctly. For formerly both Greeks and Jews were accustomed to be joined by the law of marriage with two and three and even more wives at the same time. Nay, even now, although Imperial laws prohibit taking two wives at once, they have dealings with concubines and harlots.' They said, therefore, that the divine Apostle meant that he who cohabits chastely with one wife alone is worthy to be ordained Bishop. For he did not reject marriage, they say, who often ordered it to be done. For the woman, he says, is bound by the law as long as her husband lives. But if the husband has died, she is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. And again: I say to the unmarried and widows, and to both orders joined together, he established one law. For in truth, if a vow of continence has been made, a second marriage is not in the power of the will. For if he himself, having put away his former wife, had been joined to another, he would be worthy of being reproved and would rightly be liable to accusation. But if the force of death has separated the former, and urgent nature has compelled him to be joined to a second wife, the second marriage proceeded not from will, but from circumstance. Considering these things, I admit the interpretation of those who understood it thus. Justin in his Dialogue with Trypho says: 'Your Rabbis, to this very day, permit each of you to have four and five wives.' Scaliger in his notes on the New Testament has this to say about this heresy: 'The Jews at that time, as we learn from Josephus, either took several wives or took concubines in addition to one, as the Jews living today under the Turkish Empire do.' But if I should try to prove that the Pagans took concubines in addition to a wife, I would be wasting my time. Paul, therefore, rejects from ecclesiastical office a man who either had two wives, like the Jewish Neophytes, or who had a wife and a concubine while professing Christ from paganism. Baronius also concedes, ad ann. 58, that polygamy was still customary among the Jews in the time of Christ. Therefore, marriage is not prohibited here to Presbyters, but permitted; only polygamy properly so called, or simultaneous, is excluded, not successive, which is improperly called so, as the ancients teach us. Theodoret here, as we have seen, is entirely on our side, who also appeals to the consensus of others, nor did Cornelius à Lapide take his consensus away from us; but he contends that the common exposition of other Fathers is his own: that polygamy is excluded here. Another thing is clear from Theodoret, who praised the interpretation of others, certainly not of heretics, but of Catholics. Another thing from Chrysostom also, who is of one mind with us, not with the Papists. The Apostle does not say this as if establishing it, as if it were not lawful to become a Bishop without a wife, but establishing the manner of that matter. For it was lawful for the Jews even to be joined in a second marriage, and to have two wives at the same time. For marriage is honorable. And also from Theophylact: 'Some,' he says, 'assert that he enjoined the Bishop to be away from a woman: which if it cannot be done, he commanded him to have one, just as if he had none, that is, that nothing is attached to him on account of venereal pleasures, since he thinks otherwise, nor does he deem it necessary that a Bishop be coupled to a wife. For how would he have enjoined this, who says: "I wish all to be as I am"? But because that time required such a thing, therefore if a Bishop takes a wife, he says, let him be the husband of one, not of many.' Add also from Jerome: whose suffrage and that of others Claud. Espensæus generously grants us in this place, fol. 86. Lest you think this is a Greek invention, Jerome also argues thus, but according to the common proverb, seeking a bad wedge for a bad knot. 'The Apostle,' he says in his Epistle to Oecumenius, 'was from the Jews.' The first Church of Christ was gathered from the remnants of Israel. He knew it was granted by law, and familiar to the people by the example of the Patriarchs and Moses to scatter children among many wives; the license for which was also open to the priests by their own discretion. He commanded, therefore, that the priests of the Church should not claim the same license for themselves, that they should not take two or three marriages at once, and that they should have single wives at one time. He also subjoins the letter of the author on the seven grades of the Church, which circulates under the name of Jerome; nor is it argued as spurious by Bellarmine in his Ecclesiastical History, the opinion: 'Let the Bishop observe everything, if he is the husband of one woman, that is, content only with his own, let him not seek the allurements of another's body.' From the more recent ones, many are brought forward by Estius, not denying that Bishops and Deacons were then married, at verse 12 of this chapter. Therefore it is more probable, as concerning the wives of the aforementioned, viz. Of Bishops and Deacons, let this part be accepted: for since it admits them as married, it thought it necessary to give instructions also concerning their wives, what sort they ought to be; just as it also gave instructions concerning their children, saying: having children subject with all chastity. For just as he is to be kept from the episcopate who has a bad reputation on account of his children; so also he who has one on account of his wife, if she be either unchaste, or a slanderer, or given to wine, or not of proven faith. Thus do Peter Lombard, St. Thomas, Cajetan, and other moderns explain it after the interlinear gloss. Whence it is not to be entirely disapproved that Erasmus translates not 'women' but 'wives'; since the Greek word γυναῖκες is ambiguous for both, but he would have more correctly translated 'women', which is likewise ambiguous. Cajetan, Guillaud, Salmero, Justinianus, Hesebius, Saa, Cornelius à Lapide, and others admit that the wives of Bishops and Deacons are being dealt with there. What of the fact that Pope Leo the Great himself, in Epistle 95, supports us here: The Apostle saying, that among other rules of election, that man be ordained Bishop, whom he established to have been or to be the husband of one wife. So severe has this precept always been held, that even concerning the woman The same condition should be understood to be observed for choosing a priest. But what Soto says with Cornelius a Lapide, that bishops and deacons abstained from the use of wives, Salmero says is only probable, but it is in no way probable, since it is clearly contrary to the Apostolic sanction, 1 Cor. VII. 5: 'Do not defraud one another, except by consent for a time.' And from where, asks Claud. Espensæus, l. 1 de continent. c. 8, does this certainty come, that the Apostles rejected their wives from the marriage bed?

The things which Grotius brings forward to the contrary for the exposition of the Papists are easily disposed of. First, he compares the passage 1 Tim. V. 9, because she who was read among the orders of elder women is commanded to be γεγονυῖα ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς γυνὴ, having experienced one husband; but there, since the discourse is about a widow, what she was, or what she ought to have been, is explained: here, however, what kind of person a bishop is, and ought to be in the present, even after ordination, is taught. Nor, however, is it required there of a widow that she should not have had several husbands successively, but that she should not have had several at the same time; indeed, it was not unusual among the Romans and others for women to be involved with several husbands. See Seneca de benef. c. 9; Caelius in Cicero, lib. IIX, Ep. fam. 7; Juvenal, l. II, Satyr. 6. Nor does it happen in only one way that a woman is the wife of only one man: namely, if she has two husbands at the same time. There are also other ways. Namely, if she departs from her husband, whether willing or unwilling, and marries another; if, having been repudiated by her husband outside the case of adultery, she contracts with another while the former is still alive. If, while the marriage stands, she cohabits with another. He brings forward the 2 Constitutions of Clement. But what will he gain by these, when Athanasius in the Synopsis Script. and Bellarmine himself in his book de Script. Eccles. p. 59, reckons them among the spurious and reprobate, and wishes the same judgment to be held of them as of the books of Recognitions, which he, in lib. II de R. P. c. 2, § Adde huc, reckons among the Apocrypha, and professes of them that they have almost no name in the Latin Church, and the later Greeks themselves in the Trullan Council, C. 2, disapprove of their constitutions as corrupted by heretics, and when in these Constit. l. III, c. 2, it is said that trigamy is an argument of incontinence, that which is above trigamy is manifest fornication. Bellarmine, on the contrary, l. 1 de matrim. c. 9, testifies: that Catholics teach that third and fourth marriages, and others thereafter, are lawful and true marriages. What of the fact that l. II Constit. c. 2, it is thus decreed: 'Let a bishop be chosen if he has an honest wife, or has had one.' And l. VI c. 17: 'We say that a bishop, and a presbyter, and a deacon ought to be appointed as the husband of one wife, whether their wives are living or have died.'

Thirdly, he appeals to Clem. Alexandr., who, not indeed in book IV, but in III Stromat., although he ascribes this to perfection, if anyone remains by himself, keeping the union which is dissolved by death undefiled, yet he does not consider it a vice, whether in a cleric or in a layman, as they say, to pass to other vows, but rather arguing against Tatian in favor of marriage: 'It is good,' he says in the Heinsius edition, p. 337, 'to remain as I am. But also those who use it with thanksgiving, and he who again does not use it, he also lives with thanksgiving, and with a modest and temperate perception, conveniently to reason.' And to speak in summary, all the Apostles' epistles, which teach moderation and continence, since they contain innumerable precepts about marriage, and the procreation of children, and the administration of a house, never prohibited or abrogated honest and moderate marriage, but keeping the consistency of the Law with the Gospel, they admit both: both him who, giving thanks to God, uses marriage moderately; and him who, as the LORD wills, lives in chastity, just as each one has been called, choosing unoffensively and perfectly. And further, p. 338: 'But what, is it not permitted even to those who please their wife according to God, to give thanks to God? Is it not permitted even to him who has taken a wife, along with marriage, also to be solicitous about those things which are of the Lord?' Indeed, he even explains the present passage similarly with us: 'va; μὴν καὶ τὸν τεκνογονίας.' Moreover, (the Apostle) also admits the husband of one wife, whether he be a Presbyter, or a Deacon, or a Layman, using marriage without reproach; it will be preserved, however, through the procreation of children. And p. 344: 'What do they say to these things, who inveigh against the law, and against marriage, as to why it is only permitted by the law, but not also in the New Testament? What can they say to these laws that have been laid down, who abhor procreation and generation, when he also appoints as a leader of the Church a bishop who rightly presides over his house?' Finally, p. 327: 'Do they also reprove the Apostles? For Peter and Philip procreated children: and Philip even gave his daughters to husbands. And Paul indeed certainly is not afraid in a certain epistle to call his spouse, whom he did not carry about, because there was no need for great ministry for him. He says, therefore, in a certain Epistle: "Do we not have the power to lead about a sister, a woman, as also the rest of the Apostles?"'

Fourthly, he brings forward encomiums of monogamy: some of which were also produced on Luke XI, v. 36: (1) Of the Gentiles: of the Romans, who abstained from second marriages: and of other nations: because among all nations second marriages were less honored, and in some places even restrained by punishments. But here Grotius, playing the Papist, should have come to an agreement with his Catholics, whom Bellarmine just said teach: that a third, fourth, etc., marriage is lawful: indeed, with the Canon Law, C. Aperiant, caus. 31, quæst. 1, from Jerome: 'I do not condemn digamists, indeed not even trigamists, and if it can be said, octogamists: I now proclaim with my voice that it is free, that digamy is not condemned in the Church, indeed not even trigamy, and thus it is lawful to marry a fifth and sixth and beyond, just as it is rightly to marry a second husband.' Grotius's argument, however, must be inverted; and since that disapproval of second marriages, especially among priests, draws its origin from paganism: whence Grotius, along with Bellarmine, derives it, the prohibition of second marriages or successive polygamy is deservedly suspect to Christians: in which not Catholics, but rather heretics, have followed the pagans. There was indeed the ancient error of Montanus, says Bellarmine, book on matrimony, ch. 9, of Tertullian, and of the Novatians, that second marriages are illicit: but Catholics, both by word and deed, teach that second marriages, and indeed even third ones, etc., are licit. Citing the passages Rom. VII, 1 Cor. ch. VII, 1 Tim. V. If therefore those are in themselves pious, legitimate, and not illicit, how will they be illicit for ministers of the word? (2) of Christians, from whom he praises the Canons of the Apostles, the Council of Neocaesarea, Basil the Great, and the Novel of Justinian. Grotius says that the Canons of the Apostles were collected at the end of the second century. But Baronius, at the year 92, no. 16, admits that they were scarcely known in the Church before the end of the seventh century, having been received in the sixth general council, which, however, Baronius himself teaches was rejected by the Roman Church, at the year 156, no. 40, and the year 182, no. 40. Yet all of them (even if they are at variance with one another) support our opinion. For in Canon VI, the marriage of bishops, presbyters, and deacons is approved. The Council of Neocaesarea, as Bellarmine himself acknowledges in book II on councils, ch. 8, response to the 4th, speaks of him who has two wives at the same time, and prohibits presbyters from attending the weddings of such digamists.

The authority of Tertullian is of no account here; for he was infected with the heresy of Montanus, an enemy of marriage, and yet he himself had a wife when he was a Presbyter, and when in book 1 to his wife he had given her a precept, that she should renounce marriage after his departure with as much license as she could, for her own benefit; but in the second book, chapter 1, having turned to second counsels out of respect for human infirmity, he exhorts that if she is not willing to abstain entirely from remarrying, she should at least abstain from a Gentile marriage. Therefore, Pamelius assigned an argument for book II of Tertullian that is entirely contrary to his intent. Moreover, Tertullian was more hostile to second marriages in his book De Monogamia after he passed into the camp of Montanus; therefore, he reproached the Catholics, whom he calls Psychics, because among them digamists are baptized and digamists preside. From which, however, it is clear that in his time Catholic Presbyters were established in office who had taken a second wife after the death of the first. For as Bellarmine holds in book 1 De Clericis, chapter 23, those who had a second wife before Baptism were considered digamists by Tertullian. But Ambrose, Innocent, and Augustine, as the same Cardinal notes, contend that a bigamist, who has had two wives, whether before Baptism or after Baptism, must be entirely excluded.

νηφάλιον) In the Glosses, νηφάλι@ means sober. Thus also below in II and Titus II. 2, it is signified not as one who is without wine, but who is moderate, as appears below in V. 23. Angels are called עירים ἐγρήγοροι, because they are always attentive to their duty.

Although νηφάλι@ is said of the sobriety of both the mind and the body, and thus implies both vigilance and prudence of spirit at the same time—whence Chrysostom explained νηφάλιον as vigilant, one who has care not only for himself but also for others, and Erasmus and Beza translate it as vigilant—it is clear that here it is taken as sobriety of the body, both because the word most frequently denotes sober, and because it is opposed to τῷ μεθύοντι (the drunkard), and the following word σώφρων deals with the sobriety of the mind, and because vigilance pertains to the duty of a minister, which is distinguished from the virtues of a minister. Therefore, Blessed Luther, with the Vulgate, interpreted it as sober.

σώφρονα) Modest; see above II. 15. Not a fanatic, such as the חסידים were.

σώφρων is said by Chrysostom in Homily XX on the Epistle to the Romans, noting ἀπὸ τῶ σώας ἔχειν τὰς φρένας, that he is endowed with a sound mind; therefore it is rightly rendered by the Vulgate as prudent (not, as Beza notes by a slip, sober and prudent). Jerome interpreted it as chaste. Beza as prudent, although in his notes he explains it as one who moderates his affections: just as Blessed Luther rendered it mäßig, because σωφροσύνη is also called moderation by Aristotle, book 6, Ethics, chapter 5. Theophylact explained it as abstinent and moderate.

Κόσμιον) In the Glossary: κόσμι@ means decorous. Understand it as one who does all things κατὰ τὸ πρέπον (according to what is fitting). Plato also uses this word in that sense. The Rabbis call such a one הגון or נאה.

Blessed Luther rightly rendered it sittig (decent), one who is composed and adorned in his manners. The Vulgate says adorned, concerning which in dist. XLI in the beginning: It behooves a Bishop to be adorned, even in external matters of dress and gait. In dress, so that he does not adorn himself with flashy or filthy clothes. Theophylact says adorned, i.e., grave and honest.

φιλόξενον) This was also a duty of Presbyters, to receive at their own homes Christians arriving from elsewhere. Josephus on the Essenes, Jewish War II. 12: "They have no one city, but in every city many dwell; and to those of their sect who come from elsewhere, their possessions are opened just as if they were their own, and they enter into the houses of those whom they have not seen before as if they were most familiar. Therefore, they carry nothing at all when they travel, but they are armed on account of robbers. And in every city, a steward is appointed for the strangers."

For if, says Theophylact, he shows himself upright and hospitable only to his own fellow citizens, he will be following the affection of his kin. It is necessary, therefore, that he show himself liberal even to strangers. Which is certainly a greater indication of brotherly charity. This is required in general of all Christians, 1 Pet. 4:9, but especially of Bishops, since not even a widow is to be received who has not welcomed the poor with hospitality. As it is said in the beginning of dist. 42, he cannot be an exhorter of hospitality who closes his own house to guests. For if a Priest ought first to demand of himself and of his own domestic Church what he later commands the people; if he ought first, by imitating Christ, to do himself what he later teaches the people, it is necessary that he receive the poor with hospitality, so that he may more easily attract his subjects to hospitality by his own example.

Apt to teach) Thus also 2 Tim. 2:24, who is fit for instructing others.

These were the positive moral requirements. This now pertains to doctrine. And it is most necessary and proper for a Bishop, since other things are common. What was said above, says Theophylact, is required even of subjects. But this office of teaching must especially be present in Bishops. Concerning which the blessed Hunnius says: You may find those who are liberally and elegantly learned: but what they know, they know for themselves, destitute of the gift of communicating to others the things they hold. Therefore, this is a singular gift of God, that you may propose what you have conceived in your mind, aptly and clearly in a certain order, having preserved the distinction between Law and Gospel, and having employed that popular method of teaching which lowers itself entirely to the grasp of the uneducated common people, in such a way that meanwhile you nowhere deviate from the path of truth. Nothing, says Jerome, book 1 against Jude ch. 20, does it profit to enjoy the consciousness of virtues, unless one can also instruct the people entrusted to him, so that he may be able to exhort in doctrine and refute those who contradict. It is fitting for a Bishop to be a teacher, it is said in the law, dist. 86, lest the fault of the inferiors be cast back upon him who accepted the office of teaching, which he does not know how to execute, or neglects. All the work of Priests, it is said in § Ignorantia from the 4th Council of Toledo, ch. 24, should consist in preaching and doctrine, and they should edify all as much by the knowledge of the faith as by the discipline of works. How these things suit Papal presbyters, let the Papists see. Most are certainly as fit for teaching as an ass is for the lyre. But in order for someone to be able to teach others, and be a good teacher, it is necessary that he himself first learn. For if the Levites were to be instructed for five years beforehand, which they gather from the collation of Num. 4:47 and 8:24, how much more do they need instruction who wish to turn out to be Teachers of the word; therefore Gregory Nazianzen vehemently inveighs against them in oration 1, for whom the mere will suffices to be Teachers of the Church, whom he teaches to learn the potter's craft in the jar, that is, with danger to the souls which are entrusted to them, to first draw out the things necessary for the administration of the office.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Δεῖ ὖν τὸν Ἐπίσκοπον ἀνεπίληπτον εἶναι) Su- mendus est ex iis, qui post baptismum lapsi nunquam funt. Sic mystice impletur lex Lev. 21, 17. per quam sa- cerdotio fungi quis vetatur: Ἐὰν ᾖ ἐν αὐτῷ μῶμος. Hinc ἱερεῖς ἀμώμυς nominat Scriptor prioris Maccabaici c. 4, 41. Philo περὶ μοναρχίας de ea re hæc dicit: Νόμοι ἱερῶν εἰσιν οἷδε, παντελῆ καὶ ὁλόκληρον εἶναι τὸν ἱερέα προστέτακται, μη- δεμίαν ἐν τῷ σώματι λώβην ἔχοντα, μή τε κατ᾽ ἔνδειαν ἐπιλεί- ποντός που κὰι ἀκρωτηριασθέντος μέρους, μήτε κατὰ πλεονασμὸν ἅ- μα τῇ γενέσει περιττεύσαντος, ἢ ὕστερον ἐκ νόσυ προσφύντος, μήτε τῆς χρόας μεταβαλόντος εἰς λέπραν, ἢ λευχηίαν, ἢ ἀγρίας, ἢ μυρμηκίας, ἤ τινας ἄλλας ἐξανθηκότων ἐκφύσεις, ἃ μοι δοκεῖ πάντα σύμβολα τῆς περὶ ψυχὴν εἶναι τελειότητος. Cicero de Senatu: Is ordo vitio vacat.

In genere primum requirit Apostolus, ut E- piscopus, vel Presbyter sit ἀνεπίληπτος: Quod non est nunquam lapsum esse post baptismum: Sic enim nullus facile admittendus ad pastora- tum vel Presbyterium erit. Nam in multis la- bimur omnes, Jacob. 3, 2. Ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι est re- prehendere. Ἀνεπίληπτος apud Thucydidem, qui reprehensioni obnoxius non est ob crimen ali- quod perpetratum. Ἐπίληπτοι dicuntur, qui mor- bo comitiali laborant, quo ita corripiuntur, ut nullum membrum movere possint: Unde hæc appellatio non rapienda ad omnes, qui post ba- ptismum lapsi. Iidem Paulo ἀνέγκλητοι vocantur, Tit. 1, 16. quibus nullum crimen juste objici pos- sit. Τὰ ἐγκεκλημένα sunt, quæ in judiciis ceu crimina & probra publice objiciuntur, id de gravioribus criminibus, iisque non occultis sed publicis explicant: quia secundum Rabanum ad Heribaldum scandalum est populo DEI, tales personas supra se positas habere, quas ultra mo- dum vitiosas esse constat. Non dicit Apostolus, inquit Augustinus tract. XLI. in Johannem, si quis sine peccato est. Hoc enim si diceret, omnis homo reprobaretur, & nullus ordinaretur, sed ait, sine crimine est, sicuti est homicidium, adul- terium, aut aliqua immunditia fornicationis, fur- tum, fraus, sacrilegium, & cætera hujusmodi. Crimen enim est grave peccatum accusatione & damnatione dignissimum. Agnoscit & Bellarmi- nus libr. I. de Clericis, cap. 24. nomine hoc ex- cludi crimen grave, & peccatum lethale, inter- pretationem Augustini laudans loco citato, & libr. I. contra duas epistolas Pelag. cap. XIV. Ideo Gregorius M. apud Gerhardum pag. 295. Hi, inquit, qui adhuc vitiorum bello subjacent, nequa- quam per prædicationis usum præesse magisterio ca- terorum debent. Et excipiunt præterea pœniten- tiam, quod exemplo Davidis Hieronymus probat in cap. 3. Mich. qui etiam post gravissima crimi- na adulterii & homicidii pœnitentia acta Psal. 51. profitetur: Docebo iniquos vias tuas, Et Gregor. M. exemplo Petri libr. VII. Epist. LIII. (cujus verba in jure Canonico repetita dist. 50.) Quid gravius inveniuntur, aut Dei Filium jurejurando negare, in quo ipsum Petrum lapsum esse cognovimus: Sed post negationem pœnitentia sequuta est, & post pœni- tentiam misericordia data est, quia ab Apostolatu non expulit, qui ante quidem ipsum se negare prædixit. In quibus vero imprimis circumstantiarum cum in admittendis ad officium sacrum, tum in tolerandis aut restituendis habenda est ratio, & quod secun- dum ἀκριβοδικαιόν non licet, quandoque secun- dum ἐπιείκειαν prudenter dispensatur: quemad- modum Deus ipse in Aarone post μοχολατρίαν, Jona post gravissimam inobedientiam, aliisque dispensavit.

μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα) Sic infra de ea, quæ in seniorum fœ- minarum ordinem legebatur, jubetur esse γεγονῦα ἑνὸς ἀν- δρὸς γυνὴ, unum virum experta. Ita hic in presbytero exi- gitur, ut unam tantum fœminam expertus sit. In Constitu- tionibus Clementis τοιῦτοι δὲ δεῖ εἶναι τὸν ἐπίσκοπον, μιᾶς ἄν- δρα γεγενημένον γυναικὸς μονόγαμον. Clemens Alexandri- nus Strom. IV. Καὶ εἴ τινι ὁ ἀπόστολος δι ἀκρασίαν κὰι πύρωσιν, κατὰ συγγνώμην δευτέρῳ μεταδίδωσι γάμῳ, ἐπεὶ οὐχ ἁμαρ- τάνει μὲν κατὰ διαθήκην, ὀὐ γὰρ κεκώλυται πρὸς τῦ νόμῳ. ὀὐ πλη- ροῖ δὲ τῆς κατὰ τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον πολιτείας τὴν κατ’ ἐπίτασιν τε- λειότητα. δόξαν δὲ αὑτῷ οὐράνιον περιποιεῖ μένας ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ, κὰι διαλυθεῖσαν θανάτῳ συζυγίαν ἄχραντον φυλάττων, κὰι τῇ οἰκο- νομίᾳ πειθόμενος ἐυπρεπῶς, καθ’ ἣν ἀπερίσπαστος τῆς τῦ Κυρίυ γέγονε λειτυργίας. Adde alia, quæ dicta Luc. II. 36. Plutarchus quæstionibus Romanis: Ζηλωτὸς ὁ πρῶτος γάμος, ὁ δὲ δέυ- τερος ἀπευκταῖος. Apud omnes gentes nuptiæ secundæ minus honoratæ: alicubi & pœnis nonnullis coërcitæ: Vi- de titulum Codicis de secundis nuptiis. Servium ad illud Virgilii: Huic uni forsan poteram succumbere culpæ. Chrysostomum sermone de Virginitate c. 37. & altero libro ad Viduam, & ad Furiam Hieronymum. Neque vero Chri- stiani in illa laudis parte cedere debebant gentibus, apud quorum multas ad fœminina sacerdotia non admissæ nisi univiræ, ut Tertullianus nos docet de Monogamia, & ad u- xorem priore libro, & exhortatione castitatis: & ad Ge- rontium Hieronymus: Neque honeste presbyteri in seipsis eam sprevissent regulam, quam in eligendis fœminis serva- bant. Hinc factum est, ut unius matrimonii oporteret esse eos, qui allegebantur in ordinem sacerdotalem: & si qui di- gami fierent, loco dejicerentur, ut Tertullianus testatur in illa castitatis exhortatione: &, ad hunc ipsum locum respi- ciens, priore ad uxorem: Quantum detrahant fidei, quan- tum obstrepant sanctitati nuptiæ secundæ, disciplina Ecclesiæ & præscriptio Apostoli declarat, cum digamos non sinit præsidere, cum viduam allegi in ordinem, nisi univirum non concedit. I- dem in illo de monogamia libro, eos qui in clero sunt Monogamiæ jugo ab Apostolo adstrictos ait. In Canoni- bus Apostolicis, qui collecti videntur fine seculi secundi, hunc Canonem habemus: ὁ δυσὶ γάμοις συμπλακεὶς μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα, ἢ πολλακτὴν κτησάμενος, ὐ δύναται εἶναι ἐπίσκο- πος, ἢ πρεσβύτερος, ἢ διάκονος, ἢ ὅλως τῦ καταλόγου τῦ ἱερα-τικῦ. Ubi additum illud μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα ex consuetudi- ne quarundam Ecclesiarum, quæ nuptias ante baptismum admissas nolebant venire in calculum. Itaque tales, qui vi- dui ante baptismum facti, postea nuptias fecerant, interdum ad clerum admissos etiam Hieron. nos docet. In sequente Canone à clero excluditur, ὁ χήραν λαβὼν, quia nimirum pa- ria sunt facere aliquid, aut alteri, ut id faciat, causam dare. Itaque διγάμοις æquatur qui fœminam fecit δίγαμον. Vide Basilii Can. X. ad Amphilochium, & Novellam Justiniani XXIII. & XXXVII. Non autem verba hæc exigunt ut presbyter uxorem habeat, aut habuerit, sed id permittit, dum ne plures una habuerit.

Quod ad specialia Episcopi requisita attinet. (1) Unius uxoris vir sit: Quod non intelligen- dum positivè, quasi necessario eligendus uxo- rem habeat, sed negativè, ne qui præficitur, aut qui præest Ecclesiæ, plures habeat uxores, quam unam: ut ita excludantur digami aut po- lygami; quod primum est προσκείμενον, ut sit ἀνεπίληπτος. Quo pacto explicat B. Lutherus in proposit. de digam. accipiendo verba Apostoli non positive, sed negative, ita ut non teneatur Epi- scopus habere unam, sed teneatur non habere plures fœminas cum uxore. Vigilantius quidem cum aliis nonullis Episcopis, Hieronymo teste, ita do- cuit, neminem ad Episcopatum promovendum esse, qui solutus conjugio viduus, nec ordinandas personas, nisi prius uxores duxerint. Sed illam sententiam nostrates nunquam fecerunt suam. Papistæ, quo cœlibatum, quem Pontifex Roma- nus Clericis præscripsit, ut Anti-Christi notam, de qua ad cap. IV. v. 1. impleret, sacerdotum tue- antur, aut cum Ambrosio libr. de dignitat. Sa- cerdot. cap. IV. hæc exponunt de spirituali con- jugio Episcopi cum Ecclesia, quomodo Papa Ca- lixtus Tom. I. Conc. 7. Epist. II. uxorem inter- pretatur de Ecclesia, ut Episcopo prohibitum in- telligatur, ne plures quam unam regat Eccle- siam. Quæ vero glossa inepta est, cum de tali uxore hic sermo sit, ex qua liberos suscipit Epi- scopus & Presbyter, eique ideo præscribatur, quomodo illi gubernandi sint: aut id exigi vo- lunt, quod hic cum Papistis defendere satagit Grotius, ut unam tantum fœminam expertus fue- rit, quemadmodum Bellarminus ab Apostolo requiri contendit, ut Episcopi non habeant aut habuerint, scil. ante ordinationem, plures uxo- res, quam unam. Sed ea interpretatio violenta est. Nam primo non loquitur Apostolus in præterito, admittens eum solum ad presbyterium, qui plures una non HABUERIT uxores. Sed requirit ut Episcopus non sit nisi unius uxo- ris vir. De præsenti ergo cum sit, aut est Episcopus, qualis esse debeat, non de præteri- to, qualis fuerit, sermo est. Quod porro ex aliis requisitis manifestissimum est: quis enim illa in præterito accipienda diceret? quod Episcopus an- tea debuerit esse vigilans, sobrius, benè composi- tus, hospitalis,non vinosus, non percussor,non tur- pis lucri cupidus; non autem in præsenti, quod talis esse debeat, cum in Episcopatu jam constitu- tus est? Nimirum designantur quidem requisita ejus, qui eligendus est, & præficiendus presbyte- rio, non autem sensu exclusivo, quasi tantum de requisitis eligendi, non de requisitis in officio con- stituti agatur. Nam talis esse debet, non minus cum præest, quam cum præficitur primum Epi- scopatui. Præficiendus est ἀνεπίληπτος; ma- nere etiam debet in Episcopatu ἀνεπίληπτος. Sic non præficiendus plurium uxorum vir, nec in Episcopatu plurium vir esse debet. Tertio ad τὸ esse ἀνεπίληπτον requiritur speciatim esse μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα. Nec plurium, quam unius uxoris vir sit. Quod utique non ita tantum, quod plures una non habuerit, intelligendum, sed quod nec plures una habeat, itaque si habeat plures, non fore ἀνεπίληπτον, innuitur. Pro- inde quarto polygamia simultanea hic excluditur, non successiva. Hæc enim probe consistere po- test cum τῷ esse ἀνεπίληπτον. Nec Apostolus dicit δεῖ εἶναι μονόγαμον, sed μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄν- δρα, non nuptiarum, sed uxoris singularitatem exigit. Nec est, quod excipiunt Bellarminus & Cornelius à Lapide irreprehensibilem intelligi non tantum carentem crimine, sed etiam iis, quæ signum habent incontinentiæ, & suspicionem pro- pensionis in libidinem. Nam ἀνεπίληπτος non ea ratione dicitur, ut omnis etiam vitii, infir- mitatis & imperfectionis species excludatur, ut Cornelius vult, aut ut nec suspicio incontinentiæ subsit, quod contendit Bellarminus, quum reme- dium paratum sit libidinis, si quis se non con- tineat, nimirum conjugium 1. Cor. cap. VII. v. 2. 9. Continentia vel est abstinentia à quovis congres- su, vel ab illicito congressu. Prioris continen- tiæ mandatum nulli datum; ideo hîc locum non habet peccatum. Posterioris quidem re- quiritur ab omnibus, sed ea cum matrimo- nio probe consistere potest. Neque transitus ad secunda vota statim certum est incontinentiæ vitiosæ signum, cum aliæ etiam possint e- jusdem causæ: Nec donum continentiæ sit omnium, aut Presbyterorum saltem o- mnium: Non enim omnes capiunt verbum hoc

Matth. c. XIX. Nuptiæ secundæ uti vitium minimè sunt, nisi secundum Cataphrygas, ita nullum sta- tum, ac ne Sacerdotalem quidem vitiare possunt. Conveniunt divinæ institutioni: quia bonum non est hominem esse solum Gen. II. Neque uspiam Sa- cerdotibus prohibitæ sunt, imo approbatæ à Deo 1. Cor. VII. 39. 1. Tim. V. 14. à Paulo injunctæ omni- bus, qui dono continentiæ instructi non sunt. 1. Cor. VII. 9. & v. 2. propter fornicationem unus- quisque habeat uxorem suam. Taceo, quod Apo- stolus ipse videatur sese inter viduos numerare 1. Cor. VII. 8. quem viduum fuisse Ignatius Epist. ad Philad. & Clemens Alexandrinus l. III. Strom. as- serunt. Nec tamen dubitavit, se potestatem habere circumducendi uxorem, sicut Cephas, & reliqui Apostoli 1. Cor. IX. 15. Quî ergo pro crimine aut re illicita haberi valuisset digamia successiva? Quinto permittitur hic Episcopo, ut maritus sit unius uxoris, sive cum præficiendus, sive cum præ- fectus est Episcopatui; Non ergo excludi possunt isti, qui in conjugio vivunt, nec qui successive plu- res una habuerint conjuges. Nam qui post obi- tum conjugis aliam ducit, æque est unius uxoris vir, ac qui priori adhuc junctus est matrimonio. Mortuæ enim conjugis maritus esse desiit, soluta per mortem lege conjugii. Rom. VII. 2. 3 Sexto cau- sam hujus permissionis ac præcepti reddit Theodo- retus ex sua, & aliorum sententia: Illud autem unius uxoris virum, mihi videntur quidam recte dixisse. Olim enim consueverant & Græci, & Ju- dæi, cum duabus & tribus & pluribus etiam uxori- bus simul jungi lege matrimonii. Quin etiam nunc cum leges Imperatoriæ prohibeant duas simul uxores ducere, rem habent cum concubinis & meretricibus. Dixerunt ergo divinum dixisse Apostolum, qui cum una sola uxore pudice cohabitat, dignum esse qui ordi- netur Episcopus. Neque enim secundum, inquiunt, rejecit matrimonium, qui illud sæpe jussit fieri. Mu- lier enim, inquit, alligata est legi, quamdiu vivit vir ejus. Sin autem vir mortuus fuerit, libera est, ut, cui vult, nubat, tantum in Domino. Et rursus: Dico autem innuptis & viduis, & utroque ordine conjuncto, unam legem constituit. Revera enim si factum fuerit votum continentiæ, non est in volun- tatis potestate secundum matrimonium. Si enim ipse priore expulsa uxore, fuisset alii conjunctus, di- gnus esset, qui reprehenderetur, & jure esset accusa- tioni obnoxius. Sin autem vis mortis priorem dis- junxerit, urgens autem natura ut secundæ uxori con- jungeretur, coëgerit, non ex voluntate, sed ex casu processit secundum matrimonium. Hæc conside- rans, admitto eorum interpretationem, qui sic intel- lexerunt. Justinus in Dial. cum Tryphone: Rab- bini vestri, inquit, ad hunc usque diem quatuor & quinque vestrûm quemque uxores habere permit- tunt. Scaliger in notis ad N. T. de hac αἱρεσει sic habet: Judæi eo tempore, ut ex Josepho discimus, aut plures uxores ducebant, aut uni concubinas superin- ducebant, ut hodie Judæi sub Turcico Imperio viven- tes. Paganos vero concubinas uxori superinduxisse si coner probare, abutar otio meo. Paulus ergo rejicit hominem à munere Ecclesiastico, qui aut duas uxores haberet, ut Judæi Neophyti, aut qui uxorem & con- cubinam ex paganismo Christum profitentes. Con- cedit & Baronius ad ann. 58. Polygamiam adhuc tempore Christi apud Judæos usitatam fuisse. Ideo non prohiberi hîc Presbyteris, sed permitti conjugium, excludi solùm Polygamiam proprie dictam, vel simultaneam, non successivam, quæ improprie ita vocatur, nobiscum veteres do- cent. Theodoretus hic, ut vidimus, ex asse no- ster est, qui ad aliorum etiam consensum pro- vocat, nec ejus consensum nobis devexit Cor- nelius à Lapide; At communem aliorum Pa- trum expositionem suam esse contendit: quod po- lygamia hic excludatur. Aliud è Theodoreto patet, qui aliorum interpretationem laudavit, non certe hæreticorum, sed Catholicorum. A- liud è Chrysostomo etiam, qui nobis, non Pa- pistis ὁμόψηχος. Non hoc veluti sanciens dicit Apostolus, quasi non liceat absque uxore Episco- pum fieri, sed ejus rei modum constituens. Judæis quippe licitum erat etiam secundo matrimonio jungi, & duas κατὰ ταὐτὸ simul habere uxores. Ho- norabiles enim nuptiæ. Nec non è Theophy- lacto: Nonnulli, inquit, asserunt à muliere ab- esse Episcopum injunxisse: Quod fieri si nequeat, habere hunc unicam sic præcepisse, perinde ac si nullam haberet, hoc est, nihil illi addictum esse ob venereas voluptates, cum aliter sentiat, nec ne- cessarium ducat, ut uxori copuletur Episcopus. Quo enim pacto hoc indixisset, qui ita inquit: Volo autem omnes esse atque ego sum? Sed quia illud tempus hujusmodi rem exigebat, propterea si duxerit (inquit) uxorem Episcopus, unius sit, non multarum maritus. Adde & ex Hierony- mo: cujus & aliorum suffragium nobis προθύμως largitur Claud. Espensæus in h. l. f. 86. Ne putes commentum hoc Græcanicum esse, sic quoque dis- serit Hieronymus, sed juxta vulgi, quod ait, proverbium, malo nodo malum quærens cuneum. Ex Judæis, inquit in Epist. ad Oecumen. erat Apostolus. Prima Christi Ecclesia de Israel re- liquis congerebatur. Sciebat lege concessum, & exemplo Patriarcharum ac Mosis familiare po- pulo in multis uxoribus liberos spargere; cujus etiam licentia sacerdotibus patebat arbitrium. Præcepit ergo ne eandem licentiam sibi Ecclesiæ vindicent Sacerdotes, ne bina pariter & trina sortiantur conjugia, & ut singulas uno tempore habeant uxores. Subjungit etiam autoris de se- ptem gradibus Ecclesiæ Epistolam, quæ sub no- mine Hieronymi circumfertur; nec à Bellar- mino inde Histor. Eccles. νοθείας arguitur, sen- tentiam: Observet omnia Episcopus, si unius mulieris vir est, id est, suâ tantum contentus, alieni corporis illecebras non requirat. E re- centioribus plures adducuntur ab Estio, Episco- pos & Diaconos tum uxoratos fuisse non diffitente, ad vers. 12. hujus capitis. Itaque probabilius est, ut de uxoribus prædictorum, scil. Episcoporum & Diaconorum, hac pars accipiatur: cum enim eos uxoratos admittat, putavit etiam de uxoribus præcipiendum, quales esse debeant; quemadmo- dum & de filiis præcepit, dicens: filios habentem subditos cum omni castitate. Nam sicut arcen- dus est ab episcopatu, qui propter filios male au- dit; ita & qui propter uxorem, si vel impudica sit, vel obrectatrix, vel vinosa, vel non probæ fidei. Sic exponunt post glossam interlinearem, Petrus Lombardus, S. Thomas, Cajetanus, aliique neoterici. Unde nec plane improbandum, quod Erasmus non mulieres, sed uxores vertit; cum Græca vox γυναῖκες anceps sit ad utrumque, sed rectius vertisset mulieres, quod similiter est an- ceps. De uxoribus Episcoporum & Diacono- rum illic agi admittunt & Cajetanus, Guillau- dus, Salmero, Justinianus, Hesebius, Saa, Cor- nelius à Lapide & alii. Quid, quod ipse P. R. Leo M. Ep. XCV. nobis hic suffragetur: Dicente Apostolo, ut inter alias electionis regulas is Episcopus ordinetur, quem unius uxoris vi- rum fuisse aut esse, constituit. Tam severa sem- per habita est ista præceptio, ut etiam de muliere Sacerdotis eligendi eadem intelligatur servanda conditio. Quod vero Soto cum Cornelio a Lapide dicit, Episcopos & Diaconos uxorum usu abstinu- iffe, Salmero tantum probabile hoc esse ait, sed nul- lo modo id probabile est, cum plane contrarium sit sanctioni Apostolicæ, 1. Cor. VII. 5. Ne fraudate alter alterum, nisi si quid ex consensu ad tempus. Et unde indubia quærit Claud. Espensæus l. 1. de con- tinent. c. 8. isthæc certitudo, quod Apostoli conju- ges a toro rejecerint.

Quæ in contrarium affert pro Pontificiorum expositione Grotius, facile expediuntur. Primum confert locum 1. Tim. V. 9. quod ea, quæ in senio- rum fœminarum ordinum legebatur, jubeatur esse γεγονυῖα ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς γυνὴ, unum virum experta, sed ibi cum de vidua sermo sit, qualis illa fuerit, aut qualem fuisse oportuerit, exponitur: hic autem qualis Episcopus sit, & esse debeat in præsenti etiam post ordinationem docetur. Nec tamen ibi a vidua requiritur, ut non habuerit successive plu- res maritos, sed ne simul plures habuerit; equidem fœminas pluribus maritis misceri apud Romanos, aliosque non inconsuetum fuerit. Vid. Seneca de be- nef. c. 9. Cœlius apud Ciceronem lib. IIX. Ep. fam. 7. Juvenalis l. II. Satyr. 6. Neque ut mulier unius tan- tum viri uxor sit, uno solum modo fit: nempe si duos simul habeat maritos. Dantur & alii modi. Nempe si discedit a marito vel volente vel nolente, & alii nubit, si a viro repudiata extra casum adulte- rii dimissa cum alio contrahit, illo adhuc super- stite. Si stante matrimonio cum alio consuescit. Adfert 2. Constitutiones Clementis. Sed quid hisce proficiet, quum illas nothis & reprobis accenseat Athanasius in Synopsi Script. ac Bellarminus ipse lib. de Script. Eccles. p. 59. idem velit de illis esse judi- cium, quod de libris recognitionum, quos lib. II. de R. P. c. 2. §. Adde huc. Apocryphis accenset, ac de illis profiteatur, eas in Ecclesia Latina nullum fere nomen habere, ipsosque Græcos posteriores in Concilio Trullano C. 2. improbare suas constitutio- nes ab hæreticis depravatas, ac cum in his constit. l. III. c. 2. dicitur, trigamiam esse argumentum in- continentiæ, id, quod supra trigamiam esse manife- stam scortationem. Bellarminus ex adverso l. 1. de ma- trim. c. 9. testatur: Catholicos docere, tertias & quar- tas nuptias, & alias deinceps esse licitas, & vera matri- monia. Quid, quod l. II. Constit. c. 2. ita sancitum sit: Episcopus eligatur, si uxorem honestam habeat, vel habuerit. Et l. VI. c. 17. Episcopum & Presbyte- rum, & Diaconum dicimus unius uxoris debere con- stitui, sive vivant eorum uxores, sive decesserint.

Tertio provocat ad Clem. Alexandr. qui non li- bro quidem IV. sed III. Stromat. etsi perfectioni hoc adscribat, si quis apud se manserit, eam quæ est ex morte dissoluta, impollutam servat conjunctionem, non tamen sive in Clerico, sive in Laico, ut loquun- tur, pro vitio id habet, ad alia vota transire, sed con- tra Tatianum potius pro conjugio disputans: Bonum est, inquit in edit. Heinsii p. 337. manere sicut ego. Sed & qui utuntur cum gratiarum actione, & qui rursus non utitur ipse quoque cum gratiarum actione, & cum modesta ac temperanti vivat per- ceptione, rationi convenienter. Et ut in summa dicam, omnes Apostoli epistolæ, quæ moderationem docent & continentiam, cum & de matrimonio, & de liberorum procreatione, & de domus admi- nistratione innumerabilia præcepta contineant, nusquam honestum moderatumque matrimonium prohibuerunt aut abrogarunt, sed legis cum Ev- angelio servantes convenientiam, utrumque admit- tunt: & eum, qui Deo agendo gratias, moderate utitur matrimonio: & eum, qui, ut vult DO- MINUS, vivit in castitate, quemadmodum vo- catus est unusquisque inoffense & perfecte eli- gens. Et porro pag. 338. Quid vero annon li- cet etiam eis, qui secundum Deum placent uxori, Deo gratias agere? Annon permittitur etiam ei, qui uxorem duxit, una cum conjugio, etiam esse solicitum de iis, qui sunt Domini? Imo etiam lo- cum præsentem similiter nobiscum explicat: va; μὴν καὶ τὸν τεκνογονίας. Quin & unius quoque uxoris virum admittit (Apostolus), seu sit Presby- ter, seu Diaconus, seu Laicus, utens matrimonio ci- tra reprehensionem; servabitur autem per Filiorum procreationem. Et pag. 344. Quid ad hæc di- cunt, qui in legem invebuntur, & in matrimo- nium, ut quid sit solum à lege concessum, non au- tem etiam in Nov. Test. Quid ad has leges latas possunt dicere, qui fationem abhorrent & generatio- nem, cum Episcopum quoque, qui domui recte præsit, Ecclesiæ ducem constituat? Denique pag. 327. An etiam reprobant Apostolos? Petrus enim & Phi- lippus filios procrearunt: Philippus autem filias quoque suas viris tradidit. Et Paulus quidem certe non veretur in quadam epistola suam appel- lare conjugem, quam non circumferebat, quod non magno ei esset opus ministerio. Dicit itaque in quadam Epistola: Nonne habemus potestatem, soro- rem mulierem circumducendi, ut & reliqui Apo- stoli?

Quarto Encomia adducit monogamias: quorum nonnulla etiam ad Luc. XI. v. 36. producta: (1) Gen- tilium: Romanorum, qui abstinuerunt à secun- dis nuptiis: & aliarum gentium: quod apud omnes gentes minus honoratæ secundæ nuptiæ, alicubi & pœnis coërcitæ. Sed hic transigere debuisset Grotius Papizans cum Catholicis suis, quos docere modo dixit Bellarminus: licitum esse tertium, quartum &c. matrimonium: imo cum Jure Canonico C. Aperiant. caus. 31. quæst. 1. Ex Hieronymo: Non damno digamos, imo nec trigamos, & si dici potest octogamos: Ego nunc voce proclamo liberum, non damnari in Ecclesia diga- miam, imo nec trigamiam, & ita licere quinto & sexto & ultra, quomodo & secundo marito recte nubere. In- vertendum autem argumentum Grotii; & cum è gentilitio illa reprobatio nuptiarum secunda- rum, imprimis sacerdotum origenem trahat: unde cum Bellarmino eam deducit Grotius, merito inter- dictum secundarum nuptiarum, vel polygamiæ successivæ suspectum esse Christianis: In quo non Catholici, sed hæretici potius gentiles secuti sunt. Fuit quidem antiquus error Montani, inquit Bel- larm. l. de matrim. c. 9. Tertulliani, & Novatiano- rum, secundas nuptias esse illicitas: Catholici vero & verbo & facto docent secundas nuptias, imo etiam & tertias &c. esse licitas. Adferens loca Rom. VI. 1. Cor. c. VII. 1. Tim. V. Si ergo illæ per se piæ, legitimæ, nec illicitæ sunt, quomodo ministris verbi erunt illici- tæ? (2) Christianorum, è quibus Canones Apostolo- rum, Consilium Neo-Cæsariense, Tertullianum, Basi- lium M. & Novellam Justiniani laudat. Canones Apostolorum collectos dicit Grotius fine secundi seculi. Sed Baronius ad ann. 92. n. 16. fatetur vix ante finem seculi septimi innotuisse in Ecclesia rece- ptos in Concilio generali sexto, quod tamen Baro- nius ipse ab Ecclesia Romana reprobatum docet ann. 156. n. 40. ann. 182. n. 40. Illi tamen omnes (etsi à se invicem discordes) nostræ sententiæ pa- trocinantur. Nam Can. VI. Conjugium Episcopo- rum Presbyterorum & Diaconorum approbatum est. Concilium Neo-Cæsariense Bellarmino ipso l. II. de concil. c. 8. resp. ad 4. agnoscente loquitur de eo: qui duas simul uxores habet, & talium di- gamorum nuptiis interesse Presbyteris prohibet.

Tertulliani autoritas hic nulla est; Infectus enim fuit hæresi Montani nuptiarum hostis, & uxorem tamen ipse habuit, cum Presbyter esset, & cum lib. 1. ad uxorem suam præceptum ipsi dedisset, quanta posset cum licentia post excessum suum nuptiis renuntiet sibi ipsi profutura; altero autem libro c. 1. ad secunda consilia respectu humanæ in- firmitatis conversus hortatur, si à repetendis nu- ptiis adeo abstinere non velit, saltim à matrimo- nio gentili ut abstineat. Ideo sine fraude argu- mentum libr. II. Tertulliani prorsus contrarium assignavit Pamelius. Nuptiis autem secundis ini- quior fuit Tertullianus lib. de Monogam. post- quam in Montani castra transiit, ideo Catholicis, quos Physicos vocat, objecit, quod digami apud eos tingant, digami præsideant. E quo vero patet, quod ipsius tempore Catholici Presbyteri in offi- cio constituti fuerint, qui alteram post defunctam priorem uxorem duxerunt. Nam ut Bellarminus habet l. 1. de Cler. c. 23. illi, qui alteram uxorem ha- buerunt ante Baptismum, à Tertulliano digami censebantur. Ambrosius vero, Innocentius, & Augustinus, notante eodem Cardinali, conten- dunt, omnino habendum bigamum, qui duas uxo- res habuit, sive ante Baptismum, sive post Ba- ptismum.

νηφάλιον) In Glossis νηφάλι@ sobrius. Sic & infra II. & Tit. II. 2. significatur, non qui nullius sit vini, sed qui modi- ci, ut apparet infra V. 23. Angeli dicti עירים ἐγρήγοροι, quod semper sint ad officium attenti.

Etsi νηφάλι@ dicatur tum de mentis tum de corporis sobrietate, atque ita vigilantiam atque prudentiam animi simul inferat, unde & Chrysofto- mus νηφάλιον exposuit vigilantem, qui non solum sui, verum etiam reliquorum curam habet, ac Era- smus & Beza vertit vigilantem: hic tamen de corpo- ris sobrietate accipi patet, tum quia frequentissime sobrium vox notat, tum quia τῷ μεθύοντι opponi- tur, ac de sobrietate mentis requisitum sequens σώφρων agit, tum quia vigilantia ad officium mini- stri pertinet, quod à virtutibus ministri distinguitur. Ideo B. Lutherus cum Vulgata Sobrium interpre- tatus est.

σώφρονα) Modestum vide supra II. 15. non fanaticum, quales erant חסידים.

Dicitur σώφρων Chrysostomo hom. XX. in Epist. ad Rom. notante, ἀπὸ τῶ σώας ἔχειν τὰς φρένας, qui sana mente præditus est, ideo recte à Vulgato redditur prudens, (non ut Beza per παρόραμα notat, sobrius & prudens) Hieronymus interpretatus est castum. Beza prudentem, etsi in suis notis explicet suos affectus moderantem: quemadmodum B. Lu- therus reddidit mäßig/ quia σωφροσύνη etiam mo- deratio Aristoteli dicta. l. 6. Eth c. 5. Theophyl. abs- tinentem & moderatum exposuit.

Κόσμιον) In Glossario: κόσμι@ decorus. Intellige eum, qui omnia faciat κατὰ τὸ πρέπον. Utitur & Plato hac voce eo sensu. Rabbini talem dicunt הגון aut נאה.

Rectè B. Lutherus sittig reddidit, qui moribus est compositus & ornatus. Vulgata ornatum, quo de dist. XLI. in princ. Oportet Episcopum esse orna- tum, etiam in exterioribus habitu & incessu. Ha- bitu, ut nec fulgidis, nec fædis vestibus se ornet. Theophylactus ornatum h. e. gravem & honestum.

φιλόξενον) Erat & hoc Presbyterorum, advenientes aliun. de Christianos domi suæ excipere. Josephus de Essenis belli Judaici II. 12. Μιὰ δ' ἐκ ἔστιν αὐτοῖς πόλις, ἀλλὰ ἐν ἑκάστῃ με- τοικοῦσι πολλοὶ, καὶ τοῖς ἑτέρωθεν ἥκουσιν αἱρετισταῖς ἀναπέπταται τὰ παρ' αὐτοῖς ὁμοίως ὥσπερ ἴδια, καὶ πρὸς ὓς ἐ πρότερον εἶδον, εἰσίασιν ὡς συνηθεστάτους διὸ καὶ ποιοῦνται τὰς ἐπιδημίας, ἐδὲν μὲν ὅλως ἐπικομιζόμενοι. διὰ δὲ τὰς λῃστὰς ἔνοπλοι. Κηδεμὼν δὲ ἐν ἑκάστῃ πόλει ἐξαίρετ@ τῶν ξένων ἀποδείκνυται.
