Si enim suis civibus, inquit Theophylactus, se duntaxat probum præstiterit & hospitalem, generis affectionem sequetur. Oportet itaque, ut in alienos etiam liberalem se praebeat. Quod sane majus est fraternae charitatis indicium. Requiritur id in ge- nere ab omnibus Christianis 1. Petr. IV. 9. sed ma- xime ab Episcopis, cum ne vidua quidem accipi- enda, quae pauperes non excepit hospitio. Quo- modo dicitur in princip. dist. XLII. hospitalitatis ex- hortator non poterit esse, qui domum propriam hospi- tibus claudit. Si enim Sacerdos primum à seipso & à domestica sua Ecclesia debet exigere, quod postea populis imperet; si primum imitando Christum ipse debet facere, quae postea populum doceat, necesse est, ut pauperes hospitio recipiat, quo ad hospitalitatem facilius suo exemplo subditos attrahat.

διδακτικὸν) Sic & 2. Tim. II. 24. qui aptus sit aliis insti- tuendis.

Fuere requisita positiva moralia. Hoc ad do- ctrinam jam pertinet. Et vel maxime necessarium, ac proprium est Episcopo, cum alia sint communia. Quae dicta superius sunt, inquit Theophylactus, vel à subditis exiguntur. Hoc autem docendi officium omnium praecipue ut insit Episcopis necesse est. Quo de B. Hunnius: Invenias qui liberaliter & eleganter docti sunt: Verum quod sciunt, sibi sciunt, destituti do- no, ea quae tenent, cum aliis communicandi. Itaque singulare hoc est donum Dei, ut quae animo concepe- ris, apte etiam & perspicue certo quodam ordine, ser- vato discrimine legis & Evangelii, adhibitaque popu- lari illa ratione docendi, quae se totam ad captum ru- dis plebeculae demittat, ratione, ita proponas, ut inte- rim à semita veritatis nullibi deflectas. Nihil, in- quit Hieronymus l. 1. adv. Jud. c. 20. prodest, con- scientiâ virtutum frui, nisi & creditum sibi populum possit instruere, ut valeat exhortari in doctrinâ, & eos, qui contradicunt, redarguere. Doctorem Episco- pum esse decet, dicitur in jure dist. XXCVI. ne infe- riorum culpa in eum refundantur, qui docendi offi- cium accepit, quod exequi nescit, vel negligit. Omne opus Sacerdotum, dicitur §. Ignorantia ex Concil. Toletano IV. c 24. in praedicatione, & doctrinâ con- sistat, atque aedificent cunctos tam fidei scientia, quam operum disciplina. Quæ quomodo Papalibus pres- byteris conveniant, Papistæ viderint. Plerique certe ad docendum tam apti sunt quam asinus ad lyram. Ut autem alios docere quis possit, ac bo- nus sit didacticus, necessum est, ut ipse prius discat. Quod si Levitae per quinquennium prius infor- mandi erant, quod colligunt è collat. Num. IV. 47. & IIX. 24. quanto magis informatione opus ha- bent, qui Doctores verbi evadere volunt, ideo ve- hementer invehitur in eos Greg. Nazianz. orat. 1. quibus sola voluntas sufficit ad id, ut sint Doctores Ec- clesiae, quos figulinam in dolio discere, h. e. cum peri- culo animarum, quae ipsis creditae sunt, primum ne- cessaria ad muneris administrationem haurire, do- cet.

## 3:3
Verse 3. Not given to wine) In the Glossary, given to wine. The same word paroinios in Aristophanes, that is, a drunkard, a violent person, as the Scholiast explains on the Acharnians.

Among the negative requirements is not given to wine, which he explains in verse 8, not addicted to much wine. Compare Titus ch. 3, verse 7. And thus paroinos is called by Athenaeus, book 10, sitting by the wine to drink heavily and to carouse. By that reason, intemperance of the gullet is simultaneously forbidden. Dist. 44, in the beginning. When one is forbidden to be given to wine, intemperance of the gullet is by no means permitted to be held: for drunkenness is not forbidden while gluttony is permitted. Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret paroinos as the violent person: because paroinia is insult, petulance. μὴ πλήκτην) Hesychius explains it as pugnacious. In the Glossary, πλήκτης is a striker, מכה or פריץ.

μὴ αἰσχροκερδῆ) It is missing in the Manuscript, as also in the Syriac and the Latin.

ἀλλ' ἐπιεικῆ) See Phil. IV. 5. Tit. III. 2. Jas. III. 17. 1 Pet. ch. II. 18. Ἐπιεικής in the Glossary is mild, modest. To Aristotle, the ἐπιεικής is described as one who is not strictly just to the worse side, but rather yielding, even though he has the law as an aid. Among the interpreters of the Old Testament, it corresponds to the Hebrew סלח, as in Ps. LXXXVI. 5. God is spoken of in this way, just as ἐπιείκεια is attributed to Him in Baruch II. 21, the Song of the Three Holy Children 13, Wis. XII. 18, 2 Macc. II. 23, X. 4.

It is derived from πλήττειν, to strike, meaning one who is ready to strike: to which is opposed ἀλλὰ ἐπιεικὴς, but equitable, mild, and gentle, who prefers equity even to strict law, who would rather yield from his own right than urge rigor, much less strike. Budé explains ἐπιεικῆ as a clement granter of pardon. Cf. 1 Pet. II. 18. Jerome and Chrysostom refer it to the insults of the tongue. Which explanation can be joined, so that he may strike neither with words nor with blows. B. Luther: Ein Bischoff soll nicht pochen. ἰατρός ἐστιν ὁ διδά- σκαλος τῶν ψυχῶν, says Chrysostom, ὁ δὲ ἰατρὸς ὐ πλήττει, ἀλλὰ τὰ πεπληγότα διορθῶταί τε θεραπεύει. He is the physician, the Teacher of souls. Furthermore, the physician does not strike at all; but rather corrects and heals the sick person who has been struck. What is inserted, μὴ αἰσχροκερδῆ, is not only absent from the Syriac and Latin, but is not found in Chrysostom or Theophylact, nor in Jerome. Ep. 85, nor was it found in Beza's five codices; and it seems to be gathered from the opposite member, and transferred here from Tit. I. v. 7: since this ἀφιλάργυρος follows next, by which αἰσχροκερδίας is also excluded, just as Budé warns that the vice of αἰσχροκερδίας is twin to πλεονεξίᾳ, because the good odor of gain comes from any source whatsoever.

ἄμαχον) This word among the Greeks is sometimes taken passively, to signify one who cannot be fought against, and sometimes actively, to signify one who does not fight, as in Xenophon and in this place. But μάχεσθαι, corresponding to the Hebrew רוב, often also signifies to litigate: so that ἄμαχος is one who abstains from lawsuits and quarrels, ἄμαχος ענו: without strife, says Jerome, where he cites this passage.

ἀφιλάργυρον) You have the same word in Heb. ch. XIII. v. 5. In Hebrew it would be לא בצע, not greedy of gain: גרב.

Ἄμαχοι are those who are far from fights, or are not contentious. B. Luther: nicht haderhafftig. Far from fights and contentions in teaching (2 Tim. II. 23, 24) and in rebuking, whether publicly or privately, out of carnal affections. Ἀφυλάργυροι are those who are not avaricious, not lovers of silver: to this vice of Φιλαργυγίας is opposed αὐτάρκεια (Heb. XIII. 5), since one is easily content with present things. He did not say 'possessing nothing,' says Theodoret; for he establishes what is convenient and suitable for them, but 'not loving money.' For it is possible that we may indeed possess them, but administer and dispense them as is right, and not be slaves to them, but be their masters.

Latin:

Vers. 3. μὴ πάροινον) In Glossario πάροινος vinolentus. Idem παροίνιος Aristophani, id est μέθυσος, ὑβρισὴς, expo- nente Scholiaste ad Acharnenses.

Inter negativa requisita est μὴ πάροινον, quod exponit vers. 8. μὴ οἴνῳ πολλῷ προσέχοντα. Conf. Tit. cap. III. vers. 7. Atque ita πάροινος Athenaeo dicitur l. X. vino assidens ad perpotandum & per- graecandum. Ea ratione simul gula intemperantia probita. Dist. XLIV. in princ. Cum vinolen- tus esse prohibetur, gula intemperantia nequaquam haberi permittitur: neque enim ebrietas prohibetur & voracitas permittitur. Chrysostomus & Theo- phylactus πάροινον interpretantur τὴν ὑβρισὴν : quia παροινία est contumelia, petulantia. μὴ πλήκτην) μαχιμὸν exponit Hesychius. In Glossario πλήκτης percussor מכה aut פריץ

μὴ αἰσχροκερδῆ) Deest in Manuscripto, ut & Syriaco, & Latino.

ἀλλ' ἐπιεικῆ) Vide Phil. IV. 5. Tit. III. 2. Jac. III. 17. 1. Petr. c. II. 18. Ἐπιεικής in Glossario mitis, modestus. Aristoteli ὁ ἐπι- εικὴς describitur, ὁ μὴ ἀκριβοδίκαιος ἐπὶ τὸ χεῖρον, ἀλλ' ἐλαττω- τικός καίπερ ἔχων τὸν νόμον βοηθόν. Apud interpretes Vet. Test. respondet Ebræo סלח ut Ps. LXXXVI. 5. Deus sic dicitur, sicut eidem ἐπιείκεια tribuitur Baruch. II. 21. Can- tico puerorum 13. Sap. XII. 18. 2. Maccab. II. 23. X. 4.

Dicitur à πλήττειν percutere, qui promtus est ad percutiendum: cui opponitur ἀλλὰ ἐπιεικὴς, sed æquus, mitis, & lenis, quæ etiam stricto juri æqui- tatem præferat, qui de jure suo potius cedat, quam rigorem urgeat, nedum percutiat. Budæus ἐπιεικῆ clementem veniæ concessorem exponit. Conf. 1. Petr. II. 18. Hieronymus & Chrysost. ad linguæ con- vitia referunt. Quæ explicatio conjungi poterit, ne vel verbis vel verberibus percutiat. B. Lutherus: Ein Bischoff soll nicht pochen. ἰατρός ἐστιν ὁ διδά- σκαλος τῶν ψυχῶν, inquit Chrysost. ὁ δὲ ἰατρὸς ὐ πλήττει, ἀλλὰ τὰ πεπληγότα διορθῶταί τε θεραπεύει. Medicus est animarum Doctor. Porro. Medicus minime percutit; sed ægram percussum potius emendat & curat. Quod inseritur μὴ αἰσχροκερδῆ non modo abest à Syro ac Latino, sed nec reperitur apud Chry- sost. aut Theophyl. nec apud Hieronym. Ep. 85. nec in Bezæ quinque codicibus inventum fuit; & ex op- posito membro videtur colligi, atque è Tit. I. v. 7. huc traductum: Siquidem sequatur deinde hic ἀφιλάργυρος, quo excluditur etiam αἰσχροκερδίας, quemadmodum Budæus monet αἰσχροκερδίας vi- tium geminum esse τῇ πλεονεξίᾳ, quia lucri bonus odor est ex re qualibet.

ἄμαχον) Vox ista apud Græcos modo passive sumitur, ut significet eum, cui repugnari nequit, modo active, ut signi- ficet τὸν μὴ μαχόμενον, ut apud Xenophontem & hoc loco. Sed μάχεσθαι respondens Ebræo רוב sæpe etiam litigare si- gnificat: Ita ut ἄμαχος sit litium & rixarum abstinens, ἄμαχος ענו : absque jurgio, ait Hieronymus, ubi hunc lo- cum citat.

ἀφιλάργυρον) Habes eandem vocem Ebr. c. XIII. v. 5. Ebraice esset לא בצע, non cupidus habendi: גרב.

Ἄμαχοι sunt, qui à pugnis alieni, vel non conten- tiosi sunt. B. Lutherus nicht haderhafftig. A pugnis & contentionibus in docendo 2. Tim. II. 23. 24. & redarguendo sive publice, sive privatim ex affecti- bus carnalibus. Ἀφυλάργυροι, qui non avari, non argenti cupidi: huic vitio Φιλαργυγίας opponitur ἀυτάρκεια Ebr. XIII. 5. cum præsentibus facile quis contentus est. Non dixit nihil possidentem, inquit Theodoreius; quæ sunt enim commodenra ac eis con- venientia constituit, sed, non amantem pecuniæ. Fieri enim potest, ut possideamus quidem, ea autem, ut par est, administremus ac dispensemus, & eis non servia- mus, sed earum simus Domini.

## 3:4
Vers. 4. τοῦ ἰδίου ὄικου καλῶς προϊστάμενον) Sophocles, Antigone: 'For whoever is a good man in his own house, will appear just also in the city.' Aeschines against Timarchus: 'For he who has managed his own house badly, he considered would manage the common affairs of the city in like manner.' Xenophon says this very thing in the third book of his Commentaries.

having children in subjection with all gravity) Apollonius in Philostratus V., giving precepts to a Prince: 'You have children; rule them above all. For the sins committed by them bring reproach upon the father.' Therefore the priest's daughter was most severely punished if she dishonored her father's house, Lev. XXI. 9. And Eli, id., because he had neglected the faults of his sons, 1 Sam. II. And Joseph, the son of Jacob, first ruled his house well, then the kingdom. Sons ought to learn both the obedience due to parents and upright morals, which is 'gravity' here.

Latin:

Vers. 4. τοῦ ἰδίου ὄικου καλῶς προϊστάμενον) Sophocles An- tigone: Ἐν τοῖς γὰρ ὀικείοισιν ὅςις ἔς' ἀνὴρ Χρηστὸς, φανεῖται κἀν πόλει δίκαιος ὤν. Æschines contra Timarchum: τὸν γὰρ τὴν ἰδίαν ὀικίαν κακῶς ὀικήσαντα, καὶ τὰ κοινὰ τῆς πόλεως παραπλησίως ἡγήσατο δια- θήσειν. Hoc ipsum dicit Xenophon Tertio Commenta- riorum.

τέκνα ἔχοντα ἐν ὑποταγῇ μετὰ πάσης σεμνότητος) Apol- lonius apud Philostratum V. dans præcepta Principi: παῖ- δές ἐισί σοι ἄρχε τούτων μάλιστα. τὰ γὰρ ἐκείνοις ἁμαρτηθέντα τῷ δήπῳ διαβάλλει. Ideo Sacerdotis filia gravissime punita, si domum paternam dehonestaret Levit. XXI. 9. Et Heli id. eo quod filiorum neglexisset culpas 1. Sam. II. Et Josephus Jacobi Filius, primum domo bene præfuit, deinde regno. Fi- lii debent addiscere, & obedientiam parentibus debitam, & probos mores, quæ hic σεμνότης.

## 3:5
Vers. 5. 'But if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?' Thus also, he who has managed his own private affairs badly should not be entrusted with the republic, said Apollodorus in the Iambics, which are in Stobaeus, and Aeschines against Timarchus. Basil the Emperor to his son: 'Use as counselors those who have deliberated and managed their own affairs well, but not those who have managed their own poorly through lack of judgment; for he who is ill-disposed toward his own affairs will never deliberate well about the affairs of others.'

Thus far the requirements, both positive and negative. There follow the relative ones: which have respect partly to the household, partly to age and time. Here it is required that, since a Bishop can also be married and support a family, he should rule his own house well, and especially educate his children properly in the instruction and admonition of the Lord, Eph. VI. v. 4, and have them obedient and devoted to honesty. It was necessary, as Chrysostom says, that from his neighbor and domestic life he should provide evidence of his virtue. For who would believe that he would have all strangers in subjection who has not had his own sons in subjection? 'Ruling his own house well,' he says. External wisdom authors also say this, that he who has rightly administered his own family affairs could also appropriately handle the business of the state. For the Church is like a certain house (1 Tim. III. 15). But it is far easier to rule a house than a Church. He, therefore, who does not know how to dispense family matters, as I said, how is he to be thought capable of presiding over the Church appropriately? Bernard, Sermon XXX on the Canticles: 'I marvel,' he says, 'at the audacity of many, whom we see gathering nothing but thorns and thistles from their own vineyards, yet who do not fear to thrust themselves upon the vineyards of all.'

Latin:

Vers. 5. Εἰ δέ τις τοῦ ἰδίου ὀικοῦ προστῆναι ὐκ οἶδε, πῶς ἐκ- κλησίας Θεοῦ ἐπιμελήσεται) Sic etiam ei, qui privatas res suas male curaverit, non esse committendam rempublicam, dixit Apollodorus in Jambis, qui sunt apud Stobæum, & Æ- schines contra Timarchum. Basilius Imperator ad filium: συμβούλοις δὲ χρῶ τοῖς καλῶς περὶ τῶν οἰκείων βουλευσαμένοις καὶ διοικήσασιν, ἀλλὰ μὴ τοῖς κακῶς ἐξ ἀβουλίας τὰ ἑαυτῶν οἰ- κονομήσασιν· ὁ γὰρ κακῶς περὶ τὰ οἰκεῖα διατεθεὶς, οὐδέποτε καλῶς βουλεύσεται περὶ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων.

Hactenus requisita tùm positiva, tùm negativa. Succedunt relata: quæ respectum habent partim ad domesticos, partim ad ætatem & tempus. Ibire- quiritur, ut cum Episcopus etiam uxoratus esse possit, & familiam alere, domui suæ bene præsit, & imprimis liberos suos probe educet in institu- tione & commonefactione Domini, Ephes. VI. v. 4. eosque obsequentes & honestati deditos habeat. Oportebat nempe, Chrysostomo dicente, ut ex vicino & re domestica, virtutis suæ præberet indicia. Quis enim crederet illum alienos quosque subjectos habi- turum, qui filios non habuerit subditos. Suæ, inquit, domui bene præpositum. Hoc & externa sapi- entia auctores ajunt, ut qui rem familiarem suam rite administraverit, rei quoque publica convenienter posset contrectare negotia. Est enim Ecclesia veluti domus quædam (1. Tim. III. 15.) Est autem longe facilius domum quam Ecclesiam regere. Qui igitur rem, ut dixi, familiarem dispensare congrue nescit, is quo pacto Ecclesiæ præesse convenienter posse putandus est? Bernardus Serm. XXX. in Cant. Miror, inquit, audaciam plurimorum, quos videmus de suis vineis non colligere nisi spinas & tribulos, vineis tamen cunctos ingerere se non vereri.

## 3:6
Vers. 6. 'Not a novice') The LXX are accustomed to translate נטע thus, which signifies a new plant. Truly, it is excellently referred here to discipline, but the word is placed as an adjective, in the way Pollux reported it to be used even in Aristophanes. The Syrian translates it as a boy in doctrine, that is, a recent one.

This respects age, that he should not be recently implanted, either into the Christian religion, to which he may have perhaps converted, or even into those things which are required for preparation for the office. For he did not wish to signify the age of adolescence here, as Chrysostom warns, but one who had been newly instructed, like a certain new planting. Compare 1 Tim. IV. 12. Chrysostom adds: Because at that time most people were coming to the Church from the Gentiles and were being baptized, he warned that one should take care not to promote a man newly imbued with the sacraments of the Church to bear the burdens of this leadership immediately. For if a man were taken as a master before he was a disciple, he would soon be lifted up in the pride of arrogance: if he were placed in the order of rulers before he had learned to be subject, he would quickly swell up. And afterwards, Hom. XI. It is very inept and absurd if, when we bring a purchased slave into the house, we do not first entrust him with some domestic furniture before he has given many proofs of his judgment and will through long experience: [that] we do not use the same diligence in the Church of God, but rather we establish a novice immediately in the first order, before he has given proofs of his faith and life.

lest being puffed up he fall into the judgment of the Devil) 'Puffed up' [is] מתנאה. Those who suddenly arrive at honors are easily inflated. The judgment of the Devil, that is, the punishment such as happened to the Devil, who was cast down from heaven, 2 Pet. II. 4, namely on account of pride. Sirach X. 15.

Thus also Chrysostom: This is: lest he incur the same condemnation which Satan himself suffered through arrogance. Others understand the slanderer in general, i.e., lest he fall into rash and tumultuous judgment. The former explanation, which is considered not inconvenient, [is in] distinct. XLIIX. C. 'Let them be prohibited.' Novices are prohibited from being ordained as Bishops, so that he who was a catechumen yesterday does not become a Bishop today, he who was in the theater yesterday does not sit in the Church today, etc. The cause of this prohibition, however, is lest the elected [man] fall into pride, as if religion If a Christian is greatly in need of this, he falls into the ruin of the Devil. For a momentary priest does not know humility, and the manners of persons, or how to despise himself; he has not fasted, he has not wept, he has not corrected himself, he has not distributed to the poor: he falls into arrogance, which is the ruin of the Devil, he who in a moment, indeed, not yet being disciples, becomes a Master. B. Hunnius in this place has it thus: Because he has recently come to the Church, if he is immediately adorned with that honor, it can easily happen in a moment that he both thinks more magnificently of himself than is right, and, puffed up by the poison of ambition, attempts new things to the ruin of the Church; and thus an opportunity is given to slanderers, both to speak ill of this novice, and to disparage and revile the very office which has been entrusted to him.

Latin:

Vers. 6. μὴ νεόφυτον) Solent LXX. sic vertere נטע, quæ plantam novam significat. Egregie vero hic ad disciplinam refertur, sed adjective posita voce, quomodo eam etiam apud Aristophanem positam retulit Pollux. Puerum in do- ctrina, id est recentem, vertit Syrus.

Hoc ætatem respicit, ne recens implantatus sit, sive religioni Christianæ, ad quam conversus for- te, sive etiam iis, quæ ad præparationem ad offi- cium requiruntur. Hic enim ætatem adolescentiæ, Chrysostomo monente, significare noluit, sed eum, qui noviter esset instructus, veluti novella quædam plan- tatio. Confer 1. Tim. IV. 12. Addit Chrysostom. Quia enim ex gentilibus tunc plerique ad Ecclesiam acce- debant, ac baptizabantur, cavendum admonuit, ne continuo noviter imbutum ecclesiæ sacramentis ad hujusce principatus onera ferenda proveheret. Si enim antequam discipulus esset, magister affumere- tur, quam primum tolleretur in arrogantia fastum: si priusquam subjici didicisset, in rectorum ordine lo- caretur, cito intumesceret. Et postea hom. XI. Per- quam ineptum & absurdum est, si cum emptitium servum introducimus domum, non prius illi aliquid suppellectilis domesticæ tradimus, quam longo expe- rimento sententiæ suæ atque voluntatis plurima indi- cia dederit: In Ecclesia Dei non eadem utamur dili- gentia, cæterum novitium adhuc in primo statim constituimus ordine, antequam fidei suæ & vitæ de- derit documenta.

ἵνα μὴ τυφωθεὶς εἰς τὸ κρῖμα ἐμπέσῃ τοῦ Διαβόλου) Τυφωθεὶς מתנאה. Facile inflantur, qui subito ad honores per- veniunt. Judicium Diaboli, id est pœna, qualis Diabolo evenit, qui de cœlo dejectus est 2. Petr. II. 4. nempe ob su- perbiam. Sirach. X. 15.

Sic etiam Chrysostomus: Hoc est: ne in eandem incurrat damnationem, quam ipse Satanas per arro- gantiam pertulit. Alii Calumniatorem in genere in- telligunt h. m. ne in judicium temerarium & tu- multuarium incidat. Prior explicatio, quæ non incommoda habetur distinct. XLIIX. C. prohi- beatur. Prohibentur Neophyti in Episcopos ordi- nari, ut qui heri erat Catechumenus, hodie non fiat Episcopus, qui heri erat in theatro, hodie non sedeat in Ecclesia, &c. Causa autem hujus prohibitio- nis est, ne electus in superbiam, tanquam religio Christiana plurimum eo egeat, incidat in ruinam Diaboli. Momentaneus nempe Sacerdos nescit humi- litatem, & modos personarum, vel sese contemnere, non jejunavit, non flevit, non se correxit, non paupe- ribus erogavit: In arrogantiam, quæ est ruina Dia- boli, incidit, qui in puncto sane nec dum discipuli fiunt Magistri. B. Hunnius in h. l. ita habet: Quia recens ad Ecclesiam accessit, si protinus honore illo de- coretur, facili momento fieri potest, ut & de se sentiat magnificentius, quam par sit, & ambitionis afflatus veneno res moliatur novas, in perniciem Ecclesiæ; atque sic calumniatoribus ansa detur, cum de novitio hoc loquendi male, tum munus ipsum, quod ei credi- tum est, extenuandi & sugillandi.

## 3:7
Vers. 7. Moreover, he must also have a good testimony from those who are outside) οἱ ἔξωθεν, who are οἱ ἔξω, 1 Cor. V. 12, 13, 1 Thess. IV. 12, that is, those who are not in the Church. Even those who had been of bad reputation could be received into Christianity, but the Apostle does not want such to be received into the presbytery, and he gives the reason. Thus also in the Jewish people, the Senators had to be ידועים, that is, well-born. Latin: whose conversation is approved most highly. Such are called by the Rabbis בעלי שמועה לטובה.

Chrysostom not without reason notes the particle καὶ. What then if he has a good testimony and a good reputation, and he himself is not of this kind? But that is indeed especially difficult. For it can scarcely be obtained that even those who are good have a good testimony among their enemies, but he himself has now also taken care of this. For he does not say, 'but he must have testimony,' but, 'but he himself must also have good testimony,' so that along with the other things which are required in him, not even this may be lacking. For solid testimony alone is not enough. For he who has been conspicuous by the splendor of his life must also be revered by them, since the truth stops the mouths of the enemies themselves. Just as no one would call the sun obscure, not even if he were blind, for he blushes to oppose the opinions of all; so also, no one surely presumes to blame him who has been conspicuous by excessive beauty and illustrious by the honesty of his morals.

ἵνα μὴ εἰς ὀνειδισμὸν ἐμπέσῃ) I take ὀνειδισμὸν here passively, in the way the Hebrew כלמה is translated. The sense is: lest at some time his former life be cast in his teeth.

καὶ παγίδα Διαβόλε) that is, lest, irritated by insults, he seeks to avenge himself; all occasions of sin are παγίδες Διαβόλε, as below VI. 9, 2 Tim. II. 26, מוקשים.

For the more holy the office that is committed to him, the more studiously is the Devil intent upon occasions, both to blacken his reputation because of a life not lived very well beforehand, and through his side to also dishonor the Church of God, and to deform the office itself, which was entrusted to such an unworthy person, as our B. Hunnius says here. Crocius, along with Theodoret, also understands this as the snare of Satan: which the Apostle shows is prepared for the infamous, and says there is a danger that he might return to his former iniquity, with the Devil plotting to bring this about.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Δεῖ δὲ αὐτὸν καὶ μαρτυρίαν καλὴν ἔχειν ἀπὸ τῶν ἔξωθεν) οἱ ἔξωθεν qui οἱ ἔξω 1. Cor. V. 12. 13. 1. Thess. IV. 12. ii, qui in Ecclesia non sunt. Ad Christianismum recipi poterant etiam, qui malæ famæ fuerant, at non vult Aposto- lus tales in presbyterium recipi, & causam reddit. Sic & in Judaico populo Senatores esse debebant ידועים, id est bene nati. Latinus: quorum conversatio sit probata optime. Ta- les Rabbinis dicuntur בעלי שמועה לטובה.

Chrysostomus non abs re notat particulam καὶ. Quid igitur si testimonium habeat bonum, bonamque famam: & ipse hujusmodi non sit? At id quidem imprimis difficile est. Vix enim obtineri potest, ut & qui boni sunt, apud inimicos bonum habeant testi- monium, cæterum hoc ipse nunc quoque cavit. Neque enim ait, oportet autem eum testimonium habere: sed, oportet autem ipsum & testimonium habere bonum, ut cum cæteris, quæ in illo requiruntur, ne istud quidem desit. Neque enim solidum testimo- nium sufficit. Qui enim fuerit vita fulgore con- spicuus, & illis verendus sit necesse est, quippe veri- tas ipsis quoque ora obstruit inimicis. Quemadmodum nemo obscurum diceret solem, ne si cæcus quidem fue- rit, erubescit quippe opinionibus omnium adversari: ita & eum, qui nimio fuerit decore conspicuus, atque morum honestate illustris, nullus profecto culpare præsumit.

ἵνα μὴ εἰς ὀνειδισμὸν ἐμπέσῃ) ὀνειδισμὸν hic passive sumo, quomodo vertitur Ebræum כלמה. Sensus est: ne ali- quando ei exprobretur prior vita.

καὶ παγίδα Διαβόλε) id est, ne contumeliis irritatus quæ- rat se ulcisci, omnes peccandi occasiones sunt παγίδες Δια- βόλε, ut infra VI. 9. 2. Tim. II. 26. מוקשים.

Etenim quo sanctius ei munus committitur, eo stu- diosius in occasiones intentus est Diabolus, tum ipsius denigrandi famam ob vitam non optime antehac a- ctam, tum per illius latus dehonestandi quoque Eccle- siam Dei, & munus ipsum tam indigna personæ cre- ditum deformandi, ut hic B. Hunnius noster. De laqueo Satanæ etiam accipit Crocius cum Theodo- reto: quem infami paratum monstrat Apostolus, & periculum esse dicit, ne ad priorem iniquitatem revertatur, Diabolo ut hoc efficiat, machinante.

## 3:8
Vers. 8. Deacons likewise) That is, χρὴ εἶναι from the preceding. See the החזנים, Acts VI, Phil. I. 1.

σεμνὺς) See Philipp. IV. 8.

μὴ διλόγυς) The same as διγλώσσυς. The Hebrews call them רכילים, as can be seen in Proverbs ch. XI. v. 13, ch. XX. v. 22. Ephesus was a very mercantile city, as we said to the Ephesians. Merchants, however, are for the most part vain, as noted by Cicero, and רכל, from which that word רכיל comes, is to trade. And in Homer, a Phoenician, that is, a merchant, ἀπατήλια εἰδὼς, τρώκτης. Tyrians are double-tongued to Virgil.

μὴ οἴνῳ πολλῷ προσέχοντας) That is, μὴ παροίνυς, as he spoke above. προσέχειν is to devote effort to some thing, as can be seen above I. 4, below IV. 1, 13, Tit. I. 14, Heb. II. 1, VII. 13.

μὴ αἰσχροκερδεῖς) That is, those who practice neither an unjust nor a shameful trade. Of that kind are usurers and informers: of this kind are gamblers, actors, parasites. Αἰσχροκερδὴς is בוצע בצע Prov. XV. 27. To the Rabbis, שאני ממון.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Διακόνυς ὡσάυτως) Nempe χρὴ εἶναι ex superio- ribus. החזנים Vide Act. VI. Phil. I. 1.

σεμνὺς) Vide Philipp. IV. 8.

μὴ διλόγυς) Idem quod διγλώσσυς. Ebræi eos vocant רכילים, ut videre est Proverb. cap. XI. v. 13. c. XX. v. 22. Ephesus erat urbs valde mercatrix, ut ad Ephesios dixi- mus. Mercatores autem plerumque vani, ut Ciceroni no- tatum, & רכל, unde illa vox רכיל est mercari. Et Ho- mero Phœnix, id est, mercator, ἀπατήλια εἰδὼς, τρώκτης. Ty- rii bilingues Virgilio.

μὴ οἴνῳ πολλῷ προσέχοντας) Id est μὴ παροίνυς, ut locutus est supra. προσέχειν est operam alicui rei dare, ut videre est supra I. 4. infra IV. 1. 13. Tit. I. 14. Ebr. II. 1. VII. 13.

μὴ αἰσχροκερδεῖς) Id est, qui neque injustum neque tur- pe artificium faciunt. Illius generis sunt fœneratores & dela- tores : hujus aleatores, scenici, parasiti. Αἰσχροκερδὴς בוצע בצע Prov. XV. 27. Rabbinis שאני ממון.

## 3:9
Vers. 9. having the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience) ἔχοντας i.e. κατέχοντας, as above I. 19. Through a pure conscience, faith is also guarded. For those who neglect this are accustomed to lose that also, as we have already heard I. 19. Concerning the word mystery, see Eph. ch. VI. 19, Col. IV. 3. See also below 16. For this doctrine is hidden from the impious, 2 Cor. IV. 3.

Deacons are immediately subjoined to Bishops, by a certain indication, because at that time Presbyters were not distinct from Bishops. Moreover, they are deacons who minister not only by preaching the word in the Church, but by performing other duties which pertain to the εὐχημοσύνην [decency] of the Church, to the care of the poor, of the Jews and Greeks, to the distribution of resources, and to ecclesiastical accounts and the like; such were those of whom Acts VI speaks, which kind of dispensers of resources were especially necessary while the communion of goods was still in force. Although even afterwards, among the Gentiles, in whom the communion of goods was not received, deacons were employed. Nor yet do they seem to have been entirely excluded from the duty of teaching, because when necessity burned, they also held discourse in the Church, who were endowed with the gift of ἑρμηνείας [interpretation] or were διδακτικοὶ [apt to teach]. That they also pertained to the ecclesiastical order is clear from Phil. I. Although otherwise the word διακόνος [deacon] is more general, not only concerning any other ministers serving, but also as it relates to ministers of the Church, and is attributed even to those who preach the word in the Church, who in respect to God and Christ are called deacons (1 Cor. III. 5, 2 Cor. III. 6, Col. I. 7), and is also used concerning Timothy (1 Tim. IV. 5). But here the Apostle teaches both what kind of deacons themselves, and what kind of wives they ought to have. He assigns these requirements for the former: that they should be (1.) σεμνοὶ [grave], i.e., grave and honest, and alien to all levity: (2.) not double-tongued, saying one thing now, denying another then, not simulators, not deceitful, as Chrysostom has it. For almost nothing makes us degenerate so much from spiritual nobility as fraud and deceit, and nothing harms the Church more than crafty simulation. (3.) not given to wine or drunkenness. For drunkenness, as the blessed Hunnius rightly says: stands very much in the way of the σεμνότητι [gravity] just required, makes them light and dissolute, and inept for managing affairs or sustaining public office in the Church, and produces scandals, by which both doctrine and the Ministry are besmirched with a foul stain. (4.) not given to filthy lucre, for how shall those be entrusted with the goods of the Church who, given to the disease of avarice, seek their own advantages from public revenues. (5.) Faithful. For to the unfaithful or those alien to the faith of the Church, how are the goods of the Church to be committed? (6.) Of a good conscience. For they have and cherish the mystery of the faith in a good conscience, who, with the truly mystical doctrine of the faith, strive to retain a good conscience. Theophylact. That is, after having received the correctness of dogma, they should also lead a life that cannot be accused of crime. For a purer conscience is situated in an irreprehensible life.

Latin:

Vers. 9. ἔχοντας τὸ μυσήριον τῆς πίστεως ἐν καθαρᾷ συνειδή- σει) ἔχοντας i. e. κατέχοντας, ut supra I. 19. Per puram conscientiam custoditur & fides. Nam qui hanc negligunt, solent & illam amittere, ut jam audivimus I. 19. De voce mysterii vide Eph. c. VI. 19. Col. IV. 3. Vide & infra 16. Est enim hæc doctrina occulta impiis 2. Cor. IV. 3.

Diaconi immediate subjunguntur Episcopis, certo indicio, quod tum Presbyteri ab Episcopis diversi non fuerint. Diaconi autem sunt, qui ministrant non tantum verbum prædicando in Ecclesia, sed alia munia præstando, quæ ad εὐχημοσύνην Ecclesiæ, ad curam pauperum, Judæorum & Græcorum, ad distributionem facultatum, & rationes Ecclesiasticas & similia pertinent; quales erant illi, de quibus Act. VI. cujusmodi dispensatores facultatum maxime vigente adhuc communione bonorum necessarii erant. Quanquam etiam postea penes gentes, in quibus non recepta fuit bonorum communio, Diaconi adhibiti. Nec tamen à docendi munere exclusi omnino fuisse videntur, quia necessitate flagrante etiam sermonem haberent in Ecclesia, qui dono ἑρμηνείας præditi vel διδακτικοὶ erant. Pertinuisse eos etiam ad Ecclesiasticum ordinem è Phil. I. patet. Quanquam alias vox διακόνος generalior sit, non tantum de quibusvis ministris aliis inservientibus, sed etiam quod ad ministros Ecclesiæ, ac illis quoque tribuatur, qui verbum prædicant in Ecclesia, qui respectu Dei & Christi dicuntur Diaconi 1. Cor. III. 5. 2. Cor. III. 6. Col. I. 7. & de Timotheo quoque adhibeatur 1. Tim. 1. IV. 5. Docet autem hic Apostolus tum quales ipsi Diaconi, tum quales uxores eorum esse debeant. Illorum requisita hæc assignat: ut nempe sint (1.) σεμνοὶ i. e. graves & honesti, & ab omni levitate alieni: (2.) non bilingues, modo ajentes quiddam, modo negantes, non simulatores, non dolosi, ut habet Chrysost. Nihil enim ferme nos ita degenerare à spirituali nobilitate facit, ut fraus atque dolus, nihilque in Ecclesia nocet magis, quam versuta simulatio. (3.) non vino vel ebrietati dediti. Ebrietas enim, ut recte B. Hunnius: σεμνότητι modo requisitæ plurimum obstat, leves ac solutos, & ad res gerendas, aut officium publicum in Ecclesia sustinendum ineptos efficit, & scandala parit, quibus & doctrina, & Ministerio macula tetra aspergitur. (4.) non turpi lucro dediti, quomodo enim illi bona Ecclesiæ credentur, qui avaritiæ morbo deditus, ex publicis reditibus sua quærit commoda. (5.) Fideles. Nam infidelibus seu alienis à fide Ecclesiæ, quomodo bona Ecclesiæ committenda? (6.) Bonæ conscientiæ. Nam mysterium fidei habent & fovent in bona conscientia, qui cum fidei doctrina vere mystica student bonam retinere conscientiam. Theophyl. Hoc est, post susceptam dogmatis rectitudinem, & vitam degant, quæ criminis nequeat incusari. Est namque purior conscientia in vita irreprehensibili sita.

## 3:10
Vers. 10. καὶ οὗτοι δοκιμαζέσθωσαν πρῶτον [and let these also be proved first]) The sense is: The names of those who seem not unsuitable for the presbytery should be published in the Church for δοκιμασίαν [probation], so that if anyone has anything to blame in them, he may bring it forth. The word δοκιμάζεσθαι [to be proved] is transferred from Attic law, which the Ephesians, as descendants of the Ionians, imitated. Δοκιμασία [probation] is the same as ἀνάκρισις [examination] in Pollux: an investigation of the morals of each one, which you have well described in Lysias. That this was accustomed to be done in the Church in the way I have said, Lampridius teaches us first in the life of Severus: for when he wished to give some as governors to provinces, or to make them prefects, he proposed their names, exhorting the people that if anyone had any charge of crime, he should prove it with manifest facts: and he said it was a grave matter that this was not done in the case of provincial governors, when Christians and Jews did it in the proclaiming of priests who are to be ordained: where incidentally we learn that this custom also is from the Synagogue. But the priests of the Jews are improperly called here οἱ πρεσβύτεροι [the elders], and that by σύγχυσιν [confusion], because the presbyters of the Christians were also called priests. The Council of Chalcedon teaches us the same thing that we have said: ὃ χειροτονούμενος ἐπικηρύττοιτο [that he who is to be ordained should be publicly proclaimed]. This is the power of refusing the unworthy, which Cyprian attributes to the laity, adding that in the presence of the laity either the crimes of the wicked may be detected, or the merits of the good may be proclaimed: because the laity knows the life of each one most fully, and has perceived the act of each one concerning his conversation. Of the same Cyprian is that: In ordaining Clerics, dearest brothers, we are accustomed to consult you beforehand, and to weigh the morals and merits of each one by common counsel.

But when the Apostle, dealing with Deacons here, says κj ὗτοι, he shows that presbyters must be measured by that standard much more. And therefore in Timothy, known to him for some time, Paul kept this form for himself, Acts XVI. 2, so that he might show the Churches that which they did not indeed always follow, but ought to have followed. This δοκιμασία is called by the Rabbis בְּדִיקָה or בְּדִיקוּתָא.

Εἶτα διακονείτωσαν) After such an examination let them be admitted to their ministry. Theophylact says: Just as I did not ask for a neophyte as Bishop, so I would not wish these deacons to be brought to minister unless they are approved. Moreover, I would say that these men must be tested by the passage of time, to see if they are free from harm and crime, just as no one entrusts the management of a house to a slave who has been recently bought, before he appears honest after a trial has been made for some time.

Ἀνέγκλητοι ὄντες) That which appears openly is often said to be. Take ἀνεγκλήτοι ὄντες here in this way: after it has appeared that nothing can be objected against them. Here ἀνέγκλητοι, who are above ἀνεπίληπτοι. So also Tit. I. 6. 7. see also 1 Cor. I. 8. Col. I. 22. In the Glossary ἀνέγκλητος, unaccusable.

B. Hunnius refers this to the preceding word. Εἶτα διακονείτωσαν: He warns, therefore, that future Deacons must be tested first, and thus, once approved, this ministry is to be committed to them, so that they may perform it in such a way that they minister blamelessly, i.e., so that neither diligence nor faith can be found wanting in them.

Latin:

Vers. 10. καὶ οὗτοι δοκιμαζέσθωσαν πρῶτον) Sensus est: Eorum, qui presbyterio videntur non inidonei nomina ad δοκιμασίαν publicentur in Ecclesia, ut si quid habet, quod in eis culpet, id proferat. Verbum δοκιμάζεσθαι ex jure Attico, quod & Ephesii Jonum traduces imitati sunt, traductum est. Δοκιμασία idem quod ἀνάκρισις apud Pollucem: de moribus cujusque exploratio, quam bene descriptam habes apud Lysiam. Eam in Ecclesia fieri solitam eo quo dixi modo, docet nos primum Lampridius in vita Severi: ubi enim aliquos voluit vel rectores provinciis dare, vel præpositos facere nomina eorum proponebat, hortans populum, ut si quis quid haberet criminis, probaret manifestis rebus: dicebatque grave esse non fieri in provinciarum rectoribus, cum id Christiani & Judæi facerent, in prædicandis sacerdotibus, qui ordinandi sunt: ubi obiter discimus & hunc morem esse ex Synagoga. Sacerdotes autem Judæorum improprie hic vocantur οἱ πρεσβύτεροι, idque per σύγχυσιν, quia Christianorum presbyteri etiam sacerdotes vocabantur. Docet, nos idem quod diximus Chalcedonensis Synodus: ὃ χειροτονούμενος ἐπικηρύττοιτο. Hæc est potestas indignos recusandi, quam plebi tribuit Cyprianus, addens ut plebe præsente vel detegantur malorum crimina, vel bonorum merita prædicentur: quia plebs singulorum vitam plenissime novit, & uniuscujusque actum de ejus conversatione perspexit. Ejusdem Cypriani est illud: In ordinandis Clericis, fratres charissimi, solemus vos ante consulere, & mores ac merita singulorum communi consilio ponderare.

Cum autem dicit Apostolus de Diaconis hic agens, κj ὗτοι, ostendit multo magis ad eam normam exigendos presby- teros. Et ideo in Timotheo, pridem sibi noto, hanc for- mam sibi servavit Paulus, Act. XVI. 2. ut Ecclesiis monstra- ret id quod non quidem secutæ sunt semper, sed sequi de- buerunt. Hæc δοκιμασία Rabbinis dicitur בְּדִיקָה vel בְּדִיקוּתָא.

Εἶτα διακονείτωσαν) Post talem explorationem admit- tantur ad suum ministerium. Theophylactus: Quemadmodum, inquit, Episco- pum depoposci haudquaquam neophytum, sic nolim diaconos istos nisi probatos deduci ad ministrandum. Quin etiam & temporis processu periclitandos hos dixerim, si noxa vacant & crimine, quemadmo- dum nec servo quispiam, qui nuper sit emptus, non ante domus gubernationem demandat, quam per aliquod tempus periculo facto probus appareat.

Ἀνέγκλητοι ὄντες) Sæpe esse dicitur id, quod palam appa- ret. Ita hic sume ἀνεγκλήτοι ὄντες: postquam apparuerit, ni- hil illis posse objici. Hic ἀνέγκλητοι, qui supra ἀνεπίληπτοι. Sic & Tit. I. 6. 7. vide & 1. Cor. I. 8. Col. I. 22. In Glossario ἀνέγκλητος, inaccusabilis.

B. Hunnius id ad præcedens verbum refert. Εἶτα διακονείτωσαν: Monet ergo futuros Diaconos probari prius, & sic probatis ministerium hoc com- mitti, quod sic obeant, ut ministrent inculpati, i. e. ut nec diligentia, neque fides in eis desiderari queat.

## 3:11
V. 11. Γυναῖκας ὡσαύτως) Supply διακόνους: which must be repeated ἀπὸ κοινῆ, as Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and Theophylact rightly saw. For there were also female διάκονοι, as can be seen in Rom. XVI. 1, whom Pliny called ministers. See Law 'nulla' in the Code concerning Bishops and Clerics, and the things said there by the learned. Female διάκονοι were taken from the younger women: πρεσβύτιδες from the older. You may easily understand, however, that the things which the Apostle requires in female διακόνοις are required much more in those who were called πρεσβύτιδες or προκαθήμεναι, and who in their own way corresponded to τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις, of whom we spoke in Philippians IV. 16, and will speak below in IV. 9.

Σεμνάς) It becomes men too, but especially women, to have a certain moderate gravity.

Μὴ διαβόλους) He does not add this in vain. For he notes the customs of women, especially in Greece and Asia. 'A fault-finding thing is the nature of women, and if they receive small pretexts for words, they bring in more; and it is a certain pleasure to women to say nothing sound to one another,' says Euripides in the Phoenissae. See below V. 13, which passage explains this.

Νηφαλίους) Drunkenness is most unbecoming to women.

Πιστὰς ἐν πᾶσι) Namely, those who have shown such faith in all business that the entire distributions of the Churches can be entrusted to them.

By γυναῖκας, wives are understood, as is clear from the usage of the word and verse 2, as also below in verse 12. Wives, namely, of both Bishops and Deacons. For the name is relative: and since the Apostle warned concerning Bishops in verse 2 that they should be husbands of one wife, he informs us, intending to warn the same in verse 12 concerning Deacons, so that they might not be ignorant of what kind of wives they ought to have, so that they may be such as the men, equal to them in honesty and gravity, so that they may not be slanderers, but given to sobriety, and faithful in all things, not only in marriage but also in the administration of household affairs. For it contributes greatly to authority

The levity and bad faith of wives detracts from Presbyters and Deacons. But Cornelius à Lapide is in vain when he affirms that Deacons abstained from the use of wives after ordination, citing, but falsely, Lombard and Thomas. It is certain, at any rate, that in the sixth century Deacons still used their wives, and indeed Presbyters too. For not only in the fourth century did the Nicene Ecumenical Synod, at the persuasion of Paphnutius, permit the use of marriage to sacred ministers, and the Synod of Gangra strike with anathema the Eustathians, because they affected the marriage of priests, just as Athanasius, Gregory of Nyssa, and Gregory Nazianzen lived in marriage, as also Hilary of Poitiers, Bishops, and Jerome himself admits that even after the interdict of Pope Siricius, very many priests still lived in matrimony. In the fifth century also, after the interdict of Siricius was renewed by Pope Innocent, Prosper was Bishop of Reggio, as were Sidonius Apollinaris, Bishop of the Arverni, and Simplicius of Bourges, etc. What of the fact that Synesius would not undertake the Bishopric of Cyrene in Africa, unless on the condition that he be openly permitted to retain his wife, according to Nicephorus, lib. XIV. Hist. Eccles. c. 59. Among our ancestors also throughout Germany for over a thousand years the marriage of Ministers of the word was approved, until Gregory VII, having thrown almost the entire Christian world into turmoil, forced celibacy upon the whole Ecclesiastical order.

Latin:

V. 11. Γυναῖκας ὡσαύτως) Supple διακόνους : quod ἀπὸ κοινῆ repetendum, quod recte viderunt Chrysostomus, Oe- cumenius, Theophylactus. Nam erant & fœminæ διάκονοι, ut videre est Rom. XVI. 1. quas ministras dixit Plinius. Vi- de L. nulla C. de Episcopis & Clericis, & ibi dicta ab eru- ditis. Fœminæ διάκονοι sumebantur ex junioribus: πρεσβύ- τιδες ex senioribus. Facile autem intelligas ea, quæ exigit Apostolus in fœminis διακόνοις, multo magis exigi in iis, quæ πρεσβύτιδες sive προκαθήμεναι dicebantur, & quæ suo modo respondebant τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις, de quibus diximus Philipp. IV. 16. & dicemus infra IV. 9.

Σεμνάς) Decet & viros, sed fœminas maximè modera- ta quædam gravitas.

Μὴ διαβόλους) Non frustra hoc addit. Notat enim mo- res mulierum maximè in Græcia Asiæque. Φιλόψογον δὲ χρῆμα θηλειῶν ἔφυ, Σμικρὰς δ᾽ ἀφορμὰς ἢν λάβωσι τῶν λόγων Πλείως ἐπεισφέρουσιν ἡδονὴ δέ τις Γυναιξὶ μηδὲν ὑγιὲς ἀλλήλαις λέγειν. Ait in Phœnissis Euripides. Vide infra V. 13. qui locus hunc explicat.

Νηφαλίους) Vinositas fœminas maximè dedecet.

Πιστὰς ἐν πᾶσι) Nempe quæ ita fidem in negotiis omni- bus præstiterint, ut totæ ipsis Ecclesiæ largitiones credi possint.

Per γυναῖκας uxores intelliguntur, ut è vocis usu & v. 2. ut & infra v. 12. liquet. Uxores scil. tum Epi- scoporum, tum Diaconorum. Nomen enim rela- tivum est: & cum de Episcopis v. 2. monuerit A- postolus, ut sint unius uxoris viri, moniturus idem v. 12. de Diaconis, ne nesciant, qualesnam uxores habere debeant, informat, ut nempe tales sint quales viri, gemini ipsis honestate, gravitate, ne sint calumniatrices, sobrietati deditæ, ac fidæ sint in omnibus, non solum in conjugio, sed & in rei fami- liaris administratione. Plurimum enim autoritati

Presbyterorum & Diaconorum derogat uxorum levitas & mala fides. Frustra autem est Corn. à Lap. cum Diaconos post ordinationem abstinuisse ab usu uxorum affirmat, adducens, sed falsò, Lombar- dum & Thomam. Constat utiq; seculo adhuc sexto Diaconos usos esse uxoribus, imò & presbyteros. Nam non seculo quarto tantum Nicena Oecumeni- ca Synodus Paphnutii suasu ministris sacris usum conjugii permisit, ac Synodus Gangrensis Eusta- tianos, quod conjugium sacerdotum afficiebant anathemate percussit, quemadmodum in conju- gio vixêre Athanasius, Gregorius Nyssenus, & Gre- gorius Nazianzenus, ut & Hilarius Pictaviens. Epi- scopi, ac Hieronymus ipse fatetur, etiam post Si- ricii Papæ interdictum plurimos adhuc sacerdotes in matrimonio vixisse. Quinto etiam seculo post renovatum ab Innocentio P. R. Siricii interdictum Prosper Regiensis Episcopus fuit, ut & Sidonius Apollinaris Arvernorum Episcopus, & Simplicius Biturigum &c. Quid, quod Synesius Cyrenes in Africa Episcopatum subire noluerit, nisi ea condi- tione, ut sibi palam liceret uxorem suam retinere, apud Nicephor. lib. XIV. Hist. Eccles. c. 59. Majo- ribus etiam nostris per Germaniam ultra mille an- nos conjugium Ministrorum verbi probatum est, usque dum Gregorius VII. universo propè orbe Christiano turbato, cælibatum toti ordini Eccle- siastico obtruderet.

## 3:12
Vers. 12. Let the deacons be) He returns to the true Deacons. After that digression, as it were, interposed concerning Deaconesses. Husbands of one wife) Interpret, as above 2. Ruling their children and their own houses well) See above 3. & 4.

Now he returns to the Deacons: For the preceding things pertained to their wives just as much as to those of Bishops. Therefore he continues his exhortations concerning Deacons: he requires that they ought not to be of many wives, but that each one be a monogamous husband of one wife only, and that he preside well over his children and his own families.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Διάκονοι ἔστωσαν) Redit ad veros Diacones. Post illam velut παρέκβασιν de Diaconissis interpositam. Μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρες) Interpretare, ut supra 2. Τέκνων καλῶς προϊστάμενοι καὶ τῶν ἰδίων οἴκων) Vide su- pra 3. & 4.

Nunc redit ad Diaconos: Nam præcedentia ad uxores eorum pertinebant æque ac Episcoporum. Proinde continuat hortationes suas de Diaconis: quod debeant esse non plurium uxorum, sed ut quisque μονόγαμος unius uxoris maritus tantum sit, liberisque ac familiis suis benè præsit, requirit.

## 3:13
Vers. 13. For they who have served well) They make for themselves an honest degree, namely to the presbyterate. For such was the custom of those centuries, that from the best of the Christian people deacons were made, from the best deacons presbyters, from the best presbyters presidents. They acquire a degree. In the constitutions of Clement there are prayers for a deacon, in which we read these things pertaining to this: vouchsafe that he, having served well the ministry entrusted to him, without turning, without blame, without reproach, may be deemed worthy of a greater degree.

For those who have been more diligent in the lowest matters, says Theophylact, will soon reach the highest summits. Thus before him Chrysostom and after him Oecumenius. And also from the Papists Cornelius à Lapide, Estius, others: from the Reformed Bullinger, Hyperius, Beza, Tossanus: Calvin however, (and Beza not denying it) explain the degree simply as dignity and honor, not precisely as a higher degree of Ecclesiastical Ministry: for whether Deacons were so restricted to sacred order in the primitive Church that they could not be raised to political offices of greater dignity, is not certain. Those from the Papists who draw it to the highest degree in the kingdom of heaven are refuted here by Estius: because it is unusual for these things to be signified by a good degree in Scripture.

And much boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus) Those who have performed the office of deacon well, if they become presbyters, preached the Gospel to others more freely and with greater confidence. For faith here is put for the doctrine itself, as Gal. III. 23. and often elsewhere.

Estius wishes the liberty of acting frankly to be signified, which a mind conscious of right is accustomed to produce, to which we easily agree, which however Hunnius explains more fully, that namely from a rightly administered office they bring back this most pleasant use, they enjoy a joyful and clear conscience, by which, relying on God on high, they perform their duty with greater alacrity and also with more successful results, they despise the calumnies and hatreds of the world with an unbroken spirit, raising themselves in all adversities by the testimony of a good conscience, the approval of God, and the most ample retribution of happiness provided, which they know is laid up for them in heaven by the promise of the Lord. Nor does Crocius depart to a different view: I would prefer, he says, to refer it to God and men so that it promises liberty in both respects; namely, that they may both conduct their cause before God with great confidence, and that they may fear neither accusation, nor detraction, nor the unjust judgment or insults of any man, that they may move fearlessly without dread among the faithful and the unfaithful, professing CHRIST, and doing what belongs to their office. For the Apostle seems entirely, as Beza noted, to oppose liberty to accusation, to reproach and to oppose the snare of the Devil. By faith, however, he understands with Piscator saving faith, which, namely, expects all good things from the gratuitous mercy of God on account of CHRIST. Where this faith is joined with good ministry, there is true and solid liberty. For it is called faith in Christ Jesus, because it tends to Him alone, and relies on Him alone.

PART II. Instruction of Timothy concerning conduct in the house of God.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Οἱ γὰρ καλῶς διακονήσαντες βαθμὸν ἑαυτοῖς κα- λὸν περιποιοῦνται) Gradum sibi honestum faciunt, nempe ad presbyterium. Ita enim mos erat illorum seculorum, ut ex optimis de Christiana plebe diaconi fierent, ex dia- conis optimis presbyteri, ex presbyteris optimis præsiden- tes. Περιποιοῦνται קנו βαθμὸν מעלה. In Clementis con- stitutionibus sunt preces pro diacono, in quibus hæc legi- mus huc pertinentia: καταξίωσον αὐτὸν εὐαρέστως λειτουργή- σαντα τὴν ἐγχειρισθεῖσαν αὐτῷ διακονίαν ἀτρέπτως, ἀμέμ- πτως, ἀνεγκλήτως, μείζονος ἀξιωθῆναι βαθμοῦ.

Nam qui infimis, inquit Theophyl. fuerint in re- bus solertiores, ad summa mox pertingent fastigia. Sic ante ipsum Chrysostomus & post eum Oecume- nius. Nec non è Pontificiis Cornel. à Lap. Estius, alii: è Reformatis Bullingerus, Hyperius, Beza, Tossanus: Calvinus tamen, (nec abnuente etiam Beza) simpliciter gradum de dignitate ac honore exponunt, non præcise de superiori Ministerii Ec- clesiastici gradu: num enim ita Diaconi ad sacrum ordinem in primitiva Ecclesia adstricti fuerint, ut ad politica officia majoris dignitatis evehi non potuerint, haud constat. Qui è Pontificiis ad gra- dum summum in regno cœlorum trahunt ab Estio hic refutantur: quod ut ista per gradum bonum in Scriptura significentur insuetum sit.

Καὶ πολλὴν παῤῥησίαν ἐν πίστει τῇ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) Qui diaconi munere bene functi sunt, si presbyteri fiant, libe- rius & cum majore fiducia aliis Evangelium prædicabant. Nam πίστις hic ponitur pro doctrina ipsa, ut Gal. III. 23. & alibi sæpe.

Libertatem potius ingenuè agendi significari vult Estius, quam parere solet mens conscia recti, cui facilè annuimus, quam tamen plenius explicat Hunnius, quod nempe ex recte administrato officio hunc jucundissimum usum reportantes, læta fruan- tur, & exporrecta conscientia, qua Deo excelso freti majore cum alacritate, successu quoq́; feliciori suum munus obeunt, calumnias odiaque mundi infracto animo contemnunt, erigentes se in omnibus adversi- tatibus testimonio bonæ conscientiæ, approbatione Dei, & præstita felicitatis amplissima retributione, quam ex promisso Domini sibi repositam in cœlis esse norunt. Nec in diversum abit Crocius: Ego, inquit, malim referre ad Deum & homines ut utrobiq́; mul- tum polliceatur libertatem; nempe tum ut magna cum fiducia apud Deum agant causam suam, tum ut nec criminationem, nec obtrectationem, nec ullius hominis nec iniquam sensuram sive probra extime- scant, intrepide sine metu inter fideles & infideles versentur, profitentes CHRISTUM, & agentes quæ sunt sui officii. Videtur enim omnino Apostolus, ut annotavit Beza libertatem criminationi, probro & laqueo Diaboli opponere. Per fidem autem intel- ligit cum Piscatore fidem salvificam, quæ scil. ex gratuita Dei misericordia propter CHRISTUM omnia bona expectat. Ubi hæc fides cum bono ministerio conjuncta est, ibi vera & solida libertas. Dicitur enim fides in Christum Jesum, quia in il- lum solum tendit, illo solo nititur.

PARS II. Informatio Timothei de conversatione in domo Domini.

## 3:14
Ver. 14. These things I write to you) In Macedonia, as the learned judge. He had delivered instruction concerning the Bishop or Presbyter and Deacons, and their wives. For ancient simplicity in the Church was ignorant of other ranks. For what purpose he delivered these things, he now subjoins, namely, so that Timothy the Bishop himself may know how he ought to conduct himself with the Deacons in the house of God. For he was a young man still in need of instruction, and especially of Apostolic authority. Nor indeed is the little word ταῦτα to be restricted only to the preceding. It pertains also to the following, indeed to those things which have been delivered throughout the whole Epistle. But the subscription teaches that these were not written in Macedonia, but in Phrygia Pacatiana, concerning which in the Prolegomena. Hoping to come to you sooner) Paul did not come to Ephesus, but to Troas: and there Timothy saw him. In the Manuscript for τάχιον there is in the same sense ἐν τάχει, as Luke XVIII. 8. Acts XII. 7. XXII. 18. XXV. 4. Rom. XVI. 20. Rev. II. 5. XXII. 6. Deut. XXVIII. 29. Josh. VIII. 19. Ps. IV. 13. What is to be held concerning it, we have already warned in the Prolegomena: which should be compared here. V. 15. If however I delay) If anything should intervene: which often happened to Paul. See 2 Cor. XII. 14. XIII. 3. That you may know) That warned by these letters you may know those things which otherwise I was about to say in person. How one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God) ἀναστρέφεσθαι, as 2 Cor. I. v. 12. Eph. II. 3. Heb. X. 33. XIII. 18. 1 Pet. I. 17. corresponds to the Hebrew הָלַךְ as is to be seen in Prov. XX. 7. if individual pious persons are the temple of God 1 Cor. III. 16. VI. 19. Eph. II. 21. therefore also the assembly of the pious. For the sake of greater clarity he adds an explanation of this metaphor. Which is the church of the living God) Not of false gods, but of the true God אֵל חַי Matt. XXVI. 63. Rom. IX. 26. 2 Cor. VI. 16. 1 Thess. I. 9. below IV. 10. VI. 17.

The Church is called the house of God on account of a typical adumbration, because where God manifested Himself in the Old Testament, it was believed to be the house of God, as for instance Gen. XXVIII. v. 17. in Bethel: and therefore the tabernacle and temple of the Lord was called the house of GOD, because God deigned to manifest Himself peculiarly in the same, Exod. XXIII. 19. XXXIV. 26. Deut. XXIII. 18. 1 Kings II. 36. III. 1. just as heaven itself, in which God manifests Himself in an excellent manner to the Angels and the elect, is called the house of GOD, John XIV. 2. Since therefore in the Church or assembly and communion of saints God deigns to be present and to manifest Himself through the word and Sacraments, the Church is deservedly called the house of God, in which the stewards are the ministers of the word, 1 Cor. IV. 1. The head of the household is God, the domestics are the faithful, Eph. II. 19. who are called the domestics of the faith Gal. VI. 10. The principal foundation is Christ, 1 Cor. III. 9. But the organic [foundation] is the doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles, Eph. II. 20.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ταῦτά σοι γράφω) In Macedonia, ut eruditi censent. Tradiderat informationem de Episcopo vel Presbytero & Diaconis, eorumque uxoribus. Alios enim gradus ignorabat prisca simplicitas in Ecclesia. Quo fine hæc tradiderit, jam subjun- git, ut scil. Timotheus Episcopus ipse sciat, quo- modo sibi cum Diaconis versandum in domo Dei sit. Erat enim juvenis adhuc informatione, maxime autem autoritate Apostolica, indigens. Neque vero vocula ταῦτα tantum ad præcedentia restringenda. Pertinet etiam ad sequentia, imò ad ea, quæ per totam Epistolam tradita. Non au- tem scripta hæc esse in Macedonia, sed in Phry- gia Pacatiana, subscriptio docet, quo de in Pro- legomenis. Ἐλπίζων ἐλθεῖν πρός σε τάχιον) Venit non Ephesum Pau- lus, sed Troada: & ibi eum vidit Timotheus. In Manu- scripto pro τάχιον est sensu eodem ἐν τάχει, ut Luc. XVIII. 8. Act. XII. 7. XXII. 18. XXV. 4. Rom. XVI. 20. Apoc. II. 5. XXII. 6. Deut. XXVIII. 29. Jos. VIII. 19. Ps. IV. 13. Quid de eo habendum sit, in Prolegomenis jam monuimus: quæ hic conferantur. V. 15. Ἐὰν δὲ βραδύνω) Si quid intercesserit: quod sæpe eveniebat Paulo. Vide 2. Cor. XII. 14. XIII. 3. Ἵνα εἰδῇς) Ut his literis monitus noris ea, quæ alioqui coram fueram dicturus. Πῶς ἐν οἴκῳ Θεῦ ἀναστρέφεσθαι) ἀναστρέφεσθαι, ut 2. Cor. I. v. 12. Eph. II. 3. Ebr. X. 33. XIII. 18. 1. Petr. I. 17. respondet Ebræo הָלַךְ ut videre est Prov. XX. 7. si pii singuli tem- plum Dei 1. Cor. III. 16. VI. 19. Eph. II. 21. ergo & cœtus piorum. Majoris claritatis ergo μεταφορᾶς hujus addit explicationem. Ἥτις ἐστὶν ἐκκλησία Θεῦ ζῶντος) Non falsorum deo- rum, sed Dei veri אֵל חַי Matth. XXVI. 63. Rom. IX. 26. 2. Cor. VI. 16. 1. Thess I. 9. infra IV. 10. VI 17.

Ecclesia dicitur domus Dei ob typicam adum- brationem, quia ubi Deus sese in Vet. Testam. ma- nifestabat, domus Dei esse credebatur, utpote Gen. XXIIX. v. 17. in Bethel: & ideo tabernaculum ac templum Domini dicebatur domus DEI, quod pe- culiariter se Deus in eodem manifestare dignatus est, Exod. XXIII. 19. XXXIV. 26. Deut. XXIII. 18. 1. Reg. II. 36. III. 1. quemadmodum cælum ipsum, in quo excellentissima ratione Deus Angelis, & electis sese manifestat, domus DEI vocatur, Joh. XIV. 2. Quum itaque in Ecclesia vel cœtu ac communione sanctorum Deus præstò esse, ac sese manifestare per verbum ac Sacramenta dignetur, Ecclesia domus Dei merito vocatur, in qua œco- nomi sunt verbi ministri, 1. Cor. IV. 1. Paterfa- milias est Deus, domestici sunt fideles, Eph. II. 19. qui fidei domestici dicuntur Gal. II. 16. Funda- mentum principale est Christus, 1. Cor. III. 9. Or- ganicum vero est doctrina Prophetarum & Aposto- lorum, Eph. II. 20.

## 3:15
pillar and ground of the truth) These are titles of the Church: and it is a wonder how those who begrudge them to her labor to connect these words with the following period. Other things are repugnant to them, as well as that article, which is placed before τῆς εὐσεβείας μυ- στήριον, which article shows that it is a new sense, not a continuation of the titles with the following, and that that mystery is placed subjectively, not predicatively, as the Schools speak. The Apostle, having made mention of the Temple, took up a new similitude from the Temple. In the Temple there were columns עַמּוּדִים. Those columns had their bases or ἑδραιώ- ματα: אֲדָנִים but just as the column [rests] on the base, so the work above rested on the column. He compares the truth here to the work above: the Church, especially the universal one, but also those parts which adhere to the universal, to the column and the base, that is, καὶ ἑ- δραιώματι, the column having a base. The Church sustains and lifts up the truth, it causes it not to slip from minds, it causes it to be seen far and wide. For the testimony of many upright men, who all say that they received those dogmas, those precepts from the Apostles, has great force among men who are not obstinate. Nor should this title given to the Church seem invidious, since a wife is also called the pillar of her husband Sir. XXVI. 16. Tob. VIII. 5. a support.

The Lord Dr. Sebastian Schmid in his Collegium Biblicum post. p. 301. (2 Kings VII. Jer. LII.) wishes us to look at the columns made in the temple of Solomon for the sake of ornament, whose function was not to sustain anything, but they were in themselves a notable work and an ornament of the temple: and he notes that the Church is called the column and firmament of the truth passively, (as the house of God is taken passively, because it was built by God, and God dwells in it,) partly because it was erected by the heavenly truth, partly because it holds and professes the same truth dwelling in it, which he proves from the scope, because the Apostle exhorts Timothy to conduct himself in the Ephesian Church according to the divine word, by this argument, that the Church is the column of the truth, erected by it, and to be further built up through it. Whence the Church is not considered by reason of the office which it performs for the truth, but by reason of the edification through the Ecclesiastical ministry, and so passively, as to be built up into a column and firmament of the truth, so that, built up through the truth, it may firmly hold the truth, and have the same dwelling within itself. There is no reason, therefore, why we should begrudge these titles to the Church, nor do Camero and others, who refer these titles to the mystery of godliness, do so out of envy toward the Church. But neither should more than is just be attributed to these titles of the Church with Grotius, as if the Church sustains and lifts up the truth. For the Apostle does not call it the base or foundation, but a pillar or firmament. The only foundation is Christ, 1 Cor. III. 9. and His word, in which He is prominent, and Christ sustains the role of its cornerstone, Eph. II. 20. Since this is the foundation of the Church, it cannot be established that this (I mean the Church) is the foundation of Holy Scripture, which is the word of God and heavenly truth. Therefore, Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 1, calls Scripture the foundation of faith, not the Church. We have known the disposition of our salvation through no others than those through whom the Gospel came to us, which indeed they then proclaimed, but afterwards by the will of God handed down to us in the Scriptures, to be the foundation and pillar of our faith. If by hendiadys the Church is called στύλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα, a pillar resting on a base, it is not the base itself, for nothing rests upon itself. If, therefore, the pillar of truth were to be taken not passively, but actively, the Church would be a pillar resting upon the base or foundation of Scripture, or built upon the foundation of Scripture, and a pillar of truth in that, like a pillar, it supports, sustains among men, interprets, guards, preserves from destruction, and transmits to posterity the same by its ministry; which sense Blessed Gerhard defends in his work on the Church, § 116, against Bellarmine. Or, if one prefers with Blessed Meisner, in his treatise on the Church, to depart from this architectural meaning and take 'pillar' in the forensic sense, just as in courts or before praetoria laws and decrees of the magistrate are posted on pillars by public authority, the Church performs the role of such a pillar, by which heavenly edicts [are posted], regarding which use of pillars see Josephus, book 1 of Antiquities, chapter 49; Pliny, book 6 of Natural History, chapter 29; Alexand. ab Alex., book 3 of Genialium Dierum, chapter 7. To the former explanation

The passage cited from St. Irenaeus agrees excellently with Mr. Schmid, nor is that one inconsistent, in our judgment at least.

Latin:

στύλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα τῆς ἀληθείας) Tituli hi sunt Eccle- siæ: cui qui eos invident, mirum quam laborent ut hæc verba sequenti periodo connectant. Eis tum alia repu- gnant, tum illud τὸ, quod ponitur ante τῆς εὐσεβείας μυ- στήριον, qui articulus ostendit novum esse sensum, non ti- tulorum cum sequentibus continuationem, & illud μυ- στήριον poni subjective, non prædicativè, ut Scholæ lo- quuntur. Apostolus, mentione facta Templi, novam de Templo sumpsit similitudinem. In Templo erant colu- עַמּוּדִים. Iis columnis suæ erant bases sive ἑδραιώ- ματα: אֲדָנִים at sicut columnæ basi, ita opus superius columnæ innitebatur. Veritatem hic comparat operi su- pero: Ecclesiam maxime universalem, sed & eas partes, quæ universali adhærent, columnæ & basi, id est, καὶ ἐ- δραιώματι columnæ basim habenti. Veritatem sustentat atque attollit Ecclesia, efficit ne elabatur ex animis, efficit ut longe lateque conspiciatur. Magnam enim vim apud homines non contumaces habet testimonium multorum hominum proborum, qui omnes ajunt se ista dogmata, ista præcepta ab Apostolis accepisse. Nec invidiosus videri de- bet hic datus Ecclesiæ titulus, cum & uxor dicatur viri στύ- λος Sir. XVI. 36. Tob. VIII. 5. ἕρεισμα.

Columnas in templo Salomonis ornatus causa factas respici vult Dn. D. Sebast. Schmidius Colleg. Bibl. post. p. 301. (2. Reg. VII. Jer. LII.) quarum of- ficium non erat, ut aliquid sustentarent, sed per se insigne erant opus, & templi ornamentum: no- tatque columnam & firmamentum veritatis Eccle- siam passivè dici, (ut oἶκος Dei passivè sumitur, quod à Deo extructa sit, & Deus in ea habitet,) partim quod à veritate cælesti erecta sit, partim quod eandem veritatem in se habitantem teneat, & profiteatur, quod probat à scopo, quia hortatur Apostolus Timotheum, ut in Ecclesia Ephesina secundum verbum divinum conversetur, argu- mento hoc, quod Ecclesia sit columna veritatis, ab ea extructa, & per eam porrò exædificanda. Un- de Ecclesia non consideratur ratione officii, quod ræstat veritati, sed ratione ædificationis per mini- sterium Ecclesiasticum, adeoq; passivè, ut exædi- ficanda in columnam & firmamentum veritatis, ut per veritatem extructa firmiter teneat veritatem, eandemq; in se habeat habitantem. Non ergo est, quod invideamus titulos hosce Ecclesiæ, neque Camero & alii, qui ad mysterium pietatis referunt hos titulos, invidiæ erga Ecclesiam causa id faci- unt. Sed nec plus justo tribuendum est cum Gro- tio titulis istis Ecclesiæ, quasi veritatem sustentet atque attollat Ecclesia. Non enim basin seu fun- damentum, sed στύλον vel firmamentum dicit Apo- stolus. Fundamentum unicum est Christus, 1. Cor. III. 9. & verbum ejus, in quo eminet, & lapidis ejus angularis vicem sustinet Christus, Eph. II. 20. Quod cum Ecclesiæ fundamentum sit, hæc (Eccle- siam dico) fundamentum Scripturæ S. quæ ver- bum Dei & veritas cælestis est, statui non potest. Ideo Irenæus lib. 3. cap. 1. Scripturam vocat funda- mentum fidei, non Ecclesiam. Non per alios dispo- sitionem salutis nostræ cognovimus, quam per eos, per quos Evangelium pervenit ad nos, quod quidem tunc præconiarunt, postea vero per Dei voluntatem in Scripturis nobis tradiderunt fundamentum & co- lumnam fidei nostræ futurum. Si per hendyaden Ec- clesia dicitur στύλος καὶ ἑδραίωμα columna basi in- nixa non est ipsa basis, nec enim sibi ipsi idem in- nititur. Si itaque maxime non passivè, sed activè columna veritatis acciperetur, columna erit basi vel fundamento Scripturæ innixa, vel super funda- mentum Scripturæ extructa Ecclesia, & columna veritatis, quod instar columnæ eandem suo mini- sterio suffulciat, inter homines sustentet, inter- pretetur, custodiat, ab interitu vindicet, & ad po- steros transmittat, quem sensum B. Gerhardus de Ecclesia §. 116. contra Bellarminum vindicat, vel si discedere quis cum B. Meisnero tract. de Ecclesia, malit ab hoc significatu architectonico, & columna sensu forensi accipere, prout in curiis, vel ante præ- toria in columnis leges & decreta Magistratus pu- blica autoritate appenduntur, columnæ ejusmo- di vicem præstat, quà cælestia edicta, de quo usu columnarum Josephus lib. 1. antiquit. cap. 49. Plinius lib. VI. Ant. Histor. cap. 29. Alexand. ab Alex. l. III. Genial. dier. c. 7. Priori explicationi

Dn. Schmidii convenit eximiè locus laudatus S. Irenæi, nec inconcinna est ea, nostro quidem ju- dicio.

## 3:16
Ver. 16. And confessedly great is the mystery of godliness) He says, it is not a matter here of just any truth, but of that which no man could discover by himself, and which has the greatest power to generate piety in us, before which all the precepts and dogmas of the law and of the philosophers vanish, confessedly. The Latins say undoubtedly, plainly, beyond controversy, assuredly; for the same thing is put ὁμολόγως. The Gospel is often called a mystery, not only because it lay hidden for so long, but also because it cannot be discovered by human industry, Matt. XVI. 17. The genitive εὐσεβείας here designates the effect. In the same sense this truth is said to be, according to godliness 1 Tim. I. Here GOD is said to have given us in Christ all things that pertain to piety, Romans I. ver. 3.

God was manifested in the flesh) Ancient interpreters, the Latin, the Syrian, the Arab, and Ambrose, make this reading suspect to us, all of whom read ὃ ἐφανερώθη. Hincmar adds in his Opusculum LV that this word God was placed here by the Nestorians. That ὃ ἐφανερώθη makes good sense. That heavenly Gospel was made known first, not through angels, but through mortal men, and as far as the outward appearance went, weak ones, Christ and His Apostles. ἐφανερώθη is דאתגלי in the Syrian. That word agrees well with a mystery, that is, a hidden thing. So also Coloss. I. 26. Σὰρξ, בשר, signifies mortal man. 2 Cor. II. 16. See 1 John IV. ver. 2 and what will be said on that passage.

He was justified in the spirit) That truth was approved by very many miracles. Πνεῦμα are divine miracles, by metonymy, which is also in 1 Cor. II. 4 and elsewhere. Δικαιωθῆναι, however, here is to approve, as in Matt. XI. 19, where see the remarks. Thus he is called הצדיק who is the victor in a lawsuit, because his cause is approved, Deut. XXV. 1. Add Ps. CXVI.

He was seen by angels) Namely, with the greatest admiration. The angels learned this secret through mortal men, Eph. III. 10, 1 Pet. I. 12. To see is transferred among the Hebrews to every mode of knowing.

He was preached among the nations) That truth was announced not only to the Jews, but also to those nations which had been most alien from God. Eph. II. 12, Coloss. I. 21, ἐν ἔθνεσι among the nations, לגויים.

He was believed on in the world) that is, in a great part of the world, Roman. I. 8, Col. I. 6.

He was received up in glory) It was exalted most gloriously, namely because it brought much greater holiness than any dogmas before it; ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι is to be taken up and sublimely elevated, and it corresponds to the Hebrew words נטל and נעלה. Ἐν δόξῃ gloriously, Phil. IV. 19, Col. III. 4. See also 2 Cor. III. 8. Thus ἐδόξαζον τὸν λόγον τῦ κυρίε. Acts XIII. 48.

This detestable audacity must be attributed to the Socinian heresy: which we already defeated twenty-nine years ago in the chief of its champions in the Apodixis of the Deity of Christ: but because that has not yet seen the light, we have decided to insert the same here.

And thus the argument for the eternal Deity of CHRIST, taken from this truly classic Apostolic passage, stands.

He who appeared in the flesh is true and essential GOD. But the Son of God appeared in the flesh. Therefore the Son of God is true and essential God. The major premise is established by the words of the Apostle. For He who appeared in the flesh (1) is called God absolutely, which name we have proved elsewhere to be significative of the divine essence, and not to be used absolutely in the singular except of the true and essential God. (2) He is called God subjectively. God appeared in the flesh. But the adversaries hold this as an undoubted mark of the true and essential God, when the word God occurs somewhere subjectively. (3) He is celebrated here as the confessedly great mystery of godliness, that God appeared in the flesh. But for some God, named so nominally and metaphorically, to be flesh, or to be manifested in the flesh, is no mystery at all, much less a great mystery of piety beyond controversy. For what? Is it not sufficiently known that many others, who are called Gods nominally, are flesh? It is acknowledged that magistrates, Moses, and other mortal men have been so called nominally. It follows (4) that whenever it is mentioned simply that God appeared, it is to be understood that God himself, the most high, appeared and manifested himself. Which is shown without difficulty by an induction of passages. Thus, therefore, this most high God is likewise to be understood here with the Apostle: θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκὶ. (5) Furthermore, who could be understood besides the most high God? Perhaps some created Angel? But GOD, who appeared in the flesh, is contradistinguished from the Angels: while this also is celebrated as a great mystery of godliness, that God, who was manifested in the flesh, willed to appear to the Angels and to be seen by them. It is certain, therefore, that an Angel cannot be understood. But perhaps some man? But a man does not appear in the flesh, but is flesh himself, nor is he more sublime than the Angels, nor is it to be believed that he is a mere man, just as it is not to be believed that he is an Angel, nor finally is this a great mystery of godliness, that a man consists of flesh and is seen in the flesh: since there is no one among men who does not consist of flesh and blood. Who then is left to be understood, if not the most high God, especially because the name of God is personal, and the predicates which occur here can be understood only of a person? Moreover, it is well known that besides God, men, and Angels, no other persons exist. (6) He is understood by the name of God who ἐκηρύχθη ἐν ἔθνεσιν, ἐπισεύ- θη ἐν κόσμῳ, preached among the nations, believed in the world. But what God, besides the one true God, has both been preached among the nations and believed in the world? The Apostle certainly professes that there is only one true God of the Christians, 1. Cor. VIII. 4. nor will it be taught that more gods were ever preached by the Apostles or believed in by Christians, since it was the way of the Gentiles, not of Christians, to worship many gods. (7) But the preceding context also sufficiently teaches that no one else is understood than that one God who is called the true God, and to whom the Church is claimed as his house, v. 15. (8) Why many words? The adversaries themselves admit that by the name θεῦ, that one true God is to be understood in this place: as can be seen in Enjedinus, Socinus, and all the others without exception. But as for the minor premise, although it is clear in itself, yet all things, even the most manifest, are called into doubt by the adversaries; therefore, we note these things for the sake of confirmation: (1) That this appearance in the flesh which occurred in the time of the New Testament is ascribed and claimed in the Holy Scriptures to no one else who is designated as God, except the Son of GOD: who is also designated as God, John I., c. XX. 28, Acts XX. v. 28. Rom. IX. 5. etc., and is said to have been made flesh, John I. 14. Made a partaker of flesh and blood, Heb. II. 14. According to the flesh he is from the Fathers, Rom. IX. 5. Born of the Seed of David according to the flesh, Rom. I. 3. Came in the flesh, 1 John IV. 2, 3, etc., and thus God manifested in the flesh is rightly said according to the tenor of the Holy Scriptures. (2) Wherever flesh is attributed in the N.T. to him who is also established by the scriptures to be God, there Christ is understood. Which is evident from an induction of passages, John I. 14, VI. 53, Acts II. 31, Rom. I. 3, VIII. 3, IX. 5, Eph. II. 14, 15, Col. I. 22, Heb. II. 14, v. 7, X. 19, 20, 1 Pet. III. 18, IV. 1, 1 John IV. v. 2, 3, 1 John V. 6, etc. (3) He is understood here as manifested in the flesh, who exerted and manifested his divine power and glory in the time of the N.T., in the flesh and through the flesh, and rendered his glory conspicuous to all, and demonstrated himself as GOD. But it cannot be denied that this was done in the Son of God in the days of his flesh, in the time of the New Testament, which various miracles and the Evangelical history most clearly testify, John I. 14, ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο, and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, John 2:11. Christ ἐφανέρωσε manifested his glory and his disciples believed in him. Cf. John 7:3 and the sermons of Christ in John 5 and 10, etc. (4) This discourse is about that Φανέρωσῃ Θεῦ ἐν σαρκὶ [manifestation of God in the flesh], which was finally brought to pass in the time of the New Testament, and which ought to be considered, beyond controversy, a great mystery of godliness. But what other manifestation of this kind could be brought forth from the Scriptures, besides the very appearance of the Son of God in the flesh?
