(5) Scripture explains this very manifestation elsewhere, and ascribes the same to the Son of God. 1 John 1:2, the life ἐφανερώθη, was manifested, appeared, and we saw it and testify to it, and we announce to you that eternal life which was with the Father, and appeared to us. With a great display of words it describes that appearance, as a new and admirable mystery; just as here Paul celebrates as a great mystery of godliness the Φανέρωσιν Θεῦ ἐν σαρκὶ [manifestation of God in the flesh]. What? That τὸ Φανερωθῆναι [the being manifested] is always ascribed in the New Testament to the Son of God when the discourse is about his person, but never to God the Father, as is evident from the induction of passages: Mark 16:12, 14; John 7:4; ch. 21:1, 14; Col. 3:4; Heb. 9:26; 1 Pet. 1:20; ch. 5:4; 1 John 3:5 & 8. Therefore, this manifestation must also be understood here as concerning Christ, because of the perpetual tenor of Scripture, not the Father. (5) Who can doubt that the God who was justified in the Spirit in the time of the New Testament is Christ? For was not Christ ἐδικαιώθη justified, acknowledged as the true Messiah, and celebrated? And was not that done ἐν πνεύματι in the Spirit and through the Spirit, whether through his own Deity or through the power of the Spirit by which he was anointed? For that word 'to be justified' is often the same as to be acknowledged as true, praised, and celebrated, as in Luke 7:19, Matt. 11:19, Rom. 3:4. which latter passage Smalcius himself compares here, and acknowledges that 'God was justified in the Spirit' is nothing other than that he was acknowledged as true through the divine power exerting itself in Christ. But that is taught everywhere concerning Christ, that by such proofs the Spirit showed him to be that true Messiah, and truly the Son of God, and that he was sufficiently acknowledged and celebrated from that, not only by the Apostles but also by other believers. (6) Furthermore, of whom will it be more rightly explained that he was seen particularly by angels, ὤφθη ἀγγέλοις, than of Christ? Who saw the Son of God manifested in the flesh lying in a manger, Luke 2:13; who saw him prevailing in the desert against the Devil, Matt. 4:11; who saw and strengthened him struggling in his agony, Luke 22:43; who saw him rising from the dead, Matt. 29:2, Mark 16:1, Luke 24:4; they saw him gloriously ascending, Acts 1:10. (7) Who, moreover, does not know that Christ was particularly preached to the Gentiles as the great mystery of godliness? We preach, says the Apostle in 1 Cor. 1:23-24, Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles foolishness, but to those who are called, both Jews and Gentiles, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God: and 1 Cor. 2:2, For I did not judge myself to know anything among you, εἰ μὴ EXCEPT Jesus Christ, and him crucified. v. 7, We speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, hidden, etc. The whole New Testament Scripture testifies concerning him that Christ was particularly preached to the Gentiles in the time of the New Testament, Luke 24:46-47, Acts 3:20, ch. 8:5, ch. 9:20, ch. 19:13, 1 Cor. 15:12, Heb. 1:19, ch. 4:5, ch. 11:4, Phil. 1:15. Who, therefore, would doubt, when the discourse is about him who was particularly preached to the Gentiles in the time of the New Testament, in the apostolic phraseology frequently used everywhere, that Christ is understood? (8) Who, furthermore, is there who in the time of the New Testament was particularly believed in the world, if that is not Christ? Since the whole New Testament Scripture is full of the faith to be placed in Christ, and particularly what was written and done tends to this, that we might believe that Jesus is the Christ, and through faith in his name might have life, John 20:20-21. Therefore, if anything else is inculcated and required, certainly the command of faith in Christ is not; John 1:12, ch. 2:11, ch. 3:17, 18, 35, 36, ch. 6:40, Acts 10:43, ch. 16:3, Rom. 3:22, ch. 10:8, 9, Gal. 2:16, 1 John 1:5, and elsewhere everywhere in all New Testament writings, so that there can be no doubt again that, according to the tenor of the apostolic style, this ἐπιστεύθη 'was believed in the world' also looks to Christ and pertains to the same. (9) Who, finally, ἀνελήφθη 'was taken up' in glory in the time of the New Testament besides Christ, whose ascension into heaven is expressly called ἀνάληψις in Luke 9:51 was taken up into heaven, Mark 16:19, and absolutely ἀνελήφθη 'was taken up' in Acts 1:11, etc. Which ascension of Christ was done ἐν δόξῃ 'in glory,' just as he is to return with glory, Luke 21:27. For he will come in the same way as you saw him ascending into heaven, Acts 1:11. He ascended with angels serving him, a cloud taking him up in a manner as miraculous as it was entirely glorious, Acts 1:10. He ascended in such a way that he sat down at the right hand of majesty and glory in the highest. He was not carried up to heaven in the manner of Elijah, but in glory, explains Theophylact: While he was being taken up, angels were ministering to him in the clouds. Thus also Beza: He was received up into glory. (Smalcius asserts in his disputation on the refutation of the incarnation, p. 21, that the Greek word ἐν is perhaps never taken in that way, or at least very rarely, but Smalcius is refuted by not a few examples: Mark 1:15, Luke 1:17, ch. 2:12, ch. 21:22, Rom. 1:23, 24, 25, 1 Thess. 4:7, 1 John 4:9, Heb. 4:10 &c.) For this reason he says 'in glory': because the very being taken up is glorious. Ὅτι καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ἀναληφθῆναι ἔνδοξόν ἐστι, says Oecumenius in this place. The Syriac translates: He was lifted up into glory. B. Luther: taken up into glory. Which can be understood and explained of no one else but Christ. (10) Finally, the holy Church has always and with unanimous suffrage understood this mystery of godliness, this manifestation in the flesh, to be understood of Christ, from whose interpretation, fortified by so many reasons, it is a capital danger for us to depart. All Greek commentators have accepted it as concerning Christ. Chrysostom, homily 2 on 1 Tim. 3; Cyril to the Kings; Theodoret, Oecumenius, Theophylact in this place, etc. The Latins also, although they read in the Latin editions, 'which (sacrament) was manifested in the flesh,' nevertheless accepted it with a constant and unanimous opinion concerning the Son of God made visible in the flesh, and by the word 'Sacrament' understood Christ himself, metonymically, because the mystery is about Christ, as the object, as Guil. Estius notes in h. l. B. Hieron. Tom. VIII. in Comment. h. l. p. m. 384. He explains the 'Sacrament of godliness' as the Sacrament of the incarnation of Christ, through which godliness was conferred upon the human race, etc. August. Comm. in h. l. T. V. oper. p. m. 395. 'The sacrament of the mystery of God, which is Christ, he says was manifested in the flesh, which was hidden in the Spirit.' For the Son of God, born man, who was in secret with God, declared himself to the creature by work and preaching, and this is, 'justified in the Spirit' by works and mighty works, that he who was in the flesh had shone forth, that he was, etc. Nor did Anselm, and others, think otherwise. What of the fact that Erasmus himself, however much he may drag certain attributes toward the preaching of the Gospel by the neck, nevertheless could hardly explain some things otherwise than of Christ, his birth and ascension into heaven, along with the orthodox Fathers and the whole Church of Christ; inasmuch as he says it was seen by the angels, who sang (at the birth of Christ, not at the manifestation of the Gospel made to the whole world) 'Glory to God in the highest,' and received after the resurrection into heaven, from whence it had proceeded, which he could not say except of the Word and Son of God.

The adversaries object, (1) That the Latin editions have the pronoun 'Quod' [which] instead of the word GOD, and refer the manifestation in the flesh not to God, but to the mystery of godliness, the Syriac reading also supporting this: which reading Socinus says seems much more convenient to him (contr. Volan. p. 249), and Smalcius appeals to the same (homil. IIX. in 1. Joh. p. 89), as do also Volckel (de ver. relig. p. 462) and Enjedinus, who wishes to teach that the Latin word is a corruption of the Greek reading, and that it is ancient, by the argument that the ancients, who fought fiercely against Arius, placed no support in this testimony (p. 361); and then, having admitted the word 'God', they contend that it must be taken not of the Son of God, but of the Father, since there is nothing at all that cannot be accommodated to God the Father, which Socinus pursues at greater length. Smalcius: what absurdity is there, he says (ref. thes. de incarnat. p. 6). if it be said that the will of God was manifested through weak and mortal men? (3) Whatever is said here concerning manifestation and justification ought to be accepted in such a way that it pertains not to discussing the essence of God, but to commending the authority of the doctrine of Christ, from the reason of the preceding words and the purpose of the Apostle, says Enjedinus, since it is a matter of the excellence of the Church and of the ecclesiastical office. (4) The same Enjedinus objects that those things—to be seen, to be beheld, to be justified, to be taken up into heaven—do not befit the eternal and infinite Word, since an invisible spirit fills all things, and can neither be seen nor transferred from place to place. (5) Schlichting (de Trin. p. 479) also urges that manifestation under the New Testament is not accustomed to signify the exhibition of a divine person, but only the revelation of those things which pertain to the knowledge of God and His will. (6) That this is no mystery, that God incarnate was seen by Angels, or taken up on high and into heaven. (7) That, finally, those things are in no sense said, nor do they cohere: God is incarnate, and justified in the Spirit. (8) Finally, Smalcius (contr. Grav. p. 9) urges that that God, who was manifested in the flesh, is said to have been received into glory after He was preached to the Gentiles and believed on in the world. But Christ was received into glory on high before He was preached to the Gentiles. Thus also Enjedinus in this place, as also Socinus in the place cited. These, therefore, are the things which the adversaries object to our proof: which are, however, easily dissolved.

As to (1) I reply: The Christomachs cannot rely sufficiently safely on the Latin version, since it is also admittedly certain to them that not the Latin translation, or any other version whatsoever, but only the Greek text in the Scripture of the New Testament ought to be held as divinely inspired. The reading of the Latin interpretation, says Crell (l. de un. Deo pat. sect. 2. c. 10. p. 154), ought to yield to the reading of the Greek codices, which agree among themselves, and be corrected from it. (2) But that which Enjedinus argues concerning the corrupted Greek text, he can show by no document; certainly, the corruption of the Greek text is most ineptly inferred from the different reading of the Latin version. Nor is it right to argue from that, that the ancients are not read to have used this testimony against the Arians, since many other proofs of the divinity of Christ are read in the authentic texts, Hebrew and Greek, which the ancients did not produce against the Arians. But must it be concluded immediately that those things did not exist of old in the Hebrew and Greek text? What? That the Greek interpreters did not doubt that both the Deity of the Son of God and His incarnation were insinuated in this place, as can be seen from Cyril, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and others. Indeed, says Chrysostom, the mystery is most truly preached as great. For God made man, and man God, man appeared without sin, man was taken up, was preached in the world, the Angels saw Him with us. Add that Theophylact dares to profess, concerning this place, that no one passes over that God is incarnate. Compare also Athanasius de resurr. Carnis. (3) But because the adversaries harp on the variant reading, in order to conclude that nothing certain can be concluded from this place, since Smalcius (ref. disp. de incarnat. p. 6) asserts that it is more true than it needs to be proved that nothing certain can be concluded from places whose reading is variant. In the Old Testament, indeed, there are not a few places of different readings indicated by the Masoretic marginal notes, Qere and Ketiv. But that far more occur in the New, the Observations of Stephanus, Valla, Beza, Casaubon, Ludovicus de Dieu, Johannes Morinus, and others teach. But if you should wish to value not only those different readings which happen to be found in the sources, but also those which are detected by the contention of the ancient interpreters—the LXX, the Vulgate, and also the Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, Coptic, and others in the New Testament (as here Smalcius points out a different reading of the Vulgate version itself)—you will collect a monstrous number of differently read sayings of Scripture! Apply now to all these the Smalcian axiom, and infinite testimonies of Scripture will be rendered uncertain, and will be able to prove nothing. Not to mention that the Socinians themselves sometimes call upon those places in proof whose reading occurs as variant, not only if you compare among themselves the editions of the Vulgate Latin and other ancient translations, but also different copies of the authentic text itself. But they will by no means admit that all those proofs are uncertain and vain. Therefore, that postulate must necessarily be corrected, which we restrict thus: From places whose reading is variant, nothing certain can be concluded, if, namely, first, that variety of reading is in the sources or the authentic text, not only in the translations themselves: and if, secondly, it is so constituted that which of the variant readings is the truer is altogether uncertain, and cannot be defined: if, finally, thirdly, they do not only differ word for word, but also render different meanings. But that a various reading occurs here in the Greek sources themselves, not even Smalcius himself dared to assert with certainty. Although Volckelius indeed contends more boldly that the word God is by no means contained in all Greek codices, he was nevertheless unable to name any in which it was missing. Nor has anyone been found thus far who has testified that he has discovered any Greek codex, whether manuscript or printed, ancient or modern, in which that word was missing. Robert observed no discrepancy here among the Greek copies. Stephanus, who collated seventeen Greek codices most diligently, and among them the most ancient ones sought out with the greatest care; the authors of the Complutensian edition, who employed the most corrected and ancient archetypal copies in every respect, as well as the most ancient codices of the Vatican Library, noted no discrepancy; Hervagius, who annotated various discrepant readings from a collation of the best copies and appended them to the Basel edition of the year 1545, noticed none. Laurentius Valla compared the Vulgate version with various Greek codices, but found no Greek codex omitting the word θεὸς; therefore he notes in his collation of the New Testament at this passage: What is read in the neuter (in the Vulgate) should be read in the masculine, and GOD should be added. For so it is in Greek. Aldus, who published the Greek text at Venice in the year 1518 after collating many most ancient copies, retained the word Θεὸς. Theodore Beza, who not only in his second revision most accurately collated the 17 Greek codices cited by Robert Stephanus, but also used the Claromontane copy of wonderful antiquity, observes in his edition of the N.T. that all Greek Codices PERPETUALLY by consensus disagree with the Latin Vulgate reading. Sebastian Castellio also read in his own Codices & rendered according to the Greek Exemplars 'God appeared in the flesh.' Erasmus himself, who likewise used various and most ancient Greek Codices, did not dare to deny that the word Θεῦ is read in all Codices, but rather confesses that it is so held in Greek, Θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκὶ, and that the things which follow refer to God. Finally, the modern Pontificians, who after the decree of the Council of Trent strive in every way to defend the Vulgate reading, and who defend the translation of their Interpreter against the common Greek reading by the authority of certain Greek exemplars, such as they can, nevertheless cannot deny here that the Greek exemplars constantly retain the word τῦ Θεῦ, nor can they bring forward any Greek Codex that supports the Latin translation. And therefore, even against their will, Corn. à Lapide and Guil. Estius in their Commentaries on this passage yield the palm here to the Greek reading. Furthermore, that this reading is not at least of the modern Greek Codices, as Enjedinus cavils, but also of the most ancient ones, is testified both by the most ancient exemplars collated by the aforementioned authors, and by the monuments of the ancient Greek Interpreters, from whom not one can be brought forward who read otherwise. And Corn. with Estius professes that the Greek expositors read it thus. à Lap. and Erasmus acknowledges, such as Cyril, Chrysostom, Theophylact. Nor did Athanasius in his work on the resurrection of the Flesh, or any other of the Greek Doctors, read it differently. To which is added the consideration of the subjects of this matter, which are indeed so arranged that God ought rather to be placed beneath them in the place of the subject, than that the mystery of godliness should appear. For what? Has Doctrine appeared in the flesh? Has it been seen by Angels? Has it been received up again into glory? Furthermore, the description of the mystery favors the Greek reading more than the Latin. For that God was made visible in the flesh, and whatever else is said there about God, is most deservedly designated as μυσήριον τῆς εὐσεβείας, and indeed a confessedly great mystery, concerning which Dionysius c. 2 of the Divine Names says: The appearance of Jesus in the flesh is ineffable in all speech, and unknown to all intelligence, not known even to the prince of the Angels himself. But that the doctrine of God was manifested in the flesh, that is, through weak men, is by no means a mystery of such a kind and hidden, or a secret of righteousness, as the Syrian and Arab render it, great and stupendous by the confession of all the pious. (5) As regards the Syriac translation, that it not rarely deviates from the true and genuine reading, these examples among others teach: Matt. VI. 18, ch. IX. 13, ch. XI. 23, ch. XXIV. 36, ch. XXV. 13, Mark I. 2, ch. II. 17, Luke IV. 8, V. 7, VI. 43, John VIII. 1 seqq., Acts VIII. 37, 1 John V. 8. Although I do not know whether in this place a differing reading occurs in all editions of the Syriac interpretation. For although in the Cothenian exemplar in quarto format, as also in the Plantinian of smaller format expressed in Hebrew character, the word God does not appear, nevertheless it seems to be concluded from his translation that the word אלהא was read by Tremellius, rather than that we should conclude with Socinus that this most learned and diligent man had fallen significantly, because he expounded it: especially since we see that others also read the Syriac text thus, among whom are Cornel. à Lap. and Guil. Estius. And so it is likely that the other reading drew its origin from the Latin Vulgate, which one may observe also in other places of this interpretation. We judge that the same is to be determined concerning the Arabic translation in this place, which we have noted elsewhere to depart from the fountains of truth in quite a few places. (6) But as concerns the Latin Vulgate, it is very well known that it lies in very many errors, after the Sixtine and Clementine correction, and in almost countless places disagrees with the θεοπνεύστοις words. And so it is no wonder if it also deviates from the true reading in this place. And we judge that this is rather to be maintained (whatever the cause of this discrepancy may be) than that the faith of the holy Ancients should be called into question with Erasmus, who, it rightly smells, says that 'God' was added against the Arian heretics; although a little before he was still ambiguous as to which reading is truer, the Greek or the Latin? So prone is he to suspicion in such matters, which can also be seen in his annotations on Matt. XXIV. 36 and John V. 7. But Beza more correctly believes that the name of God was removed by those who denied either the divinity of Christ, or the union of both natures from the very moment of conception. Which Cornelius à Lap. also approves, and brings forward this reason for the matter: namely, that some Greek Codices formerly read ὁ θεὸς or ὃς θεὸς; but Macedonius the Nestorian corrupted this passage, reading ὡς for ὃς, and thus interpreted it, so that (the man Jesus could be called, and) he was God, God appeared through the flesh and dwelt in the body of Jesus. Some Codices formerly read ὁ θεὸς or ὃς θεὸς; but Macedonius the Nestorian corrupted this passage, reading ὡς for ὃς, and thus interpreted it, so that (the man Jesus could be called, and) he was God, God appeared through the flesh and dwelt in the body of Jesus. Estius confirms this with his own vote, and brings forward Liberatus the Deacon in Breviar. c. XIX as a witness to that fact. And therefore he notes that the Vulgate interpreter accepted the word 'Quod' as a determinative conjunction and that the word 'God' ought to be understood in his translation, having taken the conjecture from the Syriac interpretation, which he says holds it thus: 'Great is this mystery of righteousness, that God was manifested in the flesh.' What of the fact that Smalcius says that not all, but only very many exemplars of the Latin translation omit the word 'God,' and therefore he easily admits a various reading in the Latin editions, whence not undeservedly the constant reading of the Greeks is preferred to the doubtful Latin exemplars. Which the Racovians also expressed in their German Translation of the New Testament: GOtt ist geoffenbaret worden im Fleisch. Thus also Franc. Davidis, a fellow-soldier of the Socinians in attacking the supreme Deity of the Son of God in Art. Colloqu. Transylv. dec. 3. Deus manifestatus est in carne. Nay, Smalcius even acknowledged the sincerity of the Greek reading, and ingenuously professed that it is to be preferred to the Latin, in his book de verb. incarn. c. 18. All the Greek Exemplars, he says, CONSTANTLY HAVE THE WORD GOD. And furthermore: We judge that the Greek text is to be preferred by far to the Vulgate; but it has that God was manifested in the flesh. And therefore he repeatedly asserts, We confess with Paul that God appeared in the flesh; And we say that God was manifested in the flesh. I pass over the fact that a universal corruption of all modern Greek Codices must be posited, if anyone should say that the word Θεὸς, which is read in all of them, is an interpolation? Which is contrary to divine wisdom, nor is it admitted by the Socinians themselves; And these things concerning the reading of the text.

As to (2) Resp. We showed above that the word God in this place is to be taken concerning the Son of God. Ex abundanti, that it is not to be understood concerning God the Father, and that the Socinian gloss ought by no means to be admitted (namely, that they wish the will of God the Father to have been manifested through weak and mortal men, Christ and the Apostles, as Enjed. and Smalcius de verb. incarnat. c. 18. p. 107. and others wish) we teach by these points. (1) Because since this gloss is new, and hitherto unheard of in the Church, it can be established or supported by no firm reason. For that which they uniquely bring forward, that where the word θεὸς holds the place of the subject, the Father is perpetually understood, is slippery, begs the question, and has been solidly destroyed heretofore. (2) Because nowhere in the New Testament is the manifestation in the flesh attributed to God the Father: nowhere is God the Father said to have been manifested in the flesh, using the works of men to declare His will. Smalcius babbles in vain in the place cited. How can God conveniently manifest Himself to flesh, that is, to mortal men, except through flesh? For, not to mention that God manifested Himself in the Old Testament in many parts and in many ways, not only through flesh, but through voice, through visions, etc., it is one thing to be manifested through flesh, and another to appear in the flesh, en sarki, which Smalcius confuses most wretchedly. He indeed argues against Gravius, p. 7, that 'in the flesh' can be the same as 'through the flesh,' that the word 'en' is very frequently taken for 'dia': but the consequence from 'can be' to 'is' is not valid. Even if the passages were brought forward, it would be evident that they are far different, and it is not right to depart from the proper meaning of words. Finally, no passage can be brought forward where God is said to have appeared in the flesh, because He revealed His will through the mediation of men. (3) To appear in the flesh implies presence in the flesh, that is, to exist in the flesh and to exhibit Himself to be seen in it, just as when God is said to have appeared in the burning bush, His singular presence is noted; that, however, does not befit God the Father, but the Son of God, to appear in the flesh in this way. Nor is there any reason for Smalcius to say that a manifestation of God is given even if God Himself, as to His essence, is absent, in his book on the Incarnate Word, p. 104, since God can neither be absent anywhere as to His essence, nor is He said simply to have been manifested here, but ephanerothe en sarki, He appeared IN THE FLESH. But that it does not befit God the Father to exist in the flesh and to exhibit Himself to be seen in it, the adversaries themselves acknowledge. It is certain, says Smalcius in the place cited, that God the Father can have no flesh in which He Himself might appear. It is irrelevant that Smalcius draws this in here with Socinus from John 14:9, 'He who sees me, sees also the Father.' For there it is implied that God the Father and Christ are one, but it is not said that God the Father appeared in Christ, as He is flesh. There is nothing there about the flesh of Christ, or about the appearance of the Father in the flesh of Christ. How, therefore, will these things be very remarkably to the point, as Smalcius says? (4) The opposition of flesh and Spirit has no place in God the Father, but in the Son, for that diverse respect of flesh and Spirit is not assigned to the Father in the Scriptures, but to Christ, Rom. 1:4, 9:5, 1 Pet. 3:18. (5) It is not a question here of the will of God revealed, but God Himself is said to have appeared in the flesh. But what reason compels or at least persuades that the word GOD is not to be taken properly, but metonymically for the will of GOD? From the propriety of a word, one certainly should not depart without necessity. (6) The phrase en sarki from the usage of Scripture denotes human nature, received by synecdoche. But nowhere is Christ denoted by the word sarkikos, but 'sarx' (flesh), that is, human nature, is attributed to Christ, John 1:14, Heb. 2:14. For Christ, even if He consists of flesh, is not, however, merely flesh, nor is He called flesh, or understood absolutely by the name of flesh. Let suitable examples of this matter be brought forward from the Scriptures? Again, if flesh signifies human nature, as Enjedius thinks, p. 368, then it will not designate only the will of the Father.

Smalcius here compares 1 John 4:2, 'Christ came in the flesh,' which he indeed renders, that is, 'surrounded by infirmity.' But nowhere in the Scriptures is flesh the same as infirmity, because infirmity is distinguished from flesh, Galatians 4:13, 'di' astheneian tes sarkos' (through the infirmity of the flesh). Nor is anyone ever said to have come in infirmity. And therefore something essential is introduced here, in which He came, just as the name of flesh properly signifies a substance; Christ therefore came in the flesh, that is, in human nature as a true man. Whence we conclude: He who came in the flesh, in the same He was also manifested; Christ came in the flesh, not the Father. Therefore, the things which the adversaries compare here are irrelevant: such as that 2 Cor. 4:7, for there men are said to have the treasure in earthen vessels. Here not man, but God is said to be manifested in the flesh. Nor does verse 10 & 11 imply that Christ was preached in mortal flesh, that is, through infirm men, but the discourse is about a mortal body: in which the Apostles carried about the mortification of the Lord Jesus, so that the life also might be manifested in that body of theirs; but what is this to the present passage? Other things are not even worthy of examination, since everyone can see that they are too irrelevant. (7) If nothing else is implied here than that the will of God was manifested through mortal and infirm men, this was certainly not a mystery proper to the New Testament, nor to be proposed with such a great apparatus of words: 'homologoumenos mega mysterion tes eusebeias'; without controversy great is the mystery of godliness. For was not the will of God already revealed in the Old Testament through infirm men, through Moses and the Prophets, Ps. 147:9, 10? Was this a new and hidden secret? Had that not been the ordinary method of revealing the divine will? Where is it said for that reason that God appeared in the flesh as a great mystery, because He revealed His will through mortal men? What Smalcius acknowledged, he says is not said in the Old Testament for that reason, because the will of God is at least imperfectly revealed there, but here perfectly concerning the salvation of the human race, of which elsewhere. But who will admit that the foreshadowing made through Moses and the Prophets was worth just as much as if there had been no revelation, and that none of those who existed then understood those things? What a paradox Smalcius blurted out against Gravius, p. 7. And what a transformation of words is this? First, that the word GOD is to be taken of God the Father, because it is placed subjectively. Secondly, that not God Himself, but the will of God the Father is noted: Finally, not just any will, but the perfect one (as if there were also an imperfect will of God) or concerning the salvation of the human race. But where does the word GOD denote the same as the will of GOD concerning our salvation? Why are passages or examples not brought forward from the Scriptures, since the adversaries never cease to appeal to the Scriptures elsewhere? That nothing is more frequent than for 'God' to be taken for 'the will of God,' Smalcius indeed says, but he could not bring forward any passage of Scripture. For who does not see that the passages noted in the margin, Acts 4:6, 7, retain the proper meaning of the word 'God'? (8) That God the Father is seen by the angels is not a great mystery of godliness, that is, according to the interpretation of Smalcius himself, a new, wonderful, and unknown thing, an admirable and unusual thing, according to the interpretation of Enjedinus, since the angels always see the face of the Father who is in heaven, Matt. 18:10. Nor is this discourse merely about a purely intellectual vision. It is not merely the knowledge of God that is noted, but the vision of God made conspicuous in the flesh is pointed out, which must be understood not of the Father, but of the Son of God, whom the angels saw in the flesh, as sacred history testifies. The emphasis of the word ὤφθη implies more than a mere and pure knowledge of the mind. Whence Enjedinus twists himself: at one moment he says the reading varies here, and that in certain codices 'men' is read instead of 'angels,' which indeed is so much the less suitable to God the Father, who certainly was not seen by the eyes of men made manifest in the flesh in the time of the New Testament, but is most rightly attributed to the Son of God: at another moment he observes that the word ὤφθη must be explained according to the propriety of the Hebrew language, 'was made to be seen,' that is, rendered conspicuous, was shown to men by the angels. But that which he himself with

Socinus, as also Smalcius, take refuge in the revelation of the will of God, as if they had not previously had the benevolent will of God toward the nations acknowledged; it is a vain refuge. Because the Apostle does not say that the will of God was made known to the Angels; nor could the Angels have been ignorant of the benevolent will of God toward the nations, already predicted by so many oracles of the Prophets in the Old Testament; nor is it implied in Eph. III. 10 that they were ignorant, even if it is signified that the manifold wisdom of God was made known more clearly, namely, through experimental knowledge, the actual fulfillment of the Prophets having been perceived. To say nothing of the fact that to Smalcius, in his book De Incarn. Verb. p. 105, it seems that demons are understood, not good Angels. Furthermore, here he is said to have been seen by the Angels, after he was preached among the nations. Therefore, it is not a question of that knowledge by which the calling of the nations became known to them, which in the order of nature presupposes and follows the calling itself and the preaching among the nations. Finally, the Apostle does not say, ἀποκαλύφθη, but ὤφθη τοῖς ἀγγέλοις, he was not manifested, but he was seen by the angels: and who will doubt, if it was revealed in the Church through Christ and the Apostles, that the will of God became known to the Angels? Was there any need to recount this as a wondrous mystery? (9) If the will of God revealed through the flesh is understood, through the Φανέρωσιν Θεῦ ἐν σαρκὶ, it follows that a tautology has been committed in this so vigorous exposition of the mysteries of godliness. Since afterwards it is added ἐκυρήχθη ἐν ἔθνεσιν, preached among the nations. For what else can the adversaries understand by this preaching than the manifestation and revelation of the will of God made through the Apostles? But shall we believe that the Apostle was tautological in this aphorism, so that in such a vigorous period a phrase entirely unusual is placed first, which is followed by another clearer one of the same sense, with several other diverse predicates interposed? (10) It is added that nowhere in the scriptures of the New Testament is God the Father said to be taken up or taken up in glory; it is so far from being proclaimed as a manifestly great mystery of godliness. But neither is the Gospel of Christ ever said to be taken up in glory. Let the passages be produced; to those who assert nakedly outside and beyond the Scriptures, we do not give credence. When the word of God is said to be received, the word δέχεσθαι is used, Acts II. 4, ch. VIII. 14, XI. 1. But ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι ἐν δόξῃ is nowhere said of the reception of the Word of God, which is not simply to be received, but as the Syrian was taken up, and Beza was received upward. Thus Scapula in his Lexicon: τὸ ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι is to be taken up; and he observes that τὸ ἀνὰ is frequently placed for ἄνω, upward. Osorodus against Tradel. part 2, cap. 5: that God was gloriously received, i.e., with the glorious exaltation of himself. Smalcius against Grav. That God is received in glory is the same as saying that the Gospel of Christ is admitted eagerly, quickly, and with the zeal of true piety. But by what documents of Scripture, by what reasons do they prove this? By none. With what ease, therefore, it is asserted, with the same it is also deservedly rejected. (11) What of the fact that the adversaries again make the Apostle tautological with this gloss of theirs? For the Apostle had already said before, ἐπιστεύθη ἐν κόσμῳ, believed in the world. But is not he in whom one believes received with the glorious exaltation of his name? Acts XIII. 48. And since true faith cannot exist without the zeal of true piety, is not he also received with the zeal of true piety? However, such a redundancy does not suit a brief, succinct, and vigorous review of mysteries, nor can it be held to be an explanation or a declaration of the prior assertion, as Smalcius wishes, since it is much more obscure and less obvious that by τὸ ἀνελήφθη ἐν δόξῃ the reception of the Gospel is understood than by τὸ ἐπιστεύθη ἐν κόσμῳ: And will this be a new and distinct mystery, that the Gospel was received in glory, from that, that it was believed in the world? Whence Erasmus himself stuck here, so that he could not explain those things concerning the Gospel, but declared them concerning the reception of Christ into heaven, from whence he had departed. But Francis David had to acknowledge in Act. Colloq. Transylv. §. 3 that those things could not be understood of any other person than the man Jesus Christ, who is God manifested in the flesh, and taken up into glory and preached to the nations. And Andr. Fricius professes in Sylv. I. p. 42. That his adversaries concede that it is said of Christ, God appeared in the flesh, but deny that he is God of himself, and that he is essentially one with the Father. Nor does Smalcius agree sufficiently with Enjedinus. For the latter asserts that that mystery in Col. I. 26 is different from this which is described in 1 Tim. III, and is only a part of this, that the nations also were admitted to the grace of God. De incarn. verb. p. 108. On the contrary, Enjed. p. 373: without any doubt, he says, by mystery in this place is understood the doctrine of the Gospel concerning the recovery of the nations, and that there is no other matter here than in Col. I. 26. What of the fact that Smalcius is not even consistent with himself: And when he sometimes understands the will of God by the word God, when God is said to be manifested in the flesh, sometimes when it is added, justified in the Spirit, he says it means God is just, that is, acknowledged as true, sometimes when it is subjoined he was seen by angels, he again takes refuge in the will of God revealed to the angels, etc.

To (3) I reply: Even if it is admitted that the Apostle is engaged in commending the dignity and sublimity of the doctrine of the Church, does not the review of the principal chapters of that doctrine, which are most sublime and most worthy of admiration, also contribute to that end? Nor do we assert that the essence of God is described here, but rather the economy, which venerable antiquity has so called. The description of which fits the scope and purpose of the Apostle most excellently; namely, to teach what principal chapters that truth embraces, of which the Church is the pillar and ground. Theodoret in this place is excellent: Having said these things concerning the Church, he necessarily brought in the dogmatic discourse. Chrysostom and Theophylact look to the mention of the Church, because it is compared with the temple of the Jews, and the High Priest of the Church with the Levites, because God himself, manifested in the flesh, presides over these. If anyone should urge with Smalcius that the Apostle does not recount the death and resurrection of Christ; Resp. Although it is not expressly recounted, both are nevertheless implicitly insinuated. Because for this reason the Son was manifested in the flesh, that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, Heb. 2:14, and his glorious ascension presupposes his resurrection from the dead; his preaching also, which was done among the Gentiles, comprised chiefly the doctrine concerning Christ's death and resuscitation. Nor is faith in Christ required otherwise than that it be believed that he was delivered for our sins and raised for our justification, Rom. 4:25.

To (4) Resp. A distinction must be made between those things which pertain to the eternal Son of God according to his essence, and those which pertain according to the economy. Although as to his essence he is invisible and is not moved by place, yet by dispensation he appeared in the flesh, was seen, and was taken up into heaven. For what? Is it not certain that even in the Old Testament God was seen, and changed place in his appearances, without prejudice to his infinite and invisible essence? To deny which is surely too rash, as Augustine teaches in book II of De Trinitate, ch. 17. Furthermore, these predicates must be distinguished. For as God is said first to have appeared in the flesh, afterwards to have been seen, and again to have been taken up into glory, so the later predicates are to be understood not of the Word, as regards his simple Deity, but of God manifested in the flesh. Concerning whom he says most correctly, who would doubt that he was seen, and that he was assumed into heaven in glory?

To (5) Response. Passages ought to have been produced by Schlichting to the effect that Φανέρωσις Θεῦ denotes only the knowledge of the will of God in the Scriptures: nor is this passage only about the Φανέρωσις Θεῦ, but about the Φανέρωσις Θεῦ ἐν σαρκὶ, which the adversaries have not yet proven from the Scriptures must be understood solely as the revelation of the will of God. But we have proven the contrary above. And why would an appearance in the N.T. not imply the exhibition or presence of a divine person, when it is established that in the O.T. the appearance of GOD implied the presence of GOD himself? Therefore, just as when God is said to have appeared in the O.T., his singular presence was implied, not only the revelation of his will, so when it is said here that God appeared in the flesh, likewise not only the revelation of his will, but his singular presence in the flesh is denoted. Add that concerning Christ, whom the adversaries do not deny to be God and a divine person, it is said even in the New Testament, when his presence is designated, ἐφανερώθη Mark XVI. v. 12, 14. John III. 11. ch. XXI. 1, 14. Col. III. 4. Heb. IX. 26. 1 Pet. I. 20. Indeed, never or nowhere is Christ or God said to be Φανερωθῆναι in the N.T. without it always being understood as the appearance of a real presence: and therefore the argument can be inverted and firmly retorted against the adversaries from the perpetual usage of Scripture. Finally, just as in Mark XVI. 12 it is said of Christ ἐφανερώθη ἐν ἑτέρᾳ μορφῆ, so that the assumption of an alien (extrinsic) form and an appearance in the same is implied, so also here, by the force of the identity of the phrase, when Θεὸς ἐφα- νερώθη ἐν σαρκὶ is used, the assumption of flesh and an appearance in the same is implied.

To (6) Response. The Church venerates both of those as a great mystery, both that God in the flesh was made conspicuous and willed to be seen particularly by angels, and that he was assumed into heaven. But what kind of mystery is this! the adversaries grumble. For those things which were seen by the Angels were also seen by others, and therefore they cannot be commended by that as something new and wonderful, that they were seen by the Angels, says Smalcius contr. Grav. p. 21. Add that no part of the mystery of godliness would rightly be in the fact that Christ ascended into heaven. For this would necessarily have happened if Christ was the Savior of the world, as Smalcius says again de Incarn. verb. p. 105. A great mystery indeed here, that God manifested in the flesh ὤφθη to the Angels: both because angels are read to have descended from heaven for the sake of seeing him, and because they did not, as before, behold the Son of GOD ἄσαρκον, but now saw with amazement the same one conspicuous in the flesh, and because, having been seen first by the Angels, he was then announced by them as heralds to men, Luke II, and because they themselves offered the ministry of angels to him in fragile flesh and appearing in the form of a servant as to their Lord; these and other things of this kind pertain here as confessedly great mysteries of godliness. But as for the ascension into heaven, who can rightly doubt that it was a great mystery, whether we look at the person ascending, who is not a mere man, but the Lord of heaven himself, God blessed forever, who fills heaven and earth; or whether we look at the manner of the ascension: for is it not a great mystery for a man to ascend to heaven by his own power, indeed to penetrate the heavens gloriously? Or whether we consider the end of the ascension: in that as true man by nature he was assumed into glory, and raised to the right hand of Majesty on high, all of which are without controversy great mysteries of godliness. The reason brought to the contrary is utterly futile, because even

other things were and would necessarily be, if Christ was the Savior of the world, such as that he had to die for our sins, that he had to rise from the dead, that he had to be preached among the nations, which nevertheless cannot be denied to be mysteries; thus also, according to the Smalcian consequence, no part of the mystery of godliness would rightly be in the fact that the will of GOD was gloriously received, or the religion of Christ. For this would necessarily have happened if Christ was the Savior of the world.

To (7) Response. Both the sense and the coherence of the words are perfectly consistent with the faith of the Church; if it is said that it is implied that God not only willed to be made conspicuous in the flesh, or in the assumed human nature, but also to be justified at the same time, that is, to be acknowledged, revealed, and celebrated as the true Messiah in the Spirit or by reason of his Deity, and as he is of divine nature; since the promised Messiah ought not only to have appeared in the flesh, and to be of the same substance as us, but also to be justified, acknowledged, and celebrated in the Spirit as the true God, as one in whom flesh and Spirit, that is, divine and human nature, appear at the same time, and who is made conspicuous and justified, or truly and in reality acknowledged, both in the flesh and in the Spirit, as true man by nature and true God by nature. The interpretation of Chrysostom looks to this, that wisdom is justified by her children. Others understand the divine nature by the Spirit, by which he exerted himself through miracles, and they place the force of the opposition in the fact that it exerted itself in the weak flesh of Christ, so that it was manifest that Christ, however much a weak man, was God: as Beza, Piscator, and Junius and Tremellius in this place. Others wish to indicate the divine nature, by which he kept the human nature he assumed free from sins: so that he is understood to be justified, indeed as to the flesh, but in the Spirit, by the power of the divine nature, so that he was devoid of sin and perfectly just, as with Theodoret, Chrysostom, Cyril, Theophylact, Anselm, with whom also Oecumenius explains the word justified, namely by reason of the thing, not only by reason of acknowledgment, that he was immune from sins and just according to the flesh; Oecumenius adds that he fulfilled the legal justifications: and likewise that he was justified by those who saw his glory as of the only-begotten from the Father. However the justified may be understood, whether that he was sanctified, or that he fulfilled the legal requirements of righteousness, or that he was acknowledged and celebrated as righteous, holy, and fulfilling all righteousness, or that he was acknowledged and celebrated as the true Messiah, that is, such as he proclaimed himself to be, and thus justified, righteous, and found not to be a deceiver: our exposition will be perfectly consistent, that by the word Spirit the divine nature is designated, as is the context itself: that God indeed appeared in the flesh, but at the same time was sanctified in the Spirit or by the power of the divine nature, fulfilled the legal requirements of righteousness, and was truly acknowledged as the righteous and true Messiah; or just as the appearance in the flesh implies the presence of God in the flesh, and in the same a manifestation, so it is implied that he not only existed in the Spirit, in the divine form, as the Apostle speaks in Phil. II. 6, but also that he manifested himself in the Spirit, that he is righteous, and our righteousness, the promised Messiah. Moreover, we do not deny that some explain the word ἐν πνεύματι otherwise, either concerning the Holy Spirit, that he was praised and commended through the Holy Spirit in the Gospel or in the testimonies of the Holy Spirit, or even by miracles, as Blessed Luther and others, or that he was judged righteous not by human eyes, but by the eyes of the Spirit, who searches even the deep things of God, as Oecumenius; or that he was justified not indeed by carnal men, but by those who were confirmed by the Spirit of God; as Oecumenius again, or that he fulfilled the righteousness of the law not by the spirit of bondage, but by the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of adoption, which he received according to his humanity, which interpretation Oecumenius likewise handed down: Either concerning divine virtue, so that in the Spirit it is the same as by power, or by divine virtue, by which He demonstrated Himself in such a way that He was justified, or acknowledged as just: or concerning the mode, that in the Spirit, that is, spiritually, He was acknowledged as just, or also spiritually exposition is likewise read in Oecumenius at this place. But indeed all those expositions are proposed by the Doctors of the Church in such a way that the force of the preceding proposition of the Apostolic aphorism nevertheless remains, that God was made visible in the flesh, nor does the connection waver, even though the opposition of flesh and spirit in the manifested God stands more correctly for itself, if as the former is understood and explained concerning human nature, so this latter is understood and explained concerning divine nature, just as we have already shown.

If anyone should say with Enjedinus p. 321 that Christ was entirely proven and received: therefore not at least in the Spirit, that is, as regards the divine nature, that He was justified. I reply: the 'in the Spirit' is not accepted exclusively, but inclusively, because the Messiah had to be not only true man, but also God, and was acknowledged and revealed as such, as one who both appeared in the flesh (by which human nature is designated) and was at the same time justified in the Spirit, that is, acknowledged as being true God. Add that He is said to be justified particularly according to the divine nature, because the human nature itself also had glory from this.

Finally, it is answered to (8): There would be no absurdity, even if a hysteron proteron were admitted in the fact that the preaching among the Gentiles is named before the assumption into glory. Because it cannot be denied that hysteron proteron exists in the Scriptures. Smalcius indeed says in his book 'De Verb. Incarn.' p. 105, that to attribute hysteron proteron to the Apostles is to cast ignominy upon the Holy Spirit, by whose authority they spoke, not upon them. Nevertheless, elsewhere in his 'refut. disp. de Incarn.' p. 24, he himself confesses that a hysteron proteron is sometimes found in the Sacred writings, as also on p. 17. A figure, he says, of hysteron proteron we do not deny exists, but it is rare, and such that anyone can detect it by himself and easily judge it; now indeed, who would doubt that, if the same were admitted in this place, it could be easily detected; especially since it is established from elsewhere that Christ was assumed into heaven before He was preached among the Gentiles? 2. Nor indeed is only that which is written in one place in a prior position required to be recounted in a posterior position in the Sacred writings; But that is also placed in a posterior position which was done first, (which is to be observed against Smalcius's exception, l. c. p. 24) as can be seen in historical narratives Gen. II. 1, chap. XII. 1, chap. XXX. 22, 23, Isa. XXXVIII. 21. In Luke IV. 9, the abduction of Christ onto the pinnacle of the temple by the Devil is commemorated after his translation onto the mountain, when nevertheless the former preceded the latter, as is evident from Matt. IV. 5, 8. 3. But if hysteron protera also occur in historical narratives, how much less absurd will it be to establish the same here, where no historical narrative is being woven, nor is there a need for the Apostle's speech to be bound to the order and series in which things were done? 4. Although there is no need for the same, if it be said that he did not recount those things according to the order of time, but by another arbitrary and sufficiently harmonious order, so that just as he deservedly assigned the first place to the appearance made on earth in the flesh, by which God, descending from the heavens, willed to become visible in the flesh and to appear in time, so he might conclude everything with the reception of Christ into heaven. 5. Add that He was already preached among the Gentiles and believed in the world in part before He was assumed into heaven, since He Himself made the beginnings of the preaching of the Gospel among the Gentiles in the days of His flesh, nor were there lacking those by whom He was believed, as is evident from the Evangelical history. See Matt. IV. 15, 23, Luke VI. 6, John IV. 39, 41, 42, chap. XII. 20, 21. 6. Finally, Theodoret's observation on these words is not to be rejected: He was assumed in glory. This indeed, he says, was done before the preaching, but he placed it last, teaching that the preaching was rightly believed. For He is in the heavens who ordered this to be done, and sits at the right hand. But these things also concerning that classic passage.

Latin:

Verf. 16. Καὶ ὁμολογουμένως μέγα ἐσὶ τὸ τῆς ἐυσεβείας μυ- σήριον) Non hic, inquit, de quavis veritate agitur, sed de ea, quam nemo hominum per se reperire potuit, & quæ vim ad pietatem nobis ingenerandam habet maximam, præ qua evanescant omnia legis, omnia philosophorum præcepta & dogmata, ὁμολογυμένως. Latini dicunt haud dubie, plane, extra controversiam, profecto, pro eodem ponitur ὁμολόγως. Μυσήριον sæpe vocatur Evangelium, non modo quia tamdiu latuit, verum etiam, quia humana industria nequit reperiri, Matth. XVI. 17. Genitivus εὐσε- βείας hic effectum designat. Eodem sensu hæc veritas dici- tur esse, κατὰ εὐσέβειαν 1. Tim. I. hic DEUS in Christo nobis omnia dicitur donasse, quæ ad pietatem pertinent, Roman. I. verf. 3.

Θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκὶ) Suspectam nobis hanc lectio- nem faciunt interpretes veteres, Latinus, Syrus, Arabs, & Ambrosius, qui omnes legerunt ὃ ἐφανερώθη. Addit Hinc- marus Opusculo LV. illud Θεὸς hic positum à Nestorianis. Sensum bonum facit illud ὃ ἐφανερώθη. Evangelium illud cœleste innotuit primùm, non per Angelos, sed per homi- nes mortales, & quantum extera species ferebat, infirmos, Christum & Apostolos ejus. ἐφανερώθη דאתגלי Syro. Id verbum bene convenit mysterio, id est, rei latenti. Sic & Coloff. I. 26. Σὰρξ בשר hominem significat mortalem. 2. Cor. II. 16. vide 1. Joh. IV. verf. 2. & quæ ad eum locum dicentur.

Ἐδικαιώθη ἐν πνεύματι) Per plurima miracula approba- ta est ea veritas. Πνεῦμα sunt miracula divina, per μετω- νυμίαν, quæ est & 1. Cor. II. 4. & alibi. Δικαιωθῆναι autem hic est approbare ut Matth. XI. 19. ubi dicta vide. Sic הצ- דיק dicitur, qui in lite victor est, quia causa ejus appro- batur, Deut. XXV. 1. Adde Pf. CXVI.

Ὢφθη ἀγγέλοις) Nempe cum admiratione maxima. Angeli hoc arcanum per homines mortales didicere, Eph. III. 10. 1. Petr. I. 12. Videre apud Ebræos ad omnem co- gnoscendi modum transfertur.

Ἐκηρύχθη ἐν ἔθνεσι) Non Judæis tantum arnunciata est ista veritas, sed & gentibus illis, quæ à Deo alienissimæ fuerant. Ephef. II. 12. Coloff. I. 21. ἐν ἔθνεσι apud gentes לגויים.

Ἐπισεύθη ἐν κόσμῳ) id est, in magna mundi parte, Ro- man. I. 8. Col. I. 6.

Ἀνελήφθη ἐν δόξῃ) Gloriose admodum exaltatum est, nempe quia multo majorem attulit sanctitatem, quam ulla antehac dogmata, ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι & sublimiter evehi, re- spondetque Ebræis verbis נטל & נעלה. Ἐν δόξῃ glorio- se, Phil. IV. 19. Col. III. 4. Vide & 2. Cor. III. 8. Sic ἐδόξα- ζον τὸν λόγον τῦ κυρίε. Actor. XIII. 48.

Detestanda hæc σφελότης hærefi Socinianæ accepta ferenda est: quam in præcipuis ejus pro- pugnatoribus ante hos XXIX. annos jam profli- gavimus in Apodixi Deitatis Christi: quia verò illa lucem nondum aspexit, hic eandem inferendam duximus.

Ita autem habet argumentum æternæ Deitatis CHRISTI ex hoc loco Apostolico verè classico petitum.

Qui apparuit in carne, est verus & essentialis DEUS. At Filius Dei apparuit in carne. Ergo Filius Dei est verus, & essentialis Deus. Major verbis Apostoli constat. Nam is, qui apparuit in carne, (1) dicitur Θεὸς absolutè, quod nomen es- sentiæ divinæ significativum esse, nec nisi de vero & essentiali Deo absolutè in singulari usurpari, alibi probavimus. (2) dicitur Θεὸς subjectivè. Deus apparuit in carne. At hoc pro indubitata nota veri & essentialis Dei habent adversarii, cum vox Dei subjectivè alicubi occurrit. (3) Celebra- tur hic ceu ὁμολογυμένως μέγα τῆς ἐυσεβείας μυ- sήριον, quod Deus apparuerit in carne. At DEUM aliquem nuncupativè & metaphoricè ita dictum carnem esse, vel in carne manifestatum esse, nihil est mysterii, nedum citra controversiam magnum pietatis mysterium. Quid enim? anne satis notum, quod plures alii, qui nuncupativè Dii dicantur, caro sint? Magistratus, Mosen, aliosque morta- les homines nuncupativè ita vocatos fuisse in con- fesso est. Accedit (4) quod semper, ubi comme- moratur simpliciter, Deum apparuisse, intelli- gendum sit, quod ipse Deus altissimus apparue- rit, seseque manifestarit. Quod è locorum in- ductione haud difficulter ostenditur. Ita ergò pa- riter hic Deus altissimus intelligendus venit cūm Apost. θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκὶ. (5) Præterea quis- nam præter altissimum Deum intelligi posset? Num Angelus aliquis creatus? At DEUS, qui apparuit in carne, contradistinguitur ab Angelis: dum id quoque ceu magnum pietatis mysterium celebratur, quod Deus, qui patefactus est in carne, apparere Angelis & videri ab iisdem voluit. Cer- tum ergo, quod Angelus intelligi non possit. Num vero homo quispiam? At homo non apparet in carne, sed ipse caro est, nec sublimior est Ange- lis, nec in hominem merum, uti ne in Angelum quidem credendum est, nec denique magnum hoc est pietatis mysterium, quod homo carne constet, & carne videatur: quum nullus non hominum carne & sanguine constet. Quis ergo relinquitur intelligendus, nisi Deus altissimus, præsertim quia Dei nomen personale est, & prædicata, quæ hic occurrunt, non nisi de persona intelligi possunt? Præter autem Deum, homines, & Angelos, nullas alias personas dari notissimum. (6) Is nomine Dei intelligitur, qui ἐκηρύχθη ἐν ἔθνεσιν, ἐπισεύ- θη ἐν κόσμῳ, prædicatus inter gentes, creditus in mundo. Quis autem Deus præter unum verum Deum & prædicatus est inter gentes, & creditus in mundo? Apostolus certè non nisi unum Chri- stianorum esse verum Deum profitetur, 1. Cor. VIII. 4. nec plures Deos prædicatos esse uspiam ab Apostolis aut creditos à Christianis docebitur, quum gentilium non Christianorum fuerit, plu- res colere Deos. (7) Sed & antecedentia satis do- cent, nullum alium quàm Deum illum unum in- telligi, qui Deus verus dicitur, & cui Ecclesia ceu domus ejus vindicatur, v. 15. (8) Quid multis? Fa- tentur adversarii ipsimet, nomine θεῦ intelligen- dum esse hoc in loco unum illum verum Deum: ut videre est apud Enjedin. Socinum, & cæteros ad unum omnes. Minorem vero quod attinet, licet ea per se luculenta sit, ab adversariis tamen omnia etiam manifestissima in dubium revocantur, hæc ergò confirmationis gratia advertimus: (1) Quod nulli alii, qui Deus indigitetur in Scripturis appa- ritio hæc in carne Nov. Test. tempore facta adscri- batur & vindicetur in S. literis, nisi Filio DEI: qui & Deus indigitatur Joh. I. c. XX. 28. Act. XX. v. 28. Rom. IX. 5. &c. & caro factus dicitur Joh. I. 14. Carnis & sanguinis particeps factus Ebr. II. 14. Secundum carnem est ex Patribus, Rom. IX. 5. è Se- mine Davidis natus est secundum carnem, Rom. I. 3. venit in carne, 1. Joh. IV. 2. 3. &c. adeoque Deus in carne manifestatus secundum tenorem S. literarum recte dicitur. (2) Ubicunque caro in N. T. tribui- tur illi, quem Deum esse simul è scripturis con- stat, ibi Christus intelligitur. Quod ex locorum inductione patescit, Joh. I. 14. VI. 53. Act. II. 31. Rom. I. 3. VIII. 3. IX. 5. Eph. II. 14. 15. Col. I. 22. Ebr. II. 14. v. 7. X. 19. 20. 1. Petr. III. 18. IV. 1. 1. Joh. IV. v. 2. 3. 1. Joh. V. 6. &c. (3) Is hic intelligitur manifestatus in carne, qui divinam potentiam & gloriam suam tempore N. T. exeruit, & manife- stavit, in carne ac per carnem, omnibusque glo- riam suam conspicuam reddidit, ac se ceu DEUM demonstravit. At hoc in Filio Dei factum esse ne- gari nequit diebus carnis ejus, tempore Novi Te- stamenti, quod varia miracula, & historia Evan- gelica luculentissimè testantur, Joh. I. 14. ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο, & habitavit in nobis, & vidimus glo- riam ejus, gloriam veluti unigeniti à Patre, Joh. II. v.11. Christus ἐφανέρωσε manifestavit gloriam suam & crediderunt in eum discipuli. Conf. Joh. VII. 3. & conciones Christi Joh.V. & X.capp. &c. (4) De ea Φανερώσῃ Θεῦ ἐν σαρκὶ hic sermo est, quæ & N. T. tempore demum facta sit, & magnum citra controversiam haberi debeat pietatis mysterium. At quænam alia è scripturis proferri poterit Φανέ- ρωσις ejusmodi, præter ipsam Filii Dei in carne ap- paritionem? (5) Explicat Scriptura alibi hanc ipsam Φανέρωσιν, eandemque adscribit Filio Dei. 1. Joh.I.2. vita ἐφανερώθη, manifestata est, apparuit, & illam vidimus & testamur, & annunciamus vo- bis vitam illam æternam, quæ erat apud Patrem, & apparuit nobis. Magno verborum apparatu de- scribit eam apparitionem, ut novum & admiran- dum mysterium; perinde ut hic Paulus celebrat ceu magnum pietatis mysterium Φανέρωσιν Θεῦ ἐν σαρκὶ. Quid? quod semper τὸ Φανερωθῆναι in N. T. adscribatur Filio Dei, cum de persona sermo est, nunquam autem Dei Patri, ut ex locorum in- ductione constat, Marc. XVI. 12. 14. Joh. VII. 4. c. XXI. 1. 14. Col. III. 4. Ebr. IX. 26. 1. Petr. I. 20. c. V. 4. 1. Joh. III. v. 5. & 8. Proinde etiam hic de Christo Φανέρωσις illa intelligenda venit, ob per- petuum scripturæ tenorem, non de Patre. (5) Deum qui justificatus est in Spiritu N. Test. tem- pore, quis ambigere potest Christum esse? Annon enim Christus ἐδικαιώθη justificatus, verus Messias agnitus, & celebratus fuit? Annon id ἐν πνεύματι in Spiritu & per Spiritum factum, sive per Deita- tem ipsius, sive per Spiritus, quo unctus fuit, po- tentiam: Verbum enim illud justificari sæpe idem est, quod pro vero agnosci, laudari, & celebrari, ut Luc.VII.19. Matth.XI.19. Rom.III.4. quem poste- riorem locum Smalcius ipse hic confert, nihilque aliud esse, quod Deus justificatus sit in Spiritu, agnoscit, quam quod pro vero sit agnitus per vir- tutem divinam in Christo sese exerente. Id autem de Christo passim docetur, quod documentis ejusmodi Spiritus ostenderit sese esse verum illum Messiam, & verè Filium Dei, quodque satis inde agnitus sit, & celebratus non tantum ab Aposto- lis, sed & ab aliis fidelibus. (6) Porrò de quonam rectius exponetur, quod peculiariter visus sit An- gelis, ὤφθη ἀγγέλοις, quam de Christo? Qui vi- derunt Filium Dei in carne manifestatum in præ- sepi jacentem, Luc. II. 13. qui viderunt eum in de- serto adversus Diabolum prævalentem, Matth. IV. 11. qui viderunt, & confirmarunt eum in ago- ne luctantem, Luc. XXII. 43. qui viderunt à mor- tuis resurgentem, Matth. XXIX. 2. Marc. XVI. 1. Luc. XXIV. v. 4. viderunt gloriosè ascendentem, Act. I. 10. (7) Quis præterea nescit, quod gentibus peculiariter prædicatus sit Christus pro magno mysterio pietatis? Prædicamus, inquit Apostolus 1. Cor. I. 23. 24. Christum crucifixum, Judæis qui- dem scandalum, gentibus vero stultitiam, ipsis verò vocatis Judæis & gentibus Christum Dei potentiam & Dei sapientiam: & 1. Cor. II. 2. Non enim judi- cabam me scire quicquam inter vos, εἰ μὴ NISI Je- sum Christum, & hunc crucifixum. v. 7. Sapientiam Dei loquimur in mysterio absconditam &c. Testa- tur de eo tota N. Test. Scriptura, quod peculia- riter Christus prædicatus sit gentibus N. T. tem- pore, Luc. XXIV. 46. 47. Act. III. 20. cap. IIX. 5. c.IX. 20. c.XIX. 13. 1.Cor.XV.12. Ebr.I. 19. c.IV. 5. c.XI.4. Phil.I.15. Quis ergo dubitaret, cum sermo est de eo, qui peculiariter prædicatus gentibus N. T. tempore, phrasi Apostolica passim frequenta- ta, intelligatur Christus? (8) Quis insuper est, qui tempore N. T. peculiariter creditus fuit in mundo, si Christus is non est? quum tota N. T. Scriptura plena sit de fide in Christum locanda, & peculia- riter quae scripta & gesta sunt eo tendant, ut cre- damus Jesum esse Christum, & per fidem in nomine ejus vitam habeamus, Joh. XX. 20. 21. Ideo si quic- quam aliud, fidei certe in Christum praeceptum non inculcatur, & requiritur; Joh. I. 12. cap. II. 11. c. III. 17. 18. 35. 36. c. VI. 40. Act. X. 43. cap. XVI. 3. Rom. III. 22. c. X. 8. 9. Gal. II. 16. 1. Joh. I. 5. & alibi passim in omnibus N. T. scriptis, ut nullum iterum dubium esse possit, quin juxta tenorem styli Apo- stolici & hoc ἐπιστεύθη creditus est in mundo Chri- stum respiciat, & ad eundem pertineat. (9) Quis denique ἀνελήφθη assumptus est in gloria tempore N. T. praeterquam Christus, cujus ascensio in coe- lum ἀνάληψις expresse vocatur Luc. IX. 51. ἀνελή- φθη εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν, Marc. XVI. 19. & absolute ἀνε- λήφθη Act. I. 11. &c. Qui ascensus Christi ἐν δόξῃ in gloria factus est, uti cum gloria rediturus est, Luc. XXI. 27. Nam ita veniet, quemadmodum vidistis eum ascendentem in coelum, Act. I. 11. Ascendit An- gelis sibi servientibus nube sese suscipiente modo ut mirabili, ita prorsus glorioso, Act. I. 10. Ascendit ita ut consederit ad dexteram majestatis & gloria in excelsis. Non ad Eliae modum ad coelum subvectus est, sed in gloria, exponit Theophylactus: Ipsi dum as- sumebatur, ministrabant Angeli in nubibus. Sic & Be- za: Sursum receptus est in gloriam. (Vocem Grae- cam ἐν nunquam ita fortassis, vel saltim rarissimè accipi asserit Smalcius disput. de incarnat. refut. p. 21. sed refellitur Smalcius exemplis non paucis. Marc. I. 15. Luc. I. 17. c. II. 12. c. XXI. 22. Rom. I. 23. 24. 25. 1. Thess. IV. 7. 1. Joh. IV. 9. Ebr. IV. 10. &c.) Propter hoc dicit in gloria: quia & ipsum assumi gloriosum est. Ὅτι καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ἀναληφθῆναι ἔνδοξόν ἐστι, ait Oecumenius in h. l. Syrus vertit: Sublatus est in gloriam. B. Lutherus: auffgenomen in die Herr- lichkeit. Quod de nullo alio, quam de Christo in- telligi, & explicari potest. (10) Tandem de Chri- sto intelligi hoc pietatis mysterium, hanc Φανέρω- σιν ἐν σαρκὶ semper & unanimi suffragio sancta Ec- clesia intellexit, a cujus interpretatione tot ratio- nibus munita discedere capitale periculum nobis est. De Christo accepere Graeci tractatores omnes. Chrysost. homil. II. in 1. Tim. III. Cyrillus ad Reg. Theodoret. Oecumen. Theophyl. in h. l. &c. Latini quoque etsi legerunt in editionibus Latinis, quod (sacramentum) manifestatum est in carne, con- stanter tamen & unanimi sententia de Filio DEI conspicuo facto in carne acceperunt, voceque Sacramenti Christum ipsum intellexerunt, meto- nymice, quia mysterium de Christo est, ut objecto, ut notat Guil. Estius in h. l. B. Hieron. Tom. VIII. in Comment. h. l. p. m. 384. Pietatis Sacramentum explicat Sacramentum incarnationis Christi, per quam generi humano pietas collata est &c. August. Comm. in h. l. T. V. oper. p. m. 395. Sacramentum mysterii Dei, quod est Christus, in carne dicit mani- festatum, quod latebat in Spiritu. Natus enim homo Filius Dei, qui in secreto erat apud Deum, opere & praedicatione declaravit se creaturae, & hoc est, justi- ficatum esse in Spiritu operibus & virtute, claruisse eum, qui erat in carne, quod esset &c. Nec aliter Anshelmus, & alii. Quid quod Erasmus ipse, utut attributa quaedam ad Evangelii praedicationem ob- torto collo trahat, nonnulla tamen aliter, quam de Christo, ejus nativitate & ascensione in coelum cum orthodoxis Patribus, & tota Christi Ecclesia, explicare haud potuerit; utpote quod visum An- gelis dicat, qui canebant (in nativitate Christi, non in Evangelii manifestatione universo mundo fa- cta) Gloria in excelsis Deo, & acceptum post resurre- ftionem in cœlum, unde profectum fuerat, quod non nisi de verbo & Filio Dei dicere poterat.

Excipiunt adversarii, (1) Quod Latinæ editio- nes pro voce DEUS habeant pronomen Quod, & manifestationem in carne, non ad Deum, sed ad pietatis mysterium referant, suffragante etiam Sy- riaca lectione: quam lectionem sibi convenientio- rem multò videri ait Socinus contr. Volan. p. 249. provocatque ad eandem Smalcius homil. IIX. in 1. Joh. p. 89. ut & in refut. thes. de incarnat. pag. 6. nec non Volckel. de ver. relig. pag. 462. Enjedinus Græca lectione corruptam Latinam vocem esse, & antiquam eo docere vult argumento, quod in hoc testimonio veteres, qui contra Arium acriter pugnarunt, nihil præsidii collocarint p.361. & deinde admissa voce Dei, eam non de Filio Dei, sed de Pa- tre accipiendam esse contendunt, quum nihil pror- sus sit, quod ad Deum Patrem accommodari nequeat, quod prolixius prosequitur Socinus. Smalcius: quid absurdi est, ait ref. thes. de incarnat. p.6. si di- catur Dei voluntatem esse manifestatam per homi- nes infirmos, & mortales? (3) Quicquid hîc de ma- nifestatione & justificatione dicitur, ita accipi debe- re, ut non ad Dei essentiam discutiendam, sed ad do- ctrinæ Christi autoritatem commendandam perti- neat, ex ratione priorum verborum & proposito A- postoli ait Enjed. quum agatur de excellentia Eccle- siæ, & muneris Ecclesiastici. (4) Objectat idem En- jed. λόγῳ æterno & infinito non competere illa conspectum esse, visum, justificatum, assumtum in cœ- lum, quum invisibilis spiritus omnia compleat, nec cerni, nec de loco in locum transferri possit. (5) Schlichting. de Trin. p. 479. urget quoque, quod manifestatio sub N. T. non soleat significare personæ divinæ exhibitionem, sed tantum eorum, quæ ad co- gnitionem Dei, ejusq; voluntatis spectant revelatio- nem. (6) Quod nullum hoc sit mysterium, quod Deus incarnatus ab Angelis visus fuerit, vel sursum, & in cælis assumtus. (7) Quod deniq; illa nullo sen- su dicantur, aut cohæreant, Deus incarnatus est, & justificatus in Spiritu. (8) Tandem Smalcius contr. Grav. p. 9. urget, quod Deus ille, qui in carne ma- nifestatus fuit, dicatur receptq in gloriam, postquam p千ædicatus fuit gentibus & creditum illi in mundo. Christus autem in gloria sursum acceptus fuerit,an- tequam gentibus prædicaretur. Sic & Enjed. in h. l. ut & Socinus l. c. Hæc ergo sunt, quæ excipiunt ad nostrum ἀπόδειξιν adversarii: quæ v. εὐδιάλυτα.

Quod ad (1) Resp. Versione Latina non possunt satis tuto niti Christomachi,quum id ipsis quoque ὁμολογημένως certum sit,non Latinam translatio- nem, vel aliam quamcunque versionem, sed solum Græcum textum in Scriptura N. T. pro θεοπνεύστῳ haberi debere. Lectio interpretationis Latinæ, ait Crell. l. de un. Deo pat. sect. 2. c. 10. pag. 154. lectioni Græcorum codicum, sibi inter se consentient cedere debet, & ex illa corrigi. (2) Quod vero de Græco textu corrupto arguit Enjedinus, nullo docu- mento ostendere potest; è diversa certè lectione Latinæ versionis corruptio Græci textus non nisi ineptissimè colligitur. Nec inde eam fas est argue- re, quod hoc testimonio non legantur usi veteres contra Arianos, quum & alia non pauca in texti- bus authenticis, Ebræo & Græco, legantur di- vinitatis Christi documenta, quæ veteres contra Arianos non produxere. Num verò ilicò conclu- dendum, illa olim non extitisse in textu Ebræo & Græco? Quid? quod & Deitatem Filii Dei, & in- carnationem ejusdem hoc loco insinuari haud du- bitarint Græci Interpp. ut è Cyrillo, Chrysostomo, Theophyl. & aliis videre est. Profectò,inquit Chry- sostomus, verissime magnum prædicatur mysterium. Homo enim factus Deus, & Deus homo, homo appa- ruit absq; peccato, homo assumptus est, prædicatus est in mundo, viderunt eum Angeli nobiscum. Adde quod Theophylactus profiteri ausit, circa hunc lo- cum, neminem præterire, quod Deus incarnatus sit. Conf. & Athanasius de resurr. Carnis. (3) Quod autem variam lectionem inculcant adversarii, ut concludant, nihil certi concludi posse ex hoc lo- co, quum nihil certi è locis, quorum lectio varia est, concludi posse verius esse, quam ut probari debeat, asserat Smalcius ref. disp. de incarnat. p. 6. In Vet. sanè Test. non pauca sunt loca diversarum lectio- num indicata notis marginalibus Masorethicis תכ קרי & כתיב. In Novo verò longe plura occurrere, Observationes Stephani, Valle, Bezæ, Casauboni, Lud. de Dieu, Joh. de Morini, aliorumq; edocent. Quod si non tantum eas æstimare velis diversas le- ctiones, quæ fortè in fontibus reperiuntur, sed & quæ contentione facta veterum Interpp. LXX. Vul- gati, nec non Syri, Arabis, Æthiop. Coptici & alio- rum in N. T. deprehenduntur, (uti hic Smalcius vulgatæ ipsius versionis diversam lectionem indi- gitat) immanè quantum dictorum Scripturæ di- versimodè lectorum colliges numerum! Applica jam hisce omnibus axioma Smalcianum, & infi- nita Scripturæ testimonia incerta reddentur, ni- hilque probare poterunt. Ne dicam, quod ipsi Sociniani nonnunquam in probationem advocent ea loca, quorum varia occurrit lectio, non tantum si componas inter se vulgatæ Lat. aliarumq; vete- rum translationum editiones, sed & ipsius textus authentici diversa exemplaria. Eas autem omnes probationes incertas vanasque esse haud admit- tent. Itaque castigandum necessario illud postula tum, quod ita restringimus: Ex locis, quorum va- ria est lectio, nihil certi concludi potest, si scilicet primò ea varietas lectionis sit in fontibus vel textu authentico, non tantum in ipsis translationibus: sique secundò ita comparata sit, ut utra è lectioni- bus variis verior sit, prorsus incertum sit, nec de- finiri possit: Si denique tertio non tantum verbo- tenus eædem discrepent, sed diversas etiam red- dant sententias. Hic autem variam occurrere le- ctionem in ipsis fontibus Græcis, certò asseverare ne ipse quidem Smalcius ausus fuit. (4) Quan- quam verò Volckelius audacius vocem Dei nequa- quam in omnibus Codd. Græcis haberi contendat, nullum tamen, in quo defuerit, nominare potuit. Nec repertus fuit hactenus, qui ullum Codicum Græcorum sive manuscriptum, sive typis editum, antiquum vel neotericum sese deprehendisse testa- tus sit, in quo vox ista desiderata fuerit. Nullam hic Græcorum Exemplarium discrepantiam ob- servavit Rob. Stephani, qui septendecim Codices Græcos contulit diligentissimè, & inter eos vetu- stissimos quosque summa diligentia conquisitos; nullam editionis Complutensis autores notarunt, qui castigatissima omni ex parte, vetustissimaque ex- emplaria architypa, ut & Vaticanæ Bibliothecæ Co- dices antiquissimos adhibuerunt: nullam Herva- gius advertit, qui ex optimorum exemplarium collatione varias discrepantes lectiones annota- vit editioni Basiliensi An. 1545. subjunctas. Lau- rentius Valla vulgatam versionem cum Græcis Codicibus diversis contendit, sed nullum Græco- rum Codd. vocem θεὸς omittentem invenit, idcir- co annotat in collat. N. T. ad hunc locum: Quod neutraliter legitur (in Vulgata) masculinè legen- dum est, addendumque DEUS. Sic enim est Græcè. Aldus, qui multis vetustissimis exemplaribus col- latis Græcum textum edidit Venetiis Anno 1518. vocem Θεὸς retinuit. Theodorus Beza, qui non so- lum secundâ curâ 17. Codd. Græcos à Rob. Ste- phano citatos accuratissimè contulit, sed & Cla- ramontanum mirae antiquitatis exemplar adhibuit, in editione N. T. observat omnes Graecos Codd. PERPETUO consensu repugnare Vulgatae lectioni Latinae. Sebastianus Castellio legit quoque in suis Codd. & reddidit juxta Graeca Exemplaria Deus apparuit in carne. Erasmus ipse, qui varios itidem & antiquissimos Codd. Graecos adhibuit, vocem Θεῦ legi in omnibus Codd. non ausus fuit inficiari, sed potius fatetur Graecè sic haberi, Θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκὶ, & quae sequuntur ad Deum referri. Pon- tificii deniq; moderni, qui post decretum Concilii Tridentini omnibus modis id agunt, ut vulgatam lectionem tueantur, & Graecorum quorundam ex- emplarium, quâ possunt, auctoritate, adversus vul- gatam Graecam lectionem sui Interpretis transla- tionem propugnant, infiteri tamen hic non pos- sunt, Graeca exemplaria constanter retinere vo- cem τῦ Θεῦ, nec ullum adducere queunt Latinae translationi suffragantem Graecum Codicem. Ideoque palmam hic vel inviti deferunt Graecae le- ctioni Corn. à Lapide & Guil. Estius in Comm. ad h.l. Eam porro lectionem non Neotericorum sal- tem Codicum Graecorum esse, ut cavillatur En- jedinus, sed & vetustissimorum tum antiquissima exemplaria à praedictis autoribus collata testan- tur, tum veterum Graecorum Interpp. monumen- ta loquuntur, è quibus nullus adferri potest, qui secus legerit. Sic autem legisse Graecos exposito- res cum Estio profitetur Corn. à Lap. & agnoscit Erasmus, utpote Cyrillum, Chrysostom. Theophyla- ctum. Nec diversum legit Athanasius de resurr. Carn. aut alius quisquam è Graecis Doctoribus. Quibus accedit praedicatorum hujus Subjecti con- sideratio, quae sanè ita comparata sunt, ut subjecti loco potius iis substerni debere Deum, quàm my- sterium pietatis appareat. Quid enim? An Doctri- na apparuit in carne? Num visa est Angelis? Num rursum recepta in gloriam? Descriptio praeterea mysterii favet magis Graecae, quam Latinae lectio- ni. Nam Deum in carne conspicuum factum esse, & quicquid porro de Deo illic dicitur, μυσήριον τῆς εὐσεβείας, & quidem ὁμολογυμένως μέγα μυσή- ριον meritissime indigitatur, de quo Dionysius c.2. de Divin. nominib. Jesu in carne apparitio & inef- fabilis est sermone omni, & omni ignota intelligentia, ipsi quoque Angelorum primati non cognita. Doctri- nam autem Dei manifestatam esse in carne, id est, per infirmos homines, neutiquam est arcanum ejus- modi & absconditum mysterium, vel secretum ju- stitiae, ut Syrus & Arabs reddit, omnium piorum confessione magnum & stupendum. (5) Syriacam quod attinet translationem, eam non raro à vera & genuina lectione exorbitare, haec inter alia do- cent exempla, Matth. VI.18. cap. IX. 13. c. XI. 23. c. XXIV. 36. c. XXV. 13. Marc. I.2. c. II.17. Luc. IV. 8. V. 7. VI. 43. Joh. IIX. 1. seqq. Act. IIX. 37. 1. Joh. V.8. Quanquam haud sciam, annè hoc in loco discrepans occurrit in Syrae interpretationis edi- tionibus omnibus lectio. Nam licet in exemplari Cotheniano in forma Quarta, ut & in Plantiniano minoris formae Ebraeo charactere expresso non compareat vox Dei, tamen vocem אלהא lectam fuisse Tremellio, è translatione illius colligendum potius videtur, quam cum Socino virum istum doctissimum & diligentissimum, quod eam expo- neret, insigniter lapsum statuendum: praesertim quum & alios sic legisse textum Syriacum videa- mus, è quibus sunt Cornel. à Lap. & Guil. Estius. Itaque verisimile est, alteram lectionem è vulgata Latina originem traxisse, quod etiam in aliis locis hujus interpretationis observare licet. Idem quo- que de Arabica translatione hoc in loco statuen- dum censemus, quam pariter in plusculis abire à veritatis fontibus alibi notavimus. (6) Vulgatam verò Latinam quod concernit, notissimum est, quod & in mendis cubet plurimis, post Sixtinam & Clementinam correctionem, & innumeris penè locis à verbis θεοπνεύστοις discrepet. Itaq; non mi- rum, si etiam hoc in loco deflectat à vera lectione. Idque potius statuendum arbitramur, (quæcunq; hujus discrepantiæ sit causa) quam S.
