Veterum fi- dem solicitandam cum Erasmo, qui, rectè subolet, inquit, Deum additum fuisse adversus Arianos hæ- reticos; tametsi paulò ante ambiguus adhuc fue- rit, utra lectio sit verior, Græcanè an Latina? Ita proclivis est in ejusmodi suspicio, quod & in annot. ejus ad Matth. XXIV. 36. & Joh. V. 7. videre est. Rectius autem Beza Dei nomen sublatum cre- dit ab iis, qui vel divinitatem Christi, vel utriusque naturæ unionem inde ab ipso conceptionis momento negabant. Quod etiam Cornelius à Lap. approbat, ejusque rei hanc adfert rationem: quod nempe Græc. Codd. nonnulli olim legerint ὁ θεὸς vel ὃς θεὸς; Macedonius autem Nestorianus hunc locum corruperit, legens ὡς pro ὃς, sicq; interpretatus sit, ut (homo Jesus dici posset, &) esset Deus, appa- ruit Deus per carnem & in corpore Jesu habita- vit. Suffragio suo comprobat hæc Estius, & in te- stimonium ejus rei adducit Liberatum Diaconum in Breviar. c. XIX. Ideoque advertit, Vulgatum interpretem vocem Quod accepisse ut conjun- ctionem determinativam & subintelligi debere in ejus translatione vocem Dei sumtâ conjectura è Syra interpretatione, quam sic habere ait, ma- gnum est mysterium hoc justitiæ, quod Deus manife- status est in carne. Quid quod Smalcius non omnia, sed plurima tantum Latinæ translationis exemplaria vocem Dei omittere dicat, ideoq; & in Latinis editionibus variam lectionem facilè ad- mittat, unde non immeritò dubiis Latinis exem- plaribus constans Græcorum lectio antefertur. Quam etiam Racovienses in sua Translat. Germ. Nov. Test. expresserunt: GOtt ist geoffenbaret worden im Fleisch. Sic & Franc. Davidis Soci- nianorum συστρατιώτης in oppugnanda suprema Deitate Filii Dei in Art. Colloqu. Transylv. dec. 3. Deus manifestatus est in carne. Quin etiam Smalcius agnovit sinceritatem Græcæ lectionis, ean- demque Latinæ præferendam esse, ingenuè pro- fessus est libr. de verb. incarn. c. 18. Omnia, inquit, Exemplaria Græca CONSTANTER VOCEM DEI habent. Et porrò: Nos Græcum textum Vul- gatæ longè anteponendum esse censemus; Is verò ha- bet Deum in carne esse manifestatum. Ideoque ite- rato adserit, Deum apparuisse in carne una cum Paulo confitemur; Et Deum in carne manifesta- tum esse dicimus. Taceo, quod universalis omnium modernorum Codicum Græcorum corruptio statu- enda sit, si vocem Θεὸς, quæ in omnibus legitur, irreptitiam quis dixerit? Quod divinæ refragatur prudentiæ, nec ab ipsis admittitur Socinianis; Atque hæc de lectione textus.

Quod ad (2) Resp. Vocem Dei hoc loco de Fi- lio Dei accipiendam esse, supra ostendimus. Ex- abundanti, quod de Deo Patre intelligenda non sit, quodque glossa Sociniana minimè admitti de- beat (nimirum Dei Patris esse manifestata per ho- mines infirmos & mortales Christum & Apostolos voluntatem, ut vult Enjed. & Smalcius de verb. in- carnat. c. 18. p. 107. aliiq;) hisce docemus. (1) Quia cum nova sit, & inaudita antehac in Ecclesia hæc glossa, nulla ratione firma stabiliri, vel fulciri potest. Ea enim quam unicè adferunt, quod ubi vox θεὸς subjecti locum obtinet perpetuò, Pater intelligatur, lubrica est, principium petit & antehac solidè destructa est. (2) Quia nuspiam in N. Test. Deo Patri Fanerosis en sarki tribuitur: Nuspiam Deus Pater opera hominum usus ad declarandam voluntatem suam, manife- status dicitur in carne. Frustra oggannit Smal- cius l. c. Quomodo Deus carni, hoc est, hominibus mortalibus seipsum manifestare commodè potest, nisi per carnem? Nam ne dicam, quod Deus po- lymeros kai polytropos sese manifestavit in V.T. non tantùm per carnem, sed per vocem, per visio- nes &c. aliud est manifestari per carnem, aliud ap- parere in carne, en sarki, quæ pessime confundit Smalcius. Regerit quidem contra Grav. p. 7. in carne idem esse posse, quod per carnem, creberrimè vocem en pro dia accipi: sed à posse ad esse non va- let consequentia. Loca etiam si afferantur, pateret longè esse dissimilia, nec fas est à propria verbo- rum significatione recedere. Denique nullus ad- ferri locus poterit, ubi apparuisse in carne Deus dicatur, quod mediantibus hominibus volunta- tem suam patefecerit. (3) To apparere in carne infert præsentiam in carne, existere scil. in carne, & se in ea videndum exhibere, ut cum apparuisse in rubo ardente dicitur Deus, singularis ejus præ- sentia notatur; id vero Deo Patri non convenit, sed Filio DEI, sic apparere in carne. Nec est, quod Smalcius dicat, manifestationem Dei dari, etiam si Deus ipse, quoad essentiam suam, absit, libr. de Verb. incarnat. p. 104. quum nec uspiam Deus, quoad essentiam, abesse possit, nec simpliciter hic manifestatus dicatur, sed ephanerothe en sarki, appa- ruit IN CARNE. Quod autem Deo Patri non conveniat to existere in carne, & in ea se viden- dum exhibere, agnoscunt ipsimet adversarii. Cer- tum est, inquit Smalcius l. c. Deum Patrem car- nem nullam habere posse, in qua ipsemet appareat. Alienum est, quod cum Socino huc trahit Smal- cius è Joh. XIV. 9. Qui videt me, videt & Patrem. Ibi enim Deum Patrem, & Christum unum esse innuitur, non autem Deus Pater in Christo, quà caro est, apparuisse dicitur. Nihil ibi de carne Chri- sti, aut de apparitione Patris in carne Christi. Quî ergò peregregiè ista huc facient, ut ait Smalcius? (4) Oppositio carnis & Spiritus locum non habet in Deo Patre, sed in Filio, non enim Patri in Scri- pturis assignatur ille diversus carnis & Spiritus respectus, sed Christo Rom. I. 4. IX. 5. 1. Pet. III. 18. (5) Non agitur hic de voluntate Dei patefacta, sed Deus ipse dicitur apparuisse in carne. Vocem autem DEI, non esse propriè, sed metonymicè de voluntate DEI accipiendam, quæ cogit aut suadet saltim ratio? A proprietate utiq; vocis non est di- sccdendum citra necessitatem. (6) Vox en sarki ex usu Scripturæ notat humanam naturam, per Syn- ecdochen receptam. Nuspiam autem Christus voce sarkikos notatur, sed tribuitur Christo sarx caro h. e. humana natura, Johan. I. 14. Ebr. II. 14. Christus enim etsi carne constet, non tamen merè caro est, nec caro esse dicitur, aut absolutè intel- ligitur nomine carnis. Proferantur hujus rei exempla è Scripturis idonea? Rursus si caro hu- manam significat naturam, ut censet Enjed. p. 368. non ergò voluntatem tantùm Patris designabit.

Smalcius hic confert 1. Joh. IV. 2. Christus venit in carne, quod reddit quidem, id est, circumda- tus infirmitate. Sed nuspiam caro in Scripturis idem est, quod infirmitas, quia infirmitas distin- guitur à carne, Galat. IV. 13. di' astheneian tes sar- kos per infirmitatem carnis. Nec uspiam aliquis dicitur venisse in infirmitate. Ideoque hic aliquid ousiodes infertur, in quo venerit, uti nomen car- nis propriè substantiam significat; venit igitur Christus in carne, id est, in humana natura tan- quam verus homo. Unde concludimus: Qui venit in carne, in eadem quoque manifestatus est; Christus venit in carne, non Pater. E. Quæ præ- terea hic conferunt adversarii, ἀλλότρια sunt: Quale est illud 2. Cor. IV. 7. ibi enim homines di- cuntur habere thesaurum in testaceis vasis. Hic non homo, sed Deus manifestari dicitur carne. Nec vers. 10. & 11. innuitur, quod Christus in car- ne mortali, id est, per homines infirmos prædicatus sit, sed de corpore mortali sermo est: in quo cir- cumferebant Apostoli mortificationem Domini Jesu, ut etiam vita in illo suo corpore manifestaretur, quid verò hoc ad præsentem locum? Alia ne excussione quidem digna sunt, quum nimis alie- na esse nemo non videat. (7) Si nihil aliud hic innuitur, quàm quod voluntas Dei manifestata sit per homines mortales & infirmos, non erat certè hoc mysterium N. Test. proprium, nec tanto ver- borum apparatu proponendum : ὁμολογουμένως mέγα μυστήριον τῆς εὐσεβείας; citra controversiam magnum est pietatis mysterium. Annon enim in V. T. jam voluntas Dei per homines infirmos, per Mosen & Prophetas erat revelata, Ps. CXLVII. 9. 10. Num hoc novum & absconditum arcanum erat? Annon ordinaria illa fuerat patefaciendæ volun- tatis divinæ ratio? Ubinam dicitur eapropter Deus apparuisse in carne pro magno mysterio, quod per homines mortales voluntatem suam re- velavit? Quod agnovit Smalcius, id idco non dici in V. T. ait, quod voluntas Dei saltem imperfecta ibi sit revelata, hic autem perfecta de salute generis hu- mani, de quo alias. Quis vero admittet, adumbra- tionem per Mosen & Prophetas factam tantundem valuisse, ac si nulla fuisset revelatio, neminemque illo- rum, qui tunc extabant, illa intellexisse; Quod Pa- radoxon effutiit Smalcius contr. Grav. p. 7. Et quæ est vocum μεταμόρφωσις? Vocem Θεõ primum accipiendam esse de Deo Patre, quia subjectivè po- nitur. Secundò non Deum ipsum, sed Dei Patris voluntatem notari: Denique non quamvis volun- tatem, sed perfectam (quasi detur etiam Dei volun- tas imperfecta) vel de salute generis humani. Ubi verò vox Θεõ idem notat, quod voluntatem DEI de salute nostra? Cur non proferuntur è Scriptu- ris loca vel exempla, quum nunquam non provo- cent aliàs adversarii ad Scripturas? Nihil crebrius esse, quam Deum pro voluntate Dei accipi, ait qui- dem Smalcius, sed nullum tamen Scripturæ locum proferre potuit. Nam qui in margine notantur Act. IV. 6. 7. vocis Dei propriam significationem retinere quis non videt? (8) Deum Patrem videri Angelis, non est magnum pietatis mysterium, hoc est, interprete ipso Smalcio, res nova, mira & in- cognita, res admirabilis & inusitata, interprete En- jedino, quum Angeli διὰ παντὸς videant faciem Patris, qui in cælis est, Matth. X IIX. 20. Nec de vi- sione tantum merè intellectuali hic sermo est. Non notatur tantum cognitio Dei, sed visio Dei conspi- cui facti in carne indigitatur, quæ non de Patre, sed de Filio Dei, quem in carne viderunt Angeli, teste historiâ sacrâ, intelligenda sunt. Emphasis vocis ὤφθη plus quàm meram & puram mentis no- titiam infert. Unde torquet se Enjedinus: modò lectionem hic variare dicit, & in quibusdam codici- bus pro Angelis legi hominibus, quod quidem tan- tò minus convenit Deo Patri, qui certe oculis cor- poreis non est conspectus ab hominibus patefa- ctus in carne tempore N. T. sed Filio Dei rectiffi- mè tribuitur: modò observat vocem ὤφθη secun- dum proprietatem Ebrææ linguæ exponendam esse, videri factus est, hoc est, conspicuus redditus, osten- sus hominibus est ab Angelis. Quod vero ipse cum

Socino, ut & Smalcius confugiunt ad voluntatis Dei revelationem, quasi antea benignam Dei erga gentes voluntatem agnitam non habuerint, vanum est κρησφύγετον; Quia non voluntatem Dei, ait A- postolus, innotuisse Angelis; nec ignorare potuêre Angeli voluntatem Dei benignam erga gentes tot vaticiniis Prophetarum jam prædictam in Vet. Test. nec Eph.III.10. id innuitur, quod ignorarint, etsi clarius innotuisse significetur multiformem Dei sapientiam scil. per experimentalem cognitio- nem, actuali Prophetarum complemento depre- henso. Ut taceam, quod Smalcio videatur l. de Incarn. Verb. p.105. Eph.III.10. Dæmones intelligi, non Angelos bonos. Præterea hic prius visus dicitur Angelis, post ἐκηρύχθη ἐν ἔθνεσιν prædicatus inter gentes. Non ergò de ea cognitione agitur, qua gen- tium vocatio ipsis innotuit, quæ ordine naturæ ipsam vocationem & prædicationem inter gentes præsupponit & consequitur. Deniq; non ait Apo- stolus, ἀποκαλύφθη, sed ὤφθη τοῖς ἀγγέλοις, non manifestata est, sed visa est angelis:& quis dubitabit, si patefacta est in Ecclesia per Christum & Aposto- los, quin Angelis innotuerit voluntas Dei? Num hoc opus erat ceu mirum mysterium recensere? (9) Si voluntas Dei revelata per carnem intelligitur, per Φανέρωσιν Θεῦ ἐν σαρκὶ, sequitur ταυτολογίαν commissam esse in hac tam nervosa mysteriorum pietatis enarratione. Quandoquidem postmodum addatur ἐκυρήχθη ἐν ἔθνεσιν, prædicatus inter gentes. Quid enim aliud intelligere possunt adversarii per hanc prædicationem, quam voluntatis Dei pate- factionem & revelationem per Apostolos factam? Num verò credemus in hoc aphorismo tavtolo- gum fuisse Apostolum, ut in ejusmodi nervosâ pe- riodo præmittitur phrasis plane inusitata, quam sequatur alia clarior ejusdem sensus, nonnullis aliis interjectis diversis prædicatis? (10) Accedit, quod nuspiam Deus Pater in scripturis N. T. dica- tur ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι vel ἐν δόξῃ ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι; tantum abest, ut id deprædicetur ceu manifestè magnum pietatis mysterium. Sed nec Evangelium Christi uspiam dicitur ἀναληφθῆναι ἐν δόξῃ. Pro- ducantur loca, nudè asserentibus extra & citra Scripturas non adjungimus fidem. Cum verbum Dei recipi dicitur, vox δέχεσθαι adhibetur, Act.II.4. c.IIX.14. XI.1. At ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι ἐν δόξῃ de Verbi Dei receptione nuspiam dicitur, quod non est sim- pliciter recipi, sed ut Syrus sublatus est, & Beza sur- sum receptus est. Ita Scapula in Lexic. τὸ ἀναλαμ- βάνομαι est sursum sumor; & observat τὸ ἀνὰ fre- quenter poni pro ἄνω sursum. Osorodus contra Tradel. part. 2. cap. 5. Deum gloriosè receptum esse, h. e. cum gloriosa sui exaltatione. Smalcius contra Grav. Deum recipi in gloria, idem est, quod alacri- ter, celeriter, & cum studio veræ pietatis admitti Christi Evangelium. Sed quibusnam Scripturæ do- cumentis, quibus rationibus id probant? Nullis. Quâ ergò facilitate id asseritur, eâdem quoq; me- ritò rejicitur. (11) Quid, quod denuo tavtologum faciant Apostolum adversarii hâc suâ glossâ. Jam enim anteà dixerat Apostolus, ἐπιστεύθη ἐν κόσμῳ, creditus in mundo. Annon vero cum gloriosa no- minis exaltatione accipitur is, in quem creditur? Act. XIII. 48. Et quum fides vera esse non possit absque studio veræ pietatis, annon suscipitur is et- iam cum studio veræ pietatis? Non congruit au- tem brevi, succinctæ, & nervosæ mysteriorum re- censioni περισσολογία ejusmodi, nec haberi potest ἐξήγησις vel prioris assertionis declaratio, ut vult Smalcius, quum multo obscurius minusq; obvium sit per τὸ ἀνελήφθη ἐν δόξῃ intelligi receptionem Evangelii, quam per τὸ ἐπιστεύθη ἐν κόσμῳ : Et num novum hoc atq; distinctum erit mysterium, quod receptum Evangelium sit ἐν δόξῃ ab eo, quod ei creditum sit in mundo: Unde Erasmo ipsi hîc aqua hæsit, ut non posset de Evangelio ista explicare, sed de receptione Christi in cœlum, unde profectus erat, declararet. Franciscus verò David agnoscere necessum habuit in Act. Colloq. Transylv. §. 3. non posse illa de aliâ aliqua persona intelligi, quàm homine Jesu Christo, qui est Deus manifestatus in carne, & assumptus in gloriam & gentibus prædi- catus. Et profitetur Andr. Fricius in Sylv. I. p. 42. Concedere adversarios suos de Christo dici, Deus apparuit in carne, sed negare, eum Deum esse à se, esseq; essentialiter unum cum Patre. Nec satis con- venit Smalcio cum Enjedino. Ille enim mysterium illud Col. I. 26. aliud esse ab hoc, quod 1. Tim. III. de- scribitur, & partem tantum hujus esse asserit, quod gentes etiam admissæ sint ad gratiam Dei. De in- carn. verb. p. 108. E contra Enjed. p. 373. procul omni dubio, ait, per mysterium hoc in loco intelligi doctrinam Evangelii de recuperatione gentium, neq; hic alia de re agi, quam Col. I. 26. Quid quod neque sibi ipsi constet Smalcius: Et cum modo per vo- cem θεῦ voluntatem Dei intelligit, cum Deus dici- tur manifestatus in carne, modò cum additur, ju- stificatus in Spiritu Deum justum, id est, pro vero agnitum ait, modò cum subjungitur visus angelis, iterum ad voluntatem Dei refugit angelis reve- latam &c.

Ad (3) Resp. Licet admittatur versari Aposto- lum in commendandâ Ecclesiæ doctrinæ dignita- te, & sublimitate, annon eò etiam facit recensio præcipuorum doctrinæ illius capitû maxime sub- limium, & admiratione dignissimorum? Nec verò Dei essentiam describi hîc asserimus, sed potius tὴν οἰκονομίαν, quam ita vocavit veneranda anti- quitas. Cujus descriptio optimè scopo, & proposi- to Apostoli congruit; ut doceat nempe, quænam complecteretur illa veritas præcipua capita, cujus σύλος ἅ̓ ἑδραίωμα est Ecclesia. Optimè Theodoret. in h. l. Ταῦτα περὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας εἰπὼν ἀναγκαίως τὸν δογματικὸν προσήγαγε λόγον. Postquam hæc dixit de Ecclesia, necessario etiam induxit orationem dogmaticam. Chrysost. & Theophyl. respiciunt men- tionem Ecclesiæ, quod ea cum Judæorum templo conferatur, & Pontifex Ecclesiæ cum Levitis, quod his præsideat ipse Deus manifestatus in carne. Si quis urgeat cum Smalcio, quod Christi mortem & resurrectionem non recenseat Apostolus; Resp. Licet expressè non recenseatur, implicite tamen insinu- atur utraq;. Quia ideo ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκὶ Filius, ut per mortem destrueret eum, qui mortis habebat im- perium, Ebr. II. 14. & ascensio gloriosa præsupponit ejusdem à mortuis resurrectionem, prædicatio quoq; ejus facta inter gentes complectebatur præcipuè doctrinam de Christi morte & resuscitatione. Nec aliter in Christum fides requiritur, quam ut creda- tur traditum propter peccata nostra, & resuscita- tum propter justificationem nostram, Rom. IV. 25.

Ad (4) Resp. Distinguendum est inter ea, quæ conveniunt æterno Dei Filio κατ' οὐσίαν, & quæ κατ' οἰκονομίαν. Licet quà essentiam invisibilis sit, nec loco moveatur, per dispensationem tamen appa- ruit in carne, visus est, & assumtus in cœlum. Quid enim? Annon constat etiam in V. T. Deum visum fuisse, locumque in apparitionibus mutasse, salvâ suâ infinitâ & invisibili essentiâ? Quod negare profectò nimis temerarium est, docente Augustino l. II. de Trin. c. 77. Distinguenda adhæc prædicata. Nam ut Deus primum dicitur in carne apparuisse, post visus esse, iterumque assumtus in gloriam, ita posteriora prædicata non de λόγῳ, quoad simpli- cem Deitatem, sed de Deo in carne manifestato ac- cipienda. De quo rectissime dicit, quis ambigeret, quod visus sit, quodq; in gloria in cælum assumt9?

Ad (5) Resp. Producenda erant à Schlichtin- gio loca, quod Φανέρωσις Θεῦ tantum cognitionem voluntatis Dei denotet in Scripturis: nec de Φανε- ρώσει̃ Θεῦ hic tantum agitur, sed de Φανερώσει̃ Θεῦ ἐν σαρκὶ, quam de sola voluntatis Dei revelatio- ne accipiendam esse, nondum è Scripturis evice- re adversarii. Contrarium verò supra probatum dedimus. Et cur apparitio in N. T. non inferret divinæ personæ exhibitionem, vel præsentiam, quum constet in V. T. apparitionem DEI præ- sentiam ipsius DEI importasse? ut ergò cum in V.T. Deus apparuisse dicitur, præsentia ejus infe- rebatur singularis, non tantum voluntatis ejus re- velatio, ita cum hic dicitur Deus apparuisse in carne, pariter non tantum voluntatis ejus reve- latio, sed singularis præsentia in carne denota- tur. Adde, quod de Christo, quem Deum & per- sonam esse divinam non diffitentur adversarii, in Novo etiam Testamento dicatur, cum præsentia ejus designatur, ἐφανερώθη Marc. XVI. v. 12. 14. Joh. III. 11. cap. XXI. 1. 14. Col. III. 4. Ebr. IX. 26. 1. Pet. I. 20. Imò nunquam vel nuspiam Christus vel Deus dicitur Φανερωθῆναι in N. T. quin semper intelligatur apparitio realis præsentiæ: ideoque ar- gumentum inverti & firmiter retorqueri potest contra adversarios ex usu Scripturæ perpetuo. Denique ut Marc. XVI. 12. de Christo dicitur ἐφα- νερώθη ἐν ἑτέρᾳ μορφῆ, ita ut assumtio alienæ formæ (extrinsecæ) & in eadem apparitio innuatur, ita etiam hic, vi identitatis phraseos, cum Θεὸς ἐφα- νερώθη ἐν σαρκὶ, assumtæ carnis & in eadem appa- ritio innuitur.

Ad (6) Resp. Utrumque illud ceu magnum veneratur Ecclesia mysterium, & quod Deus in carne conspicuus factus videri peculiariter volue- rit ab angelis, & quod in cælum assumtus sit. Qua- lenam verò hoc mysterium! obganniunt adversarii. Nam quæ ab Angelis conspecta, ea ab aliis etiam conspecta, & proinde commendari per id nequeunt tanquam aliquid novum, & mirum, quod ab Ange- lis visa fuerint, ait Smalcius contr. Grav. pag. 21. Adde, quod nulla pars mysterii pietatis jure in eo esset, quod Christus in cælum afcendit. Hoc enim necessario futurum erat, si Christus Servator mundi fuit, ut iterum Smalcius de Incarn. verb. p. 105. Resp. Magnum omnino hic mysterium, quod Angelis ὤφθη Deus manifestatus in carne: tum quod angeli de cœlo descendisse legantur, ipsum videndi causa, tum quod non, ut antea, intuiti sint Filium DEI ἄσαρκον, sed cum stupore jam viderint eundem in carne conspicuum, tum quod primitus ab Angelis visus, per eosdem deinde ceu præco- nes annunciatus sit hominibus, Luc. II. tum quod ipsi in carne fragili, & forma servi apparenti an- geli ministerium præbuerint ceu suo Domino, quæ & id genus alia huc pertinent ὁμολογυμένως magna pietatis mysteria. Ascensionem verò in cæ- lum, qui jure ambigi potest magnum fuisse my- sterium sive personam ascendentem spectemus, quæ non ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος, sed ipse cœli Dominus, Deus benedictus in secula, qui cœlum & terram implet; sive ascensionis modum respiciamus: Annon enim hominem propriâ virtute cœlum conscendere, imò cœlos gloriose penetrare μέγα μυσήριον; sive ascensionis consideremus terminum: quà verus na- tura homo in gloriam assumtus est, & ad dexteram Majestatis in excelsis erectus, quæ omnia citra con- troversiam magna pietatis sunt mysteria. Ratio in contrarium adducta prorsus futilis est, quia &

alia erant & necessariò futura, si Christus Servator mundi, utpote quod mori pro peccatis nostris, quod resurgere à morte, quod prædicari debuerit inter gentes, quæ tamen mysteria esse negari haud potest, sic & nulla pars mysterii pietatis in eo jure erit, juxta Smalcianam consequentiam, quod voluntas DEI gloriose recepta fuerit, vel religio Christi. Hoc enim necessario futurum erat, si Christus Servator mundi fuit.

Ad (7) Resp. Optime sibi constat & sensus & verborum cohærentia juxta fidem Ecclesiæ; si dicatur id innui, quod non tantum voluerit Deus conspicuus fieri in carne, seu naturâ humanâ assumtâ, sed & justificari simul, hoc est, ceu verus Messias agnosci, patefieri & celebrari in Spiritu vel ratione Deitatis, & quâ naturam divinam; quum Messias promissus non debuerit tantum apparere in carne, nobisque esse ὁμούσιός, sed etiam justificari, agnosci & celebrari in Spiritu verus Deus, ut in quo simul caro & Spiritus, id est, divina & humana natura appareant, quique & in carne & in Spiritu conspicuus fiat, & justificetur, vel agnoscatur verè, ac reapse verus naturâ homo, & verus naturâ Deus. Huc respicit interpretatio Chrysostomi, quod sapientia justificata sit à filiis suis. Alii divinam naturam intelligunt per Spiritum, qua sese exeruit per miracula, & oppositionis vim in eo locant, quod in infirmâ Christi carne ea sese exeruit, ut Christum quantumvis hominem infirmum, palam fuerit esse Deum: ut Beza, Piscator & Junius ac Tremel. in h. l. Alii divinam naturam indigitare volunt, qua ea humana suscepta eandem liberam servavit à peccatis: ut justificatus intelligatur, quá carnem quidem, sed in Spiritu, virtute divina naturæ, ut expers esset peccati, & perfecte justus, ut cum Theodoreto, Chrysost. Cyril. Theophyl. Anshelmus, quibuscum etiam Oecumenius vocem justificatus explicat, ratione rei sc. non ratione agnitionis tantum, quod immunis à peccatis, justusque secundum carnem fuerit; Addit Oecumenius, quod legales compleverit justificationes: itemque quod justificatus sit ab his, qui viderunt gloriam ejus ceu unigeniti à Patre. Quocunq; autem modo intelligatur justificatus, sive quod sanctificatus fuerit, sive quod legales justitias compleverit, sive quod justus, sanctus, & omnem implens justitiam agnitus, sive quod Messias verus, h. e. talis, qualem sese prædicavit, agnitus & celebratus fuerit, atque ita justificatus, justus, non fallax deprehensus: optimè sibi constabit nostra expositio, quod voce Spiritus divina designetur natura, ut & ipse contextus: quod Deus quidem apparuerit in carne, at simul in Spiritu vel virtute divinæ naturæ sanctificatus, legales justitias impleverit, vereque justus & verus Messias agnitus fuerit; aut veluti apparitio in carne infert præsentiam Dei in carne, & in eadem manifestationem, ita in Spiritu non solum fuisse, in forma divina, ut Phil. II. 6. loquitur Apostolus, extitisse, sed & in Spiritu sese manifestasse innuitur, quod justus sit, & justitia nostra, Messias promissus. Cæterùm non diffitemur, nonnullos vocem ἐν πνεύμαsi etiam aliter explicare, vel de Spiritu S. quod per Spiritum S. collaudatus sit & commendatus in Evangelio vel in testificationibus Sp. S. aut etiam miraculis, ut B. Lutherus, & alii, vel quod non ab humanis oculis justus judicatus sit, sed oculis Spiritus, qui scrutatur etiam profunda Dei, ut Oecumenius; vel quod, non quidem carnalibus, sed his, qui Spiritu DEI confirmati erant, justificatus sit; ut iterum Oecumenius, vel quod compleverit legis justitiam non Spiritu servitutis, sed Spiritu S. qui est Spiritus adoptionis, quem accepit juxta humanitatem, quam interpretationem itidem tradidit Oecume- nius: Vel de virtute divina, ut in Spiritu idem sit, quod potentiâ, vel virtute divina, qua sese ita demonstravit, ut justificaretur, seu justus agnosce- retur: vel de modo, quod in Spiritu, id est, spiri- tualiter agnitus sit justus, vel etiam spiritualiter justitiam compleverit, quæ expositio itidem legi- tur apud Oecumenium in h. l. Verumenimvero omnes illæ expositiones ita proponuntur à DD. Ecclesiæ, ut sua tamen maneat vis antecedenti aphorismi Apostolici propositioni, quod Deus conspicuus factus sit in carne, nec vacillet συνέ- χεια, tametsi oppositio rectius sibi constet carnis & spiritus in Deo manifestato, si ut illa de huma- na natura, ita hic de divina intelligatur & explice- tur naturâ, quemadmodum jam ostendimus.

Si quis dicat cum Enjedino p. 321. Christum totum esse comprobatum & receptum: non ergò sal- tim in Spiritu, h. e. quoad divinam naturam eum esse justificatum. Resp. τὸ in Spiritu non accipi exclusivè, sed inclusivè, quod non solum verus homo, sed & Deus esse debuerit Messias, talisque agnitus & patefactus sit, ut qui & in carne appa- ruerit (quâ humana natura designatur) & in Spi- ritu simul justificatus sit, h. e. agnitus, quod esset verus Deus. Adde quod peculiariter juxta divi- nam naturam dicatur justificatus, quia ab hac glo- riam quoque habuit ipsa humana natura.

Ad (8) denique respondetur: Nulla foret ab- surditas, etiamsi admitteretur ὑστερολογία in eo, quod prius nominetur prædicatio inter gentes, quàm assumtio in gloriam. Quia ὑστερολογίας in Scripturis dari, negari non potest. Smalcius ait quidem libr. de Verb. Incarn. p. 105. ὕστερα πρό- τερα Apostolis tribuere, esse Spiritum Sanctum, quo autore illi locuti sunt tantum, non ignominia afficere. Veruntamen alibi in refut. disp. de Incarn. p. 24. ipsemet fatetur dari interdum in Sacris ὑστερολο- γίαν, ut & p. 17. Figuram, inquit, ὑστέρꙋ προτέρꙋ dari non negamus, sed & raro, & talem quam quivis per se deprehendere, & facile dijudicare potest; jam verò quisnam ambigeret, hoc loco admissa eadem facile eam deprehendi posse; præ- sertim cùm aliunde constet, prius assumptum esse Christum in cœlum, quam prædicatum inter gen- tes? 2. Nec verò tantum id, quod alicubi priori loco scriptum est, alibi posteriori loco requiritur recensitum in Sacris; Sed id etiam posteriori loco ponitur, quod prius factum est, (quod con- tra Smalcii exceptionem l. c. p. 24. observandum) ut in narrationibus historicis videre est Gen. II. 1. cap. XII. 1. cap. XXX. 22. 23. Esa. XXXVIII. 21. Luc. IV. 9. abductio Christi super pinnam templi à Diabolo facta commemoratur post translatio- nem ejus in montem, quum tamen illa præcesse- rit hancce, ut patet è Matth. IV. 5. 8. 3. Quod si in historicis etiam narrationibus ὑσερολογίαι occurrunt, quantò minus absurdum erit hic, ubi non texitur historica narratio, nec opus est, ut ad ordinem & seriem, quâ gesta sunt, adstringa- tur oratio Apostoli, eandem statuere? 4. Quan- quam non opus sit eâdem, si dicatur, non juxta ordinem temporis illa recensuisse, sed alio arbi- trario, satisque concinno ordine, ut quemadmo- dum primum locum assignavit meritò apparitio- ni in terris factæ in carne, quâ Deus è cœlis de- scendens in carne conspicuus fieri voluit, & in tempore apparere,ita concluderet receptione Chri- sti in cælum omnia. 5. Adde, quod & ex parte prædicatus jam fuerit inter gentes, & creditus in mundo, antequam in cælum assumeretur, quum initia prædicationis Evangelii inter gentes ipse fecerit in diebus carnis suæ, nec defuerint, à quibus creditus est, ut ex historia Evangelica constat. Vid. Matth. IV. 15. 23. Luc. VI, 6. Joh. IV. 39. 41. 42. cap. XII. 20. 21. 6. Denique non reprobanda est Theodoreti observatio ad hæc verba: Assumtus est in gloria. Hoc quidem, inquit, factum est ante prædicationem, postremo autem id posuit, docens, prædicationem jure creditam fuisse. Est enim in cælis, qui hoc jussit fieri, & à dextris considet. Sed hæc etiam de loco illo classico.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle exhorts Timothy, regarding the predicted apostasy of many from the true faith and demonic seduction concerning the prohibition of marriage and certain foods, which are good creatures of God, to persist in the doctrine of the faith to which he has adhered, to flee profane old wives' fables, to exercise himself in piety, to place his trust in God alone, the Savior of all men, and to teach others the same, nor to allow himself to be despised, then to conduct himself in such a way that he may provide a pattern to others, and to that end to insist on reading and instruction, so that he may be able to have regard for his own salvation and that of others.

There are two parts: I. A prophecy concerning the apostasy of the last times, up to verse 5. II. An informative precept for the Bishop, set forth with distinct admonitions, up to verse 16.

PART I. A prophecy concerning the Apostasy of the last times.

Vers. 1. The Spirit) is given to Paul and to other Prophets of the Christian Church.

He says expressly) He signifies openly: not through ambiguities or enigmas, that is, through חידות or משל. See what was said at Num. XII. 8. More elegant Greeks would say διαῤῥήδην. But ῥητῶς is also found in Dioscorides and others. In the Glossary, ῥητῶς is openly.

That in later times) That is, hereafter. For that is the sense of the Hebrew expression אחרית הימים, which the Seventy are accustomed to translate, ἐσχάται τῶν ἡμερῶν.

Some shall depart from the faith) Many, tempted by philosophical arguments, shall fall away from the Christian faith, סוררי. The Patriarchs of heretics are philosophers, says Tertullian against Hermogenes. Professors of wisdom, from whose talent every heresy is armed, says the same Tertullian against Marcion I. He fortifies Timothy against those things which were to happen while he himself was still alive: This is evident below in verse 6. Compare 1 Pet. II. verse 2.

Giving heed to seducing spirits) Thus, to give heed to fables, above I. 4. Tit. I. verse 14. For πνεύματι πλάνης, the Latin has πνεύμασι πλάνης. Most Greeks have πνεύμασι πλάνοις, just as not a few Latins read it. Now, those who say they have prophecy from God, when they nevertheless truly speak from themselves or from the dictates of Satan, are accustomed to be called such by the Apostles. See 1 John IV. 1. and following. Πλάνοι, seducers, מתעים, Isaiah III. 12. IX. 16.

And doctrines of demons) He indicates the Pythagoreans especially, whose leaders were magi, and had commerce with demons. Among these, Apollonius of Tyana was notable, who is here expressly denoted. For he came to Ephesus while Timothy was still alive. Clem. Alexandr. Strom. III. 'Indeed, it is a matter of concern even to the magi to abstain from wine, and from living things, and from sexual pleasures.'

Latin:

CAP. IV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Prædicta apostasia plurium à vera fide, & seductione Dæmoniaca, quoad prohibitionem conjugii, & ciborum certorum, quæ bona Dei creaturæ sunt, hortatur Apostolus, ut Timotheus in doctrina fidei, cui adbæsit, persistat, prophanas aniles fabulas fugiat, seque in pietate exerceat, in Deum solum Salvatorem omnium hominum fiduciam suam collocet, aliosque id doceat, nec contemni se patiatur, tum ita se gerat, ut aliis typum præbeat, eaque fini lectioni & informationi instet, ut tum suæ, tum aliorum salutis rationem habere possit.

PArtes duæ sunt: I. Vaticinium de apostasia novissimorum temporum, ad vers. 5. II. Præceptum Episcopi informatorium monitis distinctis expeditum, usque ad vers. 16.

PARS I. Vaticinium de Apostasia novissimorum temporum.

Vers. 1. Τὸ πνεῦμα) Spiritus Paulo, & aliis Christianæ Ecclesiæ Prophetis datur.

Ῥητῶς λέγει) Apertè significat: non per ambages aut ænigmata, id est, per חידות aut משל. Vide, quæ dicta Num. XII. 8. Græci elegantiores dicerent διαῤῥήδην. Sed ῥητῶς etiam apud Dioscoridem est, & alios. In Glossario ῥητῶς apertè.

Ὅτι ἐν ὑστέροις καιροῖς) Id est, posthac. Nam is sensus est locutionis Ebrææ אחרית הימים, quod septuaginta solent vertere, ἐσχάται τῶν ἡμερῶν.

Ἀποστήσονταί τινες τῆς πίστεως) Deficient à Christiana fide multi Philosophicis ratiunculis tentati סוררי. Hæreticorum Patriarchæ Philosophi, ait Tertullianus adversus Hermogenem. Sapientiæ professores, de quorum ingenio omnis hæresis armatur, ait idem Tertullianus adversus Marcionein I. Munit Timotheum adversus ea, quæ ipso adhuc vivente erant eventura: Patet id infra 6. Confer. 1. Petr. II. vers. 2.

Προσέχοντες πνεύμασι πλάνης) Sic προσέχειν μύθοις supra I. 4. Tit. I. vers. 14. Pro πνεύματι πλάνης Latinus habet πνεύμασι πλάνης. Græci plerique πνευμασι πλάνοις, quomodo & Latini non pauci legere. Solent autem sic appellari ab Apostolis ii, qui Prophetiam se à Deo habere dicunt, cum tamen verè de suo, aut de Satanæ dictatis loquantur. Vide 1. Joh. IV. 1. & seqq. Πλάνοι מתעים, Esaiæ III. 12. IX. 16.

Καὶ διδασκαλίαις δαιμονίων) Pythagoricos maximè indicat, quorum præcipui erant magi, & cum dæmonibus habebant commercium. Inter hos insignis fuit Apollonius Tyanæus, qui hic eximie denotatur. Venit enim Ephesum vivente adhuc Timotheo. Clem. Alexandr. Strom. III. ἀμέλει διὰ φροντίδος ἐστὶ καὶ τοῖς μάγοις, οἴνου τε ὀμῶ, καὶ ἐμψύχων, καὶ ἀφροδισίων ἀπέχεσθαι.

## 4:2
Vers. 2.

In hypocrisy of liars) These things indeed have the appearance of holiness: But those who use it are false Teachers, and they do not observe these things except in the sight of men to deceive the common people. Ὑπόκρισις, hypocrisy, חלקות; ψευδολόγος, falsidicus, a liar in the Glossary. Athenaeus uses it. Plautus said 'falsiloquum' (liar), which word Ambrose used here. Having their own conscience seared) Having a conscience branded with the marks of crimes, of which they are conscious to themselves. Claudian: Inwardly branded stains deform the breast, and the image of vice has grown in. See other things which we have brought to bear on this matter at the end of the annotations to book 1 of the truth of the Christian religion.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Ἐν ὑποκρίσει ψευδολόγων) Speciem quidem ista habent sanctimoniæ: Sed qui eam usurpant, falsi sunt Doctores, neque ista observant, nisi in conspectu hominum ad fallendam plebem. Ὑπόκρισις חלקות, ψευδολόγος, falsidicus, mendax in Glossario. Utitur Athenæus. Plautus dixit falsiloquum, quam vocem hic posuit Ambrosius. Κεκαυτηριασμένων τὴν ἰδίαν συνείδησιν) Conscientiam habentes inustam notis criminum, quibus sibi sunt conscii. Claudianus: Pectus inusta Deformant maculæ, vitiique inolevit imago. Vide alia, quæ ad eam rem attulimus fine annotatorum ad libr. 1. pro veritate religionis Christianæ.

## 4:3
Verse 3. Forbidding to marry) They were not dissuading from marriage because they preferred celibacy: for that is fitting for Christians: but they were saying plainly that marriages are illicit, and that those who are in wedlock are alienated from salvation. To forbid is from the Hebrew כלה. It is attributed, however, to teachers just as 'laying on a burden', 'to say' and similar things; 'they set aside marriage', says Clement of the same people, Constitutions IV. 8. 'they teach celibacy' VI, 10.

To abstain from foods) There is here an ellipsis of the contrary. For 'commanding' is missing, which Epiphanius adds when citing this passage: or 'doing', which the Syrian adds. There is an almost similar ellipsis in 1 Cor. XIV. 34. and here above 11. 12. Thus Phaedrus: 'Not to dismiss these, but to be tortured by hunger.' Supply, 'I command'. This is Simplicius: although meanwhile it is true, as the Greeks say, that after verbs of prohibiting it is customary to add either particles or negative verbs, just as a double negative among them denies. Wherefore there is no need to change the reading, so that for 'to abstain' we read 'to hold fast', which Isidore of Pelusium contends in his letters IV. 101. By foods here understand those which are from animals. This is the abstinence from living things observed by the Pythagoreans, about which Porphyry's book exists. Alexis mentions it in the Atthis. Clement Stromata I, concerning the Sarmatians among the Persians: 'They neither live in cities, nor have roofs, but they clothe themselves in the barks of trees, and eat tree-fruits, and drink water with their hands, and know neither marriage nor procreation, just like the present-day Encratites.' In Clement's Constitutions VI. 8: 'they loathe some foods'; and VI. 26: 'they disparage certain foods.' These two abstinences, from marriage and from the most important part of food, are as it were the horns of the lamb, Rev. XIII. v. 11. Christians praised these things, but did not demand them, as can be seen in Apostolic Canon LI, in the Synod of Ancyra and Gangra, to which places Zonaras and Balsamon are to be consulted. Since the Encratites are so openly denoted here, it is no wonder if they did not receive Paul's Epistles, which Origen teaches us.

began to be fulfilled in Corinth, yet especially in the heretics who followed, impugning both the Deity of CHRIST and the meritorious satisfaction, which we have treated by institution in a special dissertation at Königsberg in Prussia. It is a question of apostasy not private, but public, not of a few, but notable and remarkable, which is to be in the extreme times, notorious: for who is ignorant that a particular apostasy has occurred in all ages in these or those regions, but this one, above others, is to be everywhere in the world, and almost ecumenical. But what more public, more universal, more notable apostasy from the faith was ever heard of in the Christian Church than that of the Roman Anti-Christ, who has made almost all his own heresies, just as has been shown everywhere by our people. The Apostle points to no other Apostasy here than that which 2 Thess. II. is predicted in the description of that great Anti-Christ, of whom we spoke there at verse 3. Which indeed is the very apostasy of the Roman Pontiff. Are the Pythagoreans therefore noted here, and the Magi especially, as will be taught? To be agitated by an evil spirit, by a spirit of seduction, or by seduction, is common to all false Prophets and Teachers, but it properly belongs to those who falsely boast of the Holy Spirit, which is done by the Pope, pretending an infallible direction of the Holy Spirit in all things, whatsoever he sanctions and decrees, both regarding faith and Christian life, to be observed under anathema; such as is also the decree prescribed for ecclesiastics concerning abstinence from marriage, and concerning the distinction of foods. That Apollonius of Tyana is especially denoted here is rashly asserted. For what reasons for this invention can he bring forward? None. Did he not himself at Matt. XV. verse 11. judge that the Jewish law prescribing a distinction of foods is referred to in this place, which is to be abolished? Did he not in book III of the truth of the Christian Religion, near the beginning, refer these things to the times of the Bishops contending for the highest sees, by whom Judaism regarding rites began as it were to be brought back? And what other traditions are those, about which Grotius at Matt. XXIV. verse 29, which after the death of the Apostles, and of the last of them, John, began to be scattered here and there, and in succeeding centuries received greater and greater increase, until at last the sun of the Evangelical truth itself was covered with darkness, Rev. XIX. verse 12, IX. verse 2, than those Papal ones concerning marriage and the distinction of foods? Furthermore, how do these things concerning Apollonius of Tyana, and other Pythagoreans, in the time of Timothy, square with the appendix of Grotius, where he draws this to the dogmas of the Encratites, whose parent Tatian, a disciple of Justin, finally emerged in the year 174, as noted at that year n. 3. by Baronius: but that these things look to the last times, both the letter of the text teaches, and the Greek Interpreters observe from the same. Chrysostom says, do not wonder if now some departing from the faith are still detained by Jewish superstition, there will be a time when those who are partakers of the faith will do that with greater blindness, when they will bring in a pernicious counsel not only as far as foods, but will also condemn marriages, and all things of this kind. And further: He does not say these things about the Jews, for in what way would it have a place in the last times: because of that same 'some will depart from the faith.' Theophylact says: Since it is established, he says, that some have made shipwreck concerning the faith, do not by any means wonder, he says, if some Christians from this time maintain the rites of the Jews. For it is to be that they will fall into worse things, who seem to follow CHRIST. These things indeed are not about the Jews

In this chapter he specifically instructs Timothy concerning matters pertaining to the office of a Bishop, not only for his own sake, but also for the sake of other Presbyters and Bishops, who are instructed in his person. Since he had already looked toward what kind of men those ought to be who are to be assumed into the Holy ministry: now he instructs what kind of men they ought to conduct themselves as in office. Since he had indicated to Timothy how he ought to behave in the house of the living GOD: now he teaches further what things are to be observed by him. He had warned at the end of the preceding chapter concerning the mystery of godliness regarding Christ, in which the sum of the Gospel is contained. Now, before he delivers other exhortations pertaining to the office, he instructs concerning the mystery of the Anti-Christ, and the doctrines of the same, as being the τὲ ἀντικειμένς of Christ and of the divine mysteries, so that it may be recognized by certain characteristics. Grotius, so that we might no longer believe that the Roman Pontiff is designated as the Anti-Christ, transforms the ὑσέρες καιρὲς, the last times, into times immediately impending, but with no example brought forward for that purpose, whether from Hebrew custom or from Greek, as if a prophecy were being delivered concerning those things which were to happen even in Timothy's time; and he snatches away what is said concerning those who apostatize from the faith, if not to the Philosophers, the professors of wisdom, then to their children. But by what argument? First, he seeks it from verse 6, whom Timothy ought to warn concerning that time of his. But were not the Apostles commanded to warn in their own time concerning prophecies suggested by the Spirit, even if they were to have their fulfillment in the last times? Was not Saint John also commanded the same, even though it is beyond ambiguity that those things which pertain to the last times were inspired in him by the Holy Spirit? Then he brings forward the saying of Peter in 2 Epist. II. 2, which, however, even if in the age of the Apostles in Ebion and Ce-

He predicts [this] to the Jews, inasmuch as they were in earlier times, but [he speaks] of the Marcionites and Manichaeans, and other followers of heresies. For by their suggestion and work, they both rejected food and marriage. Nor is any one of the ancients found who believed that these things were fulfilled in the time of Timothy. Many judged that they began to be fulfilled in the Manichaeans and Encratites, the mystery of Papal impiety not yet being so detected: but Lyranus expressly confesses at this place that the Apostle speaks most especially of those who will seduce with false doctrines around the times of the Anti-Christ: and Bellarmine himself confesses, in these words: 'In the last times is signified the whole final age from Christ even to the judgment,' just as Justinian also has in his paraphrase, he declares that it will be that those things will come in the following and almost final times. Let the Jesuits reconcile, if they can, with these things which Tirinus has, that those who absolutely condemn marriage and lived in the first times of the Church are noted, such as Saturninus, the Marcionites, the Encratites, the Manichaeans. Add that the Apostle joins the prohibition of foods with the interdict of marriage: But who ever prohibited all foods to all people? Whence it is clear that not a simple prohibition of marriages, just as neither of foods, is designated: But both are to be understood in a certain respect, the former concerning a certain kind of men, the latter concerning a certain kind of foods and certain times, just as also Alcibiades, a companion of Montanus, previously observed a choice of foods according to Eusebius, book V, 3, μὴ χρήμενος τοῖς κτίσμασι τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ἄλλοις τύπον σκανδάλου ὑπολειπόμενος, not using the creatures of God, and leaving to others an example of scandal, until he was corrected by Attalus the Martyr; but other companions of Montanus, boasting of prophecies, passed laws concerning fasts and prophecies. But the Manichaeans deterred their 'elect' from the eating of meat and the use of marriage, leaving it to their 'auditors,' whose rank was second. See Augustine, Epistle LXXIV, and On the Morals of the Manichaeans, chapter 18. From whom, therefore, the Roman Anti-Christs have their origin, namely from the Marcionites, Encratites, Montanists, Manichaeans, and others of that kind, forbidding marriage to priests; and observing a distinction of foods, under obligation of conscience, unless a dispensation is redeemed by a price. For these characters of the apostates of the last time are very notable, and striking the eyes most especially, even of the ruder common people, and they do not fit anyone as they do the Roman Anti-Christ. They certainly do not fit Apollonius of Tyana, nor were they observed in him, and it is to be noted especially that by the word κωλυόντων it is not expressed that they will condemn marriages, but they are designated as those who prohibit them with legislative authority and power. For neither, as Theodoret says, does he disparage celibacy and continence, but he accuses those who, by a law having been passed, compel [people] to follow them. Just as was done by the Roman Pontiff in the Council of Trent, Session XXIV, Canon IX: 'If anyone shall say that Clerics constituted in holy orders, or Regulars who have solemnly professed chastity, can contract marriage, and that the contract is to be ratified, notwithstanding the Ecclesiastical law or vow, and that the opposite is nothing else than to condemn marriage, and that all can contract marriage who do not feel that they have the gift of chastity, even if they have vowed it, let him be anathema.' Add that in the same session, Canon VI, he defined that a ratified marriage is dissolved by the solemn profession of some religion through another marriage; and that the Papists are very unjust to second marriages, they deny them the blessing of the Church, nor do they admit priests to be present at them, nay, they truly pronounce them to be fornication, C. Hac causa XXXI. q. 1. Finally, they think impiously concerning marriage itself. 'If it is good not to touch a woman,' it is said in C. Hospitiolum, dist. XXXII, 'therefore it is evil to touch [one]': Item, 'the presence of the Holy Spirit is not given at the time when conjugal acts are exercised.' Can. Quicquid & C. connubia caus. XXXII. q. 2. 'even the marriage of Saints is not exercised without a certain pollution and filthiness.' Bellarmine, book 1, On Clerics, chapter 18. To which they drag that [saying] of the Apostle: 'Those who are in the flesh cannot please GOD.' See Can. Decernimus &c. dist. XXXIII. Can. Tenere. dist. XXXI. Can. proposuisti, & Plurimos dist. LXXXII, to say nothing of the profane voices of Campegius, Pighius, Hosius, three Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church: 'That a priest sins more grievously if he takes a wife than if he commits fornication,' which the Jesuits are not afraid to defend. See Costerus in Enchiridion, chapter XVIII. Cornelius à Lapide on 1 Corinthians VII. Similarly, laws have been sanctioned in the Papacy concerning the choice of foods, which cannot be violated without the most grievous sin. Whence Bellarmine contends, book II, On the Good Works, chapter 7, that the faithful are bound in conscience to certain fasts and a choice of foods. But also certain foods were prohibited as unclean and execrable by Gregory II & the Epistles of Zachary to Boniface of Mainz, when on the contrary, by the testimony of the Apostle, every creature of GOD is good, nay, it is punished more severely in the Papacy against those who use prohibited foods than against those who impinge upon the law of GOD, just as in Rome at the time of Lent the meat market is indeed closed, but prostitutes are offered, and brothels are open. What do the Pythagoreans have to do with this? What do the Persian Sarmani? Did they fall away from the Christian faith? More rightly those two horns, as of the Lamb in Apocalypse XIII, verse 11, are brought here, which are truly the horns of the Anti-Christ himself, who keeps saying that he is like the Lamb, like Christ himself, that Lamb of GOD. If Christians only praised abstinence from marriages and certain foods, they would not demand it; does not the Roman Pope proclaim himself to be less of a Christian when he demands them? However, Apostolic Canon LI is rashly cited by Grotius, since the Apostolic Canons are reckoned among the apocrypha by Gelasius, dist. XV, c. Sancta Romana; nor are more than 50 canons asserted by Leo IX in Gratian, dist. XVI, c. Clementis. And the rest added to them are rejected as spurious and heretical by Bellarmine, De Script. Eccl., and Baronius, ad ann. CII, n. 7. And since abstinence is not imposed by that canon upon either clergy or laity as if it were from the Pope, but is left to their own judgment, which is also observed in the Xth and XIVth Canons of the Synod of Ancyra, and in the Synod of Gangra, with Grotius not dissenting here; it does not appear how these canons and these councils can assist the Papacy, whose defender Grotius acts. In the Council of Ancyra, Canon X allows deacons already ordained to take wives, if at the very ordination they have protested that they have need of wives. Do the Roman Pontiffs allow that? Nor is abstinence from meats commanded in Canon XIV, even for the clergy themselves: since, on the contrary, the Roman Pontiff sanctions abstinence by his own laws. In the Council of Gangra, Eustathius, Bishop of Sebaste, is condemned, as witnessed by Socrates, book II, chapter 3, and Sozomen, book III, chapter 13, among other things, because he forbade marriage and taught abstinence from foods. Thus, therefore, the Roman Pontiff will also have to be condemned. Anathema is also said in Canon II to one eating meat. Therefore, let the same be said of the Roman Pontiff. That this is not said of the Encratites, he proved

B. Gerhard on this passage: The Apostle does not speak of those who were going to condemn marriage and foods; but of those who, through hypocrisy and the appearance of singular perfection, were going to forbid marriage and certain foods. For it is one thing to condemn, which the Marcionites, Tatianists, and Manichaeans did; it is another to forbid, which the Papists do. For Paul does not speak of those who, with open blasphemy against God, the author of marriage, and the Creator of foods, would condemn marriage and certain foods (which those ancient heretics did), but of those who, in hypocrisy, under the appearance of a certain feigned holiness, would interdict marriage to certain men and prescribe abstinence from certain foods. And further: The Apostle speaks of those who do this with a seared conscience. This fits the Papists most especially, since they know that this distinction is not divinely commanded. But let us suppose these things fit the Encratites in a certain way; it must not therefore be denied that the Roman Pontiff is designated here: since he has had many precursors, and it is evident that the sink of ancient heresies has flowed into the Roman ἀκρισίαν [lack of judgment] and ἀποστασίαν [apostasy]. Which is here not obscurely insinuated concerning the apostasy of the last times. For although those two special doctrines are expressed as certain and notable characteristic marks, from which the Anti-Christ can be recognized without difficulty by anyone, yet in general, διδασκαλίαι δαιμωνίων [doctrines of demons] denotes false doctrines adverse to heavenly truth originating from the Demon, of which there is such an abundance in the Papacy as is not easily found in any heresy dispersed throughout the universal Church. And what wonder, that doctrines of demons proceeded from and were sanctioned by the Roman Pontiffs, who themselves gave themselves over to demons and were addicted to magic, such as it is established that Sylvester II, Benedict VIII, Gregory VII, the chief author of the Papal Monarchy, Benedict IX, John XX, and John XXI, and others were?

Now if hypocrisy is also a peculiar character of the Anti-Christ, where does hypocrisy in doctrine and life reign more among all the heresies in the world than in the Papacy, which is entirely composed of hypocrisy and frauds? A great part of these things can be testified to by the many dogmas of the Canon decrees, and the multivolume works of moralists and casuists, rituals, ceremonials, processionals, and other such public Papist writings, the countless miracles which are bandied about in the Papacy, the cult of relics, fictitious fasts, the peddling of indulgences, penitential taxes, satisfactions, pilgrimages, flagellations, and especially the throngs of religious orders, etc., which are living images of hypocrisy.

Furthermore, do the Roman Anti-Christs not betray a seared conscience when they run to Scripture, to the Vicariate of Christ, to the chair of Peter, and to the succession in that same see; even though they know that Scripture, Christ, and Peter are in most things diametrically opposed to them, as well as they know their own fingers or feet, which those servants of servants expose to the kisses of the great, and they are not ignorant that that succession is so uncertain that it cannot be more uncertain, the vanity and nullity of which has been demonstrated to the eyes often enough. In particular, the hypocrisy shines through, and the seared conscience of the Anti-Christ is betrayed in the decrees of abstinence from marriage and certain foods. For in C. Si quis docuerit dist. XXVII, the Canon of the Apostles is praised: If anyone shall teach that a priest, under the pretext of religion, should despise his own wife, let him be anathema. C. Lege Imperatorum dist. X.

from Pope Nicholas this sentence is brought forward: Blessed Gregory writes to Theoctista the Patrician, among other things; If, he says, marriages are said to be dissolved for the sake of religion, it must be known that, although human law has conceded this, divine law has nevertheless forbidden it. Book VI, Constit. chap. 17. We say that a Bishop, Presbyter, and Deacon ought to be appointed as the husband of one wife, whether their wives are living or have departed. See also the sentence of Innocent C. Deinceps dist. XXVI, of Pelagius C. de Syracusana dist. XXIIX, of Leo IX C. omninò dist. XXXI, etc. John Hofmeister, against the Augsburg Confession, art. on the Marriage of Priests, approves the sentence of Aeneas Sylvius, later Roman Pontiff: That Pope Pius II rightly and without doubt said: We believe there were causes why marriage was taken away from priests, but there are much greater causes why it ought to be granted. Do they not therefore act against their conscience, because they do not restore it? They forbid priests to have wives under the pretext of holiness, just as Popes Siricius and Innocent ordered them to be celibate, because it is written: Be holy, for I am holy; likewise: Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. C. decernimus dist. XXXVII, C. Tenens dist. XXXI, etc. But yet they find it necessary to admit that more married men live holily than are found holy among the celibate. See Confess. Cathol. B. Gerh. l. II. part. II. pag. 92. seq. So also the matter stands regarding those masked fasts, which are instituted by the choice of foods. The Canon Law, Roman Catholic Pontiffs and Bishops, and other notable Papists openly betray the seared conscience of the Anti-Christ along with hypocrisy. C. Qui Episcopus dist. XXIII. From the Council of Carthage, among other things, it is required of a Bishop that he should not condemn second marriages, and should not blame the partaking of meat C. Si quis carnem &c. dist. XXX. the decree of the Council of Gangra is cited. C. If anyone believes that one eating meat is to be condemned both in faith and religion as having no hope, let him who eats it be anathema. C. What it says in dist. XLI. the opinion of Augustine is praised: It does not matter at all what kind of food you take to relieve the necessity of the body, provided it is consistent in the kinds of food with those with whom one must live, etc. Eleutherius in the time of Antoninus Commodus, as Platina testifies in his rite, decreed that no one should reject any kind of food on account of superstition, by which human custom might be overcome. Gregory the Great, Vol. III. part 3. Adm. 20. Food does not commend us to GOD. Let those hear, some will depart from the faith and truth, etc. Anastasius the Bishop, Vol. I. Bibl. Patr. fol. 98. If anyone abstains from meats indeed, but nourishes the body with other foods and drinks, and renders it filled with fat, fasting profits him nothing. Guilhelm. Lindanus l. III. Panopl. l. 9. Our fasts, which swim with an abundance of wine, and overflow with plenty, and surpass the delights of meats with a variety of fish, and so, as Jerome also complained about the customs of his own age, seem to play with GOD, while for the heat that arises from eggs, they stuff the gluttonous stomach with flames of oil, the heat of wine, and fires of every kind of spice, we think it is better known to all pious people who consider the truth than that any words need to be brought forth about the matter, that these were not only unknown to the ancient Christians, but also intolerable, and even abominable. Similar things to these are read in Erasmus in ἰχθυοφαγίῃ and in Epist. ad Basil. Episcop. CXIV. Although these things are entirely so, the Pope nevertheless dared, through the Council of Toledo in the year 653, as Cardinal Baronius reports in that year no. 3. to define: Whoever without inevitable necessity, and evident languor of frailty, or even impossibility of age, shall presume to attend to the eating of meats on the days of Lent, will not only be guilty of the Lord's resurrection, but also a stranger to the communion of the same holy day. abstinence from certain foods and especially from meat pertains to the reason of fasting. Can this hypocrisy not be felt with the hands, can the cautery of the conscience not be usurped by the very eyes? But when Grotius tries to draw this to Apollonius of Tyana and to the Encratites, so that they might not be believed to touch the Roman Pontiffs, he agrees neither with himself, nor with the Apostolic prediction, because he wishes it to have been fulfilled in the time of Timothy. But the Encratites arose only a century later: and the words of the Apostle clearly teach that he looked here to the last times; who therefore can restrict these things to the Encratites or to the times of Timothy? Apostasy from the faith does not fit Apollonius, because he was a Pythagorean philosopher: but Theodoret here: He shows that those who were later false prophets were once joined to the Ecclesiastical body. For this is what that signifies: 'some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error.' The hypocrisy designated by Paul does not fit him, because he was an open Magician: nor the doctrine forbidding marriages and distinguishing foods, for which no authentic documents exist. But the thing itself speaks that the dogmas and hypocrisy of the Encratites dominate under the Roman Anti-Christ, so that that great champion of the Pope could not manage the desperate cause of the Papacy here.

Concerning the phrase κωλυόντων βρωμάτων, the observations of Oecumenius are worthy: It is not an error or a slip from the elegance of speech that he says 'to abstain from foods,' as it has seemed to some, nor is it the Apostle's negligence: But the speech is rightly expressed according to the Attic usage also. Just as when it is said ἐκώλυσεν αὐτὸν μὴ ποιεῖν τὰ ἄτοπα, that is, 'he prevented him from committing absurdities,' it is not signified that he exhorted him to absurdity, and when it is said, ἀπέτρεπεν ἀυτὸν μὴ προσκρόειν Φίλοις, 'he deterred him from resisting friends,' it is not hinted that he exhorted him to resist friends, but rather the contrary. Again when it is said: ἐκώλυσε μὴ κλέπτειν, that is, 'he prevented from not stealing,' it is not signified that he exhorted to theft. Furthermore when it is said: ἐκώλυσεν ἀπέχεσθαι ἀῥῥητοποιΐας, that is, 'he prevented from abstaining from unspeakable deeds,' this is, he drove him away from such an action. For thus ἐκώλυον ἀπέχεσθαι βρωμάτων, that is, 'they prevented from abstaining from foods,' that is, they prevented from foods. Conformable to this exposition of Oecumenius is that of Budaeus in his commentary on the Greek language, fol. 935. To verbs which are in themselves negative (ἀποφατικὰ καὶ ἀπαγορευτικὰ) the Attics add a negation, as with ἀπαγορεύω, with κωλύω, and ἀρνῦμαι and ἀπέχω. Hence the rule: The verb κωλύειν joined with a negative particle or a verb having a negative signification contains a greater force of commanding and ordering according to Attic custom.

which God created for partaking) That is, he created with this intention, that he might grant their use to men, if not from the beginning, at least after the flood, Gen. IX. verse 3. and more openly in the Gospel. But it is said very properly here εἰς μετάληψιν. For μεταλαμβάνειν τροφῆς is to eat, Acts II. verse 46. XXVII. verse 33. So also καρπῶν μεταλαμβάνειν 2. Timothy II. verse 6. and ἀγαθῶν above XVIII. verse 9.

With thanksgiving to the faithful. A transposition for ἔκτισε τοῖς πιϛοῖς εἰς μετάληψιν μετ' εὐχαριστίας: That food may not be taken unless thanks have been given to GOD, who created these things for our uses, is an ancient custom of the Hebrews, which Christ approved by his own example. See what is said in Matthew XIV. 19. XV. 36. XXVI. 26.

And to those who have known the truth) To whom this truth is known, which now follows.

Whose partaking and use, therefore, God himself granted, which the Roman Pope prohibits, does he not thus exalt himself above GOD? Therefore John of Wesel (around the year of Christ 1464) rightly warned: That which is not prohibited in Scripture is not to be held as a sin: it is also lawful to eat meat on Green Thursday. Master Johannes Ibenhagen around the year 1480 taught that it is lawful for Christians to eat meat on all days. For all things, he says, were created by GOD for the use of man, and no such precept is found in the Holy Scriptures: therefore men are not obligated to observe it. Erasmus in his paraphrase on 1. Corinthians VIII. I approve what you say: Food does not commend us to GOD. For since GOD created all things for human uses, and no one demands anything from us besides the piety of life, what does it matter to him whether one eats the meat of fish, or of quadrupeds, or of birds? For the choice of foods neither adds nor subtracts anything from piety. It can make one superstitious, but by no means pious; Christ taught no such distinction. Therefore it is an act of rashness if any little man (the Roman Pontiff) attempts to burden anyone with such constitutions. The estates of the Holy Roman Empire in the Grievances of the German Nation, offered at the Diet of Nuremberg in the year 1523, among other burdens (they say) this is not to be placed in the last position, that by human constitutions many things are prohibited and commanded, even many things which have been neither forbidden nor commanded by any divine precept, of which kind are marriage, etc., and the prohibited use of foods, which God created for the necessity of man, and which the Apostle taught should be taken indiscriminately with thanksgiving. Concerning which, see the Theodoretian notes on this place. After he shows the ruinous nature of their doctrines, he predicts how execrable their laws also are: For they call marriages execrable, and many foods, so that they may do injury to the Creator. But he made them for use, so that those who are partakers of them might take from it an occasion of giving thanks, and of praising him who provides them. Grotius asks here: Why does the Apostle refute not both, but only one species of the Diabolical doctrine? From Danaeus he brings the reason, that he foresaw that that evil (of forbidding marriage) was not yet imminent. From Hyperius, that he judged that error, as being contrary to nature itself, unworthy of refutation; he himself, however, observes that it is sufficient that elsewhere the Apostle brings a grave judgment against the prohibition of marriage, and excellently asserts the freedom of contracting it, Heb. XIII. 1 Cor. VII. But the arguments of the Apostle are so constructed that, by parity of reasoning, they can be applied equally to the other species. For if you look at the efficient cause, from where do all foods come, if not from GOD, from where marriage, if not from the author GOD? Use, therefore, depends not on the will and ordination of men, but of GOD. If the final cause, εἰς μετάληψιν, they were ordained for participation by all men in the Protoplasts, not for abstinence. The ultimate end is the glory of GOD, which is born from participation, when we use these gifts of GOD with thanksgiving; which they hinder who forbid their use, or that of any men, no less than those who abuse the same for the lusts of the flesh. If you look at the object, they are ordained for all the faithful, and those who acknowledge the divine truth, without distinction. Therefore, they are not against piety, nor against the faith, with respect to any order or status. But they testify to an apostasy from the faith and heavenly truth who define other things against that ordinance of GOD.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Κωλυόντων γαμεῖν) Non dehortabantur à nuptiis, ideò quod cælibatum præferrent: id enim Christianis convenit: sed plane dicebant illicitas esse nuptias, alienos esse à salu- te eos, qui in conjugio sunt. Κωλύειν ab Ebræo כלה. Tri- buitur autem doctoribus sicut ἐπιτιθέναι βάρος, dicon & si- milia, τὸν γάμον ἀθετῦσιν, ait de eisdem Clem. Constit.IV.8. ἀγαμίαν διδάσκουσι VI, 10.

Ἀπέχεσθαι βρωμάτων) Est hic ἰσχνησις contrarii. De- est enim κελευόντων, quod addit hunc locum citans Epi- phanius: aut ποιούντων, quod addit Syrus. Similis fermè Ellipsis 1.Cor.XIV. 34. & hic supra 11. 12. Sic Phædrus: Non hæc dimitti, verum cruciari fame. Supple, jubeo. Hoc Simplicius: quanquam interim ve- rum est, quod ajunt Græci, post verba prohibendi solere addi aut particulas, aut verba negantia, sicut duplex ne- gatio apud eos negat. Quare nihil opus mutare lectio- nem, ut pro ἀπέχεσθαι legamus ἀντέχεσθαι, quod conten- dit Isidorus Pelusiota epistolarum IV. 101. Βρώματα hic intellige ea, quæ sunt ex animalibus. Hæc est ἀποχὴ ἐμ- ψύχων observata Pythagoristis, de qua extat Porphyrii li- ber. Meminit Alexis Atthide. Clemens Strom. I. de Sar- manis apud Persas: ὕτε πόλεις οἰκῦσιν, ἔτε στέγας ἔχουσιν, δενδρῶν δὲ ἀμφιέννυνται φλοιοῖς, καὶ ἀκρέδρυα σιτῦνται, καὶ ὕδωρ ταῖς χερσὶ πίνουσιν, 8 γάμον, 8 παιδοποιΐαν ἴσασιν, ὥσ- περ οἱ νῦν ἐγκρατῖται. In Clementis Constitutionibus VI. 8. τινὰ τῶν βρωμάτων βδελύσσονλαι· & VI. 26. βρώματά τι- να φαυλίζυσι. Hæ duæ abstinentiæ à nuptiis, & à ciborum parte potissima, sunt cornua velut agni, Apoc. XIII. v. 11. Christiani ista laudabant, sed non exigebant, ut videre est Canone Apostolico LI. in Synodo Ancyrana & Gangrensi, ad quæ loca videndi Zonaras & Balsamo. Cum tam aper- te hic denotentur Encratitæ, nihil mirum, si illi Pauli Epi- stolas non recepere, quod nos Origenes docet.

rintho impleri cœpit, maximè tamen in hæreti- cis subsecutis, cum Deitatem CHRISTI, tum satisfactionem meritoriam impugnantibus, ad- impletum, quo de peculiari dissertatione Regio- monti Borussorum ex instituto egimus. De apo- stasia agitur non privata, sed publica, non pau- corum, sed insigni ac notabili, quæ temporibus ex- tremis futura sit, notoria: nam alias apostasiam particularem omnibus seculis in his illisve regio- nibus contigisse, quis ignorat, sed hæc præ aliis passim in orbe, ac ferè œcumenica futura. Quæ verò magis publica, magis universalis, magis insignis à fide apostasia unquam in Ecclesia Chri- stiana audita est, quàm Romani Anti-Christi, qui omnes propemodum hæreses suas fecit, quemadmodum passim à nostratibus ostensum. Non aliam Apostasiam hîc indigitat Apostolus, quam eam, quæ 2. Thessal. II. prædicta est in de- scriptione magni illius Anti-Christi, quâ de illic ad vers. 3. diximus. Quæ vero est ipsissima Ro- mani Pontificis Apostasia. Pythagoricos ergò hîc notari, & Magos præcipuè, quomodo do- cebitur? A maligno spiritu, à spiritu seductio- nis, vel seductione agitari, commune est omnibus falsis Prophetis & Doctoribus, sed illis propriè convenit, qui Spiritum Sanctum falso jactant, quod à Papa fit, infallibilem Spiritus Sancti di- rectionem prætendente, in omnibus, quæcunque sancit ac decernit, quà fidem, & qua vitam Chri- stianam, sub anathemate observanda; quale et- iam decretum est de abstinentia conjugii Eccle- siasticis præscriptum, & de ciborum discrimine. Apollonium Thyanæum hic eximiè denotari teme- rè asseritur. Quas enim hujus commenti ratio- nes proferre potest? Nullas. Annon ipse ad Matth. XV. vers. 11. Judaicam legem ciborum discrimen præcipientem respici h. l. censuit, quas abolenda sit? Annon l. III. de verit. Relig. Christ. sub initium ad tempora Episcoporum de sum- mis sedibus certantium hæc retulit, quibus Ju- dæismus circa ritus quasi reduci cœperit? Et quænam aliæ sunt istæ traditiones, de quibus Grotius ad Matth. XXIV. vers. 29. quæ post mor- tem Apostolorum, eorumque ultimi Johannis spargi hic, illic cœptæ procedentibus seculis ma- jus, majusque augmentum accepêre, donec tan- dem ipse sol veritatis Evangelicæ caligine obdu- ctus fuit Apoc. XIX. vers. 12. IX. vers. 2. quàm Papales illæ de conjugio & ciborum discrimine. Porrò quomodo hæc de Apollonio Thyanæo, & aliis Pythagoræis, tempore Timothei, quadrant cum appendice Grotii, ubi ad dogmata Encra- titarum hoc trahit, quorum Parens Tatianus Ju- stini discipulus demum anno 174. emersit, no- tante ad illum annum n. 3. Baronio: ad tempora autem novissima hæc spectare, cùm litera textus docet, tùm Græci Interpretes ex eodem obser- vant. Chrysostomus, ne mireris, inquit, si modo quidam à fide discedentes adhuc Judaica supersti- tione detineantur, tempus erit, cum hi, qui fidei participes sunt, istud majore cum exæcatione fa- cient, cum non modò ad cibos usque perniciosum consilium inferent, verum nuptias quoque, & hu- jusmodi cuncta damnabunt. Et porro: Non de Judæis hæc dicit, quo enim pacto locum haberet in novissimis temporibus: ob illud idem recedent. quidam à fide. Theophylactus: Cum constet, in- quit, circa fidem naufragium fecisse nonnullos, ne- quaquam, inquit, mireris, si quidam ex hoc tempo- re Christiani Judæorum ritus tueantur. Est nam- que ut in deteriora prolabantur futurum, qui fectæ- ri CHRISTUM videntur. Hæc quidem non de Judæis

Hoc capite peculiariter informat Timotheum de rebus ad officium Episcopi spectantibus, non tantùm ipsius, sed etiam aliorum Presbyterorum & Episcoporum causâ, qui in ejus persona insti- tuuntur. Quum antea ed etiam respexerit, qua- les esse debeant, qui assumendi ad S. ministeri- um: Jam quales in officio sese gerere debeant, instruit. Quum Timotheo indicarrit, quomodo conversari in domo DEI viventis debeat: nunc ulterius, quæ ab ipso sint observanda, docet. De mysterio pietatis de Christo, quo summa contine- tur Evangelii, sub finem præcedentis capitis mo- nuerat. Nunc antequam paræneses alias ad offi- cium spectantes tradat, de mysterio Anti-Christi, & doctrinis ejusdem, utpote τὲ ἀντικειμένς Chri- sti & mysteriorum divinorum, ut per characte- res certos cognoscatur, informat. Grotius ne Romanum Pontificem Anti-Christum designa- ri amplius credamus, ὑσέρες καιρὲς tempora no- vissima in tempora imminentia proximè trans- format, sed nullo eam in rem adducto sive ex Ebraicâ consuetudine, sive è Græcâ, exemplo, quasi de iis vaticinium tradatur, quæ Timothei adhuc tempore eventura sint; & quæ de aposta- tis à fide dicuntur, abripit, si non ad Philoso- phos, sapientiæ professores, ad eorum filios. Sed quo argumento? Primum è vers. 6. quos monere de eo tempore suo debebat Timotheus, petit. At annon de vaticiniis à Spiritu suggestis, etsi temporibus extremis complementum habi- turis, suo tempore monere jubebantur Aposto- li? Nonne etiam idem jussus est S. Johannes, etsi citra ambiguum ea ipsi à Spiritu Sancto sint inspirata, quæ ad novissima tempora spectant? Deinde Petri dictum adfert 2. Epist. II. 2. quod verò etsi Apostolorum ætate in Ebione & Ce-

Judæis prædicit, quippe, qui superioribus fuêre tem- poribus, sed de Marcionistis & Manichæis, & cæte- ris hærefium fectatoribus. Horum namque fugge- stione & opera, & escam detrectabant & nuptias. Nec quisquam reperitur veterum, qui Timothei tempore impleta crediderit. Plerique impleri cœ- pta in Manichæis, & Encratitis censuere, non- dum ita detecto Papalis impietatis mysterio: Ly- ranus vero fatetur disertè ad hunc loc. Aposto- lum loqui potissime de iis, qui circa tempora An- ti-Christi falsis doctrinis feducent: & fatetur Bel- larminus ipse, verbis: In novissimis temporibus significari totam ultimam ætatem à Christo usque ad judicium, quemadmodum & Justinianus in pa- raphrasi habet, denunciat, fore, ut in sequenti- bus ac penè postremis temporibus veniant illa. Concilient, si possunt, Jesuitæ cum his, quæ Ti- rinus habet, notari eos, qui conjugium absolutè damnant, ac primis Ecclesiæ temporibus vixerunt, utpote Saturninum, Marcionistas, Encratitas, Manichæos. Adde quod Apostolus cum inter- dicto conjugii ciborum prohibitionem conjungat: At omnes cibos ecquis unquam prohibuit omni- bus? unde patet, quod non simplex nuptia- rum, uti nec ciborum prohibitio designetur: Sed utraque secundum quid intelligenda, illa de certo hominum genere, hæc de certo genere ciborum certisque temporibus, quemadmodum & Alcibiades Montani socius prius delectum ciborum observabat apud Eusebium l. V. 3. μὴ χρήμενος τοῖς κτίσμασι τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ἄλλοις τύπον σκανδάλου ὑπολειπόμενος, non utens creaturis Dei, & aliis exemplar offendiculi relinquens, donec ab Attalo Martyre emendaretur; at alii Montani Socii Prophetias jactantes, leges de jejuniis & Prophetiis tulerunt. Manichæi verò electos suos à carnium esu, & usu conjugii absterrebant, audi- toribus suis, quorum erat secundus gradus, eum relinquentes. Vid. August. Ep. LXXIV. & de moribus Manichæorum cap. 18. E quibus proin- de ortum suum habent Anti-Christi Romani Marcionitis nempe, Encratitis, Montanistis, Ma- nichæis & id genus aliis, sacerdotibus conjugi- um vetantibus; & discrimen ciborum obser- vantibus, sub conscientiæ obligatione, nisi pre- tio redimatur dispensatio. Hi enim characteres apostatarum novissimi temporis valdè insignes, & maximè in oculos, etiam rudioris plebeculæ, incurrentes, in neminem ita conveniunt, ut in Romanum Anti-Christum. Apollonio certè Thy- anæo non quadrant, nec in eo sunt observati, & notandum imprimis, quod voce κωλυόντων non exprimantur damnaturi nuptias, sed designen- tur cum autoritate ac potestate νομοθετικῇ eas- dem prohibentes. Neque enim, Theodoreto dicen- te, cælibatum ac continentiam vituperat, sed eos accusat, qui lege lata ea sequi compellunt. Quem- admodum Roman. Pontif. in Concilio Tridenti- no factum Sess. XXIV. Can. IX. Si quis dixerit Clericos in sacris ordinibus constitutos, vel Regula- res, castitatem solenniter professos, posse matrimo- nium contrahere, contractumque ratificandum esse, non obstante lege Ecclesiastica, vel voto, & oppositum nihil aliud esse, quàm damnare matrimonium, posséque omnes contrahere matrimo- nium, qui non sentiunt, se castitatis, etsi eam vo- verint, habere donum, anathema sit. Adde quod in eâdem sessione Can. VI. matrimonium ratum dirimi definivit, solemni religionis alicujus pro- fessione per alterum conjugium; quodque secundis nuptiis valde sint iniqui Papistæ, benedictionem Ecclesiæ iis derogent, nec presbyteros iisdem interesse admittant, imò verè eas fornicationem esse pronuncient C. Hac causa XXXI. q. 1. de Conjugio denique ipso impie sentiant. Si bonum est, mulierem non tangere, dicitur in C. Hospi- tiolum, dist. XXXII. malum est ergò tangere: Item, non dari presentiam Spiritus Sancti tempo- re, quo actus conjugales exercentur. Can. Quic- quid & C. connubia caus. XXXII. q. 2. etiam Sanctorum matrimonium non exerceri sine pollu- tione quadam & turpitudine. Bellarmin. lib. 1. de Cler. cap. 18. Quò trahunt illud Apostoli: Qui sunt in carne, DEO placere non possunt. Vid. Can. Decernimus &c. dist. XXXIII. Can. Tenere. dist. XXXI. Can. proposuisti, & Plurimos dist. LXXXII. ut taceam Campegi i, Pighii, Hosii, Cardinalium trium E. R. voces profanas: Gra- vius peccare Sacerdotem, si uxorem ducat, quam si scortetur, quas defendere Jesuitæ non veren- tur. Vid. Costerus in Enchir. cap. XVIII. Corne- lius à Lapide in 1. Corinth. VII. Similiter de cibo- rum delectu leges sancitæ sunt in Papatu, quæ citra gravissimum peccatum violari non possint. Unde Bellarminus contendit l. II. de B. O. cap. 7. fideles in conscientia obligari ad certa quædam je- junia & ciborum delectum. Sed & prohibiti qui- dam cibi tanquam immundi & execrabiles à Gre- gorio II. & Zachariæ Epistolis ad Bonifacium Moguntinum,quum contrà, Apostolo teste, omnis creatura DEI bona sit, imò severius animadver- titur in Papatu in eos, qui prohibitis cibis utun- tur, quam qui in legem DEI impingunt, quem- admodum Romæ quadragesimæ tempore macel- lum quidem clausum est, sed scorta prostant, & lupanaria patent. Quid huc faciunt Pythagori- cæ? Quid Sarmani Persæ? Num illi à fide de- fecerunt Christiana? Rectius duo illa cornua velut Agni Apocal. XIII. vers. 11. huc adferun- tur, quæ vero ipsiusmet Anti-Christi cornua sunt, qui sese instar Agni, instar ipsius Christi, agni illius DEI, esse dictitat. Si laudarent tan- tum Christiani abstinentiam à nuptiis & cibis qui- busdam, non exegerunt, annon Papa Romanus se minùs Christianum esse clamat, cum ea ex- igit. Canon autem Apostolicus LI. temerè addu- citur à Grotio, cum Canones Apostolici Apo- cryphis accenseantur à Gelasio dist. XV. C. San- cta Romana: Nec nisi L. Canones à Leone IX. asseruntur apud Gratianum dist. XVI. C. Cle- mentis. Cæterique illis additi ceu spurii & hæ- retici à Bellarmino de Script. Eccl. & Baronio ad ann. CII. n. 7. rejiciuntur. Et cum abstinentia illo canone nec clericis, nec laicis, ut à Papa sit, imponatur, sed eorum arbitrio relinquatur, quod etiam in Ancyrana Synodi Can. X. & XIV. & in Synodo Gangrensi observatum est, non dissiten- te hic Grotio; non apparet, quid hi Canones, & hæcce Concilia juvare possint Papatum, cujus hyperaspisten agit Grotius. In Concilio Ancyra- no conceditur Canon. X. Diaconis jam ordinatis uxores ducere, si in ipsa ordinatione protestati sint sibi uxoribus opus esse. Num id concedunt Pontifices Romani?
