Nec abstinentia à carnibus præcepta est Can. XIV. vel ipsis Clericis: cum ex adverso legibus suis sanciat Romanus Ponti- fex abstinentiam. In concilio Gangrensi damna- tur Eustathius Sebastæ Episcopus teste Socrate l. II. cap. 3. Sozomeno l. III. cap. 13. inter alia, quod γαμεῖν ἐκόλυε, καὶ βρωμάτων ἀπέχεσθαι ἐδο- γμάτιζεν. Sic ergo damnandus erit etiam Pon- tifex Romanus. Anathema etiam dicitur Canon. II. ἐσθίοντι κρέα. Idem ergo dicatur & Romano Pontifici. De Encratitis hoc non dici probavit

B. Gerhardus in h. loc. Non loquitur Apostolus de iis, qui damnaturi essent nuptias & cibos; sed qui per hypocrisin, & singularis perfectionis spe- ciem nuptias & certos cibos prohibiţuri. Aliud enim est damnare, quod Marcionitæ, Tatiani & Manichæi fecerunt; aliud prohibere, quod faci- unt Pontificii. Neque enim de iis loquitur Paulus, qui cum aperta blasphemia in autorem matrimo- nii Deum & ciborum Creatorem, nuptias & ci- bos quosdam damnarent (quod veteres illi hæretici fecerunt) sed qui in hypocrisi sub ementitæ cujus- dam sanctitatis specie certis quibusdam hominibus matrimonio interdicerent, ciborumque quorun- dam abstinentiam præciperent. Et porro: Loqui- tur Apostolus de iis, qui id faciunt cauteriata con- scientia. Hoc maximè convenit Pontificiis, quippe qui norunt, non esse divinitus præceptum hoc dif- crimen. Sed ponamus hæc certa ratione Encra- titis convenire, non tamen ideo Pontificem Ro- manum hìc designatum esse negandum: quum ille multos habuerit præcursores, & hæresium an- tiquarum colluvies in ἀκρισίαν & ἀποστασίαν Ro- manam confluxisse, in aprico sit. Quod hìc non obscurè de ἀποστασίᾳ novissimorum temporum insinuatur. Nam etsi speciales illæ doctrinæ duæ expressæ sint, tanquam certæ & insignes notæ cha- racteristicæ, è quibus dignosci à quibusvis haud difficulter possit Anti-Christus, in genere tamen διδασκαλίαι δαιμωνίων notatæ doctrinas falsas ac veritati cælesti adversas à Dæmone oriundas desi- gnant, quarum tanta est in Papatu copia, quanta non facile in ulla hæresi per Ecclesiam univer- sam dispersa. Et quid mirum, doctrinas dæmo- niorum à PP. RR. profectas, & sancitas, qui ipsi dæmoniis sese dedidère, ac Magiæ addicti fuère, quales Sylvestrum II. Benedictum VIII. Grego- rium VII. præcipuum Papalis Monarchiæ aucto- rem, Benedictum IX. Johannem XX. & Johannem XXI. aliosque fuisse constat?

Jam si hypocrisis character etiam peculiaris est Anti-Christi, ubi magis hypocrisis in doctrina, ac vita regnat inter omnes hærefes in orbe, quàm in Papatu, qui totus ex hypocrisi & fraudibus conflatus est. Testari magnam partem de his- ce possunt dogmata plurima decretorum Ca- nonicorum, & moralistarum & casuistarum, vo- lumina multivaria, ritualia, ceremonialia, proces- sionalia, & id genus alia scripta publica Papisti- ca, miracula innumera, quæ in Papatu ventilan- tur, reliquiarum cultus, jejunia fictitia, nundi- nationes indulgentiarum, taxæ pœnitentiariæ, sa- tisfactiones, peregrinationes, flagellationes, impri- mis ordinum religiosorum agmina &c. quæ vivæ imagines hypocrisæos.

Porrò annon cauteria- tam produnt conscientiam Romani Anti-Chri- sti, cum ad Scripturam, ad Vicariatum Christi, ad Petri cathedram, & successionem in ejusdem se- de procurrunt; etsi Scripturam, Christum ac Pe- trum sibi καδδιάμετρον in plerisque adversari tam norint, quam proprios digitos, vel pedes suos, quos osculis magnatum exponunt servi illi ser- vorum, successionem illam tam incertam esse, ut non possit esse incertior, haud ignorent, cujus vanitas & nullitas sæpius ad oculos est demon- strata. In specie pellucet hypocrisis, & prodi- tur cauteriata conscientia Anti-Christi in decre- tis abstinentiæ conjugii, & ciborum nonnullorum. Nam C. Si quis docuerit dist. XXVII. laudatur Canon Apostolorum: Si quis docuerit, Sacerdo- tem sub obtentu religionis propriam uxorem con- temnere, anathema sit. C. Lege Imperatorum dist. X.

ex Nicolao Papa adducitur hæc sententia : B. Gre- gorius scribit ad Theoctistam Patritium inter cæ- tera ; Si, inquit, religionis causa debere dissolvi conjugia dicuntur, sciendum est, quia etsi hoc lex humana concessit, lex divina tamen prohibuit Libr. VI. Constit. cap. 17. Episcopum & Pres- byterum ac Diaconum dicimus unius uxoris debe- re constitui, sive vivant eorum uxores, sive dis- cesserint. Vid. & Innocentii sententia C. Dein- ceps dist. XXVI. Pelagii C. de Syracusana dist. XXIIX. Leonis IX. C. omninò dist. XXXI. &c. Johan. Hofmeisterus contra August. Confessio- nem art. de Conjugio Sacerdotum approbat Æneæ Sylvii postea Pontificis Romani sententiam: Rectè haud dubiè Pium II. Papam dixisse : Credimus fuisse causas, cur adimeretur Sacerdotibus conju- gium, sed multò majores esse causas, cur concedi debeat. Annon ergò contra conscientiam agunt, quod non reddunt ? Prohibent uxores habere Sacerdotes prætextu Sanctitatis, ut Siricius & Innocentius Papæ cælibes eos esse jusserunt, quia scriptum est : Sancti estote, quia ego sanctus; item : Qui sunt in carne, Deo placere non possunt. C. de- cernimus dist. XXXVII. C. Tenens dist. XXXI. &c. At fateri tamen necesse habent plures conjuga- tos sanctè vivere, quam sancti inter cælibes in- veniantur. Vid. Confess. Cathol. B. Gerh. l. II. part. II. pag. 92. seq. Ita etiam sese res habet, quoad larvata illa jejunia, quæ ciborum delectu instituuntur. Cauteriatam conscientiam Anti- Christi cum hypocrisi palam produnt jus Cano- nicum, Pontifices & Episcopi Romano-Catho- lici, aliique insignes Papistæ. C. Qui Episcopus dist. XXIII. Ex Concilio Carthaginensi inter alia requiritur ab Episcopo, ut secunda matri- monia non damnet, ac carnium perceptionem non culpet C. Si quis carnem &c. dist. XXX. adfertur decretum Concilii Gangrens. C. Si quis carnem manducantem & fide & religione crediderit, con- demnandum tanquam spem non habentem, qui eam manducat, anathema sit. C. Quod dicit dist. XLI. laudatur Augustini sententia : Non interest omninò, quid alimentorum sumas, ut succurras necessitati corporis, dummodo congruat in gene- ribus alimentorum his, cum quibus vivendum est, &c. Elevtherius tempore Antonini Com- modi, teste Platina in ritu ejus definivit, ne quis ob superstitionem cibi genus ullum resspueret, quo humana consuetudo vinceretur. Gregorius M. Tom. III. part. 3. Adm. 20. Esca nos non com- mendat DEO. Audiant illi, discedent quidam à fide & veritate &c. Anastasius Episcopus Tom. I. Bibl. Patr. fol. 98. Si quis à carnibus quidem abstinet, aliis autem cibis potibus corpus alit, & adipe repletum reddit, ei nihil prodest je- junium. Guilhelm. Lindanus l. III. Panopl. l. 9. Jejunia nostra, quæ & vini copia natant, abun- dantiaque redundant, & piscium varietate car- nium superant delitias, adeoque, quod & Hiero- nymus de suæ ætatis moribus conquerebatur, cum DEO ludere videntur, dum pro intercepto, qui ex ovis oritur, calore, olei flammas, vini æstum, omnisque aromatum generis ignes beluoni infar- ciunt stomacho, veteribus Christianis omninò fu- isse non modo incognita, sed & intolerabilia, at- que adeò abominanda, piis omnibus veritatem co- gitantibus arbitramur notius, quàm ut ea de re ulla sint verba proferenda. Similia his leguntur apud Erasmum in ἰχθυοφαγίῃ & in Epist. ad Basil. Episcop. CXIV. Hæc quanquam ita se omninò habeant, ausus tamen Pontifex per concilium Toletanum anno 653. referente Cardin. Baronio ad illum annum num. 3. definire: Quisquis abs- que inevitabili necessitate, atque fragilitatis evi- denti languore, seu etiam ætatis impossibilitate die- bus Quadragesimæ esum carnium præsumpserit at- tendere, non solum reus erit resurrectionis Domi- nicæ, verum etiam alienus ab ejusdem diei sanctæ communicatione, Audent Papales Advocati cum Bellarmino lib. II. de B. O. in part. cap. 5. tueri, ad rationem jejunii abstinentiam à certis cibis ac potissimum à carne pertinere. Annon hæc hypocrisis manibus palpari, annon conscientiæ cauterium oculis ipsis usurpari potest? Cum verò hoc ad Apollonium Thyaneum, & ad Encrati- tas trahere conatur, ne Pontifices Romanos tangere credantur, nec secum ipso convenit Gro- tius, neque cum Apostolica prædictione, quia tempore Timothei vult impletæ esse. Encratitæ autem seculo post demum exorti sunt: & Apo- stolum hic respexisse novissima tempora, verba ejus luculenter docent, qui ergo hæc ad Encræ- titas, aut ad tempora Timothei restringi pos- sunt? Apollonio non convenit Apostasia à fide, quia Philosophus Pythagoreus fuit: Theodoro- tus autem hic: Ostendit quod Ecclesiastico corpori olim conjuncti fuerunt, qui fuerunt postea Pro- phetæ mendaces. Hoc enim significat illud defi- cient quidam à fide attendentes Spiritui erroris. Non convenit ipsi hypocrisis à Paulo designata, quia Magus apertus fuit: non doctrina prohi- bens conjugia, & discernens cibos, quo de avthen- tica nulla prostant documenta. Encratitarum autem dogmata & hypocrisin sub Anti-Chri- sto Romano dominari, res ipsa loquitur, ut hic causam Papatus desperatam agere magnus ille Papæ hyperaspistes nequiverit.

De Phrasi κωλυόντων βρωμάτων digna sunt, quæ observat Oecumenius: Non est error aut lapsus à venustate sermonis, quod ait, abstinere à cibis, ut quibusdam visum est, neque Apostoli negligentia: Sed rectè ad Atticum etiam usum expressus est sermo. Quemadmodum cum dici- tur ἐκώλυσεν αὐτὸν μὴ ποιεῖν τὰ ἄτοπα, hoc est, prohibuit eum, ne perpetraret absurda, non signi- ficatur, quod ad absurditatem eum exhortatus est, & cum dicitur, ἀπέτρεπεν ἀυτὸν μὴ προσκρόειν Φίλοις, deterruit eum, ne resistat amicis, non in- nuitur, quod hortatus sit ad resistendum amicis, sed contrarium potius. Rursus cum dicitur: ἐκώ- λυσε μὴ κλέπτειν, id est, prohibuit non furari, non significatur, quod adhortatus sit ad furtum. Præterea cum dicitur: ἐκώλυσεν ἀπέχεσθαι ἀῥ- ῥητοποιΐας, id est, prohibuit à nefandis abstinere, hoc est, abegit à tali actione. Ita enim ἐκώλυον ἀπέχεσθαι βρωμάτων, id est, prohibebant absti- nere à cibis, hoc est, prohibebant à cibis. Huic Oecumenii expositioni conforme est illud Bu- dæi in comm. lingu. Græcæ fol. 935. Verbis, quæ sunt per se negantia (ἀποφατικὰ καὶ ἀπαγορευτι- κὰ) Attici negationem addunt, ut τῷ ἀπαγο- ρεύω, τῷ κωλύω, καὶ ἀρνῦμαι κὰὶ ἀπέχω. Inde regula: Verbum κωλύειν conjunctum cum parti- cula negativa vel verbo negationis significationem habente majorem vim præcipiendi & jubendi ex Attica consuetudine continet.

ἃ ὁ θεὸς ἔκτισεν εἰς μετάληψιν) Id est, condidit eo animo, ut eorum usum, si non ab initio, at certè post diluvium hominibus indulgeret, Gen. IX. vers. 3. & in Evangelio apertius. Est autem valdè propriè hic dictum εἰς μετάληψιν. Nam μεταλαμβάνειν τροφῆς est vesci, Act. II. vers. 46. XXVII. vers. 33. Sic & καρπῶν μεταλαμ- βάνειν 2. Timoth. II. vers. 6. & ἀγαθῶν supra XVIII. vers. 9.

Μεθ' εὐχαριστίας τοῖς πιϛοῖς. Transpositio pro ἔκτισε τοῖς πιϛοῖς εἰς μετάληψιν μετ' εὐχαριστίας : Ne cibus sumatur, nisi actis DEO gratiis, qui ista nostris usibus condidit, mos est Hebræorum ve- tus, quem Christus exemplo suo probavit. Vide, quæ dicta Matth. XIV. 19. XV. 36. XXVI. 26.

Καὶ ἐπεγνωκόσι τὴν ἀλήθειαν ) Quibus nota est veritas ista, quæ jam sequitur.

Cujus ergò μετάληψιν & usum concessit Deus ipse, qui prohibet Papa Romanus, annon ita ex- tollit se supra DEUM? Ideò Johannes de Ve- salia (circa annum Christi 1464.) meritò mo- nuit: Quod in Scriptura non est prohibitum, pro peccato non est habendum: licitum etiam esse die Viridium carne vesci. M. Johannes Ibenhagen circa ann. 1480. omnibus diebus licere Christianis vesci carnibus docuit. Omnia enim in usum ho- minis, inquit, à DEO sunt creata, & non inve- nitur in Scripturis S. ejusmodi præceptum: ideò & homines, ut id servent, non obligantur. Era- smus in paraphr. 1. Corinth. VIII. Approbo, quod dicis: Esca non commendat nos DEO. Cum enim DEUS universa creaverit ad usus humanos, neque quisquam à nobis exigat præter vitæ pieta- tem, quid illius refert, an piscium, an quadru- pedum, an volatilium carnibus vescatur? Nihil enim pietati quicquam vel addit vel detrahit cibo- rum delectus. Superstitiosum facere potest, pi- um nequaquam, Christus nullum horum discri- men docuit. Proinde temeritatis est, si quis ho- munculus (P. R.) conetur, quenquam hujus- modi constitutionibus onerare. S. Romani Impe- rii status in Gravaminibus Nation. German. in Comitiis Noriberg. Anno 1523. oblatis, inter reliqua onera (inquiunt) vel illud minime po- stremo loco est collocandum, quod constitutioni- bus humanis multa prohibentur, imperantur, etiem multa, quæ nullo divino præcepto vel inter- dicta sunt, vel imperata, quod genus sunt matri- monium &c. ciborum usus interdictus, quos Deus ad hominis necessitatem creavit, ac cum gratia- rum actione promiscue sumendos docuit Aposto- lus. Quo de Theodoretiis in hunc loc. Postquam eorum dogmatum ostendit perniciem, quam execrandæ etiam sint eorum leges prædicit: Exe- crables enim nuptias, & plurimos cibos appellant, ut Creatorem injuria afficiant. Eos autem fecit ad usum, ut ii, qui sunt eorum participes, ex eo sumant occasionem agendi gratias, & laudandi eum, qui eos suppeditat. Quærit hìc Grotius: Cur non utramque, sed unam tantùm speciem Dia- bolici dogmatis refellat Apostolus? Ex Danæo caufam adfert, quod illud malum (prohibendi conjugii) nondum vicinum esse præviderit. Ex Hyperio, errorem illum ceu naturæ ipsi adver- sum, refutatione indignum judicarit, ipse autem sufficere observat, quod alibi Apostolus gravem contra prohibitionem conjugii ferat sententiam, & contrahendi libertatem egregiè adferat, Ebr. XIII. 1. Corinth. VII. Sed argumenta Aposto- li fic comparata sunt, ut à paritate rationis ap- plicari alteri speciei æquè possint. Nam si cau- sam efficientem spectes, undenam cibi omnes, nisi à DEO, unde conjugium, nisi ab autore DEO? Usus ergo non ex hominum, sed ex DEI voluntate & ordinatione dependet. Si fi- nalem, εἰς μετάληψιν, ad participationem omni- bus hominibus in Protoplastis ordinati sunt non ad abstinentiam. Ultimus finis est DEI gloria, quæ ex participatione nascitur, cum utimur istis DEI donis cum gratiarum actione; cui officiunt, qui usui eorum, vel ulli hominum interdicunt, non minùs ac qui abutuntur iisdem ad carnis concupiscentias. Si objectum respicias, omnibus fidelibus, & veritatem divinam agnoscentibus sine discrimine ordinata sunt. Non ergò contra pietatem, contra fidem sunt, respectu ullius ordinis aut status. Apostasiam autem à fide, & veritate cœlesti, testantur, qui contra illam DEI ordinationem alia definiunt.

## 4:4
Ver. 4. For every creature of God is good) Gen. I. ver. 31.

And nothing to be rejected.

Thus it translates the Hebrew פגול; which is elsewhere translated as pollution, an unoffered thing, or a profane thing. There is nothing that is פגול in itself and apart from the law of God. Moreover, the law of GOD concerning this matter was never given to the Gentiles, and it was taken away from the Jews through Christ. See Rom. VII. and what is said there.

Received with thanksgiving.

He repeats this law, lest anyone should forget it. See Deut. VIII. ver. 10. Is. LXII. 9. Joel II. 26.

The previous arguments are confirmed by the condition of created things: because all things which GOD created were very good, as Moses testifies, and nothing of them is to be rejected or is inconvenient and profane. Which things, as they apply to all foods established by GOD, so also they apply to marriage, which is equally a creature or ordinance of GOD. There is nothing that is פגול in itself and apart from the law, says Grotius. Moreover, there is no law of GOD that binds us, whether to abstinence from certain foods or from marriage. The Gentiles indeed, being superstitious, along with Jewish sects adding their own traditions to the divine law, observed such things: but to introduce those superstitions into Christianity, and to bind the consciences of the faithful to them, was not a proof of piety, but of the apostasy of the Anti-Christ. To which pertains the observation of Polydore Vergil, book III, de rerum invent. chap. 5. and of Josephus, that the Essenes are celebrated because they always abstained from wives and wine, and, as Jerome pleases, from meats, and of Baronius to the year 57, num. 191, that Pythagoras was the first author of the superstitious distinction of foods. If everything that GOD created is good, and nothing is abominable or unclean, why do the Popes make marriage unclean, and the use of certain foods abominable? The former of which was observed before regarding Innocent and Siricius, the latter regarding Gregory and Zacharias, the Roman Pontiffs.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ὅτι πᾶν κτίσμα Θεῦ καλὸν) Gen. I. vers. 31.

Καὶ ὐδὲν ἀπόβλητον.

Sic vertit Hebræum פגול; quod μίασμα, ἄθυτον, βέβηλον alibi vertitur. Nihil est פגול per se & citra Dei legem. Lex autem DEI hac de re neque gentibus unquam data est, & à Judæis per Christum est ablata. Vide Rom. VII. & ibi dicta.

Μετ' εὐχαριστίας λαμβανόμενον.

Repetit hanc legem, ne quis ejus obliviscatur. Vide Deut. VIII. vers. 10. Es. LXII. 9. Joel. II. 26.

Argumenta priora confirmantur à rerum creatarum conditione: quia omnia, quæ creavit DEUS, valdè bona fuêre, teste Mose, nec quicquam eorum rejiculum aut incommodum & prophanum. Quæ ut cibis omnibus à DEO conditis, ita etiam conjugio, quod æque DEI est creatura, vel ordinatio, conveniunt. Nihil est פגול per se & citra legem, ait Grotius. Nulla autem lex DEI, quæ nos obstringat, sive ad ciborum quorundam, sive ad conjugii abstinentiam. Gentiles quidem superstitiosi, cum Judaicis sectis legi divinæ suas δευτερώσεις adjicientibus talia observarunt: sed illas superstitiones in Christianismum invehere, & conscientias fidelium iis alligare, non pietatis fuit, sed ἀποστασίας Anti-Christi documentum. Quò pertinet observatio Polydori Virgilii lib. III. de rerum invent. cap. 5. & Josephi, quod Essæi celebrentur, quod ab uxoribus & vino, &, ut Hieronymo placet, carnibus semper abstinuerint, & Baronii ad ann. 57. num. 191. quod Pythagoras primus autor fuerit superstitiosi ciborum discriminis. Si omne, quod condidit DEUS, bonum, nihil abominabile, aut immundum est, cur Pontifices immundum faciunt conjugium, abominabilem quorundam ciborum usum? quorum prius de Innocentio, & Siricio, posterius de Gregorio & Zacharia PP. RR. antea observatum.

## 4:5
Ver. 5. For it is sanctified by the word of God, and prayer.

It is sanctified, that is, the use of those things is pleasing to GOD: just as we had 'is sanctified' regarding husband and wife in 1 Cor. VII. ver. 14. It is pleasing to GOD for two reasons: first, because he who uses it certainly persuades himself that it is lawful for him on account of the word of GOD, which we have in Acts X. ver. 15. Secondly, because he calls upon GOD as the author of the gift. 'Prayer' is taken here more generally than above in II. 1, as also 'to intercede' in Wisd. VII. ver. 1, 21, and XVI. ver. 28. They are joined together, thanksgiving and prayers: the former for things given; the latter so that things may be profitable. Both are comprehended under the name of blessing.

Food is therefore sanctified, not because it is unclean in itself: because everything that GOD created is good: But so that its use may not result in profanation and abuse of a good creature of GOD. It is not sanctified like a man, who, being polluted by sin, has need of sanctification, and after the fall is unclean in himself: But it is to be sanctified for the sake of man, not for its own sake: which is done through the Word and prayers, because the word instructs us how we ought to use the creature of GOD, and we are sanctified through the word, and then to the pure all things are pure. Prayers, however, procure the divine blessing, so that it may result in our salvation, not in the harm of the use of foods. Which must be held likewise regarding marriage. Concerning which Augustine speaks in his Elenctics against the heresy of the Manichaeans. It is foreign to the truth what Cornelius says: that to be sanctified is to be offered to GOD through a blessing, as it were, and to be consecrated. It is not offered to GOD, but is received from GOD; it is sanctified, not so that it may be offered to GOD, but so that we may enjoy it, as if received from the hand of GOD, with a grateful mind and a good conscience, Deut. VIII. ver. 3, Matt. IV. ver. 4. Nor do Lombard, Thomas, or Hugo Cardinalis conveniently understand the Word of GOD the Son here. For it is manifest that the manner of thanksgiving through the word and prayer and the means of sanctification are designated by the same. Therefore, others more correctly understand the Word that goes forth from the mouth of GOD, as is held in the cited place. For our heart ought to be firm, Heb. XIII. ver. 9, which is done through faith, Rom. XIV. ver. 23, which is nothing without the word of GOD. That Word, therefore, is pointed out by which we are made certain that every creature of GOD is good. That Word through which He granted it to man and established the use of all foods. Through which that right of dominion, which he lost on account of sin, was in turn restored to him, sin having been destroyed. Which word is to be received by faith: Thus to those purified by faith all things will be pure. Compare on this entire passage B. Luther, Vol. II, Jena, German treatise on human traditions, fol. 110, which namely flourish under the Roman Anti-Christ, whom he concludes with these words: Who has ever heard human doctrine so horribly blamed in every way, that they are apostate, unbelieving, unchristian, heathen, erroneous, devilish, false, hypocritical, harmful to the conscience, ungrateful, against the honor and creature of God, harmful fables and old-wives' chatter. Flee, whoever can flee from this judgment of God. Theodoret: That thing, however, he says, which is good by nature, if it is taken with thanksgiving, is rendered holy also through the memory of God. Theophylact, following Chrysostom: Therefore, he says, will it be unclean, unless it is sanctified? By no means. But he posits that by way of permission. For first, by asserting that nothing is unclean: Then let us concede, he says, that it becomes unclean, you still have the remedy which you can apply.

PART II.

An informative precept for a Bishop.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Ἁγιάζεται γὰρ διὰ λόγω Θεῦ, καὶ ἐντεύξεως.

Ἁγιάζεται, id est, usus illarum rerum gratus est DEO: quomodo ἡγίασται de viro & uxore habuimus 1. Corinth. VII. vers. 14. Gratus autem est DEO duas ob causas: primùm, quia is, qui utitur, certò sibi persuadet id sibi licere propter verbum DEI, quod habemus Actor. X. vers. 15. Deinde quia DEUM invocat ut doni auctorem. Ἔντευξις hic generalius sumitur, quam supra II. 1. ut & ἐντυγχάνειν Sap. VII. vers. 1. 21. & XVI. vers. 28. Conjuncta sunt, gratiarum actio & preces: illa pro rebus datis: hæ ut res prosint. Utrumque comprehenditur sub nomine ברכה.

Sanctificatur ergò cibus, non quod per se immundus sit: quia omne, quod DEUS condidit, bonum est: Sed ut usus ejus ne cedat nobis in prophanationem, & abusum bonæ DEI creaturæ. Non sanctificatur ut homo, qui per peccatum pollutus sanctificatione opus habet, ac post lapsum per se immundus est: Sed hominis, non sui causa, sanctificandus est: quod per Verbum fit & preces, quia verbum instruit nos, quomodo creaturâ DEI uti debeamus, nosque sanctificamur per verbum, ac mundis tùm omnia sunt munda. Preces verò conciliant benedictionem divinam, ut saluti nostræ cedat: ciborum usus, non damno. Quod pariter de conjugio habendum. Quo de Augustinus in Elencticis suis contra Manichæorum hæresin. Alienum est, quod Cornelius dicit: Sanctificari esse DEO per benedictionem quasi offerri, & consecrari. Non offertur DEO, sed accipitur à DEO; sanctificatur, non ut DEO offeratur, sed ut eo, tanquam à manu DEI accepto, grata mente, ac bona conscientia fruamur, Deut. IIX. vers. 3. Matth. IV. vers. 4. Nec commodè per Verbum DEI Filium hic intelligunt Lombardus, Thomas, Hugo Cardinalis. Nam modum gratiarum actionis per verbum, & orationem ac media sanctificationis per eadem designari manifestum est. Rectius ergo alii Verbum, quod egreditur ex ore DEI, ut l. c. habetur, intelligunt. Cor enim nostrum firmum esse debet, Ebr. XIII. vers. 9. quod fit per fidem, Roman. XIV. vers. 23. quæ sine verbo DEI nulla est. Verbum itaque illud indigitatur, quo certi reddimur, omnem creaturam DEI bonam esse. Verbum illud, per quod concessit homini, & usum ciborum omnium constituit. Per quod illud, quo excidit ob peccatum, jus dominii, ei restitutum vicissim est, destructo peccato. Quod verbum fide suscipiendum: Ita purificatis per fidem omnia erunt pura. Confer de hoc integro loco B. Lutherum Tom. II. Jenens. Germ. tract. de tradit. human. fol. 110. quæ scil. sub Anti-Christo Romano vigent, quem hisce verbis concludit: Wer hat nun Menschen-Lehre je gehöret so greulich auff alle Weise tadeln / daß sie abtrünnig / ungläubig / unchristlich / heyndnisch / irrig / teufflisch / falsch / gleißnerisch / verschrlich am Gewissen / undanckbar / wider die Ehre / und GOttes Creatur / schädliche Fabeln und altvettelisch Geschwätze sind. Fleuch wer fliehen kan aus diesem Urtheil GOttes. Theodorestus: Illud autem, inquit, quod natura bonum, si cum gratiarum actione sumitur, per DEI memoriam etiam sanctum redditur. Theophylactus præeunte Chrysostomo: Ergò, inquit, immundum erit, nisi sanctificetur? Nequaquam. Sed ex permissu id ponit. Nam primùm asseverando nihil dicit immundum: Deinde concedamus, inquit; immundum id fieri, habes tamen quam adhibere possis medelam.

PARS II.

Præceptum Episcopi informatorium.

## 4:6
Ver. 6. Ταῦτα ὑποθέμενος τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς) If you admonish the Christians about these things, whom those philosophers and likewise magicians wish to lead to themselves. Ὑποτίθεσθαι for to command is frequent in Homer. Aristotle also uses it.

Καλὸς ἔσῃ διάκονος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Ἔσῃ, that is, you will show yourself to be such. Διάκονος is taken here as in 1 Thess. III. ver. 2.

The philosophers and magicians are strangers here. And this doctrine is not only inculcated to Timothy: But in his person to all Presbyters or Bishops: since the idea of a Good Teacher is handed down here. Ταῦτα, these things, also do not pertain only to those times, but for a good part especially to the last times, about which, however, so that the believers of that time might be informed, it was also of interest, as from 2 Thess.

II. 1. 2. 3. novimus. Ταῦτα, these things, Theophylact indeed refers to the preceding matters concerning marriage and foods, and others which he foretold. Crocius refers them also to those mysteries which he delivered in verse 16 of the preceding chapter. But they are to be referred to all things which he suggests to him in this Epistle, even to those which follow thereafter. For he delivers these things to him, and in him to other teachers, to this end, that they may be proposed to others by the ministers of the word: and the Apostle used the present participle ὑποτιθέμενος, that he might intimate a continuous act, that these things are not to be submitted once, but that such things are to be proposed continuously and assiduously: that we may proceed to be good teachers rather than seem and be acknowledged as such. For it is the proper duty of him who ministers to fulfill those things which are commanded, and to transmit divine precepts to those who are of the same faith.

Ἐντρεφόμενος τοῖς λόγοις τῆς πίστεως, καὶ τῆς διδασκαλίας ᾗ παρηκολούθηκας. You will show yourself nourished by the words both of the faith and of that discipline which you have followed until now. Fides refers to things to be believed, διδασκαλία to things to be done. Παρακολυθεῖν refers sometimes to things, sometimes to persons. See 2 Tim. III, verse 10, and 2 Macc. IX, verse 27. In the manuscript it is, οἷς παρηκολούθηκας.

The reason is brought forward why he continues to be such; inasmuch as he was nourished from his earliest cradle by maternal instruction in the words of faith and discipline. I do not disapprove that faith is referred to things to be believed, and διδασκαλία to things to be done. For he prescribed concerning both in this Epistle. And so also do Hugo Cardinalis and Thomas. But why does Grotius omit the epithet, τῆς καλῆς διδασκαλίας? It pleases Crocius more that by the words of faith the whole form of the Christian religion is denoted, so that faith is true doctrine, as above in v. 1. Yet he wishes faith to be named rather than anything else, because faith reigns in the whole of Theology. It is a doctrine, he says, not which is measured by the rule of the senses and reason, but which is received by humble faith, (would that the Calvinists always observed this concerning heavenly doctrine, or the Word of GOD!) But it seems more to be approved that we should understand these things as said κατ’ ἐπεξήγησιν. For ἡ καλὴ διδασκαλία, which Timothy had followed from childhood, 2 Tim. III. verse 15, embraced not only those things which are to be done, but even especially those which pertained to the doctrine of faith, as is clear from that book. Therefore, the words of faith, in which Timothy had been nourished, are commended because they exhibit a good and salutary doctrine, which, just as he had imbibed it ἀπὸ βρέφυς and as it were with his mother’s milk, so he ought also to dispense the same to others, that they may be instructed through faith in CHRIST unto salvation. Theophylact also notes the emphasis of the Greek verb, and he said "nourished" for this reason, to show his unceasing attention to these things, so that just as we always partake of food for the body, so also we may be nourished by the constant words which pertain to faith.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Ταῦτα ὑποθέμενος τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς) Si de his moneas Christianos, quos isti Philosophi idemque magi ad se volunt perducere. Ὑποτίθεσθαι pro præcipere frequens Homero. Utitur & Aristoteles.

Καλὸς ἔσῃ διάκονος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ. Ἔσῃ, id est, ostendes te esse talem. Διάκονος hic sumitur ut 1. Thessal. III. vers. 2.

Alieni hic sunt Philosophi & Magi. Nec tantùm doctrina hæc Timotheo inculcatur: Sed in ipsius persona omnibus Presbyteris vel Episcopis: quum idea hic tradatur Boni Doctoris. Ταῦτα etiam hæc non ad illa tantum tempora pertinent, sed bonam partem imprimis ad novissima tempora, de quibus tamen, ut istius temporis fideles informarentur, etiam intererat, ut è 2. Thess.

II. 1. 2. 3. novimus. Ταῦτα hæc refert quidem Theophylactus ad priora de nuptiis & cibis, & alias, quæ prædixit. Crocius ad illa etiam myste- ria, quæ vers. 16. cap. præced. tradidit. Sed re- ferenda ad omnia, quæ in hac Epistola ei sug- gerit, etiam ad ea, quæ deinceps sequuntur. Nam eo fine & ipsi, & in ipso aliis Doctoribus hæc tradit, ut aliis proponantur à ministris ver- bi: & præsenti usus Apostolus est participio ὑπο- τιθέμενος, ut actum continuum innueret, non semel hæc subjicienda, sed continuè & assiduè talia proponenda esse: ut boni magistri magis pergamus esse, quàm videamur & agnoscamur. Est enim ejus, qui ministrat proprium ea imple- re, quæ imperantur, & ad eos, qui sunt ejusdem fidei, divina præcepta transmittere.

Ἐντρεφόμενος τοῖς λόγοις τῆς πίστεως, καὶ τῆς διδασκαλίας ᾗ παρηκολούθηκας. Ostendes te innutritum verbis & fidei, & ejus disci- plinæ, quam sectatus es hactenus. Fides ad credenda re- fertur, διδασκαλία ad facienda. Παρακολυθεῖν modo ad res, modo ad personas refertur. Vide 2. Timoth. III. vers. 10. & 2. Maccab. IX. vers. 27. In Manuscripto est, οἷς παρηκολούθηκας.

Ut talis esse pergat, ratio adfertur; utpote qui innutritus à primis cunabulis per maternam in- formationem verbis fidei & disciplinæ. Non improbo, quod fides refertur ad credenda, δι- δασκαλία ad facienda. Nam de utrisque præscri- psit in hac Epistola. Atque ita etiam Hugo Car- dinalis & Thomas. Sed cur Epithetan præter- mittit Grotius, τῆς καλῆς διδασκαλίας? Crocio magis placet, per sermones fidei notari totam reli- gionis Christianæ formam, ut fides sit vera do- ctrina, ut supra v. 1. Fidem tamen potius, quàm quodvis aliud nominari vult, quia in tota Theo- logia regnat fides. Est doctrina, inquit, non quæ ad sensus & rationis regulam exigitur, sed quæ fide humili suscipitur, (utinam id Calviniani circa doctrinam cœlestem, vel Verbum DEI, sem- per observarent!) Magis autem id probandum videtur, ut κατ’ ἐπεξήγησιν hæc dicta intelligamus. Nam ἡ καλὴ διδασκαλία, quam sectatus erat Ti- motheus à puero, 2. Timoth. III. vers. 15. non tantùm ea, quæ facienda sunt, complectebatur, sed vel maximè ea, quæ ad doctrinam pertine- bant fidei, ut ex libro illo liquet. Commendan- tur itaque sermones fidei, quibus innutritus erat Timotheus, quod bonam & salutarem doctri- nam exhibeant, quam uti ἀπὸ βρέφυς & veluti cum lacte materno imbiberat, ita eandem etiam aliis propinare debebat, ut instruantur per fi- dem in CHRISTUM ad salutem. Notat & Theo- phylactus emphasin Græci verbi, innutritus verò ideo dixit, ut indefinentem ejus in his attentionem ostenderet, ut quemadmodum semper corporis ali- mento percipimus, sic etiam assiduis, quæ ad fidem faciunt, verbis enutriamur.

## 4:7
Verse 7.

"But refuse profane and old wives' fables." He understands that doctrine concerning the transmigration of souls, which is the foundation of that abstinence. These fables are, first, profane, because they rest upon no revelation of GOD: then, old wives' tales, that is, absurd, no less than those which little old women recite to small children. Cicero spoke of old wives' absurdities in the Tusculans; παραιτεῖsθαι is ἀποσρέφεsθαι. You have this word in the same sense in 2 Tim. II. 23, Tit. III. 10.

The office of a Bishop & Doctor, or of a good Minister, ought first to be occupied in the teaching of the divine word, so that he may deliver those things which he has received from GOD through the Apostles, or through Prophetic and Apostolic Scripture, and by which he himself has been instructed and nourished from the word of GOD for the teaching of others: on the other hand, however, he should avoid all things contrary to these, as profane dogmas, and teach that they are to be avoided. They are profane for the very reason that they are contrary to the word of GOD, or indeed even when they are merely foreign to the word of GOD, and are peddled as the word of GOD, Gal. I. vers. 8. 9. Who would doubt that they are even doctrines of demons? For every lie is from the Devil, who is the father of it, Johan. VIII. vers. 44. Old wives' tales, or old wives' lies, are spoken of with regard to those dogmas which were to be spread in the latter times, such as indeed are those which are disseminated in the Papacy, e.g., concerning the infallibility of the Pope, concerning purgatory, concerning the apparitions of spirits, concerning traditions and revelations, concerning various exorcisms and consecrations, concerning invocations and heavenly patrons, concerning the most diverse Masses, concerning fictitious miracles and most fabulous histories, concerning indulgences, and other trifles and nonsense of that kind, with which the whole Papacy is filled. For what are these other than βέβηλοι καὶ γραώδεις μῦθοι? Or let these gems be shown elsewhere in any heresy or sect. It will not be permitted to find even the hundredth part of such old wives' tales in any other! Nothing regarding those Pythagorean commentaries περὶ ψυχῶν μετενσωματώσεως, which may even now refer to a hidden meaning or something μυστικώτε- ρόν, but those Papal fables are truly and entirely profane, because they not only rely on no revelation of GOD, but fight with a hostile front against divine Prophetic and Apostolic revelation, and are truly impious, against the glory of GOD, the merit of Christ, and the voice of the Holy Spirit; truly senseless, that is, absurd, no less, nay, sometimes much more so than those which old women recite to little children. Meanwhile, we do not deny that Jewish doctrines are included here, which for a good part were also profane and old wives' fables, and are considered to be designated here by Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Theophylact: and likewise we think that the μύθες of philosophers and poets, which crept into the Church, are to be excluded: or the fables of the Simonian heretics and others concerning the creation of things, concerning the battles of angels, concerning the marriages of the Gods, about which Irenæus, Epiphanius, and Augustine write. But we deny that these alone are being referred to. Nay, we consider that these things pertain most especially to the very last times.

Γύμναζε δὲ σεαυτὸν πρὸς εὐσέβειαν. Γυμνάζειν properly means to be exercised in a gymnasium. From there it began to be transferred to all those things which we learn by doing, and we are said both γυμνάζειν τὸ σῶμα, as in Plato’s Laws, and γυμνάζειν τὴν ψυχὴν, as in Isocrates. To piety, that is, to all the virtues of the soul, which is accomplished by frequent pious actions.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Τὸς δὲ βεβήλυς καὶ γραώδεις μύθυς παραιτῦ. Intelligit doctrinam illam περὶ ψυχῶν μετενσωματώ- σεως, quæ fundamentum est istius ἀποχῆς. Hæ fabulæ primùm sunt profanæ, quia nulla DEI revelatione nitun- tur: deinde aniles, id est, absurdæ, non minus quam illæ, quas aniculæ puerulis recitant. Aniles ineptias dixit Ci- cero in Tusculanis, παραιτεῖsθαι est ἀποσρέφεsθαι. Eodem sensu hanc vocem habes 2. Tim. II. 23. Tit. III. 10.

Episcopi & Doctoris, vel Ministri boni offi- cium primùm in doctrina verbi divini occupari debet, ut ea tradat, quæ à DEO per Aposto- los, vel Scripturam Propheticam, & Apostolicam accepit, & quibus ipse ad alios docendos instru- &us è verbo DEI & innutritus fuit: ex adverso autem omnia his contraria, ceu dogmata profa- na, devitet, ac devitanda esse doceat. Profana eo ipso sunt, quod verbo DEI contraria, imò etiam cum aliena tantum à verbo DEI, & pro verbo DEI venditantur, Gal. I. vers. 8. 9. Dæmoniorum quin sint doctrinæ, ecquis dubitaret? Nam men- dacium omne à Diabolo est, qui ejusdem pater est, Johan. VIII. vers. 44. Aniles fabulæ, vel anilia mendacia dicuntur respectu habito ad ea dogma- ta, quæ novissimis temporibus spargenda, qua- lia profectò sunt illa, quæ in Papatu disseminan- tur, v. g. de Papæ infallibilitate, de purgatorio, de apparitionibus spirituum, de traditionibus & revelationibus, de Exorcismis & consecrationibus variis, de invocationibus & Patronis cælestibus, de Missis diversissimis, de miraculis fictitiis & hi- storiis fabulosissimis, de indulgentiis, & id genus aliis næniis & affaniis, quibus totus Papatus re- pletus est. Quid enim hæc aliud sunt, quàm βέ- βηλοι καὶ γραώδεις μῦθοι? Aut monstrentur alibi in ulla hæresi vel secta hicce gemmæ. Ne cente- simam quidem partem talium anilium fabularum in ulla alia reperire licebit! Nihil ad illas Pytha- gorica commenta περὶ ψυχῶν μετενσωματώσεως, quæ adhæc absconditum sensum, vel μυστικώτε- ρόν τι referre possunt, sed illæ Papales fabulæ ve- rè & ex asse profanæ, quia non modo nulla DEI revelatione nituntur, sed cum revelatione divi- na Prophetica & Apostolica adversa fronte pu- gnant, & verè impiæ sunt, in gloriam DEI, me- ritum Christi & vocem Spiritus Sancti; verè ani- les, id est, absurdæ, non minus, imò multò ma- gis quandoque quàm illæ, quas aniculæ puerulis recitant. Interim non negamus doctrinas Ju- daicas hic comprehendi, quæ bonam partem etiam profanæ & aniles fabulæ erant, & à Chry- sostomo, Theodoreto, ac Theophylacto hic designa- ri censentur: itemque Philosophorum & Poëta- rum μύθες, qui in Ecclesiam irrepserunt, exclu- dendas putamus: aut hæreticorum Simonianorum & aliorum fabulas de rerum creatione, de pu- gnis angelorum, de conjugiis Deorum, de qui- bus Irenæus, Epiphanius, Augustinus. Sed eas so- las respici negamus. Imò maximè ad tempora no- vissima hæc spectare censemus.

Γύμναζε δὲ σεαυτὸν πρὸς εὐσέβειαν. Γυμνάζειν est propriè exerceri in gymnade. Inde cœpit transferri ad omnia ea, quæ agendo discimus, dicimurque & γυμνάζειν τὸ σῶμα, ut apud Platonem in legibus, & γυμνάζειν τὴν ψυχὴν, ut apud Isocratem. Ad pietatem, id est, ad omnes animi virtutes, quod fit crebris actio- nibus piis.

## 4:8
Verse 8.

For bodily exercise is profitable for a little. מעט יסכן the Rabbis say concerning such things. He does not despise bodily exercises, such as abstinence from better foods, and from wine, and from marriage. For these have a certain utility within their own limits, concerning which it is said in Colossians 2:23.

But godliness is profitable for all things. It is never not, and nowhere not useful. This sentiment is opposed to the saying of the wicked in Job 34:9.

Having promise of the life that now is. עולם הזה, namely in peace of conscience and good hope. For as Pindar says: 'Whoever lives his life piously and justly, sweet hope, the nurse of old age, accompanies his heart, which most of all steers the shifting mind of mortals.'

Against the impious Antiphon: 'For he who is impious and transgresses against the gods and deprives himself of hope itself (which is the greatest good for men in life), deprives himself.' The Hebrews say there are four things which have a reward in both lives: honor and obedience shown to parents, beneficence toward the needy, hospitality, and the effort to reconcile those who are at odds. Well, provided that those things which are equal to these are not excluded.

And of the one to come.

The world to come. For eternal life is promised to piety.

Next to doctrine is the exercise of piety in a good minister of the Word. But it is rash that not Prophets, but Poets are brought forward for this exercise, who know nothing of the peace of conscience and good hope, which Grotius scarcely leaves to the Prophets. Eternal life is perversely promised to piety. It is indeed promised to the pious, but to be obtained through faith, not through piety. Piety also has the promise of the future life, but even if the exercises of virtues also contribute to piety, the first and most important thing in it is faith, which must be exerted and exercised most of all, especially in the struggle and in various temptations, in which the faithful are bound to prove themselves good athletes by faith, by fighting in faith, by contention through the Word, and by constant perseverance, fighting the good fight. We have examples of such a struggle of faith in the Old Testament: Jacob, Gen. 32; Job throughout his various scenes; in the New Testament: the Canaanite woman, Matt. 15; Paul, 2 Cor. 12, and others. Add that Chrysostom and Theophylact understand by piety a pure faith and an upright life, to whom Bullinger and Crocius accede, asserting that the whole of Christianity is comprehended, as in 2 Tim. 3:12, whence B. Hunnius: 'This is wrongly twisted by the Papists to establish the justification of works. For what belongs to the whole in respect to some one part is not immediately to be ascribed to the other parts as well.' There are several parts of piety, among which new obedience and the pursuit of good works are contained. But that it is said to have the promise of eternal life is said synecdochically, in respect to the saving knowledge of God, which is called faith. Although neither do its other parts lack their own reward (though a gratuitous one) even in the blessed life. In which respect and sense the clause concerning the promise of the future life is not absurdly accommodated even to the pursuit of new obedience, yet with this distinction: that eternal life itself does not come to us from any works, not even those produced after regeneration, but is and remains the gift of God through Christ Jesus our Lord, Rom. 6, Eph. 2. Good works, however, are crowned by God IN THE blessed life, and are weighed with eternal rewards, considering the differences in glory (of which Paul speaks in 1 Cor. 15). And it is not life itself, but the degrees of glory in eternal life that stand forth from the exercises of virtues by the promise of divine grace. But the merits of virtues are injurious to the merit of Christ, which Grotius, a Papist, not obscurely favors here, and which he asserts more openly elsewhere. 'There is no reason,' says Bernard in Sermon 68 on the Song of Songs, 'why you should ask by what merits we hope for good things, especially when you hear from the Prophet:' 'Not for your sake, but for my sake I will do it, says the Lord.' It was the duty of Timothy as a Bishop to ask that, but since no one trains another unless he has first trained himself, the Apostle exhorts Timothy to that. The Greek word, derived from 'naked,' was appropriate for those who exercised themselves naked in the gymnasia, so that they might be more agile. It warns that we should be naked of human traditions, naked of passions, of the cares of the world, and of all impediments. But Cornelius à Lapide and Justinianus wrongly understand the exercises of athletes by 'bodily exercise.' For it was not the Apostle's place to prescribe anything about those. Sounder is the explanation of Grotius, which fits both the context and the information about abstinence from marriage and foods, and has been noted by Ambrosiaster, indeed it has pleased Bernard in his Apology to Abbot William, Anselm, Lombard, Hugh, Thomas, Lyranus, most Papists, and even our own and Reformed interpreters. And the Papists acknowledge that external actions undertaken for the sake of religion are meant, and among others, long fasts, vigils, sleeping on the ground, walking barefoot, etc. 'Bodily exercise,' says Lombard, 'in which you weary yourself by fasting, watching, abstaining, which are the bridles of the flesh, is useful for a little, unless piety is added to this.'

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Ἡ γὰρ σωματικὴ γυμνασία πρὸς ὀλίγον ἐστὶν ὠφέλιμος. מעט יסכן dicunt de talibus Rabbini. Non spernit corporis exercitationes, puta abstinentiam à cibis melio- ribus, & à vino, & à conjugio. Habent enim ista utilita- rem quandam intra suos limites, de quibus dictum Coloss. II. vers. 23.

Ἡ δὲ εὐσέβεια πρὸς πάντα ὠφέλιμός ἐστιν. Nunquam non, & nusquam non est utilis. Est hæc sen- tentia opposita dicto impiorum Job. XXXIV. 9.

Ἐπαγγελίαν ἔχουσα ζωῆς τῆς νῦν. עולם הזה, nempe in pace conscientiæ & spe bona. Nam ut ait Pindarus: Ὅς ὢν ὁσίως καὶ δικαίως τὸν βίον Διάγῃ, γλυκεῖα οἱ καρδίαν Ἀτιτάλλουσα γηροτρόφος ξυναορεῖ Ἐλπὶς, ἅ μάλιστα θνατῶν Πολύστροφον γνώμαν κυβερνᾷ.

Contra de impio Antiphon: ἀσεβῶν γὰρ καὶ παραβαίνων τὰ εἰς τὸς Θεὸς καὶ ἀυτῆς ἐλπίδος (ὅπερ ἐςὶ μέγισον ἀνθρώποις τῦ βίε ἀγαθὸν) ἀυτὸς ἀυτὸν ἀποσερεῖν. Ajunt Ebræi res esse quatuor, quæ in utraque vita habeant ἀνταπόδοσιν: honorem & obsequia parentibus præbita: beneficentiam in egenos, hospitalitatem, studium reconciliandi dissiden- tes. Benè, dum ne excludantur, quæ his sunt paria.

Καὶ τῆς μελλύσης.

עולם הבא. Pietati enim vita æterna promittitur.

Proximum à doctrina est pietatis γύμνασμα in bono verbi ministro. Temerè autem ad hoc γύ- μνασμα non Prophetæ, sed Poëtæ adferuntur, qui de pace conscientiæ & spe bona nihil novêre, quam vix Prophetis Grotius relinquit. Perversè pietati vita æterna promittitur. Piis quidem pro- missa est, sed per fidem, non per pietatem obti- nenda. Habet & pietas promissionem vitæ fu- turæ, sed etsi ad τὴν ἐυσέβειαν faciant etiam τὰ γυμνάσματα virtutum, primum tamen & potis- simum in ea est fides, quæ exerenda & exercen- da maximè est, imprimis in agone, & tentatio- nibus variis, in quibus fideles se bonos athletas præstare tenentur fide, pugna in fide, contentione per Verbum, ac constante perseverantia, militiam bonam militando. Exempla talis pugnæ fidei habemus in V. T. Jacobum, Genes. XXXII. Jo- bum passim in ejus scenis diversis; in N. T. mu- lierem Cananæam, Matth. XV. Paulum, 2. Cor. XII. & alios. Adde, quod Chrysostomus & Theophyla- ctus per pietatem fidem puram & vitam rectam intelligant, quibus accedunt Bullingerus, & Cro- cius, totum Christianismum comprehendi asse- rens, ut 2. Tim. III. vers. 12. unde B. Hunnius: Perperam hoc à Pontificiis torquetur ad justifica- tionem operum constituendam. Non enim quod toti respectu unius alicujus partis competit, id con- festim cæteris quoque partibus adscribendum est. Sunt pietatis partes complures, inter quas & nova obedientia, studiumque bonorum operum continen- tur. Quod autem habere dicitur vitæ æternæ pro- missionem, synecdochicè dicitur, respectu salvificæ agnitionis DEI, quæ fides nuncupatur. Quanquam nec cæteris ejus partibus sua defit remuneratio (gra- tuita tamen) etiam in vita beata. Quo respectu atque sensu particula de promissione futuræ vitæ non absurdè ad nova etiam obedientiæ studium ac- commodatur, hoc tamen discrimine, ut ipsa per se vita æterna non proveniat nobis ex ullis operi- bus, ne quidem post regenerationem editis, sed sit maneatque donum DEI per Christum Jesum Do- minum nostrum, Roman. VI. Eph. II. Bona opera vero, IN VITA beata coronentur à DEO, & pensentur æternis præmiis, in gloria differentiæ (cu- jus Paulus 1. Cor. XV. meminit) consideratis. Nec ipsa vita, sed in vita æterna gradus gloriæ ex pro- misso divinæ gratiæ prostant virtutum γυμνά- σμασι. Merita autem virtutum in meritum Chri- sti injuriosa sunt, quibus tamen haud obscurè hic Papista favet Grotius, quæque alibi apertius asserit. Non est, quod quæras, inquit Bernhar- dus Serm. LXIIX. in Cant. quibus meritis spere- mus bona, præsertim cum audias apud Prophe- tam: Non propter vos, sed propter me ego fa- ciam, dicit Dominus: Timothei ceu Episcopi erat illud quærere, sed cum nemo alium exerceat, nisi seipsum prius exercuerit, ad id hortatur Timo- theum Apostolus. Græcum verbum à γυμνὸς nu- dus deductum iis conveniebat, qui nudi se in Gymnasiis exercebant, ut expeditiores essent. Id monet, ut nudi simus ab humanis traditioni- bus, nudi ab affectibus, à curis seculi, omnibusque impedimentis. Perperam autem per γυμνασίαν σω- ματικὴν athletarum exercitia intelligunt Cornelius à Lapide & Justinianus. Non enim Apostoli erat de istis aliquid præscribere. Sanior est Grotii ex- plicatio, quæ & contextui & informationi de abstinentia à conjugio, & cibis convenit, & Am- brosiastro notata est, imò Bernardo in Apolog. ad Guilhelm. Abbatem, Anshelmo, Lombardo Hugoni, Thomæ, Lyrano, plerisque Pontificiis, nostris etiam ac Reformatis Interpp. placuit. Et agnoscunt Pontificii externas actiones religio- nis causa susceptas respici, atque inter alia lon- gas inedias, vigilias, humicubationes, nudipedia &c. Corporalis exercitatio, inquit Lombardus, in qua te fatigas jejunando, vigilando, abstinendo, quæ sunt frena carnis, ad modicum est utilis, nisi huic addatur pietas.

## 4:9
Verse 9.

Faithful is the word and worthy of all acceptance. Some refer this to the preceding. I would prefer to refer it to the following. For we have the same words with the following 'that' above in 1:15. But in this way these things must be included by a parenthesis.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Πιρὸς ὁ λόγος καὶ πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιος. Referunt quidam ad præcedentia. Ego ad sequentia referre malim. Nam & sic eadem verba subsequente ὅτι habemus supra I. 15. Sed ita per παρένθεσιν includendæ sunt ista.

## 4:10
Verse 10.

For to this end we both labor and are reproached. For that which I am now about to say, we endure labors and insults. Concerning labors, see Acts XX. 35. 1 Cor. XVI. 16. Col. I. 29. 1 Thess. V. 12. In the Manuscript: Καὶ ἀγωνιζόμεθα, not badly, as in Col. I, 29.

Because we have hoped in the living God. באל חי. He who has life in Himself by the fullest right, is able to confer it upon whom He wills. See below VI. 17.

Who is the Savior of all men, especially of believers.

He wills all to be saved, namely if they believe: but He wills to save Christians, because they believe: namely if faith is effective through love. Compare what we had above II. 4. The writer on the calling of the Gentiles V. 31. Since whether secretly or manifestly, He Himself is (as the Apostle says) the Savior of all men, especially of the faithful. Which sentiment, with the most subtle brevity and most valid strength, if it is considered with a tranquil gaze, settles this whole controversy of which we are treating: for by saying, who is the Savior of all men, he confirms that the goodness of GOD is general over all men. But by adding, especially of the faithful, he shows that there is a part of the human race which, by the merit of faith divinely inspired, is promoted to the highest and eternal salvation by special benefits. We have seen the word σωτῆρ attributed to God the Father also above I. 1. That to the Hebrews is מושיע.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Εἰς τῦτο γὰρ καὶ κοπιῶμεν καὶ ὀνειδιζόμεθα. Ob id, quod jam dicturus sum, perferimus labores ac contumelias. De laboribus vide Actor. XX. 35. 1. Cor. XVI. 16. Col. I. 29. 1. Thess. V. 12. In Manuscripto: Καὶ ἀγωνιζόμεθα, non male, ut Col. I, 29.

Ὅτι ἠλπίκαμεν ἐπὶ Θεῷ ζῶντι. באל חי. Qui vitam in se habet plenissimo jure, is eam potest quibus vult conferre. Vide infra VI. 17.

Ὅς ἐσι σωτὴρ πάντων ἀνθρώπων, μάλιςα πισῶν.

Vult omnes servari, nempe si credant: Christianos autem servare vult, quia credunt: nempe si fides per di- lectionem sit efficax. Confer, quod supra habuimus II. 4. Scriptor de vocatione gentium V. 31. Quoniam sive oc- cultè, sive manifestè, ipse est (ut Apostolus ait) salvator omnium hominum, maximè fidelium. Quæ sententia sub- tilissima brevitate, & validissimi roboris, si tranquillo consi- deretur intuitu, totam hanc, de qua agimus, controversiam dirimit: dicendo enim, qui est salvator omnium hominum, confirmatvit bonitatem DEI super universos homines esse ge- neralem. Adjiciendo autem, maxime fidelium, ostendit esse partem generis humani, quæ merito fidei divinitus inspiratæ ad summam atque æternam salutem specialibus beneficiis pro- vehitur. Vocem σωτῆρ tribui Deo Patri vidimus etiam supra I. 1. id Hebræis est מושיע.

## 4:11
Vers. 11. Command these things, and teach) Admonish privately: teach publicly.

He had exhorted to the good doctrine and the faith to be handed down, and also to piety to be exercised in practice: here he repeats again what doctrine of the faith ought especially to be inculcated, even though in ch. I. v. 15 he had already presented the same. That which is never sufficiently learned is never sufficiently said. For the sake of this doctrine, one had to labor and suffer. This was the foundation of hope in the living GOD, this was that faithful saying which Timothy had learned from a boy, which is most worthy of all acceptance, from which Satan desired to draw away those who had embraced that Evangelical truth, through his demonic doctrines, so that they might not seek salvation in Christ alone, but in the observations of human traditions, in which he would wish the state of Christian perfection to be placed. Which he has achieved in these most recent times especially through the Papacy. But when God is called the Savior of men, it can be understood either of GOD the Father, or of the whole SS. Trinity, so that the Son of GOD is included, or also singularly of Christ, who is the true GOD and eternal life, 1 John V. verse 20. Which sense the parallel passage in chapter I. verse 15 seems to confirm. Thus from the Reformed, Bullinger: I preach only the truth of the Gospel, teaching that Christ the Lord came not for any one nation, but to save all who do not by their own faithlessness make themselves unworthy of this Salvation. Here the Apostle, says Crocius, provides an illustrious argument by which he confirms that the pursuit of piety is not in vain, nor does one bear all things without cause with hope placed in GOD alone, because, clearly, God is so good that He desires the salvation of all, does good to all, and indeed bears a singular care for believers, not only here, but will also in the future bring them into the full possession of eternal life. The more common interpretation, however, is concerning God the Father, which is favored by similar passages: 1 Tim. II. verses 3, 4; Tit. I. verse 3; II. v. 10; III. v. 4; Jude v. 25; in which manner GOD the triune is the Savior of all men, according to His antecedent will; but peculiarly of believers, according to His consequent will. Meanwhile, He is called the Savior of all men, especially of believers, but not the Savior of all men, if they believe. Concerning this hypothetical, it has been laboriously discussed at John III. verse 16. He is the Savior of the world, 1 John IV. verse 16; the propitiation for the sins of the whole world, 1 John II. v. 2; the Savior πάντων τῶν λαῶν, Luke II. verse 31. He does not only will that all men be saved if they believe, but He wills that all be saved, and that all believe, or arrive at the knowledge of the truth, 1 Tim. II. verse 4. Nor does He truly will to save those who believe, if faith is effective through charity. For charity does nothing for salvation. By grace you have been saved through faith: and this is not of yourselves: for it is the gift of GOD, not of works, lest anyone should boast, Eph. II. verses 8, 9. Although Piscator and Tofsanus wish for σωτῆρα to be understood not as the giver of eternal salvation, but as the author of deliverance from the dangers of this life, to which Estius agrees, it is nevertheless clear from the context and scope that eternal salvation is being discussed here: since that temporal deliverance does not always befall the pious, as is evident from the example of the Martyrs; add that the word σωτὴρ in the New Testament, when used of GOD or Christ, always denotes a spiritual savior, Luke I. verse 47; II. verse 11; John IV. verse 42; Acts VI. verse 31, etc.; therefore Theophylactus rightly explains this passage by that one in 1 Tim. II. verse 4.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Παράγγελλε ταῦτα, καὶ δίδασκε) Mone priva- tim: doce publicè.

Exhortatus erat ad doctrinam bonam & fidem tradendam, nec non ad pietatem in praxi exer- cendam: hîc iterum repetit, quæ præcipuè do- ctrina fidei debeat inculcari, tametsi c. I. v. 15. jam eamdem exhibuerit. Nunquam satis dicitur, quod nunquam satis discitur. Ob hanc doctri- nam laborandum & patiendum erat. Hæc fun- damentum erat spei in DEO vivo, hæc erat fide- lis ille sermo, quem didicerat Timotheus à pue- ro, qui omni acceptione maximè dignus, à quo per prophanas & aniles fabulas abstrahere Sata- nas cupiebat eos, qui veritatem illam Evange- licam amplexi erant, per doctrinas suas dæmo- niacas, ut non in Christo uno salutem quærant, sed in observationibus humanarum traditionum, in quibus statum perfectionis Christianorum collocari vellet. Quod hisce imprimis novissi- mis temporibus per Papatum consecutus est. Cum autem Deus Servator hominum dicitur, vel de DEO de Deo Patre id intelligi potest, vel de tota SS. Trinitate, ut Filius DEI includatur, vel etiam singulariter de Christo, qui verus DEUS & vita æterna est, 1. Joh. V. vers. 20. Quem sensum fir- mare videtur locus parallelus cap. I. vers. 15. Sic è Reformatis Bullingerus: Solam Evangelii ve- ritatem prædico docens, Christum Dominum ve- nisse non uni alicui genti, sed servandis omnibus, qui modo perfidia seipsos non fecerint indignos hac Salute. Hic Apostolus, inquit Crocius, illustre præ- bet argumentum, quo confirmat, non frustraneum esse pietatis studium, nec se citra causam spe in solo DEO collocata omnia ferre, quia videlicet Deus tam bonus sit, ut omnium salutem expetat, omnibus bene faciat, singularem verò credentium curam gerat, non tantùm hic, sed & olim eos in plenam vitæ æternæ possessionem sit immissurus. Communior tamen interpretatio est de Deo Pa- tre, cui favent loca similia 1. Tim. II. vers. 3. 4. Tit. I. vers. 3. II. v. 10. III. v. 4. Jud. v. 25. quo pacto DEUS triunus Salvator est omnium ho- minum, quoad voluntatem antecedentem: pecu- liariter autem credentium, quoad voluntatem con- sequentem. Interim Salvator omnium hominum dicitur, maximè credentium, non autem Salva- tor omnium hominum, si credant. De qua hy- pothetica ad Johan. III. vers. 16. operosè dictum. Salvator est mundi, 1. Johan. IV. vers. 16. propi- tiatio pro peccatis totius mundi, 1. Johan. II. v. 2. Salvator πάντων τῶν λαῶν, Luc. II. vers. 31. Non tantum vult, homines omnes salvari, si credant, sed vult, ut omnes salventur, & ut credant, vel ad agnitionem veritatis perveniant omnes, 1. Tim. II. vers. 4. Nec vero salvare eos vult, qui cre- dunt, si fides per charitatem sit efficax. Nam ad salutem nihil facit charitas. Gratia salvati estis per fidem: & hoc non ex vobis: DEI enim do- num est, non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur, Eph. II. vers. 8. 9. Quanquam verò Piscator & Tof- sanus per σωτῆρα intelligi velint non æternæ sa- lutis datorem, sed liberationis ex periculis hujus vitæ autorem, quibus annuit Estius, è contextu tamen & scopo patet de salute æterna hic agi: Siquidem illa liberatio temporalis non semper piis obtingat, ut exemplo Martyrum constat, adde, quod vox σωτὴρ in Nov. Test. cum de DEO vel Christo adhibetur, semper spiritualem salvatorem notet, Luc. I. vers. 47. II. vers. 11. Jo- hann. IV. vers. 42. Actor. VI. vers. 31. &c. ideo recte Theophylactus hunc locum exponit per il- lum 1. Tim. II. vers. 4.

## 4:12
Vers. 12.

Μηδείς σε τῆς νεότητος καταφρονείτω.

In those times, Presbyters were accustomed to be what they were called, that is, of much advanced age. Timothy had been made an Evangelist before such an age, because both prophecies had indicated him, and the gifts of the Spirit commended him. But it does not therefore follow that Timothy was clearly a youth when Paul wrote these things. For בחורה to the Hebrews, νεότης to the interpreters, is military age, and it comprises civil age, and is opposed only to old age. This, therefore, is what he means: what you lack in the customary age of presbyters, supply that with the gravity of your character. Let no one despise your age: that is, conduct yourself in such a way that it cannot be despised: ὅτι σοὶ ἔδωκεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ πρεσβυτέρων, Wisd. XVI. 51.

Ἀλλὰ τύπος γίνου τῶν πιστῶν.

As Paul himself did, Phil. III. verse 17. A similar admonition is in 1 Pet. V. verse 3.

Ἐν λόγῳ) In serious and useful conversations, Eph. V. 4.

Ἐν ἀναστροφῇ.

בְּדֶרֶךְ that is, ἐν τῇ ὁμιλίᾳ, in pleasant conversation. Thus Jas. III. 10; 1 Pet. I. 15.

Ἐν ἀγάπῃ, ἐν πίστει.

The Latin does not have that ἐν πνεύματι, nor does the Syriac, nor Chrysostom. Understand 'love' here as the works of love; and understand 'faith' as the sincere profession of faith.

Ἐν ἁγνείᾳ) Thus also below V. 22. Add also Philipp. IV. 8. 1. Cor. VI. 6.

The Apostle had warned how Timothy ought to exercise himself in piety: now he teaches what kind of person he ought to show himself to others. He prefaces this, however, so that he might not suffer himself to be despised, by observing the authority of his office, so that it might not be held in contempt, and also by preserving it with an exemplary life. 'Let no one despise your youth.' But, says Theodoret, this is not mine, why then do you command me things that are suitable for others? 'But be an example of the believers.' You wish, he says, not to be despised if you command things to be done, you living law, show that you rightly execute the law, have a life that bears witness to your speech. Be, says Chrysostom as interpreter, εἰκὼν ἔμψυχος, καὶ ὅρος εὐζωΐας, an animated law, and a rule and norm of living well and rightly. Let him be a pattern of the believers or of the flock of the Lord, 1. Petr. V. 3. in speech, in conduct, in love, not feigned, but which is done in Spirit and in truth, Eph. IV. 3. 1. Joh. III. 18. (constantly in the Greek. Codd. those words ἐν πνεύματι are read) in a sincere profession of faith, and in purity, the first two are general: the rest are special, love concerns the neighbor, faith God, purity concerns ourselves. Blessed Hunnius explains those words 'in Spirit and in faith' a little differently: In Spirit, he says, by which he wishes him to be fervent in bringing forth heavenly truth, in refuting errors, and in chastising vices. In faith, so that it may be kept sound, so that it may be fixed in God alone and the Lord Jesus Christ, which allows itself neither to be cast down in troubles, nor to be hidden in time of persecution, but rather to bring itself forward through an ingenuous confession of doctrine, having spurned all adversities and dangers. There is no reason for us to reject this exposition: especially since it is not a private person who is being instructed here, but a public one, namely a Bishop or Doctor of the Church. Thus also Calvin and Crocius understand Spirit as the fervent zeal of God and his glory. Conf. Rom. XII. 11. The Vulgate rendered purity as chastity. But that is too narrow. Not only that, but also candor and simplicity are indicated according to Crocius. We judge that purity of mind and body is noted.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Μηδείς σε τῆς νεότητος καταφρονείτω.

Solebant illis temporibus Presbyteri esse id quod dice- bantur, id est, multum provectæ ætatis. Timotheus ante talem ætatem factus erat Evangelista, quia & prophetiæ eum indicaverant, & Spiritus dona eum commendabant. At non ideo sequitur plane juvenem fuisse Timotheum, cum hæc Paulus scriberet. Nam בחורה Hebræis, νεότης Interpretibus, est ætas militaris, & civilem ætatem com- prehendit, solique senectuti opponitur. Hoc ergò vult, quod tibi ad solitam presbyterorum ætatem deest, id sup- ple morum gravitate. Nemo tuam ætatem contemnat: id est, ita te gere, ne contemni possit: ὅτι σοὶ ἔδωκεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ πρεσβυτέρων, Sap. XVI. 51.

Ἀλλὰ τύπος γίνου τῶν πιστῶν.

Ut ipse fecit Paulus Philipp. III. vers. 17. Similis moni- tio 1. Petr. V. vers. 3.

Ἐν λόγῳ) Sermonibus seriis & utilibus, Eph. V. 4.

Ἐν ἀναστροφῇ.

בְּדֶרֶךְ id est, ἐν τῇ ὁμιλίᾳ, in suavi conversatione. Sic Jac. III. 10. 1. Petr. I. 15.

Ἐν ἀγάπῃ, ἐν πίστει.

Illud ἐν πνεύματι non habet Latinus, neque Syrus, ne- que Chrysostomus. Dilectionem autem hic intellige, di- lectionis opera: & fidem intellige, fidei sinceram pro- fessionem.

Ἐν ἁγνείᾳ) Sic & infra V. 22. Adde & Philipp. IV. 8. 1. Cor. VI. 6.

Monuerat Apostolus, quomodo sese exercere debeat in pietate Timotheus: jam qualem sese aliis præbere debeat, docet. Præmittit autem, ne sefe contemni patiatur, autoritatem muneris sui observando, ne eadem despicatui habeatur, nec non vitæ exemplari eam conservando. Nemo ado- lescentiam tuam contemnat. Atqui, inquit Theo- doretus, hoc non est meum, cur ergò mihi præcipis, quæ aliis conveniunt? Sed exemplum esto fide- lium. Vis, inquit, non contemni si præcipias effi- cere, lex animata, ostende te legem rectè exequi, habe vitam, quæ de sermone ferat testimonium. Esto, inquit Chrysostomo interprete, εἰκὼν ἔμψυ- χος, καὶ ὅρος εὐζωΐας, animata lex, & regula ac norma bene recteque vivendi. Typus sit fidelium vel gregis Domini, 1. Petr. V. 3. in sermone, in con- versatione, in dilectione, non fucata, sed quæ in Spiritu & veritate fiat, Eph. IV. 3. 1. Joh. III. 18. (constanter in Græc. Codd. leguntur illa ἐν πνεύ- ματι) in sincera fidei professione, & in puritate, priora duo generalia sunt: Reliqua specialia, dile- ctio proximum, fides Deum, puritas nos ipsos con- cernit. Illa in Spiritu & in fide paulò aliter ex- plicat B. Hunnius: In Spiritu, inquit, quo vult esse ardentem in afferenda veritate cælesti, in refellendis erroribus, castigandisque vitiis. In fide, ut ea ser- vetur sana, ut sit defixa in solo Deo & Domino Jesu Christo, quæ se nec dejici patiatur in ærumnis, nec tempore persecutionis occultari, quin per ingenuam Confessionem doctrinæ sese proferat, spretis omni- bus adversis atque periculis. Quam ἔκθεσιν non est, ut reprobemus: maximè, cum hic informe- tur non privata persona, sed publica, Episcopus nempe vel Doctor Ecclesiæ. Sic etiam Calvinus & Crocius Spiritum de fervente zelo Dei ejusque gloria intelligunt. Conf. Rom. XII. 11. Puritatem Vulgatus reddidit castitatem. Sed id angustius. Non ea solum, sed & Candor ac simplicitas juxta Crocium indicatur. Nos puritatem animi & cor- poris notari censemus.

## 4:13
Vers. 13. Ἕως ἔρχομαι, πρόσεχε τῇ ἀναγνώσει.

Be assiduous in reading the Prophets, the Psalms, and other books. See 2. Tim. III. vers. 15. מקרא for the Hebrews is reading, namely of the law. He adds, 'until I come,' that is, then I will instruct you more fully. He consoles his labor. Paul hoped, however, that he would come to Ephesus: but that did not happen for him.

Τῇ παρακλήσει, τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ.

In admonishing others privately, in teaching publicly, as above 11.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ἕως ἔρχομαι, πρόσεχε τῇ ἀναγνώσει.

Assiduus esto in legendis Prophetis, Psalmis, aliisque li- bris. Vide 2. Tim. III. vers. 15. מקרא Hebræis lectio, nempe legis. Addit, dum venero, id est, tunc ego te ple- nius instruam. Solatur ejus laborem. Speravit autem Paulus venturum se Ephesum: sed id ei non contigit.

Τῇ παρακλήσει, τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ.

In monendis aliis privatim, docendis publicè, ut supra 11.

## 4:14
Vers. 14. Μὴ ἀμέλει τῦ σοι χαρίσματος.

I think this concerns the gift of tongues; such gifts must be solicitously guarded by thanksgiving, prayers, and holy use, 1. Thess. V. 19. 2. Tim. I. 6.

ὃ ἐδόθη σοι διὰ προφητείας.

That is, that the gift was pre-signified to be about to be given to you through the prophecy of others: see above on I. 8. Prophets are said to do what they predict, Jer. I. 10.

Μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τῦ πρεσβυτερίυ.

That is, to the prophecy was added a serious invocation of divine help, at the time when hands were laid upon you. Paul himself had laid hands on Timothy, 2 Tim. I. 6, but it was the custom that the Presbyters who were present should lay on hands together with the head of their assembly. Clement, Constitutions VIII. 16: 'When ordaining a presbyter, O bishop, lay your hand upon his head, with the presbytery and the deacons standing by you.' Africa retained this custom for a long time. For in the Acts of the Council of Carthage we read: 'When a presbyter is ordained, while the bishop blesses him and holds his hand upon his head, let all the presbyters who are present also hold their hands beside the hand of the bishop upon his head.' Where Apostles or the assistants of the Apostles were not present, ordination was performed by the president of the assembly, with the consent of the presbytery. But where Apostles or their assistants were present, this honor and the presidency itself belonged to them. Yet they did these and such things together with the Presbytery, as we see here. Thus among the Hebrews, the הנשיא, the prince of the Sanhedrin, used to lay on hands for the Sanhedrin upon elected judges. Concerning the imposition of hands, see what we have said on Matt. IX. v. 18.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Μὴ ἀμέλει τῦ σοι χαρίσματος.

Puto agi de dono linguarum; talia dona sollicite cu- stodienda sunt gratiarum actione, precibus, sancto usu, 1. Thess. V. 19. 2. Tim. I. 6.

ὃ ἐδόθη σοι διὰ προφητείας.

Id est, quod donum præsignificatum est tibi datum iri per aliorum prophetiam: supra I. 8. Prophetæ facere di- cuntur, quod prædicunt Jer. I. 10.

Μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τῦ πρεσβυτερίυ.

Id est, ad prophetiam accessit seria invocatio opis divi- næ, tunc cum manus tibi imponerentur. Paulus ipse Ti- motheo manus imposuerat, 2. Tim. I. 6. sed mos erat, ut qui adessent Presbyteri, una cum cœtus sui principe manus imponerent. Clemens Constitutionum VIII. 16. Πρεσβύτε- ρον χειροτονῶν, ὦ ἐπίσκοπε, τὴν χεῖρα ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς ἐπίθες αὐτῶν, τῦ πρεσβυτερίε παρεστῶτος σοι, κὴ τῶν διακόνων. Hunc morem diu retinuit Africa. In Synodi enim Carthaginensis Actis legimus: Presbyter cum ordinatur, Episcopo eum benedicente, & manum super caput ejus tenente, etiam omnes Presbyteri, qui præsentes sunt, manus suas juxta ma- num Episcopi super caput illius teneant. Ubi Apostoli, aut Apostolorum adjutores non aderant, fiebat ordinatio per Præsidem cœtus, consentiente Presbytero. At ubi aderant Apostoli, aut eorum adjutores, hic honor & ipsa præsiden- tia ad illos pertinebat. Faciebant tamen hæc & talia una cum Presbyterio, ut hic videmus. Sic apud Hebræos ju- dicibus electis manus pro Synedrio imponebat הנשיא princeps Synedrii. De manuum impositione vide, quæ diximus ad Matth. IX. v. 18.

## 4:15
Verse 15. Meditate on these things (Hebrew: Hagah, Psalm 1, verse 2). Be in these things (Latin: Sic Horatius: totus in illis). The supports and means, both of this exercise and of the presentation of the model, so that this may come about with fruit, are both the reading of Holy Scripture, and frequent exhortation and instruction, and the solicitous care and guarding of the gifts divinely granted; not, however, the gift of tongues, but by enallage all gifts, as B. Hunnius rightly observes, are understood to be granted to Timothy for the useful performance of the Ecclesiastical office: which he says were granted through prophecy, that is, according to the prophecy previously published concerning Timothy, so that using it healthfully he might be a distinguished vessel and instrument of divine glory, but increased and completed when he was ordained a minister of the Church of GOD by the solemn rite of the laying on of hands. Theophylact explains 'through prophecy' as 'the Holy Spirit commanding'; but the Hunnian interpretation is more suitable. Crocius deserts his Beza here: Beza, he says, in the first edition, which I use, translates 'to prophesy,' how it could be accepted, Bullinger had noted before him. And the matter indeed holds well: For the gift, which Timothy received, was given to him so that he might be fit for prophesying, or interpreting Holy Scripture. It seems, however, rather harshly said, 'through prophecy' for 'unto prophecy.' He says the sense is: he ought to stir up the gift given, with which it was established that he was endowed by divine revelation, when he was designated Bishop from it. But Cornelius à Lapide is most foolish, understanding the Sacrament of order through prophecy, which is unworthy of refutation.

That your progress may be manifest to all. 'Prokope' is also for philosophers 'Progress in virtue.' See Philippians 1, verse 25, and Sirach 51:23. The matter stands thus in Christian piety, as in one who has made a journey against an opposing river. If he has not progressed, - - - if he has perhaps relaxed his arms, the current carries him forward against the opposing river. 'In all' (Hebrew: be-kol) among all. For to be exercised in spiritual things, so that we may receive increase in divine matters, brings it about, says Theodoret: 'not in life only, but also in the word of teaching,' as Chrysostom has it. These therefore understand it concerning the person of Timothy, and so also the Commentary attributed to Ambrose, Lombard, Hugo Card., Aretius. Others explain it concerning the effect of the ministry with Calvin and Bullinger. Crocius joins both, because the more Timothy progressed in himself, the more he progressed in the work of the Church, to which sense the following last verse favors: 'and you will save yourself, and those who hear you.' 'In all,' although it can be understood of persons, 'among all,' is nevertheless more rightly accepted of the thing, in all parts of doctrine and of the sacred Ministry. You see, says Chrysostom, how he wanted him to become great and admirable in these things also, from which he knew the benefits of the Church would proceed. In all, not only in the rectitude of life, but also in the abundance of doctrine. Thus also Theophylact. B. Hunnius: so that it may become clear from the thing itself, that you do not grow sluggish in idleness, nor do the things of your office negligently, but that you aim at this, that both by the knowledge of doctrine, and the administration of office, and the dexterity of government, you may continually surpass yourself.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Ταῦτα μελέτα) הגה Psalm. I. vers. 2. Ἐν τούτοις ἴσθι) Sic Horatius: totus in illis. Adminicula & media & γυμνάσματος istius, & exemplaris præsentationis, ut hæc cum fructu eveniat, sunt tum lectio Scripturæ Sacræ, tum ad- hortatio & informatio frequens, tum donorum di- vinitus concessorum solicita cura, & custoditio; Non autem linguarum donum, sed per enallagen dona omnia, ut rectè observat B. Hunnius, ad mu- nus Ecclesiasticum utiliter obeundum Timotheo concessa intelliguntur: quæ per Prophetiam, id est, secundum Prophetiam de Timotheo pridem editam concessa ait, ut eo salutariter utens insi- gne possit esse divinæ gloriæ vas atque organum, aucta verò & completa, quando solenni ritu im- positionis manuum ordinatus est Ecclesiæ DEI minister. Theophylactus per Prophetiam exponit, jubente Spiritu Sancto; Sed convenientior est Hunniana interpretatio. Bezam suum hic dese- rit Crocius: Beza, inquit, in prima editione, qua utor vertit, ad prophetandum, quomodo accipi pos- se, ante illum notaverat Bullingerus. Et res qui- dem habet bene: Nam donum, quod accepit Timo- theus, ei datum erat, ut esset idoneus ad prophetan- dum, seu interpretandam sacram Scripturam. Du- riusculè tamen videtur dictum, διὰ προφητείας, pro εἰς προφητείαν. Sensum esse dicit: excitare debere donum datum, quo ipsum præditum esse divina re- velatione constiterit, quando ex ea designatus est Episcopus. Ineptit autem maxime Cornelius à La- pide, Sacramentum ordinis per Prophetiam intelli- gens, quod refutatione indignum.

Ἱνα σου ἡ προκοπὴ φανερὰ ἧ ἐν πᾶσι) προκοπὴ etiam Phi- losophis est Profectus in virtute. Vide Philipp. I. v. 25. & Sirach. LI. 23. Ita se res habet in Christiana pietate, ut in eo, qui amne adverso iter fecit. Si non profecit, - - - si brachia forte remisit Atque illum adverso prorius rapit alveus amne. ἐν πᾶσι בכל apud omnes. In spiritualibus enim exerceri, ut in rebus divi- nis incrementum accipiamus, efficit, ait Theodore- tus: μὴ ἐν τῷ βίῳ μόνῳ, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ διδασκαλικῷ, ut habet Chrysostomus. Hi ergò de Timothei persona intelligunt, atque ita etiam Commentarius Ambrosio tributus, Lombardus, Hugo Card. Aretius. Alii de effectu ministerii explicant cum Calvino & Bullingero. Crocius utrumque conjungit, quia quo magis Timotheus proficiebat in se, eo magis proficiebat in opere Ecclesiæ, cui sensui favet vers. sequens ultimus: & te ipsum servabis, & eos, qui te audiunt, ἐν πᾶ- σι, etsi de personis intelligi possit, apud omnes, rectius tamen de re accipitur, in omnibus parti- bus doctrinæ, & sacri Ministerii. Vides, inquit Chrysostomus, ut in his quoque illum magnum fieri volebat, atque mirabilem, ex quo scilicet Ecclesiæ commoda provenire sciebat. In omnibus, non modo in vitæ rectitudine, sed etiam in doctrinæ uber- tate. Sic & Theophylactus. B. Hunnius: ut ex ipsa re perspicuum evadat, te non torpere ocio, nec quæ sunt muneris tui, facere negligenter, sed eo specta- re, ut & cognitione doctrinæ, & administratione offici, & dexteritate gubernationis, teipsum sub- inde vincas.

## 4:16
Verse 16.

Take heed to yourself and to the doctrine. Eustathius noted that 'epechein' is put for 'prosechein,' that is, to attend with the mind. Thus Luke 14:7, Sirach 31:1, 2, 35:11. Attend with your mind to yourself, how you live, and to the doctrine, what you teach. In sacred matters it was said: 'Do this,' which Plutarch translates 'proseche.' He was ordered to attend to himself, not only how he lives, but also how he progresses in doctrine, as much as pertains to the 'prokope' of spiritual intelligence, therefore he had warned in verse 13: 'attend to reading': and he repeats that, so that he may understand how necessary that is. We concede that the office of teaching is noted here by Synecdoche. Thus the Apostle commanded in Acts 20:28 to the Ephesian Presbyters: 'take heed to yourselves and to all the flock.'

Ἐπίμενε αὐτοῖς) Remain with them. Thus we have ἐπιμένειν in Acts X. 48, XXI. 4, 10, XXVIII. 12, 14, 1 Corinthians XVI. 8, Galatians I. 18. He does not command him to remain with the Ephesians, but to persist in those things which the Apostle had commanded: in attention to himself, and care for the committed flock, indeed in all the admonitions which he had delivered: thus ἐπιμένειν τῇ χάριτι Θεοῦ is found in Acts XIII. 43, ἐπιμένειν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ in Romans VI. 1, ἐπιμένειν τῇ χρηστότητι in Romans XI. 22.
