When a place is implied, a preposition is added and the place is indicated: as 1 Corinthians XVI. 7, ἐπιμεῖναι πρὸς ὑμᾶς, Galatians I. 18, πρὸς αὐτὸν, 1 Corinthians XVI. 8, ἐπιμενῶ ἐν Ἐφέσῳ, Philippians I. 24, ἐπιμένω ἐν σαρκὶ. Which is not the case here. Nor was it necessary for Timothy to remain at Ephesus forever; other churches also had to be won. That he was appointed bishop at Ephesus is a begging of the question from the beginning. And the resulting fruit teaches that Timothy is being admonished to persist in those things, not to remain there, with the Ephesians.

For in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you. He who instructs others, instructs himself also. He saves others also, namely by exhorting those standing, by raising up those who have fallen. It is not new that words which belong to GOD by supreme right, or to Christ, are attributed to men in a certain subordinate sense, as we said at Matthew 16:18. Thus likewise this 'sozein' is attributed to men, Romans 11:14. Thus also 'ekpeiphein' Luke 1:16.

Compare Obadiah verse 21. But Cornelius à Lapide wrongly gathers from these words that saints (inhabitants of heaven) are called saviors without injury to Christ. What have these to do with the saints in heaven? Those who preach the word of God in the Church 'diakonikos' (ministerially), are said to save us through the word. Therefore do the heavenly saints also save us as our Mediators and Patrons? A corpse of a consequence, not a consequence! GOD alone is the author of salvation, but because He saves us not immediately, but through the word, 1 Corinthians 1:21. The same effect is attributed to the ministers of the word, not for the sake of honor, or at least only in title, as some Calvinists say, but truly as a ministerial cause, through which the principal cause produces something. For thus it is truly a cause, it truly acts, even if only 'diakonikos,' not 'kyrios' (properly) or 'autoenergetikos' (by its own power). See 1 Corinthians 11:5 seq., 4:25, 2 Corinthians 5:20, Galatians 4:19, Philemon verse 10.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Ἔπεχε σεαυτῷ κὶ τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ) ἐπέχειν poni pro προσ- έχειν, id est, animum attendere, notavit Eustathius. Sic Luc. XIV. 7. Sirach. XXXI. 1. 2. XXXV. 11. Animum attende tibi ipsi, quomodo vivas, & doctrinæ, quid doceas. In sacris dicebatur: Hoc age, quod Plutarchus vertit πρόσεχε. Attendere sibi ipsi jubebatur, non tantum quo- modo vivat, sed etiam quomodo in doctrina profi- ciat, quantum ad προκοπὴν spiritualis intelligentiæ, ideò monuerat vers. 13. attende lectioni: repetitq; ac illud, ut quam necessarium id sit, intelligat. Διδα- σκαλίαν autem officium hic notari per Synecdo- chen concedimus. Sic præcepit Apostolus Act. XX. 28. Ephesinis Presbyteris: προσέχετε ἑαυτοῖς καὶ παντὶ τῷ ποιμνίῳ.

Ἐπίμενε αὐτοῖς) Mane apud Ephesios. Sic ἐπιμένειν ha- bemus Actor. X. 48. XXI. 4. 10. XXIIIX. 12. 14. 1. Corinth. XVI. 8. Galat. I. 18. Non penes Ephesios manere jubet: Sed in illis persistere, quæ præceperat Apostolus: in attentione sui ipsius, & curâ commissi gregis, imò omnibus in monitis, quæ tradiderat: Sic ἐπιμένειν τῇ χάριτι Θεῦ habetur Act. XIII. 43. ἐπιμένειν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ Rom. VI. 1. ἐπιμένειν τῇ χρηστότητι Rom. XI. 22. Cum locus innuitur, præpositio addita, & locus indica- tus est: ut 1. Cor. XVI. 7. ἐπιμεῖναι πρὸς ὑμᾶς Gal. I. 18. πρὸς αὐτὸν 1. Cor. XVI. 8. ἐπιμενῶ ἐν Ἐφέσῳ, Phil. I. 24. ἐπιμένω ἐν σαρκὶ. Quod hic non sit. Ne- que Timotheo manendum semper Ephesi fuit, lu- crandæ etiam erant aliæ Ecclesiæ. Episcopum E- phesi constitutum fuisse, αἴτησίς est τῶ ἐν ἀρχῇ. Et consequens fructus docet moneri Timotheum, ut in illis persistat, non ut illic, apud Ephesios.

Τῦτο γὰρ ποιῶν καὶ σεαυτὸν σώσεις, καὶ τὺς ἀκούοντάς σου) Qui alios instruit, & se instruit. Servat & alios, nempe stantes hortando, lapsos erigendo. Non novum est, ver- ba, quæ DEO summo jure competunt; aut Christo, sen- su quodam subordinato tribui hominibus, ut diximus ad Matth. XVI. 18. Sic item hoc σώζειν hominibus tribuitur, Rom. XI. 14. Sic & ἐκπείφειν Luc. I. 16.

Conf. Obad. v. 21. Perperam autem ex his ver- bis colligit Cornelius à Lapide, citra Christi inju- riam sanctos (cœlites) servatores dici. Quid hæc ad sanctos in cœlis? Qui verbum Dei prædicant in Ecclesia διακονικῶς, per verbum salvare nos di- cuntur. Ergonè & sancti cœlites nos salvant eeu Mediatores & Patroni nostri? Cadaver conse- quentiæ, non consequentia! DEUS solus au- ctor est salutis, sed quia salvat nos non immediatè, sed per verbum, 1. Cor. I. 21. Verbi ministris idem effectus tribuitur, non honoris causa, seu titulote- nus saltem, ut Calviniani quidam ajunt, sed verè ut causæ ministeriali, per quam causa principalis ali- quid producit. Ita enim verè causa est, verè agit, etsi διακονικῶς solum, non κυρίως vel αὐτοενεργη- τικῶς. Vid. 1. Cor. XI. 5. seq. IV. 25. 2. Cor. V. 20. Gal. IV. 19. Philem. v. 10.

## 5:1 Argument
PART II. OF THE SPECIAL EPISTLE, Concerning persons of different kinds. CHAPTER V.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle teaches how one should deal with the elders, how with the juniors of both sexes, how with widows, and which are true widows, and at what age, and what kind are to be chosen for the ministry of the saints; but he commands that the younger ones, who ought to marry, be avoided. He adds concerning the honoring and supporting of presbyters, and that complaints against them are not to be easily entertained, then concerning public rebuke, concerning the circumspect laying on of hands, and sobriety, concerning manifest sins, and good works.

There are three parts: namely, Ecclesiastical matters to be done. I. Concerning the manner of rebuking, to verse 3. II. Concerning the care of widows, to verse 16. III. Concerning presbyters, their honor, support, rebuke, and ordination, to verse 25.

PART I. Ecclesiastical Agenda concerning the manner of rebuking.

Vers. 1. Do not rebuke an elder) The word πρεσβυτέρῳ here is to be taken as referring to age, not to office: the following words show this. Ἐπιπλήττειν here is נזף, frequent among the Rabbis, whence נזיפה, a certain harsher rebuke, which elders are accustomed to use against juniors, not the contrary. In the Glossary: ἐπιπλήττω, I chastise, rebuke, interrupt, chide; both Socrates and Demosthenes use this word.

But exhort him as a father) Admonish gently, and with a certain sign of reverence. Thus Peter I. 1: The elders who are among you I exhort. It is a custom among all nations to call older men by the name of Fathers, and women by the name of Mothers.

The younger as brothers) Brother is a kindly appellation for equals among themselves, in Martial, and in the Greek Epigram.

Latin:

PARS II. EPISTOLÆ SPECIALIS, Quà diversi generis Personas. CAP. V.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Docet Apostolus, quomodo cum Senioribus, quo- modo cum Junioribus utriusque sexus, quo- modo cum viduis agendum, & quæ veræ viduæ, & qua ætate, ac quales eligendæ sint ad sanctorum ministerium; juniores au- tem vitari jubet, quæ nubere debeant. Ad- dit de Presbyteris honorandis, & sustentan- dis, nec suscipienda facilè adversus illos que- rela, tum de correptione publica, de cir- cumspecta manuum impositione, ac sobrie- tate, de manifestis peccatis, bonisŕ, operibus.

PArtes tres sunt: Agenda nempe Ecclesiastica I. De modo corripiendi, ad v. 3. II. De cura vi- duarum, ad v. 16. III. De Presbyteris, eorum ho- nore, sustentatione, correptione, ac ordinatione, ad v. 25.

PARS I. Agenda Ecclesiastica de modo corripiendi.

Vers. 1. Πρεσβυτέρῳ μὴ ἐπιπλήξῃς) Vox πρεσβυτέρῳ hic de ætate sumenda est, non de functione : monstrant id sequentia. Ἐπιπλήττειν hic est נזף frequens Rabbinis, unde נזיפה durior quædam objurgatio, qua seniores uti solent adversum juniores, non contra. In Glossario : ἐπι- πλήττω, castigo, increpo, obstrepo, objurgo, utuntur ea voce & Socrates & Demosthenes.

Ἀλλὰ παρακάλει ὡς πατέρα) Blandè admone, & cum quadam reverentiæ significatione. Sic Petrus I. 1. πρεσβυ- τέρους τοὺς ἐν ὑμῖν παρακαλῶ. Mos est apud omnes gentes seniores viros appellare Patrum, fœminas autem Matrum vocabulo.

Νεωτέρους ὡς ἀδελφοὺς) Frater benigna appellatio pa- rium inter se, apud Martialem, & in Epigrammate Græco.

## 5:2
Vers. 2.

The elder women as mothers, the younger as sisters, in all purity) He wishes the same distinction of ages to be observed among women, but there is more caution, lest any window be opened by blandishments either to love or to suspicion.

He had warned in the preceding chapter about corruptions of doctrine: Now he warns about corruptions of morals, and first of all about the manner of reproof according to the reason of different age, so that, namely, old men may be admonished as Fathers, younger men as brothers and sisters: whether the correction is to be instituted privately or publicly.

He therefore presents distinct canons: The first is: Do not rebuke elders. Elders are understood by reason of age, not office. The cause is the reverence which is owed to them, Lev. XIX. vers. 32. Τὸ ἐπιπλήσσειν properly is to strike with the fists: figuratively, to treat with harsher words, which is forbidden here. But what if some elder is in need of rebuke? The Apostle answers, rebuke him as a Father, i.e., interpreting Chrysostom, speak to him modestly, and admonish him with a certain mixed reverence. That is of great prudence. He is to be admonished in such a way that he understands the admonition proceeds not from affection, but from duty. If, however, moderate exhortation profits nothing, there is need of a more severe rebuke, especially when others are affected by scandals: Concerning which Gregory the Great, book VII, Ep. I: This rule is to be observed when the fault of the Elder does not draw the hearts of the juniors to destruction by his example. But where an Elder offers an example of destruction to the young, there he must be struck with a sharp rebuke: for it is written: a snare to the young are you all, Is. XLII. and again the Prophet says: And the child of a hundred years shall be accursed, Is. LXV.

The second Canon is: Rebuke younger men as brothers. He commands that younger men, as those equal in age to Timothy, who was of a youthful age, be exhorted as brothers, so that they may be more easily brought back to the path of duty by friendly admonition.

The third Canon is: Admonish older women as mothers; by which he wishes older women to be addressed with reverence as mothers, even if they are in need of admonition, so that they do not think they are being despised on account of their old age.

The fourth is: Rebuke younger women as sisters, and that with all purity of mind, words, and gestures. Which can also be referred to all the preceding: So that in any admonition or correction, every suspicion of either austerity, or cruelty, or hatred, or even of less than chaste love is avoided. And therefore it is less aptly rendered by the Vulgate as 'in all chastity,' even if this is entirely included. But what does this mean? Are you commanding these things to Timothy? These things indeed, he says, with Chrysostom saying, for through him I address the whole world. But if he is enjoining these things upon Timothy, let everyone now consider what sort of person he ought to be, so that, namely, he may offer no place for suspicion, and not even give a shadow of an occasion to those wishing to slander. Let Ecclesiasticus 42:13-14 be compared. Jerome to Nepotian, Epistle 2: Let the feet of women rarely or never tread your lodging. Do not stay under the same roof: nor trust in past chastity. You cannot be holier than David, nor stronger than Samson, nor wiser than Solomon. Beware of all suspicions, and whatever can probably be imagined, avoid it beforehand so that it may not be imagined.

PART II. Of the Widows of the Church.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Πρεσβυτέρας ὡς μητέρας, νεωτέρας ὡς ἀδελφὰς, ἐν πάσῃ ἁγνείᾳ) Vult idem discrimen ætatum in fœminis obser- vari, sed plus est cautionis, ne qua ex blanditiis aut amori aut suspicioni pateat fenestra.

Monuerat capite præcedente de corruptelis do- ctrinæ: Jam de morum corruptelis monet, ac pri- mum quidem de modo reprehensionis pro ratione diversæ ætatis, ut nempe senes ceu Parentes, ju- niores ceu fratres & sorores commonefiant: sive privatim seu publicè instituenda sit correptio.

Canones ergo distinctos exhibet: Primus est: Se- niores ne increpaveris. Seniores intelliguntur ætatis, non muneris ratione. Causa est reveren- tia, quæ illis debetur, Lev. XIX. vers. 32. Τὸ ἐπι- πλήσσειν propriè est pugnis cædere : tralatitie, ver- bis durioribus tractare, quod hic vetatur. Quid si vero senior aliquis objurgatione indigeat ? Respondet Apostolus, tanquam Patrem repre- hende, h. e. interprete Chrysostomo, modeste al- loquere, mixtaá, quadam reverentia admone. Est illud magnæ prudentiæ. Sic admonendus est, ut intelligat non ex affectu, sed officio proficisci commonefactionem. Si tamen moderata adhor- tatio nihil proficiat, opus est increpatione seve- riori, maximè, cum scandalis alii afficiuntur: Quo de Gregorius M. l. VII. Ep. I. Hac regula tunc ser- vanda est, cum culpa Senioris exemplo suo non tra- hit ad interitum corda juniorum. Ubi autem Se- nior juvenibus exemplum ad interitum præbet, ibi districta increpatione feriendus est: nam scriptum est: laqueus juvenum omnes vos, Es. XLII. & rur- sus Propheta dicit: Et puer centum annorum male- dictus est, Es. LXV.

Secundus Canon est : Juniores corripe ut Fra- tres. Juniores ceu ætate pares Timotheo, qui ætate juvenili erat, ut fratres hortari jubet, ut amica commonefactione facilius in viam officii reducantur.

Canon tertius est: Mulieres senes ut Matres admone; quo vult mulieres natu grandio- res cum reverentia compellari ut Matres, etsi ad- monitione indigeant, ne se ob senectam suam pu- tent despici.

Quartus est : Juniores ut Sorores cor- ripias, idque cum omni puritate animi, verborum & gestuum. Quod etiam ad omnia præcedentia referri potest: Ita, ut in quavis admonitione, vel correptione vitetur omnis suspicio vel austerita- tis, vel sævitiæ, vel odii, vel amoris etiam minus pu- dici. Ideoque minus commodè à Vulgata reddi- tur in omni castitate, etsi hæc omnino includatur. Quid vero hoc sibi vult? Istane Timotheo imperas? Ista sane, inquit, Chrysostomo dicente, per ipsum enim orbem alloquor universum. Sin vero ista Ti- motheo præcipit, consideret jam quisque cujusmodi debeat esse, ut scil. nullum suspicioni præbeat locum, ne umbram quidem occasionis calumniari volen- tibus det. Conferatur Ecclesiastic. XLII. vers. 13. 14. Hieronymus ad Nepot. Epistol. H. Hospitio- lum tuum aut raro, aut nunquam mulierum pedes terant. Ne sub eodem tecto mansites: nec in præteri- ta castitate confidas. Nec sanctior David, nec Sam- sone fortior, nec Salomone potes esse sapientior. Ca- veto omnes suspiciones, & quicquid probabiliter fingi potest, ne fingatur ante devita.

PARS II. De Viduis Ecclesiæ.

## 5:3
Verse 3. Honor widows) And here the name of widows is general, and does not signify a function, but lost marriage. 'Honor' here is, give sustenance from the Church's largesse, namely so that they may serve the Church, which he says below 'to be enrolled,' that is, to be inscribed in the white list or register. Compare what is below at 17. They say the Hebrews include the precept of feeding in the precept of honoring parents. See what is at Matthew 15:4. Jerome to Gerontius: Honor is taken either for alms or for a gift. See 2 Maccabees 8:28 & 30.

The widows indeed) Destitute of all help. There is also here a 'ploke' (interweaving), a figure familiar to Paul. Thus in Sophocles 'widowed of a foot,' that is, solitary, as the Scholiast explains. And to be a widow is to be desolate, orphaned. Thus in Plautus: 'widowhood of all resources, and of wealth, of help, of protection holds us.' For which Cato said 'viduertatem' (widowhood) in his 'De Re Rustica.' Thus also a widowed tree, a widowed bed, widowed nights, a widowed Apollo with his quiver among the poets. And so shortly, for the sake of explanation, he will add 'left alone'.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Χήρας τίμα) Et hic χηρῶν nomen est generale, neque functionem significat, sed amissas nuptias. Τίμα hic est, da de Ecclesiæ largitionibus alimenta, nempe ut Ecclesiæ inserviant, quod infra dicit καταλέγεσθαι, inscri- batur albo, sive matriculæ. Confer, quæ infra 17. Alendi præceptum includi in præcepto honorandi Parentes ajunt Heb . Vide, quæ ad Matth. XV. 4. Hieronymus ad Ge- rontium: Honor vel pro eleemosyna, vel pro munere accipitur. Vide 2. Macc. IIX. 28. & 30.

Τὰς ὄντως χήρας) Ab omni auxilio destitutas. Est & hic πλοκὴ figura Paulo familiaris. Sic Sophocli χηρεύων μο- λόποδι, id est, μονάζων, ut explicat Scholiastes. Et χηρεῦ- est desolare, ὀρφάνευον. Sic apud Plautum: omnium copia- rum, atq; opum, auxilii, præsidii, viduitas nos tenet. Pro quo viduertatem dixit in Re Rustica Cato. Sic & arbor vi- dua, viduus lectus, viduæ noctes, viduus Pharetra Apol- lo apud Poetas. Itaque mox explicationis causa addet μεμονωμένη.

## 5:4
Verse 4. But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them learn first to show piety to their own house) They were chosen for the order of 'presbytides' (elder women), who were the instructors of women, sometimes also mothers and educators of children, as Tertullian teaches us in 'On the Veiling of Virgins'; but rarely such, and where others were lacking. Why not also mothers of families? Because they had at home what they should do. Why not virgins? Because since they do not have the experience of marriage from childbirth, they are less able to help others with counsel and comfort. Thus Tertullian in the cited book: 'children or grandchildren' (Hebrew: 'nin ve-neched') 'to show piety' here is in the manner of Jews speaking Greek for the Hiphil, that is, to make pious. And here we have what is often elsewhere in collective nouns, a transition from the singular to the plural. Elsewhere the opposite.

And to render returns to their ancestors) Wisely said. Thus Valerius Maximus: Parents, by feeding us, have bound us to the debt of feeding our grandchildren. 'To render returns' is 'to render a reward' to ancestors (Psalm 68:7).

For this is good and acceptable before God) Thus also above 2:3.

In another place he gives instructions concerning widows, who are to be supported according to the circumstances of that time from the common treasury of the Church, or to be chosen for sacred ministries. He prescribes certain Canons: The first is: Widows are to be honored; by which he requires that they be treated with both the veneration due to them and the necessary beneficence. For there is no reason why honor should be restricted to sustenance alone. Nor does Jerome exclude honor in Matt. XV. But he desires it to be joined with alms. Honor, he says, in the Scriptures is understood not so much in greetings and services rendered, as in alms and the offering of gifts: Honor, says the Apostle, widows who are truly widows, here a gift (especially, that is) is understood. That Chrysostom, however, understands by honor only the necessary provision of things (which Crocius claims) does not appear. For because, he says, they do not have husbands, it seems to many to be a reproach, and therefore he orders that she be honored by the Priest with greater zeal, and not only for that reason, but also because she is worthy. The Apostle, however, adds a limitation: But if they are truly widows: that is, if they have lived chastely in widowhood, and furthermore are worthy of compassion, truly bereaved, and destitute of help. He therefore makes a distinction between true widows, ὄντως χήρας, which we have already mentioned, and false ones, who abuse widowhood for the license of the flesh, which marriage used to prohibit. He designates the former again as twofold, for some are indeed bereaved of husbands, but not of children; some are entirely bereaved of children and husbands. The second Canon therefore concerns the former: Let widows instruct their children and grandchildren in piety, let them learn to manage their own household piously, and to repay their elders in turn. The Church, he says, with Theodoret as interpreter, ought to provide support for those who have no help or comfort from elsewhere, and they, because they are freed from cares, are perpetually occupied in divine prayers. But those who have children or grandchildren ought to be concerned about them, and just as their parents took care of them, they too should take care of them, so that they may repay the remuneration that is owed to them, and receive mutual help from them as well. Chrysostom explained it thus: They educated you, and brought you to maturity, and treated you with great honor. They have departed from life, and you could not return the favor to them: for you did not yourself give birth to them in turn: nor did you nourish them: show this at least to your grandchildren, and return the favor. Theophylact, however, here departs from Chrysostom, beside the point and contrary to custom, in a different direction: as if it were not the duty of widows toward their own that is being described, but that of children toward their mothers and grandmothers: Let them learn, therefore, he says, as much children as grandchildren to show honor to their mothers, and to provide food for them and do them good: B. Hunnius agrees with this same explanation, which also pleased Ambrosiaster and Grotius here: Beza, Danaeus, Tossanus, and Piscator follow the latter. But the Apostle is not teaching what kind of children they should have, namely, those who know how to manage a house, but how widows ought to instruct them for that purpose: and this is πρωτον, first, so that when they have performed this, if they have any left over, they may be admitted to the benefits of public alms: when they can no longer be helped by the work of their children, for whom their own family must be cared for. They ought, however, to inform them primarily of αντιπελαργίαν (filial piety): which is good, and honest, and acceptable to God, Eph. VI. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Εἰ δέ τις χήρα τέκνα ἢ ἔκγονα ἔχει, μανθανέ- τωσαν πρῶτον τὸν ἴδιον οἶκον εὐσεβεῖν) Eligebantur ad ordi- nem πρεσβυτίδων, quæ mulierum essent σωφρονίστριαι, in- terdum & matres & educatrices filiorum, ut nos Tertul- lianus docet de Virginibus velandis; sed raro tales, & ubi aliæ deerant. Cur non & Matresfamilias? quia domi ha- bebant, quod agerent. Cur non Virgines? quia cùm expe- rimenta matrimonii ex puerperio non habeant, minus pos- sunt alias consilio & solatio juvare. Ita Tertullianus dicto libro: τέκνα ἢ ἔκγονα נין ונכד εὐσεβεῖν hic est more Ju- dæorum Græca loquentium pro Hiphil, id est, εὐσεβῆ ποιεῖν הצדיק. Et hic habemus, quod alibi sæpe in collectivis no- minibus transitum à singulari ad plurale. Alibi contra.

Καὶ ἀμοιβὰς ἀποδιδόναι τοῖς προγόνοις) Sapienter dictum. Sic Valerius Maximus: Parentes, nos alendo, nepotum nu- triendorum debito alligarunt. Ἀμοιβὰς ἀποδιδόναι est גמל גמולות τοῖς προγόνοις להורים Ps. LXIIX. 7.

Τοῦτο γάρ καλὸν καὶ ἀποδεκτὸν ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ) Sic & su- pra II. 3.

Altero loco de Viduis præcipit, quæ alendæ pro ratione istius temporis ex communi Ecclesiæ æra- rio, vel deligendæ ad sacra ministeria. Certos præscribit Canones: Primus est: Viduæ honoran- dæ sunt; quo requirit, ut tum veneratione sibi de- bita tum beneficentia necessaria afficiantur. Nam cur ad alimenta solum restringatur honor, causa nulla est. Nec excludit Hieronymus honorem in Matth. XV. Sed Eleemosynis conjunctum esse cu- pit. Honor, inquit, in Scripturis non tantum in sa- lutationibus & officiis deferendis, quantum in E- leemosynis ac munerum oblatione sentitur: Honora, inquit Apostolus, viduas, quæ verè viduæ sunt, hic non donum (præcipuè sc.) intelligitur. Chrysosto- mum verò per honorem necessariam rerum procu- rationem solùm intelligere, (quod Crocius vult) non apparet. Quia enim, inquit, viros non habent, probro esse plerisque videtur, atque ideo illam à Sacer- dote jubet majori cum studio honorari, neque ob eam tantum rem, verum quia etiam digna est. Addit autem limitationem Apostolus: Sed si verè viduæ sint: h. e. in viduitate castè vixerint, adhæc com- miseratione digna, verè orbatæ, & auxilio desti- tutæ. Facit ergò discrimen inter viduas veras ὄν- τως χήρας, quas jam diximus, & fictas, quæ vidui- tate abutuntur ad licentiam carnis, quam prohi- bebat conjugium. Illas iterum duplices designat, quædam enim maritis quidem orbæ, sed non libe- ris; quædam omninò orbæ liberis & maritis. Priores ergo concernit Canon secundus: Viduæ instruant liberos & nepotes in pietate, discant propriam domum piè tractare, ac vicem repen- dere majoribus. Ecclesiasticam, inquit, Theodo- reto interprete, subventionem oportet eas consequi, quae nullum habent aliunde subsidium aut solatium, ea autem eo, quod sint a curis liberatae, in divinis precationibus perpetuo versantur. Eas autem, quae habent filios vel nepotes, oportet esse de iis sollici- tas, & quam parentes earum curam gesserunt, eas quoque illorum curam gerere, ut qua illis debetur rependant remunerationem, ab eis quoque mutuum auxilium recipiant. Sic etiam exposuit Chryso- stomus : Educarunt te illi, atque ad incrementa perduxerunt, magnoque honore prosecuti sunt. Mi- grarunt illi ex vita, nec vicem eis reddere potuisti: non enim & ipsa illos vicissim genuisti: neque enu- tristi: hoc saltem nepotibus exhibe, vicesque redde. Theophylactus vero hic a Chrysostomo praeter rem & morem in diversum abit: quasi non officium viduarum erga suos, sed liberorum erga matres & avias describatur: Ediscant igitur, inquit, tam filii quam nepotes eorum matribus honorem defer- re, hisque & alimenta praebere & benefacere: Ex- plicationi eidem, quae etiam Ambrosiantro & Gro- tio hic placuit, accedit B. Hunnius: posteriorem sequitur Beza, Danaeus, Tossanus, Piscator. At non quales habere liberos, qui scilicet regere do- mum norint, sed quomodo eos ad id instruere de- beant viduae, docet Apostolus: idque πρωτον, primum, ut quum hoc praestiterint, si superent, admitti ad beneficia eleemosynarum publicarum possint: cum liberorum opera amplius juvari non poterunt, quibus propria curanda familia. Informare autem eosdem imprimis ad αντιπε- λαργίαν debent: quae bona, atque honesta, & Deo accepta est, Eph. VI. 2.

## 5:5
Ver. 5.

But she who is truly a widow and left alone) A more obscure word is explained by a clearer one. See what was said above at 3. Thus גלמוד is translated by certain Greek interpreters as μεμονωμενη (left alone) in Job III. ver. 7. But גלמודה is a widow in Is. XLIX. ver. 21. Philo says in his work On Monarchy at the end, 'destitute of husband and children.' Psalm LXIIX. v. 7. יחידים (solitary ones) are μονοτροπες (living alone), which means the same as μεμονωμενος (left alone). The same sense is in רוקם (empty) in Ruth I. v. 21, which the LXX translate as κενην (empty), and in שכולה (bereaved) in Is. XLIX. 21. As much as the Greeks use χηρειν (to be a widow), the Latins use viduare (to bereave) and desolare (to make desolate), to be alone.

She has hoped in God and continues in supplications night and day) That is, hoping in God she continues, etc. A double Hebraism: for the past tense is used for the present, as in Matt. III. v. 2, and the verb with a conjunction takes the place of a participle. The sense, however, is: because she has no human helpers, and among them she is אלמונה (a widow), that is, mute, therefore she has her refuge in GOD alone, she looks only to Him, as Anna the daughter of Phanuel, Luke II. 36, night and day, that is, as assiduously as possible. See the same passage in Luke and 1 Thess. II. v. 9, III. 10, 2 Thess. III. 8, 2 Tim. I. 3, and so also Rev. IV. ver. 8 and other places in that book. Προσμενειν (to continue) here is the same as προσκαρτερειν (to persevere) in Acts I. ver. 14.

But they are called alone, not precisely those who are ατεκνοι (childless), but those who are solitary and desolate, deprived of all help from both husband and family, to whom the third Canon refers; Let a widow comfort her bereavement with prayers and piety toward GOD: By which at the same time the marks of a true widow are exhibited. Under the word hope, faith is simultaneously included, without which there is no solid hope. He preferred, however, to name hope, because he is dealing with afflicted persons, whom hope strengthens, lest they distrust GOD when things have collapsed. Furthermore, the exercise of a true widow is added, by which she declares her hope placed in GOD alone and her piety, namely, supplications and prayers, with a continuous προσμονη (perseverance) in them, night and day; so that, having set aside other cares, she may give herself entirely to prayers, both those by which she may pray against public and private evils, and those by which she may entreat for necessary goods. Jerome, in his Epistle to Ageruchia, describes true widows from this passage thus: Those who are destitute of all help from their own, who cannot work with their hands, whom poverty weakens and age consumes: for whom God is their hope, and their whole work is prayer. By which, however, he does not approve of the superstition of the Euchites and Psallians, nor that of the nuns, which is similar to them, in perpetual prayers or those restricted to Canonical hours. Compare what was said at 1 Thess. V. v. 16, 17. Anna is said to have served GOD with fastings and prayers night and day, Luke II. v. 37: Must we believe that she fasted perpetually, i.e., that she abstained from all food? Scripture knows of no other fasting.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Η δε οντως χηρα και μεμονωμενη) Vox obscurior per clariorem explicatur. Vide, quae supra 3. sic גלמוד Grae- cis quibusdam interpretibus μεμονωμενη Job. III. vers. 7. At גלמודה χηρα Es. XLIX. vers. 21. ανδρος και παιδων ερημ@ ait Philo περι μοναρχιας in fine. Psalm. LXIIX. v. 7. יחידים μονοτροπες, idem valet, quod μεμονωμενος. Idem sensus in רוקם Ruth. I. v. 21. quod κενην vertunt LXX. & in שכולה Es. XLIX. 21. Tam Graecis χηρειν quam Latinis viduare quam desolare, μονων.

Ηλπικεν επι τον Θεον και προσμενη ταις δεησεσι νυκτος και ημερας) Id est, ελπιζουσα εις τον Θεον προσμενη &c. Du- plex Hebraismus: nam & praeteritum est pro praesenti, ut Matth. III. v. 2. & verbum cum copula vice participii. Sensus vero : quia homines opitulatores non habet, & apud eos est אלמונה, id est, muta, ideo in uno DEO perfugium habet, illum solum respicit, ut Anna Phanue- lis, Luc. II. 36. noctu diuque, id est, tam assidue, quam fieri potest. Vide eundem Lucae locum & 1. Thessal. II. v. 9. III. 10. 2. Thessal. III. 8. 2. Tim. I. 3. sic & Apoc. IV. vers 8. & aliis ejus libri locis. Προσμενειν hic quod προσ- καρτερειν Actor. I. vers. 14.

Solae autem dicuntur, non praecise, quae ατε- κνοι, sed quae sunt solitariae ac desolatae omni tum viri, tum familiae subsidio privatae, ad quas spe- ctat tertius Canon; Vidua orbitatem suam preci- bus & pietate in DEUM soletur: Quo simul γνωρισματα verae viduae exhibentur. Sub spei vo- cabulo fides simul comprehenditur, sine qua nul- la est spes solida. Maluit autem spem nominare, quia de afflictis personis agit, quas spes corro- borat, ne rebus accisis DEO diffidant. Addi- tur autem exercitium verae viduae, quo spem in solo DEO collocatam & pietatem suam decla- rat, supplicationes & orationes, cum προσμονη in iisdem continua, nocte atque die; ut nempe aliis curis sepositis, totam se det orationibus, tum qui- bus mala publica & privata deprecetur, tum quibus bona necessaria exoret. Hieronymus E- pift. ad Ageruchiam ex hoc loco vere viduas ita describit: Quæ omni suorum auxilio destitutæ sunt, quæ manibus suis laborare non possunt, quas paupertas debilitat, ætasque conficit : quibus Deus spes est, & omne opus oratio. Quo tamen nec Evchetarum, & Psallianorum, nec monialium illis geminam superstitionem in perpetuis, aut ad Canonicas horas adstrictis precibus approbat. Conf. quæ ad 1. Thessal. V. v. 16. 17. Luc. II. v. 37. Hanna noctes & dies jejuniis & precibus DEO serviisse dicitur: Num credenda perpetuò jeju- nasse, h. e. ab omni cibo abstinuisse? Aliud jeju- nium ignorat Scriptura.

## 5:6
Ver. 6.

But she who lives in pleasure) We have the same word in James V. ver. 5. In the Glossary, σπατάλη is wantonness, delights. Σπαταλῶ means I live in pleasure. You have that word in Greek in Ezek. XVI. ver. 48 and Sirach XXI. ver. 17. In the same sense it is said עֲדִינָה (delicate) or τρυφερά (luxurious). He understands her who remains a widow for this reason, that, being freed from the authority of a husband, she may more freely do what she pleases.

Living she is dead) Excellently said. Seneca on the tranquility of the mind: Curius Dentatus used to say that he would rather be dead than not live; it is the ultimate of evils to depart from the number of the living before you die. The same in Epistle XCIII: he perished before death. See what we said at Matt. IIX. 22, Eph. II. 11. He lives truly who lives for GOD. He who is without hope of eternal life has already perished.

A true widow, as B. Hunnius advises, described only in her bereavement and in the pursuits and exercises of piety, now opposes impious, forward widows, steeped in lusts: who, after they have been released from the halter of matrimony, live according to their own pleasure and surrender themselves entirely to the pleasures of the flesh, whom (although they seem to themselves to live beautifully) he nevertheless says are dead while living, cut off, indeed, from the life which is from GOD, and devoid of His eternal life of the elect. The fourth Canon, therefore, is: A wanton widow is to be held as dead. She who is in delights, that is, not only has the goods of fortune, but also abuses the same for luxury, this one is dead while living: that is, she lives for her belly, dead to the remaining senses, or rather the flesh lives in her, the Spirit is extinguished. For immoderate delights, as Theodoret says, overwhelm reason and cause it to lie in the body as if in some sepulcher. The life of your flesh, says Augustine in Tractate XLIII on John, is your soul: the life of your soul is your God: just as the flesh dies when the soul is lost, because it is its life, so the soul dies when God is lost, because He is its life.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Ἡ δὲ σπαταλῶσα) Idem verbum habemus Jacob. V. vers. 5. In Glossario, σπατάλη lascivia, delitiæ. Σπατα- λῶ delicias ago. Habes eam vocem in Græco Ezech. XVI. vers. 48. & Sirach. XXI. vers. 17. Eodem sensu dici- tur עֲדִינָה τρυφερά. Intelligit eam, quæ ideo vidua ma- net, ut à mariti imperio soluta liberius faciat, quæ lubet.

Ζῶσα τέθνηκε) Egregie dictum. Seneca de tranquil- litate animi: Curius dentatus dicebat, malle se esse mor- tuum, quam non vivere; ultimum malorum est, ex vivorum numero exire, antequam moriaris. Idem epistola XCIII. ante mortem periit. Vide, quæ diximus ad Matth. IIX. 22. Eph. II. 11. Vivit verè, qui DEO vivit. Qui sine spe est vitæ æternæ, jam nunc periit.

Vidua vera, B. Hunnio monente, modo in sua orbitate, pietatisque studiis & exercitiis descripta nunc opponit viduas impias, procaces, libidini- bus delibutas: quæ postquam matrimonii capistro solutæ sunt, pro libitu suo vivunt, & voluptati- bus carnis se totas mancipant, quas (etsi pulchre sibi vivere videntur) tamen corporaliter viven- tes ait esse mortuas, abscissas, quippe à vita, quæ ex DEO est, & illius sempiterna vita electorum exortes. Quartus ergo Canon est: Vidua lasci- va habeatur pro mortua. Quæ in delitiis est, hoc est, non tantum habet bona fortunæ, sed & abutitur iisdem ad luxuriam, hæc vivens mor- tua est: id est, ventri vivit, reliquis sensibus mortua, vel potius caro in ea vivit, Spiritus ex- tinctus est. Immodicæ enim deliciæ, Theodoreto di- cente, rationem obruunt & efficiunt, ut in corpore tanquam in aliquo sepulchro jaceat. Vita carnis tuæ, inquit Augustinus tr. XLIII. in Joh. anima tua: Vita animæ tuæ Deus tuus est: quomodo mori- tur caro amissa anima, quia vita est ejus, sic ani- ma amisso Deo, quia vita est ejus.

## 5:7
Ver. 7. Καὶ ταῦτα παράγγελλε, ἵνα ἀνεπίληπτοι ὦσι)

Admonish, moreover, both men and women, that they give no occasion for a bad name regarding themselves. We had the word ἀνεπίληπτος also above at III. 2. He will now unfold the general word through species.

B. Balduinus fixes the fifth Canon here: A widow should be irreproachable. Not undeservedly. For that the Apostle is pursuing the subject of widows is evident from verse 9, even though these Canons can also be adapted to men, and indeed to virgins and adolescents, comprehended in the sixth and seventh verses. For that is especially the duty of widows, who can easily be tempted on account of their solitude, and upon whom the eyes of others are fixed, so that they do not commit what is worthy of reproach. Widows are often accustomed to be oppressed by others: let them take care, therefore, that they do not bring that upon themselves by their own fault. GOD takes care of widows in a peculiar way: let them therefore conduct themselves so that they do not offend this Patron, and lose their provider. Thus also Blessed Hunnius: Because such voluptuous widows are never not found: diligently inculcate what is becoming for widows, and what judgment is to be expected by those who serve the pleasures of the flesh: teach and command that they be irreproachable, lest they contaminate their reputation by the wickedness of their life, and Evangelical doctrine, says that they might disgrace the profession of evangelical doctrine. Therefore, those things [illa] and these things [ταῦτα] are to be understood cumulatively; command ALSO THESE, namely, besides those things about which it has already been commanded.…

Latin:

Vers. 7. Καὶ ταῦτα παράγγελλε, ἵνα ἀνεπίληπτοι ὦσι)

Mone præterea tum viros, tum fœminas, ne ullam dent mali nominis de se occasionem. Vocem ἀνεπίληπτος habui- mus & supra III. 2. Vocem generalem jam per species evolvet.

Quintum hic Canonem figit B. Balduinus: Vi- dua sit irreprehensibilis. Non immerito. Nam per- sequi Apostolum materiam de viduis è vers. 9. pa- tet, etsi hi Canones adaptari etiam viris possint, imò & virginibus & adolescentibus, sexto nempe & septimo versu comprehensi. Nam id impri- mis viduarum est, quæ tentari facile ob solitudi- nem possunt, & in quas aliorum oculi defixi sunt, ut non committant, quod reprehensione di- gnum sit. Opprimi alias sæpè solent viduæ: caveant ergo, ne id jumento suo sibi accersant. Curam viduarum peculiariter DEUS gerit: ita ergo se gerant, ut ne hunc Patronum offen- dant, nutritium amittant. Sic & Beat. Hun- nius: Quia nunquam non reperiuntur ejusmo- di voluptuosæ viduæ: tu quid deceat viduas, & quod judicium sit expectandum iis, quæ volu- ptatibus carnis deserviunt, diligenter inculca: doce & præcipe, ut sint irreprehensibiles, ne vita improbitate famam suam contaminent, & Evangelicæ doctrinæ professionem dehonestent. Illa ergò ὴ ταῦτα cumulativè intelligenda, ETIAM HÆC præcipe, scil. præter illa, de quibus præ- cipiendis jam dictum.

## 5:8
Ver. 8.

If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. This is a sentiment pertaining to both sexes, and its meaning is the same as that in Ecclesiasticus 56:7. He gravely accuses both rich men and women who allowed those whom they themselves ought to have supported to be a burden to the Church, that is, those joined by blood, who are ἴδιοι [your flesh], and especially parents, who are also οἰκεῖοι [household members], Ecclesiasticus 4:5. Προνοεῖν means to take care, namely, that they have the means to live: which the Latins also call 'prospicere' (to provide for). But what he says, 'he has denied the faith,' is to be understood as such a man destroying by his deeds the Christianity which he professes. Thus also 2 Tim. 3:5, Tit. 1:16; just as one is said to 'choose' [ἐκλογεῖν] who does good, so one is said to 'deny' [ἀρνεῖσθαι] who neglects, by a translation taken from words to deeds. But he is worse than an infidel, because although he knows the will of God more accurately, he nevertheless does not accommodate himself to it. See Luke 2:48 and what is said there.

That these things were said specifically about widows, a comparison of verse 4 with the continuation of the same subject matter in the following verses teaches; therefore, it is permitted to establish the sixth canon: Widows who do not provide for their own, if they are able, are to be held as infidels. Thus Theophylact with Chrysostom: She, he says, who lives in pleasures is dead, and has utterly perished, who cares for nothing else but herself, when all household members, that is, the faithful, ought to be cared for, and especially here, those who are nearest to us by birth and joined by consanguinity. But B. Hunnius wishes to censure those who neglect to provide that duty of nourishment to mothers or grandmothers, now widows, worn out by old age and weary with years. The matter for the Apostle, says Crocius, is with children and relatives who foisted widows to be supported by the Church, whom they themselves could conveniently support; he urges them with a general sentiment which concerns both superiors and inferiors. He is said to have denied the faith not by words, but by deeds, because his works, as Theophylact says, are by no means those of one believing in God: worse than an infidel, because by the same author, he who lacks faith, even if he despises strangers, yet does not spurn his own, obeying nature. But this man is most opposed to the law, both human and divine. Therefore, the Gentiles are healthier, who, led by the law of nature, cherish their own and provide for them. Therefore, those who do not do this from among Christians are worse than them. Furthermore, from the fact that such a one is said to deny the faith and become worse than an infidel, it is clear that faith is lost through mortal sin. Estius and the Council of Trent indeed deny this. But how can he have faith who is worse than an infidel? Where there is no charity, there is no faith. In such a case, for those who do not have care for their own, there is no charity, Gal. 5:6.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Εἰ δέ τις τῶν ἰδίων, καὶ μάλιςα τῶν οἰκείων ὀ προνοεῖ, τὴν πίσιν ἤρνηται, κὶ ἔσιν ἀπίσυ χείρων) Sententia est ad utrum- que sexum pertinens, & sensus ejusdem, cujus illud EC LVI. vers. 7. Graviter accusat & viros & mulieres divi- tes, qui sinebant Ecclesiæ oneri esse eos, quos ipsi alere debebant, id est, junctos sanguine, qui sunt ἴδιοι בשרך ac præcipue parentes, qui οἰκεῖοι etiam EC. IV. 5. Προνοεῖν est curam gerere, nempe ut habeant, unde vivant: quod & Latini dicunt prospicere. Quod autem ait, τὴν πίσιν ἤρνηται, intelligendum est talem hominem factis destrue- re Christianismum, quem profitetur. Sic & 2. Tim. III. 5. Tit. I. 16. sicut ἐκλογεῖν dicitur, qui benefacit, ita ἀρνεῖ- σθαι, qui contemnit, à verbis ad facta ducta translatione. Pejor autem infideli est, quia cum exactius norit volun- tatem Dei, ei tamen se non accommodat. Vide Luc. II. v. 48. & ibi dicta.

De viduis hæc specialiter dicta, collatio v. 4. cum continuatione materiæ ejusdem in sequen- tibus docet; ideo canonem sextum constituere licet : Viduæ, quæ non prospiciunt suis, si possint, habeantur pro infidelibus. Ita cum Chrysostomo Theophylactus: Ea, inquit, quæ in deliciis diver- satur, mortua est, & planè interiit, quæ præter seipsam nihil aliud curat, cum & domestici omnes, hoc est, fideles curandi sint, & hic præcipuè, qui ge- nere nobis proximi sunt, & consanguinitate conjun- cti. B. Hunnius verò eos perstringi vult, qui ma- tribus aut aviis, jam viduis, senio confectis, & ætate fessis illud nutricationis officium præstare negligunt. Res Apostolo, inquit Crocius, cum fi- liis & cognatis, qui viduas obtrudebant alendas Ecclesiæ, quas ipsi commode poterant alere; illos urget sententia generali, quæ concernit tam supe- riores, quàm inferiores. Fidem abnegâsse dicitur non verbis, sed factis, quia ejus opera, dicente Theophylacto, nequaquam sunt in Deum creden- tis : Infideli deteriores, quia eodem autore, qui fide caret, etsi alienos contemnit, suos tamen, natu- ræ obediens, non adspernatur. Hic vero legi ut hu- manæ, ita & divinæ maximè adversatur. Gentes ergo saniores ductu legis naturæ suos fovent, iis- que prospiciunt. Illis ergo deteriores sunt, qui è Christianis id non faciunt. Porro ex eo, quod talis fidem negare, ac infideli parte pejor fieri dicatur, patet fidem per mortale peccatum amit- ti. Negat id quidem Estius & Conc. Trid. Sed quomodo fidem habere potest, qui infideli dete- rior? ubi non est charitas, ibi non est fides. In tali causa, qui suorum curam non habent, cha- ritas non est, Gal. V. 6.

## 5:9
Ver. 9.

Let a widow be enrolled [Χήρα καταλεγέσθω]. Let her be admitted to the order of the presbyteresses, who lived from the offerings of the faithful no less than the presbyters. Tertullian says this about placing them in the order of widows in his book 'On the Veiling of Virgins': to enroll a widow in the order, in his first book 'To His Wife': the Greek Fathers say 'to appoint to the clerical order' [τάσσειν εἰς τὸ χηρικόν] or 'to the register' [εἰς τὸν κατάλογον]. Hermas also mentions such widows, and names one of them Grapta.

Not less than sixty years old [Μὴ ἔλαττον ἐτῶν ἑξήκοντα]. Tertullian teaches us that this was observed in his own times in the aforementioned book 'On the Veiling of Virgins'.

Having been the wife of one man [Γεγονυῖα ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς γυνὴ]. The meaning is clear, about which we already began to say something above at 3:2. Christians ought not to yield to the Gentiles in any part of praise. Pausanias in his 'Achaica': 'A woman receiving the priesthood from then on remains chaste, if she has not arrived at the flower of age having been with more than one man.' Minutius: 'The univira (one-husband woman) crowns the sacred rites of Asia.' Opposed to this is the old woman of many marriages. Epist. ad Atticum 13.29. Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 13. Those who had been content with one marriage were honored with a crown of modesty. For they thought that a matron should have a mind of sincere faith, by which she would not know how to leave the chaste bed of her surrendered virginity: believing the experience of many marriages to be, as it were, a legitimate sign of a certain intemperance. Which meaning Athenagoras expressed a little more harshly: 'A second marriage is a specious adultery.' Tertullian to his wife: There is a priesthood of widowhood and celibacy among the Nations. The same author in 'On Exhortation to Chastity': Finally, Monogamy is in such high honor among the heathens that even for virgins marrying legitimately, a univira is employed as a bridesmaid: and if it is for the sake of omens, it is certainly a good omen. Likewise, that in certain solemn duties the place of the univira is first. Certainly, the Flaminica is only a univira. The same in 'On Monogamy': Certainly, both monogamy and widowhood appear to the idols. It does not impose a crown on 'Fortuna Muliebris' (Womanly Fortune) unless she is a univira: just as neither to 'Mater Matuta'. Festus also said concerning 'Fortuna Muliebris' that it is a sacrilege for it to be touched except by her who has married once. And among Propertius it is: 'On this stone I shall be read to have been married to one.' Likewise: 'See that you hold to one, imitate us, a husband.' See Canon 18 of Basil to Amphilochius.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Χήρα καταλεγέσθω ) Admittatur ad ordinem τῶν πρεσ- βυτίδων, quæ de fidelium oblationibus non minus, quam presbyteri vivebant. Hoc Tertullianus dicit in viduata collocare, libro de Virginibus velandis: Viduam allege- re in ordinem, libro ad uxorem priore : τάσσειν εἰς τὸ χη- ρικὸν vel εἰς τὸν κατάλογον Græci Patres. Talium vi- duarum meminit & Hermas, & unam earum Graptam nominat.

Μὴ ἔλαττον ἐτῶν ἑξήκοντα) Id ad sua tempora obser- vatum docet nos Tertullianus, dicto libro de Virgini- bus velandis.

Γεγονυῖα ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς γυνὴ) Sensus apertus est, de quo jam aliquid dicere cœpimus supra III. 2. Non debebant Christiani in ulla laudis parte cedere Gentibus. Pausa- nias Achaicis : Γυνὴ δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν ἱερωσύνην λαμβάνουσα ἀγί- σεύῃ μὲν ἀπὸ τότε, εἰ μὴ δὲ πρὸ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἐπὶ πλέον ἢ ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς εἰς πῶραν ἀφιγμένη. Minutius : Asiæ sacra coronat univira. Huic opponitur vetula multarum nuptiarum. Epist. ad Atticum XIII. 29. Valerius Maximus lib. II. cap. 13. Quæ uno contenta matrimonio fuerant, corona pu- dicitia honorabantur. Existimabant enim cum præcipuè ma- trona sincera fide esse animum, quo depositæ virginitatis cubile pudicum egredi nesciret : multorum matrimoniorum experien- tiam, quasi legitima cujusdam intemperantiæ signum esse cre- dentes. Quem sensum paulo durius extulit Athenagoras : ὁ δεύτερος γάμος εὐπρεπὴς μοιχεία. Tertullianus ad uxorem: Sacerdotium viduitatis & cælibatum est apud Na- tiones. Idem de exhortatione castitatis : Denique Mono- gamia apud Ethnicos ita in summo honore est, ut & virginibus legitime nubentibus univira pronuba to adhibeatur: & si au- spiciis causa, utique boni auspicii est. Item ut in quibusdam solemnibus officiis prior sit univira locus. Certè Flaminica non nisi univira est. Idem de Monogamia : Idolis certè & monogamia & viduitas apparent. Fortunæ muliebri coronam non imponit, nisi univira: sicut nec Matri Matutæ. De for- tuna muliebri, nefas eam attingi, nisi ab ea, quæ semel nu- psit, dixit & Festus. Et apud Propertium est : In lapide hoc uni nupta fuisse, legar. Item : Fac teneas unum, nos imitare, virum. Vide Canonem XVIII. Basilii ad Amphilochium.

## 5:10
Verse 10.

Ἐν ἔργοις καλοῖς μαρτυρουμένη) That is, having a good testimony, as he was speaking above in III. 17. Which the fame of good works accompanies.

Εἰ ἐτεκνοτρόφησεν) If she has neither caused an abortion for herself, nor exposed her children because of poverty, as was accustomed to be done among the Gentiles, but has raised all born to her, and indeed honestly and piously. See above III. 3.

Εἰ ἐξενοδόχησεν) If she has received the pious into hospitality, as Lydia did in XVI. 15. Euripides also uses the word ξενοδοχεῖν. Xenophon uses the noun ξενοδοχίας. The Rabbis say this with a word which is corrupted from the Latin, אושפיזינך.

Εἰ ἁγίων πόδας ἔνιψεν) Proverbial: that is, if she has lowered herself even to the lowest ministries, so that she might relieve holy men. There is no need here to repeat what we said at John III. verse 5. Tertullian, in his letter to his wife, places among the duties of Christian women the offering of water to the feet of the saints.

Εἰ θλιβομένοις ἐπήρκεσεν) The Rabbis would say רפס. Thus Euripides said Φίλοις ἐπαρκεῖν without an accusative case. See also in the following. You have this verb with an accusative in Maccab. VIII. 26, XI. 35. Women were accustomed to send small gifts to those who were in chains because of their piety.

Εἰ παντὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ ἐπηκολούθησε) ἐπακολυθεῖν is what the Hebrews call הלך or מלא סדוא אחרי. If she has followed after, pursued, all occasions of good work, as Jerome cites elsewhere.

The Seventh Canon holds thus: A widow is not to be chosen for the ministries of the saints, or to be fed at the expense of the Church, unless she is approved by certain years of age and life. Compare Acts VI. and IX. verse 37, 51, where the observation of the blessed Hunnius must be held: That in the primitive Church, selected widows sustained certain offices, such as (as far as can be gathered from the circumstances) ministering to the sick in Xenodochia, and that the instruction of young girls in the first beginnings and rudiments of Christian doctrine was committed to them, especially since the Apostle otherwise warns in Tit. II. that older women should teach what is honest, so that they might render young women honest. And thus some part of both instruction and discipline was entrusted to them: and there were undoubtedly, according to the custom of those times, certain other things, in the carrying out of which they could provide service to the pastors of their churches. To which the blessed Hunnius refers the διακονίαν of Phoebe, Rom. XVI. See. concerning such Deaconesses, Epiph. haer. LXXVI. As to age, that she be of sixty years. Where, however, the blessed Balduinus rightly observed that a certain number seems to be put for an uncertain one, because such a widow is understood who is no longer fit for the labors by which anyone can provide food for themselves; whence Jerome, epistle 9 to Salvinia: He wishes those to be sustained by the resources of the Church who cannot labor with their own hands, who are truly widows, whom both age and life approve. Similar is that which, as Jerome observes in the same place in the Hebrew Traditions in the book of Chronicles, from the sixtieth year both Levites were to minister and a soldier was to fight they defined it, as if that age seems more suited to rest than to labor.

Regarding a proven life (1) That she has had one husband, not more at the same time. It can happen in many ways that a woman is not the wife of one man. First, when she departs from her husband, either willingly or unwillingly, and marries another. Second, when, having been repudiated by her husband, she contracts with another while the former is still alive. Third, if, while the marriage stands, she has relations with another. Fourth, if she openly acknowledges several husbands at the same time. Whoever is such, the Apostle excludes her. Crotius is more correct than Grotius. For it is not to be understood as having been married only once. The sense is entirely the same as in chapter III, verse 2, concerning the Bishop, that he must be a man of one wife. There is no praise in it that she did not enter into another marriage after the first, just as there is no disgrace if she lived successively in different marriages. The laws of the nations are not to be heard here against the judgment of God: It is not good for man to be alone, Gen. II, and because of fornication let each one have his own wife, 1. Cor. VII. verse 2. Therefore Chrysostom calls those heretics who condemn second marriages. August. de fide ad Petr. cap. III. Because a sick person must always be trusted, therefore if it happens that he is deprived of his first marriage, if he wishes to enter into second or third marriages, he will have no sin from them, if he has kept them chastely. Jerome, Epist. XI to Gerantia, although more severe toward repeated marriages, nevertheless comes to the aid of such incontinent histories: namely, that he saw at Rome two pairs of spouses, one who had buried twenty wives, the other who had had a twenty-second husband. And it is clear from the Julian and Papian law that, just as rewards were set before marriages, so heavy penalties were established at Rome for the unmarried, the childless, and widows: whence the 'vidurium' and 'uxorium' money, those fines which men paid for those reasons, in Scipio Gentilis, tract. de secund. nupt. cap. I. If any things contrary to these were sanctioned by Christians, that must be attributed to the kingdom of the Anti-Christ. But how would the Apostle have excluded the 'digamos' here, when he orders younger widows to marry, whom, at any rate, once they had become widows again, he would have most excluded from the benefits of the Jews. Therefore Theodoret: Hence it is also manifest that he does not reject second marriages, but decrees that they should live chastely in marriage. Nor did he, who established the second marriage by law above, prohibit that she who has followed a second marriage should not obtain bodily support: who openly commands that we do good to all men.

(2) Who has a testimony of good works. That, indeed, can make her worthy of the College of widows, says Theophylact. He does not express whose testimony she ought to have: but without doubt he desires the testimony of both the faithful and outsiders, as in the case of Bishops, 1 Timoth. III. verse 7. Some think that good works are to be understood with Theophylact, which now follow. But it is considered more correct that the praise of moral virtues and an honest reputation are required.

(3) Who has brought up children, where Theophylact rightly says: To bring up children is not to feed children, but to instruct them, so that they may remain in faith and holiness, namely. I would think, however, that care of both body and soul is noted. He does not demand that they feed them, but also that they nourish them piously. GOD also says this about Abraham, that he commanded his children and his house after him, that they should keep all the judgments of the Lord GOD; says Theodoret. By which very thing, however, he does not exclude the sterile. For he does not say 'eteknogonesen' (she bore children), but 'eteknotrophesen' (she brought up children), so that it is clear that not sterility, but the half-hearted nullity of mothers is noted; who wish to give birth, but do not wish to carry the burden of their offspring. But why would he require this, and other things that follow further, if only food were provided by the Church to the widows, and they themselves performed no works, e.g., regarding the poor, the sick, etc. Tertullian, book de vel. virg. cap. 9. Mothers are chosen, and indeed educators of children, namely so that, built up by the experiences of all affections, they may easily know how to help others with both counsel and consolation, and so that they have nonetheless run through those things by which a woman can be proven.

(4) If she has been hospitable, not in preparing splendid banquets, but in receiving exiles with hospitality: which duty was very necessary in the primitive Church because of the abundance of exiles.

(5) Who has washed the feet of the Saints: Which is to be taken not so much proverbially as synecdochically, so that any extreme services are included. Such was the washing of feet, Gen. XIII. v. 4, c. XIX. verse 12, Luke VII. verse 44. Chrysostom notes that the washing is understood which is done by one's own hands, not that which is done by maids. Theophylact follows, whose commentary is this: He brought this in, for example, because although some admit strangers to hospitality, they nevertheless use the work of maids, not their own, in receiving them. Since, therefore, he wants the widow to be active here and exercised, not languid and soft, he orders this very one to serve the guests herself. Languor and softness itself is rather for her who lives in luxuries. Furthermore, lest anyone excuse poverty entirely for exercising this hospitality, just as if she does not have a home where she can receive guests, if she has washed the feet of the saints, he says. For such an ablution demands neither expense nor wealth. And saints are as many as have attained the right faith with works, even if they perform no miracles.

(6) If she has helped those suffering tribulation, either by intercession, or by counsel, or by subsidy. He seeks not the quantity of the supply, but the quality of the mind. Such were the two mites of the widow in the Holy Gospels, says Theodoret. (7) If she has followed every good work. He had begun from the testimony of good works. Now he ends in the pursuit of every good work, which is openly known. And he requires not only the will to do good, but also constancy in pursuing the good work: and not only in this and that, but in everything. Then we also leave room for the explanation of Jerome, namely that she has also followed and pursued all occasions for good work. Theophylact has added yet another member: If she has ministered: with this interpretation: namely, if she has spread the bed for guests for rest, and facilitated other things of that kind, for which women are more suited. But that addition is found in no place. Nor is it sufficiently agreed: for already the precision has preceded, which the Apostle broke off from the further enumeration of good works, and by the appellation of the genus he apprehended all those things which could have been piously and rightly done by such a matron.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Ἐν ἔργοις καλοῖς μαρτυρουμένη) Id est, μαρτυρίαν καλὴν ἔχουσα, quomodo supra loquebatur III. 17. Quam fama comitatur bonorum operum.

Εἰ ἐτεκνοτρόφησεν) Si nec abortum sibi fecerit, nec ob paupertatem exposuerit liberos, ut inter Gentes fieri sole- bat, sed omnes sibi natos educaverit, & quidem honestè ac piè. Vide supra III. 3.

Εἰ ἐξενοδόχησεν) Si hospitio pios excepit, ut Lydia XVI. 15. Verbum ξενοδοχεῖν usurpat & Euripides. Nomen ξε- νοδοχίας Xenophon. Rabbini id dicunt voce, quæ ex La- tino corrupta est אושפיזינך.

Εἰ ἁγίων πόδας ἔνιψεν) Proverbiale : id est, si ad infima etiam ministeria se demisit, ut viros sanctos sublevaret. Nihil opus hic repeti, quæ diximus ad Johan. III. vers. 5. Tertullianus ad uxorem inter Christianarum fœminarum officia ponit, aquam Sanctorum pedibus offerre.

Εἰ θλιβομένοις ἐπήρκεσεν) רפס dicerent Rabbini. Sic Φίλοις ἐπαρκεῖν sine casu accusativo dixit Euripides. Vi- de & in sequentibus. Cum accusativo habes hoc verbum, Maccab. VIII. 26. XI. 35. Solebant fœminæ munuscula mittere iis, qui ob pietatem in vinculis erant.

Εἰ παντὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ ἐπηκολούθησε) ἐπακολυθεῖν est quod Ebræi dicunt הלך aut מלא סדוא אחרי. Si omnes boni operis occasiones sectata est, persecuta est, ut alibi citat Hieronymus.

Septimus Canon ita habet: Vidua non nisicer- tis ætatis & vitæ annis probata, ad sanctorum mi- nisteria, vel ut Ecclesiæ sumptu alatur, deligen- da. Conf. Actor. VI. & IX. vers. 37. 51. ubi ob- servatio B. Hunnii tenenda : In primitiva Eccle- sia viduas selectas sustinuisse quædam officia, ut quod (quantum ex circumstantiis colligi potest) in Xenodochiis ministrabant ægrotis, quod commis- sa eis erat institutio puellarum in primis initiis & rudimentis doctrinæ Christianæ, præsertim cum alioquin Apostolus Tit. II. moneat, ut anus hone- sta doceant, quo possint honestas reddere adole- scentulas. Atque sic pars aliqua cum institutio- nis, tum disciplinæ fuit eis concredita : & fuerunt haud dubiè, pro ratione illorum temporum, quæ- dam alia, circa quæ expedienda potuerunt Pasto- ribus Ecclesiarum suarum navare operam. Quo refert B. Hunnius Phœbæ διακονίαν, Rom. XVI. Vid. de talibus Diaconissis Epiph. hær. LXXVI. Quoad ætatem, ut sexaginta annorum sit. Ubi tamen rectè observavit B. Balduinus, videri nu- merum certum pro incerto positum, quia talis intelligatur vidua, quæ ad labores, quibus ali- menta sibi quilibet parare potest, non amplius apta est; unde Hieronymus epist. 9. ad Salvi- nam : Illas vult Ecclesiæ opibus sustentari, quæ propriis manibus non possunt laborare, quæ ve- rè viduæ sunt, quas & ætas probat & vita. Simile est, quod observante ibidem Hieronymo in Tradit. Hebraic. in lib. Paralip. ab anno sexa- gesimo & Levitæ ministrare, & miles pugnare- definebant, quasi ea ætas quieti magis, quam la- bori apta videatur.

Quoad vitam probatam (1) Ut unum non plu- res simul habuerit maritos. Multis modis fieri potest, ut mulier non sit unius viri uxor. Primò cùm discedit à viro, vel volente, vel nolente, & al- teri nubit. Secundò cùm à viro repudiata cum alio contrahit priore superstite. Tertiò si stante matri- monio cum alio consuescat. Quartò si plures si- mul maritos palam agnoscat. Quæ talis fuerit, eam arcet Apostolus. Ut rectius Crocius, quam Grotius. Non enim semel tantùm nupta intelli- genda. Sensus omninò idem, qui cap. III. v. 2. de Episcopo, quod eligendus sit unius uxoris vir. Nulla in eo laus est, quod post primum ma- trimonium aliud non inierit, quemadmodum contra nullum dedecus, si successive in diversis vixerit matrimoniis. Gentium leges hîc non au- diendæ contra Dei sententiam: Non est bonum, hominem esse solum, Genes. II. & propter fornica- tionem unusquisque habeat suam uxorem, 1. Cor. VII. vers. 2. Ideo Chrysostomus hæreticos vocat, qui secundas nuptias damnant. August. de fide ad Petr. cap. III. Quia ægroto hinc semper est confidendum, propterea si primo contigerit privari conjugio, si voluerit secundas vel tertias inire nuptias, nullum de illis peccatum habebit, si eas castè servaverit. Hieronymus Epist. XI. ad Gerantiam etsi iniquior iteratis nuptiis, incontinentibus tamen ejusmodi historiis succurrit: quod nempe Romæ viderit duo inter se paria conjugum, unum, qui viginti sepelis- set uxores, alteram, quæ vigesimum secundum ha- buisset maritum. Et ex lege Julia & Papia con- stat, ut præmia matrimoniis præposita, ita cælibi- bus & orbis, ac viduis graves pœnas Romæ con- stitutas esse: unde vidurium & uxorium æs mul- tæ illæ, quas viri ob eas causas pendebant, apud Scipionem Gentilem tract. de secund. nupt. cap. I. Si quæ his contraria à Christianis sancita, id re- gno Anti-Christi acceptum ferendum. Quî ve- rò Apostolus διγάμως hic exclusisset, cum jubeat viduas juniores nubere, quas utique, ubi iterum viduæ factæ, à Judæorum beneficiis maximè ex- clusisset. Ideo Theodoretes: Hinc etiam manife- stum est, quod non rejicit secundas nuptias, sed decernit, ut in matrimonio castè vivant. Neque enim, qui secundum matrimonium lege superius constituit, prohibuit, ut quæ secundas sit secuta nuptias, non assequatur corporale subsidium: qui apertè præcipit, ut bonum faciamus omnibus ho- minibus.

(2) Quæ testimonium habeat bonorum ope- rum. Id sanè hanc potest viduarum Collegio di- gnam efficere, inquit Theophylactus. Non expri- mit, quorum testimonium habere debeat: sed sine dubio & fidelium & extraneorum desiderat testimonium, ut in Episcopis, 1. Timoth. III. vers. 7. Nonnulli bona opera intelligi cum Theophylacto putant, quæ jam sequuntur. Sed rectius vir- tutum moralium laus, & fama honesta requiri censetur.

(3) Quæ liberos educavit, ubi rectè Theophy- lactus: Filios educare non est filios enutrire, sed instituere, ut in fide scilicet & sanctitate perma- neant. Putarim tamen curam & corporis & ani- mi notari. Non exigit ut alant, sed etiam ut pie nutriant. Hoc etiam dicit DEUS de Abraham, quod mandavit filiis suis, & domui suæ post se, ut servarent omnia judicia Domini DEI; ait Theodoretes. Quo ipso tamen non excludit steri- les. Non enim ait, ἐτεκνογόνησε, sed ἐτεκνοτρόφησε, ut constet non sterilitatem, sed nullitatem dimi- diatam matrum; quæ parere volunt, partus cæ- rum gerere non volunt, notari. Cur autem hoc, & alia, quæ porrò sequuntur, requireret, si tan- tum victus ab Ecclesia viduis præberetur, nulla vero opera ipsæ fungerentur, v. g. quoad paupe- res, ægrotos &c. Tertullianus libr. de vel. virg. cap. 9. Eliguntur matres, & quidem educatrices filiorum, scilicet ut experimentis omnium affe- ctuum structæ facile norint cæteras & consilio & solatio juvare, & ut nihilo minus ea decucurrerint, per quæ fæmina probari potest.

(4) Si fuit hospitalis, non in apparandis splen- didis conviviis, sed excipiendis hospitio exu- libus: quod officium in Ecclesia primitiva ob exulum copiam valdè necessarium erat.

(5) Quæ Sanctorum pedes laverit: Quod non tam proverbialiter, quam synecdochicè accipiendum, ut extrema quævis ministeria comprehendan- tur. Qualis erat lotio pedum, Gen. XIII. v. 4. c. XIX. vers. 12. Luc. VII. vers. 44. Chrysostomus notat, lotionem intelligi, quæ propriis mani- bus fiat, non quæ per ancillas. Sequitur Theo- phylactus, cujus hic est commentarius: Id v. g. intulit, quia etsi alienos hospitio admittunt non- nullæ, ancillarum tamen, non sua in illis exci- piendis utuntur opera. Cum itaque viduam actuo- sam hic esse velit & exercitam, non languidiorem & mollem, hanc ipsam per se jubet hospitibus in- servire. Languorem & mollitiem ipsam, ejus est potius, quæ in deliciis agit. Quin etiam ne quis inopiam omnino excuset ad hospitalitatem hanc exercendam, perinde ac domicilium non habeat, quo hospites queat excipere, si pedes inquit sancto- rum lavit. Istiusmodi namque ablutio, nec sum- ptus deposcit, nec opes. Sancti autem sunt, quot- quot fidem sunt rectam cum operibus consecuti, etiamsi nulla edant miracula.

(6) Si patientibus tribulationem subvenit, vel intercessione, vel consilio, vel subsidio. Non quantitatem suppeditationis, sed mentis quæ- rit qualitatem. Talia erant in Sacris Evange- liis viduæ duo minuta, ait Theodoretus. (7) Si omne opus bonum sectata est. A testimonio bonorum operum cœperat. Jam finit in studio omnis bo- ni operis, quod palam notum sit. Nec volun- tatem tantum benè operandi, sed constantiam etiam in persequendo bono opere: nec in hoc & illo tantum, sed in omni requirit. Deinde etiam locum relinquimus explicationi Hiero- nymi, nempe omnes boni operis occasiones etiam sectata sit & persecuta. Theophylactus ad- huc aliud membrum adjecit: Si subministravit: cum hoc interpretamento: scil. si lectum stravit hospitibus ad quietem, & alia ejusmodi facilitavit, quibus fœminæ sunt accommodatiores. Sed il- la προσθήκη in nullo loco reperitur. Nec satis convenit: jam enim præcessit præcisio, quam enumerationem bonorum operum ulteriorem abrupit Apostolus, & generis appellatione ap- prehendit ea omnia, quæ à tali matrona piè re- cteque potuerunt fieri.

## 5:11
Vers. 11.

Νεωτέρας δὲ χήρας παραιτũ) Younger than sixty. Παραιτũ, that is, do not admit to that order of presiding women. In the Glossary: παραιτẽμαι I refuse. Plutarch and others use it thus.

Ὅταν γὰρ κατασρηνιάσωσι τẽ χριςẽ γαμẽιν θέλουσιν) That is, ὅταν σρηνιάσωσι κατὰ τẽ χριςẽ. And by Christ understand the Church, concerning which manner of speaking we have spoken at Rom. IX, 3. After it began to weary them of that servitude which they had promised to the Church. For it is σρηνιᾷν, as they teach us

The Greek grammarians, στρηνινίας. Thus Apoc. XVIII. 7. And the noun שְׁאָנַן for סְאָנָן is in 2 Kings XIX. 28. The Syrian here uses that word which is placed in the Syriac of the Old Testament, where in the Greek it is ὑβρίζειν. In a similar matter, the Council of Chalcedon can. 15. ὑβρίσασα ἐπὶ τῇ Θεῦ χάριτι. And Oecumenius: ὅταν καθάπερ ἀκκίσωνται τῷ χριστῷ. They want then to marry again, ἡ φορτητὴ γὰρ νέας χρηστία, says Thano.

ἔχουσα κρῖμα) κρῖμα here calls the judgment a disgrace, dissenting from their deed. Similar is that of Chrysostom, Hom. LXIII on John: ἐκ οἶδας ὅτι οἱ μετὰ τ' τελευτὴν τῶν ἑαυτῶν ἑτέραι ἐπεισαγόμενοι, παρὰ πολλῶν καταγινώσκονται, καίτοι ἐ κόλασιν ἔχει τὸ πρᾶγμα.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Νεωτέρας δὲ χήρας παραιτũ) Minores sexagenariis. Πα- ραιτũ, id est, ne admitte ad ordinem illum fœminarum præsidentium. In Glossario: παραιτẽμαι recuso. Utun- tur sic Plutarchus & alii.

Ὅταν γὰρ κατασρηνιάσωσι τẽ χριςẽ γαμẽιν θέλουσιν) Id est, ὅταν σρηνιάσωσι κατὰ τẽ χριςẽ. Et per Christum intel- lige Ecclesiam, de quo loquendi genere diximus ad Rom. IX, 3. Postquam tædere eos cœpit istius servitutis, quam Ecclesiæ promiserant. Est enim σρηνιᾷν, ut nos docent

Græcorum Grammatici, στρηνινίας. Sic Apoc. XVIII. 7. & nomen שְׁאָנַן pro סְאָנָן est Reg. XIX. 28. Syrus hic eo verbo utitur, quod in Syriaco Veteris Testamenti poni- tur, ubi in Græco est ὑβρίζειν. In re pari Synodus Chal- cedonensis can. 15. ὑβρίσασα ἐπὶ τῇ Θεῦ χάριτι. Et Oecy- menius : ὅταν καθάπερ ἀκκίσωνται τῷ χριστῷ. Volunt den- de nubere rursum, ἡ φορτητὴ γὰρ νέας χρηστία, ait Thano.

ἔχουσα κρῖμα) κρῖμα hic vocat judicium probrum ab earum facto dissentatiss. Simile Chrysostomi illud Hom. LXIII. ad Johannem : ἐκ οἶδας ὅτι οἱ μετὰ τ' τελευτὴν τῶν ἑαυτῶν ἑτέραι ἐπεισαγόμενοι, παρὰ πολλῶν καταγινώσκονται, καίτοι ἐ κόλασιν ἔχει τὸ πρᾶγμα.

## 5:12
Ὅτι τὴν πρώτην πίστιν ἠθέτησαν) for the faith which they had given to the Church, having professed that they wished to serve it. παρέβησαν τὰς συνθήκας says Chrysostom here: ἐψεύσαντο τὴν συμφωνίαν, Theophylact: Oecumenius [says] a covenant toward Christ: Epiphanius [says] a promise: Ambrose [says] a profession. Thus διαθήκην ἀθε Gal. III. 15. In the Constitutions of Clement III. 1: If a younger woman is appointed to the diaconate, and not bearing the widowhood in youth, she marries, she will bring reproach upon the word of the diaconate, and will render an account to God, not because she was joined in a second marriage, but because she did not keep her own promise, having waxed wanton against Christ, because she did not come with faith and the fear of God to keep the promise, wherefore it is necessary not to pray for her sooner, or to pray and not accept. Tertullian on Monogamy explains this passage thus: He directs [this] to those whom he denotes above, young widows, who, having been included in widowhood and having affected it for some time, after they have had Christ in delights, wish to marry, having judgment, because they have rescinded their first faith: that is to say, the one which, having been found in widowhood and professed, they do not persevere in. On account of which he wishes them to marry, lest they afterwards rescind the first faith of the widowhood they had undertaken. Cyprian has a similar [passage] concerning virgins, epist. LXX. If they have dedicated themselves to Christ by faith.

This is the eighth Canon: Let younger widows be kept away from the College of widows of the Church: The Apostle gives grave reasons for this: namely, that they might κατὰ τοῦ χριστοῦ στρηνεύσωσι, i.e., begin to grow fierce with insolences, as if having broken and cast off the reins. A metaphor taken from beasts of burden, which, well-fed from excessive satiety and luxury, break all barriers and bridles. Thus Erasmus, Chemnitius, Balduinus. Theophylact and Oecumenius explain that word by ἀκκιῶσι, which is derived from the manners of a most petulant woman, whose name was Acco. To Camerarius, στρηνιᾶν signifies the swelling of surfeit and luxury, and the obscene titillation of lust, against CHRIST, or faith in Christ. But what need is there to understand the Church through Christ? For it pleased the Apostle to name the head himself: because they break not only the reins of the Church, but of Christ. Those who, thus lascivious, when they desire to marry in turn, incur the judgment not only of other widows, but of GOD himself, by violating that faith which they had given to Christ: because they were accustomed to consecrate themselves to the Church for their whole life. Thus faith is understood as fidelity to be kept in promises, as Rom. III. verse 3. The first faith, that is, the one given earlier, as Apoc. II. v. 4. 5. is understood by B. Hunnius in his treatise on Law and Gospel, page 82. Tossanus and Beza on Polygamy, page 206. Others explain it concerning the faith of religion with B. Luther, book on the Babylonian Captivity, Vol. II. Lat. Jen. f. 514. B. Chemnitius, examination of the Council of Trent, part 3, page 59. Calvin, Whitaker, etc., [who explain] that such younger women denied the faith of Christ for the sake of lasciviousness. How ineptly these are dragged to monastic vows by the Papists is obvious to all who understand them. For here the discourse is about widows; the Papists bind virgins with a vow; here those who are under sixty years of age are not admitted: The Papists thrust tender girls, who are not known to themselves by reason of age, into cloisters: here widows are assigned to sacred ministries. The Papists, by an opinion of worship and religion, and also of merit, bind their Nuns with a vow of continence.

Verf. 12.

Latin:

Ὅτι τὴν πρώτην πίστιν ἠθέτησαν) nam fidem, quam Ecclesiæ dederant, professæ se ei so lérvire velle. παρέ- βησαν τὰς συνθήκας ait hic Chrysostomus: ἐψεύσαντο τὴν συμφωνίαν, Theophylactus: πρὸς τὸν χριστὸν συνθήκην Oecumenius: Epiphanius ἐπαγγελίαν: professionem Am- brosius. Sic διαθήκην ἀθε Gal. III. 15. In Constitutio- nibus Clementis III. 1 Εἰ δὲ νεωτέραι καταστήσεται εἰς τὸ χηρικὸν, καὶ μὴ φέρεσα τὴν ἐν νεότητι χηρείαν γαμηθῇ, ἀπεί- κεισιν ἐμποιήσει τῇ γῇ τοῦ χηρικοῦ, καὶ λόγον ὑφέξει τῷ Θεῷ, ἐχ ὅτι δευτέρῳ μῳ συνήφθη, ἀλλ' ὅτι τὴν ἑαυτῆς ἐπαγγε- λίαν ἐκ ἐφύλαξε, καταστρηνιάσασα τοῦ χριστοῦ, διότι μετὰ πί- στεως καὶ ́ῶς τοῦ Θεῦ ἐκ ἦλθε φυλάξαι τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν, διὸ χρὴ μὴ πρότερον αὐτῇ ἐπι μὴ ἔυξασθαι, ἢ ἔυξασθαι καὶ μὴ ἀπο- δεῖ. Tertullianus de Monogamia hunc locum sic ex- plicat: Ad eas dirigit, quales suprà denotat, juvenculas vi- duas, quæ in viduitate comprehensa, & aliquandiu affectata, postquam in deliciis habuerunt Christum, nubere volunt, ha- bentes judicium, quod primam fidem resciderunt: illam vi- delicet, quæ in viduitate inventa & professa eam, non perse- verant. Propter quod vult eas nubere, ne primam fidem susce- pta viduitatis postea rescindant. Simile de Virginibus habet Cyprianus epist. LXX. Si ex fide se Christo dicaverunt.

Octavus hic Canon est: Juniores viduæ à Colle- gio viduarum Ecclesiæ arceantur: Cujus causas graves reddit Apostolus: quod nempe κατὰ τοῦ χριστοῦ στρηνεύσωσι, h. e. insolentiis protervè quasi ruptis, & abjectis habenis ferocire incipiant. Me- taphora sumpta ex jumentis, quæ bene pasta exi- mia satietate & luxurie omnia repagula & frena frangunt. Sic Erasmus, Chemnitius, Balduinus. Verbum illud per ἀκκιῶσι explicant Theophy- lactus & Oecumenius, quod deducitur à moribus petulantissimæ mulieris, cui nomen Acco. Ca- merario στρηνιᾶν significat crapula ac luxuria tumo- rem, ac obscœna libidinis titillationem, contra CHRISTUM, vel fidem in Christum. Quid autem opus est per Christum Ecclesiam intellige- re? Placuit enim Apostolo, caput ipsum nomina- re: quia non tantum frena Ecclesiæ, sed Christi rumpunt. Quæ ita lascivientes, ubi vicissim nu- bere cupiunt, judicium non tantum aliarum vi- duarum, sed ipsius DEI incurrunt, violando il- lam fidem, quam Christo dederant: quia per to- tam vitam se consecrare Ecclesiæ solebant. Sic fides pro fidelitate in promissis servanda, ut Rom. III. vers. 3. fides prima, id est, prius data, ut Apoc. II. v. 4. 5. intelligitur à B. Hunnio tr. de Leg. & Evangel. pag. 82. Tossano & Beza de Polygam. pag. 206. Alii de fide religionis cum B. Luthero lib. de capt. Babylon. Tom. II. Lat. Jen. f. 514. B. Chemnit. exam. Conc. Trid. part. 3. pag. 59. Calvino, Witta- kero &c. explicant, quod tales Juniores fidem Christi abnegarint lascivia causa. Quæ quam in- eptè ad vota monastica trahantur à Papistis, omni- bus obvium est, ea intelligentibus. Nam hic de viduis sermo est; Papistæ virgines voto obstrin- gunt; hic non admittuntur, quæ infra sexaginta annos sunt: Papistæ puellas teneras, quæ per æta- tem sibi ipsis notæ non sunt, in claustra detru- dunt: hic ad ministeria sacra allegantur viduæ. Papistæ opinione cultus & religionis, necnon meriti Moniales suas voto continentiæ obstrin- gunt.

Verf. 12.

## 5:13
Ἅμα δὲ καὶ ἀργαὶ μανθάνουσι) He notes also other vices frequent in younger women. Since they have nothing to do, he says, they become busybodies. Μανθάνειν here is to inquire, as in 1 Tim. V. 13. See what we have said on 2 Thess. III. verse 11. True is that: Ὡς πολλὰ θνητοῖς ἡ σχολὴ ποιεῖ κακά.

Περιερχόμεναι τὰς οἰκίας) Which Alexis called περινοστεῖν, in the verses which we produced at that place which we have already mentioned on the Thessalonians. You have a description of such a gadabout woman in Prov. VII, 1. And such a one is called by the Hebrews הַמִּיָּה וְסוֹרְרָה. But the ancients made the tortoise, never leaving its shell, a figure of a good woman. For they ought to be οἰκουροὶ, as the same Apostle says here to Titus II. v. 5. Euripides in Meleager: Ἔνδον μένουσαν τὴν γυναῖκ’ εἶναι χρεὼν Ἐσθλὴν· θύρησι δ’ ἀξίαν τοῦ μηδενός.

Verf. 13.

Οὐ μόνον δὲ ἀργαί.) This is an Epanorthosis, as if he were saying, it is too little that I said they are idle, for that would have been more tolerable. For it is better to be idle than to do evil.

Ἀλλὰ καὶ φλύαροι) In the Glosses, φλύαρος is a chatterer, φλυαρεῖ is to chatter, which word we have in 3 John verse 10. These things are connected, as we have said, to pry and to chatter.

Καὶ περίεργοι) See the things said on that passage to the Thessalonians; they busy themselves with other people's affairs.

Λαλοῦσαι τὰ μὴ δέοντα) מדברות הכאי of Maimonides, where they have nothing else to say, they begin to slander. 'The race of women is naturally fond of fault-finding,' says Euripides.
