A second reason is now given why younger widows are not to be admitted into the College of Deaconesses, because they easily indulge in idleness and other vices emerging from it: For idleness has taught every evil, as Theophylact says here. Idleness introduces wickedness, says Theodoret. Which B. Balduinus has succinctly summarized here: Thus, indeed, vice is born from vice: from the untimely maintenance of the Church, idleness; from idleness, curiosity; from curiosity, the frequenting of other houses to catch novelties; from that frequenting, garrulity and foolishness: for they would hardly be welcome in other people's houses unless they knew how to play the fool and chatter about things that are not fitting. For they often traduce men, lie, slander, or bring forth fabrications, only so that they might be welcome through some novelty: because of which vices St. Jerome, in his Epistle to Eustochium, named certain matrons as if they were plagues.

Latin:

Ἅμα δὲ καὶ ἀργαὶ μανθάνουσι) Notat & alia vitia foeminis junioribus frequentia. Cum nihil habeant, quod agant, inquit, fiunt percunctatrices. Μανθάνειν hic est sciscitari, ut Efth. IV. 5. Vide, quæ diximus ad 2. Theff. III. verf. 11. Verum illud: Ὡς πολλὰ θνητοῖς ἡ σχολὴ ποιεῖ κακά.

Περιερχόμεναι τὰς οἰκίας) Quod περινοστεῖν dixit Alexis, in verfibus, quos ad illum quem jam diximus locum ad Theffalonicenses produximus. Talis discurfatricis foeminæ descriptionem habes Prov. VII, 1. Et dicitur talis Ebræis המיל היב וסוררה At veteres testudinem de tecto suo nunquam egredientem figuram fecere bonæ foeminæ. Debent enim esse οἰκουροὶ, ut ait idem hic Apostolus ad Tit. II. v. 5. Euripides Meleagro: Ἔνδον μένουσαν τὴν γυναῖκ’ εἶναι χρεὼν Ἐσθλὴν· θύρησι δ’ ἀξίαν τοῦ μηδενός.

Verf. 13.

Οὐ μόνον δὲ ἀργαί.) Est Epanorthosis, quasi dicat, pa- rum est, quod dixi eas effe otiofas, fuerat enim id tolerabi- lius. Satius enim est otiofum esse, quàm male agere.

Ἀλλὰ καὶ φλύαροι) In Glossis φλύαρος garrulus, φλυαρεῖ garrio, quod verbum habemus Epist. III. Johannis verf. 10. connexa sunt ista, ut diximus, percunctari & garrire.

Καὶ περίεργοι) Vide dicta in eum locum ad Theffaloni- censes, aliena negotia curant.

Λαλοῦσαι τὰ μὴ δέοντα) מדברות הכאי Maimonidæ, ubi aliud non habent, quod dicant, calumniari incipiunt. φιλόψογον δὲ χρῆμα θηλειῶν ἔφυ. ait Euripides.

Altera jam ratio redditur, cur non adsciscen- dæ in Diaconissarum Collegium sunt juniores vi- duæ, quod facilè otio, & inde emergentibus aliis vitiis indulgeant: Otium enim omne malum edo- cuit, ut hic Theophylactus. Otium introducit ne- quitiam, ait Theodoretus. Quæ succincte hic com- plexus est B. Balduinus: Ita nimirum vitium ex vi- tio nascitur: ex intempestiva nimirum alimentatio- ne Ecclesiæ otium, ex otio curiositas, ex curiositate frequentatio aliarum ædium, ad captandas novita- tes, ex frequentatione ista garrulitas & ineptia: vix enim grata essent in alienis domibus, nisi ine- ptire scirent, & garrire, quæ non oportet. Sæpe enim traducunt homines, mentiuntur, calumnian- tur, aut figmenta afferunt, tantum ut novitate qua- dam gratæ sint: ob quæ vitia tales viduas D. Hiero- nymus in Epistola ad Eustachium matronarum quasdam quasi pestes nominavit.

## 5:14
Verf. 14.

Βούλομαι δὲ ὖν νεωτέρας χήρας γαμεῖν) βούλομαι is to be taken comparatively here, I prefer: namely, rather than that these things which I have said should happen. Thus θέλω in 1 Cor. 14:19.

Τεκνογονεῖν) Not to perform abortions, as some were doing, so that they might live more luxuriously; others, so that they might preserve their figure all the better. 'So that the belly may be free from the crime of wrinkles,' says the Master of such things in 2:14.

Οἰκοδεσποτεῖν) Namely, under a husband. It is the man's business to manage things outside; the woman's to preserve what has been acquired. Aristotle, Economics I. 3.

The ninth Canon is: Let younger widows marry, so that they may have something to do. The Apostle had established two kinds of widows; one of which he wishes to be admitted to the ministries used in those times, the other he rejects and wishes to be sent back to enter into marriage in turn. But this is not a mere indulgence here: for marriages do not need indulgence. Nor is it an absolute and universal precept, but hypothetical and restricted. It is limited in 1 Corinthians 7:9: 'Those who do not contain themselves, let them contract marriage.' But it will also be a precept in this way, (Bellarminus insists), τεκνογονεῖν, to bear children. Setting aside Grotius's explanation: the precept can be said to be, not indeed to procreate children in act, but to give aid for procreating them, and for rightly educating the same: just as it is commanded, not to acquire a house and family, but if a widow has a family, to administer and rule it. The exhortation of Jerome to Celantia is to be observed, Ep. 14: 'Rule and cherish your family in such a way that you wish to seem more a mother to your own than a mistress, from whom you should exact reverence by kindness rather than by severity.' The end of marriage is therefore expressed as twofold: one is the procreation of offspring: for marriage is to be entered into not for the sake of increasing but of restraining lust, and for the sake of procreating offspring: which end is opposed to the wantonness and luxury of younger widows, concerning which see verse 12. The other is the governance of the house, which is opposed to idleness, concerning which see verse 13.

To give no occasion to the adversary for the sake of reproach.

To give no pretext to enemies for curses. ἀφορμή is a pretext, 2 Cor. 5:2, 11:12, Gal. 5:13. ὁ ἀντικείμενος by excellence is the Devil: but it is also accustomed to be said of others who imitate him, as can be seen in 1 Cor. 16:9, Phil. 1:28. It is customary, however, for the singular with the article to be placed for the whole genus, as we said on Mark 3:26 and elsewhere. λοιδορίας χάριν, that is, εἰς λοιδορίαν, for reproach.

Latin:

Verf. 14.

Βούλομαι δὲ ὖν νεωτέρας χήρας γαμεῖν) βούλομαι sic com- parative sumendum est, malo: nempe quam fiant ista, quæ dixi. Sic θέλω 1. Cor. XIV. 19.

Τεκνογονεῖν) Non abortus facere; ut quædam facie- bant, quo lautius viverent: aliæ, quo formam eò melius servarent, Scilicet ut careat rugamm crimine venter. ait Magister talium II. 14.

Οἰκοδεσποτεῖν) Nempe sub marito. Viri est res extra gerere; foeminæ servare quæsita. Aristoteles Oeconomi- corum I. 3.

Nonus Canon est: Viduæ juniores nubant, ut habeant, quod agant. Duo constituerat Aposto- lus viduarum genera; {quorum unum ad mini- steria iis temporibus usitata admitti, alterum ab eo rejici, & ad conjugium vicissim ineun- dum remitti vult. Non autem hic nuda est in- dulgentia: nam nuptiæ non indigent indulgen- tia: Nec est præceptum absolutum & universa- le, sed hypotheticum & restrictum. Limitatur 1. Corinth. VII. verf. 9. Qui se non continent, ma- trimonium contrahant. Sed ita præceptum etiam erit, (instat Bellarminus) τεκνογονεῖν, liberos pro- creare. Missâ Grotii explicatione: præceptum esse dici potest, non quidem actu procreare li- beros, sed opem dare procreandis, iisdemque re- cte educandis: quemadmodum præceptum est, non domum & familiam comparare, sed si viduis sit familia, eam administrare, ac regere. Hie- ronymi observanda parænesis ad Celant. Ep. XIV, Familiam tuam ita rege & confove, ut te matrem magis tuorum, quam dominam videri velis, à qui- bus benignitate potius, quam severitate exige re- verentiam. Finis itaque conjugii geminus expri- mitur: unus procreatio sobolis: non enim au- gendæ sed refrænandæ libidini, & sobolis pro- creandæ gratia ineundum est conjugium: qui fi- nis opponitur proterviæ & luxuriæ juniorum vi- duarum, de qua v. 12. Alter est gubernatio domus, quæ opponitur otiositati de qua v. 13.

Μηδεμίαν ἀφορμὴν διδόναι τῷ ἀντικειμένῳ λοιδορίας χάριν.

Nullum dare prætextum inimicis ad maledicta. Ἀφορ- μὴ est prætextus 2. Cor. V. 2. XI, 12. Galat. V. 13. ὁ ἀντι- κείμενος per excellentiam Diabolus: sed solet & de aliis dici, qui eum imitantur, ut videre est 1. Cor. XVI. v. 9. Philipp. I. 28. Solet autem singulare cum articulo poni pro toto genere, ut diximus ad Marcum III. 26. & alibi λοι- δορίας χάριν, id est, εἰς λοιδορίαν לרבר.

## 5:15
Ver. 15. For already some have turned aside after Satan.

Not only have they fallen into those vices which I mentioned, but also, when they saw that this change of life of theirs was disapproved of by good Christians, they deserted Christianity. ἐκτρέπεσθαι for Paul is to turn aside from the straight path: above 16, within 6:20, 2 Tim. 4:4. ὀπίσω, or 'after' or 'behind', added to verbs of going and similar ones, signifies to follow. They have followed, he says, Satan, who presides over the world, 2 Cor. 4:4.

This tenth Canon can be established: Let younger widows beware, lest they leave an occasion of accusing to the adversary. This rule is general, by which younger widows, whether they marry again or not, are told what they ought to avoid. The Apostle therefore wishes that they cut off every pretext and occasion for detraction. Where by ἀντικείμενον is understood not the Devil, but any reviler whatsoever. Maresius in 'Anti-Christo revel.', p. 1, c. 17, p. 315, approves the conjecture of those who, since ὁ ἀντικείμενος is placed absolutely, and is also expressly distinguished from Satan, of whom he speaks in the following verse, thinks that the same one who is called ὁ ἀντικείμενος in 2 Thess. 2 is designated; as if the Apostle, having indicated the marks of the future ἀποστασία in the Church by the prohibition of marriages and the interdiction of foods, 1 Tim. 4:7, now commands the young women to marry, lest they give an occasion to τῷ ἀντικειμένῳ, that is, to the Anti-Christ, the enemy of matrimony, for his reproach. Which we leave in its place. The reason added by the Apostle teaches that at that time there was no lack of examples of younger widows who not only did not avoid every occasion of calumny, but also, having followed Satan, the author of all seduction, were turned away from Christ, from piety, and from faith to sins of every kind. Some refer these things to the precept about marrying, and to those vices which were noted in young widows if they were fed at the expense of the Church. But it is better to be understood generally, since it has already been acted upon above concerning that Canon, that such women are to be kept away from the College of Deaconesses because of the danger of lasciviousness against CHRIST, and of seduction to vices.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Ἤδη γάρ τινες ἐξετράπησαν ὀπίσω τοῦ Σατανᾶ.

Non tantum in ea vitia delapsæ sunt quæ dixi, verum etiam cum viderent suam istam vitæ mutationem à bo- nis Christianis improbari, Christianismum deserere. Ἐκ- τρέπεσθαι Paulo est declinare à via recta: supra 16. intra VI. 20. 2. Tim. IV. 4. ὀπίσω vel אחרו vel אחרי verbis eun- di & similibus additum significat sequi. Secutæ sunt, in- quit, Satanam, qui sæculo præsidet 2. Cor. IV. 4.

Hic decimus Canon constitui potest: Viduæ juniores caveant, ne occasionem criminandi adver- sario relinquant. Hæc regula generalis est, quà viduas juniores, sive iterum nubant, sive non: quid nempe vitare debeant. Vult ergò Aposto- lus, ut omnem detrahendi prætextum, atque oc- casionem præscindant. Ubi per ἀντικείμενον non Diabolus, sed quivis maledicus intelligitur. Ma- resius in Anti-Christo revel. p. I. c. XVII. p. 315. eorum approbat conjecturam, qui cum absolutè ὁ ἀντικείμενος ponatur, expresse etiam à Satana, de quo sequenti commate, distinguatur, eundem, qui 2. Thessal. II. ὁ ἀντικείμενος vocatur, designa- ri putans; quasi Apostolus indicatis τῆς ἀποστα- σίας futuræ in Ecclesia notis prohibitione nu- ptiarum & ciborum interdictione 1. Tim. IV. 7. nunc præcipiat juvenculis, ut nubant, ne dent oc- casionem τῷ ἀντικειμένῳ, id est, Anti-Christo, matrimonii Inimico, ad λοιδορίαν illius. Quod suo loco relinquimus. Ratio ab Apostolo addi- ta docet, illo tempore exempla non defuisse vi- duarum juniorum, quæ non modo non cave- rint omnem occasionem calumniæ, sed etiam Sa- tanam sequutæ, omnis seductionis autorem, à Christo aversæ sint, à pietate, à fide ad omnis ge- neris peccata. Nonnulli hæc ad præceptum de nubendo, & ad vitia illa, quæ in juvenculis vi- duis, si Ecclesiæ sumptu alantur, notata erant, referunt. Sed præstat generaliter intelligi, quum de isto Canone, quod tales arcendæ sint à Col- legio Diaconissarum, ob periculum lasciviæ con- tra CHRISTUM, & seductionis ad vitia, jam su- pra actum fuerit.

## 5:16
V. 16. If any believer, man or woman, has widows) Has, namely, those belonging to them by proximity of blood or affinity. ἐπαρκείτω αὐταῖς) Let him relieve them, as above 10, lest they burden the Church. See how much care Paul takes, lest the liberalities of the Church be spent on others than those who can in no way lack them.

And let not the church be burdened) βαρεῖσθαι is to be taken here as ἐν βάρει εἶναι in 1 Thess. 2:6. Ἵνα ταῖς ὄντως χήραις ἐπαρκέσῃ) That the Church may have wherewith to relieve those who are widows in such a way that they have no one to care for them. See above 3 and 5.

This is the eleventh Canon: Let everyone provide for his own widows, lest the Church be burdened by them: The cause of which, without doubt, was that many would decline the burden of feeding their own, and would burden the Church with the same. Add that it would by no means be fitting for the widows of the faithful, as Theophylact warns, to be fed by infidels, lest they seem to be in need of their help. He commands, however, that what is sufficient be supplied to them, implying that nothing is to be given to them for luxury, as Theophylact also warns with Chrysostom.

PART III. Concerning the honor and order of the Presbytery.

Latin:

V. 16. Εἴτις πιστὸς, ἢ πιστὴ ἔχει χήρας) Habet, nempe ad se pertinentes, propinquitate sanguinis aut affinitatis. Ἐπαρκείτω αὐταῖς) Subveniat illis, ut supra 10. ne Ec- clesiam onerent. Vide quantam curam gerat Paulus, ne Ecclesiæ liberalitates in alios impendantur, quam qui ca- rere eis nullo modo possunt.

Καὶ μὴ βαρείσθω ἡ ἐκκλησία) Sumendum hic βαρεῖσθαι quomodo ἐν βάρει εἶναι 1. Thess. II. 6. Ἵνα ταῖς ὄντως χήραις ἐπαρκέσῃ) Ut Ecclesia habeat, unde subveniat iis, quæ ita viduæ sunt, ut nullos habeant, qui ipsos curent. Vide supra 3. & 5.

Undecimus hic Canon est: Unusquisque suis prospiciat viduis, ne eis gravetur Ecclesia: Cujus causam citra dubium id dedit, quod multi suos alendi onus declinarent, & eodem Ecclesiam onerarent. Adde quod fidelium viduas, monente Theophylacto, haudquaquam deceat, ut ab infidelibus alantur, ne illorum ope videantur egere. Jubet autem ut subministretur eis, quod satis est, innuens, nihil illis ad luxum tribuendum esse, monente itidem cum Chrysostomo, Theophylacto.

PARS III. De Presbyterii honore atque ordine.

## 5:17
Vers. 17. Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor.

All elders are worthy of honor, as we have seen, but especially those who preside over the Churches, the הפרנסים [Parnasim], who are also κατ' ἐξοχὴν [by way of eminence] זקנים [Zekenim], are worthy of double honor, both on account of their age and on account of the judgment which the Church has made concerning them. And rightly διπλῆς τιμῆς [double honor]. For they are as it were the firstborn among their brothers. See Deut. 11:17. Ἀξιούσθαι [to be counted worthy] here, as also in Heb. 10:27, is used passively: just as in Virgil.

Deemed worthy of the proud marriage of Venus.

So also Gen. 31:28. It seems, however, that by double honor he means also sustenance, which itself is given to them with honor, as tributes are to kings. Consider the following, and those things at Matt. 15:4. Plato in the fifth book of the Laws said: πλέον ἢ διπλασίας τιμῆς ἄξιος ἐκείνῳ [worthy of more than double honor to him].

Especially those who labor in the word and doctrine.

That is, the leaders of the Presbyters, whose duty it was properly to speak to the people and thus to teach them. If they were not sufficient due to illness or age, they took others to themselves, mostly from the Presbyters, rarely from the laity. But it is to be noted that formerly in one large city, just as there were many Synagogues, so there were also many Churches, that is, assemblies of Christians. And each Church had its own president, who would address the people and ordain Presbyters. Sozomen (1.14) teaches us that only at Alexandria was there the custom that there was one president in the whole city, who would distribute Presbyters throughout the city for teaching; and Epiphanius, where he deals with Arius, says that there were never two Bishops at Alexandria, with that word taken κατ' ἐξοχὴν [by way of eminence], so that it signifies that right which ὁ ἄρχων τῆς συναγωγῆς [the ruler of the synagogue] had. In those words ἐν λόγῳ καὶ διδασκαλίᾳ [in word and doctrine] there is a ἓν διὰ δυοῖν [one through two], for ἐν λόγῳ διδασκαλίας [in the word of doctrine]. We had a similar one above at 4:1. In the Constitutions of Clement 2.28. And to the Presbyters, as those who labor concerning the word of doctrine, let a double portion also be set apart for them.

These things concerning the leaders of the Presbyters and Bishops κατ' ἐξοχὴν [by way of eminence] were foreign to the age of the Apostles. Therefore they do not fit here. Others more correctly say that a double kind of Presbyters is established. Namely, some ruling, others teaching. They call the former Lay Presbyters, the latter Clerical. For they too were in the dignity of an ecclesiastical office, who, having been appointed by the Magistrate, attended to ecclesiastical discipline, or external morals, to the order of Christians in the Church, and to the preservation of public doctrine, and presided over others in the external government of the Church, and took cognizance of them together with the Pastors. Just as also in 1 Cor. 12:28, besides Teachers, helps and governments are introduced, and the elders of the people took care of the Jewish external worship besides the Priests. Matt. 21:23. Thus in Augustine, book 3 against Cresconius, the Elders are read of.

The Church of the Masticana region: and concerning such things Canon C occurs in the Code of Canons of the African Church. The Apostle therefore prescribes canons concerning both kinds of Presbyters. The first is: Let the Presbyters who rule well be accounted worthy of double honor: All Elders are to be honored: But those who rule the Church are to be held worthy of double honor. Which is not to be restricted to sustenance: for what would double sustenance be? But to the ἐξοχὴν (preeminence) of honor before other promiscuous or plebeian Elders: to which honor, however, he confirms in v. 18 that retribution for labor also pertains. There is therefore no reason for anyone to trifle with the word διπλῆς (double), and to understand it either with Ambrose as sublime and thin honor, that is, support, or with Hugh of St. Cher and Lombard as spiritual obedience and temporal provision. Theodoret and Theophylact more conveniently explain it as double from much. But we acquiesce to the former comparative sense. Moreover, another Canon is added specifically concerning teaching Presbyters. Let those who labor in word and doctrine be held worthy of maximum honor. For this office of teaching the word of GOD is more worthy than taking care of ecclesiastical discipline and other external matters in the Church. Doctrine is such a praiseworthy thing, says Theodoret. And from this it is also the case that more liberal stipends are provided to such men: since they themselves must labor more than others. For authority and discretion, which are the two chief things in those who rule, do not suffice for doctrine: but there is need for reading and meditation on the scriptures, so that they may not only be able to speak, but also to speak well to the people, who perceive more benefit from the doctrine of a Doctor than from the governance of a president: B. Balduinus says. It is certainly a great labor to meditate well on the Word, to rightly divide it, to apply it conveniently: and it is as much more excellent than other labors as the soul is more excellent than the body.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Οἱ καλῶς προεστῶτες πρεσβύτεροι διπλῆς τιμῆς ἀξιούσθωσαν.

Omnes senes honore digni, ut vidimus, maxime vero, qui præsident Ecclesiis הפרנסים qui & κατ' ἐξοχὴν זקנים, digni sunt duplici honore, tum propter ætatem, tum propter judicium, quod de ipsis fecit Ecclesia. Et bene διπλῆς τιμῆς. Sunt enim velut primogeniti inter fratres suos. Vide Deuter. XI. 17. Ἀξιούσθαι hic ut & Ebr. X. 27. dignari passive: quomodo apud Virgilium.

Conjugio Veneris dignate superbo.

Sic & Gen. XXXI. 28. Videtur autem duplicem honorem dicere & alimenta, quæ & ipsa illis cum honore dantur, ut regibus tributa. Considera sequentia, & quæ ad Matth. XV. 4. Plato de legibus quinto dixit: πλέον ἢ διπλασίας τιμῆς ἄξιος ἐκείνῳ.

Μάλιστα οἱ κοπιῶντες ἐν λόγῳ καὶ διδασκαλίᾳ.

Id est, principes Presbyterorum, quorum proprie erat munus loqui ad populum, & fic eum docere. Si per morbum aut ætatem non sufficerent, affumebant sibi alios, de Presbyteris plerumque, raro de laicis. Sed notandum olim in una urbe magna, sicut plures Synagogas, ita & plures fuisse Ecclesias, id est, conventus Christianorum. Et cuique Ecclesiæ fuisse suum præsidem, qui populum alloqueretur, & Presbyteros ordinaret. Alexandriæ tantum eum fuisse morem, ut unus esset in tota urbe præses, qui ad docendum Presbyteros per urbem distribueret, docet nos Sozomenus I. 14. & Epiphanius, ubi de Ario agit, dicitque Alexandriæ nunquam duos fuisse Ἐπισκόπους, voce ea sumpta κατ' ἐξοχὴν, ita ut significet iliud jus, quod habebat ὁ ἄρχων τῆς συναγωγῆς. In illis verbis ἐν λόγῳ καὶ διδασκαλίᾳ est ἓν διὰ δυοῖν, pro ἐν λόγῳ διδασκαλίας. Simile habuimus supra IV. 1. In Clementis Constitutionibus II. 28. τοῖς δὲ Πρεσβυτέροις ὡς ἂν κάμνουσι περὶ τὸν τῆς διδασκαλίας λόγον διπλῆ καὶ αὐτοῖς ἀφοριζέσθω ἡ μοῖρα.

Hæc de principibus Presbyterorum & Episcopis κατ' ἐξοχὴν aliena fuere ab ætate Apostolorum. Non ergo huc quadrant. Rectius alii duplex genus Presbyterorum constitui ajunt. Alios nempe regentes, alios docentes. Illos Presbyteros Laicos vocant, hos Clericos. Nam & illi in dignitate muneris Ecclesiastici erant, qui à Magistratu constituti disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ, vel moribus externis, Christianorum ordini in Ecclesia, & conservationi doctrinæ publicæ intendebant, aliisque in regimine externo Ecclesiæ præerant, ac de illis unà cum Pastoribus cognoscebant. Quemadmodum & 1. Corinth. XII. 28. præter Doctores opitulationes & gubernationes introducuntur, & Judaicum externum cultum præter Sacerdotes curarunt Seniores populi. Matth. XXI. vers. 23. Sic apud Augustinum libr. III. contra Cresconium leguntur Seniores

Ecclesia Masticana regionis: & de talibus occur- rit Canon C. in Codice Canonum Ecclesia Africana. Canones ergo præscribit Apostolus de utriusque generis Presbyteris. Primus est: Presbyteri, qui bene præsunt, honore duplici afficiantur: Hono- randi sunt omnes Seniores: Sed qui Ecclesiæ præ- sunt, duplici honore digni habendi. Quod non ad sustentationem restringendum: quid enim esset duplex sustentatio? Sed ad ἐξοχὴν honoris præ aliis Senioribus promiscuis, vel plebejis: ad quem ta- men honorem etiam retributionem pro labore pertinere v. 18. confirmat. Non ergo est, quod tricetur quis in voce διπλῆς, & vel cum Ambrosio honorem sublimem & tenuem, id est, subsidium, vel cum Hugone Card. ac Lombardo obedientiam spiritualem, & providentiam temporalem intelli- gat. Convenientius Theodoretus, & Theophyla- ctus duplicem de multo explicant. Sed acquie- scimus priori comparativo sensui. Additur autem peculiariter de Presbyteris docentibus Canon alter. Qui laborant in sermone & doctrina maxi- me honore digni habentor. Nam dignius hoc of- ficium est docere verbum DEI, quam curam ge- rere disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ, & aliorum externo- rum in Ecclesia. Usque adeo res laudabilis est do- ctrina, ait Theodoretus. Atque inde etiam est, ut talibus liberaliora præbeantur stipendia: Siqui- dem plus aliis ipsis laborandum sit. Neque enim sufficit ad doctrinam autoritas & discretio, quæ duo in iis, qui præsunt, palmaria sunt: sed lectione & meditatione scripturarum opus est, ne loqui saltem possint, sed & bene loqui ad populum, qui plus com- modi percipit ex doctrina Doctoris, quam ex gu- bernatione præsidis: B. Balduinus ait. Magnus utique labor est Verbum bene meditari, recte se- care, commode applicare: isque tanto præstan- tior est aliis laboribus, quanto præstantior est cor- poribus animus.

## 5:18
Vers. 18. For the scripture says: thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. Deut. XXV. vers. 4. which passage we have had and explained in 1 Cor. IX. vers. 9. And the laborer is worthy of his reward.

It is a common sentiment among the Hebrews, as can be seen in Matt. X. vers. 10. Luke X. 7. The words are not in Scripture, that is, in the Old Law, to which Paul here looks back: but the sense is found in Lev. XIX, 13. Deut. XXIII. 14. where in Hebrew שׂכיר and in Greek μισθωτός, it is worth the same as ἐργάτης. For it signifies him whose work is hired for a wage. See Mark I. vers. 20. John X. v. 12. 13.

It is permitted to establish this as the third canon: Just stipends are to be provided to Doctors of the Word. For although the reason for double honor is brought forward here, the supply of the means of living is nevertheless referred specifically to the honor owed to Presbyters, the necessity of which is confirmed both from the law, Deut. XXV. 4. thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn: Because the ancients were accustomed to drive oxen in a closed threshing floor, who would crush the ears of corn with their hooves, where those more attentive to the matter would muzzle the oxen with baskets, so that they could not snatch the ears of corn, according to Cato on agriculture c. 54. which inhumanity that law indeed prohibits. Whence, not indeed through a mystical exposition of the senses, but from the lesser to the greater it is gathered: If food is not to be denied to the ox that treadeth out the corn, much more are necessary foods to be supplied to the Doctor of the Church: then from the equity which that common sentiment exhibits: The laborer is worthy of his reward, which was also brought forward for this purpose by Christ in Matt. X. Luke X. Compare what is at 1 Cor. IX. Note, however, warns Theophylact: just as he who teaches is compelled to sweat on all sides. For as it is no small labor to break up the grain and subsequently grind it into flour, so also it is necessary for him who instructs others to prepare himself for the tolerance of anguish and poverty and labors. When he discourses about the laborer, he shows that he ought by no means to seek out luxuries and rest.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Λέγει γὰρ ἡ γραφή: βῦν ἀλοῶντα ἐ φιμώσεις. Deut. XXV. vers. 4. quem locum habuimus & exposui- mus 1. Cor. IX. vers. 9. Καὶ ἄξιος ὁ ἐργάτης τῦ μισθῦ αὑτῦ.

Est sententia inter Ebræos trita, ut videre est Matth. X. vers. 10. Luc. X. 7. Verba non sunt in Scriptura, id est, in Veteri lege, ad quam hic respicit Paulus: at sensus reperitur Levit. XIX, 13. Deut. XXIII. 14. ubi in Ebræo שׂכיר in Græco μισθωτός, idem valet, quod ἐργάτης. Significatur enim is, cujus opera mercede conducta est. Vide Marc. I. vers. 20. Joh. X. v. 12. 13.

Canonem tertium constituere hunc licet: Ver- bi Doctoribus justa præbenda sunt stipendia. Quan- quam enim hìc ratio duplicis honoris adferatur, peculiariter tamen ad honorem Presbyteris de- bitum refertur subministratio mediorum viven- di, cujus necessitas confirmatur tum è lege, Deut. XXV. 4. non refrenabis os bovi trituranti: Quia solebant veteres boves in area clausa circumage- re, qui spicas ungulis contererent, ubi atten- tiores ad rem fiscellis capistrabant boves, ne spi- cas præcerpere possent, apud Catonem de re rusti- ca c. 54. quam vero inhumanitatem lex illa prohi- bet. Unde, non quidem per sensus mysticam ex- positionem, sed à minori ad majus colligitur: Si bovi trituranti non est denegandus cibus, multo magis Ecclesiæ Doctori subministranda sunt neces- saria alimenta: tum ex æquitate, quam trita illa sententia exhibet: Operarius est dignus mercede sua, quæ etiam eam in rem à Christo adducta Matth. X. Luc. X. Conf. quæ ad 1. Cor. IX. Ad- verte autem, monet Theophylactus: quemadmo- dum undique cogitur insudare, qui docet. Nam ut frumenta dissolvere, & in grana deinceps com- minuere, non mediocris est labor, sic & qui alios instruit, necesse est ad angoris & penuriæ & laborum se tolerantiam præparet. Cum vero de operario dis- serit, ostendit nequaquam hunc oportere delicias & quietem conquirere.

## 5:19
Vers. 19.

Against a Presbyter do not receive an accusation, except if it be upon two or three witnesses) It appears here that the president is being instructed, who is called by way of excellence the Bishop; for it was the duty of such to direct the actions of the Presbytery. Understand here 'presbyter' by honor: read that by the law of Moses no one could be condemned of a crime, unless the cause was proven by two witnesses. But a common man could be seized at the word of one witness, or an inquiry could be begun against him: not so, however, against a Senator, to whom a Presbyter is equated: And why not? Because the judgment for him is that of the whole people, when he is elected, which easily outweighs one witness. Furthermore, those who correct the crimes of others are accustomed to be exposed to the hatreds of many. And note, it is not said, do not condemn: but do not receive the accusation, repel the informers. Nicolaus Damascenus: among the Tarsians it is not permitted to bear witness against a younger presbyter. In these words of Paul there is a double negation, 'except, if not', as 1 Cor. XIV. v. 5. XV. v. 2.

Let this be the fourth canon: Against a Presbyter let no accusation be admitted without two or three witnesses. Some Papists, along with Chrysostom and Theophylact, understand 'Presbyter' by age, and therefore they wish for power in secular matters to be attributed to Bishops even over the Laity: But 'Presbyter' is understood here by dignity and office, as Theodoret, Ambrose, Hugo Card., and Lombard explain. Some infer that because they could be accused before Timothy, he was the 'proestos' and Bishop of the Ephesian Church: But the Apostle is not so much prescribing laws to Timothy, as to the Ecclesiastical Magistrate in his person: He is not indeed referring to mitred Papal Bishops, but to any prelates of the sacred order, and he teaches what ought to be done in an Ecclesiastical Council. Nor indeed is it to be inferred from this, with Justinian, that a judge of Presbyters cannot be constituted by the authority of a Prince and Magistrate: because Timothy was not constituted by that authority, for at that time there was no Christian Magistrate, whence a judge could not be constituted by him. But from where will it be taught that the Episcopacy itself, and the judgment of Ecclesiastical persons, was constituted by Peter? Moreover, Paul does not claim the vindication of causes for Timothy in any other way than he required the composition of lawsuits between brothers from the Corinthians: Nor is he who judges another immediately superior in power, since an equal can be judged by an equal, and indeed a superior can be judged by an inferior. The reasons for the Canon can be brought forward, both from the law of Deut. XIX. 15, 'in the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word stand', and from equity: because (1) an accusation of a minister easily redounds to the whole Church (2) nor does it rarely arise from a just correction of vices and a desire for vengeance, which cause Theodoret brings forward (3) Add that the Order of Doctors is exposed to calumnies more than others; (4) Finally, the Apostle wished to provide for the honor and authority of the Holy Ministry, which is the office of the Holy Spirit, in this way. Ambrose: 'Since the honor of this Order is sublime, therefore an accusation against this person ought not to be easily admitted.' And therefore the prudence of Constantine the Great is praised by Socrates, because he sealed the libels of accusations of Bishops with his ring, and did not read them, but consigned them to the flames of reconciled concord. For, he says, it is not fitting for the exorbitances of Priests to become known to the common people, lest those offended by them be rendered more bold to commit offenses. And it is added that if by chance he had seen with his own eyes a Bishop undermining another's marriage bed, he would cover the wicked deed with his cloak, lest to anyone who might happen to see it, that sight should do harm, as attested by Theodoret, Book 1, Ecclesiastical History, Chapter II. He does not say, as Chrysostom warns: Do not condemn, but do not receive an accusation, nor sit in judgment.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Κατὰ Πρεσβυτέρου κατηγορίαν μὴ παραδέχου, ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ ἐπὶ δύο ἢ τριῶν μαρτύρων) Apparet hîc instrui præsi- dem, qui dictus κατ' ἐξοχὴν ὁ Ἐπίσκοπος; nam talium erat dirigere Presbyterii actiones. Intellige hic πρεσβύτε- ρον honore: lege Mosis nemo damnari poterat criminis, nisi causa probata per testes duos. At poterat ad unius te- stis dictum vir plebejus capi, aut contra eum inquisitio in- cipi: non ita autem contra Senatorem, cui æquiparatur Presbyter: Et cur non? Quia judicium pro illo totius populi, cum electus est, facile uni testi præponderat. De- inde solent, qui aliorum crimina corrigunt, multorum pa- tere odiis. Et nota, non dici, ne damna: sed ne recipe ac- cusationem, repelle delatores. Nicolaus Damascenus πα- ρὰ ταρτησίοις νεωτέρῳ πρεσβυτέρῳ καταμαρτυρεῖν οὐκ ἔξεστι. In verbis his Pauli duplex negatio, ἐκτὸς, εἰ μὴ, ut 1. Cor. XIV. v. 5. XV. v. 2.

Canon quartus hic esto: Adversus Presbyte- rum citra duos vel tres testes nulla admittatur ac- cusatio. Presbyterum ætate intelligunt Pontificii nonnulli cum Chrysostomo & Theophylacto, adeo- que etiam in Laicos Episcopis potestatem in re- bus secularibus tribui volunt: Sed intelligitur hîc Presbyter dignitate, & munere, ut Theodo- retus, Ambrosius, Hugo Card. Lombardus expo- nunt. Qui accusari coram Timotheo quum po- tuerint, eundem Ecclesiæ Ephesinæ προεςῶτα, & Episcopum fuisse, nonnulli colligunt: Verum Apostolus non tam Timotheo leges præscribit, quam in persona ejus Magistratui Ecclesiastico: Non quidem mitratos Episcopos Papales, sed quosvis Antistites ordinis sacri referenti, & quid in Consilio Ecclesiastico fieri debeat, do- cet. Neque vero cum Justiniano hinc colligen- dum, judicem Presbyterorum autoritate Principis, & Magistratus constitui non posse: quia Timo- theus ea autoritate constitutus non fuit, nam illo tempore non erat Christianus Magistratus, unde ab eo judex constitui non potuit. A Petro au- tem ipsum Episcopatum constitutum esse, & ju- dicium personarum Ecclesiasticarum, unde do- cebitur? Causarum autem vindicationem non vindicat aliter Timotheo Paulus, quam à Corin- thiis compositionem litium inter fratres requi- rebat: Neque statim superior est potestate, qui alium judicat, cum & æqualis ab æquali, imo su- perior ab inferiori judicari possit. Causæ Cano- nis adferri possunt, tum è lege Deuter. XIX. 15. in ore duorum aut trium stabit omne verbum, tum ex æquitate: quia (1) accusatio ministri in totam facile redundat Ecclesiam (2) nec raro ex justa ἐπανορθώσει vitiorum, & vindićtæ studio nascitur, quam causam adfert Theodoreţus (3) Adde quod Ordo Doctorum calumniis præ aliis expositus sit; (4) Denique honori & autoritati S. Ministerii, quod officium est Spiritus S. ita cavere voluit Apostolus. Ambrosius: Quoniam hujus Ordinis sublimis honor est, idcirco non facile de hac persona accusatio debet admitti. Ideoque laudatur à So- crate Constantini M. prudentia, quod libellos accu- sationum Episcoporum annulo obsignavit, nec legerit, sed conciliatæ concordiæ flammis tradiderit. Non enim, inquit, Sacerdotum exorbitationes vulgo in- notescere oportet, ne illis offensi ad delinquendum reddantur audaciores. Additurq; se si forte oculis con- spexisset suis Episcopũ alienum torum labefactantem, obtecturum paludamento sceleratum facinus, ne cui forte cernentium illud visum noceret, teste Theo- doreto l. 1. Hist. Eccl. cap. II. Non ait, monente Chrysostomo: Noli condemnare, sed ne accusatio- nem recipias, neque ad judicium sedeas.

## 5:20
Verse 20.

“Them that sin rebuke before all.” Tertullian, where he describes the Churches in his Apologetic: “There also are exhortations, corrections, and divine censure. For judgment is passed with great weight, as is fitting among those who are certain of the sight of GOD: it is the highest judgment, which is a foretaste of the future judge, if anyone has so sinned that he is banished from the communion of prayer, and of the assembly, and of all holy commerce.” The approved elders preside. Therefore, the criminals were admonished by the elders while the people stood by and listened: “by the many” (2 Cor. II. 6). If he was repentant, a penalty (ἐπιτιμία) was imposed upon him. If he were contumacious, he was cut off from the Church.

“That the others also may have fear.” We have said elsewhere that there are three ends of punishments: instruction, satisfaction, and example. In ecclesiastical punishments, these three concur. For it is done so that he who has fallen may become better, and that the honor of the Church, injured by him, may be restored, and that others may be deterred by his example. This is also taken from the law in Deut. XIII. 11 and elsewhere.

This is the fifth canon: Those sinning publicly are to be rebuked before all by the Presbyters. Some wish for the sinning Presbyters to be noted: but the rule is more general, concerning the ecclesiastical discipline prescribed for those who are set over it. For just as the Church does not judge private matters, so, when someone sins publicly with scandal to the Church, a public correction is also necessary, so that the scandal may be removed. Theophylact, along with Theodoret, understands it thus: “Those who persist in wicked deeds, and whom you discover by inquiry to have sinned, rebuke openly, not to satisfy your anger, but so that others, affected by fear, may abstain from sins.” It is therefore necessary that the Bishop be a terror to others. For as it is rash and imprudent to condemn anyone without cause, so it is pestiferous not to rebuke the wicked and harmful. For the disease will be disseminated to many in the future.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Τὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας ἐνώπιον πάντων ἔλεγχε. Tertullianus, ubi in Apologetico Ecclesias describit: Ibidem etiam exhortationes, cogitationes, & censura divina. Nam & judicatur magno cum pondere, ut apud castra de DEI conspectu: summum, quæ futuri judicis præjudicium est, si quis ita deliquerit, ut à communicatione orationis, & conventus, & omnis sancti commercii relegetur. Præsident probati quique seniores. Admonebantur ergo criminosi à senioribus adstante & audiente plebe: ὑπὸ τῶν πλειόνων 2. Cor. II. 6. Si doleret, imponebatur ei ἐπιτιμία. Si con- tumax esset, abscindebatur ab Ecclesia.

Ἵνα κὰι οἱ λοιποὶ φόβον ἔχωσι. Diximus alibi pœnarum tres esse fines, νοθεσίαν, ἀπο- πλήρωσιν, παράδειγμα. In pœnis Ecclesiasticis tria hæc concurrunt. Nam & agitur, ut melior fiat is, qui lapsus est: & ut honos Ecclesiæ per eum læsus refarciatur, & ut alii exemplo absterreantur. Sumptum autem & hoc de lege Deut. XIII. 11. & alibi.

Canon quintus hic est: Publice peccantes co- ram omnibus à Presbyteris arguendi sunt. Peccan- tes Presbyteros notari nonnulli volunt: Sed re- gula generalior est, de disciplina Ecclesiastica præ- scripta illis, qui eidem præfecti sunt. Uti enim de privatis non judicat Ecclesia, ita, cum publice quis peccat cum scandalo Ecclesiæ, publica et- iam opus est correptione, ut tollatur scandalum. Sic accipit cum Theodoreto Theophylactus: Eos qui in pravis facinoribus perseverant, & quos inqui- rendo deliquisse compereris, propalam objurgato, non ut iracundiæ medearis, sed ut cæteri affecti for- midine, à peccatis abstineant. Oportet itaque ut aliis terrori Episcopus sit. Nam ut sine causa quem- piam condemnare, temeritatis est, & imprudentiæ, sic fontes & noxios non increpare, pestiferum. Nam in plures morbus in posterum disseminabitur.

## 5:21
Verse 21.

“I charge thee before GOD and the Lord Jesus Christ.” I adjure you of this, with GOD and Christ listening. You have the same form of speaking in 2 Tim. II. 14, IV. 1.

“And the elect angels.” Therefore, the Angels also hear what we say (Matt. XVIII. 10, Luke XV. 10, 1 Cor. XI. 10). Angels are often accustomed to be joined to God, so that His supreme Majesty may be more rightly conceived (Deut. XXXIII. 2). “Elect angels” are those whom God loves. For the Hebrew בָּחוּר is often taken in this way, as in Num. I. 28, 1 Chron. XVI. 13, and often elsewhere. But they are the same as those who are called saints elsewhere, as in Mark VIII. 38, Luke IX. 27. See what was said at 1 Thess. III. 13. For these are opposed to the angels of Satan (2 Cor. XII. 7, Rom. VIII. 38), who sinned and fell away from God (2 Pet. II. 4, Jude 6).

“That thou observe these things.” These things which I have said concerning ecclesiastical judgments.

“Without prejudice.” πρόκριμα is what the Latins call a prejudgment, as in that verse: “It is a grave prejudice, which has no judgment.” That has a place where a judge condemns someone unheard or undefended: to which that refers: “When you judge, haste is criminal.”

And: “Do not judge a case until you have heard the story of both.” And that which we have in Exodus XXIII. 1. The passage in Psalm L. 18 tends to the same.

Μηδὲν ποιῶν κατὰ πρόσκλισιν) Doing nothing out of partiality, that is, in favor of either the person for whose sake the action is taken, or a colleague, or one who recommends. Reference is made to the law of Exodus XXIII, where there is לִנְטֹת: In Greek ὥστε ἐκκλῖναι.

Although this most serious adjuration can be referred to other Canons as well, it seems, however, to be referred primarily to those things which he includes in certain Canons concerning ecclesiastical judgments: To which, therefore, he wished this sixth one to be added by the force of the same adjuration, to be properly observed regarding all those things: In ecclesiastical judgments, prejudice is to be avoided, and one must in no way pronounce judgment out of partiality. Both are indeed to be observed and are necessary in every judgment, but all the more so in ecclesiastical judgments, the more holy the things they treat and the more worthy the persons they concern. Erasmus explained Χωρὶς προκρίματος as 'without precipitation of judgment'; Castellio as 'without any discrimination' or 'partiality' (προσωποληψίᾳ), just as Beza had also previously translated it as 'without, so that you prefer one to another.' But the Vulgate and the Syriac are more correct with 'without prejudice' or 'without preoccupation'. For prejudice is a judgment not sought from a known cause, but brought from home, with the cause not yet examined. In the word πρόσκλισις, a metaphor is noted from a balance, which ought not to incline to one side, but be established in equilibrium. Hugo the Cardinal understands an equilibrium between justice and mercy, so that it does not incline to the other side, either by extending justice too much or by relaxing mercy; or to the other side alien to justice. It is necessary for a judge to be, with respect to both parties, as if in equilibrium, so that he does not incline toward either one out of favor, by which method partiality (προσωποληψία) is prohibited, or, as the Syriac has it, 'acceptance of the face.' Cf. 1 Chron. XIX. Two vices are especially to be avoided by judges, says Blessed Gerhard, namely, both precipitation in judging and partiality. The Apostle excludes both vices.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Διαμαρτύρομαι ἐνώπιον τῷ Θεῶ κὰι κυρίυ Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ) Hoc te obtestor, audiente & DEO & Christo. Idem lo- quendi genus habes 2. Tim. II. 14. IV. 1.

Καὶ τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν ἀγγέλων) Ergo & Angeli audiunt, quæ dicimus Matth. XVIII, 10 Luc. XV. 10. 1. Cor. XI. 10. Solent Deo sæpe adjungi Angeli, ut eo rectius concipia- tur ejus summa Majestas Deut. XXXIII, 2. Ἄγγελοι ἐκλεκτοὶ funt ii, quos Deus diligit. Ita enim sæpe sumitur Hebræum בָּחוּר ut Num. I. 28. 1. Paral. XVI. 13. & alibi sæpe. Ii au- tem sunt iidem, qui alibi dicuntur sancti, ut Marc. VIII. 38. Luc. IX. 27. Vide quæ dicta ad 1. Thessal. III, 13. Oppo- nuntur enim hi Angelis Satanæ 2. Cor. XII. 7. Rom. VIII. 38. qui peccarunt & à Deo defecgrunt, 2. Pet. II. 4. Jud. 6.

Ἵνα ταῦτα φυλάξῃ) Hæc quæ de judiciis Ecclesia- sticis dixi.

Χωρὶς προκρίματος) πρόκριμα est, quod præjudicium Latini vocant, ut in illo versu: Gravé præjudicium est, quod judicium non habet: Id locum habet, ubi inauditum, aut indefensum judex damnat: quo illud spectat: Te judicante criminofa est celeritas.

Et: Μήδε δίκην δικάσῃς πρὶν ἀμφοῖν μῦθον ἀκούσῃ· Et id, quod habemus Exodi XXIII. 1. Eodem tendit lo- cus Psal. L. 18.

Μηδὲν ποιῶν κατὰ πρόσκλισιν) Nihil propensione faciens, id est in gratiam, aut ejus, cujus causa agitur, aut collegæ, aut commendantis. Respicitur lex Exodi XXIII. ubi est לִנְטֹת: In Græco ὥστε ἐκκλῖναι.

Quanquam hæc gravissima obtestatio ad alios etiam Canones referri possit, videtur tamen im- primis ad ea, quæ de Ecclesiasticis judiciis certis Canonibus comprehendit, referenda: Quibus proinde sextum hunc adjectum voluit vi ejusdem obtestationis, probe circa ista omnia observan- dum: In judiciis Ecclesiasticis vitandum præjudi- cium, nec ullatenus ex affectu pronunciandum. Utrumque in omni quidem judicio observan- dum & necessarium, sed eo magis in judiciis Ec- clesiasticis, quo sanctiora tractant necessaria, ac digniores concernunt personas. Χωρὶς προκρίμα- τος exposuit Erasmus sine præcipitatione judicii; Castellio sine ullo discrimine, vel προσωποληψίᾳ, quemadmodum & Beza prius verterat absque, ut unum alteri præferas. At rectius Vulgata & Syrus sine præjudicio, vel sine præoccupatione. Nam præ- judicium est judicium, non à causa cognita peti- tum, sed domo allatum, causâ nondum perspectâ. In voce πρόσκλισις notatur metaphora à balance, quæ non debet in unam partem præpendere, sed in æquilibrio constituta esse. Hugo Cardinalis æquilibrium inter justitiam & misericordiam in- telligit, ne in alteram partem inclinet, vel nimis extendendo justitiam, vel remittendo misericor- diam; vel in alteram partem alienam à justitia. Oportet judicem esse respectu utriusque partis quasi in æquilibrio, ne in alterutram favore pro- pendeat, quo pacto προσωποληψία prohibetur, vel, ut Syrus habet, acceptio vultus. Conf. 1. Par. XIX. Duo vitia præcipue cavenda judicibus, ait B. Ger- hardus, videlicet, tum judicandi præcipitantia, tum affectus. Utrumque vitium Apostolus excludit.

## 5:22
Vers. 22. Lay hands suddenly on no man, neither be partaker of other men's sins. Some of the ancients understand this of absolution: others of ordination. For both were performed through the imposition of hands. I approve of it being taken as ordination: for there is a similar sentiment in the Talmud. A similar sense is found in Horace: 'Look again and again at the kind of man you recommend, lest soon others' sins bring fear upon you.' For ordination is also a certain solemn recommendation, coming from the custom of the Jews. He who is set over the Church must be explored for a long time, lest if he has any vice in doctrine or life, the ordainer comes into a share of the guilt as an ערב, that is, a surety. Isocrates to Demonicus: 'When established in authority, use no wicked man for administrations. For whatever he commits, they will attribute the causes to you.' Basil in Canon LXXXIV: 'Let us not wish to be destroyed together with the sins of others.' See also the rest there.

The seventh canon, therefore, is: No one is to be admitted to ordination without a just examination. The Papists cannot prove that the laying on of hands (χειροθεσίαν) was received in absolution. Therefore, Salmero, T. XI, tr. 18, rashly infers the sacrament of penance from this passage. Justinian acknowledges that this is done without any firm argument, because no testimony of the use of the imposition of hands exists in the Holy Scriptures: indeed, Salmero himself in this place admits that there is no mention of it in the Holy Scriptures, and therefore teaches that the present passage is to be understood concerning ordination, and he proves this from Acts VI. 13, 14. And most of the Ancients and more recent Interpreters agree that ordination is understood, because it was done by the laying on of hands (χειροθεσίᾳ) of the presbytery, chapter IV. 14. And that with a prior examination of both doctrine and life, lest it be precipitated without just exploration, Leo the Great, Epistle LXXXVII to the African Bishops, chapter 1. What is it to lay on hands quickly, if not to bestow priestly honor upon those not proven, before the maturity of age, before the time of examination, before the merit of labor, before the experience of discipline? So also Gregory the Great, lib. V. Moral. cap. 30. Thomas, Diana, Cajetan, Gagnæus, Guillaudius, Tirinus: Theophylact: By no means quickly, that is, rashly, or as soon as you have tested someone once or twice or thrice, but often, so that having diligently investigated everything, you may lay hands on someone. For this matter is not devoid of danger. For you are liable for the faults of others, namely those which he whom you have ordained shall commit in the future. Nor does the gloss of those among the Papists, who snatch these things for the laying on of hands (χειροθεσίαν) of exorcists, deserve support: for it is a matter of appointing ministers of the Church. Some at the same time concerning the sins of the promoters they understand, when out of blind affection promoters call someone to the sacred office who is unworthy of it. Which is not undeservedly noted: For he also communicates in the sins of others, who quickly lays on hands: But because the Examiner cannot discuss the causes of the calling, and inquires only into the doctrine and life of the candidate, he is prohibited from communicating in the sins of this man properly.

Keep yourself pure) See Phil. IV. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Χεῖρας ταχέως μηδενὶ ἐπιτίθει, μηδὲ κοινώνει ἁμαρτίαις ἀλλοτρίαις. Alii veterum de absolutione intelligunt: alii de ordi- natione. Utrumque enim per manuum impositionem per- agebatur. Probem ego de ordinatione accipi: nam est & in Thalmude par sententia. Similis apud Horatium sensus: Qualem commendas etiam atque etiam abspice, ne mox Incutiant aliena tibi peccata timorem. Nam & ordinatio est solennis quædam commendatio, à more Judæorum veniens. Diu explorandus est, qui præ- ficitur Ecclesiæ, ne si quod habeat vitium in dogmate, aut vita, veniat ordinator in culpæ partem tanquam ערב, id est obfirmator. Isocrates ad Demonicum: εἰς ἀρχὴν κα- τασταθεὶς μηδενὶ χρῶ πονηρῷ πρὸς τὰς διοικήσεις. ὧν γὰρ ἐκεῖνος ἁμάρτῃ σοὶ τὰς αἰτίας ἀναθήσουσι. Basilius Canone LXXXIV. μὴ θελήσωμεν ἁμαρτίαις ἀλλοτρίαις συναπόλλυσθαι. Vide & cætera ibi.

Canon ergo septimus est: Ad ordinationem nemo sine justo examine admittendus. Χειροθεσίαν in absolutione receptam fuisse, probare nequeunt Papistæ. Temere ergo Salmero T. XI. tr. 18. Sacra- mentum pœnitentiæ ex hoc loco colligit. Justi- nianus id nullo firmo argumento fieri agnoscit, quia usus manus impositionis nullum extat in S. literis testimonium: imo & Salmero ipse in h. l. fatetur, nullam ejus in S. literis mentionem esse, ideoque de ordinatione præsentem locum intelli- gendum esse docet, idque probat ex Act. VI. 13. 14. Et consentiunt plerique Veteres, & recentiores Interpretes, ordinationem intelligi, quia χειροθε- σίᾳ Presbyterii fiebat cap. IV. 14. Idque prævio examine tum doctrinæ, tum vitæ, ne illa præci- pitetur sine justa exploratione Leo M. Epist. LXXXVII. ad Episcopos Africanos cap. 1. Quid est cito manus imponere, nisi ante maturitatem ætatis, ante tempus examinis, ante meritum laboris, ante experientiam disciplinæ, sacerdotalem honorem tribuere non probatis. Ita & Gregorius M. lib. V. Moral. cap. 30. Thomas, Diana, Cajetanus, Ga- gnæus, Guillaudius, Tirinus: Theophylactus: Haud quaquam cito, id est, temere, vel cum primum quempiam fucris secundove aut tertio periclitatus, sed sæpe, ut diligenter omnibus investigatis, ma- nus cuiquam imposueris. Neque enim expers peri- culi ea res est. Es enim alienis delictis obnoxius, his scilicet, quæ ille in futurum commiserit, cui manus imposuisti. Neque suffragium meretur eorum è Pontificiis glossa, qui ad χειροθεσίαν Exorcista- rum hæc rapiunt: Agitur enim de ministris Ec- clesiæ præficiendis. Nonnulli simul de peccatis promotorum intelligunt, cum ex affectu cæco promotores aliquem ad sacrum officium vocant, qui indignus eodem sit. Quod non immerito notatur: Nam & illorum peccatis communicat, qui cito manus imponit: Sed quia causas voca- tionis discutere nequit Examinator, & in candidati tantum doctrinam & vitam inquirit, hujus proprie peccatis communicare prohibetur.

Σεαυτὸν ἁγνὸν τήρει) Vide Phil. IV. 8.

## 5:23
Ver. 23. No longer drink water.

It coheres with the preceding. I do not wish, however, for that reason that you be a drinker of water alone. The word ὑδροποτεῖν is good Greek; Dioscorides uses it.

But use a little wine) Use wine indeed, but well diluted. See on this matter the excellent dissertation of Chrysostom, the first on the statues. Justin to Zenas: 'And let not wine be smelled so as to be persuaded to drunkenness, nor let it be sought after like water, for both are God's creations. But water is necessary: wine, however, has been made for the sake of the body's assistance.'

For your stomach's sake) Cornelius Celsus recommends thin and austere wine for those suffering from stomach ailments. In a similar way, Marinus says that Proclus was warned by the philosophers not to abstain from eating meat, 'so that the body might also have the ability to serve the soul's activities.' Plato, however, in Laws II, advises using wine, 'unless for the sake of physical training or illness.'

And your frequent infirmities) For many kinds of infirmities are accustomed to follow those who digest poorly. Justin in the aforementioned place: 'It is necessary in winter, because of the cold, to drink until one is not shivering. And in summer, for the sake of the internal healing,' see also other things there. Add the excellent things said by Clement, Pedagogue II. 2. The Greek sentiment is: 'Wine increases great strength for a weary man.' Jerome to Demetrias gives a general rule: 'We do not command you immoderate fasts and enormous abstinence from food, by which delicate bodies are immediately broken: and they begin to be sick before they have laid the foundations of a holy conversation.' It is also the opinion of the philosophers that 'moderations are virtues, and excesses are vices,' which the Latin language can express thus: that virtues are moderate, and things exceeding measure and proportion are reckoned among vices. Whence also one of the seven wise men: μηδὲν ἄγαν, that is: 'Nothing in excess,' he says, which has become so famous that it has been expressed even in a comic verse. You ought to fast in such a way that you do not tremble, and are either carried or dragged by the hands of your companions: but so that with the appetite of the body broken, you do nothing less than usual in reading, or in Psalms, or in Vigils.

The eighth Canon is: Let Presbyters be zealous for purity and abstinence, yet let them not be wanting to the necessity of the body. Augustine, book I, On Grace and Free Will, chapter 4, renders it: 'Contain yourself.' In the Greek it is ἁγνὸν, which signifies pure and whole, in purity of mind and body, for which abstinence is necessary. Therefore a Bishop is prohibited from being παροινὸς (a drunkard). Yet the exception is added by the example of Timothy for the sake of curing his health: for whose sake the use of wine, but moderate, is granted. Compare Psalm CIV. 15. Sirach XXXI. 33. Ephesians V. 18. Romans XIII. 14. God wills that He be served prudently, as Ambrose warns, lest we be made weak by excess, and afterwards require the help of physicians. Therefore, under a special warning, suitable to Timothy, a general caution is to be understood. It must be weighed, says Gregory, book XX, Moral. chapter 31, that a string on a lyre, if it is stretched too little, does not sound: if too much, it sounds raucous, because undoubtedly the virtue of abstinence is either none at all, if each person does not adorn the body as much as he is able, or it is very disordered, if he wears out the body more than he is able. For through abstinence the vices of the flesh are to be extinguished, not the flesh, and each person ought to preside over himself with such moderation that the flesh does not grow proud toward guilt, and yet remains for the affection of righteousness. That ἁγνότης (purity), when compared with the preceding warning, teaches that Presbyters must apply themselves to this, that others also may be kept pure, lest they communicate in their sins, and if that cannot be obtained, at least let each one take pains that he keeps himself pure.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Μηκέτι ὑδροπότει.

Cohæret cum superioribus. Nolo tamen ea de causa te solius aquæ esse potorem. Vox ὑδροποτεῖν bene Græca est, utitur ea Dioscorides.

Ἀλλ’ οἴνῳ ὀλίγῳ χρῶ) Utere quidem vino, sed bene diluto. Vide hac de re egregiam dissertationem Chry- sostomi prima de statuis. Justinus ad Zenam: ὁ δὲ οἶνος μήτε ὀσφρέσθω ἐπὶ τὸ μεθύειν πέπεισθαι, μηδὲ ὡς ὕδωρ ἐπι- ζητείσθω, ἑκάτερα μὲν γὰρ Θεῦ ποιήματά ἐστιν. Ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν ὕδωρ ἀναγκαῖον: ὁ δὲ οἶνος βοηθείας χάριν τῷ σώματος γέγονεν.

Διὰ τὸν σόμαχόν συ) Stomacho laborantibus vinum tenue & austerum commendat Cornelius Celsus. Pari modo Proclum ait Marinus à Philosophis monitum, ne carnium esu abstineret, ὅπως ἂν καὶ τὸ σῶμα ὑπηρετεῖν ἔχῃ ταῖς ψυχικαῖς ἐνεργείαις. Plato vero legum II. suadet vino uti, εἰ μὴ σωμασκίας ἡ νόσων ἕνεκα.

Καὶ τὰς πυκνάς συ ἀσθενείας) Multa enim infirmitatum genera consequi solent male concoquentes. Justinus di- cto loco : δέον τῷ μὲν χειμῶνι· διὰ τὸ κρύος· πίνειν, μέ- χρι τῦ μὴ ῥιγῦν. Τῷ δὲ θέρει διὰ τὴν τῶν ἐντὸς θεραπείαν, vide & alia ibi. Adde egregie dicta à Clemente Pædagogi II. 2. Græca est sententia: Ἀνδρὶ δὲ κεκμηῶτι μένος μέγα οἶνος ἀέξει. Hieronymus ad Demetriadem generalem dat regulam : Neque vero immoderata tibi imperamus jejunia, & enormem ciborum abstinentiam, quibus statim corpora delicata fran- guntur: & ante ægrotare incipiunt, quam sanctæ conver- sationis jacere fundamenta. Philosophorum quoque sententia est μεσότητας, ἀρετὰς, ὑπερβολὰς, κακίας εἶναι, quod Latinus ita potest sermo resonare, moderatas esse virtutes, excedentia modum atque mensuram inter vitia deputari. Unde & unus de septem sapientibus: μηδὲν ἄγαν, id est: Ne quid, ait, ni- mis, quod tam celebre factum est, ut comico quoque versu expressum sit. Sic debes jejunare ut non palpites, & comitum tuorum vel porteris, vel traharis manibus: sed ut fracto corporis appetitu, nec in lectione, nec in Psalmis, nec in Vigiliis, solito quid minus facias.

Octavus Canon est : Puritati & abstinentiæ studeant Presbyteri, corporis tamen necessitati ne defint. Augustinus lib. I. de grat. & lib. arb. cap. 4. reddit: Contine Teipsum. In Græco est ἁγνὸν, quod significat purum & integrum, puritate mentis & corporis, ad quam abstinentia opus est. Ideò prohibetur Episcopus esse παροινὸς. Additur ta- men exemplo Timothei exceptio ob curandam valetudinem: cujus gratia usus vini, sed modicus, conceditur. Conf. Psalm. CIV. 15. Syr. XXXI. 33. Ephes. V. 18. Rom. XIII. 14. vult Deus prudenter sibi serviri, monente Ambrosio, ne nimietate de- biles efficiamur, & postea medicorum suffragia re- quiramus. Sub speciali ergo monito, Timotheo convenienti generalis intelligenda est cautio. Pensandum, inquit Gregorius l. XX. Moral. cap. 31. quod chorda in cythara, si minus tenditur, non so- nat: si amplius, raucum sonat, quia nimirum vir- tus abstinentiæ aut omnino nulla est, si tantum quisque corpus non adornat, quantum valet, aut val- de inordinata est, si corpus atterit plus, quam va- let. Per abstinentiam quippe sunt carnis vitia ex- tinguenda, non caro, & tanto quisque sibimet debet moderamine præesse, ut & ad culpam caro non su- perbiat, & tamen ad affectum rectitudinis subsistat. Illa ἁγνότης cum præcedenti monito collata, do- cet, Presbyteris in id incumbendum esse, ut & alii puri serventur, ne peccatis ipsorum commu- nicent, ac si obtineri id non possit, operam saltem quisque det, ut ipse purum se servet.

## 5:24
Ver. 24. The sins of some men are manifest, going before to judgment) He returns to that matter concerning ordinations, as if by an inserted parenthesis. And he calls judgment ἀνάκρισιν, or that examination which was done concerning those to be ordained. See above III. 10. He silently warns Timothy to inquire diligently into those things which preceded that time.

Τισὶ δὲ καὶ ἐπακολουθοῦσιν) Some, while hoping for the Presbyterate, do not remove their vices, but cover them up, to break forth when they have obtained what they desired; the ordainer is not held responsible for such men: but when he has learned of it, he shall take pains that Ecclesiastical censure does not sleep. Therefore, the ordainer shall always keep watchful eyes upon those whom he has ordained.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Τινῶν ἀνθρώπων αἱ ἁμαρτίαι πρόδηλοί εἰσι προ- άγουσαι εἰς κρίσιν) Redit ad illud de ordinationibus, velut interposita παρενθέσει. Et κρίσιν vocat ἀνάκρισιν, sive δο- κιμασίαν illam, quæ fiebat circa ordinandos. Vide supra III. 10. Tacite monet Timotheum, ut diligenter inquirat in ea, quæ id tempus præcessere.

Τισὶ δὲ καὶ ἐπακολουθοῦσιν) Quidam dum Presbyterium sperant, vitia sua non tollunt, sed obtegunt, eruptura ubi cupito erunt potiti, de talibus non tenetur ordinator: sed ubi resciverit, dabit operam, ut ne Ecclesiastica censura dormiat. Ideo ordinator in eos, quos ordinavit, intentos semper habebit oculos.

## 5:25
V. 25. Ὡσαύτως καὶ τὰ καλὰ ἔργα πρόδηλά ἐστι) You ought to inquire not only about him who is to be ordained, whether he has done nothing evil, but also whether he has done much good. And you will trust this matter most of all. For those who are truly pious, their pious deeds do not lie hidden.

Καὶ τὰ ἄλλως ἔχοντα κρυβῆναι ὐ δύναται) הבה לוא יוכל Jerem. XLIX. 10. If the affairs of some are otherwise, they cannot be hidden. That is, if any have produced no good works, such as by admonishing others, serving the sick, or relieving the poor, it will be easy for you to know this and to beware of such men. For they are deservedly suspicious.

This is the ninth and final Canon. One must diligently inquire into those things, whether evil or good, which the candidate has done before his vocation. Theophylact handed down this sense of the Canon, which Grotius has exhibited here well enough. Theophylact also handed down another sense of these words from Basil the Great: If by chance anyone commits fornication or theft, this alone of his offenses precedes him, dragging him to judgment. But if anyone teaches perverse things and brings forward a study of more pernicious wisdom and discipline, this sin truly follows him. Which, indeed, is not extinguished or ended in him, but such pestilent doctrines have successors: of which kind are the wise men of the Greeks, as are all the rest who write many things beyond the truth of the Ecclesiastical dogma. But these men are about to pay the penalty, not only because they themselves are entangled in errors, but because they provided the cause of error for those who follow them. But the former explanation is more suitable and accords better with the present information concerning Presbyters. Which also pleased the blessed Hunnius: These things also, he says, spoken on the occasion of the preceding, pertain to the ministers of the Church: These are not of the same mark: some are good, some are evil, and among these others are openly evil, whose impiety so manifests itself in words or deeds that it can be judged, and just severity can be exercised against those impious ministers. But some are evil, not openly, but secretly. For they can draw a mask of holiness over their impiety. But, even if they lie hidden for some time, yet at length their wickedness is brought to light: just as, conversely, the things that are done well by the good cannot be hidden, however much they may be weighed down for a time by the slanders of the impious. The exposition of the blessed Gerhard also agrees.

Latin:

V. 25. Ὡσαύτως καὶ τὰ καλὰ ἔργα πρόδηλά ἐστι) Non tan- tum de eo, qui ordinandus est, inquirere debes, an nihil mali egerit, sed an etiam multum boni. Et huic rei potis- simum credes. Qui enim vere pii sunt, eorum pia facta non latent.

Καὶ τὰ ἄλλως ἔχοντα κρυβῆναι ὐ δύναται) הבה לוא יוכל Jerem. XLIX. 10. Si quorum res aliter se habent, ex latere non possunt. Id est, si qui nulla ediderint bona opera, puta monendo alios, inserviendo ægrotis, suble- vando pauperes, facile id tibi erit scire, & tales cavere. Merito enim suspecti sunt.

Nonus & ultimus hic Canon est. Diligenter in- quirendum de iis, qua sive mala, sive bona Candida- tus egerit ante vocationem. Hunc Canonis sen- sum tradidit Theophylactus, quem probe satis hic exhibuit Grotius. Tradidit & alium e Basilio M. horum verborum sensum Theophylactus: Si for- san quispiam fornicetur, fureturve, hunc id solum delicti præcedit, ad judicium trahens. Verum, si pra- va quis edocet, & perniciosioris sapientiæ studium affert, & disciplinam, hunc sane peccatum subse- quitur. Quod utique non in ipso extinguitur, vel finitur, sed restant ejusmodi pestilentes doctrinæ suc- cessores: cujusmodi sunt Græcorum sapientes, qua- les & reliqui omnes, qui præter Ecclesiastici dogma- tis veritatem multa conscribunt. Daturi autem hi pœnas sunt, non solum quia ipsimet erroribus sunt involuti: sed quia se subsequentibus erroris causam præbuere. Sed prior explicatio convenientior est, magisque congruit informationi præsenti de Pres- byteris. Quæ etiam placuit B. Hunnio: Hæc quoq;, inquit, ex occasione præcedentium dicta pertinent ad Ecclesiæ ministros: Hi non sunt ejusdem notæ: quidam boni sunt, quidam mali, & inter hos alii sunt aperte mali, quorum impietas dictis aut factis ita se profert, ut judicari ea, & in ministros impios illos justa severitate animadverti possit. Quidam vero sunt mali, non palam, sed occulte. Possunt enim suæ impietati larvam obducere sanctimoniæ. Verum, etsi aliquandiu latent, tamen vel tandem in lucem producitur improbitas eorum: quemadmodum vi- cissim, quæ bene fiunt a bonis, occultari nequeunt, quantumvis aliquandiu calumniis impiorum præ- graventur. Consonat etiam B. Gerhardi expositio.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

After certain admonitions concerning servants, he adds precepts concerning those who do not remain in the doctrine of Christ, that they are to be avoided, and concerning contentment, and the avoiding of avarice, and also concerning the pursuit of piety, and fighting the good fight of faith, with a most grave adjuration, and he teaches what must be prescribed to the rich of this world, and lastly, he gives a reminder about guarding the deposit of faith, and ends with a prayer.

There are six parts. I. Concerning servants, v. 1 and 2. II. A precept concerning avoiding the heterodox, v. 3, 4, 5. III. Information concerning contentment and avarice, to verse 10. IV. A reminder of what the man of God ought primarily to avoid and what to pursue, to verse 17. V. Mandates to be prescribed to the rich, to verse 19. VI. An exhortation to guard the deposit of faith.

Latin:

CAPUT VI.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Post monita quædam de servis, addit præcepta de iis, qui non permanent in doctrina Chri- sti, vitandis, deque ἀυταρκείᾳ, & fugienda avaritia, nec non de studio pietatis, & mili- tanda bona fidei militia, cum gravissima ob- testatione, ac qua divitibus seculi præcipien- da sit, docet, novissime de custodiendo fidei deposito commonefacit, & voto finit.

PArtes sunt sex. I. De servis, v. 1. & 2. II. Præceptum de heterodoxis fugiendis v. 3. 4. 5. III. Informatio de ἀυταρκείᾳ, & avaritia, ad vers. 10. IV. Commonefactio, quid imprimis vitare, quid prosequi homo DEI debeat, ad vers. 17. V. Mandata divitibus præscribenda ad vers. 19. VI. Adhortatio ad custodiendum fidei depositum.

## 6:1
Vers. 1. As many as are under the yoke are slaves.

He added this for the sake of distinction. For all Christians are servants of GOD and of Christ: and because of this, also servants of one another. Under the yoke, that is, under the authority of a master. Thus also the word is used in Levit. XXIX. 13, Is. IX. 3, and elsewhere.

Let them count their own masters worthy of all honor.

As their domestic magistrates. See Romans XIII. vers. 7, 1 Peter II. vers. 17.

He treats first of the servants of unbelievers: then of believers. Regarding the former, some perhaps were persuaded that Christian liberty removes the servitude to be rendered to unbelievers. He wishes, therefore, that servants be warned that they are bound to sustain not only servitude, but also the yoke—that is, a heavier servitude, if the masters are harsher—1 Peter II. vers. 18, without prejudice to Christian liberty, which ensures that we do not become servants of men in matters of religion, 1 Cor. VII. 23, but it does not remove the authority of a master, just as the Gospel does not abolish civil government. Add that the servants of the Hebrews were accustomed to be set free after six years, Exod. XXI. 2. Lest Christians should therefore think the same, instruction seemed necessary, as Augustine warns in Quæst. LXXVII. in Exod. Finally, the scandal of the Gentiles had to be countered, which would have arisen if Christian servants had not honored their unbelieving masters. Therefore, they are commanded to show every honor, both of reverence and of obedience. For they should not, as Theophylact says here, believe that they will be free because they have received the faith of Christ. Rather, they use their liberty when they are free from wicked deeds, while in body they are subject to servitude. Which servitude is to be held as liberty, when someone has undergone it for the name of Christ.

That the name of God and the doctrine be not blasphemed.

The name of GOD is attacked with curses when those who call themselves his worshippers live wickedly. See Rom. II. 24, Is. LII. 5, Ezek. XXXVI. vers. 23; for outsiders say: what kind of God do these people have? Thus also the doctrine, the Evangelical doctrine, is slandered as a destroyer of empires.

A most serious reason is added, lest the name of the Lord and the Evangelical doctrine, which is called the doctrine by antonomasia in 1 Tim. V. 17, be blasphemed. For Gentiles are accustomed to judge dogmas not from words, but from the things themselves and from life. Concerning which Theophylact says: For then especially would unbelievers detest this most holy dogma of Christ, when they saw it being attacked by the believers themselves: for it instructs its followers in tolerance and placability, and does not permit them to be contumacious. But if servants show themselves to be kind and easy to obey, the unbelieving masters will undoubtedly marvel and be astonished at the virtue of the Christian religion, which is of such value that it makes even the characters of servants, which cannot easily be composed and corrected, so compliant that they soon obey the one commanding.

Latin:

Vers. 1. Ὅσοι εἰσὶν ὑπὸ ζυγὸν δῦλοι.

Hoc ad distinctionem addidit. Omnes enim Christia- ni servi DEI & Christi: & propter hoc etiam servi alii alio- rum. Ὑπὸ ζυγὸν, id est, sub imperio herili. Sic & vox usurpatur Levit. XXIX. 13. Es. IX. 3. & alibi.

Τοὺς ἰδίους δεσπότας πάσης τιμῆς ἀξίους ἡγείσθωσαν.

Tanquam Magistratus suos domesticos. Vide Roman. XIII. vers. 7. 1. Petr. II. vers. 17.

Primùm de servis infidelium: Deinde fidelium agit. De illis forte nonnulli persuasi erant, liber- tatem Christianam tollere servitutem infidelibus præstandam. Monitos ergo servos vult, quod non servitutem tantùm, sed & jugum, h. e. graviorem servitutem, si domini duriores sint, sustinere te- neantur, 1. Petr. II. vers. 18. salva libertate Chri- stiana, quæ, ne in rebus religionis servi hominum fiamus, præstat, 1. Cor. VII. 23. non autem pote- statem herilem tollit, quemadmodum Evange- lium non abolet politiam. Adde quod servi E- bræorum post sexennium liberi reddi solebant, Exod. XXI. 2. Ne idem ergo Christiani opina- rentur, informatione opus videbatur, monente Au- gustino quæst. LXXVII. in Exod. Denique occur- rendum etiam erat scandalo gentilium, quod oritu- rum erat, nisi honorassent servi Christiani Domi- nos infideles. Omnem itaque honorem tum re- verentiæ, tum obedientiæ exhibere jubentur. Ne- que enim, ut hic Theophylactus, quia Christi fidem exceperint, credant se liberos fore. Verum libertate utuntur, cum à pravis sunt facinoribus liberi, corpore vero servituti obnoxii. Quæ servitus pro libertate habeatur, cum eam pro Christi nomine quisquam subierit.

Ἵνα μὴ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ ἡ διδασκαλία βλασφημῆται.

Nomen DEI maledictis impetitur, cum male vivunt, qui ejus se dicunt cultores. Vide Rom. II. 24. Es. LII. 5. Ezech. XXXVI. vers. 23. dicunt enim extranei: qualem isti Deum habent? Sic & ἡ διδασκαλία doctrina Evangelica traducitur, velut imperiorum dissolutrix.

Additur causa gravissima, ne nomen Domini, & Doctrina Evangelica, quæ κατ' ἀντονομασίαν do- ctrina vocatur 1. Tim. V. 17. blasphemetur. Nam Gentiles non ex verbis dogmata, sed ex ipsis re- bus & vita judicare solent. Quo de Theophyla- ctus: Nam tum maxime detestarentur infideles Christi Domini hoc sanctissimum dogma, cum illud per fideles ipsos oppugnatum iri conspicerent: quip- pe quod ad tolerantiam & placabilitatem sectatores suos instituit, nec contumaces esse permittit. Quod si benignos se servi præstiterint, & ad parendum faciles erunt, demirabuntur haud dubie domini in- fideles, & obstupescent Christiana religionis virtu- tem, quæ tanti sit, ut servorum etiam mores, qui componi, & castigari haud facile possunt, tum faci- les reddat, ut imperanti mox pareant.

## 6:2
Vers. 2. And they that have believing masters, let them not despise them, because they are brethren) Let them not despise them for the reason that they are brothers among themselves in Christ. That equality does not remove the other distinctions of persons.

— Ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον δουλευέτωσαν) Serve them all the more zealously. Civil laws prescribed nothing to slaves, because masters compelled them sufficiently to do what was for the masters' use. Now, since through the Gospel masters had become much milder, precepts had to be given to slaves as well.

Ὅτι πιστοί εἰσι καὶ ἀγαπητοὶ οἱ τῆς εὐεργεσίας ἀντιλαμβανόμενοι) First, because they are endowed with faith in God; secondly, they are to be loved for this reason, that they take care to benefit you, that is, to clothe you, feed you, and protect you from injuries. ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι means to take care of someone. Thus ἀντιλαβόμενοι ἀληθείας, Isa. XXVI. 3.

This rule concerns slaves who were under the yoke of faithful masters. Three reasons for it are given: (1) Because they are believers. For if one must serve unbelievers, how much more those who are of the same faith as we are; for we are bound to perform the duties of charity more to them, Gal. V. 10. (2) Because they are worthy of love, because they treat their slaves equally as brothers with sincere love. Therefore, a great zeal for love excites one to return duties mutually. But when he says 'beloved,' he removes fear from the slaves, as Theophylact warns, and introduces charity. For those whom they revere and fear, they generally also hate. Rather, he says, let slaves serve and obey their masters the more willingly, the more they have been made partakers of benefits. But masters are faithful and beloved in this, because they take care that slaves are made partakers of benefits. (3) Because τῆς εὐεργεσίας ἀντιλαμβανόμενοι: which others explain concerning the benefits with which they are affected by Christ the Lord: Thus blessed Balduinus, and our blessed Gerhard, who understands the inheritance of eternal life, which Christ merited for all; or also by having a relation to the masters, because they are partakers of the benefit of Christ equally as the slaves are. Others prefer to interpret it concerning the beneficence which slaves partake of from their masters, by whom, as Christians and brothers in the Lord, services are compensated more liberally to them: which explanation of the Greek interpreters pleased Grotius, but in such a way that there is no need for the hyperbaton that others posit. But because taking care of slaves is common to faithful and unfaithful masters, and the force of the argument is not constituted in comparison, and the meaning of the Greek word is more common in the sense of participation, the exposition of blessed Luther is to be preferred, 'die der Wohlthat theilhafftig seyn,' just as Ambrose understood it concerning the beneficence of GOD, which faithful masters and slaves equally partake of in Christ, whom Lombard, Thomas, and the Reformed follow, interpreting it as the divine benefit: not to mention that some add the word 'God' to 'beneficence.' For this is not found in the Greek codices. For why should slaves not more readily perform the duties which they are bound to perform for unfaithful masters to those who are partakers of the same grace with them and co-heirs of salvation? Crocius also agrees, making the argument of blessed Balduinus his own: For the care for slaves was common to faithful and unfaithful masters. The Apostle, however, wishes here to note those things which are exceptional among the faithful. Slaves were using the communion of the divine benefit, that is, the calling to Christ, as a pretext for their liberty; the Apostle makes an argument by which they are obligated to serve more promptly.

Ταῦτα δίδασκε, καὶ παρακάλει) I say this to you thus, because it is your duty also to teach slaves.

These things can be referred in general to those things which the Apostle has warned about until now, not only concerning slaves, but also concerning widows, Presbyters, etc., indeed to all things that preceded these. For those things partly concern διδασκαλίαν, or doctrine and information, and partly παράκλησιν, or exhortation, so that this is a general conclusion of the admonitions. Crocius explains it thus: Teach these things to those who are ignorant, or are in doubt. And exhort those who know and do not do; others do so more remissly, and more sluggishly. Theophylact: There is need, therefore, not only of authority and dogma for teaching, which indeed he implies when he says 'teach,' but also of kindness and gentleness, which is preferred when he says 'exhort.' For the teacher performs the office of a physician. Since he now soothes, now irritates the ulcers. He teaches that it is to be taken in a general sense, both by the collation in chapter I, verse 3, and by the antithesis subjoined. For since he has hitherto prescribed what is to be taught by sincere Doctors, he now, by way of antithesis, warns concerning false Doctors, and their heterodoxy and life and custom, or perverse negotiation, especially the avarice to be detested and diligently fled, and from the opposite side commends true gain and contentment of piety, and sincerity in confession, in the office of exhortation, and in the preservation of the doctrine of faith, he inculcates again as a finishing touch. Therefore follows

PART II. OF CHAPTER VI. Antithesis or Collation of false Doctors with the true Doctor.

Latin:
