Vers. 2. Οἱ δὲ πιστοὺς ἔχοντες δεσπότας μὴ καταφρονείτω- σαν, ὅτι ἀδελφοί εἰσι) Ne ob id eos contemnant, quod in- ter se fratres sunt in Christo. Ista paritas cætera persona- rum discrimina non tollit.

— Ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον δουλευέτωσαν) Eo impensius illis servite. Leges civiles nihil præcipiebant servis: quia domini satis eos cogebant facere, quod ex usu dominorum esset. Nunc cum per Evangelium domini facti essent multo leniores, præcepta etiam servis danda fuêre.

Ὅτι πιστοί εἰσι καὶ ἀγαπητοὶ οἱ τῆς εὐεργεσίας ἀντιλαμβανό- μενοι) Primum, quia fide in Deum sunt præditi: dein- de diligendi eo nomine, quod curam gerant, ut vobis be- nefaciant, id est, ut vos vestiant, pascant, ab injuriis prote- gant, ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι est curam alicujus gerere. Sic ἀντι- λαβόμενοι ἀληθείας Esa. XXVI. 3.

Hæc regula servos concernit, qui sub jugo erant Dominorum fidelium. Tres autem ejus ratio- nes redduntur: (1) Quia fideles sunt. Nam si in- fidelibus serviendum, quanto magis illis, qui fidei ejusdem nobiscum sunt, illis enim magis chari- tatis officia præstare tenemur, Gal. V. 10. (2.) Quia dilectione digni sunt, quod servos pariter ceu fra- tres dilectione prosequantur sincerâ. Multum ergo dilectionis studium ad mutuo reddenda of- ficia excitat. Cum vero dilectos inquit, servis, monente Theophylacto, formidinem demit, & charitatem inducit. Nam quos verentur & timent, eos plerumque & odio habent. Quin potius inquit eo libentius servi dominis obsequantur & servant, quo & beneficiorum sint effecti participes. Domini vero eo fideles sunt & dilecti, quippe qui, servi ut beneficiis efficiantur, curent. (3) Quia τῆς εὐεργεσίας ἀντιλαμβανόμενοι: quod de beneficiis, quibus à Christo Domino afficiuntur, alii explicant: Ita B. Balduinus, & B. Gerhardus noster, qui intelli- git hæreditatem vitæ æternæ, quam Christus o- mnibus promeruit; vel etiam relatione ad Do- minos habita, quia beneficii Christi participes sunt æque ut servi: Alii malunt interpretari de bene- ficentia, quam ab heris suis participant servi, à quibus utpote Christianis & fratribus in Domino liberalius ipsis compensantur servitia: quæ Græ- corum Interpp. explicatio Grotio placuit, sed ita, ut hyperbato, quod alii ponunt, opus non sit. Sed quia curam gerere servorum fidelibus & in- fidelibus Dominis commune est, nec in compa- ratione ἐνέργεια & vis argumenti constituitur, ac significatio verbi Græci sensu participationis com- munior est, præferenda B. Lutheri expositio, die der Wohlthat theilhafftig seyn, quemadmodum Ambrosius de beneficentia DEI, quam in Chri- sto æque Domini ac servi fideles participant, in- tellexit, quem sequuntur Lombardus, Thomas, Re- formati, de divino beneficio interpretantes: ut taceam, quod nonnulli vocem Dei ad beneficen- tiam addant. Hæc enim non reperitur in Græcis codd. Quidni enim officia, quæ infidelibus Do- minis præstare tenentur servi, promtius iis, qui secum ejusdem gratiæ participes, & cohæredes salutis sunt, exhibeant? Annuit & Crocius B. Bal- duini argumentum suum faciens: Cura enim pro servis communis erat fidelibus & infidelibus Domi- nis. Apostolus autem hic ea notare vult, quæ fidelium sunt eximia. Servi communionem divini beneficii, id est, vocationis ad Christum prætexebant suæ li- bertati; Apostolus facit argumentum, quo ad prom- ptius serviendum obligentur.

Ταῦτα δίδασκε, καὶ παρακάλει) Hoc ita tibi dico, quia tuum est etiam servos docere.

Hæc referri possunt in genere ad ea, quæ ha- ctenus non de servis tantum, sed etiam de vi- duis, Presbyteris &c. monuit Apostolus, imo ad omnia, quæ his præcessere. Illa enim partim διδασκαλίαν, seu doctrinam & informationem, partim παράκλησιν, seu adhortationem concer- nunt, ut generalis sit hæc monitorum conclu- sio. Crocius sic explicat: Hæc doce, eos, qui ignorant, aut dubitant. Et exhortare; Eos, qui sciunt & non faciunt; alii remissius faciunt, segniusque. Theophylactus: Non itaque autho- ritate solum, & dogmate docendi est opus, quod sane cum doce inquit, prætendit, sed & benigni- tate & mansuetudine, quod cum exhortare dicit, præfertur. Fungitur quippe præceptor medici mu- nere. Siquidem modo lenit, modo exasperat ulce- ra. In genere accipienda esse docet tum colla- tio cap. I. vers. 3. tum antithesis subjuncta. Nam quum hactenus docenda Doctoribus sinceris præscripserit, jam κατ' ἀντίθεσιν de falsis Docto- ribus, eorumque heterodoxia ac vita & consue- tudine, vel negotiatione perversa, imprimis de- testanda avaritia sedulo fugienda, commonefa- cit, atque ex adverso verum quæstum & ἀυτάρ- κειαν commendat pietatis, & sinceritatis, in con- fessione, adhortationis munere, ac doctrinæ fi- dei conservatione colophonis loco iterum incul- cat. Sequitur itaque

PARS II. CAPITIS VI. Ἀντίθεσις vel Collatio falsorum Doctorum cum vero Doctore.

## 6:3
Verse 3. If any one teaches otherwise) See above I. v. 3.

After the Apostle has sincerely proposed the teaching which is to be delivered in the Church: he now warns concerning heterodoxy, which is to be fled by all means: describing both the doctrine of the heterodox, as being different from those things which he had delivered concerning Christ, sent into the world to save sinners, concerning the one GOD the Saviour of all, and the one mediator of GOD and men, concerning the great mystery of piety, and concerning the Anti-Christ: and thus alien from the sound words of Christ, and the doctrine of piety, v. 3. as well as their morals, pursuits, and life, as being vain pride, a craving for questions, and disputes of words most harmful, and execrable avarice, while they hunt for gain from piety, verses 4 and 5. To which he therefore opposes the true gain of piety, to be uniquely aimed at by sincere Doctors, and indeed by all the faithful, with a serious flight from avarice, which is the root of all evils, and makes one wander from the faith, from verse 6 to 10. and the pursuit of justice and other virtues not sluggishly to be followed by the man of GOD, verse 11, as also the battle to be fought bravely for the faith by the power of the calling and the divine promise and the example of the profession of Christ, verses 12, 13, so that he may remain devoid of every stain and fault, until the illustrious coming of Christ, which the only blessed and immortal God will show, verses 14, 15, 16. And this as much as concerns the life and pursuits of the man of GOD, or the minister of the word. Regarding doctrine and duty, he especially commends these to Timothy, and in his person to all men of GOD, concerning whom he warns the rich of this age, verses 17, 18, 19, and warns that they ought to sincerely guard the deposit of heavenly doctrine, verses 20, 21, so that thus true Doctors may show themselves no less different from the false by their exhortation than by their teaching, as those who make gain from piety, and convert the faith into profane babblings and antitheses of knowledge falsely so called. Crocius notes that there are those who interpret 'teaching otherwise' as the untimely and obstinate defense of true dogma not always accepted by everyone, which is to be distinguished from 'false teaching': But there is no doubt for him that the Apostle here notes 'false teaching.' But that is not only when something contrary to Apostolic doctrine is taught to be believed, but also when something different from it is taught. Gal. I. 8, 9.

And does not consent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ.

He consents [approaches] קרב, which is said of those who come to the altar, Levit. IX. verse 7, and elsewhere. The Gospel is to be treated with no less reverence: whose words are truly sound as above I. 10, 2. Tim. I. 13, IV. 3, Tit. I. 9, II. 1, because they have nothing unwholesome mixed in, which the dogmas of the Rabbis and Philosophers do not lack.

Words are called sound, not only because they contain nothing unwholesome, but also because they uniquely make for spiritual health, which we have in the wounds of Christ, Eph. LIII. 5, and in his Evangelical sermons, Luke IV. 18: nor are they opposed only to the tenets and doctrines of the Rabbis and Philosophers, but especially to those of heretics and false doctors. Some understand the words of Christ, which he himself had in the days of his flesh: But they are more rightly understood as words about Christ: unless you call the words of Christ more generally, which were delivered through the Spirit of Christ to the Prophets and Apostles, 1 Pet. I. 11, III. 2. He understands an approach not of the feet, but of the mind. He is said to approach who approves, holds, professes, and acquiesces. He does not approach who does not approve, does not acquiesce. He does not say, who rejects, but who does not approach, implying that those who by the very fact do not deliver or profess sound doctrine, even if they do not reject it, are to be avoided. Those also do not approach who are neutral, or are silent when they ought not to be silent.

And to the teaching according to godliness.

Here 'καὶ', as often, is explanatory. For the words of Christ are truly doctrine making for godliness. 'Κατ’ εὐσέβειαν' is that which is suitable to godliness, as in Tit. I. 1.

There is no reason why, having abandoned the proper meaning, which is copulative, we should depart to the meaning of explanation. For the doctrine of Christ, and concerning Christ, also makes for the health of the soul, providing us with medicine against spiritual diseases, and 'Φάρμακα τῆς ψυχῆς' [remedies of the soul]; and it informs us about true godliness, lest, falling away from it, we suffer a relapse, John V. verse 14; nor does it only make us wise unto salvation regarding faith in Christ, 2 Tim. III. verse 15, but it also exhibits those things which make for godliness and the sincere worship of GOD. Therefore, we have here a description of theology, which is doctrine according to godliness, in which the true sense concerning GOD and the sincere worship of GOD is handed down.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Εἴ τις ἑτεροδιδασκαλᾶ) Vide supra I. v. 3.

Postquam τὴν διδασκαλίαν sincere proposuit Apostolus, quæ tradenda in Ecclesia: jam de ἑτεροδιδασκαλία monet, quæ omnibus modis fu- gienda: describens tum heterodoxorum doctri- nam, ceu diversam ab iis, quæ de Christo, in mundum misso ad servandum peccatores, de uno DEO Salvatore omnium, & uno mediatore DEI & hominum, de magno pietatis mysterio, & de Anti-Christo tradiderat: adeoque alienam à sa- nis sermonibus Christi, & doctrina pietatis, v. 3. tum mores, studia, & vitam, utpote vanam su- perbiam, pruritum quæstionum, & pugnas ver- borum maxime noxias, & avaritiam execrandam, dum lucrum è pietate aucupantur vers. 4. & 5. Quibus proinde opponit verum pietatis quæstum à sinceris Doctoribus, imo omnibus fidelibus unice intendendum, cum seria avaritiæ, quæ radix est malorum omnium, & à fide aberrare facit, fuga, à vers. 6. ad 10. & justitiæ ac aliarum vir- tutum studium non segniter homini DEI sectan- dum vers. 11. ut & prælium vi vocationis & pro- missionis divinæ atque exempli professionis Chri- sti fortiter pro fide depugnandum vers. 12. 13. ut maneat maculæ & culpæ omnis expers, usque ad illustrem adventum Christi, quem exhibiturus est solus beatus & immortalis Deus v. 14. 15. 16. Atque hoc quantum ad vitam & studia hominis DEI, vel ministri verbi. Quoad doctrinam & officium ea imprimis commendat Timotheo, & in ejus persona omnibus DEI hominibus, de quibus divites hujus seculi commonefacere vers. 17. 18. 19. & monet, quod depositum doctrinæ cœlestis sincere custodire debeant vers. 20. 21. ut ita non minus τῇ παρακλήσει quam τῇ διδα- σκαλίᾳ veri Doctores à falsis se diversos præbe- ant, utpote qui e pietate quæstum faciunt, fidem in prophanas κενοφωνίας, & ἀντιθέσεις τῆς ψευδω- νούκυ γνώσεως convertunt. Crocius notat esse, qui ἑτεροδιδασκαλίαν intempestivam, obstinatam- que veri dogmatis non semper ab omnibus re- cepti defensionem interpretentur, quæ à ψευδο- διδασκαλίᾳ distinguatur: Sed dubium non est ipsi, quin Apostolus ψευδοδιδασκαλίαν hic notet. Ea autem non est tantum cum contrarium quid doctrinæ Apostolicæ, sed etiam cum diversum ab eadem credendum traditur. Gal. I. 8. 9.

Καὶ μὴ προσέρχηται ὑγιαίνουσι λόγοις τοῖς τῦ Κυρίυ ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ χρισῦ.

Προσέρχεται קרב, quod dicitur de iis, qui ad altare ve- niunt, Levit. IX. vers. 7. & alibi. Non minori reveren- tia tractandum est Evangelium: cujus sermones vere sunt ὑγιαίνοντες ut supra I. 10. 2. Tim. I. 13. IV. 3. Tit. I. 9. II. 1. quia nihil insalubre admixtum habent, quo non carent do- gmata Rabbinorum & Philosophorum.

Sermones dicuntur ὑγιαίνοντες, non modo quia nihil insalubre continent, sed etiam quia ad sa- nitatem spiritualem, quam in vulneribus Christi Ef. LIII. 5. & concionibus ejus Evangelicis Luc. IV. 18. habemus, unice faciunt: nec tantum Rab- binorum & Philosophorum, sed imprimis hæreti- corum & falsorum doctorum placitis & doctrinis opponuntur. Nonnulli sermones Christi intelli- gunt, quos ipse in diebus carnis habuit: Sed re- ctius intelliguntur sermones de Christo: nisi ge- neralius sermones Christi dicas, qui per Spiri- tum Christi Prophetis & Apostolis traditi 1. Petr. I. 11. III, 2. Accessum non pedum, sed mentis in- telligit. Accedere dicitur, qui approbat, tenet, profitetur, & acquiescit. Non accedit, qui non approbat, non acquiescit. Non ait, qui rejicit, sed qui non accedit, innuens, qui facto ipso non tra- dunt aut profitentur sanam doctrinam, etsi eam non rejiciant, vitandos esse. Non accedunt et- iam qui neutrales sunt, vel tacent, cum tacen- dum non est.

Καὶ τῇ κατ’ εὐσέβειαν διδασκαλίᾳ.

Hic καὶ, ut sæpe, est ἐξηγητικός. Nam verba Christi ve- re sunt doctrina ad pietatem faciens. Κατ’ εὐσέβειαν est, quod pietati convenit, ut Tit. I. 1.

Non est, cur relicta propria significatione, quæ est copulativa, ad significationem ἐξηγήσεως abea- mus. Nam doctrina Christi, ac de Christo, & ad sanitatem animæ facit, nobis medicinam adver- sus morbos spirituales sufficiens, & Φάρμακα τῆς ψυχῆς; & de vera pietate nos informat, ne ab ea deficiscentes recidivam patiamur Joh. V. vers. 14. nec solum de fide in Christum ad salutem nos sapientes reddit 2. Tim. III. vers. 15. sed etiam, quæ ad pietatem, ac sincerum DEI cultum faciunt, exhibet. Theologiæ itaque descriptionem hic ha- bemus, quæ doctrina est secundum pietatem, in qua verus de DEO sensus, & sincerus DEI cul- tus traditur.

## 6:3
verse 3. & the root of immortality, Wisdom XV. verse 3. Theodoret understands the possession of future goods itself by the foundation. He says, he called the possession of riches uncertain, but he called the perception of future things the foundation: For those are immutable and immovable. But because a foundation is spoken of relatively to those things which lean upon the foundation, and those goods are of the future age, the foundation must be distinguished from the goods themselves and their perception. Others make this a peculiar precept: charge the rich in the present age; that they may lay hold of eternal life, by which method the argument of Grotius and the Papists clearly falls: nor is the apprehension of eternal life attributed in any way either to alms or to good works. For they are only commanded to lay hold of eternal life, that is, to do that by which they may one day possess heavenly treasures, that they may lay up treasures for themselves in heaven, Matt. V. verse 20. but it is not taught by what method that apprehension is made, which elsewhere is taught to be made through the apprehension of that incomparable treasure, namely Christ, and his righteousness, which is done through faith. But even if you refer these to the preceding words, so that they cohere with them as a final cause, and do not take it as a peculiar precept, since they can be referred neither to good works in general, nor to alms in particular, as if eternal life were apprehended through them, which is claimed by the Apostle for faith alone; they can not inconveniently be referred, with the Blessed Baldwin, to that precept by which the rich are commanded to hope in the living GOD, that is, to trust in GOD, who provides all things abundantly for enjoyment, not only bodily, but also spiritual and heavenly goods, the end of which trust is eternal life, by which that very thing is apprehended.

The Blessed Hunnius explains the words of the Apostle in this way; for thus they store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that is, by their liberality and beneficence they attain to laying a good and safe foundation for their affairs, not only so that wealth may be durable, but even especially so that by this exercise of beneficence they may take on more and more increments in spiritual things, in piety, in faith, which is accustomed to be active through love, and in the remaining related virtues. He understood the rest in the same way as they are explained by the Blessed Baldwin. Who, moreover, handed down this exposition: He opposes a good foundation to the uncertainty of earthly wealth. For future goods are solid and perpetual, and what he understands by them, he soon adds by epexegesis, namely eternal life, which is sought and apprehended as a certain treasure by doing good from the goods of this age, not as if alms merit eternal life, but because by our liberality we exercise faith and bind others to us, so that they may both pray for us and at some time bear witness of true piety toward the needy: to whom this happens, they can have a certain hope of eternal life. In the same sense Christ said in Matt. XIX. verse 21. Give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.

The Blessed Gerhard does not depart from our explanation, saying that that foundation is faith in CHRIST, from which flow works of mercy, done out of charity, which GOD promised he would most bountifully reward: not, however, from merit, but from grace. For he adds those things which refer to our explanation, that namely he understands faith by reason of the object which it apprehends, not as it is a quality in us, when he disputes against Estius, who does not indeed profess faith to be the foundation of good works and righteousness, but refers good works and the foundation of salvation, which we expect in the future. For he answers: Faith is not only the foundation of righteousness, but the instrumental cause through which we apprehend the righteousness of Christ, so that it may be imputed to us. And further: Good works are the fruits of faith, meanwhile CHRIST alone apprehended by true faith is the foundation of our salvation, Acts IV. v. 12. 1. Corinth. III. verse 11. likewise: as our works are not the foundation of election, but CHRIST: so also the foundation of justification and glorification is CHRIST alone, 1. Timoth. I. verse 9. Tit. III. verse 6.

Latin:

vers. 3. & radix ἀθανασίας, Sapient. XV. vers. 3. Theodoretus ipsam bonorum futurorum possessio- nem intelligit per fundamentum. Divitiarum, inquit, possessionem appellavit incertam, futuro- rum autem perceptionem appellavit fundamen- tum : Illa enim sunt immutabilia & immobilia. Sed quia fundamentum relative dicitur ad ea, quæ innituntur fundamento, & illa bona sunt futuri seculi, fundamentum ab ipsis bonis, eo- rumque perceptione distinguendum est. Alii præceptum peculiare istud faciunt παράγγελλε τοῖς πλουσίοις ἐν τῷ νῦν αἰῶνι; ἵνα ἐπιλάβωνται τῆς αἰωνίꙋ ζωῆς, quo pacto plane cadit argumen- tum Grotii & Papistarum : nec ullatenus tri- buitur vitæ æternæ apprehensio sive eleemosy- nis, sive operibus bonis. Jubentur enim tan- tum, ut apprehendant vitam æternam, id est, id agant, quo thesauros cœlestes olim possi- deant, ut thesauros sibi in cœlis colligant, Matth. V. vers. 20. non autem docetur, qua ra- tione fiat illa apprehensio, quæ alibi per appre- hensionem thesauri illius incomparabilis, Chri- sti nempe, & justitiæ ejus, quæ per fidem fit, fieri docetur. Sed etiamsi ad verba præceden- tia hæc referas, ut cohæreant cum illis ut causa finalis, nec ut peculiare præceptum accipias, quum neque ad bona opera in genere, neque ad eleemosynam in specie referri possint, quasi per ea apprehendatur vita æterna, quod non nisi fidei vindicatur ab Apostolo; non incom- mode cum Beato Balduino ad illud præceptum referri possunt, quo divites sperare jubentur in DEO vivo, hoc est, DEO confidere, quod præstat omnibus abunde ad fruendum, non tantum corporalia, sed etiam spiritualia & cœ- lestia bona, cujus fiduciæ finis est vita æterna, qua illa ipsa apprehenditur.

Beatus Hunnius hoc modo explicat verba A- postoli; sic enim recondunt sibi ipsis fundamen- tum bonum imposterum, hoc est, sua liberali- tate & beneficentia consequuntur, ut rerum sua- rum bonum ac tutum fundamentum ponant, non modo ut opes sint durabiles, sed vel maxime, ut isto beneficentiæ exercitio magis magisque in spiri- tualibus incrementa sumant, in pietate, in fide, quæ per charitatem operosa soles esse, & in reli- quis cognatis virtutibus. Cætera eodem modo intellexit, quo exponuntur à Beato Balduino. Qui præterea hanc tradidit ἔκθεσιν: Fundamen- tum bonum opponit incertitudini opum terrena- rum. Nam futura bona solida sunt & perpetua, & quid per ea intelligat, per epexegesin mox ad- dit, vitam nimirum æternam, quæ quasi thesau- rus quidam conquiritur & apprehenditur bene- faciendo de bonis hujus seculi, non quasi eleemo- syna mereatur vitam æternam, sed quia libem- litate nostra fidem exercemus aliosque nobis de- vincimus, ut & pro nobis orent, & testimonium aliquando veræ pietatis erga egenos perhibeant: quod quibus contingit, bi certam vitæ æternæ spem habere possunt. Eodem sensu Christus dixit Matth. XIX. vers. 21. Da pauperibus, & habebis thesaurum in cælo.

A nostra explicatione non abit Beatus Ger- hardus, illud θεμέλιον, inquiens, est fides in CHRISTUM, ex qua promanant opera mi- sericordiæ, ex charitate facta, qua DEUS lar- gissime se recompensaturum promisit: non tamen ex merito, sed ex gratia. Addit enim ea, quæ nostram referunt explicationem, quod nempe fidem intelligat ratione objecti, quod appre- hendit, non ut qualitas est in nobis, cum con- tra Estium disputat, qui fidem bonorum ope- rum ac justitiae fundamentum quidem non pro- fitetur, sed bona opera ac fundamentum salutis, quam in futuro expectamus, refert. Respondet n. Fides non solum est fundamentum justitiae, sed causa instrumentalis, per quam Christi justitiam apprehendimus, ut ea nobis imputetur. Et por- ro : Bona opera sunt fructus fidei, interim solus CHRISTUS vera fide apprehensus est salutis nostrae fundamentum, Actor. IV. v. 12. 1. Corinth. III. versu 11. item : ut electionis fundamentum non sunt nostra opera, sed CHRISTUS: ita quoque justificationis & glorificationis fundamen- tum est solus CHRISTUS, 1. Timoth. I. vers. 9. Tit. III. vers. 6.

## 6:4
V. 4. Τετύφωται [He is puffed up]) See what happens to those, he says, who depart from the Gospel; they are puffed up, to be sure, as unhealthy bodies are wont to be. See above III. 6. they become 'κατῆς οἰήσεως ἔμπλεοι ἄτικοι' [full of conceit, senseless].

Μηδὲν ἐπιστάμενος [Knowing nothing]) Knowing nothing, namely, of those things which have the greatest power for godliness. That is to be supplied from the preceding.

This spiritual inflation is pride properly, because the persuasion of knowledge puffs up, 1 Cor. VIII. 1, 2 Cor. XII. 20, which has precipitated most into heterodoxies and heresies. They derive the word 'τετύφωται' from the typhonic wind, which was believed to take away the mind and reason, to such an extent that those seized by that wind go insane, whence it is called a 'δεινὸς καὶ ὑβριστὴς ἄνεμος' [terrible and insolent wind]. What else happens to those seized and puffed up by the typhus of pride, who please themselves and are inflated by the persuasion of knowledge, so that they often cling to their opinions to the point of insanity, and proudly despise others, nay, prefer their own senses to the Apostolic doctrine itself? Such are in reality 'μηδὲν ἐπιστάμενοι', knowing nothing truly, however much they may swell with wisdom. Nothing of those things which pertain either to faith or to true godliness. Compare here what is in James III. 13. Theodoret: It is necessary, he says, to stand in those things which have been decreed by the Lord. For he who indeed dares to transgress, but follows his own reasonings and thoughts, knows nothing indeed of those things which it is necessary to know, but serves only pride and arrogance. Therefore, the pride of the false teacher is not from excessive wisdom, but from great ignorance. For he who wishes to be wise beyond Christ, not content with his words may seem wise to himself and his associates. Moreover, he knows nothing either theoretically, because he is ignorant of what is necessary for salvation while he is occupied with other less necessary things, or practically, because he is destitute of the practical knowledge of God, as is this B. Balduinus.

Ἀλλὰ νοσῶν) He is delirious, as sick people often are. For he pursues the simile he has begun. Moreover, νοσεῖν is accustomed to be constructed in that sense with περὶ; thus Plutarch says περὶ σφραγῖδα πολυτελῆ νοσεῖν.

περὶ ζητήσεις) Concerning physical matters, of course, as Socrates used to say, which have nothing to do with us—namely, making us better—how great the uncertainties of opinions have been in these matters, see the book in Plutarch's works περὶ τῶν ἀρεσκόντων τοῖς φιλοσόφοις. And in the physics of Stobaeus. Hermas, book 3, 9. These are they who have quarrels among themselves, and because of their complaints they languish in the faith.

Questions not so much about physical matters as about the faith and about things handed down in Scripture; or those that are detrimental to the Christian faith are indicated. For when the mysteries of the faith are called into question by the subtleties of reason, which exalts itself against the word of God, and when questions outside the word of God—whether useless, vain, curious, or profane and scandalous—are stirred up, the holiness of faith is lost, and delirium follows. What is reason in sacred matters if not a delirium of things? Which Irenaeus observed especially regarding the ancient heretics, and which abundant experience testifies regarding the Scholastic disputations. Faith is an eye; he who has no eyes finds nothing, he only seeks, says Theophylact. When the soul, says Chrysostom, is burned by the fever of thoughts, when it is tossed by the fluctuation of ambiguity, then it seeks: but when it is healthy, it does not seek, but faithfully believes. Such people are truly sick in soul and intellect, they are corrupted in sense and mind, indeed they are truly insane, as Erasmus rendered the word νοσῶν, so that the antithesis might appear more clearly between the holiness of the doctrine of Christ and the insanity of the doctrine of the heterodox. Conf. 2 Tim. II. 14, 17, 23.

Καὶ λογομαχίας) There were many disputations among the philosophers about words. Those things which conduce to the body and to the conduct of life are good to Plato and Aristotle. The Porch does not want them to be called so, but προηγμένα. The Platonic and Aristotelian wise man feels pity. The fool does not feel pity, but spares. The greatest part of Stoic disputations, says Cicero, is consumed about names. But it is vicious to intend a controversy because of a change of names, says the author of Ad Herennium. Aristotle in the Topics is not wrong: Εὐλαβητέον πρὸς τοῦτο μὴ διαλέγεσθαι. You have the word λογομαχεῖν also among Greek writers, and below in 2 Timothy II, verse 14.

These are rashly restricted to the disputations of philosophers about words. The subject here is heterodox teachers, those who do not acquiesce in the sound words of Christ, not those who are entirely ignorant of Christ, and their frivolous and not rarely dangerous fights and disputations about words are noted. For often he who invents new words simultaneously begets new dogmas. Therefore, λογομαχίαι are to be avoided in the Church of God by all means, and one must adhere precisely to the sound words of Christ, nor depart from the τύπῳ τῶν ὑγιαινόντων. One must abstain not only from questions adverse to sound doctrine, but also from forms of speaking that are alien to the form of sound words. The Apostle teaches so prolifically what great damages λογομαχίαι drag along with those unhealthy questions, so that we may flee them all the more studiously.

Ἐξ ὧν γίνεται φθόνος, ἔρις, βλασφημίαι) Envy, strife, railings, frequent among philosophers, about whom Timon says: Ποίων ἔκ τ' ἐρίδων καὶ λεσχομάχων πεπλάνησθε; And elsewhere: Φοιτᾷ δὲ βροτολοιγὸς ἔρις κενεὸν λελακῦα. Νείκεος αἰνδροφόνοιο κασιγνήτη καὶ ἐριθος.

Ὑπόνοιαι πονηραὶ) Evil opinions: for ὑπονοεῖν is put for שכל, which is to think. Such were the opinions of Diagoras, that there is no God; of Epicurus, that God does not care for human affairs, which seems also to have been the opinion of Aristotle in his esoteric discourses. Of the younger Academy and the skeptics, that nothing can be perceived, that nothing is base in itself.

Envy is of the heart, contention and blasphemy of the mouth, an evil opinion of the soul and mind. Thus follow manifold sins among those who indulge in questions of this kind and λογομαχίαις (word-battles); they envy others out of the pride of their heart; for the mother of envy is ambition. They contend with others out of a zeal for Φιλονεικίας (love of strife). Contention is placed under it, not because it always follows envy, for sometimes it precedes it, but because it is more bitter after the more fervent mind, laboring, approaches to disputing. They traduce others, nay, they blaspheme the very word of GOD itself, when they not only impugn the dogmas delivered in the same, but also tear them apart with various insults; in the heat of contention, insults against men and blasphemies against GOD himself are often poured forth. There follow also depraved and impious opinions about GOD. Not only blasphemies, which perhaps slip out, but also profane opinions, which remain fixed in the minds. Which, again, were said not to philosophers ignorant of the true GOD, but to heretics turning away from the word of GOD, and perverting it.

Latin:

V. 4. Τετύφωται) Vide quid illis eveniat, inquit, qui ab Evangelio abscedunt; inflantur nempe, ut solent corpo- ra male sana. Vide supra III. 6. fiunt κατῆς οἰήσεως ἔμπλεοι ἄτικοι.

Μηδὲν ἐπιστάμενος) Nihil sciens, nempe earum rerum, quæ maximam vim habent ad pietatem. Id supplendum ex præcedentibus.

Inflatio spiritualis hæc superbia proprie est, quia persuasio scientiæ inflat 1. Cor. IIX. 1. 2. Cor. XII. 20. quæ plerosque in heterodoxias, & hæreses præcipitavit. Vocem τετύφωται à vento typhonicœ deducunt, qui creditus est mentem ac rationem adimere, adeo, ut vento isto correpti insaniant, unde δεινὸς καὶ ὑβριστὴς ἄνεμος dictus. Quid aliud contingit typho superbiæ correptis, & inflatis, qui sibi placent, & suffexi sunt scientiæ persuasio- ne, ut opinionibus suis ad insaniam sæpe inhæ- reant, aliosque superbe contemnant, imo sensus proprios ipsi Apostolicæ doctrinæ præferant. Quales revera sunt μηδὲν ἐπιστάμενοι, nihil verè scientes, quantacunque etiam sapientia turgeant. Nihil earum rerum sive quæ ad fidem, sive quæ ad veram pietatem spectant. Conf. h. l. quæ Jac. III. 13. Theodoreius: Oportet, inquit, stare in iis, quæ sunt decreta à Domino. Qui enim ea quidem audent transgredi, proprias autem rationes & cogi- tationes sequuntur, nihil quidem sciunt eorum, quæ scire oportet, soli autem superbiæ & arrogan- tiæ serviunt. Est ergo superbia falsi Doctoris non ex nimia sapientia, sed ex magna inscitia. Nam qui ultra Christum sapere vult, non contentus ser- monibus ejus, eum desipere oportet, utut sibi sociisque suis sapere videatur. Nihil autem scit vel theo- retice, quia, quæ necessaria sunt ad salutem, igno- rat, dum aliis minus necessariis est occupatus, vel præctice, quia præctica Dei cognitione destitutus, ut hic B. Balduinus.

Ἀλλὰ νοσῶν) Delirat, ut sæpe solent ægroti. Persequi- tur enim cœptam similitudinem. Solet autem νοσεῖν illo sensu construi cum περὶ, sic Plutarchus dicit περὶ σφραγῖδα πολυτελῆ νοσεῖν.

περὶ ζητήσεις) De physicis scilicet rebus, uti Socrates aje- bat, quæ nihil ad nos, nempe meliores reddendas quanta in his fuerint opinionum incerta, vide librum in Plutarchi operibus περὶ τῶν ἀρεσκόντων τοῖς φιλοσόφοις. Et in physi- cis Stobæi. Hermas ill. 9. Hi sunt, qui inter se habent lites, & propter querelas suas in fide languent.

Quæstiones non tam de physicis, quam circa fidem, & de rebus in Scriptura traditis; vel fidei Christianæ affutis indigitantur. Nam & cum mysteria fidei in quæstionem vocantur, argutiis rationis, adversus verbum Dei sese efferentis, & cum quæstiones extra Dei verbum sive inutiles, vanæ, curiosæ, sive prophanæ, ac scandalosæ moventur, Sanctitas fidei deperditur, ac deli- ratio sequitur. Quid ratio in Sacris nisi delira- tio rebus? Quod de hæreticis antiquis Irenæus im- primis observavit, & de Scholasticis disputatio- nibus locuples testatur experientia. Fides est oculus, qui non habet oculos, nihil invenit, solum- modo quærit, inquit Theophylactus. Quando ani- ma, inquit Chrysostomus, cogitationum uritur fe- bri, quando ambiguitas jactatur fluctu, tunc quæ- rit: cum vero illa sana est, non quærit, sed fideli- ter credit. Tales vere laborant animo, & intel- lectu, corrupti sunt sensu & mente, imo vere in- saniant, ut Erasmus vocem νοσῶν reddidit, ut ma- gis antithesis appareat, inter sanctitatem doctri- næ Christi, & insaniam doctrinæ heterodoxo rum. Conf. 2. Tim. II. 14. 17. 23.

Καὶ λογομαχίας) Multæ inter philosophos erant dispu- tationes de vocabulis. Ea quæ corpori & vitæ agendæ conducunt, bona sunt Platoni & Aristoteli. Non vult porticus ea sic appellari, sed προηγμένα. Miseretur sapiens Platonicus & Aristotelicus. Stoltus non miseretur; sed parcit. Maxima pars Stoicarum disputationum, ait Ci- cero, circa nomina consumitur. Vitiosum autem est, con- troversiam intendere propter nominum mutationem, ait ad Herennium Scriptor. Aristoteles in topicis non male: Εὐλαβητέον πρὸς τοῦτο μὴ διαλέγεσθαι. Verbum λογομαχεῖν habes & apud Græcos Scriptores, & infra 2. Timoth. II. vers. 14.

Temere hæc restringuntur ad Philosophorum disputationes de vocabulis. Agitur hic de hete- rodidascalis, de iis, qui non acquiescunt sanis Christi sermonibus, non de iis, qui Christum pla- ne ignorant, notanturque eorum frivolæ, & non raro periculosæ pugnæ & disputationes de ver- bis. Sæpe enim, qui fingit nova verba, simul no- va dogmata gignit. Vitandæ ergo sunt in Eccle- sia Dei omnibus modis λογομαχίαι, & inhæren- dum præcise sanis sermonibus Christi, nec à τύπῳ τῶν ὑγιαινόντων recedendum. Non tantum à quæstionibus salubri doctrinæ adversis, sed etiam à loquendi formulis, à fanorum verborum for- ma alienis, abstinendum. Quanta damna cum quæstionibus illis male sanis secum trahant λογο- μαχίαι, tam prolixe docet Apostolus, ut tanto studiosius illas fugiamus.

Ἐξ ὧν γίνεται φθόνος, ἔρις, βλασφημίαι) Invidia, lites, maledicta frequentia Philosophis, de quibus Timon: Ποίων ἔκ τ' ἐρίδων καὶ λεσχομάχων πεπλάνησθε; Et alibi: Φοιτᾷ δὲ βροτολοιγὸς ἔρις κενεὸν λελακῦα. Νείκεος αἰνδροφόνοιο κασιγνήτη καὶ ἐριθος.

Ὑπόνοιαι πονηραὶ) Opiniones malæ : nam ὑπονοεῖν ponitur pro שכל quod est cogitare. Tales opiniones Diagoræ, non esse Deum; Epicuri, Deum non curare res humanas, quæ videtur etiam Aristotelis fuisse sententia ἐν τοῖς ἐσωτερικοῖς λόγοις. Academiæ adolescentioris & scepticorum, nihil posse percipi, nihil esse turpe per se.

Invidia cordis est, contentio, & blasphemia oris, opinio mala animi, & mentis. Ita sequuntur peccata multivaria, penes illos, qui quæstionibus ejusmodi, & λογομαχίαις indulgent; invident aliis præ superbia cordis; invidiæ enim mater est ambitio. Cum aliis contendunt ex studio Φιλονεικίας. Contentio subjugitur, non quod semper invidiam sequatur, interdum enim præcedit, sed quod acerbior sit, postquam animus fervidior laborans accedit ad disputandum. Traducunt alios, imo ipsummet DEI verbum blasphemant, cum dogmata in eodem tradita non modo impugnant, sed variis etiam convitiis proscindunt, in æstu contentionis sæpe effunduntur tum convitia in homines, tum blasphemiæ in DEUM ipsum. Sequuntur etiam opiniones pravæ atque impiæ de DEO. Non solum blasphemiæ, quæ forte excidunt, sed opiniones etiam prophanæ, quæ animis fixæ hærent. Quæ iterum non Philosophis veri DEI ignaris, sed hæreticis à verbo DEI deflectentibus, idque pervertentibus, dicta sunt.

## 6:5
Vers. 5.

Διαπαρατριβαί) In other books παραδιατριβαὶ, which is correct: Διατριβὴ is a word proper to philosophers, a disputation: Whence Gellius called the very place where one disputes a διατριβὴν. Paul added παρὰ, which not rarely in composition signifies that which is not correct, as when we say παράγραμμα or παραγραμματισμὸς, παραλογίζεσθαι, παρενοίκησις, and the like.

Διεφθαρμένων ἀνθρώπων τὸν νῦν) that is, having a mind alienated from piety, which is truly φθείρεσθαι 2 Cor. XI. 3.

It is certain that παραδιατριβαὶ is read by most codices, and the principal editions retain it in the text: Why therefore did Grotius substitute another, which he judged less correct, in the text? He does not, however, say διατριβαὶ, by which are understood disputations, which are not condemned in themselves, but have the greatest utility; nay, they are necessary, employed by Christ and the Apostles themselves: But παραδιατριβαὶ are useless disputations, Erasmus renders them superfluous; others explain them as perverse disputations: by which truth is obscured, intellect is blunted, judgment is corrupted, faith is overturned. To Chrysostom and Theophylact they seem to be called διαπάρατριβαὶ, which are constant rubbings and frictions, because the heterodox wear each other down and infect others with their scab. For just as infected and diseased sheep, says Theophylact, if they associate with healthy and sound ones, infect them also with the disease; so also these, who are imbued with perverse morals or depraved dogmas, will corrupt those with whom they have taken up association. Theodoret has it thus: For those who depart from the truth and follow their own thoughts, they indeed attempt to teach things that are convenient, but from this follows contention and envy, and from contention blasphemy against GOD is undertaken, and with faith cast out, evil suspicions arise, and from this are generated certain strifes, which infect those who approach. For this signifies that: The contagion of those who are corrupt in mind. For just as sick sheep, if they associate with the healthy, infect them with the same disease: so also these fill those who associate with them with the same evil. Whence he also exclaims in prohibiting him: Withdraw from those who are of this kind. They are therefore of a corrupt mind, and they indicate a corrupt mind, and render it further more corrupt: such as he calls φρεναπάτας in Tit. I. verse 10. however much such questioners may seem wise to themselves above others. Which corruption of the mind indeed draws with it the corruption of the will, because the mind is the guide of the will, yet this is not directly indicated.

And destitute of the truth) Deprived of the knowledge of that truth which is of the greatest importance.

Supposing that godliness is a way of gain) They think that piety, that is, Christianity, ought to serve their own profit. The passage in Is. LVII. 11 seems to be referred to.

It is not precisely a στέρησις or privation of truth previously known that is inferred; those who have never known the Evangelical truth can also come under this designation. But those have piety for gain who, under the guise of the profession of the Christian faith, seek profit and their own advantages, Tit. I. verse 11, 2 Pet. II. verse 3. You see, says Theophylact: how also contentious words produce shameful gain, since men of this sort, by contending and disputing, draw many disciples after themselves, and claim wealth, and entice many to themselves by art and glibness. He notes avarice, to which false teachers were addicted, and who abused the Christian religion, and gain, especially also through the multiplication of questions and disputes, enticing the ignorant under the guise of singular wisdom. By piety is to be understood the doctrine of faith and

of piety. But they are called 'supposing,' not because they truly think so, but because they present themselves as such, as if that opinion regarding the doctrine of faith and piety clung to them, and they express this sense of theirs by the very deed. Indeed, they betrayed their opinion by a shameful act, so that anyone who considered it could not doubt that they considered piety to be a trade from which profit is honestly captured. Which is an indication that they are truly corrupt in mind. But Cornelius applies these things to us ineptly. Certainly, princes who drive idle bellies from monasteries and destine the revenues for the better uses of Churches, Schools, and the poor, do not have piety for gain, but rescue it from gain.

Withdraw from such) This is not in the best Manuscript. It is also missing in many others, and in the Latin. Those who thought the sense was not full without these added it: when the matter is to the contrary: For τετύφωται, which had preceded, was not a description of the subject, but a predicate, as they say.

There is no reason why we should suspect it was added by another hand. It is found in all Greek Codices. It was read by the Greek interpreters, Theodoret, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius. And by the Latins, Ambrose, and others. But because the Apostle is occupied in warning, this addition is required. For he does not only teach what kind of false Teachers they are, but also commands that they be avoided. But he did not say, as Theophylact advises, contend with words, and oppose these, but depart, just as if he were inquiring. When you have admonished them once or twice, let them go. For how will you be able to overcome men who are disputing for the sake of money and gain? Therefore, since these cannot be corrected, decline them. Let Tit. III. verse 10 be compared.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Διαπαρατριβαί) In aliis libris παραδιατριβαὶ, quod rectum: Διατριβὴ vox propria Philosophorum, disputatio: Unde locum ipsum, ubi disputatur, διατριβὴν vocavit Gellius. Addidit Paulus παρὰ, quod non raro in compositione id significat, quod rectum non est, ut cum dicimus παράγραμμα sive παραγραμματισμὸς, παραλογίζεσθαι, παρενοίκησις, & similia.

Διεφθαρμένων ἀνθρώπων τὸν νῦν) id est, mentem habentium alienam à pietate, quod vere est φθείρεσθαι 2. Cor. XI. 3.

Legi à plerisque Codd. παραδιατριβαὶ, certum est, idque in textu retinent Editiones præcipuæ: Cur ergo aliud, quod minus rectum censuit, in textu substituit Grotius? Non autem dicit διατριβαὶ, quo disputationes intelliguntur, quæ per se damnatæ non sunt, sed utilitatem maximam habent; imo necessariæ sunt, à Christo & Apostolis ipsis adhibitæ: Sed παραδιατριβαὶ inutiles disputationes, Erasmus reddit supervacaneas; alii perversas disputationes exponunt: quibus veritas obscuratur, ingenium obtunditur, judicium cor rumpitur, fides evertitur. Chrysostomo & Theophylacto dictæ videntur διαπάρατριβαὶ, quæ sunt confricationes & attritus assidui, quod heterodoxi se mutuo atterant, & alios sua scabie inficiant. Nam quemadmodum infectæ & morbidæ oves, inquit Theophylactus, si cum sanis & integris diversentur, & illas morbo inficiunt; ita & bi, qui perversis sunt moribus vel dogmatibus pravis imbuti, eos corrumpent, quibuscum consuetudinem ceperint. Theodorettus ita habet: Qui enim à veritate recedunt, & sequuntur proprias cogitationes, ea quidem docere conantur, quæ conveniunt, hinc autem sequitur contentio & invidia, ex contentione autem adversus DEUM blasphemia suscipitnr, ejecta autem fide, oriuntur malæ suspiciones, hinc autem procreatur quædam lites, quæ inficit eos, qui appropinquant. Hoc enim si- gnificat illud: Contagio eorum, qui sunt mente corrupti. Quemadmodum enim oves ægrotæ, si cum sanis versantur, eodem eas morbo inficiunt: ita etiam hi eos, qui ipsis utuntur, eodem malo re- plent. Unde etiam ei prohibendo exclamat: Re- cede ab iis, qui sunt ejusmodi. Mente ergo cor- ruptorum sunt, & mentem corruptam indicant, & corruptiorem porro reddunt: quales φρενα- πάτας vocat Tit. I. vers. 10. utut præ aliis sibi sa- piant ejusmodi quæstionarii. Quæ mentis φθορὰ trahit quidem secum corruptionem voluntatis, quia mens voluntatis dux est, non tamen hæc directe indicatur.

Καὶ ἀπεστερημένων τῆς ἀληθείας) Destituti cognitione ejus veritatis, quæ maximi momenti est.

Νομιζόντων πορισμὸν εἶναι τὴν εὐσέβειαν) Existimant pie- tatem, id est, Christianismum quæstui suo servire debere. Respici videtur locus Es. LVII. 11.

Non στέρησις vel privatio veritatis antea co- gnitæ præcise infertur, possunt eo nomine ve- nire etiam, qui nunquam veritatem Evangeli- cam cognovere. Quæstui autem pietatem ha- bent, qui sub specie professionis fidei Christia- næ lucrum & commoda propria quærunt, Tit. I. vers. 11. 2. Petr. II. vers. 3. Vides, inquit Theophy- lactus: quemadmodum & verba contentiosa turpe pariant lucrum, quippe cum homines istiusmodi contendendo & altercando plures post se trahant discipulos, & opes vendicent, arte & dicacitate ad se alliciant multos. Notat avaritiam, cui falsi doctores erant dediti, & qui religione Christia- na abutebantur, & quæstum, imprimis etiam quæ- stionum & disputationum multiplicatione, sub specie singularis sapientiæ ignaros allicientes. Per pietatem intelligenda est doctrina fidei &

pietatis. Νομίζοντες autem dicuntur, non quod revera censeant, sed quod tales se præbeant, ac si ea ipsis de doctrina fidei & pietatis hæreat opinio, ac opere ipso istum suum sensum refe- rant, Nimirum opinionem suam facto turpi prodebant, ut, qui id consideraret, dubitare non posset, quin pietatem ducerent esse mercaturam, ex qua lucrum honeste captetur. Quod indi- cium est, vere corruptos esse mente. Inepte au- tem hæc applicat nobis Cornelius. Principes cer- te, qui otiosos ventres monasteriis pellunt, & re- ditus melioribus usibus Ecclesiarum, Scholarum, & pauperum destinant, non pietatem habent quæstui, sed à quæstu vindicant.

Ἀφίστασο ἀπὸ τῶν τοιούτων) Hoc non est in Manuscripto optimo. Deest & in aliis multis, & in Latino. Addide- runt ii, qui sensum putarunt sine his non plenum: cum contra res se habeat: Nam τετύφωται, quod præcesserat, non erat descriptio subjecti, sed prædicatum, ut lo- quuntur.

Non est, cur suspicemur, aliena manu addi- tum. Reperitur in Codd. Græcis omnibus. Le- ctum est ab interpretibus Græcis, Theodoreto, Chrysostomo, Theophylacto, Oecumenio. Et à La- tinis, Ambrosio, & aliis. Sed quia in monendo occupatur Apostolus, requiritur hæc προσθήκη. Non enim solum docet, quales sint falsi Docto- res, sed etiam eos vitari jubet. Non autem dixit, Theophylacto monente, verbis contendito, & hos oppugna, sed discede, perinde ac si inquirat. Cum semel aut bis istos commonefeceris, missos facito. Qui enim poteris homines pecuniarum & lucri gratia altercantes pervincere? Hos itaque, cum corrigi nequeant, declina. Conferatur Tit. III. vers. 10.

## 6:6
But godliness is a great gain) From Is. XXXIII. v. 6. יִרְאַת יְהוָה הִיא אוֹצָרוֹ The fear of the Lord is his treasure. It is a great gain to gain a soul. Matt. XVI. 26.

With contentment) An old saying: thrift is a great income: But more truly. That it is a great gain to be content with one's own, for that is to be in need of nothing. See 2 Cor. IX. verse 8. Thus the Hebrews say. He is rich who rejoices in his lot. Polybius and others use the word αὐταρκείας.

He had exhorted [them] away from the company of false teachers: afterwards he also exhorts [them] away from the very commerce of vices customary to them. He had noted as wicked the gain from piety, as they called it. Now, on the contrary, he celebrates the gain of true piety. This is a rhetorical correction, by which he turns what he had blamed into its opposite with a changed sense, i.e., if anyone estimates the matter rightly, piety itself is great gain, not earthly, but heavenly, not bodily, but spiritual. He calls piety both faith and the worship of GOD, not excluding, but including love of neighbor. For piety toward one's neighbor is also a kind of piety, nor can love of GOD exist without love of neighbor, 1 John IV. v. 20. Moreover, to declare the truth of great gain, αὐτάρκεια (self-sufficiency) is added to piety. For the faithful so hold piety for gain, that they are content with God alone, Job XXII. verse 25. Genesis XV. verse 1. Psalm LXXIII. verse 25. Therefore they acquiesce in the will of God, and are entirely content with the goods and gifts of GOD. Danaeus notes that the Apostle did not say πόρον, that is, income and revenue, which is received only once a year, or in a whole lifetime, but πορισμὸν, that is, a foundation and a perennial or inexhaustible fountain, which always pours forth and produces for us the highest and most abundant yields. The impious, however, are poor, because they are not rich in GOD, Luke XII. verse 21. Matthew XVI. verse 26. False teachers gape after gain; ἀχροκερδία (not being greedy for gain) ought to be most especially alien to true teachers, 1 Timothy III. verse 3. Titus I. verse 7. 1 Peter V. verse 2. whence the Apostle warns that they should study τῇ αὐταρκείᾳ (self-sufficiency), and certainly be content with their own. They, he says, with Theophylact as interpreter, are far deceived when they wrongly think piety is gain. There is indeed gain in piety, but by no means of the kind they imagine, but far more excellent. Since piety is said to be gainful, not when it abounds in money, but when it lacks it. For sufficiency and what is enough is considered in the place of huge and stable wealth. Therefore, let those who pursue piety by no means lose heart because they abound in no riches, nor possess money. Chrysostom, Homily XXXIX on 1 Corinthians XV, says: it is not affluence that produces pleasure, but a rightly instructed mind, without which, if anyone possesses everything, he will be made as if deprived of everything.

Latin:

Ἔστι δὲ πορισμὸς μέγας ἡ εὐσέβεια) Ex Es. XXXIII. v. 6. יִרְאַת יְהוָה הִיא אוֹצָרוֹ Timor Domini Thesaurus ejus. Magnus est quæstus lucrari animam. Matth. XVI. 26.

Μετὰ αὐταρκείας) Vetus dictum : magnum vectigal par- simonia : At verius. Magnum esse quæstum suo conten- tum esse, id enim est nullius rei indigere. Vide 2. Cor. IX. vers. 8. Sic dicunt Ebræi. Dives est, qui sua sorte gaudet. Utuntur voce αὐταρκείας Polybius & alii.

A falsorum Doctorum consortio dehorta- tus erat: Postmodum etiam à vitiorum ipsis so- lemnium commercio dehortatur. Quæstum è pietate quam vocabant, improbum notaverat. Jam contra verum pietatis veræ quæstum cele- brat. Quæ correctio est Rhetorica, qua quod culpaverat, in contrarium vertit sensu mutato, q. d. si quis rem recte æstimet, ipsa pietas est ma- gnus quæstus, non terrenus, sed cœlestis, non corporalis, sed spiritualis. Pietatem autem vo- cat tum fidem, tum cultum DEI, non exclusa, sed inclusa charitate proximi. Nam & pietas in proximum quædam est, nec sine amore proxi- mi amor DEI constare potest, 1. Johan. IV. v. 20. Additur autem pietati, ad quæstus magni veri- tatem declarandam, αὐτάρκεια. Nam fideles ita pietatem pro quæstu habent, ut solo Deo con- tenti sint, Job. XXII. vers. 25. Genes. XV. vers. 1. Psalm. LXXIII. vers. 25. Ideo acquiescunt in Dei voluntate, ac bonis & donis DEI conten- ti omnino sunt. Danæus notat, Apostolum non πόρον, id est, reditum & vectigal dixisse, quod semel tantum in anno, vel in tota vita perci- piatur, sed πορισμὸν, id est, fundum & peren- nem sive inexhaustum fontem, qui semper sum- mos, uberrimosque proventus fundat nobis & producat. Impii vero pauperes, quia non sunt divites in DEO, Luc. XII. vers. 21. Matth. XVI. vers. 26. Falsi Doctores quæstui inhiant; aliena à veris Doctoribus vel maxime esse debet ἀχρο- κερδία 1. Timoth. III. vers. 3. Tit. I. vers. 7. 1. Pet. V. vers. 2. unde τῇ αὐταρκείᾳ student, ac certe suo contenti sint, monet Apostolus. Illi inquit, Theophylacto interprete, longe falluntur, cum quæstum male existimant pietatem. Inest quidem pietati & lucrum, sed nequaquam cujusmodi bi opinantur, sed longe præstantius. Quandoquidem lucrifacere pietas dicitur, non cum pecuniis affluit, sed cum his caret. Sufficientia enim & quod sat est, ingentium opum & stabilium ducitur loco. Nequaquam ergo animo concidant, qui pietatem sectantur, quod nullis abundent divitiis, nec pe- cuniis potiantur. Chrysostomus homil. XXXIX. in 1. Corinth. XV. non est affluentia, inquit, quæ voluptatem parit, sed animus recte institutus, quo fine, si quis omnia possideat, tanquam omnibus pri- vatus efficietur.

## 6:7
Vers. 7.

For we brought nothing into the world; it is clear that we can carry nothing out) The sense is the same as Job I. 21 and Ecclesiastes V. 14. But it is applied here to mock avarice. Such is that of Martial: Seize, heap up, carry off, possess, it must be left behind. And the Greek is of no different sense: I stepped upon the earth naked; naked I shall go under the earth. And why do I toil in vain, seeing the end is naked? Add what is at Luke XII. 20.

He shows in this place, says Theophylact, that the gain to which they lean and apply themselves is of no moment, since it is something that is to remain on earth after our death, and will not migrate with us. What need, therefore, have we of an excess of things, if we are to carry nothing of these things into the true Fatherland. He proves, therefore, first of all that self-sufficiency is a great gain. He proposes, however, the beginning and the end of life. Let those who measure everything by secular gain consider what kind of beings nature brings us forth as, and what kind it receives. What kind does it bring forth? Not clothed in purple and fine linen, not shining with gold and silver, not burdened with food and drink, but naked and needy: Maternal blood is our purple: Filth is our gold and silver. As is the entry, so is the exit. We brought nothing with us except filth, we shall carry nothing away; as Crocius says here. Let Ecclesiastes V, verse 14 be compared.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Οὐδὲν γὰρ εἰσηνέγκαμεν εἰς τὸν κόσμον· δῆλον ὅτι οὐδὲ ἐξενεγ- κεῖν τι δυνάμεθα) Sensus idem, qui Jobi I. 21. & Eccl. V. 14. Applicatum autem hic ad irridendam avaritiam. Tale il- lud Martialis : Rape, congere, aufer, posside, relinquendum est. Et Græcum non disparis sensus : Γῆς ἐπέβην γυμνὸς· γυμνὸς δ’ ὑπὸ γαῖαν ἄπειμι. Καὶ τι μάτην μοχθῶ γυμνὸν ὁρῶν τὸ τέλος. Adde quæ ad Luc. XII. 20.

Ostendit hoc loco, inquit Theophylactus, id quæ- stus, cui illi incumbunt, & student, nullius esse momenti, quippe quod nostrum post obitum in terris sit remansurum, non nobiscum commigra- turum. Quid ergo opus est nobis nimia rerum abundantiæ, si nihil sumus ex his veram in Pa- triam delaturi. Probat igitur imprimis αὐτάρκειαν esse quæstum ingentem. Proponit autem vitæ initium & exitum. Considerent, qui omnia ex quæ- stu seculari metiuntur, quales nos natura gignat, quales recipiat. Quales gignit? non purpura & bysso indutos, non auro & argento fulgentes, non cibo & potu onustos, sed nudos & inopes: Sanguis maternus est nostra purpura: Sordes sunt aurum & argentum. Qualis ingressus, talis est egressus. Nihil nobiscum tulimus præter sordes, nihil effe- remus; ut hic Crocius. Conferatur Ecclesiast. V. vers. 14.

## 6:8
Verse 8.

But having food and clothing, we shall be content with these) Philo on rewards. Plato says that food and shelter are sufficient for nature. Aristides: for I think we need clothing, and shelter, and food. Where Aristides placed shelter for a roof: For shelter or covering is everything by which we are covered. Jacob asks only for bread and clothing, Genesis XXVIII, verse 20. That Cyprian translates food as maintenance, in that he followed legal terminology. For to maintain is to feed. Law 'si qua' § 'sed si' Digest on acknowledging and feeding children.

Jerome, book II against Jovinian. Having food and clothing. He commands Timothy and other teachers to be content, not to imitate false teachers intent on gain. Which warning, however, is delivered in such a way that it is suitable for all. For we all entered the world naked, and naked we shall in turn depart. The Apostle does not here forbid the abundance of riches, as is evident from verse 17, but in the lack of abundance he commends self-sufficiency.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Ἔχοντες δὲ διατροφὰς καὶ σκεπάσματα τούτοις ἀρκεσθη- σόμεθα) Philo de præmiis. Πλάτων δὲ ὁ μὲν τῆς φύσεως ἐντελής ἐστι τροφὴ καὶ σκέπη. Aristides : ἐσθῆτος γὰρ, οἶ- μαι, καὶ σκέπης, καὶ τροφῆς δεόμεθα. Ubi σκέπην Aristides posuit pro tecto: Est enim σκέπη sive σκέπασμα צל hoc o- mne quo tegimur. Jacobus panem tantum & vestem po- stulat Genes. XXVIII. vers. 20. Quod Cyprianus διατρο- φὰς vertit exhibitionem, in eo locutionem juris secutus est. Nam exhibere est alere. L. si qua §. sed si D. de Agnosscen- dis & alendis liberis.

Hieronymus libr. II. contra Jovin. Habentes victum & amictum. Timotheum aliosque Do- ctores contentos esse jubet, non imitari falsos Doctores quæstui intentos. Quæ monitio ta- men ita tradita, ut omnibus conveniat. Omnes enim nudi ingressi mundum sumus, nudi vi- cissim egrediemur. Non autem prohibet hic Apostolus opum abundantiam, ut è versu 17. constat, sed in defectu abundantiæ commendat αὐτάρκειαν.

## 6:9
Verse 9.

But those who wish to be rich) Proverbs XXVIII:22. He whose sole study it is to become rich is a slave to Mammon. See Matthew VI, verse 24.

They fall into temptation and a snare) that is, into a snare of temptation. They are ensnared by the Devil: whose name certain interpreters added here for the sake of clarity: to fall into temptation is the same as to enter, about which we spoke at Matthew V, verse 13.

And many foolish and harmful desires) Thus the Latin reads, not 'unprofitable'. These desires not only do no good (for one does not live on superfluous things) but they even do harm. For they hinder us from serving God as we ought, Matthew VI, verse 13, in which are all things.

Which drown men in destruction and perdition) A simile taken from a punishment, not indeed among the Jews, but customary in the East, 2 Maccabees XII, verse 4. You have mention of this punishment also in Eusebius. See what was said at Matthew XIII, verse 6. They sink them into the deep, from which there is no exit, destruction and perdition, that is, irreparable ruin. Thus 1 Kings VIII, verse 24, into destruction and desolation.

He does not say, those who are rich, lest he seem to condemn the possession of riches, which are a gift of God, but those who wish to be rich, who in all ways cling to earthly goods, and direct all their thoughts to this, that they may amass riches. They do not only fall into the dangers of this life, but into the temptations of Satan: and not only into temptations, but into a manifold snare, by which snare they are led as captives, 2 Timothy II, verse 26, and are precipitated into destruction. The Vulgate added the name of the Devil, but against the good rules of translation, because it is not found in any Greek codex. They also fall into many and absurd desires, as the Syriac rendered it: which reading Grotius rashly changed to 'unprofitable' for the sake, as it appears, of the Vulgate. For the Greeks read not 'unprofitable' but 'foolish'.

Interpreters, and truly foolish, as the blessed Luther rendered it, are both the desires and those addicted to them. For they have no regard for their own person, status, dignity, lot, nor for place, nor time; from every thing a sweet odor: with eyes as if blind against divine and human laws they covet everything, as if stung by a gadfly. Nothing so absurd can be imagined that the lovers of wealth will not seize upon, provided it contributes anything to increasing their wealth: as Crocius truly says here: Let Proverbs XXVII, verse 20 and Sirach XIV, verse 9 be compared. And they fall not only into foolish, but also into harmful desires, which drown men, in soul and body, into destruction and perdition. Danaeus joins these words, either to designate temporal and eternal destruction, or to denote insuperable ruin. Theophylact has: so that they neither enjoy goods in this age, and in the future are utterly despaired of, and are adjudged to death. The word βυθίζουσι is emphatic, as being proper to those who are submerged in waters, so that they can no longer emerge. Nor does the similarity of the punishment brought forward by Grotius displease.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Οἱ δὲ βουλόμενοι πλουτεῖν) נבהל להון Prov. XXVIII. 22. Cui id unicum studium est, ut ditescat, Mammonæ servus. Vide Matth. VI. vers. 24.

Ἐμπίπτουσιν εἰς πειρασμὸν καὶ παγίδα) id est, εἰς παγί- δα πειρασμοῦ. Illaqueantur à Diabolo: cujus nomen hic claritatis causa addidere interpretes quidam : ἐμπίπτειν εἰς πειρασμὸν, idem quod εἰσέρχεσθαι, de quo diximus ad Matth. V. v. 13.

Καὶ ἐπιθυμίας πολλὰς ἀνοήτους καὶ βλαβεράς) Sic legit Latinus, non ἀνοήτους. Cupiditates istæ non modo nihil prosunt (neque enim vivitur de supervacuis) ve- rum nocent insuper. Impediunt enim nos DEO, ut oportet, servire Matth. VI. vers. 13. in quo sunt τὰ πάντα.

Αἵ τινες βυθίζουσι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους εἰς ὄλεθρον εἰς ἀπώλειαν) Similitudo sumpta ex supplicio, non quidem apud Ju- dæos, sed in Oriente usitato, 2. Maccab. XII. vers. 4. Ha- bes & apud Eusebium ejus supplicii mentionem. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. XIII. vers. 6. Demergunt eos in profundum, unde nullus est exitus, ὄλεθρον καὶ ἀπώλειαν id est interitum irreparabilem. Sic 1. Reg. VIII. vers. 24. εἰς ὄλεθρον καὶ ἀφανισμόν.

Non ait, qui divites sunt, ne divitiarum pos- sessionem, quæ donum DEI sunt, damnare vi- deatur, sed qui volunt divites esse, omnibus mo- dis inhærent terrenis bonis, in id omnes inten- dunt cogitationes, ut divitias congerant. Non incidunt tantum in pericula hujus vitæ, sed in tentationes Satanæ: nec in tentationes solum, sed in laqueum multiplicem, quo laqueo velut captivi ducantur, 2. Timoth. II. vers. 26. & in exi- tium præcipitentur. Vulgata nomen Diaboli addidit, sed præter leges bonas translationis, quia in nullo Codice Græco habetur. Incidunt & in desideria multa & absurda, ut Syrus red- didit: quam lectionem ἀνοήτους temere immuta- vit Grotius in gratiam, ut apparet, Vulgatæ. Non enim ἀνονήτους inutiles, sed ἀνοήτους legêre Græci

Interpretes, & verè ἀνόητοι, thöricht/ ut Beatus Lutherus reddidit, sunt tum cupiditates, tum illis dediti. Non enim habent rationem suæ per- sonæ, status, dignitatis, sortis, non loci, non tem- poris; Ex qualibet re suavis odor: cæcis quasi oculis adversus divina & humana jura appetunt omnia, quasi æstro perciti. Nihil tam absurdum singi potest, quod φιλόπλυτοι non arripiant, mo- do ad rem augendam quicquam conferat: ut ex vero hic Crocius: Conferatur Proverb. XXVII. vers. 20. Syrach. XIV. vers. 9. Nec in stultas tan- tum, sed etiam damnosas cupiditates incidunt, quæ demergunt homines, anima & corpore, εἰς ὄλεθρον καὶ ἀπώλειαν, in exitium & interitum. Danæus istas voces conjungit, sive ut tempora- lem ac æternum interitum designet, sive ut in- superabile exitium denotet. Theophylactus ha- bet: ita, ut neque hoc sæculo bonis fruantur, in fu- turo plane desperent, & morti adjudicentur. Ver- bum βυθίζουσι emphaticum est, ceu proprium βυθίζεσι eorum, qui aquis immerguntur, ut emergere amplius non possint. Nec displicet similitudo supplicii à Grotio adducta.

## 6:10
Verse 10.

For the love of money is the root of all evils) That is, there is no evil which cannot be born from avarice. See what we said at Eph. IV. 19. Apollodorus: But you have spoken almost the sum of evils; for in the love of money all things are contained. Therefore, for Philo, the love of money is the metropolis of vice. Greek philosophers indeed spoke much about the contempt of riches: but more philosophers were seen at the doors of the rich than rich men at the doors of the philosophers.

Just as various branches sprout from a root: so many sins from avarice. But not only evils of fault, but also evils of punishment are understood, and not only evils of punishment of the future, but also of the present age, says Blessed Gerhard. Some understand only the evils of fault, to whom Crocius accedes: The root provides the vital sap to the tree, by the benefit of which it pushes forth leaves and bears fruit. Avarice provides fuel for all vices; thence leaves and fruits are born. There is nothing more wicked than a miser: for he holds even his own soul for sale, Eccl. X. verse 9. But the evil of punishment is not to be excluded. For the Apostle previously named not only the snare of sins, but also destruction, and he confirms both in this sentence. Blessed Gerhard teaches this more fully in his Schola pietat. book V. chapter XI. page 1036. that avarice, as far as the evil of fault is concerned, has a universal influence on all sins, that it is a very bad mother, who has many daughters likewise very bad: (1) aversion from God Job XXVII. verse 10. Matt. VI. verse 25. (2) contempt of the divine word, Psalm X. verse 3. Ezek. XXX. verse 31. Hos. II. verse 2. (3) corruption of doctrine Isa. LVI. verse 11. Jer. XVII. verse 13. VIII. verse 10. Ezek. XIII. verse 19. 2 Pet. II. verse 1. foll. Jude v. 4. (4) inhumanity Prov. XII. verse 10. (5) rapacity Mic. II. verse 19. Isa. XXXII. verse 7. (6) iniquity Mic. VI. verse 12. Sirach XXVII. verse 1. There is no trace of justice in that heart in which avarice makes a dwelling for itself, says Leo, Sermon IX. (7) Murder 1 Kings XX. verse 10. Prov. I. verse 29. Ezek. XXII. verse 25. 27. (8) Impostures and frauds Mic. II. verse 1. and 2. (9) Lies and perjuries Mic. VI. verse 12. (10.) Simony Acts VIII. verse 18. 19. 20. But concerning the evil of punishment, he brings this forward, that in general indeed avarice is followed by destruction, Prov. 29:12, Sir. 31:6 & 7. In particular, indeed: (1) constant restlessness, Eccles. 5:11, Sir. 31:1-2; (2) the curse of the people, Prov. 11:26; (3) the destruction of the house, Prov. 15:27, Hab. 2:10-11; (4) the plundering and scattering of resources, Job 20:15, 18, 20, Jer. 17:11; (5) the overthrow of empires, Sir. 10:8; (6) the acceleration of public punishments, Amos 9:1, Mic. 2:2-3; (7) excommunication, 1 Cor. 5:11; (8) eternal damnation, 1 Cor. 6:9, Eph. 5:5, Col. 3:5. That these things are said of the philosophers in the present passage is contrary to the context. For he had begun to speak of heretics, and is now about to finish, having commemorated the examples of those who wandered from the faith, led by avarice.

Ἧς τινες ὀρεγόμενοι) Thus ὄρεξις πορισμοῦ, Wis. 14:3. ὀρέγειν is properly said of things, such as money: but by a certain metaphor, of the very vices which we love. You would not translate it badly: 'To which some, striving.'

Ἀπεπλανήθησαν ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως) See above 1:19 & 5:15. Having spoken thus far about those philosophers who inserted themselves into Christian assemblies, he adds that they adulterate the word of GOD and hunt for advantages, and that from this it happened that some even deserted Christianity. Hence he shows how great a matter of danger this is.

There is no evidence that the Apostle was dealing with philosophers inserting themselves into Christian assemblies. He brings forward examples of those who believed in Christ, but, being desirous of money, deserted the Christian faith for its sake: so that he may show how great an evil redounds from φιλαργυρία (love of money), where the pronoun ἧς (of which) is placed for the object, avarice for the things coveted, or money; but they fall away from the faith: for out of avarice they have a venal religion, both through apostasy from the Christian religion and through idolatry, when they place their trust not in GOD, but in gold, Job 31:24, Matt. 6:25, Col. 3:5.

Καὶ ἑαυτοὺς περιέπειραν ὀδύναις πολλαῖς) In the Glossary: περιπείρω, I fasten to. They have entangled themselves in many sorrows. For first, there is great trouble in seeking money, then greater in keeping it. See Matt. 13:22. Added to this are the hatreds of others, often lawsuits, and sometimes even punishments.

The word περιπείρειν implies being pierced through, as when one falls upon a sword, i.e., they have pierced themselves through on every side with many sorrows, both by the stinging cares of enriching and preserving resources, and by the goads and pangs of conscience on account of unjustly acquired things, which are a kind of hell, but a bitter foretaste. Those who are held by this greed, says Theophylact, mourn while they live, and grieve because they cannot satisfy the most voracious power of having. For the cares of riches are like thorns, as the Lord has testified. Which, wherever you touch them on any side, make the hands bleed with innate prickles, and inflict wounds, and torment with pains.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ Φιλαργυρία) Id est nullum est malum, quod non ex avaritia nasci possit. Vide quæ diximus Eph. IV. 19. Apollodorus: Ἀλλὰ σχεδόν τι τὸ κεφάλαιον τῶν κακῶν Εἴρηκας· ἡ φιλαργυρία γὰρ πάντ᾽ ἔνι. Ideo φιλαργυρία Philoni, κακίας μητροπόλις. Philosophi Græci multa quidem de contemptu divitiarum loqueban- tur: sed plures Philosophi spectabantur ad fores divitum, quam divites ad fores Philosophorum.

Sicut ex radice varii pullulant rami: sic ex avaritia multa peccata. Non solum vero mala culpa, sed etiam mala pœnæ intelliguntur, nec so- lum mala pœnæ futuri, sed etiam præsentis seculi, ait Beatus Gerhardus. Nonnulli tantum de ma- lis culpæ intelligunt, quibus accedit Crocius: Ra- dix arbori suggerit succum vitalem, cujus bene- ficio folia protrudit & fructum fert. Avaritia fomentum præbet omnibus vitiis; inde folia & fructus nascuntur. Avaro nihil est scelestius: hic enim & animam suam venalem habet Eccl. X. vers. 9. Sed non excludendum est malum pœ- næ. Nam non laqueum tantum peccatorum, sed & exitium nominavit antea Apostolus, & utrum- que hac sententia confirmat. Id plenius docet Beatus Gerhardus in Schola pietat. libr. V. cap. XI. pag. 1036. quod avaritia, quantum ad malum culpæ, universalem influentiam habeat ad omnia peccata, quod pessima sit mater, quæ plures ha- bet filias itidem pessimas: (1) aversionem à Deo Job. XXVII. vers. 10. Matth. VI. vers. 25. (2) contemptum verbi divini, Psalm. X. vers. 3. Ezech. XXX. vers. 31. Hos. II. vers. 2. (3) corru- ptelam doctrinæ Esa. LVI. vers. 11. Jerem. XVII. vers. 13. IIX. vers. 10. Ezech. XIII. vers. 19. 2. Petr. II. vers. 1. sequ. Judæ v. 4. (4) inhumanitatem Proverb. XII. vers. 10. (5) rapacitatem Mich. II. vers. 19. Esa. XXXII. vers. 7. (6) iniquitatem Mich. VI. vers. 12. Syrach. XXVII. vers. 1. Nul- lum est justitiæ in illo corde vestigium, in quo avaritia sibi facit habitaculum, inquit Leo Serm. IX. (7) Cædem 1. Reg. XX. vers. 10. Proverb. I. vers. 29. Ezech. XXII. vers. 25. 27. (8) Impostu- ras & fraudes Mich. II. vers. 1. & 2. (9) Menda- cia & perjuria Mich. VI. vers. 12. (10.) Simonia Actor. IIX. vers. 18. 19. 20. De malo autem pœ- næ hæc adfert, quod in genere quidem avaritiam sequatur exitium Proverb. XXIX. vers. 12. Syr. XXXI. vers. 6. & 7. in specie vero (1) assidua in- quietudo Ecclesiast. V. vers. 11. Syr. XXXI. vers. 1. 2. (2) Populi maledictio Proverb. XI. vers. 26. (3) Domus destructio Proverb. XV. vers. 27. Hab. II. vers. 10. 11. (4) Facultatum direptio ac dispersio Job. XX. vers. 15. 18. 20. Jerem. XVII. vers. 11. (5) Imperiorum eversio Syrach. X. vers. 8. (6) Pœna- rum publicarum acceleratio Amos IX. vers. 1. Mich. II. vers. 2. 3. (7) Excommunicatio 1. Cor. V. vers. 11. (8) æterna damnatio 1. Corinth. VI. vers. 9. Ephes. V. vers. 5. Coloss. III. vers. 5. De Phi- losophis hæc dicta in præsenti esse, repugnat con- textui. Nam de hæreticis dicere cœperat, & jam finiturus est, commemoratis exemplis eorum, qui à fide aberrarunt, inducti avaritia.

Ἧς τινες ὀρεγόμενοι) Sic ὄρεξις πορισμοῦ, Sap. XIV. v. 3. ὀρέγειν proprie quidem dicitur de rebus, ut de pecuniis: sed per translationem quandam de ipsis, quæ amamus, vi- tiis. Non male verteris: Cui quidam studentes.

Ἀπεπλανήθησαν ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως) Vide supra I. 19. & V. vers. 15. Hactenus locutus de Philosophis illis, qui se Christianis cœtibus inserebant, addit eos adulterare ver- bum DEI, & venari commoda, atque inde evenisse, ut etiam quidam Christianismum deseruerint. Hinc osten- dit, quanti sit res ista periculi.

De Philosophis Christianis cœtibus se inge- rentibus egisse Apostolum, nullo constat indi- cio. Exempla profert eorum, qui in Christum crediderunt, sed pecuniæ appetentes ejus causa Christianam fidem deseruere: ut quantum è Φιλαργυρίᾳ redundet malum, ostendat, ubi quod ad pronomen ἧς affectus ponitur pro ob- jecto, avaritia pro rebus concupitis, vel pecu- nia; à fide autem deficiunt: Ex avaritia enim ve- nalem habent religionem, tum per apostasiam à religione Christiana, tum per idololatriam, cum fiduciam non in DEUM, sed in aurum collo- cant, Job. XXXI. vers. 24. Matth. VI. vers. 25. Co- loss. III. vers. 5.

Καὶ ἑαυτοὺς περιέπειραν ὀδύναις πολλαῖς) In Glossario: περιπείρω adfigo. Multis doloribus se implicuere. Primum enim magna est molestia in quærendis pecuniis, deinde major in servandis. Vide Matth. XIII. 22. Accedunt odia aliorum, sæpe lites, interdum & pœnæ.

Vox περιπείρειν confossionem infert, cum quis in mucronem incidit, q. d. undiquaque transfi- xerunt se multis doloribus, tum qua curas acu- leatas de locupletandis & conservandis facul- tatibus, tum qua stimulos & angores conscien- tiæ propter injuste acquisita, qui sunt gehennæ quædam, sed acerba prælibatio. Quî hac cu- piditate tenentur, inquit Theophylactus, mœrent, dum vivunt, & dolent, quod explere avidiffi- mam habendi vim nequeant. Sunt namque sen- tibus similes curæ divitiarum, ut testatus est Do- minus. Quæ undiquaque ubi ipse attigeris, innatis aculeis manus cruentant, infliguntque vulnera, & doloribus angunt.

## 6:11
Vers. 11.

Σὺ δὲ ὦ ἄνθρωπε τοῦ Θεοῦ) He addresses him with a very honorable title, in the way that the Prophets were accustomed to be addressed, as in the inscription of Ps. 90, 2 Kings 4:40, and elsewhere.

Ταῦτα φεῦγε) Be far removed even from the borders of such vices.

Add 1 Sam. 2:27, 3:17, 9:6, 1 Kings 12:22, 13:1. He addresses him with such a distinguished title, however, so that he may lift his mind from earthly things upward to GOD more and more: and he tacitly opposes the man of GOD to the men of the Devil; for those are φιλάργυροι (lovers of money).

The pronoun ταῦτα designates not only avarice, but also all those vices which sprout from this unhappy root. For murders and deceits, as Theodoret teaches, thefts and rapine, frauds and lies, the violation of oaths, and other kinds of iniquity sprout from this root.

Δίωκε δὲ δικαιοσύνην) The same expression is in Rom. 9:36 and 2 Tim. 2:22. So also διώκειν ἀγάπην, 1 Cor. 14:1. The Hebrews use רדף in this way. Δικαιοσύνη in this place is innocence. Εὐσέβειαν) Piety toward God. Πίστιν ἀγάπην) benevolence toward men. Ὑπομονὴν) Patience in adversities. Πραότητα) Gentleness in offenses. In the Manuscript it is πραοπάθειαν. And Hesychius seems to have read it thus. For with him, πραοπάθεια is πραότης.

Grotius omitted πίσιν, or his copyist did, perhaps through carelessness. The Apostle therefore commands that the man of GOD should pursue righteousness, namely imputed, as is gathered from the parallel in 2 Timothy 2:22, and piety and faith, without which there is none, as regards GOD, then piety, charity, as regards one's neighbor, then patience, and gentleness, by which we govern our own affections, lest we harm ourselves through either impatience or anger. Ambrose explains πραότητα as tranquility, and most others as gentleness. Oecumenius commends the order thus: Καλὴ δὲ ἡ τάξις τῆ λόγε, ἀπὸ μὲν γὰρ πίστεως ἀγά- πη τίκτεται· ἀπὸ δὲ ἀγάπης ὑπομονὴ, ἡ δὲ ὑπο- μονὴ ὁδῷ βαδίζεσα πρᾶες ποιεῖ. From charity, says Theophylact, patience and gentleness are derived. Charity also sustains all things out of a certain greatness of soul. Διώκειν is a hunting term: it corresponds to the Hebrew רדף, which is used for a similar admonition in Psalm 34:14. Implying vigilance and diligent zeal in pursuing virtues, just as hunters are accustomed to pursue wild beasts.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Σὺ δὲ ὦ ἄνθρωπε τοῦ Θεοῦ) Honorifico admodum eum appellat vocabulo, quomodo Prophetæ appellari solebant, ut in inscriptione Psalm. XC. 2. Reg. IV. v. 40. & alibi.

Ταῦτα φεῦγε) Longe abesto etiam à collimitiis ta- lium vitiorum.

Adde 1. Sam. II. vers. 27. III. v. 17. IX. vers. 6. 1. Reg. XII. vers. 22. XIII. vers. 1. Compellat au- tem eum tam præclaro titulo, ut animum ejus à terrenis sursum ad DEUM magis magisque elevet: ac tacite hominem DEI simul oppo- nit hominibus Diaboli; ii enim Φιλάργυροι sunt.

Pronomen ταῦτα non tantum Φιλαργυρίαν, sed etiam omnia illa vitia, quæ ex hac infelice ra- dice propullulant, designat. Cades enim & præ- stigia, Theodoreto docente, furta & rapina, frau- des & mendacia, jurisjurandi violatio, & alia gene- ra iniquitatis ex hac radice pullulant.

Δίωκε δὲ δικαιοσύνην) Eadem locutio Roman. IX. v. 36. & 2. Timoth. II. vers. 22. Sic & διώκειν ἀγάπην 1. Cor. XIV. vers. 1. Hebræi רדף sic usurpant. Δικαιοσύνη hoc loco est innocentia. Εὐσέβειαν) Pietatem in Deum. Πίσιν ἀγάπην) benevolentiam in homines. Ὑπομονὴν) Patientiam in adversis. Πραότητα) Lenitatem in offensis. In Manuscripto est πραοπάθειαν. Et videtur sic legisse Hesychius. Est enim apud eum πραοπάθεια πραότης.

Grotius prætermisit πίσιν, seu ejus exscri- ptor, forte per incuriam. Præcipit ergo Apo- stolus, ut homo DEI sectetur justitiam, impu- tatam nempe, ut è parallelo, 2. Timoth. II. vers. 22. colligitur, & pietatem ac fidem, fine qua ea nul- la est, quod ad DEUM, tum pietatem, charita- tem, quod ad proximum, tum patientiam, & man- suetudinem, qua affectus proprios, ne vel impa- tientia, vel ira nobis ipsis officiamus. Πραότητα Ambrosius tranquillitatem, ac plerique lenitatem exponunt. Oecumenius ordinem ita commendat: Καλὴ δὲ ἡ τάξις τῆ λόγε, ἀπὸ μὲν γὰρ πίστεως ἀγά- πη τίκτεται· ἀπὸ δὲ ἀγάπης ὑπομονὴ, ἡ δὲ ὑπο- μονὴ ὁδῷ βαδίζεσα πρᾶες ποιεῖ. A charitate, inquit Theophylactus, patientia & mansuetudo derivantur. Omnia etiam sustinet, ex quadam animi magnitudine charitas. Διώκειν est ver- bum venatorium: respondet Ebræo רדף quod simili admonitioni adhibitum, Psalm. XXXIV. vers. 15. Vigilantiam & studium sedulum per- sequendi virtutes, uti venatores solent feras per- sequi, importans.

## 6:12
Verse 12.

Fight the good fight of faith) You have come to that contest where one must fight without intermission 1 Cor. 9:25, Phil. 1:29, Col. 1:29, 2:1, 2 Tim. 4:7. נפתלי נפתל אלהים as it is in Gen. 30:8.

He commands, says Theodoret, that he should exercise himself; now he persuades him to contend. The hunting and pursuit of virtues will not happen without a contest. For many obstacles are thrown in the way by enemies, both internal and external: but there is need of the contest of faith. Because faith is the victory that overcomes the world 1 John 5:4. He alludes to the Greek contests 1 Cor. 9:24, Phil. 3:14, 2 Tim. 2:5. But those were undertaken out of ambition: just as the contests of false teachers. We must fight by faith, for the faith of CHRIST, out of the faith of the divine word. Blessed Gerhard correctly expresses the sense. Remain constant in the true faith, and through it bravely resist depraved desires and temptations 1 Cor. 9:25, Eph. 6:16, 1 Tim. 1:18, 2 Tim. 4:7.

Lay hold of eternal life) So also shortly in verse 19, an expression similar to that in Proverbs 4:13, החזק במוסר where the Greeks say, ἐπι- λαβοῦ ἐμῆς παιδείας, hold fast. But it is to be noted that by the name of eternal life here, and elsewhere, is signified the right to eternal life. The sense is the same in Phil. 3:14.

He persists in the metaphor.
