He does not say you will earn life by contending; but lay hold: not as the wages of merit, but as the goal, or the gratuitous reward proposed to those who hold fast to the faith. An ample inheritance of paternal goods is, by reason of the succession, the reward of filial obedience, but not the reward of merit. But he is commanded to embrace that reward with as certain a confidence as if GOD, with outstretched hand, as the umpires were accustomed to do, were offering it, and to embrace it in such a way that he holds it firmly, and lets it go on no account. Apocal. III. 11.

to which you were called) Thus, in the place spoken to the Philippians, of the upward calling of God. And you confessed the good confession before many witnesses) Here 'and' signifies 'when': namely, in baptism, to which many witnesses were applied. Concerning this profession, see what we have said at Matth. XXIX. 19. Tertullian, in his book on Baptism, calls this confession a testimony of faith.

Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius among the Greeks, and Ambrosiaster, Primasius, and Haymo, and others among the Latins, as well as our blessed Balduinus, also explain it as the profession in Baptism: Lombard, Thomas, and Hugo Cardinalis explain it as the profession in ordination to the ministry: Theophylact explains it as the profession made in great dangers, and others as the profession in the whole of life. But all those professions of faith are most correctly taken together by Theodoret, Bullinger, Crocius, and others.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Ἀγωνίζω τὸν καλὸν ἀγῶνα τῆς πίστεως) Ad id certamen ve- nisti, ubi sine intermissione pugnandum est 1. Cor. IX. 25. Philipp. I. 29. Coloss. I. 29. II. 1. 2. Timoth. IV. 7. נפתלי נפתל אלהים ut est Gen. XXX. 8.

Præcipit, inquit Theodoretus, ut se exerce- ret, nunc persuadet, ut decertet. Venatio & per- secutio virtutum sine certamine non fiet. Mul- ta enim injiciuntur impedimenta, ab hostibus tam internis, quam externis: Certamine autem fidei opus est. Quia fides est victoria, quæ mun- dum vincit 1. Johan. V. vers. 3. Alludit ad Græ- corum certamina 1. Corinth. IX. vers. 24. Philipp. III. vers. 14. 2. Timoth. II. vers. 5. Sed illa ex am- bitione suscipiebantur: quemadmodum & fal- sorum Doctorum certamina. Nobis fide pu- gnandum est, pro fide CHRISTI, ex fide ver- bi divini. Sensum recte exprimit Beatus Ger- hardus. Constans permane in vera fide, ac per eandem pravis concupiscentiis, ac tentationibus for- titer resiste 1. Corinth. IX. vers. 25. Eph. VI. 16. 1. Tim. I. 18. 2. Tim. IV. 7.

Ἐπιλαβοῦ τῆς αἰωνία ζωῆς) Sic & mox 19. locutio simi- lis isti Proverb. IV. vers. 12. החזק במוסר ubi Græci, ἐπι- λαβοῦ ἐμῆς παιδείας, firmiter tene. Sed notandum, vitæ æternæ nomine hic, & alibi significari jus ad vitam æternam. Sensus idem Phil. III. 14.

Persistit in metaphora. Non dicit certando mereberis vitam; sed apprehende: non ut merce- dem meriti, sed ut metam, vel præmium fidem retinentibus gratuitum propositam. Ampla hæ- reditas bonorum paternorum ratione sequelæ est merces obedientiæ filialis, non autem merces meriti. Amplecti autem praemium illud jubetur tam certa fiducia, ac si DEUS exporrecta manu, ut brabeutae solebant, porrigeret, idque ita am- plecti, ut firmiter teneat, nulloque casu missum faciat. Apocal. III. 11.

ἐὶς ἧν ἐκλήθης) Sic τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως τῦ Θεῦ dicto ad Phi- lippenses loco. Καὶ ὡμολόγησας τὴν καλὴν ὁμολογίαν ἐνώπιον πολλῶν μαρ- τύρων) Hic καὶ valet quando: nempe in baptismo, cui multi adhibebantur testes. De hac professione vide, quae diximus ad Matth. XXIX. 19. Hanc ὁμολογίαν testatio- nem fidei vocat in libro de Baptismo Tertullianus.

De professione in Baptismo etiam exponunt Chrysostomus, & Theophylactus, Oecumenius e Graecis, Ambrosiafter, Primasius, & Haymo, aliique e Latinis, ut & Beat. Balduinus noster: de professione in ordinatione ad ministerium Lombardus, Thomas, Hugo Cardinalis: de pro- fessione in magnis periculis edita, Theophylactus, in tota denique vita, alii. Sed omnes illae profes- siones fidei conjunctim accipiuntur rectissime a Theodoreto, Bullingero, Crocio, aliis.

## 6:13
Ver. 13.

I charge you) I command you. The same word is in 1 Cor. VII. v. 10, XI. v. 17, 1 Thessalon. IV. v. 11, 2 Thess. III. v. 4, 6, 10, 13, above IV. 11, v. 7, and the noun 'charge' in 1 Thess. IV. 2, above I. 5, 18. Before God who gives life to all things) Concerning the sense, see above v. 21, to that GOD who gives life to all things that live, and, giving it as He wills, preserves it. He is the one who can also restore it, John V. v. 21. In the Manuscript it is 'giving life' in a similar sense. For Greek interpreters use 'to give life' and 'to make alive' interchangeably for the Hebrew החיה. And of Christ Jesus who witnessed the good confession before Pontius Pilate) He gave you an example, he himself having confessed at the peril of his life that he was the king of the heavenly kingdom, sent for this purpose, that he might bear witness to the truth, John XVI. v. 37. Do you likewise; profess yourself a Bishop, a witness of the same truth. 'Before' [is used of] one standing in his own character before a Judge, Acts XXV. 9, 10.

A most severe adjuration follows the exhortation. For it concerns matters of the greatest difficulty, both for Timothy and for others who were looking to their own salvation. Theophylact also observes that in the description of GOD who gives life, regard is had primarily to the resurrection, by the intuition of which all adversities are overcome by the faithful: he says, with these words he encourages him to undergo dangers, and reminds him of the resurrection, just as if he were saying, do not fear death at all: for you are a servant of GOD, who can grant life to all. But Christ is introduced as a Confessor, so that Timothy may not only retain faith in his heart, but also, by the example of Christ, profess it with an intrepid mouth. But he preferred to name Pilate rather than the Priests, not only for the truth of the Evangelical history, but also to express the magnitude of the danger and the fear of death which was observed before the eyes of Christ, and also because the Majesty of civil Magistrates terrifies Christians above all.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Παραγγέλλω σοι) Denuntio tibi. Eadem vox 1. Cor. VII. v. 10. XI. v. 17. 1. Thessalon. IV. vers. 11. 2. Thess. III. v. 4. 6. 10. 13. supra IV. 11. vers. 7. & nomen παραγγελία 1. Thess. IV. 2. supra I. 5. 18. Ἐνώπιον τῦ Θεῦ τῦ ζωοποιῦντος τὰ πάντα) De sensu vide supra vers. 21 illi DEO, qui omnibus, quae vivunt, vitam dat, & dans ut vult servat. Is est, qui eam potest & reddere Joh. V. vers. 21. In Manuscripto est ζωογονῦν- τος pari sensu. Interpretes enim Graeci pro Ebraeo החיה promiscue ponunt ζωογονεῖν & ζωοποιεῖν. Καὶ χριστῦ Ἰησῦ τῦ μαρτυρήσαντος ἐπὶ Ποντίυ Πιλάτυ τὴν καλὴν ὁμολογίαν) Dedit tibi exemplum, ipse cum vitae periculo professus, se esse regem regni coelestis, in hoc missum, ut veritati testimonium perhiberet Johan. XVI. vers. 37. Sic & tu fac, profitere te Episcopum, te- stem ejusdem veritatis. Ἐπὶ nota propria stantis apud Ju- dicem Act. XXV. 9. 10.

Exhortationem sequitur severissima obtesta- tio. Res enim maxime arduas concernens, tum Timothei, tum aliorum, qui ipsorum respicie- bant salutem. In descriptione DEI τῦ ζωοποιῦν- τος imprimis respectum haberi ad resurrectio- nem, cujus intuitu omnes adversitates superan- tur a fidelibus, observat etiam Theophylactus: his verbis, inquit, hunc ad pericula subeunda hor- tatur, & resurrectionis commonefacit, perinde ac si diceret, nil prorsus mortem horresce: DEI enim es servus, qui vitam potest omnibus donare. Chri- stus vero ut Confessor introducitur, ut non tan- tum fidem corde retineat, sed etiam, exemplo Christi, ore intrepido profiteatur Timotheus. Maluit autem Pilatum, quam Sacerdotes nomi- nare, non solum propter historiae Evangelicae veritatem, sed etiam, ut periculi magnitudinem; & metum mortis, quae Christi oculis observa- batur, exprimeret, tum quod Majestas Magi- stratuum civilium imprimis terreat Christianos.

## 6:14
V. 14. That you keep the commandment without spot) Namely, in your profession. 'Without spot', without any stain. Thus James I. v. 27, 1 Peter III. v. 1 and 4. The Hebrews say 'without blemish' in the same sense.

Others refer this commandment to the profession of faith commanded in verse 12, or to that which he enjoined upon Timothy in his office: But it is more correctly referred to all things which he commands him to observe, whether by reason of faith, or by reason of life, or by reason of his Ecclesiastical office. The Vulgate understood the epithets 'without spot' and 'blameless' as referring to the commandment, as did Lombard and Hugo Cardinalis. But Chrysostom, whom Theophylact follows, is more correct. This is, that you do not imprint any stain upon it, neither for the sake of dogmas nor of life. For the reason of the adjuration demands this, by which the Apostle wished to conclude the admonitions concerning Timothy's doctrine, office, and life, and the condition of the precepts, because all things are enjoined by the same authority, with the same obligation, and under the same servitude.

Until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ) And here it appears that Paul speaks to Timothy as one who could live until the time when Christ was to come for judgment. See what we have said at 1 Cor. XV. 52, 2 Cor. V. 23, 1 Thessal. IV. 15. See the same word 'appearing' in this excellent sense in 2 Timoth. I. v. 10, IV. v. 8, Tit. II. v. 13. In Hebrew it is 'appearances'.

Latin:

V. 14. Τηρῆσαί σε τὴν ἐντολὴν ἄσπιλον) Nempe in pro- fessione tua. ἄσπιλον, sine ulla macula. Sic Jac. I. vers. 27. 1. Petr. III. vers. 1. & 4. Hebraei eodem sensu dicunt בלא מום.

Referunt alii hoc mandatum ad professionem fidei praeceptam vers. 12. vel ad id, quod injun- xit Timotheo in officio: Sed rectius ad omnia, quae ipsi praecipit tum ratione fidei, tum ratio- ne vitae, tum ratione muneris Ecclesiastici ob servanda refertur. Epitheta ἄσπιλον, ἀνεπίλη- πτον Vulgata intellexit de mandato, ut & Lom- bardus, & Hugo Cardinalis. Sed rectius Chryso- stomus, quem sequitur Theophylactus. Hoc est, nec dogmatum neque vitæ gratia labem illi aliquani imprimas. Nam id poscit obtestationis ratio, qua concludere voluit Apostolus commonitio- nes Timothei doctrinam, officium, & vitam concernentes, & præceptorum conditio, quia ea- dem autoritate, eadem obligatione sub eadem servitute omnia injunguntur.

Μέχρι τῆς ἐπιφανείας τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ) Et hic apparet loqui Paulum ad Timotheum, tanquam qui vivere posset ad tempus, quo Christus ad judicium erat venturus. Vide quæ diximus ad 1. Cor. XV. 52. 2. Cor. V. 23. 1. Thessal. IV. 15. Vide eandem vocem ἐπιφάνειας hoc sensu eximio 2. Timoth. I. vers. 10. IV. v. 8. Tit. II. vers. 13. Hebraice est נראות.

## 6:15
Ver. 15.

which in his own times he will show) He will make it appear יראה. Καιροῖς ἰδίοις, בעתו, at the time which he himself knows. See above II. verse 16.

But that does not appear in the least. For the things we said regarding chapter II, second to the Thessalonians, can show that this was not the opinion of the Apostle. And he handed down in the cited place that the καιροὺς ἰδίους (appointed times) are not imminent, but that other things are still to intervene; indeed, he also designated in chapter IV, verse 1 above, that other things would follow in the last days; some understand the day of ἐπιφανείας (appearing) as the day of anyone's death, which we admit can be done by way of accommodation: but the literal sense looks to that illustrious ἐπιφάνειαν (appearing) which is expected in the last days.

the blessed one.) See above I. 11.

And the only potentate) That is, he who alone has power over all things, שליט. Thus 2 Maccabees III. 24. the potentate of all power. In the same place XII. verse 15 he is called the potentate of the world and the potentate who is in heaven, in the same book XV. 2. 23.

the king of those who reign) Thus the Hebrews say מרא מלכין as in Daniel III. 27.

And the lord of those who rule) אדני האדנים Deuteronomy X. verse 17. Psalm CXXXVI. verse 3. Do not fear those lesser lords, while you obey him who has authority even over them.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

ἣν καιροῖς ἰδίοις δείξει) Faciet apparere יראה. Και- ροῖς ἰδίοις, בעתו, tempore quod ipse novit. Vide supra II. vers. 16.

Id vero minime apparet. Nam eam non fuis- se sententiam Apostoli, ea, quæ ad c. II. poster. ad Thessalon. diximus, docere possunt. Et καιροὺς ἰδίους non imminere, sed alia adhuc iisdem in- tercessura loco laudato tradidit, imo & cap. IV. vers. 1. supra, alia consecutura diebus novissimis designavit; nonnulli diem ἐπιφανείας de die mor- tis cujusvis intelligunt, quod per accommodatio- nem fieri admittimus: Sensus autem literalis re- spicit illustrem illam ἐπιφάνειαν, quæ diebus no- vissimis expectatur.

ὁ μακάριος.) Vide supra I. 11.

Καὶ μόνος δυνάστης) Id est, qui solus potest omnia, שליט. Sic 2. Macc. III. 24. πάσης ἐξουσίας δυνάστης. Ibidem XII. v. 15. dicitur κόσμου δυνάστης & ὁ ἐν οὐρανῷ δυνάστης, in eodem libro XV. 2. 23.

ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν βασιλευόντων) Sic Hebræi dicunt מרא מלכין ut Dan. III. 27.

Καὶ κύριος τῶν κυριευόντων) אדני האדנים Deut. X. vers. 17. Psalm. CXXXVI. vers. 3. Ne timete minores illos Dominos, dum ei paretis, qui & in ipsos imperium habet.

## 6:16
Verse 16.

He who alone has immortality) Namely, of himself. Thus the word μόνος (only) is used, and Romans XVI. verse 27. 1 Timothy I. verse 17. The word ἀθανασίας (immortality) is found several times in the book of Wisdom, and in Paul 1 Corinthians XV. verses 53 and 54. Menander also uses it: the opinion of Plato does not depart far from this, which Proclus explains thus in his Theological works, speaking of the lesser gods, whom we do not call angels: 'neither to be immortal, nor to obtain a share of death.' Plato himself in the Timaeus introduces the supreme GOD himself speaking thus: 'but those things which have been made by me, are indissoluble while I will it.' Thus Justin, disputing with Trypho, denies that souls are immortal (namely, of themselves) and yet denies that they die. The author of the responses to the Orthodox says not badly: 'God is said to be the only one having immortality, because it is not by will, but by his own essence.' GOD has it from his own nature and not from the will of another, says the response to the Greek questions.

Dwelling in unapproachable light) That highest heaven removed from our sight, which the Hebrews call the light under the throne of glory, נהירא עמה שרא Daniel II. verse 22, where the Greek is 'the light is with him.' Jachiades ואור חונה עמו. Virgil called it 'inaccessum' (unapproachable).

(Whom no man hath seen, nor can see) Namely, of mortals, 1 John IV. 12.

to whom be honor, eternal power, amen) You have here again an asyndeton in two joined nouns. Such as we noted in Luke II. verse 14 and elsewhere. In Psalm XXIX. 1 with the conjunction כבוד ועז but here 'eternal' is added as also in 2 Timothy II. 10 and 1 Peter V. 10. Ὧι κράτος (to whom power) here signifies empire, δυναστείαν (dominion), for thus עז is translated, Job XXXVII. 6. Psalm LXXXVIII. 14. Daniel XI. 31.

Although this description without controversy fits GOD the Father: yet since the Father and the Son are one, and indeed the Holy Spirit also, John X. verse 30, 1 John V. verse 7, it must not be denied, To belong to the Most Holy Trinity, and not inappropriately, with Chrysostom and Theophylact, the Blessed Baldwin here refers the same to the Son of GOD. Moreover, there is attributed to him both the exhibition of ἐπιφανείας, of the apparition: because he himself will exhibit his presence, who is already present to us, but invisibly, Matt. 18, last verse; for then he will show himself present gloriously; and a periphrasis or description from divine attributes, and these are (1) Supreme beatitude and happiness, which certainly befits the Son of GOD, because from him, and in him, we have every beatitude, Psalm 2, last verse, and salvation, Is. 45, verse 23, Acts 4, verse 12. He is the שדי, the all-sufficient, Gen. 17, verse 1, to whom is εὐλογία, καὶ τιμὴ, καὶ κράτος, Apoc. 5, v. 13. (2) Supreme power, on account of which he is called the only potentate, because he is ὁ παντοκράτωρ, Apoc. 1, verse 8, to whom all authority belongs in heaven and on earth, Matt. 28, verse 19, and who can render all things subject to himself by his power, Phil. 3, verse 21. (3) Supereminent Majesty: that he is ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν βασιλέων, καὶ κύριος τῶν κυριευόντων, which dignity is attributed to Christ in the same words, Apoc. 17, verse 14, 19, v. 16. (4) Immortality. Who is ὁ μόνος ἔχων ἀθανασίαν: because he alone is the true GOD, and eternal life, 1 John 5, verse 20, whence divine immortality, divine, eternal and independent life befits him, no less than the Father. Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has given also to the Son to have life in himself, John 5, verse 26. (5) Inaccessibility of the seat: He dwells in unapproachable glorious light; for he himself is the splendor of the glory of GOD the Father, Heb. 1, verse 3, he is in the eternal bosom of the Father, John 1, verse 18, he appeared on Mount Sinai in unapproachable light, Exod. 19, as the Lord of glory, 1 Cor. 2, verse 8. Compare also Psalm 97, verse 1, following. Not that a material or corporeal heaven is noted in the highest place: because the heaven of heavens do not contain GOD, 1 Kings 8, Jer. 23. But the incomprehensible majesty of GOD, because GOD himself is Light, and the Son of GOD is light from light, 1 John 1, verse 5, that unapproachable light is spoken of, says Dionysius the Carthusian, because it can be comprehended by no created intellect, whence it is also said to make darkness his hiding place. (6) Divine invisibility. For he is the image of the invisible God, Col. 1, verse 15. ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτῦ, Heb. 1, verse 3, whose face no mortal can see, Exod. 33, verse 20. Finally (7) divine doxology and celebration, to whom be honor and eternal power, amen. The Son is to be honored, just as the Father, John 5, 23. The strength and empire is the same for him as with the Father, Apoc. 5, 13.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Ὁ μόνος ἔχων ἀθανασίαν) Nempe per se. Sic vox μό- νος ponitur, & Roman. XVI. vers. 27. 1. Timoth. I. v. 17. Ἀθανασίας vox est aliquoties in libro Sapientiæ, & apud Paulum 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 53. & 54. utitur & Menan- der: non longe hinc abit sententia Platonis, quam sic ex- plicat in Theologicis Proclus, loquens de Diis minoribus, quos non Angelos dicimus: μήτε ἀθανάτους εἶναι, μήτε τεύξεσθαι θανάτου μοίρας. Plato ipse in Timæo, DEUM ipsum summum sic inducit loquentem: ἃ δὲ ἐμοῦ γενό- μενα, ἄλυτα ἐμοῦ γε θέλοντος. Sic Justinus cum Trypho- ne disputans negat esse animas immortales, (nempe per se) & tamen negat eas mori. Scriptor responsorum ad Orthodoxos non male: Μόνος ἔχων τὴν ἀθανασίαν λέγεται ὁ Θεὸς, ὅτι οὐκ ἐκ θελήματος, ἀλλ᾿ ἐκ τῆς οἰκείας οὐσίας. Habet eam DEUS ἐκ τῆς οἰκείας φύσεως καὶ οὐκ ἐκ τῆς ἑτέρου βουλῆς, ait responsum ad quæstiones Græcas.

Φῶς οἰκῶν ἀπρόσιτον) Summum illud cœlum à conspe- ctu nostro remotum, quod lucem sub solio gloriæ appel- lant Hebræi, נהירא עמה שרא Dan. II. vers. 22. ubi Græca τὸ φῶς μετ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἐστι. Jachiades ואור חונה עמו ἀπρόσιτον inaccessum dixit Virgilius.

Ὃν εἶδεν οὐδεὶς ἀνθρώπων, οὐδὲ ἰδεῖν δύναται) Mortalium scil. 1. Joh. III. 7.

ᾧ τιμὴ, κράτος αἰώνιον ἀμήν) Habes hic iterum asynde- ton in nominibus duobus junctis. Quale notavimus Luc. II. vers. 14. & alibi. In Psalm. XXIX. 1. cum copula כבוד ועז sed hic additur αἰώνιον ut & 2. Timoth. II. 10. & 1. Petr. V. 10. Ὧι κράτος hic significat, imperium, δυνα- στείαν, nam sic עז vertitur, Job. XXXVII. 6. Ps. LXXXVIII. 14. Dan. XI. 31.

Quamvis hæc descriptio citra controversiam DEO Patri conveniat: tamen cum Pater & Fi- lius unum sint, imo & Spiritus sanctus Johan. X. vers. 30. 1. Johan. V. vers. 7. negandum non est, Sacrosanctae Trinitati competere, nec inconve- nienter cum Chrysostomo & Theophylacto Beat. Balduinus hîc eandem ad Filium DEI refert. Tribuitur autem ei tum exhibitio ἐπιφανείας, ap- paritionis: quia praesentiam suam exhibebit ipse, qui jam praesens nobis est, sed invisibiliter Matth. XIIX. vers. ult. tum enim praesentem * sese gloriosè ostendet; tum περίφρασις seu de- scriptio ab attributis divinis, eaque sunt (1) Su- prema beatitudo & felicitas, quae utique Filio DEI convenit, quia ab eo, & in eo beatitudi- nem omnem habemus Psalm. II. vers. ult. & sa- lutem Es. XLV. vers. 23. Act. IV. vers. 12. Ipse est שדי omnisufficiens. Genes. XVII. vers. 1. cui est εὐλογία, καὶ τιμὴ, καὶ κράτος, Apoc. V. v. 13. (2) Summa potestas, ob quam dicitur μόνος δυνάστης, quia est ὁ παντοκράτωρ Apoc. I. vers. 8. cui omnis ἐξουσία convenit in coelo, & in terra Matth. XXIIX. vers. 19. quique omnia sibi subjecta red- dere potest δυνάμει, virtute sua Philipp. III. vers. 21. (3) Supereminens Majestas: quod sit ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν βασιλέων, καὶ κύριος τῶν κυριευόν- των, quae dignitas iisdem verbis Christo tribui- tur Apocal. XVII. vers. 14. XIX. v. 16. (4) Immor- talitas. Qui ὁ μόνος ἔχων ἀθανασίαν: quia so- lus ipse est verus DEUS, & vita aeterna 1. Johan. V. vers. 20. unde divina immortalitas, divina, aeter- na & independens vita ei competit, non minus, quam Patri. Sicut Pater vitam habet in semet- ipso, ita dedit & Filio vitam habere in semetipso Johan. V. vers. 26. (5) Sedis inaccessibilitas: Ha- bitat lucem gloriosam inaccessam; Est enim ipse splendor gloriae DEI Patris Ebr. I. vers. 3. est in sinu aeterno Patris Johan. I. vers. 18. apparuit in monte Sinai in luce inaccessa, Exod. XIX. ceu Dominus gloriae 1. Corinth. II. vers. 8. Confer. & Psalm. XCVII. vers. 1. sequ. Non coelum in su- premo loco materiale aut corporeum notatum: quia coeli coelorum DEUM non comprehen- dunt 1. Reg. IIX. Jerem. XXIII. Sed incompre- hensibilis DEI majestas, quia DEUS ipse Lux est, & Filius DEI lumen est de lumine, 1. Johan. I. vers. 5. dicitur lux illa inaccessibilis, inquit Dionysius Carthus. quia à nullo intellectu creato comprehendi potest, unde etiam dicitur tenebras ponere latibulum suum. (6) divina invisibilitas. Est enim imago Dei invisibilis Coloss. I. vers. 15. ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστά- σεως αὐτῦ Ebr. I. vers. 3. cujus faciem nemo mor- talium videre potest Exod. XXXI. vers. 30. De- nique (7) divina δοξολογία & celebratio ᾧ τιμὴ, καὶ κρατὸς αἰώνιον ἀμήν. Honorandus est Filius, sicut Pater Joh. V. 23. Robur ac imperium idem ipsi est cum Patre Ap. V. 13.

## 6:17
Verse 17.

To the rich in the present age) When he had now finished the epistle, it came into his mind that those rich merchants, who were very numerous at Ephesus, had need of a special admonition: But he well said rich of this age: because there are also other riches, about which Matt. 6, 20, and 19, 21, Mark 10, 21, Luke 12, 21, 33, 18, 22.

Charge) See above 13.

Not to be high-minded) We had this word also in Rom. 11, verse 20, for ὑψηλὰ φρονεῖν, Rom. 12, verse 16, that is, to carry oneself high, which vice especially follows riches: Sosiphanes: 'But if you are fortunate, being nothing here, do not think yourself equal to heaven.' Euripides: 'Wealth begets insolence.' Menander: 'Proudly exulting in wealth and birth.'

The same: 'For excessive nourishment makes men arrogant.' Hence the warning of the same Menander: '-- nor, if you are very well-off, trust in this, nor again despise us poor.' Grotius seems to consider Paul not as a divine, but as a human writer, not as an amanuensis of GOD and inspired, but as one who writes whatever happens to come into his mind without inspiration, bringing forward what pleases him by human will, and not indeed carried by the Holy Spirit, which is against the Petrine sentence, 2 Pet. 1, verse 21, and the pronouncement of Paul, 2 Tim. 3, verse 16. The Apostle had spoken against those who wish to become rich out of avarice; now, lest it be believed that riches cannot consist with piety and αὐταρκείᾳ (self-sufficiency), he teaches concerning the possession of riches; prescribing rules for the rich of this age, whom he distinguishes from the rich of the future age, or rather from those who are rich in GOD, as those who are rich in the world and only with respect to the treasures of the world, Luke 12:21. Therefore, this admonition is not accidental and παραφυαδικὴ (incidental), but is required for the preceding exhortation, and he explains the same further. Moreover, there are in these things, which the Apostle wishes to be prescribed to the rich of this age, certain things which are to be prohibited, and certain things which are to be commended. The former are both pride and vain confidence in riches. The latter are (1) trust in the true GOD (2) Spiritual opulence. (3) Liberal beneficence toward others. (4) The excellence of a good foundation for the future. verses 18 & 19. Concerning pride, Chrysostom says: Nothing, he says, makes one so proud, nothing so begets pride and arrogance, as wealth. Money makes courage. Psalm 49. Matthew 6:20.

Μηδὲ ἠλπικέναι ἐπὶ πλύτε ἀδηλότητι) On the uncertainty of riches, instead of uncertain riches, or fleeting ones. For an example of a man trusting in wealth, see Psalm 39:7. Luke 12:17, 18, & 19.

The possession of riches, says Theodoret, is uncertain. For now they come to this person, now indeed they pass to that one; and that which has many masters is the possession of no one. However, he necessarily used a distinction. For there are also rich people of the future age, who possess stable and sufficient riches. Chrysostom on this passage: Nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches: For from that primarily arrogance is born, just as on the contrary, he who hopes in GOD is always a stranger to haughtiness. Why do you hope in that which is suddenly transferred? For such are riches: You who place hope in those things in which you cannot trust at all? How indeed will they be able to avoid pride? If they see how weak they are, how unstable; if they attend to how a firm hope in GOD surpasses all wealth, if they understand that GOD is the author of these things also. Augustine, book 5, De Civitate Dei, chapter 18. Earthly riches do not make us or our children happy, being either to be lost while we are living, or to be received by those we do not know or those we do not wish when we are dead; but GOD has made happy, who is the true opulence of minds. How many were rich yesterday, says Augustine on the word of the Lord in Matthew 10, who are poor today? How many sleep rich, and with thieves awake and taking everything away, they are therefore poor. Compare Psalm 68:11.

Ἀλλ᾽ ἐν τῷ Θεῷ τῷ ζῶντι) Which is also subjoined to the aforementioned place of the Psalm. The epithet of GOD is ὁ ζῶν (the living one). 1 Thessalonians 1:9.

Above III. ver. 15. IV. ver. 10. Thus to the Hebrews אל חי and not in vain is this placed here, riches perish, He remains: riches are inanimate things, GOD is living and the cause of life. For ἐν τῷ Θεῷ, the Manuscript has ἐπὶ τῷ Θεῷ. After the word ἐλπίζειν, sometimes ἐν, sometimes ἐπὶ is accustomed to be placed, for the Hebrew ב: sometimes also εἰς. See Matt. XII. 2. John V. ver. 45. Rom. XV. 12. 1 Cor. XV. 15. 2 Cor. I. 10. Phil. II. ver. 19. Above IV. 20. 1 Pet. III. 5.

To Him who provides us richly with all things for enjoyment) In Him hope must be placed, who even to us poor people gives all those things which nature needs, and with which we are content. For that is ἀπολαύειν, to use with a certain delight. πλουσίως that is, abundantly, as Col. III. ver. 16. Tit. III. ver. 6. 2 Pet. I. ver. 11. He gives the Sun and the heaven, and the stars and the fountains, and the fruit-bearing lands.

Beautifully, as Chrysostom advises, he said all things abundantly, signifying the annual conversions and changes, the air, water, light, and all other things. You see how He provides all things abundantly with ineffable plenty. Theodoret, in that, he says, trust is to be placed, who indeed always lives, but supplies good things for all to enjoy. Nor indeed are only temporal goods included, but also heavenly ones, as Augustine says in his sermon on the Words of the Lord in Matt. X. He includes, he says, temporal and eternal, but more for enjoying the eternal, for using the temporal: temporal as for travelers, eternal as for inhabitants: Temporal, from which we may do good: eternal, from which we may be made good.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Τοῖς πλουσίοις ἐν τῷ νῦν αἰῶνι) Cum epistolam jam absol- visset, venit ei in mentem speciali admonitione opus habere divites illos mercatores, qui plurimi erant Ephesi: Bené autem dixit divites hujus seculi: quia sunt & aliae divitiae, de quibus Matth. VI. 20. & XIX. 21. Marc. X. 21. Luc. XII. 21. 33. XVIII. 22.

Παράγγελλε) Vide supra 13.

Μὴ ὑψηλοφρονεῖν) Habuimus hoc verbum & Roman. XI. vers. 20. pro ὑψηλὰ φρονεῖν Rom. XII. vers. 16. id est al- tos gerere Spiritus quod vitium maxime divitias sequitur: Sosiphanes: Αἳ δ᾽ εὐτυχῆτε μηδὲν ὄντες ἐνθάδε Ἴσ᾽ ὀρανῷ φρονεῖτε. Euripides: Ὕβριν τε τίκτει πλοῦτος. Menander: Λαμπρῶς τε πλούτῳ καὶ γένει γαυρούμενοι.

Idem Ὑπερήφανοι γὰρ γίνεθ᾽ ἡ λίαν τροφή. Inde ejusdem Menandri monitum: - - μηδ᾽ αὐτὸς εἰ σφόδρ᾽ εὐπορεῖς, πίσευε τούτῳ, μήτε τῶν πτωχῶν πάλιν ἡμῶν καταφρόνει. - - - Confiderare videtur Grotius Paulum non tan- quam divinum, sed tanquam humanum Scri- ptorem, non tanquam DEI amanuensem & θεόπνευςον, sed tanquam eum, qui quicquid in mentem forte venit citra θεοπνευςίαν scribit, vo- luntate humana adferens, quæ placent, non vero ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε φερόμενος, quod est con- tra Petrinam sententiam, 2. Petr. I. vers. 21. & Pauli pronunciatum 2. Timoth. III. vers. 16. Di- xerat Apostolus adversus eos, qui divites fieri volunt ex avaritia, jam, ne credatur, non posse divitias consistere cum pietate, & αὐταρκείᾳ, docet de possessione divitiarum; Regulas præ- scribens divitibus hujus seculi, quos à divitibus futuri seculi, vel potius iis, qui in DEO divi- tes sunt, distinguit, ceu eos, qui in mundo, & quoad mundi thesauros tantum divites sunt, Luc. XII. vers. 21. Non ergo accidentalis hæc est admonitio, & παραφυαδικὴ, sed ad adhortatio- nem præcedaneam requiritur, eandemque ulte- rius explicat. Sunt autem in his, quæ diviti- bus hujus seculi præscribi vult Apostolus quæ- dam, quæ prohibenda sunt, & quædam, quæ com- mendanda. Illa sunt tum superbia, tum vana in divitiis confidentia. Ista sunt (1) in DEO vero fiducia (2) Spiritualis opulentia. (3) Liberalis erga alios beneficentia. (4) Fundamenti boni in futurum præcellentia. vers. 18. & 19. De super- bia Chrysostomus: Nihil ita, inquit, superbum absolvit, nihil ita superbiam & arrogantiam gi- gnit, atque opes. Gut machet Muth. Psal. XLIX. Matth. VI. v. 20.

Μηδὲ ἠλπικέναι ἐπὶ πλύτε ἀδηλότητι) Incerto divitia- rum, pro divitiis incertis, sive fluxis. Exemplum homi- nis fidentis opibus vide Psalm. XXXIX. vers. 7. Luc. XII. vers. 17. 18. & 19.

Incerta est, inquit Theodoreius, possessio divi- tiarum. Nunc enim ad hunc veniunt, nunc ve- ro ad illum transeunt, quæ autem multos habet Dominos, nullius est possessio. Distinctione autem necessario usus est. Sunt enim futuri etiam secu- li divites, qui stabiles divitias & sufficientes possi- dent. Chrysostomus in hunc loc. Neque spera- re incerto divitiarum: Ex eo enim imprimis arro- gantia nascitur, sicut contra, qui in DEUM sperat, à fastu semper alienus est. Quid in eo spe- ras, quod repente transfertur? Id quippe divitiæ sunt: Qui in illis spem ponis, quibus confidere omnino non potes? Quomodo vero cavere super- biam poterunt; Si viderint, quam infirmæ illæ, quam instabiles sint: si attenderint, quam omnes opes exuperet firma in DEUM spes, si intelli- gant, harum etiam autorem esse DEUM. Au- gustinus libr. V. de C. D. cap. 18. Felices vel nos vel filios nostros non faciunt divitiæ terrenæ, aut nobis viventibus amittendæ, aut nobis mortuis, à quibus nescimus, vel à quibus nolumus, accipi- endæ, sed DEUS felices fecit, qui est mentium vera opulentia. Quam multi heri divites, inquit Augustinus de verbo Domini in Matth. X. ho- die pauperes? Quam multi dormiunt divites, & vigilantibus latronibus, & auferentibus omnia, ergo pauperes sunt. Conferatur Psalm. LXVII. vers. 11.

Ἀλλ᾽ ἐν τῷ Θεῷ τῷ ζῶντι) Quod subjungitur etiam dicto Psalmi loco. Ἐπίθετον est DEI ὁ ζῶν 1. Thessal. I. 4.

Supra III. verf. 15. IV. verf. 10. Sic Hebræis אל חי nec inaniter hic id positum, divitiæ pereunt, ille manet: divitiæ res inanimes, DEUS vivus & vitæ causa. Pro ἐν τῷ Θεῷ, Manuscriptus habet ἐπὶ τῷ Θεῷ. Post vo- cem ἐλπίζειν modo ἐν, modo ἐπὶ solet poni, pro Ebræo ב: interdum & εἰς. Vide Matth. XII. 2. Johan. V. v. 45. Roman. XV. 12. 1. Cor. XV. 15. 2. Corinth. I. 10. Philipp. II. v. 19. Supra IV. 20. 1. Petr. III. 5.

Τῷ παρέχοντι ἡμῖν πλουσίως πάντα εἰς ἀπόλαυσιν) In illo spes reponenda est, qui etiam nobis pauperibus dat omnia ista, quibus natura indiget, & quibus nos con- tenti sumus. Id enim est ἀπολαύειν, uti cum quadam delectatione. πλουσίως id est large, ut Coloss. III. verf. 16. Tit. III. verf. 6. 2. Petr. I. verf. 11. Dat Solem & cœlum, & sidera & fontes, & terras frugiferas.

Pulchre, monente Chrysostomo, dixit affluen- ter omnia, conversiones annuas, vicesque signifi- cans, aërem, aquam, lucem, & cætera omnia. Vides, ut affluenter præstet omnia cum ineffabili copia. Theodoretius, in eo, inquit, collocanda est fiducia, qui semper quidem vivit, bona autem fru- enda omnibus suppeditat. Nec vero temporalia tantum bona, sed etiam cælestia comprehen- duntur, ut Augustinus serm. de Verb. Dom. in Matth. X. Complectitur, inquit, temporalia & æ- terna, sed magis ad fruendum æterna, ad utendum temporalia: temporalia tanquam viatoribus, æter- na tanquam habitatoribus: Temporalia, unde bona faciamus: æterna, unde boni efficiamur.

## 6:18
Ver. 18.

᾿Αγαθοεργεῖν) The same as ἀγαθοποιεῖν Mark III. ver. 4. Luke VI. ver. 9, 33, and 35. Acts XIV. ver. 17, and among Peter several times: it corresponds to the Hebrew הטוב, as can be seen in Num. X. ver. 32. Judg. XVII. ver. 13. Zeph. I. ver. 13. but it signifies to confer benefits, which is easy for the rich, and indeed toward men of any fortune. This infinitive is constructed here with that παραγγέλλων.

Πλουτεῖν ἐν ἔργοις καλοῖς) To abound in good deeds. For that is πλουτεῖν Rom. X. 12. עשר.

Others also explain that as concerning beneficence. But it is more correctly understood as concerning good works in general, because it follows them next in particular, with the words to give easily, to communicate. Namely, he commands first to do good, that is, not only to be good, but also to act well: because the rich think that all things are permitted to them in any way, or at least they are tempted by various desires. But he wishes further that the rich of this world should also be rich in good works: that is, that they may acquire a habit of good works by continually acting well, and thus procure for themselves certain riches of virtues. There are many rich people, says Crocius, full of evil works; they are greedy, unmerciful, unjust, fraudulent, they swear rashly, they perjure themselves, they neglect their neighbor, they exhaust with wicked usury, they live in luxury, they are lustful: To these evil works he opposes the riches of good works, with which the mind may be filled: From the fact, however, that they are commanded to abound in good works, Estius gathers that nothing of our opinion is true, that the good works of the just are sins: because we do not say this in any other sense than that good works are imperfect and unclean, and thus contaminated by sin: for the common stain is not lacking.

᾿Ευμεταδότους εἶναι) To give liberally to the poor, according to that saying:

Remember, while rich, to benefit the poor.

Κοινωνικούς) Also to invite the poor, so that they may commonly enjoy the things that have been shared. Prov. XXII. 8. Isa. LVIII. 7. Luke XIV. 12. Thus Hermes is called κοινωνικὸς by Aristotle. Certain beginnings of these precepts were in the laws concerning gleaning and grape-gathering, and the Sabbatical year.

There are not wanting those who, with Theodoret and Theophylact, refer the word κοινωνικοὺς to manners, and interpret it as friendly and affable. For moroseness is a great vice in a rich man; he listens to no one willingly, much less does he succor the needy, or if he does any of this, he does it with resentment and reproach: as Blessed Baldwin says. But that word signifies communication, by which one shares generously from his own resources, Num. XII. verse 13, 2 Cor. VIII. verse 4, Gal. VI. verse 6, Heb. XIII. verse 16. It is joined, however, with the word εὐμεταδότης, by which a ready communication is implied, so that the rich may share their goods both willingly and opulently. Nor indeed are the beginnings of these precepts found only in the Old Testament: but the same liberality which is commanded in the New Testament was also prescribed there, Deut. XV. verses 7, 8, 10, and 11, Prov. III. verse 27, chap. V. verse 16, Dan. IV. verse 14. Sirach IV. verse 1, following, VII. verse 11, XIV. verses 13 and 14, XXIX. verses 12, 13, and 14. In this sense, as Estius notes, Latin expositors interpret the word for communicating. Hervaeus, Aquinas, Lyranus, Cajetan, Catharinus, and others. To communicate, says Aquinas, is to have riches as if they were common. Whence the same doctor, 2. Sec. quest. 66, art. 2, proves from this Scripture that no one ought to have external things, as far as use is concerned, as his own but as common; so, namely, that he may easily communicate them for the needs of others. And Cajetan also diligently noted this in his commentary.

Latin:

Verf. 18.

᾿Αγαθοεργεῖν) Idem quod ἀγαθοποιεῖν Marc. III. verf. 4. Luc. VI. verf. 9, 33. & 35. Actor. XIV. verf. 17. & apud Petrum aliquoties: respondet Hebræo הטוב, ut videre est Num. X. verf. 32. Jud. XVII. verf. 13. Soph. I. verf. 13. significat autem beneficia conferre, quod facile diviti- bus, & quidem in cujusvis fortunæ homines. Construi- tur hic infinitivus cum illo παραγγέλλων.

Πλουτεῖν ἐν ἔργοις καλοῖς) Piis factis abundare. Id enim πλουτεῖν Roman. X. 12. עשר.

Illud alii etiam de beneficentia explicant. Sed rectius intelligitur de bonis operibus in genere, quia de illis sequitur deinceps in specie, verbis facile tribuere, communicare. Nimirum bene operari primum jubet, id est, non bonum tan- tum, sed & bene agere: quia divites omnia sibi quovis modo licere putant, vel certe tentantur variis cupiditatibus. Vult autem ulterius, ut di- vites hujus seculi divites etiam sint in bonis ope- ribus: id est, habitum bonorum operum con- tinuo bene agendo acquirant, adeoque divitias quasdam virtutum sibi comparent. Sunt ple- rique divites, inquit Crocius, pleni malorum ope- rum; sunt avari, immisericordes, injusti, frau- dulenti, temere jurant, pejerant, negligunt pro- ximum, exhauriunt iniquis usuris, luxuriant, libidinantur: His malis operibus bonorum operum divitias opponit, quibus impleatur animus: Ex eo autem, quod abundare jubeantur bonis operibus, ne quicquam colligit Estius, falsam esse nostram sententiam, bona opera justorum esse peccata: quia alio sensu hoc non dicimus, quam quod bo- na opera imperfecta, & immunda sint, adeoque peccato contaminata: communis enim labes non deest.

᾿Ευμεταδότους εἶναι) Liberaliter dare pauperibus, secun- dum dictum illud:

Μέμνησο πλουτῶν τοῖς πένητας ὠφελεῖν.

Κοινωνικούς) Etiam vocare pauperes, ut communiter rebus partis fruantur. Proverb. XXII. 8. Esa. LVIII. 7. Luc. XIV. 12. Sic κοινωνικὸς Ἑρμῆς Aristoteli. Horum præ- ceptorum initia quædam erant in legibus de spicilegio & racematione, & anno Sabbatıco.

Non desunt, qui vocem κοινωνικοὺς cum Theo- doreto & Theophylacto ad mores referant, & in- terpretantur amicos & affabiles. Magnum enim vitium in divite est morositas, neminem libenter audit, multo minus egentibus succurrit, aut si quod hujus facit, cum stomacho & exprobratione facit: ut Beatus Balduinus. Sed vox ea signi- ficat communicationem, qua quis largiter de facultatibus suis impertit, Num. XII. versu 13. 2. Corinth. IIX. versu 4. Galat. VI. vers. 6. Hebr. XIII. versu 16. Conjungitur autem cum voce εὐμεταδότης, qua prompta communicatio infertur, ut & libenter & opulenter bona sua communi- cent divites. Nec vero tantum initia istorum præceptorum in Veteri Testamento reperiun- tur: Sed eadem liberalitas, quæ in Novo Te- stamento præcipitur, illic etiam præscripta fuit Deuteronom. XV. versu 7. 8. 10. & 11. Proverb. III. vers. 27. cap. V. versu 16. Dan. IV. vers. 14. Syrach. IV. vers. 1. sequ. VII. vers. 11. XIV. vers. 13. & 14. XXIX. vers. 12. 13. & 14. In hunc sen- sum, notante Estio, interpretantur communican- di verbum expositores Latini. Hervæus, Aqui- nas, Liranus, Cajetanus, Catharinus, & alii. Communicare, ait Aquinas, id est, habere di- vitias sicut communes. Unde idem ductor 2. Sec. quæst. 66. artic. 2. probat ex hac Scriptura, non debere quenquam res exteriores, quantum ad u- sum attinet, habere ut proprias sed ut communes; ita scilicet, ut facile eas communicet in necessita- tes aliorum. Idque etiam Cajetanus in suo com- mentario diligenter annotavit.

## 6:19
Verse 19.

Laying up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold on eternal life) θησαυρίζειν and ἀποθησαυρίζειν are used by allusion concerning everything that is deposited secretly, such as alms among the poor. Thus this word is placed in Rom. II. verse 5, Jas. V. verse 3, 2 Pet. III. verse 7. It also agrees with this foundation, because foundations are hidden so that they do not appear. But works of mercy are compared to a foundation because, just as a house rises on high from hidden foundations, so from those works rises that sublime and heavenly life. See Matt. XIX. verse 21. We had the word ἐπιλαβέσθαι joined with eternal life also above in 12. But there the name of the thing received the right to the thing: here the thing itself is signified. In the manuscript, for τῆς αἰωνίυ ζωῆς, there is τῆς ὄντως ζωῆς, with the same sense. For those things which always remain are called ὄντα and Ἀληθῆ by way of excellence. And the Latin reads thus: for it translates it as true life.

This is a Papistical distortion, and entirely alien to the mind of the Apostle, and contrary to the Holy Scriptures. For he does not call works of mercy the foundation of eternal life: he had already dealt with beneficence in the previous words εὐμεταδότης, κοινωνικὸς: there is no reason, therefore, for him to repeat what has been done, and to inculcate the same thing again in such succinct admonitions. Nor is there any word here further either about works of mercy, or beneficence, or, as pleases other Papists, about good works in general: because he had already commanded those with the word ἀγαθοεργεῖν. Nor are good works ever called the foundation of eternal life; indeed, because they labor under many defects, they foster too weak a foundation. The Apostle knows no other foundation, he denies that any other can be laid, than that which is laid, which is CHRIST JESUS, 1 Cor. III. verse 11. This is that treasure which we ought to acquire for ourselves, putting all others behind, Matt. XIII. verse 44. If we possess Him, we can hold all things in heaven and on earth as of no account, Ps. LXXIII. verse 19; in Him alone the rich ought to glory, Jer. IX. verse 24, 1 Cor. I. verse 31; the knowledge of Him is better than all the treasures of the world, because it is the knowledge of salvation, Luke I. verse 77, and eternal life, John XVII.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

'Αποθησαυρίζοντας ἑαυτοῖς θεμέλιον καλὸν εἰς τὸ μέλλον, ἵνα ἐπιλάβωνται τῆς αἰωνίας ζωῆς) θησαυρίζειν, & ἀποθη- σαυρίζειν per allusionem de omni re, quæ clam deponi- tur, ut eleemosynæ apud pauperes. Sic ponitur hæc vox Roman. II. vers. 5. Jac. V. vers. 3. 2. Petr. III. vers. 7. Convenit autem & hoc fundamento, quia fundamenta abduntur, ita, ut non appareant. Opera autem miseri- cordiæ ideo comparantur fundamento, quia sicut ex fun- damentis latentibus domus in altum assurgit, ita ex illis operibus assurgit vita illa sublimis atque cœlestis. Vi- de Matth. XIX. vers. 21. Vocem ἐπιλαβέσθαι conjunctam cum vita æterna habuimus & supra 12. Sed ibi jus ad rem rei nomen accepit: hic res ipsa significatur. In Manu- scripto pro τῆς αἰωνίυ ζωῆς, est τῆς ὄντως ζωῆς, sensu eodem. Nam ὄντα & Ἀληθῆ dicuntur κατ’ ἐξοχὴν ea quæ semper manent. Et Latinus sic legit: vertit enim statum vitam.

Papistica hæc detorsio est, & prorsus à men- te Apostolica aliena, & Scripturis Sacr. contra- ria. Non enim opera misericordiæ fundamen- tum dicit vitæ æternæ: egerat jam prioribus verbis ἐυμεταδότης, κοινωνικὸς de beneficentia: Non ergo est, quod actum agat: & idem ite- rum in tam succinctis monitis inculcet. Neque ullum verbum hic amplius vel de operibus mi- sericordiæ, seu beneficentia, vel quod Papistis aliis placet, de bonis operibus in genere: quia etiam illa jam verbo ἀγαθοεργεῖν præceperat. Nec uspiam bona opera fundamentum vitæ æ- ternæ dicuntur: imo, quia multis defectibus laborant, nimis infirmum fovent fundamen- tum. Nescit Apostolus aliud fundamentum, negat aliud poni posse, quam quod positum est, quod est CHRISTUS JESUS, 2. Corinth. III. versu 11. Hic est thesaurus ille, quem nobis omnibus aliis posthabitis comparare debemus, Matth. XIII. vers. 44. Si illum possidemus, o- mnia in cœlo & in terra fusque deque habere possumus, Psalm. LXXIII. versu 19. in uno il- lo gloriari oportet divites, Jerem. IX. vers. 24. 1. Corinth. I. vers. 31. illius cognitio omnis the- sauris mundi potior est, quia est cognitio salu- tis, Luc. I. vers. 77. & vita æterna, Johan. XVII.

## 6:20-21
vers. 20. 21. If a trichotomy pleases, the Apostle teaches what must be enjoined to servants, vers. 1. 2. Then, what must be observed, both regarding heterodoxy in doctrine and regarding the practice of life, such as in self-sufficiency, justice, etc., up to vers. 16. Finally, an exhortation to duty, both regarding the instruction of the rich and regarding the keeping of the deposit of faith, up to vers. 21. Lastly, this chapter can be explained by a dichotomy, which (I) contains an admonition concerning servants. (II) Institutes an antithesis and comparison of false and true teachers.

PART I. Admonition concerning servants.

Latin:

vers. 20. 21. Si placeat τριχοτομία, docet Aposto- lus, quæ servis præcipienda vers. 1. 2. Deinde, quæ observanda, tum quoad heterodoxian in doctrina, tum quòd praxin vitæ, utpote in ἀυταρκείᾳ, justi- tiâ &c. ad vers. 16. Tandem hortatio ad officium, tùm qua instructionem divitum, tùm qua custo- diendum fidei depositum ad vers. 21. Denique per διχοτομίαν exponi potest hoc caput, quod (I) Commonefactionem de servis continet. (II) An- tithesin & collationem falsorum & verorum Do- ctorum instituit.

PARS I. Commonitio de servis.

## 6:20
Verse 20.

O Timothy) A gentle address, with the proper name added.

Keep the deposit) A manuscript here and in 2. Timoth. I. verse 12. has deposit. In the Glossary, deposit is this trust. And this word is described thus in Levit. c. IV. verse 2. & 4. where in the Hebrew it is פקדון 2. Maccab. III. verse 10. & 15. And Phrynichus wants it to be called deposit, not trust; he calls the sacred doctrine of the Gospel a deposit: because it is also the thing of another, namely of Christ, and its faithful custody rests upon the pastors. Wherefore we also have the verb to entrust in the same matter above I. 18. 2. Timoth. II. verse 2. And others have noted in the book Musar, that precepts are called a deposit.

Theodoret explains it concerning the talent, or the grace of the Holy Spirit, which Timothy had received through ordination. But it is manifest that it concerns the deposit of doctrine. For the Apostle wished to warn of this still by way of a conclusion, that he should diligently guard that saving deposit, and he confirms this by the antithesis concerning avoiding profane novelties of words, and oppositions of falsely named knowledge: and also by the collation of similar passages, 2. Timoth. I. verse 13. chap. II. verse 2. chap. III. verse 14. Therefore Theophylact with Chrysostom takes it concerning all things which the Apostle had handed down here: so that nothing of them may be diminished, among which those things which pertain to faith were especially prominent. But Lyranus and Thomas wrongly understand by the deposit the Church, or the flock of the Corinthians. Scripture speaks nowhere in that way. Furthermore, Timothy is commanded to guard that deposit in such a way that nothing is added to it, nothing taken away. For the very name of a deposit demands that which is to be faithfully kept. Beware lest you diminish it, says Chrysostom, for they are not yours, but another's, which you have received to be kept. And this deposit can also be adulterated through additions, Galat. 1. vers. 8. We learn from this passage, says Estius, that guardians of doctrine have been appointed, and as it were depositaries, to whom therefore it is permitted neither to change anything in it, nor to diminish, nor to add. For this also is contrary to the nature of a deposit, that something be added to it. Whence Basil said that Bishops are guardians of the deposit, not inventors of any doctrine, as is held in the Historia Tripartita, lib. 7. cap. 36. Hence therefore it follows, that to the faith once delivered by Christ, and received from the Apostles, nothing at all can be added.

Vincent of Lérins against profane novelties, haeres. cap. XXIV. What is, he says, a deposit? That is, what has been entrusted to you, not what has been invented by you; what you have received, not what you have devised; a matter not of wit, but of doctrine: not of private usurpation, but of public tradition: a matter brought to you, not brought forth by you: in which you ought to be an author, but a guardian; not an originator, but a follower; not leading, but following. The deposit, he says, guard; the talent of the Catholic faith, keep inviolate and unblemished. What has been entrusted to you, let it remain with you, let it be handed on by you. You have received gold, return gold; I do not want you to substitute one thing for another for me. of Vincent, who in chapter XXVI, through this Apostolic passage, says that all the wicked novelties of all heresies are, as if by a certain spiritual sword, often cut down and must always be cut down.

Avoiding profane babblings.

Those genealogies of which I spoke above: which are both empty, for they profit nothing toward piety, and profane, because they are not divinely revealed. The same profane myths [are mentioned] above in IV. 7. 'Kenophonia' is the same as in the Glossary. 'Kenologein' is vain-speaking: Theophylact at this place [calls it] 'mataiologia' [vain-speaking].

He rightly departs from the Vulgate version, which rendered it 'profane novelties of words,' as if the Apostle had written 'kainophonias' [novelties of words]; for the Greek codices consistently have 'kenophonias,' that is, emptinesses of words, and Estius admits that Theophylact and Oecumenius read and expounded it thus, and that more recent interpreters also translate it so, and he observes that it conforms to the word of the same meaning, 'mataiologia,' in chapter I: And that the same word recurs in 2 Timothy II, verse 16, where the Vulgate rendered it 'vain-speakings': Why then does he prefer 'novelties of words' here? Because he says that vain-speakings, whatever they may be, are a fault. Therefore, there was no need to add 'profane'. It is rightly added, because he wished to note not so much empty words in general, but especially those which are profane, just as Estius himself adds: But if we read 'emptinesses of words,' the sense will be that the futile, empty, and clamorous loquacity of certain people is noted, and that it is profane, that is, impure and harmful to piety, as the Greeks expound it, and that it is commanded to Timothy that he should avoid and reject that kind. Which sense is more convenient than Grotius's. For it is not the case that the warning should be restricted to genealogies. For there is no doubt that 'profane babblings' extends much further. However, the Apostle does not say 'abstain,' but 'ektrepomenos' [turning away], flee with abomination, just as we turn our nostrils and eyes away from foul and impure things.

And oppositions) For they were also fighting among themselves, as we said in I. 4. In the Glossary: 'antithesis' is opposition. The Greeks interpret 'antitheses' as 'antilogias' [contradictions].

Of the falsely named knowledge.

You see here how old the name of the Gnostics is, which those philosophers, mingling themselves with Christian assemblies, took upon themselves, and despised others as rude in comparison to themselves: we spoke about them at the beginning of John, and at chapter V, verse 4 of this Epistle. But they falsely claimed for themselves the praise of knowledge, whence Irenaeus at the beginning says, 'leading them away under the pretext of knowledge.' Eusebius, book V, chapter 7, says that the books of Irenaeus are for the 'refutation and overturning of the falsely named knowledge.' Against these is also that statement of Justin to Diognetus: 'For he who thinks he knows something without knowledge that is true and testified to by life, has not known; he is deceived by the serpent.' And that statement of Clement in the Pedagogue, book 1: 'For we are called children and infants, in relation to the childish and contemptible nature of learning, just as those who are puffed up into knowledge have slandered us.' The same [Clement] in Stromata I says that this Epistle was for this reason rejected by the Gnostics, because they recognized themselves noted in it with such vivid colors: 'Just as,' he says, 'pride and conceit have slandered philosophy, so too has false knowledge slandered knowledge, and that which is called by the same name.' Then he produces this passage which we have in our hands. True knowledge is that which profits toward eternal salvation.

Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret it as being about the Gnostics, who called themselves such at that time: Theodoret says that those who proceeded from Simon were called Gnostics. Estius agrees that the Gnostics are noted; he admits, however, that that name was not yet in use at that time, just as Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 10, teaches that the falsely named knowledge received its beginnings only from the Simonians: And Epiphanius, after the Simonians, Menandrians, and Basilidians, finally lists the Nicolaitans and then the Gnostics. Theophylact says here that they were those Nicolaitans. But no one, as far as I know, among the ancients, with Grotius, maintains that they were philosophers mixed with Christians; because they consider them to be Christians by profession. It is certain that at that time neither was the heresy of the Gnostics known, nor were philosophers called by that name, and so it is better to say that what is designated is a falsely named knowledge, which opposes itself to the truth of the divine word: as Theodoret notes, I rightly call it falsely named knowledge, which has the darkness of ignorance, but not the light of divine cognition. For it cannot be true knowledge which is contrary to the truth. 'Antitheses.' The Vulgate rendered it 'oppositions': just as 'antithesis' is called a proposition which is opposed to a true 'thesis'; such as the 'heterodidaskaliai' [different teachings] from chapter 1, verse 3, can be named. B. Gerhard, with Estius, thinks that objections are noted, which are brought forward against the doctrine of the faith under the specious title of knowledge, but falsely. Haymo and Cajetan suspect that the questions of the Jews are signified, which they moved against Christians from that falsely named knowledge, which they call Cabalistic. But Estius doubts whether that doctrine is so ancient. Others interpret Sophistry, which Estius admits, provided that Dialectic is not censured, along with Pelagius, who denies that it is a science in the true sense of the word.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Ώ Τιμόθεε ) Blanda compellatio, addito nomine proprio.

Τὴν παρακαταθήκην φύλαξον ) Manuscriptus & hic & 2. Timoth. I. versu 12. παραθήκην. In Glossario παρα- θήκη hoc depositum. Et ita describitur haec vox Levit. c. IV. vers. 2. & 4. ubi in Hebraeo פקדון 2. Maccab. III. vers. 10. & 15. Et Phrynichus vult παραθήκην dici, non παρακαταθήκην ; vocat autem depositum sacram doctri- nam Evangelii : quia & res est alterius, nempe & Chri- sti, & pastoribus fida ejus custodia incumbit. Quare & verbum παρατίθεσθαι in eodem negotio habemus supra I. 18. 2. Timoth. II. vers. 2. Et notarunt alii in libro Mu- sar, praecepta vocari depositum.

Theodoretus de talento, seu gratia Spiritus san- cti, quam per ordinationem Timotheus accepe- rat, explicat. Sed manifestum est, de deposito doctrinae agi. Nam coronidis loco id adhuc mo- nere voluit Apostolus, ut depositum illud sa- lutare diligenter custodiat, idque confirmat an- tithesis de vitandis prophanis vocum novitatibus, & oppositionibus falsi nominis scientiae : nec non collatio locorum similium, 2. Timoth. I. vers. 13. cap. II. vers. 2. cap. III. vers. 14. Ideo Theophyla- ctus cum Chrysostomo accipit de omnibus, quae hic tradiderat Apostolus : ne quicquam eorum imminuatur, inter quae praecipue eminebant, quae ad fidem spectant. Perperam autem Lyra- nus & Thomas per depositum Ecclesiam, seu gre- gem Corinthiorum intelligunt. Nuspiam ita lo- quitur Scriptura. Caeterum ita illam παρακατα- θήκην custodire jubetur Timotheus, ut ei nihil ad- datur, nihil dematur. Id enim nomen depositi postulat, quod fideliter servandum. Cave ne minuas, ait Chrysostomus, non enim tua sunt, sed aliena, quae servanda accepisti. Et potest depo- situm hoc etiam per additamenta adulterari, Galat. 1. vers. 8. Discimus ex hoc loco, inquit E- stius, constitutos esse doctrinae custodes, ac velut depositarios, quibus proinde nec mutare quicquam in ea liceat, nec minuere, nec addere. Nam & hoc praeter depositi rationem est, ut ei aliquid ad- datur. Unde Basilius Episcopos esse dixit custodes depositi, non alicujus doctrinae inventores, ut ha- betur historia trip. lib. 7. cap. 36. Hinc ergo sequi- tur, fidei semel a Christo tradita, & ab Apostolis accepta nihil prorsus addi posse.

Vincentius Lyrinensis adversus prophanas no- vitates haeres. cap. XXIV. Quid est, inquit, de- positum ? id est, quod tibi creditum est, non quod a te inventum, quod accepisti, non quod excogi- tasti, rem non ingenii, sed doctrinae : non usur- pationis privatae, sed publicae traditionis : rem ad te perductam, non a te prolatam : in qua non autor debes esse, sed custos, non institutor, sed sectator, non ducens, sed sequens. Depositum, inquit, custodi, Catholicæ fidei talentum invio- latum, illibatumque conserva. Quod tibi cre- ditum est, hoc penes te maneat, hoc à te trada- tur. Aurum accepisti, aurum redde; nolo mi- bi alia pro aliis adjicias. Hæc Vincentius, qui cap. XXVI. per hoc Apostolicum ait, omnes omnium hæreseon sceleratas novitates velut quo- dam spirituali gladio, sæpe truncatas, semperque trucandas esse.

Ἐκτρεπόμενος τὰς βεβήλους κενοφω- νίας.

Illas γενεαλογίας de quibus supra: quæ & inanes sunt, nihil enim ad pietatem proficiunt, & profanæ, quia non sunt divinitus revelatæ. Iisdem βέβηλοι μῦθοι supra IV. 7. κενοφωνία idem quod in Glossario. κενολογεῖν va- niloquium: Theophylacto ad hunc locum ματαιο- λογία.

Merito discedit à Vulgata versione, quæ red- didit prophanas vocum novitates, quasi καινο- φωνίας scripserit Apostolus; nam Græci Cod. constanter habent κενοφωνίας, id est, vocum ina- nitates, atque ita legisse atque exposuisse Theo- phylactum & Oecumenium, ita etiam interpre- tari recentiores fatetur Estius, idque consona- re vocabulo ejusdem significationis ματαιολογία cap. I. observat: Et recurrere eandem vocem, 2. Timoth. II. versu 16. ubi Vulgatus reddidit va- niloquia: Cur ergo præfert hic vocum novita- tes ? Quod ait vaniloquia, quæcunque sint, in vitio esse. Ideo non opus fuisse, addere τὰς βε- βήλους: Resp. Addi merito, quia non tam in ge- nere inanes voces, quam eas etiam imprimis quæ prophanæ sunt, notare voluit, quemadmo- dum Estius ipse subjicit: Quod si legimus vo- cum inanitates, sensus erit, notari quorundam futilem, inanem, & clamosam loquacitatem, eamque profanam, id est, impuram, & pietati noxiam, ut Græci exponunt, ac Timotheo præci- pi, ut id genus devitet, ac respuat. Qui sensus commodior est Grotiano. Non enim est, ut restringatur monitum ad Genealogias? Nam lon- gelatius patere κενοφωνίας βεβήλους dubium nul- lum est. Non autem ait Apostolus abstine, sed ἐκτρεπόμενος avertere, cum abominatione fuge, sicut avertimus nares & oculos à fœtidis & impuris.

Καὶ ἀντιθέσεις) Nam & ipsi inter se pugnabant, ut dixi- mus I. 4. In Glossario: ἀντίθεσις oppositio. Græci ἀντιθέσεις interpretantur ἀντιλογίας.

Τῆς ψευδωνύμως γνώσεως.

Vides hic quam vetus nomen Gnosticorum, quod isti Philosophi Christianis cœtibus se immiscertes sibi inde- bant, spernebantque præ se cæteros ut rudes: diximus de iis ad Johannis initium, & ad hujus Epistolæ l. v. 4. falso autem scientiæ laudem sibi vindicabant, unde Ire- næus initio ait ἀπάγοντες ἀυτὸς προφάσει γνώσεως. Eu- sebius libr. V. 7. libros Irenæi ait esse ἐλέγχου καὶ ἀνα- τροπῆς τῆς ψευδωνύμως γνώσεως. Adversus hos est & Ju- stini illud ad Diognetum: ὁ γὰρ νομίζων ἐιδέναι τι ἄνευ γνώσεως ἀληθῶς καὶ μαρτυρουμένης ὑπὸ τῆς ζωῆς, ἐκ ἔγνω. ὑπὸ τῆ ὄφεως πλανᾶται. Et illud Clementis Pædago- gi l. 1. γὰρ παῖδες ἡμεῖς καὶ νήπιοι, πρὸς τὸ παιδαριῶδες κὴ ἐυκαταφρόνητον τῆς μαθήσεως, προσηγορεύμεθα, καθὼς οἱ εἰς γνῶσιν πεφυσιωμένοι διαβεβλήκασι. Idem Stro- matum I. ait hanc Epistolam ob id à Gnosticis repudia- tam, quod in ea se tam vivis coloribus notatos agno- scerent : καθάπερ, inquit τὴν φιλοσοφικὸ ὁ τύφος κὴ ἡ οἴησις διαβέβληκεν, ὕτως κὴ τὴν γνῶσιν ἡ ψευδὴς γνῶσις ἥ τε ὁμω- ύμως καλυμένη. Deinde producit hunc, quem in mani- bus habemus locum. Vera scientia est, quæ ad salutem æternam proficit.

De Gnosticis, qui ita se tunc appellarunt, Chrysostomus & Theophylactus interpretantur: Theodoretus, qui à Simone processerunt, appellati sunt Gnostici. Annuit Estius, Gnosticos notari; fatetur tamen id nomen tum nondum in usu fuisse, quemadmodum Irenæus libr. 1. cap. 10. do- cet, à Simonianis demum falsi nominis scientiam accepisse initia: Et Epiphanius vere post Simo- nianos, Menandrinos, Basilidianos, Nicolaitas demum recenset Gnosticos. Theophylactus hic Nicolaitas illos fuisse dicit. Nemo autem, quod sciam, veterum cum Grotio, eos Philosophos fuisse Christianis mixtos statuit; quia professione Christianos eosdem censent. Id certum, quod isto tempore nec Gnosticorum hæresis nota, nec Philosophi eo nomine appellati fuerint, adeoque præstat dicere, designari quamvis falso nominatam scientiam, quæ sese opponit veritati verbi divini: ut Theodoretius notat, jure voco fal- so nominatam scientiam, quæ ignorationis habet caliginem, non autem lucem divinæ cognitionis. Non enim vera scientia esse potest, quæ veritati contraria est. Ἀντιθέσεις. Vulgata oppositiones reddidit: quemadmodum ἀντίθεσις dicitur sen- tentia, quæ opposita est veræ θέσει; quales ἑτερο- διδασκαλίαι è cap. 1. 3. nominari possunt. B. Ger- bardus cum Estio censet, objectiones notari, quæ contra fidei doctrinam specioso scientiæ ti- tulo proferuntur, sed falso. Haymo & Cajeta- nus suspicantur, significari quæstiones Judæorum, quas Christianis movebant ex ea falsi nominis scientia, quam Cabalisticam vocant. Sed Estius dubitat, an ea doctrina tam antiqua sit. Sophisti- cam alii interpretantur, quod admittit Estius, dummodo non notetur Dialectica, cum Pelagio, qui eam veri nominis scientiam esse negat.

## 6:21
Ver. 21. Ἥν τινες ἐπαγγελλόμενοι) Professing, as above in ver. 10. B. Balduinus notes that the word ἐπαγγελόμενοι pertains not only to the tongue, but also to all gestures of the body and the whole life, so that the sense is that they do not merely promise such vanities with their voice, but also display them with every gesture and their whole life, in which sense this was used above in a good sense regarding Christian women, ch. II. 10.

Περὶ τὴν πίστιν ἠστόχησαν.

Some, he says, of them, from their very pride and contempt for others, finally arrived at the point where they even abandoned Christianity. This is what he said above about others, ἀπεπλανήθησαν ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως [they have wandered from the faith]; and I. 19, περὶ τὴν πίστιν ἐναυάγησαν [they have made shipwreck concerning the faith]. We have had the word ἀστοχεῖν [to miss the mark] regarding the faith also above in 6. Thus also 2 Tim. II. v. 18. Others wish to note not indeed a defection from the Christian religion, but nevertheless grave errors concerning the faith, by which one wanders from the integrity of the faith, as if from a target, as the phrase implies.

Ἡ χάρις μετά σου

Namely of GOD the Father & of CHRIST. Briefly stated, as also in Ephesians VI, verse 24. In the Manuscript it is μεθ' ὑμῶν [with you all], as in Colossians IV, verse 18, 2 Timothy IV, verse 22, Titus III, verse 15. Paul had added these last words with his own hand.

Whether he added only these words with his own hand, we leave to its proper place. However, it is pleasing to finish with the words of Theodoret: He added the customary benediction: It behooves all who have attained the Priesthood to diligently keep this doctrine, and to always propose it to themselves as a kind of rule, and to direct to it what is said and done by them. For thus it will be possible that, with the blessed Timothy, and indeed with the most divine Paul, we may obtain a portion by the grace and kindness of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. With whom, to the Father with the Most Holy Spirit, belongs glory and magnificence now and always, and for ever and ever, Amen.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Ἥν τινες ἐπαγγελλόμενοι) Profitentes, ut supra V. vers. 10. Vocem ἐπαγγελόμενοι notat B. Balduinus, non tantum ad linguam, sed & ad omnes gestus corpo- ris, totamque vitam pertinere, ut sensus sit, quod non voce tantum hujusmodi vanitates promit- tant, sed & omni gestu, totaque vita præ se fe- rant, quo sensu hæc supra in bonam partem de mulieribus Christianis usurpata fuerit, c. II. 10.

Περὶ τὴν πίστιν ἠστόχησαν.

Quidam, inquit, eorum ex ipso fastu & aliorum contemptu tandem eo pervenere, ut etiam Christiani- smum desererent. Hoc est, quod supra dixit de aliis, ἀπεπλανήθησαν ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως· & I. 19. περὶ τὴν πίστιν ἐναυάγησαν. Vocem ἀστοχεῖν de fide habuimus & supra 6. Sic & 2. Tim. II. v. 18. Alii non quidem defectionem à religione Chri- stiana, errores tamen de fide graves, quibus ab in- tegritate fidei, velut à scopo, ceu phrasis infert, aberratur, notari volunt.

Ἡ χάρις μετά σου

Nempe DEI Patris & CHRISTI. Breviter di- ctum ut & Ephes. VI. versu 24. In Manuscripto μεθ' ὑμῶν, quomodo Coloss. IV. versu 18. 2. Timoth. IV. vers. 22. Tit. III. vers. 15. Hæc ultima verba adscripserat Paulus sua manu.

An hæc solum verba manu sua adscripserit, suo loco relinquimus. Finire autem placet verbis Theodoreti: Benedictionem consuetam addidit: O- portet omnes, qui Sacerdotium sunt consecuti, hanc doctrinam diligenter servare, & eam veluti quan- dam regulam sibi semper proponere, & ad eam di- rigere, quæ ab ipsis dicuntur & fiunt. Ita enim fieri poterit, ut cum beato Timotheo, quin etiam cum di- vinissimo Paulo partem consequamur gratia & be- nignitate Domini & Servatoris nostri Jesu Christi. Cum quo Patri cum Sanctissimo Spiritu convenit gloria & magnificentia nunc & semper, & in secula seculorum, Amen.

# 2 Timothy

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N. J. ANNOTATIONS ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY.

Latin:

I. N. J. ANNOTATA AD POSTERIOREM EPISTOLAM AD TIMOTHEUM.

## 1:1 Introduction: A Brief Grotian Preface
A BRIEF GROTIAN PREFACE.

This Epistle was written, as the Ancients believed, at Rome, when Paul had already returned from his journey, and with Nero raging more daily, he always had death before his eyes. It was written after the Epistle to Titus: And many things from the Epistle to Titus and the former one to Timothy have been transcribed here.

Π Ρ Ο Λ Ε Γ Ο Μ Ε Ν Α of the Author.

Grotius dealt with only three things: Namely, the place and time of the writing: about which there is no need for us to advise. (For in these matters Interpreters easily agree, that the Apostle wrote this Epistle at Rome in his final chains and shortly before his ἀνάλυσιν [departure], except that Baronius and Estius depart into a different view, whom the blessed Gerhard here refutes from Cosmas Magalianus:) and about the subject matter, which he touched upon only, observing that some of the contents of this Epistle were transcribed here from the former one to Timothy and from that which the Apostle had given to Titus. But although it did not irk the Apostle to write the same things, Philipp. III. verse 1, yet it was not his custom to repeat those things which he wrote either to others or to the same people in the same way, but rather, because of the circumstances of the occasion, place, time, and persons, he would even deliver or apply similar things in different ways, let alone transcribe certain things from one Epistle into another, as Grotius speaks quite contemptuously, but to write in such a way as the Holy Spirit suggested, by whose impulse he wrote everything. However, it must still be noted here concerning the occasion, scope, argument, and parts of this Epistle.

The status of the Apostle provided the occasion, who was held in chains at Rome, and so he asked Timothy to come to him, chapter IV, verse 9, and being about to be sacrificed shortly, chapter IV, verse 6, which he knew from the revelation of the Holy Spirit, he was again reminding him of his duty and encouraging him against imminent afflictions. The scope, therefore, was to inform, exhort, and console Timothy, and in his person furthermore a teacher of the Church, and to arrange and remind him of certain private matters still. The argument, therefore, is by no means obscure, namely that he primarily commends the sincerity of doctrine, exhorts to constancy in the faith, warns about seducing spirits, instructs about performing one's duty, about his own imminent ἀνάλυσιν [departure], and some other things: Which Theophylact has encompassed here in the prologue: The reason why he writes the second epistle to Timothy is this. For he had said in the former Epistle: I hope to see you very quickly, which, that he might not execute according to his will as he had promised, was intercepted because he was being detained in chains by Nero; since therefore he was by no means free to go where he most desired, he approaches him, and consoles him through letters, lest perhaps. Both because he was deprived of the presence of Paul his teacher, and also because the care of the Church was pressing him too much, the burden undertaken was already weighing upon him, to the governing of which even more excellent men might succumb, especially at that time when the faithful were being agitated by storms on all sides, and were being attacked most fiercely from every direction. Therefore, the Apostle calls Timothy back to himself, because he was now closer to death.

The parts therefore can be established according to the number of chapters, four. In the first, he gives instructions concerning keeping the deposit of faith. In the second, he excites him to fortitude in the execution of his office and lifts him up with divine promises. In the third, he predicts concerning the last times, and because of seducers who have already arisen, he admonishes him to persist in those things which he learned from childhood. In the fourth, he adds a grave adjuration concerning the parts of his office, primarily because the time of ἀναλύσεως is imminent for him, and he summons him to himself by a commemoration of his own state. Blessed Baldwin makes two parts: The first is παρανετικὴ up to chapter IV, verse 6. The other adds some things concerning certain private matters.

Latin:

PRÆFATIUNCULA GRO- TIANA.

SCripta est hæc Epistola, ut Veteres credidere Ro- mæ, cum jam iterum venisset ab itinere Paulus, & magis indies sæviente Nerone, mortem semper ob oculos haberet. Est scripta post Epistolam ad Titum: Multaque ex Epistola ad Titum, & priore ad Timothe- um huc sunt transcripta.

Π Ρ Ο Λ Ε Γ Ο Μ Ε Ν Α Autoris.

DE tribus tantum egit Grotius: De loco nempe atque tempore scriptionis: de qui- bus non est quod moneamus. (In his enim fa- cile consentiunt Interpretes, quod Romæ in vinculis postremis & paulo ante ἀνάλυσιν hanc Epistolam scripserit Apostolus, nisi quod Ba- ronius & Estius in diversum abeant, quos hic è Cosma Magaliano refellit Beatus Gerhardus:) & de materia, quam attigit solum, observans, quod contenta hujus Epistolæ nonnulla è prio- ri ad Timotheum, & ex ea, quam ad Titum dederat Apostolus huc transcripta sint. Sed quanquam eadem scribere non piguerit Apo- stolum Philipp. III. vers. 1. non tamen mos ejus fuit, repetere ea, quæ sive ad alios, sive ad eos- dem perscripsit eadem ratione, quin ob cir- cumstantias occasionis, loci, temporis, perso- narum similia etiam diversimode traderet, aut applicaret, nedum quædam ex una Epistola in aliam transcribere, ut satis contemptim loqui- tur Grotius, sed ita scribere, prout suggerebat Spiritus sanctus, quo motore omnia scripsit. Est autem hic adhuc monendum de Epistolæ hujus occasione, scopo, argumento, & partibus.

Occasionem præbebat status Apostoli, qui in vinculis hærebat Romæ, adeoque Timotheum rogabat, ut ad se veniret, cap. IV. versu 9. eun- demque brevi immolandus, cap. IV. versu 6. quod ex revelatione Spiritus Sancti cognitum habebat, denuo de officio suo commonefacie- bat, & adversus imminentes afflictiones erige- bat. Scopus ergo erat Timotheum, & in per- sona ejus porro Ecclesiæ doctorem informare, exhortari, consolari, ac de quibusdam priva- tis adhuc disponere, ac commonefacere. Ar- gumentum itaque minime obscurum est, quod nempe imprimis sinceritatem doctrinæ com- mendet, ad constantiam in fide exhortetur, de Spiritibus seductoribus præmoneat, de facien- do officio, de sua imminente ἀναλύσει, aliisque nonnullis instruat: Quæ hic complexus est in prologo Theophylactus: Cur secundam ad Ti- motheum conscribat epistolam, id causa est. Di- xerat nempe in priori Epistola: Spero me celer- rime te conventurum, quod ne uti pollicitus est, pro voluntate exequeretur, eo est interceptum, quia in vinculis à Nerone detinebatur, cum ita- que sibi nequaquam liber pateret, quod maxime cupiebat, accessit, eundem per literas consolatur, neforsan forsan. Tum quia Pauli præceptoris privatus esset præsentia, tum etiam, quia nimis eum Ecclesiæ cura urgeret, onus susceptum jam premeret, cui moderandæ vel viri præstantiores succumberent, eo præsertim tempore, cum pro- cellis undique agitarentur fideles, oppugnarentur undiquaque acerrime. Revocat itaque ad se Ti- motheum Apostolus, quia morti jam erat pro- pinquior.

Partes ergo constitui pro numero capitum possunt IV. In primo de deposito fidei servando præcepit. In secundo ad fortitudi- nem in executione officii excitat ac promissis di- vinis erigit. In tertio de novissimis temporibus prædicit, & ob jam exortos seductores ad per- sistendum in iis, quæ à puero didicit, commo- nefacit. In quarto gravem obtestationem addit de partibus officii, imprimis quia sibi immineat tempus ἀναλύσεως, eumque ad sese commemo- ratione status sui accersit. Beatus Balduinus duas facit partes: Prima est παρανετικὴ usque ad cap. IV. vers. 6. Altera nonnulla de privatis qui- busdam subjicit.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

With a vow and thanksgiving for Timothy premised, he commends his faith for the sake of stirring up the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and for suffering- NOTES ON 2 TIMOTHY, CHAPTER 1, VERSES 1, 2, 3. For the sake of the Gospel, by the gracious calling of God, and for the guarding of the deposit of faith, he exhorts by his own example; and having noted the faithlessness of Phygellus and Hermogenes, he praises Onesiphorus and prays for the Lord's mercy upon him.

There are three parts: I. The Preparatory part, consisting of a vow, of thanksgiving, and of a declaration of his desire for Timothy, as well as a commendation of his faith, extending to verse 5. II. The Hortatory part, concerning stirring up the gift, and preserving the deposit with patience amid afflictions, extending to verse 14. III. The Historical part, concerning those who had fallen away, and those who themselves had remained faithful, extending to verse 18. THE PREPARATORY PART. Verse 1.

PART I.

PREPARATORY.

Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ.

So also in both epistles to the Corinthians, and in that to the Ephesians, and in that to the Colossians.

He ascribes his apostleship not to his own merits, but to the will and gratuitous election of God. Moreover, he calls himself an Apostle, so that immediately at the threshold he may again testify that he acts not in his own name but in another's, and may secure just authority for the epistle. But what Salmero notes is inept: that he does not call himself an Apostle κατ' ἐξοχήν (by way of eminence), because he omits the article, since Peter was the Prince of the Apostles. For neither does Peter prefix the article ὁ Ἀπόστολος, whether in his first or second epistle; and Chrysostom sufficiently indicates Paul as the Apostle κατ' ἀντονομασίαν (by way of antonomasia), saying, "When you have said 'the Apostle,' you have understood Paul."

According to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus. Κατά here signifies that for the sake of which the Apostle is constituted, i.e., the end or purpose.

In the same way the particle is used in 1 Timothy 6:3 and Titus 1:1. Therefore God willed me to be an Apostle, that I might announce to all the promised eternal life, which comes to us through CHRIST. See 1 Timothy 4:6. This is a tacit ἀνθυποφορά (anticipatory objection): Why should we be terrified by adversities, when we have such great promises? ...of mixture?

Therefore, at the outset, as Theophylact advises, he immediately lifts up and raises Timothy's spirit, then says: "I would not have you recount to me the perils of this life, which, if they are endured by us, would undoubtedly produce for us everlasting life. For we discharge this office of apostleship to this end, that being struck by death we may live eternally." Moreover, lest Timothy should be consumed with grief instead of expected consolation, if he perceived that his teacher was in danger, in order to console him now, the Apostle begins thus: "If that perpetual life is promised to us, do not seek it from these earthly things, since this life is in CHRIST JESUS, and is to be with CHRIST." Therefore this life is in CHRIST both by reason of acquisition, and by reason of possession and fruition, who both here and especially in the future life is all things to us.

Latin:

CAPUT I. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.
