Christo? turam. In CHRISTO ergo eſt hæc vita tum ratione acquifitionis, tum ratione poſſeſſionis, & fruitionis, qui & hic & maxime in futura vita nobis est omnia.

## 1:2
Verse 2. To Timothy, beloved child. So he calls Timothy also in 1 Corinthians 4:17.

Grace, mercy, peace, from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. So also in 1 Timothy 1:2.

Latin:

Verf. 2. Τιμοθέῳ ἀγαπητῷ τέκιῳ) Sic Timotheum appellat & 1. Corinth. IV. v. 17.

Χάρις, ἔλεθ, εἰρήνη ἀπὸ Θεῦ πατρὸς κὶ Χρισῷ Ἰησὲ τὰ κυρία ἡμῶν) Sic & 1. Timoth. I. v. 2.

## 1:3
Verse 3. I thank God. Namely, for the gifts bestowed upon you. See Philemon 4.

Whom I serve from my forefathers.

For he served the same GOD whom his ancestors had served, from Benjamin onward. For the GOD of the Jews is not one God, and the GOD of the New Testament another. Acts 22:14; 26:2. The word προγόνων (forefathers) is found in Plato and Sirach 8:5, and 2 Maccabees 8:19; 11:25. Cicero renders it "Generatores" (begetters); Paul, a legal expert, renders it "majores" (ancestors).

With a pure conscience.

This seems to refer to both periods of Paul's life, both in Judaism and in Christianity. For even when he lived as a Jew, he worshipped the same GOD according to the measure of his knowledge.

Here, however, there is rightly a question: how did Paul serve GOD with a pure conscience who had not known CHRIST? Theophylact advises: "In this place, put 'conscience' for 'life,' which, although he was a Jew and observed Jewish rites, he passed most honorably, even though he persecuted the Church." This indeed he did in order to uphold the paternal traditions, not led by desire for glory, as is customary for those who stir up heresy. Meanwhile, while he professes himself an Apostle, he acknowledges with a grateful mind that he is now better instructed after his conversion to CHRIST. Others also note that the conscience is not called pure simply and absolutely, i.e., purified by faith, but sincere, and such that he was conscious of no deceit or prevarication in his worship of GOD.

As without ceasing I have remembrance of thee in my prayers night and day.

You may rightly render it: "as also I have perpetual remembrance of you in my prayers day and night." For what is here ὡς ἔχω (as I have), the same thing is μνείαν ποιούμενος (making mention), as said in the passage to Philemon.

Therefore they say κατά is placed for εἰς or παρά (for, or with respect to), as in Titus 1:1. For nowhere was a promise made concerning Paul's calling, which was fulfilled in his being called. But the end of that calling is to announce that promise—not the legal promise, of which Moses was the minister, but the evangelical one. For that promise was made under the condition of fulfilling the law, a condition which no one could keep. Hence, therefore, a new promise of lost life, i.e., of gratuitous salvation, was made to believers through the Prophets, in CHRIST JESUS, as the one who is the foundation and fountain of life and salvation, John 14:6, and by His death, as the Prophets foretold, He brought forth the same for us, which it was the office of the Apostles to announce. Thus he intimates the matter and end of his apostleship.

Crocius rightly observes on this passage: "He does not say 'which is in Moses,' nor does he say 'in Moses,' but 'in CHRIST JESUS.' This was the mixture of the false apostles." CHRIST is opposed both to Moses and to all other inventions which men devise. Why then does he himself with his followers profess good works as necessary for salvation? Was this not the teaching of the false apostles? Indeed, the Commentary ascribed to Ambrose connects these things with the preceding in this way, which Blessed Luther followed, as also Theodoret: "I give thanks to my GOD, that as often as I pour out prayers to Him, so often I am mindful of you, and pray for you: for my doing this is a divine gift, and therefore worthy of thanks." But here Blessed Gerhard rightly prefers the opinion of others, who explain it thus: "I give thanks to GOD for you, my dearest son, a faithful συνέργῳ (fellow-worker) in the Gospel, signifying to you that in my prayers to God I have constant..."

Volume II. (PPPP) 3 I have remembrance of you, praying that what He began in you, He may perfect. To these here also Grotius has been added.

ἐι καθαρά συνειδήσει

Videtur hoc referri ad tempus Pauli utrumque in Ju- daismo & in Christianiſmo. Nam & cum Judaice viveret, DEUM eundem colebat pro modo cognitionis.

Merito autem hic dubium, quomodo in pu- Quomodo ra conscientia DEO ſerviverit, qui CHRI-in pura STUM ignorarat, monet Theophylactus: Con-conferentia Scientiam bos loco pro viza ponie, quam eisi Ju Paulius in deus esset, & Judaicos ritus fervaret, bonestiffime, Fudaismo transigebat, tametfi Ecclesiam persecutus fit. Interim dum ſe Apostolum profitetur, grata mente agnoscit, ſe nunc poſt ſuam ad CHRI STUM converfionem melius inſtructum. No- tant & alii, non nominari puram simpliciter & abfolute, ſeu fide purificatam conscientiam, sed finceram, & talem, ut nullius doli & præ- varicationis sibi conscius fuerit in DEOcolendo.

ὡς ἀδιάλυπτον ἔχω τὴν περί σε μνείαν ἐν ταῖς δεήσεσί με νυκτός καὶ ἡμέρας.

Vertas recte: sicut & perpetuam tui memoriam in precibus meis babeo diu wottugue. Nam quod hic elt ὡς ἔχω mar, id ipsum est μίαν ποιώμεν, dicto ad Philemo nem loco.

Ideo κατὰ pro εἰς vel παρὰ poſitum dicunt, ut Tit. I. verfu 1. Nusquam enim promissio facta de Pauli vocatione, quæ impleta fuerit vocando. At is finis vocationis, annunciare illam promissionem, non legalem, hujus miniſter fuit Mofes, sed Evangelicam. Illa enim fub legis implendæ conditione facta, quæ conditio à nemine ſervari poterat: Inde ergo nova promiſſio vitæ deperditæ, seu ſalutis gratuita facta credentibus per Prophetas, in CHRISTO JES II, utpote qui fundamentum & fons vi- tæ & salutis, Joban. XIV. verfu 6. ac morte ſua, ut prædixere Prophetæ, eandem nobis peperit, quod annunciare erat Apostolorum officium. Materiam itaque & finem Apostolatus ſui innuit. Recte Crocius obſervat hoc loco: Non ait que est in Mose, nec ait, in Mose JESU CHRISTO: Hacerat falforum Apostolorum mixtum. CHRISTUM opponit cum Moss, tum omnibus aliis mtionibus, quas bomines comminiscuntur. Cur ergo ipſe cum suis bona opera ad salutem neceſſaria profitetur. Annon hæc erat falforum Apostolo-

Connetit quidem hæc cum fuperioribus ita Commentarius Ambrofio adscriptus, quem, ut & Theodoretum ſequutus Beatus Lutherus est: Gratias ago DEO meo, quod quoties ad eum preces fundo, toties tui fum memor, ac pro te oro: boc enim me facere, divini muneris est, ideoque dignum, de quo gratias agam. Sed merito hic aliorum præfert sententiam Beatus Gerhardus, qui sic exponunt: Gratias ago DEO pro te filio mibi charissimo, fideli in Evangelio συνέργῳ ſignifi cans tibi, quod in precibus meis ad Deum assiduam

Tom. II. (PPPP) 3 babeo habeo tui memoriam, orans, ut quod in te cœpit, perficiat. Quibus hic etiam accessit Grotius.

Νυκτὸς καὶ ἡμέρας) Non hæc pertinent ad verba se- quentia, de desiderio videndi Timotheum, quod non- nullis visum, sed ad preces Pauli. Conf. Rom. I, 9. 10. 1. Thessalon. I. 2. III. 10. 1. Timoth. V. vers. 5.

## 1:4
Vers. 4.

Ἐπιποθῶν σε ἰδεῖν) Thus also Roman. I. 11.

Μεμνημένος σου τῶν δακρύων. This is inserted by way of a parenthesis. For the following words cohere with the preceding ones. He understands the tears at the departure of Paul. Similar to Acts XXI. 13.

It seems that this should be understood not of tears from contrition for sins, not of those which he shed out of συμπαθείᾳ on account of the calamities of the Apostle, but of those which were shed at the departure of Paul.

Ἵνα χαρᾶς πληρωθῶ) Namely, from the sight of you. Thus also Roman. I. 12. & XV. 32.

Not only, as Theophylact interprets, he says, do I desire to see you while calling your tears to memory, but also while remembering your faith, which is entirely devoid of hypocrisy and deceit. That also compels me most of all, that I may with the best right pursue you with benevolence and embrace you with charity.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Ἐπιποθῶν σε ἰδεῖν) Sic & Roman. I. 11.

Μεμνημένος σου τῶν δακρύων. Hoc per παρένθεσιν interjectum est. Nam sequentia cum præcedentibus cohærent. Lacrymas intelligit in discessu Pauli. Simile Actor. XXI. 13.

Id non de lacrymis ex contritione de peccatis, non de illis, quas ex συμπαθείᾳ propter calami- tates Apostoli fuderit, sed de illis, quæ sub disces- sum Pauli fusæ sunt, accipiendum videtur.

Ἵνα χαρᾶς πληρωθῶ) Nempe ex tui conspectu. Sic & Ro- man. I. 12. & XV. 32.

Non solum, interprete Theophylacto, inquit, lachrymas tuas memoria repetens videre te cupio, quin & tuæ fidei reminiscens, quæ simulatione prorsus caret & dolo. Id etiam me vel plurimum cogit, ut jure optimo te benevolentia prosequar, & charitate complectar.

## 1:5
Vers. 5. Ὑπόμνησιν λαμβάνων.

The manuscript has λαβών. Taking a remembrance, namely in the mind, that is, calling to mind for myself your faith. Thus we have the word ὑπομνήσεως in 2. Petr. I. v. 13. III. 1. Wisd. XVI. 11. 2. Macc. VI. 16.

Τῆς ἐν σοὶ ἀνυποκρίτου πίστεως.

Of the sincere faith, which I have seen and known in you. He gave the same title to faith in 1. Tim. I. 5. It is also given to love in Rom. XII. 9. 2. Corinth. IX. 6. 1. Petr. I. 22. To wisdom, Jas. III. 17. To judgment, Wisd. XVIII. 16.

That it is Ἀνυπόκριτον [unfeigned], the Apostle does not judge from the judgment of charity, but has it from the revelation of the Holy Spirit, through whom these things were suggested: Therefore this judgment is not probable, but certain and infallible. Which is to be observed against Estius, who asserts that the Apostle was not certain that unfeigned faith dwelt in Timothy, but that, taught by long experience, he held it to be certain only in a human way. He does not, however, speak of perseverance in faith: but as the words sound, of faith in the present, that it dwells in him Ἀνυπόκριτον [unfeigned].

Which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice.

One must read Ἐυνίκῃ, which name is also found in Theocritus. ἥτις here signifies the kind of faith, that is, the Christian faith: these women therefore were among the first Christians. The Hebrew name Λωῒς seems to have been מאר־טוב, but that of Ἐυνίκης, רחב. By that ἐνῴκησεν [dwelt] he understands that the Christian faith remained in those women until the end.

And I am persuaded that also in thee.

Supply ἐνοικήσει [it shall dwell]. I trust also that that faith will remain in thee until the end. Πέπεισμαι is in a similar sense in Rom. VIII. v. 38, XV. v. 14.

If it be asked: how was faith propagated from grandmother and mother into Timothy, since Christians are made, not born? I answer: This was done not through carnal generation, but through faithful doctrine and instruction. They did not, however, have that faith outside of Christianity, as Calvin wishes, but were informed about Christ. But as to the fact that both have now died, whence is it certain? And why must the name of Eunice be written with an ι? Who does not know that proper names are sometimes varied in writing by one letter or another? But faith is said to have dwelt, because it remained fixed and firm in Eunice as if in a dwelling. That πέπεισμαι [I am persuaded], most explain as a merely probable persuasion. But if it is a question of the present indwelling of faith, why could it not have been held infallibly from infallible revelation, that sincere faith certainly dwells in the heart of Timothy? But concerning the future perseverance of Timothy in the faith, of which the word which he wishes to be supplied here, ἐνοικήσει [it shall dwell], Grotius takes it, it is not likely that GOD revealed anything to Paul, or that Paul wished to make Timothy certain of this here. Why could he not say that he was certainly persuaded that faith also dwells in him, so that the word πέπεισμαι [I am persuaded] brings with it a persuasion no less certain than in Romans VIII. verse 38? The Apostle will exhort to perseverance in the faith in what follows.

PART II. EXHORTATORY.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Ὑπόμνησιν λαμβάνων.

Manuscriptus habet λαβών. Sumens commemoratio- nem, nempe in animo, id est, mihimetipsi commemorans tuam fidem. Sic vocem ὑπομνήσεως habemus 2. Petr. I. v. 13. III. 1. Sap. XVI. 11. 2. Macc. VI. 16.

Τῆς ἐν σοὶ ἀνυποκρίτου πίστεως.

Fidei sinceræ, quam in te vidi atque cognovi. Eundem titulum fidei dedit 1. Tim. I. 5. Datur & dilectioni Rom. XII. 9. 2. Corinth. IX. 6. 1. Petr. I. 22. Sapientiæ, Jac. III. 17. Judicio Sap. XVIII. 16.

Ἀνυπόκριτον esse, non ex judicio charitatis cen- set, sed à revelatione Spiritus S. habet Aposto- lus, per quem hæc suggesta: Ideo non probabi- le hoc est judicium, sed certum atque infallibile. Quod contra Estium observandum, qui asserit, certum non fuisse Apostolum, fidem non fictam in Timotheo habitare, sed id longa experientia edoctum humanitus tantum certum tenuisse. Non loquitur autem de perseverantia in fide: sed ut verba sonant, de fide in præsenti, quod ea in ipso habitet ἀνυπόκριτος.

Ἥτις ἐνῴκησε πρῶτον ἐν τῇ μάμμῃ σου Λωΐδι, καὶ τῇ μητρί σου Ἐυνίκῃ.

Legendum Ἐυνίκῃ, quod nomen est & apud Theocri- tum. ἥτις hic genus fidei significat, id est, fidem Chri- stianam: fœminæ ergo istæ ex primis Christianis fuere. Nomen Hebræum Λωῒς videtur fuisse מאר־טוב Ἐυνίκης vero רחב Per illud ἐνῴκησεν intelligit fidem Chri- stianam in illis fœminis ad finem usque mansisse.

Πέπεισμαι δὲ ὅτι καὶ ἐν σοὶ.

Supple ἐνοικήσει. Confido etiam in te mansuram eam fidem ad finem usque. Πέπεισμαι pari sensu est Rom. VIII. v. 38. XV. v. 14.

Si quæratur: quomodo fides ab avia, & ma- tre in Timotheum propagata sit, quum fiant, non nascantur Christiani? Respond. Factum hoc non per carnalem generationem, sed per fidelem doctrinam & institutionem. Non habuere au- tem illam fidem extra Christianismum, ut Cal- vinus vult, sed informati fuere de Christo. Quod vero jam diem obierit utraque, unde constat? Et cur per ι scribendum nomen Eunices? Quis nescit variari quandoque nomina propria in scri- ptione una vel altera literula? Inhabitasse autem fides dicitur, quod fixa & firma velut in habi- taculo in Eunice manserit. Illud πέπεισμαι per- suasus sum, de persuasione tantum probabili ex- plicant plerique. Sed si de præsenti fidei inhabi- tatione agatur, quidni ex infallibili revelatione haberi potuerit infallibiliter, habitare certo fi- dem sinceram in corde Timothei? De futura au- tem perseverentia Timothei in fide, de qua ver- bum, quod hic suppleri vult ἐνοικήσει accipit Gro- tius, DEUM Paulo quid revelasse, aut per Pau- lum Timotheum hic certiorem reddere voluisse, non est verisimile. Quidni dicere potuit, se cer- to persuasum esse, quod etiam in ipso fides habi- tet, ut vox πέπεισμαι non minus certam persua- sionem inferat, quam Roman. IIX. vers. 38. Ad perseverantiam in fide hortabitur Apostolus in sequentibus.

PARS II. ΠΑΡΑΙΝΕΤΙΚΗ.

## 1:6
Ver. 6.

Δι ἣν αἰτίαν [For which cause]) לָכֵן; wherefore? namely, so that this may happen, which I desire and hope for. He seems to have feared something for Timothy, whom he had previously called γνήσιον [genuine], but here ἀγαπητὸν [beloved]. Consider the following.

᾿Αναμιμνήσκω σε [I remind thee]) מַזְכִּיר Gen. XLI. 9. ᾿Αναζωπυρεῖν τὸ χάρισμα τοῦ Θεοῦ [To stir up the gift of God]) In the Manuscript τὸ χάρισμα τοῦ χριστοῦ [the gift of Christ]. To the Thessalonians he says V. 19, 'quench not the Spirit.' Here, however, ἀναζωπυρεῖν [to stir up]. ᾿Αναζωπυρεῖν, he who stirs up fires that have gone to sleep. This word is in Gen. XLV. verse 27, and ζωσυρεῖν, 2 Kings VIII. verse 15, for וַיְחִי. That Spirit is stirred up, however, by prayers, diligent meditation, and constant pious action.

Ὃ ἐστιν ἐν σοὶ [Which is in thee]) It has not yet departed. See that you retain it.

The meaning is: Since I am certain that sincere faith dwells in you, I advise that you stir up more and more the gifts of the Holy Spirit, namely, that through your ministry others also may become partakers of this faith: ἀναζωπυρεῖν. Since these things, says Theodoret, are confirmed to me, I exhort you that by the readiness and alacrity of your mind you stir up the grace of the Spirit, which you received through my ordination; for just as oil makes the flame of a lamp more intense, so the readiness and alacrity of the mind attracts the grace of the Spirit. And Theophylact: Since (he says) your faith is proven and well-attested to me, I would indeed wish to exhort you as much as possible, and to incite you, that you may revive, and render vivid and flourishing, the grace of the Spirit which you have received for the protection of the Church, and for performing miracles, and finally for every virtue befitting a Bishop. For just as fire needs wood in order to burn, so the grace of the Spirit requires readiness of mind and demands zeal and vigilance, so that it may burn perpetually. If it lacks these, it is easily extinguished. Estius, following the mind of the Apostle, judges what those gifts of grace are which Timothy ought to stir up, when he says that they received a spirit of power, of love, and of self-control; which gifts a minister of the Church certainly has need of, but they are not proper to ministers of the word, nor are they conferred through the laying on of hands in ordination, from which it is clear that ordination is not a Sacrament. For every Sacrament properly so called is instituted for this end, that it may apply and seal the promise of saving grace.

Through the laying on of my hands) With me solemnly calling upon God, with the presbytery approving. See what was said at 1 Tim. IV. v. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Δι ἣν αἰτίαν) לָכֵן; quapropter? nempe ut hoc fiat, quod opto ac spero. Videtur timuisse aliquid pro Timo- theo, quem ante γνήσιον vocarat, hic vero ἀγαπητὸν. Considera sequentia.

᾿Αναμιμνήσκω σε) מַזְכִּיר Gen. XLI. 9. ᾿Αναζωπυρεῖν τὸ χάρισμα τοῦ Θεοῦ) In Manuscripto τὸ χάρισμα τοῦ χριστοῦ. Thessalonicensibus dicit V. 19. τὸ πνεῦμα μὴ σβέννυτε. Hic vero ἀναζωπυρεῖν. ᾿Αναζωπυρεῖν qui sopitos suscitat ignes. Est hoc verbum Genes. XLV. vers. 27. & ζωσυρεῖν, 2. Reg. VIII. vers 15. pro וַיְחִי. Sus- citatur autem Spiritus ille precibus, diligenti meditatio- ne, & jugi pia operatione.

Ὃ ἐστιν ἐν σοὶ) Nondum abiit. Vide retineas.

Sensus est: Cum certus sim, fidem ἀνυπόκρι- τον in te habitare, moneo, ut magis magisque dona Spiritus S. excites, scilicet, ut hujus fidei per ministerium tuum alii etiam consortes fiant: διαζωσυ- Hæc cum mihi, inquit Theodoretus, sint persuasa, ρεῖν. hortor te, ut animi tui promptitudine & alacrita- te excites gratiam Spiritus, quam accepisti per meam ordinationem, quemadmodum enim oleum lampadis flammam efficit vehementiorem: ita ani- mi promptitudo & alacritas attrahit gratiam Spi- ritus. Et Theophylactus: Quoniam (inquit) spe- ctata tua est mihi, & testatior fides, velim equi- dem te hortari quam maxime, & incitare, ut Spi- ritus gratiam, quam ad tutandam Ecclesiam, & si- gna operanda, & omnem denique Episcopum de- centem virtutem acceperis, resuscites, & vividam reddas & floridam. Nam quemadmodum ignis ligno, ut ardeat, indiget, sic Spiritus gratia animi exigit promptitudinem studiumque, & vigilantiam poscit, ut perpetuo ferveat. Quibus si careat, ex- tinguitur facile. Quæ illa gratiæ dona sint, quæ ἀναζωπυρεῖν debeat Timotheus, ex mente Apo- stoli, censet Estius, quando ait, quod acceperint Spiritum virtutis, dilectionis, sobrietatis, quibus donis omnino quidem opus habet minister Ec- clesiæ, sed ea non sunt ministrorum verbi pro- pria, nec per manuum impositionem conferun- tur in ordinatione, unde patet ordinationem non esse Sacramentum. Omne enim Sacramentum proprie dictum eo fine institutum est, ut pro- missionem gratiæ salutiferæ applicet & obsignet.

Διὰ τῆς ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν μοῦ) Me solemniter invo- cante Deum, approbante presbyterio. Vide quæ dicta ad 1. Tim. IV. v. 13.

## 1:7
Verse 7. For God has not given us a spirit of cowardice) He has not given us a weak spirit, which would allow us to fear death and adversities. He says these things because he was somewhat afraid that Timothy, having observed those perpetual evils which were pressing upon Paul and the Christians, might on that account waver. Δειλία is not fear, but timidity. And it is so translated in the Glossary.

But of power.

Sufficiently strong so that we may resist those temptations, provided we are not cowards. See 1 Cor. XII. 9. Micah III, 8.

Καὶ ἀγάπης) Full of the love of God and neighbor, from which that fortitude is born 1 John IV. 18.

Καὶ σωφρονισμῦ) Of a tranquil mind, as the Syrian rightly translates here, not because the word does not have a wider meaning, but because this sense fits this passage best. Thus σωφρόσυης is used in Wisdom IX. 11. Among other things, this is the power of that Spirit, that it calms us in evils, provided it is rightly cultivated.

Some wish to refer ministering gifts here, and restrict these to the Ministers of the Church, to which view Blessed Gerhard accedes, as does Crocius. But that by the pronoun ἡμῖν not only the Ministers of the word are understood, is clear from verse 9, and those gifts are so constituted that they belong to all believers. Hence they have not received the Spirit of bondage, but of adoption Rom. VIII. 15. The Spirit of fortitude and power Ephesians III. verse 16. The Spirit of love Gal. V. 22. and of moderation of mind Gal. VI. 1. For the fact that he is able to stir up those gifts, which he obtained in ordination through the laying on of hands and prayers, and to use them strenuously for a salutary and brave purpose, is confirmed by the fact that he himself, along with other believers, has been instructed by the Spirit of adoption, of power, of love, and of prudent moderation. Thus Theodoret: God has given us the grace of the most Holy Spirit, not so that we may fear dangers for the sake of piety, but so that, filled with divine power, we may love Him ardently, and may chasten the insolent movements of our mind's perturbations. And Theophylact, with Chrysostom leading: For he says, we have not received the Spirit for this, that we should be contracted by fear, but that we might be stronger against temptations, and might boldly and freely offer ourselves to dangers. And of love: Namely, that which he was to have toward himself and his neighbor, for even that we worship God as Father, we have from the Spirit, who makes us say Abba Father. But that nothing is to be separated from the charity of the neighbor is a result of grace and divine truth: as on the contrary, to be offended by a neighbor, and not to tolerate him patiently, is of a fearful, pusillanimous, and inconstant mind. And of Sobriety: That is, that we may be sober and continent, and of an integral and stable mind. Or that we may have the Spirit Himself as our moderator. And when some temptation is offered, we may receive it for chastisement, or choose others for continence. Blessed Balduinus agrees with this interpretation, and therefore provides this sense and connection: that Timothy ought not to remit anything of the alacrity of his mind, because he is full of the Holy Spirit, who does not work such δειλίαν, torpor, sloth, and trepidation; but rather true strength of mind, love of God and neighbor, and a just moderation of all actions, from which follows constancy in adversities. We have Grotius agreeing here.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Οὐ γὰρ ἔδωκεν ἡμῖν ὁ Θεὸς πνεῦμα δειλίας) Non dedit nobis Spiritum tenuem, qui nobis permittat timere mortem & adversa. Hæc ideo dicit, quod aliquantum me- tuebat, ne Timotheus, conspectis illis perpetuis malis, quæ Paulum & Christianos premebant, ob id labasceret. Δειλία non est timor, sed timiditas. Atque ita vertitur in Glossario.

᾿Αλλὰ δυνάμεως.

Satis validum ut illis tentationibus resistamus, modo ne simus ῥιψάσπιδες. Vide 1. Cor. XII. 9. Mich. III, 8.

Καὶ ἀγάπης) Plenum dilectionis Dei proximi, unde illa fortitudo nascitur 1. Joh. IV. 18.

Καὶ σωφρονισμῦ) Animi tranquilli, ut hic recte vertit Syrus, non quod non latius pateat vox, sed quod is sen- sus huic loco optime conveniat. Sic σωφρόσυης sumitur Sap. IX. 11. Spiritus illius inter alia & hæc vis est, quod nos in malis tranquillat, modo recte colatur.

Nonnulli huc dona ministrantia referri vo- lunt, & ad Ecclesiæ Ministros hæc restringunt, quibus accedit B. Gerhardus, ut & Crocius. Sed pronomine ἡμῖν non solos verbi Ministros intel- ligi, è v. 9. liquet & dona illa ita comparata sunt, ut competant omnibus credentibus. Hinc non Spi- ritum servitutis acceperunt, sed τῆς ὑοθεσίας Rom. IIX. 15. Spiritum fortitudinis & virtutis Ephes. III. vers. 16. Spiritum dilectionis Gal. V. 22. & mode- rationis animi Gal. VI. 1. Quod enim dona illa, quæ in ordinatione per manuum impositionem & preces consequutus est, exsuscitare, & iisdem ad strenue exequendam salutariter & fortiter uti possit, confirmatur inde, quod ipse cum aliis fi- delibus instructus sit Spiritu ὑοθεσίας, virtutis, di- lectionis, & moderationis prudentis. Ita Theo doretus: Sanctissimi Spiritus gratiam dedit nobis Deus, non ut pericula pro pietate timeamus, sed ut divina virtute referti, ipsum quidem ardenter ame- mus, nostri autem animi perturbationum motus in- solentes castigemus. Et Theophylactus præeunte Chrysostomo: Non enim eo inquit, Spiritum ipsi ac- cepimus, ut formidine contrahamur, sed ut adver- sum tentationes simus validiores, audenterque & libere nos periculis offeramus. Et dilectionis: Ejus videlicet, quam erga se ac proximum esset habitu- rus, nam & quod Deum colimus ut Patrem, ex Spi- ritu habemus, qui Abba Pater dicere nos facit. Nil vero à proximi charitate sejungi, gratia est & di- vina veritate effectum: ut contra, à proximo offen- di, nec patienter hunc tolerare, formidolosi & pu- silli animi & inconstantis. Et Sobrietatis: Ut scil. sobrii simus & continentes, & mente integra & sta- bili. Vel ut Spiritum ipsum nostri habeamus mode- ratorem. Et cum aliqua offertur tentatio, hanc ad castigationem excipiamus, vel alios ut ad continen- tiam eligamus. Annuit huic interpretationi B. Balduinus, ideo hunc sensum & nexum tradit: Timotheum ideo nihil de alacritate animi sui re- mittere debere, quia Spiritu S. plenus sit, qui non ejusmodi δειλίαν, torporem, ignaviam & trepida- tionem operetur; sed potius verum animi robur, dilectionem Dei atque proximi, & justam omnium actionum moderationem, unde sequitur constantia in adversis. Habemus hic Grotium consentientem.

## 1:8
Vers. 8.

Μὴ ἓν ἐπαισχυνθῇς τὸ μαρτύριον τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν. Ἐπαισχύνεσθαι governs the accusative, as can be seen in Mark VIII. 38, Luke IX. 26, Rom. I. 16, and so below 16. It is also constructed with ἐπὶ and the third case as in Rom. VI. 21. In Latin we would say: let you not be ashamed of the Gospel, for that is what he here calls the testimony of Christ, or about Christ as in 1 Cor. XVI, which is also the testimony of God 1 Cor. II. verse 1.

Some understand the confession of CHRIST by the word testimony, but it is more correctly explained as the preaching of the Gospel, which is a testimony about Christ John XV. 27, Acts I. 8. For it is the cross, says Theodoret, which is preached, and contumely, and curses, and passion, and death. But these things, to those who do not believe, seem to be disgraces and ignominy. For the word of the cross, he says, seems indeed to those who are perishing, foolishness. Wherefore he himself also, writing to the Romans, said: For I am not ashamed of the Gospel, for it is the power of GOD unto salvation to every one that believeth.

Μηδὲ ἐμὲ.

Nor let you be ashamed of me, let you not be ashamed to be called a disciple of Paul, for the reason that I suffer such things. He touches the very sore.

Τὸν δέσμιον ἀυτᾶ.

Who now again am dragged bound for his sake; for this genitive signifies the cause on account of which. Thus also Eph. II. 1. & Philem. 1. & 9 for which elsewhere he says δέσμιον ἐν Κυρίῳ. Eph. IV. 1. on account of Christ, that is, his doctrine.

But suffer hardship together with the Gospel.

Κακοπαθεῖν רע עמל Jonah IV. 11. is to be affected with trouble, whence κακοπαθεῦντα μόρια to physicians. In the Glossary κακοπαθῶ, I am vexed. But for the most part such words, signifying passion in themselves, among our writers signify at the same time a mind prepared for this. Thus we have κακοπαθεῖν below II. 3. 9. IV. 5, James V. verse 13. Συγκακοπαθεῖν is of the same form as συγκακουχεῖσθαι Hebr. XI. v. 25. But after his custom Paul personifies the Gospel, and attributes to it a sense, as elsewhere to the Law, to Death, to Sin. Blessed Gerhard does not disapprove of this prosopopoeia, yet he observes that it can also be explained in this way: Not only let my bonds not shame you, but also patiently endure your portion of adversities for the sake of the Gospel. If circumstances should so bring it about that you also must endure something on account of the preaching of the Gospel, patiently bear it by my example. Which sense Theodoret prefers. He called the passion of the preachers the passion of the Gospel, since they endured all kinds of punishments on account of it. Theophylact: Or that, he says, & labor with me for the sake of the Gospel. Or he calls the Gospel the heralds of the Gospel itself, and participants of the divine mysteries.

According to the power of GOD.

That is, by the power of GOD, as the Syrian here, by the powers given by GOD. Paul uses that κατὰ in many ways. Here in the way in which the Greeks say something is done κατὰ Θεὸν, or κατὰ τύχην. Since δύναμις Θεῦ can be explained in two ways: namely, of the powers given to man by GOD, and of the virtue by which God works in man; here the latter sense seems more congruent. Because the Apostle's scope is to recall Timothy from trust in his own powers, and on the contrary to exhort the same, that he should trust in God alone and in his virtue: by whose grace alone he was both saved and called to the communion of salvation. Not by your own, he says, with Theophylact as interpreter, but by Christ's virtue will you labor for the Gospel. He adds spirit, says Theodoret, from the remembrance of divine power. For he who called for the sake of salvation, also provides the powers, measuring them to those who receive grace by faith.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Μὴ ἓν ἐπαισχυνθῇς τὸ μαρτύριον τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν. Ἐπαισχύνεσθαι regit accusativum, ut videre est Marc. VIII. 38. Luc. IX. 26. Rom. I. 16. sic infra 16. Construi- tur & cum ἐπὶ & tertio casu ut Rom. VI. 21. Latine dicere- mus: ne te pudeat Evangelii, id enim est, quod hic vocat testimonium Christi, sive de Christo ut 1. Cor. XVI. quod & μαρτύριον τῦ Θεῦ 1. Cor. II. vers. 1.

Nonnulli intelligunt confessionem CHRISTI per μαρτύριον, sed rectius explicatur de prædica- tione Evangelii, quod est testimonium de Chri- sto Joh. XV. 27. Act. I. 8. Crux est enim, in- quit Theodoretus, quæ prædicatur, & contume- lia, & maledicta, & passio, & mors. Hæc autem iis, qui non credunt, videntur esse dedecora & igno- minia. Sermo enim crucis, inquit, videtur iis quidem, qui pereunt, stultitia. Quamobrem ipse etiam scribens ad Romanos dixit: Non enim me pudet Evangelii, est enim DEI virtus ad salu- tem omni credenti.

Μηδὲ ἐμὲ.

Neque te mei pudeat, ne pudeat, te dici discipulum Pau- li, ideo, quod tanta patior. Tangit ipsum ulcus.

Τὸν δέσμιον ἀυτᾶ.

Qui nunc iterum vinctus trahor ipsius causa; nam ge- nitivus hic causam ob quam significat. Sic & Eph. II. 1. & Philem. 1. & 9 pro quo alibi dicit δέσμιον ἐν Κυρίῳ. Eph. IV. 1. propter Christum, id est, doctrinam ipsius.

᾿Αλλὰ συγκακοπάθησον τῷ Ἐυαγγελίῳ.

Κακοπαθεῖν רע עמל Jonæ IV. 11. est molestia affici, un- de κακοπαθεῦντα μόρια medicis. In Glossario κακοπαθῶ, sea- xor. Sed plerumque voces tales, per se passionem signi- ficantes, apud nostros Scriptores simul significant animum ad hoc paratum. Sic κακοπαθεῖν habemus infra II. 3. 9. IV. 5, Jac. V. vers. 13. Συγκακοπαθεῖν eadem forma, quæ συγκακουχεῖσθαι Hebr. XI. v. 25. More autem suo Paulus προσωποποιεῖ Evangelium, seique sensum tribuit, quomo- do alibi Legi, Morti, Peccato. Non improbat hanc prosopopœiam B. Gerhar- dus, observat tamen, posse etiam hoc modo expo- ni: Non solum non te pudeat meorum vinculorum, verum etiam tuam portionem adversitatum pati- enter sustine propter Evangelium. Si res ita tulerit, ut tibi quoque propter Evangelii prædicationem aliquid sustinendum, meo exemplo patienter illud perfer. Quem sensum præfert Theodoret. Prædi- catorum passionem Evangelii passionem vocavit, quoniam propter illud omnis generis supplicia su- stinuerunt. Theophylactus: Vel illud, inquit, & laborem mecum propter Evangelium inhume. Vel Evangelium dicit Evangelii ipsius præcones, & di- vinorum arcanorum participes.

Κατὰ δύναμιν τῶ Θεῦ.

Id est, per vim DEI, ut hic Syrus, per vires à DEO datas. Multis modis usurpat Paulus illud κατὰ. Hic eo modo, quo Græci dicunt, aliquid fieri κατὰ Θεὸν, aut κατὰ τύχην. Cum bifariam δύναμις Θεῦ exponi queat: de viribus nempe à DEO homini datis, & de virtu- te, qua Deus in homine operatur; hic posterior sensus videtur magis congruus. Quia Apostoli scopus est, revocare Timotheum à fiducia pro- priarum virium, & ex adverso hortari eundem, ut in solo Deo & in virtute ejus confidat: cujus solius gratia & salvatus sit & vocatus ad salutis communionem. Non tua inquit, Theophylacto interprete, sed Christi virtute Evangelio insudabis. Addit animum, inquit Theodoretus, ex recorda- tione divinæ potentiæ. Qui enim vocavit propter salutem, præbet etiam vires, eorum, qui suscipiunt fide gratiam metiens.

## 1:9
Vers. 9.

Τῦ σώσαντος ἡμᾶς) Who delivered us from vices. Thus σώζεσθαι is taken also in Eph. II. verse 8. Salvation is understood, as in Ephes. II. v. 8. which brings not only liberation from sins, or the remission of sins, but also the donation and imputation of the righteousness of Christ, and also the collation of hope and certainty of salvation, as is evident from Rom. III. IV. V. VIII. He saved, he says, although certain acts of saving still remain, preservation in faith, liberation from evil through death, and from death through resurrection, and leading to eternal life: Because he wishes to perfect the work which he began, provided we do not reject his grace. His gifts are, as far as he is concerned, ἀμεταμέλητα Romans XI. v. 29. There is no need here to establish a digression with some, since those things follow in order, as Theodoret has already observed. Blessed Baldwin handed down this connection: But in order that it may be clear what that testimony of our GOD is, or the Gospel, of which the world is ashamed, adds the sum: who saved us, etc. For he is occupied in that doctrine concerning our liberation and calling: Liberation was made from the kingdom of darkness, calling to the kingdom of light, or the Church. In the Greek, for him who saved us, it is τοῦ σώσαντος ἡμᾶς, and it embraces the whole work of our salvation, which consists in the remission of sins and eternal justice: which, since it is begun in this life and continued until death, therefore he says in the present, τοῦ σώσαντος, and because it is not found outside the Church, therefore he adds our calling to salvation. This is the blessed predecessor, Johan. Crocius: Not without grave cause, he says, does the Apostle add this; and he says grace was given from eternity; it could be a strong stimulus and sweet consolation. Is not his Gospel constantly preached? For his sake are not all things endured, for a short time, for a moment the adversities, by him who not today, or the day before yesterday, not with the beginning of our life, but from eternity gave grace, when we did not exist, much less had we deserved anything? Timothy could be excellently armed from this. To whom was he present, when he did not yet exist, who gave grace to one not yet born, nay, to the world not yet founded, and holds it stored up with himself, kept for the ages, would he desert one laboring strenuously, bravely suffering evils together with the Gospel? He who from eternity kept the same mind and benevolent affection, would he change thereafter?

And who called us with a holy calling.

That 'and' here is, as often elsewhere, explanatory. For Paul explains how we have been liberated from vices, namely because God called us by that holy word of his, which is called here from its effect 'calling' קראן.

The 'and' here is not explanatory. The benefits of salvation and calling are distinct. Nor does the mode of salvation, or even of liberation from vices, consist in the calling, but the end of the calling here is that we may be saved. Moreover, the calling is holy, both because it is done by the most holy GOD, and because it is through the most holy word and the ministry of the Word, and because it is to the holy Church, and the communion of saints, and to sanctification and holiness 1 Thess. IV. verse 7. that we may be holy Eph. I. verse 4.

not according to our works.

Our works had not moved him to call us in this way, for in the greatest part there were more evil than good works. See Eph. II. verse 9. Polycarp in his Epistle: that by grace you are saved, not from works, but by the will of God through Jesus Christ.

Nay, there were no good works, nor could there be, before calling, before regeneration and faith, Roman. XIV. last verse, Heb. XI. v. 6. Estius himself also acknowledges that the grace of GOD is not given according to our merits. Yet the same man denies that eternal salvation is not from works: But if the grace of GOD is not given according to merits, neither is eternal life, which is a gift Roman. VI. last verse, and is given out of grace Eph. II. verse 8. obtained according to merits by way of opposition Roman. XI. v. 5. What of the fact that Estius acknowledges here that our predestination is not from merits, but from the mere good pleasure of the grace of GOD? How then can salvation be from merits? For the execution of the decree does not behave otherwise than the decree; and for the same causes for which God saves us in time, for those same causes he also determined from eternity to save us. What of the fact that Estius adds to the following words: The Apostle wishes every respect of our merit to be excluded from our salvation and calling, and only the purpose and grace of GOD to be considered. Behold the power of the truth, that EVERY respect of MERIT is excluded, and

indeed FROM SALVATION. How were you called, he says? (thus Chrysostom clarifies this place) with a holy calling, that is: he made those holy who were sinners and enemies, and this is not from us, but is from a divine gift. If therefore he is both powerful in calling and good, and does this through grace, not out of debt, there is nothing for us to fear. For he who, when we were lost and enemies, made us saved through grace, much more when he sees us working, does he approach as a co-worker. He will work together, not according to our works, he says, but according to his purpose. With no one compelling, and no one advising, but out of his own purpose, impelled by the sole power of his goodness, he made us saved.

But according to his own purpose) From his own purpose. See Eph. III. verse 11.

And the grace given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times.

He explains what that purpose is. First, he says it was made long ago, before Abraham, of whom the Jews boasted. See what we said at John 8:58. You have the same manner of speaking in Titus 1:2. By the interpreters of the Old Testament, αἰώνιος is used both of that which is to last a long time and of that whose origin must be sought far back, as Psalm 77:5, Prov. 22:28, Isa. 58:12, 61:4, Ezek. 35:9, 36:2, Micah 2:9, Hab. 3:5, and elsewhere. Then he says it is a benefit given in Christ by metonymy. For he wishes to say that that purpose is concerning the benefit of God to be given to us through Christ Jesus. We had a similar manner of speaking in Eph. 1:4.

That purpose was made not only before many times, but before all times, Eph. 1:4. He calls the series of times from the very foundation of the world χρόνους αἰωνίους. But grace was given πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων. Wherefore, before all times, and consequently from eternity. For before times there was nothing but mere eternity, and what is before times is truly eternal; for thus eternity is wont to be described, Psalm 90:2, Rom. 8:23, 24. He understands, however, by 'his own purpose' (which the Vulgate rendered less emphatically as 'his purpose') the purpose by which God decreed from eternity to make the believer in Christ safe, Rom. 8:28. But this πρόθεσις is not the decree of predestination itself, inasmuch as by it He chose from eternity to salvation those whom He foresaw would believe in Christ: but it is distinguished from the same; for predestination was made κατὰ πρόθεσιν, according to purpose; just as also πρόγνωσις, according to which election was made, is not predestination itself, Rom. 9:29, Eph. 1:11, 1 Pet. 1:2. Nor is χάριν to be understood as the infused habit of charity, but the mercy of God, as Estius himself admits, which is said to be given to us in Christ from eternity, because in view of the merit of Christ apprehended by true faith, God chooses us from grace to eternal life. Is this not a clear exhibition, or the highest manifestation of grace, that He inscribed us in the book of life and predestined us to eternal salvation, the force of which that explanation of Estius does not exhaust: 'Grace or mercy, as regards its effects, given to us through Christ, that is, prepared in view of the merits of Christ from eternity'? For the Apostle says not only that He prepared or decreed to give grace to us, but that He actually gave grace to us before secular times. Salvation was prepared from eternity: but grace was given from eternity. And although we were not actually in existence from eternity, yet to God, who is always the same and is never not, they are most present; who, just as He chose us in Christ from eternity, so, since this is a work of immense grace, grace is rightly said to be given to us in Christ from eternity. That grace to us, who are predestined, was given in election, when He chose us for eternal life in CHRIST, or on account of CHRIST apprehended by faith, which, because it was done before secular times, that grace was given to us from eternity. πρόθεσις concerning those to be saved who believe in Christ is common. But the grace given to us in election, whom He foresaw would believe in Christ, is proper to those who are chosen. However, election is not here constituted as the cause of vocation and salvation, because the grace of election did not come to us except in Christ, whom He foresaw would believe in Christ: therefore election does not precede vocation in the order of nature and causality, but presupposes in the divine προγνώσει (foreknowledge) the vocation and faith, which receives the grace of vocation. Nothing else is therefore implied, when we are said to be called and saved according to His own purpose and grace exhibited and given to us before the ages, than that temporal vocation and the leading to salvation are in such a state as the eternal purpose of GOD and the eternal predestination to salvation: or that the execution is entirely in accordance with the decree, which was made from eternity.

Johannes Crocius denies that πρόθεσις here is the decree of saving: because πρόθεσις is the same according to which we are predestined. Philipp. I. v. 11. but this is not a decree concerning those to be saved who believe. But why not? For he says, the predestining One did not look upon men as those who would believe, but chose them so that they might believe, just as He did not look upon them as holy, but chose them so that they might be holy and blameless. But here the reasoning is distinct. For holiness follows election, but faith in the divine προγνώσει (foreknowledge) does not; just as the latter precedes justification; the former, however, is a consequence of the same. For the causes of justification are not other than the causes of salvation: nor are we saved by one cause and chosen for salvation by another; for there must be a harmony of the decree and the execution of the decree: Therefore that explanation of Crocius is not correct: πρόθεσις is for the Apostle a serious, certain, immovable will, by which GOD called us to faith, holiness, and salvation. For πρόθεσις is that gracious gift of GOD, by which He did not decree to call us to faith out of an absolute good pleasure, but by which He determined to save those who would believe in CHRIST Ephes. 1. verse 11. Bullinger himself explained it thus: Moreover, that grace and that purpose of GOD is such that He wills to save believers through the Son: This purpose of GOD is mere grace. For before this world was made, GOD by His eternal decree, not on account of our merits, but on account of His own goodness, decreed to save us, and that through CHRIST, whom He recently exhibited to the world, just as He once promised through the Prophets. Estius acknowledges that the grace given to us in CHRIST is not, as the Greeks explain, with Christ, or with Him consenting and supporting, thereby concluding the eternity of CHRIST, but in Christ, as Mediator, that is, on account of CHRIST, as Hyperius holds. Therefore, the grace which is given on account of Christ is not absolute. Therefore, the gloss of Cornelius à Lapide was not to be approved by Crocius, that the giving here is nothing other than the efficacious and ABSOLUTE will of giving. Let us suppose that grace is said to be given IN PREDESTINATION, which Crocius wants, alleging the Papists Lyranus, Salmeron, Sasbouth, Magalianus, Justinianus, Cornelius. While he also explains with Piscator, what GOD decreed to give to us: these are certainly not simply the same: For grace was exhibited to us in election, because God chose us out of grace: but not because He decreed to give us efficacious grace, which he calls the grace of vocation, much less that He decreed to give irresistible grace, and that He decreed this out of absolute good pleasure. Ἀνάρχως ταῦτα προετύπιντο ἐν Χριςῷ Ἰησοῦ γενέσθαι; without any beginning these things were prefixed in Christ Jesus to come to pass, explains Chrysostom. Theophylact followed him here as is his custom.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Τῦ σώσαντος ἡμᾶς) Qui nos à vitiis liberavit. Sic σώ- ζεσθαι sumitur & Eph. 11. vers. 8. Salvatio intelligitur, ut Ephes. II. v. 8. quæ non tantum liberationem à peccatis, vel remis- sionem peccatorum, sed etiam justitiæ Christi donationem & imputationem, nec non spei & certitudinis salutis collationem infert, ut è Rom. III. IV. V. IIX. constat. Servavit, dicit, etsi actus quidam servandi adhuc restent, conservatio in fi- de, liberatio a malo per mortem, & à morte per resurrectionem, & ad æternam vitam perductio: Quia quod incepit opus, perficere vult, modo ipsius gratiam non reprobemus. Dona ejus sunt, quod ad ipsum attinet, ἀμεταμέλητα Roman. XI. v. 29. Non opus est hic digressionem statuere cum quibusdam, siquidem ista ordine sequan- tur, ut observavit jam Theodoretus. B. Balduinus hunc nexum tradidit: Ut autem constet, quod- nam illud sit testimonium DEI nostri, vel Evan- gelium, cujus mundum pudet, summam addit : qui nos liberavit &c. Versatur enim in illa doctri- na circa liberationem & vocationem nostram : Li- beratio facta est ex regno tenebrarum, vocatio ad regnum lucis, seu Ecclesiam. In Græco pro eo, qui liberavit nos, est τοῦ σώσαντος ἡμᾶς, complectiturque totum opus salutis nostræ, quæ in remissione pecca- torum & justitia æterna consistit : quæ cum in hac vita inchoetur, & continuetur usque ad mortem, ideo in præsenti dicit, τοῦ σώσαντος, & quia extra Ecclesiam non reperitur, ideo salvationi vocatio- nem nostram addit. Hæc B. Antecessor. Johan. Crocius : Non sine gravi causa, inquit, hoc addit Apostolus; & gratiam datam ab æterno dicit; Po- terat esse fortis stimulus & suavis consolatio. An- non ipsius Evangelium constanter prædicetur? An illius causa non omnia sustineantur, ad tempus bre- ve, ad momentum adversa, qui non hodie, aut nudius tertius, non cum vita nostra initio, sed ab æterno gratiam dedit, cum non existeremus, nedum quicquam meriti essemus ? Armari hinc poterat egregie Timotheus. Cui præsens fuit, cum nondum esset, qui gratiam dedit nondum nato, imo mundo nondum condito, & apud se repositam ha- bet, servavit seculis, num desereret strenue laboran- tem, fortiter patientem mala una cum Evangelio? Qui ab æterno eandem servavit mentem & affectum benevolum, num deinceps mutaret?

Καὶ καλέσαντος κλήσει ἁγίᾳ.

Illud καὶ hic est, ut alibi sæpe ἐξηγητικὸν. Explicat enim Paulus quomodo liberati simus à vitiis, nempe quia Deus nos vocavit sermone illo suo sancto, qui hic ex effectu dicitur κλῆσις קראן.

Non est καὶ hic ἐξηγητικὸν. Distincta sunt be- neficia salvationis & vocationis. Nec modus sal- vationis, aut etiam liberationis à vitiis consistit in vocatione, sed vocationis finis hic est, ut sal- vemur. Sancta autem est vocatio, tum quia à DEO sanctissimo fit, tum quia per Sacrosanctum verbum, & Verbi ministerium, tum quia ad Ec- clesiam sanctam, & communionem sanctorum, & ad sanctificationem & sanctitatem 1. Thess. IV. vers. 7. ut sancti simus Eph. I. vers. 4.

ὐ κατὰ τὰ ἔργα ἡμῶν.

Non nostra opera eum moverant, ut nos sic vocaret, erant enim maximæ partis mala plura quam bona opera. Vide Eph. II. vers. 9. Polycarpus in Epistola : ὅτι χάριτί ἐστε σεσωσμένοι, ὐκ ἐκ ἔργων, ἀλλὰ θελήματι Θεῦ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.

Imo nulla erant, nec esse poterant bona ope- ra ante vocationem, ante regenerationem & fi- dem, Roman. XIV. vers. ult. Ebr. XI. v. 6. Agno- scit etiam Estius ipse, gratiam DEI non dari se- cundum merita nostra. Negat tamen idem, æter- nam salutem non esse ex operibus : Sed si gratia DEI non datur secundum merita, nec vita æter- na, quæ est χάρισμα Roman. VI. vers. ult. & ex gratia datur Ephes. II. vers. 8. secundum merita obtingit vi oppositionis Roman. XI. v. 5. Quid, quod agnoscat hic Estius, prædestinationem no- stram non esse ex meritis, sed ex mero benepla- cito gratiæ DEI. Qui ergo salvatio esse potest ex meritis? non enim aliter sese habet executio decreti, quam decretum; & propter quas causas nos Deus in tempore salvat, propter easdem etiam nos ab æterno constituit salvare. Quid quod Estius ad verba sequentia addat : Vult Apo- stolus omnem meriti nostri respectum à salute & vocatione nostra excludi, & solum cogitari pro- positum & gratiam DEI. En vim veritatis, OMNEM respectum MERITI excludi, &

quidem A SALUTE. Quomodo vocatus es, inquit? (ita hunc locum dilucidat Chrysostomus) vocatione sancta, hoc est: sanctos effecit, qui pec- catores & inimici eramus, & hoc non ex nobis, sed ex divino munere est. Si igitur ille & potens est vocando & bonus, idque per gratiam, non ex debito faciendo, nihil est, cur metuamus. Qui enim nos, cum perditi inimicique essemus, salvos per gratiam fecit, multo magis cum operantes vi- derit, cooperator accedit. Συμπράξει, non secun- dum opera nostra, inquit, sed secundum propo- situm suum. Nemine cogente, nemineque consu- lente, sed ex proposito suo, sola vi bonitatis suae im- pulsus, salvos nos fecit.

̓Αλλὰ κατ' ἰδίαν πρόθεσιν) Ex suo proposito. Vide Ephes. III. vers. 11.

Καὶ χάριν τὴν δοθεῖσαν ἡμῖν ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων.

Explicat, quod sit illud propositum. Primum ait fa- ctum esse ante plurima tempora, ante Abrahamum, de quo Judaei gloriabantur. Vide quae diximus ad Johan. VIII. vers. 58. Idem loquendi genus habes Tit. I. vers. 2. Veteris Testamenti interpretibus αἰώνιος dicitur, & de eo, quod diu duraturum est, & de eo, cujus origo longe pe- tenda, ut Psalm. LXXVI. vers. 4. Prov. XXII. vers. 28. Es. LVIII. vers. 12. LXI. vers. 4. Ezech. XXXV. vers. 9. XXXVI. vers. 2. Michae II. vers. 9. Abac. III. vers. 5 &amp; alibi. Deinde dicit esse beneficium datum in Christo per μετωνυμίαν. Vult enim dicere, illud propositum esse de DEI beneficio dando nobis per Christum Jesum. Par loquendi genus habuimus Ephes. I. vers. 4.

Non ante plurima tantum, sed ante omnia tempora factum est illud propositum Eph. I. 4. χρόνους αἰωνίους vocat temporum seriem jam inde ab orbe condito. At gratia data est πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων. Quapropter ante tempora omnia, ac pro- inde ab aeterno. Ante tempora enim non fuit ni- si aeternitas mera, & quod ante tempora est, id vere aeternum est, sic enim describi solet aeter- nitas Psal. XC. 2. Rom. IIX. vers. 23. 24. Intelli- git autem per proprium propositum (quod mi- nus emphatice suum propositum Vulgata reddidit) propositum, quo Deus decrevit credentem in Christum salvum facere ab aeterno Roman. IIX. vers. 28. Quae vero πρόθεσις non est ipsum decre- tum praedestinationis, utpote quo illos, quos cre- dituros praevidit in Christum, ab aeterno elegit ad salutem : sed ab eodem distinguitur : facta enim est praedestinatio κατὰ πρόθεσιν, juxta pro- positum; quemadmodum etiam πρόγνωσις, juxta quam facta est electio, non est ipsa praedestinatio Rom. IX. 29. Eph. I. 11. 1. Petr. I. 2. Nec per χά- ριν intelligendus est habitus charitatis infusus, sed DEI misericordia, fatente ipsomet Estio, quae data nobis in Christo ab aeterno dicitur, quia intui- tu meriti Christi vera fide apprehensi ex gratia eligit nos Deus ad aeternam vitam. Annon haec est exhibitio luculenta, vel praestatio summa gra- tiae, quod nos in librum vitae inscripserit, & ad aeternam salutem praedestinavit, cujus vim non exhaurit illa explicatio Estii: Gratia seu mise- ricordia quoad effectus suos nobis per Christum da- ta, id est, intuitu meritorum Christi praeparata est ab aeterno; non enim tantum praeparasse nobis aut decrevisse dare gratiam, sed revera dedisse gratiam nobis ante tempora secularia, dicit Apo- stolus. Salus ab aeterno praeparata : gratia autem data ab aeterno. Etsi autem nos non fuerimus actu ab aeterno, Deo tamen, qui semper idem est, nun- quam non est, sunt praesentissima; qui uti nos elegit in Christo ab aeterno, ita, cum hoc sit immen- sae gratiae opus, gratia utique in Christo ab aeterno nobis data merito dicitur. Gratia illa nobis, qui prædestinati sumus, data est in electione, quando in CHRISTO, vel propter CHRISTUM fide apprehensum nos elegit ad æternam vitam, quod quia ante secularia tempora factum, gratia illa nobis ab æterno data est. πρόθεσις de salvandis in Christum credentibus communis est. Sed gra- tia nobis in electione data, quos prævidit credi- turos in Christum, propria est illis, qui electi sunt. Non autem electio hic causa constituitur vocationis, & salvationis, quia electionis gratia non nisi in Christo contigit nobis, quos in Chri- stum credituros prævidit: non ergo electio an- tecedit, ordine naturæ & causalitatis vocatio- nem, sed præsupponit in προγνώσει divina, vo- cationem & fidem, quæ suscipit vocationis gra- tiam. Nihil ergo aliud innuitur, cum secundum proprium propositum & gratiam ante secula no- bis exhibitam & donatam vocati & salvati di- cimur, quam quod ita se habeat temporalis vo- catio, & ad salutem perductio, quemadmodum æternum DEI propositum, & æterna ad salu- tem prædestinatio: vel quod ex asse executio, quæ consonat decreto, quod factum est ab æter- no.

Johannes Crocius negat πρόθεσιν hic esse de- cretum salvandi: quod πρόθεσις eadem sit, secun- dum quam prædestinati sumus. Philipp. I. v. 11. hæc autem non sit decretum de salvandis cre- dentibus. Cur autem non? Non enim, inquit, prædestinans spectavit homines ut credituros, sed elegit ut credant, sicut non spectavit ut sanctos, sed elegit ut essent sancti & inculpati. Sed hic di- stincta est ratio. Sanctitas enim consequitur ele- ctionem, non item fides in προγνώσει divina; quemadmodum hæc justificationem antecedit; illa vero consequens ejusdem est. Non enim aliæ sunt justificationis, aliæ salutis causæ: nec ex alia causa salvamur, ex alia electi sumus ad sa- lutem; oportet namque harmoniam esse decre- ti, & executionis decreti: Non ergo recte se habet illa Crocii explicatio: πρόθεσις est Aposto- lo seria, certa, immota voluntas, qua DEUS nos vocavit ad fidem, sanctimoniam & salutem. Nam πρόθεσις est gratiosum illud DEI donum, quo non ex absoluto beneplacito nos vocare ad fidem decrevit, sed quo credituros in CHRI- STUM salvare constituit Ephes. 1. vers. 11. Ita exposuit ipse Bullingerus: Cæterum illa gratia, & illud propositum DEI tale est, quod per Fi- lium vult salvare credentes: Hoc propositum DEI mera gratia est. Nam priusquam hic mundus fieret, DEUS æterno suo decreto non propter me- rita nostra, sed propter bonitatem suam decrevit nos servare, idque per CHRISTUM, quem nuper orbi exhibuit, quemadmodum olim per Pro- phetas promisit. In CHRISTO datam nobis gratiam agnoscit Estius, non esse, cum Christo, vel eo consentiente & suffragante, uti Græci ex- plicant, inde æternitatem CHRISTI confluden- tes, sed in Christo, ut Mediatore, id est pro- pter CHRISTUM, ut habet Hyperius. Non er- go absolute est gratia, quæ data propter Chri- stum. Non approbanda itaque erat à Crocio Cor- nelii à Lapide glossa, quod datio hic nihil aliud sit, quam donandi efficax & ABSOLUTA voluntas. Ponamus, datam dici gratiam IN PRÆDESTINATIONE, quod vult Cro- cius allegans Pontificios Lyranum, Salmeronem, Sasbouth, Magalianum, Justinianum, Cornelium. Dum & explicat cum Piscatore, quam nobis de- crevit dare DEUS: hæc utique non simplici- ter idem sunt: Nam exhibita est nobis gratia in in electione, quod Deus ex gratia nos elegit : non vero quod decreverit nobis dare gratiam effica- cem, quam vocat, vocationis, nedum quod de- creverit dare gratiam irresistibilem, quodque ex absoluto beneplacito id decreverit. Ἀνάρχως ταῦτα προετύπιντο ἐν Χριςῷ Ἰησοῦ γενέσθαι; absque ullo principio in Christo ista præfixa sunt, ut fie- rent, exponit Chrysostomus. Quem secutus hic pro more est Theophylactus.

## 1:10
Vers. 10. But now made manifest.

The purpose, that long lay hidden in GOD, but now has been made manifest. Thus also Roman. XVI. verse 26. and Tit. I. 3. Φανεροῦν is נִגְלָה (revealed).

Through the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ.

After Christ appeared to the world. At which time both the grace and Truth of GOD are said to have appeared to men Tit. II. verse 11. III. verse 4. Elsewhere ἐπιφάνεια (appearing) is taken for the judicial advent. But the word is general, as we said elsewhere.

That eternal purpose of GOD has been manifested in time, which concerns the saving of men through Christ: or that grace given from eternity has been manifested. Concerning which I would prefer to understand this. Φανερωθεῖσα, however, is what this ἰδία πρόθεσις is called, or even χάρις in time according to some, through ἐπιφάνειαν, or Φανέρωσιν ἐν σαρκὶ through the advent of the Son of GOD our Savior JESUS CHRIST: which Theodoret explains concerning the execution of this gracious purpose: This, he says, GOD of the universe predetermined indeed from the beginning and before the ages, but now He has imposed an end upon those things which were predetermined and decreed. Others, however, understand it concerning the manifestation which is made through the proclamation of this divine προθέσεως, καὶ χάριτος: not that that grace was unknown before: but that it was manifested more illustriously through the advent of CHRIST, partly by the breadth of the object, partly by the clarity of the circumstances of the manifestation. Those who observe that the word ἐπιφανείας implies that the Son of GOD was indeed already in the world before the ἐνσάρκωσιν, Job 1. verse 20. But that His presence was manifested through the assumption of visible flesh. That manifestation of the decree in the former sense, by which Christ fulfilled it, was real, with the work of redemption promised through the Prophets indeed performed by Christ in the fullness of time: but this manifestation through the Gospel announced by CHRIST is verbal, which is done by the proclamation of the word. But a comparison of the passage Romans XVI. verse 26 favors this latter sense, which is also more accepted. Although such grace was predestined, it has now become known, where also the Savior has shone forth, says Theophylact. Which Blessed Gerhard also embraced: and from the Reformed, Bullinger. Nevertheless, Blessed Balduinus seems to agree with the former: CHRIST by His advent into the world showed what counsel GOD had concerning our eternal salvation, to execute which He Himself appeared, without whose advent there would have been no need for anything else. We note here that Crocius also admits that ἐπιφάνειαν presupposes a presence, which the Son of GOD manifested by His advent into the flesh. Whence from the Epiphany of CHRIST in the last advent, concerning which 1 Tim. VI. verse 14, 2 Tim. II. verse 8, Tit. II. verse 13, it is rightly inferred that Christ who will then be manifested is not absent, but is already present to us: Whose presence is also said to be manifested then, 2 Thess. II. 8.

Having abolished death.

Death is here personified. Death had dominion over men alienated from GOD. Romans VI. verse 23.

1 Cor. 15:26, Christ takes away that dominion, that right from him: he is also to take away his very power in his own time; as we are taught in the same place to the Corinthians. Thus Christ in Heb. 2:14 is said to καταργῆσαι τὸν κράτος ἔχοντα τοῦ θανάτου, that is, to have taken away his right בטל. Thus the law is said to be καταργεῖσθαι in Eph. 2:15, when the right of binding us is taken away from it.

He took away not only the dominion and right, but also the very power, namely by reason of merit, whence Theodoret explains it concerning the power of death, expounding it thus: 'For when the only-begotten Word had become man, he poured out and routed the power of death, but gave us the promise of eternal life': Because by his death he acquired for us liberation from death, both temporal and eternal, which liberation we enjoy through faith: For although we are subjected to temporal death, yet to believers it is not a punishment and penalty, but grace and a benefit: because they are freed from the evils of this life, and through death they pass into the blessed life, John 5:24. Death is not an exit, says Cyprian in Sermon 4 on mortality, but a transition, and having run the course of a temporal journey, a crossing over to the eternal. Chrysostom, Homily 45 on Genesis: Death is a transmigration from worse things to better. The Greek verb καταργήσαντος implies an abolition, by which something is made void and of no effect. Blessed Luther rendered it: 'zunicht gemacht' [made to nothing]; but in order to destroy death, sin had to be destroyed, through which death entered into the world, Rom. 5:10, 11. The Devil had to be destroyed, who had the τὸ κράτος of death, i.e., strength and power through sin, which was done through the death of Christ, Heb. 2:14, which was the death of death.

Hos. 13:14. But with death destroyed, life is returned: for if it did not return, one would have to remain in death forever, nor would death be fully conquered. Therefore, the restoration of life is consequently introduced here, which the following words also imply. For life could not have been brought to light or announced through the Gospel, unless it had been restored to us. As the illumination of immortal life through the Gospel includes at the same time the announcement of the destruction of death: So through CHRIST both death is destroyed and life is restored, through his meritorious satisfaction, when he gave his flesh for the life of the world, John 6:51. He said, therefore, that death was destroyed rather than sin, because death is wont to terrify the pious; even if they are certain of the remission of sins. Therefore, lest Timothy should fear even to undergo death for the sake of the Gospel, he says that not only eternal death, but even temporal death is abolished, inasmuch as it is not death, but an entrance and gate of life.

Φωτίσαντος δὲ ζωὴν καὶ ἀφθαρσίαν διὰ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου.

There is here an ἐν διὰ δυοῖν [one thing through two]. For he said ζωὴν & ἀφθαρσίαν [life and incorruption] for ζωὴν ἄφθαρτον [incorruptible life], concerning which life there had indeed been some hope from conjectures, but no clear promise without shadows. And so Christ is rightly said to have brought that life, which knows not how to be corrupted, as it were out of darkness into light. For whatever the Philosophers, whatever the Rabbis say about that matter, it is darkness if compared to the light of the Gospel.

Some understand these things concerning the merit of life and immortality, others concerning the announcement and promise. But because 'through the Gospel' is added, the latter explanation is to be preferred. However, it is not said to be illuminated or brought to light through the Gospel because there had previously been only shadows and conjectures of incorruptible life in the Old Testament: but no promise—an error we have often noted in Grotius; but because eternal life, as it has been restored and reinstated through CHRIST, after it had been lost through Adam, 1 Cor.

15:22, Rom. 5:18, has now become known: namely, the restoration of life made through JESUS of Nazareth. He does not say, 'and he acquired life,' says Crocius: There was no need. For he who abolishes death, he acquires life. He says, he brought life to light, namely, not from another, but obtained by himself by dying, and confirmed by rising again; Thus, he illuminated, he made it shine, so that it might show itself to us, as if raised from the dead, and so that we might know in what it consists, and how it is obtained. Before, it was as if dead in us, with death reigning over us, but Christ, by abolishing death, as it were raised it from the dead. But it was necessary that it should become known to the whole world, which was sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, Isa. 9, Matt. 4. He accomplished this through the Gospel, as a lamp hung in a high place, by whose benefit life is seen. I would like that to be noted in the Calvinian man because of the confession of the universal preaching of the word. Φωτίζειν here means to bring into the light; not, however, as the Vulgate rendered it, to illuminate. Some distinguish ζωὴν καὶ ἀφθαρσίαν here, so that by the former is understood spiritual life in this age, through which we revive from the death of sins, Eph. 2:5, and by the latter, heavenly life in the future age: but a hendiadys pleases me: For as the destruction of death is an argument for liberation from sin, which is called ἀθέτησις τῆς ἁμαρτίας in Heb. 9:26, yet the destruction of death is not formally the very cessation or destruction of sin: So also the restoration of incorruptibility, or the bringing of eternal life into the light, is not either the spiritual life itself, or the revival from the death of sin: or the Φωτισμὸς of the same, but an indication and argument of the same: For unless spiritual life had been obtained for us, eternal life would not have been restored to us: unless the Φωτισμὸς of spiritual life were obtained through the Gospel, nor would the Φωτισμὸς of eternal heavenly life be obtained for us through the Gospel; one presupposes the other; yet one is not formally the other, or, by the same word and phrase by which one is signified, the other is also signified.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Φανερωθεῖσαν δὲ νῦν.

Propositum, illud diu in DEO latuit, nunc vero pa- tefactum est. Sic & Roman. XVI. vers. 26. & Tit. I. 3. Φανεροῦν est נִגְלָה.

Διὰ τῆς ἐπιφανείας τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριςοῦ.

Postquam Christus mundo apparuit. Quo tempore & DEI gratia & Veritas in homines apparuisse dicuntur Tit. II. vers. 11. III. vers. 4. Alibi ἐπιφάνεια sumitur de judiciali adventu. Sed vox est generalis, ut alibi dixi- mus.

Propositum illud DEI æternum manifestatum est in tempore, quod est de salvandis hominibus per Christum: vel manifestata gratia illa ab æter- no data. De qua malim hoc intelligere. Φανερω- θεῖσα autem dicitur hæc ἰδία πρόθεσις, vel etiam χάρις in tempore secundum nonnullos, per ἐπι- φάνειαν, vel Φανέρωσιν ἐν σαρκὶ per adventum Fi- lii DEI Salvatoris nostri JESU CHRISTI: quod de executione propositi istius gratiosi expli- cat Theodoretius: Hæc ab initio quidem, inquit, & ante secula præfiniit universorum DEUS, nunc autem iis, quæ præfinita ac decreta fuerunt, finem imposuit. Alii autem de manifestatione, quæ fit per annuntiationem hujus divinæ προθέσεως, καὶ χάριτος, intelligunt: non quod ante gratia illa ignota fuerit: sed quod illustrius per adventum CHRISTI manifestata sit, partim qua ob- jecti latitudinem, partim qua manifestationis cir- cumstantiarum claritatem. Qui observant ἐπι- φανείας vocem inferre, quod Filius DEI qui- dem ante ἐνσάρκωσιν jam tum fuerit in mundo Job. 1. vers. 20. Sed per carnis visibilis assum- ptionem manifestata fuerit ejus præsentia. Ma- nifestatio illa decreti sensu priori, qua id imple- vit Christus, realis fuit, promisso quidem per Prophetas redemptionis opere præstito à Chri- sto in plenitudine temporis: hæc autem manife- statio per Evangelium à CHRISTO annuncia- tum verbalis est, quæ præconio verbi fit. Sed collatio loci Roman. XVI. vers. 26. huic posterio- ri sensui favet, qui etiam receptior est. Etsi emt istiusmodi gratia prædestinata, nunc tamen inno- tuit, ubi & Salvator illuxit, inquit Theophyla- ctus. Quam etiam amplexus est B. Gerhardus: & è reformatis Bullingerus. Videtur tamen prio- ri accedere B. Balduinus: CHRISTUS suo in mundum adventu ostendit, quodnam consilium DEUS de æterna salute nostra habuerit, ad quod exequendum ipse apparuit, cujus adventu alias opus haud fuisset. Notamus hic, quod & Crocius ἐπιφάνειαν præsupponere præsentiam fateatur, quam Filius DEI manifestavit suo in carnem ad- ventu. Unde ex Epiphania CHRISTI in ultimo adventu, de qua 1. Tim. VI. vers. 14. 2. Tim. II. vers. 8. Tit. II. vers. 13. recte colligitur Christum qui tum manifestabitur, non absentem, sed præ- sentem jam nobis esse: Cujus etiam præsentia tum manifestanda dicitur 2. Thessal. II. 8.

Καταργήσαντος μὲν τὸν θάνατον.

Mors hic προσωποποιεῖται. Mors dominium habebat in homines à DEO abalienatos. Roman. VI. vers. 23.

1. Corinth. XV: 26, Id dominium, id jus ei Christus ade- mit: vim quoque ipsam ei adempturus suo tempore; ut eodem ad Corinthios loco docemur. Sic Christus Ebr. II. vers. 14. dicitur καταργῆσαι τὸν κράτος ἔχοντα τοῦ θα- νάτου, id est jus ei ademisse בטל. Sic lex dicitur καταρ- γεῖσθαι Eph. II. 15. Cum ei adimitur jus nos obligandi.

Non tantum dominium & jus ademit, sed vim etiam ipsam scil. ratione meriti, unde de mortis potentia explicat Theodoretus ita exponens: Cum enim homo factus esset Sermo unigenitus, mortis quidem fudit ac profligavit potentiam, æterna au- tem vitæ nobis dedit promissionem : Quia morte sua acquisivit nobis liberationem à morte, tum temporali, tum æterna, qua liberatione fruimur per fidem: Nam etsi morti subjiciamur tempo- rali, non tamen illa credentibus est pœna & sup- plicium, sed gratia & beneficium: quia liberan- tur à malis hujus vitæ, & per mortem transeunt in vitam beatam Joh. V. vers. 24. Mors non est exitus, ait Cyprianus serm. IV. de mortalitat. sed transitus, & temporali itinere decurso ad æter- nam transgressus. Chrysost. homil. XLV. in Gen. Mors est transmigratio à deterioribus ad melio- ra. Verbum Græcum καταργήσαντος abolitio- nem, qua cassum & irritum quid fit, infert. B. Lutherus reddidit: zunicht gemacht/ ut autem mortem destrueret, destruendum erat peccatum, per quod mors intravit in mundum Roman. V. vers. 10. 11. Destruendus erat Diabolus, qui ha- bebat τὸ κράτος mortis, h. e. robur & potestatem per peccatum, quod factum est per mortem Christi, Ebr. II. vers. 14. quæ fuit mortis mors.

Os. XIII. 14. Morte autem destructa vita red- ditur: nam si non rediret, perpetuo in morte manendum foret, nec mors plene devicta esset. Ideo consequenter vitæ reparatio hic infertur, quam etiam sequentia important. Nam non po- tuisset per Evangelium in lucem proferri vita, vel annunciari, nisi eadem nobis reparata esset. Ut illuminatio vitæ immortalis per Evangelium complectitur simul annunciationem destructio- nis mortis: Sic per CHRISTUM & mors de- structa, & vita reparata est, per satisfactionem ejus meritoriam, cum dedit carnem suam pro mundi vita, Johan. VI. vers. 51. Mortem ergo potius destructam dixit, quam peccatum, quia mors terrere solet pios; etsi de remissione pec- catorum certi sint. Ideo ne vel mortem subire Evangelii causa vereretur Timotheus, mortem non æternam tantum, sed temporalem etiam abolitam dicit, utpote quæ non mors est, sed introitus & janua vitæ.

Φωτίσαντος δὲ ζωὴν καὶ ἀφθαρσίαν διὰ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου.

Est hic ἐν διὰ δυοῖν. Nam ζωὴν & ἀφθαρσίαν dixit pro ζωὴν ἄφθαρτον, de qua vita spes quidem fuerat aliqua ex conjecturis, sed non difertum & sine umbris promissum. Itaque recte dicitur Christus vitam illam corrumpi ne- sciam tanquam ex tenebris in lucem eruisse. Quicquid enim Philosophi, quicquid Rabbini ea de re dicunt, tene- bræ sunt, si ad lucem Evangelii comparantur.

Nonnulli de merito vitæ & immortalitatis hæc intelligunt, alii de annunciatione ac promisso. Sed quia additur διὰ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου, posterior explicatio est præferenda. Non autem per Ev- angelium illuminata vel in lucem producta dici- tur, quod antea in Vet. Testamento solum umbra & conjecturæ vitæ incorruptibilis fuerant: nul- la vero promissio, quem errorem in Grotio sæpe notavimus; sed quod æterna vita, prout ea- dem reparata est ac restituta per CHRISTUM, postquam amissa erat per Adamum 1. Corinth.

XV. vers. 22. Roman. V. vers. 18. jam innotue- rit: Reparatio nempe vitæ per JESUM Nazare- num facta. Non ait, & vitam acquisivit, inquit Crocius: Non opus erat. Qui enim mortem ab- olet, is vitam acquirit. Dicit, vitam in lucem pro- duxit, nempe non ab alio, sed à se moriendo par- tam, & resurgendo confirmatam; Sic, illustravit, fecit illucescere, ut se nobis exhibeat, quasi à morte resuscitata, & ut cognoscamus, qua in re posita sit, & quomodo obtineatur. Antea erat in nobis quasi emortua, morte in nos regnante, sed Christus mor- tem abolendo quasi è morte suscitavit. Opus au- tem erat, ut mundo toti innotesceret, qui sedebat in tenebris & umbra mortis Jes. IX. Matth. IV. Id præstitit per Evangelium, tanquam lampadem in loco excelso suspensam, cujus beneficio vita vi- detur. Id in homine Calviniano notari velim ob confessionem universalis prædicationis verbi. Φω- τίζειν hic est in lucem producere; non vero ut Vul- gata reddidit, illuminare. Ζωὴν καὶ ἀφθαρσίαν hic nonnulli distinguunt, ut per illam vita spiritua- lis in hoc seculo per quam à morte peccatorum reviviscimus Ephes. II. vers. 5. per hanc vita cœ- lestis in futuro seculo intelligatur: sed placet hendyade: Nam ut destructio mortis argumen- tum est liberationis à peccato, quæ ἀθέτησις τῆς ἁμαρτίας dicitur Ebr. IX. vers. 26. non tamen formaliter mortis destructio est ipsa peccati de- stitutio vel destructio: Sic etiam incorruptibili- tatis restitutio, vel vitæ æternæ in lucem produ- ctio, non est vel ipsa vita spiritualis, seu revivi- scentia à morte peccati: vel ejusdem Φωτισμὸς, sed indicium & argumentum ejusdem: Nisi enim nobis parta esset vita spiritualis, nec æterna vita nobis reparata foret: nisi per Evangelium ob- tingeret Φωτισμὸς spiritualis vitæ, nec Φωτισμὸς vitæ cœlestis æternæ per Evangelium nobis ob- tingeret, unum præsupponit alterum; non ta- men unum formaliter est alterum, vel, qua voce ac phrasi significatur unum, eadem significatur & alterum.

## 1:11
Verse 11.

Εἰς ὃ ἐτέθην ἐγὼ κήρυξ, καὶ ἀπόστολος, καὶ διδάσκαλος ἐθνῶν.

That ὃ refers to all that which preceded. A parallel passage is 1 Tim. 2:7. In the manuscript, ἐθνῶν is absent here.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Εἰς ὃ ἐτέθην ἐγὼ κήρυξ, καὶ ἀπόστολος, καὶ δι- δάσκαλος ἐθνῶν.

Illud ὃ totum illud, quod præcessit, respicit. Par locus 1. Tim. II. vers. 7. In Manuscripto hic abest ἐθνῶν.

## 1:12
Verse 12.

Δι ἣν αἰτίαν καὶ ταῦτα πάσχω.

These chains, these hatreds of the Jews, the wrath of the idolaters, and the dangers of death.

Ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐπαισχύνομαι.

Having warned of what preceded above in 8, he adds his own example. Cf. Mark 8:38, Luke 9:26, Rom. 1:16.

The Vulgate renders εἰς ὃ as 'in quo' (in which): which Primasius understands of Christ illuminating. But εἰς ὃ is to be referred to the Gospel, not to Christ, for thus it would have had to be said εἰς ὃν. Having made mention of the Φωτισμὸς of life through the Gospel, he mentions his ministry, which God deigned to use in the same, and in the same, the patience by which he sets forth the toleration of afflictions as an example to Timothy, because he was ashamed to suffer such things, that is, by meiosis, because he held it for glory, as one may read concerning the Apostles in Acts 5:41. A κήρυξ is called a herald, a messenger, an ein Herold, who promulgated not his own commands, but those ordered by a superior, by public faith, which if it were injured, had the sender as the avenger of injuries. The Apostle therefore testifies that he has been placed as a public interpreter of such a joyful message, by which life and immortality have been brought into the light, and therefore has Christ as his avenger, nor is there any reason why Timothy should be ashamed of his own, or be deterred by adversities from the common cause. As Crocius says here. And therefore, he says, I suffer these bonds, according to Theophylact’s interpretation, because I preach to the Gentiles, not because I have committed any wicked crime. At the same time, he also vindicates his faith by his own words, just as if he were saying: If I did not believe that death had been overcome, I would by no means suffer these things. Theodoret, regarding those words, ‘for which cause I also suffer these things,’ says: He openly shows both the crime of their ungrateful spirit and the fortitude of his own spirit. For when they received the good news, and it was fitting that they should treat him well and receive him kindly, they punished him, but he himself endured the punishments with joy.

For I know whom I have believed) to GOD, who is truthful in His promises: וְאַשֶׁׁר בָּחַתִּי בוֹ שׁπεπίσευκα. And I am persuaded) here ‘I am persuaded’ is used for ‘I hold for certain,’ as in Romans VIII, verse 38. That He is able) In order for us to trust in one who makes a promise, two things are required: that he be of good faith, and that he be able to fulfill what he wills. He has already dealt with the former; now he adds the latter.

O the confidence, exclaims Theophylact, and the hope that is clearly indubitable! I know, he says, and I am certain. Which expressions are to be noted against the Popish doubt regarding salvation. I know whom I have believed, not to whom I have entrusted a deposit, but in whom I have placed my trust, which we understand to be Christ and His merit and grace, in which all his trust rested: and I hold for certain—I do not undertake this with a wavering or doubtful mind—that He both wills it, as one truthful in His promises and gracious, and is able, as one who can subject all things to Himself. Phil. III, last verse. To keep my deposit: Ambrose teaches that by the word πισεύειν, trust is denoted, and Cosmus Magalianus admits this.

My deposit. Both here and below the Manuscript has παραθήκην, as in 1 Tim. VI, verse 20. We also have in this 14th verse a mention of a double deposit. God deposits His word with us; we deposit our spirit with God, Luke XXIII, verse 40; Acts VII, verse 59. To keep until that day. To keep uncorrupted until the day of the universal judgment. Which day is called ‘that day’ by way of excellence, as in 2 Thess. I, verse 10, and below in IV, 8. Elsewhere, the day of the Lord.

Others more correctly explain the deposit as the crown of righteousness, which the Apostle testifies in chapter IV, 18 (ἀπόκειταί μοι ὁ τῆς δικαιοσύνης σέφανος) is laid up for him in heaven, to be rendered on the last day: which Peter called τετηρημένην ἐν ὐρανοῖς εἰς ὑμᾶς in 1 Ep.
