I, 4. Theophylact teaches that this should be taken either as faith, along with Chrysostom, or as the preaching of the Gospel. That is to say: Christ, who entrusted this task to me, will keep this very thing, and I endure all things so that my treasure may not be taken away from me here: or it may refer to the faithful, whom Paul commended to the Lord with the word παρατίθεμαι, ‘I commend you to GOD,’ Acts XX, verse 32. That is to say: I am not ashamed of my bonds, since I hope that I shall offer many to the Lord, whom He will protect and grant salvation. Chrysostom had also brought forward this explanation. Thomas and Lyranus understand the grace of faith to have been committed to the pastors. But faith was about keeping the deposit, yet faith was not the deposit itself: And the preaching of the Gospel is openly distinguished from the deposit, because he was not ashamed of the Gospel of Paul, and of the sufferings for the Gospel, provided he testifies that he was certain not of the proclamation of the Gospel, but of the preservation of his deposit: which B. Balduinus also interprets as doctrine: But as for this eager defense, that God will keep it until that day, that is, until the last moment of life, so that he may constantly defend it. But because it is thus, eagerness is rather to be noted as constancy in keeping the defense: I am of good spirit, he says, according to Theodoret’s interpretation, and I am confident, looking to His power, that He will keep intact the grace of the Spirit which He has granted me until His coming. It is better, with Ambrose, B. Gerhard, Piscator, Osiander, and the Vinar. Paraphrase, to take it as the deposit of heavenly grace, especially also because by ‘that day’ is understood the day of the Lord’s last coming: which he hoped for; not because he merits it either by his proclamation or by his sufferings, but because he was made certain through the Holy Spirit that it was to be rendered to him out of grace. Cf. Rom. VIII, verse 38. Crocius presents the connection thus: The Apostle does not put forth this persuasion of his in vain: Timothy ought to have been wonderfully moved by it, for why should he be ashamed of his Master, who, relying on divine power, is certain of obtaining salvation? Why should he be ashamed of the Gospel, from which certainty is drawn? Why should he succumb to dangers, when none can interfere with the deposit? For whatever was the Apostle’s reasoning in this part, the same was that of Timothy and the other faithful.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Δι ἣν αἰτίαν καὶ ταῦτα πάσχω.

Hæc vincula, hæc odia Judæorum, iram Idololatra- rum, & mortis pericula.

Ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐπαισχύνομαι.

Monito quod præcessit supra 8. addit suum exemplum. Conf. Marc. VIII. vers. 38. Luc. IX. vers. 26. Rom. I. vers. 16.

Εἰς ὃ Vulgata reddit in quo: quod Primasius de Christo illuminante intelligit. At εἰς ὃ refe- rendum ad Evangelium, non ad Christum, sic enim dicendum fuisset εἰς ὃν. Mentiore facta τοῦ Φωτισμοῦ τῆς ζωῆς διὰ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου suum mini- sterium, quo Deus in eodem uti dignatus est, & in eodem patientiam, qua tolerandas afflictio- nes in exemplum sistitit Timotheo, quod pudue- rit talia pati, hoc est, per μείωσιν, quod pro glo- ria habuerit, ut de Apostolis legere est Actor. V. vers. 41. κήρυξ dicitur fecialis, caduceator, ein Herold / qui non sua, sed à superiori imperata promulgabat, fide publica, quæ si læderetur, mitten- tem habebat injuriarum vindicem. Testatur igi- tur Apostolus, se tam læti nuncii, quo vita & im- mortalitas in lucem sit producta, esse positum inter- pretem publicum, proinde Christum habere vindicem neque esse, cur Timotheum sui pudeat, aut adver- sis absterreatur à communi causa. Ut hic Crocius. Ideoque Vincula hæc patior, inquit, Theophylacto interprete, quia gentibus prædico, non quia pra- vum aliquod admiserim facinus. Simul etiam & suis dictis vindicat fidem, perinde ac si dicat : Si minus crederem mortem esse devictam, nequaquam hæc paterer. Theodoretius ad illa, ob quam cau- sam etiam hæc patior: Aperte, inquit, ostendit, & eorum ingrati animi crimen, & suam animi fortitudinem. Cum illi enim bonum nuncium ac- ciperent, oporteret autem bene cùm eo agere & hu- mane excipere, eum supplicio affecerunt, ipse vero cum gaudio supplicia subiit.

Οἶδα γὰρ ᾧ πεπίσευκα) DEO veraci in promissis : וְאַשֶׁׁר בָּחַתִּי בוֹ שׁπεπίσευκα. Καὶ πέπεισμαι) πέπεισμαι hic est pro certo habeo, ut Roman. VIII. vers. 38. Ὅτι δύνατός ἐςι) Ut promissori confidamus, duo re- quiruntur, ut & is bonæ fidei sit, & ut possit, quod vult, implere. De priori jam egit, nunc addit alterum.

O confidentiam, exclamat Theophylactus, & spem plane indubitatam! Scio, inquit & certus sum. Quæ voces contra Papisticam dubitatio nem de salute notandæ sunt. Scio cui credidi, non cui depositum credidi, sed in quem fiduciam meam collocavi, quod de Christo ejusque me- rito & gratia, in qua omnis ejus fiducia recum- bebat, intelligimus: & pro certo habeo, non fluctuanti aut dubia mente id suscipio, quod & velit, ceu verax in promissis, & gratiosus, & pos- sit, utpote qui omnia sibi subjicere potest. Phil. III. ult. meum depositum servare: Ambrosius docet verbo πισεύειν fiduciam notari, idque ad- mittit Cosmus Magalianus.

Τὴν παρακαταθήκην με. Et hic & infra παραθήκην habet Manuscriptus, ut 1. Tim. VI. vers. 20. Habemus & in hoc 14. commate mentio- nem depositi duplicis. Deus apud nos deponit verbum suum, nos apud Deum deponimus spiritum nostrum Luc. XXIII. vers. 40. Act. VII. vers. 59. Φυλάξαι εἰς ἐκείνην τὴν ἡμέραν. Servare incorruptum ad diem usque judicii universa- lis. Quæ dies per excellentiam dicitur illa dies ut 2. Thess. I, vers. 10. infra IV. 8. Alibi dies Domini.

Depositum rectius alii explicant de corona ju- stitiæ, quam repositam sibi in cœlis esse testatur Apostolus cap. IV. 18. (ἀπόκειταί μοι ὁ τῆς δικαιο- σύνης σέφανος) in die novissimo reddendam : quam τετηρημένην ἐν ὐρανοῖς εἰς ὑμᾶς dixit Petrus 1. Ep. I. 4. Theophylactus vel de fide id cum Chry- sostomo accipiendum esse docet, vel de Evangelii prædicatione. q. d. Christus, qui mihi id nego- tii demandavit, hoc ipsum servabit, & omnia to- lero, ne mihi thesaurus meus hic subtrahatur : vel etiam de fidelibus, quos Paulus Domino com- mendabat voce παρατίθεμαι vos DEO Act. XX. vers. 32. q. d. Nil equidem vincula erubesco, quippe qui sperem me plurimos Domino obla- turum, quos ille tuebitur, & salute donabit. Quam explicationem adduxerat & Chrysostomus. Thomas & Lyranus gratiam fidei pastoribus com- missam esse intelligunt. Sed fides erat de deposito custodiendo, non vero fides erat ipsum deposi- tum: Et Evangelii prædicatio aperte à deposito distinguitur, quia non erubuit Paulum Evange- lii, atque passionum ob Evangelium, siquidem certus fuerit non de Evangelii præconio, sed de depositi sui conservatione testetur: quod de do- ctrina interpretatur etiam B. Balduinus: Sed quo- ad alacrem defensionem hanc Deum servaturum usque ad diem illum, h. e. usque ad ultimum vitæ momentum, ut constanter eam defendat. Sed quia ita alacritas potius est constantia in defensione servanda notaretur: Bono inquit, Theodoreto in- terprete, sum animo, & confido respiciens ad il- lius potentiam, quod quantum mihi præbuit Spiri- tus gratiam, integram servabit usque ad suum ad- ventum. Præstat cum Ambrosio, B. Gerhardo, Pis- catore, Osiandro & Paraphrasi Vinariens. ac- cipere de deposito gratiæ cœlestis, imprimis etiam, quia per τὴν ἡμέραν intelligitur dies adventus Do- mini novissimi: quod sperabat; non quod merea- tur sive præconio, sive passionibus suis, sed quia id ex gratia sibi reddendum esse per Spiritum S. certus reddebatur. Conf. Rom. IIX. vers. 38. Ne- xum ita exhibet Crocius: Hanc suam persuasio- nem non frustra promit Apostolus: Ea mirifice po- tent ac debebat affici Timotheus, cur enim puderet ipsum Magistri, qui fretus divina potentia certus est de salute consequenda? Cur Evangelii ipsum puderet, ex quo hauriatur certitudo? Cur pericu- lis succumberet, cum nulla possint depositum inter- vertere? Quæ enim Apostoli hac parte ratio, ea- dem erat Timothei cæterorumque fidelium.

## 1:13
Verse 13. Hold the pattern of sound words.

Pattern is an exemplar, as in 1 Tim. I, verse 16, but understand it as an exemplar fixed in the mind, which the Platonists call an idea. He calls ‘sound words’ here, and in 1 Tim. II, v. 3, ‘sound doctrine,’ 1 Tim. I, 10, and here below in IV, 3, Tit. I, 9, that doctrine which has nothing unhealthy mixed in, such as many things were in the doctrine of the Rabbis and Philosophers.

Which you have heard from me. In the way you have often heard me speaking. In faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.

He shows in what matters that doctrine is occupied, namely first in faith. Then in love, not just any kind, but for the sake of Christ. This is that excellent συζυγία, from which our salvation hangs. See Gal. V. 6. Eph. VI. 23. 1. Tim. I. 14. This pair is prefigured in the ancient Urim & Thummim.

That salvation hangs from faith and love does not taste of the ὑποτύπωσις τῶν ὑγιαινόντων λόγων. For this is that we are saved by faith alone, not by love, Rom. III. 28. IV. 6. Eph. II. 8. Nor do all admit that these things are to be understood concerning the object of the ὑποτύπωσις or of the sound words, because they are concerned with faith and love. For some join them with the words immediately preceding, 'which you heard from me,' because he heard in faith and love, not only applying faith to the words of the Apostle, but also adding the affection of charity: by which he would seek not his own things, but the things of Christ. Others refer it to the hypotyposis, but understand it thus: have the form of sound words in faith and charity, so that the manner of having the same is noted, not its object, because it is performed through faith and charity, so that one does not depart from that form. But we easily admit that the object is noted; however, we deny that those things from which salvation hangs are expressed. For not only are the causes of salvation exhibited in that hypotyposis, but also its adjuncts, consequences, and other things: These words of mine (thus the paraphrase of Theophylact has it) embrace faith and charity, that is, the dogmas themselves brought forth by me, explained how one must live. If therefore anything will be for you either to be decided, or to be deferred, or something to be carried out for the sake of truth, you will be able to take a form from such words of mine. Furthermore, the Vulgate has interpreted ὑποτύπωσιν as 'form' here, which word in 1 Tim. I. verse 16 it rendered as 'information,' others expound it as 'expressed form,' others as 'image and delineation': because it is a metaphor taken from painters, who first adorn some outline, before they introduce living colors. But not here is a rough outline only, just as it is not only a form of teaching that is noted: But primarily the very substance of heavenly doctrine: therefore it is not inappropriately rendered as an idea: just as also through λόγος ὑγιαίνοντας the Apostle designated not only the words themselves and the modes of speaking, but the sense of the divine word, or words taken not only materially, but primarily formally, or rather taken collectively, in which way indeed the Word of GOD is received both materially and formally. Theodoret explains it thus: Imitate painters, and just as they, attending to patterns, perfectly describe their images: So also do you have as it were a certain archetypal pattern, that doctrine concerning faith and charity which has been handed down to you by me. This is the paraphrase of Theophylact: As a painter I have described and formed for you an image, which you yourself, attending to it with your mind, may depict, and have the form of sound words, which in no way deviate from the truth, in the place of a pattern, so that if anything is to be fashioned by you in the future, you may take it from that. For in that form of words all things are stored up. There were those who, as Crocius says, deviating from the sum of the commandment as if from a target, were turning aside to vain talk, 1 Tim. 1:6-7, who were languishing about frivolous, curious, useless questions, 1 Tim. 6:4, who were following profane clamors and oppositions of falsely named science, 1 Tim. 6:20. Their speeches were not sound in themselves; they were corrupt and were corrupting both the health, or integrity, of faith, and the souls of men. Whence languor is attributed to them. Thence the Apostle commends to Timothy a hypotyposis, that is, a brief and express outline of sound words, that is, of doctrine, which is sound in itself, that is, whole and incorrupt, not infected by human inventions, and which leads to the effecting and preserving of the health of the soul. Whence Estius in vain wishes this to refer to the unwritten word rather than to Holy Scripture. For who denies that that hypotyposis is expressed in Holy Scripture? But besides Scripture, Papists cannot teach by even a single example that some hypotyposis of sound words exists, handed down divinely and to be believed by divine faith, different regarding the necessary heads of faith and Christian life, unless perhaps such things are stored in the secret chest of the Papal breast: but how can these be received with equal reverence as Scripture, when they never proceed from it?

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ὑποτύπωσιν ἔχε ὑγιαινόντων λόγων.

Ὑποτύπωσις exemplar, ut 1. Tim. I. vers. 16. sed intelli- ge exemplar in animo fixum, quod ἰδέαν Platonici vocant. Λόγος ὑγιαίνοντας hic & 1. Tim. II. v. 3. διδασκαλίαν ὑγιαί- νουσαν, 1. Tim. I. 10. hic infra IV. 3. Tit. I. 9. vocat eam doctrinam quæ nihil insalubre habet admixtum, qualia multa erant in doctrina Rabbinorum & Philosophorum.

Ὧν παρ’ ἐμῦ ἤκυσας. Quomodo me dicentem sæpius audisti. Ἐν πίσει καὶ ἀγάπῃ τῇ ἐν Χρισῷ Ἰησῦ.

Ostendit in quibus rebus occupetur illa doctrina, nem- pe in fide primum. Deinde in dilectione, non qualicunque, sed propter Christum. Hæc est egregia illa συζυγία, unde Salus nostra pendet. Vide Gal. V. 6. Eph. VI. 23. 1. Tim. I. 14. Hæc biga figurata in vetere Urim & Thumim.

Salutem pendere à fide & dilectione, non fa- pit ὑποτύπωσις τῶν ὑγιαινόντων λόγων. Nam hæc est sola fide, non dilectione nos salvari Rom. III. 28. IV. 6. Eph. II. 8. Nec omnes admittunt de obje- cto τῆς ὑποτυπώσεως vel τῶν ὑγιαινόντων λόγων hæc intelligi, quod illi versentur circa fidem & dilectionem. Nonnulli enim cum verbis imme- diate præcedentibus, quæ audisti à me, ea con- jungunt, quod audiverit in fide & dilectione, non fidem solum adhibens sermonibus Apostoli, sed etiam charitatis affectum adjungens: qua non quæ sua sunt, sed quæ Christi, quæreret. Alii re- ferunt ad bypotyposin, sed ita accipiunt: formam habe sanorum verborum in fide & charitate, ut modus habendi eadem notetur, non objectum ejus, quia per fidem & charitatem præstatur, ut ab illa forma non recedatur. Sed admittimus facile ob- jectum notari; negamus autem exprimi ea, è qui- bus salus pendet. Non enim in hypotyposi illa tantum exhibentur salutis causæ, sed etiam ejus- dem adjuncta, consequentia, & alia: Mea hæc di- cta (ita habet paraphrasis Theophylacti) fidem complectuntur & charitatem, hoc est, dogmata ipsa per me lata, quemadmodum vivendum sit, expli- cavunt. Si quid itaque tibi erit vel decernendum, vel differendum, vel pro veritate aliquid peragen- dum, poteris ex meis illiusmodi verbis formam de- sumere. Ceterum ὑποτύπωσιν per formam hic interpretatus est Vulgatus, quam vocem 1. Tim. I. vers. 16. informationem reddidit, alii expres- sam formam, alii imaginem & delineationem expo- nunt: quod metaphora sit à pictoribus petita, qui primum delineationem aliquam adornant, an- tequam vivos colores inducant. Sed non hic ru- dis tantum delineatio, uti nec sola docendi for- ma notatur: Verum imprimis ipsa doctrinae coe- lestis substantia: ideo non incommode idea red- ditur: quemadmodum etiam per λόγος ὑγιαίνον- τας non ipsa modo verba, & modos loquendi designavit Apostolus, sed sensum verbi divini, seu verba non materialiter tantum, sed imprimis formaliter, aut magis complexive sumpta, qua nempe materialiter & formaliter accipitur Ver- bum DEI. Theodoretus ita explicat: Imitare pi- ctores, & quemadmodum illi attendentes exempla- ria, perfecte eorum imagines describunt: Ita et- iam Tu habe veluti quoddam exemplar archety- pum, eam, quae a me Tibi tradita est, doctrinam de fide & charitate. Theophylacti haec est peri- phrasis: Tanquam pictor descripsi tibi & formavi imaginem, quam ipse advertens animo tuo depin- gas, & sanorum verborum formam a vero nil aber- rantium, exempli habeas loco, ita ut si tibi quid in posterum erit effigiandum, ab ea desumas. In ea namque verborum forma omnia reconduntur. Erant qui, dicente Crocio, a mandati summa tanquam scopo aberrantes ad vaniloquentia deflectebant, 1. Tim. I. vers. 6. 7. qui languebant circa quaestiones frivolas, curiosas, inutiles, 1. Timoth. VI. vers. 4 qui sectabantur profanos de rebus inanibus clamo- res & oppositiones falso nominatae scientiae 1. Tim. VI. vers. 20. Illorum sermones non erant in se sani; erant corrupti & corrumpebant tum sanitatem, seu integritatem fidei, tum hominum animas. Un- de languor illis tribuitur. Inde Apostolus Timo- theo hypotyposin, id est, brevem expressamque de- lineationem verborum sanorum commendat, id est, doctrinae, quae in se sana, id est, integra est atque incorrupta, non infecta commentis humanis, & ad sanitatem animae efficiendam conservandamque con- ducit. Unde frustra haec Estius verbum non scri- ptum magis, quam Scripturam S. respicere vult. Nam in Scriptura S. ὑποτύπωσιν illam expressam esse, ecquis negat? Praeter autem Scripturam ὑπο- τύπωσιν aliquam sanorum verborum haberi divi- nitus traditam, & fide divina credendam, diver- sam quoad fidei, & vitae Christianae capita ne- cessaria, docere non possunt Papistae vel unico exemplo, nisi in scrinio pectoris Papalis forte talia recondantur: quae vero quomodo pari re- verentia cum Scriptura suscipi queant, cum nun- quam inde prodeant?

## 1:14
Ver. 14.

Guard the good deposit.

A manuscript [has] παραθήκην, as above: Thus he calls that Evangelical doctrine, as in 1 Tim. 6:20, where see what is said. For the word deposit, Ambrose in citing this passage uses the word commendation. It signifies the same thing. See the passage of Modestinus in the collation of Mosaic and Roman laws, under the title concerning deposit.

Theodoret again understands alacrity and promptness of mind by the grace to be preserved by faith: but he nowhere notes it as a deposit: but that the Evangelical doctrine is noted by it is sufficiently evident from the parallel passage 1 Tim. 6:20, and is commonly acknowledged, even by Theophylact, although he also brought forward another exposition: a deposit, he says, this is the precepts which have been handed down to you by me concerning life and faith: or he calls the grace which he had received a deposit. He calls it a good deposit, as the blessed Baldwin notes, because it has a good author, its contents are good and salutary, it also makes men good, and it has a good and most wholesome end, namely, life and eternal salvation. Papists understand not so much Holy Scripture as Apostolic doctrine handed down by word: indeed Estius speaks quite contemptuously of Scripture: What kind of deposit, he says, is that which is common to almost all sects of heretics! But although Scripture is common to all materially, as regards the words, it is not however formally, as regards the genuine sense of the words: but where today is that Apostolic doctrine handed down by word without Scripture, not written? Produce it, whoever you are, champion of traditions! I pass over the fact that Papists vary greatly in explaining that deposit: Thomas and Lyranus, as also Cajetan, explain it concerning the flock committed to the fidelity of the Pastor: the interlinear Gloss concerning the office entrusted to Pastors, which they ought to guard by diligent execution. Salmero brings forward many interpretations in Disputation 16 on 1 Timothy. The deposit according to Oecumenius is either the precept of GOD concerning doctrine proposed to Timothy through Paul, or the grace received through ordination. Haymo understands the grace of faith and spiritual [grace], which the Apostle commended to Timothy. Others [understand] the deposit, that is, the care entrusted to the Church to be guarded by the Holy Spirit, etc.

Through the Holy Spirit) As if he were to say: do not distrust: You have a great helper, above [verse] 7.

Which dwells in us) As if he were to say: He who is not deserted, will not desert us. Rom. 8:11.

Estius wishes the pronoun ἡμῖν to designate the prefects of the Church, by whose ministry that deposit entrusted to them through the Holy Spirit is preserved in the Church. But it is more correctly understood of all the faithful collectively, and of the whole Church, because the grace of the Holy Spirit is promised to all and each. Theophylact says, in what way will you guard this very grace? Certainly not by those human strengths, but through the Holy Spirit, who dwells in us by the grace of baptism. He commands us to guard this deposit, which is the duty of a faithful depositary, to whom an account must one day be rendered of how he has cared for the thing committed to him. Moreover, this custody is not the work of human strength, but of the Holy Spirit, whom he says dwells in us, because the saints are called temples of the Holy Spirit. 1. Cor. III. v. 16. VI. 19. who works in them, and bestows strengths, so that we may not only faithfully receive sound doctrine, but also constantly retain it against all the wisdom of the world and the fury of the Devil, as Blessed Balduinus says.

PART III. Historical.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Τὴν καλὴν παρακαταθήκην φύλαξον.

Παραθήκην Manuscriptus, ut supra: Sic vocat doctri- nam illam Evangelicam, ut 1. Timoth. VI. vers. 20. ubi dicta vide. Pro depositi voce Ambrosius in hoc loco ci- tando usurpat vocem commendati. Idem ea significat. Vide locum Modestini in collatione legum Mosaicarum & Romanarum, titulo de deposito.

Theodoretus iterum alacritatem & promptitu- dinem animi intelligit per gratiam fide confer- vandam: sed eam παρακαταθήκην nuspiam notat: doctrinam vero Evangelicam ea notari e loco pa- rallelo 1. Tim. VI. vers. 20. satis constat, & com- muniter agnoscitur, etiam a Theophylacto, etsi alteram is quoque attulerit expositionem: depo- situm, inquit, hoc est praecepta, quae tibi sunt per me de vita, fideque tradita: vel depositum gratiam dicit, quam ille acceperat. Bonum depositum, no- tante B. Balduino, vocat, quia autorem bonum habet, contenta sunt bona & salutaria, bonos et- iam facit, & bonum saluberrimumque finem ha- bet, vitam nimirum & salutem aeternam. Papistae non tam Scripturam S. quam Apostolicam do- ctrinam verbo traditam intelligunt: imo Estius de Scriptura satis contemptim: Quale, inquit, de- positum, quod omnibus pene sectis hæreticorum commune est! Sed quamvis communis sit Scri- ptura omnibus materialiter, quoad verba, non tamen formaliter, quoad germanum verborum sensum: ubi autem hodie est illa doctrina Aposto- lica verbo ἄτερ γραφῆς tradita, non scripta? Ce- do illam, quisquis es traditionum propugnator! Taceo, quod in deposito illo explicando maxi- mopere varient Papistæ: Thomas & Lyranus, ut & Cajetanus explicant de grege fidelitati Pastoris commisso: Glossa interlin. de officio Pastoribus concredito, quod diligenti executione debeant custodire. Salmero plures adfert ἐκθέσεις disp. XVI. in 1. Tim. Depositum secundum Oecume- nium est vel præceptum DEI de doctrina Timo- theo per Paulum propositum, aut gratia per or- dinationem accepta. Haymo intelligit gratiam fidei & spiritualem, quam Apostolus Timotheo commendavit. Alii depositum, id est, curam creditam Ecclesiæ per Spiritum Sanctum custo- diendam, &c.

Διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίε) Quasi dicat: ne diffide: Ma- gnum habes opitulatorem, supra 7.

Tῆ ἐνοικῦντος ἐν ἡμῖν) Quasi dicat: Qui non deser- tus, nec nos deferet. Rom. VIII. 11.

Estius pronomine ἡμῖν designari vult præfectos Ecclesiæ, quorum ministerio depositum illud per Spiritum Sanctum eis permissum in Ecclesia con- servatur. Sed rectius de fidelibus quibusvis con- junctim intelligitur, & de tota Ecclesia, quia o- mnibus & singulis promissa est Spiritus Sancti gratia. Theophylactus, quo pacto, inquit, gratiam hanc ipsam tutaberis? Certe non humanis viribus illis, sed per Spiritum Sanctum, qui nobis baptismi inhabitat gratia. Depositum hoc custodire jubet, quod fidelis est depositarii, cui aliquando ratio red- denda quomodo rem sibi commissam curarit. Cu- stodia autem hæc non est humanarum virium, sed Spiritus S. opus, quem dicit habitare in nobis, quia sancti vocantur templa Spiritus S. 1. Cor. III. v. 16. VI. 19. qui operatur in ipsis, & vires largitur, ut doctrinam sanam non tantum fideliter recipiamus, sed & contra omnem mundi sapientiam & Diaboli furorem constanter retineamus, ut B. Balduinus ait.

PARS III. Ἱστορικὴ.

## 1:15
Vers. 15. You know this) The more Timothy may be attentive to himself, he shows him both good and bad examples, the former, so that he may beware; the latter, so that he may not yield to others.

That all who are in Asia turned away from me. All those teachers: who are in Asia, not in Ephesus, where you are: but in the places around Ephesus: whence he says you know; you cannot be ignorant of this, they turned away from me, they loathed me, my authority and office of teaching being despised, they opposed, namely, on account of dangers.

Theophylact: He explains, he says, into what evils he has been immersed. Not to terrify the disciple, but rather to persuade him, if he should fall into the same, that he should not, as if suffering something unusual, abhor and fear it, but bear it with an even mind. For Paul, when he was apprehended by Nero, was soon deserted by all who were in Asia, that is, who had gone with him from Asia to Rome. Thus Theophylact and other Greeks interpret the particle IN Asia as FROM Asia. Others, however, retaining the proper meaning of the word ἐν, understand it either of those who had adhered to the Apostle while he was preaching in Asia, but when they saw him a captive coming to Rome, deserted him, or of those who were then in Asia, where Timothy was staying, and therefore he could not know them. He points to Asia Minor, and Chrysostom understands all those Asians who were then at Rome to be converts from the Jews, not from the Gentiles.

of whom are Phygellus and Hermogenes) Tertullian mentions these in his Prescription against Heretics and in his work on the resurrection of the flesh. The Hermogenes against whom Tertullian wrote a special book is different from this one. Perhaps this Hermogenes is the one whom the scholiast of Apollonius says wrote about Phrygia. There was also a Sophist by that name. I think, however, that the name Phygellus is a corruption of the Latin Figulus.

We dismiss Grotius's Figulus: and leave them to those who perhaps take delight in it. Tertullian, writing in Latin in his book on Prescription, ch. 3, named not Figulus, but Phygellus. Phygellus is said as if one to be fled from: Hermogenes, however, is born of Mercury, i.e., talkative and a liar. They were, without doubt, prominent among the Doctors. The passage of Tertullian concerning such deserters of the Church is remarkable: Let them fly away, as much as they will, the chaff of light faith with any breath of temptations, the purer mass of grain will be stored in the barns of the Lord. Did not some of the disciples themselves, scandalized, turn away from the Lord himself? Yet the others did not for that reason think they should depart from his footsteps, but those who knew that he was the word of life, and had come from God, persevered in his company until the end: although he had offered them, if they wished to depart, to do so quietly. It is a lesser thing if some, Phygellus and Hermogenes, abandoned his Apostle; and Philetus and Hymenaeus abandoned him, the very betrayer of Christ was of the Apostles. We wonder at his churches if they are deserted by some, since those things which we suffer show us to be Christians, after the example of Christ himself: They went out from us, he says, but they were not of us. If they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us: It is doubtful, however, whether Phygellus and Hermogenes were turned away from the faith? Nor does that seem likely, since the Apostle says of all of them that they turned away, and the Gospel does not say they deserted, but that they withdrew because of the scandal of his chains. Hermogenes, against whom Tertullian wrote expressly, lived under Antoninus Caracalla, 140 years after the birth of Christ. But this one lived in the time of Nero, whom Dorotheus in his Synopsis made Bishop of Megara, as he made Phygellus Bishop of Ephesus; let the credit rest with the Author.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Οἶδας τῦτο) Quo magis Timotheus sibi at- tennat, ostendit ei & bona & mala exempla, illa, ut sibi caveat: hæc ut aliis non cedat.

Ὅτι ἀπεστράφησάν με πάντες οἱ ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ. Πάντες omnes illi doctores: οἱ ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ qui sunt non Ephesi, ubi tu es: sed in locis circa Ephesum: unde ait οἶδας· non potes hoc nescire, ἀπεστράφησάν με fastidierunt me, spreta mea auctoritate & docendi munere, obstitite- runt, ob pericula scilicet.

Theophylactus: Explicat, inquit, quibus sit ma- lis immersus. Non ut discipulum terreat, quin ut suadeat potius, si in eadem ille inciderit, non tan- quam insolens aliquid patiatur, abhorreat, & for- midet, sed æquo animo ferat. Paulus enim cum esset à Nerone comprehensus, à cunctis mox est desti- tutus, qui in Asia erant, fidelibus, hoc est, qui ex Asia secum Romam concesserant. Ita Theophyla- ctus & alii Græci particulam IN Asia interpretan- tur EX Asia. Alii tamen propriam vocis ἐν signi- ficationem retinentes, vel de iis, qui Apostolo in Asia prædicanti adhæserint, sed Romam venien- tem, cum viderent captivum, ipsum deseruerint, intelligunt, vel de illis, qui tunc in Asia erant, ubi Timotheus versabatur, ideoque eos ignorare poterat. Asiam minorem indigitat, & conversos ex Judæis, non ex Gentibus Chrysostomus illos omnes intelligit Asianos, qui tunc Romæ erant.

ὧν ἐστι Φύγελλος καὶ Ἑρμογένης) Meminit horum Tertul- lianus Præscriptione adversum hæreticos, & de resurre- ctione carnis. Alius ab hoc Hermogene est is, contra quem librum specialem scripsit Tertullianus. Forte hic Hermo- genes is est, quem de Phrygia scripsisse ait Apollonii Scho- liastes. Fuit & Sophista eo nomine. Phygelli autem puto corruptum esse nomen ex Latino Figulus.

Mittimus Grotii Figulum: illisque relinqui- mus, qui eo forte delectantur. Tertullianus Lati- ne scribens lib. de Præscript. c. 3. non Figulum, sed Phygellum nominavit. Φύγελλος dicitur quasi fu- giendus: Ἑρμογένης autem à Mercurio genitus, i. e. loquax, & mendax. Fuerunt autem illi fine dubio præcipui è Doctoribus. Locus Tertulliani de ta- libus Ecclesiæ desertoribus insignis est: Avolent, quantum volent, palea levis fidei quocunque affla- tu tentationum, eo purior massa frumenti in hor- rea Domini reponetur. Nonne ab ipso Domino qui- dam discentium scandalizati diverterunt? Nec tamen propterea cæteri quoque discedendum à ve- stigiis ejus putaverunt, sed qui scierunt illum vita esse verbum, & à Deo venisse, perseverarunt in co- mitatu ejus usque ad finem: cum illis si vellent & ipsi, discedere, placide obtulisset. Minus est, si & Apo- stolum ejus, aliqui Phygellus & Hermogenes reli- querunt; & Philetus & Hymenæus reliquerunt, ipse traditor Christi de Apostolis fuit. Miramur de Ec- clesiis ejus, si à quibusdam deseruntur, cum ea nos ostendunt Christianos, quæ patimur ad exemplum ipsius Christi: Ex nobis, inquit, prodierunt, sed non fuerunt ex nobis. Si fuissent ex nobis, permansissent utique nobiscum: Dubium tamen est, an à fide aver- si fuerint Phygellus & Hermogenes? Nec id vide tur verosimile, cum de omnibus dicat Apostolus ἀπεστράφησαν, nec Evangelium illos dicat dese- ruisse, sed ob vinculorum scandalum subduxisse. Hermogenes, contra quem ex professo scripsit Tertullianus, sub Antonino Caracalla vixit 140. an. post Christum natum. Hic vero vixit Neronis tempore, quem Megarensem Episcopum, ut Phy- gellum Ephesinum fecit in Synopsi Dorotheus, fides sit penes Autorem.

## 1:16
V. 16. May the Lord grant mercy to the house of Onesiphorus) It seems to me that this Onesiphorus was dead when Paul wrote these things. For here prayers for his family and for him are distinguished: and below he greets the family of Onesiphorus, IV. 19, but not Onesiphorus: Add that he said in the past tense, he refreshed. May he grant mercy, that is, may he grant many good things. ויתן חסד for we have seen ἔλεος placed thus in Gal. VI. 11. and elsewhere οἶκος for family, is also frequent among the Greeks. Thus also 1 Cor. XVI. 19, 1 Tim. III. 4, 5, V. 4.

Papists say that Onesiphorus was dead at that time, in order to prove that prayers were accustomed to be made for the dead, and Estius and Fevardentius brought forward the same reasons as Grotius here. But those are weak. For Onesiphorus could have been included when his family was named. Just as Stephen is included when his family is said to have been baptized. And perhaps he did not explicitly mention Onesiphorus because he was absent from home at that time. He prays well, says Theophylact, for him who had undertaken the care of his own sustenance: and not for him alone, but for his whole family and house, so much did all the household of Onesiphorus excel in virtue, and were already very well instructed by him. Baronius, with Dorotheus, asserts that he held a bishopric at that time. Justin says that the same man was made Bishop of Ephesus after Timothy, which Alphonsus Salmero had also handed down before him. Therefore he was not yet dead. Nor did Estius dare to affirm that with certainty: it can be said probably, he says, nay, it must be known, he warns, that this good prayer of the Apostle for him did not lack effect. For as it is reported in the Martyrologies, both Greek and Latin, Onesiphorus was finally crowned with martyrdom in the Hellespont for the name of Christ, if indeed he is the same one whom those commemorate. He was an Asian, who is praised in this passage. He is therefore excepted from the number of those who deserted Paul.

For he often refreshed me) He comforted. A translation taken from shade or a light breeze in hot places. It is placed for בלג Psalm XXXIX. 14, for חרה Jud. XV. 14, for נפש Exod. XXIII. 12, 2 Sam. XVI. 14. Hence ἀνάψυξις Exod. VIII. 15, Acts III. 20.

Without doubt, he refreshed Paul in prison not only with consolation, but also with beneficence. Cf. Jas. II. 16. Onesiphorus signifies a man who is thrifty and light-bringing; truly such was Onesiphorus to Paul.

Καὶ τὴν ἄλυσίν μου οὐκ ἐπῃσχύνθη) He was not ashamed of this military chain, by which I am dragged, as fountains are wont to be. What he often called bonds elsewhere, he here calls ἄλυσιν more distinctly, and Eph. VI. 20; for in the same way Paul was bound again as he was when he first arrived. Acts XII. 6, 7; XXI. 33; XXVIII. 20. Concerning the word ἐπαισχύνεσθαι, see above 8.

Latin:

V. 16. Δώη ἔλεος ὁ Κύριος τῷ Ὀνησιφόρου ὄικῳ) Videtur mihi hic Onesiphorus fuisse mortuus, cum hæc Paulus scri- beret. Nam hic distinguuntur preces pro familia ipsius & pro ipso: & infra Onesiphori familiam salutat IV. 19. non autem Onesiphorum: Adde quod in præterito dixit ἀνέψυξε. Δώη ἔλεος, id est, det multa bona. ויתן חסד nam ἔλεος sic poni vidimus Gal. VI. 11. & alibi οἶκος pro familia, frequens et- iam Græcis. Sic & 1. Cor. XVI. 19. 1. Tim. III. 4. 5. V. 4.

Mortuum tum fuisse Onesiphorum Papistæ a- junt, ut probent orationes fieri solitas pro defunctis, Et easdem rationes, quas hic Grotius, adduxit E- stius & Fevardentius. Sed illæ infirmæ sunt. Nam potuit Onesiphorus comprehendi nominata fami- lia. Sicut Stephanus comprehenditur, cum fami- lia ejus baptizata dicitur. Et forte non expressit diserte Onesiphorum, quod tunc domo abfuerit. Ei, inquit Theophylactus, qui sui alendi susceperat curam, bene precatur: nec illi solum, sed familiæ universæ & domui, adeo Onesiphori domestici omnes virtute præstabant, & ab eo jam optime erant instru- cti. Baronius cum Dorotheo Episcopatum tum ges- sisse asserit. Eundem Justinus post Timotheum Episcopum Ephesinum factum dicit, quod Al- phonsus Salmero ante ipsum etiam tradidit. Non ergo jam defunctus fuit. Neque certo id ausus est affirmare Estius: probabiliter, inquit, dici potest, imò sciendum est, monet, bonam hanc Apostoli pro eo precationem effectu non caruisse. Nam ut refer- tur in Martyrologiis tam Græcis quam Latinis, Onesiphorus tandem in Hellesponto pro Christi nomine martyrio coronatus est, si tamen est idem, quem illa commemorant. Asianus fuit, qui hoc loco prædicatur. Excipitur ergo è numero illo- rum, qui Paulum deseruerunt.

Ὅτι πολλάκις με ἀνέψυξε) Consolatus est. Translatio sumpta ab umbra aut ventulo in locis æstuosis. Ponitur pro בלג Psalm. XXXIX. 14. pro חרה Jud. XV. 14. pro נפש Exod. XXIII. 12. 2. Sam. XVI. 14. Hinc ἀνάψυξις Exod. VIII. 15. Act. III. 20.

Sine dubio non tantum consolatione, sed etiam beneficentia refocillavit Paulum in carcere. Conf. Jac. II. 16. Onesiphorus significat hominem fru- gi, & luciferum, vere talis Onesiphorus fuit Paulo.

Καὶ τὴν ἄλυσίν μου οὐκ ἐπῃσχύνθη) Non puduit eum catenæ hujus militaris, qua trahor, ut fontes solent. Quod alibi sæpe vincula dixit, id distinctius ἄλυσιν hic, & Eph. VI. 20. nimirum eodem modo iterum vinctus fuit Paulus, quo cum primum adveniret. Actor. XII. 6. 7. XXI. 33. XXVIII. 20. de voce ἐπαισχύνεσθαι, vide supra 8.

## 1:17
v. 17. Ἀλλὰ γενόμενος ἐν Ῥώμῃ) For Ephesian merchants had many dealings in Rome.

Σπουδαιότερον) A comparative for a superlative, frequent among the Greeks.

Ἐζήτησέ με) He ran about through the whole city of Rome to seek me.

He had need of inquiry, either because there was not one, but several prisons in Rome, or because it was perhaps permitted to Paul, as in his first captivity, Acts XXVIII. 16, to go about with the soldier guarding him.

Καὶ εὗρε) GOD favoring: namely, in the little lodging where he was with his guard.

Latin:

v. 17. Ἀλλὰ γενόμενος ἐν Ῥώμῃ) Nam Ephesini mercato- res multa negotia Romæ habebant.

Σπουδαιότερον) Comparativus pro Superlativo, frequens Græcis.

Ἐζήτησέ με) Per totam urbem Romam cursitavit, ut me quæreret.

Inquisitione opus habuit, sive quia non unus, sed complures carceres erant Romæ, sive quia permissum forte Paulo, ut in prima captivitate, Act. XXIX. 16. ut circumiret cum custodiente se milite.

Καὶ εὗρε) DEO favente: nempe in diverforiolo, ubi erat cum suo custode.

## 1:18
v. 18. Δῴη αὐτῷ ὁ Κύριος) Christ, to whom the power of judging has been given.

Εὑρεῖν ἔλεος) that he may receive good things, namely eternal ones; we have already said what ἔλεος is. Εὑρίσκειν is מצא, to obtain. See Luke I. 30.

Παρὰ κυρίου) A Hebrew idiom, for from himself, or by his own giving. You have similar expressions in Gen. IV. 23; Exod. X. 11; XXIII. v. 18, 19; XXIV. 1, 2; Num. X. 29; Zach. I. 17; Ps. XIII. 6; LXXXII. verse 1.

There is no reason why we should admit that Hebraism here: since by such expressions, according to Canon XVI of the Council of Sirmium, a distinction of persons in the Godhead is asserted: and Paul prays to Christ the Lord that he himself may grant Onesiphorus to find mercy before the Lord, God the Father. Concerning which, more in the Diatribe on the plurality of divine persons. Crocius, with Theophylact leading the way, proves this sense, having set aside other interpretations of the faithful and Calvin himself. Theophylact has it thus: In this place, because Paul puts 'Lord' twice, those who suffer from the disease of Marcion insult, and assert that there are two Lords. Which is certainly far otherwise. For there is one Lord, as the Apostle testifies elsewhere. Yet the Sacred letters are accustomed to repeat that name of Lord quite often, as also elsewhere. The Lord rained from the Lord, that is, from himself. Nor is it otherwise in this place: for if you take the Father and the Son to be signified by this iteration of Lord, there will be nothing absurd. For the Father is Lord, and the Son is Lord, and indeed the Spirit is called Lord, but in three substances one Lord is demonstrated.

Ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ) See above 12.

Fevardentius therefore wrongly refers these to prayers for the dead in purgatory: If they pertain to the last day: which cannot be denied. For in that judgment that fire will already be extinguished according to the fables of the Papists. And therefore Cajetan preferred to interpret: he prays for eternal retribution. Mercy is divine grace, from which eternal life will be obtained by anyone in Christ Jesus Rom. VI. 23. He has had mercy, he says, with Theophylact saying, on me. I would therefore wish, and I desire it greatly, that he may receive the retribution of this mercy on that horrible day, when all, even those who excel in holiness, will stand in need of mercy. If, therefore, that Onesiphorus, who exposed himself to dangers for the sake of Christ, is saved by the compassion of God, far more shall we also obtain salvation through the clemency of God.

And how much he ministered in Ephesus, you know better. It was not a new thing for Onesiphorus to serve me and the Church. Long ago at Ephesus he had done the same. I do not repeat the history. For it is known to you who were there with me. He ministered, namely, to the saints, which is added in a not dissimilar matter in Rom. 15:25, Heb. 6:10. Thus also elsewhere after διακονεῖν the dative is understood, as in John 12:2. But διακονεῖν with the accusative is a Greek construction. Therefore, for ὅσα, you will rightly translate in Latin: in how many things.

Thus also, with the Censor in the additions to Estius, the blessed Gerhard [says], in how many things he ministered at Ephesus, that is, how officious he was in his ministry. The Vulgate, contrary to the authority of the Greek [texts] and many Latin codices, adds 'to me.' The addition is not appropriate. For it is more consistent that Paul himself should have known the benefits conferred upon him than Timothy. And thus his charity appears greater, because he ministered not to Paul alone, but to many saints, or helped them with his labor, consolation, and aid.

Latin:

v. 18. Δῴη αὐτῷ ὁ Κύριος) Christus cui judicandi pote- stas data est.

Εὑρεῖν ἔλεος) ut bona, nempe æterna accipiat, ἔλεος quid sit, jam diximus. Εὑρίσκειν מצא est consequi. Vi- de Luc. I. 30.

Παρὰ κυρίου) Hebræa locutio, pro à se, sive ipso dante. Similes locutiones habes Gen. IV. 23. Exod. X. 11. XXIII. v. 18. 19. XXIV. 1. 2. Num. X. 29. Zach. I. 17. Ps. XIII. 6. LXXXII. vers. 1.

Nulla causa est, cur hic Ebraismum illum ad- mittamus: quum talibus locutionibus juxta Con- cilii Sirmicensis Can. XVI. adseratur distinctio per- sonarum in divinitate: ac à Christo Domino prece- tur Paulus, det ipse Onesiphoro misericordiam invenire coram Domino, Deo Patre. Quo de plu- ribus in Diatrib. de pluralit. person. divinar. Pro- bat hunc sensum posthabitis aliis fidei sociennis, & Calvino ipso, Crocius, Theophylacto præeunte. Theophylactus ita habet: Hoc loco, quia Paulus bis Dominum ponit, insultant qui Marcionis morbo la- borant, asseruntque duos Dominos esse. Quod sane longe secus se habet. Unus namque Dominus, ut alibi testatur Apostolus. Consuevere tamen literæ Sacræ id Domini nomen sæpius iterare, ut & alibi. Pluit Dominus à Domino, hoc est à se ipso. Nec se- cus hoc loco fuisse constas: quod si Patrem & Filium significari Domini iteratione hac ceperis, nil erit absurdum. Est namque & Pater Dominus, & Fi- lius Dominus, quin & Spiritus Dominus nuncupa- tur, sed in tribus substantiis unus Dominus demon- stratur.

Ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ) Vide supra 12.

Ad orationes ergo pro defunctis in purgatorio hæc perperam refert Fevardentius: Si ad diem novissimum ea pertinent: quod negari non potest. In judicio enim illo extinctus jam erit ignis ille juxta fabulas Papistarum. Ideoque Cajetanus ma- luit interpretari: orat pro æterna retributione. Mi- sericordia est gratia divina, ex qua cuivis obtinget in Christo Jesu vita æterna Rom. VI. 23. Miser- tus, inquit, Theophylacto dicente, est mei. Velim itaque, & id admodum concupisco, ut hujusce mise- ricordiæ retributionem, in die illa horribili capiat, cum omnes, vel qui sanctimonia pollent, miseri- cordia indigebunt. Si itaque Onesiphorus ille, qui Chri- sti ob gratiam periculis se objecitavit, ex Dei com- miseratione salvatur, longe magis & nos salutem sumus ex Dei clementia habituri.

Καὶ ὅσα ἐν Ἐφέσῳ διηκόνησε, βέλτιον σὺ γινώσκεις) Non novum fuit Onesiphoro servire mihi & Ecclesiæ. Jampri- dem Ephesi idem fecerat. Historiam non repeto. Est enim ibi nota, qui ibi mihi adfuisti. Διηκόνησε nempe τοῖς ἁγίοις, quod in re non dissimili additur Rom. V. 25. Hebr. VI. v. 10. Sic & alibi post διακονεῖν subauditur Dativus, ut Joh. XII. 2. Διακονεῖν autem cum accusativo, constructio Græca. Ita- que pro ὅσα Latine recte verteris, in quantis rebus.

Sic & cum Censore in addit. ad Estium B. Ger- hardus, in quam multis rebus Ephesi ministraverit, id est, quam fuerit in ministerio officiosus. Vulgata præter Græcorum fidem, & multos Latinos Codd. addit mihi. Non convenit additamentum. Con- sentaneum enim est Paulum ipsummet potius no- visse in se collata beneficia, quam Timotheum. Et major ita apparet charitas, quod non uni Paulo, sed pluribus Sanctis ministravit, vel operâ, sola- tio & auxilio subveniret.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He exhorts to alacrity in duty, that he may strive patiently and with secular matters set aside, that he may obtain the crown and fruit of his labors, that he may keep the resurrection of Christ in memory, that he may follow his own example, with the promise of eternal life added, and he orders him to warn [others] to avoid fighting over words, and to study the blameless administration of his office: he defeats the injuries of the heterodox, notes the gangrene of errors, and designates the seal of the divine foundation, and commands that we be vessels sanctified for the Lord; finally, he reminds Timothy to flee from lusts, and to pursue justice, to avoid useless and anxious questions, and with meekness to correct those who contradict.

There are two parts: I. An exhortation concerning the administration of the office, up to verse 21. II. A reminder concerning the pursuit of piety and meekness.

PART I. Exhortation concerning the administration of the office.

verse 1. You therefore, my child) See with what affection, as in 1 Tim. 1:18. Be strengthened (Ἐνδυνάμου)) עזז. For it is translated thus in Psalm 52:9. Thus also both active and passive [forms] are used indiscriminately by the Hebrews, whether writing in Hebrew or in Greek, for reciprocal [meanings]. For the sense is: strengthen yourself, namely, by assiduous effort.

He requires for the administration of the office (1) Alacrity, both that Timothy may strengthen himself and that he may excite others to the sacred ministry, verse 2. (2) Tolerance of evils and labors, with a triple similitude proposed, namely, of soldiers, who do not entangle themselves in the affairs of the world, being intent on their military service, verses 3, 4; of athletes, verse 5; and of farmers, verse 6; with a prayer for divine illumination, verse 7; with the resurrection of the Lord from the dead also proposed, verse 8; as well as his own, which he sets forth by way of example, in patience, verses 9, 10; and finally, the most certain promise of divine life, verses 11, 12, 13. (3) The due exhortation of others, both to patience and to avoiding logomachy, verse 14. (4) Blameless operation in his office, both in general and in particular, regarding the right handling of the word of truth, verse 15; the flight from profane empty talk, verse 16, such as was that of Hymenaeus and Philetus, verse 17, who contend that the resurrection has already taken place, verse 18, with a reason brought forward from the divine care of the faithful, verse 19, and the similitude of the different vessels in the house of the Lord, verses 20, 21. He derives his exhortation to execute his office manfully from the preceding [instructions] about stirring up the gift which he had received through the laying on of hands, and about the Spirit not of fear, but of power, with which GOD instructs men, 2 Tim. 1:6, 7, and also about guarding the deposit, verse 14. The Vulgate renders: You therefore, my Son, be strengthened in the grace which is in Christ JESUS. The same word is used of all the faithful in Eph. 6:10, be strengthened in the Lord. Here, primarily, strength and alacrity of office are regarded in the grace, which some, like Sasbouth and Justinian, understand as the doctrine of the Gospel, which is the word of grace, Acts 14:3; others [understand it] as faith, by which we apprehend the grace of GOD in Christ; many also think it is the grace of the ministry, just as the grace of the Apostleship is celebrated in Romans 1:5. The blessed Luther, looking to the Hebraism, translates, 'through the grace.' Theophylact, with Chrysostom preceding him, also explains the strengthening from grace, so that he may have it as a helper in this struggle: who has it thus: He brings in that admonition with the greatest affection, while he says, 'child': and not only that, but he adds, 'my child.' If you are a son, he says, imitate the Father; if you are a son, be strengthened from these things which I have said, and not from these only, but from the grace of Christ. Be strengthened, he says, in the grace which is in Christ JESUS, that is, through the grace of Christ, as if he were saying, persist strongly, you have the grace of GOD helping you and struggling along with you: with great alacrity of purpose, with great constancy of will, undertake your duty. Similarly Theodoret. These things, he says, since you know them, stand strongly: for the grace of Christ sustains you. This grace, however, by the force of the Greek text, is more correctly explained as the grace of GOD, which is in Christ JESUS. He exhorts Timothy, therefore, that having cast aside all timidity, he should act strongly in the office he has undertaken, and do so leaning upon the aid of the grace of GOD, which is given through Christ, as the blessed Gerhard [says] here. He designates the grace that strengthens, sustains, defends, and perfects, 'fighting with and struggling along with,' as Chrysostom calls it, which is proper to the reborn. In vain, therefore, do the Pelagians and those who Pelagianize bring forward this exhortation for the powers of free will.

Latin:

CAPUT II. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Hortatur ad alacritatem in officio, ut patienter, & posthabitis secularibus certet, ut coronam & fructum laborum consequatur, resurre- ctionem Christi in memoria habeat, exem- plum suum sequatur, addita promissione vitæ æternæ, & monere jubet de vitanda verbo- rum pugna, ac studere inculpatæ muneris administrationi: profligat heterodoxorum injurias, errorum gangrænam notat, ac sigil- lum fundamenti divini designat, præcipitque ut vasa simus Domino sanctificata, denique commonefacit, ut fugiat Timotheus concu- piscentias, ac sectetur justitiam, vitet in- utiles & anxias quæstiones & cum mansue- tudine corrigat contradicentes.

Partes duæ sunt I. Adhortatio de officii ad- ministratione, ad v. 21. II. Commonefactio de stu- dio pietatis & mansuetudinis.

PARS I. Adhortatio de officii administratione.

vers. 1. Σὺ οὖν τέκνον μου) Vide quanto affectu ut 1. Tim. I. vers. 18. Ἐνδυνάμου) עזז. Id enim sic transfertur Psal. LII. v. 9. Sic & activa & passiva promiscue Hebræis, tum Hebraice, tum Græce scribentibus, usurpantur pro reciprocis. Sensus enim est: robora temet, assiduo nempe studio.

Requirit ad officii administrationem (1) Ala- critatem, tum ut seipsum Timotheus roboret, tum ut alios excitet ad sacrum ministerium, vers. 2. (2.) Malorum & laborum tolerantiam, propo- sitâ triplici similitudine, utpote militantium, qui negotiis seculi se non implicant militiæ suæ intenti vers. 3. 4. athletarum vers. 5. & agricola- rum vers. 6. cum voto illuminationis divinæ v. 7. propositâ item resurrectione à mortuis Dominica vers. 8. ut & propriâ, quam exempli loco sistit, patientiâ, vers. 9. 10. & denique promissione vitæ divinæ certissima, vers. 11. 12. 13. (3) Adhor- tationem aliorum debitam tum ad patientiam, tum ad vitandam λογομαχίαν, vers. 14. (4.) In- culpatam in munere operationem tum in genere tum in specie qua verbi veritatis ὀρθοτομίαν vers. 15. prophanæ κενοφωνίας fugam vers. 16. qualis fuit Hymenæi & Phileti vers. 17. resurrectionem jam factam contendentium vers. 18. adducta ratione a divina fidelium cura vers. 19. & Simi- litudine de diversis vasis in domo Domini v. 20. 21. Deducit autem parænesin suam ad officium viriliter exequendum e superioribus de excitan- do dono, quod acceperat per impositionem ma- nuum, & de Spiritu non timoris, sed virtutis, quo instruit homines DEUS 2. Timoth. I. vers. 6. 7. nec non de custodiendo deposito vers. 14. Vulgata reddit: Tu ergo Fili mi confor- tare in gratia, quæ est in Christo JESU. Idem verbum adhibitum de omnibus fidelibus Eph. VI. vers. 10. ἐνδυναμοῦσθε ἐν κυρίῳ, Confortamini in Domino. Hic imprimis robur & alacritas effi- cii respicitur ἐν τῇ χάριτι, in gratia, quam de doctrina Evangelii, quod est verbum gratiæ, Actor. XIV. vers. 3. nonnulli ut Sasbouth & Ju- stinianus intelligunt, alii de fide, qua gratiam DEI in Christo apprehendimus, multi etiam putant gratiam ministerii, uti gratia Apostola- tus Romanorum I. vers. 5. celebratur. Beat. Lu- therus Ebraismum respiciens vertit, durch die Gnade. De confortatione ex gratia, ut eam ha- beat adjutricem in hoc certamine, etiam expli- cat Theophylactus, præeunte Chrysostomo: qui ita habet: Summo vero affectu eam admonitio- nem infert, dum dicit, fili: neque id tantum, sed adjicit, fili mi. Si filius es, inquit, Patrem imitare; si filius es, ex his confortare, quæ di- xi, neque ex his tantum, sed ex gratia Christi. Confortare, inquit, in gratia, quæ est in Chri- sto JESU, hoc est, per gratiam Christi, ac si di- cat, persiste fortiter, habes adjuvantem gratiam DEI, unaque certantem: Magna propositi ala- critate, magna constantia, voluntatis munus tuum aggredere. Similiter Theodoretes. Hæc, inquit, cum scias, sta fortiter: Te enim susten- tat Christi gratia. Hæc tamen gratia vi Græ- ci textus rectius exponitur gratia DEI, quæ est in Christo JESU. Adhortatur ergo Timo- theum, ut abjecta omni timiditate fortiter agat in suscepto munere, idque faciat, innixus auxi- lio gratiæ DEI, quæ datur per Christum, ut hic Beat. Gerhardus. Gratiam corroborantem, susten- tantem, propugnantem, perficientem, συμμα- χοῦσαν καὶ συναγωνιζομένην, ut Chrysostomus vo- cat, designat, quæ renatorum propria. Frustra ergo hanc parænesin pro liberi arbitrii viribus ad- ducunt Pelagiani, & Pelagianizantes.

## 2:2
Verse 2.

And the things which you have heard from me by many witnesses) By many witnesses brought forward, the Prophets, who had predicted these things, Heb. XII. verse 1.

He refers to the deposit of doctrine which he had commended in chapter I, verse 14. By witnesses some understand the presbyters who were present at the ordination of Timothy to the Sacred ministry, translating it as 'among many witnesses': others understand others whom the Apostle instructed along with Timothy: as, after Tertullian in De Praescriptione, Theodoret, Chrysostom, Theophylact. You did not hear these things in private, he says, nor in secret, but openly with everyone standing by. Theophylact, however, also brings forward the Grotian explanation. Some, indeed, he says, have taken 'many witnesses' to mean the Law and the Prophets, just as if he were inquiring, 'My words were confirmed by the testimony of the Sacred Writers.' But the former explanation is simpler.

The Apostle instructed Timothy among many, so that the fruit might redound to more, and that there might not be lacking witnesses of those things which he had handed down. He is not, therefore, dealing with more secret perfect things handed down only, and that by word of mouth alone, as Magalianus wishes: for he handed them down publicly. And thus Thomas: who understands the Law and the Prophets through many witnesses: The nerve of the argument, which is sought from here for traditions, is clearly cut: for the Law and the Prophets pertain to the written word.

Commit these things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also. From this we see that Timothy performed the office not only of a Bishop, but also of a Metropolitan, no less than Titus: for to teach was the duty of the leaders, the presiding ones, the angels, as before, the Bishops, as the Church later called them by way of eminence. Timothy was therefore truly the great Rabbi. We have here the word parathou, command. See Psalm 36:5. who will be able to teach others also: apt to teach, 1 Timothy 3, verse 2, below here 2.

He did not say 'narrate' or 'teach', as Chrysostom and Theophylact advise, but 'commend' as a royal treasure. For whatever is commended to the faith of another is placed in safety. The Apostle wishes, therefore, that Timothy not only teach faithfully, but also grant the power of teaching to others. For the deposit had been commended to those who are both faithful and fit to teach others. For he speaks of Presbyters and Bishops: and thus he teaches that these two things are necessary for a Doctor, that he be faithful in teaching, so that he may conceal or suppress nothing, add or change nothing of his own, and fit and suitable to teach others. For what does it profit, says Theophylact, if someone is faithful and gives out everything, omitting nothing, when he cannot bring forth doctrine to others? And again, neither brings forth words here, nor can make others equal to himself by teaching? Neither the ancient Interpreters observed that Timothy was a Metropolitan, nor does it appear from the text. For whence would that be gathered? For even those who are not Metropolitans can give others the power of teaching. What of the fact that at that time there were none yet.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Καὶ ἃ ἤκουσας παρ’ ἐμοῦ διὰ πολλῶν μαρτύρων) Multis addu- ctis testibus Prophetis, qui hæc prædixerant, Ebr. XII. vers. 1.

Respicit depositum doctrinæ, quam commen- darat cap. I. vers. 20. per testes nonnulli intel- ligunt presbyteros, qui adfuerint ordinationi Timothei ad Sacrum ministerium vertentes 18- ter multos testes: alii alios, quos informavit A- postolus cum Timotheo: ut post Tertullianum de Præscript. Theodoretus, Chrysostomus, Theophy- lactus. Non ea clam, inquit, audiisti, nec in secreto, sed palam omnibus adstantibus. Ad- fert tamen Theophylactus etiam Grotianam expli- cationem. Nonnulli vero, inquit, multos testes pro lege & Prophetis acceperunt, perinde ac inquirat, Sa- crorum Scriptorum testimonio dicta mea confirma- bantur. Sed prior explicatio simplicior est.

Instituit Apostolus Timotheum inter multos, ut ad plures redundaret fructus, & ut non deeffent testes de iis, quæ tradiderat. Non ergo de secretioribus perfectis tantum traditis, idque viva solum voce, ut Magalianus vult, agit: Publice enim ea tradidit. Et sic Thomas: qui per multos testes legem & Prophetas intelligit: Inciditur plane nervus argumenti, quod petitur hinc pro traditionibus: Lex enim & Prophetæ ad verbum scriptum pertinent.

Τᾶυτα παράθυ πιστοῖς ἀνθρώποις οἵ τινες ἱκανοὶ ἔσονται καὶ ἑτέρυς διδάξαι) Hinc videmus Timotheum, non Episcopi tantum, sed & Metropolitæ functum officio, non minus quam Titum: nam docere erat τῶν ἡγυμένων, προῗσαμένων, ἀγγόλων, ut prius, Episcoporum, ut posterius per eminentiam eos vocavit Ecclesia. Erat ergo Timotheus verè רב הגדול. Habemus hic verbum παράθυ, פקוד. Vide Psal. XXXVI. 5. οἵ τινες ἱκανοὶ ἔσονται καὶ ἑτέρυς διδάξαι• qui possint & alios docere: διδακτικοῖς, 1. Timoth. III. vers. 2. infra hic 2.

Non dixit enarra vel doce, monente Chrysostomo & Theophylacto, sed commenda velut thesaurum regium. Quodcunque enim alterius fidei commendatur, in tuto reponitur. Vult ergo Apostolus, ut Timotheus non solum fideliter doceat, sed etiam aliis docendi potestatem concedat. Illis autem commendatum erat depositum qui & fideles sunt,& alios docere idonei. Loquitur enim de Presbyteris & Episcopis: adeoque duo hæc necessaria Doctori esse docet, ut nempe πιςὸς fidelis sit in docendo, ut nihil sileat, vel subticeat, nihil de suo addat, vel immutet, & ἱκανὸς καὶ ἑτέρυς διδάξαι, aptus & idoneus ad alios docendos. Quid enim prodest, inquit Theophylactus, si quispiam fidelis sit & omnia erogans nil excipiat,cum nequeat aliis proferre doctrinam? Rursumque nec verba hic edat, nec alios possit pares sibi docendo efficere? Metropolitanum fuisse Timotheum nec veteres Interpretes observarunt, nec è textu apparet. Unde enim id colligetur? Nam aliis potestatem docendi dare possunt etiam qui Metropolitani non sunt. Quid, quod illo tempore nulli adhuc fuerint.

## 2:3
Verse 3.

You therefore endure hardship. See what we said above 1, v. 8. In the Manuscript here it is: suffer hardship together. As a good soldier of Jesus Christ. See 1 Cor. 9, verse 7. 2 Cor. 10, verse 34. 1 Tim. 1, verse 18. Under that leader, under those standards, we must do military service.

The Vulgate rendered it 'labor': But the Greek word properly implies the endurance of evils. You see how a soldier must sweat, says Theophylact, and endure evils. Therefore, it will not be the duty of a soldier to dwell in idleness. Nor indeed is it to be borne with an impatient mind if he who has been placed in the number of soldiers labors and is pressed. But how great is the dignity of being a soldier of Christ? Since some value highly serving in the military under some earthly Emperor.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Σὺ ůν κακοπάθησον) Vide quæ diximus supra I, v. 8. In Manuscripto est hic: συγκακοπάθησον. Ὡς καλὸς στρατιώτης Ἰησῦ χρισῦ) Vide 1. Cor. IX. vers. 7. 2. Cor. X, vers. 34. 1. Tim. I. vers. 18. Sub illo duce, sub illis signis nobis militandum est.

Vulgata reddidit labora: Sed Græcum verbum infert proprie malorum tolerantiam. Vides quemadmodum militi sit insudandum, inquit Theophylactus, & mala perpetienda. Non ergo erit officium militis in otio diversari. Nec est quidem animo iniquo ferendum, si laborat & premitur, qui fuerit in militum numero constitutus. Verum quanta illud est dignitatis, Christi militem esse? Quandoquidem nonnulli plurimi faciant, sub terreno aliquo Imperatore militiam exercere.

## 2:4
Verse 4.

No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of this life. Entangles, that is, involves himself: passive for reciprocal. He draws the comparison from secular military service, as in the cited places, that is, from the lesser to the greater. Emperor Leo in Law 'Soldiers', Code concerning Military Affairs, book 12. Soldiers who are armed and fed by the Republic ought to be occupied only with public utilities, and not with the cultivation of fields, and the guarding of animals, or the profit of merchandise: but to sweat at their own military duties. The same Emperor, Law 'Soldiers', Code 'Hired'. We prohibit our soldiers from becoming conductors, or procurators and guarantors, or mandatories of conductors of other people's affairs, lest, having omitted the use of arms, they betake themselves to rustic work. Then: But let them be occupied with arms, not private business. Ambrose, book 1, on duties. He who serves as a soldier for the Emperor is prohibited by human laws from the undertaking of lawsuits, the acting of forensic business, and the sale of merchandise. Vegetius, book 2. Nor were soldiers appointed to any services, nor were private businesses entrusted to them: since it seemed incongruous for a soldier of the Emperor, who was fed by public clothing and rations, to be free for private utilities. Moreover, there are ancient laws which forbid this. For Florus narrates that Postumius, a man of Consular rank, was condemned because he had used the labor of soldiers on his own field. Diocletian and Maximian, Law 'If a soldier', Code concerning the recovery of things given for a cause, say: If you have made a soldier a procurator for your business, since this has been forbidden by the laws. See also the law of Honorius and Arcadius: No soldier, under the said title of the Code concerning military affairs. The title of the Code tends to the same: 'That traders may not serve as soldiers': in a similar matter, the last law of the Code concerning the Fabricenses. Cassiodorus 2.31. Those who have given their name to the military ought to sweat at public matters. The word 'entangles' is found in the Greek Proverbs 28:18. Thus 'entangled in labors' in Plato, 'involved in occupations' in Cicero. He said the same thing about being involved in business in more than one place.

Ἵνα τῷ στρατολογήσαντι ἀρέσῃ) that he may please him who has made the levy, that is, the commander, who is מפקד צבא in Isaiah 13:4. In the Glossary, στρατολογία is a levy. In the Latin we read 'that he may please him, to whom he has approved himself': But the interpreter who wrote 'approved himself' must have written it. For there are also letters of approval concerning this matter in the Code.

Persisting in the metaphor, as Theodoret advises, he prepares a benefit from it: Those who embrace the military life are separated from the pursuits of trade, and take care only of military discipline. Theophylact says: These words are addressed to all bishops and teachers. But when he says 'entangles,' he makes the matter clearer: For certainly the businesses of this life are in the place of shackles. And when he says 'businesses,' he designates various perturbations and troubles of the mind, and exhorts us to decline from these: just as if he were to say: Why do you entangle yourself in more troublesome things and businesses? Devote yourself only to the militia; in this way you will have obeyed Christ, who chose you for that duty of the militia. Grotius ought to have reminded the Papal bishops of this, who entangle themselves in various secular matters, and are at once politicians, nay, secular soldiers; concerning which see the 'Ecclesiastical Iron-wood' of our Dn. D. Ziegler: The Bishop as Soldier. Whence Claud. Espencæus has frankly confessed in his digression 2 on chapter 1 of Titus, according to this postulate, that France would have no bishops or presbyters, since they are immersed in secular businesses. Nicholas I certainly wrote to the Emperor Michael in the year 858, which is cited in C. Cum ad verum, Dist. 96, and C. Quoniam, Dist. 10, under the name of Cyprian, proves from this saying that the offices of both powers are distinct, separated by their own proper acts and dignities, which was also repeated in the Synod of Macra in the year 881. Compare also C. Placuit, Caus. 21, q. 3. And let these things also be noted against the Pontificians, who arrogate secular power to themselves. Claud. Espencæus in this place also praises the opinion of Ambrose in this place: 'But let the ecclesiastic therefore present himself to God, that, devoted to Him, he may fulfill the office which he promised, solicitous in the things of God, alien from secular business. For it is not fitting for one to have a double profession.' These things were indeed said, says Chrysostom, to Timothy, but they are said through him also to all masters and disciples. Let no one therefore endowed with a bishopric refuse to hear these things, but let him refuse to do them plainly. Estius indeed turns aside the necessity by way of excuse, which was also done by Bellarmine, book 5, De Romano Pontifice, chapter 9. But what necessity can excuse that which is prohibited by divine law? And O miserable religion, which relies not except on secular power and the human arm of bishops. But Estius rightly notes the Vulgate, which has: 'No one warring to God': The little word 'TO GOD' is not only absent from the Greek and Syriac codices, but it is not in all Latin ones, nor does it pertain here at all: just as Robert Bellarmine, book 5, De Romano Pontifice, last chapter, learnedly noted after others. And although it is found in the written text of the Ambrosian, Pelagius, Primasius, and Sedulius, from their own commentaries it is sufficiently apparent that it was not acknowledged by them. For the comparison here is: If a soldier endures all things for the sake of earthly pay, and rejects from himself all business that might hinder him from military service, how much more does this devolve upon the spiritual soldier? Bellarmine and Torrensis, however, ineptly abuse this saying for the interdiction of priestly marriage. For marriage is not a secular business of such a kind that it would hinder either bodily or spiritual warfare; indeed, Bellarmine does not hesitate to place its essence in the nature of a Sacrament (de Sacr. matr. cap. II. & XXXII.). Nor are all secular businesses prohibited, but only an anxious immersion in secular affairs, which Thomas and Erasmus teach from the word ἐμπλέκεσθαι. Espensæus and Justin teach; and as Salmeron observes, the Apostle seems to note certain Doctors and Bishops of his own age who served their own interests and involved themselves in the secular affairs of this world through pride, or avarice, or the flesh, and did not have leisure for the occupations of their office. What of the fact that Corn. à Lapide and Estius, as well as Bellarmine himself (lib. V. de R. P. c. ult.), wish these things to be said as much to a Bishop as to other men, since all laymen ought to be soldiers of Christ? Is marriage therefore interdicted to all men? Not undeservedly, therefore, is a spirit of giddiness noted here in Bellarmine, who, in order to despoil Bishops of the right of marriage, restricts the sense of this saying to Bishops alone: whereas when we oppose that to the secular power of Bishops, Bellarmine replies: These things are said by Paul as much to a Bishop as to other men.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Οὐδεὶς στρατευόμενο ἐμπλέκεται ταῖς τῦ βίε πραγματείαις) ἐμπλέκεται, id est, se implicat: passivum pro reciproco. Similitudinem ducit à militia seculari,ut dictis locis,id est,à minori ad majus. Leo Imperator in L. Milites. C. de Re militari, libr. XII. Milites qui à Republ. armantur & aluntur, solis debent utilitatibus publicis occupari, nec agrorum cultui, & custodia animalium, vel mercimoniorum quæstui: sed propria munia insudare militia: Idem Imperator L. Milites. C. Locati. Milites nostros alienarum rerum conductores, seu procuratores & fidejussores, vel mandatores conductorum fieri prohibemus, ne omisso armorum usu ad opus ruste se conferant. Deinde: Armis autem,non privatis negotiis occupentur. Ambrosius libr. I. de offic. Is qui Imperatori militat, à susceptionibus litium, actu negotiorum forensium, venditione mercium prohibetur humanis legibus. Ve- getius lib. II. Nec aliquibus milites instituti deputabantur obsequiis, nec privata iisdem negotia mandabantur: siquidem incongruum videbatur Imperatoris militem, qui veste & an- nona publica pascebatur, utilitatibus vacare privatis. Veteres autem sunt leges, quæ hoc vetant. Nam Postumium virum Consularem damnatum narrat Florus, quod opera militum in agro suo usus esset. Diocletianus & Maximilianus L. Si militem, C. de condictione ob causam datorum ajunt: Si militem ad negotium tuum procuratorem fecisti, cum hoc legi- bus interdictum sit. Vide & legem Honnorii & Arcadii : Nemo miles, dicto titulo Codicis de re militari. Eodem ten- dit titulus Codicis : Negotiatores ne militent : in re simili, lex ultima C. de Fabricensibus. Cassiodorus II. 31. Publi- cis debent insudare, qui nomen dedere militiæ. Verbum ἐμ- πλέκεται habetur in Græco Prov. XXVIII. 18. Sic ἐμπλα- κεὶς πόνοις apud Platonem, occupationibus implicatus est apud Ciceronem. Idem negotiis implicari dixit non uno loco.

Ἵνα τῷ στρατολογήσαντι ἀρέσῃ) ut ei placeat qui delectum fecit, id est, imperatori, qui מפקד צבא Es. XIII. v. 4. In Glossario στρατολογία delectus. In Latino legimus ut ei pla- ceat, cui se probavit : Sed scripserit interpres qui se probavit. Nam & literæ ea de re probatoriæ in Codice.

Persistens in Metaphora, monente Theodoreto, ex ea parat utilitatem : Qui vitam militarem am- plectuntur, sunt à mercimoniorum studiis separa- ti, solius autem militaris disciplinæ curam gerunt. Theophylactus: Ad universos, inquit, hæc verba ha- bentur Episcopos & Præceptores. Cum vero impli- cat inquit, magis rem patefacit: Certe enim vitæ hujus negotia compedum loco sunt. Negotia vero cum dicit, varias animi perturbationes molestiasque designat, ab hisque ut declinemus hortatur: perinde ac si dicat : Quid te molestioribus rebus & negotiis implicas ? Militiæ duntaxat vaca, hoc pacto Christo morem gesseris, qui te ad id militiæ munus elegit. De eo commonefacere debuerat Grotius Papales Episcopos, qui variis secularibus sese immiscent, ac Politici simul, imo milites seculares sunt; quo de vid. Dn. D. Ziegleri nostri σιδηρέξυλον Ecclesia- sticum : Episcopus miles. Unde Claud. Espensæus ingenue est fassus in digress. 2. in cap. I. ad Titum juxta hoc postulatum nullos habituram Galliam Episcopos, vel Presbyteros, cum secularibus ne- gotiis isti sint immersi. Nicolaus I. certo ad Im- perat. Michaelem anno 858. quod citatur C. Cum ad verum Dist. XCVI. & C. Quoniam Dist. X. sub nomine Cypriani ex hoc dicto probat, offi- cia utriusque potestatis actibus propriis, ac digni- tatibus distinctis discreta esse, quod etiam in Syn- odo Macrensi anno 881. repetitum. Confer. & C. Placuit. Caus. XXI. quæst. 3. Et notentur hæc et- iam contra Pontificios, qui secularem potestatem sibi arrogant. Claud. Espensæus in h. l. laudat & Ambrosii in h. l. sententiam: Ecclesiasticus autem idcirco se præstet Deo, ut huic devotus officium im- pleat, quod spopondit in DEI rebus solicitus, à secu- lari negotio alienus. Non enim convenit unum ha- bere duplicem professionem. Dicta quidem sunt, in- quit Chrysostomus, ista ad Timotheum, dicuntur antem per illum quoque Magistris omnibus, atque discipulis. Nullus ergo Episcopatu præditus hæc audire detrectet, sed agere ea plane detrectet. Ob- vertit quidem Estius excusationis gratia necessita- tem, quod & à Bellarmino l. V. de R. P. c. 9. factum. Sed quæ necessitas excusare potest id, quod lege divina prohibitum ? & ô miseram religionem, quæ non nisi seculari potestate ac brachio huma- no Episcoporum nititur. Recte autem notat Estius Vulgatam, quæ habet: Nemo militans Deo: Vo- cula DEO non solum à Græcis & Syris Codicib. abest, verum, nec in omnibus est Latinis, nec omnino huc pertinet: quemadmodum post alios docte annotavit Rob. Bellarm. l. 5. de Rom. Pont. cap. ult. Et quam- vis apud Ambrosianum, Pelagium, Primassium & Sedulium in textu scripto reperiatur, ex ipsorum tamen commentariis satis apparet, ab iis agnitam non fuisse. Nam similitudo hic est: Si miles pro- pter terrenum salarium omnia tolerat, & omnia negotia, quæ à militia ipsum impedire possint, à se rejicit, quanto magis spirituali militi id incum- bit? Inepte autem hoc dicto abutuntur Bellar- minus, & Torrensis ad interdictum conjugii sacer- dotalis. Nam conjugium non est ejusmodi secu- lare negotium, quod militiam vel corporalem vel spiritualem impediat, imo ejus essentiam in ratione Sacramenti collocare non dubitat Bel- larmin. de Sacr. matr. cap. II. & XXXII. Nec prohibentur omnia secularia negotia, sed dun- taxat solicita in secularia negotia immersio, quod è verbo ἐμπλέκεσθαι Thomas, Erasmus Cl. Espensæus, & Justin. docent; & Salmerone observante, videtur Apostolus notare quos- dam sui seculi Doctores, & Episcopos, qui suis commodis serviebant, & secularibus negotiis hu- jus mundi per superbiam, vel avaritiam, vel car- nem se implicabant & occupationibus sui muneris non vacabant. Quid quod Corn. à Lapide & E- stius, ut & Bellarminus ipse lib. V. de R. P. c. ult. hæc dici velint tam Episcopo, quam aliis homi- nibus, siquidem omnes laici milites Christi esse debeant. Num ergo omnibus hominibus con- jugium interdictum? Non immerito itaque in Bellarmino hîc notatur spiritus vertiginis, qui ut jure conjugii Episcopos spoliet, sensum hujus dicti ad solos Episcopos restringit: Cum vero nos illud Episcoporum seculari potestati oppona- mus, Bellarminus respondet: Dicuntur hæc à Paulo tam Episcopo, quam aliis hominibus.

## 2:5
Verse 5.

If anyone also competes as an athlete, he is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules) A second comparison taken from public contests; for there are also gymnastic laws, of which Aristotle makes mention at the end of the Nicomachean Ethics. A frequent comparison of the σπουδαῖος (earnest man) and the ἀθλητής (athlete) is found among the philosophers. Andronicus, or whoever is the best paraphrast of the Nicomachean Ethics: X, 11. 'In the same way, it is necessary for the athlete of virtue not only to love these words, from which it is possible to learn what each thing is, but also to teach how it might be possible to accomplish this, thinking that in this way one would truly become a teacher of virtue. For it is fitting for the trainer to arrange his words toward the perfection of the one being trained; and the perfection of the athlete of virtue would be for him to become good himself, and a practitioner of noble things.' Marcus Tyrius, Diatriba XXXII. For at the Olympics it is not possible to receive an olive wreath, nor to obtain an apple, if they are lying there by themselves, but there must be an opponent for the proclamation; but in the stadium of life and the struggle here, who could be an opponent to a good man, except the experience of difficulties? See, if you have leisure, the following as well. Hierocles: 'For first, athletes do not receive a crown by competing, but by having competed and won.'

It is not enough, he says, with Chrysostom as interpreter, if anyone merely descends into the contest, if he only anoints himself or merely engages, but unless he has kept the law of the contest in all things—so that he is sober, grave, and constant—and observes absolutely everything that is appropriate for those competing, he will never be crowned. And observe, I pray, the wisdom of Paul; he makes mention of the contest and of soldiers, partly to persuade them to be prompt and eager for slaughter, blood, and death for the sake of the faith, and partly to exhort them to endure all things constantly and bravely, and to be always in training. The athletic art also has, says Theodoret, certain laws according to which athletes must compete; but he who wrestles contrary to them does not attain the crowns. Augustine, ad fratr. in erem. serm. 8. No one fights rightly except he who perseveres in the place of battle until the end. Prosper Aquitanicus, Epigramm. 30. vers. 7. For to him who does not compete, a crown is not to be hoped for.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Ἐὰν δὲ καὶ ἀθλῇ τις, μὴ στεφανοῦται, ἐὰν μὴ νομίμως ἀθλήσῃ) Altera similitudo à publicis certaminibus desumpta, sunt enim & gymnicæ leges, quarum meminit Aristoteles fine Nicomachiorum. Frequens autem comparatio σπουδαίου & ἀθλητοῦ apud Philosophos. Andronicus aut quisquis est Nicomachiorum optimus Paraphrastes: X, 11. Τὸν ἶσον δὴ τρόπον καὶ τὸν τῆς ἀρετῆς ἀθλητὴν ἀνάγκη μὴ τύτοις μόνον ἀγαπᾷν τοῖς λόγοις, ὅθεν ἔνι μαθεῖν ἕκαστα τί ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅπως γένοιτο κατορθῶσαι τοῦτο διδάσκειν, οἰόμενον ὕτως ἂν ἀληθῶς γενέσθαι διδάσκαλον ἀρετῆς. πρὸς γὰρ τὴν τελείω- σιν τοῦ γυμναζομένου τὸν παιδευτὴν προσήκει τάττειν τοὺς λόγους· τελείωσις δ' ἂν εἴη τοῦ τῆς ἀρετῆς ἀθλητοῦ, τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἀυτὸν γενέ- σθαι, καὶ πρακτικὸν τῶν καλῶν. Marcus Tyrius Diatriba XXXII.
