Ὀλυμπιάσι μὲν γὰρ ἔνεστι οὐκ ὄντσι κότινον λαβεῖν, ὀὐδὲ μῆλον τυχεῖν ἀυτὸν, ἐφ' ἑαυτοῦ κεισαμένους, ἀλλ' ἀντα- γωνιστὴν δεῖ τῷ κηρύγματι· ἐν δὲ τῷ βίω σταδίω καὶ τῇ δεῦρο ἀγωνίᾳ, τίς ἂν γένοιτο ἀνταγωνιστὴς αἱρεῖ ἀγαθῷ, πλὴν τῆς πεί- ρας τῶν δυσχερῶν. Vide, si vacat, & sequentia. Hierocles: πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ ἀθληταὶ στέφανον ἐκ ἀγωνιζόμενοι ὀὐ λαμβάνουσιν, ἀλλ' ἀγωνισάμενοι καὶ νικήσαντες.

Non sufficit inquit, Chrysostomo interprete, si quis in certamen tantummodo descendat, si so- lummodo ungatur, aut congrediatur tantum, sed nisi per omnia certaminis servaverit legem, ut sobrius, gravis, constansque sit, omnia prorsus ob- servet, quæ certantibus congruunt, nunquam co- ronabitur. Et intuere quæso sapientiam Pauli, certaminis atque militantium mentionem facit, partim ut promptos atque alacres ad cædes, san- guinem ac mortem suaderet fidei, partim ut con- stanter & fortiter omnia perferre hortaretur, ac semper in exercitatione esse. Habet etiam ars ath- letica, inquit Theodoretus, leges quasdam, ex qui- bus oportet Athletas decertare, qui autem præter eas luctatur, coronas non assequitur. Augustinus ad fratr. in erem. serm. 8. Nemo recte pugnat, nisi qui in loco pugnæ ad finem usque perseverat. Pro- sper Aquitanicus Epigramm. 30. vers. 7. Nam non certanti non est speranda corona.

## 2:6
v. 6. The laboring farmer must be the first to partake of the fruits) 'First' here signifies 'only then.' A third comparison is added. If a farmer has labored, only then will it be right for him to eat of the fruits. A similar comparison is in 1 Cor. IX. verse 10. But there it is shown what is owed to the worker: here, what is required so that one may rightly feed himself from the fruits. There is no doubt that Paul had reasons for saying these things: for it is also added

Latin:

v. 6. Τὸν κοπιῶντα γεωργὸν δεῖ πρῶτον τῶν καρπῶν μετα- λαμβάνειν) πρῶτον hîc significat, ita demum. Tertia simi- litudo attexitur. Agricola si laboraverit, ita demum par erit eum de fructibus vesci. Par similitudo 1. Cor. IX. vers. 10. Sed ibi ostenditur, quid operanti debeatur: hic quid exigatur, ut quis de fructibus se jure pascat. Non dubium est, quin causas habuerit, cur haec diceret Pau- lus: nam & additur

## 2:7
Verse 7.

Understand what I say) A similar admonition in Mark XIII. v. 14. Understand (הבן or בין) Dan. IX. v. 23. Pay attention to the words.

For may the Lord give you understanding in all things) In such great matters, there is need not only of attention but also of divine illumination, which we ought to pray for both for ourselves and for others. Dan. II. verse 21. As if to say: you already understand many things, but not all. There is that in which you still need greater light. A similar prayer in Coloss. I. verse 9. But in the Manuscript it is δώσει (will give), as if wishing well. In which way the Syriac also seems to have read it: although with him the future can be taken as a precative, according to the custom of the people.

Although Chrysostom also explains it concerning the sustenance of the ministers of the word, the scope of the Apostle nevertheless teaches that he is animating Timothy with an excellent hope—namely, of glory in heaven and of rewards—for the sake of labors and evils to be endured for the office; indeed, also with the hope of the gain of souls, as Theophylact notes, observing with Chrysostom that this third Simile is proper to teachers: for the things he said about the soldier and the competitors are also appropriate for subjects and for men of another's jurisdiction. But the farmer studies nothing for himself, but intends to cultivate the land. Whence he also receives a not mediocre return of benefit, on account of the abundance of fruits. Thus also the teacher does not labor in vain, but he himself enjoys his own labors above others, with GOD abundantly rendering him a return. Let no one, therefore, take this delay of future reward heavily; you are already, he says, receiving this. For there is a recompense even in the labor itself. But if no other utility were to come of it, the progress of souls from your industry and labor will nevertheless bring you great profit. He adds: Understand what I say. Since (Theophylact continues) he had brought forward everything in the manner of riddles, whether concerning the soldier, or the athlete and the farmer, he says, understand. For I have explained these things in this way for this reason, that I might sharpen and stir you up. Finally, he prays well for his own son. May the Lord give you understanding in all things, not only in these things which I have said, but in all things, namely in words and actions.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Νόει ἃ λέγω) Similis admonitio Marc. XIII. v. 14. Νόει הבן vel בין Dan. IX. v. 23. Attende dictis.

Δῴη γάρ σοι Κύριος σύνεσιν ἐν πᾶσιν) In rebus tantis, non tantum attentione, sed & illuminatione divina opus est, quam & nobis ipsis, & aliis precari debemus. Dan. II. vers. 21. quasi dicat, multa jam intelligis: Sed non omnia. Est in quo adhuc luce majore indigeas. Similis precatio Coloss. I. vers. 9. At in Manuscripto est δώσει, quasi be- ne ominantis. Quomodo & Syrus videtur legisse: quan- quam potest apud eum futurum pro precativo accipi, mo- re gentis.

Quanquam & Chrysostomus explicet de su- stentatione ministrorum verbi, scopus tamen Apostoli docet, Timotheum spe eximia nempe gloriae in caelis ac praemiorum ad labores & mala officii causa toleranda animare, imo & spe lucri animarum, ut Theophylactus notat, cum Chry- sostomo observans tertium hoc Simile proprium esse doctoribus: Nam quae de milite dixit, & certatoribus, vel subditis competunt, & alieni juris hominibus. Agricola vero nil sibi studet, sed terrae excolendae intendit. Unde & beneficii vi- cissitudinem recipit non mediocrem, ob fructuum copiam. Sic & praeceptor non incassum laborat, quin ipse prae caeteris propriis sudoribus perfruatur, DEO hubertim illi vicem reddente. Nemo itaque hanc futurae mercedis tarditatem graviter tulerit, jam, inquit, hanc capis. Inest namque vel in ipso labore & retributio. Quod si aliud nihil obventu- rum esset utilitatis, animarum tamen ex tua indu- stria & labore profectus, magnum tibi allaturus est lucrum. Addit: Intellige quae dico. Cum in aenigmatis modum (pergit Theophylactus) omnia sive de milite, sive de certatore & agricola protu- lisset, intellige inquit. Haec enim ideo sic explicavi, ut te acuam concitemque. Demum ut proprio filio bene precatur. Det autem tibi Dominus intelle- ctum in omnibus, non in his solum quae dixi, sed in omnibus, in verbis scilicet & actionibus.

## 2:8
Vers. 8.

Μνημόνευε Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐγηγερμένον ἐκ νεκρῶν) Do not be surprised even if something rather grievous happens to me. Christ also died an ignominious death. But he was raised by GOD to a glorious life. The same will happen to me, and to you, if, terrified by nothing in adversity, you persist in faith and profession.

Ἐκ σπέρματος Δαβίδ) Thus also Romans 1, verse 3. This is not placed here in vain. For if David, destined for the kingdom, endured such great evils, if Jesus endured greater ones, in whom all those promises made to the posterity of David had their most perfect fulfillment, why should you be surprised if such things happen to us? See Acts 13:23.

This also seems to have been added on account of those who attacked the genealogy of Christ, as if he were not sprung from the tribe of Judah and the family of David, and also on account of those who attributed to him a celestial body or a phantastical flesh, as Theophylact notes, or were about to attribute it: and especially on account of those who contend that Christ rose again not in the same, but in a different body, as regards substance. To which pertains what Epiphanius observes, that the Gnostics are also refuted here, who said that flesh perishes and does not rise again. And the remembrance of Christ's resurrection from the dead was to be cherished not only for the sake of comfort, but also for the sake of doctrine, because it is the foundation, as the Apostle teaches in 1 Cor. 15, of our own resurrection from the dead, which some at that time were calling into doubt: and it is the chief head of Christian doctrine, which was to be handed down in the Church,

1. Cor. XV. verses 1, 2, 3. And therefore it seemed that it should be commended to Timothy, as a Doctor of the Church, above all else, which Chrysostom observes was necessary at that time even because of heretics. For thus had some then begun to overturn the mystery of the divine dispensation, considering the magnitude of the divine goodness a cause for shame (ἐπαισχυνόμενοι τῷ μεγέθει τῆς τῦ Θεῦ Φιλανθρωπίας). For GOD conferred such benefits upon us that men were ashamed to attribute them to GOD, and did not believe that He had descended to our weaknesses. Theodoret commemorates Simon, who at that time had begun to sow heretical thorns. For he, and all who descended from him, denied the assumption of flesh, and said that the taking up of human nature was done by a vision. For which cause the divine Apostle, the divine nature being for the present passed over, wrote to him concerning the economy of the incarnation alone, commanding that he should always remember the generation from the seed of David according to the flesh, and the resurrection from the dead; but he set forth both, the generation and the passion, and indeed he even added the lineage, since the enemies of truth openly denied all these things.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Μνημόνευε Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐγηγερμένον ἐκ νεκρῶν) Ne mira- re etiam, si quid mihi gravius eveniat. Mortuus est etiam Christus morte ignominiosa. Sed à DEO ad vitam glorio- sam resuscitatus est. Idem & mihi eveniet, & tibi, si ad- versis nihil territus in fide & professione perstiteris.

Ἐκ σπέρματος Δαβίδ) Sic & Roman. I. vers. 3. Non frustra autem istud hoc loco positum est. Nam si David regno destinatus tanta mala pertulit, si Jesus majora, in quo omnia illa promissa Davidis posteritati facta perfe- ctissimum habebant implementum, quid mirere, si nobis talia eveniant? Vide Act. XIII. 23.

Additum etiam hoc videtur ob eos, qui Christi genealogiam impugnabant, quasi non esset ex tri- bu Juda, & familia Davidis oriundus, nec non ob illos, qui corpus coeleste aut carnem phan- tasticam ipsi tribuebant, ut Theophylactus notat, vel tributuri erant: & imprimis ob eos, qui non eodem, sed diverso corpore, quod ad substan- tiam resurrexisse Christum contendunt. Quo facit, quod Epiphanius observat, Gnosticos etiam hic confutari, qui carnem dixerint perire, non resurgere. Neque tantum solatii, sed & doctrinae causa memoria erat fovenda Christi è mortuis resuscitatio, quia fundamentum illa est, docente Apostolo, 1. Cor. XV. nostrae è mortuis resuscita- tionis, quam tum temporis in dubium nonnulli revocabant: & praecipuum doctrinae Christia- nae caput, quod in Ecclesia tradendum erat,

1. Cor. XV. vers. 1. 2. 3. ideoque Timotheo ceu Ecclesiæ Doctori imprimis commendandum vi- debatur, quod isto tempore etiam ob hæreticos necessarium fuisse observat Chrysostomus. Ita enim tunc cœperant quidam mysterium divinæ dispen- sationis evertere, magnitudinem divinæ bonitatis pudori ducentes (ἐπαισχυνόμενοι τῷ μεγέθει τῆς τῦ Θεῦ Φιλανθρωπίας) Talia quippe in nos benefi- cia contulit DEUS, ut ea homines DEO appli- care erubescerent, neque illum ad infirma nostra descendisse crederent. Theodor. Simonem commemorat, qui tum temporis cœperit semi- nare spinas hæreticas. Is enim, & omnes qui ex eo descenderunt, negarunt carnis assumptionem, & di- cebant visione factam esse naturæ humanæ susceptio- nem. Quà de causa divinus Apostolus, divina natura in præsentia prætermissa, scripsit ad eum de sola incarnationis œconomia, jubens, ut semper me- minisset generationis ex semine David secundum carnem, & resurrectionis ex mortuis, utraque autem posuit, generationem, & passionem, quin etiam genus adjecit, quoniam hæc omnia aperte negabant veritatis inimici.

## 2:9
Verse 9.

(Κατὰ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιόν μυ) Just as I have announced and do announce the commands of Christ to all. A similar locution is in Romans II. v. 16, XVI. v. 25, which is explained thus: τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον τὸ ἐυαγγελισθὲν ὑπ᾽ ἐμῦ, Galatians I. verse 11; thus also the Apostle says 'our Gospel', associating his helpers with himself, 1 Thessalonians I. verse 5, 2 Thessalonians II. 14.

The Gospel is not the commands of Christ, but the proclamation of the grace exhibited in Christ, who was delivered up for our sins and raised for our justification, Romans IV. 25. This Gospel, of which the Apostle speaks at present, some among Jerome understand as the Gospel of Luke, which had been dictated by Paul, but Paul speaks of the Gospel preached by himself, to which, according to Chrysostom, he refers Timothy, because there were also those who preached other gospels, whom he notes and reproves in another place, Galatians I. 8.

(Ἐν ᾧ κακοπαθῶ) ἐν ᾧ here is in the Hebrew manner, 'on account of which'. κακοπαθῶ: I bear many evils, and I bear them with an even mind. For we have also said above that this is present in this verb in these places.

(Μέχρι δεσμῶν) It is a heavy thing for free men to be bound. He shows that what he was suffering was not light. See above 8.

(Ὢς κακῦργος) For against such people handcuffs and fetters were invented. Thus also Christ is equated with evildoers in his punishment, Luke XXIII. 32, 33, 39.

That word κακῦργος will scarcely admit of this. For Christian patience does not suit them so well. Therefore Theophylact speaks simply. Again, he consoles his disciple from his own example, when he says that he is being worn out and suffering evil, just as if he had committed some crime. Moreover, in the verb κακοπαθῶ ὡς κακῦργος there is an elegant paronomasia: I suffer evil as an evildoer. But he adds that he sustains persecutions for the sake of the Gospel, so that he may confirm the truth of the Gospel. For no prudent person would wish to risk his reputation and life for a doubtful and uncertain matter.

(Ἀλλὰ ὁ λόγος τῦ Θεῦ ὐ δέδεται) I speak with the same freedom as if I were not bound. The mind is not bound, and it still uses the tongue. If I do this while bound, how much more ought you to do this while free?

There is here both a paronomasia and an antanaklasis in the words δεσμῶν and δέδεται: chains have indeed been cast upon me, but the word is not bound. Compare Isaiah LV. verses 10, 11; Philippians I. verse 12. For if, he says (with Chrysostom as interpreter), we were soldiers of the world, if we were fighting carnal wars, chains that bound our hands would have some strength. But then he did not make us such that nothing can cast us down. The hands are bound, but the tongue remains free, which no one can bind except fear alone and infidelity. As long as that is absent, no matter how many chains one may cast, the voice of preaching is not bound. And further: It is indeed most full of miracles that he who is bound performs the duty of the free, bound he conquers all, bound he overcomes those who bound him. For the word of GOD is not ours. Furthermore, human bonds cannot bind the word of God. The word is truly a divine thing (says Theophylact in his paraphrase of this passage); for us who are bound, it is released and free; and it runs everywhere. Behold, even though we ourselves are constrained by chains, we nevertheless perform the duty of writing and preaching. See therefore the miracle, note what profit emanates from it.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Κατὰ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιόν μυ) Sicut ego Christi mandata o- mnibus annunciavi, & annuncio. Par locutio Roman. II. v. 16. XVI. v. 25. quod explicatur sic, τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον τὸ ἐυ- αγγελισθὲν ὑπ᾽ ἐμῦ, Gal. I. vers. 11. sic & Εὐαγγέλιον ἡμῶν di- cit Apostolus, adjutores suos secum socians, 1. Thess. I. vers. 5. 2. Thess. II. 14.

Evangelium non sunt Christi mandata, sed præ- conium gratiæ in Christo exhibitæ, qui propter peccata nostra traditus est, & propter justitiam nostram resuscitatus, Rom. IV. 25. Hoc Evan- gelium, de quo in præsenti Apostolus, nonnulli apud Hieronymum de Evangelio Lucæ, quod à Paulo dictatum fuerit, intelligunt, sed Paulus de Evangelio à se prædicato loquitur, ad quod se- cundum Chrysostomum remittit Timotheum, quia fuerint etiam qui alia evangelizarent, quos alio in lo- co notet & reprobet, Gal. I. 8.

Ἐν ᾧ κακοπαθῶ) ἐν ᾧ hic more Ebræo est cujus causa. κα- ποπαθῶ multa mala fero, & æquo animo fero. Nam & hoc huic verbo his locis inesse etiam supra diximus.

Μέχρι δεσμῶν) Grave vinciri hominibus liberis. Often- dit non levia esse, quæ patiebatur. Vide supra 8.

Ὢς κακῦργος) Nam adversus tales inventæ manicæ & compedes. Sic & Christus κακύργοις æquatur in supplicio, Luc. XXIII. 32. 33. 39.

Id verbum κακῦργος vix admittet. Illis enim patientia Christiana non adeo convenit. Ideo simpliciter Theophylactus. Rursus ex sui ipsius ex- emplo discipulum consolatur, cum defatigari se di- cit, & male pati, perinde ac si aliquid commisisset. Cæterum in verbo κακοπαθῶ ὡς κακῦργος est e- legans παρονομασία, mala patior ut maleficus. Id- eo autem addit, se Evangelii causa persecutiones sustinere, ut veritatem Evangelii, confirmet. Ne- mo enim prudens ob rem dubiam & incertam fa- mæ & vitæ periculum velit adire.

Ἀλλὰ ὁ λόγος τῦ Θεῦ ὐ δέδεται) Loquor eadem liber- tate, quasi vinctus non essem. Animus vinctus non est, is- que lingua adhuc utitur. Si ego hoc facio vinctus, quan- to magis tu hoc facere debes solutus?

Est hic & paronomasia, & ἀντανάκλασις, in verbis δεσμῶν & δέδεται: mihi quidem injecta sunt vincula, sed verbum vinctum non est. Conf. Es. LV. vers. 10. 11. Phil. I. vers. 12. Nam si qui- dem inquit, (Chrysostomo interprete) sæculi milites essemus, si bella carnalia bellaremus, habe- rent aliquid virium vincula, quæ manus obligas- sent nostras. At tunc tales non fecit, ut nihil nos dejicere possit. Vinciuntur manus, sed manet lin- gua libera, quam nemo ligare possit, nisi formido sola, atque infidelitas. Quandiu ea abest, quan- talibet quis injiciat vincula, prædicationis vox alligata non est. Et porro: Est quippe mira- culis plenissimum, quod is, qui vinctus est, so- lutorum exercet munus, vinctus omnia vincit, vin- ctus eos, qui se vinxerant, superat. Verbum quippe DEI, non nostrum est. Porro humani nexus Dei verbum ligare non possunt. Res sane divina est ser- mo (inquit in paraphrasi hujus loci Theophylactus) nobis ligatis solutum est illud & liberum; per- curritque passim. Ecce etsi ipsi adstringimur vincu- lis, scribendi tamen & prædicandi fungimur mu- nere. Vide ergo miraculum, adverte quod inde lu- crum emanet.

## 2:10
Verse 10.

Διὰ τοῦτο) for this very Gospel. Πάντα ὑπομένω) And these evils, and many others, I bear patiently. ὑπομένω יכלתי. See also below 12. Hebr. XII. 2. 3. Jas. V. 11. 1. Pet. II. 20.

Διὰ τοὺς ἐκλεκτοὺς) For the good of the Christians, who are confirmed in the faith by my example, and are encouraged to a like endurance. Concerning the word ἐκλεκτῶν see what was said at Matt. XXIV. 22.

Ἵνα καὶ αὐτοὶ σωτηρίας τύχωσι τῆς ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ μετὰ δόξης αἰωνίε) that they too, by walking in the same footsteps, may arrive at salvation and eternal glory, Christ granting it. See above I.

Paul says, therefore, that he endures afflictions for the sake of the elect, not that he might make satisfaction for them, but because he endeavored to promote their salvation by the preaching of the Gospel; which was the procatarctic cause why the infidels persecuted him; and he offered himself to them as an example of patience and constancy, so that they might be confirmed in the faith, which is the final cause of the affliction patiently endured. Moreover, that salvation is called 'in Christ,' not only because salvation is conferred on account of Christ as the meritorious cause, but also because we are saved in Christ, as being the one in whom we are justified; the Vulgate rendered μετὰ δόξης αἰωνίε as 'with heavenly glory.' The Syriac more correctly as 'with eternal glory.' This qualification, however, as Blessed Gerhard notes, is to be referred to the word 'salvation': that they may obtain salvation, joined with eternal happiness and glory, of which they will be partakers in Christ, through Christ, and with Christ. He says (according to Theophylact) not only that they may be saved, but what is more excellent, that they may claim glory with us forever. Whence, even though these bonds seem ignominious, they nevertheless provide glory to those who are elect, and that indeed heavenly and everlasting. If, therefore, they produce glory for others, much more so for me, who am led and bound for their sake. Let no care for me, therefore, vex you because I am afflicted with evils. Which, however, is not to be understood as if the sufferings of the ministers of the Church were either merits or means of salvation, but that salvation is certainly obtained if they persevere in the faith, as is evident from verse 11. They are the way to the kingdom, not the cause of reigning. For eternal life is a grace in Christ Jesus. Romans VI. verse 23. They are testimonies of heavenly doctrine, by which the pious are confirmed in the faith; they are examples of the constancy of faith, which others imitate, to obtain salvation and glory with them through faith.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Διὰ τοῦτο) ob hoc ipsum Evangelium. Πάντα ὑπομένω) Et hæc mala, & multa alia patienter fero. ὑπομένω יכלתי. Vide & infra 12. Hebr. XII. 2. 3. Jac. V. 11. 1. Petr. II. 20.

Διὰ τοὺς ἐκλεκτοὺς) Bono Christianorum, qui meo exem- plo confirmantur in fide, & ad parem sufferentiam animan- tur. De voce ἐκλεκτῶν vide quæ dicta ad Matth. XXIV. 22.

Ἵνα καὶ αὐτοὶ σωτηρίας τύχωσι τῆς ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ μετὰ δόξης αἰωνίε) ut ipsi quoque per eadem incedendo vestigia per- veniant ad salutem gloriamque æternam, dante Christo. Vide supra I.

Propter electos ergo sustinere sese afflictiones ait Paulus, non ut pro iis satisfaciat, sed quia præ- dicatione Evangelii salutem ipsorum promovere conatus est; quæ causa erat προκαταρκτικὴ, cur ipsum persequerentur infideles; iisque se patien- tiæ ac constantiæ exemplum, ut in fide confirmen- tur, præbuit, quæ causa est τελικὴ afflictionis patienter toleratæ. Cæterum quod σωτηρία dici- tur ἡ ἐν χριστῷ, non tantum quod propter Chri- stum, ceu causam meritoriam, salus conferatur, sed etiam, quod in Christo salvemur, utpote in quo unice justificamur, μετὰ δόξης αἰωνίε Vulgata reddidit cum gloria cælesti. Rectius Syrus cum gloria æterna. Referendus autem hic προσδιορισμὸς, notante Beat. Gerhardo, ad vocem σωτηρίας: ut salutem consequantur, conjunctam cum æterna felicitate & gloria, cujus in Christo, per Chri- stum & cum Christo erunt participes. Non solum inquit (juxta Theophylactum) ut salvi fiant, sed quod præstantius est, ut nobiscum perpetuo & glo- riam vendicent. Unde etsi ignominiosa videntur hæc vincula, gloriam tamen his, qui electi sunt, subministrant, & eam quidem cælestem & sempi- ternam. Si itaque cæteris gloriam pariunt, longe magis & mihi, qui illis obducor, constringorque. Nulla ergo te mei cura divexet, quia malis af- flictor. Quæ tamen non ita intelligenda, quasi ministrorum Ecclesiæ passiones vel merita, vel media sint salutis, sed quod certo consequatur salus, si in fide perseverent ut è v. 11. constat. Sunt via regni, non causa regnandi. Vita enim æterna χάρισμα est in Christo Jesu. Roman. VI. vers. 23. testimonia sunt doctrinæ cælestis, quibus pii in fide confirmantur, sunt exempla constantiæ fidei, quæ alii imitantur, per fidem cum ipsis salu- tem & gloriam consequuturi.

## 2:11
Verse 11.

Πιστὸς ὁ λόγος) Namely that which follows. For he is accustomed to preface these words before an excellent sentiment. See 1 Tim. I. 15. III. 1. IV. 7.

Εἰ γὰρ συναπεθάνομεν) γὰρ is placed here for אכן, certainly. Isaiah XLV. 1. To die here means to undergo supreme miseries and dangers of death. A similar expression is in 2 Cor. IV. verse 10, where see what is said.

Καὶ συζήσομεν) We shall live with Him that immortal life.

Not only by reason of the soul, but also by reason of the body, in which we sustain various sufferings, to be resurrected one day to life. To die with Christ, although some may refer it to the spiritual and salutary death, by which we die to sin, Romans VI, verse 1: it is clear, however, from the context, that the discourse here is about the afflictions and death which are sustained with Christ. Compare 2 Corinthians IV, verses 10, 11. What kind of assertion is that of Paul? Certainly, as he says, if we are his companions in harsher and sadder things, but by no means in good and joyful ones, not even a mortal would do this, how much less God, who is the fountain of justice and goodness, says Theophylact. Therefore, it is not fitting that he explains the same word 'died with' regarding Baptism (however much that may have pleased Theodoret). He says, he calls that death which is undergone both through Baptism and through many sufferings and temptations. How can such disparate meanings have a place at the same time? But that the discourse is about bodily death is clear from what follows: If we endure, we shall also reign with him; which he interprets thus: For it is not enough that one should offer himself to death once, but it is necessary that he should always do so. For he says, I die daily. There is need, therefore (he says), of patience, so that one may be able to escape with us, and to arrive at that point, that he may obtain that heavenly kingdom.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Πιστὸς ὁ λόγος) Nempe is, qui sequitur. Solet enim hæc verba præfari ante egregiam sententiam. Vide 1. Tim. I. 15. III. 1. IV. 7.

Εἰ γὰρ συναπεθάνομεν) γὰρ hic ponitur pro אכן certe. Esaiæ XLV. 1. Mori hic vocat miserias summas ac mor- tis pericula subire. Par locutio 2. Cor. IV. vers. 10. ubi dicta vide.

Καὶ συζήσομεν) Vivemus cum illo vitam illam immor- talem.

Non tantum ratione animæ, sed etiam ratione corporis, in quo passiones varias sustinemus, olim ad vitam resuscitandi. Commori cum Christo, etsi nonnulli ad mortem spiritualem & salutarem, qua peccato morimur, Roman. VI. vers. 1. referant: liquet tamen è contextu, de afflictionibus & morte, quæ cum Christo sustinentur, hîc ser- monem esse. Confer. 2. Corinth. IV. vers. 10. 11. Qualis est illa Pauli asseveratio? Certe ut dicat, si durioribus & mæstis in rebus illi socii sumus, in bonis vero & lætis nequaquam, nec mortalis qui- dem hoc quispiam egerit, quanto magis nec Deus, qui justitiæ & bonitatis fons est, inquit Theophy- lactus. Non ergo convenit, quod de Baptismo idem verbum commortui exponit (utut id etiam Theodoreto placuerit) Mortem, inquit, eam dicit, quæ cum per Baptismum, tum per passiones multas & tentationes subitur. Tam disparatæ si- gnificationes quomodo simul locum habeant? De morte autem corporali sermonem esse vel quæ è sequentibus patet: Si sustinemus, & con- regnabimus; quæ ita interpretatur: Neque enim sat est, ut semel quis morti se offerat, sed semper id agat necesse est. Inquit enim, quotidie morior. Est itaque (inquit) patientia opus, ut queat quis evadere nobiscum, & eo evadere, ut regnum cœle- ste illud adipiscatur.

## 2:12
Εἰ ὑπομένομεν.

See above 10. An accusative is understood here, for example σταυρὸν as in Hebrews XII, 2, or πειρασμὸν as in James I, 12.

Καὶ συμβασιλεύσομεν.

He made two opposites. For as he opposed life to death, so he opposed the kingdom to suffering, which he just called glory, that is, a state not only safe, but also exalted. See Romans V, verse 17. In the Martyrology we have: When Saint Nestor answered with great joy: with my Christ I was, and am, and shall be. Then the hardened Praetor passed sentence against him, that because he confessed Jesus Christ crucified under Pontius Pilate, as one devoted to his GOD, he should undergo his sentence and, being crucified on the wood, be released from life. He, giving thanks to GOD, when he was already fixed to the gibbet, was teaching the Christian people standing by, that they should persist in the faith and charity of Christ, and most willingly suffer with him, so that they might also be glorified together.

The Vulgate renders it, if we shall endure. But in the Greek text it is the present: which the Apostle's sense requires: If in this life we tolerate afflictions, insults, crosses, deaths with Christ, it will come to pass that we shall reign with him in heaven, Romans VIII, verse 17. Not only shall we reign with others, who still endure afflictions, but also with Christ, who already reigns.

Εἰ ἀρνούμεθα) Namely him: which is to be understood, as is clear from the opposite member, and from Matthew X, 33.

Κἀκεῖνος ἀρνήσεται ἡμᾶς.

He will not acknowledge us as his own, and therefore he will not admit us to the communion of his things. See the cited passage of Matthew.

Latin:

Εἰ ὑπομένομεν.

Vide supra 10. Subauditur hic accusativus, puta σταυ- ρὸν ut Ebr. XII. 2. aut πειρασμὸν ut Jac. I. 12.

Καὶ συμβασιλεύσομεν.

Duo fecit ἀντίθετα. Nam ut morti opposuit vitam, ita sufferentiæ regnum, quod modo dixit gloriam, id est, statum non tutum tantum, sed & excelsum. Vide Rom. V. vers. 17. in Martyrologio habemus: Cum sanctus Ne- stor cum magno gaudio respondis: cum Christo meo & eram, & sum, & ero. Tunc induratus Prætor dedit adversus eum sententiam, ut quia Jesum Christum crucifixum sub Pontio Pilato fateretur, tanquam devotus DEO suo, illius subiret sententiam & ligno crucifixus resolveretur à vita. Ille gratias agens DEO, cum jam affixus esset patibulo, docebat assisten- tem populum Christianum, ut persisterent in fide & charitate Christi, & libentissime compaterentur, ut & simul glorifica- rentur.

Vulgata reddit, si sustinebimus. Sed in textu Græco est præsens: quod requirit Apostoli sen- sus: Si in hac vita cum Christo toleramus affli- ctiones, contumelias, cruces, mortes, futurum est, ut cum ipso in cœlo regnemus, Rom. VIII. vers. 17. Non tantum cum aliis regnabimus, qui adhuc sustinent afflictiones, sed etiam cum Chri- sto, qui jam regnat.

Εἰ ἀρνούμεθα) Nempe ipsum: quod subintelligendum liquet ex membro opposito, & ex Matth. X. 33.

Κἀκεῖνος ἀρνήσεται ἡμᾶς.

Pro suis nos non agnoscet, ac proinde ad rerum sua- rum communionem nos non admittet. Vide dictum Mat- thæi locum.

## 2:13
Verse 13.

Εἰ ἀπιστοῦμεν) if we are unfaithful to him. Just as πιστὸς in these books sometimes signifies a believer, sometimes faithful, as Matt. XXIV. v. 45, XXV. v. 21, 23, Luke XII. v. 42, XVI. 10, 11, 12, XIX. 17, so also ἀπιστεῖν has a double meaning. But the opposition shows that the one we have stated is proper to this passage.

ἐκεῖνος πιστὸς μένει) Namely, no less in threats than in promises.

He cannot deny himself.

He cannot deny that he said what he said; there is a metonymy in ἑαυτὸν. For he named the speaker instead of the words of the speaker.

That 'if we are unfaithful,' therefore, is not to be restricted, with Chrysostom, to the resurrection of Christ, if we do not believe that Christ has risen: or, with others in Justinian, to the preceding, 'if we endure, we shall reign.' It is more general: If we are unfaithful in doctrine, life, persecution. Athanasius, orat. III, explained πιστὸς as ἀμετακίνητον (immovable): But although faithfulness follows from immutability, and he who is not faithful and true is not immutable, formally, however, these are different, and God is called faithful on account of constancy and truth in promises and threats, so that the sense is, if they do not keep faith with him, he nevertheless remains faithful. Cf. Rom. III. v. 3. He cannot deny himself, not because of impotence, but because of immutability and insuperable power, just as for that reason he can neither sin nor die. Therefore GOD is omnipotent, says Augustine, book 1 de Symbolo, chap. 1, because he cannot do these things. For if he could do these things, he would not be omnipotent. There is, therefore, great power in God, not to be able to lie. Anselm, book Cur DEUS homo, chap. 17: As often as GOD is said not to be able, no power is denied in him, but insuperable power and strength are signified. The commentary of the Greeks is more alien here: that of Theodoret, and what Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius have similar to it. For we do not make God himself believers, nor if we do not believe do we cast him out from the divine nature; but whether we believe or do not believe, he himself is GOD. For, as I said, it is not the immobility of GOD that is properly asserted here, but his veracity. But there is no need for a metonymy. For in truth he has denied himself if his words are not true: for thus he would not be immutable, nor even GOD himself: whose name is this: אהיה אשר אהיה Exod. III.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Εἰ ἀπιστοῦμεν) si nos in illum infidi sumus. Sicut πιστὸς in his libris modo credentem significat, modo fidelem, ut Matth. XXIV. vers. 45. XXV. vers. 21. 23. Luc. XII. v. 42. XVI. 10. 11. 12. XIX. 17. ita & ἀπιστεῖν duplicem habet si- gnificationem. Sed eam, quam diximus huic loco esse pro- priam ostendit oppositio.

ἐκεῖνος πιστὸς μένει) Nempe non minus in comminatio- nibus, quam in promissis.

Ἀρνήσασθαι ἑαυτὸν ὀ δύναται.

Non potest negare, se dixisse quæ dixit, est μετωνυμία in ἑαυτὸν. Nam loquentem nominavit pro verbis lo- quentis.

Illud ergo si infidi sumus, non restringendum cum Chrysostomo ad resurrectionem Christi, si non credimus Christum resurrexisse: aut cum aliis apud Justinianum ad præcedens, si sustinemus, re- gnabimus. Generalius est: Si infidi sumus in do- ctrina, vita, persecutione. πιστὸς Athanasius orat. III. exposuit ἀμετακίνητον: Sed quanquam fide- litas ex immutabilitate consequatur, nec immuta- bilis sit, 'qui fidelis & verax non est, formaliter tamen hæc diversa sunt, & fidelis dicitur Deus ob constantiam & veritatem in promissionibus & comminationibus, ut sensus sit, si fidem illi non servant, ille nihilominus fidelis manet. Conf. Rom. III. vers. 3. Seipsum abnegare non potest, non propter impotentiam, sed propter immutabilita- tem, & insuperabilem potentiam, quemadmodum ideo etiam nec peccare, nec mori potest. Ideo DEUS omnipotens est, inquit Augustinus libr. 1. de Symbolo cap. 1. quia ista non potest. Nam si posset ista, non esset omnipotens. Magna ergo in Deo potentia est, non posse mentiri. Anselmus lib. Cur DEUS homo, cap. 17. Quoties DEUS dici- tur non posse, nulla negatur in eo potestas, sed insu- perabilis significatur potentia & fortitudo. Alienior hic est Græcorum commentarius: Theodoreti, & quæ illi similia habent Chrysostom. Theophyl. Oe- cumen. Neque enim credentes ipsum Deum effi- cimus, nec si non credamus à divina natura ejici- mus; sed sive credamus, sive non credamus, ipse DEUS est. Nam, ut dixi, non immobilitas DEI proprie hic adstruitur, sed veracitas. Non autem opus est μετωνυμίᾳ. Nam revera seipsum negavit, si verba ejus vera non sunt: Sic enim non immutabilis ipse ac ne DEUS quidem esset: cujus hoc est nomen : אהיה אשר אהיה Ex- odi III.

## 2:14
Vers. 14.

Ταῦτα ὑπομίμνῃσκε) הזכיר; Bring this to the memory of those who hear.

Διαμαρτυρόμενος ἐνώπιον τοῦ Κυρίου) The same expression 1 Tim. V. v. 21.

Μὴ λογομαχεῖν) See 1 Tim. VI. 4.

Εἰς οὐδὲν χρήσιμον) Fighting about words has no use.

Ἐπὶ καταστροφῇ τῶν ἀκουόντων). For the hearers are split into factions by these contests: they lose mutual love. That, indeed, is in this business הפכה καταστροφὴ, subversion. In the Glossary: καταστροφὴ subversion, destruction. Timon: Who then brought these together to fight in deadly strife? The crowd, a companion of noise; for he, angered at those who are silent, stirred up a bad disease against the men.

Now, according to the blessed Gerhard, λογομαχεῖν is (1.) to contend odiously about words when the thing itself is agreed upon, (2.) to use a contentious and litigious method of disputing, (3.) to seek the praise of victory in disputing, not the truth. Augustine, book 4 of Christian Doctrine, chapter 28: To contend with words is not to care how error may be overcome by truth, but how your own speech may be preferred to the speech of another. The words εἰς οὐδὲν χρήσιμον seem to be included in a parenthesis: 'admonish them, that they contend not in words (which is to no profit) to the subverting of the hearers.' But even without a parenthesis they hold up correctly: 'that they contend not in words, it is to no profit, to the subverting of the hearers,' namely, it causes it: or as the Syrian has it, 'that they contend not with useless speeches, to the subverting of those who hear them.' The discourse rises: λογομαχίαι (logomachies) not only lack all fruit, but do much harm to the hearers, who are disturbed by those contentions and begin to doubt those things which they believed, by which process their faith is subverted and converted into skepticism. For not only, says Theophylact, does a contentious disputation of this kind profit nothing at all, nor will it bring any fruit, but rather will do much harm. For when the faith of the hearers is finally overturned by scrutinizing and searching, it is no different than how a tower is usually demolished by iron and levers.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Ταῦτα ὑπομίμνῃσκε) הזכיר; Hoc in memoriam reduc audientibus.

Διαμαρτυρόμενος ἐνώπιον τοῦ Κυρίου) Eadem locutio 1. Tim. V. v. 21.

Μὴ λογομαχεῖν) Vide 1. Tim. VI. 4.

Εἰς οὐδὲν χρήσιμον) Pugna de verbis nihil habet utile.

Ἐπὶ καταστροφῇ τῶν ἀκουόντων). Nam auditores per ista certamina scinduntur in partes: amittunt dilectionem mutuam. Id vero est in hoc negotio הפכה καταστροφὴ, everfio. In Glossario: καταστροφὴ subversio, excidium. Timon: Τίς δ' ἂρ τύσδ' ὀλοῇ ἔριδι ξυνέηκε μαχέσθαι; Ἠχοῦς σύνδρομος ὄχλος· ὁ γὰρ σιγῶσι χολαθὼς. Νῦσον ἐπ' ἀνέρας ὦρσε κακήν.

Est autem λογομαχεῖν juxta Beat. Gerhardum (1.) cum de re ipsa constat de verbis odiose contende- re, (2.) uti ratione disputandi contentiosa & liti- giosa, (3.) in disputando laudem victoriæ, non veri- tatem quærere. August. libr. 4. de doctr. Christ. cap. 28. Verbis contendere est non curare, quomodo error veritate convincatur; sed quomodo tua di- ctio dictioni præferatur alterius. Verba εἰς οὐδὲν χρήσιμον videntur parenthesi includenda: admo- ne illos, ne contendant verbis (quod ad nihil utile est) ad subversionem audientium. Sed sine παρεν- θέσει etiam recte se habent, ne contendant verbis, ad nihil utile est, ad subversionem audientium, scil. facit: vel ut Syrus, ne contendant sermonibus inutilibus, ad subversionem eorum, qui audiunt eos. Assurgit oratio: λογομαχίαι non solum carent omni fructu, sed multum nocent auditori- bus, qui contentionibus illis turbantur, ac dubi- tare incipiunt de iis, quæ credebant, qua ratio- ne ipsorum fides subvertitur, & in scepticismum convertitur. Non enim solum, inquit Theo- phylactus, nil prorsus proficit contentiosa hujusmodi disputatio, nec ullum allatura est fructum, quin plurimum est obfutura. Quippe cum audientium fides scrutando conquirendoque tandem evertitur, haud secus ac solet turris aliqua ferro & vectibus dirui.

## 2:15
Verse 15.

Σπούδασον σεαυτὸν δόκιμον παραστῆσαι τῷ Θεῷ) The Latin correctly translates παραστῆσαι as 'to present' (exhibere). Take δόκιμον as in Romans 16, verse 10; 1 Corinthians 11, verse 19; 2 Corinthians 10:18; James 1, verse 12. The sense is: make yourself approved to God. In the manuscript, it is παραστῆσαι τῷ χριστῷ.

Ἐργάτην ἀνεπαίσχυντον.

Doing those things of which one ought not to be ashamed. See Romans 6, verse 21.

Ὀρθοτομοῦντα τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας) A simile drawn from victims, which had to be cut according to a certain rite, as we showed regarding Leviticus. Moreover, the proclamation of the Gospel is also a sacrifice, and indeed an excellent one. With a slightly different translation, interpreters have called Proverbs 3, verse 6 and 11, verse 5 ὀρθοτομεῖν ὁδὸν, where in the Hebrew there is ישׁר, which is elsewhere translated as και τευθύνειν or κατορθοῦν, for we also say 'to cut a path.' But one 'rightly cuts' (ὀρθοτομεῖ) the Gospel who adapts to each person those admonitions which are most suitable to him: just as with victims, some parts were given to the priests, others to private individuals. In the Constitutions of Clement VII, verse 33: ὀρθοτομοῦντας ἐν τοῖς Κυρίου δόγμασιν. Philo on Cain and Abel: ὅτως ὁ τιμιώτερον τῷ χυσίῳ λόγον, ἐκ ποικιλμάτων καὶ μυρίων ἰδεῶν τελειουργητότα, ὅταν ἄχρι τῶν λεπτοτάτων κεφαλαίων τμηθεὶς τρόπον τινὰ τούματων δέξηται, καθάπερ ἡγεμὼν ἀποδείξεως ἐναργεστάτης.

Theodoret explains it with another metaphor: We praise farmers who plow straight furrows. So also the teacher is worthy of praise who follows the rule of the divine utterances. Others seek the metaphor from tanners, who cut away the superfluous parts from the skins they prepare for use, as Theophylact and Oecumenius did, following Chrysostom. Theophylact: Circumcise all useless things, and remove with the sword of the word those things that are alien to the preaching of the Gospel. Some, however (we do not deny), derive it from the Greek phrase τέμνειν ὁδὸν, to pave or open a way. That is to say, to open a straight path, as it were, of the word of truth, or to open the discourse of truth as a straight journey. But the explanation concerning the priests who dissected victims according to a certain rite is more suitable, which was also approved by Grotius: to which is similar the metaphor from the organizers of a banquet, or rather the distributors of food, which they carve, and the comparison from the head of a household distributing rations to children and servants as is fitting, Luke 12, verse 42. Compare 1 Corinthians 3, verse 1; Hebrews 5, verse 12. The Vulgate explains the matter itself well: 'rightly handling,' as if the meaning were transferred from species to genus, as Fuller notes in Miscellanea Sacra, book 3, chapter 16, because καινοτομεῖν according to the usage of the Greek language is to devise or undertake new things, and ὀρθοτομεῖν by the same reasoning is to approach or do things rightly; and the Syriac rendered it, 'rightly preaching the word'; referring here to the passages from Proverbs 3 and 11, in which ישׁר is rendered ὀρθοτομεῖν, to direct or to make straight. Add also the explanation of Theophylact: Even if many tear that word apart and translate it otherwise, you nevertheless handle it rightly yourself. More alien, however, is that conjecture of Fuller, that τμήματα denotes segments, which are called פסקים from פסק, to cut, whence the הפיסקים בתורה are called οἱ τέμνοντες τὸν νόμον, who cut the law, or were occupied in treating the law. Furthermore, those are said to 'rightly cut' or handle the word of truth in this place, not those who through διχοτομίαν (dichotomy) dissect everything into smaller parts—although even that, when it is done according to the sense of the Holy Spirit and one does not indulge too much in such διχοτομίαις, by which the text is often not so much illustrated as obscured, not so much cut rightly as miserably torn apart, and deprived of its use—but those who, having resolved everything according to the intention, context, and emphasis of the words, expose them to be grasped as if by the eyes themselves, so that all things are open, καὶ γυμνὰ, καὶ τετραχηλισμένα, through that 'orthotomy,' a sacrificial phrase which the Apostle also used in Hebrews 4, verse 13. For the just distinction between Law and Gospel contributes primarily to that orthotomy, so that they are not confused with one another, as was done by the Pseudo-Apostles; and of other things which are distinct in Scripture, which Osiander rightly observed here. For here also holds that oft-repeated saying: He who distinguishes well, teaches well.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Σπούδασον σεαυτὸν δόκιμον παραστῆσαι τῷ Θεῷ) παραστῆ- σαι recte Latinus vertit exhibere. Δόκιμον sume ut Roman. XVI. vers. 10. 1. Cor. XI. v. 19. 2. Cor. X. 18. Jac. I. vers. 12. Sensus est: fac te probes Deo. In Manuscripto παραστῆσαι τῷ χριστῷ.

Ἐργάτην ἀνεπαίσχυντον.

Ea agentem, quorum pudere non debeat. Vide Roman. VI. v. 21.

Ὀρθοτομοῦντα τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας) Similitudo ducta a victimis, quæ certo ritu secari debebant, ut ad Leviticum ostendimus. Est autem & Evangelii annuntiatio sacrifi- cium & quidem egregium. Translatione paulum diversa interpretes Proverb. III. vers. 6. & XI. vers. 5. ὀρθοτομεῖν ὁδὸν dixere, ubi in Hebræo est ישׁר quod alibi vertitur και τευθύνειν aut κατορθοῦν, nempe etiam secare viam dicimus. Evangelium autem ὀρθοτομεῖ qui cuique accommodat ea monita, quæ ei maxime conveniunt: quomodo de victi mis aliæ partes dabantur sacerdotibus, aliæ privatis. In Clementis Constitutionibus VII. v. 33. ὀρθοτομοῦντας ἐν τοῖς Κυρίου δόγμασιν. Philo de Caino & Abele: ὅτως ὁ τι- μιώτερον τῷ χρυσίῳ λόγον, ἐκ ποικιλμάτων καὶ μυρίων ἰδεῶν τελειουργητότα, ὅταν ἄχρι τῶν λεπτοτάτων κεφαλαίων τμη- θεὶς τρόπον τινὰ τούματων δέξηται, καθάπερ ἡγεμὼν ἀποδεί- ξεως ἐναργεστάτης.

Alia metaphora explicat Theodoretus: Lauda- mus agricolas, qui rectos sulcos proscindunt. Ita etiam Magister est laude dignus, qui sequitur re- gulam divinorum eloquiorum. Alii a coriariis metaphoram petunt, qui superflua resecant a pellibus, quas ad usum parant, ut Theophylactus & Oecumenius Chrysostomum secuti. Theophyla- ctus: Circumcide inutilia quæque, & deme gladio verbi, quæ ab Evangelii prædicatione sunt aliena. Nonnulli tamen (non diffitemur) & phrasi Græca τέμνειν ὁδὸν viam patefacere vel aperire deducunt. q. d. Verbi veritatis rectam quasi viam aperire, aut sermonem veritatis, quasi iter rectum pate- facere. Sed convenientior est explicatio de sa- cerdotibus, qui certo ritu victimas dissecabant, quæ & Grotio probata: cui similis metaphora ab instructoribus convivii, vel potius distributo- ribus dapum, quas dissecant, & comparatio a Patrefamilias, liberis & servis demensum, prout convenit, distribuente, Luc. XII. vers. 42. Confer. 1. Corinth. III. vers. 1. Ebræor. V. vers. 12. Rem ipsam probe explicat Vulgata: recte trans- latam, velut a specie ad genus traducta signifi- catione, notante Fullero libr. III. miscell. Sacr. cap. 16. quod καινοτομεῖν ex usu linguæ Græcæ sit res novas moliri, vel suscipere, & ὀρθοτομεῖν pari ratione sit res rectas aggredi vel facere, & Syrus reddidit, recte prædicare sermonem; huc referens loca e Proverb. III. & XI. quibus ישׁר redditur ὀρθοτομεῖν dirigere, aut rectum facere. Adde & explicationem Theophylacti: Etsi ple- rique id verbum discerpent, traducuntque alio, tu tamen id ipsum recte pertracta. Alienior au- tem illa Fulleri conjectura, quod τμήματα sig- menta, quæ פסקים vocantur à פסק τέμνειν scin- dere denotentur,unde dicti sunt הפיסקים בתורה οἱ τέμνοντες τὸν νόμον, qui legem secabant, vel in lege tractanda occupati erant. Cæterum recte secare aut tractare sermonem veritatis hoc loco dicuntur, non qui per διχοτομίαν omnia in mi- nutiores partes dissecant, quanquam nec id cum juxta sensum Spiritus sancti fit, nec nimis in- dulgetur talibus διχοτομίαις, quibus sæpe tex- tus non tam illustratur, quam obscuratur, non tam secatur recte, quam discerpitur misere, suo usu destituatur: Sed qui omnia juxta in- tentionem, contextum, & emphasin verborum resoluta ipsis veluti oculis usurpanda exponunt, ut aperta sint omnia, καὶ γυμνὰ, καὶ τετραχη- λισμένα per illam orthotomiam, qua phrasi iti- dem sacrificiali usus est Apostolus Ebræor. IV. vers. 13. Ad eam enim orthotomiam imprimis facit legis & Evangelii justum discrimen, ne illa inter se confundantur, quemadmodum a Pseudo- Apostolis fiebat; & aliorum, qui in Scriptura distincta sunt, quod hic recte observavit Osian- der. Nam & hic valet illud πολυθρύλλητον: Qui bene distinguit, bene docet.

## 2:16
Verse 16.

But avoid profane babblings) We have 'avoid' for περιΐστασο, both in Tit. III. v. 9 and in Josephus, because we are accustomed to fence off those things from which we fear harm. In the Manuscript here, as also above in 1 Tim. VI. v. 20, it is κενοφωνίας, not καινοφωνίας; there it is ἐκτρεπόμενος, which is περιΐστασο here, and what is παραιτᾶ in 1 Tim. IV. v. 7. Elsewhere it is 'profane fables,' which here is 'profane babblings,' the inventions of men concerning divine things, without any revelation.

The Vulgate inserted a conjunction, 'profane, and babblings': But it is found neither in the Greek, nor, as Salmeron admits, in most Latin codices. The Ambrosian Commentary, Augustine, and Vincent of Lérins, and also, as Theophylact notes, Basil the Great, have 'profane novelties of words,' as if it read καινοφωνίας. Chrysostom also reads it thus: 'But avoid profane novelties of words: for they will not stop there. For when something new has been invented, it always gives birth to something new, and the error of him who has left the tranquil and faithful station of the shore and begun to wander through devious paths is infinite.' But since the Greek codices consistently have κενοφωνίας, one must not depart from them. The Apostle therefore acts against empty talk, or clamors about vain things. As the Blessed Luther says: 'Rid yourself of unspiritual, loose chatter.'

For they will proceed to more ungodliness.

These things do not stand where they begin; what seems a small error in the beginning becomes great in its progress, as the Dialecticians say. προκόπτειν is said of good, as often, and of evil, as below in III. 13. The Hebrews would say רבו.

Grotius understands this of 'babblings.' Others, with the Greek interpreters, more correctly understand it of the persons themselves who are given to these things: since it is added, 'and their word spreads like a gangrene.' Namely, of those who proceed to greater impiety. Cf. below chapter III. v. 13. He understands those, says Theodoret, who attempt to teach things contrary to the truth, often corrupting even those who are free from the passion, like a gangrene.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Τὰς δὲ βεβήλους κενοφωνίας περιΐστασο) περιΐστασο pro cavere habemus & Tit. III. vers. 9. & apud Josephum, quia circumcludere solemus ea, a quibus nobis metui- mus. In Manuscripto hic, ut & supra 1. Tim. VI. v. 20. κενοφωνίας, non καινοφωνίας· ibi ἐκτρεπόμενος, quod hic περιΐστασο, & quod παραιτᾶ, 1. Timoth. IV. vers. 7. Ali- bi βέβηλοι μύθοι, qui hic βέβηλοι κενοφωνίαι, hominum commenta de rebus divinis, sine ulla revelatione.

Vulgata interjecit copulam, prophana, & vaniloquia: Sed ea nec in Græcis, nec fatente Salmerone in plerisque Latinis Codd. reperitur, Commentarius Ambrosianus, Augustinus & Vincentius Lyrinensis, nec non notante Theo- phylacto, Basilius M. habent prophanas vocum novitates, quasi legeretur καινοφωνίας. Legit etiam ita Chrysostomus: Prophanas autem vocum novitates devita: Neque enim eatenus subsistent. Nam cum quid novi fuerit inventum, semper nova id parturit, infinitusque sit error ejus, qui tranquillam fidamque stationem litoris egressus per devia cœperit vagari. Sed cum constanter Græ- ci Codd. habeant κενοφωνίας, ab iis discedendum non est. Agit ergo Apostolus contra vaniloquen- tiam, seu clamores de rebus inanibus. Ut Beat. Lutherus: Des ungeistlichen losen Geschwätzes entschlahe dich.

Ἐπὶ πλεῖον γὰρ προκόψουσιν ἀσεβείας.

Non stant ista, ubi incipiunt; qui initio parvus vi- detur error, magnus sit processu, ut ajunt Dialectici. προ- κόπτειν & de bono dicitur ut sæpe, & de malo, ut infra III. 13. Hebræi dicerent רבו.

De κενοφωνίαις intelligit Grotius. Rectius alii cum Græcis interpp. de personis iisdem deditis: quum addatur, & sermo eorum serpit ut gangræ- na. Illorum scil. qui ad majorem impietatem procedunt. Conf. infra cap. III. vers. 13. Illos intelligit, inquit Theodoretus, qui contraria veri- tati docere conantur, sæpe etiam eos corrumpunt, instar gangrænæ, qui sunt a passione liberi.

## 2:17
Vers. 17.

And their word will have pasture like a gangrene) Gangrene is not the same as cancer, but something similar. But 'will have pasture' (νομὴν ἕξει) is well used, that is, it will widely consume healthy flesh; פשה as in Levit. XIII. v. 22 and elsewhere. For the Greeks also say that gangrene is called from γραίειν, which is to eat. The Latin interpreter 'spreads' (serpit), not by the word, but by the sense well expressed. Lucilius:

To spread like a gangrene to the evil to which you might be able to [apply] a poultice.

Varro: We do not blame, when we know that a finger ought to be cut off, if on that account a gangrene is not to follow to the arm. He says this: That philosophical evil spreads widely, especially because many embrace that way of living, so that they may avoid the punishments which threaten Christians on all sides. Nothing has so harmed Christianity, as those institutions, which approached quite closely to Christianity, and softened πολυθείαν [polytheism] through certain interpretations. But the reason why many men embraced those institutions rather than Christianity was not that there was anything more certain in them: but that the cross, which pressed upon Christians, was avoided in that way. Tertullian, Præscript. adversus hæreticos. And fruitless questions, and words spreading like a cancer, from which the Apostle, restraining us, testifies by name that Philosophy must be avoided. Another evil, not unlike this, exercised the early Church from those who, likewise for the sake of avoiding the cross, wished to impose the necessity of Jewish rites upon the Gentiles, concerning which we have spoken in those [epistles] to the Galatians and Philippians. One who wishes to understand Paul correctly must have these things before his eyes.

Grotius deserves no credit, asserting without document or witness that philosophers and certain Judaizers are being noted. The examples adduced indicate whom the Apostle understands. Namely, heretics, of whose number were Hymenaeus and Philetus. It appears from the analogy of other Epistles that he also has regard for false apostles, who confound the Law and the Gospel: especially from those which were written to the Romans, to the Galatians, and to the Philippians, which are not so much illustrated as obscured by that observation of Grotius. How much darkness Grotius attempted to introduce into them, these annotations of ours, by which those [darknesses], by the grace of God, have been dispelled, will teach.

Concerning gangrene, Chrysostom says: A disease, he says, truly horrible, and which cannot be contained by medicine, but daily corrupts and destroys everything: therefore no remedy can be applied to it. By these things he shows that those who have willingly wandered from the truth cannot be corrected and amended. The Vulgate, as also the Blessed Luther, translating it as cancer, judged that gangrene, as a disease spreading like a cancer and devouring the neighboring members of the body, is a species put for the genus. For physicians call cancer καρκῖνον [karkinon], and distinguish it from gangrene, which is said to be from γέγγειν [genglein], to eat or to devour. It is also called ἕρπης [herpes], because it creeps like a serpent. Anselm, deceived by the homonymy of the word cancer, took it for an animal. Gangrene, however, properly so called, is the mortification and extinction of some part in the body, arising from the vehemence of inflammation, infecting the joined parts at the same time, not even leaving the bones, which, permeated by a vicious humor, also rot and begin to die. Pustules appear first, but when no remedy is brought, it creeps and devours the neighboring members until it reaches the heart itself, nor does it cease before it has destroyed the man. Error in faith is compared to it (1.) by reason of its small beginning (2.) by reason of its great increase, because it creeps from member to member (3.) by reason of the damage, because, just as gangrene extinguishes the native color, so error in faith extinguishes the spiritual life by which we live in the faith of Christ, Gal. II, verse 20; just as gangrene devours the body, so error devours the mystical body of the Church. The Vulgate translates it νομὴν ἕξει [nomen hexei], it creeps. But it is more correctly explained as devours. Let Arius be an example, who, as Jerome says, was one spark, but because it was not immediately suppressed, its flame ravaged the whole world.

Ὧν ἐστι Ὑμέναιος καὶ Φιλητὸς [Of whom are Hymenaeus and Philetus]) It is a zeugma. The names are Greek, such as are many in the cities of Asia founded by the Greeks. Hymenaeus is from the god of weddings. Philetus is a name such as Amatus, Optatus, Desideratus among the Latins: among the Greeks, Ἐραστός [Erastus].

Concerning Hymenaeus, 1 Tim. I, verse 20, the Apostle says that he delivered him with Alexander to Satan, that is, he excommunicated him. Who Philetus was, is not certain. He expresses the heretics by name, however, so that they may be avoided. Without doubt there were more, which the little word ὧν [of whom] indicates. But he wished to name at least the principal ones.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Καὶ ὁ λόγος αὐτῶν ὡς γάγγραινα νομὴν ἕξει) Gangræna non idem est quod cancer, sed vicinum aliquid. Bene autem νομὴν ἕξει, id est, late carnem sanam depascet; פשה ut Levit. XIII. vers. 22. & alibi. Nam & Græci γάγγραιναν dictam ajunt παρὰ τὸ γραίειν, quod est ἐσθίειν. Latinus interpres serpit, non voce, sed sensu bene expresso. Lucillius:

Serpere uti gangræna malo ad quem herpetica posses.

Varro: Non bituperamus, cum sciamus digitum præcidi oportere, si ob eam rem gangræna non sit ad brachium secutura. Hoc dicit: Late serpit illua philosophicum malum,præcipue quod mul- ti illam vivendi rationem amplectantur, ut pœnas evitent, quæ undique Christianis imminent.Nihil tam Christianismo- nocuit, quam illa instituta, quæ ad Christianismum sa- tis prope accedebant, & πολυθείαν per interpretationes quasdam molliebant. Sed causa cur homines multi illa in- stituta præ Christianismo amplecterentur, non erat, quod in iis esset certius aliquid: sed quod crux, quæ Christianos premebat, eo modo vitaretur. Tertullianus Præscript. adversus hæreticos. Et quæstiones infructuosa, & sermo- nes serpentes velut cancer, à quibus nos Apostolus refrænans nominatim Philosophiam contestatur caveri oportere. Huic malo alterum non dispar primam Ecclesiam exercuit ab iis, qui similiter crucis vitandæ causa Judaicorum rituum neces- sitatem imponere gentibus volebant, de quo diximus in il- las ad Galatas & Philippenses. Hæc ob oculos habere de- bet, qui Paulum recte velit intelligere.

Philosophos, & Judaizantes quosdam notari sine documento, aut teste asserens Grotius fidem non meretur. Quales intelligat Apostolus, ex- empla adducta indicant. Hæreticos nempe, è quo- rum numero fuere Hymenæus & Philetus. Pseu- do - Apostolos, Legem & Evangelium confun- dentes etiam respici ex aliarum Epistolarum Analogia apparet: Imprimis ex ea, quæ ad Ro- manos, ad Galatas, ad Philippenses exaratæ, quæ per istam Grotii observationem non tam illu- strantur, quam obscurantur. Quantum tene- brarum inducere illis conatus fuerit Grotius, hæc nostra annotata, quibus istæ, per DEI gra- tiam, discussæ sunt, docebunt.

De Gangræna Chrysostomus: Morbus, inquit, utique horren- dus, & qui medicina contineri nequit, sed omnia indies corrumpit ac perimit: ideo nullum ei reme- dium valet adhiberi. Ostendit per hæc eos cor- rigi emendarique non posse, qui sponte à veritate aberrarunt. Vulgata, ut & Beat. Lutherus can- crum vertentes gangrænam pro morbo cancri instar serpente, & vicina corporis membra de- pascente, speciem pro genere poni censuere. Medici enim Cancrum καρκῖνον vocant, & à Gan- græna, quæ à γέγγειν edendo, vel depascendo di- citur, distinguunt. Vocatur etiam hæc ἕρπης, quia serpentis instar serpit. Anshelmus ὁμω- νυμίᾳ vocis cancri deceptus pro animali habuit. Gangræna autem proprie dicta, est partis alicu- jus in corpore mortificatio, & extinctio ab inflammationis vehementia oriunda, partes conjunctas simul inficiens, ne ossibus quidem relictis, quæ vitioso humore perfusa etiam pu- trescunt, emorique incipiunt. Apparent primo pustulæ, sed ubi non affertur remedium, serpit & depascitur vicina membra, donec ad cor ipsum pertingat, nec cessat prius quam hominem ex- tinxerit. Ei confertur error in fide (1.) ratio- ne exigui initii (2.) ratione magni incrementi, quod de membro in membrum serpat (3.) ratio- ne damni, quod, ut gangræna colorem nativum, sic error in fide vitam spiritualem, qua in fide Christi vivimus Gal. II. vers. 20. extinguat; ut gangræna corpus, ita error Ecclesiæ corpus mysticum depascitur. νομὴν ἕξει, serpit, Vulgata vertit. Sed rectius exponitur depascitur. Exem- plo sit Arius, qui, Hieronymo dicente, una scintil- la fuit, sed quia non statim oppressa est, totum or- bem ejus flamma populata est.

Ὧν ἐστι Ὑμέναιος καὶ Φιλητὸς) Est πρόζευγμα. Nomina sunt Græca, qualia multa in urbibus Asiæ per Græcos con- ditis. Hymenæus à nuptiarum Deo. Philetus nomen quale Amatus, Optatus, Desideratus apud Latinos: apud Græcos Ἐραστός.

De Hymenæo 1. Timoth. I. vers. 20. dicit Apo- stolus, quod eum cum Alexandro Satanæ tra- diderit, hoc est, excommunicarit. Quis Phile- tus fuerit, non constat. Exprimit autem hære- ticos κατ' ὄνομα, ut caveri possint. Sine dubio plures fuêre, quod vocula ὧν indicat. Sed præ- cipuos nominare faltem voluit.

## 2:18
Verse 18.

Οἵτινες περὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἠςόχησαν [Who concerning the truth have erred]) Frustrated concerning the truth, as Tertullian [says] concerning the resurrection of the flesh. The Latin [translation] well [renders it] 'have wandered': in which way he translates the same word, 1 Tim. I. 6, VI. 2.

Λέγοντες ἀνάςασιν γεγονέναι [Saying that the resurrection has happened]) See 1 Cor. XV, verse 2. Just as for the philosophers a bad life is called death, so a corrected life is called ἀνάςασις [resurrection], as also παλιγγενεσία [regeneration], concerning which we have spoken at John III, verse 3. But in the Gospel, the resurrection of the dead, or from the dead, is described so openly and in so many places that it cannot be understood as anything other than that which will be after the separation of the body from the soul, which separation is called death in the common sense. And certainly, unless that is hoped for, not even that other resurrection of morals will be such as it was in the Apostles and their faithful disciples. Wherefore, these innovations, which exclude the most necessary sense, must be resisted in every way. Tertullian: He equally touches those who would say that the resurrection has already happened. The Valentinians assert this concerning themselves.

Καὶ ἀνατρέπουσι τήν τινων πίςιν [And they overturn the faith of some]) They overturn the faith of many. ἀνατρέπουσι [they overturn] is הרפו [they have weakened], as in Proverbs X, verse 3. See a similar [passage] 2 Thess. II. 11.

He said that Hymenaeus had made shipwreck of the faith, 1 Tim. 1:19: they asserted that the resurrection had already taken place, that is, they so corrupted the things that are handed down in the sacred writings concerning the resurrection from the dead that they were to be understood as concerning a certain resurrection which has already taken place, which most people, along with Augustine in Epistle 119 to Januarius, explain as the spiritual resurrection which happens daily through repentance and faith: there are not lacking, however, those who say that they maintained that no other resurrection was to be expected than that by which men are reborn daily through the procreation of children, and as it were revive in their children: such a heresy Augustine ascribes to the Seleucians in his work to Quodvultdeus, Heresies 59. Thus Theodoret says, 'The wretches called the succession which happens through the procreation of children the resurrection.' Sedulius wished it to be noted as the passage of souls into other and other bodies according to the opinion of the Platonists. Primasius, in the passage of Ezekiel, proves that they were deceived and interpreted the resurrection as the return of the Jews to the land of Canaan from Babylon. Cornelius à Lapide notes that Theophylact observes that they understood by the resurrection the renewal of all things which happens annually in the Spring, around Easter. But that is found neither in the London edition nor in the Latin commentary of Theophylact published at Cologne by Christopher Porsena the Roman in the year 1528. Thomas thinks that they understood by the resurrection the glorification which has already taken place, and happens daily, when any believer dies, or even when they are baptized and rise again from the death of sins. Which explanation coincides with the former one of Augustine; and is approved by Anselm and the Glossa Ordinaria; just as a similar error was noted by Tertullian in his book on the resurrection of the Flesh, chapter 19, that in his time there were not lacking those who twisted the resurrection of the dead, clearly announced, into an imaginary resurrection, saying from that, that men had attained the resurrection by faith with the Lord when they put on Baptism. Cornelius à Lapide prefers to understand by the resurrection, according to Hymenaeus and Philetus, Christianity, and the freedom and joy of the Christian life, which Christ introduced and established: because that has already been done by Christ: and he refers to the error of the Judaizing Cerinthus, that the carnal delights of this life are the resurrection and blessedness, and that no other is to be expected, but these are most distant from the carnal delights of Cerinthus, and the pleasure sanctioned by Christ, which is certainly spiritual: nor was it an error concerning blessedness, but resurrection; but who will admit that the freedom of Christian life and pleasure are called resurrection? It can, however, be said that he spoke of the resurrection as already having happened, because in himself and others baptized, they believed that the resurrection had already occurred and that no other was to be expected. But that they fell from the truth of the faith, and overturned the faith of many, that is, of the changeable, is easily evident, because they thus denied the resurrection of the dead, concerning which Tertullian says: The hope of Christians is the resurrection of the dead. If (as they affirm) the resurrection has happened, then both the future judgment and retribution are clearly taken away, and the upright and holy are indeed affected by sorrows and evils. But the wicked have paid the penalties through luxury and delights: What need then will there be for virtue, if these are the remunerations.

Latin:

Verf. 18.

Οἵτινες περὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἠςόχησαν) Frustrati circa veri- tatem, ut Tertullianus de Resurrectione carnis. Latinus bene aberraverunt: quomodo vocem eandem vertit, 1. Tim. I. 6. VI. 2.

Λέγοντες ἀνάςασιν γεγονέναι) Vide 1. Cor. XV. verf. 2. Sicut Philosophis mala vita mors dicitur, ita vita corre- cta ἀνάςασις ut & παλιγγενεσία, de quo diximus ad Joh. III. verf. 3. At in Evangelio ἀνάςασις νεκρῶν, aut ἐκ νε- κρῶν tam aperte & tot locis describitur, ut non possit alia intelligi, quam quæ erit post corporis ab animo sejunctio- nem, quæ sejunctio vulgari sensu mors dicitur. Et certe illa nisi speretur, ne altera quidem illa morum ἀνάςασις talis erit, qualis fuit in Apostolis, & eorum fidelibus di- scipulis. Quare istis ἀκαινολογίαις sensum maxime necessa- rium excludentibus omni modo obsisti debet. Tertullia- nus: Æque tangit eos, qui dicerent factam jam resurrectio- nem. Id de se Valentiniani asseverant.

Καὶ ἀνατρέπουσι τήν τινων πίςιν) Multorum fidem ever- tunt. ἀνατρέπουσι הרפו ut Proverb. X. verf. 3. Vide simi- le 2. Thess. II. 11.

Naufragium fidei fecisse Hymenaeum 1. Tim. I. verf. 19. dixit: Resurrectionem jam factam esse asseruêre, hoc est, quæ de resurrectione à mor- tuis futura traduntur in sacris, ita depravarunt, quod de resurrectione quadam, quæ jam facta sit, intelligenda sint, quod de spirituali resurre- ctione plerique cum Augustino Epist. CXIX. ad Januar. explicant, quæ quotidie fit per pœni- tentiam & fidem: non desunt tamen, qui non aliam resurrectionem expectandam statuisse di- cant, quam qua quotidie per liberorum procrea- tionem homines renascuntur, & quasi reviviscunt in liberis: qualem hæresin Augustinus ad Quod vult DEUM hær. LIX. Seleucianis adscribit. Ita Theodoreius successionem, inquit, quæ fit per liberorum procreationem resurrectionem miseri appellarunt. Sedulius animarum in alia & alia corpora transitum juxta Platonico- rum opinionem notari voluit. Primasius pro- bat loco Ezechielis deceptos resurrectionem reditum Judæorum in terram Cananææ è Baby- lone interpretatos. Cornelius à Lapide notat, Theophylactum observare, eos per resurrectio- nem intellexisse renovationem omnium rerum, quæ quotannis in Vere fiat, circa Pascha. Sed id nec in Londinensi, nec in Latina Coloniæ à Chri- stophoro Porsena Romano ann. 1528. edito com- mentario Theophylacti reperitur. Thomas putat, eos per resurrectionem intellexisse glorificatio- nem, quæ jam facta, & quotidie fit, cum quis fidelis moritur, vel etiam cum baptizantur, & à peccatorum morte resurgunt. Quæ explicatio cum priori Augustini coincidit: ac Anselmo & Glossæ ordinariæ probata; quemadmodum à Ter- tulliano etiam similis error notatus fuit libr. de resurrect. Carnis cap. 19. quod suo tempore non defuerint, qui resurrectionem mortuorum ma- nifeste annunciatam in imaginariam resurrectio- nem detorquerent, dicentes exinde, homines resurrectionem fide consecutos cum Domino esse, cum Baptisma induerint. Cornelius à Lapide mavult per resurrectionem secundum Hyme- næum, & Philetum intelligere Christianismum, & Christiana vitæ libertatem, ac jucunditatem, quam induxit & sanxit Christus: quia illa jam facta est à Christo: & eò refert Cerinthi Judai- zantis errorem, quod deliciæ carnales hujus vitæ resurrectio & beatitudo sint, nec alia sit expectanda, sed hæc maxime distant carnales delicia Cerinthi, & jucunditas à Christo sancita, quæ utique spiritualis est : nec error fuit de bea- titudine, sed resurrectione, libertatem autem Christianæ vitæ, ac jucunditatem resurrectio- nem nuncupatam, ecquis admittet? Dici au- tem potest, jam factam resurrectionem dixisse, quod in se & aliis Baptismo tinctis, resurrectio- nem jam factam nec aliam expectandam credi- derint. A veritate autem fidei excidisse eosdem, & multorum, scilicet mutabilium, fidem ever- tisse, facile constat, quia ita negarunt resurre- ctionem mortuorum, de qua Tertull. Spes Chri- stianorum est resurrectio mortuorum. Si (ut illi as- firmant) facta est resurrectio, & futurum plane judicium tollitur & retributio, & probi quidem & sancti doloribus sunt & malis affecti. Improbi vero per luxum & delicias pœnas luerunt: Quid ergo opus virtute erit, si istiusmodi sunt remune- rationes.

## 2:19
Verse 19.

ὁ μὸν τοι στερεὸς θεμέλιος Θεῦ ἕστηκεν) Just as those who build palaces are accustomed to lay firm foundations, so GOD, constructing that eternal city, laid down certain decrees as foundations, which remain unshaken, which is the property of a foundation. In the same way, Cicero often spoke of the foundations of the Republic, of liberty, of peace, of justice, of defense, namely those things upon which each thing rests.

Ἔχων τὴν σφραγῖδα ταύτην) For it was customary for certain sentences of good omen to be inscribed on the stones of foundations. See something similar in Zech. III. verse 9, ch. IV. verse 10, and what is said there. Σφραγὶς is that which is inscribed on a stone, just as elsewhere it is that which is carved in a ring. The Latins call that a signum: Pliny calls it ἀποσφράγισμα, and gives an example, a quadriga. Such are in other rings, a sphinx, a lion, a frog, and many others. There are also letters in rings, such as those ἡν με φιλέιτα φιλᾶς, etc. These are to the Hebrews חותם as in Exodus XXVIII, 11, where the Greeks said σφραγῖδα. Hence also a coin-tessera, because it has something inscribed חותם in the Talmud of Shekels.

Ἔγνω Κύριος τὺς ὄντας ἁυτῦ) From Numbers XVI. verse 5, where in the Greek it is Ἔγνω Θεὸς τὺς ὄντας ἁυτῦ. For they read ידע in the Kal, not in the future Hiphil, as others do. Paul cites two sentences as foundations of the calling into the heavenly city. The former is that GOD does not regard that external profession, but chiefly the heart, which He alone sees. What is attributed to GOD there is here attributed to Christ: which is solemn for our writers.

Καὶ ἀποσήτω ἀπὸ ἀδικίας πᾶς ὁ ὀνομάζων τὸ ὄνομα τῦ Κυρίε) The other sentence is: that external profession profits nothing if evil works are present. The same sense is in Matt. VII. verses 21, 22, 23, where see what is said. He who says he is of Christ, so that he may truly and for his own good be such, let him be far from an impure life. Christ does not acknowledge others than such as His own. ὀνομάζειν τὸ ὄνομα τῦ Κυρίε is he who, being asked of whose discipline he is, names Christ as Master. See 1 Cor. I, 2.

The Calvinists here think they have found that election, by which GOD, out of mere grace, foreordained those whom He specially loved to faith, perseverance, justice, and glory—that is, His absolute decree of election, which is the heart and palladium of the Reformed Church—is the foundation, because it is laid under faith, grace, and glory, as Crocius has it in this place, i.e., Let the unstable be subverted: the counsel of GOD concerning the salvation of the Elect is not turned aside for that reason. But that absolute election is a pure figment of the Calvinistic brain. If it has the foundation of that seal, The Lord knows who are His, but GOD does not acknowledge as His own except those who believe, whom it is impossible to please without faith, Hebrews XI. v. 6, the foreknowledge of faith in the decree of election cannot be excluded. And that counsel of God concerning those to be saved, whom He foresaw would believe, τὺς μέλλοντας πισέυειν, it is certain that it does not fail; but that a believer cannot fall from grace is entirely contrary to the Scriptures.

and is clearly refuted by the examples of David, Peter, and sinners in the Holy Scripture. Wherefore that explanation concerning the elect is to be corrected with Scripture as Osiander handed it down: This is the immovable foundation before God, and it is like a seal by which letters or diplomas are confirmed: namely, that the Lord knows all those perfectly whom He has predestined to eternal life. Therefore, those who are in their number will either not be seduced by false doctrine, or they will not persevere in fatal error until the end. Meanwhile, however, whoever professes that he belongs to Christ, let him most diligently beware of all corruptions, both of doctrine and of morals. For impious doctrine or wicked morals cannot stand with true saving faith. If these passages are compared with the decree of Grotius concerning the foundation of the house or the heavenly city, namely the divine decree concerning saving those who believe in Christ, whom GOD foresaw from eternity, the sense will be more clearly revealed than if faith itself were said to be the foundation with others, which rather rests upon this counsel, or the decree of GOD concerning salvation to be obtained only in Christ and through Christ apprehended by faith, or the sacred Prophetic and Apostolic Scriptures, which explain that counsel of GOD, as that foundation in which Christ is the cornerstone, Eph. II. verse 20, or the Church: for this is not the foundation, but is founded upon Christ and the word of GOD, exhibiting the counsel concerning Christ, as upon an immovable rock, Matt. XVI. v. 16. Therefore, the election of individual persons itself, such as Abraham, Paul, or Peter, is not the foundation, but that counsel of GOD concerning the saving of the faithful through faith in Christ, or the πρόθεσιν of GOD, according to which the election was made, insofar as it is considered in the antecedent will of GOD, as they call it, the seal of which—as far as we are concerned, namely regarding the gracious will of GOD toward us, by which each of the faithful is sealed through the Holy Spirit—is the divine πρόγνωσις, by which He specifically knows and embraces with His grace His own, that is, those who believe in Christ: For we are made certain of that eternal counsel of GOD through the internal sealing of the grace of GOD in our heart, through the testimony of the Holy Spirit, who testifies that we, on account of Christ and through Christ, are in the grace of GOD, so that we may believe that He is our Father and that we are the children of GOD. He who receives the testimony concerning Christ through faith, seals that GOD is true, John 3:33. We are also made more certain through the operation of faith outwardly, by which, namely, those who believe in Christ and profess this faith strive to depart from all unrighteousness: which is a sign both of true faith and of divine grace, which cherishes us as its own, and thus through our example seals the counsel of GOD concerning the saving of His own, that is, those who believe in Him. To this point also returns the opinion of Thomas and Cajetan, who deduce this saying of the Apostle, as a second seal, likewise from Numbers 16:21, 26: 'Separate yourselves from the midst of this congregation, and depart from the tabernacle of these wicked men, lest you be involved in their sins,' in this way: Whoever says that he is Christ's, let him depart from unrighteousness; and he who does this perseveringly can firmly conclude from this mark that he is in the number of the elect. By ἀδικίαν is not understood falsehood opposed to virtue, as in Romans 2:8, which seemed so to some, but ἀνομία, since any sin against conscience, which is truly ἀδικία, faith be shaken, and so it is necessary that he abstain from it, whoever desires to be certain of his own election, and to be among those who are the Lord's, and whom the Lord knows peculiarly. These things cohere with the preceding in this way: Although the faith of not a few may be subverted by heretics, yet the foundation is not therefore overturned, nor the counsel of GOD concerning saving those who believe in Christ. For God knows and guards his own in faith, who as they call upon the name of the Lord Jesus through faith, (by which reason faith itself is described, 1 John II. 32. Rom. X. 13.) so they devote effort diligently, that they may be as alien as possible from all iniquity: who by that very fact seal the eternal counsel of God concerning salvation through faith. For neither is that practical knowledge of God joined with a gracious affection, unless of the faithful, who are said to be the Lord's, because they adhere to the Lord through faith, nor do they depart from injustice, unless they are inserted into the Lord by faith. Without me, says the Lord, you can do nothing, John XV. 6. Theophylact has it thus on this place: By no means are all perverse, but only the weak and inconstant: for if they had not been of this kind, they would not have fallen at all. But those who are well-founded remain stable and unmoved. Note, however, that one must adhere to faith no differently than to some most firm foundation. Of faith, that is, of the doctrine of faith, or of the faith which is believed. Having a seal, that is, having as if an epigram on a stone, and some mark inscribed, suitable to him from the very works and deeds performed. The Lord knows, that is, those who are of his lot were known by him long before, and these indeed are therefore pre-elected, lest they perish with those rotting and defiled ones. Let him depart from iniquity, he says, that is, from the error of dogmas, or from any injustice whatsoever. For he who is more iniquitous: will have stood neither on the foundation, nor in God. For he does not have the mark of God, who is more wicked and unjust. Note, however, that it will be necessary that he who is about to call upon the name of God, depart from any unjust thing whatsoever: from which he who has not turned away, is not worthy to be able to call upon the Lord faithfully by right. For praise and confession are neither becoming nor acceptable to sins.

Latin:

Vers. 19.
