ὁ μὸν τοι στερεὸς θεμέλιος Θεῦ ἕστηκεν) Sicut qui palatia struunt, solent firmà subjicere fundamenta, ita DEUS moliens civitatem illam æternam, decreta quædam sub- stravit, velut fundamenta, quæ manent inconcussa, quod fundamenti est proprium. Pari modo fundamenta Rei- publicæ, libertatis, pacis, justitiæ, defensionis, sæpe dixit Cicero, ea scilicet, quibus res quæque innititur.

Ἔχων τὴν σφραγῖδα ταύτην) Solebant enim fundamen- torum lapidibus sententiæ quædam inscribi, boni ominis causa. Vide simile quid Zach. III. vers. 9. c. IV. vers. 10. & ibi dicta. Σφραγὶς est id, quod lapidi inscribitur, sicut alibi id, quod sculptur in annulo. Id signum vocant La- tini: Plinius ἀποσφράγισμα, & exemplum dat, quadri- gam. Talia in aliis annulis, sphinx, leo, rana, aliaque multa. Sunt & literæ in annulis, ut illæ ἡν με φιλέιτα φιλᾶς, &c. Hæc Hebræis חותם ut Exodi XXVIII, 11. ubi Græci σφραγῖδα dixêre. Hinc & tessera nummaria, quia aliquid insculptum habet חותם in Thalmudo Siclis.

Ἔγνω Κύριος τὺς ὄντας ἁυτῦ) Ex Numer. XVI. vers. 5. ubi Græcis Ἔγνω Θεὸς τὺς ὄντας ἁυτῦ. Legerunt enim ידע in Kal, non in futuro Hiphil, ut alii. Duas sententias reci- tat Paulus, velut fundamenta allectionis in civitatem cœlestem. Prior est, DEUM non professionem illam externam, sed cor præcipue respicere, quod solus videt. Quod ibi DEO tribuitur, id hic Christo: quod solemne nostris scriptoribus.

Καὶ ἀποσήτω ἀπὸ ἀδικίας πᾶς ὁ ὀνομάζων τὸ ὄνομα τῦ Κυ- ρίε) Altera sententia est: professionem externam nihil prodesse, si adsint mala opera. Idem sensus Matth. VII. vers. 21. 22. 23. ubi dicta vide. Qui se Christi esse dicit, ut vere & cum suo bono talis sit, longe absit à vita impura. Alios quam tales Christus pro suis non agnoscit. ὀνομάζειν τὸ ὄνομα τῦ Κυρίε qui rogatus cujus sit disciplinæ, Christum nominat ut Magistrum. Vide 1. Cor. I, 2.

Calviniani hic putant se invenisse, electionem, quâ DEUS, quos specialiter dilexerit, ad fidem, perseverantiam, justitiam & gloriam præordi- narit ex mera gratia, hoc est, absolutum suum ele- ctionis decretum, quod cor, & palladium est Ec- clesiæ Reformatæ, esse fundamentum, quia sub- sternitur fidei, gratiæ, & gloriæ, ut Crocius hoc loco habet, q. d. Esto, subvertantur instabiles: non ideo DEI consilium de salute Electorum vertitur. Sed illa absoluta electio purum est com- mentum cerebri Calvinistici. Si fundamentum habet illud sigillum Deus novit, qui sunt sui, pro suis autem non agnoscit DEUS, nisi eos qui credunt, cui placere, sine fide, impossibile est Hebræor. XI. v. 6. πρόγνωσις fidei in decreto electionis excludenda non erit. Atque illud Dei consilium de salvandis, quos prævidit creditu- ros in Christum τὺς μέλλοντας πισέυειν, non ex- cidere certum est; fidelem autem excidere non posse gratia, Scripturæ prorsus contrarium est.

& Davidis, Petri, ac peccatorum in Scriptura sacra exemplis luculenter refellitur. Quapropter ita corrigenda illa de electis explicatio cum Scri- ptura: ut eam Osiander tradidit: Hoc est immo- tum fundamentum apud Deum, & est instar si- gilli, quo literæ aut diplomata confirmantur: quod videlicet Dominus omnes illos optime novit, quos ad vitam æternam prædestinavit. Ergo qui in eo- rum sunt numero, aut non seducentur falsa do- ctrina, aut in errore exitiali non perseverabunt usque ad finem. Interim tamen, quicunque pro- fitetur, se pertinere ad Christum, is ab omnibus corruptelis iam doctrinæ quam morum sibi dili- gentissime caveat. Non enim stare possunt cum vera salutari fide, impia doctrina, aut scelerati mores. Quæ si cum Grotii de fundamento do- mus, vel civitatis cœlestis decreto divino de salvandis iis, qui in Christum credunt, quos DEUS ab æterno prævidit, conferantur loci, sensus illustrius patebit, quam si cum aliis vel fides ipsa fundamentum dicatur, quæ potius in- nititur huic consilio, vel decreto DEI de salute non nisi in Christo & per Christum fide ap- prehensum obtinenda, aut Scripturis sacr. Pro- pheticis & Apostolicis, consilium illud DEI exponentibus, utpote in quo fundamento lapis angularis est Christus Ephes. II. vers. 20. vel Ecclesia: nam hæc non est fundamentum, sed fundata super Christum, & verbum DEI, con- silium de Christo exhibens, ceu supra petram immobilem Matth. XVI. v. 16. Non ergo ipsa electio singularium personarum, puta Abrahami, Pauli, Petri est fundamentum, sed consilium illud DEI de salvandis fidelibus per fidem in Chri- stum vel πρόθεσιν DEI, secundum quam facta est electio, quatenus in voluntate DEI anteceden- te, quam vocant, respicitur, cujus sigillum, quoad nos nimirum de gratiosa DEI erga nos voluntate, qua quisque fidelium per Spiritum sanctum obsignatur, est divina πρόγνωσις, qua speciatim novit, & gratia sua complectitur suos, hoc est credentes in Christum: Certi enim red- dimur, de æterno illo DEI consilio per ob- signationem internam gratiæ DEI in corde nostro, per testimonium Spiritus sancti, qui nos propter Christum, & per Christum in gratia DEI esse testatur, ut credamus, ipsum esse Pa- trem nostrum, nosque DEI esse filios. Qui per fidem suscipit testimonium de Christo, ob- signat, quod DEUS verax est Johan. III. vers. 32. Certiores etiam reddimur, per operationem fi- dei ad extra, qua nempe credentes in Christum, & fidem hanc profitentes ab omni injustitia recedere satagunt: quod signum est tum fidei veræ, tum gratiæ divinæ, quæ nos tanquam suos fovet, adeoque per nostrum exemplum obsignat consilium DEI de servandis suis, hoc est, qui in se credunt. Quo redit hactenus etiam Thomæ, & Cajetani sententia, qui hoc dictum Apostoli, ceu alterum signaculum pariter de- ducunt è Numeror. XVI. vers. 21. 26. Separamini de medio congregationis hujus, & recedite à ta- bernaculo hominum impiorum istorum, ne in- volvamini peccatis eorum, hoc modo: Quicun- que se Christi esse dicit: recedat ab injustitia, quod qui perseveranter facit, ex hac nota firmiter col- ligere potest, se esse in numero electorum. Per ἀδικίαν non falsitas virtuti opposita, ut Roma- norum II. vers. 8. intelligitur, quod quibusdam visum, sed ἀνομία, quum per peccatum quod- vis contra conscientiam, quod vere est ἀδικία, fides excutiatur, adeoque necessum sit abstineat ab ea, quisquis de sua electione certus esse cupit, & inter eos esse, qui sunt Domini, & quos pecu- liariter novit Dominus. Cohærent hæc cum su- perioribus hoc modo : Etsi per hæreticos fides non paucorum subvertatur, non tamen ideo ever- titur fundamentum, vel consilium DEI de salvan- dis credentibus in Christum. Novit enim & cu- stodit Deus suos in fide, qui ut invocant nomen Domini Jesu per fidem, (qua ratione fides ipsa describitur, 1. Joh. II. 32. Rom. X. 13.) sic operam navant sedulo, ut ab omni iniquitate sint quam alienissimi: qui eo ipso obsignant consilium æter- num Dei de salute per fidem. Nam nec practica illa Dei notitia cum affectu gratioso conjuncta est, nisi fidelium, qui Domini esse dicuntur, quod per fidem Domino adhæreant, nec ab injustitia rece- dunt, nisi fide inserti Domini sint. Sine me, inquit Dominus, nihil potestis facere Joh. XV. 6. Theophy- lactus in hunc locum ita habet: Haudquaquam omnes perversi sunt, sed infirmi duntaxat & incon- stantes: nam si non fuissent bujusmodi, minime con- cidissent. Qui vero bene fundati sunt, stabiles perma- nent & immoti. Adverte autem non secus esse fidei inbærendum, quam firmissimo alicui fundamento. Fidei, id est, doctrinæ fidei, vel fidei, quæ credi- tur. Habens signaculum, hoc est, habens tanquam in lapide Epigramma, & insigne aliquod insculptum, ex ipsis operibus, rebusque gestis illi conveniens. No- vit Dominus, hoc est, ab eo longe ante sunt cogniti, qui ejus sunt sortis, & hi quidem idcirco sunt præ- electi, ne cum putrescentibus illis corruant, & inqui- netis. Ab iniquitate, inquit, discedat, hoc est, à dogmatum errore, vel à quavis plane injustitia. Nam qui iniquior est: nec in fundamento, nec in Deo constiterit. Non enim Dei habet insigne, qui nequior sit & injustus. Adverte autem necesse fore, ut qui Dei sit nomen invocaturus, à re quavis injusta abscedat: à qua qui non declinaverit, nec dignus fide- liter, qui jure possit Dominum invocare. Nil enim decora est vel accepta peccatis laus & confessio.

## 2:20
Vers. 20.

In a great house) Such as this world is to God. Are there not only gold and silver vessels) Such as were the eating and drinking vessels of the rich. L. Supellectili §. Vitrea D. de Supellectile legata. But also wooden) such as hooks and siphons against fires, shovels. And earthen) Think of chamber pots, basins, urinals. And some for honor) Such as those from which we eat. And some for dishonor) such as those into which we cast filth. But to this tends the ἀναγωγία (allegorical interpretation), it is no wonder if GOD even allows some to insinuate themselves into the Church, who then betray themselves by evil deeds. Nothing escapes God, because he knows how to use both the good and the bad. Compare what are in Rom. IX. 21. 22.

Because mention was made of the foundation, now the house of God, the Church, which rests upon it, in which in their own way were also those who were overturning the faith, before they were excommunicated and cast out of the Church, Hymenaeus and Philetus, is exhibited: as being that in which there are vessels of different kinds. Therefore he understands the house not as the world, but as the Church, which Grotius himself acknowledges in these latter points: how do Cyprian lib. III. Epist. 3. lib. IV. Epist. 2. Augustine lib. III. de Bapt. contra Donatistas cap. 18. & 19. lib. IV. cap. 12. lib. VII. cap. 51. &c. not understand the world, but the Church, in a broad way, as it embraces all who call upon the name of Christ, as Chrysostom and Theophylact do. Certainly no one is surprised or troubled that there are evil men in the world, but that they are in the Church; which Estius notes here, observing: that there is nothing absurd if we confess that heretics, as long as they are either entirely hidden, or not so manifest that they are not still tolerated in the assembly of the faithful, are in the Church in a certain respect, namely, according to external profession. That this should be said, reason itself compels. For it happens that heretics are prelates and heads of churches; and therefore in some respect at least members. Nor indeed could they exercise jurisdiction in the Church, unless they were in it at least by external profession. The scope therefore of the Apostle, as noted with Estius by the blessed Gerhard, is to teach that it should not seem strange to anyone that in the external society of the Church there are mixed with truly believing and holy people those who are not holy, who subsequently fall away from the faith, or lead a flagitious and impious life. It is so far from being the case that it should seem strange to anyone that the bad are mixed with the good in the Church, that it should rather be considered to pertain to the order of divine providence, which knows how to use even the bad well for ends proposed to divine goodness and wisdom, just as a householder has vessels of every kind in his house, which he knows how to use for certain ends. Nor indeed do Chrysostom and Theophylact deny this; but they use the word Church more strictly, for the communion of saints.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Ἐν μεγάλῃ δὲ οἰκίᾳ) Qualis Deo est hic mundus. ἐκ ἔςι μόνον σκέυη χρυσᾶ καὶ ἀργυρᾶ) Qualia erant divi- tum escaria & potoria. L. Supellectili §. Vitrea D. de Supel- lectile legata. Ἀλλὰ καὶ ξύλινα) ut hami & siphones adversus incendia, rutra. Καὶ ὀςράκινα) Puta Lasana, Scaphia, matulæ. Καὶ ἃ μὲν εἰς τιμὴν) Ut de quibus vescimur. ἃ δὲ εἰς ἀτιμίαν) ut in quæ sordes egerimus. Huc au- tem tendit ἀναγωγία, non mirum si DEUS etiam aliquos sinat se insinuare in Ecclesiam, qui deinde malis factis se prodant. Deo nihil abscedit, quia novit & bonis & malis uti. Confer quæ sunt Rom. IX. 21. 22.

Quia mentio facta fundamenti, jam domus Dei Ecclesia, quæ illi innititur, in qua suo modo erant, etiam, qui fidem evertebant, antequam excommu- nicarentur, & ejicerentur ex Ecclesia, Hymenæus & Philetus, exhibetur : utpote in qua diversi gene- ris vasa sunt. Domum ergo non de mundo, sed de Ecclesia intelligit, quod hisce posterioribus ipse Grotius agnoscit : quomodo non cum Chrysost. & Theophyl. mundum, sed Ecclesiam, largo quodam modo, prout omnes complectitur, qui Christi nomen invocant, intelligunt Cyprianus libr. III. Epist. 3. libr. IV. Epist. 2. Augustinus libr. III. de Bapt. contra Donatistas cap. 18. & 19. libr. IV. cap. 12. libr. VII. cap. 51. &c. Nemo certe miratur aut turbatur, quod in mundo sint homines ma- li, sed quod in Ecclesia; quod hic notat Estius observans: nihil absurdi esse, si fateamur, hære- ticos, quamdiu vel omnino occulti sunt, vel non ita manifesti, quin adhuc in cœtu fidelium tolerentur, secundum quid, nempe secundum externam pro- fessionem, in Ecclesia esse. Quod ut dicatur, ipsa ratio cogit. Contingit enim hæreticos Eccle- siarum esse prælatos & capita; ac proinde quadam saltem ratione membra. Nec sane jurisdictionem exercere possent in Ecclesia, nisi saltem externa professione in ea essent. Scopus ergo Apostoli, no- tante cum Estio Beat. Gerhardo, docere, non de- bere cuiquam mirum videri, quod in externa Ecclesia societate vere credentibus ac sanctis ad- mixti sint non sancti, qui à fide postmodum defi- ciunt, vel flagitiosam & impiam vitam ducunt. Tantum abest, ut alicui mirum videri debeat, malos in Ecclesia bonis esse admixtos, ut potius ad ordinem divina providentiæ hoc pertinere censen- dum sit, quippe quæ novit etiam malis bene uti ad fines divinæ bonitati & sapientiæ propositos, sicut Paterfamilias omnis generis vasa in domo sua ha- bet, quibus ad certos fines uti novit. Neque vero id negant Chrysostomus & Theophylactus; Sed Ecclesiæ voce strictius utuntur, pro communione sanctorum.

## 2:21
Vers. 21.

If therefore anyone cleanses himself from these) He shows that this simile has something dissimilar. For those bronze vessels contribute nothing of themselves as to why they are of this kind or that kind. But man contributes something. For he can always resist by the help of GOD, and thus bring it about that he is an honorable vessel, accommodated to noble uses. Just as the word of converting, so also of purifying, is sometimes attributed to GOD, as the primary cause, sometimes to man himself, as the secondary cause. See Psalm LXXIII. verse 13. James IV. 8. 1. Peter I. verse 22. 1. John III. 3.

He shall be a vessel for honor) Do not be terrified by that distinction which I have brought. There is in this matter something that is up to us.

Sanctified) As the vessels of the temple.

And useful to the Master, prepared for every good work) Christ can also be called Master: but GOD, the Father of Christ, is more often called so, as in Luke 2:29, Acts 4:24, Jude 4. See also Gen. 11:2, Josh. 5:14, Isa. 1:24, 3:1, 10:31, and very often in the books of Wisdom, Sirach, and Second Maccabees. Ἡτοιμασμένον is מוכן. Thus, in the opposite sense, we have κατηρτισμένα in Rom. 9:22. It is a great honor for a man to become an instrument of divine goodness.

Let care be taken that the powers of free will are not introduced here after the manner of the Arminians, Socinians, and other remnants of Pelagius. The faithful can cleanse themselves from those vain babblings and injustice, not by the powers of free will, but through the grace of the Holy Spirit, who dwells in them: and then they will be, that is, they will show themselves to be, vessels unto honor. For things are said to be in the Scriptures when they are manifested. Such vessels, which are divinely preserved for honor, both here in the kingdom of grace and hereafter in the kingdom of glory, being indeed sanctified to the Lord, that is, purged from the corruptions of doctrine and morals, and consecrated to the Lord, useful to the Lord, or adapted to the uses of the Lord for every good work in the Church. However, it does not appear why Christ should not be understood here by δεσπότην, who is the Master of this great house, Heb. 3:6, 2 Pet. 2:1. A vessel is said to be prepared (ἡτοιμασμένον) for honor through the grace of regeneration, and also of renewal. For of ourselves we are truly useless: but the grace of GOD alone prepares us, see Luke 17:10, 1 Cor. 4:7, 2 Cor. 3:5, so that God may use those vessels (as pure and good furniture), & through it may effect good works of every kind. (Those therefore who depart from errors, & who piously amend their own life, are not cast away by GOD on account of prior errors, or excesses: but are received into grace, & are reputed among sacred and clean vessels, and are set aside, as here Osiander. He does not say, that he prepared himself, but that it is prepared, viz. by the Lord, as Justinianus himself observes, that this participle ἡτοιμασμένον is placed, so that it may signify not only prompt and ready, but that it had been prepared by the Lord for this very use. Conf. Ephes. II. 20. Bellar. also adds his vote to the truth here, lib. II. de grat. & lib: arbitr. c. 13. The Apostle does not say that vessels are made into vessels for dishonor through cleansing into vessels for honor, but he shows by what sign vessels for honor can be known, and he says that vessels for honor have two seals, one internal, which cannot be perceived by us in this life, the knowledge of all divine approval; the other external, the avoidance of iniquity and errors, (I have already said that those seals are not of the vessels, but of the foundation of GOD.) Likewise the Apostle does not say, if anyone shall have cleansed himself from them, he will become a vessel (much less will he make himself a vessel) for honor, but he will be a vessel for honor, that is, he will be known to be a vessel for honor. These things Bellarmine. Therefore Bailius in Catech. controv. tr. 17. qu. 6. wrongly gathers from this place that we can render ourselves vessels for honor; others gather that the foreknowledge of works is the cause that one is a vessel for honor, that is, elected. The Apostle (on the contrary), as Estius says, placed predestination through the signification of a vessel of honor as an effect, and that a chief one, that is, of eternal life, which he also expressed in Romans II. by the name of glory and honor. Whence some wrongly strive to prove from this place that predestination is from the foreknowledge of works. Crocius also explains τὸ ἕσαι concerning manifestation: comparing the places John XV. v. 8. c. IIX. 31. James I. 12.

PART II. Admonition of Timothy concerning pursuing piety and showing gentleness.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Ἐὰν οὖν τις ἐκκαθάρῃ ἑαυτὸν ἀπὸ τούτων) Ostendit, si- militudinem hanc habere aliquid dissimile. Nam vasa illa ærea nihil de se conferunt, cur sint hujusmodi aut istius- modi. Homo autem confert aliquid. Potest enim DEI ope semper repugnare, & ita efficere, ut sit vas hone- stum, accommodatum ad egregios usus. Sicut verbum convertendi, ita & purificandi, modo DEO tribuitur, ut causæ principi, modo ipsi homini, ut causæ secunda- riæ. Vide Psal. LXXIII. vers. 13. Jacob. IV. 8. 1. Petr. I. vers. 22. 1. Job. III. 3.

Ἔσται σκεῦος εἰς τιμὴν) Ne terrere isto quod attuli discri- mine. Est in hac re aliquid ἐφ' ἡμῖν.

Ἡγιασμένον) Sicut vasa templi.

Καὶ εὔχρηστον τῷ δεσπότῃ, εἰς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἡτοιμα- σμένον) δεσπότης potest & Christus dici: sed sæpius sic vo- catur DEUS Christi Pater, ut Luc. II. 29. Actor. IV. v. 24. Judæ 4. Vide & Gen. XI. vers. 2. Jos. V. vers. 14. Esai. I. vers. 24. III. vers. 1. X. vers. 31. & sæpissime in libris Sapi- entiæ, Sirachidæ, & secundo Maccabaico. Ἡτοιμασμένον מוכן. Sic in contrariam partem κατηρτισμένα habemus Rom. IX. v. 22. Magnus honos homini, divinæ bonitatis fieri instrumentum.

Caveatur ne Arminianorum, & Socinianorum, aliarumque Pelagii reliquiarum more ingeran- tur hic vires liberi arbitrii. Emendare seipsos à vaniloquiis illis & injustitia possunt fideles, non viribus liberi arbitrii: Sed per gratiam Spiri- tus sancti, qui in ipsis habitat: & tum erunt, id est, ostendent se esse vasa in honorem. Nam res tum esse dicuntur in Scripturis, cum manifestan- tur. Vasa talia, quæ asservantur divinitus in hono- rem, tum hic in regno gratiæ, tum olim in regno gloriæ, sanctificata quippe Domino, h. e. à corru- ptelis doctrinæ & morum expurgata, ac Domino consecrata, utilia Domino, vel usibus Domini ad omne opus bonum in Ecclesia accommodata. Non apparet autem, cur per δεσπότην hic non intelligendus sit Christus, qui est δεσπότης ma- gnæ hujus domus Ebræor. III. vers. 6. 2. Petr. II. vers. 8. ἡτοιμασμένον præparatum dicitur vas ad honorem per gratiam regenerationis, nec non renovationis. Ex nobis enim ipsis vere inutiles sumus: sola autem DEI gratia nos præparat vid. Luc. XVII. 10. 1. Cor. IV. 7. 2. Cor. III. 5. ut Deus illa vasa, (tanquam pura & bona supellectili) utatur, & per illud omnis generis bona opera efficiat. (Qui itaque ab erroribus discedunt, & qui vitam suam pie emendant, non abjiciuntur à DEO propter priores errores, aut excessus: sed recipiuntur in gratiam, & inter sacra & munda vasa reputan- tur, & reponuntur, ut hic Osiander. Non ait, quod se pararit, sed quod paratum est, scil. à Domino, ut Justinianus ipse observat, hoc par- ticipium ἡτοιμασμένον positum esse, ut non modo promptum atque expeditum, sed à Domino in hunc ipsum usum præparatum fuisse significet. Conf. Ephes. II. 20. Veritati hic etiam calculum addit Bellar. lib. II. de grat. & lib: arbitr. c. 13. Non di- cit Apostolus, vasa in contumeliam fieri per emunda- tionem vasa in honorem, sed oftendit, quo signo possint cognosci vasa in honorem, ac dicit vasa in honorem habere duo signacúla, unum internum, quod à nobis in hac vita cerni non potest, notitiam omnem divinæ approbationis; alterum externum, vitationem iniquitatis, & errorum, (signacula illa non va- sorum, sed fundamenti DEI esse, jam dixi- mus.) Item Apostolus non dicit, si quis emunda- verit se ab eis, fiet vas (multo minus faciet se- ipsum vas) in honorem, sed erit vas in honorem id est, cognoscetur esse vas in honorem. Hæc Bel- larminus. Perperam igitur ex hoc loco colligit Bailius in Catech. controv. tr. 17. qu. 6. nos posse nos ipsos reddere vasa ad honorem; colligunt alii prævisionem operum esse causam, ut quis sit vas in honorem, hoc est electus. Apostolus (contra) dicente Estio, prædestinationem per vas honoris si- gnificationem pro effectu posuit, eoque præcipuo, id est, vitæ æternæ, quam & Romanor. II. nomine gloriæ & honoris expressit. Unde male ex hoc loco nonnulli probare nituntur, prædestinationem esse ex operum prævisione. De manifestatione etiam exponit τὸ ἕσαι Crocius: conferens loca Joh. XV. v. 8. c. IIX. 31. Jac. I. 12.

PARS II. Commonitio Timothei de sectanda pietate, ac exhibenda lenitate.

## 2:22
Vers. 22.

Flee youthful desires) By νεωτερικὰς ἐπιθυμίας תאבת נעורים, I think vainglories are understood, those who are eager for which are called νεανιεύεθαι by the Greeks. All languages command us to flee them. That which must be guarded against with all zeal. See 1 Cor. VI. 18. X. 14. 1 Tim. VI. 11. Opposed to this is διώκειν רדף, which we shall have now.

The Apostle now exhorts to the pursuit of piety, admonishing him concerning those things which are to be fled and which are to be pursued by him. He is commanded to flee youthful desires, as the Vulgate renders it, which command indeed seems to be general, and to prohibit desires especially of lusts and pleasures, to which young men incline; if, however, we look at the person of Timothy, who was most abstinent, and the things which are noted in the opposite member, as well as the circumstances of the office, it must be judged with Estius, Cornelius à Lapide, and Blessed Gerhard that it refers rather to certain vices of the mind, for example, pride, animosity, the desire for fame, vain glory, rashness, etc., with which young men who preside over others, or have undertaken the duty of teaching and disputing, are wont to be troubled. Our Domin. Wandalinus diatrib. de feria passion. after Salmasius, in appar. ad libros de primat. Pap. page 57. to which Schlichtingius also added his vote in this place, though he is by no means approved by his own Dan. Bremius in Notes to the Old & New Testament, fol. 23., who thinks that vain desires for innovating and cravings for new things are noted. Since the word νεωτερικὸς signifies new, or one who is innovating, but not truly youthful, and νεωτερίζειν for Thucydides book II. and Herodotus book I. is to innovate, for Philo book III. de Vita Mosis it is to pursue new things: whence he judges that νεωτερικὰς ἐπιθυμίας signifies desires which are concerned with τὰ νεώτερα, and are affected by novelties. Aristotle indeed in Ethic. Nicomach. book VII. cap. 4. calls youthful impulse νεανικὴν ἐπιθυμίαν, but nowhere is youthful craving called νεωτερικὴν. He misses, therefore, in the Grotian explanation, that he has taught that signification of the word νεωτερικὰς by no example from the Greeks: But in truth the Greek interpreters all explain it concerning youthful desires, not concerning a study of novelty or φιλοκαινίᾳ, who without doubt were most skilled in Greek literature, Theodoret, Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius, and Greek Lexicons interpret νεωτερικὸν as youthful, likewise foolish, because youthful age is often led by foolish affections, and for Hesychius νεωτερίζειν is to imitate the manners of the younger; for Suidas νεώτερος is said as a comparative for a positive, young, we acquiesce in the common exposition, approved by both ancients and moderns, which Blessed Luther, Beza, Er. Schmidius, and who not among interpreters, have also followed. Such youthful desires are ambition, the desire to excel and to become famous, and the contempt of others which is wont to arise from this: says Blessed Gerhard. By ἐπιθυμίας, says Blessed Balduinus, he understands whatever desires can disturb anyone from the path of right, such as gluttony, drunkenness, ambition, pride, petulance, lust, precipitation of mind, and whatever are alien to Christian gravity. He calls them youthful desires, not only because Timothy himself was a young man, but also because younger people are more frequently tempted by these desires, and are more easily overcome. The Apostle is about to warn him concerning those things which pertain to his office, and now he treats of those things which pertain to life and the pursuit of piety. For in the following verse he commands that foolish and unlearned questions be avoided, such as those who are led by a desire for novelty are wont to stir up, and he prohibits fights and contentions. All of which a love of novelty especially begets. Furthermore, the opposite, in that those things which are to be pursued do not correspond to τῇ φιλοκαινίᾳ or a desire for novelty; but rather to depraved lusts, such as pursuing righteousness, faith, charity, peace: Finally, the parallel passage is clear; concerning which lust 1 Timothy VI. verse 9. ταῦτα Φεῦγε, among which he had also reckoned foolish and harmful desires, verse 11. δίωκε δὲ δικαιοσύνην &c. While we have thus explained these things, there was offered to us the learned Exercise on this passage by Mr. Bohsius, the Polyhistor of Jena, from which it will have been worth the effort to observe a few more things. He proved, however, that the word νεώτερον is not accepted in the New Testament otherwise than as a young man, an adolescent, or a junior, as Luke XV. verses 12, 13, John XXI. verse 18, 1 Timothy V. verses 1, 2, I. verses 11, 14, Titus II. verses 4, 6, 1 Peter V. verse 5, as also Acts V. verse 6. Add also Luke XXII. verse 26, nor among the LXX Interpreters. signify anything other than one younger in age, such as this age is accustomed to be, unrefined, despised, and vile, but nowhere new, from an induction of the passages. For it corresponds to τῷ ילד 2 Samuel X. verse 14, to τῷ נער Judges 11. verse 20, & 2 Chronicles XIII. verse 7, Job XXIV. verse 5, Psalm XXXV. verse 26, Psalm CXLVIII. verse 9, Psalm CXLVIII.

Eccl. X. 16. Eph. XL. 30. Jer. I. 6. 7. τῷ צעיר Gen. XIX. vers. 31. 34. 35. 38. cap. XXIX. vers. 26. XLIII. 33. XLIIX. 14. 1 Reg. XVI. 34. Job. XXXII. 6. Ps. CXIX. v. 14. Jer. XIV. 3. τῷ קטן Gen. IX. 24. c. XXVII. 15. 42. &c. nor is it used among the Apocryphal writers for 'new', but for 'younger', Syr. LI. History of Susanna v. 44. Psalm. CLI. 1. Baruch. III. 19. 20. Regarding the word itself, νεωτερικὸς, he also brought forward examples in ch. V. §. II. from Eusebius in Append. b. IIX. Hist. Eccles. and from the end of Josephus, Antiquities XVI, who mentions ἀυθαδείας νεωτερικῆς; JUVENILE ARROGANCE of Alexander and Aristobulus; and from the author of the book περὶ παρθενίας ἢ περὶ ἀσκήσεως among the works of Athanasius: and also from Gellius, book XIII. c. 25, that it is used in the sense of youthful age. He observed, moreover, that Neoteric writers are not only those who treat of new things, but whoever has recently written about the most ancient things, whatever they may be. Which example those of the opposite opinion had also brought forward for their own cause. To whom, therefore, the most famous Bofius not undeservedly replied: just as 'carnal' is one thing and 'flesh' is another; 'the world' is one thing, and 'worldly things' are another: so likewise 'new' and 'that which pertains to new things' or 'that which is carried toward new things' are distinct. He teaches, furthermore, from the examples brought forward (by them), that at most it can be elicited that νεωτερικὰς ἐπιθυμίαι are to be explained as 'new desires', not likewise—even if you apply the rack—that the pursuit of new things is indicated. But who, he says, would say that new desires are forbidden in this place? Was Timothy to desire nothing more from then on than what he had desired before? And why would only 'new' ones be forbidden? Were the old ones, and those which were so frequent among the young, seen as harmless? He adds: I will say more: It is not even necessary to admit that it can be clearly demonstrated from the examples brought forward that νεωτερικὸς ever designates 'new'. Nay, I confidently affirm that in both cases it can be understood regarding age. For as to the fact that certain writers are called 'neoteric', there is no need to explain them as 'recent'. They can also be called so for the reason that they are younger. In the Epistles of Ignatius, too, it is so far from my thinking that νεωτερικὴν τάξιν ought to be explained as 'a new order' with Salmasius, Andreas Rivetus, and D. Blondellus, that I would almost dare to affirm that 'youthful' is designated by that word, as it is in Paul. He therefore discourses at length on the passage of Ignatius. And he proves that his discourse is not about the novelty of an order, but about the youth of the Bishop. He considers that the custom of the Holy Scriptures aids the received interpretation not a little, because ἐπιθυμίαι in the N.T.—and indeed in the manner of speaking which the Apostle used here—are never denominated from the object alone, but always from the subject and the cause: observing this from an induction of passages, especially that the object of desires is never designated by an adjective alone, but always the subject of them, or their nature or quality is indicated, as for instance Jas. I. 14, 2 Tim. IV. 3, 1 Pet. IV. 3, Jude v. 18, Tit. II. 12, 1 Pet. II. 11, 1 John III. 5, 1 Tim. VI. 9, 2 Tim. III. 6, Tit. III. 3. Which he executes in ch. III. He also used the argument which we brought forward, from the Apostle's opposite exhortation, which he proposed thus in ch. VII: 'Follow after righteousness', etc. You see that it is not constancy or the zeal of defending and preserving those things which are received by custom that is opposed to νεωτερικαῖς ἐπιθυμίαις (which ought to have been the case if the Apostle had wished to designate a desire for innovation by them), but those virtues which you would seek in vain in most young people, that is, as the interpreters explain, justice and innocence of life; faith, which without curious investigation receives the mysteries revealed by GOD; charity, which does not envy, is not puffed up, is not ambitious; likewise concord, meekness in bearing with those who think differently, patience in tolerating the faults and infirmities of others, abstinence from quarrels and foolish, immodest, excessive, and useless questions: Finally, if we believe Cyprian, Anselm, and others, docility, i.e., that they allow themselves to be taught willingly. To all these are opposed injustice, excessive curiosity, envy, pride, ambition, boasting, irascibility, a lust for contending and quarreling, impatience, rashness, youthful impulse, immodesty, a pursuit of useless questions, and an opinion of singular erudition: which usually tend to inhere in the minds of the young, especially those who either preside over others or have undertaken the duty of teaching and disputing; such as Timothy also was. Finally, he also took an argument from the person of Timothy, that there was no reason why the Apostle should dissuade him from the pursuit of new things, as he was well instructed in the doctrine of the faith.

The word διώκειν is a hunting term, a metaphor from the chasing of wild beasts; it must be done circumspectly, strenuously, fervently. Cf. Job. XV. 20, Rom. XIV. vers. 19, Phil. III. vers. 14, Apocal. XII. vers. 13. By 'righteousness' can be understood either imputed or begun justice. Chrysostom understands this: he calls righteousness any virtue, namely of piety, which consists in a right life: whom Theophylact follows. But the Apostle seems rather to understand that: for by the name of love, which is the fulfilling of the law, every virtue is comprehended. But we are commanded to pursue righteousness, which is apprehended by faith, therefore it is placed before faith, Rom. IX. vers. 31, 'Pursuing the law of righteousness', and vers. 30, 'those who did not pursue righteousness', where mention of faith is also added, 'attained righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith'. A similar passage is 1 Tim. VI. vers. 11. By πίστιν therefore in this place we understand justifying faith: which it is necessary to pursue, so that we may attain that righteousness. This faith, which through love ἐνεργουμένη Gal. V. ver. 6. follows the love of GOD and neighbor, which we are commanded to pursue 1. Cor. XIV. 1. διώκετε τὴν ἀγάπην, this implies a zeal for concord: by which we seek and pursue peace, as Peter commands 1. Ep. III. 11. ζητησάτω εἰρήνην, καὶ διωξάτω ἀυτὴν, and that with all, Heb. XII. 14. Here, however, spiritual concord is primarily regarded, which [is to be maintained] not with enemies of the truth, such as Hymenaeus and Philetus were, whom he ought to have fled and turned away from, but μετὰ τῶν ἐπικαλομένων τὸν κύριον ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας, with the truly faithful, because hearts are purified through faith, Acts XV. ver. 9. calling upon the Lord from a pure heart, which is a description of the faithful, Rom. X. 11. who believe with the heart unto righteousness, and confess with the mouth unto salvation v. 10. Therefore the object, or correlate of peace, and not indeed the communion and partners of peace (as Thomas and Cajetan wished), is denoted by this periphrasis, as is evident from a similar passage in Hebrews XII. ver. 14. Thus Chrysostom: Trust only those who call upon [Him] not rashly, but without guile and simulation, in whom there is no fraud, who proceed to prayer with peace, who do not litigate: therefore approach as a partner only to them, and mingle prayers with them, abstain from the rest. Thus also Theophylactus, and before them Theodoret: who says that while all are to be loved, yet sincere peace, which has need of common choice and will, or in the consensus of minds consists in being cultivated with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart. There is one kind of external and political peace, another internal and mystical. The former all are bound to exercise toward everyone; the latter exists mutually only between GOD and His pious faithful. The bond of the former depends both on the law of nature and on the calling to the communion of grace; the foundation of the latter consists both in agreement concerning heavenly truth and in the pious conjunction of wills and minds. Concerning the former, Heb. XII. 14; concerning the latter, 2 Cor. VI. v. 14. Syncretists do not attend to this distinction when they order those who err to be distinguished from their errors, and the foundation of doctrine from the persons inserted into the same. See Bergius, Stereom. p. 250. For spiritual communion does not regard persons so much as faith, or certainly persons on account of faith. For this is not the mystical conjunction by which men bear with one another and act peacefully in some external society, but that which ensures that they are one in the Spirit. Cons. Beat. Luth. Tom. III. Jen. Germ. f. 341.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

Τὰς δὲ νεωτερικὰς ἐπιθυμίας φεῦγε) Per νεωτερικὰς ἐπι- θυμίας תאבת נעורים, puto gloriolas intelligi, qui- bus qui student, νεανιεύεθαι Græcis dicuntur. Linguæ o- mnes fugere nos jubent. Id quod omni studio cavendum est. Vide 1. Cor. VI. 18. X. 14. 1. Tim. VI. 11. Huic op- positum est διώκειν רדף, quod jam habebimus.

Ad pietatis studium jam hortatur Apostolus, de iis commonefaciens, quæ fugienda, quæ pro- sequenda ipsi sint. Fugere jubetur juvenilia desideria, ut reddit Vulgatus, quod præce- ptum generale quidem esse, ac desideria maxi- me libidinum & voluptatum, ad quæ juvenes propendent, prohibere videtur; Si tamen Ti- mothei personam, qui abstinentissimus erat, & quæ in membro opposito notantur, nec non officii circumstantias spectamus, vitia quædam ani- mi potius respicere cum Estio, Cornelio à Lapi- de & Beat. Gerhardo censendum, verbi gratia, superbiam, animositatem, inclarescendi studium, inanem gloriam, temeritatem &c. quibus labo- rare solent juvenes, qui præsunt aliis, aut do- cendi ac disputandi munus susceperunt. Noster Domin. Wandalinus diatrib. de feria passion. post Salmasium, in appar. ad libros de primat. Pap. pag. 57. cui calculum etiam addidit Schlich- tingius in hoc loco, à suo tamen Dan. Bremio in Notis ad V. & Nov. Testam. fol. 23. minime probatus, vana innovandi desideria ac novarum rerum cupiditates notari putat. Siquidem vox νεωτερικὸς novum, vel novaturientem, non ve- ro juvenilem significet, & νεωτερίζειν Thucidi- di libr. II. & Herodoto libr. I. est innovare, Philoni libr. III. de Vita Mosis nova consectari sit: unde νεωτερικὰς ἐπιθυμίας significare censet desideria, quæ circa τὰ νεώτερα versantur, & novitatibus afficiuntur. Juvenilem impetum quidem Aristotel. Ethic. Nicomach. libr. VII. cap. 4. νεανικὴν ἐπιθυμίαν dicere, nuspiam au- tem νεωτερικὴν nuncupari juvenilem cupiditatem. Desiderat ergo id in Grotiana explicatione, quod eam vocis νεωτερικὰς significationem è Græcis nullo exemplo docuerit: Verum enim vero Græci interpp. omnes de juvenilibus cupiditatibus, non de novitatis studio, aut φιλο- καινίᾳ explicant, qui sine dubio Græcæ litera- turæ peritissimi fuêre, Theodorelus, Chrysosto- mus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius, & νεωτερικὸν Lexica Græca juvenilem interpretantur, item stultum, quod juvenilis ætas sæpe stultis affe- ctibus ducatur, & Hesychio νεωτερίζειν est junio- rum mores imitari; Suidæ νεώτερος pro νεός com- parativus pro positivo juvenis dicitur, commu- ni expositioni, tam antiquis, quam recentiori- bus probatæ, quam secutus etiam Beat. Luthe- rus, Beza, Er. Schmidius, & quis non inter- pretum? acquiescimus. Juveniles ejusmodi cu- piditates sunt ambitio, cupiditas eminendi, atque inclarescendi, & qui hinc oriri solitus, aliorum contemptus: inquit Beat. Gerhardus. Per ἐπιθυ- μίας, inquit Beat. Balduinus, intelligit quascun- que cupiditates, quæ aliquem à tramite recti de- turbare possunt, ut est gula, crapula, ambitio, fastus, petulantia, libido, animi præcipitantia, & quæcunque à gravitate Christiana sunt aliena. Νεωτερικὰς ἐπιθυμίας vocat, non tantum, quia ipse Timotheus juvenis erat, sed &, quia ado- lescentiores hisce desideriis crebrius tentantur, & facilius vincuntur. De illis, quæ ad officium spectant dehinc moniturus est, jam ea, quæ ad vitam & pietatis studium pertinent, tractat A- postolus. Nam vers. sequ. de stultis & ἀπαιδεύ- τοις quæstionibus vitandis præcipit, quales mo- vere solent maxime, qui novitatis studio du- cuntur, & pugnas ac contentiones prohibet. Quas omnes præcipue φιλοκαινία gignit. Porro oppositum, qua ea quæ persequenda sunt, non respondet τῇ φιλοκαινίᾳ vel studio novitatis; Sed potius concupiscentiis pravis, utpote sectari ju- stitiam, fidem, charitatem, pacem: Denique locus parallelus luculentus est; de qua concu- piscentia 1. Timoth. VI. vers. 9. ταῦτα Φεῦγε, inter quæ etiam censuerat ἐπιθυμίας ἀνοήτως καὶ βλαβερὰς vers. 11. δίωκε δὲ δικαιοσύνην &c. Dum hæc ita expedivimus, oblata nobis fuit erudita de hoc loco Dn. Bohsii Polyhistoris Jenerisis Ex- ercitatio, è qua nonnulla adhuc observare operæ pretium fuerit. Probavit autem vocem νεώτερον non aliter in Nov. Testam. quam de juvene ado- lescente aut juniori accipi, ut Luc. XV. vers. 12. 13. Job. XXI. vers. 18. 1. Tim. V. vers. 1. 2. I. vers. 11. 14. Tit. II. vers. 4. 6. 1. Petr. V. v. 5. ut & Actor. V. v. 6. Adde & Luc. XXII. vers. 26. nec apud LXX. In- terpp. aliud significare, quam ætate minorem, velut hæc ætas solet, rudem, contemptumque ac vilem, nullibi vero novum, ex inductione loco- rum. Respondet enim τῷ ילד 2. Sam. X. vers. 14. τῷ נער Juda 11. vers. 20. & 2. Chronic. XIII. vers. 7. Job. XXIV. vers. 5. Psalm. XXXV. vers. 26. Psalm. CXLIIX, vers. 9. Psal. CXLIIX.

Eccl. X. 16. Ef XL. 30. Jer. I. 6. 7. τῷ צעיר Gen. XIX. vers. 31. 34. 35. 38. cap. XXIX. vers. 26. XLIII. 33. XLIIX. 14. 1 Reg. XVI. 34. Job. XXXII. 6. Pf. CXIX. v. 14. Jer. XIV. 3. τῷ קטן Gen. IX. 24. c. XXVII. 15. 42. &c. nec apud Apocryphos Scriptores pro Novo adhibetur, sed pro juniori, Syr. LI. Hiftor. Susan- na v. 44. Psalm. CLI. 1. Baruch. III. 19. 20. De voce ipsa præsenti νεωτερικὸς exempla etiam ad- duxit cap. V. §. II. ex Eusebio in Append. l. IIX. Hist. Eccles. Josepho extremo XVI. antiqu. qui ἀυθαδείας νεωτερικῆς; JUVENILIS ARRO- GANTIÆ Alexandri & Aristobuli meminit; & autore libri περὶ παρθενίας ἢ περὶ ἀσκήσεως apud Athanasium: nec non è Gellii lib. XIII. c. 25. quod juvenilis ætatis sensu ea usurpata sit. Obser- vavit præterea, quod Neoterici Scriptores non illi sint modo, qui res novas tractant, sed qui- cunque nuper de antiquissimis quamlibet rebus scripsere. Quod exemplum etiam pro sua ad- duxerant οἱ ἐξ ἐναντίας sententia. Quibus proinde celeberrimus Bofius non immerito respondit: ut aliud est carnalis, aliud caro: mundus aliud, aliud res mundana: ita distant pariter novum, & quod est rerum novarum, sive quod in res novas fertur. Do- cet insuper ex adductis (ab iisdem) exemplis ad summum illud elici posse, νεωτερικὰς ἐπιθυμίας ex- poni novas cupiditates, non item, etsi fidiculas ad- hibeas, studia rerum novarum indicari. At quis, inquit, dixerit, novas cupiditates hoc loco vetari? An nil amplius appetere deinceps Timotheus, quam quod ante concupierat, debuit? Et cur solum novæ vetarentur? num veteres, & quæ tam frequentes inter juvenes erant, innoxiæ videbantur? Addit: Dicam amplius: Ne id quidem necesse est admitte- re, adductis exemplis liquido demonstrari posse νεωτε- ρικὸς unquam novum designare. Quin imo fiden- ter affirmo, utrobique de ætate posse accipi. Nam quod Scriptores quidam neoterici vocantur, id non opus est recentes exponere. Possunt & ideo sic dici, quod sint juniores. In Epistolis quoque Ignatii tan- tum abest, ut putem νεωτερικὴν τάξιν cum Salmasio, Andrea Riveto, & D. Blondello exponi debere no- vellum ordinem, ut pene ausim affirmare, juve- nilem, ut apud Paulum, ea voce designari. Prolixe itaque differit de loco Ignatii. Et id probat, non de novitate ordinis, sed de juventute Episcopi ei sermonem esse. Non parum autem receptam in- terpretationem juvare consuetudinem S. litera- rum censet, quod ἐπιθυμίαι in N. T. & quidem lo- quendi genere, quo Apostolus hîc usus est, nus- quam à solo objecto, ubique vero à subjecto & cau- sa denominentur: id ex inductione locorum im- primis observans, nusquam nomine adjectivo so- lum objectum ἐπιθυμιῶν designari, semper autem subjectum earum, aut naturam vel qualitatem in- dicari, utpote Jac. I. 14. 2. Tim. IV. 3. 1. Pet. IV. 3. Jud. v. 18. Tit. II. 12. 1. Petr. II. 11. 1. Joh. III. 5. 1. Tim. VI. 9. 2. Tim. III. 6. Tit. III. 3. Quæ exequitur c. III. Usus est & eo argumento, quod à nobis adductum, ab opposita adhortatione Apostoli, quod ita pro- posuit cap. VII. Δίωκε δὲ δικαιοσύνην &c. Vides, non constantiam aut studium tuendi conservandique ea, quæ usu receptæ sunt, νεωτερικαῖς ἐπιθυμίαις oppo- ni (quod fieri debebat, si per eas innovandi cupidinem designare Apostolus voluisset) sed illas virtutes, quas in plerisque junioribus frustra quæras, hoc est, ut interpretes exponunt, justitiam, vitæque inno- centiam; fidem, quæ sine curiosa disquisitione re- cipit mysteria à DEO revelata; charitatem, quæ non æmulatur, non inflatur, non est ambitiosa; Concordiam item, mansuetudinem in ferendis, qui diversum sentiunt, patientiam in tolerandis con- vitiis & infirmitatibus aliorum, abstinentiam a rixis & quæstionibus stultis, immodestis, immo- dicis, & inutilibus: Denique si credimus Cypria- no, Anselmo & aliis, docilitatem, h. e. ut libenter doceri se patiantur. Quibus omnibus adversantur injustitia, nimia curiositas, æmulatio, superbia, ambitio, jactantia, iracundia, contendendi rixan- dique libido, impatientia, temeritas, impetus juve- nilis, immodestia, studium inutilium quæstionum, & opinio singularis eruditionis: quæ plerumque ju- venum animis inhærere solent, præsertim eorum, qui aut præsunt aliis, aut docendi disputandique munus susceperunt; qualis & Timotheus fuit. Denique argumentum etiam desumsit a Timothei persona, quod nulla fuerit causa, cur eum a novarum rerum studiis dehortaretur Apostolus, utpote in doctrina fidei bene instructum.

Verbum διώκειν est venatorium, Metaphora ab insectatione ferarum, fieri necessum est cir- cumspecte, strenue, fervide. Conf. Job. XV. 20. Rom. XIV. vers. 19. Phil. III. vers. 14. Apocal. XII. vers. 13. Per δικαιοσύνην intelligi potest vel justi- tia imputata, vel inchoata. Hanc intelligit Chry- sostomus: justitiam dicit quamlibet virtutem, pieta- tis scil. quæ in recta vita consistit: quem sequitur Theophylactus: Videtur autem potius illam intel- ligere Apostolus: Nam dilectionis nomine, quæ impletio legis est, omnis virtus comprehendi- tur. Sectari autem jubemur justitiam, quæ fide apprehenditur, ideo fidei præmittitur, Rom. IX. vers. 31. Διώκων νόμον δικαιοσύνης, & vers. 30. τὰ μὴ διώκοντα δικαιοσύνην, ubi additur etiam mentio fidei, κατέλαβε δικαιοσύνην, δικαιοσύνην δὲ τὴν ἐκ πίστεως. Similis est locus 1. Tim. VI. vers. 11. Per πίστιν ergo hoc loco fidem justificantem intelligi- mus: quam sectari oportet, ut justitiam illam con- sequamur. Fidem hanc, quæ per charitatem ἐν- εργουμένη Gal. V. vers. 6. sequitur dilectio DEI & proximi, quam prosequi jubemur 1. Cor. XIV. 1. διώκετε τὴν ἀγάπην, hæc concordiæ studium im- portat: quo pacem quærimus & persequimur, jubente Petro 1. Ep. III. 11. ζητησάτω εἰρήνην, καὶ διωξάτω ἀυτὴν, idque μετὰ πάντων, Ebr. XII. 14. Hic tamen imprimis respicitur concordia Spiritua- lis, quam non cum hostibus veritatis, qualis Hy- meneus, & Philetus erant, quos fugere & aversari debuit, sed μετὰ τῶν ἐπικαλομένων τὸν κύριον ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας, cum vere fidelibus, quia per fi- dem purificantur corda, Actor. XV. vers. 9. ex puro corde invocantibus Dominum, quæ descriptio est fidelium, Rom. X. 11. qui corde credunt ad justitiam, ore confitentur ad salutem v. 10. objectum ergo, vel correlatum pacis, non vero communio, & socii pa- cis (ut Thomas & Cajetanus voluere) hac περι- φράσει notatur, ut e simili loco Ebræor. XII. vers. 14. patet. Ita Chrysostomus: Illis solum confide, non qui temere, sed absque dolo & simulatione in- vocant, quibus nihil inest fraudis, qui cum pace ad invocandum pergunt, qui non litigant: illis itaque tantum accede socius, & cum eis preces misce, a cæteris abstine. Sic etiam Theophylactus, & ante illos Theodoretius: qui diligendos quidem omnes ait, sed pacem sinceram, qua opus habet commu- ni electione & voluntate, vel in consensu animorum consistit cum iis coli, qui ex puro corde Dominum invocant. Aliud est pax externa & politica, aliud pax interna & mystica. Illam omnes exercere de- bent erga quoslibet, hæc soli DEO atque ejus pie fidelibus ultro citroque intercedit. Illius vin- culum dependet tum è naturæ lege, tum è voca- tione ad gratiæ communionem: hujus fundamen- tum tum in consensu de veritate cœlesti, tum in voluntatum atque animorum pia conjunctione consistit. De illa Ebr. XII. 14. de hac 2. Cor. VI. v. 14. Quod discrimen non attendunt Syncreti- stæ, cum errantes jubent distinguere ab erroribus, firmamentum doctrinæ à personis eodem insertis. Vid. Bergii Stereom. pag. 250. Nam spiritualis communio non tam respicit personas, quam fi- dem, vel certè ob fidem personas. Non enim hæc est mystica conjunctio, qua homines sese mu- tuo ferunt, & in externa quadam societate paca- tè agunt, sed quæ præstat, ut unum sint Spiritu. Cons. Beat. Luth. Tom. III. Jen. Germ. f. 341.

## 2:23
Vers. 23.

Τὰς δὲ μωρὰς ϰὴ ἀπαιδεύτους ζητήσεις παραιτῶ) This is the same admonition as 1 Tim. I. 4 and VI. 4. He calls those questions μωρὰς (foolish) because they pertain nothing to true and saving wisdom. ἀπαιδεύτους is אין מוסר as in Prov. V. 23, those who reject correction, as is said in Prov. XV. 4. ἀπαί- δευτος is also accustomed to be put for כסל as in Prov. VIII. v. 5, XV. 15, and לץ in Prov. XV. 13, and for נבל in Prov. XVII. 22; it is also read in Wisd. XVII. 1 and several times in Sirach. Paul understands here immodest questions: for the Greeks also say ἀπαίδευτον for ἀκόλαστος, because ϰολάζειν and παιδεύειν are the same.

Εἰδὼς ὅτι γεννῶσι μάχας) That is, strifes, quarrels. So also Tit. III. 9. The Hebrew מדון is sometimes translated as ἀντιλογίαν (contradiction), sometimes as μάχην (strife).

Latin:

Vers. 23.

Τὰς δὲ μωρὰς ϰὴ ἀπαιδεύτους ζητήσεις παραιτῶ) Est eadem admonitio, quæ 1. Tim. I. 4. & VI. 4. μωρὰς vocat illas quæstiones, quia ad veram & salutarem sapientiam nihil pertinent. ἀπαιδεύτους אין מוסר ut Prov. V. 23. qui re- spuunt correctionem, ut dicitur Prov. XV. 4. Solet & ἀπαί- δευτος poni pro כסל ut Prov. VIII. v. 5. XV. 15. & לץ Prov. XV. 13. & pro נבל Prov. XVII. 22. legitur & Sap. XVII. 1. & apud Sirachidem aliquoties. Intelligit hic Pau- lus quæstiones immodestas: nam & Græci pro ἀκόλαστος dicunt ἀπαίδευτον, quia idem est ϰολάζειν & παιδεύειν.

Εἰδὼς ὅτι γεννῶσι μάχας) Id est, lites, jurgia. Sic & Tit. III. 9. Hebræum מדון modò ἀντιλογίαν vertitur, modo μάχην.

## 2:24
v. 24. Δῦλον δὲ Κυρίε) Of Christ, who is so patient and peaceful.

ἐ δεῖ μάχεσθαι) To wrangle: גור as in Gen. XXVI. 20. So also John VI. 52. So also in Aristophanes: ἐ μαχῦμαί σοι, I will not contend with you in words.

So far those things which concerned the person of Timothy: now those which look to his office follow. Where again he first removes what is to be avoided, then demands what is to be observed. He removes, just as useless contentions and fights, so also foolish questions, and those which arise from contention, and not for any utility, as Theodoret explains ἀπαιδεύτους. See, says Theophylact, how he everywhere averts him from inquiring and disputing: and not indeed because he trusted less that Timothy could refute others, but because it seemed altogether useless to enter upon a contest of this kind, which had nothing of good in it besides contentions and hatreds. These, therefore, he calls foolish questions, although it is established that they are otherwise not insipid in the sacred scriptures. Chrysostom had preceded him thus: You see how he everywhere keeps him away from questions, not that he was not fit to overturn them: otherwise he would have said, be fit to overturn them, just as when he said: Attend to reading: for by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear. But he knew that it was altogether useless to undergo contests of this kind, and that they would have no end except quarrels, hatreds, injuries, and curses; these, therefore, he says, avoid these questions. But there are other very useful questions about the Scriptures, about other necessary things, from which he by no means prohibits us: but so that in inquiring, strifes, quarrels, and wrangles cease. For these things ought to be far from him who is a servant of the GOD of peace. The Vulgate renders ἀπαιδεύτους as 'without discipline.' Ambrose as 'senseless and unlearned.' Crocius rightly: He calls them foolish, not those which seem such before the world, nor those which have no sharpness, but those which have nothing of divine wisdom, nor make one wise unto salvation. He calls them unlearned, not because they are moved by the unskilled or unlearned, but because they are not useful for teaching truth and piety, or for edification, which is according to piety. Ambrosiaster refers that to the questions of the Gentiles and heretics. Salmero adds Judaizers too narrowly. Still too narrowly. Sometimes others also slip into them. Therefore he does not name them the foolish questions of Judaizers, pagans, and heretics, but absolutely foolish, i.e., by whomever they may be proposed. Immodesty, and when correction is rejected, pertain to the manner of the disputations, not to the object or the periphrasis of the same. The Vulgate rendered παραιτẽ as 'avoid': But it is more emphatic: Reject, disapprove, exclude from the Church. He commands, therefore, that he neither bring them onto the stage of the Church himself, nor allow them to be produced and agitated by others. Which beget only fights and word-battles, as in 1 Tim. VI. v. 4. For it is not rarely the case that there is more ardent contention about those things which contribute nothing to piety than about matters of faith. He therefore gives the reason for the command: because it does not befit a servant of the Lord, or a minister of the word, to wrangle and fight about matters of no moment: inasmuch as he ought to study gentleness. GOD is not of dissension, but of peace, 1 Cor. XIV. 33. From His servants, therefore, contentions ought to be absent, since they ought to imitate their Lord.

ἀλλ᾽ ἤπιον εἶναι πρὸς πάντας) To be gentle. So 1 Thess. II. v. 7. And Homer, 'and he was gentle as a father.' In the Glossary: ἤπιος, tranquil, meek, ענו.

Now it demands what things are to be observed: It requires, namely, that the Servant of the Lord be first ἤπιος πρὸς πάντας. But does this also apply to the enemies of the truth? These, at any rate, he ought to refute and confute ἀποτόμως, severely. Tit. I. verse 3. But that is perfectly consistent with gentleness: For severity shows zeal for the heavenly truth, which must be propagated in such a way that love for it is not lukewarm, but is perceived by true faith and piety toward God, and the correction of the heterodox is instituted with becoming authority and ardor; but gentleness, for the sake of testifying to love toward the salvation and conversion of one's neighbor, demands moderation of emotions and words, so that he may understand that the correction and refutation proceed from a friendly affection, and it may be recognized that the reduction of the erring one to the path is sought, not his confusion: For this also belongs to meekness, (ἀποτόμως ἐλέγχειν) when it is done in such a way that one does not depart from meekness, it is that which is most accustomed to work excellently, which is its own. For it is indeed permitted to rebuke more sharply with meekness than to confound with audacity and ferocity.

Διδακτικὸν) See 1 Tim. III. 2.

According to this is the requirement of the Servant of the Lord, which the Vulgate wrongly rendered as 'teachable.' For it denotes him who is apt for teaching others, πρὸς πάντας τὲς βυλομένυς διδαχθῆναι, as Chrysostom speaks; such as are not heretics, upon whom, therefore, there is no reason for us to spend effort in instructing, since oil and labor are lost where they have been warned once and again, Tit. III. verse 10.

Ἀνεξίκακον) In the Glossary ἀνεξίκακος, patient; ἀνεξικακία, clemency, patience. What in the Digests is 'to accommodate patience,' that in the Basilics is ἀνεξικακεῖν. Wisd. II. verse 19, the Latin translates ἀνεξικακία as patience. This ἀνεξικακία is to be understood concerning those things which are done outside of ecclesiastical censure.

Chrysostom also understood it thus, that the Servant of the Lord must indeed be patient. For that, he says, is absolutely necessary, otherwise the rest is done in vain: For if fishermen, when they have often cast their nets all day in vain, do not yet desist, nor despair: much more does it befit us to do so.

And see how usefully this is done. It often happens that while constant teaching lets fruit slip into the mind, the vice by which it is disturbed falls away. Blessed Gerhard notes that the Vulgate translates it as patience, but more correctly as tolerance, and he responds to the ἐναντιοφάνειαν from Apoc. II. v. 2: The wicked ought not to be tolerated in such a way that we wish to flatter their vices and wink at them; but so that their perversity may be overcome by gentleness, as long as there still remains some hope of conversion. Not all are good in the Church. The wicked are mixed with the good. There are modest ones, there are immodest and importunate ones, there are tractable ones, there are hard, stubborn, and perverse ones: There are detractors; these one ought to tolerate, no differently than a physician tolerates the ravings and foolishness of a madman or even of one suffering from a fever. Nor are all who will one day be good always good. There are sometimes very wicked people who eventually become good. They hardly behave well toward the Ministry. If a minister wished to thunder immediately, or to abandon such people, he would lose those who are corrected by gentleness. But some also remain wicked. Here the Apostle brings the law of tolerance to the servant of the Lord, namely, as long as any hope of conversion remains, says Crocius here.

Latin:

v. 24. Δῦλον δὲ Κυρίε) Christi adeo patientis atqúe pa- cifici.

ἐ δεῖ μάχεσθαι) Rixari: גור ut Gen. XXVI. 20. Sic & Joh. VI. 52. Sic & apud Aristophanem: ἐ μαχῦμαί σοι non contendam tecum verbis.

Hactenus ea, quæ personam Timothei concer- nebant: Jam quæ ad officium ejus spectant, sequun- tur. Ubi iterum primum removet, quæ vitanda, deinde postulat, quæ observanda. Removet, ut contentiones & pugnas inutiles, ita & quæstiones stultas, & quæ ex contentione fiunt, & non pro- pter aliquam utilitatem, ut ἀπαιδεύτους exponit Theodoretus. Vide, inquit Theophylactus, quem- admodum ubique hunc ab inquirendo & disce- ptando avertat: Nec eo quidem quod minus con- fideret Timotheum alios posse refellere, sed quia prorsus videretur inutile hujusmodi certamen ad- ire, quod præter contentiones & odia nil in se boni haberet. Has itaque stultas nuncupat quæstiones, cum aliàs esse non insulsas in sacris literis constet. Cui sic præiverat Chrysostomus: Vides ut ubique illum quæstionibus arceat, non quod ille idoneus non fuerit eas evertere: alioqui dixisset, curæ idoneus fieri ad eas evertendas, sicuti cum dixit: Intende lectioni: hoc enim faciens & teipsum salvum fa- cies, & eos, qui audiunt. Verum noverat, esse pror- sus inutile hujusmodi subire certamina, nullumque finem habitura, nisi rixas, odia, injurias, male- dicta, has ergo, inquit, quæstiones devita. Sunt au- tem alia perutiles quæstiones de Scripturis, de aliis necessariis, à quibus ille nos minimè prohibet: sed ita, ut in conquirendo cessent lites, jurgia, rixæ. Procul enim ista esse debent ab eo, qui DEI pacis servus est. Ἀπαιδεύτους Vulgatus reddit sine disci- plina. Ambrosius insensatas & ineruditas. Rectè Crocius: Vocat stultas, non quæ coram mundo tales videntur, nec quæ nihil habent acuminis, sed quæ nihil habent divinæ sapientiæ, nec sapientem red- dunt ad salutem. Ineruditas vocat, non quod ab imperitis seu indoctis moveantur, sed quæ non utiles sunt ad docendam veritatem, pietatemque, seu ad ædificationem, quæ est secundum pietatem. Id ad Gentilium & hæreticorum quæstiones refert Am- brosiaster. Nimis angustè Salmero addit Judai- zantes. Adhuc nimis angustè. Interdum & alii ad eas dilabuntur. Ideo non nominat, stultas Ju- daizantium, paganorum & hæreticorum quæstio- nes, sed absolutè stultas, scil. à quocunque tandem proponantur. Immodestia, & cum respuitur, corre- ctio, ad modum disputationum, non ad objectum vel περίφρασιν ejusdem pertinent. παραιτẽ Vulg. wacai- reddidit devita: Sed ἐμφατικώτερον illud est: Reji- ce, improba, exclude ab Ecclesia. Præcipit ergò, ut nec ipse eos in Ecclesiæ proscenium adducat, neque ab aliis produci, & agitari sinat. Quæ pu- gnas tantum & λογομαχίας gignunt, ut 1. Tim. VI. v. 4. Non rarò enim fit, ut ardentiori conten- tione dimicetur de iis, quæ ad pietatem nihil fa- ciunt, quàm de rebus fidei. Reddit itaque cau- sam præcepti: quod servum Domini, vel ministrum verbi non deceat de rebus nullius momenti ri- xari, ac pugnare: utpote qui lenitati studere de- beat. DEUS non dissensionis est, sed pacis, 1. Cor. XIV. 33. Ab ejus ergò servis contentiones abesse decet, cum Dominum suum imitari de- beant.

ἀλλ᾽ ἤπιον εἶναι πρὸς πάντας) Lenem esse. Sic 1. Thess. II. vers. 7. Et Homerus, πατὴρ δ᾽ ὡς ἤπιος ἦεν. In Glossario: ἤπιος tranquillus, mansuetus, ענו.

Jam postulat, quæ observanda: Requirit nem- pè, Servus Domini sit primò ἤπιος πρὸς πάντας. Sed num etiam erga veritatis hostes? Hos utique ἀποτόμως severè redarguere, ac refutare debet. Tit. I. vers. 3. Sed id cum lenitate probe confi- stit: Nam severitas zelum ostendit pro cœlesti veritate, quæ ita propaganda est, ut amor ejusdem non tepidus, sed vera fide, ac pietate erga Deum deprehendatur, ac decenti autoritate, atque ar- dore correptio heterodoxorum instituatur; le- nitas vero amoris erga salutem & conversionem proximi testandi causa moderationem affectuum, & verborum postulat, ut ab amico affectu corre- ptionem, & confutationem proficisci intelligat, & reductionem errantis in viam, non confusionem quæri agnoscatur: Nam & hoc mansuetudinis est, (ἀποτόμως ἐλέγχειν) Quando ita fit, ut à man- suetudine non discedatur, ea maximè est, quæ ope- rari consuevit egregiè, quod suum est. Licet enim profectò acrius cum mansuetudine carpere, quàm cum audacia & feritate confundere.

Διδακτικὸν) Vide 1. Tim. III. 2.

Secundum hoc requisitum est Servi Domini, quod docibilem Vulgata perperam reddidit. No- tatur enim is, qui ad docendum alios aptus est, πρὸς πάντας τὲς βυλομένυς διδαχθῆναι, ut Chry- sostomus loquitur; quales non sunt hæretici, qui- bus proinde informandis non est, quod operam impendamus, quum oleum atque opera perda- tur, ubi semel atque iterum moniti sunt, Tit. III. vers. 10.

Ἀνεξίκακον) In Glossario ἀνεξίκακος, patiens, ἀνεξικακία clementia, patientia. Quod in Digestis est patientiam ac- commodare, id in Basilicis ἀνεξικακεῖν. Sap. II. vers. 19. ἀνεξικακίαν Latinus vertit patientiam. Hæc ἀνεξικακία in- telligenda de iis, quæ fiunt extra censuram Ecclesiasti- cam.

Ita etiam intellexit Chrysostomus, quod nempe patiens esse debeat Servus Domini. Id quippe, in- quit, prorsus necessarium est, alioqui cætera in cas- sum fiunt: Si enim piscatores cum sæpe die tota frustra jactaverint retia, non tamen desistunt, ne- que desperant: multò magis nos id facere convenit.

Et vide, quam id utiliter fiat. Sæpe fit, ut dum as- sidua doctrina fructus illabitur animo, vitium, quo ille perturbatur, excidat. Vulgatus patientiam sed rectius exponi tolerantiam notat Beat. Ger- bardus, & ad ἐναντιοφάνειαν ex Apoc. II. v. 2. respondet: Non debent mali tolerari eo modo, ut velimus eorum vitiis abblandiri, & ad ea con- nivere; sed ut mansuetudine eorum protervia su- peretur, quamdiu adhuc aliqua conversionis spes superest. Non omnes Boni in Ecclesia. Mali bonis permixti. Sunt modesti, sunt immodesti ac impor- tuni, sunt tractabiles, sunt duri, pervicaces, proter- vi: Sunt obtrectatores, hos tolerare debet, non aliter, ac medicus tolerat phrenetici, aut etiam fe- bricitantis convitia, atque ineptias. Nec omnes, qui aliquando futuri sunt boni, omnes semper sunt boni. Sunt interdum valde mali, qui tandem fiunt boni. Illi vix bene se gerunt erga Ministerium. Si mini- ster vellet mox fulminare, aut tales deserere, per- deret, qui lenitate corriguntur. Sed etiam aliqui manent mali. Hic tolerandi legem fert servo Domi- ni Apostolus, scil. quamdiu spes ulla conversionis superest, ait hic Crocius.

## 2:25
Vers. 25.

Ἐν πραότητι παιδεύοντα τὰς ἀντιδιατιθεμένους. See 1 Tim. VI. vers. 11. Those who err are to be treated gently, not exasperated with curses. Ἀντιδιατιθεμένους, those otherwise disposed than we are. For τὴν γνώμην διατεθῆναι for διακεῖσθαι is also found in Isocrates.

This is the fourth requirement of a Doctor, that he show modesty and gentleness above all in the instruction of those for whom there is some hope. For through quarrels, as Theophylact says, and contentions, nothing good is learned: There is therefore a certain special modesty to be maintained toward him whom you are teaching. Someone will say: In what way can anyone show himself human and mild toward one who is reckless and contumelious? In what way, you ask, if you have driven away one who is ensnared by some heresy after one or two rebukes? For he cannot be corrected, and is incurable. But in this place he is discoursing about those who are not yet to be despaired of, so that some capacity for returning to health remains. Which is surely clear from what follows. Thus far Theophylact. Regarding ecclesiastical censure also, Blessed Gerhardus: Although according to the nature of the objects, and likewise of time and place, a minister of the Church must sometimes apply rigor; yet he ought to temper that rigor with gentleness, and perpetually retain the affection of gentleness fixed in his mind. The Vulgate translates πραότη͵τα as modesty: but that word properly signifies gentleness. παιδευον͵τα, which it rendered as correcting, is more correctly explained in this place as instructing. For instruction ought to precede correction in those who are still ignorant of the truth. August. ad Gal. VI. tom. III. How in modesty? How correcting? Unless we retain gentleness in our heart, and sprinkle some sharpness of medicine with the word of correction. The Vulgate translates ἀντιδιατιθεμένους as those who resist the truth. But the name of truth is not in the source, nor in the more corrected Latin codices, as Salmeron and Justin admit. The dative, VERITATI, says Estius, was added either by the interpreter, or rather by the scribes, because it seemed that something of the sort was missing, or certainly it flowed from the following chapter, where it is said: so also these resist the truth. For the Greek and Syriac do not recognize it, just as the Greek commentators do not, and among the Latins, the one bearing the title of Ambrose, and some others, it is not read in many MSS. codices of the bibles. Ambrosiaster explains it as those who think differently, and so does August. lib. de corrept. & grat. c. 5. l. 1. contr.

Cresc. Grammat. c. 6. The Apostle does not mean the malicious, or even obstinate heretics: But those who, either from perverse upbringing, or from the company of the wicked, or from elsewhere, have imbibed false opinions, and have either not recognized the truth, or if they have recognized it, have been led into error by the cunning persuasions of heretics. The Apostle had previously dealt with gentleness in general, now he warns specifically regarding the manner of treating τοὺς ἐναντιοφρονοῦντας, prescribing the manner of instruction. Augustine noted somewhere that not only those who resist the truth are understood, but also those who oppose themselves by wicked works: since few contradict with their tongues, but most by living badly. However, it is to be believed that these are especially noted by that,

Μηποτε δω αυτοις ο Θεος μετανοιαν) By testing whether GOD may give them repentance, as the rightly learned have explained. For we have μηποτε for 'whether' in Luke III. vers. 15. John VII. v. 8. We have the omission of a similar verb before ειποτε, Acts XXVII. v. 12. Rom. XI. 14. The Hebrews would say אולי. God does not give repentance to all who resist the calling. For some He takes from life either among their sins, or even hardens them. In whom this is to be done, and in whom not, it is for Him alone to know: It is for men to try everything for the salvation of others.

Εις επιγνωσιν αληθειας) A manuscript adds ελθειν, so that these words may be an explanation of what preceded μετανοιαν, if by chance, he says, GOD may give them a better mind, that is, so that they may arrive at the acknowledgment of that truth which they now oppose.

The end of the gentle instruction of those who oppose themselves is both repentance from errors, when they are soundly convinced of them, and the acknowledgment of the truth, to which they are to be soundly led by the addition of information. Εις επιγνωσιν is not 'through acknowledgment': but what the customary meaning of the preposition implies, 'to the acknowledgment of the truth.' Estius very rashly gathers from these words that faith is prior to repentance in the justification of man: for neither is justification being treated here, nor saving faith, which is not prior to repentance, but a part of it: but dogmatic or historical [faith], as they call it, to the acknowledgment of the doctrine of faith, which we do not deny is prior to repentance. Nor, finally, are those who resist, or who think differently, to be led through faith to repentance, but through gentle instruction to repentance from errors, and thence further to the acknowledgment of the doctrine of faith, and at length to sobriety from the snares of the Devil: so that they may acknowledge both the manner of the seduction, because they have been ensnared by false doctrines; and the danger of the snares by which they are entangled, when they are led captive by the Devil at his will: so that these things may be referred to repentance not only of errors, but also of vices and sins. Μετανοια is understood either as entire repentance, or as only the acknowledgment of the false and the evil, which is a step toward acknowledging the truth, which belongs both to doctrine and to life, see John 3:20-21, Eph. 4:21, 23. Which acknowledgment of the truth is to be understood with affection, by which, having abandoned error, we embrace the truth, and having abandoned sin, we embrace righteousness. It is therefore more fitting to understand μετανοιαν here partially rather than wholly, so that the particle Εις may be taken as indicating the end.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

Ἐν πραότητι παιδεύοντα τὰς ἀντιδιατιθεμένους. Vide 1. Tim. VI. vers. 11. qui errant, leniter tractandi, non maledictis exasperandi. Ἀντιδιατιθεμένους, aliter affectos, quam nos sumus. Nam τὴν γνώμην διατεθῆναι pro διακεῖσθαι est etiam apud Isocratem.

Quartum hoc est Doctoris requisitum, ut im- primis modestiam & mansuetudinem ostendat in informatione eorum, de quibus spes aliqua super- est. Per jurgia namque, dicente Theophylacto, & contentiones nil boni perdisciter: Est itaque præci- pua quædam erga eum, quem doceas, servanda mo- destia. Dicet aliquis: Quo pacto poterit quispiam erga eum, qui temerarius sit, & contumeliosus, humanum se, & mitem præbere? Quo pacto, in- quis, Si eum, qui sit hæresi aliqua irretitus, post unam alteramque castigationem abegeris? Is nam- que corrigi nequit, & insanabilis est. Verum hoc loco de his, qui nondum sunt desperandi, quo minus aliqua restet ad sanitatem redeundi facultas, edisse- rit. Quod sane ex sequentibus patet. Hactenus Theophylactus. De censura etiam Ecclesiastica recte monet Beat. Gerhardus: Quamvis pro ra- tione objectorum, temporis item ac loci minister Ecclesiæ quandoque rigorem adhibere debeat; ta- men rigorem illum mansuetudine debet temperare, & mansuetudinis affectum animo infixum perpetuò retinere. Πραότη͵τα Vulgata vertit modestiam: sed vox illa propriè significat mansuetudinem. παι- δευον͵τα, quam reddidit corripientem, rectius expo- nitur hoc loco erudientem. Præcedere enim de- bet informatio correptionem in illis, qui verita- tem adhuc ignorant. August. ad Gal. VI. tom. III. Quomodo in modestia? quomodo corripientem? nisi cum lenitatem corde retinemus, & aliquam medi- camenti acrimoniam verbo correptionis aspergi- mus. Ἀντιδιατιθεμένους Vulgata vertit, qui resistunt veritati. Sed veritatis nomen non est in fonte, nec in emendatioribus Latinis Codd. fatente Sal- merone, ac Justin. Dativus, VERITATI, inquit Estius, additus est vel ab interprete, vel potius a scribis, quod videretur aliquid tale deesse, aut certe affusus ex capite sequenti, ubi dicitur: ita & hi resi- stunt veritati. Nam Græca & Syriaca non agno- scunt, uti nec Græci commentatores & inter Lati- nos Ambrosii titulum habens, aliiqve nonnulli, in multis etiam MSS. bibliorum codicibus non legi- tur. Ambrosiaster exponit, qui diversa sentiunt, sic & August. lib. de corrept. & grat. c. 5. l. 1. contr.

Cresc. Grammat. c. 6. Non intelligit Apostolus maliciosos, aut obstinatos etiam haereticos: Sed qui vel ex prava institutione, vel malorum con- versatione, vel aliunde falsas hauserunt opiniones, & veritatem vel non agnoverunt, vel si agnove- runt, in errorem abrepti sunt callidis haeretico- rum persuasionibus. Prius de lenitate communiter egerat Apostolus, jam quoad modum tractandi τους εναντιοφρονουντας, peculiariter monet τροπον παιδειας praescribens. Non tamen solum eos, qui veritati resistunt, sed etiam, qui se opponunt, operibus malignis, intelligi, Augustinus alicubi monuit: cum pauci contradicant linguis, plurimi male vivendo. Illo autem praecipue hos notari, credendum,

Μηποτε δω αυτοις ο Θεος μετανοιαν) Experiendo an det: illis DEUS poenitentiam, ut recte eruditi exposuere. Nam μηποτε pro an habemus Luc. III. vers. 15. Joh. VII. v. 8. Reti centiam vero verbi similis ante ειποτε habemus, Act. XXVII. v. 12. Rom. XI. 14. Hebraei dicerent אולי. Non omnibus, qui vocationi reluctantur, dat Deus poeniten- tiam. Nam quosdam aut inter peccata e vita eripit, aut etiam obdurat. In quibus autem hoc faciendum, in quibus non, ipsius solius est nosse: Hominum tentare omnia pro aliorum salute.

Εις επιγνωσιν αληθειας) ελθειν addit Manuscriptus, ut haec verba εξηγησις sint ejus, quod praecessit μετανοιαν, si forte, inquit, det DEUS illis mentem meliorem, id est, ut per- veniant ad agnitionem ejus veritatis, quam nunc oppu- gnant.

Finis mansuetae παιδειας των αντιδιατιθεμενων est tum poenitentia ab erroribus, cum de iisdem solide convincuntur, tum agnitio veritatis, ad quam perducendi solide sunt accedente informa- tione. Εις επιγνωσιν non est per agnitionem: sed quod usitata praepositionis significatio infert, ad agnitionem veritatis. Valde temere Estius colligit ex hisce verbis, priorem in hominis justificatione fidem esse, quam poenitentiam: nam nec de justi- ficatione hic agitur, nec de fide salutifera, quae non est prior poenitentia, sed pars ejus: sed de dogmatica vel historica, quam vocant, ad agnitio- nem doctrinae fidei, quam priorem esse poeniten- tia, non negamus. Nec denique per fidem ad poe- nitentiam, sed per παιδειαν mansuetam ad erro- rum poenitentiam, & inde porro ad doctrinae fidei agnitionem, adducendi sunt, qui resistunt, aut qui diversa sentiunt, tandem ad sobrietatem a laqueis Diaboli: ut agnoscant etiam tum modum sedu- ctionis, quia illaqueati sunt falsis doctrinis; tum periculum laqueorum, quibus implicati sunt, cum a Diabolo pro voluntate ipsius captivi ducuntur: ut haec referantur ad poenitentiam non errorum tantum, sed etiam vitiorum & peccatorum. Με- τανοια vel de integra poenitentia accipitur, vel de sola falsi, & mali agnitione, quae gradus est ad agnoscendam veritatem, quae & doctrinae est, & vitae, vid. Johan. III. vers. 20. 21. Eph. IV. 21. 23. Quae veritatis agnitio intelligenda cum affectu, qua relicto errore veritatem, relicto peccato justitiam amplectimur. Magis ergo convenit μετανοιαν hic μερικως intelligere, quam ολικως, ut particula Εις finaliter accipiatur.

## 2:26
Vers. 26.

Και ανανηψωσιν εκ τῆς του διαβολου παγιδος) ανανηφειν is the same as εκνηφειν, Gen. 9:4, 1 Sam. 25:27, Joel 1:5, properly to return to oneself from wine, but by metaphor it is used for liberation from all other things that disturb the mind, as can be seen in Hab. 2:7, 1 Cor. 11:34. The snare of the Devil is pleasures, which make a man as if intoxicated. We are freed from these through Christ, Isa. 42:7.

Εζωγρημενοι ὑπ' αυτου) For they are held captive by the Devil. Ζωγρειν is a word properly used in war. 'Spare them, son of Atreus,' but it began to be used more broadly, as can be seen in Luke 5:10.

This repentance, as the Vulgate translates it, or rather awakening, or sobriety, because both are signified by that word, from the snares of the Devil, is a consequence of the acknowledgment of the truth, or an adjunct, because when someone is brought to the acknowledgment of the truth, he awakens from that drunkenness by which he had been ensnared through errors or crimes: and he returns to sobriety and is freed Νήφειν is opposed to τῷ μεθύειν, to be drunk, and it is also to awaken: therefore ἀνανήφειν is to return to sobriety of mind, and to awaken. Beza translates, 'that they may recover their sanity of mind,' because of the words which are brought forward, 'that they may escape' (from the Devil's snare). Concerning which he holds thus: The translation is from the sense of the body to the mind by consequence, because those who are sober and temperate are also sound in mind, whereas in the drunk neither the mind nor the body performs its duty. For τὸ νήφειν and τὸ μεθύειν are opposed both properly concerning the body, and metaphorically concerning the mind. I would prefer, however, to interpret it as sanity rather than sobriety of mind; it is both more perspicuous and more Latin. I expressed the participle 'evasuri' [that they may escape], so that I might soften the harsher construction of the preposition ἐκ, concerning which Hebrew idiom I have spoken elsewhere at length, but especially in Matt. IV. verse 8, and I shall speak in Heb. V. 7. The Syrian interpreter, however, not ineptly, if you look at the sense, took τὸ ἀνανήφωσιν for 'to be mindful of oneself,' that is, to return to oneself, and he also supplied the ellipsis with these words, with our Tremellius as interpreter, 'that they may be mindful of themselves, and may escape from the Devil's snare.' Blessed Luther: 'that they may become sober again from the Devil's snare.' The following words

having been taken alive by him, are metaphorical, as is also the noun παγίδος, taken from hunters, who entangle and wrap wild beasts in snares or nets, so that they may take them alive; for ζωγρεῖν properly signifies to be taken alive, i.e., ζῶντα ἀγρεῦσαι. For the Devil, that infernal hunter, takes men alive when he wraps them in the nets or snares of his temptations. Which fits better than if it were taken as a military term; for in war men are not accustomed to be taken by snares. Theophylact holds it here thus, having closely followed Chrysostom: Understand that these things are said not only concerning the doctrines themselves, but concerning a more upright manner of living. For mortals are ensnared by the devil not only by the error of the doctrines themselves, but by the vices of life. Whence it happens that those who are deceived as to how this life should be led, are to be corrected more modestly and kindly.
