For as a sparrow, if it is grasped by even one part of its foot, is under the power of him who has set the trap, so also they, even if we are less ensnared by both feet, namely by faith and life, yet by mere wicked actions of life, we will be subject to the dominion of the devil.

To His will) OF GOD; for this must be construed with that ἀνανήψωσι, with a mark of distinction placed after ὑπ᾽ αὐτȣ. To the will OF GOD, namely to be done, Eph. VI. 6.

Theophylact also explained it concerning the will of GOD, and Beza understands it of that, even if in his translation he followed the more common opinion, which is concerning the pleasure of the Devil: referring this pronoun to the nearest noun: which Theophylact also brought forward, and seems to have approved, and Chrysostom seems to look to it in Homily XXXVII on Matthew: 'All men, before we sin, indeed have free will, whether we wish to follow the will of the Devil or not. But if, once sinning, we have bound ourselves to his works, we can no longer escape by our own virtue: but just as a ship with a broken rudder is led thither where the storm wills: so also man, having lost the help of divine grace through sin, does not do what he wills, but what the Devil wills, and unless GOD with the mighty hand of His mercy shall have loosened him, he will remain in the bonds of his sins until death,' etc. Anselm, book on Similitudes, chapter 189. Like a boy (who keeps a little bird tied by a thread, and lets it fly hither and thither, but soon pulls it back), the Devil plays with sinners, whom, ensnared in his snares, he drags according to his own will into various impediments of vices. For there are many who are avaricious, drunken, lustful, who propose to abandon avarice, gluttony, and lust, and think that like a bird they will fly away freely, but because they are held by the enemy, ensnared by the practice of sin, they are cast back into the same vices against their will, and this happens quite often, nor are they liberated in every way, unless by great effort and the grace of GOD the thread of wicked habit is broken.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

Και ανανηψωσιν εκ τῆς του διαβολου παγιδος) ανανηφειν idem quod εκνηφειν, Gen. IX. 4. 1. Sam. XXV. 27. Joel. I. vers. 5. proprie e vino ad se redire, sed per translationem usurpatur ad liberationem ab omnibus rebus aliis, quae mentem turbant, ut videre est Abac. II. 7. 1. Cor. XI. vers. 34. Laqueus Diaboli sunt voluptates, quae hominem faciunt velut temulentum. Ab his liberamur per Christum, Es. XLII. v. 7.

Εζωγρημενοι ὑπ' αυτου) Capti enim a Diabolo tenen- tur. Ζωγρειν vox proprie bellica. Ζωγρει Ατρεος ὑιε, sed la- tius usurpari coepit, ut videre est Luc. V. 10.

Haec resipiscentia, ut Vulg. vertit, vel potius evigilatio, vel sobrietas, quia utraque significatur illa voce, à laqueis Diaboli, est consequens agni- tionis veritatis, vel adjunctum, quia cum ad ve- ritatis agnitionem perductus quis est, evigilat ab illa ebrietate, qua per errores, aut crimina illa- queatus fuerat: & ad sobrietatem redit ac libera- tur à laqueis, quibus erat implicatus. Νήφειν op- ponitur τῷ μεθύειν ebrium esse, estque etiam evigi- lare: ideò ἀνανήφειν est ad sobrietatem mentis redire, & evigilare. Beza vertit, sanitatem mentis recipiant, ob ea, quæ adducuntur, verba, evasuri (ex Diaboli laqueo.) Quo de ita habet: Transla- tio est à corporis sensu ad animum ex consequenti, quod sobrii & temperantes animo quoque valeant, contra in ebriis neq; mens neq; corpus officium faciat. Opponuntur enim & propriè de corpore, & metapho- ricè de animo τὸ νήφειν & τὸ μεθύειν. Malim tamen sanitatem, quàm sobrietatem mentis interpretari; magis tum perspicuè, tum Latinè. Participium au- tem evasuri, expressi, ut duriorem constructionem præpositionis ἐκ emollirem, de quo Ebræorum idio- tismo passim alibi dixi, at præsertim Matth. IV. vers. 8. & dicam Ebr. V. 7. Syrus autem interpres τὸ ἀνανήφωσιν non ineptè, si sensum spectes, accepit pro memorem esse sui, id est, ad se redire, & ellipsin quoque supplevit, his verbis, Tremellio nostro inter- prete, ut memores sint sui, & eripiant ex Diaboli laqueo. Beat. Lutherus: daß sie wieder nüchtern werden aus des Teuffels Strick. Verba sequentia

ἐζωγρημένοι ὑπ᾽ αὐτȣ, capti ab ipso, metaphorica sunt, ut & nomen παγίδος, à venatoribus desum- pta, qui feras laqueis vel retibus implicant & In- volvunt, ut easdem vivas capiant; ζωγρεῖν enim propriè significat vivum capi, q. d. ζῶντα ἀγρεῦσαι. Nam Diabolus venator ille infernalis vivos capit homines, quando illos tentationum suarum re- tibus, vel laqueis involvit. Quod magis conve- nit, quàm si accipiatur ut vox bellica; nam in bello laqueis homines non solent capi. Theo- phylactus hic ita habet, Chrysostomum pressè secutus: Hoc non solùm de ipsis dogmatibus, sed de rectiori vivendi modo dicta esse intellige. Quip- pe cum non solum dogmatum ipsorum errore, sed vita vitiis à diabolo irretiuntur mortales. Quo fit, ut qui quemadmodum sit ducenda hæc vita, falluntur, modestius sint & benignius castigandi. Nam ut passer, si vel una pedis parte comprehendi- tur, sub ejus est potestate, qui pedicam fixerit, ita & ipsi, etsi minus utroque pede fide scilicet illa- queamur & vita, at solis pravis vitæ actionibus, dia- boli erimus ditioni subjecti.

Εἰς τὸ ἐκείνου θέλημα) DEI; nam construenda hæc cum illo ἀνανήψωσι posito διαστολῆς signo post ὑπ᾽ ἀυτȣ. Ad DEI voluntatem, nempe faciendam, Eph. VI. 6.

De voluntate DEI etiam Theophylact. exposuit deque ea Beza intelligit, etsi in translatione communiorern sententiam secutus sit, quæ est de libitu Diaboli: ad nomen proximum referens hoc pronomen: quam adduxit quoque Theo- phylactus, & probasse videtur, ac respicere Chry- sostomus homil. XXXVII. in Matth: omnes ho- mines, antequam peccemus, liberum quidem ha- bemus arbitrium, si volumus sequi voluntatem Diaboli, an non. Quod si semel peccantes obliga- verimus nos operibus ejus, jam nostra virtute evudere non possumus: sed sicuti navis fracto gu- bernaculo illuc ducitur, ubi tempestas voluerit: sic & homo divinæ gratiæ auxilio perdito per pecca- tum, non quod vult agit, sed quod Diabolus vult, & nisi DEUS valida manu misericordiæ suæ sol- verit eum, usque ad mortem in peccatorum suorum vinculis permanebit, &c. Anshelmus l. de Simi- lit. cap. 189. Instar pueri (qui aviculam filo liga- tam retinet, & huc illuc avolare sinit, sed mox retrahit,) jocatur Diabolus cum peccatoribus, quos irretitos suis laqueis pro sua voluntate in diversa vitiorum impellimenta pertrahit. Sunt enim multi avari, ebriosi, luxuriosi, qui proponunt avaritiam, gulam, libidinem deserere, & putant instar avis se libere avolaturos, sed quia peccati usu irretiti ab hoste tenentur, nolentes in eadem vitia dejiciuntur, sitque hoc sæpius, nec omnimodis liberantur, nisi magno conatu, & gratia DEI funis rumpatur pra- væ consuetudinis.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He prophesies concerning the corrupt state of the last times, as to time and doctrine, and by his own example and the argument of the salutary Scripture, he exhorts that he may persist constantly in the office and doctrine which he has drawn from the Holy Scriptures.

There are two parts: I. A prophetic prediction concerning the last times, up to verse 9. II. A serious exhortation to constancy in duty and faith, up to the final verse 17.

PART I. A prophetic prediction concerning the last times.

verse 1. Τῦτο δὲ γίνωσκε) Bishops are greatly strengthened to avoid and refute errors that arise when they have been forewarned about those errors beforehand. Thus, Christ and John gave excellent warnings against false Christs.

Ὅτι ἐν ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις) באחרית הימים, that is, hereafter. The same is ἐν ὑστέροις καιροῖς, 1 Tim. IV. v. 1. For that אחרית is translated in both ways. It is clear, however, that Paul is dealing with those things which he thought would happen while Timothy was alive, from what is below in verse 5.

ἐνστήσονται καιροὶ χαλεποὶ) ἐνστῶτα are present things, Rom. VIII. verse 38, 1 Cor. III. verse 23, VII. v. 36, Gal. I. verse 4. ἐνστήσονται will be present. Καιροὶ χαλεποὶ, the same as ἡμέραι πονηραὶ, Eph. V. 16, and Gen. XLVII. 9, and Psalm XLIX. 6. Formidable times, says Cicero.

This prediction concerns not so much the times of Timothy as the last times, although it also embraces those, and looks toward the entire age up to the consummation of the world, according to the opinion of Augustine in Epistle XXI and most interpreters. Since (1) it expressly names ἐσχάτας ἡμέρας, which phrase cannot be restricted to the times of Timothy, or those following shortly after this prediction; (2) the parallel passage 1 Tim. IV. v. 1 speaks not of those times, but of the last days; (3) Scripture is accustomed to express the times after Christ up to the end of the world in this way, 1 Cor. X. verse 11, 1 John II. verse 18, Heb. I. verse 1; (4) this prophecy was delivered not only for the sake of Timothy, but also for the sake of subsequent centuries, to which this Epistle was to be propagated. Why does he predict this here, asks Chrysostom, so that Timothy, and none of us, might be troubled if there are evil men. Theophylact: Do not, he says, paraphrasing this text, consider this a new thing yourself, since this multitude of most wicked men will not end even at your own age. Compare what is said at verse 5. Although, therefore, it is evident from verses 5 and 6 that these things also apply in a certain way to the times of Timothy, the Apostle testifies with a clear voice that they pertain primarily to the last days. Thus he applies these things particularly to his own times, Theodoret, who flourished in the fifth century after Christ was born: I think this time has been predicted. Modern interpreters not undeservedly apply it to our time, and if there are any to come hereafter, they rightly accommodate it to their own times. They are called, however, what the Vulgate explains as dangerous, others as troublesome. Dr. Luther [calls them] greuliche Zeiten [horrible times], which, however, only fits the times metonymically: for no times are evil in themselves, but because of the men who live in them. Not the days indeed, says Chrysostom, nor the times, but the men who are to be then, he criticizes, for we too are accustomed to speak in this way, when we call times either evil or good from those things which have happened in them.

Latin:

CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Vaticinatur de statu novissimorum temporum corrupto, quà tempus & doctrinam, ac suo exemplo & argumento usus salutaris Scripturæ hortatur, ut in officio, & do- ctrina, quam è S. literis hausit, constan- ter persistat.

Partes duæ sunt: I. Prophetica de novissimis temporibus prædictio, ad vers. 9. II. Seria ad con- stiam in munere, ac fide exhortatio, ad vers. 17. finalem.

PARS I. Prophetica de novissimis temporibus prædictio.

vers. 1. Τῦτο δὲ γίνωσκε) Multum confirmantur Episcopi ad vitandos & refellendos errores, qui subnascuntur, ubi de iis erroribus antè præmoniti sunt. Sic adversus Pseudo- Christos egregia monita dedere Christus & Johannes.

Ὅτι ἐν ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις) באחרית הימים, id est, post- hac. Idem ἐν ὑστέροις καιροῖς, 1. Tim. IV. v. 1. Nam utro- que modo transfertur illud אחרית. Patet autem agere Paulum de iis, quæ Timotheo vivente eventura putabat ex eo, quod infra est 5.

ἐνστήσονται καιροὶ χαλεποὶ) ἐνστῶτα sunt præsentia, Rom. IIX. vers. 38. 1. Cor. III. vers. 23. VII. v. 36. Gal. I. vers. 4. ἐνστήσονται aderunt. Καιροὶ χαλεποὶ, idem quod ἡμέραι πονηραὶ, Eph. V. 16. & Gen. XLVII. 9. & Psalm. XLIX. 6. Formidolosa tempora, ait Cicero.

Prædictio hæc non tàm tempora Timothei, quàm novissima concernit, etsi illa etiam com- plectatur, & universam ætatem, usque ad con- summationem seculi respiciat, juxta Augustini Epist. XXI. & plerorumque interpp. sententiam. Siquidem (1) expressè nominet ἐσχάτας ἡμέρας, quæ phrasis non potest restringi ad tempora Timothei, vel brevi post hanc prædictionem sequutura (2) locus parallelus 1. Timoth. IV. v. 1. non de illis temporibus, sed de novissimis diebus loquatur. (3) Solet Scriptura ita tempora post Christum usque ad mundi finem exprimere, 1. Cor. X. vers. 11. 1. Joh. II. vers. 18. Ebr. I. vers. 1. (4) non Timothei tantum causa hæc prophetia tradita, sed ob sequentia etiam secula, ad quæ propaganda erat hæc Epistola. Cur hîc prædicit, quærit Chrysostomus, ne scilicet turbetur Timotheus, nec quispiam nostrum, si sint homines mali. Theo- phylactus: Noli, inquit παραφράζων hunc textum, novum id ipse existimare, quando neque ad tuam usque ætatem nequissimorum hominum multitudo hæc terminabitur. Conf. quæ ad vers. 5. Quamvis ergò temporibus Timothei hæc etiam certa ratio- ne convenire, è vers. 5. & 6. pateat, ad novissimos tamen dies imprimis ea pertinere clara voce Apo- stolus testatur. Ita applicat hæc peculiariter suis temporibus Theodoretus, qui seculo quinto à Chri- sto nato floruit: Existimo prædictum esse hoc tempus. Moderni interpretes nostro non immerito ap- plicant tempori, & si qui posthac futuri, suis rectè accommodant temporibus. Dicuntur au- tem, quod Vulg. exponit periculosa, alii molesta. D. Lutherus greuliche Zeiten/ quod verò non nisi metonymicè temporibus convenit: nulla enim tempora per se mala sunt, sed ob homines, qui vivunt in illis. Non dies profectò, inquit Chry- sostomus, neque tempora, sed homines, qui tunc fu- turi sunt, carpit, quippe & nos ita loqui consuevi- mus, quum tempora vel mala, vel bona ex his, quæ in illis contigere, appellamus.

## 3:2
Ver. 2.

For men will be lovers of self) Even among Christians there were some such, and therefore the easier to be deceived. οἱ ἄνθρωποι. בני אדם [sons of men]. Φίλαυτοι [lovers of self] is a word, if we take it philosophically, neutral in itself: but one which by usage has been drawn to the worse side, so that a lover of self is understood as, 'he who does everything for his own sake according to what is advantageous,' says Aristotle, adding elsewhere, 'or according to what is pleasant.' These are those 'seeking their own, not what is another's,' contrary to what Paul wishes Christians to do, 1 Cor. X. 24.

He is not dealing with those who are clearly outside, but with those who will be in the Church at least by external profession, and first indeed about the wicked in general, yet so that the morals of false teachers are particularly regarded. Whence Augustine, tract. CXXIII. in John, applied everything particularly also to false teachers: then he treats of the false teachers themselves and their doctrine and pursuits. He places first in the catalogue of the wicked Φιλάυτους, that is, lovers of self, which Estius explains as those who study their own private advantages. But that word regards not only actions and pursuits, but primarily also the mind and affection, that they are lovers of themselves only, as Ambrosaster rendered it. For this vice is the cause of all others, as Chrysostom notes: He immediately added the cause of all evils, and the root and fountain, from which all other things are born: when individuals seek not those things which are their neighbor's, but their own: from which it happens that they neglect both equally, for thus they do not even look to their own: for just as he who seeks the things that are his neighbor's, also rightly arranges his own: so also if he neglects those things which are his, he despises his own as well. For if we are members one of another, the salvation of a neighbor is not his alone, but also the rest of the body, and his detriment does not reach to him alone, but also occupies the whole body with pains. If we are a building, if any part suffers, the remaining structure totters: but if it remains firm and inviolable, it can support the remaining structure: so also in the Church, if you despise a brother, you have neglected yourself. In what way? Your member has suffered no small loss. If anyone does not wish to count out money, he is sent into hell: he who sees one in danger regarding necessary things, and does not stretch out a hand: does he not suffer this much more than that man? And so much more, by which this detriment will be made of greater things? For there will be, he says, men lovers of self. He who loves himself, he is primarily the one who is convicted of not having loved himself. But he who loves his brother, this man most of all loves himself. From this avarice is born: for this plague contracts and constricts charity, which is spread by nature and is diffused everywhere: avarice subdues even the mediocre and the weak: from it elation is born, from elation pride, whose offspring is blasphemy, from which arrogance proceeds, which is not of obeying. For he who exalts himself against men: is easily impious against GOD himself: thus also sins are born, so that they more often ascend from the lower to the higher. He who has been pious toward men, will be much more so toward GOD: he who will be gentle toward associates and fellow-servants, how much more toward the Lord? But he who spurns fellow-servants, will gradually reach the point that he despises the Lord himself. Augustine in the beginning of his books on the City of God teaches: that the love of self built the city of the Devil, just as the love of GOD built the city of GOD. Theophylact, however, observes with Chrysostom, that it happens to him who is drawn only by the love of himself, that he does not even love himself: For just as it is accustomed to happen also in members, of which when one is harmed, it is necessary that the rest are also harmed, which indeed buildings also suffer: So it can be said also in the Church, that he who neglects his neighbor, and cares for himself, harms himself.

Augustine applies these things thus in book 5 to false teachers: Let them not be lovers of themselves: let those who feed the sheep of Christ not feed them as if they were their own, but as His, and let them not wish to derive their own gains from them, like lovers of money, or to lord it over them like the arrogant, or to glory in the honors which they receive from them, like the proud, or to progress so far as even to create heresies, like blasphemers. Φιλάργυροι is rendered by the Vulgate as 'cupidi' (covetous), but this is too general, for there are also those covetous of honor, etc. Here, however, lovers of money, those covetous of riches, are noted. When you have explained the root of evils, says Theophylact, he enumerates the branches one by one, among which the first and by far the most powerful is avarice. For just as all good things proceed from charity toward others, so also do evils proceed from private affection, which is entirely separated from true charity. For that [charity] is both most ample and is diffused overflowing everywhere: but this [private affection] is confined to a narrow space and terminates in some one thing. Ἀλαζόνες is explained by the Vulgate as 'elati' (arrogant); but this refers rather to the following vice. Blessed Luther more correctly rendered it 'ruhmredig' (boastful), and Grotius as 'jactatorem' (boaster). They derive it from ἄλη and ζῆν, so that it properly means one who seeks a living by wandering, like ἀγύρται, that is, charlatans, and consequently a boastful, empty-talking ostentator. Ulpian, explaining Demosthenes, says that ἀλαζονεία is of men promising more than they can perform. Suidas says ἀλαζὼν is πλάνος, ὑπερήφανος, ψευδὴς· παρὰ τὸ ἐν ἄλῃ ζῆν, because he lives in error: ἢ ἀλαζὼν ἄλλως ζῶν, ὃ ἐςι ματαίως, otherwise, that is, living rashly: ἀλαζὼν ὁ μείζονα τ' ἑαυτῦ ἀξίας κομιτάζων κὶ φρονῶν: one who boasts and thinks greater things than his own dignity and merit warrant. ὑπερήφανοι, the Vulgate 'superbi' (proud), who despise the humble and lowly; ἀλαζονεία, boasting and arrogance in words and gestures, arises from ὑπερηφανείᾳ, pride lurking in the mind. Suidas says that a virtue is opposed to every vice, but no virtue is opposed to pride alone, on account of the supereminent malice of that evil, διὰ τὴν ὑπερβάλλεσαν κακίαν, God Himself opposes Himself to it. βλάσφημοι, Vulgate 'blasphemi' (blasphemers). Although others may take this generally regarding those who speak evil, it is more correctly understood, by the force of the order, of those who are blasphemous against God, especially because later 'διάβολοι' (slanderers) are distinctly named.

Parents are next to GOD. See the same crime Rom. I. 30.

By saying ungrateful, you have named every crime. See Luke VI. 35. Wis. XVI. 24. Sir. XXIX. 19. 28.

Those who commit foul deeds. See 1 Tim. I. 7.

Concerning these see Rom. I. 31. And perhaps they were stuffed in here from there. For they are missing in the Syriac.

שׂטנים. Thus are they called, who oppose themselves to good men, especially by slandering. Among these are the whisperers, backbiters, in the aforementioned chapter to the Romans, v. 30.

Incontinent are those who are constant neither in good nor in evil: such as that man, of whom Horace says: Nothing was consistent in that man. See Aristotle and the interpreters. Nicom. VII. 1.

The opposite of that praise which we have, Tit. I. verse 8. in the Glossary: φιλάγαθος [is] benign. Thus πνεῦμα φιλάνθρωπον, Wisd. VII. 22.

These things are accommodated to false teachers by Augustine in this way: They do not yield to the holy Fathers, just as those disobedient to parents, and to those who wish to correct them, because they do not want to perish, they return evil for good, just as the ungrateful kill both their own souls and those of others, just as the wicked, and they dissipate the eternal bowels of the Church, just as the prodigal, they do not sympathize with the infirm, just as those without affection they attempt to stain the reputation of the holy, just as detractors, they do not restrain the worst desires, just as the incontinent, they engage in strife, just as the harsh, they do not know how to help, just as those without kindness. γονεῦσιν ἀπειθεῖς. This properly signifies those who do not suffer themselves to be persuaded to render due obedience to parents. Ἀχάριστοι, ungrateful. ἀπειθεῖς and ἀχάριστοι are joined, because disobedience arises from ingratitude. Ἀνόσιοι, Vulg. wicked, the Greek, as Estius admits, is properly profane, nefarious: who have no regard for what is right and holy, so as not to dare to perpetrate any evils. ἄστοργοι, Vulg. without affection, in whom natural affections toward parents, children, and brothers are utterly extinguished. Blessed Luther: störrige [stubborn]. ἄσπονδοι, Vulg. without peace, ἀσπονδὶην denotes familiarity and friendship: ἄσπονδοι, those who do not keep pacts, who are implacable. B. Luther: unversöhnliche [irreconcilable]. Suidas says: ἀσόργες, the harsh and unfriendly. But ἀσπόνδες, the irreconcilable, or those who hold a grudge; that is, they call the unpraised and those lacking natural love ἀστόργες, but they call the irreconcilable ἀσπόνδες. There is no sufficient reason to believe these were interpolated. The Syriac interpreter does not prejudice the original Codices, which agree here. And it is easier for something to fall out than to be inserted. These follow one another, and one overflows from the other in this way, according to Theophylact: For if they curse GOD, how will they venerate their parents? But those who venerate parents not at all, nor obey them, it is necessary that they also show themselves ungrateful toward others. But those who are of this kind will both lack religion and be oppressed by any wickedness. Since they keep nothing of what they owe. Furthermore, they are to be without affection. For whom will they cherish, who spurn and reject those who are beneficent to them? Without peace, that is, those who are joined to no one by friendship: not even to those who have conferred benefits upon them. διάβολοι, accusers, who oppress the innocence of others with lies and fabricated crimes: from which vice the prince of the Cacodæmons received his name. Theophylact: Detracting from all. For he who is conscious of no good in himself, like an envious person, carps at and accuses everyone, continually devising some remedy for his own evils. Ἀκρατεῖς, Vulg. incontinent. Estius says that Chrysostom understands by them those who pour themselves into any kind of carnal pleasure, whether they make a habit of it, or are overcome by passions. But Chrysostom, as also Theophylact, wish incontinence to be designated not only of the belly, but also of the tongue, and of all other things. But the incontinence of the tongue pertains rather to the name of accusers. Ἀνήμεροι, which Grotius passed over, Vulg. harsh, B. Luther: wilde [wild], endowed with beastly manners. See, says Theophylact, what kind of people this excessive self-indulgence (incontinence) and desire itself makes, and how it turns men into beasts? Ἀφιλάγαθοι, Vulg. without kindness. More correctly, Ambrose: enemies of the good. The Syriac: haters of the good. Luther: ungütige [unkind]. B. Gerhard, with Estius, notes that it can be taken of persons and things, but it is more probable that it is taken of persons, so that those are noted who, because of a discrepancy in morals, abhor the friendship of the good, and hate them.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

˄Ἔσονται γὰρ οἱ ἄνθρωποι φίλαυτοι) Etiam inter Christia- nos tales erant quidam, eoque faciliores decipi. οἱ ἄνθρωποι. בני אדם Φίλαυτοι vox est, si philosophicè eam sumamus, per se media: sed quæ usu tracta est in partem pejorem, ita ut φίλαυτⓒ intelligatur, ὁ αὑτῦ ἕνεκα πάντα πράττων κατὰ τὸ λυσιτελὲς ait Aristoteles, addens alibi, ἢ πρὸς τὸ ἡδύ. Hi sunt ζητῦντες τὰ ἑαυτῶν, ὐ τὰ τῶ ἑτέρω, contra quam facere vult Christianos Paulus, 1. Cor. X. 24.

Agit non de iis, qui planè foris sunt, sed de iis, qui saltem externa professione in Ecclesia futuri sunt, & primum quidem de malis in genere, ita tamen, ut mores falsorum Doctorum peculia- riter spectentur. Unde Augustinus tract. CXXIII. in Johann. omnia ad falsos Doctores peculiariter etiam applicavit: deinde de ipsis falsis doctoribus eorumque doctrina, & studiis tractat. Præmit- tit autem in catalogo improborum Φιλάυτυς, hoc est, sui amantes, quod explicat Estius de iis, qui privatis suis commodis student. Sed vox ea non actiones & studia tantum, sed imprimis etiam animum & affectum, quod sui tantum amatores sint, ut Ambrosaster reddidit, respicit. Hoc enim vitium causa est aliorum omnium, notante Chry- sostomo: Causam malorum omnium, atque ra- dicem ac fontem protinus addidit, unde alia gignuntur omnia: quum non ea, quæ proxi- mi, sed quæ sua sunt, singuli quærunt: ex quo fit, ut utrumque pariter negligant, ita enim ne sua quidem aspiciunt: sicuti enim, qui ea, quæ proximi sunt, quærit, sua quoque ritè disponit: ita & si quæ illius sunt, negligit, sua quoque despicit. Nam si sumus invicem membra, proximi salus non illius saltem est, sed & corporis reliqui, illiusque detrimentum non ad ipsum pertingit solùm, sed & corpus omne doloribus occupat. Si ædificatio su- mus, si qua patitur pars, reliqua constructio ti- tubat: sin verò firma, & inviolabilis durat, stru- cturam ferre reliquam potest: ita & in Ecclesia, si fratrem despicis, teipsum neglexisti. Quo pacto? Membrum tuum jacturam baud exiguam pertulit. Si qui pecunias connumerare non vult, in gehen- nam mittitur: qui in rebus necessariis periclitan- tem videt, manumque non porrigit: nonne multò magis quàm ille hoc patitur? atque adeo amplius, quo de majoribus detrimentum hoc fiet? Erunt enim, inquit, homines sui amantes. Qui seipsum amat, ille inprimis est, qui se non amasse convin- citur. Qui verò diligit fratrem, hic maximè se- ipsum amat. Ex hoc avaritia nascitur: charita- tem enim, quæ per naturam lata est, & ubique diffunditur, contrahit atque constringit hæc pe- stis: mediocres quoque ac tenues avaritia subigit: ex eo elatio gignitur, ex elatione superbia, cujus proles blasphemia est, ex qua arrogantia prodit, quæ non obtemperandi est. Qui enim contra ho- mines se effert: facile in DEUM ipsum impius est: ita quoque peccata nascuntur, ut sæpius ad inferioribus ad superna conscendant. Qui fuerit in homines pius, multo magis in DEUM erit: qui in socios, atque conservos erit mansuetus, quan- to magis in Dominum? Qui verò aspernatur con- servos, ad hoc sensim pertinget, ut ipsum quoque despiciat Dominum. Augustinus in principio libro- rum de civitate DEI docet: quod amor sui ædifi- caverit civitatem Diaboli, sicut amor DEI ædifi- caverit civitatem DEI. Observat autem cum Chrysostomo Theophylactus, eum, qui suiipsius dun- taxat trahitur charitate accidere, ut nec ipse se amet: Nam quemadmodum solet & in membris continge- re, quorum cum unum aliquod læditur, & reliqua lædantur necesse est, quod utique & ædificia patiun- tur: Sic dici & in Ecclesia potest, qui proximum negligat, & ipsum se curet, sibiipsi officere.

Hæc ita applicat Augustinus l. 5. ad falsos Do- ctores: Non sint seipsos amantes: qui pascunt oves Christi, nec tanquam suas, sed tanquam ipsius eas pascant, & velint ex iis sua lucra concipere, sicut amatores pecuniæ, vel eis dominari sicut elati, vel gloriari de honoribus, quos ab eis sumunt, sicut su- perbi, vel in tantum progredi, ut etiam hæreses faciat, sicut blasphemi. Φιλάργυροι à Vulg. red- duntur cupidi, sed hoc nimis generale est, nam & cupidi honoris sunt, &c. hic verò amantes pe- cuniarum, cupidi divitiarum notantur. Cum ma- lorum, inquit Theophylactus, explicasses radi- cem, & ramos sigillatim enumerat, inter quos prior, & longè potentior avaritia est. Nam uti ex charitate in alios universa bona proveniunt, sic & mala ex privato affectu, qui prorsus est à vera charitate sejunctus. Illa siquidem & amplissima est, & ubique redundans diffunditur: Hæc verò in an- gusto versatur, & in uno aliquo terminatur. Ἀλα- ζόνες elati à Vulg. exponuntur; verum hoc ad se- quens vitium potius spectat. Rectius B. Luthe- rus ruhmredig reddidit, & Grotius jactatorem. Deducunt ab ἄλη & ζῆν, ut propriè, qui vagando victum quærit, veluti ἀγύρται, hoc est, circulato- res, per consequens autem jactator vaniloquus ostentator. Ulpianus Demosthenem enarrans ἀλα- ζονείαν ait esse hominum plura, quam præstare possunt, pollicentium. Suidas ἀλαζὼν, inquit, πλά- νος, ὑπερήφανος, ψευδὴς· παρὰ τὸ ἐν ἄλῃ ζῆν, quod in errore vivat: ἢ ἀλαζὼν ἄλλως ζῶν, ὃ ἐςι ματαίως, aliter, id est, temerè vivens: ἀλαζὼν ὁ μείζονα τ' ἑαυτῦ ἀξίας κομιτάζων κὶ φρονῶν: qui majora jactat & sentit, quam ipsius dignitas, meri- tumq́ ferat. ὑπερήφανοι Vulgata superbi, qui hu- miles ac tenues despiciunt, ἀλαζονεία jactantia & arrogantia, in verbis & gestibus, oritur ex ὑπερη- φανείᾳ superbia in animo latente. Suidas, omni, in- quit, vitio virtus opponitur, soli vero fastui nulla op- ponitur virtus, propter supereminentem ejus mali- tiam, διὰ τὴν ὑπερβάλλεσαν κακίαν, ipse Deus se- ipsum ei opponit. βλάσφημοι Vulg. blasphemi. Quod etsi alii generaliter accipiant de maledicis, rectius tamen de iis, qui maledici sunt in Deum, vi ordinis intelligitur, imprimis quia postmodum διάβολοι criminatores distinctè nominati sunt.

Proximi DEO parentes. Vide idem crimen Rom. I. 30.

Ingratum dicens, omne crimen dixeris. Vide Luc. VI. 35. Sap. XVI. 24. Sir. XXIX. 19. 28.

Qui fœda patrant. Vide 1. Tim. I. 7.

De his vide Rom. I. 31. Et for-te inde huc infarcita sunt. Nam defunt in Syriaco.

שׂטנים. Sic dicuntur, qui viris bonis se op-ponunt præsertim calumniando. In his sunt ψιθυρισταὶ, κα-τάλαλοι dicto capite ad Rom. v. 30.

ἀκρατεῖς sunt, qui nec in bono, nec in malo sibi constant: qualis ille, de quo Horatius: Nil æquale fuit bomini illi. Vide Aristotelem & interpretes. Nicom. VII. 1.

Oppositum ei laudi quam habemus, Tit. I. vers. 8. in Glossario: φιλάγαθος benignus. Sic πνεῦμα φιλάν-θρωπον, Sap. VII. 22.

Ad falsos doctores hæc sic accommodantur ab Augustino: Non cedunt sanctis Patribus, sicut parentibus non obedientes, & eis, qui illos corrigere volunt, quia perire nolunt, mala pro bonis reddunt, sicut ingrati interficiunt animas & suas & alienas, sicuti scelesti, ac æterna Ecclesiæ viscera dissipant, sicut prodigiosi, non compatiuntur infirmis, sicut sine affectione famam sanctorum maculare conantur, sicut detractores, cupiditates pessimas non refrenant, sicut incontinentes, exercent lites, sicut immites, ne-sciunt subvenire, sicut sine benignitate. γονεῦσιν ἀπειθεῖς. Hoc propriè significat eos, qui non pa-tiuntur sibi persuaderi, ut debitam obedientiam parentibus præstent. Ἀχάριστοι, ingrati. Con-junguntur ἀπειθεῖς & ἀχάριστοι, quia ἀπείθεια ori-tur ex ἀχαριστίᾳ. Ἀνόσιοι Vulg. scelesti Græcum fatente Estio propriè est profani, nefarii: qui recti & sancti nullam habent rationem, quò minus au-deant quævis mala perpetrare. ἄστοργοι Vulg. sine affectione, in quibus storgæ naturales erga paren-tes, liberos & fratres prorsus extinctæ. Beat. Lu-therus störrige. ἄσπονδοι Vulg. sine pace, ἀσπονδὶην familiaritatem & amicitiam notat: ἄσπονδοι, qui pacta non servant, qui sunt implacabiles. B. Lu-therus unversöhnliche. Suidas ἀσόργες, inquit, τὲς ἀπηνεῖς καὶ ἀφίλες. ἀσπόνδες δὲ τες ἀδιαλλά-κτες, ἢ μνησικάκες, hoc est, ἀστόργες vocant illau-datos, & naturali amore carentes, ἀσπόνδες verò irreconciliabiles. Cur hæc infarcita credamus, ratio nulla est idonea. Syrus interpres non præjudicat Codicibus originalibus, qui hic consentiunt. Et facilius quid excidere, quam ingeri potest. Con-sequuntur hæc sese, & unum ex alio redundat hoc modo, juxta Theophylactum: Si enim DEO ma-ledicunt, quo pacto genitores venerabuntur? Qui verò parentes nil venerantur, nec illis obtemperant, vel in cæteros ingratos se præstent, necesse est. Qui verò istiusmodi erunt & religione carebunt, & quo-vis scelere opprimuntur. Quandoquidem, quod de-bent nil servant. Sunt præterea sine affectione futu-ri. Quem enim bi colent, qui in se beneficos asper-nantur, & respuunt? Sine pace, id est, qui nemini juncti sunt amicitia: neque his quidem, qui in se contulerint beneficia. διάβολοι criminatorese, qui mendaciis & confictis criminibus aliorum inno-centiam premunt: à quo vitio Cacodæmonum princeps nomen accepit. Theophylact. Omnibus detrahentes. Qui enim sibi nullius est boni conscius, omnes ut invidus carpit, & criminatur, subinde aliquam suis malis medelam excogitans. Ἀκρατεῖς Vulg. incontinentes. Estius Chrysostomum eos in-telligere ait, qui in quodcunque genus carna-lium voluptatum sese effundunt, sive consuetudi-nem faciant, sive à passionibus superati. Sed Chrys. ut & Theophyl. incontinentiam non tantum ven-tris, sed etiam linguæ, & cæterorum omnium designari volunt. Linguæ autem incontinentia potius ad nomen διαβολῶν pertinet. Ἀνήμεροι, quod præteriit Grotius, Vulg. immites, B. Lutherus wilde/ ferinis moribus præditi. Vide ne quis, in-quit Theophyl. quales nimia hac suiipsius indulgen-tia (incontinentia) & cupiditas ipsa efficiat, atque ex hominibus beluas reddat? Ἀφιλάγαθοι Vulg. sine benignitate. Rectius Ambrosius bonorum ini-mici. Syrus bonorum osores. Lutherus ungütige. B. Gerhardus cum Estio notat de personis & rebus accipi posse, sed probabilius sumi de personis, ut notentur, qui ob morum discrepantiam abhor-rent ab amicitia bonorum, eosque oderunt.

## 3:4
Vers. 4.

Προδόται) Those who betray their closest friends, such as Judas, Luke VI. 16. See also 2 Macc. V. 15. X. 13. 22. Προπετεῖς) προπετὲς is said of everything that is not well thought out and premeditated, as Acts XIX. verse 36. And they are accustomed to be called προπετεῖς, both those who assent and those who become angry for a slight cause. But by a certain excellence, the headstrong, forward, and petulant are called προπετεῖς, as it is in the Glossary, and in this sense, among the interpreters of Proverbs, it corresponds both to the word פוחר X. verse 15, and to פשע XIII. verse 3. Τετυφωμένοι) Inflated with a vain opinion of themselves, which is τῦφος to the Greeks. See 1 Tim. III. 6. VI. 4.

Προδόται, those who betray even friends and well-wishers, according to Theophylact, others: deserters of friendship. Προπετεῖς, Vulg. forward. Blessed Luther, more emphatically: Freveler [transgressors]. Theophylact: those having no thought or consideration. τετυφωμένοι, Vulg. inflated, those who swell with pride, puffed up with themselves.

Φιλήδονοι μᾶλλον ἢ φιλόθεοι) Equal to those whose god he said was their belly, Phil. III. 17. Both words are well-formed according to the Greek style. For that necessarily follows, as Theophylact says, that where the desire for worldly pleasures exists, the love or desire for GOD cannot exist. Augustine, l. c. on false Doctors: They indicate, he says, to the enemies of the pious what they have learned in secret, like traitors: they disturb human modesty with shameless thought, like the forward; they do not understand either what they say or about what they affirm, like the blinded: they prefer carnal joys to spiritual delights, like lovers of pleasures more than of GOD. Estius says these pertain particularly to the love of pleasures in the family of Simon, and from Epiph. haer. XXVI. he notes that it was said by the Apostle because of the Gnostics, who taught things similar to Simon.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Προδόται) Qui amicissimos produnt, qualis Judas, Luc. VI. 16. Vide & 2. Macc. V. 15. X. 13. 22. Προπετεῖς) προπετὲς dicitur omne id, quod non bene co-gitum atque præmeditatum est, ut Act. XIX. vers. 36. So-lentque προπετεῖς dici, tum qui assentiuntur, tum qui ira-scuntur levi de causa. Sed per excellentiam quandam προπετεῖς dicuntur protervi, procaces, petulantes, ut est in Glossario, respondetque in hoc sensu, apud Proverbio-rum interpretes, tum voci פוחר X. vers. 15. tum פשע XIII. vers. 3. Τετυφωμένοι) Inflati vana de se opinione, quæ τῦφος Græcis. Vide 1. Tim. III. 6. VI. 4.

Προδόται, qui vel amicos & benevolos prodant, Theophylacto, aliis amicitiæ defectores. Προπε-τεῖς Vulgato protervi. Beat. Luthero magis em-phaticè Freveler. Theophylacto nil rati aut pensi habentes. τετυφωμένοι Vulg. inflati, qui fastu tu-ment, sibiipsis suffeni.

Φιλήδονοι μᾶλλον ἢ φιλόθεοι) Pares illis, quorum Deum esse dixit ventrem Philipp. III. 17. utraque vox bene effi-cta ad Græcam formam. Id enim necessariò, Theophyl. dicente, sequi-tur, ut ubi mundanorum incrit oblectamentorum cupiditas, DEI inesse amor vel desiderium inesse ne-queat. Augustinus l. c. de falsis Doctoribus: In-dicant, inquit, inimicis piorum, quæ occulmndà cognoverint, sicut proditores: humanam verecun-diam inverecunda excogitatione perturbant, sicut-procaces non intelligunt, neque quæ loquuntur, ne-que de quibus affirmant, ficuti excæcati: lætitias-carnales Spiritualibus gaudiis anteponunt sicut vo-luptatum amatores magis, quam DEI. Peculia-riter hæc de voluptatum amore quadrare in fami-lia Simonis, ait Estius, & ex Epiph. hær. XXVI. notat ab Apostolo propter Gnosticos dicta, qui similia cum Simeone docuere.

## 3:5
Verse 5.

“Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof.” Thus he opposed μόρφωσιν [form] and δύναμιν [power], just as Tacitus often opposes appearance or image and force. We had μόρφωσιν also in Rom. II, v. 20. But there it has nothing opposed to it, from which its meaning might be narrowed. The Syriac here has אסכמא [form/likeness], a conformity. Those are said to deny here who destroy something by their deeds, just as the Hebrews are accustomed to make metaphors from words to deeds. See what is said regarding deeds in 1 Tim. V. 8. Others, with Estius, understand ἔχοντας μόρφωσιν in terms of doctrine, because μόρφωσις signifies a method of instructing and informing, comparing Matt. XXIII, verse 3, Rom. II, verse 20. But the Greeks more correctly explain it as the external appearance of the piety of hypocrites. They present, says Theophylact, only the figure and shadow of piety and feign it, but in their works they deny and abhor it. Furthermore, he warns: Observe, however, that the power of piety, and (if I may so say) its sinews, are displayed in actions themselves and in deeds, whence it is also deservedly said that faith without works is dead.

“And from such turn away.” סור מהם [turn away from them], to turn away, to be averse, as Cicero speaks. Elegant Greeks also use the verb ἀποτρέπεσθαι instead of φεύγειν. The Vulgate renders it 'avoid'; the Greek is properly 'turn away from,' as Estius admits, which means (1) by not consenting, not approving, (2) by withdrawing yourself from them. by not dragging the yoke with them. A doubt proposed here by Theophylact must be noted, and his answer: Someone will ask: If such men are to be in the last times, why does Paul say, avoid these? For it is possible that some such were there at that time. Who, even if they were less outstanding in the magnitude of their crimes, were nevertheless to be wicked and depraved, just as if he were saying, either avoid these very ones, who are found to be of such a kind even at this time, just as he infers, for of these are they who penetrate; or Paul speaks of the future and last days, which are to occur after his death, to which Timothy was to be a survivor, or (which is truer, and Basil judges) under the person of Timothy he reminds the others that they should avoid such men. Chrysostom is more succinct: It is certainly allowed to be understood that there were some of this kind even then, even if not so many, yet they were: But perhaps we say more truly, that through him all are admonished that they should avoid these.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Ἔχοντες μόρφωσιν ἐυσεβείας, τὴν δὲ δύναμιν ἀυτῆς ἠρνη-μένοι) Ita opposuit μόρφωσιν & δύναμιν, quomodo spe-ciem aut imaginem, & vim, sæpe Tacitus. Μόρφωσιν ha-buimus & Rom. II. v. 20. Sed ibi nihil habet oppositum, unde significatio ejus contrahatur. Syrus hic אסכמא convenientiam. Ἀρνεῖσθαι hic dicuntur, qui factis aliquid destruunt, sicut solent Ebræi à dictis ad facta μεταφορὰς facere. Vide, quæ dicta ad facta 1. Tim. V. 8. Alii cum Estio ἔχοντας μόρφωσιν ratione doctri-næ intelligunt, quia μόρφωσις instituendi infor-mandique rationem significat, conferentes Matth. XXIII. vers. 3. Roman. II. vers. 20. Sed rectius Græci de specie externa pietatis hypocritarum explicant. Figuram, inquit Theophylactus, dunta-xat, & umbram præferunt pietatis & simulant, ope-ribus verò hanc abnegant, & abominantur. Monet porrò: Adverte autem pietatis potentiam, & (ut ita dixerim) nervos, in actionibus ipsis & factis præ-serri, unde & meritò dicitur, fides sine operibus mortua est.

Καὶ τάτες ἀποτρέπε) סור מהם avertere, ἀφυλικὸ, ut Cicero loquitur. Verbo ἀποτρέπεσθαι pro φεύγειν utun-tur & elegantes Græci. Vulgata reddit devita: Græcum propriè est aversare, fatente Estio, quod sit (1) non consen-tiendo, non approbando (2) ab illis te subducendo. (3) jugum cum illis non trahendo. Observandum hic dubium à Theophylacto propositum, ejusque responsum: Quæret aliquis: Si novissimis tempo- ribus futuri sunt istiusmodi homines, cur Paulus inquit, istos devita? Fieri enim potest, ut tales essent nonnulli tunc temporis. Qui etsi minus præstarent scelerum magnitudine, iniqui tamen & improbi sint futuri, perinde ac si dicat, vel hos ipsos devita, qui vel hoc tempore istiusmodi reperiuntur, quemad- modum infert, ex his enim sunt, qui penetrant; vel posteros & novissimos dies Paulus dicit, qui ejus post obitum sunt obventuri, quibus superstes futurus erat Timotheus, vel (quod verius est, & Basilius censet) sub Timothei persona cæteros commonefacit, ut ejusmodi viros devitent. Succinctius Chrysosto- mus: Intelligi profectò datur, & tunc hujusmodi fuïsse quosdam, etsi non tam multos, fuisse tamen: Sed verius fortasse dicimus, per illum admoneri omnes, ut hos devitent.

## 3:6
v. 6. For of these they are) Of the number of these they will be: the present for the future. Those penetrating into houses) They want to know the secrets of the house, and thence to be feared. penetrating. Physicists say to enter in the same sense. Ambrose: creeping in. And taking captive silly women laden with sins, led away by various desires) These were following the old art of the Pharisees, of whom Josephus XVII. 3. for there was a certain portion of Jewish men, priding themselves greatly on the exactness of the ancestral law, to whom the women's quarters were subject, pretending that the divine was pleased with them. The Scholiast on Horace's first epistle says that some who pretended to be Stoics practiced the same art. And it is excellently said taking captive, because they make women beholden to them, as if they had been captured by a word. We have similar translations in the same word or an equal one in Rom. VII. 23. 2 Cor. X. 3. & Judith XVI. 7. & in to take alive above II. 6. And he preferred to say silly women, rather than women, so that he might show more the abject lot of those women, who were not only vicious, but also overwhelmed with vices. For that is what laden means, as can be understood from Prov. XXV. 23. Thus the Jewish people heavy with iniquity Is. I. 4. where the Greeks full of sins. He adds led away by many desires, not only those of their own sex, but also by rapacity, luxury, pride. But the Manuscript has more distinctly: By desires and various pleasures.

Why should the present tense not be retained, or why should an enallage be admitted? The Apostle commands to avoid: implying the present ones of course: And furthermore in the present those who penetrate. Meanwhile, it is undoubtedly also indicated that such will be in the last times. For he describes their morals, pursuits, and character, both of those who were then, and of those who will be in the future. By the word to penetrate, which the Vulgate renders to penetrate, their impudence is noted, in that they craftily insert and intrude themselves into others' families, for the sake of the belly, of whom Tit. I. 11. that they subvert whole houses, of which Theophylact. He reveals their impudence and life not liberal, but filled with deceitful flatteries, because they would invade others' houses. And taking captive, thoroughly subjecting to themselves silly women, either by striking fear into them, or by deceiving them with flatteries, by which their fraudulence is noted, and its effect, that they thus render them captive to themselves, so that they may be able to lead them wherever they wish, into errors, and into crimes. For he did not say deceiving, says Theophylact, but leading captive (silly women) so that they might use them as slaves. For he who is deceived, plays the part of the one deceiving. He calls them laden with sins, either because the silly women had previously led a dishonest life, and had laden themselves with sins, and so could be seduced all the more easily: which is the opinion of Chrysostom: Or rather, because being seduced by false Teachers they are burdened with the load of sins. For they do not only seduce wicked women, but also sometimes pious and honest ones. led away by various desires, which by various vicious desires, to wit, & detestable, they are led like brutes, they allow themselves to be driven to the same, as Theophylact interprets.

Latin:

v. 6. Ἐκ τούτων γάρ εἰσιν) Ex horum numero erunt: præ- sens præ futuro. Οἱ ἐνδύνοντες εἰς τὰς οἰκίας) Scire volunt secreta domus, atque inde timeri. ἐνδύνοντες penetrantes. εἰσδύειν eodem sensu dicunt Physici. Ambrosius: irrepentes. Καὶ αἰχμαλωτίζοντες γυναικάρια σεσωρευμένα ἁμαρτίαις, ἀγόμενα ἐπιθυμίαις ποικίλαις) Sequebantur hi veterem artem Pharisæorum, de quibus Josephus XVII. 3. ἦν γάρ μόριόν τι Ἰουδαϊκῶν ἀνθρώπων, ἐπ᾽ ἀκριβώσει μέγα φρονοῦν τοῦ πατρῴου νόμου, οἷς χαίρειν τὸ θεῖον προσποιουμένων ὑπῆκτο ἡ γυναικωνῖτις. Ean- dem artem factitasse quosdam, qui se Stoicos simularent, dicit Scholiastes ad Horatii epistolam primam. Et egregiè dictum αἰχμαλωτίζοντες, quia fœminas faciunt sibi obno- xias, quasi verbo captæ essent. Similes in eadem voce aut pari translationes habemus Rom. VII. 23. 2. Cor. X. 3. & Ju- dith XVI. 7. & in ζωγρεῖν supra II. 6. Et maluit γυναικάρια dicere, quàm γυναῖκας, ut illarum mulierum abjectam sor- tem magis ostenderet, quæ non tantum vitiosæ erant, sed & obrutæ vitiis. Id enim est σεσωρευμένα, ut intelligi potest Prov. XXV. 23. Sic populus Judaicus כבד עון Es. I. 4. ubi Græci πλήρης ἁμαρτιῶν. Addit abreptas multis cupi- ditatibus, non illis tantum sexus sui, sed & rapacitate, lu- xu, superbia. At Manuscriptus distinctius habet: Ἐπιθυ- μίαις καὶ ἡδοναῖς ποικίλαις.

Cur non retineatur tempus præsens, aut cur ad- mittenda enallage? Devitare jubet Apostolus: præ- sentes utique innuens: Et porro in præsenti qui penetrant. Interim tales etiam futuros novissimis temporibus sine dubio quoque indicatur. Nam mores, studia & ingeniū eorum describit, tum qui tunc erant, tum qui olim futuri erunt. Voce ἐνδύ- νειν, quam Vulg. reddit penetrare, impudentia eo- rum notatur, quod callidè sese insiquent & inge- rant in alienas familias, ventris causa, de quibus Tit. I. 11. quod integras domus subvertant, de quo Theophylact. Horum impudentiam & vitam non li- beralem, sed assentationes dolo refertas, quod alienas domos invaderent patefacit. Καὶ αἰχμαλωτεύοντες, penitus sibi subjicientes mulierculas, iis vel timo- rem incutiendo, vel blanditiis fallendo, quo no- tatur eorum fraudulentia, ejusque effectus, ut ita sibi captivas reddant, ut quò libet, ducere valeant in errores, & in scelera. Non enim fallentes dixit, ait Theophylactus, sed captivas ductantes (mulier- culas) ut quibus pro mancipiis uterentur. Qui enim decipitur, morem fallenti gerit. Oneratas peccatis vocat, sive quod mulierculæ antea egerint vitam inhonestam, seque peccatis oneraverint, adeoque eo facilius seduci potuerint: quæ Chrysostomi est sententia: Sive potius, quod seductæ à falsis Do- ctoribus onere peccatorum graventur. Nam non seducunt tantum improbas mulieres, sed etiam quandoque pias, & honestas. ἀγόμενα ἐπιθυμίαις ποικίλαις, quæ variis concupiscentiis vitiosis scil. & detestandis, aguntur brutorum instar, ad easdem se impelli patiantur, ut Theophylactus interpretatur.

## 3:7
v. 7. Always learning) Those women were present at the assemblies of the Christians, where they received the best precepts.

And never able to come to the knowledge of the truth) Understand that active knowledge, which is shown by things. And take able, as Matth. XII. 34. & Mark VI. 9. where see the things said. They were given over to passion, as Clement speaks Strom. II. and the teachers, who ought to have shaken them out of this lethargy with severe threats, were fostering those vices, promising that they would effect by their prayers that those women would have God propitious. See Matth. XXIII. 14. where the precursors of these are described. And would that there were not many such even now. See concerning such women Plato at the end of the sixth book of the Laws.

These things are falsely referred by certain Latins to false Teachers: For the Greek construction teaches that it pertains to the silly women, whom he says always learn, but never arrive at the knowledge of the truth: either because they only hear false Teachers, from whom they cannot draw the truth: or because not content with Apostolic doctrine, out of curiosity and instability of mind they always seek new things, and those accommodated to their own desires, as Estius explains, or if they theoretically acknowledge the truth, they do not however arrive at the practical knowledge of the truth, heaping up for themselves teachers itching in their ears according to their own desires, as is had in c. IV. 3.

Latin:

v. 7. Πάντοτε μανθάνοντες) Intererant illæ fœminæ con- ventibus Christianorum, ubi optima accipiebant præcepta.

Καὶ μηδέποτε εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας ἐλθεῖν δυνάμενα) Ἐπί- γνωσιν intellige illam activam, quæ rebus ostenditur. Et δυ- νάμενα sume, ut Matth. XII. 34. & Marc. VI. 9. ubi dicta vide. Erant ἔκδοτοι τῷ πάθει, ut Clemens loquitur Strom. II. & doctores, qui eas severis comminationibus excutere ex hoc veterno debuerant, fovebant ista vitia, pollicentes se preci- bus suis effecturos, ut illæ Deum haberent propitium. Vide Matth. XXIII. 14. ubi horum præcursores describuntur. Et utinam non & nunc multi sint tales. Vide de hujusmodi fœminis Platonem fine sexti de legibus.

Falsò hæc referuntur à Latinis quibusdam ad falsos Doctores: Constructio enim Græca docet, pertinere ad mulierculas, quas dicit semper disce- re, nunquam autem ad agnitionem veritatis per- venire: sive quod tantum falsos Doctores audiant, à quibus veritatem haurire nequeunt: sive quod non contentæ doctrina Apostolica, præ curiosita- te, & instabilitate animi semper nova quærunt, ea- que suis desideriis accommoda, ut Estius explicat, aut si theoreticè veritatem agnoscant, non tamen ad veritatis agnitionem practicam perveniant, ad sua desideria coacervantes sibi magistros prurien- tes auribus, ut habetur c. IV. 3.

## 3:8
v. 8. And in the manner that Jannes and Jambres) The Greek exemplar of the Latin Interpreter had Mambres. And thus that Magician is called by Numenius, as we showed in the annotations from book I. for the truth of the Christian Religion. Nor otherwise in the Talmudic, under the title of Oblations. The other is Jannes, as even the best books of Apuleius have: in Tanchuma. The name is Egyptian, for which in the Talmud. These are the priests above Memphis to Artabanus. These names Paul had, not from the Scripture of Moses, for there the magicians are mentioned, not with names expressed, but from tradition, or the writings of the ancients.

Withstood Moses) Exod. VII. 11. & following. See also the place indicated by Artabanus. Numenius says thus: To Moses (thus he calls Moses) at any rate the one who interpreted for the Jews, a man who had become most powerful in prayer to God, those who were deemed worthy to stand against him by the multitude of the Egyptians. See a similar thing Acts XIII. 8. where there is withstood.

Why not rather from divine revelation? As Theophylact holds. For he wrote, 'borne along by the Holy Spirit.' In vain also is the Vulgate silently excused. For why is the different spelling of the name referred to another reading of the Codex, rather than to a slip of the interpreter, or an error of the copyist, when no codex reads it so, nor the Syriac, nor Chrysostom. 'Who,' he says, 'are Jannes and Jambres?' Magicians, who lived in the times of Moses: whom Theophylact likewise understood. Aretius, however, understands rebellious Jews rather than Egyptian Magicians, such as were Dathan and Abiram, since this discourse is about domestic enemies and hypocrites, who wished both to be and to be considered Christians, nay, to be considered teachers among Christians. Magicians, however, although they opposed themselves to Moses, nevertheless did that as open enemies, dissenting from him both in the profession of religion and in their manner of life and studies. Camerarius says these are the proper names of those who opposed themselves to Moses, whether Egyptians at the court of Pharaoh, or others elsewhere. Nor does the opinion of Aretius seem improbable. Without doubt, not a few from among the Jews resisted the truth proposed by Moses, of whom this account of the Apostle can teach that those were the chief ones. Magicians are not read to have resisted the truth of the Mosaic doctrine so much as to have wished to emulate and elude the miracles of Moses, whence consequently the faith of his legation could be rendered suspect.

So also these resist the truth) Again the present for the future, as often among the Prophets. They too will have their Pharaohs, whom they are about to harden.

Men corrupted in mind) Thus 'men corrupted in mind,' 1 Tim. VI. 5, where see the things said.

Reprobate concerning the faith) Adulterated, rejected regarding the faith. See Rom. I. 28.

Latin:

v. 8. Ὃν τρόπον δὲ Ἰαννῆς καὶ Ἰαμβρῆς) Latini Interpretis Græcum exemplar habuit Μαμβρῆς. Et sic Magus iste voca- tur Numenio, ut oftendimus in annotatis ab lib. I. pro veri- tate Religionis Christianæ. Nec aliter in Thalmudico, titulo de Oblationibus. Alter est Jannes, quomodo & Apuleji ha- bent optimi libri: יניס in Tanchuma. Nomen est Ægy- ptium, pro quo יוחני in Thalmude. Hi sunt sacerdotes su- pra Memphim Artabano. Hæc nomina Paulus, non ex Scri- ptura Mosis, ibi enim magi memorantur, non expressis no- minibus, sed ex traditione, aut veterum scriptis habuit.

Ἀντέστησαν Μωσῇ) Exod. VII. 11. & sequentibus. Vide & locum indicatum Artabani. Numenius sic ait: Μωσαίῳ (ita Mosen vocat) γοῦν τῷ Ἰουδαίων ἐξηγησαμένῳ, ἄνδρι γενο- μένῳ Θεῷ εὔξασθαι δυνατωτάτῳ οἱ παραστῆναι ἀξιωθέντες ὑπὸ τοῦ πλήθους τῶν Αἰγυπτίων. Simile vide Act. XIII. 8. ubi est ἀνθίστατο.

Cur non potius ex revelatione divina? ut Theo- phylactus habet. Scripsit enim Φερόμενος ὑπὸ πνεύ- ματος ἁγίου. Frustra etiam tacite excusatur Vulga- ta. Cur enim diversa nominis scriptio ad Codicis aliam lectionem potius, quàm ad παρόραμα inter- pretis, aut σφάλμα exscriptoris refertur, cum nul- lus codex ita legat, nec Syrus, neq; Chrysostomus. Quinam sunt, inquiens, Jannes & Jambres? Magi, qui vixerunt temporibus Mosis: Quos pariter in- tellexit Theophylactus. Aretius tamen rebelles po- tius Judæos, quàm Magos Ægytios intelligit, quales fuere Datan & Abiram, cum hic sermo sit de hostibus domesticis, & hypocritis, qui Christiani & esse & haberi volebant, imo Doctores inter Christianos ha- beri. Magi autem, quamvis se opposuerunt Mosi, fe- cerunt tamen id, tanquam aperti hostes, & religionis professione, & genere vitæ ac studiorum ab eo dissiden- tes. Camerarius propria, inquit, nomina hæc sunt eo- rum, qui se Mosi opposuerunt, sive Ægyptii apud Pharaonem, seu alii alibi. Nec improbabilis vide- tur Aretii sententia. Restiterunt sine dubio ex Ju- dæis veritati à Mose propositæ non pauci, è quibus præcipuos illos fuisse, hæc Apostoli relatio docere potest. Magi non tam veritati doctrinæ Mosaicæ restitisse leguntur, quàm miracula Mosis æmulari & eludere voluisse, unde consequenter fides lega- tionis ejus suspecta reddi poterat.

οὕτως καὶ οὗτοι ἀνθίστανται τῇ ἀληθείᾳ) Rursum præsens pro futuro, ut sæpe apud Prophetas. Habebunt & illi suos Pha- raones, quos obduraturi sunt.

Ἄνθρωποι κατεφθαρμένοι τὸν νοῦν) Sic διεφθαρμένων ἀνθρώ- πων τὸν νοῦν, 1. Tim. VI. 5. ubi dicta vide.

Ἀδόκιμοι περὶ τὴν πίστιν) Circa fidem adulterini, rejiculi. Vide Rom. I. 28.

## 3:9
v. 9. But they shall not progress further) They will make some progress, but not for long. In like manner Thucydides: 'they go forth to the greatest extent': they proceed very far: לא יכלו הוציא הכנס

For their folly shall be manifest to all) Shortly it will be revealed the madness of those who conduct their own affairs under the name of GOD. Fictitious things do not last long. *In the Manuscript ἡ γὰρ δίανοια. as also theirs became) Of those magicians who withstood Moses.

Whose mind is clouded and corrupted by preconceived false opinions and vicious affections: who understand nothing in matters of faith, nor can they judge rightly concerning them: But they will not progress far, before their errors and frauds are detected by sincere Doctors, so that their folly is exposed everywhere and openly; which explanation Estius approves as being in agreement with the commentaries of the Greeks and with experience itself. But here, says the Apostle, with Theophylact as interpreter, he is by no means weaving these deceits to deceive others, nor will it happen that they corrupt many, for even if they seem to circumvent, they are nevertheless going to be tolerable. And further: Presently, he says, if you do not give credence to these words, you will learn how it was dealt with those magicians. For these are they who, by certain tricks, were found to have produced certain wondrous things for the sake of deception, when Moses produced truer ones. Whence it can be understood that these fallacies flourish for some short time.

Others refer it to the method of instructing, since, as Aristotle teaches in Book I of the Rhetoric, ἀγωγὴ signifies the leading and sense of a law, when a preceptor and Master leads the disciple, as it were, to the sense of some matter. But B. Gerhard admits that both meanings, both that imitation and the conversation of life and the manner of living, are signified by this word. Estius prefers the explanation concerning the manner of living, even though the Vulgate translated it as instruction. The Apostle had already spoken about information, τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ, which the Vulgate rendered as doctrine. Doctrine indeed, says Theophylact, he said regarding the discourse, but instruction regarding life and conversation. Chrysostom had preceded him, understanding doctrine as the word of preaching, and instruction as that of life, and Theodoret: Doctrine, i.e., the truth through preaching: Instruction, the translation of my life. Granted, if anyone should think that conversation is regarded not only as a general vocation, which is that of all the faithful, but especially also as a special one, that is, in the parts of duty, we will not object.

PART II. Exhortation to constancy in duty and in the acknowledged faith.

Latin:

v. 9. Ἀλλ' οὐ προκόψουσιν ἐπὶπλεῖον) Progressus aliquos facient, sed non diu. Pari modo Thucydides: ἐπὶ πλεῖστον ἐξέρχονται: longissimè procedūt: לא יכלו הוציא הכנס

ἡ γὰρ ἄνοια ἀυτῶν ἔκδηλος ἔσται πᾶσιν) Brevi patescet amentia illorum res suas sub DEI nomine agentium. Ficta non durant diu. *In Manuscripto ἡ γὰρ δίανοια. ὡς καὶ ἡ ἐκείνων ἐγένετο) Illorum magorum, qui Mosi obsti- terunt.

Quorum mens præconceptis falsis opinionibus, & vitiosis affectibus est obnubilata & corrupta: qui in rebus fidei nihil intelligunt, nec de illis rectè judicare possunt: Sed non proficient ita, quin à sinceris Doctoribus errores & fraudes eorum de- tegantur, ut passim & palàm eorum insipientia tra- ducatur; quam explicationem ceu Græcorum com- mentariis, atque ipsi experientiæ consentaneam ap- probat Estius. Hic verò inquit Apostolus, Theophy- lacto interprete, nequaquam hos dolos nectere, ut alios fallant, nec fore ut multos corrumpant, quin etsi videantur circumvenire, tolerabiles sunt tamen fu- turi. Et porro: Subinde, inquiens, si dictis his fidem non adhibueris, edisces, quemadmodum cum magis biscc actum sit. Hi namque sunt præstigiis quibusdam, mira quædam ad deceptionem edidisse deprehensi, cum Moses ederet veriora. Unde comprehendi po- test, ad tempus aliquod breve fallacias istas florere.

Ad instituendi rationem alii referunt, quum, Aristotele lib. I. Rhet. docente, ἀγωγὴ ductum & sensum legis significet, quando præceptor & Magister ad sensum alicujus rei discipulum in- formandum quasi ducit. Sed utrumque, & illam imitationem, & conversationem vitæ, ac rationem vivendi significari hâc voce, utramque admittit B. Gerhardus. Estius præfert explicationem de viven- di ratione, etsi Vulgata institutionem transtulerit. De informatione jam dixerat Apostolus, τῇ διδα- σκαλίᾳ, quam doctrinam reddidit Vulgatus. Do- ctrinam quidem, inquit Theophylactus, quoad ser- monem dixit, institutionem verò quoad vitam & con- versationem. Præiverat Chrysost. doctrinam de verbo, prædicationis intelligens, institutionem de vitâ, & Theodoretius: Doctrinam, h. e. veritatem per prædicationem: Institutionem vitæ meæ traductio- nem. Esto, conversationem non tantum quà gene- ralem vocationem, quæ est fidelium omnium, sed im- primis etiam quà specialem, hoc est, in partibus offi- cii respici, quis censeat, non refragabimur.

PARS II. Adhortatio ad Constantiarn in officio, & fide agnita.

## 3:10
V. 10. Σὺ δὲ παρηκολούθηκάς μυ τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ) But you have a far different model by which to form yourself, all my actions, at which you were present. Thus Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and Theophylact take it here. Thus Demosthenes concerning the poorly conducted embassy: παρηκολουθηκὼς ἅπασι κατηγορῶ, I accuse because I was present at all those things. The same: Ὅσα τυγχάνω δι' ἐμπειρίας καὶ τῷ παρηκολουθηκέναι τοῖς πράγμασιν εἰδώς. What I know by experiencing, and therefore, because I was present at the events. Timothy, commended by his mother, I believe, and grandmother, had followed Paul from a boy, so that he might observe his life and compose himself to it. Luke indeed makes the first mention of Timothy when Paul came to Lystra, Acts XVI. 1, because Timothy was ordained as an Evangelist at that time. But that Timothy had been present with Paul before that time also appears from the fact that it is said that Timothy was already with Paul at Iconium, and at Antioch, before he was at Iconium. But Paul was at Iconium before he was at Lystra, as can be seen in Acts XIII. 52, XIV. 1, XVI. 1. You were a witness, he says, of my doctrine, from the beginning, which the Greek Interpreters add here. *

Chrysostom, whom Theophylact follows as is his custom, understands a ready will and alacrity of mind. For he says, I did not speak those things and fail to fulfill them in deed, nor did I philosophize only with words. But Grotius's explanation, which was also Theodoret's, is more fitting; You have rightly learned my scope and intent, to which B. Gerhard also agrees: By πρόθεσιν the end and scope of the Apostolic actions is understood, namely, that he had proposed to himself not his own glory, nor his own advantage, but the glory of God and the advantage of his neighbor in all the actions of his Ministry. Beza: You not only know what I have taught, what I have done, but also what my mind and will have been, you know thoroughly.

Now therefore he opposes his own example to the perverse doctrines and morals of the heretics, and by the same he excites Timothy to perform his duty constantly and to persevere in the acknowledged doctrine. But you have followed, and sufficiently understood my doctrine, instruction, and purpose, that is, since you have been an inseparable companion of my journey and a partner in my actions, therefore all my affairs are thoroughly perceived and known to you. Thus our B. Gerhard with Erasmus and Estius. But that Timothy was always present with them cannot be certainly gathered from this passage. Not without reason does Beza ask, what is it to follow someone's doctrine and manner of life? Furthermore, even if

Others understand it as constancy of mind: But since the Apostle has handed down those things which he proposed to Timothy to be imitated in his office, he now seems to proceed to those things which can also serve as an example to all the pious, just as he also dealt with the occupations not only of ministers of the word, but of all the faithful in v. 12, and proposed his own example of constancy to them: and by πίστιν, that which he is commonly accustomed to understand in these Epistles, namely the πληροφορίαν (full assurance) of faith, which exerts itself through sincerity as well as strength and constancy of mind. The expositions of the Greeks favor this sense. Theodoret: Faith, what affection I have toward the Lord: Chrysostom: None of these things disturbed me. Theophylact, who explains it the same way: Faith, that is, firmness either in deciding the truth or in facing dangers: which caused me not to lose heart. But rather that I should trust more and more in God, that I would eventually be set free.

even if that explanation of the word παρηκολούθηκάς is admitted, it is not necessary, however, that he was present with the Apostle during that whole time, always and in all places and actions and sufferings; it is sufficient if he was present for most of them, but learned other things from the Apostle's report. Nor was Luke present at those things about which he wrote, even though he used this same word in ch. III. 3, which therefore sometimes implies only the knowledge which one has obtained, even if he was not present at the event, but received it from elsewhere. In which sense it is certain that the word is also used in 1 Tim. IV. Budé also observed that that word is used regarding the understanding of the mind, just as those things are called δυσπαρακολούθητα which we cannot easily attain by understanding. It is, however, he says in Comment. lingu. Græc. page 346, παρακολυθεῖν to attain by observation and understanding; which that man most skilled in the Greek language proves from Aeschines, Galen, and others.

This pertains primarily to the office, nor is it excluded in this place. The word is more general, however, in that sense, and extends itself to more objects of μακροθυμία (long-suffering). The blessed Gerhard understands it as lenity of mind and moderation toward persecutors and enemies of the truth. Chrysostom and Theophylact toward heretics. Theodoret toward brothers. in bearing with their offenses, which becomes all the faithful, Matt. 18. Gal. 6.

Τῇ ἀγάπῃ) Which elsewhere is taken generally, so as to comprehend all virtues, but here more specifically for brotherly affection toward all Christians: But this is absent in the Manuscript.

Why should not Christian love toward all men be understood, along with Theodoret: How I wish well to all: Why not in general love toward God and men? Charity toward God ought certainly not to have been omitted, since the Apostle sets himself as an example to Timothy and others.

Τῇ ὑπομονῇ) How I am in no way changed by adversities: which adversities he now explains.

That not only tolerance in adversities and persecutions, but also patience, or patient constancy is understood, the use of the word ὑπομονῆς in the writings of the New Testament teaches, Luke 8:15, 21:19, Heb. 11:35.

Latin:

V. 10. Σὺ δὲ παρηκολούθηκάς μυ τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ) Tu verò longe aliud habes exemplar, ad quod te formes, actiones omnes meas, quibus præsens fuisti. Ita hic accipiunt Chry- sostomus, Oecumenius, Theophylactus. Sic Demosthenes de male obita legatione: παρηκολουθηκὼς ἅπασι κατηγορῶ, ideò accuso, quia omnibus istis præsens adfui. Idem: Ὅσα τυγχάνω δι' ἐμπειρίας καὶ τῷ παρηκολουθηκέναι τοῖς πράγμασιν εἰδώς. Quæ novi experiendo, & ideo, quod rebus adfui. Timo- theus, à matre, credo, & avia commendatus, à puero se- ctatus erat Paulum, ut ejus vitam spectaret, & ad eam se componeret. Lucas quidem primam Timothei mentio- nem facit, ubi Paulus Lystra venit, Act. XVI. 1. quia tunc in Evangelistam ordinatus fuit Timotheus, At ante id tem- pus Timotheum adfuisse Paulo, etiam inde apparet, quod jamjam dicatur Iconii cum Paulo fuisse Timotheus, & An- tiochiæ, antequam Iconii. Iconii autem Paulus fuit, ante- quam Lystris, ut videre est Act. XIII. 52. XIV. 1. XVI. 1. Testis, inquit, fuisti meæ doctrinæ, ab initio, quod hic ad- dunt Græci Interpretes. *

Chrysostomus, quem Theophylactus pro more se- quitur, promtam voluntatem & alacritatem animi intelligit. Non enim, inquit, ista locutus sum, & ope- re minimè implevi, nec verbis tantummodo philoso- phatus sum. Magis autem convenit Grotii explica- tio, quæ etiam Theodoreti fuit; Recte didicisti sco- pum meum ac institutum, cui annuit etiam B. Ger- bardus: Per πρόθεσιν finis & scopus actionum Apo- stolicarum intelligitur, quod scil. non suam gloriam, nec suum commodum, sed Dei gloriam & proximi commodum in omnibus Ministerii sui actionibus sibi propositum habuerit. Beza: Tu non modo quid do- cuerim, quid egerim, sed etiam quæ mea mens ac vo- luntas fuerit, prorsus nosti.

Jam ergò perversis hæreticorum doctrinis & moribus suum ipsius opponit exemplum, eodem- que Timotheum ad officium constanter peragen- dum, & perseverantiam in doctrina agnita excitat. Tu verò assectatus es, ac satis intellexisti meam do- ctrinam, institutionem, & propositum, id est, cum fueris individuus itineris mei comes, & actionum mearum socius, ideo omnia mea tibi probe per- specta sunt, & cognita. Ita cum Erasmo & Estio B. Gerhardus noster. Quod autem illis semper adfue- rit Timotheus, certò ex hoc loco colligi non po- test. Non immerito quærit Beza, quid sit affectari alicujus doctrinam, & vita rationem? Porro etiamsi

Alii animi constantiam intelligunt: Sed cum Apostolus ea, quæ in officio Timotheo imitandæ proposuit, tradiderit, nunc ad ea, quæ omnibus piis etiam exemplo esse possunt, quemadmodum & de occupationibus non solum ministrorum verbi, sed omnium fidelium egit v. 12. suumque constantiæ exemplum illis proposuit, accedere videtur: ac per πίστιν id, quod in his Epistolis communiter so- let intelligere, πληροφορίαν nempe fidei, quæ se per sinceritatem pariter ac animi robur ac con- stiamtiam exerit. Cui sensui favent Græcorum ἐκθέσεις. Theodoreti: Fidem, Quamnam habeo in Dominum affectionem: Chrysostomi: Nihil me horum perturbavit. Theophylacti, qui eandem ex- plicat: Fidem, id est, vel in decernenda veritate, vel in adeundis periculis firmitudinem: quæ ne animo conciderem, effecit. Quin ut Deo magis ac magis confiderem, iri me aliquando liberatum.

ea admittatur vocis παρηκολούθηκάς μυ explicatio, non tamen necesse est, ut toto illo tempore semper ac in omnibus locis & actionibus, ac passionibus ejus præstò fuerit Apostolo, sufficit, si plerisque affuerit, alia verò è relatione Apostolica cogno- verit. Nec Lucas illis adfuit, de quibus scripsit, etsi hoc eodem verbo usus sit c. III. 3. quod proinde quandoque solam notitiam, quam quis consecu- tus est, infert, etsi rei gestæ non interfuerit, sed ali- unde eam acceperit. Quo sensu etiam verbum 1. Tim. IV. adhiberi certum est. Observavit & Bu- dæus, verbum illud de animi intelligentia adhiberi, quemadmodum δυσπαρακολούθητα dicta sunt, quæ non facilè intelligentia possumus assequi. Est au- tem, inquit Comment. lingu. Græc. pag. 346. πα- ρακολυθεῖν animadversione & intelligentia assequi; quod ex Æschine, Galeno, & aliis probat Vir Græ- cæ linguæ peritissimus.

Hæc imprimis ad officium pertinet, nec excluditur hoc loco. Generalior tamen vox est eo sensu, & ad plura sese perrigit μακροθυμία objecta. Beat. Gerhardus de lenitate animi, & moderatione erga persecutores & veritatis hostes intelligit. Chrysostomus & Theophyla- ctus erga hæreticos. Theodoretus erga fratres in delictis eorum ferendis, quæ decet omnes fide- les, Matth. XIIX. Gal. VI.

Τῇ ἀγάπῃ) Quæ alibi generaliter sumitur, ut omnes vir- tutes comprehendat, hîc verò specialius pro fraterno affe- ctu in Christianos omnes: Sed in Manuscripto abest hoc.

Cur non Christiana ergà omnes homines dile- ctio intelligatur cum Theodoreto: Quàm omnibus benè velim: Cur non in genere dilectio ergo Deum & homines? Non fuit sane prætermittenda cha- ritas erga Deum, cum exemplar se Timotheo, aliis- que sistit Apostolus.

Τῇ ὑπομονῇ) Quomodo adversis mutatus nihil sim: quæ adversa jam explicat.

Non tolerantiam modò in adversis & persecu- tionibus, sed etiam patientiam, vel patientem constantiam intelligi, vocis ὑπομονῆς usus in Scri- ptis Nov. Test. docet, Luc. IIX. v. 15. XXI. v. 19. Ebr. XI. 35.

## 3:11
Vers. 11.

Τοῖς διωγμοῖς) You have seen the hatreds kindled against me. See Matt. 3:21, 2 Cor. 12:10.

Τοῖς παθήμασι) You have seen what inconveniences have happened to me. See 2 Cor. 1:6, 7, Col. 1:24, Phil. 3:10.

Οἷά μοι ἐγένοντο ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ) Of Pisidia. For Paul had been there before he came to Iconium, Acts 13:14. But the history is touched upon here which is in Acts 13:45 and 50, where you see Paul cast out from there by force.

(In Iconium) The history is touched upon, which is in Acts XIV. 2. 4. 5., where Paul was also stoned.

Ἐν Λύστροις) The history is touched upon which is in Acts 14:18, where Paul was stoned again.

Οἵυς διωγμὺς ὑπήνεγκα) How great were the storms of Jews and Gentiles that poured themselves upon me.

He seems to have made mention of these persecutions specifically, both because they were better known to Timothy, since he was born in Lystra, a city near the other two, as Theodoret and Theophylact judge; and because they were particularly stirred up against Paul by the Jews.

Καὶ ἐκ πάντων με ἐῥῥύσατο Κύριος) A Hebrew construction for ἐξ ὧν πάντων ὁ Κύριός με ἐῥῥύσατο. Christ saved me from greater things.

God does not deliver from adversities in only one way; sometimes He removes them, sometimes He mitigates them, whether by consolation, or by work and help: He always works patience in the heart of the faithful, and finally grants a blessed ἔκβασιν, if not in life, then through death, Rom. VIII. 28. 2 Tim. IV. 18. Both, says Chrysostom, are full of consolation, that I have shown extraordinary cheerfulness, and have not been abandoned. Nor can it be said that GOD has destroyed me, but rather that He has woven a brighter crown for me.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Τοῖς διωγμοῖς) Vidisti accensa in me odia. Vide Matth. III. 21. 2. Cor. XII. 10.

Τοῖς παθήμασι) Vidisti, quæ mihi incommoda evene- rint. Vide 2. Cor. I, 6. 7. Col. I. 24. Philip. III. 10.

Οἷά μοι ἐγένοντο ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ) Pisidiæ. Nam ibi Paulus fuerat, antequam Iconium veniret, Act. XIII. 14. Tangitur autem hîc Historia, quæ est Act. XIII. 45. & 50. ubi vides vi ejestum inde Paulum.

Ἐν Ἰκονίῳ) Tangitur Historia, quæ est Act. XIV. 2. 4. 5. ibi lapidatus etiam Paulus.

Ἐν Λύστροις) Tangitur Historia, quæ est Actor. XIV. 18. ubi rursum lapidatus Paulus.

Οἵυς διωγμὺς ὑπήνεγκα) Quantæ se Judæorum & Gen- tium procellæ in me effuderint.

Videtur harum persecutionum in specie men- tionem fecisse, tum quia istas notiores Timotheo fuère, quum ex Lybiis oriundus fuerit, urbe re- liquis duabus vicina, ut Theodoretus & Theophy- lactus censent; tum quia illa peculiariter à Judæis in Paulum concitatæ fuère.

Καὶ ἐκ πάντων με ἐῥῥύσατο Κύριος) Hebraica constructio pro ἐξ ὧν πάντων ὁ Κύριός με ἐῥῥύσατο. Servavit me Christus rebus majoribus.

Non uno modo Deus ex adversis liberat, quan- doque eadem aufert, quandoque mitigat, sive solatio, sive opere & auxilio: Semper patientiam in corde fidelium operatur, & beatam tandem ἔκβασιν, si non in vita, tamen per mortem conce- dit, Rom. IIX. 28. 2. Tim. IV. 18. Utraque, inquit Chrysostomus, consolationis plena sunt, quod alacri- tatem eximiam præstiti, neque derelictus sum. Nec dici potest, quod me perdiderit DEUS, sed coronam mihi texuerit clariorem.

## 3:12
Vers. 12.

Καὶ πάντες οἱ θέλοντες εὐσεβῶς ζῇν ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, διωχθήσονται) The son of Sirach said: 'My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation.' II. 1. But Paul prudently adds here, 'in Christ Jesus,' because this way according to the Gospel has this peculiar property above others, that it stirs up the hatred of the world against itself, and therefore is exposed to many vexations, even the most savage: which first appeared in the very author of that way, Jesus Christ, who foretold that the same would happen to his own, Matt. X. v. 17, 18. XXIII. 24. John XVI. 33. XVII. 14.

This particle can be taken causally. καὶ πάντες δὲ. For indeed all. He adds this, lest by chance Timothy, or anyone else, should believe that he would be exempt, or if persecutions should arise, that it should seem a wonder. Gregory the Great, lib. VI. Epist. 27. 'I say confidently,' he says, 'that you live less piously if you suffer fewer persecutions.' But by persecutions, as Theophylact warns, he means in this place not only those which are brought by infidels, but any pressures and labors whatsoever, which those who have devoted themselves to virtue undergo. For this life is, according to Job, a certain temptation, and one which proceeds through narrow ways, and is necessarily pressed. 'In Christ,' he says, because there is no true piety except in Christ, John XV. 6, and in the faith of Christ, Heb. XI. 6.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Καὶ πάντες οἱ θέλοντες εὐσεβῶς ζῇν ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, διωχ- θήσονται) Dixit Syrachides: τέκνον εἰ προσέρχῃ δυλεύειν τῷ Κυρίῳ, ἑτοίμασον τὴν ψυχήν σε εἰς πειρασμόν. II. 1. Sed providè hic addit Paulus, ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ, quia ista via se- cundum Evangelium supra cæteras hoc habet proprium, quod mundi odia in se concitat, ideoque multis vexatio- nibus, etiam sævissimis, objacet: quod in ipso autore ejus viæ Jesu Christo primum apparuit, qui suis idem eventu- rum prædixit, Matth. X. v. 17. 18. XXIII. 24. Joh. XVI. 33. XVII. 14.

Particula hæc accipi potest αἰτιολογικῶς. καὶ πάντες δὲ. Enim verò omnes. Hoc addit, ne fortè se exemtum fore Timotheus, aut quisquam alius credat, vel si persecutiones ingruant, id mirum videatur. Gregorius M. lib. VI. Epist. 27. Ego, inquit, fidenter dico, quia minus piè vivis, si minus persecutiones pateris.
