Persecutiones autem, mo- nente Theophylacto, hoc loco dicit, non eas solum, quæ ab infidelibus inferuntur, sed pressuras quasli- bet & labores, quos subeunt, qui virtuti se addixere. Est namque hæc vita, secundum Job, tentatio quæ- dam, & quæ per angusta incedit, & neceffariò pre- mitur. In Christo, inquit, quia nulla est vera pie- tas, nisi in Christo, Joh. XV. 6. & in fide Christi, Ebr. XI. 6.

## 3:13
v. 13. Πονηροὶ δὲ ἄνθρωποι) הרשעים men given to all vices.

Καὶ γόητες) Deceivers. Thus λόγοι γοητικοὶ of Aquila, Prov. XXVI. 22, which others call μαλακοὶ מתלהמים. In the Glossary, γόης is ὁ κόλαξ, a flatterer. Thus Demosthenes calls Aeschines a γόης.

Προκόψουσι ἐπὶ τὸ χεῖρον) They will become more and more shameless, and first they will introduce questions: then they will overturn the very foundations of Christianity.

Πλανῶντες) For those teachers deceive the common people.

Καὶ πλανώμενοι) The same are deceived by philosophers, especially by the Pythagoreans, who were many in Ephesus, as we said regarding the Epistle inscribed to the Ephesians. Πλανῶντες καὶ πλανώμενοι, מתעים ונתעים

The connection and sense here is: There is no reason for us to hope that persecutions will cease during this age, because evil men and seducers always progress for the worse, whence persecutions against the pious do not cease, but grow heavy. γόητες denotes seducers of such a kind, who soothe and deceive others with their tricks. They do not indeed progress according to their wish, so as to prevail by faith, but they progress in evil arts, tricks, and methods of persecution, while they continually lead others into error, just as they themselves wander and are seduced. πλανῶντες καὶ πλανώμενοι, or if you prefer to understand that elegant polyptoton, it means: while they seduce others, they themselves suffer this by the just judgment of God, that they continually fall into graver errors, so that there is no need to change the series with the Vulgate. Theodoret has this to say about these: 'All who wish to live piously, etc.' For the common enemy wages war either through men with men, or through their own thoughts with them. But evil men, etc. For the destructive enemy of the human race brings aid to his own: and like a certain trainer of boys, whose duty it is to exercise boys, he anoints and strengthens them for the practice of vice.

Latin:

v. 13. Πονηροὶ δὲ ἄνθρωποι) הרשעים homines omnibus vitiis dediti.

Καὶ γόητες) Deceptores. Sic λόγοι γοητικοὶ Aquilæ Prov. XXVI. 22. qui aliis μαλακοὶ מתלהמים. In Glossario γόης ὁ κόλαξ blanditor. Sic Demosthenes γόης Æschini.

Προκόψουσι ἐπὶ τὸ χεῖρον) Magis magisque fient invere- cundi, & primum quæstiones inferent : deinde ipsa everrent Christianismi fundamenta.

Πλανῶντες) Doctores enim illi plebem decipiunt.

Καὶ πλανώμενοι) Decipiuntur iidem à philosophis, præ- sertim à Pythagoristis, qui multi Ephesi, ut ad Epistolam Ephesiis inscriptam diximus. Πλανῶντες καὶ πλανώμενοι, מתעים ונתעים

Nexus & sensus hic est: Non est, quod spere- mus persecutiones durante hoc seculo cessaturas, quia homines mali ac seductores in pejus semper proficiunt, unde persecutiones in pios non desi- nunt, sed ingravescunt. γόητες seductores ejusmodi notat, qui præstigiis suis alios demulcent ac deci- piunt. Non proficiunt quidem ex voto, ut præ- valeant fide, proficiunt autem in malis artibus, præstigiis, & persecutionis modis, dum in errorem inducunt subinde alios, quemadmodum ipsi er- rant, & seducti sunt. πλανῶντες καὶ πλανώμενοι vel si mavis elegans illud polyptoton intelligere h. m. dum alios seducunt, ipsi justo Dei judicio hoc pa- tiuntur, ut subinde in graviores errores incidant, ut opus non sit cum Vulgata seriem mutare. Theo- doretus de hisce ita habet: Omnes, qui volunt piè vivere, &c. Communis enim hostis, vel per homines cum hominibus, vel per proprias cogitationes cum eis bellum gerit. Mali autem homines, &c. Suis enim opem fert exitialis humani generis hostis: & veluti quidam pædotriba, cujus munus est exercere pueros, ad vitii exercitationem eos ungit ac confirmat.

## 3:14
v. 14. But you, continue in the things which you have learned) A similar admonition in 1 Tim. VI. v. 14.

And you were assured) The received reading had been ἃ ἐπιστώθης. But it is a construction according to sense, where something is said commonly about two things, which according to an exact rule applies only to one.

But you, says the Apostle, do not follow those seducers, separate yourself from them, and persist in those things which you have once been taught. The Vulgate rendered the word ἐπιστώθης as 'were believed': others, 'which were entrusted to you.' Both are less apt in the judgment of Fuller, Misc. Book I, ch. 19. A different word would have been more appropriate here. See Rom. III. 2. Gal. V. 7. 1 Tim. I. verse 11. The Apostle said neither ἐπιστεύθης, nor ἃ ἐπίστευσας, nor ἃ ἐπιστώθης, but ἐν οἷς ἐπιστώθης. Hesychius interprets ἐπιστώθης most excellently as ἐπληροφορήθης. For it is a greater thing to be fully assured (πιστευθῆναι) than to have learned (μαθεῖν), to be fully certified or to be certain, than to have learned in a general way. For the latter belongs to anyone, the former only to true believers, whose characteristic is full assurance (πληροφορία). Whence Fuller advises that the words of the Apostle should be translated thus: And what firm (or full) faith has been made to you, and that the Syrian looked to this by using the word אשתררת, which also means you were confirmed or established. Our Camerarius on this passage. continue in the things in which, ) i.e., continue in these things which you have learned. An elliptical phrase, which the Greeks often use a great deal; but it says that which is in the former epistle, 'continue in them.' And presently ἐπιστώθης is 'you were made faithful,' so that it may be understood that mention is made of the doctrine of the faith. For it is not ἐπιστεύθης, and the Greeks interpret ἐπιστώθης, that is, 'you were fully assured': Not simply all things, says Theophylact, following Chrysostom, have you learned, as one who has learned thoroughly those things which you received from us, and which were entrusted with certainty and faith. Therefore, if things turn out contrary to what was instituted, you yourself should look to it, do not bear it with a troubled mind, since even Abraham, when he had heard, 'in Isaac your seed shall be called,' yet when commanded to sacrifice him, was not at all disturbed.

Knowing from whom you have learned) He means to say, from me, a man by no means a liar, and very well-wishing to you. In the Manuscript παρὰ τινων, by me and Barnabas.

A single manuscript cannot prejudice all other codices. By me, he says, an Apostle of Jesus Christ, as the title of chapter I, verse 1 had it; which is a far more ample and certain document of divine and infallible information.

Latin:

v. 14. Σὺ δὲ μένε ἐν οἷς ἔμαθες) Similis admonitio 1. Tim. VI. v. 14.

Καὶ ἐπιστώθης) Receptus sermo fuerat ἃ ἐπιστώθης. Sed est constructio κατὰ σύνεσιν, ubi quid communiter de duo- bus dicitur, quod secundum exactam regulam alteri tan- tum convenit.

Tu verò, inquit Apostolus, ne illos seductores sequaris, sejunge te ab illis, ac persiste in iis, quæ semel edoctus es. Verbum ἐπιστώθης Vulg. reddidit cre- dita sunt : alii, quæ tibi concredita sunt. Minus aptè utrique judicio Fulleri l. I. Misc. c. 19. Alia hic op9 fuisset λέξις. Vide Rom. III. 2. Gal. V. 7. 1. Tim. I. vers. 11. Apostolus nec ἐπιστεύθης dixit, nec ἃ ἐπί- στευσας, vel ἃ ἐπιστώθης, sed ἐν οἷς ἐπιστώθης. Optimè Hesychius ἐπιστώθης interpretatur ἐπληροφορήθης. Majus quippe est πιστευθῆναι, quàm μαθεῖν, plenè certiorari, aut certum esse, quàm in genere didicisse. Hoc enim quorumvis est, illud vere credentium duntaxat, quorum propria est πληροφορία. Unde ita vertenda esse verba Apostoli monet Fullerus: Et quàm firma (seu plena) fides tibi facta est, eoq; spectasse Syrum adhibito verbo אשתררת, quod & ἐβεβαιώθης confirmatus, vel stabilitus es. Camerari. noster ad h. l. μένε ἐν οἷς, ) i. e. μένε ἐν τούτοις ἃ ἐμ . ἐλλειπτικὴ φράσις, qua Græci sæpe multum q́; utan- tur, id autem dicit, quod in priore epistola, ἐπίμενε αὐτοῖς. Et mox ἐπιστώθης est πιστὸς ἐγενήθης, ut in- telligatur fieri mentionem doctrinæ fidei. Non enim est ἐπιστεύθης, & interpretantur Græci ἐπιστώθης, id est, ἐπληροφορήθης: Non omnia simpliciter, inquit Theophylactus, præeunte Chrysostomo, didicisti, ut qui ea, quæ à nobis acceperas, & credita sunt cum certitudine & fide perdidicisti. Itaque si contra res evenire ac institutæ es, ipse prospexeris, noli id mo- lesto animo ferre, quandoquidem & Abraham, cùm audisset, in Isaac vocabitur tibi semen, eundem ta- men jussus ut immolaret, nil est obturbatus.

Εἰδὼς παρὰ τίνος ἔμαθες) Vult dicere, à me, homine minimè minimè mendaci, ac tibi optimè volente. In Manuscripto παρὰ τινων, à me & Barnaba.

Manuscriptum unicum præjudicare nequit aliis codicibus omnibus. A me, inquit, Apostolo Jesu Christi, ut habebat titulus cap. I. v. 1. quod longè amplius, certumque divinæ, & infallibilis infor- mationis documentum.

## 3:15
v. 15. And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures) What those holy scriptures are, we shall now hear. It was and is now also the custom of the Jews, from the earliest age capable of letters, to give the holy scriptures to boys to read.

Why therefore does the Roman Pontiff interdict the reading of the Sacred letters to the Jews themselves, even if they were then most corrupt, and worse, not only to boys, but even to adults, if they are laymen? Claudius Espencaeus on this passage: Some think the Scriptures are too difficult to be worn out by the hands of the Laity. But it seemed otherwise to the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments. The Jews adapted their five-year-old sons to the Holy Bible, and gave the first place to instructing boys in the Holy letters, from which they began, which Eusebius writes that they preserved from the ancient custom of the Jews to his own times. Let Christians therefore be ashamed to be strangers to this care, and this is not new, but is the complaint of the ancient Fathers. Estius on this passage. This passage, he says, teaches that neither boys are to be kept away from the reading of Holy Scripture. Nay, from the fact that Timothy was not instructed in the holy letters by his father (inasmuch as he was a Gentile, and he had not suffered him to be circumcised) but, as is likely, by his mother and grandmother, whose sincerity of faith the Apostle praised in chapter I, it is gathered that neither are women to be prohibited from the reading of Holy Scripture. He adds indeed: Which, however, understand in such a way, provided such persons are according to the Ecclesiastical rule, who are known to be able to take from such reading not damage, but an increase of faith and piety: just as the Pontiff prescribes. But how will he apply this to this warning about boys? And who will admit that anyone by himself perceives damage from this reading? That is by accident. Claudius Espencaeus on this passage. Origen, he says, observes that John writes to four ages, boys, adolescents, youths, fathers, 1 John II. Jerome distinguishes between Philosophers and Apostles thus, that Plato for example wrote certain things, but for a few, not for the people. But the Apostles and Evangelists did not write for a few, but for the whole people. So also the Lord Christ spoke, not so that a few, but so that all might understand. For Prosper's little verse about Scripture is well known: Which suits no minds, no ages not. Jodocus Coccius Vol. I, Thes. Book VI, art. 30, page 753, praises that of Basil the Great, Exhortation to Leon the Son, ch. 17. O son, just as a tender plant irrigated by fountains grows green, and bears flowers and fruits: so your mind irrigated by the studies of the Sacred letters will grow more and more, and for fruits will bring forth excellent virtues. Is this to bring damage? Ederus in Oecon. Bibl. page 76, teaches: that Holy Scripture is accommodated to all, and exhibits manifold and life-giving utilities, having adduced Chrysostom, Homily XLI on Matthew. Chrysostom explains ἀπὸ βρέφες in this passage as ἐκ πρώτης ἡλικίας, from the first age, he says, immediately you learned the holy letters. What are the Holy letters? Divine Scriptures. In these, he says, you were educated, so that through them also a greater virtue of faith might be added to you, and thus it has prevailed, resting on the deepest roots, solidified by long time.

Which are able to make thee wise unto salvation, through faith which is in Christ Jesus) He says this: those letters lead you to Christ, who confers salvation upon those believing in him. The same sense in John V:39, where see the sayings. σοφίσαι, to instruct. Thus David concerning the Law, Ps. XIX:8, making wise the simple.

For the sake of the Papists, the passage is perverted. They do not only lead Holy Scripture to Christ, from whom salvation is had: But they CAN not only instruct us, as the Vulgate rendered it, but make us WISE, and thus they even make us wise unto salvation: which is through faith in Christ. Therefore that wisdom, which is necessary for salvation, can be had from the Scriptures: nay, even faith itself in Christ is had from Scripture. For the Holy letters teach and require faith in Christ: they teach what faith in Christ is: and Timothy had learned that from a child from Scripture. Theophylact on this passage. For not as this exterior worldly science instructs a man for fallacies, circumventions, and contentions of words, so that divine one instructs us, but rather it instructs us unto salvation. Which if you seek, it is certainly not that which consists in works and words, but that which consists in faith in Christ Jesus. For when these Sacred Writings induce a man to believe in Christ, they produce for him undoubted salvation. Estius here assigns another cause, but only an accessory one, why Timothy should not recede from the doctrine once received. He had therefore received saving doctrine from thence from a child, he had not only learned it finally from Paul. Furthermore, saying unto salvation, he shows, says Estius, the scope of the reading and study of the Scriptures: Which indeed he expressed more fully in the mentioned passage (1 Tim. IV) when he says: For in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee. But what he says: The words, which is through faith, were added then, so that it might be signified that from the Holy Scriptures, both because of their obscurity, and because of the blindness and dullness of our intellect, and the depravity of the affections with which we labor, no one can draw sound and incorrupt doctrine, unless he is fortified by the faith of Christ, and uses it as a guide to understand them; is a false interpretation, and from a preconceived false opinion. If Holy Scripture is obscure, how could Timothy be instructed from it from infancy by its reading? And is not that blindness of our intellect, and depravity of affections, dispelled by Scripture itself, which converts souls, and gives wisdom to the simple, Ps. XIX, v. 8, to which one must attend, as St. Peter warns, 1 Epist. I:19, as to a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawns, and the day star arises in our hearts. The Apostle does not say that the reader of Holy Scripture must be forearmed with faith: but rather he teaches that faith arises from the reading of Scripture, because through it are had doctrine and righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, instructed for every good work, so that it may otherwise lead to faith and salvation. This is therefore not merely an accessory cause, but the principal one, why Timothy must persist in the doctrine of the Gospel, inasmuch as it was not only handed down by the Apostle, but, lest any doubt arise concerning the Apostle's tradition, drawn from the sacred writings from infancy: just as the Apostle himself also protested that he taught nothing else than what Moses and the Prophets (in their writings) teach, Acts XXVI. v. 22. In this volume, says Gregory the Great, Bishop, Rom. l. IX. in Ez., all things that edify, all things that instruct are contained in the writings, and lib. XIIX. cap. 14. Those who desire to speak truly must take from the pages of the authority of Scripture what they say. Anselm of Canterbury (others make Herveus the author) on this passage: Sacred letters can instruct you, that is, render you sufficiently learned for salvation. Cardinal Cajetan on this passage: The discourse is about the Holy Scriptures of the New Testament, which can instruct you through wisdom, to teach for salvation through faith. For they have the power of teaching wisdom, not of this world, but for eternal salvation, so that the man of God may be perfect, that is, whole, consisting of all the requisites for the perfecting of a man of GOD. Laurent. Villarinc. lib. de rat. stud. Theol. cap. 3. Scripture, and indeed it alone, can instruct us unto salvation through faith in Christ. Consult also what is to be brought forward from Claud. Espensæus on the following verse. Two causes, says Theophylact here, he brings forward, by which he ought to show himself immovable: since not only because he learned these things not from a man of little importance, but from Paul himself, which is the same as saying as if he had received them from Christ; but also because he had been taught them not recently or yesterday, but from his youth. As if he were to say, divine knowledge is rooted in you, and so, that it is by no means some insane and stupid act that you undergo what is permitted, and such as many suffer. For he who has been instructed in the sacred letters as is fitting, will never be changed once a purpose has been accepted. He calls the sacred letters the divine writings.

Latin:

v. 15. Καὶ ὅτι ἀπὸ βρέφες τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα οἶδας) Quæ sint ista ἱερὰ γράμματα jam audiemus. Mos erat & est nunc quoque Judæorum, à prima ætate, quæ literarum capax est, sacra scripta legenda dare pueris.

Cur ergò Pontifex Romanus ipsis Judæis, etsi tum corruptissimis, pejor, non pueris tantum, sed adultis etiam, si laici sint, Sacrarum literarum le- ctioni interdicit? Claudius Espensæus in hoc loco: Aliqui existimant Scripturas difficiliores esse, quàm ut debeant Laicorum manibus conteri. Sed aliter visum est Patribus V. & Nov. Testam. Judæi filios suos quinquennes ad S. Biblia adaptabant, & pri- mum locum informandis pueris S. literis, unde au- spicabantur, tribuebant, quod ex prisca consuetu- dine Judæorum ad sua tempora servasse Eusebius scribit. Pudeat igitur Christianos ab hac cura alie- nos esse, neque hæc nova, sed est Patrum antiquo- rum querimonia. Estius in hunc loc. Locus hic, inquit, docet, nec pueros arcendos esse à lectione Scripturæ S. Quin ex eo, quod Timotheus non à Patre fuerit institutus in sacris literis (utpote qui gentilis erat, nec passus fuerat eum circumcidi) sed, ut verisimile est, à matre & avia, quarum fidei sin- ceritatem laudavit Apostolus cap. I. colligitur, nec mulieres à lectione Scripturæ S. prohibendas esse. Addit quidem: Quod tamen ita intellige, modo se- cundum regulam Ecclesiasticam tales sint personæ, quæ cognoscantur ex hujusmodi lectione non da- mnum, sed fidei atque pietatis augmentum capere posse: quemadmodum præscribit Pontifex. Sed quomodo hæc applicabit huic monito de pueris? Et quis admittet, è lectione hâc quempiam per se damnum percipere? Id ex accidenti est. Clau- dius Espensæus in h. l. Origenes, inquit, observat, Jobannem quatuor ætatibus scribere, pueris, ado- lescentibus, juvenibus, patribus, 1. Joh. II. Hie- ronymus inter Philosophos & Apostolos sic distin- guit, quod Plato exempli gratia scripsit quædam, sed paucis, non populo. At Apostoli & Evangelistæ non scripserunt paucis, sed universo populo. Ita etiam Dominus Christus locutus est, non ut pauci, sed ut omnes intelligerent. Scitum enim est Prosperi ver- siculus de Scriptura: Quæ nullis animis, nullis non convenit annis. Jodocus Coccius Tom. I. Thes. l. VI. art. 30. pag. 753. laudat illud Basilii Magni Exhort. ad Leon. Fil. c. 17. O filii, quemadmodum tenera planta fontibus irrigata virescunt, floresque & fructus ferunt: ita mens tua Sacrar. literarum studiis irrigata magis ac magis augefcet, ac pro fru- ctibus egregias virtutes proferet. Estne hoc da- mnum afferre? Ederus in Oecon. Bibl. pag. 76. docet: Scripturam S. esse omnibus accommodatam, & multiplices, atque vivificas utilitates exhibere, adducto Chrysostomo hom. XLI. in Matth. ἀπὸ βρέφες Chrysost. hoc loco explicat ἐκ πρώτης ἡλι- κίας, à prima, inquit, statim ætate sacras literas di- dicisti. Quid sunt S. literæ? Scripturæ divinæ. In his, inquit, educatus es, ut per eas quoque major tibi fidei virtus accesserit, adeoque invaluerit, ut nihil jacturæ possit incurrere, altissimis radicibus nixa, longo tempore solidata.

Τὰ δυνάμενά σε σοφίσαι εἰς σωτηρίαν, διὰ πίσεως τῆς ἐν Χρι- σῷ Ἰησοῦ) Hoc dicit: literæ istæ te ducunt ad Christum, qui sin se credentibus confert salutem. Idem sensus Joh. V 39. ubi dicta vide. σοφίσαι מחכימ instruere. Sic David de Lege, Ps. XIX. 8. מחכימת פתי σοφίζεσα νήπια.

In Papistarum gratiam locus insignis perverti- tur. Non adducunt tantum S. Scripturae ad Chri- stum, a quo salus habetur: Sed POSSUNT nos non instruere modo, ut Vulg. reddidit, sed SA- PIENTES reddere, adeoque sapientes etiam nos reddunt ad salutem: quae est per fidem in Christum. Sapientia ergo illa, quae ad salutem necessaria est, e Scripturis haberi potest: imo ipsa etiam fides in Christum ex Scriptura habetur. Nam docent & requirunt S. literae fidem in Chri- stum: docent, quid sit fides in Christum: idque ex Scriptura didicerat a puero Timotheus. Theo- phylactus in h. l. Non enim ut exterior haec mun- dana scientia hominem ad fallacias, circumven- tiones, & concertationes verborum erudit, sic di- vina illa nos instruit, quin potius ad salutem insti- tuit. Quam illam si quaeras, non ea certe, quae ope- ribus constat & verbis, sed quae in Christo Jesu fide consistit. Nam cum Sacra haec Scripta hominem in Christum ut credat, inducunt, salutem ei haud du- biam pariunt. Estius hic alteram causam, sed tan- tum accessoriam assignat, cur Timotheo non sit a doctrina semel accepta recedendum. Acceperat ergo inde salutarem doctrinam a puero, non tan- tum a Paulo didicerat demum. Porro dicens ad salutem ostendit, inquit Estius, scopum lectionis & studii Scripturarum: Quem quidem plenius ex- pressit loco memorato, (1. Tim. IV.) cum ait: Hoc enim faciens & teipsum salvum facies, & eos, qui audiunt te. Quod autem ait: Verba, quae est per fidem, addita tum esse, ut significetur ex Scripturis S. tum ob earum obscuritatem, tum ob intellectus nostri caecitatem & hebetudinem, atque affectuum, quibus laboramus, pravitatem, non posse quen- quam haurire doctrinam sanam & incorruptam, nisi fide Christi praemunitus sit, eaque ductrice ad illas intelligendas utatur; a ψευδεγμηνεία est, & e praecepta falsa opinione. Si Scriptura S. obscura est, quomodo inde ab infantia ex ejusdem lectio- ne instrui potuit Timotheus? Et an non illa in- tellectus nostri caecitas, & affectuum pravitas per ipsam Scripturam discutitur, quae animas conver- tit, & sapientiam praestat parvulis, Ps. XIX. v. 8. cui attendendum, monente S. Petro, 1. Epist. I. 19. quasi lucerna lucenti in loco caliginoso, ut dies illu- cescat, & lucifer oriatur in cordibus nostris. Fide praemunitum esse debere lectorem S. literarum, non ait Apostolus: sed fidem potius oriri e Scripturae lectione docet, quia per eam habetur doctrina, & justitia, ut perfectus sit homo DEI ad omne opus bo- num instructus, ut alias ad fidem & salutem per- ducat. Non ergo haec accessoria tantum causa est, sed praecipua, cur persistendum Timotheo sit in doctrina Evangelii, utpote non tantum ab Apostolo tradita, sed ne qua de Apostoli tra- ditione dubium oriatur, e sacris literis ab ipsa infantia hausta: quemadmodum & Apostolus ipse protestatus est, se nihil aliud docere, praeterquam quod Moses & Prophetae (in scriptis suis) docent, Act. XXVI. v. 22. In hoc volumine, inquit Grego- rius M. Episcopus, Rom. l. IX. in Ez. cuncta, quae aedificant, omnia quae erudiunt scripta, continentur, & lib. XIIX. cap. 14. Qui vere loqui desiderant, ex Scripturae autoritatis paginis desumere debent, quod loquantur. Anshelmus Cant. (alii Hervaeum fa- ciunt autorem) in h. loc. Sacrae literae possunt te instruere, hoc est, sufficienter doctum reddere ad salutem. Cajetanus Card. ad hunc loc. Sermo est de S. literis Nov. Test. quae te possunt instruere per sa- pientiam, docere ad salutem per fidem. Habent enim facultatem docendi sapientiam non hujus mundi, sed ad aeternam salutem, ut sit homo DEI perfectus, hoc est, integer constans ex omni- bus requisitis ad perficiendum hominem DEI. Lau- rent. Villarinc. lib. de rat. stud. Theol. cap. 3. Scriptura & quidem sola possunt nos ad salutem erudire per fidem Christi. Cons. & quæ è Claud. Espensæo ad seq. vers. adducenda. Duas causas, inquit hìc Theophylactus, affert, quibus debeat ille immobilem se præstare: cùm quia non ab aliquo parvi momenti viro, sed à se Paulo ea didicerit, quod perinde est dicere, ac si à Christo acceperit: tum quia non nuper aut pridie, sed à parvis fuisset edoctus. Quasi dicat, irradicata est in Te divina scientia, & ita,ut nequaquam sit insanum aliquod & stolidum facinus, ut subeas permissum, & qualia multi perpetiuntur. Nam qui sacris literis fue- rit ut decet instructus, nunquam accepto proposito immutabitur. Sacras autem literas dicit divina scripta.

## 3:16
Ver. 16.

All scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching) The Syrian well expressed the sense: every scripture, which is inspired by GOD, is also useful for teaching, etc. For GOD does nothing in vain, nor does He inspire men, except to teach us. Now, scripture that is θεόπνευστος is that which was written either by those who performed the duties of Prophets, such as Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, or by those who, although they were in another walk of life, were nevertheless inspired by GOD at certain times, such as David and Daniel. In place of an accession to these, and to fulfill either moral wisdom or history, some other books were added, approved by the great Synagogue, as agreeing best with those θεοπνεύστοις. The Christian Church, both Greek and Latin by consensus, added others to these very ones afterwards. Πρὸς διδασκαλίαν למלמדה. See Rom. XV. 4. Those Prophetic books do not teach us everything that Christ did, but yet some things pertaining to it, Gal. III. 24. 2. Pet. I. 19.

Πρὸς ἔλεγχον) לתוכחה as in Proverbs several times. It is useful for showing the baseness of graver crimes. Thou shalt not kill: Thou shalt not commit adultery, etc. He said ἔλεγξις in the same sense 2. Pet. II. 16. You will see what ἐλέγχειν is, Matth. XVIII. ver. 15. Luc. III. ver. 19. Joh III. v. 20. 1. Cor. XIV. ver 24. 1. Tim. V. ver. 20. below IV. v. 2. Tit. I. ver. 9. 13. II. 15.

πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν) There is a certain distinction between ἔλεγχον and ἐπανόρθωσιν. The shameless are rebuked (ἐλέγχονται): the tender and fragile are set right (ἐπανορθῦνται). ὀρθῦν or ἐπανορθῦν is עשק, to sustain one who is tottering.

Πρὸς παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ) למוסר בצדק. Those scriptures direct those who have already begun well, more and more to persist in the path of innocence.

Not one corruption of this famous passage occurs here. First, as far as the subject is concerned, to the Scripture of which the Apostle speaks, there are referred, as appears from Grotius, not only the Canonical Scriptures of the O. Test., but also the Apocryphal, which were added by the consensus of the Christian Church, both Greek and Latin. Which Papistic error we have refuted in the Critico S. The Church did not add them by universal consensus, nor did it have the power of adding anything to the Canon accepted by the Jewish Church, approved by Christ and the Apostles, which is to be received with equal affection of piety, or deserves to be referred to τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα, which are commended by θεοπνευσία and truly divine authority, and admits the same predicates. If it be said that the Church added the O. Test. to the writings of the Evangelists and Apostles, those were not properly added by the Church, but by the Holy Spirit, by whom they were inspired, and collected by St. John, who put the final hand to the Canon, as we showed in the Critic. S. But Grotius seems in this place to restrict it rather to the Prophetic books, which are here predicated of Scripture. But Scripture knows no other Prophetic books, nor does the truly Catholic Church, outside of those which were written in the Hebrew language by the Prophets, to whom that was proper, and entrusted to the Jewish Church, Rom. III. v. 2. Luc. XVI. v. 29. 2. Pet. I. v. 19. Furthermore, just as the Scriptures of the New Testament are not to be excluded from those to whom those predicates apply, there is no doubt, so it is not to be denied that the same must be applied to these. For although τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα, which Timothy had known from infancy, are only the Scriptures of the O. T., there had nevertheless been added in the meantime, while he progressed more and more from the Scriptures, the writings of the Evangelists and the Apostolic writings, which could not have been unknown to Timothy. For Timothy had ascribed his salvation to the Epistle to the Romans, he had brought the former to the Corinthians, he had subscribed to the latter to the Corinthians, to both to the Thessalonians, as also to that which is to the Philippians, that to the Colossians, that to Philemon, and he had read the former written to himself, and those which he perhaps had not yet read of the Apostolic scriptures, he himself, and others to whom Scripture is commended in his person, were entirely about to read. Whether therefore the reason is given here that the S. letters make us wise, or the use of Scripture is simply commended, these things are perfectly consistent. For the reason that the O. T. Scripture provides that wisdom will be this, that Scripture was inspired for that end, and therefore also the O. T. Scripture, which alone was [Scripture] before the N. T. Scripture was added. For if every truly Sacred Scripture, which is here implied from the preceding, by reason of its efficient cause, matter, and end, because it is from a holy author, concerning holy things, and because through it a man is sanctified, is immediately inspired by GOD, and has such uses as the Apostle brings forward here, then the O. T. Scripture must also have been θεόπνευστος and ὠφέλιμος: but that which is such, there is no doubt that it provides wisdom unto salvation through faith in Christ. Estius, however, likes to present the connection thus: Since he was exhorting to the reading of S. Scripture, he now commends it with a distinguished encomium, first from its authority, then from the utility which proceeds from it. Which appears more expressly in the Greek: Every Scripture divinely inspired, and useful, supply, is. Therefore two things are affirmed, that every Scripture is divinely inspired, and that the same is useful for those things which follow. He understands Sacred Scripture, of which he had said: You have known the sacred letters: For by the name of Scripture, Sacred Scripture is signified throughout the Bible by antonomasia, as Matt. XXII. You err, not knowing the Scriptures, John V. Search the Scriptures, and X. The Scripture cannot be broken. Rightly therefore and most truly is it established from this passage, that every Sacred and Canonical Scripture was written with the Holy Spirit dictating, so indeed, that not only the sentences, but also the individual words, and the order of the words, and the whole arrangement is from God, as if speaking or writing through Himself. For this is what it is for Scripture to be divinely inspired. But he explains the utility thereafter. Which refute quite solidly Grotius, who makes one out of two predicates, and converts the copulative particle into the substantive verb IS.

If it be said that it should not be rendered EVERY Scripture, but whole, or universal, because it is false that every scripture has these uses: Estius answers: It is to be noted that the Apostle does not mean that every single part of sacred Scripture is useful for these four (for here the sense is clearly false) but that in the universal Scripture these four utilities are found, so indeed, that one part of Scripture brings one utility, and that there is no Scripture which does not avail for some of these. We add that these uses can be asserted of every sentence of scripture as well. For they all certainly inform about something, and thus are apt to refute those asserting the contrary to what they teach, by the authority of the speaker, the Holy Spirit, or by the power of θεοπνευστίας. And since information in the Scriptures, by the intention of the supreme author, is not theoretical, but practical, they all inform with respect to the end of the Holy Scriptures for the sake of faith, to which all things have their relation, to the righteousness which is in Christ, that through faith in Christ we may have salvation, John 20, v. last. Hence, therefore, those who neglect or pervert that intention of the Holy Scriptures also detract from the faith, whether directly or indirectly, whence there is a need for correction, which use emerges from the comparison be considered here that the sentences of Scripture are to be regarded not separately, but as they are viewed in the body of Scripture, not in a divided sense, but a composite one, and as they are compared with others, having proceeded from the same author and for the same end. Nevertheless, those things may also be understood relatively or respectively, so that in respect to some, utility is implied for teaching, for others for refuting, for others for correcting, for others for instructing in righteousness.

Furthermore, as to the predicates, they pertain not only to those things which are said concerning utility, but also to the θεόπνευσία (God-breathed nature) itself, which Grotius indeed refers to the subject, but the particle καὶ teaches that it constitutes a distinct predicate, which the Vulgate rashly neglected. The Syriac rendered θεόπνευστος as 'written by the Holy Spirit,' implying that not only the sentences, but also the written words, and the order and disposition of the words, are from GOD, as the blessed Gerhard says here; which we have opposed elsewhere to Grotius and Calixtus. Cf. System. Theol. Vol. I, p. 561. Now Grotius also perverts the use of Scripture: first, διδασκαλίαν (teaching), as if the prophetic books only taught some things pertaining to doctrine; which is rashly gathered from Galatians 3, verse 14, and 2 Peter 1, verse 20. We spoke of the meaning of that passage there. But here the plain opposite is taught: namely, when we attend to the Scripture of the Old Testament. that we are illuminated by it, so that the day-star may arise in our hearts: nor did Christ refer elsewhere than to Moses and the Prophets, and taught that from them the Jews could be instructed unto eternal salvation and concerning escaping eternal condemnation, John 5, verse 39; Luke 16, verse 29. The Apostle, however, testified that he taught nothing outside of Moses and the Prophets, Acts 26, verse 22, although he delivered the whole counsel of GOD concerning salvation, Acts 20, v. 27. But we have refuted that Socinian error concerning the Scripture of the Old Testament in 'Socinismo profligato,' in the 'System. Theol.,' and elsewhere. Next, Grotius calls ἔλεγχον (reproof) a demonstration of the baseness of graver crimes. But ἐλέγχειν and ἔλεγχος, according to the usage of Scripture and the consensus of interpreters, is the refutation of false doctrine. Cf. 1 Cor. 14, verse 24; Tit. 1, v. 9. And the context demands this: since the uses of Scripture, both theoretical and practical, are enumerated here. Similarly Theophylact: (for teaching) It is profitable, he says, because it instructs us what must be learned thoroughly. For there is nothing that cannot be resolved by the Scriptures. (for reproof) If, namely, lies must be refuted, (for correction, for instruction in righteousness) If it is necessary, he says, that something either be corrected or instructed, that is, to render one continent and sober unto righteousness, and to execute those things which are just, all that will be supplied from the sacred writings. Therefore, as to the third use, τὴν ἐπανόρθωσιν (correction), it is rashly restricted to the tender and fragile; the Greeks refer it in general to correction. Ambrosiaster: that it may restore the deformed. Finally, he restricts παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ (instruction in righteousness) with equal rashness to those who have already begun well, when it also pertains to those who have not yet begun well, Tit. 2, verse 12. Ambrosiaster rendered it, 'drawing the unrighteous to righteousness.' Our people not undeservedly build the perfection of sacred Scripture from this, to which the Papists also sometimes accede, constrained by the force of truth. Scripture, says Claudius Espencaeus, if there is anything to bear, if there is anything to do, teaches what is true, corrects what is false, leads back from evil, leads to good, and indeed they do not make one good in any way, but they perfect, and can instruct men unto salvation, and render one sufficiently learned. Leonhard Marius, Prolegomena in Sacr. Script. q. 2, sect. 5, said of the Holy Scriptures: The blessed Apostle Paul, in the 2nd Epistle to Timothy, chapter 3, says they can instruct you unto salvation, and adds that through them it comes to pass that the man of GOD may be perfect, instructed unto every good work. And indeed it is so. For we learn from these, not only what to believe, but also what to do, how to be helped, and what we ought to hope for and fear, in which the whole perfection of human life consists. Guilelmus Popik, Dominican, in Postill., Dom. II. Adv. Conc. I. This Scripture alone teaches perfectly and plainly what is to be believed, as are the articles of faith; what is to be done, as are the divine precepts; what is to be shunned, as are vices; what is to be feared, as are eternal torments; what is to be sought and desired, as are heavenly joys.

Therefore, there is no reason why you should except, with Bellarmine and Estius, that Scripture is indeed useful for these things, but not sufficient. For that which is useful for all the duties that are required of a teacher of the Church, there is no doubt that it suffices for the entire institution of the doctrine of faith. That which is so useful for teaching, etc., that the man of GOD may be rendered perfect, instructed unto every good work, ought to be considered sufficiently useful and perfect in every way. That which is so useful that it makes us wise unto salvation through faith, it is certain beyond a doubt that it suffices for salvation. If you say with Estius: the same would have to be said concerning the Scripture of the Old Testament: Response: That the Canon of the Old Testament was entirely sufficient in its own time, and yet the Old Testament is not unnecessary for us in the time of the New Testament, because we must believe that what was believed in the Old Testament to be about to be fulfilled has been fulfilled; nor, therefore, does the New Testament deliver anything different from the Old Testament, but only exhibits its complement. For it delivers nothing outside of those things which were written in Moses and the Prophets, Acts 26, verse 22. Furthermore, we invert the argument: If the writings of the Old Testament could instruct unto salvation, why should not the same be said of the universal Scripture of the Old and New Testament? Thomas acknowledges this, part 1, quest. 29, art. 3, from Dionysius, saying, universally, one must not believe or think anything beyond those things which have been divinely expressed to us from the Holy utterances: and in Comment. III. sent. dist. 3, quest. 1. art. 1. from Jerome: Do not believe me, if I say anything to you which you cannot find in either the Old or New Testament, and lect. III. in this place. The effect of Holy Scripture is fourfold, namely: to teach the truth, to refute falsehood, regarding the speculative; to snatch from evil, and to lead to good, regarding the practical: its final effect is that it may lead men to perfection, it does not indeed make them good in any way whatsoever, but it perfects them. Ludovicus Soto Major asserts the perfection of Scripture even more fully from the present passage in his commentary. Every Scripture, he says, inspired by God is apt or suitable, that is, it provides the faculty, or supplies abundant material for teaching, for refuting, for correcting, for instructing. In it, therefore, you will easily, and as if ready at hand, find what you may teach the people, the faithful, and the clergy, with which you may refute heretics, with which you may correct even depraved morals and speech, or depraved dogmas, with which, moreover, you may instruct and train little ones, who like infants have need of milk. Finally, it is useful for all things which are necessary and consistent for the attainment of true justice, piety, and salvation, that is, that the man of God may be perfect, instructed for every good work.

We dealt with this apostolic eulogy of Scripture in a special disputation published here in the year 1568. But the begun treatment, because of the unexpected departure of the respondent, who had left no copy, could not be continued: However, it is pleasing to append to these what was published at that time, so that that work may not perish entirely. But that treatment is arranged in paragraphs as follows.

§. I. Holy Scripture is celebrated with many eulogies; which are read in Scripture itself. And no wonder; because no one is a more worthy herald of the word of God than God himself, who speaks in the Scriptures. But after the lyre of David, who destined an entire Psalm, and that a most prolix and beautiful one, which you might call the alphabet of alphabets, to the praises of Scripture, it is not easy to find anything more excellent in the whole of Scripture than what we now have in hand: which the trumpet of the Gospel, the roar of our Lion, the thunder of the nations (thus Jerome names Paul in his letter to Pammachius) proclaims. For this so clearly sets forth both the divinity of the holy letters, and their necessity, and their all-manner and most absolute perfection, and their altogether divine utility, and at the same time describes all the causes of Holy Scripture so graphically, that even this one truly apostolic axiom might abundantly suffice to powerfully confound all haters of writing.

§. II. But it stands thus in the Greek sources: πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος, καὶ ὠφέλιμος πρὸς διδασκαλίαν, πρὸς ἔλεγχον, πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν, πρὸς παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ. Ἱνα ἄρτιος ἦ ὁ τῦ θεῦ ἄνθρωπος, πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐξηρτισμένος. The Vulgate renders it thus: All Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in justice, that the man of God may be perfect, instructed for every good work. The Syriac version, from the interpretation of Tremellius, stands thus: For in Scripture, which is written by the Spirit, there is utility for doctrine, and for reproof, and for correction, and for training, which is in justice: that the son of man of God may be perfect and absolute for every good work. The interpretation of the Trostian Syriac version is this: For all Scripture, which is written by the Spirit, is useful for doctrine, and for reproof, and for correction, and for training, which is in justice, etc.

§. III. A certain diversity appears. First, the Syrian and the Vulgate employ the causal conjunction ENIM (for), which is not held in the original text; added without doubt for the sake of sense and connection. For they do not always render it word for word. Then in the Syriac version, the readings vary in the first word, which variety has no place in the original text, nor can it have. Tremellius renders: In SCRIPTURA. For thus, he says, the Syriac words sound על כתב etc. He adds: I would not dare to say that על is placed for כל (although it would correspond better to the Greek text) because not only the printed, but also the manuscript Heidelberg Codex, which appears to be very ancient, reads על. But Francis Junius proves that others read 'all Scripture', and rightly so. Which diverse reading Trostius observed in the various readings at the foot of the New Testament, because a certain Viennese Codex and the Tremellius MSS read על, but Guido Fabricius has כל. Which reading, as being consonant with the source, is entirely to be preferred. A slip is easy in these similar letters in the inscription. Hence, thirdly, a difference has arisen. For since Guido and Trostius have מותרנא הו (it is useful), so that it may correspond to the subject, 'all Scripture': in the Viennese and Tremellius MSS it is noted by Trostius that מותרנא הן (utility is) is read. But the former corresponds to the original text: saying that all Scripture is useful, not merely placing utility in Scripture. Fourthly, the Greek text has two predicates, which are uttered concerning Scripture, that it is divinely inspired and useful. πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος καὶ ὠφέλιμος, all Scripture is divinely inspired and useful: the Vulgate refers the former predicate to the description of the subject, omits the copulative particle, and leaves only one predicate. All Scripture divinely inspired is useful. And so also the Syrian interpreter. But because the Greek Codices agree, there is without doubt a slip of the interpreters here, or too much boldness. Grotius, however: The Syrian well expressed the sense, 'all Scripture, which is inspired by God, is also useful for teaching.' In the same way Erasmus had reconciled it: It appears there is a tacit force of arguing in the conjunction. Scripture, as it is divinely inspired, is also effective for many things, whereas human doctrine is ineffective. But in the Greek text those two predicates are connected by an interposed comma, πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος, καὶ ὠφέλιμος, which Grotius omitted, so that by rendering the particle καὶ as 'also', he might make the sense in the Greek consonant with the Syriac interpretation. Wrongly. For the original text is not to be adapted to the versions, but the versions to the original text. And it is manifest that two predicates are uttered here concerning Scripture, in the commending of which the Apostle is engaged, both its divine inspiration and its truly divine utility. And Erasmus acknowledges this in the cited place. Meanwhile, it is certain that the latter redounds from the former, and that Scripture therefore possesses these utilities because it is divinely inspired. Fifthly, Grotius reads the last word ἐξαρτυμένος; with Arias Montanus, who rendered it 'prepared', from ἐξαρτύομαι, just as Castellio translates it 'composed'. The Latin Vulgate seems to have followed yet another reading, according to Erasmus and Beza, as if it had been written ἐξηρτημένος from ἐξαρτάω, which is to construct and prepare, as Beza observed it is also read in the Complutensian edition. For the Vulgate rendered it 'instructed'. But most of the better Codices all have ἐξηρτισμένος, which reading Beza and Junius follow, rendering it 'perfectly instructed'. Which Grotius also approves: 'Better,' he says, 'other Codices [read] ἐξηρτισμένος.' Sixthly, some difference is detected in the Syrian in the last words, but a slight one, and one which does not change the sense. For he places a comma after ἔργον ἀγαθὸν and a conjunction before ἐξηρτισμένος. And he translates that ἄρτιον as גמיר, which is consummatus or perfectus, so that it may be perfectus filius hominis Dei, that is, a man of GOD in the manner of speaking of the Syrians, which is extremely familiar: but he explains the latter, ἐξηρτισμένος, by prefixing the conjunction ומשלמן, which has almost the same meaning; Trostius rendered it with Tremellius as absolutus. Seventhly, it may be observed that the Syriac version rendered the word θεόπνευστος according to the sense alone, דברוחא אתכתב, which is "written by the Spirit." These declare one another. For because the holy men of GOD wrote by divine inspiration, holy Scripture is written by the Spirit: for this is peculiarly appropriated to the Holy Spirit. Nor were the sacred writers only inspired in that divine revelation was made to them, but they also wrote those things which were revealed by the same Spirit who disclosed them to them.

So that whatever was written by them, even all the words by which it was written, may be from Him. The Greek is nevertheless still more emphatic: because it makes divine inspiration the efficient cause; and in it also establishes the form of Holy Scripture, as it is divine, in that it is θεόπνευστος (God-breathed). Eighth, the Latin reading can be corrected from a collation of the Greek and Syriac text. St. Ambrose, says Erasmus, translates πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν as 'for restoration,' for which our codices have 'for correcting.' But I do not know whether the interpreter wrote 'for correcting.' And what I guessed in the fourth edition I found in the Constance copies: 'for correcting.' For the Greek word sounds like 'to set upright' what was crooked: and thus also the emendations of the Popes Sixtus V and Clement VIII have 'for correcting.' Which agrees with the Greek and Syriac word. It is a trivial matter that in place of the nouns 'for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction,' the Vulgate used the verbs 'for teaching, for arguing, for correcting, for instructing.' It is better, however, as far as possible, if word is rendered by word, which was therefore done here by the Blessed Luther. This is the reason why we cannot approve of Beza's translation, because he rendered the word πᾶσα as 'the whole.' Concerning which he has this in the annotations to this place. The Vulgate and Erasmus: 'All Scripture,' with ambiguity dangerous in this place. For it is certain that the Apostle is dealing with specific Scriptures, namely, that which we call the Canon of the Hebrews. But that ambiguity is not removed by this translation. Then, whether you render it 'all' or 'the whole' Scripture, it detracts nothing from the mind of the Apostle, because he speaks only of Canonical Scripture: for in both translations the word 'holy' is to be understood from the preceding verse. More correctly, therefore, the Syrian, the Vulgate, Erasmus, and the Blessed Luther retain the word 'all.' But how that is to be explained, we shall see hereafter. It is one thing to act as a metaphrast, another as a paraphrast. And there is greater emphasis in the word 'all': by which the whole of Holy Scripture could thus be designated, so that it might be hinted, however, that even everything which is contained in Holy Scripture is useful, if not for all those four uses, at least for one of them, just as not only is the whole of Holy Scripture θεόπνευστος (God-breathed), but also everything that is held in Holy Scripture. But these things are about the collation of versions with the source: which ought not to seem useless. For it contributes to asserting the authenticity and majesty of the original text, and can sometimes help us in investigating the true sense. Sacred criticism is never superfluous, provided it is instituted with κρίσει (judgment).

§. IV. Now to the explanation of the text. First, the connection with the preceding text must be considered, which the interpreters expressed with a copulative particle. Then the subject, which is πᾶσα γραφὴ, ALL SCRIPTURE. Third, the predicate, which is twofold: the former θεόπνευστος, divinely inspired; the latter, ὠφέλιμος, and is useful. Which utility is understood and how, is explained by the Apostle by parts: that it is indeed fourfold, for doctrine, and for reproof, and for correction, and for instruction, but that which is in righteousness. Which, in what sense, not in what word, seems to be able to be referred to all those things; properly, however, it pertains to the last, πρὸς τὴν παιδείαν. For the end of all those uses is righteousness; therefore it teaches true things, therefore it reproves, therefore it corrects wrong things, so that true righteousness may prevail. And this παιδεία ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ (instruction in righteousness) is as it were the apex of the rest. Fourth, the consequence of the latter predicate; that the man of God may be perfect, instructed for every good work. For it provides his sufficiency for all these uses and for true righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, not only attaining true perfection by himself, but, being instructed for every good work, he becomes abundant even regarding others. Therefore, the entire exegesis, all parts of which cohere like rings in a chain, is completed in eleven members. The first concerns the συνέχειαν (continuity) of the text. The second, the scope and περιφέρεian (circumference) of all Scripture. The third, the θεοπνευσίαν (divine inspiration) of all Holy Scripture. The fourth, the ὠφέλειαν (utility) of the God-breathed Scripture. The fifth, the highly useful διδασκαλίαν (teaching) of divine Scripture. The sixth, the truly divine ἔλεγχον (reproof) or ἔλεγξιν of Holy Scripture. The seventh, the likewise entirely divine ἐπανόρθωσιν (correction) of Holy Scripture. The eighth, the no less truly divine παιδείαν (instruction) of Holy Scripture. The ninth, the object and scope of instruction, τὴν δικαιοσύνην, true righteousness. The tenth, the ἀποτέλεσμα (result) and former fruit of the utility of Scripture, the all-around perfection of the man of GOD. The eleventh and last, the latter fruit of the same, perfect instruction for every good work. It is now in the open how concisely the individual parts cohere: Namely, Holy Scripture is most worthy of study, which Timothy cultivated, and it provides wisdom for salvation through faith in Christ, because all Holy Scripture is divinely inspired to this end. Nor is anything in Scripture to be neglected or esteemed lightly. For all Holy Scripture is both divinely inspired and useful. Indeed, because all is inspired, all is also useful. But useful first for doctrine. Which is the fountain and spring of the remaining uses. Then, when true doctrine is drawn from there, the false flows away of its own accord. Therefore it is also useful for the ἔλεγχον (reproof) of the false. And because the doctrine which it delivers, and which it powerfully asserts, is not merely theoretical, but practical, therefore it is useful for our correction. Since after the fall we first have need of ἐπανόρθώσει (restoration) and correction. Which being expedited, instruction succeeds, so that we may be instituted not only in righteousness, but be formed to the same, by the heavenly Pedagogue: both to imputed righteousness, and to our own, as that which redounds from that imputation, and is indeed begun here; but in the other life it is consummated. These five uses the Word of GOD provides through the sacred ministry, therefore it perfects first the man of GOD, that is, the minister of the Word, so that he himself may both understand true things and discern them from false, and not be ignorant of human depravity needing correction, and the righteousness which Scripture intends, indeed so that he himself may be able to emerge perfect from Scripture and through Scripture in all these things, as much perfection as falls to man here, or as much as is required: Then indeed it also renders the man of God equipped for every good work committed to him, which is confined within the compass of these four principal hinges: so that he may be perfectly equipped for teaching others every truth, and for refuting others regarding whatever is false, adverse, and harmful to faith, justice, and salvation, and also for correcting all things that deviate from the line, and for recalling and leading back all who deviate from any exorbitance and depravity: Finally, for instructing all concerning true justice, so that all may thus be rendered wise unto salvation through the faith which is in Christ JESUS: who ought to be the end of the Holy Scripture, of the ministers of the word, and of us all. It is now clear how many things the Apostle embraces in these few words, so that he may seem to have wished to exhibit here to Timothy and to any minister of the word a σωματοποίησιν of the Christian religion, since there is almost no article of faith that is not comprehended by the same. If a beginning is made from the Holy Scripture through the intermediate chapters of faith up to the last, which is eternal salvation. But here fixed limits are set for us, so that it is permitted to pursue scarcely one or two members, which, however, we shall explain in such a way that the whole aphorism may be easily understood from it.

§. V. Therefore, as to the first point regarding the συνέχειαν: The Apostle had predicted the worst fates of the last times, verse 1. He had revealed the source of all evils, the seduction of false teachers, who, by the example of Jannes and Jambres, resist the truth: such as he had indicated were even then, in his own time, thrusting themselves in and creeping into houses everywhere, verse 6. He therefore warns Timothy that, since he had followed his truly Apostolic doctrine and manner of life, purpose, faith, long-suffering, charity, patience—all of which were fruits of true doctrine, in which the Apostle had shown himself an example to all, even to his own Timothy—he should remain in those things which he had learned and which had been entrusted to him, καὶ ἐπισεύθης; Grotius on this passage. The received reading had been ἇ ἐπισώθης, but it is a construction κατὰ σύλληψιν, where something is said commonly about two things, which according to exact rule fits only one; Hesychius explains it as ἐπείσθης, ἐπληροφορηθεὶς. In the same way the Syriac, according to the interpretation of Tremellius and Trostius, 'in which you have been confirmed.' They render the sense, as Chrysostom explains: you have not only learned these things, but they have also been entrusted to you: that is, you have believed that this is life. He uses more than one argument why one should remain in them. The first is from the dangerous and harmful state, which he had insinuated before, namely the condition and qualities of the false teachers, and their end. Whose madness will eventually be evident, just as that of Jannes and Jambres, and that they drag whomever else they can with them into errors, and only progress for the worse, to their own greater destruction. προκόψυσιν ἐπὶ τὸ χεῖρον. Grotius, they will become more and more impudent and will first introduce questions, then they will overturn the very foundations of Christianity. Which he (Grotius) himself proved by his own example. Whence it cannot be but that their madness will eventually become πᾶσιν ἔκδηλος. Fictions do not last long. As Chrysostom says in this place: For although error may seem to prevail on every side for a time, it does not remain until the end: for such things are those which are not good by nature, but seem to be good: they flourish for a time, but are quickly detected. But our things are not such, and you are a witness of these. For all error is absent from us. For who would want to die for an error? Grotius thinks that by these πλανῶντας καὶ πλανωμένυς are indicated those who were deceived by the Philosophers, especially by the Pythagoreans, who were many in Ephesus: or by the followers of Heraclitus, who had been an Ephesian: who had persuaded the Christians that men could both live rightly and attain eternal life by following the tenets of the Philosophers, as Grotius had said in the argument of the Epistle written to the Ephesians. But it does not appear from this Epistle written to Timothy that the Apostle had especially looked at those seduced by the Philosophers. He had predicted, towards his departure, that men speaking διεςραμμένα (perverse things) would arise from the Ephesian teachers themselves, and would draw away disciples after them. Therefore he had warned that one must be vigilant, Acts XX, verse 31. He expressly designates Phygellus and Hermogenes, 2 Tim. I, verse 16. Then he had also expressed Hymenaeus and Philetus, who had fallen from the truth, saying that the resurrection had already taken place. He complained that these had subverted the faith of some, and that their speech was spreading like a cancer, chapter II, verses 17, 18. There is no doubt, therefore, that he noted such men here. He spoke of them in the same way there; And further, they will progress to impiety: verse 16, just as here in chapter III, verse 13, 'Evil men and seducers will progress for the worse.' He also notes their fables in chapter IV, verse 4, such as were various among the Jews (Tit. I, 14; 1 Tim. I, verse 4) and heretics, such as the Simonians and others, so that there is no need, with Grotius, to understand specifically fables about the expiation of sins from the Chaldean and Orphic discipline, which he lists on this passage. More correctly, therefore, Chrysostom, in homily 1 on this Epistle, observes that heresies are being referred to which took their beginnings from Jewish observances, which he had also signaled in the former Epistle, which, along with the novelties of Hymenaeus and Philetus, were troubling the faithful. There was not as much danger threatening them from Ethnicism, from which they had been converted, as from Judaism. Meanwhile, I would not deny that the Ethnic philosophers, whom Tertullian and others called the patriarchs of the heretics, also contributed their ἐπιβάλ- λον μέρος (share) to perverting those who subsequently progressed more and more toward impiety.

§. VI. But how he said in 2 Tim. II, verse 16, 'they will progress further to impiety,' but here in chapter III, verse 9, 'they will progress no further,' I prefer to explain with the words of Chrysostom rather than my own: He spoke thus to them, he says, because these who are eager for novelties will nowhere find an end to error, but will always bring forth new inventions and a corrupted dogma, for such is the power of error that it cannot be stopped. But here he says they will not deceive, nor will they carry others with them, although in the beginning they may seem to have deceived some: But they will be most easily detected. For their madness will become clear to all. Let those who are agitated by an itch for novelties observe this, and think it said to themselves, so that they do not flatter themselves with the easy propagation of the same among others. The Spirit does not deceive: ἡ γὰρ ἄνοια ἀυτῶν ἔκδηλ(ος) ἔσται πᾶσιν.

§. VII. One thing still, but ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ, must be added. Regarding the names Jannes and Jambres, Grotius, as is his custom, questions the original text in order to assert the reliability of the Vulgate. In this, he has the Papist Estius as his predecessor. The Latin interpreter, he says, had the Greek exemplar Μαμβρῆς. But from where does he prove this? Because the Magus was so called by Numenius; and no differently by the Jews in the Talmudic tractate on offerings. Estius adds that R. Nathan reads it in the same way, according to Genebrardus. But that the more recent Jews follow the Talmud, what is surprising about that? And it is very well known that proper names in the Talmud are often severely corrupted. Just as the name Jannes is read differently in the Talmud, יוחני. This happens especially in languages translated into Greek: whence no one will easily wonder that the reading in Numenius is slightly different, and therefore corrupted. Jerome certainly considers both names, Jambres and Mambres, to be the same in his interpretation of Hebrew names. But not only do the Greek codices consistently read Jambres, but so does the ancient Syriac interpreter, as well as Chrysostom in Homily VIII. In vain, therefore, does Grotius here gratify the Papists: he who was also in vain in that he affirms, as it appears, for the sake of Papist traditions, that Paul had all these things from tradition or the writings of the ancients. It is likely that Paul learned them from Chrysostom, either by tradition or from the Holy Spirit. Both could be joined, if it were certain that such a tradition had flourished at that time. For he wrote these things at the dictation of the Holy Spirit; who inspired the Apostles not only with dogmas, but also with historical matters, not only with sentiments, but also with words, and impelled them to write even those things which were not unknown, and how they were to be written he bestowed upon the same. All Scripture is God-breathed. No word of Holy Scripture, no jot is excepted, but that it is from divine inspiration. Not to mention that Papists ineptly argue from historical traditions to dogmatic ones.

§. VII. To return to the arguments of the Apostolic exhortation, the second is taken from the honorable, that it is right to remain in those things which he had learned and which were entrusted to him, on account of the instructor and Master, the Apostle: That he knows from whom he has learned, verse 14. Certainly not such a one as the false teachers are described, but one whose not only doctrine and instruction, but also purpose, faith, longsuffering, love, patience—all things contrary to the ways of the false teachers—as well as the persecutions and sufferings, from all of which, however, the Lord delivered him, he knew; in a word, whom Timothy most clearly recognized as a true Apostle of Jesus Christ. He confidently and with boasting alleges the persecutions and sufferings, by which he believed his doctrine was rendered illustrious, just as by the gifts of the Spirit, but as Chrysostom observes, for the consolation of the disciple, not for boasting. For these two things especially disturb the mind of a teacher: namely, the multitude of heretics and the impatience of sufferings. What kind of persecutions, he says, I endured. Both are full of consolation, because I showed remarkable cheerfulness and was not forsaken. Nor can it be said that God betrayed me, but rather that He wove a brighter crown for me.

§. IX. The third argument is taken from the useful: because that doctrine which Timothy had learned, as it rested upon the foundation of Holy Scripture—outside of which Paul taught nothing, Acts 26:13—and which Timothy had known from infancy with the sacred letters, agreed perfectly, so it possessed the same power, nay, it was equally divine, equally God-breathed. Some wish this to be the nerve of the argument, that Timothy imbibed this doctrine with his first mother's milk, which he ought not so easily to cast away. But although it also recalls that to his memory, the power of the doctrine must be added above all, which he had felt in himself from infancy. For nowhere does he not explain the same word where he finds a place. The Apostle himself adds it: Which are able to instruct you unto salvation. Chrysostom seems to hint at that force already insinuated by the word 'you were entrusted': You have not only learned these things, but they have also been ENTRUSTED to you: that is, you have believed this to be life. If, therefore, at the present time you perceive things contrary to these which you have believed, do not be troubled. Others, however, prefer that the CONTRUSTED Deposit be required here (which fits the phrase better. Cf. Gal. 2:7; 1 Tim. 1:11). Estius, Menochius, Grotius, so that this reasoning should be considered to pertain to the other argument from the honorable, or if you wish to distribute it with the blessed Balduinus, a twofold reason is contained therein: By two arguments, says the blessed predecessor, he exhorts him to constancy: 1. Because the heavenly doctrine was committed to him as a deposit. 2. Because he received it from a faithful Master, who fought for it even unto blood. To the former of which greater strength is gathered if the office of Timothy is added. That this deposit was entrusted to him as a Bishop, and committed to be guarded. 1 Tim. 6:20; 2 Tim. 1:14.

§. X. Furthermore, there is no reason for us to invent a hyperbole with Estius in the phrase 'from infancy.' For since we teach even infants themselves, as they begin to speak, to recite the sayings of Scripture, which is wont to be the care especially of pious mothers, the mother of Timothy, Eunice, and his grandmother Lois, without a doubt informed him from his tender years, in whom dwelt unfeigned faith, as the Apostle proclaims, 2 Tim. 1:5. His mother was a Hebrew, even though his father was a Gentile, who did not want him to be circumcised, Acts 16:1. It was, and still is, the custom of the Jews not only to give the Holy Scriptures to boys to be read from the first age capable of letters, which Grotius observes here, but also to accustom even infants themselves to recite the sayings of Scripture. Concerning which, in the book 'Chin.' page 161, cited by Hottinger in 'Thesaurus Philologicus,' book 1, chapter 2, page 90, it is read thus: The wise men of blessed memory say, when does a father begin to instruct his son in the law? Then when he begins to speak, the father also makes a beginning of his instruction, which Moses commanded us.

§. XI. But the truth itself extorted this from the Papist Estius, that he wished to have it observed here; namely, that this passage teaches that neither boys nor women should be kept away from the reading of Holy Scripture, since it is likely that Timothy was instructed in the Holy Scriptures by his mother and grandmother. However, the caution which he adds—provided that such persons are, according to Ecclesiastical rule, known to be able to receive not harm, but an increase of faith and piety from such reading, as the Pontiff prescribes in Rule IV of the Index of Prohibited Books—is shameful to Holy Scripture, nor does it agree with the observation of Estius. For what evil genius ordered the Pontiff to refer Holy Scripture, which has been entrusted to all to be read, among prohibited books? Who gave him the power to decide to whom the reading of Biblical books should be permitted, and to whom less? How can Scripture, divinely inspired, which can make us wise unto salvation, be said to bring harm to anyone, without notable insult to Scripture, nay, blasphemy against GOD, the author of Scripture? That which GOD willed to be a good common to all, that cannot be taken away from most by any Ecclesiastical law, nor restricted to certain ones; whoever does this opposes himself to GOD, and demonstrates himself to be the Anti-Christ by the very deed. Moreover, that He willed Scripture to be common to all: Deut. 31:11; Psalm 1:1; Psalm 119; Hab. 2:2; John 5:39; 2 Pet. 1:14. It was common among the Jews, as we have already noted; which Peresius denies in vain along with Harding: That the crown of the law has been left so that whoever wishes may come and take it, that is, to which access is open to everyone; Buxtorf teaches this from the book Joma in 'Lexicon Thalmudicum,' p. 690. In Pircke Aboth, chapter 6, it is held thus: Whoever does not devote effort to the study of the law is called a reprobate. Nor indeed did Lois or Eunice need to seek the faculty of reading it from the Supreme Pontiff: Scripture was common to Christians in the early Church along with the Apostolic [writings], Acts 17:11, 2 Peter 1:19, and those that followed, as witnessed by Ignatius to the Philadelphians and Polycarp to the Philippians. There was no need for a dispensation there. Wisdom concerning Christ, faith in Christ, and salvation through faith pertain to all by the intention of GOD. How, therefore, can Scripture be restricted to a few, or taken away from any, by which we are made wise, from which we draw faith in Christ, and through which we obtain salvation? Nor indeed can Scripture have anything harmful, which was prepared by GOD for these uses; which is the common apothecary of souls, as Basil says in Psalm 1, the reading of which is a great fortification against sin, as Chrysostom witnesses. Homily 3 on Lazarus: Scripture is life-giving and has no stumbling block for the faithful, says Epiphanius, heresy 69, which is that of the Ariomanites. But by the work and instinct of evil demons, the punishment of death [was directed] against the readers of the Prophets Gentiles to have established. Justin, Apol. II. pro Christ., is the authority. What kind of persecution they ascribe to Trajan against the Jews, lest they read the Scripture, about which R. Zakuth also complained: the Jews indeed exclude Christians from the reading of the Law, a Gentile (so they call a Christian) who devotes effort to the Law is guilty of death, Sanh. c. 7. It is manifest by what Spirit the Pontiffs are ruled, when they prohibit the reading of Scripture, and in their Inquisition they also establish this interrogative article, whether anyone has read the Bibles?

§. XII. The power and utility of the Holy Scriptures is excellently expressed by the Apostle, when the τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα are said to be able to make one wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus. For three supreme effects are attributed to them. First, most eminent WISDOM, not concerning worldly matters for common life, but concerning God and divine things, for salvation and eternal life. Scripture can not only instruct us, and educate us unto salvation, but σοφίσαι, to make us wise: which is the highest peak of erudition. For nothing is more sublime than wisdom. Therefore, a perfect information is noted, which we have from the Holy Scriptures concerning faith unto salvation. For whatever makes us wise unto salvation, it must instruct us perfectly concerning those things which are necessary for salvation. What is that WISDOM which is lacking in necessary things, and how could Holy Scripture make one wise unto salvation if it passed over even one article of faith, without which salvation cannot be obtained? Therefore Anselm of Canterbury on this passage: The Holy Scriptures can instruct you, that is, make you SUFFICIENTLY learned unto eternal Salvation. So that Bullinger's exception against du Plessis is vain, that τὸ σοφίσαι is not properly to make wise, but to instruct. For the Greek word imports wisdom; and therefore Erasmus on this passage: σοφίσαι i.e., to educate, to make wise. Salmero: σοφίσαι i.e., to make wise, or to educate, as Ambrose reads: Nor do the Latin Vulgate translators explain the word otherwise than to instruct, Cajetan, Estius, and others.

§. XIII. The second effect is saving Faith, which is in Christ Jesus, John III. 16, ch. XX. 31. For this arises from the Scriptures, John V. 39, 46, Rom. III. 21, ch. X. v. 17. Since faith consists of knowledge, assent, and trust, and neither can knowledge of Christ be had from elsewhere than from Scripture, Rom. XVI. v. 26, nor can assent be provided, except by the efficacy and power of Holy Scripture itself, which convinces our hearts of the truth which it delivers, 1 John V. 6, much less can trust be conceived, except by the efficacious operation of the word, John VI. 63, Gal. III. 2, Heb. IV. 12, through which we are enlightened, Ps. XIX. 9, Acts XXVI. 18, Eph. III. v. 9, we are regenerated, 1 Pet. I. 23, James I. 21, we are converted, Jer. XXIII. 29, Isa. VI. 10, John XII. 40.

§. XIV. It is a mere perversion, diametrically contrary to the words of the Apostle, when Estius says that the words 'through faith, which is believed in Christ' are added so that the Apostle may teach against the Judaizers that knowledge of the Law without faith in Christ is worth nothing for salvation, or to signify that from the Holy Scriptures, both because of their obscurity and because of the blindness and dullness of our intellect and the depravity of the affections with which we labor, no one can draw sound and uncorrupted doctrine unless he is fortified by faith in Christ and uses that as a teacher to understand them. For (1) the Apostle does not teach that knowledge of the Law with faith is of value for salvation; he requires faith alone for salvation: for the righteousness of faith has been manifested χωρὶς νόμου without the law, Rom. III, verse 21. (2) Nor does he wish faith to be brought to the reading of Scripture from elsewhere for salvation, but he commends the Holy Scriptures, as they are able to make us wise unto salvation through faith. But unless they instructed us clearly

and sufficiently, how could they be able to make one wise unto salvation, which is not obtained except through faith? It is necessary that wisdom, just as faith, be drawn from the Scriptures: otherwise, Scripture does not make anyone wise unto salvation. (3) Scripture is not obscure in those things which pertain to faith and salvation. If it were obscure, it could not instruct or educate anyone unto salvation. And from where else can faith be sought, if not from the Scriptures, indubitably and infallibly? And those things which are open, says Augustine, l. de unit. Eccles. c. V., let us choose as manifest, which if they were not found in the Holy Scriptures, there would be NO way from which the closed could be opened and the obscure illustrated. And therefore, l. II. de Doctr. Christ. cap. 9, he delivers this axiom: In those things which are placed openly in Scripture, are found all those things which contain faith and the morals of living. (4) Scripture itself heals the blindness of our intellect and the depravity of our affections: while it illuminates minds and purifies hearts. The law of the Lord is immaculate, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones. The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes, Ps. XIX. verse 8. Divine Scripture, says Cyril, l. VII. contr. Julian., is sufficient so that those who are educated in it may turn out wise, and upright, and endowed with the fullest prudence, nor do we need foreign teachers for that at all. (5) Therefore, we do not approach Scripture fortified by faith, but we are instructed and fortified in faith by Scripture, John V. 39, 46, ch. XX. verse 31, and the Wisdom of salvation, which is of faith. Scripture knows no other wisdom of salvation, or unto salvation, than the knowledge of faith, John XVII. verse 3, the knowledge of Christ, Isa. LIII. verse 11, the knowledge of salvation concerning the remission of sins through Christ, Luke I. verse 77. (6) Therefore, the effect of faith cannot be separated here from Scripture, but faith also is attributed to Holy Scripture along with wisdom. Which Claude Espence acknowledges in this passage: if there is anything to know, if there is anything to do, they teach the true, they refute the false, they lead back from evil, they lead into good, and they do not just make good in any way, but they perfect, and they are able to educate a man unto salvation and make him sufficiently learned. And Leonhard Marius the Jesuit, prolegom. in Script. S. q. II. sect. 5: The Blessed Apostle Paul said of the Holy books, 2 Tim. III, they can instruct you unto salvation, and he adds, that through them it comes to pass that the man of GOD may be perfect, instructed unto every good work. And it is truly so; for we learn from them not only what we ought to believe, but also what we ought to do, what to avoid, and what to hope for and fear, in which the sole perfection of human life consists. Laurentius Villavicent. lib. 1. de rat. stud. Theol. cap. 3. The Scriptures, and indeed THEY ALONE, can instruct us unto salvation through faith in Christ.

§. XV.
