The third effect is eternal SALVATION: which stands not only by way of the ultimate end of divine revelation and the Holy Scriptures, but also by way of effect: because in the Scriptures we have eternal life, John V. verse 39. The word of GOD is Spirit and life, John VI. verse 63. The Gospel is the power of GOD unto salvation to every one that believeth, Rom. I. verse 16. The word of Life, Acts V. 20. Phil. II. v. 16. The word of salvation, Acts XIII. verse 26. Ephes. I. 15. But since the discourse here is concerning the Scriptures of the O. T., which Timothy had learned from infancy, it is manifest from this that eternal salvation was not only proposed in the O. T., which the Socinians wrongly deny, but that the Scriptures of the Old Testament also sufficiently instructed unto eternal salvation, and indeed through faith in Christ: whence the doctrine concerning the Deity of Christ must have been clearly proposed in the O. T. without which faith in Christ cannot consist. Which is to be observed against the Calixtine Innovators. That was the voice of Julian the impious Apostate, that in Moses & the Prophets there is nothing concerning the Deity of Christ, or the Trinity, but the blessed Cyril refutes him at length in book VIII & IX against Julian, when Moses, he says in book IX, Tom. VI, p. m. 294, & the Prophets confess the holy & consubstantial Trinity, and neither did those Princes of wisdom then (he understands the gentile Philosophers, from whom Cyril had brought similar things) not know this, how does it happen, I pray you, that you do not perceive that you labor under a hard & stubborn ignorance?

§. XVI. And thus the continuity of the text is now established: For he wishes to explain & confirm more fully what the Apostle had said concerning the wisdom which is had from the Holy Scriptures. Therefore he employed a causal particle. For all Scripture is divinely inspired, & is useful: He used a double argument: The first is taken from the origin & divine constitution of Holy Scripture, because it is θεόπνευςος, and therefore since it has proceeded from GOD the most perfect author and is animated by the divine spirit, for the sake of our salvation, it cannot but exhibit perfect wisdom, and perfectly instruct us for salvation. Thus Irenaeus concludes in book II against heresies, chapter 7. The Scriptures, he says, are perfect, inasmuch as they are dictated by the word of GOD and His Spirit. And Hilary in book XII on the Trinity. The word of GOD and the true doctrine of wisdom, which speaks, are both perfect and absolute. John Trithemius acknowledges this consequence in book VIII of Questions, q. IV to Maximilian. All Scripture divinely inspired is a perfect work of divinity preordained before all time, written in time no otherwise than GOD willed, who inspired men so that it might be written. But all the works of GOD are perfect. And therefore since the Scripture, of which we speak, is the work of GOD, it is necessary that it be considered perfect in all things. The latter is taken from an induction of the uses of Scripture: which make for perfect divine wisdom: since Scripture is useful for teaching, & for arguing & for instructing in justice, that the man of GOD may be perfect, instructed for every good work. Whatever Scripture provides all these uses, it can undoubtedly render us wise unto salvation.

§. XVII. As for the second head of our treatment, namely the subject, which here is πᾶσα γραφὴ ALL SCRIPTURE, and its scope, that the discourse is about all HOLY Scripture is manifest from the preceding verse, from the predicate, and the whole context. Which he had expressed by ἱερὰ γράμματα. Thus Holy Scripture is called absolutely γραφὴ John XIX, verse 31, or in the plural γραφαὶ Matthew XXII, verse 29, John V, verse 39, just as among the Hebrews it is likewise called κατ’ ἐξοχὴν כְּתָב, מִכְתָּב and also by the Chaldeans כְּתָבָא scripture, because this stands out among all Scriptures, compared to which the remaining writings are to be esteemed as nothing, indeed for its sake alone all other writings ought to be made: just as also for that reason κατ’ ἀντονομασίαν it is called by the Hebrews מִקְרָא reading from Nehemiah VIII, verse 8, because it ought to be read by all, and it alone is worthy to be read: תּוֹרָה doctrine or instruction Psalm XIX, verse 9. John X, v. 34, because it alone teaches us, and instructs us, and is to be taught in those things which make for salvation. Likewise מְגִלָּה a volume or מְגִלַּת סֵפֶר a volume of a book Psalm XL, verse 8, whence by Greeks, Latins, Gauls, Germans, English, βιβλια Biblia are called κατ’ ἐξαίρετον λόγον. Synonymously therefore another name is accepted here for Scripture, τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα: which are also called γραφαὶ ἁγίαι Romans I, verse 2, and τὰ βιβλια τὰ ἅγια 1 Maccabees XII, v. 9. By the Hebrews כִּתְבֵי הַקֹּדֶשׁ Scriptures of Holiness, or holy and books of Holiness, or holy. By which name it is called (1) because of the author, God thrice holy (2) because of the amanuenses, holy men of God, through whom the Scripture was written 2 Peter I, 21, (3) because of the matter: which are sacred dogmas, sacred Precepts, sacred examples. For there is nothing that is not sacred in Scripture. It is immune from all error, from all uncleanness, and thus truly holy. (4) because of the form. Because the manner in which those things are proposed is truly sacred, and the whole structure is holy: that it is therefore elegantly called מִקְדַּשְׁיָה sanctuary of the Lord by the Hebrews: just as there the structure was holy, the apparatus holy, the presence and habitation of GOD especially holy, so God united Himself with this sanctuary of Holy letters in a holy and inseparable union, so that the word is Spirit and life John VI, verse 6, and the power of God Romans I, v. 16. Therefore it is separated very far from every other Scripture (5) because of the effect, because it sanctifies us John XVII, verse 17, (6) because of the adjunct: because it is to be kept holily, to be treated holily, and to be separated from all profane things, and in no way to be contaminated by profane uses.

§. XVIII. The Apostle prefixes the particle πᾶσα, which embraces both the whole Scripture, and in a certain respect everything that is contained in Scripture. For the whole Scripture is also divinely inspired and useful for teaching, rebuking, etc., and there is nothing in Scripture which is not divinely inspired, which is not useful, if not for all those ends, certainly for some of them: of which it can be said what the Rabbis pronounce concerning the Law, that there is no letter in Scripture from which great mountains of doctrines are not suspended. These predicates are therefore said of the whole Scripture, as it is whole, and according to all its parts. The word πᾶσα therefore comprehends 1. the universality or totality of the Canonical Scripture: that it is all inspired by GOD, and useful for these ends, and thus is sufficient for salvation. Thus Athanasius explains in the Synopsis πᾶσα γραφὴ ἡμῶν χρισιανῶν θεόπνευσός ἐςω: ἐκ ἀόρισα δὲ ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ὡρισμένα καὶ κεκανονισμένα ἔχει τὰ βίβλια: All our Scripture, we who are Christians, is divinely inspired: and it has books not infinite, but finite and comprised in a certain canon. Thus Chrysostom, Theophylact, & Oecumenius: And no otherwise from the Pontificals Dionysius the Carthusian, Adam Sasbout, Guilb. Estius, Jacob Tirinus. ALL, that is, THE WHOLE scripture is useful, that is, it conduces, it is founded for this end. Will Tanner say that they all distort Scripture, as he accuses our people, because they interpret the word πᾶσα as WHOLE? See T. III. Theol. Scholast. disp. I. q. 5. page 340.

§. XIX. We can also say that the universality of the sacred Scriptures is included here too, so that every sacred Scripture is adorned with these praises, indeed that nothing is taught to be in Holy Scripture which is not θεόπνευσον, not ὠφέλιμον: Nor does Tanner's reasoning warn us: If the word useful meant sufficient, then every Scripture, and thus any book of divine Scripture, would be sufficient for salvation and instruction, because all Scripture and every book of Scripture is useful for teaching. For we say that the whole Scripture is endowed with these praises, as it is a whole, and as regards individual parts, but for a different reason. To the whole Scripture and to all its parts pertains τὸ εἶναι θεόπνευσον: because in that, as such, the formal aspect of Holy Scripture is situated: to the whole Scripture and also to all its parts looks τὸ ὠφέλιμον: because Scripture divinely inspired cannot but be useful, and the uses also, which are enumerated, belong to the whole Scripture, then by a certain reasoning also of the parts of Scripture: All together are of the whole Scripture: But of the parts of Scripture in such a way that there is none of them which does not make for and conduce to some one or some of these uses. But since from that utility of Scripture its sufficiency and perfection is inferred, regarding those things which are necessary to be known for salvation, not only is the word ὠφέλιμος considered, nor should we adhere precisely to an interpretation of the word πᾶσα, which ought to be explained as WHOLE, but we believe that the συνέχειαν of the text must be looked to first; which the Apostle proves and explains, that the τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα, the Holy Scriptures, are able to make us wise unto salvation through faith in Christ: because all Holy Scripture is divinely inspired, and useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, and indeed in such a way that the man of GOD may be perfect, instructed unto every good work. Since for this end Scripture was inspired by GOD, and the utility of Scripture tends to this, and such a perfect ἀποτέλεσμα is from Scripture, how will Scripture itself not be perfect and sufficient?

§. XX. Although indeed the matter concerns specifically those holy letters which Timothy had learned from childhood, v. 15, yet the reasoning which the Apostle brings forward to prove this faculty or utility of the Holy Scriptures is universal, as the syllogistic principle of 'of all and of none' requires. Add that the same reasoning applies to Canonical Scripture, as far as origin, form, and efficacy are concerned. And the Scripture of the New Testament is useful, just as the Scripture of the Old Testament; indeed, since the light of the New Testament is greater and more illustrious, how would it possess less virtue and efficacy? Then indeed, if the Scripture of the Old Testament can perfectly instruct us and make us wise unto salvation, how much more the whole Scripture, after Apostolic Scripture was added to the letters of the Holy Prophets? so that therefore there is no need to inquire solicitously which writings of the New Testament had been published at that time, so that it might be established which are comprised within the scope of the word ALL in Scripture; for whether more or fewer had been published then, indeed if none had yet been written, the force and δεινότης of the Apostle's statement remains, that Scripture alone sufficiently instructs us, because it is therefore divinely inspired and adapted to all kinds of uses, so that we may be rendered perfect thereby: since even the writings of the Old Testament themselves would have sufficed then, when they alone were divinely destined for that same end.

§. XXI. It is false, however, what Tiletanus thinks, that no writings of the New Testament yet existed when the Apostle wrote this: nor should one think with others that the Apostle here looked only to the Old Testament because only those existed when Timothy was still an infant; for he is said to have learned the holy letters not only in infancy, but from infancy, and that whole period from infancy is indicated here: nor can there be any doubt that other holy writings, which had appeared in the meantime from the Evangelists and Apostles, were known to him who himself subscribed to most of the Apostolic Epistles: such as the latter to the Corinthians, that which was written to the Philippians, that to the Colossians; both to the Thessalonians and the Epistle to Philemon: he brought the former to the Corinthians, he added greetings in the Epistle to the Romans: and who would doubt that Timothy, most desirous of the Holy Scriptures, had also studiously perused other writings? for there had appeared then, if you take the calculation of Cornelius a Lapide here, already almost all the writings of the New Testament, such as the Gospel of Matthew written in the year of Christ XLI: the Gospel of Mark, and the first Epistle of Peter in the year XLVI. The first to the Thessalonians in the year of Christ LII and the following, LIII, the latter: in the year LVII the first to the Corinthians and to Timothy. In the year LIIX the Epistle to Titus with the latter to the Corinthians. Baronius judges that Luke wrote his Gospel in the same year; but Cornelius a Lapide shows at Acts XVI that the Gospel of Luke was already published and famous then, and that it was written between the year LI, when Luke began to adhere to Paul, and LIIX, when the Apostle asserts in 2 Cor. IIX, v. 18 that it was praised by the mouth of all. In the year of Christ LIX the Epistle to the Philippians and to the Ephesians was written: in the year LX the Epistle to Philemon, to the Colossians and to the Hebrews; in the year LXI the Acts of the Apostles were finished. In the year LXIII James was crowned with martyrdom, who wrote the Canonical Epistle. Cornelius, in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, p. 28, wishes that the Epistle which is to the Romans was written after the Epistles to the Corinthians, but before other Pauline ones. Chrysostom and Baronius judge that the Epistle to the Galatians was written before the Epistle to the Romans, the time of which Cornelius a Lapide says is the most uncertain of all, in his proem to the Epistle to the Galatians. Since therefore this latter to Timothy was written only in the year LXIIX, and it is the last of all among the Pauline ones, in which year Cornelius also wishes the latter Epistle of Peter and that of Jude to have been written (but before this Pauline one), it is manifest from this chronotaxis, which Cornelius placed before the Acts of the Apostles, that all the writings of the New Testament, if you except only the Johannine ones, existed at the time when Paul wrote this.

§. XVII. Wherefore it can be said not without reason that the Apostle, by this eulogy, wished to celebrate the canon of the New Testament Scriptures alongside the canon of the Old Testament and to commend it to the Church through Timothy. That the Johannine writings, which were added later, are not inferior to these eulogies, St. John himself testifies, when he openly teaches in chapter XX, 31 that faith and salvation can be had from those things which he wrote in the Gospel: but concerning the Epistles, in 1 Ep. I, verse 4, 'These things,' he says, 'I write to you, that your joy may be perfect': finally the Apocalypse, the last of the books of the New Testament, and with the same the whole canon of the New He thus seals the Testament, so that it can be doubtful to no one that it is perfect, inasmuch as he testifies concerning that book that nothing is to be added to it, nothing is to be taken away (which is an argument of perfection), unless we wish for the plagues written in it to be added to us, or for our part to be taken away from the book of Life; but he pronounces him blessed who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book, Ap. XXII. 7. 18. 19. whence it is left that salvation or blessedness can be obtained from this book. St. Cyril writes excellently concerning the writings of the Evangelists towards the end of his commentaries on John: Not all things which the Lord did are written down, but those which the writers thought SUFFICIENT for both morals and dogmas, so that, shining with right faith, and works, and virtue, we might arrive at the kingdom of heaven: as it has in the Basel edition of the year 1546. The interpretation of George of Trebizond: They are read a little differently in the Paris edition of the year 1638 in the Greek text, but with the same meaning: γεγράϕασι γεμὴν τῶν εὐαγγελίων οἱ κήρυκες τὰ ἐν τοῖς γεγονόσι λαμπρότερα, καὶ ἄγε τὸ εἰκὸς, καὶ δι' ὧν ἦν μάλιςα τοῖς ἀκροωμένοις δύνασθαι βεβαιοῦσθαι πρὸς πίσιν τὸν ἀπαράϕθορον, καὶ παίδευσιν ἔχειν ἠθικήν τε καὶ δογματικὴν, ἵνα πίσει μὲν ὀρθῇ διαπρέποντες, ἔργοις δὲ τοῖς εἰς εὐσέβειαν βλέποισι πολυτρόπως ἠγλαϊσμένοι, καὶ εἰς ἀυτὴν κατατήσευτες τὴν ἄνω πόλιν, καὶ τῇ τῶν πρωτοτόκων ἐκκλησίᾳ συναπτόμενοι, καὶ εἰς ἀυτὴν εἰσελεύσειαν τὴν τῶν ὀρανῶν βασιλείαν, ἐν χρισῷ. The Latin translation of Jean Aubert has it thus: For one must think that many thousands of miracles were done by the power of our Savior: nevertheless, only the more illustrious ones [were recorded] by the Gospels were written, it seems, for heralds, and by which the hearers could be most effectively strengthened in an uncorrupted faith and instructed in the doctrine of both morals and dogmas, so that, conspicuous in right faith and variously illuminated by works pertaining to piety, and raised up to that very heavenly city, and joined to the firstborn of the Church, they might also penetrate into the very kingdom of Heaven in Christ.

§. XXIII. But it must be observed first of all that the Apostle vindicates these praises for Scripture alone. Some observe that the word 'all' sometimes occurs in this sense, so as to indicate at the same time that the attribute applies only to the thing to which it is joined. See Matt. XXIX [sic]. verses 19, 20; John III. 16; chap. VI. 45; 2 Pet. I. 21. Here, certainly, it is in the open that the Apostle bestows these praises on HOLY Scripture ALONE. For he warns him to remain and persist in the sacred Scriptures and those things which he had learned from them: not to allow himself to be carried away to other things. He teaches that the sacred scriptures are powerful and sufficient to instruct unto salvation through faith in Christ. He shows that the sacred Scriptures are therefore divinely inspired and adapted and adorned for all kinds of necessary uses. He testifies that through them, and from them, the man of GOD is made perfect, instructed unto every good work. He requires no other principle of instruction, nor does he teach that any is necessary: he attributes all of this to Scripture alone, so that nothing is more certain than that Scripture alone is sufficient and perfect for these things. The Apostle alleges the sacred letters alone as the ordinary medium of saving wisdom: with them alone he fortifies the Bishop against any seduction whatsoever of false teachers, of whom he had forewarned him: and he attributes those axioms to the sacred Scriptures for the reason that holy Scripture is θεόπνευστος (God-breathed). Therefore, they do not apply to any word except the θεόπνευστον (God-breathed) word. But what other word can be called θεόπνευστον (God-breathed) outside of and beyond sacred Scripture, which is now to be held infallibly as such? And the ancient Doctors, Chrysostom in this place, acknowledge that Timothy is here referred to nothing but Scripture alone, as that unique, ordinary, undoubted, and infallible principle of divine saving wisdom. If there is anything that needs to be learned or ignored, we shall learn that in Holy Scripture: If to refute falsehood, we shall draw it from there. If to be corrected, if to be chastised, for exhortation, for consolation, if anything is LACKING and needs to be obtained, we learn it nonetheless from it. So that the man of GOD may be perfect. Therefore, he cannot be perfected without it. For my part, says Paul, you have the Scriptures; if you desire to learn anything, you will be able to from here. Therefore, he does not refer him to traditions, but the Apostle wished Scripture to be in his place, as Chrysostom interprets. Now the Apostle was a most sufficient teacher for Timothy. Chrysostom adds: But if he writes these things to Timothy, being full of the Holy Spirit, how much more ought we to think they are said to us. Theophylact follows Chrysostom, as he does in most other things, along with Oecumenius: whose commentary, however, is a little fuller here, and may be considered a most solid refutation of the Papistic calumny, or blasphemy, concerning the imperfection of the sacred letters. Therefore, we shall transcribe it in its entirety. Lest he (Timothy) lose heart, as one who is about to be deprived of his teacher, who is consoling him a little later, you have, he says, the Scriptures in my stead, which can both lift you up and profit you. Scripture profits, he says, for teaching. Because it instructs us what must be learned thoroughly. For there is NOTHING that cannot be resolved by the Scriptures. For refuting: if, that is, lies must be refuted. For correcting, for training in righteousness: If it is necessary, he says, that something be either corrected or instructed, that is, to be rendered continent and sober unto righteousness, and to execute those things which are just, from the sacred letters, and EVERYTHING will be supplied. So that the man of GOD may be perfect. Correction, he says, is prepared from the Scriptures, so that NOTHING IS LACKING TO THE MAN who has walked according to God. If, therefore, you yourself desire to be made WHOLE, and MORE PERFECT, and to be rendered sound and always equable, and you do not wish to be contracted by adversities nor puffed up by prosperous things (for that signifies perfection of mind and equality), consult these sacred letters when you will lack my presence. But if he wrote about such reading to Timothy, who was filled with the Holy Spirit, how much more are we to be exhorted to it, who are in need of this Spirit. Observe, however, how he teaches that unless the sacred letters help us, we cannot be rendered whole and PERFECT. Instructed unto every good work. For he is not simply a participant in good works, but instructed by these very things, and ABSOLUTE. Nor will he be more perfect in one thing and least of all in others, but he is more instructed unto every work that is right, and unto each and every thing. The Jesuit Tirinus embraces the commentary of Chrysostom here: Now I am girding myself for martyrdom, O Timothy, you will henceforth lack my instruction: But INSTEAD OF IT I commend to you the study of the sacred letters; in them you will hear GOD speaking and admonishing. Thus St. Chrysostom. In the same way, the Angelic Doctor Thomas Aquinas explains it in this place. He shows that the sacred letters are the WAY TO SALVATION. And he posits three things: for he commends the Scriptures by reason of their principle, by reason of their useful effect, and by reason of their ultimate fruit and progress. The effect of Holy Scripture is fourfold: to teach the truth, to refute falsehood, as regards the Speculative; to snatch from evil, and to induce to good, as regards the Practical: its ultimate effect is to lead men to perfection. For it does not do good in just any way, but it PERFECTS; Heb. VI, let us be borne unto perfection. And therefore he says, so that the man of God may be perfect. For PERFECT is that to which NOTHING IS LACKING. Then, therefore, a man is perfect when he is instructed, that is, prepared, unto every good work. Gabriel Biel in the Canon of the Mass, lesson 7, has it thus: How could the soul of man live the life of righteousness and grace, unless it knew the will of GOD and those things which are just or unjust according to it, what things are to be done and what are to be fled; what are to be loved, what are to be despised, what are to be feared, and what are to be dared, and what are to be believed, and what are to be hoped for, and other things NECESSARY for our Salvation, all of WHICH Holy Scripture alone teaches. But these things also concern the second Chapter. And the said dispute had progressed only that far. We return from the digression to the Grotius text.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος καὶ ὠφέλιμος πρὸς διδασκαλίαν) Benè expressit sensum Syrus: omnis scriptura, quæ à DEO inspirata est, etiam utilis est ad docendum, &c. DEUS enim nihil frustra facit, nec inspirat homines, nisi ad nos docendos. Scriptura autem θεόπνευστος ea est, quæ scripta est aut ab iis, qui Prophetarum munia obiêre, ut Mose, Esaia, Jeremia, Ezechiele, aut ab iis, qui licet in alio essent vitæ genere, à DEO tamen certis temporibus afflati fuêre, ut David & Daniel. His accessionis vice, & ad implendam aut sapientiam moralem, aut historiam, additi sunt libri nonnulli alii, probati à magna Synagoga, tanquam optime convenientes cum illis θεοπνεύστοις. Addidit his ipsis & alios postea Christiana Ecclesia, tum Græca, tum Latina con- sensus. Πρὸς διδασκαλίαν למלמדה. Vide Rom. XV. 4. Docent nos libri isti Prophetici non omnia, quæ Christus, sed tamen aliqua eò pertinentia, Gal. III. 24. 2. Pet. I. 19.

Πρὸς ἔλεγχον) לתוכחה ut in Proverbiis aliquoties. Utilis est ad monstrandam turpitudinem graviorum crimi- num. Non occides: Non Mœchaberis, &c. ἔλεγξις eodem sensu dixit 2. Pet. II. 16. quid sit ἐλέγχειν videbis, Matth. XVIII. vers. 15. Luc. III. vers. 19. Joh III. v. 20. 1. Cor. XIV. vers 24. 1. Tim. V. vers. 20. infra IV. v. 2. Tit. I. vers. 9. 13. II. 15.

πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν) Est quoddam discrimen inter ἔλεγ- χον & ἐπανόρθωσιν. Ελέγχονται inverecundi: ἐπανορθῦνται teneri, fragiles. ὀρθῦν vel ἐπανορθῦν est עשק, labantem sustentare.

Πρὸς παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ) למוסר בצדק. Eos, qui jam bene cœpere, magis magisque dirigunt scripturæ illæ ad insistendum iter innocentiæ.

Non una hîc loci illustris occurrit corruptela. Primum quod ad subjectum attinet, ad Scriptu- ram, de qua Apostolus, referuntur, ut apparet à Protio, non modò Scripta Canonica V. Test. sed etiam Apocrypha, quæ Christianæ Ecclesiæ tum Græcæ tum Latinæ consensu adjecta. Quem er- rorem Papisticum in Critico S. profligavimus. Non adjecit Ecclesia consensu universali, nec facultatem habuit adjiciendi aliquid Canoni ab Ecclesia Judaica accepto, à Christo & Aposto- lis approbato, quod pari pietatis affectu susci- piendum sit, aut ad τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα, quæ à θεοπνευσία & autoritate verè divina commen- dantur, referri mereatur, eademque prædicata admittat. Si dicatur adjecisse Ecclesiam V. Test. Scriptis Evangelistarum & Apostolorum scripta, ea non propriè ab Ecclesia adjecta sunt, se à Spiri- tu S. à quo inspirata ea sunt, & collecta à S. Johan- ne, qui Canoni ultimam manum imposuit, ut in Critic. S. ostendimus. Sed restringere videtur hoc loco Grotius potius ad libros Propheticos, quæ hic prædicantur de Scriptura. Propheticos autem libros nullos alios novit Scriptura, nec Ec- clesia verè Catholica extra eos, qui lingua E- bræa à Prophetis, quibus illa propria, scripti, & Ecclesiæ Judaicæ concrediti sunt, Rom. III. v. 2. Luc. XVI. v. 29. 2. Pet. I. v. 19. Cæterum uti non excludenda Scripta Novi Testamenti ab his, qui- bus prædicata illa convenire, nullum dubium est, ita etiam his eadem applicanda negandum non est. Nam etsi τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα, quæ ab infantia noverat Timotheus, sola sint Scripta V. T. acces- serant tamen interim, dum è Scripturis magis ma- gisque ille profecit Scripta Evangelistarum & A- postolica, quæ Timotheo non poterant ignota es- se. Epistolæ enim ad Romanos salutem suam ad- scripserat Timotheus, priorem ad Corinthios attu- lerat, posteriori ad Corinthios, utrique ad Thes- salonicenses, ut & illi, quæ est ad Philippenses, quæ ad Colossenses, quæ ad Philemonem subscripserat, & priorem ad se scriptam legerat, ac quæ tum fortè nondum legit de scripturis Apostolicis, ipse, alique quibus in persona ejus Scriptura commendatur lecturi omninò erant. Sive ergo ratio hic redda- tur, quod sapientes nos faciant S. literæ, sive sim- pliciter commendetur usus Scripturæ, optime hæc sibi constant. Ratio enim, quod V. T. Scriptura sapientiam eam præstet, hæc erit, quod Scriptura eum in finem inspirata sit, ideoque & V. T. Scri- ptura, quæ sola, antequam accederet N. T. Scri- ptura, erat. Nam si omnis Scriptura verè Sacra, quod hic subintelligitur ex antecedentibus, ratio- ne sc. efficientis causæ, materiæ & finis, quod à san- cto autore, de sanctis rebus sit, & quod per eam homo sanctificetur, est à DEO immediatè inspi- rata, habet tales usus, quos hic adducit Apostolus, Scriptura ergò V.T. ita θεόπνευστος & ὠφέλιμος etiam fuerit, necesse est: quæ verò talis est, eam dubitandum non est sapientiam præstare ad salu- tem per fidem in Christum. Placet autem Estio nexum ita exhibere: Quoniam ad Scripturæ S. le- ctionem hortabatur, nunc eam insigni encomio com- mendat, primum ab autoritate, mox ab utilitate, quæ ex ea provenit. Quod expressius apparet in Græco: Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata, & utilis, subaudi, est. Itaque duo affirmantur, omnem Scripturam esse divinitus inspiratam, & eandem esse utilem ad ea, quæ sequuntur. Scripturam in- telligit Sacram, de qua dixerat: Sacras literas nosti: Nam Scripturæ nomine passim in Bibliis Sacra Scri- ptura per antonomasiam significatur, ut Matt. XXII. Erratis nescientes Scripturas, Joh. V. Scrutamini Scripturas, & X. Non potest solvi Scriptura. Rectè igitur & verissimè ex hoc loco statuitur, omnem Scri- pturam Sacram & Canonicam Spiritu S. dictante esse conscriptam, ita nimirum, ut non solum senten- tiæ, sed & verba singula, & verborum ordo, ac tota dispositio sit à Deo, tanquam per semetipsum loquen- te, aut scribente. Hoc enim est Scripturam esse divi- nitus inspiratam. Utilitatem vero deinceps expli- cat. Quæ solidè satis Grotium ex duobus prædi- catis unum efficientem, & particulam copulandi in verbum substantivum EST convertentem, re- fellunt.

Si dicatur, non reddendum esse OMNIS Scri- ptura, sed tota, vel universa, quia falsum est, omnem scripturam hosce usus habere: Respondet Estius: Notandum id velle Apostolum non quod unaquæque pars Scripturæ sacræ sit utilis ad ista quatuor (hic n. sensus liquidò falsus est) sed quod in universa Scri- ptura hæ quatuor utilitates reperiantur, ita nimirū, ut alia Scripturæ pars aliam adferat utilitatē, quod- que nulla sit Scriptura, quæ non ad aliquid istorum valeat. Addimus, de omni etiam scripturæ sen- tentia hos usus adstrui posse. Nam omnes utique de aliquo informant, & ita contrarium ei, quod docent, adserentes refellere aptæ sunt, autori- tate loquentis ea Spir. Sancti vel vi θεοπνευστίας. Et cum informatio in Scripturis ex intentione autoris supremi non sit θεωρητικὴ, sed πρακτικὴ, in- formant omnes respectu finis S. S. fidei causâ, ad quam omnia suam σχέσιν habent, ad justitiam, quæ est in Christo, ut per fidem in Christum salutem habeamus, Johan. XX. v. ult. hinc ergò, qui eam intentionem S. S. negligunt, vel pervertunt, etiam fidei derogant, sive directè, sive per indire- ctum, unde ἐπανορθώσεως opus est, qui usus è col- latione Scripturarum aliarum emergit. Cogitan- dum enim hic, sententias Scripturæ non seorsim, sed prout in corpore Scripturæ spectantur, non in sensu diviso, sed composito, & prout cum aliis conferuntur, ab eodem autore, eodem fi- ne profectæ, respici. Poterunt tamen & illa σχετικῶς, vel respectivè intelligi, ut aliorum qui- dem respectu utilitas innuatur ad docendum, alio- rum ad refutandum, aliorum ad emendandum, aliorum ad informandum in justitia.

Porrò quod ad prædicata, non tantum ad ea pertinent, quæ de utilitate dicuntur, sed & ipsa θεόπνευσία, quam ad subjectum quidem refert Grotius, sed distinctum prædicatum constitue- re particula καὶ docet, quam temerè neglexit Vulgata. Syrus θεόπνευστος reddidit per Spiritum Sanctum scripta, innuens, non solum sententias, sed & verba scripta, ac verborum ordinem & dispositionem à DEO esse, ut hic Beat. Ger- hardus; quod alibi Grotio & Calixto opposuimus. Conf. System. Theol. Tom. I. pag. 561. Jam usus quoque Scripturæ pervertit Grotius : pri- mò διδασκαλίαν, quasi prophetici libri tantum aliqua ad doctrinam pertinentia doceant; quod temerè è Galat. III. vers. 14. 2. Petr. I. vers. 20. colligitur. De illius loci sententia isthic dixi- mus. Hic verò planè contrarium docetur : nimi- rum cum attendimus Scripturæ Vet. Testament. nos illuminari per eam, ut lucifer in cordibus oriatur : nec Christus remisit aliò, quam ad Mosen & Prophetas, indeque instrui posse Judæos ad salutem æternam & de effugienda æterna con- demnatione docuit, Joh. V. vers. 39. Luc. XVI. vers. 29. Apostolus verò testatus, se extra Mosen & Prophetas nihil docere, Actor. XXVI. vers. 22. tametsi omne consilium DEI de salute tradiderit, Actor. XX. v. 27. Sed errorem illum Socinianum de Scriptura Vet. Testam. in Socinismo proflig. in System. Theol. & aliàs profligavimus. Deinde ἔλεγ- χον Grotius demonstrationem dicit turpitudinis gra- viorum criminum. At ἐλέγχειν & ἔλεγχος ex usu Scripturæ & consensu interpp. confutatio est falsæ doctrinæ. Conf. 1. Cor. XIV. vers. 24. Tit. I. v. 9. Idque poscit contextus : cum usus Scripturæ tum theoretici, tum practici hic recenseantur. Simi- liter Theophylactus : (ad docendum) Prodest, inquit, quia nos instruit, quid sit perdiscendum. Ni- bil est enim, quod nequeat Scripturis dissolvi. (ad arguendum) Si coarguenda scil. fuerint mendacia, (ad corripiendum, ad erudiendum in justitia) Si necesse est, inquit, ut aliquid vel corrigatur, vel instruatur, hoc est, ad justitiam reddi continentem & sobrium, & ea, quæ justa sunt, exequi, ex sacris literis id omne suppeditabitur. Quod ergò ad tertium usum, τὴν ἐπανόρθωσιν, temere restringi- tur illa ad teneros & fragiles; in genere ad corre- ctionem referunt Græci. Ambrosiafter : ut instau- ret deformes. Denique παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ parili temeritate restringit ad eos, qui jam benè cœpere, cum etiam ad illos pertineat, qui non- dum cœpere benè, Tit. II. vers. 12. Ambrof. reddidit, attrahens iniquos ad justitiam. Perfectio- nem Scripturæ sacræ inde non immerito Nostra- tes extruunt, quibus etiam Pontificii accedunt quandoque, vi veritatis constricti. Scriptura, in- quit Claud. Espensæus, si quid ferre, si quid agere opus est, verum docent, falsum corrigunt, redu- cunt à malo, inducunt ad bonum, nec verò quali- tercunque bonum faciunt, sed perficiunt, atque possunt homines ad salutem erudire, & sufficienter doctum reddere. Leonh. Marius prolegom. in Sacr. Script. q. 2. sect. 5. de S. literis dixit Beat. Apostolus Paulus, Epist. II. ad Timotheum cap. 3. possunt te instruere ad salutem, additque per eas fie- ri, ut perfectus sit homo DEI ad omne opus bonum instructus. Et verò ita est. Discimus enim ex his, non tantum, quid credere, sed etiam quid agere, quo- modo juvari, & quid sperare ac metuere debea- mus, in quibus tota vitæ humanæ perfectio consti- stit. Guilelmus Popik Dominicanus in Postill., Dom. II. Adv. Conc. I. Sola hæc Scriptura docet perfectè & planè, quid credendum, ut sunt arti- culi fidei; quid agendum, ut sunt divina præcepta; quid fugiendum, ut sunt vitia, quid timendum, ut sunt æterna tormenta: quid appetendum & deside- randum, ut sunt cælestia gaudia.

Non ergo est, quod cum Bellarmino & Estio ex- cipias, quod utilis quidem ad ista Scriptura sit, non autem sufficiens. Nam quod ad omnia officia, quæ requiruntur ad doctorem Ecclesiæ, utile est, id quin sufficiat ad institutionem omnem doctrinæ fidei, dubitandum non est. Quod ita utile est ad docendum, &c. ut homo DEI perfectus redda- tur, ad omne opus bonum instructus, id sufficien- ter omninò utile ac perfectum censeri debet. Quod ita utile est, ut nos sapientes reddat ad sa- lutem per fidem, id sufficere ad salutem, certo certius est. Si dicas cum Estio; de Scriptura Ve- teris Testamenti idem dicendum fore: Resps Omnino suo tempore sufficientem fuisse Canonem Veteris Testamenti, nec tamen non necessarium esse Vetus Testamentum nobis tempore Novi Testamenti, quia nobis credendum est, impletum esse, quod in Veteri Testamento credebatur im- plendum; neque ergò Novum Testamentum ali- quid diversi à Vet. Testam. tradit, sed ejus tantum exhibet complementum. Nihil enim extra ea, quæ in Mose & Prophetis scripta, tradit Actor. XXVI. vers. 22. Porro invertimus argumentum: Si V. Test. Scripta ad salutem instruere potuere, quidni id de universa Scriptura Vet. & Nov. Test. dicendum? Agnoscunt id Thomas part. 1. quæst. 29. art. 3. ex Dionysio, universaliter, inquiens, non est credendum aliquid dicere, nec cogitare præ- ter ea, quæ divinitus nobis ex Sanctis eloquiis sunt expressa: & in Comment. III. sent. dist. 3. quæst. 1. art. 1. ex Hieronymo: Non mihi credas, si quod tibi dixero, quod vel ex Vet. vel ex N. T. haberi non pos- sis, & lect. III. in h. l. Quadruplex est effectus S. Scri- pturæ, scil. docere veritatem, arguere falsitatem, quantum ad speculativam: eripere à malo, & in- ducere ad bonum, quantum ad practicam: ultimus ejus effectus est, ut perducat homines ad perfectum, non verò qualitercunque bonum facit, sed perficit. Plenius adhuc è præsenti loco perfectionem Scri- pturæ adserit Ludov. Soto major in commentar. Omnis Scriptura, inquit, divinitus inspirata apta seu idonea est, id est, facultatem præbet, vel materiam suppeditat uberem ad docendum, ad redarguendum, ad corrigendum, ad erudiendum. In ea igitur facile, & quasi ad manum paratum invenies, quod doceas populum, fidelem & clerum, quo redarguas hære- ticos, quo pravos etiam mores, atque sermones cor- rigas, sive prava dogmata, quo insuper erudias, & instituas parvulos, qui velut infantes lacte opus ha- bent. Denique utilis est ad omnia, quæ necessaria, & consentanea sunt, ad consequendam veram justi- tiam, pietatem, atque Salutem, id est, ut perfectus sit homo DEI ad omne opus bonum instructus.

Egimus de elogio hoc Scripturae Apostolico peculiari disputatione Anno cIɔ Iɔ c LXIIX. hic edita: Sed cepta tractatio, propter Respon- dentis inopinatum discessum, qui nullum exem- plar reliquerat, continuari haud potuit: Ea ta- men, quae tum edita sunt, his subjicere placet, ne opera illa prorsus pereat. Sic autem habet illa tractatio in paragraphos distributa.

§. I. Multis celebratur elogiis Scriptura sacra; quae in ipsa Scriptura leguntur. Nec mirum; Quia nemo dignior praeco est verbi DEI, quam Deus ipse, qui in Scripturis loquitur. Sed post Davidis plectrum, qui integrum Psalmum, eumque pro- lixissimum ac pulcherrimum, quem alphabetum alphabetorum dixeris, Encomiis Scripturae desti- navit, non est facile praestantius in universa Scri- ptura, quam quod nunc sub manibus habemus: quod tuba Evangelii, rugitus Leonis nostri, toni- tru gentium (ita Paulum nominat Hieronymus ad Pammachium,) ebuccinat. Hoc enim & divini- tatem S. literarum, & necessitatem earundem, & omnimodam atque absolutissimam perfectionem, & divinam prorsus utilitatem tam praeclare expo- nit, causasque omnes Scripturae S. tam graphice si- mul describit, ut vel hoc unum axioma vere Apo- stolicum, ad confundendos potenter omnes μι- σογράφους, abundantissime sufficiat.

§. II. Sic autem habet in fontibus Graecis: πᾶ- σα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος, καὶ ὠφέλιμος πρὸς διδα- σκαλίαν, πρὸς ἔλεγχον, πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν, πρὸς παιδείαν τὴν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ. Ἱνα ἄρτιος ἦ ὁ τῦ θεῦ ἄνθρωπος, πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐξηρτισμένος. Vulgata ita reddit: Omnis enim Scriptura divinitus inspirata utilis est ad docendum, ad arguendum, ad corrigendum, ad erudiendum in justitia, ut perfe- ctus sit homo DEI ad omne opus bonum instructus. Syriaca versio, ex interpretatione Tremelliana, sic habet: In Scriptura enim, quae per Spiritum scripta est, utilitas est ad doctrinam, & ad redargutionem, & ad correctionem, & ad eruditionem, quae est in justitia: ut sit perfectus filius hominis DEI ad omne opus bonum & absolutus. Trostiana versionis Syrae interpretatio haec est: Omnis enim Scriptura, quae per Spiritum scripta est, utilis est ad doctrinam, & ad redargutionem, & ad correctionem, & ad erudi- tionem, quae est in justitia, &c.

§. III. Apparet diversitas quaedam. Primo Syrus & Vulgatus conjunctionem causalem גיר ENIM adhibent, quae in textu originario non habetur; Addita sine dubio sensus & connexionis gratia. Non enim semper κατὰ πόδας reddunt. Tum in Syriaca versione variant lectiones in prima voce, quae varietas in originali textu locum non habet, nec habere potest. Tremellius reddit: In SCRI- PTURA. Sic enim, ait, sonant Syra verba על כתב &c. Addit: dicere n. non ausim על esse positum pro כל (licet ita melius responderet Graeco textui) quia non modo impressus, sed etiam manuscriptus Codex Heidelbergensis, quem antiquissimum esse apparet, le- git על. Franciscus vero Junius probat, alios lege- re omnis Scriptura, & recte. Quam diversam le- ctionem Trostius in variis lectionibus ad calcem Novi Testamenti observavit, quod Codex quidam Viennensis & Tremell. MSS. legat על, at Guido Fabricius habeat כל. Quae lectio ceu fonti con- sona omnino praeferenda. Facilis in his literis similibus inscriptione lapsus. Hinc porro tertio enata differentia. Quum enim Guido & Trostius habeant מותרנא הו utiliis est, ut respondeat subjecto, omnis Scriptura: in Viennensis & Tre- mell. MSS. legi מותרנא הן utilitas est, à Tro- stio notatur. Sed prius textui primigenio re- spondet: Scripturam omnem utilem dicenti non solum utilitatem in Scriptura ponenti. Quarto Graecus Textus duo praedicata habet, quae de Scriptura efferuntur, quod sit inspirata divinitus & utilis. πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος καὶ ὠφέλιμος, omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata & utilis est: Vulgata prius praedicatum ad subjecti descriptio- nem refert, particulam copulativam omittit, ac unum tantum praedicatum relinquit. Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata utilis est. Atque ita etiam Syrus interpres. Sed quia consentiunt Graeci Codices, sine dubio παράοραμα hîc inter- pretum, aut nimia παῤῥησία. Grotius tamen: Bene expressit sensum Syrus, omnis Scriptura, quae à DEO inspirata est, etiam utilis est ad docen- dum. Eodem modo conciliarat Erasmus: Appa- ret subesse tacitam vim argumentandi in conjun- ctione. Scriptura, ut est divinitus inspirata & efficax est ad multa, quum humana doctrina sit inef- ficax. Sed in Graeco textu per interpositum comma nectuntur duo illa praedicata, πᾶσα γραφὴ θεό- πνευστος, καὶ ὠφέλιμος, quod omisit Grotius, ut particulam καὶ per Etiam reddendo, sensum in Graeco consonum Syriacae interpretationi faceret. Male. Non enim ad versiones aptandus est tex- tus originalis, sed ad textum originalem versio- nes. Et manifestum est, duo praedicata hic de Scriptura, in qua commendanda versatur Apo- stolus, efferri, cum θεοπνευσίαν, tum utilitatem ejus verè divinam. Idque agnoscit Erasmus loco citato. Interim certum est, quod posterius e priori redundet, quodque ideo Scriptura hisce utilitati- bus polleat, quia inspirata est divinitus. Quinto, postremam vocem Grotius legit ἐξαρτυμένος; cum Ariamontano, qui reddidit conditus, ab ἐξαρ- τύομαι, uti Castellio vertit compositus. Vulgatus La- tinus adhuc aliam lectionem sequutus Erasmo & Bezae videtur, quasi scriptum fuerit ἐξηρτημένος ab ἐξαρτάω, quod est construere, & apparare, uti legi etiam in Complutensi editione Beza observavit. Reddidit enim Vulgatus instructus. Sed meliores Codices plerique omnes habent ἐξηρτισμένος, quam lectionem sequitur Beza, & Junius red- dentes, perfectè instructus. Quam etiam probat Grotius: Melius, inquit, alii Codices ἐξηρτισμέ- νος. Sexto in Syro deprehenditur in postremis verbis differentia aliqua, sed levis, & quae sensum non mutet. Ponit enim Comma post ἔργον ἀγα- θὸν & copulam ante ἐξηρτισμένος. Atque illud ἄρ- τιον vertit גמיר quod est consummatus, vel perfectus: ut sit perfectus filius hominis Dei, id est, homo DEI modo loquendi Syro perquam fami- liari: Posterius vero ἐξηρτισμένος exponit prae- fixa copula ומשלמן, quod eundem fere sen- sum habet, Trostius reddidit cum Tremellio, & absolutus. Observari Septimo potest, quod versio Syriaca vocem θεόπνευστος ad sensum solum red- diderit, דברוחא אתכתב quae per Spiritum scripta est. Quae se invicem declarant. Nam quia inspiratione divina scripserunt sancti DEI homines, per Spiritum scripta est sacra Scriptu- ra: Spiritui Sancto enim peculiariter hoc ap- propriatur. Neque tantum inspirati sunt sacri Scriptores, quà illis divina facta revelatio, sed scripserunt etiam ea, quae revelata sunt, per eundem Spiritum, qui illis patefecit.

Ut quicquid ab ipsis scriptum, omnia etiam ver- ba, quibus id scriptum, ab eo sint. ἐμφατικώτερον tamen adhuc est Græcum: quia & causam efficien- tem inspirationem divinam facit; & in eo etiam formam Scripturæ Sacræ, uti divina est, con- stituit, quod sit θεόπνευστος. Octavo corrigi potest lectio Latina è collatione textus Græci & Syriaci. D. Ambrosius, inquit Erasmus, πρὸς ἐ- πανόρθωσιν vertit ad redintegrationem, pro quo No- stri Codices habent ad corripiendum. Sed haud scio, an interpres scripserit ad corrigendum. Et quod divinarem in quarta editione comperi in ex- emplaribus Constantiensibus, ad corrigendum. Nam Græca vox sonat erigere, quod erat incurvum: At- que ita habent etiam emendationes Pontificum Sixti V. & Clementis IIX. ad corrigendum. Quod Græcæ & Syriacæ voci congruit. Leviculum est, quod loco nominum ad doctrinam, ad redargu- tionem, ad correctionem, ad eruditionem verba adhibuerit Vulgatus ad docendum, ad arguen- dum, ad corrigendum, ad erudiendum. Præstat ta- men, quoad fieri potest, si verbum reddatur ver- bo, quod proinde hic à Beat. Luthero factum. Quæ causa est, quod probare etiam non possimus Bezæ translationem, quod vocem πᾶσα reddi- derit tota. Quo de ista habet in annot. ad h. l. Vulg. & Erasmus. Omnis Scriptura, ambiguita- te hoc loco periculosa. Constat enim de certis Scri- ptis agere Apostolum, nempe de eo, quem Canonem Hœbræorum vocamus. Sed ea ambiguitas ista translatione non tollitur. Tum sive reddas omnis, seu tota Scriptura, nihil id derogat menti Apo- stoli, quod loquatur solum de Scriptura Canoni- ca: nam in utraque translatione subaudienda est è versu præcedenti vox sacra. Rectius ergo Sy- rus, Vulgatus, Erasmus, Beat. Lutherus vocem omnis retinent. Quomodo vero ea explicanda sit, deinceps videbimus. Aliud est Metaphrasten agere, aliud Paraphrasten. Et major emphasis est in voce omnis: quo ita tota designari potuit Scriptura sacra, ut innuèretur tamen etiam omne, quod in Scriptura S. continetur, utile esse, si non ad omnes illos quatuor usus, ad aliquem saltem eorundem, uti non tantum tota Scriptura S. est θεόπνευστος, sed etiam omne quod in Scriptura S. habetur. Sed hæc de collatione versionum cum fonte: quæ frustranea videri non debet. Fa- cit enim ad asserendam textus originalis authen- tiam & majestatem, & juvare quandoque nos po- test in indagando vero sensu. Crisis sacra nun- quam est supervacanea, modo cum κρίσει insti- tuatur.

§. IV. Nunc ad textus explicationem. Conside- randum occurrit primo vinculum cum præcedenti textu, quod particula copulativa interpretes ex- pressere. Tum subjectum, quod est πᾶσα γρα- φὴ, OMNIS SCRIPTURA. Tertio prædicatum quod geminum: prius θεόπνευστος divinitus inspirata est; Posterius vero ὠφέλιμος & utilis est. Quæ utilitas intelligatur & quon o- do, per partes explicatur ab Apostolo: quod nempe quadruplex ea sit, ad doctrinam, & ad re- dargutionem, & ad correctionem, & ad eruditio- nem, sed eam, quæ est in justitia. Quod qua sen- sum, non qua vocem referri posse videtur ad o- mnia illa; proprie tamen ad postremum πρὸς τὴν παιδείαν pertinet. Omnium enim illorum usuum finis est justitia, ideo docet vera, ideo redar- guit, ideo corrigit prava, ut justitia vera obtineat. Estque hæc παιδεία ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ apex veluti cæterorum. Quarto prædicati posterioris con- sectarium; ut perfectus sit homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum instructus. Sufficientiam enim suam ad istos usus universos & ad veram justitiam præ- stat, ut perfectus sit homo Dei, non modo per se veram perfectionem adipiscatur, sed ad omne opus bonum instructus, etiam quoad alios, abunde fit. Undecim ergo membris universa ἐξήγησις, quæ omnia, velut annuli in catena cohærent, absolvitur. Primum concernit textus συνέχειαν. Alterum Scripturæ omnis ambitum & περιφέ- ρειαν. Tertium omnis Scripturæ Sacræ θεοπνευ- σίαν. Quartum Scripturæ θεοπνεύστꙋ ὠφέλειαν. Quintum Scripturæ divinæ summe utilem διδα- σκαλίαν. Sextum Scripturæ sacræ ἔλεγχον vel ἔλεγξιν vere divinam. Septimam Scripturæ sa- cræ ἐπανόρθωσιν itidem prorsus divinam. Octavum Scripturæ sacræ παιδείαν, non minus vere divi- nam. Nonum παιδείας objectum & scopum τὴν δικαιοσύνην, veram justitiam. Decimum uti- litatis Scripturæ ἀποτέλεσμα & fructum priorem hominis DEI perfectionem omnimodam. Un- decimum & postremum fructum ejusdem poste- riorem, instructionem perfectam ad omne opus bonum. In aprico jam est, quam concinne co- hæreant singula: Nimirum studio dignissima Scri- ptura sacra est, quam coluit Timotheus, & sa- pientiam præstat ad salutem per fidem in Chri- stum, quia omnis Scriptura sacra est divinitus ad hunc finem inspirata. Nec quicquam post- habendum in Scriptura, aut leve æstimandum. Omnis enim Scriptura sacra & inspirata divini- tus & utilis est. Imo quia inspirata omnis, utilis etiam omnis est. Sed utilis primum ad doctri- nam. Quæ fons & scaturigo reliquorum usuum. Tum ubi vera inde hauritur doctrina, falsa spon- te diffluit. Ideo etiam utilis ad falsæ ἔλεγχον. Et quia doctrina, quam tradit, quamque poten- ter adserit, non est mere Theorica, sed Practi- ca, ideo utilis est ad nostri correctionem. Quan- doquidem post lapsum prius nobis opus sit ἐπα- νορθώσει & correctione. Qua expedita, succedit παιδεία, ut instituamur non tantum in justi- tia, sed efformemur ad eandem, à Pædaggo cœlesti: tum ad justitiam imputatam, tum ad pro- priam, utpote quæ ex imputatione illa redundat, & hic quidem inchoatur; in altera autem vita consummatur. Hos v. usus præstat Verbum DEI per sacrum ministerium, ideo perficit primum hominem DEI, id est, ministrum Verbi, ut nempe ipse tum vera intelligat & à falsis discernat, tum pravitatem humanam correctionis indigam, & quam intendit Scriptura justitiam non ignoret, imo ut perfectus ipse è Scriptura & per Scriptu- ram in his omnibus evadere possit, quanta in ho- minem hic cadit perfectio, aut quanta requiritur: tum vero instructum etiam reddit hominem Dei ad omne opus bonum sibi commissum, quod intra ambitum horum quatuor cardinum principalium coërcetur: ut perfecte instructus sit ad docendum alios vera quaque, & ad redarguendum alios qua falsa quæcunque, fidei, justitiæ, saluti ad- versa & noxia, nec non ad corrigendum omnia, quæ exorbitant à linea, omnesque à quacunque exorbitantia & pravitate revocandos, & redu- cendos: Denique ad erudiendum omnes de vera justitia, ut ita sapientes reddantur omnes ad salutem per fidem, quæ est in Christo JESU: qui Scripturæ sacræ, qui Ministrorum verbi, qui omnium nostrum finis esse debet. Liquet nunc, quam multa paucis hisce verbis complectatur Apostolus, ut integram Timotheo & cuivis verbi Ministro hic videri possit exhibere vo- luisse σωματοποίησιν religionis Christianæ, quum nullus fere sit articulus fidei, qui eàdem compre- hensus non sit. Si exordium fiat à Scripturæ S. per intermedia capita fidei usque ad novissimum, quod est æterna salus. Sed nobis hic angusti fixi sunt limites, ut vix unum atque alterum membrum prosequi liceat, quod tamen ita expediemus, ut de toto aphorismo inde haud difficulter constare queat.

§. V. Quod itaque primo ad συνέχειαν: Prædi- xerat Apostolus fata temporum novissimorum pessima vers. 1. Aperuerat fontem malorum o- mnium, seductionem falsorum Doctorum, qui, exem- plo Jannis & Jambri veritati resistunt: quales tum etiam, suo nempe tempore sese ingerere, & in domos irrepere passim, indicârat, vers. 6. Monet itaque Timotheum, ut quum assecutus fuerit doctrinam suam vere Apostolicam, & vitæ ratio- nem, propositum, fidem, longanimitatem, charita- tem, patientiam, quæ omnia fructus veræ doctrinæ erant, in quibus sese exemplum omnibus, etiam Timotheo suo, exhibuerat Apostolus; in iis, quæ didicerat, permaneat, & quæ ipsi concredita erant, καὶ ἐπισεύθης; Grotius ad hunc loc. Receptus ser- mo fuerat ἇ ἐπισώθης, sed est constructio κατὰ σύλλη- ψιν, ubi quid communiter de duobus dicitur, quod secundum exactam regulam alteri tantum conve- nit, Hesychius exponit ἐπείσθης, ἐπληροφορηθεὶς. Eodem modo Syrus juxta Tremell. & Trostii in- terpretationem, in quibus confirmatus es. Sen- sum reddunt, uti exponit Chrysostomus: non tan- tum ea didicisti, sed & credita sunt tibi: hoc est, credidisti, hanc esse vitam. Argumento utitur non uno, cur in iis permanendum sit. Primum à peri- culoso & noxio, quod antea insinuarat, statu nempe & qualitatibus falsorum Doctorum, eorumque exi- tu. Quorum amentia tandem evidens sit, sicuti Jannis & Jambris, quodque ipsi quoscunque alios secum abripiant in errores, in pejus solum proficiant, majori suo exitio. προκόψυσιν ἐπὶ τὸ χεῖρον. Grotius, magis magisque fient impu- denti & primum quæstiones inferent, deinde ipsa evertent Christianismi fundamenta. Quod ipse (Grotius) suo exemplo comprobavit. Unde fieri non potest, quin amentia ipsorum tandem fiat πᾶσιν ἔκδηλος. Ficta non durant diu. Quo- modo Chrysost. in h. l. Quamvis enim omni ex parte videatur error invalescere ad tempus, ad finem tamen usque non permanet: bujusmodi quippe sunt, quæ per naturam bona non sunt, sed bona esse viden- tur: ad tempus florent, sed cito deprehenduntur. At nostra talia non sunt, horumque tu testis es. Abest enim à nobis error omnis. Quis enim velit pro er- rore mori? Grotius existimat indigitari per hos πλανῶντας καὶ πλανωμένυς, illos, qui à Philo- sophis, præsertim à Pythagoristis, qui multi Ephesi, decepti: vel ab Heracliti sectatoribus, qui Ephe- sius fuerat: qui persuaserant Christianis, posse homi- nes & recte vivere & vitam æternam consequi se- quendo Philosophorum scita, uti in argumento ejus, quæ ad Ephesios scripta, dixerat Grotius. Sed non apparet ex hâc ad Timotheum exaratâ Epi- stola, quod seductos à Philosophis præcipue respe- xerit Apostolus. Prædixerat sub discessum suum, ex ipsis Ephesiis Doctoribus exsurrecturos viros loquentes διεςραμμένα perversa, & discipulos abdu- cturos post se. Ideo vigilandum esse monuerat, Actor. XX. vers. 31. Phigellum & Hermogenem expsesse designat, 2. Tim. I. vers. 16. Tum Hy- menæum quoque & Philetum expresserat, qui à veritate exciderint, dicentes, resurrectionem jam esse factam. Hos subvertisse quorundam fidem, & sermonem eorum instar cancri serpere, questus est cap. II. vers. 17. 18. Tales ergo ipsum hîc no- tasse, dubitandum non est. Eodem modo de illis loquutus ibi est; Et amplius, proficient ad impie- tatem: vers. 16. uti hic cap. III. vers. 13. Mali ho- mines & seductores proficient in pejus. Quorum fabulas etiam notat cap. IV. vers. 4. quales variæ erant apud Judæos Tit. I. 14. 1. Tim. I. vers. 4. & hæreticos, utpote Simonianos & alios, ut non opus sit, cum Grotio peculiariter fabulas de ex- piationibus peccatorum ex Chaldaica & Orphica disciplina intelligere, quas ad h. l. recenset. Re- ctius ergo Chrysostomus homil. l. in hac Epist. hæreses observat respici, quæ ex Judaicis observa- tionibus initia trahebant, quas & in priori signarit Epistola, quæ cum novellis Hymenei & Phileti turbabant fideles. Tantum illis ab Ethnicismo, à quo conversi erant, periculum non imminebat, quantum à Judaismo. Interim non negarim, Eth- nicos Philosophos, quos hæreticorum Patriarchas Tertullianus & alii dixere, suum quoque ἐπιβάλ- λον μέρος contulisse ad pervertendum eos, qui sub- inde ad impietatem magis magisque proficiebant.

§. VI. Quomodo autem 2. Tim. II. vers. 16. dixerit, proficient amplius ad impietatem, hic ve- ro cap. III. vers. 9. ultra non proficient, Chrysosto- mi hic malo verbis explicare, quam meis: Illis, inquit, ita locutus est, quia hi, qui novitatibus student, nusquam erroris finem invenient, sed nova semper commenta, & corruptum dogma proferent, ea enim est erroris vis, ut sisti non queat. Hic au- tem dicit non fallent, neque secum rapient, licet ini- tio quosdam decepisse videantur: Sed facillime de- prehendentur. Eorum enim amentia cunctis fiet perspicua. Observent id, qui novitatum pruritu agitantur, sibique dictum putent, ne facili earun- dem penes alios propagatione sibi blandiantur. Non fallit Spiritus: ἡ γὰρ ἄνοια ἀυτῶν ἔκδηλ(ος) ἔσται πᾶσιν.

§. VII. Unum adhuc, sed ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ adden- dum. In nominibus Jannes & Jambres textum originalem pro more solicitat Grotius, ut vulgatæ fidem adserat. In quo Estium Papistam præun- tem habet. Latini Interpretis, inquit, Græcum exemplar habuit Μαμβρῆς. Unde vero id probat? Quia ita Numenio Magus vocatus; nec aliter Ju- dæis in Thalmudico, titulo de oblationibus. Addit Estius, eodem modo legere R. Nathan, teste Ge- nebrardo. Sed Judæos recentiores Thalmud sequi, quid mirum? in Thalmode vero nomina pro- pria sæpe vehementer esse corrupta, notissimum est. Uti etiam nomen Jannes aliter in Thalmode lectum יוחני. Quod in Græcam imprimis transla- tis linguam accidit: Unde illud apud Numenium aliter paulo lectum, adeoque corruptum esse, ne- mo facile mirabitur. Hieronymus certe utrum- que nomen Jambres & Mambres pro eodem ha- bet, in interpretatione Ebraicorum nominum. Jambres autem non modo Codices Græci con- stanter legunt, sed Syrus etiam Interpres antiquus, ut & Chrysostomus homil. IIX. Frustra ergo hic gratificatur Papistis Grotius: qui in eo quoque frustra fuit, quod traditionum Papisticarum, ut apparet, causa ex traditione aut veterum Scriptis hæc omnia Paulum habuisse, affirmat. Chryso- stomo vel ex traditione, vel à Sp. S. Paulum ea didicisse, verisimile est. Posset utrumque con- jungi, si certo constaret, talem tum viguisse traditionem. Spiritu enim sancto dictante hæc scripsit; qui non dogmata solum, sed & histo- rica, non solum sententias, sed & verba inspira- vit Apostolis, ac ea etiam, quæ non ignota erant, ut scriberent, impulit, & quomodo scribenda erant, iisdem indidit. πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος. Nullum Scripturæ S. verbum, nullus apex excipi- tur, quin à divina sit inspiratione. Ut taceam quod à traditionibus historicis ad dogmaticas inepte arguant Papistæ.

§. VII. Ut ad argumenta Apostolicæ exhorta- tionis redeamus, desumtum alterum est ab hone- sto, quod fas sit permanere in illis, quæ didicerat & quæ credita sunt ipsi, ob præceptorem & Magistrum Apostolum : Quod sciat, à quo didicerit vers. 14. non certe tali, quales descripti sunt falsi Doctores, sed cujus non modo doctrinam & institutionem, sed & propositum, fidem, longanimitatem, dilectio- nem, patientiam, omnia falsorum Doctorum mo- ribus contraria, tum persecutiones quoque & pas- siones, è quibus tamen omnibus ipsum Dominus eripuit, noverat, uno verbo, quem verum Jesu Christi Apostolum planissime agnoscebat Timo- theus. Allegat confidenter & μετὰ καυχήσεως per- sequutiones, ac passiones, quibus æque, uti doti- bus Spiritus, doctrinam suam illustrem reddi cre- didit, sed quod Chrysostomus observat, ad conso- lationem discipuli, non ad jactantiam. Duo enim ista imprimis doctoris animum perturbant, hareti- corum scilicet multitudo, & impatientia passionum. Quales, inquit, persequutiones sustinui. Utræque consolationis plena sunt, quod alacritatem eximiam præstiti, neque derelictus sum. Nec dici potest, quod me prodiderit Deus, sed coronam mihi texuerit clariorem.

§. IX. Tertium argumentum ab utili petitum est: quia doctrina illa, quam didicerat Timotheus, uti fundamento Scripturæ S. nitebatur, extra quam nihil Paulus docuit Act. XXVI. 13. & cum sa- cris literis ἀπὸ βρέφους noverat Timotheus, ex as- se congruebat, ita eadem prorsus virtute pollebat, imo æque divina erat, æque θεόπνευστος. Non- nulli argumenti nervum hunc esse volunt, quod Timotheus doctrinam hanc cum primo lacte ma- terno imbiberit, quam tam facile abjicere non de- beat. Sed quanquam id eidem in memoriam etiam revocet, addenda tamen imprimis est virtus do- ctrinæ, quam inde ἀπὸ βρέφους etiam in semetipso senserat. Nusquam enim non explicat eandem ver- bum, ubi locum invenit. Eam addit ipse Aposto- lus: Quæ te possunt instruere ad salutem. Chryso- stomus vim illam insinuatam jam voce ἐπιστεύθης innuere videtur: Non tantum ea didicisti, sed & CREDITA sunt tibi: hoc est, credidisti hanc esse vitam. Si igitur impræsentiarum contraria his, quæ credidisti, evenire perspexeris, noli turbari. Alii ta- men malunt hîc CONCREDITUM Depositum requiri, (quod phrasi magis convenit. Conf. Gal. II. 7. 1. Tim. I. 11.) Estius, Menochius, Grotius, ut ad alterum argumentum ab honesto ratio hæc pertinere censenda sit, vel si cum B. Balduino illud distribuere velis, gemina ibi ratio contineatur: Duobus, inquit Beatus Antecessor, argumentis hortatur ipsum ad constantiam: 1. Quia doctrina cælestis ipsi ut depositum sit commissa. 2. Quia à fi- deli Magistro, qui super ea ad sanguinem usque pu- gnavit, eam accepit. Quorum priori majus robur conciliatur, si Timothei officium addatur. Quod ipsi ut Episcopo hæc παρακαταθήκη credita sit, & commissa asservanda. 1. Tim. VI. vers. 20. 2. Tim. I. vers. 14.

§. X. Cæterum non est, quod hyperbolen fin- gamus cum Estio in phrasi ab infantia. Quum enim infantes etiam ipsos, dum fari incipiunt, dicta Scripturæ proferre doceamus, quæ ma- trum cumprimis piarum cura esse solet, mater Timothei Eunice, & avia Lois dubio procul à teneris unguiculis eundem informarunt, in qui- bus fides non ficta habitavit, præcone Apostolo 2. Tim. I. verf. 5. Erat mater Ebræa, etsi genti- lis Pater esset, qui eum circumcidi noluit, Act. XVI. v. 1. Mos autem erat, & est nunc quoque Judæorum non tantum à prima ætate, quæ lite- rarum capax est, Sacra scripta legenda dare pue- ris, quod hic observat Grotius, sed infantes et- iam ipsos ad dicta Scripturæ recitanda assueface- re. Quo de in libr. Chin. pag. 161. laudante Hot- tingero Thefaur. Philol. lib. 1. cap. 2. pag. 90. ita legitur: Dicunt sapientes p. m. quando incipit Pater Filium suum instituere in lege? Tunc cum fari incipit, Pater quoque institutionis suæ facit ini- tium, id quod Moses nobis præcepit.

§. XI. Id vero Estio Papista veritas ipsa extor- sit, quod hic observatum voluit; locum nempe hunc docere, nec pueros arcendos esse à lectione Scri- pturæ S. nec mulieres, quum verisimile sit à matre & avia in S. literis institutum fuisse Timotheum. Cautela tamen, quam addit, modo secundum regulam Ecclesiasticam tales sint personæ, quæ co- gnoscantur ex hujusmodi lectione non damnum, sed fidei atque pietatis augmentum capere posse, quem- admodum præscribit Pontifex Regul. IV. in indic. libr. prohibit. S. Scripturæ probrosa est, nec observationi Estii convenit. Quis enim malus genius jussit Pontificem Scripturam S. quæ omni- bus demandata est legenda, inter libros prohibitos referre? Quis ei potestatem dedit, cuinam per- missam velit lectionem librorum Biblicorum, cui minus? Quomodo Scriptura divinitus inspirata, quæ nos potest ad salutem sapientes reddere, ulli damnum inferre dici potest, citra insignem con- tumeliam in Scripturam, imo blasphemiam in DEUM Scripturæ autorem? Quod DEUS omnibus commune esse voluit bonum, id nulla lege Ecclesiastica plerisque adimi, ad certos re- stringi potest; Qui vero id facit, DEO se op- ponit, & Anti-Christum se opere ipso demon- strat. Communem autem omnibus Scripturam esse voluit Deut. XXXI. verf. 11. Psalm. I. verf. 1. Psal. CXIX. Hab. II. verf. 2. Johan. V. verf. 39. 2. Petr. I. verf. 14. Communis erat ea penes Ju- dæos, uti jam notavimus; quod frustra negat cum Hardingo Peresius: Coronam legis relictam esse, ut quisque voluerit accipere, veniat, & acci- piat eam, id est ad quam cuique pateat aditus; è libro Joma docet Buxtorf. in Lex. Thalm. p. 690. In Pircke Aboth. cap. 6. ita habetur: Quicun- que non dat operam studio legis, vocatur repro- bus. Neque vero opus habuit facultatem eam legendi expetere Lois aut Eunice à summo Pon- tifice: Communis erat Scriptura Christianis in veteri Ecclesia cum Apostolica Actor. XVII. v. 11. 2. Petr. I. verf. 19. tum subsequa, teste Ignatio ad Philad. Polycarpo ad Philipp. Nulla ibi opus erat dispensatsone. Sapientia de Christo, fides in Chri- stum, & Salus per fidem ad omnes pertinent ex intentione DEI. Quomodo ergo ad paucos restringi, aut ulli adimi potest Scriptura, qua sapientes reddimur, è qua fidem in Christo hau- rimus, per quam salutem consequimur? Nec vero noxii quid habere potest Scriptura, quæ à DEO ad hos usus adornata; quæ communis est Medica animarum officina, dicente Basilio in Psal. I. cujus lectio magna est adversus peccatum munitio, teste Chrysost. hom. III. de Lazaro: Scriptura vitalis est & nihil offendiculi habet fide- libus, ait Epiphanius hær. LXIX. quæ Ariomanit. est. Opera autem & instinctu malorum Dæmonum mortis supplicium adversus Prophetarum lectores Gentiles constituisse. Justinus Apol. II. pro Christ. autor est. Qualem persequutionem in Judæos, ne Scripturam lectitarent, Trajano adscribunt, de qua etiam R. Zakuth conquestus fuit: Judæi vero excludunt Christianos à lectione legis, Gentilis (ita Christianum vocant) operam dans legi reus est mortis Sanh. c. 7. Manifestum est, quo regantur Spiritu Pontifices, cum Scripturæ lectionem pro- hibent, & in Inquisitione sua hunc etiam articu- lum interrogativum constituunt, an aliquis Bi- alia legerit?

§. XII. Præclare autem S. literarum vis & uti- litas exprimitur ab Apostolo, cum τὰ ἱερὰ γράμ- ματα dicuntur δυνάμενα σοφίσαι εἰς σωτηρίαν διὰ πίστεως τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ. Tribuuntur enim ipsis tres summi effectus. Primo SAPIENTIA emi- nentissima, non de rebus mundanis ad vitam com- munem, sed de Deo & divinis rebus, ad salutem & vitam æternam. Non instruere nos tantum po- test scriptura, & erudire ad salutem, sed σοφίσαι, sapientes reddere: qui est supremus eruditionis apex. Nihil enim sapientia sublimius. Notatur ergo perfecta informatio, quam è S. literis de fide ad salutem habemus. Quicquid n. sapientes nos reddit ad salutem, id perfecte de iis, quæ ad salu- tem necessaria sunt, nos instruere oportet. Quæ- nam est illa SAPIENTIA, quæ in necessariis defi- cit, & quomodo ad salutem sapientes reddere pos- set Scriptura S. si vel ullum fidei caput, sine quo salus obtineri non possit, præteriret? Ideo Anshel- mus Cantuariens. in h. l. S. literæ te possunt instruere, hoc est, SUFFICIENTER doctum reddere ad æter- nam Salutem. Ut vana sit Bullingeri contra Plessæ- um exceptio, τὸ σοφίσαι non esse proprie sapientem reddere, sed instruere. Vox enim Græca impor- tat sapientiam; Ideoque Erasmus ad h. l. σοφίσαι i. e. erudire, sapientem reddere. Salmero σοφίσαι i. e. sapientem reddere, vel erudire, ut legit Ambrosius: Nec aliter exponunt vocem Latinam vulgatæ in- struere, Cajetanus, Estius, alii.

§. XIII. Secundus effectus est Fides salvifica, quæ est in Christum Jesum, Joh. III. 16. cap. XX. 31. Hæc enim è Scripturis oritur Joh. V. 39. 46. Rom. III. 21. cap. X. v. 17. Quum fides notitia, assensu & fiducia constet, neque notitia de Christo aliunde haberi potest, quam è Scriptura Rom. XVI. v. 26. neque assensus præberi, nisi efficacia & virtute ipsius Scripturæ S. quæ corda nostra de veritate, quam tradit, convincit, 1. Joh. V. 6. nedum fiducia concipi potest, nisi efficaci operatione verbi, Joh. VI. 63. Gal. III. 2. Ebr. IV. 12. per quod illumina- mur, Psal. XIX. 9. Act. XXVI. 18. Eph. III. v. 9. regeneramur, 1. Pet. I. 23. Jac. I. 21. convertimur Jer. XXIII. 29. Es. VI. 10. Joh. XII. 40.

§. XIV. Mera perversio est, καδδιάμετρον Apo- stoli verbis contraria, cum Estius verba per fidem, quæ in Christum creditur, addi, ait, ut doceat Aposto- lus contra Judaizantes scientiam legis sine fide Christi nihil valere ad salutem, vel ut significet, ex Scri- pturis S. cum ob earum obscuritatem, tum ob intel- lectus nostri cæcitatem, & hebetudinem atque affe- ctuum, quibus laboramus, pravitatem, non posse quenquam haurire doctrinam sanam & incorru- ptam, nisi fide Christi præmunitus sit, eaque doctrice ad illas intelligendas utatur. Nam (1) non docet Apostolus, scientiam legis cum fide ad salutem vale- re, solam fidem requirit ad salutem: justitia enim fidei χωρὶς νόμου sine lege manifestata est, Rom. III, vers. 21. (2) Nec aliunde ad Scripturæ lectionem ad- ferri vult fidem ad salutem, sed sacras literas com- mendat, utpote quæ possint nos sapientes reddere ad salutem per fidem. Nisi autem de fide nos perspicue

& sufficienter instruerent, quomodo ad salutem sapientes reddere valerent, quæ non nisi per fi- dem obtinetur? ut sapientia, ita fides salvifica è Scripturis hauriatur, necessum est: alias scriptura non reddit quenquam sapientem ad salutem, (3) Obscura non est Scriptura in his, quæ ad fidem & salutem pertinent. Si obscura esset, neminem ipsa instruere vel erudire posset ad salutem. Et unde alias fides, quam è Scripturis indubitato, atque infallibiliter peti potest? Quæque aperta, inquit August. l. de unit. Eccles. c. V. & manifesta deligamus, quæ si in S. Scripturis non invenirentur, NULLO modo esset, unde aperirentur clausa, & illustrarentur obscura. Ideoque l. II. de Doctr. Christ. cap. 9. hoc tradit axioma: In his, quæ aperte in Scriptura posita sunt, inveniuntur illa omnia, quæ continent fidem, moresque vivendi. (4) Intellectus nostri cæcitati, affectuum pravi- tati Scriptura ipsa medetur : dum mentes illumi- nat, & corda purificat. Lex Domini immaculata, convertens animas; testimonium Domini fidele sa- pientiam præstans parvulis. Præceptum Domini lu- cidum illuminans oculos, Psal. XIX. vers. 8. Di- vina Scriptura, inquit Cyrillus l. VII. contr. Julian. sufficit, ut sapientes, ac probi, ac plenissi- ma prudentia præditi evadant, qui in ea educati sunt, nec ad illud prorsus egemus Doctoribus pere- grinis. (5) Non ergo per fidem præmuniti ad Scripturam accedimus, sed per Scripturam fide instruimur, & munimur Joh. V. 39. 46. cap. XX. vers. 31. & Sapientia salutis, quæ est fidei. Nullam etiam aliam sapientiam salutis, vel ad salutem no- vit Scriptura, quam notitiam fidei, Joh. XVII. vers. 3. notitiam Christi Es. LIII. vers. 11. scientiam salutis de remissione peccatorum per Christum Luc. I. vers. 77. (6) Ideo separari hîc effectus fidei non potest à Scriptura, sed cum sapientia fides quoque Scripturæ S. accepta fertur. Quod a- gnoscit Claudius Espensæus in hoc loco si quid scire, si quid agere opus est, verum docent, fal- sum coarguunt, reducunt à malo, inducunt ad bonum, nec vero qualitercunque bonum faciunt, sed perficiunt, eaque possunt hominem ad salutem erudire, & sufficienter doctum reddere. Et Leonh. Marins Jesuita prolegom. in Script. S. q. II. sect. 5. De S. libris dixit B. Apost. Paulus 2. Tim. III. pos- sunt te instruere ad salutem, additque, per eos fieri, ut perfectus sit homo DEI ad omne opus bonum in- structus. Et vere ita est; Discimus enim ex iis non tantum, quid credere, sed etiam, quid agere, quid vitare, & quid sperare ac metuere debeamus, in quibus sola vita humana perfectio consistit. Lau- rentius Villavicent. l. 1. de rat. stud. Theol. cap. 3. Scriptura & quidem SOLÆ possunt nos ad salutem erudire per fidem Christi.

§. XV. Tertius effectus & SALUS æterna: quæ non tantum se per modum finis ultimi habet, re- velationis divinæ & S. literarum, sed etiam per modum effecti : quia in Scripturis habemus vitam æternam, Joh. V. vers. 39. Verbum DEI Spiri- tus est & vita Joh. VI. vers. 63. Evangelium est potentia DEI ad salutem omni credenti Rom. I. vers. 16. Verbum Vitæ Act. V. 20. Phil. II. v. 16. Verbum salutis, Actor. XV. vers. 26. Ephes. I. 15. Quum vero hîc de Scripturis V. T. sermo sit, quas ab infantia didicerat Timotheus, manife- stum hinc est, salutem æternam non tantum in V. T. propositam fuisse, quod Sociniani perpe- ram negant, sed sufficienter etiam ad salutem æternam erudiisse Scripturas Vet. Testam. & quidem per fidem in Christum: unde doctrinam de Deitate Christi oportuit in V. T. clare propositam fuisse, sine qua fides in Christum constare non potest. | Quod contra Novatores Calixtinos observan- | dum. Juliani impii Apostatæ ea erat vox, in Mose | & Prophetis nihil de Deitate Christi, aut Trinitate | haberi, sed eum refellit prolixe B. Cyrillus l. IIX. | & IX. contr. Julian. cum Moses, inquit l. IX. Tom. | VI. p. m. 294. & Prophetæ sanctam & consubstan- | tialem Trinitatem fateantur, neque istud tum isti | sapientiæ Principes (gentiles intelligit Philoso- | phos, è quibus similia adduxerat Cyrillus) igno- | raverint, quî fit, amabò te, ut durâ & pertinaci igno- | rantia te laborare non sentias?

§. XVI. Atque ita constat jam συνέχεια textus: Vult enim explicare & confirmare uberius, quod dixerat Apostolus de sapientiâ, quæ è S. literis habetur. Ideo particulam causalem adhibuit. Omnis enim Scriptura divinitus inspirata, & u- tilis est: Gemino usus argumento: Prius ab ori- gine & constitutione divinâ S. Scripturæ petitum, quia θεόπνευςος est, ideoque quum à DEO au- tore perfectissimo profecta & spiritu divino animata sit, nostræ salutis causa, non poterit non perfe- ctam sapientiam exhibere, nosque perfecte ad salutem instruere. Ita colligit Irenæus l. II. ad- vers. hæres. cap. 7. Scripturæ, inquit, perfectæ sunt, quippe à verbo DEI & Spiritu ejus dictatæ. Et Hilarius l. XII. de Trinit. DEI sermo & vera sapientiæ doctrina, quæ loquitur, & perfecta, & ab- solutæ sunt. Agnoscit hanc consequentiam Joh. Trithem. in libr. IIX. Quæst. q. IV. ad Maximil. Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata perfectum di- vinitatis opus est ante tempus omne præordinatum, in tempore scriptum non secus, quam DEUS voluit, qui ut scriberetur hominibus inspiravit. DEI au- tem omnia opera sunt perfecta. Ideoque cum Scri- ptura, de quâ loquimur, DEI sit opus, necessa- rium est, eam in omnibus consueri perfectam. Po- sterius ex inductione usuum Scripturæ desumptum: qui ad perfectam divinam sapientiam faciunt: si- quidem Scriptura utilis sit ad docendum, & arguen- dum & erudiendum in justitia, ut perfectus sit homo DEI ad omne opus bonum instructus. Quæ Scri- ptura hos omnes usus præstat, ea indubie nos sapientes reddere potest ad salutem.

§. XVII. Quod ergo secundum tractationis no- stræ caput attinet, subjectum nempe, quod hìc est πᾶσα γραφὴ OMNIS SCRIPTURA, ejusque ambitum, de Scripturâ omni SACRA sermonem esse, è versu præcedenti, è prædicato, totoque contextu manifestum est. Quam per ἱερὰ γράμ- ματα expresserat. Sic Scriptura S. vocatur abso- lute γραφὴ Johan. XIX. vers. 31. vel πληθυντικῶς γραφαὶ Matth. XXII. vers. 29. Joh. V. vers. 39. uti Ebræis pariter κατ’ ἐξοχὴν vocatur כְּתָב, מִכְתָּב nec non Chaldais כְּתָבָא scriptura, quia hæc inter Scripturas omnes eminet, ad quam collatæ scriptæ reliqua nihili æstimanda sunt imo ob eam solam omnia alia scripta fieri debent: quemadmodum etiam ideo κατ’ ἀντονομασίαν Ebræis dicitur מִקְרָא lectura è Neb. IIX. vers. 8. quia ab omnibus legi debet, & sola digna est, quæ legatur: תּוֹרָה do- ctrina vel institutio Psal. XIX. vers. 9. Joh. X. v. 34. quia sola nos docet, atque instituit ac docenda est in bis, quæ ad salutem faciunt. Item מְגִלָּה volumen vel מְגִלַּת סֵפֶר volumen libri Psal. XL. vers. 8 unde Græcis, Latinis, Gallis, Germanis, Anglis, βιβλια Biblia κατ’ ἐξαίρετον λόγον dicta. Συνωνύμως ergo Scripturæ hic accipitur alterum nomen τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα: quæ γραφαὶ ἁγίαι etiam dicantur Rom. I. vers. 2. & τὰ βιβλια τὰ ἅγια 1. Macc. XII. v. 9. Ebræis כִּתְבֵי הַקֹּדֶשׁ Scripturæ Sanctitatis, vel san- cta & libri Sanctitatis, vel sancti. Quo nomine vocatur (1) ob autorem, Deum ter sanctum (2) ob amanuenses, sanctos Dei viros, per quos exarata est Scriptura 2. Petr. I. 21. (3) ob materiam: quæ sunt sacra dogmata, sacra Præcepta, sacra exempla. Nihil enim non sacrum est in Scripturâ. Immu- nis est ab omni errore, ab omni immundicie, adeoque vere sancta. (4) ob formam. Quia modus quo proponuntur illa, vere sacer est, & structura tota sancta: id eleganter ideo מִקְדַּשְׁיָה sanctuarium Domini vocetur ab Ebræis: quemad- modum illic sancta erat fabrica, sanctus appara- tus, sancta imprimis præsentia & habitatio DEI, ita univit sese cum hoc sanctuario S. literarum Deus unione sancta, & inseparabili, ut verbum sit Spiritus & vita Joh. VI. vers. 6. & potentia Dei Rom. I. v. 16. Ideo ab omni alia Scriptura lon- gissime separata est (5) ob effectum, quia sanctifi- cat nos Joh. XVII. vers. 17. (6) ob adjunctum: quia sancte custodienda, sancte tractanda est, & ab omnibus prophanis separanda, nec prophanis usibus ullatenus contaminanda.

§. XVIII. Præmittit Apostolus particulam πᾶ- σα, quæ complectitur tum totam Scripturam, tum certo respectu omne illud, quod in Scripturâ con- tinetur. Nam & Scriptura tota est divinitus in- spirata atque utilis ad docendum, redarguen- dum &c. nihilque in scriptura est, quod non sit in- spiratum divinitus, quod non sit utile, si non ad omnes illos fines, ad aliquem certe eorundem: de quâ id dici queat, quod de Lege Rabbini pro- nunciant, quod nulla sit in Scripturâ litera, à qua non suspensi sint magni doctrinarum montes. Di- cuntur ergo hæc prædicata de Scripturâ tota, qua tota est, & secundum omnes sui partes. Compre- hendit itaque vox πᾶσα 1. universalitatem seu to- talitatem Scripturæ Canonicæ: quod ea tota à DEO sit inspirata, & utilis ad hosce fines, adeoque suf- ficiens sit ad salutem. Sic explicat Athanasius in Synopsi πᾶσα γραφὴ ἡμῶν χρισιανῶν θεόπνευσός ἐςω: ἐκ ἀόρισα δὲ ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ὡρισμένα καὶ κεκανονισμένα ἔχει τὰ βίβλια: Omnis nostra, qui Christiani sumus, Scriptura divinitus inspirata est, librosque habet non infinitos, sed finitos ac certo ca- none comprehensos. Sic Chrysost. Theophyl. & Oecumen: Nec aliter è Pontificiis Dionysius Car- thusian. Adamus Sasbout, Guilb. Estius, Jacob. Tirinus. OMNIS, hoc est, TOTA scriptura utilis est, id est, conducit, ad hunc finem condita est. Num illos omnes Tannerus distorquere Scripturam di- cet, uti nostros accusat, quod vocem πᾶσα in- terpretentur TOTA? Vid. T. III. Theol. Scho- last. disp. I. q. 5. pag. 340.

§. XIX. Dicere etiam possumus, compre- hendi hic quoque universalitatem Scriptorum sacrorum, ita ut omne Scriptum sacrum hisce elogiis ornetur, imo nihil in Scripturâ Sacra esse doceatur, quod non sit θεόπνευσον, non ὠφέλι- μον: Neque nos monet Tanneri ratio: Si vox utilis significaret sufficiens, tunc omnem Scripturam, adeoque quemlibet divina Scripturæ librum fore sufficientem ad salutem & instructionem, quia omnis Scriptura & omnis Scripturæ liber est utilis ad do- cendum. Nam totam Scripturam dicimus his elogiis mactari, qua tota est, & quoad singulas par- tes, sed diversa ratione. Ad totam Scripturam per- tinet & ad omnes ejus partes τὸ εἶναι θεόπνευσον: quia in eo Scripturæ S. qua talis, formale situm est: ad totam Scripturam etiam omnesque ejus partes spectat τὸ ὠφέλιμον: quia Scriptura divi- nitus inspirata non potest non utilis esse, usus etiam illi, qui enumerantur, tum totius Scripturæ sunt, tum certa ratione etiam partium Scripturae : Omnes conjunctim totius sunt Scripturae : Par- tium Scripturae autem ita, ut nulla sit earum, quae non ad aliquem aut aliquos horum usus faciat & conducat. Cum autem ex utilitate ista Scriptu- rae infertur ejusdem sufficientia & perfectio, quoad ea, quae ad salutem scitu necessaria sunt, non tan- tum vox ὠφέλιμος spectatur, neque praecise in- haereamus, opus est, interpretationi vocis πᾶσα, quod explicari debeat TOTA, sed imprimis re- spiciendam συνέχειαν textus censemus; quod pro- bet atque explicet Apostolus τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα Scripturas S. sapientes nos reddere posse ad salutem per fidem in Christum : quia omnis Scriptura Sacra divinitus inspirata est, & utilis ad doctrinam, ad re- darguitionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem in justitia & quidem ita, ut perfectus sit homo DEI ad omne opus bonum instructus. Quum hoc fine a DEO inspirata sit Scriptura, eoque utilitas Scri- pturae tendat, atque istud tam perfectum ἀποτέλε- σμα a Scriptura sit, quomodo Scriptura ipsa non erit perfecta atque sufficiens?

§. XX. Quanquam vero de sacris literis illis, quas a puero didicerat Timotheus, specialiter v. 15. actum sit, ratio tamen, quam adfert Apostolus, ad probandam hanc facultatem vel utilitatem S. li- terarum universalis est, ut requirit principium Syl- logisticum de omni & nullo.
