Adde, quod eadem ratio sit Scripturae Canonicae, quantum ad origi- nem, formam, & efficaciam. Atque Scriptura N. T. utilis est, uti Scriptura V. T. imo quum lux major atque illustrior N. T. sit, quomodo mi- nori polleret virtute atque efficacia ? Tum vero si Scriptura Veter. Testam. perfecte nos instruere ac sapientes reddere potest ad salutem, quanto magis Scriptura universa, postquam accessit ad S. Prophetarum literas Scriptura Apostolica? ut proinde opus non sit solicite disquirere, quaenam tum edita fuerint N. T. scripta, quo constet, qua- nam Scripturae vocis OMNIS ambitu compre- hendantur; sive enim plura, seu pauciora tum fue- rint edita, imo si nulla adhuc fuissent tum conscri- pta, vis tamen & δεινότης effati Apostoli manet, Scripturam solam nos sufficienter instruere, quia ideo divinitus inspirata & ad usus omnigenos aptata est, ut inde perfecti reddamur : Siquidem ipsa etiam V. T. scripta tum suffecerint, cum illi fini eadem sola destinarentur divinitus.

§. XXI. Falsum tamen est, quod existimat Ti- letanus, tum nulla adhuc extitisse N. T. scripta, cum haec scriberet Apostolus: neque cum aliis putan- dum, sola V. T. hic respexisse Apostolum, quia sola illa extiterunt, cum Timotheus adhuc infans esset ; Non enim tantum in infantia, sed inde ab infan- tia literas sacras didicisse dicitur, totusque ille ab infantia tractus hic indigitatur : neque dubi- um esse potest, alia Scripta sacra, quae interea prodierunt ab Evangelistis & Apostolis, cogni- ta eidem fuisse, qui plerisque Epistolis Apostoli- cis subscripsit ipse: utpote posteriori ad Corinthi- os, ei quae ad Philippenses, quae ad Colossenses per- scripta; utrique ad Thessalonicenses & Epistolae ad Philemonem: priorem ad Corinthios attulerit, in Epistola ad Romanos salutem adscripserit: & quis ambiget alia etiam scripta studiose volvisse Timo- theum S. literarum cupidissimum : prodierant e- nim tum, si calculum Cornelii a Lapide hic assumas, jam pleraque omnia N. T. scripta, utpote Evan- gelium Matthaei Anno Christi XLI. scriptum : Mar- ci Evangelium, & prior Epistola Petri An. XLVI. Prior ad Thessalon. Anno Christi LII. & seq. LIII. posterior : An. LVII. prior ad Corinthios & ad Timo- theum. Anno LIIX. Epistola ad Titum cum po- steriori ad Corinthios. Eodem ann. Lucam scripsisse Evangelium suum Baronius censet; Sed Cornelius a Lapide ostendit ad Act. XVI. tum jam vulga- tum & celebre fuisse Lucae Evangelium, & inter annum LI. quo Lucas Paulo adhaerere coepit, & LIIX. quo illud ore omnium laudari asserit Apo- stolus 2. Cor. IIX. v. 18. id conscriptum esse. An- no Christi LIX. scripta est Epistola ad Philippen- ses & ad Ephesios: Anno LX. Epistola ad Philemo- nem, ad Colossenses & ad Ebraeos; Anno LXI. Acta Apostolica finita sunt. Anno LXIII. Jacobus mar- tyrio coronatus est, qui Canonicam scripsit Epi- stolam. Eam, quae est ad Romanos Epistolam post Epistolas ad Corinthios, sed ante alias Paulinas scriptam vult Cornelius Comm. in Epist. ad Rom. p. 28. Ante Epistolam ad Romanos Chrysostomus & Baronius censent scriptam Epistolam ad Galatas, cujus tempus omnium incertissimum dicit Corne- lius a Lapide, in prooem. in Epist. ad Gal. Quum ergo An. demum LXIIX. posterior haec ad Timo- theum scripta, eaque omnium inter Paulinas ul- tima sit, quo anno etiam posteriorem Petri & Judae Epistolam scriptam vult Cornelius (sed ante hanc Paulinam) manifestum est ex hac Chronotaxi, quam Actis Apostolicis praemisit Cornelius, o- mnia scripta Nov. T. si Johannea sola exceperis, tum, cum haec scriberet Paulus, extitisse.

§. XVII. Quapropter non abs re dici potest, Apostolum hoc elogio Scripturarum Novi Test. canonem juxta cum canone Veteris Testam. ce- lebrare & Ecclesiae per Timotheum commendare voluisse. His vero elogiis non inferiora esse Jo- hannea, quae post accesserunt, scripta, S. Johan- nes ipse testatur, cum ex iis, quae in Evangelio scripsit haberi posse fidem & salutem cap. XX. 31. aperte docet: de Epistolis vero, 1. Ep. I. vers. 4. Haec scribo vobis, inquit, ut gaudium vestrum sit per- fectum: Apocalypsin denique librorum N. Test. ultimum, & cum eadem totum canonem Nov. Te- stamenti sic obsignat, ut perfectum eundem esse nulli dubium esse queat, siquidem contestetur de libro illo, ei nihil apponendum, nihil demendum es- se, (quod argumentum perfectionis est) nisi ap- poni nobis plagas in illo scriptas, aut auferri partem nostram velimus de libro Vitae; Beatum vero pro- nunciet illum, qui verba propheta libri istius custodit Ap. XXII. 7. 18. 19. unde relinquitur ex hoc libro salutem vel beatitudinem obtineri posse. Praecla- re de Scriptis Evangelistarum S. Cyrillus sub finem commentariorum suorum in Johannem: Non omnia, quae Dominus fecit, conscripta sunt, sed quae scribentes tam ad mores quam dogmata putarunt SUFFICERE, ut recta fide, & operibus, ac virtute rutilantes ad regnum caelorum perveniamus: ut ha- bet in editione Basileensi Anno 1546. Gregorii Trapezuntii interpretatio: Paulo aliter ea legun- tur in editione Parisiensi Anno 1638. in Graeco textu, sed sensu eodem: γεγράϕασι γεμὴν τῶν εὐαγγελίων οἱ κήρυκες τὰ ἐν τοῖς γεγονόσι λαμ- πρότερα, καὶ ἄγε τὸ εἰκὸς, καὶ δι' ὧν ἦν μάλιςα τοῖς ἀκροωμένοις δύνασθαι βεβαιοῦσθαι πρὸς πίσιν τὸν ἀπαράϕθορον, καὶ παίδευσιν ἔχειν ἠθικήν τε καὶ δογ- ματικὴν, ἵνα πίσει μὲν ὀρθῇ διαπρέποντες, ἔργοις δὲ τοῖς εἰς εὐσέβειαν βλέποισι πολυτρόπως ἠγλαϊ- μένοι, καὶ εἰς ἀυτὴν κατατήσευτες τὴν ἄνω πόλιν, καὶ τῇ τῶν πρωτοτόκων ἐκκλησίᾳ συναπτόμενοι, καὶ εἰς ἀυτὴν εἰσελεύσειαν τὴν τῶν ὀρανῶν βασι- λείαν, ἐν χρισῷ. Latina translatio Johannis Au- berti sic habet: Multa quippe miraculorum millia virtute Servatoris nostri facta esse cogitandum est: verumtamen illustriora tantum ab Evangeliorum preconibus, ut videtur, scripta fuere, & per quæ ma- xime possent Auditores ad incorruptam fidem firmari & doctrina tam morum quam dogmatum institui, ut recta fide conspicui & operibus ad pietatem spectan- tibus varie illustrati, & ad ipsam supernam civita- tem evecti, atque primogenitorum Ecclesiæ conjun- cti, in ipsum quoque regnum Cælorum penetrarent in Christo.

§. XXIII. Sed imprimis observandum, quod hæc elogia Apostolus soli Scripturæ vindicet. Quo sen- su vocem omnis quandoque occurrere, ut simul indicet, soli illi rei attributum competere, cui ad- jungitur, nonnulli observant. Vide Matth. XXIX. vers. 19. 20. Joh. III. 16. cap. VI. 45. 2. Pet. I. 21. Hic certe SOLAM scripturam S. istis elogiis ma- ctari ab Apostolo, in aprico est. Monet enim ut in Scripturis sacris & his, quæ ex illis didicerat, per- maneat, & persistat: non ad alia se abripi patiatur. Docet, scripturas sacras potentes esse, atque suffi- cientes, ut instruant ad salutem per fidem in Chri- stum. Ostendit Scripturas Sacras ideo divinitus inspiratas esse, atque ad omnigenos usus necessarios aptatas, & adornatas. Testatur, per illas, & ex illis hominem DEI perfectum reddi, ad omne opus bonum instructum. Nullum aliud principium instructio- nis requirit, aut necessarium esse docet: Soli Scri- pturæ id tribuit omne, ut nihil certius sit, quam, quod Scriptura sola ad ea sufficiens sit, atque per- fecta. Solas literas Sacras allegat Apostolus, tan- quam ordinarium Sapientiæ salutiferæ medium: illis solis munit Episcopum adversus quamcunque falsorum Doctorum, de quibus præmonuerat, sedu- ctionem: eaque ἀξιώματα Scripturis sacris ideo tribuit, quia scriptura S. θεόπνευστος est. Nulli er- go, nisi θεοπνεύστῳ verbo ea conveniunt. Quod- nam vero aliud vocari potest verbum θεόπνευστον extra & præter Scripturam Sacram, quod nunc infallibiliter tale habendum sit? Nec nisi ad solam Scripturam, ceu unicum illud ordinarium, indu- bitatum atque infallibile sapientiæ divinæ saluti- feræ principium Timotheum hic remitti agno- scunt veteres Doctores: Chrysostomus in h. l. Si quid vel discere vel ignorare opus sit, illud in Sacra Scriptura addiscemus: Si arguere falsitatem, inde hauriemus. Si corrigi, si castigari, ad exhortatio- nem, ad solatium si quid DESIT & oporteat adi- pisci, ex ea nihilominus addiscimus. Ut perfectus sit homo DEI. Non ergo sine illa perfici potest. Pro me, inquit Paulus, Scripturas habes, si quid addisce- re cupis, hinc poteris. Non ergo ad traditiones re- mittit, sed sui loco Scripturam esse voluit Aposto- lus, interprete Chrysostomo. Erat autem Apo- stolus Timotheo præceptor sufficientissimus. Ad- dit Chrysost. Si autem Timotheo ista scribit Sancto Spiritu plenus, quanto magis nobis dicta putare de- bemus. Sequitur Chrysostomum ut in plerisque aliis cum Oecumenio Theophylactus: cujus com- mentarius tamen hic paulo plenior est, ac solidis- sima Papisticæ de imperfectione S. literarum ca- lumniæ, vel blasphemiæ refutatio censeri queat. Ideo adscribemus integrum. Ne animo concidat (Timotheus) utpote qui præceptore sit paulo post se consolante privandus, habes, inquit, in mei vicem Scripturas, quæ & levare te possunt & prodesse. Scri- ptum prodest, inquit, ad docendum. Quia nos in- stituit, quid sit perdiscendum. NIHIL est enim, quod nequeat Scripturis dissolvi. Ad arguendum: si coarguenda sc. fuerint mendacia. Ad corripien- dum, ad erudiendum in justitia: Si necesse est, in- quit, ut aliquid vel corrigatur, vel instruatur, hoc est, ad justiciam reddi continentem, & sobrium, & ea, quæ justa sunt exequi ex S. literis & OMNE suppe- ditabitur. Ut perfectus sit homo DEI. Emendatio, inquit, ex Scripturis paratur, ut NIHIL HOMINI DESIT, qui secundum Deum incesserit. Si itaque ipse INTEGER fieri, & PERFECTIOR cupis sanusque & semper æquabilis reddi, nec contrahi adversis exoptas, nec prosperis rebus efferri (id enim præsert perfectionem mentis & æqualitatem) has sacras literas consule, cum mea carebis præsentia. Atqui si Timotheo S. S. oppleto de ejusmodi lectione conscripsit, quanto magis sumus & nos ad eam hortandi, qui Spiritu hoc indigemus. Adverte autem quemadmodum, ni S. literæ opitulentur, integros nos & PERFECTOS reddi non posse doceat. Ad omne opus bonum instructus. Non enim simpliciter bonorum est operum particeps, sed instructus his ipsis, & ABSOLUTUS. Neque una aliqua in re erit ille perfectior in aliis vero minime, sed ad omne opus quod rectum sit, & ad rem unamquamque est instructior. Chrysostomi commentarium amplectitur hic Jesuita Tirinus: Jam ad martyrium accingor, ô Timothee, mea instructione carendum tibi deinceps : Sed VICE ILLIUS commendo tibi studium S. literarum, in iis audies loquentem & monentem DEUM. Ita S. Chrysost. Eodem modo explicat Doctor Angelicus Thomas de Aquino in h. l. Ostendit, quod S. literæ sunt VIA AD SALUTEM. Et tria ponit: nam commendat Scripturas ratione principii, ratione effectus utilis, & ratione ultimi fructus & profectus. Effectus quadruplex est S. Scripturæ, docere veritatem, arguere falsitatem, quantum ad Speculativam, eripere à malo, & inducere ad bonum, quantum ad Practicam: ultimus ejus effectus est, ut perducat homines ad perfectum. Non enim qualitercunque bonum facit, sed PERFICIT, Hebr. VI. ad perfectionem feramur. Et ideo dicit, ut perfectus sit homo Dei. PERFECTUM enim est, cui NIHIL DEEST. Tunc ergo homo est perfectus, quando est instructus, id est, paratus, ad omne opus bonum. Gabriel Biel in Canone Missæ lection. 7. ita habet: Quomodo anima hominis vivere posset vita justitiæ, & gratiæ, nisi cognosceret DEI voluntatem & ea, quæ secundum hanc justa sunt, vel injusta, quæ agenda, & quæ fugienda; quæ amanda, quæ contemnenda, quæ timenda, & quæ audenda, & quæ credenda, & quæ speranda, cætera Saluti nostræ NECESSARIA, quæ OMNIA SOLA docet S. Scriptura. Sed hæc etiam circa secundum Cap. Atque eo usque tantum progressa fuit dicta disputatio. Revertimur è digressione ad textum Grotianum.

## 3:17
V. 17. That the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.) Other codices have better ἐξηρτισμένος. The following member here is an explanation of the preceding, as above II, 21. Men of God were formerly called Prophets: now with better right the Doctors of the N. T. as we said at 1 Tim. VI. 11. Add Luke X. 24. where those Doctors are preferred to the ancient Prophets. ἄρτιος is the same as τέλειος, שלם or נכון κατηρτισμένος. Luke VI. 40. The Syrian placed a comma after ἔργον ἀγαθὸν, and a conjunction before ἐξηρτισμένος, and translated that ἄρτιος as כליל, which is consummated. But that ἐξηρτισμένος as משלם which has the same or a neighboring sense with the other. And it is the custom of the Hebrews to express with more words those things which they wish to impress deeply upon readers. Him who is ἄρτιος or ἐξηρτισμένος for every good work, the Rabbis call: ממולא בכל מדות.

By the man of God others understand the minister of the word, just as Prophets were called men of God throughout 1 Sam. IX. 6. 1 Kings 17. 18. etc. and ἄνθρωποι Θεοῦ in 2 Pet. I. Others say that the man of God is any faithful person, just as Claudius Espencaeus says, not badly that Cajetan understands by the man of God any faithful person, whoever has given himself to God, of whatever rank he may be, whether he is subject or in authority, because he can be consummated through scripture to exercise his own good work. In favor of the former opinion, which is confirmed from 1 Tim. VI. verse 11, some observe that those former things in verse 15 concern any believers, but these latter things in verses 16 and 17 concern the duties of a Doctor of the Church, because Paul exhorts Timothy both to constancy in faith and to patience and faithfulness in his office, and for the sake of both he celebrates Holy Scripture, because it can make all wise unto salvation through faith, and is sufficient for all things that are necessary for Doctors of the Church to undertake the parts of their office, so that he may be perfectly instructed for every good work of his ministry: as Chrysostom says, for me, he says, I have Holy Scripture, if you desire to learn anything, from here you will be able. Why then would Holy Scripture not be sufficient and perfect? And Theophylact: Do not, he says, let Timothy lose heart, as one who is about to be deprived of a Teacher shortly after, you have, he says, in my place the Scriptures, which will be able both to lift you up and to profit you. And further: that the man of GOD may be perfect.) Amendment, he says, is prepared from the scriptures, so that nothing is lacking to the man who has walked according to GOD. If therefore you desire to become whole yourself, and more perfect, and to be rendered sound and always equable, and you do not wish to be contracted by adversities, nor puffed up by prosperous things, for that prefers perfection and equability of mind, consult these sacred letters, when you will lack my presence. From that, however, it is easy to gather that any believer is rendered perfect through Scripture. But if he wrote to Timothy, continues Theophylact, filled with the Holy Spirit, about such reading, how much more are we also to be exhorted to it, who are in need of this spirit? And note, he commands, unless the sacred letters help, we cannot be rendered whole and perfect. Instructed for every good work.) For he is not simply a participant of good works, but instructed by these very things and made complete. Nor will he be more perfect in one single thing, but in others not at all, but for every work that is right, and for each and every thing he is more instructed. These things Theophylact, not simply participating, says Chrysostom, but equipped with accuracy. Estius explains it concerning the Bishop. But to our argument: If Holy Scripture ensures that the man of GOD may be perfect, and instructed for every part of his office; therefore whatever he ought to teach the people is contained in the sacred letters, nor is there any need for him of doctrines or unwritten traditions; he answers: that the Apostle, saying for every good work, does not wish by that universal sign to include individuals, but the kinds of individuals. But the Apostle first says simply that the man of God is perfect through Scripture, and from this assigns the end of scripture. Arta, says Suidas, are called those things which are fitted, perfect and sound. Estius calls him artion who holds all the parts of his office, for that is whole which consists of all its parts. Then he adds further pros pan agathon ergon, for every good work, which is to say, whatever is necessary for him, perfectly instructed. From artios is derived artizo, that is, I perfect, I render perfect and absolute, or I perfectly instruct, therefore he is called artios, and exartismenos, who is whole, and sufficiently instructed for every work of his office. The Syrian has the word gmir, which denotes perfect and absolute. Oecumenius explains it as filled. And before he had said that Holy Scripture makes us wise unto salvation: whence an indissoluble argument: Whatever scripture is so useful for all parts of the office of Doctors, that the man of GOD is rendered perfect from it, perfectly prepared for every good work, and can instruct and make all wise through faith unto salvation, that must fully exhibit all things which are necessary for the parts of the Ecclesiastical ministry, for leading men to eternal life, and whatever is necessary for all men for faith and for salvation.

But the Apostle testifies about scripture with a clear voice beforehand. The latter therefore must be entirely conceded. It is one thing, as the blessed Gerhard warns, to be in any way useful for teaching, reproving, correcting, and training in righteousness; but it is another thing to be so useful for teaching, reproving, correcting, and training in righteousness, that the man of GOD may be perfect, i.e., that perfection is joined with that utility. The Apostle attributes to Scripture not only the utility of the former, but also of the latter kind joined with perfection. Therefore he determines that utility not only for the kinds of individuals, but also for the individuals of the kinds. If anyone therefore raises a doubt, because the use of consolation is omitted here, which is preached in Romans 15:3, it can easily be answered that paraklesis is included under didaskalia. For he who consoles another teaches him about the Wisdom of GOD in governing the elect, and about the blessed outcome or conclusion of adversities; and what greater consolation is there than from the wisdom by which we are instructed unto salvation, and from the faith which is in Christ?

Latin:

V. 17. Ἵνα ἄρτιος ᾖ ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος, πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐξηρτυμένος.) Melius alii Codices ἐξηρτισμένος. Sequens membrum hic, ἐξήγησις est præcedentis, ut supra II, 21. ἄνθρωποι Θεοῦ olim vocabantur Prophetæ: nunc meliori jure Doctores N. T. ut diximus ad 1. Tim. VI. 11. Adde Luc. X. 24. ubi isti Doctores Prophetis veteribus præferuntur. ἄρτιος idem quod τέλειος, שלם aut נכון κατηρτισμένος. Luc. VI. 40. Syrus comma posuit post ἔργον ἀγαθὸν, & copulam ante ἐξηρτισμένος, & illud ἄρτιος vertit כליל, quod est consummatus. Illud vero ἐξηρτισμένος משלם quod eundem aut vicinum cum altero habet sensum. Et mos est Hebræorum pluribus verbis ea eloqui, quæ penitus imprimere lectoribus volunt. Eum qui est ἄρτιος aut ἐξηρτισμένος πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν, Rabbini vocant: ממולא בכל מדות.

Per hominem Dei alii ministrum verbi intelligunt, uti Prophetæ viri Dei passim 1. Sam. IX. 6. 1. Reg. 17. 18. &c. & ἄνθρωποι Θεοῦ 2. Petr. I. dicti sunt. Alii hominem Dei quemvis fidelem esse ajunt, quomodo Claudius Espensæus ait, non male Cajetanum per hominem Dei quemvis fidelem intelligere, quicunq; seipsum Deo dedit, cujuscunque sit gradus, sive subsit, sive præsit, quod is per scripturam ad suum opus bonum exercendum consummatus esse possit. Pro sententia priori, quæ è 1. Timoth. VI. vers. 11. confirmatur, observant nonnulli priora ista vers. 15. quosvis fideles, hæc vero po- steriora vers. 16. 17. officia Doctoris Ecclesiæ con- cernere, quia Paulus Timotheum tum ad constan- tiam in fide, tum ad patientiam & fidem in officio hortatur, & utriusque gratia scripturam S. cele- brat, quod ea ad salutem omnes sapientes red- dere possit per fidem, & sufficiat omnia quæ Do- ctoribus Ecclesiæ necessaria sunt, ad subeundas officii partes, ut ad omne opus bonum muneris sui perfecte instruatur: quomodo Chrysostomus, pro me, inquit, habeo Scripturam S. si quid ad- discere cupis, hinc poteris. Quidni ergo suffi- ciens esset & perfecta Scriptura sacra? Et Theo- phylactus: Ne itaque, inquit, animo concidat Ti- motheus, utpote qui Præceptore paulo post se conso- lante privandus, habes, inquit, in mei vicem Scriptu- ras, quæ & levare te poterunt & prodesse. Et porro: ut perfectus sit homo DEI.) Emendatio, inquit, ex scripturis paratur, ut nihil homini desit, qui se- cundum DEUM incesserit. Si itaque ipse integer fieri, & perfectior cupis, sanusque & semper æqua- bilis reddi, nec contrahi adversis exoptas, nec pro- speris rebus efferri, id enim præfert perfectionem & mentis æquabilitatem, has sacras literas consule, cum mea carebis præsentia. Ex eo tamen in promtu est colligere, quemvis fidelem perfectum reddi per Scripturam. Atqui si Timotheo, pergit Theoph. Spi- ritu S. oppleto, de ejusmodi lectione scripsit, quanto magis sumus & nos ad eam hortandi, qui spiritu hoc indigemus? Et adverte, jubet, ni sacræ literæ opi- tulentur, integros & perfectos nos reddi non posse. Ad omne opus bonum instructus.) Non enim simpliciter bonorum est operum particeps, sed instru- ctus his ipsis & absolutus. Neque una aliqua in re erit ille perfectior, in aliis vero minime, sed ad omne opus quod rectum sit, & ad rem unamquamque est ille instructior. Hæc Theophylactus ἐκ ἁπλῶς με- τέχων, inquit Chrysostomus, ἀλλὰ μετ᾽ ἀκριβείας ἐξηρτισμένον. De Episcopo explicat Estius. Ad no- strum vero argumentum: Si scriptura S. præstat ut perfectus sit homo DEI, & ad omnem officii sui partem instructus; ergo quicquid populum docere debet, sacris literis est comprehensum, nec quic- quam opus ei est doctrinis, aut traditionibus non- scriptis; respondet: Apostolum dicentem ad omne opus bonum, eo signo universali non velle com- prehendere singula, sed genera singulorum. Verum Apostolus primum simpliciter perfectum esse homi- nem Dei per Scripturam ait, & hinc finem scriptu- ræ assignat. Ἄρτια, inquit Suidas, λέγεται τὰ ἠρμο- σμένα, τέλεια καὶ ὑγιῆ. Estius ἄρτιον appellat eum, qui tenet omnes officii sui partes, integrum enim est quod omnibus partibus constat. Deinde addit adhuc πρὸς πᾶν ἀγαθὸν ἔργον, ad omne opus bo- num, quodcunque scil. ipsi necessarium est, per- fecte instructum. Ab ἄρτιος derivatur ἀρτίζω h. e. perficio, perfectum & absolutum reddo, aut perfecte instruo, dicitur ergo ἄρτιος, & ἐξηρτι- σμένος, qui totus, & ad omne opus officii sui suf- ficienter instructus est. Syrus habet vocem גמיר, quæ perfectum & absolutum notat. Oecumenius exponit πεπληρωμένον. Et antea Scripturam S. sapientes nos reddere ad salutem dixerat: unde ar- gumentum ἀδιάλυτον: Quæcunque scriptura ita utilis est ad omnes partes officii Doctorum, ut perfectus inde reddatur homo DEI ad omne opus bonum perfecte comparatus, omnesque instruere ac sapientes reddere possit per fidem ad salutem, illam oportet plene exhibere omnia, quæ ad par- tes muneris Ecclesiastici, ad perducendum homi- nes ad vitam æternam, & quæcunque omnibus hominibus ad fidem, & ad salutem necessaria sunt.

Prius autem de scriptura testatur λευκάδι φωνῇ Apostolus. Posterius ergo omnino conceden- dum. Aliud est, monente B. Gerhardo, esse qua- vis modo utile ad docendum, redarguendum, cor- rigendum, & erudiendum in justitia; aliud vero est, ita esse utile ad docendum, redarguendum, corrigen- dum & erudiendum in justitia, ut homo DEI sit perfectus, i. e. ut cum utilitate illa perfectio sit con- juncta. Apostolus non solum prioris, sed etiam po- sterioris generis utilitatem cum perfectione conjun- ctam Scripturae tribuit. Ergo non solum ad genera singulorum, sed etiam ad singula generum utilita- tem illam determinat. Si quis ideo dubium moveat, quod consolationis usus hic praetermissus sit, qui Rom. XV. 3. praedicatur, responderi facile potest, παράκλησιν sub διδασκαλίᾳ comprehendi. Qui enim alium consolatur, docet eum de Sapientia DEI in gubernandis electis, & de beata adversita- tum ἐκβάσει, vel clausula; & quae major παράκλη- σις, quam è sapientia, quâ ad salutem instruimur, & è fide, quae est in Christum?

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle adjures Timothy concerning the faithful execution of the parts of his office. Because very many will readily receive false Doctors, and the time of his own departure is imminent, he warns him therefore to come to him, having been left by almost everyone, and to beware of Alexander: reporting that in his first defense no one stood by him, but the Lord by assisting him provided strength, from whom he now also expects deliverance; finally, having added greetings, he seals the Epistle with a vow.

There are two parts: I. The adjuration concerning performing the office up to verse 8. II. The admonition concerning visiting him, and the cause of it up to verse 21, with the conclusion.

PART I. An adjuration concerning the performance of duty.

Ver. 1.

Διαμαρτύρομαι ὖν ἐγὼ ἐνώπιον τῦ Θεῦ καὶ τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ) A very serious adjuration, and having the force of a great oath. Similar to 1 Tim. V. ver. 21. and above, II. 14.

The Vulgate wrongly omits the illative particle: for this adjuration is deduced from the preceding: Theodoret: After, he says, he thus showed the utility which proceeds from scripture inspired by GOD, he commands him to deliver it to all, and thus terrifies with an adjuration. Now this is the third adjuration of Timothy: the two former are read in the preceding Epistle ch. V. ver. 21. and ch. VI. v. 13. How greatly, therefore, it is incumbent upon the teachers of the word to perform their duty faithfully is evident from that triple adjuration made to Timothy himself, of whose faith there was no doubt; for in his person all teachers of the word are, without ambiguity, reminded and terrified by this adjuration. And from this appears the remarkable solicitude of Paul for the Church, and the care of the Holy Spirit himself adjuring through Paul.

Τῦ μέλλοντος κρίνειν ζῶντας καὶ νεκρὲς. He could not have expressed the majesty of Christ more than by this title. For how much should he be esteemed, who will judge all. See John V. 25. Acts X. 42. XVII. 31. 1 Cor. XV. 51. 1 Thess. IV. 19. The living and the dead, that is, both those who shall then be living, and those previously dead, 1 Cor. XV. 52. 1 Thess. IV. ver. 15. 17.

The majesty of Christ could indeed have been expressed more, and it was expressed elsewhere by the Apostle in Rom. IX. 15, Heb. I. 2, seq., and elsewhere: but the description of the universal judge, before whom an account must be rendered by all, served for the adjuration, 2 Cor. V. 20. He adjures by the greatest witnesses, the triune GOD and JESUS Christ, through whom God has appointed to judge the whole world, Acts XVII. 31, whence all judgment has been given to him according to his human nature, John V. 26, 27, Acts X. 42. Cajetan gathers from this passage that not only the elect, of whom in 1 Thess. IV, but also the reprobate who shall be found at the coming of Christ, without any death intervening, are to be judged alive, which does not please Estius. He prefers to posit that those whom he finds living will perish by a conflagratory fire, so that they may soon rise again together with the other dead. Perhaps it would be better here to τὸ ἐπέχειν (withhold judgment).

At his appearing, and his kingdom) The Syrian does not explain this badly by an ἐν διὰ δυοῖν (one through two), as if it were, at the appearing of his kingdom. In a similar way, the appearing of his glory. Christ indeed already reigns, but that does not appear in all things, as it will appear then. The same appearing is called κατ' ἐξοχὴν (by way of eminence), as can be seen in 1 Tim. VI. 14, above I, 10, IV, 1, 8. κατὰ here signifies time: as in Rom. V. 6 and IX. 19. And Paul uses κατὰ for many prepositions.

The Latins generally refer these words, at his appearing, to the more remote I adjure. But the preposition διὰ, which is used in adjurations, should rather have been employed in that way. For this κατὰ, joined to the accusative, frequently serves for time, never for adjuration or entreaty; the Syrian also renders it: in the appearing of his kingdom.

Latin:

CAPUT IV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Obtestatur Apostolus Timotheum de partibus officio fideliter exequendis. Quod plurimi falsos Doctores promte suscepturi sint, & tempus obitus sui immineat, monetque ideo, ut ad se veniat derelictum fere ab omni- bus, utque Alexandrum caveat: referens, quod in prima defensione nemo sibi adfue- rit, Dominus vero assistendo robur suffe- cerit, à quo jam etiam liberationem expe- ctet; additis denique salutationibus, voto obsignat Epistolam.

Partes duae sunt I. Obtestatio de officio prae- stando ad vers. 8. II. Admonitio de se visitan- do, ejusque causae ad v. 21. cum conclusione.

PARS I. Obtestatio de officio praestando.

Vers. 1.

Διαμαρτύρομαι ὖν ἐγὼ ἐνώπιον τῦ Θεῦ καὶ τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ) Seria admodum obtestatio, & maximi juramenti vim habens. Similis 1. Tim. V. vers. 21. & su- pra, II. 14.

Vulgata particulam illativam omittit perperam: Deducitur enim haec obtestatio è superioribus: Theodoretus: Postquam, inquit, sic ostendit utili- tatem, quae ex scriptura à DEO inspirata proficisci- tur, jubet eam omnibus tradere, & testatione sic ter- ret. Tertia autem haec est Timothei obtestatio: priores duae leguntur in praecedente Epistola c. V. vers. 21. & cap. VI. v. 13. Quantopere ergo Do- ctoribus verbi hoc incumbat, ut fideliter officium suum faciant, ex trina illa obtestatione, Timo- theo ipsi, de cujus fide non erat dubium, facta patet, in ipsius enim persona omnes verbi Do- ctores hac obtestatione commonefieri, atque terreri, ambiguo vacat. Et apparet hinc insignis Pauli pro Ecclesia solicitudo, & ipsius Spiritus S. per Paulum obtestantis cura.

Τῦ μέλλοντος κρίνειν ζῶντας καὶ νεκρὲς. Non potuerat magis exprimere majestatem Christi quam hoc titulo. Quanti enim fieri debet, qui omnes judica- bit. Vid. Joh. V. 25. Act. X. 42. XVII. 31. 1. Cor. XV. 51. 1. Thess. IV. 19. Vivos & mortuos, id est, tum eos qui tum vivent, tum praemortuos, 1. Cor. XV. 52. 1. Thess. IV. vers. 15. 17.

Majestas Christi magis quidem exprimi pote- rat, & expressa est alias ab Apostolo Rom. IX. 15. Ebr. I. 2. seq. & alibi: sed ad obtestationem fa- ciebat descriptio judicis universalis, coram quo reddenda omnibus erit ratio, 2. Cor. V. 20. Obte- statur per testes maximos, DEUM triunnum & JESUM Christum, per quem Deus constituit judicare orbem universum A&. XVII. 31. unde ei secundum humanam naturam datum est omne ju- dicium Job. V. 26. 27. A&. X. 42. Cajetanus ex h. l. colligit, quod non solum electi, de quibus 1. Theff. IV. sed etiam reprobi, qui in adventu Christi re- perientur, nulla morte intercedente, vivi judi- candi sint, quod Estio non placet. Mavult, quos viventes deprehendet, igne conflagratorio inte- rituros statuere, ut mox una cum aliis mortuis re- surgant. Præstiterit fortassis hîc τὸ ἐπέχειν.

Κατὰ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν ἀυτῶ, καὶ τὴν βασιλείαν ἀυτῶ) Syrus non male hoc explicat per ἐν διὰ δυοῖν quasi esset, κατὰ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν έ βασιλείας ἀυτῶ. Pari modo ἐπιφάνεια έ δόξης. Regnat quidem jam Christus, sed id non in omnibus ap- paret, sicut tunc apparebit. Eadem ἐπιφάνεια dicitur κατ' ἐξοχὴν, ut videre est 1. Tim. VI. 14. supra I, 10. IV. 1. 8. κα- τὰ hîc tempus significat: ut Rom. V. 6. & IX. 19. Et Pau- lus pro multis propositionibus κατὰ usurpat.

Latini fere hæc κατὰ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν ad remo- tius διαμαρτύρομαι referunt. Sed ita potius ad- hibenda fuisset propositio διὰ, quæ in obtesta- tionibus usurpatur. Hæc enim κατὰ accusativo juncta frequenter tempori subservit, nunquam obtestationi, aut obsecrationi; Syrus reddit et- iam: in apparitione regni sui.

## 4:2
Verse 2.

Preach the word) That is, the gospel, as in Matt. IV. verse 23, XXIV. 14, Mark I. 14, XIII. 10, XVI. 15, which elsewhere is called to preach Christ. Paul inculcates this, however, because he saw that Timothy might become more timid by the example of the evils which Paul himself and others were bearing.

Be instant) Namely, to them: just as Demosthenes also said to urge him on. The Syrian has well expressed the force of this verb.

In season, out of season) That is, in leisure or in business: for opportunity is put for leisure. Sirach XXXVIII. 26, 1 Macc. XI. 42. Seneca, letter XXIX: Is the hand to be scattered? It cannot be that it does not sometimes succeed for one who attempts many things.

Some take in season, out of season adverbially, that is, assiduously and incessantly. Theophylact brings forward this sense, i.e., preach the Gospel at any time. Others think that regard is had to those to whom it is preached, not to those who preach. Thus Augustine in Ps. CXXVIII: Let the word of God sound in season to those who are willing: out of season to those who are unwilling. To the Greeks, however, the time of peace is called opportune, that of persecution importune, namely, to the preachers themselves: the opinion of Augustine pleases Estius and B. Gerhard and others more, which he explains more fully in Gal. VI. Be instant in season, which if you do not succeed in this way, be instant out of season, and although you may seem importunate to him who does not willingly hear what is said to him, you nevertheless know that this is opportune for him, and keep the love and care for his health in a gentle, modest, and brotherly mind. Nor, however, is spiritual prudence to be neglected, which does not reject the diversity of hearers and times, but perpetually attends to what is convenient and salutary for the hearers. Luke XII. 42. For then a word in season is best, Prov. XV. 23, not that which is opportune to the carnal sense of the hearers, but to the spiritual judgment of the Pastors. Sometimes also something is obtained by an opportune importunity; as it is commonly said that one must solicit importunately among the Great, if we wish anything to be granted. See Luke XVIII. verse 5.

Reprove) Show the wicked what shameful things they are doing; above III. 19.

Rebuke) Correct. Above III. 16. Chastise the less wicked with words. Thus also this word is taken in Gen. XXXVII. 10, and elsewhere in the Glossary: I rebuke, I chastise.

Παρακάλεσον) Exhort those who have begun well. This is missing in the Syriac.

Ἐν πάσῃ μακροθυμίᾳ καὶ διδαχῇ) See above III. 10. The sense is: ἐν διδαχῇ μακροθύμῳ, that is, by teaching them gently: ἐν διὰ δυοῖν as just now.

It is wrongly missing. For those four parts of the Ecclesiastical office, which the Apostle had designated in chapter III. 6, are repeated here and commanded to Timothy: (1) διδασκαλία through the first imperative κήρυξον. (2) ἔλεγχος through the second, ἔλεγξον. (3) ἐπανόρθωσις through the third, ἐπιτίμησον. (4) παιδεία through the fourth, παρακάλεσον. Therefore, since he wished to repeat in the same order by commanding what he had previously designated by informing, the Vulgate does not well invert the order: preach, argue, observe, rebuke. But the addition ἐν πάσῃ μακροθυμίᾳ should pertain both to ἐπανόρθωσιν or ἐπιτίμησιν or rebuke, and to παιδείαν. See 2 Tim. II. v. 25, it is established ἐν πραότητι παιδεύοντα: since indeed instructions and rebukes ought to be joined with gentleness and meekness of spirit, so that they may be more easily admitted: but διδαχὴ should be referred to κήρυγμα and ἔλεγξιν, in all patience and doctrine. For it is, as Theophylact says, not to be rashly despaired of concerning those who have committed wicked things, but one must persist either with prayers, so that they cease to do evil, or with doctrine, so that they may at last repent and be admonished. And in all patience, that is, in any kind of patience, and which is so performed that it shines forth in all ways, as much by works as by words and gesture. Prosp. l. II. de vit. integrit. cap. 5. He who is lightly chastised shows reverence to the one chastising, but he who is offended by excessive harshness receives neither the rebuke nor salvation.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Κήρυξον τὸν λόγον) Id est, τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον ut Matth. IV. vers. 23. XXIV. 14. Marci I. 14. XIII. 10. XVI. 15. quod alibi dicitur κηρύσσειν τὸν χριστὸν. Hoc autem ideo inculcat Paulus, quod videret malorum, quæ ipse Paulus & alii fere- bant exemplo Timotheum posse timidiorem fieri.

Ἔπίςηθι) Nempe ἀυτοῖς : quomodo & Demosthenes di- xit ἐφιςάναι δ' ἀυτῷ, urgebat eum. Syrus vim hujus verbi bene expressit.

Εὐκαίρως, ἀκαίρως) Id est, in otio, vel negotio: Nam ἐυκαιρία pro otio ponitur. Sirach. XXXIIX. 26. 1. Macc. XI. 42. Seneca epistola XXIX. Spargenda est manus? non po- test fieri ut non aliquando succedat, multa tentanti.

Nonnulli ἐυκαίρως, ἀκαίρως adverbialiter acci- piunt, id est, assidue & incessanter. Quem sensum adfert Theophylactus, h. e. quovis tempore Evange- lium prædica. Alii respectum haberi ad eos qui- bus prædicatur, non ad eos qui prædicant, censent. Ita Augustinus in Ps. CXXIIX. Sonet verbum Dei volentibus opportune: nolentibus importune. Græ- cis tamen tempus pacis opportunum, persecutionis importunum, sc. ipsius prædicantibus dicitur: Estio & B. Gerhardo, aliisque magis placet Augustini sententia, quam plenius explicat Gal. VI. Insta opportune, quod si hoc modo non proficis, importune, & licet illi videaris importunus, qui non libenter au- dit, qua in eum dicuntur, tu tamen scias, hoc illi esse opportunum, & dilectionem, curamque sanitatis ejus animo teneas mansueto, modesto, & fraterno. Ne- que tamen spiritualis prudentia negligenda, quæ diversitatem auditorum, & temporum non re- spuit, sed perpetuo, quod commodum & salutare auditoribus sit, attendit. Luc. XII. 42. Tum enim sermo opportunus est optimus, Prov. XV. 23. non qui opportunus carnali auditorum sensui, sed spi- rituali Pastorum judicio. Nonnunquam etiam importunitate opportuna aliquid obtinetur; ut vul- go dicitur importune apud Magnates solicitandum esse, si quid impetratum volumus. Vid. Luc. XIIX. vers. 5.

Ἔλεγξον) ostende flagitiosis quam agant turpia; Su- pra III. 19.

Ἐπιτίμησον) ἐπανόρθυ Supra III. 16. Minus malos verbis castiga. Sic & verbum hoc sumitur Gen. XXXVII. 10. & alibi in Glossario: Ἐπιτιμῶ castigo.

Παρακάλεσον) Hortare eos qui bene cœperunt. Deest hoc apud Syrum.

Ἐν πάσῃ μακροθυμίᾳ καὶ διδαχῇ) Vide supra III. 10. Sensus est: ἐν διδαχῇ μακροθύμῳ, id est, docendo eos le- niter: ἐν διὰ δυοῖν ut jam modo.

Male deest. Nam repetuntur hîc quatuor illæ partes officii Ecclesiastici, quas cap. III. 6. designa- rat Apostolus, ac imperantur Timotheo, (1) διδα- σκαλία per imperativum primum κήρυξον. (2) ἔλεγ- χος per alteram ἔλεγξον. (3) ἐπανόρθωσις per terti- um ἐπιτίμησον. (4) παιδεία per quartum παρακά- λεσον. Ideo cum eodem ordine repetere voluerit imperando, quæ antea designavit informando, non bene ordinem invertit Vulgatus, prædica, argue, observa, increpa. Sed addita ἐν πάσῃ μακροθυμίᾳ, tum ad ἐπανόρθωσιν vel ἐπιτίμησιν vel increpatio- nem, tum ad παιδείαν pertineat. Vide 2. Tim. II. v. 25. constat ἐν πραότητι παιδεύοντα: Siquidem institutiones & increpationes cum animi lenitate ac mansuetudine conjuncta esse debeant, ut faci- lius admittantur: διδαχὴ autem ad κήρυγμα & ἔλεγξιν referenda sit, in omni patientia & doctri- na. Est namque, dicente Theophylacto, baud te- mere de his & mox desperandum, qui prava commi- serint, sed vel precibus est insistendum, ut desinant ma- lefacere, vel doctrina, ut tandem resipiscant, admo- nendi. Et in omni patientia, hoc est, in quovis pa- tientiæ genere, & qua ita præstetur, ut omnibus modis eluceat, tam operibus, quam verbis & gestu. Prosp. l. II. de vit. integrit. cap. 5. Leviter castigatus exhibet reverentiam castiganti, asperitate autem nimia offensus, neque increpationem recipit, neque salutem.

## 4:3
V. 3. Ἔσται γὰρ καιρός) I did not say this in vain: Times will come which will need both reproof and chastisement.

Ὅτε τῆς ὑγιαινούσης διδασκαλίας ὀυκ ἀνέξονται) Namely, many will not endure sound doctrine, that is, that which requires life to be according to the standard of the Gospel. A description of similar men, Is. XXX. 10.

Ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας τὰς ἰδίας) They will seek advocates according to their own evil desires: one for luxury, another for lust, another for drunkenness. See Rom. I. 24. Jude 16.

Ἑαυτοῖς ἐπισωρεύσουσι διδασκάλους) They will find many such teachers: therefore he says ἐπισωρεύσουσι, they will heap up. In the Glossary ἐπισωρεύω, I gather together, I heap up, I accumulate. They will run together from everywhere μαντευόμενοι τὰ πρὸς χάριν, as it is in the Greek of Ezekiel XII. 24.

Κνηθόμενοι τὴν ἀκοήν) As if they were lepers: for itching is their characteristic. He elegantly says that those have itching ears who seek speeches that tickle their vices. Flatterers of the people, tickling the levity of the multitude as if with pleasure, says Cicero.

The cause is now explained why he reminds him of the parts of the office with such a grave adjuration, since not only are many to depart from sound doctrine, namely false teachers, but also those from the flock or the people who are not going to hear the same, and who, not content with one, are going to heap up for themselves many false teachers, just as their own evil desires will impel them. It is reckless, says Theophylact in his paraphrase: and when they heap up an ill-advised crowd of teachers, he says, here he reveals that they are gathered by the common people, which relies on no reasons, but is carried along inconsiderately as the mind has inclined. And they extol with praises and choose those teachers who favor their own desires, and who defer and perform everything for their thanks and pleasure. Since they themselves are given to gluttony and lust, they will also seek such teachers who will not so much rebuke those carnal desires, but are dumb regarding vices, Is. LVI. verse 10, or sew pillows, Ez. 13, 18. seq., concerning whom Gregory the Great, l. 18. Moral. c. 4. Whoever flatters those acting wickedly, places a pillow under the head or elbow of the one lying down; so that he who ought to have been corrected for his fault, might rest softened by the praises of such a one in that fault. Some prefer to take the words κνηθόμενοι ἀκοὴν as referring to ears itching to hear novelties, with Eslio, rather than to those who in their depraved desires seek out flatterers, so that another reason is now brought forward why they turn their ears away from sound doctrine and heap up false teachers for themselves: by which vice the Athenians were marked, Acts XVII. Theophylact explains: 'Merely delighting the ears.' For men of this kind, once beguiled, desire to hear what will always please them and cause them less sorrow. A metaphor taken from those with the itch, as Crocius notes, who scratch the itching part of the body even to the point of blood, not at all concerned about the pain that will follow. Thus, whatever impulse carries those who are weary of the truth, they will turn themselves to gather those who speak pleasant things, by which they pleasantly tickle their ears.

Latin:

V. 3. Ἔσται γὰρ καιρός) Non frustra hoc dixi: Venient tempora quæ & exprobatione & castigatione egeant.

Ὅτε τῆς ὑγιαινούσης διδασκαλίας ὀυκ ἀνέξονται) Nempe πολλοὶ, non ferent salubrem doctrinam, id est, eam quæ vitam exigit ad Evangelii amussim. Similium hominum descriptio, Es. XXX. 10.

Ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας τὰς ἰδίας) Malis cupiditatibus suis quærent advocatos: hic luxui, ille libidini: alius e- brietati. Vide Rom. I. 24. Jud. 16.

Ἑαυτοῖς ἐπισωρεύσουσι διδασκάλους) Multos reperient ta- les Doctores: ideo dicit ἐπισωρεύσουσι, cumulabunt. In Glossario ἐπισωρεύω, coaggero, congero, cumulo. Concur- rent undique μαντευόμενοι τὰ πρὸς χάριν, ut est in Græco Ezechielis XII. 24.

Κνηθόμενοι τὴν ἀκοήν) Tanquam leprosi: nam eorum est κνησμός. Eleganter autem prurire eos dicit auribus qui sermones quærunt vitia sua titillantes. Assentatores popu- li, multitudinis levitatem voluptate quasi titillantes, ait Cicero.

Exponitur jam causa, cur tam gravi obtestatio- ne de partibus officii commonefaciat, siquidem non tantum multi à sana doctrina discessuri, falsi nempe Doctores, sed etiam qui è grege vel populo eandem non audituri, & falsos Doctores complu- res, uno non contenti, sibi coacervaturi sint, prout ipsos pravæ cupiditates impellent. Temerarium, in- quit in paraphrasi sua Theophylactus: & inconsul- tam præceptorum turbam cum coacervabunt inquit, Hic patefacit, quod à vulgo bi congerantur, qui nullis nititur rationibus, sed ut animus tulerit, inconside- rate defertur. Et eos efferunt laudibus & eligunt præceptores, qui suis favent cupiditatibus, ipsorum- que ad gratiam cuncta & voluptatem defferunt & exequuntur. Cum ipsi sint gulæ & libidini dediti, tales quoque quærent Doctores, qui cupiditates illas carnales non adeo reprehensuri sunt, sed mu- ti ad vitia, Es. LVI. vers. 10. aut pulvillos consuunt Ez. 13, 18. seq. de qualibus Gregorius M. l. 18. Moral. c. 4. Quisquis male agentibus adulatur, pulvillum sub capite vel cubito jacentis ponit; ut qui corripi ex culpa debuerat, in ea talis laudibus mollicet quiescat. Verba κνηθόμενοι ἀκοὴν alii de auribus ad novitates audiendas prurientibus accipere, cum Eslio, ma- lunt, quam de iis, qui in suis pravis concupiscen- tiis assentatores desiderant, ut altera jam ratio adferatur, cur à doctrina sana aures avertant, & falsos Doctores sibi coacervent: quo vitio notati sunt Athenienses Act. XVII. Theophylactus expli- cat: Aures duntaxat oblectantes. Homines enim istiusmodi deliniti, qui juvent semper, & minus contristent, audire percupiunt. Metaphora à sca- biosis desumpta, notante Crocio, qui partem cor- poris prurientem usque ad sanguinem scabunt, de do- lore consecuturo minime soliciti. Sic quo illos perta- sos veritatis feret impetus, se vertent, ut colligant eos, qui loquuntur placentia, quibus aures jucunde ti- tillent.

## 4:4
Verse 4.

And from the truth they will turn away their hearing) they will turn away their hearing. יסירו אזן as it is in Prov. XXVIII. 19. from the truth, from the Gospel, which assents to no one.

And they will turn aside to myths) Those fables were about the expiation of sins from Chaldean and Orphic discipline. In these, sea water held the first place: then also spring water: squill, sulfur, bitumen, the mention of which is in the poem of Diphilus, which is in our Excerpts, and of squill also in Pliny, Dio, Chrysostom, Artemidorus, Lucian; of sulfur and pitch in Juvenal and Claudian in the sixth consulship of Honorius, where there is also mention of bitumen and water. Added to these were the Ἐφέσια γράμματα. Concerning which we spoke at Acts XIX. verse 19. Such myths are מהתלות Is. XXX. v. 10.

From where will Grotius teach that such fables are to be understood? This restriction is purely arbitrary. In general, those things are called fables which are destitute of truth, and here are implied not so much the fables of philosophers as those of heretics, and those which were creeping into the Church and bore the appearance of truth. B. Gerhard says: They can, he says, be understood in general as any old wives' tales, whether they proceeded from Jews, or from Gentiles, or from heretics. From the truth:) that is, from the word of God, which is the truth, or from the Doctrine proposed by the ministry of the Prophets and Apostles. This does not provide what they desire and seek exclusively. It does not favor sins, it does not foster them; it does not flatter the flesh, it does not satisfy its depraved desires. It does not soothe soft minds: it does not tickle the ears. Therefore they turn their ears away from it. They will also turn away their mind: yet the Apostle preferred to name the ears, so as to exaggerate the hatred of the truth. They will not stop at that, so as not to obey the truth, not to love it; they will pursue it with such hatred that they will not even endure to hear it. They do not want to seem to be all; they will deny that it is the truth: yet Paul says they turn their ears away from the truth, since it does not depend at all on the ears and judgment of men. To fables) that is, to human inventions, which, as they have not proceeded from GOD, so they have nothing of truth, nothing of utility, they only tickle the ears, they pleasantly affect minds corrupted by depraved desires. He exhorted against these, 1 Tim. 4, he commands to reject them, 1 Tim. IV. verse 7. To Titus he names Jewish fables: but he adds: the commandments of men who turn away from the truth, chap. I. v. 14. Here he speaks more generally, so that we do not restrict it to the fables of one sect, as Crocius does here.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Καὶ ἀπὸ μὲν τῆς ἀληθείας τὴν ἀκοὴν ἀποστρέψουσι) ἀποστρέ- ψουσι τὴν ἀκοήν. יסירו אזן ut est Prov. XXVIII. 19. ἀπὸ τῆς ἀληθείας ab Evangelio, quod nemini assentatur.

Ἐπὶ δὲ τοὺς μύθους ἐκτραπήσονται) Fabulæ illæ erant de expiationibus peccatorum ex Chaldaica & Orphica disci- plina. In his primum locum habebat aqua marina: deinde & fontana: scilla, sulphur, bitumen, quorum mentio in carmine Diphili, quod est in nostris Excerptis, scillæ etiam apud Plinium, Dionem, Chrysostomum, Artemidorum, Lucianum, sulphuris & facis apud Juvenalem & Claudia- num in sexto consulatu Honorii, ubi & bituminis & aquæ mentio: Accedebant ad hæc Ἐφέσια γράμματα. De qui- bus diximus ad Actor. XIX. vers. 19. Tales μῦθοι מהתלות Es. XXX. v. 10.

Tales fabulas intelligi, undenam docebit Gro- tius? Mere arbitraria est hæc restrictio. In genere fabula dicuntur, quæ veritate destituuntur, nec tam philosophorum, quam hæreticorum, & eo- rum, quæ in Ecclesiam irrepebant, & μόρφωσιν ve- ritatis præ se ferebant, fabulæ hìc innuuntur. B. Gerhardus. Possunt, inquit, in genere intelligi quæ- vis aniles fabulæ sive à Judæis, sive à gentibus, sive ab hæreticis profectæ. A veritate:) id est à verbo Dei, quod est veritas, seu à Doctrina Propheta- rum & Apostolorum ministerio proposita. Hæc non præstat, quæ illi optant, quæruntque unice. Non fa- vet peccatis, non fovet; non blanditur carni, non sa- tisfacit pravis ejus desideriis. Non demulcet animos molles: Non titillat aures. Ideo aures ab ea aver- tent. Etiam avertent animum: Maluit tamen Apostolus aures nominare, ut odium veritatis exag- geret. Non in eo subsistent, ut non obtemperent veritati, non ament; tanto prosequentur odio, ut ne quidem audire sustineant. Non omnes videri vo- lent; negabunt esse veritatem: Paulus tamen dicit à veritate aures avertere, quippe quæ ab hominum auribus & judicio minime pendet. Ad fabulas) id est, ad humana commenta, quæ ut à DEO non sunt profecta, ita nihil habent veritatis, nihil utilitatis, tantum titillant aures, suaviter afficiunt animos corruptos pravis desideriis. Ab his dehortatus est, 1. Tim. 4. jubet rejicere, 1. Tim. IV. vers. 7. Ad Titum nominat Judaicas fabulas: sed addit: man- data hominum aversantium veritatem cap. I. v. 14. Hìc generalius loquitur, ne ad unius sectæ fabulas restringamus, ut hic Crocius.

## 4:5
Verse 5.

But you, be sober in all things) See 1 Thess. V. 6.

Some draw the word 'in all things' to what follows with the Vulgate, 'labor in all things,' but it is more correctly referred to what precedes: Be vigilant in all parts of your duty.

Endure hardship) Let no evils deter you, as above II. 3. There is added here in the Manuscript, 'as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.'

It is not 'labor,' as the Vulgate renders it, but 'suffer evils,' or 'endure afflictions': or if you join labors, 'endure in afflictions and labors.' But it is believed more correctly that, as the former warning was about vigilance, so this is about the endurance of evils, and the following is about diligent exertion in the work of the Gospel.

Do the work of an evangelist) That is, of a helper of the Apostles, which is indeed a great dignity. Acts XXI. 8. Eph. IV. 11. 'Do the work' means do what is the duty. See 1 Tim. III. 1.

Τὴν διακονίαν σου πληροφορησον) Fulfill, as below 17, the same as πληρῶσαι. Col. I. 25. מלא perform well all parts of the ministry, especially in pointing out the dangers from sins.

Some understand the preaching of the Gospel in a general sense: but that special acceptance of the Evangelist pleases me, agreeing with Timothy, because the genus is added afterwards by the word τῆς διακονίας, which he wishes to be dispatched with full confidence of mind, μετὰ πληροφορίας καὶ παῤῥησίας, as he will show by the work itself, that he is a true and faithful minister, performing all parts of his office with great confidence. πληροφορησον, make full assurance (of your ministry), is not from φορᾶν, but φέρειν. It brings in faith and certainty Rom. XIV. 5. This therefore is to bring or make full assurance, as Luke I. 1. πεπληροφορημένα πράγματα, of which full assurance is faith. That the Vulgate adds 'be sober', Estius himself rejects: saying, The Greek does not have this part, just as the Syrian interpreter and the Ambrosian do not acknowledge it. But it is not in all Latin Manuscripts either. Finally Pelagius, Primasius and Haymo, since they do not explain it, are argued not to have read it: it is more than likely that it was added by occasion, since for it: 'But you watch', some Latin version would have: 'But you be sober', as is also read in the Ambrosian text, according to the older editions.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Σὺ δὲ νῆφε ἐν πᾶσι) Vide 1. Thess. V. 6.

Nonnulli vocem ἐν πᾶσι ad sequentia trahunt cum Vulgata, in omnibus labora, sed rectius re- fertur ad præcedentia: Esto vigilans in omnibus officii partibus.

Κακοπάθησον) Nullis malis absterretor, ut supra II. 3. Additur hìc in Manuscripto, ὡς καλὸς στρατιώτης Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ.

Non est labora, ut Vulg. reddit, sed mala patere, vel afflictiones tolera: aut si labores jungas, in af- flictionibus & laboribus obdura. Sed rectius ut priori monito, vigilantia; ita hoc malorum tole- rantia, & sequenti strenua in opere Evangelico di- ligentia injuncta creditur.

Ἔργον ποίησον Ἐυαγγελισοῦ) Id est adjutoris Apostolorum, quæ magna sane dignitas. Act. XXI. 8. Eph. IV. 11. ἔργον ποίησον fac quod officium est. Vide 1. Tim. III. 1.

Τὴν διακονίαν σου πληροφορησον) Imple, ut infra 17. idem quod πληρῶσαι. Col. I. 25. מלא omnes partes ministerii bene exequere, præsertim in ostendendis periculis à pec- catis.

Prædicationem Evangelii in genere intelligunt nonnulli: sed placet illa Evangelistæ specialis ac- ceptio, Timotheo congruens, quia additur dein- de genus voce τῆς διακονίας, quam plenâ animi fidu- ciâ, μετὰ πληροφορίας καὶ παῤῥησίας vult expediri, ut opere ipso ostendet, se esse verum ac fidelem ministrum, magna fiducia, partes quascunque mu- neris sui obeundo. πληροφορησον, plenam fidem (ministerii tui) facito, est non à φορᾶν, sed φέρειν. Infert fidem ac certitudinem Rom. XIV. 5. Hic er- go est plenam fidem afferre, vel facere, ut Luc. I. 1. πεπληροφορημένα πράγματα, quorum plena fi- des est fides. Quod Vulgata addit sobrius esto, re- probat Estius ipse: Hanc partem, inquiens, Græca non habent, ut nec agnoscunt Syrus interpres & Am- brosianus. At neque in omnibus est Manuscriptis La- tinis. Denique Pelagius, Primasius & Haymo, cum non exponant, arguuntur non legisse: plusquam ve- risimile est ex occasione additam esse, cum pro eo: Tu vero vigila, quædam Latina versio haberet: Tu ve- ro sobrius esto, ut & legitur in Ambrosiano textu, se- cundum editiones antiquiores.

## 4:6
Vers. 6.

Ἐγὼ γὰρ ἤδη σπένδομαι) You ought to apply yourself to your duty the more, because hereafter you will not have help from me, for whom death is imminent. Σπένδεσθαι is said of wine which is sprinkled upon a victim. A vine in a Greek Epigram is introduced speaking thus: Κἄν με φάγῃς ἐπὶ ῥίζαν ὅμως ἔτι καρποφορήσω Ὅσσον ἐπισπεῖσαί σοι τράγε θυομένῳ. There is also at Philippians II. 17 a comparison drawn from libations, but in another way, if I am not mistaken. There σπονδὴ, or libation, is considered as an accession to the victim. Here as a preparation for the slaughter. Now I am being sprinkled with wine, that is, I am being prepared for death, as victims are accustomed to be. Legal victims are prefigurations of the martyrs. Therefore the souls of the martyrs are under the altar Apoc. VI. 7. because the blood of the victims was poured out under the altar. Levit. I. 5. 15. III. 28. and elsewhere.

Others explain that he says he is being libated, i.e., that he is now about to be libated, or that his blood is to be poured out, to sanction the truth of the doctrine of the Gospel, just as covenants were sanctioned by libations: or that he is to be offered in sacrifice to GOD in this way. For our death is a sacrifice, which must be offered to GOD with a ready mind: for sacrifices had to be voluntary. There does not appear to be a cause for a different meaning here and in the other place, at Philippians. To Suidas, σπένδομαι is in general 'I am immolated', just as 'I am dedicated to God', as he said σπένδοντες, θύοντας, προσφέροντας. Theophylact notes: he did not say 'I am immolated', but 'I am libated', which is certainly more excellent. Since by no means are all things which belong to immolation referred to God, but all things of a libation are.

Καὶ ὁ καιρὸς τῆς ἐμῆς ἀναλύσεως ἐφέστηκε) ἀναλύσεως, of migration, פטירה or rather of return. See what we said at Philipp. I. 23. ἐφέστηκε, it is imminent, it is near, as 1 Thess. V. 3. Paul said this, not only because all things which he saw at Rome and in the court of Nero commanded it to be believed; but moreover, as I think, having been taught by God concerning what was about to happen, such as we read happened to Cyprian and Chrysostom.

Ἐξήγησις prioris sententiæ. ἀναλύειν, although sometimes it is to return, the meaning of 'solution' is nevertheless more accepted, as is evident from the Commentaries of Budaeus: and that occurs in Athenaeus book 1 and Appian on the Civil Wars book IV, only with the preposition ἀπὸ or ἐξ; and therefore it should be judged that the solution of the soul from the bonds of the body is rather denoted. But it is manifest from this place that this Epistle was written not long before Paul's martyrdom, which Estius and indeed deny Baronius [uses] certain arguments: but they are not of such importance that they should move us from the common opinion of Eusebius, Hist. Eccles. Book II, ch. 2, and most interpreters, which Cornelius a Lapide also proves in this place. For as to what (1) they say, that Paul wished to make his disciple Timothy, than whom he had no one dearer, certain at least of the success of his first defense. I answer: That could have been done long before, even if here a comparison (σύγκρισις) is instituted again, as to how he was once abandoned by his companions, v. 17, yet not by the Lord, so also the Lord would not fail him, even if he had only Luke present, v. 17, 18. As to what (2) they say: that in ch. IV, v. 19 & 20, the things which he left at Troas, Corinth, and Miletus are mentioned: I do not see what stands in the way of our opinion: since those places could have been visited and those things and persons left there on another journey after his first captivity. (3) As to v. 17 of this chapter, where the Apostle says that he is still being reserved to fulfill the office of preaching among the Gentiles, it is perhaps not necessary to refer this to the time of his final captivity, since it can be taken relatively concerning his first apology, which was instituted a decade earlier. But more on this in its proper place. That gloss of Estius on this passage, that the Apostle does not mean that he is about to be snatched away to martyrdom, but only signifies that he is being prepared little by little for the victim through prisons and tribunals, does not fit. For he says expressly ἤδη σπένδομαι, I AM ALREADY BEING POURED OUT: likewise the time of my departure (ἀναλύσεώς) is at hand, which he had entirely from divine revelation, and writes to Timothy from the suggestion of the Holy Spirit. Because he adds that he has already fought the good fight, or his contest, that he has already finished his course: that a crown is already laid up for him. He would have sung a triumph before the victory, if he had still had to struggle and do military service for a decade.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Ἐγὼ γὰρ ἤδη σπένδομαι) Eo magis debes officio incum- bere, quia posthac auxilium non habebis à me, cui mors instat. Σπένδεσθαι dicitur vinum quod aspergitur victimæ. Vitis in Epigrammate Græco sic loquens inducitur: Κἄν με φάγῃς ἐπὶ ῥίζαν ὅμως ἔτι καρποφορήσω Ὅσσον ἐπισπεῖσαί σοι τράγε θυομένῳ. Est etiam ad Philippenses II. 17. comparatio ducta à liba- mentis, sed alio, ni fallor, modo. Ibi σπονδὴ, sive libamen consideratur ut accessio victimæ. Hic ut præparatio ad mactationes. Jam nunc aspergor vino, id est, præparor ad mortem, ut victimæ solent. Victimæ legales martyrum præfigurationes. Ideo animæ martyrum sub altari Apoc. VI. 7. quia sanguis victimarum effundebatur sub altari. Levit. I. 5. 15. III. 28. & alibi.

Alii exponunt, dicere se libari, h.e. jam jam li- batum iri, vel sanguinem suum profusum iri, ad sanciendam veritatem doctrinæ Evangelii, sicut fœdera sanciebantur libaminibus: vel ita in sacri- ficium DEI oblatum iri. Mors enim nostra est sacrificium, quod DEO promto animo offeren- dum: sacrificia enim debuerunt esse voluntaria. Non apparet causa diversæ significationis hic, & altero loco, ad Philipp. Suidæ σπένδομαι est in ge- nere immolor, ut & Deo dicor, ut σπένδοντες, θύον- τας, προσφέροντας dixit. Theophylactus notat: non immolor, dixit, sed delibor, quod sane præstantius est. Siquidem baudquaquam, quæ immolationis sunt, ad Deum omnia referuntur, libationis vero universa.

Καὶ ὁ καιρὸς τῆς ἐμῆς ἀναλύσεως ἐφέστηκε) ἀναλύσεως, mi- grationis, פטירה aut potius reditus. Vide quæ diximus ad Philipp.I.23. ἐφέστηκε, imminet, prope est, ut, 1.Thess V.3. dixit hoc Paulus, non tantum, quia omnia quæ videbat Romæ & in aula Neronis id credi jubebant; verum insuper, ut arbitror, à Deo de eo, quod futurum erat edoctus, quale quid & Cypriano & Chrysostomo evenisse legimus.

Ἐξήγησις prioris sententiæ. ἀναλύειν, etsi quan- doque reverti sit, receptior tamen est solutionis si- gnificatio, ut è Comment. Budæi constat: & illa apud Athen. l. 1. & Appian. de bell. civ. l. IV. cum præpositione ἀπὸ vel ἐξ tantum occurrit; ideoque solutionem animæ à vinculis corporis potius notari censendum. Manifestum autem est ex hoc lo- co, Epistolam hanc non multo ante Pauli martyri- um exaratam esse, quod negant quidem Estius & Baronius argumentis quibusdam: sed quae tanti momenti non sunt, ut nos a communi Eusebii l. II. Histor. Eccles. c. 2. & Interpp. plerorumque sen- tentia dimoveant, quam etiam probat Cornelius a Lapide in hoc loco. Nam quod (1) ajunt, Pau- lum discipulum suum Timotheum, quo chario- rem non habuit ullum, saltim de successu primae suae defensionis certum redditum voluisse. Re- spond. Pridem id fieri potuisse, etiamsi hic denuo σύγκρισις instituta, quomodo olim derelictus fuerit a sociis, vers. 17. non tamen a Domino, ita etiam sibi non defuturum Dominum, utut Lucam solum praesentem habeat v. 17. 18. Quod (2) ajunt: Cap. IV. vers. 19. & 20. quae Troade, Corinthi, ac Mileti reliquerit, commemorari: non video, quid obstet nostrae sententiae: siquidem alia post primam captivitatem via illa loca visitari, & res ac personae istae ibidem relinqui potuerint. (3) Quod ad vers. 17. hujus capitis, quod Apo- stolus adhuc se reservari ad implendum praedica- tionis officium in gentibus ait, id forte necessum non est, referre ad tempus postremae captivitatis, cum relative de prima apologia accipi possit, quae ante decennium instituta. Sed de hoc suo loco. Glossa illa Estii ad hunc loc. Apostolum non sen- tire, se jamjam rapiendum ad martyrium, sed hoc tantum significare, se per carceres & tribunalia paulatim parari ad victimam, non congruit. Di- serte enim ἤδη σπένδομαι JAM IMMOLOR, in- quit: item tempus ἀναλύσεώς mea ἐφέστηκε, quod omnino e revelatione divina habuit, & ex Spiri- tus sancti suggestione ad Timotheum perscribit. Quia addit, se decertasse jam agona, vel certamen suum, se jam consummasse cursum suum: sibi jam repositam esse coronam. Triumphum autem cecinisset ante victoriam, si adhuc per decennium ipsi certandum, & militandum fuisset.

## 4:7
Verse 7.

I have fought the good fight (Τὸν ἀγῶνα τὸν καλὸν ἠγώνισμαι) — would that many, with death approaching, could truly declare this of themselves, and not wish to deceive themselves through imputed or ceremonial righteousnesses. A noble contest indeed, which is undertaken for the Gospel, against the snares of the Devil, the examples of the world, and the allurements of the flesh: and full of hope, in that he always conducted himself well. See 1 Tim. VI. 12 & Gen. XXX. 8.

Let Grotius rebuke the imputed righteousnesses of the Papists, who believe that the merits and satisfactions of Francis and others are imputed to others and to themselves. Let him rebuke the ceremonial righteousnesses of the Papists, who constitute righteousnesses, nay, Evangelical perfections, in their rites, ceremonies, and orders instituted as merely fanatical. We believe that no other righteousness is imputed to us except the obedience of Christ, by which many are constituted righteous, as the Apostle testifies in Rom. V, v. 19; in ceremonies, however, we place no righteousness, nor do we admit that ceremonies are necessary for salvation. But that noble contest, which the Apostle hints at by a metaphor taken from athletes, we do not deny to be waging a battle against the Devil, the world, and the flesh; we know that we must struggle primarily by faith, with the Apostle as our authority, Eph. VI, v. 16, by which we must resist the Devil, as St. Peter admonishes in 1. Epistle V, v. 9, by which also the world is overcome, 1 John V. 1, seq.

I have finished the course (Τὸν δρόμον τετέλεκα) — I was never weary. I always ran in this stadium. See 1 Cor. IX. 24, 26; Gal. II. 2; Phil. II. 16; Heb. XII. 1.

He does not say he was never weary: for the infirmity of the flesh does not admit that, Matt. XXVI, v. 41, and the struggle of the flesh and Spirit, of which he complained vehemently in Rom. VII. 14, seq., but, he says, I have finished the course: using a metaphor taken from runners, who must run in the stadium and within the barriers to the goal, 1 Cor. IX. 24; Phil. III. 14; in which course there is need again primarily of faith, so that we may look to Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith (ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν τῆς πίστεως), and his passion, Heb. XII, v. 2, by which the business of our redemption was FINISHED. John XIX. 3.

I have kept the faith (Τὴν πίστιν τετήρηκα) — I never failed even in the slightest from the faith or the Christian profession: which many others have done. See above I. 15.

He hints that faith is needed for both of those things, namely, that the good fight must be fought and the course finished, and therefore he says that he has kept the faith, that he has fought in the faith, and that he has finished the course in the faith. Some here assign a third metaphor or similitude, taken from a good soldier, whose duty it is to keep the faith given to his Emperor. But this contest, both that which commonly lies upon all men, whose whole life is a perpetual contest, Job VII. 1, that which must be struggled by the faithful specifically, and finally that which had to be endured singularly by Paul, as an athlete of Christ, in his office, is designated here, just as the course in the stadium and the career of life and Christianity, as well as the Apostolic duty, is to be finished: yet the military service, to which the faith was given, looks only to the Christian profession, and the faith in it, which is carried toward Christ and must be kept unto death for Christ's sake, and the Apostolic office, namely, that he kept the faith by constantly believing in Christ and faithfully executing those things which had been entrusted by Christ, 1 Cor. IV, v. 2, and thus he proved his faith to Christ in every way.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Τὸν ἀγῶνα τὸν καλὸν ἠγώνισμαι) utinam multi morte in- stante hoc de se praedicare vere possent, & non se vellent decipere per justitias imputatas, vel ceremoniales. Prae- clarum utique certamen, quod pro Evangelio suscipitnr, contra Diaboli insidias, mundi exempla, & carnis illece- bras: & spei plenum, in eo bene se semper gessisse. Vid. 1. Tim. VI. 12. & Gen. XXX. 8.

Reprehendat Grotius justitias imputatas Papi- colarum, qui Francisci & aliorum merita, & satis- factiones aliis, sibique imputari credunt. Repre- hendat Papicolarum justitias ceremoniales, qui in ritibus, ceremoniis, & ordinibus suis institutis mere fanaticis justitias, imo perfectiones Evan- gelicas constituunt. Nos nullam aliam justi- tiam imputari nobis credimus, nisi obedientiam Christi, qua justi constituuntur multi, teste A- postolo Rom. V. vers. 19. in ceremoniis vero nullam collocamus justitiam, nec ad salutem ne- cessarias esse ceremonias admittimus. Certamen vero illud praeclarum, quod similitudine ab ath- letis desumta innuit Apostolus, pugnam contra Diabolum, mundum & carnem inferre, non negamus, ita fide imprimis decertandum esse, Apostolo autore, novimus, Ephes. VI. vers. 16. qua resistendum esse Diabolo, monet Sanct. Pe- trus 1. Epist. V. vers. 9. qua etiam mundus vin- citur 1. Joh. V. 1. sequ.

Τὸν δρόμον τετέλεκα) Nunquam defatigatus fui. Sem- per cucurri in hoc stadio. Vide 1. Cor. IX. 24. 26. Gal. II. 2. Philipp. II. 16. Ebr. XII. 1.

Non ait se nunquam defatigatum: id enim non admittit infirmitas carnis Matth. XXVI. vers. 41. & lucta carnis & Spiritus, de qua questus est vehe- menter Rom. VII. 14. seq. sed cursum, inquit, con- summavi: similitudine a cursoribus desumta, qui- bus in stadio, & intra carceres currendum est ad metam 1. Cor. IX. 24. Phil. III. 14. in quo cursu cumprimis opus iterum fide, ut nempe eadem re- spiciamus Jesum ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν τῆς πίστεως, ejusque passionem Ebr. XII. vers. 2. qua CON- SUMMATUM est redemtionis nostræ nego- tium. Job. XIX. 3.

Τὴν πίστιν τετήρηκα) Nunquam à fide, vel professione Christiana vel minimum defeci : quod alii fecere multi. Vide supra I. 15.

Ad utrumque illud, certamen, nempe, bonum decertandum, & cursum consummandum fide opus esse, ita innuit, ideoque fidem se servasse, in fide decertasse, in fide cursum consummasse, ait. Non- nulli hic tertiam metaphoram, vel similitudinem assignant, desumptam à bono milite, cujus est ser- vare fidem Imperatori datam. Hoc autem certa- men, tum quod communiter omnibus hominibus incumbit, quorum tota vita est perpetuum cer- tamen Job. VII. 1. quod specialiter fidelibus est cer- tandum, quod denique singulariter Paulo, ceu athletæ Christi, in officio erat exantlandum, hic designatur, ut cursus in stadio, & curriculo vitæ, & Christianismi, ut & muneris Apostolici consum- mandus : militia tamen, cui fides data, professio- nem tantum Christianam, & in ea fidem, quæ in Christum fertur, & propter Christum ad mor- tem servanda, & officium Apostolicum respicit, quod nempe fidem servarit, constanter in Chri- stum credendo, & fideliter ea, quæ à Christo cre- dita erant, exequendo 1. Cor. IV. vers. 2. adeoque Christo fidem suam undiquaque probavit.

## 4:8
V. 8. Λοιπὸν, ἀπόκειταί μοι ὁ τῆς δικαιοσύνης στέφανος) Namely, immortal and heavenly life: which is also called by the name of a crown, Jas. I. 12, 1 Pet. V. 4, Rev. II. 10, VI. 2, and elsewhere: also to the Rabbis עטרת λοιπὸν, that is, what remains, what is left. I have fulfilled my parts, it remains that God fulfill His.

Δικαιοσύνη) Here it is taken so broadly that it comprehends everything that is owed to God and men, or is performed with praise, as 2 Cor. III. 9, V. 21, IX. 10, and elsewhere, ἀπόκειται, it does not appear, but is kept in good faith. See Col. I. 5 and what is said there. Here you have the mystical sense of the saying in Prov. XIV. verse 31, חסה במותו צדיק.

He does not say, it is decreed: He prefers, it is laid up; thus He indicates that it is not only decreed, but also acquired and placed in safety. He does not say nakedly, it is laid up, but laid up for me: thus He shows that it will not yield to another, nor will it be taken away by anyone, nor will anyone hinder him from receiving it. This contributed much to diminishing Timothy's grief and strengthening his spirit against the impending difficulties. For why should he envy the Teacher his migration to the crown? Furthermore, it was easy for him to gather that he himself would not be struggling, running, and keeping the faith in vain, as Grotius says here.

Grotius understands righteousness as the righteousness of debt or the obedience which we perform, but he does not prove that sense from the Scriptures. For as to the passage 2 Cor. III. 9, V. 21, it treats there of Evangelical righteousness, which the ministry of reconciliation proclaims, which is the righteousness of Christ, in whom we are made righteous, Rom. V. 18, 1 Cor. I. 30, Phil. III. 9. In the third passage, however, 2 Cor. IX. 10, the word righteousness is taken for beneficence or mercy, nor does the passage Prov. XIV. 31 contribute anything to the matter in a literal sense. He honors God who has mercy on the poor. But what mystical sense can be carved out from here that would apply to this sentiment of the Apostle, does not appear. Others by righteousness here understand the righteousness of God, not that which judges according to the merits of works, but according to which God is constant in His promises, and which brings about a debt, not of merit, but of gratuitous promise: which sense the blessed Gerhard explains in this place. To which also contributes that saying of Bernard in his book on Grace and Free Will, 'Promised out of mercy,' but nevertheless to be paid out of justice. Therefore, the crown of justice which Paul expects is indeed a crown of justice, but of the justice of GOD, not his own. It is indeed just that He should render what He owes, and He owes what He has promised; but this is the justice of God, upon which the Apostle presumes, on account of the mercy of God: And what John Ferus has in ch. XX of Matthew: He promised freely, He will render freely and out of justice; therefore he understands that justice which regards the truth of the promise, not that which regards the dignity of works. Moreover, it seems to be called a crown of justice by reason of the justice of Christ, which Christ, namely, earned for us by His own justice, and which is imputed to us through faith for our justification and salvation, Rom. X. 4. seq. Cor. V. 21. both because the righteous judge, in view not of our inherent justice, but of that which is given and imputed to us, confers the crown of glory: but that rendering does not regard our merit, but solely the merit of Christ: and because the Apostle implies that we obtain the same by faith: for after he said that he had kept the faith, he added immediately that the crown of justice was laid up for him: Faith and the justice of Christ are related, and as faith apprehends the justice of Christ, so through faith also, by which it apprehends the justice of Christ, we obtain the crown which Christ earned for us by His own justice. Therefore, it is not a crown of justice in the same way that it is called a crown of life and glory, which is evident even from the opinion of Grotius himself. For it is called a crown of life and glory because it brings life and glory, or because it either consists in or has its place in the blessed life and heavenly glory: but it is called a crown of justice because it is owed to him: which Grotius indeed interprets as our own, or proper to us, against the Apostolic faith, but we interpret it as the justice of Christ imputed to us, according to the analogy of faith. Concerning which, Johannes Lorinus on 2 Pet. I. verse 1. The appellation of the crown of justice, which the Lord the righteous judge will render, is admitted. But because that, whatever it is, even though founded on the merits of Christ of infinite value, depends upon the divine will and covenant, and there is always an infinite gap between the creature and GOD, an exact and rigorous account of justice cannot have a place in this sort of contract, so that Thomas rightly calls it not a requirement, but a fittingness of divine goodness. And Bellarmine on Psalm XXIII. verse 5. Eternal life and the kingdom of heaven is justice for Christ, but mercy for His faithful ministers. From which the blessed Gerhard concludes in lib. II. Conf. Cathol. part. III, art. XXIII. c. 8. Therefore, with respect to the merit of Christ, eternal life is said to be given out of justice, but with respect to us, it is mercy, because eternal life is a gift of God, Rom. VI. last verse, which saying Bellarmine cites in the same place. It must be observed, therefore, on account of the Papists, who abuse this saying for their own merits, that justice, because it is called absolutely the crown of justice, and no mention is made of GOD or of us, can be explained either concerning the justice of GOD or concerning our own. Concerning that of GOD, either insofar as equity and rectitude are denoted by justice in general, which they call universal justice: or insofar as justice is designated in the sayings; and it embraces truthfulness, faithfulness, and constancy in fulfilling promises, or insofar as it is particular justice, whether distributive or commutative. None of these acceptations, if the explanation is made according to the analogy of faith, favors our merits. For if justice denotes the universal goodness of GOD, and grace imputing the merit of Christ to us, and truthfulness, faithfulness, and constancy, what have these to do with the merits of our works? For the crown of justice is not so called because it is bestowed upon us out of our merit, but out of the gracious covenant of GOD: and that GOD is moved by His truth and faithfulness to give it to us out of His promise. If, finally, particular justice is noted, remuneration is designated, rewarding us who are justified by the merit of Christ, and perfectly righteous by His justice. For justice gives to each his own. But the crown of eternal life for the believer is from the merit of Christ, which he apprehends through faith and holds as his own. Therefore, He bestows the crown of life upon believers out of justice. But if it is called a crown of justice with respect to us, it must be understood not of infused justice and the justice of works, but of the justice of Christ, which, apprehended through faith, becomes ours and makes us worthy of that crown, or the due reward, in that the merit of Christ is regarded. For it is clear that the justice of works cannot be regarded, even from the fact that we are not saved even by grace, let alone by right and merit, whether that merit is estimated from the nature of works performed by the regenerate, which are not properly our own, and furthermore are owed, and finally are unclean and imperfect, since the law promises life only to perfect justice, Lev. XVIII. verse 5, Luke X. verse 28.

Moreover, by the crown of justice to be rendered in that day, that is, the last day, the Apostle understands the perfect blessedness to be given to him not only by reason of the soul, but also by reason of the body, or to the whole person, which he expected through the appearing of Christ, or His glorious coming, not denying meanwhile that he would attain the blessedness of the soul immediately after his departure: since for that reason he desired in Phil. I. verse 23 to depart, that he might be with Christ in heavenly glory. Cf. Luke XXIII. verse 43, Rev. XIV. verse 13. Some also refer this day to the day of death, such as Justinianus. But the word appearing refers to the day of the Lord's last coming, in which we shall be crowned in soul and glorified body, and that publicly and solemnly in the sight of all the Angels and holy men.
