In death, the coronation begins with respect to the soul: it is completed in the glorification of the body on the last day: as Crocius does here with Aretius. Cornelius à Lapide also explains it concerning the day of the final judgment.

which the Lord will render to me in that day) He will render for the labor, although the thing itself exceeds the labor expended. Thus you have 'will render' in Matt. VI. 6, 18, Rom. II. 6. 'In that day' as in 1 Thess. I. 10. Above I. 12, 18.

Ἀπόδοσις either regards the subject, Paul, to whom it will be rendered; or the cause, for which this glorious crown will be rendered. In respect of the former, it is rendered out of grace, because Paul acknowledges no merit of his own, but professes eternal life to be a gratuitous gift, Rom. VI. v. ult. In respect of the latter, however, ἀπέδοσις is either referred to the merit of Christ, which is owed to the righteousness of Christ performed for us, and to us solely, on account of Christ's, not our own righteousness, as the meritorious cause. Concerning this latter relation we have already spoken, but concerning the former, Augustine in Ps. CIX: God is faithful, who has made Himself our debtor, not by receiving anything from us, but by promising us so much. Whatever He promised, He promised to the unworthy, so that the reward might not be promised as if for works, but that grace might be given freely in His name. It is therefore a debt not of justice, but of gracious divine promise. Where furthermore it is to be observed that the verb ἀποδώσει, according to the usage of Scripture, does not always imply retribution, but sometimes simple giving or donation. Basil the Great in Psalm VII: It is the custom, he says, of Scripture to use the name of retribution not only for some reward of good and evil, but also at the beginning of actions, as 'render to thy servant,' for 'give.' See Matt. XXVII. v. 58, Acts IV. 33, Col. III. v. 24, where it has no meaning other than that of giving. In which way eternal life is only a gift, and not retribution, as the Apostle teaches Rom. 6:23 and Eph. 2:8. Ὁ δίκαιος κριτής) The title of Judge is given to Christ, Acts 10:42. He is called just, however, because it is of justice, and this is to fulfill promises. See what we said in Book II of the Law of War and Peace, ch. XI. Then the saying of Ps. 7:12 will be most fully fulfilled: אלהים שופט צדיק. Papists are also accustomed to seek the foundation of their merits in this title of a just judge. But Grotius understands it, nevertheless, as justice in words, or truthfulness in promises, or even fidelity and constancy, which is exercised not only toward a hireling, but also toward a beneficiary. If, however, regard is had to universal justice, CHRIST is a just judge because He does what is consistent with His goodness, and does nothing for the sake of merits. For what is given freely out of goodness and grace is not given on account of a work, Rom. 11:6. Finally, even if it were conceded that regard is had to commutative justice, CHRIST is a just judge in eternal life for believers, to judge them not on account of faith itself or works, but on account of His own justice apprehended by faith by the believers and imputed to them as justice: for thus He most perfectly affects the just afterward with rewards worthy of justice. What does this have to do with our merits again? These are as far apart as heaven is from earth: the justice or obedience of Christ, and our justice or works. The former is the service of a just servant performed for us, the knowledge or faith of which constitutes us just, Is. 43:25, ch. 53:11, and it does not admit, but excludes, our merit. For if justice is through the law or from our works, CHRIST died for nothing, Gal. 2:21. You have been emptied of Christ, you who wish to be justified by the law: you have fallen from grace, Gal. 5:4. What Estius says: that Paul still doubted in the Epistle written to the Philippians, ch. 3, v. 11, he rashly assumes in that, that this Epistle is later than that one, and he feigns a doubt where there is none: for Paul was entirely certain of his perseverance, Rom. 8:38. Nor is the particle εἴ truly dubitative: but rather significant of the difficulties and afflictions which still press upon the pious here. Οὐ μόνον δὲ μοι) This is well said, so that he may also stir up others to share in the labor, under the hope of a common reward. Ἀλλὰ καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ἠγαπηκόσι τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν αὐτοῦ) By ἐπιφάνειαν he understands that excellent one, of which he spoke just now, at the beginning of this chapter. They are said to love it, that is, חפץ, which is translated both by ἀγαπᾷν and by ὀνχιέσθαι and by ἐπιθυμεῖν, who desire that it may come to pass, because they hope for all the best things from it: which only those can rightly do who have ordered their lives according to Christ's prescription. To them, however, that saying is appropriate: אַשרי כל־חוכי לו Is. 30:18. Add Dan. 11:12. He said ἠγαπηκόσι, however, not ἀγαπῶσι, referring the mind to that time of judgment, as if he were saying: those who shall then be found to have hoped for His advent. That hope and love of the apparition of Christ argues faith in CHRIST, for faith is ἐνεργουμένη through charity, Gal. 5:6; it also argues the certainty of grace and salvation, which they expect from Christ, concerning which, just as the Apostle testified for himself that a crown of justice would be given to him, so he now testifies that other believers also certainly expect the same and will obtain it. But this is not merely moral certainty, nor that which arises from the testimony of conscience and the memory of a life well lived, as Cornelius à Lapide wishes. For the conscience of a believing man can indeed appear before the tribunal of God, but not unless veiled with the garment of Christ's justice: for it cannot set inherent justice and the goodness of life before the eyes of God the Judge because of its imperfection. But the certainty of his own conscience, recognizing the experiments of faith in Christ according to the norm of true faith expressed in the divine word, and relying on the merit of Christ imputed through faith, is by no means moral, but infallible and resting on a divine foundation. Cf. 1 John 4:12.

Moreover, the Vulgate rashly omitted the particle πᾶσι. For it is found in the Greek codices and in the text of the Greek interpreters, even of Oecumenius, who infers with Chrysostom and Theophylact: If He will give the crown to all who love His advent, much more to himself. Indeed, even in the Council of Trent itself, Sess. VI, c. 16, and Estius himself acknowledges that the sense seems to demand it.

PART II. Admonition concerning the arrival of Timothy.

Latin:

V. 8. Λοιπὸν, ἀπόκειταί μοι ὁ τῆς δικαιοσύνης στέφανος) Nem- pe vita immortalis & cœlestis : quæ coronæ nomine voca- tur etiam, Jac. I. 12. 1. Petr. V. 4. Apoc. II. 10. VI. 2. & alibi : Rabbinis etiam עטרת λοιπὸν, id est, quod restat, quod re- liquum. Explevi meas partes, restat Deus suas impleat.

Δικαιοσύνη) Hic ita large sumitur, ut omne id compre- hendat, quod Deo & hominibus debetur, aut cum laude præstatur, ut 2. Cor. III. 9. V. 21. IX. 10. & alibi, ἀπόκειται כמס, non apparet, sed bona fide asservatur. Vide Col. I. 5. & ibi dicta. Hic habes sensum mysticum dicti Prov. XIV. vers. 31. חסה במותו צדיק.

Non dicit, decretus est : Mavult, reposita est ; Ita non tantum decretam esse, sed & acquisitam & in tu- to esse collocatam, indicat. Non nude ait, reposita est, sed reposita mihi : Sic ostendit, non alii cessuram esse, nec à quoquam præceptum iri, nec quemquam impe- diturum, quo minus accipiat. Hoc multum faciebat ad minuendum Timothei dolorem & roborandum animum contra instantes difficultates. Cur enim migrationem ad coronam Præceptori invideret ? Præ- terea promtum illi erat colligere, quod nec ipse esset frustra certaturus, cursurus, fidem servaturus, ut hic Grotius.

Justitiam Grotius de justitia debiti vel obedientia, quam nos præstamus, intelligit, sed sensum illum è Scripturis non probat. Quod enim ad locum 2. Cor. III. 9. IV. 21. ibi de justitia Evangelica, quam ministerium reconciliationis prædicat, quæ Christi justitia est, in quo nos effi- cimur justi Rom. V. 18. 1. Cor. I. 30. Phil. III. 9. agitur. In tertio vero loco 2. Cor. IX. 10. justitiæ vox pro beneficentia, vel misericordia sumitur, neque ad rem quicquam sensu literali facit locus Prov. XIV. 31. Deum honorat, qui pauperis miseretur. Quis vero hinc mysticus sensus exculpi queat, qui ad hanc Apostoli sententiam faciat, non apparet. Alii per justitiam hic Dei justitiam intelligunt, non illam, quæ judicat secundum merita operum, sed secundum quam Deus constans est in promis- sionibus, quæque debitum infert, non meriti, sed gratuitæ promissionis : quem sensum explicat B. Ger- hardus in h. l. Quo etiam facit illud Bernhardi lib. de Grat. & lib. arbitr. Promissum ex misericordia, sed tamen ex justitia persolvendum. Est ergo quam Paulus expectat corona justitiæ, sed justitiæ DEI, non suæ. Justum quidem est, ut reddat quod debet, debet autem quod pollicitus est, at hæc est justitia Dei, de qua præsumit Apostolus, pro misericordia Dei: Et quod habet Joh. Ferus in c. XX. Matth. Gratis promisit, gratis & ex justitia reddet, proinde in- telligit illam justitiam, quæ promissionis veritatem, non quæ operum dignitatem respicit. Videtur autem corona justitiæ dici ratione justitiæ Christi, quam scilicet Christus justitia sua nobis promeruit, quæ- que nobis imputatur per fidem ad nostri justifica- tionem & salutem, Rom. X. 4. sequ. 1. Cor. V. 21. tum quia ὁ δίκαιος κριτὴς justus judex, intuitu non nostræ inhærentis justitiæ, sed quæ nobis donatur & im- putatur, coronam gloriæ confert: at ἀπόδοσις illa non respicit nostrum, sed unice Christi meritum: tum quia fide eandem nos consequi innuit Apo- stolus: nam postquam fidem se servasse dixit, ad- jecit statim, repositam sibi esse coronam justitiæ: Fides autem & justitia Christi relata sunt, & ut fides apprehendit justitiam Christi, sic per fi- dem etiam, qua Christi justitiam apprehendit, consequimur coronam, quam justitia sua Chri- stus nobis promeruit. Non ergo ita corona ju- stitiæ, ut corona vitæ & gloriæ dicitur, quod ex ipsa etiam Grotiana sententia constat. Nam vita & gloria corona dicitur, quod vitam & glo- riam adferat, vel in vita beata, & gloria cœlesti aut consistat, aut locum habeat: justitiæ autem, quod ei debeatur: quod Grotius quidem de no- stra, vel propria contra fidem Apostolicam, nos autem de Christi nobis imputata justitia accipi- mus, secundum analogiam fidei. De quo Jo- hannes Lorinus in 2. Petr. I. vers. 1. Admit- titur appellatio coronæ justitiæ, quam reddet Do- minus justus judex. Sed quia illud, quicquid est, etiam fundatum in infiniti pretii meritis Christi, à divina pendet voluntate ac pacto, estque semper creaturæ ac DEI interstitium infinitum exacta & rigorosa justitiæ ratio locum hunc habere nequit, in isto veluti contractu, ut idcirco satu bene Tho- mas appellat non exigentiam, sed condecentiam bonitatis divinæ. Et Bellarm. in Psal. XXIII. vers. 5. Vita æterna ac regnum cœlorum Christo justitia, fidelibus ejus ministris misericordia est. Ex quo concludit Beat. Gerhardus l. II. Conf. Cathol. part. III, art. XXIII. c. 8. Ergo respectu meriti Christi dicitur vita æterna dari ex justitia, sed respectu nostri est misericordia, quia χάρισμα Θεῦ vita æterna, Rom. VI. v. ult. quod dictum ibi- dem Bellarminus allegat. Observandum ergo propter Pontificios, hoc dicto pro meritis suis abutentes, justitiam, quia absolute corona justi- tiæ dicitur, nec DEI vel nostri fit mentio, vel explicari posse de DEI justitia: vel de nostri. De DEI, vel prout per justitiam in genere æquitas & rectitudo notatur, quam vocant universalem justitiam: vel prout designatur justitia in dictis; & veracitatem, fidelitatem, & constantiam in præstandis promissis complectitur, vel prout ju- stitia particularis, sive distributiva, sive commu- tativa. Nulla ex istis acceptionibus, si κατ' ἀνα- λογίαν τ̃ πίςεως fiat explicatio, favet nostris me- ritis. Nam justitia notatur universalis bonitas DEI, & gratia meritum Christi nobis imputans, ac veracitas, fidelitas & constantia, quod hæc ad operum nostrorum merita? Non enim ita coro- na justitiæ dicitur, quod ex merito nostro sed ex gratioso DEI pacto nobis tribuatur: quodque veritate & fidelitate sua DEUS moveatur, ut eam ex promisso nobis det. Si denique notetur justitia particularis, remuneratio designatur, re- munerans nos ex merito Christi justificatos, & justitia ejus perfecte justos. Justitia enim tri- buit cuique suum. Sed corona vitæ æternæ cre- denti est ex merito Christi, quod ille per fi- dem apprehendit, & tenet ut suum. Ergo cre- dentibus coronam vitæ tribuit ex justitia. Si autem nostri respectu dicatur corona justitiæ, in- telligendum id non de infusa & operum justitia, sed de justitia Christi, quæ per fidem apprehen- sa fit nostra, & nos facit dignos illa corona, seu debito præmio, qua nempe Christi meri- tum respicitur. Justitiam enim operum respici non posse vel ex eo liquet, quod eadem ne qui- dem per gratiam salvemur, nedum ex jure & merito, sive meritum illud æstimetur ex operum à renatis præstitorum natura, quæ proprie no- stra non sunt, ad hæc debita, denique immunda & imperfecta, cum lex non nisi perfectæ justitiæ vitam promittat Lev. XIIII. vers. 5. Luc. X. v. 28.

Cæterum per coronam justitiæ in die illa, hoc est novissima, reddendam Apostolus intelligit beatitudinem perfectam sibi non tantum ratione animæ, sed etiam ratione corporis, seu toti sup- posito donandam, quam expectabat per appari- tionem Christi, seu adventum ejus gloriosum, non negans interim, se beatitudinem animæ ra- tione adepturum statim post ἀνάλυσιν: Siqui- dem ideo Phil. I. vers. 23. desiderarit τὸ ἀναλῦσαι, ut cum Christo esse possit in gloria cœlesti. Conf. Luc. XXIII. v. 43. Apoc. XIV. vers. 13. Nonnulli etiam hunc diem referunt ad diem mortis, utpote Justinianus. Sed ἐπιφανείας vox respicit diem no- vissimi adventus Domini, in quo coronabimur anima & corpore glorificato, idque publice & so- lenniter in omnium Angelorum & sanctorum ho- minum conspectu. In morte coronatio incipit respectu animæ: completur in corporis glorifica- tione in extremo die: ut hic cum Aretio Crocius. De die extremi judicii etiam explicat Cornelius à Lapide.

ὃν ἀποδώσει μοι ὁ κύριος ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ) Reddet pro labore, quanquam res ipsa laborem impensum exce- dit. Sic ἀποδώσει habes Matth. VI. 6. 18. Rom. V. 6. ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ uti 1. Thess. I. 10. Supra I. 12. 18.

Ἀπόδοσις vel respicit subjectum, Paulum, cui reddetur; vel causam, ob quam reddetur hæc co- rona gloriosa. Istius respectu ex gratia redditur, quia Paulus nullum sui agnoscit meritum, sed vi- tam æternam profitetur donum gratuitum Rom. VI. v. ult. Hujus respectu autem ἀπέδοσις vel refer- tur ad Christi meritum, quod debeatur justitiæ Christi pro nobis præstitæ, & nobis unice, ob Christi, non ob nostram justitiam, ceu causam meritoriam. De hac posteriori σχέσει jam diximus, de priori autem Augustinus in Ps. CIX. Fidelis Deus, qui se nostrum debitorem fecit, non aliud à nobis accipiendo, sed tanta nobis promittendo. Quicquid promisit, indignis promisit, ut non quasi operibus merces promitteretur, sed gratia in suo nomine gratis daretur. Est ergo debitum non ju- stitiæ, sed promissionis divina gratiosa. Ubi por- ro observandum verbum ἀποδώσει ex usu Scri- pturæ non semper retributionem, sed simplicem quandoque dationem vel donationem inferre. Basilius M. in Psalm. VII. Mos est, inquit, Scri- pturæ retributionis nomen non solum in præmium aliquod boni, & mali, accipere, sed etiam in Actio- num principio, ut retribue servo tuo, pro tribue. Vid. Matth. XXVII. v. 58. Act. IV. 33. Col. III. v. 24. ubi non nisi dandi significatio locum habet. Quomodo vitam æternam donum tantum esse, non retributionem Apostolus docet Rom. 6, 23. & Eph. 2, 8. Ὁ δίκαιος κριτής) Judicis titulus Christo datur Act. 10. 42. Justus autem dicitur, quia justitiæ & hoc est, im- plere promissa. Vide, quæ diximus lib. II. de Jure Belli & Pacis cap. XI. Tunc plenissime implebitur dictum Psal. 7, 12. אלהים שופט צדיק Solent etiam in hoc justi judicis titulo Papistæ meritorum suorum fundamentum quærere. Sed Grotius eam tamen intelligit de justitia in dictis seu veracitate in promissis, vel etiam fidelitate ac constan- tia, quæ exercetur non tantùm erga mercena- rium, sed etiam erga beneficiarium. Si autem ad universalem justitiam respectus habeatur, justus judex CHRISTUS est, quia facit, quod congruum est suæ bonitati, & nihil facit ad merita. Quod enim ex bonitate ac gratia gratis datur, non datur propter opus, Rom. 11, 6. Denique etiamsi con- cederetur, respectum haberi ad justitiam commu- tativam; Justus judex CHRISTUS est in vita æ- terna credentibus ad judicandum non propter fi- dem ipsam, aut opera, sed propter justitiam suam fide à credentibus apprehensam, & in justitiam il- lis imputatam: Sic enim perfectissimè justos post- ea præmiis justitia dignis afficit. Quid hoc ite- rum ad merita nostra? Toto hæc cœlo distant ju- stitia vel obedientia Christi, & justitia vel opera nostra. Illa est servitium servi justi pro nobis im- pensum, cujus cognitio seu fides nos justos con- stituit, Es. 43, 25. cap. 53, 11. nec admittit, sed excludit nostrum meritum. Nam si per legem vel ex operibus nostris justitia, CHRISTUS gratis mortuus est, Galat. 2, 21. Evacuati estis à Christo, qui vultis lege justificari: gratia excidistis, Galat. 5, 4. Quod Estius ait: Adhuc dubitasse Paulum in Epist. ad Philippenses exarata, cap. 3. vers. 11. in eo temerè assumit, illam Epistolam hac poste- riorem esse, ac dubitationem fingit, ubi nulla est: erat enim de perseverantia sua Paulus omninò certus, Rom. 8, 38. Nec verò particula εἴ dubita- tiva est: sed significativa potius difficultatum, & afflictionum, quæ piis hic adhuc incumbunt. Οὐ μόνον δὲ μοι) Bene hoc, ut & alios excitet ad par- ticipandum laborem, sub spe communis præmii. Ἀλλὰ καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ἠγαπηκόσι τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν αὐτοῦ) Ἐπι- φάνειαν intelligit illam eximiam, de qua egit modò, initio hujus capitis. Eam diligere dicuntur, id est, חפץ, quod & per ἀγαπᾷν & per ὀνχιέσθαι, & per ἐπιθυμεῖν ver- titur, qui exoptant, ut ea eveniat, quia inde omnia sperant optima: quod facere illi soli jure possunt, qui ad Christi præscriptum vitam instituerunt. Iis verò illud convenit אַשרי כל־חוכי לו Esa. 30, 18. Adde Dan. 11. 12. Dixit autem ἠγαπηκόσι, non ἀγαπῶσι animum referens ad tempus illud judicii, quasi dicat; qui tunc deprehen- dentur adventum ejus sperasse. Spes illa & dilectio apparitionis Christi, arguit fi- dem in CHRISTUM, fides enim per charitatem est ἐνεργουμένη, Gal. 5, 6. arguit etiam certitudinem gratiæ & salutis, quam expectant à Christo, de qua uti testatus Apostolus quoad se, donatum sibi iri coronam justitiæ, ita etiam certò eandem expecta- re, ac consecuturos esse alios fideles jam testatur. Non autem hæc est tantùm moralis certitudo, nec quæ oritur ex testificatione conscientiæ, & memoria vita benè actæ, ut Cornelius à Lapide vult. Con- scientia enim hominis credentis coram tribunali Dei potest quidem comparere, sed non nisi velata vestimento justitiæ Christi: inhærentem verò justitiā, & vitæ bonitatem ante oculos Dei judicis statue- re non potest propter ejus imperfectionem. Con- scientia autem sua in Christum fidei experimenta ad normam fidei veræ, verbo divino expressam, reco- gnoscentis, & merito Christi per fidem imputato fretæ certitudo nequaquam est moralis, sed infalli- bilis, ac divino fundamento nixa. Conf. 1. Joh. 4, 12.

Cæterum particulam πᾶσι temerè omisit Vulgata. Habetur enim in Græcis Codd. & in textu inter-pretum Græcorum, etiam Oecumenii, qui infert cum Chrysostomo & Theophylacto: Si omnibus, qui diligunt adventum ipsius, dabit coronam, multo ma-gis sibi. Imò in ipso Concil. Trident. Sess. VI. c. 16. & agnoscit Estius ipse, sensum eam postulare videri.

PARS II. Commonitio de adventu Timothei.

## 4:9
V. 9. Σπούδασον ἐλθεῖν πρός με ταχέως) Namely, to Rome. And Timothy did this, as appears from Col. 1:1, Philem. v. 1, Heb. 3:23, Phil. 2:19.

That these things were fulfilled there cannot be admitted: for the present Epistle is later than the others, and is deservedly held by Eusebius, Chrysostom, and others to be the last. He summoned Timothy, however, because he wished to use his ministry to promote the business of Christ, which was destitute of other helpers: That ταχέως is declared later, v. 21, before winter, so that he might not, namely, defer his departure to another year. He had already been present before. Yet he seeks a meeting again. He knew that the Asian Church could ill afford to lack his work and presence; yet he urges his arrival. Which is not to be taken as if the Apostle had more regard for himself than for the Churches. He wishes to come in such a way that in the meantime the Churches may be provided for from elsewhere. As Crocius says here.

Latin:

V. 9. Σπούδασον ἐλθεῖν πρός με ταχέως) Nempe Romam. Et hoc fecit Timotheus, ut apparet Col. 1, 1. Philem. v. 1. Ebr. 3, 23. Philipp. 2, 19.

Hæc ibi impleta referri admitti nequit: nam præsens Epistola posterior est reliquis, & pro ultima merito habetur ab Eusebio, Chrysostomo, & aliis. Accersivit autem Timotheum, quod voluerit ejus ministerio uti ad promovendum Christi negotium, quod aliis destituto erat adjutoribus: Illud ταχέως declaratur postea v. 21. ante hyemem, ne scil. in alte-rum annum differat profectionem. Jam ante ad-fuerat. Iterum tamen expetit congressum. Sciebat Ecclesiam Asianam ipsius opera & præsentia agrè ca-rere; urget tamen adventum. Quod non sic est acci-piendum, quasi Apostolus potiorem sui, quam Eccle-siarum habeat rationem. Sic vult venire, ut interim Ecclesiis aliunde consulatur. Ut hic Crocius.

## 4:10
V. 10. Δημάς γάρ με ἐγκατέλιπεν) He abandoned the office of evangelist. He did as those did, of whom above c. 1:5. He deserted me, that is, he did not wish to be my helper. We have said, however, that Δη-μᾶς is a shortened name from Δημήτριος. Is this the same one whose mention is at the end of John 12? See here also how good men are sometimes changed by fear or bad examples. Wherefore let him who stands take heed lest he fall. But we also gather that Demas repented of this fault from the passage Philem. v. 24 and Col. 4:14.

Ἀγαπήσας τὸν νῦν αἰῶνα) Matt. 13:22.

Καὶ ἐπορεύθη εἰς Θεσσαλονίκην) so that he might make money there by trading. For it was a noble emporium.

Although Demas was still with Paul at that time, when he was sending letters from Rome to the Colossians and to Philemon, he could nevertheless have abandoned Paul afterwards and chosen worldly pleasures: but it is not established that he repented. That Demas went to Thessalonica only for the sake of trade, and put the care of the Gospel after private interests, as Estius wishes, denying with Baronius that his apostasy is implied, does not seem consistent with the phrase of the Apostle, ἀγαπήσας τὸν νῦν αἰῶνα. What it means to love the world is known from 1 John 2:15; and the opposition, as it appears, is implied with respect to the description of the pious, who are said to love not the present age, but the appearing of Christ; not to mention what Epiphanius reports in Heresy 51: that Demas, having abandoned the way of truth, became a heretic, holding the same views as Cerinthus, Ebion, and others, who asserted that Christ was a mere man. Dorotheus in his Synopsis mentions that he became a worshiper of the idols of the Thessalonians and a priest. It is said by Grotius that Demas is Demetrius, but it is not proven: just as it is not proven by Estius that the Demas who is the bishop of the Magnesians in Ignatius' Epistle to the Magnesians is this same Demas.

Crescens into Galatia) Namely, for the evangelical harvest. Galatia is an ambiguous name: for Gaul is also called so by the Greeks, and a part of Asia inhabited by Gauls in ancient times. That Gaul should rather be understood here is suggested by the proximity of Italy, where Paul was, and the ancient tradition among the Gauls. Epiphanius teaches us that in the codices of his time it was written Gallia. The Greeks, who have no names ending in -ens, write Poudēs, Klēmēs for Pudens, Clemens. Also that Cynic, the enemy of Justin Martyr, is called Kriskes by Tatian, just as some codices have it here. This name is read incorrectly as Crispus in the Syriac, and Crisicus in the Arabic.

Epiphanius' reading is to be rejected: for all Greek codices consistently read Galatias.

Titus into Dalmatia) Which is opposite Italy.

Latin:

V. 10. Δημάς γάρ με ἐγκατέλιπεν) Dereliquit munus Evangelistæ. Fecit, ut illi, de quibus supra c. 1, 5. Me de-seruit, id est, adjutor meus esse noluit. Diximus autem Δη-μᾶς esse curtatum nomen ex Δημήτριος. An hic idem cujus mentio ult. Joh. 12. Vide hic etiam bonos interdum metu aut malis exemplis mutari. Quare qui stat, videat ne cadat. Sed & culpæ hujus pœnituisse Demam colligi-mus ex loco Philem. v. 24. & Col. 4, 14.

Ἀγαπήσας τὸν νῦν αἰῶνα) Matth. 13, 22.

Καὶ ἐπορεύθη εἰς Θεσσαλονίκην) ut ibi mercando rem faceret. Erat enim nobile emporium.

Quamvis Demas Paulo tum adhuc adfuerit, cum Roma ad Colossenses & ad Philemonem daret li-teras, postea tamen Paulum dereliquisse potuit, & mundanas voluptates elegisse: quem vero pœni-tuisse non constat. Mercaturæ causa tantum De-mam Thessalonicam concessisse, & Evangelii cu-ram commodis privatis postposuisse, ut Estius vult, negans cum Baronio apostasiam ejus innui, non vi-detur phrasi Apostoli, ἀγαπήσας τὸν νῦν αἰῶνα, consentaneum. Quid sit ἀγαπᾶν τὸν κόσμον ex Joh. 1. Ep. 2, 10. notum est: & oppositio, ut apparet, innuitur respectu descriptionis piorum, qui dicun-tur amare non præsens seculum, sed apparitionem Christi; ut taceam, quod Epiphanius hær. LI. re-ferat: Demam relicta veritatis via factum fuisse hæ-reticum, eadem sentientem cum Cerintho, Ebione & aliis, qui Christum nudum hominem asserebant. Do-rotheus in Synopsi memorat, eum Thessalonicen-sium simulacrorum cultorem & Sacerdotem fa-ctum fuisse. Demam esse Demetrium dicitur à Grotio, non probatur: æquè ut ab Estio Damam Ignatius in Epist. ad Magnes. Episcopum eorun-dem esse hunc ipsum Demam.

Κρήσκης εἰς Γαλατίαν) Nempe ad Evangelicam mes-sem. Γαλατίας ambiguum est nomen: nam & Gallia sic vocatur Græcis, & Asiæ pars à Gallis antiquitus habitata. Ut Gallia potius hîc intelligenda sit, facit Italiæ, ubi Pau-lus erat, vicinitas, & vetus apud Gallos fama. Epipha-nius in sui temporis Codicibus Γαλλίαν scriptam fuisse nos docet. Græci, qui nulla nomina habent in ENS desinen-tia, scribunt Πούδης, Κλήμης pro Pudens, Clemens. Etiam Cynicus ille Justini martyris hostis Tatiano Κρίσκης, quo-modo & hîc Codices habent nonnulli. Nomen hoc in Sy-riaco malè legitur Crispus, in Arabico Crisicus.

Epiphanii lectio reprobanda: Omnes enim Græci Codices constanter legunt Γαλατίας.

Τίτος εἰς Δαλματίαν) Quæ objecta Italiæ.

## 4:11
V. 11. Luke is alone with me) For after that journey, which he described at the end of the Acts, he remained in Italy with Paul. Col. 4, 14. Philem. v. 24.

Luke had so attached himself to Paul, as Theophylact teaches, that he never departed from him. Furthermore, the same man wrote both the Gospel and the entire Acts of the Apostles; Paul also makes mention of this one, saying, Whose praise is in the Gospel throughout all the churches. Jerome in his Catalogue calls Luke a follower of the Apostle Paul, and an inseparable companion of all his travels. Regarding this, Crocius ad h. l. He is named among the helpers Phil. 24. That beloved physician Coloss. 4, 14. Yet let it be the same: The ancients understand the same person, Chrysostom, Theodoret, the Commentary inscribed to Ambrose, Jerome, namely the author of the Evangelical and Apostolic history, who Eusebius affirms was an Antiochene, lib. 3. Hist. Eccles. cap. 4. Origen lib. 1. de recta in DEUM fide, Epiphan. haer. 57. Dorotheus in his Synopsis affirms that he was one of the seventy-two disciples of CHRIST: that he was a companion of Cleopas on the journey to Emmaus is the opinion of Gregory the Great in the preface to Job c. 1. Theophylact on Luke 24. Nicephorus lib. 2. hist. cap. 43. report that he was converted to the faith by Paul. That he has his history from those who conversed with CHRIST, he himself indicates not obscurely Luke 1, 2.

Taking Mark, bring him with you) Namely, that kinsman of Barnabas. And this desire of Paul was fulfilled. See Philem. 24. Coloss. 4, 16.

This is asserted without proof regarding the present desire of Paul being fulfilled. For the Apostle wrote the Epistle to Philemon, and to the Colossians before, when Timothy was present with him, together with Timothy. That Paul wrote any Epistle to Timothy after this one, when he had come to him, is supported by no document.

For he is useful to me for the ministry) Namely, of the Gospel, perhaps because of the custom of the Latin language.

Latin:

V. 11. Λουκᾶς ἐστι μόνος μετ' ἐμοῦ) Nam post iter illud, quod fine Actorum descripsit, mansit in Italia cum Paulo. Col. 4, 14. Philem. v. 24.

Lucas sic Paulo adhaeserat, Theophylacto docen- te, ut ab eo nunquam discederet. Idem praeterea & Evangelium & Apostolorum Acta universa con- scripsit, de hoc item & Paulus meminit, dicens, Cujus laus in Evangelio est per omnes Ecclesias. Hiero- nymus in Catalogo Lucam vocat Apostoli Pauli se- ctatorem, & omnis ejus peregrinationis comitem in- dividuum. De hoc Crocius ad h. l. Nominatur inter adjutores Phil. 24. Medicus dilectus ille Co- loss. 4, 14. Sit tamen idem: Eundem intelligunt ve- teres Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, Commentarius Ambrosio inscriptus, Hieronymus, auctorem scilicet historiae Evangelicae & Apostolorum, quem Antio- chenum fuisse, affirmat Eusebius lib. 3. Hist. Eccles. cap. 4. Origenes lib. 1. de recta in DEUM fide, Epiphan. haer. 57. Dorotheus in Synopsi ex septua- ginta duobus CHRISTI discipulis fuisse, affirmant: Cleophae comitem fuisse in Emauntico itinere, placet Gregorio M. in praefat. in Job. c. 1. Theophylacto in Luc. 24. Nicephorus lib. 2. hist. cap. 43. à Paulo ad fidem conversum esse, tradunt. Ab iis habere historiam, qui cum CHRISTO sunt conversati, ipse non obscure indicat Luc. 1, 2.

Μάρκον ἀναλαβὼν, ἄγαγε μετὰ σεαυτοῦ) Illum nempe Barnabae consanguineum. Et hoc desiderium Pauli im- pletum est. Vide Philem. 24. Coloss. 4, 16.

Gratis hoc adseritur de praesenti desiderio Pauli adimpleto. Nam Epistolam ad Philemo- nem, & ad Colossenses antea, cum Timotheus ipsi praesens esset, exaravit, unà cum Timotheo, Apo- stolus. Post hanc ad Timotheum aliquam Paulum cum Timotheo, ubi ad eum venerat, Epistolam scripsisse, nullo documento constat.

Ἔστι μοι γὰρ εὔχρηστος εἰς διακονίαν) Nempe Evangelii, fortè ob Latini sermonis consuetudinem.

## 4:12
Vers. 12.

But Tychicus I have sent to Ephesus) That appears in Eph. 6. verse 21.

He designates the Evangelical ministry, for which he had previously seemed useless to the Apostle, Acts 15, 37. He does not lead him into leisure, according to the interpretation of Theophylact, but into the ministry of the Gospel. For the Apostle, even though he was bound in chains, had not interrupted that duty of preaching, and for that reason he recalls Timothy not without cause, but for the sake of the Gospel, so that the faithful might not be disturbed at the time of his passing, since there were many among his disciples who were afflicted, who might calm and confirm the crowd and tumults, if any should happen to arise, who might bear his death more intolerably. For it was necessary that there be men of great importance, to whom Rome might be entrusted for care.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Τυχικὸν δὲ ἀπέστειλα εἰς Ἔφεσον) Apparet id Ephes. 6. vers. 21.

Ministerium Evangelicum designat, ad quod an- tea visus Apostolo erat inutilis, Act. 15, 37. Non in otium ducit, interprete Theophylacto, sed in Evan- gelii ministerium. Apostolus namque etsi vinculis erat constrictus, praedicandi tamen id munus non in- termiserat, eoque & Timotheum non sine causa revo- cat, sed Evangelii, ut nihil fideles sui obitus tempore obturbarentur, cum multi essent ex ejus discipulis af- flicti, qui turbam & tumultus, si qui forte oboriren- tur, sedarent, confirmarentque, qui ejus mortem fer- rent intolerantius. Erat enim necesse, ut magni es- sent momenti viri, quibus Roma demandaretur in curam.

## 4:13
Vers. 13.

The cloak) A Greek word made from a Latin one: and that already long ago, since even the Comic Rhetorician used it in the times of the Ptolemies. It is written, however, as external words are wont to be, variously, φαινόλης, as in Athenaeus, φανόλας, Φελώνης. In the Glossary φαινόλης, τὸ φελόνιον, a cloak. We also read φελόνιον in the Liturgy of Chrysostom, and in the books of later Greeks.

Chrysostom understood it as a small chest or book-case, which the Syrian, in the Hebrew manner, calls a house of writings. Jerome explained it as a volume of the Old Testament in his Epistle 125 to Damasus, q. 2; which opinion, B. Gerhard says, is confirmed by the fact that Φέλλov denotes a book, that is, the bark of a tree, from which volumes were once made. Ambrosiaster explains it as a Senator's garment. Others explain it as a consular mantle. Neither suits the Apostle. Others wish it to be understood as a sacred garment or a chasuble; but that is called Φαινόλη by the Greeks. Most interpret it as a penula, a garment suitable for warding off rain and cold; which Jerome, in Dial. 3 against Pelagius, calls a lacerna. But shall we believe that the Holy Spirit dictated even such things to the Apostle? Although they may seem carnal, yet since all Scripture is θεόπνευςτος, one must not doubt even this particle of Scripture. It also has its own teaching: that even lighter things are not to be despised, and that a penula could still be of use in winter, and so that we may not be ignorant of the poverty of such a great Apostle, which is also wont to console us in our own indigence: and what such consolations might perhaps have been. Theophylact: A penula, that is, a garment: for he laid this aside, lest he be forced to demand garments from others. For everywhere he took the greatest care not to be in need of the help of others, or to be a burden to anyone. Some, however, say that this was a small chest in which books were stored. But what need had he of books, who was soon to depart to GOD? Namely, that he might leave them to the faithful after his death, to have them in his place.

Ὃν ἀπέλιπον Τρωάδι) A city, of course, for it was not only the name of a region at that time, but also of a city, as we have said regarding the Acts. He had left this penula at that time, which is mentioned in Acts 20:6.

It is by no means fitting to refer this to that time. For that preceded this captivity of the Apostle by a long time, and was before the first captivity. But could not the Apostle, having been freed from the former, have come to Troas again? Who would believe, says Grotius, that after his liberation from his first bonds he did not return to Greece and Asia?

Παρὰ Κάρπῳ) It is a Roman name, so called, who was picking food in Petronius.

Ἐρχόμενος φέρε) Behold the poverty of such a great Apostle, who considered such a small thing, left so far away, among his losses.

Καὶ τὰ βιβλία) Small books written by the interpreters of the Old Testament, in which were legal customs and rites, the names of Jannes and Mambres, and the like.

But where did Grotius get the idea that these were such books, and contained such things? This is a mere arbitrary assertion. Those who wish a volume of Old Testament Scripture to be denoted by Φελώνην, understand by the books other codices written on paper: yet they are not of such rashness as to define it.

Μάλιστα τὰς μεμβράνας) This word is also Latin. They were skins adapted for the same use that papers exhibit, by the invention of King Attalus, whence they were also called Parchments. Varro, Pliny, and others are witnesses. The Greek interpreters here explain them as σωμάτια, διφθέρας. Many wrote on such membranes. Horace: 'With the membranes placed inside, you will be able to erase what you have not published.' Cicero to Atticus teaches us that indices were made from them. Paul did not have a library of Greek books: nevertheless, he had excerpted them on membranes for his own use, some from Epimenides, some from Aratus, some from Menander.

The Syrian rendered it as a bundle of volumes. Membranes are parchment sheets, and they seem to be designated as those on which Paul noted something for his memory, for which reason he was singularly concerned about them.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Τὸν φελόνην) Vox Graeca facta ex Latina: idque jam olim, cum & Rhetor Comicus Ptolemaeorum tempori- bus ea sit usus. Scribitur autem, ut solent externae vo- ces, variè, φαινόλης, ut apud Athenaeum, φανόλας, Φελώνης. In Glossario φαινόλης, τὸ φελόνιον, penula. Φελόνιον legi- mus etiam in Liturgia Chrysostomi, & in posteriorum Graecorum libris.

Chrysostomus de scriniolo, seu arcula libraria in- tellexit, quam Syrus more Ebraeo domum scripto- rum vocat. De volumine V. T. exposuit Hierony- mus ad Damas. Epist. CXXV. q. 2. quam senten- tiam inde confirmari ait B. Gerhardus, quia Φέλλov librum, id est corticem arboris notat; unde volu- mina olim fiebant. Ambrosiafter de veste Senato- ris. De pallio consulari alii explicant. Neutrum convenit Apostolo. Alii vestem sacram, vel ca- sulam notari volunt; sed illa Graecis Φαινόλη vo- catur. Plerique penulam vestem aptam imbri- bus ac frigori depellendo; quae lacerna Hierony- mo, Dial. 3. contra Pelag. interpretantur. Sed an etiam talia dictasse Apostolo Spiritum S. crede- mus? Etsi carnalia videantur, Scriptura tamen omnis quum θεόπνευςτος sit, nec de hac particula scripturae dubitandum. Habet ea etiam suam doctrinam: quod nec leviora aspernanda sint, quodque in hyeme adhuc usui penula esse possit, & ut paupertatem tanti Apostoli ne ignoremus, quae nos etiam soletur in nostra indigentia: & quae forte ejusmodi consolationes esse poterant. Theo- phylactus: Penulam, id est, vestem: Hanc enim de- posuit, ne ab aliis exigere indumenta cogatur. Ubi- que enim plurimum cavit, ne aliorum ope indigeret, aut cuiquam oneri esset: Nonnulli vero arculam hanc esse dicunt, qua libri reconderentur. Verum quid libris indiguit, qui propediem esset ad DEUM demigraturus? ut illos nimirum fidelibus post suam mortem relinqueret, quos sui loco haberent.

Ὃν ἀπέλιπον Τρωάδι) Urbs scilicet, nam non regionis id tantum nomen fuit eo tempore, sed & urbis, ut ad Acta diximus. Reliquerat autem hanc penulam eo tempore, cujus est mentio Act. 20. 6.

Ad illud tempus hoc referri minime convenit. Nam id longe antecessit secundum hanc captivi- tatem Apostoli, & prius fuit prima captivitate. Annon vero potuit Apostolus e priori liberatus denud Troadam venire? Quis credat, inquit Gro- tius, post liberationem ex primis vinculis non rever- sum esse in Graeciam & Asiam?

Παρὰ Κάρπῳ) Nomen est Romanum, ita vocatus, qui cibum carpebat apud Petronium.

Ἐρχόμενος φέρε) Vide paupertatem tanti Aposto- li, qui rem tantillam, tam longe relictam, inter damna censuerit.

Καὶ τὰ βιβλία) Libellos scriptos ab interpretibus Vet. Test. in quibus mores ritusque legales, nomina Jannis & Mambris similia.

Unde vero habuit Grotius, quod tales libri hi fuerint, & talia continuerint? Est haec mera ar- bitraria assertio. Qui per Φελώνην volumen Scri- pturae V.T. denotatum volunt, intelligunt per Bi- blia alios codices in chartis descriptos: ejus tamen temeritatis non sunt, ut definiant.

Μάλιστα τὰς μεμβράνας) Etiam haec vox Latina. Erant autem pelles aptatae in usum eundem, quem chartae exhi- bent, Attali Regis invento, unde & Pergamenae dictae. Testes Varro, Plinius & alii. Graeci hic interpretes ex- plicant σωμάτια, διφθέρας. In talibus membranis scribe- bant multi. Horatius: Membranis intus positis delere licebit, Quod non edideris. Cicero ad Atticum nos docet Indices inde factos. Paulus Bibliothecam librorum Graecorum non habebat: attamen in membranis ad usum suum excerpserat, alia ex Epimeni- de, alia ex Arato, alia ex Menandro.

Syrus fasciculum voluminum reddidit. Mem- branae sunt schedae pelliceae, & designari videntur ejusmodi, in quibus Paulus aliquid pro memoria annotavit, ideo singulariter de illis solicitus fuit.

## 4:14
Vers. 14.

Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils) The same man, of whom we spoke in Acts 19:33 and 1 Tim. 1:20. He did not wish well to Paul, when he was at Ephesus, falsely reporting many things heard from him. Ἐνδείξασθαι κακὰ and ποιεῖν for to do, so that someone might experience evils; You have also Gen. 50:15 and 17. ἔδειξας σκληρὰ Ps. 60:5. הראית.

Without doubt for this reason, because he had been excommunicated by Paul as a heretic, whence he also prepared a harsher winter for Paul in Nero's court, arguing that he was a seditious man and was attacking the ancient religion of the Jews, which had been permitted at Rome, (which is the conjecture of some,) and he resisted him and the doctrine of the Gospel more and more, as is held in v. 15. To some it seems ambiguous whether this is the same Alexander who is commemorated in 1 Tim. 1, 21.

May the Lord repay him according to his works) Both what he has done and what he will do. This is not of one cursing, but of one permitting all judgment to God, ἀποδῴη גמל. It is a prediction befitting an Apostle, says the respondent to the orthodox, CXXV. Perhaps he reads ἀποδώσει, as the Manuscript has, and the Syriac reads. But Clement of Alexandria reads ἀποδῴη and says in Strom. VII: even if one must use such a prayer, it should not be for the harm of men, unless one is aiming at the turning back of justice, and he should manage the request for those who have become past feeling in an orgiastic way.

Even not a few Latin MS. Codices, as Estius admits, and the Latin interpreters, Ambrosiaster, Pelagius, Primasius, Sedulius, as also Jerome in book III of the Dialogue against the Pelagians, c. 1, and in the exposition of chapter VIII of Ecclesiastes, read 'reddat' (may he repay): why therefore did the Canonized Vulgate depart from all of them as well as from the Greek Codices? Augustine varies. For in book XVI against Faustus, c. 22, he reads 'reddat', as Estius observes: since he teaches there how such imprecations are to be received, even though he used a faulty Latin Codex in book 1 of the Sermon on the Mount, c. 37, where he reads in the future 'reddet' (he will repay): He does not say, 'reddat', but 'the Lord will repay him according to his works', which is the word of one stating a fact, not of one cursing. But even if it is read in the Optative, which the Greek Codices allow, that does not stand in the way of the Apostle's piety: because since he understands from the prophetic Spirit that the repayment will certainly follow, as he testified to the Apostle's zeal when he was resisting those who were resisting the truth of the Gospel, with no hope of amendment remaining, he imprecates divine vengeance upon him insofar as it is just, both for the sake of others who ought to be terrified by his example, and for the sake of those who ought to be freed from his snares, and thus for the public good of the Church.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ χαλκεὺς πολλά μοι κακὰ ἐνεδείξατο) Idem ille, de quo diximus Actor. 19. 33. & 1. Tim. 1, 20. Noluit autem Paulo, cum is Ephesi esset, multa ab illo audita fal- so referens. Ἐνδείξασθαι κακὰ & ποιεῖν pro facere, ut quis mala sentiat; Habes & Gen. 50, 15. & 17. ἔδειξας σκλη- ρὰ Ps. 60, 5. הראית.

Sine dubio ideo, quod a Paulo ceu haereticus ex- communicatus esset, unde & Paulo in aula Neronis acriorem hyemem paravit, eum hominem seditio- sum, & veterem Judæorum religionem, quæ Ro- mæ permissa erat, impugnantem arguit, (quæ con- jectura quorundam est,) ac sibi & doctrinæ Evan- gelii magis magisque restitit, ut v. 15. habetur. Nonnullis ambiguum videtur, anne idem sit Ale- xander, qui 1. Tim. 1, 21. commemoratur.

Ἀποδῴη αὐτῷ ὁ Κύριος κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶ) Tam quæ fecit, quam quæ faciet. Hoc non est imprecantis, sed Deo judicium omne permittentis, ἀποδῴη גמל. Esse πρόῤῥησιν πρέπουσαν ἀνδρὶ Ἀποστόλῳ, ait responsor ad or- thodoxos CXXV. legit forte ἀποδώσει, quomodo habet Manuscriptus, & legit Syrus. At Clemens Alexandri- nus legit ἀποδῴη aitque Strom. VII. κἄν ἐκ ἐπὶ τῇ τῶν ἀνθρώπων βλάβῃ τῇ τοιᾷδε χρηστέον εὐχῇ ποτε πλὴν εἰ μὴ τὴν ἐπιστροφὴν τ̃ δικαιοσύνης τοχασζομένοις, τοῖς δὲ ἀπαλγη- κόσιν ὀργιαστικῶς οἰκονομοίη τὴν αἴτησιν.

Etiam Latini Codd. MS. non pauci fatente Estio, ac Interpp. Latini, Ambrosiafter, Pelagius, Prima- sius, Sedulius, ut & Hieronymus lib. III. Dial. contra Pelag. c. 1. & in exposit. cap. VIII. Eccles. legêre reddat: cur ergo ab illis omnibus ut & à Græcis Codd. recessit Vulgata Canonizata? Augustinus variat. Nam lib. XVI. contra Faust. c. 22. legit reddat, observante Estio: siquidem ibi doceat, quomodo eju modi imprecationes accipiendæ sint, tametsi vitioso Latino Codice usus l. 1. de serm. Dom. in monte cap. 37. legat in futuro reddet: Non ait, reddat, sed reddet illi Dominus secundum opera ejus, quod verbum pronunciantis est, non impre- cantis. Etsiarnsi autem legatur in Optativo, quod Græci Codd. possunt, non id pietati Apostoli ob- stat: quia cùm è prophetico Spiritu intelligat certo consequuturam ἀπόδοσιν, ut zelum Aposto- li cum adversus tales testaretur veritati Evangeli- cæ resistentes, nulla restante spe emendationis, di- vinam vindictam quatenus justa est, ipsi impreca- tur, tum aliorum causa, qui exemplo ejus terreri, tum istorum, qui ab ejus insidiis liberari debeant, adeoque publico Ecclesiæ bono.

## 4:15
Verse 15.

Whom you also beware of) Beware of him, as a man of dangerous habits: Theocritus also has φυλάττειν for 'beware'. See also Luke 12, 15.

Not so that he may not harm you through seduction, but primarily, so that he may not bring losses upon the Church through the agitation of others. For that error seems to have stirred up the Jews against the Church of Christ.

For he has greatly withstood our words) He will do the same to you if he finds any handle.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Ὃν καὶ σὺ φύλασσε) Cave eum, ut periculosæ consue- tudinis hominem: φυλάττειν pro cave habet & Theocri- tus. Vide & Luc. 12, 15.

Non ut ne noceat tibi per seductionem, sed im- primis, ut ne Ecclesiæ damna inferat per aliorum commotionem. Videtur enim error ille utique Judæos adversus Ecclesiam Christi excitasse.

Λίαν γὰρ ἀνθέστηκε τοῖς ἡμετέροις λόγοις) Idem tibi fa- cturus si quam ansam invenerit.

## 4:16
Verse 16.

In my first defense) Namely, after he had come to Rome again. A defendant is said to 'apologize' (ἀπολογεῖσθαι) when he pleads his case. In the Glossary: ἀπολογοῦμαι I defend. See Luke 21, 14. Acts 19, 33. c. 24, 10. c. 25, 8. c. 26, 1. 2. 21.

Estius cannot conclude from this that this Epistle was written immediately after his first arrival in the city, because it is not likely that he would signify this to Timothy only after many years: But neither is it necessary that we should think he signified it to him here for the first time, since he could have commemorated it here for another reason, and Cajetan replies: that Paul is speaking of a defense not the first of all, but the one which he had as the first after his second arrival in Rome. Which Grotius also admitted here. Theophylact agrees. In the first defense, which does he call that? This one, clearly: for when he was first brought before the most savage Nero, he escaped death, and in such a way that from that time he had the opportunity of preaching. But when he had instructed in the faith the man whom Nero had at home as his wine-taster, soon that man, raging with madness, both threw Paul into prison and a little later cut off his head.

No one stood by me, but all abandoned me) His acquaintances, clearly, fearing Nero's savagery. See Psalm 88, 9.

It seems it should be taken restrictively. Almost no one. For that is perhaps not to be said of Luke, because he did not stand by him.

Μὴ αὐτοῖς λογισθείη) Let it not be imputed, namely to this end, that they might not be allowed to fall into more serious sins on account of this. May there be for them a quick return to a better mind, as for Peter, לא נחשב See what we said regarding Luke ch. 23, 34.

Others more simply: Let this not be imputed to them, that is to say, as a fault. See Acts 7, 26.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ με ἀπολογίᾳ) Nempe postquam iterum Romam venerat. Ἀπολογεῖσθαι dicitur reus cum causam dicit. In Glossario: ἀπολογοῦμαι defendo. Vide Luc. 21, 14. Act. 19, 33. c. 24, 10. c. 25, 8. c. 26, 1. 2. 21.

Non potest hinc Estius colligere, hanc Episto- lam statim post primum adventum in urbem scri- ptam, eò quod post annos plures id Timotheo de- mum significatû, non sit verosimile: Sed nec neces- sum est, ut censeamus hic primum id ei significasse, cum alia de causa id hic commemorare potuerit, & respondet Cajetanus: Paulum loqui de defensione non omnium prima, sed quam primam habuit post secundum suum in Romam adventum. Quod et- iam Grotius hic admisit. Consentit Theophylact. Prima defensione, quam illam dicit? Hanc scilicet: nam cum primùm esset Neroni sævissimo adstitutus, mortem evasit, & ita, ut eo ex tempore prædicandi sibi esset facultas. Sed cum instruxisset ad fidem, quem Nero vini habebat domi prægustatorem, mox ille ve- fania furens, & Paulum conjecit in carcerem, & paulo post ei caput præcidit.

Οὐδείς μοι συμπαρεγένετο, ἀλλὰ πάντες με ἐγκατέλιπον) Familiares scilicet, Neronis sævitiam extimescentes. Vi- de Psalm. 88, 9.

Restrictè accipienda videtur. Nullus fere. Nam de Luca id forte non dicendum, quod ei haud adstiterit.

Μὴ αὐτοῖς λογισθείη) Ne imputetur, nempe in hoc, ut in graviora peccata, ob hoc labi sinantur. Sit illis citus ad meliorem mentem reditus, ut Petro, לא נחשב Vide, quæ ad Lucam diximus c. 23, 34.

Simplicius alii: Ne illis hoc imputetur, scili- cet ad culpam. Vide Act. 7, 26.

## 4:17
Ver. 17.

Ὁ δὲ Κύριός μοι παρέστη) He was a help: Thus you have παρέστη, Psalm 109, 30.

Καὶ ἐνεδυνάμωσέ με) עזר. See 1 Tim. 1, 12. Christ gave me strength according to the promise, Matt. 10, 19. 20.

Which seems rather to have been done by some peculiar apparition, as also the present [passage] Acts 27, 23 and the similar word ἐπιστὰς in Acts 23, 11 implies.

Ἵνα δι᾽ ἐμοῦ τὸ κήρυγμα πληροφορηθῇ) That the preaching might be fulfilled, that is, might attain its completion, resounding in the very court of Caesar. See above ch. 5.

Καὶ ἀκούσῃ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη) Many from the most diverse nations, who had business in the court; Martial, when he had enumerated very many peoples who were in the court of Caesar, adds: A diverse voice sounds: yet the voice of the peoples is one, When you are called the true Father of the Fatherland.

You may not inappropriately refer this, with Theodoret, to the time of the first captivity, as we hinted at v. 6: When he used his right of appeal and was sent to Rome by Festus, his defense was heard, he was acquitted, and he set out for Spain, and running to other nations brought them the light of doctrine. Therefore he called that the first defense which he used during that journey. Jerome, says Crocius, in the Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers: Eusebius book 2, Ecclesiastical History ch. 22, Bede, and others refer it to the earlier chains, when he had been bound in chains at Jerusalem and led to Rome, and lived for two years in free custody. Salmero, Baronius, and those who follow them, eagerly seize upon this to prove that the Epistle was written from the first chains. They do not prove it. For why would he not have mentioned those things which had happened a decade before? However, the explanation which pleased Grotius, concerning the first defense in this second captivity, not disapproved even by the blessed Gerhard: That the proclamation concerning Christ might be set forth with full confidence, namely through a free and public confession before Caesar: because in Paul's confession, so solemn and extraordinary, the Spirit of God was working, so much so that the spirits of those already believing were confirmed, and even those not yet believing were moved. Whether that was done immediately before Caesar Nero, or before an inferior judge. Estius here imagines the speech of the narrator: what had been said to him by the Lord through revelation, namely these or similar words: Be constant, do not fear: For it is still necessary that the preaching be fulfilled through you and that all nations hear. For thus this passage, when explained in this way, has the greatest possible similarity with both the passages of Acts already cited before. It is fulfilled in Greek πληροφορηθῇ, which some other person translates as 'confirmed', another renders the meaning thus: that through me the faith of the proclamation or preaching might be made. The opinion about the meaning of the Greek word, about which we have spoken enough elsewhere, deceives them. Erasmus, Lonicerus, and Hentenius are more correct in this place, who, with our interpreter, translated it as 'fulfilled' or 'completed'. Thus earlier in this same chapter: Fulfill your ministry. And the commentary of Theophylact and Oecumenius corresponds to this meaning. Finally, he explains it as that which here is added. And let all nations hear. But he invents this meaning τῇ ὑποθέσει δουλεύων, that this Epistle was written from the first captivity, which he himself established with Sasbaut, but he proves nothing from the present words, as Crocius notes: For they say that when he came to Rome a second time, he was not condemned in the first defense, but finally after nine months, when Nero had learned that Paul had converted his cupbearer, and had drawn away his concubines to the Christian faith.

And I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion) That is, of Nero, whom Seneca also called a lion, as the scholiast on Juvenal records. It is the custom of Scripture to call idolatrous princes, and those raging on account of idolatry, by the names of wild beasts, as Jacchiades notes on Daniel, where the Chaldean kings are described by the name of a Lion, and the Hebrews feel that Nebuchadnezzar is specially denoted under this name by Amos ch. 5, 19. See also Jerem. 2, 30. Joel 1, v. 6. Nah. 2, 12. Concerning Tiberius, it is in Josephus XXVIII. 8. The lion is dead. The Libyan lion Hannibal is in Silius Italicus. The idolatrous empire is described with lion's teeth, Rev. 13, v. 12. God did here what is in the proverb: To snatch prey from the mouth of a hungry lion. At the same time, there is an allusion to the passage in Daniel 6, 22.

He is called delivered not from chains, for he wrote this Epistle from chains, but from the present danger of death, which was not yet decreed for him at that time. He called Nero a lion, according to Chrysostom's interpretation, because of his ferocity, the strength of his empire, and his supreme power. From whom he was snatched, he does not express verbatim here. There are those who think he escaped by the zeal and effort of Seneca, who was familiarly known to Paul; whence also the Epistles of Seneca to Paul, and of Paul to Seneca, were already circulating in Jerome's time. But it can hardly be doubted that they are supposititious. And if human effort had intervened, perhaps the Apostle would not have been silent. Crocius.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Ὁ δὲ Κύριός μοι παρέστη) Auxilio fuit: Sic παρέστη ha- bes, Psalm. 109, 30.

Καὶ ἐνεδυνάμωσέ με) עזר. Vide 1. Tim. 1, 12. Christus vires mihi dedit ex promisso, Matth. 10, 19. 20.

Quod potius videtur factum apparitione qua- dam peculiari, uti & præsens Act. 27, 23. & simile verbum ἐπιστὰς Act. 23, 11. innuit.

Ἵνα δι᾽ ἐμοῦ τὸ κήρυγμα πληροφορηθῇ) Ut impleretur prædicatio, id est, consummationem suam consequeretur, in ipsa aula Cæsaris sonans. Vide supra c. 5.

Καὶ ἀκούσῃ πάντα τὰ ἔθνη) Multi ex diversissimis gen- tibus, quibus in aula negotium erat, Martialis, cum plurimos numerasset populos, qui in aula erant Cæsa- ris, addit: Vox diversa sonat: populorum vox tamen una est, Cum verus Patriæ d: ceris esse Pater.

Non incommode id referas cum Theodoreto ad tempus primæ captivitatis, ut ad v. 6. innuimus: Quando appellatione usus Romam à Fausto missus est, defensione audita fuit absolutus, & in Hispaniam profectus est, & ad alias gentes excurrens eis doctrinæ lucem attulit. Primam ergò vocavit defensionem, qua in illa profectione usus est. Hieronymus, inquit Crocius, in Catalogo Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum: Eusebius lib. 2. Hist. Eccles. c. 22. Beda, alii ad priora vincula referunt, cum Hierosolyma catena vinctus Romam esset deductus, & biennio in libera viveret custodia. Hoc Salmero, Baronius, & qui eos sequun- tur, arripiunt cupide, ut Epistolam ex primis vincu- lis scriptam esse evincant. Non evincunt. Cur enim non meminisset eorum, quæ ante decennium erant fa- cta? Explicatio tamen, quæ Grotio placuit, de pri- ma defensione in altera hac captivitate, non im- probata etiam B. Gerhardo: Ut præconium de Chri- sto plena fiducia proponeretur per liberam scil. & pu- blicam coram Cæsare confessionem: quia in Pauli con- fessione tam solenni extra ordinem Spiritus Dei ope- rabatur, adeò ut confirmarentur animi jam creden- tium, ac moverentur etiam nondum credentes. Sive immediate coram Cæsare Nerone, sive coram ju- dice inferiori id factum sit. Estius hic fingit ser- monem narrantis: quid sibi à Domino per revelatio- nem dictum fuerit, nimirum hæc aut similia verba: Constans esto, ne timeas: Adhuc enim oportet, ut per te prædicatio impleatur & audiant omnes gen- tes. Sic enim expositus hic locus maximam omnino similitudinem habet cum utroque loco Act. jam ante citato. Impleatur Græcè πληροφορηθῇ, quod alius quidam vertit confirmetur, alius sic reddit sententia: ut per me fieret fides præconii seu prædicationis. Fallit hos opinio de significatione vocabuli Græci, de quo satis alibi diximus. Rectius hoc loco Erasmus, Lonicerus, & Hentenius, qui cum nostro interprete, impleretur, aut expleretur, verterunt. Ita superius hoc eodem capite: Ministerium tuum imple. Et huic significationi respondet Theophylacti & Oecu- menii Commentarius. Deniq; eam explicat, quod hic adjungitur. Et audiant omnes gentes. Sed hunc sensum fingit τῇ ὑποθέσει δουλεύων, quod hæc Epi- stola è prima captivitate scripta sit, quod cum Sasbauto ipse statuit, sed è verbis præsentibus ne- quicquam probat, notante Crocio : Dicunt enim cum secundo venisset Romam, in prima defensio- ne non esse condemnatum, sed demum post no- vem menses, cum Nero cognovisset, Paulum con- vertisse suum Pincernam, & concubinas ab ipso abstractas ad fidem Christianam traduxisse.

Καὶ ἐῤῥύσθην ἐκ στόματος λέοντος) Id est, Neronis, quem leonem vocavit & Seneca, memorante ad Juve- nalem Scholiaste. Mos Scripturæ Principes idolola- tras, & ob idololatriam sævientes appellare ferarum nomine, ut notat ad Danielem Jacchiades, ubi Leonis nomine describuntur reges Chaldæi, & specialiter sub hoc nomine denotari Nabuchodonosorum ab Amoso cap. 5, 19. sentiunt Hebræi. Vide & Jerem. 2, 30. Joel. 1. v. 6. Nah. 2, 12. De Tiberio est apud Josephum XXVIII. 8. Τέθνηκεν ὁ λέων. Annibal Lybicus leo apud Silium Ita- licum. Imperium idololatricum describitur cum den- tibus Leoninis Apoc. 13. v. 12. Fecit hic Deus, quod in proverbio est : Esuriente Leone ex ore exsculpere prædam. Simul allusio est ad locum Danielis 6, 22.

Liberatus vocatur non è vinculis, nam ex vincu- lis hanc Epistolam scripsit, sed ex præsenti mortis discrimine, quæ tum nondum ei decreta. Leonem Neronem dixit, Chrysostomo interprete, pro feri- tate, & imperii robore, summaque potentia. A quo ereptus fuerit, hic verbatim non exprimit. Sunt, qui putent, studio ac opera Senecæ evasisse, qui Paulo fue- rit familiariter notus; unde etiam Epistolæ Senecæ ad Paulum, & Pauli ad Senecam jam Hieronymi tempore circumferebantur. Sed supposititias esse vix dubitari potest. Et si humana intervenisset opera, fortasse Apostolus non tacuisset. Crocius.

## 4:18
Ver. 18.

And the Lord will deliver me from every evil work) He does not say, he will deliver me always from the mouth of the lion: but he will deliver me, so that I may do nothing unworthy of a Christian, nothing unworthy of an Apostle. He will deliver, namely, by the powerful aid of the Spirit. See what is on Matth. 6, 16. In the manuscript, there is a new period here: ῥύσεταί με, without καὶ.

The Vulgate indeed has it in the past tense, he delivered me, but with the Greek codices, the Ambrosian, and other Latin MSS. opposing it, and the future tense is demanded by the added word σώσει. Estius acknowledges this, having disregarded the Tridentine Canonization; as do also Cornelius à Lapide and Magalianus. Although Blessed Gerhard also takes it concerning preservation from falling: yet with Blessed Luther he admits it can also be taken concerning deliverance from all evils, which is through death, which explanation is more convenient because of the following words, even if I should not be free from persecutions and dangers in this life, yet Christ the Lord will give me constancy in the faith and a final outcome, and will snatch me from all evils and dangers. And therefore Theophylact joins both evils, both of sin and of affliction: At that time, he says, he exempted me from bodily death: But after I have preached enough, I hope that he will undoubtedly deliver me not only from this bodily slaughter of mine, since I am already being poured out, but even from every evil work, that is, every sin, just as if he were saying: He will by no means allow me to grow weak in enduring this death, but will supply strength to resist sins even unto blood. For to be able, says Chrysostom, to stand against sin even unto blood, and not to yield, is to be rescued from another lion, namely the Devil: therefore it is a greater salvation than the former, when he is seen to be exposed and given over to death. Theodoret: He did not say, he will deliver me again from the Lion, but, from every evil work. For he knew that his life would come to an end entirely.

And will save me into his heavenly kingdom) It is a shorthand way of speaking, for he will save me and bring me into the kingdom. We have had a similar way of speaking in Acts 7, 9. and elsewhere. Concerning the word heavenly, see 1 Cor. 15, 4. Eph. 1, 3. 20. 2 Cor. 3, 10. ch. 6, 12. Philipp. 2, 10.

To whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.) We have had a similar doxology near the end of an Epistle in Rom. 16, v. 27. Philipp. 4, 20. and sometimes in the middle of epistles.

Behold, says Theophylact, now he imparts glory to the Son no less than to the Father, and praise: for he is the Lord.

Greet Priscilla and Aquila) For Paul had left them at Ephesus, Acts 18, 19.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Καὶ ῥύσεταί με ὁ Κύριος ἀπὸ παντὸς ἔργου πονηροῦ ) Non dicit, liberabit me semper ex ore Leonis : sed li- berabit me, ne quid agam Christiano, ne quid Apostolo indignum. Liberabit, nempe potente auxilio Spiritus. Vide, quæ ad Matth. 6, 16. in Manuscripto nova hic est periodus : ῥύσεταί με, sine καὶ.

Vulgata quidem habet in præterito, liberavit me, sed refragantibus Græcis codicibus, Ambrosiano, & aliis MS. Latinis, ac futurum postulat verbum additum σώσει. Agnoscit id Estius, susque deque habita Canonizatione Tridentina; nec non Cor- nelius à Lapide, & Magalianus. Quanquam vero B. Gerhardus etiam de conservatione à lapsu acci- piat: Cum B. Luthero tamen de liberatione ex omnibus malis, quæ per mortem sit, accipi etiam posse admittit, quæ explicatio ob verba sequentia convenientior, si vel maximè à persecutionibus & periculis in hac vita non sim liber futurus, dabit ta- men mihi Christus Dominus constantiam in fide & finalem ἔκβασιν, ac eripiet ex omnibus malis & periculis. Ideoque utrumque malum tum pec- cati, tum afflictionis conjungit Theophylactus: Tunc quidem, inquit, me à corporis morte exemit: Post- quam verò satis jam prædicavero, hunc haud dubie spero non modo mea corporea hac internecione libera- turum, quippe qui delibando jam sim, sed vel ab omni opere malo, hoc est, omni peccato, proinde ac si dicat: Nequaquam me sinet in morte hac toleranda flaccesce- re, sed ad usque sanguinem vires suppeditabit obsisten- di peccatis. Nam posse, inquit Chrysostomus, usque ad sanguinem stare adversum peccatum, nec cedere, ab alio leone, videlicet Diabolo, erui est: major itaq; salus, quam prior est, quando videtur exponi, atq; ad mortem dari. Theodoretus: Non dixit, liberabit me rursus à Leone, sed, ab omni opere malo. Scie- bat enim fore, ut vita omnino finem caperet.

Καὶ σώσῃ εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν ἀυτοῦ τὴν ἐπουράνιον) Est compendium loquendi, pro σώζων ἄξει με εἰς τὴν βασι- λείαν. Simile loquendi genus habuimus Actor. 7, 9. & alibi. De voce ἐπουρανίε vide 1. Cor. 15, 4. Eph. 1, 3. 20. 2. Cor. 3, 10. c. 6, 12. Philipp. 2, 10.

ᾯ ἡ δόξα εἰς τὲς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.) Similem δοξολογίαν circa finem Epistolæ habuimus Rom. 16. v. 27. Philipp. 4, 20. interdum & in mediis epistolis.

Ecce, inquit Theophylactus, nunc haud secus filio gloriam,quam Patri & laudem impartitur : is nam- que Dominus est.

Ἄσπασαι Πρίσκιλλαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν) Nam hos Paulus Ephesi reliquerat, Act. 18, 19.

## 4:19
Ver. 19.

Καὶ τὸν Ὀνησιφόρε οἶκον) Not Onesiphorus himself, as one who had already departed from this life. See above ch. 1, 16.

Theodoret held a different view: Because Onesiphorus was with Paul, he greeted his house, and through the greeting brought a blessing. And Chrysostom: For he himself was in Rome then, as he says elsewhere: May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord in that day. By this greeting, however, he makes his household more ready to imitate the virtues of the head of the family. Theophylact: (Onesiphorus' house,) he says, that is, those whom he has at home. For he himself was in Rome, having received him when detained in prison and chains. Compare what is said at ch. 1, 16. Dorotheus makes Prisca a man, and Bishop of Colophon: The others make her a woman. Theodoret has Priscilla from Acts 18, 26.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Καὶ τὸν Ὀνησιφόρε οἶκον) Non ipsum Onesiphorum, ut qui jam ex hac vita excessisset. Vide supra c. 1, 16.

Aliud visum Theodoreto: Quia erat apud Pau- lum Onesiphorus, salutavit illius domum, & per sa- lutationem benedictionem attulit. Et Chrysosto- mo: Ipse enim Roma tunc erat, sicut alibi dicit : Det ei Dominus invenire gratiam à Domino in die illa. Hac autem salutatione promptiores ejus dome- sticos facit ad patrisfamilias virtutes imitandas. Theophylacto: (Onesiphori domum,) inquit, hoc est,quos domi habet. Ipse nanq; Romæ erat,car- cere & vinculis detenti, susceperat. Conf. quæ ad c. 1, 16. Priscam Dorotheus virum facit, & Colo- phonæ Episcopum: Cæteri fœminam. Theodore- tus habet Priscillam ex Act. 28, 26.

## 4:20
Vers. 20.

Ἔραστος ἔμεινεν ἐν Κορίνθῳ) For he was the treasurer of that city, Rom. 16, 23. He had been sent into Macedonia by Paul, Acts 19, 22. Then he had returned to Corinth: and there he had remained, and had not come to Rome.

Since in the preceding, says Theophylact, he had made no mention of these, now he mentions them, and argues that he is destitute on all sides, so that he may soon compel Timothy to return to him.

Τρόφιμον δὲ) An Ephesian, Acts 20, 5. ch. 21, 29. He had accompanied Paul as far as Jerusalem.

Ἀπέλιπον ἐν Μιλήτῳ ἀσθενῶντα) I entirely agree with the most learned Beza, who reads ἐν Μελίτῃ. For the Arab also has this word here, by which he calls Melite in Acts 28, 1. On the journey from Jerusalem, Paul reached Melite, not Miletus. We see here incidentally that God, because He had given such gifts of healing to the Apostles, willed that some bodily infirmities should remain both in them and in their friends, so that it might appear that they were human. Thus Chrysostom here. Concerning the word ἀσθενεῖν see John 11, 1. 2.

But why must we necessarily depart from the received reading? Indeed, Baronius also, at the year 58, n. 144, wishes to read ἐν Μελίτῃ: But others say that Trophimus, coming from Jerusalem, from where he departed with Paul to Miletus, see Acts 20, 17. ch. 21, 29, returned to Miletus, and was there seized by illness. Bartholom. Petri in his annotations to Estius on this passage notes that there was also a city in Crete named Miletus, according to Homer, Iliad β, and Strabo, who was a Cretan, book XII, where Trophimus could have been left sick when Paul was sailing as a captive to Crete, Acts 27, 7. He writes these things not from the first, but from the last chains. Therefore, he could have left Trophimus at Miletus on another occasion. It is probable, therefore, says Crocius, that having been freed there in the first chains, he returned to Asia, Macedonia, and Greece, and then left the sick Trophimus at Miletus. Certainly, when he was in his first chains at Rome, he gives hope of his arrival to the Philippians, Phil. 2, 24. Philem. v. 22. To the Hebrews, Heb. 13, 23. With these statements, Salmero confirms the Pauline journey, vol. 12, tract. 59, page 380. What Baronius says, that Miletus crept into the text, is more easily said than proven. The things which Paul said in Acts 20, 25 about his face not being seen again can be understood in such a way that Paul did not know otherwise at that time, nor did the Holy Spirit reveal to him then that he would see Miletus again, Although he speaks not of Miletus, but of the Elders summoned there from Ephesus, who, or some of whom, might have died before he returned there. Chrysostom, whom Theophylact also followed, says: Miletus is near Ephesus; therefore, either he left him while sailing to Judea, or when he had been at Rome, he set out again for Spain. But whether he came again from there to these parts, we do not know.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Ἔραστος ἔμεινεν ἐν Κορίνθῳ) Erat enim urbis ejus arca- rius, Rom. 16, 23. Fuerat in Macedoniam missus a Pau- lo, Actor. 19, 20. Deinde Corinthum redierat : ibique manserat, nec venerat Romam.

Cum in superioribus, inquit Theophylactus, nul- lam horum mentionem fecisset,nunc meminit,arguit- que,se undique destitutum, ut Timotheum mox co- gat ad se redire.

Τρόφιμον δὲ) Ephesium, Act. 20, 5. c. 21, 29. Is Paulum comitatus erat Hierosolyma usque.

Ἀπέλιπον ἐν Μιλήτῳ ἀσθενῶντα) Omninò assentior do- ctissimo Bezæ, legenti ἐν Μελίτῃ Nam & Arabs hic eam vocem habet, qua Melitem appellat Actor. 28, 1. In iti- nere Hierosolymis Paulus Meliten attigit non Miletum. Videmus hic obiter Deum, quia tanta dona sanationum Apostolis dederat, aliquas voluisse corporis infirmitates & in ipsis, & in ipsorum amicis manere, ut appareret, eos esse homines. Ita hic Chrysostomus. De voce ἀσθε- νεῖν vide Joh. 11, 1. 2.

Cur verò necessariò à recepta lectione disce- dendum ? Ita quidem & Baronius ad ann.58.n.144. legi vult ἐν Μελίτῃ : Sed alii dicunt, Trophimum Hierosolymâ, quo cum Paulo Mileto discedens ve- nit, vid. Act. 20, 17. c. 22, 29. Miletum rediisse, ibique morbo correptum esse. Bartholom. Petri in annotatiunc. ad Estium in h. l. notat, etiam in Creta fuisse urbem,cui nomen esset Miletus, teste Ho- mero Iliad. β. & Strabone,qui Cretensis fuit, lib.XII. ubi relinqui potuerit Trophimus ægrotus, cum Cretam adnavigaret Paulus captivus, Actor. 27,7. Scribit hæc non è primis, sed postremis vinculis. Mileti ergo Trophimum alia occasione reliquisse potuit. Probabile igitur, inquit Crocius, illuc in primis vinculis liberatum, in Asiam, Macedoniam, & Greciam rediisse, ægrotum Trophimum tunc Mi- leti reliquisse. Certe cum in primis vinculis versa- retur Romæ adventus sui spem facit Philippensibus, Philipp.2, 24. Philem. v. 22. Hebræis, Ebr. 13, 23. His dictis Salmero Paulinam peregrinationem con- firmat tom. 12. tract. 59. pag. 380. Quod Baronius dicit, Miletum irrepsisse in textum, facilius dicitur, quam probatur. Quæ Act. 20, 25. Paulus dixit de facie sua haud videnda, ita intelligi possunt, quod tum aliter haud sciverit Paulus, nec Spiritus S. ipsi tum revelavit,quod illuc Miletum iterũ visurus sit, quanquam non de Mileto, sed de Senioribus ex E- pheso eo accersitis loquatur, qui vel quorum aliqui potuerint, antequam eo reverteretur, diem obiif- se. Chrysostomus, quem etiam secutus Theophyla- ctus est, Miletus, inquit, Epheso vicina est: aut igitur in Judæam navigans reliquit illum, aut cum fuisset Romæ, rursus in Hispaniam profectus est. An autem inde iterum ad has partes venerit, ignoramus.

## 4:21
Ver. 21.

Σπούδασον πρὸ χειμῶνος ἐλθεῖν.) Namely to Rome. See above 9, where we showed that Timothy obeyed this command. But here Paul adds 'before winter,' because navigation is dangerous in winter.

For since I am deserted on all sides (so Theophylact), as may be perceived, hasten your return to me with all zeal. And he says, do not come before I die. For that would bring him sorrow. But do not be prevented by winter so that you cannot be present, nor have the opportunity of visiting me. For that ought to be understood, even though he expressed it less clearly.

Ασπάζεταί σε ἕυβυλος.) It is an Attic name, by which a writer of comedies is called, another a historian, and another an opponent of Demosthenes.

Καὶ Πύδης ) Pudens. It is a Roman name found in Martial.

Καὶ Λῖνος) A presbyter at Rome. Clement mentions him in the Apostolic Constitutions: Irenaeus III. 3. Eusebius III, 2. 4. V, 6. and others. It is a Greek name.

Καὶ Κλαυδία) Claudia or Clodia (for both are the same) is a frequent female name at Rome.

No mention of Eubulus is made elsewhere in the sacred writings. Pudens

is said to have been a man of Senatorial rank among the Romans, the father of Praxedes and Potentiana, according to the Martyrology on the 14th of the Kalends of June: Claudia was his wife. Concerning Pudens and Claudia, there exists a Syntagma by Franc. Moncaeus under the title 'The Royal Cradles of the Ancient British Church,' with observations here by Bartholom. Petri.

Καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ πάντες) Who were already many at Rome, as appears in Rom. 1, 8. Philipp. 4, 22.

None of these, as Theophylact says, does he express by name. For since there was a very great multitude of the faithful, he explains by name only those who were both more illustrious, and had already escaped every desire for human things, and were burning with the ardor of the Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Σπούδασον πρὸ χειμῶνος ἐλθεῖν.) Nempe Romam. Vi- de supra 9. ubi ostendimus paruisse huic præcepto Timo- theum. Hic vero Paulus addit ante hyemem, quia peri- culosa est hyeme navigatio.

Cum enim undiq; deferor (ita Theophylactus) ut percipi licet, omni studio tuum ad me accelera redi- tum. Nec priusquam moriar, inquit, accedito. Id namque mœrorem illi adferret. Sed ne hyeme inter- ceptus adesse nequeas, nec me visendi habeas faculta- tem. Id enim subintelligi debet, tametsi minus ex- pressit.

Ασπάζεταί σε ἕυβυλος.) Nomen est Atticum, quo ap- pellatur Comœdiarum scriptor, historicus alter, & alius Demosthenes adversator.

Καὶ Πύδης ) Pudens. Nomen Romanum est apud Martialem.

Καὶ Λῖνος) Presbyter Romæ. Meminere Clemens constitutionibus Apostolicis: Irenæus III. 3. Eusebius III, 2. 4. V, 6. & alii. Nomen est Græcum.

Καὶ Κλαυδία) Claudia sive Clodia (nam idem est utrumque) nomen muliebre frequens Romæ.

Eubuli in sacris nulla aliàs facta mentio. Pudens

Vir Senatorii ordinis dicitur fuisse apud Roma- nos, Pater Praxedis, & Potentianæ, teste Martyro- logio ad 14. Cal. Junii: Claudia uxor ejusdem. De Pudente ac Claudia extat Franc. Moncæi Syntagma sub titulo Ecclesiæ Britannicæ veteris incunabula Regia, observante hic Bartholom. Petri.

Καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ πάντες) Qui multi jam erant Romæ, ut apparet Rom. 1, 8. Philipp. 4, 22.

Horum neminem, dicente Theophylacto, nomine exprimit. Nam cum maxima esset fidelium multi- tudo, illos duntaxat nomine explicat, qui & clariores essent, & humanarum rerum omnem jam evasissent cupidinem, & Spiritus ardore pollerent.

## 4:22
The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit) Thus also Gal. 6:18. Philem. v. 25. The Lord be with you, Ruth 2:4. There God is called Lord: here, however, Christ.

May he save and guard your soul. So also Crocius: He names the principal part of man, to which when the Lord is present, he cannot but be present to the whole man. Therefore he does not say, with your body, not because he had no regard for the body, but because the soul is the better part, and spiritual aid prevails over bodily, nor can it go ill with the body of him with whose spirit the Lord is.

Grace be with you) This Paul added with his own hand. See 2 Thess. 3:18. Thus also Col. 4:18. Tit. 3:15.

The Greek interpreters explain it as with you. But the Greek codices consistently retain that reading; and by the same reasoning the Epistle to Titus is concluded.

Glory be to the Father, glory be to the Son, glory to the Holy Spirit, glory be to the Sacred Trinity!

Latin:

Ὁ Κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματός σου) Sic & Gal. 6, 8. Philem. v. 25. Dominus vobiscum, Ruth, 2, 4. ibi Deus dicitur Dominus: hic vero Christus.

Servet & custodiat animam tuam. Ita & Crocius: Partem hominis principem nominat, cui cum adest Dominus, non potest non adesse toti homini. Ideo non ait, cum corpore tuo, non quod nullam corporis ha- buerit rationem, sed quia anima pars potior, & auxi- lium spirituale prævalet corporali, neq; potest male il- lius corpori esse, cum cujus Spiritu Dominus est.

Ἡ χάρις μεθ' ὑμῶν) Hoc Paulus addidit manu sua. Vide 2. Thess. 3, 18. Sic & Coloss. 3, 18. Tit. 3, 15.

Græci interpretes exponunt μεθ' ὑμῶν. Sed Co- dices Græci constanter istam lectionem retinent; & eadem ratione concluditur Epistola ad Titum.

Gloria sit Patri, sit Nato gloria, sancto Gloria Spiritui, Triadi sit gloria Sacra!

# Titus

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N. J. ANNOTATIONS ON THE EPISTLE TO TITUS.

Latin:

I. N. J. ANNOTATA AD EPISTOLAM AD TITUM.

## 1:1 Introduction: Grotian Preface
GROTIAN PREFACE.

I do not see that the Apostle Paul was in Crete, except on that journey on which he was taken from Jerusalem to Rome, Acts 27:7. But there were many who, out of love for Paul, added themselves as companions to his voyage, among whom were Tychicus and Trophimus, 2 Tim. 4:20, and Aristarchus, Col. 4:10, and many others, among whom was also Titus, 2 Tim. 4:10. Paul, when he was passing Crete, seeing the beginnings of churches there, I believe from that dispersion after Stephen, had left him behind to do those things which were of a Metropolitan. I think Chrysostom and others do not judge badly that this Titus was a Corinthian by birth, because his name is in many codices, Acts 18:7. It seems to me, however, as it did to others before me, that this epistle was written either at Rome, or from some other place in Italy, between Paul's first and second imprisonments, at which time he was free and serving the Gospel. At that time, however, his intention was to cross into Epirus. For Jerome, and other Latins, more correctly understand here the Nicopolis of Epirus, which took its name from Augustus's victory at Actium, than the Greeks, who send us into Thrace.

Latin:

PRÆFATIO GROTIANA.

IN Creta non video fuisse Paulum Apostolum, nisi in illo itinere, quo ab Hierosolymis tractus Romam, Actor. 27, 7. Multi autem erant, qui amore Pauli se navigationi ejus addiderunt comites, quorum fue re Tychicus & Trophimus, 2. Tim. 4, 20. & Aristar- chus, Col. 4, 10. & multi alii, inter quos & Titus, 2. Tim. 4, 10. Eum Paulus, cum Cretam transiret, initia ibi Ec- clesiarum videns, credo ex illa dispersione post Stephanum, reliquerat, ad ea agenda, quæ erant Metropolitæ. Puto non male arbitrari Chrysostomum & alios, fuisse hunc Ti- tum domo Corinthium, quia nomen ejus est in multis co- dicibus, Act. 18, 7. Videtur autem mihi, ut & aliis ante me, scripta hæc epistola aut Romæ, aut ex alio aliquo Ita- liæ loco, inter prima & altera Pauli vincula, quo tempore liber serviebat Evangelio.
