Eo autem tempore proposi- tum illi erat transire in Epirum. Nam Epiri Nicopolim, quæ ab Actiaca Augusti victoria nomen habuit, rectius hic intelligit Hieronymus, & Latinorum alii, quam Græci, qui nos in Thraciam mittunt.

## 1:1 Introduction: Observations with Other Prolegomena
OBSERVATIONS WITH OTHER PROLEGOMENA.

Grotius has prefaced five chapters: I. On the Church in Crete. II. On Titus, his office and fatherland. III. On the place where this epistle was written. IV. On the time of writing. V. On Nicopolis, of which he made mention. To which we will add five others, namely: VI. On the occasion of the epistle. VII. On the scope. VIII. On the Argument. IX. On the Authority. X. On the Partition.

As to I. regarding the Church in Crete. This island, which today is called Candia, became a seat of the Church, if you listen to Grotius; not so much by the work of the Holy Apostle Paul as from an accidental confluence. For he says that the Apostle already found the beginnings of churches there; which he believes arose from the dispersion of the Jews after Stephen. But that it was Jews, not Gentiles, who first professed the faith of Christ in Crete is in no way made likely, much less that they flowed there from that ἐ διασπορᾷ. For how will faith be reconciled to these ἐνγήμασι or αἰτήμασι? Did not Paul rather devote effort to preaching the Gospel where the name of Christ was not known, so as not to build upon a foreign foundation? Rom. 15, 20. Was he not appointed Doctor of the Gentiles rather than of the Jews? Acts 9, 15. Rom. 15, 16. Gal. 1, 6. ch. 2, 8. 1 Tim. 2, 7. But if it be asked when the Apostle came to the island of Crete? Grotius confuses the times. He says he was not in Crete, except on that journey in which he was dragged from Jerusalem to Rome, Acts 27, 7. But it is not said there that he came to Crete then, but ὑπεπλεύσαμεν, says Luke, the companion of the Apostle, τὴν Κρήτην κατὰ Σαλ- μώνην, we sailed by Crete near Salmone, the Vulgate rendered; from v. 4 it is clear that it signifies we sailed under Crete near Salmone, where the Vulgate has, we sailed under Cyprus, or we went around near Crete, according to the Syriac and the Arab: Beza explained, we sailed along Crete. It is added: μόλις τε παραλεγόμενοι αὐτὴν ἤλθομεν &c. Vulgate: And with difficulty (that is, laboriously) sailing by it we arrived. Beza: And with difficulty sailing past it we arrived. From that account it is clear that at that time the Apostle did not come to Crete; Luke does not narrate that Tychicus and Trophimus were present with Paul, much less does he claim Aristarchus was present, ch. 27, 2. Trophimus is indeed said to have been left at Miletus, 2. Tim. 4, 10. where he prefers to read Melita, and that regard be had to

Acts 28:1. But history does not testify that Trophimus was present with Paul in Malta, nor should it be read there otherwise than as the Greek Codices have it. If, however, Trophimus was then with the Apostle on the island of Malta and in Crete, when he came to Rome and was thrown into the chains from which he wrote his second epistle to Timothy, it must be that the present epistle to Titus is in that way later than the second epistle to Timothy; but because the latter was written from his final chains, it is manifest that the voyage in Acts 27, by which he was being taken to Rome when he was first to be thrown into chains there, has nothing to do with this. Nothing could be brought forward regarding Tychicus's presence in Crete either, whom he says he sent alone from Rome to Ephesus, 2 Tim. 4:12, which was likewise done during Paul's second captivity, and he promises that he wishes to send him to Titus, Tit. 3:12. Finally, neither is Titus said to have been present as Paul's companion or associate when he was being taken to Rome, of whom no mention is made anywhere in the Acts, nor in the approved Codices, ch. 18:17. It is indeed read there in some copies that Paul came to the house of someone at Corinth by the name of Τίτε Ἰέστε; but most Codices omit the name of Titus, nor is it established that this Titus, the Bishop of the Cretans, was called Justus; so far is it from being the case that one should believe that this Justus, the Corinthian host of Paul, was Titus. However, the opinion of those who think that Paul, when he had departed from Ephesus and was traveling through Macedonia and Greece, passed through Crete on that journey and first preached the Gospel there, is more likely. But that he could not remain there for long, because he had to hasten to other places, and therefore left Titus, as his faithful disciple, there on the island of Crete. Which most noble island, situated in the middle of the Pontus, which according to Strabo the Cretan is washed by the Aegean and Cretan seas from the North, by the Libyan from the South, and they say it encompasses 589 miles in circumference, nowhere exceeds fifty miles in width, and in the middle part of itself, where it is most wide, fills 270 miles in length, and contains one hundred cities, whence Homer called it ἑκατόμπολιν in Iliad β.

II. Concerning Titus.

As for II to Titus, he was a Gentile by both parents, and a Greek, Gal. 2:2, converted by Paul to the faith of CHRIST, therefore he is called his son, Tit. 1:4, whom nevertheless he did not wish to circumcise because of false brothers, who were urging the necessity of circumcision, although he had circumcised Timothy to avoid the scandal of the Jews, Gal. 3: v. 2. Whether he was a Corinthian is in doubt, nor does Chrysostom affirm it for certain: He was, he says, perhaps a Corinthian, unless there was some other person among them by the same name. However, there is no doubt that he was very familiar to the Corinthians, just as he also seems to have been a teacher of that Church for a time, whom they received with fear and trembling, 2 Cor. 7:15, and who, having set out for Paul from Corinth, when he had not found him in Troas, and had come into Macedonia for the sake of seeking him, reported how much the Corinthians were held by a longing for him, 2 Cor. 11, 12, 13, ch. 7:6, 7, 13, 14, whom he also sent to the Corinthians to collect alms, 2 Cor. 8:6, 16, 17, and into Dalmatia for the sake of the Church, 2 Tim. 4:10. He was not only a beloved disciple of Paul, but also a faithful companion and helper, as 2 Cor. 8:23.

concerning him, he says, my partner and fellow-worker for you, whom he also calls a brother in 2 Cor. 2:13, who walked with him in one Spirit and in the same footsteps, 2 Cor. 12:18. Grotius says that he was left in the churches of the island of Crete to do those things which belonged to a Metropolitan or Archbishop. But in that age those names and offices of Bishops, Archbishops, and metropolitans were not in use: as they imply, namely, a superiority of jurisdiction in the Papacy, and finally began to be introduced after the age of the Apostles. One may, however, call him a Bishop or General Superintendent, as they are called among us today, of all Candia: left there by the Apostle for that end, that he might set in order, ἐπιδιορθώσῃ, what the Apostle could not set in order due to the shortness of time, and might appoint Presbyters throughout the cities. Paul called him out of Crete, so that he might come to him at Nicopolis, into which Paul, having traveled through Macedonia, had decided to settle and to winter there. Afterwards, Chytræus in his Onomasticon thinks that Paul, having changed his plan, ordered Titus to come to him at Troas, where, when Paul had not found Titus (2 Cor. 2), he had crossed into Macedonia. See Jerome, Questions to Hedibia. Meanwhile, continues B. Chytræus, Titus of his own accord (2 Cor. 8) had sailed to Corinth, where, having explored the mind of that Church toward Paul, he sets out for Macedonia, where Paul, then staying there, was wonderfully refreshed by the arrival of Titus (2 Cor. 7). At that time Paul wrote the second epistle to the Corinthians, and sent it to Corinth by Titus and Luke the Evangelist, 2 Cor. 8:13. Afterwards he was present with Paul the captive at Rome for some time. Thence he set out for Dalmatia, 2 Tim. 4. In the readings of the saints it is written that he returned to Crete and died there, in the 94th year of his age. These are the words of B. Chytræus; who also says that he was present at the Council of Jerusalem, Acts 15. Jerome notes in his preface that his place in the Cretan oversight was committed to others for a time: The Apostle, he says, commands Titus that when either Artemas or Tychicus has arrived in Crete, he himself should come to Nicopolis. For it was just that he who had said, my anxiety for all the churches: and who, setting out from Jerusalem, had founded the Gospel of Christ as far as Illyricum, should not suffer both himself and the Cretans to be deserted by the absence of Titus, from whom the seeds of idolatry first sprouted; but that he should send to them in his and Titus's place Artemas or Tychicus, by whose teaching and comfort they might be cherished.

As for III, regarding the place of this written epistle, it seems to Grotius that it was written either at Rome or at some other place in Italy. But whence does Grotius have that? Why indeed not at Nicopolis, as the subscription has it? Crocius says that it is supposititious, and that this epistle was not written at Nicopolis, is evident even from this, that he does not write, ch. 3, 12, Ἐνταῦθα γὰρ κέκρικα παραχειμάσαι, but ἐκεῖ γὰρ κέκρικα παραχειμάσαι. He was not yet, therefore, at Nicopolis when he wrote these things. But it could be said that these things were written at the beginning of winter, as if to say, at Nicopolis, where I am now, you will find me. For I am going to remain there the whole winter. Be that as it may, says Estius, this at least appears, that this epistle was sent from Achaia. It seems safest here to leave the location undecided.

As for IV, regarding the time, Grotius says it was written between the first and second imprisonments, at which time he was serving the Gospel, and it was his intention to go to Nicopolis, Tit. 3, 16. Most say it was written before the first bonds. Concerning which Crocius says: The epistle to Titus, he says, is thought to have been written within a six-month space, after the Ephesian tumult, stirred up by Demetrius, after the second epistle to the Corinthians and before the epistle to the Romans. Baronius refers it to the fifty-eighth year of Christ, the second of Nero. Baronius clearly thinks that the Apostle, at that time when he set out from Macedonia (as is read in Acts 20) into Greece, did not come immediately by a direct route into Greece, but having used a voyage, first landed in Crete, and having preached the Gospel there, and having left his disciple Titus to take care of the Church of that region, finally arrived in Greece or Achaia; where Luke in the same chapter 20 of Acts testifies that Paul stayed for three months. Therefore he thinks this epistle was written at that time. Now that time falls in the second year of Nero's reign: as Estius has it here. Who indeed adds: But it must be seen whether this opinion of Baronius sufficiently agrees with those things which are read in 2 Cor. 11. Others refer it to the eighth year of Nero, the sixty-third of Christ, the twenty-eighth of Paul's apostleship.

As for V. to Nicopolis, concerning which Tit. 3, 12, Grotius thinks it is not of Thrace, as the Greeks wish, but of Epirus, with Jerome and other Latins, bordering on Greece; since that was not far distant from Philippi. Concerning which Büntingius in his Itinerary, page 262: Nicopolis, a city of Macedonia, where the Apostle Paul wrote his epistle to Titus, is situated at the river Nessus, not far from Philippi, in the borders of Thrace, two hundred and thirty miles from Jerusalem towards the North-West wind, which blows partly from the West and partly also from the North. B. Chytreus seems to leave the matter in the middle in his Onomasticon, under the word Nicopolis: which in an obscure matter is perhaps the safest.

VI. We approach the occasion, which is assigned as threefold: Athanasius brings forward the former in his Synopsis: that in the island of Crete many, under the pretext of the law, tried to seduce the believing people; when the Apostle learned of this, he wrote this epistle to Titus, concerning which chapter 1, 10, 14. Others give a second, that his authority was held in contempt by the contumacious and ambitious no less than by the seducers, so that he could less execute the pious and salutary commands of the Apostle according to the Apostle's wish. Therefore, so that he might apply himself to his duty all the more powerfully, and perform it happily, the Apostle arms him through this epistle with his authority, as if he were imposing his own supreme person upon him, or were already presenting himself in person, as Flacius has it here. Nor were there lacking those who neglected the political order and the pursuit of good works under the pretext of the Gospel, whom he notes in chapter 2, 12, chapter 3, 18. To which, thirdly, was added that it had to be guarded against that, in the passage of time, less suitable persons should intrude themselves into ecclesiastical offices, whence the Apostle wished to prescribe here the rules concerning the appointing of Presbyters.

VII. The scope therefore proposed to the Apostle was, both that the sincere doctrine might be propagated in that island, to repeat its summary and heads, and that the seducers, as well as the contumacious, might be countered, to instruct Titus with authority and counsel, and to prescribe certain canons for all estates, and that none but the worthy should be placed in charge of the duties of teaching, to hand down the requirements for Bishops or Doctors.

VIII. Whence the argument of the epistle is not obscure: which it pleases to subjoin from the Synopsis of Athanasius: In the beginning, he says, having given thanks to God on account of his piety, he indicates that faith in Christ is not a recent invention: but prepared from the age and promised by God. Then he teaches concerning the appointing of clerics, how they ought to conduct themselves, and what kind they ought to be. He also commands him to rebuke those who contradicted the sound faith, especially those who were of the circumcision, and to know that the Cretans are idle, and have need of rebuke. And after he taught that all kinds of food are clean to the clean, and what kind the older women ought to be, whose duty it is to chastise the young women, he admonishes how servants ought to be subject to their masters. Finally, when he has admonished that the grace of the Savior has justified us not from works, but from Divine kindness, and has declared that he should avoid legal strifes as rash and impudent, he signifies to him that as soon as he has sent Artemas to him, he should come to him. He also commands that he should teach his hearers to excel in good works, and thus he ends the epistle.

IX. Jerome reports in Vol. VI, in the Preface to Paula and Eustochium, that Marcion and Basilides called the authority of the epistle into doubt. But with no reasons brought forward: But for the establishing of the same, there serves 1. The Author called and illuminated immediately by God. 2. The truth, holiness, and entirely Divine nature of the oracles of the doctrine. 3. The Apostolic style. 4. The efficacy of the doctrine. 5. The consensus and conformity with the remaining undoubtedly Divine writings, especially with both to Timothy, concerning which epistles Augustine writes in book IV of Christian Doctrine, chapter 16: Which three epistles he who has the role of Teacher in the Church imposed upon him ought to have before his eyes. 6. The received sign of an Apostle, at the end of the epistle, concerning which 2 Thess. 3:17. 7. The unanimous consensus of the Church. 8. The testimony of the Holy Spirit, persuading the faithful that this epistle is truly Divine. Jerome appeals here to the assertion of Tatian: But Tatian, the Patriarch of the Encratites, who himself also rejected some of Paul's epistles: believed this one most of all, that is, the one to Titus, to be proclaimed as the Apostle's, thinking little of the assertion of Marcion and others who agree with him in this part.

X. Three parts of the epistle can be assigned: I. The title or inscription. II. The treatment. III. The conclusion of the epistle; But a dichotomy pleases, when we look especially at the Apostolic treatment. The former is didactic, containing instruction, both concerning the requirements of Teachers of the Church, chapter 1, and concerning the duties of Hearers in any kind of life, chapter 2. The latter is hortatory, in which are common and particular memoranda, and also some singular things concerning Titus, Titus 3. However, the individual chapters have evangelical sentences intermixed, like very distinguished gems. In the first, in the title itself, concerning the evangelical ministry: In the second, concerning the mystery of redemption: In the third, concerning justification and salvation given freely on account of Christ: Which render the epistle, although short, most precious.

PART I. DIDACTIC. SECTION I. CONCERNING THE REQUIREMENTS OF TEACHERS. CHAPTER I. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

The inscription having been premised, but with the dignity of the evangelical ministry shining more brightly, in the The Apostle recalls to Titus the memory of why he left him in Crete, and assigns the requirements of the Presbyters or Ministers of the Church, both moral and intellectual virtues, for instructing, exhorting, and refuting, given the necessity brought about by various seducers, especially the Jews, and the notorious character of the Cretans, so that they might not attend to Jewish fables and the commandments of men concerning the distinction of foods, since to the pure all things are pure, and such holiness of theirs is mere hypocrisy.

There are two parts: I. The inscription with a prayer up to verse 4. II. The description of the Doctors of the Church, what sort of men they ought to be, regarding life up to verse 8, and regarding doctrine up to verse 16.

PART I. The title of the Epistle and the inscription.

Ver. 1.

Paul, a servant of God) All Christians are indeed servants of God, 1 Pet. 2:16. But this title belongs especially to the Apostles, who are often elsewhere called servants of Christ. But here the Apostle wished to begin from the Principal cause.

In the title those three customary things occur: The subscription or designation of him from whom the epistle is written: The inscription, peculiarly so called, to whom it is inscribed: and the prayer or salutation. The subscription is made in more august words than is almost ever the case, if you except the epistle to the Romans, by which he professes himself both a servant of God and an Apostle or legate of Christ, in such a way that he wonderfully describes the dignity of his ministry, which he held in common with Titus, and indeed with all the Presbyters of whom he was about to speak, and places an idea of it, as it were, before the eyes in the very frontispiece of the epistle. He calls himself a servant of God, not in the general sense by which all creatures, or even men by right of creation, serve God, nor in the special sense by which all are indeed bound to serve God on account of redemption, but the faithful, born of God, serve Him in the very act, Luke 1:74, 1 Pet. 2:6. Rev. 19:5, but in a singular sense and one proper to the ministry of the Word, by which reason Moses is called the servant of God on account of his legation, Deut. 34:5, Acts 15:3, and the Apostles, Acts 4:29, and other Ministers of the Word on account of the calling which they have from God, and the peculiar servitude which they render to God, as Stewards of the mysteries of God, 1 Cor. 4:1, 2 Tim. 2:24. But when Paul calls himself a servant of God, he by no means designates God the Father as the Principal cause with respect to the Son: for of those whose essence is one, the notion of a Principal cause and one different from the principal has no place: But rather, because elsewhere they are similarly called servants of CHRIST, as the Apostle says of himself, Rom. 1:1, Gal. 1:10, where he opposes CHRIST to men (which was also done in chap. 1, ver. 1), and of himself and Timothy, Phil. 1:1, and likewise Peter, 2 Epist. 1:1, James, chap. 1:1. Jude v. 1. professes, concludes Chrysostom, with Theophylact agreeing: that there is οὐδεμίαν διαφορὰν (no difference) between the Father and the Son. See, he says, how indifferently he puts these things, while he sometimes calls himself a servant of God and an Apostle of CHRIST: but at other times he calls himself a servant of CHRIST, saying: Paul, a servant of JESUS CHRIST, so little does he know of any difference between the Father and the Son.

And an Apostle of Jesus Christ) This title is in almost all the openings of the Pauline epistles.

Not content to call himself a servant of God, which all Ministers of the Word are, he also professes himself an Apostle of Jesus Christ, because that grace and dignity of Apostleship fell to him in a peculiar way, than which there is no greater in the order of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, so that he might win authority for the epistle through the Apostolic legation over all the Churches of Crete. Concerning which St. Jerome says in this place: Furthermore, what he says: 'But an Apostle of Jesus Christ.' It seems to me as if he had said: Prefect of the praetorium of Augustus Caesar, master of the army of Tiberius the Emperor. For just as the judges of this world, the more noble they appear to be from the Kings whom they serve, and from the dignity with which they swell, the more they obtain titles: So also the Apostle, claiming for himself a great dignity among Christians, prefixed the title of Apostle of Christ, so that he might terrify those about to read by the very authority of the name, indicating that all who believed in Christ ought to be subject to him.

According to the faith of God's elect) Κατὰ here signifies that toward which the Evangelical function tends, 2 Tim. 1:1, namely, to the sowing of that faith through which men become the elect of God, that is, most dear to God. The genitive ἐκλεκτῶν here signifies the effect. And they are called the elect of God, just as they are called διδακτοὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ (taught of God) John 6:45.

The ministry is described by reason of all its causes. For as the efficient cause is Jesus Christ, who chooses, calls, and appoints the Apostles and other Ministers, whose legates and ministers they are, 1 Cor. 4:1, 2 Cor. 5:20, so the material cause is designated by the words κατὰ πίστιν ἐκλεκτῶν Θεοῦ, because it is occupied with the Elect of God and their faith. By the Elect of God some understand other believers, others—since believers can also be πρόσκαιροι—those who are elected to eternal life. The commentary which is ascribed to Jerome has it thus: According to that faith by which the believers are elected, when they acknowledged the truth, which acknowledgment is not from merit, but from the Lord's truth. With B. Balduinus as author, he calls it the faith of the Elect, which is the principal requirement of election. For He chose us in the faith of the truth, 2 Thess. 2:13, and it is the perpetual mark of the Elect, who are not found outside the assembly of the faithful. Therefore it is called the faith of the Elect of God, because it is the faith of all these, and is kindled and fostered through the mere work of the Apostleship and evangelical ministry; although saving faith and salvation itself are intended for all men. But Chrysostom's explanation is more foreign, as if the Apostle were saying by these words that the elect were entrusted to him; unless it is understood that he is an Apostle for the sake of the elect, who were certainly entrusted to him, so that they might be led to faith. But the words do not imply that. Only κατὰ πίστιν, that is, either 'concerning,' as B. Balduinus from Rom. 8:15, or rather 'to faith,' because the scope and end of the ministry is faith, and indeed such as is that of the Elect of GOD, that is, truly saving, which they would wish to generate in all, as much as lies within them, just as Camerarius: κατὰ πίστιν is 'to faith,' so that κατὰ sounds like πρός. And Osiander: I am sent that I may teach the true faith in CHRIST: not that which the reprobate boast of, but that which the elect have, whom GOD from eternity predestined to receive perpetual happiness: I teach, I say, that faith by which heavenly truth is acknowledged. Flacius says it can be explained 'according to faith': That Paul professes himself to be an Apostle and Teacher according to faith, not against or outside of faith of the elect, as if he were saying: that his faith and doctrine agree with those of all the elect and saints from the foundation of the world, or that it is plainly orthodox and catholic. And Beza had also explained it thus in this place.

And the knowledge of the truth) Faith precedes. A greater knowledge follows daily. So also Eph. 4:13. From faith to knowledge, says Clement, Strom. IV.

Of that which is according to godliness) Again, kata signifies that toward which one tends. For both faith and knowledge are given for this purpose, that one may live piously. So also 1 Tim. 6:3, 'the doctrine which is according to godliness'.

Saving faith does not precede, but includes knowledge; otherwise faith would be blind, being utterly destitute of the knowledge of the thing which is to be embraced by faith—the sort of blind and 'coal-heaver' faith that Papists require. It is therefore a hendiadys for faith and the knowledge of the truth, that is, for a fiducial knowledge, because a bare awareness of the truth does not suffice, but it must be joined with trust: which tends entirely toward piety. Because without piety, faith is not living and true, but dead and spoken of equivocally, as is taught in James 2. Beza observes in this place that epignosis implies not only knowledge, but the recognition of the truth, which is entirely required for faith. By the mention of truth, with Chrysostom as authority, he seems to teach that the Apostle is not such a servant as Moses, who was occupied with shadows and ceremonies, but one who is occupied with the truth, John 1:16. For evangelical truth is understood, which is accustomed to be called so by way of excellence, Gal. 3:1, Col. 1:5.

Verse 2.

In hope of eternal life) 'In hope', which is a locution found in 1 Cor. 9:10. You have 'the hope of eternal life' also below in chapter 3, verse 7.

The ultimate end of the evangelical ministry is commemorated here, eternal life, just as faith, piety or charity, and hope are the intermediate ends. For these are joined together: but hope looks toward future things. For we do not hope for present things, but for those which we expect. The faith of the elect tends toward piety in the hope of eternal life, insofar as it looks toward the gratuitous promise of God, and hopes for the promised thing out of grace. For faith looks at the promise, but hope expects the promised thing, Heb. 6:18. 'My preaching,' says Osiander in his paraphrase, 'teaches men true piety, so that they may rightly worship God and live innocently, and it creates a certain and indubitable hope of eternal life for all who believe and obey my preaching.'

Which the God who cannot lie promised) El Ne'eman. The hope is firm which relies upon the promise of Him who knows not how to deceive. Therefore God is called Tsur, that is, a rock. You have the word apseudes also in Wisd. 7:18. In the Glossary, apseudes is 'truthful'.

Before eternal times) Not from eternity, but before many ages. For it has the same value as 'from ancient days', Acts 15:7, 'from ancient generations', ch. 15:21. See what we said on 2 Tim. 1:9. However, he does not mean by this name that eternal life was promised, but that great goods were promised, under which wrapping eternal life lies hidden, unfolded through Christ. Reference is made especially to that which is in Gen. 15:1, ch. 17:7, ch. 22:18.

Others understand the promise 'before eternal times' as 'before secular times', with Jerome, which the pseudo-Jerome explains thus: 'Before all times He proposed within Himself to save believers through the Son.' Thus Beza: 'Before the whole series of ages, or before this world existed, as in John 17:5, that is, from eternity.' For because all things are present to God, and that which God has decreed will be is absolutely certain to happen: therefore God is said to have done from eternity what is finally revealed to us in its own time. Thus it is said

GOD chose us before the foundations of the world were laid, (Ephes. 1:4) that is, He proposed to choose. Thus it is said that He gave us eternal life in CHRIST before the times of the ages, that is, He proposed to give it, 2 Tim. 1:9. Thus the blessed Balduinus: There the promise of eternal life was made, when God promised that He would give it to the faithful: For promise is here put for decree, just as the giving of life is put for predestination, 2 Tim. 1:9. For since the outcome of the matter was most certain, GOD is said both to promise and to give, when He decreed that He would give it, although those to whom He would give it did not yet exist. Others understand it thus: before many ages, because the promise was made immediately at the cradle of the world. Thus Athanasius in his Synopsis, referring it to faith, indicates that faith in CHRIST is not a recent invention, but was prepared from the age and promised by God. Thus also Flacius: 'Before the times of the ages' signifies before any age elapsed, so that it may note the promise given in Paradise. As also Osiander: God promised eternal life to those believing in CHRIST. 'Before the times of the ages,' before some ages or before some centuries of years, when He said to our first parents: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. According to the former explanation, a metonymy will be necessary, in this way: He promised, that is, He decreed to promise, before the times of the ages, to give eternal life to the faithful. In the latter, however, the proper sense of the word is retained. More subtle than solid is Jerome's explanation concerning the promise made to the Son: 'Before all these times, which neither speech can utter, nor mind comprehend, nor silent thought dare to touch, God the Father promised to His Wisdom, His Word, and to that very Wisdom of His, and to the life of those who were to believe, that it was to come into the world:' (where he also wishes eternal life to be the Word itself, which in the beginning was with God: Which interpretation concerning the promise made to the Son, Anselm joined with the first in this place. How did He promise, since He surely promised to men who did not yet exist before the times of the ages, unless because in His eternity, and in His co-eternal Word, it was already fixed by predestination what was to be in its own time? Or to whom did He promise, unless promising to His Wisdom, that all who were to believe in it would have eternal life. But it is altogether better to explain that πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων with Augustine, Book XII, De Civitate Dei, ch. 16, and Jerome in this place, as 'before all ages,' that is, before the world was founded, when the ages began, Heb. 11:3, ch. 1:3, as Ephes. 2:4, ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, John 17:5, πρὸ τοῦ τὸν κόσμον εἶναι, and thus 2 Tim. 1:9, grace is said to be given πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων, not that there were ages before the world was founded in which the angels served God, as Jerome, perhaps fascinated by the error of Origen, says in this place, but so that a catachresis may be admitted in the word of the promise given from eternity. Absolutely nothing could be promised when there was no one to whom it could be promised. But because those who promise determine to give what they promise, hence the Apostle used this word for a decree, namely, that God determined to give eternal life to believers. The word ἐπηγγείλατο has greater emphasis than the Latin 'promisit'; because ἐπαγγελία introduces the promise of grace, as Beza notes. However, Grotius's Pelagian opinion is by no means to be admitted: that only great goods were promised, because the Apostle teaches that not great goods, under whose covering eternal life might lie hidden, but eternal life itself was promised, which we have taught in their proper places is contained in those promises, Gen. 15, 17, and 22, not in a mystical sense, but in a native and literal one, if they are understood according to the mind of the Holy Spirit.

Ver. 3.

'Εφανέρωσε δὲ καιροῖς ἰδίοις τὸν λόγον ἀυτῶ) He revealed the long-hidden decree, Rom. 16, 26. Λόγον that is דבר a decree, just as to speak is to decree. Καιροῖς ἰδίοις, that is, at the time destined by Himself for this. So also 1 Tim. 2, 6.

It is not said simply that the decree was either long hidden or now finally opened: But it implies that the promise made many ages ago has now been set forth, brought into open light at its own time, or more clearly manifested: otherwise these things would be ἀσύςατα: that the promise was announced many ages ago, and that the promise was opened only at these times. By τὸν λόγον Jerome understands the λόγον ὑποστατικὸν; but the context teaches that the promise already announced before, but now more clearly manifested through the proclamation of the Gospel, is being referred to.

'Εν Κηρύγματι) Through that message. Thus the preaching of the Gospel is called 1 Cor. 16, 25. 1 Cor. 1, 21. ch. 2, 4. ch. 15, 14. 2 Tim. 4, 17.

Ὃ ἐπιστεύθην ἐγὼ) The same manner of speaking Gal. 2, 7. 1 Thess. 2, 4. 1 Tim. 1, 11.

The Apostle expressed the means through which we may attain that hope of eternal life, both the ἐπαγγελίαν exhibited before Christ, according to the exposition of some, insofar as that promise was indeed made in the Messiah many ages before, and the ἐυαγγέλιον designated by the κήρυγμα, insofar as after the Φανέρωσιν of the Son of God in the flesh, eternal life was manifested far more clearly through the proclamation of the Gospel Word, and how Christ acquired the same for us, and we possess the same through Christ. For the promise of eternal life is viewed not merely by the consideration of its existence and truth, but with the manner of attaining it.

Κατ' ἐπιταγὴν τῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεῦ) He ascends again to the Principal cause. Thus κατ' ἐπιταγὴν τῦ ἀιωνίου Θεῦ, Rom. 16, 26. Κατ' ἐπιταγὴν Θεῦ σωτῆρος, 1 Tim. 1, 1. where see the things said.

The Principal cause is God, our Savior: But the name of the Lord can be understood essentially; there is no need for it to be restricted personally to the Father. For the Son of God also professes Himself to be the Savior, besides whom there is no other, Is. 45, 22. Cf. Acts 4, 12. and the blessed Baldwin judges that Christ is also adorned with that title in ch. 2, 10, 11, ch. 3, 4, from which Savior the Apostle had received his calling immediately, Acts 9, 15, ch. 22, 14. Therefore, the Son of God seems to be noted here particularly, just as it is explained shortly in ver. 4, that Christ is that Savior whom he had mentioned.

Ver. 4.

Τίτῳ γνησίῳ τέκνῳ) He is here made equal to Timothy. See 1 Tim. 1, 2.

Κατὰ κοινὴν πίσιν) Thus ἐν πίστι in the passage said to Timothy. He shows in what matter he is Paul's son. And he says common faith, because it was common both to Jews, such as Paul, and to Greeks, such as Titus.

This is the inscription. He is called a genuine son, so that he may be distinguished from false teachers, who even sold themselves as sons of the Apostles. For they were spurious, not genuine sons: who were neither begotten from the word of truth, nor were they twins to those whom they boasted as progenitors in doctrine or life. Therefore, it is added κατὰ κοινὴν πίσιν, which was not only common to him with Paul, nor only common to the Gentiles and Jews, but to all the Elect of all times. For there is only one faith, Eph. 4, 6. Acts 15, 11. It is indicated, therefore, that regeneration and communion with the saints are obtained only through that faith.

Grace, mercy, peace, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. You have these also in the same place to Timothy. But we learn from Origen and others that mercy was absent here in certain codices, and the Syriac does not read it.

Of our Savior) The title which he had just given to God, he now gives to Christ, because whatever the Father did for our salvation, he did through Christ: what Christ did, he did by the command of the Father.

This is the Apostolic greeting, the third part of the entrance or exordium, by which the fruits of the Evangelical ministry are also designated, or the proper object, because it revolves around grace, mercy, and peace, which comes to the faithful from God the Father, but only through the Lord Jesus Christ, and thus through faith in Christ. However, the Vulgate is excused in vain for omitting the word mercy, which the Greek codices consistently have. The grace of God is a benevolent affection toward us: Mercy, which is affected by our miseries, overflows from grace: Peace with God above and internal peace of conscience and grace and mercy come to us: and these have their origin from the Father: But the foundation is in Christ Jesus, our Savior, who brought it about by his merit and obedience that God should be well-disposed toward us, be affected by our misery, and tranquilize our conscience: In Christ alone we have both grace and mercy and peace, Eph. 1, 6. Heb. 4, 16. Rom. 5, 1. Those things of Grotius concerning the authority of the Father, unless they are understood of Christ according to his human nature, will not agree with the consubstantiality of the Son of God.

PART II. Instruction concerning the requirements of the Ministers of the Word.

Ver. 5.

For this cause I left you in Crete) The manuscript has I departed, namely as Timothy at Ephesus. Paul had left him in Crete at the time we have already mentioned. I left you in Crete, said the Latin Interpreter, less customarily, yet not without example. For Varro also says: It is said that there is a plane tree in Crete at Gortyna. And Virgil, Aeneid III: Or Apollo ordered us to settle in Crete. And Jerome speaks thus throughout.

That you might set in order the things that are lacking) The manuscript has set in order, and proceed to arrange the rest, namely those things which I, because of the shortness of time and impediments from guards, could not arrange. For to set in order is not always to correct, but often to arrange.

The Apostle brings forward a twofold cause for Titus being left in Crete: The first concerns the ordination of those things which, due to the narrowness of time, could not be ordained by Paul; not indeed because of the impediments of guards, for Paul was undoubtedly free at that time, concerning which in the Prolegomena, but because of other impediments and causes calling him away. The particle epi implies super-ordering or proceeding in ordering, as Jerome, Erasmus, Beza, and others have expressed its force. However, the meaning of ordination pleases more than that of correction in this place: For Paul had begun to ordain first, not to amend or correct. For he had found no church there.

And that you may appoint elders in every city, זקנים or פרנסין, among whom the one who labors in the word, as Paul calls him, held the place of Prince, who by excellence is the one presiding. To Justin, just as by a similar excellence the bishop is the Angel in the Apocalypse. His duty was to teach, or even to give the power of teaching to suitable persons, whether Presbyters or Laity: clearly as was done in the synagogue. And note κατὰ πόλιν, because Titus had been set over all of Crete, which on account of the frequency of its cities was once called the hundred-citied. Καταστήσῃς is הפקד as in Genesis 39:4, 5, chapter 41:34, Deuteronomy 19, and elsewhere.

This is the second reason for the appointment of Presbyters throughout the individual cities. However, it does not imply that several Presbyters were to be appointed in any given city, and a Prince-Bishop among them: for that plurality is to be understood not with regard to individual cities, but with regard to all of them collectively. Nor is a Bishop immediately the one who labors in the word, or in the age of the Apostle was there any Bishop different from a Presbyter, whose duty it was to teach, or to give the power of teaching to suitable Presbyters or even to Laity: which is here at length from proved by Jerome from sacred authority, among others, from this text: Let us diligently, he says, weigh the words of the Apostle, saying: That you should appoint Presbyters through the cities, as I have arranged for you. Who, what kind of Presbyter ought to be ordained, differing in the following, he says this: If any is without crime, the husband of one wife, & the rest: Afterwards he brought in: For… a Bishop must be without crime, as the steward of GOD. The Presbyter is therefore the same as the Bishop, and before, by the instinct of the Devil, studies were made in religion, and it was said among the people: I am of Paul, I am of Apollo, but I of Cephas, the Churches were governed by the common counsel of the Presbyters. And a little later: As therefore Presbyters know that they, by the custom of the Church, are subject to him who has been set over them: So let Bishops know that they are greater than Presbyters more by custom than by the truth of the Lord's arrangement. Which are repeated again dist. 95. It is vain what Bartholomew of Peter says in this place: That Jerome extols the dignity of the Presbyterate in an oratorical manner and as if by a certain Hyperbole. The opinion of Jerome here and in the epistle to Evagrius is clear. Estius is more ingenuous, although he falsely pronounces Jerome's opinion to be consistent with neither sacred scripture nor the antiquity of history, who indeed was forced to admit here that the Apostle warns Titus to appoint Presbyters through the cities, namely individual Bishops through individual cities, and that he was not yet solicitous about Presbyters who are not Bishops: But when was the Apostle ever solicitous or thinking about such? Theodoret on this place: Hence also it is manifest that they called Presbyters Bishops. For when he had said, that he should appoint Presbyters in the city, he subjoined: For a Bishop must be without crime. But in each city it is the custom not to have many Bishops, but Presbyters. But what Estius thinks is sufficiently shown from this place, that it does not pertain to the secular magistrate to appoint the Ministers of the Church: But to the Prefects of the Church itself, such as Titus was, is vain and frivolous. For the condition of that time was different, when there were no magistrates addicted to the Christian faith. But when there were Christian magistrates, their vote was also employed in the calling of Ministers. But in the progress of time, the Roman Bishops through tyranny snatched that right to themselves alone. See B. Hunn. on this place in LL. CC. num. 7.

some are moral, others doctrinal. But in general he first requires that he should appoint to the Church only him who has been ἀνέγκλητος, no less in life than in doctrine. But it is not required of a Bishop that he be immune from every sin, but only that nothing be blamed in his external conversation. For as Augustine speaks in book I against two epistles of the Pelagians, chap. 14, no Minister could be rightly ordained in the Church if the Apostle had said, if anyone is without sin, where he says, if anyone is without crime, or if he had said, having no sin, where he says, having no crime: For many baptized believers are without crime, but you would call no one without sin in this life, as Balduinus page 1472. For this reason he also wishes that a Bishop be the husband of one wife, not, as Grotius perverts it, of one marriage (concerning which we spoke on 1 Tim. 5, 2). we have said) having faithful children, who do not deserve to be accused of intemperance and disobedience, for by this τεκμηρίῳ they will be able to be distinguished, whether they are able to preside over the Church of God or not. See 1 Tim. 3, 5. With what liberty, says Jerome here, can we rebuke the children of others, and teach what is right, when he who has been rebuked can immediately throw back at us, teach your own children first. Where, as B. Hunnius notes, the Apostle does not prohibit the approach to this function, provided they are otherwise fit to handle the rudders of the Church, and live chastely. But he opposes this mark to those who withdraw themselves from marriage because of its difficulties, even if they are deprived of the gift of continence: Similarly also to those who are bigamists or polygamists. He wishes the former to have their wives, if only they wish to be tolerated in the Ministry. But these latter, who had taken more than one wife, he judges should be simply excluded from the ministry. Concerning which we have spoken more fully in the l. c. Jerome adds a mystical interpretation: but one which savors of nothing but the Origenic cacoethes of allegorizing: That in the scriptures by sons are understood λογισμοὺς, that is, thoughts, by daughters πράξεις, that is, works, and that now it ought to be commanded that a Bishop be made who has both thoughts and works in his power, and truly believes in Christ, and is not stained by any blemish of creeping vices.

Vers. 7.

Δεῖ γὰρ τὸν Ἐπίσκοπον ἀνέγκλητον εἶναι) For all πρεσβύτεροι are also Ἐπίσκοποι of the flock, Acts 20. v. 28. But he who was the Prince, κατ' ἐξοχὴν occupied the common name, as they feel in Africa.

He truly acknowledges that all Presbyters are Bishops, but he asserts ἄτερ γραφῆς, that he who was the Prince, κατ' ἐξοχὴν, occupied the common name in the Apostolic age, that was to be proven. The contrary has been proven in entire writings against the Papists, especially by Claudius Salmasius under the name of Walo Messalinus against Petavius in the tract on Bishops and Presbyters, by David Blondel, etc. What? That the Jesuits themselves openly taught that it is false that any particular Church needs a Bishop, and handed down that France, England, and Spain can lack Bishops, and added moreover that monks, in order to hear confessions, have no need of Episcopal approval. See Theologia moralis Jesuitarum, and others praised by Maresius in Anti-Tirinum Contr. XXVI. T. II. page 864. The ordinary and interlinear gloss observe here that Bishops are designated by the name of Presbyters. Hugo Cardinalis as well as Cajetan on this place. say that Presbyters and Bishops were the same. It should be known, says Lyra on this place, that the Apostle under the name of Presbyters understands also Bishops, and conversely under the name of Bishops understands Presbyters.

Ὡς ἐγώ σοι διεταξάμην) Departing thence I commanded. The same word 1 Cor. 7, 17. c. 11, 34. c. 16, 1. שִׁמֵּר.

Verse 6.

If any is blameless (ἀνέγκλητος) [is] irreproachable, 1 Timothy 3, 2. You have the word ἀνέγκλητος in 1 Corinthians 1, 8; Colossians 1, 22; 1 Timothy 3, 10. In the Glossary, ἀνέγκλητος [is] inaccusabilis (unaccusable).

The husband of one wife, 1 Timothy 3, verse 2.

Having faithful children, not in accusation of riot, or unruly (ἀνυπότακτα) [is] having children in subjection with all gravity, 1 Timothy 3, 4. That is a sign of both his probity and his diligence, to have instructed his children in faith, in obedience, in temperance: so that deservedly a greater rule ought to be entrusted to him who has shown himself such in a lesser one, Matthew 25, 21. It is said to be ἐν κατηγορίᾳ (in accusation), just as ἐν αἰτίᾳ (in fault). For what ἀσωτία (riot) is, see Luke 15, 13; Ephesians 5, 18; 1 Peter 4, verse 4. Ἀταξ- (disorderly) [is] הוֹלֵל וְסוֹבֵא (a glutton and a drunkard) Deuteronomy 21, 20. Ἀνυπότακτος (unruly) [is] אֵינֶנּוּ שֹׁמֵעַ (he will not obey) in the same place.

Although the Apostle had already delivered instructions (διατάξεις) to Titus by word of mouth, as to what kind of Bishops or Presbyters were to be appointed; yet he wished to include it in writing, so that he might always have a certain rule before his eyes. He delivers, however, the requirements of good Presbyters.

Mich. Medina, book I, on the origin and contents of the sacraments of men; Bellarmine himself admitting it, he says that Ambrose, Augustine, Sedulius, Primasius, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Oecumenius, and Theophylact held this opinion with Jerome. And Essensaeus, book I, digression on 1 Timothy 1, acknowledges that the Canonists in C. Legimus dist. 93, and others among the Papists, establish that Presbyters are by Divine right equal to Bishops.

As God's steward) that is, steward of the mysteries of God, as 1 Cor. 4:1.

All Presbyters, therefore, of whom the Apostle speaks here, are stewards of God: It is the duty of all of them to teach the Word of God, to labor in the Word, not only of Bishops, whom Grotius, along with the Papists, distinguishes from Presbyters.

Not self-willed) Authadēs by origin is 'pleasing to oneself,' autoadēs as Aristotle explains in the Great Ethics. In the Glossary it is translated as 'stubborn.' In Theophrastus, authadeia is 'a roughness of manner in speech.' Euripides: 'Nor did I praise whoever, having become self-willed, is bitter to the citizens through ignorance.' Certain ancient Latins translate it in this passage as 'insolent.'

Not quick-tempered) Orgiloi are 'irascible' according to Aristotle in the Nicomachean Ethics, book 10, who 'are angry quickly, and with whom they ought, and at what they ought, and more than they ought.' In Hebrew: אִישׁ חֵמָה Proverbs 29:21, where the Greeks: 'An irascible man.'

Not a drunkard, not violent, not greedy for gain) You have these also in 1 Tim. 3:3.

There follow the moral requirements of Presbyters in particular, partly proposed negatively, partly positively. To the former belong the following, namely that a Bishop or Presbyter should not be 1. self-willed, which although some derive from autos and adein, as if 'pleasing to oneself,' while despising others with a high brow: others, however, think it is said from autos and en heautō, 'the same from himself.' And they are properly such as are 'opinionated,' clinging to their own opinions, which arises from pride and is usually joined with stubbornness; therefore the Vulgate rendered it here as 'proud': as 2 Pet. 2:10, 'pleasing himself': Jerome 'insolent,' elsewhere 'impudent'; Erasmus in 2 Pet. 2:10 'fractious,' and 'of his own head and mind,' here 'fractious,' that is, hard, and more than enough tenacious of his own mind. To Camerarius, authades is 'obstinate' or 'stubborn,' who thinks nothing right except what he himself does and thinks: and the same in another form, 'self-loving,' such as are generally the unskilled and unlearned. The Syriac rendered it 'elated,' 'led by the will of his own soul,' B. Luther, 'stubborn.' The LXX in Genesis 49:7 thus render the word 'az, 'obstinate.' Hesychius has these synonyms: authades, hyperphantos, thymōdēs, paranomos, autareskos, exousiastikos, proud, irascible, lawless, self-pleasing, of one's own right. Suidas says: Authades, autareskos, thymōdēs, thrasys, hyperoptēs: Who pleases himself, irascible, bold, a contemner of others. 2. Orgilos, irascible. Concerning whom Jerome: 'An irascible man is one who is always getting angry, and at the slightest breath of a reply and sin is moved like a leaf by the wind.' And in truth, he adds, there is nothing more foul than a furious Teacher, who, when he ought to be gentle, and according to that which is written: But the servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be humble toward all, a patient teacher, instructing in meekness those who oppose. He, on the contrary, with a grim face, trembling lips, wrinkled brow, unbridled reproaches, his face varying between pallor and redness, makes a clamor with shouting; and he does not so much draw back the erring to the good, as he precipitates them into evil by his cruelty. Hence it is that Solomon also says: 'Anger also destroys the wise': And 'the anger of man does not work the righteousness of GOD.' (Proverbs 21.) Nor indeed is he who is sometimes angry 'irascible': But he is called irascible who is frequently overcome by this passion. Therefore the habit of anger, as B. Baldwin says, or irascibility is forbidden here, not the affection, or anger itself. For anger falls even upon a good man, and is sometimes necessary by reason of duty. Irascibility, however, is from an immoderate perturbation of the mind without a legitimate cause, often over a very slight matter, which vice ought especially to be alien to all Doctors of the Church, because it destroys the wise, and does many disordered things, for it does not work righteousness, James 1:20. 3. Paroinos, violent, concerning whom, after many other things, Jerome: 'Let it suffice to have said this now, that according to the Apostle, in wine there is luxury. And wherever satiety and drunkenness are, there lust dominates.' 4. Plēktēs, which

Jerome prefers the understanding of the striking of words rather than of blows, with Erasmus not disapproving: It is better, he says, that we do not call him a striker who, being gentle and patient, knows in time what must be said and what must be kept silent: nor does he strike the conscience of the weak with useless speech. For the Apostle, in forming a Prince of the Church, does not forbid him to be a pugilist and a pancratiast: which, even if it were in a commoner or any gentile, is reprehended, but this, as I said, so that he who is insulting and garrulous does not destroy him whom he could have corrected with modesty and gentleness. Chrysostom: In this place he wished to signify an insulting person. For it is fitting to do all things by correcting rather than by striking or by inflicting insults. For what need is there, I beseech you, of injury? It is necessary to terrify with the threat of Gehenna, and to amend those of this kind with terrors. For he upon whom an insult is inflicted becomes more bold and more impudent: And he who has so affected himself that he may despise more is introduced. For a physician, Chrysostom continues, is a Doctor of souls; furthermore, a physician does not strike at all, but even if the sick man by chance has struck himself, he corrects, amends, and cures. To Camerarius, however, and others it is pleasing that it be understood properly as a striker, so that just as writing to Timothy he orders a Bishop to be ἄμαχον, which signifies one fleeing fights and quarrels: So let us understand again now that it is forbidden for him to lay violent hands on anyone. Both real and verbal injuries, as they are called, or strikes, can be understood: But those things which pertain to the mode of doctrine do not look to this. The Apostle is not yet engaged in moral matters. 5. Αἰσχροκερδῆς, Erasmus rendered it, given over to base gain, but Estius prefers to interpret him as desirous of base gain, who seeks gain from anywhere, even with the reason of honesty resisting. Chrysostom: Not desirous, he says, of base gain, that is, so that he may present a great contempt for money. For there is, as Theophylact teaches, any gain for a Bishop, even if it be just, that is indecorous. The proud and stubborn are easily irascible; drunkenness is accustomed to stir up quarrels and fights. Therefore, it is necessary that not only all the faithful, but especially the Ministers of the word, be alien to these vices, and no less also to avarice and the desire for base gain, which is the root of all evils, 1 Tim. 6, v. 10.

…1 Pet. 5, verse 2. Since hospitality cannot consist with avarice, which the Apostle requires above all things in a Bishop, 1 Tim. 3, v. 2, and in this place

Ver. 8.

̓Αλλὰ φιλόξενον) And he has this there too.

Φιλάγαθον) The Latin translator correctly explained it as benign, as can be seen from those things which we said at 1 Tim. 3:3.

Σώφρονα) Thus also 1 Tim. 3:2.

Δίκαιον, ὅσιον) צדיק וחסיד. For thus the Hebrews distinguish those terms, so that the latter contains more in itself than the former. And thus among the Apostles, the former is δικαιοῦσθαι (to be justified), the latter ἁγιάζεσθαι (to be sanctified).

̓Εγκρατῆ) One who restrains himself even from lawful things for the sake of some good. Thus τὸ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι (self-control) is used in 1 Cor. 7:9, ch. 9:25. That word corresponds to the Hebrew התאפק, Genesis 43:30, 1 Samuel 13:12. Add Acts 24:26, Galatians 5:23.

Positive requirements now follow, and after the vices that must be absent, the virtues that must be present, so that a Presbyter or Bishop, that is, any Minister of the Word, may be 1. Φιλόξενος (hospitable). For if all desire to hear that from the Gospel: I was a stranger, and you took me in, how much more so a Bishop, whose house ought to be a common hospice for all.

2. Φιλάγαθος, which the Vulgate renders as benign, Erasmus as a student of good things, and Augustine in book XIV of The City of God, ch. 7, as a lover of good. But since kindness toward the good coheres better with the preceding, and the Greek ἀγαθὸς is used more commonly of persons than of things, according to Estius. And a lover of the good is included in the predicates just and holy.

3. Σώφρων, which the Latin translator formerly rendered as prudent, as Jerome notes, which the Ambrosian also has; some codices today have prudent, sober; the Clementine edition, with the epithet of prudent omitted, has sober: As the first two are opposed to greed, so the present one is opposed to addiction to wine or drunkenness. Therefore, we do not understand this here as chaste or modest with Jerome, but as sober with the Syrian. Wherefore, Bellarmine's argument from this passage for the celibacy of the priesthood in his book On the Clergy, ch. XIX, falls to the ground. Because the Vulgate itself rendered it sober, which sense Salmero and Justinianus also provide. And beyond the mind of the ancient interpreters of this passage, both Greek and Latin, Claud acknowledges that the law of clerical continence is urged from this passage. Espencaeus on this passage, to say nothing of the fact that Bellarmine himself concedes that celibacy in the time of the Apostles was still left to liberty, but was finally imposed upon the Clergy by the Church of a later time.

4. Δίκαιος, one who devotes effort to justice toward his neighbor, with whom it is not fitting to be πλήκτην (a striker). But he also wants a just man, who, as B. Hunnius says, in external conversation or in contracts permitted to a Minister, does injury to no one in any matter: he should not indulge in private affections, or sin in those things which he does with his hearers by reason of his ministry through προσωποληψίᾳ (respect of persons), which is the enemy of all justice and equity.

5. Ὅσιος, one who is devoted to holiness or piety toward GOD. 6. Ἐγκρατὴς, one who is zealous for continence regarding his own soul and body. Jerome renders it 'abstinent,' others 'temperate': Estius understands it as 'alien to lust and gluttony': But it also seems to be opposed to τῷ ὀργίλῳ (the irascible man): Whence Jerome: 'Let the Bishop also be abstinent, not only (as some think) from lust and the embrace of a wife, but from all perturbations of the mind, lest he be stirred to anger, lest sadness cast him down, lest terror agitate him, lest immoderate joy lift him up.' Abstinence, however, is numbered by the Apostle among the fruits of the Spirit. And if it is required of all, how much more of a Bishop, who, being patient and gentle, ought to bear the vices of sinners, console the faint-hearted, sustain the weak, render to no one evil for evil, but overcome evil with good. Not him, says Chrysostom, who is zealous for fasting, did he wish to signify here, but him who has overcome every vice, and has chastened both tongue and hand and unchaste eyes. For this is indeed continence, to be subject to no evil.

Verse 9.

Ἀντεχόμενον τῶ κατὰ τὴν διδαχὴν πιστῶ λόγου) Ἀντέχεσθαι with the Genitive, corresponding to the Hebrew הֶחֱזִיק, is to embrace something firmly, as appears in Isaiah 56:2, 4, 6; Proverbs 3:18. It is a truly Greek word. For Euripides and Plato use it thus. Κατὰ τὴν διδαχὴν, as they received it from the Apostles. עַל-לִמּוּד. Here also Ambrose reads ἀνθεκτικῶς λόγου, which error we said arose from a compendium of writing at 1 Timothy 1:15, chapter 3:1.

Ἵνα δυνατὸς ᾖ) We often have this locution, δυνατός ἐστι for δύναται. Romans 4:21, chapter 11:23, chapter 14:4, and elsewhere. So also Numbers 22:38 in the Greek.

Παρακαλεῖν) to exhort to perseverance and increase in piety.

Ἐν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ) By that pure, wholesome Evangelical doctrine, 1 Timothy 1:10, chapter 6:3, 2 Timothy 1:13, chapter 4:3. But the Manuscript has for these words, τοὺς ἐν πάσῃ θλίψει, which if we accept, then παρακαλεῖν will not be to exhort, but to console, as it often is. See 2 Corinthians 1:4.

Καὶ τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν) He who can convince the Jews through the ancient prophecies and miracles; but the Greeks partly through miracles, partly through the testimonies of the learned among themselves. These are not ordinary things.

The Apostle now subjoins the doctrinal requirements for all, and demands 1. As regards διδασκαλίαν (teaching), that the Bishop be ἀντεχόμενος, which according to Estius properly signifies one who adheres to something, as if fixed by his fingernails, and does not allow himself to be torn away. Whence the Ambrosian version rendered it 'tenacious'. The Vulgate less emphatically 'embracing', since the sense is, as Estius admits: It behooves the Bishop to be such a one who tenaciously and stubbornly adheres to the faithful word, by which he may hand down saving doctrine to others. He calls it the 'faithful word' in his own manner, that which is of certain and explored truth. Theophylact in this place has: 'Providing', that is, having the business; so that he may lean upon the word which is faithful, that is, true, not that which is brought forth by opinions and quibbles. Whence also he added 'according to the doctrine', arguing that he is able to instruct others without the support of this external and worldly wisdom. For there is no need for swelling words, but for skill in the sacred scriptures, and for the power and sense of a deeper understanding. For from these, doctrine, such as Paul's was, is advanced. B. Hunnius: He describes the Word of God by a certain periphrasis, calling it πιστὸν λόγον (faithful word), not only because it stands above the grasp of reason, so that it is rather to be believed than understood: but also because it is, in respect of its Author, a certain, faithful, and indubitable word, namely, brought forth from the mouth of God, and therefore also worthy of faith, to be religiously received by faith. And he writes that this word is 'according to the doctrine', that is, so constituted that men can be usefully taught from it to confirm faith, to nourish piety, and to rightly institute the ways of life, nay rather, for eternal life. Of this faithful word, therefore, he wishes the Bishop to be tenacious, lest he either allow it to be snatched from his heart by the fraud of Satan, and opinions dissenting from the truth to be instilled, or for the sake of men cast away the truth, or out of fear of them change anything, or suppress it by silence, and betray the truth before his hearers and not keep silent, but constantly profess it from the sacred scriptures. Therefore, as B. Balduinus warns, this epithet requires three things: (1) Assent to sound doctrine, in which there is nothing adulterated. (2) The gift of proposing it, for he calls it the discourse which is according to doctrine, that is, which can be taught among others. (3.) Constancy in that doctrine, to which he wishes the Minister of the Church to adhere tenaciously. 2. As to παράκλησιν or exhortation, which flows from doctrine, whence it is added ἵνα δυνατὸς ἦ͂ καὶ παρακαλεῖν, so that he may also be powerful ἐν τῇ͂ διδασκαλίᾳ (by applying the doctrine in practice) in doctrine for exhorting. Ἐν τῇ͂ διδασκαλίᾳ τῇ͂ ὑγιαινούσῃ in sound doctrine, lest less sound or vain doctrines be used for exhortations. The sense is, according to Estius: I wish the Bishop to be instructed in the word of truth for this purpose, that he may not only be able to teach others, but also be powerful, that is, sufficient and fit to exhort to piety and to every kind of virtue, and that through the sound, whole, and incorrupt doctrine of the Gospel. Jerome understands it concerning consolation: That he may also be able to console those who are agitated by the storms of this age, and to destroy weak precepts through sound doctrine. But it is called sound doctrine in contrast to weak and languid doctrine. Chrysostom observes that by sound doctrine is noted the skill of the scriptures. Therefore, not with those pompous words, but with that supreme skill of the scriptures is there need, so that he may search out the hidden senses and understandings.

3. As to conviction, not indeed through miracles, as Grotius, perhaps wishing to gratify the Papists, whether the matter be with Jews or with Gentiles. For it is in no Presbyter's power to perform miracles, but through the ἀνέλγεγκτον of the scriptures. This passage, says Jerome, makes against those who, giving themselves to sloth, and leisure, and sleep, think it is a sin if they read the scripture: And who despise those who meditate in the law of the Lord day and night as if they were garrulous and useless: not noticing that the Apostle, after the catalog of the Bishop's conduct, had likewise commanded doctrine. Chrysostom, regarding these things and refuting those who contradict, has it thus: For unless he can do this, all things perish: for unless one has learned to fight against enemies, and to take captive every thought into the obedience of CHRIST, and to destroy reasonings. He who, he says, is ignorant of the right and sound doctrine, as it ought to be delivered, let him be far removed from the Episcopal seat. For it is easy to find other things also in subordinates, for instance, to be without crime, to have children subject, to be hospitable, just, and holy. But this is what most expresses a Teacher, namely, to be able to instruct with words and to refute adversaries: of which thing we see almost no care being taken now, and we groan. If the saint felt it necessary to groan about the Bishops of his own time, how much more would he groan if he saw the Bishops of our age? Estius here pleads the cause of his Presbyters, who are for the most part very ignorant; not that all these things are required from any Presbyters whatsoever (opposing a passage, which is irrelevant here, about Presbyters not laboring in the Word, but attending to the external affairs of the Church, 1 Tim. 5), which, however, that the Apostle requires from all Presbyters, is clearer than the sun. But he wishes it to be required from all Bishops: But in that way, for most Bishops in the Papacy, the Episcopal miter would have to be taken off, and the pallium would hardly be left.

Ver. 10.

For there are many and insubordinate) The 'and' is better absent in the Manuscript: There are, he says, among you מורים men, impatient of that discipline which is in the Church.

Vain talkers) deceivers, 2 Tim. 3, 15. In the glossary: Vain talker, one who speaks in vain. They turned aside to vain talking, 1 Tim. 1, ver. 6. Those who devise iniquity, Ezek. 11, ver. 2.

And mind-deceivers) those who lead astray, Isa. 9, 16. Deceiving and being deceived, 2 Tim. 3, 13. We have the verb to deceive the mind in Gal. 6, 3.

Especially those of the circumcision) We have this phrase in the circumcision also in Acts 10, 45, ch. 11, 2, Gal. 2, 12, Col. 4, 11. He indicates those who taught that all Israelites would have a part in the other world, than which no doctrine is more pernicious. And there are those who wish to be called Christians, and under other names teach the same thing. Josephus and Luke in Acts 2, 11 teach us that there were many Jews in Crete in many places.

The reason is given, according to some, why it is necessary for a Bishop to be equipped with the faculty both of exhorting τοὺς ἀνυποτάκτους (the insubordinate), and of convincing τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας (the gainsayers). Although some here assign the third section of the chapter, so that the second indeed treats of the properties of Presbyters to be appointed, but the third of repelling Pseudo-Apostles; which was done by B. Hunnius. The particle καὶ seems to favor this opinion, as if he were saying, appoint such as I have mentioned, not other Bishops. For there are also many who are not such, but if you look at their character, they are ἀνυπότακτοι (insubordinate), if their tongue, ματαιολόγοι (vain talkers), if their pursuits, φρεναπάται (deceivers of minds); especially from among the Jews, these are by no means to be set over the Church, nay rather they are to be rebuked, and their mouths must be stopped. There is, however, a silent transition here to the rebuke of heretics, and thus this causal particle properly respects the necessity of the Refutation, and the copulative implies that not only true Teachers, but also false ones are to be found, for the convincing of whom the Minister of the Word ought to be suitable. See, says Chrysostom: how significantly he expressed whence such as these are. They do not want, he says, to be ruled, but to rule: for he wished that to be understood. Since, therefore, you have not been able to persuade, do not fear or dread such as these, but for the sake of the utility of others, rebuke them, and impose silence upon them. Such men, says Jerome in this place, the Doctor of the Church, to whom the souls of the people have been entrusted, ought to overcome by the reason of the scriptures, and impose silence upon them by the weight of testimonies. When he said evil-speaking, says Theophylact, he expressed the root of all evils. For he who is unwilling to obey another, and cannot endure authority, but rather invades others so that he may preside, will profess that he has learned nothing right or sound. He who endures nothing so that he may be instructed by others, he is truly both a vain talker and a deceiver, who deceives both himself and others. Jerome explains φρεναπάτας as deceivers of minds, who strengthen perverse doctrine, because garrulity without the authority of the scriptures would not have credibility, even with Divine testimonies. By the circumcision, however, he understands the Jews, who at that time were striving to subvert the nascent Church of Christ, and to introduce legal precepts, concerning which Paul treats more fully both to the Romans and to the Galatians, teaching about the differences of foods, and about the injury of circumcision. He noted the Pseudo-Apostles in the aforementioned epistles, both as requiring the observance of the law or good works for salvation, and as burdening consciences with Mosaic ceremonies, e.g., concerning the distinction of foods, which is noted in this place v. 15, and concerning certain external things, by which they hypocritically boasted of piety, v. 16. Whether they also introduced atheism, by promising salvation to all indiscriminately, is not certain. We have taught elsewhere that the Syncretistic opinion of Grotius was not far removed from atheism.

Verse 11.

Whose mouths must be stopped) To shut the mouth. Ἐπιδέειν τὸ στό- μα (To bind the mouth). Pollux interprets ἐπιστομίζειν as to restrain one who is speaking. This is called סתם in the Zohar on Deuteronomy, and among other Rabbis.

Who subvert whole houses) They overturn: That is, they lead away from salvation: which is ἀνατρέπειν τὴν πίσιν (to subvert the faith), 2 Timothy 2:18.

Teaching things which they ought not) Those things which favor vices. See Ezekiel 13:18. Τὰ μὴ δέοντα (things not fitting), 1 Timothy 5:13.

For the sake of filthy lucre) Truly filthy lucre, which is made from doctrine that corrupts souls. See what is said in Matthew 23:14, 2 Timothy 3:6, Romans 16:18, Philippians 3:19.

The necessity of refutation therefore appears. The Apostle does not leave the stopping of mouths free or arbitrary, but when there is danger from deceivers, he says it is necessary to stop their mouths, that is, according to the interpretation of Theophylact, they are to be severely rebuked, and in such a way that their mouths are closed; because the detriment which they bring to the Church is not light. For they do not pervert a few believers with their doctrine, but subvert whole families, removing the foundation of the spiritual edifice, which is faith. The metaphor is taken from a material house, which is subverted when the foundation is torn out, as Estius says here. Someone will say: (thus Theophylact in his paraphrase:) What profit will come from this, if silence is enjoined upon them, since they are contumacious and rebellious? To them indeed it will be able to profit nothing, but to others very much, who could be both corrupted and defiled by them, if the Bishop were to remain silent. For he is going to render an account for them. Therefore they must be restrained and curbed. But he who cannot do this, let him not assume the dignity of the Episcopate. Chrysostom explains the cause: For if someone receives the grace of doctrine, but is not sufficient to withstand them, nor to impose silence upon them, who are so impudent, he will draw upon himself the damages of those who are perishing, and will be the author of perdition for each one. On those words: Who subvert whole houses. You see, says Theophylact, how to disobedience there has also been added the greed of possessing, and filthy lucre, or that the houses themselves are to be overturned. For with these levers and mattocks the Demon strives to overturn the house of God. FOR THE SAKE OF FILTHY LUCRE. He signifies that they, blinded by avarice, teach falsely, while they think that godliness is a means of gain, as he says in 1 Timothy 6. For Teachers, who compose themselves for gain, easily persuade others that those things are true and agreeable to godliness which are pleasing to the hearers, into whose hands they look, as Estius says here. Jerome adds another sense concerning the gain of men, because all heretics, when they teach perversely, are accustomed to assert that they are gainers of men, when it is not gain, but perdition, to kill the souls of the deceived. But that is more foreign.

Verse 12.

One of themselves) One of the Cretans, among whom you live, said this, who knew them well.

Their own prophet) Epimenides, whom Cicero in his De Divinatione counts among those who prophesy through frenzy: Dio of Prusa also calls him a prophet. Let his book have the name: Oracles: Clinias in Plato's Laws: For perhaps you have heard that Epimenides was a divine man, who was known to us. And coming to you ten years before the Persian wars, according to the oracle of God, he performed certain sacrifices, which God had declared. And indeed, when the Athenians feared the Persian fleet, he said that they would not come for ten years; but when they do come, they will depart having accomplished nothing of what they hoped, but having suffered and done more evils. Diodorus Siculus calls him a Theologian in book V. He performed a purification through the years; Strabo says of him in book X. Plutarch in his Life of Solon: 'Thus, indeed, Epimenides the Phaestian came to them, having been sent for from Crete; whom some of those who prefer him to Periander count as the seventh among the wise men. He seemed to be a man beloved of God and wise in divine matters, possessing an inspired and ritualistic wisdom; for which reason the people of that time called him the son of the Nymph Balte and a new Curete.' See also the following likewise. Laërtius says he was most knowledgeable, and Apuleius calls him a prophet. Maximus Tyrius, Diatriba XXII: 'He came to Athens, a Cretan man, by name Epimenides; nor could anyone say he had a teacher, but he was skilled in divine matters, so that he saved the city of the Athenians, which was suffering from famine and sedition, by performing sacrifices.' He is called a Prophet by Paul, because he was held as such by his own people, just as the Prophets of Baal; but the things which Epimenides predicted were such as could certainly be known by the help of demons, if what Aristotle says of him in Rhetoric III. 17 is true: 'He did not prophesy about things to come, but about things that had happened, yet were unknown.' The word 'prophets' is also in use among the Greeks. Plutarch calls the priests of Ammon by this term. And among the Latins, Julius Tragicus called the ministers of the temples thus, as Festus testifies.

Cretans are always liars) Favorinus also cites this verse. The Cretans have been infamous by this name from every age. Callimachus: 'Cretans are always liars; for even a tomb, O King, the Cretans built for you.' Ovid: 'Can deceitful Crete deny this to him?' And elsewhere: '-- -- the Cretans do not feign everything.' Hence the proverb: 'To play the Cretan against a Cretan.'

Evil beasts) That is, men similar to wild beasts in this, that they secretly harm others. 'The beast itself,' says Aeschines regarding Demosthenes.

Idle bellies) Idle bellies. Thus the common interpreters: not badly. Favorinus cites 'idle bellies' and explains it as 'gluttons.' For he seems to have taken the word 'idle' in the sense of strenuousness. From 'to rush,' as if Epimenides had said 'strenuous eaters.' Even among the Latins, men are called 'bellies' for whom that part is the most important.

This coheres with the preceding (about which Jerome discourses here), not that those false teachers were from among the lying Cretans, but that many even from among the Cretans belonged to those 'insubordinate,' 'vain talkers,' and 'deceivers,' along with the seducers from the circumcision, whom he therefore wished to be marked by this excellent eulogy of their own prophet. Jerome says the Apostle called him a prophet either in mockery, because such Christians deserve to have such prophets, just as there were prophets of Baal, etc., or because he wrote about oracles, and the book of Epimenides was entitled with the name of oracles. There were those, as Jerome observes, who said the verse was taken from the poet Callimachus of Cyrene, who, writing in praise of Jupiter against the Cretans who boasted of having his tomb, says, 'Cretans are always liars.' But that entire verse is not found there: nor was he a Cretan by birth, but a Cyrenian. Jerome rendered the sense in this way: 'Wherefore rebuke them sharply,' he says. 'For they are liars, and evil beasts, and gluttons, who persuade others of false things, who in the manner of wild beasts thirst for the blood of the deceived, and not working in silence, they eat their own bread, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame; rebuke them, that they may be sound in the faith.' But in one verse, says Blessed Hunnius, the poet Epimenides notes three vices in his countrymen: First, their levity in believing things that are brought from everywhere, and their vanity in spreading lies. Next, he attacks their malice, because they are treacherous and perverse men. Hence he calls them 'evil beasts.' Thirdly, he notes luxury joined with sloth in doing what is proper, and therefore calls them 'idle bellies.'

Verse 13.
