Cohæret id cum præcedentibus, (de quo folici- te Hieronymus hic disquirit,) non quod falsi illi Doctores è Cretenfibus mendacibus fuerint, sed quod ad illos ἀνυποτάκτυς, vaniloquos, & excepto- res multi etiam è Cretenfibus pertinuerint, juxta cum seductoribus è circumcisione, quos proinde notatos voluerit hoc eximio proprii ipsorum pro- phetæ elogio. Quem Prophetam dixisse Aposto- lum, ait Hieronymus, vel illudendo, quod scilicet ta- les Christiani tales mereantur habere Prophetas, quo- modo & Prophetæ erant Baal &c. vel quod de ori- culis scripserit, & oraculorum titulo prænotatus sit li- ber Epimenidis. Fuerunt, observante Hieronymo, qui è Callimacho Cyrenensi Poëta versum desum- ptum dixere, qui in laudibus Jovis adversus Cre- tenses, sepulchrum ejus se habere gloriantes, scri- ptitans ait, Cretenses semper mendaces. Sed ibi integer ille versus non habetur: Nec is patria Cre- tensis, sed Cyrenensis fuit. Sensum reddidit Hiero- nymus hoc modo: Quamobrem increpa, ait, illos acriter. Mendaces quippe sunt, & malæ bestiæ, & pin- gri, qui falsa persuadeant, qui ferarum ritu sanguinem sitiunt deceptorum, & non cum silentio operantes pa- nem suum manducant, quorum Deus venter est, & glo- ria in confusione eorum, increpa eos, ut sani sint in fide. Uno autem versu, inquit B. Hunnius, tria no- tat vitia in popularibus suis Epimenides Poëta: Pri- mo quidem ipsorum levitatem in credendis iis, quæ un- dique afferuntur, & vanitatem in spargendis menda- ciis. Deinde malignitatem illorum carpit, quod sint homines infidi & perversi. Hinc κακὰ θηρία nomi- nat. Tertio luxuriam conjunctam cum ignavia, in fa- ciendis iis, quæ decet, ideoque ventres pigros dicit.

Vers. 13.

Ἡ μαρτυρία αὕτη ἐστὶν ἀληθής) Quasi dicat: Epime- nidis verba adduxi, non quod ipsi sit multum fidei tri- buendum, sed quod experientia idipsum & me docuerit & alios. Etsi testes domestici in laudando exiguam fi- dem mereantur: Ubi tamen propriam confiten- tur culpam vi veritatis coacti, reprobandi non sunt. Et probe hic observat Hieronymus, Apo- stolum circumspecte loquutum esse: Testimo- nium, inquit, hoc verum est, non totum carmen, de quo testimonium sumptum, non universum opus: Sed tantum hoc testimonium, hic versiculus, quo mendaces vocantur. Unde disquisitio hic de Jo- vis sepulchro instituitur a Chrysostomo, Theophy- lacto, & ab Hieronymo, quomodo Cretenses, quod Jovis sepulchrum inane construxerint, Jovem se- pultum in sua insula ceu gentes mendaces, Divina non sentientes, comprobarint? in spongiam in- cumbit; quanquam nec e Callimacho de laudibus Jovis, sed Epimenide versus ille adductus sit, ut an- te monuimus.

Δι' ἣν αἰτίαν) Cum tales sint.

Ἔλεγχε ἀυτὸς ἀποτόμως) הַכְרֵךְ Severe eos admo- ne. Sic ἀποτόμως habemus 2. Cor. 13, 10. Et ἀποτομίας vocem, Roman. 11, 22. Et nomen ἀπότομος & adverbium ἀποτόμως habetur apud Sapientem Ebræum. In glossario: Ἀποτόμως, præcise.

Ἵνα ὑγιαίνωσιν ἐν τῇ πίςει) · Ut doctrinam servent sa- nam, id est, incorruptam. Nam doctrinæ fidei nomen datur per Μετωνυμίαν. Sic infra cap. 2, 2. ὑγιαίνοντας τῇ πίςει. Notat Aristoteles, sanum primum dici de homine, ἀναλόγως de iis, quæ ad sanitatem conferant. Sic διδα- σκαλία ὑγιαίνεσα supra cap. 1, 9. infra cap. 2. vers. 1. 2. Ti- moth. 1, 13.

Vult quidem Apostolus infirmos circa usum indifferentium tolerari, Rom. 14. Sed hic de fal- sis Doctoribus & Seductoribus non infirmis fratri- bus sermo est, qui legem ceremonialem urgebant, & bona opera necessaria esse ad salutem conten- debant; quales exscindi optavit, Gal. 5, 12. Porro illud increpa illos acriter, monente hic Theodoreto, non est contrarium ejus, quod dixit, in lenitate docen- tem. Iis enim, qui nondum crediderunt, placide ac leniter tradenda est doctrina: Eos autem, qui credere profitentur, & ea, quæ fidei repugnant, facere conan- tur, medicamentis paulo asperioribus medicari con- venit. Ἀποτόμως, ut inquit Crocius, quasi trunca- tim. Nam sicut qui mitem & moderatum acrius feriat, perdit eum; sic qui impudenti adulatur, cum corrumpit, ne se ipsum agnoscat, inquit Theophylactus in h. l. Metaphora transsumpta a chirurgis, qui puti- dam carnem in vulneribus ad vivum usque resecant, ut mederi possint.

Vers. 14.

Μὴ προσέχοντες Ἰυδαϊκοῖς μύθοις) De Messia Rege terreno, de resurrectione priore in his terris, de bello Gog & Magog; de Behemotho & Leviathano ac simili- bus. Προσέχειν μύθοις habuimus & supra 1. Timoth. 1. vers. 4.

Καὶ ἐντολαῖς ἀνθρώπων ἀποςρεφομένων τὴν ἀλήθειαν) Etiam quæ Deus per Mosen præceperat, sunt præcepta ho- minum, ubi gentilibus imponuntur, quibus lex illa data non fuerat: imo etiam cum a Judæis hoc tempore exigun- tur ut ad salutem necessaria, Eph. 2, 15. Aversantium ve- ritatem, id est Evangelium. De voce ἀποςρέφειν vel ἀπο- τφέφεσθαι vide 2. Tim. 4, 4.

Vulgata vertit, non intendentes. Hieronymus & Ambrosianus habent, non attendentes: quod conve- nientius. Quia sensus est: ne seductoribus illis ex circumcisione fabulas suas venditantibus aures præbeant, neque mandatis hominum, quales erant traditiones variæ apud Judæos Matth. 15. & 23. δευτερώσεις, quas vocant, veritatem aversantes, ut Græcus & Syrus habent, quod, fatente Estio, & latius dicitur, & significantius, cujus loco Vulgata posuit aversantes a veritate. Fabulæ autem non sunt so- lum tales ineptiæ Judaicarum nugarum, quales hic

Grotius affert, de Leviathan & Behemoth, sed quæ- vis falsæ doctrinæ ipsorum, quia quicquid veritati cœlestis doctrinæ contrarium est, id inter fabulas recte computatur, etiam verborum lenocinio mirifice pingatur, & qui sunt humanarum traditio- num Autores, hanc sc. commendationem ab Apo- stolo amiserunt, quod avertant se a veritate, ut re- cte hic Osiander.

Vers. 15.

Πάντα μὲν καθαρὰ τοῖς καθαροῖς) Quod generaliter dixerat, applicat ad leges de cibis vetitis. De iisdem Roman. 14, 20. Πάντα μὲν καθαρὰ, nempe per Evange- lium. Hic additum est τοῖς καθαροῖς, id est Christianis, pu- ro corde & conscientia Deum colentibus, Matth. 5, 8. 1. Ti- moth. 1, 5. c. 3, 9. 2. Tim. 1, 3. c. 2, 22.

Τοῖς δὲ μεμιασμένοις( נִטְמָאִים vel חֲנֵפִים): Eis, qui vitæ sunt impuræ. Est enim Pallivum in sensu reciproco, ut Ebr. 12, 11.

Καὶ ἀπίσους) id est, qui a priori, impuritate per fidem se non purificant.

Οὐδὲν καθαρὸν) Non placent Deo, quæ agunt etiam circa res medias: quia actiones tales Deus ex animo æsti- mat. Vide 1. Cor. 7, 14. 1. Tim. 4, 5. & ibi dicta.

Omnia pura dicit puris, non indefinite, de omni- bus, sed de rebus indifferentibus, quales erant cibi, post abdicatam legem eæremonialem, universi: Nihil quicquam ergo mundis, hoc est, fidelibus, & de adiaphoris recte edoctis, immundum esse pro- nunciat: Ex adverso immundis, qui Christi sangui- ne ob ἀπιστίαν nondum erant mundati, & de liber- tate Evangelica minus recte sentiebant, nihil pu- rum erat. Ipsi enim erant polluti, utpote infide- les, vera fide destituti, qua sola purificantur corda, Act. 11, 10. Puris, inquit Beza, opponit non eos ex Judæis, qui ex ignorantia beneficii Christi, vel infir- mitate adhuc ista legalia observabant, ac exemplo suo ubique mones, ut qui firmi sunt, maximam ubiq; infir- morum habeant rationem: Sed opponit hypocritas, & malitiose ac pertinaciter veritati obsistentes, quibus ne tantillum quidem cedendum esse, sed fortiter obsi- stendum ex ipso Apostolo didicerat Titus Galat. 2, 3. Theophylactus: Non enim per naturam vel munda vel immunda res sunt, sed pro eorum voluntate, qui illis vescuntur. Nam qui puriores sunt & fideles, cuncta pro mundis habent, ut quæ a Deo condita sint, flagitia duntaxat immunda duxerint. Si vero im- puri sunt, qui immundis in cibum utuntur & infide- les, hic plane universa erunt immunda. Fit enim ut mens inquinatior de his male existimans, quæ nobis sunt in usum creata, sibi ipsi stulte ista confingat im- munda, cum suapte natura nequaquam sint. Nec secus agunt istiusmodi homines, ac solet, qui affecto sit stomacho, tum cibos, etsi suavissimi sint, insuaves ta- men existimat. Deducit hanc impuritatem Theo- phylactus ex persuasione hominum, qui cibos hos vel illos immundos habent: Sed deducenda potius videtur ex ipsa impuritate personarum, quæ cum non sint fide purificatæ, omnia ipsarum impura sunt. De quo B. Hunnius: De natura infidelitatis monemur, quæ homini universa polluit: Contaminat mentem ipsius & conscientiam, ut hic ait Apostolus: Personam ejus, quia impossibile est, placere Deo sine fide, Ebr. 11. Opera ipsius, quia quicquid ex fide non est, peccatum est, Rom. 14. Omnem cultum corrum- pit & inutilem reddit Esa. 1. Ipsam denique orationem hominis in peccatum convertit, Psal. 109. Ergo pe- tamus a Deo, ut corda nostra purificet fide Jesu Christi, atque sic opera nostra fide commendata placebunt ei. Quam sententiam confirmat, quod addit Aposto- lus. Monet autem Hieronymus: Ne ista tractantes occasionem demus illi hæresi, quæ juxta Apocalypsin & ipsum quoque Apostolum Paulum scribentem ad Corinthios putat de idolothytis esse vescendum, quia omnia munda sunt mundis. Nunc enim Apostolo non fuit propositum, de his, quæ immolantur dæ- monibus, disputare: Sed adversus Judæos, qui se- cundum legis abolitæ disciplinam quædam munda, quædam arbitrabantur immunda.

Ἀλλὰ μεμίανται αὐτῶν καὶ ὁ νῦς καὶ ἡ συνείδησις) Pas- sivum hic sumitur pro verbo substantivo & participio. נטמא apud Ebræos. Illud secundum καὶ hic valet ὥσ- περ, more itidem Ebræo. Non mirum est, mentem eorum sordibus obsitam non videre, quod verum est, quia ma- la vita, cujus ipsi sibi sunt conscii, sordes istas in mentem advehit.

Non assequitur mentem Apostoli Grotius. Non enim ait Apostolus, mentem infidelium non videre, quod videre est, nedum causam ejus reddit vitæ impuritatem: Et quid vitæ impuritas ad id facit, ut non agnoscant, cibos per se immundos nullos esse? Sed explicat, quomodo infidelibus, adeoque impuris nihil purum sit. Nimirum tan- tum abesse, ut pura sint, quæ agunt illi etiam circa res medias, aut DEO placere possint, ut etiam ipsa eorum & mens, & conscientia contamina- ta sit immunditie tum originali, tum multifaria actuati. Unde nihil ab ipsis proficisci potest, quod in oculis DEI purum sit, aut DEO placeat, cui sine fide impossibile est DEO placere, Ebr. 11. v. 6. Impurus enim animus etiam res, quæ per se im- puræ non sunt, contaminat. Hieronymus in h. l. Si mundi sumus, munda nobis est creatura. Si au- tem immundi & infideles, nobis omnia fiunt com- munia, sive per inhabitantem in cordibus nostris hæresin, sive per conscientiam delictorum. Porro si conscientia nostra nos non reprehenderit, & habue- rimus fiduciam pietatis ad Dominum: orabimus Spiritu, orabimus & mente: psallemus Spiritu, psallemus & mente, & procul erimus ab his, de quibus nunc scribitur: Polluta est eorum mens & conscientia. Inutilem ergo esse docet, B. Baldui- no observante, Apostolus observationem ceremo- niarum Leviticarum, nisi cor sit mundum coram Deo; non necessariam vero iis, qui cor habent mundum. Nihil enim ad illam mundiciam cordis facit, quæ consistit in vera fide, qua purificantur corda, Act. 15, 9. Fidelibus igitur omnia munda sunt, non possunt contaminari usu ciborum aut dierum, vel intermissione lotionum Judaicarum; non etiam of- fenduntur ullis ritibus, quia in quo consistat liber- tas Christiana intelligunt: qui vero fide in CHRI- STUM destituuntur, quales illi erant Cretensium matæologi, iis nihil proderit externa illa ablutio, & ciborum dierumque observatio: Sed mens ipsorum est impura, quia nihil recte credunt de Deo, vivunt absque CHRISTO & fide, nihil intelligunt de li- bertate Christiana, nihil de vera ratione salutem consequendi: ipsorum conscientia etiam est impu- ra, quia peccatis se contaminant gravissimis, qui- bus conscientia vulneratur, & tamen in externa il- la ceremoniarum Leviticarum observatione salutem qurunt. Beza, (& ex eo Crocius) mentis no- mine, inquit, declarat intelligentiam θεωρητικὴν, in qua collocatur συντήρησις, quæ propositiones suppe- ditat. Συνείδησις vero, id est, conscientia, colloca- tur in intelligentia πρακτικῇ, & assumptiones pro- mit. Quod si utraque illa facultas est depravata, quæ tandem erit conclusio τῶν κριτηρίς? Loquitur autem de mente & conscientia, quatenus istos oportuit lu- ce Dei illustrari ad recte de rebus Divinis judican- dum. Verum de cordis ac conscientiæ puritate ac impuritate, ut actiones emergant, sive puræ sive impuræ: Mundis, inquit, omnia munda. Coinquinatis autem nihil mundum. Eodem etiam antithefin refpicere oportet, sed inquinata sunt eorum mens & conscientia.

Vers. 16.

Θεὸν ὁμολογῆσι εἰδέναι) Judæi scilicet isti dicunt se agnoscere Deum verum, mundi opificem, autorem legis per Mosen datæ, Inspiratorem Prophetarum: Rom. 2, 17. Ὁμολογῆσι prædicant, profitentur, Rom. 10, 9. 1. Tim. 6, v. 12. 1. Joh. 4, 2. 3.

Τοῖς δὲ ἔργοις ἀρνῦνται) Faciunt contra legis præcepta. De hac loquutione vide 2. Tim. 3, 5.

Hæc sunt manifesta indicia, inquit B. Baldui- nus, impuræ conscientiæ. Nam vote quidem se ve- ros DEI cultores profitentur, Abrahæ filios, Mosis discipulos, si vitam vero spectes, omnis religionis sunt expertes.

Βδελυκτοὶ ὄντες) Digni, quos omnes execrentur. Sic- ut תועבה, quod proprie est βδέλυγμα. Sed etiam per βδελυκτὸς vertitur Prov. 17, 15.

Καὶ ἀπειθεῖς) Ne illi quidem parent legi, quam Divi- nam esse dicunt, Rom. 2, 21. 22. 23.

Καὶ πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἀδόκιμοι) Rabbini dicerent פסולים, inutiles, non minus, quam nummi, rejiciun- tur. Vide Rom. 1, 28. 1. Cor. 9, 27. 2. Cor. 13, 5. 6. 2. Ti- moth. 3, 8. Ebr. 6, 8. Tales autem sunt profani omnes: et- iamsi quid faciant, quod oportet, non faciunt tamen, ut oportet.

Hieronymus recte execrabiles & inobedientes ex- posuit. Vulgata autem barbare abominatos & incredibiles. Sunt autem βδελυκτοὶ, qui sic vi- vunt, ut DEO sint abominabiles, quia sinceræ doctrinæ nec credunt nec obediunt, & ad vere bona opera facienda prorsus non sunt idonei. Videntur autem mihi, inquit Beza, vocari βδελυκτοὶ, qui sibi videbantur omnium sanctissimi. Ἀπειθεῖς, qui se jactabant supra legem aliquid facere. Ἀδόκι- μοι, qui quum videri vellent tenere justitiæ regulam, omnium tamen minime norant, quæ vera sit justi- tia. Audiendus hic iterum Hieronymus: Hi ve- ro, quorum polluta est mens & conscientia, DEUM se nosse confitentur, factis autem negant, secundum id, quod in Esaia dicitur: Populus hic labiis me ho- norat, cor autem eorum longe est à me. Quomodo igitur labiis quis honorat, & corde procul recedit: Ita DEUM sermone quis confitens operibus negat. Negans autem operibus DEUM, confessione simu- lata, recte execrabilis & profanus est, & nulla ve- ritatis ratione persuasus inobediens & incredulus appellatur. Unde evenit, ut ad omne opus bonum reprobus sit, quod scilicet & ea, quæ naturali bonita- te superatus forte bona fecerit non sint bona, dum mentis perversitate sunt reproba. Existimant qui- dam, in eo tantum DEUM negari, si quis in perse- cutione comprehensus à gentilibus, se renuerit Chri- stianum. Sed ecce Apostolus omnibus quæ perver- sa sunt factis, DEUM asserit denegari. CHRI- STUS sapientia est, justitia, veritas, sanctitas, forti- tudo. Negatur per insipientiam sapientia, per ini- quitatem justitia, per mendacium veritas, per tur- pitudinem sanctitas, per imbecillitatem animi for- titudo. Et quotiescunque vincimur vitiis atque pec- catis; toties DEUM negamus. Et è contrario: Quoties bene quid agimus, toties DEUM confi- temur.

SECTIO II.

De OFFICIIS AUDITORUM.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

Canons are prescribed for inculcation in the aged, both male and of the weaker sex, as well as in the younger, both women and men, to all of whom Titus ought to shine as a light by his own example: likewise for servants, that the doctrine of God our Savior may be adorned in all things, whose saving grace has appeared to all men, and instructs all to renounce impiety and worldly pleasure, but to pursue chastity, justice, and piety, with the expectation of the final appearing of God our Savior, who not only redeemed us, but also cleanses us for His own peculiar people.

There are two parts: I. Exhortations for different ages, chapters or points, up to v. 10. II. Reasons or arguments for the exhortations, up to v. 15.

PART I. Exhortations for

of the Gospel and the law, much less is the Gospel to be transformed into the law.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Praescribuntur canones inculcandi senibus Ma- sculini, & sequioris sexus, ut junioribus tum foeminis, tum viris, quibus omnibus Titus pralucere exemplo suo debeat: Ser- vts item, ut ornetur per omnia doctrina Dei Salvatoris, cujus gratia salutifera apparuit omnibus hominibus, omnesque informat de abneganda impietate & mundana volupta- te, sectanda autem castitate, justitia & pie- tate, cum expectatione novissimae apparitio- nis Dei Salvatoris, qui nos non redemit tan- tum, sed etiam mundat in peculium suum.

Partes duae sunt: I. Adhortationes pro diversis aetatibus capita vel momenta, ad v. 10. II. Ad- hortationum rationes vel argumenta, ad v. 15.

PARS I. Adhortationes pro diversis aetatibus ca- pita vel momenta.

angelii & legis, nedum Evangelium transmutan- dum in legem est.

## 2:1
Ver. 1.

Σὺ δὲ λάλει) that is, teach. For thus the Hebrews say אמר, when they treat of Teachers.

Νηφαλίως εἶναι) that is, using wine, no more than health requires. The Greeks say that for old men wine is instead of milk. But they ought to observe moderation, first so that they may consult their own health and mind; then so that as much as they excel others in age, they may excel them also in examples. Concerning the word νηφαλίως see 1 Tim. 3, 2. 11.

Σεμνός) See 1 Tim. 3, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 1.

Σὺ δὲ λάλει) id est, doce. Sic enim Ebraei dicunt אמר, ubi de Doctoribus agunt.

Νηφαλίως εἶναι) id est, vino utentes, non plus, quam valetudo requirit. Senibus vinum pro lacte ajunt esse Graeci. Sed modum servare debent, primum ut valetudini suae & menti consulant; deinde ut quantum aetate praestant caeteris, tantum praestent & exemplis. De voce νηφαλίως vide 1. Tim. 3, 2. 11.

Σεμνός) Vide 1. Tim. 3, 8.

## 2:1
Ἃ πρέπει τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ διδασκαλίᾳ) Which agree with that holy discipline, of which I spoke before in chap. 1, 9.

Which teach sound doctrine; for this is κατ' εὐσέβειαν, directed toward piety v. 1. just as also the mystery concerning Christ, 1 Tim. 3, v. 16. is called the mystery of piety. The reason is rendered in the whole other part of this chapter v. 10. 12. 14. It is one thing therefore, as Jerome warns in this place, to speak sound doctrine, another to teach those things which soundly agree with doctrine: because in the one there is only simple instruction, in the other, along with what you teach, there is also the correction of life. Therefore the doctrine of the Cretans is not to be confused with the Republic, which among many excellent laws also had those which prescribed sobriety, and gravely prohibited drunken drinking bouts and wine-bibbing, to which belonged the law of Minos, whose words are recited by Plato, not to drink together to drunkenness. But because, with the observance of laws having gradually slipped away, morals had gone for the worse, the Apostle judges that faithful old men in Crete are to be recalled to sobriety by the authority of God, which they ought to have maintained from the old institution, and were neglecting. For it is excessively shameful for those converted to Christ not to pursue sobriety, to which a King ignorant of the true God had bound their infidel ancestors, as Crocius says here. The Vulgate rendered the word σεμνὸς as chaste. Jerome interpreted it as honest, the Ambrosian as grave: But that word nowhere denotes chaste, even if chastity is also required for honesty and gravity, so that old men may be alien to all lasciviousness. Σεμνότης is gravity of manners, which is opposed to levity, with which unchaste manners and speech are joined, such as are sometimes heard in youthful age; but old men in their manners and speech and indeed in their whole life ought to be venerable, lest they luxuriate in another's age, lest, with blood already cold to lust, they be examples to adolescents for ruin, as Jerome speaks. We understand Σώφρονας not as the moderation of the affections with Chrysostom, of which later, but as prudence in counsels and circumspection in all actions, which is the more proper ornament of that age.

Sound in faith) Above ch. 1, 13. In love, in patience) Which follow faith, 2 Tim. 3, 10. Health in these is sincerity.

He who is sound in faith, says Jerome, who is sound in charity, let him also be sound in patience, and patience, which is especially proven in temptations: because it is of no use to have what we enumerated above, unless all the riches and merchandise with which the ship is laden are saved in a storm, and while the winds blow hither and thither, those things which were well acquired are delivered without shipwreck. For he who shall have persevered unto the end, he shall be saved. But these things must be inculcated particularly to old men, because old men for the most part are cold in faith: hence charity is more relaxed, and patience more difficult. For these flow from faith. Chrysostom: Most rightly, he says, he added altogether: And patience: That indeed is most fitting for old men. To the elders, says Theophylact, tolerance is especially enjoined: and not undeservedly, as those in whom black bile sits upon the highest nostrils, and they are disturbed by the smallest things. Theodoret: That they themselves may both believe sincerely, and shine forth in charity toward their neighbor, and bear with a strong and excellent spirit the troubles which are brought upon them by the enemies of the truth. See concerning old men Isa. 45, 20. Sir. 25, 4. Eccles. 4, 13. It is truly a ridiculous thing, says Chrysostom homil. VII in Heb., to be adorned outwardly with gray hair: but inwardly to have the sense of a boy.

Latin:

Ἃ πρέπει τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ διδασκαλίᾳ) Quae conveni- unt cum ista sancta disciplina, de qua ante dixi cap. 1, 9.

Quae docent sanam doctrinam; haec enim est κατ' εὐσέβειαν, ad pietatem directa v. 1. quemad- modum & mysterium de Christo, 1. Tim. 3, v. 16. dicitur τῆς ἐυσεβείας μυστήριον. Causa redditur in tota parte altera hujus capitis vers. 10. 12. 14. A- lind ergo est, monente Hieronymo in h. l. sanam do- ctrinam loqui, aliud ea, quae sane conveniunt doctri- nae, docere: quia in altero simplex tantum institutio est, in altero, cum eo, quod doces, vita quoque corre- ctio est. Non itaque confundenda doctrina Ev- Cretensium Respublica inter multas praeclaras leges & illas habebat, quae sobrietatem praecipiebant, com- potationes temulentas ac vinolentiam graviter pro- hibebant, ad quas pertinebat Minois lex, cujus verba a Platone recitantur, μὴ συμπίνειν ἀλλήλοις εἰς μέ- θην. Quia vero prolapsa sensim legum observatio- ne mores in deterius iverant, Apostolus fideles senes in Creta ad sobrietatem Dei autoritate revocandos cen- set, quam tueri debebant ex veteri instituto, ac negli- gebant. Nimiis enim turpe, ad CHRISTUM con- versos sobrietati non studere, ad quam veri Dei igna- rus Rex majores ipsorum infideles obstrinxerat, ut hic Crocius. Vulgata vocem σεμνὸς pudicos red- didit. Honestos interpretatus est Hieronymus, graves Ambrosianus: Vox autem illa nuspiam pu- dicos notat, etsi ad honestatem & gravitatem re- quiritur etiam pudicitia, ut senes ab omni lascivia alieni sint. Σεμνότης est gravitas morum, quæ op- ponitur levitati, cum qua conjuncti sunt impudici mores & sermones, quales in juvenili interdum ætate audiuntur; Senes vero in moribus ac ser- monibus adeoque totâ vita sua debent esse vene- randi, ne in aliena ætate luxurient, ne jam fri- gido ad libidinem sanguine, exempla sint adolescen- tibus ad ruinam, ut Hieronymus loquitur. Σώ- φρονας non de moderatione affectuum cum Chryso- stomo, qua de postea, sed de prudentia in consi- liis, & circumspectione in omnibus actionibus intelligimus, quæ proprius ætatis illius ornatus est.

Ὑγιαίνοντας τῇ πίσει) Supra c. 1, 13. Τῇ ἀγάπῃ, τῇ ὑπομονῇ) Quæ fidem sequuntur, 2. Tim. 3, 10. Sanitas in his est sinceritas.

Qui sanus in fide, ait Hieronymus, qui sanus in charitate, sanus quoque sit in patientia, & pa- tientia, quæ maxime in tentationibus comprobatur: quia nihil prodest habere, quæ supra enumeravi- mus, nisi omnes divitiæ & merosmonia, quibus onusta est navis, in tempestate serventur, & ventis hinc inde perflantibus, absque naufragio ea, quæ bene parta sunt, liberentur. Qui enim perseveraverit usque in finem, hic salvus erit. Senibus autem peculiariter hæc inculcanda, quia senes plerum- que frigent fide: Hinc remissior charitas est, & patientia difficilior. Hæc enim ex fide fluunt. Chrysostomus: Rectissime, inquit, omnino sub- junxit: Et patientia: Id quippe maxime senibus con- venit. Senioribus, inquit Theophylactus, præci- pue injungitur tolerantia: nec immerito, ut qui- bus atra bilis summis insideat naribus, & minimis obturbentur. Theodoretius: Ut ipsi & sincere credant, & charitate in proximum resplendeant, &, quæ à veritatis hostibus inferuntur, molestias forti & excellenti animo ferant. Vide de senibus Esa. 45, 20. Sir. 25, 4. Eccles. 4, 13. Vere est res ridicula, inquit Chrysostomus homil. VII. in Ebr. extrinsecus quidem ornari canis: Intrinsecus autem habere sensum pueri.

## 2:2
Ver. 2.

Πρεσβύτας) It seems that age is to be understood here rather than dignity. And the word πρεσβύτης is frequent in that sense among the interpreters of the Old Testament. What follows below in verses 4 and 6 moves me to take it so.

Age is altogether to be understood here. For he had already instructed the Presbyters by reason of their office in chapter 1. And therefore he proceeds now from the Ecclesiastical state to the Oeconomic state: Or rather from the office of the Teachers to the duties of the hearers, and among them of different ages and orders: Or if you prefer it so, from the requirements of the Presbytery or of those to be chosen for the Presbytery, to the parts of Christianity both in general and in particular. Generally, says Jerome on this passage, having previously instructed Titus what he himself ought to speak to all, in that which he says: But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine: now he explains by individual species what becomes each age. First, things suitable for old men: then what becomes old women, thirdly what things are apt for young people, namely both males and females, although in the precept for old women he has subjoined commands concerning young women: so that he might not so much teach the young women himself, as explain what they should be taught by the old women. Finally, concerning servants, he establishes precepts so decently for each age and condition, that his speech may be a rule of life and morals.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Πρεσβύτας) Videtur potius hic aetas intelligenda quam dignitas. Et frequens est eo sensu vox πρεσβύτης apud Interpretes Veteris Testamenti. Movet me, ut ita sumam, id, quod sequitur infra 4. & 6.

Omnino aetas hic intelligenda. Nam Presby- teros ratione officii jam informarat cap. 1. Ideo- que a statu Ecclesiastico progreditur nunc ad statum Oeconomicum: Vel potius ab officio Doctorum ad officia auditorum, & inter eos diversarum aetatum atque ordinum: Aut si ita mavis, a requisitis Pres- byterii seu eligendorum ad Presbyterium, ad partes Christianismi tum in genere, tum in specie. Ge- neraliter, inquit Hieronymus h. 1. Tito ante prae- cipiens, quid ipse loqui deberet ad cunctos, in eo quod ait: Tu vero loquere, que decet sanam doctrinam: nunc per singulas species, quid unamquamque aetatem deceat, exponit. Primum senibus viris convenien- tia: deinde anus quid deceat, tertio quae adolescen- tibus apta sint, tam maribus scilicet, quam foeminis, licet in praecepto mulierum vetularum de adolescenti- bus foeminis mandata subjecerit: ut non tam ipse do- ceret adolescentulas, quam quid a vetulis docerentur, exponeret. Extremo de servis & per singulas aeta- tes & conditiones sic decenter praecepta constituit, ut sermo ejus vita morumque sit regula.

## 2:2
Σώφρονας) See the same.

The canons which are to be prescribed to old men concern morals both common and proper to Christians. Of these there are three. For there is required 1. sobriety, 2. honesty, 3. prudence: which, as they become everyone, so they are especially fitting for old men: Of these likewise three occur, requiring soundness in faith, charity, and patience.

He had just taught concerning refuting false Doctors, so that they might be avoided, and what kind of doctrines and morals they have: Now on the contrary, what true Doctors ought to inculcate and teach, both as to morals and life, according to the reason of different ages, and as to doctrine, which leads to true piety and inflames it, and for that reason it is here exhibited in summary, especially what it explains regarding the grace of redemption, sanctification, and glorification, and demonstrates to other Presbyters in the example of Titus. The Apostle had commended two things especially to the care of Titus, leaving him in Crete, namely the constitution of the ministry and the ἐπιδιόρθωσιν. He dealt with the former in the first chapter. He is about to deal with the latter in the present chapter, and indeed in this verse generally. For since impostors were strenuously doing their duty in deceiving minds, in subverting whole families, by teaching things which they ought not. He opposes Titus as a wall against ruin, saying: But do you speak. Chrysostom refers these things to the preceding chapter, and therefore paraphrases thus: Those men indeed are unclean, but do not you be silent on their account: Even if they do not respect you, he says, yet you, perform what is your duty; and if they do not obey, you admonish, you advise. Yet they are more correctly referred to what follows.

He wishes old men therefore to be sober, according to Jerome's interpretation, or vigilant: because νηφάλιος among the Greeks sounds both: Honest, so that the gravity of their morals may adorn the gravity of their age. Chaste, so that they may not be wanton in an age not their own, so that they, with blood already cold for lust, may not be an example to adolescents for ruin. Old age, says Chrysostom, has certain proper vices and diseases, which youth lacks. And indeed old age itself is a disease: yet there is in it besides a certain sluggishness and slowness, deep forgetfulness, and dullness of the senses and irascibility. Theophylact seems to understand vigilance by sobriety, which we do not deny is consequently implied. For sobriety is required so that we may be able to be vigilant. Since, he says, by the vice of age old men are slower, forgetful and torpid, and quite difficult, for that reason, he says, let them be sober, that is, alert, and in those things which are of God, more perceptive and diligent.

Latin:

Σώφρονας) Vide idem.

Canones, qui senibus viris praescribendi sunt, concernunt moralia tum communia, tum Christia- nis propria. Illorum tres sunt. Requiritur enim 1. sobrietas, 2. honestas, 3. prudentia: quae cum o- mnes deceant, tum vero maxime senibus conve- niunt: Horum itidem tres occurrunt, sanitatem in fide, charitatem, & patientiam requirentes.

De falsis Doctoribus redarguendis, ut fugian- tur, & quales eorum sint doctrinae ac mores proxime docuerat: Jam contra, quid veri Do- ctores inculcare ac docere debeant, tum qua mo- res ac vitam, pro ratione diversarum aetatum, tum qua doctrinam, quae ad veram pietatem ducit, & inflammat, ejusque gratia hic summatim exhibe- tur, imprimis quod ad gratiam redemptionis, san- ctificationis, & glorificationis, exponit, & in ex- emplo Titi aliis Presbyteris demonstrat. A- postolus duo potissimum Titi cura commendaverat, eum relinquens in Creta, scilicet ministerii consti- tutionem & ἐπιδιόρθωσιν. De illa egit capite pri- mo. De hac acturus capite praesenti, & quidem hoc versu generaliter. Cum enim impostores stre- nue facerent officium in decipiendis mentibus, in subvertendis integris familiis, docendo quae non o- portet. Titum opponit tanquam murum adversus ruinam, inquiens: At tu loquere. Chrysostomus refert haec ad caput praecedens, ideoque ita παραφράζει: Isti quidem immundi sunt, caeterum tu eorum causa ne taceas: Etsi illi non suspiciant, inquit, tamen tu, quod tui est muneris, perfice; & si illi non obtemperent, tu admone, consule. Re- ctius tamen ad consequentia referuntur.

Senes igitur sobrios esse vult, interprete Hieronymo, sive vigilantes: quia νηφάλιος apud Graecos utrum- que sonat: Honestos, ut aetatis gravitatem morum gravitas decoret. Pudicos, ne in aliena aetate luxu- rient, ne jam frigido ad libidinem sanguine, exemplo sint adolescentibus ad ruinam. Habet senectus, in- quit Chrysostomus, vitia quaedam propria & mor- bos, quibus juventus caret. Et ipsa quippe senectus morbus est: inest tamen illi praeterea segnities qua- dam ac tarditas, oblivio profunda, & obtusio sensuum atque iracundia. Theophylactus vigilantiam vide- tur intelligere per sobrietatem, quam consequen- ter innui non abnuimus. Nam sobrietas requiritur, ut vigilantes esse possimus. Cum aetatis, inquit, vitio senes tardiores sint, obliviosi & torpidi, & ad- modum difficiles, eo, inquit, & sobrii sint, id est, exciti, & in his, quae Dei sunt, perspicaciores & diligentes.

## 2:3
Ver. 3.

Aged women likewise) They are also called thus by way of excellence, those who preside. But we have already indicated why this should be taken here concerning age. And Aeschines uses that word in this sense.

It is certain that age is regarded from the relation of old men and young men, aged women and younger women. But Grotius does not seem to be consistent here, since he thinks that the σωφρονίστριαι or teachers of manners are being instructed: concerning whom he also took this word in his annotations on the Gospels in the history of Anna, Luke 2, 37. From this order of widows, he says, it was customary to read not only the deaconesses, who cared for poor women, but also the aged women, who were also called those who preside, of whom Paul makes mention as teachers of manners and instructors of other women, Tit. 2, 3. These things Grotius in the same place.

In holy attire) Κατάσημα according to Hesychius, which in the glossary is translated as status, signifies both gesture and habit. Ἱεροπρεπεῖς as if they were always occupied in the temple, like those Jewish aged women, concerning whom see what was said at Luke 2, 37. Thus ἱεροπρεπής πίσσα in Lucian. Ἱεροπρεπῶς, θεοπρεπῶς, Hesychius.

Chrysostom also took these things concerning holy habit in general, so that from the very habit and clothing the interior ornament might be shown. Similarly Theodoret understood an honest habit, and no less Theophylact, who nevertheless adds another interpretation besides of others concerning a holy habit: he says that aged women ought to carry before them decorum and modesty even from their very gesture and habit. But some say that these are those who perform the duty of ministering in the Church, whom even their very clothing demands that they should carry forward the decorum of holiness, that is, those who are congruent with sacred ministries. The former pleases, and not undeservedly, Jerome, which he nevertheless joins with the prior requirements of old men on account of the word ὡσαύτως; and he explains it more fully in this way: Aged women likewise, that is, in such a way as the old men, in all things honest, sober, chaste, sound in faith, and charity, and patience: And for their sex let them have this as proper, that they be in holy attire, or, as it is read better in the Greek, ἐν καταστήματι ἱεροπρεπεῖς, so that their very gait and movements, countenance, speech, silence, may carry forward a certain dignity of sacred decorum.

Not slanderers) 1 Tim. 3:11.

Concerning which Jerome beautifully says: Because this type of woman is accustomed to be garrulous, according to that: At the same time they are idle, they learn to go about from house to house; and not only idle, but also talkative and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not. Therefore he wishes them not to be slanderers, that is, not accusers, not such as, in order to please others, disparage others: Or certainly because they themselves have already passed youth, they dispute about the states of young women and say: she is adorned thus, she is accompanied thus; she proceeds thus, she loves him, she is loved by him, when even if these things are true, they ought not to accuse them before others as much as to correct them secretly with the love of CHRIST, and rather teach them not to do it, than to accuse in public what she has done.

Not given to much wine) The same as sober in the aforementioned place to Timothy. • Given to wine, Proverbs 23:30. Habit makes men slaves of vices, John 8:34, Rom. 7:14. A woman who drinks much and drinks pure wine in Plautus.

Concerning this vice of old women, and the connection of this vice with the former in the same persons, Jerome says thus: These ages are accustomed to give themselves to wine, according to their desire, and when they have seemed to themselves wise and eloquent among their cups, they assume a sort of austerity of morals, speaking that which they seem to themselves to be, and not remembering that which they were. Therefore let old women be prohibited from the excessive drinking of wine, since what lust is in adolescents, drunkenness is in the elderly. Or how can an old woman teach young women chastity, when if a young woman has imitated the drunkenness of an old woman, she cannot be modest. He significantly expressed: not given to much wine. For it is a kind of slavery, and an extreme condition, for the senses of men to be occupied by wine, and not to be their own, but the wine's. Chrysostom: For the same, he says, is the peculiar vice of women and old age. For because they grow cold with age, they devote themselves to a great zeal for drinking. Wherefore he admonishes them here especially, that they should cut off the vice of drunkenness from all parts, desiring them to be most remote from this disease, and to escape the mockery which arises from this. For vapors are more easily carried from the lowest parts to the higher, and occupy the brain, and the head is harmed from this (in that they are already worn out by age) and from there drunkenness especially occurs.

This age does indeed have need of wine, since it is very weak, but it must be temperate. The same admonition touches young women, though not for the same reason, but because from the drinking of wine the vehement flame of lust is kindled.

Καλοδιδασκάλους) Teaching right things. Such a woman is praised in Proverbs 31:25, ותורת־חסד לשונה. Not such as those of whom Hermione complains in Euripides: Κακῶν γυναικῶν εἴσοδοί μ᾽ ἀπώλεσαν.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Πρεσβύτιδας ὡσαύτως) Appellantur & sic κατ᾿ ἐξοχὴν αἱ προκαθήμεναι. Sed cur de ætate potius hic sumendum sit, jam indicavimus. Et utitur hoc sensu ea voce Æschi- nes.

Respici ætatem è relatione senum & juvenum, anuum & juniorum fœminarum, certum est. Sed non constare hic videtur sibi Grotius, quum infor- mari τὰς σωφρονιςρίας vel morum magistras cen- seat: De quibus etiam hanc vocem accepit in annot. ad Evangel. in historia Hannæ Luc. 2, 37. Ex hoc viduarum, inquit ordine legi solebant non tantum αἱ διάκονοι, quæ fœminas pauperes curabant, sed & πρεσβύτιδες, quæ & προκαθήμεναι dicebantur, aliarum mulierum σωφρονίςριαι & morum magistrarum meminit Paulus, Tit. 2, 3. Hæc ibidem Grotius.

Ἐν κατασήματι ἱεροπρεπεῖς) Κατάσημα Hesychio, quod in glossario vertitur status, & gestum & habitum significat. Ἱεροπρεπεῖς quasi semper in templo versaren- tur, ut anus illæ Judaicæ, de quibus vide quæ dicta ad Luc. 2, 37. Sic ἱεροπρεπής πίσσα apud Lucianum. Ἱερο- πρεπῶς, θεοπρεπῶς, Hesychius.

Hæc de habitu sancto in genere Chrysostomus etiam accepit, ut ex ipso habitu atque amictu in- terior ostendatur ornatus. Similiter ho- nestum habitum intellexit Theodoretus, nec minus Theophylactus, qui tamen & aliam præter- ea aliorum addit interpretationem de habitu sa- cro: Aniculas vel ex gestu ipso & habitu dicit debere præ se decorem & modestiam ferre. Nonnulli vero, quæ in Ecclesia ministrandi munere funguntur, has esse dicunt, quas vel ex ipso amictu deposcit, ut san- ctitatis præferant decus, id est, quæ sacris congru- ant ministeriis. Prius placet, nec immerito, Hie- ronymo, quod tamen ob vocem ὡσάυτως cum prioribus senum requisitis conjungit; pleniusque explicat hoc modo: Anus similiter, hoc est, ita, ut viri senes, in omnibus honestæ, sobriæ, pudicæ, sanæ in fide, & charitate, & patientia: Et pro sexu suo hoc habeant proprium, ut sint in habitu sancto, sive, ut melius legitur in Græco, ἐν καταστήματι ἱεροπρε- πεῖς, ut ipse quoque earum incessus & motus, vul- tus, oratio, silentium, quandam decoris sacri præfe- rant dignitatem.

Μὴ διαβόλυς) 1. Timoth. 3, 11.

De quo pulchre Hieronymus: Quia hoc genus muliercularum solet esse garrulum, juxta illud: Si- mul & otiosæ discunt circumire domos; non autem solum otiosæ, sed & verbosæ, & curiosæ, loquentes quæ non oportet. Propterea eas vult esse non incentri- ces, id est, non accusatrices, non tales, quæ ut aliis pla- ceant, de aliis detrahant: Aut certe quia ipsæ ado- lescentiam jam transgressæ sunt, de adolescentularum statibus disputent ac dicant: illa sic ornatur, illa sic comitatur; sic illa procedit, amat illum, amatur ab illo, cum etiam, si hæc vera sint, non debeant tant apud alios accusare, quam ipsam secrete CHRISTI charitate corripere, & magis docere, ne faciat, quam in publico accusare quod fecerit.

Μὴ οἴνῳ πολλῷ δεδυλωμένας) Idem quod νηφαλέυς dicto ad Timotheum loco. • Οἴνῳ δεδυλωμένοι מאחרים על־היין, Proverb. 23, 30. Con- suetudo homines vitiorum servos facit, Joh. 8, 34. Rom. 7, 14. Anus multibiba & merobiba apud Plautum.

De hoc anuum vitio, & vitii hujus cum priori in iisdem commercio ita Hieronymus: Solent hæ ætates vino se dedere, pro libidine, & cum inter po- cula sibi prudentes visæ fuerint & facundæ, morum quasi austeritatem assumere, loquentes hoc, quod sibi videntur esse, & non recordantes illud, quod fuerunt. A vini ergo nimio potu anus prohibeantur, quo- niam quod in adolescentibus libido, hoc in senibus ebrietas est. Aut quomodo potest anus adolescen- tulas docere castitatem, cum si ebrietatem vetulæ mulieris adolescentula fuerit imitata, pudica esse non possit. Signanter autem expressit: non vino multo servientes. Servitus enim quædam est, & extrema conditio, vino sensus hominum occupari, & non suum esse, sed vini. Chrysostomus: Idem quippe, inquit, mulierum atque senectutis proprium vitium est. Nam quod ætate frigescent, magno potationis inserviant studio. Quocirca eas hic maxime admonet, ut omnibus ex partibus ebrieta- tis vitium amputent, eas ab hoc morbo remotissi- mas esse cupiens, atque irrisionem, quæ hinc ex- surgit, effugere. Namque facilius vapores ex infimis ad superiora feruntur, ac cerebrum oc- cupant, & caput hinc læditur (eo quod jam ætate confecta sint ipsæ) atque inde maxime ebrietas fit.

Habet quidem vino opus hæc ætas, quum maxime infirma sit, cæterum temperato. Eadem admoni- tio adolescentulas tangit, verum non eadem ex cau- sa, sed ideo, quod ex vini potatione vehemens libidi- nis incenditur flamma.

Καλοδιδασκάλους) Recta docentes. Talis fœmina lau- data in Proverb. 31, 25. ותורת־חסד לשונה. Non tales, de quibus queritur apud Euripidem Hermione : Κακῶν γυναικῶν εἴσοδοί μ᾽ ἀπώλεσαν.

## 2:4
Verse 4.

Ἵνα σωφρονίζωσι τὰς νέας) Theano: To you younger women, authority is given by the law to rule over the servants as soon as you are married. But instruction comes from the elders, being obliged to advise always concerning the household management, and what follows. Σωφρονισταὶ were called at Athens those who formed the characters of the youth.

It is not necessary that we restrict these things specifically to teachers of morals. For it is the duty of all older women to inform the morals of the young, where the occasion arises. Any older woman, says Chrysostom, should moderate and rule a young woman. Estius acknowledges that Καλοδιδασκάλους is more correctly rendered 'teaching good things,' as the Ambrosian and Jerome read, than 'teaching well,' as the Vulgate has it: and he says that the Greek expression signifies masters of good arts. The Vulgate rendered the verb σωφρονίζωσι as 'that they may teach (the young women) prudence,' although some Latin codices begin a new period and admonition with the word 'young women,' that Titus ought to admonish the young women, with the agreement of Thomas and Lyranus, but against the Greek truth and the reading of Jerome: because the Greek verb is transitive, which Jerome rendered 'let them instruct in chastity,' and the Ambrosian, 'let them simply institute.' Moreover, according to Estius (even if the Vulgate has it otherwise), it signifies to render one modest and sober, or temperate, which older women ought to do both by example and by doctrine. The Syriac explained: 'And let them render those who are young women honest.' However, I would easily prefer the interpretation of the Ambrosian: for the chapters of instruction follow only afterwards, among which is also chastity and sobriety. Beza rendered it: 'That they may teach them to be wise.' The Vulgate, he says, 'that they may teach prudence': Erasmus: 'That they may be able to render young women modest.' Neither is correct, as I think. And here σωφροσύνη seems to extend more broadly than in the previous and the immediately following verse, being opposed, of course, to youthful lasciviousness and other vices of that age and sex, to which are opposed the virtues which he describes later. Moreover, it seems that the Apostle does not immediately entrust this instruction to the Presbyters, so that scandal may be avoided: since it does not befit a Bishop to approach young women, or to call them to himself, which easily gives rise to suspicion. He wishes, therefore, for it to be done through older women.

Φιλάνδρους εἶναι). That they may be lovers of their husbands, in which sense Lucian spoke of φιλανδρία in praise. Ἀνὴρ signifies both a husband and any person of the male sex, in which respect a woman is called φίλανδρος for the sake of reproach, 'man-crazy'.

That chief thing, says Chrysostom, is the foundation of domestic peace and of all good things, if a wife is in all things in agreement with her husband. For where this is, nothing sad can happen. For in what way, when the head is connected and joined to the body, could any sedition or any dissension arise there? Necessarily, indeed, all other things are in peace. For when the leaders are at peace, who could now divide and tear apart the peace? Just as, on the contrary, when these are in disagreement with each other, nothing can be healthy, and the whole family will totter at once. Nothing, therefore, is greater than this thing, and nothing more necessary; indeed, it surpasses both money and noble birth and power, and is by far the most useful of all other things. For he does not say simply 'to be in peace,' but 'to love their husbands.' For such is the power of love, that wherever the scent of its fragrance breathes, nothing at all sad, nothing unpleasant can break in. For from this also the rest of the good things arise. But what doctrine is it, asks Jerome, to love one's husbands? Since this is established not in the speech of the teacher, but in the heart of the lover? He wishes them to love their husbands chastely: he wishes there to be a modest love between woman and man, so that she may render the debt to her husband with modesty and shame and as if by the necessity of sex, rather than she herself demanding it from him, and she may believe that she is performing the work of children before the eyes of God and the Angels. But why should not young women also be informed to love their husbands, even if this is established in the heart of the lover? Can the heart itself not be instructed, convinced, and amended through the energy of the information of the Divine Word? Should they not also be informed about Φιλοτεκνίᾳ, even if that affection is natural?

Φιλοτέκνυς) Lovers of children. Greek epigrams give this name to the swallow.

For she who loves the root, says Chrysostom, is much more going to love the fruit. And to that love pertains primarily a good education, concerning which Jerome says: They love their children in such a way if they instruct them in the discipline of God. However, to be unwilling to sadden them by teaching what is good, and to grant them the freedom to sin, is not to love one's children, but to hate them.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Ἵνα σωφρονίζωσι τὰς νέας) Theano: Ταῖς νεωτέραις ὑμῖν ἡ μὲν ἐξουσία παρὰ τοῦ νόμου δίδοται, τῶν οἰκετῶν ἄρ- χειν ἅμα τῷ γήμασθαι. Ἡ δὲ διδασκαλία παρὰ τῶν πρεσβυ- τέρων ἀπαντᾷ, ὀφείλουσα περὶ τῆς οἰκονομίας ἀεὶ παραινεῖν, & quæ sequuntur. Σωφρονισταὶ dicebantur Athenis, qui Juve- num mores formabant.

Non necessum est, ut hæc speciatim restringa- mus ad morum magistras. Nam anuum omnium est, juvenum mores informare, ubi fert occasio. Anus quælibet, inquit Chrysostomus, adolescentulam modcretur & regat. Καλοδιδασκάλυς rectius red- di bona docentes, ut Ambrosianus & Hieronymus legerunt, quam bene docentes, ut Vulgatus habet, agnoscit Estius: Et Græcam dictionem significa- re ait, bonarum artium magistros. Verbum σωφρονίζωσι Vulgatus reddidit, ut prudentiam do- ceant (adolescentulas) quanquam nonnulli Codi- ces Latini voce adolescentulas novam periodum & monitionem, quod Titus adolescentulas mone- re debeat, inchoet, annuente Thoma & Lyrano, sed invita Græca veritate & lectione Hieronymi: quia verbum Græcum transitivum est, quod reddidit Hieronymus, ad castitatem erudiant, Ambrosianus, simpliciter instituant. Significat autem secun- dum Estium (etsi aliter Vulgatus habeat) modestum, ac sobrium, seu temperantem reddere, quod & exem- plo & doctrina facere debent anus. Syrus expo- suit: Et honestas reddant eas, quæ sunt juvenculæ. Cæterum prætulerim facile interpretationem Am- brosiani: Nam capita institutionis deinceps demum sequuntur, inter quæ est etiam castitas & sobrietas. Beza reddidit: Ut sapere doceant. Vulgatus, in- quit, ut prudentiam doceant: Erasmus: Quo possint modestas reddere adolescentulas. Neutrum recte, ut opinor. Et hic σωφροσύνη videtur latius patere, quam superiori & mox sequenti versiculo, opposita nimirum juvenili lasciviæ, & aliis ejus ætatis ac se- xus vitiis, quibus opponuntur virtutes, quas postea describit. Videtur autem ideo Apostolum hanc institutionem non immediate committere Pres- byteris, ut vitetur scandalum: Siquidem non de- ceat Episcopum, ut adeat adolescentulas, vel eas ad se vocet, quod facile suspicionem parit. Vult ergo id per anus fieri.

Φιλάνδρους εἶναι). Ut sint maritorum amantes, quo sen- su Lucianus φιλανδρίαν in laude dixit. Ἀνὴρ & maritum si- gnificat, & quemvis virilis sexus, quo respectu mulier φίλαν- δρος dicitur probri causa, virosa.

Præcipuum illud, inquit Chrysostomus, est domesti- cæ pacis, ac bonorum omnium fundamentum, si uxor viro per omnia consentiens sit. Nam ubi hoc sit, nihil triste contingere poterit. Quo pacto enim, quum ca- put corpori connexum conjunctumque sit, ulla ibi sedi- tio, ulla dissensio oriri poterit? Necessario profecto re- liqua omnia in pace sunt. Principibus namque pa- catis quis jam pacem dividere possit atque discindere? Quemadmodum è contrario his invicem dissentienti- bus nihil salubre esse poterit, totaque simul nutabit fa- milia. Nihil igitur hac re majus, nihilque magis ne- cessarium, verum præstat id & pecuniis & ingenuitati, atq; potentiæ, atq; cæteris omnibus longe utilissimum est. Neque enim ait simpliciter in pace esse: sed amare viros. Ea quippe dilectionis est vis, ubicunque illius fragrantiæ odor afpirat, nihil omnino triste, nihil ingratum irrumpere poterit. Ex hac enim & reliqua oriuntur bona. Quæ vero, quærit Hieronymus, doctrina est, amare viros? Cum hoc non in eloquio docentis, sed in corde amantis constitutum sit? Vult eas amare viros suos caste: Vult inter mulierem & virum esse pudicam dilectionem, ut eum pudore & verecundia & quasi necessitate sexus reddat debitum viro potius, quam ipsa exigat ab eo, & opera liberorum ante oculos Dei & Angelorum perpetrare se credat. Sed quidni informandæ etiam adolescentulæ sint, ut ament viros, etsi in corde amantis hoc constitutum sit? Annon cor ipsum per informationis ἐνέργειαν Verbi Divini instrui, convinci, emendari potest? Nonne etiam de Φιλοτεκνίᾳ informandæ, etsi ille affectus naturalis sit?

Φιλοτέκνυς) Liberorum amantes. Hirundini hoc nomen dant Græca epigrammata.

Quæ enim radicem diligit, multo magis, dicente Chrysostomo, & fructum amatura est. Ad eum autem amorem imprimis pertinet bona educatio, de qua Hieronymus: Filios ita diligunt, si eos erudiant in Dei disciplina. Cæterum nolle eos contristare docendo, quæ bona sunt, & libertatem tribuere peccandi, non est amare filios, sed odisse.

## 2:5
Verse 5.

Σώφρονας) Modest. See 1 Tim. 2:15, ch. 3:2.

Sobriety is primarily regarded here, so that it is not neglected in the instruction of young women. We judge that modesty is included in the word ἀγαθὰς, or certainly in the word ἁγνὰς, because those who are alien to modesty cannot be considered ἁγναὶ or ἀγαθαὶ. The Vulgate translated σώφρονας with two words, prudent, sober, which it nevertheless separated from each other, interposing chaste. Estius acknowledges that this arose from two interpretations, because one person translated it as prudent, another as sober. The Syriac agrees with the Greeks. Estius, however, wishes it to be correctly translated in either way, prudent, or sober, or even temperate. But the latter interpretation of sobriety and temperance is without doubt more suitable.

Ἁγνὰς)

About whom fame fears to lie.

Theophylact seems to understand it as chaste. For she who has loved her husband, he says, will show herself chaste and pure in mind and body. The Vulgate rendered it as chaste, that is, according to the interpreter Estius, observant of modesty and conjugal fidelity.

Οἰκουρὸς)

Not going about the houses, like those about whom 1 Tim. 5:15 and Proverbs 7:12 speak. Philo on special laws: 'For markets and council chambers and gatherings, and assemblies of crowded throngs, and life in the open air, through words and deeds in wars and in peace, are suitable for men; but for women, keeping the house and staying within, for virgins indeed making the inner door the boundary, but for women already mature, the outer door,' which last things are from those of Menander: '-- -- For the outer door of the house is considered the limit for a free woman.'

With which that saying of Meleager in Euripides agrees not badly: 'A good woman ought always to remain within, but outside she is worth nothing.'

The Vulgate, 'having care of the house,' Erasmus, 'keepers of the house,' that is; those who are assiduous at home, and take care of domestic matters, remaining at home. Which is the chief praise of women. Whence among the ancient matrons the tortoise was a symbol, because that animal never departs from its shell, and does not even put out its head, unless the care of the body requires it. To this pertains the story that Phidias made a Venus for the Eleans, which was treading on a tortoise with its feet.

Ἀγαθὰς) φιλαγάθυς, as he speaks of the Presbyter above 1, 8. Such was Tabitha, Acts 9:36, 'full of good works.' There is no reason for us to say that the simple is used for the compound. Grotius produced none. Jerome is more correct: 'Because it could happen that the diligence of the house might be governed with austerity, and through this the Apostle's precept might make a matron too severe toward her servants: therefore he coupled "kind," so that she might believe she is ruling the house well for her husband if she commands the servants with kindness, not in terror.' Yet the Greek word implies more than what the Vulgate rendered as 'kind.' Beza says 'good': Stephanus prefers it to be read conjunctively with the preceding οἰκυρὰς ἀγαθὰς, that is, 'good keepers of the house,' namely, faithful and diligent matrons, nor does Beza disapprove. It is better, however, to distinguish them according to the Greek Codices and Interpreters: 'Kind,' that is, placid and mild toward the household, not clamoring at their husbands, but tolerating and excusing their manners and faults, such as is commended in Abigail, 1 Samuel 25. 'For they become good and keepers of the house from love, and from the affection and friendship toward the husband.' A wife who has care of the house, Chrysostom further says, must also be chaste, serving such a dispensation and care, and will never occupy herself with delights, or with untimely and wicked proceedings, or anything else of this kind.

Ὑποτασσόμενας τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν) And here the passive is used for the reciprocal, which is frequent in the verbs τάσσεσθαι and those derived from it, but especially in ὑποτάσσεσθαι, Luke 2:51, Romans 8:7, 10:13, 13:1, 5. And specifically concerning women, Ephesians 5:22, Colossians 3:18, which places you should consult. He does not only want them to show themselves kind and agreeable to their husbands, but also obedient and compliant, because the husband is the head of the woman, 1 Corinthians 11, Ephesians 5. Jerome observes here that it was not said (Genesis 3) to the man, 'you shall rule over your wife,' but to the woman herself: 'Your turning shall be to your husband, and he shall rule over you,' so that (GOD) might leave her a reward for obedience, while she is in his power, if she wishes to obey the precepts of God. To serve the man, and to be subject to the husband: so that it might be in a way a free servitude, and full of love: therefore she is a servant to the man, while she fears to offend him. For man was not created for the woman, but the woman for the man. And since the husband is the head of the woman: but Christ is the head of the husband, whatever wife is not subject to her husband, that is, to her head, is guilty of the same crime as the husband, if he is not subject to Christ, his head.

Ἱνα μὴ ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ βλασφημῆται) So also Romans 2:24, 1 Timothy 6:1. For if any Christian woman had lived too licentiously, the Greeks were immediately going to say: 'What does this new discipline profit her?' But they were in danger of this especially if the husband were either a Pagan or a Jew. Concerning which Jerome in this place: 'But the word of God is blasphemed, either while the first sentence of God is despised and held for nothing. Or the Gospel of Christ is defamed, while, contrary to the law and the faith of nature, she who is a Christian, and subject by the law of God, desires to rule over her husband. Since even Gentile women serve their husbands by the common law of nature.'

Τὺς νεωτέρες) נערים: Ωσαύτως παρακάλει σωφρονεῖν) Excite them to modesty.

You see, says Chrysostom, how doctrine everywhere preserves decorum? For he permitted the teaching of women to women for the most part, appointing older women as teachers of the younger ones. Furthermore, he permits the entire care of instructing the male sex to himself. For nothing can be so difficult and so hard for this age as to overcome harmful and deadly pleasures. For neither the love of money, nor the pursuit of glory, nor the concupiscence of any other thing, disturbs this age as much as the love of bodies and insane lust. Therefore, omitting all other things, the admonition is occupied with that which was more pressing and more necessary. Chrysostom therefore understands temperance and continence. Concerning which Theophylact: 'But what, someone will say, are they to be exhorted to continence? Because at that age especially, the fire emanating from pleasures infests the young men themselves, which must certainly be extinguished and chastity must be pursued.' Nor indeed is this the only thing to be inculcated in young men. Decency shows more things that befit that age, but which they have to lay aside from the type or pattern, concerning which he therefore warned Titus, and not for the sake of the young men only, but of all whom Titus was over. Jerome from the word ὡσαύτως gathers that it is required that young men have the sobriety of old men, and be good and honest and chaste and sound in faith and charity and patience. But that older women be in holiness of behavior, that they be not accusers, not given to much wine, teaching well, and the rest. But that he (the Apostle) placed this as proper to adolescents, that they be chaste in all things, namely, as much in mind as in body, as much in work as in thought, so that there may be no suspicion of turpitude in an adolescent. But Jerome wants that 'IN ALL THINGS' to be referred to the preceding, in this way: 'Exhort them to be chaste in all things:' since continence is necessary not only in the work of the flesh and in the continence of the mind, but in all things, lest we desire undue honors, lest we be inflamed by avarice, lest we be overcome by any passion. But in this Jerome has no one supporting him. For all the Greeks and Latins, with the Syrian, refer these 'all things' to what follows. For after he had instructed the old men, the older women, the young women, and the adolescents, the Apostle warns Titus to show himself as an example in all things which he had prescribed, so that his life may inform no less than his doctrine, and his exhortation may be more effective.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Σώφρονας) Modestas. Vide 1. Tim. 2, 15. c. 3, 2.

Sobrietas imprimis hic respicitur, ne in adolescentularum institutione illa negligatur. Modestiam in voce ἀγαθὰς comprehendi censemus, aut certe in voce ἁγνὰς, quia non possunt ἁγναὶ aut ἀγαθαὶ haberi, quæ à modestia alienæ sunt. Vulgatus σώφρονας exposuit duabus vocibus, prudentes, sobrias, quas tamen à se invicem divulsit, castas interponens. Ex duabus autem interpretationibus hoc ortum agnoscit Estius, quod alius prudentes, alius sobrias transtulerit. Syra Græcis consonant. Utrovis autem modo recte verti vult Estius, prudentes, aut sobrias, aut etiam temperantes. Sed posterior interpretatio sobrietatis & temperantiæ sine dubio convenientior est.

Ἁγνὰς)

De queis fama mentiri veretur.

Castas intelligere videtur Theophylactus. Quæ enim virum dilexerit, inquit, castam se, & puram mente præstabit, & corpore. Castas reddidit Vulgatus, id est, Estio Interprete, pudicitiæ fideique conjugalis observantes.

Οἰκουρὸς)

Non περιερχομένας τὰς οἰκίας, ut illæ, de quibus 1. Tim. 5, 15. & Proverb. 7, 12. Philo de legibus specialibus: Ἀγοραὶ γὰρ καὶ βουλευτήρια καὶ θίασοι, καὶ σύλλογοι πολυανθρώπων ὁμίλων, καὶ ὁ ἐν ὑπαίθρῳ βίος, διὰ λόγων καὶ πράξεων κατὰ πολέμους, καὶ κατὰ εἰρήνην ἀνδράσιν ἐφαρμόζουσι· Θηλείαις δὲ οἰκουρία καὶ ἔνδον μονὴ, παρθένοις μὲν εἴσω κλισιάδων τὴν μεσαύλιον ὅρον πεποιημέναις· Τελείαις δὲ ἤδη γυναιξὶ τὴν αὔλιον, quæ ultima ex illis sunt Menandri: -- -- Πέρας γὰρ αὔλιος θύρα Ἐλευθέρᾳ γυναικὶ νενόμιστ᾽ οἰκίας.

Qui cum non male convenit illud Meleagro Euripidis: Ἔνδον μένουσαν τὴν γυναῖκ᾽ ἀεὶ χρεὼν Ἐσθλὴν, θύρασι δ᾽ ἀξίαν τὸ μηδενός.

Vulgatus, domus curam habentes, Erasmus, do- mus custodes, hoc est; quae assiduae sint domi, rem- que curent domesticam, domi manentes. Quae mulierum praecipua laus est. Unde apud antiquas matresfamilias symbolum erat testudo, quod illud animal nunquam e cortice discedat, ac ne caput quidem exerat, nisi cura corporis id exigente. Huc pertinet, quod Phidiam narrant Eliensibus Vene- rem fecisse, quae testudinem pedibus calcaret.

Ἀγαθὰς) φιλαγάθυς, ut de Presbytero loquitur supra 1, 8. Talis Tabitha Act. 9, 36. πλήρης ἀγαθῶν ἔργων Adhiberi simplex pro composito, causa non est, cur dicamus. Nullam protulit Grotius. Rectius Hieronymus: Quia poterat evenire, ut diligentia do- mus cum austeritate regeretur, & per hoc Apostoli praeceptum, matrona severior fieret in servulos: ideo copulavit, benignas, ut tunc se crederet mariti bene domum regere, si cum benignitate imperet servulis, non in terrore. Infert tamen amplius quid vox Graeca, quam Vulgatus reddidit benignas. Beza bonas: Stephanus mavult conjunctim legi cum praecedenti οἰκυρὰς ἀγαθὰς, id est, bonas custodes domus, fidae videlicet, ac diligentes matresfamilias, nec improbat Beza. Praestat tamen eas juxta Grae- cos Codices & Interpretes distinguere: Benignas, id est, placidas ac mites erga domesticos, nec ob- strepentes maritis, sed mores eorum ac vitia tole- rantes & excusantes, qualis commendatur Abigail 1. Samuel. 25. Καὶ γὰρ ἀγαθαὶ καὶ οἰκυραὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγάπης, καὶ τῆς περὶ τὸν ἄνδρα φιλίας γίνονται. Bonae enim & curatrices domus ex dilectione & a- more circa virum (manendi) fiunt, Uxor quae domus curam habet, inquit porro Chrysostomus, pu- dica quoque sit necesse est, hujusmodi dispensationi & cura inserviens, nunquam vel circa delicias, vel circa intempestivos improbosque processus aut aliud aliquid hujusmodi se occupabit.

Ὑποτασσόμενας τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν) Et hic passivum est pro reciproco, quod in verbis τάσσεσθαι & inde derivatis fre- quens, maxime vero in ὑποτάσσεσθαι, Luc. 2. v. 51. Roman. 8, 7. c. 10, 13. c. 13, 1. 5. Et nominatim de mulieribus Eph. 5, 22. Col. 3, 18. quibus locis dicta consule. Non solum vult, ut benignas & commodas se viris exhibeant, sed etiam obsequentes & morigeras, quia vir caput est mulieris, 1. Corinth. 11. Ephes. 5. Ob- servat hic Hieronymus, non esse dictum (Genes. 3.) viro, dominaberis uxori tuae, sed ipsi mulieri: Ad vi- rum tuum conversio tua; & ipse tui dominabitur, ut illi praemium relinqueret (DEUS) obsequela, dum in potestate ejus est, si Dei velit obedire praeceptis. Servire viro, & marito esse subjecta: ut quodam- modo esset libera servitus, & dilectione plena: Ideo serviens est viro, dum eum metuit offendere. Ete- nim non creatus est vir propter mulierem, sed mulier propter virum. Et cum caput mulieris vir sit: caput autem viri Christus, quaecunque uxor non subji- citur viro suo, hoc est, capiti suo, ejusdem criminis rea est, cujus & vir, si non subjiciatur Christo, ca- piti suo.

Ἱνα μὴ ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ βλασφημῆται) Sic & Rom. 2, 24. 1. Tim. 6, 1. Nam si qua mulier Christiana vixisset licen- tius, continuo dicturi erant Graeci: Quid ei proficit nova haec disciplina? Maxime vero in hoc periclitabantur, si ma- ritus esset aut Paganus aut Judaeus. De quo Hieronymus in h. l. Verbum autem Do- mini blasphematur, vel dum contemnitur Dei prima sententia, & pro nihilo ducitur. Vel Christi infama- tur Evangelium, dum contra legem fidemque naturae ea quae Christiana est, & ex Dei lege subjecta, viro im- perare desiderat. Cum etiam gentiles foeminae suis viris serviant communi lege naturae.

Τὺς νεωτέρες) נערים: Ωσαύτως παρακάλει σωφρονεῖν) Ad modestiam eos excita.

Vides, inquit Chrysostomus, quomodo ubique do- ctrina servet decorem? Nam docendas mulieres mulieribus magna ex parte permisit, anus adolescen- tularum magistras esse constituens. Porro sexus vi- rilis instruendi curam omnem ipsi permittit. Nihil enim ita difficile tamque durum ætati huic esse potest, ut superare noxias ac mortiferas voluptates. Neque enim aut pecuniæ amor aut gloriæ studium, aut cujus- libet rei alterius concupiscentia, ita hanc perturbat æ- tatem, sicuti corporum amor, vesanaque libido. Id- circo omnibus aliis omissis, circa id, quod urgebat ma- gis plusque erat necessarium versatur admonitio. Temperantiam ergo Chrysostomus intelligit & con- tinentiam. Quo de Theophylactus: Quid vero, inquiet aliquis, ad continentiam cohortandi sint hi? Quia ea præcipue ætate ex voluptatibus ignis ema- nans, juvenes ipsos infestat, qui & restinguendus est utique & castitati studendum. Nec vero hoc uni- cum juvenibus inculcandum. Plura monstrat eam ætatem decentia, sed quæ è typo vel exempla- ri deponere habeant, de quo proinde monuit Ti- tum, nec id juvenum tantum, sed omnium causa, quibus Titus præerat. Hieronymus è voce ὡσαύ- τως colligit requiri, ut juvenes senum habeant so- brietatem, & boni honestique sint & pudici & sani in fide & charitate & patientia. Anuum autem in habitus sanctitate, ut non sint accusatores, non vino multo servientes, bene docentes, & cætera. Pro- prium autem adolescentibus hoc posuisse (Aposto- lum) ut pudici sint in omnibus, scilicet tam mente, quam corpore, tam opere, quam cogitatione, ut nulla sit in adolescente suspicio turpitudinis. Illud autem IN OMNIBUS ad superiora referendum esse vult Hieronymus, hoc modo: Hortare, ut pudici sint in omnibus: Siquidem continentia non solum in carnis opere & in animi continentia, sed in omnibus rebus necessaria sit, ne honores indebitos appetamus, ne ac- cendamur avaritia, ne ulla passione superemur. Sed in eo Hieronymus neminem habet suffragantem. Græci enim & Latini omnes cum Syro hæc πάντα ad sequentia referunt. Nam postquam senes, anus, fœminas juvenculas, adolescentes instruxe- rat, in omnibus, quæ præscripserat, Titus se exem- plum præbeat, monet Apostolus, ut non minus vi- ta, quam doctrina informet, & exhortatio ejus sit efficacior.

## 2:7
Vers. 7.

Περὶ πάντα σεαυτὸν παρεχόμενος τύπον καλῶν ἔργων) You must lead not only by words, but also by example. We have τύπος for a pattern, which is proposed to be imitated, Phil. 3, 17. 1. Thess. 1, 7. 2. Thess. 3, 9. 1. Petr. 5, 3.

Let the doctrine, he says, with Chrysostom as interpreter, and the example of your virtue be a mirror of life, which is proposed to all for imitation, like a certain primitive image, having in itself all things that are good and honest: which, with great ease, may be ready to always provide examples to those wishing to imitate some of its beauty. Jerome in Epitaph. ad Heliodor. Upon you the eyes of all are directed; your house and conversation, established as if in a mirror, are a teacher of public discipline; whatever you do, men think that they must do the same. Beware lest you commit that which those who wish to find fault may see that they have labored in vain, or those who are compelled to imitate may be led to sin.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Περὶ πάντα σεαυτὸν παρεχόμενος τύπον καλῶν ἔργων) Non verbis tantum præire debes, sed & exemplo. Τύ- πος pro exemplari, quod imitandum proponitur, habemus Phil. 3, 17. 1. Thess. 1, 7. 2. Thess. 3, 9. 1. Petr. 5, 3.

Sit omnibus, inquit Chrysostomo Interprete, do- ctrina, exemplárque virtutis tuæ speculum vitæ, quod omnibus proponitur ad imitandum, veluti primiti- va quædam imago, omnia in se habens, qua bona & honesta sunt: quæ magna cum facilitate volentibus aliquid sui decoris imitari, exempla semper præbere parata sit. Hieronymus in Epitaph. ad Helio- dor. In te omnium diriguntur oculi, domus tua, & conversatio quasi in speculo constituta, magistra est publicæ disciplinæ, quicquid feceris, id sibi homines faciendum putant. Cave ne committas, quod aut reprehendere volunt, qui seque laborasse videantur, aut qui imitari coguntur, delinquere.

## 2:8
Verse 8.

In teaching, incorruptness, gravity, immortality, sound speech, that cannot be condemned) In the Manuscript, ἄφθορίαν, the interpretation of which is that ἀφθαρσίαν, which is absent from many Codices, nor do Chrysostom, Oecumenius, or Theophylact read it. These accusatives are governed by that παρεχόμενος, without repeating σεαυτὸν. ἄφθορος is accustomed to be said of a virgin. Therefore, ἄφθορία ἐν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ is unblemished purity. Σεμνότης is gravity in teaching, as 1 Timothy 2:2, chapter 3:4. Λόγος ὑγιὴς ἀκατάγνωστος is speech in which there is not only nothing harmful, but also nothing that could be taken badly. See Galatians 2:11. You have the word ἀκατάγνωστος also in 2 Maccabees 4:47.

That he who is of the contrary part may be ashamed, having nothing to say evil of you) ὁ ἐξ ἐναντίας is he who is of the opposing party: Aristotle also speaks thus. The article ὁ here signifies generality, as often elsewhere. Concerning the word ἐντρέπεσθαι, see 2 Thessalonians 3:14. Φαῦλον, עול, John 3:20, chapter 5:29, James 3:16.

Theophylact understands these things concerning the incorrupt integrity of doctrine, and that which is alien to all falsehood: namely, that the things you teach should not be corrupt and false, but integral and proceeding from right reason. In gravity. Namely, that your instruction should have nothing that is new and unusual, and that offends the unwise, but that all things should be religious and brought forth according to the dignity of God. But they are more correctly explained concerning life, as if to say: in this province of teaching, see that you provide integrity of life corrupted by no vice, and also gravity of manners, which may commend the authority of the teacher. For it follows next concerning sound and irreprehensible speech, so that the adversaries, terrified by the soundness of our life and doctrine, may not dare to accuse, that is, to fabricate nothing plausible in an accusation, as Jerome has it, who confirms this with examples of his own age. And in truth, even to this day we see some in the Church, although this is a rare bird, to be of such gravity and continence that they have a testimony even from their adversaries, and it is said, 'He is a great man, and of holy conversation and upright morals, were he not a heretic.' For there is no one of such immoderate impudence that he can accuse the rays of the sun of being dark, and pour the clear light into the gloom of night.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Ἐν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ ἀδιαφθορίαν, σεμνότητα, ἀφθαρσίαν, λόγον ὑγιῆ, ἀκατάγνωστον) In Manuscripto ἄφθορίαν, cujus interpretamentum illud ἀφθαρσίαν, quod à plu- ribus Codicibus abest, neque id legere Chrysostomus, Oecumenius, Theophylactus. Reguntur hi accusativi ab illo παρεχόμενος, non repetito σεαυτὸν. Solet ἄφ- θορος dici de virgine. Est ergo ἄφθορία ἐν τῇ διδασκα- λίᾳ puritas illibata. Σεμνότης est in docendo gravitas, ut 1. Timoth. 2, 2. cap. 3, 4. Λόγος ὑγιὴς ἀκατάγνωστος is sermo, in quo non modo nihil sit noxium, sed nec quod male accipi posset. Vide Galat. 2,11. Vocem ἀκατάγνωστος habes & 2. Macc. 4, 47.

Ἵνα ὁ ἐξ ἐναντίας ἐντραπῇ, μηδὲν ἔχων περὶ ὑμῶν λέγειν φαῦλον) ὁ ἐξ ἐναντίας est is, qui adversæ est partis: lo- quitur sic & Aristoteles. Articulus autem ὁ hic genera- litatem significat, ut alibi sæpe. De voce ἐντρέπεσθαι vide 2. Thessal. 3, 14. Φαῦλον עול Johan. 3, 20. cap. 5, 29. Jac. 3. v. 16.

Hæc de doctrinæ integritate incorrupta, & ab o- mni falsitate aliena intelligit Theophylactus: Ne scilicet corrupta sint & falsa, quæ doces, sed integra, & à recta ratione prodeuntia. In gravitate. Ut nihil scilicet habeat tua instructio, quod novum sit & insolitum, & insipientes offendat, sed cuncta & re- ligiosa sint & pro Dei dignitate deprompta. Sed re- ctius de vita explicantur, q. d. in hac docendi pro- vincia fac præstes integritatem vitæ nullo vitio corruptæ, nec non gravitatem morum, quæ docen- tis autoritatem commendet. Sequitur enim de- inceps de sermone sano & irreprehensibili, ut Ad- versarii vitæ & doctrinæ nostræ sanitate perterriti, non audeant accusare, hoc est, nihil verisimile in accusatione confingere, ut habet Hieronymus, qui hoc confirmat exemplis suæ ætatis. Et revera usque hodie videmus nonnullos in Ecclesia, quanquam hæc rara avis sit, tantæ gravitatis continentiæque esse, ut etiam ab adversariis habeant testimonium, & dica- tur, vir magnus est ille, & conversationis sancta, pro- bisque moribus, nisi esset hæreticus, Nemo enim est tam immoderatæ impudentiæ, ut solis radios possit ac- cusare tenebrosos, & clarum lumen caligine noctis ef- fundere.

## 2:9
Verse 9.

Exhort servants to be obedient to their own masters) One must repeat 'exhort' from the previous passage. Again, here you have ὑποτάσσεσθαι in a reciprocal sense. The sense is the same as Ephesians 6:5, Colossians 3:22.

There follow the Canons to be prescribed to servants, as a part of the Church and members of the body of Christ. First, concerning due subjection. Jerome reads: 'Servants, be subject to your own masters in all things.' But the Greek texts consistently refer those words 'in all things' to the second Canon, even though Jerome testifies that he read it otherwise in the Greek: 'in all things being pleasing,' so that they may indeed strive to gratify their masters and please them in all things which are not contrary to God, who is the supreme Lord, Acts 5. Jerome's interpretation is less suitable: 'Servants, let them please THEMSELVES, because they are servants,' or in their condition, so that they do not bear servitude harshly.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Δούλους ἰδίοις δεσπόταις ὑποτάσσεσθαι) Repetendum ex superiori loco παρακάλει. Rursum hic habes ὑποτάσ- σεσθαι in sensu reciproco. Sensus idem, qui Ephes. 6, 5. Col. 3, 22.

Sequuntur Canones, servis, ut parti Ecclesiæ, membrisque corporis Christi præscribendi. Pri- mum de subjectione debita. Hieronymus legit: Servi Dominis suis subditi sint in omnibus. Sed Græca constanter illa ἐν πᾶσιν ad secundum Cano- nem referunt, etsi in Græco aliter se legisse testetur Hieronymus, in omnibus sint placentes, ut nempe studeant Dominis suis gratificari, & placere in o- mnibus, quæ scilicet Deo, qui supremus Dominus est, adversa non sunt, Actor. 5. Minus convenit Hieronymi interpretatio: Servi complaceant SIBI, quod servi sint, vel in conditione sua, ut non aspere fe- runt servitutem.

## 2:9
To be well-pleasing in all things) Namely, to their masters, which is understood as the Dative from the preceding. Moreover, εὐάρεστος is accustomed to have a Dative after it, Wisdom 4:10, Romans 12:1, 2, chapter 14:18, 2 Corinthians 5:9, Ephesians 5:10, Philippians 4:18, Colossians 3:20. He wants servants to act in every way so that they may please their masters and prove themselves to them. Take 'in all things' as in Colossians 3:22.

Not answering back: For thus Plautus speaks.

The very greatest vice of servants, says Jerome, is to contradict their masters, so that when they have ordered something, they mutter to themselves. Therefore I warn Titus, that through his teaching he may remove such a passion from those who are Christian servants. For if a servant has a necessity to fulfill what the Lord commands: why does he not do this very thing with a good will, but both offends the Lord, and finally does what is commanded. The Ambrosian also rendered it 'not answering back'. B. Luther elegantly: 'Do not bark back'.

Latin:

Ἐν πᾶσιν εὐαρέστους εἶναι) Nempe τοῖς δεσπόταις, qui Dativus ex præcedenti subintelligitur. Solet autem εὐάρεσ- τος Dativum habere post se, Sap. 4, 10. Rom. 12, 1. 2. cap. 14, 18. 2. Cor. 5, 9. Eph. 5, 10. Phil. 4, 18. Col. 3, 20. Vult servos omni modo id agere, ut Dominis placeant, iisque se probent. Ἐν πᾶσι sume, ut Col. 3, 22.

Μὴ ἀντιλέγοντας) Non responsatores: Ita enim Plautus loquitur.

Vel maximum servorum vitium est, inquit Hie- ronymus, Dominis contradicere, ut cum aliquid jus- serint, secum mussitare. Itaque Titum commoneo, ut per doctrinam suam ab his, qui Christiani servi sunt, istiusmodi auferat passionem. Si enim quæ Domi- nus imperat, necesse habet servus implere: cur hoc ipsum non cum bona faciat voluntate, sed & Dominum offendat, & tandem faciat, quod jubetur. Ambrosianus etiam reddidit non responsatores. B. Lutherus eleganter: Nicht widerbellen.

## 2:10
Verse 10.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

## 2:10
Μὴ νοσφιζομένους) He does not mean thieves, but has used a milder word, as when the Jurisconsults say, 'removed things'. See 2 Maccabees 4:32. In the Glossary: Νοσφίζομαι, I embezzle, I usurp.

The Vulgate rendered it 'not defrauding', Jerome, 'not stealing'. It would have been better, in Estius's judgment, to be 'not pilfering', because in Greek he is called νοσφίζεσθαι who secretly picks or takes away something, when he does not dare to take the whole thing. B. Luther neatly: 'Do not embezzle'. Suidas: νοσφιζόμενον, ὑφαιρέμενον, ἰδιοποιούμενον, that is, translated by Aemilius Portus, 'purloining, diverting, misappropriating'; that person who makes some things his own, pilfering.
