Ἀλλὰ πίστιν πᾶσαν ἐνδεικνυμένους ἀγαθὴν) Ἀγαθὴν πίστιν from the Latin, 'good faith'. Take ἐνδείκνυσθαι as in 2 Timothy 4, verse 14.

The Vulgate with the Syriac rendered the sense: 'But in all things showing good faith', whereas literally it sounds: 'But showing all good faith', as Jerome and the Ambrosian read. B. Luther beautifully and as if 'step by step': 'But show all good loyalty'. By the Hebrew phrase, says Estius, 'all' is said of that which is perfect, and is lacking in no part. Therefore servants show all good faith when they do not defraud their masters in any part, but in all things provide complete fidelity. Whence in a sense entirely similar in 1 Timothy 3 it is read in the Greek, 'faithful in all things'.

Ἵνα τὴν διδασκαλίαν τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεοῦ κοσμῶσιν ἐν πᾶσιν) That they may adorn their profession, that they may commend it by good morals. For he calls their profession 'teaching' by metonymy. And he calls this teaching the teaching of Christ our GOD, because it was commanded to him by God the Father. Concerning the title 'Savior' attributed to the Father of Christ, see 1 Timothy 2:3, chapter 4:10, above chapter 1:3.

There is no reason why we should interpret διδασκαλίαν otherwise than as it sounds, concerning doctrine. For the doctrine of Christ is adorned by the holy conduct of Christians; just as the same is disgraced by the wickedness of life, not in itself, but in the eyes of others. By the name of our Savior God, Christ is understood here; who was called Σωτὴρ, Savior, by the Angel specifically in Luke 2:11, as also by Peter, Acts 5:31, 2 Peter 1:11, chapter 2:20, chapter 3:2, chapter 5:18, by Paul in Acts 13:23, Philippians 3:20, 1 Timothy 1:1, 2 Timothy 1:20, Titus 1:1, chapter 2:13, chapter 3:6, and he is called 'the Savior of the world', John 4:42, 1 John 4:14, and 'of his body' Ephesians 5:23, etc., so that this name is almost proper and perpetual to him in the books of the New Testament. For those remaining passages are also conveniently understood of CHRIST, Luke 1:47, Titus 1:3, chapter 3:4, Jude v. 25. Whom Paul also calls by the name of 'our great God and Savior' below in verse 13. He who delivered this doctrine, which is to be adorned, and appointed Paul the Apostle to propagate it. And this reason seems to be referred to all the preceding warnings, which he prescribed concerning an irreproachable life for different ages and states. For it is fitting for all that they should adorn, according to the prescribed canons, the doctrine of our Savior GOD, not servants alone, just as the saving grace has also shone for all. He adorns the doctrine of the Lord, says Jerome, who does those things which are suitable to his condition. Which reason, proposed succinctly, the Apostle now executes.

PART II. Reasons or arguments for merits.

Latin:

Μὴ νοσφιζομένους) Non furaces vult dicere, sed leniori verbo usus est, ut cum JurisConsulti dicunt, res amotas. Vid. 2. Maccab. 4, 32. In Glossario: Νοσφίζομαι, peculor, usurpo.

Vulgata reddidit non fraudantes, Hieronymus, non furantes. Melius, Estio Judice, erat non suffurantes, quia Græcis νοσφίζεσθαι dicitur, qui furtim aliquid decerpit, aut detrahit, cum totam rem tollere non ausit. B. Lutherus concinne: Nicht veruntreuen. Suidas νοσφιζόμενον, ὑφαιρέμενον, ἰδιοποιούμενον, id est, interprete Æmilio Porto, surripientem, intervertentem, traducentem; illum, qui res aliquas suas facit, suffurantem.

Ἀλλὰ πίστιν πᾶσαν ἐνδεικνυμένους ἀγαθὴν) Ἀγαθὴν πίστιν ex Latino, bonam fidem. Ἐνδείκνυσθαι sume ut 2. Tim. 4, vers. 14.

Vulgatus cum Syro sensum reddidit: Sed in omnibus fidem bonam ostendentes, quum ad verbum sonet: Sed fidem omnem ostendentes bonam, ut Hieronymus & Ambrosianus legere. B. Lutherus pulchre & si κατὰ πόδας: Sondern alle gute Treu erzeigen. Ebræ phrasi, inquit Estius, omnibus dicitur, quod perfectum est, & nulla parte deficit. Igitur omnem bonam fidem servi ostendunt, quando nulla parte fraudant heros suos, sed in omnibus integram præstant fidelitatem. Unde sensu prorsus simili 1. Tim. 3. legitur in Græco, fideles in omnibus.

Ἵνα τὴν διδασκαλίαν τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεοῦ κοσμῶσιν ἐν πᾶσιν) Ut professionem suam ornent, ut commendent bonis moribus. Nam professionem μετωνυμικῶς vocat διδασκαλίαν. Et doctrinam hanc Christi DEI Patris doctrinam vocat, quia ipsi a Deo Patre fuit mandata. De titulo Σωτῆρος tributo Patri Christi, vide 1. Timoth. 2, 3. cap. 4, 10. supra c. 1, 3.

Non est, cur διδασκαλίαν aliter, quam ut sonat, de doctrina interpretemur. Ornatur enim doctrina Christi conversatione sancta Christianorum; quemadmodum eadem dedecoratur vitæ improbitate non in se, sed penes alios. Nomine Salvatoris nostri Dei hic Christus intelligitur; qui Σωτὴρ, Servator ab Angelo dictus est peculiariter Luc. 2, 11. ut & à Petro, Actor. 5, 31. 2. Petr. 1. v. 11. cap. 2, 20. cap. 3, 2. cap. 5, 18. à Paulo Actor. 13, 23. Phil. 3, 20. 1. Timoth. 1, 1. 2. Timoth. 1, 20. Tit. 1. v. 1. cap. 2, 13. cap. 3, 6. & ὁ Σωτὴρ τοῦ κόσμου vocatur, Joh. 4, 42. 1. Joh. 4, 14. & τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ Eph. 5, 23. &c. adeo ut fere proprium ac perpetuum ipsi hoc nomen sit in libris Novi Testamenti. Nam & illa, quæ supersunt loca, commode de CHRISTO accipiuntur, Luc. 1, 47. Tit. 1, 3. cap. 3, 4. Jud. v. 25. Quem etiam nomine τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ καὶ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν appellat Paulus infra v. 13. Qui tradidit hanc doctrinam, quæ ornanda est, eique propagandæ Paulum Apostolum constituit. Et videtur hæc ratio referenda ad omnia præcedentia monita, quæ de vita inculpata diversis ætatibus & statibus præscripsit. Omnibus enim id convenit, ut ornent, juxta præscriptos scilicet canones doctrinam Salvatoris nostri DEI non servis solis, quemadmodum etiam illuxit ideo omnibus gratia σωτήριος. Ornat doctrinam Domini, inquit Hieronymus, qui ea, quæ conditioni suæ apta sunt, facit. Quam rationem succincte propositam jam exequitur Apostolus.

PARS II. Meritorum rationes vel argumenta.

## 2:11
Verse 11.

For the grace of God has appeared) The supreme goodness of God, which has appeared in the Gospel, desires also the supreme purity of life. He compares this goodness to some star that suddenly shines forth. See Luke 1:29, Acts 27:20, below ch. 3:4. נגלה, as in Genesis 25:7. The Greeks have the passage of Zephaniah 2:11 thus: The Lord will appear over them, and will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth, and each one from his own place shall worship him. Which words, slightly changed, Chrysostom cites in his second work against the Jews.

Which is salutary for all men) which is saving for all men, namely, those who accept it.

The reasons are now set forth why the Apostolic admonitions are to be observed; both because of the appearance of saving grace, which has already taken place, v. 11, 12; and because of the manifestation of the glory of the Savior, which we await, v. 13; and because of the satisfactory redemption of Christ, and its end, our sanctification, v. 14. Regarding the first reason, Chrysostom refers it especially to the exhortation concerning servants, the grace shown to us who were servants of sin. For if anyone, having obtained a servant who has offended in many things, has not beaten him with scourges, but, having pardoned his sins, has warned him to avoid future ones and to take care in the future not to fall into the same, and has also further illustrated him with great gifts and cherished him with benefits: what, I pray, will be so treacherous a mind, so ungrateful a soul, that would not be sufficient to be provoked by such grace to pursue better things? More correctly, the preceding admonitions are viewed generally, as if to say, in the interpretation of the blessed Balduinus: We no longer dwell in darkness, he wishes to say, so that it is permitted to commit the works of darkness with impunity, which was once almost done among the Gentiles, but the time of grace has shone upon all men, of whatever rank they may be; therefore it is right that all should live worthily of their calling, worthily of this light, worthily of the Gospel. The grace of a great Prince impels us to do what we understand to be pleasing to him. Much more the grace of God. For if it is the grace of God, it is immovable and constant, to be preferred to all things. He calls it salutary, as if it were the bringer of salvation, with respect to us and in its end. For since we have fallen from salvation through sin, through it we are led back to eternal salvation, and it is provided to us for this end, that we may not perish, but be saved, as Crocius says here.

Moreover, the appearance of the grace of God is presented 1. by reason of its greatest clarity, by the word ἐπεφάνη, which implies that grace has appeared in an illustrious manner. For what could be more illustrious than that manifestation of grace by which the sunrise from on high visited us, Luke 1:78, the sun of righteousness, Malachi 3:1, that great light illuminating all men, John 1:9, the glory of the Lord has risen upon us, the Lord himself has risen, Isaiah 60:1, 2, God was manifested in the flesh, 1 Timothy 3:16. 2. by reason of supreme goodness: The grace of God, infinite indeed and purely gratuitous, which is called the kindness and love of God our Savior, and his mercy, ch. 3:4, 5. 3. by reason of the fullest salvation. For it is called saving grace, which brings all and perfect salvation. For it would not be truly saving if it did not bring perfect salvation. And that salvation is truly perfect, because outside of it there is no true salvation, Isaiah 45:23. Acts 4:12. 4. by reason of all-encompassing universality: because it has shone upon all men, no one excepted, no one excluded. Grace has shone upon all, and indeed the same grace, namely, saving grace, which can be understood both as having shone upon all men and as being saving for all men, not only those who accept it, but also those who do not accept it. For that true light, if you look at its power and virtue, if you look at the divine gracious intention, if you look at the price, efficacy, and value of the merit of Christ, illuminates every man, John 1:9. It shines in the darkness, even if the darkness does not apprehend it, v. 5. Christ came into the world so that the world might be saved through him, John 3:17, even if very many in the world are not saved: the reason is that the light came into the world, but men loved darkness more than the light, v. 19. Which appears from the coherence of our text, which Jerome presents thus: After the catalog of doctrine to Titus, what he ought to teach the old men, what the old women, what the young women and the young men, and finally the servants, he rightly added now: For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all men. For there is no difference between free and slave, Greek and barbarian, circumcised and one having uncircumcision, woman and man, but we are all one in Christ, we are all called to the kingdom of God: We are all to be reconciled to our Father after the offense, not through our merits, but through the grace of the Savior. 5. by reason of a common end, because grace has appeared and shone upon all, instructing all. For this reason the Apostles announce Christ, admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, so that they may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus, Colossians 1:28, 29. For Christ gave himself for all for this reason, that he might free all from all iniquity, and that he might purify for himself a peculiar people, below verse 14, cf. 2 Corinthians 5:15. However, as much as the name of God in this verse 11 can be understood as God the Father, or even if it is permitted to take that name essentially concerning the Triune God; yet it seems that the Son of God is particularly designated by that name in this place, but as they say, hypostatically, because that God the Savior is noted, who is designated in verse 10: whom we have previously taught to be the Son of God: whose saving grace is celebrated here, and to whom this appearance is particularly attributed from the oracles of the Old Testament, Isaiah 9:2, ch. 60:1, 2, Malachi 3:1, and the oracles of the New Testament, Luke 1:79, John 1:9, ch. 8:12, 1 Timothy 3:15, 2 Timothy 1:10. All which passages, and many more akin to these, speak of the Son of GOD, whose χάρις also in the business of our τῆς σωτηρίας is partly proclaimed, namely the grace of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, which the Apostle prays for all, 2 Corinth. 13, 13. the grace by which we are spiritually enriched, 2 Corinth. 8. verse 9. the grace by which we are saved just as the Fathers of the Old Testament, Acts 15. verse 11. Which indeed is the saving grace ἡ σωτήριος, since outside of CHRIST there is no σωτηρία, nor is any other name given, in which it behooves us σωθῆναι, Acts 4, 12. Furthermore, that CHRIST is that God the Saviour is evident from Isaiah 45. v. 23, whom the Apostle calls GOD blessed forever above all, Romans 9. verse 5. who, by the same author, is that GOD whose flock we are, and peculiar possession, who acquired us for himself with his own blood, Acts 20. verse 28. Cf. below verse 14. where CHRIST is called the great GOD and our Saviour for the same reason. It is added that CHRIST by his ἐπιφανείᾳ has become our Teacher and Prophet, to whom τὸ παιδεύειν, as a pedagogue, as he is called by Clement of Alexandria, properly belongs, as to the hypostatic wisdom of GOD, Luke 23, 16. 22. Revelation 3, 19.

Finally, that former appearing of grace has a mutual relationship here, which has already occurred, and the most recent appearing of glory, which is still to come, is appropriate to the same person. Since the latter belongs to the Son of God, why should we doubt that the former also belongs to the same? For, as Chrysostom warns, he shows two advents in this place: for there are indeed two, the former of grace; the following, however, of retribution and justice. Whence Jerome in this place warns: That this is the grace of Christ God the Savior, and we have not been saved by our own merit: according to that which is said in another place: You shall save them for nothing, Psalm 55.

Latin:

Verf. 11.

Ἐπεφάνη γὰρ ἡ χάρις Θεοῦ) Summa Dei bonitas, quæ in Evangelio apparuit, summam etiam vitæ puritatem desiderat. Comparat hanc bonitatem astro alicui, quod subito illucet. Vide Luc. 1, 29. Actor. 27, 20. infra c. 3, 4. נגלה, ut Genes. 25, 7. Locum Sophoniæ 2, 11. sic habent Græci: Ἐπιφανήσεται ὁ Κύριος ἐπ’ αὐτὺς, καὶ ἐξολοθρεύσει πάντας τὺς Θεὺς τῶν ἐθνῶν γῆς, καὶ προσκυνήσεσιν αὐτῷ ἕκα- στος ἐκ τῦ τόπυ αὑτῦ. Quæ verba paululum mutata citat Chrysostomus II. adversus Judæos.

Ἡ σωτήριος πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις) quæ salutaris est omni- bus hominibus, nempe eam acceptantibus.

Rationes jam exponuntur, cur monita Aposto- lica observanda; tum ob gratiæ salutiferæ appari- tionem, quæ jam facta, v. 11. 12. tum ob gloriæ Sal- vatoris manifestationem, quam expectamus, v. 13. tum ob satisfactoriam Christi redemptionem, ejusque finem, nostri sanctificationem vers. 14. Quod ad primam rationem Chrysostomus eam imprimis ad parænesin de servis refert, gratiam nobis peccati servis exhibitam. Nam si quis servum nactus, qui in mul- tis offenderit, eum non flagris ceciderit, verum pecca- tis indultis, futura vitare monuerit, atque cavere im- posterum, ne in eadem decidat, magnis quoque mune- ribus præterea illustraverit, ac beneficiis foverit: quæ- nam obsecro futurum est tam perfida mens, tam ingrata anima, quæ hujusmodi gratia non ad meliora sectan- da provocari sufficeret? Rectius generaliter respi- ciuntur antecedentia monita, q. d. interprete B. Balduino: Non amplius versamur in tenebris, vult dicere, ut opera tenebrarum impune liceat patrare, quod olim inter gentiles fere fiebat, sed tempus gra- tiæ omnibus illuxit hominibus, cujuscunque sint ordi- nis, ideo omnes digni vocatione sua, digne luce ista, digne Evangelio vivere fas est. Gratia magni Principis nos impellit, ut faciamus, quod illi gratum esse intelligimus. Multo magis gratia Dei. Si e- nim Dei est gratia, immobilis est & constans, omni- bus rebus anteferenda. Salutiferam appellat, quasi σωτηρίας πρόξενον, respectu nostri & à fine. Cum enim à salute exciderimus per peccatum, per illam ad salutem æternam reducimur, atque hoc fine no- bis præstatur, ne pereamus, sed servemur, ut hic Cro- cius.

Cæterum apparitio gratiæ Dei exhibetur 1. ratio- ne maximæ claritatis, voce ἐπεφάνη, quæ illustri modo gratiam apparuisse innuit. Quid enim il- lustrius esse poterat illa gratiæ manifestatione, qua visitavit nos oriens ex alto, Luc. 1, 78. sol justitiæ, Malach. 3, 1. lux illa magna illuminans omnes ho- mines, Joh. 1, 9. gloria Domini super nos orta est, Dominus ipse ortus est, Esa. 60, 1. 2. Θεὸς ἐφανερώ- θη ἐν σαρκὶ, 1. Timoth. 3, 16. 2. ratione summæ bo- nitatis: Ἡ χάρις τῦ Θεῦ, gratia Dei, infinita utique ac mere gratuita, quæ ἡ χρηστότης καὶ ἡ Φιλανθρω- πία τῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεῦ dicitur, & ἔλεος αὐτῦ. cap. 3. 4. 5. 3. ratione plenissimæ salutis. Dicitur enim χάρις σωτήριος, quæ omnem ac perfectam salutem infert. Non enim vere salutifera esset, nisi perfectam salutem affeffet. Et vere illa per- fecta est salus, quia extra eam nulla est vera salus, Esa. 45, 23. Actor. 4, 12. 4. ratione omnimoda universalitatis: quia illuxit πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις, o- mnibus hominibus, nemine excepto, nemine ex- cluso. Omnibus illuxit gratia, & quidem eadem gratia, nempe σωτήριος, quæ & illuxisse omnibus hominibus intelligi potest, & salutifera omnibus hominibus, non solum eam acceptantibus, sed etiam iis, qui non acceptant. Nam lux illa vera, si vim & virtutem ejusdem, si Divinam gratiosam in- tentionem, si meriti Christi pretium, efficaciam & valorem respicias, illuminat omnem hominem, Joh. 1, 9. Lucet in tenebris, etiamsi tenebræ non apprehendant eam, v. 5. Venit Christus in mun- dum, ut salvetur mundus per ipsum Johan. 3, v. 17. etsi plurimi in mundo non salventur: ratio, quia lux venit in mundum, sed homines magis dile- xerunt tenebras quam lucem, v. 19. Quod ex cohærentia textus nostri apparet, quam sic exhi- bet Hieronymus: Post catalogum doctrinæ ad Titum, quid senes, quid anus, quid adolescentulas & juvenes, quid ad extremum servos erudire deberet, re- cte nunc intulit: Illuxit enim Dei gratia Salvatoris DEI omnibus hominibus. Non est enim aliqua dif- ferentia liberi & servi, Græci & barbari, circumcisi & habentis præputium, mulieris & viri, sed cuncti in Christo unum sumus, universi ad Dei regnum voca- mur: Omnes post offensam Patri nostro reconcili- andi sumus, non per merita nostra, sed per gratiam Salvatoris. 5. ratione communis finis, quia ap- paruit & illuxit gratia omnibus, omnes παιδεύου- σα. Ideo enim annunciant CHRISTUM Apo- stoli νουθετοῦντες πάντα ἄνθρωπον, καὶ διδάσκοντες πάντα ἄνθρωπον ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ, ut scilicet sistant omnem hominem perfectum in CHRISTO JESU, Coloss. 1, 28. 29. Nam ideo se pro omnibus de- dit CHRISTUS, ut liberaret omnes ab omni iniquitate, & ut omnes mundaret sibi λαὸν πε- ριούσιον infra vers. 4. conf. 2. Corinth. 5, 15. Quan- tum vero nomine τοῦ Θεοῦ in hoc commate 11. intelligi possit DEUS Pater, vel etiam οὐσιωδῶς de DEO Triuno id nomen accipere liceat; vi- detur tamen peculiariter Filius DEI nomine il- lo hoc loco designatus, sed ut loquuntur ὑποστα- τικῶς, quia DEUS ille ὁ Σωτὴρ notatur, qui v. 10. designatur: quem esse Filium DEI antea do- cuimus: cujus σωτήριος ἡ χάρις hic celebratur, & cui hæc ἐπιφάνεια ex oraculis Veteris, Esa. 9. v. 2. cap. 60, 1. 2. Malach. 3, 1. & oraculis Novi Testamenti peculiariter tribuitur, Luc. 1. v. 79. Johan. 1, 9. cap. 8, 12. 1. Timoth. 3, 15. 2. Timoth. 1. vers. 10. Quæ loca omnia, & his gemina plura de Filio DEI loquuntur, cujus etiam χάρις in negotio τῆς σωτηρίας nostræ partim deprædica- tur, gratia nempe Domini nostri JESU CHRI- STI, quam omnibus precatur Apostolus, 2. Co- rinth. 13, 13. gratia, qua nos ditamur spiritualiter, 2. Corinth. 8. vers. 9. gratia, qua nos juxta cum Patribus Veteris Testamenti salvamur, Actor. 15. vers. 11. Quæ vero est gratia ἡ σωτήριος, quum extra CHRISTUM nulla sit σωτηρία, nec datum aliud nomen, in quo oporteat σωθῆναι, Actor, 4, 12. Porro CHRISTUM esse Deum illum Salvatorem, ex Esa. 45. v. 23. luculentum est, quem Apostolus DEUM benedictum in sæcula super omnia dicit, Roman. 9. vers. 5. qui, eodem autore, DEUS ille est, cujus grex su- mus, & peculium, qui nos proprio suo sangui- ne sibi acquisivit, Actor. 20. vers. 28. Conf. infra vers. 14. ubi CHRISTUS eadem ratione ma- gnus DEUS atque Salvator noster dicitur. Accedit, quod CHRISTUS sua ἐπιφανείᾳ no- ster factus sit Doctor, & Propheta, cui τὸ παι- δεύειν ceu Pædagogo, ut à Clemente Alexandri- no vocatur, proprie convenit, tanquam sapien- tiæ DEI hypostaticæ, Luc. 23, 16. 22. Apocal. 3, 19.

Denique relationem mutuam hic habet prior illa τῆς χάριτος ἐπιφάνεια, quæ jam facta & noviffi- ma τῆς δόξης ἐπιφάνεια, quæ adhuc futura est, ei- dem personæ conveniens. Quæ posterior cum sit Filii Dei,priorem etiam ejusdem esse,cur ambige- remus? Nam duos in hoc loco,monente Chrysofto- mo,ostendit adventus: Duo enim revera sunt,gra- tiæ prior; sequens vero retributionis atque justi- tiæ. Unde Hieronymus in h. l. monet: Quod Chri- sti Dei Salvatoris hæc sit gratia, & non nostro meri- to salvati sumus : secundum illud, quod in alio loco di- citur: Pro nihilo salvabis eos, Psal.55.

## 2:12
Verse 12.

Instructing us) Namely, through Christ.

Nay, Christ is that very God the Savior, whose grace has shone upon all for the salvation of all, the God who acquired us with his own blood, Acts 20:28. For this grace is understood as both of redemption and of calling, which, so that we do not receive it in vain, Christ informs and instructs us as to what should be avoided by us and what should be done, and to that end the grace of Christ is directed, whence it itself is called instructing us. Not that the grace of Christ, as Estius warns, consists in doctrine, as Pelagius wished, but because the manifestation of grace or the beneficence of God ought to be to us in place of an institution for living a holy life. Nevertheless, neither that institution, nor any doctrine brought to the ears, however much it is applied for persuasion, will ensure that we live holily, unless God effectively works this very thing in us through his grace. To instruct is to train ignorant children in letters and morals. And the Apostle uses this word conveniently, because in divine matters we are all infants and children, who have need of a pedagogue, for which reason the whole Christian discipline is not ineptly called pedagogy, as here the blessed Baldwin.

That having denied ungodliness and worldly desires) Having denied here is renouncing, by that locution which we discussed in 2 Timothy 3:5. Ungodliness is accustomed to follow idolatry, as appears from Cicero's disputations on the nature of the gods. Worldly desires are called those cravings which the greater part of men follow. For that greater part is often called by the name of world in these books.

That we may live soberly and righteously and godly in this present age) With three words he briefly concluded all parts of our duty. For they pertain either to us, or to another man, or to God. Philo, in the book 'That the good man is free': Using triple boundaries and rules, the God-loving, the virtue-loving, and the man-loving; for the God-loving, there are provided countless proofs, a continuous and successive purity throughout the whole life, the not swearing, the truthfulness, to consider the divine as the cause of all good things, but of no evil. For the virtue-loving, the lack of love for money, the lack of love for glory, the lack of love for pleasure, self-control, endurance, and furthermore, moderation, ease, lack of arrogance, lawfulness, stability, and whatever is similar to these. For the man-loving, goodwill, equality in every word, superior fellowship, etc. The same shows the coherence of piety and justice thus: It is of the same nature to be both pious and man-loving. And concerning the same things, each is considered: holiness toward God, but justice toward men. Concerning which matter we have said much in Book II of the Law of War and Peace, XX. 44 and following, both in the text and in the annotations.

There must be avoided both impiety toward God against the first table of the Decalogue, and the perverse desire of the age against the second table. For the Apostle understands denial, not that which is done by voice only, but that which is done in the thing itself. Denial, says Chrysostom, of this kind indicates a great distance, a huge interval, the greatest execration, so that, namely, with as much zeal as we have turned away from idols, we may likewise flee worldly desires. But the things to be done the Apostle embraces in those three words, that namely we must live soberly regarding ourselves, righteously regarding our neighbor, and godly regarding God. See Fulgentius, Book I, on the remission of sins, chapter 28. Worldly desires are, says Jerome, those which are suggested by the Prince of this world, and since they are of the age, they pass away with the cloud of this age. We, however, when we have lived in Christ chastely and justly, and not with the mind of a sinner, will also live godly in this age. He adds in this present age, so that all may remember that now is the time for doing good and avoiding sins. When one has departed from this life, all things are closed; then there is no place for faith or repentance; as Crocius has here.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Παιδεύουσα ἡμᾶς) Nempe per Christum.

Imo Christus est ipse Deus ille Servator, cujus gratia omnibus illuxit ad omnium salutem, Deus qui proprio suo sanguine nos acquisivit Act. 20,28. Nam hæc intelligitur gratia tum redemptionis tum vocationis,quam ne frustra accipiamus,informat ac erudit nos Christus, quæ fugienda nobis sint, quæ facienda, eoque directa est gratia Christi, unde ipsa dicitur παιδεύουσα ἡμᾶς. Non quod gratia Christi, quod monet Estius, consistat in doctrina, quemadmodum volebat Pelagius, sed quia manifesta- tio gratiæ seu beneficentia Dei nobis esse debet vice in- stitutionis ad vitam sancte agendam. Veruntamen nec ea institutio, nec ulla doctrina auribus admota, quantumvis ad persuadendum apposita, præstabit, ut sancte vivamus, nisi Deus hoc ipsum per gratiam suam in nobis efficaciter operetur. Παιδεύειν est pueros ignorantes in literis & moribus instituere. Et com- mode utitur Apostolus hac voce, quia in rebus Divinis omnes sumus infantes & pueri, qui Pædagogo opus habent, quam ob causam tota Christiana disciplina haud inepte pædagogia appellatur, ut hic B. Baldui- nus.

Ἵνα ἀρνησάμενοι τὴν ἀσέβειαν καὶ τὰς κοσμικὰς ἐπιθυμίας) Ἀρνησάμενοι hic est abdicentes, ea loquutione, de quæ e- gimus 2. Timoth. 3, 5. Ἀσέβεια solet εἰδωλολατρείαν sequi, ut apparet ex Ciceronis disputationibus de natura Deo- rum. Κοσμικαὶ ἐπιθυμίαι dicuntur eæ cupiditates, quas major pars hominum sequitur. Ea enim pars major sæpe in his libris κόσμος vocatur nomine.

Σωφρόνως καὶ δικαίως καὶ εὐσεβῶς ζήσωμεν ἐν τῷ νῦν αἰῶνι) Tribus verbis breviter omnes officii nostri partes con- clusit. Nam ea aut ad nos pertinent aut ad hominem alterum, aut ad Deum. Philo: libro Virum bonum esse liberum: Ὅροις καὶ κανόσι τριττοῖς χρώμενοι τῷ τε φιλοθέῳ, καὶ φιλαρέτῳ, καὶ φιλανθρώπῳ, τῶ μὲν οὖν φιλο- θέῳ δείγματα παρέχονται μυρία, τὴν παρ᾽ ὅλον τὸν βίον συνεχῆ καὶ ἐπάλληλον ἁγνείαν, τὸ ἀνώμοτον, τὸ ἀψευδὲς, τὸ πάντων μὲν ἀγαθῶν αἴτιον, κακῶ δὲ μηδενὸς νομίζειν εἶ- ναι τὸ θεῖον. Τῶ δὲ φιλαρέτῳ τὸ ἀφιλοχρήματον, τὸ ἀφι- λόδοξον, τὸ ἀφιλήδονον, τὸ ἐγκρατες, τὸ καρτερικὸν, ἔτι δὲ ὀλιγόδειαν, εὐκολίαν, τὸ ἄτυφον, τὸ νόμιμον, τὸ εὐ- σταθὲς, καὶ ὅσα τούτοις ὁμοιότροπα. Τῶ δὲ φιλανθρώπῳ, εὔνοιαν, ἰσότητα παντὸς λόγω, κρείττονα κοινωνίαν &c. I- dem pietatis & justitiæ cohærentiam sic ostendit: Τῆς ἀυ- τῆς φύσεώς ἐστιν, εὐσεβεῖ τε εἶναι καὶ φιλάνθρωπον. Καὶ πε- ρὶ τῶν ἀυτῶν ἑκάτερον ὁσιότης μὲν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, δικαιοσύνη δὲ πρὸς τῆς ἀνθρώπως θεωρεῖται. Qua de re multa diximus libr. II. de jure belli & pacis XX. 44. & sequentibus, tum in textu, tum in annotatis.

Fugienda sunt tum impietas erga Deum contra tabulam primam Decalogi, tum prava seculi cupi- ditas contra secundam tabulam. Abnegationem enim intelligit Apostolus, non quæ voce tantum fit, sed quæ re ipsa. Abnegatio, inquit Chrysofto- mus, hujusmodi magnam distantiam indicat, ingens intervallum, plurimam execrationem, ut videlicet quanto studio idola aversati sumus, cum tanto secula- ria itidem desideria fugiamus. Facienda vero tribus illis verbis complectitur Apostolus, quod nempe vivendum nobis sit σωφρόνως quoad nos- ipsos, δικαίως, quoad proximum, καὶ εὐσεβῶς quo- ad Deum. Vid. Fulgentius libr. I. de remiss. pecc. cap. 28. Secularia desideria sunt, inquit Hierony- mus, quæ à mundi istius Principe suggeruntur, & cum sint seculi, cum hujus seculi nube prætereunt. Nos autem cum pudicè & justè, nec mente peccantis vixerimus in Christo: piè quoque vivemus in hoc secu- lo. Addit in præsenti seculo, ut omnes meminerint, nunc esse tempus benefaciendi, & peccata vitandi. Cum excessum fuerit ex hac vita, clausa sunt omnia, tunc nec fidei, nec pænitentiæ est locus; ut hic habet Crocius.

## 2:13
Verse 13.

Looking for the blessed hope) There is also a metonymy here. For the name of hope is given to the thing hoped for, as also in Galatians 5:5, Colossians 1:5. And hope, that is, eternal life, is called blessed, because it contains in itself everything that can make a man blessed.

Καὶ ἐπιφάνειαν τῆς δόξης) Here again καὶ is explanatory. And ἐπιφάνεια δόξης, according to the Hebrew custom, is a glorious appearing. See Matt. 25, 30; Mark 13, 26.

Τῦ μεγάλυ Θεῦ καὶ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χρισῦ) That appearing is said to be not only of Christ, but also of God: because God bestows that Majesty upon Christ. Therefore Christ is said to be about to come ἐν τῇ δόξῃ τῦ Πατρός, Matt. 16, 27; Mark 8, 38. Thus Ambrose rightly understood this passage. Those who think that τῦ Σωτῆρος should have been said if the Apostle had distinguished these, should know that in these books the articles are often placed where there is no need, and often omitted where they would be used by custom.

The appearing of the glory of the great God and our Savior will follow the appearing of the saving grace: Grace, which in this age saves us from sins and instructs us that we should flee iniquity and depraved desire, and live soberly, justly, and piously in this age, is followed, if we receive that grace by faith and do not neglect His discipline so as not to fall from the same, by a blessed life in the other age; which, however, is not to be confused with the glorious appearing of CHRIST Himself, who is about to appear on the last day to render that blessedness to us. The hope of blessedness is connected with faith in the grace of GOD the Savior, which has shone upon all men, and with the reception of that discipline, which is comprised in charity toward GOD and neighbor, through which saving faith is active, Galat. 5, 6. For these three follow one another: Faith, charity, and hope. Piety, says Jerome on this passage, awaits the blessed hope and the advent of the glory of the great GOD and our Savior JESUS CHRIST. For just as impiety dreads the advent of the great GOD, so piety, secure in its work and in faith in Him, awaits it. But Grotius rashly separates what the Apostle has joined, τῦ μεγάλυ Θεῦ καὶ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χρισῦ, with the Arians and Socinians, making one great GOD here and another Savior JESUS CHRIST: whereas, on the contrary, this is one person according to the Apostle, from which an indissoluble argument for the Divine nature of CHRIST results. As we asserted this in another, though unpublished, work thirty years ago, so it seems worth the effort to repeat those vindications at present.

That argument stands thus: He who is designated by the name τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ, of the great GOD, is the supreme GOD. But CHRIST is designated by the name τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ, of the great GOD. Therefore Christ is the true GOD. The major premise is evident: Because (1) by the name of the great God absolutely and κατ' ἐξοχὴν (by way of eminence) none other is designated than that great GOD Jehovah. And he who would be called the great GOD absolutely, [would not be] one who depends on another, and who is by nature a mere man, and a mere creature. Great, says Oecumenius on this passage, not because he is also a small GOD, but because he is absolutely great, and because a greater than he cannot be conceived. Τὸ μέγας ἐπὶ Θεοῦ ὅταν λέγῃ οὐ πρός τι μέγας φησὶ, ἀλλ' ἀπολύτως μέγας μεθ' ὃν οὐκ ἂν εἴη μέγας, says Chrysostom on this passage. (2) Because in the Scriptures the name of the great GOD is appropriated to and claimed by the one and only supreme GOD. For that it is said of none but that one GOD, the induction of places teaches, Exodus 18, verse 11. The Lord is great above all gods. Deuteronomy 7, verse 21. The Lord your GOD is in the midst of you, a great and terrible GOD. Ezra 5, verse 8, to the House of the great GOD. Nehemiah 1, verse 5, O Lord God of heaven, strong, great and terrible. Chapter 8, verse 6, Ezra blessed the Lord the great GOD. Chapter 9, verse 32, Now therefore our GOD, great, strong and terrible. Job 36, verse 26, Behold, GOD is great, surpassing our knowledge. Psalm 95, verse 3, For the Lord is a great GOD. Daniel 2, verse 45, The great GOD has shown the King what things are to come. Chapter 9, verse 4, O Lord God, great and terrible. Revelation 19, verse 17, Gather yourselves to the supper of the great GOD τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ, etc. (3) Because the Socinians say that the name τοῦ Θεοῦ with the article is proper to the one and only supreme GOD. But here the name τοῦ Θεοῦ occurs with the article. (4) Crellius admits in his book on GOD and divine attributes, chapter 27, page 272, that the word 'greatness' when referred to GOD signifies, according to the common custom of speaking, eminence or excellence: nor do most of the disciples of Socinus deny that in this passage the supreme GOD is designated by the phrase 'great God'.

We confirm the minor premise, (1) Because the very sense of the words indicates that the ἐπιφάνειαν τῆς δόξης (appearing of the glory) is referred to one and the same subject, namely JESUS CHRIST, and that the same is designated by the words τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ, καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν (of the great God and our Savior), since only one article is employed, which denotes nothing but one subject, according to the propriety of the Greek language. If there were diverse subjects, the great GOD and the Savior JESUS CHRIST, the article would have been repeated in this manner: τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ, καὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ; Just as there is one subject in 2. Peter 3, verse 18, when it is said: Grow in the knowledge of our Lord and Savior JESUS CHRIST, and our Lord is not one, and the Savior JESUS another, but this one is designated both as our Lord and as Savior: so here likewise there is one subject, when mention is made of τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ, καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ (of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ), and the great GOD is not one, and our Savior JESUS CHRIST another, but this one is called both the great GOD and our Savior. They certainly could not be referred to two distinct persons with any more probability than that expression, ὁ Θεὸς, καὶ πατὴρ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ (the God and Father of Jesus Christ), as the excellent Philologist Theodore Beza says on this passage. (2) Because ἐπιφάνεια (appearing), or illustrious advent, as Beza renders it, is not ascribed in the Holy Scriptures to the Father, but perpetually to the Son, who is said to be about to come to judgment and to appear on the last day, whence we conclude. He is designated by the name of the great GOD, whose ἐπιφάνεια, appearing, and illustrious advent is expected on the last day. But this, according to Scripture, is not the Father, but the Son, as may be read everywhere in the Scriptures. John 5:22, The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son. The name of the appearing, which occurs here, is nowhere used of the Father, but always of the Son. 2 Thessalonians 2, verse 8, CHRIST will destroy by the appearing of his coming. 1 Timothy 6, verse 14, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. 2 Timothy 1, verse 10, Through the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ. Chapter 4, verse 1, at his appearing (of the Lord Jesus Christ). Verse 8, not to me only, but also to all who love his appearing, namely of the Lord Jesus Christ. (3) It is added that a little before, verse 10. CHRIST was likewise called GOD our Savior, that they might adorn the doctrine of God our Savior in all things. For who is that GOD our Savior, whose doctrine we ought to adorn? Is not CHRIST our Savior designated by that name, from whom we have received the doctrine, to whom for that reason the name of Teacher is appropriated in the New Testament, Matthew 8, verse 19, 9, verse 11, John 3, verse 2, 13, verse 13, etc., whose doctrine is read to be so accurately described in the New Testament? (4) The Apostle's argument must not be deprived of its weight: For he means to say this: My Titus, see to it that your Cretans think of redemption, and they will have the most urgent cause for living piously. For since that great GOD and at the same time true man gave himself to death in our stead for this end, that he might release us from the bonds of sin and every liability, with what conscience shall we indulge in sins any longer? (5) Finally, it adds momentum to this opinion that the Greek Fathers as well as the Latin defend the same with great consensus: Where is the serpent Arius, says Jerome on this passage, where is the viper Eunomius? Jesus Christ is called the great Savior. He named Christ the great GOD, says Theodoret on this passage, refuting the heretical blasphemy. Πῶς εἰσιν οἱ τῦ Πατρὸς ἐλάττονα τὸν ὑὸν λέγοντες : τῦ μεγάλε, φησὶ, Θεῦ ᾄ σωτῆρος (How are they who say the Son is lesser than the Father: of the great, he says, God and Savior), says Chrysostom on this passage. Similar things are read in Oecumenius and Theophylact. Augustine and others from the choir of the Fathers, most of them all, agree. What of the fact that even the Arians acknowledged that CHRIST is called the great GOD here, even though they denied that the same should therefore be held to be the supreme GOD, as Erasmus observes in his annotation on this passage, as also Andreas Fricius in Sylv. tract. 1, page 42.

Enjedinus objects here, p. 374: (1) Even if it were granted that JESUS is called the great GOD, he is nevertheless not the eternal GOD, because nothing prevents one from being Greater, according to Erasmus, and because it does not befit the supreme GOD to give himself unto death, which is said here of the great GOD, whom Enjedinus therefore concludes is said to have died only insofar as he was the great God. (2) He contends that the minor premise is false, for the reason that mention is made here of two, the great GOD, that is, the Father, and the Savior Christ, which he considers the conjunction and the interposed comma to demonstrate quite clearly, as in Philip. I. v. 6. (3) Enjedinus takes exception to the arguments brought forward for the confirmation of the minor premise, to the first indeed, that a single article is also applied to two nouns signifying different things in this very verse, τὴν μακαρίαν ἐλπίδα καὶ ἐπιφάνειαν, as also 1. Tim. V. verse 21. chapter VI. verse 13. Similarly Socinus denies in Anti-Wujeck: that that rule in the Greek language concerning one article bringing in only one person is perpetual, and that the testimony of Erasmus alone, a man in the judgment of all most expert in the Greek language, ought to be enough to convince. He adds the passages Matt. XXI. verse 12. Eph. V. verse 5. Schlichtingius against Meisner on the Trinity page 254 produces these examples to the contrary Eph. IV. verse 11. Matt. III. verse 7. 16. 17. chapter XXVII. verse 56. Eph. II. verse 20. chapter III. v. 5. 1 Thess. I. verse 8. Heb. IX. verse 19. (4) To our other argument Enjedinus objects, Tit. II. verse 11. that the word ἐπιφανείας is referred to the Father, as also chapter III. verse 4. (5) Socinus urges that the word παρουσία, which is commonly rendered advent both here and elsewhere in the New Testament, signifies presence more properly, although it is sometimes used for advent. (6) That Paul does not say that we are awaiting the advent of the great GOD, but the advent of the glory of the great GOD. But that the glory of GOD the Father can be said to be about to come when CHRIST the judge shall have arrived, Matt. XVI. v. 27. Mark VIII. verse 38. Schlichtingius: There are two things, he says, which we expect to appear, one is the glory of that great GOD, the other is our Savior or CHRIST. For that great GOD himself will not indeed appear, but only his glory with CHRIST, who is to come in the glory of his Father: but again, not only the glory of our Savior, or CHRIST, will appear, but also the Savior or CHRIST himself. (7) It is not absurd, says Socinus, if GOD the Father is said to be about to come when Christ shall come, because Christ in judging the world will sustain the person of GOD the Father, John V. verse 27. Acts XVII. verse 31. (8) Finally Socinus also objects Ambrose, who refers the name of the great GOD to God the Father in his commentary on this passage. These are the adversaries': Otherwise it is easy to satisfy each of those exceptions.

As to (1) we have already proven that the name of the great God brings in the supreme God: nor does it stand in the way that that great GOD is said to have delivered himself for us unto death. For although the supreme GOD, as such, or by reason of his Deity, cannot undergo death, he could nevertheless undergo death in the flesh personally proper to himself, just as he is also said to have shed his own blood Acts XX. verse 28. Finally there is no ἀκολουθία: It is said of the great GOD that he delivered himself unto death; therefore insofar as he is the great GOD, or by reason of his Deity, he has died. Just as it does not follow, when it is said of an animated man that he has been wounded and bruised, therefore by reason of his soul he has been wounded and bruised.

To (2) Resp. The argument taken from the particle καὶ is slippery and frivolous, since nothing is more known and common than that it is used even when it is about one subject. For must it be explained as about two, for example, εὐλογητὸς ὁ θεὸς, καὶ πατὴρ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν, because of the interposed particle καὶ, must that be held as a sufficiently manifest demonstration that one is GOD, and another the Father of our Lord, to say nothing of countless others, for there is no need for prolixity in a manifest matter.

To (3) Resp. If we look to the ordinary tenor of the Greek language, those most expert in Greek literature, both ancient commentators and more recent Philologists, testify that the Greek words τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ, καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ bring in one and the same subject, nor could Erasmus himself deny it. Although, he says, the omitted article in the Greek books makes SOMETHING for the different opinion μεγάλυ Θεῦ καὶ σωτῆρος. He would have distinguished the persons more evidently if he had said, καὶ τῦ σωτῆρος. Nor indeed do we rely only on that argument from the omission of the article. There are also others, which viewed together solidly establish our opinion: so that there is no need now to look into the contrary examples.

To (4) Resp. It remains certain and solid that the word ἐπιφανείας is nowhere used of the Father. Tit. II. verse 11. ἐπεφάνη ἡ χάρις τῦ θεῦ ἡ σωτήριος is said, and Tit. III. verse 4. ὅτε δὲ ἡ χρησότης καὶ ἡ Φιλανθρωπία ἐπεφάνη τῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεῦ. But the apparition of the grace of GOD and kindness is one thing, the apparition of GOD himself is another. Nor is there any reason for Enjedinus to retort that here too the ἐπιφάνεια of GOD himself is not described, but τῆς δόξης τῦ Θεῦ, of the glory of GOD: because he has already cut the nerve of this objection, for he admitted that the advent of glory is said, as if it were a glorious advent, whence it remains that the glorious advent of GOD himself is commemorated here. Add that the word ἐπιφανείας concerning the advent to judgment is nowhere used of GOD the Father, always of GOD the Son, which can be infringed by no objection. But here it is a question of the advent to judgment. The passages adduced, however, look to the manifestation of the grace of God made in the Gospel, which are far different.

To (5) Resp. He committed an inexcusable oversight, since the word here is not παρεσίας, but ἐπιφανείας. Thus he was indeed carried away by a blind desire to corrupt, so that he did not even look at the Greek text, although, as Beza observed, not even the word παρεσίας is ever attributed to GOD the Father in the New Testament, but only to the Son. See Matt. XXIV. verse 3. XXVII. verse 39. 1 Cor. XV. v. 23. 1 Thess. II. v. 19. III. verse 13. IV. verse 15. V. verse 23. 2 Thess. II. verse 1. Jas. V. verse 7. & 8. 2 Pet. III. verse 4. 1 John II. verse 18.

To (6) Resp. The advent of the glory of the great GOD, through a received Hebraism, is the same as the glorious advent of the great GOD, which Enjedinus does not deny, but admits. Nor is it said anywhere that the glory of God the Father is about to come, even if CHRIST is said to be about to come in the glory of God the Father; much less is the glory of God the Father said to be about to come separately, so that it is added that CHRIST himself is also about to come. Schlichtingius, however, presupposes a false hypothesis, that namely the great GOD is not about to come and appear, but only his glory; which is entirely inconsistent, because the glory of the great God is entirely inseparable from the great God himself, to say nothing of the fact that it is not for the glory to come, but for the glorious GOD himself, since that is a personal predicate, bringing in a subject. And what is that paraphrase: awaiting the apparition of the glory of the great GOD, in which CHRIST is about to come, and of the Savior, or Christ? Can there be any doubt that the Savior Jesus Christ will appear and come on the last day, assuming that the glory of the most high GOD is to come and appear, and that it is not to appear otherwise than in so far as Christ is to come in it: What of the fact that as the glory of the Father and the Son is one and the same, so also the Father and the Son are one τῇ ὐσίᾳ, John X. verse 30, 1 John V. verse 7. Finally, the appearance on the last day, where it is described in the sacred scriptures, is not about GOD the Father, but the Son, who was made visible in the flesh, and will then appear in a visible form, just as he visibly ascended into heaven, concerning whose visible appearance in the clouds, in the glory of GOD the Father, and his own, [the Scriptures speak] everywhere, but nowhere concerning a visible appearance of the Father in the clouds must be distinguished: that by which it is viewed in GOD, and that by which the same is communicated to CHRIST as man. The ἐπιφάνεια (manifestation) of the glory of GOD at the coming of CHRIST to judgment is attributed not to the former, but to the latter mode, because the Son of man will then be revealed, coming in the clouds of heaven, with power and great glory, Luke XVII. verse 3. Matthew XXIV. v. 30. See Dan. VII. verse 13. Matthew XVI. verse 27. XIX. verse 28. XXVI. verse 64. But if CHRIST is to come in the glory of the Father, it is necessary that he be endowed with infinite and immense glory, since the glory of the Father is infinite and immense glory.

To (7) Resp. We admit that it is not absurd for GOD the Father to be said to be coming: but we add that nowhere in the New Testament is the coming to judgment and appearance on the last day spoken of concerning God the Father, but always concerning the Son of God. This is so perpetual that not only the word ἐπιφανείας (manifestation), but also related words are claimed uniquely for the Son of GOD, such as παρουσίας (presence), concerning which [we spoke] above, Φανερώσεως (revelation) Col. III. verse 4, 1 Pet. V. v. 4, 1 John II. v. 28, III. verse 2, as also ἀποκαλύψεως (revelation), 1 Corinth. I. v. 7, 2 Thessal. I. verse 7, 1 Pet. I. verse 7, 13, chap. IV. verse 13. However, one must not attend to what might perhaps be said without absurdity, but to what is said in the Scriptures, and what is accustomed to be said. Furthermore, it is nowhere said in the Scriptures that Christ must sustain the person of God in the final judgment. GOD the Father gave Christ the power of performing judgment, in that he is the Son of man, John V. verse 23. and he is said to be about to judge the world through him, Acts XVII. verse 31. But it by no means follows from that that Christ will solely sustain the person of God the Father in the act of judgment. Scripture teaches that the Son and the Father are one: it does not teach that the Son sustains the person of the Father. The power communicated to Christ is not a vicarious and delegated power, but the same infinite and immense power which is that of the Father himself, since on that account he ought to be honored as the Father. Therefore, it cannot be a lesser or inferior power which brings about equal or equivalent honor and glory. But more on these things elsewhere.

To (8) Resp. The commentary on the Pauline Epistles which bears the name of Ambrose is not by Ambrose, but by some other person, which both the style teaches, and Antonio Possevino, Johann Maldonatus in chapter Matth. IX. and in John III., and Bellarmine, book 4 de just. chapter 8, admit. Maldonatus attributes the same commentaries to Remigius of Lyons, who lived around the year of our Lord 870, and thus was long after Ambrose. Finally, the authority of one Ambrose cannot prejudice the consensus of most Greek Doctors and the opinion most received in the Church. And so much for that argument.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Προσδεχόμενοι τὴν μακαρίαν ἐλπίδα) Est & hic Metony- mia. Nam rei speratæ datur spei nomen, ut & Galat. 5, 5. Col. 1, 5. Et spes, id est, vita æterna dicitur μακαρία, quia omne id, quod beatum facere hominem potest, in se continet.

Καὶ ἐπιφάνειαν τῆς δόξης) Hic rursus καὶ est ἐξηγητι- κόν. Et ἐπιφάνεια δόξης more Ebræo est gloriosa apparitio. Vide Matth. 25, 30. Marc, 13, 26.

Τῦ μεγάλυ Θεῦ καὶ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χρισῦ) Illa apparitio dicitur non Christi tantum futura, sed & Dei: quia Deus Majestatem illam Christo tribuit. Ideo Chri- stus dicitur venturus ἐν τῇ δόξῃ τῦ Πατρός, Matth 16, 27. Marc. 8, 38. Ita hunc locum recte accepit Ambrosius. Qui putant τῦ Σωτῆρος dici debuisse, si hæc distinxiffet Apostolus, norint in his libris τὰ ἄρθρα sæpe poni, ubi non est opus, & sæpe omitti, ubi ex usu pone- rentur.

Sequetur apparitionem gratiæ salutiferæ appari- tio gloriæ Dei Salvatoris: Gratiam, quæ in hoc se- culo nos salvat à peccatis, & informat, ut iniqui- tatem & pravam cupiditatem fugiamus, sobrie, juste, ac pie vivamus in hoc seculo, excipit, si fide illam gratiam suscipiamus, & ne eadem excida- mus, παιδίαν ejus non negligamus, beata vita in altero seculo; quæ vero confundenda non est cum ipsa apparitione CHRISTI gloriosa, ad redden- dam nobis illam beatitudinem, in novissimo die comparituri. Spes beatitudinis connexa est cum fide in gratiam DEI Servatoris, quæ omnibus hominibus illuxit, ac παιδίας illius susceptio- ne, quæ charitate erga DEUM & proximum comprehenditur, per quam fides salvifica ope- rosa est, Galat. 5, 6. Hæc enim tria consequun- tur se invicem: Fides, charitas, & spes. Pie- tas, inquit Hieronymus in hunc locum, expe- ctat beatam spem, & adventum gloriæ magni DEI, & Salvatoris nostri JESU CHRISTI. Sic- ut enim impietas magni DEI reformidat ad- ventum: Ita secura de opere suo & de fide illius pietas præstolatur. Illa vero quæ copulavit A- postolus τῦ μεγάλυ Θεῦ καὶ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χρισῦ temere sejungit cum Arianis & Socinia- nis Grotius, alium magnum DEUM, alium Sal- vatorem JESUM CHRISTUM hic faciens: quum ex adverso una hæc sit persona secundum Apostolum, unde argumentum ἀδιάλυτον pro Divina CHRISTI natura resultat. Quod uti in alio sed ἀνεκδότῳ, & in completo opere ante ipsos triginta annos asseruimus: Ita vindicias illas inpræsentiarum repetere inde operæ pre- tium videtur.

Argumentum illud ita habet : Is qui indigitatur nomine τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ, magni DEI, est summus DEUS. At CHRISTUS indigitatur nomine τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ, magni DEI. Ergò Christus est verus DEUS. Major patet: Quia (1) nomine magni Dei absolutè & κατ' ἐξοχὴν non nisi magnus ille DEUS Jehovah designatur. Et qui absolutè magnus DEUS diceretur is, qui ab alio dependet, quique natura purus homo, & mera creatura est. Magnus, inquit Oecumenius in hunc loc. non quia etiam parvus sit DEUS, sed quia absolutè magnus, & quia major ipso cogitari nequit. Τὸ μέγας ἐπὶ Θεοῦ ὅταν λέγῃ οὐ πρός τι μέγας φησὶ, ἀλλ' ἀπολύτως μέγας μεθ' ὃν οὐκ ἂν εἴη μέγας, ait Chrysostomus in h. l. (2) Quia in Scripturis nomen magni DEI appropriatur & vendicatur uni & soli summo DEO. Non enim nisi de uno illo DEO dici, locorum inductio docet, Exod. XIIX. versu 11. Magnus Dominus super omnes Deos. Deuteronom. VII. vers. 21. Dominus DEUS tuus in medio tui est, DEUS magnus & terribilis. Esdr. V. vers. 8. ad Domum DEI magni. Nehem. I. vers. 5. Domine Deus cœli fortis, magne atque terribilis. Cap. IIX. vers. 6. Benedixit Esdras Domino DEO magno. Cap. IX. vers. 32. Nunc itaque DEUS noster magne, fortis & terribilis. Job. XXXVI. v. 26. Ecce DEUS magnus vincens scientiam nostram. Psalm. XCV. vers. 3. Quoniam DEUS magnus Dominus. Dan. II. vers. 45. DEUS magnus ostendit Regi, quæ ventura sunt. Cap. IX. vers. 4. Domine Deus magne & terribilis. Apocal. XIX. v. 17. Congregamini ad cœnam magni DEI τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ, &c. (3) Quia nomen τοῦ Θεοῦ cum articulo uni & soli DEO summo proprium esse ajunt Sociniani. At hic occurrit nomen τοῦ Θεοῦ cum articulo. (4) Fatetur Crellius lib. de DEO & attributis divinis cap. 27. pag. 272. magnitudinis vocem ad DEUM relatam ex vulgari loquendi consuetudine, eminentiam seu excellentiam significare : nec inficiantur Socini discipuli plerique omnes, hoc loco voce magni Dei DEUM summum designari.

Minorem confirmamus, (1) Quia unius ejusdemque subjecti ἐπιφάνειαν τῆς δόξης referri, nimirum JESU CHRISTI, eandemque vocibus τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ, καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν designari, ipse verborum sensus indicat, cùm unicus tantum adhibeatur articulus, qui non nisi unum subjectum denotat, secundum Græcæ linguæ proprietatem. Si diversa subjecta forent magnus DEUS, & Servator JESUS CHRISTUS, repetitus fuisset articulus hoc pacto, τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ, καὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ; Quemadmodum unum est subjectum 2. Petr. III. vers. 18. cum dicitur: Crescite in cognitione τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν, καὶ σωτῆρος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, nec aliud est Dominus noster, alius Salvator JESUS, sed hic & Dominus noster, & Salvator indigitatur: ita hic pariter unum est subjectum, cum mentio fit τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ, καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, nec alius est DEUS magnus, alius Salvator noster JESUS CHRISTUS, sed hic & DEUS magnus dicitur, & Salvator noster. Non magis certè probabiliter poterunt ad duas distinctas personas referri, quam illa locutio, ὁ Θεὸς, καὶ πατὴρ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, ut ait eximius Philologus Theodorus Beza in h. l. (2) Quia ἐπιφάνεια apparitio, vel illustris adventus, ut Beza reddit, ad judicium non adscribitur in Sacris literis Patri, sed Filio perpetuò, qui adventurus dicitur ad judicium & appariturus in novissimo die, unde concludimus. Is nomine τῶ μεγάλΰ Θεῦ indi- gitatur, cujus ἐπιφάνεια, apparitio, & adventus illustris in novissimo die exspectatur. At hic secundum Scripturam non est Pater, sed Filius, ut passim in Scripturis legere est. Johan. V. 22. Pater non judicat quenquam, sed omne judicium dedit Filio. Nomen ἐπιφανείας, quod hic occur- rit, nuspiam de Patre, semper de Filio adhibe- tur. 2. Thessalon. II. vers. 8. CHRISTUS de- struet τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ τῆς παρεσίας αὑτῦ 1. Tim. VI. vers. 14. μεχρὶ τῆς ἐπιφανείας τῦ κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ. 2. Timoth. I. v. 10. Διὰ τῆς ἐπιφα- νείας τῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ. Cap. IV. vers. 1. κατὰ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν αὑτῦ (τῦ Κυρίε Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ.) Vers. 8. non mihi tantum, sed & omni- bus diligentibus τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν αὑτῦ, scilicet τῦ κυρίε Domini Jesu Christi. (3) Accedit, quod paulò ante v. 10. CHRISTUS itidem DEUS Servator noster dictus fuerit, ἵνα τὴν διδασκα- λίαν τῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεῦ κοσμῶσιν ἐν πᾶσιν. Quisnam enim ille DEUS Salvator noster est, cujus διδασκαλίαν ornare debemus? Annon eo designatur nomine CHRISTUS Servator noster, à quo διδασκαλίαν accepimus, cui ea- propter nomen διδασκάλε appropriatur in No- vo Testamento, Matth. IIX. vers. 19. IX. vers. 11. Joh. III. vers. 2. XIII. vers. 13. &c. cujus διδασκα- λία in Novo Testamento tam accurate descri- pta legitur? (4) Argumentum Apostoli suo non est privandum pondere : Id enim vult dicere : Mi Tite, effice, ut tui Cretenses redemptionem cogitent, & habebunt causam piè vivendi urgen- tissimam. Cum enim magnus ille DEUS idem- que verus homo hoc fine seipsum vice nostra in mortem dederit, ut nos à vinculis peccati & reatu omni exolveret, qua conscientia peccatis indulgebimus ampliùs? (5) Momentum denique addit huic sententiæ, quod magno consensu eandem Patres Græci pariter ac Latini propu- gnent: Ubi est serpens Arius, inquit Hierony- mus in h. l. ubi Eunomius coluber ? Magnus Jesus Christus Salvator dicitur. Magnum DEUM, ait Theodoretius in h. l. nominavit Christum hære- ticam blasphemiam redarguens. Πῶς εἰσιν οἱ τῦ Πα- τρὸς ἐλάττονα τὸν ὑὸν λέγοντες : τῦ μεγάλε, φη- σὶ, Θεῦ ᾄ σωτῆρος, ait Chrysostomus in h. l.-Similia leguntur apud Oecumenium & Theophylactum. Consentiunt Augustinus, aliiqve è Patrum cho- ro, plerique omnes. Quid quod Ariani etiam agnoverint CHRISTUM hic magnum DEUM dici, etsi negarint, eundem summum DEUM ideò habendum esse, ut observat Erasmus in annotatione ad h. l. ut & Andreas Fricius in Sylv. tract. I. pag. 42.

Obvertit hic Enjedinus pag. 374. (1) Etiamsi concederetur, JESUM dici magnum DEUM, non tamen esse æternum DEUM, quod nihil vetet, alterum esse Majorem, secundum Era- smum, quodque DEO summo non competat se dare in mortem, quod hic de magno DEO di- citur, quem proinde eatenus mortuum dici con- cludit Enjedinus, quatenus erat magnus Deus. (2) Minorem falsam esse contendit, eò quod duorum hic mentio fiat, magni DEI, id est, Pa- tris, & Salvatoris Christi, quod satis manifestè demonstrare conjunctionem, & interpositum com- ma censet, ut Philip. I. v. 6. (3) Excipit Enje- dinus ad rationes pro minoris confirmatione adductas, ad primam quidem, quod unicus quo- que articulus appositus sit duobus nominibus di- versum significantibus in hoc ipso versu, τὴν μακαρίαν ἐλπίδα καὶ ἐπιφάνειαν, ut & 1. Tim. V. vers. 21. cap. VI. vers. 13. Similiter negat Soci- nus in Anti-Wujeck: regulam illam esse perpe- tuam in Graeca lingua de uno articulo unam in- ferente tantum personam, idque vel solum Era- smi, hominis, omnium judicio, linguae Graecae peritissimi, testimonium satis persuadere debere. Addit loca Matth. XXI. vers. 12. Ephes. V. vers. 5. Schlichtingius contra Meisnerum de Trinitate pag. 254. exempla haec producit in contrarium Ephes. IV. vers. 11. Matth. III. vers. 7. 16. 17. cap. XXVII. vers. 56. Ephes. II. vers. 20. cap. III. v. 5. 1. Thessal. I. vers. 8. Ebr. IX. vers. 19. (4) Ad al- teram nostram rationem excipit Enjedinus, Tit. II. vers. 11. vocem ἐπιφανείας ad Patrem re- ferri, ut & cap. III. vers. 4. (5) Socinus urget, quod vox παρουσία, quae & hic, & alibi in No- vo Testamento vulgo redditur adventus, magis proprie praesentiam significet, licet aliquando pro adventu usurpetur. (6) Non dicere Pau- lum, nos expectare adventum magni DEI, sed adventum gloriae magni DEI. DEI Patris autem gloriam venturam dici posse, cum CHRISTUS judex advenerit, Matth. XVI. v. 27. Marc. VIII. vers. 38. Schlichtingius: Duo sunt, inquit, quae apparitura expectamus, unum est gloria illius ma- gni DEI, alter est Servator noster vel CHRI- STUS. Nam ipse quidem magnus ille DEUS non apparebit, sed tantum ejus gloria cum CHRISTO, qui in gloria Patris sui venturus est: rursus vero non tantum gloria Servatoris no- stri, sive CHRISTI apparebit, sed etiam ipse Servator vel CHRISTUS. (7) Non absurdum esse, ait Socinus, si DEUS Pater venturus di- catur, cum Christus veniet, quia Christus in mundo judicando DEI Patris personam sustine- bit, Johan. V. vers. 27. Actor. XVII. vers. 31. (8) Denique obvertit quoque Socinus Ambrosium, nomen magni DEI in commentatione ad h. l. ad Deum Patrem referentem. Haec adversa- rii: Caeterum facile est singulis illis exceptioni- bus satisfacere.

Quod ad (1) jam evicimus nomen magni Dei summum Deum inferre: nec quicquam obstat, quod magnus ille DEUS se tradidisse dicatur pro nobis in mortem. Etsi enim DEUS sum- mus, qua talis, seu ratione Deitatis mortem sub- ire nequeat, potuit tamen in carne sibi perso- naliter propria subire mortem, uti etiam pro- prium sanguinem effudisse dicitur Actor. XX. vers. 28. Nulla denique est ἀκολουθία: De DEO magno dicitur, quod in mortem se tradiderit; ergo eatenus, quatenus est DEUS magnus, vel ratione Deitatis mortuus est. Quemadmodum non sequitur, quando de homine animato dici- tur, quod vulneratus sit, & contusus, ergo ra- tione animae vulneratus & contusus est.

Ad (2) Resp. Lubricum & frivolum est ar- gumentum a particula καὶ petitum, cum nihil notius ac tritius sit, quam quod adhibeatur ea- dem etiam, ubi de uno subjecto est. Num enim de duobus exponendum, verbi gratia, εὐλογητὸς ὁ θεὸς, καὶ πατὴρ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν, ob interpositam particulam καὶ, num ea satis manifesta haben- da demonstratio, alium esse DEUM, alium Patrem Domini nostri, ut alia innumera ta- ceam, non opus enim in re manifesta prolixi- tate.

Ad (3) Resp. Ordinarium tenorem Graecae linguae si respiciamus, verba Graeca τοῦ μεγάλου Θεοῦ, καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ unum idem- que subjectum inferre, testantur Graecae litera- turæ longè peritissimi, tum veteres tractatores, tum recentiores Philologi, nec diffiteri id po- tuit ipse Erasmus. Quanquam, inquit, omissus articulus in Græcis libris facit NONNIHIL pro diversa sententia μεγάλυ Θεῦ καὶ σωτῆρος. Evi- dentius distinxiffet personas, si dixisset, καὶ τῦ σω- τῆρος. Nec verò solo illo argumento ab arti- culi omissione nitimur. Sunt & alia, quæ con- junctim spectata sententiam nostram solide ad- struunt: ut non opus sit jam de contrariis exem- plis dispicere.

Ad (4) Resp. Certum, & solidum manet, vo- cem ἐπιφανείας nuspiam de Patre adhiberi. Tit. II. vers. 11. ἐπεφάνη ἡ χάρις τῦ θεῦ ἡ σωτήριος dicitur, & Tit. III. vers. 4. ὅτε δὲ ἡ χρησότης καὶ ἡ Φιλανθρωπία ἐπεφάνη τῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεῦ. Aliud autem est apparitio gratiæ DEI, & beni- gnitatis, aliud apparitio ipsius DEI. Nec est, quod regerat Enjedinus, hic etiam non ipsius DEI ἐπιφάνειαν describi, sed τῆς δόξης τῦ Θεῦ, gloriæ DEI: quia nervum jam incidit huic ob- jectioni, nam adventum gloriæ fassus est dici, quasi gloriosum adventum, unde relinquitur glo- riosum adventum DEI ipsius hic commemo- rari. Adde, quod vox ἐπιφανείας de adventu ad judicium nuspiam de DEO Patre usurpetur, semper de DEO Filio, id quod nulla ἐνςάσει infringi potest. Hic autem agitur de adventu ad judicium. Loca autem adducta manifestatio- nem gratiæ Dei in Evangelio factam respiciunt, quæ longè diversa sunt.

Ad (5) Resp. Facinus παρόραμα commisit non excusandum, quum hic non παρεσίας, sed ἐπιφανείας vox legatur. Ita scilicet cæca depra- vandi libidine abreptus fuit, ut ne Græcum qui- dem textum inspiceret, quanquam, ut Beza ob- servavit, ne παρεσίας quidem vox DEO Patri uspiam tribuatur in Novo Testamento, sed tan- tum Filio. Vid. Matth. XXIV. vers. 3. XXVII. vers. 39. 1. Corinth. XV. v. 23. 1. Thessalon. II. v. 19. III. vers. 13. IV. vers. 15. V. vers. 23. 2. Thessalon. II. vers. 1. Jac. V. vers. 7. & 8. 2. Petr. III. vers. 4. 1. Johan. II. vers. 18.

Ad (6) Resp. Adventus gloriæ magni DEI per Ebraismum receptum, idem est, atque ad- ventus gloriosus magni DEI, quod non diffite- tur, sed admittit Enjedinus. Nec dicitur uspiam Dei Patris gloria ventura, etsi CHRISTUS in Dei Patris gloria venturus dicatur; multò minus Dei Patris gloria ventura separatim dicitur, ita ut addatur etiam ipsum CHRISTUM ventu- rum. Schlichtingius verò præsupponit falsam hypothesin, quod nempe DEUS magnus ven- turus & appariturus non sit, sed tantum ejus gloria; quæ prorsus ἀσύςατα, quia magni Dei gloria ab ipso magno Deo est prorsus insepa- rabilis, ut taceam, quod venire non sit gloriæ, sed ipsius DEI gloriosi, quum id sit prædicatum personale, suppositum inferens. Et quænam ista παράφρασις: expectantes apparitionem gloriæ ma- gni DEI, in qua venturus est CHRISTUS, & Servatoris, vel Christi? Num dubium esse pote- rit Servatorem Jesum Christum appariturum, & venturum in novissimo die, supposito, quod adventura & apparitura sit gloria DEI sum- mi, eaque non aliter, quam in quantum Chri- stus in ea venturus est, apparitura sit: Quid quod ut una eademque est gloria Patris & Filii, sic & unum sint Pater & Filius τῇ ὐσίᾳ, Johann. X. vers. 30. 1. Johan. V. vers. 7. Denique apparitio in novissimo die, ubi describitur in sacris literis, non de DEO Patre, sed Filio sermo est, qui conspicuus factus est in carne, & tum in visibili forma apparebit, quemadmodum visibiliter in cœlum ascendit, de cujus apparitione visibili in nubibus, in gloria DEI Patris, & sua, passim in Scripturis, nuspiam autem de Patris appari- tione visibili in nubibus. Distinguenda ergo gloria divina, qua spectatur in DEO, & qua eadem CHRISTO homini communicata est. Non priori, sed posteriori modo tribuitur ἐπι- φάνεια gloriæ DEI in adventu CHRISTI ad judicium, quia revelabitur tum Filius hominis, veniens in nubibus cœli, cum virtute & gloria magna, Luc. XVII. vers. 3. Matth. XXIV. v. 30. Vid. Dan. VII. vers. 13. Matth. XVI. vers. 27. XIX. vers. 28. XXVI. vers. 64. Quod si autem CHRISTUS venturus est in gloria Patris, oportet eum gloria infinita & immensa prædi- tum esse, quum gloria Patris sit infinita & im- mensa gloria.

Ad (7) Resp. Fatemur, non absurdum esse, DEUM Patrem dici venturum: sed addimus nuspiam in Novo Testamento de Deo Patre, sed semper de Filio Dei adventum ad judicium & apparitionem in novissimo die efferri. Quod ita perpetuum est, ut non tantum vox ἐπιφανείας, sed etiam cognatæ unice Filio DEI vindicen- tur, utpote παρουσίας, de qua supra, Φανερώσεως Col. III. vers. 4. 1. Petr. V. v. 4. 1. Johan. II. v. 28. III. vers. 2. ut & ἀποκαλύψεως, 1. Corinth. I. v. 7. 2. Thessal. I. vers. 7. 1. Petr. I. vers. 7. 13. cap. IV. vers. 13. Non autem attendendum, quid fortè absque absurditate dici, sed quid in Scripturis dicatur, & dici consueverit. Cæterum Christum personam Dei sustinere debere in judicio extremo, nuspiam in Scripturis dicitur. Dedit DEUS Pater Christo potestatem judicium faciendi, qua est Filius hominis, Johan. V. vers. 23. & ju- dicaturus per ipsum orbem dicitur, Actor. XVII. vers. 31. At ex eo minimè sequitur, Christum solummodo personam Dei Patris sustenturum in actu judicii. Filium & Patrem unum esse Scriptura docet: Filium Patris sustinere perso- nam, non docet. Potestas Christo communi- cata est non vicaria & delegata potestas, sed ea- dem infinita & immensa potestas, quæ ipsius Pa- tris, quum eapropter honorari debeat, ut Pa- ter. Non ergò minor, vel inferior potestas esse potest, quæ parem, vel æqualem infert honorem & gloriam. Sed de his alias plenius.

Ad (8) Resp. Commentarius super Episto- las Paulinas, qui Ambrosii nomen refert, non est Ambrosii, sed alterius cujusdam, quod & stylus docet, & fatetur Antonius Possevinus Johann. Maldonatus in cap. Matth. IX. & in Johan. III. Bellarm. l. 4. de just. cap. 8. Maldo- natus Remigio Lugdunens. qui circa annum Do- mini 870. vixit, adeoque longe posterior Am- brosio fuit, adscribit eosdem Commentarios. Denique unius Ambrosii autoritas non potest præjudicare consensui plerorumque Græcorum Doctorum & sententiæ in Ecclesia receptissimæ. Atque hæc de isto argumento.

## 2:14
Verse 14.

Ὃς ἔδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν) Who Jesus devoted himself to death for our sake.

Ἵνα λυτρώσηται ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ πάσης ἀνομίας.

Namely, through the preaching of the Apostles supported by that Spirit whom CHRIST had obtained for them. See 1 Pet. I. verse 18.

That is, having purged them from vices, he might make them for himself an excellent people: עַם סְגֻלָּה Exod. XIX. v. 5, Deut. VII. v. 6, XIV. verse 2, XXVI. verse 18. It is translated λαὸς περιούσιος from περιῆναι, which means to excel, as in Plutarch's Lycurgus, τοσούτον περιῆν τῇ πόλει. Hence also περιουσιασμὸς Ps. CXXV. verse 14, Ecclesiastes II. verse 8. Most excellent of possessions. Symmachus said ἐξαίρετον for the same, as Jerome teaches us.

The Apostle has thus explained a second reason from the appearance of the glory of the Savior, which will one day be the cause of our eternal blessedness, which we await with firm and immovable hope, and with great desire, which indeed ought deservedly to excite us to observe the prescribed admonitions. He now adds a third from the satisfactory redemption of CHRIST, which at the same time illustrates the former. For that saving grace of CHRIST, which appeared to us, shone forth most of all in the redemption of CHRIST, and the end of the same, our satisfaction.

Three things are therefore to be noted here: 1. The satisfaction of CHRIST, which is expressed by the sacrificial phrase, ἔδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, he delivered himself up, namely to death for us, as Galat. II. verse 20: Christ loved me, and delivered himself up for me. Eph. V. verse 2: CHRIST loved us and παρέδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν προσφορὰν καὶ θυσίαν θεῷ εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας (delivered himself up for us as an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savor): And in verse 25: Καθὼς καὶ ὁ χριστὸς ἠγάπησε τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν, καὶ παρέδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς (Just as Christ also loved the Church, and delivered himself up for it). Roman. IV. verse 25: ὃς παρεδόθη διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα ἡμῶν (who was delivered up for our trespasses). Chap. VIII. 32: ὃς τᾶ ἰδίκ ὑἓ ἐκ ἐφείσατο, ἀλλὰ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν πάντων παρέδωκεν αὐτόν (who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all). All of which imply the satisfaction of Christ for us, that is, performed in our place and stead, and on account of the merit of our sins. See on these things copiously in Soci- nismus Profligatus. For that great God, says Crocius here in sufficiently orthodox language, provided he did not cherish the Zwinglian notion of ἀλλοιώσεως, and our Savior CHRIST JESUS gave, namely unto death, and that truly, not apparently, not compelled, but willingly made obedient to the Father. For he was not dragged to death rashly, not by the weakness of nature, not by the violence of enemies, he who gave himself. But what did he give? Not gold or silver, not calves, not another man, but himself, namely as a price, who was innocent, and could have enjoyed perpetual joy and honor, Heb. XII. verse 2. Compare Ephes. V. verse 25. 1. Timoth. II. verse 6. Elsewhere he is named flesh, John VI. verse 51. elsewhere body, Luke XXII. v. 19. blood, in the same place verse 20. Here a part is not named, but the whole CHRIST, offering, not only body, not soul, but his whole self, body and soul, GOD and man, so that all may consider the magnitude of his love. But let there be absent here also the Nestorian distraction, the Zwinglian ἀλλοίωσις, and the Piscatorian Synecdoche.

Furthermore: For whom? Not for himself, for he had no sin, but for us. The preposition 'pro' is taken in two ways; sometimes it is the same as 'vice' or 'in the place of', at other times it denotes the end. In the latter sense, he is said to have given himself for our sins, namely to be expiated, Galat. I. verse 4. Let 1. John I. verse 7, chapter II. verse 2 be compared. In the former sense, he gave himself for us, just as he is said to have suffered and died for us, that is, in our place, 1. Peter IV. verse 1. Romans V. verse 8. For us, that is, for human sinners turned away from GOD, formerly enemies under the wrath of God, the curse, the slavery of sin, established in the power of Satan, finally guilty of eternal damnation, namely whether we are men or women, free or slaves, Jews or Gentiles. We were all such, GOD willed to have mercy on all, Romans XI. verse 33. For all He gave His Son, Romans VIII. verse 32. For all CHRIST died, 2. Corinthians V. verse 19. Not only for the kinds of individuals, but also for the individuals of the kinds. See what we said on John III. verse 16. 2. CHRIST'S redemption. The end of Christ's satisfaction is λύτρωσις, our redemption, by which He Himself, as our גאל & λυτρωτὴς, redeemed us not with gold or silver, but with the precious λύτρῳ of His blood, delivering His soul εἰς λύτρον for us, Matthew XX. verse 28. Mark X. verse 45. & Himself ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων, 1. Timothy II. verse 6. He redeemed us, however, ἀπὸ πάσης ἀνομίας, from all iniquity, or rather, from all that which is adverse and contrary to the law, from all sin. For ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἡ ἀνομία, 1. John III. verse 4. namely from the guilt of every sin, because with His blood He cleanses us from all sin, 1. John I. verse 7. & He was made a propitiation for our sins, 1. John II. verse 2. and also from the dominion of sin, so that we might not be slaves of sin, but having been made free ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας, from sin, we might serve τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ, Romans VI. verse 18.

3. CHRIST'S sanctification. Another end of Christ's satisfaction is καθαρισμὸς, a purification unto a peculiar people: Which embraces the whole sanctification. For as through λύτρωσιν all men have been freed from sin, as far as concerns the acquisition of liberty, which pertains to the second article of the Christian faith concerning Redemption: So there is need of the application of this redemption according to the third article of the Apostles' Creed concerning sanctification: to which pertains the purification, which is done both by faith through the sprinkling & cleansing of the blood of CHRIST, 1. Peter I. verse 1. 1. John I. verse 7. Hebrews IX. verse 14. chapter X. v. 22. chapter XII. verse 24. Acts XV. verse 9. in our justification, and by consecration εἰς λαὸν περιούσιον in renewal. Theophylactus: By the laver of baptism, he says, & the operation and power of His divine and cleansing precepts, He makes the people both purer, and renders them familiar and acceptable. Grotius's commentary on these such great benefits of CHRIST the Savior is too meager, when he says that CHRIST devoted Himself to death only for our sake, who more correctly, when dealing with the satisfaction of CHRIST against Socinus, once explained the force of that phrase: And he thinks that λύτρωσιν is attributed to Christ through the preaching of the Apostles, because that preaching was done through the Spirit obtained for them by Christ. But that λύτρον, λύτρωσις & ἀπολύτρωσις are attributed to CHRIST in the cause of salvation in a far different way, is most testified by the scriptures, and asserted in that same treatise of Grotius. Concerning which also expressly in Socinismo Profligato. Finally, the manner of the purgation from vices done by CHRIST or the καθαρισμὸς of CHRIST is not explained by Grotius, who here preferred to foster some ὑποκλόν, rather than to profess the Catholic faith clearly. Concerning the word περιούσιος, Jerome in this place notes indeed that it was rendered by Symmachus ἐξαίρετον, that is, excellent or chief; he prefers, however, another explanation of his in another Latin volume, by which he interpreted it as peculiar. Rightly therefore, he says, CHRIST JESUS our great GOD and Savior redeemed us with His blood, that He might make for Himself a peculiar Christian people, who could then be peculiar, if they were zealous of good works. The Ambrosian also has peculiar. The word is proper to the LXX. Interpreters in this sense, in place of the Hebrew סגלה, which is proper & peculiar, rare & dear, as if someone should have a singular treasure dear above other things. Sant. Pagnin. peculium, Rab. Abr. Desirable thing. Concerning the people it occurs in Exodus XIX. verse 5. Deuteronomy VII. verse 5. chapter XIV. verse 2. chapter XXVI. verse 18. The same Hebrew word is rendered also περιβιασμὸς, possession, Psalm CXXXIV. v. 4. concerning Israel, Ecclesiasticus II. verse 8. concerning treasure: and also περιποίησις, possession, concerning the faithful, Malachi III. verse 7. The Vulgate here rendered it an acceptable people, which Beza corrects, because the Greeks call that περιουσίαν, which, when it remains over, is stored away. Therefore he rendered it peculiar. Theophylactus: What has been interpreted in Latin as acceptable, the Greeks call περιούσιον and more significantly: In such a way that a people is expressed who are occupied about the care of their Lord's substance and wealth, as one chief person chosen by the master, who is like nothing of the rest. We must not doubt, says Estius, but that the LXX. Interpreters, and the others, translating περιούσιον, wished to express that which is signified by the Hebrew word. But that is a peculium, that is, something acquired by industry, price, labor, as a proper possession. Rabbi Solomon explains it as a beloved treasure, just as Pagninus also translates it in Exodus XIX. For what one has acquired with much labor & price, that he holds dear as a treasure. Although therefore the other meanings, such as acceptable, excellent, rare, abundant or copious, are not alien to the Greek word and its derivatives, yet he who translated it peculiar expressed properly that which is in the original language. Just as Jerome himself also interpreted it in the places cited above. For there is no doubt that Paul alluded here to such places, especially since according to that which he says elsewhere: all things happened to them in a figure, 1. Corinthians X. he would not be ignorant that the ancient Israelite people, liberated by the wondrous power of GOD and singular benefit from the Egyptian servitude, and by this fact having become peculiar to GOD, was a type of the Christian people, redeemed by the death of CHRIST, and the price of His blood, and that by a far greater benefit from the Diabolical captivity, which people, therefore, as peculiar, he deservedly claims for himself.

Ζηλωτὴν καλῶν ἔργων.

קנא, that is, vehemently zealous. See concerning this word Acts XXI. verse 20, chapter XXII. verse 3, 1 Corinthians XIV. verse 2, Galatians I. verse 14.

The Vulgate rendered it 'follower', but Jerome more correctly explained the Greek Ζηλωτὴν as 'zealot', and the Ambrosian text also reads it thus. 'Do you see,' says Chrysostom, 'how works of virtue are not simply required of us?' For he added 'follower', that is, one who undertakes works of virtue with great alacrity and with huge zeal and spirit, in which matter a certain vehemence is present, which is necessary and altogether praiseworthy. For to rescue those who are oppressed by evils and languishing in despair is the property of that kindness, but the works and progress in virtue that follow are both ours and His.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Ὃς ἔδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν) Qui Jesus morti se devo- vit nostra causa.

Ἵνα λυτρώσηται ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ πάσης ἀνομίας.

Nempe per prædicationem Apostolorum fultam illo Spiritu, quem CHRISTUS ipsis impetraverat. Vide 1. Petr. I. vers. 18.

Id est, purgatos à vitiis, eos sibi faceret populum præ- stantem : עַם סְגֻלָּה Exod. XIX. v. 5. Deut. VII. v. 6. XIV. vers. 2. XXVI. vers. 18. Vertitur λαὸς περιούσιος à περιῆναι, quod est præstare, ut apud Plutarchum Lycur- go, τοσούτον περιῆν τῇ πόλει. Hinc & περιουσιασμὸς Pf. CXXV. vers. 14. Ecclesiastæ II. vers. 8. Possessionum præstantissima. Symmachus pro eodem dixit ἐξαίρετον, ut nos docet Hieronymus.
