Rationem alteram à gloriæ Servatoris appari- tione, nostræ æternæ beatitudinis causa olim futura, quam spe firma & immota, & magno cum desiderio expectamus, ita expedivit Apo- stolus, quæ scilicet nos ad observanda monita præscripta excitare merito debeat. Subjungit nunc tertiam à satisfactoria CHRISTI red- emtione, quæ illustrat simul priorem. Nam gratia illa σωτήριος CHRISTI, quæ nobis ap- paruit, illuxit maximè in CHRISTI redem- ptione, ejusdemque fine, nostri satisfactione.

Notanda ergo hic tria, 1. CHRISTI satisfactio, quæ exprimitur phrasi sacrificiali, ἔδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, tradidit semetipsum, in mortem scili- cet pro nobis, ut Galat. II. vers. 20. Christus di- lexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me. Eph. V. vers. 2. CHRISTUS dilexit nos & παρέ- δωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν προσφορὰν καὶ θυσίαν θεῷ εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας : Et versu 25. Καθὼς καὶ ὁ χριστὸς ἠγάπησε τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν, καὶ παρέδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς. Roman. IV. vers. 25. ὃς πα- ρεδόθη διὰ τὰ παραπτώματα ἡμῶν. Cap. VIII. 32. ὃς τᾶ ἰδίκ ὑἓ ἐκ ἐφείσατο, ἀλλὰ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν πάν- των παρέδωκεν αὐτόν. Quæ omnia satisfactio- nem Christi pro nobis, id est, nostri loco & vi- ce, ac propter peccatorum nostrorum meritum præstitam inferunt. Vid. de his copiose Soci- nismus Profligatus. Qui nempe magnus ille Deus, inquit Crocius hic lingua satis orthodoxa, mo- do non mentem ἀλλοιώσεως Zwinglianæ fove- ret, & Servator noster CHRISTUS JESUS dedit, scilicet in mortem, idque vere, non appa- renter, non coactus, sed volens obediens factus Pa- tri. Non enim temere, non naturæ imbecillitate, non hostium violentia ad mortem est pertractus, qui se dedit. Quid autem dedit? Non aurum argentumve, non vitulos, non alium hominem, sed semetipsum, nempe in pretium, qui erat in- nocens, & frui poterat gaudio & honore perpe- tuo, Ebr. XII. vers. 2. Confer. Ephes. V. vers. 25. 1. Timoth. II. versu 6. Alibi nominatur caro, Johan. VI. vers. 51. alibi corpus, Luc. XXII. v. 19. sanguis, ibidem vers. 20. Hic non pars nomina- tur, sed totus CHRISTUS, offerens, non tan- tum corpus, non animam, sed seipsum totum, corpus & animam, DEUM & hominem, ut considerent omnes amoris magnitudinem. Ab- sit autem hic etiam distractio Nestoriana, ἀλλοίωσις Zwingliana, & Synecdoche Piscato- riana.

Porrò: Pro quibus? Non pro se, peccatum enim non habebat, sed pro nobis. Præpositio pro dupliciter accipitur, interdum idem est, quod vi- ce seu loco, alias finem notat. Posteriori sensu dicitur dedisse semetipsum pro peccatis nostris scili- cet expiandis, Galat. I. vers. 4. Conferatur 1. Joh. I. vers. 7. cap. II. vers. 2. Priori sensu dedit semet- ipsum pro nobis, sicut pro nobis, id est, loco nostri passus & mortuus dicitur, 1. Petr. IV. versu 1. Roman. V. versu 8. Nobis, id est, hominibus peccatoribus à DEO aversis, olim inimicis sub ira Dei, maledictione, peccati servitute, potesta- te Satanæ constitutis, denique reis æternæ damna- tionis, nempe sive simus viri, sive foemina, libe- ri sive servi, Judaei sive gentiles. Omnes era- mus tales, omnium misereri voluit DEUS, Roman. XI. vers. 33. Pro omnibus dedit Filium, Roman. VIII. vers. 32. Pro omnibus mortuus est CHRISTUS, 2. Corinth. V. vers. 19. Non pro generibus tantum singulorum, sed etiam pro sin- gulis generum. Vide, quae ad Joh. III. vers. 16. diximus. 2. CHRISTI redemptio. Finis sa- tisfactionis Christi est λύτρωσις, redemptio no- stri, qua ipse, ut גאל & λυτρωτὴς noster, non auro vel argento, sed pretioso sanguinis sui λύ- τρῳ nos redemit, tradens suam animam εἰς λύ- τρον pro nobis, Matth. XX. vers. 28. Marc. X. vers. 45. & semetipsum ἀντίλυτρον ὑπὲρ πάντων, 1. Timoth. II. vers. 6. Redemit autem nos ἀπὸ πάσης ἀνομίας, ab omni iniquitate, vel potius, ab omni illo, quod legi adversum, & contra- rium est, ab omni peccato. Nam ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἡ ἀνομία, 1. Johan. III. versu 4. nimirum ab omnis peccati reatu, quia sanguine suo mundat nos ab omni peccato, 1. Johan. I. vers. 7. & pro- pitiatio factus est pro peccatis nostris, 1. Johann. II. vers. 2. nec non à peccati dominio, ut non ser- vi simus peccati, sed liberi facti ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρ- τίας, à peccato, serviamus τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ, Rom. VI. vers. 18.

3. CHRISTI sanctificatio. Alter finis sa- tisfactionis Christi est καθαρισμὸς purificatio in populum περιούσιον : Quae totam sanctificatio- nem complectitur. Nam ut per λύτρωσιν omnes homines liberati sunt à peccato, quantum ad li- bertatis acquisitionem, quae ad articulum fidei Christianae secundum de Redemptione perti- net: Ita opus est redemptionis hujus applica- tione juxta tertium Symboli Apostolici articulum de sanctificatione : ad quam pertinet purifica- tio, quae fit tum fide per aspersionem & emunda- tionem sanguinis CHRISTI, 1. Petr. I. vers. 1. 1. Johan. I. vers. 7. Ebr. IX. vers. 14. cap. X. v. 22. cap. XII. vers. 24. Actor. XV. vers. 9. in nostri justificatione, tum consecratione εἰς λαὸν περιούσιον in renovatione. Theophylactus: Per baptismi la- vacrum, inquit, & divinorum ipsius & pur- gantium praeceptorum operationem & virtutem populum & puriorem efficit, & familiarem & acceptabilem reddit. Jejunus nimis est Grotii commentarius de hisce tantis CHRISTI Sal- vatoris beneficiis, cum nostra causa tantum se devovisse morti CHRISTUM ait, qui rectius olim de satisfactione CHRISTI contra Soci- num agens vim istius phraseos exposuit : Et λύτρωσιν per Apostolorum praedicationem factam Christo ideo tribui putat, quod praedicatio ista fa- cta sit per Spiritum à Christo ipsis impetratum. Longe autem aliter λύτρον, λύτρωσις & ἀπολύ- τρωσις in causa salutis CHRISTO tribui, per scripturas testatissimum est, eodemque Grotii tractatu adsertum. De quo etiam ex professo in Socinismo Profligato. Denique modus pur- gationis à vitiis à CHRISTO factae vel καθα- ρισμᾶ CHRISTI non exponitur à Grotio, qui hic maluit ὑποκλόν τι fovere, quam fidem Ca- tholicam diserte profiteri. De voce περιούσι̇ος Hieronymus in hoc loc. notat quidem redditam eam à Symmacho ἐξαίρετον, id est, egregium vel praecipuum; praefert tamen alteram in volumine alio Latino ejus explicationem, qua peculiarem interpretatus est. Rectè igitur, inquit, CHRI- STUS JESUS magnus DEUS noster atque Salvator redemit nos sanguine suo, ut sibi Chri- stianum populum peculiarem faceret, qui peculia- ris tunc esse posset, si bonorum operum æmulator esset. Ambrosianus etiam habet peculiarem. Vox est LXX. Interpp. hoc sensu propria, lo- co Ebræi סגלה, quod est proprium & peculia- re, rarum & charum, ut si quis habeat singula- rem thesaurum præ aliis rebus charum. Sant. Pagnin. peculium, Rab. Abr. Res desiderabilis. De populo occurrit Exod. XIX. versu 5. Deute- ronom. VII. versus 5. cap. XIV. vers. 2. cap. XXVI. versu 18. Redditur eadem vox Ebræa etiam περιβιασμὸς, possessio, Psalm. CXXXIV. v. 4. de Israële, Ecclesiastic. II. vers. 8. de thesauro: necnon περιποίησις possessio de fidelibus, Malach. III. vers. 7. Vulgatus hic reddidit populum acce- ptabilem, quem castigat Beza, quod περιουσίαν vocent Græci, quod quum supersit, recondi- tur. Ideo reddidit peculiarem. Theophylactus: Quod Latine acceptabilem interpretatum est, πε- ριούσιον Græci & significantius dicunt: Perinde populus is exprimatur, qui circa Domini sui sub- stantiam curandam & opes versetur, tanquam præcipuus unus ab hero electus, qui nihil cætero- rum sit similis. Nobis non est ambigendum, in- quit Estius, quin LXX. Interpretes, ac cæteri, vertentes περιούσιον, id exprimere voluerint, quod Ebræa voce significatur. Id autem est peculium, hoc est, aliquid industria, pretio, labore compa- ratum, ut propria possessio. Rabbi Salomon expo- nit thesaurum dilectum, quomodo & vertit Pa- gninus Exod. XIX. Quod enim quis multo labore & precio comparavit, id charum habet velut the- saurum. Quamvis igitur cætera significata, ut acceptabile, egregium, rarum, abundans seu co- piosum, à Græca voce atque ejus derivatis non sint aliena, proprie tamen id, quod in originali lingua est, expressit, qui vertit peculiarem. Sicut & ipse Hieronymus interpretatus est locis citatis supra. Nam ad ejusmodi loca Paulum hic allu- sisse, nullum est dubium, præsertim cum juxta id, quod alibi dicit: omnia in figura contingebant il- lis, 1. Corinth. X. non ignoraret antiquum popu- lum Israëliticum mira DEI virtute ac singulari beneficio liberatum è servitute Ægyptiaca, & per hoc factum DEO peculiarem fuisse typum populi Christiani, morte CHRISTI, pretioque sanguinis ejus, idque beneficio longe majori redem- pti è captivitate Diabolica, quem proinde popu- lum ut peculiarem merito sibi vendicat.

Ζηλωτὴν καλῶν ἔργων.

קנא, id est, vehementer studiosum. Vide de hac voce Actor. XXI. vers. 20. cap. XXII. vers. 3. 1. Corinth. XIV. vers. 2. Galat. I. vers. 14.

Sectatorem reddidit Vulgata, sed Græcum Ζηλωτὴν rectius exposuit Hieronymus æmulato- rem, atque ita etiam legit Ambrosianus. Vides, inquit Chrysostomus, ut non simpliciter à nobis opera virtutis exigantur? Addidit nempe sectato- rem, hoc est, magna cum alacritate, atque ingen- ti studio & animo virtutis opera capessentem, qua in re vehementia quædam adsit, necesse est, omnino laudabilis. Nam eos quidem, qui ma- lis pressi sunt, atque desperabiliter languent, eri- pere, illius benignitatis est proprium, quæ vero sequuntur opera profectusque virtutis, nostra simul atque illius sunt.

## 2:15
Vers. 15.

Ταῦτα λάλει καὶ παρακάλει) Take λάλει as above in I. In the manuscript, instead of λάλει, there is δίδασκε.

Καὶ ἔλεγχε μετὰ πάσης ἐπιταγῆς.

Namely, commanding in the name of God that they abstain from sins, in the way that ἐπιταγὴ is used in 2 Corinthians II. 8.

He concludes, therefore, the present treatise with these things, and as he had required in a good Doctor διδασκαλίαν, παράκλησιν καὶ ἔλεγχον: Thus Titus, in the present, warns that he should set himself as an example to any Presbyters whatsoever. Jerome accepted παράκλησιν as consolation; but that meaning suits neither the preceding nor those things which follow, μετὰ πάσης ἐπιταγῆς. He adds, however, with authority, because, as Chrysostom warns, there are certain sins which it is necessary to restrain even with authority: and not simply with authority, but with all authority. You see, says Chrysostom, with what authority and license he arranges that these things be commanded to them. It is necessary, says Theodoret, that he who is learned in divine disciplines should not do this sluggishly and remissly, nor with any timidity, but should teach and rebuke with freedom where this is necessary. Theophylact here: Since the Cretans were difficult toward the good, he commands that he show himself harder and sharper against them. There are, however, many things which do not require austerity, but are overcome only by warnings and persuasion, as when we say that money is to be despised. But some things, which require the sharpest castigation, such as adultery, thefts, avarice, and magical arts.

Μηδείς σου περιφρονείτω.

That is, conduct yourself in such a way that you can be despised by no one. A similar warning is in 1 Timothy 4:12, where it is καταφρονείτω, which is περιφρονείτω here. The scholiast of Aristophanes on the Clouds says that περιφρονῶ is equal to καταφρονῶ.

Theophylact refers this to opportunity: when, namely, you have shown yourself austere at the right time, you will be a laughingstock to no one by rebuking. Just as, on the contrary, he who is accustomed to attack others by rebuking them at a less necessary time is wont to be held in low esteem. The interpretation of Grotius is not displeasing. Which returns to the same thing more briefly, that which the Hieronymian [interpretation] does through circumlocutions: Let no one of those who are in the Churches live in such a way, while you act sluggishly, that he thinks himself to be better. For what kind of edification will there be for a disciple if he understands himself to be greater than his master? Which sense he had succinctly rendered in the parallel passage, 1 Timothy 4: 'Let no one despise your youth,' that is, I do not want you to show yourself such that you can be deservedly despised by anyone. Nevertheless, the interpretation of those who press the literal meaning is to be preferred. It is indeed certain, says Crocius, that authority is gained for a Doctor by the integrity of his morals, and his doctrine is rendered more pleasing. Life gives authority to doctrine, says Primasius. But the very sound of the words shows that it is prescribed not so much what Titus ought to do, as what others ought not to do. Some, therefore, think that account should be taken of age, as with Timothy, whose youth ought not to be despised. I would prefer to take it thus, that the Apostle is addressing not so much Titus as the whole Cretan Church, and ordains that, since he is commanded to combat vices and errors, but to defend truth and piety, and that gravely, no one ought to be so prodigal of his own salvation as to spurn either the person of Titus or the office which he discharges, or to prefer himself to him as if he were better and more worthy. Regarding the word περιφρονείτω, I am pleased with what Jerome brings from the adage: Περιφρόνησις sounds that, when someone, trusting in himself, [thinks] himself to be better than another, despises him whom he thinks to be inferior, and, being 'over,' that is, wiser, thinks the humbler person to be worthy of contempt. Something of this sort, swelling with the vanity of pride and despising the very heaven and sun, is mocked as having been said by someone among the Greeks. Ἀεροβατῶ καὶ περιφρονῶ τὸν ἥλιον, which we can say in Latin: I walk through the air, and I know myself to be of more value than the Sun.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Ταῦτα λάλει καὶ παρακάλει) Sume λάλει ut supra I. In Manuscripto pro λάλει est δίδασκε.

Καὶ ἔλεγχε μετὰ πάσης ἐπιταγῆς.

Nempe imperans Dei nomine, ut à peccatis absti- neant, quomodo ἐπιταγὴ sumitur 2. Cor. II. 8.

Concludit ergo hisce præsentem tractatio- nem, & ut in bono Doctore requisiverat διδα- σκαλίαν, παράκλησιν καὶ ἔλεγχον: Ita exemplo seie sistat Presbyteris quibusvis Titus, in præ- senti monet. Hieronymus de consolatione πα- ράκλησιν accepit; sed ea significatio nec superio- ribus convenit, nec iis, quæ sequuntur, μετὰ πάσης ἐπιταγῆς. Cum imperio autem addit, quia monente Chrysostomo, sunt quædam peccata, quæ etiam imperiis arcere oportet: neque sim- pliciter cum imperio, sed cum omni imperio. Vides, inquit Chrysostomus, quanta cum auto- ritate atque licentia hæc illis imperanda dispo- nat. Oportet, inquit Theodoretus, eum, qui est in divinis disciplinis eruditus, non ignave ac re- misse, nec cum ulla timiditate hoc facere, sed cum libertate docere, atque increpare, ubi hoc opus est. Theophylactus hic: Cum essent Cretenses ad bonum difficiles, ut duriorem se & acrem ad- versus hos præbeat, mandat. Sunt autem ple- raque, quæ austeritate non indigent, sed monitis tantum & persuasione vincuntur, ut cum dici- mus, contemnendas esse pecunias. Nonnulla ve- ro, quæ acerrima egent castigatione, quemadmo- dum adulterium, furta, avaritia, & magicæ artes.

Μηδείς σου περιφρονείτω.

Id est, ita te gere, ut à nemine contemni possis. Si- milis monitio 1. Timoth. IV. vers. 12. ubi καταφρονείτω, quod hic περιφρονείτω. Scholiastes Aristophanis ad Ne- bulas περιφρονῶ ait ἴσον esse τῷ καταφρονῶ.

Theophylactus id ad opportunitatem refert: Cum opportune scilicet austerum te exhibueris, objurgando nemini eris derisui. Ut contra solet, qui minus necessario tempore alios increpando in- cesserit, parvi fieri. Non displicet Grotiana interpretatio. Quæ eodem brevius redit, quòd Hieronymiana per anfractus: Nemo eorum, qui in Ecclesiis sunt, te segniter agente sic vivat, ut se putet meliorem esse. Qualis enim ædificatio erit discipuli, si se intelligat magistro esse majorem. Quem sensum in loco parallelo, 1. Timoth. IV. succincte ita reddiderat: Nemo adolescentiam tuam contemnat, id est, nolo te talem exhibeas, ut possis ab aliquo merito contemni. Præferenda tamen eorum interpretatio, qui τὸ ῥητὸν pre- munt. Certum quidem est, inquit Crocius, mo- rum integritate Doctori autoritatem conciliari, & doctrinam reddi gratiorem. Autoritatem do- ctrinæ facit vita, inquit Primasius. Verum so- nus ipse verborum ostendit, præscribi non tam, quid Titus facere debeat, quam quid alii facere non debeant. Aliqui ergo ætatis haberi rationem censent, ut ad Timotheum, cujus juventus con- temni non debeat. Ego sic accipere malim, quod Apostolus non tam Titum, quam totam Creten- sem Ecclesiam alloquatur, & sanciat, cum ille vitia & errores debellare, veritatem autem atque pietatem, idque graviter, tueri sit jussus, nemi- nem salutis suæ tam prodigum esse debere, ut aspernetur sive Timothei personam sive officium, quo fungatur, aut se illi tanquam meliorem & di- gniorem anteferat. De voce περιφρονείτω pla- cet, quod ex adagio Hieronymus affert: Περι- φρόνησις illud sonat, cum quis confidens sibi, se alio esse meliorem, despicit eum, quem inferiorem pu- tat, & super, id est, plus sapiens, humiliorem existimat dignum esse contemptu. Tale quid in- tumescens superbiæ vanitate, & cœlum ipsum so- lemque despiciens apud Græcos quidam dixisse de- luditur. Ἀεροβατῶ καὶ περιφρονῶ τὸν ἥλιον, quod nos Latine possumus dicere: Seando per aërem, & pluris me novi esse, quam Solem.

## 3:1 Argument
PART II. THE PARENETIC EPISTLE. CHAPTER III. AND LAST. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He exhorts Titus concerning the admonishing of any persons whatsoever to render obedience to the Magistrate, and to perform any good works, by a comparison of the former state before regeneration and the modern state after regeneration and the renewal made through baptism: And that he should propose the doctrine concerning divine grace in justification and salvation in such a way that he may at the same time remind them of good works, and avoid useless questions, and heretics who do not know how to be corrected. Finally, he solicits Titus to come to him, and with salutations added, he seals the epistle with a vow.

There are three parts: I. The exhortation of Titus concerning those things of which the regenerate ought to be warned, up to verse 7. II. The admonition of the same concerning the doctrine to be chiefly handed down, and concerning the fleeing of empty questions and heretics, up to verse 11. III. The solicitation concerning his arrival, up to verse 15. Whoever desires a dichotomy may say that other things concern others, and are common, up to verse 11. Other things concern Titus, which namely pertained to that time and the present state, which especially demanded the arrival of Titus.

PART I. The exhortation of Titus concerning those things of which the regenerate ought to be warned.

Verse 1. Ὑπομίμνησκε αὐτὸς.

See 2 Timothy 2:14. He wishes the Cretans to be warned about those things of which they were most in need.

To be subject to principalities and powers.

Here ὑποτάσσεσθαι is again used as in 2:9. He calls governors ἐξουσίας. But Ἀρχὰς are τὰς ὑπερεχούσας ἐξουσίας, as he speaks in Romans 13:1. In like manner, the Apostle here distinguishes βασιλείας, that is, Emperors, and τὰς ἐν ὑπεροχῇ ὄντας. Peter, however, distinguishes kings and governors, 1 Peter 2:14. Thus the King is called ראש by the Hebrews, as in Ezekiel 38:21. Crete was always very seditious.

To obey.

To comply with authorities. See Acts 5:29.

Jerome gives this as the reason for the admonition: because the dogma of Judas the Galilean was still flourishing at that time and had many followers, [who held] that no one ought to be called Lord except God alone, and that those who brought tithes to the temple should not pay tribute to Caesar.

To be ready for every good work.

Contrary to those who were affected as they were, of whom [it is spoken] above in 2:16. Ἑτοίμους, נכונים, well prepared. In the Glossary: Ἕτοιμος, ready, prepared.

Jerome wishes this to be added, as does Theodoret, that Princes are to be obeyed only in those things which are good, which also pleases Estius, and indeed even Baldwin. Theophylact: That those who are prone to evil should less obey the commands of Princes. But it is properly a peculiar rule, by which the reborn are commanded to be reminded of beneficence, as some please: or rather to any good whatsoever. By a hypothesis, says the Blessed Hunnius, he subjoins a thesis, and to a special precept a general one, by which he wishes men converted to the faith of the Gospel to be with instructed minds and duties for every good work, by whatever name it may come. And he illustrates this by the contention of vices opposed to good works.

Latin:

PARS II. EPISTOLÆ PARÆNETICA. CAPUT III. ET ULTIMUM. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Hortatur Titum de admonendis quibusvis ad obsequia Magistratui præstanda, & quævis opera bona, comparatione status pristini ante regenerationem, & moder- ni post regenerationem & renovatio- nem per baptismum factam : Et ut do- ctrinam de gratia divina in justifica- tione & salute ita proponat, ut simul de bonis operibus commonefaciat, & vi- tet quæstiones inutiles, & hæreticos cor- rigi nescios. Denique solicitat Titum, ut ad se veniat, & additis salutationibus voto obsignat epistolam.

Partes tres sunt: I. Adhortatio Titi de iis, quæ renati moneri debeant, ad vers. 7. II. Com- monitio ejusdem de doctrina præcipue tradenda, & de fugiendis inanibus quæstionibus & hæreticis, ad vers. 11. III. Solicitatio de adventu, ad v. 15. Qui διχοτομίαν desiderat, alia dicat concerne- re alios, & communia esse, usque ad vers. 11. Alia Titum, quæ scilicet ad tempus illud, & præsentem statum pertinebant, qui imprimis Titi adventum postulabat.

PARS I. Adhortatio Titi de iis, quæ renati moneri debeant.

Vers. 1. Ὑπομίμνησκε αὐτὸς.

Vide 2. Timoth. II. vers. 14. De eis vult moneri Cre- tas, quorum maxime indigebant.

Ἀρχαῖς καὶ ἐξουσίαις ὑποτάσσεσθαι.

Rursum hic ὑποτάσσεσθαι sumitur, ut II. 4. 9. Ἐξουσίας vocat Præsides. Ἀρχὰς autem τὰς ὑπερεχούσας ἐξουσίας, ut loquitur Roman. XIII. vers. 1. Pari modo distinguit hic Apostolus βασιλείας, id est, Imperatores, & τὰς ἐν ὑπεροχῇ ὄντας. Petrus vero βασιλέας & ἡγεμόνας, 1. Petr. II. 14. Sic Rex dicitur ראש Ebræis, ut Ezech. XXXIIX. vers. 21. Valde seditiosa semper fuit Creta.

Πειθαρχεῖν.

Imperiis obtemperare. Vide Actor. V. vers. 29.

Hieronymus causam admonitionis hanc red- dit, quod Judæ Galilæi per tempus illud dogma adhuc viguerit, & plurimos sectatores habuerit, nullum debere Dominum, nisi solum DEUM vocari, & eos, qui ad templum decimas affer- rent, Cæsari tributum non reddere.

Πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἑτοίμους εἶναι.

Contra affectos, quam illi erant, de quibus supra II. 16. Ἑτοίμους נכונים, bene paratos. In Glossario: Ἕτοιμος, paratus, præparatus.

Addi hoc vult Hieronymus, ut & Theodore- tus, quod in iis tantum, quæ bonà sunt, obe- diendum Principibus sit, quod & Estio pla- cet, imo & Balduino. Theophylactus : Quod qui ad malum prompti sunt, Principum juf- sis minus obtemperent. Est autem proprie pe- culiaris regula, qua ad beneficentiam commo- nefieri jubeantur renati, ut nonnullis placet: vel potius ad quodvis bonum. Hypothesi, in- quit Beatus Hunnius, subjungit thesin, & spe- ciali præcepto generale, quo vult homines ad fidem Evangelii conversos instructis animis & officiis es- se ad omne bonum opus, quocunque nomine id ve- niat. Idque vitiorum operibus bonis oppositorum contentione illustrat.

## 3:2
Ver. 2. Μηδένα βλασφημεῖν.

That they should speak evil of no one. Thus that word is taken in Matt. XXVII. verse 39. Mark XV. verse 29. Luke XXIII. verse 39. Acts XIII. verse 45. chapter XVIII. verse 6. Romans III. verse 8. 1. Corinthians IV. verse 13. chapter X. verse 30. 2. Peter II. verse 10. The Hebrews say גִדֵּף: And so here the Syrian.

Theophylact also took blasphemy as speaking evil against one's neighbor: Indeed, I would also wish you to warn them, that they should not assail anyone with curses, not even him who habitually does evil. For it is necessary that our mouth be kept immune from any abuse. Which even if it is rightly brought, it is nevertheless no concern of ours to judge others: But if it is an injury, it is permitted to foresee what great danger may hang over us from it.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Μηδένα βλασφημεῖν.

Ut nemini maledicant. Sic vox ista sumitur Matth. XXVII. versu 39. Marc. XV. versu 29. Luc. XXIII. versu 39. Actorum XIII. versu 45. cap. XVIII. versu 6. Roman. III. versu 8. 1. Corinth. IV. vers. 13. cap. X. vers. 30. 2. Petr. II. vers. 10. Ebræi dicunt גִדֵּף : Et ita hic Syrus.

Blasphemiam etiam de maledicentia in pro- ximum accepit Theophylactus : Quin etiam mo- neas velim, ut neminem maledictis incessant, nec eum quidem, qui factitet mala. Est enim ne- cesse, ut à quovis convicio os nostrum immune servetur. Quod vel si jure infertur, nihil ta- men interest nostra alios judicare : At si inju- ria, licet prospicere, quam summum ex eo nobis impendat discrimen.

## 3:3
Ἀμάχυς εἶναι) 1. Timothy III. v. 3. Ἐπιεικεῖς) Ibid. Πᾶσαν ἐνδεικνυμένυς πραότητα πρὸς πάντας ἀνθρώπυς.

Not only against those who share the faith, but also against those who contradict it. We have already spoken about the word ἐνδείκνυσθαι in 2. Timothy IV. verse 14. above II. 10. Πᾶσαν πραότητα, that is, the highest gentleness. See Ephesians I. verse 8. Colossians I. verse 9. 1. Timothy I. verse 15.

We are children of peace, says Jerome, and we wish peace to rest upon us, and we have approached the heavenly Jerusalem, which received its name from peace, let us have peace with those who hate peace, and, as much as is in us, let us be at peace with all men: not only with the modest, but also with the quarrelsome: because there is no virtue in bearing with the gentle: and let us give place to wrath, showing all gentleness to all men, not that we ought to show ourselves gentle to all men out of a desire for vain glory, but while we bear with all, and do not repay injury for injury, the works themselves become known to all. Someone may, because of boasting and the opinion of the common people, simulate gentleness before some, and feign goodness. But where there is no true and genuine and solid gentleness, I do not know whether it can be persuaded to all that he is gentle. Moreover, he exhibits all gentleness toward them, not he who nowhere applies severity, but he who, having observed the circumstances of place, time, and persons, fails in no part of the duty of this virtue, observing also the precept of Christ: do not resist evil, Matt. V. Furthermore, the Blessed Hunnius rightly warned: Just as he opposed these mentioned vices generally to the zeal for good works: so he contends with the virtues directly opposed to the vices with an elegant antithesis. For to the disease of evil-speaking he opposes ἐπιείκειαν or equity, to the desire for fighting he opposes πραότητα or gentleness: by the cultivation of which virtues those vices can easily be overthrown. He says therefore: But human. In Greek it is ἐπιεικεῖς. By which word is noted equity opposed to excessive rigor in judging and criticizing anything. Showing all gentleness. As much, that is, as piety permits. For sometimes the reason of duty compels one to be severe. Which severity itself, however, in rebuking should be so tinged with gentleness, that it may be clear that we hate the vices of persons, not the persons themselves.

Ver. 3. Ἦμεν γάρ ποτε καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀνόητοι.

This pertains to tolerating those who contradict the faith. We too were such, he says. A regard for ourselves will make us more moderate, if we have consulted ourselves, says Seneca on anger II. 28. When Paul says ἡμεῖς, he does not so much understand himself as those who had been called from the Gentiles, through a κοίνωσιν sufficiently familiar to him, and not too forced, since all Christians are members of one body. Such is that of Brutus to Cicero: But if we had remembered that we are Romans. But he calls them ἀνοήτους, not understanding divine things: for it is about these things that it is treated here. See Luke XXIV. 25. Romans I. 24.

Why does the Apostle not also count himself, without a figure of speech, among the τοῖς ἀνοήτοις before his conversion? For there was indeed in him a zeal for the law, but not according to knowledge. Does not, says Jerome, Paul seem to you to have been foolish, when he had zeal, but not according to knowledge, and was persecuting the Church, or could he have any virtues without the virtue of GOD Christ Jesus? Or to extinguish the burning flame of desires: when he was not a temple of GOD? But what greater malice or envy can there be, than to take up letters against those who are absent, and everywhere to devastate the disciples of Christ? To be unwilling for him to be saved, and to envy others who could be saved? To hate Christians and consequently to deserve hatred from all. But what greater error, and disobedience or madness, than after the day has breathed again, and the shadows have passed, to wish to keep the abolished law and to say: Do not handle, do not touch, do not taste, and while solid and manly food is appearing, to desire to be fed with the milk of infancy. Here is commonly described the state of the unregenerate, in whom reign ignorance, incredulity, various errors in the mind, and desires of manifold pleasures in the will, whose life also was led by malice and envy, and these were almost taken for life, whence we were worthy of hatred, inasmuch as we also pursued one another with hatred. The Apostle wished here, as Estius admits, to declare what kind of men those are who are not yet illuminated by the faith of Christ, and that there is no one who does not first serve desires, although not all are addicted to the same ones, nor equally. B. Hunnius gives this connection: We ought not to be too rigid censors of the vices of others. For we also formerly, when we were still ignorant of Christ, were subject to various sins. He wishes the impious to be called foolish, who, deprived of the saving knowledge of God and Christ, and void of the fear of God (which is the beginning of wisdom), are ruled by their own affections, and relish nothing but earthly and carnal things, and without any fear of the Divine Being rush into sins of every kind, ignorant of the punishments which they are hastening upon themselves, both temporal and eternal. For such people, in their stupidity, surpass the most dull-witted fools by many parasangs, so that this is a genus of spiritual folly, which the Apostle later unfolds more deeply through the explanation of its species.

Ἀπειθεῖς) Not even obedient to those laws of God which are called natural, and which human society requires.

Πλανώμενοι) Those are called πλανᾶσθαι in a special sense who worship idols, Deut. IV. 19. XXX. 17. נדחים.

This explanation is more restricted. For GOD has shut up all εἰς ἀπείθειαν (in disobedience), that he might have mercy on all, Romans XI. verse 32. Ephesians II. verse 23, ὑοὶ τῆς ἀπειθείας (sons of disobedience) not converted. Nor are only πλανώμενοι (those wandering) understood here, who worship idols, but those infected with any errors whatsoever. For generally, as we have said, the state of the unregenerate is described, such as we are before conversion: Wandering from the truth of GOD, from the way of righteousness, from the path of eternal life: Because we are ignorant of Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life, immersed in errors, idolatry, and the deadly darkness of ignorance. We were wandering as much in the way of morals as of doctrine, Isaiah LIII.

Δουλεύοντες ἐπιθυμίαις καὶ ἡδοναῖς ποικίλαις (Serving various lusts and pleasures).

That is, ἐπιθυμίαις ἡδονῶν (with the lusts of pleasures). Δουλεύοντες (serving) means addicted, enslaved, in the way we had δεδουλωμένοι (enslaved) above II. 3. Add what is in Matthew VI. verse 24, Romans VI. verse 6.

The word for serving is emphatic, by which Paul denotes the exquisite zeal with which they were entirely carried away, and were seized by a certain impulse toward carnal pleasures. To these they were intensely devoted. To these they served uniquely, and while they wished to wander freely with unbridled license, they greedily bound themselves with the chains of a most miserable servitude, namely, to depraved desires, as here Blessed Hunnius.

Ἐν κακίᾳ καὶ φθόνῳ διάγοντες (Living in malice and envy).

See Romans I. verse 29. Διάγοντες (living) is a brief expression. For βίον (life) is understood, which you have explained in 1 Timothy II. verse 2. Thus διάγειν ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ (to live in quietness), διάγειν ἡδέως (to live pleasantly) are frequent among the Greeks.

Malice for the Apostle is the desire to harm one's neighbor; envy is a malignant disease of the soul, by which one envies the prosperous fortunes of a neighbor.

Στυγητοὶ (Hateful).

Worthy of hatred. For verbal adjectives of this kind have such a meaning: And thus Jerome interprets ἀγαπητὸν (beloved) as worthy of love in his Commentaries on Philemon.

Μισοῦντες ἀλλήλους (Hating one another) Mutually hostile, in the manner of wild beasts. See 1 John II. verse 9.

Depraved desires look to the internal motions of the soul, the rest seem to be referred to external acts. For when depraved desires break out into action, malice is formed, which is joined with προαιρέσει (purpose) and seeks the harm of the neighbor. A notable species of this is envy, which grieves because of a neighbor's happiness. The fruit of this is the hatred of others, whom they ought to love, whence they also make themselves worthy of hatred.

Latin:

Ἀμάχυς εἶναι) 1. Timoth. III. v. 3. Ἐπιεικεῖς) Ibidem. Πᾶσαν ἐνδεικνυμένυς πραότητα πρὸς πάντας ἀνθρώπυς.

Non tantum adversus fidei consortes, sed etiam ad- versus contradictores. De voce ἐνδείκνυσθαι jam diximus 2. Timoth. IV. vers. 14. supra II. 10. Πᾶσαν πραότητα, id est, summam lenitatem. Vide Ephes. I. vers. 8. Coloff. I. vers. 9. 1. Timoth. I. vers. 15.

Filii sumus pacis, inquit Hieronymus, & volumus super nos pacem requiescere, & accessi- mus ad Hierusalem cœlestem, qua ex pace no- men accepit, cum his, qui oderunt pacem, ha- beamus pacem, &, quantum in nobis est, cum omnibus hominibus pacati simus : non solum cum modestis, sed etiam cum rixosis : quia nulla vir- tus est ferre mansuetos : locumque demus iræ, omnem ostendentes mansuetudinem ad omnes ho- mines, non quod vana gloria desiderio nos esse mansuetos omnibus hominibus ostendere debea- mus, sed dum omnes ferimus, & injuriæ vicem non rependimus, ipsa opera notiora universis fi- ant. Potest aliquis ob jactantiam & opinionem vulgi quamque popularem simulare apud quos- dam mansuetudinem, & fingere bonitatem. Sed ubi non est vera & genuina & solida mansuetu- do, nescio, an eum esse mansuetum possit omnibus persuaderi. Omnem autem erga eos mansue- tudinem exhibet, non qui nusquam severita- tem adhibet, sed qui servatis circumstantiis lo- ci, temporis, personarum ab hujus virtutis of- ficio nulla parte deficit, Christi etiam præce- ptum observans : non resistite malo, Matth. V. Cæterum recte monuit Beatus Hunnius : Sicut generatim modo bonorum operum studio memo- rata hæc vitia opposuit : sic cum vitiis virtutes directe oppositas eleganti antitheto contendit. Nam maledicentiæ morbo ἐπιείκειαν seu æquita- tem pugnandi cupiditati πραότητα mansuetudi- nem opponit : quarum virtutum cultu vitia illa facile profligari possint. Dicit ergo: Sed huma- ni. In Græco-est ἐπιεικεῖς. Quâ voce notatur æquitas nimio rigori censendi & carpendi quævis opposita. Omnem exhibentes mansuetudinem. Quantum scilicet pietas permittit. Interdum enim officii ratione cogit esse severos. Quæ ipsa tamen severitas in redarguendo sic tincta sit man- suetudine, ut pateat nos odisse vitia personarum, non personas ipsas.

Vers. 3. Ἦμεν γάρ ποτε καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀνόητοι.

Hoc pertinet ad tolerandos eos, qui fidei contradi- cunt. Fuimus & nos tales, inquit, Faciet nos modera- tiores respectus nostri, si consuluerimus nos, ait Seneca de ira II. 28. Cum dicit Paulus ἡμεῖς, non tam se intel- ligit, quam eos, qui ex gentibus vocati erant, per κοί- νωσιν satis ipsi familiarem, neque nimium obtortam, cum Christiani omnes unius corporis membra sint. Tale il- lud Bruti ad Ciceronem: Quod si Romanos nos esse me- minissemus. Ἀνοήτους autem vocat non intelligentes re- rum divinarum: nam de iis rebus hic agitur. Vide Luc. XXIV. 25. Roman. I. 24.

Cur non se accenseat etiam Apostolus ci- tra figuram dicendi τοῖς ἀνοήτοις ante conversio- nem? Nam erat quidem in illo zelus legis, sed non secundum scientiam. Annon, inquit Hieronymus, Paulus vobis videtur fuisse stultus, quando habebat zelum, sed non secundum scien- tiam, & persequebatur Ecclesiam, aut ullas po- terat habere virtutes sine virtute DEI Christi Jesu? aut æstuantem flammam restinguere volu- ptatum: cum non esset templum DEI? Quæ au- tem major potest esse malitia aut invidia, quam contra absentes epistolas sumere, & ubique Christi vastare discipulos? Nolle ipsum salvum fieri, & cæteris, qui salvi esse poterant, invidere? Odisse Christianos & consequenter ab omnibus odium pro- mereri. Quis autem major error, & inobedientia aut vecordia, quam postquam respiravit dies, & præterierunt umbræ legem abolitam velle servare & dicere: Ne attrectaveris, ne contigeris, ne gu- staveris, & apparente solido cibo & virili, infan- tiæ lacte cupere potari. Describitur autem hic communiter status non renatorum, in quibus re- gnant ignorantia, incredulitas, errores varii in mente, concupiscentiæ voluptatum multiplicium in voluntate, quorum etiam vita agebatur mali- tia & invidia, & hæc fere pro vita ducebantur, unde digni odio eramus, utpote qui & nos in- vicem odio persequebamur. Voluit hic Apo- stolus, fatente Estio, declarare, quales sint ho- mines, fide Christi nondum illuminati, nec quenquam esse, qui prius cupiditatibus non ser- viat, tametsi nec omnes iisdem, nec æqualiter addicti sint. B. Hunnius hanc reddit συνέχειαν: Non debemus esse nimis rigidi censores in aliorum vitia. Nam & nos quondam, cum adhuc Chri- stum ignoraremus, eramus variis peccatis obnoxii. Stultos autem vocari vult impios, qui salvifica agni- tione Dei & Christi orbati, & timore Dei, (qui sapientiæ initium est) vacui, suis affectibus regun- tur, & nihil nisi terrena carnaliaque sapiunt, ac sine omni metu Numinis ruunt in omnis generis peccata, nescii pænarum, quas sibi temporales & æternales accelerant. Tales enim stoliditate quos- vis stupidissimos moriones multis parafangis an- tecedunt, ut hoc stultitiæ spiritualis vitium ge- nus sit, quod postea specierum explicatione pe- nitius evolvat Apostolus.

Ἀπειθεῖς) Ne illis quidem Dei legibus obsequentes, quæ naturales dicuntur, & quas societas humana exigit.

Πλανώμενοι) πλανᾶσθαι dicuntur eximie illi, qui colunt idola, Deut. IV. 19. XXX. 17. נדחים.

Restrictior hæc explicatio. Nam omnes conclu- sit DEUS εἰς ἀπείθειαν, ut omnium misereretur, Roman. XI. vers. 32. Ephes. II. vers. 23. ὑοὶ τῆς ἀπειθείας non conversi. Nec tantum πλανώ- μενοι hic intelliguntur, qui idola colunt, sed qui- buscunque erroribus infecti. Nam generaliter, ut diximus, status non renatorum describitur, qua- les simus ante conversionem: Errantes à verita- te DEI, à via justitiæ, ab æternæ vitæ semita: Quia Christum, qui via, veritas, & vita; ignora- mus, immersi erroribus, idololatriæ, & lethi- feris ignorantiæ tenebris. Eramus errantes tam in via morum, quam doctrinæ, Es. LIII.

Δουλεύοντες ἐπιθυμίαις καὶ ἡδοναῖς ποικίλαις.

Id est ἐπιθυμίαις ἡδονῶν. Δουλεύοντες addicti, mancipati, quomodo δεδουλωμένοι habuimus supra II. 3. Adde, quod Matth. VI. vers. 24. Roman. VI. vers. 6.

Serviendi vox emphatica est, qua Paulus ex- quisitum studium notat, quo toti ferebantur, & quodam rapiebantur impetu ad voluptates carna- les. His impense erant dediti. His serviebant uni- ce, & dum effreni licentia vagari libere volebant, cupide se alligabant tristissimæ servitutis vinculis, videlicet desideriis pravis, ut hic B. Hunnius.

Ἐν κακίᾳ καὶ φθόνῳ διάγοντες.

Vid. Roman. I. vers. 29. Διάγοντες est brevis loquutio. Subauditur enim βίον, quod expositum habes 1. Timoth. II. vers. 2. Sic διάγειν ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ, διάγειν ἡδέως frequentia apud Græcos.

Malitia Apostolo est studium nocendi pro- ximo; invidia malignus animi morbus, quo proximi fortunæ secundæ invidetur.

Στυγητοὶ.

Digni odio. Nam talem sensum habent verbalia ejus- modi: Et sic ἀγαπητὸν dignum amore interpretatur Hie- ronymus in Commentariis ad Philemonem.

Μισοῦντες ἀλλήλους) Mutuo infesti, ferarum more. Vid. 1. Joh. II. vers. 9.

Concupiscentiæ pravæ ad internos animi motus spectant, cætera ad externos actus referenda vi- dentur. Quando enim desideria prava in ner- vum erumpunt, fit malitia, quæ cum προαιρέσει conjuncta est, & proximi damnum quærit. In- signis ejus species est invidia, quæ dolet ob pro- ximi felicitatem. Hujus fructus est aliorum odium, quos amare deberent, unde & seipsos odio dignos faciunt.

## 3:4
Verse 4. Ὅτε δὲ ἡ χρηστότης καὶ ἡ φιλανθρωπία ἐπεφάνη τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεοῦ (But when the kindness and the love of God our Savior appeared).

This same χρηστότης καὶ φιλανθρωπία Θεοῦ [kindness and love for mankind of God], which is just now χάρις Θεοῦ [grace of God], II. 11. There is also here a καὶ rursus ἐξηγητικόν [an explanatory 'and' again]. For the general noun χρηστότης is explained by the more specific φιλανθρωπία, just as the Rabbis are accustomed to say טובה וחעלתי. Plutarch also notes that God is not called Φίλιππος [lover of horses], but φιλάνθρωπος [lover of mankind]. See Psalm VIII. verse 5. Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεοῦ [of our Savior God], as above II. v. 10.

There is no reason why we should consider χρηστότητα & Φιλανθρωπίαν as synonyms. They are more correctly distinguished, as our blessed Hunnius explains them thus: He calls it χρηστότητα or goodness. But God would have remained immutably good if He had not shown Himself especially kind to us sinners, but had left us in misery according to the rigor of justice, just as the fallen Angels. But now, to illustrate His goodness, this certain addition, as it were, comes as a heap, because He is not only good, considered within Himself with a certain immutable goodness, but He also opens the fountain of that goodness of His to us men, so that He is now χρηστὸς to us, usefully good, while He brings forth eternal benefits to us from the treasures of His goodness. The other word is Φιλανθρωπία. Which, as the Latin language cannot render with one word, so no human power of eloquence is able to attain its emphasis. It designates, however, that admirable love by which the eternal God deigns to favor with His heavenly grace mortal man, the Creator the needy creature, justice and holiness itself miserable sinners, and even His own enemies, and with all memory of offenses completely erased, He establishes a grace of ἀμνησίαν [oblivion] joined with a perpetual zeal for doing good. By the word τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεοῦ [of our Savior God] most understand God the Father: yet some explicitly understand it of the Son of God, who elsewhere always comes by this name in the New Testament, to whom also that ἐπιφάνεια [manifestation], χρηστότης [kindness], & Φιλανθρωπία [love for mankind] eminently belongs, which shone forth first in the work of redemption to all men, and afterwards also shines forth in the work of sanctification, illumination, regeneration, & renovation, where we are made actual participants of the redemption accomplished through Christ. Which explanation did not displease Bernard, sermon I on the nativity. of the Lord: Power had appeared before in the creation of things, wisdom appeared in their governance; but kindness and mercy have now appeared most of all in humanity. And sermon I on the Epiphany. Before humanity appeared, kindness lay hidden. Theophylact among the Greeks agrees with this, paraphrasing it thus: When the kindness & humanity of our Savior God appeared, that is, when the Only-begotten was incarnate, & was made like unto us. Estius says it is clear from the following words that these things are said of the Father, because it is added that God poured out upon us abundantly the Holy Spirit through Jesus Christ our Savior, which cannot be understood of any other than the Father. But why not? Does not the Son also pour out the Holy Spirit upon us? But that it is said here to be poured out through Jesus Christ our Savior, by that it is only noted that this outpouring was acquired for us by the merit of Christ. Christ is also the primary Efficient cause with the Father by reason of theology, insofar as He is the same God with the Father, and the meritorious cause, by reason of the economy, insofar as He is our Mediator, the God-man, God and man. This phrase, says Estius later, 'through Jesus Christ,' signifies the meritorious cause both in the Pauline Epistles and in the prayers of the Church. Therefore the sense is: that Christ as man by His passion merited for us the abundance of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which we are renewed. For the same reason He calls Christ our Savior, because, to be sure, our entire salvation from the beginning of faith to the consummation of glory is from His merit. These things could be the more attributed to Estius, since he constitutes Christ as our Mediator only according to His human nature. But because in the Scriptures, when God is said to save through God, when the Lord is said to do something by the Lord or through the Lord, as here the Savior God is said to pour out the Holy Spirit through the Savior Christ, a distinction of persons is indicated, it is better to acquiesce in the common explanation, which is handed down by the great consensus of the ancients and moderns, and flows from the words themselves, that God the Father causes His kindness & Φιλανθρωπία [love for mankind] to shine upon us in the business of our conversion, whose χρηστότης [kindness] is celebrated in Rom. II. 4, XI. 22, Eph. II. 7, as also His love toward the human race, John III. 16, 1 John IV. 16, Rom. V. 8, and also ἔλεος [mercy] or pity in the ἐπιφανείᾳ [manifestation] of the sunrise from on high upon those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death, Luke I. 78, 79, & v. 50, 51, 52, in calling & conversion, Rom. XV. 9, in salvation, Eph. II. 4, and regeneration, 1 Peter I. 3, and that according to His mercy He saved us, of which grace, love, and mercy and kindness of the same, with a great abundance of words Paul [speaks] Eph. II. 4. 5. 7. 8. and that he pours out the Holy Spirit upon us, Acts II. 17. (Joel II. 28. Isa. XLIV. 3.) by whose grace also we are justified, below v. 7. and Rom. III. 24. Crocius rightly [says]: By our Savior God in this place is understood God the Father. For he is distinguished by reason of person and mode, or order of acting, from Christ and the Holy Spirit, verses 5. 6. and is said to pour out the Spirit through Christ. He is called Savior not only because he commonly saves all, as Creator, but primarily because he restores our salvation in Christ. For he proposed Christ, that he might be a propitiation through faith in his blood, Rom. III. 25. he reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, 2 Cor. V. 18. Truly the Son saves us by his compassion, merit, and efficacy, John XVII. 12. Matt. I. 21. The Father by his compassion and efficacy. Thence the Son asks the Father that he may save us from evil in his name, John XVII. 15. Whence the pious Ancients everywhere observe here the testimony of the Holy Trinity, which has also been done in our System of Theology, Vol. III. Let us attend more diligently, says Jerome, and we shall find in the present chapter a most manifest Trinity. For the kindness and clemency of our Savior God, of no other than God the Father: through the washing of regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Spirit, which he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, he has quickened us into eternal life. The salvation of believers is the mystery of the Trinity: But this ἐπιφάνεια τῆς χρηστότητος καὶ φιλανθρωπίας [manifestation of the kindness and love toward man] was made to Paul, made to Titus, and to the Cretans in the manifestation of the Gospel, illumination, and conversion, made also to the faithful in the Old Testament, and to us all, to whom that saving grace is preached, to wish to deprive the ancients of whose proclamation and manifestation is to deprive them of eternal salvation, since we are saved only through that word and proclamation of grace, and the faith held in it, Acts XV. v. 11. There is no doubt, however, that the ἐπιφάνεια [manifestation] is more illustrious in the New Testament.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ὅτε δὲ ἡ χρηστότης καὶ ἡ φιλανθρωπία ἐπεφάνη τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεοῦ.

Idem hic χρηστότης καὶ φιλανθρωπία Θεοῦ, quod modo χάρις Θεοῦ, II. 11. Est & hic καὶ rursus ἐξηγητικόν. Nam χρηστότης nomen generale explicatur per specialius φιλαν- θρωπίας, sic Rabbini solent dicere טובה וחעלתי. No- tat etiam Plutarchus, Deum non dici Φίλιππον, sed φιλάν- θρωπον. Vide Psalm. VIII. vers. 5. Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεοῦ, ut supra II. v. 10.

Non est cur χρηστότητα & Φιλανθρωπίαν pro Synonymis habeamus. Rectius ea distinguuntur, quæ sic explicat B. Hunnius noster: Appellat χρη- στότητα seu bonitatem. Mansisset autem Deus im- mutabiliter bonus, si maxime se nobis peccatoribus benignum non ostendisset, sed secundum justitiæ ri- gorem nos reliquisset in miseria, sicut lapsos Angelos. Jam vero ad illustrandam ipsius bonitatem hic qui- dam veluti cumulus accedit, quod non tam intra se consideratus incommutabili quadam bonitate bo- nus est, sed etiam bonitatis illius suæ fontem nobis hominibus aperit, ut jam nobis sit χρηστὸς, utiliter bonus, dum ex bonitatis suæ thesauris æternas com- moditates ad nos profert. Altera vox est Φιλαν- θρωπία. Quam ut Latina lingua voce una redde- re non potest: Sic emphasin ejus nulla vis humana eloquentia valet affequi. Designat autem admi- randum illum amorem, quo æternus Deus mortalem hominem, Creator egenam creaturam, ipsa justitia & sanctitas peccatores miseros, adeoque hostes ini- micos suos cælesti favore suo dignatur, omnique me- moria offensarum penitus inducta gratiam ἀμνη- σίαν sancit cum perpetuo benefaciendi studio con- junctam. Voce τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Θεῦ plerique Deum Patrem intelligunt: explicite tamen non- nulli de Filio Dei, qui alibi semper hoc nomine in Novo Testamento venit, cui & illa ἐπιφάνεια, χρηστότης & Φιλανθρωπία eximie convenit, quæ illuxit primum in opere redemptionis omnibus ho- minibus, postmodum etiam illucescit in opere sanctificationis, illuminationis, regenerationis, & re- novationis, ubi actu participes reddimur redem- ptionis per Christum factæ. Quæ explicatio non displicuit Bernardo serm. I. de natal. Domini: Apparuerat antea potentia in rerum creatione, ap- parebat sapientia in earum gubernatione; sed be- nignitas misericordia nunc maxime apparuit in humanitate. Et serm. I. de Epiphan. Priusquam appareret humanitas, latebat benignitas. Cui è Græcis Theophylactus consonat, hæc ita παραφρά- ζων: Cum benignitas & humanitas apparuit Salva- toris Dei nostri, id est, cum incarnatus est Unige- nitus, & similis nobis effectus. Estius è verbis se- quentibus patere ait, de Patre hæc dici, quia ad- ditur, Deum effudisse in nos abunde Spiritum San- ctum per Jesum Christum Salvatorem nostrum, quod de alio, quam de Patre intelligi non possit. Quidni vero? Annon & Filius in nos effundit Spiritum Sanctum? Quod autem hic effusus di- citur per Jesum Christum Salvatorem nostrum, eo id solum notatur, merito Christi hanc effusionem nobis acquisitam. Est autem Christus & causa Efficiens prima cum Patre hujus effusionis ratio- ne Θεολογίας, quatenus idem cum Patre Deus, & causa meritoria, ratione τῆς οἰκονομίας, quatenus Mediator noster θεάνθρωπος, Deus & homo. Hic sermo, inquit Estius postea, per Jesum Christum, tam in Epistolis Paulinis, quam in orationibus Ec- clesiæ causam promerentem significat. Itaque sensus est: Christum ut hominem sua passione nobis pro- meruisse affluentiam donorum Spiritus Sancti, qui- bus renovamur. Ob eandem causam Christum vo- cat Salvatorem nostrum, quia nimirum universa salus nostra ab initio fidei usque ad gloriæ consum- mationem, est ex illius merito. Hæc ita Estio eo magis reponi possent, quum Christum solum se- cundum humanam naturam Mediatorem nostrum constituat. Sed quia in Scripturis, cum Deus per Deum salvare, cum Dominus à Domino vel per Do- minum quid agere dicitur, ut hic Servator Deus per Servatorem Christum effundere dicitur Spiri- tum S. discrimen personarum indicatur, præstat communi explicationi acquiescere, quæ magno veterum & recentiorũ consensu traditur, & è ver- bis ipsis fluit, quod Deus Pater illucescere nobis saciat benignitatem & Φιλανθρωπίαν suã in nego- tio conversionis nostræ, cujus χρηστότης celebratur Rom. II. 4. XI. 22. Eph. II. 7. ut & amor erga genus humanum, Joh. III. 16. 1. Joh. IV. 16. Rom. V. 8. nec non ἔλεος vel misericordia in ἐπιφανείᾳ orientis ex alto penes eos, qui in tenebris sedebant, & um- bra mortis, Luc. I. 78. 79. & v. 50. 51. 52. in vo- catione & conversione, Rom. XV. 9. in salvatione, Eph. II. 4. ac regeneratione, 1. Petr. I. 3. quodque secundum suam misericordiam salvavit nos, de qua gratia, dilectione & misericordia ac benigni- tate ejusdem magna verborum copia Paulus Eph. II. 4. 5. 7. 8. & quod effundat Spiritum Sanctum super nos, Act. II. 17. (Joël. II. 28. Es. XLIV. 3.) cujus etiam gratia justificamur, infra v. 7. & Rom. III. 24. Recte Crocius: Per Servatorem nostrum Deum hoc loco intelligitur Deus Pater. Distingui- tur enim ratione personae & modi, seu ordinis agen- di à Christo & Spiritu Sancto vers. 5. 6. ac dicitur effundere Spiritum per Christum. Servator dictus non solum, quia communiter servat omnes, ut Crea- tor, sed imprimis, quia in Christo salutem nostram instaurat. Ille enim proposuit Christum, ut esset placamentum per fidem in sanguine, Rom. III. 25. ille reconciliavit nos sibi per Jesum Christum, 2. Cor. V. 18. Nempe servat nos Filius sua miseratione, me- rito, & efficacia, Joh. XVII. 12. Matth. I. 21. Pa- ter sua miseratione & efficacia. Inde Filius Patrem rogat, ut in suo nomine nos servet à malo, Johan. XVII. 15. Unde hic testimonium SS. Trinitatis observant pii Veteres passim, quod etiam in Sy- stem. nostro Theol. T. III. factum. Diligentius attendamus, inquit Hieronymus, & inveniemus in praesenti capitulo manifestissimam Trinitatem. Be- nignitas quippe atque clementia Salvatoris nostri Dei, non alterius, quam Dei Patris: per lavacrum regenerationis & renovationem Spiritus Sancti, quem effudit super nos abunde per Jesum Christum Salvatorem nostrum, vivificavit nos in vitam aeter- nam. Salus credentium mysterium Trinitatis est: Haec autem ἐπιφάνεια τῆς χρηστότητος καὶ φιλαν- θρωπίας facta Paulo, facta Tito, & Cretensibus in manifestatione Evangelii, illuminatione, & conversione, facta etiam fidelibus in Veteri Te- stamento, & nobis omnibus, quibus praedicatur gratia illa σωτήριος, cujus praeconio & manifesta- tione privare velle veteres est eosdem aeterna sa- lute privare, quum non nisi per illud verbum & praeconium gratiae, fidemque illi habitam salve- mur, Actor. XV. v. 11. Illustriorem tamen ἐπι- φάνειαν esse in Novo Test. dubium nullum est.

## 3:5
Vers. 5.

Not by works of righteousness which we have done.

For the works of most had been evil. Ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ [in righteousness] after the Hebrew manner for κατὰ δικαιοσύνην [according to righteousness]. The sense is the same as Eph. II. 9. It alludes to Deut. VII. 7.

But according to his own mercy.

This is what is called in the cited passage to the Ephesians Θεῦ τὸ δῶρον [the gift of God]. חן אלהים [grace of God], Galat. I. 12. διὰ τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ [through his grace]. He bestowed benefits of his own accord; to those asking for nothing of the kind, 1 Pet. I. 3. In the Manuscript: Κατὰ τὸ αὑτῦ ἔλεος [according to his own mercy].

He saved us.

It is a metonymy. For he said 'he saved' for 'he placed in the way of salvation.' Thus Eph. II. verse 5. and II. verse 8. χάριτί ἐσι σεσωσμένοι [by grace you are saved].

Salvation here is claimed for grace and divine mercy alone, to the exclusion of the merits of works of justice, if indeed they were present at all. Therefore, not only are the moral works of nature and of the law, which the Papists call such, excluded, but even the works τῆς δικαιοσύνης of justice. Estius twists this into a completely contrary sense: namely, that the Apostle means that we were not made safe through Christ by the merit of any works, as if they were just, which might have been done by us, because, forsooth, there was no justice of ours, unless it were false, and no just works. For he says, he does not mean that we did works of justice, from which, however, we were not made safe, but because works of justice bring salvation, he simply intends to remove works of justice from us. But although it is certain that our works are nothing before justification, whence the merits of congruity of Papistic justification must necessarily collapse; yet here works of good are simply removed, even from the business of salvation or being saved, even the works τῆς δικαιοσύνης of justice. Nor do we assert that those words, ὧν ἐποιήσαμεν ἡμεῖς, imply that, as if any works of justice had been done before conversion: but rather that he means this, that even if they could have been done (and we acknowledge that such works could not have been), they would contribute nothing to salvation: for Estius observes that the Greek is more conveniently translated by others thus: Not from works which were in justice, which we might have done. Paul is not dealing here with justification alone, but with salvation, just as there are no other causes of salvation than of justification: and yet he excludes from it works of justice, and ascribes it solely to the gratuitous beneficence or mercy of GOD, inasmuch as it is here opposed adequately and ἀντιδιῃρημένως to works in Romans 11:6. Rightly, therefore, in the judgment of Estius, and solidly do Augustine, Thomas, and other orthodox writers teach from this Scripture that GOD predestined us to salvation not from any foreknowledge of our works, but from his mercy alone. For just as he made us safe, says Thomas, I. p. q. 23. art. 5, so he predestined us to be made safe. Therefore, if he made us safe not from works, but from his mercy alone, so also he predestined us: these things are clearly ἀσύςατα with the merits of eternal life, about which he immediately subjoins, nor can they be reconciled any more than the North Pole with the South Pole: whatever may be said of the dictum of Pope Celestine: The goodness of God is so great that he wishes our merits to be his gifts. For where does Paul say this? He who rather says the opposite: If by grace, he says, not by works: otherwise grace would not be grace, Romans 11:6. And the gift of GOD in Christ Jesus is eternal life, Romans 6: last verse, to which one should rather acquiesce than to Celestine? Nor is there any reason why we should explain ἔσωσεν by metonymy as 'placed in the way of salvation.' For through baptism we are not only justified, or obtain remission of sins, but we are also saved: Nor is salvation any less a gift of GOD than justification, Eph. 2:5, 8. And do not those who depart in infancy after baptism obtain salvation, even if the merits of good works are not found in them? It is better also to say of others that God has saved them, even if they have not yet attained eternal blessedness, which belongs to the fatherland, but are still in the state of wayfarers: not only because of the certainty of future blessedness, but also because of the foretaste and preliminary draught of the same in this life, and because they possess all things from which they can be blessed from now on, and it only remains that through death, as the door of life, they should penetrate into blessedness; therefore Christ says of the faithful who believe in him, that they have passed from death into life, John 5:24.

Διὰ λυτρῦ παλιγγενεσίας. In the Manuscript: Δια τῦ λυτρῦ. He understands baptism joined with the doctrine of baptism. See also Eph. 5:6 and 1 Pet. 3:21, where baptism is said to save. A part of the new birth is the exaction of vices, which is promised in baptism. See what is said on John 3:3 and Matt. 28:19. Add Gal. 3:27, Col. 2:12, where baptism is similarly considered with doctrine and the thing signified. Theophilus of Antioch: Ἔτι μὲν καὶ ἐνλογῖθη ὑπὸ τῦ Θεῦ τὰ ἐκ τῶν ὑδάτων γενόμενα, ὅπως ᾖ καὶ τῦτο εἰς δεῖγμα τῦ μέλλειν λαμβάνειν τὺς ἀνθρώπες μετάνοιαν καὶ ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν διὰ ὕδατὸς ϗ λυτρῦ παλιγγενεσίας, πάντας τὺς προσιόντας τῇ ἀληθείᾳ καὶ ἀναγεννωμένες καὶ λαμβάνον- τας ἐνλογίαν παρὰ τῦ Θεῦ. By the washing of regeneration, baptism is rightly understood. For in it and through it we are regenerated, as Christ testifies, John 3:5. But it is not correctly said that the doctrine of baptism is understood at the same time. For nowhere in the Scriptures is the doctrine of baptism called λουτρὸν παλιγγενεσίας [washing of regeneration], or by a similar name, nor is it fitting that both baptism and the doctrine of baptism be understood together by the same word. The passages cited, Eph. 5:6 and 1 Pet. 3:21, likewise deal only with baptism. But from where is it established that the casting off of vices, which is promised in baptism, is designated by regeneration? Regeneration is not promised in baptism, but is obtained through baptism by divine grace and power, which is therefore called the washing of regeneration, because through this washing we are truly regenerated, just as Christ teaches that we are regenerated of water and the Spirit, John 3:5, and St. Peter: that baptism saves us, 1 Epist. 3:21. Nor indeed is that casting off of vices, which Grotius calls regeneration or new birth, the gracious operation of God, when it is taken actively, conferring spiritual life and the strength to believe upon a man dead in sin, the consequence of which is the casting off of vices, which pertains to renovation rather than regeneration, as these are distinguished. Crocius distinguishes these not inappropriately: Regeneration is not the generation of a new substance, which succeeds in the place of the old substance, as Illyricus invented: But it is the action of God, by which He endows men dead in sin with spiritual life, through the communication of faith, so that they may be able to produce the works of the Spirit. What is born of the flesh in the first generation is flesh: the second is born of the Spirit as a spiritual man, not by reason of substance, but by quality, gifts, and motions. Renovation properly concerns morals, and is the action of the same God, by which He gradually abolishes the old man, that is, the corruption of nature, by His grace, and adorns all faculties with new powers, so that, progressing more and more in new obedience, we may exercise ourselves in the pursuit of good works.

Socinus understands repentance by the washing of regeneration. But that is never called a washing in the Scriptures, nor is it taught anywhere that regeneration is brought about through repentance. Scripture knows no other washing by which we are washed from sins or regenerated than baptism; see Zech. 13:1, Rom. 6:4, Acts 22:16, 1 Cor. 6:11, Eph. 5:25, Col. 2:11, 1 Pet. 3:21. Smalcius and the Racovian Catechism wish for regeneration itself to be denoted by this washing. But regeneration is one thing, and the washing of regeneration is another. And nowhere is washing called regeneration. And here the effect of the washing of baptism is established as regeneration: but the washing itself is not regeneration. Therefore, the gloss of Schlichtingius on this passage is vain and subtle: 'by the washing of regeneration and renovation,' that is, 'by the washing, which is regeneration and renovation.' Nor is it less vain and futile when he adds that by this very thing it is signified that we are saved by just works. For what, he says, is regeneration and renovation other than the change of the former impure, vice-polluted, and profane state into a pure and holy one? But what is this other than to contradict Paul to his face? Who in express words denies that we are saved by works of righteousness, and teaches that we are not saved except by the χρηστότητα [kindness], Φιλανθρωπίαν [love for mankind], and ἔλεος [mercy] of God, vindicating this with such an apparatus of words here and in Eph. 2:4, 5, 7, 8, that it would be impious to deny it and to wish to divide salvation between grace and our works, which is to deny that grace so highly celebrated by the Apostle, Rom. 11:6. The Apostle teaches that we are not saved by regeneration, not by renovation, much less by the change of an impure life into a pure one, and least of all by just works: But by the washing of regeneration,

and renovation, that is, baptism, through which we are regenerated and saved, as Christ testifies, John 3:5, we obtain the remission of sins, Acts 2:38, we are washed from sins, Acts 22:16, we are purified, 1 John 1:7, we put on Christ, Gal. 3:27, and we are saved, 1 Pet. 3:21. It is vain and futile that Schlichtingius says the water, of whose washing he admits is treated here, is the Holy Spirit, for regeneration and renovation are said to be of the Holy Spirit, and God is said to save us by the washing of regeneration and renovation, but Scripture does not say that the Holy Spirit is water, either here or anywhere else. He is said to be poured out like water by metaphor, on account of the abundance of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which redundantly flow into us in large measure, not drop by drop, through this washing, but the Holy Spirit Himself is not called water or washing, so far is it from the case that we have Paul here as an interpreter of the words of Christ John 3:5. That water, from which we are born and generated, is the Holy Spirit, who is truly and expressly distinguished by Christ from water, and here by Paul from the washing of water, by which there is no doubt that baptism is denoted to him who knows that no other washing of water is found in the Scriptures except the sacrament of baptism, just as Schlichtingius himself could not deny here that the washing of water, which is contained in baptism, pertains to this, insofar as it is the divinely instituted sign and sacrament of the washing of regeneration and renovation, which is done through the Holy Spirit. But as for what he adds, that those who refer all their salvation to the baptism of water, and do not lay aside their vices and evil morals, to do which they bound themselves in the baptism of water, are held by a greater crime, so far is it from the case that they can be helped at all by the baptism of water, that they strike at us. For although we believe that baptism is a means of salvation and a sacrament divinely instituted for regeneration and the remission of sins, and that through baptism we obtain perfect salvation and enter into the kingdom of heaven, we nevertheless teach that vices must be laid aside and the flesh with its depraved desires must be mortified, unless we wish to fall from the grace of God and eternal salvation, which happens through sins against conscience: Indeed, we assert the efficacy of baptism in such a way that we believe no crimes are so great that they cannot be washed away through baptism, which is evident even from the example of Paul, Acts 20:16, and indeed even of those who are said here to have been foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, hating one another, and yet they were saved through baptism.

And of the renewing of the Holy Spirit) After baptism the Holy Spirit is given, acting toward all greatest things. This is the second part of the new birth, which is here called ἀνακαίνωσις, as also in Rom. 12:2, Col. 3:10. The passage in Ezek. 36:26 is referred to. The ancients note in this place a sufficiently express mention of the Trinity.

The Apostle teaches here that the Holy Spirit is given not after baptism, but through baptism, because he calls baptism the washing of regeneration and of the renewing of the Holy Spirit, both of which, just as they are done through the Holy Spirit as the principal cause, so both are also done through baptism as the instrumental cause. Renovation, however, is not properly a part of the new generation, because here it is distinguished from regeneration: By the latter we conceive faith and are begotten as children of God: By the former, however, we are changed into a new man and are renewed to the image of God situated in righteousness and holiness. Regeneration precedes, renovation follows; because, justified through faith, we are renewed and sanctified, so that we may walk in newness of life; and we are rendered a new creature in Christ, putting off or laying aside the old man which corrupts itself through the lusts of deceit, and we are renewed

by the spirit of our mind, and we put on the new man, who according to God is created in righteousness and holiness of truth, Eph. IV. 22, 23, 24. Joh. Piscator only wishes the Apostle to allude to baptism, as if to say: God has saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, that is, through the regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit as if through a certain washing, by which, namely, we are washed from the filth of sin: the seal of which washing is baptism. But here there is no indication of an allusion, and that 'AS IF' and 'AS' is rashly thrust into the text; there is no trace of a seal in it, nor is regeneration or renewal compared to a washing, or called by that name, but it is said to be done through the washing of baptism, as that which Christ instituted as a means to this end, and through which the Holy Spirit works effectively; not only by testifying and sealing and proving regeneration and renewal in us, but by conferring or effecting it. For it is not only a significant sign, but an effective and communicative means.

That Herborn Piscator also gratifies the Arians, whether prudently or imprudently, when he says that the ministering causes in this place, with respect to God the Father, are two: Christ and the Holy Spirit: For these three are one, 1 Joh. V. 7. And therefore their consubstantiality does not admit the notion of a Principal cause and ministering causes: For Arius draws into his fellowship those who say there are three causes, and make the Son and the Holy Spirit ministers of God the Father.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων τῶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ, ὧν ἐποιήσαμεν ἡμεῖς.

Plerorumque enim mala fuerant opera. Ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ Ebraeo more pro κατὰ δικαιοσύνην. Sensus idem Eph. II. 9. Alluditur ad Deut. VII. 7.

Ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸν αὑτῦ ἔλεον.

Hoc est, quod dicto ad Ephesios loco dicitur Θεῦ τὸ δῶ- ρον. חן אלהים, Galat. I, 12. διὰ τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ. Beneficia ultro ingessit; nihil tale petentibus, 1. Petr. I. 3. In Manuscripto: Κατὰ τὸ αὑτῦ ἔλεος.

Ἔσωσεν ἡμᾶς.

Est Μετωνυμία. Nam servavit dixit, pro in via salutis collocavit. Sic Ephes. II. vers. 5. & II. vers. 8. χάριτί ἐσι σεσωσμένοι.

Salus hic vendicatur uni gratiae & misericor- diae divinae, exclusis operum justitiae, si omnino adfuissent, meritis. Non ergo tantum opera mo- ralia naturae & legis, quae vocant Papistae, exclu- duntur, sed opera etiam τῆς δικαιοσύνης justitiae. In contrarium plane sensum haec detorquet Esti- us: Sentire nempe Apostolum, non ex ullo ope- rum, quasi justorum, merito, quae à nobis facta essent, nos salvos factos esse per Christum, quia ni- mirum nulla erat nostra justitia, nisi falsa, nulla opera justa. Neque enim, inquit, significat, nos fecisse opera justitiae, ex quibus tamen non simus salvi facti, sed quia opera justitiae salutem afferunt, ideo simpliciter intendit à nobis opera justitiae re- movere. Sed licet certum sit, opera nostra nulla esse ante justificationem, unde corruere neces- fum est merita ex congruo Papisticæ justificatio- nis; hic tamen simpliciter removentur opera bona, etiam à negotio salutis vel salvatione, etiam opera τῆς δικαιοσύνης justitiæ. Nec vero illa, ὧν ἐποιήσαμεν ἡμεῖς id innuere asserimus, quasi facta aliqua opera justitiæ fuerint ante conver- sionem: Sed id potius velle, etiamsi fieri po- tuissent, (uti non potuisse agnoscimus talia ope- ra) nihil tamen illa ad salutem: Nam Græca commodius ita ab aliis verti observat Estius: Non ex operibus, quæ essent in justitia, quæ fe- cissemus nos. Non de justificatione solum agit hic Paulus, sed de salute, quemadmodum nec aliæ salutis sunt causæ, quam justificationis: & exclu- dit tamen ab illa opera justitiæ, eamque gratui- tæ DEI beneficentiæ vel misericordiæ, utpote quæ hic opponitur adæquate & ἀντιδιῃρημένως operibus Roman. XI. vers. 6. unice adscribit. Re- cte igitur, Estio Judice, & solide Augustinus, & Thomas, alique Scriptores orthodoxi docent ex hac Scriptura, DEUM nos ad salutem prædestinasse non ex ulla operum nostrorum præscientia, sed ex sola sua misericordia. Sicut enim salvos nos fe- cit, ait Thomas I. p. q. 23. art. 5. ita prædestina- vit nos salvos fieri. Igitur si salvos nos fecit non ex operibus, sed ex sola sua misericordia, sic quoque prædestinavit: Hæc cum meritis vitæ æternæ, de quibus statim subjungit, plane ἀσύςατα sunt, nec magis componi possunt, quam Polus Arcticus cum Ant-Arctico: quicquid sit de dicto Papæ Cœlestini: Tanta est Dei bonitas, ut nostra velit esse merita, quæ sunt ipsius dona. Ubi enim ita Paulus? Qui ex adverso potius: Si ex gratia, in- quit, non ex operibus: alioquin gratia non esset gratia, Roman. XI. 6. Et donum DEI in Christo Jesu vita æterna, Roman. VI. vers. ult. cui potius acquiescendum, quam Cœlestino? Nec est, quod ἔσωσεν per Metonymiam explicemus, in salutis via collocavit. Nam per baptismum non tantum justificamur, vel remissionem peccatorum con- sequimur, sed etiam salvamur: Nec minus salus est donum DEI, quam justificatio, Eph. II. v. 5. 8. Et annon illi, qui post baptismum in infantia decedunt, salute potiuntur, etsi bonorum ope- rum merita in iis non inveniantur? Præstat et- iam de aliis dicere, quod salvarit eos Deus, etsi nondum æternam beatitudinem, quæ patriæ est, consequuti, sed in statu viatorum adhuc sint: non tantum ob certitudinem futuræ beatitudinis, sed etiam ob πρόγευσμα ϗ προποτισμὸν ejusdem in hac vita, & quod omnia, ex quibus beati à mo- do esse queant, possideant, ac solum restet, ut per mortem, ceu januam vitæ, in beatitudinem pene- trent; ideo de fidelibus in se credentibus ait Christus, quod transierint de morte in vitam, Johan. V. vers. 24.

Διὰ λυτρῦ παλιγγενεσίας. In Manuscripto: Δια τῦ λυτρῦ. Baptismum intelligit junctim cum doctrina baptismi. Vide & Ephes. V. vers. 6. & 1. Petr. III. 21. ubi βάπτισμα σώζειν dicitur. Pars novæ nativitatis est exactio vitiorum, quæ in baptismo promit- titur. Vide, quæ ad Johan. III. vers. 3. & Matth. XXVIII. vers. 19. Adde Galat. III. vers. 27. Coloff. II. vers. 12. ubi similiter baptismus cum doctrina & re significata consi- deratur. Theophilus Antiochenus: Ἔτι μὲν καὶ ἐνλογῖθη ὑπὸ τῦ Θεῦ τὰ ἐκ τῶν ὑδάτων γενόμενα, ὅπως ᾖ καὶ τῦτο εἰς δεῖγμα τῦ μέλλειν λαμβάνειν τὺς ἀνθρώπες μετάνοιαν καὶ ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν διὰ ὕδατὸς ϗ λυτρῦ παλιγγενεσίας, πάντας τὺς προσιόντας τῇ ἀληθείᾳ καὶ ἀναγεννωμένες καὶ λαμβάνον- τας ἐνλογίαν παρὰ τῦ Θεῦ. Per lavacrum regenerationis recte baptismus intelligitur. In eo enim & per illum regenera- mur teste Christo, Joh. III. 5. Sed non recte ba- ptismi doctrinam simul intelligi dicitur. Nuspiam enim baptismi doctrina λουτρὸν παλιγγενεσίας in Scripturis, aut simili nomine vocatur, nec conve- nit eadem voce junctim & baptismum & baptismi doctrinam intelligi. Loca adducta Eph. V. 6. & 1. Petr. III. 21. itidem solum de baptismo agunt. Per regenerationem autem designari exactionem vitiorum, quæ in baptismo promittatur, unde- nam constat? Regeneratio in baptismo non pro- mittitur, sed per baptismum divina gratia ac vir- tute obtingit, qui ideo lavacrum regenerationis dicitur, quod per hoc lavacrum vere regenere- mur, quemadmodum docet Christus, nos ex aqua & Spiritu regenerari, Joh. III. 5. & S. Petrus: Ba- ptismum nos σώζειν servare, 1. Epist. III. 21. Nec vero regenerationis vel novæ nativitatis est illa vitiorum exactio, quam vocat Grotius, quæ est operatio Dei gratiosa, cum active sumitur, ho- mini in peccato mortuo vitam spiritualem vires- que credendi conferens, cujus consequens est vitiorum exactio ad renovationem potius, quam regenerationem, prout hæc distinguuntur, per- tinens. Quæ non incommode distinguit Crocius: Regeneratio non est generatio novæ substantiæ, quæ in veteris substantiæ locum succedat, sicut commen- tus Illyricus: Sed est actio Dei, qua homines in pec- cato mortuos donat spirituali vita, communicatio- ne fidei, ut opera Spiritus edere queant. Quod pri- ma generatione ex carne gignitur, caro est: Secun- da ex Spiritu spiritualis homo nascitur, non ratione substantiæ, sed qualitate, donorum, motuum. Re- novatio mores proprie respicit, estque ejusdem Dei actio, qua veterem hominem, id est, naturæ corru- ptionem sua gratia abolet paulatim, & novis viri- bus facultates omnes ornat, ut magis magisque in nova obedientia proficientes nos exerceamus in bo- norum operum studio.

Socinus per lavacrum re- generationis pœnitentiam intelligit. Sed ea nec lavacrum unquam in Scripturis dicitur, nec rege- nerationem per pœnitentiam fieri uspiam doce- tur. Nullum etiam aliud lavacrum, quo à pecca- tis abluamur aut regeneremur, novit Scriptura, quam baptismum; vid. Zach. XIII. 1. Rom. VI. 4. Act. XXII. 16. 1. Cor. VI. 11. Eph. V. 25. Col. II. 11. 1. Petr. III. 21. Smalcius & Catechesis Racov. re- generationem ipsam per hoc lavacrum notari vo- lunt. Sed aliud est regeneratio, aliud lavacrum regenerationis. Nec uspiam lavacrum dici- tur regeneratio. Et hic effectus lavacri baptismi constituitur regeneratio: non vero lavacrum est ipsa regeneratio. Vana ergo & subtilis est glossa Schlichtingii in h. l. per lavacrum regenerationis & renovationis, id est, per lavacrum, quod est re- generatio ac renovatio. Nec minus vanum & futi- le, cum addit hoc ipso significari, nos esse per opera justa servatos. Quid enim, inquit, aliud est rege- neratio & renovatio, quam prioris impuræ & vi- tiis pollutæ, ac profanæ in puram ac sanctam mu- tatio? Quid vero hoc aliud est, quam Paulo in os contradicere? Qui diserta voce negat, per ope- ra justitiæ nos salvari, docetque non salvari, nisi per χρηστότητα, Φιλανθρωπίαν, ἔλεος τοῦ Θεοῦ, tanto verborum apparatu hic & Ephes. II. 4. 5. 7. 8. id vindicans, ut impium sit, id negare, ac salutem inter gratiam & opera nostra partiri velle, quod est, gratiam illam tantopere ab Apostolo cele- bratam esse gratiam inficiari, Roman. XI. vers. 6. Non per regenerationem, non per renovationem, nedum per vitæ impuræ in puram mutationem, minime omnium per opera justa nos servari do- cet Apostolus: Sed per lavacrum regenerationis,

& renovationis, hoc est, baptismum, per quem regeneramur ac salvamur, teste Christo, Joh. III. v. 5. remissionem peccatorum consequimur, Act. II. v. 18. à peccatis abluimur, cap. XX. 16. purifi- camur, 2. Joh. v. 26. Christum induimus, Galat. III. 27. & salvamur, 1. Pet. III. 21. Vanum est at- que futile, quod Schlichtingius aquam, de cujus lavacro hic agi fatetur, Spiritum Sanctum esse di- cit, nam regeneratio & renovatio dicitur Spiritus Sancti esse, & lavacrum regenerationis & renova- tionis salvare nos dicitur Deus, non autem Spiri- tum Sanctum aquam esse vel hic vel uspiam alias Scriptura dicit. Effundi dicit instar aquæ per Me- taphoram, ob copiam donorum Spiritus Sancti, quæ largiter, non guttatim, in nos redundant per hoc lavacrum, non autem Spiritus Sanctus ipse vel aqua vel lavacrum dicitur, tantum abest, ut Paulum hic habeamus interpretem verborum Christi 1. Joh.
