III. 5. aquam istam, ex qua nascimur & generamur, Spiritum S. esse, qui vero diserte à Christo distinguitur ab aqua, & à Paulo hic à la- vacro aquæ, per quod baptismum notari dubium nullum est ei, qui novit in Scripturis nullum aliud lavacrum aquæ, nisi baptismatos sacramentum re- periri, uti nec ipse Schlichtingius hic diffiteri po- tuit, lavacrum aquæ, quod baptismo continetur, huc pertinere, quatenus lavacri regenerationis ac reno- vationis, quæ per Spiritum S. fit, signum ac sacra- mentum est divinitus institutum. Quod vero ad- dit, qui salutem suam omnem ad baptismum aquæ referunt, nec deponunt vitia ac malos mores, ad quod faciendum baptismo aquæ sese obligarunt, ma- jori tenentur crimine, tantum abest, ut baptismo aquæ juvari quicquam possint, nos feriunt. Etsi enim credamus, baptismum esse medium salutis ac sacramentum divinitus institutum ad regene- rationem ac peccatorum remissionem & per ba- ptismum nos salutem perfectam consequi, ac in- trare in regnum cœlorum, docemus tamen depo- nenda esse vitia, carnemque cum pravis concupi- scentiis mortificandam esse, nisi gratia Dei & sa- lute æterna excidere velimus, quod fit per pecca- ta contra conscientiam: Ita vero baptismi effi- caciam adserimus, ut nulla crimina tanta esse cre- damus, quæ non ablui possint per baptismum, quod vel Pauli exemplo constat, Act. XX. 16. imo etiam eorum, qui hic dicuntur fuisse ἀνόητοι, ἀπειθεῖς, πλανώμενοι, δελεύοντες ἐπιθυμίαις καὶ ἡδοναῖς ποικί- λαις ἐν κακίᾳ καὶ φθόνῳ διάγοντες, συγητοὶ, μισῶντες ἀλλήλες, & salvati tamen sunt per baptismum.

Καὶ ἀνακαινώσεως πνεύματος ἁγίε) Post baptismum da- tur Spiritus S. agens ad omnia maxima. Hæc est pars altera novæ nativitatis, quæ hic ἀνακαίνωσις, ut & Rom. XII. v. 2. Col. II. 10. Respicitur locus Ezech. XVIII. 26. Notant ve- teres in h. l. τῆς τριάδος mentionem satis expressam.

Non post baptismum, sed per baptismum dari Spiritum Sanctum hic Apostolus docet, quia Ba- ptismum lavacrum regenerationis & renovationis Spiritus S. vocat, quæ utraque uti per Spiritum S. fit, ceu causam Principalem, ita utraque etiam per baptismum ceu causam mediam fit. Renovatio autem non est proprie pars novæ generationis, quia hic à regeneratione distinguitur: Hac fidem concipimus & filii DEI gignimur: Illa vero in novum hominem mutamur, & ad imaginem DEI in justitia & sanctitate sitam renovamur. Regeneratio præcedit, renovatio sequitur; quia per fidem justificati renovamur, & sanctifica- mur, ut in novitate vitæ ambulemus; & nova creatura reddimur in Christo, exuentes vel de- ponentes veterem hominem corrumpentem se- se per concupiscentias erroris, & renovamur

Spiritu mentis nostræ, ac induimus novum ho- minem, qui secundum Deum conditus est in ju- stitia & sanctitate veritatis, Ephes. IV. 22. 23. 24. Joh. Piscator alludere tantum vult Apostolum ad baptismum, q. d. Deum servasse nos per lavacrum regenerationis & renovationis Spiritus Sancti, id est, per regenerationem & renovationem Spiri- tus S. tanquam per lavacrum quoddam, quo scil. abluimur a peccati sordibus: cujus lavacri sigil- lum est baptismus. Sed hic nullum indicium al- lusionis, & illud QUASI & TANQUAM temere in- geritur in textum, nullum in eo sigilli vestigium, nec regeneratio aut renovatio comparatur lava- cro, vel eo nomine vocatur, sed per lavacrum baptismatis dicitur fieri, utpote quod medium in hunc finem instituit Christus, & per quod effica- citer operatur Spiritus Sanctus; non tantum te- stificando & obsignando ac arguendo regenera- tionem & renovationem in nobis, sed eam confe- rendo vel efficiendo. Est enim non tantum signum σημαντικὸν, sed medium ἐνεργητικὸν κὶ μεταδοτικὸν.

Arianis etiam seu prudens seu imprudens grati- ficatur Piscator ille Herbornensis, cum causæ mini- strantes, inquit, h. l. respectu Dei Patris sunt duæ, Christus & Spiritus Sanctus: Hi enim tres unum sunt, 1. Joh. V. 7. Ideoque ὁμοουσία ipsorum non admittit causæ Principalis & causarum ministran- tium notionem: Nam tres causas qui dicunt, & Filium ac Spiritum S. ministros DEI Patris fa- ciunt, eos in societatem suam rapit Arius.

## 3:6
Ver. 6. Which He poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior.

He poured out by itself signifies a large communication, as can be seen in Acts II. 17, 18, 33; X. 45. Furthermore, Paul added 'richly,' which in his speech is 'abundantly.' Through Jesus, because Jesus obtained this very thing from the Father. Therefore, the Holy Spirit is poured out abundantly upon us in baptism, regenerating and renewing us through baptism, and richly instructing us with various gifts, as the Apostle testifies. Which is done through Jesus the Savior, not only by reason of Mediatorial impetration, because He obtained this for us from the Father both by merit and by the efficacy of His intercession; but also of communication, because the Holy Spirit is also poured out, sent, and given to us by Christ, because having been exalted to the right hand of God and having received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father, He poured out the Holy Spirit, Acts II. 33, whom He promised He would send from His Father, Joh. XV. 26.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Οὗ ἐξέχεεν ἐφ' ἡμᾶς πλουσίως διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν.

Ἐξέχεεν per se largam communicationem significat, ut videre est Act. II. 17. 18. 33. X. 45. Præterea addidit Pau- lus πλουσίως, quod in ipsius sermone est, abundanter. Διὰ Ἰησοῦ, quia Jesus hoc ipsum a Patre obtinuit. Effunditur itaque Spiritus Sanctus largiter in baptismo super nos, nos per baptismum regene- rans & renovans, donisq; variis opulenter instru- ens, teste Apostolo. Quod per Jesum Salvatorem fit, non tantum ratione impetrationis Mediatoriæ, quia id obtinuit nobis a Patre tum merito, tum intercessionis suæ efficacia; sed etiam communi- cationis, quia a Christo etiam effunditur, mittitur ac donatur nobis Spiritus Sanctus, quia ad dex- tram DEI exaltatus ἐπαγγελίαν τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύ- ματος λαβὼν παρὰ τοῦ Πατρὸς ἐξέχεεν effudit Spi- ritum Sanctum, Act. II. 33. quem se a Patre suo missurum promisit Joh. XV. 26.

## 3:7
Ver. 7. That being justified by His grace) Cleansed of vices through faith, which came to us by faith as His gift, Rom. III. 28; V. 1; Gal. II. 16. See our Prolegomena to the Epistle to the Romans.

That we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life) We are said to be heirs here also, but by right and certain hope. Therefore, 'according to hope' is added here. Thus Rom. VIII. 24: We were saved by hope.

Justification is not a cleansing of vices, but is defined by the Apostle through the remission or non-imputation of sins, and through the imputation of righteousness, which is without the works of the law, that is, the righteousness of Christ, as is evident from Rom. III and IV, as also Philipp. III. 9. And in this place is contained a complete description of justification according to its causes. The Principal efficient cause is God the Father, our Savior, not excluding the Son or the Holy Spirit, if indeed we are said to be justified by His grace, which can be understood of the Son no less than of the Father, whose mention immediately preceded, cf. Acts XV. 11. And the Holy Spirit is expressly designated as the cause of our regeneration and renewal, and therefore also of our justification. The internal impulsive cause is the kindness, love for mankind, mercy, and grace of God: The external is the merit of Christ our Savior, who is therefore called our Savior. Regarding this, Piscator explains that 'justified by His grace' by understanding metonymically by grace that benefit of CHRIST which He performed for us out of grace and love, namely by dying for us. For by His death Christ obtained for us from the Father the remission of sins or justification: so that, namely, the Father might hold us as righteous, with sins remitted because of the death of Christ, by which they were expiated. The material cause or object of justification and salvation are men who are foolish, disobedient, etc., because God justifies the ungodly, Rom. IV. 6. The organic cause on the part of God is both the doctrine of the Gospel, by which the grace of God has shone upon us, and baptism, which is the washing of regeneration, through which God saves us, and through which He pours out the Holy Spirit into us for our regeneration and renewal. The organic cause on our part is faith, which the Holy Spirit works in us when He regenerates us, and which is included in the word hope, or is presupposed, because to hope in the phrase of Scripture is to trust, or at least it requires faith before it, nor can the heavenly inheritance be hoped for except through faith in Christ the Savior: whom we have or claim as our Savior solely through faith, just as we are also justified solely through faith, Rom. III. 28, and saved, Eph. II. 8. Therefore, the final cause of justification is the inheritance of eternal life. There remains the formal cause, which is signified by the very word δικαιωθέντες, inasmuch as it is forensic, and brings about absolution from sin and the punishment of sin, Rom. VIII. 33. Thus, with a wonderful but illustrious brevity, and with a truly divine artifice, the Apostle has exhibited the entire mystery of our justification and salvation in most emphatic and august words. Therefore, so that we may receive these things fully by faith, he adds its confirmation and admonitions concerning the doctrine that must be most inculcated in the Church.

PART II. An admonition concerning the doctrine that is to be inculcated above all, and concerning those things which are to be avoided.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἵνα δικαιωθέντες τῇ ἐκείνου χάριτι) Mundatis vitiis per fidem, quæ ipsius dono nobis fide contigit, Rom. III. 28. V. 1. Gal. II. 16. Vide Prolegomena nostra in epistolam ad Romanos.

Κληρονόμοι γενώμεθα κατ' ἐλπίδα ζωῆς αἰωνίου) Hæredes etiam hic esse dicimur, sed jure, ac certa spe. Ideo hic additur κατ' ἐλπίδα. Sic Rom. VIII. 24. Τῇ ἐλπίδι ἐσώ- θημεν.

Justificatio non est mundatio vitiorum, sed ab Apostolo definitur per remissionem vel non im- putationem peccatorum, & per imputationem ju- stitiæ, quæ est sine operibus legis, hoc est, justitiæ Christi, ut e Rom. III. & IV. constat, ut & Philipp. III. 9. Et habetur hoc loco integra descriptio justificationis secundum causas suas. Causa Prin- cipalis efficiens est Deus Pater, Servator noster, non excluso Filio aut Spiritu Sancto, siquidem τῇ χάριτι ἐκείνου δικαιωθέντες, gratia illius justificati dicamur, quod de Filio non minus intelligi po- test, cujus immediate antegressa est mentio, quam de Patre, conf. Actor. XV. 11. Et Spiritus Sanctus diserte designatur ceu causa regenerationis & re- novationis, adeoque etiam justificationis nostræ. Causa impulsiva interna est χρηστότης, Φιλανθρω- πία, ἔλεος καὶ χάρις τοῦ θεοῦ: Externa est Christi Servatoris nostri meritum, qui ideo Σωτὴρ ἡμῶν Servator noster dicitur. De quo explicat Pisi a- tor illud justificati gratia ipsius Metonymicè per gratiam intelligens beneficium illud CHRISTI, quod ex gratia & amore nobis præstitit, mori- endo scilicet pro nobis. Etenim sua morte Chri- stus nobis apud Patrem impetravit remissionem peccatorum seu justificationem: ut nimirum Pa- ter nos pro justis habeat, remissis peccatis pro- pter mortem Christi, qua illa sunt expiata. Causa materialis vel objectum justificationis & salvatio- nis sunt homines ἀνόητοι, ἀπειθεῖς &c. quia Deus justificat impium, Rom. IV. 6. Causa organica ex parte DEI est tum doctrina Evangelii, qua illu- xit nobis gratia DEI, tum baptismus, qui lava- crum regenerationis est, per quod nos salvat Deus, & per quem effundat Spiritum Sanctum in nos ad nostri regenerationem & renovationem. Cau- sa organica ex parte nostri est fides, quam opera- tur in nobis Spiritus Sanctus, cum nos regenerat, quæque spei voce comprehenditur, vel præsup- ponitur, quia sperare phrasi Scripturæ est con- fidere, aut certe fidem ante se requirit, nec hæ- reditas cœlestis sperari potest, nisi per fidem in Christum Salvatorem: quem Salvatorem nostrum habemus vel nobis vindicamus unice per fidem, quemadmodum unice per fidem etiam tum ju- stificamur, Rom. III. 28. tum salvamur, Eph. II. 8. Causa itaque justificationis finalis est hæreditas vitæ æternæ. Superest causa formalis, quæ voce ipsa δικαιωθέντες, utpote quæ forensis est, & abso- lutionem à peccato & pœna peccati infert, Rom. VIII. 33. significatur. Ita mira, sed illustri brevi- tate, divino prorsus artificio exhibuit Apostolus universum justificationis & salutis nostræ myste- rium verbis maxime emphaticis & augustis. Ideo ut plena hæc fide suscipiamus, addit ejus confir- mationem & monita de doctrina maxime incul- canda in Ecclesia.

PARS II. Commonefactio de doctrina, inprimis incul- canda, deque iis, quæ fugienda.

## 3:8
Verse 8. Πιστὸς ὁ λόγος) Namely that which follows, as in 1 Tim. I. 15, III. 1, IV. 9, 2 Tim. II. 11. That which follows, however, is that it behooves those who believe in God to take care to excel in honest labors. Καὶ περὶ τούτων βούλομαί σε διαβεβαιοῦσθαι) That is, concerning these things I wish you to speak with the greatest asseveration, as concerning most certain matters. Διαβεβαιοῦσθαι in 1 Tim. I. 7 is to speak with certainty, see Heb. VI. 16, בצמיתת.

Grotius, however, rashly draws these to the following things, which entirely pertain to the preceding ones. The reason for the passages which are compared is different, namely 1 Tim. I. 15, chap. III. 1. For here the particle καὶ occurs, which teaches that the phrase πιστὸν τὸν λόγον should not begin here: for a discourse is not accustomed to begin with a copulative particle. Indeed, the passage 1 Tim. IV. v. 9, 10 teaches the contrary, if it is held as a parallel; namely, that those things which are adorned with the eulogy λόγῳ πιστῷ have preceded, not followed. The passage 2 Tim. II. v. 11 also, because of the particle γὰρ, refers itself at the same time to the preceding things and confirms their certainty, that no one is crowned unless he competes lawfully, v. 5, which Paul had taught by his own example how it ought to be done, verse 10. Now, therefore, he confirms that word, that it is faithful, because if we suffer with him and live with him, if we endure, we shall also reign with him. And the words of the Apostle in this place clearly teach that these things pertain to the preceding ones. And concerning these things

I desire you to affirm, where we do not disapprove of the translation of Grotius, though the copulative particle omitted by him has been added: This is a faithful saying. I also want you to speak about these things with the greatest assurance, as about most certain matters. This doctrine, therefore, concerning the Word of the Gospel, which by the grace of God has shone upon us, concerning the kindness, φιλανθρωπίᾳ, and mercy of GOD the Father, concerning the merit of Christ the Savior, concerning Jesus Christ, and his person and office, concerning the Holy Spirit and his benefits, regeneration and renewal, concerning the sacrament of baptism, concerning the conversion and justification of the sinful man before God, concerning salvation and the hope of the inheritance of eternal life, are most certain and must be taught most strongly in the Church, which the Apostle here seriously inculcates to Titus, and in the person of Titus to all faithful Teachers of the Word, to whom πιστὸς ὁ λόγος should be most highly commended.

A faithful saying, as the promises made to David are πιστὰ, faithful, Acts 13:34, and Rev. 21:5, ch. 22:6, the words are faithful and true. Blessed Balduinus beautifully compares here the Hebrew word נאם, which should not be explained so much verbally, 'the Lord said,' or 'the saying of the Lord,' as nominally: 'The certain saying of the Lord,' observing from the opinion of certain Doctors that this word in the scriptures is attributed to and befits only GOD and those divinely inspired.

That they who have believed in God may be careful to maintain good works) Thus he begins the sentence here with ἵνα, just as he does with ὅτι, 1 Tim. 1:15 and 4:10. Προΐστασθαι with the dative signifies to preside, as in 1 Tim. 3:5. To preside over good works, however, is nothing other than to make one's house a workshop of some honest craft, to exercise all one's own in honest labors, not to lead the life of pimps, parasites, actors, soothsayers, or anything similar. The same sentence repeated below in verse 14, with the addition εἰς τὰς ἀναγκαίας χρείας, shows us this sense. These things are opposed to what he had just said about the Cretans: 'Slow bellies.'

The reason is added why he wants Titus to speak about these things μετὰ βεβαιώσεως, with the greatest assurance, namely, that trusting in God, in the divine grace and mercy which he had said had shone forth, embracing it with true confidence of heart, and relying solely upon it, they may be wise, or prudent from the information and παιδείᾳ of the saving grace of GOD, Tit. 2:11, and from the instruction of Titus and other heralds of the Word, to preside over good works. The reason is thus twofold: The first is trust in God, or saving faith: for these things are related to πιστὸς ὁ λόγος, the faithful saying of the Gospel, and πίστις, or the faith which is applied to the Word of the Gospel: according to that Vulgate saying: Word and faith are related. The second is the pursuit of good works. Therefore, the sentence is not begun here by ἵνα. It had already been handed down what the Apostle wants to be done by Titus. The final cause of his doctrine is now subjoined; so that the Word of the Gospel may be received by faith, and that that saving grace of God may excite and inflame the hearers to the pursuit of true piety. Nor indeed is the exercise in honest labors denoted only by this phrase ἵνα φροντίζωσι καλῶν ἔργων προΐστασθαι: but since καλὰ ἔργα are good works in general, to which those justified by grace, through the operation of the Holy Spirit who is poured out abundantly upon them—by whom they are not only regenerated to faith but also renewed to true holiness—ought to apply themselves. Whence Blessed Luther elegantly rendered it: 'This I want you to teach firmly, so that those who have become believers in GOD may now be found in the state of good works.' You have thus καλὰ ἔργα in Matt. 5:16, 1 Tim. 5:10, 25, ch. 6:18, Tit. 2:7, 14, Heb. 10:24, 1 Pet. 2:12, Matt. 26:10, Mark 14:6. John 10:32, nor do these words easily occur otherwise in the New Testament. We shall see later about the passage below in verse 14. And so this exhortation is general, because those who believe in God had to be warned about good works, which must be joined with faith and inculcated jointly by Teachers, whose doctrine ought to be most occupied in teaching the article of justification, as it is that upon which the Church stands or falls, as Blessed Luther used to say, and in the exhortation or encouragement to the pursuit of good works, which is most effectively sought from the Apostolic doctrine of justification. This sense is confirmed by the argument from honesty and utility subjoined; as well as the antithesis concerning the avoiding of foolish and useless questions from the opposite side, and the avoiding of heretics who pervert that Evangelical doctrine. In which sense I see that Interpreters also easily agree, except that Chrysostom and Theophylact interpret these specifically concerning beneficence, which in our opinion is not excluded, but pertains entirely to τὰ καλὰ ἔργα. 'This which he says,' says Jerome, 'a faithful saying, is to be joined to the preceding things: in which he had premised that, being justified by his grace, we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life. For the saying concerning the inheritance of GOD and the hope of eternal life is worthy of faith. Whence it is necessary for one not to be doubtful, not fearing, but to believe it himself, and to confirm it so that others may believe. But those who have believed these things to be true, it is necessary that they have a care for good works.' Regarding the word φροντίζωσι, Beza says: 'That is, let them strive with the greatest zeal.' For true charity toward God and neighbor does not grow cold, and the struggle between flesh and blood is great and very difficult, as the Apostle himself testifies, Rom. 7:24. Regarding the phrase καλῶν ἔργων προΐστασθαι, which he interpreted as 'to lead by doing good': That is, he says, to be leaders in a holy and upright life, just as in Quintilian, Sulpitius is the leader of law, and in Pliny, Plato is the leader of wisdom. The Vulgate and Erasmus, 'to preside over good works,' is quite obscure, although προΐστασθαι is taken this way in 1 Tim. 3:4. But the notation of this verb is varied. The Syriac seems to have accepted it in such a way that in Latin it is said to 'perform' something, he who accomplishes it: which I do not think is said by this verb in Greek. Some explain the Apostle's phrase thus: 'That they may strive to precede, or to excel others in good works, just as it befits professors of good works.' But in the judgment of Estius, the Greek does not easily admit this sense. Estius explains it thus: This doctrine, he says, not only ensures the integrity of the faith, but also contributes to this, that those who have believed in God as the Author of salvation may take care of good works, and be solicitous that they not only practice them, but also promote them with all zeal, as exactors and overseers of works. For if we have been regenerated, renewed, and justified by the grace of God, we must certainly henceforth walk in newness of life and works of righteousness, so that we may attain the promised salvation.

These things are good and profitable to men) These are honorable in themselves, as Hesiod says: Work is no disgrace. They bring utility to this life. See Sir. 38, verse 36, and what is said there.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Πιστὸς ὁ λόγος) Nempe id, quod sequitur, ut 1. Tim. I. 15. III. 1. IV. 9. 2. Tim. II. 11. Id autem, quod sequitur, est, oportere eos, qui Deo credunt, curam gerere, ut præsint honestis laboribus. Καὶ περὶ τούτων βούλομαί σε διαβεβαιοῦσθαι) Id est, de his volo te loqui cum maxima asseveratione, ut de rebus cer- tissimis. Διαβεβαιοῦσθαι 1. Tim. I. 7. est loqui μετὰ βε- βαιώσεως, vide Ebr. VI. 16. בצמיתת.

Temere autem hæc trahit Grotius ad sequen- tia, quæ omnino ad præcedentia pertinent. Lo- corum, quæ conferuntur, alia est ratio, nempe 1. Tim. I. 15. cap. III. 1. Nam hic particula καὶ oc- currit, quæ docet, non hic ordiendum esse πιστὸν τὸν λόγον: Non enim oratio à particula copulati- va incipere solet. Locus vero 1. Tim. IV. v. 9. 10. contrarium docet, si parallelus habeatur; nimi- rum præcessisse ea, quæ λόγῳ πιστῷ elogio ornan- tur, non consequi. Locus etiam 2. Tim. II. v. 11. ob particulam γὰρ ad præcedentia simul se re- fert, eorumque certitudinem confirmat, quod nemo coronetur, nisi legitime certet, v. 5. quod quomodo fieri debeat, exemplo suo docuerat Paulus vers. 10. Jam ergo λόγον, sermonem istum confirmat, quod πιστὸς sit, quia si compatimur & convivemus, si sustinemus, etiam conregnabimus. Et docent hoc loco id verba Apostoli luculenter, quod ad præcedentia hæc pertineant. Καὶ περὶ τούτων

βέλομαί σε διαβεβαιȣσθαι, ubi non improbamus translationem Grotii, addita tamen ab ipso præ- termissa particula copulativa: Sermo hic fidelis est. Etiam de his volo te loqui cum maxima asse- curatione, ut de rebus certissimis. Hæc ergo do- ctrina de Verbo Evangelii, quod gratia Dei illuxit nobis, de benignitate, φιλανθρωπίᾳ & misericor- dia DEI Patris, de merito Christi Servatoris, de Jesu Christo, ejusque persona, & officio, de Spi- ritu Sancto, ejusque beneficiis, regeneratione & renovatione, de baptismatis sacramento, de con- versione ac justificatione hominis peccatoris coram Deo, de salute & spe hæreditatis vitæ æternæ, cer- tissimæ, & maxime tradendæ sunt in Ecclesia, quod hic serio inculcat Tito Apostolus, & in Titi persona omnibus Verbi fidelibus Doctori- bus, quibus πιστὸς ὁ λόγος sit quam commenda- tissimus.

Πιστὸς ὁ λόγος, ut promissa Davidi fa- cta πιστὰ fidelia, Act. XIII. v. 34. & Apoc. XXI. 5. cap. XXII. 6. οἱ λόγοι πιστοὶ καὶ ἀληθινοὶ. Pulchre hic confert B. Balduinus vocem נאם Ebræorum, quæ non tam verbaliter exponenda sit, dixit Do- minus, vel dictum Domini; quam nominaliter: Sermo certus Domini ex sententia Doctorum quorundam observans vocem hanc in scripturis tantum DEO & divinitus inspiratis tribui, & convenire.

Ἵνα φροντίζωσι καλῶν ἔργων προΐστασθαι οἱ πεπιστευκότες τῷ Θεῷ) Ita hic per ἵνα inchoat sententiam, quomodo per ὅτι, 1. Tim. I. 15. & IV. 10. Προΐστασθαι cum Dativo significat præesse, ut 1. Tim. III. 5. Præesse autem bonis operibus non est aliud, quam domum suam facere hone- sti alicujus opificii officinam, omnes suos exercere in la- boribus honestis, non agere vitam lenonum, parasitorum, scenicorum, aruspicum, aut his similem. Hunc sensum no- bis monstrat eadem sententia repetita infra 14. cum addi- tamento εἰς τὰς ἀναγκαίας χρείας. Opponuntur hæc ei, quæ modo de Cretenfibus dixerat: Γαστέρες ἀργαί.

Additur causa, cur velit de istis loqui Titum μετὰ βεβαιώσεως cum maxima assecuratione, ut nempe confidentes Deo, divinæ gratiæ & mise- ricordiæ, quam illuxisse dixerat, vera cordis fidu- cia amplectentes, eique unice innitentes, sapi- ant, vel prudentes sint ex informatione ac παι- δείᾳ gratiæ DEI salutiferæ, Tit. II. v. 11. & in- stitutione Titi, aliorumque Verbi præconum, præesse bonis operibus. Causa ita gemina invol- vitur: Prior est fiducia in Deum, vel fides salvi- fica: Hæc enim relata sunt πιστὸς ὁ λόγος, fidelis sermo Evangelii, & πίστις vel fides, quæ adhibe- tur Verbo Evangelii: juxta illud Vulgatum: Ver- bum & fides sunt relata. Altera est, studium bo- norum operum. Non ergo hic inchoatur per ἵνα sententia. Traditum jam erat, quod velit fieri à Tito Apostolus. Causa autem finalis ejus do- c衍生 jam subjungitur; ut tum fide suscipiatur Verbum Evangelii, tum gratia illa Dei σωτήριος excitet atque inflammet auditores ad veræ pieta- tis studium. Nec verò hac phrasi ἵνα φροντίζωσι καλῶν ἔργων προΐστασθαι tantum denotatur exerci- tium in laboribus honestis: sed quum καλὰ ἔργα sint opera bona in genere, quibus justificati per gratiam ope Spiritus Sancti, qui largiter effunditur in eosdem, per quem non tantum regenerantur ad fidem, sed etiam renovantur ad veram sanctita- tem, studere debeant. Unde B. Lutherus elegan- ter reddidit: Solches will ich, daß du fest lehrest, auff daß die, so an GOTT glaubig sind worden, nun im Stand guter Werck funden werden. Ha- bes ita καλὰ ἔργα Matth. V. 16. 1. Tim. V. 10. 25. cap. VI. 18. Tit. II. 7. 14. Ebr. X. 24. 1. Petr. II. 12. Matth. XXVI. 10. Marc. XIV. 6. Joh. X. 32. nec facile aliter in Novo Testamento voces hæ oc- currunt. De loco infra 14. postea videbimus. Et generalis ergo est haec exhortatio, quia monen- di erant de bonis operibus credentes in Deum, quae cum fide oportet conjuncta esse, & conjun- ctim a Doctoribus inculcari, quorum doctrina maxime occupari debeat in tradendo articulo de justificatione, utpote, qui stantis & cadentis est Ecclesiae, ut ajebat B. Lutherus, & in paraenesi vel adhortatione ad studium bonorum operum, quae efficacissime petitur e doctrina Apostolica de ju- stificatione. Quem sensum confirmat argumen- tum ab honestate & utilitate subjunctum; necnon antithesis de fugiendis ex adverso quaestionibus stultis & inutilibus, ac vitandis haereticis, doctri- nam illam Evangelicam pervertentibus. In quo sensu video etiam facile convenire Interpretes, nisi quod Chrysostomus & Theophylactus haec in specie de beneficentia, quae nostra sententia non excluditur, sed ad τὰ καλὰ ἔργα omnino perti- net, interpretentur. Hoc quod ait, inquit Hiero- nymus, fidelis sermo, ad superiora jungendum est: in quibus praemiserat, ut justificati illius gratia hae- redes efficiamur secundum spem vitae aeternae. Di- gnus enim fide super haereditate DEI sermo, & su- per spe vitae aeternae. Unde oportet de his non dubi- um, non timentem & ipsum credere, &, ut credant caeteri, confirmare. Qui autem ista vera esse cre- diderint, necesse est, ut curam habeant bonorum operum. De voce φροντίζωσι Beza: Id est, summo studio enitantur. Nec enim friget vera in Deum & proximum charitas, & magnum ac perdifficile est certamen inter carnem & sanguinem, teste ipso Apostolo, Rom. VII. 24. De phrasi καλῶν ἔργων προίσασθαι, quam interpretatus est, bene agendo praecire: Id est, inquit, sancta & recta vita antisti- tes esse, ut apud Quintilianum Sulpitius juris, & apud Plinium Plato sapientiae Antistes. Vulgatus & Erasmus bonis operibus praeesse, obscure admo- dum, quamvis προίσασθαι sic accipiatur 1. Tim. III. vers. 4. Sed varia est hujus verbi notatio. Syrus videtur sic illud accepisse, ut Latine dicitur ali- quid praestare, qui illud efficit: quod non puto Grae- ce hoc verbo dici. Nonnulli phrasin Apostoli sic explicant: Ut studeant praecedere, sive prae aliis eminere bonis operibus, sicuti decet operum bonorum professores. Sed hunc sensum, Estio Judice, Graeca non facile admittunt. Estius ita exponit: Non tantum, inquit, haec doctrina prae- stat integritatem fidei, verum etiam eo conducit, ut qui in Deum tanquam salutis Autorem credide- runt, curam habeant bonorum operum, ac soliciti sint, ut ea non exe:ceant solum, sed etiam omni stu- dio promoveant, tanquam operum exactores & prae- fecti. Si enim per gratiam Dei regenerati, reno- vati & justificati sumus, utique deinceps ambulan- dum nobis est in novitate vitae & operibus justitiae, ut promissam salutem assequamur.

Ταῦτά ἐστι τὰ καλὰ κὰὶ ὠφέλιμα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις) Haec per se honesta sunt, sicut ait Hesiodus: Ἔργον δ' οὐδὲν ὄνειδος. Ea utilitatem ad hanc vitam afferunt. Vid. Sir. XXXIIX. vers. 36. & ibi dicta.

## 3:9
Verse 9. But foolish questions.

Vain questions, contributing nothing to piety, 2 Tim. II, verse 23. מבעיות to the Rabbis.

And genealogies) Those various emanations of properties or מדות, the business of idle Jews. See 1 Timothy I, verse 4.

And contentions and strivings about the law) That is, contentions arising from legal strivings, disputes born from the diverse interpretation of the places of the law, 2 Tim. II. 23. 1 Tim. VI. 4. The Jews of Ephesus and Crete were suffering from the same diseases.

Avoid) See regarding this word 2 Tim. II. 16.

These are those things good and profitable to men, Beza rendered. Thus these are referred to those things which were to be delivered in the Church, both as to the doctrine of faith, then as to a Christian life worthy of the faith: To which are opposed accordingly foolish questions about faith and genealogies, as well as legal contentions and strife, which contribute nothing to a Christian life, inasmuch as they are neither good, but μάταιοι [vain], nor useful, but ἀνωφελεῖς [unprofitable]. These things can also be referred to the admonition, concerning τὰ καλὰ ἔργα [good works] in particular, or to the good works themselves: As Jerome says: For it is necessary that they have a care for good works, which, when fulfilled and performed with all zeal, are good and useful to believers. And Theophylact: Those very things which are rightly done are right, and very profitable. But the former sense is more coherent. Nor is there considered here only the honesty and utility of the present life, but primarily what is both becoming or beautiful with respect to the Christian faith, and useful to believers, so that they may not fall from the heavenly inheritance, cf. 1 Tim. IV. 16. Tit. II. 10., These things are good and useful to men, to believe in GOD, and to order one's life by his laws, says Theodoret here. We have spoken of others in the epistle to Timothy. For the unconverted, as well Jews as Gentiles, had their own τὸ καλὸν [good]. The former placed it in the traditions of the elders, in the external noise of ceremonies, in bodily discipline, sacrifices, etc. The latter in the external splendor and pomp of virtue. For they did not want to seem to be contemners of virtue: But they were grasping at a shadow instead of the truth. The Apostle proposes to the faithful another τὸ καλὸν, which consists not in the appearance of virtue, but in its truth, says Grotius here. As to τὸ ὠφέλιμον [the useful], he could, he says, have said that they were thus useful for the glory of God, Matt. V. 13. He does not rise so high, content to have pointed a finger at the utility that would return to men from it; for he says also useful to men. Namely, first to those to whom they do good. For they are much helped by the good works of the pious, and that both corporally and spiritually. For they are relieved in their necessities, and receive consolation. Then to others who see. For they are instructed by example unto piety, and are often won over without a word, as Peter testifies 1 Pet. III. 1. 2. Finally to those who do them. For their faith shines forth, but the reward, indeed gratuitous and great, is laid up in the heavens.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Μωρὰς δὲ ζητήσεις.

Quaestiones inanes, ad pietatem nihil facientes, 2. Tim. II. vers. 23. מבעיות Rabbinis.

Καὶ γενεαλογίας) Varias illas emanationes proprie- tatum sive מדות, Judaeorum otiosorum negotia. Vid. 1. Timoth. I. vers. 4.

Καὶ ἔρεις κὰὶ μάχας νομικὰς) Id est, ἔρεις ἐκ μαχῶν νο- μικῶν, lites ex diversa locorum legis interpretatione natas, 2. Tim. II. 23. 1. Tim. VI. 4. Iisdem morbis laborabant Judaei Ephesini & Cretae.

Περιίσασο) Vide de hac voce 2. Tim. II. 16.

Haec illa sunt bona & utilia hominibus, reddidit Beza. Ita referuntur haec ad ea, quae traden- da erant in Ecclesia, tum qua fidei doctrinam, tum qua vitam Christianam fide dignam: Quibus opponuntur proinde quaestiones stultae de fide & genealogiis, necnon contentiones ac pugna legales, quae nihil faciunt ad vitam Christianam, utpote quae nec bonae, sed μάταιοι, nec utiles, sed ἀνωφε- λεῖς. Referri etiam haec possunt ad monitum, τὰ καλὰ ἔργα in specie concernens, vel ad ipsa bo- na opera: Uti Hieronymus: Necesse est enim, ut curam bonorum operum habeant, quae adimpleta, & omni studio perpetrata, sunt bona utiliaque cre- dentibus. Et Theophylactus: Ea ipsa, quae recte ge- runtur, recta sunt, & admodum profutura. Sed concinnior est prior sensus. Nec vero spectatur hic solum honestas & utilitas praesentis vitae, sed imprimis quid & condecens vel pulchrum sit fidei Christianae respectu, & utile credentibus, ut ne excidant haereditate coelesti, conf. 1. Tim. IV. 16. Tit. II. 10., Haec sunt bona & utilia homi- nibus, DEO credere, & ejus legibus vitam in- stituere, ait hic Theodoretus. De aliis diximus in epist. ad Timoth. Habebant enim non conversi tam Judaei, quam Gentiles suum τὸ καλὸν. Illi po- nebant in traditionibus majorum, in externo cere- moniarum strepitu, in disciplina corporali, sacrifi- ciis &c. Isti in externo virtutis splendore atq; pom- pa. Nolebant enim videri virtutis contemptores: Sed umbram apprehendebant pro veritate. Aposto- lus fidelibus aliud τὸ καλὸν proponit, quod consistit in virtutis non specie, sed veritate, inquit hic Cro- tius. Quod ad τὸ ὠφέλιμον, poterat, inquit, di- cere, quod ita essent utilia ad Dei gloriam, Matth. V. 13. Non eo usque assurgit, contentus digitum intendisse in utilitatem ad homines inde redituram; ait enim & hominibus utilia. Nempe primo illis, quibus benefaciunt. Illi enim multum juvantur piorum bonis operibus, idque tum corporaliter tum spiritualiter. Sublevantur enim in necessitatibus, & consolationem accipiunt. Deinde aliis qui vi- dent. Illi enim instruuntur exemplo ad pietatem, & saepe lucrifunt sine verbo, teste Petro 1. Petr. III. 1. 2. Denique illis, qui faciunt. Illorum enim fi- des clarescit, merces autem gratuita quidem illa & magna reposita est in caelis.

## 3:10
Vers. 10. A heretical man) The Syrian has here αἱρεσιώτην, the Arab גאהל, that is, ignorant. The word αἵρεσις in itself is neutral, where it is taken in a bad sense, it signifies the same as σχίσμα [schism], except that that generality of schism is contracted by the word αἵρεσις to those parties which are made from a diversity of opinions. Therefore, a heretic here is he who makes parties through opinion about the Church, who disputes to the end that he may prepare disciples for himself, with unity despised: who is זקן מורה [a rebellious elder], as the Hebrews speak, פריש [Pharisee] as the Rabbis, from a word which signifies appearance.

After a first and second admonition reject) He does not say excommunicate. For they themselves of their own accord desert the communion. Therefore such are to be warned once and again according to the precept of Christ, Matt. XVIII. 16. 17. 18. If that does not avail, more familiar association with them is to be broken off, as 1 Cor. V. vers. 9. Παραιτοῦ, that is, avoid. In the Glossary παραιτοῦμαι, I avoid.

We have distinguished schism and heresy elsewhere. Jerome in this place: They think that between heresy and schism there is this difference, that heresy has a perverse dogma, schism is separated from the Church on account of Episcopal dissension, which indeed in the beginning can be understood in some part; However, there is no schism that does not invent for itself some heresy, so that it may appear to have rightly withdrawn from the Church. The opposition teaches that a heretical man is said in the present to be one who errs in the faith or in those principal doctrines which are to be delivered in the Church, such as those previously recounted. A schismatic is one who for light causes rends the unity of the Church. Therefore, a heretic after one and a second νουθεσία [admonition], which some render correction, others a warning, which is without rebuke, which the latter Jerome prefers, but the former seems to agree more with the Greek word, Rom. XV. 14. Ephes. IV. 1. 2. Thess. III. 15. (νυθεσία is as it were a putting back of the lost mind) He warns that he is to be avoided, both because Titus ought to flee the same, and also to warn others to flee. Therefore it can also be done with the threat of excommunication. Certainly, it is not excluded here. For even if such people of their own accord desert the communion, and virtually exclude themselves from it, it is nevertheless in the interest of others that they be formally excluded from the communion of the Church through excommunication, so that they may be guarded against and avoided. But the Apostle wishes that one and a second νυθεσία precede, because he is not to be rejected unless it has first been attempted whether he can be recalled to the way of truth. Nor can he be held for obstinate unless information with due warning or correction has preceded. After one and a second correction, which namely Jerome warning, it is not enough to correct or warn only once one who has been depraved by some error, but a second teaching must also be applied to him: that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand. Augustine book IV against the Donatists ch. 16. If anyone, he says, thinks the same thing about Christ that Photinus opined, and believes this to be the Catholic faith, I do not yet say he is a heretic, unless he prefers to resist the manifested doctrine of the Catholic faith, and chooses that which he held: namely, materially such a one is a heretic, but not formally. Therefore Augustine book XVIII of the City of God ch. 57. Those who in the Church of Christ think something morbid and depraved, if, when corrected so that they may think what is sound and right, they resist contumaciously, and do not want to amend their pestiferous and deadly dogmas, but persist in defending them, they are heretics: formally, that is, such. Chrysostom: Just as, he says, it is great sloth and great negligence to despise those whom we do not despair of being changed for the better: So to strive to cure those who languish desperately is of huge folly and extreme madness: For from this, more audacity and rashness is added to them. Concerning the insipid proof of capital punishment produced from this passage by a certain senior Papal theologian in the Council, see Erasmus on this passage and B. Balduinus: How much Justin and Cornel are ashamed of it, as if it were 'devita', take it from 'de vita', and it were a Latin word 'devitare'.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Αἱρετικὸν ἄνθρωπον) αἱρεσιώτην habet hic Sy- rus, Arabs גאהל, id est, ignarum. Αἱρέσεως vox per se media, ubi in malam partem sumitur, significat idem, quod σχίσμα, nisi quod illa generalitas σχίσματ@ voce αἱρέ- σεως contrahitur ad eas partes, quae fiunt ex opinionum di- versitate. Est ergo hic haereticus is, qui per opinionem de Ecclesia partes facit, qui in id disputat, ut sibi disci- pulos paret, unitate contempta: qui est זקן מורה, ut loquuntur Ebraei, פריש ut Rabbini, à voce, quae speciem significat.

Μετὰ μίαν καὶ δευτέραν νουθεσίαν παραιτοῦ) Non dicit excommunica. Nam ipsi ultro communionem deserunt. Ergo tales monendi sunt semel atque iterum ex praece- pto Christi, Matth. XVII. 16. 17. 18. Id si non prosit, ab- rumpenda cum eis familiarior consuetudo, ut 1. Cor. V. vers. 9. Παραιτοῦ, id est, ἀποτρέφου. In Glossario παραι- τοῦμαι, evito.

Schisma & haeresin alias distinximus. Hierony- mus hoc loco: Inter haeresin & schisma hoc esse arbitrantur, quod haeresis perversum dogma habeat, schisma propter Episcopalem dissensionem ab Ec- clesia separetur, quod quidem in principio aliqua ex parte intelligi potest; Caeterum nullum schisma non sibi aliquam confingit haeresin, ut recte ab Ec- clesia recessisse videatur. Oppositio docet, haere- ticum hominem in praesenti dici, qui in fide vel doctrinis illis praecipuis, quae in Ecclesia tra- dendae sunt, quales antea recensitae sunt, errat. Schismaticus est, qui ob leves causas unitatem Ecclesiae scindit. Haereticum ergo post unam & alteram νουθεσίαν, quod alii correptionem reddunt, alii commonitionem, quæ absque increpatione sit, quod posterius præfert Hieronymus, prius autem Græcæ voci magis convenire videtur, Rom. XV. 14. Ephes. IV. 1. 2. Thess. III. 15. (νυθεσία est quasi mentis amissæ repositio) Devitandum esse mo- net, tum quod Titus eundem fugere debeat, tum alios etiam commonefacere, ut fugiant. Ea er- go etiam cum comminatione excommunicatio- nis fieri potest. Certe ea hic non excluditur. Et- iamfi enim tales ultro communionem deserant, & semetipsos ab eadem excludant virtualiter, in- terest tamen aliorum, ut formaliter è commu- nione Ecclesiæ per excommunicationem ipsi ex- cludantur, ut caveri & vitari possint. Vult autem Apostolus, ut una atque altera νυθεσία præcedat, quia rejiciendus non est, nisi prius tentatum fue- rit, an revocari possit in viam veritatis. Nec ha- beri potest pro pertinaci, nisi præcesserit infor- matio cum debita admonitione, vel correptione. Post unam atque alteram correptionem, quod scil. Hieronymo monente, non sufficiat tantum semel cum corripi aut commoneri, qui aliquo sit deprava- tus errore, sed & secunda sit ei adhibenda doctrina: ut in ore duorum vel trium testium stet omne ver- bum. Augustinus l. IV. contr. Donat. c. 16. Si ali- quis, inquit, hoc idem sentiat de Christo, quod Pho- tinus opinatus est, & hoc credit esse fidem Catholi- cam, eum nondum dico esse hæreticum, nisi mani- festata doctrina Catholicæ fidei resistere maluerit, & illud, quod tenebat elegerit: scilicet materiali- ter quidem talis hæreticus est, non autem forma- liter. Ideo Augustinus libr. XIIX. de Civ. Dei cap. 57. Qui in Ecclesia Christi morbidum aliquid pravumque sapiunt, si correpti, ut sanum rectumque sapiant, resistant contumaciter, suaque pestifera & mortifera dogmata emendare nolunt, sed defensare persistunt, hæretici sunt: formaliter scilicet tales. Chrysostomus: Quemadmodum, inquit, magna de- sidia, magnaque socordia est, eos despicere, quos im- mutandos in melius non desperamus: Ita eos, qui desperabiliter languent, curare contendere, stultitiæ ingentis est, atque extrema dementiæ: Quippe ex hoc plus illis audaciæ & temeritatis adjicitur. De insulsa probatione capitalis supplicii ex hoc loco à quodam Pontificio Seniore Theologo in Con- cilio producto vid. Erasmus in h. l. & B. Baldui- nus: Quantopere ejus pudeat Justin. & Cornel. quasi devita sit, de vita tolle, & Latinum verbum sit devitare.

## 3:11
Verse 11. Εἰδὼς ὅτι ἐξέστραπται ὁ τοιοῦτος) And here the passive is used for the reciprocal; ἐξέστραπται is the same as ἐξεστραμμένος ἐστιν. אִישׁ תַּהְפֻּכֹת from Deut. XXXII. 20. The Latins also call such a one perverse: a depraved mind.

Καὶ ἁμαρτάνει ὢν αὐτοκατάκριτος) He knows himself that he is sinning. Within, he cannot but condemn himself. Why? Because he affirms many things about divine matters without revelation, and he does this so that he may make a party for himself out of the Church, whose peace he ought to have consulted, in which he may reign. Heresy is the madness of an obstinate mind in the Justinian Code, Book II, on the supreme Trinity. A heretic, according to Augustine, is one who, for the sake of some temporal advantage and especially for his own glory and leadership, either creates or follows false and new opinions. Αὐτοκατάκριτος, in the Jerusalem Talmud, under the title of the Sanhedrin, מתחיב. Justin to Zenas: For I would say that it seems to me that everyone who is worldly in his mind, and who is outside of right things, is self-condemned, knowing what he does by design, and knowing the war within himself, but not drawing peace into his bowels. Tertullian translates αὐτοκατάκριτον as 'sibi damnatum', that is, in his own judgment.

Why he is to be avoided after the first and second admonition, (so Jerome has it) He gives the reasons, saying: Because such a one is subverted, and sins, being condemned by himself. For he who, having been admonished once and twice, does not wish to be corrected, adding to his error, thinks the one correcting him is in error, and on the contrary preparing himself for battles of words, when he wishes to gain profit from the one by whom he is taught. For such a one (according to B. Balduinus) is a subverted man, that is, clearly desperate and lost, in whom, in recalling him to the way, effort and oil are wasted: He is also ἐυτοκατάκριτος, condemned by himself, partly because he is convicted of error in his own conscience, although he fears to confess it publicly; partly also, because he separates himself of his own accord from the assembly of the faithful, having been removed by no one as yet. For as Cyprian writes in epistle LXXV, it is manifest that all have condemned themselves, and before the day of judgment have pronounced an inexcusable sentence against themselves. Heretics, as Jerome says, bring sentence upon themselves, withdrawing from the Church by their own choice, which withdrawal seems to be a condemnation of their own conscience. Chrysostom asks here: How does the Apostle command that these be avoided, when he has ordered that those who contradict be refuted? And he answers: This concerns those who pervert themselves. For, he says, we shall never be able to gain those who are perverted, and who sin not out of ignorance, but out of perversity of judgment. What if these have also infected others with the poisons of their doctrine? It is necessary to stand against them, and to fight, and to overcome them with great fortitude and authority. If, therefore, such a necessity has been proclaimed, and you see others being corrupted by such a plague, now take care that you do not remain silent, but stop the mouths of these, bearing the care of those who are perishing.

PART III. The summoning of Titus concerning the arrival.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Εἰδὼς ὅτι ἐξέστραπται ὁ τοιοῦτος) Et hic passi- vum est pro reciproco ἐξέστραπται idem quod ἐξεστραμμένος ἐστιν. אִישׁ תַּהְפֻּכֹת ex Deut. XXXII. 20. Latini quo- que talem perversum vocant: prava mens.

Καὶ ἁμαρτάνει ὢν αὐτοκατάκριτος) Scit ipse se peccare. Intus non potest se non damnare. Cur? Quia de rebus divinis affirmat multa sine revelatione, & hoc facit, ut de Ecclesia, cujus paci consulere debebat, partem sibi faciat, in quo regnet. Est hæresis obstinationis animi dementia in Codice Justinianeo L. II. de summa Trinitate. Hæreti- cus Augustino, qui alicujus temporalis commodi & maxi- me gloriæ principatusque sui gratia falsas ac novas opi- niones vel gignit vel sequitur. Αὐτοκατάκριτος, Thalmu- de Hierosolymitana, titulo de synedrio, מתחיב. Justi- nus ad Zenam: Τὸ γὰρ ἐμοὶ δοκεῖν εἴποιμι ἂν, ὅτι πᾶς ὁ τὴν γνώμην κοσμικός, καὶ τὰ ὀρθὰ κατόπιν ἔξω γινόμενος, αὐτο- κατάκριτός ἐστι, εἰδὼς ὃ πράττει καθ' ἐπιτήδευσιν, καὶ γινώ- σκων μὲν τὸν ἐν αὐτῷ πόλεμον, τὴν δὲ εἰρήνην ἐν τοῖς σπλάγ- χνοις μὴ ἐπισπώμενος. Tertullianus αὐτοκατάκριτον vertit, sibi damnatum, id est, apud se.

Quare post primam & secundam correptionem devitandus sit, (ita habet Hieronymus) Reddit causas dicens: Quod subversus est ejusmodi, & peccat, cum sit à semetipso damnatus. Qui enim semel bisque correptus addito errore suo non vult corrigi, errare existimat corrigentem, & econtrario se ad pugnas verborum parans, cum vult lucrifa- cere, a quo docetur. Talis enim, (secundum B. Balduinum) est homo subversus, hoc est plane de- speratus, & perditus, in quo in viam revocando ope- ra & oleum perditur: Est etiam ἐυτοκατάκριτος, a seipso damnatus, partim, quia in conscientia sua erroris convictus est, licet publice fateri vereatur; partim etiam, quia sponte se a fidelium cœtu sejun- git, a nemine adhuc remotus. Nam ut Cyprianus epist. LXXV. scribit, omnes manifestum est a se- metipsis damnatos esse, & ante diem judicii inex- cusabilem sententiam adversus semetipsos dixisse. Hæretici, dicente Hieronymo, in semetipsos senten- tiam ferunt, suo arbitrio de Ecclesia recedentes, quæ recessio propria conscientiæ videtur esse damna- tio. Chrysostomus hic quærit: Quomodo vitandos hos esse præcipiat Apostolus, quum jusserit con- tradicentes redarguere? Et respondet: Hoc con- cernere eos, qui semetipsos pervertunt. Neque enim eos, inquit, lucrari unquam poterimus, qui perversi sunt, peccantque non ex ignorantia, sed ex perversitate sententiæ. Quid si isti alios quoque do- ctrina sua venenis infecerint, stare ex adverso opor- tet, atque pugnare, eosque magna cum fortitudi- ne atque autoritate revincere. Si igitur hujusmo- di indicta fuerit necessitas, viderisque alios hujus- modi tabe corrumpi, jam cave, ne taceas, sed ora istis obstrue, curam pereuntium gerens.

PARS III. Sollicitatio Titi de adventu.

## 3:12
Ver. 12. Ὅταν πέμψω ᾿Αρτεμᾶν πρός σε) A name contracted from Artemidorus. See what [is said] at the beginning of Luke.

Ἢ Τυχικὸν) He had been among the companions of Paul from Judea all the way to Rome, and from there he was sent by him now here, now there. See Acts XX. 4, Eph. VI. 21, Col. IV. 7, 2 Tim. IV. 12.

Σπύδασον ἐλθεῖν πρός με εἰς Νικόπολιν) Namely, from Crete into Epirus, where Paul hoped he would come, and as some think, he came in that middle time, between those two imprisonments of his.

Ἐκεῖ γὰρ κέκρικα παραχειμάσαι) κέκρικα [means] I have decided, as in Acts XX. verse 16. παραχειμάσαι here is, as in the Glossary, to winter, to pass the winter.

For the sake of which thing, says Theophylact, does he call Titus back to himself again, and tear him away from the work, to which he had entrusted such a great and most ample island to be cared for? Doubtless to benefit him more, and to render him more perfect. And no less to examine the work entrusted to him, and [to see] whether he had conducted himself rightly in handling it or not? I do not do this, he says, with Chrysostom as interpreter, to remove him from his study and ministry, but so that he may depart from me more instructed and more learned. For as to why he does not call him to himself for that reason, that he might lead him around with him and have him as a companion everywhere, hear what follows: For I have decided to winter there. He does not, therefore, summon Titus so much for his own sake, although he could also be of use to him, as for the sake of the Church: that he might confer with him in person about the state of the Cretan Churches, so that if any things required correction, they might be amended with mature counsel and remedy applied. Jerome therefore notes here the fatherly affections of the Apostle toward the Cretans: For he has need of Titus, he says, for the ministry of the Gospel: Yet he does not wish him to come to him before Artemas and Tychicus, his successor, have arrived. Concerning Nicopolis, it was said before. Nicopolis, says Theodoret, is a town of Thrace, and it is bordering on Macedonia. It is clear, therefore, that the epistle was written at the time when he was staying in Macedonia and Achaia. He does not say, however, 'I have decided to betake myself there, and to pass the winter there.' For he could have already been there, and [written] these things from Nicopolis, as the subscription holds; he says to Titus simply: 'I have decided to winter there,' which can be understood of the winter impending, or [the winter] begun, to be passed there further.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ὅταν πέμψω ᾿Αρτεμᾶν πρός σε) Contractum nomen ex Artemidoro. Vide quæ ad initium Lucæ.

Ἢ Τυχικὸν) Is inter Comites Pauli fuerat à Judæa Ro- mam usque, & inde ab eo nunc huc, nunc illuc mittebatur. Vid. Act. XX. 4. Eph. VI. 21. Col. IV. 7. 2. Tim. IV. 12.

Σπύδασον ἐλθεῖν πρός με εἰς Νικόπολιν) Nempe ex Cre- ta in Epirum, quo Paulus venturum se sperabat, & ut qui- dam putant, venit medio illo tempore, inter illas duas ejus vincturas.

Ἐκεῖ γὰρ κέκρικα παραχειμάσαι) κέκρικα constitui, ut Actor. XX. vers. 16. παραχειμάσαι hic est, ut in Glossario, hybernare, hyemem transigere.

Cujus rei gratia, inquit Theophylactus, iterum ad se revocat Titum, & ab opere divellit, cui tan- tam & tam amplissimam insulam mandasset curan- dam? Nimirum ut illi magis prodesse, & perfe- ctiorem reddere. Nec minus ut & creditum illi opus examinet & si in eo tractando recte sese gesse- rit, nec ne? Non inquit, Chrysostomo interprete, hoc ago, ut illum a suo removeam studio & mini- sterio, sed ut a me instructior doctiorque recedat. Nam quod illum non idcirco ad se vocet, ut secum circumducat, & ubique comitem habeat, audi quid sequitur: Illic enim hyemare decrevi. Non ergo tam sui causa Titum accersit, quamvis et- iam sibi usui esse possit, quam Ecclesiæ gratia: ut coram de statu Creticarum Ecclesiarum cum illo conferret, ut si quæ correptionem postula- rent, maturo consilio remedioque adhibito emen- darentur. Notat ergo hic Hieronymus paternos Apostoli erga Cretenses affectus: Necessarium enim, inquit, habet Titum in Evangelii ministe- rium: Tamen non eum ante ad se vult venire, nisi prius Artemas & Tychicus successor advenerit. De Nicopoli antea dictum. Nicopolis, inquit Theodo- retus, est oppidum Thraciæ, est autem finitimum Macedoniæ. Clarum ergo est, scriptam fuisse epi- stolam eo tempore, quo versabatur in Macedonia & Achaia. Non ait autem, constitui eo me con- ferre, ibique hyemem transigere. Poterat enim jam illic egisse, & hæc e Nicopoli, ut subscriptio habet, ad Titum simpliciter ait: Constitui ibi hybernare, quod intelligi potest de hyeme immi- nente, aut coepta ibi porro transigenda.

## 3:13
Ver. 13.

Ζηνᾶν τὸν νομικὸν) This name is contracted from Zenodorus: Νομικὸς ὁ νόμως εἰδὼς, a jurisperitus, a legiperitus in the Glossary. The Stoics defined νομικὸν as τὸν ἐξηγητικὸν τῶ νόμω. The Greeks also learned Roman law, such as Tryphoninus, Callistratus, Menander, Arcadius. Nor do I doubt that many from the Priests of the Law became Priests of Christ, because they saw all the precepts of the law to be contained eminently in that religion. Among them was Tertullian, full of the locutions of Roman law, although he is not the one whose [writings] we have in the digests.

But why should we either make Zenas from Zenodorus, or not believe what the common opinion holds, that Zenas was a Jew from those νομικοῖς who are known to be called so everywhere among the Jews? For the word νομικὴ is always used thus in the New Testament, never, so far as I know, concerning an expert in Roman law. Whence it is gathered that this Zenas was converted from Judaism to the faith of Christ, since he is called a legiperitus, that is, one versed in the law of Moses. Zenas the Doctor of the Law, says Jerome, from another place in Scripture, we cannot say who he was, except only this, that he himself, an Apostolic man, had that work which Apollos exercised, of building up the Churches of Christ. Chrysostom and Theophylact say he was an expert in the Jewish law.

Καὶ Ἀπολλὼ) I suspect that he too was with Paul in Rome: for the man in chains had need of many helpers in so great a city.

Σπεδαίως πρόπεμψον) They, if I am not mistaken, were going from Rome through Crete into Judea and Syria, at Paul's mission. Προπέμπειν here means to take care that they may set out, namely by providing, as follows, those things which are necessary for the journey, such as a ship, travel money, and provisions. Thus the word προπέμπειν is used in Wisdom XIX. 2, 1 Corinthians XVI. 11, and elsewhere. Σπεδαίως means diligently, earnestly in the Glossary. See Luke VII. 4 and Wisdom II. 6.

Ἵνα μηδὲν ἀυτοῖς λείπῃ) Namely, what is necessary for the journey, as we have already said; λείπῃ for ἐλλείπῃ, as in Luke XVIII. verse 22.

It is assumed without foundation that this epistle was written at Rome: there is no reason why we should depart from the subscription, which names Nicopolis. Apollos is likewise celebrated for his skill in the Scripture of the Old Testament; Acts XVIII. verse 24, who was held in high regard in the Corinthian Church, 1 Cor. I. verse 12, whom the Apostle joins to himself in the ministry of Christ, 1 Cor. III. 6, 'I planted, Apollos watered.' See also concerning him Acts XIX. 1, 1 Cor. XVI. verse 12. However, it does not appear that he and Zenas went from Rome to Syria and Judea at Paul's mission. Jerome renders πξόπεμψον as 'send forward,' with this added interpretation of the text: 'He commands Titus that, since they were about to sail from Crete to Greece, he should not let them lack provisions, but that they should have those things which are necessary for the journey.' For he thinks that Apollos, whom he calls Bishop of the Corinthians, because of the dissensions which were in Corinth, had crossed over to the neighboring island of Crete with Zenas the lawyer, and that, with the dissensions which had arisen in Corinth having been tempered by Paul's epistle, he had returned again to Corinth. Chrysostom says: 'Send them forward,' that is, that they may enjoy more abundant teaching. Our B. Hunnius says: 'He wishes these two to be sent forward for certain reasons, which he does not express here.' In general, we know that Paul, in missions of this kind, sought nothing else than to communicate his plans for planting churches with pious teachers, and in turn to hear their judgments. Wherefore he asks that these two be sent and diligently escorted, so that nothing may be lacking to them for completing that journey. Here Estius prefers the translation of others to the Vulgate, which is authentic through the Council of Trent: 'What we have, soli-' cite, send ahead, others translate better from the Greek, diligently escort or accompany. This duty is usually performed for departing guests; in which sense this Greek word occurs not rarely elsewhere, both in the Acts and in the Apostolic Epistles, where we always have 'deducere' [to escort] in Latin, so that it is a wonder that the Interpreter rendered it otherwise here. He therefore commends Zenas and Apollo to Titus, so that he may take care that travel provisions are supplied to them as they are about to travel through Crete, so that they lack nothing.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Ζηνᾶν τὸν νομικὸν) Est hoc nomen contractum ex Ze- nodoro: Νομικὸς ὁ νόμως εἰδὼς, jurisperitus, legiperitus in Glossario. Stoici νομικὸν definiebant τὸν ἐξηγητικὸν τῶ νό- μω. Jus Romanum etiam Graeci didicere, ut Tryphoni- nus, Callistratus, Menander, Arcadius. Neque dubito, quin multi ex Juris Sacerdotibus Christi Sacerdotes facti sint, quod in ea religione omnia juris praecepta viderent eminenter contineri. Inter eos fuit Tertullianus, plenus loquutionum juris Romani, quanquam non is est cujus quaedam in digestis habemus.

Cur vero vel e Zenodoro Zenam faciamus, vel non credamus, quod communis fert sententia, Zenam Judaeum fuisse e νομικοῖς illis, quos ita passim inter Judaeos appellari constat. Semper enim vox νομικὴ sic usurpatur in Novo Testam. nuspiam, quod sciam, de perito juris Romani. Unde a Judaismo ad Christi fidem Zenam hunc conversum fuisse colligitur, quandoquidem legis- peritus, hoc est, in lege Mosis versatus dicitur. Zenam legis Doctorem, inquit Hieronymus, de alio Scripturae loco, quis fuerit, non possumus dicere, nisi hoc tantum, quod & ipse Apostolicus vir id operis, quod Apollo exercuit, habuerit Christi Ecclesias ex- truendi. Legis Judaicae peritum fuisse dicunt Chrysostomus & Theophylactus.

Καὶ Ἀπολλὼ) Etiam hunc apud Paulum Romae fuisse suspicor: Multis enim adjutoribus in tanta urbe opus ha- bebat homo vinctus.

Σπεδαίως πρόπεμψον) Illi ni fallor, Roma per Cre- tam ibant in Judaeam & Syriam, Pauli missu. Προπέμπειν hic est curare, ut proficiscantur, nempe subministratis, ut sequitur, iis, quae ad iter necessaria, ut navi, viatico, ciba- riis. Sic vox προπέμπειν sumitur Sap. XIX. 2. 1. Corinth. XVI. 11. & alibi. Σπεδαίως sedulo, enixe in Glossario. Vide Luc. VII. 4. & Sap. II. 6.

Ἵνα μηδὲν ἀυτοῖς λείπῃ) Nempe quod ad iter sit necessa- rium, ut jam diximus, λείπῃ pro ἐλλείπῃ, quomodo Luc. XVIII. vers. 22.

Romae scriptam hanc epistolam citra funda- mentum supponitur: Causa nulla est, cur a sub- scriptione, quae Nicopolin nominat, discedamus. Apollo celebratur itidem a peritia in Scriptura Veteris Testamenti; Actor. XIIX. vers. 24. qui magni habitus est in Ecclesia Corinthiaca 1. Cor. I. vers. 12. quem sibi jungit in ministerio Christi Apostolus, 1. Cor. III. 6. Ego plantavi, Apollo rigavit. Vide & de ipso Act. XIX. 1. 1. Cor. XVI. vers. 12. Hunc autem & Zenam Romam Pauli missu in Syriam & Judaeam ivisse non apparet. Hieronymus πξόπεμψον reddit premitte, hac textus addita interpretatione: Praecipit Tito, ut quoniam de Creta ad Graecam navigaturi erant, non eos fa- ciat sitarceis indigere, sed habere, ea, quae ad viati- cum neceffaria sunt. Censet enim Apollo, quem Corinthiorum Episcopum dicit, propter dissen- siones, quae in Corintho erant, ad vicinam insu- lam Cretam cum Zena legis Doctore transfre- tasse, & Pauli epistola, dissensionibus, quae Co- rinthi ortae fuerant, temperatis, rursum Corin- thum revertisse. Chrysostomus: Praemitte, inquit, eos, hoc est, ut uberiore doctrina perfruantur. B. Hunnius noster: Hos duos, ait, certis de causis, quas hic non exprimit, vult premitti. In genere scimus, Paulum sub hujusmodi legationibus, nihil quaesivisse aliud, quam ut cum piis Doctoribus sua consilia in plantandis Ecclesiis communicaret, & ipsorum judicia vicissim audiret. Quare hos duos mitti petit, & studiose deduci, ne quid eis desit ad iter illud conficiendum. Praefert hic Estius alio- rum translationem Vulgatae, per Tridentinum Concilium authenticae: Quod nos habemus, soli- cite præmitte, melius alii vertunt ex Græco, studiose deducito seu prosequere. Quod officium solet hospi- tibus abeuntibus exhiberi; in qua significatione & alibi non raro Græcum hoc verbum occurrit tam in Actis, quam Epistolis Apostolicis, ubi nos Latine semper habemus deducere, ut mirum sit Interpretem hic aliud reddidisse. Commendat igitur Tito Ze- nam & Apollo, ut per Cretam iter facturis viaticum subministrari curet, ne quid eis desit.

## 3:14
Vers. 14.

Μανθανέτωσαν δὲ καὶ οἱ ἡμέτεροι.

Ours, that is, Apollos, Tychicus, and others whom we are sending, if they have settled in any place.

Καλῶν ἔργων προΐστασθαι.

Let them become accustomed, he says, to having some workshop at home, imitating me, Acts XX. vers. 34.

Εἰς τὰς ἀναγκαίας χρείας.

For the necessities of life. Thus we have χρείας in Acts XX. vers. 34, Rom. XII. 13, and in the singular in Phil. II. 25, IV. 6. But he well added ἀναγκαίας, that is, food and clothing, which nature desires, 1 Tim. VI. 8.

Ἵνα μὴ ὦσιν ἄκαρποι) That they may not be - - Slothful to others' pastures.

καρπὸς is called gain from work, Proverbs XXXI. v. 16.

A new gloss about having a workshop at home, in which they may labor: which Grotius also wished to insert at verse 8. But where is 'to preside over good works' the same as 'to make one's home a workshop of some honest craft, to exercise all one's own in honest labors'? The Greeks indeed explain it concerning beneficence, but not concerning the exercise of a craft. Chrysostom: 'What is it, that they should take care to preside over good works, so that they do not wait until the needy approach them? But that they should diligently seek out of their own accord those who are in need of their help.' For that is most rightly said to be 'taking care.' For he will do that diligently and with great zeal. For that matter produces not so much profit for those who receive the benefit, as for those who bestow it; for it provides them with a most abundant confidence toward God, and acquires huge gains. He teaches them, according to the interpretation of Theodoret, who have believed, to take care of them, and to provide the necessities for those to whom the divine office of teaching has been entrusted; it is fitting that they also bear fruits of this kind. He calls them 'ours,' says Jerome, who had believed in Christ, who because they were CHRIST'S, rightly deserved to be called both Paul's and Titus's. 'You have,' he says, 'power over the disciples; teach them not to be unfruitful, but to minister to the Evangelists and Apostolic men who serve in good works; and to minister, not in any causes whatsoever, but in necessary uses: For having food and clothing, let us be content with these. And those who serve the altar, let them live from the altar, and those who have been made partakers of our spiritual things, ought to share their carnal things with us.' And lest perhaps they might despise either the epistle of Paul or the command of Titus, he calls them unfruitful, whoever shall not have ministered to the Evangelists. Solomon also says in Proverbs: But the fruit is alms. And Paul himself calls charity the first fruit of the Spirit. Charity, however, is most proven in communication or in ministry. So that, he says, they may not be unfruitful. For every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire. But I say this: Because he who sows sparingly, shall also reap sparingly. To be unwilling to contribute to the necessary uses of the apostolic men, the evangelizers of Christ; is to condemn oneself to sterility. Similarly our countrymen, from whom B. Hunnius: He transfers the hypothesis to the thesis, and what he had said about Titus, that he should provide that nothing be lacking to those whom he was about to send ahead, he now adapts to the rest, whether Cretans or other Christians, that they may excel in good works, assisting with their resources and expenses the course of the Gospel, and all those things which pertain to promoting the doctrine of the Gospel. He had accepted the same phrase in verse 8 generally regarding good works; here he explains it specifically regarding beneficence. So also Piscator and others. Since it does not seem necessary that it be taken in exactly the same way in both places, especially because in this place a determination has been added, εἰς τὰς ἀναγκαίας χρείας. Others, however, explain it not inconveniently in a general sense in this place as well. Thus Estius: Let our people, he says, that is, the Christians who are with you, learn at your exhortation to excel in and devote themselves to good works, wherever necessity demands, such as that which was the case of sending off the apostolic men Zenas and Apollos. So also Camerarius: καλῶν ἔργων προΐστασθαι εἰς τὰς ἀναγκαίας χρείας. The same also above, ἵνα φροντίζωσι καλῶν ἔργων προΐστασθαι, and higher up, λαὸν περιούσιον, ζηλωτὴν καλῶν ἔργων. For he does not want his own, that is, the Christians, to be a gathering of common and vulgar condition, but an excellent and peculiar one, whose zeal may burn in performing duty and the cultivation of virtue. Whose most beautiful works are those of liberality and kindness, so that others may be relieved, and the necessary things, which are now called ἀναγκαῖαι χρεῖαι, may be supplied to the needy. For in no way does the Apostle suffer those to be named Christians who are ἄκαρποι, that is, sterile, who will be, of course, of no thing or use. So also B. Balduinus: He calls this excelling in good works, that is, to progress in good, to maintain good works in such a way that from their very beneficence it may appear that their faith has not been unfruitful.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Μανθανέτωσαν δὲ καὶ οἱ ἡμέτεροι.

Nostri, id est, Apollos, Tychicus, & alii, quos mit- timus, si quo in loco resederint.

Καλῶν ἔργων προΐστασθαι.

Assuescant, inquit, habere domi officinam aliquam, me imitantes, Actor. XX. vers. 34.

Εἰς τὰς ἀναγκαίας χρείας.

Ad vitæ subsidia. Sic χρείας habemus Act. XX. vers. 34. Rom. XII. 13. & in singulari Phil. II. 25. IV. 6. Bene au- tem addidit ἀναγκαίας, id est, victum & tegmen, quæ na- tura desiderat, 1. Tim. VI. 8.

Ἵνα μὴ ὦσιν ἄκαρποι) Ne sint - - Segnes aliena ad pabula furi.

καρπὸς dicitur quæstus ex opera, Proverb. XXXI. v. 16.

Nova glossa de officina domi habenda, in qua laborent : quam etiam vers. 8. ingerere voluit Grotius. At ubinam præesse bonis operibus est, facere domum suam honesti alicujus opificii offi- cinam, omnes suos exercere in laboribus hone- stis. De beneficentia quidem Græci explicant, at non de exercitio opificii. Chrysostomus : Quid est, ut curent bonis operibus præesse, ne scilicet ex- pectent, dum se inopes adeant. Verum illud per se studiose requirant eos, qui suo auxilio indigent. Id quippe curare rectissime dicitur. Im enim diligen- ter & magno cum studio id operabitur. Namque ea res non tantum emolumenti eis parit, qui bene- ficium sumunt, quantum eis, qui impendunt; quip- pe confidentiam illis ad Deum uberrimam præstat, & lucra acquirit ingentia. Docet eos, interprete Theodoreto, qui crediderunt, eorum curam gerere, & necessaria providere iis, quibus divinum docen- di munus creditum est; convenit eos quoque fru- ctus ferre ejusmodi. Nostros suos vocat, inquit Hieronymus, qui in Christo crediderant, qui quia CHRISTI erant, recte & Pauli & Titi appel- lari merebantur. Habes, inquit, in discipulos po- testatem, doce eos non esse infructuosos, sed Evan- gelistis & Apostolicis viris, qui bonis operibus ser- viunt, ministrare; & ministrare, non in quibus- cunque causis, sed in necessariis usibus : Habentes quippe victum & vestimentum, his contenti simus. Et qui altari serviunt, de altari vivant, & qui participes spiritualium nostrorum facti sunt, debent nobis participare sua carnalia. Et ne forsitan vel epistolam Pauli, vel præceptum Titi contemnerent, infructuosos vocat, quicunque Evangelistis non mi- nistraverint. Dicit & Salomon in Proverbiis : Fru- ctus vero Eleemosyna. Et Paulus ipse primum Spi- ritus fructum charitatem vocat. Charitas autem in communicatione vel in ministerio maxime com- probatur. Ut non, inquit, infructuosi sint. Omnis enim arbor, quæ non facit fructum bonum, exci- detur & in ignem mittetur. Hoc autem dico : Quia qui parce seminat, & parce metet. Apostolicis vi- ris Evangelizatoribus Christi necessariis usibus nol- le tribuere; sterilitatis seipsum est condemnare. Si- militer nostrates, è quibus B. Hunnius : Hypothe- sin ad thesin transfert, & quod de Tito dixerat, pro- videret, ne quid deesset his, quos præmissurus erat, nunc ad reliquos, sive Cretenses, sive alios Christia- nos accommodat, ut præsint bonis operibus, adju- vantes suis facultatibus & sumptibus, Evangelii cursum, atque omnia ea, quæ ad promovendum Evangelii doctrinam pertinent. Phrasin eandem vers. 8. in genere de bonis operibus acceperat, hic in specie de beneficentia explicat. Sic etiam Piscator & alii. Quum non videatur necessari- um, ut utrobique eadem ratione prorsus accipia- tur maxime, quod hoc loco determinatio addita sit, εἰς τὰς ἀναγκαίας χρείας. Generaliter tamen & hoc loco eandem non incommode explicant alii. Sic Estius: Discant, inquit, te hortante, no- stri, id est, Christiani, qui apud te sunt, bonis ope- ribus præesse atque intendere, ubicunque postulat necessitas, qualis ista erat viros Apostolicos Zinam & Apollo deducendi. Sic & Camerarius: καλῶν ἔργων προΐστασθαι εἰς τὰς ἀναγκαίας χρείας. Idem & supra, ἵνα φροντίζωσι καλῶν ἔργων προΐστα- σθαι, & superius, λαὸν περιούσιον, ζηλωτὴν καλῶν ἔργων. Non enim vult suos, id est, Christianos esse communis & vulgaris conditionis cætum, sed exi- mium atque peculiarem, cujus studium ardeat in præstando officio & cultu virtutis. Cujus pulcher- rima opera sunt liberalitatis & benignitatis, ut alii subleventur, & suppeditentur egentibus necessaria, quæ nunc ἀναγκαῖαι χρεῖαι dicuntur. Nullo enim modo patitur, eos nominari Christianos Apostolus, qui sunt ἄκαρποι, id est, steriles, qui erunt scili- cet nullius rei aut usus. Sic etiam B. Balduinus: Hoc vocat præesse bonis operibus, hoc est, in bono proficere, bona opera ita tueri, ut ex ipsorum be- neficentia appareat, fidem ipsorum non fuisse in- frugiferam.

## 3:15
Verse 15.

All who are with me greet you) Luke, Timothy, Epaphras, and others. But from where is it certain to Grotius that Luke, Timothy, and Epaphras were then present with Paul? From where are they understood to be co-workers in the ministry of the Word? Since any believers who were with the Apostle can be understood. Since the Apostle does not determine, it is not for us to determine.

Greet those who love us in faith.

That is, the brothers, as in Colossians 4:15, 1 Thessalonians 5:26. Every saint in Christ, as in Philippians 4:21. Greet, he says, those who love us because of our common faith. For that is what ἐν signifies in this place, in the Hebrew manner. The more accepted sense of the particle ἐν should not be abandoned without cause. For they are said to love in faith, because true love redounds from faith, which is active through charity, Galatians 5:6. Compare 2 Peter 1:5, 7. If everyone who loves, loved in faith, and there were not others who loved without faith, Paul would never have added faith to love, saying: Greet those who love us in faith. For he does not want, as Theodoret says, the Master of truth to be loved otherwise than from the sole purpose and intent of piety. Therefore he understands true Christians, who not only boast of faith with their mouth, but also demonstrate it by works of charity. He adds in faith, says Estius, not because there were those among the Cretans who loved Paul otherwise than in faith, but to intimate what the love of all Christians ought to be, namely, progressed and directed by faith.

Grace be with you all. Amen.

In Colossians 4:18 and 2 Timothy 4:22 we have, grace be with you. Here, in addition, we have all, as also in Hebrews 13:25, namely, so that no one might complain that they were excluded. The Vulgate adds the name of GOD: The grace of GOD be with you all. Amen. That, however, even if it is understood, is found neither in the Greek nor in the Syriac. Estius observes this. He also observed in his own time in the Latin Codices, Jerome says: It must be known, he says, that in the Greek Codices it is written thus: Grace be with you all, so that neither 'Lord' nor 'our' is carried in the authentic books. What kind of Papal emendation was it, therefore? We conclude the epistle with the words of Theodoret: The divine Apostle wrote these things indeed to the blessed Titus. which proceeds from them. For we enjoy them as common treasures. Would that we too might be able to preserve those things which have been gathered in Christ Jesus our Lord. WITH WHOM TO THE FATHER together with the MOST HOLY SPIRIT be glory, honor, and power now and always, and unto the ages of ages, Amen.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

᾿Ασπάζονταί σε οἱ μετ᾽ ἐμοῦ πάντες) Lucas, Timotheus, Epaphras, & alii. Unde vero constat Grotio, Lucam, Timo- theum & Epaphram Paulo tum adfuisse? Unde coadjutores in Verbi ministerio intelligi? Quum qui erant cum Apostolo credentes quivis intel- ligi possint. Non determinante Apostolo no- strum non est determinare.

᾿Ασπάσαι τοὺς φιλοῦντας ἡμᾶς ἐν πίστει.

Id est, fratres, ut Coloss. IV. vers. 15. 1. Thess. V. 26. Πάντα ἅγιον ἐν χριστῷ, ut Phil. IV. 21. Saluta, inquit, eos qui nos amant ob communem fidem. Nam id valet hoc loco ἐν more Ebræo. Particulæ ἐν sensus receptior citra causam non deserendus. Amare in fide enim dicuntur, quia verus amor ex fide redundat, quæ per charita- tem operosa est, Galat. V. vers. 6. Conf. 2. Petr. I. vers. 5. 7. Si omnis, qui amat, amaret in fide, & non essent alii, qui absque fide diligerent, nunquam Paulus ad amorem fidem apposuisset, dicens: Saluta eos, qui nos amant in fide. Non vult enim, dicen- te Theodoreto, aliter amari veritatis Magister, præ- terquam ex solo scopo atque instituto pietatis. Ve- ros itaque Christianos intelligit, qui non tan- tum fidem ore jactant, sed & operibus charita- tis eam demonstrant. Addit in fide, inquit Estius, non quod essent apud Cretenses, qui Paulum ali- ter quam in fide amarent, sed ut innuat, qualis omnium Christianorum amor esse debeat, scilicet profectus & directus à fide.

῾Η χάρις μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. ᾿Αμήν.

Coloss. IV. 18. 2. Tim. IV. 22. habemus, ἡ χάρις μεθ᾽ ὑμῶν. Hic præterea habemus πάντων, ut & Ebr. XIII. 25. nempe ne quis se exclusum quereretur. Vulgatus addit nomen DEI: Gratia DEI cum omnibus vobis. Amen. Id vero, etsi subaudia- tur, nec in Græco, nec in Syro reperitur. Ob- servat id Estius. Observavit etiam suo tempore in Latinis Codicibus Hieronymus: Sciendum, inquit, quod in Græcis Codicibus ita scriptum est: Gratia cum omnibus vobis, ut nec Domini nec nostri in libris feratur Authenticis. Qualis ergo Papalis fuit emendatio? Concludimus epistolam verbis Theodoreti: Hæc beato quidem Tito scripsit divinus Apostolus. Nobis autem omnibus, quæ ex illis proficiscitur, utilitatem præbuit. Iis enim tanquam thesauris communibus fruimur. Utinam possimus & nos conservare ea, quæ collecta sunt in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. CUM QVO PATRI una cum SANCTISSIMO SPIRITU gloria, honor & potentia nunc & semper, & in secula seculorum, Amen.

# Philemon

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N. J. [In the Name of Jesus] ANNOTATIONS ON THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON.

Latin:

I. N. J. ANNOTATA IN EPISTOLAM AD PHILEMONEM.

## 1:1 Introduction: Preface
PREFACE.

It was doubted by some concerning the author and authority of the epistle, as Jerome testifies in the preface: But [it was doubted] for frivolous arguments, that it was written only for the office of commending, not of teaching: that it is short, and that it is simple: Which are easily solved. For he commends in such a way that he teaches: It is so short that what Jerome proclaims about certain short prophets, Obadiah, Nahum, Zephaniah, can rightly be said of this epistle: namely, that it is doubtful whether you ought to admire the brevity of the words in them, or the magnitude of the meanings. And if those who reject the epistle to Philemon understood this, they would never despise the brevity, which, as Jerome says, was written with Evangelical decorum instead of the wordy works of the law.

But those who argue that the epistle is simple, betray their own ignorance, in the judgment of Jerome, not understanding what virtue and wisdom lie hidden in the individual words. Chrysostom produced some proofs of it, but more occur.
