For it shows not only Apostolic gravity tempered with gentleness, but also in a humble argument it treats of sublime things, and through the hypothesis of receiving Onesimus, a fugitive, back into favor from his master, it forms the duties of charity in the thesis, and by that example it clearly teaches that to no man, not even to a fugitive slave, not even to a thief, is the approach to grace closed; that one must act gently with penitent sinners; that care must be taken even for slaves; that slaves are not to be torn away from their masters under the pretext of piety; it reminds us of forgiving injuries, of helping brothers even with the loss of one's own goods, of the restitution of stolen things, of satisfaction for others out of the law of charity, and, which are more sublime, of the efficacy of the Gospel, of faith in Christ, of the communion of saints, of the joy and consolation arising from it, of thanksgiving and prayer for the faith and charity of the brothers, of regeneration and other necessary and useful things; and thus it pertains not only to Philemon, but is a κειμήλιον [treasure] of the whole Church, just as Tertullian [says] against Marcion. To all, he says, the Apostles wrote, while to some [they wrote]. We have in this epistle all the internal κριτήρια [criteria] of divinely inspired Scripture. We have the inscription and the Apostolic salutation: We have the sign of the Pauline epistles proper to 2 Thess. III. Philemon and other faithful Colossians had the character of his own hand, not unknown, with which the Apostle wrote this epistle, which has been preserved in the Church: They also had the testimony of Onesimus, who brought the epistle, and of his companion Tychicus. Nor is anything lacking that might be desired here regarding the γνωρίσματα [marks] of divine Scripture. This epistle contains mysteries concerning the ὁμοουσία [consubstantiality] and ὁμοτιμία [equal honor] of God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, concerning the grace of God the Father and Jesus Christ, concerning peace to be obtained uniquely from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, as the best gift of grace, concerning faith in Christ, and confession and martyrdom for Christ, concerning the demonstration of faith, concerning its communion and union, concerning the Church, and other things of this kind. For there is no verse that does not contain some doctrine of faith. In it are handed down most holy admonitions and most illustrious examples of true piety concerning prayer, thanksgiving, faith, and joy in the Lord, and unfeigned charity toward all the saints and their needs, that our bowels ought to be held [as theirs], and their bowels ought to be refreshed by us, and also [matters] of justice and equity concerning rendering to each his own. This epistle exhibits a most lucid mirror of love in the Apostle; a clear example of the intercession of Christ and the imputation of justice through Christ in the intercession and promised satisfaction for Onesimus; an excellent document of our debt for such a benefit in Onesimus, who is restored to Philemon forever. Therefore, this epistle was also received by the whole Church along with the other Pauline ones as truly apostolic and divine. Marcion himself, as Jerome testifies, when he either did not accept the other epistles of the Apostle, or changed and gnawed away certain things in them, did not dare to lay hands on this one alone, because its brevity defended it.

Onesimus, the slave of Philemon, gave the occasion for the epistle; he, having added theft to his flight, had betaken himself to Italy, and at Rome had been converted to the faith of Christ by Paul. After Paul had been served by him for some time in prison, he sent him back to his master, as one sufficiently confirmed in faith and piety, with a distinguished recommendation, interceding for him most earnestly and with a great apparatus of words and arguments woven with wonderful art, omitting nothing of those things which seem to have any moment or force for obtaining pardon for a fugitive and unfaithful slave.

…Who Philemon was is not so certain. Most, with Jerome, make him a citizen of Colossae; whose house at Colossae even until his own time Theodoret testifies that he remained in the argument of the epistle: Chrysostom calls him a faithful man, noble and admirable in virtue, and says that this is evident primarily from the fact that his whole house was also faithful, and so faithful that it was even called a Church. He is celebrated in v. 7 for his liberality: The hearts of the saints have been refreshed by you, brother. It is believed he was not a Jew, but a Gentile; because the Apostle calls Onesimus his brother in the flesh, whom they judge to have been a Gentile, having been appointed Bishop of Gaza after, as Dorotheus relates in his Synopsis; Phil. Pareus, however, [says] of the Colossians. Neither enjoys any certainty or authority of the ancients. Grotius, however, makes Onesimus Bishop of the Ephesians. Estius affirms that he succeeded Timothy in this bishopric, and both prove this from the blessed Ignatius's epistle to the Ephesians. Thus the God-bearer commends him to the Ephesians: Since I have received your multitude in the name of GOD in Onesimus, your beloved Teacher (in the Codex and the English [version] of Ussher, and the Florentine [version] of Vossius it reads: Τῷ ἐπ' ἀγάπῃ ἀδιηγήτῳ, who is inexpressible in love) and your Bishop. I beseech him according to Jesus Christ to love you, and [that] you all be in his concord in Him. For blessed is God, who granted you to have such a Bishop in Christ. Ado, in his book on the festivals of the Apostles on the 14th of the Kalends of March, affirms that this is the same [person] of whom Paul speaks in the present epistle: with whom also Bede, Notker, and the Roman Martyrologies agree. The wonder of God's grace, that from a runaway slave and a thief he was made such a great Bishop! In the Greek Menologies, however, and in Simeon Metaphrastes, his Ephesian bishopric is not acknowledged: and Gaius, not Onesimus, is established by Dorotheus as the successor of Timothy in that bishopric. Which Gaius, James Ussher also observed in his annotations to the epistles of Ignatius, the unpublished book of Hippolytus on the LXX disciples makes Bishop of the Ephesians. But who succeeded Onesimus, he relates, although in the Clementine Constitutions, book VII, chapter 48, that Onesimus of Philemon is said to have been appointed Bishop by the Apostles at Beroea in Macedonia.

This epistle was written at Rome from chains, which he mentions five times, and was sent through Onesimus together with the epistle to the Colossians handed to Tychicus to be delivered; Estius proves it was sent thus: because both join Timothy to Paul at the beginning, both address Archippus, and finally both have the same greeters at the end—Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke. Let it be added to these that the epistle to the Colossians is said to have been transmitted through Tychicus and Onesimus in the note added to it at the bottom: Which, if it deserves credit, there is no doubt that both presented it inscribed to the Colossians: Thus Onesimus, to whom the same were handed, offered his own letters of commendation and intercession to Philemon.

The time of the written epistle, however, was the time of Paul's captivity, not the first, as Cornelius a Lapide and others, including our Grotius, wish: But the later one; because he calls himself an old man in this epistle, verse 9. Nor does it stand in the way that he ordered a lodging to be prepared for him at Colossae, verse 22, which does not seem to correspond to the final captivity, from which he had no hope of liberation, but wrote to Timothy that he was already being offered up. For the times in the second captivity must be distinguished, because when he was first presented in the same before Nero's judgment, the Apostle's hope of liberation was not entirely dashed; whom some, according to Grotius at 2 Timothy IV, v. 17,

say that when he had come to Rome a second time, he was not condemned in the first defense, but finally after nine months, when Nero had recognized that Paul had converted his cupbearer and had led away his concubines to the Christian faith. The whole epistle is completed in one chapter of 25 verses.

Latin:

PRÆLOQVIIM.

Dubitatum à quibusdam fuit de Autore & autoritate epistolæ, teste Hieronymo in procemio: Sed argumentis frivolis, quod commendandi tantum scribatur officio, non docendi: quod brevis, & quod simplex sit: Quæ facile solvuntur. Nam ita commendat,ut doceat: Ita brevis est, ut quod de Prophetis quibusdam brevibus Obadia, Nabum, Sophonia prædicat Hieronymus, jure de hac epistola dici possit: quod nempe dubium sit, utrum brevitatem sermonum in illis admirari debeas, an magnitudinem sensuum. Quod si intelligerent hi, qui epistolam ad Philemonem repudiant,nunquam brevitatem despicerent, quæ pro laciniosis legis operibus Evangelico decore, dicente Hieronymo, conscripta est.

Qui vero epistolam simplicitatis arguunt, suam imperitiam, judice Hieronymo, produnt, non intelligentes, quid in singulis sermonibus virtutis ac sapientiæ lateat. Produxit nonnulla ejus Chrysostomus documenta, sed plura occurrunt. Ostendit enim non tantum Apostolicam gravitatem mansuetudine temperatam, sed & in argumento humili sublimia tractat, & per hypothesin de Onesimo fugitivo ab hero in gratiam recipiendo format in thesi charitatis officia, atque exemplo illo luculenter docet, quod nulli homini, ne quidem servo fugitivo, ne furi quidem aditus ad gratiam sit præclusus, quod cum pœnitentibus peccatoribus mansuete agendum sit, quod fervorum etiam cura haberi debeat, quod servi à Dominis suis prætextu pietatis non sint avellendi, commonefacit de injuriis condonandis, de fratribus etiam cum jactura rerum suarum juvandis, de restitutione ablatorum, de satisfactione pro aliis ex lege charitatis, &, quæ sublimiora sunt, de efficacia Evangelii, de fide in Christum, de communione sanctorum, de gaudio & solatio inde oriundo, de gratiarum actione & precatione pro fide ac charitate fratrum, de regeneratione & aliis necessariis & utilibus rebus, adeoque non ad Philemonem solum pertinet, sed totius Ecclesiæ κειμήλιον est, quemadmodum Tertullianus contra Marc. Ad omnes, inquit, Apostols scripserunt, dum ad quosdam. Habemus in hac epistola omnia κριτήρια interna divinitus inspiratæ Scripturæ. Habemus inscriptionem, & salutationem Apostolicam: Habemus fignum Epistolarum Paulinarum proprium 2. Theff. III. Habuerunt Philemon & alii Colossensium fideles characterem manus pro- pria non ignotum, qua epistolam hanc exararit Apostolus, qui asservatus in Ecclesia est: Habuerunt & testimonium Onesimi epistolam afferentis, & socii ejus Tychici. Nec deest quicquam, quod ad γνωρίσματα Scripturæ divinæ hic desideretur. Continet hæc epistola mysteria de ὁμοο sia & ὁμοτιμία Dei Patris & Domini nostri Jesu Christi, de gratia Dei Patris & Jesu Christi, de pace à Deo Patre & Domino nostro Jesu Christo unice obtinenda, ceu dono gratiæ optimo, de fide in Christum, ac confessione & martyrio pro Christo, de fidei demonstratione, de ejusdem communione & unione, de Ecclesia, & alia ejusmodi. Nullus enim versiculus est, qui non doctrinam aliquam fidei contineat. Traduntur in eadem monita sanctissima, & exempla illustrissima veræ pietatis de precatione, gratiarum actione, fide ac gaudio in Domino, & infucatæ charitatis erga omnes sanctos & necessitates eorum, quod ut viscera nostra haberi, & viscera ipsorum refocillari à nobis debeant, nec non justitiæ & equitatis de suo unicuique reddendo. Exhibet hæc epistola lucidissimum amoris speculum in Apostolo; præclarum intercessionis Christi & imputationis justitiæ per Christum exemplum in intercessione ac promissa satisfactione pro Onesimo; egregium debiti nostri pro tanto beneficio in Onesimo, qui Philemoni in æternum restituitur, documentum. Ideo etiam ab Ecclesia tota recepta est cum cæteris Paulinis hæc epistola ceu vere apostolica & divina. Marcion ipse, Hieronymo teste, quum cæteras Apostoli epistolas vel non susceperit, vel quædam in his mutaverit atque corrosserit, in hanc solam manus non est ausus mittere, quia sua illam brevitas defendebat.

Occasionem epistolæ dedit Onesimus servus Philemonis, qui fugam furto cumulans in Italiam se receperat, & Romæ à Paulo ad fidem Christi conversus erat: Quem Paulus postquam ipsi in carcere aliquandiu inserviisset, ceu satis in fide ac pietate confirmatum hero suo cum commendatione insigni remittit, impensissime ac magno verborum ac rationum miro artificio contextarum apparatu pro eo intercedens, nihilque eorum prætermittens, quæ ad impetrandam servo fugitivo & infido veniam, momentum aut vim aliquam habere videntur.

Quis Philemon fuerit, non adeo constat. Plerique eum cum Hieronymo civem Colossensem faciunt; cujus domum Colossis ad sua usque tem- pora mansisse testatur in argumento epistolae | Theodoretus : Chrysostomus virum fidelem, nobilem ac virtute mirabilem dicit, idque ex eo imprimis constare ait, quod domus quoque ejus omnis fidelis erat, atque adeo fidelis, ut Ecclesia etiam appellaretur. Celebratur v. 7. a liberalitate: Vi- scera sanctorum per te requieverunt frater. Cre- ditur non Judaeus fuisse, sed gentilis; quia Apo- stolus Onesimum fratrem ejus carne vocat, quem gentilem fuisse censent, post Gazae Episcopum constitutum, ut Dorotheus in Synopsi tradit; Phil. Pareus vero Colossensium. Neutrum certitudine vel autoritate aliqua veterum gaudet. Onesimum vero Ephesiorum Episcopum facit Grotius. In quo Episcopatu Timotheo ipsum successisse affirmat Estius, idque e B. Ignatii ad Ephesios epistola uterque probat. Ita cum Ephesiis commendat ȯ Θεοφόρο̇ς : Quoniam ego suscepi multitudinem vestram in nomine DEI in Onesimo dilecto Praece- ptore nostro (in Cod. & Anglic. Usserii, & Flo- rent. Vossii legitur : Τῷ ἐπ' ἀγάπῃ ἀδιηγήτῳ, qui in charitate inenarrabilis est) vestro autem Epi- scopo. Obsecro eum secundum Jesum Christum di- ligere vos, & vos omnes in concordia ejus in ipso esse. Benedictus enim Deus, qui vobis talibus ta- lem Episcopum donavit habere in Christo. Hunc eundem esse, de quo in praesenti epistola Paulus, in libello de festivitatibus Apostolorum ad XIV. Kal. Mart. affirmat Ado : cui etiam Beda, Not- keri, & Romanum Martyrologia consonant. Mi- ra DEI gratii, quod ex servulo fugitivo & furti reo tantus factus sit Episcopus! In Graecorum ta- men Mensis, & Simeone Metaphrasta Episco- patus ipsius Ephesinus non agnoscitur : ac suc- cessor Timothei in illo Episcopatu a Dorotheo Gajus, non Onesimus constituitur. Quem Ga- jum etiam Hippolyti de LXX. discipulis libellum ineditum Ephesiorum Episcopum facere obser- vavit in annot. suis ad epistolas Ignatii Jacobus Usserius. Qui vero Onesimum successisset Gajo tradit, tametsi in Clementinis Constitut. l. VII. cap. 48. ille Philemonis Onesimus Beroeae in Ma- cedonia ab Apostolis constitutus fuisse dicatur Episcopus.

Scripta Romae est haec epistola e vinculis, quo- rum quinquies meminit, & per Onesimum trans- missa una cum epistola ad Colossenses Tychico ad perferendum tradita missam esse ita probat Esti- us : quia utraque Timotheum Paulo conjungit in principio, utraque Archippum compellat, deni- que utraque eosdem habet salutatores in fine Epa- phram, Marcum, Aristarchum, Deman, & Lu- cam. Addatur his, quod epistola ad Colossenses dicatur per Tychicum & Onesimum transmissa in nota sub calcem ei addita : Quae si fidem mere- tur, haud dubium est, ut Colossensibus inscri- ptam uterque exhibuit : Ita suas systaticas & in- tercessorias Onesimum, cui eaedem traditae, Phi- lemoni obtulisse.

Tempus autem scriptae epistolae fuit tempus captivitatis Pauli, non primae, ut vult Cornelius a Lapide, & alii, etiam Grotius noster : Sed po- sterioris; quia senem se vocat in hac epistola, vers. 9. Nec obstat, quod hospitium Colossis sibi parari jusserit vers. 22. quod non videtur con- gruere postremae captivitati, e qua nullam libe- rationis spem habuit, sed se jam immolari ad Ti- motheum scripsit. Distinguenda enim sunt tem- pora in altera captivitate, quia quum primum in eadem sisteretur coram Neronis judicio, spes non omnino decollabat liberationis Apostoli; quem nonnulli apud Grotium ad 2. Tim. IV. v. 17

dicunt, cum secundo venisset Romam, in pri- ma defensione non esse condemnatum, sed de- mum post novem menses, cum Nero agnovis- set Paulum convertisse suum pincernam, & con- cubinas ab ipso abstractas ad fidem Christianam traduxisse. Absolvitur tota epistola uno capite versibus 25.

## 1:1 Argument
ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Paul, after the inscription and the vow, gives thanks to GOD and pours out prayers for Philemon, and having testified to his joy over his charity, he intercedes for Onesimus, that he might be received again, whom, although useful to himself, he did not wish to detain, but to send back to his master, with a promise of satisfaction at the same time for those things which he had taken, having given this his own handwritten note, and asking for a lodging to be prepared for himself, he greets the same in the name of his companions, sealing the epistle with the customary vow.

There are two parts. The former is preparatory, up to v. 7. The latter is intercessory, up to v. 25. To which, although other things concerning the arrival of Paul and the greetings of others are added, all things are nevertheless directed to adding weight to the intercession.

PART I. PREPARATORY.

Ver. 1.

Παῦλος δέσμιος Χριστῦ Ἰησοῦ.

Living at Rome under the guard of a soldier bound by the same chain, Acts XXVIII. ver. 16. The genitive here signifies the cause, as also below 9. Eph. III. ver. 1. 2 Tim. I. ver. 8. for which Eph. IV. ver. 1. δέσμιος ἐν Κυρίῳ.

Grotius assumes that the first captivity is referred to. But that does not fit the old age of Paul so well; and since the present epistle was written and sent with the epistle to the Colossians, these chains must be referred entirely to the later captivity of Paul. He mentions his own chains, however, both so that prayers might be more effective, and that affliction might not be added to one already afflicted by the denial of them, and also because the chains, which he hints he endures even for Philemon's sake, might move his own heart. He called himself a prisoner, says Theodoret, making his petition worthy of belief through his chains. For on your account, he says, have chains been cast upon me. For if I had wished to live a life of leisure, and not to travel the world and preach the Gospel to all, I would not have undergone these things. He calls himself a prisoner not because of some crime, but because of the confession of the name of Christ, therefore he calls himself a prisoner of Christ. He has used this periphrasis nowhere else in his epistles; but here he wished to use it, so that he might move Philemon by his martyrdom. For almost all the words are composed with wonderful care to win effectiveness for his intercession. A prisoner of Christ, says Chrysostom: for indeed he had been bound on His account. Who now would not revere him? Who would not shudder, hearing of the chains of Christ? Who would not even lay down his soul, out of reverence for this name, let alone one little slave?

Καὶ Τιμόθεος ὁ ἀδελφὸς.

Christians called each other brothers because of their common regeneration. Timothy was almost the constant companion of Paul, as can be seen in 2 Tim. III. 10. He was also present with him at Rome, Eph. I. 1. Col. I. 1.

He calls Timothy a brother not only because of their common regeneration, but also because of his office

the fellowship of the Gospel. He joins him, however, to himself in the frontispiece, both so that the intercession of two, one expressed, the other interpretative, may penetrate more deeply, and so that he may employ him as an ἀξιόπιστον [trustworthy] witness of his caution, or of his obligation for Onesimus. He takes another with him as well, so that, being entreated by more, he might yield more easily, and grant the favor, says Chrysostom.

Φιλήμονι τῷ ἀγαπητῷ.

Philemon is a Greek name, by which both a noble poet and a certain writer on natural things mentioned by Pliny were called. He seems to have lived at Ephesus, where Onesimus later served in the episcopate, as both the letters of Ignatius and other writers report. Paul calls this Philemon beloved or most dear, because he embraced him with a certain inner friendship, as a man who was very pious.

He adds the name of beloved τῷ ἀγαπητῷ by antonomasia, and by that, so that he who loves him intensely may not deny the petition, he reminds him. For a friend does not easily deny a friend anything that he has in his power. If he is most dear, it is not a matter of audacity or rashness to trust, but a sign of singular friendship.

Καὶ συνεργῷ ἡμῶν.

That is, one of those presbyters who were many at Ephesus, Acts 20:17. But the Apostles called all presbyters, and even the presbyteresses, who devoted effort to calling women to Christ, fellow workers of their own work, Rom. 16:3, 9; Phil. 2:25; Col. 4:11.

It is not certain that Philemon was at Ephesus. It is more likely, as we said in the introduction, and is believed by most interpreters, that he was at Colossae. He calls him a fellow worker, not because he was then established in the sacred ministry, about which nothing is certain, but because he had cooperated in his own place in promoting the doctrine of the Gospel, which can be done by political persons or even by anyone at all who lives outside the sacred ministries, when they enjoy that power and ability. Therefore, he ought also to have readily received this neophyte as a fellow worker in promoting the Gospel. Theophylact and Chrysostom think he was a minister of the Church, and they present the nerve of the argument as such: If Philemon is a worker, he will not keep the slave; but will send him back again to the ministry of the Word, of which he himself is also a fellow worker. But Epaphras seems to have been the pastor of the Colossians rather than Philemon, Col. 1:7, ch. 4:16. Ambrosiaster therefore thinks he was called by that name only because he faithfully promoted the affairs of the Church, and on his part helped the course of the Gospel not a little: the ardor of whom in promoting the Gospel some gather from the fact that he had a domestic Church, and that he was very liberal in refreshing the hearts of the saints.

Latin:

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Paulus post inscriptionem, & votum gratias DEO agit, & preces fundit pro Philemo- ne, testatusque gaudium suum super ejus charitate, intercedit pro Onesimo, ut iterum recipiatur, quem, etsi utilem sibi, detine- re noluerit, sed Domino suo remittere, promissa simul satisfactione pro iis, quae abstulerat ille, dato hoc suo chirographo, ac petens praeparari sibi hospitium salutat eundem sociorum nomine, voto consueto obsignans epistolam.

PArtes duae sunt. Prior est praeparatoria, ad v. 7. Altera intercessoria, ad v. 25. Cui etsi alia adventum Pauli & salutationes aliorum concet- nentia accedant, omnia tamen ad pondus inter- cessioni addendum directa sunt.

PARS I. PREPARATORIA.

Vers. 1.

Παῦλος δέσμιος Χριστῦ Ἰησοῦ.

Romae agens sub militis eadem catena vincti custodia, Actor. XXVIII. vers. 16. Genitivus hic causam significat, ut & infra 9. Ephes. III. vers. 1. 2. Tim. I. vers. 8. pro quo Ephes. IV. vers. 1. δέσμιος ἐν Κυρίῳ.

Assumit Grotius, primam captivitatem respici. Sed ea non adeo convenit senio Pauli; & quum scripta ac missa sit cum epistola ad Colossenses praesens epistola, ad posteriorem Pauli captivita- tem omnino haec vincula referenda. Vinculorum autem suorum meminit, tam ut preces efficacio- res essent, nec denegatione earum afflicto adde- retur afflictio, tum quod vincula, quae etiam Phi- lemonis causa sese sustinere innuit, commoverent ipsius viscera. Vinctum seipsum appellavit, ait Theo- doretus, per vincula suam petitionem fide dignam efficiens. Propter vos enim, inquit, mihi injecta sunt vincula. Si enim voluissem in otio vitam age- re, & non orbem terrarum obire, & praedicare Ev- angelium omnibus, hec ego non subiisssem. Vin- ctum autem non ob scelus quoddam, sed ob con- fessionem nominis Christi se dicit, ideo vinctum Christi vocat. Qua περιφράσει nuspiam in ἐπισλα- ρῇ usus est; hic autem uti voluit, ut martyrio suo moveret Philemonem. Ad efficaciam enim intercessioni conciliandam omnia fere verba mi- rabili studio composita sunt. Vinctus Christi, in- quit Chrysostomus : Propter ipsum quippe fuerat vinctus. Quis jam non revereatur? Quis non ex- horreat, Christi audiens vincula? Quis non & ani- mam poneret, hujusce reverentia nominis, nedum servulum unum?

Καὶ Τιμόθεος ὁ ἀδελφὸς.

Fratres vocabant se mutuo Christiani ob communem regenerationem. Timotheus perpetuus ferme Pauli co- mes, ut videre est 2. Tim. III. 10. etiam Romae ipsi ad- erat, Eph. I. 1. Col. I. 1.

Fratrem dicit Timotheum non tantum ob communem regenerationem, sed etiam ob muneris

Evangelii communionem. Adjungit autem eun- dem sibi in frontispicio, tum ut duorum inter- cessio, altera expressa, altera interpretativa magis penetret, tum ut cautionis, vel obligationis suae pro Onesimo testem adhibeat ἀξιόπιστον. Assu- mit & alterum secum, ut à pluribus oratus facilius cedat, & gratiam tribuat, ait Chrysostomus.

Φιλήμονι τῷ ἀγαπητῷ.

Philemon nomen est Graecum, quo appellatus fuit & Poëta nobilis, & rerum naturalium Scriptor quidam Pli- nio memoratus. Videtur habitasse Ephesi, ubi Onesimus postea Episcopatu functus est, ut & Ignatii literae, & alii Scriptores tradunt. Hunc Philemonem dilectum sive cha- rissimum vocat Paulus, quod eum interiore quadam ami- citia, ut virum valde pium, complecteretur.

Addit τῷ ἀγαπητῷ dilecti nomen κατ' ἀντονο- μασίαν, eoque ut sibi impense diligenti non de- neget petitionem, commonefaciat. Amicus enim amico nihil facile denegat, quod in potestate sua habet. Si charissimus, non audaciae neque temeri- tatis est fidere, sed amicitiae singularis indicium.

Καὶ συνεργῷ ἡμῶν.

Id est, uni Presbyterorum illorum, qui Ephesi plures erant, Actor. XX. 17. Omnes autem πρεσβυτέρους, atque etiam πρεσβύτιδας, quae foeminis ad Christum vocandis dabant operam, Apostoli sui operis adjutores vocabant, Rom. XVI. 3. 9. Phil. II. 25. Col. IV. 11.

Ephesi Philemonem fuisse, non constat. Ve- risimilius est, ut in prooemio diximus, & à ple- risq; Interpretibus creditur, fuisse Colossis : Quem συνεργὸν dicit, non quod in sacro ministerio con- stitutus tum fuerit, de quo nihil constat, sed quod promovendae doctrinae Evangelii suo loco coo- peratus fuerit, quod à Politicis personis vel et- iam quibuscunque, qui extra sacra ministeria vivunt, cum ea potestate & facultate gaudent, fieri potest. Ideo etiam hunc neophytum ceu συνεργὸν in promovendo Evangelio prompte sus- cipere debebat. Theophylactus & Chrysostomus Ecclesiae Ministrum fuisse putant, atque nervum argumenti talem exhibent: Si operarius est Phi- lemon, non retinebit servum; sed rursus remit- tet ad Verbi ministerium, cujus & ipse συνεργὸς est. Sed Epaphras Pastor potius Colossensium videtur fuisse, quam Philemon, Col. 1. 7. cap. IV. vers. 16. Ambrosiasster itaque eo solum nomine eum vocatum censet, quod res Ecclesiae fideliter promoverit, suaque ex parte Evangelii cursum non parum adjuverit : cujus ardorem in promo- vendo Evangelio colligunt nonnulli ex eo, quod domesticam habuerit Ecclesiam, quodque ad- modum liberalis fuerit in sanctorum visceribus refocillandis.

## 1:2
Vers. 2.

Καὶ Ἀπφίᾳ τῇ ἀγαπητῇ) Appia is a Roman name changed into φ in the Hebrew manner.

Some think this was the wife of Philemon, whom the Latin version calls the beloved sister. But the word for sister is not read in the source, but she is called beloved in the faith. Theodoret also notes that the intercessory letter is inscribed to her as well, not without cause. He also joins the wife to him, as one who was a participant in the faith: It was likely, moreover, that she, if she had been passed over, would have been one to oppose those things which were being written. The wife, says Chrysostom, as far as I judge, was this one of Philemon. Observe more diligently the humility of Paul. He takes Timothy with him as a petitioner, and he does not only entreat the man, but also the wife, and another certain necessary person.

He seems to have performed the office of an evangelist here, acting now at Ephesus, now at Colossae, Col. 4:17, where Ambrose testifies that he later settled, and thus was made a bishop. Paul was accustomed to call such men his fellow soldiers because of the burden of the office, as can be seen in Phil. 2:25.

The opinion of Ambrosiaster is not approved by others: who are more pleased that Epaphras remained Bishop of the Colossians. Whatever may have been the case, the Apostle joined that fellow-soldier to himself in the ministry of the Word in his intercession, which had much value in the Colossian Church, Coloss. IV. 17, and therefore also as a chief member of the same before Philemon. Archippus, says Jerome, I believe to have been a victor, fighting against adversaries for the name of Christ with Paul and Timothy, and for that reason is now called a fellow-soldier, because he overcame in the same struggle and war. If you are a companion in the militia, says the Apostle, as interpreted by Chrysostom, it is necessary that you also show yourself a companion in these things.

And to the church in your house.

This is to be referred to Philemon, to whom this epistle is chiefly inscribed. In his house there were many Christians. Even three make a church, as Tertullian testifies. Thus, those who were in the house of Aquila and Priscilla are called a church, Romans XV. verse 15, 1 Corinthians XVI. verse 19, and those in the house of Nymphas, Coloss. IV. verse 15.

Blessed Balduinus wishes to note not only the whole family, but also all who had gathered in his house for the sake of sacred things, and thus he observes that so many intercessors are employed for the sake of the salvation of one fugitive slave, so that he might be received back into favor by his master, as a singular example of gentleness. The Greeks, however, interpret it only as his family; Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, who holds as follows: He calls all the church who were believers in Philemon's house, and it embraces both children and slaves at the same time. Note what humility the Apostle displays, so that he might even entreat Philemon's domestics, insofar as they might assist with their prayers and vows, and intercede for him before Philemon the Lord. For he knew, as Chrysostom says, that it often happens that the words of servants change the mind of masters, and that most especially when one is asked for on behalf of a slave, when perhaps they themselves had been the first to provoke the Lord against him. Furthermore, while he embraces even slaves under the title of the Church, he hints that in Christ there is neither free nor slave, concerning which Chrysostom warned here: See how great is the prudence of his usage, that by mentioning them he honored them in such a way that the Lord would have nothing at which he could be angry. For the name of the Church does not allow masters to be indignant if they are numbered together with slaves. For the Church knows no difference between Lord or slave.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Καὶ Ἀπφίᾳ τῇ ἀγαπητῇ) Appia nomen est Romanum mutatur in φ more Ebraeo.

Hanc conjugem Philemonis nonnulli censent, quam Latina versio sororem dilectam nuncupat. Sed vox sororis in fonte non legitur, dilecta au- tem dicitur in fide. Theodorettus etiam eidem, non praeter causam, intercesssoriam epistolam inscribi notat. Conjugem quoque illi conjungit, ut quae essset fidei particeps: Erat autem verisimile, eam, si fuisset praetermissa, fuisse etiam repugnaturam iis, quae scribebantur. Uxor, inquit Chrysosto- mus, quantum ego arbitror, Philemonis haec fuit. Intuere diligentius humilitatem Pauli. Timothe- um assumit secum precatorem, nec modo virum deprecatur, sed etiam uxorem, & alium quen- dam necessarium.

Evangelistæ munus hic obiisse videtur, modo Ephesi agens, modo Colossis, Col. IV. 17. ubi postea eum rese- disse, ac sic Episcopum factum testatur Ambrosius. Tales ob molestiam muneris commilitones suos vocare Paulus solebat, ut videre est Phil. II. 25.

Ambrosiastri sententia aliis non probatur: qui- bus magis placet, Epaphram Colossensium Episco- pum mansisse. Quicquid ejus fuerit, commili- tonem illum in Verbi ministerio sibi junxit Apo- stolus in intercessione sua, quod multum value- rit in Colossensi Ecclesia, Coloss. IV. 17. adeoque etiam apud Philemonem membrum ejusdem præ- cipuum. Archippum, inquit Hieronymus, arbi- tror cum Paulo & Timotheo contra adversarios pro Christi nomine dimicantem extitisse victorem, & propterea nunc commilitonem dici, quod in eo- dem certamine belloque superaverit. Si militiæ so- cius es, ait Apostolus, interprete Chrysostomo, in his quoque te socium exhibeas, necesse est.

Καὶ τῇ κατ᾿ οἶκόν σε Ἐκκλησίᾳ.

Ad Philemonem hoc referendum, cui præcipue inscri- bitur hæc epistola. In ejus domo complures erant, Chri- stiani. Etiam tres Ecclesiam faciunt, teste Tertulliano. Sic in Aquilæ & Priscillæ domo qui erant, Ecclesia dicuntur, Roman. XV. vers. 15. 1. Corinth. XVI. vers. 19. & qui in Nymphæ domo, Coloss. IV. vers. 15.

Non tantum familiam universam, sed etiam omnes, qui in domo ejus sacrorum causa con- venerant, notari vult B. Balduinus, adeoque tot deprecatores observat adhiberi, ob unius servuli fugitivi salutem, ut ab hero suo in gratiam reci- piatur, singulari mansuetudinis exemplo. Græci tamen de familia ejus solum interpretantur, Chry- sostomus, Theodorelus, Theophylactus, qui ita ha- bet: Ecclesiam omnes dicit, qui in Philemonis do- mo erant fideles, & liberos simul & servos comple- ctitur. Adverte quam præ se ferat humilitatem Apostolus, ut vel Philemonis domesticos deprece- tur, quatenus & precibus suis & votis opitulentur, & apud Philemonem Dominum pro se intercedant. Sciebat enim, dicente Chrysostomo, sæpe fieri, ut servorum verba Domini sententiam immutarent, idque tunc maxime, quum pro servo rogatur, quum illi fortassis in primis adversus eum irrita- verint Dominum. Porro dum Ecclesiæ titulo servos etiam complectitur, in Christo non esse liberum vel servum innuit, quo de hic monuit Chrysostomus: Vide quanta sit usus prudentia, ut illos memorando ita honoraret, ut Dominus nihil haberet, quod succensere posset. Namque non sinit Ecclesiæ nomen indignari Dominos, si servis con- numerentur. Non enim novit Ecclesia Domini aut servi differentiam.

## 1:3
Vers. 3. Grace to you and peace from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ.

He prays for them for the favor of God, and of Christ, and for all prosperous things, which the Hebrews are accustomed to call by the name of peace. Paul often uses this prayer, as in 1 Cor. I. 3, 2 Cor. I. 2, Gal. I. 3, Eph. I. 2, 1 Thessal. I. 1.

Grace is the first principle and source of our salvation, Tit. III. verse 5; peace is the consequence of grace, by which, although any prosperous things can be noted by the Hebrew phrase, yet it is familiar to the Apostle, when it is joined to divine grace, to designate primarily the peace of conscience, in which the kingdom of God consists, Romans XIV. verse 17, concerning which Romans V. v. 1. Grace, says Jerome, is that by which we are saved by no work or merit. Peace is that by which we are reconciled to God through Christ. Theophylact, with Chrysostom leading, also directs these things to the aim of the intercession: In what way, he says, will the grace of GOD be present to us? Certainly thus, if we forgive the debts to those who are bound to us by debt. How also will you obtain the peace of the Lord Jesus, unless you are reconciled to the servant Onesimus? But since the Apostle prays for grace and peace from Jesus Christ our Lord, no less than from God the Father, he confirms that the divine nature of both is the same: just as it is not lawful to worship any other than the God who is true by nature without idolatry, nor can we obtain grace and peace except from GOD who is true by nature. Therefore Jerome in h. l. From which it is shown that the nature of the Son and the Father is one, since the Son can perform that which the Father does, and the Father is said to perform that which the Son does. Paul prays for both from God and from Christ, because they are of the same essence and power, and the Son performs the same thing as the Father, yet with this distinction of order, that the Father is considered as the efficient cause, the Son as the meritorious cause of our salvation: Therefore the Father is also called God, the Son Lord, not that the Son is not God, nor the Father Lord, but because the Son by the merit of his obedience acquired a peculiar lordship over men. Victors in war have lordship over those whom they have snatched from the hand of enemies and restored to liberty, as the blessed Baldwin neatly puts it here.

indeed in the Lord Jesus, but that one toward all the saints: by which he shows both the necessity of intercessions before God for the faithful, and thanksgiving for them, when grace is obtained with them, and at the same time the bond of charity toward the saints with faith in Jesus: Thus all these things contribute to the admission of his intercession for Onesimus. For they testify to the holy and sincere brotherly love of the intercessor, and set before God an example of one who hears the intercessions of men: and that true faith cannot exist without charity, and compassion, and forgiveness due to one's neighbor: and that this charity is borne especially toward the saints and the household of faith. Furthermore: in this place, as Theophylact says, he praises him as a merciful man: For the fame of this man would not have been carried from Phrygia all the way to the city, had he not been outstanding and excellent. He says therefore, since you are affected with charity toward all the saints, you ought also to embrace this Onesimus with love, who is now a believer, so that in this way you may seem to pursue God himself with worship and benevolence. Do you see what power these words have in deprecating and persuading? St. Chrysostom observed the art of Apostolic oratory very well here: He did not immediately from the beginning and the very principles demand the favor, but first admired the man, and followed his virtues with worthy praises, and when he had added no small argument of his charity toward him, that he always remembered him in his prayers, and had said that many found rest in him, and that he obeyed and yielded in all things; then at last he asked for the favor itself, thereby preparing an easy approach for himself. Then, lest he should seem to be writing only for the sake of this man, as if he would not have written otherwise unless Onesimus urged him, see how prudently he added other reasons for the letter. First indeed he insinuates his charity, then he asks that hospitality also be prepared for himself. Hearing, he says, of your charity. This is no common praise, but clearly distinguished, and greater than if he had seen it in person. For it is certain that this virtue, had it not been extraordinary in him, could not have become so well known that it reached even his ears, when such a great distance of land and sea separated them both. For he, as it seems to me, was in Phrygia, of which fact Archippus is the indication, about whom he writes to the Colossians. Indeed the Colossians are Phrygians. There is no need for that transposition, or that knowledge be taken as manifestation: or that all these things be referred either to the commendation of Philemon's love or to thanksgiving. They are accepted by others either as the scope of the Apostle's prayers for Philemon, or as an amplification of the fame concerning Philemon. In the former way the blessed Hunnius explains it: That is to say, I strive in this prayer of mine before God with ardent vows, that the faith, which is common to you with me and with the rest of the Christians, may be effective, and not rely on the title alone, but on the solid truth of the thing itself, manifesting itself through effects, namely the fruits of faith and the works of charity. From which, as from the least doubtful indications, true faith in Christ and unfeigned charity may powerfully shine forth, and that through Jesus Christ, the sole author and restorer of every good in us. In the latter way Estius with Thomas: I hear of your faith in Christ, I hear also of your charity toward all the saints, so much so indeed, that that beneficence of yours toward the saints, having proceeded from faith, can by no means be hidden, but becomes evident and manifest to all, as they acknowledge and proclaim your good works, which you value highly. But that former explanation is better, especially as it is proposed by Osiander: I pray to God, says Paul, that the communication of your faith may become evident, or more correctly, effective in the acknowledgment of every work, in Greek, in the acknowledgment

Vers. 3. Χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ Θεῦ Πατρὸς ἡμῶν, καὶ Κυρίε Ἰησῦ Χριςῦ.

Precatur illis favorem DEI, & Christi, & prospera o- mnia, quæ Ebræi pacis nomine solent appellare. Utitur sæpe hac precatione Paulus, ut 1. Cor. I. 3. 2. Cor. I. 2. Gal. I. 3. Eph. I. 2. 1. Thessal. I. 1.

Gratia est primum principium & fons salutis nostræ, Tit. III. vers. 5. pax est consequens gra- tiæ, per quam etsi possint notari quævis prospera, phrasi Ebræa; tamen Apostolo familiare id est, imprimis pacem conscientiæ, in qua regnum DEI consistit, Roman. XIV. vers. 17. cum jungitur di- vinæ gratiæ, designare, de qua Roman. V. v. 1. Gratia est, inquit Hieronymus, qua nullo opere nec merito salvamur. Pax, qua reconciliati Deo per Christum sumus. Theophylactus, præeunte Chry- sostomo, hæc etiam ad scopum intercessionis di- rigit : Quo pacto, inquit, DEI nobis est affutura gratia? Sic certe, si debito nobis obstrictis debita condonemus. Quomodo & Domini Jesu pacem tu assequere, nisi servo Onesimo conciliahere? Cæte- rum cum à Jesu Christo Domino nostro, non mi- nus quam à Deo Patre, gratiam & pacem precatur Apostolus, eandem naturam divinam utriusque esse confirmat: quemadmodum nec adorare ali- um, quam verum natura Deum citra idololatriam fas est, nec gratiam & pacem obtinere nisi à vero natura DEO possumus. Ideo Hieronymus in h. l. Ex quo ostenditur, unam esse Filii Patrisque natu- ram, cum id potest Filius præstare quod Pater, & dicitur id Pater præstare, quod Filius. Utrumque precatur Paulus à Deo & à Christo, quia ejusdem sunt essentia & potentia, & Filius idem præstat, quod Pater, hoc tamen cum discrimine ordinis, quod Pater, ut causa efficiens, Filius ut meritoria salutis nostræ consideratur : Ideo & Pater appella- tur Deus, Filius Dominus, non quod Filius non sit Deus, nec Pater Dominus, sed quia Filius merito suæ obedientiæ peculiare dominium in homines sibi acquisivit. Victores in bello dominium habent in eos, quos è manu hostium ereptos in libertatem asse- ruerunt, ut hic concinne B. Balduinus.

quidem in Dominum Jesum, illam vero in omnes sanctos : quibus ut necessitatem intercessionum apud Deum pro fidelibus, & εὐχαρισίαν pro iis- dem, cum iis obtingit gratia, ac nexum simul cha- ritatis in sanctos cum fide in Jesum ostendit : Sic omnia ista faciunt ad intercessionis suæ pro One- simo admissionem. Testantur enim sanctam & sinceram Φιλαδελφίαν intercessoris, ac Deum si- stunt exemplum, hominum intercessiones exau- dientem: fidemque veram esse non posse sine cha- ritate, ac commiseratione ac condonatione pro- ximo debita : eamque charitatem ferri maxime erga sanctos & fidei domesticos. Porro : hoc loco, Theophylacto dicente, ut misericordem hunc laudat : Non enim è Phrygia ad usque urbem hu- jus esset fama perlata, nisi præstans ille & excellens fuiffet. Ait itaque cum erga omnes sanctos sis cha- ritate affectus, debes & Onesimum hunc amore complecti, qui fidelis jam sit, ut hoc pacto & Deum ipsum cultu & benevolentia prosequi videare. Vi- desne, quam habeant vim in deprecando & persua- dendo hæc verba ? Optime autem hic observavit Oratoriæ Apostolicæ artificium S. Chrysostomus : Non statim ab exordio ipsique principiis gratiam flagitavit, sed antea virum admiratus, ejusque vir- tutes dignis prosequutus laudibus, quum charitatis & in eum suæ non parvum addidisset argumen- tum, quod semper in orationibus suis ejus memi- nisset, dixissetque, quod multi in eo requiescerent, quodque in omnibus obtemperaret & cederet ; tunc & ipsam postremo postulast gratiam, eo ipso faci- lem sibi aditum parans. Deinde ne videretur hu- jus tantum gratia scribere, quasi non alias scri- pturus, nisi Onesimus impelleret, vide quam pru- denter & alias epistolæ adjecit causas. Primum quidem ipsius charitatem insinuat, deinde sibi et- iam parari petit hospitium. Audiens, inquit, cha- ritatem tuam. Non vulgaris hæc laus est, sed insi- gnis plane, majorque, quam si coram se vidisset. Constat enim hanc virtutem, nisi in eo fuisset exi- mia, non adeo potuisse innotescere, ut ad ejus quoque aures perveniret, quum tanta utrumque terra ma- risque intercapedo dirimeret. Nam hic, ut mihi quidem videtur, in Phrygia fuit, cujus rei indi- cium Archippus est, de quo scribit Colossensibus. Quippe Colossenses Phryges sunt. Non opus est illa trajectione, vel ut ἐπίγνωσις de patefactione accipiatur: aut hæc omnia sive ad dilectionis Phi- lemonis commendationem sive ad εὐχαρισίαν re- ferantur. Accipiuntur autem ab aliis vel ut sco- pus precum Apostoli pro Philemone, vel ut am- plificatio famæ de Philemone. Priori modo ex- plicat B. Hunnius : Q. d. Hoc in precatione mea apud Deum ardentibus votis contendo, ut fides, quæ tibi una mecum & cum cæteris Christianis communis est, sit efficax, & non innitatur solo ti- tulo, sed ipsiusmet rei solida veritate, proferente se per effecta fructus nimirum fidei charitatisque ope- ra. E quibus tanquam minime dubiis indiciis fi- des vera in Christum & charitas non simulam po- tenter elucescat, idque per Jesum Christum, omnis boni in nobis autorem & instauratorem unicum. Posteriori Estius cum Thoma : Audio fidem tuam in Christum, audio & charitatem in omnes sanctos, adeo sane, ut illa tua in sanctos beneficentia ex fide profecta neutiquam latere possit, sed omnibus evi- dens ac manifesta fiat, agnoscentibus & prædican- tibus opera tua bona, quæ plurimi facis. Sed præ- stat illa prior explicatio, maxime, ut ea ab Osian- dro proposita est: Precor autem Deum, inquit Pau- lus, ut communicatio fidei tuæ evidens, rectius effi- cax fiat in agnitione omnis operis, Grace, in agni-

## 1:4
Vers. 4.

Εὐχαριςῶ τῷ Θεῷ με.

We owe thanks to God for gifts, not only bestowed upon us, but also upon others, Romans 1:8. 1 Corinthians 1:4. Ephesians 1:16.

Πάντοτε μνείαν σου ποιέμενος ἐπὶ τῶν προσευχῶν με.

You have the same words in the mentioned place Eph. 1:16. From which you may learn that prayers are called here all addresses to God, even those through which nothing is asked, but thanks are given.

Vers. 4.

Εὐχαριςῶ τῷ Θεῷ με.

Gratias Deo debemus pro donis, non tantum in nos, sed & in alios collatis, Roman. I. 8. 1. Corinth. I. v. 1. 4. Ephef. I. vers. 16.

Πάντοτε μνείαν σου ποιέμενος ἐπὶ τῶν προσευχῶν με.

Eadem verba habes dicto loco Eph. I. 16. Unde discas προσευχὰς hic dici omnes ad Deum alloquutiones, etiam per quas non poscitur aliquid, sed gratiæ aguntur.

## 1:5
Verse 5.

Hearing of your love and faith.

He gives the reason for his thanksgiving, such as you will see in the stated passages, Romans I. 8. 1. Cor. I. 4. Ephes. I. 16. Here a remarkable pair is named, love and faith. See 1. Cor. XIII. Gal. V. verse 6. Ephes. VI. v. 23. 1. Thess. III. v. 6. 1. Tim. I. verse 14. VI. v. 11. 2. Tim. I. v. 13. II. v. 22.

Which you have toward the Lord Jesus.

This refers to faith.

And toward all the saints.

This refers to love. All Christians are called saints, as in Ephes. I. verse 1. and often elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

᾿Ακέων σε τὴν ἀγάπην καὶ τὴν πίσιν.

Causam reddit suæ gratiarum actionis, qualem videbis dictis locis, Roman. I. 8. 1. Cor. I. 4. Ephef. I. 16. Egregia hic biga nominatur dilectio & fides. Vide 1. Cor. XIII. Gal. V. vers. 6. Ephes. VI. v. 23. 1. Thess. III. v. 6. 1. Tim. I. vers. 14. VI. v. 11. 2. Tim. I. v. 13. II. v. 22.

Ἣν ἔχεις πρὸς τὸν Κύριον Ἰησῶν.

Hoc ad dilectionem. Sancti vocantur Christiani omnes, ut Ephes. I. vers. 1. & alibi sæpe.

## 1:6
Verse 6.

That the fellowship of your faith may become active in the knowledge of every good thing which is in you in Christ Jesus.

There is first a transposition here. For those words 'in Christ Jesus' pertain to that which preceded, 'your faith'. Then 'fellowship of faith' is put for faith itself, which Philemon had in common with those other Christians. And 'in knowledge' is taken here passively, and has the meaning of becoming known. For the sense is: That love of yours looked to this, that the faith which is common to you with other saints might become active, and thus be known through those good works which proceed from you and others. 'May become active' is said here in the same sense as 'faith working through love', Gal. V. verse 6. Thence follows 'knowledge', that is, the manifestation of the same faith. For faith is shown through works, James II. 18.

The Apostle makes Philemon so certain about his thanksgiving for his faith and charity, that he believes the duty of his own prayers is also perpetually destined for him. Thus Theodoret, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and others. There is no need, therefore, that we confuse prayers and thanksgivings. Namely, since he always made mention of him in his prayers or intercessions before God, he testifies that he deservedly gives thanks to his GOD for the gracious hearing of them. Since he perceives his charity and faith, which he himself has, this acknowledgment of every good in you, in Christ Jesus. i. e. I ask the Lord, that your faith, which you have in common with us, may continually grow, and demonstrate its efficacy (through love): but especially, and more and more, that you may acknowledge with a grateful mind all those spiritual goods which are given to us for the sake of and through CHRIST. In these words, however, and the preceding ones, Philemon is tacitly warned to demonstrate the efficacy of faith through love also in receiving Onesimus. Ἐις χριστὸν, says Camerarius, is either the Apostle's customary ἐναλλαγὴ, that is, ἐν χρισῷ Ἰησῦ. Or it is παντὸς ἀγαθῦ εἰς χρισὸν, so that it may be τείνοντος εἰς χριστὸν, that is, pertaining to the praise of Christ and the truth of Christian doctrine. The Vulgate deviation from the Greek truth has produced diverse interpretations, and those not at all fitting for the text; even the Grotian one, which inserts ἔργον, against the faith of many Codices. Chrysostom has it thus: I pray that the fellowship of your faith may be effective. You see how, before he asks for a favor, he has bestowed a greater one upon him: As he says, that the fellowship of your faith may be effective in the acknowledgment of every good which is in you in CHRIST JESUS. This is, that you may fulfill every form of virtue, and suffer nothing to be lacking to you. For thus faith is effective, if you have works. For without works faith is dead: Nor does he say your faith, but the fellowship of your faith, joining him to himself, and showing them to be one body, and by this very thing most greatly and most aptly agreeing with him. If you are a partner, he says, in faith, you ought also to be a partner in other things.

Vers. 6. For we have great joy and consolation.

Deservedly, he says, we give thanks to God for these virtues of yours, because from them comes to us the greatest joy, and in the evils which we endure for the sake of the Gospel, comfort. Thus also 2 Cor. VII. 4, 13, 1 Thess. III. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Ὅπως ἡ κοινωνία τῆς πίσεώς σε ἐνεργὴς γένηται ἐν ἐπιγνώσει παντὸς ἔργε ἀγαθᾶ τῶ ἐν ὑμῖν εἰς Χρισὸν Ἰησῶν.

Est primum hic trajectio. Nam verba illa εἰς Χρισὸν Ἰησῶν pertinent ad id quod præcessit τῆς πίσεώς σε. Dein- de κοινωνία τῆς πίσεως, positum est pro ipsa fide, quæ Phi- lemoni cum aliis illis Christianis erat communis. Et ἐν ἐπιγνώσει hic παθητικῶς sumitur, habetque innotescendi significationem. Sensus enim est : Eo spectabat tua ista dilectio, ut fides, quæ tibi cum aliis sanctis communis est, actuosa fieret, ac sic cognosceretur per bona illa opera, quæ abs te aliisque procedunt. Ἐνεργὴς γένηται hic dici- tur eodem sensu, quo πίσις δι ἀγάπης ἐνεργεμένη. Gal. V. vers. 6. Inde sequitur ἐπίγνωσις, id est, patefactio ejusdem fidei. Ostenditur enim fides per opera, Jac. II. 18.

De gratiarum actione pro fide ac charitate Philemonis ita certum reddit ipsum Apostolus, ut precum etiam suarum officium sibi perpetuum destinatum esse credat. Sic Theodoreius, Chryso- stomus, Theophylactus alii. Non opus est ergo προσευχὰς καὶ εὐχαρισίας confundamus. Nimi- rum quum semper memoriam ipsius in precibus vel intercessionibus suis apud Deum faceret, gra- tias sese merito DEO suo pro gratiosa earum exauditione agere, testatur. Siquidem percipiat charitatem ejus & fidem, quam habeat ipse, hanc tione omnis boni in vobis, in Christo Jesu. i. e. Rogo Dominum, ut fides tua, quam nobiscum commu- nem habes, subinde crescat, & suam (per charita- tem) efficaciam demonstret: imprimis autem, & ma- gis magisque grata mente agnoscas omnia illa bona spiritualia, quae propter & per CHRISTUM nobis donantur. In his autem verbis & superio- ribus tacite monetur Philemon, ut fidei efficaciam per charitatem etiam in Onesimo recipiendo de- monstret. Ἐις χριστὸν, inquit Camerarius, vel est usitata Apostolo ἐναλλαγὴ, id est, ἐν χρισῷ Ἰησῦ. Vel est παντὸς ἀγαθῦ εἰς χρισὸν, ut sit τείνοντος εἰς χρισὸν, id est pertinentis ad laudem Christi & veritatem doctrinae Christianae. Vulgata deviatio a veritate Graeca diversas interpretationes, eas- que textui haud convenientes procreavit; etiam Grotianam, quae ἔργον inserit, praeter plurium Codd. fidem. Chrysostomus ita habet: Oro, ut efficax sit societas fidei tuae. Vides ut antequam gratiam postulet, majorem ipsi praestiterit: Ut in- quit societas fidei tuae efficax sit in agnitione omnis boni, quod in vobis est in CHRISTO JESU. Hoc est, ut omnem virtutis speciem impleas, ni- hilque tibi deesse patiaris. Ita enim fides efficax est, si habes opera. Nam sine operibus fides mortua est: Nec ait fides tua, sed societas fidei tuae, il- lum sibi ipsi conjungens, & corpus unum osten- dens, atque hoc ipso illum maxime aptissimeque con- veniens. Si socius, inquit, es in fide, debes & in cateris esse socius.

Vers. 6. Χαρὰν γὰρ ἔχομεν πολλὴν καὶ παρά- κλησιν.

Merito, inquit, gratias Deo pro istis vestris virtuti- bus habemus, quia nobis maximum inde gaudium, & in malis, quae Evangelii causa toleramus, solatium prove- nit. Sic & 2. Cor. VII. 4. 13. 1. Thessal. III. 7.

## 1:7
Because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed by you, brother.

Σπλάγχνα here for mind, as Sirach XXX. 7, XXXIII. v. 5. And so ἀναπέπαυται τὰ σπλάγχνα, and below 20, ἀνάπαυσόν με τὰ σπλάγχνα has a similar sense to that, ἀνέπαυσαν τὸ ἐμὸν πνεῦμα, 1 Cor. XVI. 18. The poor, he says, are of a tranquil mind, because they have learned by experience that in your riches there is provision ready for their needs.

The Osiandrian paraphrase is also most pleasing here: For I have had great joy, more correctly: we have, and consolation (that is, most sweet recreation) in your love which is not at all feigned: because the hearts of the saints, (that is, the hearts of believers) have rested, more correctly: have been refreshed by you, by your singular kindness and the services with which you have hitherto followed the faithful, my dearest brother: wherefore I do not doubt that you will always be like yourself, so that you may willingly and promptly grant me a favor, as I ask something of you. Compare also B. Hunnius. Nothing can so move his mind, says Chrysostom, as to recount benefits communicated to others, especially when he is here far more worthy and venerable than them. He does not indeed say, when you do these things for others, how much more ought you not to deny me what you provide for others: But he has nevertheless admonished this very thing in other words, seeking that which is in some way milder and more pleasing. You, he says, have given me the confidence to ask from these things which you have bestowed upon others. And much, he says, consolation, that is, we are not only joyful, but we are also affected with consolation: for they are our members. If therefore there ought to be such concord and harmony of members, that in the rest of others, these also, who are in tribulation, though destitute of rest, nevertheless rejoice for their sake, as if the benefit of rest were flowing into the whole body: How much more have you also granted rest to us? Nor does he indeed say, because you yield, because you are obedient, but much more vehemently and expressively: Because, he says, the hearts of the saints have been refreshed by you. For as if a little child were too dear and lovable to its parents: So the love and affection and indulgence of those who have been set free indicates that he had been too much loved by the saints. And these things for the sake of preparation, but in such a way that many arguments for the intercession to be admitted have already been insinuated, before it is proposed.

PART II. INTERCESSORY.

Latin:

Ὅτι τὰ σπλάγχνα τῶν ἁγίων ἀναπέπαυται διὰ σῦ ἀδελφέ.

Σπλάγχνα hic pro animo, ut Sirach. XXX. 7. XXXIII. v. 5. Itaque ἀναπέπαυται τὰ σπλάγχνα, & infra 20. ἀνά- παυσόν με τὰ σπλάγχνα parem sensum habet cum illo, ἀνέπαυσαν τὸ ἐμὸν πνεῦμα, 1. Cor. XVI. 18. Pauperes, in- quit, tranquillo sunt animo, eo quod experiendo didi- cerint, in tuis divitiis paratum esse suis necessitatibus subsidium.

Placet hic etiam maxime Osiandrina para- phrasis: Gaudium enim magnum habui, rectius: habemus, & consolationem (id est recreationem suavissimam) in charitate tua minime simulata: quia viscera sanctorum, (id est, corda creden- tium) requieverunt, rectius: recreata sunt per te, singulari tua humanitate & officiis, quibus hactenus prosequutus es fideles, charissime mi fra- ter: quare non dubito, quin semper tui similis sis futurus, ut mihi, petenti a te aliquid, libenter & prompte gratificeris. Confer. & B. Hunnius. Nihil ita ejus animum movere potest, inquit Chrysostomus, ut beneficia in alios communicata retexere, maxime cum eis hic longe dignior & venerabilior sit. Non quidem ait, quum haec aliis facias, quanto magis mihi denegare non debes, quod caeteris praestas: Sed hoc ipsum tamen aliis verbis admonuit, lenius id quodammodo & gra- tius expetens. Tu mihi, inquit, dedisti fiduciam postulandi ex his, quae in alios contulisti. Et mul- tam, inquit, consolationem, id est non solum lae- tamur, sed etiam consolatione afficimur: membra enim nostra illi sunt. Si igitur tantam esse opor- tet concordiam consonantiamque membrorum, ut in aliorum requie, hi quoque, qui in tribulatione sunt, quietis exortes, illorum tamen gratia exul- tent, quasi in totum corpus manante quietis bene- ficio: Quanto magis & tu nobis requiem tribui- sti? Neque vero ait, quoniam cedis, quoniam ob- temperans, sed multo quidem vehementius atque expressius: Quoniam inquit viscera sanctorum per te requieverunt. Ac si enim parvulus charus nimium atque amabilis parentibus sit: Ita chari- tas & affectio & indulgentia liberatis eum indicat à sanctis nimium fuisse dilectum. Atque haec πα- ρασκευῆς ἕνεκα, sed ita, ut argumenta plurima jam insinuata sint admittendae intercessionis, an- tequam ea proponatur.

PARS II. INTERCESSORIA.

## 1:8
Vers. 8. Therefore, having much boldness in Christ, to command what is fitting.

The apostolic function enjoined upon me by Christ gives me this right, that I may be able to enjoin upon you, and other Christians, those things which are of your duty. The word Παῤῥησίας came from the Greek language to the Syrians with a broader meaning, so that it often signifies right and authority.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Διὸ πολλὴν ἐν χριστῷ παῤῥησίαν ἔχων, ἐπιτάσσειν τὸ ἀνῆκον.

Apostolica functio mihi à Christo injuncta hoc jus mi- hi dat, ut tibi, Christianisque aliis ea praecipere possim, quae officii vestri sint. Παῤῥησίας vox ex Graeco sermo- ne ad Syros venit latiore significatu, ita ut saepe jus au- toritatemque significet.

## 1:9
Vers. 9. For love's sake I rather beseech.

I prefer to beseech as a friend through the necessity of our friendship.

Being such a one.

That is, I descend to entreaties, since I am such as you know me to be.

As Paul,

The founder of so many churches.

An old man,

Now also of advanced age, to whom even strangers grant many things.

But now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.

That is, bound on account of Christ, as we have just said. Great reverence is owed to those who endure hardships for the most honorable causes, Col. IV. 18. Eph. IV. 1.

With many praises having been premised, to use the words of Jerome now on Philemon, since the matter for which he is about to ask is such that it is both excellent and useful, and to the one asking, Paul could have commanded more than requested. And this came from that confidence, that he who had performed such great works for Christ, certainly could not be unequal to himself in other things. But he wishes to request rather than to command, with the great authority of the petitioner set forth, through which he both as an Apostle beseeches, and as an old man, and as a prisoner of JESUS CHRIST. Chrysostom has executed a more prolix artifice of speech: Observe, I pray, how cautiously he proceeds. For lest anything, though expressed with the greatest force of charity, might perhaps strike the hearer, and therefore be taken heavily, and therefore before he said, to command thee, because that seemed heavy, and although it could rather be taken care of as having proceeded from charity, yet out of an abundance of caution he fortifies himself, saying, having confidence: Which is surely an indication of Philemon being of great merit, and as if he were to say: thou hast given us confidence, and not this alone, but in Christ. Not therefore because thou art more famous and powerful in the world, do we presume concerning this matter: But because of the faith which thou hast in CHRIST. And so at last he adds: To command thee; not even that alone, but also what is expedient, that is, a reasonable thing. And observe, I beseech thee, from how many places he prepares for himself an approach to his heart. Others, he says, and myself thou dost cherish with benefits both for Christ's sake, and because the matter is reasonable, and because charity gives: For the sake of which I rather beseech; as if he were to say: I know indeed, that even by commanding I would easily effect what I intend, which I gather from thy previous works, but because I have a great zeal for this matter, I beseech. He shows both at once, that he both trusted him, because he obtained it, and that this concern was vehemently at his heart. For he beseeches, Such, he says, being as Paul the aged. O ineffable goodness! in how many ways does he approach him? From how many parts does he proceed to entreat? From the quality of the person. For Paul [proceeds] from his age, because he is an old man; from the fact that he persuades all men more justly and powerfully. Since he is a prisoner of Jesus Christ. Who, I ask, would not receive with open arms such an athlete, famous for countless victories? Who, beholding one in chains for Christ, would not offer him countless thanks? Revere, he says, according to Theodoret the Interpreter, Paul, revere his old age, revere the chains with which I am bound as a preacher of the truth! The Vulgate version reads wrongly here, 'cum talis sis' [since you are such], which Thomas explains thus: If you were a boy, I would command you; since you are an old man, I entreat you: Whom Justinian refutes here, because by this [interpretation] Paul cannot be excused from a solecism.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Διὰ τὴν ἀγάπην μᾶλλον παρα- καλῶ.

Malo ut amicum precari per necessitudinem amicitiae nostrae.

Τοιοῦτος ὤν.

Id est ad preces descendo, cum talis sim, qualem me esse nosti.

Ὡς Παῦλος,

Tot Ecclesiarum conditor.

Πρεσβύτης,

Jam & provecta aetate cui multa concedunt etiam ignoti.

Νῦν δὲ καὶ δέσμιος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.

Id est, propter Christum vinctus, ut modo diximus. Magna debetur reverentia iis, qui dura ferunt honestissi- mis de causis, Col. IV. 18. Eph. IV. 1.

Multis, ut Hieronymi verbis jam utar, in Philemonem laudibus ante praemissis, cum res ta- lis sit, pro qua rogaturus est, quae & praestanti u- tilis sit & roganti, poterat Paulus magis impera- re quam petere. Et hoc ex fiducia illa veniebat, quod qui tanta ob Christum opera perpetrarat, utique impar sui in caeteris esse non poterat. Sed vult magis petere quam jubere, grandi petentis autoritate proposita, per quam & Apostolus ob- secrat & senex & vinctus JESU CHRISTI. Prolixius orationis artificium exequutus est Chrysostomus: Inspice quaeso, quam cautus ince- dat. Ne quid enim, maxima licet vi charitatis expressum, auditorem forte feriret, atque ideo gra- viter ferret, ideoque antequam diceret, imperan- di tibi, quia id grave videbatur, ac licet ex cha- ritate profectum curare potius posset, ex abun- dantia tamen magis secura praemunit, dicens, fi- duciam habens: Quod profecto Philemonem ma- gni esse meriti indicantis est, ac si dicat: fidu- ciam tu nobis dedisti, neque hoc solum, sed in Chri- sto. Non ideo quod sis in seculo clarior & poten- tior, de re ista praesumimus: Sed propter fidem quam habes in CHRISTUM. Sicque demum addit: Imperandi tibi; etiam ne id quidem so- lum, sed etiam quod expedit, hoc est, rationabilem rem. Et inspice obsecro, quam multis ex locis sibi ad cor ejus aditum parat. Alios, inquit, & me ipsum beneficiis foves & propter Christum, & quia res rationabilis est, & quia charitas dat: Propter quam magis obsecro; ac si dicat: Scio quidem, quod etiam imperans facile efficaciam, quod intendo, quod ex praecedentibus tuis ope- ribus colligo, sed quia mihi hujus rei magnum studium est, obsecro. Utrumque simul ostendit, quod & ipsi confideret, quia impetravit, & quod ea cura sibi vehementer cordi esset. Obsecrat enim, Talis, inquit, existens ut Paulus senex. O ineffa- bilem bonitatem! quantis hunc modis aggreditur? Quot ex partibus exorare pergit? Ex persona qua- litate. Paulus enim ex ætate, quia senex; ex eo, quod omnibus justius potentiusque persuadet. Quo- niam vinctus Jesu Christi. Quis, oro, hujusmodi athletam innumeris victoriis clarum non obviis exciperet manibus? Quis intuens vinctum pro Christo, non ei innumeras deferret gratias? revere- re, inquit Theodoreto Interprete, Paulum, reve- rere senectutem, reverere vincula, quibus ut veri- tatis prædicator adstrictus sum! Vulgata versio perperam hic legit, cum talis sis: quam ita Tho- mas explicat: Si puer esses, præciperem tibi, cum sis senex, precor: Quem refellit hic Ju- stinianus, quod per eam nequeat Paulus à Solœ- cismo excusari.

## 1:10
Vers. 10. I beseech thee.

Here 'Παρακαλῶ σε' has the meaning of praying or rather of entreating. If servants had committed any fault, they were accustomed to provide themselves with an intercessor, as Donatus notes on Terence. Similar to this is Pliny's entreaty for the freedman of Sabinianus, in the twenty-first letter of the ninth book.

When therefore, Chrysostom continues, he had prepared and mitigated his mind in so many ways, he did not immediately add the name, but after such a remarkable admonition of this kind, he still delays. For you know the indignation of masters against runaway servants, and especially if they have fled after plundering the household goods: however mild they may have been, anger grows from the loss sustained. He strives, therefore, to soothe this in every way. And first, by persuading him to provide everything, whatever it may be, readily. When he had now prepared his mind for every obedience, then he adds what he wants, and says, 'I beseech thee.' And he added praises when he introduces, 'for my son, whom I have begotten in my chains.'

Concerning my child, whom I begat in my bonds.

Whom I made a Christian here in Rome, while I am in chains. It is the work of God to regenerate a man. But such is His goodness that He admits His ministers into the fellowship of His name, 1 Cor. 4:15, Gal. 4:19. Thus also the Apostles are said to 'save,' Rom. 11:14, and others, 1 Cor. 7:16.

Again, says Chrysostom, [he uses] things that have the power of placating and entreating, and only then is the name appended. For he not only extinguished his anger, but also filled him with great joy. I would by no means, he says, call him a son, unless he were highly approved and useful. Finally, I call him and Timothy by the same name. But when he had declared his affection in many places, he also indicates his reverence from the time of his birth. 'In chains,' he says, 'I begat him': so that from this love he may be deemed more worthy of honor, and because he was brought forth amidst the very struggles and in the very temptations for CHRIST: Wishing, says Jerome, to obtain what he asks, he asserts that he is now entreating not for Philemon's servant, but for his own son, and that son whom he begat in the chains of the Gospel, that is, which he was enduring for the Gospel of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Παρακαλῶ σε.

Παρακαλῶ σε hic precandi aut potius deprecandi ha- bet significationem. Servi si quid deliquissent, precato- rem sibi parare solebant, ut notat ad Terentium Donatus. Similis est huic deprecatio Plinii pro liberto Sabiniani e- pistola libri IX. una & vicesima.

Quum itaque, pergit Chrysostomus, tam mul- tis modis præparasset & mitigasset illis animum, non continuo adjecit nomen, sed post hujusmodi adeo insignem admonitionem differt adhuc. No- stis quippe Dominorum adversus profugos servos indignationem, & maxime si re familiari expi- lata diffugerint: quamlibet illi mites fuerint, ex accepto detrimento ira succrescit. Hanc igitur le- nire modis omnibus contendit. Ac primum per- suadens omnia, quæcunque illa sint, alacriter sub- ministrare. Quum jam animum ipsius ad omnem parasset obedientiam, tunc jam quid velit, ad- jungit, & dicit, obsecro te. Et adjecit laudes, quum infert, pro filio meo, quem ego genui in vin- culis meis.

Περὶ τῦ ἐμῦ τέκνε, ὃν ἐγέννησα ἐν τοῖς δεσμοῖς μγ.

Quem hic Romæ, dum vinctus sum, Christianum fe- ci. Dei opus est regignere hominem. Sed tanta est ejus bonitas, ut in nominis sui consortium ministros suos ad- mittat, 1. Cor. IV. 15. Galat. IV. 19. Sic & σώζειν dicun- tur Apostoli, Rom. XI. 14. & alii, 1. Cor. VII. 16.

Rursus, inquit Chrysostomus, quæ placandi ac exorandi vim habent, & dum demum nomen ap- ponitur. Non modo enim extinxit iram, ve- rum & magna jucunditate replevit. Nequaquam inquit illum vocarem filium, nisi esset valde ap- probatus & utilis. Illum denique ac Timotheum eodem appello nomine. Ubi vero plurimis in locis affectum suum declarasset, ex partus quoque tem- pore sui reverentiam indicat. Vinctus, inquit, illum genui: ut ex hoc amore dignior honore cen- seatur, & quod esset inter ipsa certamina, & in ipsis pro CHRISTO tentationibus editus: Vo- lens, inquit Hieronymus, impetrare quod postulat, jam non pro servo Philemonis, sed pro filio suo se asserit deprecari, & illo filio quem genuerit in vinculis Evangelii, hoc est, quæ pro Christi Evange- lio sustinebat.

## 1:11
Vers. 11. Him who was once to thee unprofitable.

It is the custom of those who entreat to soften the harshness of things with words. Onesimus had not only been useless to Philemon, but had also caused him loss. Flight and theft are usually joined together. Therefore, in the Justinian Code, the title concerning runaway servants is followed by that concerning thefts. Martial: 'From the feet, the wanton hands have learned to sin: I do not wonder at the thief, who was a runaway.' And those who sold a servant were accustomed to promise that he was not a thief, that he was not a runaway. L. Cum in venditione, L. Lucius §. ult., L. Evicta re. §. ult., L. Si ita quis, L. Quia dicitur. D. de Emptionibus. L. quoties. D. si familia furtum fecisse dicatur. L. Et emptor §. venditorem D. de act. empt. Varro II. de re Rustica. Seneca Controv. III. 21.

See how prudently, says Chrysostom, he confesses his fault, so that by that very thing he may extinguish the master's anger. 'I know,' he says, 'that he was useless. But now he will be useful both to you and to me.' He does not say: 'but then he will be useful to you': lest he should not believe it, but he also introduced his own person, so that from this he might more worthily hope for better things. 'But now,' he says, 'he will be useful both to you and to me.' For if he is to be useful to Paul, who demands such great diligence of virtue and perfection, how much more to his Master! Who, although before, as Jerome says, he was only useless to his Master—for a servant who is a thief or a runaway did not harm another, except his Master—now, on the contrary, by the compensation of utility, by which he is useful to the Master himself and to Paul, and through Paul to others, he deserves more charity than he had previously deserved hatred. Whence he says: 'Who was once useless to you,' to you, he says, alone, not to others, 'but now he is useful both to me and to you.' Useful to the Master in this, because he can also serve Paul in place of his Master; but useful to Paul in this, because while he is detained in prison and chains, he could minister to him in the Gospel. At the same time, one must admire the magnanimity of the Apostle, and his mind fervent toward Christ. He is held in prison, bound by chains, constricted by the squalor of his body, the separation from loved ones, and penal darkness, and he does not feel the injury, he is not tortured by pain, he knows nothing else but to think of the Gospel of CHRIST. He knew the servant, he knew the runaway, he knew the one who was once a robber had been converted to the faith of Christ. It is a work of great labor for such a man to persevere in what he has begun. Therefore, he inculcates and repeats that he is his son, and the son of his chains, and a minister of the Gospel of one established in chains, so that Philemon, who was prudently and diplomatically praised only in the preface, would not dare to refuse, lest he appear unworthy of his own praises.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Τὸν ποτέ σοι ἄχρηστον.

Deprecantium mos est rerum asperitatem verbis leni- re. Onesimus non inutilis modo Philemoni fuerat, sed & damnum dederat. Conjuncta esse solent fuga ac fur- tum. Itaque in Codice Justinianeo titulum de servis fu- gitivis sequitur ille de furtis. Martialis: A pedibus didicere manus peccare protervæ: Non miror furem, qui fugitivus erat. Et qui servum vendebant, promittere solebant furem non esse, fugitivum non esse. L. Cum in venditione, L. Lucius §. ult. L. Evicta re. §. ult. L. Si ita quis. L. Quia dicitur. D. de Emptionibus. L. quoties. D. si familia furtum fecisse di- catur. L. Et emptor §. venditorem D. de act. empt. Var- ro II. de re Rustica. Seneca Controv. III. 21.

Vide quam prudenter, inquit Chrysostomus, ipsius delictum confitetur, ut eo ipso extinguat ira- cundiam Domini. Scio, inquit, quod inutilis fue- rit. Nunc autem & tibi & mihi utilis erit. Non ait: tunc autem tibi utilis erit: Ne ille non cre- deret, sed personam quoque induxit suam, ut ex hoc dignius sperare meliora possit. Nunc autem, in- quit, & tibi & mihi utilis erit. Si enim Paulo futurus est utilis, qui tantam virtutis & perfe- ctionis diligentiam exigit, quanto magis Domino! Qui cum ante, dicente Hieronymo, inutilis tan- tum Domino suo fuerit, nec enim servus fur aut fugitivus alteri nocuit, nisi Domino suo: nunc è contrario utilitatis compensatione, qua ipsi Do- mino & Paulo utilis est, cæterisque per Paulum plus charitatis meretur, quam odii ante meruerat. Un- de ait: Qui tibi aliquando inutilis fuit, tibi, in- quit, soli, non cæteris, nunc autem & mihi & ti- bi utilis. Utilis Domino in eo, quia possit & Pau- lo servire pro Domino suo; Paulo vero in eo uti- lis, quia illo in carcere vinculisque detento posset ei in Evangelio ministrare. Simul autem admi- randum de magnanimitate Apostoli, & in Chri- stum mente ferventis. Tenetur in carcere, vin- culis stringitur, squalore corporis, charorum sepa- ratione, pœnalibus tenebris coarctatur, & non sentit injuriam, non dolore cruciatur, nihil novit aliud, nisi de CHRISTI Evangelio cogitare. Sciebat servum, sciebat fugitivum, sciebat ali- quando raptorem ad Christi fidem esse conversum. Grandis laboris est talem hominem in eo perseve- rare quod cœpit. Idcirco filium suum, & filium vinculorum & ministrum Evangelii in vinculis constituti inculcat ac replicat, ut Philemon ille prudenter & dispensatorie tantum in præfatione laudatus, non auderet negare, ne suis laudibus vi- deretur indignus.

## 1:12
Vers. 12. But now to you and to me useless. Because he was useful to Paul, he was also to Philemon. For the things of friends are common. He alludes to the name of Onesimus. ὃν ἀνέπεμψα) Namely with this letter. And in this respect, according to Chrysostom, he mitigates anger, when he delivers him into the hands of the master. For then masters are most accustomed to be indignant, when prayers are offered to them on behalf of the absent. This, therefore, is the very thing above all that restrains his entire spirit and fury. Theophylact: Just as if he said, I deliver him to you, use him at your own discretion. For thus he placates even the somewhat angry spirit of Philemon. Blessed Hunnius observes that Paul wished by this token also to declare his honorable judgment concerning Onesimus: as if to say, If I thought that he would be useless to you hereafter as well, believe me, I am of such a mind toward you that I would never have sent him back to you. But now because I fear nothing in sending him back to you, you have a most abundant testimony of my opinion concerning him, which is by no means vain. Furthermore, while Paul sends the slave back to his master, he does not act against the law of Deuteronomy 23:15. For there it concerns slaves driven away by their masters, who could not be saved except by fleeing.

Σὺ δὲ ἀυτὸν, τουτέσι τὰ ἐμὰ σπλάγχνα προσ- λαβοῦ. Προσλαμβάνεσθαι has various meanings, all pertaining to benevolence and benefits, as appears in Acts 18:26, Romans 14:1, 3, chapter 15:7. Here the interpreters: To receive kindly into the home, as in Acts 28:2. Τὰ ἐμὰ σπλάγχνα, that is, as beloved to me as we love our own bowels. Artemidorus: Τὰ σπλάγχνα signifies a child. Thus in Plautus: My little heart.

The proposition, which he finally submits after the arguments constructed with singular art, so that it may be so much the more pleasant may flow into the mind of Philemon. He asks that he receive him back into his former favor. The act of Philemon ought to correspond to his own remission: therefore he says: But you, but you, praised by me for so many reasons, receive him, namely with a benevolent mind. He has inserted, however, a very effective argument into the proposition. For he does not say nakedly, receive him, nor as a servant henceforth to be useful, or as one repenting, but him, that is, my own bowels. Oecumenius: What do I say, that you should receive him? Receiving him, you will receive my bowels. I love him so much, he says, that I call him my bowels. Thus he wishes him to be received not just as his son, but as a beloved one. This has more strength than if he had nakedly named him son. If he were to reject him, he would reject Paul himself, he would be hard toward his very bowels, whom he was accustomed to venerate as another parent.
