He had refreshed the bowels of the saints, and would he keep the bowels of Paul, an old man and a prisoner of JESUS CHRIST, away from his own family? By this act he would draw away from himself all the praise with which he was adorned by the Apostle, as Crocius says here. It is pleasant to hear the golden mouth again. And here again he did not simply place the name, but also added the voice of one exhorting, which has far more strength than if he said son. He had said son, he had said whom I have begotten in bonds, so that he might seem especially lovable from the fact that he was begotten in pressures and in temptations. For that we are especially affected by those sons whom we beget among dangers or even after dangers is proved by the testimony of Scripture, which reveals Benjamin as a son delicate to his father Jacob from the fact that his mother bore him while dying, and called him Benoni, that is, son of my sorrow. But you, he says, receive him, that is, my own bowels. From these words he shows the magnitude of his charity. He does not say receive, he did not say, do not be angry, but take him to yourself, that is, he merits not only pardon, but also honor. For he is made the son of Paul. Jerome says: Bowels signify the internal affection of the heart, and a full will from the soul, when everything that is in us is received by the one asked. Otherwise, however, all children are the bowels of their parents. Which latter is more convenient. He is mine, he says according to Theodoret, a son born from my bowels. It can, however, be illustrated from the former. Thus you will receive my very bowels, my heart, and whatever is in me. Theophylact has it thus: But you receive him as my bowels, that is, receive with charity this very person, whom I myself follow with benevolence and hold in my heart no differently than myself. We easily acquiesce here to the Grotian explanation.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Νυνὶ δὲ σοι κὶ ἐμοὶ ἄχρηστον. Quia Paulo utilis erat, erat & Philemoni. Communia enim sunt τὰ τῶν φίλων. Alludit ad nomen Onesimi. ὃν ἀνέπεμψα) Nempe cum hac epistola. Et hac ex parte, Judice Chrysostomo, iracun- diam mitigat, quum illum in manus Domini tra- dit. Tunc enim maxime Domini indignari so- lent, quum sibi pro absentibus preces porriguntur. Hoc igitur ipsum imprimis est, quod ejus animum furoremque compescit omnem. Theophylactus: Perinde, inquit, ac si dicat, hunc tibi trado, pro tuo utere arbitratu. Sic enim vel subiratum Phi- lemonis animum placat. Beatus Hunnius obser- vat, hoc quoque symbolo suum de Onesimo ho- norificum judicium declarare voluisse Paulum: q. d. Si existimarem, ipsum tibi posthac etiam inu- tilem fore, crede mihi, sum ego eo in te animo, ut nunquam illum ad te remissurus fuerim. Nunc vero quia nihil metuo illum tibi remittere, habes meæ de ipso opinionis haudquaquam vanæ testi- monium locupletissimum. Cæterum dum Paulus servum remittit hero, non agit contra legem Deuteronom. XXXIII. vers. 15. Ibi enim agitur de servis ab heris abactis, qui non nisi fugiendo servari potuerunt.

Σὺ δὲ ἀυτὸν, τουτέσι τὰ ἐμὰ σπλάγχνα προσ- λαβῦ. Προσλαμβάνεσθαι varias habet significationes, omnes ad benevolentiam & beneficia pertinentes, ut apparet Actor. XVIII. vers. 26. Roman. XIV. vers. 1. 3. cap. XV. vers. 7. Hic Interpretes: Benigne in domum recipere, quo- modo Actor. XXVIII. vers. 2. Τὰ ἐμὰ σπλάγχνα, id est, ita mihi dilectum quomodo viscera nostra diligimus. Ar- temidorus: Τὰ σπλάγχνα τὸν παῖδα σημαίνει. Sic apud Plautum: Meum corculum.

Propositio, quam arte singulari præstructis argumentis demum subjicit, ut tanto jucundius in Philemonis animum influat. Petit ut eum in pristinam recipiat gratiam. Suæ remissioni re- spondere debet actus Philemonis: ideo ait: Tu au- tem, tu autem mihi tot nominibus laudatus eum excipe animo scilicet benevolo. Insevit autem pro- positioni argumentum valde efficax. Non enim nude ait, excipe eum, nec servum deinceps uti- lem futurum, aut resipiscentem, sed eum, id est, viscera mea. Oecumenius: Quid dico, ut eum suscipias? Hunc suscipiens mea viscera suscipies. Adeo inquit, diligo, ut eum mea appellem vi- scera. Sic non utcunque ut filium suum, sed ut di- lectum vult recipi. Hoc plus habet roboris, quam si nude nominasset filium. Si rejiceret, ipsum Pau- lum rejiceret, in ipsius viscera esset durus, quem tanquam alterum parentem solebat venerari. Re- focillaverat sanctorum viscera, & à sua familia arceret viscera Pauli, senis & captivi JESU CHRISTI? Ipse hoc facto sibi omnem laudem detraheret, qua ornatus ab Apostolo, ut hic Cro- cius. Juvat iterum audire os aureum. Et hic rursus non simpliciter posuit nomen, sed etiam vo- cem adhortantis adjecit, quæ longe plus habet vi- rium, quam si filium diceret. Dixerat filium, dixerat quem in vinculis genui, ut ex eo maxi- me videretur amabilis, quod esset in pressuris & in tentationibus genitus. Quod enim illis maxime filiis afficiamur, quos inter pericula vel etiam post pericula gignimus, testimonio Scripturæ probatur, quæ Benjamin delicatum Patri Jacob filium ex eo manifestat, quod hunc mater moriens edide- rit, appellavitque Benoni, hoc est, filium dolo- ris. Tu autem ipsum, inquit, hoc est, viscera mea suscipe. Ex his verbis magnitudinem chari- tatis ostendit. Non ait recipe, non dixit, ne ira- scaris, sed suscipe, hoc est, non modo veniam, sed honorem quoque promeretur. Est enim Pauli filius effectus. Hieronymus inquit: Viscera significant in- ternum cordis affectum, & plenam ex animo vo- luntatem, cum totum, quicquid in nobis est, sus- cipitur à rogato. Alias autem omnes liberi visce- ra sunt parentum. Quod posterius est conve- nientius. Meus est, inquit secundum Theodo- retum, filius natus ex visceribus meis. Illustrari tamen è priori potest. Ita suscipies ipsa viscera mea, cor meum, & quicquid in me est. Theo- phylactus sic habet: Tu vero illum ut viscem mea suscipe, id est, cum charitate hunc ipsum excipito, quem ipse haud secus ac meipsum & benevolentia prosequar & cordi habeo. Facile autem hic ac- quiescimus Grotianæ explicationi.

## 1:13
Vers. 13. Whom I wished to keep with myself.

Here is an Indicative for a Subjunctive in the Greek manner. I would have wished to retain him with me, namely, had other reasons not stood in the way, which will now follow. Concerning this kind of speaking, see what we have said at Matt. XXVI. 39.

He brings forward another argument, according to B. Hunnius, by which he may conquer the mind of Philemon and lead him to enter into a pious reconciliation with Onesimus. For it is shown by these words that Onesimus had served Paul the prisoner with such zeal, assiduity, diligence, and highest fidelity that, if it had been permitted to retain him with the good peace of Philemon, the Apostle would have altogether retained him. Therefore, by this example and by his own most honest judgment concerning him, the Apostle insinuates this reasoning to Philemon, so that he may weigh with himself that, because such an Apostle judges and feels so honestly about Onesimus, that judgment and testimony will by no means be for nothing, but that the fact is clearly such as Paul proclaims.

That he might serve me in your stead. That he might perform for me those things which you, if you were here, would be about to perform for me in all things.

In these bonds, which I sustain for the sake of the Gospel. The same kind of speaking which we had above at 9.

Attend, Theophylact warns, how wisely and gradually he places the servant in the place of the Lord, so that, he says, he might serve me for you. He shows besides that he desires those things which will be of use to Philemon, as if he were saying this: for if you are bound to me by the duty of serving, and Onesimus indeed performs this very thing for you, will that not be a gain for you? You owe me, he says, with Theodoret as interpreter, a ministry, as a disciple to a Master; I wished therefore to retain him for you, so that he might discharge the debt of your ministry to me. One can see the power of the Gospel; it makes the servant equal to the Lord. Now, is it not also clear from this that Paul brought the saving preaching to the Colossians, because he writes to Philemon as to a disciple?

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ὃν ἐγὼ ἐβουλόμην πρὸς ἐμαυτὸν κατέχειν.

Est hic Indicativus pro Subjunctivo more Græco. Vo- luissem eum mecum retinere, nempe nisi obstitissent ra- tiones aliæ, quæ jam sequentur. De hoc loquendi gene- re vide quæ diximus ad Matth. XXVI. 39.

Aliud argumentum, secundum B. Hunnium, profert, quo Philemonis animum expugnet, & ad piam reconciliationem cum Onesimo ineun- dam traducat. Ostenditur enim hisce verbis, Onesimum studio, sedulitate, diligentia & fide summa ita ministrasse Paulo captivo, ut si bona cum pace Philemonis illum retinere licuisset, o- mnino retenturus illum fuerit Apostolus. Hoc igi- tur exemplo suo facto que honestissimo de eo judicio hanc ratiocinationem insinuat Apostolus Phile- moni, ut secum perpendat, quia tantus Aposto- lus tam honeste judicet & sentiat de Onesimo, ne- quaquam id judicium ac testimonium fore de ni- hilo, sed plane talem esse factum, qualem Paulus deprædicet.

Ἵνα ὑπὲρ σῦ διακονῇ μοι. Ut mihi præstaret, quæ tu, si hic esses, præstiturus mihi omnia esses.

Ἐν τοῖς δεσμοῖς τῦ Εὐαγγελίυ. In his vinculis, quæ Evangelii causa sustineo. Idem loquendi genus, quod habuimus supra 9.

Attende, monet Theophylactus, quam sapie- nter & sensim in Domini loco servum adstituat, ut pro te, inquit, mihi ministraret. Ostendit præterea, ea se cupere, quæ Philemoni usui sint futura, tanquam id diceret, si enim tu mihi ob- strictus es ministrandi officio, Onesimus vero pro te hoc ipsum exequitur, nonne id tibi futurum est lucro? Debes, inquit, Theodoreto Interprete, mihi ministerium, ut discipulus Magistro, volui ergo eum pro te retinere, ut tui ministerii mihi debitum exolveret. Videre potentiam Evangelii efficit servum æqualem Domino. Jam non & hoc etiam clarum esse, Paulum prædicationem salu- tarem attulisse Colossensibus, quia ad Philemo- nem scribit, tanquam ad discipulum.

## 1:14
Vers. 14.

But without your opinion I did not wish to do anything) I did not want to use him, unless you were willing to do so of your own accord.

That it might not be as if by necessity your good deed, but by your own free will.

For if Paul had kept him, the will of Philemon would not have appeared as much as if he himself, having been sent to him, sent him back to Paul. Seneca II. de Benef. IV. If you wish to know whether I am willing, make it so that I am able to be unwilling. Ἑκύσιον & ἀναγκαῖον, or τὸ κατ᾽ ἀνάγκην are opposed to one another, as in 1 Peter 5:2. Thus, to perform something by free will and out of necessity, Paul the Jurisconsult opposes them in L. Atqui natura §. Si libero D. de negotiis gestis. Praise, however, is not owed except to free actions.

This, says Chrysostom, is what primarily moves the Lord, when the matter is both useful, and yet is not attempted without His opinion. And he adds: So that your good deed might not be as if by necessity, but voluntary. For I knew, he says, that if you had not been forewarned, but had suddenly learned that it was done, not even then would you have taken it ill or indignantly: but I preferred to move you out of abundance, so that your good deed might not be as if by necessity. Τὸ ἀγαθὸν, as Camerarius says, is ἡ ἀγαθεργία or ἀγαθοποιία. So that the work of your kindness might be voluntary, not forced by necessity. Estius gathers from this that it is likely that Paul expected that Onesimus would either be gifted to him or simply manumitted. For he thinks that is what is noted by the word τὸ ἀγαθὸν. But why does the Apostle not ask directly that Onesimus be manumitted? Estius answers: This was done 1. lest Onesimus should seem to have derived an advantage from his wrongdoing, namely, having obtained liberty from theft and flight. 2. because perhaps the request would have been too burdensome for Philemon. For slaves were very useful to their masters, and a good part of their property. 3. The Apostle would have seemed to act against his own doctrine in 1 Corinthians 7: Were you called as a slave? Do not let it be a concern to you. That Onesimus was manumitted, however, is taught by those things which are handed down concerning his bishopric.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Χωρὶς δὲ τῆς σῆς γνώμης ἐκ ἠθέλησα ποιῆσαι) Nolui eo uti, nisi te ultro id volente.

Ἵνα μὴ ὡς κατὰ ἀνάγκην τὸ ἀγαθόν σε, ἀλλὰ κατὰ ἑκύσιον.

Si enim Paulus retinuisset, non tam apparuisset vo- luntas Philemonis, quam si eum ad se missum ipse ad Paulum remitteret. Seneca II. de Benef. IV. Si vis sci- re, an velim, effice ut possim nolle. Ἑκύσιον & ἀναγκαῖον, sive τὸ κατ᾽ ἀνάγκην inter se opponuntur, ut 1. Petr. V. vers. 2. Sic libera voluntate aliquid exequi & ex ne- cessitate, inter se opponit Paulus Jurisconsultus L. Atqui natura §. Si libero D. de negotiis gestis. Laus autem non debetur, nisi liberis actionibus.

Istud, inquit Chrysostomus, est quod impri- mis Dominum flectit, quando & res utilis est, & sine illius tamen sententia non attentatur. Et ad- dit: Uti ne velut ex necessitate tuum bonum es- set, sed voluntarium. Sciebam enim, inquit, quod si non fuisses præmonitus, sed repente factum cognovisses, ne sic quidem ægre aut indigne fer- res: verum te malui ex abundanti commovere, uti ne veluti ex necessitate bonum tuum esset. Τὸ ἀγαθὸν dicente Camerario, ἡ ἀγαθεργία seu ἀγαθοποιία σε. Ut esset opus benignitatis tuæ vo- luntarium non expressum necessitate. Colligit in- de Estius, verisimile esse, Paulum expectasse, ut Onesimus aut sibi donaretur, aut simplici- ter manumitteretur. Id enim voce τὸ ἀγαθὸν notari censet. Sed cur id directè non petit A- postolus, ut manumittatur Onesimus? Respon- det Estius: Id factum esse 1. ne videretur Onesi- mus ex maleficio commodum reportasse, videlicet ex furto & fuga libertatem adeptus. 2. quia for- sitan nimis onerosa erat futura Philemoni petitio. Nam servi erant Dominis suis valde utiles, & bo- na pars possessionis eorum. 3. Visus fuisset Apo- stolus facere contra suam doctrinam 1. Corinth. VII. Servus vocatus es? Non sit tibi curæ. Manumis- sum autem Onesimum esse, ea quæ de Episco- patu traduntur, docent.

## 1:15
Verse 15. For perhaps for this reason.

As if he were saying, perhaps that was the counsel of God, when He permitted him to flee. Compare Genesis 45:5.

He was separated.

You see here also, what we just said, that what is harsh in the matter is mitigated by the gentleness of the word. He said Ἐχωρίσθη, instead of 'he fled.' Such are the things which the Greeks call euphemisms.

Rightly, in the judgment of Chrysostom, he used 'perhaps.' Sometimes, says Jerome, evil becomes an occasion for good, and God turns the wicked counsels of men to the right. What I say will become clearer by an example. Joseph’s brothers, incited by the stings of jealousy, sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of gold. This was the beginning of all good things for the father, the brothers, and all of Egypt. Finally, he himself later said to his brothers: You, he said, thought evil against me, but God thought good for me. We can understand something similar about Onesimus, that bad beginnings were the occasions for a good thing. For if he had not fled from his Master, he would never have come to Rome, where Paul was bound in prison. If he had not seen Paul in chains, he would not have received faith in Christ; if he had not had faith in CHRIST, he would not have been made a son of Paul and sent to the work of the Gospel. From which, little by little and by its own steps, the sentence reciprocating, Onesimus was made a Minister of the Gospel because he fled from his Master. But by adding 'perhaps,' he tempered the sentence. For the judgments of GOD are hidden, and it is rash to pronounce as certain what is doubtful. 'Perhaps,' he says, he departed for this reason—cautiously, timidly, tremblingly, and not with a firm step—so that if he had not added 'perhaps,' it would have to be that all servants must flee so that they might become Apostolic. This is Jerome. Therefore, that διὰ τῦτο is not to be referred to the counsel of the fleeing Onesimus, who certainly had not fled from his master with that intention, but to the disposition of GOD, who accommodates and directs this flight to a salutary outcome. These things, therefore, have the force of a prolepsis, as the blessed Hunnius warns, since he forestalls by anticipation that which could have been a hindrance to his purpose, and by interpreting it in a better light, he renders it useful for the attainment of his goal, while he warns that the furtive departure of Onesimus is not to be weighed so much by the mind of the fugitive servant as by the outcome, which followed as most salutary, and thus from the providence of GOD, which governed this flight in such a way that by this occasion he arrived at the Apostle, and being taught by his preaching the way of eternal salvation, he was afterwards returned to his Master far better and more faithful than he had been when he departed from him.

Πρὸς ὥραν.

That is, for a little time. The same kind of speaking is found in 2 Cor. 7:8, Gal. 2:5, 1 Thess. 2:17.

Ἵνα αἰώνιον αὐτὸν ἔχῃς.

So that, corrected by me, he may be useful to you forever. Αἰώνιον is said here in the same way as in Horace: 'He will serve eternally.' Evangelical doctrine does not abolish the differences of status and the authority of masters over servants, as appears in 1 Tim. 6:1, Tit. 2:9, 1 Pet. 2:10, Eph. 6:5-6, Col. 3:22. There is, therefore, no reason why a Christian, who as a master can have authority over servants, cannot have it over subjects as a Prince. The master in the house and the King in the kingdom are on equal footing. Seneca, De Beneficiis III. 18: 'If necessity and the fear of ultimate suffering prevent a slave from reaching the name of a free man, the same thing will hinder him who has a King and him who has a Duke; for although under a different title, cruelty is permitted against them.' And therefore Peter equates the authority of Kings and Masters. For masters could also torture, and indeed even kill, servants who deserved ill without approaching a magistrate (L. 1. D. de his qui sui, vel alieni juris sunt, Instit. eod. tit. §. In potestate). Nor was this right only at Rome, but also in Greece. See Seneca, Controversiae V. 35. For this came from the law of nations, as the cited legal passages teach us. How masters ought to use this right since they became Christians, Paul taught them, intending to say the same things to Kings if Kings had been as many Christians then as many of the masters were Christians: Both Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were Senators, with authority and the power to punish. For the senate, as much the public one of the people as that of the city of Jerusalem, had the right of scourging, as appears in Matt. 10:17, Acts 5:48, 2 Cor. 11:24, and indeed even of punishing with death, if the Romans ever permitted it, just as the Jews had a general permission to kill a foreigner who had entered within the precincts of the temple. Yet CHRIST never warns these Senators, his disciples, to desist from that duty. And if he had done so, he would undoubtedly have broken the law, which commanded those called by legitimate custom to such a duty to perform that duty, which was far from him, who while he lived a mortal life was made under the law, Gal. 4, nor did he himself break any part of it, nor was he the author of others breaking it.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Τάχα γὰρ διὰ τῦτο.

Quasi dicat, forte id Dei consilium fuit, cum eum fugere permisit. Conf. Gen. XLV. 5.

Ἐχωρίσθη.

Vides & hic, quod modo diximus, lenitate verbi mi- tigari id, quod in re est asperum. Ἐχωρίσθη dixit, pro fugit. Talia sunt, quæ Græci ἐυφημισμὺς vocant.

Recte, judicio Chrysostomi, forsitan posuit. Non- nunquam, ait Hieronymus, malum occasio fit bono- rum, & hominum prava consilia Deus convertit ad rectum. Quod dico manifestius exemplo fiet. Jo- seph fratres sui stimulis zeli incitati, Ismaëlitis vi- ginti aureis vendiderunt. Hoc initium & Patri & fratribus & toti Ægypto omnium bonorum fuit. De- nique ipse postea ad fratres: Vos, inquit, cogitastis de me mala, & Deus cogitavit de me bona. Si- mile quid de Onesimo possumus intelligere, quod ma- ta principia occasiones rei bonæ fuerint. Si enim Dominum non fugisset, nunquam venisset Romam, ubi erat Paulus vinctus in carcere. Si Paulum in vinculis non vidisset, non recepisset fidem in Chri- stum; Si CHRISTI fidem non habuisset, non Pauli filius effectus in Evangelii opus mitteretur. Ex quo paulatim & per gradus suos reciprocante sententia ideo Minister Evangelii factus est One- simus, quia fugit à Domino. Pulchre autem addens forsitan sententiam temperavit. Occulta sunt quippe judicia DEI & temerarium est quasi de certo pronunciare, quod dubium est. Forsitan, inquit, ideo discessit, caute, timide, trepidanter, & non toto fixo gradu, ut si non posuisset forsitan, omnibus servis fugiendum esset, ut Apostolici fie- rent. Hæc Hieronymus. Illud ergo διὰ τῦτο non referendum est ad consilium Onesimi fugi- entis, qui eo certe animo ab hero suo non pro- fugerat, sed ad dispositionem DEI fugam hanc accommodantis, & dirigentis ad eventum salu- tarem. Habent ergo ista vim προλήψεως, monen- te Beato Hunnio, siquidem id, quod instituto suo incommodare poterat, occupatione prævertit, & in meliorem interpretando partem ad propositi sui consecutionem utile sibi reddit, dum furtivum O- nesimi discessum non tam ex fugitivi servuli men- te pensicandum monet, quam ab eventu, qui lon- ge saluberrimus est insecutus, adeoque ex DEI providentia, quæ hanc fugam ita gubernavit, ut ista occasione perveniret ille ad Apostolum, ejus- que contione ad salutis æternæ viam edoctus, post- modum suo Domino redderetur longe melior ac fi- delior, quam ab illo discesserat.

Πρὸς ὥραν.

Id est ad modicum tempus. Idem loquendi genus 2. Cor. VII. 8. Galat. II. v. 5. 1. Thessalonic. II. v. 17.

Ἵνα αἰώνιον αὐτὸν ἔχῃς.

Ut à me correctus perpetuo tibi sit utilis. Αἰώνιον ita hic dictum, quomodo apud Horatium : Serviet æter- num. Doctrina Evangelica non tollit statuum differen- tias & imperia Dominorum in servos, ut apparet 1. Ti- moth. VI. vers. 1. 2. Tit. II. vers. 9. 1. Petr. II. versu 10. Ephes. VI. vers. 5. 6. Col. III. vers. 22. Nulla ergo causa est, cur Christianus, qui ut Dominus in servos habere imperium potest, non possit in subditos habere ut Prin- ceps. Paria sunt in domo Dominus, in regno Rex. Se- neca III. de Benef. 18. Si servo, quo minus in nomen me- viti perveniat, necessitas obest & patiendi ultima timor, idem istud obstabit & ei, qui Regem habet, & ei, qui Ducem; quoniam quanquam sub dispari titulo sævia in illos licent. Ideoque Petrus imperia Regum & Domi- norum inter se æquat. Nam & servos male meritos Domini non adito magistratu torquere, imo & occide- re poterant L. 1. D. de his qui sui, vel alieni juris sunt Instit. eod. tit. §. In potestate. Nec Romæ tantum id jus fuit, sed & in Græcia. Vide Senecam Controv. V. 35. Venit enim hoc ex jure gentium, ut nos docent dicta juris loca. Hoc jure quomodo Domini uti deberent, ex quo Christiani facti sunt, Paulus eos docuit, eadem dicturus Regibus, si tam Reges tunc fuissent Christiani, quam multi Dominorum erant Christiani: Et Nicode- mus & Josephus Arimathensis Senatores fuere, cum im- perio & puniendi potestate. Nam senatus tam publicus populi, quam urbis Hierosolymitanæ jus verberandi ha- bebat, ut apparet Matth. X. vers. 17. Actor. V. vers. 48. 2. Corinth. XI. vers. 24. imo & morte puniendi, si quando id Romani permitterent, sicut generalem permissum ha- bebant Judæi occidendi alienigenam, qui intra templi septa intrasset. Hos tamen Senatores, discipulos suos, CHRISTUS nunquam monet, ut ab eo munere desi- sterent. Et si id fecisset, rupisset haud dubie legem, quæ legitimo more ad tale munus vocatis præcipiebat, fungi eo munere, quod longe ab ipso absfuit, qui dum vitam egit mortalem factus fuit sub lege, Gal. IV. nec ullam ejus partem infregit ipse, aut aliis infringendi autor fuit.

## 1:16
Verse 16. Οὐκ ἔτι ὡς δῦλον.

Supply only what the following words show. Often among all nations, but especially among the Hebrews, this particle is understood; then it must be repeated from the preceding words: παραλαβῇ.

But above a slave.

Belonging to you not only by right of master, but also

A beloved brother.

Namely to all Christians.

Especially to me.

Who have experienced his faithful service.

How much more to you.

He ought to be much dearer to you than to me, because he will always be for your use, as long as you wish.

And in the flesh.

The body of Onesimus is not so much his own as it is yours, by possession and by use. In Aristophanes, Cario says: 'For the spirit does not allow the master to control the body, but the one who bought it.' Flesh and body are accustomed to be interchanged, as appears from the Hebrew, Soph. I. 17, Ezech. X. 12, and elsewhere, when the Greek and Latin versions are compared.

Yet the observation of Jerome does not seem to be rejected: 'No master is eternal to his slave, for his power and the condition of both are ended by death. But Onesimus, who through faith in Christ has become eternal, began to be an eternal brother to Philemon, because he himself had also believed in Christ and received the Spirit of liberty; he began to be no longer a slave, but a brother, a most dear brother, an eternal brother, to the Apostle himself, and to his own Lord, to whom the condition of the flesh formerly joined Onesimus, just as the Spirit joined him afterwards: And then indeed, when he was subject to him in the flesh, he was not joined to him in the Lord, but now he is joined to him both in the flesh and in the Lord.' From which we understand that a slave who has believed in Christ is bound by the law to his double master, so that he is joined to him by the necessity of the flesh for a time, and is joined to him eternally by the Spirit. Theophylact has things similar to these: 'His flight was profitable for much: since he himself obtained him as eternal, instead of one who was momentary and about to die shortly after. For if even all the courses of this human life are to be made of no account in the contemplation of that eternal one, much more will the time of his flight, during which he was away from you, be very small and short. For you have a brother instead of a slave, and instead of one who had been of no use, you have claimed one most loving to you and most useful. And in the flesh, that is, in carnal ministries, love is worthy: since he is also suitable for comforting: And in the Lord, that is, in spiritual matters.' We add the commentary of Chrysostom: 'And time is shortened, and the sin is confessed, and he converts that into a dispensation. That you might receive him forever, he says. Not only in the present age, but also in the future. That you may always have him now not as a slave, but as one far dearer than a slave.' He is indeed a slave, but you will cherish him with greater benevolence than if he were a brother. Therefore, you have gained in terms of both time and quality. For now he will no longer recoil from you. You had lost a slave for a little while, and you have found a brother forever, a brother not only yours, but also mine. A great testimony of exceptional virtue from this: My, he says, brother he is; surely you will not be ashamed to have him as a brother. From the fact, therefore, that he called him son, he gave a sign of singular love; but from the fact that he called him brother, he surely judged him worthy of great benevolence and equal honor with himself.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Οὐκ ἔτι ὡς δῦλον.

Supple tantum, quod sequentia ostendunt. Sæpe apud omnes gentes, maxime vero apud Ebræos, hæc particula subauditur, deinde repetendum ex superioribus παρα- λαβῇ.

Ἀλλ’ ὑπὲρ δῦλον.

Pertinentem ad te non solo jure herili, sed &

Ἀδελφὸν ἀγαπητὸν.

Nempe Christianis omnibus.

Μάλισα ἐμοί.

Qui ejus operam fidelem sum expertus.

Πόσῳ μᾶλλόν σοι.

Multo tibi charior, quam mihi esse debet, quia in tuo usu semper futurus est, dum voles.

Καὶ ἐν σαρκὶ.

Corpus Onesimi non tam ipsius est, quam tuum est, κτήσει καὶ χρήσει. Apud Aristophanem Cario: Τῶ σώματος γὰρ ὐκ ἐᾷ τὸν Κύριον. Κρατεῖν ὁ δαίμων, ἀλλὰ τὸν ἐωνημένον. Solent inter se permisceri σὰρξ & σῶμα, ut apparet ex Ebræo, Soph. I. 17. Ezech. X. 12. & alibi, collatis versio- nibus Græcis & Latinis.

Nec reprobanda tamen videtur Hieronymi observatio: Nullus æternus Dominus servi sui, potestas quippe ejus & utriusque conditio morte fi- nitur. Onesimus vero, qui ex fide Christi factus æternus est, æterno Philemoni, quia in Christum & ipse crediderat Spiritu libertatis accepto jam non servus, sed frater cœpit esse de servo, frater charisfiimus, frater æternus, æterno & ipsi Apo- stolo, Dominoque suo, cui Onesimum ut carnis an- te conditio; ita postea Spiritus copulabat: Et tunc quidem quando ei erat subjectus in carne, non erat ei junctus in Domino, nunc autem ei & in carne junctus est, & in Domino. Ex quo intelligimus, servum, qui crediderit in Christo duplici Domi- no suo lege constringi, ut ei & carnis necessitate jungatur ad tempus, & in æternum Spiritu copu- letur. Similia his habet Theophylactus: Ad mul- tum bujus profuit fuga: quippe cum ipse hunc pro momentaneo & paulo post morituro æternum fis nactus. Nam si vel omnia vitæ bujus humanæ curricula nihili sunt facienda æternæ illius con- templatione, longe magis & fugæ tempus, quo à te abfuit, perexiguum erit & breve. Habes enim pro servo fratrem, & pro eo, qui nulli usui fue- rat, amantissimum tui & utilissimum vendicasti. Et in carne, hoc est, in carnalibus ministeriis, amor est dignus: Quippe qui sit & ad consolan- dum idoneus: Et in Domino id est in spirituali- bus rebus. Addimus Chrysostomi commentari- um: Et tempus conrembit, & peccatum confictur, illudque in dispensationem convertit. Ut in æter- num illum reciperes, ait. Non in præsenti tantum seculo, sed in futuro etiam. Ut eum semper ba- beas jam non ut servum, sed ut servo longe chario- rem. Servus quidem est, sed majori illum benevo- lentia fovebis, quam si frater esset. Itaque & tem- poris & qualitatis ratione lucratus es. Jam enim abs te ultra non resiliet. Servum ad modicum ami- seras, & fratrem perpetuo reperisti, fratrem non modo tuum, sed etiam meum. Magnum ex hoc eximia virtutis testimonium, S: meus, inquit, frater est, profecto non erubesces & tu, illum fratrem habere. Ex eo igitur, quod hunc filium dixit, singularis amo- ris indicium dedit; ex eo autem quod fratrem ap- pellavit, magna illum benevolentia & pari secum honore dignum profecto judicavit.

## 1:17
Vers. 17. Ἐι ὖν ἐμὲ ἔχεις κοινωνὸν) If you hold me as a friend, and consequently as a partner in your affairs. λαμβάνου αὐτὸν) Do not only forgive him the punishment which you could have exacted by your right, but also receive him kindly. You have received him into your house, into your heart, said Pliny in a clearly similar matter in Epistle IX. 24.…

It is a σχῆμα παρασιωπήσεως, or reticence, when we say we wish to omit what we are most strongly stating. Paul says he could have said that he is a debtor to me not only for your things, but also for yourself: namely, because Philemon, if he had been without Paul, would have remained in thick darkness and vices, far from the hope of salvation.

Ὡς ἐμὲ. For since Onesimus was a friend to Paul, what is bestowed upon him seemed to be bestowed upon Paul himself.

What is more apt for persuasion than these words? says Theodoret: And what is more vehement and more forceful? If you consider that some account should be taken of my fellowship, receive him, who has undertaken a change of life, as you would receive me. Who, even the most savage, says Theophylact, would not such words soften? And who would not receive Paul kindly? Chrysostom, however, says excellently: Nothing can have such power to persuade as not asking for everything at once. For see after what praises, after what preparation he placed this great thing. When he had called him his son and partner in the Gospel, when he had called him his own heart, and had said: Receive him as a brother, and have him as a brother: then he added: As you would me. Nor was Paul ashamed of this: For because the servant of the faithful is not ashamed to be called so, not only is he not ashamed, but he professes it freely and openly; much less did he feel ashamed to profess it about himself. That, however, is: If you feel the same as I do, if you run the same path as I do, if you consider me a friend, receive him whom I have also received as my own. We also add the commentary of our blessed Hunnius, no less ἀξιομνημόνευτον: In the admirable brevity which Paul uses, he omits nothing that might seem to pertain to softening Philemon, and by a most effective argument through inference from the preceding, he demonstrates that Onesimus is worthy of being forgiven. At the same time, he indicates that he does not bear being distracted from Onesimus in that part of love, but that it is absolutely necessary that either Philemon loves both, or is equally averse to both.

See, as Chrysostom warns, how cautiously he finally added the fault. For because the loss of money is wont to trouble men most, lest he should object to anything of this kind, since the money had perhaps been consumed or taken by theft: He does not say, if he has stolen anything, but, if he has harmed you in any way. At the same time, he confesses the sin, and not as the sin of a servant, but as of a friend to a friend, using the term injury rather than theft. Impute this to me, he says, that is, exact from me what is owed. With what spiritual grace did he do this? I, says Paul, have written it with my own hand. He strikes him with shame too gratefully, if indeed he himself would refuse to admit him for whom Paul had not refused to write such a letter. And from what follows, he repelled every sense of anger from him: With my hand, he says, I have written. Nothing is more pleasing or vehement than these bowels of compassion, nothing that shows a greater force of zeal and eagerness. For one man, what excellent providence he shows? Not to say, he says, that you owe me even yourself. Then, lest it be thought that an insult was being admitted against the one who was being asked, if he had not dared to pray for the theft, and had despaired of obtaining what he was praying for: how beautifully he also consoles this, (παραμυθεῖται) not to say, he says, that you owe me even yourself, not only your things, but also yourself. And he said this out of charity, and out of the law of friendship, and because he trusted him greatly. Jerome says that what he says is like this: What Onesimus took by theft, I pledge myself to repay: of which pledge this letter and my own hand is witness, which I did not dictate in the usual manner, but wrote myself with my own hand. Believe me, therefore, promising for Onesimus. But I say this as if speaking to a stranger. Otherwise, if I return to my right on account of the word of CHRIST, which I preached to you, and you have become a Christian, you owe me yourself. But if you are mine, and all your things are mine. Onesimus also who is yours, is mine. I could therefore use him as my own, but I leave it to your will, so that you may have a reward by forgiving. The sense of these words is, as interpreted by our blessed Hunnius: I offer myself abundantly for the liberal discharge of all those things which Onesimus owes you, however much, if the account is balanced, it must be confessed by you yourself which of us owes more to the other. Whether I to you in place of Onesimus, or indeed you to me, you yourself must confess that you owe me more, in that by my work and ministry I brought you to the knowledge of GOD (than which there is no treasure more precious under the Sun) like a torch for knowing GOD. So that not only the little bit, whatever it may be, that Onesimus owes, but you owe me yourself besides. Which things, however, the Apostle does not mention with the intention of reproaching, but directs the style of his writing solely to this end, that Philemon, in consideration of such great benefits which he received from Paul, may remember in turn not to act so rigidly with Onesimus, but to consider that detriment by which he was afflicted as already abundantly compensated by so many and such great merits flowing to him from Paul. It is clear from this passage that Philemon was led to the faith of Christ by the Apostle. Which is clearer from verse 19.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ἐι ὖν ἐμὲ ἔχεις κοινωνὸν) Si me habes pro amico, ac proinde tuarum rerum participe. Προσλαβοῦ αὐτὸν) Non modo pœnam, quam tuo jure exigere poteras, ei condona, sed & benigne eum excipe. In domum, in animum recepisti, dixit in re plane simi- li Plinius in epist. IX. 24.

Est σχῆμα παρασιωπήσεως, sive reticentiæ, cum di- cimus omittere nos velle, quod maxime dicimus. Pote- ram dicere ait Paulus, se non tantum rerum tuarum, sed & tui ipsius mihi esse debitorem : nempe quia Phile- mon, si absque Paulo fuisset, mansisset in crassis tenebris vitiis&que longe a spe salutis.

Ὡς ἐμὲ. Nam amicus Paulo cum esset Onesimus, quod ipsi præ- statur, Paulo ipsi præstari videbatur.

Quid est his verbis ad persuadendum aptius? inquit Theodoretus: Et quid vehementius ac ma- gis violentum? Si meæ societatis rationem ali- quam habendam esse ducis, eum, qui suscepit alie- nam mutationem, tanquam me suscipe. Quem vel inatissimum, inquit Theophylactus, hujusmo- di verba non mollirent? Et quis Paulum beni- gne non susciperet? Eximie autem Chrysosto- mus: Nihil tantam impenendi vim habere potest, quantum non simul omnia petere. Vide enim post quantas laudes, post quantum apparatum magnum hoc posuit. Quum dixisset illum Fili- um suum & Evangelii socium, quum sua eum appellasset viscera, & dixisset: Ut fratrem illum recipe, & ut fratrem illum babe: tunc addidit: Sicut & me. Nec istud erubuit Paulus: Quia enim fidelium servus non erubescit appellari, ne modo non erubescit, verum & libere & aperte id profitetur; multo minus ita profiteri de se ve- nuit. Id autem est: Si mecum eadem sentis, si eadem mecum curris via, si amicum arbitraris, su- scipe illum, quem & ego meum suscepi. Addimus & Beat. Hunnii nostri commentarium, non mi- nus ἀξιομνημόνευτον : In admiranda brevitate, qua Paulus utitur, nihil omittit, quod ad emol- liendum Philemonem pertinere videatur, ac effica- cissimo argumento per illationem e superioribus de- monstrat, dignum esse Onesimum, cui ignoscatur. Simul indicat, non se ferre, ut ab Onesimo in ista parte dilectionis distrahatur, sed omnino alteru- trum esse necesse, ut Philemon aut utrumque dili- gat, aut utrumque pariter aversetur.

Vide, monente Chrysostomo, quam caute postremo addidit culpam. Quia enim maxime rei pecuniariæ jactura angere bomines solet, ne quid hujusmodi obticeret, consumptæ quippe for- te erat pecunia furto sublata: Non ait, si quid furatus est, sed, si quid te læsit. Simul & pecca- tum confitetur, & non veluti servi peccatum, sed quasi amici ad amicum, injuria magis usus, quam furti nomine. Hoc mihi, inquit impu- ta, id est a me debitum exige. Quanta vero cum spiritali gratia id egit? Ego, inquit Pau- lus, scripsi manu mea. Grate nimium illi vere- cundiam incutit, siquidem ipse illum detrectaret admittere, pro quo Paulus literas hujusmodi scri- bere non renuisset. Atque ex eo, quod sequitur, omnem iracundiæ sensum ab eo repulit: Manu, inquit, mea scripsi. Nihil hisce visceribus gra- tius vel vehementius, nihil quod majorem vim studii & alacritatis ostendat. Pro viro uno quam eximiam ostendit providentiam? Ut non dicam, inquit, quod & te ipsum mihi debes. Deinde ne putaretur contumelia in eum qui rogabatur ad- mitti, si pro furto non ausus esset orare, & quod orabat, consequi desperasset: quam pulchre & istud consolatur, (παραμυθεῖται) ut non dicam, inquit, quod & teipsum mihi debes, non modo tua, sed & teipsum. Et hoc ex charitate, & ex amicitia lege, & quod illi valde consideret dixit. Hieronymus, quod dicit, inquit, tale est: Quod Onesimus furto rapuit, ego me spondeo redditu- rum: Cujus sponsionis epistola hæc & manus te- stis est propria, quam non solito more dictavi, sed mea manu ipse conscripsi. Crede igitur mihi pro Onesimo pollicenti. Hoc autem dico, quasi ad extraneum loquens. Cæterum si ad jus meum redeam propter sermonem CHRISTI, quem tibi evangelizavi, & Christianus effectus es, te- ipsum mihi debes. Quod si tu meus es, & tua omnia mea sunt. Onesimus quoque qui tuus est, meus est. Poteram igitur eo uti, ut meo, sed voluntati tuæ relinquo, ut mercedem habeas igno- scendo. Sensus horum verborum est, interprete Beat. Hunnio nostro: Ex abundanti me ad li- beralem omnium eorum, quæ tibi debet Onesi- mus, dissolutionem offero, quantumvis si ratio subducatur, uter nostrum utri plus debeat. Ego- ne tibi loco Onesimi, an vero tu mihi, ipsemet fatearis necesse sit, te mihi plus debere, eo quod opera, ministerioque meo tibi ad cognoscendum DEUM (quo non alius est sub Sole pretiosior thesaurus) ceu facem quandam prætuli ad cogno- scendum DEUM. Adeo ut non modo tantil- lum, quantum forte est, quod debet Onesimus, sed teipsum mihi debeas insuper. Quæ tamen Apostolus non exprobrandi animo commemorat, sed eo scriptionis stylum unice dirigit, ut Phile- mon consideratione tantorum beneficiorum, quæ accepit a Paulo, meminerit vicissim, non ita rigide agere cum Onesimo, sed detrimentum illud, quo affictus est abunde jam tot tantisque meritis in il- lum a Paulo profectis largissime compensatum sta- tuat. Constat ex hoc loco, Philemonem ab A- postolo ad fidem Christi perductum esse. Quod clarius e versu 19. patet.

## 1:18
Vers. 18.

Εἰ δὲ τι ἠδίκησέ σε) If he has taken anything while fleeing. Ἢ ὀφείλει. Or if he was a debtor from your accounts. The name of the genus for the species.

Τοῦτο ἐμοὶ ἐλλόγει) Impute that to my accounts, make your name mine for him.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Εἰ δὲ τι ἠδίκησέ σε) Si quid fugiens abstulit. Ἢ ὀφείλει. Aut si ex rationibus tuis reliquator erat. Nomen ge- neris pro specie.

Τοῦτο ἐμοὶ ἐλλόγει) Id meis rationibus imputa, Me pro eo fac tuum nomen.

## 1:19
Verse 19.

Ἐγὼ Παῦλος ἔγραψα τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ (I, Paul, have written it with my own hand). So that you may be certain, you have my hand here. You will be able to summon me, wherever you wish, by this handwriting. This is what the Scholiast calls writing a security in L. Titius. D. quæ res pignori. Add L. lect. D. si certum petatur, & L. Aurelius §. quidam D. de lib. leg.

Ἐγὼ ἀποτίσω (I will repay).

In Latin, this is called 'constituting money,' concerning which there is a title in the Digest. The Greeks say ᾿Αναδέχεσθαι, as Demosthenes against Lacritus. The form itself is contained in these words: Ἐγὼ ἀποτίσω, or 'I will satisfy you,' as Novella CXV. 6 has it. Which is accustomed to be inserted in the title of the Code 'de pecunia constituta.' Thus in L. Eum qui §. Julianus, this formula is read: 'I have written according to the mandate of Seius, but whatever will be approved as owed to you, I will provide security and pay to you without controversy.' And another, L. quidam, in the same title: 'Ten, which Lucius Titius had received as a loan from your chest, saving the account of interest, you have in my possession, Master.' Moreover, money can be constituted even that which is only naturally owed. L. I. §. debitum. D. in the said title. Slaves can owe their masters, not indeed civilly, but by nature. l. stipulatus. §. adhiberi, with the following law. Thus also for a natural obligation a surety is rightly accepted, L. fidejussor, §. fidejussor. D. de fidejussoribus. Donatus on that passage of Terence's Phormio: 'It shall be done, look to me.' Because in law he promises and interposes his faith, which we say, 'you have me.'

Ἵνα μὴ λέγω σοι, ὅτι καὶ σεαυτόν μοι προσοφείλεις (Not to mention to you that you owe me even your own self).

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Ἐγὼ Παῦλος ἔγραψα τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Ut certus sis, habes hic manum meam. Poteris me, ubi voles, convenire ex chirographo. Hoc est, quod scri- bere cautionem vocat Scholiastes ad L. Titius. D. quæ res pignori. Adde L. lect. D. si certum petatur, & L. Au- relius §. quidam D. de lib. leg.

Ἐγὼ ἀποτίσω.

Hoc Latine dicitur pecuniam constituere, de quo ti- tulus est in digestis. ᾿Αναδέχεσθαι dicunt Græci, ut De- mosthenes contra Lacritum. Forma ipsa continetur his verbis: Ἐγὼ ἀποτίσω, aut satisfaciam tibi, ut habet Novella CXV. 6. Quæ inseri solet titulo Codicis de pecunia constituta. Sic in L. Eum qui §. Julianus, for- mula hæc legitur: Scripsi secundum mandatum Seji, sed quid tibi debitum approbatum erit, me tibi cauturum & solu- turum sine controversia. Et alia L. quidam, eodem tit. Decem quæ Lucius Titius ex arca tua mutua acceperat, salva ratione usurarum, habes penes me, Domine. Consti- tui autem pecunia potest, etiam quæ naturaliter tan- tum debetur. L. I. §. debitum. D. dicto titulo. Servi Dominis debere possunt, non quidem civiliter, sed na- tura. l. stipulatus. §. adhiberi, cum lege sequente. Sic & pro obligatione naturali recte fidejussor accipitur L. fidejussor, §. fidejussor. D. de fidejussoribus. Donatus ad illud Terentii Phormionis : Fiet, me vide. Quia in jure promittit & interponit suam fidem, quod nos di- cimus, me habes.

Ἵνα μὴ λέγω σοι, ὅτι καὶ σεαυτόν μοι προσοφεί- λεις.

## 1:20
Verse 20.

…Ναὶ ἀδελφὲ (Yes, brother) Ναὶ here is of one beseeching, as among the Hebrews, Concerning which Jerome: The Latin language does not explain the Greek property. For what he says ναὶ ἀδελφὲ, ναὶ is a certain adverb of one as if coaxing. But we, interpreting, say 'yes brother', more weakly and more dilutedly, I know not what else, than that which is written. For just as that Hebrew אנא, for which the LXX Interpreters frequently translated ὠδὴ, signifies in their language the affection of one entreating, whence sometimes Symmachus translated for anah δέομαι, that is, I beseech: So also we suffer the same force in the Greek language, which the Greeks sustain in the Hebrew. Chrysostom: And for the repetition of the former request: Yes brother: What does this mean for itself? Receive him. But what more does this particle bring in the present, concerning which rightly Beat. Hunnius: The particle ναὶ is at once of one asking and of one hoping well, nay, of one certainly confessing, as if Paul were saying: I plainly hope, my brother, that my intercession with you will not be in vain, but will have such weight and force that it may be permitted to enjoy your equanimity in forgiving and your liberality in showing kindness: Which I would wish you to be asked in a greater manner.

Ἐγώ σε ὀναίμην ἐν κυρίῳ.

That is, may it be permitted to me to rejoice in your progress in CHRIST, Sir. XXX. vers. 2. 'he that nurtureth his son shall have joy in him.' Ignatius to the Magnesians: 'of the Saviour, in whom I may have joy.' The same to the Ephesians: 'May I have joy of you always.'

Which fruition indeed primarily here looks to the works of charity and mercy, concerning which he had also warned his Colossians, the citizens of Philemon, Coloss. III. vers. 12, 13, and 14. But it can nevertheless be taken generally, with respect to παντὸς ἀγαθᾶ vers. 6. Concerning which Jerome: But what he says, 'I may enjoy you, in the Lord', something much different is understood than is thought. The Apostle does not enjoy, except him who has many and harmonious virtues in himself. And all that is said of CHRIST for the variety of causes, namely wisdom, justice, continence, meekness, temperance, chastity: these he prays for Philemon, that when he shall have abounded with these, he himself, enjoying him, may be filled. And lest you think that fruition is meant, by which we are often delighted by the presence of our own among us: he added 'in the Lord', so that from the fact that the name of the Lord is joined, it might be understood that there is also another fruition, by which one might enjoy without the Lord. So also Theodoret: That 'I may enjoy in the Lord', for that which is 'I may enjoy all your good actions in CHRIST, I may see you rich in all spiritual goods.' To the words: Σὲ ὀναίμην: Camerarius: 'May this advantage from you befall me.' That is, 'I may take this fruit from you.' Namely, 'so that by Onesimus being received by you, my bowels may be refreshed.'

Ἀνάπαυσόν με τὰ σπλάγχνα ἐν κυρίῳ.

That is, for the sake of CHRIST make me tranquil in this matter.

Jerome judges that by the bowels of Paul, Onesimus can be understood, who was to be refreshed: But from verse 7 the sense is clear, by which he had praised Philemon, because through him the bowels of the saints had been refreshed by works of charity: therefore now he asks that he might deign to refresh his own bowels also by charity and mercy, not shown to himself, but to his son, whom he cherished in his own bowels. 'Refresh this heart of mine for the sake of CHRIST', as Theophylact has it among others. He would have said simply, says the Blessed Hunnius, 'I ask you through the Lord, that you forgive Onesimus.' But he brings forth this proposition in such a way that he declares at the same time that his bowels, that is, his heart, will be refreshed. Thus he might deign to restore to his former favor and benevolence him whom he had named his bowels in the preceding.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Ναὶ ἀδελφὲ) Ναὶ hic est precantis ut apud Ebræos, Quo de Hieronymus: Proprietatem Græcam Latinus sermo non explicat. Quod enim ait ναὶ ἀδελφὲ, ναὶ quoddam adverbium quasi blandien- tis est. Nos autem interpretantes, ita frater, aqua- tius & dilutius nescio quid aliud, quam id, quod est scriptum, sonamus. Sicut enim אנא illud Ebraicum, pro quo frequenter LXX. Interpretes ὠδὴ transtulerunt, in lingua sua significat deprecantis affectum, unde nonnunquam Symmachus pro anah δέομαι, hoc est, obsecro, transtulit: Ita & nos eandem in Græca lingua patimur vim, quam Græci sustinent in Ebræa. Chrysostomus: Et pro repetitione prioris petiti: Ita frater: Quid sibi hoc vult? Suscipe eum. Amplius autem quid infert hæc particula in præsenti, de qua recte Beat. Hunnius: Particula ναὶ rogantis simul est & bene sperantis, quin certo confitentis, ac si di- cat Paulus: Plane spero, mi frater, intercessio- nem meam apud te non fore irritam, sed habitu- ram pondus atque vim eam, ut frui liceat tua igno- scendi æquanimitate & in gratificando liberali- tate: Id quod te majorem in modum rogatum velim.

Ἐγώ σε ὀναίμην ἐν κυρίῳ.

Id est, liceat mihi gaudere de tuis in CHRISTO pro- fectibus, Sir. XXX. vers. 2. ὁ παιδεύων τὸν υἱὸν αὑτῶ, ὀνή- σεται ἐπὶ ἀυτῷ. Ignatius ad Magnetios: Διαιοὺς Σωτῆ- ρος, ᾧ ἐγὼ ὀναίμην. Idem ad Ephesios: Ὀναίμην ὑμῶν διὰπαντὸς.

Quæ fruitio quidem imprimis hic respicit charitatis & misericordiæ opera, de quibus & Colossenses suos, Philemonis cives monuerat, Coloss. III. vers. 12. 13. & 14. Sed generaliter ta- men accipi potest, respectu παντὸς ἀγαθᾶ vers. 6. De quo Hieronymus: Quod autem ait, ego te fruar, in Domino, aliud multo intelligi- tur, quam putatur. Apostolus non fruitur, nisi eo, qui multas in se habet concinentesque virtu- tes. Et totum quod CHRISTI dicitur pro va- rietate causarum, sapientiam videlicet, justitiam, continentiam, mansuetudinem, temperantiam, ca- stitatem: has imprecatur Philemoni, ut cum his abundaverit, ipse eo perfruens impleatur. Et ne putes illam fruitionem dici, qua nos sæpe nostri inter nos præsentia delectamur: addidit in Domi- no, ut ex eo, quod Domini nomen adjunctum est, intelligeretur, & alia esse fruitio, qua quis absque Domino perfruatur. Ita & Theodoreius: Illud fruar in Domino, pro eo, quod est fruar omni- bus tuis bonis in CHRISTO actionibus, vi- deam te locupletem in omnibus bonis spirituali- bus. Ad verba: Σὲ ὀναίμην: Camerarius: Hæc mihi à te commoditas obtingat. Id est fructum istum ex te capiam. Nimirum, ὥςε τῆ Ὀνησί- με προσληφθέντος ὑπὸ σε ἀναπαυθῆναι τὰ σπλάγχνα με.

Ἀνάπαυσόν με τὰ σπλάγχνα ἐν κυρίῳ.

Id est, propter CHRISTUM fac me tranquillum hac de re.

Hieronymus per viscera Pauli Onesimum in- telligi posse censet, qui reficiendus erat: Sed e versu 7. sensus luculentus est, quo Philemo- nem laudarat, quod per ipsum viscera sancto- rum operibus charitatis refocillata sint: itaque jam rogat, ut sua etiam viscera refocillare di- gnetur charitate & misericordia, non sibi, sed filio suo, quem in visceribus suis fovebat, ex- hibita. Refice hoc cor meum CHRISTI ob gratiam, ut habet inter alia Theophylactus. Sim- pliciter dixisset, inquit Beatus Hunnius, rogo te per Dominum, ut ignoscas Onesimo. Hanc au- tem propositionem sic effert, ut simul declaret, viscem sua, id est, cor suum refocillatum iri. Sic eum, quem in præcedentibus viscera sua nomi- naverat, condonato delicto dignatus fuerit antiquo suo favore & benevolentia.

## 1:21
Vers. 21. Πεποιθὼς τῇ ὑπακοῇ σου ἔγραψά σοι.

The knowledge of that obedience of yours, which you show to the Gospel, has given me confidence. Thus ὑπακοὴ is taken in Romans I. vers. 5, chap. XV. 18, chap. XVI. 19, 26, 2 Corinth. VII. 15, chap. X. 5, 6, 1 Petr. I. 14, 22.

Knowing that you will do even more than I say.

I hold it for certain that you will do more than I dare to ask.

Jerome says beautifully: He who presumes, by that very presumption, in a way prejudges the one he is about to ask, so that it is not permitted for him to deny what is requested. Furthermore, if he who asks knows that the one asked will do more than he requested, he asks for less, so that the one asked may have a voluntary and greater reward for his performance. The conclusion is, as Blessed Hunnius says, by which he declares that he cherishes no doubtful hope concerning his readiness, namely that he will not only not deny the requested service, but will even perform more than the Apostle demands. A sign of the confidence conceived about him is that he wrote to him so confidently and familiarly. He uses the word 'obedience' not without singular emphasis. For he indicates conversely that Philemon could not escape the mark of disobedience if he did not comply with the Apostle of CHRIST, who is asking for things so fair, so honest, and so pious, which he could even have commanded by Apostolic authority. Nor indeed, as Chrysostom has it, do I write these things using command and authority, but 'trusting in your obedience I have written to you,' which he had also said in the beginning, having confidence: he does this also now when he signs the letter: 'Knowing that you will do even more than I say.' These things have great power to exhort and to entreat. For he would surely blush, if for no other reason, not to do what he advises, if only from the fact that he has this opinion of him, beyond which he himself said he would do.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Πεποιθὼς τῇ ὑπακοῇ σου ἔγρα- ψά σοι.

Fiduciam mihi fecit, cognita illa tua, quam Evange- lio præstas, obedientia. Ita ὑπακοὴ sumitur Roman. I. vers. 5. cap. XV. 18. cap. XVI. 19. 26. 2. Corinth. VII. 15. cap. X. 5. 6. 1. Petr. I. 14. 22.

Εἰδὼς ὅτι καὶ ὑπὲρ ὃ λέγω, ποιήσεις.

Pro certo habeo, plus te facturum, quam ego au- deam poscere.

Pulchre Hieronymus: Qui præsumit, de eo, quem rogaturus est, ipsa quodammodo præsum- ptione præjudicat, ne ei negare liceat, quod roga- tur. Porro si scit ille, qui postulat, plus quam ro- gavit, rogatum esse facturum, ideo minora petit, ut habeat rogatus voluntariam & majorem præ- statione mercedem. Conclusio est, Beato Hun- nio dicente, qua se de ipsius promptitudine spem non dubiam fovere perhibet, quod videlicet peti- tum officium non modo denegaturus non sit, sed plus etiam præstiturus, quam Apostolus efflagi- tet. Cujus de illo conceptæ fiduciæ signum sit, quod tam ad illum scripserit confidenter & familiari- ter. Utitur autem obedientiæ vocabulo non sine singulari emphası. Subindicat enim è converso inobedientiæ notam Philemonem effugere baud posse, si non obsecundet Apostolo CHRISTI, tam æqua, tam honesta, tamque pia roganti, quæ etiam ex Apostolica autoritate mandare poterat. Neque vero, ut Chrysostomus habet, imperio usus, atque autoritate hæc scribo, sed confidens de obedientia tua scripsi tibi, quod etiam in principio dixerat, fiduciam habens: hoc & modo quum signaret epi- stolam: Sciens quoniam & super id, quod dico, facies. Habent ista magnam hortandi atque exo- randi vim. Erubesceret enim profecto, & si ob nihil aliud non id faceret, quod admonet, vel ex eo certe, quod hanc ille de se habet opinionem, su- per quam diceret ipse esse facturum.

## 1:22
Verse 22. But at the same time prepare a lodging for me.

Prepare a lodging. Thus 'xenia' is used in Acts 28:23 and in Josephus and others.

That he arranges a lodging for himself at Philemon's is both an argument of confidence and at the same time obliquely contributes to the principal cause, not only because the Apostle wishes to deign to honor him with the love and honor of that visit; but also because Philemon, recognizing that he will soon have Paul in his own house, may the more readily grant what is requested, lest the Apostle, upon arriving, find the state of Philemon's domestic affairs far different than he had expected. And this, says Chrysostom, was an indication of one vehemently confident; indeed, it also made primarily for Onesimus, so that they would not neglect him, but knowing that he would certainly come and hear how they had behaved toward him, they would lay aside all memory of injury and be more ready for thanks. For great was the honor and grace of the present Paul. Of Paul, I say, after his old age was expressed, after his chains were often commended. It will not be beside the point to add here also Jerome's commentary: I do not think the Apostle was so rich and occupied with such great burdens that he would act to prepare a lodging, and not content with one small room, would consider very large houses for the short space of his body. But so that while Philemon looks forward to his coming to him, he may the more readily do what is asked. But if anyone thinks that this was commanded not by way of dispensation, but truly, that he should prepare lodging for himself, then lodging must be prepared for the Apostle rather than for Paul. About to come to a new city, about to preach the crucified one and to bring forth unheard-of doctrines, he knew that very many would flock to him: And it was necessary first, that he should be in a famous place of the city, to which one might easily gather: Then that it should be free from all annoyance, that it should be spacious, which might hold very many of the listeners, so that it would not be detestable because of the nearby places of spectacles, nor because of a shameful neighborhood: finally that it should be situated on level ground rather than in an upper room.

For I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you. I hope it will come to pass that God will grant me (that is, my arrival to you) to you at your prayers. Similar to 1 Timothy 3:14. There are those who think this hope of Paul was fulfilled, and that he, having been freed from chains, went into Asia and returned to Rome.

The hope was not fulfilled: For this was Paul's last captivity, as was said before. The hope, therefore, as Crocius holds, is conditional and of opinion. He speaks thus because he commits himself entirely to God, and implies His permission, which he expresses in 1 Corinthians 16:7. The nature of the thing hoped for shows this: which is promised in the word not absolutely but with a condition, the definition of which was unknown to Paul. He does not hope for his own sake. For he was prepared for either. Prepared to die, prepared to labor longer. He hopes for the sake of Philemon and other believers. Therefore he says, I hope I am granted to you. He calls it a gift, and thus a singular benefit. He certainly knew that he could not be freed by human strength. He hoped that he would be granted out of mere grace. Nor indeed is there need that what he had said to them themselves, to Philemon, Apphia, and Archippus, and the Church which was in Philemon's house, about being granted at their prayers, should be explained concerning the arrival of Paul. For whether he came to them freed from chains and the danger of death, or not, he would still be granted to them: since he could have managed their care by prayers, and counsels, and even by work while absent. To declare the confidence of love, and to commend their piety, he adds what is added, by the help of your prayers: And as he hoped their prayers would not be in vain before God: So also he seems to tacitly hint that his own intercession for Onesimus would have a place among them.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Ἅμα δὲ καὶ ἑτοίμαζέ μοι ξενίαν.

Hospitium para. Ita ξενία sumitur Actor. VIII. v. 23. & apud Josephum & alios.

Quod hospitium sibi conducit apud Phile- monem, & confidentiæ argumentum est, & ad principalem causam simul oblique conducit, non modo quia amore & honore illo visitatio- nis dignari velit ipsum Apostolus; sed etiam Philemon agnoscens, quod propediem in suis tectis habiturus sit Paulum, eo promptius det expeditum, quod petitur, ne veniens Aposto- lus statum rei domesticæ Philemonis offendat longe alium, quam expectaverat. Et hoc, in- quit Chrysostomus, vehementer confidentis erat in- dicium, imo & pro Onesimo imprimis faciebat, ne illi negligerent, sed scientes, illum omnino ven- turum atque auditurum, ut sese habuerint adver- sus eum, omnem injuriæ memoriam deponerent, & promptiores ad gratiam essent. Grandis enim erat præsentis Pauli honor & gratia. Pauli, inquam, post ætatem senectutis expressam, post commen- data sæpius vincula. Non abs re erit hic adjice- re etiam Hieronymi commentarium: Non pu- to tam divitem fuisse Apostolum, & tantis sarci- nis occupatum, ut de præparando ageret hospitio, & non una contentus cellula, breve corporis sui spatium, ædes amplissimas existimaret. Sed ut dum eum spectat Philemon ad se venturum esse, magis faciat quod rogatus est. Si autem hoc non dispensatorie, sed vere quis existimat im- peratum, ut sibi hospitium paret, Apostolo magis, quam Paulo hospitium parendum est. Venturus ad novam civitatem, prædicaturus crucifixum & in- audita dogmata delaturus sciebat ad se plurimos concursuros: Et necesse erat primum, ut in celebri esset urbis loco, ad quam facile conveniretur: De- inde ut ab omni importunitate vacua, ut ampla, quæ plurimos caperet audientium, ne proximæ spe- ctaculorum locis, ne turpi vicinia detestabilis: po- stremo ut in plano potius esset sita, quam in cœna- culo.

Ἐλπίζω γὰρ, ὅτι διὰ τῶν προσευχῶν ὑμῶν χαρι- σθήσομαι ὑμῖν. Spero fore, ut ad preces vestras Deus me (id est, ad- ventum ad vos meum) vobis concedat. Simile 1. Timoth. III. 14. Sunt qui spem hanc Pauli impletam putant, & libe- ratum eum a vinculis ivisse in Asiam, rediisse Romam.

Non impleta est spes: Hæc enim ultima erat Pauli captivitas, ut antea dictum. Spes ergo, ut Crocius habet, conditionalis & opinionis. Sic loquitur, quia se totum permittit Deo, & subintel- ligit ejus permissionem, quam exprimit 1. Corinth. XVI. 7. Id ostendit natura speratæ rei: quæ in ver- bo non absolute sed cum conditione promissa, cujus definitio Paulo fuit ignota. Non sua causa sperat. Paratus enim erat ad utrumque. Paratus mori, pa- ratus longius laborare. Sperat Philemonis & alio- rum fidelium causa. Ideo ait, spero donari me vo- bis. Donum vocat, adeoque beneficium singulare. Humanis viribus liberari non posse certe sciebat. Ex mera gratia se donatum iri sperabat. Neque vero opus est, ut quod de se dixerat ipsis, Phile- moni, Appiæ, & Archippo, & Ecclesiæ, quæ in domo Philemonis erat, ad preces ipsorum donan- do, de adventu Pauli explicetur. Nam sive libe- ratus e vinculis & capitis periculo ad ipsos ve- niret, seu non, donaretur tamen ipsis: quum vi- vus eorum curam & precibus, & consiliis & ope etiam absens gerere potuerit. Ad fiduciam a- moris declarandam, & ad pietatem ipsorum com- mendandam facit, quod additur, auxilio precum vestrarum: Et ut preces ipsorum sperabat apud Deum non fore irritas: Ita etiam intercessionem suam pro Onesimo apud ipsos locum habituram tacite innuere videtur.

## 1:23
Verse 23. Epaphras greets you. The full name is Epaphroditus, Phil. 2:25, 4:18. Contracted Epaphras, Col. 1:7, 4:12. We have brought forward many names of this kind contracted in -as at the beginning of Luke.

My fellow prisoner. One of those whose mention is in Acts 27.

In Christ Jesus. That is, on account of Jesus Christ, as above at 20.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Ἀσπάζονταί σε Ἐπαφρᾶς) Nomen plenum est Ἐπαφρόδιτος, Phil. II, 25. IV. 18. Contractum Ἐπαφρᾶς, Coloss. I. 7. IV. 12. Cujus generis nomina in ᾶς contracta multa adduximus ad Lucæ initium.

Ὁ συναιχμάλωτός με) Unus eorum, quorum mentio Actor. XXVII.

Ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ) Id est propter Jesum Christum, ut supra 20.

## 1:24
Mark. He whose mention is in Acts 12:12, 25, 15:37, 39, Col. 4:10.

It is not clear that Epaphras was with Paul on that voyage: nor do these things pertain to the former captivity of Paul, in which it will be taught whence Epaphras was Paul's fellow prisoner? But this man was sent by the Colossians, Col. 1:7, who it is certain was a minister of Christ among them, commended highly by the Apostle in chapter 4:12, whom Chrysostom thinks is called a fellow prisoner because he himself was in much pressure with Paul. But the proper notion of the word implies that the same man was also a prisoner for Christ, as Paul was. It appears from this place, says our B. Hunnius, that Epaphras, who first planted the Church of the Colossians, was accused by the enemies of the Gospel, and led to Rome, and cast into chains. Therefore his name, which he adds with Chrysostom hinting, not doubting that the same would also add some weight to his prayers, especially since this also brings shame to Philemon, if his fellow citizen and fellow prisoner is afflicted at the same time, while he himself, asked for a servant, is unwilling to grant a favor. Jerome recounts this fable or history concerning Epaphras: We have received such a fable as to who Epaphras, the fellow prisoner of Paul, is: They say that the parents of the Apostle Paul were from the region of Gyscalis of Judea, and that they, when the whole Roman province was being devastated by hand and the Jews were being dispersed in the world, were transferred to the city of Tarsus in Cilicia; that the adolescent Paul followed the condition of his parents: And thus that which he himself testifies about himself can stand: They are Hebrews, and I am. And again elsewhere: A Hebrew of Hebrews, and the rest, which indicate him to be a Jew rather than a Tarsian. But if this is so, we can also suspect that Epaphras was captured at that time when Paul was captured, and was settled with his parents in the city of Colossae in Asia, and later received the word of Christ. Whence it is written to the Colossians, as we said above: Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, greets you, always solicitous for you in prayers. If this is the case, and Aristarchus, who is called his fellow prisoner in the same epistle, will be led to the same understanding. But these things without doubt look to captivity for Christ. Let us therefore leave that fable to its authors.

Mark was the cousin of Barnabas. His most pious mother Mary was accustomed to provide lodging to the disciples of the primitive Church in Jerusalem, and to receive them into her house, and to allow meetings to be held there, Acts 12:12. Jerome understands Mark the author of the Gospel. But he is believed to have adhered to Peter rather than to Paul.

Verse 24. Aristarchus

Whom he likewise names his fellow prisoner, and in whose name he also greets the Colossians, Colossians IV, verse 10. Mention of him is made in Acts XIX, verse 29, chapter XX, verse 4, chapter XXVII, verse 2.

Demas) whose full name is Demetrius. He is named in Colossians IV, 14; 2 Timothy IV, 10.

Who at that time was still a constant follower of the evangelical doctrine: but afterwards he withdrew from Paul, having embraced the present world, 2 Timothy IV, verse 11. From which it is to be gathered that the second epistle to Timothy was written some time after this one, which is under our hands.

Luke) The physician who gave us the Gospel and the Acts. See Colossians IV, 14; 2 Timothy IV, 11.

Concerning whom Jerome says: And Luke the physician, who leaving the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles to the churches, just as the Apostles were made from fishers of fish into fishers of men: so he was turned from a physician of bodies into a physician of souls, concerning whom also in another place: He sent, he says, with him the brother, whose praise is in the Gospel through all the churches, whose book as often as it is read in the churches, so often his medicine does not cease.

My fellow workers) See above 1.

Who labor faithfully with me in propagating the Gospel of Christ. Paul added their greetings also for this reason, that Philemon might understand that these excellent men were interceding together with Paul for Onesimus. Which is also the observation of Chrysostom: And from these therefore he greets him, so that he may be more inclined to grant the favor. He calls them fellow workers, however, so that he may add spurs to him for that purpose.

Latin:

Μᾶρκος) Is cujus mentio Actor. XII. 12. 25. XV. 37. 39. Coloss. IV. 10.

Epaphram in illa navigatione Paulo adfuisse non liquet: neque hæc pertinent ad priorem Pau- li captivitatem, in qua Epaphram Pauli συναιχμά- λωτον fuisse, unde docebitur? Fuit autem hic a Colossensibus missus, Col. I. 7. quem Ministrum Christi penes ipsos fuisse constat, commendatus eximie ab Apostolo cap. IV. 12. quem concapti- vum vocari putat Chrysostomus, quod & ipse in multa fuerit pressura cum Paulo. Sed propria vocis notio infert, eundem etiam captivum fuisse pro Christo, ut Paulum. Apparet ex hoc loco, inquit B. Hunnius noster, Epaphram, qui primus Eccle- siam Colossensium plantavit, fuisse ab hostibus Ev- angelii accusatum, & Romam ductum, atque in vincula conjectum. Ejus ergo nomen, quod Chry- sostomo innuente addit, idem precibus suis etiam pondus aliquod additurum non dubitans, impri- mis quum & hoc Philemoni verecundiam addu- cat, si civis ejus & concaptivus simul affligitur, ipse vero pro servo rogatus gratiam praestare nolit. Hieronymus de Epaphra hanc recenset fabulam vel historiam: Quis sit Epaphras concaptivus Pauli, talem fabulam accepimus : Ajunt parentes Apostoli Pauli de Gyscalis regione fuisse Judae, & eos, cum tota provincia Romana vastaretur manu & dispergerentur in orbe Judaei, in Tarsum urbem Ciliciae fuisse translatos; parentum conditionem adolescentulum Paulum secutum : Et sic posse stare illud, quod de se ipse testatur: Ebraei sunt, & Ego. Et rursum alibi: Ebraeus ex Ebraeis, & caetera, quae illum Judaeum magis indicant, quam Tarsensem. Quod si ita est, possumus & Epaphram illo tempore captum suspicari, quo captus est Paulus, & cum parentibus suis in Colossis urbe Asiae collocatum, Christi postea recepisse sermonem. Unde ad Colossenses, ut supra diximus, scribitur: Salutat vos Epaphras, qui est ex vobis, servus Christi, semper solicitus pro vobis in orationibus. Hoc si se ita habeat, & Aristarchus, qui concaptivus ejus in eadem epistola dicitur, ad eandem intelligentiam deducetur. Sed his ad captivitatem pro Christo sine dubio respicitur. Linquamus ergo illam fabulam autoribus suis.

Marcus consobrinus Barnabae erat. Ejus mater pientissima Maria primitivae Ecclesiae discipulis Hierosolymis hospitium praebere, & in domum suam recipere, ac conventus agendos concedere solita erat Actor. XII. vers. 12. Marcum Evangelii conditorem intelligit Hieronymus. Sed ille Petro potius, quam Paulo adhaesisse creditur.

Vers. 24. Ἀρίσταρχος

Quem itidem concaptivum suum nominat, & cujus nomine etiam Colossenses salutat, Coloss. IV. vers. 10. mentio ejus fit Actor. XIX. vers. 29. cap. XX. vers. 4. cap. XXVII. v. 2.

Δημᾶς) cui plenum nomen Demetrius. Nominatur Col. IV. 14. 2. Tim. IV. 10.

Qui eo tempore adhuc erat constans Evangelicae doctrinae sectator : at post secessit à Paulo, complexus praesens seculum, 2. Tim. IV. vers. 11. Unde colligere est, epistolam ad Timotheum posteriorem aliquanto post hanc, quae sub manibus est, scriptam esse.

Λουκᾶς) Medicus qui Evangelium & Acta nobis dedit. Vide Col. IV. 14. 2. Tim. IV. 11.

De quo Hieronymus: Et Lucam medicum, qui Evangelium & actus Apostolorum Eccleslis derelinquens, quomodo Apostoli de piscatoribus piscium piscatores hominum facti sunt: Ita de medico corporum in medicum est versus animarum, de quo & in alio loco: Misit, inquit, cum illo fratrem, cujus laus est in Evangelio per omnes Ecclesias, cujus liber quotiescunque legitur in Ecclesiis, toties ejus medicina non cessat.

Οι συνεργοί μου) Vide supra 1.

Qui in propagando Christi Evangelio fideliter mecum laborant. Horum salutationes eam etiam ob causam adscripsit Paulus, ut Philemon intelligeret hos praestantes viros una cum Paulo pro Onesimo intercedere. Quae etiam Chrysostomi est observatio: Et ex his ergo illum salutat, ut ad dandam gratiam pronior sit. Cooperatores autem vocat, ut ei ad id stimulos addat.

## 1:25
Ver. 25. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ) The favor of Christ.

He had prayed for grace and peace from GOD the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ at the beginning. Now he wishes only for the grace of our Lord JESUS Christ at the end of the epistle. For grace is the fountain of all good things. He who enjoys the grace of GOD is not destitute of peace with GOD and tranquility of conscience, nay, he rejoices in all the rivulets of divine benefits which spring from this fountain, Ps. 36:8 ff. Furthermore, the final prayer, by which one prays for the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, must be equally effective, equally sufficient, and equally salutary as the initial one, by which one prayed for the same from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. Which comparison again confirms the ὁμοουσίαν (consubstantiality) of God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. For it is of GOD alone that that grace is sufficient, from which spiritual benefits flow as from a fountain, and which is truly σωτήριος (saving) and salutary. Cf. Acts 15:11; 2 Cor. 13:13.

Μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν (With your spirit) That is, may it be with you. The same expression is in Gal. 6:18. Elsewhere he said for it: Μεθ' ὑμῶν, καὶ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν (With you, and with all of you).

The whole man can certainly be understood synecdochically through the Spirit, with Jerome. For the grace of Christ holds both body and soul, who redeemed not only our soul but also our body, and saves not only our soul but also our body. Specifically, however, mention of the Spirit is made here because His grace illuminates, regenerates, and renews our soul and mind to the image of GOD, and confirms and preserves us in true faith, so that we may attain the end of faith, the salvation of our souls, 1 Pet. 1:9. Therefore, the spirit illuminated by the Holy Spirit, and the new man, is understood.

Ἀμήν (Amen) It is the word which the Church used to respond when the epistles were read. Therefore, it began to be appended to all of Paul's epistles. See what is at Matt. 6:13.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Η χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) Favor Christi.

Gratiam, & pacem à DEO Patre & Domino nostro Jesu Christo sub initium precatus erat. Jam gratiam Domini nostri JESU Christi solum optat sub finem epistolae. Gratia enim fons omnium bonorum est. Qui gratia DEI fruitur, pace cum DEO & tranquillitate conscientiæ non de- stituitur, imo omnibus rivulis beneficiorum di- vinorum, qui ex hoc fonte scaturiunt, gaudet, Psal. XXXVI. 8. seqq. Porro æque efficax, æque sufficiens ac salutiferum finale votum esse oportet, quo gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi precatur atque initiale, quo à Deo Patre, & Domino no- stro Jesu Christo eandem precatus est. Quæ col- latio iterum ὁμοουσίαν Dei Patris & Domini no- stri Jesu Christi confirmat. Solius enim DEI est, gratiam eam sufficere, è qua beneficia spiritualia, tanquam è fonte redundant, quæque vere σωτή- ριος ac salutifera est. Conf. Actor. XV. vers. 11. 2. Corinth. XIII. vers. 13.

Μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ὑμῶν) Id est, sit vobiscum. Eadem loquutio Gal. VI. vers. 18. Alibi pro eo dixit: Μεθ' ὑμῶν, καὶ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν.

Potest utique Synecdochice per Spiritum intel- ligi totus homo cum Hieronymo. Nam & corpus & animam atinet Christi gratia, qui non animam modo, sed & corpus nostrum redemit, non ani- mam modo, sed & corpus nostrum salvat. Spe- cialiter tamen hic Spiritus mentio facta, quia ani- mam mentemque nostram gratia sua illuminat, regenerat, atque renovat ad imaginem DEI, & in vera fide confirmat ac conservat, ut finem fidei animarum salutem consequamur, 1. Petr. I. v. 9. Spiritus ergo à Spiritu Sancto illuminatus, & no- vus intelligitur.

Ἀμήν) Est vox quam Ecclesia respondebat lectis epi- stolis. Ideo omnibus Pauli epistolis cœpit adscribi. Vi- de quæ ad Matth. VI. 13.

# Hebrews

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
YEAR IN THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

Latin:

ANNO IN EPIS AD EB

## 1:1 Introduction: Grotius's Preface
GROTIUS'S PREFACE.

Whose writer this Epistle is, it is no wonder that it is doubted today, since even the Ancients doubted it. The most ancient are divided into three parts; for some attribute it to Barnabas, others to Clement of Rome, others to Luke. Many later writers ascribed it to Paul. This last opinion is the easiest to refute, for the reason that Paul's Epistles are akin to one another in equal character and mode of speech: but this one clearly differs from them, having more select Greek words, and flowing more smoothly, and not broken by short, choppy, and rugged clauses. Moreover, certain locutions familiar to Paul never appear here; on the contrary, others appear that are not Pauline, such as παραῤῥυεῖσθαι (to drift away) and αἰῶνες (ages) for the world. Furthermore, it disqualifies this Epistle from being Paul's, because its writer counts himself among those who received knowledge of the Gospel not from Christ but from His disciples (II. 3), whereas, on the contrary, Paul adds authority to himself from the fact that he received this knowledge from Christ Himself. It also differs much from the speech of Barnabas, if that Epistle which we have is truly Barnabas's, partly Greek, partly Latin, but which it appears is the same one that Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and others used. For that diction of Barnabas is, compared to this, rude, unpolished, and βαρβαρίζουσα (barbarizing). The speech of Clement of Rome approaches our own more closely: but he seems, as one called from the Gentiles, to have been much less versed in the literature of the Hebrews than this writer; nor does there seem to be any other reason why some of the ancients ascribed this epistle to Clement of Rome, except that they saw certain words in the epistle of Clement to the Corinthians which also appear here. But that is weak, since Clement also frequently uses Pauline words. And nothing else follows from that than that this Epistle was both read at Rome and held in esteem at the time when Clement was writing to the Corinthians: although it was received into the Canon by the Romans late. There remains, therefore, from those whom the ancients named, Luke, to whom I would willingly attribute this epistle. For just as this epistle is good Greek and flowery, so too is the speech of Luke, where he does not report the words of Christ or the Apostles

- If that word was added by someone other than an Apostle, - it will not be θεόπνευστος (God-breathed), nor will it belong - to the canon. Which is inconvenient.
