But it is evident from - the comparison of 2 Thess. 3:17-18 and Rom. 16:24 - that it was customary for it to be added by the Apostle himself, and that it pertains - to the sign and character of Apostolic - letters. We end for the present with the words and εὐλο- - γίᾳ (blessing) of Theophylact on this epistle: You see therefore - how much utility redounds from this - epistle, even if it has been considered lighter (which it is held to be by some), - although it has seemed clearer and more open. Whence it happens that there is nothing of such scriptures - that should not be searched out more accurately. For there is - in these also, with the Spirit suggesting, some very useful sense. For this, that Paraclete has undoubtedly - foretold. And to us who are seeking the truth, - He is about to give the ability to comprehend. By whom we ourselves, illuminated, are led to the truth itself, so that we may both speak of GOD and lead an immortal life, not at all circumvented by any perverse opinions, or enticed by these false pleasures of the world. It is necessary, therefore, that we ourselves, even if we are Princes and rule over others, when we see that servants have become holy and perform the office of the Apostolate, strive with all zeal that we be found in no way inferior to them in the kingdom of Christ. Who, when He had come into the world for our sake, took upon Himself the form of a servant, and is our true God: To whom be power and empire forever: To whom, therefore, be honor and glory forever with the Father and the Holy Spirit, Amen.

Latin:

PRÆLOQVIUM GROTII.

CUjus scriptoris sit hæc Epistola, non mirum est hodie dubitari, cum etiam Veteres dubitaverint. Vetustissimi in tres partes scinduntur, alii enim Barnabæ eam tribuunt, alii Clementi Romano, alii Lucæ. Posteriores multi eam Paulo adscripsere. Facil- lima refutatu est postrema hæc opinio, ideo quod Paulinæ Epistolæ inter se sint germanæ pari charactere & dicendi modo: hæc vero manifeste ab iis discrepet, selectiores ha- bens voces Græcas, leniusque fluens, non autem fracta brevibus incisis ac salebrosa. Tum vero locutiones quæ- dam Paulo familiares hic nusquam apparent, contra ap- parent aliæ non Paulinæ, ut παραῤῥυεῖσθαι, & αἰῶνες pro mundo. Præterea Paulo hanc Epistolam abjudicat, quod hujus scriptor se eis annumeret, qui non a Christo sed ab ejus discipulis notitiam Evangelii accepere II. 3. cum con- tra Paulus autoritatem sibi addat inde, quod hanc noti- tiam à Christo ipso acceperit. A Barnabæ quoque sermone multum distat, si vere Barnabæ ea Epistola est, quam nos habemus, partim Græcam, partim Latinam, sed quam ap- paret eandem esse, qua usi sunt Clemens Alexandrinus, Origenes & alii. Est enim illa Barnabæ dictio præ hac ru- dis & incompta & βαρβαρίζουσα. Clementis Romani oratio ad hanc nostram propius accedit: sed videtur is, ut voca- tus è gentibus, in literis Ebræorum multo minus quam hic scriptor fuisse versatus; neque alia videtur causa, cur veterum nonnulli epistolam hanc Clementi Romano ad- scriberent, nisi quod verba quædam viderent in epistola Clementis ad Corinthios, quæ & hic apparent. Sed id in- firmum est, cum & Paulinis verbis frequenter utatur Cle- mens. Nec aliud inde sequitur, quam Epistolam hanc & le- ctam fuisse Romæ, & in pretio habitam quo tempore ad Corinthios scribebat Clemens: quanquam in Canonem à Romanis sero recepta est. Restat ergo ex iis, quos veteres nominarunt, Lucas, cui ego hanc epistolam libens tribue- rim. Nam sicut hæc epistola bene Græca est, & florida, ita & sermo Lucæ, ubi non Christi, aut Apostolorum refert

- Si vox illa ab alio, quam Apostolo, addita, - non erit illa θεόπνευστος, nec ad canonem perti- - nebit. Quod inconveniens. Patet autem è - collatione 2. Thess. III. 17. 18. Rom. XVI. 24. Eam - ab ipso Apostolo addi consuevisse, ac pertinere - ad signum & characterem literarum Apostolica- - rum. Finimus impræsentiarum verbis & εὐλο- - γίᾳ Theophylacti hanc epistolam: Vides itaque - quantum ex leviori (quæ talis habita nonnullis est) - epistola hac, etsi clarior visa est & aperta, redun- - det utilitatis. Quo fit, ut nihil ex scripturis hujus- - modi non accuratius sit perscrutandum. Inest - enim & his Spiritu suggerente, perutilis semper aliquis sensus. Hæc siquidem Paracletus ille haud dubie præfatus est. Et conquirentibus nobis veri- tatem, comprehendendi daturus est facultatem. A quo & ipsi illuminati ad veritatem ipsam tra- ducimur, ut & loqui de DEO possimus & vitam ducere immortalem, nullis prorsus aut pravis opi- nionibus circumveuti, aut mundi voluptatibus his falsis illecti. Necesse est igitur, ut ipsi vel si Prin- cipes simus & aliis dominemur, cum servos spe- ctamus evasisse sanctos, & Apostolatus munere fungi, omni studio contendamus, nihil illis in Chri- sti regno inferiores deprehendi. Qui nostri gratia cum in mundum venisset, formam præ se tulit ser- vi, & verus noster sit Deus: Cui perpetuo & po- testas & imperium: Cui proinde perpetuo sit cum Patre, ac Spiritu Sancto honor & gloria, Amen.

## 1:1 Introduction: In. J. Otata Epistle to the Hebrews
IN. J. OTATA EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS.

words, but in narrating other matters, for instance Paul's voyage, he wanders more freely. It appears that this epistle was written from Italy, since below at XIII. 24 he makes no mention of Paul, because Paul at that time had been freed from his bonds and had departed outside of Italy into Epirus, as it seems at Tit. III. 12. Now Paul, when he was in Rome, had had with him both Luke and Timothy. Concerning Luke it appears at Col. IV. 14, 2 Tim. IV. 11, Philem. 24; concerning Timothy at Eph. I. 1, Phil. II. 19, Col. I. 1, Philem. 1. These Paul, when he departed from Italy, left in Italy to cultivate the seed which Paul had sown and to spread it more widely. While Timothy was attending to his duty, he was bound: but he had soon been released from his bonds; below at XIII. 23. Luke meanwhile, who himself had also previously been bound, but had emerged from his bonds below at X. 33, while in some part of Italy devoting effort to converting or confirming the Italians, found time to write to those Christians whom he had formerly known in Judea and Syria, being himself a Syrian by origin. Now not a few of them, pressed by the burden of persecutions, had withdrawn themselves from the congregations. Therefore, in order to bring these back to the path, and to support others who were still standing, he shows in many ways that all the ancient histories and the sayings of the Prophets are occupied, by a certain hidden dispensation of God, in prefiguring Christ and his affairs. And it is possible that he drew the explanation of these mysteries partly from the mouth of Paul, partly from Barnabas, so that some part of this epistle may rightly be ascribed to them as well. And indeed not only in this matter, but in all ways this writer strives to fix deeply in their minds the superiority of Christianity over Judaism, and he opposes eternal rewards to afflictions: moreover, certain words and modes of speaking, as if proper to Luke, also show Luke to be the writer of this epistle. Εὐλαβεῖσθαι and εὐλάβεια for to fear and fear, Acts XXIII. 10, Heb. V. 7. εἰς τὸ παντελὲς Luke XIII. 11, for εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς we have in Hebrews VII. 7. μαρτυρούμενος and μαρτυρεῖσθαι, Acts VI. 3, XVI. 2, Heb. VIII. 8, XI. 2, 5, 30. χρηματίζεσθαι, Luke II. 26, Acts X. 22, Heb. VIII. 5. ἡγεῖσθαι, Luke XXII. 26, Heb. XIII. 7, 17. ἀρχηγὸς, Acts III. 15, V. 31, Hebrews II. 10, XII. 2. πρὸς in place of the particle περὶ, Luke XVIII. 1, XIX. 42, XX. 19, Acts XXVIII. 25, Heb. I. 7, 8. Furthermore, this writer for the most part strictly follows the LXX version, which is also Luke's. The inscription to the Hebrews is old. For thus Tertullian in 'De pudicitia' and Clement in 'Stromata' VI name this Epistle. By Hebrews, however, are understood the Jews, as in Acts 6:1, 2 Cor. 11:22, Phil. 3:5. Thus also the Hebrew language is Jewish, Luke 23:38, Acts 21:40, 22:2, 26:14. This epistle, however, was written in Greek, because that language was more familiar to Luke. Most Jews, moreover, also knew Greek; some of them, indeed, only Greek, as is clear from Acts 6:1.

PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS.

Grotius deals with three things in his preface. I. The Author. II. The inscription to the Hebrews. III. The language in which it was written. He also introduces something, though quite incidentally, about its reception into the Canon. To these, however, some things must be added regarding the Scope, which was touched upon briefly by Grotius, and regarding the Argument and division of the epistle: but succinctly, since most of these things were taught thirty-four years ago at the Königsberg Academy, when I was performing the duties of a theological professor there, and were published at Danzig in the year 1659 under the title 'Vestibulum in portam Veteris, et munimentum Novi Testamenti, divinam S. Pauli ad Ebræos Epistolam'.

As far as the author of the Epistle is concerned, Grotius first of all strives to render him doubtful, and then to persuade that the most ancient writers attributed it to someone other than Paul, namely either to Barnabas, or to Clement of Rome, or to Luke: furthermore, he clearly denies it to the Apostle Paul: finally, he maintains that it is not by Barnabas, nor by Clement of Rome, but by Luke.

That Grotius says at the beginning that it is doubted today whose epistle this is, we do not wonder without cause, since he could not have been ignorant that such doubt opposes the definition of the Council of Trent, which was without doubt sacrosanct to him. For in its Fourth Session it was decreed that there are fourteen Epistles of Paul, and that the one inscribed to the Hebrews is among the Epistles of Paul, and anathema was pronounced upon him who did not receive it as Canonical. Nor was the polymath ignorant that this contrary doubt is opposed to the authority of more ancient Councils, by which it was defined that this Epistle is by St. Paul, namely the Council of Laodicea around the year of Christ 394, Canon 59, and the Third Council of Carthage around the year 400, Canon 47, as well as the Second of Ancyra, and also the Roman one convened by Gelasius in the year 494, not to mention the councils of later ages, which in no way dissent from them.

Now if we consult the ancient authors or doctors, it is certainly established that they attributed this Epistle to the Apostle Paul. In the very first century after Christ was born, all the elders of Origen, who appeals to them in Psalm 1 and in his preface to this Epistle, just as St. Athanasius, or whoever the author of the book is, in 'Dialogus 1 de Trinitate' testifies, believed that it is Paul's, from the time the Gospel of Christ was announced. In the second century, Clement of Alexandria attributes it to Paul (in Eusebius, 'Hist. Eccl.' book 6, ch. 13), as do Heraclius, Origen, and Dionysius in his Epistle to Titus. In the third century, Epiphanius in heresy 76, Athanasius in his 'Synopsis', Eusebius of Caesarea, Gregory Nazianzen in his poem, Didymus of Alexandria, and other principal doctors. In the fourth century, Chrysostom and his disciple Constantine of Antioch, Cyril of Alexandria, 'Thesaurus' book 12, ch. 19. Amphilochius in his poem to Seleucus, Theodoret of Heraclea and Cyrrhus, Hilary in book 2 'de Trinitate', Ambrose in book 2 'de Cain' ch. 11, Philastrius of Brescia, Jerome, Augustine in book 11 'de doctrina Christiana' ch. 8, and others. Furthermore, in subsequent centuries, this Epistle was constantly attributed to St. Paul by both Greek and Latin Fathers. Among the more recent ones, Peter Lombard, Hugh of St. Victor, Peter of Tarentaise, Thomas Aquinas, Alexander of Hales, and others among the Scholastics have also vindicated it for Paul; and among the subsequent Papists, Claudius Guillandus, Eduardus Loeus, Nic. Tacitus Zigenus, Johannes Gagnejus, Ambrosius Catharinus, Gregorius Primaticensis, Franc. Lucas Brugensis, Adamus Sasbouth, Emanuel Saa, Mutius Angelus, Nicolaus Grandis, Hieronymus Veronensis, Cardinal Bellarmine, Johannes Mariana, Guilielmus Lindanus, Gabriel Vasquez, Franc. Ribera, Cornel. à Lapide, and who else? Since by the decree of the Council of Trent it was not permitted for Papists to think otherwise. Among the Reformed, Andreas Hyperius, Georgius Sobnius, Johannes Piscator, David Pareus, Bartholomaeus Keckermannus, Franc. Gomarus, Mart. Frieder. Wendelinus, and others have also acknowledged this Epistle as Pauline. Among the Neo-Photinians, the leader and standard-bearer of the rest, Faustus Socinus, in 'Solutio Scrupulorum' p. 70. Nor do Matthias Flacius Illyricus, David Chytreus, Salomo Gesnerus, and B. Gerhard, among the doctors of the Augustan Confession, deny it, to say nothing of many others. Grotius would certainly have found few in his own time who doubted that Paul was the author, in comparison with those who acknowledged Paul as the author, since it is a matter of conscience for Papists to doubt it after the Council of Trent, and others, if any were found, would have been of no account to him. And what is to be thought of the doubt of those for whom it was perhaps ambiguous in the previous century has been sufficiently explained in the aforementioned 'Vestibulum'. Grotius named no one, therefore there is no need to examine it specifically.

He appeals to the most ancient: but who those are among the most ancient who denied this to Paul, he does not explain at all. Nor is it easy to find among the Greeks anyone who denied that this Epistle is Pauline. Eusebius mentions one Gaius in 'Hist. Eccl.' book 6, ch. 20, and Jerome in 'De viris illustribus' ch. 9, who was a contemporary of Origen, but who seems to have assumed this opinion not so much from his own mind as for the sake of argument, if you weigh the words of Eusebius correctly. Nor is he to be referred to the Greeks. For he wrote at Rome under Zephyrinus. Whence it is clear from Eusebius (loc. cit. and book 3, ch. 3) as well as from Jerome (loc. cit. and in the same book, ch. 5) that some in the Latin Church, and especially the Roman, denied it. But who those were among the Romans, besides Gaius, and whether they denied that the present Epistle was Pauline simply or in a qualified sense, is not clear. Jerome, writing to Dardanus, when he had asserted that the Epistle to the Hebrews was accepted as Paul's by the Churches of the East (of his time), nay, by all Churches and Greek writers of the past, adds that although many think it to be either Barnabas's or Clement's. And Origen, in his homily on this Epistle, in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book VI, chapter 24, says that the men of old handed it down as Pauline, although some of them said it was written by Clement, Bishop of Rome, and others by Luke, who also gave us the Gospel and the Acts. How this is to be understood according to the mind of the Ancients is perhaps not uselessly inquired into. There were, however, some among the Ancients who held that the archetypon and original text should be attributed to Paul, but others that an ektypon or translation into the Greek language should be attributed to someone else: as Jerome in the Catalogue, chapter 5. Doctor, chapter 5, says that Paul wrote to the Hebrews in Hebrew, that is, in his own tongue most eloquently, but that those things which had been written eloquently were translated even more eloquently into Greek. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book VI, chapter 13: 'Since Paul,' he says, 'wrote to the Hebrews in his native tongue, some say Luke the Evangelist, others Clement'

They say that it was interpreted by a Roman, which is also more consonant with the truth: And Clement of Alexandria taught in his Hypotyposes that the Epistle to the Hebrews was written by Paul in Hebrew for the sake of the Hebrews, and was diligently translated by Luke, and set before the Gentiles, according to Eusebius, Book VI, ch. 13. Yet some others have said that Paul was the author of the Epistle only in respect of the thoughts or sentiments, but another, rather than the Apostle, in respect of the structure, such as Origen, as cited by Eusebius, Book VI, ch. 34, who nevertheless professes it to be credible that the things which Paul wrote eloquently in the Hebrew language, a Greek interpreter, whoever he may have been, translated even more eloquently into the Greek language. It is not, therefore, to be admitted except with a grain of salt what Grotius says, that the most ancient writers are divided into three parts, for some attribute this Epistle to Barnabas, others to Clement of Rome, others to Luke.

Now as far as Barnabas is concerned, no one was easily found who attributed this Epistle to him, except for what Jerome noted in his Catalogue, ch. 5, that this was done by Tertullian, which, however, in the same place he seems to have understood only in respect of the translation into the Greek language. But Grotius himself does not deny that the present Epistle differs much from his style. But what he gathers from the Epistle of Barnabas which exists today, he thinks is the same one that Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and others used. But Eusebius, even in his own time, reckoned the Epistle which was carried under the name of Barnabas among the least legitimate Scriptures, H.E. Book III, ch. 19, and that it is read among the Apocrypha, Jerome, Book 12, on writers. Eccl., as also Book XIII on Ezekiel, ch. 43, observed; And whatever may be the case regarding the opinion of Isaac Vossius, in his notes on the Epistle of Barnabas, Hugo Menander himself, who brought this Epistle out of darkness and illustrated it with notes, published at Paris in the year 1645, confesses at the beginning of his observations that it is rightly placed among the Apocryphal Scriptures; both because it is uncertain whether it is by Barnabas, and because there are found in it things which are by no means free from difficulty, and he observes that Clement of Alexandria and Origen often use apocryphal works, although it is certain to him that this epistle which he edited is the one which St. Jerome, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen once had in their hands, which we leave in its place, although that argument is of little strength which is sought from the places cited by them found in it: since those things could have been filled in by the compiler from their own writings. What, therefore, can be judged about the style of Barnabas from a spurious and adulterated writing? But whatever may be the case regarding it, does the style of our Epistle correspond to the diction of Barnabas or not? Whence Tertullian had it that this Epistle was translated by Barnabas does not appear. Origen certainly, in Eusebius, H.E. Book VI, ch. 34, reports that a story had reached him that some said it was written by Clement of Rome, others by Luke. But of Barnabas, neither Origen nor anyone else makes mention. I pass over the fact that Cornelius a Lapide, I know not by what author, says that this Epistle was handed over by Paul to Barnabas, so that he might publish it as if in his own name.

Furthermore, as regards Clement of Rome, not only Origen but also Eusebius observed that this Epistle was attributed to him by some, but in respect of the translation from Hebrew into Greek, which he also judges to be more consonant with the truth than that the version was made by Luke, H.E. Book VI, ch. 13; yet it seems otherwise to Grotius. He thinks, namely, that Clement of Rome, as one called from the Gentiles, was much less versed in the literature of the Hebrews than this writer, and he denies that the agreement of some words in this Epistle and in Clement's Epistle to the Corinthians is sufficient for proof that this Epistle proceeded from Clement. But we have sufficiently proven in our preface to Paul's Epistle to the Corinthians that that Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians is spurious. Others add that Clement of Rome did not have such authority among the Hebrews, as a Gentile man, (which is a wonder that Estius pronounced this about a Roman Pontiff), and that the style of this Epistle is that of a man not Roman, but a Hebrew, skilled in Greek; indeed, while Clement of Rome in his Epistle, which they admit, recites certain sentiments from this one of ours, he testifies that this Epistle of ours is of another author, not his own.

Grotius confesses, therefore, that he is willing to attribute it to Luke. But what evidence does he bring forward? First, he appeals to the ancients. But he did not name which of the ancients, let alone the most ancient, attributed it to Luke as the author. We have observed something similar regarding Clement of Alexandria and Eusebius, but they only look to the translation in that place: And Eusebius speaks only comparatively, that it was translated by Luke rather than Clement of Rome: indeed, Eusebius, Book III, ch. 34, judged not undeservedly that it should be reckoned among the remaining writings of the Apostle: And he praises Clement of Alexandria, Book VI, ch. 11, who pronounced this to be MANIFESTLY Paul's Epistle.

Secondly, Grotius alleges the style: that this Epistle is good Greek and flowery, just as is the speech of Luke. But that agreement of style moved at least the ancients to attribute the translation to Luke, but it is not evident that they therefore judged this Epistle away from Paul. Otherwise, that argument about the style is not sufficiently firm. Origen, certainly an accurate observer of style, could not judge from that that it was a translation by Luke, but left the matter in the middle: but to Eusebius, from the style, it seemed more consistent that Clement of Rome rather than Luke had interpreted this Epistle, with Theodoret, Oecumenius, and Nicephorus not denying it, H.E. Book IV, ch. 33. Nor was Paul less eloquent in the Greek language than Luke, so that he could use a flowery style, as one being carried by the Holy Spirit. concerning whose eloquence we treated in the inaugural oration prefixed to the Vestibulum, and Flacius, skilled beyond others in discerning sacred literature, inverted the argument, concluding not only from the grand eloquence of this Epistle that none but Paul is the author, but also contending that this Epistle was written with the Pauline ones to the Corinthians, and rendering the reason why the Apostle used a clearer and, as it were, more splendid style here, namely, because he did not write to any single church or person, as in the other Epistles, but to the whole nation of the Hebrews, then dispersed throughout the world, so that he might teach and admonish such varied hearers, he could use a clearer and more illustrious style, as writers are accustomed to compose lucidly those things which are proposed to a more frequent audience, which rhetoricians also prescribe.

But as to what Grotius brings forward thirdly concerning the place. Be it that this Epistle was written from Italy: be it that Paul had been liberated at that time, that he had both Luke and Timothy as companions, but whence is it proved that Paul was not then in Italy? Whence is it certain that Luke was bound in Rome? Grotius assumes these things precariously and gratuitously: but all the other things agree more correctly with Paul than with Luke.

As to what is fourthly derived from certain words and modes of speaking, the argument is truly too weak: forsooth, to collect a peculiar mode of speaking and a genuine author from four or five words: and how easily could many Pauline words be noted in this Epistle, and indeed even axioms peculiar to Paul? Nor are those little words so peculiar to Luke that they have not been used by others, or could not have been employed. The word μαρτυρόμενος is familiar to Paul, Rom. III. 21, Col. II. 21, 1 Thess. II. 12, 1 Tim. V. 10. χρηματίζεσθαι occurs in Matt. II. 12, 22, Rom. XI. 4. ἡγύμενος in Matt. II. 6. The word ἀρχηγὸς is Petrine, Acts III. 15, ch. V. 31, and it occurs among the LXX Interpreters, Jud. V. 15, Neh. II: verse 9, Isa. XXX: verse 4.

Fifthly, regarding the claim that this Epistle follows the version of the LXX Interpreters for the most part slavishly, as Grotius says, and that this is also done by Luke, I respond: Luke is not the only one who loves to follow the LXX version. That is common to most writers of the New Testament, including the Apostle Paul. Compare what we have said about these matters in the Critico S., p. 720 seq., of the first edition.

Estius notes that the fact that Luke is not to be believed as the author of this Epistle is hindered by the fact that he did not have such authority among the Hebrews that he would give them letters to instruct them on the deep mysteries of the Christian faith. Moreover, the reason for the composition suggests that he is not the same author, since the style here is grander than in the Gospel and Acts of Luke, which Estius likewise acknowledges; furthermore, this reason thoroughly persuades one, because it is in no way likely that two men inspired by God (θεοπνεύστους) labored in one and the same Epistle—namely, Paul and Luke—in such a way that the former provided the hand, while the latter elaborated it, the former prescribed the order, while the latter wrote the Epistle according to that order, and that by the immediate inspiration of the Holy Spirit, by whom both were moved in this work, whose grace certainly knows no slow delays. If Paul wished and was obligated to consign these prescriptions to the Hebrews by the instinct of the Holy Spirit, what, I ask, could have been the reason why he himself did not write out the whole Epistle, but only dictated the material and prescribed the order? But if Luke was moved by the Holy Spirit to write to the Hebrews, what need had he for some other Apostle to suggest the material or prescribe the order? Could these things not have proceeded from the Holy Spirit inwardly suggesting and dictating to Luke? Certainly, nothing even seemingly akin to the truth can be brought forward here that could serve as a reason.

But we see at last, in reverse order (καθ' ὕστερον πρότερον), what reason Grotius has for denying this Epistle to Paul. The first is that the Pauline Epistles are akin to one another, with an equal character and mode of speaking, whereas this one manifestly differs from them. But neither of these is granted. For if one were to compare the Corinthian Epistles with others, he would not find an equal character and mode of speaking in all respects, nor would such a manifest discrepancy from them appear in this one of ours. Moreover, Grotius has not yet demonstrated that the other Epistles are broken up by rough and short clauses, nor that they do not flow so clearly, nor has he brought forward those more select Greek words that are more suitable to Luke than to Paul. Furthermore, why could Paul not have adapted himself with a more flowery diction to the studies and genius of the Hebrews, who delighted in a more elegant Hellenism in that dispersion (διασπορᾷ), or even to the material itself, which was so illustrious and seemed to require a greater apparatus of diction? Finally, is not the Holy Spirit the best Master of speech, who spoke through Paul, able to bring these things forth through the Apostle in such a way as Grotius believes they could have been brought forth through Luke? He is certainly not restricted to the instruments he uses, but gives them the ability to speak as the occasion arises, as He wills, Acts II. 4; He gives a mouth and wisdom, Luke XXI. 15.

Next, he says that certain locutions familiar to Paul nowhere appear. But this argument is futile, as such arguments from negative testimony usually are. And what are those words that should have appeared if the discourse were Pauline? On the contrary, he says, others appear that are not Pauline, such as παραῤῥυῆναι and αἰῶνες for the world. But the former is not in Luke anywhere; as for the latter, why should it not occur in Paul in the same sense (1 Cor. I. 20, II. 6, 7, 2 Tim. IV. 10, Tit. II. 10) as it does in Luke (ch. XVI. 8, XX. 34)? Thirdly, he says that it adjudges this Epistle away from Paul because its writer counts himself among those who received knowledge of the Gospel not from Christ, but from His disciples (ch. II. 3), whereas, on the contrary, Paul adds authority to himself from the fact that he received this knowledge from Christ Himself. This argument, I do not deny, was the reason for some to adjudge this Epistle away from Paul, even for our blessed Luther, but it is less firm, let alone sufficient to prejudice others who make Paul its author. For could not the author, by the figure of communication, count himself among others who received knowledge of the Gospel from the disciples, which is not infrequent? And what prevents one from saying that the fellowship (κοινωνίαν) pertains not to the person of Paul, but to the Church? Does he not also, on the contrary, affirm that God has spoken to us in the last days in His Son (ch. I. 2)? And was St. Luke not equally inspired by God (θεόπνευστος) as Paul, or how does it conflict with divine inspiration (θεοπνευσίᾳ) that the word of the Gospel reached the author of the Epistle even through the disciples? Paul was certainly not present with Christ when that word began to be brought forth and announced by Him, and it was confirmed (ἐβεβαιώθη), without doubt also through communication with the Apostles who had heard Christ teaching in the days of His flesh, into the Apostle the word of the Gospel, even if Paul received the Gospel immediately from Christ; for these are not opposites. Nor is it absurd if an Apostle is said at some time to have heard another Apostle, or even his companion Barnabas preaching, or to have watched their miracles; nor is it inconsistent if it is said that Paul had not indeed the certainty of divine confirmation (βεβαιώσεως), of which he speaks in Gal. I. 1 and II. 6, but experimental knowledge from others who were eyewitnesses (αὐτόπται); such a historical confirmation (βεβαίωσις) came to him from Ananias (Acts IX. 17, XXII. 12, 13). But this argument, which Schlichtingius urged more laboriously along with many others opposed to Paul as author, we have already expressly refuted in the aforementioned Vestibulum, Title II. We do not wish to do what has already been done. On the other hand, we have produced there arguments very numerous in number, and most weighty in importance for this Author, namely the Apostle Paul: I. From the fervor of Apostolic zeal. II. From the quality of the prayer. III. From the designation of the disciple Timothy. IV. From the commemoration of the bonds. V. From the comparison of the life of Paul. VI. From the observation of the Method. VII. From the introduction of certain phrases and axioms. VIII. From the sealing of the Epistle. IX. From the inscription. X. From the approval of Peter. XI. From the testimony of the ancient Fathers. XII. From the definition of the Councils. XIII. From the assent of recent doctors. Which still stand unmoved. And so much for the present concerning the first chapter of the prolegomena.

But indeed, because there is mixed in with three words something concerning Canonical authority, namely that this Epistle was received into the Canon by the Romans late, this does not seem to be passed over with a silent foot. For besides the fact that it smacks of Papism—that the Church, and indeed the Roman Church, has the power to receive into the Canon some book which had been outside the Canon for some centuries from the Apostolic age, which hypothesis we have otherwise refuted—it is foreign to the truth that the Canonical authority of this Epistle was recognized late by the Romans. For those who recognized it as Pauline, such as many already noted, did not in the least doubt its Canonical authority. Which is evident primarily concerning Clement of Rome from Eusebius. Although indeed Jerome in his own age, in chapter VIII of Isaiah, is the author of the statement that some did not hold the same among the Canonical Scriptures; yet that was not the mind of the ancients was: just as Jerome added there: We, however, accept the same, following by no means the custom of this time, but the authority of the ancients, who for the most part use its testimonies, not as they are sometimes wont to do concerning the Apocrypha, but as if they were Canonical and Ecclesiastical. And that there were very few who contradicted this epistle, we gather from Eusebius, when compared with Jerome: for he does not enumerate the same among those spoken against by some, without doubt because those whom Jerome noted were so few and obscure, but rather among the undisputed, canonical, and genuine [books], Hist. Eccl. Book III, ch. 22. Cf. Book III, ch. 3. Moreover, arguments for its divine authority appear no less illustrious in this Epistle than in other writings that are undoubtedly canonical, partly from internal and partly from external criteria; the internal are 1. truth, 2. sublimity in divine mysteries and their proof, 3. holiness in most sweet admonitions and examples, 4. singularity of style, 5. efficacy in instruction, etc. The external are both certain documents and testimonies. The former: 1. That it was written in the time of the Apostles. 2. That it was by some Apostle. 3. That it was commended to the Church by Peter, 2 Ep. III. 15. 4. That it has been preserved with the Canonical [books] by singular divine providence. These, indeed, are both of particular Doctors, who have testified to its divine authority through all ages; and of Councils, not only provincial, but also general or Ecumenical, from which it is permitted to observe 1. that this Epistle has been celebrated as Canonical throughout the whole world, 2. by all Greek and Latin Doctors, 3. by particular and Ecumenical Synods, representing the Church, 4. and that this tradition has been propagated by continuous succession. All of which, together with the resolution of contrary objections, we have executed in the aforementioned book. Friederich Spanheim also dealt at length with the authority and author of the Epistle to the Hebrews in a special treatise, which was published this year in London, annexed to the commentaries of Ludovicus Tenà on the same. How weakly, however, Grotius felt about the authority of this Epistle is clear even from what he says about Luke: That it is possible that he drew the explanation of the mysteries partly from the mouth of Paul, partly from Barnabas, so that from these a certain part of this Epistle may rightly be ascribed [to them]. For these things cannot consist with the divine inspiration of this Epistle: For who would believe that those things which are inspired by the Holy Spirit, which perhaps were patched together by someone from those things which he received at times from various people, are not those things whose sentiments and words were divinely suggested to the writer, nor proceeded in all things from the immediate impulse of GOD, or the movement of the Holy Spirit?

As regards the inscription, which is 'to the Hebrews', which is the second chapter of the prolegomena, Grotius repeats that denomination from Tertullian 'de pudicitia' and Clement 'Strom. VI', but it must be repeated much further back. For, to touch upon them at least lightly, those whom Grotius, the champion of the Papists, perhaps would not have rashly opposed, Bellarmine, Book 1 'de verbo DEI', ch. 17, praised Dionysius the Areopagite for producing the Epistle to the Hebrews; Sixtus Senensis, Book VII, 'Bibl. S.', heresy 8, alleged from the decretal epistles, which are held in esteem by not a few in the Papacy, Clement of Rome, Pope Evaristus, and Hyginus I. Alphonsus Salmeron, Vol. 15, 'Comment. in N. T.', on the Epistle to the Hebrews, disp. 1, produces the following Roman Pontiffs, close to the age of the Apostles: Clement in the epistle to James, Anacletus in epistle 2, Evaristus in the epistle to Africanus, Soter, Cornelius, Marcus, Julius, Liberius, Felix. Irenaeus, in the century next to the Apostle, cited the Epistle to the Hebrews, as witnessed by Eusebius, Book V, ch. 24, as did Clement of Alexandria, witnessed by the same, Book VI, ch. 17, and also Heraclius, who, according to Sixtus Senensis, wrote a commentary on the same. In the possession of Athanasius, Dial. I 'de Trin.', we read this: The Anomoean asks: Where is it written that the Son is the character of the hypostasis? The Orthodox responds: In the Apostle Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews. The Anomoean replies: It is not received in the Church; the Orthodox responds, 'from the time the Gospel of Christ was announced, this Epistle has been believed to be Paul's.' Which Origen also professed, according to Eusebius, Book VI, Eccl. ch. 24, namely, that the men of old (who in his own age, the third century, were already considered ancient) had handed down that this Epistle to the Hebrews was Pauline. What of the fact that Beza observed that all Greek copies except one had this inscription: 'The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Hebrews.' That this inscription is Paul's, there is no doubt. But that it is not found in the body of the Epistle itself, as the Apostle's name is prefixed in the remaining Pauline Epistles, this, without a doubt, had its causes, such as can be, in the judgment of some, that the Epistle was not directed to a particular Church or individual persons, but to all Hebrews dispersed throughout the whole world, and that he wished to remain hidden among some, by the omission of his name, lest, seeing a title and name hateful to them, they might immediately cast away the Epistle. See Jerome, preface to the Epistles of Paul; Athanasius, Dial. I 'de Trinit.'; Theophylact on Rom. I.

That by Hebrews, Jews are understood, is beyond controversy. There were, however, Jews of two kinds. Others, whom they called Hellenists, who lived here and there in Egypt, Asia, and Europe; others who were in the East, Babylonia, Persia, and beyond, who adhered to the Hebrew text. The Epistle was written to the former rather than to the latter, as being closer and better known to Paul, and in the dispersion of Pontus, Asia, Galatia, Bithynia, etc.

The third chapter concerns the language: Grotius acknowledges that this Epistle was written in Greek, for a twofold reason: the former is false, namely that the speech is more familiar to Luke: because he gratuitously assumes Luke to be its author: the latter is admitted, because most Jews also knew Greek, and indeed some of them only Greek, Acts VI. 1. for the Epistle pertained to all, and was to be read by all. However, Clement of Alexandria, book IV, observes that this Epistle was written in the original in Hebrew, not Greek; and in the hypotyposes cited by Eusebius, book VI, Hist. Eccl. c. 34, Origen in Ps. I, Eusebius book III, Hist. Eccl. c. 34, Jerome in Catal. c. 5, Theodoret and Oecumenius in the preface, Nicephorus book II, Hist. Eccl. c. 46. book IV. c. 45. assert this, and not a few of the more recent writers agree with them, especially the Papists, but they do not bring forward reasons for the Hebrew writing, except slippery ones and of lighter moment, namely that Paul was not so eloquent in the Greek language, and that it was written to the Hebrews: For as to the first, that Paul was equally eloquent in the Greek and Hebrew language is testified both by many other Epistles, and by his native land, because he was a Tarsian, and had lived among Greeks as long as among Hebrews, which answer is given by Schlichting; moreover, one should not stop there, for one must look primarily to the author, the Holy Spirit, the artificer of eloquence and of all languages. As to the other reason, both the first of James and John and of Peter were also written to the Hebrews, yet in the Greek language, not Hebrew: Grotius also acknowledges that the use of the Greek language was very widespread, and thus flourished among the Jews, since all knew Greek, not all knew Hebrew, or even the Chaldean idiom itself, which was then in use. Valid reasons to the contrary exist, that this Epistle was not written in the Hebrew language, such as from the character of the diction, from the cited passages of the Old Testament, from the emphasis of the Greek words, from the Greek interpretation of the Hebrew words, and also from certain inconveniences. Arguments of the most serious moment are also at hand, because it was written in the Greek language in the original: namely from the divine destination for the Canon of the N.T., from the induction of the remaining Pauline [epistles], from the collation of the Petrine Epistle, from the commonality of the Greek language, from the dispersion of the Jews among the nations, from the intention or dedication of the Holy Spirit, from the negation of a similar example, that any book should be θεόπνευστος both in the sources and in the translation, from the divine preservation of the original text, from the authority of the Greek text, and finally from the common calculation and consensus of other authors, concerning which [see] in the Critico Sacro, the Systemate Theologico, and the aforementioned Vestibulo.

Fourthly, as regards the scope and occasion of the Epistle, Grotius observes only παραϕυαδικῶς [incidentally] that not a few from among the Jews and Syrians, pressed by the burden of persecutions, withdrew themselves from the Christian party, whom he wished to recall to the way, and to support those still standing by his writings: and therefore he shows to many that all the histories of the Ancients and the sayings of the Prophets are occupied, by a certain hidden dispensation of God, in prefiguring Christ and his affairs. Although indeed we do not deny that the persecutions which those converted from the Hebrews endured, especially from the men of their own nation, provided the occasion for them, it is nevertheless certain that they did not avert themselves from the Christian Church; but that they were disturbed in the Christian faith by others, both Jews and heretics, there seems to be no doubt, with those also persecuting them—the Roman governors permitting it (which Constantinus Antiochenus in the works of Chrysostom, and Theophylactus observe)—as Apostates who had defected from the law of Moses, and despoiling them of their goods; to which is added that occasion which Athanasius noted in his Synopsis, that the Jews were leaning upon the law and its shadows, even those who had been converted to Christ, and as Anselm hands down, judged that faith alone without the admixture of legal ceremonies was not sufficient for salvation. Who could also easily conceive, or had conceived, a scruple concerning the doctrine of the Gospel, concerning the person and office of Christ, concerning his passion and cross, by which very many were offended, concerning justification through Christ, especially because the opinion stuck with many that sins still ought to be expiated by victims, and that the Priesthood of the O.T. was to be perpetual, and that the Messiah was about to administer a worldly kingdom, and that it had been impressed upon some from Pharisaism and the perversion of the Pseudo-Apostles that our works are a cause of salvation and necessary for salvation, and therefore that one is by no means justified by faith alone in Christ the man: which are evident from the reading and analysis of the Epistle.

Therefore, in order to assist all those, the Apostle, at the impulse of the Holy Spirit, wrote this Epistle to the converted Hebrews, the didactic scope of which Athanasius makes in his Synopsis, inasmuch as it is instructed with declarations and proofs concerning the advent of Christ and concerning the shadow of the law, that it has ceased. Moreover, although we acknowledge the primary scope of the Epistle to be didactic, yet that question, whether the Messiah has come, and whether Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah—which has been established most especially by the Evangelists as the primary foundation of Christianity—is not properly treated here. But as in other Epistles, so also in this one of ours, that is primarily dealt with: what sort of person the Messiah ought to have been, and who Christ is, both in person and by reason of his office; whence the Greek Scholiast, Oecumenius, Primasius, and Sedulius assign this scope to Paul, that he wished to draw the Hebrews entirely and perfectly from Judaism to Christianity: and Anselm observes that Paul discourses on the eminence of Christ and the uselessness of the law for justification and salvation. However, there can be added to this didactic scope, as a primary one, a secondary hortatory one, namely for which this Epistle is called in ch. XIII. 22 a word of exhortation, provided that the Apostle subjoins to each doctrinal part, or infers from it, an exhortation flowing from the doctrine: by which name some make the scope of this Epistle mixed: yet so that it is primarily occupied in the doctrine concerning Christ and his person and office, especially the Priestly one, for the sake of which he institutes a comparison with the Priests and sacrifices of the O.T.; and also concerning the faith by which we apprehend the righteousness of his obedience, passion, and death: and for that reason the Epistle may deservedly be compared to those to the Romans and to the Galatians; meanwhile the Apostle himself seems to hint at the primary scope in chapter VIII. 1: This is the sum of the things of which we speak, that we have such a High Priest.

Therefore its primary argument is the Priesthood of Christ, for the sake of which it is occupied in describing the Priest of the new covenant, that he is God-man, sent immediately by God to expiate sins, to appease the wrath of God by the offering of the sacrifice of his body, and to pray for us, so that we may be reconciled with God, with righteousness and eternal life acquired for us, and the covenant of grace is sanctioned, for which there is need of faith in this our High Priest and his unique propitiatory sacrifice.

Schlichtingius says that it primarily exhorts to constancy in the Christian religion, and thus to remove especially those things which seemed to undermine it, and to invite the Hebrews to prefer the Gospel to the law: namely both the excellence of the Mosaic law and discipline, and the various afflictions that are companions of the Christian profession: the economy of which, both as to the thing itself and as to the method, we discussed in the Vestibulo p. 79 seq.

Three parts of the Epistle can be established: The first is concerning the person of Christ, which is completed in two chapters, I & II, up to the middle of v. 9, with an exhortation inserted to receive Christ. The second is concerning the Regal office of Christ from c. II.9 up to X.19, with a double hortatory digression inserted, however, for the double treatment: the first of which is general up to the end of chapter II, to which is subjoined an exhortation concerning receiving the Apostle and High Priest of our royal confession: who is preferred to Moses, because he is the house of God and the Architect, and the master, and leads us to eternal rest: c. III & IV. The other explains the Priesthood of Christ more specifically, with a parenesis inserted, however, at the end of c. V, and c. VI, that they may be carried on to perfection, and not indeed deny Christ once acknowledged. The third is concerning saving faith in Christ, c. X & XI, with an exhortation subjoined not only to constancy and patience, but also to other virtues by which faith is declared, c. XII & XIII. However, the present Epistle, just like the first of John, omits the things of the epistle which the Apostles were otherwise accustomed to place at the beginning, such as not only the personalia, or personal matters, the mention of the Author from whom, and of those to whom it was written, but also the realia, or real matters, whether votive or congratulatory, or as they are commonly indicated, the subscription, inscription, and salutation. Since, indeed, the subscription of the name was to be omitted on purpose, he also omitted the inscription and salutation, which the Apostle was accustomed to attach to them. Toward the end of the Epistle, however, he did not neglect those things with which he was accustomed to conclude his Epistles, so that it might be evident even from the closing that it is an Epistle.

We present the economy of the whole Epistle more fully in this way, namely that it consists both of the principal parts up to the last chapter, v. 21, and of the secondary parts, which are added as if by way of an addition (προσθήκην) to the last four verses. The principal parts, however, are: Proposition and Treatment. If anyone prefers to call them three parts: Proposition, treatment, and conclusion of the Epistle, we do not object. The Proposition concerns both the person and the office of Christ: The person of Christ Christ, which is treated here, is both Doctoral and Sacerdotal. In the proposition (προθέσει) therefore, he presents Christ as our Teacher and Priest, the Son of God, in whom God has spoken to the Hebrews in these last days, when he was made man, who made purification for our sins by himself, and sat down at the right hand of God. Therefore, as regards his person, he teaches that he is the same Son of God, through whom he created the ages, the radiance of his glory, and the character of his hypostasis, which pertain to describing the divine nature: the heir of all things, who sat down at the right hand of the Majesty of God on high, having become more sublime than the Angels, with respect to his human nature. As to the Doctoral office, that in him GOD has most recently spoken to the Hebrew people, after he had formerly spoken in many ways and in many manners to the Fathers through the Prophets: As to the Sacerdotal office, however, that the Son of God made purification for our sins by himself, and sits at the right hand of GOD. c. I. v. 1. 2. 3. 4.

The exposition (Ἔκθεσις) or treatment is bipartite. First, didactic, with the name taken from the more important part, up to c. X. 18. Then hortatory (pænetica) to c. XIII. 12. There, first, the person of Christ is treated demonstratively (ἀποδεικτικῶς) in c. I. & II. so that the supreme eminence and sublimity of our Teacher and Priest may be demonstrated: Then the office, both Doctoral in chapters III. & IV. and Sacerdotal in c. V. VI. VII. VIII. IX. X., is treated explanatorily (ἐξηγητικῶς), so that the greater glory and truth of the office may be explained. Moreover, that entire treatment is instituted comparatively (συγκριτικῶς); with a comparison made, as far as the sublimity of his person is concerned, with the Angels, and as far as the dignity and nature of the office is concerned, with Moses regarding the Doctoral office, and with the priests of the Old Testament regarding the Sacerdotal office: Just as in the exhortation the Apostle likewise presents examples from the Old Testament, which are to be imitated by Christians, by reason of faith, constancy, and holiness in the New Testament, so that he may exhibit to the Hebrews the Harmony of both, and stir them up by the example of the Ancients to a like faith, because Jesus is the same yesterday and forever. The demonstration (Apodixis) concerning the person of Christ, as it is instituted regarding his divine nature, is from c. I. up to v. 12; regarding the eminence of his human nature, from v. 13 & 14 and the following chapter to v. 9. The divine nature of Christ is demonstrated first from the generation of the Son of God, which befits none of the Angels, v. 5, by a double testimony of the Old Testament: the one concerns the theology (τὴν θεολογίαν), as the ancients call it, from Ps. II. 7; the other pertains at the same time to the economy (τὴν ὀικονομίαν) from 2 Sam. VII. 14. For there the Son of GOD is viewed within the simplest complex of the Deity; here the Son of David is taught to be the Messiah himself, the natural Son of GOD. Secondly, from the axiom of adoration, v. 6, because that firstborn is to be adored by all the Angels, by virtue of Ps. XCVII. 4; thirdly, from the name, throne, and divine scepter, by which he again exceeds all Angelic dignity in a most eminent manner, v. 7, 8, 9, by a comparison made between Ps. CIV. v. 4 and Ps. XLV. 7. Fourthly, from the divine work of the creation and consummation of the world, and the divine immutability of the Son of GOD, v. 10, 11, 12. Which are confirmed from Ps. CII. 26.

As regards the sublimity of the human nature of Christ, according to which, having been exalted to the right hand of God, he received a name more eminent than the Angels, it is proved by a double testimony: a comparison being instituted again with the Angels: The one is brought forward in c. I. 13 & 14 from Ps. CX. 1, because it was said to none of the Angels, 'sit at my right hand,' as they are only ministering Spirits, sent forth for our salvation: on the occasion of which is subjoined by way of application (παραθετικῶς), as if at the beginning of chapter II. 1, 2, 3, an exhortation to receive the word announced by such a Teacher, if we wish to escape divine punishment; as it was preached not through Angels, but immediately through the Lord himself (who was made flesh, ἐνσαρκωθέντα). The other saying, to demonstrate the subjection of all things in the world to come not to the Angels, but to the Son of Man, Christ Jesus, is taken from v. 5 seq. from Ps. VIII. 5 seq., which he illustrates from the fulfillment, namely, Jesus being crowned, through the suffering of death, with glory and honor, who had been made lower than the Angels for a short time, v. 9. And thus far concerning the person of Christ. Concerning the office of Christ, it is treated first in general, regarding the congruity of the divine Economy, apart from the author of our salvation: namely, that it was fitting that he who brings many sons to glory, the very GOD, for whom are all things and through whom are all things (for the Apostle had already demonstrated this concerning Christ), should be made perfect through sufferings; To which contribute (1) the identity and brotherhood of origin (ταυτότης & συναδελφία), that it is fitting that he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified should all be from one, whence he also calls us his brothers, v. 11, 12, according to Psalm XXII. 23, 26. (2) Common boldness (παρρησία) and confidence toward God, v. 13, 14, from Ps. XVIII. 3, Is. VIII. 17, 18. (3) The likeness (ὁμοιοσία) of Christ with the children given to him by GOD, and the cause of the same, namely, that through death he might destroy him who has the power of death, and liberate his captives, v. 14, 15. (4) The taking hold (ἐπίληψις) of the seed of Abraham: Since it is nowhere said in the Scriptures that he takes hold of Angels, but the seed of Abraham (Gen. XII. 3, etc.). (5) The fellow-suffering (ὁμοιοπάθεια) of Christ with his brothers: By which it is taught that there was need for the execution of the Priesthood, v. 17, 18. These things concerning the person of our Teacher and High Priest.

After those things, the Apostle treats more specifically of his office: and first indeed of the Doctoral office, that he is the same Apostle who is the High Priest of their confession, whom the Hebrews confessed, c. III. 1. Whose, therefore, the Apostle's, both fidelity and dignity he sets forth by a comparison made with Moses, the former teacher of the people of the Hebrews: the former, because he is like the faithful Moses in the whole house of the Lord, v. 5; the latter, both because he is of greater honor, inasmuch as he prepared the house of the Lord, v. 2, 4, and because Moses was only a minister, but Christ is the Son over the house of the Lord, v. 5, 6, and because all the faithful are his house, v. 6; whence an exhortation is deduced concerning observing this Teacher, drawn partly from the command of the Holy Spirit, v. 6, 7, following to the end of the third chapter, namely from Psalm XCV. 7, which is illustrated in chapter IV, v. 1, following, from the rest still remaining for us, to be attained only through faith, by a comparison of the rest and the Sabbath of creation, v. 3, Gen. II. 2, XXII. 11, the rest into which the Hebrews were introduced by Joshua, the possession of the land of Canaan, v. 5, 6. and the rest into which they are to be introduced through Jesus, according to David's prediction, v. 7, following, established: that they should strive to enter into the same, and not be excluded from it by unbelief, v. 11, partly from the power and efficacy of the word of God, v. 12, partly from the omniscience of Christ, v. 13, to whose constant confession, as the Great High Priest who penetrated the heavens so that he might intercede for us there, and who is the very Son of God, tempted in all things so that he might be able to sympathize with our infirmities, and to a confident approach to the throne of grace, the Apostle exhorts, v. 14, 15, and 16, by that very fact [opening] an approach for himself preparing for a fuller discourse on the priestly office of Christ, to be established in the following chapters.

Wherefore he has executed these things concerning the priestly office: First, in general, he delivers the definition of a priest in chapter V, verses 1, 2, 3; then he confirms his vocation and its necessity by the example of Aaron, because a comparison with the Levitical priesthood had to be established, verse 4; namely, that he was called by God the Father: as being He from whom (1) the Messiah was begotten from eternity, or that Anointed One of the Lord, verse 5, according to Ps. II. 7; (2) by whom he was constituted Priest, verse 6, according to Ps. CX. 4; (3) to whom he prayed in the days of his flesh; (4) to whom his Son was made obedient, inasmuch as he learned obedience in his passion, verses 7, 8; (5) by whom he was made perfect, the cause of salvation to those who obey, verse 9, and thus was deservedly called a Priest according to the order of Melchizedek, verse 10. Then, in particular, he set forth the explanation of that priesthood (according to the order of Melchizedek). But before he approaches that, he anticipates that many things must be said about it, but that the Hebrews are still weak, kindly noting their infancy in matters of faith, c. V. 11, 12, 13, 14; and having designated those things which pertain to the foundation, c. VI. 1, 2, 3, he tacitly dissuades them from apostasy, having proposed the danger of the sin against the Holy Spirit, testifying to a better confidence concerning them, verses 9, 10; and he exhorts them to constancy, verse 11, setting before them both the example of faithful predecessors, verse 12, and the promise made to Abraham, confirmed by a divine oath, verse 13, seq. Moreover, he explains the priesthood of Christ first from the type of Melchizedek, chapter VII, and that both tacitly, regarding the office, the blessing of Abraham, from whom he also received tithes, and the name of King and his seat, as well as his origin and end, c. VII. 1, 2, 3; and expressly, regarding the dignity of Melchizedek above the Levites, who were tithed by him, verse 4, seq., and the diversity of the priesthood, verse 11, 13, which is clear in Christ from the diversity of the tribe, verses 13, 14. and even clearer, because he was constituted High Priest not according to the law of the Levitical priesthood, but according to the promise of power, verses 15, 16, to show the infirmity and uselessness of the law in the cause of salvation, verses 18, 19; and because he was made Priest not without an oath (as those Levitical priests were), but with a divine oath intervening, verses 20, 21, according to Ps. CX. 4; whence it is concluded that he is the sponsor of a better testament, verse 22; furthermore, that he is a unique and eternal Priest, verses 23, 24, 25; finally, that he is holy and free from sin, and thus offered himself once, not for himself, but only for us, as the Son of God and perfect, verses 26, 27, 28.

Secondly, the priesthood of Christ and its eminence and prerogative are explained from the sitting of the Priest at the right hand of God. Which pertains to the other duty of the priesthood of Christ, namely, intercession for us at the right hand of the Majesty on high, because of the expiation made through death; to which two things pertain, concerning the truth of which he treats in c. VIII, but concerning the quality and nature in c. IX, as being both a λειτουργία in the heavens, because, namely, he is the administrator of the holy things and of the true tabernacle, inasmuch as he not only offered himself (in death: cf. c. VII. 26), since it is the duty of a priest to offer a sacrifice, but also is a λειτουργὸς in the heavens, no longer performing the priesthood on earth, as the Aaronic priests, who only served shadows, as Moses testifies (Exod. XXV. 40), and the mediation of a better Testament, verse 6, seq., because he is the Mediator of the Testament of grace, and of the New, which was promised by the Holy Spirit (Jer. XXXI. 24.) and brings about the antiquity and ἀφανισμὸν of the old, verse 6, to the end of the chapter.

But to explain the nature and character of both the λειτουργία of Christ and the μεσιτεία of the New Testament, there contributes, regarding the former, a comparison of the Old Testament, whose laws and worship with the apparatus of the tabernacles are designated, especially regarding the annual entry into the holy of holies, which are taught to have been typical, chapter IX. 1, seq., of the future good things of Christ the High Priest, who, having entered through the true tabernacle with his own blood into the holy (of holies) with his sacrifice, purified our consciences, verse 11, seq.

Regarding the latter, however, that he was made Mediator of the N. T., this reason is given, that, namely, through his death we were freed from the sins which oppressed us under the O. T., so that we might obtain the promised inheritance, verse 15; whence also the new Testament had to be confirmed by the death of the testator, just as the Old was sanctioned by the blood of beasts, verse 16, seq. (Ex. XXIV. verse 8), with the addition also of the end of Christ's entry into the holy of holies, heaven itself, namely, intercession for us, verse 24, where is noted at the same time the diversity of the Levitical High Priest's entry, that it had to be repeated annually, as also the sacrifices had to be repeated with whose blood he entered: whereas Christ offered himself only once to take away sins, and entered once, verse 25, seq., as also the fruit of the sacrifice, the taking away of sins, and of the mediation of the Testament of grace, the final appearance for the salvation of the faithful.

Thirdly, the priesthood of Christ and its prerogative are explained from the comparison of Christ's sacrifice with the sacrifices of the O. T., because that was only a type and shadow, c. X, which is deduced (1) from the repetition of the Levitical sacrifices, which is an argument that those sacrifices did not of themselves perfect those who offered them, verse 2, nor take away sins, verse 4; (2) from the testimony of Christ, verse 5, seq., from Ps. XL. 7, seq., which is explained concerning the sacrifice of the body of Christ, verse 10; (3) from the eternal value of the sacrifice of Christ, verses 11, 12, 13, 14; (4) from the reason of the New Testament, situated in the fact that he no longer wishes to remember sins, verses 15, 16, 17, from Jer. XXXI. 33, whence there is no need for a repetition of a sacrifice for sins, verse 18. And thus far the didactic part of the Epistle has been set forth.

The second Parænetic part begins at v. 19, c. X, and is inferred πορισματικῶς (as a corollary) from the former, an entrance into heaven with παῤῥησίᾳ (boldness): which is confirmed both from the manner and merit of the entrance, because it is made in the blood of Christ v. 19, because it is opened to us through the veil, i.e., the body of Christ v. 20, and from the means on our part, which is πληροφορία τῆς πίςεως (full assurance of faith) v. 21, and on the part of GOD, which is Baptism v. 22. And therefore the Hebrews are excited to constancy in the confession of Christ, which is established by the faithfulness of God who calls v. 23, as also to mutual exhortation to charity and good works v. 24, and not to desert the Church v. 25. Moreover, causes for perseverance in the saving faith of Christ, and for not deserting the Church, are added, both from the nearness of the last day v. 25, and from the extreme danger of those who sin willfully v. 26, 27, which is confirmed by a comparison of the punishment for prevarication against the Mosaic law, and the trampling underfoot of the Son of God v. 28, 29. and by the threatening of divine vengeance v. 30, 31, from Deut. XXX. 11, 35, 36, then from the struggle of past times v. 32, 33, 34, then from the gracious retribution, and the attainment of the promise v. 35, 36, established by the testimony of Habakkuk concerning the just man who shall live by faith v. 37, seq.

Furthermore, to these arguments in chap. XI, examples of the O.T. are subjoined, so that the Hebrews may be confirmed in faith in Christ, and the promise concerning life to be attained through faith may be corroborated: to which is prefixed a definition of faith v. 1, 2, and its illustration from the article of creation v. 3, but the Apostle presents to them the example of the faith of Abel offering a sacrifice v. 4, of Enoch, who through faith pleased God, so that he did not see death, v. 5. 6. Of Noah, who was made heir of the righteousness which is through faith, v. 7. Of Abraham, who by faith obeyed God when he called, by faith was a stranger in the land of promise, expecting the heavenly city with Isaac and Jacob, vers. 9. 10. Of Sarah, who by faith embraced the promise: and with the said Patriarchs, although the promised Messiah was not yet actually obtained, expected the heavenly country, vers. 11. seq. likewise of the offering of Isaac attempted by faith by Abraham, whom he received back alive as a figure of the resurrection of Christ, v. 17. 18. 19. and furthermore of the blessing of Isaac, vers. 20. and of Jacob, v. 21. Of the commandment of Joseph concerning the translation of his bones into the promised land, made by faith, v. 22. of the hiding of Moses by his parents, which was likewise done by faith, v. 23. of the faith of Moses in choosing the reproach of Christ over the treasures of Egypt, v. 24. seq. in leaving Egypt, v. 27. in the celebration of the Passover, v. 28. in the crossing through the Red Sea, v. 29. of the faith of Joshua in the throwing down of the walls of Jericho, v. 30. of the faith of Rahab in the receiving of the spies, v. 31. finally of the faith of other righteous men, whose names he only brings forward, Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, or their office, such as Prophets, or deeds proceeding from faith with various sufferings, v. 32. 33. seq.

To this primary exhortation to faith in the Messiah and perseverance by the example of the ancestors, the Apostle subjoins other exhortations, both to patience and to holiness, and in general in chapter XII, and in particular in chapter XIII. There, in the course of patience, he presents the comfort of divine love toward those whom he chastens, from Prov. III. 11. 12. which is explained in vers. 5. seq. and the fruit of chastening, vers. 10. 11. and thus he exhorts that they strengthen the slack hands and lift up the feeble knees, vers. 12. Here he commends holiness with a zeal for peace, and also that we do not fall short of the grace of God, vers. 15. through contention, fornication, impiety, vers. 14. 15. 16. 17. since we have come not to Mount Sinai, in which there is terror and trembling, v. 18. 19. 20. 21. But to Zion, and the communion of the church militant and triumphant, to God himself and the Mediator of the New Testament. Jesus, and his blood, which speaks not of vengeance, but of grace, v. 22. 23. 24. then that we do not despise the voice of the Lord speaking from heaven, v. 25. 26. who shook heaven and earth, Hag. II. 7. by whose grace we receive an immovable kingdom, that we may serve God, and who is a consuming fire to the disobedient, v. 27. 28. 29. Deut. IV. 24.

To the general exhortations are added special precepts concerning certain virtues of the Christian life in chapter XIII, namely first regarding the neighbor: I. of Φιλαδελφίᾳ, v. 1. love toward brothers; II. Φιλοξενίᾳ, hospitality toward strangers, v. 2.; III. συμπαθείᾳ toward the afflicted, v. 3.; IV. honor of marriage and faithfulness toward spouses, v. 4. Then regarding ourselves, namely both ἀυταρκείᾳ, in conduct, with confidence toward GOD, v. 5. 6. from Job I. 5. Psalm LVI. v. 12. and imitation of those who were in charge in the Old Testament, who died piously, and the avoidance of false teachers, who are to be fled, and especially those who were attempting to lead the Hebrews away from Christ Jesus, and faith in him, to ceremonies, e.g., concerning foods, v. 8. 9. because those who still wish to serve the (shadowy) tabernacle cannot partake of the true altar, after Christ suffered outside the gate, that he might sanctify the people with his blood, just as (in type) the blood of animals was carried into the sanctuary, whose bodies were burned outside the camp: then a constant profession of Christ, and also the endurance of exile and reproach, because we do not have a lasting city here, v. 13. 14. Thirdly regarding GOD, who is to be honored both with spiritual sacrifices of praise, v. 15. and with beneficence, vers. 16. and also with obedience toward the ministers of GOD: to which he subjoins prayers for himself and his companions, v. 18. 19. All of which he ends with a vow, containing a recapitulation of the doctrine concerning the Shepherd of souls brought back from the dead through the blood of the eternal Testament, and constituted Lord by the God of peace, and an exhortation to the pursuit of perfection in every good work, and of divine complacency, with a doxology, v. 20. 21.

To these, in place of a conclusion, is subjoined an admonition concerning receiving the word of exhortation, v. 22. as also a notification concerning the release of Timothy, and the intention to visit the Hebrews with him, v. 23. and also a commission of greeting to the teachers and all other saints, with the addition of a greeting in the name of the brothers from Italy, v. 24. and a final prayer for grace, v. 25.

PART I. OF THE EPISTLE, DOGMATIC. OF THE PERSON AND OFFICE OF CHRIST.

SECTION I. OF THE PERSON OF CHRIST.

Latin:

IN. J. OTATA STOLAM BRÆOS.

verba, sed in aliis rebus narrandis, puta Pauli navigatione, liberius spatiatur. Ad hoc scriptam apparet ex Italia hanc epistolam infra XIII. 24. Pauli non facit mentionem, quia nempe Paulus eo tempore vinculis liberatus extra Italiam erat profectus in Epirum, ut videtur Tit. III. 12. Habuerat autem Paulus, Romæ cum esset, secum & Lucam & Timo- theum. De Luca apparet Col. IV. 14. 2. Tim. IV. 11. Philem. 24. de Timotheo Eph. I. 1. Phil. II. 19. Col. I. 1. Philem. 1. Hos Paulus, cum ab Italia discessit, in Italia reliquit ad per- colendam eam, quam Paulus fecerat latiusque spargendam semeutem. Horum Timotheus dum suo muneri instat, vin- ctus: sed mox è vinculis exemptus fuerat; infra XIII. 23. Lu- cas interim, qui & ipse antea vinctus fuerat, sed ex vinculis exierat infra X. 33. in aliqua parte Italiæ dans operam con- vertendis aut confirmandis Italis, tempus reperit scribendi ad illos Christianos, quos in Judæa & Syria quondam no- verat, Syrus & ipse origine. Eorum autem non pauci per- secutionum onere pressi a cœtibus se subduxerant. Ut ergo hos in viam reducat, alios vero adhuc stantes fulciat, mul- tis ostendit, omnes veteres historias, & dicta Prophetarum, occulta quadam Dei dispensatione in Christo ejusque rebus figurandis occupari. Et fieri potest, ut istorum mysterio- rum explicationem ex ore partim Pauli, partim Barnabæ hauferit, ita ut & istis pars hujus epistolæ aliqua ascribi re- cte possit. Neque vero hac tantum re, sed omnibus modis id agit hic scriptor, ut Christianismi præ Judaïsmo præstan- tiam alte infigat animis, & afflictionibus opponit æterna præmia: Lucam autem hujus epistolæ scriptorem osten- dunt etiam vocabula & loquendi genera quædam Lucæ velut propria. Εὐλαβεῖσθαι & εὐλάβεια pro metuere & me- tu Act. XXIII. 10. Ebr. V. 7. εἰς τὸ παντελὲς Luc. XIII. 11. pro εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς habemus Ebræor. VII. 7. μαρτυρούμενος & μαρτυρεῖσθαι Actor. VI. 3. XVI. 2. Ebr. VIII. 8. XI. 2. 5. 30. χρηματίζεσθαι Luc. II. 26. Act. X. 22. Ebr. VIII. 5. ἡγεῖσθαι Luc. XXII. 26. Ebr. XIII. 7. 17. ἀρχηγὸς Actor. III. 15. V. 31. Ebræor. II. 10. XII. 2. πρὸς loco particulæ περὶ Luc. XVIII. 1. XIX. 42. XX. 19. Act. XXVIII. 25. Ebr. 1. 7. 8. Præterea scriptor hic verfionem LXX. plerumque addicte sequitur, quod & ipsum Lucæ est. Inscriptio ad Ebræos vetus. Ita enim hanc Epistolam nominant Tertullianus de pudicitia, & Clemens Strom. VI. Per Ebræos autem intelliguntur Judæi, ut Act. VI. 1. 2. Cor. XI. 22. Phil. III. 5. Sic & lingua Ebræa est Judaica Luc. XXIII. 38. Actor. XXI. 40. XXII. 2. XXVI. 14. Græce autem scripta est hæc epistola, quia is sermo Lucæ familiarjor. Judæi autem plerique etiam Græce norant: nonnulli vero eorum tantum Græce, ut liquet Actor. VI. vers. 1.

OBSERVATIONES PRÆLIMINARES.

De tribus agit Grotius in procœmio. I. De Autore. II. De inscriptione ad Ebræos. III. De lingua, qua eadem scripta. Nonnihil etiam, quanquam obiter admodum, de receptione in Canonem ingerit. Quibus vero addenda nonnulla de Scopo, paucis tacto à Grotio, deque Argumento, & partitione epistolæ: sed succincte, quum pleraque ante hosce XXXIV. annos in Academia Regiomontana, quum Theologicâ ibidem fungerer professio- ne, tradita & Anno ↆĵ IƆc LIX. sub titulo Vestibuli in portam Veteris, & munimentum Novi Testamenti, divinam S. Pauli ad Ebræos Epistolam Dantisci edita sint.

Quod primum Autorem Epistolæ attinet, ante omnia id agit Grotius, ut eundem dubium reddat, tum vero persuadeat, vetustissimos alii potius quam Paulo, nimirum aut Barnabæ, aut Clementi Romano, aut Lucæ eandem tribuisse: Porro eam Apostolo Paulo planè abjudicet: denique nec Barnabæ, nec Clementis Romani, sed Lucæ eam esse obtineat.

Quod autem initio, hodie dubitari, cujus scriptoris hæc sit Epistola, Grotius ait, id non immerito miramur, siquidem eam dubitationem Concilii Tridentini definitioni, quæ sine dubio ipsi Sacrosancta fuit, adversari, haud ignorârit. In eo enim Sessione IV. decretum fuit, quatuordecim esse Pauli Epistolas, & inter Pauli Epistolas eam esse, quæ ad Ebræos inscribitur, & anathema dictum ei, qui illam non susceperit, ut Canonicam. Neque ignoravit Polyhistor, contrariam esse dubitationem illam autoritati antiquiorum Conciliorum, à quibus hanc Epistolam S. Pauli esse definitum fuit, utpote Concilii Laodicensis circa annum Christi ccc xciv. Can. 59. & Concilii Carthaginensis III. circa annum cccc. Can. 47. nec non Amsicani II. ut & Romani à Gelasio An. ccccxciv. coacti, ut sequiorum ætatum Concilia taceamus, quæ minime ab illis dissentiunt.

Jam si Autores vel Doctores antiquos consulamus, sane Apostolo Paulo hanc Epistolam tribuisse constat. Ipso primo à Christo nato seculo, majores omnes Origenis, qui ad illos provocat in Ps. I. & præfatione super hanc Epistolam, quemadmodum & S. Athanasius vel quisquis libri Autor est, Dial. 1. de Trin. perhibet, eandem Pauli esse, creditum esse, ex quo annunciatum est Evangelium Christi. Seculo vero secundo Paulo eandem tribuit Clemens Alexandrinus apud Eusebium l. VI. Hist. Eccl. c. 13. Heraclius, Origenes, ut & Dionysius in Epist. ad Titum. Seculo tertio Epiphanius hæresi LXXVI. Athanasius in Synopsi, Eusebius Cæsariensis, Gregorius Nazianzenus in carmine, Didymus Alexandrinus, aliique præcipui Doctores. Seculo quarto Chrysostomus, ejusque discipulus Constantinus Antiochenus, Cyrillus Alexandrinus l. XII. Thesaur. c. 19. Amphilochius in Carm. ad Seleucum, Theodoretus Heracliensis, & Cyrensis, Hilarius l. II. de Trin. Ambrosius l. 2. de Cain c. 11. Philastrius Brixiensis, Hieronymus, Augustinus l. 11. de doct. Christ. c. 8. aliique. Porro seculis subsequentibus à Patribus tum Græcis tum Latinis constanter tributa est hæc Epistola S. Paulo. E recen- tioribus etiam Paulo eandem vindicarunt è Scho- lasticis Petrus Lombardus, Hugo de S. Victore, Pe- trus de Tarantasio, Thomas de Aquino, Alexander Alensis aliique; & subsequis Pontificiis Claudius Guillandus, Eduardus Loeus, Nic. Tacitus Zigenus, Johannes Gagnejus, Ambrosius Catharinus, Grego- rius Primaticensis, Franc. Lucas Brugensis, Adamus Sasbouth, Emanuel Saa, Mutius Angelus, Nico- laus Grandis, Hieronymus Veronensis, Cardinalis Bellarminus, Johannes Mariana, Guilielmus Lin- danus, Gabriel Vasquez, Franc. Ribera, Cornel. à Lapide, & qui non alii? Siquidem per decretum Concilii Tridentini Papistis aliter sentire non li- cuit. E Reformatis etiam pro Paulina hanc Epi- stolam agnovêre Andreas Hyperius, Georgius Sob- nius, Johannes Piscator, David Pareus, Bartholo- mæus Keckermannus, Franc. Gomarus, Mart. Frie- der. Wendelinus, & alii. E Neophotinianis cætero- rum Dux & Antesignanus Faustus Socinus in Solut. Scrupul. p. 70. Neque abnuunt ex August. Con- fessionis Doctoribus Matthias Flacius Illyricus, David Chytreus, Salomo Gesnerus, B. Gerhardus, ut alios plurimos taceam. Paucos utique suo tem- pore invenisset Grotius, qui dubitarint de Paulo Autore comparatione eorum, qui Paulum Auto- rem agnoverunt, cum Papistis post Concilium Tridentinum de eo dubitare religio sit, alii vero, si forte inventi sint, in nullo censu apud ipsum fue- rint. Et quid de dubitatione eorum, quibus su- periori seculo forte id ambiguum fuit, habendum sit, in Vestibulo prædicto satis expositum. Ne- minem nominavit Grotius, ideo peculiariter de eo dispicere, opus non est.

Provocat ad Vetustissimos: Qui vero illi sint, qui è vetustissimis Paulo eandem abjudicarint, non o- mnino explicat. Neque facile inter Græcos reperi- re est, qui Paulinam hanc Epistolam esse negarit. Unum Cajum commemorat Eusebius l. VI. Hist. Eccl. c. 20. & Hieronymus in Catalogo Illust. Doct. Eccl. c. 9. qui Origenis σύγχρονος fuit, qui vero non tam ex propria mente hoc inficiatus, quam disputandi causa assumsisse hanc sententiam vide- tur, si Eusebii verba recte expendas. Nec ille ad græ- cos referendus. Scripsit enim Romæ sub Zepherino, Unde in Latina quidem Ecclesia, & cumprimis Ro- manâ quosdam id negasse, ex Eusebio l. c. & l. III. c. 3. ut & Hieronymo l. c. & lib. eod. c. 5. constat. Sed quinam illi apud Romanos, præter Cajum, fuerint, & anne simpliciter, an v. secundum quid Epistolam præsentem Paulinam esse negarint, haud constat. Hieronymus ad Dardanum scribens quum asseruis- set ab Ecclesiis Orientis (sui temporis) imo ab omni- bus retro Ecclesiis & Græcis scriptoribus Epistolam ad Ebræos quasi Pauli suscipi, addit, licet plerique eam vel Barnabæ, vel Clementis esse arbitrentur. Et Ori- genes in homil. super hanc Epist. apud Eusebium lib. VI. Hist. Eccl. c. 24. priscos, ait, viros eam Pau- linam esse tradidisse, tametsi quidam eorum à Cle- mente Romano Episcopo, alii vero à Luca, qui & Evangelium, & acta dedit, scriptam esse dixerunt. Quod quomodo accipiendum sit ex mente Vete- rum forte non inutiliter disquiritur. Fuere autem, qui ita censuere è Veteribus, Paulo ἀρχέτυπον & originalem textum tribuendum esse, alii vero cui- piam ἔκτυπον vel translationem in linguam Græ- cam: quomodo Hieron. in Catalog. III. Doct. c. 5. ait Paulum Ebræum scripsisse Ebrais Ebraice, id est suo eloquio disertissime, ea autem, quæ eloquenter scripta fuerant, adhuc eloquentius translata esse in Græcum. Eusebius lib. VI. Hist.
