Eccl. c. 13. Cum E- bræis, inquit, Paulus scripteo hoc Patria lingua lo- cutus sit, alii Lucam Evangelistam, alii Clementem

Romanum interpretatum esse, ajunt, id quod & magis veritati consonum : Et Clemens Alexandri- nus Epistolam ad Ebræos Ebræorum gratia à Pau- lo Ebraice scriptam esse docuit in hypotyposibus, & à Luca studiose conversam, gentibusque opositam apud Eusebium l. VI. c. 13. Alii tamen nonnulli Paulum autorem Epistolæ dixêre tantum ratione sensuum, vel sententiarum, alterius vero quam A- postoli ratione structuræ, utpote Origenes, citante Eusebio l. VI. c. 34. qui tamen profitetur credibile esse, quæ Paulus Ebraica lingua eloquenter scripse- rit, Græcum Interpretem, quisquis ille fuerit, elo- quentius adhuc in Græcum sermonem transtulisse. Non ergo nisi cum grano salis admittendum, quod Grotius ait, vetustissimos in tres partes scindi, alios enim Barnabæ hanc Epistolam tribuere, alios Cle- menti Romano, alios Lucæ.

Jam quod ad Barnabam attinet, nemo facile inventus fuit, qui eidem hanc Epistolam tribuit, nisi quod annotavit Hieronymus in Catalogo c. 5. Tertulliano id factum, quod tamen ibidem vide- tur solum ratione translationis in Græcum ser- monem intellexisse. Sed non diffitetur Grotius ipse à sermone ejus multum distare præsentem Epistolam. Quod vero colligit ex Epistola Barna- bæ quæ hodie extat, quam eandem esse, qua usi sunt Clemens Alexandrinus, Origenes, & alii, exi- stimat. Sed Eusebius jam suo tempore Epistolam, quæ nomine Barnabæ ferebatur, Scripturis mini- me legitimis accensuit l. III. H. E. c. 19. eamque in- ter Apocryphas legi, Hieron. l. 12. script. Eccl. ut & l. XIII. in Ezech. c. 43. observavit; Et quicquid sit de Isaaci Vossii sententia, in notis ad Epistolam Barnabæ, fatetur ipse Hugo Menander, qui è te- nebris Epistolam hanc eruit, notisque illustravit, editam Parisiis An. 1645. sub initium observatio- num, jure inter Scripturas Apocryphas collocari; tum quia an Barnabæ sit, incertum est, tum quia in eadem reperiuntur, quæ minime difficultate ca- rent, & Clementem Alexandrinum & Origenem sæpe apocryphis uti observat, tametsi certum ei sit, hanc epistolam, quam edidit, illam esse, quam S. Hieronymus, Clemens Alexandrinus, & Origenes olim præ manibus habuerunt, quod nos suo loco relinquimus, quanquam argumentum illud exigui roboris sit, quod è locis ab ipsis citatis in ea in- ventis petitur : quum illa ex ipsorum scriptis com- pleri à consarcinatore potuerint. Quid ergo de stylo Barnabæ è scripto notho & adulterino ju- dicari poterit? Quicquid autem de eo sit, con- gruatne stylus nostræ Epistolæ dictioni Barnabæ, annon? unde habuerit Tertullianus, quod Epi- stola hæc à Barnaba translata sit, non apparet. Ori- genes certe apud Eusebium l. VI. H. E. c. 34. tradit, historiam ad se pervenisse, quod quidam à Clemente Romano Episcopo, quidam vero à Luca eam scri- ptam dixerint. De Barnaba vero nec Origenes nec alius quisquam meminit. Taceo, quod Cor- nelius à Lapide, nescio quo autore, dicat Epi- stolam hanc à Paulo traditam Barnabæ, ut eandem quasi suo nomine vulgaret.

Porro quod ad Clementem Romanum non tan- tum Origenes, sed etiam Eusebius eidem Episto- lam hanc à quibusdam tribui observavit, sed ra- tione translationis ex Ebræo in Græcum, quod et- iam veritati magis consonum censet, quam à Luca factam esse versionem l. VI. H. E. c. 13. secus tamen videtur Grotio; Nimirum Clementem Romanum ut vocatum è gentibus censet, multo minus in lite- ris Ebræorum versatum fuisse, quam hunc scripto- rem & verborum nonnullorum convenientiam in hac & Clementis ad Corinthios Epistola sufficere negat, ad probationem, quod hæc Epistola à Cle- mente profecta sit. Nos vero Epistolam illam Cle- mentis ad Corinthios spuriam esse in præfat. ad Epist. Pauli ad Corinthios satis evicimus. Addunt alii, Clementem Romanum tantæ non fuisse autori- tatis apud Ebræos, ceu hominem gentilem, (quod mirum de Pontifice Romano pronunciasse Estium) & stylum hujus Epistolæ hominis esse non Romani, sed Ebræi, Græce periti, imo dum Clemens Romanus in sua Epistola, quam illi admittunt, sententias quas- dam ex hac nostra recitat, eundem testari hanc Epi- stolam nostram alterius autoris esse, non suam.

Lucæ ergo eam se libenter tribuere velle fate- tur Grotius. Sed quæ profert documenta? Pri- mum ad veteres provocat. At non nominavit qui- nam è veteribus, nedum è vetustissimis Lucæ eam tribuerint, ceu Autori. Affine quid de Clemente Alexandr. & Eusebio observavimus, sed illi so- lum translationem ibidem respiciunt: Et Euse- bius comparate tantum loquitur potius à Luca, quam Clemente Romano translatam: imo Euse- bius l. III. c. 34. judicavit non immerito eam reli- quis Apostoli scriptis accenseri: Et Clementem Alexandrinum laudat l. VI. c. 11. qui MANIFE- STE Pauli hanc esse Epistolam pronunciavit.

Secundo stylum allegat Grotius: quod hæc Epi- stola bene Græca & florida sit, uti & sermo Lucæ. Illa vero styli convenientia movit saltim veteres, ut translationem Lucæ tribuerint, non vero ideo abjudicasse hanc Epistolam Paulo constat. Cæte- rum argumentum illud de stylo non satis firmum est. Origenes certe styli observator accuratus non potuit inde dijudicare, quod Lucæ ea esset trans- latio, sed rem in medio reliquit: Eusebio vero è stylo magis consentaneum visum Clementem Ro- manum, quàm Lucam hanc interpretatum esse E- pistolam, non abnuente Theodoreto, Oecumenio, Nicephoro l. IV. H. E. c. 33. Nec minus eloquens fuit Paulus in Græca Lingua, quam Lucas, ut stylo florido uti potuerit, utpote ἀπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε φερόμενος; de cujus eloquentia egimus in oratio- ne auspicali Vestibulo præmissa, & invertit argumen- tum Flacius in discernenda literatura sacra præ ali- is peritus, non modo ex grandi eloquentia hujus Epistolæ nonnisi Paulum autorem esse conclu- dens, sed contendens etiam hanc Epistolam cum Paulinis ad Corinthios exaratis, causamque reddens cur clariori ab splendididore quasi sermone hic usus Apostolus sit, quod scil. non scripserit ad unicam aliquam Ecclesiam, aut personam, ut in cæteris Epistolis, sed ad totam gentem Ebræorum, tunc per orbem terrarum dispersam, ut quo tam varios au- ditores doceret & moneret clariori & illustriori sermone eum uti potuerit, uti solent scriptores ea luculenter componere, quæ frequentiori audito- rio proponuntur, quod etiam Rhetores præcipiunt.

Quod autem tertio de loco adfert Grotius. Esto, scriptam esse hanc Epistolam ex Italia: Esto, libe- ratum fuisse eo tempore Paulum, quod habuerit comitem & Lucam & Timotheum, unde vero pro- batur, Paulum tum non fuisse in Italia? Unde con- stat, Lucam Romæ vinctum fuisse? Precario ac gratis hæc sumit Grotius: Cætera vero omnia rectius Paulo, quam Lucæ conveniunt.

Quod quarto è vocabulis quibusúam & loquendi generibus desumitur, nimis profecto infirmum est argumentum: nimirum ex quatuor vel quinque vo- cabulis colligere proprium loquendi genus, & au- torem germanum: & quam facile possent plures notari voces Paulinæ in hac Epistola, imo & axio- mata Paulo propria? Neque illæ voculæ Lucæ sunt adeo propriæ, ut ab aliis ex adhibitæ non fuerint, aut adhiberi non potuerint. Vox μαρτυρόμενος Paulo familiaris Rom. III. 21. Col. II. 21. 1. Thessal. II. 12. 1. Tim. V. 10. χρηματίζεσθαι occurrit Matth. II. 12. 22. Rom. XI. 4. ἡγύμενος Matth. II. 6. Vox ἀρχηγὸς Petrina est Actor. III. 15. c. V. 31. & apud LXX. Interpp. occurrit Jud. V. 15. Neh. II: vers. 9. Esa. XXX. vers. 4.

Quinto quod Epistolam hanc versionem LXX. Interpretum plerumque addicte sequi, ait Grotius, quod & à Luca fiat, Resp. non solus Lucas amat sequi versionem LXX. Commune id plerisque est scriptoribus N. T. etiam Paulo Apostolo. Conf. quæ de his diximus Critico S. p. 720. seq. primæ edit.

Lucæ autem, quo minus is credendus sit autor hujus Epistolæ, obstare notat Estius, quod tantæ non fuerit autoritatis apud Ebræos, ut de profundis Christianæ fidei mysteriis ad eos instruendos literas daret. Compositionis autem ratione eundem auto- rem non esse tum stylus innuit, qui hic grandior quam in Evangelio, & Actis Lucæ, quod itidem agnoscit Estius: tum ratio hæc penitus persuadet, quod nullatenus verisimile sit duos viros θεοπνεύ- στος ita in una eademq; Epistola laborasse, Paulum scil. & Lucam, ut ille quidem manum subministra- rit, hic autem eandem elaborarir, ille ordinem præscripserit, hic autem Epistolam juxta illum or- dinem conscripserit, idque immediato afflatu Spi- ritus S. quo uterque in hoc opere actus fuit, cujus certe gratia nescit tarda molimina. Si Paulus vo- luit & debuit hæc præscripta ad Ebræos instinctu Spiritus S. consignare, quid obsecro causæ fuerit, cur ipse non integram Epistolam exararit, sed tan- tum materiam dictarit & ordinem præscripserit? Si autem Lucas agitatus fuit à Spiritu S. ut scriberet ad Ebræos, quid habuit opus, ut ipsi alius quidam Apostolus suggereret materiam vel ordinem præ- scriberet. Num hæc à Spiritu S. intus suggerente & dictitante Lucæ proficisci non poterat? Nihil certè vel in speciem tantum vero affine hìc in me- dium afferri poterit, quod causæ loco esse queat.

Videmus autem tandem, καθ' ὕστερον πρότερον, quid causæ habeat Grotius, cur Paulo hanc Epi- stolam deneget? Prima hæc est, quod Epistolæ Pau- linæ inter se germanæ sint, pari charactere & dicen- di modo: hæc vero manifeste ab iis discrepet. Qua- rum vero neutrum conceditur. Nam si Corinthia- cas Epistolas quis contendat cum aliis, non per omnia parem characterem, & dicendi modum de- prehendet: nec manifesta adeò ab illis in hac no- stra discrepantia apparebit. Salebrosas autem bre- vibusque incisis fractas esse alias Epistolas, nec adeo luculenter fluere nondum demonstravit Grotius, neque adduxit illas selectiores voces Græcas, Lucæ potius quam Paulo convenientes. Porro quidni po- tuisset sese Paulus attemperare dictione floridiori studiis, & genio Ebræorum, qui delectabantur elegantiori Græcismo in ista διασπορᾷ aut mate- riæ etiam tam præclaræ, quæ majorem dictionis apparatum requirere videbatur? Denique annon Sp. S. dicendi optimus Magister, qui per Paulum locutus est, ea ita per Apostolum proferre potuit, uti per Lucam ea proferri potuisse, credit Gro- tius? Non sane adstrictus est ad organa, quibus utitur, sed iis dat pro re nata cloqui, prout vult, Act. II, 4. dat ςόμα καὶ σοφίαν Lucæ XXI, 15.

Deinde ait locutiones quasdam Paulo familia- res nusquam apparere. Sed futile hoc argumen- tum est, qualia solent esse à testimonio negativo. Et quænam illæ voces sunt, quæ comparere debue- rint, si Paulinus sit sermo? Contra, ait, apparere alias non Paulinas, ut παραῤῥυῆναι, & αἰῶνες pro mundo. Sed illa nec Lucæ est alicubi: hæc vero quidni tam apud Paulum occurrat eodem sensu 1. Cor. I. 20. II. 6. 7. 2. Tim. IV. 10. Tit. II. 10. quam apud Lucam c. XVI. 8. XX. 34. Tertio ait, id abjudicare Paulo hanc Episto- lam, quod hujus scriptor se eis annumeret, qui non à Christo, sed ab ejus discipulis notitiam Evan- gelii accepêre c. II. 3. cum contra Paulus autorita- tem sibi addat inde, quod hanc notitiam à Chri- sto ipso acceperit. Hoc argumentum, haud diffi- teor, nonnullis causa fuit, cur abjudicarent Epi- stolam hanc Paulo, etiam B. Luthero nostro, sed ea minus firma est, nedum aliis, quæ Paulum au- thorem ejus faciunt, præjudicare sufficiens. An- non enim per figuram communicationis se Autor aliis annumerare potuit, quæ non infrequens, qui scil. à discipulis notitiam Evangelii accepêre? Et pertinere κοινωνίαν non ad personam Pauli, sed ad Ecclesiam quid prohibet dicere? Annon etiam contrà novissimis diebus ad se locutum esse Deum in Filio affirmat c. I. 2. Et annon S. Lucas æque fuit θεόπνευστος ut Paulus, aut quomodo pugnat cum θεοπνευσίᾳ id, quod sermo Evangelii etiam per discipulos ad Autorem Epistolæ pervenerit? Paulus certe non adfuit Christo, cùm sermo ille cœpit ab ipso proferri & annunciari, & ἐβεβαιώθη, sine dubio etiam, per communicationem cum A- postolis, qui Christum in diebus carnis audierant docentem, in Apostolum sermo Evangelii, etsi immediate Evangelium à Christo acceperit Pau- lus; non enim hæc sunt opposita. Nec absurdum, si Apostolus dicatur aliquando alium audivisse Apostolum, aut etiam Barnabam socium concio- nantem, aut miracula etiam eorum spectasse: aut inconveniens si dicatur Paulus non quidem βε- βαιώσεως certitudinis divinæ, de qua Gal. I. 1. & II. 6. sed experimentalis notitiæ ab aliis, qui αὐτόπται fuê- re, habuisse: qualis Historica βεβαίωσις ei contigit ab Anania Act. IX. 17. XXII. 12. 13. Sed hoc argu- mentum, quod operosius ursit Schlichtingius cum aliis pluribus Paulo autori oppositis ex professo jam profligavimus laudato Vestibulo, Titulo II. Nolumus actum agere. Ex adverso autem produ- ximus illic argumenta numero plurima, pondere gravissima pro hoc Autore, Paulo nempe Apostolo, I. A zeli Apostolici fervore. II. Ab orationis qua- litate. III. A Timothei discipuli designatione. IV. A vinculorum commemoratione. V. A vitæ Pauli collatione. VI. A Methodi observatione. VII. A phrasium & axiomatum nonnullorum in- ductione. IIX. Ab Epistolæ obsignatione. IX. Ab inscriptione. X. A Petri approbatione. XI. A Pa- trum veterum testificatione. XII. A Conciliorum definitione. XIII. A doctorum recentiorum assen- sione. Quæ adhuc prostant immota. Et tantum in præsenti de primo τῶν προλεγομένων capite.

Cut vero, quia admixtum est tribus verbis quid de autoritate Canonica, sero nempe hanc Epistolam à Romanis in Canonem receptam esse, id tacito pla- ne pede prætereundum non videtur. Nam præter- quam quod id Papismum resipit, potestatem habe- re Ecclesiam, & quidem Romanam, librum aliquem, qui extra Canonem aliquot ab ætate Apostolica seculis fuerit, in Canonem recipere, quam hypo- thesin alias profligavimus, à vero alienum est, quod sero à Romanis agnita fuerit hujus Epistolæ autoritas Canonica. Qui eam enim agnovêre Pau- linam, quales multi jam notati, de Canonica ejus autoritate minime dubitarunt. Quod imprimis de Clemente Romano ex Eusebio constat. Quan- quam v. sua ætate Hieronymus in c. IIX. Es. inter Scripturas Canonicas nonnullos eandem haud habuisse, autor sit; non tamen veterum ea mens fuit: quemadmodum addidit ibi Hieronymus: Nos autem suscipimus eandem, nequaquam hujus temporis consuetudinem, sed VETERUM autorita- tem sequentes, qui plerumque ejus utuntur testimo- niis, non ut interdum de Apocryphis facere solent, sed quasi Canonicis, & Ecclesiasticis. Et paucissi- mos fuisse, qui epistolæ huic contradixerint, ex Eusebio colligimus, cum Hieronymo collato: nam is annumerat eandem non τοῖς ἀντιλεγομένοις ὑπὸ τινῶν, sine dubio quod tam pauci & obscuri fuerint illi, quos notavit Hieronymus, sed potius τοῖς ἀναμ- φιλέκτοις ἐνδιαθήκοις, κὴ γνησίοις l. III. Hist. Eccl. c. 22. Conf. l. III. c.3. Argumenta autem divinæ auto- ritatis non minus illustria in hac Epistola compa- rent, quam in aliis scriptis indubitato ἐνδιαθήκοις, partim ab internis partim ab externis κριτηρίοις; in- terna sunt 1. veritas 2. sublimitas in divinis myste- riis eorumque probatione 3. sanctitas in monitis & exemplis suavissimis 4. styli singularitas 5. effica- citas in informatione &c. Externa sunt tum docu- menta nonnulla, tum testimonia. Illa 1. Quod Apo- stolorum tempore conscripta sit. 2. Quod ab Apo- stolo quopiam. 3. Quod à Petro Ecclesiæ commen- data sit 2. Ep. III. 15. 4. Quod conservata sit cum Canonicis singulari divina providentia. Hæc vero sunt tum Doctorum particularium, qui per omnia se- cula de divina ejus autoritate testati sunt; tum Con- ciliorum, non tantum provincialium, sed etiam gene- ralium, vel Oecumenicorum, è quibus observare licet 1. per totum orbem celebratam esse Canoni- cam hanc Epistolam 2. ab omnibus Græcis & La- tinis Doctoribus 3. à Synodis particularibus & Oecumenicis, Ecclesiam repræsentantibus 4. eam- que traditionem continua successione propaga- tam fuisse. Quæ omnia una cum διαλύσει objectio- num contrariarum exequuti sumus l. c. Prolixe et- iam de auctoritate, & autore Epistolæ ad Ebræos egit peculiari tractatu Fried. Spanhemius, qui hoc anno Londini Ludovici Tenà commentationibus in eandem annexus prodiit. Quam tenuiter vero de autoritate hujus Epistolæ senserit Grotius, vel ex eo liquet, quod de Luca ait: Fieri posse, ut mysterio- rum explicationem ex ore partim Pauli, partim Barnabæ hauserit, ita ut ex istis pars aliqua Episto- læ hujus jure adscribi possit. Hæc enim cum θεο- πνευσίᾳ hujus Epistolæ consistere non possunt: Qui namque credenda per Spiritum S. inspirata, quæ forte ab aliquo ex iis, quæ à diversis aliquan- do accepit, consarcinata, non vero quæ sententias & verba divinitus scriptori suggesta, nec ab im- mediato DEI impulsu, vel Spiritus Sancti φορᾷ per omnia profecta est?

Inscriptionem quod attinet, quæ est ad Ebræos, quæ alterum caput est τῶν προλεγομένων, deno- minationem illam à Tertulliano de pudicitia, & Clemente Strom. VI. repetit Grotius, sed al- tius omnino repetenda. Nam ut eos attingam saltim leviter, quibus non temere forsan se oppo- suisset Papistarum hyperaspistes Grotius, Bel- larminus l. 1. de verbo DEI, c. 17. Dionysium Areo- pagitam laudavit Epistolam ad Ebræos producen- tem, Sixtus Senensis l. VII. Bibl. S. hær. IIX. allega- vit ex Epistolis decretalibus, quæ apud non paucos in Papatu in pretio sunt, Clementem Romanum, Evaristum Papam, & Hyginum I. Alphonsus Salme- ron Tom. 15. Comment. in N. T. in Epistolam ad Ebræos disp. I. sequentes producit Romanos Pon- tifices, Apostolorum ætati vicinos, Clementem in epist. ad Jacobum, Anacletum epist. 2. Evaristum in Epist. ad Aphricanum, Soterem, Cornelium Mar- cum, Julium, Liberium, Felicem. Irenæus proximo ab Apostoli seculo Epistolam ad Ebræos adduxit, teste Eusebio l. V. c. 24. ut & Clemens Alexandrinus testa eodem l. VI. c. 17. nec non Heraclius, qui teste Sixto Senensi in eandem commentatus est. Penes Athanasium Dial. I. de Trin. hæc legimus: Ano- mæus quærit: Ubi scriptum est, Filium esse chara- Eterem hypostaseos? Orthodoxus respondet: apud Apostolum Paulum in Epistola ad Ebræos. Anomæus reponit: Non recipitur in Ecclesia; respondet Ortho- doxus, ἀφ' ὗ κατήγγελται τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον Χριστὲ Παύλῳ εἶναι πεπίςευται ἡ ἐπιϛολὴ. Ex quo annun- ciatum est Evangelium Christi, credita est hæc Epi- stola Pauli. Quod professus etiam est Origenes apud Eusebium l. VI. Eccl. c. 24. priscos nempe viros, (qui sua ætate seculo III. prisci jam habebantur) hanc ad Ebræos Epistolam Paulinam esse tradidisse. Quid, quod Beza observavit exemplaria Græca omnia præter unicum hanc inscriptionem habuis- se: Παύλꙋ τῦ Ἀποϛόλꙋ ἡ πρὸς Ἑβραίꙋς ἐπιϛολή. Quam inscriptionem Pauli esse, dubitandum non est. Quod vero in ipso corpore Epistolæ non inve- niatur, ut in reliquis Epistolis Paulinis Apostoli no- men præmissum, id suas, procul ambiguo, habuit causas, quales esse possunt nonnullorum judicio, quod Epistola non ad particularem Ecclesiam, vel singulares personas, sed ad Ebræos omnes per totum orbem dispersos, directa fuerit, & quod latere a- pud nonnullos, omissione nominis sui, voluerit, ne viso titu'o & nomine sibi inviso statim abjice- rent Epistolam. Vid. Hieron. præfat. in Ep. Pauli. Athanas. Dial. I. de Trinit. Theophyl. in Rom. I.

Per Ebræos Judæos inteligi, extra controver- siam est. Fuêre autem Judæi duplicis generis. Alii, quos Hellenistas dixêre, qui passim in Ægypto, Alia, Europa habitarunt, alii qui in Oriente, Baby- lonia, Persia, & ultra, qui Ebræo textui inhæsere. Ad illos potius quam ad hosce scripta Epistola, utpote propiores, & Paulo notiores, & in dia- σπορᾷ Ponti, Asiæ, Galatiæ, Bithyniæ, &c.

Tertium caput linguam concernit: Græce scti- ptam esse hanc Epistolam agnoscit Grotius, ob causam geminam: prior falsa est, quod nempe sermo is Lucæ familiarior sit: quia gratis sumit Lu- cam ejus autorem esse: posterior admittitur, quod Judæi plerique etiam Græce norint, nonnulli vero eo- rum tantum Græce Act. VI. 1. ad omnes enim per- tinebat, & ab omnibus legenda erat Epistola. In originali tamen Ebræaice non Græce hanc Epistolam scri- ptam Clemens Alexand. l. IV. observat; & in hypot. citante Eusebio l. VI. Hist. Eccl. c. 34. Origenes in Ps. I. Eusebius l. III. Hist. Eccl. c. 34. Hieron. in Catal. c. 5. Theodoretius & Oecume- nius in præfat. Nicephorus l. II. Hist. Eccl. c. 46. l. IV. c. 45. asserunt, iisque consentiunt non pauci e recentioribus, im- primis vero Pontificii, sed nec rationes proferunt Ebraicæ scriptionis, nisi lubricas, & levioris momenti, nempe quod Paulus non tam eloquens fuerit in Græca lingua, & quod ad Ebræos ea scripta fuerit: Nam quod ad primum, Paulum, eloquentem æque in Græca, ac Ebræa lingua fu- isse tum Epistolæ aliæ plurimæ testantur, tum patria, quia Tarsensis erat, & æque diu inter Græcos versatus, atque Ebræos, quæ responsio redditur à Schlichtingio; cæterum in ea non subsisten tum, respici enim imprimis debet autor Spiritus S. elo- quentiæ & linguarum omnium artifex. Quod ad alteram rationem Jacobi & Johannis I. & Petri na utraque exaratæ etiam ad Ebræos sunt, lingua ta- men Græca, non Ebræa: Latissime etiam Græcæ linguæ usum tum patuisse, adeoque inter Judæos vi- guisse agnoscit Grotius, cum omnes Græce, non omnes Ebraice noverint, ipsum Chaldaicum etiam idioma, quod tum in usu erat. Rationes ex ad- verso validæ prostant, quod Ebræâ lingua exarata non sit hæc Epistola, utpote à charactere dictio- nis, ab allegatis Veteris Testamenti, à Græcarum vocum emphasi, ab Ebraicarum vocum Græca interpretatione, nec non à quibusdam incommo- dis. Argumenta etiam gravissimi momenti in promptu sunt, quod scripta sit lingua Græca in originali: utpote à divina in Canonem N. T. desti- natione, à reliquarum Paulinarum inductione, à Petrina Epistolæ collatione, à Græcæ linguæ com- munitate, à Judæorum inter gentes dispersione, à Spiritus S. intentione, vel dedicatione, à similis ex- empli negatione, quod liber aliquis & in fontibus, & in translatione θεόπνευστος sit, à textus origi- nalis divina conservatione, à Græci textus autori- tate, denique ab aliorum autorum communi cal- culo & consensione, de quibus in Critico Sacro, Sy- stemate Theologico, & prædicto Vestibulo.

Quarto Scopum & occasionem Epistolæ quod attinet, Grotius tantum παραϕυαδικῶς id obser- vat, quod nempe non pauci è Judæis & Syris per- secutionum onere pressi se à partibus Christianis subduxerint, quos in viam revocare, alios vero ad- huc stantes fulcire scriptis voluerit: ideoque mul- tis ostendat, omnes Veteres historias, & dicta Pro- phetarum occulta quadam Dei dispensatione in Christo ejusque rebus figurandis occupari. Quan- quam vero non abnuamus, persecutiones, quas conversi ex Ebræis sustinuere, maxime à suæ gentis hominibus occasionem illis præbuisse, non tamen ab Ecclesia Christiana eosdem sese avertisse, con- stat, turbatos autem fuisse in fide Christiana, ab aliis tum Judæis, tum hæreticis, dubium haud vi- detur, illis etiam, permittentibus Romanis præ- sidibus (quod Constantinus Antiochenus in ope- ribus Chrysostomi, & Theophylactus observant) eos persequentibus ceu Apostatas, qui à lege Mo- sis defecerint, bonisque suis spoliantibus, qui- bus accedit ea occasio, quam Athanasius in sua Synopsi notavit, quod Judæi legi & umbris illius incumberent, etiam qui ad Christum conversi erant, & ut Anshelmus tradit, judicarint fidem so- lam sine admixtione ceremoniarum legalium ad sa- lutem non sufficere. Qui scrupulum etiam facile concipere poterant, aut conceperant de doctrina Evangelii, de persona & officio Christi, de passione & cruce ejus, qua offendebantur plurimi, de ju- stificatione per Christum, imprimis quia hærebat multis opinio, quod peccata victimis expiari ad- huc debeant, quodque Sacerdotium V. T. perpe- tuum futurum sit, ac Messias regnum administru- turus mundanum, & quod ex Pharisaismo & Pseudo-Apostolorum perversione quibusdam impressum fuerat, opera nostra causam salutis, & ad salutem neceffaria esse, ideoque sola fide in Christum hominem minime justificari: quæ è lectione & ἀναλύσει Epistolæ patent.

Illis ergo omnibus ut succurreret Apostolus, hanc Epistolam impulsu Spir. S. exaravit ad con- versos Ebræos, cujus Scopum didacticum facit A- thanasius in Synopsi, utpote ideo instructam de- clarationibus & probationibus de Christi ad- ventu, & de legis umbra, quod illa desierit. Cæ- terum quanquam præcipuum Epistolæ scopum didacticum esse agnoscamus, non tamen quæstio illa, anne Messias venerit, & an Jesus Nazarenus Messias sit? quæ potissimum per Evangelistas ceu primum Christianismi fundamentum stabilita est, proprie hic tractatur. Sed ut in aliis Epistolis, ita etiam in hac nostra id potissimum agitur, qualis esse debuerit Messias, & quis Christus sit tum per- sona, tum officii ratione, unde Scholiastes Græ- cus, Oecumenius, Primasius, & Sedulius scopum Pauli hunc assignant, quod Ebræos à Judaismo integre & perfecte ad Christianismum trahere voluerit: & Anshelmus observat: Paulum de emi- nentia Christi & inutilitate legis ad justificationem & salutem differere. Addi tamen potest huic sco- po didactico ceu primario secundarius paræneti- cus, nempe ob quem hæc Epist. c. XIII. 22. dici- tur λόγος τῆς παρακλήσεως, siquidem unicuique parti doctrinali subjungat, aut ex ea inferat Apo- stolus adhortationem è doctrina profluentem: quo nomine nonnulli scopum mixtum hujus Epi- stolæ faciunt: ita tamen ut πρώτως occupetur in doctrina de Christo, ejusque persona & officio, ma- xime Sacerdotali, cujus gratia comparationem cum Sacerdotibus & sacrificiis V. T. instituit; nec non de fide, qua justitiam obedientiæ, passionis & mortis ejus adprehendimus: eaque de causa meri- to Epistola ad Romanos & ad Galatas conferatur; interea præcipuum scopum innuere videtur Apo- stolus ipse cap. IIX. 1. Hæc est summa, de qua loqui- mur, quod Pontificem ejusmodi habemus.

Argumentum ergo ejus præcipuum est Sacer- dotium Christi, cujus gratia occupatur in descri- bendo Sacerdote novi fœderis, quod sit θεάνθρω- πος immediate à Deo missus ad peccata expianda, iram Dei placandam sacrificii corporis sui obla- tione, & ad orandum pro nobis, ut nos cum Deo reconciliemur, acquisitâ nobis justitiâ ac vita æ- terna, & fœdus gratiæ sanciatur, ad quod fide opus est in hunc Pontificem nostrum, ejusque sa- crificium unicum propitiatorium.

Schlichtingius primario hortari, ait, ad constan- tiam in religione Christiana, adeoque amoliri po- tissimum ea, quæ illam labefactare videbantur, E- bræosque ut legem Evangelio præferant, invitare: utpote tum legis & disciplinæ Mosaicæ præstantiam, tum afflictiones varias Christianæ professionis comi- tes: Cujus oikovoμíav tum qua rem ipsam, tum qua methodum discussimus in Vestibulo p. 79. seq.

Partes Epistolæ tres constitui possunt: Prima est de persona Christi, quæ duobus capitibus I. & II. absolvitur usque ad medium v. 9. insertâ adhor- tatione ad Christum suscipiendum. Altera de officio Christi Regali à c. II.9. usque ad X.19. interjecta ta- men digressione adhortatoria gemina, pro duplici tractatione: quarum prima generalis est ad finem usque cap. II. cui subjungitur adhortatio de susci- piendo Apostolo & Pontifice nostræ confessionis Re- gio: qui præfertur Mosi, quod domus Dei sit & Architectus, & herus, nosque ad æternam requiem perducat: cap. III. & IV. Altera specialius explicat Sacerdotium Christi, inserta tamen parænesi, c. V. extremo, & c. VI. ut ad perfectionem ferantur, non vero Christum agnitum abnegent. Tertia de fide salvifica in Christum c. X. & XI. subjuncta adhor- tatione non ad constantiam tantum & patientiam, sed ad alias etiam virtutes, quibus fides declaratur c. XII. & XIII. Prætermittit autem præsens Epi- stola perinde ut Johannis prior ἀνεπίγραφος τὰ τῆς ἐπισολῆς, quæ alias Apostoli præmittere con- sueverunt, ut puta non modo τὰ προσωτικὰ, seu personalia, mentionem Autoris à quo, & eorum ad quos perscripta, sed & τὰ πραγματικὰ seu rea- lia, sive votiva, sive gratulatoria, vel prout vul- go indigitantur ὑπογραφὴν, ἐπιγραφὴν & ἀσπα- σμὸν, subscriptionem, inscriptionem, & salutationem. Quum n. nominis ὑπογραφὴ consulto prætermit- tenda esset, inscriptionem quoque & salutationem, quam illi annectere consueverat Apostolus, præ- termisit. Sub finem autem Epistolæ non neglexit ea, quibus concludere solitus erat Epistolas suas, ut E- pistolam esse vel ex clausula constaret.

Plenius οἰκονομίαν totius Epistolæ ita exhibe- mus, quod nempe constet tum partibus princi pa- libus usque ad cap. ult. v. 21. tum secundariis, quæ veluti per προσθήκην adjiciuntur quatuor postre- mis commatibus. Principales vero partes sunt: Propositio & Tractatio. Si quis malit tres partes di- cere: Propositionem, tractationem, & conclusionem Epistolæ, non repugnamus. Propositio concernit tum personam, tum officium Christi: Persona Chri- sti constat naturâ divina & humana: Officium Christi, quo de hic agitur, est tum Doctorale, tum Sacerdotale. In προθέσει ergo Christum Doctorem & Sacerdotem nostrum Filium Dei sistit, in quo in novissimis diebus locutus est Ebræis Deus, cum homo factus est, qui expiationem peccatorum no- strorum per semetipsum fecit, & consedit ad dextram Dei. Quod itaque ad personam, eundem docet esse Filium Dei, per quem secula condidit, effulgescen- tiam gloriæ, & characterem hypostaseos ejus, quæ ad describendam divinam naturam pertinent: hæredem omnium, qui consedit ad dextram Maje- statis Dei in excelsis, sublimior factus Angelis, re- spectu humanæ naturæ. Quod ad officium Docto- rale, quod in eodem DEUS novissime locutus sit populo Ebræo, postquam olim multivariam, & multis modis locutus est Patribus in Prophetis: Quoad Sacerdotale vero officium, quod Filius Dei purificationem peccatorum nostrorum fecerit per semetipsum, & ad dextram DEI sedeat. c. I. v. 1. 2. 3. 4.

Ἔκθεσις sive tractatio bipartita est. Primo di- dactica, denominatione à potiori petita, usque ad c. X. 18. Deinde pænetica ad c. XIII. 12. illic pri- mum de persona Christi agitur ἀποδεικτικῶς c. I. & II. ut demonstretur Doctoris, & Sacerdotis nostri summa eminentia, & sublimitas: Deinde de offi- cio tum Doctorali cap. III. & IV. tum Sacerdotali c. V. VI. VII. VIII. IX. X. ἐξηγητικῶς tractatur, ut explicetur uberior muneris gloria & veritas. U- niversa autem illa tractatio συγκριτικῶς instituta est; comparatione, quantum ad sublimitatem per- sonæ, factâ cum Angelis, quantum ad dignitatem & rationem muneris, cum Mose, quoad Doctorale, cum Sacerdotibus Vet. Test. quoad Sacerdotale offi- cium: Quemadmodum in parænesi Apostolus exempla itidem sistit Vet. Test. quæ Christianis imitanda sint, ratione fidei, constantiæ, & sancti- moniæ in N. T. ut Ebræis Harmoniam utriusque exhibeat, eosque exemplo Majorum ad parilem fidem excitet, quia Jesus, heri idem & in secula. Apodixis de persona Christi, quod ad divinam ejus naturam instituitur c. I. usque ad v. 12. quoad hu- manæ naturæ eminentiam v. 13. & 14. & seq. capite ad v. 9. Natura divina Christi demonstratur pri- mo à Filii Dei generatione, nulli Angelorum con- venienti v. 5. gemino V. T. testimonio: alterum concernit τὴν θεολογίαν, quam veteres vocant, è Ps. II. 7. alterum pertinet simul ad τὴν ὀικονομίαν è 2. Sam. VII. 14. Ibi enim spectatur Filius DEI in- tra simplicissimum complexum Deitatis; hîc Da- vidis Filium Messiam ipsummet naturalem DEI Filium esse docetur. Secundo ab adorationis axio- mate v. 6. quia primogenitus ille ab omnibus An- gelis adorandus est, vi Ps. XCVII. 4. tertiò à no- mine, throno, & sceptro divino, quibus iterum eminentissima ratione omnem Angelicam di- gnitatem excedit v. 7. 8. 9. collatione facta Ps. CIV. v. 4. cum Ps. XLV. 7. Quarto à divino creationis & consummationis mundi opere, Filiique DEI di- vina immutabilitate v. 10. 11. 12. Quæ è Ps. CII. 26. confirmantur.

Quod attinet humanæ naturæ Christi sublimi- tatem, secundum quam ad dexteram Dei evectus eminentius nomen præ Angelis acceperit, ea pro- batur gemino testimonio: instituta iterum com- paratione cum Angelis: Alterum c. I. 13. & 14. adducitur è Ps. CX. 1. quod nulli Angelorum di- ctum sit sede ad dextram meam, utpote qui admi- nistratorii tantum Spiritus sint, emissi ob salutem nostram: cujus occasione subjungitur παραθετικῶς quasi sub initium cap. II. 1. 2. 3. adhortatio ad verbum à tanto Doctore annunciatum suscipi- endum, si effugere velimus poenam divinam; ut- pote non per Angelos, sed immediate per Domi- num ipsum (ἐνσαρκωθέντα) prædicatum. Alterum dictum ad demonstrandam rerum omnium in mundo futuro subjectionem non Angelis, sed fi- lio hominis Christo Jesu factam, v. 5. seq. petitum est è Ps. IIX. 5. seq. quod à complemento illustrat, coronato nempe Jesu, per passionem mortis, glo- ria & honore, qui infra Angelos minoratus ad breve tempus fuerat, v. 9. Atque hactenus de per- sona Christi. De officio Christi primum in genere agitur, quoad congruentiam divinæ Oeconomiæ, citra autorem Salutis nostræ: quod nempe decuerit, ut ille, qui multos filios ad gloriam adducit, ipse DEUS, propter quem omnia, & per quem omnia (hoc enim de Christo jam demonstrarat Aposto- lus) per passiones consummaretur; Quo faciunt (1) Originis ταυτότης & συναδελφία, quod conve- niat, ut is qui sanctificat, & illi qui sanctificantur, ex eodem omnes sint, unde etiam nos fratres suos vocat v. 11. 12. secundum Psalmum XXII. 23. 26. (2) Communis erga Deum παρρησία & fiducia v. 13. 14. è Ps. XIIX. 3. Es. IIX. 17. 18. (3) Christi cum liberis sibi à DEO datis ὁμοιοσία, ejusdemque causa, ut nempe per mortem destrueret vim mortis haben- tem, & mancipia ejus liberaret v. 14. 15. (4) Seminis Abrahæ ἐπίληψις: Siquidem nuspiam in Scripturis dicatur Angelos assumere, sed semen Abrahæ (Gen. XII. 3. &c.) (5) Christi cum fratribus ὁμοιοπάθεια: Quâ ad Sacerdotii executio- nem opus fuisse docetur, v. 17. 18. Hæc de persona Doctoris & Pontificis nostri.

Post illa de officio ejus specialius tractat Apo- stolus: & primum quidem de Doctorali, quod idem etiam Apostolus sit, qui Pontifex confessio- nis ipsorum, quem Ebræi confitebantur c. III. 1. Cujus proinde Apostoli, tum fidelitatem, tum dignitatem comparatione cum Mose Doctore quondam populi Ebræorum facta sistit: illam quod similis Mosi fideli in tota domo Domini sit v. 5. hanc tum quod majoris honoris sit, quippe qui domum Domini præparavit vers. 2. 4. tum quod Moses tantum minister fuerit, Christus vero Filius super domum Domini, v. 5. 6. tum quod domus ejus sint omnes fideles v. 6. unde exhortatio deducitur de hoc Doctore observando, petita partim à mandato Spiritus S. v. 6. 7. seq. ad finem usque capitis tertii, videlicet è Psal. XCV. 7. quod cap. IV. v. 1. seq. illustratur è requie nobis adhuc reliqua, non nisi per fidem consequenda, collatione requiei, & Sabbati creationis v. 3. Gen. II. 2. XXII. 11. requiei, in quam Ebræi per Josuam introducti sunt possessionis terræ Canaan v. 5. 6. & requiei, in quam per Jesum introducendi sint, secundum Davidis prædictionem vers. 7. seq. instituta: ut studeant in eandem ingredi, nec excludantur ab eadem per incredulitatem v. 11. partim à verbi DEI vi, & efficacia vers. 12. partim à CHRISTI omniscentia, v. 13. ad cujus, ceu Magni Pontificis, qui cœlos penetravit, ut pro nobis illic intercedat, atque ipse Dei Filius est, tentatus per omnia, ut nostris infirmitatibus compati possit, constantem confessionem, & ad fiducialem throni gratiæ accessionem hortatur Apostolus vers. 14. 15. & 16. eo ipso aditum sibi- parans ad pleniorem de officio Christi Sacerdotali διήγησιν, seqq. capp. instituendam.

Quapropter de officio Sacerdotali hæc execu- tus est : Primo in genere Sacerdotis tum defini- tionem tradit cap. V. vers. 1. 2. 3. tum vocationem ejusque necessitatem exemplo Aaronis, quia com- paratio cum Sacerdotio Levitico instituenda erat, confirmatam v. 4. quod nempe vocatus sit à Deo Patre: utpote à quo (1) ab æterno genitus Messias, vel unctus ille Domini vers. 5. secundum Ps. II. 7. (2) à quo Sacerdos constitutus v. 6. se- cundum Ps. CX. 4. (3) ad quem oravit in diebus carnis. (4) cui obediens factus est, Filius ejus, siquidem in passione didicit obedientiam v. 7. 8. (5) à quo consummatus factus est obedientibus causa salutis v. 9. adeoque merito vocatus est Sa- cerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech v. 10. Deinde in specie expedivit Sacerdotii istius (se- cundum ordinem Melchisedeci) explicationem. Antequam autem illam aggreditur, præoccupat multa de illo dicenda esse, sed infirmos adhuc esse E- bræos, comiter notans eorum in rebus fidei infan- tiam c. V. 11. 12. 13. 14. & designatis iis, quæ ad fun- damentum pertinent c. VI. 1. 2. 3. tacite dehorta- tur ab apostasia, proposito periculo peccati in Spi- ritum S. testatus meliorem de ipsis fiduciam v. 9. 10. & adhortatur ad constantiam v. 11. sistens illis & exemplum prædecessorum fidelium v. 12. & pro- missum Abrahamo factum jurejurando divino confirmatum v. 13. seq. Explicat autem Sacerdo- tium Christi primum è typo Melchisedeci cap. VII. idque tum tacite, quoad officium, benedictio- nem Abrahami, à quo & decimas accepit, Regis- que & sedis ipsius nomen, ejus item originem, & terminum, c. VII. 1. 2. 3. tum expresse, quoad di- gnitatem Melchisedeci præ Levitis, qui decimati ab ipso sunt v. 4. seq. ac diversitatem Sacerdotii, v. 11. 13. quæ in Christo luculenta est è diversitate tribus v. 13. 14. & adhuc luculentior, quod non se- cundum legem Sacerdotii Levitici, sed secundum promissionem virtutis constitutus est Pontifex v. 15. 16. ad ostendendam legis infirmitatem & inutili- tatem in causa salutis v. 18. 19. quodque non sine juramento (ut illi Levitici Sacerdotes) sed inter- veniente juramento divino factus est Sacerdos v. 20. 21. secundum Psal. CX. 4. unde concluditur, melioris testamenti sponsorem esse v. 22. adhæc quod unicus & æternus sit Sacerdos v. 23. 24. 25. denique quod sanctus & peccati expers sit, adeoque non pro se, sed tantum pro nobis sese semel obtulerit, ut- pote Filius DEI & perfectus v. 26. 27. 28.

Secundo explicatur Sacerdotium Christi ejus- que eminentia & prærogativa, è confessu Sacerdo- tis ad dextram Dei. Quæ ad alterum munus Sacer- dotii Christi facit, intercessionem nempe pro no- bis ad dextram Majestatis in excelsis, propter ex- piationem per mortem factam; ad quam perti- nent duo, de quorum veritate agit c. IIX. de qua- litate vero atque indole c. IX. utpote tum λειτουργία in cælis, quod scil. administrator sit sanctorum, & tabernaculi veri, siquidem non tantum obtu- lerit sese (in morte: Conf. c. VII. 26.) quum Sa- cerdotis sit offerre hostiam, sed etiam in cælis λει- τουργὸς sit, non amplius in terra Sacerdotio fun- gens, ut Aaronici Sacerdotes, qui tantum umbræ inservierunt, teste Mose (Exod. XXV. 40.) tum Testamenti melioris mediatio v. 6. seq. quia Me- diator est Testamenti gratiæ, & Novi, quod pro- missum à S. S. (Jer. XXXI. 24.) & vetustatem atque ἀφανισμὸν veteris inducit, v. 6. ad finem capitis.

Ad naturam autem atque indolem & λειτουργίας Christi, & μεσιτείας Novi Test. explicandam fa- ciunt, quoad illam quidem, collatio veteris Testa- menti, cujus jura, & cultus cum tabernarum ap- paratu designantur, imprimis quoad annuum in- gressum in sanctum sanctorum, quæ typica fuisse docentur cap. IX. 1. seq. Christi Pontificis futuro- rum bonorum, qui per tabernaculum verum in- gressus sanguine proprio in sanctum (sanctorum) cum sacrificio suo conscientias nostras purifica- vit v. 11. seq.

Quoad hanc vero, quod Mediator N. T. factus sit, causa hæc redditur, ut nempe per mortem ejus liberati à peccatis, quæ sub V. T. nos premebant, hæreditatem promissam consequeremur v. 15. unde etiam morte testatoris confirmandum fuit Testa- mentum novum, quemadmodum sanguine pe- cudum Vetus sancitum fuit v. 16. seq. (Ex. XXIV. vers. 8.) addito etiam fine ingressus Christi in san- ctum sanctorum, cœlum ipsum, nempe interpel- latione pro nobis v. 24. ubi notatur simul diversi- tas ingressus Levitici Pontificis, quod iterandus quotannis fuerit, uti & iteranda sacrificia, cum quorum sanguine ingrediebatur: quum Christus semel tantum ad tollenda peccata se obtulerit, & semel ingressus sit v. 25. seq. ut & fructus sacrificii, sublatio peccatorum, ac mediationis Testamenti gratiæ, apparitio novissima ad salutem fidelium.

Tertio explicatur Christi Sacerdotium, ejus- que prærogativa è sacrificii Christi comparatione cum sacrificiis V. T. quod illic tantum typus fuerit & umbra c. X. quod deducitur (1) è Sacrificio- rum Leviticorum repetitione, quæ argumentum est, quod sacrificia illa per se, non perfecerint eos, qui offerebant v. 2. nec peccata sustulerint v. 4. (2) è Christi testificatione v. 5. seq. è Ps. XL. 7. seq. qui explicatur de sacrificio corporis Christi v. 10. (3) ex æterno sacrificii Christi valore v. 11. 12. 13. 14. (4) è Testamenti Novi ratione, sita in eo, quod peccatorum amplius nolit meminisse v. 15. 16. 17. è Jer. XXXI. 33. unde opus non est repeti- tione sacrificii pro peccatis v. 18. Atque huc us- que expedita est pars didactica Epistolæ.

Pars altera Parænetica v. 19. c. X. incipit, & è priori πορισματικῶς infertur, è παῤῥησίᾳ ingres- sus in cœlum: quæ confirmatur tum è modo, & merito ingressus, quod in sanguine Christi fiat v. 19. quod per velamen, h. e. corpus Christi nobis aperta sit v. 20. tum è medio ex parte nostri, quod est πληροφορία τῆς πίςεως v. 21. & ex parte DEI, quod est Baptismus v. 22. Ideoque Ebræi ad con- stantiam excitantur Gonfessionis Christi, quæ à fidelitate Dei vocantis stabilitur v. 23. ut & ad mu- tuam exhortationem ad charitatem & bona opera v. 24. ac ne deserant Ecclesiam v. 25. Adduntur autem causæ perseverantiæ in fide Christi salvifica, & non desertionis Ecclesiæ, tum à propinquitate diei extremi v. 25. tum à voluntarie peccantium extremo periculo v. 26. 27. quod confirmatur com- paratione pœnæ prævaricationis in legem Mo- saicam, & conculcationis Filii Dei v. 28. 29. & comminatione vindictæ divinæ v. 30. 31. è Deut. XXX. 11. 35. 36. tum à præteritorum temporum cer- tamine v. 32. 33. 34. tum à gratiosa retributione, & promissionis consecutione v. 35. 36. stabilita Habacuci testimonio de justo fide victuro v 37. seq.

His argumentis porro cap. XI. exempla V. T. subjunguntur, ut confirmentur Ebræi in fide in Christum, ac promissio de vita per fidem conse- quenda corroboretur: quibus præmissa est fidei definitio v. 1. 2. ejusque ab articulo creationis illu- stratio v. 3. sistit autem Apostolus ipsis exemplum fidei Abelis hostiam offerentis vers. 4. Enochi, qui per fidem Deo placuit, ut mortem non vide- rit, v. 5. 6. Noachi, qui hæres justitiæ, quæ est per fidem, factus est v. 7. Abrahami, qui fide Deo vo- canti obedivit, fide in terram promissionis hospes fuit expectans cœlestem civitatem cum Isaaco, & Jacobo vers. 9. 10. Saræ, quæ fide promissionem complexa est: & cum dictis Patriarchis, etsi non- dum reipsa impetrato Messia promisso, patriam cœlestem expectarit vers. 11. seq. oblationis item Isaaci per fidem ab Abrahamo tentatæ, quem in figuram resurrectionis Christi vivum recepit, v. 17. 18. 19. ac porro benedictionis Isaaci vers. 20. & Jacobi v. 21. Præcepti Josephi de translatione os- sium suorum in terram promissam per fidem fa- ctæ v. 22. occultationis Mosis à Parentibus, quæ itidem per fidem facta v. 23. fidei Mosis in electio- ne opprobrii Christi præ thesauris Ægypti v. 24. seq. in relictione Ægypti v. 27. in celebratione Paschatos v. 28. in transitu per mare rubrum v. 29. fidei Josuæ in dejectione murorum Jericho v. 30. fidei Rachab in susceptione exploratorum v. 31. fidei denique aliorum justorum, quorum vel no- mina tantum adfert, Gideonis, Baraci, Samsonis, Jephthæ, Davidis, Samuelis, vel officium, utpote Prophetarum, vel facta è fide profecta cum variis passionibus v. 32. 33. seq.

Huic primariæ exhortationi ad fidem in Mes- siam & perseverantiam exemplo Majorum sub- jungit Apostolus alias paræneses, tum ad patien- tiam, tum ad sanctimoniam & in genere cap. XII. & in specie cap. XIII. Illic in curriculo patientiæ exhibet solatium amoris divini erga eos, quos castigat è Prov. III. 11. 12. quod explicatur vers. 5. seq. & Castigationis fructum vers. 10. 11. adeoque hortatur, ut manus remissas confortent, & genua lassa erigant vers. 12. Hîc cum pacis studio sancti- moniam commendat, tum ne gratia Dei excida- mus vers. 15. per contentionem, scortationem, im- pietatem vers. 14. 15. 16. 17. siquidem accesserimus non ad montem Sinai, in quo terror & tremor, v. 18. 19. 20. 21. Sed Sion, & communionem Eccle- siæ militantis & triumphantis, ad Deum ipsum & Mediatorem Novi Test. Jesum, ejusque sangui- nem, non vindictam, sed gratiam postulantem, v. 22. 23. 24. tum ne vocem Domini de cœlo lo- quentis contemnamus v. 25. 26. qui cœlum & ter- ram commovit Hag. II. 7. cujus gratia regnum immobile consequimur, ut Deo serviamus, qui- que immorigeris ignis consumens est v. 27. 28. 29. Deut. IV. 24.

Generalibus adhortationibus succenturiantur præcepta specialia de quibusdam virtutibus vitæ Christianæ cap. XIII. utpote primo quoad pro- ximum I. de Φιλαδελφίᾳ v. 1. amore erga fratres, II. Φιλοξενίᾳ, hospitalitate erga peregrinos v. 2. III. συμπαθείᾳ erga afflictos v. 3. IV. honore con- jugii & fide erga conjuges, v. 4. Deinde quoad nos ipsos, utpote tum ἀυταρκείᾳ, in conversatione, cum fiducia erga DEUM, v. 5. 6. è Job. I. 5. Psal. LVI. v. 12. tum imitatione præpositorum in Vet. Test. pie defunctorum, tum vitatione falsorum Do- ctorum, qui fugiendi, & imprimis illi, qui à Chri- sto Jesu, & fide in ipsum, ad ceremonias v. g. de cibis, abducere conabantur Ebræos, v. 8. 9. quia participare de vero altari non possunt, qui adhuc servire volunt tabernaculo (umbratili) postquam Christus extra portam passus est, ut sanctificaret sanguine suo populum, quemadmodum (in ty- po) sanguis pecorum in sanctum portabatur, quorum corpora extra castra comburebantur: tum constanti Christi professione, nec non exilii atque opprobrii tolerantia, quia civitatem ma- nentem hîc non habemus v. 13. 14. Tertio quoad DEUM, qui honorandus & sacrificiis spiritualibus laudum v. 15. & beneficentia vers. 16. nec non obedientia erga Ministros DEI: quibus subjungit preces pro se & sociis v. 18. 19. Quæ omnia finit voto, recapitulationem doctrinæ de Pastore animarum per sanguinem æterni Testamenti è mortuis educto, atque Domino constituto à Deo pacis, & adhortationem ad studium perfectionis in omni opere bono, & complacentiæ divinæ, continente, cum δοξολογίά v. 20. 21.

His Coronidis loco subjicitur admonitio, de suscipiendo verbo adhortationis v. 22. ut & notificatio de liberato Timotheo, & proposito Ebræos invisendi cum eodem v. 23. nec non commissio salutationis Doctorum, & aliorum sanctorum omnium, addita salutatione nomine fratrum ex Italia v. 24. ac finali comprecatione gratiæ v. 25.

PARS I. EPISTOLÆ ΔΟΓΜΑΤΙΚΉ́. DE PERSONA ET OFFICIO CHRISTI.

SECTIO I. DE CHRISTI PERSONA.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Having premised a comparison of the revelation through the Prophets to the Fathers, and the speaking done in these last days to the Hebrews, in which a proposition is artfully implicated: that the Doctor and Priest of the N. T., namely Christ, is the eternal Son of God, through whom He created the ages, and who has been made heir of all things according to his human nature; by reason of the former, he teaches that he is the same as the brightness of the glory of God, and the express image of his hypostasis, and that he upholds all things by the word of his power, but with respect to the latter, that after he had made purification of our sins, he sat down at the right hand of God: and thus, as to his person, Christ is true God, true man, but constituted over all, and exalted to the right hand of GOD, and having obtained a most eminent name: as to his office, he is the Doctor and propitiator of our sins. Then the Apostle undertakes the confirmation, both of the true Deity of Christ, that he is the Son eternally begotten by God (Ps. II. 7. 2. Sam. VII. 14.) and to be worshipped by the Angels (Ps. XCVII. 17.), who are created by God and are his ministers, whereas the Son is God, and his throne is eternal (Ps. XLV. 7.), and he himself is the Lord, who founded the earth and made the heavens, and while they shall perish, he remains always immutable (Ps. CII. 26. seq.), and also of his exalted humanity, according to which it was said to him, which was said to none of the Angels, sit at my right hand, whereas they are only ministering spirits.

There are two parts. I. The proposition to v. 4. II. The treatment concerning the person of Christ, according to his eternal and true Deity, and also according to his human nature exalted to the right hand of God to v. 14.

PART II. PROPOSITION.

V. 1. Πολυμερω̃ς) In the Glossary πολυμερω̃ς means in many ways, that is, at many times: in the time of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob: in the times of Moses, Joshua, the Judges: in the times of David, Solomon & the Prophets: and finally in the times of Daniel, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. Καὶ πολυτρόπως) By giving daily or nightly visions, or internal inspirations, or heard voices, sometimes through figures, sometimes openly. See what is said in Num. XII. 6. The Apostle's proposition is two-membered: I. Concerning the Teacher of the New Testament. II. Concerning the High Priest of the New Testament. I. The proposition concerning Christ the Teacher is presented by the Apostle, at the very threshold & beginning, by a comparison of the Old & New Testament, or rather of the time before CHRIST was exhibited, which was of promise, & from the advent of CHRIST, which is of completion & exhibition, πλήρωμα τῶν χρόνων, Galat. IV. verse 4. πλήρωμα τῶν καιρῶν, Ephes. I. verse 10. The sum of the exordium is: That same JESUS, who spoke to the ancestors of the Hebrews, or the Israelite people, in past ages, through the Prophets, who foretold the advent of the Messiah, and bore witness concerning the free remission of sins in his name according to the measure of divine revelation, which also consisted of diverse parts of heavenly doctrine, revealed one thing after another to some and others, and insinuated itself in various ways and forms: in recent, and those the final times of the world, has added the completion and colophon of all revelations, where he has proposed the mysteries of faith lastly and most perfectly, and what he had promised of old, he has at length deigned to exhibit in his Son manifested in the flesh, announcing and providing the advent of the Kingdom of heaven, and the completion of all predictions. Two things therefore are insinuated by this exordium; the one is expressly posited, and is a comparison of the manifestation of GOD made to the Fathers of old in the Prophets, and the most recent manifestation of GOD in the Son exhibited in the flesh; the other is tacitly hinted at, that in the advent of the Son those things which had been predicted through the Prophets have been fulfilled; since he indicates that the prophetic λαλιὰν, which was of prediction, and the advent of the Son, as its completion and end, looked primarily to this, that now through the advent of the Son himself, the Teacher, and that Great Prophet, it has attained its end and completion. Moreover, this πρόθεσις is conformable, even as to the manner of proposing, to the διήγησις itself, in which he institutes various συγκρίσεις, and especially has diligently exposed the difference between the Old and New Testament, and demonstrated the completion of the prophecies and of the many types of the Old Testament in CHRIST. He therefore sets out to speak concerning the Son of GOD, in so far as he was of old proposed under various oracles and types, but now by the exhibition of himself has brought light to the same, and provided completion, and thus by a collation of predictions and types, and of the proclamation or doctrine, as well as of those things which Christ provided, he undertakes to declare the primary article of faith concerning the person and office of CHRIST. By which proposition he immediately prepares attention for himself, both among the afflicted, to whom he testifies that a greater grace has been exhibited by God than to the Fathers, and adds courage by the commemoration of the instant end of all things and the fulfilled promises, and among the infirm, whom the Evangelio-mastiges, the other Jews, were trying to render more and more doubtful in the faith of CHRIST by the divine authority of the Prophets and the variety of prophetic visions and revelations. The Apostle therefore comes to the rescue at the very threshold: that the Jews can indeed boast of the prophetic doctrine, but those converted to the faith of CHRIST far more: who not only venerate the prophetic doctrine as the forerunner of the Messiah, but also hear the Messiah himself, the Son of GOD, as foretold by the Prophets, and thus not under various wrappings, but αὐτοπροσώπως exhibited in the flesh, the most eminent teacher of the grace which they predicted, and of the salvation which the Prophets sought.

Moreover, in this first part of the Apostolic proposition there occurs first the description of the past state, by reason of the divine manifestation made of old, in which these things are designated in order: (1) The mode of manifestation, (2) the time, (3) the supreme Author, (4) the Act, (5) the Object, (6) the intermediate Authors.

As regards (1) the mode of divine manifestation, it is hinted at by two words: πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως. Which the Vulgate interpreter takes as synonyms, rendering them 'at sundry times and in divers manners'. But they are distinct. For as μέρος is one thing, and τρόπος is another; so πολυμερὲς is one thing, and πολύτροπον is another. And therefore Beza renders the former (πολυμερῶς) 'at many times', others prefer 'multipartitely', or 'in many parts'. The Syriac interprets both as 'in all parts, in all forms', or because it does not precisely understand a universal particle, as Junius notes, by the custom of the Hebrews, or because it indicates that God spoke through the Prophets in all parts and all forms which He judged to befit the revelation of those times before CHRIST was exhibited, so that no part, no form of divine revelation, and thus no divine revelation at all, was outside the ministry of the θεοφόρων and ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε φερομένων Prophets. Moreover, by the former word πολυμερῶς three things seem to be insinuated: (1) the multitude of divine manifestations, that GOD spoke of old not just once, but at many times in diverse seasons, as Grotius here, (2) the diversity of degrees of intension and remission in divine revelation, that He revealed Himself by degrees and moments, now more obscurely, now more illustriously, and especially (3) the partition of the revelation of divine mysteries, that not all things, nor the same things, were revealed to all the Prophets, but as if the parts of the mysteries were distributed, some things inspired to some, others to others; e.g., to Isaiah the birth of the virgin and the satisfactory passion of Christ, to Jeremiah the mystery of the incarnation, to Daniel the time of his advent, to Zechariah the place, to Malachi his forerunner, etc., and again more to some, fewer to others.

As regards the other word πολυτρόπως, Bullinger notes an emphasis in it, and following him Cornelius à Lapide, who has it thus: πολυτρόπως, that is, multiformiter [in many forms], as if turning itself into various forms, modes, and similitudes. For thus Homer calls Ulysses πολύτροπον, because he was of a versatile disposition, and knew how to accommodate himself to every place, time, and person. Thus GOD turns Himself among the Prophets into all forms and figures, so that He might teach, soften, and bend the hard and rude people of the Jews. But πολύτροπος in Homer designates a crafty and versatile man, which Eustathius derives ἀπὸ τροπῆς from conversion, not from τρόπῳ or from mode; but the most perfect goodness and the immutable and most simple nature of GOD does not admit attributing that to HIM, since with GOD there is no παραλλαγὴ ἢ τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα [variation or shadow of turning], James 1:17. Wherefore the little word πολυτρόπως is more correctly referred here to the variety of the mode of revelations, than to the description of GOD revealing: and by it is noted both the variety of the announcement

Prophetic, which is the manifold and various manner of the revelation made to the Prophets. For as GOD revealed mysteries in a manifold manner, so also the Prophets set them forth in the same way, πολυτρόπως, according to the will of God. This must be understood both of the diverse forms of manifestations and of the various means of revelations. For GOD at one time set forth mysteries and heavenly doctrine nakedly and openly, as if a garment were removed, and at another time willed to exhibit the same as if covered by a garment and through wrappings. To these were added the various forms of the apparitions of GOD: who appeared to Isaiah on a high throne, with Seraphim flying around; to Ezekiel in the chariot of the Cherubim; to Daniel in the likeness of the Ancient of Days; to Zechariah and others in other symbols and forms. Again, as to the means by the intervention of which He made His revelations known, they are various and manifold, not only speech and visions, or sensible apparitions, but also ecstasies, dreams, figures, enigmas, signs and symbols, sacrifices, and other things of that kind. From the words of God

In Numbers XII, verse 6, divine revelation can be established as both extraordinary and ordinary. The former is either singular, such as that which is commemorated as proper and peculiar to Moses, namely, the aspect and friendly conversation from mouth to mouth: or common: which, by reason of the subject, was both of those who were awake and those who were asleep. The latter is said to have been done through a dream, the former through a vision: And one vision is external, such as that of the burning bush, Exod. III, another is internal, when the mind itself saw the Prophetic object represented by heavenly light. (2) With respect to the modes, one is symbolic, another open. The symbolic was done both through images of things, in a figure or idea, and through enigmas; in the former, the same things were signified as were seen, in the latter, other things than those which were seen. The open [revelation], which was ordinary, is omitted in Num. XII, where GOD commemorates only the extraordinary revelations made to the Prophets. Moreover, that [revelation] is made either through the word, whether internal or external, or announced to men by God ἀμέσως through Angels: or through Urim and Thummim; of this latter kind we have treated elsewhere. As to the former, when GOD speaks immediately, it is either through a sensible or imaginary representation, from which concepts are born, or through the infusion of knowledge, which does not take its origin from sense or imagination, but arises immediately through light poured into the intellect through intellectual species newly imparted, or even pre-existing ones, but employed or applied by divine power to form some concept of the mind. Concerning that kind of revelation by which GOD spoke to the Prophets through Angels as legates, nothing is held in Num. XII, verse 6, and therefore Schlichtingius wrongly weaves the revelation itself into his paraphrase of the Mosaic passage at this place: indeed, it does not seem to have a place even in the present Apostolic text, since it treats of the speech of GOD Himself made to the Prophets in various ways, and not of the Angels sustaining the person of GOD, as Schlichtingius wishes, in conversations with the Prophets.

πάλαι) מקדם. He says this here, because the oracles had ceased for a long time before the times of Christ.

II. The time is expressed by the word πάλαι, of old: by which Thomas wishes to imply in this place that the things which they said about Christ were not manifested suddenly, but with the increase of times, because they were great: but the word πάλαι is opposed only to the present time, not however to haste or to simultaneous revelation. And although the things which were proposed concerning Christ were very great, they could nevertheless have been delivered by God and believed by men once and at the same time, if GOD had so willed, just as was done by Christ in the time of the New Testament. Three things are implied by this word: (1) A respect for the time that preceded the advent of Christ, because it is opposed to the last days, in which GOD spoke in His Son. (2) The lapse of some centuries: to the times immediately preceding the advent of CHRIST, but to ancient times, in which the Prophets still flourished. Therefore the Syrian rendered it from the beginning, not of creation, but of Prophetic manifestation. (3) The cessation of Prophecies and various revelations, as Burgensis notes in his annotations to Lyranus, that by the word OF OLD it is implied that prophecy had already ceased for some time before the advent of CHRIST.

ὁ θεὸς) III. The supreme Author is expressed as ὁ θεὸς, that GOD of Israel, whom the Hebrews worshipped as the one true GOD. The Apostle adds the commemoration of the supreme Author, ὁ θεὸς, so that he may profess immediately at the outset that he by no means intends a defection from that true GOD, or from the revelations of Moses and the writings of the Prophets. The Photinian Schlichtingius remarks here that that supreme and only God was indeed of old the GOD of Israel, but now is called the GOD and Father of our Lord JESUS CHRIST. But although we do not deny that the appellations of the God of Israel are more frequent in the Old Testament and of the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ in the New Testament, it is nevertheless false that He was called only the GOD of Israel in the Old Testament, and nowhere in the New Testament, and conversely only the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ in the New Testament, and nowhere in the Old, which Schlichtingius seems to intend. For mention is also made of God the Father of Jesus Christ in the O. T., 2 Sam. VII. 14. (Cf. also 1 Chron. XVII. 13. Ps. LXXXIX. 26.) whence Christ is called the Son of God Ps. II. 7. Prov. XXX. 4. and from no other source than the O. T. does this Epistle demonstrate that Christ is the Son of GOD, and therefore that God is the Father of Christ: for these things are relative, and imply one another. Likewise God is called the Lord of Jesus Christ frequently in the Old Testament Ps. XXII. 1. Cf. Matt. XXVII. 46. Ps. XL. 6. (Cf. Heb. X. 5.) Ps. XLV. 7. (Cf. Heb. I. 8.) Ps. LXIX. 4. (Cf. John II. 17. with v. 10. & Matt. XXVII. 34. with v. 22. Ps. LXXXIX. 26. (Cf. 2 Sam. VII. 14. Heb. I. 5.) etc. Again, in the New Testament also, God is designated as the God of Israel, Matt. XV. 31. Luke I. 16. & 68. But that the mention of God the Father of Jesus Christ is not so frequent in the books of the Old Testament, that is not because the grace of God exhibited in Christ Jesus in the Old Testament had no place, for this is against the decree of the Synod of Jerusalem, Acts XV. verse 11. & the Axiom of the Apostle, Heb. XIII. verse 8. since He was also called the God of Israel especially for this reason, namely that in the seed of Israel all the nations of the earth might be blessed, but because the grace of God in Christ Jesus was more clearly declared, and indeed to the whole world, not only to the Israelites, but also to the Gentiles, and the fulfillment of the promises made in the Old Testament was provided in Christ; whence since the Israelites rejected this constitution of grace, which the Gentiles accepted with exultation, Acts XIII. 47. God is not so much designated as the God of Israel in the writings of the New Testament, much less the Lord of all, which the Apostle explains excellently, Rom. X. 14. seq.

Λαλήσας) IV. The act of manifestation is designated by the word λαλήσας, which is wrongly rendered by the Vulgate as 'loquens' in the present tense, therefore the ordinary gloss in vain seeks the mystery in this, that the present is placed regarding the past, namely regarding the Prophets, and the past regarding the present, namely regarding the Son, although in both cases in Greek there is an Aorist, obtaining the signification of the past. But since it is said that God spoke in many ways, it is easily understood that λαλιὰν τοῦ Θεοῦ is to be accepted concerning all those ways of divine revelations which were made to the Prophets. Therefore, divine revelation, whatever it may have been and however it may have been made, is called λαλιὰ, or the speech of God, because just as word and speech is for us the medium through which we most powerfully manifest our mind's concepts and our will, so through those various kinds of revelations God acts so that his mind and will might be established. But the speech of GOD can be distinguished into internal and external. Internal [speech] occurs either through the inscription of the word of GOD, Heb. 8:10, or through another expression of the will of GOD, whether of concepts immediately exhibiting things, or of symbols mediately signifying them (which for the sake of distinction can be called primary or secondary notions), by interior representation; which if it happens while awake, is called ὀπτασία, Luke 1:22. But if in sleep, it is called ὅραμα, Acts 10:17. External speech or the external word of God is either uttered or committed to letters; the former occurs either immediately, whereby God either presents to the sight some notable sign, or an articulated voice to the hearing, whether by forming the same in the air, or by placing words into the mouth of the Prophet; or mediately, whether by the intervention of the ministry of Angels, appearing either to those awake or to those sleeping, or through the ministry of other men. But this is the written word of GOD. For even concerning the Scriptures the word λαλεῖν occurs, Acts 2:31, ch. 3:21, 24. 1 Cor. 2:6, 7:13, 9:8, 2 Cor. 11:23, 12:19, 13:3. And through the Scriptures God and his Prophets speak to us, and when we read the Scriptures we are said to hear them, Acts 13:27, Heb. 3:7 & 15, 4:7, Luke 16:29. Here are understood all those λαλιαὶ by which God spoke to the Prophets, especially indeed internally; and without doubt the Apostle looks most to those by which God spoke concerning Christ as the primary goal of the Prophets, as those which he had decided to treat in the whole Epistle.

To the fathers.

Namely of the Hebrews, to whom this discourse is addressed.

V. The object, to whom he spoke through the Prophets, is expressed by the following little word τοῖς πατράσιν, to the fathers, by which name some also include the Patriarchs, but GOD did not speak to them through the Prophets; but either immediately αὐτοπροσώπως, or through the mediation of the ministry of Angels, and therefore we understand rather the ancestors of the Hebrews who lived in the times of the Prophets through whom God spoke. For the name of fathers, according to the custom of the Hebrews, designates any ancestors, Ps. 22:5, Ps. 106:6, etc., John 4:20, Heb. 3:9, 8:9, etc.

In the prophets.

Through the Prophets explaining to the people those things which we have said.

VI. Finally, he points out the intermediate authors, by whose labors and intervention God formerly spoke to the fathers: ἐν τοῖς προφήταις: in the prophets, the particle ἐν, just as the prefix ב, which the Syrian uses here, is accustomed sometimes to be equivalent to the preposition διὰ or through, as Numbers 12:2, בְּמשֶׁה through Moses spoke Jehovah, is it not also בָנוּ through us. Thus here in the prophets, that is, God is said to have spoken to the Israelite people through the prophets. Thus the Greek Scholia, as also Ambrose and Chrysostom, take ἐν as διὰ, in for through. Moreover, it is hinted at the same time both at the singular indwelling of God in the Prophets, as

Matt. 10:20, Christ says concerning the Apostles, it is not you who are speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you, who also indwells you in a singular way, and at the same time speaks in you and through you; and also the interior revelation, or suggestion, by which he instilled or manifested to the Prophets interiorly what they ought to bring forth to the people exteriorly, which David says, 2 Sam. 23:2, The Spirit of the Lord spoke בִּי, in me, that is, he spoke in my heart first, whatever he then brought forth through me: for the interior concepts of the mind are prior in the order of nature to the external symbols of words, and words represent those things which are within in the mind. We do not, however, object if anyone refers this also to the external word, because GOD speaks to the heart, or to hearts, also through external appearances and manifestations, since the word penetrates the soul; and indeed the Prophets admitted the divinely made manifestations, whatever they were, to their soul before they brought them forth externally and set them before the people. For they did not prophesy unknowingly like Caiaphas, John 11:51. Therefore, every revelation of the Prophets made in the Prophets was through an internal information of persuasion, by which God, even with external means employed, instructed them internally, etc. Furthermore, by the name of Prophets are understood those who are specifically called Prophets, and were not only enunciators of the words of GOD, as Augustine calls them, Quest. 17 in Exod., but speaking by the inspiration of the divine Spirit, who prophesied future things which needed to be fulfilled, as Justin describes them in Trypho from Deuteronomy. 19:22 and 2 Peter 1:21, but especially those who prophesied concerning Christ, which we believe have been fulfilled, and see being fulfilled, and trust will be fulfilled, as Augustine says in Book 7 of The City of God, chapter 32. For as the primary object of the whole Holy Scripture is CHRIST, and thus He is established as the end of the entire law, Romans 10:4, so also all the Prophets bore witness of Him, Acts 10:43, and Augustine says in Book 12 against Faustus, chapter 7, that all things contained in the writings of the Prophets were said either about Christ or for the sake of Christ. Therefore Peter teaches that the Prophets searched and prophesied about the future grace and the times of the New Testament, 1 Epistle 1:10, 11, and Acts 3:24 testifies that all the Prophets from Samuel onwards, as many as have spoken, have predicted these days. That Peter begins the series of Prophets from Samuel is because not only did Prophets not flourish so much before Samuel, when the word of God was precious and prophecies were rare, 1 Samuel 3:1, but also because he had previously introduced the testimony of Moses, the highest and most eminent of the Prophets, and therefore now adds to it the concurring votes of all the remaining Prophets, since just as he was either the only one before Samuel specifically called a Prophet, or certainly could be considered as one equal to all, so those who followed in order from Samuel onwards, all the Prophets equally with Moses, the leader of the Prophets, prophesied concerning Christ.

There is no doubt, however, that Moses is included here in the number of the Prophets through whom GOD spoke to the Fathers. Therefore, right at the very beginning, Moses is brought into the order of those who are lesser than CHRIST; which the Apostle does tacitly, and only under a general name, lest some be offended at the threshold. And most here extend the denomination of Prophets even to the Patriarchs, who judge that here the discourse is concerning the the station of GOD from the beginning of the world, they think the discourse is here. Their opinion seems to be supported by the fact that Abraham is called a Prophet in Gen. XX. verse 7, (Compare Psalm CV. verse 15,) where this name is not assigned to him because he knew as a Prophet that his wife was untouched by Abimelech, as Junius notes on this passage. For that he could not know as a Prophet; nor does he seem to be designated a Prophet by God merely for that reason, in the way that heralds of the divine word are generally so called; but also in a special sense, because through divine revelation he knew and foretold many future things, such as that a son would be born to him from the barren Sarah, that the Messiah would arise from his seed, and that in him all the nations of the earth would be blessed, that his descendants would serve in Egypt, would be liberated from that servitude in the fourth generation, and would be introduced into the land of Canaan, etc. Meanwhile, after Moses, the coryphaeus of the Prophets, in the New Testament, the Prophets are generally placed, specifically and properly so called, and the series of Prophets is begun from Samuel, as Peter is the author, nor is another place easily found in the New Testament where the name of Prophets, when the discourse is about the Prophets of the Old Testament, is used with such breadth that it also fits the Patriarchs, but rather about those who are called by the Hebrews Prophets, both ראשונים, or the former, and אחרונים, or the latter, that is, those who followed Moses up to the schism of the Israelite kingdom, and those who flourished after the schism of the ten tribes from the rest. Therefore, some think that interpretation is to be preferred by which the present passage is understood of those Prophets: but if anyone should urge Acts

verse 25, that the descendants of the Patriarchs are called the sons of the Prophets, which seems so to some: they respond that the sons of the Prophets are not called there otherwise than they are called the sons of the testament, or of the covenant, that is, not by nature, but by culture, not by propagation, but by instruction, and inheritance, or communion; that those are the Israelites to whom the Prophets were peculiarly destined and with whom the covenant was sanctioned, according to common Hebraism. However, in our judgment, those who wish the name of Prophets to be extended here even to the Patriarchs approach more closely to the mind of the Apostle; and they embrace here the entire divine revelation made before Christ was exhibited, which I see is approved by most interpreters: just as the blessed Dorscheus also says, in his commentary begun and unpublished, that by Prophets are understood all those immediately illuminated, as in 2 Peter I, the prophetic word, and prophecy, verses 19, 20, 21, is every word that is θεόπνευστον (God-breathed). Therefore the ante- and post-diluvian Patriarchs, Moses the founder and legislator of the Israelite Republic, and the rest. In this way, David Pareus assigns a fourfold variety, which is indicated here for the different ages and times of divine revelation: I. Before the flood, by which the first rudiments were handed down. II. Before the law, by which the promises were given to Abraham somewhat more illustriously. III. After the law, or under the law, with further doctrine of the Church and the form of the Republic instituted: which finally IV. he accumulated and perfected at various times and in parts, up to the times of Malachi. For just as that πάλαι (of old) is extended to all times before the Messiah was exhibited, as the name of Fathers extends itself to any fathers whatsoever, even the first parents, since there is no restriction, as the speaking done by GOD in various ways and parts sounds most broadly, and is adequately contradistinguished from the most recent speaking done in the Son: so the word of the Prophets must be taken with that same breadth which fits any intermediate authors of divine revelation who pertain to the Fathers and Elders, or their predecessors, from the first revelation about the Messiah. For even among the first Patriarchs, God spoke πολυμερῶς & πολυτρόπως (in many parts and in many ways) to the domestic Church: and the Fathers can be understood most broadly, otherwise than Schlichtingius thinks, who under the Patriarchs pertained to the Church of GOD, or were called to the same, and those who were properly and more closely the ancestors of the Hebrews. Two things, however, are gathered from these. I. The discourse made through the Prophets denotes the extraordinary ministry of the Prophets for propagating or restoring the Church. II. With the Canon of the Old Testament established, the prophetic gift and that of extraordinary illumination concerning matters of faith ceased until Christ.

In these last days.

That is, finally now. See Acts II. verse 17, 2 Timothy III. verse 1. In the Manuscript it is ἐπ’ ἐσχάτυ τῶν ἡμερῶν τύτων, as in Num. XXIV. 14, Ezech. XXXVIII. 16.

He has spoken to us by the Son.

He has spoken to us by the Son, he did not entrust the greatest and heavenly things to servants, but to the Son. See Matthew XXI. 37, John I. 18, III. 16, John XV. 15, 1 Peter I. 10.

Here is the second member of the first part of the τῆς προθέσεως concerning the great Doctor or Prophet, by which is presented a comparison or opposition of the present state with respect to the divine manifestation made formerly: Which member is connected by the Syrian with a copulative particle, but it is to be taken in an adversative sense, as it is accustomed to vary in sense, a most common Hebraism, which is not expressed in the Greek. And it contains (1) the Mode, (2) the Time, (3) the Author, (4) the Act, (5) the Object, (6) the Messenger of the same, of which members some are expressly stated: But the rest are partly repeated ἀπὸ κοινῷ, and partly left to be gathered from the antithesis.

Therefore, as to I. the mode of divine manifestation in the New Testament made through Christ, it is not expressed, but is gathered ἀντιθετικῶς from the description of the Prophetic revelation. Namely, just as that was 1. πολυμερῶς and by turns, and according to different degrees of intensity and remission, and κατὰ μέρη, or made by parts: so, on the contrary, the manifestation in Christ happened ἐφάπαξ καὶ σαφῶς once and openly, or ἐσχάτως μονοειδῶς lastly and uniformly, and thus it must be held as unique, having been done at the last. And that both most clearly and most fully, as regards all and singular parts, so that no other, much less a clearer or more perfect one, is to be expected in the Church of God established on this earth until the consummation of the age. (2) Just as GOD spoke πολυτρόπως in many ways, both to the Prophets and through the Prophets, to the Fathers, or the people, using various forms and means of revelations: so in the New Testament the speech is uniform and the same, by which GOD spoke not through symbols, through signs, ecstasies, dreams, figures, enigmas, sacrifices, types, visions, Urim and Thummim, and other things of that kind, but with an open voice in the Son. Furthermore, the same doctrine of Christ is uniform, such as it was first made by the Lord himself in the flesh, and afterwards propagated by those who heard the Lord, Heb. II. 3. It will endure, and will be propagated in the Church, nor is any other external mode of divine revelation to be expected in these times.

II. The time is noted by this periphrasis ἐπ’ ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν τύτων. The Complutensian Codex reads ἐπ’ ἐσχάτυ. Whence a double interpretation: The Syrian renders it ܒܝܘܡܬܐ ܗܪܝܐ in the last in these last days, according to the former reading; but the Vulgate, 'most recently in these days,' according to the latter: as if in the last, or extreme day of these days. Estius the Papist, however, judges the former to be better, and therefore to be preferred to the Vulgate version. Moreover, 'day' is used for 'time' by a synecdoche familiar to the Scriptures, Psalm 18, verse 19; Psalm 102, verse 12; Isaiah 4, verse 1; Matthew 12, verse 1; Hebrews 8, verses 8, 10, etc. But 'last' are not said only with respect to time past, as Schlichtingius renders it, 'in the extreme of these days,' but also by reason of the impending end of the times, because although regard is had to the word πάλαι, yet that opposition involves both the term, or the extreme day of things past, and the end or term of all days.
