For the last days, the last hour, or the last times are called in Scripture those after which nothing else is to be expected than the end and term of the world, and the advent of Christ the Judge, as being those to which, by His first advent, Christ brought the completion of all prophecies. For the times of the Messiah are wont to be called 'the last' simply; and by that phrase is designated in the Scriptures either the time itself of the advent of the Messiah, or the entire time after Christ was exhibited until the end of the world. Compare Isaiah 2, verse 2; Joel 2, verses 28, 31; Micah 4, verse 1; Acts 2, verse 17. Where, because the Prophets call the last days the time of the advent of the Messiah, it can indeed be accepted by reason of that time, which at last, in the extreme of all prophecies, was to come, which also brought an end to the law and to the Jewish polity; but especially the times of the Messiah or of Christ exhibited and the times of the New Testament are called 'the last,' partly by reason of the manifestation of the latest grace made in Christ, because in the Old Testament one revelation succeeded another, one prophet succeeded another, but in the New Testament, by the revelation made through Christ, nothing more is to be expected: partly by reason of the appearance of glory now impending in the last day, because, as the prophecy of Elijah Levita has it, the times of the Messiah are the final ones, whence also John says, 'Little children, it is now the last hour,' 1 Epistle 2, verse 18. and the Apostle in our Epistle does not hesitate to call this time, in which Christ offered Himself, συντελείαν τῶν αἰώνων, the consummation of the age, chapter 9, verse 26, and he points out that that last day is ἐγγίζουσαν, or already approaching, chapter 10, verse 25, because ἐτὶ μικρὸν ὅσον, in a short or within a short space of time, Christ will come to judgment, chapter 10, verse 37. Compare 1 Corinthians 10:11 and 1 Peter 4:7. And so Chrysostom and Theophylact note that in this way Paul at the same time stirs up the Hebrews to hope and constancy in the struggles and afflictions to be endured for the faith of Christ. For a combatant, even if he be somewhat sluggish, when he understands that the struggle is now about to be finished, breathes a little and regains his strength, because he knows that the end of the labor is at hand, and that the time of rest and reward is present.

III. Who spoke in the last times is evident from the former member: namely, that same GOD who formerly spoke in the Old Testament, from which it is gathered that the author of the revelation of the Old and New Testaments is the same, namely, that true and supreme GOD. For just as GOD spoke in the Prophets to the Fathers when they preached, so also it must be believed that what they consigned to writing, and proposed to the people through the Scriptures, they consigned and proposed with GOD speaking in them, or through divine revelation and inspiration. Since, therefore, that same GOD is the author of the manifestation made in the New Testament, which is contained in the writings of the New Testament, there is no doubt that the Scripture of the Old and New Testaments proceeded from the same author; and therefore in this identity, as Burgensis says in his additions to Lyranus, two errors are refuted, namely, those of the Manichaeans and the Jews. For the Manichaeans attributed the Old Testament to an evil principle, but the New to a good one; the Jews, however, conversely, said the Old Testament was from GOD, but the New was not; whence, refuting both errors, the Apostle asserts the aforementioned identity. Moreover, from this repetition of the word it is manifest that the same is here taken ὑποστατικῶς or personally concerning GOD the Father, because it is said that GOD spoke in the Son. Furthermore, he establishes GOD as the author of the revelation made in the New Testament, so that he immediately raises it to the pinnacle of authority and Canonical authority, and teaches that all things which were preached by Christ to the Apostles are ἀξιόπιστα, καὶ ἀυτόπιστα (worthy of belief and self-evidencing). Therefore, since the latest revelation proceeded no less from GOD than the Prophetic manifestation, the Hebrews ought by no means to oppose that twofold revelation, and judge this latest revelation to be alien from that ancient revelation of GOD, since GOD cannot be opposed to Himself. Finally, he thus also adds courage to the afflicted Hebrews, because just as their Fathers or ancestors rejoice in the revelation and speech of GOD made to them, they are happier than their immediate progenitors, and those of their ancestors who, with prophecy ceasing, had no immediate divine revelation.

IV. The act of manifestation is expressed again by the speech ἐλάλησεν. God manifested Himself in the Old Testament through speech. But the λαλιὰ of GOD, because it was then πολύτροπος (manifold), does not only embrace speech properly so called, but any signification and representation of the divine will: but here in the New Testament, where it is μονότροπος (uniform), it designates that act by which God manifested Himself to us in CHRIST, which, with respect to us, was done only through the Word properly so called, and not through various symbols, which by an analogy of proportion at least come under the name of the divine word. But how did GOD speak in the Son, since the Son Himself is דבר יהוה: Psalm 33, verse 6; 1 Samuel 7, verse 20; 2 Chronicles 17, verse 19; and ὁ λόγος, the Word of GOD, John 1, verses 1, 2, 14; 1 John 1, verse 1, chapter 5, verse 7; Revelation 19, verse 13? Answer. Because the Son of God is a Word not προφορικὸν, but ὑποστατικὸν or substantial, and the same is that great Prophet, Evangelist, and Teacher of peoples, Deut. XVIII. 15. Is. XLI. 27. chap. LV. 4.

V. The object ἡμῖν, to us, Chrysostom restricts to the Apostles: But Paul understands the Hebrews, among whom he counts himself. The opposition is between the Hebrews, to whom the Apostle writes, and the Fathers, that grace is now shown to the Hebrews no less than it was shown to their ancestors formerly. The Apostle speaks, however, as if the Hebrews to whom he writes had heard Christ himself teaching ἀυτοπροσώπως, both because He spoke in their time, so that He could be heard by them, and because, speaking in the writings of the Apostles, He is heard by them, in which latter sense God still speaks to us in the Son.

VI. Finally, the Intermediary is expressed by the phrase ἐν ὑιῷ: But He has spoken in one way in the Son, and in another in the Prophets. The prophets were only legates, servants, not authors of the doctrine. The Son, as legate, is the Lord and the author of the doctrine himself. In the prophets GOD spoke, because He was singularly present to them by His Spirit; in the Son, because in Him dwells bodily the whole fullness of the Deity, Coloss. II. verse 9. In the prophe He revealed to them what they ought to speak. In the Son: because the Son is in the Father, and the Father in the Son through an essential περιχώρησιν [indwelling], and existing in the bosom of the Father, He manifests Him to us, John I. verse 18. In the prophets spoke the Spirit of CHRIST Himself, who was in them, 1 Pet. I. verse 11. nor did the prophets know anything except what the Son revealed to them: because no one knows the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal Him, Matt. XI. verse 27. The Son sent the prophets, Luke XI. verse 49. Matt. XXIII. verse 34. & He instituted them as the substantial Wisdom of GOD, Prov. I. verse 21. chap. IX. verse 32. Therefore GOD is said to have spoken in the Son as in hypostatic wisdom, and the splendor of glory, and the character of His substance, but not as a separate person outside of GOD. Furthermore, the Son is opposed to the prophets: Because although the Son of GOD is also a prophet, and spoke to us by reason of the prophetic office, He is not, however, of the common number of prophets, but κατ' ἐξοχὴν [by way of excellence] that great Prophet, Deuteronomy XVIII. verse 15. and the Lord of the remaining prophets, by whom they were sent, Luke XI. verse 49. Isa. VI. verse 8. Confer. John XII. verse 41. 42. and who is not only an internuncio of the divine will, but with GOD the Father is one and the same author of the divine word, 2 Sam. XXIII. verse 3. 4. therefore the word of GOD is called the word τῦ κυρίε [of the Lord], Acts VIII. verse 25. XIII. verse 48. 49. XV. verse 36. XIX. verse 20. 1 Thessal. I. verse 8. 2. Thess. II. verse 1. τῦ κυρίε τῦ Χριςῦ [of the Lord Christ], as is expressed Apocal. XIX. verse 10. Col. III. verse 16. 1 Timoth. VI. verse 3. Again, although the prophets were also sons of GOD, there is nevertheless an infinite difference between the prophets and Christ the Son of GOD. They are sons by adoption, He by nature. They by spiritual regeneration, He by eternal generation. They through a certain τῆς θείας φύσεως κοινωνίαν [participation of the divine nature], and that merely gracious, 2 Pet. I. verse 4. but He truly καθ' ἑνότητα τῆς ὐσίας [according to the unity of essence] as regards essential unity with the Father, John X. v. 30.

Nor is there any reason why Socinus, from the fact that GOD is said to have spoken in the Son, should conclude that the Son is not God. For the personal distinction of the Father and the Son is not to be opposed to the essential unity: nor does the preposition ἐν [in] necessarily imply any inferiority or respect of instrumental cause. For the Son is also said to be in the Father, John XVII. v. 21. nor is the Father inferior, but an essential περιχώρησις [indwelling] is noted: and the Son performed miracles in the Holy Spirit, Matt. XII. v. 48. But the adversaries do not admit that the Holy Spirit is inferior to the Son. And it was observed before, that GOD spoke in one way in the Son, and in another in the prophets. Finally, it is implied here that He spoke in the Son not as ἀσάρκῳ [without flesh], but as ἐνσάρκῳ [in the flesh]: because the most recent manifestation was made through human nature, according to which the Son of GOD was also constituted κληρονόμς πάντων [heir of all things]. Those, therefore, are in vain who, with Calixtus, trifle that all the apparitions of the Son of GOD in the Old Testament are taken away by these words: namely, that GOD spoke to us in the Son only in the last days. Certainly the λογοφανείαι [manifestations of the Word] are too illustrious to be called into doubt, by which the Son of GOD was seen and spoke especially to the Patriarchs and other faithful of the Old Testament; as the consoler of Hagar, Gen. XVI. verse 17. seq. the entertainer of Abraham, Gen. XVIII. the savior of Isaac, Gen. XXII. verse 11. seq. the sponsor of Jacob, Gen. XXIX. verse 13. who was also his antagonist and wrestler, Gen. XXXII. verse 24. and Redeemer, Gen. XLVIII. verse 16. the Lord of Moses, and leader of the people, Exod. III. verse 34. chap. XIX. verse 3. XXIII. verse 20. the Prince and defender of the Israelite army, Josh. V. verse 13. the helper of Gideon, Jud. VI. verse 12. How then did He speak through the Son only in the last times? The following things are to be noted here: (1) It is not so much the times of the Patriarchs and the Messiah that are opposed, as the times of the Prophets and the New Testament, according to Schlichting. Although, therefore, He appeared in the time of the Patriarchs, yet with respect to the time of the Prophets, He is rightly said to have spoken in the last of the days. (2) The ΛόγοΦανείαι [manifestations of the Word] in the Old Testament were 1) Types foreshadowing the most recent manifestation. 2) Preludes of the ἐνανθρωπήσεως [incarnation]. 3) Extraordinary and particular, done to a few. But in the New Testament GOD was manifested in the flesh to all, and the Son of GOD was made flesh: The true body and substance succeeded the types, and that manifestation was ecumenical and universal, and at the same time perfect and ordinary, up to the last day. Therefore (3) one must distinguish between the λόγον ἄσαρκον [Word without flesh], who also manifested Himself in the Old Testament, even if sometimes by an assumed visible form for a time οἰκονομικῶς [economically], not however ὑποσατικῶς [hypostatically] united to Himself in flesh, which was the most recent manifestation: But παρασατικῶς [by way of appearance], which was only πρόσκαιρος [temporary] and a passing assumption of a visible form, such as was also done by the angels. Therefore, GOD is said to have spoken most recently here in the Son, namely, in the One manifested in the flesh, 1 Timoth. III. verse 16. and conversing among men, and preaching the Gospel after His ἐνσάρκωσιν [incarnation], John I. verse 14. Since then the Father spoke to men through His Son, as He conversed as true man among men, and as the Word made flesh declared GOD, John I. 18.

Concerning the Son of GOD therefore manifested in the flesh, in whom and through whom in these last days GOD has spoken to the Hebrews, in order to set forth the eminence of this Teacher of the New Testament, the Apostle treats further here, describing his person, both as regards his human nature and his divine nature. By reason of the former, he calls him the appointed heir of all things; but with respect to the latter, he says that GOD created the ages through him. However, he wished to designate the human nature by that periphrasis rather than by an express name. For what did it matter to mention so nakedly that CHRIST, the latest herald of divine grace, had been a man, when that very fact was neither in doubt to anyone, nor did it seem to contribute anything to the dignity of the latest Revelation. And therefore he used that periphrasis rather, primarily because he did not intend so much to propose CHRIST as Man, as regards his nature viewed nakedly, as regards the state both of his Humiliation and of his Exaltation, which brought no little authority and dignity to the latest revelation. For which reason he says that CHRIST was appointed by GOD as heir of all things, which it is certain pertains to him by reason of his human nature, which alone admits of different states, and to which the promise of the inheritance of all things had been made after the preceding humiliation, but not by reason of his divine nature, which not through the gracious appointment of GOD the Father, but through the omnipotent creation of all things possessed all things. Furthermore, the divine nature of the Son of GOD is insinuated here, when the ages are said to have been created through him; since CHRIST is the Creator of the world as GOD, or by reason of his divine nature, by the power of which the inheritance of all things also fell to CHRIST as man. For if CHRIST were by nature a ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος, a mere man, and not at the same time in the unity of his person true GOD by nature, the Creator of all things, he could never have obtained or administered the inheritance of all things in respect of his human nature, which is indeed separate from GOD, inasmuch as divine and infinite wisdom and power are required for it. The Apostle describes the divine nature of CHRIST from the creation of the ages, for this reason above all, that he instituted a σύγκρισιν (comparison) of the former times of old and the most recent ones, and that he testified that the Son manifested in the flesh has spoken to us in these last days; therefore, to demonstrate the dignity of this revelation, he teaches that the Son was not only constituted heir of all things, but is also the author and founder of all things, and of the ages and times themselves, and he undertakes to confirm this further. Wherefore it is determined by the Apostle to treat of CHRIST, true GOD and true man, who as GOD created the ages, and as man was constituted heir of all things, and to demonstrate his supreme dignity, which he obtains both κατὰ φύσιν, by nature, as the true GOD and Creator of the universe, and κατὰ χάριν, by grace, as the true man raised to the inheritance of all things.

Latin:

CAPUT I.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Præmissa comparatione revelationis per Prophetas ad Patres, & locutione novissimis diebus ad Ebræos facta, cui artificiose implicatur propositio: quod Doctor & Sacerdos N. T. nempe Christus, sit Dei Filius æternus, per quem secula condidit, quique hæres factus est omnium secundum humanam naturam; illius ratione eundem esse splendorem gloriæ Dei, & characterem hypostaseos ejus, & omnia ferre verbo virtutis suæ tradit, hujus vero respectu, post factam purificationem peccatorum nostrorum consedisse ad dextram Dei docet: adeoque quod ad personam Christum verum Deum, verum hominem, sed constitutum super omnia, & evectum ad dextram DEI, nomenque eminentissimum consecutum: quoad officium Doctorem, & propitiatorem peccatorum nostrorum. Deinde confirmationem aggreditur Apostolus, tum veræ Deitatis Christi, quod sit Filius à Deo ab æterno genitus (Ps. II. 7. 2. Sam. VII. 14.) & ab Angelis adorandus (Ps. XCVII. 17.) qui creati à Deo, ejusque ministri sunt, quum Filius Deus, ac thronus ejus æternus (Ps. XLV. 7.) & ipse Dominus sit, qui terram fundavit, & cœlos fecit, illisque desituris immutabilis semper manet (Ps. CII. 26. sequ.) tum exaltatæ humanitatis, secundum quam dictum eidem, quod Angelorum nulli, sede ad dextram meam, cum illi tantum Spiritus ministratorii sint.

PArtes duæ sunt. I. Propositio ad v. 4. II. Tractatio de persona Christi, juxta præternam & veram ejus Deitatem, nec non juxta humanam naturam ad dextram Dei evectam ad v. 14.

PARS II. PROPOSITIO.

V. 1. Πολυμερω̃ς) In Glossario πολυμερω̃ς plurifariam, id est, pluribus temporibus: tempore Abrahami, Isaaci, Jacobi: temporibus Mosis, Josuæ, Judicum: temporibus Davidis, Salomonis & Prophetarum: ac postremo tempori- bus Danielis, Aggæi, Zachariæ, Malachiæ. Καὶ πολυτρόπως) Dando visa diurna aut nocturna, aut afflatus internos, aut voces auditas, interdum per figuras, in- terdum aperte. Vide quæ dicta Num. XII. 6. Propositio Apostoli bimembris est I. de Do- ctore Novi Testamenti. II. De Novi Testamenti Pontifice summo. I. Propositio de Christo Doctore exhibetur ab Apostolo, in ipso limine & exor- dio, comparatione Vet. & Novi Test. vel potius temporis ante CHRISTUM exhibetum, quod erat promissionis, & à CHRISTI adventu, quod com- plementi & exhibitionis πλήρωμα τῶν χρόνων, Galat. IV. vers. 4. πλήρωμα τῶν καιρῶν, Ephes. I. vers. 10. Summa exordii est: Eundem illum JESUM, qui majoribus Ebræorum, seu populo Israelitico locutus est antegressis ætatibus, per Prophetas, adventum Messiæ prænunciantes, & de gratuita remissione peccatorum in nomine ejus testimo- nium perhibentes pro modulo revelationis di- vinæ, quæ & partibus diversis doctrinæ cœlestis constabat, alia aliis subinde revelata & variis mo- dis atque formis sese insinuabat: nuperis, iisque extremis mundi temporibus, complementum & colophonem omnium revelationum addidisse, ubi ultimo & perfectissime mysteria fidei pro- posuit, & quod promiserat olim, id exhibere tandem dignatus est in Filio suo in carne ma- nifestato, Regni cœlorum adventum, prædi- ctionumque omnium complementum annun- ciante, atque præstante. Duo itaque insinu- antur hoc exordio; alterum expresse ponitur, estque comparatio manifestationis DEI Patri- bus olim factæ in Prophetis, & manifestationis DEI novissimæ in Filio in carne exhibito; alte- rum tacite innuitur, in Filii adventu ea, quæ per Prophetas prædicta erant, adimpleta esse; quan- doquidem λαλιὰν propheticam, quæ erat prædi- ctionis, & adventum Filii, ceu complementum, finemque suum potissimum respiciebat, nunc per adventum ipsius Filii Doctoris, & Prophetæ il- lius Magni finem & complementum suum con- secutam esse indicet. Est autem πρόθεσις hæc conformis, etiam quoad modum proponendi ipsi διηγήσει, in qua va- rias συγκρίσεις instituit, ac præcipue diligenter exposuit discrimen Veteris & Novi Testamen- ti, & complementum vaticiniorum, ac typo- rum plurium Vet. Testam. in CHRISTO de- monstravit. De Filio ergo DEI dicere insti- tuit, in quantum is olim sub oraculis, typisque variis propositus, nunc autem sui ipsius exhi- bitione lucem iisdem attulit, & complemen- tum præstitit, adeoque collatione prædictio- num & typorum, ac præconii seu doctrinæ, nec non eorum, quæ Christus præstitit, articulum fidei primarium de CHRISTI persona & officio declarare suscipit. Qua propositione statim attentionem sibi parat, cum apud afflictos, qui- bus & majorem divinitus exhibitam contesta- tur gratiam, quam Patribus, & adimpletis pro- missionibus instantis finis rerum omnium com- memoratione animum addit, tum apud infirmos, quos Prophetarum divina autoritate, visionum- que ac revelationum Propheticarum varietate objecta conabantur Evangelio - mastiges, Ju- dæi cæteri, magis magisque dubios reddere in fide CHRISTI. Succurrit itaque Apostolus in ipso limine: gloriari quidem posse Judæos de Prophetica doctrina, sed longe magis ad fi- dem CHRISTI conversos: qui non tantum doctrinam propheticam venerantur, ut præ- in nunciam Messiæ, sed & ipsum Messiam, DEI Filium audiunt ut prænunciatum à Prophetis, adeoque non sub involucris variis, sed αὐτο- προσώπως in carne exhibitum, gratiæ, quam præ- dixerunt, salutis, quam inquisiverunt Prophe- tæ, doctorem eminentissimum.

Occurrit autem in hac prima parte proposi- tionis Apostolicæ primo status antegressi descri- ptio, ratione manifestationis divinæ olim factæ, in qua ordine hæc designantur: (1) Manifesta- tionis modus, (2) tempus, (3) Autor summus, (4) Actus, (5) Objectum, (6) Autores inter- medii.

Quod (1) ad modum attinet divinæ manife- stationis, innuitur is duabus vocibus: πολυμε- ρῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως. Quas pro Synonymis ha- bet vulgatus interpres, reddens multifariam, multisque modis. Sed distinctæ sunt. Nam ut aliud est μέρος, aliud vero τρόπος; sic aliud est πολυμερὲς, aliud πολύτροπον. Ideoque reddit Beza priorem (πολυμερῶς) multis vicibus, alii malunt, multipartite, vel multis partibus. Sy- rus interpretatur utramque omnibus partibus, omnibus formis, sive quod particulam universa- lem non præcise intelligat, ut Junius notat, Ebræorum consuetudine, sive quod indiset, omnibus partibus, omnibusque formis, quas Deus temporum istorum ante CHRISTUM exhi- bitum revelationi convenire judicabat, locutum esse Deum per Prophetas, ut nulla pars, nulla forma revelationis divinæ, adeoque nulla pror- sus divina revelatio fuerit extra Prophetarum θεοφόρων, & ὑπὸ πνεύματος ἁγίε φερομένων mi- nisterium. Cæterum priori voce πολυμερῶς tria insinuari videntur (1) multitudo divinarum ma- nifestationum, quod non semel tantum, sed mul- tis vicibus olim locutus sit DEUS diversis tem- poribus, ut hic Grotius, (2) graduum intensionis & remissionis in divina revelatione diversitas, quod per gradus & momenta, modo obscurius, modo illustrius sese revelarir, cumprimis vero (3) revelationis mysteriorum divinorum partitio, quod non omnia, nec eadem omnibus Prophe- tis revelata sint, sed quasi partibus mysteriorum distributis, alia aliis inspirata, Esaiæ e. g. partus virginis, & passio satisfactoria Christi, Jeremiæ incarnationis mysterium, Danieli tempus ad- ventus ejus, Zachariæ locus, Malachiæ præcur- sor ejusdem, &c. ac rursum aliis plura, aliis pau- ciora.

Alteram vocem πολυτρόπως quod attinet, em- phasin in ea notat Bullingerus, & ex eo Cornelius à Lapide, qui ita habet: πολυτρόπως, id est, mul- tiformiter, quasi vertens se in varias formas, mo- dos, similitudines. Sic enim Homerus Ulyssem vocat πολύτροπον, quia versatili erat ingenio, noveratque se omni loco, tempori & personæ accommodare. Sic vertit se DEUS apud Pro- phetas in omnes formas & figuras, ut populum Ju- dæorum durum & rudem doceret, molliret & fle- cteret. Sed πολύτροπος apud Homerum homi- nem versutum & versatilem designat, quod Eu- stathius ἀπὸ τροπῆς à conversione, non à τρόπῳ seu à modo deducit; id vero DEO attribuere bonitas ejus perfectissima, & natura immuta- bilis ac simplicissima non admittit, cum apud DEUM nulla sit παραλλαγὴ ἢ τροπῆς ἀποσκία- σμα Jac. I. vers. 17. Quocirca rectius hic vocula πολυτρόπως refertur ad modi revelationum varie- tatem, quam ad DEI revelantis descriptionem: notaturque eâdem tam varietas annunciationis

Prophetica, quam revelationis Prophetis factae multiplex, & multifaria ratio. Nam ut DEUS multiplici ratione arcana revelavit, sic & Prophetae eadem πολυτρόπως ex voluntate Dei proposuerunt. Quod & de formis manifestationum diversis, & de mediis revelationum variis accipiendum. DEUS enim modo nude & aperte veluti veste detracta proposuit mysteria, & coelestem doctrinam, modo vero veluti veste operta, & per involucra exhibere voluit eandem. Ad haec apparitionum DEI variae fuerunt formae: qui Esaiae apparuit in throno excelso, circumvolutantibus Seraphim; Ezechieli in curru Cherubim, Danieli in specie antiqui dierum, Zachariae & caeteris aliis symbolis & formis. Rursus quod ad media, quorum interventu revelationes suas patefecit, varia & multiplicia ea sunt, non sermo tantum & visiones, aut apparitiones sensibiles, sed & ecstases, somnia, figurae, aenigmata, signa & symbola, sacrificia & id genus alia. E verbis Dei

Numeror. XII. versu 6. revelatio divina constitui potest tum extraordinaria, tum ordinaria. Illa vel singularis est, qualis erat, quae ceu Mosi propria & peculiaris commemoratur, aspectus nempe, ac conversationis amicae ab ore ad os: vel communis: quae subjecti ratione cum vigilantium erat, tum dormientium. Haec per somnium, illa per visionem facta dicitur: Estque visio alia externa, qualis erat rubi ardentis, Exod. III. alia interna, cum mens ipsa vidit objectum Propheticum coelesti lumine repraesentatum. (2) Modi respectu alia symbolica est, alia aperta. Symbolica fiebat tum per rerum imagines, in figura, seu idea, tum per aenigmata; ibi eadem quae videbantur, hic alia, quam quae videbantur, significata. Aperta quae ordinaria erat Num. XII. praetermittitur, ubi extraordinarias solum revelationes Prophetis factas DEUS commemorat. Est autem illa facta vel per verbum, sive internum, sive externum, sive a Deo ἀμέσως per Angelos hominibus annunciatum: vel per Urim & Thumim; de hoc posteriori genere alias actum. Quod ad prius, cum immediate DEUS loquitur, sive per sensibilem, vel imaginariam repraesentationem, ex qua conceptus nascuntur, sive per cognitionis infusionem, quae non ducit originem a sensu vel imaginatione, sed oritur immediate per lumen intellectui affusum per species intellectuales de novo inditas, aut praeexistentes etiam, sed divina virtute ad aliquem mentis conceptum formandum adhibitas vel applicatas. De illo revelationis genere, quo DEUS Prophetis locutus est per Angelos ceu legatos, nihil habetur Num. XII. vers. 6. ideoque perperam Schlichtingius h. l. in paraphrasi loci Mosaici revelationem ipsam intexit: imo nec in praesenti Apostolico textu eadem locum habere videtur, quum de loquela ipsius DEI in Prophetis variis modis facta, non vero de Angelorum DEI persona, ut vult Schlichtingius, sustinentium colloquia cum Prophetis agat.

πάλαι) מקדם. Ideo hic dicit, quia ante Christi tempora diu oracula cessaverant.

II. Tempus exprimitur voce πάλαι olim: qua id innui hoc loco vult Thomas, quod non subito, sed cum incremento temporum, ideo quia magna erant, quae de Christo dicebant, manifestata sunt: sed vox πάλαι praesenti tantum tempori opponitur, non autem festinationi, vel simultaneae revelationi. Et licet maxima fuerint, quæ de Christo proponebantur, potuissent ta- men eadem semel ac simul à Deo tradi, & ab ho- minibus credi, si DEUS ita voluisset, quemad- modum Novi Testamenti tempore à Christo fa- ctum. Innuuntur autem tria hac voce (1) Tem- poris Christi adventum antegressi respectus, quia opponitur novissimis diebus, quibus DEUS in Filio locutus est (2) Lapsus aliquot seculorum: temporibus immediate adventum CHRISTI antegressis, sed antiquis, quibus viguerunt ad- huc Prophetæ. Ideo Syrus reddidit ab initio, non creationis, sed Propheticæ manifestationis. (3) Cessatio Prophetiarum & revelationum va- riarum, uti Burgensis in annotatis ad Lyranum notat, voce OLIM innui, quod ante adventum CHRISTI per aliquod tempus jam cessaverit Prophetia.

ὁ θεὸς) III. Autor summus exprimitur ὁ θεὸς, DEUS ille Israelis, quem Ebræi venerabantur, ceu unum verum DEUM. Addit Apostolus ὁ θεὸς Autoris summi commemorationem, ut profitea- tur statim in aditu, se neutiquam intendere defe- ctionem à DEO illo vero, vel à revelationibus Mosis, & Prophetarum scriptis. Advertit hic Schlichtingius Photinianus, Deum illum sum- mum & unicum olim quidem DEUM Israelis, nunc vero DEUM & Patrem Domini JESU CHRISTI appellatum. Sed quanquam haud diffiteamur, frequentiores appellationes esse Dei Israelis in Veteri Testamento & Dei & Patris Domini nostri Jesu Christi in Novo Testamento, id tamen falsum est, quod tantum DEUS Israelis in Veteri Testamento dictus sit, nuspiam in Novo Testamento, & rursus tantum Deus & Pater Do- mini nostri Jesu Christi in Novo Testamento, nus- piam in Veteri, quod intendere videtur Schlich- tingius. Nam & in V. T. Dei Patris Jesu Christi mentio fit, 2. Sam. VII. 14. (Conf. & 1. Par. XIIX. 12. Ps. XXCIX. 27.) unde Christus Dei Filius vocatur Ps. II. 7. Prov. XXX. 4. nec aliunde, quam è V. T. demonstrat Epistola hæc, Christum esse Filium DEI, adeoque Deum esse Patrem Christi: hæc e- nim relata sunt, & se mutuo inferunt. Pariter di- citur Deus Dominus Jesu Christi sæpicule in Vet. Test. Psal. XXII. 2. Conf. Matth. XXVII. 46. Psal. XL. 6. (Conf. Ebr. X. 5.) Ps. XLV. 8. (Conf. Ebr. I. 8.) Ps. LXIX. 4. (Conf. Job. II. 17. cum v. 10. & Matth. XXVII. 34. cum v. 22. Psalm. XXCIX. 17. (Conf. 2. Sam. VII. 14. Ebr. I. 5.) &c. Rursus in Novo quoque Testamento Deus, Deus Israel in- digitatur, Matth. XV. 31. Luc. I. 16. & 68. Quod autem non ita frequens sit in libris Vet. Test. Dei Patris Jesu Christi mentio, id non inde est, quod Gratia Dei in Christo Jesu exhibita in Vet. Test. locum non habuerit, hoc enim est contra decre- tum Synodi Hierosolymitanæ, Act. XV. vers. 11. & Axioma Apostoli, Ebr. XIII. vers. 8. quum & ideo Deus Israelis potissimum dictus, quod nempe in semine Israelis benedicantur omnes gentes ter- ræ, sed quod gratia Dei in Christo Jesu luculen- tius declarata fuit, & quidem toti terrarum orbi, non tantum Israelitis, sed & gentibus, & comple- mentum promissionum in Vet. Test. factarum præstitum in Christo; unde cum Israelitæ hanc gratiæ constitutionem reprobarint, quam gentes cum tripudio acceptarint, Act. XIII. 47. non adeo Deus Israelis indigitatur in Scriptis Novi Test. nedum omnium Dominus, quod egregie expli- cat Apostolus, Rom. X. 14. seq.

Λαλήσας) IV. Actus manifestationis designatur voce λαλήσας, quæ perperam à vulgat. loquens in præsenti redditur, ideo frustra glossa ordinaria mysterium in eo quærit, quod præsens de præ- terito, nempe de Prophetis, & præteritum de præsenti positum sit, nempe de Filio, cum utro- bique in Græco Aoristus sit, præteriti significa- tionem obtinens. Quum autem dicatur locutus esse Deus multis modis, facile intelligitur λαλιὰν τοῦ Θεοῦ de omnibus istis modis revelationum divi- narum, quæ Prophetis factæ sunt, accipiendam esse. Dicitur itaq; revelatio divina, quæcunq; fue- rit & quomodocunq; facta sit λαλιὰ, sive loquela Dei, quia uti verbum & loquela nobis est medium, per quod potissimum nos animi conceptus & vo- luntatem nostram manifestamus, ita per varia ista revelationum genera id agit Deus, ut de mente & voluntate ejus constaret. Loquela verò DEI di- stingui potest in internam & externam. Interna fit vel per verbi DEI inscriptionem, Ebr. IIX. 10. vel per aliam voluntatis DEI expressionem, sive conceptuum immediatè res exhibentium, sive Symbolorum mediatè significantium, (quæ di- stinctionis causa notiones primæ vel secundæ di- ci queunt) interiori repræsentatione; quæ si fiat in vigiliis, ὀπτασία dicitur Luc. I. 22. Si vero in so- mno, ὅραμα vocatur Act. X. 17. Externa loquela seu externum Dei verbum est, tum prolatum, tum in literas relatum; Illud vel immediate fit, quo Deus vel visui objicit signum aliquod notabile, vel vo- cem articulatam auditui, sive formando eandem in aëre, sive verba in os Prophetæ ponendo; vel mediate, sive interventu ministerii Angelorum, apparentium vel vigilantibus, vel dormientibus, sive per aliorum hominum ministerium. Hoc verò est scriptum DEI verbum. Nam & de Scripturis verbum λαλεῖν occurrit Act. II. 31. cap. III. 21. 24. 1. Cor. II. 6. VII. 13. IX. 8. 2. Cor. XI. 23. XII. 19. XIII. 3. Et per Scripturas Deus, & Prophetæ ejus nobis loquuntur, & nos cum legimus Scripturas eos audire dicimur, Actor. XIII. 27. Ebr. III. 7. & 15. IV. 7. Luc. XVI. 29. Hic intelliguntur omnes istæ λαλιαὶ, quibus Deus Prophetis locutus est, præsertim verò internè; & procul dubio eas ma- xime respicit Apostolus, quibus de Christo ceu primario Prophetarum scopo locutus est Deus, utpote de quibus in universa Epistola agere con- stituerat.

Τοῖς πατράσιν.

Nempe Hebræorum, ad quos est hic sermo.

V. Objectum, ad quos per Prophetas locutus est, exprimit sequens vocula τοῖς πατράσιν Patri- bus, quo nomine complectuntur quoque nonnulli Patriarchas, sed illis non locutus est DEUS per Prophetas; sed vel immediate αὐτοπροσώπως, vel mediante Angelorum ministerio, ideoque intelli- gimus potius majores Ebræorum, qui tempori- bus Prophetarum, per quos locutus est Deus, vi- xerunt. Nomen enim Patrum ex Ebræorum mo- re majores quosvis designat, Ps. XXII. 5. Ps. CVI. 6. &c. Joh. IV. 20. Ebr. III. 9. IIX. 9. &c.

Ἐν τοῖς προφήταις.

Per Prophetas populo exponentes ea, quæ diximus.

VI. Denique autores intermedios, quorum ope- ra & interventu Deus Patribus quondam locu- tus est, indigitat: ἐν τοῖς προφήταις: in Prophetis, particula ἐν, uti & præfixum ב, quod hic Syrus adhibet, solet interdum æquipollere præpositio- ni διὰ seu per, ut Numer. XII. vers. 2. בְּמשֶׁה per Mosen locutus est Jehovah, annon etiam בָנוּ per nos. Ita hic in Prophetis, id est, per Prophetas loquutus dicitur Deus ad populum Israeliticum. Ita Scho- lia Græca, ut & Ambrosius & Chrysostomus, ἐν διὰ in pro per accipiunt. Cæterum innuitur simul tum inhabitatio Dei singularis in Prophetis, uti

Matth. X. vers. 20. de Apostolis dicit Christus, non vos estis loquentes, sed Spiritus Patris vestri lo- quens in vobis, qui etiam inhabitat vos singulari modo, & simul in vobis, & per vos loquitur; tum interior revelatio, vel suggestio, qua indidit vel manifestavit Prophetis interius, quod proferre debebant ad populum exterius, quod David ait, 2. Sam. XXIII. vers. 2. Spiritus Domini loquutus est בִּי, in me, hoc est, in corde meo locutus est prius, quicquid per me deinde protulit: nam interiores animi conceptùs, ordine naturæ priores sunt ex- ternis verborum symbolis, & verba repræsen- tant ea, quæ intus sunt in animo. Non refraga- mur támen, si quis ad externum quoque verbum id referat, quia per externas quoque apparitio- nes, & manifestationes DEUS loquitur in cor, seu cordibus, cum penetret verbum animum, & sanè prius ad animum admiserunt Prophetæ manifestationes divinitus factas, quæcunque illæ fuerint, quam ad extra eas protulêre, populoque exposuêre. Non enim prophetabant nescii ut Cajaphas, Johan. XI. vers. 51. Itaque omnis re- velatio Prophetarum in Prophetis facta per in- formationem persuasionis internam, qua Deus etiam externis mediis adhibitis interius eosdem instruxit, &c. Porrò Prophetarum nόmine in- telligúntur ii, qui Prophetæ speciatim appellan- tur, erantque non tantum enunciatores verbo- rum DEI, ut vocat eos August. Quæst. XVII. in Exod. sed divini Spiritus afflatu loquentes, qui futura vaticinabantur, quæ impleri oporteret, ut Justin. in Tryphon. eos describit è Deuteronom. XIX. vers. 22. & 2. Petr. I. vers. 21. præcipue ve- rò, qui de Christo prophetabant, quæ & impleta credimus, & impleri cernimus, & implenda con- fidimus, dicente Augustino lib. VII. de Civitate DEI cap. XXXII. Nam uti totius Scripturæ Sacræ objectum primarium est CHRISTUS, adeoque legis universæ finis constituitur Roman. X. vers. 4. ita & Prophetæ omnes testimonium de' eo perhibuêre, Act. X. vers. 43. & quæ in Pro- phetarum scriptis continentur, omnia vel de Chri- sto, vel propter Christum dicta esse ait Augusti- nus L. XII. contra Faust. cap. VII. Idcirco docet Petrus, Prophetas scrutatos & vaticinatos esse de futura gratia & temporibus Novi Testamen- ti 1. Epistola I. 10. 11. & Actor. III. vers. 24. testa- tur, omnes Prophetas à Samuele usque & deinceps, quotquot loquuti sunt, de hisce diebus prædixisse. Quod autem Petrus seriem Prophetarum ordia- tur à Samuele, inde est, quod non modò ante Samuelem ita non viguerint Prophetæ, ubi ser- mo Dei pretiosus erat, & rara vaticinia, 1. Sam. III. vers. 2. sed & quia Prophetæ summi ac emi- nentissimi Mosis antea induxerat testimonium, ideoque jam addit eidem ὁμόψηφα reliquorum omnium Prophetarum suffragia, quum ut ille, vel unicus erat ante Samuelem Propheta specia- tim dictus, vel certe unus instar omnium haberi poterat, ita qui deinceps à Samuele ordine con- secuti sunt, Prophetæ omnes pariter cum Mose, Prophetarum Antesignano, de Christo vaticinati sint.

Dubium autèm non est, hîc Mosen numero Prophetarum comprehendi, per quos locutus est DEUS Patribus. Proinde statim in ipso ingressu Moses in ordinem redigitur eorum, qui CHRISTO sunt minores; quod tamen A- postolus tacitè facit, ac tantum sub nomine ge- nerali, ne in limine nonnulli offenderentur. Et extendunt hic plerique Prophetarum denomi- nationem usque ad Patriarchas, qui de manife- statione DEI inde ab origine mundi hic sermonem esse arbitrantur. Quorum sententiam juvare videtur, quod Abraham Gen. XX. vers. 7. Propheta dicatur, (Confer. Psalm. CV. vers. 15.) ubi non ideo nomen hoc ei assignatur, quod ut Propheta sciret, uxorem suam ab Abimelecho intactam, ut Junius annotat ad h. l. Id enim quà Propheta scire non poterat; nec saltim ea ratione Propheta indigitari videtur à Deo, prout generaliter præcones verbi divini sic vocantur; sed speciali quoque sensu, quia ex Dei revelatione multa futura noverit, atque prædixerit, utpote filium ex Sara sterili sibi nasciturum, Messiam è semine suo oriturum, & in eodem omnes gentes terræ benedictum iri, posteros suos in Ægypto servituros, generatione quarta ex ea servitute liberandos, & in terram Canaan introducendos &c. Interim post Mosen Prophetarum Coryphæum in Nov. Testam. plerumque collocantur Prophetæ speciatim, & propriè ita dicti, ac Prophetarum series inchoatur, à Samuele, Autore Petro, nec alius facile in Novo Testamento locus reperitur, uti Prophetarum nomen, cum de Prophetis Veteris Testamenti sermo est, ea usurpatur amplitudine, ut Patriarchis quoque conveniat, sed potius de iis, qui Ebræis dicuntur Prophetæ tum ראשונים, seu priores, tum אחרונים, sive posteriores, hoc est, qui Mosen secuti, usque ad scissionem regni Israelitici, & qui post scissionem decem tribuum à cæteris floruere. Ideò præferendam potius censent nonnulli eam interpretationem, quâ de Prophetis illis accipitur præsens locus: Si quis autem urgeat Act.

III. vers. 25. Prophetarum filios dici posteros Patriarcharum, quod nonnullis videtur: respondent, Prophetarum filios ibi non aliter dici, quam dicuntur testamenti, seu fœderis filios, hoc est, non naturâ, sed culturâ, non propagatione, sed informatione, & hæreditate, vel communione; quod Israelitæ illi sint, quibus peculiariter destinati erant Prophetæ, & quibuscum fœdus sancitum, ex Ebraismo usitato. Cæterum nostro judicio ad mentem Apostoli propius accedunt, qui etiam ad Patriarchas extensum hic volunt Prophetarum nomen; & universam revelationem divinam ante Christum exhibitum factam hic complectuntur, quod plerisque interpretibus probari video: quemadmodum & Beatus Dorscheus, Intelliguntur autem, inquit in Comment. inchoato, & ἀνεκδότῳ, per Prophetas omnes immediatè illuminati, ut 2. Petr. I. Propheticus sermo, & Prophetia, vers. 19. 20. 21. est omne verbum θεόπνευστον. Itaque Patriarchæ ante- & post-diluviani Moses fundator & legislator Reip. Israel, & cæteri. Quo pacto David Pareus quadruplicem assignat varietatem, quæ hic indicata sit pro diversis ætatibus & temporibus revelationis divinæ, I. Ante diluvium, quâ prima rudimenta tradita. II. Ante legem, quâ Abrahæ promissiones aliquantò illustriores datæ. III. Post legem, vel sub lege, institutâ ulteriori doctrinâ Ecclesiæ & Reipubl. forma: quam denique IV. variis vicibus & partibus cumulavit ac perfecerit, usque ad Malachiæ tempora. Ut enim illud πάλαι olim ad omnia tempora ante exhibitum Messiam extenditur, ut Patrum nomen ad Patres quos cunque, etiam primos parentes, sese porrigit, quum nulla sit restrictio, ut loquutio variis modis, & partibus facta à DEO amplissimè sonat, & adæquatè novissimæ loquutioni in Filio factæ contradiftinguitur: ita vox Prophetarum eâ etiam amplitudine accipienda, quæ conveniat autori- bus patefactionis divinæ intermediis quibusque, qui ad Patres & Majores, vel antecessores eorum pertinent, inde à prima de Messia revelatione. Nam & in Patriarchis primis Deus πολυμερῶς & πολυτρόπως loquutus est ad Ecclesiam domesticam: & Patres amplissimè intelligi possunt, secus atque Schlichtingius existimat, qui sub Patriarchis ad Ecclesiam DEI pertinuêre, vel ad eandem vocati sunt, & illi, qui propriè, & propius majores Ebræorum fuêre. Duo autem ex hisce colliguntur. I. Eloquium per Prophetas ad homines factum notare ministerium Prophetarum extraordinarium ad propagandam vel restaurandam Ecclesiam. II. Canone Veter. Testament. constituto donum Propheticum & extraordinariæ illuminationis circa res fidei usque ad Christum cessasse.

Ἐπ’ ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν τύτων.

Id est, tandem nunc. Vide Actor. II. vers. 17. 2. Timoth. III. vers. 1. In Manuscripto est ἐπ’ ἐσχάτυ τῶν ἡμερῶν τύτων, quomodo Num. XXIV. 14. Ezech. XXXVIII. 16.

Ἐλάλησεν ἡμῖν ἐν ὑῖῷ.

Locutus nobis est per Filium, res maximas & cœlestes non servis credidit, sed Filio. Vide Matth. XXI. 37. Johan. I. 18. III. 16. Joh. XV. 15. 1. Petr. I. 10.

Alterum hic est partis prioris τῆς προθέσεως de Doctore vel Propheta magno membrum, quo exhibetur status præsentis collatio vel oppositio ratione manifestationis divinæ olim factæ: Quod membrum connectitur à Syro particulâ copulativâ, sed sensu adversativo, quemadmodum sensu variare solet, usitatissimo Ebraismo, accipienda, quæ in Græco non exprimitur. Continetque (1) Modum, (2) Tempus, (3) Autorem, (4) Actum, (5) Objectum, (6) Internuncium ejusdem, quorum membrorum nonnulla disertè exprimuntur: Reliqua vero partim ἀπὸ κοινῷ repetuntur, partim ex antithesi colligenda relinquuntur.

Quod itaque I. ad modum manifestationis divinæ in Nov. Test. per Christum factæ, is non exprimitur, sed ἀντιθετικῶς colligitur è descriptione revelationis Propheticæ. Nimirum quemadmodum illa 1. πολυμερῶς & per vices, ac secundum intensionis & remissionis diversos gradus, & κατὰ μέρη, seu per partes facta est: ita ex adverso manifestatio in Christo ἐφάπαξ καὶ σαφῶς semel & aperte, vel ἐσχάτως μονοειδῶς postremo & uniformiter contigit, adeoque unica haberi debet, ultimò facta. Idque tum luculentissimè, tum plenissime, quoad omnes ac singulas partes, ut nec alia ulla, nedum luculentior aut perfectior expectanda sit in Ecclesia Dei in his terris constituta usque ad consummationem seculi. (2) Quemadmodum πολυτρόπως multis modis locutus est DEUS, tum ad Prophetas, tum per Prophetas, ad Patres, seu populum variis adhibitis revelationum formis & mediis: ita in Novo Testamento uniformis & eadem est loquela, qua DEUS non per Symbola, per signa, ecstases, somnia, figuras, ænigmata, sacrificia, typos, visiones, Urim & Thumim, & id genus alia, sed apertà voce locutus est in Filio. Eadem porrò doctrina Christi uniformis, qualis primum per ipsum Dominum in carne facta est, post per eos, qui Dominum audierunt, propagata, Ebr. II. 3. Durabit, & in Ecclesia propagabitur, nec expectandus ullus alius revelationis divinæ modus externus hisce temporibus.

II. Tempus hac periphrasi notatur ἐπ’ ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν τύτων. Complutens. Codex legit ἐπ’ ἐπ’ ἐσχά- ἐσχάτυ. Unde gemina interpretatio: Syrus reddit ܒܝܘܡܬܐ ܗܪܝܐ novissi- novissimis diebus istis, juxta priorem lectionem; | Vulgatus autem, novissimè diebus istis, juxta po- | steriorem: quasi in novissimo, seu extremo die- | rum istorum. Priorem tamen potiorem, adeo- | que versioni vulgatæ anteponendam censet E- | stius Pontificius. Dicitur autem dies pro tempo- | re Synecdoche scripturis familiari, Psalm. XIIX. | vers. 19. Psalm. CII. vers. 12. Es. IV. vers. 1. Matth. | XII. vers. 1. Ebr. IIX. vers. 8. 10. &c. Novissimi | autem non tantum respectu temporis ante acti, | dicuntur, ut Schlichtingius reddit, in extremo | dierum istorum, sed etiam ratione instantis finis | temporum, quia licet respectus habeatur ad vo- | cem πάλαι; involvit tamen illa oppositio & | terminum, seu extremum diem præteritorum, & | finem sive terminum dierum omnium. Nam no- | vissimi dies, novissima hora, vel novissima tem- | pora Scripturæ dicuntur, post quæ aliud nihil | expectandum, quam finis & terminus mundi, & | adventus Christi Judicis, utpote quibus adven- | tu primo Christus omnium Prophetiarum com- | plementum attulerit. Solent enim tempora Mes- | siæ dici novissima simpliciter; eaque phrasi desi- | gnatum in Scripturis aut tempus ipsum adven- | tus Messiæ, aut universum tempus post exhibi- | tum Christum usque ad finem mundi. Confer. | Es. II. vers. 2. Joel. II. vers. 28. 31. Mich. IV. v. 1. | Actor. II. v. 17. Ubi quod Prophetæ novissimos | dies vocant tempus adventus Messiæ, accipi qui- | dem poterit ratione temporis istius, quod novis- | simis diebus demum, & in extremo Prophetia- | rum omnium venire debuerat, quod & finem | legi adferebat, & politiæ Judaicæ, præcipuè ta- | men tempora Messiæ seu Christi exhibiti & Novi | Testamenti tempora novissima vocantur, partim | ratione manifestationis gratiæ novissimæ in Christo | factæ, quod in Vet. quidem Testamento una re- | velatio exceperit aliam, unus Propheta succes- | serit alteri, at in Novo Testamento revelatio- | ne per Christum facta nulla sit expectanda am- | plius: partim ratione apparitionis gloriæ in no- | vissimo die jam instantis, quia ut habet Eliæ | Levitæ vaticinium, tempora Messiæ ultima sunt, | unde & Johannes, Filioli, hora jam est novis- | sima, 1. Epist. II. vers. 18. & Apostolus in nostra | Epistola non dubitat, hoc tempus, quo Chri- | stus sese obtulit, dicere συντελείαν τῶν αἰώνων, | consummationem seculi, cap. IX. vers. 26. diemque | illum novissimum ἐγγίζοσαν, seu jam appropin- | quantem indigitat cap. X. vers. 25. quia ἐτὶ μικρὸν | ὅσον brevi vel intra breve temporis spatium adve- | niet Christus ad judicium, cap. X. vers. 37. Conf. | 1, Corinth. X. 11. & 1. Petr. IV. 7. adeoque adver- | tit Chrysostomus & Theophylactus hoc pacto Pau- | lum simul excitare Ebræos ad spem & constan- | tiam in certaminibus & afflictionibus, pro fide | Christi sustinendis. Certator enim, etsi hebetior | sit, cum tamen intelligit certamen propemodum ter- | minatum jam iri, parumper respirat, & vires refu- | mit, quod & laboris instare finem, ac quietis & præ- | mii tempus præsto esse cognoscat.

III. Quis locutus sit novissimis temporibus, è priori membro constat: nempe idem ille DEUS, qui olim locutus est in Vet. Testam. ex quo colli- gitur, eundem esse autorem revelationis Veteris & Novi Testamenti, DEUM scilicet illum verum & summum. Quemadmodum enim locutus est DEUS in Prophetis ad Patres, cum prædicarunt, ita etiam, quæ scriptis consignarunt, & per scri- pturas populo proposuerunt, DEO loquente in ipsis, seu per revelationem & inspirationem divinam consignasse, & proposuisse, credendum est. Quum itaque idem ille DEUS manifesta- tionis in Novo Testamento factæ autor sit, quæ scriptis Novi Testamenti comprehensa conti- netur, dubium nullum est, eodem autore pro- fectam esse Scripturam Veteris & Novi Testa- menti; Ideoque in hac identitate, ut Burgens. ait in addit. ad Lyran. refutantur duo errores, scilicet Manichæorum & Judæorum. Manichæi enim antiquum Testamentum attribuebant ma- lo principio, novum vero bono: Judæi verò è converso antiquum Testamentum dicebant esse à DEO, novum autem non, unde utrumque er- rorem refutans Apostolus, asserit prædictam identitatem. Ex hac autem repetitione vocis manifestum est, eandem hic ὑποστατικῶς seu per- sonaliter accipi de DEO Patre, quia dicitur lo- cutus DEUS in Filio. Cæterum DEUM con- stituit autorem revelationis in Novo Testamento factæ, ut statim in autoris & Canonicæ autorita- tis fastigium eandem elevat, & omnia, quæ à Christo Apostolis prædicata sunt, ἀξιόπιστα, καὶ ἀυτόπιστα esse doceat. Proinde, cum non minus à DEO profecta sit revelatio novissima, quàm Prophetica manifestatio, utique minimè oppo- nere debebant Ebræi, geminam istam revelatio- nem, ac revelationem hanc novissimam alie- nam judicare ab antiqua illa DEI revelatione, quum DEUS sibi ipsi adversus esse nequeat. Denique animum ita quoque addit afflictis E- bræis, quod perinde uti Patres vel Majores ipso- rum gaudeant revelatione, & loquela DEI ad ipsos facta, eaque feliciores sint, immediatis pro- genitoribus, & illis è majoribus suis, qui cessante Prophetia nullam habuere immediatam revela- tionem divinam.

IV. Actus manifestationis exprimitur iterum per loquelam ἐλάλησεν. Manifestavit sese Deus in Vet. Testam. per loquelam. Sed λαλιὰ DEI, quia tum πολύτροπος erat, non tantum comple- ctitur propriè ita dictam loquelam, sed quamvis voluntatis divinæ significationem, & repræsenta- tionem: hic autem in Novo Testamento, ubi μονότροπος est, eum designat actum, quo Deus in CHRISTO sese nobis manifestavit, quod respectu nostri tantum factum est per Verbum propriè ita dictum, non autem per varia Sym- bola, quæ per analogiam saltem proportionis ver- bi divini nomine veniunt. Sed quî locutus est DEUS in Filio, quum Filius ipse sit דבר יהוה: Psalm. XXXIII. vers. 6. 1. Sam. VII. v. 20. 2. Pa- ralip. XVII. vers. 19. & ὁ λόγος, Verbum DEI, Johan. I. vers. 1. 2. 14. 1. Joh. I. vers. 1, cap. V. v. 7. Apocal. XIX. vers. 13? Resp. Quia Filius Dei est Verbum non προφορικὸν, sed ὑποστατικὸν sive sub- stantiale, idemque est Propheta ille magnus, Ev- angelista, & Præceptor populorum, Deut. XIIX. 15. Es. XLI. 27. cap. LV. 4.

V. Objectum ἡμῖν nobis, restringit Chrysosto- mus ad Apostolos: Sed Paulus intelligit Ebræos, quibus sese accenset. Oppositio est Ebræorum, ad quos scribit Apostolus, & Patrum, quod non minus gratia nunc Ebræis, quàm eorum majoribus olim exhibita sit. Loquitur autem ita Apostolus veluti audiverint Ebræi, ad quos scribit, ipsummet Christum ἀυτοπροσώπως do- centem, tum quod ipsorum tempore locutus est, ut ab iisdem audiri potuerit, tum quod in Apo- stolorum scriptis loquens audiatur ab ipsis, quo posteriori sensu adhuc nobis loquitur Deus in Filio.

VI. Denique Internuncius voce ἐν ὑιῷ expri- mitur: Aliter autem in Filio, aliter in Prophetis locutus est. Prophetæ tantum fuerunt legati, servi, non autores doctrinæ. Filius legatus Dominus, & autor ipse doctrinæ. In Prophetis locutus est DEUS, quia singulariter ipsis Spi- ritu suo præsto fuit; in Filio, quia in eo habitat corporaliter tota plenitudo Deitatis, Coloss. II. vers. 9. In Prophetis superveniens eosdem ex- traordinariè, quando voluit, revelavit iis, quæ loqui debuêre. In Filio : quia Filius in Patre, & Pater in Filio per essentialem περιχώρησιν, & existens in sinu Patris, eum manifestat nobis, Johan. I. vers. 18. In Prophetis locutus est Spi- ritus ipsius CHRISTI, qui in ipsis erat, 1. Pet. I. vers. 11. nec quicquam sciverunt Prophetæ, nisi quod revelavit ipsis Filius : quia nemo novit Patrem, nisi Filius, & cui vult Filius revelare, Matth. XI. vers. 27. Filius misit Prophetas, Luc. XI. vers. 49. Matth. XXIII. vers. 34. & instituit eosdem ceu Sapientia DEI substantialis, Prov. I. vers. 21. cap. IX. vers. 32. Ideo locutus esse dici- tur DEUS in Filio ceu sapientia hypostaticâ, & splendore gloriæ, ac charactere substantiæ suæ, non autem ut personâ separatâ extrà DEUM. Por- ro Filius opponitur Prophetis : Quia licet Filius DEI etiam Prophetæ, & ratione Prophetici mu- neris nobis locutus sit, non tamen est è commu- ni Prophetarum numero, sed κατ' ἐξοχὴν ma- gnus ille Prophetæ, Deuteronom. XIIX. vers. 15. & Prophetarum reliquorum Dominus, à quo illi missi sunt, Luc. XI. vers. 49. Esa. VI. vers. 8. Confer. Johan. XII. vers. 41. 42. quique non tan- tum est internuncius voluntatis divinæ, sed cum DEO Patre unus idemque verbi divini auctor, 2. Sam. XXIII. vers. 3. 4. idcircò verbum DEI di- citur verbum τῦ κυρίε, Actor. IIX. vers. 25. XIII. vers. 48. 49. XV. vers. 36. XIX. vers. 20. 1. Thessal. I. vers. 8. 2. Thess. II. vers. 1. τῦ κυρίε τῦ Χριςῦ, ut exprimitur Apocal. XIX. vers. 10. Col. III. vers. 16. 1. Timoth. VI. vers. 3. Rursus licet Prophetæ quo- que fuerint Filii DEI, discrimen tamen infinitum est inter Prophetas, & Christum Filium DEI. Illi Filii per adoptionem, hic per naturam. Illi spirituali regeneratione, hic æterna generatione. Illi per quandam τῆς θείας φύσεως κοινωνίαν, eam- que merè gratiosam, 2. Petr. I. vers. 4. hic vero καθ' ἑνότητα τῆς ὐσίας quoad essentialem cum Patre unitatem, Joh. X. v. 30.

Nec est, quod Socinus ex eo, quod DEUS in Filio loquutus dicitur, colligat, Filium non esse Deum. Distinctio enim personalis Patris & Filii non est opponenda unitati essentiali : nec bræpositio ἐν necessario aliquam inferioritatem vel causæ instrumentalis respectum infert. Nam & in Patre Filius esse dicitur, Johan. XVII. v. 21. nec tamen Pater inferior est, sed περιχώρησις no- tatur essentialis : & in Spiritu S. miracula patra- vit Filius, Matth. XII. v. 48. Spiritum S. autem inferiorem esse Filio non admittunt adversarii. Et observatum antea, aliter DEUM in Filio lo- quutum, aliter in Prophetis. Denique hic in Fi- lio non ἀσάρκῳ, sed ἐνσάρκῳ loquutus innuitur : quia per humanam naturam facta est novissima manifestatio, secundum quam etiam Filius DEI constitutus est κληρονόμς πάντων. Frustra pro- inde sunt, qui cum Calixto omnes apparitiones Filii DEI in Vet. Test. hisce verbis tolli nu- gantur : quod nempe demum in novissimis die- bus locutus sit nobis in Filio DEUS. Illustrio- res certè sunt λογοφανείαι, quam ut in dubium vocari possint, quibus DEI Filius visus & locu- tus est cumprimis Patriarchis, aliisque fideli- bus Veteris Testamenti; utpote Hagaræ con- solator, Genes. XVI. vers. 17. seq. Abrahæ Con- vivator, Genes. XIIX. Isaaci Sospitator, Genes. XXII. vers. 11. seq. Jacobi Sponsor, Gen. XXIX. vers. 13. qui & ejusdem Antagonista & luctator, Genes. XXXII. vers. 24. & Redemptor, Genes. XLIIX. versu 16. Mosis Dominus, populique Ductor, Exod. III. versu 34. cap. XIX. versu 3. XXIII. vers. 20. Israelitici Exercitus Princeps & defensor, Jos. V. vers. 13. Gedeonis opitula- tor, Jud. VI. vers. 12. Quomodo ergò novissimis demum temporibus per Filium loquutus est? Advertenda hic sequentia: (1) Opponuntur non tam Patriarcharum tempora, & Messiæ, quàm Prophetarum & Novi Testamenti tempora, se- cundum Schlichtingium. Licet ergò Patriar- charum tempore apparuerit, tamen respectu temporis Prophetarum in novissimo dierum lo- cutus rectè dicitur. (2) ΛόγοΦανείαι in Veteri Testamento fuêre 1) Typi adumbrantes novissi- mam manifestationem. 2) Præludia ἐνανθρωπή- σεως. 3) Extraordinariæ, & particulares, paucis factæ. At in Novo Testamento omnibus DEUS manifestatus in carne, & Filius DEI caro factus est: Verum corpus & substantia typorum suc- cessit, eaque manifestatio fuit œcumenica & uni- versalis, simul & perfecta atque ordinaria, us- que ad diem novissimum. Proinde (3) distin- gui inter λόγον ἄσαρκον, qui in Veteri Testa- mento etiam sese manifestavit, utut interdum visibili forma assumta ad tempus οἰκονομικῶς, non tamen ὑποσατικῶς sibi unita carne, quæ fuit no- vissima manifestatio: Sed παρασατικῶς, quæ πρόσκαιρος, & temporaria tantum fuit formæ visibilis assumptio, qualis etiam ab Angelis fa- cta. Itaque hìc DEUS novissimè loquutus di- citur in Filio, nempe in carne manifestato, 1. Ti- moth. III. vers. 16. & inter homines conversante, atque Evangelium prædicante post suam ἐνσάρ- κωσιν, Johan. I. versu 14. Quandoquidem tum Pater locutus sit ad homines per Filium suum, uti is conversabatur ut verus homo inter homi- nes, & ceu Verbum caro factum DEUM enar- ravit Joh. I. 18.

De Filio ergò DEI manifestato in carne, in quo & per quem novissimis diebus locutus est Ebræis DEUS, ut Doctoris hujus Novi Testamenti eminentiam sistat, ulterius hic agit Apostolus, personam ejus describens, tum quoad naturam humanam, tum quoad divi- nam. Illius ratione hæredem constitutum ipsum dicit omnium; hujus verò respectu, per eum condidisse DEUM secula ait. Naturam au- tem humanam ista περιφράσει potius, quam ex- presso nomine designare voluit. Nam homi- nem fuisse CHRISTUM gratiæ divinæ præ- conem Novissimum quid intererat, ita nudè commemorare, cum id ipsum neque dubium fuerit ulli, neque ad dignitatem Revelationis novissimæ quicquam facere videretur. Ideoque potius περιφράσει illa usus est, imprimis quia non tam CHRISTUM Hominem propone- re constituit, quoad ipsam naturam nudè spe- ctatam, quàm quoad statum tum Exinanitionis, tum Exaltationis, quæ non parum auctoritatis & dignitatis revelationi novissimæ conciliabat. Quocirca CHRISTUM dicit à DEO hæ- redem omnium constitutum, quod ratione na- turæ humanæ ei competere certum est, quæ so- la diversos admittit status, & cui facta erat pro- missio hæreditatis omnium post exinanitionem præviam', non autem ratione divinæ naturæ, quæ non per gratiosam DEI Patris constitutio- nem, sed per omnipotentem rerum omnium crea- tionem possidebat omnia. Divina porro natu- ra Filii DEI hic insinuatur, cum per eum secula creata dicuntur; quandoquidem CHRISTUS mundi Creator sit quà DEUS, seu ratione di- vinæ naturæ, vi cujus obtigit quoque CHRI- STO homini hæreditas omnium. Si enim CHRISTUS natura ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος, nudus homo esset, non autem simul in unitate personæ verus natura DEUS, rerum omnium Creator, naturæ humanæ respectu, quippe à DEO sepa- ratæ, nunquam potuisset hæreditatem rerum omnium aut adipisci, aut administrare, utpote ad quam divina & infinita requiritur sapientia & potentia. Describit autem Apostolus divinam naturam CHRISTI à seculorum creatione, ea potissimum de causa, quod temporum præteri- torum quondam, & novissimorum instituerit σύγκρισιν, quodque novissimis diebus Filium in carne manifestatum nobis locutum esse testatus fuerit, proinde ut dignitatem revelationis hujus demonstret, Filium non solum hæredem esse constitutum omnium, sed & omnium rerum, ipsorumque seculorum & temporum auctorem, & conditorem esse docet, idque ulterius confir- mare suscipit. Quocirca constitutum est Apo- stolo de CHRISTO agere, vero DEO, vero- que homine, qui ut DEUS creavit secula, ut homo constitutus est hæres omnium, ejusque su- premam demonstrare dignitatem, quam obtinet tum κατὰ φύσιν, per naturam, ceu verus DEUS universi Creator, tum κατὰ χάριν, per gratiam, ceu verus homo ad hæreditatem rerum omnium evectus.

## 1:2
Vers. 2. Ὃν ἔθηκε κληρονόμον πάντων. (Whom he appointed heir of all things.)

That is, Lord. For among the Latins, heir (hæres) is the same as master (herus). Christ, raised to heaven, is Lord of all things, this right having been received from the Father, Eph. 1:20, 22; 1 Cor. 15:27. Thus below 2:8. To the Fathers a terrestrial and perishable inheritance was given, to Christ a heavenly and eternal one; here is a more sublime sense, Psalm 2 and 8.

In this description, one must look both to the subject and to the predicate. The subject is the Son, the predicate is he whom GOD has placed as heir of all things. Now the Son is understood not ἄσαρκος (without flesh), but ἔνσαρκος (in the flesh), not to be exhibited in the flesh, but exhibited and manifested in the flesh: because the discourse is about the Son, who in the last days appeared and spoke to us: the relative pronoun ὃν (whom) therefore points to him. But since there are two natures in the Son exhibited in the flesh, divine and human, from which nature the predicate is to be taken is to be learned not so much from the subject itself as from the attribute or predicate. Which is, that he has been constituted by GOD as heir of all things: in the unfolding of which one must look I. to GOD who constitutes. II. to the act of constitution. III. to the right, dignity, and privilege of the inheritance to which he has been constituted. IV. finally to the object or limit of the inheritance, or even the territory, which is the whole universe.

I. The GOD constituting Christ as heir is he whom he commemorated in the previous verse, ὁ Θεὸς, that God: which name here designates GOD the Father ὑποστατικῶς (hypostatically): as he to whom the Son of GOD was accustomed to refer all his things, as the author and principle from whom he himself also obtains his origin and being. Which, however, is not to be understood ἐκκλειστικῶς or exclusively, by excluding the other persons of the Holy Trinity, because the constitution and designation of CHRIST as heir of all things is a work common and undivided to the whole Holy Trinity: nor is it to be understood ἐξοχικῶς or eminently, because where there is supreme equality and identity of essence, there no ἐξοχὴ (pre-eminence) has a place, but πηγαίως κῂ οἰκονομικῶς (fountain-wise and economically): because GOD the Father is the source and origin of the other persons, and because the Father sent the Son into the world, and raised him up, and exalted him to the right hand of Majesty.

II. The act of constitution is noted by the word ἔθηκε: concerning which these four things are to be explained: (1) That he was not constituted from eternity, but in time. (2) At what time. (3) According to which nature, and (4) how he was constituted heir. As to

(1) The word ἔθηκε denotes not preordination and decree, but actual constitution and the execution of the decree, because the discourse is about CHRIST the Son of GOD manifested in the last times, and the explanation or confirmation of the proposition in verse 13 and chapter 2:8 teaches that it concerns that constitution by which, having been exalted to the right hand of GOD, all things are made subject to him. Therefore, as regards that threefold mode by which Pareus says in this place that CHRIST was constituted heir of all things: (a) by eternal ordination to the office of Mediator, 1 Pet. 1:20, (β) by mission into the flesh, and the heavenly command, 'hear him,' (γ) by exaltation to the right hand of Majesty in the heavens: only the last is understood here. The first is foreign, because it is not a question here of the ordination to the office of Mediator, or of the predestination of the spotless lamb, but rather of the constitution to the royal office, since the Son is constituted heir, that is, the proprietary Lord of all creatures in heaven and on earth, as Pareus explains; which is far foreign to his mediatorial office, by which he is the unique Mediator between GOD and men, giving himself as ἀντίλυτρον for us, 1 Timothy II, verse 6. The other mode also, the mission into the flesh, with the heavenly proclamation, 'hear him,' is irrelevant here, because it pertains to the Prophetic office.

As to (2) at what time CHRIST was constituted heir? Although CHRIST was King and Lord from the beginning of his conception and birth, as the Angel testifies in Luke II, verse 11, and the Prophet Isaiah in chapter IX, verse 6, yet here it is a question of the possession of the Kingdom and dominion, and of the fuller administration, which he obtained through his exaltation to the right hand of GOD, concerning which Peter also discourses in Acts II, verse 36, pronouncing that he, whom the Jews crucified, was made Lord and CHRIST; by which words Estius, in this place, struggles wrongly and foolishly to prove the contrary, that CHRIST is said to be made heir, insofar as he was born Lord and King. Whereas it is clearer than the midday sun that Peter in the Acts is discoursing about the exaltation to the right hand of GOD, and demonstrating from Psalm CX, verse 1, that he who had previously been crucified by the Jews was made Lord and CHRIST. That this is also intended here from verse 3 and 13, is most manifest; since he is likewise said to be constituted heir, in that he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty of God on high, according to the prediction of the Holy Spirit in Psalm CX, here likewise brought forward as a demonstration and explained concerning Christ. In the state of humiliation, indeed, he professed that all things were delivered into his hands, John III, verse 35, XIII, verse 3, Matthew XI, verse 27, and he was Lord from his birth; but that lay hidden in his humiliation, whereas in his exaltation it was most clearly revealed, Matthew XXVIII, verse 19, and it will be revealed even more sublimely at his second coming and the resurrection of the dead.

Furthermore, (3) it is certain that Christ is said to be appointed heir here according to his human nature: because according to his divine nature he was Lord of all, from the time he founded the ages and established the earth and formed the heavens. But because some Calvinists, especially Sadeel and others, contend that certain things apply to Christ which are to be understood only according to his person, but do not properly pertain to either of the natures, and to this they also refer the fact that Christ is called our King: it must be held here: (1) That it can be admitted that some things are said of Christ so that they do not apply to him through his natures as through primary immediate subjects, but by hypostatic reason, as when it is said that he is begotten by the Father, which belongs to the person, not the essence, since that, speaking accurately, is not begotten but communicated. (2) Moreover, it can by no means be added to these that Christ is called our King, but rather to those things which are said of Christ in such a way that they apply to him primarily and immediately through his natures, before they apply to the person himself, which must necessarily be claimed for either one or both natures, and one must by no means stop at the person alone. For this name is of an office, which does not apply to Christ according to those personal attributes which are distinguished from essential ones, such as being begotten, but applies to CHRIST rather according to both natures, according to the rule of the Council of Chalcedon. Furthermore, it is one thing to be King, another to be appointed King. Since Christ is King and Lord according to both natures; but he was appointed King through his exaltation to the right hand of God only according to his human nature. Therefore, it is worth the effort that we prove that Christ, as he is man, is said to be appointed heir here, and that by this the human nature of Christ is exhibited periphrastically. We show this by these proofs: (1) From the time of the appointment, because the Son, through whom he spoke in these last days, is said to be appointed heir of all things: and therefore it is not obscurely hinted that he was appointed in these last days, and it is a matter not of the decree, but of the execution of the decree made in time. Whatever Christ receives in time, he receives according to his humanity, to which, as he did not have it, things are conferred, as Leo says in Epistle XLI, by the consent of all antiquity. (2) From the distinction of the divine nature, for that is indeed insinuated in the following words, with the Calvinists not dissenting, and is described by the Apostle by a distinct periphrasis, as that according to which Christ is said to have founded the ages. Wherefore, since the Apostle here proposes those things which he intends to explain later: and it is undoubted that he discourses not only about the divine but also about the human nature in this Epistle, and that especially in chapter II, as if expressly, it must certainly be admitted that the human nature is insinuated here, according to which he is said to be appointed heir of all things. (3) From the concession of the inheritance: Because as God he is Lord of all not by appointment and by grace, but by the creation of all things, and by nature, or as he founded the ages and the whole universe, not in so far as he is appointed over all things by GOD. Primasius elegantly says in chapter II of Hebrews: In that he is man, he received the inheritance of the world, he was crowned with honor in the confession of eternal majesty; just as all things were created by the Word, so that man assumed by the Word possesses all things with the Word. (4) From the improvement of Christ over the Angels: For he is said to be made more excellent than the Angels, verse 4, without doubt in that respect in which he is appointed heir of all things. But that improvement, by which he was made more excellent than the Angels, applies to Christ not according to his divine nature, which is most perfect, immutable, and can in no way be made more excellent, but according to his human nature. Athanasius says in Oration 2 against the Arians: The divine nature, as being perfect and absolute, is in need of nothing: How then was he exalted, who, before he was exalted, was most high? And how did he receive what he always had before he received it? For the improvement did not come to the Word on account of the flesh, but to the flesh on account of the Word. (5) From the attainment of a more excellent name. Since it is said without controversy that he is appointed heir of all things with respect to that nature, with respect to which it is said in verse 4 that he has inherited a name far more excellent than any of the Angels: for these explain each other, when he is said to be appointed heir by GOD, and that he has inherited a more different, that is, more excellent name. Theodoret in Psalm XXI: He inherited a more excellent name for his human nature. For as GOD he is the maker of the Angels and Lord, as man he was lower than the Angels on account of the suffering of death. But after he rose again and ascended into heaven, he was made more excellent than the Angels, for he sat down above every principality. (6) From his sitting at the right hand of GOD. For he is made heir of all things, in so far as he is placed at the right hand of GOD, as is manifest from the collation of verses 3 and 13. But that applies to Christ not according to his divine, but solely according to his human nature. Athanasius in Theodoret, Dialogue 2: Those words, sit at my right hand, are said concerning the Lord's body. For if God fills all things, in what seat does he sit? It is therefore the body to which the Lord says, sit at my right hand. And Theodoret in Psalm CX: Sit at my right hand: This is great, and not only exceeds all human nature, but even the whole universe: But this also is said in a human way, for as the Son of GOD he has an everlasting empire, but as man he receives what he had as GOD; as man, therefore, he hears, sit at my right hand. (7) From the collation of his emptying and exaltation. Because he is made heir and exalted according to that nature according to which he was emptied. But he was emptied according to his human nature. Therefore he is also made heir according to his human nature. The major premise is confirmed from chapter II, 7 and 8. The minor shines with its own light. Cyril, book 8, Thesaurus. c. I. To whom humility is appropriate, this which is said about being exalted: but the thing is humble for human nature: therefore it itself is also understood to be exalted. (8) From the clarification of similar passages. Various things could be compared: But especially from the Old Testament the words of David v. 6. Ps. II. which Theophylact compares here for this reason: In what way he made him Lord, namely as man, just as in the second Psalm he addresses him in this same way: Ask of me, and I will give thee the nations for thine inheritance. He received therefore this inheritance, which as heir he asked for, or sought the same. Cf. John XVII. 5. From the N. T. we especially compare here the words of Peter Acts II. 36. by which Christ is said to have been made Lord, Peter looking to τὴν ὐσίαν τῶ λόγʋ, ἀλλὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπον, which Athanasius demonstrates at length in orat. 2. & 3. & 4. against the Arians, as also in the tract on the saving advent of Christ, and the preface to book IV against Eunomius, and Gregory Nazianzen in orat. IV on Theology. Epiphanius against heresies Vol. II. book 11. heresy LXIX. against the Arians, Ambrose Vol. III. on the death of his brother Satyrus, Gregory of Nyssa in Theodoret in Dial. 2. as well as Theophylact and Oecumenius on this passage, and they admit from the Calvinists, Pellican, Calvin himself, Beza, Marloratus on this passage, constrained by the evidence of the context: since the discourse here is about Christ according to that nature according to which he was crucified, resurrected, exalted, and enriched with the promise of the Holy Spirit, which things befit him not according to his divine, but according to his human nature. When Peter says that Christ was made by God Lord and Christ, he is not speaking of his divinity, but of his humanity. For the Logos was always Lord, he was not first made Lord after the cross, says Athanasius, Orat. 4 contr. Arian. (10) From the explanation of the orthodox Fathers. For thus the better antiquity received this inheritance of all things. Cyril, book XI on John, ch. XV: He who possesses all things as God, begins to possess all things as man, to whom reigning is adventitious, that is, not natural. Theodoret on Ps. II: As God he has an innate kingdom, as man he receives it by decree. Idem: Since he is Lord by nature as God, he also receives the empire of all things as man; and on Ps. XXI: He is the maker of all things as God, the heir of all things as man. Vigil, book V against Eutych. According to the nature of the flesh he was exalted, honored, crowned, and attained the dignity of a better name, he who according to the nature of the Word lacked none of these things at any time, so that, namely, he might receive from time the excellent inheritance of heaven and earth and the subjection of all things. For did the Creator not have power and dominion over his own creature, so that in the last times he might possess these by the grace of a gift? Oecumenius from Chrysostom, Heb. I: Insofar as he is God, he has an eternal throne, Ps. 45, but what he had as God, he received as man. And long before these, Eusebius Emissenus in his homily after the Lord's passion: He who according to his divinity always had power over all things together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now also receives power over all things according to his humanity, so that that man, who recently suffered, might rule over heaven and earth. Finally, we add here the calculation and confession of Calvin on this passage. The name of heir is attributed to Christ manifested in the flesh. For insofar as he was made man, he put on the same nature as us, he receives this inheritance, and that so that he might recover for us what we had lost in Adam, etc. And Pareus acknowledges this on this passage, to pass over others now. From the Papists, Cornelius à Lapide confesses the same: Christ as he is God is born heir, Lord, and maker of all things, but as he is man, he is not born, but constituted by God as heir, that is, Lord, and is an equal sharer and possessor of all creatures with the Father. To which William Estius agrees on this passage. Those things which are noted against Bellarmine, book III de Christo ch. XV, asserting that the excellence and glory of God were not given to the humanity of Christ in itself, but in the suppositum. Since these things are sophistically opposed to him, that these things were granted to the flesh as it subsists in the hypostasis of the Word, and that they were given to the flesh itself in itself: which are not opposites: since they are said to be given to the flesh itself, not separately and outside the Word, but in the hypostasis of the Word; but in such a way that they look not only to the hypostasis, or to the suppositum, but to the flesh itself. For the suppositum does not sit at the right hand of God, as it is constituted over all things by reason of subsistence, but by reason of the subsisting nature, and indeed that which was raised into the subsistence of the Word, as has been demonstrated thus far.

4. Finally, in what manner is Christ heir as man? It is indicated by the word ἔθηκε, that he is constituted heir by God, that is, (1) by right of constitution, not succession. (2) Not by merit of his own virtue or obedience, since that is entirely assigned to our eternal salvation, and not to the glory of Christ, but he is heir before and outside of any respect of merit, since he is heir of all things even from his birth. The Papists, and among them Estius in this place, as also the Socinians, keep saying that Christ earned for himself the inheritance and possession of all things, but without scripture, and I add, contradictorily: because what has fallen to one by inheritance, that person to whom it has fallen cannot be said to have earned it: what is received by the title of inheritance is received without one's own labors and merits.

III. The dignity, right, and privilege of Christ's inheritance is designated here by the word κληρονόμꙋ, of which one must note 1. its varied usage. For it is called κληρονόμꙋ, either specifically, one who obtains his lot by hereditary right through succession, or generally, of any possessor and Lord, in which sense Festus notes that the Latins also take the word for heir. Furthermore, κλῆρꙋ, or inheritance, in the Scriptures denotes either properly goods received by right of succession from dead parents or other relatives; or figuratively, any precious and pleasing possessions, and goods whether internal or external, whether bodily or spiritual: the reason for which translation Flacius gives in Clav., because hereditary goods were more pleasing and sweet to the Jews, and were retained more zealously than is done now in Germany and elsewhere, as appears from that speech and deed of Naboth, 1. Kings XXI. verses 2, 3, and that for two reasons: both because they did not migrate so easily from their own seats or tribes elsewhere, and because that land alone received by inheritance from their ancestors had fallen to them by divine providence. Furthermore, in this latter way, inheritance is said of GOD: and that both passively, as God himself and his true religion is the inheritance of the pious, Ezech. XLIV. verse 28, Psalm XVI. 5, 6, Ps. CXIX. 174, and actively, as the Church is said to be the inheritance of GOD, that is, his sweetest possession, 1 Sam. XXV. 19, Deut. XXXII. 19, Jer. II. 7, VI. 18, XII. 7, 8, by which the love of God and his singular care for the Church is implied. Compare Exod. XIX. 6 and Deut. XI. 12, and in that manner also Ps. II. 8, the Church is called the inheritance of Christ. Otherwise, the name of heir hardly or scarcely ever occurs in the Scriptures passively, namely for one who is possessed by another, as Beza notes on Rom. IV. 13. He imagines that Abraham will be the heir of the world through a passive signification, i.e., Abraham will be inherited by the whole world, or he will be the Father of all nations, so that he may obtain that the word 'world' is used of the faithful: when rather it is taught there that Abraham is the heir of the world to come, that is, of eternal life, which he obtained through his righteousness. Certainly, nowhere in the Scriptures does the name 'heir' denote a Father, but is rather relatively opposed to a Father, so as to denote a son, or one who is in the place of a son, to whom the inheritance belongs. Indeed, sons are called the inheritance of the Father given by God, Ps. 127:3; but 'heir' for 'Father' occurs nowhere.
