Likewise, when we are called heirs of GOD, it is by reason of the inheritance of eternal life, which we obtain from God, Rom. 8:17, as Beza rightly acknowledges at the cited passage, namely that we are participants as sons of the Father's goods, but by no means by reason of the fatherhood of God, or that we are Fathers and Lords of GOD, as one must say with Beza, if the passive signification of this word is to be elicited from here. Nor less absurdly does he also compare in the same place at this passage Heb. 1:2, where Christ is called the heir of all things: because Christ is called heir not by reason of Fatherhood regarding all things, as Beza [calls] Abraham the heir, i.e., the Father of the world or of believers, but by reason of the possession of all things. And therefore that passive explanation is entirely foreign here. For he is called the heir of all things not passively, that he is possessed by all, but that he possesses all things, and thus actively, as Abraham is the heir of the world, because all the faithful are also called heirs, namely of eternal life, Romans 4:14, actively, because they obtain it and are to possess it. Since heavenly and eternal goods are κληρονομία, and the inheritance of believers, Acts 20:32, Eph. 1:14, 18, Col. 3:24.

Heb. IX. ver. 15. 1 Pet. I. ver. 4. In the same sense, that is, actively, the faithful are called heirs of GOD, Rom. VIII. ver. 17. Gal. IV. ver. 7. because they possess GOD as if by right of inheritance, and have eternal salvation in GOD, or also because they are heirs of eternal life and heavenly glory by GOD and through the grace of GOD. Cf. Tit. III. v. 7. Heb. VI. ver. 17. Jas. II. ver. 5. 1 Pet. V. v. 7. Finally, in this sense the faithful are said to inherit (κληρονομεῖν) the kingdom of GOD, Matt. XII. v. 29. XXV. ver. 34. 1 Cor. VI. ver. 9, 10. XV. ver. 50. Heb. I. ver. 14. 1 Pet. III. ver. 9. Rev. XXI. ver. 7. that is, to obtain it by grace, but not strictly by right of inheritance.

(2) The reason for this name, why is he called heir here? The Apostle preferred to say heir here, rather than possessor and Lord of all: for these reasons especially, (α) because of the relation of the Son: because he had called CHRIST the Son, for an inheritance belongs to the Son. (β) because of firm retention, because to inherit in the Scriptures is to obtain by firm possession, so that no one can stir up a lawsuit or drive one from it, as Flacius notes, in the way Theophylact does: He said heir, he says, to express the property of the Son, who cannot be driven from his dominion, therefore the throne of the Son of GOD is also unto the age of the age (τὸν αἰῶνα τ̃̃ αἰῶν̾), ver. 8. (γ) because of gracious acquisition, because one does not attain an inheritance by merit, but by right of succession or adoption, and the inheritance of all things fell to CHRIST not by the merit of the obedience which he performed for us, not for himself and his own advantage, but by the grace of GOD, who constitutes him heir. (δ) because of the appropriation of the Church: because his inheritance is especially the Church, which he acquired for himself with his own blood, Acts XX. ver. 28. which, just as it is often called the inheritance of the Lord in the Scriptures, Deut. XXXII. ver. 9. 1 Sam. XXV. ver. 19. Jer. II. v. 7. etc., so CHRIST, constituted Lord of the Church, is rightly and deservedly designated heir, (ε) because of grateful possession, because an inheritance is a grateful, precious, and lovable thing: so the possession granted to CHRIST is also grateful, of whom he himself says in Psalm XVI. ver. 5, 6, The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup. Thou art he who shall restore my inheritance: The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places, for the inheritance is pleasant to me. (ζ) but the Apostle especially wished to speak thus because of the fulfillment of the prophecy: so that the event might correspond to the prophecy, promise, and decree. Psalm II. ver. 8. Ask of me, and I will give thee the nations for an inheritance, and the ends of the earth for a possession.

(3) The rights and preeminences of this heir. CHRIST is heir, because he is the possessor and Lord of all. For he is Lord (a) proprietary, since all things are his own (τὰ ἴδια αὐτ̃), John I. 11. so that that inheritance is his own; and he himself is its proprietary Lord, which is manifest from the description of this dominion and the collation of the divine decree in Psalm II. 8. But CHRIST is the proprietary Lord of all things not only by right of creation: because all things were created through him, John I. ver. 3. but also by right of donation, Psalm II. 8. Matt. XI. 27. John III. 35. and chap. XIII. 3. The latter respect is hinted at here, because he is said to be constituted Lord of all things. (b) absolute, who can dispense of all things by his own authority (ἀυτεξουσίως) and according to his most free will, no differently than an heir can dispense of goods received by inheritance at his pleasure: Which supreme freedom of acting CHRIST himself hints at, John V. ver. 21. X. 11. by special examples indeed, but which provide the most certain proofs of his most free dispensation of the same in other matters. Cf. also Psalm CX. ver. 1. 1 Cor. XV. ver. 25. with ver. 3 and 13 of this first chapter of ours. (c) most eminent, partly (α) because of the eminence of his virtue and power, which is absolutely infinite, because he carries all things by the word of his power, as is said in ver. 3. Cf. Matt. XXVIII. ver. 18. Phil. III. ver. 21. Rev. I. ver. 8. partly (β) because of the eminence of the knowledge of his goods, and of his truly divine wisdom, because it is fitting for an heir and Lord to have knowledge of his goods: which in CHRIST is the most eminent of all, John II. ver. 25. XVI. ver. 30. XXI. ver. 27. Col. II. 3. Rev. II. v. 18, 23. partly (γ) because of the eminence of administration, and of authority and immense glory, which is seen and shines forth in the manner of the government and dispensation of that inheritance: both by reason of justice of every kind and the most exact: in which respect his scepter is called a scepter of righteousness, ver. 8. and by reason of his majestic presence, and the filling of all things, because he is not absent from his possession, but administers the same most presently by a divine method, since his throne is unlimited and immense, and he is most presently filling all things of GOD himself, Jer. XXIII. ver. 23. Ps. CXXXIX. ver. 7. seq. is his throne, as is evident from ver. 8, and being constituted at the right hand of Majesty on high, he rules in the midst of his enemies. Cf. ver. 3 and 13 with Ps. CX. ver. 2. Therefore, the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ is rightly elicited and inferred from the inheritance of all things; for Christ is not the heir of all things according to his human nature in some human way, as a King's son is heir to a kingdom, even if he cannot be present in all parts of the kingdom; but by a divine method; since there is one and the same dominion of Christ as GOD and man, as there is only one Lord. As therefore Christ is Lord of all, so that he is most presently present to all and governs them: so Christ as Man has been made Lord of all, so that alongside the divine nature of Christ, his flesh, subsisting in the hypostasis, is infinite and most presently present to all, and rules them not as absent, but as present. Cf. Matt. XVIII. ver. 20. XXVIII. 18. Rev. I. 13. which was to be noted here against the sophistry of Pareus.

Furthermore, a doubt arises: because the Son is called heir: Is he heir, in that he is the Son of God? Indeed, inheritance, insofar as it is the possession of all things, belongs to Christ both as he is God and as he is man, since the inheritance of the Church of God is ascribed also to God the Father, Deut. XXXII. 9, 1 Sam. XXV. 19. But just as God is nowhere in the Scriptures called heir, so neither is Christ, insofar as he is God, accustomed to be called heir, but simply Lord and Maker of all things: but much less is the Son of God called heir here as he is God, because he is said to be appointed heir, which, as has been proven before, designates Christ's humanity. Therefore, the Son of God is indeed called heir, not however by reason of generation, or as he is the Son of God eternally begotten by the Father, but by reason of appointment or donation, or as he is the Son of David, to whom the promise of inheritance was made, Ps. II. 8. Furthermore, since an heir succeeds to the possession of the goods of him whose heir he is; is Christ the heir of all things because he succeeded the Father, or rather because he is Lord of all things together with the Father? It was said before that heir here signifies possessor, though without excluding those respects which the emphasis of that word imports. The Son of God possesses, however, not after the Father, as is the case in human affairs, but together with the Father, which Schlichtingius rightly notes here, which is to be observed against the rest of the Socinians: who teach that God himself no longer governs the Church in his own person, but rather that Christ exercises divine judgments in it, with F. Socinus leading the way, Rel. Christ. Or. V. just. page 95, because Christ was a successor in the administration of things: whom they are also accustomed to designate as vicar and prefect. But in truth Schlichting is more correct: as I have said, CHRIST possesses all things together with the Father: because the Father did not abdicate himself from the dominion and possession of things when he granted it to Christ, but raised Christ to the throne of his rule and made him a sharer in it; nor does GOD himself therefore not govern the Church in his own person because he gave it to Christ to be governed, because the government is one and the same, the act of government of GOD and CHRIST is one and the same, just as the Lord is one and the same, and not indeed several Lords. For Christ has been made a participant in the divine power and Majesty, by which all things are governed, and he rules and governs all things by the same.

IV. Finally, the territory and limit of this inheritance and possession is expressed by the word πάντων. Which some restrict to persons, namely of all men and Angels, and those both living and dead: others refer it to things, yet in such a way that persons are also included under the breadth of things, and therefore Chrysostom and Theophylact explain it as the Ruler of the whole world; others extend it even further, so that they wish to imply that he was made heir not only of the possession of created things, but also of all divine ἀυχημάτων, of which Scripture teaches he was made a participant: And therefore that he is heir of the universe in a triple respect: (1) broadly and universally, and that both κατ' ἔσω, because the whole fullness of divinity dwells in him bodily, Coloss. II. verse 9, and κατ' ἔξω, because all creatures whatsoever are subject to him, Psalm VIII, 7. seq. (2) strictly and separately in respect to all men, whose inheritance CHRIST has obtained, both to redeem them by his passion and death, and to gather to himself a kingdom of grace, erected from the whole world, or all men, Psalm II. verse 8. and Ps. LXXII. verse 8. (3) most strictly and most specially, in respect to believers and the elect, of which inheritance Christ boasts Psalm XVI. verse 5. Conf. John VI. verse 37. 39. 40. XVII. verse 2. Although these things are most correctly said according to the analogy of faith, we do not think that all of them are equally indicated in the present passage. But that only that sense is implied here, by which all things are understood universally, over which he is established in heaven and on earth, which is especially evident both (1) from the proper signification of the universal word, which includes all things under its scope, and (2) from the relation to the Father, which is implied here by the word heir, that just as the Father is Lord of all, so the Son is established as heir over all. Moreover, the Father is Lord of all absolutely and without the exception of any creature: then (3) from the words subjoined: through whom he also made the ages: because he is established as heir of all those things whose Author and Creator he is by reason of his divine nature: then (4) from the explanation and confirmation of the proposition, made in the following, from the Royal throne and scepter of Christ, from the absolute Lord in heaven and on earth, from the session at the right hand of GOD, from the glorious coronation and constitution over all the works of the hands of GOD from Psalm XLV. CII. CX. as CII. etc. then finally (5) from the collation of similar places, where the inheritance to which CHRIST has been raised is discussed, which indeed includes under itself the Church gathered throughout the whole earth, Psalm II. verse 8. XVI. verse 5. 6. 7. and LXX. verse 8. but is extended more broadly even outside the boundaries of the Church, indeed over all creatures, Psalm VIII. verse 6. 1. Corinth. XV. v. 27. Heb. II. verse 8. For it is an absolute and Catholic dominion, which CHRIST holds together with the Father and the Holy Spirit as true GOD by nature: But the same dominion, which Christ as GOD held from the foundation of the world, CHRIST as man received in his exaltation, because as there is only one Lord, CHRIST θεάνθρωπος, GOD and man, one Ruler, so there is a single dominion, a single Rulership of all, 1. Cor. VIII. verse 6. Ephes. IV. verse 5. 1. Tim. II. verse 6. Apocal. XVII. verse 14. chap. XIX. verse 16. Therefore all things are said to be delivered into the hands of CHRIST the man, John III. verse 35. and Matth. XI. verse 27. with nothing excepted, except him who subjected all things to him, all power is given to him in heaven and on earth, Matth. XXVIII. verse 18. which is a periphrasis of divine power immense and infinite over all, Genesis XIV. verse 12. XXIV. verse 3. 7. Ezra I. v. 2. 12. V. verse 11. VI. v. 9. 10. VII. v. 12. 21. 23. Dan. VI. verse 27. Matth. XI. verse 25. Luke X. v. 21. Acts XVII. verse 24. Which must be observed here against the Socinians, who admit that CHRIST is heir and possessor and Lord only of the Church, and of those things which pertain to the Church, but not Lord of all things whatsoever that are creatures. See Smalcius on the divinity of Christ p. 114. But the Socinians teach craftily, and I add contradictorily, that Christ is not established as Lord of all, as the Father is, but only of the Church and of those things which pertain to the Church: because there is nothing that does not have some relation to the Church, either to yield to its use, or so that it is not adverse and harmful to its salvation, since all things are administered in such a way that they tend both to the praise of the divine name and to the salvation of the Church. And so in this way nothing at all will be excepted from the dominion of CHRIST. Add that CHRIST simply and universally pronounces that whatever things the Father does, the Son likewise does the same, John V. verse 19. and the Apostle is soon to subjoin that CHRIST carries all things by the word of his power, verse 3 of this first chapter to the Hebrews. Therefore Schlichting confesses that all things are understood here, of which the Father is Lord: Since the Father is Lord of all things, therefore also Christ, his only Son, has become heir and Lord of all things. He adds moreover that CHRIST alone enjoys the inheritance of all things clearly, and possesses supreme power and dominion over all, as well Angels as men.

This inheritance of CHRIST, by which he is constituted over all things, is not common, but proper, not suitable to any believers and elect whatsoever, but to Christ alone: since this is his own proper περίφρασις in this place, nor can it be said of any ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ, that he is so constituted heir of all things, as is said here of CHRIST, that is, that he is a partner of that unique and highest Dominion of GOD, and one Lord with him. For Jehovah has a divided empire with no one, nor does he concede his glory to any. Wherefore the inheritance of the faithful and of CHRIST himself is different in its whole kind, nor are the faithful called co-heirs of Christ except κατά τι, Romans 8:17, namely not by reason of all things which Christ possesses, but by reason of the glory of eternal life, to which the faithful are to be raised after the sufferings of this life, yet in such a way that this glory also, with respect to Christ and the Elect, is distinguished not only by degree, but is separated by infinite parasangs: because Christ's glory is eternal and immense glory, John XVII. verse 5, and the glory of God the Father himself, Apoc. V. verses 12, 13. The glory of the Elect, however, is finite, and is separated by an immense distance from the glory of God the Father. Which distinction Christ also indicates, among other things, when he says that he will grant the elect to sit upon his throne, just as he himself sat upon the throne of his Father, distinguishing the throne of the Father from his own throne, and asserting that he alone occupied the throne of the Father, but that he raises the Elect not to the Father's throne, but only to his own throne prepared for them. Conf. Apocal. VII. verse 17, where the Lamb is said to sit in the midst of the throne, that is, on the throne of God, at the right hand of Majesty, Heb. XII. verse 2, as the Lord of glory, 1 Cor. II. verse 8, Lord of lords, Apoc. XVII. verse 14, XIX. verse 16, Lord over all the works of God's hands, Psalm VIII. verse 7. Which befits none of the Elect, nay, not even the Angels or Archangels. For to which of the Angels did he ever say, sit at my right hand? Heb. I. 13.

Δι’ ὗ καὶ τὂς αἰῶνας ἐποίησε.

It seems that δι’ ὗ here can rightly be taken for δι’ ὅν, for thus as διὰ with the accusative is sometimes 'through', as we have shown elsewhere, and is further proven by the passage in the Apocalypse c. IV. v. 11, XII. v. 11, XIII. v. 14. Thus διὰ with the genitive sometimes signifies 'on account of'. See Beza on Romans VI. v. 4; thus δι’ ὗν is wont to be put for 'wherefore'. And that aorist ἐποίησε is most conveniently translated here by the pluperfect 'had created'. Now this interpretation commends itself to me most highly in this place, because in writing to the Hebrews he seems to look back to the old saying of the Hebrews: that the world was created for the sake of the Messiah. The same Hebrews use עלמים, which signifies αἰῶνας, for the world by a certain metonymy. Hence God is רב עלמים, thus כולי עלמא to the Chaldeans, the whole world; thus below XI. verse 3, πίσει νοῦμεν κατηρτίσθαι τὂς αἰῶνας, that is, the world. What wonder is it that he is the Lord of all, for whose sake all things were created.

The second part of the description of the person of CHRIST concerning the divine nature is proposed in these words, δι’ ὗ καὶ τὂς αἰῶνας ἐποίησε, in which occurs (1) The connection and coherence with the prior part in the particle καὶ, which here can be taken causally, so that it joins the cause of the preceding member. For the fact that CHRIST as Man was constituted heir of all things, comes from the fact that the same CHRIST as GOD is the Creator of all things: then augmentatively: so that it has the force of increasing, which Schlichtingius admits, and the thing itself teaches, as if to say. That Christ was not only constituted heir of all things, but is also the author of all things, or that he does not only possess all things by right of inheritance and by force of divine constitution, but also by right of creation and original property, and does not merely obtain the supreme dominion of things, by which in these last times he has been raised above all things, but already existed before the ages, and is the founder of all the ages, and thus from the age was Lord over all things. But it is not to be gathered from the copula that he was constituted heir of all things and created the ages in respect of the same nature, because it is most well known that the copulative particle often joins things that are most distinct and attributed in a most distinct respect, nor can anything be inferred from this, other than that both are assigned to and befit the same suppositum or person, but not the same nature.

(2) The sense and subject matter proposed in these words, namely that through Christ the ages were created. Three things are therefore noted: (1) Through whom they were created, δι' ὗ. There is no doubt that the Son of God is meant. Arians formerly contended that the particle διὰ designates a ministerial and organic cause of the first creation; today Socinians wish to imply a middle and subordinate cause of the second creation, which Schlichtingius does here in loc. p. 18, because by this preposition a difference of the Son from the Father is inferred: That the Son does not create from himself as the Father, but the Father through the Son. But that proof is of no moment. Since (1) the preposition διὰ is not used only of a middle and instrumental cause, but also of a first and principal cause, Romans VI. verse 4, 1 Cor. I. verse 9, Rom. XI. verse 36, etc., nor should one look to the bare use of this preposition, but rather to the object which is being discussed. Furthermore (2) if you look to the first creation, no middle or instrumental cause was employed: because neither in the history of creation is there mention of any instrumental cause or of any other kind by any name, but God alone is reported to have created all things, nor besides is such a thing read anywhere in the scriptures concerning an organ of creation; furthermore, all things outside of God are excluded from the work of creation, Job IX. v. 8, Is. XLIV. v. 24, XLV. 6. Finally, the infinite power of creating cannot be communicated to one who is outside of GOD, without which creation cannot be completed. I pass over the fact that CHRIST is not the middle cause of the first creation, but the first, being the same Creator with the Father, the same artificer of all things, Is. XLIV. verse 24, Prov. VIII. verse 22, John I. verse 3, 10, Coloss. I. verse 16, which will be manifest later, especially from the demonstration of our Apostle in verse 10 of this 1st Chapter to the Hebrews, made from Psalm CII. verse 26. If it be understood of the second creation or reparation, although it ought not to be understood of it, it is nevertheless certain that the Son is not a secondary cause, as of our salvation, so of our reparation and regeneration, but the primary cause, because He is the One, besides whom there is no salvation, Acts IV. verse 12. which is of the one supreme GOD, Is. XLIII. verse 11. Conf. Is. XLV. verse 22. with Rom. XIV. verse 11. Phil. II. verse 10. and He quickens us equally, as the Father, John V. verse 21. αὐτοκρατορικῶς, καὶ ἀυτεξουσίως, as the author of life and salvation, Acts III. verse 15. Heb. II. verse 10. the author and finisher of faith, Heb. XII. verse 2. and the author of eternal salvation to all, Heb. V. verse 9. Jehovah our righteousness, the author of salvation and security, Jerem. XXIII. verse 5.6. Savior and great GOD, Tit. II. verse 13. 14. Savior and Lord, through whom are all things, 1. Corinth. VIII. verse 6. Savior and only GOD, Jude verse last. Add (3) that the Apostle sufficiently explains himself, that he understands that the worlds were created through the Son, not indeed as through an instrumental or secondary cause, but as the substantial power of GOD, and the express image of the person of GOD the Father, and the brightness of His glory, who upholds all things by the word of His providence. Others explain it thus, that the Father is said to judge through the Son, because He begat the judge, so also He is said to have created through the Son, because He begat Him the maker. Most simply with the scriptures it is said that the Father founded all things through the Son, as through the hypostatic Word, Gen. I. verse 2. 1. John I. verse 3. as the architectonic wisdom, Prov. VIII. verse 30. the infinite power and potency, Luke I. verse 35. 1. Corinth. I. verse 24. and the omnipotent right hand of GOD, Ps. LXXII. 11. as therefore the right hand of GOD is not an instrument or medium of GOD, but designates the infinite power of GOD, which is GOD Himself, so neither is the Son an intermediate and instrumental cause of creation, although it is said that all things were founded by God through the Son. (4) However, by this arrangement, at least an order is noted in the Holy Trinity, that the Son is from the Father by reason of person, through whom the Father created all things: although by reason of essence the Son is one with the Father, John X. 30. John V. 7.

Grotius's gloss, that δι᾿ ὕ was said for δι ὃν, that is, on account of him, is not only new, but also departs from the common meaning of the preposition in that construction without necessity: furthermore, it relies on a Rabbinical rather than a Biblical foundation. For where in the Scriptures is the world said to have been created on account of the Messiah? And by what reason do either angels, or irrational and inanimate creatures, pertain to the Son of God as anointed into Mediator, or Priest, King, and Prophet? For he is by no means anointed for their sake, but on account of man; much less were those things created on account of the Messiah or the Lord's anointed, since not even man was created on account of the Messiah.

II. The ages, which are said to have been founded. By τοὺς αἰῶνας are understood not only times, or the ages in their entirety, as it is placed absolutely or indefinitely, just as secular times are called revelations of times, Romans XVI. verse 25. 2 Timothy I. verse 9. Titus I. verse 2. χρόνοι αἰώνιοι, and αἰῶνες, Colossians I. verse 26. but also all temporal things, or those which are measured by time, were created in time, and subsist. For the word αἰῶν is taken in two ways, (1) concerning duration and time; (2) concerning things which were created in time, and exist, or for created things and things made in the age, whatever have ever existed anywhere, exist, or will exist, just as the word עוֹלָם among the Hebrews, and age or time, and things existing in the age signifies the world and what is in the world. Flacius notes in Clav. part II. cap. 287. a rule: that the writers of the New Testament, when about to render some polysemous Hebrew words, often use one meaning for another, and the present word αἰώνων can be referred to that. For it is very well known that both the Hebrew עוֹלָם and the ages signify the world, therefore αἰῶνες, the ages, are rendered for the world; in exactly the same way the Apostle said in chapter XI. 3. that the ages were fitted by the Word: or, that the world was founded through the Word of God.

Enjedinus wishes the new Church to be understood by αἰῶνας: Schlichtingius says the ages were made through Christ, not that all the ages that ever existed were founded through him, but that some were, namely new ones, and different from the former, and far more fortunate than them. Which he pronounces to have been done, because God through Christ introduced a completely new fabric of things and the world, and one far different from the former, and that the divine author here had regard to the Greek translation of the Bibles, in which Christ in Isaiah IX. verse 6. is named the Father or Author of the future age, insofar as God was about to found through him certain future ages, and those very fortunate ones, as for example not only those which will exist after the end of the world, but also those which began to flow from Christ's kingdom, and the reformation of the whole world made through him.

But in truth, neither attains the mind of the Apostle, who does not discourse here about the constitution of the new Church, or the reformation of the world through Christ, or the origin of heavenly blessedness, but testifies that Christ is the heir of all things and also the maker and author of all things. And so we confirm with these proofs that the word αἰῶν here ought to be taken not concerning the Church, or the ages of the New Testament, or eternal life, as the aforementioned heretics wish, but concerning the universe or all the ages. (1) The word αἰώνων is placed indefinitely, and therefore all the ages are to be understood universally, and not just some. For the article here does not restrict the word to certain ages, and that it is very often added where a word placed indefinitely is to be taken universally needs no proof; (2) because αἰῶνες are nowhere said absolutely concerning the Church. Enjedinus replies in chapter II. v. 5. of this Epistle. that the future world is said to be subject to Christ, and chapter V. verse 6. that the mighty works of the future age are tasted, concerning the foretaste of eternal life: But in the former place the word αἰώνων is not had, but rather οἰκουμένης, but in the latter, not the Church, but eternal life and heavenly blessedness comes by the name αἰῶνι, in the singular, and indeed not absolutely, but with the added determination of τοῦ μέλλοντος, of the future age. (3) Because the Apostle's discourse grows here, as Schlichtingius admits: But there is less dignity in the fact that Christ is said to have founded some ages, however fortunate, than that he is the heir of all things, whatever are in heaven and on earth, and is the absolute and catholic Lord over all the works of God's hands. (4) Indeed, the reason is rendered here, on account of which Christ was rightly raised by God to the inheritance: because, namely, the ages were founded through him: But there will be no connection of this cause, if he is said to have made only some ages, whence it will seem that the inheritance of none but those of which he himself is the author and maker has devolved upon him by right. (5) Those things are without doubt founded through the Son, which he himself carries by the word of his power: since it is not only of the same one to found and to conserve, or to carry all things, but the Apostle also immediately subjoins here that Christ carries or sustains all things by his powerful word, just as he had said that the ages were created or founded through Christ. But Christ carries and sustains all things, not just some, as the Apostle says. (6) The Apostle understands that by the ages in the proposition, which he said were founded in verse 2, which he hints at in the exposition and narration of the proposition, when he teaches in verse 10 that heaven and earth were founded by Christ. Here, however, it is most manifest that it is not a new Church, or even eternal life or the future age, that is pointed out, but the very machine of the present heaven and earth. (7) A parallel passage is added from chap. XI. vers. 3. πίστει νοοῦμεν κατηρτίσθαι τοὺς αἰῶνας ῥήματι Θεοῦ. For just as the Apostle there calls τοὺς αἰῶνας the ages fashioned, so in the present passage he teaches that τοὺς αἰῶνας the ages were founded by GOD. But undoubtedly the ages are said to be fashioned concerning the creation of the world, and by no means concerning the reformation of the Church. (8) That a face of things and of the world entirely new, and far different from the former, was introduced through CHRIST, Scripture nowhere teaches, but that reformation of the whole world made through CHRIST is a figment of the Socinian brain. That CHRIST, however, is the author and maker of all things, not only does the Apostle show below from Psalm CII. vers. 26, but the universal consensus of Scripture also agrees. (9) If here by ages we are to understand not only the blessed ages of the other life, but as many as began to flow from the reign of CHRIST, then certainly not just some, but all ages universally are designated. For the kingdom of Christ began from the origin of the world, Heb. XIII. vers. 8, Apocal. XIII. vers. 8. (10) If Christ founded the blessed ages, that is, eternal life, since it is the same not only for the faithful in the New Testament, but for all who have been faithful from the foundation of the world, it is also necessary that the faithful belong to the kingdom of Christ from the very beginning of the age; indeed, since none are admitted to the blessed ages except those who have been partakers of the kingdom of Christ in this age, as the whole of Holy Scripture testifies, it is necessary that the kingdom of Christ began with the very origin of the world. (11) If the blessed ages were founded through Christ, that is, if eternal life was prepared, as Schlichting admits, it is necessary that Christ existed before the ages of time, or from the origin of the age: because blessed life was prepared for the elect ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, Matt. 25:34, and we were chosen in him, Eph. 1:4, and grace was given to us in Christ Jesus πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων, 2 Tim. 1:9, ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς, 2 Thess. 2:13. (12) Finally, what more certain interpreter shall we provide than the Holy Spirit himself, who in John 1:3 says that all things were founded through the Word, the Son of God, and in v. 10 testifies that the world was made through the Word, and in Col. 1:16 teaches that all things were created through him: just as here he declares that the ages were founded through the Son of God. Schlichting acknowledges this analogy of the passages: The sense, he says, will be the same if by the word 'ages' we understand the world. For the learned author himself also used this word below with the same meaning, so that if you look at the thing itself, the learned author here means nothing other than what John said, that the world was made through the Word, or Paul, that all things were created through Christ. But when John says that the world was made through him, or that all things were founded through him, whatever was founded, just as Paul also understands not merely some things, or points to a new Church, much less eternal life, but the whole world, all things whatsoever that were created, so that without him nothing was made that has been made, all things that are in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible. We conclude, therefore, that all those things are also denoted here by the word αἰώνων. Which, finally, the Racovians also seem to acknowledge, who in the German version render τοὺς αἰῶνας as 'die Welt'. What the enemies of the truth bring forward here to prove their depravity, we shall refute regarding the last member: We only add here that it is not at all certain that the Apostle wished here to refer to the LXX translation of Isa. 9:6 by the word αἰώνων: because there the compound word μέλλοντος αἰῶνος is used, whereas here the simple noun αἰώνων is commemorated; there Christ is called the Father of the future age, here the ages are said to have been founded through Christ, not to mention that there in the Hebrew and original text אבי עד can be rendered neutrally and ἁπλῶς, as the Chaldean interpreter seems to have understood it, rendering it גברא קים לעלמא, 'a man enduring forever,' so that he, the אל גבור, the mighty God, is said to be the eternal Father, and his eternity is truly expressed: concerning which place we have dealt at greater length in our Rostock dissertation, page 63 et seqq.

III. The act of the creation of the ages is expressed by the word ἐποίησεν, 'he made,' which here, given the subject matter, must be understood as the primary creation of things, and not, as the Socinians contend, as a reformation. For although we do not deny that it is sometimes said in the Scriptures that one thing becomes another by reason of certain qualities, and as it were puts on a new form, or of a making by reason of some quality and condition, not by reason of the nature itself, and that furthermore our restoration in Christ is called a creation (which Schlichting tries in vain to prove here), nevertheless it can by no means be inferred from this that the same meaning is obtained in this place. For the argument proceeds from a particular.

That the primary creation is meant here entirely, we show: (1) Because we have already proven that the discourse is about the creation of all things. But the reformation of all things was not performed by Christ, but only of the human race, whose reformation, if Schlichting says it is the condition of all things or of the world, he perversely confuses the part with the whole, and will not satisfy the Apostle, whom it has been shown understands 'all things' without synecdoche. (2) Because the reformation of the human race and the creation of the ages are very different: and it could not have entered the mind of anyone reading this Epistle without a preconceived opinion that, when the ages are said to have been founded through Christ, the reformation of the human race was indicated. That, however, is undoubtedly a foreign sense, which is by no means elicited from the words themselves, but is imported into them; the genuine sense of the Holy Spirit is obscure to no one who reads his words. (3) Furthermore, the context does not allow these things to be understood as our restoration, or the preparation of eternal glory, since in these introductory verses the Apostle proposes those things which he has determined to deal with in this Epistle as if expressly; it is therefore not likely that he wished to make mention here of our restoration, which he indicates only in the following verse by the mention of the purification of our sins, after, namely, the doctrine concerning the person of Christ and his nature, both human and divine, had been laid down as a foundation. And therefore the same thing would have been said twice in the Apostolic proposition if the human race restored by Christ were understood by 'the ages were founded,' which it is not necessary to admit here. Indeed, the order of things would be inverted (which Schlichting nevertheless wishes to be observed) if our restoration were placed before the purification of our sins, which was made through the blood of Christ, and his elevation to the right hand of God, because Schlichting says that this restoration was only perfected after the exaltation to the right hand of God. (4) What the Apostle wishes to be understood by this ποίησιν, his ἐξήγησις and demonstration in v. 10, which is subjoined, teaches, where he vindicates to the Son of God the foundation and creation not of a new earth and a new heaven, but of this whole universe, and teaches and proves with a clear voice that he is the same founder and creator of heaven and earth. (5) Wherever in the Scriptures a second creation or restoration is indicated, there is no mention of a simple making or production or creation of things, but with such an added declaration that it is clearly evident that a second creation is understood. But where all things are said to be produced absolutely by GOD, or the creation of the world is commemorated, it is certain that the primary creation is to be understood. That is taught even by those passages which Schlichtingius alleges, Psalm 100, verse 3: He made us, and not we ourselves; it is added, his people, and the sheep of his pasture. Ephesians 2, verse 10: Created in Christ Jesus unto good works. Thus 2 Corinthians, 5, verse 17: he who is in CHRIST is called a creature with the addition of καινὴ, new, and the added declaration of novelty. Isaiah 51, verse 16: it is called the planting of the heavens and the founding of the earth, not the restoration itself from the Babylonian captivity, but the gathering of the Church, regeneration, and the creation of the Lord's people through the word, as the subjoined explanation teaches: because God is said to plant the heaven and found the earth while He puts His word in the mouth of the Prophet and says to Zion (that is, He actually makes Zion, the Israelite people, such, just as to speak for GOD is to do, and then it is said what Scripture says, when it is actually performed): you are my people. And therefore this planting of the heavens and founding of the earth is also ascribed to the Prophet, not merely by reason of prediction, or because he foretold it with his words and prophecies, but by reason of the preaching of the divine word, and the ministerial concurrence for planting the heaven and founding the earth: because God through the ministry of the Doctors of the word plants the heaven, founds the earth, who are hence called fellow-workers of God [Θεῦ σύνεργοι] 1 Cor. 3:9, Gal. 4:19, Phil. 5:10, who are the plants of the Lord Is. 61:3, with whom the heavenly Paradise is filled Rev. 2:7, and they possess the earth forever Is. 60:21, and therefore it is permitted to understand by earth and heaven in the cited place either the kingdom of grace, or the Church in these lands, or the kingdom of glory, or the new heaven and the new earth Is. 66:22. Schlichting praises the interpretation of Musculus and others who refer these things to Christ, to whom the Father gave his words into his mouth, that he might found a new heaven and a new earth, but the series of words manifestly teaches that the discourse is about the Prophet. Whom the Lord consoles and raises up in his office with the promise of gracious assistance, and the fruit of his excellent duty. But that this ought to be referred to Christ in a mystical sense, and indeed that that creation of the ages is designated by these words of the Prophet, the adversary teaches by no argument; nay, it is the Son of God who puts these words of the Prophet into his mouth, as is clear from the comparison of the preceding chapter, verse 6. But that is entirely clear from the words themselves, that the first creation is not being looked at. Which must likewise be accepted concerning the other places of Scripture which perhaps present a second creation, which the name itself sufficiently explains. Here, however, there is no determination added, nor explanation subjoined, from which it might be established by even the slightest judgment that the discourse is about reparation. Add (6) that the adversaries can never bring forth from the Scriptures a parallel place where the ages are said to have been founded or prepared, or anything similar, concerning the reformation which he says was made through Christ. And that the first creation is insinuated by this locution is proven by a similar place, Heb. 11:3, where the ages are said to have been fitted. And therefore, while the Scripture indeed prepares us concerning the first creation, the Socinians take this phrase without Scripture [ἄτερ γραφῆς] concerning the second. Finally, we here again compare other places of the New Testament parallel to this, which interpret this making [ποίησιν], by which God created all things through Christ, as concerning the first creation of this universe, John 1:3, 10, and Col. 1:16.

Nor is it of any weight that the ages are said to have been founded through the Son, from which Schlichting infers: that the discourse is not about the old creation, which is never said to have been accomplished through any intermediate cause. For that an intermediate cause is designated by that word is too frivolous, as we noted before, and as the ancient Doctors of the Church long ago observed against the Arians. Athanasius, Sermon 3 against Arius; Cyril, Book 1 on John, chapter 3; and Basil, Book on the Holy Spirit, chapters 8 and 10; since it is also attributed to the Father, 1 Cor. 1:9, Gal. 1:1, Heb. 11:10, and to the Holy Spirit, Rom. 5:5. But we admit that the order and distinction of the Father from the Son is insinuated, as Basil taught at length in the cited place, chapter 1, signifying only this: that the Father is the principle without a principle, the Son is the principle from a principle, from which it happens that what the Father does is rightly said to be done not only by himself, but also through the Son, because the Son received from the Father both origin and Nature, and the Power of acting. But if the Adversary denies that the notion of an intermediate cause being dismissed, the old creation is said anywhere to have been made THROUGH the Word, THROUGH the Wisdom, THROUGH the Virtue of God, as also THROUGH his Spirit, he denies that the sun is shining now. THROUGH Wisdom, says Solomon, the Lord founded the earth, chapter 3:19. THROUGH HIS VIRTUE he made the earth, by his Wisdom he established the world, Jer. 10:12. Compare chapter 51:15. Through his great virtue he made the heaven and the earth, and through his high arm, Jer. 32:17. Through the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and through the Spirit of his mouth all their host, Psalm 33:6. In which manner also the Chaldean Interpreter, Is. 44:24, renders it: I the Lord, the creator of all, stretching out the heavens by my word, I founded the earth in my virtue. And in the New Testament, all things are said to have been created through the hypostatic word, John 1:3. The world was created through him, verse 10. GOD CREATED all things THROUGH Christ, Eph. 3:9, and Col. 1:16. All things were created through him. But that St. John is not dealing with the reformation of the world, as Schlichting wishes, but with the first creation, chapter 1:3 and 10, and does not merely allude to the old creation when he says that all things were created through the Word, and makes mention of light, but shows that the Word, which in the beginning of all things existed with GOD, and which is GOD himself, created all things from nothing, and created this whole universe, both the scope and the evidence of the words and the context clearly teach. And who would allude by the mention of light, which was created first of all, when he here designates the Son of God as the Great light, whom he says is not of the number of creatures, but rather the creator of all things, since nothing was created without him that was created. But Paul, when he distributes by division [κατὰ μερισμὸν] all those things which were created through the image of the invisible God, Col. 1:16, those things which are in the heavens and which are on the earth, visible and invisible, thrones, powers, dominions, etc. and says that all and each of those things were created through him and for him: with what face does Schlichting drag that to reformation or reparation? For what? Were the Angels and powers, thrones, dominions also reformed and repaired through Christ? Were all things which are in heaven and which are on earth made new through Christ, visible and invisible? But here perhaps Schlichting will say, with Socinus and Schmalz his preceptors, that the polities of the Angels were reformed, and their original dignities changed, so that they are now different from those which they had before Christ ascended into heaven, in Ex. 157. Error. page 12, and in his book on the divinity of the Son, chapter 16, page 98; nay, that even demons can be said to have been created through Christ, insofar as Christ so reformed all their power that now they are even subject to Christ and obey him, in Ex. Error. 157. Err. 133, page 53. But this is a new Theology, entirely unknown to Holy Scripture, concerning the reformation of Angels and Devils brought about by Christ, and concerning the creation of the same by Christ after his ascension into heaven, which the Socinians have recently devised solely for the purpose of refuting the most luminous testimony of Scripture. Nowhere in Scripture is there any reading concerning the reformation of Angels and demons: nowhere is a new creation extended to Angels or demons, and why does Schmalzius not say that fish, winged creatures, birds, and whatsoever things are in the world, were reformed and newly created by Christ, since all these same things are now subject to Christ through his exaltation to the right hand of God, Psalm VIII. verse 7, Hebrews II. verse 8, if that subjection is a reformation and a new creation? In Christ all things are new, as the Apostle says in 1 Cor. V. v. 17, but not universally all things which are in heaven and internal, but those which are in Christ, therefore he explains himself: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature. Schlichting further compares the words of Isaiah cited above, ch. LI, 16, that the planting of the heavens and the foundation of the earth should be ascribed to Christ, insofar as through him a new heaven, or a new earth, or a new people of GOD was to be founded, from which new ages have followed. But if it were admitted that one must explain the same things concerning Christ, whether according to the letter or in a mystical sense—which, however, for certain reasons it has been shown before should not be admitted—whence it is evident that for the Apostle the ages founded through Christ is the same thing as the new heaven and new earth in the Prophet: Whence, a new heaven, a new earth is the same as a new people, or a new Church rather than a heavenly Jerusalem? Schlichting assumes these things as indubitable, nor does he confirm them with any foundation of Scripture, and therefore they can be denied with the same ease with which they are asserted.

It remains that we refute Enjedinus's arguments, which seem to be of greater moment: they are these: (1) that it is said the world was founded through the Son (as we say) incarnate or through the Man Christ. But the Man Christ was several hundred years later than the created visible world. (2) that it is said first that GOD spoke through the Son, afterwards that he founded the world through him. But when he spoke through the man Christ, the machinery of the world had already been founded long ago. Finally he says: The purpose of the Apostle is to extol the Son of GOD above all creatures, and to proclaim his excellence. But what need is there to demonstrate that the eternal GOD is more excellent than his creatures, since that is known to all? But a response to them from the word of GOD is at hand: To the first indeed; the world is said to have been founded through the incarnate Son: because there is no other Son of GOD before the incarnation through whom the world was created, John I, verse 10. Col. I, verse 16, another after the incarnation: But it is the same Son of GOD, the same person, and therefore the creation of the world is rightly attributed to the Son of GOD incarnate, or even to the Man Christ, because of the identity of the person, just as Christ the Man asserts that he was before Abraham was, John VIII, verse 59, not by reason of the nature which he assumed in time from the Fathers, or according to the flesh, but as he is the eternal and blessed GOD for ever, Rom. IX, verse 5. He is therefore later than the created world by reason of his human nature: he who is prior to the world and the author of the world by reason of his divine nature. The second argument rests on a slippery foundation. For it is not necessary that those things which are said first be prior in order, time, or nature: Nor does the Apostle say that GOD founded the ages through Christ only in the last times, but he testifies that the Same, through whom he spoke in the last times, is the founder of the ages. The identity here is of the person, not of the time. But the Adversary does not teach that that order was observed in these predicates—the speech of GOD made through Christ, his admission to the inheritance of all things, and finally the creation of the ages likewise made through Christ—so that the creation of the ages is later than those in time. It is very well known, however, that those things are often said in a later place, as the intention of the speaker and the series of the discourse demand, which are prior to the others in time or nature. But the Apostle here intends to describe the divine nature of Christ, which he therefore subjoins to the description of the human nature; because in the following verse he has undertaken to explain the same at greater length, and, as we noted before, he wished to intensify the discourse more and more. It is a great thing that GOD spoke through the Son to the Hebrews in the last times. But it could seem a greater thing to the Hebrews that it was through that Son who has been constituted heir of all things in heaven and on earth: Finally, the greatest thing is that it was through Him who is the author and Founder of all things that are in heaven and on earth. The third argument of Enjedinus indeed bears a greater appearance of truth, yet in the background there is nothing of truth at all. Because it is not unusual in the Scriptures for God to be compared with creatures, and to be taught to be far more eminent than them, since we cannot even conceive and apprehend the supreme eminence and sublimity of GOD in our mind, or attain it by thinking, otherwise than by a comparison made with creatures, which he surpasses and exceeds by infinite reasons; nor is Scripture accustomed only to proclaim the Majesty of GOD by a comparison of creatures, but also to demonstrate and assert it, which seems absurd to Enjedinus, as also to Socinus in his response to Wujeck, page 86. That GOD is in infinite ways more excellent than the creatures, which he surpasses and exceeds by infinite reasons, that GOD is not like a man, and other things of that kind, Num. XXIII, verse 19, Is. LV, verse 9, Job IX, verse 8, ch. XXXIII, verse 12, XXXVIII, verse 18, seq., ch. XLI, verse 2. Which the adversary could have learned even from Psalm CII, brought in here by the Apostle in verse 11, where the most high God is compared with creatures in verse 27. What of the fact that GOD is most frequently compared with the idols of the nations, which are nothing but Demons, and nothing, and he contends by many arguments that he is more excellent than them by an infinite interval, 1 Kings XVIII, verse 24, Psalm XCVI, verse 15, and CXV, verse 4, seq., Is. XLII, verse 8, ch. XLIII, verse 9, XLV, verse 20, Jerem. X, verse 10, etc. Hence it must be noted: that the Son of GOD is compared with creatures, and is taught to be more eminent than them, concerning which matter a doubt had been stirred up for the Hebrews by the enemies of the Deity of Christ. Therefore the Apostle does not demonstrate that he, whom all acknowledged as the supreme God, is superior to the Angels and other creatures, but the Son of GOD, whom the heretics denied to be the supreme GOD, and whom the Hebrews had not sufficiently acknowledged to be the supreme GOD, the Lord of Angels, the creator of heaven and earth: and this according to the Scriptures of the Old Testament, whose authority the Hebrews accepted and venerated.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Ὃν ἔθηκε κληρονόμον πάντων.

Id est, Dominum. Nam & Latinis hæres idem, quod herus. Christus in cælum evectus rerum omnium est Dominus, à Patre scil. hoc jure accepto, Ephes. I. 20. 22. 1. Corinth. XV. 27. Sic infra II. 8. Patribus hæreditas da- ta terrestris & caduca, Christo cælestis & æterna, hic sen- sus sublimior, Psalm. II. & VIII.

Respiciendum in hac descriptione cum ad subjectum, tum ad prædicatum. Subjectum est Filius, prædicatum est ille, quem posuit DEUS hæredem omnium. Filius autem intelligitur non ἄσαρκος, sed ἔνσαρκος, non exhibendus in car- ne, sed exhibitus & manifestatus in carne: quia de Filio sermo est, qui novissimis diebus appa- ruit, & locutus est nobis: Eum itaque prono- men relativum ὃν innuit. Cum autem in Filio in carne exhibito duæ sint naturæ, divina & hu- mana, respectu cujus naturæ prædicatum sit ac- cipiendum, id non tam è subjecto ipso, quam at- tributo vel prædicato discendum. Quod est, con- stitutum esse à DEO hæredem omnium: in cu- jus evolutione respiciendum est I. ad DEUM constituentem. II. ad constitutionis actum. III. ad hæreditatis, ad quam constitutus est, jus, digni- tatem, & privilegium. IV. ad hæreditatis deni- que objectum seu terminum, vel etiam territori- um, quod est totum universum.

I. DEUS constituens Christum hæredem est, quem vers. præced. commemoravit, ὁ Θεὸς, Deus ille: quod nomen ὑποστατικῶς hic DEUM Pa- trem designat: utpote ad quem Filius DEI omnia sua referre consueverat, tanquam autorem & principium, à quo ipse quoque originem & esse suum obtinet. Quod tamen non ἐκκλειστικῶς sive exclusive, reliquas personas SS. Trinitatis excludendo, quia opus est illud commune & in- dividuum toti SS. Trinitati, CHRISTI hæredis omnium constitutio & designatio: neque ἐξο- χικῶς seu eminenter intelligendum, quia ubi sum- ma æqualitas, & essentiæ identitas, ibi nulla ἐξο- χὴ locum habet, sed πηγαίως κῂ οἰκονομικῶς: quod DEUS Pater sit fons & origo aliarum persona- rum, quodque Pater miserit Filium in mundum, eundemque resuscitarit, & exaltarit ad dextram Majestatis.

II. Constitutionis actus voce ἔθηκε notatur: cir- ca quam hæc quatuor expedienda: (1) Quod non ab æterno, sed in tempore constitutus sit. (2) Quo tempore. (3) Juxta quam naturam, & (4) quomodo constitutus sit hæres. Quod ad

(1) vox ἔθηκε non præordinationem, & decretum, sed actualem constitutionem, & decreti executio- nem notat, quia de CHRISTO Filio DEI novissimis temporibus manifestato sermo est, & explicatio sive confirmatio propositionis vers. 13. & cap. II. 8. docet, de ea constitutione agi, quà ad dextram DEI exaltato subjecta sunt eidem omnia. Itaque quod attinet triplicem illum mo- dum, quo Pareus hoc loco ait CHRISTUM hæ- redem omnium constitutum (a) æternâ ordina- tione ad Mediatoris officium, 1. Petr. I. vers. 20. (β) missione in carnem, & cœlesti mandato, hunc audite, (γ) evectione ad dextram Majesta- tis in cœlis: Ultimus tantum hic intelligitur. Pri- mus alienus est, quia non de ordinatione ad Me- diatoris officium, vel de prædestinatione agni im- maculati, sed potius de constitutione ad regium officium hic agitur, cum hæres sit constitutus Fi- lius, id est, Dominus proprietarius omnium creatu- rarum in cælo & in terra, explicante Pareo; quod longe alienum est ab officio ejus mediatorio, quo est inter DEUM & homines unicus Mediator, sese ἀντίλυτρον dans pro nobis, 1. Timoth. II. vers. 6. Alter quoque modus missionem in car- nem, cum promulgatione cœlesti, hunc audite, hic impertinens est, quia spectat ad officium Pro- pheticum.

Quod ad (2) quo tempore CHRISTUS hæ- res constitutus sit? Quanquam CHRISTUS ab initio conceptionis & nativitatis suæ Rex & Dominus fuerit, teste Angelo Luc. II. vers. 11. & Prophetâ Esaia cap. IX. vers. 6. hic tamen de Regni & dominii possessione, & pleniori admi- nistratione, quam per exaltationem ad dextram DEI consecutus, agitur, de qua Petrus etiam disserit Actor. II. vers. 36. ipsum, quem crucifi- xerunt Judæi, Dominum & CHRISTUM fa- ctum esse pronuncians; quibus verbis perperam & insulse contrarium probare satagit Estius h. l. CHRISTUM hæredem factum dici, prout Do- minus & Rex natus est. Quum luce meridiana clarius sit, Petrum in actis de exaltatione ad dex- tram DEI disserere, & è Psalm. CX. v. 1. demon- strare CHRISTUM ac Dominum esse factum, qui antea à Judæis crucifixus erat. Quod hic quoque intendi è vers. 3. & 13. manifestissimum est; Siquidem pariter constitutus hæres dicatur, quà consedit ad dextram Majestatis Dei in ex- celsis, secundum prædictionem Spiritus Sancti Psalm. CX. hic itidem demonstrationis loco ad- ductam & de Christo explicatam. In exinani- tionis quidem statu omnia sibi tradita in manus suas, Johan. III. vers. 35. XIII. vers. 3. Matth. XI. vers. 27. professus est, & Dominus fuit inde à na- tivitate; sed id in exinanitione latuit, in exaltatio- ne autem clarissime patuit, Matth. XXIX. v. 19. & sublimius adhuc patebit in secundo adventu, & mortuorum resuscitatione.

Porro (3) certum est, secundum humanam naturam Christum hic hæredem constitutum dici: quia secundum divinam naturam Dominus fuit omnium, ex quo secula condidit, & terram fundavit, cœlosque formavit. Sed quia Calviniani nonnulli, Sadeel præsertim & alii contendunt, quædam convenire Christo, quæ secundum personam ejus tantum intelligenda, proprie verò non pertinent ad alteram ex naturis, eoque referunt etiam, quod Christus Rex noster dicatur: tenendum hic: (1) Admitti posse, quod nonnulla de Christo dicantur, ut per naturas illi non conveniant tanquam per prima immediata subjecta, sed ratione hypostatica, ut cum dicitur à Patre genitus, quod est personæ, non essentiæ, quippe quæ accuratè loquendo non genita est, sed communicata. (2) Cæterum his accenseri minimè potest, quod Christus dicitur Rex noster, sed iis potius, quæ ita de Christo dicuntur, ut ei πρώτως & immediatè competant per naturas, priusquam ipsi personæ conveniant, quæ necessariò aut alterutri, aut utrique naturæ vendicanda sunt, minimè verò in persona tantum subsistendum est. Hoc quippe nomen est officii, quod Christo non convenit secundum illa personalia, quæ ab essentialibus distinguuntur, ut τὸ genitum esse, sed convenit CHRISTO potius secundum utramque naturam, juxta regulam Concilii Chalcedonens. Præterea aliud quoque est, Regem esse, aliud constitui Regem. Quandoquidem Rex & Dominus sit Christus secundum utramque naturam; Rex autem constitutus per exaltationem ad dextram Dei, tantum secundum humanam naturam. Proinde operæ pretium est, ut evincamus Christum, quà homo est, hæredem constitutum hic dici, eoque περιφραστικῶς exhiberi humanam Christi naturam. Quod his documentis ostendimus (1) è constitutionis tempore, quia Filius, per quem locutus est novissimis diebus, constitutus dicitur hæres omnium: Ideoque haud obscurè innuitur novissimis diebus hisce constitutum esse, agiturque non de decreto, sed de executione decreti facta in tempore. Quicquid autem in tempore Christus accipit, secundum hominem accipit, cui, qua non habuit, conferuntur, ut Leo Epist. XLI. ex consensu totius antiquitatis. (2) E divinæ naturæ distinctione, ea quippe verbis sequentibus insinuatur, non dissentientibus Calvinianis, & distincta περιφράσει, ab Apostolo describitur, utpote secundum quam Christus secula condidisse dicitur. Quocirca cum hic Apostolus proponat ea, quæ postmodum explicare constituit: indubium autem sit eundem non modo de divina, sed & de humana natura in hac Epistola disserere, idque præsertim cap. II. velut ex professo, admittendum sane, hic insinuari humanam naturam, secundum quam constitutus dicitur hæres omnium. (3) Ex hæreditatis concessione: Quia ut Deus Dominus omnium est non per constitutionem & τῇ χάριτι, sed per creationem rerum omnium, & τῇ φύσει, vel quà secula & totam universitatem condidit, non in quantum super universa constitutus est à DEO. Eleganter Primasius in cap. II. Ebr. In hoc, quod homo est, accepit hæreditatem mundi, honore coronatus est in consessione æternæ majestatis, sicut Verbo omnia creata sunt, ita homo ille assumptus à Verbo cum Verbo possidet omnia. (4) E melioratione Christi præ Angelis: Dicitur quippe κρείττων γενόμενος τῶν ἀγγέλων præstantior factus Angelis, vers. 4. eo dubio procul respectu, quo constitutus est hæres omnium. Atqui βελτίωσις melioratio illa, qua præstantior factus est Angelis, convenit Christo non secundum divinam na- - turam, quæ perfectissima, immutabilis, nullaque ratione præstantior fieri potest, sed secundum humanam naturam. Divina naturæ, inquit A- thanafius Orat. 2. contr. Arian. utpote perfecta & absoluta, nullius rei indiga est: Quo igitur ex- altabatur, qui, priusquam exaltaretur, erat altis- simus? Et quomodo accepit, quod semper habuit, priusquam acciperet? Non enim Verbo propter carnem, sed carni propter Verbum βελτίωσις ac- cessit. (5) E nominis præstantioris consecutione. Quandoquidem ejus naturæ respectu citra con- troversiam dicatur hæres constitutus omnium, cujus respectu dicitur verf. 4. hæreditasse nomen longè præstantius, quam ullus Angelorum : ex- plicant enim hæc se mutuò, cum κληρονόμ di- . citur constitutus à DEO, & quod διαφορώτερον, præstantius nomen κεκληρονόμηκεν hæreditario acceperit. Theodoretes in Psalm. XXI. Præstan- tius nomen hæreditavit naturæ humanæ. Nam ut DEUS factor est Angelorum & Dominus, ut ho- mo minor erat Angelis propter mortis perpessio- nem. Postquam autem resurrexit, & ascendit in cœlum, præstantior effectus est Angelis, consedit enim super omnem principatum. (6) E sessione ad dextram DEI. Est enim hæres effectus omni- um, in quantum ad dextram DEI collocatus est, ut è verf. 3. & 13. collatione manifestum est. Id vero convenit Christo non secundum divinam, sed secundum humanam naturam unicè. Atha- nas. apud Theodoretum Dial. 2. Illa, sede à dextris meis, de corpore Dominico dicta sunt. Si enim omnia implet Deus in quanam sede sedet? Corpus ergo est, cui dicit Dominus, sede à dextris meis. Et Theodore- tus in Psal. CX. Sede à dextris meis: Magnum est hoc, & non modo omnem humanam naturam exce- dit, verum etiam totam universitatem: Atqui & hoc ἀνθρωπείνως dictum est, ut enim Filius DEI sempiternum habet imperium, sed ut homo accipit, quod ut DEUS habebat, ut homo igitur audit, se- de ad dextram meam. (7) Ab exinanitionis & ex- altationis collatione. Quia secundum eam naturam est hæres factus & exaltatus, secundum quam na- turam exinanitus fuit. At secundum humanam naturam fuit exinanitus. Ergo secundum huma- nam naturam est etiam hæres factus. Major pro- positio è cap. II. 7. & 8. confirmatur. Minor sua luce radiat. Cyrillus l. 8. Thesaur. c. I. Cui humi- litas congruit, hic exaltari quod dicitur: Humanæ verò naturæ res humilis est: ipsa ergo quoq; exalta- ri intelligitur. (8) E locorum similium dilucida- tione. Varia conferri possent: Sed cumprimis è Vet. Testam. verba Davidis v. 6. Pf. II. quæ hic eapropter confert Theophylactus: Quo pacto fe- cit hunc Dominum, nempe ut hominem, quemad- modum & in secundo Psalmo hunc ipsum ita allo- quitur: Postula à me, & dabo tibi gentes hæredita- tem tuam. Accepit itaque hanc hæreditatem, quam hæres postulavit, sive petiit eandem. Conf. Johan. XVII. 5. E N. T. cumprimis verba Petri hic con- ferimus Act. II. 36. quibus factus dicitur Christus & Dominus, Petro ș τὴν ὐσίαν τῶ λόγʋ, ἀλλὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπον respiciente, quod prolixè demonstrat Athanas. orat. 2. & 3. & 4. contr. Arian. ut & tract. de salut. advent. Christ. & præfat. in l. IV. contra Eunom. Gregor. Nazianzen. orat. IV. de Theol. Epiphan. adv. hæres. T. II. l. 11. hæres. LXIX. contr. Arian. Ambrof. T. III. de obit. fratr. Satyr. Grego- rius Nyssenus apud Theodor. in Dial. 2. nec non Theophyl. & Oecumenius ad h. l. & admittunt è Cal- vinianis, Pelicanus, Calvin. ipse, Beza, Marloratus ad h.l. contextus evidentia constricti: quandoqui- dem de Christo secundum eam naturam hic sermo sit, fit, secundum quam crucifixus fuit, resuscitatus, ex- altatus, promissione Sp. S. ditatus, quæ ei non se- cundum divinam, sed secundum humanam natu- ram conveniunt. Cum Petrus dicit, Christum à Deo factum Dominum ac Christum, non de divinitate ejus loquitur, sed de humanitate. Λόγος enim semper erat Dominus, non post crucem primùm factus est Do- minus, ait Athanasius Orat. 4. contr. Arian. (10) E Patrum orthodoxorum explicatione. Ita enim acce- pit melior antiquitas hanc omnium hæreditatem. Cyrillus l. XI. in Joh. c. XV. Qui omnia possidet, ut Deus, omnia incipit ut homo, cui regnare adventiti- um, h.e. non naturale est. Theodor. in Ps. II. Ut Deus innatum habet regnum, ut homo decreto accipit. It. Cum natura Dominus sit ut Deus, etiam ut homo universorum imperium accipit; & in Ps. XXI. Omni- um est opifex ut Deus, omnium hæres ut homo. Vigil. l. V. contra Eutych. Secundum carnis naturam ex- altatus est, honoratus, coronatus, melioris nominis dignitatem adeptus, qui secundum naturam Verbi horum nihil eguit aliquando, ut sc. præstantem cœli & terræ hæreditatem gentium & subjectionem uni- versorum ex tempore acciperet. Nunquid enim pote- statem & dominium creaturæ suæ conditor non ha- bebat, ut novissimis temporibus muneris gratia his potiretur? Oecumenius ex Chrysost. Ebr. I. Quatenus Deus est, æternum habet thronum, Ps. 45. sed quod ut Deus habebat, accepit ut homo. Et longè ante hos Euseb. Emissen. in homil. post Dom. pass. Qui se- cundum divinitatem semper simul cum Patre & Sp. S. omnium rerum potestatem habuit, nunc etiam se- cundum humanitatem omnium rerum potestatem accipit, ut homo ille, qui nuper passus est, cœlo & ter- ræ dominetur. Denique adjicimus hic calculum & confessionem Calvini in h. l. Nomen hæredis Christo in carne manifestato tribuitur. Nam quatenus homo fact9, eandem nobiscum induit naturam, hæreditatem hanc accipit, idq; ut nobis recuperaret, quod perdide- ramus in Adamo &c. idq; agnoscit & Pareus super h. l. ut alios jam prætermittam. E Pontificiis idem fatetur Cornelius à Lapide: Christus quà Deus est, natus hæres, Dominus & opifex omnium, quà verò homo est, non natus, sed constitutus est à Deo hæres, id est, Dominus, & ex æquo cum Patre consors ac possessor creaturarum omnium. Cui adstipulatur Guilelmus Estius in h. l. Quæ contra Bellarminum lib. III. de Christo c. XV. excellentiam & gloriam Dei non humanitati Christi datam esse in se, sed in supposito adserentem, notanda. Quum hæc sibi so- phistice opponantur, carni concessa hæc esse, quà in ὑποςάσέ τῦ λόγέ subsistit, & carni ipsi in se da- ta esse: quæ opposita non sunt: quandoquidem carni ipsi data esse dicantur, non seorsim & extra λόγον, sed in hypostasi τῦ λόγέ; verum ita, ut non ad hypostasin solum, seu ad suppositum, sed ad ipsam carnem spectent. Nec enim sedet supposi- tum ad dextram Dei, ut constitutum est super o- mnia ratione subsistentiæ, sed ratione naturæ sub- sistentis, & quidem ejus, quæ in subsistentiam τῦ λόγέ evecta est, ut hactenus demonstratum.

4. Deniq; quo pacto hæres sit Christus quà ho- mo? Indigitatur verbo ἔθηκε, quod hæres sit à Deo constitutus, hoc est, (1) non successionis, sed constitutionis jure. (2) non merito suæ virtutis, vel obedientiæ, quippe quod totum nostræ æternæ sa- luti deputatum est, non autem Christi gloriæ, sed ante & extra respectum meriti hæres sit, quum et- iam inde à nativitate sit hæres omnium. Pontificii, & ex illis Estius hoc loco, ut & Sociniani Chri- stum sibi meruisse dictitant hæreditatem & pos- sessionem omnium, sed ἄτερ γραφῆς, addo & ἀν- τιφατικῶς: quia quod hæreditario obtigit, id is, cui obtigit, mereri dici non potest: quod hæredi- tatis titulo accipitur, id sine laboribus meritisque propriis accipitur.

III. Designatur hîc dignitas, jus & privilegium hæreditatis Christi voce κληρονόμꙋ, cujus notanda 1. varia usurpatio. Dicitur enim κληρονόμꙋ, vel specialiter, qui hæreditario jure per successionem obtinet sortem suam, vel generaliter, de quovis possessore & Domino, quo sensu & Latinos vo- cem hæredis accipere notat Festus. κλῆρꙋ por- ro, sive hæreditas in Scripturis notat vel propriè bona jure successionis à mortuis parentibus, aut aliis cognatis accepta; vel tralatitiè, possessiones quasvis pretiosas atque gratas, & bona sive in- terna, sive externa, sive corporalia, sive spiri- tualia: cujus translationis rationem reddit Fla- cius in Clav. quod hæreditaria bona Judæis gra- tiora & dulciora fuerint, studiosiusque retine- rentur, quam nunc in Germania & alibi fit, ut è sermone illo & facto Nabot apparet, 1. Reg. XXI. vers. 2. 3. idque duabus de causis: tùm quod non ita facilè ex suis sedibus, aut tribubus aliò migrarent, tum quod illud solum à Majoribus hæreditate acceptum illis divinitus contigerat. Porrò hoc posteriori modo hæreditas de DEO dicitur: idque tum passivè, quà ipse Deus, ejus- que vera religio piorum est hæreditas, Ezech. XLIV. vers. 28. Psalm. XVI. 5. 6. Pf. CXIX. 174. tum activè, quà Ecclesia DEI hæreditas, h. e. dul- cissima possessio dicitur, 1. Sam. XXV. 19. Deut. XXXII. 19. Jer. II. 7. VI. 18. XII. 7. 8. quo amor Dei, & singularis cura innuitur in Ecclesiam. Conf. Exod. XIX. 6. & Deut. XI. 12. eoque pacto etiam Pf. II. 8. hæreditas Christi dicitur Ecclesia. Cæte- rum hæredis nomen passivè in Scripturis vix ac ne vix quidem occurrit, nempe pro eo, qui posside- tur ab alio, uti Beza in not. ad Rom. IV. 13. Abra- hamum fore hæredem mundi comminiscitur per passivam significationem, h. m. Abrahamus hære- ditabitur à toto mundo, sive erit Pater omnium gentium, ut obtineat, vocem mundi de fidelibus usurpari: cum potius ibi doceatur, Abrahamum esse hæredem mundi futuri, id est, vitæ æternæ, quam per justitiam suam consequutus. Sane nu- spiam hæredis nomen in Scripturis Patrem notat, sed relativè Patri potius opponitur, ut filium, aut qui loco filii est, notet, ad quem pertinet hæreditas. Filii quidem dicuntur hæreditas Pa- tris à Deo data, Pf. CXXVII. 3. hæres autem pro Patre nullibi occurrit. Pariter eum nos hæredes DEI dicimur, id ratione hæreditatis vitæ æternæ, quam à Deo consequimur, Rom. IIX. 17. sit, uti re- cte agnoscit Beza ad l. cit. quod nempe participes ut filii simus bonorum Patris, minimè verò ra- tione paternitatis Dei, vel quod DEI Patres, & Domini simus, ut oportet cum Beza dicere, si hinc sit elicienda passiva vocis hujus significatio. Nec minùs absurdè quoque confert ibidem h. l. Ebr. I. 2. quo Christus hæres omnium dicitur: quia Christus non ratione Paternitatis quoad omnia, ut Beza Abrahamum hæredem, i. e. Patrem mundi sive credentium, sed ratione possessionis omnium hæres dicitur. Ideoque passiva ista explicatio hic prorsus aliena est. Dicitur enim omnium hæres non passivè, quod possideatur ab omnibus, sed quod possideat omnia, adeoque activè, ut Abra- ham hæres mundi, quia & omnes fideles hære- des dicuntur nempe vitæ æternæ, Roman. IV. vers. 14. activè, quod ea adipiscantur, & posses- suri sint. Quum bona cœlestia & æterna sint κληρονομία, & hæreditas credentium, Actor. XX. vers. 32. Ephes. I. vers. 14. 18. Coloff. III. vers. 24.

Ebr. IX. verf. 15. 1. Petr. I. verf. 4. Eodem fen- fu, hoc est, activè dicuntur fideles hæredes DEI, Roman. IIX. verf. 17. Galat. IV. verf. 7. quod velut hæreditatis jure DEUM possideant, & in DEO salutem æternam habeant, vel etiam quod à DEO & per gratiam DEI hæredes sint æter- næ vitæ, ac cœlestis gloriæ. Conf. Tit. III. v. 7. Ebr. VI. verf. 17. Jac. II. verf. 5. 1. Petr. V. v. 7. Denique κληρονομεῖν sive hæreditare hoc sensu dicuntur regnum DEI fideles, Matth. XII. v. 29. XXV. verf. 34. 1. Cor. VI. verf. 9. 10. XV. verf. 50. Ebr. I. verf. 14. 1. Petr. III. verf. 9. Apocal. XXI. verf. 7. id est, ex gratia consequi, non verò pro- priè hæreditatis jure.

(2) Nominis hujus ratio, cur hic hæres di- catur? Maluit Apostolus hic dicere hæredem, quam possessorem, & Dominum omnium: his præcipue de causis, (a) ob Filii relationem: quia Filium dixerat CHRISTUM, hæreditas enim est Filii. (β) ob firmam retentionem, quia hære- ditare in Scripturis est firma possessione obtine- re, ut nemo litem movere, vel inde depellere possit, notante Flacio, quomodo Theophyla- ctus: Hæredem, inquit, dixit, ut Filii proprieta- tem exprimeret, qui nequeat à dominatu depelli, ideo thronus Filii DEI etiam in τὸν αἰῶνα τ̃̃ αἰῶν̾, in seculum seculi, verf. 8. (γ) ob gra- tiosam adeptionem, quia hæreditatem non meri- to quis assequitur, sed successionis, vel adoptio- nis jure, & CHRISTO hæreditas omnium obtigit non merito obedientiæ, quam pro nobis præsti- tit, non sibi, suoque commodo, sed gratiâ DEI, hæredem eum constituentis. (δ) ob Ecclesiæ ap- propriationem: quia hæreditas ejus præcipuè est Ecclesia, quam proprio sibi acquisivit sanguine, Actor. XX. verf. 28. quæ uti subinde in Scriptu- ris hæreditas Domini dicitur, Deuteron. XXXII. verf. 9. 1. Sam. XXV. verf. 19. Jerem. II. v. 7. &c. ita CHRISTUS Dominus Ecclesiæ constitu- tus hæres jure meritoque indigitatur, (ε) ob gra- tam possessionem, quia hæreditas res grata, pretio- sa & amabilis est: ita grata quoque est posses- sio concessa CHRISTO, de quo Psalm. XVI. verf. 5. 6. ipse ait, Dominus est portio hæreditatis meæ, & calicis mei. Tu es, qui restitues hæredi- tatem meam: Funes ceciderunt mihi in præclaris, etenim hæreditas præclara est mihi. (ζ) præci- pue vero ita loqui voluit Apostolus ob vaticinii executionem: ut eventus respondeat vaticinio, promissioni & decreto. Psalm. II. verf. 8. Postu- la à me, & dabo tibi gentes hæreditatem, & termi- nos terræ possessionem.

(3) Hæredis hujus jura & præeminentiæ. Hæ- res est CHRISTUS, quod sit possessor & Domi- nus omnium. Est enim Dominus (a) proprieta- rius, quum omnia ei sint propria, τὰ ἴδια αὐτ̃, Job. I. 11. ita, ut hæreditas illa sit ei propria; & ipse sit Dominus ejus proprietarius, quod è dominii hujus descriptione, & decreti divini Psalm. II. 8. col- latione manifestum est. Proprietarius autem Do- minus est CHRISTUS rerum omnium non mo- dò jure creationis: quia omnia per ipsum creata sunt, Johan. I. verf. 3. sed & jure donationis, Psalm. II. 8. Matth. XI. 27. Johan. III. 35. & cap. XIII. 3. Posterior respectus hic innuitur, quia constitutus dicitur rerum omnium Dominus. (b) absolutus, qui ἀυτεξουσίως, & pro liberrima voluntate dis- pensare potest de omnibus, non secus atque hæ- res de bonis hæreditario acceptis pro libitu dis- pensare potest: Quam supremam agendi liber- tatem innuit ipse CHRISTUS, Johan. V. verf. 21. X. 11. exemplis specialibus quidem, sed quæ cer- tissima præbent documenta liberrimæ ejusdem in aliis dispensationis. Conf. & Pfalm. CX. vers. 1. 1. Cor. XV. vers. 25. cum vers. 3. & 13. hujus primâ capitis nostri. (c) eminentissimus, partim (α) ob eminentiam virtutis & potentiæ prorsus infinitæ, quia verbo potentiæ suæ omnia portat, ut vers. 3. dicitur. Conf. Matth. XXIX. vers. 18. Phil. III. vers. 21. Apocal. I. vers. 8. partim (β) ob eminen- tiam cognitionis bonorum suorum, & sapientiæ verè divinæ, quia convenit hæredem & Domi- num bonorum suorum notitiam habere: quæ in CHRISTO omnium est eminentissima, Joh. II. vers. 25. XVI. vers. 30. XXI. vers. 27. Coloss. II. 3. Apoc. II. v. 18. 23. partim (γ) ob eminentiam ad- ministrationis, & auctoritatis atque gloriæ im- mensæ, quæ in modo regiminis & dispensationis hæreditatis istius conspicitur & effulget: tum ra- tione omnimodæ & exactissimæ justitiæ: quo re- spectu sceptrum ejus dicitur sceptrum rectitudi- nis, vers. 8. tum ratione majestaticæ præsentiæ, & impletionis rerum omnium, quia non absens à possessione sua, sed divina ratione præsentissimus eadem administrat, cum thronus ejus illimitatus & immensus, & ipsius DEI omnia implentis præ- sentissimè, Jerem. XXIII. vers. 23. Ps. CXXXIX. vers. 7. seq. thronus sit, ut è vers. 8. patet, & ad dextram Majestatis in excelsis constitutus, domi- netur in medio inimicorum suorum. Conf. vers. 3. & 13. cum Ps. CX. vers. 2. Itaque rectè ex hæ- reditate omnium elicitur & infertur omnipræsen- tia carnis Christi; nec enim hæres omnium Chri- stus secundum humanam naturam est humana quadam ratione, ut filius Regis hæres regni est, etsi omnibus partibus regni præsens esse non pos- sit; sed divinâ ratione; quum unum idemque do- minium sit Christi DEI & hominis, ut unus est tantum Dominus. Ut ergo Christus Dominus omnium est, ita ut omnibus præsentissimè adsit, eaque gubernet: ita Christus Homo omnium fa- ctus est Dominus, ut juxta cum divina natura Christi caro ejus in hypostasi subsistens infinita, præsentissima sit omnibus, iisque non absens, sed præsens dominetur. Conf. Matth. XIIX. vers. 20. XXIIX. 18. Apoc. I. 13. quod hic contra sophisma Parei observandum erat.

Porro dubium oritur: quia Filius hæres dici- tur: An hæres sit, quà Filius DEI est? Equidem hæreditas, prout est possessio rerum omnium, Chri- sto convenit tum quà Deus est, tum qua homo est, cum & DEO Patri hæreditas adscribatur Ecclesia DEI, Deut. XXXII. 9. 1. Sam. XXV. 19. Sed uti Deus nuspiam in Scripturis hæres dicitur, ita nec Christus in quantum Deus, hæres vocari con- suevit, sed Dominus simpliciter, & opifex omnium: multo verò minus hic ita vocatur Filius Dei hæ- res, quà Deus est, quia hæres constitutus dicitur, quod CHRISTI humanitatem designare, antehac probatum. Quocirca Filius DEI hæres quidem vocatur, non autem ratione generationis, seu qua Filius est DEI ab æterno à Patre genitus, sed ra- tione constitutionis vel donationis, seu qua Filius est Davidis, cui promissio facta est hæreditatis, Ps.
