Respondeo hanc probatio- nem è Psal. 2, 7. desumptam neutiquam ab Apo- stolo adduci ad confirmandum hoc postremum membrum propositionis, quod excelsior Angelis factus, & excellentius nomen præ illis consequutus sit.

Non καθ᾽ ὕστερον πρότερον inchoat Apostolus suam ἀπόδειξιν, sed prius id probat, quod in προ- θέσει primum erat, circa declarationem eminen- tiæ personæ Doctoris & Sacerdotis nostri, quod nempe ipse sit Filius Dei, seculorum Conditor, splen- dor gloriæ & character personæ Dei, omnia ferens ver- bo virtutis suæ: quod primum membrorum, abso- luta vers. 4. προθέσει, vers. 5. incipit demonstra- re, quod Filius DEI æternus, ante secula genitus, qui imago Dei substantialis, ab Angelis ipsis ado- randus, DEUS ipse Jehovah, conditor & con- servator omnium sit, è Psalm. II. vers. 7. 2. Samuel. VII. vers. 14. Psalm. XCVII. vers. 8. Psalm. XLV. vers. 7. Psalm. CII. vers. 7. solidissime probans.

Qua demonstratione prioris membri eminen- tiam personæ, respectu Divinæ naturæ concer- nentis, absolutâ, aggreditur demum vers. 13. de- monstrare eminentiam personæ Doctoris & Pon- tificis nostri ratione humanæ naturæ, quod nem- pe secundum illam hæres omnium constitutus sit, quod sedeat in dextra majestatis, quod præstan- tior Angelis factus sit, quod sublimius nomen consequutus sit, quod primum è Psalm. CX. vers. 1. confirmat. Cui enim Angelorum dixit unquam, sede à dextra mea? postmodum è Psalm. VIII. vers. 5. de Filio hominis constituto super omnia opera manuum Dei, adeoque super Angelos ipsos, utpote cui omnia subjecta, ita ut nullum relin- quatur ἀνυπότακτον, cap. II. 6. seqq.

Quid ergo per nomen illud excellentius intel- ligitur? Nudum nomen haud intelligi, in confes- so est. Solius enim nominis acceptione nemo Angelis sit melior. Schlichtingius negat digni- tatem notari, quia hæc comparatio foret tautolo- gica. Quid enim, inquit, aliud est præstantio- rem esse effectum Angelis, quam majorem præ il- lis dignitatem sortitum esse? At, quidni ex nomi- ne, dignitatem maximam inferente: concludi pos- sit eminentior præstantia, quale nomen vel elo- gium est Sedentis ad dextram DEI: Vel no- men supra omne nomen, vel Dominus omnium. Quidni ex majori dignitate ac gloria inferri citra tautologiam possit, quod τῶν κρείττων melior fa- ctus sit? Grotius majorem titulum quidem nomi- nat, sed certum tamen ac mansurum jus simul de- signari vult, quia hæreditario consequutus est no- men excellentius.

Rectius nomen illud sublimius de gloria & majestate excellentiooi præ Angelis intelligitur. Nam nomen DEI est gloria & majestas DEI ex usu scripturæ, cujus particeps factus est CHRI- STUS secundum Humanam naturam, quia in ipso habitat tota plenitudo Deitatis σωματικῶς, Coloss. II. vers. 9. & visa est gloria ejus veluti gloria Unigeniti Filii DEI, Johan. I. vers. 14. coronatus & honore & gloria, Psalm. VIII. v. 6. Ebr. II. vers. 7. Quæ gloria quum æterna sit, quam ut Filius DEI habuit, antequam mundus conditus esset, Johan. 13. vers. 13. adeoque infini- ta & immensa sit, & ipsius DEI gloria, quia ab æterno non erat, nisi DEUS, nihil finiti erat, ideo venturus dicitur CHRISTUS ἐν τῇ δόξῃ in gloria DEI Patris, Matth. XXV. vers. 31. & esse in gloria Dei Patris, Philipp. II. vers. 11. infinitis modis sublimior est dignitate ac gloria Angelorum, uti finitum & infinitum in infini- tum distant.

Est nomen supra omne nomen, in quo curva- ri debent omnium genua, Philipp. II. vers. 9. & 10. quemadmodum exaltatus est supra omne, quod nominari potest, in hoc & in futuro seculo, Ephes. I. vers. 22.

Ita nomen excellentius supra omnes Angelos, id est, sublimiorem dignitatem, consequutus est ; quod non esset nomen supra omne nomen, nisi dignitas & gloria foret vere Divina. Nam alias daretur adhuc aliud nomen, alia dignitas, & glo- ria DEI infinities eminentioris gradus. Quo de Theodoretus in Psalm. XXI. Si natura assum- pta cum Divinitate assumente est copulata, etiam ejusdem gloriæ & honoris particeps & consors fa- cta est. Et in Ebr. I. ipsa humanitas post resur- rectionem Divinam gloriam est consecuta. Item ad Ephes. 1. Quod vero assumpta ex nobis natu- ra ejusdem honoris cum eo, qui assumpsit, sit particeps, ut nulla videatur adorationis differen- tia, sed per naturam, quæ cernitur, adoretur, quæ non cernitur, Divinitas, hoc vero omne mi- raculum superat. Διαφορώτερον pro præstantiori etiam Ebr. 8. vers. 6. occurrit, & apud Arrianum aliosque exoticos.

Quod ad quartum : Quando Angelis me- lior factus sit, & excellentius nomen hæredita- rit præ Angelis ? Id post expiationem pecca- torum nostrorum, cum consedit ad dextram Ma- jestatis, factum esse, sonora voce dicit Aposto- lus. Quanquam vero Majestatis & gloriæ Di- vinæ particeps factus sit CHRISTUS secun- dum Humanam naturam vi unionis personalis, intervenit tamen voluntaria κένωσις vel exinani- tio, in statu humiliationis, expiationis pecca- torum nostrorum gratiæ, ideo opus fuit, ut peracta illa expiatione CHRISTUS exaltare- tur, & ad gloriæ Divinæ plenariam usurpatio- nem admitteretur, cujus causa consedit ad de xtram Majestatis in excelsis : atque ideo di- citur melior factus Angelis, qui infra Angelos ad breve tempus minoratus fuerat, & excellen- tius nomen præ ipsis consequutus, postquam purificationem peccatorum nostrorum fecit per semetipsum: Vid. Phil. 2, 6. seqq.

Unde Eusebius Emissenus in homil. feria sexta post Pascha : Qui secundum Divinitatem sem- per simul cum Patre & Spiritu sancto rerum po- testatem habuit, nunc etiam secundum humani- tatem omnium rerum potestatem accepit, ut ho- mo ille, qui nuper passus est, cælo & terra do- minetur.

Et Theophylactus ex Chrysostomo in Matth. cap. XXVIII. Quia natura humana prius con- damnata, nunc vero juncta DEO Verbo perso- naliter, sed & in cælo & ab Angelis adoratur, merito dicit: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cæ- lo & in terra. Etenim humana natura prius serviebat, nunc in CHRISTO omnibus imperat. Ideo Cornelius à Lapide etsi Gabrielis Vasquezii sententiam non improbet: Sedere ad dextram DEI, qui est in excelsis, per Metaphoram de- notat maximum honorem, quem habuit huma- nitas CHRISTI: imo & consortium ejusdem dignitatis in eadem sede, & sic ratione unionis hypostaticæ cum Verbo humanitas CHRISTI ab initio conceptionis suæ sedit ad dextram Patris. Recte addit: Verum quia hic & in symbolo CHRISTUS post mortem, resurrectionem, & ascensionem in cælum dicitur sedere ad dextram DEI: Hinc optime humanitas CHRISTI, post- quam ad cælos afcendit, dicitur sedere ad de- xtram DEI super omnes creaturas exaltata est, ut longe transcendat Angelos, Cherubim & Se- raphim.

Quod ergo quinto attinet modum, quo pa- cto Angelis κρείττων melior factus sit CHRI- STUS, post expiationem peccatorum, quo pacto nomen excellentius consequutus sit, in- telligendum id non ratione κοινωνίας simpliciter vel ratione κτήσεως & possessionis gloriæ & Ma- jestatis Divinæ: Hanc enim ut homo com- municatam accepit per unionem hypostaticam, adeoque possedit inde à primo incarnationis momento; quum unio hypostatica cum Di- vina natura non possit fingi fine communicatio- ne vera & reali Divinæ gloriæ: Sed ratione χρήσεως, quoad usurpationem, eamque plena- riam, utpote qua se in statu humiliationis in- aniverat, teste Apostolo, Philipp. II. quo loco de hisce plenius.

Hereditasse autem nomen illud dicitur, quia non merito humiliationis id adeptus est. Ni- hil namque sibi, nobis omnia meruit, quibus natus & datus est Esa. IX. vers. 6. Neque enim hæreditas meritis obtinetur: Sed ex gratia, cui opponitur meritum, nomen supra omne nomen ei datum, (ἐχαρίσατο) Philipp. 2. vers. 9. & Humana CHRISTI natura, intra hyposta- sin Filii DEI accepta hæres facta est omnium, Ebr. 1. vers. 2. Secundum quam dictum est Filio DEI, postula à me, & dabo tibi heredita- tem gentium, Psalm. 2. vers. 8. Pro hæredita- vit Græce est κεκληρονόμηκεν, id est, sortitus est, forte accepit; forte, id est, hæreditate. Hæ- reditas enim per sortes sive fortito inter hæ- redes dividebatur, inde vocata sors hæredi- taria.

Est autem catachresis in verbo hæreditavit. Neque enim hæreditas dicitur, quæ demortuo parente aditur, aut hæres, qui illi succedat: Sed quod instar hæreditatis gloriam illam ade- ptus sit, & hæredis instar constitutus sit omnium Dominus allusione facta ad nomen Filii, cui hæreditas de jure competit.

Non ergo κρείττων melior vel præstantior factus dicitur Angelis quoad mores, sed quo- ad gloriam & dignitatem: non quoad nudam declarationem, ut Cornelius à Lapide & Estius cum Constantino Presbytero & Theophylacto; sed quoad rei veritatem. Ut evacuatio vel inani- tio fuit vera & realis: Sic & exaltatio & me- lioratio realis & vera credenda est: Nec Aria- nis hoc quicquam favet, quia secundum huma- nam naturam ei id contigit. Nonne enim admissio ad plenarium domini- um, ad perpetuam & plenariam usurpationem Majestatis Divinæ est aliquid reale? Neque nominis excellentioris hæreditatio est possessio nominis Filii DEI, sive per naturam; ut Tho- mas vult, qui commentarius, Estio judice, habere videtur aliquid offensionis; quia Theologi non conce- dunt, hominem factum esse Deum aut Filium Dei, sicut concedunt, & docent, Deum & Dei Filium fa- ctum hominem, quod etiam è Thoma probat III. p. 116. art. 7. sive per unionem, ut Cajetanus explicat: Aliud est nomen Filii Dei possidere, aliud excellentius præ Angelis nomen hæreditare. Possidet non hu- mana, sed Divina natura Christi Filii Dei nomen non per unionem, sed per generationem æternam, etsi unita sit Divinæ naturæ Humana, quæ unio fa- cit, non ut sit υἱὸς Filius Dei, sed ὑπόθεσις, in Filii Dei hypostasin suscepta, vel hypostasi Filii Dei subsistens: nomen autem excellentius post ex- piationem fortita est non Divina, sed Humana Christi natura, non per unionem, sed per exalta- tionem; quod est ipsa gloria Divina quoad ple- nariam ejus usurpationem. Nec ergo recte ex- plicat Estius hoc modo: Possessionem nominis Filii Dei velut jure debiti tunc sibi vindicavit Christus, quando eo nomine cæpit apud homines palam & passim agnosci.

Quarto, quod Psal. 2, 7. locum non modo nova versione quoad emphasin enervet, sed etiam per- versa explicatione sensum ejus evertat. Majo- rem enim fine dubio emphasin habent Græca κατὰ πόδας, ut ab aliis fit, reddita: Filius meus ès tu, hodie genui te, quam Grotiana illa: O mi Fili, hodie genui te. Ibi causa redditur τῆς υἱότητος ge- neratio Patris, hic nuda Filii compellatio habetur, deque eo aliquid effertur citra ejusmodi αἰτιολο- γίαν. Quod ad sensum verborum Psaltis fallitur Grotius, cum in Davide aliquo modo impletum hunc Psalmum dicit, quem non nisi de CHRISTO agere suo loco ostensum est: Fallitur, cum gemi- num Psalmi sensum comminiscitur, quum unius dicti non sit nisi unicus sensus: Fallitur, cum my- stico solum vel arcano & sublimiore, quem vocat, sensu, ad CHRISTUM eum pertinere ait, si- quidem literali sensu de Christo agat, & ab E- bræis quibusdam id etiam agnoscatur, ut loco ci- tato dictum.

PARS II. CAPITIS I. Divinæ Christi eminentiæ demonstratio. MEMBRUM I. Demonstratio naturæ Christi Divinæ.

## 1:3
Verse 3.

Who being the brightness of his glory) A reflection of the divine Majesty, such as that of the Sun in a cloud, which is called a parhelion. צמח here in the Syriac, that is, a sprout, not badly. Thus Jonathan interprets the passage of Isaiah IV, where the same word is used, of the Messiah: Thus wisdom is called the brightness of everlasting light, Wisd. VII. ver. 6. Clement of Rome, who described almost this entire passage, put for brightness of his glory, brightness of his majesty. There are those who think it alludes to the Rainbow, with an argument drawn from the passage of Ezek. I. ver. 28 & Zach. II. ver. 8, where see the remarks. Also Rabbi Solomon Bar-Yochai refers the Rainbow to the Messiah: which perhaps also the Apocalypse IV. 3 regards. Δόξα כבוד or גבורות Divine Majesty. Since that cannot be seen by itself, it is discerned in Christ, just as the Sun, which our eyes cannot behold directly, is discerned in water, a mirror, or a cloud, 2 Cor. IV. ver. 4. Col. I. 15. add also I. ver. 13. Lucian the Martyr. the Son of God, of essence and will, and power, and glory of God, an unchanging image. And the express image of his person) Another comparison from the seal of a ring, the form of which is impressed upon wax; a scar is called χαρακτὴρ κατὰ καύματα in Levit. XIII. ver. 28. ציר is translated χαρακτὴρ by Aquila in Psalm XLIX. ver. 15. That indeed signifies a messenger or legate, as in Prov. XIII. v. 18, XXV. v. 31, Jer. XLIX. ver. 13, because a legate represents the person of the one who sends him. χαρακτὴρ in the Glossaries is figure, illumination, but it should be read lineament. Ὑπόστασις here is not taken in such a way as the Platonists and, after Origen, Christians from among the Platonists took [these things]: but the comparison begun is continued. The Greeks are accustomed to distinguish between things by appearance (τὰ κατ’ ἔμφασιν) and things by substance (τὰ κατ’ ὑπόστασιν), as the Writer on the World [does]. Thus Philo in the book of the same title: 'a ray in itself has no substance (αὐγὴ δὲ κατ’ ἑαυτὴν ὑπόστασιν ὄυκ ἔχει),' not that it has no existence (ὑπάρξιν), but that its principality and origin is in the Sun. Thus in a ring the figure is by substance (κατ ὑπόστασιν), in wax by appearance (κατ’ ἔμφασιν). So power, justice, and truth are primarily in GOD the Father of Christ: but secondarily in Christ, yet so that these things appear evidently to us in Christ, John 15:9. There was a certain radiance (ἀπαύγασμα) above the Ark: and Moses, Isaiah, and Ezekiel saw something of the sort. But how much clearer is the effulgence in Christ, such that these things vanish before it? The Syrian translates 'substance' (ὑπόστασιως) as דְאִיתוּתֵה: how Basil and Hilary said the nature of the Father is impressed upon the Son. The Latin here [translates it as] the figure of his substance. Such things are to be interpreted conveniently, not maliciously caviled at.

Upholding also all things by the word of his power (Φέρων τε τὰ πάντα τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὑτοῦ): the Manuscripts, in which those grammatical spirits are distinguished, also have 'his' (αὑτοῦ), and Cyril reads it thus in [Book] VIII against Julian: the sense is: Christ rules all things by the word of the paternal power (that is, by command). To uphold (φέρειν) is often to rule: and, as Chrysostom adds here, with a certain ease. It is used thus also by the Hebrews [with] נשא, Num. 11:14, Deut. 1:9, whence נשיא, a prince. That 'word' (ῥῆμα) is put for 'command' is apparent, Luke 5:5 and below 11:3. So also 1 Kings 1:27. Seneca concerning GOD: 'He turns all things.' Epistle 31. See those things which are in Acts 15:29.

That all these things were put together by Grotius to whitewash Arianism or Socinianism, one would have to be blind not to see. He wishes the light of God to be only a reflected [light] of the divine majesty, such as that of the Sun in a cloud, which is called a parhelion (παρήλιος), or of a rainbow, or of the Sun in water or a mirror, and to refer only to the person of the Father, just as an ambassador refers to the person of the one who sends him; [he wishes] power, justice, and truth to be only secondarily in the Son of GOD: [he wishes] the Son to uphold, that is, to rule, all things not by the word of his own power, but by the word of the paternal power, that is, by the command of the Father; [he wishes] the name of 'substance' (ὑποςάσεως), which the Church uses in the mystery of the Trinity, not to have flowed from this passage, but from the School of Plato, and to be accepted here in a far different way. These things Grotius [says] most illustriously regarding the praises of the divinity and the consubstantiality (ὁμουσίας) of the Son of GOD with the Father: which could scarcely have been more exquisitely depraved by the most exquisite Sophists and torturers of the Holy Scriptures, the Socinians. In explaining and vindicating these things, we shall repeat what we formerly proposed in public lectures at Königsberg. But the web begun there was woven thus:

The Apostle proposes the office of Christ in the purpose (ἐν προθέσει) in verses 3 and 4, but in such a way that he first lays down his divine nature as a foundation, and then defines the parts of his office, the explanation of which he has undertaken. Therefore, the Apostle describes the divine nature of Christ in two ways, with respect to the Father, both a priori and a posteriori with respect to this universe. In the former, indicating the splendor of glory and the image of His substance; in the latter, ascribing the Rectorate or Government of the universe to Christ, laying the foundation of the expiation of sins with both, as also of the occupation of dominion through the session at the right hand of GOD, as we shall now explain more fully.

Therefore, one must look (1) to the coherence of the discourse, 'who being the brightness' (ὃς ὢν ἀπαύγασμα) etc.: by which words the discourse is connected 1. with the preceding, by the word 'who' (ὃς), while the Apostle still persists in the description of the Son through whom GOD has spoken in these last days, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages; and just as in the last place he had noted and described a more eminent nature in him, the creator of the ages, so those things which he now subjoins to this Nature to be explained more fully cohere most aptly: inasmuch as by them it is not merely declared that through the Son as the brightness of his glory and the image co-essential to himself he created everything, who also by his powerful word preserves and sustains all things: but a path is also prepared for the proposition concerning the priestly office of Christ. Nor does Constantine the Presbyter of Antioch observe the gradation here inconveniently: 'What he said, he appointed heir, is a judgment of humility.' Then, transcending to the highest and loftier degree, 'through whom,' he says, 'he also made the ages'; afterwards he comes to the one higher than all, after which you cannot find another higher degree: 'Who being,' he says, 'the brightness of glory and the character of his substance.' 2. It is also indicated that this most eminent description of the person of the Son of GOD is not put forward except because of those things which were to be said concerning the priestly office of Christ, and that the foundation of that office of Christ is exhibited and contained in them: which the participle 'being' (ὢν) insinuates: 'Since he is the brightness of glory, and the character of his substance, and upholds all things by the word of his power, he made purification of sins by himself, and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty,' etc. For 'being' (τὸ ὢν) signifies the immanence of the cause, 'since he is'; nor should it be translated in the past tense, 'since he was,' although the following verb 'sat down' (ἐκάθησεν) is of the past tense. For how can the following verb make the preceding participle in the first clause of the past tense? Schlichtingius therefore rests on a slippery foundation: when he infers from this that the excellence of Christ is described, such as he had while acting on earth: because it is said in the past, 'since he was.' But it is more likely that the Apostle wished to use participles of the present tense: 'who being' (ὃς ὢν) and 'upholding' (φέρων), because he did not describe something past or transient, but what remains, and is always the same in the present, as a continuous and permanent act is wont to be designated by the notion of the present tense. Not only was he the brightness of the glory of the Father and the character of his person, as also the Rector and Preserver of the universe, before the purification of sins and the session at the right hand of GOD, but he is the same, and remains perpetually: just as Christ expressed the perpetual act of being by the word 'I am' (εἰμὶ), John 8:58. & D. John by the word ὁ ὢν designates the perpetual existence of GOD, Apoc. I. verse 4. & the S. Apostle soon below chap. I. verse 12. from Psalm CII. verse 26. thus expresses the immutability of GOD σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ, whence also Plato in the Sophist and Parmenides calls GOD τὸ ὢν. For present things are properly the only ones that are, past things have passed away, they are no longer, future things are not yet, but will be at last; that alone is said to be, which is perpetually.

One must look (2) to the meaning of the present words: which I have called a description of the divine nature of Christ. 1. With respect to the Father & a priori, that he is the brightness of his glory, & the express image of His hypostasis, to wit, of GOD the Father, who having spoken through him, appointed him heir, nay, and through him also once made the ages. For these words express partly the distinction of the Son from the Father, that he is from the Father as a certain effulgence of his glory, and as an image expressed by the same, as these names denote an origin, or a certain relation of possession and origin: partly the communion of the nature of the Father himself, or the unity of essence, by which he participates in and most perfectly represents both the glory and the Essence of his Father (for in GOD glory and his essence are the same). Constantine elegantly explains these from Chrysostom: by brightness, he declared the nearness of the essence. Understand therefore the subtlety of the words: He took one essence, and one substance, so that he might reveal two subsistences. Whence he also adds: Who is a character: For a character is indeed distinct from its own exemplar, yet it is not distinct in all respects, but according to that by which it subsists in itself. For this character also provides an indication of likeness of every kind to that of which it is the character, and it does not admit at all of any suspicion of even a small dissimilarity. But let us investigate the proper emphasis of each word, and the genuine meaning of the Apostolic proposition, as far as this part is concerned, will be in the open. He employs a double periphrasis, metaphorical indeed, but especially suitable for illustrating this most sublime mystery. First, he calls him ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης: which name, as it is most magnificent, is also subject to various explanations.

I. Enjedinus the Photinian inverts the construction: he says that the Son is called the splendor of glory by a Hebraism, that is, glorious, just as the son of perdition, that is, the lost one: and the character of His ὑπόστασις, not of GOD, but of the splendor, so that the very substance of the splendor is shown, or the whole of that which can be called, conceived, and be splendor, is inherent in CHRIST, so that nothing more splendid than CHRIST himself can be thought of or imagined, just as if we were to say by some hyperbole that Aristotle was the soul of Philosophy. Wherefore he infers that the splendor of glory is spoken of absolutely in this sense, and not respectively as the splendor of the glory of the Father, and he boasts of this literal, not at all distorted, and interwoven meaning of the very words. But all Greek and Latin interpreters alike refute this distortion; they with unanimous consent profess that it is the splendor of the glory of GOD, and the character of His ὑπόστασις, namely, of GOD, so that the relative αὐτοῦ is referred both to the splendor of glory and to the character of the ὑπόστασις, and looks to the preceding name of GOD, with whom the Apostle compares the Son, whom he declares to have spoken in the Son, to have constituted the Son heir, and to have founded the ages through the Son. 2. Furthermore, splendor is spoken of relatively, and is the splendor of something. If, therefore, by a Hebraism, the splendor of glory, or most glorious, were said, nevertheless the splendor of GOD would have to be understood as most glorious, and thus the Son would be designated as the most glorious splendor of the Father. For the Son is the splendor of no one except GOD the Father. Wherefore the Son will be most glorious, as is the Father, whence also the Son of GOD is called the Lord of glory no less than the Father, 1 Corinthians. chapter II, verse 8, that is, most glorious, and when Isaiah saw the most eminent glory and Majesty of GOD, chapter VI, John is witness that the same most eminent glory and Majesty belonged to the Son of GOD, chapter XII, verse 41. 3. But that this is to be admitted only hyperbolically in that sense, we utterly deny: since it is certain beyond doubt that, without any hyperbolic manner of speaking, nothing more splendid, more glorious, or more eminent can be conceived, said, or thought of than the Son of GOD himself. Compare Exodus XVI, verse 7, and 1 Corinthians X, 9.

II. Socinus, in his book on the Savior Christ, page 175, admits that Christ is the splendor of the glory of GOD, but in this sense, that through CHRIST glory, and God himself, has appeared to us in a very remarkable way. Akin to this is Beza's interpretation: ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, that is, he in whom that glory and Majesty of the Father, otherwise infinite and invisible, shines forth, or he in whom alone the Father offers his splendor to be seen, who therefore in Colossians I, verse 15, is called the image of the invisible GOD, as also in 2 Corinthians IV, verse 4, and that in the Gospel. To this opinion Beza also brings Tertullian against Praxeas, who says that CHRIST showed himself to be the Vicar of the Father, through whom the Father might also be seen in his deeds, and heard in his words, and the deeds and words of the Father might be known in the Son who administers them. And he further illustrates this with these words: The Son, therefore, having been made man, so that we might not be absorbed by the naked contemplation of GOD, is to us like a mirror, in which there appears not some empty, abject image of a thing from a reflection of rays, but in whose intimate and substantial splendor, which we perceive from his effects in that visible flesh, the Father himself offers to us his own infinity and omnipotent majesty, that immense and incomprehensible philanthropy to be contemplated, and looked upon, and even to be touched. But, although these things are said truly, they are not sufficient to express the emphatic description of the Son of GOD, nor are they primarily intended here by the Apostle, who, just as he had designated the divine nature of the Son of GOD in the preceding words as the creator of the world, so he describes it here; and he places it underneath as a base and foundation for the most eminent office of CHRIST. It does not appear that Tertullian, even with the words cited, intended this epithet of the Son of GOD to be explained. He rather illustrates by this similitude of splendor the mystery of the ὁμοουσία of the Son of GOD with the Father, and his eternal generation from the Father, chapter VIII against Praxeas, page 497. But, says Beza, the Apostle adds this without any mention of the incarnation, which only befits him when incarnate. He is speaking, therefore, of the Son clothed in flesh. But who would deny that he is discoursing about the Son clothed in flesh? That was not what Beza had to prove, but rather this: that the present epithet uniquely befits the Son by reason of his human nature, or that it does not befit the Word in his essential Deity. If he wishes to infer this, then the preceding attribute of the Son, that the world was created through Him, will not befit the Son in his essential Deity. Furthermore, if he made no mention of the incarnation, it should rather be concluded that these things are said of the Son of GOD, without regard to the incarnation, with respect to His essential Deity: just as the other things which are subjoined, that He made purification of sins by Himself, that He sat at the right hand of the Majesty on high, pertain more to the human nature of Christ; just as Flacius notes in the gloss; the first three attributes in this verse pertain properly to the divinity, that He is the brightness of glory, or light from light, that He is the character, or most express image of His substance, and that He rules and preserves all things by His word and omnipotence; but the two latter, namely the expiation of all sins through His propitiatory sacrifice and His glorious ascension, indeed agree to the whole person, but yet more by reason of the humanity. But CHRIST is likewise called the image of the invisible GOD Coloss. I. verse 16. & 2. Corinth. IV. verse 4. not by reason of the human nature chiefly, but by reason of the divine, by which He is the substantial image of the Father, ὁμούσιος to Him. The Son is the image showing the whole Father in Himself, for the eternal Deity, power, Wisdom and Majesty of GOD the Father shines in the Son, says Basil in his sermon on the Trinity, and in that part the ὁμόνοια of the orthodox Fathers is sweet, that with respect to the divine nature He is and is called the image of the Father. Which the Apostle hints at expressly, when he joins to that appellation another, that namely He is εἰκὼν τῶ Θεῶ τῶ ἀοράτω, by which He is πρωτότοκος πάσης κτήσεως, that is, begotten before any things, as Beza himself explains, and he proves in his Notes on that passage, by which all things were created through him, which are in the heavens and which are on the earth, which is immediately subjoined; but those things do not agree with CHRIST by reason of his human nature. What is it, therefore, that Beza draws the being the image of the invisible GOD, against the unanimous consent of the Ancients and the continuity of the text itself, to the human nature of CHRIST? Truly, he knows how to bring forward nothing else, except the authority of his Arianizing Calvin, which he does not hesitate to prefer to the solid and constant interpretation of the Ancients. The Ancients, he says, more subtly refer this to the mutual relation of the Father and the Son, to which that saying of Christ is referred, John XII. v. 45 and XIV. v. 9. But to me, the opinion of the most learned interpreter seems simpler and more appropriate. Clearly, he is the αὐτὸς ἔφα, more learned than all Antiquity, nay, the most learned interpreter of Scripture κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν, whom whoever follows cannot err. Finally, it is false that no mention is made of the Son clothed in flesh. For was not the Son clothed in flesh, when in these last times GOD spoke through him, and whom he constituted heir of all things? Although, therefore, an open mention of the incarnation is not made, Beza will hardly deny that these things were said of the Son, as he was incarnate.

III. Calvin is still more barren in explaining this description, as if the Son were called the radiance of the glory of the Father only with respect to the manifestation made through the Son. Which David Pareus, a disciple of Calvin, refutes in Socinus, although Socinus had said something more, as was reported before. Let us therefore oppose him to his Preceptor: True, he says, this is, but it is neither the whole, nor is it enough. For the Apostle had already said before that GOD spoke to us through the Son, namely not πολυμερῶς, καὶ πολυτρόπως, as formerly through the Prophets, but most openly, most clearly, which pertained to his prophetic office. Here, however, he wished to designate the person of the Son as the cause and basis of his office. Add that by the same reasoning this description would also suit the Apostles, and especially Paul, the Author of this Epistle, by reason of the manifestation of the glory of GOD made through his preaching, just as he asserts that through himself was made the Φωτισμὸν τῆς γνώσεως τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ, 2 Corinthians IV. v. 6. But who will say that the Apostle is the ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χαρακτῆρα τῆς ὑποστάσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ? Could the Apostle also make purification of sins through himself, the foundation of which is here laid down as τὸ εἶναι ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ. Away with such obscurations of the most illustrious Names of the eternal Son of God! The Apostle rather distinguishes, 2. Cor. IV. v. 4, most openly τὸ αὐγάσαι τὸ Φωτισμὸ τοῦ ἐυαγγελίε τῆς δόξης τοῦ χριστοῦ, and Christ, who is εἰκὼν τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης ἀυτοῦ: And he ascribes that to himself also, but this, far be it that he should wish to arrogate to himself, which is most proper to Christ, the Lord of glory, whom he calls, 1 Cor. II. 8.

IV. But the opinion of the Photinian Schlichting approaches more closely to the truth. Who, in his Commentary on this passage, page 25, acknowledges that the gloss of Calvin and others, that this appellation was attributed to Christ because he himself declared to us the divine will, which no one could see, is less than sufficient, and thinks that this description should be extended more broadly, to be referred to the universal likeness which Christ, living on earth, had with GOD, and by which he related and represented GOD to us, so that this is the same as that which Paul wrote about Christ, that he was in the form

of God, and equal to God. He was of such wisdom that he knew the secrets of GOD, and in the name of God uttered oracles and gave answers, so that he had the thoughts and hearts of men known; of such holiness that he was without any stain; of such power that he commanded all things on earth, even demons, as God. Hence rightly John says, We have seen, he says, His glory, the glory as of the only-begotten from the Father. These are Schlichting's words. Which indeed appear to be said quite orthodoxly and magnificently about Christ, but because he believes Christ is by nature a mere man (ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον), they are entirely false and conflict with the perpetual analogy of Scripture. For that καρδιογνωσία, or inspection of hearts, how would it suit a mere man, when God claims the same for himself alone, Jer. XI. v. 20, ch. XVII. v. 10, ch. XX. v. 12, Ps. VII. v. 10, 1 Kings VIII. v. 39. That power, by which he commanded all things as GOD with sovereign authority, what does it argue but that he was that supreme GOD, because he worked all things ὁμοίως as GOD, John V. v. 17, and who besides that one and supreme GOD would command all things as GOD, when God does not wish his glory to be attributed to anyone outside himself, and wishes to be acknowledged as supreme GOD by this his power and authority over all things? Is. XLII. v. 8. Finally, that which is equal to GOD the Father, which the only-begotten Son of GOD is, manifestly proves him to be the supreme GOD, of the same nature and essence as the Father. Therefore, these things are contradictorily snatched away for Christ as a mere man.

The Syriac Interpreter renders the word ἀπαύγασμα as צמחא, that is, a sprout; which Cornelius à Lapide says did not sufficiently express the force of the Greek word: for ἀπαύγασμα is properly the same as the Hebrew זהר, brightness, splendor, radiance, refulgence. But the Syriac word also denotes the rising or exit of light, and the splendor of the rising Sun, as Junius rightly notes on this passage. And the name צמח is usually assigned to the Son of GOD in the Holy Scriptures, as can be seen in Zech. III. v. 8, ch. VI. v. 12, where צמח is pointed out: whom also Jeremiah ch. XXIII. v. 5 calls צמח צדיק, a righteous sprout, and ch. XXXIII. v. 15, צמח צדקה, a sprout of righteousness, in which places the Chaldean paraphrases teach that the Messiah is looked to. The LXX Interpreters, however, They interpret the word צמח as ἀνατολὴ, which generally indeed signifies the rising of any thing, and is used of things born from the earth, Gen. II. verse 5, III. 10; but specially and properly it denotes the rising of the Sun, and in that sense Zechariah called Christ ἀνατολὴν ἐξ ὕψους, the day-spring from on high, enlightening those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, Luke I. verse 78, who is that Sun of righteousness, Mal. IV. verse 2. In this sense, therefore, the present appellation of the Son of GOD could be compared, by which the Syriac Paraphrast calls him צמחא דשובחה, the splendor of his glory, or of GOD, with Isa. IV. verse 2, where it is called צמח יהוה, the Splendor or Branch of Jehovah, or of GOD, so that his eternal origin and generation from the Father may be expressed; although here it could also be rendered by apposition: צמח יהוה, the Branch or splendor, who is Jehovah. For so is Christ the Son of GOD, that he himself is GOD: so is he the splendor of the glorious GOD, that he himself is the most glorious Lord. Most interpreters wish Christ to be called the splendor of the Father's glory, or the refulgence, with respect to his eternal generation from the Father; although some also join the respect of eternal manifestation.

There is, however, a twofold interpretation of the latter word τῆς δόξης to be noted here. The first is: by which it is taken for the Majesty and glory of GOD: which, as it is not distinct in God from His Essence, Thus here he denotes the majestic and most glorious Deity of the Father; that the Son is the splendor, or refulgence, of the most glorious divine essence. For it is frivolous what Enjedinus objects here: If the Son is called the splendor of the glory of GOD, he would be the accident of an accident, since both splendor and the glory of GOD are accidents; which is said most ineptly in both cases: for the splendor of GOD is hypostatic and substantial, as the image of GOD in the following verse, and 2 Corinthians IV, verse 4, Colossians I, verse 15; that splendor is the Sun of righteousness itself, Malachi IV, verse 2, the Dayspring from on high, Luke I, verse 78, the Star out of Jacob, Numbers XXIV, verse 17, the most splendid Morning Star, Revelation XXII, verse 16. The glory of GOD is likewise no less substantial, since an accident cannot fall into God. Although those words indeed denote accidents in creatures, they are nevertheless used to explain the Essence of GOD in Holy Scripture, because our mind cannot attain to the infinite nature of GOD by thinking, except through such analogical names and similitudes taken from created things, which, however, we must explain in a manner worthy of God, lest we place any imperfection in God. Therefore, the glory of GOD is the same as the majestic and glorious essence of GOD. For the glory of GOD is accustomed to be taken either essentially and absolutely, to denote the Eminence and Majesty of GOD; or relatively and respectively, to designate the acknowledgment and celebration of the Majesty of GOD; this is properly called glorification, Psalm XXIX, verse 6, Luke II, verse 14, chapter XIX, verse 38, when glory is given to GOD by creatures, men, or Angels. But the former is the essential glory of GOD, and therefore, on the part of the thing, the very essence of GOD, Acts VII, verse 2, Romans I, verse 23. The glory of GOD can also be taken in the same sense for GOD himself, as the abstract for the concrete, or the adjunct for the subject: Thus Isaiah saw the glory of the Lord, John XII, verse 41, when he saw the Lord GOD Zebaoth, Isaiah VI, verse 1, or God of glory, as he is called in Acts VII, verse 2. The other interpretation of glory, as regards the thing itself and materially, coincides with the former, yet formally and by reason of the mode of speaking it is different: that glory is copious light, and as it were a fountain of light in a luminous substance, as the blessed Gerhard accepts it in part III of his Harmony continuation, chapter CLXXVII, page 403. Which explanation seems to be confirmed partly (1) from the preceding word apaugasma, for it is the splendor of light: partly (2) from the meaning of the word glory used elsewhere in the Scriptures, such as Luke II, verse 9. the glory of the Lord shone round about the Bethlehemite shepherds, which is most splendid light, 1 Corinthians XV, verse 41, another glory of the Sun, another glory of the Moon, another glory of the stars: for star differs from star in glory, that is, in splendor; partly (3) from similar names of the Son of GOD, because as he is called here the splendor of light, so elsewhere he is called great light, Isaiah IX, verse 1, and John I, verse 5, the true light, chapter VIII, verse 9, the light of the world, chapter VIII, verse 12, IX, 5, XII, 35, and Isaiah LX, verse 1, the light which is the glory of the Lord is called, as also light and glory, which words seem to alternate equally in Luke XI, 32, as in Isaiah glory and light in the cited place, the Dayspring from on high, Luke I, verse 78, the Morning Star, Revelation XXIV, verse 17, the Sun of righteousness, Malachi IV, 2, partly (4) from the parallel passage Wisdom VII, 26, which the Apostle seems to have had in mind here, or, as Cornelius à Lapide wishes, to have cited. For as in that same place the hypostatic Wisdom of the Son of GOD is called the brightness of everlasting light, so here the brightness of the glory of God: as there he is further called the unspotted mirror of the power of God, and the image of his goodness, so here the express image

of his person, so that each epithet corresponds to the other, a collation of both passages having been made. What therefore the book of Wisdom understands by the name of everlasting light, the Apostle seems to understand by the word of glory: partly (5) from the appellation of the Nicene Creed, by which it calls the Son of GOD God of God, and light of light, which appellation does not seem to be taken from anywhere more than from this passage, as Constantine of Antioch hints in this place; just as also Justin, or whoever is the author of the book: thus, he says, we understand the Son to have been begotten of the Father, as Light shone forth from Light, and Nazianzen in oration I on the Son. The splendor of the Sun is born from the Sun, is of the same nature as the Sun, emerges together with the Sun, and expresses the light of the Sun exactly: Thus the Son begotten of the Father is himself coeternal and consubstantial, showing the whole in himself. This explanation pleases the blessed Chemnitz in the cited places, part I. But glory, he says, is copious light, as 2 Corinthians III, verse 7, and Exodus XXXIV, verse 30, it is read concerning the glory of the face of Moses, and Luke II, verse 9, it is said: the glory of the Lord shone round about the shepherds. Brightness is the refulgence from that light, because brightness signifies radiance, so that glory is as it were the fountain of light, in the body of the Sun: but brightness is the splendor propagated from thence: just as rays are scattered from the body of the Sun. But, as I said, the matter comes to the same thing, whether you take the word glory for glory, or for the light of GOD, in the former or the latter way. Because light in GOD designates nothing other than the most splendid Majesty and glory of GOD, which in 1 Timothy VI, verse 16, is said to inhabit unapproachable light, that is, it possesses such glory and Majesty that no creature can either have or comprehend it, James I, verse 17, GOD is called the Father of lights on account of his essential Majesty, which some wish to be a periphrasis of the Sun, some with Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis VII, wish the Father of lights to be called Father, because the Son and the Holy Spirit are lights from the Father, as Paëzius, Justinianus, Lorinus, Estius. But the Father is nowhere called the Father of the Holy Spirit, nor are the Son and the Holy Spirit two lights, but one light, and therefore the most holy Majesty of GOD is more simply designated, as also 1 John I, verse 5, God is light.

Furthermore, various reasons can indeed be brought forward for this appellation; that the Son is ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, the refulgence and splendor of the glory of the Father, or of His most eminent Majesty, but these, as we hinted before, are conveniently referred both to the eternal generation of the Son from the Father, and to the temporal manifestation of the Majesty of GOD in the Son. Most Doctors of the Church agree that the Son is called the splendor of the glory of the Father on account of the eternal generation of the Son from the Father; because as splendor arises from light, so the Son exists from the Father through eternal generation, and has His essence, glory, and Majesty communicated. And this most eminent mystery of the Son of GOD is indeed beautifully illustrated by this appellation. (1) by reason of origin, both in Himself: because as generation is, as it were, that certain emanation of splendor and light from light, an origin, so through eternal generation the Son is from the Father as the splendor of glory, or of that divine light, and light from light, GOD from GOD begotten of the Father, that essential and unbegotten light, and the word ἀπαύγασμα hints at that origin by the force of the preposition. Whence the passage in Wisdom VII, verses 25, 26 can be compared, where wisdom is called ἀπόῤῥοια τῆς τοῦ παντοκράτορος δόξης εἰλικρινής· ἀπαύγασμα Φωτὸς ἀϊδίου and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty, and the splendor of eternal light: then (2) with respect to the mode of generation: and as to (1) necessity: for just as the rays of the Sun proceed from the Sun not freely but necessarily and naturally, so the generation of the Son is natural and necessary, although above all nature. How Cyril, book X, chapter VIII, demonstrates from this that the Son of GOD was generated from the Father not by a preceding will and choice, but according to nature; and (2) as to eternity: Just as rays exist with the Sun, and persist simultaneously with it, they are from the Sun, but not after the Sun; they are coeval with the Sun, and the emanation of the splendor is from the Sun, while the Sun is: So the Son is ὁμοαιώνιος [co-eternal] with the Father, existing from eternity to eternity with the Father; eternally from the Father, and (3) as to immutability. For the ray flows from the Sun without change and immutably, without flowing away or separation: Thus the Son is generated from the Father without any change of passion, or diminution, or division; ὀὐ γὰρ κατὰ τομὴν ἡ ῥεῦσιν ἢ διάσασιν τῶ Φωτὸς ἡ ἔκλαμψις γίνεται, ἀλλ’ ἐκ τῆς ὐσίας αὐτῆς ἀπαθῶς προέρχεται [for the shining of the light does not occur by cutting or flowing or separation, but it proceeds from the essence itself without passion], says Justin in the exposition of the faith in the declaration of this similitude. Ambrose explains the same respects of comparison in book I, de fid. ad Gratian., chapter IV. and (4) as to purity: because the splendor proceeds from the Sun without any dross or mixture, as a spiritual and most pure quality: so also the Son is generated from the Father without any mixture, as Cornelius à Lapide hints in this place, and (5) as to immediate procession: because the Son proceeds immediately from the Father by generation from the essence itself without the intervention of another, or some medium, just as the splendor and ray of light proceed immediately from the essence itself, as Justin says in the loc. cit., which Damascene hints in book I, Orthodox. fid., chapter IX, when he says that λόγον ἀπαύγασμα [the Word as radiance] is called among other things διὰ τὸ ἄνευ συνδυασμῦ γεγεν- νῆσθαι ἐκ τῧ πατρὸς [because he was generated from the Father without conjunction], which is generated from the Father without a bond or medium. and (6) as to immanence, and inseparability: because the splendor is from the Sun and light, in such a way that it remains with the Sun and light, it is from the Sun by emanation, but not by a real separation from the Sun. Thus the Son is from the Father, but in such a way that he is and remains in the Father; he proceeds from the Father, yet not as a part separated from the Father. Which I am pleased to explain with the words of Cyril from book III, in Johan., chapter XXIX, he says that the Son is naturally in the Father, although he is also from him, since he subsists, just as perhaps splendor is in a thing, and from the thing which shines: For one is understood to be another by reason, and the thing itself which shines is another, but not a different thing, if you look to the nature of both, since the splendor is from the shining thing, and is in it again, nor because they are the same in nature, will it be believed that anything is from him. For those things which are thus from another proceed separated, nor cut off. Damascene joins these members of the comparison for the most part in l. I, Orth. fid., c. IX, λόγος μὲν ὧν καὶ ἀπαύγασμα λέγεται διὰ τὸ ἄνευ συνδυασμῦ καὶ ἀπαθῶς καὶ ἀχρόνως, καὶ ἀῥῥεύστως καὶ ἀχωρίστως γεγεννῆθαι ἐκ τῧ πατρὸς, &c. [The Word is called radiance because he was generated from the Father without conjunction and without passion and timelessly, and without flowing and inseparably, etc.].

Secondly, this appellation is appropriate to the Son of GOD by reason of the representation of the glory and divine Majesty, by which the Son contains, exhibits, and represents the glory and Majesty of the Father in himself, or as a certain express image and character of the glory and Majesty of the Father, as the subsequent description teaches. For as the ray and splendor is of the same essence as the Sun, and as it were exhibits and represents its glory: So also the Son of GOD, the splendor of the glory of the Father, is of the same essence with the Father, and exhibits and represents His glory and Majesty in himself: the splendor of the Sun, says Nazianzen, Orat. I, de Filio, expresses the light of the Sun exactly, thus the Son generated from the Father is ὁμοούσιος [consubstantial] to him, τὸν ὅλον ἐν ἑαυτῷ δει- κνὺς [showing the whole in himself] representing the whole in himself. For just as the Father has life ἐν ἑαυτῷ [in himself], οὕτως [so] he has also given to the Son to have life ἐν ἑαυτῷ [in himself], says Christ, John V, verse 26. It is exhibited, however, thus (1) Unity of essence, John X, verse 30, 1 John V, verse 7. (2) Eternity, that the Son is ὁμοαιώνιος [co-eternal] with the Father, Micah V, verse 2, Prov. VIII, verse 23, seq. (3) Immutability, that he is no less immutable than the Father, Psalm CII, verse 26, Heb. I, verse 10, 11. (4) Purity and holiness: Because as GOD is light, and there is no darkness in him, 1 John I, verse 5, so the Son of GOD is the true light, John I, verse 5, 8, 9. The Holy of Holies, Dan. IX, verse 24, that thrice holy one, Is. VI, verse 3. (5) Majesty, because he is also the splendor or light and glory of the Lord, Is. LX, verse 1, and the Lord of glory, 1 Cor. II, verse 8, of the same honor and glory with the Father, John V, verse 23, Is. XLV, verse 23, Rom. XIV, verse 10, Psalm XCVI, v. 8, Heb. I, verse 6, Apoc. V, verse 12. Theophylact not undeservedly opposes these to the subtleties of the Arians in his commentary on this place. When therefore he understands that the Arians are babbling that, and arguing in this manner, since the Son is from the Father. Therefore he is also inferior to the Father, I would have you object to them of this kind: Either the splendor is emitted from the Sun, yet this splendor does not proceed after the Sun, but shines simultaneously. For the radiance arises together with the Sun.

Thirdly, by reason of origin and personal relation, the name ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης [radiance of the glory] is assigned to the Son of GOD, because an immediate procession or origin from the Father is indicated, which he has through eternal generation, Ps. II, verse 7, Micah V, verse 2, Prov. VIII, verse 23, John I, verse 14, and the origin or procession which the Holy Spirit has no less from the Son than from the Father: For just as heat is from the splendor and likewise from the Sun, so the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Son and from the Father, light, splendor, and heat are simultaneously of the same nature, although the splendor is from the light, and the heat is from the splendor and from the light: so the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of the same divine essence, even though the Son is in the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, as the Spirit of both. Bullinger speaks thus of this mystery in this place: Just as the ray is not separated from the Sun: So neither is the Son from the Father. Meanwhile, the sphere or globe is not the ray, nor is the ray the globe, and neither of these is the heat, nor is the heat the globe or the ray: yet these three are not three Suns, but one Sun. Thus, in any case, there is also one magnificent glory (for by this name the Apostle adorns GOD), not two or three. Yet there are two substances or persons from it, but not separated from it. These, therefore, are the principal reasons for this name, by which regard is had to the mystery of the eternal Deity of the Son of God, which we believe is here primarily indicated, where, however, that which Justin says must be considered: ἁρμόδιον γε τὸ παράδειγμα εἰ μὴ κατὰ πάντα κατὰ τι νῦν, It is enough if the likeness agrees at least in something, even if it does not agree in all things.

But I have not denied that the temporal manifestation of the Majesty of GOD in the Son is secondarily designated by this appellation: and that not merely regarding the preaching or verbal manifestation of the divine glory and majesty, of which Christ says, No one has seen the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him, Matt. XI. verse 27. Just as therefore the Sun communicates itself through rays and introduces itself to our senses, so the Father in the Son and through the Son has revealed his essence and will to us: Because, as Augustine says, light is known through splendor, and the weak eyes of mortals bear splendor more gently than the brightness of light; But also regarding the real manifestation, or representation of the glory of GOD, made in the flesh, because he is God manifested in the flesh, 1 Tim. III. verse 16. and he made the glory to be seen, as the glory of the only-begotten from the Father, John I. verse 14. For since no one has ever seen God, the Son of GOD, who is in the bosom of the Father, has revealed him to us. Theophylact wishes to suggest τὴν γνησιότητα, καὶ τὸ ἀχώρισον, καὶ συναΐδιον τοῦ υἱοῦ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα. The Son of GOD himself ἐξηγήσατο, which is properly led forth, from ἐξηγέομαι, made manifest, and as it were conspicuous in himself. For he who sees me, says Christ, he sees the Father, John XIV. v. 9. Which we have previously explained in a way with the words of Beza: although with Constantine of Antioch, and the Blessed Jerome. Weller in this place, it is finally not a shame to confess, that we cannot attain by thinking the ἔμφασιν, ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης of these words, how much less express it by speaking.

A second denomination follows, which the Apostle wished to be joined to this, so that the mystery already insinuated might become more illustrious, when he teaches that the Son of GOD is the splendor of the glory of GOD his Father in such a way that he is also χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ, the image of his substance.

What therefore is χαρακτὴρ to the Apostle, what is ὑποστάσεως, what is χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως, and what is it called? It must be investigated.

I. χαρακτὴρ is called either figure, as the old interpreter translates, or what expresses the emphasis of the word more, express figure, as Augustine renders in the book on the incarnation of the Word, chapter XII, or express image, as Erasmus interprets, or inscribed form, which Beza prefers παρὰ τὸ χαράσσειν, so that it may be distinguished from every shadowed or empty image: Although he acknowledges that the Greek word χαρακτὴρ is still fuller; and therefore he retains it in the version. (1) Burgensis took it from figure, the fourth species of quality, which contains the whole determined quality, he suggests that it can be taken, but ineptly. (2) The Blessed Chemnitius, part I. Loci Communes, page 131, writes about this matter thus: The Son of GOD is not a vanishing image just as the species of a body shining in a mirror is εἰκὼν, and indeed a vanishing one, James I. verses 21, 22. But an express and permanent effigy, just as a coin is the character of its matrix. But because a coin is the χαρακτὴρ of the form of the matrix only, not of the substance, therefore is added χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως, that is, an image not of qualities in GOD, but a substantial and entire image of the essence communicated to him. (3) Erasmus applies the likeness of the image of a seal, which, impressed upon the same, expresses the archetype. So also Bullinger. Just as a seal is most properly expressed in wax, so the Paternal substance most properly shines forth in Christ. (4) Others prefer the seal itself to be denoted, rather than the image impressed from the seal into the wax, in the sense that the Father intimately, as it were, inscribed his whole essence and majesty into the Son begotten by him from eternity, and as it were effigied himself in the Son, so that he might be his substantial image: Thus Mr. Glassius in Rhet. Sac. page 159, and by that name they wish to express both the secret of the eternal generation and the affection of the heavenly Father, as a seal is wont to be loved and guarded above others, whence he is also compared to a seal in the type of Zerubbabel, to whom GOD says in Hag. II. 24, I will set you as a seal; and also the business of communicated salvation, just as a seal is impressed upon wax, so Christ is the seal by which salvation is sealed to us, and he impresses upon us his image lost through sin.

(5) Cornelius à Lapide compares here that saying of Christ about himself, John VI. verse 27, that the Father ἐσφράγισεν, sealed, and as it were expressed the Son with a seal, upon which place Beza annotates in this way: he sealed, that is, with the as it were impressed seal of his own inherent power, he both distinguished him from other men, so that GOD the Father might appear in him as in a visible image, and also destined him for the performing of this thing, namely, the reconciling of men to GOD unto eternal life: not indeed badly, but less sufficiently and fully: For GOD the Father also sealed the Son as the Son contains in himself the whole fullness of the paternal form of the sealing GOD, as Hilary says, book VIII. de Trinitate, and therefore Cyril also understands the Son as sealed unto the immutable identity of GOD. Because as a signet is similar to the sealing seal, so the Son is as it were the signet of the eternal Father. Therefore, the opinions of the interpreters could perhaps be joined here. subordinated: that the Father sealed the Son with eternal generation, and the impression of his image, according to Hilary and Cyril, then with the anointing of the Holy Spirit by which he was anointed above his fellows, so that he might be separated from all other men, in which way Augustine and the Blessed Luther understand it, then by the operation of miracles, which were as a seal, by which GOD long ago wished the Messiah to be sealed, Is. XXXV. verse 5, as Chrysostom explains, then by the meritorious passion, by which he was sealed, and the stone carved, Zech. III. 9. We therefore prefer to take character for an express image, rather than for a seal: so that the archetype (may all imperfections be absent) is the eternal Father, the eternal ectype is his Son, i.e., the substantial image of the Father: because (1) χαρακτὴρ is not so accustomed to be taken for the seal itself, but rather for an image and effigy, or express form, and it speaks of a relation to the Exemplar, of which it is the image. (2) Paul called the Son of GOD the image εἰκόνα, Coloss. I. verse 16, not the seal of GOD. (3) The Book of Wisdom, whose description is very similar to ours, expresses it in the same place through εἰκόνα, chapter VII. verse 26, εἰκὼν ἀγαθότητος τῦ Θεῦ, as also through ἔσοπτρον ἀκηλίδωτον, an unspotted mirror. (4) most all interpreters, the Syrian, the Arab, the Vulgate, Erasmus, and the commentators render it through figure and image. (5) the similar place, John VI. verse 27, that God ἐσφράγισεν, sealed, agrees more with an express image than with a seal. It is the Apostle's purpose to set forth the Deity of the Son of GOD and to deliver the periphrasis of the mystery of eternal generation by both denominations, for the illustration of this sublime mystery; for just as he called him the effulgence of divine light and the splendor of the Father's glory by reason of the emanation and procession of the Son from the Father, as also of the representation of the Father's glory in the Son, so also he calls him the character of his hypostasis, both by reason of origin, that the Son is from the Father an express image through eternal generation; and by reason of representation, that the Son represents the hypostasis of the Father, no otherwise than as an image represents its archetype.

II. The word Ὑποστάσεως is ambiguous, and ἐκ τῶν πολλαχῶς λεγομένων, to omit other acceptations outside of Scripture; as regards the use of the word in Canonical Scripture and in the New Testament codex, it is used in three ways: (1) concerning boasting, 2 Corinthians 9:4 and chapter 11:17, ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ ὑποστάσεως τῆς καυχήσεως, in that hypostasis of boasting, that is, in the support of boasting, or that upon which boasting leans and is sustained; then concerning faith, Hebrews 3:14, τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς ὑποστάσεως, the beginning of the hypostasis of faith, as is clear from verse 6, or that beginning by which we are sustained; and Hebrews 11:1, Faith is ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, the hypostasis of things to be hoped for, or that by which things that are hoped for exist, or their support, not because it is the substance of the mind, but because it is the substance of the object in the mind, or in the heart of believers. Phil. Melanchthon renders it the expectation of things to be hoped for, or the confidence by which we determine that the promises of GOD are happening to us. And this is from the grammatical meaning of the word, because indeed ὑπόστασις most commonly denotes expectation, see Conf. Theol. page 137. The third use of this word is in the present description of the Son of GOD, where the Syrian interprets it as איתותה, which word, just like the Greek ὑποστάσεως, is explained here in two ways. Tremellius expounds it as Essence. Junius, however, prefers substance. Because the Syrians call essence rather ישו. Likewise, since the Greek word occurs among ecclesiastical writers sometimes for Essence or substance, sometimes for person, it is ambiguous in which meaning it ought to be taken here: There are those who wish for the same to be understood here as divine substance or essence. Epiphanius, book 2, Tom. 2, heresy 69, explains hypostasis as essence, and so do as many as assert that the word Hypostasis, in the usage and meaning received by the Church, by which it is employed in the article concerning the mystery of the three Hypostases or persons in the divine Essence, is ἄγραφον, as they say it is taken not from the phrasing of Scripture, but from common custom of speaking. See Cyril, dial. 1, on the Trinity. How also Socrates, book III, Tripart. chap. XXI, teaches that the word hypostasis was first received in the Church in this mystery in the time of Athanasius. Add also the opinion of the Council of Ephesus, which in the Synod. Epist. to Nestorius says that the Son, on account of one and the same substance, exists as the image and character of the splendor of glory. to Nestorius says that the Son, on account of one and the same substance, exists as the image and character of the splendor of glory. And Nazianzen, Orat. 5, on the Son, Tom. I, page 165, says the Son is called the image of the Father, as being of the same essence with the Father. To which also pertains what Nazianzen narrates in the oration on the praise of Athanasius, q. XXXI, that the Greeks who said three ὑποστάσεις seemed to the Latins to be saying three ὀὐσίας or essences: And what Jerome testifies, that the whole school of profane Greeks is ignorant of the distinction between hypostasis and ὀὐσία, Tom. II, Ep. 57, to Damasus, whence Jerome writes among other things in the same place concerning the three hypostases: Who, I ask, of the Apostles handed these things down? What new Teacher of the Gentiles, Paul, taught these things? Augustine also says in book V, de Trin. chap. 8, that the Romans cannot distinguish between ὀὐσία and hypostasis. Nicephorus also recognizes no distinction between ὑπόστασιν and ὀὐσία, book X, chap. XIII, to omit others. The Vulgate version also renders it by substance: and the Blessed Luther, as well as the Racovians, ein Abdruck seines Wesens. And Domin. Chemnitius in his Common Places and Domin. D. Menzerus, Tom. III, disp. Giess. IV, Th. 58, bring forward this meaning of the word here. Estius in his Commentary on this place. Others, however, prefer to take the same here for person. Which opinion is embraced from the ancients by Gregory of Nyssa in his book on the difference of Essence and Person. Basil, Epist. 45, and Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, and Oecumenius in their Commentaries on this place. Varimus and Suidas in their Lexicons, and from the more recent ones, Thomas, and likewise Cajetan, Salmeron, Bellarmine, Ribera, Cornelius à Lapide: and likewise Calvin, Zanchius, Ursinus, Pareus, and from our own, D. Hutterus in his Common Places, D. Gravverus in his Commentary on chapter I to the Hebrews. D. Meisnerus, part II, Phil. Sobr. page 417. To which latter opinion we also add our vote in the disp. on the A. Conf. IV, th. XI, and in the dissert. Rostoch. page 20. Crellius also, in his book on the one GOD the Father, renders it the character of the person of GOD. We prove and explain it in this way: because character is a relative name. Augustine, book 7, de Trinit. chap. 1, and from him Thomas, quest. XXXV, art. 1. Image is a personal name, since image is not said of itself, but to another: and therefore it presupposes a foundation and implies a correlate. That, therefore, of which it is called the character or image is immediately the correlate or its exemplar; that on account of which it is the foundation. Since, therefore, the Son is called the image of the ὑπόστασις, it is certain that the correlate is noted, but not the foundation, except indirectly, in so far as the same is presupposed. Moreover, the exemplar of the Son is the first person of the Godhead, the Father, but the foundation is the origin of the Son from the Father, or the communication of essence, by which the image of the Father is as it were impressed upon the Son, whence we conclude: That, by reason of which the Son is distinct from the Father and represents the Father, by that reason he is called the character and image of the Father. Because image implies (1) distinction; for the image of a thing is not the thing of which it is the image, by the nature of opposites; and (2) representation. For it is of the nature of an image to be a likeness, or to imply its exemplar, of which this origin is the foundation. But by reason of person, not of essence, the Son is distinct from the Father and represents the Father most exactly, because he has everything in his person that the Father has in his person, John XVI, verse 15, and as the Father has life in himself, so he has given to the Son to have life in himself. Syr. בִּקְנוֹמֵהּ in his person. For קנומה is properly person to the Syrians, as if you were to say that very one, incommunicable, so that there is not another, as Masius warns. Therefore, by reason of person, the Son is the character of the Father; or what is the same, the Son is the character of the person of the Father. Hence, by reason of relation, he is called the image of the person of the Father: meanwhile, we admit that he is called an essential or substantial image, but not because he is referred immediately to the essence of the Father, but because he refers to the Person of the Father as regards essence. But he is not called a personal image: for he is called the image of the person of the Father, not because he has the person of the Father communicated to him: for person is one thing, and the character of a person is another; but because the Son has the same essence in his person that the Father has in his person, and thus he represents, or refers to, the person of the Father as regards essence, as the Blessed Gravverus rightly says on page 17. This can be illustrated in a certain way by a similar example, when among humans a son is called the image of the hypostasis of the father; it is not understood immediately that the son is the image of the essence of the father, but rather of the suppositum, or person, yet identity or agreement is mediately inferred, because he is an image, by which he reflects the person of the father, that is, of the paternal nature. But much less in the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity is the Son to be called the image of the essence of the Father: since there is one and the same essence in number of the Father and the Son, nor is the essence of the Son only similar to the essence of the Father, but the same essence in number. In what therefore, and in respect to what, the Father and the Son are most simply one, in that and in respect to that the Son is not the image of the Father; since he cannot be called an image by reason of himself. It is added that the λόγῳ is said to be an image for the same reason that the Son is: Now the Son is said to be so not in respect to the essence, but to the person of the Father, because the essence does not properly beget, but the person. Finally, ὑπόστασις properly, and in its native signification, denotes something subsistent, and is distinguished from οὐσίᾳ, which designates nature common to several individuals: therefore Suidas defines ὑπόσασιν, because it is τὸ ἰδικὸν παρὰ τὸ κοινὸν, the particular above the common. And it is from ὑφίσασθαι, to subsist. Although, however, the Latins have not distinguished ἰσίαν & ὑπόσασιν, yet among the Greeks they are distinguished: which can be seen even from the etymology itself: and in that part the authority of the most learned Greeks, Gregory, Basil, Chrysostom, Theodoret, and others, is weightier for us than that of Jerome.

It must be noted, however, that 'person' is understood not abstractly and formally, concerning personality, or taken precisely for the incommunicable mode of subsisting, but rather concretely and materially, as it implies the essence marked with a hypostatic character, or for a person having essence. Because the Son does not represent the personality of the Father, or ἀγεννησίαν, but is distinguished from the Father by its relation. But he represents the person of the Father, because whatever the Father has in his person, that the Son also has; and therefore as he is called ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, not the effulgence of personality, but of Majesty terminated in the person of the Father, so also [he is] χαρα- κτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως or of Majesty, essence, and divinity in respect to the person of the Father: If you say, will he thus still be the image of himself? We answer: that the same thing cannot be called the image of itself in the same respect, but in a different way, nor is the Son called his own image, but the image of the Father's substance, which he reflects in himself most exactly: and to that extent those different opinions can be reconciled.

Franciscus David denies that either essence or person is signified in this place, because in other places it denotes neither, for faith is not a person or a substance. But the word is taken differently when it is said of the Father or a person in this place, and differently when it is said of things.

(3) What is the character of the hypostasis? 1. Enjedinus: He wishes the character of the hypostasis to be called not of GOD, but of the splendor, that is, the very substance of the splendor, because nothing is more splendid than Christ: which perverse explanation or depravation we have noted and refuted above. Schlichtingius also rejects the same: teaching that the pronoun αὐτοῦ, His, looks also to the name of glory, and ought to be construed with it no less than with the word hypostasis. 2. The same compares the character of the hypostasis with a footprint, and as no one calls a footprint a foot, so if the Son is the character of the hypostasis, he is not the hypostasis of the Father itself, but distinct from the Father τῇ ὑποστάσει; but we deny that a character implies merely a footprint. The word 'image' indeed seems to the Latins, from the nature of speech, to denote only a certain shadowy picture, and what represents the thing itself at least by some appearance; yet from the Hebrew mode of speaking, which Flacius rightly observes, it designates also a true and real existence, or the form of the thing itself, and a true and essential expression, and therefore 'image' is taken not only accidentally, but also substantially. Furthermore, a footprint and an image are distinguished, in that an image represents clearly that of which it is an image; but a footprint represents obscurely that of which it is a footprint. Concerning which more has been treated in Metaph. divin. How in all creatures certain footprints of divine goodness, power, and wisdom are said to be seen, but man is called the image of God. But the Son of God is called not the footprint of the Father, but the image, Col. I. verse 16, and χαρακτὴρ or expressed form, and that not accidental, but hypostatic and personal. Nor is the heretic's argument of any moment: If the character of a person is a person, it will be the person of a person, which seems absurd to the Samosatenian man. For because he would deny that the Son, who is a person distinct from the Father, when the discourse is about men, can be called the image of the Father, as a distinct person, and therefore that a person is the person of a person, or that a person has a person by virtue of the relation which intervenes between both, as that in respect of which the relative is said to be the relative of the correlate, the person of the Son is called the person of another person or the Father, from whom the Son has his being, and to whom he involves the relation by which he is the Son.

III. Calvin, just as he wishes the splendor of the Father's glory, so also the image of his hypostasis to be called only in respect of the manifestation and revelation of the Father, which we refuted above from Pareus. Beza does not depart much from his interpretation in the annotations.

That image of the hypostasis of GOD, he says, I consider not in the divinity of the Son by itself, as that which is also itself inscrutable by itself, but insofar as it offers itself to be seen in the flesh, and he explains it in this way: namely, that in CHRIST we contemplate the living, expressed, and engraved countenance of the most kind and most beneficent Father GOD. Finally, the Apostle seems to Beza to be already alluding to the ark of the covenant, and other symbols of the presence of GOD, which he will later compare with Christ. But in truth, Beza's little argument, that the divinity of the Son is no less inscrutable in itself than that of the Father, is not of such moment that we should make a divorce from the common and venerable antiquity received, and from an explanation not alien to the Apostle's purpose, and accede to the opinion of the Arians and Socinians. For he is called the image, not by reason of the knowing power, but by reason of his exemplar, or in respect of the conformity which he has with the archetype, and therefore as the Son from eternity is most similar to his Father, nay even ὁμοούσιος to the same, so also from eternity he is the image of the Father, however much κατ' ὑμᾶς he may not represent the Father, and indeed is inscrutable no less than the Father. Furthermore, it is too jejune: that the Son is called the image or character of the Father's hypostasis only by reason of the announcement or manifestation of the Father's grace made through the Son: thus CHRIST should rather have been called the character not of the hypostasis, but of the will and grace of GOD. Moreover, if the similar passage in Colossians 1:16, which Beza compares here, is consulted, it will be manifest ὀφθαλμοφανῶς that the reference is not to the human nature of CHRIST, but to his pre-eternal Deity. For it is said in the same place that he is the image of the invisible GOD, who is πρωτότυπον πάσης κτίσεως, and by whom all things were created. That this is certainly said of him not according to his human, but his divine nature, Beza himself is forced to acknowledge. Furthermore, by what evidence is it established that there is an allusion here to the ark of the covenant? Was the ark of the covenant the character of the hypostasis of GOD? And what, pray, does this allusion mean? But that the Apostle is rather occupied here in describing the eternal Deity of the Son of GOD, as was declared in the former epithet, is manifest here also from those things which were said in the preceding: and we shall treat of it more fully later. What of the fact that Beza himself seems finally to acknowledge this: when he proves from Calvin that ὑπόστασιν does not here designate Essence: because it would be absurd to say that the essence of the Father was impressed upon Christ: and he adds: that it is truly and aptly said that whatever the Father has as his own is expressed in Christ. Finally, he confirms from this not only the distinction of the hypostasis against Sabellius, but also the ὁμοούσιον against the Arians: Which would be brought forward ineptly and ἀσυλλογίςως [illogically], if Christ were called the Character of the hypostasis of the Father solely on account of his preaching, or the manifestation of his will, or only in respect of his human nature.

IV. Of the same flour is the depravity of the Neo-Photinians. Socinus, in his response to Chapter 8 of Wieki, page 116: Christ is called the image, or character of the hypostasis of GOD, because he exhibits to us the very GOD, otherwise invisible, to be looked upon, that is, he shows us his will and power, most perfectly revealed to himself, and, as far as can be and as far as it pertains to us, most perfectly communicated with himself, and which he places before our eyes. Ostorodus, in his Unterricht, chapter XX, page 141, wishes Christ to be called the character of the hypostasis of GOD, because he visibly showed the invisible GOD, i.e., his will and power (since to show the essence of GOD, as it is impossible, so also, having considered the counsel of GOD, it is entirely useless to men), as far as it concerned salvation. Schlichtingius also in his Commentary, page 25. GOD, as it were, imprinted his own form upon Christ, so that he might represent the very GOD to us; for which reason he himself also said, 'He who sees me, sees also my Father': because he both spoke the words of GOD and performed his works. And therefore Schlichtingius understands the image πρὸς ὑμᾶς [towards you] by which he represented GOD to us both by words and works, with Crellius leading the way in Book I, 'On the one GOD the Father', f. II, page 283: that Christ is called the image of GOD in respect to us, because he undoubtedly represented to us in himself the will, goodness, power, and wisdom of GOD, and exhibited its splendor in a certain way. Which Crellius says was further done, page 284, insofar as he expressed the will of God by his teaching and his power by admirable works, and clearly proclaimed the faith and truth by both.

To this Socinian corruption we oppose the following foundations. First, the word χαρακτῆρος [character] provides it, which the Socinians admit designates an image here. But that the Son of GOD is the character and image of GOD, and that the Son of GOD manifested the will and power of GOD by preaching and performing miracles, are things very different.
