A character is a form imprinted by some archetype. God, or the hypostasis of God, is the ἀρχέτυπον [archetype]; Christ is the character of that, or the ἔκτυπον [ectype]. God, as it were, imprinted his own form upon him, says Schlichtingius, and rightly so far: if all imperfections are absent from the denomination of ἀρχετύπυ [archetype] and ἐκτύπυ [ectype], as is proper in divine matters. Therefore, he is not called the character of GOD by reason of the proclamation of the word and works, but because GOD, as it were, imprinted his form upon him. Which the very appellation of image imports. For an image is, as Justin Martyr truly defines in his Questions and Answers, εἰκών ἐστιν ἧς ἡ γένεσις διὰ μιμήσεως [an image is that whose generation is through imitation], which Festus, and Andr. Placus render it thus: an image is properly called that whose generation is through imitation. And Thomas requires this for an image from Augustine: the reason for an image is likeness with expression. Which agree with the Son of GOD insofar as GOD imprinted his own form upon him, as Crellius speaks, but not insofar as Christ shows us the will and power of GOD by preaching and working.

The second: that the Son of GOD is called χαρακτὴρ [character] or image in the nominative case, and absolutely, but is not said to have been made to the image of God: that he does not represent the image of the Father in any way whatsoever, but is the most perfect image of GOD; that he is not merely a μιμητικὴ [imitative], accidental, and incomplete image, but Φυσικὴ [natural], essential, and complete κατ᾿ ὁμοουσίαν [according to consubstantiality]; which therefore is to be understood not of Christ by reason of his Prophetic office, but rather by reason of his essence and Deity: since in that respect he is most of all the image of GOD.

The third: that he is called the character τῆς ὑποστά- σεως [of the hypostasis], of the substance and person, but not of the will or power of the Father; therefore he is not called the character by reason of the announcement of the will or the manifestation of the power, but because he exhibits in himself the very substance of the Father: But since Socinus denies that the hypostasis of GOD in this place signifies the substance itself truly and properly, but that it is the same as if it had been said: that Christ is the character of God himself: and that he further thinks this is the same as the will of God. Is this not to play with the most holy word of God? For where is substance not truly and properly understood? And where is the hypostasis of God the same as the will of God? Or where at least is God the same as the will of GOD? And shall we think that the particle ὑποστά- σεως [of the hypostasis] was added in vain, so that it is the same as if he had said, the image of GOD? Therefore the Racovians also render it Wesen [substance], not Willens [will]; they do indeed add Unterstands [understanding] in the margin; but here this is not the same as will; nor did any of the interpreters before these Innovators take hypostasis for will.

The fourth: that he is called the character of the hypostasis of GOD in such a sense that he is understood to be the substantial character or image of GOD the Father. For by what reason would he be called the character of the substance, unless he were a substantial character and image? But in respect of his Prophetic office, he would have to be called not a substantial, but only an accidental image. For an office refers to actions, not to substance.

The fifth: that the Apostle is not differing here about a declaration, that he behaved and declared himself to be the image of the Father, but about the very truth of the matter, that he is in reality the image of the substance of God: Therefore, although it may be admitted that by word and work he showed himself to be the Son of God, and the image of the substance of GOD, so that it was permissible to infer and conclude with invincible force that he is the Son of GOD ὁμοούσιον [consubstantial], the substantial image of the Father, just as he proved it most often by his teaching and miracles, as if a posteriori: yet the τὸ εἶναι [the being], or the being itself of the image of the substance of GOD, even of the Son of GOD, did not consist in that. But the reason for the image of the essence of GOD consists in that, in respect of which the Son also has his origin from GOD through a certain procession or expression as if from an archetype, and has a likeness or agreement with GOD, which certainly cannot be said of the preaching and manifestation of God in respect to us.

Sixth: That the Son of God himself is called the image of the Father's substance, but not his doctrine or miracles, or his Prophetic office: yet that this should rather be said according to the mind of the Socinians, because in the doctrine, in the miracles, and thus in the office of Christ, the grace and power of GOD shone forth, but not in the Son of GOD himself, viewed substantially.

Seventh: that he is called the image of the substance of GOD in the same way as the brightness of the glory of GOD: but that the Son of GOD is called brightness at least by reason of his proclamation or Prophetic office is false, which has been shown above, and Schlichting the Socinian acknowledges. E.

Eighth: that he is called an image not with respect to us, but by reason of the substance of GOD: in that he contains the same expressed in himself, and is most similar to GOD in that; that he also represents God himself to us, this is accidental to that, that he is the image of the substance of God. Nor is it mentioned here by the Apostle, just as it is incidental, that we should understand the splendor of the glory of God to be the same thing, which would be such, even if it were never acknowledged.

The ninth is provided by the continuity of the Apostolic discourse: for this, that the Son is the image of the substance of God, is established here as the foundation of the expiation and purification of sins, which he made by himself, and of his sitting at the right hand of the Majesty of God on high. But that the Son of God preached the will of God, and exhibited the power of God by miracles, is not the foundation for why he made the purification of sins BY HIMSELF, and sat at the right hand of the Majesty: since that also applied to the Apostles and other ministers of God.

The tenth we derive from the comparison of the Apostolic passage Col. 1:15, which Socinus and Ostorodus institute here: By the same reason that Christ is called the image of the invisible God, Col. 1:15, by that same reason he is also called the character of the hypostasis of God: But not because he exhibits God to us to be seen, i.e., the will and power of God, but because he is called the πρωτότοκος τῆς πάσης κτίσεως [firstborn of all creation], he is called the image of God. Therefore.

Eleventh, again from this parallel statement: The Son of God was the image of the invisible God before all creatures, before he created those things which are in heaven and on earth, as the Apostle testifies in Col. 1:15-16, and therefore he existed as the character of the hypostasis of God before all creatures. Therefore, he is not the character by reason of the proclamation of the word and miracles, or the revelation of the will and power of God.

Twelfth: Because nowhere in the Holy Scriptures is the Son of God called the image of God, or by a similar appellation, on account of the mere manifestation of the grace and power of God, and therefore there is no reason why we should admit here the same explanation, which is foreign to the Scriptures and to the manner of speaking of the Holy Spirit. As for the passage 2 Cor. 4:4, we deny that the Son of God is called the image of God there on account of our illumination alone. For the light of the Gospel concerning the glory of Christ is not primarily, much less solely, this, that the Son of God revealed the will of God, but that he is the substantial image of God by reason of his nature, and our Lord by reason of his office, both of which the Apostle designates quite clearly as the object.

Thirteenth. If the Son of God is called the image of the Father by reason of the announcement of his will, or the manifestation of his grace and power, then by the same reason he would also have to be called the image of himself, as well as the image of the Holy Spirit. Because by reason of his prophetic office he announced to us the will not only of God the Father, but also his own and that of the Holy Spirit concerning our salvation, and manifested grace and power. But the Son of God, according to Scripture, is not and is not called the image of himself or of the Holy Spirit, but only of God the Father. Therefore.

Fourteenth: If the Son of God is called the image of the substance of God by the reason that, having performed his prophetic office on earth, he announced the will of God and declared the grace and power of God by word and miracles, then the Apostles would also be called the image of the substance of God by that same reason. But according to Holy Scripture, not the Apostles, but Christ alone is the image of the substance of God. Therefore.

Finally, to pass over other things that could be urged, it will follow that the Son of God will not be, and will not remain, the image of the substance of God for eternity, because he will declare neither the power nor the grace of God by the preaching of the word nor by miracles, but God will be there all in all to us, 1 Cor.

15:25, and we shall be ἰσάγγελοι [equal to the angels], Luke 20:36, and will have no need to be taught the will of God concerning our blessedness through the proclamation of Christ.

What else is interwoven into this gloss by its authors in the aforementioned place should be weighed, unless the nature of the undertaking suggested otherwise. That God is not known by essence is contrary to the Scriptures: no less is the claim that the knowledge of the essence of God is useless to us for salvation, John 17:3, 1 John 5:11. Compare 1 John 2:23. Furthermore, Christ also shows the essence of God no less ὁρατῶς [visibly], i.e., by miraculous operation, or ἀκουσῶς [audibly] and by the preaching of the word, than his power and grace: since that is also evident from the very contemplation of creatures, Rom. 1:20. But as for the words of Christ, 'He who sees me, sees also the Father,' John 12:45, they are to be understood not of the knowledge of the divine will alone, but of the ὁμοουσία [consubstantiality] of the Father and the Son. Which Cyril, Augustine, and Theophylact defended against the Arians. For it is not absurd that one seeing the person of Christ sees God the Father, not because the person of Christ is the very person of the Father, but because the Father and the Son are one in divine essence, John 10:30. Just as he who saw Christ in the days of his flesh as a man, saw also the Word himself, not only with the mind, but also with bodily eyes: not indeed immediately in the Deity itself, but in the assumed flesh, as John testifies, 1 Epist. 2:2, so also he consequently saw God the Father, because the Son is the character of the hypostasis of the Father, not that God the Father was seen in a body, but that the Son, who is one in essence with the Father, was manifested in the flesh, 1 Tim. 3:16. But if that is understood of the knowledge of the divine will alone: then the Apostle could also have said: 'He who sees me, sees the Father,' because he too revealed the whole counsel of God concerning salvation, Acts 20:27.

D. Pareus wishes the Son to be called the image of the Father here both in respect to the Father, in that from eternity He is the substantial image of the same, and as it were another self from Theodoret: and in respect to us, in that the Son manifested in the flesh expressed to us the nature and will of the Father to the life by His divine wisdom, doctrine, and works: Although indeed it is not to be denied that He can be called the image of the Father in both respects, yet we deny that He is called the image of the Father's substance in the latter respect, and that this is the Apostle's purpose here, as he teaches, how the Son through the incarnation became for us an image, nor do the arguments which we have just brought forward admit this.

VI. It remains, therefore, that we conclude the Son of God is called the character of the substance or person of the Father, with the unanimous suffrage of the whole of the better Antiquity and the orthodox Church, by reason of His essential Deity, or in that He is a divine person ὁμο&́σι® to GOD the Father, so that respect is had both to the origin of the Son from the Father, the first person of the Deity, through eternal procession or generation: and to the representation of the paternal substance, in that the Son reflects His eternal Father. For to be the image of another is to proceed to the likeness of another; and therefore it implies two things: Origin, or dependence, with this word taken more loosely and improperly: and likeness and agreement with Him from whom He depends or proceeds. For mere likeness does not suffice, since many things are similar to one another which are not images of one another: But in addition, origin or procession from an exemplar or antitype is required. These things, however, by purifying terms from all imperfection, and by applying them through the analogy of perfection and eminence, best suit this mystery. As far as origin and procession are concerned, the Son of GOD, speaking properly, proceeds from the hypostasis of the Father, or the first person of the Most Holy Trinity, from eternity, or has his origin in an ineffable manner according to Scripture, Psalm II, verse 7; Micah V, verse 2; Proverbs VIII, verse 23; John I, verse 18, etc., as the image of the same substantial being. Crellius, however, accuses this of involving a contradiction, lib. I, s. II, de Uno DEO, cap. XX, p. 299. No image, he says, is of the same numerical essence as that of which it is an image; otherwise, it would be an image of itself. Therefore, since Christ is the image of GOD, he cannot be of the same numerical substance as GOD, and furthermore, not GOD, namely that supreme one. Clearly, because reason invents contradictions for itself, the letter of Scripture and its constant meaning must be deferred to. But whence is the principle of Crellius established: That no image is of the same numerical essence as that of which it is an image? Is it because it involves some contradiction in itself? Let him show it, then. Or is it certain by an induction of all examples? But there is controversy about certain examples, and specifically it is now asked about this one, when the Son is called the image of the Father. Therefore, the induction is not perfect and consistent with itself. Thus, that supreme agreement and the procession proper to the Son, on account of which he is called an image, should be derived from the Scriptures rather than contradicting Scripture with such reasons. Furthermore, if the same thing can be a sign of itself, given at least some difference of reason, which is considered under one respect and another, why could not the Son, really and personally distinct from the Father, although coessential with the Father, be called the image of the Father? Divine concepts can be called images, or ὁμοιώματα of the object which is conceived in the divine mind: But are the concepts by which GOD contemplates and understands himself of a different essence from GOD, so that we may speak ἀνθρωποπαθῶς (in a human manner)? And this further becomes manifest from the nature of an image. Because an image as such brings with it nothing but agreement with the exemplar and an origin or procession from the same, but neither of these imports a numerically distinct essence of the image and the exemplar. But they are relatives, says Crellius, and therefore the image and that of which it is an image are opposites: But opposites as such must differ at least in number, l. c. p. 281. Truly, this is absurd. For it is equally false that what is assumed as a principle: Opposites and relatives must differ at least in number. A subject and an adjunct, a sign and the thing signified, a principle and that which is from a principle are relatively opposites, which nevertheless, as such, do not differ in number. A genus with respect to that of which it is a genus, a species, or an individual, is called πρός τι (relative), and is a relative. But it is not really, much less essentially, different from the same; but only formally. Therefore, however much a formal respect and difference may be required at a minimum, a real, much less an essential, difference is not precisely inferred. Nevertheless, Crellius insists: If the image and the exemplar are the same, then the same will be an image of itself. Resp. If the image and the exemplar are the same essentially, yet so that he from whom the image is, is not the same personally, it is by no means inferred that the same will be an image of itself. Thus the Son is the image of the Father, from whom he is personally distinct, but he is not an image of himself. He is the same as the Father by reason of essence, the image of the Father by reason of person; whence he is called the character of the Father's person. The adversary replies again: Our people admit that the Son is similar to the Father by reason of essence, and therefore his image. But the answer from the above is easy. The Son is called the image by reason of essence at least mediately, or as the foundation, the communication of the same essence is indicated: But by reason of person, he is immediately the image of the Father, because thus the correlate is noted, in respect of which the image is distinct from the exemplar. Furthermore, since there are two requirements of an image, origin and likeness; by reason of origin, the image is distinguished from the exemplar, the Son from the Father; by reason of likeness, the image agrees with its exemplar, the Son with the Father, or rather he is a participant of the same divine essence. Finally, Crellius urges that it is in vain to distinguish a person from his essence, since a person is the same as his essence, and therefore if the person of the Son is the image of the person of the Father, the essence of the Son is also the image of the paternal essence: Resp. but it must be entirely distinguished between person and essence, although essence and person in divine matters do not differ really. For they still admit contradictory predicates, since a person is incommunicable in subsisting, but an essence as such is not incommunicable in subsisting. It is true that everyone is the same as his essence, but it does not yet follow that a person is simply the same as the essence. Materially indeed and concretely, a person involves the essence. But formally and abstractly, it is contradistinguished from the essence, as a mode of a thing. For it is one thing to be an incommunicable mode of subsisting, another thing to be the thing itself which subsists in this mode. Then, indeed, the Son is the image of the Father as to essence, but the essence of the Son itself is not rightly called the image of the essence of the Father. For these are distinct, and are wrongly and sophistically confused by Crellius: to the former is inferred the foundation of the image, to the latter the very thing of being an image formally.

Therefore, as to the other requirement of an image, or the representation of the archetype and agreement with the exemplar, since the Son most exactly and perfectly represents the Father in himself, and is to him not only ὁμούσιον (of the same substance) but absolutely ὁμούσιον, because he is called the image of the Father in the most perfect manner, there is no room for doubt. But Schlichtingius inverts this here: that the Apostle seems to have used the word hypostasis in this place to express what exists between GOD and Christ, who is otherwise most similar to GOD and represents him: because, namely, Christ is the character, but GOD is the hypostasis itself. As the heretic asserts this to hint at a diversity of divine essence and glory, so he is in vain in that presumption. For the Apostle used the word ὑποστάσεως rather to note not some accidental, but a substantial image of the Father, which the word imports. However, it is not that he wished the hypostasis itself to be something more sublime and eminent than its character, for the very reason of the name does not imply that, nor can it be gathered from elsewhere: nay, the Apostle is rather occupied in asserting, proposing, and proving the supreme Majesty of the Son of GOD. For this reason he had also called him ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, the splendor of the Father's glory.

Statorius, however, of the same Sect, denies that Christ according to his Deity is the image of the Father: because he is not visible: and therefore cannot represent the Father. But he is far more inept in this part than the others. For (1) it is not even of the nature of an image that it should represent to us, provided that in itself it is representative of another. (2) But it is much less required that it should represent to our sight, or be visible, even assuming that according to you it is an image: Concepts certainly in the mind are images of things which are, and yet not visible, to pass over other things; and therefore we have noted in the Metaphysics that visibility is entirely accidental to an image, nor is there any reason why we should dwell on these things in this place.

Therefore, let these things suffice concerning the former description of the Son, in which he is considered with respect to the Father, and as regards his essence; we proceed to the second, in which he is viewed with respect to this universe, and as regards the Rectorship which he has over all things, proposed in these words: Φέρων τε τὰ πάντα τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὑτοῦ.

The Apostle wished this to be joined, because he is laying for himself a foundation for discoursing on the enthronement of Christ the man to the plenary rule of the whole universe, no less than on the purification of our sins, which Christ PER HIMSELF as the principal cause most omnipotently accomplished. The particle τε retains its customary meaning here, and is copulative, not exceptive, which is what Schlichtingius wants: For the Son of GOD is not the character of the hypostasis of GOD, or as Schlichtingius says: He refers primarily to the likeness and Majesty of GOD, insofar as he carries all things by his powerful word, but before he carried τὰ πάντα, he was the image and character of the Father: and to carry all things pertains to the actions of the Son of GOD, that being the Image of GOD does not pertain to actions, was demonstrated just now. Thus, the description of the principal work of the Son of GOD is joined here with the description of his Nature, which are certainly different. Enjedinus denies that this is a description of Deity, or that it can be inferred: Christ carries, governs, administers all things; Therefore he is the eternal and omnipotent GOD. Because all power is given to him, Matt. XXVIII. verse 19. and John XIII. verse 3. All things delivered into his hands by the Father; But to the eternal GOD no one gave anything. Resp. (1) Given according to his human nature: But that power is divine, supreme, infinite. Therefore it presupposes a divine nature. (2) Nor could it have been given, unless he were the supreme GOD, Is. XLII. verse 8. I argue: He who sustains and governs all things by a powerful word is the true GOD, because this belongs to the true GOD alone. But the Son of GOD sustains and governs all things by a powerful word. Therefore he is the true GOD. Fr. David, denying the Trinity of persons, likewise denies that two should be posited as having equal power and rule, denying that Christ takes care of the Church, and he takes these and similar passages concerning the bringing of all, that is, Jews and Gentiles, to the kingdom of GOD, that Christ brought them to it through the knowledge of himself. Resp. to Faust. Socin. p. 69. and concerning the power of Christ delivered, which is now exercised by the virtue of that word. That most pestilential error. Thus Christ is dislodged from his throne, deprived of his kingdom, imagined to be idle, and all things which are said concerning the sitting at the right hand of GOD and the rule of Christ are denied. See the cited disputation, page 75.

But three things are hinted at in that description: (1) The action of carrying. (2) The object of the action. (3) The medium of the same, by which the Son of GOD is said to carry all things. As to the former: The Son of GOD is called Φέρων or carrying, which is variously explained here, (1) concerning conservation, that he as it were carries, bears, and sustains all things: Which the Syrian אֲחִיד, that is, embracing, holding, sustaining, and restraining all things. Which is also among the names of GOD, noting his omnipotence, by which he sustains and preserves all things, so that unless GOD were Φέρων or אֲחִיד, all things must collapse and return to nothing, which was nothing before, and which is nothing, or consists outside of the powerful conservation of GOD. (2) Concerning the government of all things, how Erasmus seems to take it, explaining this by the word of moderating, by which he acts, moves, and governs all things. Cornelius à Lapide joins this explanation with the former, that the Son of God, as the supreme King and Moderator of all things, both carries and sustains, as well as acts upon and moves this whole universe: And he wishes the Apostle here to allude to the chariot of the Cherubim, Ezek. I., from Hieronymus Prado, since he who sits and presides in the chariot there is said to have been similar to the Son of man, which is the same as that which the Apostle says here, that the Son carries all things by the word of his virtue. Calvin takes 'to carry' here as 'to protect,' and to cause that creatures remain in their state. For he understands that all things would soon fall, unless they were sustained by his virtue. (3) Concerning sustentation, by which he fosters, feeds, and sustains all things, like a pious mother, which meaning Cornelius likewise notes here. And B. Luther proposed this in Enarr. on this place, f. 69. That 'to carry' is that which nourishes and fosters all things, so that he may acknowledge, not only that all things were made through him, which he said above, but also that all things are preserved through him, etc. Thus Beza in his notes, who says that φέρων is the same as the Hebrew מכלכל. But Cornel. à Lap. thinks rather that the Hebrew נשׂו has a place here, as a prince is called נשׂיא among the Hebrews. Cf. Num. XI. verse 12. and Is. IX. verse 6. Moreover, this third meaning can also be joined with the preceding ones, by which it is noted that the Son of GOD preserves, governs, and sustains all things.

On the contrary, Socinus and Franc. David oppose the subordinate meanings, and wish the Son of GOD to be said here to govern all things at least. Wherefore Socinus distinguishes these things thus: that this does not concern the universal and especially the interior and essential conservation of all things; but only the government, by which he preserves them either externally or only for their well-being: and this for the sole purpose of eliding the ἀπόδειξιν (demonstration) which this Apostolic assertion provides for the supreme Deity of the Son of GOD. He relies on two reasons: The first is that the word φέρων, according to Erasmus, has the meaning of acting or moving and moderating rather than carrying; because those things are called φερόμενα by the Greeks which are driven by a certain impulse, whence they also call an impulse φορὰν, and they say ἄγειν καὶ φέρειν of one who moderates someone at his own discretion. And therefore Socinus concludes that it should be said that government is being discussed here rather than conservation. The second is, that those things which are added to the word of his power indicate a command and authority, which do not so openly suit preservation and government. Who does not see upon how weak a foundation these rest? (1) That preservation and government can be distinguished by that reasoning, if it be admitted at all, which however the adversary has not yet proved ought to be admitted, it is nevertheless certain that when the Scriptures treat of the government of all things, that interior preservation is not excluded, but rather included, or presupposed. Why therefore should the same be excluded here? (2) Furthermore, it is not said simply that the Son of GOD bears all things, but by the word of his power, that is, by an omnipotent nod, and government, and most efficacious power; but he who thus administers, rules, and governs all things, he at the same time sustains and preserves, lest those things which he rules and governs should perish. Moreover, among τὰ πάντα [all things] is also the Church, which he preserves not only outwardly, but rather by an interior efficacious influx: without which the Church cannot even be said to be ruled and governed by him. (3) Furthermore, he who governs powerfully or by an omnipotent word, and efficaciously, he preserves not only for well-being, but even for being itself, because the preservation of the existence of things depends solely upon him, who rules and governs all things by his powerful word according to his nod and will.

And thus to govern is to bestow and provide the powers of subsisting, and consequently to preserve as regards being itself. (4) Whoever preserves all things as regards well-being, he certainly also preserves them internally, since well-being also pertains to internal preservation. (5) Since the same power is required for the government of all things and for their preservation, for well-being and for preserving the being of things, that power by which all things are preserved in their being will certainly belong to Christ. (6) Add that GOD claims for Himself alone in the Scriptures the government of all things no less than their preservation, Is. XLIII. verse 13, chap. XLIV. verse 47. Therefore, He who governs all things is as true and eternal a GOD as He who preserves all things. (7) That the discourse here is about preservation is evident from the very confirmation subjoined by the Apostle: for he does not merely prove that Christ moderates and governs all things, but that He preserves the whole universe, and indeed in such a way that He could destroy all things, and change them like a garment, and wear them out, verse 12, from Psalm CII. verse 27. But He who so bears and sustains all things by the word of His power, that He can change them at will and utterly destroy them, is the cause not only of exterior preservation, which makes for well-being, but of interior preservation, which pertains to being. (8) Furthermore, creation is also ascribed to the Son of GOD, verse above, of all things. But He who, as Creator and Author of all things, bears them by His own power, is not only the moderator of all things, but also their preserver. (9) A similar phrase is added, Deuteronomy I. verse 31. The Lord thy GOD bore thee, and chap. XXXII. verse 11. As an eagle bears its young upon its wing, the Lord alone led him. Cf. Exod. XIX. verse 4, which is manifest to belong to Christ as the Leader of the Israelite people from Exod. XXIII. verse 20, Is. LXIII. verse 9, 1. Corinthians X. verse 4. As therefore the sustenance and preservation of the Israelites in the desert is ascribed to the Son of GOD by the word of bearing, so in this place He is said to bear all things by the word of His power, that is, to preserve and sustain them. (10) A place of the Apostle clearly similar is also to be compared, Coloss. I. verse 17, as it is one in which there is likewise the same description of the Son, that He is the image of God, etc., verse 15, and the attribution of the work of creation, verse 16, & the preservation of all things is found assigned to the Son of GOD, as in this very place: and this indeed in these words, τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκε, all things consist in Him, because the whole System of the world is contained in Him, and if it were without His containment and preservation, it would immediately collapse: which certainly implies the interior preservation of all things: and therefore here the bearing of all things by the word of power ought not to be explained otherwise than of that sustaining and preservation by which all things are preserved, as far as their essence is concerned, so that upon the withdrawal of this power, every creature would cease to be, to become, and to subsist, as Thomas says in this place. (11) And in that way all interpreters understood this word, who, although they explain it in some places as moderation and government, do not however exclude preservation, but wish it to be understood as the same. The Syriac and Arabic paraphrases explain it with a word that has the force of containing. Chrysostom explains Φέρων τε τὰ πάντα, τῶτ᾽ ἔστι κυβερνῶν διαπίπτοντα συγκρατεῖ: and compares with one another the work of creation and

preservation, because this is here of no less moment and power than that, in these words, τῷ γὰρ ποιῆσαι τὸν κόσμον ἐκ ἠττόν ἐσι τὸ συγκρατεῖν, ἀλλ᾽ εἰδέ τι καὶ θαυμασὸν εἰπεῖν, καὶ μεῖζον: τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἐξ ἐκ ὄντων, ἐσί τι παράγειν; τὸ δὲ τὰ γεγονότα, εἰς τὸ μὴ εἶναι μέλλοντα ἀναχωρεῖν συνέ- χων καὶ συνάπτειν πρὸς ἄλληλα διασασιάζοντα, τῦτό ἐσι τὸ μέγα καὶ θαυμασὸν καὶ πολλῆς δυνά- μεως τεκμήριον. Theophylact follows him according to his custom, and reduces it to a summary, that the Son moderates and contains all things by His word. Nay rather, to restrain and coerce those things which dissent from one another and are about to proceed into nothingness is far greater than to produce all those things. Nor does Ambrose, to whose authority Socinus appeals here, think otherwise; because he interprets the word bearing as governing: because he adds what kind of government he understands, by which those things that have been made are contained, lest they return to nothing, and those things which are repugnant to one another are fitted together. Erasmus also, upon whose interpretation Socinus also relies here, sufficiently explains how he interprets the word Φέρων not as bearing or carrying, but rather as acting, or moving and moderating: because, forsooth, to bear and to carry belongs to one who is passive, and implies a burden: here, therefore, he prefers to understand one who is acting, moving, and moderating. For Paul, or whoever was the Author of the Epistle, feels (these are the words of Erasmus in the notes cited on this place) not only that this world was founded through the Son, just as he had just said: Through whom He also made the ages; but that it is ruled and administered, being founded, and that not with effort, care, and industry, as men show it, but by a word, that is, by the nod of His power. And therefore he approves in that part the interpretation of Chrysostom: (whom we have already said accepted it concerning preservation) For someone governs with effort, he bears, who moves wherever he pleases without effort. Whence it is evident that Erasmus does not understand it of government, which is only exterior preservation, but of the motion and moderation of all things, which are both preserved in their being and are driven according to the will of Christ the Moderator. Finally, Socinus himself confesses: If the word all things be accommodated to the kingdom of Christ and the Church, it can truly be said that Christ sustains, nourishes, and preserves all things by His power; Since the heretic has once admitted that, why does he turn himself again into another form: unless it be to render everything doubtful, as far as lies in him? But with a vain attempt. For the reasons brought forward by Socinus are of no moment, so far are they from being able to derogate in any way from the arguments already made. The former, as it relied on the authority of Erasmus, so with the opinion of Erasmus explained, it collapses entirely. Let those things be called Φερόμενα, which are driven by a certain impulse, that is, are effectively moved, as Erasmus hints; and let Φέρειν be to move according to one's own will, does it not therefore follow that Φέρων will fit the preservation as well as the government, or the moderation of all things? I do not think so: For even when GOD preserves all things, this is not a passion, but an action, not a burden or business for GOD, but an ἀυτεξέσιος and most free, and to GOD most easy, motion and agitation of all things: since the preservation of GOD is most closely joined and bound up with moderation and governance. Moreover, the Apostle wished to use the word Φέρων for this reason, as the better interpreters observe, because the preservation of all things causes no business for GOD: Εἶτα τὸ εὔκολον δηλῶν εἶπε, Φέρων, continues Chrysostom l. c. οὐκ εἶπε,

κυβερνῶν, from the metaphor of those who simply move and cause something to be carried by a finger, here he also showed the mass of the possession to be great, and that the great is nothing to him. And Theophylact the abbreviator from the version of the person: He did not say governing, but carrying as if by fingers this great mass of the world, he carries it no differently than if it were established that it is nothing. And the ordinary Gloss from the same: By saying this he wished to designate the ease of containing through the metaphor of those who, without any labor, move or effect something with a word or a finger. Thus Christ contains and governs the mass and magnitude of creation without labor. One may compare the passage in Isaiah chapter XL: Who has measured the waters in his fist, and meted out the heavens with a span, or held the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance? Where it is discussed concerning the sustenance and conservation of this universe, as a thing most easy for GOD, the Ruler and conservator of the universe, in words taken from the midst of men, because he performs this as if with small instruments, that is, without any labor. Cf. Prov. XXX. verse 4. Furthermore, it is indicated by the word Φέρων that the sustenance of all things is to be understood not as an impetuous carrying, but as a gentle bearing, which the blessed Luther rightly notes. It is an eloquent word, he says, which he uses: He carries all things, he does not urge, he does not impel, he does not tumultuate, but he carries and bears gently, so that all things may enjoy his goodness and gentleness.

The other argument of Socinus is also fig-like; because he is said to carry all things by the word of his power, that is, by his command and authority, and therefore it is not conveniently accepted concerning the internal and essential conservation itself, but rather concerning the government of all things. For what, is not power required, and the word of power, as much for conservation as for government? Just as all things were created by a word, so also all things are most powerfully conserved by a word. Why then would the Apostle not say concerning conservation, he carries all things by the word of his power? For it is not implied by this expression only the authority of governance, by which he moves and acts all things at his pleasure by his command and authority, but the same also applies to the sustenance and conservation of all things, by which he sustains, protects, and conserves all things by a bare, but far most powerful, word.

Schlichting compares the Petrine use of this word, 2 Epist. I. last, where the prophets are said to be Φερόμενοι, moved by the Holy Spirit, that is, stirred and agitated: and he explains it concerning Christ still acting on earth: Christ was carrying all things, insofar as all things were moved at his nod and pleasure, there was nothing that did not yield, did not obey his authority. And therefore he wishes the participle Φέρων, just as the earlier ὢν, to be explained by the past tense. But there is no reason why these things should be restricted to past time: rather, the perpetuity of the act of carrying is insinuated in the present time, as we said regarding the word ὢν. Because as the Son of GOD created all things, so from creation he carries, conserves, sustains, and moderates all things by one and the same continuous and perpetual act of conservation and moderating sustenance. Furthermore, if this is compared with that internal impulse and agitation of the Holy Spirit, by which holy men of GOD are said to have spoken while Φερόμενοι: it will be more likely that not only external, but internal conservation is implied. For as that φορὰ caused them to be teachers, and gave them to speak both by the internal formation of the mind and the formation of their speech, Acts II. verse 4, so this φορὰ of all things likewise causes all things to be, and grants them substance, and does not only moderate and rule them from the outside. Finally, that there was nothing that did not yield to the authority of Christ when he acted on earth, that was only because the Son of GOD carries all things by the word of his power, that is, he sustains, conserves, and governs omnipotently together with the Father: and therefore the Son himself testifies concerning this, John V. verse 17. My Father works until now by conserving and governing all things, and I work, whence the Jews also concluded: that he was making himself equal to GOD, v. 18, ascribing and claiming this universal conservation and government of things no less to himself than to the Father, but Christ adds apologetically in verse 19: Whatsoever the Father does, the same the Son also does likewise. And how could Christ have moved all things by his authority, by a mere nod and a little word, calmed the winds, stilled the seas, driven away any diseases, restored life to the dead, commanded unclean spirits, which Schlichting wishes to be implied here, unless he had existed as the supreme and absolute Lord of all things, the Ruler of this universe? But the same power by which he absolutely commanded all things, or the moderating and ruling power of all things, is the very power of GOD; by which all things are sustained, conserved, and supported, or the conservator of all things. And therefore those things which Christ did on earth are proofs of the divine power that conserves and governs all things, but they do not exhaust here what is said, the Son of GOD τὰ πάντα φέρων, which can be established from the arguments previously opposed to Socinus; but it will be more evident from the designation of the object of this action of the Son of GOD: to which we now proceed.

Therefore (II.) Regarding the object of this action, the Apostle expresses it with the word τὰ πάντα: which Socinus restricts to the Church, and to the kingdom of Christ, with the Racovian Catechism, Germ. chap. I. page 100, and that by the argument that this concerns the kingdom of Christ. But this is a mere begging of the question, for where is it concerned with the kingdom of Christ, and indeed exclusively? In the preceding words? But there αἰῶνες, that is, all the ages, are said to have been created through him. In the following ones? But they are either irrelevant, or certainly do not restrict the word τὰ πάντα. Finally, in these very words? But this is what we said, that this very thing is begged which is in the beginning. And therefore Schlichting does not restrict the word, but seems to take all things absolutely, and outside the Church: and he refers it to this, that he moved all things by his single nod and little word; and that at his nod the seas had to grow calm, the winds to cease, diseases to flee away, life to return, unclean spirits to yield; which things pertain to universal dominion in heaven and on earth, and not merely to the government of the Church. That nothing may be lacking for the proving of our thesis, we show the same further (1) from the proper signification of the universal note; for this, when properly accepted and absolutely placed, embraces all things universally, and therefore is to be accepted universally, absolutely, and simply, unless some restriction appears from the context itself and the underlying subject matter: of which here not even a trace is seen. (2) from a peculiar observation, which here especially deserves to be noted: As often as this universal particle is used in the New Testament with verbs that signify either the first creation, or preservation, or government, so often is it to be accepted universally and absolutely, and it admits of no restriction. See John 1:3.

Romans 11:36; 1 Corinthians 8:6; Ephesians 3:9; Colossians 1:16, 17; Philippians 3:21; Hebrews 2:8, 10. Since, therefore, this is joined here to the verb of carrying, which introduces conservation and governance, it must also be taken universally concerning all created things. (3) From the dominion and inheritance of all things. The Son of God carries all those things by the word of His power, of which He is the heir and Lord. But He is the heir and Lord of all creatures, κληρονόμον πάντων, verse 2. Therefore, just as there πάντων was called heir without the article, so here τὰ πάντα is said to carry with the article, lest by chance someone seek a restriction from the article, as Smalcius does on 1 Corinthians 8:6, ref. l. de Err. Arian. p. 63. The article does not restrict, but has emphasis, all those things which ever are, Romans 11:36; Hebrews 2:10. (4) From the creation of things. But He is understood to carry all those things which He created, by virtue of immediate connection; but by the creation of the ages, He is indicated to have created all things that are, both those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible, Colossians 1:16. Therefore. (5) From the scope and intention. For the Apostle proposes the foundation of the exaltation to the right hand of God, because He says He sat at the right hand of God, for the reason that He carries all things: since He carries all things by the word of His power, having made purification of sins by Himself, He sat down at the right hand of the majesty of God on high; how far, therefore, the dominion of Christ sitting at the right hand of God extends, so far also does that governance by which He carries all things by the word of His power. But that is universal, in that He commands all, is established over all, fills all in all, Ephesians 1:21, 23; He rules in the midst of His enemies, Psalm 110:2, and has all things subject to Himself, Psalm 8:7; 1 Corinthians 15:27. Therefore. (6) From the Apostolic treatment in verse 10 and following, subjoined, where by virtue of the creation of His power, by which He sustains heaven and earth, He is said in turn to be about to destroy them and reduce them to nothing. Therefore, He is understood to carry by the word of His power all those things which He is indicated to have created, verse 10, and over which He has such power that He can change them and in turn destroy them. (7) From the confirmation of the Apostle made from Psalm 8:7 and following, by which it is taught that Christ is established absolutely and infinitely ἐπὶ τὰ ἔργα, over the works of the hands of God, (2) all things subject to His feet, (3) living creatures, birds, fish, etc., which are not in the Church. (4) Nothing is ἀνυπότακτον. Compare 1 Corinthians 15:27. (8) From the collation of the parallel passage, which we indicated before from Colossians 1:17. For as the Apostle there says that all things, whatsoever they are, were founded by the Son of God Himself, and thus are conserved, so also here he asserts that all things are conserved and carried by Him, as by whom all things were founded. But Socinus objects, l. c., that all things in that place ought to be restricted to things endowed with intelligence, and that not insofar as they simply are, but insofar as they have been in some way reformed through Christ Himself. Resp. This fiction about the reformation of all intellectual things has already been exploded before. But that τὰ πάντα is not restricted there, but taken universally, there are many things that teach: the appellation πάσης κτίσεως, verse 15; (2) the creation of τῶν πάντων, verse 16; (3) and the distribution of creatures, all things that are in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible; (4) the emphatic repetition, that all things were founded through Him and for Him, as in Hebrews 2:10. δί ὃν τὰ πάντα, κὰι δί ὗ τὰ πάντα is said of all things absolutely and simply, or universally. (5) Existence before all things: Compare Proverbs 8:23; John 1:1.

that the Son of God was, before anything was. (6) Whence finally is subjoined the consistency of all things in the Son of God, namely of all those things of which mention had been made so frequently until now. Finally, in the following verse, the Apostle at last betakes himself to explaining the special dominion of Christ, which He has in the Church, as the head of the same, and the reformation, for the purification of all things, which is far different from the creation and conservation of all things already commemorated. (9) From the agreement of other passages, by which Christ is called Lord of all, Acts 10:36; the Lord, through whom are all things, 1 Corinthians 8:6, equally as God, from whom are all things: and all things are said to be delivered into the hands of Christ, John 3:36; chapter 13:5; Matthew 11:27; and He can subject all things to Himself, Philippians 3:21. (10) From the creation of things. He is the conservator of those things of which He is the creator. But He is the creator of all things, John 1:3; Colossians 1:16. Ephesians 3:9. (11) From the confession of the adversaries, Schlichtingius seems to understand all things here. Andr. Veidovius contradicts Socinus, and contends that Christ has dominion not only in the Church, but over all things. Epist. 101, page 574. Socinus himself admits there that Christ has power over all things.

The third medium, through which He carries all things: it is said to be done τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὑτοῦ. Where by the word ῥήματι there were those who understood the Son of God Himself, because the Son of God carries all things by Himself as the word of the power of the Lord; especially the Latins, and among these Thomas; who also takes that of Christ in John 12:48, 'The word which I have spoken will judge him,' concerning Christ the Word of God, i.e., I myself, who am the Word of power: whom others not undeservedly desert and refute. For the Son here is ὁ φέρων, who carries, not the medium through which He carries: nor is the Son of God ever called ῥῆμα in the Scriptures, but ὁ λόγος, nor does the name ῥῆμα suit Him as the word τῷ λόγῳ does, nor finally can the Son be called the word of His power, and therefore this word cannot be taken concerning the Son Himself. Thomas also ineptly judges, John 12:45, that Christ is understood by λόγον: for how would Christ be called ὁ λόγος, that word which He Himself spoke? And it is too evident that the discourse there is about the spoken word, which he who despises has a judge, Christ saying, 'He who does not receive my words, has one who judges him: the word which I have spoken, that will judge him.'

No less inconvenient is the other interpretation of those who think that it is taught from this passage that the Holy Spirit is sometimes called in Holy Scripture the word of the Son, just as the Son is called the word of the Father. For this manner of speaking is entirely unusual and unknown to Scripture, that the Holy Spirit is called ῥῆμα, or the word of the Son of God. He is indeed called the Spirit of Christ's mouth, 2 Thess. II, verse 8, the Spirit of his lips, Is. XI, verse 4, but he is nowhere called the word of Christ.

Therefore, by the word τῷ ῥήματι here, the word of God is meant, and indeed not the word of grace or of doctrine, θεόπνευςον, which Christ announced, John VI, verse 63, which is spirit and life, and the word of eternal life, verse 68. But the word of power and of might, παντοκρατορικὸν: The word by which the ages were framed and all things created, Heb. XI, verse 3. The word by which all things are preserved and blessed, Matt. IV, verse 4. The word by which nature alone is restored, Matt. VIII, verse 8, Luke VII, verse 7. The word by which Christ cast out demons, and healed all those who were ill, Matt. 8:16. The word by which Christ most powerfully restrained the winds and calmed the sea, Matt. 8:26. The word by which Christ raised the dead, Mark 5:41. The word which those who are in the graves will hear and come forth from the monuments, John 5:28. In one word, τῷ ῥῆμα τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτõ, as the Apostle himself explains. But if you wish for the word ῥῆμα here also to designate a command and order, as in Luke 5:5, ἐπὶ τῷ ῥήματί σꙋ, 'at your command,' I will not object: but that command is to be understood in such a way that, with Socinus, it is not introduced as being in the least inconsistent with preservation, but only with governance. Because by his nod and command, just as he does all things that he wills, so he also sustains and preserves no less than he moderates and governs all things. Moreover, he is said to preserve and govern by a word, so that it may be understood how easy it is for Christ to preserve and moderate all things, not needing any medium, but only a word; for it is far easier for Christ to sustain all things than for us even to utter a word, and therefore Christ possesses no less power than the Father, but just as he here sustains and rules all things by a word. Psalm 107:20: 'He sent his word and healed them.' Ps. 148:8: 'Fire, hail, snow, storm, etc., execute his word.' Psalm 33:9: 'He himself spoke, and it was; he himself commanded, and it stood'; so also the Son is said to sustain and preserve all things by the word of his power. Chrysostom on this passage: καλῶς εἶπε τῷ ῥήματι˙ ἐπειδὴ γὰρ τὸ ῥῆμα παῤ ἡμῖν ψιλὸν εἶναι δοκεῖ, δείκνυσι, ὅτι ὐκ ἔστι ψιλὸν ἐπὶ Θεõ: naturally, because it is added, τῷ ῥῆματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτõ: But he rightly adds: τῷ δὲ πῶς τῷ ῥήματι Φέρει, ὐκέτι προσέθηκεν. ὐδὲ γὰρ δυνατὸν εἰδέναι. For who could explain the manner by which all things are sustained? Job 26:7 says he hangs the earth בלימה, 'upon nothing,' as if בלימה were not something that does not subsist by itself, because it rests on no support, but only on the word sustaining all things, and after he had explained the admirable preservation and governance of things at length, he adds in verse 14: 'Behold, these are parts of his ways, but what a small particle of the matter do we hear of him? Who then understands the thunder of his supreme power?' Isaiah, in the same consideration, exclaims likewise in ch. 40:13: 'Who has weighed the Spirit of Jehovah?' And Solomon, the wisest of kings, confesses in these tables that he is a brute and without any intelligence, Proverbs 30:2. But let us return to ῥῆμα, about which we began to speak. Blessed Luther hints that ῥῆμα, 'word,' can also be taken for 'work.' Christ carries all things by the word of his power, that is, by the work of his power. For by the operation of his power all things are preserved. How ῥῆμα, 'word,' is used for 'work' or 'thing' is most well-known from Hebraism. See Gen. 18:17, Exod. 9:4, 1 Sam. 14:12, Judg. 1:37, ch. 9:28, etc. Moreover, Blessed Luther adds that 'word of power' is the same as 'power itself,' or 'a word powerful and efficacious in power.' The rule of the Hebrew idiom is known: of two substantives placed in a state of regimen, sometimes the former, or the governing one, and sometimes the latter, or the governed one, is in the place of an adjective: and therefore it can be rendered both 'by the word of power,' or 'most powerful,' and 'by the power of the word,' or 'most efficaciously,' all things are sustained.

Δύναμις, therefore, here denotes infinite and immense virtue and power: for it is required either for the preservation of the Church or for the sustenance of the whole universe. It is, therefore, the infinite power of the Son of God by which he carries all things. It is proper to the Son of God, not alien; which the Apostle hints clearly enough, that the Son of God carries all things by his own, not an alien, power and virtue, while he says, 'by the word of his power.' Both are to be diligently noted because of the enemies of celestial truth, both the Socinians and, furthermore, the Calvinists and Papists.

Regarding I, to the Socinians: That the δύναμις or power of the Son of God, by which he sustains all things, is divine and infinite, as may be established somewhat more fully, we show by these proofs. (1) From the act of preservation. For preservation is a work of divine and infinite virtue, being nothing other than the continuation of existence given in the first creation, as Scaliger, Exerc. 250. Anselm in Monologion: 'Just as nothing was made except through the creative essence, so nothing flourishes except through the preserving power.' Cf. Ps. 36:7, Isa. 43:13, ch. 44:7, 24, Acts 17:28, Rom. 11:36, Wisd. 12:13. (2) From the general object of preservation; because to preserve and govern all things requires, ἐξ ἀνάγκης, an omnipotent and infinite virtue. If the preservation of one, even the smallest thing, is of infinite virtue and power, much more does the preservation of all things argue for infinite virtue and power. (3) From the special object. For it is certain that to preserve and govern the whole Church, dispersed throughout the entire world, is an argument of divine omnipotence, since to that preservation pertains both the interior influx of the gifts of grace and the external protection from all evils and defense against all kinds of adversities: neither is of human virtue, but both are of infinite and divine virtue: the former indeed because God is ὁ ἐνεργῶν τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν, 'the one who works all things in all' in the Church, as the Apostle says in 1 Cor. 12:6, which surely is not even to be thought of as belonging to anyone other than the supreme God: the latter, moreover, because it is claimed for God alone in the Scriptures, Deut. 32:12, Ps. 77:21, 1 Tim. 4:10, Isa. 43:1, etc. And how could the guardianship and protection of the Church against the gates of hell befit a mere creature, Matt. 16:18? (4) From the medium of preservation. For that all things whatsoever that are in heaven and on earth, or the universal Church or its individual members, and those things which in any way pertain to the same, are preserved by the word alone, is again a proof of infinite power. For none but GOD alone can perform those things by His word alone. For of GOD alone can that be said, Psalm XXXIII. v. 9: He spake and they were made; and Psalm CXLVIII. verse 8: Fire and hail, snow and vapor, stormy wind fulfill His word. Since therefore the same is said here of Christ, He upholds all things by the word of His power, who would further doubt that He is also that supreme GOD? (5) from the attribute of the preserving Word. It is called the word of power, because it is the omnipotent word of GOD, by which nothing cannot be performed: as Christ is able to subject all things to Himself most powerfully, according to the efficacy of His strength, Phil. III. verse 21. And that phrase, by the word of power, implies a governance or sustentation that is altogether divine and superior to every created power. To whom finally will the word of power belong, if not to the one omnipotent GOD, whose alone is πᾶσα δύναμις, Matt. VI. verse 13, and παντοκρατορία, Apoc. IV. verse 8. Since therefore this δύναμις is attributed to Christ, is it not most evidently implied that Christ is that supreme GOD? (6) from the consequence of this power. For the Apostle implies that Christ, by the force of this preserving and moderating power of all things, made expiation for sins, and indeed by Himself. But this is a work of infinite divine power. Conf. Is. XLIII. verse 24, chap. XLIV. verse 23. (7) from the description of His power. Scripture teaches what kind of power it is by which He sustains all things: namely, that it is all power in heaven and on earth, Matt. XXVIII. v. 18; power over all flesh, John XVII. verse 2; eternal power, Daniel VII. verse 14; by which He is able to subject all things to Himself, Phil. III. verse 21, and to render them subjected, Ps. VIII. verse 7, 1 Cor. XV. verse 27; by which He has all things in His hands, John III. verse 35; by which He is above every power, and whatever can be named, Eph. I. verse 20, above every name, Phil. II. v. 9, not only by reason of dignity and eminence, but also of virtue and power; whence it follows invincibly that it is an infinite power, and furthermore that of the infinite GOD Himself, since there can be only one supreme power.

II. Moreover, the Apostle hints that this power is proper to Christ the Son of GOD, and not foreign to Him, when Christ is said to uphold all things by the word of His power; where, although Guilh. Estius thinks it not irrelevant that some observe it could be translated by the word of His power, so that the Greek ἀὐτῶ, with only the breathing changed, might be referred to the Father, and the sense might be: that the Son, through whom the Father made all things, contains, preserves, and rules all those same things by the command and power of His Father, yet it could not be said that He upholds all things, as Estius adds in the same place, unless He possessed in common with the Father the power and potency of His Father, by which He upholds all things. But it must not be admitted that the pronoun here refers to the Father, because it is impious and a profane audacity to change even a tittle in the word of GOD, and to substitute a smooth breathing for a rough one, or vice versa: since any tittle whatever, as Christ testifies, is more powerful than heaven and earth; nor will any certainty of Scripture remain if this license of changing is admitted. But it is well that Schlichtingius, in Socin., acknowledges that this refers to the Son, who upholds all things by the word of his power, just as the Vulgate version also reads. Socinus, however, objects that Christ does not have this power from himself, but has obtained it from the gift of GOD. But we reply: (1) That this power and potency is ascribed to Christ here as no less his own than it is assigned to the Father anywhere else. For the Apostle says, he upholds all things by the word of his power. It is therefore the power of the Son. (2) The power of the Son and of the Father is one and the same, as Socinus elsewhere contends regarding John 10:30, that the Son is one with the Father, namely in power. And it has been shown that the virtue and power is infinite, which is not but one, and the same as the Father’s virtue. (3) But how does that common power differ by reason of the mode of possession: is it that the Father has it intrinsically and by nature, but the Son only extrinsically and by indwelling? Or does the Son also have the same by nature and intrinsically? If the latter, then he also has an infinite essence by nature, and thus is an infinite and eternal GOD. But if by reason of indwelling only: it will follow that all the saints can be said to uphold all things by the word of his power, because GOD dwells in all by his power. But it is absurd to say of the saints that they uphold all things by the word of their power. (4) Mr. [Dn.] also urges this argument. Grawerus: If the Son works through a power granted by GOD, and indeed governs all things, that power will be either finite or infinite. It cannot be finite, since to preserve and govern the whole world is not of a created, but of an infinite power; nay, it is of GOD alone: which we have previously taught at length. GOD, however, does not have a finite power. But if it is an infinite power, the Son will work by it either as his own, or as another’s, and thus as an instrument. But the latter is absurd. For thus it would follow that the infinite and uncreated power of GOD would be the instrument of a creature, which it is impious to assert. (5) From the Scriptures it is to be held thus: that this power belongs to Christ as his own, not another’s, intrinsically, not extrinsically, both by nature and by the grace of communication. The former, as he is GOD; the latter, as he is man. Moreover, it could not befit Him in this latter way—that is, in that divine power was not communicated to Him as man—unless that man were in the unity of person the true and supreme GOD. Because the human nature of Christ does not have divine power subjectively in itself, but in the person of the Son of GOD, or λόγος, to whom it is united: because there is one ὑπόστασις of the flesh and τῆς λόγε, John 1, verse 14. (6) But it cannot be said with the Socinians that infinite power was bestowed upon a ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ, because it cannot be that divine power and infinite potency should be communicated to a creature subjectively, as is shown elsewhere at greater length.

Against the Calvinists, however, this must be noted, insofar as they attribute to Christ a certain ἐξυσία devoid of δύναμις, or even imagine a middle power of Christ, or one distant from infinite virtue. But there belongs to Christ not only ἐξυσία, Matt. XXVIII. verse 18, John XVII. verse 2, Dan. VII. verse 14, but also δύναμις, as is said in this place; nor is that only according to the divine nature, such that only a bare ἐξυσία belongs to the human, because divine δύναμις and ἐξυσία are not distinguished, but are really the same; and thus the Lamb is said to be worthy to receive δύναμις, Apoc. V. verse 12, nor can the human nature of Christ be excluded from the government of all things, after it has been made a sharer of the divine throne, and exalted to the right hand of power, Matt. XXVI. verse 64, Heb. I. verse 3. But here Pareus snarls in his commentary on this passage that Christ sustains all things not with human hands or arms, but by the word and nod of His divine power. As if these were opposites, that Christ according to his human nature governs all things, and that he governs by the word of his power: the medium by which he governs, or the mode of government, and the nature according to which he governs. But he retorts that we are playing the part of heretics in eluding this argument for the Deity of the Son of GOD, and sharpening the weapons of heretics against the Son of GOD. Mere calumnies these! To which we respond: (1) The Calvinists pour cold water on the Anti-Trinitarian heretics when they invent a mediating and infinite power inferior to the power of Christ’s office. For this office belongs to Christ, in that he is GOD. (2) We say that the power by which he upholds all things is not communicated κατὰ μετέκβασιν, or by way of inherence in the Human Nature, but κατὰ μετάδοσιν, and by common possession, Col. II. verse 9, not κατ' ἀλλοποίησιν, but κατὰ συνδύασιν. Not, however, by a titular attribution at least: by which the thing itself is denied, as Pareus here expressly denies that the Son preserves the world by his humanity: but by a real and most true predication, concerning which more is treated in the cited passages.

Δι' ἑαυτῦ καθαρισμὸν ποιησάμενος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν) After he had by his death provided the cause of that faith, through which we are purged from sins, which neither Moses had done, nor the Prophets. See what is said at Rom. III. 25. But it is said very significantly δι ἑαυτῦ. He did not offer other victims, as the Levitical Priests, but himself: concerning that purgation see below X. 12. and 1 Pet. I. 22. This δι ἑαυτῦ is, however, absent from the Manuscript.

A very jejune gloss. He did not merely provide the cause of justifying faith by his death in any way whatsoever, for instance by confirming doctrine by his death, or whatever respect Grotius may have had in mind, who in these Annotations on the Epistles gladly Socinianizes, but by expiating our sins, while he satisfied GOD the Father for them. Nor are these synonyms to perform the purification of the sins of the human race by himself, and by his death to provide the cause of that faith, through which we are purified from sins. Nor is a σύγκρισις (comparison) instituted here with Moses and the Prophets, but if there is a comparison here, it concerns the Levitical priests, with whom he then proposed in the treatment to compare Christ, just as he proposed to compare the sacrifice of Christ with their expiations. But we shall proceed to add those things which we have previously proposed concerning these matters.

After the Apostle laid the foundation in the proposition of this Epistle regarding the most eminent Office of Christ: both that by nature he is ὁμούσιος (consubstantial) with the Father, and the radiance of his glory, and the image of his substance, and that he is the supreme Preserver and Governor of all things; he now proceeds to describe the parts of Christ's office, which he had intended to treat in this Epistle. Theophylact thus explains the συνέχειαν (connection), when he had discoursed on the magnitude of the divinity of the Word himself: he says how he looked out for men through his assumption of flesh, which is surely more excellent than bearing all things. Cornelius à Lapide notes that four forms are noted here by the Apostle, and as it were the faces of Christ, which Ezekiel in chapter I designated by the four faces of the Cherubim. The first was of a Man, by which he signifies the human nature, which the Apostle notes when he says, whom he appointed heir of all things. The second of an Eagle, by which he notes the divine nature expressed by the Apostle, that he is the radiance of glory. The third of a Calf, by which he expresses the priestly office of Christ, of which the Apostle says, making a purgation of sins. The fourth of a Lion, by which the kingdom and triumph of Christ, of which the Apostle says, he sits at the right hand of Majesty; and Cornelius concludes: He himself therefore is the quadriform Cherub, in whom lies the multiform wisdom of GOD. Let these be worth as much as they can. We have simply indicated the connection, conformable to the Apostolic proposition and treatment. He describes, however, the twofold office of Christ: namely, Priestly and Royal. The former he indicates by the expiation of our sins, which Christ performed by himself, i.e., ἀυτοενεργητικῶς (by his own energy), and by his own power, not as in the Old Testament types and figures, σημαντικῶς (significantly), or τυπικῶς (typically), not as an instrumental and secondary cause, but as the principal and primary cause, which we shall teach afterwards. This he designates by the sitting at the right hand of Majesty on High, and the exaltation above every angelic power.

Concerning the Priestly office, therefore, the Apostle has it thus in verse 3: δι' ἑαυτῶ καθαρισμὸν ποιησάμενος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν, BY HIMSELF he made purification of our sins, or having made purification he sat down, etc. By which words are expressed (1) the Act, (2) the Object, (3) the Mode, (4) the Time.

As to the Act, καθαρισμὸν ποιησάμενος, the Vulgate renders it, making a purgation: but ποιησάμενος is of the past tense, whence it ought to have been translated having made a purgation of sins, lest by sitting at the right hand of God he might seem to be purifying. For he first purified by his death, then he sat down at the right hand, as Erasmus notes, and before him the Greek Doctors Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, Oecumenius: Which is to be noted against the Socinian heresy, who contend that the purification of sins is being done by Christ in the heavens, and not that it was done by the oblation of Christ on earth. Schlichtingius indeed objects: That indefinite participles, when they adhere to a verb of past tense, ought not always to be rendered by the past, but often by the present tense, as Heb. VI. verse 13, XI. 9, as c. I. 4 & 2. Petr. II. 6, and therefore the participle ποιησάμενος does not necessarily argue that Christ had performed the purification of our sins before he sat down at the right hand of the throne of GOD, much less while still on the cross. But who here would not rather give credence to the most learned Greek Interpreters, by far the most skilled in Greek literature, than to Schlichtingius, who does not even sustain their shadow, in those things which concern the propriety of the Greek language? Moreover, that Rule or observation of Schlichtingius is particular: That participles of the past tense sometimes express the present tense: and therefore it cannot be inferred that the present tense is noted here as well. But it follows from that, that the usual, ordinary, and proper manner of signifying is not here either alien or uncertain, because it might perhaps sometimes be used otherwise; because that signification is to be retained and embraced until it is shown by firm reasons that there is no place for it. I pass over the fact that Schlichtingius's examples are less certain, or equally doubtful, and that nothing prevents the proper and usual force of the aorist from having a place in them. The word γενόμενος is certainly of the past tense in the following verse, although it does not imply that Christ was made more excellent than the Angels before he sat down, and why should it imply that, when he is said to have sat down first, or to have occupied the throne of Majesty; but here he is said to have made purification of sins first, and afterwards it is added that he sat down. But this is the craftiness of the Socinians, to turn the words of Scripture at will, so that the present Φέρων may be of the past, and conversely the past ποιησάμενον may be of the present tense, when it pleases them. But it is well, because Schlichtingius finally concedes, forced no doubt by the power of truth, that it is said here that Christ performed the purification of our sins before he sat down at the right hand of the throne of GOD. Socinus, however, replies that mention of Christ's death is made here, but in such words as to show how great and how huge a fruit has flowed from it to us, when it is said that Christ made purification of sins by himself. He concedes that by these words both the oblation of Christ and the sacrifice are signified, namely described from the effect, which is the purification of sins, because sins were purified by oblation and sacrifice. But if you infer from this that the oblation was made by the death of Christ, that the death of Christ was that sacrifice by which the purification of sins was made, and that this effect flowed from the death of Christ as an expiatory sacrifice, the heretic, lest he be forced to admit that, pretends that the death of Christ is not included here otherwise than as it was a certain necessary antecedent of the oblation, but not that the sacrifice and oblation of Christ were situated in it; which Schlichtingius here strives to illustrate with several examples. In which part he not only contradicts all Christian interpreters, who with unanimous consent acknowledge that this purification of sins was made by the death of Christ, not as some antecedent of an offering, but as an expiatory sacrifice, and by the very offering of Christ; but the heretic strikes at the throat of the Catholic faith of the whole Christian Church, concerning the expiatory death of Christ, the unique sacrifice of the New Testament. But since this very scope is easily the primary one of the present Epistle, as we showed in the prolegomena, to assert and explain and demonstrate the power of the expiatory sacrifice of Christ through his death and offering on the altar of the cross, it will not only be worth the effort, but necessity itself demands that we weigh in this place the mind and opinion of the Socinians, and having made a contention for the Catholic faith and Apostolic truth, we may thoroughly dissipate and undermine the same: But dià βραχέων [briefly], and lest we wander and stray too much outside the bounds of the commentary. The Apostle therefore said Καθαρισμόν [purification] or the effect of the offering

of Christ, or the offering itself described by its effect: and this word is accustomed in the Old Testament to correspond to the word אשם and to the word כפר or expiation, and to the expiatory sacrifice, and therefore it was also retained by the Apostle to signify the expiatory sacrifice of Christ. Moreover, καθαρισμὸς is attributed to Christ in two ways, when there is discourse concerning spiritual purification: (1) by reason of merit and acquisition or of the expiation and purification made through his death, (2) by reason of efficacy or application, and of the purification which is made through faith by the merit of the blood of Christ. In the former way, καθαρισμὸς was made once. In the latter, it is made daily until the consummation of the age: in the former, it is universal for all men: in the latter, although, if you look at the intention of GOD and the efficacy of the καθαρισμὸς of Christ, it may be universal, yet from the event it becomes particular, and of some only, namely, of the faithful. The former καθαρισμὸς is of the offering and sacrifice of Christ; the latter is not immediately the effect of the offering of Christ, although it comes to pass through the mediation of the offering and the merit of the sacrifice of Christ. The former is described by ἀπολύτρωσιν, by ἱλασμὸν, by καταλλαγὴν, by ἀγορασμὸν, προσφορὰν and θυσίαν, and other such synonymous paraphrases. The latter, however, is expressed by the remission of sins, absolution from sins, sanctification, and similar things. Wherefore Christ purified us, in that he redeemed us from the curse of the law, in that he expiated the wrath of GOD, in that he reconciled us to GOD, in that he was made a propitiation for our sins, in that he offered himself as an expiatory victim for the sins of the human race, in that he obtained for us from GOD the remission of sins and purification. Then Christ also purifies, in as much as he imparts to us the remission of sins and the purification of the conscience from dead works by the virtue of his merit. Both meanings are deduced not obscurely from Hellenistic usage. For καθαρισμὸς was said by the Hellenists also of the calf of sin, and of the Levitical purifications, Exod. XXIX. verse 37, Levit. XIV. verse 4. But the legal sacrifices and Levitical purifications did not declare expiation or cleansing, but they took away guilt. Thus καθαρίζειν is explained in Heb. IX. verse 21, that it is to take away guilt and to effect the remission of sins, and indeed through αἱματεκχυσίαν or the shedding of blood, and when in Heb. IX. verse 14, Christ καθαρίζει the conscience from dead works, Socinus himself interprets this in his book on the service of Christ, chap. XV., as to liberate the conscience from guilt and punishment, and from the terror of punishment. Thus also 1 John I. verse 7. The blood of Christ καθαρίζει purifies us from all sin, not as regards the declaration of cleansing, but as regards the cleansing itself and the remission of sins: as in verse 9 it is explained by ἀφιέναι; for it is confessed, even by the Socinians themselves, that guilt is signified everywhere by the name of uncleanness: Therefore, purification is the removal of guilt, whether as regards merit or as regards the act. Let Ephes. V. verse 26, Tit. II. verse 14, Acts XV. verse 9 be compared. Here the Apostle designates καθαρισμὸν by reason of merit: Because he speaks of a καθαρισμῷ already made, before he sits at the right hand of Majesty on high.
