Which, as Schlichting the Socinian acknowledges: so those things which he adds here concerning the purgation of sins can be admitted in a sound sense. By the purgation of sins, he says, in this place is signified the removal of the guilt and punishment of sins, just as also by the offering made by the legal High Priest, the guilt and punishment of all sins for which expiation was then granted were taken away. But it is to be noted, Schlichting continues, that the matter stands otherwise in the offering and sacrifice of Christ, as far as the removal of sins itself pertains, and otherwise in the legal offering and sacrifice. For from the latter, the removal of sins followed immediately by the very act, because the other conditions necessary for that matter were already placed: but from the offering of Christ, the removal of sins does not follow otherwise than that it has the power and efficacy to take away all our sins; but the effect does not follow before, or does not remain otherwise than if we in turn do our duty, that is, believe in Christ and obey him. In which words of Schlichting we note (1) that he concedes that the removal of the guilt and punishment of sins is designated here, and (2) that it was made through the offering and sacrifice of Christ. (3) That the offering of Christ has the power and efficacy to take away all our sins. (4) That as regards the effect, however, our sins are taken away by the very act, if faith is added, or we believe in Christ. All of which, rightly understood, we admit and approve. But his master F. Socinus twists and perverts this passage far otherwise in book II. of the Savior. Christ, chap. XX., when he strives to teach that Christ did not expiate our sins in any other way than by those things by which, having been performed, we have already obtained from GOD the pardon of our offenses, which was already spontaneously decreed and promised to us, or even that it has been declared that we have obtained that pardon, i.e., that he did not expiate sins by obtaining and meriting the pardon or remission of sins, but partly by revealing the divine will concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, partly by moderating all things, and by sitting at the right hand of God, whence it is evident that Christ, whose members we are, dwelling in the heavens, has all things in his hand, and that we dwell together with him in the heavens: Whither he drags the preceding words by the head and feet, who, since he is the brightness of glory and the express image of his substance, and carries all things by the word of his power: that he declares that both of those things of the expiation of sins were made through the intervening death of Christ, first, in so far as we have seen in Christ the expressed will of GOD toward us, not only because he revealed it to us, but also because we know that what GOD promised to us was truly fulfilled in him, and therefore it is now said most openly that our sins have been remitted and blotted out. Which Socinus wishes to be signified when Christ is called the brightness of glory and the express image of the substance of GOD: Secondly, in so far as he moderates and rules all things by his powerful command: For thus also Socinus says that our sins have been truly expiated, and that we dwell together with Christ in the heavens, and that no punishment remains for our sins. That both of these things, however, came to pass through the intervention of death, by which both the love and will of GOD towards us were wonderfully commended, and Christ himself attained to the dominion of all things, insomuch that he now sits in the heavens at the right hand of the supreme Majesty on high. Thus far the Gloss of Socinus, with which he is so greatly pleased that he writes he cannot sufficiently wonder that the ancient and more recent interpreters of this Epistle, whom it has been his lot to read, did not notice that connection of these words, when nevertheless all things are wonderfully connected, but thought that the Apostle had written of Christ in one context things that were diverse, or had explained it too coldly. We are to believe, forsooth, that Socinus has found it, not what boys find in a bean, and that he alone is wise here, while the rest of the interpreters, Greeks as well as Latins before him, flit about like shadows. Truly wonderful is the connection which Socinus has devised, and therefore it is no wonder that it could not have come into the mind of anyone before him: it is to be wondered at more perhaps, how it could have come into Socinus's mind, were it not that his admirable πανεργία [craftiness] and cunning in perverting the Scriptures had been more than sufficiently perceived by the Christian world. But to the point! For it does not help to refute at length the inanities of Socinus, which he himself commends so lengthily, in order to give them a value in praise which they do not possess in themselves. We previously indicated the connection in the Apostolic proposition as most evident; nor was there any need for us of this wonderful συνεχεία [continuity] of Socinus, and others have shown the coherence of the Apostle's words quite neatly; far more suitable, indeed, than that laborious and inept gloss of Socinus. Schlichting himself, however much he may otherwise revere the tenets of Socinus and hold them in high regard, here, having disregarded that same person's so-called brilliant and excellent connection, establishes the συνεχεία [continuity] of the Apostolic context in a far different way, namely, that by those words 'the brightness of his glory, the express image of the substance of GOD, upholding all things by the word of his power,' it is not the expiation of sins, or the manner of the expiation of sins, that is described, but the dignity and excellence of Christ, and indeed that which he had even while existing on earth, from which the Apostle passes to those things which he obtained after death, mention also being made of death, since its fruit, the purification of sins, is expressed: Let Schlichting therefore see to it regarding this: why did he choose to so subordinate the very force and construction of the words, the context by which all things are wonderfully connected, and the Artifice of the Apostle—by which, in Socinus's own judgment, the manner of the expiation of our sins could not be explained more divinely, magnificently, and clearly—and why did he refuse to give credence to Socinus when he pointed out the same? As for us, we are compelled to give him less credence both by the force and construction of the words, and by the context itself, and by the Apostle's discourse, which is utterly divine, magnificent, and most evident, if those things which precede—that Christ is the brightness of glory and the express image of the hypostasis of GOD, and that he upholds all things by the word of his power—are accepted as the foundation of Christ's office, and as they describe his divine eminence, by the power of which Christ was able both to make purification of sins by himself and to sit down at the right hand of the Majesty on high: all of which things perish and are utterly enervated if, with Socinus, one says that those words explain the manner of the expiation of our sins made by Christ. (1) For Christ is called the brightness of glory and the express image of the substance of GOD, not because we see the will of GOD expressed and fulfilled in him, but because he exhibits in himself the substance and Majesty of GOD the Father, which has been shown before by many arguments: Much less (2) is he called the brightness and image by reason of the expiation of sins. For how would the expiation of sins be designated by the fact of being the brightness of glory and the image of the substance of GOD? Whence is it established that this is the force and meaning of those words? Where in the Scriptures is the expiation of sins explained in such a way, or declared by even a similar line of reasoning? Indeed (3) the expiation was made by the death of Christ according to the Scriptures, through the offering of Christ; but that it was made through the expression of the paternal glory and hypostasis in Christ is taught nowhere, not even obscurely. (4) But see what circumlocutions and tricks Socinus needs in order to extort this sense, which he calls most clear and most suitable. To be the brightness of glory and the image of the hypostasis is to be allowed to see and contemplate the glory of GOD and GOD himself in Christ. For us to see the glory of GOD and GOD in Christ is for Christ to have revealed by word the benevolent will of GOD toward us, and for us to have thoroughly known the will of GOD through Christ: and that we know that what God promised us through him has been fulfilled in Christ in reality. Therefore he is the image and brightness because he is the example and pledge of the divine goodness toward us. Again, in that declaration and demonstration of the will, we see that our sins have been remitted to us. Finally, that this is what it means for Christ to have expiated our sins and to have made purification of our sins: that he declared and made it testified that our sins have been remitted to us. And therefore [is he] called the brightness of glory and the image of the substance by reason of the expiation of sins? How many windings and circumlocutions are needed here for Socinus to be able to arrive at that? And are we to believe that this is the simplest, most certain, and most evident sense? (5) Consequently, these are most distinct: the announcement and demonstration of the gracious divine will, and the expiation and purification of sins; nor is Christ said to have expiated our sins on account of the revelation of the will of God, which pertains to the Prophetic office of Christ, since this pertains not to the Prophetic, but to the Priestly office of Christ. (6) Christ is said to have accomplished the expiation or purification of sins not through others, but by himself. But it is established that the revelation of the divine will was made not only by Christ himself, but by his Apostles, and before them by the Prophets. (7) And therefore only Christ is called the Expiator of our sins, whereas the Prophets and Apostles are by no means the expiators of our sins, nor are they called such. But they would not only have to be called so, but they could also be called the brightness of glory and the image of the hypostasis of GOD for the same reason, if this name belonged to Christ because of the announcement of the divine will. (8) The purification of sins was made through the death of Christ, therefore not through the announcement of the divine will. Because the death of Christ is not the announcement of the will of GOD, as is established. If you say that the death of Christ was a confirmation of the will of God, not only will that be difficult to prove from the Scriptures, which do not assign this end to the death of Christ, let alone wish it to be the primary and chief one, but it will still be permissible to urge: that sins were not expiated through the death of Christ insofar as the death was a testimony, martyrdom, and consecration of the will of God, but insofar as it was a λύτρον [ransom], or the price of redemption, Matt. XX. verse 28, Mark X. verse 45, 1 Timothy II. v. 6. For without doubt, the purification of sins pertains more to the death of Christ in that respect in which the reconciliation of God, the redemption from the curse of the law, and the propitiation were made, than in that in which the will of GOD toward the human race was merely declared: since that respect touches more upon this effect, the expiation and purification of sins. Furthermore, as to that mode of the expiation of sins through Christ, by which we see fulfilled in Him that which GOD promised to us, there is nothing to be seen anywhere in the Scriptures concerning it: namely, that Christ purifies our sins by the very fact that we have in Him an example of the divine grace by which He was raised to eternal glory, which is what Socinus indicates here. There is deep silence on that matter in the Scriptures. Moreover, that grace of GOD by which sins are purified, expiated, or remitted does not shine forth in this example of Christ raised to the kingdom of GOD: because it is not through the remission of the sins of Christ, who was devoid of all sin and separated most widely from sinners, Johan. VIII. vers. 46. 1. Petr. II. vers. 22. 2. Cor. V. ult. Ebr. VII. vers. 26. but through the expiation of our sins that he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. Therefore, we do not have in Christ an example of how GOD wills to remit the offenses of sinners, and, having made a purification or expiation of their sins, to raise them up to His kingdom. (11) But much less does the expiation of our sins consist in this, that we see salvation, which God willed to be promised to us through Christ: For what knowledge of our exaltation would be the formal cause or reason or mode of the purification of our sins, which Christ is said to have made here by Himself? Did Christ therefore make the purification of our sins by Himself, because we see or know GOD to be truthful in His promises by the example of Christ? The knowledge of the exaltation of Christ, which is an act of our mind, and the purification of sins made through Christ, which is an ἐνέργημα of the Savior Christ, are separated by the whole heaven; nor does the latter consist in the former, or is it manifest from it: because 1. the expiation was made before He sat at the right hand of the Majesty, but our knowledge depends upon the exaltation and session of Christ at the right hand of GOD. 2. that the expiation was made through the offering and sacrifice of CHRIST, but the knowledge of the exaltation of Christ does not exist through the offering and sacrifice of Christ. 3. that the expiation is the removal of the guilt and punishment of sins, but the knowledge of the exaltation of CHRIST is not the removal of the guilt and punishment of sins. (12) Least of all, finally, does Christ, as the splendor of the glory and the character of the person of the Father, purify and expiate our sins, as Socinus wills, so that CHRIST is understood to make the purification of sins by Himself when we gaze upon and see in Christ the splendor of the divine glory and the express image of the substance of the Father. In the other, more blessed life, we shall see that far more fully and perfectly: yet there will not be a purification of our sins in the other life: what of the fact that many know the Son of GOD in such a way, who are not actually purified from sins? The Demons also know that the Son of GOD is the splendor of the glory of the Father. The holy Angels know it, yet the sins of the Demons or Angels have not been expiated through CHRIST; because these are subject to no sins, but the sins of the former cannot be expiated for eternity. Where it is also to be noted that the opinion of Socinus is ἀσύςατον, and that it is not at all consistent with itself. For if CHRIST is called the splendor of the glory, etc., by reason of the announcement of the grace of GOD, and by that very fact made the purgation of sins by Himself, how is the splendor of the glory, etc., understood by reason of the exaltation of Christ, and by the knowledge of it is He said to have made the purgation of our sins by Himself? For the announcement was made by CHRIST, according to the mind of Socinus, while He was acting on earth, but the exaltation and the consequent knowledge of the same befits CHRIST raised from the earth into heaven. If, therefore, the Apostle hints by this sentiment that CHRIST, while still existing on earth, made the expiation of sins, how does the same sentiment with the same words hint that this very expiation of sins was made through the exaltation of CHRIST in the heavens, and indeed insofar as it is an example of the divine grace that expiates sins? These things concerning the former member of the depravation of Socinus.

As to the second member, namely that CHRIST made the expiation of our sins, by which He is said to uphold all things by the word of His power: besides that here the mode of the expiation of our sins according to the opinion of Socinus seems no less ἀσύστατος, nor does it consist with the former: we observe (1) That by those words, by which He is said to uphold all things, the preservation and government of the universe is designated, which was previously declared and shown. Therefore, the mode of the expiation of our sins is not designated by the same. For those things are most diverse. The former is universal of all creatures, the latter only concerns the human race: the former regards the sustenance of nature, the latter the destruction of sins: the former pertains to the article of creation and providence: the latter to the article of redemption. (2) That Christ expiates our sins insofar as He preserves and rules all things, so that under this formal respect He is said to make the purification of sins, the holy Scripture nowhere asserts. (3) Distinguish between the foundation of the expiation of sins, which Christ made by Himself, and the formal reason or mode by which the expiation of sins was made. The foundation indeed of the purification of sins made through Christ consists in this, that Christ is the absolute and supreme Rector and Lord of all things: But the formal reason and mode of the expiation of our sins is not at all situated in that. (4) The upholding and government of all things pertains to the Dominion of the universe, or even to the Kingly office of Christ. But the expiation of sins pertains to the Priestly office of Christ. (5) That Christ upholds all things by the word of His power, that is common to Him with the Father and the Holy Spirit. But Christ is said to have made the expiation and purification of our sins by Himself, not the Father, not the Holy Spirit. (6) Not insofar as Christ governs and moderates all things, but insofar as He offered Himself as a Sacrifice, does He expiate our sins. But the regimen and government of the universe and the expiatory Sacrifice of Christ differ greatly, and therefore the mode of expiation does not consist in that either. (7) Therefore, Scripture explains the mode of the purification of our sins far otherwise, namely that Christ took our sins upon Himself, Is. LIII. v. 6, that He was made sin for us, 2 Cor. V. v. last, that He bore our sins, John I. v. 29, that He bore the same in His body on the wood of the cross, 1 Pet. II. v. 24, that He died on account of sins, Rom. IV. v. last. & he laid down his soul as a sacrifice for guilt, Is. LIII. ver. 14. because he offered himself for the abolishing of sin through the immolation of himself, Heb. IX. ver. 26. because he gave himself as a price of redemption in our stead, Matt. XX. ver. 28. & became an expiation for our sins, 1 John II. ver. 1. because he was delivered unto death for sinners & for our sins, and by his own death reconciled us to GOD, Rom. V. verse 10. & what things are here twin-like delivered everywhere in the Scriptures. Therefore he does not expiate sins because he upholds all things by the word of his power, but because he was made sin, was slain on account of sin, bore sins, and laid down his soul as a sacrifice for sins, &c. (8) Hence it is that the purification of sins is ascribed not to the glory & Majesty of Christ, by which he upholds all things, but to the cross & blood of Christ, by which he was made the most abject of all and a curse for us, Galat. III. ver. 12. (9) That Christ, dwelling in the heavens, holds all things in his hand, that very thing is not the expiation of our sins. For although we also dwell with Christ in the heavens, as regards the hope of the heavenly kingdom, that is a consequence of the expiation of sins, not the same thing, nor an antecedent, nor a formal cause; for the hope of eternal life does not cause the expiation or purification of sins to be made through Christ, but because the expiation and purification of sins has been made through Christ, hence hope is spoken of as eternal life for those redeemed from the curse (10) The exaltation of Christ in the heavens indeed contributes to the certainty of our faith concerning the expiation of sins made through Christ. For neither would Christ our Mediator have been raised from the dead, nor taken up into heaven, had our sins, which he had taken upon himself, not been expiated through him; meanwhile, the exaltation of Christ is not the expiation of our sins itself: although the exaltation of Christ to the right hand of God and the governance and moderation of things, by which he upholds all things, are also different: for this was fitting for Christ even before he sat at the right hand of God, which Schlichtingius acknowledges: concerning which Christ says in John 5:19, 'My Father is working until now, and I am working.' But the Father was not exalted to the right hand of Majesty. Most poorly, therefore, are all these things confused by Socinus. (11) Finally, the distinction must be repeated between the expiation or purification of sins by reason of merit, and by reason of act or efficacy: or between the acquisition and imputation of the remission of sins, and the application of the same, or the actual forgiveness of sins: As regards this, we do not deny that Christ, exalted to the right hand of God, actually applies to us the benefit of the remission of sins that has been obtained: But neither is the exaltation or glory of Christ the application itself; as if our sins were actually expiated by the very fact that Christ, dwelling in the heavens, has all things in his hand, as Socinus maintains: nor is the expiation or actual purification of our sins primarily from the fact that Christ dwells in the heavens, since it ought not to be attributed so much to the glory in which Christ is established, as to the intercession of Christ for us in the heavens, Romans 8:34, 1 John 2:1. and to the efficacious operation through the ministry on earth, by means of which we are reconciled to God, and our hearts are purified through faith, 2 Corinthians 5:14, Acts 15:9. But the acquisition itself of pardon and the remission of sins must by no means be ascribed to the exaltation or glory of Christ, but to his most perfect obedience even unto the death of the cross, and to his blood shed for us for the remission of sins, Matthew 26:28. For the expiation of Christ was already made in such a way, and indeed before he sat at the right hand of Majesty, namely through the oblation and expiatory sacrifice of Christ, although as to the effect or the act itself, our sins are finally taken away if faith is added or we believe in Christ, just as Schlichtingius himself distinguished above.

But Socinus replies here: That the expiation has already been made and that Christ is said to have already performed the purification of our sins by himself, because this was done through Christ's entry into heaven, whence we are moved to embrace the forgiveness of offenses offered by God, and Christ has the power to actually grant us that forgiveness, from which then the expiation itself and true liberation from the punishments of sins perpetually flows. But in truth we respond: These are far (1) different: that the expiation of our sins has been made through Christ, and that Christ moves us to do that from which expiation can follow, or even that Christ has obtained the power to expiate our sins. (2) Neither of these, according to Socinus, was done before Christ sat at the right hand of Majesty on high: but the expiation of sins is said to have been made before he sat down. (3) By the fact that Christ entered heaven, we are not moved to embrace the forgiveness of offenses, but according to Socinus we are moved only by the fact that we know that Christ was raised from the dead and taken up into heaven. (4) According to the ὑποτύπωσιν ὑγιαινόντων λόγων (pattern of sound words), faith is not excited because we are moved of our own accord to embrace the divine promise by the example of the exalted Christ, but because Christ, by the power of his Spirit, works faith in us out of grace, Phil. 1:6, 29, 1 Thess. 1:4. (5) If Christ is said to have made expiation by himself to the extent that by his entry into heaven he moved us to do that from which the expiation of sins arises, Christ would not be understood to have made the expiation of sins by himself so much as we, given Christ's entry into the heavens, make the expiation of our sins by ourselves. Which is absurd. (6) Christ indeed makes us partakers of his benefit through the Holy Spirit after he has entered heaven: But he offered a sacrifice for us beforehand, and made purification for our sins. For by his merit he refashions us with his Spirit, so that we may receive with a grateful heart the liberation obtained through this oblation and his sacrifice, and he brings it about with his Father that He receives us into favor, through his intercession, Rom. 8:34, 1 John 2:2. (7) The power to forgive sins belonged to Christ even while he acted on earth, by virtue of which it is often read that he forgave sins, Matthew 9:11, etc., and granted to others the power to forgive sins ministerially and in his name, Matt. 16:17, John 20:23; therefore he did not finally obtain it through his entry into the heavens. (8) But it is manifest that that power is not the expiation of sins itself: nor is the expiation said to have been made for that reason, because Christ has the power to forgive sins, but rather, because Christ made the expiation of sins by himself, for that reason he obtains the power to forgive sins and to actually apply the benefit of expiation to us. For that is prior in the order of nature. (9) Therefore, the expiation or Redemption of the whole human race, which Scripture testifies was accomplished by the blood and death of Christ, does not flow from this, that Christ has the power of remitting sins, and that we are moved by the glory of Christ to accept the forgiveness of sins: indeed, even with that power placed in Christ, the expiation itself does not follow in act, unless faith in Christ is added on our part, for which it is most false that the mere knowledge of Christ's entry into heaven or of his exaltation suffices, since it is evident that many have this, yet are destitute of true and saving faith. (10) Thus, indeed, it must be established from the Scriptures concerning this matter: The expiatory sacrifice of Christ reconciled God to the human race: and therefore Christ is said to have made the expiation, or purification, of the sins of the whole world by himself. But in order that our sins may be taken away by the act itself, Schlichtingius saying and conceding, faith must be added, or that we believe in Christ: which Christ excites in us through the internal operation of the Holy Spirit and the ministry of reconciliation. In which manner the Apostle distinguishes in 2 Cor. 5:19, 20, making a twofold reconciliation: that which is announced by the word, and that which is done through the word: The former is of impetration, the latter of application. The former is prior to the word, the latter is posterior in the order of nature. And the Apostle treats here of the former, when he asserts that Christ made the expiation of sins, but not of the latter, which is perpetually done, even until the consummation of the age; namely through the word of the cross, 1 Cor. 1:18, and faith in Christ and him crucified, 1 Cor. 2:2. (10) This, therefore, must always be urged against the Socinians: that Scripture ascribes the remission of sins, expiation, redemption, and that former reconciliation to the death of Christ, not to Christ's entry into heaven not to Christ's kingly office or dignity and glory, which are rashly and absurdly mixed together and confused by the Socinians.

But the Racovian Catechism insists here, as does Schmalz in his book on the divinity of Christ, ch. XXIII, p. 134, that by the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ nothing else is understood than that Christ wishes to take care of us, and does so; and that this differs from his kingdom only in that Christ, insofar as he is King, can take care of us, but insofar as he is High Priest, he also wishes to, and does. Schmalz supports this assertion with this argument: This whole thing, he says, can appear from the fact that if one considers that in the Epistle to the Hebrews alone, in a certain way, is mention made of Christ insofar as he is Priest and of his priesthood, and yet it is impossible that the other Apostles in their writings should make no mention of a thing so significant, without which the dignity of Christ cannot consist. Hence he infers that for the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews to say that JESUS CHRIST is our High Priest is nothing other than what Christ promised, that he would be with his own until the end of the age, Matt. 18:20, and things similar to these in John 14:18, Matt. 10:20, Rev. 1:17, and Acts 18:9-10. And what the Apostles say, that he is the head of his Church, etc., Eph. 1:22, ch. 5:29, 1 Thess. 1:10. We answer, however: (1) that the claim that being a priest is nothing other than wishing to take care of, and taking care of, someone, and that sacrifice is nothing other than help, is an unheard-of paraphrase, and one completely unknown to the sacred scriptures, where no such definition of a priest or sacrifice is handed down in the sacred texts, either in the Old or in the New Testament. (2) The priest of the Old Testament had to plead the cause of the people before God, but his office did not consist in this general description of his function; for not everyone who pleaded the cause of the people before God was a priest. (3) Therefore, our Epistle hands down the special mode and proper parts of this care and office, which consisted both in offering sacrifices and in interceding before God for the people, Heb. 5:1, and applies them to Christ, the unique High Priest of the New Testament, Heb. 7:25, 27. (4) It does not, however, define the sacrifice of Christ by his help, but that he offered himself once in the consummation of the ages to abolish sin, Heb. 9:24, and that by a single oblation he perfected forever those who are sanctified, Heb. 10:14. (5) But as for the claim that this whole matter, which is described by the priesthood of Christ, is figurative and to be taken improperly, whence does Smalzius show this? The opposing party will never teach that Christ is called a priest only figuratively. And (6) indeed, that Christ is also High Priest insofar as he is King, or at least that the High Priesthood and the kingly office of Christ are so distinguished that he wishes to take care of us according to the former, and can do so according to the latter, is a figment hitherto new and unheard of in the Church of God. (7) Furthermore, to the kingly office belongs not only the faculty or power, but also the will to help, and the actual help itself. For it is the mark of a King not only to be able, but also to wish to take care of, and to aid and succor his subjects. But CHRIST is our King, Isa. 33:22, Hos. 3:5, Zech. 9:9, Luke 1:33, Heb. 7:2, and Ruler, Mic. 5:2. (8) The kingdom of Christ, namely the kingdom of power, extends itself to all things and over all things, Ps. 8:7.

Eph. 1:22, over and against the enemies of the Church, Ps. 110:2, 1 Cor. 15:27. The priesthood of Christ, however, does not extend itself to all things, not to destroying or subduing the enemies of the Church, etc. (9) The kingdom of Christ also includes under itself the kingdom of glory in heaven, Matt. 25:34, John 5:28, 1 Thess. 4:14. But the priesthood of Christ, as far as the expiation of sins is concerned, does not pertain to the citizens of the kingdom of glory in heaven. (10) As for the kingdom of grace in the Church, which Christ governs, the will of grace toward the Church cannot and ought not to be separated or torn away from it; but the gracious will of Christ toward the Church pertains no less to that kingdom of grace than the faculty and power of protecting and preserving the Church, Ps. 2:6, Ps. 40:4, John 5:14-15, Isa. 9:6, Luke 1:33. (11) Furthermore, where Scripture treats of the High Priesthood or Priesthood of Christ, it distinguishes it most explicitly from the Kingdom of Christ, and indicates more evidently the reasons by which they are distinguished from one another. Thus, Ps. 110:2 treats of the kingly office of Christ, v. 4 of the priestly office: so, where in our Epistle the priesthood of Christ is treated, it is evident that it is described in such a way that it appears completely distinct from the government of Christ. It is described, namely, by oblation and sacrifice. That, however, does not befit Kings; it describes it by intercession, which it is confessed does not befit Christ as King. See ch. 5 and 7:9. (12) Again, to the priesthood of Christ, or to Christ as High Priest, belongs not only the will to consult and provide for our salvation, but also the power and faculty, namely, to the extent that his High Priesthood requires it: to expiate sins, to reconcile to God, to free from the guilt and punishment of sins, etc. Therefore he is called ἀρχιερεὺς μέγας, a great High Priest, who has penetrated the heavens, Heb. 4:14. He is called ἰσχῦς, who can save, and wishes to, Matt. 1:21. Master of saving, Isa. 63:1; he is called גאל, Redeemer, Gen. 48:16, Job 19:15, who is not only prepared and has promised to redeem us, but also can redeem us and redeems us from all evil, who is powerful to help, Heb. 2:18, αἴτιος of eternal salvation, Heb. 5:9, and can save εἰς τὸ παντελὲς, ch. 7:25. (13) It is false that the priesthood of Christ is discussed almost only in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Indeed we confess that this article of the Christian faith is nowhere expressly explained in the Scriptures in the same way as in our Epistle, which is as it were a complement of the more perfect doctrine of the New Testament reserved for it: meanwhile it should not be denied that the Priesthood of Christ, both in the Old Testament and in other writings of the New Testament, has been proposed and expounded, partly ῥητῶς (expressly), partly also κατὰ διάνοιαν (in meaning), as regards the functions and duties of this office, and partly finally τυπικῶς (typically), as regards the prefiguration of the office of Christ: it is delivered ῥητῶς in Ps. 110:4, that Christ is a Priest forever after the order of Melchizedek, upon which place as a foundation and proper seat of this article in the Old Testament this Epistle relies in ch. 5, 6, 10, ch. 6:20, ch. 7:1, seq. The type of this High Priest was borne partly by Melchizedek, an extraordinary Priest, and partly by the ordinary Levitical Priests, with whom Christ is compared in Gen. 14:18, which is explained in Heb. 7. & ch. 5:1, seq. of this epistle, etc., and partly the Priest Joshua in Zech. 6:13. As regards the duties or functions of this office, the priesthood of Christ is described not only in types, the Priests of the Old Testament and the acts of their office, which this Epistle applies to Christ, but also by evident sayings; both as regards the sacrifice or oblation, and as regards the intercession of Christ for us. His sacrifice is hinted at by David in Ps. 40:7, as it is explained in our Epistle in ch. 10:5. It is described by

Isaiah ch. 53. that Christ is the sacrificial lamb v. 7. namely that lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, John 1, 29. 1 Pet. 1, 19. the unblemished lamb 1 Cor. 5, 7. the Passover sacrificed for us Rev. 5, 6. 9. 12. The Lamb slain, who redeemed us with his blood. Cf. Rev. 7, 14. that he laid down his soul as a sacrifice for us Is. 53, 10. and bore our sins, which is explained 1 Pet. 2, 22, and that God cast the sins of us all upon him v. 6. just as the sins of the whole people are read to have been enumerated and imputed to the goat Azazel Lev. 16. Who gave and offered himself for us Matt. 20, 28. Gal. 2, 20. as a sacrifice and a sweet-smelling savor Eph. 5, 2. Who was made a propitiation for us 1 John 2, 1. and ch. 4, 10. by which word the adversaries concede that there is an allusion to the propitiatory sacrifices of the O.T. Because he was made sin for us 2 Cor. 5, 21. and whatever things of this kind are met with here and there in the Scriptures, looking toward the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ. To this also pertain those things which are discussed concerning the Reconciliation made through Christ, concerning the work of Mediation, concerning the Redemption of Christ, which illustrate the expiation of sins made through Christ: And likewise concerning the death of Christ endured for us, by which he was delivered up as a peculiar victim for us, slain, and died for the expiation of our sins. Which is taught here and there in the Holy Scriptures. With what face, therefore, does Schmalz say that the priesthood or sacrifice of Christ is truly treated nowhere else than in this Epistle? As to the intercession of the same, how Christ both prayed for us on this earth, and intercedes for us in heaven, is to be read in John 17 and Rom. 8, 34. 1 John 2, 2. Since, therefore, the priesthood of Christ and his offices are discussed so frequently in the Holy Scriptures, there is no reason why we should drag in foreign passages of Scripture, which deal with the Kingly office, but which make no mention, not even an obscure and implicit one, of his Pontificate.

Thus, therefore, it has now been abundantly shown that the purification of sins, or even the sacrifice, or the Pontificate of Christ ought not to be confused either with the Prophetic office of Christ, by which he revealed the gracious will of God, confirmed it, and made it attested by his own example, or with the government of the universe, or the Kingly office of Christ, by which he upholds all things by the word of his power, and takes care of his Church, otherwise than it has been said that Socinus and Schmalz do. One thing remains to be settled here, so that we may remove every scruple of doubt, namely, that the expiation, or purification of our sins, and the offering or sacrifice of Christ, by which the same was made, is not finally accomplished in heaven, but has already been accomplished on earth. I speak of the merit or acquisition of the forgiveness of sins, not of the application, as I have warned more than once. There is, however, a sharp contention about this with the Socinians, in which the hinge of the true doctrine concerning the priesthood and sacrifice of Christ consists. Let us first hear the opinion of Socinus from part II of De Servatore Christo, ch. XV. It must be noted, he says, that those words of Heb. 9, 13. 14. 'he offered himself unblemished to God' do not refer to the death of the cross alone, but to the entry at the same time into the holy places, that is, into heaven itself, where CHRIST now stands perpetually before God for us. For by the offering of Christ, that author in that whole Epistle understands nothing else than the presentation of himself for us, if we may so speak, made by Christ to GOD in heaven through the shedding of his own blood. For just as he does not want him to have truly attained his priesthood before he was introduced into heaven after his death, so that he might appear for us before God: so he maintains that he did not perfectly offer himself to God before he presented himself in heaven. For priest and offering are relative terms. Therefore, where there is not yet a true priest, there cannot be a true offering. But where there is a true priest, there must also be a true offering. Now, that Christ is not truly called a priest by that writer before his ascension into heaven can be clear to anyone who has read that Epistle even once. Thus Socinus l. c. I add also from chapter XXIII of the same book: The priesthood of Christ did indeed begin in a certain way on this earth, just as his offering began. But both were completed in the heavens, where Jesus, having entered as a forerunner for us according to the order of Melchizedek, was made a high priest forever. And chapter 21. Just as the legal priest in that annual sacrifice, although he could not enter into the holy of holies before he had slaughtered the sin offerings outside, yet had to bring the blood of those same victims into the sanctuary, and there perform the expiation before God, which was done by that blood. So Christ, although he had to deliver himself to be slaughtered as a victim for our sins before he entered into heaven, yet had to present himself, through whom the expiation was to be perfected, before God in heaven itself thereafter for us, and there perform the expiation of our sins. A little later in the same chapter he added these things: But it is so true that the expiation of our sins was not accomplished before CHRIST entered into heaven, that even after he entered into heaven, he is said to still be expiating, and indeed perpetually, our sins: not, as you believe, because of the power and efficacy of the expiation already accomplished on the cross, which is perennial, but because, being perpetually placed at the right hand of God in the heavens, he reminds us of divine liberality, and moves us constantly to embrace it; and by the supreme authority which he possesses with GOD, i.e., the supreme power granted to him by Him in heaven and on earth, he both saves us, and is about to save us, from the wrath which is repeatedly exercised from heaven against the impious and sinners, and at the same time will be exercised against all on the last day. Thus far, therefore, Socinus. The opinions of others, who follow in the footsteps of this Master, we here willingly omit for the sake of brevity; adding only the words of Schlichting, by which he explains his own mind in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews regarding these words of the Apostle. Sins, he says on p. 26, were purged by oblation and sacrifice. But oblation is not the same as slaughter; slaughter is only an antecedent to oblation and a preparation for oblation, and a certain beginning of the sacrifice. Afterwards, some things having been interposed for the sake of clarification, Schlichting continues: Therefore also the divine author (namely in this place Heb. 1:3) included death as a necessary antecedent in this oblation of Christ. But this oblation of Christ is his appearing before the face of God for us through his entry into heaven. Furthermore, having explained that comparison: By the death, he says, which Christ underwent for sinners, and the immortality which followed it, this victim was so prepared that it was thoroughly pleasing to God, and fully accommodated to his counsel and intention, and was most apt for carrying out the expiation of our sins. He adds moreover that intercession is contained in the appearing, because intercession extends more broadly than to signify only prayers offered for someone. But that the purging of our sins has followed from this oblation of Christ, not only because the oblation of Christ has the power and efficacy to take away all our sins; but because the sacrifice of Christ also moves us to faith and to rendering obedience to Christ, and effects and produces that in us, and procures for Christ the power to take away all our sins, and for us the right to obtain the forgiveness of sins: from which things, if we do our duty, the effect itself necessarily follows, the purging of our sins. Further

He adds that he concedes that this author wishes to say that Christ had performed the purgation of our sins before he sat down at the right hand of the throne of God: because Christ entered that heavenly tabernacle and stood and presented himself to God, with his death intervening, before he sat down at the right hand of the throne of God; but through that entry of his into heaven—these are the words of Schlichting—and through the offering of himself, Christ purged our sins, that is, he did that from which the most full offering or remission of our sins on the part of God was immediately obtained, and as it were secured from God, since Christ himself, our High Priest, who had offered himself for us, immediately acquired the power of taking away all the punishment of sins from us, by which very fact God, as far as it depended on him, is to be considered to have remitted our sins to us. Schlichting warns that this must be carefully observed in this Epistle, so that we may the better understand the comparison of Christ and his offering with the legal Priest and his offering. These things are indeed warned opportunely, that one must carefully attend to in what Christ's sacrifice consists, but Christian readers should much more carefully beware lest they be swept away into the reefs of errors or suffer the shipwreck of saving faith by this Socinian or Schlichting-Crellian undermining and overturning of the priesthood of Christ. Therefore, it is worth the effort to reduce to a summary those things which we have reported so prolixly in their own proper words, and to direct them to the sacred cynosure of the divine word.

But first, Schlichting's distinction is to be observed: by which, whether he is illustrating Socinus's mind or departing from Socinus, it certainly serves very much to declare the truth. For he grants that by the offering of Christ our sins have been purged, that is, that this has been done by Christ, from which the most full removal or remission of our sins on the part of God was immediately obtained, and as it were secured from God. He concedes that the remission of sins was obtained on the part of God, and as it were secured from God, because Christ's sacrifice procured for us the right of obtaining pardon for sins: and he distinguishes that offering of Christ from the actual remission and removal or expiation of our sins as the effect itself, or in so far as the guilt and punishment of our sins are actually taken away; which he likewise attributes to the offering of Christ, namely, if we believe in Christ: whence on our part there follows the removal of our sins by the power of Christ's sacrifice, in so far as it not only procured for us the right of obtaining pardon for sins, but also moves us to faith, and effects and produces it in us. This distinction having been premised, the question in this place is not about the actual removal or expiation of our sins on our part, how it happens by the same power of the offering and sacrifice of Christ? Does the sacrifice of CHRIST move us to faith, and in what way does it effect faith in us? We can certainly admit that we are moved to faith by the sacrifice of Christ, in so far as faith is excited in us by the sacrifice of Christ proposed through the Word of the Gospel, and by the fact that he offered himself for us out of the highest and most intimate love for the human race, but with the efficacious and internal operation of the Holy Spirit accompanying it. Therefore, the sacrifice of Christ does not move us to faith only morally, as it is proposed by the word of the Gospel, or the doctrine of the Gospel concerning the sacrifice and offering of Christ for us, but this doctrine is the power of God unto salvation, Rom. 1:16, and through it faith is excited and produced efficaciously, which is taught elsewhere. Likewise, we admit that our faith is excited when we hear and know that by the offering and sacrifice for us the right of obtaining pardon for sins has been procured for us: although in a different way than the Socinians do: namely, that faith is excited and generated in us by God through the word, not that we claim for ourselves the powers of exciting faith. But to inquire about that here would be foreign to the purpose. Therefore, the question is solely about the expiation of sins, as it has been obtained on the part of God and as it were secured from God, as Schlichting speaks, through the offering and sacrifice of CHRIST, and in so far as CHRIST'S sacrifice procured for us the right of obtaining pardon for sins. Nor is it my intention now to dispute laboriously and as if expressly about whether that expiation of sins was made through a satisfaction to divine justice rendered by CHRIST in the place of the whole human race. And whether the remission of sins and expiation was secured from GOD through the offering of CHRIST, and the right of obtaining pardon for sins was procured for us, by which GOD is reconciled and appeased toward the human race through the expiatory sacrifice of Christ? It would be too long a digression if I were to choose to descend into this arena. And those things have been treated expressly in *Socinismo profligato*, where we dealt diligently with the satisfaction of Christ. Therefore, we must at least see to this at present: whether that offering, through which the expiation of sins was made, and remission was obtained on the part of God, and the right of pardon and remission of sins was born for us, was performed in these lands, or whether this sacrifice is performed in heaven? Therefore, it is irrelevant what Socinus said, that CHRIST, placed in heaven at the right hand of God, still expiates our sins while he admonishes us of divine liberality and moves us continually to embrace it: since the question is not about this expiation or application of the remission of sins, which we do not deny that CHRIST, established at the right hand of Majesty on high, performs by making us partakers of the fruits and efficacy of his offering or sacrifice.

Furthermore, no orthodox person denies that CHRIST, having been raised to the right hand of GOD after He offered Himself to GOD as a sacrifice, possesses the power of remitting our sins, of freeing us from the punishments of sins, and of saving us eternally. But the question here is not about that power of Christ to impart the remission of sins to us, but about the right of pardon procured for us, and about the remission of sins on the part of God, or the expiation obtained and acquired from God through the sacrifice or oblation made to God. But since Socinus infers from that power of Christ that the expiation of sins has not yet been accomplished, he confuses again the expiation of sins on our part, by reason of the effect, and on the part of GOD by reason of the right acquired for us, concerning which those who follow Socinus here are to be more correctly informed by Schlichting, or by his preceptor Johannes Crellius. Since these men concede that Christ by His oblation has already made that expiation of sins by which the right of the remission of sins has been obtained for us, and it has been obtained on the part of God.

Therefore, the contradiction of Socinus and Crellius in this part is to be noted. The former denies that the expiation has already been accomplished, and asserts that both the oblation and the expiation are now, most properly speaking, being accomplished at last. The latter, however, with Schlichting, concedes that the expiation has already been accomplished, namely on the part of God and by reason of the right acquired for us, and asserts that the expiatory oblation of Christ is now being accomplished in heaven in some manner at least. See Crellius, book on the causes of the death of Christ, p. 7. Furthermore, he ascribes to the death of CHRIST such power and efficacy and remission of sins to be obtained, that it could even move and impel GOD, if by chance He were to repent of His promise concerning the remission of sins and the liberation from destruction to be granted to us, not to rescind His promise, but to perform in reality what He had promised: And he proves that the death of Christ has this power from Heb. 12:24, where it is said that the blood of sprinkling, namely of CHRIST, by which we have been as it were sprinkled and inscribed into the new covenant, speaks better things than Abel, that is, it does not demand vengeance from GOD, as the blood of Abel once did, but rather the forgiveness of all crimes, op. cit. page 10. Although Crellius indeed refers this efficacy to the Mediatorial office of CHRIST, which he distinguishes from the Sacerdotal, by which CHRIST as Mediator of the covenant grants us a full right to obtain the remission of sins, and binds and obliges God to grant and impart the same to us: yet he makes a divorce in that part from Socinus and his associates, because he assigns this power to the death of Christ, just as he himself quite clearly indicates his disagreement with his associates. But he attempts to excuse the same on page 11, l. c. However, Crellius is mistaken in this, that he so distinguishes the Mediatorial office of Christ from the Sacerdotal, that he says the right of pardon is procured for us by reason of the former, but not by respect of the latter. For if that right has been acquired for us through the offering of Christ, even if that power and efficacy of expiating sins belongs to the offering of Christ, as Schlichtingius admits, surely it must be that the same belongs to the priesthood of CHRIST, since it is undoubted that his offering and sacrifice properly pertain to the Priesthood, or the sacrifice of Christ.

Furthermore, the opinion of Socinus concerning the death of Christ, by which it results in the expiation of sins, inclines to this, that the death of Christ is established as a cause of the expiation of sins at least by accident, in so far as it was antecedent to the resurrection and glorification of Christ, to whom the expiation of sins especially belongs, as is gathered from chap. 21, part I, de Serv. Christi. Crellius, however, asserts that the death of CHRIST is directed not only by this pact as if by accident, but also in itself to that effect, that is, to the obtaining of the remission of sins for us or the procuring of the right of it for us, l. c. p. 35. Hence the opinions of Socinus and Crellius are diametrically opposed. Socinus, loc. cit., says: Had the resurrection of Christ not followed, as we have also said sometimes above, the death of Christ would have profited us nothing. Crellius, however, l. c. says that the death of CHRIST also in itself, that is, with the resurrection that followed entirely set aside, had great power to establish and sanction his doctrine and the promise of the remission of sins contained therein.

But these things being dismissed, that in which they agree, and of which we began to speak, must be inquired into most of all. And that is concerning the offering of Christ in the heavens. Although indeed Socinus, part II, de Serv. Christ. c. XV, seems to hint that the offering of Christ was partly performed on earth, and partly is being performed in heaven, when he says that those words of Heb. 9:14, 'he offered himself to God immaculate,' do not refer to the death of the cross alone, but to the entry at the same time into the holy places, that is, into heaven itself; yet Socinus denies altogether that the offering was made on earth, for the reason that Christ was not a true Priest on earth: And therefore he believes that he did not make a true offering there either; hence he distinguishes the beginning, or rather the preparation of the sacrifice of Christ, and the absolute or perfect and true sacrifice of Christ: that the death was only a preparation of the sacrifice of Christ, not a true sacrifice: in what way, says Socinus; that the offering of Christ indeed began in a certain way on this earth, but was completed in the heavens, l. II. de Serv. Christ. c. XXIII. And for that reason the same person pronounces the same concerning the priesthood of Christ, ibid., that the priesthood of Christ indeed began in some way on earth, but was finally completed in the heavens. So also Crellius, l. c. de caus. mortis Christi p. 13. The death of Christ was a certain propitiation of this our High Priest, and because the victim is the same as the Priest, it was also of the victim itself. Schlichtingius adds here besides the immortality of Christ, that not only by the death which he underwent, but also by the immortality that followed, this victim was prepared so that it might be apt for the expiation of our sins to be performed.

Furthermore, if it is asked here whether and when that offering and expiation of sins of Christ, by which the right of pardon was made for us, and the remission of sins was obtained or procured from God, was performed in the heavens? Schlichtingius answers that this was already done by Christ before he sat at the right hand of the throne of God, in so far as Christ, having entered heaven, presented and showed himself to God before he sat at the right hand of God, and that this is the offering and sacrifice of Christ, namely that Christ, having entered into heaven, presented himself to God, and by that our sins were purged, or the remission of sins was obtained on the part of God immediately, and was procured from God, and the power of taking away all our sins was granted to Christ: Yet that the offering of Christ is still being made perpetually, by which he appears perpetually before the face of God, and that intercession is contained in that appearance; and that the expiation of sins (on our part, or regarding the actual effect of the remission of sins) follows, namely in so far as this appearance of CHRIST moves us to faith, which is followed by the actual removal of sins: where we cannot but note a new ἀντιλογίαν of Crellius himself and Schlichtingius concerning the effect of that first appearance, or presentation made in the heavens, before Christ sat at the right hand of God, as Schlichtingius speaks. Crellius explains it in such a way that he makes no mention of the right of the pardon of sins procured for us, or of the remission of sins obtained on the part of God through this very offering or presentation, which I have commemorated from Schlichtingius. But because when Christ was carried into heaven as a most pleasing victim to God, he was presented before Him, and obtained the fullest power of granting us the remission of sins, and that furthermore whatever he might do for our salvation while appearing perpetually before God, that this most sweet victim, as if delighted by it, would be ratified by God and perfected by His power. But rather, he attributes this effect to the death of Christ, and that of itself, because it produced for us the right of obtaining the remission of sins. Whence the Socinian, or one adhering to the explanation of Socinus, could be refuted anew by his own hypotheses in this question in this manner: The oblation of Christ was made for the purpose that the right of obtaining the pardon of the remission of sins was secured for us: which is the opinion of Schlichtingius. But it is not by the appearance of Christ before the face of God, but by the death of Christ that this was obtained, which is what Crellius confesses, and indeed in such a way that the death of Christ is of itself the cause of the same. From the death of Christ the oblation of Christ was made, but not by the appearance of Christ or His presentation in the heavens.

Finally, the distinction of Schlichting will have to be diligently observed: That Christ purges sins in one way insofar as He is King; in another way insofar as He is Priest. Insofar as He is King, and has supreme power from God, in that way, he says, Christ purges or takes away sins, in the way that God takes away sins, i.e., most properly, by taking away both the guilt and the punishment of sins. But insofar as He is Priest, to take away as a Priest our sins, CHRIST, in as much as he was slaughtered, and in as much as he then entered into the inner sanctuaries of heaven, offered himself, or presented himself to God, and thus appears before God, and intercedes for us. Which must be noted against Socinus and Smalcius, who contend that the expiation of our sins belongs to Christ, by which he governs all things by the word of his power, and by which he performs the Kingly office, not attending to the distinction of Schlichting. Which therefore we can urge against the same, indeed against Socinus in this way: If Christ is said here to have made expiation for our sins, as Priest, he is certainly understood not to have made expiation for our sins, by which he carries all things by the word of his virtue. Which two things are here distinctly distinguished by Schlichting: But the former is true. Therefore also the latter. Against Smalcius: If Christ expiates our sins as God most properly, in as much as he is King, not only is the power of expiating sins contained in the Kingly office of Christ, but also the will itself, and the actual expiation. Εὔδηλον. But the former is true, according to Schlichting. Again, if Christ expiates sins as Priest in a far different manner than as King, and indeed in such a way that the expiation of sins belongs to him most properly as he is King, but belongs to him less properly as he is Priest, then the Kingly office of Christ and the Priesthood are not distinguished by reason alone, nor will they be so distinct that by reason of the Kingly office he can, and by reason of the priestly office he wills to expiate our sins. But the antecedent is true according to Schlichting. Therefore.

Against the distinction of Schlichting himself, however, it must be held from the Scriptures: that expiation belongs to Christ both as he is God of the same essence with the Father (John 10:30, 1 John 5:7), namely in the same way that it belongs to the Father: and as he is Priest, and in as much as he was slaughtered, and in as much as appearing in the heavens he intercedes for us: as Schlichting speaks with us: namely in as much as being slaughtered he acquired for us the right of remission of sins by his death; (which we said a little before that Crellius conceded,) not as Schlichting wishes, by moving us with his appearance and intercession so that we might conceive faith, and thus obtain the expiation of sins, but by moving GOD with the same, so that he might deign to confer faith upon us, and to free us from the guilt and punishment of sins by the very act. As for the Kingly office, it is clear from what has preceded that the expiation of our sins by no means pertains to it, nor does Schlichting's error arise from anywhere else, that he says Christ as King expiates our sins as God, than that he places the Deity of Christ in this Royal dignity. Who is God blessed forever.

to the [expiation] before the sitting at the right hand of God, he ascribes the purification of sins, nay, he testifies that that exaltation to the right hand of GOD immediately followed the entry into heaven, as the limit of the ascension of CHRIST, Mark 16:19. Added to this is that the entry into heaven is nothing else in the phrase of Scripture than access to the Majesty, just as the sitting at the right hand of the Majesty is access to divine glory, and it is scarcely distinguished from the entry even with respect to reason.

(2) Because CHRIST is said to have entered into heaven αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν εὑρόμενον, having found eternal redemption, Heb. 9:12. Wherefore before that entry he had already found eternal redemption, and thus that λύτρωσις and ἀπολύτρωσις is said to have been made διὰ τῦ ἅιματ© αὐτῦ, through his blood, Eph. 1:7, Col. 1:17, Rom. 3:24, and thus by the shedding of blood and his death, by which he delivered himself as a λύτρον and ἀντίλυτρον for us, Matt. 20:28, Mark 10:45, 1 Tim. 2:5, which was certainly done before the entry of CHRIST into heaven, the purification of our sins having been made by his delivery into death and the shedding of the blood of Christ, which was shed on earth, and not indeed in the heavens, Matt. 26:28, Rev. 1:5, 1 Pet. 1:2, 1 John 1:7. So also Christ is said to have redeemed us with his blood, in which he was slaughtered for us, Rev. 5:9.

(3) Because CHRIST appeared in the heavens διὰ τῆς θυσίας, through the sacrifice, Heb. 9:26. The sacrifice therefore preceded, the appearance or presentation in the heavens followed, but that presentation is not the sacrifice itself. Besides these, that appearance in the heavens is distinguished from the oblation and sacrifice of Christ itself, in this Epistle, in such a way that the appearance of Christ is indeed still taking place, [but] the sacrifice has already been made, Heb. 9:24. For although the sacrifice is eternal, if you look at the efficacy, power, and effect, yet as to the act it has already passed, and was performed only once, which our Epistle hints at more often, Heb. 7:27, ch. 9:26, 28, ch. 10:1, 12, 14. Therefore the oblation is not still being made by the appearance of Christ before the face of God.

(4) Because the sacrifice is called θυσία, Heb. 9:25, ch. 10:12, Eph. 5:2. Moreover, a θυσία is performed then when the victim is given to death: whence to slaughter signifies to sacrifice. But nowhere is θυσία or the Hebrew עב said to be merely an appearance: it always implies killing or consumption, or burning made by fire: and Crellius confesses that a θυσία is properly completed by slaughtering, and that θύειν is to slaughter, resp. to Grot. p. 533. Therefore his θυσία or sacrifice was performed on the altar of the cross, not in the heavens.

Therefore, at least for the present, it is asked whether the sacrificial oblation of Christ, through which the expiation of sins was made, and on the part of God the remission of sins was obtained, and the right of pardon and remission of sins was procured for us, was performed on the altar of the cross, or in the heavens. That it was performed in these lands and on the cross, we confirm with the following arguments: (1) Because Christ is said to have made the purification of sins before he sat at the right hand of God. Therefore he also performed the expiation of sins before the entry into heaven, and thus on earth, where Schlichting objects in vain that CHRIST first presented himself in the heavens, and by that presentation made expiation, before he sat at the right hand of GOD, for Scripture nowhere distinguishes the entry into heaven and the sitting at the right hand of God in such a way that expiation mediates between the two: (5) Because the nature of sacrifice consists mostly in the oblation, as Crellius admits in the loc. cit. page 532, the slaughtering of the sacrificial victim took place, as we are taught in Leviticus 1:3, 5, 11; chapter 3:2, 8; chapter 4:14, 15, 29, 37; chapter 6:25; chapter 7:2, so that indeed the blood of the victim, given for the life of men, might expiate their souls, Leviticus 17:11. Whence it is nowhere taught that a victim is completed by the mere presentation of the victim before God, but the very slaughtering of the host is required for the oblation, as well as its consumption, without which there is no sacrifice; however, in the heavens no consumption of the body of Christ has a place. Furthermore, no expiatory sacrifice is made without the shedding of blood; the appearance of Christ in the heavens occurs without the shedding of blood. Therefore.

(6) Because as the bringing in of the blood of the victim into the holy places corresponds to the sanctification of Christ or the application of the expiation of sins, which we do not deny is done by Christ having departed into heaven; so to the burning of sacrifices, outside the tents, by which the sacrifices were completed and consumed, corresponds the passion of CHRIST outside the gate, and that is the absolute and completed expiatory sacrifice of Christ, as the Apostle most distinctly teaches in Hebrews 13:11-12. Although, therefore, the sacrifices were by no means completed by the immolation alone, but after the same had been slaughtered, the fat and blood had to be offered to God, yet that was not done in the holy of holies, into which it is not evident that the fat was brought, nor was the blood brought in to be offered or immolated, but it was offered outside the holy of holies (Leviticus 4:17-18), and the fat was consumed by fire (Exodus 29:13-14; Leviticus 8:17; 16:17), just as the flesh was to be burned outside the camp and consumed by fire; and Crellius admits (l. c. p. 532 & 534) that the oblation was finally completed by that. But that, according to the Apostle's interpretation, corresponds to the passion of Christ, and by no means agrees with an appearance in the heavens. Therefore, it is invincibly concluded that the oblation was completed by the passion of Christ, not by an appearance in the heavens. Although indeed all those things—the slaughtering, the flaying of the victims, the pouring of the blood at the base of the altar, the removal of the fat, the burning of the blood and fat, and the reduction to dust, the burning and consumption of the flesh—were distinct in the expiatory sacrifices, yet all of them concur here κατ' ἀναλογίαν (by analogy) shown by the Holy Spirit, in the great passion of Christ, and by them his sacrifice was completed. Which is graphically described in Psalm 22:15 ff.: 'I am poured out like water, all my bones are out of joint, my heart is like wax; it is melted in the midst of my bowels. My strength is dried up like a potsherd; and my tongue cleaveth to my jaws; and thou hast brought me into the dust of death.' Likewise: 'They pierced my hands and my feet, they told all my bones. They look and stare upon me,' etc. Furthermore, it must be carefully observed that in the remaining sacrifices, and especially for the sin of any private individual, no blood was brought into either the holy place or the holy of holies. Therefore, the oblation or sacrifice did not consist in that bringing of blood into the holy place. For if the sacrifice consisted in that bringing and presentation of blood, it would follow that the sacrifices for the sins of private individuals were not sacrifices: which is contradictory and most absurd. And therefore the invention of the Socinians, that the sacrifices of the Old Testament were not perfected except in the sanctuary, is also most absurd. Furthermore, from the fact that the expiatory sacrifices were for sins, without their blood being brought into the holy place, and that they shadowed forth and figured the sacrifice of CHRIST, it follows that the sacrifice of CHRIST was not completed by the presentation of blood in heaven, but by the immolation and passion of CHRIST on the altar of the cross. Since Socinus understands this, he prefers to disparage the other sacrifices, which they were, rather than concede a place to the truth, denying that all sacrifices made for sins correspond to the death of CHRIST and figured it, but only the sacrifices which were made publicly, that is, for the whole people and at stated times, and especially that which the high priest performed once a year by entering into the holy of holies, as he thinks can be evident to anyone who reads it not sluggishly from the Epistle to the Hebrews, part II de Servat. Christ. cap. IX. But this is evidently refuted in this very Epistle, chapter 9:13, where it is taught that the blood of bulls and goats and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on the defiled sanctified to the purifying of the flesh, and by that the blood of CHRIST was shadowed forth, who offered himself without blemish to GOD through the eternal Spirit, by which our consciences are purged from dead works to serve the living GOD. And verse 22 says universally that almost all things are purged in the law with blood, and that without the shedding of blood there is no remission of sins, and it is immediately subjoined: 'It is necessary, therefore, that τὰ μὲν ὑποδεί- γματα (the patterns) of things in the heavens should be purified with these.' Likewise, the daily sacrifices are also compared with the sacrifice of CHRIST in Hebrews 10:11, the meaning of which passage Socinus attempts to shake by explaining καθ' ἡμέραν (daily) as 'yearly' in an unheard-of commentary, l. II. de Serv. Christ. cap. XVI. Compare on these matters Grotius, de satisfactione Christi, page 127. Therefore CHRIST is also called אָשָׁם (asham), that is, a sacrifice for sin, in Isaiah 53:10, which word is also used for private expiatory sacrifices in Leviticus 4:3, 5:6, 8, 16, 18. And what else were the Jews doing with all those expiatory sacrifices which they offered for sin, than by them confessing themselves guilty of death, and substituting catharmata (expiatory offerings) in their place, and by their immolation being released from guilt? There is no doubt that by this very thing the death of Christ was shadowed forth, who was made sin and a curse for us (2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13), so that we might be released from sin and the curse. Add that not only at stated times of the year, but every single day, public sacrifices were offered, morning and evening (Exodus 29:38), for the whole people, by which indeed the death of CHRIST was figured daily among the Jews. It must be observed, moreover, that not even of the blood from the sacrifices offered for the sin of the whole society or communion was anything brought into the holy of holies (except for the anniversary sacrifice, Leviticus 16), but only into the holy place, and merely sprinkled toward the holy of holies (Leviticus 4:5; 6:30; 8:15; 9:9). But it was placed upon the horns of the altar of incense, and the rest in the court of the priests at the base of the altar of burnt offering standing in the open air, to be burned. In these sacrifices, therefore, because nothing was brought into the holy of holies, there will have been no oblation according to Socinus, which is not only contradictory, as we noted before, but also contrary to the opinion of Socinus, who concedes that those sacrifices figured the oblation of Christ because they were public. From this, however, we argue again against Socinus: Those public sacrifices for sins shadowed forth the sacrifice of CHRIST, as Socinus admits. But because those public sacrifices were not made for an entry into the holy of holies, nor was their blood brought in, it is clearly evident that the sacrifice of CHRIST was not made in heaven, which corresponds to the holy of holies, but on earth on the altar of the cross, where CHRIST suffered and was delivered to death.

(7) We seek our argument from our purification and liberation. For if the purification of our sins and our redemption was accomplished before the entry into heaven, by the shedding of the blood of CHRIST on earth, or by the passion and death of Christ: then certainly the expiatory sacrifice of CHRIST was also accomplished before the entry of CHRIST into heaven by the shedding of his blood. But the former is true. Therefore, the latter is also true. The assumption is evident both from this very passage, where it is said that after the purification of sins had been made he sat down at the right hand of GOD, and from a comparison with Heb. 9:12, and all the passages which treat of the λύτρον, λύτρωσις, ἀπολύτρωσις, ἀγορασμός, and καθαρισμός of Christ, inasmuch as they are always and perpetually attributed to the death of Christ, to his passion and the shedding of his blood, and to the blood of Christ, and thus to the offering made on earth, but nowhere to an offering in heaven.

(8) From 1 Corinthians 5:7. 'Our Passover was sacrificed for us.' Which was not done in heaven, but on earth by slaughter, not by presentation, since the word itself θύειν, which is derived from slaughtering (Josh. 10:10), teaches the threefold rite of the Paschal lamb, which certainly had to be slaughtered, but was not brought into the inner sanctuary; then the comparison of the analogous text: for what Paul says, 'Passover was sacrificed,' John expresses as 'a lamb slain,' that lamb slaughtered or killed, Rev. 5:6, 12, ch. 13, v. 8. Therefore, ἐθύθη is the same as ἐσφαγίθη, and Passover is the same as 'lamb': and as 'slain you have redeemed us to God by your blood,' Rev. 5:9, so 'sacrificed for us,' says the Apostle. Add that we are said to be redeemed 'with the precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot, CHRIST,' as an immaculate and incontaminate lamb, 1 Pet. 1:19; then that lamb was sacrificed for us when He redeemed us. But He redeemed us with His own blood, as Peter teaches: and therefore He was sacrificed for us when He shed His blood for us.

(9) From the oblation of Christ, described in Eph. 5:2. 'CHRIST loved us,' says the Apostle, 'and gave Himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savor.' Therefore, the very offering and sacrifice of Christ consists in this, that He indeed 'gave Himself for us.' And that this is to be understood of the giving of CHRIST for us into death is most evident, and the Socinians admit it, and urge furthermore that CHRIST is said here to have given Himself, because He gave Himself into death, as in verse 25 of this chapter, and Gal. 2:10, Rom. 8:32. Nor do the adversaries escape the force of this demonstration by the fiction of a new construction: as if the verb 'gave' should not be joined with the word 'offering,' but the word 'offering and sacrifice' was added only by apposition, so that this act of Christ, that He gave Himself into death, was a pleasing offering and victim to GOD, but not that by that giving of the body of Christ the offering and sacrifice was accomplished. Concerning which see Socin. part II, ch. XV, on the Savior of Christ. But I will not say how much Socinus fluctuates in this interpretation, how little he attributes to it himself: since he turns himself into the most diverse forms here to blunt the force of our argument: now he says he asserts and confesses that CHRIST did not offer Himself except through death, that is, with the intervention of the death of Christ, although the oblation was not perfected until after the ascension into heaven; now he says he understands the oblation made in heaven at least concerning the oblation which is commemorated in the Epistle to the Hebrews: but that he did not have regard for all the writings of the divine authors: now finally he uses this escape of a new distinction and construction of the text: thus the Sophist nowhere had a place where he could safely plant his foot, which is an evident argument of an uncertain and fluctuating mind. But these exceptions cannot stand: for if it is granted that it is hinted here that CHRIST offered Himself as a sacrifice when He was given into death, His sacrifice was not at least begun by death but completed, nor can He be said to have offered Himself as a victim and sacrifice in heaven, because He was not given into death in heaven. If it can be demonstrated from other divine writings that the oblation of Christ was completed on earth, it will not even be to be presumed that something different is proposed in the Epistle to the Hebrews, or that it contradicts the other God-breathed writings. But that depravation of a most manifest passage, as it is entirely new and unheard of, so it collapses by its own vanity: (1) for whence will the adversaries teach,

that the act of Christ is at least commended here as a victim pleasing to GOD, but that the end of the giving of CHRIST into death is not designated, so that by this very thing an oblation and victim for our sins was made: which has been constantly believed in the Church until now. (2) By what arguments will they convince us that 'victim and oblation' here must be understood entirely improperly concerning a thing pleasing to GOD, and not properly concerning an expiatory oblation and victim. (3) In that Greek text, 'He gave Himself for us an offering' are joined without punctuation: and therefore it is noted that the 'offering and sacrifice' was completed by the very giving of CHRIST into death, or that the death of Christ was the sacrifice and oblation of Christ.
