(4) So also the Syriac translation, which is most ancient, joins them. (5) The Tigurines, although they interpose a comma between the NOUN and the verb, nevertheless do not understand that CHRIST gave Himself for us in any other way than by way of sacrifice. (6) To these, the sense of the words of the Apostle is manifest in itself: that CHRIST gave Himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to GOD, because He offered Himself as a sacrifice to God for us. For the manner of the giving of Christ is hinted at, by which He gave Himself for us. And the end; especially indeed (7) because the word 'for us' denotes the same as Matt. 20:18, 'instead of many,' which is 'in our place.' But how was He given in our place? namely as an expiatory victim, which were accustomed to be offered in the place of men. (8) From there an argument is sought for the love of Christ: but the highest love of Christ is that He was given in our place and made a victim. (9) Similar passages explaining this are added, Isa. 53:10, 2 Cor. 5:21, Heb. 9:25, 28, etc. And these things for the present concerning that passage.

(10) From the end of the incarnation, Heb. 10:5, 6, the Apostle discourses concerning the end of the coming and incarnation of the Son of God, who came into the world and assumed a human body adapted to Himself, so that it might be testified that God is not delighted by victims or sacrifices in themselves, but by the fulfillment of the divine will and the oblation or sacrifice of the body of CHRIST, made once for our sanctification. He hints, therefore, that the Son of GOD assumed a human body for this end, that by the oblation of the same made once, He might complete a sacrifice, far more excellent and ample than all the sacrifices of the Old Testament. And that sacrifice made once was an expiation for our sins, and by that one we have been sanctified forever, verse 14, which being completed, He sat down at the right hand of GOD, verse 12. But what is that oblation of the body of Christ? for whose sake a body was adapted to Christ. Certainly not that Socinian one in the heavens: because it was necessary for Him to come to earth in order to make this offering. For that which is said to have come into the world is nothing other than that He came to earth, Joh. 18, 37. 1. Tim. 1, 15. Furthermore, the offering was completed before He sat down at the right hand of God, vers. 11. Therefore, it must have been done on earth, not in the heavens, because upon entering heaven Christ sat down at the right hand of God. Nor is anything read in the scriptures as an intermediate step between the entry and the sitting down in the heavens: indeed, as we warned before, the entry into heaven is nothing other than the approach to the Majesty, and the sitting down at the right hand of the Majesty is likewise nothing other than the approach to the divine glory, so that they are scarcely distinguished from one another by any rational consideration according to the scripture’s explanation of the entry into heaven and the sitting down at the right hand of GOD. For by both modes of speaking the same thing is indicated; which

CHRIST has attained heavenly Majesty and glory, by which He sustains a most full and most powerful empire over all things: whether it be said that He has occupied His kingdom—for that is what it means for heaven to receive Him, Acts 3, verse 21—or that He has occupied the royal throne, or has sat down at the right hand of GOD. Once this equivalence of phrases is properly observed, the fiction of the Socinians regarding an offering made before the sitting at the right hand of God after the entry into heaven will vanish into thin air. For those things which are distinguished only by the manner of speaking cannot be so distinguished that an intermediate act is established and located between them.

(11) From the Prophetic explanation. For thus does Isaiah explain the propitiatory sacrifice of Christ in chapter 53: That our sins were cast upon Him; that He bore our sins; that He was slaughtered as a lamb for us; that He was wounded and killed for our sins; that He delivered up His soul for us. Because the Prophet explicitly says that this very thing was the propitiatory sacrifice of Christ, that Christ laid down His soul as a sacrifice for us, verse 10. But what could have been said more clearly? So that it might be taught that by the death of Christ and His passion, the propitiatory sacrifice of Christ was accomplished?

(12) From the unity of the sacrifice. That the expiatory sacrifice of Christ is only one, and that it has already been accomplished by Christ, or that it has already passed, if indeed you look at the act, although it is eternal if we attend to its efficacy, power, and effect. Our Epistle inculcates this frequently, ch. 7, 27: 'For this He did once for all, when He offered up Himself.' Ch. 9, 26: 'But now once at the end of the ages, for the putting away of sin, He has been manifested through His own sacrifice.' Verse 28: 'Having been offered once to bear the sins of many.' Chapter 10, 10: 'By which will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Christ, made once for all.' V. 12: 'But He, having offered one sacrifice for sins for all time.' V. 14: 'For by one offering He has perfected,' etc. If, therefore, the expiatory sacrifice and offering of Christ has already been accomplished, and it ought not to have been anything but unique without repetition or iteration, it is false that that offering is being made in the heavens, for that offering is still being made by the presentation and appearance of Christ before the face of God.

(13) From the Apostolic conclusion, Heb. 9, 26. If the sacrifice of Christ had needed to be repeated, Christ would have needed to suffer often: the nerve of which argument is that the sacrifice of Christ was accomplished by His passion.

(14) From the hypothesis of the Socinians concerning the body of Christ. They maintain that Christ stripped off and laid aside His body when He ascended into heaven. If, therefore, the sacrifice of Christ is finally accomplished in the heavens, it follows, by the force of that hypothesis, that Christ did not accomplish the sacrifice with the same body of His that was born of the Virgin Mary. (2) That the body of Christ with which He accomplished the sacrifice is not ὁμοέσιον or consubstantial to us. (3) That He does not offer that body of His which God prepared for Him when He came into the lands, or into the world, to fulfill the will of God. (4) That the sacrifice was begun in one body, and is accomplished and completed in another, and one that is indeed naturally and substantially different. (5) That there is not one and the same Priest, nor one and the same sacrifice, since the sacrifice of Christ began on earth and is continued and completed in the heavens, with the intervention not only of many other rites, but also of that change by which there is an entirely different Priest and a different sacrifice.

(15) From the parallel passage 1 Pet. 2, 24, that He bore our sins in His body upon the tree of the cross. But He bore sins as an expiatory sacrifice; and thus in this body of His, subject to death, and indeed upon the tree of the cross. But so that it may be clear what is to be answered to the contrary arguments, and those sufficiently specious ones, let the following be noted: (I) The adversaries generally confuse the meritorious expiation of sins and the application of it. And they are accustomed to oppose the sayings that deal with the application of the remission of sins to the expiation of sins acquired by Christ. (II) Some distinguish thus: That the purgation of our sins depends on the entry of Christ into the heavens by reason of the λειτουργία and dispensation, Heb. 8, 2, but not by reason of the constitution and acquisition. For thus it depends on the shedding of blood, ch. 9, 22. (III) They also distinguish the offering made in the death of Christ in the days of His flesh, Heb. 5, 7, from that which is said to have been made in the heavens, because the former is meritorious and satisfactory, and liberating from servitude: the latter is triumphal and applicatory, Heb. 9, 24, 26, which is said more correctly of expiation than of offering. For in the Scriptures, offering is spoken of only as that which was made on the altar of the cross: and therefore it was made only once, and is unique, ch. 9, 28; ch. 10, 12. Furthermore, (IV) there is that which the blessed Dorscheus rightly observed, by way of the morning and evening offering, and likewise the annual purgation of the whole people. For by these offerings a certain universal καθαρισμὸς was established for the whole people, even for those far from the temple, far removed from the sacrifices. But those who were not present at the sacrifices also had to apply that καθαρισμὸς to themselves and embrace it with a certain confidence: Hence also the Jews, distant and scattered far and wide in the world, were accustomed to perform their prayers with their eyes turned toward the Temple, in which they knew those sacrifices were being made, which custom the prophecy of Daniel, ch. 6, 11, testifies was observed by him. To them, therefore, the daily καθαρισμὸς was profitable, who in this way applied it to themselves; but those who neglected the same, in them the removal of sins did not immediately follow. But there is another reason for those offering particularly for a singular cause or fault. For in them, the offering is joined with application. (V) It is indeed true that the sacrifice of CHRIST moves us to faith, produces faith in us, has acquired for CHRIST the right to take away our sins, and has procured for us the obtaining of the forgiveness of sins. But all these things are founded upon this, that through the sacrifice of Christ a καθαρισμὸς (cleansing) has been established and completed, which, when applied particularly, cleanses consciences by the very act. (VI) CHRIST is said to have made a καθαρισμὸν (cleansing), by reason of the constitution and the act as it were signed with respect to GOD the Father, to whom he afterwards invited the whole human race. The order is explained in 2 Cor. 5. CHRIST received into himself our ἀκαθαρσίαν (uncleanness), that he might provide δικαιοσύνην καθαριστικὴν (cleansing righteousness) v. 21. In this way was established the ἱλαστήριον (propitiation) & καθαριστήριον (place of cleansing) Rom. 3, 25. To those looking upon which, sins were not to be imputed, but reconciliation with God was to be insinuated 2. Corinth. 5, 19. To that end was made the θέσις (position), ordination, and sanction of the word of reconciliation, that is, of the ministry, verse same & 20. Undoubtedly the constitution of the καθαρισμῦ (cleansing) & καταλογῆς (reconciliation) required the constitution of application through the λόγον καθαρισμῦ καὶ καταλογῆς (word of cleansing and reconciliation). Therefore, that ποίησις (making) was done before the session at the right hand. This is what Socinus openly admits against Bellarmine & Wieck, chapter 8, thesis 6, when he weighs the Greek word ποιησάμενος, which properly declares past time, even though it is otherwise true that Christ even now expiates our sins.

(VII) That this making of the purification designates a completed and past act is proven thus. 1. Because it is of the same extent as the destruction of the devil who has the power of death, which was perfected through death, and lasted as long as CHRIST was made like his brothers in infirmities, and was tempted in all things with them, Heb. 2, 14. 17. 18. 2. Because CHRIST in that oblation of his, by which he offered himself with tears to GOD the Father, which preceded his session at the right hand, is said to have been made ἄιτιος σωτηρίας ἀιωνίꙋ, so that he might be τελειωθεὶς chap. 5, 7. & 9. 3. Because if the oblation, by which the purgation of our sins is effected, were not perfect, and consummated before the session at the right hand of God, then it would be false what is said in chap. 7, 27. that CHRIST has no need of a daily oblation for sins and for obtaining the purgation of the same, since he has done this once. 4. Because the καθαρισμὸς in chapter 9 is described in such a way that, regarding the acquisition, it is said to be terminated by the shedding of blood and death. 5. Because the oblation perfecting the purgation of our sins is expressly said to have preceded the session at the right hand, chap. 10, 12. 13. (VIII) The invention of the Socinians, by which they suspend the purgation of our sins on the part of God from that moment in which Christ stood before the Father immediately before his session at the right hand of God, which was the last moment of his Ascension into heaven, is repugnant both to the article of the Ascension into heaven and the session at the right hand of GOD, since those things cannot be understood locally and according to moments, and especially also to the design of the whole Epistle: since the whole Epistle extends the purgation of sins to the passion, death, shedding of blood, assimilation to men in regard to misery and humility, and to perpetual obedience, but in no way restricts it to the exaltation and the last moment of his entry into the holy of holies. (IX) The Socinians argue that the sacrificial oblation is not completed by the slaughter alone; we concede that, but we add that it is not completed by the presentation either, because in many sacrifices there was not even such a presentation. Therefore, the burning itself is required at the same time: In the sacrifice of CHRIST, however, the passion of Christ corresponds to both the slaughter and the burning. And these things concerning the act of purification.

(II.) The Object of our sins: Where we note two things (1) The name of sins, by which, being placed absolutely, it is indicated that the expiation of all sins has been made through CHRIST: with a silent antithesis, that in the Old Testament the expiation was made only for those for whom sacrifices were offered: but here for all: namely, that the expiation is universal, not only intensively, extending itself to all sins, however great and of whatever kind: for the handwriting of all sins was nailed to the cross Coloss. 2, 14. All the works of the Devil destroyed 1. John 3, 15. Heb. 2. verse 14. therefore the blood of CHRIST cleanses us from all sin 1. John 1, 29. CHRIST redeemed us ἀπὸ πάσης ἀνομίας Tit. 2, 14. with his blood shed without guilt, the handwritings of all guilts were deleted, says Augustine book II. on the remission of sins, chap. 20. Thus also the scapegoat is said to have borne all iniquities Lev. 16, 21. seq. then extensively to the sins of all men, or of the whole world; because it is said absolutely, sins. Thus Is. 53, 6. we all have wandered like sheep, but GOD cast the sins of all upon him; where note both the universality of redemption, all: who were wandering: and the truth of universal redemption, whether we look at the intention of God or the expiation of sin. Add to these from the N. T. where (1) by the word World all are expressed John 1, 29. c. 3, 6. c. 6, 33. 51. chap. 12, 47. John 4, 42. 2. Cor. 8, 29. 1. John 4, 14. 1. John 2, 2. (2) When mention is made of all people, Luke 2, 10. of every man John 1, 9. Rom. 5, 18. 19. (3) Of that which had perished Matt. 18, 11. of those who sat in darkness, Luke 1, 79. (4) If all things are commemorated in the same sense Ephes. 1, 10. Col. 1, 20. All 2. Cor. 5, 14. 15. 1. Tim. 2, 6. c. 4, 10. Tit. 2, 10. Heb. 2, 9. The use of the former is (1) against the Papists: who contend contradictorily that Christ satisfied only for original sin and for actual sins preceding Baptism, but that for the rest we ourselves must satisfy. For a naked man to satisfy the infinite justice of God is a σιδηρέξυλον. (2) Against the Socinians, who say that in the Old Testament only light sins committed without purpose out of a certain ignorance and error were expiated, which in Heb. 5, 2. c. 9, 7. are called ἀγνοήματα: but that grave sins could not be expiated by sacrifices. Socin. p. II. de Serv. Christ. c. 11. & 12. But ἀγνοήματα are said in Heb. 9, 7. even of graver sins, and voluntary transgressions of the law: both in the Apocryphal and Hellenistic books, 1. Esdr. 8, 77. Wisd. 14, 22. Sir. 23, 2. 3. and in the N. T. 1. Pet. 1, 14. Conf. Acts 8, 17. c. 13, 27. 1. Tim. 1, 13. 2. Pet. 2, 12. And the reason for the appellation is: because to be ignorant among the Hebrews often denotes affection, and is the same as not to care, not to attend, not to observe, to pass over. And it is known that words of knowledge among the Hebrews include affection. Just as also שָׁגַג is sometimes to neglect the word of God, Ps. 119, 67. and is mixed with חָטָא. Conf. Lev. 4, 12. 13. Num. 15, 22. Besides these, שְׁגָגָה is also said of such a sin that is a transgression or scandal to the people, Levit. 4, 2. 3. so also the cognate מְשֻׁגָּה is used of a very great sin 1. Sam. 26, 21. John 6, 24. c. 12, 16. Thus also in Heb. 9, 7. all sins are called ἀγνοήματα, because all have a certain concomitant ignorance: for they are done under the appearance of an apparent good, which the intellect apprehends. Which becomes clearer from Heb. v. 2. because the office of the High Priest is said to be to offer ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν, v. 1. which ἁμαρτίαι are explained, v. 2. τοῖς ἀγνοοῦσι καὶ πλανωμένοις. Furthermore, it is added that the sins of ignorance are not always light, but also grave, as in Lev. 4, 3. c. 5, 1. 2. 3. How also the crucifixion of Christ is called ἀγνόημα, which certainly was malicious, and done with a most deliberate will, Acts 3, 17. and c. 13, 27. That, however, an expiation was made entirely even for graver sins in the Old Testament is evident (1) from the commemoration of voluntary sins, Lev. 5, 21. or c. 6, 2. which were to be expiated. (2) From the scapegoat, to which all the sins of the whole people were imputed, to which Isaiah c. 53 alludes when he says that all sins were laid upon Christ: (3) From the example of the sons of Eli 1 Sam. 3, 14. where GOD by a singular oath prevents and prohibits the expiation of the iniquity of the house of Eli, for which oath there would certainly have been no need if great sins could not have been expiated. Furthermore, by the example of David 2 Sam. 12, verse 13, whose most grave sin of adultery and homicide was expiated. Meanwhile (1) we distinguish between greater, more notorious sins and clandestine ones. The former were to be punished by death, Levit. 18, 29; the latter were expiated, even with regard to ecclesiastical communion. And why should sins not be expiated before God? For they were either forgiven or not: if they were forgiven, then they were surely expiated; for without expiation and the shedding of blood there is no remission of sins. If, however, they were not forgiven, it must be said that all who fell into graver sins perished eternally, which God forbid. (2) Hence we also acknowledge a distinction in that part between the sacrifices of the Old Testament and the sacrifice

of Christ; There the sins of those who sought expiation were expiated: Here the sins of all were expiated by reason of merit. There, in some sacrifices, the removal followed by the very act, because they were offered by faith by particular persons: That, however, does not happen here, because it is not a special application, but a general expiation made on the cross, and a καθαρισμὸς, as some say, established as if in a designated act by way of a λύτρε accepted and to be dispensed under a certain τάξει. (3) Although, however, access to grace and the remission of sins was precluded to no one in the Old Testament, it can nevertheless be said that sacrifices were not established by law distinctly and specifically for the gravest and greatest sins, so that it might be taught that such offenses ought to be very far removed from them. In general, however, sacrifices were ordained for them, such as the annual ones.

The use of the latter observation is against the Calvinists: who profess that Christ expiated only the sins of the pious and the Elect, but not those of the whole world. Yet in this way no one will be certain that his sins have been expiated: nor will the unfaithful be able to be condemned because they do not believe that their sins have been expiated, since they ought not even to believe that, as it is false.

II. The pronoun ἡμῶν: Of our sins, by which the Apostle embraces ALL: because (1) all are in an equal state both with respect to sin and with respect to divine grace and the merit of Christ, to which he refers those things which were said before: that he expiated the sins of all. (2) An antithesis is simultaneously hinted at between the typical expiation in the Old Testament and the antitype in Christ; in the Old Testament 1) The expiation was made only of those who were in the people of God and offered sacrifices: here the expiation was made for the whole world; not of ours only, says John, but of the whole world, 1 Epist. 1, 2. 2) The Priest expiated not only the sins of the people, but also his own: Christ, however, made expiation not for his own, but for ours: Which is to be noted against the Socinians, who say that as high priest he offered for himself also, from Heb. 7, 27. But the author of this Epistle nowhere says that CHRIST was made a victim for himself, but always for others, Heb. 9, 14. chap. 10, 12. In addition to these things, he offered for those who were in need of the cleansing and expiation of sins, but he himself was alien to all sins and very far removed; he knew no sin, and thus for us he was made sin, 2 Cor.

That Heb. 7, 27. CHRIST is said to have done this once, that is applied only to the oblation and sacrifice of CHRIST, but not to the object, or those for whom the sacrifice was made.

III. The mode of the expiation of sins is expressed by δι' ἑαυτῦ, by himself: Which is missing in the Vulgate version, even though it is held consistently in the Greek Codices and Syriac and other versions, which while the Pontificians acknowledge, and yet still uphold the authority of the Vulgate version, according to the decree of the Council of Trent, they involve themselves in a contradiction, while they do not hesitate to assert both: that the version is authentic in all things, and yet that it is deficient in some places from the original text. This addition is, however, of the greatest importance, designating partly (1) that CHRIST αὐτοενεργητικῶς by his own power made expiation for sins, from which the dignity of Christ shines forth. Partly (2) that αὐτοπροσώπως in his own person he made expiation, from which the charity of Christ becomes conspicuous, [whereas] the priests in the Old Testament neither expiated sins by their own power, but only τυπικῶς: nor in their own person, but by offering sacrifices, or not with their own blood, but with the blood of sacrifices.

CHRIST, however, made expiation both by himself through his own divine power and by the shedding of his own blood. Our Epistle deduces both arguments more fully, both that Christ as true GOD, or not merely a naked man, but the God-man, made expiation for sins BY HIMSELF, and that CHRIST accomplished this with his own blood, unlike the priests in the Old Testament. From the former he derives the price of this redemption and its dignity: from the latter he builds up and confirms the magnitude of Christ's love and divine mercy. The use is against the Socinians. (1) He who makes expiation by himself is true GOD, Isa. 44, 24. (2) If he made expiation by himself: he not only obtained it from GOD, but held it in his own hands.

It is asked, however, to which nature in CHRIST the Apostle looks when he says δι᾽ ἀυτõ? Resp. This work, to make expiation for sins, pertains to both Natures, like all the works of the office according to the Rule of the Council of Chalcedon. For it is not the work of the human nature alone to expiate the sins of the whole world, and indeed by itself, both because in the Scriptures this is claimed for God alone, and because it is a work of infinite power, which does not fall to a mere man. Therefore God had to shed his blood, Acts 20, verse 28. Again, this cannot be attributed to the divinity alone, because the expiation was made through the death of our Redeemer. But the Deity is not subject to death and any passion: But is entirely immutable. And therefore, as the Deity of the Word, the Son of God, was clothed in flesh, and the flesh was received into the fellowship and κοινωνίαν of the Deity, so the κοινωνία of both is seen in the expiation of sins made through Christ. For which reason, in the very treatment of both natures and their mutual κοινωνίᾳ, the Apostle wished to discourse before he undertook the explanation of this theme.

Let the diversity between Christ the High Priest and the priest of the Old Testament be noted here. (1) There, there were many priests, many sacrifices: here, one unique priest, one unique sacrifice performed once, Heb. 9:25. They were themselves liable to sin and had to offer for themselves; he, immune from sin, offers only for us, Lev. 16:17; Heb. 5:3; John 8:56; Isa. 53:29; 1 Pet. 2:22; Heb. 7:25. They were mere men; he is also true God by nature: they were priests, not kings; he is at once priest and King of the Church: they were particular priests, for a certain time, for a certain people, for certain sins, namely those for which expiation was sought; he is universal, perpetual, for all men and all the sins of all men: they offered only, they were not offered; he offers himself, Heb. 8:27. They entered the tabernacle as slaughterers; he as the slaughtered, Heb. 9:26. They entered with the blood of others and of brute animals; he with his own, Heb. 9:14. They entered with aromatic spices, burning with fire and passing into smoke, Lev. 16:12; he entered with the aroma of burning love toward the human race: they entered a tabernacle made by hands; he, a heavenly and eternal one, Heb. 9:11, that he might sit at the right hand of the Majesty: they, having gone out, completed the sacrifice, which was consumed by heavenly fire; he, before he entered, completed it by suffering, as the fire of divine wrath consumed this sacrifice: they expiated at least typically; he, truly and properly. Socinus, part II, de Serv. Christ., chapter 20, says that the expiation of sins is ascribed to Christ here in two ways: (1) Insofar as we see in Christ the will of God toward us expressed, and have it declared that our sins have been remitted; which he wishes to be signified when Christ is called the brightness of glory and the express image of the substance of God. (2) Insofar as he moderates and rules all things by his powerful command, and thus our sins are truly expiated, and we dwell together with Christ in the heavens, and no punishment for our sins remains. But this gloss has not come into the mind of any of the interpreters of this Epistle, neither ancient nor modern, which Socinus himself confesses, and says he cannot wonder enough. We, however, do not wonder at it at all, since in neither respect is that καθαρισμὸς (purification) of our sins ascribed to CHRIST, either here or elsewhere. As to the former, it was shown previously that Christ is not called the brightness of the glory of God and the character of the substance of God because we see the will of GOD from him, but because he exhibits in himself the substance and Majesty of the Father as the ὁμοούσιος (consubstantial) and ἰσότιμος (equal in honor) Son. But much less is he called the brightness and character by reason of the expiation of sins. For where is such a thing in the scriptures? And who would gather this from those words? Indeed, the expiation was made by the death and oblation of Christ, not by the expression of the glory and hypostasis of God. Moreover, the gracious announcement of the will of God and the expiation of sins are most distinct. The former pertains to the prophetic office of Christ, the latter to the priestly. CHRIST performed the former not only immediately, but also through the Apostles and the words of the Doctors, which it is also established was done by the Prophets beforehand. But the latter Christ performed not through others, but by himself. Whence he alone is called the expiator of sins: the Prophets and Apostles are by no means called so. Furthermore, the expiation of sins was made not by the announcement of the divine will, but by the death of Christ: Nor was the death of Christ merely a confirmation of the proclamation, or a μαρτύριον (testimony), but a reconciliation of God, a redemption from the curse of the law, and a propitiation and λύτρον (ransom) and ἀντίλυτρον (substitute ransom) paid for us, Rom. 5:10, Gal. 3:13, Rom. 3:24, Matt. 20:28, 1 Tim. 2:6, which respects also touch upon this effect, or the expiation of sins, more than the way in which the will of God is said to be declared only by his death. To these things, scripture nowhere teaches that CHRIST performed the purification of sins by the very fact that we have in him an example of divine grace, by which he was raised to eternal glory, nor does that grace by which sins are expiated and remitted shine forth in this example of Christ raised to the kingdom of God, as we warned before. But it is truly most absurd that the expiation of our sins consists in the fact that we see fulfilled in Christ what God has promised to us, or that Christ is raised to eternal salvation, which GOD willed to be promised to us through CHRIST. Finally, who will admit that expiation is made when we gaze upon the brightness of divine glory and the express image in CHRIST? But these glosses have already been refuted before.

As to the other respect, that Christ made the expiation of sins by bearing all things by the word of his power: that is a mere Socinian fiction. For the preservation and government of the universe is one thing, the expiation of our sins is another; the former is common to Christ with the Father and the Holy Spirit. But Christ performed the expiation by himself, not the Father, nor the Holy Spirit. The former concerns the sustenance of nature, the latter the abolition of sin. The former looks to the article of creation and providence, the latter to the article of Redemption. The former is universal to all creatures: the latter pertains only to the human race. Christ is indeed the foundation of the expiation of sins, by which he made the same by himself, because he is the Lord of the universe bearing all things by the word of his power, but it does not express the formal reason and the manner in which the expiation was made. For neither does Holy scripture teach this anywhere, and we are informed about it in a far different way, namely that he expiated sins not by bearing all things by the word of his power, but by offering himself for us: that he redeemed us from sins not by sustaining the universe, but by bearing the sin of the world, Isa. 53:6, 14, John 1:29, Heb. 9:26. And therefore the propitiation, Redemption, and purification of our sins are not ascribed to the glory and Majesty of Christ, by which he bears all things; but to the cross and blood of Christ, 2 Cor. 5:11, last verse. Therefore, that Christ, dwelling in the heavens, has all things in his hand, that itself is not the expiation of our sins. For that we also dwell with Christ in the heavens, regarding the aid of the heavenly kingdom, that is a consequence of the expiation of sins, not its antecedent or formal reason. But enough has been said before about those Socinian fictions. We do not wish to do what has been done.

He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high) The discourse ascends. He preferred Christ to the Patriarchs, Moses, and the Prophets. Now, wishing also to prefer him to the Angels, through whom God had spoken to the Patriarchs, Moses, and the Prophets, he shows that he is inferior only to God the Father. The place on the right is that of one who is next to the King. See Matt. 20:21 and what is said there. The expression ἐν δεξιᾷ (at the right hand) exists also in Romans 8:34, Ephesians 1:20, Colossians 3:1, below ch. 8:1, ch. 10:12, ch. 12:2, 1 Peter 3:22, Genesis 48:13, Judges 16:30. Θρόνου μεγαλωσύνης (throne of majesty) or δόξης (glory) to the Hebrews, כסא כבוד, signifies the supreme Majesty of God himself, Apocalypse 4:2 and following, ch. 19:4, ch. 21:5, to whom the Lamb is next, that is, Christ, v. 6, 13, ch. 7:10, 17, ch. 22:1, 3. But he well adds ἐν ὑψηλοῖς (in the highest), במרומים, that is, in the highest heaven, or above the visible parts of heaven, as below ch. 7:26. See also what is said in Eph. 1:3, 20, because David also was established by God in a certain eminent place, Ps. 89:28, but only on earth.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Ὃς ὢν ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης) Repercussus divinæ Maje- statis, qualis est Solis in nube, qui dicitur παρήλιος. צמח hic Syro, id est germen, non male. Sic locum Esaiæ IV. ubi eadem vox, Jonathan de Messia accipit: Sic sapientia dicitur ἀπαύγασμα φωτὸς ἀϊδίου Sap. VII. vers. 6. Clemens Romanus, qui totum prope hunc locum descripsit, pro ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης posuit ἀπαύγασμα τῆς μεγαλωσύνης αὐτοῦ. Sunt qui alludi putant ad Irin, argumento ducto de loco Ezech. I. vers. 28. & Zach. II. vers. 8. ubi dicta vide. Etiam Rabbi Salomo Bariochai Irin ad Messiam refert: quæ forte & respicit Apocalypsis IV. 3. Δόξα כבוד aut גבורות Ma- jeftas divina. Ea cum per se conspici nequeat, cernitur in Christo, sicut Sol, quem directe oculi nostri tueri nequeunt, cernitur in aqua, speculo, nube, 2. Cor. IV. vers. 4. Col. I. 15. adde & I. vers. 13. Lucianus Martyr. ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ, οὐσίας καὶ βουλῆς, καὶ δυνάμεως, καὶ δόξης Θεοῦ ἀπα- ράλλακτος εἰκών. Καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ) Alia comparatio a sigillo annuli, cujus forma ceræ imprimitur, cicatrix dicitur χαρακτὴρ κατὰ καύματα Levit. XIII. vers. 28. ציר verti- tur χαρακτὴρ ab Aquila Psalm. XLIX. vers. 15. Id vero nuncium sive legatum significat, ut Prov. XIII. v. 18. XXV. v. 31. Jer. XLIX. vers. 13. quia legatus mittentis personam refert. χαρακτὴρ in Glossis figura, luminamentum, sed le- gendum est lineamentum. Ὑπόστασις hic non ita sumitur, quomodo Platonici & post Origenem ex Platonicis Chri- stiani sumpsere: sed continuatur cœpta comparatio. So- lent Græci distinguere τὰ κατ’ ἔμφασιν, & τὰ κατ’ ὑπόστα- σιν, ut Scriptor de Mundo. Sic Philo in ejusdem tituli libro: αὐγὴ δὲ κατ’ ἑαυτὴν ὑπόστασιν ὄυκ ἔχει, non quod nullam habeat ὑπάρξιν, sed quod principalitas & origo ejus sit in Sole. Sic in annulo figura est κατ ὑπόστασιν, in cera κατ’ ἔμ- φασιν. Ita potentia, justitia, veritas in DEO Christi Patre sunt primario: in Christo vero secundario, sed ita ut nobis in Christo ea evidenter appareant, Joh. XV. 9. Erat super Arcam quoddam ἀπαύγασμα: & aliquid tale videre Mo- ses, Esaias, Ezechiel. At quanto clarior effulgentia in Christo, ita ut præ hoc ista evanescant? Syrus ὑπόστασιως vertit דְאִיתוּתֵה : quomodo naturam Patris impressam fi- lio dixere Basilius & Hilarius. Latinus hic figura substan- tiæ ejus. Talia commode interpretanda, non maligne ca- villanda sunt.

Φέρων τε τὰ πάντα τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὑτοῦ) αὑτοῦ habent & Manuscripti, in quibus spiritus isti Grammatica- les distinguuntur, & ita legit Cyrillus VIII. contra Julianum: sensus est: Christus verbo potentiæ paternæ (id est, jussu) regit cuncta. φέρειν sæpe est regere: &, quod hic addit Chry- sostomus, cum quadam facilitate. Sic usurpatur & Ebræis נשא Num. XI. 14. Deut. I. 9. unde נשיא princeps. ῥῆ- μα pro jussu poni apparet, Luc. V. 5. & infra XI. 3. Sic & 1. Reg. I. v. 27. Seneca de DEO: Vertit omnia. Epistola 31. Vide ea, quæ Actor. XV. 29.

Composita hæc omnia à Grotio esse ad incru- standum Arianismum, vel Socinismum, cæcus sit, qui non videat. Lumen Dei repercussum tantum divinæ majestatis esse vult, qualis est Solis in nube, qui dicitur παρήλιος, vel Iridis, aut Solis in aqua vel speculo, & referre tantum personam Patris, ut legatus refert personam mittentis, potentiam, ju- stitiam, veritatem in Filio DEI tantum secun- dario esse: Filium non verbo potentiæ suæ, sed verbo potentiæ paternæ, id est, jussu Patris cun- cta ferre, id est regere; Nomen ὑποςάσεως, quo utitur Ecclesia in mysterio Trinitatis, non ex hoc loco, sed è Platonis Schola manasse, hic longe aliter accipi. Hæc ad elogia divinitatis & ὁμουσίας Filii DEI cum Patre illustrissima Grotius: Quæ vix ab exquisitissimis Sophistis, & tortoribus S. lite- rarum Socinianis exquisitius depravari potuissent. Nos in iis exponendis & vindicandis repetemus, quæ quondam in prælectionibus publicis Regio- monti proposuimus. Sic autem ibi tela cœpta per- texta fuit:

Officium Christi proponit Apostolus ἐν προθέ- σει verf. 3. & 4. sed ita, ut primum fundamenti loco substernat naturam ejus divinam, tum vero partes officii ipsius definiat, quarum explica- tionem suscepit. Bifariam itaque describit Apo- stolus naturam Christi divinam, cum respectu Patris, & à priori, tum respectu hujus universi- tatis, & à posteriori. Illic splendorem gloriæ, & imaginem substantiæ Ejus indigitans; Hic Re- ctoratum, sive Gubernationem universi Christo adscribens, utroque fundamentum jaciens ex- piationis peccatorum, ut & occupationis dominii per sessionem ad dextram DEI, quemadmodum nunc uberius exponemus.

Respiciendum proinde (1) ad orationis cohæ- rentiam, ὃς ὢν ἀπαύγασμα &c. qui cum sit splen- dor: Quibus verbis connectitur 1. oratio cum præcedentibus, voce ὃς qui, dum Apo- stolus adhuc persistit in descriptione Filii per quem locutus est DEUS novissime, quem hære- dem constituit omnium, per quem & sæcula con- didit; & uti postremo loco eminentiorem in ipso notarat, & descripserat naturam, seculo- rum conditricem, ita cohærent aptissime, quæ nunc explicandæ uberius huic Naturæ subjungit: utpote quibus non declaratur faltim, quod per Filium ceu splendorem gloriæ suæ, & imaginem sibi coëffentialem omnis condiderit, qui etiam verbo suo potenti conservat & sustentat omnia: sed accessus quoque paratur ad propositionem de munere sacerdotali Christi. Nec incommode observat hic Constantinus Presbyter Antioche- nus gradationem: Quod dixit, hæredem posuit, humilitatis est judicium. Dein ad supremum gradum altioremque transcendens, per quem, in- quit, & secula effecit; postea ad excelsiorem omni- bus venit, post quem altiorem gradum alterum invenire non possis: Qui cum sit, inquit, splen- dor gloriæ & character substantiæ ejus. 2. Indi- catur quoque, non præmitti hanc eminentissi- mam personæ Filii DEI descriptionem, nisi ob ea, quæ de officio Christi sacerdotali dicenda erant, iisque exhiberi & contineri fundamen- tum officii istius Christi: quod particula ὢν in- sinuat: Quum sit splendor gloriæ, & character hypostaseos ejus, omniaque portat verbo virtutis suæ, fecit per seipsum purificationem peccatorum, & consedit ad dextram Majestatis, &c. Nam τὸ ὢν immanentiam causæ significat, quum sit; nec in præterito verti debet, quum esset, licet ver- bum sequens ἐκάθησεν præteriti temporis sit. Qui enim verbum sequens potest antecedens parti- cipium in priori inciso efficere præteriti tempo- ris? Lubrico ergo fundamento nititur Schlich- tingius: cum hinc infert describi Christi præstan- tiam, qualem habuit in terris agens: quia in præte- rito dicatur, cum esset. Vero autem similius est Apostolum participiis præsentis temporis uti voluisse: ὃς ὢν & φέρων, quia non descripsit ali- quod præteritum, vel transiens, sed quod per- manet, & in præsenti semper idem est, ut solet præsentis temporis notione actus continuus, & permanens quid designari. Non tantum fuit ante purificationem peccatorum & sessionem ad dextram DEI splendor gloriæ Patris, & cha- racter personæ ejus, ut & Rector & Conser- vator universi, sed idem est, manetque perpe- tuo: quomodo Christus perpetuum essendi actum voce εἰμὶ expressit, Johan. VIII. vers. 58. & D. Johannes voce ὁ ὢν DEI perpetuam exi- stentiam designat, Apoc. I. vers. 4. & S. Apo- stolus mox infra cap. I. vers. 12. è Psalm. CII. vers. 26. immutabilitatem DEI ita exprimit σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ, unde & Plato in Sophista ac Par- menide DEUM τὸ ὢν appellitat. Præsentia enim proprie tantum sunt, præterita transie- runt, non amplius sunt, futura nondum sunt, sed erunt demum, id solum esse dicitur, quod perpetuo est.

Respiciendum (2) ad præsentium verborum sententiam: quam dixi descriptionem naturæ di- vinæ Christi. 1. Respectu Patris & à priori, quod sit splendor gloriæ, & character hypostaseos Ejus, scil. DEI Patris, qui per ipsum locutus, ipsum hæredem constituit, imo & per ipsum olim fecit secula. Exprimitur quippe his verbis par- tim distinctio Filii à Patre, quod à Patre sit tan- quam effulgescentia quædam gloriæ ejus, & tan- quam imago expressa ab eodem, ut dicunt hæc nomina originem, vel relationem quandam possessionis, & originis: partim communio na- turæ ipsius Patris, seu essentiæ unitas, qua & gloriam & Essentiam Patris sui (in DEO enim idem est gloria, & essentia ejus) participat, ex- primit, ac repræsentat perfectissime. Eleganter hæc è Chrysostomo explicat Constantinus: per splendorem, propinquitatem declaravit essentiæ. In- tellige ergo subtilitatem dictorum: Unam sum- sit essentiam, unamque substantiam, ut duas sub- sistentias aperiret. Unde etiam subjungit: Qui character est : Character quippe alter est ab ipso suo exemplari, alter autem non in omnibus, sed se- cundum quod per seipsum subsistit. Nam & hic character similitudinis omnimoda præbet indicium, ad illud, cujus est character, & suspicionem vel parvæ dissimilitudinis omnino non recipit. Sed in- dagemus verborum singulorum emphasin pro- priam, & in aprico erit genuina Apostolicæ propositionis, quoad hanc partem, sententia. Geminam adhibet περίφρασιν metaphoricam quidem, sed huic mysterio maxime sublimi illu- strando apprime convenientem. Primum ἀπαύ- γασμα τῆς δόξης vocat : Quod nomen uti ma- gnificentissimum est, ita variis explicationibus obnoxium.

I. Enjedinus Photin. constructionem invertit: Filium dicit appellari splendorem gloriæ per E- braïsmum, id est, gloriosum, sicut filium perdi- tionis, id est, perditum : & characterem ὑποστά- σεως Ejus, non DEI, sed splendoris, ut ostendatur ipsissima substantia splendoris, seu totum id, quod splendor dici, concipi, & esse potest inesse CHRI- STO, ita ut nihil cogitari & fingi possit splen- didius ipso CHRISTO, ut si dicamus Aristotelem animam fuisse Philosophiæ quadam hyperbole. Quo- circa splendorem gloriæ absolute dictum hoc sensu, non autem splendorem gloriæ Patris respective in- fert, eamque literalem minime detortam, & vo- cibus ipsis implexam sententiam jactitat. Verum detorsionem hanc refellunt omnes Græci pariter & Latini Interpretes, qui unanimi consensu splendorem gloriæ DEI, & characterem hy- postaseos Ejus, DEI scil. dictum profitentur, ut relativum αὐτõ & ad splendorem gloriæ, & ad characterem ὑποστάσεως referatur, spectetque nomen antecedens tῦ Θεῦ, quo cum Filium confert Apostolus, quem locutum in Filio, hæredem constituisse Filium, per Filium secu- la condidisse prònunciat. 2. Adhæc splendor relate dicitur, & est alicujus splendor. Si ergo per Ebraïsmum splendor gloriæ, sive gloriosif- fimus diceretur, DEI tamen splendor intelli- gendus esset gloriosissimus, adeoque Filius Pa- tris splendor gloriosissimus designaretur. Nul- lius enim splendor est Filius nisi DEI Patris. Quocirca gloriosissimus erit Filius, ut Pater, unde quoque non minus dicitur Filius DEI Dominus gloriæ, quam Pater 1. Corinth. cap. II. vers. 8. id est gloriosissimus, & cum videret E- saias gloriam & Majestatem DEI eminentissi- mam, cap. VI. eandem gloriam & Majestatem eminentissimam Filii DEI fuisse testis est Jo- hannes cap. XII. vers. 41. 3. Quod autem non nisi hyperbolice id eo sensu admittendum, pror- sus negamus : Quum certo certius sit, absque ullo hyperbolico dicendi genere, nihil concipi, dici, cogitari posse splendidius, gloriosius, emi- nentius ipso Filio DEI. Conf. Exod. XVI. vers. 7. & 1. Cor. X. 9.

II. Socinus lib. de Servat. Christ. pag. 175. Chri- stum esse splendorem gloriæ DEI, admittit, sed hoc sensu, quod per CHRISTUM nobis glo- ria, Deusque ipse insigniter admodum apparue- rit. Cui affinis est Bezæ interpretatio: ἀπαύγα- σμα τῆς δόξης, id est, is, in quo resplendet gloria illa, ac Majestas Patris, alioqui infiniti, & inconspi- cui, sive is, in quo uno splendorem suum conspi- ciendum præbet Pater, qui propterea Coloss. I. v. 15. dicitur imago DEI inconspicui, ut & 2. Cor. IV. vers. 4. idque in Evangelio. In quam sententiam adfert etiam Beza Tertullianum advers. Praxeam, qui Vicarium, inquit, se Patris CHRISTUS ostendit, per quem & Pater videretur in factis, & audiretur in verbis, & cognosceretur in Filio fa- cta & verba Patris administrante. Idque porro illustrat his verbis: Filius idcirco homo factus, ne nuda DEI speculatione absorberemur, nobis est speculi instar, in quo non ex aliqua radiorum reflexione appareat inane abjecta rei simulacrum, sed in cujus intimo & substantiali splendore, quem nos ex ipsius effectis in visibili illa carne percipimus, Pater ipse nobis suam illam infinitatem & omni- potentem majestatem, immensam illam, & in- comprehensam Φιλανθρωπίαν contemplandam, & spectandam, atque adeo palpandam præbet. Sed, quanquam hæc vere dicantur, non tamen suf- ficiunt ad exprimendam Emphaticam Filii DEI descriptionem, nec primario hic intenduntur ab Apostolo, qui ut verbis præcedentibus di- vinam Filii DEI naturam, ceu conditricem mundi designarat, ita hic eandem describit; eamque baseos & fundamenti loco substernit officio CHRISTI eminentissimo. Tertullia- num etiam verbis adductis voluisse hoc Epithe- ton Filii DEI explicatum non apparet. Qui potius hac similitudine splendoris mysterium ὁμουσίας Filii DEI cum Patre, & æternæ ge- nerationis à Patre illustrat, cap. IIX. contra Praxeam pagin. 497. At, inquit Beza, nulla in- carnationis mentione facta subjicit Apostolus, quæ non nisi incarnato conveniunt. Loquitur igitur de Filio carne induto. Quis vero hoc neget, quod de Filio carne induto disseratur? Non id probandum erat Bezæ, sed hoc potius: quod Filio ratione humanæ naturæ præsens Epithe- ton unice conveniat, vel quod non conveniat λόγῳ in Deitate sua essentiali. Si hoc inferre velit, ergo nec antecedens Filii attriburum, quod per Eum mundus sit conditus, Filio con- veniet in sua essentiali Deitate. Adhæc si nul- lam mentionem fecit incarnationis, potius con- cludendum de Filio DEI hæc dici, extra re- spectum incarnationis, quoad essentialem Ejus Deitatem: uti cætera, quæ subjiciuntur, quod purgationem fecerit peccatorum per semetipsum, quod sederit ad dextram Majestatis in excelsis, magis ad humanam Christi naturam spectant; quemadmodum in glossa Flacius advertit; prio- ra tria hoc in versu attributa proprie ad divini- tatem pertinere, quod sit splendor gloriæ, aut lumen de lumine, quod sit character, aut ex- pressissima imago substantiæ ejus, quodque ver- bo ac omnipotentia sua omnia regat, & conser- vet; duo autem posteriora, nempe expiationem omnium peccatorum per suum propitiatorium sa- crificium & gloriosam ascensionem convenire quidem toti personæ, sed magis tamen ratione humanitatis. Imago vero inconspicui DEI vo- catur pariter CHRISTUS Coloss. I. vers. 16. & 2. Corinth. IV. vers. 4. non ratione humanæ præcipue naturæ, sed ratione divinæ, qua Pa- tris est substantialis imago ei ὁμούσιος. Filius est imago totum in se Patrem ostendens, splendet enim in Filio æterna DEI Patris Deitas, potentia, Sapientia & Majestas, ait Basilius serm. de Tri- nit. eaque parte suavis est ὁμόνοια Patrum or- thodoxorum, quod respectu divinæ naturæ imago Patris sit & dicatur. Quod Apostolus innuit diserte, cum conjungit ei appellationi alteram, quod nempe sit εἰκὼν τῶ Θεῶ τῶ ἀο- ράτω, qua est πρωτότοκος πάσης κτήσεως, id est, ante res ullas genitus, ut explicat ipse Beza, probatque in Notis ad istum locum, qua per eum condita sunt omnia, quæ in cœlis sunt, & quæ in terra, quod immediate subjungitur; Ea autem non conveniunt CHRISTO ratio- ne humanæ naturæ. Quid ergo est, quod τὸ esse imaginem invisibilis DEI adversus Veterum unanimem consensum, ipsiusque textus συνέχειαν trahat Beza ad humanam naturam CHRISTI? Nimirum aliud nihil adferre novit, præterquam Calvini sui Arianizantis autoritatem, quam Vete- rum interpretationi solidæ & constanti præferre non dubitat. Veteres, inquit, subtilius hoc refe- runt ad mutuam Patris & Filii relationem, quo re- fertur illud Christi dictum Johan. XII. v. 45. & XIV. vers. 9. Sed mihi videtur simplicior & accommoda- tior doctissimi interpretis sententia. Scilicet ille est αὐτὸς ἔφα, tota Antiquitate doctior, imo do- ctissimus κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν Scripturæ interpres, quem qui sequitur, errare non potest. Tandem fal- sum est, nullam fieri mentionem Filii carne induti. Annon enim Filius carne indutus fuit, cum no- vissimis temporibus per eum locutus est DEUS, quemque hæredem constituit rerum omnium. Licet ergo aperta incarnationis mentio non fiat, de Filio tamen, qua incarnatus erat, ista dicta es- se haud negabit Beza.

III. Calvinus magis adhuc jejunus est in ex- plicanda hac descriptione, quasi respectu manife- stationis tantum per Filium factæ, splendor dica- tur Filius gloriæ Patris. Quam refellit in Socino discipulus Calvini David Pareus, licet aliquid amplius dixerit Socinus ut ante relatum. Eum ergo Præceptori opponamus: Verum, inquit, hoc, sed nec totum, nec satis est. Jam ante enim dixerat Apostolus, DEUM nobis per Filium locu- tum esse, nempe non πολυμερῶς, καὶ πολυτρόπως, ut olim per Prophetas, sed apertissime, clarissime, quod ad officium ejus propheticum pertinebat. Hic vero personam Filii tanquam causam & basin officii ejus designare voluit. Adde quod eadem ratio- ne Apostolis quoque, cumprimis autem Paulo hujus Epistolæ Auctori conveniret hæc descri- ptio, ratione manifestationis gloriæ DEI per præconium ipsius factæ, quomodo asserit per se- se factum esse Φωτισμὸν τῆς γνώσεως τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ, 2. Corinth. IV. vers. 6. Ecquis vero di- cet Apostolum ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χα- ρακτῆρα τῆς ὑποστάσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ? Num etiam Apostolus purificationem peccatorum per se- metipsum potuit facere, cujus fundamentum hic substernitur τὸ εἶναι ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ. Apage ejusmodi obscurationes illustrissi- morum Nominum æterni Filii Dei! Distinguit potius Apostolus, 2. Cor. IV. vers. 4. apertissime τὸ αὐγάσαι τὸ Φωτισμὸ τοῦ ἐυαγγελίε τῆς δόξης τοῦ χριστοῦ, & Christum, qui est εἰκὼν τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης ἀυτοῦ: Illudque sibi quo- que adscribit, hoc autem absit, ut sibi arrogatum velit, quod maxime proprium est Christi, Domi- ni gloriæ, quem vocat, 1. Cor. II. 8.

IV. Magis autem ad veritatem accedit Schlich- tingii Photiniani sententia. Qui in Comment. super hunc loc. pag. 25. istam Calvini & aliorum glossam, appellationem hanc Christo ideo tribu- tam esse, quod divinam voluntatem, quam nemo videre potuerit, ipse nobis enarraverit, minus suf- ficientem agnoscit, censetque latius extenden- dam eam descriptionem, referendam ad univer- sam similitudinem, quam Christus in terris vivens habuit cum DEO, & qua DEUM nobis retu- lit & repræsentavit, ita ut hoc idem sit cum eo, quod de Christo scripsit Paulus, eum fuisse in forma

Dei, & Deo æqualem. Ea erat sapientia, ut DEI arcana nosset, & Dei nomine oracula ederet, ac re- sponsa daret, ut hominum cogitationes & corda co- gnita haberet; ea sanctitate, ut esset sine omni ma- cula; ea potentia, ut omnibus in terris rebus, etiam dæmonibus, ut Deus, imperaret. Hinc merito Jo- hannes, Vidimus, inquit, gloriam Ejus, gloriam quasi unigeniti à Patre. Hæc Schlichtingius. Quæ satis quidem orthodoxe, & magnifice de Chri- sto dicta apparent, sed quia Christum natura ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον credit, prorsus falsa sunt, & Scri- pturæ perpetuæ analogiæ refragantur. Illa enim καρδιογνωσία, sive cordium inspectio, quî puro homini conveniret, quum eandem sibi soli Deus vendicet, Jer. XI. vers. 20. cap. XVII. vers. 10. cap. XX. vers. 12. Psal. VII. vers. 10. 1. Reg. IIX. vers. 39. Ea potentia, qua αὐτοκρατορικῶς omni- bus rebus ut DEUS imperabat, quid nisi sum- mum illum DEUM fuisse arguit, quia ὁμοίως ut DEUS operabatur omnia, Johan. V. vers. 17. & quis præter illum unum & summum DEUM ut DEUS imperaret omnibus, cum Deus gloriam suam nemini extra sese velit tributam,& ab hac sua potentia & potestate super omnia ut summus DEUS agnosci velit? Es. XLII. vers. 8. Id de- nique quod æqualis DEO Patri est, quod Filius DEI μονογενὴς supremum esse DEUM, ejusdem cum Patre naturæ & essentiæ manifeste compro- bat. Proinde contradictorie hæc abripiuntur ad Christum ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον.

Syrus Interpres vocem ἀπαύγασμα reddit צמחא id est germen; Quem non satis vim Græcæ vocis expressisse ait Cornelius à Lapide: ἀπαύγα- σμα enim proprie esse idem quod Ebræum זהר clari- tas, splendor, fulgor, refulgentia. Verum vox Syriaca notat etiam ortum vel exitum lucis, & splendorem exorientis Solis, ut recte Junius ad hunc loc. advertit. Et assignari solet Filio DEI no- men צמח in S. literis, ut videre est Zach. II. v. 8. cap. VI. vers. 12. ubi צמח indigitatur: quem etiam Jerem. cap. XXIII. vers. 5. צמח צדיק germen ju- stum & cap. XXXIII. vers. 15. צמח צדקה germen justitiæ vocat, quibus locis Messiam respici para- phrases Chaldaicæ docent. LXX. autem Interpp. vocem צמח interpretantur ἀνατολὴ, quod genera- liter quidem ortum cujusque rei significat, & de terra nascentibus usurpatur Gen. II. vers. 5. III. 10. specialiter autem & proprie exortum Solis notat, eoque sensu vocavit Zacharias Christum ἀνατο- λὴν ἐξ ὕψες, orientem ex alto, illuminantem eos, qui in tenebris sedent, & in umbra mortis, Luc. I. vers. 78. qui est Sol ille justitiæ, Mal. IV. vers. 2. Hoc itaque sensu conferri posset præsens appel- latio Filii DEI, qua Syrus Paraphrastes eum vocat צמחא דשובחה, splendorem gloriæ ejus, vel DEI, cum Es. IV. vers. 2. ubi dicitur צמח יהוה Splen- dor vel Germen Jehovah, sive DEI, ut exprima- tur æterna ejus à Patre origo & generatio; quam- vis hîc etiam reddi possit per appositionem צמח יהוה Germen vel splendor, qui Jehovah est. Ita enim Filius est DEI Christus, ut ipse sit DEUS: ita splendor est DEI gloriosi, ut ipse sit Dominus gloriosissimus. Plerique interpretes Christum splendorem gloriæ Patris, vel refulgescentiam dici volunt respectu æternæ generationis à Patre; quan- quam nonnulli conjungant etiam respectum ma- nifestationis æternæ.

Est autem gemina hîc quoque interpretatio posterioris vocis τῆς δόξης notanda. Prima est: qua pro Majestate, & gloria DEI accipitur: quæ uti in Deo non est distincta ab ejusdem Essentia, ita hic Majestaticam, gloriosissimamque Deitatem Patris notat; Quod Filius sit splendor, sive re- fulgentia essentiæ divinæ gloriosissimæ. Frivo- lum enim est, quod hîc objicit Enjedinus; Si Filius splendor gloriæ DEI dicatur, fore eundem accidentis accidens, quum & splendor accidens sit & gloria DEI; Quod utrumque non nisi in- eptissime dicitur: splendor DEI quippe est hy- postaticus & substantialis, ut imago DEI vers. sequ. & 2. Corinth. IV. vers. 4. Coloss. I. vers. 15. splendor ille est ipse Sol justitiæ, Mal. IV. vers. 2. Oriens ex alto, Luc. I. vers. 78. Stella ex Jacob. Num. XXIV. vers. 17. Stella matutina splendi- dissima, Apoc. XXII. vers. 16. Gloria DEI non minus quoque substantialis est, quum in Deum non cadat accidens. Licet vero voces illæ acci- dentia notent in creaturis, adhibentur tamen ad explicandam DEI Essentiam in Scriptura S. quia non potest mens nostra infinitam DEI naturam cogitando assequi, nisi per analogica ejusmodi nomina & Similitudines à creatis rebus petitas, quas tamen θεοπρεπῶς explicare debemus, ne quicquam imperfectionis in Deo locemus. Itaque gloria DEI idem est, quod essentia DEI Maje- statica & gloriosa. Solet namque accipi gloria DEI vel οὐσιωδῶς & absolute: ut Eminentiam & Majestatem DEI notet; vel σχετικῶς & respecti- ve, ut agnitionem & celebrationem Majestatis DEI designet; Hæc proprie dicitur glorificatio, Psal. XXIX. vers. 6. Luc. II. vers. 14. cap. XIX. vers. 38. cum DEO gloria datur à creaturis, hominibus, vel Angelis. Illa vero est gloria DEI essentialis, ideoque à parte rei ipsa es- sentia DEI, Actor. VII. vers. 2. Romanor. I. vers. 23. Accipi etiam potest eodem sensu glo- ria DEI pro DEO ipso, ut abstractum pro concreto, vel adjunctum pro subjecto: Sic E- saias vidit gloriam Domini, Johan. XII. vers. 41. cum Dominum DEUM Zebaoth vidit, Esa. VI. vers. 1. vel Deum τῆς δόξης sive gloriæ, ut voca- tur Actor. VII. vers. 2. Altera τῆς δόξης interpre- tatio quoad rem ipsam, & materialiter, coincidit cum priori, formaliter tamen & ratione modi loquendi diversa est: Quod δόξα sit lux copiosa, & quasi fons luminis in substantia lucida, ut Beat. Gerhardus part. III. Harm. continuat. cap. CLXXVII. pagin. 403. accipit. Quæ expli- catio firmari videtur partim (1) è voce præce- danea ἀπαύγασμα, Splendor enim lucis est: par- tim (2) è significatione vocis δόξα alibi in Scri- pturis adhibita, utpote Luc. II. vers. 9. δόξα κυρίου περιέλαμψεν, gloria Domini circumfulgens pasto- res Bethlehemiticos, quæ lux splendidissima, 1 Cor. XV. vers. 41. ἄλλη δόξα ἡλίου, alia gloria Solis, alia gloria Lunæ, alia gloria astrorum: Stel- la enim præ stella differt gloria, hoc est splendore; partim (3) è similibus Filii DEI nominibus, quia ut hic splendor lucis dicitur, ita alibi lux magna Es. IX. vers. 1. & Johan. I. vers. 5. lux vera c. VIII. vers. 9. lux mundi cap. VIII. vers. 12. IX. 5. XII. 35. & Es. LX. vers. 1. lux, quæ gloria Domini est, vocatur, ut & φῶς καὶ δόξα, quæ voces pariter alternare vi- dentur Luc. XI. 32. ut apud Esaiam כבוד & אור l. c. Oriens ex alto Luc. I. vers. 78. Stella matutina, Apoc. XXIV. v. 17. Sol justitiæ, Mal. IV. 2. partim (4) è loco parallelo Sap. VII. 26. quem hic re- spexisse, vel quod Cornel. à Lapide vult, citasse videtur Apostolus. Ut enim ibidem dicitur Sa- pientia hypostatica Filii DEI ἀπαύγασμα Φωτὸς ἀϊδίου, ita hic ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης Θεῦ: ut illic porro nuncupatur ἔσοπτρον ἀκηλίδωτον τῆς τῦ Θεῦ ἐνεργείας, καὶ εἰκὼν τ' ἀγαθότητος, ita hic χαρακτὴρ

τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ, ut ita utrumque Epitheton respondeat sibi mutuo, facta utriusque loci col-latione. Quod ergo liber Sapientiæ Φωτὸς ἀϊδίου nomine, id Apostolus τῆς δόξης voce intelligere videtur: partim (5) è Symboli Nicæni appella-tione, qua Filium DEI DEUM de DEO, & lumen de lumine vocat, quæ appellatio non vide-tur aliunde magis, quam ex hoc loco desumpta, ut innuit Constantinus Antiochen. hoc in loco; quomodo etiam Justinus, vel quisquis est autor libri: ὕτως, inquit, νοῦμεν τὸν υἱὸν ἐκ πατρὸς γε-γεννῆσθαι, ὡς Φῶς ἐκ Φωτὸς ἐκλάμψαν, & Na-zianzenus orat. I. & Filio. Splendor Solis à Sole nascitur, est ejusdem cum Sole naturæ, simul cum Sole emergit, & lucem Solis ad amussim exprimit: Sic Filius à Patre genitus ipse est συναΐδιον καὶ ὁμοού-σιον τὸν ὅλον ἐν ἑαυτῷ δεικνὺν. Placet hæc expli-catio Beat. Chemnitio in LL. CC. part. I. Est autem δόξα, inquit, copiosa lux, ut 2. Corinth. III. vers. 7. & Exod. XXXIV. vers. 30. περὶ δόξης vultus Mosis legitur, & Luc. II. vers. 9. dicitur: δόξα Domini circumfulsit Pastores. Ἀπαύγασμα est refulgentia ex illa luce, quia ἀπαύγασμα significat fulgorem, ut δόξα sit quasi fons lucis, in corpore Solis: ἀπαύγασμα vero splendor inde propagatus: sicut radii sparguntur à corpore Solis. Verum, uti dixi, res eodem re-dit, sive priori, sive posteriori modo vocem δό-ξης pro gloria, vel pro luce DEI accipias. Quia lux in DEO nihil aliud, quam Majestatem, & gloriam DEI splendidissimam designat, quæ 1. Timoth. VI. vers. 16. Φῶς ἀπρόσιτον inhabitare dicitur lucem inaccessibilem, id est ea gloria & Majestate pollet, quam nulla creatura vel habe-re, vel comprehendere potest, Jac. I. vers. 17. DEUS dicitur ὁ πατὴρ τῶν Φώτων ob essentia-lem Majestatem, quam nonnulli volunt esse So-lis περίφρασιν, aliqui cum Cyrill. Hierosolym. Ca-tech. VII. Patrem luminum volunt Patrem dici, quia Filius & Spiritus Sanct. sunt lumina à Patre, ut Paëzius, Justinianus, Lorinus, Estius. Sed Pater Spiritus Sancti Pater nuspiam dicitur, nec duo lumina sunt Filius & Spiritus Sanctus, sed u-num lumen, ideoque simplicius Majestas sanctis-sima DEI designatur, ut & 1. Johan. I. vers. 5. ὁ Θεὸς Φῶς ἐστι.

Porro appellationis hujus; quod Filius sit ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης refulgentia & splendor gloriæ Patris, vel eminentissimæ ejus Majesta-tis, variæ quidem rationes adferri possunt, sed eæ, ut ante innuimus, commode referuntur cum ad æternam Filii à Patre generationem, tum ad temporalem Majestatis DEI in Filio manife-stationem. Propter æternam generationem Filii à Patre eundem dici splendorem gloriæ Patris, plerique Dd. Ecclesiæ consentiunt; quod ut splendor à luce oritur, sic Filius à Patre per æternam generationem existit, ejusque essen-tiam, gloriam, & Majestatem communicatam habet. Et pulchre sane illustratur eminentissi-mum mysterium hac appellatione Filii DEI. (1) ratione originis tum in sese: quia ut est ge-neratio veluti quædam illa splendoris & lumi-nis à luce emanatio origo, sic per æternam generationem est Filius à Patre ceu splendor gloriæ, vel lucis istius divinæ, & lumen de lu-mine, DEUS de DEO genitus à Patre luce illa essentiali, & ingenita, eumque originem innuit vox ἀπαύγασμα vi præpositionis. Unde locus Sap. VII. vers. 25. 26. conferri potest, ubi sa-pientia dicitur. ἀπόῤῥοια τῆς τοῦ παντοκράτορος δόξης εἰλικρινής· ἀπαύγασμα Φωτὸς ἀϊδίου & ema- natio gloriæ omnipotentis sincera, & splendor æternæ lucis: tum (2) respectu modi generatio- nis: & quoad (1) necessitatem: ut enim radii Solis à Sole non libere sed necessario & natura- liter procedunt, ita generatio Filii est naturalis & necessaria, quanquam supra omnem naturam. Quomodo Cyrillus libr. X. cap. IIX. ex eo de- monstrat, Filium DEI non præcedente volun- tate, & electione, sed secundum naturam à Pa- tre generatum esse; & (2) quoad æternitatem: Sicut radii existunt cum Sole, & cum eo simul perseverant, sunt à Sole, sed non post Solem; sunt coævi Soli, & emanatio splendoris est à Sole, dum Sol est: Ita Filius est ὁμοαιώνιος Pa- tri, ab æterno in æternum existens cum Patre; in æternum à Patre, & (3) quoad immutabilita- tem. Radius enim sine mutatione, & immu- tabiliter à Sole profluit absque defluxu & deci- fione: Sic Filius à Patre genitus est absque ulla passionis mutatione, vel diminutione, aut de- cisione; ὀὐ γὰρ κατὰ τομὴν ἡ ῥεῦσιν ἢ διάσασιν τῶ Φωτὸς ἡ ἔκλαμψις γίνεται, ἀλλ’ ἐκ τῆς ὐσίας αὐτῆς ἀπαθῶς προέρχεται, ait Justinus in exposit. fidei in declaratione hujus similitudinis. Eosdem comparationis respectus explicat Ambrosius libr.I. de fid. ad Gratian. cap. IV. & (4) quoad pu- ritatem: quia splendor à Sole propinat sine ul- la fece aut commistione, quasi spiritualis & pu- rissima qualitas: ita & generatur Filius à Patre si- ne ulla commistione, ut innuit hoc loco Corne- lius à Lapide, & (5) quoad immediatam processio- nem: quia Filius à Patre immediate procedit per generationem ex ipsa essentia sine alterius inter- ventu, vel medio quodam, ut ex ipsa essentia lu- cis splendor & radius immediate procedit dicen- te Justino l. c. quod innuit Damascen. lib. I. Or- thodox. fid. cap. IX. cum λόγον ἀπαύγασμα dici inter alia ait διὰ τὸ ἄνευ συνδυασμῦ γεγεν- νῆσθαι ἐκ τῧ πατρὸς quod sine vinculo vel medio ge- neratur à Patre. & (6) quoad immanentiam, & inseparabilitatem: quia splendor à Sole & luce est, ita, ut Soli & luci maneat, est à Sole per ema- nationem, non autem per realem à Sole separa- tionem. Sic Filius est à Patre, sed ita, ut in Pa- tre sit & maneat; procedit à Patre, non tamén separari partem à Patre. Quod Cyrilli verbis ex- plicare lubet è libr. III. in Johan. cap. XXIX. in Patre naturaliter esse Filium ait, quamvis ex eo et- iam sit, quoniam subsistit, sicut forsan splendor in re, & ex re quæ splendet: Alius enim esse ratione intelligitur, & alia res ipsa, quæ splendet, sed non aliud, si ad naturam utriusque respexeris, quoniam ex re splendente splendor est, & in ipsa rursus inest, nec quoniam idem natura sunt, ab ipso etiam esse quicquam credetur. Prodeunt enim, quæ sic ex a- lio sunt separata, neque decisa. Conjungit hæc membra comparationis pleraque Damascen. l. I. Orth. fid. c. IX. λόγος μὲν ὧν καὶ ἀπαύγασμα λέγεται διὰ τὸ ἄνευ συνδυασμῦ καὶ ἀπαθῶς καὶ ἀχρόνως, καὶ ἀῥῥεύστως καὶ ἀχωρίστως γεγεννῆθαι ἐκ τῧ πατρὸς, &c.

Secundo convenit Filio DEI hæc appellatio ratione repræsentationis gloriæ, & Majestatis di- vinæ, qua Filius gloriam & Majestatem Patris in sese continet, exhibet, atque repræsentat, vel ut expressa quædam gloriæ & Majestatis Pa- tris imago & character, ut subsequens docet descriptio. Nam ut radius & splendor ejusdem est essentiæ cum Sole, ejusdemque gloriam quasi exhibet, atque repræsentat: Sic & Filius DEI splendor gloriæ Patris ejusdem est cum Patre es- sentiæ, & in sese exhibet ac repræsentat Ejus- dem gloriam ac Majestatem: splendor Solis, in- quit Nazianz. Orat. I. de Filio, lucem Solis ad amussim exprimit, sic Filius a Patre genitus ipsi est ὁμοούσιος, sive coëffentialis τὸν ὅλον ἐν ἑαυτῷ δει- κνὺς totum in seipso repræsentans. Nam sicut Pa- ter vitam habet ἐν ἑαυτῷ in seipso, οὕτως sic dedit quoque Filio vitam habere ἐν ἑαυτῷ in seipso, in- quit Christus, Johan. V. vers. 26. Exhibetur au- tem ita (1) Essentiæ unitas Johan. X. vers. 30. 1. Johan. V. vers. 7. (2) Æternitas, quod ὁμοαιώνιος sit Filius Patri Mich. V. vers. 2. Prov. IIX. vers. 23. seq. (3) Immutabilitas, quod non minus quam Pater immutabilis sit, Psalm. CII. vers. 26. Ebr. I. vers. 10. 11. (4) Puritas & san- ctitas: Quia ut DEUS lux est, & tenebræ non sunt in illo, 1. Johan. I. vers. 5. sic Filius DEI est lux vera Johan. I. vers. 5. 8. 9. Sanctus San- ctorum Dan. IX. vers. 24. ter sanctus ille Es. VI. vers. 3. (5) Majestas, quia & splendor vel lux & gloria Domini est, Ess. LX. vers. 1. & Dominus gloriæ, 1. Corinth. II. vers. 8. ejusdem honoris & gloriæ cum Patre, Johan. V. vers. 23. Es. XLV. vers. 23. Roman. XIV. vers. 10. Psalm. XCVL v. 8. Ebr. I. vers. 6. Apoc. V. vers. 12. Hæc non im- merito Theophylactus Arianorum opponit argu- tiis in comm. super hunc locum. Cum itaque Arianos illud deblaterare intelligit, & hunc in mo- dum arguere, cum ex Patre sit Filius. Ergo & Pa- tre ille est inferior, istiusmodi velim illis objicias: Vel ex Sole splendor emittitur, haud tamen hic splen- dor prodit, post Solem, sed simul effulget. Cum So- le enim una & radians fulgor exoritur.

Tertio ratione originis, & relationis persona- lis Filio DEI assignatur nomen ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, quia & immediata processio vel origo à Pa- tre indigitatur, quam habet per æternam generatio- nem, Psal. II. vers. 7. Mich. V. vers. 2. Prov. IIX. vers. 23. Johan. I. vers. 14. & origo, vel processio, quam habet Spiritus Sanct. non minus à Filio, quam à Patre: Sicut enim calor est à splendore pariter & à Sole, ita Spiritus Sanct. & à Filio procedit, & à Patre, lux splendor & calor simul ejusdem naturæ sunt, licet splendor à luce, calor à splendore sit & à luce: ita Pater, Filius & Spi- ritus Sanct. ejusdem divinæ sunt essentiæ, utut Filius in Patre sit, & Spiritus Sanct. à Patre & Filio procedat, ceu utriusque Spiritus. Hoc de mysterio ita loquitur Bullingerus h. in l. Sicut ra- dius à Sole non separatur: Sic neque è Patre Filius. Interim Sphæra, sive globus solus non est radius, ne- que radius globus & neutrum horum calor, neque calor globus aut radius: sunt tamen hæc tria non tres Soles, sed unus Sol. Sic utique & una est ma- gnifica gloria (hoc enim nomine decorat Apostolus DEUM) non duæ vel tres. Substantiæ tamen vel personæ ex illa duæ, verum ab ea non separatæ. Hæc ergo principales sunt rationes hujus nominis, qua respectus habetur ad mysterium æternæ Dei- tatis Filii Dei, quod hic πρώτως indigitari arbi- tramur, ubi tamen cogitandum illud, quod Ju- stinus ait: ἁρμόδιον γε τὸ παράδειγμα εἰ μὴ κατὰ πάντα κατὰ τι νῦν, Satis est si conveniat saltem in a- liquo similitudo, licet non in omnibus conveniat.

Secundario autem designari hâc appellatione temporalem Majestatis DEI in Filio manifestatio- nem haud negàram: idque non quoad prædicatio- nem saltem, vel manifestationem verbalem divinæ gloriæ & majestatis, de quo Christus ait, Nemo vi- dit Patrem nisi Filius, & cui vult manifestare Filius, Matth. XI. vers. 27. Sicut itaque Sol per radios sese communicat, nostrisque sensibus ingerit, Sic Pater in Filio & per Filium sese, hoc est, effentiam & voluntatem suam nobis revelavit : Quia, ut Augustinus ait, per splendorem cognoscitur lux, & infirmi mortalium oculi placidius ferunt splendorem, quam lucis claritatem ; Sed & quoad manifestationem realem, vel repræsentationem glo- riæ DEI, in carne factam, quia est Deus mani- festatus in carne, 1. Tim. III. vers. 16. & conspi- ciendam fecit gloriam, quasi gloriam unigeniti à Patre, Johan. I. vers. 14. Quum enim nemo De- um viderit unquam, Filius DEI, qui in sinu Patris est, nobis revelavit. Theophylactus innui vult τὴν γνησιότητα, καὶ τὸ ἀχώρισον, καὶ συναΐδιον τοῦ υἱοῦ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα. Ipse Filius DEI ἐξηγήσα- το, quod est proprie eduxit, ab ἐξηγέομαι, mani- festum fecit, & quasi conspicuum in sese. Nam qui me videt, inquit Christus, is videt Patrem, Joh. XIV. v. 9. Quod antea verbis Bezæ quodammodo explicavimus : quanquam cum Constantino Antio- cheno, & Beat. Hieron. Wellero in h. l. fateri tandem haud pudeat, non posse nos istorum verborum ἔμφασιν, ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης cogitando assequi, quanto minus dicendo exprimere.

Altera succedit denominatio, quam huic con- junctam voluit Apostolus, ut eo illustrius fieret mysterium jam insinuatum, quando docet, DEI Filium ita esse splendorem gloriæ DEI Patris sui, ut & χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ Imago hy- postaseos ejus sit.

Quid ergo χαρακτὴρ Apostolo, quid ὑποστά- σεως, quid χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως sit & dicatur? indagandum.

I. χαρακτὴρ dicitur vel figura, ut vertit inter- pres vetus, aut quod magis exprimit vocis em- phasin, expressa figura, ut Augustinus reddit lib. de incarn. Verbo cap. XII. aut imago expressa, ut interpretatur Erasmus, aut insculpta forma, quod mavult Beza παρὰ τὸ χαράσσειν, ut ab omni adum- brata vel inani imagine distinguatur : Quanquam agnoscat adhuc plenius esse Græcum χαρακτῆρος vocabulum; ideoque id retineat in versione. (1) Burgensis, de figura quarta specie qualitatis ac- cepit, quæ totam qualitatem terminatam conti- net, id accipi posse innuit, sed inepte. (2) Beat. Chemnitius part. I. LL. CC. pag. 131. hac de re ita scribit : Filius DEI non est evanescens imago sic- ut species corporis resplendens in speculo est εἰκὼν, & quidem evanescens, Jac. I. vers. 21. 22. Sed ex- pressa & permanens effigies, sicut nummus est cha- racter suæ matricis. Sed quia nummus est χαρακτὴρ formæ matricis tantum, non substantiæ, ideo addi- tur χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως, id est, imago non qua- litatum in DEO, sed substantialis & integra imago communicatæ ipsi essentiæ. (3) Erasmus adhibet similitudinem imaginis sigilli, quæ eidem impressa, archetypum exprimit. Sic & Bullinger. Quem- admodum in cera propriissime exprimitur sigil- lum, ita in Christo propriissime relucet substantia Paterna. (4) Alii malunt, sigillum ipsum deno- tari, quam imaginem ex sigillo ceræ impressam, eo sensu, quod Pater totam suam essentiam, & ma- jestatem Filio à se ab æterno genito intime quasi in- sculpserit, & seipsum in Filio quasi effigiavit, ut sit substantialis imago ejus: Ita Dn. Glassius in Rhet. Sac. pag. 159. eoque nomine volunt exprimi tum generationis æternæ secretum, tum Patris cœlestis af- fectum, ut solet sigillum præ cæteris diligi & custo- diri, unde etiam sigillo comparatur in typo Zeru- babelis, cui DEUS Hag. II. 24. ponam te sicut sigillum; tum salutis communicatæ negotium, sicut sigillum ceræ imprimitur, ita Christum esse sigil- lum, quo obsignatur nobis salus, & imprimit nobis sui imaginem per peccatum deperditam.

(5) Cornelius à Lapide confert hîc illud Christi de sese, Johan. VI. vers. 27. Quod Pater ἐσφρά- γισεν signavit, & quasi sigillo expresserit Filium, in quem locum Beza hoc modo annotat, ob- signavit, id est, inditæ virtutis suæ quasi impresso sigillo, tum à cæteris hominibus distinxit, ut in eo tanquam visibili imagine DEUS Pater appareat, tum etiam huic rei præstandæ destinavit, DEO videlicet homines reconciliandi in vitam æternam: non equidem male, at minus sufficienter & plene: Nam signavit quoque DEUS Pater Filium qua Filius omnem in se paternæ formæ plenitudinem si- gnantis DEI continet, ut ait Hilarius lib. IIX. de Trinit. ideoque Cyrillus etiam Filium signatum intelligit ad immutabilem DEI identitatem. Quia ut signaculum est simile imprimenti sigillo, sic Filius est veluti signaculum Patris æterni. Con- jungi itaque hic forte possent sententiæ Interpp. subordinatæ: quod signarit Pater Filium cum æterna generatione, & imaginis suæ impressione, juxta Hilar. & Cyrill. tum unctione Spiritus Sancti qua supra consortes fuit delibutus, ut ab omnibus hominibus aliis separetur, qua ratione Augustinus & Beat. Lutherus intelligit, tum miraculorum o- peratione, quæ fuere velut sigillum, quo jam olim DEUS Messiam signatum voluit, Es. XXXV. vers. 5. ut Chrysostomus explicat, tum meritoria passione, qua signatus fuit, & exsculptus lapis, Zach. III. 9. Malumus itaque characterem accipere pro imagi- ne expressa, quam pro sigillo: ut archetypus (omnes absint imperfectiones) sit Pater æternus, ectypus æternus ejus Filius, substantialis scil. imago Pa- tris: quia (1) χαρακτὴρ pro sigillo ipso accipi non adeo consuevit, sed potius pro imagine & effigie, vel forma expressa, & respectum dicit ad Exem- plar, cujus est imago. (2) Paulus imaginem εἰκόνα DEI Filium dixit, Coloss. I. vers. 16. non sigillum DEI. (3) Liber Sapientiæ, cujus descri- ptio huic nostræ persimilis est, exprimit ibidem per εἰκόνα, cap. VII. vers. 26. εἰκὼν ἀγαθότητος τῦ Θεῦ, ut & per ἔσοπτρον ἀκηλίδωτον speculum incontaminatum. (4) plerique omnes Inter- pretes Syrus, Arabs, Vulgatus, Erasmus & Com- mentatores reddunt per figuram & imaginem. (5) locus similis, Joh. VI. vers. 27. quod Deus ἐσφράγισεν signavit, convenit magis imagini ex- pressæ, quam sigillo. (6) Propositum est Aposto- lo Deitatem Filii DEI sistere & περίφρασιν my- sterii æternæ generationis utraque denominatio- ne tradere, ad sublimis hujus mysterii illustra- tionem; ut enim effulgentiam lucis divinæ, & splendorem gloriæ Patris dixit ratione emana- tionis & processionis Filii à Patre, ut & repræ- sentationis gloriæ Patris in Filio, ita & characte- rem hypostaseos dicit, cum ratione originis, quod Filius sit à Patre expressa imago per æternam ge- nerationem; tum ratione repræsentationis, quod Filius repræsentet hypostasin Patris, non secus at- que imago repræsentat archetypum.

II. Ὑποστάσεως vox est ambigua, & ἐκ τῶν πολ- λαχῶς λεγομένων, ut alias acceptiones mittamus, extra Scripturam; usum vocis quod attinet, in Scri- ptura Canonica, & in Nov. Testam. codice tri- fariam adhibetur (1) de gloriatione, 2. Corinth. IX. vers. 4. & cap. XI. vers. 17. ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ ὑποστάσει τῆς καυχήσεως in hypostasi illa gloriationis, id est, in fulcimento gloriationis, vel eo, quo nititur & sustentatur gloriatio, deinde de fide Ebr. III. vers. 14. τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς ὑποστάσεως, principium hypostaseos fidei, ut è vers. 6. liquet, seu principium illud, quo sustentamur, & Ebræor. XI. versus 1. Fides est ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις rerum sperandarum hypostasis, sive id, quo ex- tant, quæ sperantur, aut fulcimentum eorum, non quod sit animi substantia, sed quod objecti sub- stantia in animo, sive corde credentium. Phil. Melanchthon reddit expectationem rerum speran- darum, sive fiduciam, qua statuimus nobis con- tingere promissa DEI. Idque ex Grammati- ca vocis significatione, quod nempe ὑπόστασις usitatissime expectationem notet, vide Conf. Theol. pagin. 137. Tertius vocis hujus usus est in præsenti Filii DEI descriptione, ubi Sy- rus interpretatur איתותה quæ vox perinde ut Græca ὑποστάσεως duobus modis hic explica- tur. Tremellius eam exponit Essentiam. Junius autem mavult substantiam. Quod Syri essen- tiam potius appellant ישו. Pariter cum vox Græca interdum pro Essentia aut substantia, interdum pro persona occurrat apud Ecclesia- sticos Scriptores, ambiguum est, utra signi- ficatione hîc accipi debeat: Sunt qui pro sub- stantia vel essentia divina eandem hic intelle- ctam velint. Epiphan. lib. 2. Tom. 2. hæres. 69. hypostasin exponit per essentiam, ita & quotquot vocem Hypostaseos in usu & signi- ficatione recepta Ecclesiæ, qua adhibetur in articulo de Hypostaseon trium vel personarum in Essentia divina mysterio, esse ἄγραφον asserunt, utpote non è Scripturæ phrasi, sed communi lo- quendi consuetudine desumptam esse ajunt. Vid. Cyrill. dial. 1. de Trinit. Quomodo etiam Socrates lib. III. Tripart. cap. XXI. docet, vocem hypostaseos tempore Athanasii primum in Ecclesia receptam fuisse in hoc mysterio. Adde & Concil. Ephesin. sententiam, quod in Synod. E- pistol. ad Nestor. ait, quod Filius propter unam eandemque substantiam imago & character splen- dor gloriæ existat. Et Nazianzenus Orat. 5. de Fil. Tom. I. pag. 165. Filius dicitur imago Pa- tris, tanquam ejusdem essentiæ cum Patre. Quo etiam pertinet, quod narrat Nazianzenus in orat. de laude Athanasii q. XXXI. Græcos, qui tres ὑποστάσεις dicebant, Latinis visos fuisse tres ὀὐ- σίας sive essentias dicere: Quodque Hierony- mus testatur, quod tota Græcorum prophano- rum Schola discrimen inter hypostasin & ὀὐσίαν ignoret, Tom. II. Ep. 57. ad Damasc. unde scribit inter alia ibidem Hieronymus de tri- bus hypostasibus: Qui quæso Apostoli ista pro- didere? Quis novus Magister Gentium Paulus hæc docuit? Romanos etiam ὀὐσίαν & hypostasin non posse distinguere ait Augustinus libr. V. de Trin. cap. 8. Nicephorus quoque discrimen in- ter ὑπόσασιν & ὀὐσίαν nullum agnoscit lib. X. cap. XIII. ut alios prætermittam. Vulgata ver- sio reddit etiam per substantiam: & Beat. Lu- therus nec non Racovienses ein Abdruck seines Wesens. Eamque vocis significationem hîc ad- ferit Domin. Chemnitius in LL. CC. & Domin. D. Menzerus Tom. III. disp. Giess. IV. Th. 58. Estius in Comm. ad hunc loc. Alii vero malunt eandem hîc accipere pro persona. Quam senten- tiam è veteribus amplectuntur Gregorius Nys- senus in lib. de different. Essentiæ & Personæ. Basil. Epist. 45. & Chrysostomus, Theodorecus, Theophylactus & Oecumenius in Comm. ad hunc loc. Varimus & Suidas in Lexic. è recentioribus Thomas, itemque Cajetanus, Salmeron, Bellar- minus, Ribera, Cornelius à Lapide: itemque Cal- vinus, Zanchius, Ursinus, Parœus, & è nostris D. Hutterus in LL. CC. D. Gravverus Comment. super cap. I. ad Ebr. D. Meisnerus part. II. Phil. Sobr. pag. 417. Cui sententiæ posteriori etiam nos calculum adjicimus in disp. super A. Conf. IV. th. XI. & in dissert. Rostoch. pag. 20. Crellius et- iam libr. de uno DEO Patre reddit character personæ DEI. Probamus & explicamus eam hoc pacto: quia character nomen est relatum., Au- gustinus. lib. 7. de Trinit. cap. 1. & ex eo Thomas quæst. XXXV. art. 1. Imago est nomen personale, cum imago non dicatur ad se, sed ad aliud: ideo- que supponit fundamentum, & infert correlatum. Id ergo, cujus character vel imago dicitur im- mediate est correlatum vel exemplar ejusdem; id propter quod est fundamentum. Cum ergo Fi- lius vocatur imago ὑποστάσεως, certum est no- tari correlatum, non vero fundamentum, nisi ἐμμέσως, in quantum idem præsupponitur. Est autem exemplar Filii prima persona Deitatis Pa- ter, fundamentum vero origo Filii à Patre, vel essentiæ communicatio, qua velut impressa est ima- go Patris Filio, unde colligimus: Id, ratione cujus Filius est à Patre distinctus, & repræsentat Pa- trem, ejus ratione dicitur character & imago Patris. Quia imago & (1) distinctionem infert; Imago enim rei non est res, cujus est imago ex naturâ oppositorum; & (2) repræsentationem. Nam de ratione imaginis est similitudo, vel ut inferat exemplar suum, cujus fundamentum ista origo. At personæ, non essentiæ ratione Filius est à Patre distinctus, & repræsentat exactissime Patrem, quia omnia habet in persona sua, quæ habet Pater in sua persona, Johan.
