(VIII) Commentum Socinianorum, quo purgationem peccatorum nostrorum ex par- te Dei, ab eo suspendunt momento, quo Christus immediate ante sessionem ad dextram Dei se stitit Patri, quod ultimum momentum fuerit Ascensionis ejus in cælum, repugnat tum Ascensionis in cælum, & confessus ad dextram DEI articulo, quum illa non possint localiter, & secundum momenta intelli- gi, tum imprimis etiam instituto totius Epistolæ: siquidem tota Epistola purgationem peccatorum ad passionem, mortem, sanguinis effusionem, assi- milationem, quoad miseriam & humilitatem cum hominibus, & ad obedientiam perpetuam exten- dat, nullo vero modo ad exaltationem, & ultimum momentum ingressus in sancta sanctorum restrin- gat. (IX) Disputant Sociniani oblationem sacrifi- cialem non absolvi sola mactatione, concedimus id, sed addimus non absolvi eandem præsentatione, quia in multis sacrificiis ne quidem talis præsen- tatio fuit. Proinde requiritur simul ipsa com- bustio: In CHRISTI vero sacrificio & mactatio- ni & combustioni respondet Christi passio. Atque hæc de actu purificationis.

(II.) Objectum Peccatorum nostrorum: U- bi duo notamus (1) Nomen peccatorum, quo ab- solute posito indicatur omnium peccatorum ex- piationem per CHRISTUM factam esse: taci- ta antithesi, in Vet. Testam. illorum tantum ex- piatio fiebat, pro quibus offerebantur sacrificia: hic vero omnium: nempe ut universalis sit ex- piatio, non tantum intensive, ad omnia pecca- ta, quantacunque, & cujuscunque generis sese porrigens: omnium enim peccatorum chiro- graphum cruci affixum Coloss. 2, 14. Opera Dia- boli omnia destructa 1. Johan. 3, 15. Ebr. 2. vers. 14. ideo sanguis CHRISTI mundat nos ab omni pec- cato 1. Johan. 1, 29. CHRISTUS redemit nos ἀπὸ πάσης ἀνομίας Tit. 2, 14. fuso sanguine sine cul- pa omnium culparum chirographa deleta sunt, ait Augustinus l. II. de remiss. peccator. cap. 20. Sic & Hircus emissarius omnes iniquitates dicitur por- tasse Lev. 16, 21. seq. tum extensive ad omnium ho- minum peccata, seu totius mundi; quia absolu- te dicitur peccata. Sic Es. 53, 6. nos omnes instar ovium erravimus, sed DEUS omnium peccata in ipsum conjecit; ubi nota & universalitatem re- demptionis omnes: qui errabamus: & redemptio- nis universalis veritatem, sive intentionem Dei, sive peccati expiationem spectemus. Adde his e N. T. ubi (1) voce Mundi omnes exprimuntur Joh. 1, 29. c. 3, 6. c. 6, 33. 51. cap. 12, 47. Joh. 4, 42. 2. Cor. 8, 29. 1. Joh. 4, 14. 1. Joh. 2, 2. (2) Cum mentio fit omnis populi, Luc. 2, 10. omnis hominis Joh. 1, 9. Rom. 5, 18. 19. (3) Ejus quod perierat Matth. 18, 11. eorum qui in tenebris sedebant, Luc. 1, 79. (4) Si com- memorantur eodem sensu omnia Ephes. 1, 10. Col. 1, 20. Omnes 2. Cor. 5, 14. 15. 1. Tim. 2, 6. c. 4, 10. Tit. 2, 10. Ebr. 2, 9. Usus prioris est (1) contra Ponti- ficios: qui Christum tantum pro peccato originis, & pro actualibus peccatis Baptismum antecedentibus satisfecisse, pro cæteris vero nobis ipsis satisfacien- dum esse contendunt contradictorie. Hominem enim nudum Dei infinitæ justitiæ satisfacere est σιδηρέξυλον. (2) Contra Socinianos, qui in Vet. Testam. tantum peccata levia absque proposito ex ignorantia quadam & errore admissa expiata dicunt, quæ Ebr. 5, 2. c. 9, 7. vocantur ἀγνοήματα: Delicta autem gravia sacrificia expiare non potuisse. Socin. p. II. de Serv. Christ. c. 11. & 12. At ἀγνοήματα di- Ebr. 9, 7. cuntur etiam de peccatis gravioribus, & voluntaria ἀγνοήματα. legis prævaricatione: cum in libris Apocryphis & Hellenisticis, 1. Esdr. 8, 77. Sap. 14, 22. Syr. 23, 2. 3. tum in N. T. 1. Pet. 1, 14. Conf. Act. 8, 17. c. 13, 27. 1. Tim. 1, 13. 2. Pet. 2, 12. Et appellationis ratio est: quia ignorare Ebræis sæpe affectum notat, estque idem, quod non curare, non attendere, non observare, transilire. Et notum est, verba notitiæ apud Ebræos affectum includere. Sicut & שָׁגַג aliquando est verbum Dei negligere, Ps. 119, 67. & cum חָטָא per- miscetur. Conf. Lev. 4, 12. 13. Num. 15, 22. Ad hæc dicitur שְׁגָגָה etiam tale peccatum, quod sit ad de- lictum sive scandalum populo, Levit. 4, 2. 3. sic & co- gnatum מְשֻׁגָּה usurpatur de peccato maximo 1. Sam. 26, 21. Joh. 6, 24. c. 12, 16. Sic & Ebr. 9, 7. ἀγνοή- ματα dicuntur omnia peccata, quia omnia habent concomitantem quandam ignorantiam: fiunt e- nim sub specie boni apparentis, quod apprehendit intellectus. Quod magis clarescit ex Ebr. v. 2. quia officium Pontificis dicitur offerre ὑπὲρ ἁμαρ- τιῶν, v. 1. quæ ἁμαρτίαι explicantur, v. 2. τοῖς ἀγνο- οῦσι καὶ πλανωμένοις. Accedit insuper, quod pec- cata ignorantiæ non semper sint levia, sed & gravia, ut Lev. 4, 3. c. 5, 1. 2. 3. Quomodo etiam Christi crucifixio ἀγνόημα vocatur, quæ certe malitiosa fuit, & deliberatissima facta voluntate Act. 3, 17. & c. 13, 27. Quod autem omnino pro gravioribus etiam peccatis expiatio facta sit in Vet. Testam. patet (1) e commemoratione peccatorum voluntario- rum, Lev. 5, 21. vel c. 6, 2. quæ expianda. (2) Ex hirco emissario, cui omnia peccata totius populi im- putabantur, ad quem alludit Esaias c 53. cum Chri- sto omnia peccata imposita ait: (3) Exemplo filio- rum Eli 1. Sam. 3, 14. ubi DEUS singulari jura- mento præcavet, & prohibet expiationem iniqui- tatis domus Eli, quo juramento utique minime fuiffet opus, si magna peccata expiari non potuis- sent. Davidis insuper exemplo 2. Sam. 12. verf. 13. cujus peccatum gravissimum adulterium & homi- cidium expiatum est. Interim (1) distinguimus inter peccata grandiora notiora & clandestina. Illa erant morte plectenda Levit. 18, 29. hec expiaban- tur, etiam ratione communionis Ecclesiasticæ. Et quidni peccata expiarentur coram Deo? Nam vel remittebantur, vel non: si remissa sunt, ergo fane expiata: Sine expiatione enim, & sanguinis effu- sione nulla est peccatorum remissio. Si autem non remissa, dicendum, omnes qui in graviora prola- psi peccata, æternum periisse, quod absit. (2) Dehinc agnoscimus quoque discrimen ea in par- te inter sacrificia Veteris Testamenti & sacrificium

Christi; Illic expiabantur peccata eorum, qui ex- piationem quærebant: Hic expiata sunt ratione meriti omnium peccata. Ibi in nonnullis sacrificiis actu ipso sequuta est ablatio, eo quod fide ea offer- rentur a personis particularibus: Id vero hic non fit, quia non applicatio specialis, sed generalis ex- piatio in cruce facta, & καθαρισμὸς, ut nonnulli lo- quuntur, velut in actu signato constitutus est per modum λύτρε acceptati & sub certa τάξει dispen- sandi. (3) Quanquam vero nemini in Vet. Test. aditus ad gratiam & remissionem peccatorum præcluderetur, non tamen distinctim, & in specie pro gravissimis, & maximis peccatis legi constituta esse sacrificia ideo dici potest, ut doceretur longissime ab iis talia delicta abesse debere. In genere tamen sacrificia pro iis ordinata sunt, ut anniversaria.

Usus posterioris observationis est contra Cal- vinianos: qui Christum expiasse tantum peccata piorum & Electorum profitentur, non autem totius mundi. Atqui ita nemo certus erit, sibi expiata peccata esse: nec infideles damnari poterunt, quod non credant sibi expiata esse peccata, cum id ne quidem credere debeant, quippe falsum.

II. Pronomen ἡμῶν: Peccatorum nostrorum, quo complectitur Apostolus OMNES: quia (1) omnes in pari statu sunt cum respectu peccati, tum respectu gratiæ divinæ, & meriti Christi, quo refert ea, quæ antea dicta sunt: quod omnium peccata expiarit. (2) Antithesis simul innuitur, inter ex- piationem in Vet. Testam. typicam & antitypum in Christo; in Vet. Testam. 1) Expiatio tantum eorum fiebat, qui in populo Dei erant, & sacrificia offerebant: hic expiatio facta est totius mundi; non nostrorum tantum, ait Johannes, sed totius mundi, 1. Epist. 1, 2. 2) Expiabat Sacerdos non tantum populi, sed & sua peccata: Christus autem non suorum, sed nostrorum expiationem fecit: Quod contra Socinianos notandum, qui ut sum- mus sacerdos pro se etiam obtulisse ajunt ex Ebr. 7, 27. Sed autor hujus Epistolæ CHRISTUM nu- spiam ait, pro se victimam esse factum, sed pro aliis semper Ebr. 9, 14. cap. 10, 12. Ad hæc pro iis obtulit, qui purgatione, & expiatione egebant peccatorum, ipse vero ab omnibus peccatis erat a- lienus, & longissime separatus; non noverat pecca- tum, adeoque pro nobis factus est peccatum, 2. Cor.

Quod Ebr. 7, 27. CHRISTUS hoc fecis- se dicitur semel, id applicatur tantum ad oblationem & sacrificium CHRISTI, non vero ad objectum, vel eos, pro quibus factum est sacrificium.

III. Modus expiationis peccatorum exprimi- tur δι' ἑαυτῦ per semetipsum: Quod in Vulgata ver- sione deest, etsi habeatur constanter in Græcis Codd. & Syriacis aliisque versionibus, quod dum agnoscunt Pontificii, & adhuc tamen vulgatæ versionis αὐθεντίαν sustinent, secundum Trid. Concil. decretum contradictioni sese involvunt, dum utrumque asserere non dubitant: & authen- ticam esse per omnia versionem, & deficere ta- men in nonnullis locis a textu originali. Est au- tem hæc additio maximi momenti, designans par- tim (1) quod CHRISTUS αὐτοενεργητικῶς virtute propria expiationem fecerit peccatorum, ex quo Christi dignitas elucescit. Partim (2) quod αὐτοπροσώπως in sua ipsius persona fecerit expia- tionem, ex quo Christi charitas conspicua fit, Sacerdotes in Veter. Testam. nec virtute pro- pria expiabant peccata, sed τυπικῶς saltim: nec in sua persona, sed offerendo sacrificia, sive non proprio sanguine, sed sanguine sacrificiorum.

CHRISTUS vero & per se propria divina vir- tute, & effusione sanguinis sui proprii fecit expia- tionem. Quod utrumque argumentum pleni- us deducit Epistola nostra, tum quod Christus ut verus DEUS, sive non homo nudus tantum, sed θεάνθρωπος PER SEIPSUM peccatorum fecerit expiationem, tum quod CHRISTUS proprio sanguine id præstiterit, secus atque sa- cerdotes in Veteri Testamento. Ex illo pre- tium hujus redemptionis, & dignitatem derivat: ex hoc vero amoris Christi & misericordiæ divi- næ magnitudinem astruit & confirmat. Usus est contra Socinianos. (1) Is, qui per seipsum facit expiationem, est verus DEUS Esa. 44, 24. (2) Si per semetipsum fecit expiationem: non tantum eam obtinuit à DEO, sed in manibus suis habuit.

Quæritur autem, ad quamnam in CHRISTO naturam respiciat Apostolus, cum ait δι᾽ ἀυτõ? Resp. Ad utramque Naturam pertinet hoc apo- telesma, expiationem facere peccatorum, ut omnia opera officii secundum Regulam Concilii Chalce- donens. solius quippe humanæ naturæ opus non est expiare peccata totius mundi, & quidem per seipsum, tum quia in Scripturis hoc soli Deo vin- dicatur, tum quia opus est infinitæ virtutis, quæ in hominem merum non cadit. Ideo Deus sangui- nem suum effundere debuit, Actor. 20. vers. 28. Rursus soli divinitati hoc tribui non potest, quia facta est expiatio per mortem Redemptoris nostri. Deitas autem morti & passioni ulli obnoxia non est: Sed prorsus immutabilis. Ideoque ut Dei- tas τõ λόγȣ Filii Dei carne vestita, & caro in Dei- tatis consortium & κοινωνίαν recepta, ita utriusque κοινωνία conspicitur in expiatione peccatorum per Christum facta. Quo nomine in ipsa tractatione de utraque natura, & mutua κοινωνίᾳ disserere vo- luit Apostolus, antequam aggrederetur explica- tionem hujus thematis.

Notetur itaque hic diversitas inter Christum Pontificem, & Sacerdotem Vet. Test. (1) Illic erant plures Sacerdotes, plura sacrificia: hic unicus Sa- cerdos, unicum sacrificium semel peractum Ebr. 9, 25. Illi peccato ipsi erant obnoxii, & pro se ipsis offerre debuere, hic à peccato immunis pro nobis tantum offert Lev. 16. 17. Ebr. 5, 3. Joh. 8, 56. Esa. 53, 29. 1. Pet. 2, 22. Ebr. 7, 25. Illi meri homines, hic verus natura Deus quoque est: Illi Sacerdotes, non Reges, hic Sacerdos simul, & Rex Ecclesiæ: Illi particulares Sacerdotes, certi temporis, pro certo populo, pro peccatis certis, quorum nempe expiatio petebatur, hic catholicus, perpetuus pro omnibus hominibus & omnibus omnium homi- num peccatis: Illi offerebant tantum, non offere- bantur, hic seipsum offert: Ebr. 8, 27. Illi ingre- diebantur tabernaculum, ut mactatores, hic ut ma- ctatus Ebr. 9, 26. Illi sanguine alieno, & bruto- rum ingrediebantur, hic proprio Ebr. 9, 14. Illi ingressi speciebus aromaticis, cum igne confla- grantibus & in fumos abeuntibus Lev. 16, 12. hic in- gressus est cum aromate ardentis amoris erga ge- nus humanum: Illi tabernaculum ingrediebantur manufactum, hic cœleste & æternum Ebr. 9, 11. ut consideret ad dextram Majestatis: Illi egressi con- summabant sacrificium, quod igne cœlesti consu- mebatur, hic antequam ingrederetur consum- mavit patiendo, uti ignis iræ divinæ sacrificium hoc consumsit: Illi expiabant saltem typice, hic vere & proprie. Socinus part. II. de Serv. Christ. cap. 20. Christo expiationem peccatorum duobus modis hic adscri- bi ait (1) quatenus in Christo expressam videmus Dei erga nos voluntatem, & declaratam habemus, remissa esse peccata nostra; quod significari vult, cum Christus splendor gloriæ & expressa imago sub- stantiæ Dei dicitur. (2) Quatenus omnia poten- te suo jussu moderatur & regit, sic autem & vere ex- piata esse peccata nostra, & nos una cum Christo in cœlis versari, neque ullam peccatis nostris pœnam su- pereffe. Sed hæc glossa neque veterum, neque recentiorum hujus Epistolæ interpretum ulli in mentem venit, quod fatetur Socinus ipse, & non sa- tis se mirari posse ait. Nos autem minime id mi- ramur, quandoquidem neutro respectu vel hic, vel etiam alibi adscribatur καθαρισμὸς ille pecca- torum nostrorum CHRISTO. Quod ad prio- rem, non dici Christum splendorem gloriæ Dei, & characterem substantiæ Dei, quod nos voluntatem DEI ex eo videamus, sed quod in sese exhibeat substantiam & Majestatem Patris ceu Filius ὁ- μούσιος καὶ ἰσότιμος, antea ostensum fuit. Mul- to autem minus ratione expiationis peccatorum, splendor & character dicitur. Ubi enim tale quid in scripturis? & quis hoc colliget ex verbis illis? imo expiatio morte & oblatione Christi facta, non autem per expressionem gloriæ & hyposta- seos Dei. Distinctissima insuper sunt voluntatis Dei gratiosa annunciatio, & peccatorum expiatio. Illa ad officium propheticum Christi pertinet, hæc ad sacerdotale. Illam CHRISTUS non immedia- tè solum, sed & per Apostolos, & Doctorum verba fecit, quam etiam à Prophetis antea factam con- stat. Hanc autem non per alios, sed per semet- ipsum fecit Christus. Unde ipse solus dicitur ex- piator peccatorum: Prophetæ & Apostoli sic mi- nime vocantur. Porro non per annunciationem voluntatis divinæ, sed per mortem Christi facta est expiatio peccatorum: Nec mors Christi tantum confirmatio fuit præconii, vel μαρτύριον, sed recon- ciliatio Dei, redemptio ab execratione legis, & pro- pitiatio atque λύτρον & ἀντίλυτρον pro nobis so- lutum, Rom. 5, 10. Gal. 3, 13. Rom. 3, 24. Matth. 20, 28. 1. Timoth. 2, 6. qui respectus etiam magis at- tingunt hunc effectum, sive expiationem peccato- rum, quam prout morte dicitur declarata solum Dei voluntas. Ad hæc CHRISTUM eo ipso purificationem peccatorum fecisse, quod in ipso habeamus exemplum gratiæ divinæ, qua evectus est ad æternam gloriam, nuspiam scriptura docet, nec in hoc exemplo Christi ad regnum Dei evecti gratia illa emicat, qua expiantur, & remittuntur peccata, ut antea monuimus. Id vero perquam absurdum est, peccatorum nostrorum expiatio- nem in eo consistere, quod nos videamus in Christo impleri, quod nobis Deus est pollicitus, vel Chri- stum evehi ad salutem æternam, quam nobis per CHRISTUM promissam voluit DEUS. Tan- dem vero quis admittet expiationem fieri, cum in CHRISTO gloriæ divinæ splendorem & imaginem expressam intuemur. Sed hæ glossæ jam antea pro- fligatæ sunt.

Quod ad alterum respectum, quod expiationem peccatorum fecerit Christus omnia ferendo verbo virtutis suæ: merum id commentum est Socinia- num. Aliud quippe est conservatio & gubernatio universi, aliud est expiatio peccatorum nostrorum; Illa communis est Christo cum Patre & Spiritu S. Expiationem autem Christus per seipsum fecit, non Pater, nec Spiritus S. Illa naturæ sustentationem, hæc peccati abolitionem concernit. Illa spectat ad articulum creationis, & providentiæ, hæc ad arti- culum Redemptionis. Illa universalis est creatu- rarum omnium: hæc tantum pertinet ad genus humanum. Fundamentum quidem expiationis peccatorum, qua per semetipsum eandem fecit, Christus est, quod sit Dominus universi omnia portans verbo virtutis suæ, rationem vero formalem & modum, quo facta est expiatio, id non exprimit. Nam nec scriptura S. id uspiam docet, & longe aliter quoque de eo nos informamur, quod nempe non ferendo res omnes verbo virtutis, sed offerendo sefe pro nobis peccata expiavit: quod non sustentan- do universum, sed portando peccatum mundi nos à peccatis redemerit Esa. 53, 6. 14. Joh. 1, 29. Ebr. 9, 26. Ideoque propitiatio, Redemptio & purifica- tio peccatorum nostrorum non gloriæ & Majesta- ti Christi adscribuntur, qua portat omnia; sed cru- ci & sanguini Christi, 2. Cor. 5, 11. ult. Quod ergo Christus in cælis degens omnia in manu habeat, idipsum non est expiatio peccatorum nostrorum. Nam quod nos quoque cum Christo in cælis ver- semur, quoad opem regni cælestis, id consequens est expiationis peccatorum, non ejusdem vel ante- cedens, vel ratio formalis. Sed de commentis illis Socinianis antea satis actum. Nolumus τὸ πεαχ- θὲν πράτζειν.

Ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ τẽ θρόνε τῆς μεγαλωσύνης ἐν ὑψηλοῖς) Scandit oratio. Prætulit Christum Patribus, Mosi, Pro- phetis. Jam & Angelis eum proferre volens, per quos Deus Patres, Mosen, & Prophetas fuit allocutus, osten- dit, illum solo Deo Patre minorem. Locus dexter est ejus, qui Regi est proximus. Vide Matth. 20, 21. & ibi dicta. Locutio ἐν δεξιᾷ extat & Romanor. 8, 34. Ephes. 1, 20. Co- loss. 3, 1. infra c. 8, 1. c. 10, 12. c. 12, 2. 1. Petr. 3, 22. Genes. 48, 13. Judic. 16, 30. Θρόνου μεγαλωσύνης sive δόξης Ebræis, כסא כבוד significat ipsius Dei summam Majestatem A- pocal. 4, 2. & seq. c. 19, 4. c. 21, 5. cui proximus est Agnus, id est, Christus, v. 6. 13. c. 7, 10. 17. c. 22, 1. 3. Bene autem addit ἐν ὑψηλοῖς במרומים, id est, in cælo supremo, aut supra cæli partes adspectabiles, ut infra c. 7, 26. Vide & quæ dicta Eph. 1, 3. 20. quia & David in eximio quodam loco à Deo constitutus est Ps. 89, 28. sed in terris tantum.

## 1:4
Verse 4.

Having become so much better than the angels) Insofar as he was preferred to the Angels, namely at that time when he sat down at the right hand of the Father.

By how much more excellent a name he has inherited) By how much greater a title he is distinguished, for κληρονομεῖν (to inherit), נחל or ירש, is to obtain a certain and lasting right, in the way that hereditary things were held among the Hebrews, that is, real estate, as we have said elsewhere. Διαφορώτερον (more excellent). Thus also below chapter 8:6.

More correctly here in the proposition, the Apostle is said to proceed from the Priestly office, by which he made purification or expiation of our sins, now to the other part of that office, intercession; or to the state of exaltation from the state of humiliation: because as in the state of humiliation he made expiation for our sins, so in the state of exaltation he intercedes for us, that we may actually enjoy the expiation made, since for that reason he sat down at the right hand of God, as the Apostle testifies in Rom. 8, 34. He describes, however, this exaltation of Christ, which was done for our sake, both absolutely and comparatively. Absolutely, through the sitting at the right hand of the Majesty on high, concerning which these things are to be observed: (1) When he sat down. (2) According to which nature. (3) In what manner?

As to the first, he sat down after the purification of our sins was made, and thus after his passion and death. Therefore he did not sit at the right hand of God from eternity, nor from the very moment of his incarnation: because only after his passion did he enter into his glory, Luke 24, 26; after he drank from the brook in the way, he lifted up his head, Ps. 110, last verse; after he became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross, God exalted him and gave him a name which is above every name, Phil. 2, 8, 9.

As to the second point, it is certain that the exaltation of Christ was brought about according to his human, and not according to his divine nature. For although Christ, the God-man, has sat down at the right hand of the Majesty, he has done so not as God, but as man, and therefore not by reason of both natures: both natures are the principle, but the human nature is the terminus: just as the ὑπερύψωσις (superexaltation), taken passively, belongs only to the human nature, inasmuch as it is according to this that he was anointed for the kingdom, Ps. 45:6; according to which he lifted up his head, Ps. 110:last; according to which he endured the cross, and being exalted by the right hand of God, was made CHRIST and Lord, Acts 2:32, 36; was constituted over all the works of God, Ps. 8:6; and became the heir of all things, Heb. 1:2. Christ was exalted according to that nature according to which he was emptied. But he was emptied not according to his divine, but only according to his human nature. According to his divine nature, he is devoid of all change and is utterly immutable: and therefore he could neither be emptied nor exalted according to his divine nature. Cf. Luke 24:26; Phil. 2:8, 9. According to the same nature that he died, and rose again, and ascended into heaven, according to that same nature he also sits at the right hand of God, Mark 16:19; Acts 2:33; Rom. 8:34; Eph. 1:20, seq. But he died and rose again and ascended into heaven according to his human nature, not however according to his divine nature. To this pertains that ἀπ᾽ ἄρτι (from now on) in Matt. 26:64. Furthermore, according to the same nature that he received a name more excellent than the angels, or a name above every name, according to that same nature he was exalted and sits at the right hand of God. But he received a name more excellent and above every name according to his human nature, not according to his divine nature. Cf. Phil. 2:9 with this passage. Nor is the right hand of God so distinguished from the divine nature of CHRIST that he can be said to sit at the right hand of God according to the latter: and that session is expressly referred to the human nature, according to which he will visibly administer judgment, Matt. 25:31. Compare John 5:27. All of which shine with their own light. Therefore, Basil the Great, against Eunomius, book IV: 'That the Lord is celebrated and received a name above every name must be understood of the incarnation, and not of the Deity.' St. Athanasius, oration II against the Arians: 'Scripture does not understand the substance of the Word to be exalted, but this looks to his humanity, and he is said to be exalted on account of the flesh.' Jerome on chapter II of Philippians: 'Because the assumed man deigned to be humbled, the divinity, which cannot be humbled, exalted him who had been humbled; but also a name was given to him, because he did not have it before.'

As to the third point, how he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, let it be noted (1) the sense of the verb ἐκάθισεν, which is expressed in the past tense, signifying that he occupied the seat after his death, through which the expiation of sins was made by his ascension into heaven: for this follows the resurrection and precedes the session at the right hand of God, according to the Apostles' Creed, and according to Mark ch. 16:19. Therefore, it is one thing to have sat down at the right hand, and another to sit at the right hand: the former denotes the act of sitting down; the latter, the state: the former, the occupation of the kingdom, Acts 3:21; the latter, the rule itself is designated. For it is understood not as a local session, or one properly so called, as 'to sit' is used in Lev. 24:39; but as it is explained by Paul, it is a session of rule, Ps. 111:1; 1 Cor. 15:25, 'he must reign, until he puts his enemies as a footstool for his feet,' and this session implies subjection, just as 'to rule' and 'to be subjected' are related in Ps. 8:6; Heb. 2:8; Eph. 1:20; 1 Pet. 3:last.

just as the exaltation of Christ also implies a kingdom, Acts 2:33; ch. 5:31.

(2) The meaning of the Right Hand of Majesty. The right hand of God is understood, which does not denote corporeality or any place in the heavens, as Bullinger wishes in his treatise on the words of the Supper, and in his Compendium of the Christian Religion, book 6, ch. 8; Beza on part III; Brentius on the session at the right hand of GOD, vol. I of his works, page 601; the Helvetic Confession in art. XI; because GOD is a Spirit, and has no material or corporeal right hand. What of the fact that neither the right and left hand of Christ, when the faithful are said to be set at the former and the unfaithful at the latter on the day of the universal judgment, Matt. 25:32, 33, denotes a situation, but rather the infinite Majesty of CHRIST, mercifully saving, blessing, and glorifying, so that those who are admitted to the perfect enjoyment of the same are said to be placed at the one side; while on the other hand, it designates the likewise infinite Majesty of Christ, justly avenging and condemning, at which those are said to be placed who feel its power and burden in the horror of eternal punishments, as interpreted by B. Dorscheus in his Pentadec. Disp. 12, th. 23. Nor is a finite power denoted by the right hand of God, or a vicarious, secondary, or intermediate one, as Zanchius [claims] in book II of the Nature of God, quest. 4. Bergius and others wish, or a finite beatitude, or such as is proper to the elect, to which some others among the Calvinists go with Zanchius: But it is the infinite virtue and ruling power of the Son of God: namely, that power of God which created all things, Ps. 85:5; preserves and governs all things, Ps. 21:9; Ps. 96:4; Ps. 138:7; Ps. 145:16; Amos 9:2; Acts 4:27; Isa. 40:1; ch. 48:2; can change all things, Ps. 77:11; and does wonders, Exod. 15:6; and is everywhere present, Ps. 139:9; to which is attributed the gathering of the Church, Ps. 80:16; the leading of the Israelites, Ex. 15:6; Ps. 44:4; deliverance from all evils, Ps. 138:7; all of which are as falsely taken regarding a created power as they are absurdly taken regarding a certain place in heaven. Nor is the right hand of God, taken relatively, to which CHRIST was indeed raised, said to be τοπικως (locally), or regarding a place, or regarding some finite power. For it is not right to attribute a double right hand to God, or to say that the right hand of God is one way in the Old Testament and another when Christ is said to be exalted to the right hand of God in the New Testament: rather, it is one and the same right hand of God, and Christ is said to be exalted to the right hand, that is, to the infinite power of God, not to some other right hand or power of God. Therefore, that right hand is called the right hand of Majesty in this place, the right hand of the throne of God in Heb. 12:2, the right hand of the throne of Majesty in Heb. 8:1, the right hand of the power of God in Matt. 26:64, Luke 22:69. And since it is evident from an induction of all the passages where the name of the right hand of God occurs that it always denotes the infinite power of God, and since this is undoubted regarding other passages in the Old Testament, nor is it used otherwise in Acts 4:23, ch. 5:31, what reason can there be why the name of the right hand of God should be taken in a meaning entirely different in kind, both in that single passage of the Old Testament, Ps. 110:1, and in the passages of the New Testament explaining the same? Therefore Basil the Great, in his book on the Holy Spirit, ch. 6, says: the right hand of God does not signify a place, but a state of equality; and Athanasius, in question 55 to the Antiochians, says: when you hear of the right hand of God, remember that it is divine glory and Majesty. Tertullian, on the flesh of Christ, says: the right hand of God is the seat of paternal brightness. Gregory of Nyssa, in his second oration on the Resurrection, says: the right hand of God is explained by the glory which Christ possessed as his own as God. Damascene, in book 4 on the Orthodox Faith, ch. 2, says: we understand the right hand of the Father as the glory and honor of the Godhead, and, to pass over others from antiquity, he himself confesses

Altingius, Theological Problems, part 1, problem 45, p. 185. That the right hand of God is His infinite power and glory. Johann Bergius in 'Unterscheid', etc., chapter XL, page 63, confesses that the right hand of God is not a created place, but the power and virtue of God working everywhere in all places.

(3) The force of the whole phrase, of sitting or session at the right hand of Majesty: and the formal reason of that session. It imports those two things: both the kingdom of Christ the man as truly infinite: and the mode of receiving, and the foundation of the received kingdom of CHRIST. The mode includes partly the circumstance of time, partly the preceding acts, such as the passion, death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. The foundation is both remote, namely the personal union; and proximate, the exaltation to the right hand of the Father, Phil. 2:9. It is one thing, therefore, to rule omnipotently, omnisciently, and omnipresently: it is another to sit at the right hand of God, which indeed imports such a rule, but under that modification, and arising from those causes. Divine session, which is common to the three persons of the Deity, is one thing: session at the right hand of God, which is proper to CHRIST, and indeed according to his human nature, is another: and thus it does not denote divine and infinite dominion absolutely and without limit, but [the dominion] of the second person of the Trinity, and indeed by virtue of the personal union and exaltation, exercised immediately over all creatures: because it befits the incarnate Son of God, and respects the κοινωνίαν (communion) of Majesty, and ὑπερύψωσιν (exaltation), as also the preceding κένωσιν (emptying) and ταπείνωσιν (humiliation). Moreover, it implies the dominion not of an absent, but of a truly present divine [person], which cannot be imagined without the substantial presence and nearness of the nature and person to whom it befits, and wherever the throne of God and the right hand of Majesty is, there is the nature which sits on the throne of God and at the right hand of Divine majesty. Therefore CHRIST is said to have ascended above all heavens, that HE MIGHT FILL ALL THINGS, Ephes. 4:10, by which is noted a substantial nearness and filling of all things not only by reason of power, but also by reason of nature and the subject, as is evident from Jerem. 23:24, Wisd. 1:7. Wherefore, session at the right hand of God is not a local dwelling in the kingdom of blessedness, as Zanchius wishes; not the possession of the patronage of a gracious GOD, as Enjedinus in 'Explic. loc.', page 81. and in a certain way Franciscus Davidis; not the incarnation itself, as the Weigelians wish; not subsistence in the person of the λόγος (Word), which is undeservedly imputed to us; not judicial power, or that CHRIST is constituted judge of all, as Estius explains, although that is not excluded; not some intermediate dominion, as Piscator and other Reformed; not a dignity merely less than the Father and next to him, as Grotius; not superiority in place of the Father, as if now not the Father, but the Son rules in the Church, or some eminence of the Son above the Father, as Socinus and his followers, and even the Jesuit Maldonatus contend; not the communion of one Divine nature with the Father, as Athanasius 'de communi essent.', although it cannot be denied that it can be inferred from the session at the right hand of GOD; not a bare manifestation of Majesty previously hidden, as Thummius, etc., but Divine dominion under the aforementioned reason. Which is further confirmed, both from the session attributed to GOD partly by reason of dominion and gracious presence in the Church, 1 Samuel 4:4, 2 Samuel 6:2, 2 Kings 19:15, Psalm 8:2, and Psalm 99:1, Isa. 37:15, partly by reason of the universal Divine presence in the whole universe, Psalm 5:9, Psalm 11:4, Psalm 47:9, Psalm 89:15, Psalm 93.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Τοσύτῳ κρείττων γενόμενος τῶν ἀγγέλων) In tantum prælatus Angelis, nempe illo tempore, quo ad dextram Patris consedit.

Ὅσῳ διαφορώτερον παρ’ ἀυτὲς κεκληρονόμηκεν ὄνομα) Quanto majore titulo insignitur, nam κληρονομεῖν נחל aut ירש est certum mansurumque jus adipisci, quomodo ha- bebantur apud Ebræos res hæreditariæ, id est, res soli, ut alibi diximus. Διαφορώτερον excellentius. Sic & in- fra cap. 8, 6.

Rectius hic in προθέσει ab officio Sacerdotali, qua purificationem, vel expiationem peccatorum nostro- rum fecit, jam progredi dicitur Apostolus ad offi- cii istius alteram partem, intercessionem; vel ad sta- tum exaltationis à statu exinanitionis: quia ut in sta- tu exinanitionis fecit peccatorum nostrorum ex- piationem, ita in exaltationis statu intercedit pro nobis, ut actu fruamur expiatione facta, cum ideo ad dextram Dei consederit, teste Apostolo Rom. 8, 24. Describit autem hanc exaltationem Christi, nostri causa factam cum absolute, tum comparate. Absolute per consessum in dextra Majestatis in excelsis, de quo hæc observentur: (1) Quando sederit. (2) Se- cundum quam naturam. (3) Quomodo?

Quod ad primum, consedit post factam purifica- tionem peccatorum nostrorum, adeoque post passio- nem & mortem. Non ergo ab æterno ad dextram Dei sedit: nec ab ipso incarnationis momento: quia post passionem demum ingressus est in gloriam Luc. 24, 26. postquam è torrente in via bibit exalta- vit caput Ps. 110. ult. postquam obediens factus est, usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, exaltavit eum Deus, & nomen ei dedit supra omne nomen, Phil. 2, 8. 9.

Quod ad alterum, secundum humanam, non vero secundum divinam naturam factam esse ex- altationem Christi, certum est. Nam quamvis Christus θεάνθρωπος consederit ad dextram Ma- jestatis, non tamen ut Deus, sed ut homo, adeo- que non ratione utriusque naturæ: principium est utraque natura, sed terminus est natura humana: sicuti ὑπερύψωσις passive accepta humanæ naturæ tantum convenit, utpote secundum quam unctus est ob regnum, Psal. 45, 6. secundum quam exalta- vit caput Psal. 110. ult. secundum quam crucem su- stinuit, & dextrâ Dei exaltatus, CHRISTUS & Dominus factus est Actor. 2, 32, 36. constitutus su- per omnia opera Dei Psal. 8, 6. hæres omnium Ebr. 1, 2. Secundum eam naturam exaltatus est Chri- stus, secundum quam exinanitus est. At exina- nitus est non secundum divinam, sed tantum se- cundum humanam naturam. Secundum divi- nam naturam omnis expers est mutationis, & pror- sus immutabilis: adeoque nec exinaniri, nec ex- altari secundum divinam naturam potuit. Conf. Luc. 24, 26. Phil. 2, 8. 9. Secundum quam natu- ram mortuus est, & resurrexit, & ascendit in cælum, secundum eam etiam sedet ad dextram Dei Marc. 16, 19. Actor. 2, 33. Rom. 8, 34. Ephes. 1, v. 20. seq. At secundum humanam naturam mortuus est, & resurrexit, & ascendit in cœlum, non autem secun- dum divinam naturam. Quo facit illud ἀπ᾽ ἄρτι Matth. 26, 64. Adhæc, secundum quam natu- ram accepit nomen excellentius præ Angelis, vel no- men supra omne nomen, secundum eandem exal- tatus est, & sedet ad dextram Dei. At nomen ex- cellentius & supra omne nomen accepit secundum humanam naturam, non secundum divinam. Conf. Phil. 2, 9. cum hoc loco. Nec vero dextra Dei sic à CHRISTI divina natura distinguitur, ut secundum hanc ad dextram Dei sedere dici queat: Et refertur expresse sessio illa ad humanam natu- ram, secundum quam visibiliter judicium admi- nistrabit Matth. 25, 31. Confer. Johan. 5. vers. 27. Quæ omnia luce sua radiant. Ideo Basilius M. contra Eunom. l. IV. Quod Dominus celebratur & accepit nomen super omne nomen, intelligere opor- tet de incarnatione, & non de Deitate. S. Atha- nasius orat. II. contra Arrian. Scriptura non in- telligit substantiam verbi exaltatam, sed ad huma- nitatem ejus hoc spectat, & propter carnem exaltari dicitur. Hieronymus in cap. II. Phil. Quia se as- sumtus homo humiliari dignatus est, divinitas, quæ humiliari non potest, eum, qui humiliatus fuerat, exaltavit; sed & illi donatum est nomen, quia antea non habuit.

Quod ad tertium, quomodo consederit ad dex- tram Majestatis in excelsis, notetur (1) verbi ἐκάθισεν sensus, quod in præterito effertur, quod occuparit consessum post mortem, per quam facta est expiatio peccatorum per ascensionem in cœ- lum: hæc enim resurrectionem sequitur, & ses- sionem ad dextram Dei antecedit, juxta Symbo- lum Apostolicum, secundum Marc. cap. 16. vers. 19. Aliud ergo est consedit ad dextram, aliud sedet ad dextram: illo actus consessus: hoc status: illo oc- cupatio regni Actor. 3, 21. hoc regimen ipsum de- signatur. Intelligitur enim non sessio localis, vel proprie ita dicta, ut sedere Lev. 24, 39. adhibetur; sed ut à Paulo explicatur regiminis Psal. 111. 1. Cor. 15, 25. oportet ipsum regnare, usque dum ponat inimicos scabellum pedum suorum, & infert hæc sessio subjectionem, prout relata sunt regere & sub- jici Psal. 8, 6. Ebr. 2, 8. Ephes. 1, 20. 1. Petr. 3. v. ult.

uti & exaltatio Christi regnum infert, Actor. 2, 33. c. 5, 31.

(2) Dextra Majestatis significatio. Dextra Dei intelligitur, quæ non notat corporeitatem, aut locum aliquem in cælis, ut Bulling. in tract. de verb. Cœnæ vult, & in Compend. Relig. Christ. l. 6. c. 8. Beza ad part. III. Brentii de sess. ad dextr. DEI vol. I. oper. pag. 601. Confessio Helvetit. in art. XI. quia DEUS Spiritus est, nec dextram materia- lem vel corpoream habet. Quid quod neque dextra & sinistra Christi, cum ad illam fideles & ad hanc infideles constituendi dicuntur in die Pantocritico, Matth. 25, 32. 33. tam situationem, quam Majestatem CHRISTI infinitam, miseri- corditer salvantem, beantem & glorificantem notet, ita ut ad eandem collocati dicantur, qui ad ejusdem perfectam fruitionem admittuntur ab una parte; ab altera vero Majestatem itidem infinitam Christi designet, juste vindicantem & damnantem, ad quam collocati dicuntur, qui ejus vim atque onus in horrore sempiternorum sup- pliciorum sentiunt, interprete B. Dorscheo in Pentadec. Disp. 12. th. 23. Neque per dextram Dei virtus finita denotatur, aut vicaria, secunda- ria, media, ut Zanchius l. II. de Nat. Dei quæst. 4. Bergius, & alii volunt, aut beatitudo finita, vel qualis est electorum propria, quo abeunt alii non- nulli è Calvinianis cum Zanchio: Sed infinita virtus & potestas dominatrix Filii Dei: ea nempe Dei potentia, quæ creavit omnia Psal. 85. vers. 5. conservat & gubernat omnia Psal. 21, 9. Ps. 96, 4. Psal. 138, 7. Psal. 145, 16. Amos. 9, 2. Actor. 4, 27. Esa. 40, 1. cap. 48, 2. mutare potest omnia Psalm. 77, 11. ac mirabilia facit, Exod. 15, 6. & ubique præsens est Psalm. 139, 9. cui tribuitur Ecclesiæ collectio Psal. 80, 16. Israëlitarum deductio Ex. 15, 6. Psal. 44, 4. liberatio ab omnibus malis Psal. 138, 7. quæ omnia tam falso de potestate creata, quam absurde de loco certo cæli accipiuntur. Nec vero dextra Dei relate accepta, ad quam nem- pe evectus est CHRISTUS, τοπικως, vel de loco, aut de virtute quadam finita dicitur. Non enim fas est Deo affingere geminam dextram, vel aliter se habet dextra Dei in Vet. Testam. aliter cum in Nov. Test. ad dextram Dei Christus evectus di- citur: imo una est eademque dextra Dei, & ad dextram, hoc est, potentiam Dei infinitam evectus Christus dicitur, non ad aliam aliquam Dei dex- tram, aut virtutem. Ideo dicitur ea dextra Ma- jestatis h. l. dextra throni Dei Ebr. 12, 2. dextra thro- ni Majestatis, Ebr. 8, 1. dextra potentiæ Dei, Matth. 26, 64. Luc. 22, 69. Et cum ex inductione lo- corum omnium, ubi dextræ Dei nomen occurrit, constet, semper virtutem Dei infinitam denotari, idque de locis aliis in Veter. Testam. indubium sit, nec aliter Actor. 4, 23. cap. 5, 31. usurpetur, quid causæ esse potest, cur significatione toto genere diversa nomen dextræ Dei tum in unico illo loco Vet. Testam. Psal. 110, 1. tum in locis Nov. Test. eundem explicantibus accipiendum sit? Ideo Basi- lius M. lib. de S. S. c. 6. dextra Dei, ait, non signifi- cat locum, sed æqualitatis statum: & Athanasius in quæst. LV. ad Antiochen. cum dextram Dei au- dis, divinam gloriam & Majestatem esse memineris. Tertullian. de carne Christ. dextra Dei est suggestus paternæ claritatis. Gregorius Nyssenus orat. II. de Resurr. dextra Dei per gloriam explicatur, quam CHRISTUS propriam habuit ut DEUS. Da- mascenus lib. IV. de orth. fid. c. 2. dextram Patris intelligimus gloriam & honorificentiam Deitatis, & ut alios jam taceamus ex antiquitate, fatetur ipse

Altingius probl. Theol. part. 1. probl. 45. p. 185. Dextram Dei esse infinitam ipsius potentiam, & glo- riam. Johan. Bergius im Unterscheid, &c. cap. XL. pag. 63. fatetur dextram Dei non esse creatum locum, sed potentiam & virtutem Dei ubique loco- rum operantem.

(3) Totius phraseos, consessus, vel sessionis ad dextram Majestatis, vis: & sessionis istius forma- lis ratio. Duo illa importat: Tum regnum Chri- sti hominis vere infinitum: tum modum accipien- di, & fundamentum accepti regni CHRISTI. Modus includit partim temporis circumstantiam, partim actus præcedaneos, utpote passionem, mor- tem, resurrectionem, ac ascensionem in cælum. Fun- damentum est tum remotum, unio nempe perso- nalis; tum proximum exaltatio ad dextram Patris Phil. 2, 9. Aliud ergo est omnipotenter, omniscien- ter, omnipræsenter regere: aliud sedere ad dextram Dei, quod tale regimen importat quidem, sed sub ista modificatione, & ex illis causis oriundum. Aliud sessio divina, quæ tribus Deitatis personis communis est: aliud sessio ad dextram Dei, quæ CHRISTO propria est, & quidem secundum hu- manam naturam: adeoque non absolute & illimi- tate notat dominium divinum atque infinitum, sed secunda persona Trinitatis, & quidem vi unio- nis personalis, & exaltationis, immediate in omnes creaturas exercitum: quia Filio Dei incarnato convenit, ac respicit κοινωνίαν Majestatis, & ὑ- περύψωσιν, ut & antegressam κένωσιν, καὶ ταπείνω- σιν. Dominium autem infert non absentis, sed præsentis vere divinum, quod sine adessentia ac propinquitate substantiali, naturæ ac personæ il- lius, cui convenit, fingi non potest, & ubicunque est thronus Dei & dextra Majestatis, ibi est natura, quæ sedet in throno Dei, & ad dextram majestatis Divinæ. Ideo ascendisse dicitur CHRISTUS super omnes cælos, ut IMPLERET OMNIA, Ephes. 4, 10. quo notari substantialem propinquita- tem & impletionem omnium non tantum ratione virtutis, sed etiam ratione naturæ & suppositi, è Jerem. 23, 24. Sapient. 1, 7. constat. Quapropter sessio ad dextram Dei non est localis immoratio in regno beatitudinis, ut vult Zanchius; non possessio patrocinii DEI gratiosi, ut Enjedinus in explic. loc. pag. 81. & certa ratione Franciscus Davidis; non ipsa incarnatio, ut Weigeliani volunt, non subsistentia in persona τοῦ λόγου, quod immerito nobis imputatur; non judiciaria potestas, vel quod constitutus est CHRISTUS judex omni- um, ut Estius explicat, tametsi illa nonRich exclu- tur; non media quædam dominatio, ut Piscator, aliique Reformati; non solo Patre minor, eique proxima dignitas, ut Grotius,; non superioritas vice Patris, quasi jam non Pater, sed Filius do- minetur in Ecclesia, aut eminentia quædam Filii supra Patrem, ut Socinus & asseclæ, etiam Je- suita Maldonatus contendunt; non communio unius naturæ Divinæ cum Patre, ut Athanasius de communi essent. licet eam ex sessione ad de- xtram DEI posse inferri, negandum non sit; non nuda patefactio Majestatis antea occultatæ. ut Thummius &c. sed dominium Divinum sub prædicta ratione. Quod confirmatur porro, tum è sessione DEO tributa partim ratione do- minii & præsentiæ in Ecclesia gratiosæ, 1. Samuel. 4. vers. 4. 2. Samuel. 6. vers. 2. 2. Reg. 19. vers. 15. Psalm. 8. vers. 2. & Psalm. 99. vers. 1. Esa. 37, 15. partim ratione præsentiæ universalis Divinæ, in toto universo, Psalm. 5. vers. 9. Psalm. 11. vers. 4. Psalm. 47. vers. 9. Psalm. 89. vers. 15. Psalm. 93.

## 1:5
Vers. 5.

Fifthly, Christ is not said to be the Son of GOD above all others, but is μονογενὴς, the Only-begotten Son of God, not one of many sons, above whom he might excel, but the only- and sole-begotten, and the unique Son of God by nature, whereas other sons of God are so only by grace, the unique one by generation from the essence of the Father, which belongs to none of the others. And therefore he is called the Son of God μονοτρόπως. And the Apostle observes that it was said to none of the Angels: You are my Son, namely in the proper sense. For although Angels are also called sons of God, that happens not in the proper sense but metaphorically, because they are called sons of God only by similarity to God by reason of wisdom, holiness, and power. But Christ is the Son of God properly so called and is his own, ὁμοούσιος to God the Father, of the same essence with him, Rom. 8, 32. John 5, 10. ch. 10, 30. Therefore, in the sense of the Psalmist, he is not a Son from among many, but the unique Son, by a filiation different in its whole genus from the υἱότητι of the Angels.

For to whom did he ever say of the angels) As if he were to say he not only did not give this title to common Angels, but not even to any of those אַחַד הַשָּׂרִים הָרִאשֹׁנִים of the first princes, as it is in Dan. 10, 13.

“You are my Son, today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). Which you may rightly translate: O my son, today I have begotten you. From the mystical sense of the Psalm he argues correctly, because all the Hebrews confessed that that Psalm, although fulfilled in David in some way (concerning which sense we have spoken at the Psalm itself), nevertheless pertains in an arcane and more sublime sense to the Messiah himself: who is to be called the Son of God above all, begotten by God, that is, raised to authority, not only over men, but also over the Angels, as Abarbanel acknowledges. This passage of the Psalm indeed seems to be applied by Paul to the resurrection of Christ from the dead, Acts 13:33, but there that very resurrection is considered as the beginning of the glory of Christ. That word “Today” is accustomed to be used concerning times of notable joy, as can be seen in Jeremiah 1:10, 18.

Sixthly, Grotius also perverts the word γεγέννηκα [I have begotten], because it denotes not generation, as it sounds properly, but metaphorical elevation, namely to authority. The Jew Abarbanel or any other of the Rabbis is not to be heard here; but the Holy Spirit. They are blind, and leaders of the blind; they know nothing of the eternal generation of the Son of God. But if you listen to the Holy Spirit, it is necessary to understand generation properly so-called, because one must not depart from the proper sense unless necessity compels. The generation through which the Son of God is what he is, true GOD consubstantial with the Father; because he says, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”: A generation which is not only above every angelic lot, but above every creature which has been created, or could be created, because in that eternal “today,” that is, in simple eternity, the Son was begotten before anything was, before all ages, since the Son was begotten the same [one] through whom the ages were created, who was with the Father before the world was created, had glory with the Father from eternity, the image of the invisible GOD, in whom and through whom all things were created, visible and invisible, the radiance of the glory of the Father, and the character of his hypostasis, GOD whose throne is eternal, that immutable Jehovah God, who created heaven and earth, just as [is said] here concerning the Son of GOD and elsewhere throughout.

In the Grotian gloss we find these things lacking: First, that he has not correctly observed the connection and method of the Apostle, although that is common to him with most others: Because the Apostle is not proving what he had said in the words immediately preceding concerning Christ, that he had obtained a more excellent name; but he is now undertaking the proof of his thesis concerning Christ viewed in respect of his Divine nature: which had to be proved in the first place, before he proceeds to the proof of the session of Christ at the right hand of God, by which he obtained a more excellent name, which befits him according to his Human nature.

Secondly, that he explains that more eminent name as the title of Son of GOD, when it should rather be understood of majesty and Divine and trans-Angelic glory.

Holy Scripture affirms. The Son is ὁμοούσιος (consubstantial) with the Father, because he is begotten from the essence of the Father: for generation is the communication of essence: Ὁμοαιώνιος (co-eternal), because he was begotten in the ante-mundane today πρὸ πάσης κτίσεως (before all creation), Coloss. 1, verse 15, from eternity Prov. 8, verse 32, Mich. 5, verse 2; ὁμόθρονος (co-throned), because he is King on Mount Zion, possessing the nations and all the ends of the earth; ἰσοδύναμος (equal in power) and equally with the Father ἀυτεξόσιος (self-authoritative) in confounding laws, and in binding with chains, destroying, and cutting off any enemies whatsoever; ἰσότιμος (equal in honor), because it is a sin to rebel against him just as it is against the Father, trust is to be placed in him, he is to be embraced with the religious kiss of faith, his wrath is to be feared, and blessedness is to be hoped for from him, as is clear from the context of the whole Psalm. Add that this act of the generation of the Son of God precedes the divine decree concerning the anointing of Christ, and his introduction into the kingdom of grace, nay, into the inheritance of the whole world, and is laid down as a foundation for it, Psalm 2, 7, 8. But that decree is eternal. Whence it follows that the Son of God must be eternal, and truly co-eternal with the Father.

Seventh, Grotius confuses the υἱότητα (sonship) and birth of Christ with his exaltation, which are most distinct in the Apostolic προθέσει (purpose). According to the former, he is called the Son of God, the brightness of the Father's glory, and the express image of his substance; according to the latter, he is called the heir of all things, raised to the right hand of Majesty, made better than the Angels, and endowed with a more sublime name. And would this not be a tautology: I have this day begotten thee, that is, I have placed thee at my right hand, and have subjected all things to thee? Therefore, ask of me, and I will give thee the inheritance of all things, that is, I will subject all things to thee, and I will place thee at my right hand? The Son of God was indeed addressed in this decree, who is begotten from eternity, but not as he is begotten from eternity; and his eternal generation is alleged as the foundation from which he can rightfully ask, in the order of his voluntary emptying and ineffable economy, for what he already occupies and possesses by title, whence also when Christ asked with the act, he sends away his sonship, John 17, 5.

Eighth, in Acts 13, 33, the passage of the Psalm is not explained by the raising of CHRIST from the dead, but it is taught that God raised up his Son, the Messiah, from the fathers, concerning whom David prophesied in Psalm 2.

Ninth, it is not evident from Jerem. 1, 10, 18 that the particle היום (today) is used for times of notable joy. For there it simply denotes the present time, the day of Jeremiah's calling; but here, where the discourse is about the Son of God begotten from the substance of the Father, of the same essence, power, and glory as the Father, 'today' cannot be understood temporally, because it concerns generation, which is an internal act and therefore eternal in the Father.

Therefore, היום (today) is understood differently when the discourse is about a human act, and differently when it is about a Divine act, and therefore an internal one. A temporal 'today' pertains to Angels and other creatures, in whom countless sons of God have been constituted: but this TODAY is above Angels and creatures, and it anticipates all that time in which enemies could tumultuously rise against God and the Messiah. For while the human race was contaminating itself with idolatry throughout the world, it was already decreed in the Divine 'today' to establish the kingdom of God and to constitute its head, that is, from eternity, and already before, in the order of nature, the generation of the Son of God took place in that היום, which that decree presupposes, as we observed a little earlier.

The Grotian gloss being therefore dismissed, the continuity of the text must be taught. For the Apostle had proposed to treat of two things concerning the person of CHRIST:

First, concerning his Divine nature; then, concerning the excellence or eminence of his Human nature. By reason of the former, he first attributes to him the name of the Son of GOD, through whom GOD the Father has spoken in these last days as the Teacher of the New Testament, and called him the same ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χαρακτῆρα τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ (brightness of his glory, and the express image of his substance). He also called him the same creator of the ages, and the preserver of all things, and thus the true GOD. Therefore, in order to demonstrate these things among the Hebrews, he uses testimonies of the Old Testament, arguing from a conceded principle: because those were authentic to them. And he proves that the Son of GOD is the Messiah, the Teacher, or Prophet of the New Testament from Psalm 2, 7, concerning which [he speaks] of the laws proposed by God and our Messiah, the bonds of which Kings and peoples and nations strive in vain to break, tumultuously rising against him in vain, easily to be confounded and cut off, unless they submit themselves.

The sacred singer also prophesied concerning the doctrine of salvation to be received by faith by the Kings and Judges of the earth, and by all who do not wish to perish in the way by his wrath, but to be saved by trust in him. The Apostle therefore teaches that he is the Son of GOD begotten from the Father's essence from eternity, by adducing this testimony of the Psalm, not as a Son by creation, nor by reason of a concession of power, like the Angels: But by a much more eminent reason, which far exceeds the condition and lot of all the Angels. For to which of the Angels said he at any time: Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee? But since there is nothing more eminent above the Angels except GOD, as far as nature or essence is concerned, the Son of GOD must be of the Divine nature, and thus, since there is only one GOD by nature, of the same nature and essence with God the Father: You see, says Chrysostom, that the name of Son signifies τὴν γνησιότητα (genuineness), propriety, and kinship. And certainly if he is not a proper and genuine Son, and nothing is proper and genuine other than that which is from him, how does he confirm it is from him? For if he is Son by grace, he is not only not more excellent than the Angels, but even lesser. How? Because just men also have been called sons, and the name son, unless it be a proper and genuine son, cannot show excellence. And signifying that there is a certain difference between creatures and the Creator, see what he says: For to whom did he ever say: You are my Son, today I have begotten you.

Similarly Theophylact: For when we say Son, we certainly claim that he was begotten from the Father. Wherefore if he had obtained the name of Son by grace, he would be clearly inferior to the Angels here. But that, I have begotten you today, expresses nothing else, except that from the beginning, and from the time the Father is, he has begotten the Son. For just as I am, he says, he uttered that in the present tense, so he said today, which especially befits God, so that he may show himself to be eternal. For although times may be manifold, they are nevertheless present to GOD. Therefore Estius did not render the sense badly: Which of the Angels is of such excellent nature or dignity, to whom it is read that it was ever said by GOD: You are my Son? namely singularly, and particularly: As this is accustomed to be said by the Father to the Son, whom he begat of himself, especially if he is the only-begotten. For if some rich man had adopted several sons for himself, but had one natural son, to this one and alone he would say: You are my Son, especially if he also added that, because I have begotten you. Which stands more rightly, than when Genebrardus explains it concerning the temporal generation of CHRIST, or others concerning the resurrection from the dead with the Socinians, which we have refuted in the Anti-Crellius, such as Sasboldus, Jansenius, and others among the moderns, as Estius notes and does not entirely deny; however much those may appeal to Athanasius, Theodoret, Euthymium, and Fulgentium; and these, indeed, to Origen, Hilary, and Chrysostom. Yet all of them understand that 'You are my Son' as referring to the proper and natural Son of God, even if they vary regarding the latter words. But that is beside the point: Since the reason for τῆς χότης is rendered to them, and these words are not brought forward here by the Apostle in any other sense, as he is not occupied with proving either the temporal generation of CHRIST, or the resurrection from the dead, or the placement at the right hand of God, but wishes to demonstrate this, that CHRIST is the eternal Son of GOD begotten before the ages, as being he through whom the Father founded the ages.

Similarly, Augustine, whom others follow, interprets it concerning the eternal generation of the Son of God from the substance of the Father; since eternity is most openly expressed by the word 'today,' by which the present day is signified, because eternity is one day, and the same always present, as Estius does not deny, and Cornelius à Lapide proves against the Socinians: 'Better and more aptly,' he says, 'does St. Augustine in Psalm II, and Chrysostom, Theophylact, Anselm, and St. Thomas, accept this passage here concerning the eternal and Divine generation of the Son of GOD.'

Whence TODAY signifies the present duration, which is always present, indivisible and immovable, and embraces all time past, present, and future, such as eternity is.

TODAY therefore, that is, in and from eternity, in which there is one today, one instant, one now, one stable and perennial present.

It follows, therefore, that Psalm II does not speak literally of David in himself, as the Rabbis wish, nor even of David insofar as he was a type of CHRIST, as Jansenius wishes, but that it was dictated and written properly, in itself, and primarily concerning Christ: For only to CHRIST does 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you' apply. And: 'Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession,' and many other things which are said in the Psalm.

Καὶ πάλιν) That is, in another place. Thus you have πάλιν in Matthew 4:7, Romans 15:10, 11, 12, 1 Corinthians 3:20. So also below 11:13, 10:30. Thus Virgil also used 'rursum' in the 3rd Aeneid: 'Rursum in secessu' etc. And that passage is 2 Samuel 7:14.

This is the second testimony concerning CHRIST the Son of God, which now does not deal only with the same, as he is begotten from eternity within the most simple complex of the Divine essence: But at the same time it predicts his excitation from the body of David, when he proposed to discourse concerning the Son of GOD exhibited in the flesh, and to demonstrate that JESUS is that Son of God begotten from eternity by the Father.

From this combination of passages, therefore—namely, that of David concerning the eternal generation of the Son of GOD, and the promise given to David that when he himself has slept with his fathers, God will raise up seed after him, that is, the Son, from his loins, who himself shall be the Son of God—it is clear that JESUS the Son of David, who is from his seed according to the flesh (Romans 1:3), is that Son of GOD of whom the Father said: 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you,' that is, that the Son of David and the Son of GOD are one person, and thus the eternal Son of God had to be born in time from David, according to the flesh, following the promise made to David, who would build a house for the name of the Lord, for whom GOD wishes to confirm the throne of his kingdom forever: which Gabriel interpreted as the Son of Mary from the lineage of David, who is the same Son of the Most High GOD (Luke 1:32 ff.).

It is clear secondly that that passage in 2 Samuel 7 does not deal with anyone other than CHRIST, because if it dealt with another, the demonstration sought from it by the Apostle would not hold correctly.

It is clear thirdly that the same does not deal with a certain Son of GOD by grace, or by adoption, but with the Son of GOD by nature, or by eternal generation. But if it dealt with Solomon, he could not be understood as the natural Son, or be used to demonstrate the Apostolic purpose concerning the Divine person of Christ our Teacher and Priest, namely that he is the eternal Son of GOD, through whom the ages were founded, the splendor of the glory and the character of the Father's substance, upholding all things by the word of his power. Just as the passage of the Psalm cannot be understood of anyone other than the natural Son of GOD, begotten from eternity by the Father: so that passage which is at hand cannot be taken as referring to another Son of GOD, or another respect of paternity, by virtue of the Apostolic demonstration sought from both passages, and the conclusion which the Apostle infers, as it had to be demonstrated according to the Apostolic proposition.

It is clear fourthly that it was acknowledged among the Hebrews, both in the present prophecy and in Psalm II, that it deals with CHRIST according to the literal sense; otherwise the Apostle could not have instituted a demonstration from it among the Hebrews, as he assumes this as an agreed-upon fact, that these things were said concerning CHRIST.

Ἐγὼ ἔσομαι αὐτῷ εἰς Πατέρα, καὶ αὐτὸς ἔται μοι εἰς ὑὸν) That is, I will be to him in the place of a Father, and he shall be to me in the place of a Son. I will use him as fathers use a son, and I will protect him as fathers are accustomed to protect sons. And these words taken from the Greek, Solomon, of whom the passage in question treats, in the common sense is a type of CHRIST, not in all things (the following words, which cannot be applied to CHRIST, show this) but in that he excelled in wisdom, reigned in peace, ruling over many nations, and built a temple to GOD. And in this manner Isaac Benarama adapts these words to the Messiah.

Grotius corrupts the sense of the prophecy in more than one way, because what GOD said: I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son, that is, a Son, according to a very well-known Hebraism, this Grotius perverts, saying that it is only in the place of a Father and in the place of a Son; and furthermore he renders this sense utterly jejune and foreign: I will use him as fathers use a son, and I will protect him as fathers are accustomed to protect sons.

Because 1. it is against the plain letter. It is one thing to be a Father, another to be in the place of a Father; it is one thing to be a Son, another to be in the place of a Son. It is one thing to use someone as fathers use a son, another thing entirely to be a son, just as it is altogether different to protect someone like a Father, and to be the Father of someone.

2. Against the plain intent of the prophecy. For the things which GOD predicts there concerning the seed or son of David are far more magnificent; to whom GOD promises not only protection, but whom He predicts will be a Son to Him ὁμούσιον καὶ ὁμόθρονον [consubstantial and co-throned]; because he does not have an eternal throne and kingdom, unless he is the eternal and true GOD by nature. 3. Against the open assertion of the Apostle; who teaches that this predicate is too eminent to befit any of the angels. But does it not befit the angels that God uses them as sons, protects them, nay, sustains them, as sons?

4. Against the Apostolic intention, because he intends to prove here not protection, not the use of Christ in the place of a son, but the Divine nature of Christ, that he is the true and natural Son of God, through whom he created the ages, who sustains all things, who made expiation for our sins.

5. Against the meaning of the parallel passage, Ps. 2:7, which deals with the Son of God begotten from the essence of the Father and consubstantial.

6. Against the Apostolic connection. For such a son, whom God the Father only uses as a son, and whom he only protects as fathers are wont to protect sons, can be neither the creator of the ages, nor the heir and lord of all, nor the preserver of all things, nor the expiator of our sins: nor can he sit at the right hand of the Majesty, much less be the Son of God, the brightness of his glory and the express image of his person.

7. Against the truth of the person of the Son of God. For Christ is not merely a vice-Son, but is truly the Son of God, his own Son, Rom. 8:32. The only-begotten Son, John 3:16. The Son μονογενὴς παρὰ τῶ Πατρός, John 1:18. The firstborn, as the Apostle will teach in the following testimony: Πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως, the firstborn before every creature, Coloss. 1:15. Again, God the Father is not to Christ merely in the place of a Father, but is his true and own Father, John 5:19, who begat the Son in that eternal today, Ps. 2:7, as an image to himself, of the same essence and glory, which to wish to deny is to contradict the Apostle and to cross over to the camp of the Arians. He does not merely use Christ for a Son, he does not merely protect him as a Son, but through him he created the ages, and appointed him heir of all things, and made him sit at the right hand of his Majesty, and gave him an eternal kingdom.

8. Against the office of Christ, the foundation of which the Apostle designates here: For the foundation of the doctoral office is not that Christ is some vice-son, but that he is that only-begotten Son from the Father, who is in the bosom of the Father, and has declared to us the God whom no one has ever seen, John 1:18, not a mere man, as the prophets were in the Old Testament; nor is the foundation of the priestly office that God uses him for a Son, but the Apostle placed this foundation for the fact that Christ made expiation for our sins through himself, that Christ is not a mere man, like the priests who expiated sins in the Old Testament, but the eternal and consubstantial Son of God.

9. Against the state of Christ's exaltation. For he could not place a vice-son at the right hand of the Majesty on high, he could not give to a vice-son a name which is above every name. That dignity is so great that it falls to no angel, however eminent; nor does it befit any but the only-begotten and natural Son of God, since it implies a plenary usurpation of the Divine Majesty possessed in his own person, and a glory truly Divine and immense, which does not befit, nor can befit, any vice-son, Isa. 42:8.

Secondly, Grotius is mistaken when he says that 2 Sam. 7 deals with Solomon in the literal sense, which he calls the common one, as a type of Christ, not in all things, but in that he excelled in wisdom, reigned in peace, ruled over many nations, and built a temple to God. He followed in that part Isaac

Benarama the Jew, when he ought to have followed the Holy Spirit, according to whose mind the prophecy made to David does not deal with Solomon, but with Christ: It does not have a double sense, but, like all places of Scripture, only a single one: because the Holy Spirit, not speaking ambiguously in the manner of Apollo, hid a different sense in the same words, but speaks openly in his word, and willed that there be only a single sense of one oracle, which he has revealed to us in clear words, so that we might not be tossed about in ambiguity, and so that we might not wander from his intention and mind. Nor does anything occur here which does not befit Christ, but only Solomon, or which befits Solomon as a type; the word did not deal here with the wisdom of Solomon, nor with his peaceful reign, nor with his empire over many peoples, much less did it constitute Solomon a type of Christ in this, at least in this oracle: Nor does the prophecy speak of the structure of the material Solomonic temple, but of the structure of the spiritual temple to be erected to the name of the Lord by the son to be raised up after the death of David. All of which have been sufficiently demonstrated regarding the passage 2 Sam. 7.

Guilielmus Estius and Cornelius à Lapide bring forward different explanations of the oracle here: First, that the same passage deals according to the letter with both Christ and Solomon, which opinion Cornelius à Lapide notes is that of Lyranus, Burgensis, and Abulensis. But that there are multiple senses of one statement, and those literal, is no more to be admitted than that there are multiple essential forms of one thing. And Estius admits here that there is no scripture in which multiple historical or literal senses concur at the same time. Nor can it be said that some things are said here of Solomon and some of Christ. For the subject is not diverse, but only one in that prophecy: Therefore, the predicates which occur here are all uttered concerning that one subject. If you say that one subject is expressed and another is implied, there will still have to be established a double literal sense of the same statement or word, even if placed only once, namely one overflowing from the word itself, and the other silent or implied, which is absurd.

Secondly, that according to the literal sense it treats of Solomon, according to the mystical sense of Christ: which opinion of Eucherius, Thomas, Angelomus, Cajetan, and Ribera, Estius and Cornelius make their own. But that is by no means to be approved.

For 1. a double sense of the same saying is thus still feigned, one literal, the other mystical, which is repugnant to the simplicity and perspicuity of Scripture.

2. A double subject is introduced, when it treats of only a single subject, of the seed of David, to be raised up after his death, which is Christ, Jer. 23, 6. Whence therefore is another subject brought into the text, of which no mention is made in the same? It is said that the antitype is understood under the type, but it is not proven. A type as to the fact can represent an antitype, Solomon Christ: But that something is said of the type, and at the same time is to be understood of the antitype, will be taught by no example, nor does it befit the speech of the Holy Spirit, much less that it treats of Christ somewhere, but that Solomon is simultaneously understood from the mind of the Holy Spirit.

3. The Apostle's argument is weakened, since firm arguments and proofs and demonstrations are sought only from the literal sense.

4. The sense of the oracle is overturned, because we have taught in its proper place that it treats solely of CHRIST.

5. Cornelius à Lapide confesses that it is said most properly of CHRIST: I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son. He confesses that the kingdom of CHRIST, that is, the Church, is absolutely eternal, as is said here. Certain things, he says, are more appropriate to CHRIST than to Solomon, such as what is said here: I will be to him a Father, and I will not take my mercy away from him, and thy house shall be faithful, that is, thy family and Royal progeny shall be stable, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. Which words, although they may in a certain way apply thinly and as it were by hyperbole to Solomon, in that GOD did not cast him out of the kingdom, as He cast out Saul, but continued and perpetuated his kingdom through his descendants for four centuries, namely until the Babylonian captivity, in which the state of Israel collapsed, and the people of the Jews were clearly overthrown, which is a certain kind of eternity. Yet these things apply more fully and integrally to CHRIST. For it is said most properly of CHRIST: I will be to him a Father, etc. Why, therefore, does he depart from this most proper sense without cause?

6. What is brought forward to the contrary for Solomon from 2 Chronicles 22 does not pertain to this oracle (to which the passage in 2 Chronicles 17 corresponds, but it refers to another vision, and thus it is irrelevant).

Thirdly, they bring forward the interpretation concerning CHRIST alone, which is that of Lactantius in book IV of the Divine Institutes, chapter 13, and of Rupert in book II on the book of Kings, chapter 30, of Sixtus of Siena, Sasbold, Catharinus, Galen, and several others, which is entirely to be preferred: for which these arguments are urgent:

1. That it concerns him who is to be raised up after David has died, as his seed, not indeed to be elevated to the kingdom as his successor.

2. That his throne is to be established forever, whereas the kingdom of Solomon, as regards the ten tribes, failed in his son, and finally failed completely in Zedekiah.

3. That his mercy is not to be taken away: which does not appear to be the case with Solomon, who, having abandoned the worship of God, sinned so gravely that many doubt his salvation.

4. That the Apostle affirms that this was said of none of the Angels, and thus teaches that CHRIST is therefore greater than the Angels. How, then, was it said of Solomon, a mere man? Where Estius retreats in vain to the notion of a type: These grand and magnificent things would never be said of Solomon, unless CHRIST had been prefigured in him as in a certain type and image. For besides the fact that this begs the question—that such grand things are said of Solomon, or of any type of CHRIST, which were never said of any of the Angels—Solomon was not a type of CHRIST in that he was adopted as a son, nor did either Estius or Grotius establish the notion of a type in that, nor does the notion of a type have a place here. Grant that he was a type of CHRIST in his kingdom: but to establish a type of the pre-eternal generation of CHRIST or of his natural sonship in his adoption as a son is most absurd. That this is what the Apostle is dealing with here by design is evident and undeniably certain.

Add (5) that Isaiah chapter 9:5, among other praises appropriate only to CHRIST, also recounts those which occur here. (6) And that Gabriel interprets it thus in Luke 1:32, 33. (7) As does St. Peter in Acts 2:30. (8) And also David himself in Psalm 89, etc. See what has been said regarding 2 Samuel 7 and the parallel passage in Psalm 89, as well as Psalm 72:7 ff.

& compare especially what has been observed regarding verse 19 of 2 Samuel 7. As for the present matter, the blessed Dorscheus acknowledges, even if with the blessed Glassius he refers that prophecy to Solomon at the same time, that the relationship of sonship, such as it is between God the Father and the Messiah, is far too sublime to be communicable to Angels: so far is it from being able to apply to Solomon. And so he continues, when he says: I will be to him a Father, it does not indicate a finite patronage and benefit, but infinite glory and Majesty: nay, I say, the hypostatic character of the active generation, truly divine and proper to God the Father, just as through those words, and he shall be to me a Son, the hypostatic character, which the Son as such has through passive generation, as he is the brightness of his glory and the express image of the Father's person, according to the Apostle's interpretation, is indicated.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Quinto, Christus non supra omnes Filius DEI dicitur, sed est μονογενὴς, Unigenitus Dei Filius, non unus è pluribus filiis, supra quos emineat, sed uni-& soligenitus, & unicus Dei Filius per naturam, quum alii filii Dei tantum sint per gratiam, unicus per generationem ex essentia Patris, quod nulli aliorum convenit. Ideoque μονοτρόπως dicitur Dei Fi- lius. Et nulli Angelorum dictum esse observat A- postolus: Filius meus es tu, scilicet sensu proprio. Quanquam enim Angeli etiam filii Dei dicantur, id tamen sit non sensu proprio sed Metaphorico, quia solum per similitudinem cum Deo ratione sa- pientiæ, sanctitatis, & potestatis Filii Dei dicun- tur. Christus autem Filius Dei proprie dictus & proprius est, Deo Patri ὁμοούσιος, ejusdem cum ipso essentiæ, Rom. 8, 32. Johan. 5, 10. cap. 10, 30. Sensu ergo Psaltis non est Filius è multis, sed Fi- lius unicus, filiatione toto genere diversa ab An- gelorum υἱότητι.

Τίνι γὰρ εἶπέ ποτε τῶν ἀγγέλων) Quasi dicat non mo- do vulgaribus Angelis hunc titulum non dedit, sed ne ul- li quidem ex illis אַחַד הַשָּׂרִים הָרִאשֹׁנִים τῶν χόντων τῶν πρώτων, ut est Dan. 10, 13.

Υἱός με εἶ συ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε) Ex Græco Pal. 2, 7. quod recte verteris: O mi fili, hodie te genui. Ex mystico sensu Psalmi recte argumentatur, quia Ebræi omnes fatebantur, eum Psalmum, quanquam in Davide aliquo modo impletum (quo de sensu diximus ad ipsum Psal- mum) sensu tamen arcano & sublimiore ad ipsum Messi- am pertinere: qui supra omnes Filius Dei dicendus sit, Deo genitus, id est, ad imperium evectus, non in ho- mines tantum, sed & in Angelos, ut agnoscit Abarbaniel. Videtur quidem hic locus Psalmi ad exercitationem Chri- sti è mortuis aptari à Paulo, Actor. 13, 33. sed ibi ipsa illa exitatio consideratur, ut initium gloriæ Christi. Solet illud Hodie usurpari de temporibus insignis lætitiæ, ut vi- dere est Jerem. 1, 10. 18.

Sexto, pervertit etiam Grotius vocem γεγέννηκα genui, quod non generatio, uti sonat propria, sed evectio Metaphorica, nempe ad imperium denote- tur. Non hic audiendus Judæus Abarbanel aut alius quisquam è Rabbinis; sed Spiritus sanctus. Illi cæci sunt, & cæcorum ductores, nihil norunt de generatione æterna Filii Dei. Si autem Spiri- tum sanctum audias, generationem proprie dictam intelligere oportet, quia non est à proprio sensu recedendum, nisi cogat necessitas. Generatio- nem, per quam Filius Dei est, quod est, verus DEUS Patri consubstantialis; quia ait, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te: Generationem, quæ est non modo supra omnem Angelicam sortem, sed supra omnem creaturam, quæ condita est, vel condi po- tuit, quia in æterno illo hodie, id est, simplici æterni- tate Filius genitus est, antequam quicquam esset ante omnia secula, quum Filius eadem genitus sit, per quem secula condita sunt, qui fuit apud Patrem ante conditum mundum, gloriam habuit apud Pa- trem ab æterno, imago DEI invisibilis, in quo & per quem omnia condita sunt visibilia & invisibilia, effulgescentia gloriæ Patris, & character hypostaseos ejus, DEUS cujus thronus æternus, Jehovah Deus ille immutabilis, qui cælum & terram condidit, quemadmodum hic de Filio DEI & alibi passim

In Grotiana glossa hæc desideramus: Primo quod συνέχειαν & methodum Apostoli non recte observarit, quanquam id ipsi cum aliis plerisque commune sit: Quia Apostolus non id probat, quod verbis immediate præcedentibus dixerat de Christo, quod nomen excellentius fortitus sit; sed aggrediatur jam probationem theseos suæ de Christo ratione Divinæ naturæ spectato: quæ pri- mo loco probanda erat, antequam procedat ad probationem sessionis Christi ad dextram Dei, qua ille excellentius nomen consequutus est, quæ ipsi convenit secundum Humanam naturam.

Secundo, quod nomen illud eminentius de ti- tulo Filii DEI explicet, quum potius de maje- state & gloria Divina & trans-Angelica intelli- gendum sit.

Scriptura sacra affirmat. Filius Patri ὁμοούσιος, quia ex essentia Patris genitus: Generatio enim est essentiæ communicatio: Ὁμοαιώνιος, quia in hodie antemundano πρὸ πάσης κτίσεως genitus, Coloss. 1. vers. 15. ab æterno Prov. 8. vers. 32.
