(3) He is called by the LXX translators and Paul ὁ θεὸς with the article: But the word θεὸς with the article implies the true and eternal God, as the adversaries admit. (4) An eternal throne is attributed to Him. But an eternal throne befits none but the supreme and eternal GOD. (5) His throne is described as immense and truly divine, namely by that periphrasis which in the Scriptures befits only the government and throne of the supreme GOD. Cf. Psalm 9:5, 8; Psalm 11:4; Ps. 47:9; Psalm 89:15; Ps. 97:19. What of the fact that David nowhere ascribes a throne of God, such as is indicated by him here, to any but the one and only supreme God, as is evident from the passages cited: nor does he know of a divine throne, except the unique, namely the immense and eternal throne of God. Concerning a created and finite divine throne, neither David nor any other inspired author has handed down anything; mention is always made of only one throne, which is truly eternal and immense, and proper to the supreme GOD. Cf. Isa. 6:1; 66:1; Dan. 7:9; Matt. 5:34; 23:22; Acts 7:49; Rev. 3:21; 4:7, 9, 10; 5:1, 7; 6:16; 7:10, 15; 14:5; 19:4; 21:5; 22:3. Since, therefore, a divine throne is ascribed here to the Son of God, we conclude invincibly that He is the supreme God Himself. (6) He is called אדון Lord of the Church in verse 11, which name likewise is attributed to God alone in the Scriptures. (7) The divine honor of adoration is claimed for Him in verse 12, which is inseparable and incommunicable from the divine essence, Isa. 42:8. (8) Here God, whose throne is for ever and ever, is opposed to the angels as creatures founded by God, and is therefore to be worshipped by the angels. Therefore, that God is not of the number and rank of creatures, but is God by true nature, since between creatures founded by GOD and God the Creator, there is no middle ground. (9) The same is celebrated as that one Jehovah God, whom all אלהים ought to worship, Psalm 97:8. Cf. Heb. 1:5. (10) Finally, that same God is the Lord who founded the earth in the beginning, and whose works of hands are the heavens, who will remain immutable for eternity, as is most clearly taught in the same place, Heb. 1:10. But it is certain and indubitable that that Lord who founded the earth in the beginning is the eternal and supreme God, as is universally acknowledged.

Enjedinus objects in 'Depravations of Scripture Passages', p. 389: (1) That those words, 'Thy throne, O God,' are to be taken concerning Solomon according to the literal and true sense, not only do the most learned interpreters believe, but the thing itself teaches: that they are applied to Christ only mystically and because of a similarity. (2) That the same words describe not God, but a man. For he who is anointed, who has God as his superior, who has companions, is not the eternal God, but a man, or at any rate a creature. (3) That those words can be explained conveniently in such a way that the word God is said neither of Solomon nor of Christ, and is not in the vocative, but in the nominative case, and is understood of God the Father in this sense: God is thy throne for ever, that is, God will establish a throne for thee for ever. Which gloss of Enjedinus is emulated by Grotius in his annotations on Psalm 45:7. (who is to be considered in no lower, if not rather a higher, place in distorting the testimonies of Scripture among the Neo-Photinians) where he annotates thus: It can be translated from the Hebrew: Thy seat, O God

| (enduring) for ages and generations. Seat, that is, firmness. (4) Socinus in 'Animadversions', p. 8, says that it appears from this testimony that Christ is God in that way in which a created thing can be God (because all these things were said first of Solomon) and that as God, or insofar as He is God, He has His God, and is anointed by Him above His companions. Which Schlichtingius executes at greater length in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews on this passage.

But it is answered to (1) Although the Jews, and the Judaizing Calvin, and several others of his disciples assert that Psalm 45 was written on the occasion of the wedding of Solomon with the daughter of the King of Egypt, and treats of Solomon in the literal sense; yet it is most false, as Enjedinus says, that by the consensus of all the most learned interpreters those words: 'Thy throne, O God,' are explained of Solomon according to the letter. Paræus indeed, who undertook to defend his teacher Calvin against the accusation of Dr. Aegidius Hunnius, was forced to admit in 'Calvinus Orthodoxus', book 2, chapter 31, page 227: That most of the ancients wished for the spiritual marriage of Christ with His Church to be sung according to the letter under no type, whose opinion he says he does not disapprove, not only because almost every verse has something more divine or greater than what could befit a mortal King, but also because the sounder Jews themselves admit that the Psalm treats of the Messiah, and the Chaldean Targum expressly names Christ several times, as in verse 3: 'Thy beauty, O King Christ, therefore thou hast loved justice,' etc. Furthermore, Paræus denies on p. 228 Calvin, or others, to apply everything to Solomon, but only certain things to him indeed ὡς τύπῳ [as a type], but everything fully and solidly to Christ alone, and certain things to Solomon in no way, such as that this King is absolutely called God having an eternal throne, that he is anointed above his fellows, that he has sons in number and excellence not yielding to the Fathers, whom he will set as Princes over the whole world, that finally he holds a name admirable in every generation and generation to be celebrated by the peoples forever and ever, as it is in v. 17 and 18. But if indeed these things can in no way be understood of Solomon, or any other mortal king, but pertain to Christ alone, which Pareus says Calvin teaches at length, why should the whole Psalm not be sung of one and the same subject, of one and the same King? But these things in passing. For our blessed Hunnius, who may be consulted, deservedly chastised both Calvin and his defender Pareus. Andr. Rivetus, who is likewise a not ignoble disciple of Calvin, in his Comment. in Pf. Proph. Decad. p. 301, confesses: that it is acknowledged among all interpreters of the Psalms, not even excepting the Hebrews, that Psalm XLV is an epithalamium, or nuptial song, and that a spiritual one, and therefore not to be understood σαρκικῶς [carnally], but μυsτικῶς & πνευματικῶς [mystically and spiritually] concerning the spiritual marriage between Christ and the Church: and he observes that Calvin, Bucer, Junius, and others of his own, likewise Jansenius with some other Papists, acknowledge that most things in this Psalm cannot apply to Solomon, which must necessarily be expounded of the Messiah and his bride the Church: nor would the Apostle in Heb. I have attributed two verses of this Psalm to Christ, when he was dealing with the Jews, unless it had been placed beyond controversy that this Psalm pertains to the Messiah. As for those words in particular, 'Thy throne, O God,' that they ought by no means to be understood of Solomon according to the literal sense, but are to be understood of the Messiah, most of the ancient Doctors of the Church acknowledge, the Targum and the sounder Hebrews profess, and it had been placed beyond controversy among the Hebrews at the time of the Apostles, as also among most Christian Doctors of more recent times (whatever may be the case regarding Calvin) it seems in no way can be denied: it is so far from being the case that, by the consensus of all the most learned interpreters, these things are referred to Solomon according to their true and literal sense. Nor indeed can they be referred to him: Because the name of God is not attributed absolutely to Solomon, nor to any other mortal man anywhere in the Scriptures, nor can it be attributed, since it belongs in the proper sense to no one but the one supreme God; it is also certain that nowhere is any singular created person designated in the sacred writings by the plural name אלהים: nor was the throne of Solomon eternal, since his kingdom lasted only 40 years, nor can his descendants be included, as that which follows concerning the scepter of uprightness does not apply to them, since a most wicked son succeeded Solomon, nor were his grandsons any better, with a few exceptions. What of the fact that the straight rod does not even apply to Solomon himself, since he shamefully fell away from God? But if we truly grant this to the Jews with Enjedinus, that the present saying of the Psalmist in its simple, true, genuine, and literal sense does not look to Christ, but to Solomon, the Apostolic argument in Hebrews 1:8 will be rendered utterly inept and weak for convincing the Jews or Hebrews, with whom the Apostle was dealing: finally, if even by reason of a type that divine eulogy at least fits Solomon, who does not see that it is in vain to disparage the angels through the Apostle's citation, because in its own way it is not even denied to Solomon?

To (2) Response. We can concede that he who is anointed, who acknowledges God as his superior, who has partners and companions, is not, as such, and in respect of that nature by which he is anointed, according to which he acknowledges God as superior and has companions, the eternal God. But it by no means follows from that that the same one is not the eternal God in some other respect, or if those things argue and infer the true human nature of Christ, that the divine nature does not have a place in him, unless one assumes through a vain begging of the question that the divine and human nature cannot concur in the same person.

To (3) Response. The Apostolic text itself clearly refutes the depravation of Enjedinus and Grotius, referring the name τꭢ Θεꭢ in the vocative case to the Son of GOD, ὁ θρόνος σου, ὁ Θεὸς, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τꭢ αἰῶνꚙ, thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever. For the fact that it ought to be rendered thus, and not that those things cohere as subject and predicate, thy throne is God, or the very distinction employed, which is found in all codices without diversity, proves it. For a comma or distinction is never inserted between those things which cohere as subject and predicate, which we see done here ὁ θρόνος σου, ὁ Θεὸς, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, which words, placed thus, cannot be rendered otherwise than in this way: Thy throne, O God, is for ever. (2) Rule of interpretation. For one must not deflect in one's interpretation from the customary and received manner of speaking to a new, unusual, and nowhere encountered one. But it is familiar in the Holy Scriptures that a throne is ascribed to God, and that the justice and eternity of that same throne are celebrated, when the kingdom of GOD is in question. Especially, however, in the Psalms, such as Psalm 7:5, 8; Ps. 11:4; Ps. 47:9; Ps. 89:15; Ps. 94:2; 97:19; Isa. 6:1 and 66:1; Dan. 7:9; Matt. 5:34; 23:22; Acts 7:49; Rev. 4:7, etc. But that God himself is called the throne or seat of some King is foreign to the Scriptures and utterly unusual. (3) The scope of the Apostle. The Apostle is engaged in teaching that the Son of GOD is far superior and more eminent than the angels. He uses the argument that the Psalmist testifies concerning the Angels that they were created by God and are his ministers, Ps. 104:4; but concerning the Son, that he himself is God, and his throne is eternal. But what would that opposition be, what the force of the argument, if the sense were this: Angels are created by GOD, and are ministers of GOD: but the Son of GOD's throne and seat is God, or God will establish the throne for the Son for ages. Are not lordships, powers, principalities, thrones also ascribed to angels, Col. 1:16, and do not those thrones last for ever, with God preserving them? Thus, therefore, it can be said of angels that GOD establishes angelic thrones for ever, and so the Apostolic antithesis will perish entirely, the argument for the eminence of the Son of GOD will be completely enervated. What of the fact that according to Grotius's gloss, the perpetuity of the kingdom is not even inferred by these words: Because he explains 'seat' as 'firmness,' and ascribes eternity to GOD, not to him whose seat is commemorated: Thy seat, that is, thy firmness, O God, understand 'lasting for ever.' What, therefore, could this do for the Apostle's demonstration? What sublime thing will be said about Christ? For is not God the firmness of all creatures, lasting for ever? Added to this is (4) the comparison of verse 10, where there is likewise an apostrophe directed to the Son of God, who is addressed in the vocative case. Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth, which the adversaries indeed strive to pervert, but in vain. Andreas Rivetus, on this place of the Psalm, urges the lack of a similar example. For who ever speaks thus, or what example will the adversaries bring forward in which a verb is missing that ought to have been most expressed: And in this place they want 'thy throne, O God,' to be missing, understand 'will establish': Who also will forbid, if it is permitted to supply anything at will, that someone equally impious might supply the word 'will destroy' or 'will shatter'? Add that there is no place for that ellipsis in the Apostolic citation of this oracle, where ὁ θρόνος is said in the nominative case, and not τὸν θρόνον in the accusative case. Finally, the unanimous consensus of all the Doctors of the Church, who without any doubt accept the word ὁ Θεὸς in the vocative case, and from that have always believed that Christ is called God in these words, the Christian Church has always believed. Nor did the LXX Interpreters render it otherwise, whose version the Apostle followed. Aquila expressly expressed the vocative: ὁ θρόνος σου Θεὲ εἰς αἰῶνα, κὶ ἔτι. What of the fact that Socinus admits (l. c.) that he, whose throne is described here, is pointed out as GOD in this passage, and that Schlichting acknowledges this in his Comm. on the Epistle to the Hebrews, page 62? ὁ Θεὸς is placed as a nominative for a vocative, for the speech is directed to him: as also Crellius in his book on GOD and divine attributes, chapter 13, page 10, where he asserts that ὁ Θεὸς is said for Θεὲ or ὦ Θεὲ, which finally the Racovian N.T. version renders in this way, then Stuhl, O GOtt, bleibt in alle Ewigkeit.

To (4) Response. We deny that these things were first said of Solomon. The contrary was proved above. Therefore, it is not permitted to infer from this: that Christ is God only in the way that a created thing can be God. But that Christ as God, or insofar as He is God, has His own God, and was anointed above His fellows, that does not appear in the least from the words of the Apostle: διὰ τοῦτο ἔχρισέ σε ὁ Θεὸς, ὁ Θεὸς σου, says the Apostle. Schlichting comments on this passage as follows: The first word God, ὁ Θεὸς, can also be referred to Christ, and it will be a Nominative placed for a Vocative, which often happens with this word, and to GOD Himself, the Father of Christ, just as He is first simply called God, then called the GOD of Christ, as if to say, God anointed you, that God, I say, who is your God, that is, who notably does good to you. But even if we admit the former sense, which the Latin Vulgate also exhibits, nothing else is inferred, however, than that he who is truly GOD acknowledges the Father as GOD: but not that he acknowledges him as GOD according to that nature according to which he is GOD. Whence it is easier to gather that in CHRIST there are two natures, the one according to which he is truly GOD, the other according to which he acknowledges the Father as his GOD. And these things are from scattered papers. Now what is to be desired in the distortion of Grotius is by no means obscure. Let us weigh it a little more distinctly. First, Grotius deserves censure in this, that he says Paul brought these things forth from memory. For it is established that he wrote while being borne by the Holy Spirit. And what else is it to say πῦρ φλέγον than πυρὸς φλόγα: Although the Royal copies, not like those of Caraffa, have πῦρ φλέγον, but like this Paul, πυρὸς φλόγα. (2) He perverts the sense of the passage. For neither the Psalmist nor the Apostle teaches that there is nothing great in the name of Angels and ministers: But the Apostle shows from the passage of the Psalm that Angels are creatures of GOD, and his ministers. That the names of Angels and Ministers are not attributed to wind and flame: But both indicate that Angels are of a spiritual nature, and created by GOD like a fiery flame. (3) Grotius makes the predicate from the subject and vice versa, no less against the mind of the Holy Psalmist than against the demonstration of the Apostle, nay even against his own opinion delivered on Ps. CIV. But that has already been dealt with in the Annotations on the Psalms. There are indeed others, who, with Augustine also leading the way in the Psalms and Gregory the Great in Homily III on the Gospels so transpose the words, but with a far different sense, not about the names, but about the nature of the Angels, in this way, with Estius as interpreter: He who makes those, whose nature is spiritual and fiery, that is, vehemently active, his messengers and ministers. Or, he who uses spiritual and immaterial substances for messengers, couriers, and ministers. But here Barth. Petri rightly corrects Estius, rendering this sense: He who made those whom he had decreed to be his messengers and ministers, the same he made substances entirely immaterial or clearly spiritual, the same he made as it were a burning fire, bright indeed in knowledge, and burning with charity. But that the Hebrew name ruahh also signifies a spiritual and clearly immaterial substance, although Jansenius in his annotations on Psalm CIII seems to deny it: The same nevertheless concedes it in his last annotation on the last Psalm, and it is clear that it must be conceded from Gen. XLI. v. 38, chap. XLV. v. 27. Exod. XXVIII. v. 3, chap. XXXI. v. 3, chap. XXXV. v. 31, and in many other places. Franciscus Ribera, however, refutes here at length not only the Hebrews, Calvin, and Beza, but also Vatablus and Jansenius, and requires modesty in Jansenius, a learned and pious man, who says that these things are brought forward by Paul in a different sense than that in which they were spoken by David: teaching that the words in Hebrew sound thus, who makes his angels Spirits, and observing that learned men, and those most tenacious of the Hebrew TRUTH, have explained them as being about true Angels with Paul, such as Augustinus Eugubinus, M. Antonius Flaminius, Genebrardus, and others. Benedictus Justinianus says that those are by no means to be heard who think that Paul, having followed the LXX, said something far different than David. For if Paul wished to say something other than what was written by David, he followed not the Holy Scriptures, but the sense of the LXX Interpreters, that is, having neglected the Canonical, he followed the human, or at least the non-Canonical. Which it is a sin to think about the Apostle, especially in establishing a dogma. Franciscus Junius also lashes out at his Calvin here in Parall. l. III, Piscator deserts him in the annotations on this passage. (4) The Apostle does not only aim at this, to compare the titles of the Angels and the Son; but he contends that the nature of the Angels is compared with the nature of the Son of God, and he teaches that those indeed were created by GOD; but that the Son is God by nature; and furthermore that they as creatures of GOD minister to GOD; but he demonstrates that He, as the Son ὁμοούσιον to the Father, is of the same dominion and glory with the Father. (5) That Psalm XLV is about Solomon is the mind of the Jews rather than of the Catholic Church. Yet Grotius chose to side with them here, rather than with the Christians. We have, however, dealt abundantly against that Jewish gloss in the annotations on Ps. XLV. Although indeed it could be admitted that an allegory from the Solomonic history occurs almost perpetually in this Psalm, yet that it is about the Messiah alone according to the letter is proven both by what is said about his Spouse, the Church, about her interior adornment v. 14, about the worship and veneration of the Spouse, about the subjection of the nations v. 13, about children being begotten in the place of the Fathers (the Jewish nation), and Princes being established throughout the whole world v. 17. Which in no way fit the Solomonic Spouse, and by what is sung about the Spouse, such as that he is the most beautiful among the sons of men, v. 3. (Conf. Cant. v. 10 seqq.) grace is poured out, most eminent above all, most enriched with eternal blessing, most powerful and most glorious with the word of truth and justice, as if with some equestrian and military equipment v. 4, 5, 6, most high with an everlasting and immense throne, v. 7, most august with a scepter of power and perpetual justice in the same verse: for procuring justice, and destroying iniquity, anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit without comparison and measure v. 8, most instructed for adorning the universal Church, as his Spouse, with spiritual beauty v. 9, 10. The Lord of the Israelitic Church, and of the nations throughout the whole earth to be followed with religious worship and to be celebrated forever v. 12, 13, 17, 18. Most enriched with a very copious and innumerable offspring, whom he himself will establish as princes throughout the whole world (Conf. Apoc. I. 6, c. V. 9.) all of which, as it is certain that they fit the Messiah the King, so it is clearer than the sun that none of them fit Solomon. Therefore the Chaldean paraphrast, and with Grotius admitting it, most of the ancient Jews explained the Psalm about the Messiah: nor does Chrysostom hesitate to provoke the more recent Jews as being to be convinced by the present Psalm in his Comm. on this passage, against whom also Justin used the same entire Psalm in Dial. with Trypho and Cyprian in l. II, c. Jud. c. 29. (6) It is false that the name of God was attributed to Solomon, and that Solomon was a type of CHRIST even in respect of this name of GOD, which name Elohim in the Hebrew language is in its proper meaning proper to GOD, since it denotes the adorable divinity, nor does it occur anywhere in the plural concerning any singular created person: because it denotes a person who has in common with others that same most singular essence, which alone is to be adored: such as no created person is. Grotius himself admits that that plural name, when it is attributed to one, belongs to God alone. (7) The Davidic oracle in Ps. XLV is most basely corrupted by Grotius, moved not by a Davidic spirit, but by that of the recent Jewish τῶν χριστομάχων and the Arian spirit. But because we have already discussed those fabrications in the aforementioned place of the Psalm, we do not wish to do what has already been done here. Cornelius à Lapide in Erasmus thus refutes the Grotian sense: It would be an inept and insipid sense if it were taken in the nominative: For what will be the sense, if one interprets it thus: Thy throne, O Christ, is God Himself? For God is not a seat, but one sitting on a seat or throne, and Christ does not sit in the Father, but at the right hand of the Father. Again, the Deity is not the seat of humanity, but rather on the contrary, humanity is the seat, nay, the footstool of the Deity. It is certain, therefore, that this is the meaning: O GOD, that is, O Son, who are true God, your Royal and divine throne is eternal, you are an eternal King, you have an eternal kingdom and throne. The sources indeed disagree, in which the name Elohim is distinguished by accents partly from the preceding word, partly also from the following ones, whence however the LXX may have rendered that word in the nominative, it was nevertheless done in such a way that it can be explained in the vocative case, just as Eusebius explained it in Demonstratio Evangelica, book IV, chapter 15, and Schlichting admits that the nominative is used for the vocative: provided that the speech is directed to Christ, as Aquila translates it θεέ. But nowhere is God called the throne of CHRIST in the Holy Scriptures; but the throne of GOD is described here as possessed commonly by the Father and Christ, Apoc. V. 6, 7. (8) What Grotius notes here regarding verse 9 can be judged from the same place, where they have been recalled for examination as if in their proper seat. (9) What would that gloss, 'God himself will sustain you in a kingdom that will never fail,' contribute to the demonstration of the Deity of CHRIST? But the Apostle here is occupied in demonstrating the eternal Deity of Christ. (10) That Christ therefore attained dignity above all men and Angels because he taught nothing other than what was just and honest by word and example is not taught here: but rather he is said to be anointed with the oil of gladness or of the Holy Spirit for this end, that he might administer his kingdom with divine justice, concerning which see what has been said regarding the place in the Psalm. That love of justice, as the Blessed Dorfcheus, is constitutive of justice, and hatred of iniquity is destructive of iniquity. For he understands that most singular, incomparable, and Messianic justice, from which the Messiah himself is called Jehovah our righteousness, Jer. XXIII. 6, through which we are made the righteousness of GOD in him, 2 Cor. V. 21, which is the proper effect of that admirable anointing, and flows from the union of the divine and human nature, and is that justice which the Bridegroom of his heavenly Bride communicates as the greatest ornament. It is indeed that justice of most perfect obedience, through which the divine justice is satisfied, by whose virtue heavenly things are reconciled to earthly things, Col. I. 20, which compensates for that which Adam lost, Romans V. verse 18, and is imputed to us, Rom. III. 12, c. IV. 5. This justice the Messiah loves as his own ἀποτέλεσμα (result), which he consummated in the state of his emptying. He loves it, however, not only theoretically by contemplating its perfection and admirable tempering from divine mercy, but also practically by working it, perfecting it, and for its sake bearing our injustice, Is. LIII. verse 4, 1 Pet. II. v. 24. Thus also by iniquity he understands not only some particular one, but the universal one, in which all adhere, to whomsoever the Messiah is in communion of flesh and blood, on account of which he calls them his μετόχους (partners). That, however, he hates with a hatred not of simple displeasure and aversion, but of real destruction and overthrow according to the Proto-Evangelium, in which such enmity is promised to be founded in the seed of the woman, which will advance against the whole kingdom of Satan for the destruction of his head and power, Heb. II. verse 14, 1 John III. 8. (11) Not by that, as two nominatives are brought forward אלהים אלהיך, but as in the former clause ὁ θεὸς is the vocative case; so it does not appear why it should be accepted otherwise in the latter, nor was it accepted otherwise by the Interpreters. Add Eusebius, book IV, demonstr. cap. 15, Jerome to Principia. (12) Since the Chaldean and many Rabbis accept the Psalm concerning the Messiah, as Grotius admits, why is the Christian himself worse than the Jews in it, twisting the same to Solomon in the literal sense? (13) The eternal, divine, and infinite throne ὑπεραγγελικὸς (above the angels), since even Angels are called thrones, Col. I. 16, but here the throne is above the Angels, in which is ὁ Θεὸς (God), whose ministers are the angels, that throne from which is every blessing, grace, truth, justice, Ps. XLV. 3, 5, 6, as also the Scepter not finite, but infinite (concerning which compare Psalm CX) are brought forward by the Apostle to demonstrate likewise the divine nature of the Son of GOD, and they demonstrate it solidly. Whence the Bride, the Church, is commanded to adore this King as her Lord, v. 12. And therefore this passage is most aptly subjoined to the previous Psalm XCVII concerning the same King to be adored by the Angels. Nor is it brought forward in vain also from Psalm XLV, verse 8, even if it treats of the anointing according to the human nature, according to which he is beautiful beyond the sons of men, and has lips in which grace is diffused, to be exhilarated with the oil of gladness, having partners and being in need of anointing for the right administration of his kingdom: But partly because that anointing presupposes the union of the human nature with the divine, because it brings in infinite gifts of the Holy Spirit, John III. v. 34, nay, it formally consists in the very real and total communication of the Holy Spirit regarding immense gifts, then because through this ointment he is anointed absolutely and παραμετόχως (beyond his partners), with which he dispenses his gifts in incomparable variety, Heb. II. 14, Eph. IV. 8. John I. 16, then because through this ointment Christ governs on an everlasting and divine throne, v. 8, then because through it he is made King of angels and men: since it is not a convivial anointing, as Schlichting wishes, such as Ps. XXIII. 5, Luke VII. v. 42, but Priestly and Royal and Prophetic: since here a King is celebrated, v. 2, not feasting, but reigning, girded with a sword, and riding in glorious array, equipped with arrows, established on a Throne with a Scepter, and the final cause of the anointing is assigned as the operation of justice and the destruction of iniquity, primarily indeed in the Priestly office, in which by the sacrifice exhibited he consummated justice: nevertheless also in the Prophetic, in which the Messiah rode prosperously in his splendor with the word of truth, and spoke justice, v. 5. (Compare Is. LXIII. 3.) as also in the Royal [office], in which he attacks, defeats, and drives away the enemies of his justice and the authors of injustice: partly because that anointing is the foundation of Christ's exaltation above the angels, of which the Apostle next intends to treat v. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Καὶ πρὸς μὲν τοὺς ἀγγέλους λέγει) Id est, de An- gelis, quem esse Lucæ ἰδιωτισμὸν modo annotavimus. Si- milis loqutio Jerem. XIV. Ὁ ποιῶν τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα, καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πυρὸς φλόγα) Et hoc ex Græco LXX. nisi quod hic scriptor locum memoriter citans pro πῦρ φλέγον posuit πυρὸς φλόγα, ubi Aquila πῦρ λάβρον. Symmachus πυρίνην φλόγα. Sensus hujus loci est : Nihil magnum est in no- mine Angelorum & ministrorum, cum ea nomina Scriptu- ra det etiam vento & flammæ. Nam omnes creaturæ, quibus Deus extra ordinem utitur, eo nomine venire dixi- mus ad Gen. III. 23. & Maimonides Duce dubitantium II. 6. Ac sicut ventus & flamma Angeli dicuntur: Ita con- tra Angeli quidam Seraphim, id est, flammæ, & Cherubim, quo nomine olim videntur significari venti. Confer Psalm. XVIII. 11. & LIV. 3. quia & efficacia & celeritas melius per res nobis cognitas exprimi nequit. Sed priorem sen- sum magis exigit series loci in Psalmo, nec obstat articu- lus ille τοὺς, qui creditur subjectum notare non prædica- tum. Nam & apud Atticos, & apud nostros scriptores ar- ticulus ille sæpe abundat. Vers. 8. Πρὸς δὲ τὸν υἱὸν) Hoc vult, Filio dari titulos multò eminentiores. Constabat autem inter Ebræos, quod & modo attigimus, Salomonem in multis rebus fuisse ty- pum Messiæ, & qui ei dantur tituli, eos multò sublimiore sensu in Messiam competere. Ὁ θρόνος σου, ὁ Θεὸς, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος, ῥάβδος εὐθύτητος ἡ ῥάβδος τῆς βασιλείας σου. Vers. 9. Ἠγάπησας δικαιοσύνην, καὶ ἐμίσησας ἀνομίαν, διὰ τοῦτο ἔχρισέ σε ὁ Θεὸς, ὁ Θεός σου ἔλαιον ἀγαλλιάσεως παρὰ τοὺς μετόχους σου) Pla- ne eadem verba, quæ in Græco Psalmi ejus, qui in Ebræis XLV. Græcis XLIV. nisi quod in Græco est εἰς αἰῶνα αἰῶ- νος sine articulis. Et in Manuscripto hoc loco pro ἀνο- μίαν est ἀδικίαν pari sensu. Pro ὁ Θεὸς in Ebræo est אלהים, quod nomen pluribus quidem sive Angelis sive Judicibus dari solet: at cum uni tribuitur, Deo soli con- venit, quia tunc est oratio ἑλικτικὴ pro אלהה אלהים, ut alibi diximus. Sensus ergo est: Deus ipse est sedes tua perpetua, id est, si Salomonem respicimus: Sicut sedes in- concussos tenet homines: Ita Deus te semper in regno susten- tabit. Si vero Christum: Deus ipse te sustentabit in re- gno nunquam desituro. Per sceptrum Regium in Salomo- ne μετωνυμικῶς intelligitur ratio regiminis: In Christo ser- mo Evangelii ab ipso primum publicatus. Dilexit Salomon justitiam & odit injustitiam, nempè à prima ætate: ideo præ cæteris non popularibus tantum suis, sed & fratribus electus est à Deo in Regem, 1. Paral. XXVIII. v. 5. quod unctione significatur, 1. Reg. I. v. 34. Jesus dum vitam egit mortalem, nihil aliud quam justa & honesta omnia verbo & exemplo docuit, arguens his contraria. Ideo post mortem excitatus dignitatem supra omnes homines, imo & supra Angelos est consequutus, quæ dignitas hic hu- mano more significatur unctionis vocabulo. Sic χριστὸν αὐτὸν ὁ Θεὸς ἐποίησε, Actor. II. v. 36. διὰ τοῦτο sume ut διὸ Philipp. II. v. 9. Est autem more Græco Accusativus ἔλαιον positus eo sensu, quo Latini Ablativum usurpant. Et ἔλαιον ἀγαλλιάσεως dicitur id, quod causam det summi gaudii. Vide Johan. XV. 11. XVII. 13. Verterunt alii in Psalmo ἐλαίῳ ἀγλαϊσμοῦ, alii καλωπισμοῦ, δόξης, κίσμα. Pro μετόχους Symmachus posuit ἑταίρους. Sunt autem duo nominativi אלהים אלהיך ille Deus, quem tu colis. Locum hunc de Messia interpretatur Paraphrastes Chal- dæus & Rabbini multi.

Novam jam demonstrationem, eandemque iterum per collationem cum Angelis pro asseren- da infinita Deitate CHRISTI aggreditur Apostolus, quæ est ordine quarta: quæ Angelos à Deo conditos esse, Deique ministros è Psal. CIV. 4. docet v. 7. Filium DEI autem non esse creatu- ram DEI, sed verum cum Patre DEUM, non mi- nistrum DEI, sed σύνθρονον DEI Patris, cujus thronus æternus, quique etiam secundum natu- ram humanam oleo lætitiæ, Spiritus Sancti donis immensis unctus est, è Psalm. XLV. v. 7. demon- strat, quæ unctio locum non haberet, si Christus ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος tantum esset. Quomodo enim homo merus donis infinitis Spiritus Sancti dita- ri atque ungi potest, aut ut Johan. III. vers. 34. dicitur Spiritus Sanctus ei dari ἐκ ἐκ μέτρου non ad mensuram, hoc est, immensa & infinita ra- tione. Sed duo illa priora hic proprie urgentur, immediate divinam naturam referentia, unde argumentum ἀμετακίνητον: Qui à Spiritu Sancto vocatur ὁ Θεὸς DEUS, & cui, ut DEO, tri- buitur thronus æternus, is verus sit natura Deus oportet. At de Filio DEI verum est antecedens. Ergo & consequens. Assumptum è Psalmo con- stat: E quo proinde non tantum verba illa, qui- bus vocatur Deus, & agitur de throno ejus æter- no, sed etiam alia de unctione adjecta adducun- tur, ut constet, de qua persona sacrosanctæ Tri- nitatis hæc dicantur, vel dicta esse ad Filium, ad Messiam, unctum illum Domini, eò plenius intel- ligatur. Quæ prolixe & solide adversus hæreti- cos Chrysostomus exposuit & adhibuit: Vide, quo- modo & quam dilucide dividat creaturas & Crea- torem, ministros & Dominum, verumque ac pro- prium hæredem & filium ac servos. Ad filium au- tem dicit: Thronus tuus DEUS in seculum secu- li. Ecce regni signum. Virga æquitatis virga re- gni tui. Ecce rursus quoque aliud signum regni. Deinde rursus de eo, quod est carne indutum: Di- lexisti justitiam, & odisti iniquitatem: Propterea unxit te, Deus, Deus tuus. Quid est Deus tuus? Nam quoniam magnum est loquutus, id rursus le- nit & mitigat. Hic & Judæos, & Pauli Samosateni asfeclas, & Arianos, Marcellumque & Sabellium feriit & Marcionem. Quomodo? Judæos quidem, ostendens duas personas Deum & hominem. Alios autem, Pauli, inquam, Samosateni asseclas, quod hæc dicat de æterna substantia & increata essentia. Nam ad discernendum, & ex adverso distinguen- dum illud Fecit, hoc opposuit: Thronus tuus Deus in seculum seculi. Adversus Arianos autem & rursus hoc ipsum, & quod non sit servus. Si autem creatura, servus. Adversus Marcellum autem & alios, quod sint duæ personæ divisæ per hyposta- sin. Adversus Marcionistas autem, quod divini- tas non ungitur, sed humanitas. Deinde præ par- ticipibus tuis, inquit; Quinam autem sunt partici- pes, nisi homines? Hoc est, Christus accepit Spiri- tum non ad mensuram. Vides, quemadmodum ser- moni de natura increata conjungit etiam sermonem de dispensatione. Quid est hoc dilucidius? Vides, quemadmodum non sit idem creatura, & id, quod est genitum. Non enim divisisset, & ex adverso ad distinguendum illud Fecit subjunxisset. Ad Filium autem dixit: Thronus tuus, Deus, in seculum seculi. Quem sequutus pariter est Theophylactus. Nec aliter Theodoretius: Per hæc, inquit, apertè osten- dit, Angelos quidem creatam habere naturam: U- nigenitum autem increatam & æternam. Thronus enim tuus, Deus, inquit, in seculum seculi. Atque hoc quidem certè testimonium Arii blasphemiam convicit. Ostendit enim æternum Verbi thronum, & personarum dyade exegit Sabellii confusionem. Hoc ipsum autem etiam obstruit os impudens Ju- dæorum. Hæc luculenta sunt ex consensu anti- quitatis & Ecclesiæ Catholicæ.

Sed juvat uberioris confirmationis ergò argu- mentum Deitatis Christi, prout id quondam con- trà Socinianos assertum fuit, his adjicere. Ita au- tem id habet & hoc loco. Deus ille, cujus thro- nus in seculum seculi, est verus & æternus DEUS. At Christus est Deus ille, cujus thronus in secu- lum seculi. E. Minor è contextu liquet: πρὸς δὲ τὸν ὑιὸν, ὁ θρόνος σου, ὁ Θεὸς, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶ- νος. Ad Filium verò, Thronus tuus, ó Deus, in seculum seculi, & rursus vers. 9. διὰ τοῦτο ἔχρισέ σε ὁ Θεὸς σου Vulgata reddit: Propterea unxit te, ô DEUS, Deus tuus. Sic etiam Racov. Vers. Germ. Drum hat dich, O GOTT, dein GOtt gesalbet. Similiter B. Lutherus, Beza, Piscator, Versio Belgica nupera, aliique. Majorem autem statuminant sequentia: (1) Nomen אלהים, quod Psalm. XLV. 7. unde facta est allegatio Apostolica, habetur, nunquam sen- su proprio adhibetur, nisi de summo illo, & æter- no Deo. (2) Nec ratio ulla est, quare v. 3. vel et- iam 8. nomen אלהים Deum æternum notet, hic non notet. Nullum, inquam, in contextu disparis significationis vestigium apparet. (3) Vocatur à LXX. Interpretibus, & Paulo ὁ θεὸς cum arti- culo: At vox θεὸς cum articulo infert verum & æternum Deum, fatentibus adversariis. (4) Tri- buitur ei thronus æternus. At thronus æternus non nisi summo & æterno D E O convenit. (5) Thronus ejus describitur, ut immensus, vereque divinus, ea scil. περιφράσει, quæ non nisi regimi- ni & throno summi D E I convenit in Scripturis. Conf. Psalm. IX. 5. 8. Psalm. XI. 4. Ps. XLVII. 9. Psalm. XXCIX. 15. Ps. XCVII. 19. Quid, quod nu- spiam David thronum Dei, qualis hîc ab ipso in- digitatur, adscribat, nisi soli & uni summo Deo, ut è locis adductis patet: nec divinum thronum nôrit, nisi unicum, immensum scilicet & æternum Dei thronum. De throno divino creato, & fini- to, nec David, quidquam tradidit, nec quisquam alius Autor θεόπνευστος, semper unius solum thro- ni mentio fit, qui verè æternus & immensus est, summique DEI proprius. Conf. Es. VI. 1. LXVI. 1. Dan. VII. 9. Matth. V. 34. XXIII. 22. Act. VII. 49. Apoc. III. 21. IV. 7. 9. 10. V. 1. 7. VI. 16. VII. 10. 15. XIV. 5. XIX. 4. XXI. 5. XXII. 3. Quum itaque Filio Dei hic adscribatur thronus divinus, invictè con- cludimus, ipsum summum Deum esse. (6) Dici- tur אדון Dominus Ecclesiæ Vers. 11. quod nomen itidem nonnisi soli Deo tribuitur in Scripturis. (7) Honor divinus adorationis eidem vindicatur v. 12. qui ab essentia divina est inseparabilis & in- communicabilis, Es. XLII. 8. (8) Opponitur hic angelis, ceu creaturis à Deo conditis, Deus, cujus thronus est in seculum seculi, adorandus eapro- pter ab angelis. Non ergò Deus ille è numero & censu creaturarum est, sed verus natura Deus, cum inter creaturas à DEO conditas, & Deum creatorem, non detur medium quod. (9) Ce- lebratur idem ut Jehovah Deus ille unus, quem omnes אלהים adorare debent, Psalm. XCVII. 8. Conf. Ebr. I. 5. (10) Denique ille idem Deus Dominus est, qui fundavit terram in principio, & cujus opera manuum sunt cœli, qui in æternum permanebit immutabilis, ut ibid. Ebr. I. 10. luculen- tissimè docetur. Dominum autem illu, qui terram fundavit in principio, esse æternum & supremum Deum ὁμολογουμένον certum est & indubium.

Excipit Enjedinus in depravat. loc. Script. p. 389. (1) verba illa, thronus tuus Deus, de Salomo- ne, secundum literalem & verum sensum accipi- enda esse, non tantum omnium doctiss. interpp. censere, sed rem ipsam docere: mysticè tantum, ac propter similitudinem Christo applicari. (2) Eadem non Deum, sed hominem describere. Qui enim unctus est, qui Deum se superiorem, qui consortes habet, non est Deus æternus, sed ho- mo, vel certe creatura. (3) Verba illa sic commo- de explicare posse, ut vox Deus nec de Salomone, nec de Christo dicatur, neque sit vocativi, sed no- minativi casus, & intelligatur de Deo Patre hoc sensu, Deus est thronus tuus in seculum, id est, Deus tibi thronum firmabit usque in seculum. Quam Enjedini glossam æmulatur Grotius in annotat. ad Psal. XLV. 7. (in detorquendis Scri- pturæ testimoniis Neo - Photinianis non inferio- ri, si non superiori potius censendus loco) ubi ita annotat: Potest ex Ebræo verti: Sedes tua, Deus

| ((durans) in secula & ætates. Sedes, id est, firmitas. (4) Socinus in animadv. p. 8. ex hoc testimonio apparere ait, Christum ea ratione Deum esse, qua res creata Deus esse potest, (quia de Salomone pri- mum ista omnia dicta) & tanquam Deum, seu qua- tenus Deus est, Deum suum habere, ab eoque præ suis consortibus ungi. Quæ pluribus exequitur Schlichtingius in Comment. Epist. ad Ebr. ad h. l.

Respondetur autem ad (1) Etsi Judæi, & Cal- vinus Judaizans, aliique nonnulli ejus discipuli Pfalmum XLV. occasione nuptiarum Salomonis, cum filia Regis Ægypti, scriptum esse, & de Salo- mone agere sensu literali asserant; falsissimum tamen est, quoad ait Enjedinus, omnium doctis- simorum Interpp. consensu verba illa: Thronus tuus, Deus, de Salomone explicari secundum lite- ram. Paræus sanè, qui Calvinum Præceptorem ad- versus accusationem Dn. D. Ægid. Hunnii defen- dendum suscepit, fateri coactus fuit in Calvin. orthod. l. 2. c. 31. pag. 227. Veteres plerosœ, ad lite- ram Christi spirituale connubium cum sua Ecclesia decantari velle sub nullo typo, quorum etiam sen- tentiam sese non improbare ait, non solum quia singuli ferè versiculi habent divinius, vel majus, quàm quod in Regem mortalem competere possit, sed etiam quia saniores Ebræi ipsi fatentur, Psalmum tractare de Messia, & Thargum Chaldaicum ex- pressè aliquoties nominat Christum, ut vers. 3. Pul- chritudo tua, ô Rex Christe, propterea dilexisti ju- stitiam &c. Negat insuper Pareus p. 228. Calvi- num, vel alios omnia Salomoni applicare, sed quæ- dam tantum ei quidem ὡς τύπῳ, omnia autem soli Christo plenè & solidè, quædam Salomoni nullo pacto, ut quod Rex iste absolutè vocatur Deus habens thronum æternum, quod unctus supra con- sortes suos, quod filios habens numero, & præstan- tia Patribus non cedentes, quos orbi universo Principes præficiet, quod denique tenens nomen admirabile in omni generatione & generatione ce- lebrandum a populis in seculum & usque, ut est v. 17. & 18. Quod si verò hæc nullo pacto de Sa- lomone, vel alio quovis mortali rege intelligi possunt, sed ad solum Christum pertinent, quod prolixe Calvinum docere ait Pareus, quidni de uno eodemque subjecto, de uno eodemque Re- ge totus decantetur Psalmus? Sed hæc obiter. Castigavit quippe ex merito & Calvinum, & hy- peraspistem ejus Pareum B. Hunnius noster, qui videatur. Andr. Rivetus, qui itidem Calvini disci- pulus non ignobilis, Comment. in Pf. Proph. De- cad. p. 301. fatetur: Apud omnes Interpretes Psal- morum, ne Ebræis quidem exceptis, in confesso esse, Pf. XLV. esse carmen epithalamium, sive nuptiale, idque spirituale, ac proinde non σαρκικῶς, sed μυ- sτικῶς & πνευματικῶς intelligendum de spirituali connubio inter Christum & Ecclesiam: & Calvinum, Bucerum, Junium & alios è suis, item Janseninm cum aliis nonnullis Pontificiis agnoscere, pleraque hujus Psalmi Salomoni competere non posse, quæ necessario de Messia sint exponenda, & sponsa ejus Ecclesiâ, observat: neque Apostolum Ebr. I. duos versus hujus Psalmi Christo attributurum fuisse, cum ipsi cum Judæis res esset, nisi extra controversiam positum fuisset, hunc Psalmum ad Messiam pertinere. Quod in specie verba illa, Thronus tuus, Deus, attinet, ea de Salomone se- cundum literalem sensum nequaquam intelligi debere, sed de Messia intelligenda esse, agnoscere veteres plerosque Doctores Ecclesiæ, profiteri Thargum & saniores Ebræos, extra controver- siam positum fuisse apud Ebræos tempore Apo- stolorum, ut & apud plerosque Christianos Do- ctores recentiores (quicquid sit de Calvino) nullo modo videtur negandum: tantum abest, ut de consensu omnium doctissimorum interpretum ea secundum verum & literalem sensum ad Salo- monem referantur. Nec verò referri ad eum pos- sunt: Quia nec Salomoni, nec ulli alii mortali ho- mini uspiam in Scripturis Dei nomen absolutè tri- buitur, aut tribui potest, quippe quod sensu pro- prio non nisi uni Deo summo competit, nuspiam etiam nomine אלהים plurali ullam personam sin- gularem creatam in sacris literis designari, certum est: nec thronus Salomonis æternus fuit, quum regnum ejus tantùm duravit 40. annis, nec po- steri comprehendi possint, utpote quibus non convenit, quod sequitur de sceptro rectitudinis, quum Salomoni successerit iniquissimus filius, nec meliores fuerint nepotes, exceptis paucis quibusdam. Quid quod ne ipsi quidem Salomo- ni virga recta conveniat, cum turpiter à Deo de- fecerit. Quod si vero id largiamur Judæis cum Enjedino, Psalmistæ dictum præsens sensu simpli- ci suo, vero, genuino & literali non Christum spe- ctare, sed Salomonem, argumentum Apostolicum Ebr. I. v. 8. prorsus reddetur ineptum, & elumbe ad convincendos Judæos, vel Ebræos, quibuscum res erat Apostolo: denique si vel ratione typi sal- tim divinum illud elogium Salomoni congruit, quis non videt, frustra angelis derogari per alle- gationem Apostoli, quod suo modo ne quidem Salomoni denegatur?

Ad (2) Resp. Qui unctus est, qui Deum & se superiorem agnoscit, qui consortes habet & so- cios concedere possumus, eum quâ talem, & re- spectu ejus naturæ, qua unctus est, secundum quam superiorem agnoscit Deum, & socios ha- bet, non esse æternum Deum. Sed ex eo minimè consequitur, eundem illum nullo alio respectu Deum æternum esse, vel si illa arguunt & infe- runt veram humanam Christi naturam, non ha- bere in ipso locum divinam naturam, nisi suppo- natur per vanam petitionem principii, non posse in eadem persona concurrere divinam & huma- nam naturam.

Ad (3) Respond. Depravationem Enjedini, & Grotii luculenter refellit textus ipse Apostoli- cus, referens nomen τꭢ Θεꭢ casu vocandi ad Fili- um DEI, ὁ θρόνος σου, ὁ Θεὸς, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τꭢ αἰῶνꚙ, sedes tua, ô Deus, in seculum seculi. Quod enim ita reddi debeat, non vero ceu subjectum & prædicatum cohæreant illa, thronus tuus Deus, vel ipsa distinctio adhibita, quæ in omnibus co- dicibus citra diversitatem reperitur, evincit. Nun- quam enim inter ea quæ ut subjectum & prædi- catum cohærent, interjicitur comma, vel distin- ctio, quod hic fieri videmus ὁ θρόνος σου, ὁ Θεὸς, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, quæ verba ita posita aliter reddi non possunt, quam hoc pacto, Thronus tuus, ô Deus, in seculum. (2) Regula τῆς ἑρμηνείας. Non enim à consueta & recepta loquendi ratione de- flectendum in interpretatione sua ad novam in- solentem, & nuspiam obviam. At thronum Deo adscribi, ejusdemque throni justitiam, & æterni- tatem celebrari in S. literis familiare est, cum de regno DEI agitur. Præsertim verò in Psalmis, utpote Psalm. VII. 5. 8. Ps. XI. 4. Ps. XLVII. 9. Ps. LXXXIX. 15. Ps. XCIV. 2. XCVII. 19. Es. VI. 1. & LXVI. 1. Dan. VII. 9. Matth. V. 34. XXIII. 22. Act. VII. 49. Apoc. IV. 7. &c. Deum autem ipsum- met thronum vel sedem alicujus Regis dici, alie- num est à Scripturis, & prorsus insolens. (3) Sco- pus Apostoli. Versatur in eo Apostolus, ut doceat, Filium DEI superiorem & eminentiorem longè esse angelis. Argumento utitur eo, quod de An- gelis testetur Psalmista, quod sint à Deo conditi, & ministri ejus, Psal. CIV. 4. de Filio autem, quod ipse sit Deus, & thronus ejus sit æternus. Quæ- nam vero illa foret oppositio, quæ argumenti vis, si sensus hic foret: Angeli sunt creati à DEO, & ministri DEI: Filii DEI vero thronus & sedes est Deus, vel Deus firmabit Filio thronum in secula. Annon etiam angelis adscribuntur κυριότητες, ἐξου- σίαι, ἀρχαὶ, θρόνοι, Col. I. 16. & annon throni illi in seculum durant, conservante Deo? Sic ergo de angelis dici potest, quod thronos angelicos DEUS firmet in seculum, adeoque peribit ita prorsus ἀντίθεσις Apostolica, enervabitur penitus argumentum eminentiæ Filii DEI. Quid quod secundum Grotii glossam ne quidem regni per- petuitas his verbis inferatur: Quia sedem expo- nit is pro firmitate, & DEO adscribit æternita- tem, non illi, cujus sedes commemoratur: Sedes tua, id est, firmitas tua, Deus, subintellige durans in secula. Quid ergò hoc ad demonstrationem Apostoli facere poterit? Quid sublime de Chri- sto dicetur? Nonne enim omnium creaturarum firmitas est Deus durans in secula? Accedit (4) collatio vers. 10. ubi pariter apostrophe ad Filium Dei directa habetur, qui casu vocandi compella- tur. Tu ab initio, Domine, terram fundasti, quam pervertere quidem satagunt adversarii, sed fru- stra. Andr. Rivetus in hunc Psalmi locum urget defectum similis exempli. Quis enim unquam sic loquitur, aut quod exemplum afferent adversarii, in quo verbum desit, quod maximè expressum opor- tuit: Et hoc loco deeffe volunt thronum tuum Deus, subintellige, firmabit: Quis etiam prohibebit, si quodvis pro libidine supplere liceat, ut aliquis æque impius suppleat vocem destruet, vel collidet? Adde, quod illi ellipsi locus non sit in allegatio- ne Apostolica hujus oraculi, ubi ὁ θρόνος in casu recto dicitur, non verò τὸν θρόνον in casu accu- sativo. (5) Consensus denique omnium Ecclesiæ Doctorum unanimis, qui citra ullam dubietatem vocem ὁ Θεὸς casu vocandi accipiunt, indeque Christum Deum nuncupatum esse hisce verbis, semper credidit Ecclesia Christiana. Nec aliter reddidêre LXX. Interpp. quorum versionem se- cutus est Apostolus. Aquila diserte expressit vo- cativum: ὁ θρόνος σου Θεὲ εἰς αἰῶνα, κὶ ἔτι. Quid, quod concedat Socinus l. c. eum, cujus hic thro- nus describitur, DEUM hoc loco indigitari, quodque id agnoscat Schlichtingius in Comm. Epist. ad Ebr. pag. 62. ὁ Θεὸς nominativus positus est pro vocativo, dirigitur enim oratio ad ipsum: ut & Crellius l. de DEO & attrib. divin. cap. 13. pag. 10. ubi ὁ Θεὸς dici pro Θεὲ vel ὦ Θεὲ asserit, quod deniq; hoc modo reddat Racov. N. T. ver- sio, dein Stuhl, O GOtt, bleibt in alle Ewigkeit.

Ad (4) Resp. De Salomone ista primum di- cta esse negamus. Contrarium supra probatum. Non ergò hinc colligere licet: Christum solum ea ratione Deum esse, qua res creata Deus esse potest. Quod autem Christus tanquam Deus, seu quatenus Deus est, Deum suum habeat, & un- ctus sit præ consortibus, id minimè è verbis Apo- stoli apparet: διὰ τοῦτο ἔχρισέ σε ὁ Θεὸς, ὁ Θεὸς σου, ait Apostolus. Schlichting. in h. l. ita commen- tatur: Prior vox Deus ὁ Θεὸς, & ad Christum re- ferri potest, eritque Nominativus positus pro Vo- cativo, quod sæpe in hac voce contingit, & ad ipsum DEUM Christi Patrem, sicut primò sim- pliciter Deus appelletur, deinde DEUS Christi vocetur, q. d. unxit te Deus, ille, inquam, Deus, qui Deus tuus est, hoc est, qui insigniter tibi be- nefacit. Sed etiamfi priorem admittamus sensum, quem Vulgata quoque Latina exhibet, nihil aliud tamen infertur, quàm eum, qui verè DEUS est, Patrem agnoscere DEUM: non autem quod secundum eam naturam, juxta quam DEUS est, DEUM agnoscat. Unde id potius colligere in promptu est, quod in CHRISTO duæ sint na- turæ, altera secundum quam verè DEUS est, al- tera, secundum quam DEUM agnoscit Patrem suum. Atque hæc è schediis disjectis. Jam quid in Grotiana detorsione desiderandum, minimè obscurum est. Expendamus eam paulò distinctius. Primum in eo censuram meretur Grotius, quod Paulum ex memoriâ hæc protu- lisse ait. Eum enim Spiritu Sancto φερόμενον scripsisse constat. Et quid aliud est πῦρ φλέγον di- cere,quam πυρὸς φλόγα: Quanquam Regia exem- plaria, non ut Caraffæ, habeant πῦρ ψλέγον, sed ut hic Paulus, πυρὸς φλόγα. (2) Sensum loci per- vertit. Non enim nihil magni in nomine Angelo- rum & ministrorum esse docet vel Psaltes vel Apostolus: Sed Angelos esse creaturas DEI, ejusque ministros, è loco Psalmi Apostolus osten- dit. Non nomina Angelorum & Ministrorum vento & flammæ tribui: Sed Angelos esse spiri- tualis naturæ, & instar flammæ igneæ conditos à DEO, uterque indicat. (3) Ex subjecto prædi- catum & contra facit Grotius, non minus con- tra Hiero-Psaltis mentem, quam contra Apo- stoli demonstrationem, imo etiam contra pro- priam sententiam ad Ps. CIV. traditam. Sed de eo jam in Annotatis ad Psalmos actum. Sunt qui- dem & alii, qui, præeunte etiam Augustino in Psalm. & Gregor. M. homil. III. super Evangel. sic transponunt verba, sed sensu longe alio, non de nominibus, sed de naturâ Angelorum, hoc modo, interprete Estio: Qui eos, quorum natu- ra spiritualis est & ignea, id est, vehementer acti- va, facit nuncios & ministros suos. Seu, qui pro nunciis, cursoribus & ministris utitur spirituali- bus & immaterialibus substantiis. Sed recte hic corrigit Barth. Petri Estium, sensum hunc red- dens: Qui quos decreverat esse suos nuncios ac ministros, eosdem fecit substantias penitus imma- teriales seu plane spirituales, eosdem fecit quasi ignem urentem, lucidos nimirum cognitione, & charitate ardentes. Quod autem Ebræum nomen ruahh etiam spiritualem substantiam planeque im- materialem significet, licet Jansen. in annot. ad Psalm. CIII. negare videatur: Idem tamen concedit in Psalmum ultimum annot. ult. & concedendum esse liquet ex Genes. XLI. verf. 38. cap. XLV. v. 27. Exod. XXVIII. v. 3. cap. XXXI. v. 3. cap. XXXV. vers. 31. & aliis locis multis. Franciscus verò Ri- bera non tantum Ebræos, Calvinum, & Bezam, sed etiam Vatablum, & Jansenium prolixè hic re- fellit, & in Jansenio viro docto, & pio requirit modestiam, qui alio sensu hæc à Paulo afferri di- cat, quàm quo à Davide dicta sint: Verba in Ebræo ita sonare docens, qui facit angelos suos Spiritus, & observans viros doctos, & Ebraica VERITATIS tenacissimos de veris Angelis cum Paulo exposuisse, ut Augustinum Eugubinum, M. Antonium Flaminium, Genebrardum, & alios. Benedictus Justinian. nullâ ratione, inquit, audiendi sunt, qui Paulum sequutum LXX. longè aliud dixisse, quam Davidem putant. Nam si Paulus aliud dicere voluit, quam quod scriptum est à Davide, non S.S. sed LXX. Interpp. sensum, h.e. neglecto Canonico humanum, vel certe non Canonicum secutus est. Quod nefas est in dogmate præsertim stabiliendo de Apostolo cogitare. Calvi- num etiam suum perstringit hîc Franc. Junius in Parall. l. III. deserit Piscator in annot. ad h. l. (4) Non id agit Apostolus tantum, ut titulos confe- rat Angelorum, & Filii; sed contendit naturam Angelorum cum natura Filii Dei, & illos quidem esse à DEO conditos; Filium autem natura esse Deum docet; ac porro illos ut DEI creaturas DEO ministrare; Eum vero ut ὁμοούσιον Patri Filium esse ejusdem dominationis & gloriæ cum Patre demonstrat. (5) Psalm. XLV. de Salomo- ne agi, Judæorum potius, quam Catholicæ Ecclesiæ mens est. Cum illis tamen maluit hic facere Gro- tius, quam cum Christianis. Egimus autem ab- unde adversus Judaicam illam glossam in annot. ad Ps. XLV. Quanquam vero admitti posset al- legoriam ex historia Salomonea in hoc Psalmo fe- re perpetuam occurrere, de solo tamen Messia secundum literam agi evincunt tùm quæ de Spon- sa ejus, Ecclesia, dicuntur, de interiori ejus orna- tu vers. 14. de cultu & veneratione Sponsi, de subjectione gentium vers. 13. de liberis loco Patrum (gentis Judaicæ) procreandis, & Principibus per totum orbem constituendis vers. 17. Quæ Sponsæ Salomoneæ nullo pacto conveniunt, tum quæ de Sponso decantantur, utpote quod sit inter filios ho- minum pulcherrimus, vers. 3. (Conf. Cant. vers. 10. seqq.) diffusa gratia supra omnes eminentissi- mus, benedictione æterna locupletissimus, verbo veritatis & justitiæ, tanquam equestri & militari quodam apparatu, potentissimus, & gloriosissimus vers. 4. 5. 6. solio sempiterno & immenso altissi- mus, vers. 7. sceptro potentiæ & justitiæ perpetuæ augustissimus vers. eodem: ad comparandam ju- stitiam, & destruendam iniquitatem oleo S. S. sine comparatione, ac mensura, inunctus vers. 8. ad or- nandam spirituali decore Ecclesiam universam, ceu Sponsam suam, instructissimus vers. 9. 10. Do- minus Ecclesiæ Israeliticæ, gentiumque per totam terram religioso cultu prosequendus & in æternum celebrandus v. 12. 13. 17. 18. Sobole admodum copio- sa, & innumerabili, quam universam ipse princi- pes constituet per totum orbem (Conf. Apoc. I. 6. c. V. 9.) locupletissimus; quæ omnia uti certum est Messiæ Regi convenire, ita nullum eorum in Salomonem quadrare sole clarius constat. Ideo Chaldæus paraphrastes, & fatente Grotio plerique veteres Judæi de Messia Psalmum exposuere: ne- que dubitat Chrysostom. recentiores Judæos pro- vocare ceu per Psalmum præsentem convincen- dos in Comm. ad h. l. adversus quos etiam eun- dem totum adhibuit Justinus Dial. cum Tryph. & Cyprianus l. II. c. Jud. c. 29. (6) Falsum est, Dei nomen Salomoni tributum fuisse, & Salomonem typum CHRISTI fuisse etiam respectu hujus no- minis DEI, quod nomen Elohim in lingua Ebræa significatu proprio DEO proprium est, quum notet numen adorabile, nec usquam in plurali de ulla creata persona singulari occurrit: quia perso- nam, quæ communem habeat cum aliis eandem illam singularissimam essentiam, quæ sola ado- randa est, denotat: Qualis nulla est creata per- sona. Nomen illud plurale cum uni tribuitur, soli Deo convenire, fatetur ipse Grotius. (7) Pes- simè depravatur oraculum Davidicum Ps. XLV. à Grotio, Spiritu non Davidico, sed Judæorum recentiorum τῶν χριστομάχων & Arianico agitato. Sed quia ex professo commenta illa jam dicto Psalmi loco discussimus, nolumus hic actum age- re. Cornelius à Lapide in Erasmo sensum Grotia- num sic profligat: Ineptus & insulsus esset sensus, si caperetur in nominativo: Quis enim erit sensus, si quis sic interpretetur: Sedes tua, ô Christe, est ipse- Deus? Deus enim non est sedes, sed sedens in sede sive throno, & Christus non sedet in Patre, sed ad dexteram Patris. Rursum Deitas non est sedes hu- manitatis, sed potius è contrario, humanitas est se- des, imo scabellum Deitatis. Certum ergo est, hunc esse sensum: O DEUS, id est, o Fili, qui es verus Deus, thronus tuus Regius & divinus æternus est, Rex es æternus, regnum & solium habes æternum. Repugnant utique fontes, in quibus nomen E- lohim per accentus partim ab antecedente voca- bulo, partim etiam à consequentibus distingui- tur, unde utut LXX. nominativè eam vocem red- diderint, ita tamen id factum, ut in casu vocan- di exponi possit, quemadmodum exposuit Euse- bius demonstr. Evangel. l. IV. cap. 15. & fatetur Schlichting. Nominativum positum esse pro Vo- cativo: siquidem oratio dirigatur ad Christum, uti Aquila vertit θεέ. Neque vero uspiam Deus CHRISTI thronus dicitur in S. literis; Sed thro- nus DEI hic describitur, ut communiter à Patre, ac Christo possessus, Apoc. V. 6. 7. (8) Quæ ad v. 9. hic annotat Grotius, ex eodem loco dijudicari poterunt, ubi tanquam in propria sede sub exa- men revocatæ sunt. (9) Quid ad demonstratio- nem Deitatis CHRISTI glossa illa faceret, Deus ipse te sustentabit in regno nunquam desituro? At Apostolus hic occupatur in demonstranda Chri- sti æterna Deitate. (10) Christum ideo dignita- tem supra omnes homines & Angelos consequutum esse, quod nihil aliud quam justa & honesta verbo & exemplo docuit, hic non docetur: Sed eo fine potius unctus dicitur oleo lætitiæ vel Spiritus San- cti, ut regnum suum justitiâ divinâ administraret, quo de vide, quæ ad locum Psalmi dicta sunt. Di- lectio illa justitiæ, ut recte Beat. Dorfcheus, est justitiæ constitutiva, & odium iniquitatis est ini- quitatis destructivum. Intelligit enim justitiam illam singularissimam, incomparabilem, & Mes- sianam, à qua ipse Messias Jehovah justitia no- stra appellatur, Jer. XXIII. 6. per quam nos red- dimur justitia DEI in ipso, 2. Cor. V. 21. quæ est proprius effectus unctionis illius admirabilis, fluitque ex unione divinæ, & humanæ naturæ, estq; illa justitia, quam Sponsæ suæ cœlestis Spon- sus tanquam ornatum maximum communicat. Est nimirum justitia illa perfectissimæ obedientiæ, per quam justitiæ divinæ fatisfit, cujus virtute cœ- lestia terrestribus reconciliantur, Col. I. 20. quæ eam, quam Adam perdidit, compensat, Roman. V. vers. 18. nobisque imputatur, Rom. III. 12. c. IV. 5. Hanc justitiam diligit Messias tanquam ἀποτέλε- σμα suum proprium, quod statu exanitionis suæ consummavit. Diligit autem non tantum theoretice ejus perfectionem & admirabile ex misericordiâ divinâ temperamentum contemplando, sed etiam practicè eam operando, perficiendo, ejusque cau- sa nostram injustitiam portando, Es. LIII. vers. 4. 1. Petr. II. v. 24. Sic & per iniquitatem intelligit non tantum particularem aliquam, sed universa- lem, in qua hærent omnes, quibuscunque Mes- sias est in communione carnis & sanguinis, pro- pter quem eos vocat suos μετόχους. Illam autem odit odio non simplicis displicentiæ & aversatio- nis, sed realis destructionis & eversionis juxta Prot-Evangelium, in quo inimicitia promitti- tur talis in semine mulieris fundanda, quæ toti regno Satanæ adversaria ad destructionem capi- tis potestatisque ejus grassabitur, Ebr. II. vers. 14. 1. Johan. III. 8. (11) Non illâ ut duo Nominativi adducuntur אלהים אלהיך, sed ut priori commate ὁ θεὸς est Vocativi casus; ita posteriori aliter cur accipienda sit, non apparet, nec ab Interpretibus aliter acceptum fuit. Adde Eusebium libr. IV. demonstr. cap. 15. Hieronymum ad Princip. (12) Quum Chaldæus & Rabbini multi de Messia Psal- mum accipiant, fatente Grotio, cur ipse Christia- nus in eo deterior est Judæis, sensu literali eun- dem ad Salomonem detorquens? (13) thronus æternus, divinus, & infinitus ὑπεραγγελικὸς, quum & Angeli throni dicantur, Col. I. 16. hic vero thro- nus supra Angelos sit, in quo est ὁ Θεὸς, cujus mini- stri sunt angeli, thronus ille, à quo est omnis bene- dictio, gratia, veritas, justitia, Ps. XLV. 3. 5. 6. ut & Sceptrum non finitum, sed infinitum, (quo de conf. Psalm. CX.) ad demonstrandam itidem di- vinam Filii DEI naturam adducuntur ab Apo- stolo, eamque solide demonstrant. Unde Sponsa, Ecclesia, Regem hunc ceu Dominum suum ado- rare jubetur, v. 12. Ideoque locus hic aptissime Psalmo superiori XCVII. de Rege eodem ab An- gelis adorando subjunctus est. Nec frustra addu- citur etiam è Psalm. XLV. vers. 8. etsi de unctione secundum humanam naturam, juxta quam est speciosus præ filiis hominum, & labia habet, in qui- bus diffusa est gratia, exhilarandus oleo lætitiæ, con- sortes habens & unctionis indigus est ad rectam re- gni sui administrationem, agat: Sed partim quod unctio illa præsupponat unionem humanæ naturæ cum divinâ, quia infinita dona Sp. S. infert, Joh. III. v. 34. imò formaliter consistit in ipsa reali, & totali communicatione S. S. quoad dona immen- sa, tum quod per hoc unguentum tum παραμε- τόχως absolute unctus, quibus dona sua incom- parabili varietate dispensat, Ebr. II. 14. Eph. IV. 8. Joh. I. 16. tum quod per hoc unguentum Chri- stus in throno sempiterno & divino gubernet, v. 8. tum quod per illud effectus sit Rex angelorum, & hominum: quum non sit unctio convivialis, ut Schlichtingius vult, qualis Ps. XXIII. 5. Luc. VII. v. 42. sed Sacerdotalis & Regia, ac Prophetica: si- quidem hic celebretur Rex, v. 2. non convivans, sed regnans, gladio succincto, & glorioso appara- tu inequitans, sagittis instructus, in Solio cum Sce- ptro constitutus, & causa finalis unctionis assigne- tur operatio justitiæ, & destructio iniquitatis, impri- mis quidem in officio Sacerdotali, in quo sacrificio exhibito justitiam consummavit: veruntamen etiam in Prophetico, in quo Messias prospere equi- tavit, in splendore suo cum verbo veritatis, & pro- loquutus est justitiam, v. 5. (Conf. Es. LXIII. 3.) ut & in Regio, in quo hostes justitiæ suæ, & auctores injustitiæ impugnat, debellat, & depellit: partim quod unctio illa fundamentum sit sublimationis Christi supra angelos, de qua deinceps agere in- stituit Apostolus v. 12.

## 1:10
Vers. 10. Καὶ) And in another place, namely Ps. CII. v. 26. Vers. 11. 12. Σὺ κατ᾽ ἀρχὰς, Κύριε, τὴν γῆν ἐθεμελίωσας, καὶ ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν σύ εἰσιν οἱ ὐρανοί. Αὐτοὶ ἀπολοῦνται, σὺ δὲ διαμένεις, καὶ πάντες ὡς ἱμάτιον παλαιωθήσονται, κὴ ὡσεὶ περιβόλαιον ἑλίξεις αὐτὸς, καὶ ἀλλαγήσονται. Σὺ δὲ ὁ ἀυτός εἶ, καὶ τὰ ἔτη σε ἐκ ἐκλείψυσι) And this is from the LXX, except that there the words are transposed: Κατ᾽ ἀρχὰς τὴν γῆν σὺ, Κύριε, ἐθεμελίωσας. And that in the manuscript in this place it is: Ἑλίξεις αὐτὸς ὡς ἱμάτιον καὶ ἀλλαγήσονται. Again, what had been said of God, he applies to the Messiah; because it was agreed among the Hebrews that this world was created for the sake of the Messiah (whence I should think ἐθεμελίωσας is rightly understood: you were the cause why it was founded, and the work of your hands, that is, created on your account. For על־דבר also signifies 'on account of' to the Hebrews and Chaldeans, and thus the Latin reads Job XI. 3, but translates בירך as 'for you', and that a new and better world will be founded through him. For that which is in the Hebrew לפנים, that is, 'already of old', the LXX have placed κατ᾽ ἀρχὰς, explaining this passage from the beginning of Genesis, where it is בראשית. The earth is said to be founded, with a likeness taken from buildings, whence it is also called καταβολὴ in Matthew XIII. verse 35, XXV. 34, Luke XI. 50, John XVII. verse 24, Ephesians I. verse 4, below IV. 3, IX. 26.

1 Pet. 1:20. Rev. 13:8. 17:8. By the name of the heavens here, one must not understand that highest region, the seat of the divine majesty and of the angels: but the air and the ether, which clothe the earth as it were, from which the following simile is taken. Garments, before they perish, grow old, see below 8:13. So also the powers of the air and of the ether will be diminished. Garments, when they are no longer of use, are accustomed to be folded up and cast away: so also the air and the ether will be taken away. For the Hebrew word חלף has this meaning, and is translated as 'clothes,' 'encompasses,' and 'they pass away.' The same is signified by 'change' below in 12:27. They will be 'folded up' in the same sense in 2 Pet. 3:10, although in the Hebrew it is not 'you will roll up,' but 'you will change' תחליפם, which the Latin translates as 'you will change,' and 'they will be changed,' that is, they will depart at your doing: so that it may seem that 'you will roll up' crept into the Greek text for 'you will change' from the passage in Isaiah 34:4.

This is the fifth testimony of the Deity of the Messiah, by which he demonstrates that he is the same Creator of heaven and earth, who indeed made the ages, and is the preserver of all things, who carries all things by the word of his power. For he, of whom the sacred Psalmist speaks, is Jehovah, the true God, Creator of heaven and earth, who, as he preserves them as long as it pleases him: so he will one day change and annihilate them, remaining himself immutable. But the Messiah is he of whom David speaks here, with the Apostle teaching here among the Hebrews, to whom therefore it was a matter beyond all dispute that the present Psalm speaks of the Messiah. Therefore the Messiah is Jehovah, the true God, Creator and Preserver of heaven and earth, who will one day change and annihilate them, remaining himself immutable. What could again be more clear than this demonstration? He shows, says Theodoret, that he himself is the Creator and Maker of all things. For by heaven and earth he includes all things that are in them. He taught that he is alien to conversion and change. For this is what that signifies: 'they will perish, but you remain.' He also signified that a change of the creature is to be made by him into that which is more excellent, but that he himself is without beginning and end. For you, he says, are the same, and your years will not fail. For you were not made, but you are, nor do you undergo any change. Chrysostom: Saying 'in the beginning,' not now, but already long ago; behold, again he strikes with a certain wound both Paul of Samosata and Arius. And afterwards: At the same time this is also the greatest consolation, to know that things will not be so, but all things will receive a change, and all things will be changed. But he himself remains perpetually living and infinitely living. And your years, he says, will not fail. However, one is to observe here the manifold distortion of Grotius. (1) He says that what the Psalmist had said about God is adapted to Christ. But the Apostle does not merely adapt the saying, but demonstrates his theme from the Psalm. By a mere adaptation, what would he have accomplished among the Hebrews? And it is evident from the Psalm itself that it concerns the Messiah, concerning Jehovah sitting or reigning forever, whose memory is to be celebrated from generation to generation, as one who will arise in the fullness of times or at the appointed time (Dan. 9:24; Gal. 4:4), that he may have mercy on Zion, verses 13, 14, that the nations and all the Kings of the earth may fear his glory (if indeed in the time of the N.T. the nations with the Kings of the earth were to be converted to the Messiah, Psalm 2:8; Ps. 72), concerning the Lord, who will be seen in his glory, v. 17 (cf. Is. 40:5; 60:1, 3), concerning the Lord, who was to look down from on high, v. 20 (which visitation Zechariah celebrates, Luke 1:68, 78, as the 'dayspring from on high') to hear the sighing of the prisoner, and to release those who are delivered to death, verse 21. (which Zechariah renders, Luke 1:79, that he may appear to those who are in darkness and the shadow of death: concerning that Lord, to whose worship the peoples are to gather themselves, whom Jacob predicted would be the Messiah, Gen. 49:10, and that at the time when his name will be celebrated in Zion, verses 22, 23. Cf. Luke 24:47. Add to these what we have said on Ps. 102. He cast off his gloss

Grotius seems to have drawn from the Anti-Trinitarians, from whom Enjedin in his Explanation of passages, p. 394, says: What the Psalmist, he says, had said about God the Father and the old world, the Apostle mystically applies to Christ and the new world. (2) He repeats his dream about the world being created for the sake of the Messiah. The world was created before the Messiah was promised. The Messiah was promised for the sake of man. Man, the microcosm, was not created, nor the world, the macrocosm, for the sake of the Messiah. (3) He pretends that the Messiah is called here the cause why the world was created; on the contrary, the Son of God here, by the interpretation of the Apostle, and according to the letter of the Psalmist's word 'you have founded,' is established as the author or Principal cause of the creation of the world. You, Lord, he says, have founded the earth, not, for your sake the earth was founded. (4) He brings forward another invention about a new and better world to be created through the Messiah, about which nothing appears either in the Psalm or in this Apostolic text. But since he says concerning this that it will be created through the Messiah, why does he not also acknowledge concerning that, that it was created through him? Since the Apostle expressly affirms that the ages were created through him; and proves it from the Psalm, because it is said: You, Lord, have founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. (5) He therefore perverts the intention of the Apostle, who does not teach that the ages were created for the sake of Christ, but through Christ. (6) He perverts the meaning of the sacred Psalmist, who introduces Christ as God the Creator of heaven and earth: God, because the Essential names Jehovah and El in the Psalm teach this: by which he, of whom David speaks, is distinguished. Creator of the earth: For he says that he himself founded the earth: And of heaven: For he testifies that the heavens are the works of his hands. And lest these things be taken by chance as concerning a new creation, he adds, κατ᾽ ἀρχὰς, from the beginning, namely of the primordial creation: by which the beginning of creation is pointed out, (concerning which compare Gen. 1. 1.) Grotius admits. Estius is correct here: The Apostle explains by this testimony that which he said above concerning Christ, through whom he also made the ages. Lest anyone suspect that all things were made by God through him in the way that craftsmen are accustomed to fashion their works through ministers or instruments. For he shows that all things were so made by God through him, that nevertheless he himself no less truly and properly made them. For whatever things the Father has made, these the Son also does likewise, John V. (7) By the name of the heavens he says is not understood the highest region, but the air and the ether. But that highest region is either the work of the hands of God, or it is not. If it is the work of the hands of God, it is necessary that it was created from the beginning, because these heavens, which are the works of the hands of the Lord, are said to have been produced by the Lord from the beginning. If it is not, it must be uncreated, and therefore, since there is nothing uncreated outside of the creature except God, God himself. (8) To clothe the air and the ether as if it were the earth is nowhere said in the sacred scriptures, and the reason for the metaphor is far different: For not only will those quasi-garments of Grotius, the air and the ether, grow old like garments, but the earth itself also: Not only will those be taken away and perish; but the earth also will flee away, and is about to perish, Luke XXI. 33. Acts VI. 14. chapter XXI. 1. But he names the heavens specifically in this place, as the principal part of the creature, and that which might most seem to be free from destruction and everlasting. (9) He suspects that ἑλίξεις has crept into the Greek text in place of ἀλλάξεις; But the suspicion is vain, because the Apostle himself retained the word ἑλίξεις, you will roll up. Therefore it was not held, nor is it to be held, as having crept in. Yet that rolling up of the heavens (the reason for the earth is similar) is correctly explained as concerning the change which the Hebrew word implies: And so, that a destruction is implied, not accidental, but substantial, just as he had expressly said: They themselves will perish. For when the heavens are rolled up, as a garment, or as a book are folded up, how can the expanse, or the substance itself of the heavens remain? Indeed, if the earth is thus enveloped, then certainly it cannot remain substantially, much less be able to attain a more perfect state, which Grotius, with the Papists and Calvinists and others, seems to maintain. Estius's gloss is cold: As a garment So all the heavens, as if worn out by long use and brought to old age, will undergo destruction, that is, that change by which they are to be renewed into another and better state. For when a garment grows old and is clearly worn out or cast aside, it is not necessary, but it happens, that one obtains a new garment. Much less is it to be said that an old garment is changed into a new and better one. The gloss of others is almost similar, which Estius himself refutes: Others explain it in this way: As a worn-out garment is accustomed to be turned inside out, so that it may appear new: So you will turn the heavens inside out; that is, you will renew them: But it must be known that neither the Greek word nor the Syriac properly signifies an inversion, by which what was inside becomes outside, or vice versa: But a convolution or complication, by which it is brought about that what was appearing now does not appear: For as all things were made from things not appearing: So also all things will again not appear, that is, they will have departed into non-existence. Although Estius wishes to apply it thus, from chapter VI of the Apocalypse, verse 14. As in a rolled-up book (for the Hebrews used volatile membranes for books) nothing can be read before it is unrolled: So the face of the heavens, in which the stars are like letters telling us the glory of God, will be completely covered, so that nothing appears, until it is unfolded by its renewal. But concerning that new explanation, nothing is held in this place: Indeed, the opposite is held: which the Socinians themselves, Crellius and Schlichtingius, acknowledge: commenting on the word 'they will perish' as follows: Here we have a most open testimony concerning the destruction and abolition of the heavens: so that it is a wonder that men are blind in such great light, and dream I know not what about a change of those heavens into some better form. For that which remains the same and is changed into a better form and acquires more perfect qualities is certainly not said to perish. Shall we perish when we have become immortal and incorruptible from mortal and corruptible? As GOD remains the same always in respect of substance, and immutable: So, on the contrary, heaven and earth, the works of GOD, will perish substantially and cease to be. As they were produced from nothing by infinite power: So they will be reduced again into nothing, at the consummation of the universe, by the same power. Which works of infinite power, the creation of things and their annihilation, are here vindicated for Christ as true GOD by nature, and from that testimony, therefore, the eternal and immutable Deity of Christ is demonstrated most invincibly by the Apostle. The exceptions of the Socinians have been discussed elsewhere, although the same ones, being akin to them, were overthrown at the same time in the Grotian works; whence in that part he Arianizes. Schlichtingius is hardly worthy of refutation, when he pretends that the scope here is that Christ, after he sat down at the right hand of God, was made more excellent than the angels, to which the words about creation contribute nothing. And therefore do not pertain to Christ. For what? Do we believe that the Apostle brought these things ἀσκόπως or ἀπροσδιονύσως (without aim or irrelevantly)? And do not these words about the Lord as creator of heaven and earth most fittingly agree with the scope, which is here, not that Christ was made more excellent than the Angels, but that he is the God creator of heaven and earth? It is also discordant, when the Apostle cites three verses, that only two, v. 27 and 28, are applied to the Messiah, but that verse 26 does not pertain to Christ. and 28, are applied to the Messiah, but that verse 26 does not pertain to Christ. It is unheard of for the writers of the N.T. to cite words of the O.T. and accommodate them to one to whom they in no way pertain: it is unheard of that from the cited words of the O.T. some should be accommodated and compete in an improper sense to the subject for whom they are cited, but others in a proper sense. Nor were these brought in either by way of similarity or because of subordination. Not the former, because the Socinians cannot designate anything here that Christ did which is similar to the creation of heaven and earth, or to their abolition: nor the latter: because there is no need for a mediate or subordinate cause in either creation or abolition, because infinite power is required for both.
