But Schlichtingius himself acknowledges that the words about the creation of heaven and earth, which he understands of the first creation, in no way agree with Christ, but were brought in only because they could not be separated from those which deal with the abolition. Would they not therefore have been brought in impertinently? And why could the following not have been cited alone in this manner: The heavens will perish: but you remain, what is clearer than that both are said of the same אל GOD, whom the Psalmist calls his GOD, both the creation of heaven and earth, and their abolition. Since therefore the latter is explained of Christ, the former ought not to be denied of the same, unless you say that they were not only brought in by the Apostle without sense, but also falsely attributed to the same subject in the Psalm itself: in which not even a double subject can be imagined, one primary, the other secondary, whether according to the context of the Psalmist, or according to the Apostolic interpretation: much less, without ἀκύρωτα (invalidated) sense, can they be set down contradictorily with Schlichtingius.

MEMBER II. Concerning the human nature of CHRIST'S eminence.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Καὶ) Et alio loco, nempe Ps. CII. v. 26. Vers. 11. 12. Σὺ κατ᾽ ἀρχὰς, Κύριε, τὴν γῆν ἐθεμελίω- σας, καὶ ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν σύ εἰσιν οἱ ὐρανοί. Αὐτοὶ ἀπολοῦν- ται, σὺ δὲ διαμένεις, καὶ πάντες ὡς ἱμάτιον παλαιωθήσονται, κὴ ὡσεὶ περιβόλαιον ἑλίξεις αὐτὸς, καὶ ἀλλαγήσονται. Σὺ δὲ ὁ ἀυτός εἶ, καὶ τὰ ἔτη σε ἐκ ἐκλείψυσι) Et hoc ex LXX. nisi quod ibi verbis transpositis: Κατ᾽ ἀρχὰς τὴν γῆν σὺ, Κύριε, ἐθεμελίωσας. Et quod in Manuscripto hoc loco est: Ἑλίξεις αὐτὸς ὡς ἱμάτιον καὶ ἀλλαγήσονται. Rursum quod de Deo dictum fuerat, Messisæ aptat; quia constabat in- ter Ebræos, & mundum hunc Messiæ causa conditum (un- de ἐθεμελίωσας recte intelligi putem: causa fuisti, cur fun- daretur, & opus manuum tuarum, id est, propter te f.- ctum. Nam על־דבר Ebræis & Chaldæis etiam propter significat, & sic Latinus Job. XI. 3. legit, בירך vertit au- tem tibi, & fore ut novus meliorque mundus condatur per ipsum. Pro eo, quod in Ebræo est לפנים, id est, jam olim, LXX. posuere κατ᾽ ἀρχὰς, exponentes hunc lo- cum ex initio Geneseos, ubi est בראשית. Terra dici- tur fundata similitudine sumpta ab ædificiis, unde & κατα- βολὴ dicitur Matth. XIII. vers. 35 XXV. 34. Luc. XI. 50. Johan. XVII. vers. 24. Ephes. I. vers. 4. infra IV. 3. IX. 26.

1. Petr. I. 20. Apoc. XIII. 8. XVII. 8. Cœlorum nomine hic intelligi debet non suprema illa regio, sedes divinæ ma- jestatis & Angelorum: Sed aër & æther, quæ terram velut vestiunt, unde sumpta, quæ sequitur, similitudo. Vestes antequam pereant, veterascunt, vide infra VIII. 13. Sic & aëris & ætheris vires minuentur. Vestes ubi usui amplius non sunt, solent complicari & abjici: Sic & aër & æther auferentur. Nam & hunc sensum habet חלף Ebræum, vertiturque ἀμφιέννυσι & περιέχουσιν & ἀπέρχονται. Idem per μετάθεσιν significatur infra XII. v. 27. Περιέλυ- σονται eodem sensu 2. Pet. III. 10. quanquam in Ebræo non est ἑλίξεις, sed ἀλλάξεις תחליפם, quod mutabis, ibi ver- tit Latinus, & mutabuntur, id est, te faciente abscedent: Ita ut videri possit in Græcum textum pro ἀλλάξεις irrepsif- se ἑλίξεις ex loco Esaiæ XXXIV. 4.

Quintum hoc est testimonium Deitatis Mes- siæ, quo eundem esse Creatorem cœli & terræ, qui nempe secula fecit, & omnium rerum conservato- rem, qui omnia portat verbo virtutis suæ, demon- strat. Is enim, de quo loquitur Hiero-Psaltes, est Jehovah, verus Deus Creator cœli & terræ, qui ut conservat ea, quamdiu placet: Ita olim ea immu- tabit & annihilabit manens ipse immutabilis. At Messias est is, de quo David hic loquitur, docente hic penes Ebræos Apostolo, quibus proinde id erat ἔξω πάσης συζητήσεως κείμενον, Psalmum præ- sentem de Messia loqui. Ergo Messias est Jeho- vah verus Deus Creator & Conservator cœli & terræ, qui olim ea immutabit & annihilaturus est, manens ipse immutabilis. Quid iterum hac de- monstratione luculentius esse poterat? Ostendit, inquit Theodoretus, ipsum esse universorum Creato- rem & opificem. Per cælum enim & terram com- prehendit omnia, quæ sunt in ipsis. Docuit eum à conversione & mutatione alienum. Hoc enim signi- ficat illud, ipsi peribunt, tu autem permanes. Signi- ficavit etiam ab eo faciendam creaturæ mutationem in id, quod est præstantius, ipsum autem esse prin- cipii & exitus expertem. Tu enim, inquit, idem ipse es, & anni tui non deficient. Non enim factus es, sed es, nec aliquam suscipis mutationem. Chryso- stomus: Dicens in principio, non nunc, sed jam olim; Ecce rursus certo percutit vulnere & Paulum Sa- mosatenum & Arium. Et postea: Simul etiam hoc est maxima consolatio, nosse, quod res non sic erunt, sed omnia accipient mutationem, & omnia mutabuntur. Ipse autem manet perpetuo vivens & infinite vivens. Et anni tui, inquit, non defi- cient. Multiplicem autem hic observare est Gro- tii στρεβλότητα. (1) Aptari dicit Christo, quod de Deo Psaltes dixerat. At Apostolus non nude ac- commodat dictum, sed è Psalmo thema suum de- monstrat. Nuda accommodatione quid profe- cisset apud Ebræos? Et è Psalmo ipso patet, agi de Messia, de Jehovâ in seculum sedente, vel regnan- te, cujus memoria de generatione in generationem celebranda, utpote qui surget in plenitudine temporum vel statuto tempore, (Dan. IX. vers. 24. Gal. IV. 4.) ut Sionis misereatur, vers. 13. 14. ut gen- tes, & Reges terræ omnes gloriam ejus timeant, (si- quidem tempore N. T. ad Messiam convertendæ erant gentes cum Regibus terræ, Psalm. II: 8. Ps. LXXII.) de Domino, qui videbitur in gloria sua, v. 17. (Conf. Es. XL. 5. c. LX. 1. 3.) de Domino, qui prospecturus erat de excelso, v. 20. (quam ἐπί- σκεψιν celebrat Zacharias, Luc. I. 68. 78. tanquam ἀνατολῆς ἐξ ὕψες) ad audiendum suspirium vincti, & solvendum eos, qui traditi sunt morti, vers. 21. (quod Zacharias reddit, Luc. I. 79. ut appareat il- lis, qui sunt in tenebris, & umbra mortis: de Do- mino illo, ad cujus cultum se congregaturi sunt populi, quem Messiam esse prædixit Jacob, Gen. XLIX. 10. idque tum, cum in Sion celebrabitur no- men ejus, vers. 22. 23. Conf. Luc. XXIV. 47. Adde his, quæ ad Ps. CII. diximus. Glossam suam ab jecit

Anti-Trinitariis hausisse videtur Grotius, è qui- bus Enjedin. in Explic. loc. p. 394. Quod Psalmi- sta, inquit, de Deo Patre, & veteri mundo dixerat, illud Apostolus mysticè applicat ad Christum, & novum mundum. (2) Somnium suum repetit de mundo Messiæ causa condito. Erat mundus condi- tus, antequam Messias promitteretur. Propter ho- minem promissus est Messias. Non conditus ho- mo, microcosmus, neque mundus, macrocosmus, propter Messiam. (3) Messiam hic dici fingit cau- sam, cur conditus mundus; contra Filius Dei hic, interprete Apostolo, & juxta literam Psaltis ver- bo ἐθεμελίωσας autor vel causa Principalis creatio- nis mundi constituitur. Tu Domine, inquit, terram fundasti, non, tui causa terra fundata est. (4) Aliud commentum de mundo novo ac meliori per Messiam condendo affert, de quo nihil vel in Psal- mo, vel in Apostolico hoc textu comparet. Quum autem de hoc dicat, eum conditum iri per Messiam, cur non de illo etiam agnoscit, quod per ipsum con- ditus sit? quum Apostolus disertè affirmet, secula per ipsum condita esse; idq; è Psalmo probet, quia dictum est: Tu Domine terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum cæli sunt. (5) Pervertit ergo in- tentionem Apostoli, qui non docet, secula propter Christum condita, sed per Christum. (6) Pervertit sententiam Hiero-Psaltis, qui Christum ut Deum Creatorem cæli & terræ introducit: Deum, quod nomina Essentialia Jehovah & El in Psalmo do- cent: quibus is, de quo loquitur David, insigni- tur. Creatorem terræ: Dicit enim, quod terram ipse fundavit: Et cæli: Testatur enim, quod cæli sint opera manuum ejus. Et ne de nova forte crea- tione hæc accipiantur, addit, κατ᾽ ἀρχὰς, ab initio, scilicet primævæ creationis: quo indigitari ini- tium creationis, (de quo confer Gen. 1. 1.) fatetur Grotius. Rectè hic Estius: Explicat Apostolus hoc testimonio id, quod supra de Christo dixit, per quem fecit & secula. Ne quis suspicetur, sic per eum omnia à Deo facta, quomodo per ministros, aut in- strumenta solent artifices opera sua fabricare. Osten- dit enim, sic per eum omnia à Deo facta, ut tamen ipse non minus vere ac proprie ea fecerit. Quæ- cunque enim Pater fecit, hæc & Filius similiter facit, Johan. V. (7) Cælorum nomine ait non intelligi regionem supremam, sed aërem, & æthera. Sed re- gio illa suprema aut est opus manuum Dei, aut non est. Si opus manuum Dei est, necessum est, illam creatam esse ab initio, quia hic cæli, qui opera manuum Domini sunt, ab initio à Domino produ- cti dicuntur. Si non est, oportet increatam esse, adeoque, quum extra creaturam nihil increatum sit, nisi Deus, Deum ipsum. (8) Aërem, & æthera vestire quasi terram, nuspiam dicitur in sacris li- teris, & longè alia est Metaphoræ ratio: Nam non tantum illæ quasi-vestes Grotii aër & æther vete- rascent, tanquam vestes, sed terra etiam ipsa: Non illa tantum auferentur & peribunt; sed ter- ra etiam fugiet, & peritura est, Luc. XXI. 33. Act. VI. 14. cap. XXI. 1. Cælos autem nominat pecu- liariter hoc loco, velut partem creaturæ præcipu- am, & quæ maximè videri possit ab interitu libera & sempiterna. (9) Suspicatur in textum Græ- cum pro ἀλλάξεις irrepsisse ἑλίξεις; Sed vana est suspicio, quia Apostolus ipse vocem ἑλίξεις, in- volves retinuit. Non ergo pro irreptitia habuit, aut habenda est. Recte tamen explicatur illa cæ- lorum (terræ similis est ratio) involutio de im- mutatione, quam vox Ebræa infert: Et ita, ut in- feratur interitus non accidentalis, sed substantia- lis, quemadmodum expresse dixerat: Ipsi peribunt. Cum enim cæli involvuntur, ut vestis, aut ut liber complicantur, quomodo expansum, aut substantia ipsa cœlorum manere potest? Imo si terra ita involvitur, tum utique non manere sub- stantialiter, nedum perfectiorem statum assequi poterit, quod videtur Grotius cum Papistis & Calvinianis, aliisque statuere. Frigida est glossa Estii: Sicut vestis assiduo usu & tempore vetera- scit, ut proinde renovari debeat: Ita cæli omnes velut usu longi temporis attriti, & ad vetustatem perducti interitum subibunt, hoc est, eam muta- tionem, qua renovandi sint in alium ac meliorem statum. Cum enim vestis veterascit, & plane atteritur vel abjicitur, non necessum est, sed contingit, ut quis novam vestem consequatur. Multo minus dicendum est, vestem veterem im- mutari in novam & meliorem. Similis ferè est aliorum glossa, quam refellit ipse Estius: Alii ad hunc modum exponunt: Sicut vestis detrita so- let inverti, ut nova appareat: Ita tu cælos inver- tes; id est, renovabis: Sed sciendum est, nec Gra- co verbo nec Syriaco proprie significari inversio- nem, qua quod interius erat, exterjus fiat, aut contra: Sed convolutionem seu complicationem, qua id agitur, ut quod apparebat jam, non appa- reat: Ut enim ex non apparentibus facta sunt omnia: Ita etiam omnia iterum non apparebunt, id est, in non-entia abituta sunt. Quanquam Estius id ita velit applicare, è cap. VI. Apocal. vers. 14. Sicut in libro convoluto (nam membra- nis volatilibus pro libris utebantur Ebræi) nihil legi potest, priusquam evolvatur: Ita cæli facies, in qua sunt astra velut literæ nobis enarrantes glo- riam Dei, penitus obducetur, ut nihil appareat, donec renovatione sua explicetur. Sed de illa no- va explicatione nihil habetur hoc loco: Imo ha- betur contrarium: quod agnoscunt ipsimet So- ciniani, Crellius, & Schlichtingius: ad vocem peribunt, ita commentantes: Hic habemus aper- tissimum testimonium de cælorum interitu, & ab- olitione: ut mirum sit, homines in tanta luce cali- gare, & nescio, quid de cælorum istarum in melio- rem quandam formam permutatione somniare. Quod enim idem permanens in meliorem mutatur formam & perfectiores acquirit qualitates, perire certè non dicitur. Num nos peribimus, cum ex mortalibus & corruptibilibus immortales & incor- ruptibiles fuerimus? Ut DEUS substantia ratione manet idem semper, & immutabilis: Ita ex ad- verso cœlum & terra, opera DEI, peribunt sub- stantialiter & esse desinent. Uti è nihilo illa, vir- tute infinita, producta sunt: Ita in nihilum ite- rum, in consummatione universi, eadem virtu- te redigentur. Quæ opera infinitæ virtutis, crea- tio rerum, & annihilatio, Christo ceu vero na- tura DEO hic vindicantur, & ex illo proinde testimonio æterna & immutabilis Deitas Chri- sti ab Apostolo demonstratur invictissimè. Soci- nianorum exceptiones frivolæ alias discussæ sunt, quanquam in Grotianis simul eædem profligatæ, quæ illis affines; unde ea parte Arianizat. Schlichtingius vix refutatione dignus est, cum fingit, scopum hic esse, Christum postquam ad dex- tram Dei consedit, præstantiorem angelis effectum, ad quem nihil faciant verba de creatione. Ideoque ad Christum non pertinere. Quid enim? num ἀσκόπως vel ἀπροσδιονύσως Apostolum ea addu- xisse credimus? Et annon maximè scopo, qui hic est, non præstantiorem effectum Angelis, sed Deum creatorem cæli & terræ esse CHRISTUM, con- veniunt hæc verba de Domino creatore cæli & terræ? Absonum etiam, cum tres versus alleget Apost. duos solum v. 27. & 28. ad Messiam appli- cari, versum verò 26. ad Christum non pertinere. Inauditum est, scriptores N. T. verba V. T. allega- re, & accommodare ei, ad quem nullo pacto per- tinent: inauditum ex allegatis V. T. verbis quæ- dam accommodatitio & improprio sensu subjecto, pro quo allegantur, competere, aliqua vero pro- prio. Nec vel per similitudinem, vel ob subordina- tionem hæc adducta. Non illud, quia nullum hic, quod simile creationi cœli & terræ, vel abolitie- ni fecerit Christus, designare possunt Sociniani: neque hoc: quia nec in creatione, nec in aboli- tione causâ mediâ vel subordinatâ opus, quia ad utramque virtus infinita requiritur. Sed agnoscit ipse Schlichtingius, nullo modo verba de crea- tione cœli & terræ, quæ de primâ creatione in- telligit, Christo convenire, adducta autem tan- tum, quod separari nequiverint ab iis, quæ de ab- olitione agunt. Annon ergò impertinenter addu- cta forent? Et cur non potuissent sequentia sola citari h. m. Cæli peribunt: tu autem permanes, quid luculentius, quàm de eodem אל DEO, quem DEUM suum vocat Psaltes, utrumque dici, & creationem cæli ac terræ, & abolitionem. Quum ergo hæc de Christo explicetur, illa de eodem ne- gari non debet, nisi non modo citra sensum ea adducta ab Apostolo, sed etiam falsò eidem sub- jecto utraque in ipso Psalmo tributa dixeris: in quo ne fingi quidem geminum subjectum potest, alterum primarium, alterum secundarium, sive secundum contextum Hiero-Psaltis, sive secun- dum interpretationem Apostolicam: nedum ci- tra ἀκύρωτα sensus cum Schlichtingio, contradi- ctoriè statui.

MEMBRUM II. De natura humana CHRISTI eminentia.

## 1:13
Verse 13. But to which of the angels has he said at any time.

He heaps up other praises of the Messiah, which neither were nor could be adapted to the Angels. Namely, GOD said.

Thus far the Apostle has demonstrated the divine nature of Christ from the testimonies of the Old Testament: now he proceeds to demonstrate the eminence of his human nature: That according to it Christ has been constituted our Prophet and High Priest, heir or lord of all, and has been exalted to the right hand of the Majesty on high, and has received a name more excellent than the Angels. This demonstration he institutes first from the testimonies of Scripture treating of that eminence κατὰ λέξιν [literally]: of which two have been adduced. Then indeed from those things which teach the same κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν [according to the sense] by good consequence. Among those, first is adduced the passage of Psalm CX. 1. Theodoret notes this συνέχειαν [connection]: When he had discoursed thus concerning divine things, he passed back to human things. For he does not say as to God: Sit at my right hand. For how so? For his throne is for ever and ever. As man, therefore, he is a participant of this honor. For as God he has an eternal throne. Concerning which he had also spoken before on the words: Being made so much better than the angels: This he also said regarding his humanity. For as God he is the maker and Lord of the angels: but as man, after he rose again and ascended into heaven, he became more excellent than the angels, for he was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death. For we see JESUS, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death. Just as, therefore, he was lower than the angels as man: since they indeed have an immortal nature, but he himself endured passion: So after he ascended into heaven, he was made more excellent than the angels. For he sat above all principality, etc. Eph. I. Therefore Grotius is not to be heard here, as if other praises are heaped upon the Messiah only, as if they were of the same kind as the preceding ones, whereas these are most diverse, and concern the human nature of CHRIST, while the preceding ones indeed looked to the divine nature.

Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.

From Psalm 110, which Rabbi Saadia Gaon acknowledged must be understood of the Messiah. That 'sit at my right hand' in this place signifies not only dignity, but at the same time also security. Who would not be secure at the right hand of the Most Powerful King? See John 6:63, 7:34. Compare Acts 2:34, 1 Corinthians 15:25, below 10:13. 'At the right hand' is from the right side, לימיני. The same phrase is in Deuteronomy 33:2, 1 Samuel 23:19, 2 Kings 2:14, 7:38, 43, 20:19, Matthew 20:21, 23, 22:44, 25:33, 34, 26:64, 27:38, Mark 10:37, 40, 12:36, 14:62, 15:23, 16:19, Luke 1:11, 21:42, 22:69, 23:33, Acts 2:25, 34, 7:55, 56. Be secure, God says to the Messiah: not only will nothing harm you henceforth; but furthermore I will bring it about that all your enemies are subjected to you. It was the custom of the Kings of the East to trample the conquered underfoot, Joshua 10:24, Psalm 47. Clement of Rome, describing this passage, adds: 'Who then are his enemies? The wicked and those who set themselves against God, preferring their own will to His will.' Much, however, does this pertain to the encouraging of the souls of those who were enduring hardships for the sake of the Gospel.

As to the first testimony, one must first observe the seat, namely Psalm 110, which we taught in the annotations to the Old Testament is to be taken literally concerning the Messiah. And Grotius acknowledges this here, nor did he dare to deny it at the passage of Psalm 110, verse 1. It is too clear, not only this testimony of the Apostle, but also that of Christ himself, Matthew 22:43, to which the Pharisees were therefore struck dumb. Compare also 1 Corinthians 15:25, Hebrews 10:13, and the Grotian annotations to Matthew 22:48 and to Luke 24:47, as well as 'On the Truth of the Christian Religion,' Book 5, Chapter 22, where he confesses that this Psalm CANNOT be explained of anyone other than the Messiah. Secondly, one must note the Grotian explanation of the phrase 'sit at my right hand,' which he explained in the annotations to the Psalm thus: 'Be secure in the confidence of my help.' Here he adds the signification of dignity: 'It signifies,' he says, 'not only dignity, but at the same time also security.' But the Apostle is not occupied with demonstrating the security of Christ, but rather with showing his eminence through his exaltation to the right hand of the Majesty on high, and his 'betiosis,' or improvement above all Angels, and the attainment of a name much more excellent than the Angels; nor is anything read about security in the cited passages, as if that were noted by the phrase of sitting at the right hand of GOD. Let the passages John 6:63, chapter 7:34, Acts 2:34, 1 Corinthians 15:25, Hebrews 10:13 be weighed; nothing of the sort will be found in them. But concerning that insipid gloss, it was spoken of at Psalm 110. Thirdly, it was shown before that by the words 'at the right hand' it is not understood as the right side, but the right hand of power, to which Christ was exalted, is noted. It is one thing when it concerns the right hand of a man, or with respect to some place, as in most of the passages brought forward by Grotius: It is another when it concerns the right hand of GOD, which denotes the virtue and power of GOD: and it brings in the infinite and eternal majesty of omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence, 1. because through this right hand all the enemies of the Son of GOD, as many as have been, are, and will be in all times and places, are prostrated at his feet, verse 1, which work is accomplished by no finite force, then because through this right hand the Scepter of virtue is directed by the Lord, sent forth from Zion until the consummation of the age, verse 2, and the Messiah is to rule through the same in the midst of his enemies, which dominion requires infinite power:

then because in respect to this right hand, as that which constitutes its possessor adorable, the faithful will render religious adoration, verse 3, then because from that right hand graciously working, the multiplication of the sons of God is perfected, verse 3, then because through this right hand the Priesthood of the Messiah is established eternally, verse 4, then because through the same, kings are crushed, and judgment is exercised among the nations, and the head of the great earth is shattered, verses 5, 6. Compare in the Pentadecade of dissertations of the Blessed Dorsch, dissertation 12, as also 13, which proves that the sitting at the right hand of GOD the Father is a divine dominion of infinite and immense Majesty, powerfully, graciously, and gloriously exerting itself toward creatures in the kingdom of power, grace, and glory, (1) because this sitting at the right hand of GOD the Father is nothing but a divine sitting. But every divine sitting is some divine dominion. (2) because the sitting at the right hand of GOD the Father is called this sitting for this reason, that it may be shown not to be a sitting of an inferior order, but of the highest, and therefore to be a divine dominion. (3) because the seat, which is the divine right hand itself, the throne of the all-lord himself, argues for nothing other than divine dominion. (4) because the Lord himself, who is invited to this sitting by GOD the Father, is not finitely, but infinitely Lord. (5) because the acts of this sitting are acts of infinite dominion. (6) because the height of this sitting is the height of divine dominion. For it is the height above all things, Job 3:31 and Ephesians 1:21, the height from which the rising one looked upon us, Luke 1:78, from which the Apostles were imbued with heavenly power, Luke 24:48. (7) because Psalm 2, which is clearly parallel to Psalm 110, clearly promises the Messiah a divine dominion, the Father about to ask, verse 8. (8) because the Apostle expressly interprets this sitting as ruling, 1 Corinthians 15:25, where it is proven from many circumstances of the text that the discourse is about divine dominion. To these are added special reasons found in this text of ours, namely (1) because only infinite dominion constitutes an infinite distinction between Christ and the angels. And Paul wished to constitute such a thing in this place. (2) because angels are sent by only omnipotent dominion as λειτουρ- γικὰ πνεύματα, verses 13, 14, but they are sent by the one sitting at the right hand of majesty. (3) because the preceding parts argue for infinite dominion, such as the placing above all things, and the preservation of all things. (4) because it is a sitting or dominion ἐκ δεξιᾶ as in a beginning, by which that is perfected, and so it is a dominion proceeding from infinite power. (5) because it is a filial dominion, not a servile one, and indeed that of the own Son, who is the brightness of glory, and the character of the ὑποστάσεως of the Father, begotten from eternity by the Father, and therefore it is a dominion identical with the Father's dominion, and of the same throne. Add to these that some Papists, Thomas, Salmeron, Gagnaus, Staynus, Cornelius à Lapide, as also from the Calvinists Bullinger, Theodoret, Beza, acknowledge divine dominion in this place. The blessed Dorschæus also proves in the same place that the sitting at the right hand of GOD the Father is a dominion of divine, infinite, and immense Majesty joined with the substantial nearness and presence of the one sitting, (1) because it is a divine sitting. But every divine sitting requires both the dominion and the substantial presence of the one sitting among creatures, by an induction of all the divine texts which speak of that sitting. (2) because this sitting is where the throne is, in which one sits. For nowhere is there a throne without a divine sitting, nor is a sitting outside the throne. But the throne of this sitting, as it is indivisible, so also is it illocal, nor is it excluded from any place. (3) Because the Lord sitting is Lord infinitely, namely with supreme dominion. But supreme dominion is not without substantial presence. (4) Because when by this sitting the enemies of Christ are said to be prostrated under his feet, this prostration is nowhere accomplished without the presence of the one prostrating, thus also the very hands prostrating are nowhere excluded, Psalm CXXXIX. verse 10. (5) Because this sitting is accomplished in the midst of enemies, which requires the presence not only of operation, but also of subsistence. (6) Because this sitting demands from those over whom it extends, from rational creatures, religious worship, which tends not to one substantially absent, but present. (7) Because this sitting is the filling of all things, Ephes. IV. v. 10. [2] These things being well observed, from the above, delivered in the Apostolic proposition, let the determination of the subject now follow, that he sits at the right hand of GOD the Father, that this is Christ according to his human nature is evident both from Psalm CX., because Christ arrived at this sitting by divine command, which he can receive only according to his human nature: And this sitting is declared by the exaltation of the head, after he drank from the torrent in the way, last verse, just as after his passion he entered into his glory, Luke XXIV. verse 16. and it is confirmed from the parallel passage Psalm II. v. 8., because he arrived at this sitting by asking, but Christ cannot ask, except according to his human nature; just as he asked for this glorification John XVII. verse 5. [3] then from this Apostolic passage it clearly appears, because Christ sat down at the right hand of Majesty after the expiation of sins made through death, and the foundation of that sitting is the anointing of the Holy Spirit, which was treated in Psalm XLV., which befits Christ according to his human nature.

of their hearts, even Satan himself, Romans XVI. verse 20. nay, they themselves tread upon the same with their feet, Psalm XCI. verse 13. Such a sitting is understood here, which brings not only dignity above the Angels, but also a name above every name, Phil. II. verse 9. which is an infinite dignity, as we taught above, and at Phil. II. In this sitting is attributed to CHRIST a robust Scepter to be sent forth from Zion, Psalm CX. verse 2. which in Psalm II. 9. with respect to enemies is called an iron rod, and includes all power in heaven and on earth, Matth. XXVIII. verse 18. all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Col. II. verse 3. the power of life and death, John X. v. 18. whence the Messiah as Lord of the right hand is said to be about to break Kings in the day of his wrath, to exercise judgment among the nations; and thus to place his enemies at his feet, 1. Corinth. XV. v. 24. But that word footstool, although it may be said to regard the type, Jos. X. [5] v. 24. nevertheless some understand the earth as the footstool of CHRIST, Is. LXVI. verse 1. into which enemies are prostrated, when they are subjected to CHRIST, and destroyed: But that full subjection of all things will follow on the last day, when every principality and power shall be evacuated, as the Apostle teaches 1. Corinth. XV. v. 25. seqq. But as for the particle ἕως ἂν until, it includes the time preceding the subjection of enemies in such a way that the following time is not excluded, as is not infrequently evident from its use in the Scriptures. Therefore he is said to be about to sit at the right hand of GOD εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς forever, Heb. X. v. 12. Although it can also be taken τελικῶς, as I posit, just as it seemed to the blessed Dorscheus on this passage, from 2. Peter I. verse 21. so that ἕως ἂν is placed for ἵνα.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Πρὸς τίνα δὲ τῶν ἀγγέλων εἴρηκέ ποτε.

Alia congerit elogia Messiæ, quæ Angelis nec aptata sint, nec aptari queant. Dixit nempe DEUS.

Hactenus divinam Christi naturam è testimoniis Vet. Test. demonstravit Apostolus: jam progre- ditur ad naturæ humanæ eminentiam demonstran- dam: Quod secundum eam Christus Propheta, & Pontifex noster, hæres vel herus omnium con- stitutus, & ad dextram Majestatis in excelsis evectus sit, ac nomen excellentius præ Angelis acceperit. Quam demonstrationem primum è testimoniis Scripturæ κατὰ λέξιν de ea eminentia tractanti- bus, instituit: Quorum duo adducta sunt. De- inde verò ex iis, quæ κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν per bonam consequentiam eandem docent. Inter illa primo adducitur loco Psal. CX. 1. Hanc συνέχειαν advertit Theodorethus: Cum de divinis ita disseruisset, rursus transiit ad humana. Non enim tanquam Deo dicit: Sede à dextris meis. Quomodo enim? Thronus enim ejus est in seculum seculi. Ut homo ergo hujus est honoris particeps. Ut Deus enim habet æternam se- dem. Quo de etiam antea dixerat ad verba: Tan- to melior Angelis effectus est: Hoc etiam dixit, quoad humanitatem. Ut Deus enim est effector &, Dominus Angelorum: Ut homo autem, postquam resurrexit & in cælos ascendit, Angelis præstan- stior evasit, erat enim minor Angelis, propter mor- tis perpessionem. Eum enim, qui paulò minus ab Angelis est diminutus, videmus JESUM propter perpessionem mortis. Quemadmodum er- gò erat Angelis minor, ut homo: quoniam illi quidem naturam habent immortalem, ipse vero sustinuit passionem: Ita postquam ascendit in cælos, Angelis præstantior factus est. Sedit enim super omnem principatum, &c. Ephes. I. Non ergo audiendus hic Grotius, quasi alia elogia tantum Messiae congerantur, veluti ejusdem ge- neris cum praecedentibus, quum haec maxime diversa sint, & humanam CHRISTI naturam concernant, praecedentia vero ad divinam natu- ram spectarint.

Κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν με, ἕως ἂν θῶ τοὺς ἐχθρούς σε ὑπο- πόδιον τῶν ποδῶν συ.

Ex Psalm. CX. quem de Messia intelligendum agnovit Rabbi Saadia Gaon. Illud sede ad dextram hoc loco non solam dignitatem, sed simul & securitatem signifi- cat. Quis non sit securus apud Regis Potentissimi dexte- ram? Vide Johan. VI. 63. VII. 34 Confer. Actor. II. 34. 1. Corinth. XV. 25. infra X. 13. ἐκ δεξιῶν est a dextero la- tere לימיני. Eadem locutio Deut. XXXIII. v. 2. 1. Sam. XXIII. 19. 2. Reg. II. 14. VII. 38. 43. XX. 19. Matth. XX. v. 21. 23. XXII. v. 44. XXV. 33. 34. XXVI. 64. XXVII. 38. Marc. X. 37. 40. XII. 36. XIV. 62. XV. 23. XVI 19. Luc. I. 11. XXI. 42. XXII. 69. XXIII. 33. Actor. II. 25. 34. VII. v. 55. 56. Securus esto, inquit Deus Messiae : non modo posthac tibi nihil nocebit: verum insuper efficiam, ut omnes hostes tui tibi subjiciantur. Mos erat Regum Orientis, victos calcare pedibus, Jos. X. 24. Psal. XLVII. Clemens Romanus hunc locum describens addit : Τίνες ὦν οἱ ἐχθροὶ ἀυτῦ; οἱ φαῦλοι καὶ ἀντιτασσόμενοι τῷ Θεῷ τῷ θελήματι τὸ θέλημα ἴδιον. Multum autem hoc pertinet ad erigendos eorum animos, qui ob Evangelium dura perpetiebantur.

Quod ad primum testimonium ejus obser- vanda primum sedes, Psalmus nempe CX. quem de Messia secundum literam agere in annot. ad Vet. Testam. docuimus. Idque agnoscit hic Gro- tius, nec negare ausus fuit ad locum Psalm. CX. vers. 1. Nimis luculentum est, non tantum hoc Apostoli testimonium, sed etiam ipsius Christi, Matth. XXII. vers. 43. ad quod proinde obmutue- runt Pharisaei. Confer. & 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 25. Ebr. X, vers. 13. & Grotiana annotata ad Matth. XXII. vers. 48. & ad Luc. XXIV. vers. 47. necnon de verit. Christ. relig. libr. V. cap. 22. ubi fatetur, hunc Psalmum de alio, quam de Messia exponi NON POSSE. Secundo notanda explicatio Grotiana phraseos, sede ad dextram, quam in an- not. ad Psalm. sic exposuit : Securus esto fiducia auxilii mei: Hic addit significationem dignita- tis: Non solum, inquit, dignitatem, sed simul & securitatem significat. Sed Apostolus non versa- tur in demonstranda securitate Christi, verum in ostendenda eminentia per exaltationem ad dextram majestatis in excelsis, & βελτίωσιν, vel meliorationem supra omnes Angelos, ac conse- cutione nominis multo excellentioris prae Angelis; nec quicquam de securitate in locis allegatis le- gitur, quasi ea notetur phrasi sessionis ad dextram DEI. Expendantur loca Johan. VI. vers. 63. cap. VII. vers. 34. Actor. II. vers. 34. 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 25. Ebr. X. vers. 13. nihil tale de illis inve- nietur. Sed de illa insulsa glossa dictum est ad Psalm. CX. Tertio per verba ἐκ δεξιῶν non intel- ligi a dextro latere, sed dextram potentia, ad quam exaltatus est Christus, notari, antea o- stensum. Aliud est, cum de dextra hominis agi- tur, aut respectu loci alicujus, ut in plerisque lo- cis a Grotio adductis: Aliud, cum de dextra DEI, quae virtutem & potentiam DEI notat: infert- que infinitam & aeternam majestatem omnipoten- tiae, omnisapientia, omniopulentia, omnipraesen- tia, 1. quia per hanc dextram omnes inimici Fi- lii DEI, quotquot omnibus temporibus & locis fuerunt, sunt, & erunt, ad pedes ipsius proster- nuntur, vers. 1. quod opus nulla finita vi confici- tur, tum quia per hanc dextram dirigitur, Sce- ptrum virtutis a Domino, e Sion emissum usque ad consummationem seculi, vers. 2. & dominatu- rus est Messias per eandem in medio inimicorum, quod dominium infinitam requirit potentiam:

tum quia in respectu ad hanc dextram, tanquam quæ constituit adombilem possessorem suam fide- les adorationem religiosam præstabunt, vers. 3. tum quia ab illa dextra gratio\u017sè operante filio- rum Dei multiplicatio perficitur, vers. 3. tum quia per hanc dextram Sacerdotium Messiæ æternum firmatur, vers. 4. tum quia per eandem confrin- guntur reges, & judicium exercetur inter gentes, & conteritur caput terræ magnæ, vers. 5. 6. Conf. in Pentadecade dissertat. Beat. Dorschæi disp. 12. ut & 13. quæ probat, sessionem ad dextram DEI Patris esse dominationem divinam infinitæ & immensæ Majestatis, potenter, gratio\u017sè & glo- rio\u017sè sese exerenti­s erga creaturas in regno po- tentiæ, gratiæ, & gloriæ, (1) quia hæc sessio ad dextram DEI Patris non est nisi divina sessio. Divina autem sessio omnis est aliqua dominatio divina. (2) quia sessio ad dextram DEI Patris hæc sessio propterea vocatur, ut ostendatur non esse inferioris ordinis sessionem, sed summi, adeoque esse divinam dominationem. (3) quia sedes, quæ est ipsa dextra divina, ipse thronus omnidominus, non aliam, quam divinam domi- nationem arguit. (4) quia ipse Dominus, qui ad hanc sessionem à Deo Patre invitatur, non est finitè, sed infinitè Dominus. (5) quia actus hujus sessionis sunt actus infinitæ dominationis. (6) quia altitudo hujus sessionis est altitudo divinæ domi- nationis. Est enim altitudo super omnia, Job. III. vers. 31. & Eph. I. v. 21. altitudo, ex qua nos oriens respexit, Luc. I. vers. 78. ex qua Apostoli virtute cœlesti sunt imbuti, Luc. XXIV. v. 48. (7) quia Psalm. II. qui plane est parallelus Ps. CX. plane divinam dominationem Messiæ petituro pollice- tur Pater vers. 8. (8) quia hoc sedere per do- minari diserte interpretatur Apostolus 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 25. ubi de divino dominio sermonem esse ex plurimis textus circumstantiis convinci- tur. Quibus accedunt speciales rationes in hoc textu nostro obviæ, utpote (1) quia solum infini- tum dominium constituit infinitum discrimen in- ter Christum & Angelos. Tale autem constitue- re voluit Paulus hoc loco. (2) quia à solo omnipo- tente dominio mittuntur Angeli tanquam λειτουρ- γικὰ πνεύματα, vers. 13. 14. mittuntur autem à se- dente in dextra majestatis. (3) quia anteceden- tia infinitum dominium arguunt, ut sunt colloca- tio super omnia, & conservatio omnium. (4) quia est sessio sive dominium ἐκ δεξιᾶ tanquam in principio, quo istud perficitur, itaque est do- minium ab infinita potestate proficiscens. (5) quia est dominium filiale, non servile, & qui- dem Filii proprii, qui est splendor gloriæ, & cha- racter ὑποστάσεως Patris, ab æterno à Patre geni- tus, adeoque est dominium idem cum Patris do- minio, ejusdemque throni. His adde, quod Pon- tificii nonnulli Thomas, Salmeron, Gagnaus, Stay- nus, Cornelius à Lapide, ut & è Calvinianis Bul- lingerus, Theodoretus, Beza, dominium divinum hoc loco agnoscant. Probat etiam ibidem B. Dorschæus, sessionem ad dextram DEI Patris esse dominationem divinæ infinitæ, & immen- sæ Majestatis conjunctam cum substantiali pro- pinquitate, & adessentia sedentis, (1) quia est ses- sio divina. Omnis autem sessio divina tum do- minationem, tum substantialem adessentiam se- dentis apud creaturas requirit, per inductio- nem omnium textuum divinorum, qui de sef- sione ista loquuntur. (2) quia hæc sessio ibi est, ubi est thronus, in quo sedetur. Nullibi enim thronus est sine sessione divina, nec sessio est extra thronum. Thronus vero hujus sessionis, uti indivisibilis est, ita etiam illocalis, nec ullo loco excluditur. (3) Quia Dominus sedens est Dominus infinitè, dominio scilicet summo. Sum- mum autem dominium non est sine substanria- lî præsentia. (4) quia quando per hanc sessio- nem inimici Christi dicuntur prostrati sub pedes ipsius, nullibi ista prostratio perficitur sine pro- sternentis præsentia, sic & ipsæ manus proster- nentes nullibi exclusæ sunt, Psalm. CXXXIX. vers.10. (5) quia hæc sessio perficitur in medio inimicorum, quod non tantum operationis, sed etiam subsistentiæ præsentiam requirit. (6) quia hæc sessio exigit ab illis, super quos se exten- dit, à creaturis rationalibus, cultum religio- sum, qui non ad substantialiter absentem, sed præsentem tendit. (7) quia hæc sessio est impletio omnium, Ephes. IV. v. 10. His probè observatis, è superioribus, in propositione Apostolica tra- ditis, accedat jam subjecti determinatio, quod sedet ad dextram DEI Patris, quod esse Chri- stum secundum humanam naturam tum è Psalm. CX. constat, quia ad hanc sessionem Christus pervenit ex divino imperio, quod solum secun- dum humanam naturam recipere potest: Et ses- sio hæc per exaltationem capitis, postquam de torrente in via bibit, vers. ult. declaratur, uti post passionem suam ingressus est in gloriam, Luc.XXIV. vers. 16. tùm è loco parallelo Psalm. II. v. 8. confir- matur, quia ad hanc sessionem pervenit petendo, non autem petere potest Christus, nisi secundum humanam naturam; uti hanc glorificationem pe- tiit Joh. XVII. vers. 5. tum ex hoc Apostolico loco liquidò apparet, quia Christus consedit ad dex- tram Majestatis post expiationem peccatorum per mortem factam, ejusque sessionis fundamentum est unctio Spiritus S. de qua in Psalm. XLV. actum, quæ Christo secundum humanam naturam con- venit.

dibus eorum, ipsummet etiam Satanam, Roman. XVI. vers. 20. imo ipsi calcant eundem pedibus suis, Psalm. XCI. vers. 13. Talis sessio hic intelli- gitur, quæ infert non tantum dignitatem super Angelos, sed etiam nomen supra omne nomen, Phil. II. vers. 9. quæ infinita est dignitas, ut su- pra, & ad Phil. II. docuimus. In hac sessione tri- buitur CHRISTO Sceptrum robustum è Sione emittendum, Psalm. CX. vers. 2. quod Psalm. II. 9. respectu hostium virga ferrea vocatur, & inclu- dit omnem potestatem in cælo, & in terra, Matth. XXIIX. vers. 18. omnes thesauros sapientiæ & sci- entiæ, Col. II. vers. 3. potestatem vitæ & necis, Joh. X. v. 18. unde Messias tanquam Dominus dexte- ræ dicitur fracturus Reges in die iræ suæ, judicium exerciturus inter gentes; adeoque inimicos suos positurus ad pedes, 1. Corinth. XV. v. 24. Vox au- tem illa scabellum pedum quamvis dici possit re- spicere typum, Jos. X. v. 24. nonnulli tamen sca- bellum pedum CHRISTI terram intelligunt, Es. LXVI. vers. 1. in quam prosternuntur hostes, cum CHRISTO subjiciuntur, ac destruuntur: Plena verò illa omnium subjectio in die novissima sequetur, cum omnis principatus & potestas eva- cuabitur, docente Apostolo 1. Corinth. XV. v. 25. seqq. Quod autem ad particulam ἕως ἂν donec, ea ita includit tempus, subjectionem inimico- rum præcedens, ut tamen non excludatur sequens, ut ex usu ejusdem in Scripturis non infrequen- ter constat. Ided sessurus dicitur ad dextram DEI εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς in sempiternum, Ebr. X. v. 12. Quanquam etiam τελικῶς accipi queat, ut po- nam, quemadmodum B. Dorscheo in hunc loc visum, è 2. Petr. I. vers. 21. ut ἕως ἂν positum sit pro ἵνα.

## 1:14
Vers. 14. Οὐχὶ πάντες εἰσὶ λειτουργικὰ Πνεύματα. רוחות עברת : otherwise מלאכי השרת which here the Syrian in the same sense רוחא דתשמשתא In every kingdom the son of the King excels the Satraps however great they may be. The son of the King sits, while the Satraps stand or go where they are sent.

Εἰς διακονίαν ἀποστελλόμενα διὰ τοὺς μέλλοντας κληρονομεῖν σωτηρίαν.

They serve not only Christ, but also Christians, as can be seen Acts V. 19. XII. 7. Christians are rightly called μέλλοντες κληρονομεῖν τὴν σωτηρίαν. For they are destined for that, and will arrive at it, unless they hinder themselves. Κληρονομεῖν σωτηρίαν is the same as κληρονομεῖν ζωὴν αἰώνιον, Matth. IX. v. 29. Mark X. v. 17. Luke X. v. 25. chap. XVIII. v. 18. κληρονομεῖν βασιλείαν Θεοῦ, Matth. XXV. v. 34. 1. Corinth. VI. verse 9. 10. chap. XV. verse 50. Galat. V. verse 21. κληρονομεῖν τὰς ἐπαγγελίας, below VI. verse 12. κληρονομεῖν τὴν εὐλογίαν, below XII. 17. 1. Peter III. 9. See also what we said above 1. 2. 4.

Whence Fourthly it is now clear how cold the Grotian paraphrase is. Be secure, says God to the Messiah, not only will nothing harm you hereafter, but furthermore I will cause all your enemies to be subjected to you. For the sitting at the right hand of God brings the communion of divine power and Majesty, to the full exercise of which Christ was admitted according to his human nature, in the exaltation to the government or divine dominion of infinite virtue already shown. And what was the point of speaking here about the security of Christ at the right hand of God? For who could doubt that he is secure at the right hand of God? Are not the elect men themselves secure from the right hand of God? Are not the Angels in heaven secure? What then does Christ have singular in that over them, so that the Apostle should say: To which of the Angels did he say: Sit at my right hand? [10] Fifthly, enemies are understood here not only bodily, but also spiritual, among whom the last enemy is death, 1. Corinth. XV. verse 24. who are said to be about to be subjected to Christ to show his eminence, virtue, and Majesty. Because he himself subjects them to himself, even if it is said here of the Father: Until I place. Which is asserted of the Son likewise 1. Corinth. XV. 24. ἄχρις οὗ ἂν θῇ: until he places for him. For all things which the Father does, the same the Son also does likewise, John V. and the Son can render all things subjected to himself, according to the Apostle, Phil. III. verse 21. It is a question here of that dignity and power which falls to none of the Angels, as the Apostle testifies. And therefore these things are explained very jejunely and ineptly regarding the security which GOD provides for Christ. For GOD grants this to all the faithful; for can He not also subject, and does He not subject, enemies under them? It is not a session properly so-called or a station that is regarded here, but by session is understood rule, as Psalm 110:1 was interpreted by Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:25. Although indeed among the Angels there are also found dominions and principalities, by which titles the degrees of dignity among them are designated. Yet to none of them has it been said, 'sit at my right hand'; of whatever dignity one may be, none of them obtains a divine dominion of infinite power, to which Christ according to the flesh has been exalted. All are ministering spirits, all are sent forth at the nod of Christ as ministers, and they serve not only CHRIST, but also the faithful of Christ, who are about to obtain the inheritance of salvation, and they guard them and carry them in their hands, Psalm 34:8, Psalm 91:12. It is also proven from this passage, because all Angels are πνεύματα λειτυργικὰ, that the distinction of the Scholastics between superior and inferior, assisting and ministering Angels is vain. Let us therefore confess, says Estius, after he had argued at length against Thomas, Cajetan, and others, that the Apostle's words clearly state that all angels are sent out for ministries. For he would not use such a question: Are they not all, etc., with no proof added thereafter, unless he meant that this is a notion impressed upon the minds of the faithful, that all angels are sent into ministries. that the Greek word ἀποστελλόμενα does not simply indicate that angels are sent into ministry, but that they are sent out or dispatched, as other interpreters have translated it, that is, sent abroad, from which word the Apostles are also named. He says, however, that this does not hold unless those who are sent go abroad, and Estius observes this against those who, with Thomas, say that all angels are indeed sent, but some by an exterior mission, others only by an interior one, by which they are surely ordained to this, that they transmit to those by whom they are to be executed the commands received from GOD by way of illumination. But this mode of mission applies to the superior angels. But properly, he says, one is not sent into ministry unless one contends that everyone is sent into ministry to whom something is enjoined to be done either at home or abroad, even if he does not move from his place. Which usage of speech does not have, etc. We commit these Cadmean brothers to one another, and we refer to Frid. Riber. on this passage and Estius's commentary on the II. Sentences, as also Cornel. à Lapide on this passage. Daniel VII. verse 10, angels are said to minister and assist, but in the same sense, for they assist for the sake of service, and by assisting they minister, so that when they are sent out for duty, they are always ready. Which sense Cornelius à Lapide confirms from the prayer of the Church: Grant, O Lord, that those by whom you are always assisted while they minister to you in heaven, may protect our life on earth by them. Compare Luke II. verse 9, Tob. XII. v. 15. The Vulgate rendered the verb in the perfect tense as sent into ministry, but in the source it is the Present, so that the continuous ministry of the angels is indicated, which lasts as long as this present age lasts, until the elect attain the inheritance of salvation. Furthermore, they are said to be sent on account of those who are to attain that inheritance, not because they are not sent for the sake of others, since they also serve temporary things and are sent even to the reprobate, but because the fruit of their ministry appears most in those who attain salvation, and they guard them until the very end of life, and until they attain the blessed inheritance, and carry their souls into the bosom of Abraham, Luke XVI. Whence also the end and limit of the ministry of the angels is thus expressed, which is to lead men to salvation. Although indeed the heirs of eternal salvation are the proper and primary object of the angelic mission, as those for whom the world and whatever is in it are preserved, and for whom it tolerates the servitude of corruption, to be freed from the same when the glorious liberty of the children of GOD shall appear: Because, however, the Apostle does not say that angels were sent εἰς διακονίαν τοῖς μελλᾶσι κληρονομεῖν, but διὰ τὰς μέλλοντας, from that it appears that the object of the angelic mission extends more broadly than to include only the heirs of eternal salvation. For it is understood to include everything that can benefit or harm those heirs: because they are sent also to work in the kingdom of power among those things, and concerning those things, which unless divine providence prevents, could harm the kingdom of grace: hence also angels can be ordained from heaven to men placed outside the kingdom of grace, especially to universities and kingdoms, from which many inconveniences can be brought upon the assembly of the saints. See Daniel X. Indeed, even to the remaining creatures, insofar as benefit or detriment to the saints can arise from them. Psalm CIII. verses 20, 21. Chrysostom speaks beautifully about this passage: What is the wonder, he says, if they minister to the Son, when they also minister for our salvation? See how the Spirit excites them, and shows much honor of GOD toward us, since he has ordained that the angels, who are superior to us, should have this ministry for our sake. As if someone should say: He says they are used for this: This is the duty of the angels, to minister to GOD for our salvation. Wherefore this is the work of an angel, to do everything for the salvation of the brethren. Indeed, it is the work of CHRIST himself. For he indeed gives salvation, as Lord, but they as servants, and we, even if we are servants and fellow-servants of the angels: Why, he says, do you look up at the angels with open mouths? They are servants of the Son of GOD, and they are sent to many places for our sake, and they minister to our salvation, wherefore they are our fellow-servants. Chrysostom also gathers the dignity of men from this: Think how he does not give great difference to the creatures. Although there is much difference between angels and men, he nevertheless brings them near to us, saying to us almost, they labor for our sake, they run about us, and as someone might say, they serve us. This is their ministry, to be sent into all parts for our sake. Finally, he shows the distinction of the mission of the Son and of the angels: Furthermore, the Son was also sent, but not as a minister, nor as one who was performing some duty, but as Son and Only-begotten and who wills the same things as the Father. Indeed, he was not even sent: for he did not pass from place to place, but took on flesh. The angels, however, change places, and having left the former ones in which they are, they come to others in which they were not. These are the words of Chrysostom. We only add that this comparison of the angels and the Son of GOD, which the Apostle institutes here in verses 13 and 14, does not concern the Deity of CHRIST, but his humanity, according to which he was made better than the angels, and has obtained a more excellent name, that is, a more eminent dignity, which Theodoret rightly pointed out again here: He also sufficiently shows the difference, as far as it pertains to humanity. For he, he says, sits at the right hand. They, however, are sent as ministers for the salvation of men. For that, he sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high, (as Theodoret said before) was spoken humanly. For when he was the Most High, he humbled himself, and when he was GOD, he was made man. He was not, when he was humble, raised on high: nor when he was man, was he made GOD. But as GOD he was indeed the Lord of all. But as man he received the glory which he had as GOD.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Οὐχὶ πάντες ἐσὶ λειτουργικὰ Πνεύμαζα. רוחות עברת : aliter מלאכי השרת quo hic Syrus sensu eodem רוחא דתשמשתא In omni re- gno multum præstat filius Regis Satrapis quantumvis ma- gnis. Filius Regis sedet, Satrapis stantibus aut euntibus quo mittuntur.

Εἰς διακονίαν ἀποσελλόμενα διὰ τὲς μέλλοντας κληρο- νομεῖν σωτηρίαν.

Non tantum Christo serviunt, sed & Christianis, ut videre est Actor. V. 19. XII. 7. Christiani recte dicuntur μέλλοντες κληρονομεῖν τὴν σωτηρίαν. In id enim destinan- tur, & eo pervenient, nisi ipsi sibimet obstent. Κληρο- νομεῖν σωτηρίαν idem quod κληρονομεῖν ζωὴν αἰώνιον, Matth. IX. v. 29. Marc. X. v. 17. Luc. X. v. 25. cap. XVIII. v. 18. κληρονομεῖν βασιλείαν Θεῦ, Matth. XXV. v. 34. 1. Corinth. VI. vers. 9. 10. cap. XV. vers. 50. Galat. V. vers. 21. κληρο- νομεῖν τὰς ἐπαγγελίας, infra VI. vers. 12. κληρονομεῖν τὴν εὐλογίαν, infra XII. 17. 1. Petr. III. 9. Vide & quæ diximus supra 1. 2. 4.

Unde Quartò jam liquet, quam frigida sit paraphrasis Grotiana. Securus esto, inquit Deus Messiæ, non modo posthac tibi nihil nocebit, ve- rum insuper efficiam, ut omnes hostes tui tibi sub- jiciantur. Sessionem enim ad dextram Dei infer- re potentiæ & Majestatis divinæ communionem, ad cujus plenum exercitium admissus est Christus secundum humanam naturam, in exaltatione ad regimen vel dominium divinum infinitæ virtutis jam ostensum. Et quid attinebat hic de securi- tate Christi ad dextram Dei dicere? Ecquis enim dubitare poterat, eum ad dextram Dei securum esse? Annon securi sunt ipsi homines electi à dex- tra Dei? Annon securi sunt Angeli in cælis? Quid ergo singulare in eo præ illis habet Christus, ut Apostolus: Ad quem, inquiat, Angelorum dixit: Sede ad dextram meam? Quinto hostes hic in- telliguntur non tantum corporales, sed etiam spi- rituales, inter quos novissimus hostis mors est, 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 24. qui subjiciendi Christo dicuntur ad ostendendam ejus eminentiam, vir- tutem, & Majestatem. Quia ipse eos sibi subji- cit, etsi hic de Patre dicitur : Donec ponam. Quod de Filio pariter asseritur 1. Corinth. XV. 24. ἄχρις ὗ ἂν θῇ: donec ipsi ponat. Nam omnia, quæ Pater facit, eadem facit similiter & Filius, Joh. V. & Filius omnia sibi subjecta reddere potest, secun- dum Apostolum, Phil. III. vers. 21. De ea agitur hic dignitate ac potentia, quæ in nullum Angelo- rum cadit, teste Apostolo. Ideoque perquam jejune & inepte de securitate hæc explicantur, quam præstat Christo DEUS. Hanc enim præ- stat DEUS omnibus fidelibus, annon enim illis subjicere etiam potest, ac subjicit hostes sub pe- Non hic sessio proprie dicta aut statio respici- tur, sed per sessionem intelligitur regimen, ut Psalm. CX. vers. 1. interpretatus est Paulus 1. Cor. XV. v. 25. Quanquam vero inter Angelos etiam reperiantur dominationes, & principatus, qui- bus titulis gradus inter eosdem dignitatis desi- gnantur. Nulli tamen eorum dictum est, sede ad dextram meam, quantæcunque dignitatis sit, nullus eorum dominium divinum virtutis infi- nitæ obtinet, ad quod Christus secundum car- nem exaltatus est, omnes sunt Spiritus admini- stratorii, omnes emittuntur ad nutum Chri- sti, tanquam ministri, nec CHRISTO tantum, sed & fidelibus Christi, qui hæreditatem salutis consecuturi sunt, inserviunt, eosque custodiunt & manibus suis portant, Psalm. XXXIV. vers. 8. Psalm. XCI. vers. 12. Convincitur etiam ex hoc loco, quia omnes Angeli sunt πνεύματα λειτυρ- γικὰ, vanam esse Scholasticorum distinctionem inter Angelos superiores & inferiores, assistentes & ministrantes. Fateamur ergo, inquit Estius, postquam prolixè contra Thomam, Cajetanum, & alios egerat, quod Apostoli verba diserte so- nant, omnes Angelos emitti ad ministeria. Neque enim tali uteretur interrogatione : Nonne omnes &c. nulla deinceps addita probatione, nisi signifi- caret, eam esse velut notionem fidelium animis impressam, omnes Angelos in ministeria mitti. Notat etiam inter alia, quod Græca vox ἀπο- στελλόμενα non simpliciter indicet Angelos in ministerium mitti, sed emitti vel emandari, quo- modo verterunt alii Interpretes, id est, foras mitti, à qua voce & Apostoli dicti. Hoc autem non consistere ait, nisi qui mittuntur, foras ex- eant, idque observat Estius contra eos, qui cum Thoma omnes quidem Angelos ajunt mitti, sed alios exteriori missione, alios interiore tantum, qua nimirum ad hoc ordinentur, ut accepta à DEO mandata per viam illuminationis ad eos transmit- tant, à quibus sunt exequenda. Hunc autem mis- sionis modum competere superioribus Angelis. Sed proprie, inquit, non est mitti in ministerium, nisi quis contendat omnem eum in ministerium mit- ti, cuicunque aliquid seu domi seu foris agendum injungitur, etiamsi loco se non moveat. Quod non habet usus loquendi &c. Committimus in- ter se fratres Cadmæos, ac remittimus ad Frid. Riber. in hunc loc. & Estii commentar. in II. sen- tent. ut & Cornel. à Lapide hoc loc. Daniel. VII. vers. 10. ministrare & assistere dicuntur Angeli, sed eodem sensu, assistunt enim servitii causa, & assistendo ministrant, ut cum ad obsequium emittuntur, semper sint prompti. Quem sen- sum Cornelius à Lapide confirmat ex Ecclesiæ oratione : Da Domine, ut, à quibus tibi mini- strantibus in cœlo semper assistitur, ab his in ter- ra vita nostra muniatur. Conferantur Luc. II. vers. 9. Tob. XII. v. 15. Vulgata reddidit verbum in perfecto missi in ministerium, sed in fonte est Præsens, ut continuum Angelorum ministerium indicetur, quod tamdiu duret, quam durat præ- sens hoc seculum, donec electi hæreditatem sa- lutis adeant. Porrò mitti dicuntur propter eos, qui hæreditatem illam consecuturi sunt, non quod aliorum causa non emittantur, quum etiam προσκαίροις serviant, & ad reprobos quoque mit- tantur, sed quod maximè fructus ministerii ipsorum appareat in iis, qui salutem consequun- tur, eosque ad finem usque vitæ, & donec ad- eant beatam hæreditatem, custodiant, animas- que illorum in sinum Abrahæ portent, Luc. XVI. Unde etiam ita finis & terminus ministerii An- gelorum exprimitur, qui est homines perduce- re ad salutem. Quanquam verò hæredes salutis æternæ objectum proprium & primarium sint mis- sionis Angelicæ, utpote propter quos mundus, & quæcunque in eo sunt, conservantur, & pro- pter quos servitutem corruptionis tolerat, ab eadem liberandus, ubi gloriosa libertas filio- rum DEI apparuerit : Quia tamen Apostolus non dicit, Angelos missos esse εἰς διακονίαν τοῖς μελλᾶσι κληρονομεῖν, sed διὰ τὰς μέλλοντας, inde apparet latius sese extendere objectum missionis angelicæ, quàm ut solos salutis æternæ hæredes complectatur. Intelligitur enim eam comple- cti id omne, quod hæredibus illis prodesse vel obesse potest: quod mittantur etiam ut operen- tur in regno potentiæ apud ea, & circa ea, quæ nisi providentia divina obviet regno gratiæ ob- esse possint: hinc etiam extra regnum gratiæ positis hominibus angeli cœlitus ordinari pos- sunt imprimis universitatibus, & regnis, ex quibus plurima incommoda cœtui sanctorum inferri queunt. Vid. Daniel. X. Imo etiam ad reliquas creaturas, quatenus ex illis vel emolu- mentum vel detrimentum sanctorum oriri po- test. Psalm. CIII. vers. 20. 21. Pulchre de hoc lo- co Chrysostomus: Quid mirum, inquit, si mini- strant Filio, quum etiam ministrent ad nostram salutem? Vide, quomodo eorum excitet Spiritus, & multum DEI in nos honorem ostendat, siqui- dem constituit, ut Angeli, qui sunt nobis superio- res, hoc habeant pro nobis ministerium. Ut si di- xerit quispiam: Eis inquit ad hoc utitur: Hoc est munus Angelorum, ministrare DEO ad no- stram salutem. Quamobrem hoc est Angeli opus, facere omnia ad fratrum salutem. Imo vero est opus ipsius CHRISTI. Nam ipse quidem dat salutem, ut Dominus, ipsi autem tanquam servi, & nos, etiamsi servi & conservi Angelorum: Quid, inquit, Angelos hiantes suspicitis? Sunt servi Filii DEI, & in multa loca propter nos mittuntur, & ad nostram ministrant salutem, quamobrem sunt nostri conservi. Colligit etiam hinc dignitatem hominum Chrysostomus: Cogi- tate, quemadmodum non dat creaturis magnam differentiam. Quanquam multum interest inter Angelos & homines, eos tamen prope nos dedu- cit, propemodum nobis dicens, propter nos labo- rant, circa nos cursitant, & ut dixerit quispiam, nobis serviunt. Hoc est eorum ministerium, pro- pter nos in omnes mitti partes. Denique mon- strat distinctionem missionis Filii & Angelorum: Porro autem missus quoque est Filius, sed non sicut minister, neque tanquam qui aliquo funge- retur munere, sed tanquam Filius & Unigenitus & qui eadem vult, quæ Pater. Imo vero ne fuit quidem missus: non enim à loco in locum transiit, sed carnem suscepit. Angeli vero loca mutant, & prioribus, in quibus sunt, dimissis, ad alia ve- niunt, in quibus non erant. Hæc Chrysostomus. Id tantum addimus, quod hæc comparatio An- gelorum & Filii DEI, quam hic vers. 13. & 14. instituit Apostolus, non concernat CHRISTI Deitatem, sed humanitatem, secundum quam melior factus est Angelis, & nomen excellentius, hoc est, dignitatem eminentiorem consequutus est, quod iterum hic recte monuit Theodore- tus: Satis etiam ostendit differentiam, quod ad humanitatem attinet. Ille enim, inquit, sedet à dextris. Ii vero mittuntur, ut ministri pro homi- num salute. Illud enim, sedet ad dextram Ma- jestatis in excelsis, (ut antea Theodoretus) bu- mane dictum est. Cum enim esset Altissimus, seipsum humiliavit, & cum DEUS esset, homo factus est. Non cum esset humilis, in altum eve- ctus est: neque cum esset homo, DEUS factus est. Sed ut DEUS quidem erat universorum Domi- nus. Ut homo autem accepit gloriam, quam ha- buit ut DEUS.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Having premised an admonition concerning the receiving of the word announced by Christ, from a comparison of the word brought by Angels, he proceeds to demonstrate the eminence of Christ as the Son of man above the Angels, from the subjection of the world to come, which he confirms by a new testimony (from Ps. VIII. 5. et seqq.), namely that all things are subject to him, although this does not yet appear, even though he is already crowned with honor through the passion of JESUS. He then proceeds to the expiation of sins made through the Son of GOD, that it was fitting for him, who brought many children to glory, to be perfected through suffering, as one who is of the same origin as the children, their brother, (Psalm 22:23) of the same confidence, (Psalm 18:3) to whom the children were given by GOD, (Isaiah 8:18) and who for their sake was similarly made a partaker of our flesh and blood, that he might redeem them, taking hold of the seed of Abraham, not of Angels, and thus he also had to be made like his brothers in all things, that he might become a merciful and faithful High Priest to expiate the sins of the people.

There are three parts: I. An admonition concerning receiving the Word of the Lord, to verse 4. II. A demonstration of the eminence of the Son of man from the Davidic testimony, to verse 9. III. An explanation of the congruence of the divine ordination concerning the expiation of human sin through the death of the Son of God himself, to verse 18.

PART I. Admonition concerning receiving the Word of the Lord.

Verse 1. Διὰ τῦτο.

Since, as we have already shown, that author of our doctrine is greater even than the Angels.

Since the Hebrews had need not only of information in the faith, but also of excitation and admonition, that they might hold the Word of the Lord reverently and persist in the faith, the Apostle deduces this admonition from the dignity of Christ the Prophet and Teacher of the New Testament, who is exalted far above all Angels, both by reason of his divine nature, which is of the same essence and glory with the Father, and by reason of his human nature, in which he appeared so that he himself might preach the Gospel to the Hebrews. And since he had compared that Teacher of the New Testament with the Prophets on the very threshold, in whom God spoke formerly as servants, since most recently GOD has deigned to speak in the Son, who is ὁμοούσιος to Him and manifested in the flesh, lest it be objected that God also spoke to the Fathers formerly through Angels, which might seem to be more than that He announced the Word to them through the Son of man: not content to have taught that the Son of man is the Son of God, and of the same substance and glory with the Father, and the same GOD by nature with the Father, which he demonstrated clearly from the testimonies of the Old Testament: he also asserted that the Son of man, regarding his human nature, is far more excellent than the Angels, who are sent forth for the sake of the heirs of life, as one exalted to the right hand of GOD, which happened to none of the Angels. Wherefore if the mission and announcement of the Angels had to be received reverently formerly, and was not despised with impunity: the Apostle concludes that the salvation exhibited to the Hebrews must be observed much more, to whom the Word was announced by the Lord himself in the days of his flesh, which also reached others further, and was confirmed by many signs, and miracles, and mighty works, and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit: especially because He subjected the future world, not to Angels, but to the Son of man. This he proves next, so that he may further confirm the eminence of the Son of man over the Angels. This is the scope, this is the Apostolic συνέχεια and διήγησις, which is drawn from the bowels of the text, and thus is to be accurately observed: which being observed, those things which seemed very difficult to many will be easier.

Διὰ περισσοτέρως ἡμᾶς προσέχειν τοῖς ἀκουσθεῖσι. For this reason it is fitting that we direct our mind to those things which we have perceived. See Acts 16:14.

Some wish the word περισσοτέρως to be used for the positive; but the proper comparative sense is more correctly retained, because it is clear that the Apostle instituted comparisons in the premises, from which he elicits a similar hortatory conclusion, that is, a comparative one. The more worthy the person is whom God uses in an embassy to men, the greater the attention and reverence with which those things proposed by him are to be received. Indeed, all ambassadors of God are to be esteemed, and all their propositions are to be received as divine, but where God deigns to use someone for an angelic embassy, or even that of some more eminent Angel, such as the Angel Gabriel was, who was sent to Daniel and to Mary the Θεοτόκος, such an embassy seems to be observed and received περισσοτέρως. How much more is the mission of the Son of GOD to be esteemed, who also as man and according to the flesh, in which he performed his embassy, and was made the Minister of the circumcision, that is, of the Hebrews, is far more eminent than all the Angels of the supreme order, and has been made far better, and has attained a dignity above every dignity. Tὸ προσέχειν does not only imply observation, as the Vulgate rendered it 'to observe', but primarily attention, as he explained that word in Matthew 7:15, 'to attend', and Acts 16:14, 'to direct'. Therefore, this word requires 1. prompt reception: 2. pious meditation: 3. faithful preservation in true faith and obedience: Because προσέχειν is understood with affection and effect. By τὰ ἀκουσθέντα some understand the Word of the Gospel, which Christ announced in his own person, which the Apostle says the Hebrews, to whom he had preached the same, heard. But although we judge that the Gospel is primarily indicated, or the complement of the promises handed down in the Old Testament concerning the Messiah, which we have in Jesus of Nazareth. Nevertheless, the name τῶν ἀκουσθέντων is undoubtedly more general, embracing all the doctrine which was preached by the Lord in the days of his flesh: just as the Apostle and other θεόπνευστοι men handed down not only Evangelical dogmas, but also moral ones, both here among the Hebrews and elsewhere in their sermons and letters.

Lest we drift away.

Lest we slip away like water, which flows out uselessly: which similitude is expressed in 2 Sam. XV. 8. Psal. LVIII. 8. thus Prov. III, 21. υἱὲ μὴ παραῤῥυῇς lest you turn aside from the law. Origen against Celsus VIII. "But many of those who seem to believe, and are not such, have need, for the sake of a reminder, not wishing or not being able to spend all such days in sensible examples, so that they may not completely drift away." Lest he fall away entirely. Thus Lament. IV. 9. זָבוּ they flowed, that is, they collapsed. And here the Syrian and Arab translate lest we fall, nor did Chrysostom and other Greeks take it otherwise here. Thus things that perish are compared to flowing water, Job XX. 27. You have Ἔκρεῖν in a similar sense in Plutarch in Cato the Younger. A similar admonition is that of Irenaeus IV. 45. We ought not (says that elder) to be proud, nor to criticize the ancients, lest perhaps after the acknowledgment of Christ, doing something which does not please God, we may no longer have remission of sins, but be excluded from his kingdom. We are commanded to beware of nothing here, which cannot also happen and often does happen.

Chrysostom had expressed the sense thus: "That is, lest we drift away, lest we perish, lest we fall out," neither that we perish, nor that we fall out: Because by that word not only a fall, but also the danger of destruction is designated: For those who do not observe with the attention that is fitting what is proposed by God, not only easily fall, but they can also fall in such a way that they are not easily raised up again, or preserved, but perish entirely, just like flowing waters. Concerning which Chrysostom says: He shows, he says, how grave the fall is, since it is difficult for that which has flowed away to return, inasmuch as this happens out of sloth and negligence. My son, do not flow away: showing both how easy the lapse is, and how grave the destruction. This is, clearly, that it is not without danger not to obey. The Apostle seems, however, to compare man to an earthen vessel, 2 Cor. IV, verse 7, having cracks, which flows out in such a way that it finally leaks through, and can retain no liquid at all anymore; because if we once begin to have a crack of faith, and to gape, we shall most certainly leak through entirely, and all faith will slip away just like water from a broken vessel. Estius acknowledges that this sense introduces an antithesis between attending and flowing away, yet he prefers another metaphor from water in this way: Lest we perish without hope of reparation like water, which, once it has flowed away, it is impossible to gather back. He gives this reason, that the signification of punishment occurs here at the same time. He adds: That this is also the sense of the Greek interpreters. But as this does not appear to be the case with them: So the matter of punishment is dealt with in the following words, and thus it is not necessary that the signification of it be involved here. The explanation of those who say that the Word of salvation is like a rapid river, and that one must take care lest it flow away from our eyes, Prov. III, verses 20, 21, seems less appropriate, so that the sense might be derived from the history of the flood, because he caused those not attending to the word to flow away, 1 Pet. III, 20.

Latin:

CAPUT II. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Præmissa admonitione de verbo à Christo an- nuntiato suscipiendo è comparatione ver- bi per Angelos allati pergit in demon- stranda eminentia Christi ceu Filii homi- nis supra Angelos, à subjectione orbis fu- turi, quàm novo testimonio (è Ps. IIX. 5. seqq.) confirmat, quod nempe omnia- subjecta sint eidem, quum tamen id non- dum appareat, etsi per passionem JESU jam honore coronato. Accingitur dehinc ad expiationem peccatorum per Filium DEI factam, quod decuerit eum, qui multos liberos ad gloriam perduxit, per passionem consummari, utpote qui ejus- dem cum liberis originis frater ipsorum, (Psalm. XXII. vers. 23.) ejusdem fiducia, (Psalm. XIIX. vers. 3.) cui liberi à DEO dati, (Esa. IIX. vers. 18.) quique eorum causa similiter carnis & sanguinis nostri particeps factus, ut eos redimeret, semen Abrahae, non Angelos assumendo, adeoque etiam per omnia fratribus similis fieri de- buit, ut misericors & fidelis Pontifex fie- ret ad expianda peccata populi.

Partes tres sunt: I. Admonitio de Verbo Do- mini suscipiendo, ad vers. 4. II. Demonstra- tio eminentiae Filii hominis è testimonio Davidi- co, ad vers. 9. III. Explicatio congruentia divinae ordinationis de expiando, per ipsiusmet Filii Dei mortem, hominum peccato, ad v. 18.

PARS I. De Verbo Domini suscipiendo admonitio.

Vers. 1. Διὰ τῦτο.

Cum, ut jam ostendimus, major sit etiam Angelis ille nostrae doctrinae autor.

Quum Ebraei non tantum informatione in fi- de opus habuerint, sed etiam excitatione & com- monefactione, ut Verbum Domini reverenter habeant, & in fide persistant, è dignitate Christi Prophetae & Doctoris Novi Testamenti, qui & ra- tione divinae naturae ejusdem cum Patre est es- sentiae & gloriae, & ratione humanae naturae, in qua apparuit, ut Evangelium Ebraeis ipse prae- dicaret, exaltatus longe est supra omnes Angelos, hanc commonefactionem deducit Apostolus. Et quum Doctorem illum Novi Testamenti cum Prophetis in ipso limine contenderit, in quibus Deus ceu servis loquutus est olim, quum no- vissime DEUS in Filio sibi ὁμοουσίῳ in carne ma- nifestato loqui dignatus sit, ne obverteretur, Deum per Angelos etiam quandoque Patribus olim loquutum esse, quod amplius videri pos- set, quam quod per Filium hominis eis Verbum annuntiarit: non contentus docuisse, quod Fi- lius hominis sit Filius Dei, & ejusdem cum Pa- tre substantiae & gloriae, idemque cum Patre natu- ra DEUS, quod è testimoniis Veteris Testa- menti luculenter demonstravit: Asseruit etiam Filium hominis quoad naturam humanam lon- ge excellentiorem esse Angelis, qui emittuntur ob salutem haeredum vitae, utpote exaltatum ad dex- tram DEI, quod nulli Angelorum contigit. Quapropter si Angelorum missio & annuntiatio reverenter suscipi olim debuit, nec impune con- tempta fuit: Concludit Apostolus, multò magis observandam esse salutem Ebraeis exhibitam, qui- bus à Domino ipso in diebus carnis Verbum annuntiatum fuit, quod & porrò ad alios perve- nit, confirmatumque multis signis, & miraculis, & virtutibus, & effusione Spiritus Sancti: im- primis quia orbem futurum, non Angelis, sed Filio hominis subjecit. Quod deinceps probat, ut amplius eminentiam Filii hominis prae Ange- lis confirmet. Hic est scopus, haec συνέχεια & διήγησις Apostolica, quae è textus visceribus de- prompta, adeoque accurate observanda: qua observata faciliora erunt, quæ multis visa per- quam difficilia.

Διὰ περισσοτέρως ἡμᾶς προσέχειν τοῖς ἀκουσθεῖσι Eo magis par est, nos animum intendere eis, quæ per- cepimus. Vide Actor. XVI. 14.

Vocem περισσοτέρως nonnulli pro positiva vo- lunt adhibitam; sed rectius sensus proprius re- tinetur comparativus, quia luculentum est, A- postolum in præmissis comparationes instituisse, unde similem conclusionem adhortatoriam eli- cit, hoc est, comparativam. Quo dignior est persona, qua Deus utitur in legatione ad homi- nes, eo majori attentione, ac reverentia susci- pienda, quæ ab eadem proponuntur. Omnes quidem legati Dei æstimandi, omniumque eo- rum propositiones ceu divinæ suscipiendæ, sed ubi Deus dignatur quempiam legatione Angeli- ca, aut etiam Angeli alicujus eminentioris, qua- lis erat Angelus Gabriel ad Danielem, & Ma- riam Θεοτόκον missus, tanta legatio περισσοτέρως observanda videtur, ac suscipienda. Quanto ma- gis æstimanda missio Filii DEI, qui etiam ut ho- mo & secundum carnem, in qua legatione fun- ctus, & Minister circumcisionis factus, hoc est, Ebræorum, omnibus Angelis supremi ordinis longe eminentior, longeque melior effectus est, ac dignitatem supra omnem dignitatem conse- quutus. Tὸ προσέχειν non tantum observationem infert, ut Vulgata reddidit observare, sed impri- mis attentionem, uti eam vocem Matth. VII. v. 15. exposuit, attendere, & Actor. XVI. vers. 14. inten- dere. Requiritur ergo hoc verbo 1. prompta re- ceptio: 2. pia meditatio: 3. fidelis conservatio in ve- ra fide & obedientia: Quia προσέχειν cum affectu, & effectu intelligitur. Per τὰ ἀκουσθέντα nonnulli intelligunt Verbum Evangelii, quod Christus in propria persona annunciavit, quod Ebræos, qui- bus idem prædicaverat, audivisse dicit Aposto- lus. Sed tametsi Evangelium imprimis indigita- ri censeamus, vel complementum promissionum in Veteri Testamento traditarum de Messia, quod habemus in Jesu Nazareno. Generalius tamen, sine dubio, est τῶν ἀκουσθέντων nomen, omnem doctrinam, quæ à Domino in diebus carnis præ- dicata est, complectens: quemadmodum Apo- stolus, aliique viri θεόπνευστοι non tantum Evan- gelica dogmata, sed etiam moralia, & hic penes Ebræos, & alias in concionibus & literis suis tradidere.

Μήποτε παραῤῥυῶμεν.

Ne dilabamur ut aqua, quæ inutiliter effluit: quæ simi- litudo exprimitur 2. Sam. XV. 8. Psal. LVIII. 8. sic Prov. III, 21. υἱὲ μὴ παραῤῥυῇς ne deflectas à lege. Origenes adversus Celsum VIII. Οἱ δὲ πολὺς τῶν πιστεύειν δοκούντων, καὶ μὴ τηλικοῦτοι, δέονται, ὑπομνήσεως χάριν, μὴ βουλόμενοι ἢ μὴ δυνάμενοι πάσας τοιαύτας ἄγειν ἡμέρας αἰσθητῶν πα- ραδειγμάτων, ἵνα μὴ τέλεον παραῤῥυῇ. Ne plane decidat. Sic Lament. IV. 9. זָבוּ fluxerunt, id est, conciderunt. Et hic ne cadamus vertunt Syrus & Arabs, nec aliter hic sumpsit Chrysostomus & Græci alii. Sic quæ intereunt, aquæ effluenti comparantur, Job. XX. 27. Ἔκρεῖν fermo simili sensu habes apud Plutarchum Catone Uticensi. Si- milis admonitio illa Irænei IV. 45. Non debemus (inquit ille senior) superbi esse, neque reprehendere veteres, ne forte post agnitionem Christi agentes aliquid, quod non placeat Deo, remissionem ultra non habeamus delictorum, sed exclu- damur à regno ejus. Nihil hic cavere jubemur, quod non & fieri possit & sæpe fiat.

Sensum ita expresserat Chrysostomus: Τουτέστι, παραῤῥυῶ- μεν. μήποτε ἀπολώμεθα, μὴ ἐκπέσωμεν, neque perea- mus, neq; excidamus: Quod ea voce non tantum casus, sed etiam periculum interitus designetur: Qui enim non ea, qua par est, attentione, quæ di- vinitus proponuntur, observant, non modo facile cadere, sed ita etiam cadere possunt, ut non fa- cilè iterum erigantur, vel serventur, sed omninò pereant, quemadmodum aquæ effluentes. Quo de Chrysostomus : Ostendit, inquit, quàm sit gravis ca- sus, quoniam est difficile, ut id, quod effluxit, rever- tatur, quandoquidem hoc accidit ex socordia & ne- gligentia. Dictionem autem accepit è proverbiis : Fili, inquit enim, ne pereffluas : Ostendens & quam facilis sit lapsus, & quam gravis interitus. Hoc est videlicet, quod non sine periculo est non obedire. Comparare autem videtur Apostolus hominem vasi fictili, 2. Cor. IV. vers. 7. rimas habenti, quod sic effluit, ut tandem perfluat, ac nihil omninò liquoris amplius retinere possit; quia si semel fi- dei rimam habere cœperimus, & fatiscere, toti quam certissime perfluemus, omnisque fides vel- ut aqua ex vase fracto dilabetur. Quem sensum antithesin inter attendere & effluere inferre agno- scit Estius, aliam tamen Metaphoram ab aqua præfert hoc modo: Ne quando pereamus absque spe reparationis instar aquæ, quam, ubi semel efflu- xerit, impossibile est recolligere. Rationem hanc dat, quod significatio pœnæ hic simul occurrat. Ad- dit : Hunc etiam sensum esse Græcorum Interpre- tum. Sed uti hoc penes illos non apparet : Ita de pœna verbis sequentibus agitur, adeoque ne- cessum non est, ut hic ejusdem significatio invol- vatur. Minus convenire videtur eorum expli- catio, qui Verbum salutis dicunt esse instar fluvii rapidi, & cavendum esse, ne defluat ab oculis no- stris, Prov. III. vers. 20. 21. ut ex historia diluvii sensus deducatur, quod diffluere fecit non atten- dentes verbo, 1. Petr. III. 20.

## 2:2
Verse 2. For if the word spoken through Angels, That is, the law of Moses, which was not given through the Son, but through one of the chief Angels speaking in the name of God, Acts VII, 38, with many other Angels attending, Deut. XXXII, 2, Acts VII, 53, Gal. III, 19. Josephus, book XV: We have learned the most beautiful of the doctrines and the most holy of those in the laws from God through Angels.

Grotius seems to understand the word spoken through Angels as the moral law, along with Estius, Ribera, Capello, Cameron, Schlichting, and others.
