But he falsely assumes that the moral law was not given through the Son, and that it was given through one of the chief Angels speaking in the name of God. The contrary is evident from Exodus XIX and XX: Namely, that the law was promulgated immediately by God without the intervention of angelic ministry, as far as the speech or pronunciation of the law is concerned. For the word spoken is rendered by Estius as enunciated, uttered, promulgated. But in truth, the word spoken is not the Decalogue through a created Angel, much less through many Angels, just as mention is made here of many Angels, who certainly did not enunciate or promulgate the Decalogue, as Grotius admits, who therefore made his own the invention of the Jews, Socinians, and Papists, that this was done through one of the chief Angels speaking in the name of God. But concerning this, there is not a word in the history of the promulgated law: But God himself, who also testified in his own person: I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, thou shalt have no other gods before me, enunciated these precepts in person: The Lord, says Moses, spoke all these words, Exod. XX, verses 1, 2. Nor did Stephen speak otherwise in Acts VII. For although he says in verse 38 that an Angel spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai: He does not, however, understand a created Angel, but him who had appeared to Moses in the fire of the flame of the bush, verse 31, who is called Lord by Stephen; who testified to Moses: I am the Lord of thy fathers, the God of Abraham, the God

Isaac, and the God of Jacob: Who was indeed the uncreated Angel, namely the Son of God, through whom the Father spoke when the law was promulgated, because he is the eternal Word of the Father. Stephen does indeed say, verse 53, that the Hebrews received the law by the dispositions of Angels: But this is far different from that which the Apostle says at present, the word spoken through Angels. Nor does the passage in Gal. III, verse 19, contribute to this, as we observed in the annotations to the same: For it is not said there that the law was given or enunciated, but disposed through Angels. The roles of the Angels regarding the promulgation of the law were other than pronouncing the same. The Angels were present then, says Chrysostom in this place, to whom the nation had been entrusted, and they themselves were sounding trumpets, and doing other things, namely fire and darkness. Furthermore, that comparison of the Law and the Gospel does not seem to fit so well, that we ought to attend more to the doctrine of the Gospel than to that of the law, for the reason that the former was promulgated through Angels, and the latter was announced by the Lord himself. For the doctrine of the law is of no less divine origin and authority than the Gospel: Nor is it any less to be heard, attended to, and kept: nor would the contrary have been tolerable among the Hebrews, who believed that the law was delivered by God himself, which was also frequently inculcated upon them in Moses and the Prophets. For the law was held in the highest esteem among them for the very reason that it had been promulgated with such majesty by God himself, attended by a great multitude of Angels. Which is also indicated in Deuteronomy XXXIII, v. 2: The Lord came from Sinai, and with him a host of saints. In his right hand was a fiery law. Where there is nothing about the law being promulgated by any ministering Angel, much less enunciated by many Angels. Besides, that does not seem to agree in this comparison regarding confirmation through signs and miracles. For the law was not lacking in divine confirmation through signs and miracles. Whence Chrysostom, and Theophylact following him, although they willingly interpret these words of the Apostle concerning the law, yet they do not rest in that opinion, nor do they find how the law can be called the word spoken through Angels; Or does he mean only the Decalogue, says Chrysostom. For there Moses was speaking, and God was answering: Ἢ ὅτι παρῆσαν Ἄγγελοι τῷ θεῷ διαταττομένῳ (which response of Chrysostom was rashly omitted by the German interpreter Brixius) or that the Angels were present to God ordaining or promulgating the law; ἢ ὅτι περὶ τῶν ἐν τῇ παλαιᾷ λεγομένων καὶ γενομένων ἁπάντων, ὡς Ἀγγέλων κοινωνησάντων ἐν τάτοις ταῦτα φησίν: Or he says these things concerning all that was said and done in the old [testament], inasmuch as the Angels had a share in these things. He also adds another interpretation of the word λαληθεὶς, that it denotes not pronunciation, but some οἰκονομίαν, or some other acts of the Angels concerning the promulgated law, which sense he prefers to the others: Καὶ τάχα μοι δοκεῖ τῦτο λέγειν μᾶλλον τὰ διὰ τῶν Ἀγ- γέλων οἰκονομηθέντα. Τί ἐν ἐρῦμεν; παρῆσαν οἱ Ἄγ- γελοι τότε οἱ τὸ ἔθνος ἐμπεπιστευμένοι, καὶ αὐτοὶ τὰς σάλπιγγας ἐποίεν, καὶ τὰ ἕτερα, τὸ πῦρ, τὸν γνόφον. But to me this seems perhaps more to speak of those things which were dispensed through the Angels. What then shall we say? The Angels were present then, to whom the nation had been entrusted, and they themselves sounded the trumpets and did the other things, namely the fire and the darkness. But that sense is not supported by the word λαληθεὶς, which implies speech, not other acts, nor by the Apostolic context, in which the λόγos pronounced δι' Ἀγγέλων is compared with those things which the Hebrews had most recently heard, and which began to be spoken through the Lord, verse 1. 3. is compared, it agrees, therefore there is no place for the explanation of B. Gerhard: διὰ is taken for inter, 2 Tim. II. verse 2. The law therefore was ordained among the Angels, because the clanging of the trumpet, the sound, the lightning is to be attributed to them. For that comparison does not permit the word διὰ to be explained as AMONG but requires that it be understood in its proper meaning, just as in the phrase λαλεῖσθαι διὰ τοῦ Κυρίου BY the Lord. Otherwise the opposition will not be consistent. But the theologian, never sufficiently praised, most correctly acknowledges and urges against Estius, whom he otherwise followed in these matters, that not some primary angel representing the person of GOD, but GOD himself promulgated the law, since Moses so often celebrates this benefit, that the Israelites heard God himself speaking, Deut. IV. verse 32. et seqq. And further: We urge, he says, the plural number δι᾽ ἀγγέλων. Therefore, this is not about the recitation of the Decalogue, which, as Moses testifies, was done by one, whom we have established to have been GOD himself. I have cited the explanations of others, John Cameron in his Works on the Epistle to the Hebrews, page 387, concerning the sound formed in the air through the ministry of Angels, and Ludovicus de Dieu on Acts VII, concerning the Son of GOD in angelic form veiled by the glory of the Angels from the Angelic Senate, in Vol. IV of my System of Theology, chap. II, q. XVIII, page 249. But just as this designates at least a different mode of appearance, and does not introduce another subject of the speech, which is looked at here: So that one concerning the ministry in the formation of articulate sound, not concerning the speaking subject, is perhaps more subtle than solid.

What then is to be said here? Since it is most manifest that it concerns a word spoken through Angels, not among Angels, and concerning the speaking of Angels, not other combined actions, for it is said a word spoken through Angels, and furthermore the discourse is about many Angels, about Angels sent for ministry for the sake of those who are about to inherit salvation, by the force of the context, the other explanation of Chrysostom and Theophylact seems entirely to be preferred, that the discourse is not about the Decalogue, but about any other word whatsoever announced through Angels in the name of GOD. Because it is not said the law was brought forth through Angels, but the word. Or the word, says Chrysostom, he calls the commands. For the Angels, being sent by God, commanded many things without the law, such as in the case of the weeping, in the case of the judges, in the case of Samson: For this reason he did not say law, but word. Or he calls the commands the word. For the Angels sent by GOD commanded many things without the law, as in the mourning which was in the time of the Judges, in Samson. For that reason he did not say law, but word. The examples indeed from Jud. II and XIII do not sufficiently agree, for there the Angel the Lord appeared, not the Angel of the Lord. Yet it was sufficiently established among the Hebrews that God often gave commands to the Fathers through ministering Angels, and that a word was formerly made to the Fathers through Angels: As, for example, two Angels, Gen. XIX. verses 12, 13, commanded Lot and his family to depart from Sodom. Not to mention that some other laws besides the Decalogue could have been brought through Angels; since even that single word spoken through Angels to Lot and his family suffices for this Apostolic comparison, which became entirely firm. Estius also brought forward this opinion, that some understand all the precepts, responses, and addresses of GOD dispensed to men in the Old Testament: But he opposed these two things to it: First, the scope of the Apostle, because he compares the law of Moses with the law of CHRIST: Then, because he adds that every transgression and disobedience received a just retribution of reward. But that first point is the very thing being judged. For why should he contend the law with the Gospel regarding the author, when the same Author of both is Jehovah the Triune GOD? Why should he set such a comparison before the Jews, who were strongly clinging to the ceremonial law, by which he assumes that the word of the law brought forth through Angels was firm, when he is acting to teach that the Hebrews ought to adhere to the law of Christ, as Estius speaks, more firmly and studiously than formerly to the law received through Angels; which sense and scope he himself established? But what follows, concerning every transgression being punished, it is not necessary that it have respect to the preceding words concerning the word brought through Angels, since a peculiar reason can be contained in those words; so that, namely, it may be urged that both the word announced through Angels had its firmness, and every transgression against the law was punished, and there is no need at all for that word to be the Mosaic law itself. Nor does that explanation concerning the transgression against the word announced by the Angels have any inconvenience, even if that word is not taken concerning the law, but, as it sounds, concerning the word which was made to the Hebrews through Angels, the neglect of which they did not bear with impunity, just as that was evident even by the example of the sons-in-law of Lot: Certainly, even those who explain the passage concerning the law do not admit that the promulgation of the Decalogue itself is attributed to the Angels here, such as Chrysostom, Theophylact, B. Gerhard, Camero, Ludovicus de Dieu. But others prefer that this concerns another Word brought forth through Angels, and they do not admit that the Mosaic Decalogue is necessarily understood, such as Calvin, Bullinger, Gualther, Rivetus, etc. B. Glassius: There are understood, he says in Sacred Grammar, book III, tract V, canon IX, the words and revelations which GOD formerly set forth in the Old Testament through the Angels, his ministers: These are compared with the Evangelical word, which Christ, the Mediator of the New Testament, taught and confirmed with miracles. The Theologians of Strasbourg in the Censure against Laterm, page 53. For neither, they say, can it be said of the Angels that they spoke jointly in the legislation. If the legislative speech were to be attributed to the Angels, that ministry would have been assigned to one, not to many. But there is no need for us to refer this Apostolic text to the promulgation of the law. It can be taken concerning the embassies of the Angels in the Old Testament in general. The Apostle had said in chapter I, verse 14, that angels are λειτυργικά πνέυματα. This looks to the fact that they have carried out that λειτυργία not only by fighting and defending, but also by revealing and indicating the divine will. Because in verse 1 he had said that that λειτυργία, by which the Son of GOD himself was sent for those who ought to inherit salvation, is of a higher and more eminent degree, therefore in chapter II the Apostle institutes a σύγκρισιν, and says: if those embassies of the ministering angels, by which they set forth the divine will, did not have a less than most fortunate success, to such an extent that God exercised most grave vengeance against those who despised them, the embassy of the Son of GOD to the human race cannot be despised by the same without huge danger. B. Dorschæus urges these arguments for that opinion, that whatever announcement of the angels, which they, sent from above, made either concerning future events, or imminent dangers, or even concerning other matters, may be understood: 1. Because there is nowhere any mention of νομοθεσίας in chapter I, just as there is not in chapter two, whence it is uncertain, which nevertheless most of our adversaries in this place assume, and Schlichtingius takes pains to urge, that the scope of the Apostle is to oppose the Law to the Gospel, when no trace of such an opposition appears in any way. 2. Because the words are conceived in the most general terms, and therefore are not to be rashly restricted to any single act. For it is said ὁ δι᾽ ἀγγέλων λαληθεὶς λόγος, and no circumstance of time, no circumstance of place, no circumstance of persons limits it to a certain discourse. 3. Because it is uncertain that the νομοθεσία was pronounced by many Angels. For if the νομοθεσία had been made by many Angels, yet either many would have spoken in that at the same time, or many successively. Neither is certain from the sacred writings, and it rests upon evident reason. But the Apostle says in this verse 2, δι᾽ ἀγγέλων, and thus indicates that many Angels were ministers of the λόγος of which he speaks. 4. Because the παράβασις and παρακοὴ, which the Apostle indicates were received according to the retribution of reward, are not only against the λόγον νομοθεσίας of Sinai, but extend themselves altogether more broadly. For it never went unpunished if anyone had sinned inconsiderately and thoughtlessly against the revelation made through Angels. 5. Because the βεβαιότης, which is attributed in this place to the word pronounced through Angels, also extends itself more broadly than to be able to be restricted precisely to the λόγον νομοθεσίας. 6. Because in the preceding chapter I, v. 14, there is mention of the Angelic λειτυργίας and διακονίας in general. That λαλιὰ τῶ λόγε δι᾽ ἀγγέλων in verse 2 of chapter II is therefore understood as that which was made through the λειτυργίαν and διακονίαν of the Angels in verse 14 of chapter I. And yet, through the λειτυργίαν of the Angels, not only was the law pronounced, but many other revelations were also made. 7. Because the λόγος δι᾽ ἀγγέλων λαληθεὶς is also a λόγος σωτηρίας. Those who say that the discourse is about the law in verse 2, think that an opposition is being made between the λόγον σωτηρίας, which is of the Gospel, and the λόγον θανάτε, which is of the law, 2 Corinthians III, verses 6, 7, 8, 9. But the matter is not so. For in chapter I, 14, angels are said to be sent διὰ τὲς μέλλοντας κληρονομεῖν σωτηρίαν. Therefore, angels also bring the λόγον σωτηρίας. Whence the Apostle argues: If the word of God pronounced through angels, at the time when they are sent for ministry on account of those to whom the inheritance of salvation is offered, is so firm that for any transgression of it a most certain punishment is exacted: how much more will those experience the severity of divine vengeance who neglect the inheritance of salvation, brought by the Lord himself αὐτοπροσώπως. Because, therefore, the λόγος νόμος is not the λόγος σωτηρίας, but of condemnation, 2 Corinthians III, verse 9, and therefore these words can scarcely be restricted to the νομοθεσία: This is the blessed Dorscheus.

He became certain.

ספק, that is, he had threats that were not ineffectual. Thus also promises are said to be βεβαιῦσθαι or εἶναι βέβαια, when they are fulfilled by events, Rom. IV. 16, XV. 8. He is said to have been firm, either because he held to his truth, whether in promises or in threats; or because he was confirmed by miracles. The former is more suitable. True, says Chrysostom, so to speak, and faithful at the convenient time, and all things that were said came to pass. Either he says this: or that he obtained power and dominion, and the threats were brought to effect. For what is said in the other member of the comparison in verse 3, ἐβεβαιώθη, is confirmed; although it may respect miracles and signs, inasmuch as through them the doctrine of the Gospel was confirmed, it is nevertheless manifest that it likewise denotes the truth and certainty of the doctrine. But in this place no mention is made of signs, only the word is said to be βέβαιος. To each its own βεβαιότης stood firm, yet it is not necessary that it stood firm for the same reason. Conf. 2. Petr. I. v. 19.

And every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward.

Παράβασις פשע and παρακοή מרי are said of those sins which carry with them an open contempt of the law, of which GOD declares Himself the avenger, Deut. XXXII. verse 35. Moreover, those examples of punishments which occurred in the desert, and which Paul briefly indicates in 1 Cor. X. 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, are here referred to.

Some constitute prevarication in more serious matters, and disobedience in lighter ones. In the word μισθαποδοσία there is a catachresis according to Chrysostom and Theophylact, since that word is properly taken only in a good sense, which also occurs in Rom. I. verse 27 in the word ἀντιμισθίας. He teaches, therefore, that every transgression of the divine law has had its own punishment.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Εἰ γὰρ ὁ δι᾿ Ἀγγέλων λαληθεὶς λόγος, Id est, lex Mosis, quæ non data est per Filium, sed per unum è præcipuis Angelis Dei nomine loquentem, Actor. VII. 38 multis aliis Angelis stipantibus, Deut. XXXII. 2. Act. VII. 53. Gal. III. 19. Josephus libr. XV. Ἡμῶν δὲ τὰ κάλλιστα τῶν δογμάτων καὶ τὰ ὁσιώτατα τῶν ἐν τοῖς νόμοις δι᾿ Ἀγγέλων παρὰ τῦ Θεῦ μαθόντων.

De lege morali videtur intelligere Grotius τὸν λόγον δι᾿ Ἀγγέλων λαληθέντα cum Estio, Ribera, Capello, Camerone, Schlichtingio & aliis. Sed falso assumit, legem moralem non datam esse per Filium, datam esse per unum è præcipuis Angelis Dei nomine loquentem. Contrarium è XIX. & XX. Exod. patet : Nimirum immediatè legem à Deo promulgatam esse citra interventum ministerii Angelici, quod ad λαλιὰν vel pronuntiationem le- gis. Nam λόγος λαληθεὶς redditur ab Estio enunciatus, prolatus, promulgatus. Ita vero λα- ληθεὶς non est Decalogus per Angelum creatum, nedum per Angelos plures, quemadmodum hic Angelorum plurium mentio fit, qui certe non enunciarunt, aut promulgarunt Decalogum, fa- tente Grotio, qui proinde Judæorum, Sociniano- rum, & Papistarum commentum suum fecit, per unum è præcipuis Angelis DEI nomine lo- quentem id factum esse. At de hoc in historia promulgatæ legis nullum habetur verbum: Sed DEUS ipse, qui etiam in persona propria testa- tus est : Ego sum Dominus DEUS tuus, qui eduxi te de terra Ægypti, non habebis Deos alie- nos coram me, hæc præcepta αὐτοπροσώπως enun- ciavit: Loquutus est, inquit Moses, Dominus cunctos sermones hos, Exod. XX. vers. 1. 2. Ne- que aliter Stephanus Actor. VII. cap. Quanquam enim Angelum vers. 38. dicat loquutum esse Mosi in monte Sina: Non tamen Angelum creatum intelligit, sed illum, qui in igne flammæ rubi Mo- si apparuerat, vers. 31. qui dicitur à Stephano Dominus; qui Mosi testatus : Ego sum Domi- nus Patrum tuorum, DEUS Abraham, DEUS

Isaac, & DEUS Jacob : Qui utique Angelus increatus fuit, Filius nempe DEI, per quem loquutus est Pater, cum lex promulgata est, quia est æternus Patris λόγos. Dicit quidem Stephanus, vers. 53. Ebræos legem accepisse εἰς δια- ταγὰς τῶν Ἀγγέλων : Sed hoc longe diversum est ab eo, quod in præsenti Apostolus ait, λό- γον λαληθέντα δι' Ἀγγέλων. Neque locus Gal. III, vers. 19. huc facit, quemadmodum in annot. ad eundem observavimus: Non enim dicitur ibi lex data vel enunciata, sed διαταγεὶς δι' Ἀγγέλων. Aliæ fuerunt circa legis promulgationem Angelo- rum partes, quam pronunciandi eandem. Ad- erant, inquit Chrysostomus in h. l. tunc Angeli, quibus gens fuerat credita, & ipsi tubis canebant, & alia faciebant, nempe ignem & caliginem. Porrò non convenire adeo videtur illa compa- ratio Legis & Evangelii, quod περισσοτέρως magis debeamus προσέχειν attendere Evangelii, quàm legis doctrinæ, eò, quod illa per Angelos promul- gata, hoc per Dominum ipsum annuntiatum sit. Nam legis doctrina non minus divinæ originis, & autoritatis est, quam Evangelii : Nec minus etiam audienda, attendenda, atque custodien- da : neque contrarium penes Ebræos, qui le- gem à DEO ipso traditam esse credebant, quod frequenter etiam ipsis in Mose ac Prophetis in- culcatum est, tolerabile fuisset. Summo enim ideo in pretio lex erat apud eosdem, quod tanta cum majestate à DEO ipso stipato magna An- gelorum frequentia promulgata esset. Quod etiam Deuteronom. XXXIII. v. 2. indicatur : Do- minus de Sina venit, & cum eo sanctorum mili- tia. In dextra ejus ignea lex. Ubi nihil de lege ab Angelo quopiam ministro promulgata, nedum per Angelos plures enunciata. Præterea id non videtur congruere in hac comparatione de con- firmatione per signa & miracula. Nam neque le- gi defuit divina per signa & miracula confirma- tio. Unde Chrysostomus, eumque sequutus Theo- phylactus, etsi libenter hæc Apostoli verba de lege interpretentur, in ea tamen sententia non acquiescunt, nec inveniunt, quomodo lex dici possit λόγos δι' Ἀγγέλων λαληθεὶς; Aut Decalo- gum, inquit Chrysostomus, dicit solum. Illic enim Moses loquebatur, & Deus respondebat : Ἢ ὅτι παρῆσαν Ἄγγελοι τῷ θεῷ διαταττομένῳ (quæ re- sponsio Chrysostomi ab Interprete Germano Brix- tio temere prætermissa est) aut quod aderant An- geli Deo legem ordinante, vel promulgante; ἢ ὅτι περὶ τῶν ἐν τῇ παλαιᾷ λεγομένων καὶ γενομένων ἁπάντων, ὡς Ἀγγέλων κοινωνησάντων ἐν τάτοις ταῦτα φησίν: Aut hæc dicit de omnibus, quæ dicta sunt & facta sunt in veteri, utpote quod societa- tem in his habuerint Angeli. Addit etiam aliam interpretationem vocis λαληθεὶς, quod non pro- nuntiationem, sed οἰκονομίαν aliquam, vel actus nonnullos alios Angelorum circa legem promulga- tam denotet, quem sensum cæteris præfert : Καὶ τάχα μοι δοκεῖ τῦτο λέγειν μᾶλλον τὰ διὰ τῶν Ἀγ- γέλων οἰκονομηθέντα. Τί ἐν ἐρῦμεν; παρῆσαν οἱ Ἄγ- γελοι τότε οἱ τὸ ἔθνος ἐμπεπιστευμένοι, καὶ αὐτοὶ τὰς σάλπιγγας ἐποίεν, καὶ τὰ ἕτερα, τὸ πῦρ, τὸν γνόφον. Mihi autem hoc magis forte videtur dice- re ea, quæ sunt dispensata per Angelos. Quid er- go dicemus ? Aderant tunc Angeli, quibus gens fuerat credita, & ipsi tubis canebant & alia fa- ciebant, nempe ignem & caliginem. Sed ille sensus nec verbo λαληθεὶς, quod loquelam in- fert, non alios actus, nec Apostolico contextui, quo λόγos pronunciatus δι' Ἀγγέλων, confer- tur cum iis, quæ Ebræi novissimè audierant, & quæ cœperunt λαλεῖσθαι διὰ τοῦ Κυρίου vers. 1. 3. comparatur, congruit, ideo nec explicationi B. Gerhardi locus: διὰ sumitur pro inter, 2. Tim. II. vers. 2. Lex ergo inter Angelos ordinata, quia illis tribuendus tubæ clangor, sonus, fulgur. Com- paratio enim illa non permittit vocem διὰ IN- TER exponi, sed requirit, ut propria significa- tione intelligatur, quemadmodum in phrasi λα- λεῖσθαι διὰ τοῦ Κυρίου PER Dominum. Alioquin oppositio sibi non constabit. Rectissime autem agnoscit, & urget contra Estium, quem alias in hisce sequutus est, Theologus nunquam satis laudatus, non Angelum aliquem primarium per- sonam DEI repræsentantem, sed DEUM ipsum, legem promulgaffe, siquidem Moses toties hoc be- neficium celebret, quod Israëlitæ Deum ipsum loquentem audiverint, Deuter. IV. vers. 32. feqq. Et porro: Urgemus, inquit, numerum pluralem δι᾽ ἀγγέλων. Ergo hic non agitur de Decalogi re- citatione, quæ, teste Mose, facta est ab uno, quem nos statuimus fuisse ipsum DEUM. Aliorum ex- plicationes, Johann. Cameronis in epist. ad Ebræ- os Operum pag. 387. de sono per ministerium An- gelorum in aëre formato, & Ludovici de Dieu ad Actor. VII. de Filio DEI in forma Angelica è Se- natu Angelico gloria Angelorum velato, adduxi- mus Tom. IV. System. Theol. cap. II. q. XIIX. pag. 249. Sed uti hæc modum saltem designat di- versum apparitionis, non subjectum infert aliud τῆς λαλιᾶς, quod hic respicitur: Ita illa de mi- nisterio in efformatione foni articulati, non de subjecto loquente, forte subtilior est, quam so- lidior.

Quid ergo hic dicendum? Quum manifestis- simum sit, de λόγῳ per Angelos pronunciato, non inter Angelos, & de Angelorum loquuutione, non aliis actionibus conjunctis agi, dicitur enim λόγος δι᾿ ἀγγέλων λαληθεὶς, adhæc de Angelis pluribus sermo sit, de Angelis emissis εἰς διακονίαν διὰ τοὺς μέλλοντας κληρονομεῖν σωτηρίαν, vi contex- tus videtur omnino præferenda altera explica- tio Chrysostomi, & Theophylacti, quod non de Decalogo, sed de alio quocunque λόγῳ per An- gelos nomine DEI enunciato sermo sit. Quia non dicitur lex prolata per Angelos, sed sermo. Ἢ λόγον, inquit Chrysostomus, Φησὶ τὰ προσάγ- ματα. Πολλὰ γὰρ χωρὶς νόμου προσέταξαν Ἄγ- γελοι παρὰ Θεοῦ πεμπόμενοι, οἷον ἐπὶ τοῦ κλαυθμῶ- νος, ἐπὶ τῶν κριτῶν, ἐπὶ τοῦ Σαμψών: Διὰ γὰρ τοῦτο οὐκ εἶπε νόμος, ἀλλὰ λόγος. Aut sermonem dicit jussa. Multa enim sine lege jusserunt Angeli à DEO missi, sicut in luctu, qui tempore Judicum fuit, in Sam- sone. Nam propterea non dixit lex, sed sermo. Ex- empla quidem è Jud. II. & XIII. non satis conve- niunt, ibi enim apparuit Angelus Dominus, non Angelus Domini. Satis tamen inter Ebræos consta- bat, Deum sæpe per Angelos ministros mandata Patribus dedisse, ac sermonem per Angelos olim ad Patres factum esse: Quomodo, exempli gra- tia, duo Angeli, Gen. XIX. vers. 12. 13. Lotho & familiæ ejus egressum è Sodoma præcipiebant. Ne de eo dicam, quod aliæ leges nonnullæ præ- ter Decalogum per Angelos potuerint perferri; quum vel unicus ille λόγος λαληθεὶς δι᾿ ἀγγέλων ad Lothum, ejusque familiam sufficiat huic com- parationi Apostolicæ, qui omnino βέβαιος ἐγένε- το. Adduxit & Estius hanc sententiam, quod nempe nonnulli intelligant omnia DEI præcepta, responsa, alloquia in Veteri Testamento ad homines dispensata: Sed opposuit eidem hæc duo: Pri- mo scopum Apostoli, quod comparet legem Mo- sis cum lege CHRISTI: Deinde quod addat, omnem prævaricationem & inobedientiam acce- pisse justam mercedis retributionem. Verùm prius illud est ipsum τό κρινόμενον. Cur enim conten- dat legem cum Evangelio quoad autorem, quum utriusque idem Autor sit Jehovah DEUS Triu- nus? Cur Judæis legi ceremoniali fortiter inhæ- rentibus sistat talem comparationem, qua ser- monem legis per Angelos prolatum firmum fu- isse assumat, cum id agat, ut doceat, legi Chri- sti, ut loquitur Estius, firmiter ac studiosius ad- hærere debere Ebræos, quam olim legi per An- gelos susceptæ; quem sensum & scopum ipse con- stituit? Quod autem sequitur, de punita quavis prævaricatione, non necessum est, ut ad verba antecedentia de sermone per Angelos allato re- spectum habeat, quum peculiaris ratio verbis istis contineri possit; ut nempe urgeatur, & sermonem per Angelos annunciatum suam habu- isse firmitatem, & punitam fuisse quamvis præ- varicationem adversus legem, opusque minime sit, sermonem illum esse ipsammet legem Mosai- cam. Nec incommodi quicquam habet illa de prævaricatione adversus sermonem ab Angelis annunciatum explicatio, etiamsi sermo iste non de lege accipiatur, sed, ut sonat, de verbo, quod per Angelos ad Ebræos factum, cujus neglectum illi impune non tulerint, quemadmodum id vel exemplo generorum Lothi constitit: Promulga- tionem certe ipsam Decalogi Angelis hic tribui, ne quidem, qui de lege locum explicant, ad- mittunt, utpote Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, B. Gerhardus, Camero, Ludovicus de Dieu. Alii vero malunt hic agi de alio Verbo per Angelos pro- lato, nec admittunt Decalogum Mosaicum ne- cessario intelligi, ut Calvinus, Bullingerus, Gualther. Rivetus &c. B. Glassius: Intelligen- tur, inquit Gramm. S. l. III. tract. V. can. IX. sermones & revelationes, quas DEUS per An- gelos, ministros suos, olim in Veteri Testamento ex- posuit: Eæ comparantur cum sermone Evangeli- co, quem Christus Novi Testamenti Μεσίτης do- cuit & miraculis confirmavit. Dn. Theologi Ar- gentorai. in Censura contr. Laterm. pag. 53. Ne- que enim, inquiunt, de Angelis dici potest, quod in legislatione ipsi conjunctim loquuti sint. Si An- gelis loquutio legislatoria tribuenda esset, non plu- ribus, sed uni ministerium illud assignatum esset. Sed non opus est, ut ad promulgationem legis istum Apostolicum textum referamus. Potest de legatio- nibus Angelorum in Veteri Testamento in univer- sum accipi. Dixerat Apostolus cap. I. vers. 14. Angelos esse λειτυργικά πνέυματα. Hoc eo spectat, quod non tantum propugnando & defendendo illam λειτυργίαν expediverint, sed etiam revelando & voluntatem divinam indicando. Quia vers. 1. di- xerat, altioris & eminentioris gradus esse illam λειτυργίαν, qua Filius DEI ipse emissus est pro iis, qui salutem hæreditare debent, ideoque cap. II. σύγκρισιν instituit Apostolus, & dicit, si illæ le- gationes Angelorum ministrantium, quibus divi- nam voluntatem exposuerunt, non habuerunt non felicissimum successum, adeo, ut gravissimas Deus exercuerit adversus contemptores vindicias, non poterit sine ingenti periculo legatio Filii DEI ad genus humanum ab eodem contemni. B. Dor- schæus hæc urget argumenta pro ea sententia, quod quæcunque Angelorum annunciatio, quam illi desuper missi, vel de futuris eventibus, vel imminentibus periculis, vel de rebus etiam aliis fecerunt, intelligatur: 1. Quia νομοθεσίας in c. I. nuspiam sit mentio, uti nec in capite secundo, un- de incertum est, quod tamen plerique Adversa- riorum hoc loco sumunt, & Schlichtingius opero- se urget, scopum Apostoli esse, legem opponere Ev- angelio, cùm nullatenus istius oppositionis appa- reat vestigium. 2. Quia verba sunt generalissime concepta, adeoque temere ad unicum aliquem actum non restringenda. Dicitur enim ὁ δι᾽ ἀγγέλων λα- ληθεὶς λόγος, nulla temporis, nulla loci, nulla per- sonarum circumstantia ad certum sermonem limi- tat. 3. Quia incertum est, νομοθεσίαν esse pronun- ciatam per plures Angelos. Si enim per plures An- gelos νομοθεσία facta fuiffet, tamen aut plures si- mul in ista loquuti fuissent, aut plures successive. Neutrum ex sacris literis certum est & evidenti ratione nititur. Dicit vero Apostolus hoc vers. 2. δι᾽ ἀγγέλων, adeoque plures indicat Angelos λόγο, de quo loquitur, administros. 4. Quia παράβασις & παρακοὴ, quam Apostolus juxta mercedis re- tributionem accepisse indicat, non est contra λόγον νομοθεσίας Sinaitica tantum, sed omnino latius se- se extendit. Nunquam enim impune abiit, si quis contra revelationem per Angelos factam inconsi- derate & incogitanter peccasset. 5. Quia βεβαιό- της, quæ verbo per Angelos pronunciato hoc loco tribuitur, & latius se extendit, quam ut ad λό- γον νομοθεσίας præcise restringi possit. 6. Quia in antecedentibus cap. I. v. 14. sit mentio λειτυργίας Angelica, & διακονίας in universum. Ea igitur λαλιὰ τῶ λόγε δι᾽ ἀγγέλων vers. 2. cap. II. intelligi- tur, quæ facta est per λειτυργίαν & διακονίαν An- gelorum vers. 14. cap. I. Atqui per λειτυργίαν An- gelorum non tantum pronunciata est lex, sed mul- tæ etiam aliæ revelationes factæ. 7. Quia λόγος δι᾽ ἀγγέλων λαληθεὶς est λόγος etiam σωτηρίας. Qui de lege vers. 2. sermonem esse dicunt, existi- mant oppositionem fieri inter λόγον σωτηρίας, qui est Evangelii, & inter λόγον θανάτε, qui est le- gis, 2. Corinth. III. vers. 6. 7. 8. 9. At non ita se res habet. Capite enim I, 14. Angeli mitti di- cuntur διὰ τὲς μέλλοντας κληρονομεῖν σωτηρίαν. Ergo Angeli etiam afferunt λόγον σωτηρίας. Unde Apostolus argumentatur: Si verbum Dei per An- gelos pronunciatum, tum, cum illi mittuntur ad ministerium propter eos, quibus offertur hæredi- tas salutis, firmum est adeo, ut in quamvis illius transgressionem certissima fiat animadversio: Quanto magis vindictæ divinæ severitatem expe- rientur illi, qui negligunt hæreditatem salutis, per ipsum Dominum αὐτοπροσώπως allatam. Quia itaque λόγος νόμος non est λόγος σωτηρίας, sed κα- τακρίσεως, 2. Corinth. III. vers. 9. ideoque vix ad vo- μοθεσίαν verba ista restringi poterunt: Hæc Beat. Dorspheus.

Ἐγένετο βέβαιος.

ספק, id est minas habuit non irritas. Sic & promis- sa dicuntur βεβαιῦσθαι aut εἶναι βέβαια, ubi rebus implentur Rom. IV. 16. XV. 8. Firmus dicitur fuisse, vel quod veritatem suam habuerit sive in promissis, sive in minis; vel quod confirmatus fuerit per signa. Prius convenien- tius. Verus, inquit Chrysostomus, ut ita dicam, & fidelis in tempore convenienti, & evenerunt omnia, quæ dicta sunt. Aut hoc dicit: aut quod vim & dominatum obtinuit, & minæ ad effectum sunt deductæ. Quod enim in altero comparationis membro dicitur vers. 3. ἐβεβαιώθη, confirmatur; etsi miracula & signa respiciat, utpote per quæ confirmata fuit doctrina Evangelii, manifestum tamen est, notare itidem veritatem, & certitu- dinem doctrinæ. Hoc autem in loco nulla men- tio fit signorum, solum βέβαιος dicitur λόγος. Utrique constitit sua βεβαιότης, non tamen ne- cessum est, ut eâdem constiterit ratione. Conf. 2. Petr. I. v. 19.

Καὶ πᾶσα παράβασις, καὶ παρακοὴ ἔλαβεν ἔνδικον μισθαποδοσίαν.

Παράβασις פשע & παρακοή מרי dicuntur de illis pec- catis, quæ apertum legis contemptum secum ferunt, quo- rum ultorem se DEUS profitetur, Deut. XXXII. verf. 35. Respiciuntur autem hic ea, quæ in deserto contigere, pœ- narum exempla, quæ breviter indicat Paulus 1. Cor. X. 6. 7. 8. 9. 10.

Alii prævaricationem in gravioribus, inobedi- entiam in levioribus constituunt. In voce μισθα- ποδοσία Catachresis est secundum Chrysostomum, ac Theophylactum, quum vox illa in bonam tan- tum partem proprie accipiatur, quæ etiam Rom. I. verf. 27. in voce ἀντιμισθίας occurrit. Omnem ergo legis divinæ transgressionem pœnam suam ba- buisse, docet.

## 2:3
Verse 3. How shall we escape.

How shall we escape punishment? Thus in Isaiah XX. verse 6. איך נמלט אנחנו : Πῶς ἡμεῖς σωθησόμεθα;

Having neglected so great a salvation.

That is, of the word of such a salvation. If we neglect the word, which brings such great salvation to those who obey, that is, eternal and heavenly, which the law does not bring, but only a brief and earthly salvation. Thus the Gospel is called the word of salvation, Acts 13:26; the way of salvation, Acts 16:17; and the Gospel of salvation, Eph. 1:13.

Which having received its beginning to be spoken through the Lord.

That one may judge concerning the law, its beginning must be looked at, says Josephus against Apion, II. The beginning of the Evangelical law is from the Lord God the Son himself. Great matters are accustomed to be dispatched by great persons.

Was confirmed unto you by those who heard.

In a twofold way, he says, we are certain of its truth. First, because that report did not come to us transmitted through many men, but we have as teachers those who heard these things from the Lord himself, namely the Apostles: Secondly, because miracles and gifts of the Spirit, greater and more frequent than ever, gave testimony to the same word. To be confirmed in this place is rendered 'to be made worthy of belief,' as in Mark 16:20. 'Unto you,' that is, unto us, as 'unto you' [is] unto you in 1 Pet. 1:25. We said above that it is well gathered from this passage that the epistle was written by some disciple of the Apostles, such as Luke was.

We desire three things in this explanation: First, that by 'salvation' he understands the word which brings salvation to the hearers: since there is no need for a metonymical meaning, and the literal meaning can have a place. For salvation is safety. But they are said to neglect the same who do not attend to those things which were delivered through Christ and his Apostles. The angelic word is compared directly with this notable salvation, which God announced most recently to the Hebrews in his Son, or, as it has seemed to some, the blessedness which all the righteous of old desired but did not attain, Matt. 13:16, or rather, with the coming of the kingdom of heaven, or the fulfillment of the promises concerning Christ; which salvation and happiness began to be preached in the days of the flesh by the Lord, but was confirmed unto the Hebrews of the Pauline age; to whom the doctrine of the Gospel arrived. It is not the doctrine of salvation, but salvation itself that is said to have begun to be spoken. Secondly, that Grotius denies that eternal salvation was promised in the law, which is false in both ways, both if the law is taken as the moral law: for this promised life under the condition of perfect obedience; and if by the law is understood the Scripture of the Old Testament, since in it, besides legal precepts, evangelical promises are also contained concerning the remission of sins and salvation to be obtained through faith in the Messiah. Salvation is attributed to the Gospel for this reason, because no one can fulfill the law, and therefore salvation is not had except from the Gospel, Rom. 1:16, ch. 8:3. Thirdly, that Grotius maintains that this salvation was rendered worthy of belief to the very Author of the Epistle by the hearers of Christ, as if the same could be attributed in the least to immediate divine revelation, and by that argument derogates the present epistle from the Apostle. This consequence is of no value: partly because these things can well consist together, that some doctrine was received immediately from GOD himself, and that faith was also won for it by those who heard Christ himself preaching; partly because the author of the epistle could, through the figure of Communication, such as is observed in 1 Cor. X. 8, 9, 1 Pet. IV. 3, Heb. VI. 1, ch. X. 26, ch. XII. 12, even in the preceding words, 'how shall we escape?', include the Hebrews, to whom this salvation was confirmed by the hearers of Christ, even if the reason for it was different, and he himself received his Gospel not from men, nor was he taught it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ, Gal. I. 12. By those, however, who are said to have heard Christ in this place, the Apostles are primarily understood. For these were not only hearers of Christ's sermons, but also eyewitnesses of his miracles, as they were perpetually adhering to the same, whom he chose as witnesses, that they might propagate the Gospel through the whole world, beginning from Judea and the Hebrews, Acts X. 41. The Apostle says that not the doctrine of the Gospel was confirmed, although it was also confirmed by miracles, but that salvation began to be announced through the Lord as regards those Hebrews to whom he wrote, both through eyewitnesses, the disciples of Christ, and through deeds greater than any exception, so that those who had not heard Christ teaching with his own voice, and had not seen him performing miracles in person, might be rendered more certain and established concerning salvation, which was preached by Christ, and consequently concerning the truth of the Evangelical doctrine, through the testimonies of those who had heard Christ and through truly divine deeds. Εἰς ἡμᾶς, to us, namely, who did not see or hear Christ teaching on earth; ἐβεβαιώθη, not merely announced, but faith was given to it, and it obtained firmness among us.

Latin:

Verf. 3. Πῶς ἡμεῖς ἐκφυξόμεθα.

Quomodo pœnam evademus. Sic Esaiæ XX. verf. 6. איך נמלט אנחנו : Πῶς ἡμεῖς σωθησόμεθα;

Τηλικαύτης ἀμελήσαντες σωτηρίας.

Id est λόγου σωτηρίας τηλικαύτης. Si negligamus ser- monem, qui obedientibus tantam affert salutem, id est, æternam & cælestem, quam lex non affert, sed tantum salutem brevem & terrenam. Sic Evangelium vocatur λόγος σωτηρίας Act. XIII. 26. ὁδὸς σωτηρίας Act. XVI. 17. & Εὐαγγέλιον σωτηρίας Eph. I. 13.

Ἥτις ἀρχὴν λαβοῦσα λαλεῖσθαι διὰ τοῦ Κυρίου.

Ut de lege judicetur spectandum ejus initium, ait Josephus contra Appionem II. Legis Evangelicæ initium ab ipso Domino Dei Filio. Solent res magnæ per magnos expediri.

Ὑπὸ τῶν ἀκουσάντων εἰς ὑμᾶς ἐβεβαιώθη.

Duplici modo, inquit, certi sumus de ejus veritate. Primum quia non per multos homines transfusa ea fama ad nos venit, sed eos habemus magistros, qui ab ipso Do- mino ista audivere, Apostolos scilicet: Deinde quia mira- cula & dona Spiritus majora quam unquam & frequentio- ra, testimonium dedere eidem sermoni. Βεβαιῶσθαι hoc lo- co reddi fide dignum, ut Marc. XVI. vers. 20. Εἰς ὑμᾶς id est nobis, ut εἰς ὑμᾶς vobis 1. Petr. I. 25. Diximus supra ex hoc loco bene colligi scriptam epistolam ab aliquo di- scipulo Apostolorum, qualis fuit Lucas.

Tria in hac explicatione desideramus: Primo quod per σωτηρίαν sermonem, qui affert salutem audientibus, intelligat: quum opus non sit Meto- nymica significatione, ac propria locum habere possit. Σωτηρία enim salus est. Negligere autem eandem dicuntur, qui non attendunt iis, quæ tradita sunt per Christum ejusque Apostolos. Comparatur directe λόγος Ἀγγελικὸς cum σω- τηρίᾳ hac insigni, quam Ebræis novissime annun- ciavit Deus in Filio, sive quod nonnullis visum, quam beatitudinem omnes justi veteres opta- runt, non consequuti sunt, Matth. XIII. verf. 16. seu potius, cum adventu regni cælorum, vel pro- missionum de Christo complemento; quæ salus & felicitas initio prædicari cœpit in diebus car- nis à Domino, confirmata autem fuit in Ebræos ætatis Paulinæ; ad quos doctrina Evangelii perve- nit. Non salutis doctrina, sed salus dicitur cœ- pisse λαλεῖσθαι enunciari. Deinde, quod neget Grotius in lege æternam salutem promissam, quod utroque modo falsum est, tum si lex accipiatur de lege morali: Hæc enim vitam promisit sub condi- tione perfectæ obedientiæ; tum si per legem intelli- gatur Scriptura Veteris Testamenti, quippe in qua præter legalia præcepta etiam promissiones Evan- gelica continentur de remissione peccatorum & sa- lute per fidem in Messiam consequenda. Tribuitur Evangelio salus ideo, quia legem implere nemo potest, adeoque non habetur salus, nisi ex Evan- gelio Rom. I. 16. cap. IIX. 3. Tertio quod ab au- ditoribus Christi fide dignam redditam hanc salu- tem ipsimet Autori Epistolæ, Grotius ita statuat, quasi eadem minimæ divinæ immediatæ revela- tioni accepta referri possit, eoque argumento- epistolam praesentem Apostolo deroget. Quae consequentia nauci est: tum quia probe consiste- re haec possunt, doctrinam aliquam ab ipso DEO immediate acceptam esse, & fidem ei conciliatam quoque ab illis, qui Christum ipsum praedicantem audivere; tum quia potuit sese Autor epistolae per figuram Communicationis, qualis observatur 1. Cor. X. 8. 9. 1. Petr. IV. 3. Ebr. VI. 1. cap. X. 26. c. XII. 12. etiam in verbis praecedentibus, quomo- do nos effugiemus? accensere Ebraeis, in quos ἐβε- βαιώθη haec σωτηρία ab auditoribus Christi, etsi alia ejusdem fuerit ratio, & Evangelium suum ipse ab hominibus acceperit, nec edoctus fuerit, sed per revelationem Jesu Christi, Gal. I. 12. Per illos autem, qui Christum audivisse dicuntur hoc loco imprimis Apostoli intelliguntur. Hi enim non tan- tum ἀυτήκοοι fuere concionum Christi, sed & ἀυτόπται miraculorum ejus, utpote eidem perpe- tuo adhaerentes, quos testes elegit, ut Evangelium per universum orbem propagarent, initio facto à Judaea, & Ebraeis, Act. X. 41. Confirmatam autem Apostolus dicit non doctrinam Evangelii, licet ea etiam confirmata sit per miracula, sed salutem per Dominum annunciari coeptam quoad Ebraeos illos, ad quos scripsit, tum per testes oculatos, di- scipulos Christi, tum per facta omni exceptione majora, ut qui Christum ἀυτοφώνως docentem non audierant, ipsumque miracula patrantem ἀυτο- προσώπως non viderant, & per eorum, qui Chri- stum audierant, testimonia, & per facta vere di- vina de salute, quae praedicata à Christo, ac conse- quenter de veritate doctrinae Evangelicae certio- res redditi ac stabiliti sint. Εἰς ἡμᾶς in nos, scilicet qui Christum in terris docentem non vidimus nec audivimus; ἐβεβαιώθη non nude annunciata, sed fides ei reddita, firmitatemque apud nos obtinuit.

## 2:4
Verse 4. (God also bearing witness with signs and wonders and various mighty works) You have these three also in Acts II. 22, where see the remarks, and II. 43, IV. 30. You have the word μαρτυρεῖν in the same sense in Acts XIV. 3. The old law had testimony through lightnings and thunders. The new law through very many healings.

And by distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will) Not only gifts of prophecy but also of tongues. Μερίζειν is said of these gifts in Romans XII. 3, 1 Cor. VII. 17, because God did not give all things to all, but what and how much and to whom he willed, Eph. IV. 7. Since the reason for this distinction does not appear, one rightly recurs to the will of GOD, 1 Cor. XII. v. 18.

The comparison of the old law and the new law, which he wrongly calls so with the Papists and Socinians, is purely arbitrary: because it is not clear that the Apostle made words about the Mosaic law; indeed, it appears sufficiently that he did not. Estius warns that the word συνεπιμαρτυροῦντος, composed of three parts, which the Vulgate rendered by 'contestante' (bearing witness with), is more correctly rendered by 'coattestante' (co-attesting), because to the testimony of the Apostles and others who had heard and seen Christ, there was added the testimony of God, which is twofold: both of miracles, which are called σημεῖα or signs of divine power and truth, and τέρατα, because they are supernatural, and ποικίλαι δυνάμεις, because they exerted themselves in various mighty works of healings, and the raising of the dead, and the liberation of those possessed by demons: and of the distributions of the Holy Spirit, by which the visible outpouring of the same, and the concession of the gifts of prophecy, tongues, and others, concerning which 1. Cor. XIII. 5, etc., according to his (the Holy Spirit's, for the pronoun ἀυτοῦ with the rough breathing refers to this, both from the common rule that the pronoun ordinarily looks to the immediately preceding noun; and from the analogy of the parallel passage 1 Cor. XII. 11) will, as if he were saying, with Chrysostom as interpreter: They indeed bear testimony, but God also bears testimony. How does he bear testimony? Not by speech or voice. For this would indeed be credible too. But how? By signs and wonders and various mighty works. He beautifully placed that, 'various mighty works,' signifying the abundance of gratuitous gifts or charisms. Which indeed was not done in the former, nor were there so many signs and so different. This is, they did not believe them rashly and lightly, but through signs and wonders. Wherefore we do not believe them, but God. But those co-attestations are not to be referred only to those who heard the Lord himself, or the Apostles, because they themselves made faith for their testimonies by such deeds, but also to those who shone with such gifts in the time of the Apostles; or rather to God, who through the miraculous gifts and works of the same further testified, or simultaneously with the Apostles themselves, to the Hebrews concerning the salvation that began to be preached by Christ, Mark XVI. 10, Acts V. 12, 1 Cor. XII. & XIV.

PART II. Further demonstration of the eminence of the human nature of CHRIST from the eighth Psalm.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Συνεπιμαρτυροῦντος τοῦ θεοῦ σημείοις τε καὶ τέρα- σι καὶ ποικίλαις δυνάμεσι) Haec tria habes & Act. II. 22. ubi dicta vide & II. 43. IV. 30. Verbum μαρτυρεῖν eodem sen- su habes Act. XIV. 3. Lex vetus testimonium habuit per fulgura & tonitrua. Lex nova per sanationes plurimas.

Καὶ πνεύματος ἁγίου μερισμοῖς κατὰ τὴν ἀυτοῦ θέλησιν) Non sola prophetiae dona sed & linguarum. Μερίζειν de his donis dicitur Roman. XII. 3. 1. Cor. VII. 17. quia non omnibus omnia dabat Deus, sed quae & quantum & qui- bus vellet, Eph. IV. 7. Hujus discriminis ratio cum non appareat, merito ad DEI voluntatem recurritur, 1. Cor. XII. v. 18.

Comparatio legis veteris & legis novae, quam perperam cum Papistis & Socinianis ita vocat, mere arbitraria est: quia de lege Mosaica Apo- stolum verba fecisse non liquet; imo non fecisse apparet satis. Vocem συνεπιμαρτυρῶντος tri- compositam, quam Vulgata reddidit contestante, Estius monet, rectius reddi coattestante, quod te- stimonio Apostolorum & aliorum, qui Christum audierant & viderant, accesserit testimonium Dei, quod geminum est, tum miraculorum, quae σημεῖα dicuntur vel signa potentiae & veritatis di- vinae, & τέρατα, quia supernaturalia, & ποικίλαι δυνάμεις, quia exeruere sese diversis virtutibus sa- nationum, & suscitationis mortuorum, & libe- rationis obsessorum à Daemonibus: tum distri- butionum Spiritus sancti, qua visibilem ejusdem effusionem, & donorum prophetiae, linguarum, & aliorum concessionem, de quibus 1. Cor. XIII. 5. seqq. secundum ipsius (Spiritus sancti, huc enim refert Pronomen ἀυτοῦ cum aspero spiritu, tum ex Regula communi, quod ordinarie Pronomen respiciat nomen immediate antecedens; tum ex analogia loci paralleli 1. Cor. XII. 11.) voluntatem, quasi dicat, interprete Chrysostomo: Testimonium quidem illi ferunt, fert autem Deus quoque testimo- nium. Quomodo fert testimonium? Non ser- mone neque voce. Nam esset quidem hoc quoque credibile. Sed quomodo? Signis & portentis & variis virtutibus. Pulchre posuit illud, variis virtutibus, gratuitorum donorum seu charisma- tum significans abundantiam. Quod quidem non factum est in prioribus, neque tot signa & tam differentia. Hoc est, non temere ac leviter illis cre- diderunt, sed per signa & portenta. Quamobrem non illis credimus, sed Deo. Non autem illæ coat- testationes referendæ tantum ad eos, qui Domi- num ipsum audierunt, vel Apostolos, quod ipsi talibus factis fidem fecerint suis testimoniis, sed etiam ad eos, qui Apostoli tempore donis talibus claruere; vel potius ad Deum, qui per eorundem miraculosa dona & opera Ebræis de salute à Chri- sto prædicari cœpta ulterius vel simul cum ipsis Apostolis testatus est, Marc. XVI. 10. Actor. V. 12. 1. Cor. XII. & XIV.

PARS II. Ulterior demonstratio eminentiæ naturæ CHRISTI humanæ è Psalmo octavo.

## 2:5
Verse 5. (For he did not subject to angels the world to come) After the writer of this epistle had made an inference from the arguments proposed in the first chapter, he again adds other arguments by which he might strengthen the same inference. In that super-ethereal region there are indeed Angels: but they do not rule as Christ does. He calls this the 'world to come,' not because it does not already exist, but because it is not fully known to us, nor has it yet happened. Thus the Hebrews say עולם הבא with respect to us. See the book on the death of Moses. Thus the passage of Psalm IX. 6 is mystically explained.

The Apostle, about to add another testimony of the divine eminence to which Christ was exalted according to his human nature after his passion, so that he may insist on the comparison with the Angels, says: For he did not, he says, subject the future world to Angels: When he has touched upon the Prophetic office of Christ, as regards the announcement of salvation, he subjects the testimony which pertains to the Kingly office and the majesty of the kingdom of glory, to which he was raised according to his human nature. The argument is clear: According to the nature by which the future world is subjected to Christ, according to that he excels in divine eminence: But the future world is subjected to Christ according to his human nature. Therefore Christ excels in divine eminence according to his human nature. The assumption is stated thus: The future world is subjected not to Angels but to the Son of man, which is demonstrated from Psalm VIII. because all things are subjected to the Son of man. Moreover, all things would not be subject, unless the world to come were to be subject to the same. For in that all things are subject, he leaves nothing that is not subject. By τὴν μέλλουσαν οἰκουμένην, Chrysostom indeed preferred to understand the present world, which is called 'to come' because it was then still to come, just as Christ is called the Adam to come according to the flesh, Romans 5, which Theophylactus explains thus: He called it 'to come' because the Son of God has been perpetual. But the world, because it was created and at one time had been nothing, as if it were to be made, seems 'to come' because it had not existed before. Therefore, with regard to the perpetuity of the essence of the Son, the world was also 'to come.' Although he notes here that many interpret it concerning the future heavenly world, but in this sense, that then the Angels will stand by in the manner of servants, while the Son, judging, will sit. Ribera follows the former explanation, yet not absolutely concerning the present world, but understanding it of men and other things that are on earth, of men indeed to be brought into eternal life, but of other things, insofar as they serve the salvation of men. The blessed Hunnius says: The world, he says, which according to the meaning of Psalm 8 ought to have been subjected to the Messiah, he calls the future world, and that with respect to the times of David, who prophesied these things concerning CHRIST. And indeed he calls it future on account of the restoration of the world, which was to be brought about through the Messiah. To the latter meaning accede not only those who, with those whom Theophylact designated, explain it concerning the judgment and the state after the resurrection, but also those who explain it in general concerning the Church in the heavenly kingdom, to which the exposition of Grotius tends. Osiander joins these: For he did not subject the world to the angels, not only the one which now is, but also that future new world, such as it will be after the last day. And it is certain from the meaning of the Psalmist, because he says that all things are subjected under his feet, that both are included. But what the Apostle understands here by οἰκουμένην μέλλουσαν is being discussed. The blessed Gerhard, with Estius, wishes the state of the world future after the abolition of the present world, and the Church, such as it is to be in heavenly glory after the consummation of the age, to be noted; which opinion Estius proves from Isaiah 9:6, Hebrews 13:14, chapter 11:10, 2 Peter 3:13. The blessed Gerhard also proves it from Isaiah 65:17, chapter 66:22, Romans 8:21, Revelation 21:1, and also from the consensus of Theodoret, Oecumenius, Lyranus, and Cajetan; and he says that Theophylact and Thomas also prove it, and therefore he determines that the verb in the past tense has this meaning: He predicted or promised that it was to be subjected: i.e., The principality of the world to come is not decreed or promised by God to the angels. We judge that this meaning is not to be disapproved, provided that the opinion is absent concerning the heaven and earth, or other creatures as well, being renewed on the last day, which sticks to some Papists, as being contrary to the consummation of the world, as also the fiction of Schlichting concerning the new offices and principalities of the angels, of which Scripture knows nothing; nor should those who are already in the state of glory be excluded from the kingdom of glory and the principality of Christ. For it is called the FUTURE world relatively and in a certain respect, as Grotius not badly observed, not absolutely: namely, by reason of us, who are still in the state of the militant Church, as is evident from the comparison with chapter 6:5, in which respect the verb in the past tense is also used: because it is already actually subjected to the same Church triumphant, and he has the right and principality over it, even if that [Church] is subsequently and daily increased and enriched with new citizens until the consummation of the age, when that heavenly city was also full, and the full subjection of all things to Christ the King and Lord is to be; for which reason it is said, we do not yet see all things subjected to him. Nor can we add our approval to that explanation of Estius, that the present world is indeed subjected to the angels, but not the future one, which is far more excellent and is reserved for CHRIST the Prince. For however it may be admitted that angels in a certain way preside over the provinces of the earth, this is not, however, the subjection of which the Apostle and the holy Psalmist speak, as it implies supreme dominion and divine dignity, and does not pertain so much to the rule of the angels as to the guardianship and ministry, for the sake of which they are sent out even to the princes of the earth and courts, from whence the provinces are governed. To what the mystical meaning of Grotius on Psalm 9:6 tends, we cannot fathom. By οἰκουμένην μέλλουσαν, therefore, are designated not only eternal life, which Christ has in his hand and can bestow upon whom he wills, but the state of the future age, that heavenly city with all its citizens, over whom he rules, as also those things which pertain to the same, because he is their minister by reason of distribution, and administrator, and also the Priest of future good things, Hebrews 9:11, by reason of acquisition, and for the application of intercession: and he would have dominion and power over all things, by reason of royal eminence and office: since he is not a common priest, but holds a Royal Priesthood: just as the Apostle later demonstrated that the same is a High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek, and thus both Priest and King at the same time. Camerarius explains it as the men who inhabited the world in that age, in which the Son of GOD was born on earth. Therefore he now calls that age of men in the world τὴν μέλλουσαν οἰκουμένην, into which it was to be that the Son of God, according to the prophecies, would be introduced, that is, would be born as a man, who is Jesus the Son of Mary, and therefore he added, περὶ ἧς λαλοῦμεν, that is, he did not subject the world to the angels, the future one I say, of which we are speaking. That is, into which Christ was to be introduced. So much for him. The blessed Dorsch interprets it concerning the kingdom of grace, which is called the future world, both because it was still in progress and increase, the greatest part of it still to arise, and because in the prophecies it is described as a new kingdom, a future and new earth: he acknowledges, however, that the kingdom of glory is included, and the angels, insofar as they are in the kingdom of glory, and indeed all the works of the hands of God, verses 7-8, subjected to his feet, which phrase he observes is proper to the kingdom of power: since the Church, whether militant or triumphant, the Bride of Christ, is not subjected to his feet, but is his body, acknowledging the Bridegroom as its head, even if otherwise, as creatures, all things that are the works of the hands of God are under the feet of Christ, and thus also the faithful and the elect. But the question here is not what things are subjected to Christ, to whom all things are subjected without exception, but what is properly understood by οἰκουμένην τὴν μέλλουσαν. The very sitting at the right hand of God already implied that subjection of all things, but lest there be any doubt whether the kingdom of glory is also subjected, and so that it might be proved also, by reason of it, the immense eminence of the Son of man above the angels, the Apostle institutes this demonstration from Psalm 8, as subjecting all things, without exception, to Christ; and this is what he adds: We do not yet see all things subjected, in which the scope and nerve of the Apostolic proof lies. Concerning which world also as future, for whose sake the angels are sent out, under the name of inheritance and future salvation, he had spoken in chapter 1:14, and had subjected it to the Messiah sitting at the right hand of God, just as he had subjected the angels themselves. But what he now teaches and confirms more expressly; asserting that the Son of man, who in his passion had been made lower than the angels, was crowned with glory and honor, set over ALL the works of the hands of God, and that ALL things were subjected to him without exception, even if not all things yet appear to be subjected; for this reason the Apostle omits the examples of things subjected in the kingdom of power in Ps. 8:8-9, as also the glory of the Lord to be celebrated in all the earth in the kingdom of grace v. 2 and 10, which would have been most especially brought forward here if he had understood the kingdom of grace to be properly and immediately future throughout the world, and he urges and presses only the word πάντα ALL, so that under it might be included even those things which we do not yet see subjected to him; but which we shall see one day on the last day, and in the kingdom of glory 1. Cor. 15:22, even though the Son himself shall then be subjected to Him who subjected all things to him, GOD, according to his human nature, so that God may be all in all, even in the Son of man himself, the heir and Lord of all, v. 7, 8.

Concerning which we speak) that is, we have spoken. For by the present tense those things are usually expressed which are nearest to the present, whether they are past or future. For here reference is made to that which preceded in I. 6, as others also have rightly observed.

There is no need for that Enallage. For the Apostle means this, that he is discoursing about that future world, inasmuch as he determined to treat chiefly of the future goods in this epistle, Heb. IX. 11. He refers to the passage above, Heb. I, v. 6; it does not appear, much less, as Cornelius à Lapide wishes, the words of Heb. I, verse 12.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Οὐ γὰρ ἀγγέλοις ὑπέταξε τὴν οἰκουμένην τὴν μέλλουσαν) Postquam hujus epistolæ scriptor ex argumen- tis primo capite propositis illationem fecerat, rursum alia addit argumenta, quibus firmet eandem illationem. In regione illa superætherea sunt quidem Angeli: sed non illi imperant ut Christus. Vocat hanc οἰκουμένην μέλλουσαν, non quia jam non existat, sed quia nobis ea non plene nota est, nec adhuc contigit. Sic Ebræi dicunt עולם הבא nostri respectu. Vide librum de morte Mosis. Sic mystice explicatur locus Psalmi IX. 6.

Alterum jam testimonium eminentiæ divinæ, ad quam Christus secundum humanam naturam post passionem suam exaltatus est, additurus A- postolus, ut insistat comparationi cum Angelis: Non enim, inquit, Angelis orbem futurum subjecit: Quum attigerit Christi officium Propheticum, qua salutis annuntiationem, subjicit testimonium, quod ad officium Regium & regni gloriæ Majesta- tem, ad quam secundum humanam naturam eve- ctus est, pertinet. Argumentum luculentum est: Secundum quam naturam Christo subjectus est orbis futurus, secundum eam divina eminentia præcellit: At Christo secundum humanam natu- ram orbis futurus subjectus est. Ergo Christus secundum humanam naturam divina præcellit eminentia. Assumptum ita effertur: Non Ange- lis sed Filio hominis subjectus est orbis futurus, quod demonstratur è Psalm. VIII. quia Filio hominis subjecta sunt omnia. Non essent autem subjecta omnia, nisi subjectus eidem esset futurus orbis. In eo enim, quod subjecta sunt omnia, nihil re- linquit, quod non sit subjectum. Per τὴν μέλλου- σαν οἰκουμένην Chrysostomus maluit quidem orbem terræ præsentem intelligere, qui futurus dicitur, quia tum adhuc futurus erat, uti Christus Adam futurus secundum carnem, Roman. V. dicitur, quod Theophylactus ita explicat: Futurum eo di- xit, quia Filius DEI perpetuo fuerit. Mundus vero, quia conditus est, & aliquando nihil fue- rat, quasi ut fieret, videtur futurum, quia prius non extitisset. Erat igitur quoad essentia Filii per- petuitatem, futurus & orbis terræ. Etsi hic no- tet, multos de orbe cœlesti futuro interpretari, sed hoc sensu, quod tunc Angeli servorum in mo- rem adstituri, Filius vero judicans sessurus sit. Priorem explicationem sequitur Ribera, non ta- men absolute de mundo præsenti, sed de homini- bus ac cæteris, quæ in terra sunt, intelligens, de hominibus quidem in vitam æternam adducendis, de cæteris vero, quatenus hominum saluti subser- viunt. Beat. Hunnius: Orbem terræ, inquit, qui ex sententia Psalm. IIX. Messiæ subjici debuit, futurum appellat, idque respectu temporum Davi- dis, qui hæc de CHRISTO vaticinatus est. Et quidem futurum vocat propter restaurationem or- bis, quæ per Messiam fieri debuit. Posteriori sen- sui accedunt non tantum, qui cum illis, quos designavit Theophylactus, de judicio & statu post resurrectionem, sed etiam qui in genere de Eccle- sia in regno cœlesti exponunt, quo abit Grotiana ἔκθεσις. Osiander hæc conjungit: Non enim An- gelis subjecit orbem terræ, non modo eum, qui nunc est, verum etiam futurum illum novum mun- dum, qualis post diem novissimum erit. Et cer- tum est ex sententia Psaltis, quia omnia sub pe- des ejus subjecta dicit, utrumque comprehen- di. Sed quid Apostolus hic per οἰκουμένην μέλλυ- σαν intelligat, disquiritur. Beat. Gerhardus cum Estio statum mundi futurum post præsentis mun- di abolitionem, & Ecclesiam, qualis est futura in gloria cœlesti post seculi consummationem nota- ri vult, quam sententiam Estius ex Esaiæ IX. v. 6. Ebr. XIII. vers. 14. cap. XI. vers. 10. 2. Petr. III. v. 13. Beatus Gerhardus etiam ex Esaiæ LXV. vers. 17. cap. LXVI. vers. 22. Roman. IIX. vers. 21. Apocal. XXI. vers. 1. nec non è consensu Theodoreti, Oe- cumenii, Lyrani, Cajetani probat; eumque etiam probare Theophylactum & Thomam ait, ac pro- inde verbum Præteritum subjecit hunc habere sensum statuit: Subjiciendum prædixit aut pro- misit: q. d. Principatus orbis terræ futurus non est Angelis decretus aut promissus à Deo. Quem sensum non improbandum censemus, modo ab- sit opinio de cælo & terra, vel aliis etiam crea- turis, in novissimo die renovandis, quæ Pontifi- ciis nonnullis hæret, utpote contraria consum- mationi mundi, ut & commentum Schlichtin- gii de novis officiis & Principatibus Angelorum, de quibus nihil Scriptura novit; nec excludan- tur à regno gloriæ & Principatu Christi, qui jam in statu gloriæ sunt. Dicitur enim σχετικῶς & κατά τι orbis FUTURUS, ut non male Grotius observavit, non absolute: nimirum ratione no- stri, qui adhuc sumus in statu Ecclesiæ militan- tis, ut è cap. VI. 5. collatione constat, quo respe- ctu etiam verbum Præteritum adhibetur: quia jam actu eidem Ecclesiæ triumphans subjecta, & jus ac principatum habet in eandem, etsi sub- inde illa, & indies civibus novis augeatur, & locupletetur usque ad consummationem seculi, ubi & plena erat civitas illa cœlestis, & plena o- mnium subjectio Christo Regi & Domino fu- tura est; quo nomine dicitur, nondum videmus ei omnia subjecta esse. Nec illi Estii explicationi calculum addere possumus, Angelis quidem ter- ræ orbem præsentem subjectum esse, non tamen fu- turum, qui longe præstantior est, & CHRISTO Principi servatur. Nam utut Angelos certa ra- tione præesse provinciis terræ admitti possit, non tamen hæc est subjectio, de qua Aposto- lus & Hiero-Psaltes, utpote quæ supremum do- minium & divinam dignitatem infert, & non tam illa ad regimen Angelorum, quam ad custo- diam & ministerium, cujus causa emittuntur etiam ad Principes terræ & aulas, unde guber- nantur provinciæ, pertinent. Quo tendat sen- sus mysticus Grotii Psalm. IX. vers. 6. penetrare non possumus. Per οἰκουμένην ergo μέλλουσαν non modo vita æterna, quam in manu habet Chri- stus, & tribuere potest, cui vult, sed status fu- turi seculi, civitas illa cœlestis cum omnibus ci- vibus, quibus dominatur, ut & ea, quæ ad ean- dem faciunt, designantur, quod eorum sit λει- τουργὸς ratione distributionis, & administrator, nec non Sacerdos futurorum bonorum, Ebr. IX. vers. 11. ratione acquisitionis, & pro applicatio- ne intercessionis: & in omnia dominium ac potesta- tem haberet, ratione Regalis eminentiæ, ac mu- neris: siquidem non sacerdos vulgaris sit, sed Regale Sacerdotium obtineat: quemadmodum postea Apostolus eundem Pontificem esse secun- dum ordinem Melchisedech, adeoque & Sacer- dotem, & Regem simul, demonstravit. Camera- rius de hominibus, qui ea ætate coluerunt ter- rarum orbem, explicat, qua Filius DEI in ter- ris natus est. Ideo nunc τὴν μέλλουσαν οἰκουμένην eam hominum in orbe terrarum ætatem vocat, in quam futurum erat, ut Filius Dei secundum pro- phetias introduceretur, id est nasceretur homo, qui est Filius Mariæ Jesus, ideoque addidit, περὶ ἧς λαλοῦμεν, id est, non subjecit Angelis orbem ter- ræ, futurum eum inquam, de quo loquimur. Id est, in quem deberet introduci Christus. Hæc il- le. Beatus Dorschæus de regno gratiæ interpreta- tur, quod οἰκουμένη μέλλουσα vocetur, tum quia in progressu adhuc & incremento erat, maximam sui partem adhuc oriturum, tum quia in vatici- niis tanquam regnum novum, terra futura & nova describitur: Agnoscit tamen comprehen- di regnum gloriæ, & Angelos, quatenus sunt in regno gloriæ, imo & omnia opera manuum Dei, vers. 7. 8. subjecta pedibus ejus, quam phrasin esse propriam regni potentiæ, observat: quum Eccle- sia, seu militans, seu triumphans, Christi Sponsa, non subjecta ejus pedibus, sed corpus ejus sit, Sponsum pro capite agnoscens, etsi alias ut creaturæ sub pedibus Christi sint omnia, quæcunque sunt opera manuum Dei, adeoque etiam fideles, & ele- cti. Sed non hic quæritur, quænam Christo subje- cta sint, cui subjecta omnino omnia, sed quid pro- prie per οἰκουμένην τὴν μέλλουσαν intelligatur. Ipsa sessio ad dextram Dei jam illam omnium subje- ctionem inferebat, ne autem dubium sit, anne etiam regnum gloriæ subjectum sit, & ut probare- tur etiam, ejus ratione, immensa præ Angelis Fi- lii hominis eminentia, Apostolus hanc ἀπόδειξιν è Psalmo VIII. utpote omnia, citra exceptionem, Christo subjiciente, instituit; & hoc est, quod ad- dit: Nondum videmus omnia subjecta esse, in quo scopus & nervus probationis Apostolicæ latet. De qua etiam οἰκουμένη ceu futura, cujus gratia e- mittantur Angeli, sub nomine hæreditatis, & sa- lutis futuræ, loquutus erat c. I, 14. eamque Messiæ ad dextram Dei sedenti, æque ut Angelos ipsos sub- jecerat. Quod vero nunc expressius docet, atque confirmat; Filium hominis, qui in passione mino- ratus erat infra Angelos, gloria & honore corona- tum, supra OMNIA opera manuum Dei constitu- tum, eique OMNIA citra exceptionem subjecta, etsi nondum omnia subjecta appareant, asserens; ideo prætermittit Apostolus exempla rerum subdi- tarum in regno potentiæ in Ps. IIX. 8. 9. ut & gloriam Domini in omnibus terris celebrandam in regno gratiæ v. 2. & 10. quæ maxime hic adducenda fu- isset, si proprie & immediate regnum gratiæ per orbem futurum intellexisset, urgetque ac premit tantum vocem πάντα OMNIA, uti sub ea com- prehendantur etiam, quæ nondum videmus ipsi subjecta; visuri autem sumus olim in die novis- simo, & in regno gloriæ 1. Cor. XV. 22. etsi Fi- lius ipse tum ei, qui omnia sibi subjecit, DEO, subjicietur secundum humanam naturam, ut Deus sit omnia in omnibus, etiam in ipso Filio hominis, omnium hærede, & Domino, v. 7. 8.

Περὶ ἧς λαλοῦμεν) id est ἐλαλήσαμεν. Nam per tem- pus præsens exprimi solent ea, quæ proxima sunt præsenti, sive exacta, sive ventura. Respicicur enim hic id, quod præ- cessit I. 6. ut & alii recte observarunt.

Non opus est illa Enallage. Nam id vult A- postolus, se de illo futuro orbe disserere, utpote qui præcipue de Pontifice futurorum bonorum in hac epistola agere constituit Ebr. IX. 11. Respi- ci locum superiorem Ebr. I, v. 6. non apparet, nedum, ut vult Cornelius à Lapide, verba Ebr. I, vers. 12.

## 2:6
Verse 6. But one testified somewhere saying) He says 'one,' because of those poems which are in the book of Psalms, there is not one writer, and indeed the writer is often unknown. Διεμαρτύρατο means 'he testifies,' that is, he shows, הודיע. For that word is usually translated in this way.

But why should the customary meaning of the word not be retained? The sense is certainly more convenient if you translate it 'he testifies' than if you explain it 'he shows.' The Holy Spirit has no need of showing; his testimony is sufficient. Moreover, he did not name the Author either here or elsewhere in this epistle, because he wrote to the Hebrews, who were sufficiently knowledgeable of the Holy Scriptures, as Theophylact observes here.

What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him) The very words of the LXX Interpreters from Psalm VIII, which in the first obvious sense deals with Adam and his seed, but in the mystical sense ought to be referred, and was referred by the wise Hebrews, to the Messiah and his seed. For the opinion that Adam bore the figure of the Messiah was accepted in those times, as we said in Romans V, verse 14, 1 Corinthians XV, verse 45, and following. And specifically concerning this passage of the Psalm, see 1 Corinthians XV, verse 27, Ephesians I, v. 22. The dominion over the things of the lower world given to Adam and his descendants is an image of the dominion which Christ has in the higher world, and of which those will be participants who have put on his nature and are worthy to be called by his name. Ἐπισκέπτεσθαι פקד to take special care of someone. That was wonderful concerning Adam, who, like other living creatures, was made from clay; much more wonderful is this concerning Christ, who, while living among men, displayed nothing great to those looking at external things. See Matthew VIII. 20, chapter XI. 6, Phil. II. 7, 2 Corinthians VIII. 9. That Psalm VIII, like some others, used to be sung with joy at the grape harvest. Hence they are called על־הגתית.

Because we have diligently discussed the most perverse distortions of this testimony by Grotius, as well as by Calvin, to whom they are twin, in our Annotations on the book of Psalms at Psalm VIII, v. 6, in the Illustrated Bible of the Old Testament, Vol. I, page 949 et seqq., there is no reason for us to be laborious here in refuting them: yet, so that the Apostolic demonstration may be consistent with itself, some things concerning the Grotian inventions must be noted. 1. That the Psalm does not deal in the literal sense with Adam and his seed: Because Adam was not אנוש, a miserable man, in the state of integrity. 2. The other name, 'Son of man,' does not fit him, which if Grotius draws to his seed or descendants, the predicates concerning the dignity with which the son of man is said to be crowned, or concerning dominion over all things, do not in any way apply to them, which did not even apply to Adam himself before the fall. Add that there is only one subject here with which the Hiero-Psalmist deals, and thus 'man' and 'Son of man' are the same. 3. Therefore the Psalm does not deal with both Christ and his seed. For where is there any mention of the seed of Christ in this Psalm? That it deals with only one subject is too manifest, both from the Psalm and from this Apostolic text. 4. It does not deal with Christ only in a mystical sense, but in a literal one. Because those things which are handed down in the Psalm concerning this man and this Son of man do not fit, according to the literal sense, except Christ alone, who is therefore called the Son of man in the New Testament: Nor could the demonstration of the dignity and preeminence of CHRIST have been sought from the same by the Apostle, unless he were speaking in the literal sense itself. The Apostle certainly understood three continuous verses of this Psalm concerning Christ. And it is evident from a comparison of 1 Cor. XV, verse 27 and Ephesians I, v. 22 that the Apostle understood this Psalm in no other way than concerning Christ. But Christ himself also, in Matthew XXI, verse 16, applies the third clause of the Psalm to the children crying out Hosanna to him. Finally, since there is only one sense of a single statement, and no other is to be admitted besides the literal sense, and this statement of the Psalm is understood by the Apostle concerning Christ, it is manifest that it must be taken concerning Christ in the literal sense, and cannot be drawn to another subject, unless one wishes to contradict the Apostle. 5. Grotius could not teach that it was referred to Christ by the wise Hebrews only in a mystical sense, and indeed referred to the seed of Christ at the same time. 6. Nor was Grotius himself consistent regarding the mystical sense. For he explained this passage differently in his annotations on the book of Psalms, namely, concerning man in the state of integrity, but not concerning the whole human race, or Adam and his seed. 7. Paul, 1 Corinthians XV, verse 27, did not understand the present Psalm concerning Christ according to a mystical sense, but according to the literal sense, and in that sense he also used the words of the same in Eph. I. 22. 8. Adam did not obtain dominion over the things of the lower world, which Grotius opposes to the angels as the higher world, so that this division of the world might adequately exhaust the whole universe, for it is read in Gen. I. 26 that only dominion over living creatures was granted to him; and therefore the things which are held in this Psalm concerning dominion over all things, or the subjection of all things, because nothing is left ἀνυπότακτον (unsubjected), as the Apostle interprets in this place, cannot be applied to Adam. 9. Much less, therefore, can they be applied to the seed or posterity of Adam, because the Protoplasts lost that dignity through the fall. 10. The rationale of type or image does not fit in Adam, in relation to Christ as the antitype, as far as dominion over the things of the world is concerned, nor is that figure handed down anywhere in Scripture in this third point of comparison. 11. The dominion which Christ has in the supreme world is not gathered from this passage by an inference from type to antitype, or from image to the truth of the thing shadowed forth by the image: But from the universality of subjection of all things to infer also the subjection of the world to come. For to him to whom all things are universally subjected, to him it is also necessary that the world to come be subjected. For the Apostle himself shows this rationale of the inference, ἐν γὰρ τῷ ὑποτάξαι αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα, ὀδὲν ἀφῆκεν αὐτῷ ἀνυπότακτον verse 8. Which rationale of the consequence, because it did not agree with his own opinion, Grotius passed over dry-shod. 12. The dominion which is asserted for Christ in this Psalm is not only in the supreme world, but over all things, according to the evident letter, and the Apostolic observation, superior to every exception. 13. The communion of that dominion, whether in the superior world or universal and ecumenical, in no way falls to the faithful, whom Grotius describes with a new phrase alien to the Scriptures, that they have put on the nature of Christ himself. For the dominion of Christ is of infinite power, and an omnipresent government, which does not fall to the faithful, and not even to any of the Angels, but is proper to him alone, to whom it was said, sit at my right hand. 14. I pass over that, which says that Adam, like the other living creatures, was made from clay, for where does Scripture assert that the other living creatures were formed from clay? But that God took special care of Adam in the state of integrity, what is the wonder, since he was created in the image of God. 15. Nor does the sacred Psalmist wonder at that so much, that God took special care of Christ, but because He visited him in such a way that He raised him to the highest eminence.
