By this means it is clear that Christ did not merit this by his passion, so that he might be exalted for that reason: which Estius here acknowledged from the Papists: because otherwise the Apostle would not have exclaimed about that matter: What is man, that thou art mindful of him, and the son of man, that thou visitest him? Even this verse, he says, must be accepted according to the mind of the Apostle concerning Christ, whether insofar as he bears human nature, which does not merit such a visitation and exaltation, or insofar as he was defiled by ignominy and torments. Osiander explains it concerning the human race graciously visited by God. Ah good GOD, how great a miracle is this, that with such clemency you look upon and care for the human race, that you would will to assume your only-begotten eternal Son as man, or human nature into the unity of his person? and do you deem that nature, truly miserable and subject to many infirmities, worthy of such great honor? But since he acknowledges that the things which follow must be understood concerning Christ, and yet no different subject is insinuated in the Psalm or the Apostle, but all things speak of the same subject, it is sufficiently clear that the prior words treat of Christ, not of some other. Therefore Francis Ribera in this place, page 134 in my copy: There are those who say that this Psalm is understood of man in a historical sense, but in a mystical sense of Christ, as Euthymius and Jansenius. Many interpret it of man and Christ together. My opinion is far different: For I think the Psalm was by no means written of man, but truly and properly of Christ, just as St. Thomas also explained. Jerome and Augustine also interpret everything of Christ, and say nothing of man. The Greek Fathers felt the same, as we shall say a little later. For if we wish to understand it of man, certain things will occur that are greater than the condition of man. From which it will follow that the rest, which seemed to be said of him, are to be referred not to him, but to Christ, according to the canon which we handed down in chapter 1, numbers 51 and 52. Of this kind is that: Thou hast put all things under his feet, which does not befit man, because there are many animals over which he does not rule. Furthermore, it is one thing to preside over animals, another for animals to be put under his feet: for we do not have things put under our feet except those which we use at our own discretion, and which we command at our beck and call, which, besides Christ, is granted to no man. Not even Adam himself had that power at that time, so that when he wished, he could bring fiercer birds flying to him, or call fish from the bottom of the sea to him: But he would use the service of all animals, just as we now use that of tame ones. Thus Chrysostom and Hugh of St. Victor on that passage in Genesis 1. And let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, etc., teach that through sin the animals which were not very useful were alienated from man, but those which serve our life much, and are useful and necessary, were left in their servitude and subjection. And St. Thomas, dealing with this in Part 1, question 96, article 1, says that a superior power can do many things in subjects which an inferior power cannot do. An angel, however, is naturally superior to man, whence some effect could be produced concerning animals by angelic power, which could not be produced by human power, namely, that all animals would immediately be gathered together, etc. Furthermore, when the Prophet says: Thou hast put all things under his feet, the Apostle here teaches that 'all things' is not accepted, as it is sometimes wont to be accepted for 'many', but in such a way that, besides GOD, nothing at all is understood to be excluded. For in that, he says, he put all things under him, he left nothing not subject to him. Which he explains more in 1 Corinthians. XV.

saying: For he hath put all things under his feet. But when he says: All things are subject to him, without doubt, except him who put all things under him. He understands, therefore, that all creatures are placed under his feet, which can be said of no other man. The same Apostle in this chapter 11 says: But now we do not yet see all things subject to him, by which words he openly indicates that all things are to be subjected to him at some time, but it will never happen that animals are subjected to man as in the state of innocence: for after the resurrection there will be no brute animals; therefore all things are said of Christ, not of man. And the Holy Spirit teaches this with undoubted arguments, since Christ also in Matthew 21 interprets those words as pertaining to himself: Out of the mouth of infants and sucklings thou hast perfected praise, etc. And the Apostle explains those words three times concerning Christ, Hebrews 2, 1 Corinthians 15. Ephesians 1. And what we just said, that the Apostle promises that all things are to be subjected to him at some time, which will never happen to man. The same teaches in 1 Corinthians 15 that it will happen to Christ: For he must reign, until he hath put all enemies under his feet. And the last enemy shall be destroyed, death: For he hath put all things under his feet. But when he says: All things are subject to him, without doubt, except him who put all things under him; but when all things shall be subject to him, then the Son himself also shall be subject to him who put all things under himself. These are Ribera's words: Who indeed afterwards denies that those words: What is man and the son of man? are to be accepted concerning Christ; but since he confesses that the rest are to be understood concerning Christ, and that in the Psalm there is one and the same subject, it is most manifest that he is easily convinced by his own hypothesis. Nor indeed, with Titelmann and others, does he allow a transition from species to person in those words, 'thou hast made him a little lower than the angels', so that 'what is man' is said of human nature, and 'thou hast made him lower' is said of Christ, but he always accepts 'man' in the same way, and says that the Apostle speaks of him not in himself but in Christ as made lower than the angels, and crowned with glory and honor. But 'man' is always accepted in the same way, when in those things which are said concerning the 'lowering' and those which are said concerning the 'crowning', as Ribera admits, Christ is necessarily understood in the singular, nor does any other subject befit these predicates—not, I say, human nature in the species, but that individual human nature which the Son of God assumed into his own hypostasis; it cannot be otherwise, if the subject is to remain the same, than that 'man' and 'son of man', of whom the Psalmist speaks, should likewise be understood of the one Christ. Nor do Chrysostom, Theodoret, and Oecumenius [interpret it] otherwise than that it is not a question of our nature, as it is in men in general, but of the nature of our kind, as it is in Christ: Other Fathers consequently elicit only the honor redounding to us from this, that our whole nature is honored in that very thing in Christ, which is a certain κοινωνία [communion], even if that honor, with which the Son of Man is crowned, is terminated in the person of Christ, and is proper to this individual and singular nature, which was assumed by the λόγῳ [Word], from which Christ is called man and son of man. John Cameron, from the Reformed, refutes here also the glosses of Calvin, Pareus, and others of his associates in his response to the questions on the Epistle to the Hebrews, page 389. There are many things, he says, which stand in the way of this Psalm being able to be referred to the first creation. That first [point] which contains thanksgiving, and yet it is not likely that the Church gives thanks to GOD for creation, with the work of redemption passed over in silence. Then by what benefits the pious have fallen, as often as they commemorate them with thanksgiving, so often do they acknowledge the misery into which they have fallen by their own fault, and at the same time they ask that they be restored to the place from which they were cast down, none of which happens in this Psalm. To this is added the fact that God is said in this Psalm to have spread the glory of His name everywhere throughout the whole earth, which undoubtedly pertains only to the Church of the Jews and the Gentiles: For at the first creation the glory of the name of God did not extend further than Paradise, for there were not yet any elsewhere who might celebrate the praise of the name of God. Add that those words from the mouth of infants and sucklings etc. do not fit the first creation, and these indeed much less, on account of those who oppose you to restrain the enemy etc. but also that ותחסרהו ἠλάττωσας αὐτὸν you made him lack, cannot be referred to the first creation, for they denote (if we estimate their proper force) a change of condition for the worse. Whence it also appears how rightly the LXX Interpreters translated מעט as βραχύ τι and מֵאֱלֹהִים as παρ᾽ ἀγγέλος, since מעט is also referred to time, Hos. I. 4. but this, because the whole sentence would be cold and inept if אלהים signified God, for who would think that the Prophet wished to say that man, even in the first creation, was a little lower than the supreme God. Then the antithesis is manifest, which comes to this: for a small time you made him more deficient than the Angels, but afterwards you crowned him with glory and magnificence. The rest may be sought from the lectures Tom. II. page 161. seqq. Matthias Polus in the Synopsis Criticorum not only produced the arguments which I had produced against Rivetus and Grotius in the AntiGr., but he also concluded his discussion on that famous question, as he calls it, whether these things are to be accepted only concerning Christ, with the words of Cocceius: It is a matter of conscience for us to interpret this passage otherwise than the Apostle does in Heb. II. 6. 7. For in Christ this oracle is more evidently fulfilled. Cocceius, however, does not deserve our approval in all things here: since he explains the visitation of the Son of man as the incarnation itself, which is rather a consequence of the incarnation, and happened to the incarnate Son of God, constituted in a state of emptying, of whom he himself says: He is therefore made lower than GOD, because he did not conduct himself παρατηρητῶς as the God that he was: lower than the Angels, because he was made under the law, lower than men, who are called Gods, because he obeyed them, and suffered himself to be judged by them. Hence he is called עֶבֶד מוֹשְׁלִים servant of Rulers Is. XLIX. 7. Nor can it easily be doubted that Christ, when he very frequently and very studiously called himself τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου the Son of man in the Gospel, recalled his hearers and the readers of the Gospel to this passage. Although afterwards Cocceius relapses to the opinion which we brought forward from Ribera: that the Psalm speaks generally, so as to include the faithful themselves, as participants in the cross of Christ, so now in his glory: that the Psalm speaks of man, as he is visited by God, that is, of human nature, as the divine dwells in it, and thus of Christ, and those who are of Christ, and are participants of his Spirit. But thus he interprets it altogether differently than Paul, which he had said was a matter of conscience for him. For Paul teaches apodictically that this applies to Christ alone, and from there demonstrates the eminence of Christ above all Angels, let alone above all men, from the infinite glory communicated to him, which belongs to none of the Angels, let alone men, even if the fruit of the same redounds to the faithful: Which (concerning the fruit), the Apostle does not teach there, dealing with the crown of glory of the son of man of the Hiero-Psalmist, but delivers it afterwards, when he teaches that this Son of man was therefore perfected and crowned by GOD through sufferings, so that he might bring many sons into glory. What Cocceius therefore says, that the Apostle demonstrates that this saying does not pertain primarily to any man, but to someone through whom the faithful enjoy this kingdom, he hides a double sense, primary and secondary, but against the ἀπόδειξιν of the Apostle, who most evidently teaches that this Psalm speaks not primarily, but uniquely of Christ; as Camero acknowledged with us.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Διεμαρτύρατο δέ πού τις λέγων) Τις dicit, quia illorum carminum, quæ sunt in libro Psalmorum, non unus est scriptor, imo & sæpe scriptor ignoratur. Διεμαρτύρατο testatur, hoc est, ostendit הודיע. Nam id verbum sic verti solet.

Cur vero non retinenda usitata verbi signifi- catio? Convenientior utique est sensus, si red- das testatur, quam si exponas, ostendit. Non opus habet Spiritus Sanctus ostensione, sufficit ejusdem testificatio. Non autem vel hic, vel alias in hac epistola nominavit Autorem, quia ad E- bræos, Scripturæ sacræ satis gnaros, scripsit, ut hic observat Theophylactus.

Τί ἐστιν ἄνθρωπος, ὅτι μιμνήσκῃ αὐτοῦ, ἢ υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου, ὅτι ἐπισκέπτῃ αὐτόν) Verba ipsa LXX. Interpretum ex Psalm. VIII. qui sensu primum obvio agit de Adamo & semine ejus, sensu autem mystico referri debet, & ab E- bræis sapientibus referebatur ad Messiam & semen ejus. Nam Adamum figuram gessisse Messiæ recepta erat illis temporibus sententia, ut diximus Romanor. V. vers. 14. 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 45. & sequentibus. Et specialiter de hoc loco Psalmi vide 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 27. Ephes. I. v. 22. Dominium in res mundi inferioris datum Adamo & po- steris ejus imago est dominii ejus, quod in mundo supre- mo habet Christus, & cujus participes erunt, qui ipsius naturam induerunt, & ab ipsius nomine digni sunt ap- pellari. Ἐπισκέπτεσθαι פקד curam alicujus peculiarem gerere. Mirum fuit illud de Adamo, qui ut cætera animan- tia de luto erat factus, multo magis mirum hoc de Chri- sto, qui inter homines agens nihil magni prætulit exte- riora spectantibus. Vide Matth. VIII. 20. cap. XI. 6. Phil. II. 7. 2. Corinth. VIII. 9. Psalmus iste VIII. ut alii non- nulli solebant cantari cum gaudio in vindemiis. Inde di- cuntur על־הגתית.

Quia sedulo hujus testimonii perversissimas detorsiones Grotianas, ut & Calvinianas, qui- bus illæ geminæ sunt, discussimus Annotat. in librum Psalmorum ad Psalm. IIX. v. 6. in Bibliis illustrat. Vet. Testam. Tom. I. pag. 949. seqq. non est, quod hic operosi simus in iisdem refel- lendis: Ut tamen constet sibi demonstratio Apo- stolica, nonnulla de Grotianis commentis notan- da. 1. Psalmum sensu literali non agere de Ada- mo & semine ejus: Quia Adam non fuit אנוש ho- mo miser in statu integritatis. 2. In eum non qua- drat alterum nomen Filius hominis, quod Gro- tius ad semen vel posteros ejus si trahat, illis nul- la ratione prædicata conveniunt de dignitate, qua coronatus filius hominis dicitur, vel de dominio in omnia, quæ ne quidem ipsi Adamo ante la- psum conveniebant. Adde quod unum hic tan- tum sit subjectum, de quo agit Hiero-Psaltes, adeoque idem sit homo & Filius hominis. 3. Non ergo agit Psalmus & de Christo, & de semine ejus. Ubi enim ullo verbo mentio seminis Christi in hoc Psalmo? De unico tantum subjecto eundem agere nimis manifestum tum è Psalmo, tum ex hoc Apostolico textu. 4. Non agit mystico tan- tum sensu de Christo, sed literali. Quia non conveniunt secundum literalem sensum, quæ in Psalmo traduntur de hoc homine, & hoc Filio hominis, nisi Christo unice, qui inde Filius ho- minis dictus est in Novo Testamento: Neque de- monstratio dignitatis & præeminentiæ CHRISTI peti ex eodem potuisset ab Apostolo, nisi sensu literaliter ipso loqueretur. Apostolus certe tres versus continuos hujus Psalmi de Christo intelle- xit. Nec aliter, quam de Christo, Psalmum hunc alibi intellexisse Apostolum, è collatione 1. Cor. XV. vers. 27. Ephes. I. v. 22. constat. Sed & Chri- stus ipse Matth. XXI. vers. 16. comma tertium Psalmi ad pueros Osianna sibi acclamantes, ap- plicat. Denique quum unius dicti non sit nisi unicus sensus, nec præter sensum literalem ad- mittendus alius sit, & hoc dictum Psalmi ab A- postolo de Christo intelligatur, manifestum est, sensu literali de Christo accipiendum esse, nec ad aliud subjectum trahi posse, nisi Apostolo contradicere quis velit. 5. Ab Ebræis sapienti- bus tantum mystico sensu referri ad Christum, & quidem simul ad semen Christi referri, docere haud potuit Grotius. 6. Nec ipse Grotius sibi constitit de sensu mystico. Nam aliter hunc locum exposuit in annotat. ad libr. Psalm. nimirum de homine in statu integritatis, non autem de uni- verso humano genere, vel de Adamo & semine ejus. 7. Paulus 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 27. non secun- dum mysticum sensum, sed secundum sensum li- teralem præsentem Psalmum de Christo intelle- xit, atque eo etiam sensu adhibuit verba ejusdem Eph. I. 22. 8. Dominium in res mundi inferioris, quem sedi Angelorum opponit Grotius, ceu mundo superiori, ut adæquate exhauriat hoc mundi μερισμῷ totam universitatem, non obti- nuit Adam, cui tantum dominium in animantia concessum legitur Gen. I. 26. ideoque quæ de do- minio in omnia, vel subjectione omnium in Psal- mo hoc habentur, quia nihil relictum est ἀνυπό- τακτον, interprete Apostolo hoc in loco, Adamo applicari nequeunt. 9. Multo ergo minus appli- cari ea possunt semini vel posteritati Adami, quia per lapsum dignitatem illam deperdidere Proto- plasti. 10. Non convenit typi vel imaginis ratio in Adamo, in Christum ceu antitypum, quantum ad dominium in res mundi, nec ea figura in hoc comparationis tertio uspiam in Scriptura tradita. 11. Dominium, quod in mundo supremo habet Christus, ex hoc loco non colligitur per illatio- nem à typo ad antitypum, vel ab imagine ad rei veritatem imagine adumbratam: Sed ab univer- salitate subjectionis omnium ad inferendam etiam subjectionem orbis futuri. Cui enim omnia uni- versaliter subjecta sunt, illi etiam oportet subje- ctum esse orbem futurum. Hanc enim rationem illationis monstrat ipse Apostolus, ἐν γὰρ τῷ ὑπο- τάξαι αὐτῷ τὰ πάντα, ὀδὲν ἀφῆκεν αὐτῷ ἀνυπότα- κτον vers. 8. Quam consequentiæ rationem, quod suæ non congrueret opinioni, sicco pede præter- iit Grotius. 12. Dominium, quod Christo as- seritur in hoc Psalmo, non est tantum in mundo supremo, sed super omnia, juxta evidentem lite- ram, & observationem Apostolicam, omni ex- ceptione superiorem. 13. Dominii istius sive in mundo superiori, sive universalis & œcumenici communio nullatenus cadit in fideles, quos nova phrasi à Scripturis aliena describit Grotius, quod ipsius Christi naturam induerint. Dominium enim Christi virtutis infinitæ est, & omnipræsens re- gimen, quod non cadit in fideles, ac ne in An- gelorum quidem ullum, sed ei soli proprium est, cui dictum est, sede ad dextram meam. 14. Mit- to illud, quod Adamum, ut cætera animantia de luto factum dicit, ubi enim Scriptura animantia cætera de luto formata asserit? Curam autem pe- culiarem Adami gessisse Deum in statu integri- tatis, quid mirum, quum conditus fuerit ad ima- ginem Dei. 15. Neque id adeo miratur Hiero- Psaltes, quod Christi curam peculiarem gesserit Deus, sed quod ita eundem visitarit, ut ad sum- mam eminentiam evexerit. Quo pacto liquet, non id meruisse Christum passione sua, ut ea ra- tione exaltaretur: quod è Pontificiis Estius hic agnovit: quia alioquin ea de re non exclamasset Apostolus: Quid est homo, quod memor es ejus, & filius hominis, quod visitas eum? Etiam hic versus, inquit, ad mentem Apostoli de Christo erit accipiendus, sive quatenus humanam naturam ge- stans, quæ non meretur tantam visitationem & exaltationem, sive quatenus fœdatus ignominia & tormentis. Osiander explicat de humano genere gratiose à Deo visitato. Ah bone DEUS, quan- tum est hoc miraculum, quod tanta clementia hu- manum genus respicis ac curas, ut velis unigeni- tum æternum Filium tuum assumere hominem, seu humanam naturam in unitatem personæ? eamque naturam, miseram sane & multis infirmitatibus obnoxiam tanto dignaris honore? At quum ea, quæ sequuntur, de Christo intelligenda esse agno- scat, nec tamen diversum in Psalmo vel Apostolo insinuetur subjectum, sed omnia de eodem lo- quantur subjecto, satis patet, priora verba de Christo, non de alio quodam agere. Ideo Fran- ciscus Ribera in h. l. pag. mihi 134. Sunt qui di- cant, Psalmum hunc de homine intelligi historico sensu, mystico vero de Christo, ut Euthymius & Jansenius. Multi de homine & de Christo simul interpretantur. Mihi longe alia sententia est: Pu- to enim nequaquam de homine, sed vere & proprie de Christo Psalmum scriptum esse, sicut etiam S. Thomas exposuit. Hieronymus quoque & Augusti- nus omnia de Christo interpretantur, & nihil de homine dicunt. Idem senserunt Græci Patres, ut paulo post dicemus. Etenim si de homine intelli- gere velimus, occurrent quædam majora, quam pro hominis conditione. Ex quo fiet cætera, quæ de illo dici videbantur, non ad illum, sed ad Chri- stum esse referenda, juxta canonem, quem tradi- dimus cap. 1. num. 51. & 52. Hujusmodi est illud: Omnia subjecisti sub pedibus ejus, quod homini non convenit, quia multa sunt animalia, quibus non imperat. Deinde aliud est, præesse animalibus, aliud animalia subjici sub pedibus ejus: non enim sub pedibus subjecta habemus, nisi ea, quibus pro arbitrio nostro utimur, & quibus ad nutum im- peramus, quod præter Christum nulli hominum concessum est. Ne ipse quidem Adam eam tunc potestatem habuit, ut cum vellet, ferociores aves ad se volantes adduceret, aut pisces ex imo mari ad se vocaret: Sed uteretur omnium animalium servitio, sicut nunc utimur mansuetorum. Ita Chrysostomus & Hugo S. Victoris in illud Genes. 1. Et præsit piscibus maris &c. docent, per peccatum animalia, quæ non admodum utilia erant, alienata esse ab homine, quæ vero vitæ nostræ multum ser- viunt, & utilia & necessaria sunt, relicta esse in servitute & subjectione sua. Et S. Thomas de hoc agens 1. P. quæst. 96. artic. 1. ait, in subjectos mul- ta facere potest superior potestas, qua non potest facere inferior. Angelus autem est superior natu- raliter homine, unde aliquis effectus poterat fieri circa animalia virtute Angelica, qui non poterat fieri potestate humana, scilicet, quod statim omnia animalia congregarentur &c. Præterea cum Pro- pheta dicit: Omnia subjecisti sub pedibus ejus, A- postolus hic docet, non omnia accipi, ut interdum accipi solet pro multis, sed ita, ut præter DEUM nihil omnino exclusum intelligatur. In eo enim, inquit, quod omnia ei subjecit, nihil dimisit non subjectum ei. Quod magis explicat 1. Corinth. XV.

dicens : Omnia enim subjecit sub pedibus ejus. Cum autem dicat : Omnia subjecta sunt ei, sine dubio præter eum, qui subjecit ei omnia. Intelligit ergo creaturas omnes positas esse sub pedibus ejus, quod de nullo alio homine dici potest. Idem Apostolus in hoc cap. II. ait : Nunc autem nec dum videmus o- mnia subjecta ei, quibus verbis aperte subindi- cat, aliquando ei esse omnia subjicienda, at nun- quam fiet, ut animalia ita homini subjiciantur, ut in statu innocentiæ : nam post resurrectionem nulla erunt bruta animalia, de Christo ergo omnia dicuntur, non de homine. Atque id non dubiis argumentis docet Spiritus Sanctus, quandoquidem & Christus Matth. XXI. ad se pertinere interpre- tatur illa verba : Ex ore infantium & lactentium perfecisti laudem &c. Et Apostolus ter de Christo exponit illa : Omnia subjecisti sub pedibus ejus, Ebr. II. 1. Corinth. XV. Ephes. I. Et quod modo diximus, Apostolum polliceri, omnia aliquando esse illi subjicienda, quod homini non continget unquam. Idem docet 1. Corinth. XV. fore ut Chri- sto contingat : Oportet autem illum regnare, do- nec ponat omnes inimicos sub pedibus ejus. Novis- sima autem inimica destruetur mors : Omnia enim subjecit sub pedibus ejus. Cum autem dicat : O- mnia subjecta sunt ei, sine dubio præter eum, qui subjecit ei omnia ; cum autem subjecta illi fuerint omnia, tunc & ipse Filius subjectus erit ei, qui subjecit sibi omnia. Hæc Ribera : Qui quidem postea verba illa : Quid est homo & Filius homi- nis? negat de Christo accipienda ; sed quum fa- teatur, cætera de Christo intelligenda, & in Psal- mo unum idemque subjectum esse, manifestissi- mum sit, haud difficulter ex propria hypothesi convincitur. Neque vero cum Titelmanno & aliis in verbis istis, minuisti eum paulo minus ab An- gelis, transiri à specie ad personam admittit, ita ut, quid est homo, dicatur de natura humana, & minuisti eum, dicatur de Christo, sed eodem modo semper hominem accipiat, & eum non in se sed in Christo minutum ab Angelis dicat Aposto- lus, & gloria atque honore coronatum. At heo- dem modo semper homo accipitur, quum in illis, quæ de ἐλαττώσει, & quæ de στεφανώσει di- cuntur, fatente Ribera, necessario μοναδικῶς Christus intelligatur, nec aliud subjectum istis prædicatis conveniat, non natura, inquam, hu- mana in specie, sed individualis illa natura hu- mana, quam in hypostasin suam assumpsit Filius Dei, fieri aliter non potest, si subjectum idem manere debeat, quam ut homo & Filius hominis, de quo Psaltes, itidem de uno Christo intellige- tur. Nec aliter Chrysostomus, Theodoretius, Oe- cumenius, quam quod non de natura nostra, ut est in hominibus in universum, sed de nostri gene- ris natura, ut in Christo est, agatur : Alii Patres per consequens solum in nos inde redundantem honorem eliciunt, quod tota natura nostra eo ipso in Christo honorata sit, quæ est κοινωνία quæ- dam, etsi honor ille, quo coronatus est Filius hominis, in persona Christi terminetur, sitque huic individuæ & singulari naturæ, quæ assumpta est à λόγῳ, proprius, à qua Christus homo, & filius hominis dictus est. Johannes Camero è Reforma- tis refellit etiam hic Calvini, Parei, & aliorum sociennorum suorum glossas in respons. ad quæst. in epist. ad Ebr. pag. 389. Multa sunt, inquit, quæ obstant, quo minus hic Psalmus referri possit ad primam creationem. Illud primum quod con- tinet gratiarum actionem, atqui non est verisi- mile, Ecclesiam DEO gratias agere ob creatio- nem, tacito redemptionis opere. Deinde quibus beneficiis pii exciderunt, ea quoties commemorant cum gratiarum actione, toties agnoscunt miseriam, in quam sua culpa delapsi sunt, simul etiam petunt, ut in locum, unde dejecti sunt, restituantur, quorum nihil hoc Psalmo fit. Huc & illud accedit, quod Deus dicitur hoc Psalmo propagasse usquequaque tota terra gloriam nominis sui, id quod haud dubie non nisi ad Ecclesiam Judaeorum & gentium pertinet: Nam pri- ma creatione gloria nominis Dei non latius patuit, quam Paradisus, nondum enim erant alibi, qui no- minis Dei laudem celebrarent. Adde quod non qua- drant prima creationi illa verba ex ore infantium & lactentium &c, haec vero multo minus, propter eos qui tibi adversantur ad compescendum hostem &c. sed & illa ותחסרהו ἠλάττωσας αὐτὸν fecisti illum deficere, ad primam creationem nequeunt referri, no- tant enim, (si eorum propriam vim aestimemus) con- ditionis mutationem in pejus. Unde & apparet, quam recte LXX. Interpretes מעט verterint βραχύ τι & מֵאֱלֹהִים παρ᾽ ἀγγέλες illud, quoniam מעט ad tempus etiam refertur Os. I. 4. hoc vero, quia tota sen- tentia frigida foret & inepta, si אלהים Deum signifi- caret, quis enim putet, Prophetam voluisse hominem, vel in prima creatione fuisse summo Deo paulo inferio- rem. Deinde manifesta est antithesis, quae huc redit, ad exiguum tempus eum Angelis reddidisti defectiorem, at postea gloria & magnificentia coronasti eum. Reli- qua petantur è praelectionibus Tom. II. pag. 161. seqq. Matthias Polus in Synopsi Criticorum non tantum argumenta, quae produxeram adversus Rivetum & Grotius in AntiGr. produxit, sed conclusit etiam disputationem suam de quaestione illa celebri, ut vocat, an de Christo haec tantum accipienda sint verbis Cocceji: Religio est nobis, aliter hunc locum interpretari, quam Apostolus Ebr. II. 6. 7. Nam in Christo evidentius impletum est hoc oraculum. Coc- cejus tamen his per omnia calculum non meretur: siquidem visitationem Filii hominis de ipsa incar- natione explicet, quae vero consequens potius in- carnationis est, & accidit Filio Dei incarnato, in statu exanitionis constituto, de quo ipse: Is ergo minoratus est infra DEUM, quia non παρατηρητῶς gessit se pro Deo, qui erat: infra Angelos, quia factus est sub legem, infra homines, qui dicti sunt Dii, quia paruit illis, & ab iis se judicari passus est. Hinc dici- tur עֶבֶד מוֹשְׁלִים servus Principum Es. XLIX. 7. Neque dubitari facile potest, Christum, cum se cre- berrime & studiosissime in Evangelio appellaverit τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου Filium hominis, revocasse audito- res suos & lectores Evangelii ad hunc locum. Etsi postea relabatur Coccejus ad sententiam, quam è Ribera adduximus: Psalmum generatim loqui, ut ipsos fideles etiam complectatur, ut crucis Christi, ita jam gloriae ejus participes: Psalmum loqui de homi- ne, ut visitatus est à Deo, hoc est, de humana natura, ut in ea habitat divina, atque ita de Christo, eisq́;, qui sunt Christi, ejusque Spiritus participes. Atqui sic omnino aliter interpretatur, quam Paulus, quod religioni sibi esse dixerat. Paulus enim apodictice docet, uni Christo hoc convenire, atque inde de- monstrat Christi supra omnes Angelos, nedum supra omnes homines eminentiam, è gloria infi- nita ipsi communicata, quae nulli Angelorum, ne- dum hominum convenit, etsi fructus ejusdem in fideles redundet: Quod (de fructu,) non illic, de corona gloriae filii hominis Hiero-Psaltis agens docet Apostolus, sed postmodum tradit, cum Fi- lium hominis istum à DEO ideo per passiones con- summatum & coronatum docet, ut multos filios in gloriam adduceret. Quod ergo Coccejus ait, Apo- stolum demonstrare, hoc dictum non primo perti- nere ad quemvis hominem, sed de aliquo, per quem r fideles hoc regno potiuntur, in eo geminum sensum, primarium & secundarium occultat, sed contra ἀπόδειξιν Apostoli, qui non primo, sed unice de Christo hunc Psalmum loqui evidentissime docet; uti agnovit id nobiscum Camero.

## 2:7
Vers. 7. Ἠλάττωσας αὐτὸν βραχύ τι παρ᾽ Ἀγγέλυς. The Greek Interpreters took אלהים here as Angels, whose words are placed here: not badly. See Psalm XCVII. 7. Βραχύ τι מעט has one sense κατὰ πόδας, another κατὰ τὸ ἀλληγορούμενον as often. For taken in the former way it signifies a little: (for in intellect and a certain freedom of will, as Tatian explains, man is as it were equal to the Angels, in condition of body he is inferior) but taken in this latter way it signifies for a small time, in the way that word is taken in Hosea I. 4. and elsewhere.

Δόξῃ καὶ τιμῇ ἐστεφάνωσας αὐτόν. Adam in intellect, free will; Christ in most full knowledge of divine things, perfect will, admirable power. You crowned, that is, you adorned, from species to genus.

Καὶ κατέστησας αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τὰ ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν συ. Adam over the herds and cattle, as follows in the Psalm, as can be seen in Gen. I. 28. (concerning which dominion, now diminished but not entirely taken away, see Cyril in his epistle to Calosyrius against the Anthropomorphites and Isidore lib. III. epist. 95.) but Christ over the Angels. In these mystical places not all articles correspond to the mirror. See 2. Sam. VII. 13. 14. 15.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἠλάττωσας αὐτὸν βραχύ τι παρ᾽ Ἀγγέλυς. אלהים hic de Angelis sumpsere Graeci Interpretes, quo- rum verba hic ponuntur: non male. Vide Psalm. XCVII. 7. Βραχύ τι מעט alium sensum habet κατὰ πόδας, alium κατὰ τὸ ἀλληγορούμενον ut saepe. Nam illo modo sumptum signifi- cat pauxillum: (intellectu enim & quadam volendi liber- tate, ut Tatianus explicat, homo quasi par est Angelis, corporis conditione est inferior) hoc vero modo sumptum significat ad tempus exiguum, quomodo ea vox sumitur Oseae I. 4. & alibi.

Δόξῃ καὶ τιμῇ ἐστεφάνωσας αὐτόν. Adamum intellectu, voluntate libera; Christum cogni- tione plenissima rerum divinarum, voluntate perfecta, po- testate admirabili. Coronasti, id est, ornasti, a specie ad genus.

Καὶ κατέστησας αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τὰ ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν συ. Adamum super armenta & pecora, ut in Psalmo sequi- tur, ut videre est Gen. I. 28. (de quo dominio nunc immi- nuto non plane adempto videri potest Cyrillus epistola ad Calosyrium contra Anthropomorphitas & Isidorus lib. III. epist. 95.) Christum vero supra Angelos. In istis locis my- sticis non omnes articuli ad speculum respondent. Vide 2. Sam. VII. 13. 14. 15.

## 2:8
Vers. 8. Πάντα ὑπέταξας ὑποκάτω τῶν ποδῶν αὐτῦ. The same sense as in the preceding member. For to place someone over other things is to subject those things to him. This is also from the LXX.

It is very absurd that a double sense should be attributed to the same word, placed only once, which was also done by Schlichtingius, in that βραχύ τι denotes a little by reason of inferiority, and at the same time denotes for a small time, and thus is taken both quantitatively and discretively. That the word ἠλάττωσας designates diminution or inferiority regarding the faculty of intellect and freedom of will, and the condition of the body, and at the same time signifies the humiliation in the passion and state of κενώσεως of Christ; and likewise, that the crown of glory and honor is the intellect of Adam, and free will: and yet is at the same time the most full knowledge of divine things, free will, and admirable power of Christ. Who would admit such diverse senses of the same words in the same text? Furthermore, those things which, from the reason of the words and the context, and the interpretation of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament, are held as opposites, pertaining to a different state and time, as for instance one to the state of ταπεινώσεως of Christ, the other to the state τῆς ὑπερυψώσεως, are very rashly and perversely snatched away to the same state, and the same time, and the same condition of the subject. For thus Grotius took that ἠλάττωσας αὐτὸν βραχύ τι παρ᾽ Ἀγγέλυς concerning Adam in the state of integrity, as if equal to the Angels in intellect, and a certain freedom of willing, but of an inferior condition of body: And the opposite member: Δόξῃ καὶ τιμῇ ἐστεφάνωσας αὐτὸν, Grotius explained not concerning an opposite state or opposite sense, but likewise concerning Adam's intellect and free will in the state of integrity. Finally, it is ἀθεόλογον to restrict to finite gifts of knowledge, liberty, and power those things which the Apostle interprets concerning the glory which accrued after the emptying of Christ, by which He was made better than the Angels, and obtained a name or dignity of a more excellent lot, concerning the dominion of divine power; and to determine to a constitution over the Angels, and the subjection of certain things, those things which the Apostle, with the sacred Psalmist, accepted universally concerning the constitution over all the works of the hands of GOD, and the subjection of all things, against the most clear Pauline aphorism; he omitted nothing ἀνυπότακτον not subject, and thus to completely enervate that axiom, in which the force and nerve of the Apostolic argument consists. Moreover, it is too manifest that from the Apostolic context and the comparison of the passage Phil. II, the twofold state of Christ is described here, and what was κένωσις καὶ ταπείνωσις (emptying and humiliation) for the Apostle there, is ἐλάττωσιν (lowering) here; what was ὑπερύψωσις (exaltation) there, is στεφάνωσιν (crowning) here: and the little word βραχύ τι (a little) ought not to be accepted as referring to the smallness of the lowering, but to the duration of time, which indeed lasted for a short time ἐλάττωσις παρ' Ἀγγέλυς (lowering below the angels), as Origen, Athanasius, Chrysostom, and others among the Greeks, and then Augustine among the Latins, explain. Whence the blessed Gerhard rendered this sense thus: For a short time, namely during the state of emptying, especially in passion and death, you willed him to be lesser than the angels, and cast down below the angels, as much by the condition of mortality and passion, from which the nature of angels is alien, as by external liberation from sorrows and distresses, but that time was finished in the exaltation, in which he was crowned with glory and honor. This exposition is favored by v. 9, because the Apostle teaches that Christ was made lower than the angels not because he was made man, but because he sustained passion and death, because he says he was crowned with glory and honor through passion, not 'on account of' as the Vulgate wrongly has it. Which was done not only σχετικῶς (relatively) and relatively, insofar as his name is preached everywhere and he is adored by all, as some Calvinists wish, but ἀληθῶς (truly), really and truly, insofar as divine glory was conferred upon him for plenary usurpation according to his human nature, and he himself was made better than the angels, having obtained a name or dignity above every name, and was constituted over the works of the hands of the Lord, made Lord of all, Acts II. 36. Under whose feet all things are truly subjected. Moreover, that ἐλάττωσις παρ' Ἀγγέλυς (lowering below the angels) consists not only in the subtraction and interruption of the ordinary Angelic ministry owed to Christ the King, which the Hebrew phrase 'you made him lack' introduces, namely regarding the ordinary ministry of adoration and assistance, and the opposite στεφάνωσις (crowning), by which he was crowned with glory and honor παρ' Ἀγγέλυς (above the angels), whence before it he did not have that honor of Angelic ministry incessantly and indefinitely, even though he had a right over all angels, see Matt. XXVI. 53, c. IV. 11. Luke XXII. v. 43, where the Angelic comforting shows a lack of the use of Majesty exercised indefinitely over the angels, and thus a certain degradation of Christ below the angels: But also in the admission and toleration of Diabolical dishonor: A document of which occurs in Matt. IV. 1. seqq., where he tolerated temptation not only by reason of moral acts, but primarily also physical ones, by which he permitted himself to the power of Satan, so that he might truly take him up, move him from place to place, transfer him to Jerusalem, and place him on the pinnacle of the temple, etc. Furthermore, στεφάνωσις (crowning) is not a bare Φανέρωσις (manifestation), but a real ὑπερύψωσις (exaltation), done at the very divine throne before God the Father, to whom all things are always manifest, as the ante-secular glory δόξα was given to Christ, John XVII. 5. μεγαλωσύνη ἐν ὑψηλοῖς (majesty in the heights) chap. I. 3, the actual usurpation of Majesty, omnipresence, omniscience, omnipotence, and the axiom of adoration, which is μορφὴ τοῦ Θεοῦ (form of God) Phil. II. 6, and τιμὴ (honor) the same as the honor of the Father, 1 John V. 23, whence follows the subjection of all things. When, however, Christ is said to be constituted over the works of the hands of the Father, he is not said to have been made removed or distant from the works of the Father by any great interval, but rather near and intimate to the divine works themselves in a certain way: Thus, namely, just as the Father himself is over the works of his hands, who is not far from any one of his works, in whom all things are, Acts XVII. 27, 28, such a constitution the works of the hands of God the Father themselves require, which demand divine governance and presence. Through which constitution it came to be that Christ not only has his sheep in his hands, John X. 28, but also all things, John III. 35, so that now all things depend upon him as the first cause, and subsist in him, Col. I. 17, so that he is and remains ἐπάνω πάντων (above all) John III. 31, Eph. I. 21. Thus when all things are said to be subjected to his feet, divine power and presence is indicated. That phrase looks to the custom used by the victors of the Old Testament, who were accustomed to place their feet upon the necks of conquered Kings, Josh. X. 24, where lordly and victorious presence was shown. Thus all things are said to be subjected to the feet of Christ, so that it may be indicated that he is lordly present to all. But also parallel passages. For when Isa. LXVI. 1. & Matt. V. 35, the earth is called the footstool of the feet of God, and thus under the feet of God, this very thing is indicated, that God is as truly and really present everywhere on earth as he is truly and really present at the footstool of his feet, who resides on some throne. Therefore, to be under the feet of God denotes having God really present, as the blessed Dorscheus declared this excellently in this place. The Apostle brought forward this oracle of the Psalmist all the more willingly, the more it suited his comparison instituted with the angels, because he who had been lowered below them for a short time, having been raised above them and placed in charge of them, is constituted over all the works of the hands of the Lord, and is the master of all, with the future world also subjected to him, whose primary inhabitants are the holy angels, to whom the faithful elect are also to be added, as being those who will be ἰσάγγελοι (equal to angels) Luke XX. verse 36.

Νῦν δὲ οὔπω ὁρῶμεν ἀυτῷ τὰ πάντα ὑποτεταγμένα (But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him) He means this, that those words of the Psalm had no effect either in Adam or in any of his descendants except a slight one: wherefore something greater lies hidden in them. Αὐτῷ (to him), that is, to man considered generally.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Πάντα ὑπέταξας ὑποκάτω τῶν ποδῶν αὐτῦ. Idem sensus qui in membro praecedente. Nam impo- nere aliquem supra res alias, est illas res illi subjicere. Est & hoc ex LXX.

Perabsurdum est, eidem voci, semel tantum po- sitae, geminum, quod & a Schlichtingio factum, tribui sensum, utpote βραχύ τι notare pauxillum ratione inferioritatis, & notare simul ad tempus exiguum, adeoque accipi & quantitative & discre- tive. Verbum ἠλάττωσας diminutionem vel infe- rioritatem quoad facultatem intellectus & libertatem voluntatis, ac corporis conditionem designare, idemque humiliationem in passione & statu κενώ- σεως Christi simul significare; ac pariter, coronam gloriae & honoris esse intellectum Adami, & vo- luntatem liberam: & esse tamen simul Christi co- gnitionem plenissimam rerum divinarum, volunta- tem liberam, potestatem admirabilem. Quis tam diversos sensus earundem vocum admittat in eo- dem textu? Porro quae ex verborum, & contextus ratione, & Spiritus sancti in Novo Testamento in- terpretatione habentur ceu opposita, ad statum & tempus diversum spectantia, utpote alterum ad statum ταπεινώσεως Christi, alterum ad statum τῆς ὑπερυψώσεως, ea perquam temere ac perverse ab- ripiuntur ad eundem statum, idemque tempus & ean- dem conditionem subjecti. Sic enim Grotius illud ἠλάττωσας αὐτὸν βραχύ τι παρ᾽ Ἀγγέλυς accepit de Adamo in statu integritatis, quasi pari Angelis in- tellectu, & quadam volendi libertate, corporis au- tem conditione inferiori: Et oppositum membrum: Δόξῃ καὶ τιμῇ ἐστεφάνωσας αὐτὸν, non de statu op- posito aut sensu opposito, sed pariter exposuit Gro- tius de Adami intellectu & voluntate libera in sta- tu integritatis. Denique ἀθεόλογον est, quae A- postolus de gloria, quae post exinanitionem Chri- sti accessit, qua melior factus est Angelis, ac nomen vel dignitatem excellentioris sortis con- sequutus est, de dominio divinae virtutis in- terpretatur, restringere ad finitas dotes cognitio- nis, libertatis, & potestatis; quae de constitu- tione super omnia manuum DEI opera, & sub- jectione omnium cum Hiero-Psalte Apostolus universaliter accepit, determinare ad constitutio- nem super Angelos, & rerum quarundam subjectio- nem, contra luculentissimum aphorismum Pauli- num; nihil omisit ἀνυπότακτον non subjectum, & ita axioma illud, in quo vis & nervus argumenti Apostolici consistit, penitus enervare. Nimis autem manifestum est, è contextu Apostolico & collatione loci Phil. II. describi hic statum Chri- sti geminum, & quod Apostolo ibi fuit κένωσις καὶ ταπείνωσις, hic esse ἐλάττωσιν, quod ibi fuit ὑπερύ- ψωσις, hic esse στεφάνωσιν: neque voculam βραχύ τι de exiguitate ἐλαττώσεως, sed de temporis du- ratione accipi debere, quod nempe brevi tempo- re duravit ἐλάττωσις παρ' Ἀγγέλυς, ut cum Græ- cis, Origenes, Athanasius, Chrysostomus, alii; tum è Latinis Augustinus exponunt. Unde sensum hunc ita reddidit B. Gerhardus: Ad breve tempus, durante scilicet exinanitionis statu, præsertim in pas- sione & morte voluisti eum esse Angelis minorem, ac infra Angelos abjectum, tam conditione morta- litatis & passionis, à qua aliena est Angelorum na- tura, quam externa liberatione à doloribus & an- gustiis, sed tempus illud in exaltatione finitum est, in qua fuit gloria & honore coronatus. Cui expo- sitioni favet v. 9. quia Apostolus Christum non quod homo factus, sed quod passionem & mor- tem sustinuit, Angelis inferiorem factum esse do- cet, quia per passionem, non ut Vulgata perperam, propter, gloria & honore coronatum dicit. Quod factum non σχετικῶς tantum & relative, quatenus nomen ejus ubique prædicatur, & ab omnibus adoratur, ut Calviniani nonnulli volunt, sed ἀλη- θῶς realiter & vere, quatenus divina gloria ipsi ad plenariam usurpationem juxta humanam natu- ram collata est, & melior ipse factus Angelis no- men vel dignitatem supra omne nomen consequu- tus, & constitutus est super opera manuum Domi- ni, factus Dominus omnium, Act. II. 36. Sub cu- jus pedes vere subjecta sunt omnia. Consistit au- tem illa ἐλάττωσις παρ' Ἀγγέλυς non tantum in ordinarii ministerii Angelici, Christo Regi debi- ti, subtractione & intercissione, quam infert phra- sis Ebraica, carere fecisti eum, scilicet quoad or- dinarium ministerium adorationis, & auxiliationis, & opposita στεφάνωσις, qua παρ' Ἀγγέλυς gloria & honore coronatus est, unde ante eam non ha- buit illum honorem ministerii Angelici incessan- ter & indefinenter, utut jus in omnes Angelos ha- buerit, vid. Matth. XXVI. 53. c. IV. 11. Luc. XXII. v. 43. ubi confortatio Angelica ostendit carentiam usus Majestatis indefinenter in Angelos exerciti, adeoque degradationem quasi quandam Christi in- fra Angelos: Sed etiam in dehonestamenti Diabo- lici admissione & toleratione: Cujus documentum occurrit Matth. IV. 1. seqq. ubi tentationem tole- ravit non tantum ratione actuum moralium, sed imprimis etiam physicorum, quibus sese permisit potestati Satanæ, ut se revera assumeret, loco moveret, Hierosolymam transferret, & in fasti- gium templi collocaret &c. Porro στεφάνωσις non est nuda Φανέρωσις, sed realis ὑπερύψωσις, facta in ipso throno divino coram Deo Patre, cui sem- per sunt manifesta omnia, quà data Christo δό- ξα gloria ante-secularis, Joh. XVII. 5. μεγαλω- σύνη ἐν ὑψηλοῖς cap. I. 3. actualis usurpatio Majesta- tis, omnipræsentiæ, omnisapientiæ, omniopulen- tiæ, & axiomatis adorationis, quæ est μορφὴ τοῦ Θεοῦ Phil. II. 6. & τιμὴ honor cum honore Patris idem, 1. Joh. V. 23. unde sequitur subjectio omnium. Quando autem Christus dicitur constitutus super opera manuum Patris, non dicitur ab operibus Pa- tris maximo aliquo intervallo remotus aut distans factus, sed potius ipsis operibus divinis quadam ra- tione proximus & intimus: Sic scilicet, quemadmo- dum ipse Pater est super opera manuum suarum, qui non est procul ab unoquoque suorum operum, in quo omnia sunt, Act. XVII. 27. 28. qualem con- stitutionem ipsa opera manuum Dei Patris requi- runt, quæ postulant divinam gubernationem & præ- sentiam. Per quam constitutionem factum est, ut Christus non tantum oves suas in manibus suis ha- beat, Joh. X. 28. sed etiam omnia Joh. III. 35. adeo ut jam omnia ab ipso dependeant, tanquam causa prima, & in ipso subsistant, Col. I. 17. ut adeo sit & maneat ἐπάνω πάντων Joh. III. 31. Eph. I. 21. Sic cum omnia dicuntur subjecta pedibus ipsius, divina potentia & præsentia indicatur. Phrasis illa respicit morem victoribus Veteris Testamenti usita- tum, qui devictis Regibus pedes cervicibus illorum imponere soliti sunt Jos. X. 24. ubi Dominica & victrix præsentia ostendebatur. Sic Christo omnia pedibus subjecta dicuntur, ut indicetur, illum Do- minice omnibus præsentem esse. Sed etiam loca pa- rallela. Nam quando Es. LXVI, 1. & Matth. V. 35. terra dicitur scabellum pedum Dei, adeoque sub pedibus Dei, hoc ipsum indicatur, tam verè & rea- liter Deum præsentem esse ubique terræ, quam ve- re & realiter is scabello suorum pedum præsens est, qui in solio aliquo residet. Esse itaque sub pedibus Deum, Deum habere realiter præsentem denotat, ut hæc eximie declaravit B. Dorscheus in h. l. Ad- duxit autem eo libentius Apostolus hoc oracu- lum Psaltis, quo magis id conveniebat compa- rationi suæ cum Angelis institutæ, quod, qui in- fra eos brevi tempore minoratus fuerat, supra eos evectus, iisdemque præfectus, sit constitu- tus super omnia opera manuum Domini, & he- rus omnium, subjecto ipsi etiam orbe futuro, cujus incolæ primarii sunt sancti Angeli, quibus accessuri etiam fideles electi, utpote ἰσάγγελοι fu- turi Luc. XX. vers. 36.

Νῦν δὲ οὔπω ὁρῶμεν ἀυτῷ τὰ πάντα ὑποτεταγμένα) Hoc vult, illa verba Psalmi nec in Adamo, nec in quoquam ex ejus posteris effectum habuisse nisi tenuem: quare ma- jus aliquid in iis latere. Αὐτῷ, id est, homini generaliter considerato.

## 2:9
Vers. 9.

But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor) We see, that is, we know for certain from the report of Stephen and Paul, and from the effects of the kingdom which Christ himself had predicted, namely the mission of the Holy Spirit, the calling of the Gentiles, and other things. To see in this sense is used not only among the Hebrews, but among all nations. Βραχύ τι in this place is for a short time, as we just said. Jesus is adorned with the highest honor and power: For he presides over all creatures, both heavenly and earthly, as much as the use of the Church itself required. He interposes, however, διὰ τὸ πάθημα τοῦ θανάτου, so that he may connect the following things with it. That διὰ τὸ, however, signifies not only consequence, but something more, that is, that Jesus was worthy to be raised to such a height, because he had allowed himself to be brought low even to an ignominious death, for the sake of God. See above I. 9.

A new perversion again, and that a double one: (1) that the Apostle took the words of the Psalm concerning Adam and his descendants, or man considered generally. For in this Apostolic text there is no word had concerning either Adam or his descendants: And that pronoun ἀυτῷ must be referred entirely to him of whom the Apostle had spoken, that all things were subjected to him, so that nothing is left that is not subjected, which certainly cannot be taken concerning Adam, but solely concerning Christ, concerning whose state of ὑπερυψώσεως the Apostle treats by design. (2) As if the words of the Apostle sound concerning an effect that is not but slight, which in truth look to τὰ πάντα, or all things taken universally, not that all things are indeed subjected and only slightly, but that not yet are all things subjected. Therefore, there is no objection held here, as Estius wishes, but the Apostle continues in explaining the force of his demonstration, that in truth we do not yet see all things subjected to Christ, and so that this still remains, that those things which are not yet subject may one day be subjected, and finally it may be made manifest to all that all things are subject to Him. Lest, however, because we do not yet see all things subjected, we should hesitate in the application of the prophecy concerning the Messiah to Jesus of Nazareth, the Apostle therefore adds: But Him, who was made a little lower than the angels, the Hebrews had indeed seen or known concerning Jesus of Nazareth in his emptying and passion, we see Jesus crowned with glory and honor through the passion of death. For they had known that through the passion he had entered into glory, through the apparitions made after the resurrection, and the glorious ascension into heaven, as also the miraculous outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, which some had seen in part, but all had received from elsewhere from the eyewitnesses themselves, and had accepted, confirmed by signs and miracles. He says that this passion of death took place so that by the grace of God he might taste death for all, so that he may teach that the expiation of our sins was made through him, and may prepare for himself an approach to the explanation of the priestly office and the end of the incarnation. By the particle διὰ, the meritorious cause is not indicated, as Papists, Socinians, and some Calvinists contend, but the order divinely established, so that he would not enter into glory except through passion, Luke 24:16, 1 Peter 1:11, because the crown of glory was given to him freely, which is hinted at by the verb χαρίζεσθαι, Phil. 2:9; therefore that διὰ τὸ πάθημα is explained in the following verse by διὰ τῶν παθημάτων. The words should therefore be construed thus: We see Jesus crowned with glory and honor, having been humbled a little lower than the angels on account of the passion of death, or so that he could suffer and die, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for all.

PART III. OF CHAPTER II. Explanation of the congruity of the expiation made through the death of the eternal Son of God; WHICH IS SECTION II. OF PART I. OF THE EPISTLE, CONCERNING THE OFFICE OF CHRIST. MEMBER I. GENERAL.

Ὅπως χάριτι Θεῦ ὑπὲρ παντὸς γέυσηται θανάτε) It often happens that what follows refers to something that preceded, but not immediately. For the reason is rendered here not simply why Christ was exalted, but why through such grievous sufferings even unto death. For that could have happened otherwise. To meet this objection, he says it was done out of the singular goodness of God, (for that is χάρις, חסד) because indeed it was for the benefit of the whole human race, ὑπὲρ παντὸς for ὑπὲρ πάντων. A Greek idiom like εἶγε πῶς in Aristophanes. Γεύεσθαι θανάτε is to die, as Matt. 16:28, Mark 9:1, Luke 10:27, John 7:52. For χάριτι Θεῦ some codices have long had χωρὶς Θεῦ, which some Syriac codices follow here, and Ambrose, II. de fide ad Gratianum: Whence it appears that the blame for this altered scripture should not be cast upon Nestorius or the Nestorians. Those who changed it seem to have thought that Christ died even for the angels, and thus for all things except God alone.

The Apostle now proceeds to the priestly office of Christ. The particle ὅπως does not refer to the final cause, but rather to the manner, how the passion of death stands, namely, so that as a satisfaction, by which not for his own sake, but for ours, not for the sake of a crown of his own glory, but so that he might merit a crown of glory for us, he had to taste death, and willed to. And this not χωρὶς Θεῦ, without God, as Origen once read, Tom. I. in Johann., Ambrose, book II. de fide, cap. IV., book V. cap. IV., Theodoret, Theophylact, and Oecumenius in this place, which reading the Nestorians abused, dividing the person and excluding the Λόγον, the Son of God, from passion and death; but χάριτι Θεῦ, as the genuine reading has it, because it was done only by the grace of God that he, being innocent, died for us who are guilty, the just for the unjust, 1 Peter 3:18, and that God made him sin for us, who had not known sin, 2 Cor. 5:21. Conf. John 3:16. Rom. 5:8. That the gloss and Thomas think Christ is called the grace of God is from ignorance of the Greek language, in which it is not written χάρις but χάριτι, whence Ribera refutes it, explaining it as: by the grace of God, who wills to have mercy on all men. Ὑπὲρ παντὸς for EVERY. In which way both the universality of the merit of Christ, which the Calvinists deny, is built up, and the applicability to each one is hinted at, namely, that he tasted death not only for all, but also for individuals, or for each one of men, as the Syrian adds, for EVERY MAN. Whence the Apostle wished to use this expression ὑπὲρ παντὸς rather than say ὑπὲρ πάντων, not without emphasis. Conf. 2 Cor. 5:11, 1 Tim. 2:6, 1 Tim. 1:16, 1 John 2:2. The phrase to taste death also has emphasis, namely of perception and sense, that he tasted and felt the pains of death, not only by tasting the bitterness of death, but by tasting death most fully, and by draining that bitter cup which was set before him in his passion and death, the divine wrath, even though he greatly shuddered at it, so that he might satisfy for us all, and thus experience death not only temporal, but also eternal, not by reason of time, because that βραχύ τι contradicts it, but by reason of truth, namely that he was truly forsaken by God, and truly experienced infernal pains, Matt. 26:46, 27:46. Because unless he had also sustained infernal death, in our place, who were bound to taste and experience the same, he would not have tasted death, and thus we would not yet have been freed from hell and condemnation by his passion and death. Concerning this, thus the blessed Dorfscheus in Part I. Theol. Zachar. §. 194. cap. IX. There is altogether some difference between the tasting of death and its, so to speak, consumption: For just as those who taste something participate indeed in the substance of the food or drink tasted, but not as much as those who ὅλως eat and consume the whole: So those who taste death, of which at Heb. II. 9, they indeed participate in the same by reason of χάριτος, but they do not have everything which pertains to the whole, so to speak, dish of death. The verb γεύεσθαι is used with respect to death, Matt. XVI. verse 28, Mark IX. 1, Luke IX. 17, where without doubt it is understood of bodily death. But at John VIII. 52, γεῦσις θανάτου is of eternal death, which in v. 11 is called θεωρία θανάτου, namely of that death; whose immediate and principal author is Satan, who is called ἀνθρωποκτόνος, John VIII. 44, but Satan is not the immediate author of bodily death, but of the death of the soul. For he brought in the death of the soul immediately by the poison of his malicious persuasion. Namely, of that death, the remedy for which is faith, which he regards most especially, v. 45, and faith is most especially the instrument of healing the death of the soul. Namely, of that death in which they are who are of their father, the Devil, who perform the desires of their father, v. 44, but they are primarily to be considered as sticking in the death of the soul. Namely, of that death, the antidote to which is primarily ἀλήθεια, the truth of the heavenly promises, v. 41. But that primarily concerns the death of the soul torn away from its life. Namely, of that death in which they stick who are not of God, v. 47. But those who are not of God lie most especially in the death of the soul. Namely, of that death, the abolition of which is the primary and principal reward of τηρήσεως τοῦ λόγου τοῦ χριστοῦ, v. 51. But it is not the abolition of temporal and bodily death. Namely, of that

of death, which is something other than the death of Abraham and the Prophets. For the Jews interpreted the saying of Christ badly, because they understood that which He had said about the tasting of the death of Christ, verse 52, as referring to the natural dissolution of the soul from the body. There is, therefore, a death of the soul, the tasting of which is avoided by the solicitous guardians of the divine Word. The Syrian uses the word טעם, he tasted, he savored, and by metaphor he knew, felt, understood, experienced, tested, Psalm XXXIV. טעם Thargum, אשתמודעו know, Proverbs XXXI. v. 15. Although, however, not every tasting, of which mention is made in sacred writings, is distinct from the dotal and perpetual perception of the thing tasted, but sometimes tasting connotes the entire possession of the thing tasted: Nevertheless, in this place, Heb. II. verse 9, a distinction must be established. For there is a γεῦσις θανάτου (tasting of death) attributed to Him who was afterwards crowned with glory and honor, and was constituted Lord in act over all the works of the hands of the Lord, verse 7. To whom all things are subjected under His feet, verse 8, who is δι᾽ ὃν τὰ πάντα, καὶ δι᾽ ὗ τὰ πάντα (for whom are all things, and by whom are all things): Who is ἀρχηγὸς τῆς σωτηρίας (the author of salvation), who is διὰ παθημάτων (through sufferings), and thus also διὰ πάθημα τῆς γεύσεως θανάτου τελειωθεὶς (perfected through the suffering of the tasting of death), verse 14. Who is the destroyer of death and of Satan having the power of death, v. 14, which destruction 1 Cor. 15, verse 54, calls κατάποσιν (swallowing up and absorption), that is, abolition by metaphor. But he who is thus occupied with the γεῦσις θανάτου (tasting of death), he does not feel all the adjuncts and cognates of death perennially, but rather conquers and overcomes them. And that the discourse in this place is also about spiritual death, insofar as it consists in internal sorrows, and the horror of divine dereliction, and the sense of infernal pains, is clear from the circumstances of the text. For (1) Christ tasted that death also, which we, in our entirety, with all its evils and adjuncts, were bound to receive into ourselves. For it is ὑπὲρ παντὸς (for every one), verse 9. Therefore, the thing to be endured was not changed into another, nor was another substituted for it, but the delay of endurance on account of the infinity of the person, and the person Himself also, liable and guilty for the burdens to be endured, was changed, and Jesus was substituted for it, who stood in the place of the human race with respect to that death to be endured. Dan. Chamier in Panstrat. Cathol. l. 3. l. 24. cap. 12. n. 10. weighs that expression ὑπὲρ παντός, and fears that the interpreters who rendered it 'that by the grace of God He might taste death for all' did not sufficiently notice its force. For, he says, it is not in Greek ὑπὲρ πάντων (for all) in the plural voice, but in the singular voice ὑπὲρ παντός: Therefore I would prefer 'for each one' rather than 'for all.' Although it is true for all, but distributively, and ἀνὰ ἕνα ἕκαστον (one by one). Nor as an Emperor gives a donative to soldiers, much money to all, a little to each; but as the Sun offers the same light to all for each, and indeed in such a way that, even if the blind do not use it: Nevertheless, nothing remains over, from which any treasure could be accumulated. But let the matter be manifest from the celebration of the Eucharist, Luke XXII. 'This cup is that new testament in my blood, which is poured out for you,' Matthew XXVI. 'drink,' etc. He wishes the blood to be drunk: By whom? Namely, by those for whom it is poured out. Was it to be drunk in parts? Nay, the whole, which not even the Papists deny: Therefore the whole is drunk by each, therefore the whole is poured out for each, not the whole for all, drop by drop for each. Who then would dare to deny that the whole is applied to each? etc. Thus, I say, Chamier weighs this expression, but not sufficiently consistently with his own hypotheses. But they were liable to πάντος (every) not only of bodily death, but also to those horrible infernal pains and spiritual death, as is clear. That (2) death is understood ὅλως (wholly) by reason of its οὐσίας (essence), of which the Devil had the κράτος (power), v. 14. For it is said that Christ destroyed διὰ τοῦ θανάτου τὸν τὸ κράτος θανάτου ἔχοντα (through death him who had the power of death), where the same death and of the same magnitude is understood in both cases. But the Devil has the κράτος (power) not only of bodily death, but especially of spiritual death. Therefore, by suffering also the pains of spiritual death, by feeling the φόβον θανάτου (fear of death) and δουλείαν (bondage), verse 15, by enduring the πειρασμόν (temptation) of infernal pains, verse 18, Christ destroyed him who had the κράτος θανάτου (power of death). But indeed, if Christ felt the spiritual death of the soul by reason of the fiery darts and most penetrating arrows of infernal temptations, He altogether felt also that internal and greatest of all sadness. For how could a greater sadness arise than from the sense of that most sad object?

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Τὸν δὲ βραχύ τι παρ᾽ Ἀγγέλους ἠλαττωμένον βλέπομεν Ἰησοῦν διὰ τὸ πάθημα τοῦ θανάτου δόξῃ καὶ τιμῇ ἐστεφανωμέ- νον) Videmus, id est, certo cognoscimus ex relatu Stepha- ni, & Pauli, & ex effectibus regni quos ipse Christus præ- dixerat, nempe missione Spiritus Sancti, vocatione gen- tium, rebusque aliis. Videre hoc sensu sumitur non apud Ebræos tantum, sed apud gentes omnes. Βραχύ τι hoc loco est ad breve tempus, ut modo diximus. Jesus sum- mo honore ac potestate ornatus: Præest enim creaturis omnibus & cœlestibus & terrestribus quantum exegit usus Ecclesiæ ipsius. Interponit autem διὰ τὸ πάθημα τοῦ θα- νάτου, ut cum eo connectat sequentia. Illud autem διὰ τὸ non consecutionem solam significat, sed plus aliquid, id est, dignum fuisse Jesum qui in tantum eveheretur, eo quod se deprimi passus esset ad mortem usque ignominiosam, Dei causa. Vide supra I. 9.

Nova iterum perversio, eaque gemina (1) quod verba Psalmi Apostolus acceperit de Adamo & posteris ejus, vel homine generaliter considerato. Nam in hoc Apostolico textu nullum vel de Adamo, vel de posteris ejus habetur verbum: Et pronomen illud ἀυτῷ ad eum referendum omni- no, de quo dixerat Apostolus, ei omnia esse sub- jecta, adeo ut nihil relictum sit non subjectum, quod certe non de Adamo, sed unice de Christo accipi potest, de cujus statu ὑπερυψώσεως Apo- stolus ex instituto agit. (2) Quasi de effectu non nisi tenui verba Apostoli sonent, quæ vero re- spiciunt τὰ πάντα, vel omnia universim ac- cepta, non quod subjecta quidem omnia ac te- nuiter tantum, sed quod nondum omnia subjecta sint. Non ergo habetur hic occupatio, ut Estius vult, sed pergit in explicanda vi demonstrationis suæ Apostolus, quod revera nondum videamus omnia Christo subjecta, adeoque id adhuc restet, ut quæ nunc nondum subjecta sunt, olim subji- ciantur, & tandem omnibus patefiat, omnia ipsi subjecta esse. Ne tamen ideo, quod nondum omnia videamus subjecta esse, hæreamus in applica- tione vaticinii de Messia ad Jesum Nazarenum, ideo subjungit Apostolus: Eum autem, qui mo- dico infra Angelos minoratus est, quod de Jesu Na- zareno in ejus exinanitione ac passione utique vi- derant, aut cognoverant Ebræi, videmus Jesum per passionem mortis gloria & honore coronatum. Cognoverant enim, per passionem ipsum ingres- sum in gloriam, per apparitiones post resurrectio- nem factas, & ascensionem in cœlum gloriosam, ut & effusionem Spiritus Sancti super Apostolos miraculosam, quæ ex parte viderant nonnulli, omnes vero aliunde ab ipsis testibus oculatis ac- ceperant, & signis ac miraculis confirmata sus- ceperant. Quam passionem mortis factam dicit, ut gratia Dei pro omnibus gustaret mortem, ut ita expiationem peccatorum nostrorum per ipsum factam doceat, & ad Sacerdotalis officii explica- tionem, finemque incarnationis aditum sibi paret. Per particulam διὰ non causa meritoria indica- tur, uti Papistæ, Sociniani, & Calviniani nonnul- li contendunt, sed ordo divinitus constitutus, ut nonnisi per passionem ingrederetur in gloriam, Luc. XXIV. 16. 1. Petr. I. 11. quia gloriæ corona illi gratis donata, quod verbo χαρίζεσθαι innuitur, Phil. II. 9. ideo explicatur illud διὰ τὸ πάθημα vers. sequenti διὰ τῶν παθημάτων. Verba itaque ita construantur: Videmus gloria & honore coro- natum Jesum paulisper infra Angelos propter passio- nem mortis, vel ut pati & mori posset, humilia- tum, ut per gratiam DEI pro omnibus mortem gustaret.

PARS III. CAPITIS II. Explicatio congruentiæ expiationis per mor- tem ipsius æterni Filii Dei factæ; QVÆ SECTIONIS II. PARTIS I. EPISTOLÆ, DE OFFICIO CHRISTI. MEMBRUM I. GENERALE.

Ὅπως χάριτι Θεῦ ὑπὲρ παντὸς γέυσηται θανάτε) Sæpe fit, ut id quod sequitur, respiciat aliquid quod præcessit, sed non ἀμέσως. Ratio enim hic redditur non simpliciter cur Christus evectus sit, sed cur per tam graues perpessiones ad mortem usque. Potuerat enim id & aliter fieri. Huic objectioni ut occurrat, dicit id factum ex singulari DEI bonitate, (id enim χάρις חסד) quia nimirum id è re es- set totius generis humani, ὑπὲρ παντὸς pro ὑπὲρ πάντων. Græca loquutio ut εἶγε πῶς apud Aristophanem. Γεύεσθαι θανάτε est mori, ut Matth. XVI. 28. Marc. IX. 1. Luc. X. 27. Joh. VII. 52. Pro χάριτι Θεῦ quidam Codices jam olim habuere χωρὶς Θεῦ, quod sequuntur hic nonnulli codices Syriaci, & Ambrosius II. de fide ad Gratianum: Unde ap- paret non debere hujus Scripturæ mutatæ culpam in Ne- storium aut Nestorianos conjici. Videntur, qui id muta- runt, id sensisse, Christum etiam pro Angelis mortuum, atque adeo pro omnibus extra solum Deum.

Accedit ergo jam Apostolus ad officium Christi Sacerdotale. Particula ὅπως non causam finalem, sed modum potius refert, quomodo sese habeat passio mortis, ita scilicet, ut quid satisfa- ctoria, qua non sui, sed nostri causa, non ob pro- priæ gloriæ coronam, sed ut nobis gloria coronam promereretur, mortem gustare debuit, voluit. Idque non χωρὶς Θεῦ absque Deo, ut legere quon- dam Origenes Tom. I. in Johann. Ambrosius libr. II. de fide, cap. IV. libr. V. cap. IV. Theodorestus, Theophylactus, & Oecumenius in h. l. qua lectione abusi sunt Nestoriani, dividentes personam & excludentes Λόγον DEI Filium à passione & mor- te; sed χάριτι Θεῦ, ut genuina habet lectio, quia non nisi gratia DEI factum, quod ipse innocens pro nobis nocentibus, justus pro injustis mortuus est, 1. Petr. III. 18. quodque Deus eum fecerit pec- catum pro nobis, qui peccatum non noverat, 2. Cor. V. 21. Conf. Joh. III. 16. Rom. V. 8. Quod glossa & Thomas Christum vocari censet gratiam DEI, ab ignorantia linguæ Græcæ est, in qua non scriptum est, χάρις sed χάριτι, unde Ri- bera id refellit exponens, per gratiam DEI vo- lentis omnium hominum misereri. Ὑπὲρ παντὸς pro OMNI. Quo pacto tum universalitas me- riti Christi, quam Calviniani negant, adstruitur, tum applicabilitas ad unumquemque innuitur, quod nempe mortem gustarit, non solum pro omni- bus, sed etiam pro singulis, sive pro unoquoque hominum, uti Syrus addit, pro OMNI HOMINE. Unde non absque ἐμφάσει hanc loquutionem ὑπὲρ παντὸς adhibere potius Apostolus, quam ὑπὲρ πάντων dicere voluit. Conf. 2. Cor. V. v. 11. 1. Tim. II. 6. 1. Tim. I. 16. 1. Joh. II. 2. Phrasis gu- stare mortem etiam emphasin habet, perceptionis nempe ac sensus, quod dolores mortis gustarit ac senserit, non tantum delibando mortis acerbita- tem, sed mortem plenissime gustando, & pocu- lum illud amarum, quod ipsi propositum erat in passione & morte, ira divina, etsi valde id exhor- ruerit, sic exhauriendo, ut pro nobis omnibus satisfaceret, adeoque mortem non tantum tem- poralem, sed etiam æternam experiretur non ra- tione temporis, quia repugnat illud βραχύ τι, sed ratione veritatis, quod nempe vere à DEO de- sertus, vere dolores infernales expertus fuerit, Matth. XXVI. 46. XXVII. 46. Quia nisi etiam mortem infernalem sustinuisset, nostri loco, qui eandem gustare & experiri debebamus, mortem non gustasset, adeoque ejus passione & morte nos ab inferno & condemnatione nondum liberati essemus. De hac ita B. Dorfscheus in parte I. Theol. Zachar. §. 194. cap. IX. Est omnino inter gustum mortis & ejus, ut sic dicam, comestionem aliqua differentia: Sicut enim qui gustant aliquid, de sub- stantia quidem cibi aut potus gustati participant, non vero tantum, quantum qui ὅλως comedunt & totum absumunt: Sic qui gustant mortem, de qua ad Ebr. II. 9. illi vero quidem eandem ratione χά- ριτος participant, non vero omnia, quæ totum, ut sic dicam, mortis ferculum attinent, habent. Usur- patur verbum γεύεσθαι respectu mortis, Matth. XVI. vers. 28. Marc. IX. 1. Luc. IX. 17. ubi sine dubio de morte corporali intelligitur. At Johan. VIII. 52. γεῦσις θανάτου est de morte æterna, quæ v. 11. dici- tur θεωρία θανάτου, illius scilicet mortis; cujus au- tor immediatus & principalis est Satanas, qui di- citur ἀνθρωποκτόνος, Joh. VIII. 44. non autem Sa- tanas est immediatus autor mortis corporalis, sed mortis animæ. Is enim mortem animæ veneno suæ malitiosæ persuasionis intulit immediate. Illius scil. mortis, cujus remedium est fides, quam potissimum respicit, v. 45. fides vero potissimum est instrumen- tum medendæ morti animæ. Illius scil. mortis, in qua illi sunt, qui sunt ex patre suo, Diabolo, qui concupiscentias patris sui perficiunt, v. 44. illi au- tem sunt πρώτως considerandi, ut in morte animæ hærentes. Illius scilicet mortis, cujus antidotum pri- mo est ἀλήθεια veritas promissionum cælestium, v. 41. Illa autem πρώτως concernit mortem animæ avulsæ à vita sua. Illius scilicet mortis, in qua hæ- rent, qui non sunt ex Deo, v. 47. At qui non sunt ex Deo, potissimum in morte animæ jacent. Illius scil. mortis, cujus abolitio præmium est primarium & principale τηρήσεως τοῦ λόγου τοῦ χριστοῦ, v. 51. At mor- tis temporalis & corporalis abolitio non est. Illius scil.

mortis, quæ aliud quiddam est, quam mors Abra- hæ & Prophetarum. Malè namque sermonem Chri- sti interpretati sunt Judæi, quod de naturali solutio- ne animæ à corpore id intellexerunt, quod de gustu mortis Christi dixerat, vers. 52. Est igitur mors animæ, cujus gustus evitatur à solicitis Verbi divi- ni custodibus. Syrus usurpat verbum טעם, gusta- vit, sapuit, & per Metaphoram cognovit, sensit, intellexit, expertus fuit, tentavit, Psalm. XXXIV. טעם Thargum, אשתמודעו cognoscite Proverbior. XXXI. v. 15. Quamvis autem non omnis gustatio, cujus in sacris fit mentio, distincta sit à dotali & per- petua rei gustatæ perceptione, sed interdum gusta- tio connotet universam rei gustatæ habitionem: Ta- men hoc loco Ebr. II. vers. 9. discrimen est statu- endum. Est enim γεῦσις θανάτου illi tributa, qui postea fuit coronatus gloria & honore, & actuatis Dominus constitutus super omnia opera manuum Domini, vers. 7. Cui omnia sunt sub pedes subje- cta vers. 8. qui est, δι᾽ ὃν τὰ πάντα, καὶ δι᾽ ὗ τὰ πάντα: Qui est ἀρχηγὸς τῆς σωτηρίας, qui est διὰ παθημάτων, adeoque etiam διὰ πάθημα τῆς γεύσε- ως θανάτου τελειωθεὶς vers. 14. Qui est destructor mortis & Satanæ habentis imperium mortis v. 14. quam destructionem 1. Cor. 15. vers. 54. vocat κα- τάποσιν deglutitionem & absorptionem, hoc est, abo- litionem per Metaphoram. Qui autem ita ver- satur circa γεῦσιν θανάτου, ille non omnia mortis adjuncta & agnata sentit perenniter, sed potius illa vincit & superat. Et de morte etiam spiritua- li, quatenus in doloribus internis, & horrore dere- lictionis divinæ sensuque dolorum infernalium con- sistit, hoc loco sermonem esse, patet ex circumstan- tiis textus. Nam (1) Christus eam etiam mortem gustavit, quam nos totam, cum omnibus ejus ma- lis & adjunctis in nos recipere debebamus. Est enim ὑπὲρ παντὸς vers. 9. Itaque res toleranda non est mutata in aliam, aut alia pro illa substituta, sed mora tolerantiæ propter infinitatem personæ, & ipsa etiam persona oneribus tolerandis obnoxia & rea mutata est, & pro ea substitutus Jesus, qui ste- tit in locum generis humani respectu illius mortis tolerandæ. Expendit illam loquutionem ὑπὲρ παν- τὸς Dan. Chamier in Panstrat. Cathol. l. 3. l. 24. cap. 12. n. 10. & veretur, ut non satis ejus vim adverterint interpretes, qui reddiderunt, ut bene- ficio Dei pro omnibus gustaret mortem. Non enim, inquit, Græce est ὑπὲρ πάντων plurali voce, sed singulari voce ὑπὲρ παντός: Itaque malim pro uno- quoque, quam pro omnibus. Quanquam pro o- mnibus verum, sed distributive, & ἀνὰ ἕνα ἕκαστον. Nec quomodo donativum militibus Imperator, mul- ti æris omnibus, exigui singulis; sed quomodo Sol lucem eandem omnibus pro singulis præbet, & sic quidem, ut, etsi non utantur cæci: Tamen nihil superfit, unde ullus thesaurus cumulari possit. Sed res manifesta sit ex Eucharistiæ celebratione Luc. XXII. Hoc poculum est novum illud testamentum in sanguine meo, qui pro vobis effunditur, Matth. XXVI. bibite &c. Bibi vult sanguinem: A quibus? scilicet ab iis, pro quibus funditur. An bibi per partes? Imo totum, quod nec Papistæ negant: To- tum ergo bibi à singulis, totum ergo pro singulis ef- fusum, non totum pro omnibus, guttatim pro singu- lis. Quis ergo audcat negare, totum applicari singulis? &c. Ita inquam Chamier hanc loquutio- nem expendit, sed ad hypotheses suas non satis con- corditer. At πάντος non solum mortis corporiæ, sed etiam doloribus illis horrendis inferis & mortis spi- ritualis erant obnoxii, ut patet. Illa (2) mors in- telligitur ὅλως ratione suæ οὐσίας, cujus κράτος ha- bebat Diabolus v. 14. Dicitur enim Christum de- struxisse διὰ τοῦ θανάτου τὸν τὸ κράτος θανάτου ἔχοντα, ubi eadem utrobique mors & uniusmodi am- plitudinis intelligitur. Diabolus vero non corpora- lis tantum mortis, sed imprimis spiritualis habet κράτος. Itaque patiendo etiam dolores mortis spi- ritualis, sentiendo φόβον θανάτου & δουλείαν vers. 15. tolerando πειρασμόν dolorum infernalium, vers. 18. Christus destruxit κράτος θανάτου ἔχοντα. Atqui vero si Christus mortem spiritualem animæ ratione ignitorum spiculorum & sagittarum penetrantissi- marum infernalium tentationum sensit, sensit omni- no etiam internam illam & omnium maximam tri- stitiam. Quomodo enim major tristitia oriri posset, quam ex tristissimi illius objecti sensu?

## 2:10
Vers. 10.

Ἔπρεπε γὰρ ἀυτῷ, δι᾿ ὃν τὰ πάντα, καὶ δι᾿ ὗ τὰ πάντα) (For it became Him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things)

It was fitting, he says, for the wisdom of God. Πάντα (all things) here, as also in Rom. XI. 35, are to be understood as those things which pertain to our salvation. All those things are both governed by God, which is δι᾽ ὗ (by whom), and look to His highest glory, which is δι᾿ ὃν (for whom) in this place, and in that to the Romans εἰς ἀυτόν (to Him).

About to treat of the Priestly office, and initially of the καθαρισμῷ (cleansing) of our sins, the Apostle asserts before all else the fittingness of the divine ordination. Because it became Him, through whom are all things and for whom are all things, that He, who was about to lead many sons of God to glory, the author of their salvation, should be perfected through sufferings. Tὸ πρέπον (the fitting) is not only looked at in relation to divine wisdom, but also to divine grace, both of which appear here inscrutable, Rom. XI. 13. This πρέπον (fitting), however, is not to be opposed to hypothetical necessity. For many things are fitting which are also necessary. It was necessary from the hypothesis of the divine decree, insofar as He did not ordain that we be led to glory as His sons through any other than His Son. Therefore the Son of GOD, having put on flesh, not only had to suffer for us, and taste death, in order to restore salvation to us, or to acquire life by the merit of His passion and death: But also to be raised to that preeminence after the passion; so that he might lead us in act and efficacy to salvation: for which work divine glory was necessary. Which order was also most convenient for divine wisdom and grace, namely, that he who was to lead others through passion to glory, should himself after his passion be raised to that glory, by which he could bring it to effect, that we might be conformed to the same as in passion, so also in glorification, and that he himself by that reason also might obtain the first place among the brethren, Rom. 8:29. But there is no reason why τὰ πάντα here should be restricted to those things which pertain to salvation: since they can be understood universally, just as in a similar place, Romans 11:36, they are likewise understood not restrictedly, but universally. For God is the efficient cause of all things simply, through whom, and the final cause, for whom all things are, whatsoever they are. And Christ ought to have been constituted not only over those things which make for salvation, but over all things, as is evident from Psalm 8.
