Indeed, as the blessed Dorscheus rightly warned here, it pertains to the glory and majesty of our Priest to ascribe the origin of absolutely all things to him, so that he may be able to restrain and order all things, and whatever in any way might hinder his sacrifice, or be necessary for its fruit, by his supreme Dominion. For it befits the Leader of all the sons of God to glory, to be also the Lord of all creatures. For he can most rightly lead the sons of God to glory, through whom, and for whom all things so simply are, that they follow the guidance of his wisdom. But he, for whom and through whom all things are, is not Christ according to his human nature, as Rupertus understands in book XIII on Matthew, because from Christ according to That all things were not created for human nature, nor were all things created for his own sake, as Rupert contends that for Christ as man the Angels and the whole fabric of the world were created, is consistent with Scripture. Finally, Christ in his exaltation was passive and had to be perfected by God: and therefore God is designated, who perfected the same through passion, and his eternal constitution is regarded. Yet St. Athanasius understands all these things of the Son of God himself, and wishes to provide the reason why it was not fitting for any other than the Word of GOD to become man: For it became him, etc. Those words, he says in his work on the incarnation of the Word of GOD, Tom. I. p. 62, mean this: that it was not for any other to receive men from the corruption which had already settled upon them, except the Word of God, who had created them from the beginning. On this argument, the blessed Dorscheus speaks thus: This congruity is opposed by the judgments of some, both Gentiles and Jews, who thought it was clearly incongruous and inconvenient for a person of such Majesty to be subjected to such passions, and indeed to death itself, when it would seem rather to befit him, since he was to be crowned with Royal glory and dignity, that he should flourish in perpetual happiness and tranquility, and not suffer injuries of that kind. The Apostle answers to the contrary that it most became God not to act otherwise than in the way he did, because this matter was highly suitable to his purpose, and was the most appropriate means for achieving what he had intended in his mind. For it became him, who is the final end and first efficient cause of all things, and who works and performs all things through himself, to employ such means as are most adapted to the matter: namely, that it is fitting for the most wise to act most wisely, as Schlichting well speaks in this place. Thus, therefore, he turns himself at once to the death prior to the exaltation, and the καθαρισμὸν (purification) of sins made through it, so that he may gird himself for the proper treatment of the priesthood of Christ. Furthermore, that by this periphrasis δι’ ὃν τὰ πάντα, καὶ δι’ ὗ τὰ πάντα (for whom are all things, and by whom are all things), Christ himself is understood, the blessed Dorscheus proves in this place with these reasons in his Exeget. ad h. l. That 1. predicates are ordinarily referred to the nearest subject, and are not reduced to a remote one unless there is a grave reason. Since, therefore, the Apostle in v. 10 et seqq. has taken it upon himself to explain that it was fitting for Christ to taste death, he rightly says now in verse 10 ἔπρεπε αὐτῷ (it became him), namely, γεύσαντι ὑπὲρ παντὸς θανάτου (having tasted death for everyone). 2. That was the chief point of dispute among the Gentiles and Jews, how it is πρέπον (fitting) and congruous for the Savior preached by Christians to have tasted death. 3. The phrase and the series of the text are in no way repugnant to Christ. For 1 Cor. VIII. verse 6, Christ is said to be δι’ ὗ (by whom) he also made the ages. But to bring many sons to glory is the proper office of Christ, whose office it also is to prepare a place for us in the kingdom of glory, John XIV. verse 2. For the faithful are his sons as of the light, John XII. verse 6, as of the bridegroom, Matt. XIX. verse 15. And so the sense is this: It became Christ, through whom are all things and for whom are all things, while leading sons to eternal glory, and being moreover the Leader of their salvation, to be perfected through passions or to perfect his work. Which interpretation prevails very much among the ancients, and serves greatly to confirm the majesty of Christ, and indeed even dissipates the corruption of the Nestorians, who understood the Son of God by him through whom are all things and for whom are all things, but understood Jesus by the Leader of salvation, and thus constituted two persons in Christ, as Joh. Maxentius reports in book II of the Dialogue between a Nestorian and a Catholic, chapter 10. For all these eulogies and epithets are referred to one Jesus. For it was for this reason that it became Christ to perfect the work of salvation through passions received also in himself, and to complete the τελείωσιν (perfection) of the human race, which flows from thence, because he, although he is the supreme Lord of things, through and for whom are all things, yet because he is ἀρχηγὸς (the Leader) and Leader of salvation, leading the sons of GOD to glory, he had to take upon himself and overcome passions both for the sake of satisfaction and for the sake of example. For this most becomes a Leader, that the traces of battles and victories should appear in him. Nor do those words disagreeing in case from αὐτῷ (him) stand in the way. For (α) if you take the former explanation, a discrepancy of cases between ἀγαγόντα (leading) and αὐτῷ (him) must likewise be admitted, since it should be said, ἔπρεπε αὐτῷ εἰς πολλὰς ὑὸς ἀγαγόντι (it became him, leading many sons). (β) That diversity of cases in the sacred scriptures is not destitute of examples, which see in Glassius occurring variously here and there. That could also be said for the sake of removing the ἀνωμαλίας (anomaly), that those words should be ordered thus: It was fitting for him, through whom, as one leading many sons to glory and being the Leader of their salvation, are all things, and for whom are all things, that through passions received in himself he should put an end to his office and make satisfaction, so that the Apostle might thus seem to wish to remove the repugnance and inconvenience of the passions from the person of Christ, when he indicates that both concur in the person of Christ: both that he is the absolute Lord of all, the first efficient cause and the final end, and that he is the Leader and Author of honor and glory, to acquire and perfect which latter, passions were necessary. These are the words of the blessed Dorscheus.

Πολλὰς ὑὸς εἰς δόξαν ἀγαγόντα (leading many sons to glory) is an aorist in place of a present. And God is said here to have done what he had decreed to do, as Eph. I. 4, II. 6. Since he wished to lead not a few, but many men to salvation, he found a way both very useful to them and very glorious to himself.

Τὸν ἀρχηγὸν τῆς σωτηρίας αὐτῶν διὰ παθημάτων τελειῶσαι (to perfect the Leader of their salvation through passions) τελειῶσαι (to perfect) here is the same as just now εἰς δόξαν ἄγειν (to lead to glory). For that is the highest perfection of man. Thus below V. 9, VII. 28, XI. 40. In the Glossary, ἀρχηγὸς (Leader) is author. Thus Acts III. v. 15, V. 31, below XII. 2. Which cannot be, that those who devote themselves to piety should not suffer many evils, Sirach II. 1, Acts XVI. v. 21, especially in an age so corrupt, therefore GOD willed to lead the very author of the saving doctrine through nothing but grave calamities to that state of perfect beatitude, so that we too might bear adversities the more strongly, as things which the Son of GOD himself bore before us in the highest degree.

Let us admit that the aorist is used in place of the present. For Christ, the author of our salvation, is continually in the act of leading the sons of God to glory, and the divine decree was not that after he had led others to glory, he himself should be perfected, which is the explanation of some, but if the order of nature is regarded, that he should be perfected while leading the sons of God to glory, because by the virtue of both his merit and his intercession before God the Father, which he performs, sitting at the right hand of God, having been perfected through sufferings, he himself having been made the cause of salvation, leads us to eternal glory. These things follow one another in the order of divine decrees in the sign of reason, since eternal salvation has been ordained for us in view of the merit and intercession of Christ, even though both that redemption and that intercession of Christ our Mediator is later in time. For the Lamb of God was slain from the foundation of the world, Apoc. XIII. 8. and Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever, Heb. XIII. 8. Those phrases explain each other by way of epexegesis, 'bringing many sons to glory' and 'the author of their salvation,' and thus it is implied that just as Christ is the author of salvation by the merit of his passion, so he also actually leads the sons of God to glory, having been raised to the right hand of God and perfected in glory through sufferings. For he himself, the Prince of life, also willed to be slain for us, Acts III. 15, and after his sufferings entered into his glory, Luke 24, 26. For him, who was killed, hanged on the tree, GOD exalted the Prince and Savior, Acts V, verses 30, 31; who is also said to have been made the author of eternal salvation, Heb. V, verse 9, perfected forever, chap. VII, v. 28. Concerning whom Theophylact says: Furthermore, he insists on that statement which he had said above, 'You have crowned him with glory and honor.' But what he says is of this nature: he accomplished this by his own clemency, dignity, or this is evident. For he revealed the firstborn of all the sons, who are to enjoy his glory, as most illustrious beyond the rest through his passion, so that it may appear to all that one must strive entirely for that glory. He called him the Prince, the author and cause of salvation. Therefore, τελειῶσαι is not the same as 'to lead to glory.' For the latter belongs to the sons of GOD, but the former belongs to CHRIST, the Author of salvation, who leads the sons of GOD to life, and therefore had need of τελειῶσαι, which implies not a certain finite perfection, but infinite Majesty and power. For in order to lead others to salvation, divine virtue and power are needed, which can preserve them, defend them against the power of Satan, and finally, having freed them from sin, death, and corruption, raise them into eternal glory. Let us hear Theophylact again: Observe, however, how much we differ from him. For he is called the Son, and we are named sons. He bestows salvation, but we are made saved. We are, moreover, joined to him, and we are separated by another certain reason. For we are joined to him because he leads many sons to glory, and we differ in that he becomes the Author of salvation for these sons. The blessed Hunnius has it thus: The Apostle looks to that eternal counsel of God, by which, according to his good pleasure, he determined to restore all things also through that same one through whom all things are, namely through his Son, so that by this means he might bring back many sons into the glory once lost through Adam, and thus declare CHRIST to the human race as the most perfect Leader of salvation, victor and triumpher over death. It pleased the blessed Dorscheus to explain this τελείωσιν differently in his unpublished exegesis, namely as referring to sacrificial perfection: where he has this to say about this word: τελειῶσαι is either referred to the Prince himself, as an object that is to be consummated and perfected, or as to a principle that ought to consummate and perfect. If we choose the former, this will be the meaning: It was fitting for the Prince of our salvation to present himself to us as consummated and perfected through sufferings (indeed, redemptive, satisfactory, expiatory, and having the force of a ransom), not for his own person, as if earning something for himself thereby, but constituting a most abundant and copious price for the human race, and as the Apostle speaks below in chap. IX. 12, having obtained eternal redemption. If we choose the latter, this will be the meaning: It was fitting for the Prince of salvation, and thus also for our high Priest, to consummate our salvation through sufferings, as constituting himself a victim to God his Father, and illuminating it with the shedding of blood, or, to express the nature of the word more correctly from the character of the whole epistle, to perfect his priestly operation. For it is the proper and chief work of a Priest to τελειῶσαι, and this word is clearly priestly. What the blessed Dorscheus proved more laboriously concerning that word in part 1 of his Theol. Zachar. p. 191, with this sense rendered: Therefore, Τελειῶσθαι attributed to Christ denotes that he, as a most perfect sacrifice, and one most absolute in all respects, was offered to GOD the Father in his sufferings through a bloody constitution, and thus arrived at an admirable and most happy vision through his entry into the holy places. And indeed this concerning the perfection of the sacrifice of Christ

the exposition of the blessed Dorscheus might not seem unseemly. However, the explanation of the blessed Gerhard, approved in our Osiandrian Paraphrase and the Vinariean, pleases more: Concerning which he says thus: Piscator rendered it by 'to consecrate,' in which meaning this word is taken in Exod. XXIX. 10, to which can be referred the fact that Dionysius the Areopagite calls Christian sacraments 'perfections' (τελειώσεις) throughout. But to the Apostle in this epistle, the word τελειῶσαι always signifies to consummate; to render perfect, which meaning also fits this place. Which was also the interpretation of our blessed Hunnius. The meaning, however, is this: It was fitting for him, for whom are all things, as the ultimate end of all things, and through whom are all things, as the supreme efficient cause of all things, the Son of GOD, through whom the ages were created, inasmuch as he willed and ought to bring many sons to the eternal glory which Adam had lost, as the Author and consummator of their salvation, not otherwise than to be perfected through sufferings, and to be raised to that immense majesty of the right hand of GOD, for the sake of executing his office; where the congruence is regarded not of exaltation alone, but of exaltation through sufferings, by the intervention of the passion, by which he had to taste death for all men. For (1) τελείωσις, by which Christ is said to be perfected, does not easily occur in the sense of sacrificial consummation, but rather in that of the perfection of exaltation. Heb. VII. 28. (2) It concerns that perfection which Christ ought to attain according to his human nature, being constituted over all the works of the hands of God, to be crowned with glory and honor v. 7. (3) The office of Christ is indeed regarded, of that same Royal priesthood, but not properly the sacrifice of Christ himself as regards his perfection, since this perfection tends to this, that we may be sanctified through him, who would have a common origin with us, and he is not ashamed to call us his brothers, inasmuch as he is to be perfected and exalted for this reason. That Royal priesthood of Christ, even if it includes the passion and the tasting of death for us, is not completed by it; but it also required through the suffering the crowning and perfection of this our High Priest, so that we, who have been sanctified through the death of Christ, expiatorily and meritoriously, may be sanctified by Christ raised to the right hand of GOD, effectively and by way of actual efficacy. (4) The τὸ πρέπον of both of those things had to be taught: both that it was fitting that the Son of GOD Himself should suffer for us for the sake of satisfaction, and that He should be perfected διὰ παθημάτων for the sake of our salvation, so that as the ἀρχηγὸς τῆς σωτηρίας He might make us children of GOD and bring us into glory, not only by reason of merit, but also by reason of efficacy. (5) Such an ἀρχηγὸς τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν was required, who was both the supreme Author of all things, as true God, and with us ἐξ ἑνὸς from one Father, as true man, and our brother, so that as man He could undergo suffering, and as God, by His suffering, could satisfy for us and triumph over death. (6) The Son of GOD was therefore made a partaker of our flesh and blood, so that He might not only undergo death, but also destroy the Devil himself through death, and free us from the fear of death. Which is done ἱλασικῶς by Him in His satisfactory passion and death, and ἰδιοποιητικῶς, καὶ ἐνεργητικῶς in the actual application of that satisfaction, by which He makes the same proper to each of the faithful. For this is required in order that He may bring sons to glory. (7) Christ had need of this τελειώσει, not only by reason of His Kingly office, so that He might fully administer His dominion, but also by reason of His Priestly office, so that He might intercede for us eternally at the right hand of GOD as our High Priest. Which part of the Priestly duty the Apostle subsequently pursued more specifically. 8. Add that this congruence respects both the divine nature, the truth of the Leader of our salvation, and the sublimity of human nature, namely that it was fitting both that the true GOD should be ὁ ἀρχηγὸς τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν, and that He should also enjoy divine majesty, as true man, and that He should finally be raised to the plenary χρῆσιν of the same, so that He might be our Pontiff, shining at the same time with Royal dignity: Which both congruences the collation of the first chapter teaches are designated here. 9. The blessed Dorscheus himself also acknowledges this τελείωσιν of exaltation, and refers it to the consummation of the Priesthood of Christ, when he comments thus on chapter VII. 28: For when it is said εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετελειωμένον, it refers not only to the consummated sacrifice for the sins of the whole human race, of which it was said above c. II. 10. V. 9. but also to the state of glory, by which, after overcoming the emptying and sudden death, He was exalted above all things, and thus also to the eternal Priesthood τετελειωμένον. For even if the immolation and slaughter of the sacrifice was done ἐφάπαξ above v. 27, yet the dispensation of the sacrifice and the preservation of the sanctuary, and the governance of the priestly people must be continued until the consummation of the age Matth. XXVIII. vers. 20. cap. XXVIII. vers. 20.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Ἔπρεπε γὰρ ἀυτῷ, δι᾿ ὃν τὰ πάντα, καὶ δι᾿ ὗ τὰ πάντα)

Conveniens, inquit, hoc fuit sapientiæ Dei. Πάντα hic, ut & Rom. XI. 35. intelligenda ea, quæ ad salutem nostram pertinent. Ea omnia & per Deum gubernantur, quod est δι᾽ ὗ, & ad ejus summam gloriam spectant, quod est δι᾿ ὃν hoc loco, & illo ad Romanos εἰς ἀυτόν.

De officio Sacerdotali, & initio de καθαρισμῷ peccatorum nostrorum acturus Apostolus, ante omnia adserit convenientiam divinæ ordinationis. Quia decebat eum, per quem omnia & propter quem omnia, ut is, qui plurimos Dei filios ad glo- riam perducturus erat, author salutis ipsorum, per passiones perficeretur. Tὸ πρέπον non tantum di- vinæ sapientiæ respicitur, sed etiam divinæ gratiæ, quæ utraque hic apparet imperscrutabilis, Rom. XI. 13. Hoc πρέπον autem non opponendum ne- cessitati hypotheticæ. Nam multa decent, quæ et- iam necessaria sunt. Necessarium id erat ex hy- pothesi divini decreti, quatenus non per alium, quam per Filium suum constituit nos filios suos ad gloriam perducere. Ideo Filius DEI carnem indutus non modo pati pro nobis debuit, & mor- tem gustare, ut nobis salutem repararet, vel vi- tam passionis & mortis suæ merito acquireret: Sed etiam ad istam præeminentiam evehi post pas- sionem; ut nos actu & efficacia ad salutem per- duceret: Ad quod opus erat divina gloria. Qui ordo convenientissimus etiam ideo fuit divinæ sa- pientiæ, & gratiæ, uti nempe qui alios per passio- nem ad gloriam perducturus erat, ipse post pas- sionem suam ad eam gloriam eveheretur, qua id effectui dare posset, quo conformaremur eidem ut in passione, ita & in glorificatione, utque ipse ea etiam ratione primas inter fratres obtineret, Rom. IIX. 29. Cur autem τὰ πάντα hic restringren- da sint ad ea, quæ ad salutem pertinent, causa nulla est: quum universaliter intelligi possint, quemadmodum in simili loco, Roman. XI. 36. iti- dem non restricte, sed universaliter intelliguntur. Deus enim rerum simpliciter omnium & effici- ens, per quem, & finalis causa est, propter quem omnia sunt, quæcunque sunt. Et constitui Chri- stus debuit non super ea tantum, quæ ad salutem faciunt, sed super omnia, ut è Psal. IIX. constitit. Imo, ut recte hic monuit B. Dorfcheus, ad gloriam majestatemque Sacerdotis nostri pertinet absolute omnium originem ipsi adscribere, ut ita possit o- mnia & quoquo modo ipsius sacrificium impeditu- ra effent, aut ad illius fructum neceffaria futura supremo suo Dominio coërcere & ordinare. Decet enim Ductorem omnium filiorum Dei ad gloriam, omnium creaturarum etiam Dominum effe. Rectis- sime enim ille filios DEI ad gloriam perducere po- test, per quem, & propter quem adeo simpliciter sunt omnia, ut ductum sapientiæ illius sequantur. Is au- tem, propter quem & per quem omnia, non est Chri- stus secundum humanam naturam, ut Rupertus l. XIII. in Matth. intelligit, quia à Christo secundum Humanam naturam omnia condita non sunt, nec propter ipsum condita esse omnia, uti Rupertus contendit propter Christum hominem Angelos, & totam mundi fabricam conditam esse, Scripturæ consentaneum est. Denique Christus in exalta- tione passive se habuit, & à Deo perficiendus erat: ideoque Deus designatur, qui eundem per passio- nem consummavit, ejusque æterna constitutio re- spicitur. De ipso tamen Filio Dei hæc omnia in- telligit S. Athanasius, & causam reddi vult, cur non oportuerit alium quam DEI Verbum hominem fieri: Decebat enim eum &c. Verba ista, inquit de incarnatione Verbi DEI Tom. I. p. 62. hoc sibi volunt, non alterius fuisse à corruptione, quæ jam incubuerat, homines recipere, nisi Dei Verbi, quod eos ab initio condiderat. De hoc argumento ita B. Dorscheus: Opponitur ea congruentia nonnullo- rum judiciis tum Ethnicorum, tum etiam Judæo- rum, qui existimabant, incongruum plane & in- conveniens esse, tantæ Majestatis personam tantis passionibus, imo & ipsi morti subjici, cum potius illi congruere videatur, ut quoniam Regia gloria & dignitate coronandus fuerat, in perpetua felici- tate & tranquillitate floreret, nec ejusmodi patere- tur injurias. Apostolus contra respondet, maxime decuisse Deum, ut non aliter faceret, quam eo mo- do, quo fecit, propterea quod res hæc scopo illius ap- prime conveniret, & medium esset, ad quod ani- mum intenderat, assequendum accommodatissimum. Decere namque eum, qui est rerum omnium ultimus finis & prima causa efficiens, quique cuncta per se ope- ratur, & peragit, talia media adhibere, quæ maxi- me ad rem sint accommodata: Sapientissimum scil. sapientissimeque agere convenire, ut bene Schlichtin- gius hoc loco loquitur. Sic ergo simul ad præviam exaltationi mortem, & καθαρισμὸν peccatorum per eam factum sese convertit, ut ad tractationem propriam de sacerdotio Christi accingatur. Cæ- terum quod per istam περίφρασιν δι’ ὃν τὰ πάντα, καὶ δι’ ὗ τὰ πάντα, Christus ipse intelligatur, hoc loco hisce rationibus probat B. Dorscheus in Exeget. ad h. l. Quod 1. ad proximum subjectum ordinarie referantur prædicata, nec ad remotum reducantur, nisi gravis subsit ratio. Cum itaque Apostolus v. 10. seqq. exponere sibi sumpserit, quod congruum fuerit Christo gustare mortem, recte jam vers. 10. ait ἔπρεπε αὐτῷ scilicet γεύσαντι ὑπὲρ παν- τὸς θανάτου. 2. Id potissimum inter gentes & Ju- dæos disceptabatur, quomodo Salvatori à Christia- nis prædicato πρέπον decorum & congruum sit gu- stasse mortem. 3. Phrasis & series textus nihil re- pugnat Christo. Nam. 1. Cor. VIII. vers. 6. Chri- stus dicitur δι’ ὗ per quem & secula fecit. Mul- tos autem filios ad gloriam adducere officium Chri- sti proprium est, cujus etiam est locum nobis in regno gloriæ præparare Joh. XIV. vers. 2. Sunt enim fideles filii ipsius tanquam lucis, Joh. XII. vers. 6. tanquam sponsi Matth. XIX. vers. 15. Itaque sen- sus hic est: Decuit Christum, per quem omnia sunt & propter quem omnia, ducentem filios ad sempiternam gloriam, existentem insuper Ducem salutis ipsorum, per passiones consummari vel con- summare opus suum. Quæ interpretatio inter ve- teres quam plurimum obtinet, & ad majestatem Christi confirmandam maximopere servit, imo et- iam Nestorianorum corruptelam dissipat, qui per eum, per quem sunt omnia, & propter quem omnia, Filium Dei, per Ducem autem salutis Jesum intelle- xerunt, adeoque duas in Christo personas constitue- runt, uti refert Joh. Maxentius libr. II. Dial. inter Nestor. & Catholicum cap. 10. Nam ad unum Je- sum ista elogia & epitheta omnia referuntur. Ideo enim decuit Christum per passiones in se quoque re- ceptas opus salutis consummare, & generis humani τελείωσιν, quæ exinde promanat, perficere, quia ille, quamvis sit summus rerum Dominus, per & pro- pter quem omnia, quia tamen est ἀρχηγὸς & Dux salutis, filios DEI ad gloriam deducens, passiones cum satisfactionis tum exempli causa in se suscipe- re & vincere debuit. Hoc enim maxime Ducem de- cet, ut in ipso vestigia præliorum & victoriarum compareant. Nec obstat, verba ista casu discrepare ab αὐτῷ. Nam (α) si priorem explicationem affu- mas, itidem discrepantia casuum inter ἀγαγόντα & αὐτῷ admittenda est, cum dicendum, ἔπρεπε αὐ- τῷ εἰς πολλὰς ὑὸς ἀγαγόντι. (β) Ista casuum di- versitas in sacris literis non destituta est exemplis, quæ vide apud Glassium varie hinc inde occurrentia. Pos- set & illud tollendæ ἀνωμαλίας causa dici, verba illa ita ordinanda esse: Decorum fuit ipsi, per quem, utpote multos filios ad gloriam deducentem & Du- cem existentem salutis ipsorum, sunt omnia, & pro- pter quem sunt omnia, ut per passiones in se receptas finem imponeret officio suo & satisfaceret, ut adeo Apostolus hoc ipso repugnantiam & inconvenien- tiam passionum à persona Christi amoliri velle vi- deri possit, cum indicat, in persona Christi concur- rere utraque, & quod sit absolutus omnium Domi- nus, causa prima efficiens & ultimus finis, & quod sit Dux & Autor honoris & gloriæ, ad quod po- sterius acquirendum & perficiendum passionibus opus fuerit. Hæc B. Dorscheus.

Πολλὰς ὑὸς εἰς δόξαν ἀγαγόντα) Est ἀόριστ. vice Præ- sentis. Et dicitur hic Deus fecisse, quod facere decreverat, ut Eph. I. 4. II. 6. Cum non paucos, sed multos homines ad salutem vellet perducere, rationem reperit & ipsis per- utilem & sibi pergloriosam.

Τὸν ἀρχηγὸν τῆς σωτηρίας αὐτῶν διὰ παθημάτων τελειῶσαι) τελειῶσαι hic idem est, quod modo εἰς δόξαν ἄγειν. Ea enim summa est hominis perfectio. Sic infra V. 9. VII. 28. XI. 40. In Glossario ἀρχηγὸς autor. Sic Act. III. v. 15. V. 31. infra XII. 2. Qui fieri non potest, ut qui se pietati dedunt, non multa mala patiantur, Sirach. II. 1. Act. XVI. v. 21. seculo præsertim adeo corrupto, ideo DEUS voluit ipsum autorem salutiferæ doctrinæ non nisi per graves cala- mitates perducere ad statum illum perfectæ beatitudinis, ut & nos eo fortius ferremus adversa, ut quæ ante nos in sum- mo gradu pertulerit ipse DEI Filius.

Admittamus ἀόριστον vice præsentis adhiberi. Continuo enim in eo est Christus salutis nostræ ἀρχηγὸς, ut filios DEI ad gloriam perducat, & decretum divinum erat, non ut postquam perdu- xerit ad gloriam alios, ipse consummaretur, quæ nonnullorum est explicatio, sed si respiciatur naturæ ordo, ut consummaretur perducens ad gloriam filios Dei, quia virtute & meriti & inter- cessionis suæ apud Deum Patrem, quam peragit, sedens ad dextram Dei, consummatus per passio- nes, ipse causa salutis factus est, perducit nos ad æternam gloriam. Quæ in ordine decretorum divinorum in signo rationis sese consequuntur, quum intuitu meriti & intercessionis Christi nobis ordinata sit æterna salus, etsi & redemptio, & in- tercessio illa CHRISTI Mediatoris nostri tempo- re posterior sit. Nam agnus DEI occisus est ab origine mundi, Apoc. XIII. 8. & Jesus Christus he- ri, hodie, idem & in secula, Ebr. XIII. 8. Explicant se mutuo κατ' ἐπεξήγησιν illa, adducens filios mul- tos ad gloriam, & ἀρχηγὸς salutis ipsorum, adeo- que innuitur, uti Christus merito passionis suæ est ἀρχηγὸς salutis: ita eundem etiam actu filios Dei ad gloriam perducere, evectum ad dextram Dei, & consummatum gloriâ per passiones. Nam ipse Dux vitæ & pro nobis occidi voluit, Act. III. 15. & post passiones suas intravit in gloriam, Luc. 24, 26. Illum enim, qui interemptus est, suspensus in ligno, Αρχηγὸν Principem & Salvatorem exal- tavit DEUS dextra sua Actor. V. vers. 30. 31. qui factus etiam dicitur ἄιτιον σωτηρίας ἀιωνίς Ebr. V. vers. 9. εἰς τὸν ἀιῶνα τετελειωμένον, cap. VII. v. 28. De quo Theophylactus: Adhæc dicto illi insistit, quod superius dixerat, gloria & honore coronasti eum. Quod autem dicit, tale est, pro sua clemen- tia dignitate, vel hoc patet, effecit. Quippe qui primogenitum omnium filiorum, qui ejus sunt glo- ria fruituri, præ cæteris clarissimum ex passione patefecit, ut cunctis appareat esse omnino pro ea gloria decertandum. Αρχηγὸν autem salutis auto- rem & causam dixit. Non ergo idem est τελειῶ- σαι, quod εἰς δόξαν ἄγειν. Nam hoc est filiorum DEI, illud vero est CHRISTI, Autoris salutis, qui ducit filios DEI ad vitam, atque ideo τελει- ῶσαι opus habuit, quæ non finitam quandam per- fectionem, sed infinitam Majestatem ac virtu- tem infert. Nam ut alios ad salutem perducat, divina virtute opus est ac potentia, quæ eosdem conservare, adversus potestatem Satanam tueri, & tandem liberatos à peccato, morte & corru- ptione in æternam gloriam evehere possit. Au- diamus iterum Theophylactum: Adverte autem, quantum ipsi ab illo distemus. Nam Filius qui- dem is dicitur, & nos filii nuncupamur. Salutem ille largitur, nos vero salvi efficimur. Sumus præterea & illi conjuncti, & alia quadam ratione disjungi- mur. Illi namque ideo copulamur, quia multos filios traducit ad gloriam, & eo distamus, quia filio- rum fit salutis hic Autor. B. Hunnius ita habet: Respicit Apostolus ad æternum illud consilium Dei, quo juxta beneplacitum suum constituit, per eun- dem illum, per quem sunt omnia, nempe per Fili- um suum, instaurare etiam omnia, ut hoc medio multos filios in gloriam per Adamum olim amis- sam reduceret, atque sic CHRISTUM, tan- quam perfectissimum Ducem salutis, victorem & triumphatorem contra mortem humano generi de- clararet. B. Dorscheo placuit τελείωσιν hanc ali- ter explicare in ἐξηγήσει ἀνεκδότῳ, nimirum de perfectione sacrificiali: ubi ita de hoc verbo ha- bet: τελειῶσαι vel refertur ad ipsum ἀρχηγὸν, tan- quam objectum, quod consummandum & perfici- endum est, vel tanquam ad principium, quod con- summare & perficere debet. Si prius eligamus, hæc erit sententia: Oportuit Principem salutis nostræ seipsum ita nobis sistere, tanquam per passiones (utique redemptorias, satisfactorias, expiatorias, & ἀντιλύτρα vim habentes) consummatum & perfectum, non pro sua persona, tanquam sibi exin- de aliquid promerente, sed pro genere humano a- bundantissimum, & copiosissimum pretium consti- tuentem, & ut infra cap. IX. 12. Apostolus loqui- tur ἀιωνίαν λύτρωσιν εὑράμενον. Si posterius eli- gamus, hæc erit sententia: Decebat Principem sa- lutis, adeoque etiam summum Sacerdotem nostrum, per passiones, tanquam victimam ipsum Deo Patri suo constituentes, & sanguinis profusione collustran- tes consummare salutem nostram, vel ut naturam verbi ex totius epistolæ indole rectius exprimamus, sacerdotalem suam operationem perficere. Est enim Sacerdotis proprium, & præcipuum opus τελειῶσαι, & hoc verbum plane Sacerdotale est. Quæ de ver- bo illo B. Dorscheus operosius probavit part. 1. Theol. Zachar. p. 191. reddito hoc sensu: Τελειῆ- σθαι ergo Christo tributum notat, illum ceu sacrifi- cium perfectissimum, & omnibus numeris absolu- tissimum in passionibus DEO Patri per cruentam σύστασιν oblatum esse, atque ita ad admirandam feli- cissimamque ἐπωπτίαν per εἴσοδον εἰς τὰ ἅγια perve- nisse. Et sane hæc de τελειώσει sacrificii Christi

B. Dorschei ἔκθεσις non inconcinna videri queat. Placet tamen magis explicatio B. Gerhardi no- stro, Paraphrasi Osiandrina, ac Vinariensi compro- bata: Qua de ille ita: Piscator reddidit per confe- crare, in qua significatione accipitur hoc verbum Exod. XXIX. 10. quo referri potest, quod Dionysius Areopag. sacramenta Christiana passim vocat τε- λειώσεις. Sed Apostolo in hac epistola verbum τελει- ῶσαι semper significat consummare; perfectum red- dere, quæ significatio etiam huic loco congruit. Quæ etiam B. Hunnii nostri fuit interpretatio. Sensus autem hic est: Decebat autem ipsum, propter quem omnia, ceu finem ultimum rerum omnium, & per quem omnia, ceu causam efficientem supremam o- mnium, Filium DEI, per quem secula condita sunt, utpote qui volebat & debebat multos filios ad gloriam æternam, quam Adam perdiderat, addu- cere, tanquam Autorem & consummatorem salutis ipsorum, non aliter quam per passiones perfici, & ad immensam illam majestatem dextræ DEI eve- hi, officii sui exequendi causa; ubi congruentia respicitur non exaltationis solius, sed exaltatio- nis διὰ παθημάτων interveniente passione, qua pro omnibus hominibus mortem gustare debuit, adeun- dæ. Nam (1) τελείωσις, qua Christus perfici dicitur, non facile de consummatione sacrificali, magis autem de perfectione exaltationis occurrit. Ebr. VII. 28. (2) De ea τελειώσει agitur, quam Christus secundum humanam naturam consequi debeat, constituendus super omnia opera manuum Dei, co- ronandus gloria & honore v. 7. (3) Respicitur qui- dem officium Christi, sacerdotii ejusdem Regalis, non autem proprie sacrificium ipsummet Christi quoad τελείωσιν suam, quum hæc τελείωσις eo ten- dat, ut sanctificemur per eum, qui nobiscum com- munem haberet originem, nosque non veretur fra- tres suos vocare, utpote ideo perficiendum & exal- tandum. Sacerdotium autem illud Regale Chri- sti, etsi passionem, & mortis γεῦσιν pro nobis in- cludat, eâ tamen non absolvitur; sed requirebat etiam διὰ τὸ πάθημα ςεφάνωσιν, καὶ τελείωσιν hu- jus nostri Pontificis, ut, qui sanctificati per mor- tem Christi sumus, ἱλασικῶς expiatoriè, ac meri- torie, sanctificemur à Christo ad dextram DEI evecto ἐνεργητικῶς applicatorie, ac ratione effica- ciæ actualis. (4) Utriusque illius τὸ πρέπον docen- dum erat: & quod congruum fuerit, ut patere- tur pro nobis ipse DEI Filius satisfactionis causa, & ut διὰ παθημάτων idem perficeretur, nostræ sa- lutis gratia, ut tanquam ἀρχηγὸς τῆς σωτηρίας nos filios DEI efficeret, & in gloriam adduceret, non tantum ratione meriti, sed etiam ratione efficaciæ. (5) Requirebatur talis ἀρχηγὸς τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν, qui & omnium rerum Autor summus, ut- pote verus Deus, & nobiscum ἐξ ἑνὸς ab uno Patre qua verus homo, & frater noster esset, ut qua ho- mo passionem subire, qua Deus passione sua pro nobis satisfacere, ac de morte triumphare posset. (6) Filius DEI ideo particeps factus est carnis & sanguinis nostri, ut non tantum mortem sub- ire posset, sed etiam Diabolum ipsum per mortem destrueret, nosq; à timore mortis liberaret. Quod & ἱλασικῶς ab ipso in passione & morte satisfa- ctoria factum, & ἰδιοποιητικῶς, καὶ ἐνεργητικῶς in satisfactionis istius actuali applicatione fit, qua eandem unicuique fidelium propriam facit. Hoc enim requiritur ad id, ut filios ad gloriam addu- cat. (7) Hâc τελειώσει opus fuit Christo, non tantum ratione officii Regii, ut plene dominium suum administraret, sed etiam ratione officii Sa- cerdotalis, ut ad dextram DEI pro nobis æter- num ut Pontifex noster interpellaret. Quam mu- neris Sacerdotalis partem specialius postmodum persequutus est Apostolus. 8. Adde quod congru- entia illa respiciat cum natura divina, Ducis sa- lutis nostrae veritatem, tum humana natura sub- limitatem, quod nempe convenerit, & ut verus DEUS esset ὁ ἀρχηγὸς τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν, & ut majestate divina gauderet quoque, ut verus homo, & ad ejusdem etiam tandem plenariam χρῆσιν eveheretur, ut Pontifex noster. esset, si- mul Regia coruscans dignitate: Quam utram- que congruentiam hic designari collatio capi- tis primi docet. 9. Agnoscit hanc τελείωσιν ex- altationis etiam ipse Beatus Dorscheus, eamque refert ad consummationem Sacerdotii Christi, quando ad cap. VII. 28. ita commentatur: Nam cum dicitur εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετελειωμένον non tantum ad consummatum sacrificium pro peccatis totius gene- ris humani respicitur, de quo dictum est supr. c. II. 10. V. 9. sed etiam ad statum gloriae, quo post supera- tam exanitionem & mortem subitam exaltatus est super omnia, adeoque etiam ad aeternum Sacer- dotium τετελειωμένον. Etiamsi enim immolatio, & mactatio sacrificii facta sit ἐφάπαξ supr. v. 27. dispensatio tamen sacrificii & sanctuarii conserva- tio, & populi sacerdotalis gubernatio continuanda est usque ad consummationem seculi Matth. XIIX. vers. 20. cap. XXIXX. vers. 20.

## 2:11
Vers. 11. Ὅτε γὰρ ἁγιάζων καὶ οἱ ἁγιαζόμενοι ἐξ ἑνὸς πάντες) Christ makes us holy by His doctrine and example. He was conceived of the Holy Spirit, and we obtain a new nature through the Holy Spirit: Thus we have a common origin. That the origin from Adam is not looked at here is shown by what follows. Thus the Pontiff of the Hebrews was no less from Jacob than was the people who were expiated through him. Ἁγιάζων in this book is referred sometimes to that legal purity, sometimes to the true and internal one, of which that was an image. That Eis, however, is rightly explained of God is shown by the passages John VIII. 41. 1. Cor. VIII. 6. Gal. III. 20.

Δι' ἧν αἰτίαν οὐκ ἐπαισχύνεται ἀδελφοὺς αὐτοὺς καλεῖν) That appears in Matth. XXVIII. 10. And it is well said, He is not ashamed of him, who, being greater, associates himself with the lesser. You have a similar way of speaking below XI. 16.

By him who sanctifies, some, even among our own, the blessed Gerhard, understand the Pontiff of the Old Testament, so that a comparison may be instituted with him, which the late lamented explains thus: Just as the Levitical high Priest sanctifying the people through sacrifices, and the Israelitic people sanctified by the Priest are from one, either the first parent of the human race or the Patriarch Jacob, the stock of the Israelitic people, or from the same human nature: So CHRIST, the unique Priest of the New Testament, and the believers, the sons of God, have sprung from one parent, GOD. For the scope of the Apostle is to prove that it was fitting for God to consummate His Son through sufferings. He proves that from the fact that Christ was constituted by God as the unique high Priest of the New Testament, who by offering a sacrifice would sanctify, that is, cleanse from sins, and reconcile the human race to God. But the sanctifying Priest and the people who are sanctified are from one, participants of the same human nature. Therefore the Son of God also had to assume human nature, and that indeed subject to sufferings, such as other men have. But here the sign of comparison is missing, and the Apostle has not yet embarked upon a comparison with the Pontiff of the Old Testament. Moreover, the force of the Apostolic argument according to some is this: therefore also the author of our salvation is consummated after suffering, or by the intervention of the same, so that the sons of God may be led to salvation through sufferings, because he himself is of the same origin with the sons, acknowledging one author with us. The blessed Hunnius connects these with the preceding ones thus: Since those who sanctify and those who are sanctified are all from one, that is, because Christ has constituted Himself to redeem and sanctify us from sins, and that could not be done unless the price of redemption were interposed, therefore it was necessary that he who sanctifies and we who are to be sanctified should be from one, that is, participants of the same nature. Therefore He also assumed our nature, nor is He ashamed or does He consider it base to call us His brothers because of that admirable fellowship and communion of the same flesh and blood. Therefore Grotius indeed rightly understands Christ by him who sanctifies us, but Christ does not sanctify only by doctrine and example, but especially also by merit and the efficacy of operation through the word and Sacraments as the means of sanctification. Therefore He sanctified Himself for us in passion and death, that we might be sanctified in truth John XVII. vers. 19. But Grotius does not well refer these to the comparison of the conception of Christ from the Holy Spirit, which was done so that without the congress of a man He might conceive the Son of God in the womb of the Θεοτόκῳ by the miraculous operation of the Holy Spirit, and of our regeneration and renewal, by which we obtain a new nature through the Holy Spirit, so that he may teach that we thus have a common origin. For that origin is of the humanity of Christ, as to nature, of which the Holy Spirit was the author and δημιουργὸς. But to this does not correspond the origin of our regeneration, according to which we certainly do not obtain another substance or nature, or finally receive being, but when we have been born flesh from flesh, we are regenerated from God. A common origin is therefore looked at not so much from Adam as from God, as the Greek Interpreters explain, because Christ was not born man by the virtue of the blessing made to Adam before the fall, but by the virtue of the promise made after the fall concerning the seed of the woman, which procreation happened not according to the order of nature, but according to the οἰκονομίαν and dispensation of divine grace. Theophylact in his paraphrase refers it to the Son of God, in respect of the eternal generation by which He is from the Father. For when, he says, the sanctifier, that is Christ, and the sanctified, namely we ourselves, are all from one, that is, from the Father, as He is the Son, we as created. He therefore bestows holiness, we are made holy. Whence it happens that an identity intervenes, and excellence is demonstrated. But here it is a question of Christ according to human nature. For here he regards both the birth of Christ and our own bodily birth, and confirms our ὁμοουσία [consubstantiality] with Christ, concerning which the Apostle further discourses: because he calls us his brothers on account of the same origin from God, and not indeed because of spiritual regeneration and conception from the Holy Spirit. For although the conception of Christ was brought about by the power of the divine promise and the operation of the Holy Spirit; yet because the Holy Spirit fashioned the human nature from the substance of the mother, the Virgin Mary, which the Son of God assumed into his own hypostasis, therefore he is ὁμοούσιος [consubstantial] to us, and does not doubt or blush to call us his brothers, Matt. XXVIII. verse 10. Which the Apostle now further confirms from the Old Testament. Concerning which Theophylact himself: For where he enters into flesh here, he has both entered into brotherhood with us, and put it on. Whence also the brotherhood itself comes together into one. Theodoret on this passage. He who sanctifies, and they who are sanctified, are all of one. He placed this also with regard to humanity. For the nature which was assumed was created. But there is one Creator and maker both of him and of us. But through that [nature] we are sanctified. But if the heretics may wish to understand this also concerning human nature, not even this will detract anything from the glory of the Only-Begotten. For he says, we and he both have one Father, but it is clear that he is indeed the Son by nature, but we by grace. For he teaches us this difference, that he indeed sanctifies us, but we are sanctified. Thus Theodoret: Furthermore, he who notes the emphasis in the word ἐπαισχύνεται: To show the excellence of the Son, that is sufficient: He is not ashamed. For speaking of servants and Masters and teaching the humility of Masters, we are accustomed to say: He is not ashamed to eat and drink with the servants, and to sit together, and to heal those of them who are sick by himself. He hints at this very thing here also, that he who undertook the passion for us is not ashamed to call those brothers for whom he endured the passion. Chrysostom not dissimilarly: Behold again, how he reconciles and joins them, both honoring and consoling, and making them brothers of CHRIST, from the fact that they are from one. Then again, making the matter common and showing that he is speaking of that which is according to the flesh, he added: For he who sanctifies, CHRIST: and those who are sanctified, we: You see how much difference there is. He indeed sanctifies, but we are sanctified, and above he called him the author of salvation. For there is one GOD, from whom are all things. For which cause he is not ashamed to call them brothers. You see how he again shows the excellence. For to say, he is not ashamed, shows that the whole thing is not of the nature of the matter, but of his benevolence and great humility who is not ashamed. For even if we are from one, he indeed sanctifies, but we are sanctified. And he indeed is from the Father, as the true and proper Son, that is, from his essence. But we as a creature, that is, from nothing. Therefore there is a great difference. Wherefore he says: He is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: I will declare thy name unto thy brothers. For clothed in flesh he also put on brotherhood, and at the same time brotherhood also entered. The Apostle therefore proves that it was altogether fitting that the Son of GOD should be perfected through sufferings for the sake of our salvation, inasmuch as he acknowledges us as his brothers of a common origin with us: for whose sake he did not hesitate to taste death; nay, who for this reason willed to partake of our flesh and blood, that through death he might free us from death. But he does not argue thus, (as it seemed to some) Those who are from one, they ought to have a communion of sufferings with one another. For even the Angels are from one, who have no κοινωνίαν by way of sufferings: nor is there any question in this place of the communion of the sufferings of CHRIST and ours, as in Romans 8:17, but of the fittingness of the satisfaction of Christ, in which he has no partner, and no communion with us, since he alone and by himself satisfied for all. Nor indeed is the common origin from GOD simply regarded, for in that way not only Angels, but all creatures are from GOD, but that which falls upon those to be sanctified. Who certainly are not Angels, or other creatures, but men in need of sanctification because of sin, for whom CHRIST was sent, 1 Tim. 1:16, whose brother he was not ashamed to be called. If, however, anyone does not wish to understand the word ἐξ ἑνὸς as from one parent of the human race, Adam, in whom the brotherhood is founded, which opinion the Blessed Dorschäus prefers, we will not object.

Christ is not introduced under the person of David, nor is David in Psalm 22:23 a type of Christ: But those things which are held in that Psalm uniquely befit Christ, as we have shown from the bowels and fulfillment of the Psalm in the New Testament in the passion of CHRIST, and also in the present place, and other most illustrious documents in the annotations on the book of Psalms, which arguments Matth. Polus in his Synopsis Criticorum approved with his own vote and repeated from the Reformed.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Ὅτε γὰρ ἁγιάζων καὶ οἱ ἁγιαζόμενοι ἐξ ἑνὸς πάντες) Christus nos sanctos facit doctrina sua & exem- plo. Ille ex Spiritu sancto conceptus est, & nos per Spi- ritum sanctum novam adipiscimur naturam: Ita commu- nem habemus originem. Non spectari hic originem ex A- damo ostendunt sequentia. Sic Pontifex Ebraeorum ex Jacobo non minus erat quam is, qui per eum expiabatur populus. Ἀγιάζων in hoc libro modo ad puritatem illam legalem refertur, modo ad veram atque internam, cujus illa erat imago. Eis autem de Deo recte explicari osten- dunt loca Johann. VIII. 41. 1. Cor. VIII. 6. Gal. III. 20.

Δι' ἧν αἰτίαν οὐκ ἐπαισχύνεται ἀδελφοὺς αὐτοὺς καλεῖν) Apparet id Matth. XXVIII. 10. Et bene dicitur, non eru- bescit de eo, qui major minoribus se sociat. Simile lo- quendi genus habes infra XI. 16.

Per eum, qui sanctificat, nonnulli, etiam è Nostris Beatus Gerhardus Pontificem Veteris Testamenti intelligunt, ut comparatio institua- tur cum eodem, quam ita explicat ὁ μακαρίτης: Sicut summus Sacerdos Leviticus populum sancti- ficans per sacrificia, & populus Israeliticus à Sa- cerdote sanctificatus sunt ex uno vel primo generis humani parente vel Patriarcha Jacobo Israelitici populi stipite vel ex eadem natura humana : Ita CHRISTUS unicus Novi Testamenti Sacer- dos & credentes Dei filii orti sunt ex uno parente DEO. Scopus enim Apostoli est probare, quod Deum decuerit, ut Filium suum per passiones con- summaret. Id probat ex eo, quod Christus à Deo constitutus sit unicus Novi Testamenti summus Sa- cerdos, qui oblato sacrificio sanctificaret, hoc est, à peccatis mundaret, & Deo reconciliaret genus hu- manum. At Sacerdos sanctificans & populus, qui sanctificatur, sunt ex uno ejusdem natura humana participes. Igitur & Filius Dei humanam natu- ram assumere debuit, & eam quidem passionibus obnoxiam, qualem caeteri habent homines. Sed hic signum comparationis deficit, & Apostolus nondum aggressus est comparationem cum Pon- tifice Veteris Testamenti. Vis insuper Aposto- lici argumenti secundum nonnullos haec est: ideo etiam autorem salutis nostrae post passio- nem, vel interventu ejusdem, consummari, ut filii Dei per passiones ad salutem perducantur, quia ejusdem originis ipse est cum filiis unum agnoscens nobiscum autorem. Beatus Hunnius ita haec cum praecedentibus connectit: Quando- quidem qui sanctificat & qui sanctificantur ex uno sunt omnes, hoc est, quia Christus nos à peccatis redimere & sanctificare constituit, id vero non nisi pretio redemtionis interposito fieri potuit, idcirco necesse fuit, ut ipse sanctificans & nos sanctifican- di ex uno essemus, id est, ejusdem naturæ partici- pes. Proinde nostram naturam quoque affumpsit, nec erubescit aut turpe sibi ducit nos appellare suos fratres propter admirabile illud consortium & communionem ejusdem carnis & sanguinis. Pro- inde recte quidem Grotius intelligit Christum per eum, qui nos sanctificat, non autem Christus sanctificat tantum doctrina, & exemplo, sed im- primis etiam merito & efficacia operationis per verbum & Sacramenta ceu media sanctificatio- nis. Ideo semetipsum sanctificavit pro nobis in passione ac morte, ut nos sanctificaremur in ve- ritate Joh. XVII. vers. 19. Sed non bene Grotius hæc refert ad comparationem conceptionis Chri- sti ex Spiritu S. quæ facta est, ut absque congres- su viri Θεοτόκῳ Filium Dei utero conciperet mi- raculosa operatione Spiritus Sancti, & regene- rationis ac renovationis nostræ, qua per Spiritum sanctum novam adipiscimur naturam, ut doceat communem ita nos habere originem. Illa enim origo est humanitatis Christi, quantum ad na- turam, cujus autor & δημιουργὸς fuit Spiritus S. Huic vero non respondet origo nostræ regene- rationis, juxta quam utique non substantiam vel naturam aliam consequimur, aut esse demum accipimus, sed quum ex carne caro nati simus, ex Deo regeneramur. Communis ergo origo non tam ex Adamo, quam ex Deo respicitur, ut Græci Interpp. exponunt, quia non virtute bene- dictionis Adamo ante lapsum factæ Christus ho- mo natus est, sed virtute promissionis post la- psum de semine mulieris factæ, quæ procreatio non secundum ordinem naturæ, sed secundum οἰκονομίαν & dispensationem divinæ gratiæ con- tigit. Theophylactus in sua παραφράσει ad Filium Dei, qua est ex Patre æterna generationis respe- ctu, refert. Cum enim, inquit, sanctificans, id est Christus, & sanctificati nos ipsi videlicet, ex uno omnes, hoc est, à Patre, ut Filius ipse, nos ut creati. Ille itaque sanctitatem largitur, nos sancti efficimur. Quo fit, ut identitas intercedat, & ex- cellentia demonstretur. Sed hic de Christo agitur secundum humanam naturam. Hic enim nati- vitatem & Christi, & nostram corporalem re- spici ὁμοουσία, de qua porro disserit Apostolus, nostri cum Christo confirmat: quia fratres suos ob eandem ex Deo originem nos vocat, non ve- ro propter spiritualem regenerationem & ex Spi- ritu Sancto conceptionem. Quamvis enim vir- tute promissionis divinæ & operatione Spiritus Sancti facta sit Christi conceptio; quia tamen ex substantia matris Mariæ Virginis Spiritus Sanctus operatus est humanam naturam, quam assumpsit Filius DEI in hypostasin suam, idcir- co nobis est ὁμοούσιος & consubstantialis, nosque fratres suos vocare non dubitat, aut erubescit, Matth. XXVIII. vers. 10. Quod nunc porro con- firmat è Veteri Testamento Apostolus. De quo Theophylactus ipse: Ubi enim carnem hic in it, & fraternitatem nobiscum inivit, & induit. Unde & in unum fraternitas ipsa convenit. Theodo- retus in hunc loc. Qui sanctificat, & qui san- ctificantur, ex uno omnes sunt. Hoc etiam posuit quoad humanitatem. Creata est enim natura quæ sumpta est. Unus autem est & ejus & noster Creator ac opifex. Sed per illam sanctificamur. Quod si hoc etiam de natura humana intelligere voluerint hæretici, ne hoc quidem de Unigeniti gloria quicquam detrahet. Unum enim, inquit, habemus Patrem & nos & ipse, sed clarum est, eum quidem esse Filium natura, nos autem gratia. Hanc enim nos docet differentiam, quod ille qui- dem nos sanctificet, nos autem sanctificemur. Hæc Theodoretus: Qui porro emphasin in voce ἐπαι- σχύνεται notat : Ad ostendendam Filii excellen- tiam sufficit illud : Non pudet eum. De servis enim & Dominis loquentes & Dominorum hu- militatem docentes solemus dicere : Non pudet eum cum famulis comedere & bibere, & una sedere, & eos, qui ex eis ægrotant, medicari per se. Hoc ipsum hic etiam innuit, quod qui pro nobis pas- sionem suscepit, non erubescit vocare fratres eos, pro quibus sustinuit passionem. Chrysostomus non absimiliter : Ecce rursus, quomodo eos conciliat ac conjungit, & honorans, & consolans, & eos faciens fratres CHRISTI, ex eo, quod sint ex uno. Deinde rursus rem communiens & ostendens se dicere de eo, quod est secundum carnem sub- junxit : Qui enim sanctificat, CHRISTUS: & qui sanctificantur, nos : Vides, quantum intersit. Ille quidem sanctificat, nos vero sanctificamur, & superius eum dixit autorem salutis. Unus est enim DEUS, ex quo omnia. Propter quam causam non erubescit eos vocare fratres. Vides quomodo rursus ostendat excellentiam. Dicere e- nim, non erubescit, ostendit totum esse non rei na- turæ, sed ejus, qui non erubescit benevolentia & multæ humilitatis. Nam etiamsi simus ex uno, ille quidem sanctificat, nos autem sanctificamur. Et ille quidem ex Patre, tanquam verus & pro- prius Filius, hoc est, ex ejus essentia. Nos autem tanquam creatura, hoc est, ex nihilo. Multum itaque interest. Quamobrem dicit : Non erubescit eos vocare fratres, dicens : Nuntiabo nomen fra- tribus tuis. Nam carne indutus induit etiam fra- ternitatem, & simul etiam ingressa est fraterni- tas. Probat ergo Apostolus, congruum omni- no fuisse, ut nostræ salutis causa per passiones per- ficeretur Filius DEI, utpote qui communis no- biscum originis nos fratres suos agnoscit : quo- rum causa non dubitarit mortem gustare; imo qui ideo voluit communicare carni & sanguini nostro, ut per mortem nos liberaret a morte. Non autem ita arguit, (quod nonnullis visum) Qui sunt ex uno, illi debent invicem passionum communionem habere. Nam & Angeli ex uno sunt, qui vi passionum nullam habent κοινωνίαν: neque de communione passionum CHRISTI & nostrarum agitur hoc loco, uti Roman. IIX. vers. 17. sed de convenientia satisfactionis Chri- sti, in qua neminem habet consortem, & nul- lam nobiscum communionem, quum unus ille, & solus satisfecerit pro omnibus. Nec vero ori- go communis a DEO simpliciter respicitur, nam ita non Angeli tantum, sed omnes creaturæ ex DEO sunt, sed ea, quæ in sanctificandos cadit. Qui certe non sunt Angeli, aut aliæ creaturæ, sed homines ob peccatum sanctificationis indi- gi, ob quos missus est CHRISTUS 1. Tim. I. vers. 16. quorum frater dici non erubuit. Si ta- men quis vocem ἐξ ἑνὸς de uno generis huma- ni parente Adamo, in quo fundata fraternitas, intelligere nolit, quam sententiam præfert Beat. Dorschaus, non refragabimur.

Non sub persona Davidis introducitur Chri- stus aut David Psal. XXII. vers. 23. typus Christi est: Sed quæ Psalmo illo habentur, unice Christo conveniunt, quemadmodum è Psalmi visceribus & complemento in Novo Testamento in passione CHRISTI, nec non loco præsente, aliisque documentis illustrissimis ostendimus in annot. ad libr. Psalm. quæ argumenta è Reformatis calculo suo approbavit & repetiit Matth. Polus in Synops. Critic.

## 2:12
Vers. 12. Ἀπαγγελῶ τὸ ὄνομά σε τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς με, ἐν μέσῳ ἐκκλησίας ὑμνήσω σε) Cited from the Greek, but from memory. For there, for ἀπαγγελῶ, in the same sense is διηγήσομαι, אספרה. King David, however, calls the Israelites his brothers by the prescription of the law, Deuteronomy 19:20. So also Christ by the law of the duty imposed upon him. David celebrated the praises of GOD in the midst of the Israelite people; Christ in the midst of the disciples, having been recalled from death to life. Matt. 28:18, 19. Luke 24:44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49. John 20:17, 21.

He does not bring forth the Psalm from memory, but from the suggestion of the Holy Spirit, and the sense is the same, although the words vary, to which the Holy Spirit is not bound. But the Psalm in no way treats of David: nor did he announce the name of the Lord in that great Church, of which there is speech there, consisting for the most part of Gentiles. Nor are the brothers here therefore only Jews, but primarily also the Gentiles. That they are called brothers by the prescription of the law, not by birth of blood, Deuteronomy 19:20, or that only Jews are understood, is a gloss worthy of Grotius. For what, was false testimony only not to be spoken against Jews, but was it permitted by the law to speak it against Gentiles? Nor did Christ have to announce the name of the Lord only in the midst of his disciples, who were of Jewish stock, by the power of this prophecy, but also in the midst of the Gentiles. That this might happen, he sent the Apostles into the whole world, to preach the glory of the Lord through them. Compare. Psalm 22:23, 26, 28. And what comfort would redound to us, if the brotherhood of this Leader of salvation looked only to the Israelites by the law of the duty imposed upon him, and we were excluded from the same? All the sanctified are regarded, whom he himself sanctifies, all who are sons of GOD through the grace of adoption. Rightly therefore the Blessed Gerhardus: This was fulfilled 1. by Christ immediately, when after the resurrection, appearing to his Apostles, he instructed them, full of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, and several times addressed them by the name of brothers, Matt. 28:10, John 20:17. 2. Mediately through the Apostles in the preaching of the Gospel, which confirms us concerning that blessed brotherhood, and the heavenly inheritance joined to it.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ἀπαγγελῶ τὸ ὄνομά σε τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς με, ἐν μέσῳ ἐκκλησίας ὑμνήσω σε) Ex Græco citatum, sed memoriter. Nam ibi pro ἀπαγγελῶ est sensu eodem διηγήσομαι, אספרה. David Rex, tamen Israelitas fratres suos vocat ex legis præscripto Deuteronom. XIX. vers. 20. Sic & Christus ex lege impositi sibi muneris. David in medio populi Israelitici DEI laudes celebravit; Christus in medio discipulorum à morte in vitam revocatus. Matth. XXVIII. vers. 18. 19. Luc. XXIV. 44. 45. 46. 47. 48. 49. Joh. XX. 17. 21.

Non memoriter Psalmum profert, sed ex suggestione Spiritus sancti, & sensus idem est, licet verba varient, ad quæ adstrictus non est Spiritus sanctus. De Davide autem nullo modo agit Psalmus: neque is in Ecclesia illa magna, de qua ibi sermo est, è gentibus maximam partem constante, nomen Domini annunciavit. Nec fratres hic ergo Judæi tantum, sed imprimis etiam gentes. Ex legis præscripto fratres dici, non ex ortu sanguinis, Deuteronom. XIX. vers. 20. aut intelligi tantum Judæos, glossa est Grotio digna. Quid enim, num testimonium falsum tantum non dicendum erat contra Judæos, dicere autem per legem licebat contra gentes? Neque Christus tantum in medio discipulorum suorum, qui Judaicæ erant stirpis vi hujus vaticinii debuit annunciare nomen Domini, sed etiam in medio gentium. Quod ut fieret, Apostolos in totum mundum emisit, per eosdem prædicaturus gloriam Domini. Confer. Psalm. XXII. vers. 23. 26. 28. Et quid solatii ad nos redundaret, si hujus Ducis salutis fraternitas tantum ex lege impositi sibi muneris spectaret ad Israelitas, nos autem ab eadem exclusi essemus? Respiciuntur omnes sanctificati, quos ipse sanctificat, omnes qui per adoptionis gratiam sunt filii DEI. Recte itaque Beat. Gerhardus: Hoc impletum est 1. à Christo immediate, quando post resurrectionem Apostolis suis apparens mysteriis regni cælorum plenus eos instruxit, ac aliquoties fratrum nomine eos compellavit, Matth. XXVIII. 10. Joh. XX. 17. 2. Mediate per Apostolos in prædicatione Evangelii, quod de beata illa fraternitate, eidemque conjuncta hæreditate cælesti nos confirmat.

## 2:13
Vers. 13. Καὶ πάλιν) that is, in another place, as above I. 5. Ἐγὼ ἔσομαι πεποιθὼς ἐπ' αὐτῷ) Namely, in adversity: for these are words taken from the Greek, Is. VIII. 17, as are also the following words concerning the following matters. With the King of Israel and the Syrian pressing the city, Isaiah did not cease to trust in the promises of God. So too Christ, pressed by the Jews and Romans. Those Hebrew Christians to whom these things are written, and others who wish to be reckoned by that name, ought to do the same.

Καὶ πάλιν, ἰδὲ ἐγὼ καὶ τὰ παιδία, ἅ μοι ἔδωκεν ὁ Θεὸς) Πάλιν here means 'furthermore'. For these words follow. One must understand, however, what follows further, 'for signs and wonders', or as it is in the Hebrew, 'for a sign and for a portent'. The prophets bear the image now of God, now of Christ. Isaiah did not say: 'my children', but, 'whom God has given to me': because they were begotten by the command of God. Thus GOD gives his children to Christ to be educated and cared for, John XVII. verse 12. That this passage was long ago applied to the Messiah is apparent from the words of Simeon, Luke II. verse 34, and from the Gemara.

Some prefer that Psalm XVIII. verse 3 and 2 Sam. XXII. verse 3 be cited. But the passage in Is. VIII. verse 17 can be referred to here at the same time; in both places there is a discourse concerning Christ, as we have shown in the annotations to the book of Psalms and to chapter VIII of Isaiah: And indeed not only in a typical sense, but in a literal one. But the passage which others wish to be referred to from Isaiah 12, verse 2, is foreign, for CHRIST does not sing there, but the faithful are commanded to sing a song about Christ. Theodoret teaches the connection in this passage thus: Furthermore, he also shows that those things which are said humbly are said by economy, or the dispensation of the flesh assumed. For to that which is, he is not ashamed, he joined that: I will be trusting in him. For he is not ashamed, for the sake of human salvation, to use even humble words beyond his own dignity. Chrysostom says that the Apostle teaches here that Christ shows himself to be the Father: Behold I and the children whom GOD has given me: Just as he previously showed himself to be a brother. But since in Isaiah 8, Christ joins himself at the same time with the children given to him by GOD, that is, the faithful, as in the sufferings by which they are a sign and a portent in Israel: So also in trust in GOD; not undeservedly did the Apostle bring forward that passage, where he teaches that it was fitting that CHRIST should be perfected through sufferings, just as the children of God, truly faithful, trusting in God, are led through sufferings to glory. For CHRIST also placed his trust uniquely in GOD in his sufferings, so that by this reason he might teach us to be like him, not only by origin, because both he and we are from one, and by nature, because we are his brothers; but also by trust in passion, whence it was altogether fitting that he himself should also be crowned after the passion, just as we also obtain the crown of glory after the cross has been overcome: indeed, not only for the sake of conformity, but primarily for the sake of office, so that as Priest, both by the merit of his passion and by his efficacious intercession for us in heaven, and as our King, by his gracious governing, protection, and leading of us to eternal glory, he might preside over his brothers. Thus he simultaneously prepares for himself an approach to the explanation of both the ὁμοουσίας and the ὁμοπαθείας with his brothers, since for the sake of the latter he brings forward the incarnation of the Son of GOD, but for the sake of the former, the temptations which he deigned to undergo for our sake, concerning which in verse 14. and 16. he simultaneously paves the way for the cause of the passion and death of Christ, and for explaining more fully the Sacerdotal function, concerning which in verses 14, 15, 17, 18. Therefore, the Prophet Isaiah is not speaking, but Christ in chapter 8, verse 17; the children of Isaiah born by the command of GOD are not introduced, but the children given to Christ by GOD; nor has this passage been adapted here, whether by the Apostle or by Simeon, Luke 2, verse 34, to the Messiah, but it treats of the Messiah according to the letter, concerning which see the annotations to Isaiah. The blessed Dorscheus makes the Apostle argue here as follows: He who in the work of sanctification and the founding of the Church sweats and labors even then, when the face of GOD seems hidden from the house of Jacob, so that amidst scandals he promises himself victory and the execution of his purpose out of the highest trust in God, he altogether descends into brotherhood and communion of nature with men, and thus is ἐξ ἑνὸς with them. For unless it were so, Jehovah the sanctifier could not speak of himself in this way. But from the subsequent words of the Prophet, likewise brought forward by the Apostle, he judges this to be the Apostolic syllogism: He who, having lived in the midst of communion with the saints and the faithful, as one of them, and thus exposed to scandals, and seen with the stumbling block of many, triumphantly exclaims that he has emerged with his children from those difficulties by which both were believed to be surrounded and hindered, he is a participant in the same stock and origin with his children handed over to him for sanctification. But the Messiah does this. Therefore. The minor premise is clear from what has been said. To which, moreover, this must be added, that when the Messiah says, ἰδὺ ἐγὼ καὶ τὰ παιδία &c. he clearly insinuates that not only the παιδία are to be looked at, but also himself, and thus that in both it is to be admired that, placed in such great communion and exposed to the same dangers, both nevertheless emerged beyond everyone's expectation: These indeed as sanctified and disciples, but he as the sanctifier and Immanuel.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Καὶ πάλιν) id est alio loco, ut supra I. 5. Ἐγὼ ἔσομαι πεποιθὼς ἐπ' αὐτῷ) Nempe in adversis: Sunt enim verba desumpta ex Græco, Es. VIII. 17. ut & sequentia de sequentibus. Rege Israelis & Syro urbem premente non destitit Esaias Dei promissis confidere. Sic & Christus pressus à Judæis & Romanis. Idem facere debebant Ebræi illi Christiani, ad quos hæc scribuntur, & alii, qui eo nomine censeri volunt.

Καὶ πάλιν, ἰδὲ ἐγὼ καὶ τὰ παιδία, ἅ μοι ἔδωκεν ὁ Θεὸς) Πάλιν hic est deinde. Nam hæc verba subsequuntur. Subintelligenda autem, quæ porro sequuntur ἴση σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα, aut ut in Ebræo est, in signum & in portentum. Prophetæ modo Dei, modo Christi gerunt imaginem. Non dixit Esaias: filii mei, sed, quos dedit mihi Deus: quia ex præcepto Dei erant geniti. Sic DEUS filios suos Christo dat educandos atque curandos, Joh. XVII. vers. 12. Jam olim autem ad Messiam aptatum hunc locum apparet ex verbis Simeonis Luc. II. vers. 34. & ex Gemara.

Nonnulli malunt adduci Psalm. XIIX. vers. 3. & 2. Sam. XXII. vers. 3. Sed potest simul locus Es. VIII. vers. 17. hic respici; utrobique de Christo sermo est, ut in annotat. ad libr. Psalm. & ad cap. IIX. Es. ostendimus: Nec vero tantum sen- su typico, sed literali. Locus vero, quem alii ex Esaie. XII. vers. 2. respici volunt, alienus est, Non enim illic CHRISTUS cantat, sed fideles, canticum de Christo pangere jubentur. Theo- doretus in hunc locum συνέχειαν ita docet: Por- ro autem ostendit etiam, quæ dicuntur humiliter, dici per œconomiam, seu carnis susceptæ dispenfa- tionem. Ei enim quod est, non pudet eum, con- junxit illud: Ego ero fidens in eum. Non erube- scit enim propter hominum salutem, vel humili- bus uti verbis præter suam dignitatem. Chryso- stomus hic docere Apostolum ait, Christum sei- psum ostendere Patrem: Ecce ego & pueri, quos mihi dedit DEUS: Sicut antea se ostendit fra- trem. Quum autem Esa. IIX. simul pueris sibi à DEO datis, hoc est, fidelibus se conjungat Christus, ut in passionibus, quibus sunt signo & portento in Israel: Ita & in fiducia in DEUM; non immerito illum Apostolus locum adduxit, ubi decuisse docet, ut CHRISTUS per passiones consummaretur, quemadmodum filii Dei, ve- re fideles, in Deum confidentes, per passiones ad gloriam perducuntur. Nam & CHRISTUS in passionibus suis unice in DEUM fiduciam collocavit, ut hac ratione similes nos ipsi esse doceat, non tantum origine, quia & ipse & nos ab uno, & natura, quia fratres ejus; sed etiam fiducia in passione, unde par omnino erat, ut etiam post passionem ipse coronaretur, quem- admodum & nos coronam gloriæ post supera- tam crucem consequimur: imo non tantum con- formitatis, sed imprimis officii causa, ut tanquam Sacerdos & merito passionis, & efficaci in cœ- lis pro nobis intercessione, & tanquam Rex no- ster gratiosa nostri gubernatione, protectione & ad æternam gloriam perductione fratribus suis præesset. Ita simul aditum sibi parat ad ex- plicationem tum ὁμοουσίας tum ὁμοπαθείας cum fratribus, quum illjus causa incarnationem Filii DEI adducat, hujus vero causa tentationes, quas subire dignatus est nostri gratia, de qua vers. 14. & 16. simul viam sternit ad causam passionis & mortis Christi, & functionem Sacerdotalem ube- rius explicandam, de qua v. 14. 15. 17. 18. Non ergo Propheta Esaias loquitur, sed Christus cap. IIX. v. 17. non filii Esaiæ ex præcepto DEI geniti, introducuntur, sed filii Christo à DEO dati; nec solum aptatus est hic locus sive hic ab Apostolo, sive à Simeone, Luc. II. vers. 34. Mes- siæ, sed secundum literam agit de Messia, quo de vid. annot. ad Esaiam. Beat. Dorscheus Apo- stolum hic facit ita argumentantem: Qui in o- pere sanctificationis, & fundationis Ecclesiæ etiam tum, cum absconsa videtur facies DEI à domo Jacobita, sudat & laborat, ut inter media scandala ex summa in Deum fiducia, victoriam tamen sibi polliceatur & propositi exequutio- nem, is cum hominibus in fraternitatem, & na- turæ communionem omnino descendit, adeo- que ἐξ ἑνὸς est cum illis. Nisi enim ita esset, Jehovah sanctificator ita de se loqui non posset. Ex subsequentibus vero Prophetæ verbis ab A- postolo itidem adductis syllogismum Apostoli- cum hunc esse censet: Qui in media commu- nione cum sanctis & fidelibus versatus, tanquam unus ex ipsis, adeoque scandalis obnoxius, & cum offendiculo plurimorum conspectus trium- phaliter exclamat, se cum natis suis ex istis dif- ficultatibus emersisse, quibus utrique circum- fusi atque impediti credebantur, is cum natis suis sibi ad sanctificandum traditis ejusdem stir- pis & originis particeps est. Atqui hoc facit Messias. Ergo. Minor ex dictis liquet. Quibus insuper illud addendum est, quod cum Messias inquit, ἰδὺ ἐγὼ καὶ τὰ παιδία &c. manifeste in- sinuet, non tantum παιδία spectanda esse, sed & semetipsum, adeoque in utrisque esse admi- randum, quod in tanta communione positi & iisdem periculis expositi utrique tamen emerse- rint præter omnium expectationem: Hi quidem ut sanctificati & discipuli, ille vero ut sanctifi- cator & Immanuel.

## 2:14
Verse 14.

Since therefore the children have partaken of flesh and blood) Because the children of God, that is, the pious, are subject to all the inconveniences which this mortal life can bear: Σὰρξ & αἷμα here signify neither vicious appetites nor mere matter, but quality with matter, that is, the passible, the corruptible. Thus also below in verse 7, 1 Timothy 3, verse 16, 2 Corinthians 4, verse 11.

And he himself likewise partook of the same) It was not fitting that he be exempted from that common lot. In the Glossary, παραπλησίως means likewise, similarly. Demosthenes uses it. Aristotle said παραπλησίως for the same.

This gloss is owed to the Socinians: who deny that the Apostle is treating of the incarnation of the Son of GOD, and wish for CHRIST alone to be hinted at as being subject to the common lot of the afflictions of the pious. But the Apostle rises to the proper cause of the brotherhood of the Son of God with the faithful, which is his own incarnation. For the Son of GOD would not be ὁμοόσιος with us, or our brother, unless he had been made a participant of our nature through the incarnation. Therefore, so that that Socinian gloss may be refuted more fully, we urge 1. the subject, which is the Son of GOD, whom the Apostle had called the brightness of the glory of God, and the express image of his person, and the Creator and Preserver of all things, and had demonstrated this from the testimonies of the Old Testament: To whom certainly flesh and blood do not belong, nor the passible and the corruptible, except insofar as he was made a participant of our flesh and blood through the incarnation. For the Son of GOD, as regards his own nature, is immutable, devoid of all passion and mortality: 2. The predicate, which is to be demonstrated here: namely, the gracious communication of divine dignity, which requires a suitable subject, and that is not an Angel, nor the Son of GOD by reason of his divinity: wherefore, since that βελτίωσις, στεφάνωσις καὶ τελείωσις was brought about for the same divine person, namely the Son of GOD, it was necessary that a human nature should concur in that person besides the Deity, and that the same should be united to the divine nature. For communication presupposes union. Therefore, the ἐνανθρώπησις of the Son of GOD was not to be passed over in the explanation of this mystery. 3. The title of Son of man. For this subject, crowned with glory and honor, called the Son of GOD, from Psalm VIII, the son of man, and man, and described his emptying and exaltation. That the foundation itself might not be neglected, the Apostle teaches that the Son of GOD was made the Son of man, and a man ὁμοόσιον to us through the κοινωνίαν and μετοχὴν of flesh and blood. 4. The firmament of our Συναδελφίας. It was certainly to be established, and a proper reason to be brought forward, whence arises that confraternity of the Son of GOD with ψιλοῖς ἀνθρώποις, which is nothing other than the participation of our flesh and blood. Suppose only the communion of sufferings is indicated, that principal thing, which is to be laid down in the place of a foundation, which is of nature and of our substance, must it be said that it was passed over by the Apostle with a dry foot? Which is absurd. 5. The example of the children given to CHRIST. Because παραπλησίως (in like manner) it is said that the Son of GOD was made a partaker of flesh and blood, as the children. But these are truly and ὐσιωδῶς (essentially) partakers of the substance of flesh and blood. There is certainly no participation or κοινω- νία (communion) properly between children and frailty. 6. The proper meaning of flesh and blood. For one must not depart from the propriety of words without necessity. But the proper acceptance of these words implies the very substance of flesh and blood. Flesh is indeed sometimes called man by reason of the corruption of sin, and flesh and blood as corrupt nature, for example John III. verse 5. Matthew XVI. verse 17. But in that sense it cannot be applied to Christ, who is devoid of sin. It is also called flesh and blood by reason of mortality, but not excluding nature and substance, as 1. Corinthians XV. verse 50. flesh and blood, that is, our nature, as it is mortal and corruptible, cannot inherit the heavenly kingdom. Thus the substance is included, and neither mere frailty, mortality, nor sinful corruption is signified by these words; but either our substance alone, or the same with these imperfections. Here, however, the proper meaning must be retained entirely, because the truth of our substance and of the ὁμουσίας (consubstantiality) of Christ regarding human nature had to be explained and confirmed: and it obtains the meaning not only of the body, which consists of blood and flesh, but of the whole human nature, as Isaiah XL. verse 5. Romans III. verse 20. because unless the communion of the entire human nature, to which body and soul pertain, is designated: how can our συναδελφία (brotherhood) with the Son of GOD be confirmed thereby? And a rule is to be noted here: Flesh never denotes frailty in the abstract and solitarily, but in the concrete it denotes human nature, subject to frailty. Flesh and blood nowhere in Holy Scripture denotes mere infirmity, but either human nature itself, or as it is corrupted or corruptible by sin. 7. The synonym of this word. For what is understood by flesh and blood, the word seed of Abraham declares, by which is expressed likewise human nature, according to which he is the son of Abraham from the seed of Abraham, and his μοναδικὸν (unique) seed, that blessed seed, in which all the families of the earth were to be blessed, the seed of the woman, which was to crush the head of the infernal serpent, which seed CHRIST is according to human nature, as the Apostle interprets in Galatians III. verse 16. We conclude thus: He who is μέτοχος (a partaker) of flesh and blood through a true ἀνά- ληψιν (assumption) of humanity, he is a partaker through ἐνσάρκωσιν (incarnation) and ἐνανθρώπησιν (becoming man), not through a mere participation of frailty. But the former is true of the Son of GOD. Therefore the latter is also. 8. The scope of the demonstrated participation of flesh and blood, which is here to teach that the Son of GOD himself, the ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης τῦ θεῦ (brightness of the glory of God), the Creator and Preserver of all things, might through his death snatch us from the Devil, who has the power of subjecting us to death, and might free us from the fear of death. Therefore he teaches that the Son of GOD was truly made a partaker of human nature, so that he could taste death for us, verse 9, so that by his death he might make purification of our sins by himself, so that through sufferings he might be perfected as the ἀρχηγὸς (author) of our salvation. The Apostle speaks here of such a μετοχῇ (participation) of flesh and blood, the end of which is the victory of the Devil, verse 14. But the end of the assumption of mere infirmity is not

the victory of the Devil, but rather the assumption of human nature, in which he could die, and by his death overcome him who had the empire over death. 9. The other member of the comparison instituted.
