As truly as children participate in flesh and blood, or their nature, from their parents, so truly (παραπλησίως) did the Son of GOD participate in flesh and blood, so that he became ὁμούσιος (consubstantial) with Abraham, his other progenitors, and all of us by that μετοχῇ (participation). Chrysostom: See, he says on this passage, where the likeness is, namely according to the flesh. Similarly he himself also was a partaker of the same. Let all heretics blush. Let them hide themselves for shame, who say that he came by vision and opinion, not by the very truth of the thing. For he did not only say: He was a partaker of them, and was silent. Although even if he had said so, it would be enough: But he placed something else greater, namely Similarly, not by vision and opinion, but by truth, showing that there is a brotherhood. 10. The distinct moment of ὁμοιότητος (likeness). For the Apostle deals next with ὁμοιοπα- θείᾳ (like-passion) and likeness with sufferings and temptations, with affections, in verse 17 and 18, after he had taught the ὁμουσίαν (consubstantiality) through the μετοχὴν τῆς σαρκὸς καὶ αἵματος (participation of flesh and blood), and the ἐπίλη- ψιν (taking hold) of the seed of Abraham, just as the incarnate Word, GOD manifested in the flesh CHRIST JESUS, when he was in the form of GOD, assumed the form of a servant, and ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος (being made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man), Philippians II. verse 7, 8. John I. verse 14. 1 Timothy III. verse 16. Therefore this humiliation and ἐλάττωσις (emptying) of the God-man is not to be confused with that very communion or participation of our nature, with which the Son of GOD deigned to honor the same. Just as the incarnation and personal union should not be confused with the emptying of the incarnate one: The former pertains to the suppositum, and the assumption of human nature into the hypostasis of the Son of GOD: the latter pertains to the state of the suppositum, convenient to the composite person, but not to the Son of GOD viewed by reason of his divine nature. 11. We add an ὁμό- ψηφον (unanimous) testimony from antiquity. Theodoret in this place provides this paraphrase: How, he says, could it be that he would either call himself our brother, or truly call us sons, unless he had received the same nature? For which reason, having assumed it, he broke the power of death, and took away from the midst the fear that hung over us. But he pursued all these things, teaching those who think that the Son is less than the Angels on account of suffering, that he necessarily underwent this suffering. We have already praised Chrysostom before. Following whom, Theophylact has this to say on this passage: I would wish that those who claim that the Son did not obtain a birth equal to ours in reality, but only by some outward appearance, would be ashamed at this point. For he says that he did not only partake of flesh and blood, just as the children, that is, the rest of men—although even if he had put forward that, it would surely have been enough to confirm that he had taken on true flesh—but he added 'in like manner,' so that he might show that he had a flesh very similar to our own. Athanasius, On the Incarnation of the Word, Vol. I of his Works, page 62. Moreover, that the Word himself assumed a body for himself so that it might be available to him as a victim of the same body, they also reveal in his own words. 'After, therefore, the childish, etc.' For by the immolation of his own body he both put an end to the law that was hostile to us, and renewed for us the beginning of life, with the hope of resurrection given to us. Since death had gathered its forces from among men against men, therefore again through a man the nature assumed by the Word of GOD, the dissolution of death was made, and the resurrection of life. He teaches that the same is to be understood concerning the common essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, Tom. I. of his works, page 234, here treating of the mystery of the assumed humanity. And in Oration III against the Arians, page 379: That he was made a partaker of flesh and blood, as we are, ὅτε γέγονεν ἄνθρωπος ἐνδυσάμενος τὴν ἡμετέραν σάρκα [when he became man, having put on our flesh]. And page 425: That he might undergo death for us, and that he might raise up men; and that he might dissolve the power of the Devil, the Savior came, and that is the cause of his advent in the flesh: otherwise the resurrection would not have occurred, if there had not been death: furthermore, how would death have had a place in him, if he had not borne a mortal body? When Paul had learned this from him, he burst forth into these words: Since the children were partakers of flesh and blood, he himself likewise also willed to be a partaker of the same things, that through death he might abolish him who had the power of death, the Devil, etc. I omit the testimonies of others, St. Ambrose, Augustine, etc. The explanation of the blessed Hunnius is as follows: Behold I and the children whom the Lord has given me. Where he calls his elect by the gentle and sweet name of his children, and that on account of the communion of the same blood, just as he now immediately explains the Prophetic oracle, saying: Since therefore the children, that is, the brothers of CHRIST, have a commerce, or as it is in the Greek κεκοινώνηκεν, that is, they communicate, or have communion with flesh and blood, and Christ himself likewise has been made a partaker of the same (flesh and blood), while he hypostatically joined to himself the true, entire human nature taken from the Divine Virgin Mary, and made it most proper to himself by personal union. What Schlichtingius with Crellius objects in his lectures: If the incarnation of CHRIST were asserted here, that the incarnation of the rest of the sons of GOD must be concluded from it, is εὐδιάλυτον [easily dissolved]. For because Christ is the Son of God by nature, and therefore eternal GOD: Christians are sons of God by grace; He certainly could not be a man subject to death and various calamities, except through the ἐνανθρώπησιν [incarnation], and in that part he is not similar to them. But the similarity is shown in this, that he is truly a partaker of flesh and blood or human nature, παραπλησίως [in like manner] or similarly, as his faithful are partakers of it. Although they do not agree in the mode of participating in flesh and blood specifically: Yet they agree in the truth of the thing and in a general mode, that, just as we truly draw human nature through temporal birth; so also the Son of GOD willed to be begotten by a temporal birth as a true man, and thence is equally a partaker of flesh and blood, just as we are brothers of the same. It must be observed, however, that τὸ μετέχειν σαρκὸς καὶ αἵματος [the partaking of flesh and blood] is not to be understood of a parastatic communication, as believers become partakers of CHRIST, who dwells in them through faith, Heb. III. verse 14, Eph. III. verse 17, and of the Holy Spirit, whose temples they are, Heb. VI. verse 14, 1 Cor. III. verse 16. But hypostatic, or as the blessed Gerhard speaks: He was made a partaker of flesh and blood not effectively, but substantially, like the children, to whose substance flesh and blood belong.

That through death he might destroy him who has the power of death.

He shows the benefits obtained from this counsel of GOD. Samael, that is, the Devil, is said by the Hebrews to have the power of death. You have this in the Talmud Baba-Bathra, in the book Caphthor, in the book on the death of Moses in Maimonides' Guide for the Perplexed III. 22. He is, of course, the accuser of those who give themselves to vices, as can be seen in Zech. III. verse 1, and he shows that such are to be detained in death, that is, that they ought not to be raised to a better life, Romans VI. verse 23, 1 Corinthians XV. verse 56. CHRIST, by taking away these vices in his own, at the same time took away this right from the accuser, Romans VIII. verse 2, just as he did not find in Christ what he could accuse, John XIV. verse 36, so neither in Christians, because the ἀγνοήματα [sins of ignorance] which remain in them are not called sins, in that sense, namely, that they could be condemned for them, 1 John III. verse 9.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Ἐπεὶ ὖν τὰ παιδία κεκοινώνηκε σαρκὸς καὶ αἵματος) Quia filii Dei, id est, pii omnibus subjecti sunt incom- modis, quæ ferre potest vita hæc mortalis: Σὰρξ & αἷμα hic neque vitiosos appetitus, neque solam materiam si- gnificant, sed cum materia qualitatem, id est τὸ παθητὸν, τὸ φθαρτόν. Sic & infra V. 7. 1. Tim. III. vers. 16. 2. Cor. IV. vers. 11.

Καὶ αὐτὸς παραπλησίως μετέσχε τῶν αὐτῶν) Non expe- diit eum eximi communi illi forti. In Glossario παρα- πλησίως perinde similiter. Utitur Demosthenes. Aristo- teles pro eodem dixit παραπλησίως.

Glossa hæc Socinianis debetur: qui negant de incarnatione Filii DEI Apostolum agere, ac CHRISTUM solum innui communi affli- ctionum piorum forti subjici volunt. At Apo- stolus assurgit ad propriam causam συναδελφίας Filii Dei cum fidelibus, quæ est ejusdem ἐνσάρ- κωσις. Non enim nobiscum Filius DEI esset ὁμοόσιος, aut frater noster, nisi naturæ nostræ particeps factus esset, per ἐνσάρκωσιν. Quapro- pter ut uberius refellatur glossa illa Sociniana, urgemus 1. subjectum, quod est Filius DEI, quem dixerat Apostolus ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης Θεῦ, καὶ χαρακτῆρα τῆς ὑποστάσεως ἀυτῦ, & Crea- torem ac Conservatorem rerum omnium, id- que demonstrarat è testimoniis Veteris Testa- menti: Cui certe non convenit caro & sanguis, neque τὸ παθητὸν καὶ τὸ φθαρτὸν, nisi quate- nus carnis & sanguinis nostri particeps factus est per incarnationem. Nam Filius DEI quoad naturam propriam est immutabilis, omnis pas- sionis & mortalitatis expers: 2. Prædicatum, quod hic demonstrandum: Dignitatis nempe divinæ gratiosa communicatio, quæ requirit sub- jectum conveniens, id vero non Angelus est, nec Filius DEI ratione divinitatis suæ: quapro- pter quum eidem personæ divinæ, Filio nempe DEI ea facta sit βελτίωσις, στεφάνωσις καὶ τε- λείωσις, præter Deitatem in persona illa con- currere humanam naturam, eandemque unitam esse oportuit divinæ naturæ. Communicatio enim præsupponit unionem. Ideo tacenda in ex- plicatione mysterii hujus non erat, Filii DEI ἐνανθρώπησις. 3. Filii hominis cognomentum. Nam suppositum hoc gloria & honore corona- tum, Filium DEI, è Psalm. IIX. dixit filium ho- minis, & hominem, ejusque exinanitionem & exaltationem descripsit. Ut ergo fundamentum ipsum non negligeretur, Filium DEI factum esse Filium hominis, & hominem nobis ὁμοόσιον per carnis & sanguinis κοινωνίαν & μετοχὴν, do- cet Apostolus. 4. Συναδελφίας nostræ firmamen- tum. Stabilienda ea utique erat, & ratio pro- pria afferenda, unde oritur illa confraternitas Filii DEI cum ψιλοῖς ἀνθρώποις, quæ nulla alia est, quam carnis & sanguinis nostri participa- tio. Pone solam tantum passionum communio- nem indicari, præcipuum illud, quod funda- menti loco substernendum, quod est naturæ & substantiæ nostræ participatio ficco pede ab A- postolo præteritum esse, dicendum erit? Quod inconveniens. 5. Liberorum CHRISTO da- torum exemplum. Quia παραπλησίως similiter dicitur Filius DEI particeps factus carnis & sanguinis, uti liberi. At hi vere, & ὐσιωδῶς participes sunt substantiæ carnis & sanguinis. Nulla utique proprie est participatio vel κοινω- νία inter pueros & fragilitatem. 6. Carnis & san- guinis proprium significatum. Non enim rece- dendum à proprietate vocum citra necessitatem. At propria vocum istarum acceptio infert ipsam carnis & sanguinis substantiam. Caro dicitur quidem homo quandoque ratione corruptionis peccati, & caro & sanguis corrupta natura, ex- empli gratia Johan. III. verf. 5. Matth. XVI. vers. 17. Sed eo sensu Christo peccati experti applicari nequit. Dicitur & caro ac sanguis ra- tione mortalitatis, sed non exclusa natura & sub- stantia, quomodo 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 50. caro & sanguis, id est, natura nostra, qua mortalis & corruptibilis, hereditare regnum cœleste non pos- sunt. Ita includitur substantia, neque nuda fra- gilitas, mortalitas, aut peccaminosa corruptio istis vocibus significatur; sed vel sola substantia nostra, vel ipsa tamen cum istis imperfectioni- bus. Hic vero propria omnino retinenda si- gnificatio, quia substantiæ nostræ & ὁμουσίας Christi quoad humanam naturam veritas expli- canda & confirmanda erat: neque tantum cor- poris quod sanguine & carne constat, sed totius naturæ humanæ significatio obtinet, ut Esa. XL. vers. 5. Romanor. III. vers. 20. quia nisi humanæ naturæ integræ, ad quam corpus & anima per- tinent, communio designatur: quomodo con- firmari inde συναδελφία nostra cum Filio DEI poterit? Et notanda hic regula: Caro nunquam in abstracto & solitarie fragilitatem notat, sed in concreto humanam naturam, fragilitati obnoxi- am. Caro & sanguinis nuspiam in Scriptura sacra notat solam infirmitatem, sed vel ipsam humanam naturam per se, vel prout eadem peccato est cor- rupta aut corruptibilis. 7. Vocis hujus Synonymum. Nam quod per carnem & sanguinem intelligi- tur, seminis Abrahæ vox declarat, qua exprimi- tur itidem humana natura, secundum quam est filius Abrahæ è semine Abraham, & semen ejus μοναδικὸν, semen illud benedictum, in quo omnes familiæ terræ benedicendæ erant, semen mulie- ris, quod caput infernalis serpentis contriturum erat, quod semen CHRISTUS est secundum humanam naturam, interprete Apostolo Galat. III. vers. 16. Concludimus ita: Qui est μέτοχος carnis & sanguinis per veram humanitatis ἀνά- ληψιν, is per ἐνσάρκωσιν, καὶ ἐνανθρώπησιν non per solam fragilitatis participationem μέτοχος est. At de Filio DEI verum prius. Ergo & po- sterius. 8. Demonstrata participationis carnis & sanguinis scopum, qui hic est, ut doceat, quod ipsi Filius DEI ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης τῦ θεῦ, Creator & Conservator rerum omnium per mortem suam Diabolo, potestatem nos morti mancipandi habenti, eriperet, nosque à metu mortis liberaret. Ideo ergo vere humanæ natu- ræ participem factum esse Filium DEI docet, ut mortem pro nobis gustare posset vers. 9. ut morte sua peccatorum nostrorum purificatio- nem per semetipsum faceret, ut per passiones velut ἀρχηγὸς salutis nostræ consummaretur. De tali μετοχῇ carnis & sanguinis hic loquitur Apostolus, cujus finis est victoria Diaboli, vers. 14. At assumptionis solius infirmitatis finis non est

Diaboli victoria, sed potius assumptionis hu- manæ naturæ, in qua mori possit, ac morte sua vincere eum, qui in mortem habebat impe- rium. 9. Comparationis institutæ alterum mem- brum. Quam vere pueri à parentibus suis par- ticipant carnem & sanguinem, seu naturam suam, tam vere (παραπλησίως) Filius DEI par- ticipavit carnem & sanguinem, ut Abrahæ, ali- isque progenitoribus suis, nobisque omnibus ὁμούσιος ea μετοχῇ evaserit. Chrysostomus: Vi- de, inquit ad hunc locum, ubi sit similitudo, nempe secundum carnem. Similiter ipse quoque eorundem fuit particeps. Erubescant omnes he- retici. Præ pudore se abscondant, qui dicunt, eum advenisse visione & opinione, non ipsa rei veritate. Non solum enim dixit: Eorum fuit particeps & tacuit. Quanquam etiamsi sic di- xiffet, satis esset: Sed aliquid aliud majus posuit, nempe Similiter, non visione & opinione, sed ve- ritate, ostendens esse fraternitatem. 10. Distin- ctum ὁμοιότητος momentum. Nam de ὁμοιοπα- θείᾳ & similitudine cum passionum & tentatio- num, cum affectuum, deinceps demum agit Apostolus vers. 17. & 18. postquam ὁμουσίαν per μετοχὴν τῆς σαρκὸς καὶ αἵματος, & ἐπίλη- ψιν τῶ σπέρματος Ἀβραὰμ docuisset, quem- admodum Verbum incarnatum, DEUS ma- nifestatus in carne CHRISTUS JESUS, quum esset in forma DEI, servi formam affum- psit, & ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος, Philipp. II. vers. 7.8. Johan. I. vers. 14. 1. Timoth. III. vers. 16. Non ergo hæc θεανθρώπω humiliatio & ἐλάττωσις confundenda cum ipsa naturæ nostræ commu- nione vel participatione, qua eandem dignatus est Filius DEI. Sicut confundi non debet in- carnatio & unio personalis cum incarnati ex- inanitione: Illæ ad suppositum pertinet, & as- sumptionem humanæ naturæ in hypostasin Fi- lii DEI: hæc ad suppositi statum, personæ συν- θέτῳ convenientem, non vero Filio DEI ra- tione divinæ naturæ spectato. 11. Addimus ὁμό- ψηφον ex antiquitate testimonium. Theodore- tus hoc loco hanc tradit paraphrasin: Quomo- do, inquit, fieri posset, ut vel ipse se fratrem no- strum vocaret, vel filios nos vere appellaret, nisi eandem naturam accepisset? Qua de causa, ea suscepta mortis fregit potentiam, & de medio sus- tulit timorem, qui nobis imminebat. Hæc au- tem omnia persequutus est, docens eos, qui filium esse minorem Angelis propter passionem existi- mant, quod hanc passionem necessario subiit. Chrysostomum jam ante laudavimus. Quem se- quutus Theophylactus ita habet in hunc locum: Pudeat velim hoc loco, qui afferunt, non re Fi- lium, sed apparentia quadam exteriori parem nobiscum genituram fortitum. Neque enim so- lum carnis hunc inquit & sanguinis, eque ac pueri, id est, reliqui homines participasse, quam- vis, etsi id protulisset, satis fuisset profecto ad con- firmandum veram carnem hunc accepisse, sed Si- militer adjunxit, ut nostræ carni persimilem hunc habuisse ostendat. Athanasius de incarnatione Verb. Tom. I. Oper. pagina 62. Quod autem ut victima ejusdem corporis sibi suppeteret, cor- pus sibi ipsum Verbum assumpserit, etiam in suis verbis produnt. Postquam igitur puerili &c. Immolatione enim sui corporis & legi nobis in- festæ finem imposuit, & primordium vitæ nobis renovavit, spe resurrectionis nobis data. Quan- doquidem ex hominibus adversus homines vires suas collegerat mors, ideo rursus per hominis naturam à Verbo DEI susceptam, mortis disso- lutio facta est & vita resurrectio. Idem de com- muni essent: Patris, Filii & Spir. sancti Tom. I. oper. pagina 234. hic de mysterio susceptæ hu- manitatis agi docet. Et orat. III. contr. Arian. pagina 379. Carnis & sanguinis, ut nos, parti- cipem factum esse, ὅτε γέγονεν ἄνθρωπος ἐνδυσά- μενος τὴν ἡμετέραν σάρκα. Et pagina 425. Ut prò nobis mortem susciperet, & ut homines exci- taret; atque Diaboli opem dissolveret, Salvator venit, atque illa causa est adventus illius in car- ne: Resurrectio alioqui non obtigisset, nisi mors fuiffet: Mors porro, quomodo in eo locum ha- buiffet, nisi mortale corpus gestasset? Id ubi ab eo Paulus didicerat, in hæc verba prorupit: Quo- niam pueri consortes erant carnis & sanguinis, ipse quoque itidem earundem rerum particeps effe voluit, ut per mortem aboleret eum, qui impe- rium mortis habebat, Diabolum &c. Alia alio- rum Sanct. Ambrosii, Augustini &c. suffragia prætermitto. Beati Hunnii explicatio sic ha- bet: Ecce ego & pueri, quos dedit mihi Dominus. Ubi electos suos blando & dulci nomine vocat pue- ros suos, idque propter communionem ejusdem sanguinis, quemadmodum nunc immediate ad o- raculum Propheticum enarrat, inquiens: Postea- quam igitur pueri, hoc est fratres CHRISTI commercium habent, seu ut in Græco est κεκοινώ- νηκεν, id est, communicant, seu communionem habent cum carne & sanguine, & ipse Christus similiter eorundem (carnis & sanguinis) parti- ceps est factus, dum veram humanam naturam integram ex Diva Maria virgine sumptam hy- postatice sibi copulavit, eamque sibi personali u- nione propriissimam effecit. Quód Schlichtin- gius cum Crellio in prælectionibus ipsius obje- cit: Si hic CHRISTI incarnatio assereretur, reliquorum DEI filiorum incarnationem inde con- cludendam esse, εὐδιάλυτον est. Nam quia Chri- stus est Dei Filius per naturam, adeoque æter- nus DEUS: Christiani sunt filii Dei per gra- tiam; Ille utique non potuit homo esse morti & variis calamitatibus obnoxius, nisi per ἐναν- θρώπησιν, eaque parte his similis non est. Osten- ditur autem similitudo in eo, quod vere carnis & sanguinis seu naturæ humanæ consors sit πα- ραπλησίως vel similiter, uti fideles ejus partici- pes sunt. Etsi non conveniant in modo parti- cipandi carnem & sanguinem speciali: Conve- niunt tamen in veritate rei & modo generali, quod, ut naturam humanam nos vere trahimus per nativitatem temporalem; Ita etiam Filius DEI temporali nativitate procreari voluerit ve- rus homo, & inde æque sit carnis & sanguinis particeps, quemadmodum nos ejusdem fratres. Observandum autem τὸ μετέχειν σαρκὸς ἡ αἷμα- τος non intelligendum de communicatione pa- rastatica, sicut credentes CHRISTI partici- pes fiunt, qui in ipsis habitat per fidem, Ebr. III. vers. 14. Ephes. III. vers. 17. & Spiritus san- cti, cujus templa sunt, Ebr. VI. vers. 14. 1. Cor. III. vers.16. Sed hypostatica, vel ut Beatus Ger- hardus loquitur: Particeps factus est carnis & sanguinis non effective, sed substantialiter, sicut pueri, ad quorum substantiam pertinet caro & sanguis.

Ἴνα διὰ τῦ θανάτε καταργήσῃ τὸν τὸ κράτος ἔχοντα τῦ θανάτε.

Ostendit utilitates ex hoc consilio DEI consecutaf. Samael, id est, Diabolus dicitur Ebræis habere impe- rium mortis. Habes hoc in Thalmude Baba-Bathra in libro Caphthor, in libro de morte Mosis apud Maimo- nidem directoris dubitantis III. 22. Nimirum accusator est eorum, qui vitiis se dedunt, ut videre est Zach. III. vers. 1. & tales ostendit detinendos in morte, id est, non debere excitari ad vitam meliorem, Romanor. VI. vers. 23. 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 56. CHRISTUS in suis auferendo ista vitia simul abstulit hoc jus accusatori, Romanor. VIII. vers. 2. sicut in Christo non reperit, quod accusaret, Johan. XIV. vers. 36. ita nec in Christianis, quia ἀγνοήματα quæ in illis manent, non dicuntur pec- cata, eo scilicet sensu, ut ob ea damnari possint 1. Joh. III. vers. 9.

## 2:15
Verse 15. And might deliver those who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.

Christ, whom he frees from vices, he also makes certain of eternal life. Death is the most fearful thing, says Aristotle: Man naturally loves his own preservation; therefore he fears death most of all. Nor can he not fear it, who either does not think there will be another life, or is not in such a state that he ought to hope he will be a partaker of it. But all fear carries with it servitude, that is, a servile condition. For it is the lot of servants to fear, Romans VII. verse 15.

Never is slavery a straight head. That is, he might deliver from fear, which is understood from what follows.

If Grotius understood these things correctly, they could easily be admitted. But because Grotius Socinianizes, in the sanctification of Christ, which he wishes to be done only by doctrine and example; see verse 11, and in the exposition of the participation of flesh and blood, concerning the common lot of various inconveniences with us; and likewise, when he explains these things in such a way that Christ, by taking away vices in his own, at the same time took away from the Devil the right of accusing us and detaining us in death, and that those whom Christ frees from vices he also makes certain of eternal life, hardly any other than a Socinian sense seems to underlie this. For just as Christ sanctifies us: so also he frees us from vices. But Grotius maintains that this is done only by doctrine and example. Let the commentary of Crellius be compared here with Schlichtingius, and the agreement will appear. For he expounded verse 11 here thus: That both the people, who are sanctified by Christ, that is, are thoroughly purged from all sins, and Christ, who sanctifies the people, are of one, so to speak, kind with him, begotten from the same Father, namely from GOD. And against verse 14. By flesh and blood is understood a nature and condition that is weak, fragile, perishable, and subject to corruption and various evils. However, he denies that the incarnation is concluded from this. Nor does he acknowledge the merit of CHRIST here, but attributes those effects of sanctification and the certainty of immortal life solely to his doctrine and example, which he wishes the faithful to desire, having obtained it from Christ's death and resurrection, as their own resurrection or immortality to be obtained after death and through death, and he makes that the sense of the Apostle's words, so that through the death of CHRIST they might be freed from the fear of death. Understanding the abolition of the Devil as the abolition of the powers which he has to consign men to eternal death, as being clearly enslaved to him by vices and crimes, which he explains in two ways: 1. because through death he obtained supreme power over it, by which he restrains all his enemies, of whom the Devil is the head; 2. because the death of Christ, and the resurrection that followed it, draws all men to embrace the faith of CHRIST, and implants in them a certain hope of immortality, if they have obeyed Christ, and consequently causes them, with the yoke of the Devil shaken off, to enslave themselves to CHRIST. Furthermore, he expounds the liberation from the fear of death here: To fear is the lot of those who are slaves. Moreover, whoever does not have the hope of resurrection is compelled to fear. From this servitude CHRIST has freed men by his death, as by his death he not only escaped to immortal life, but also obtained the power of restraining and abolishing the Devil. If these things are compared with the Gratian glosses, the agreement will be in the open. Let us now weigh the Socinian-Grotian [views], and let us subjoin the true sense of the Apostle to those refuted fictions. But first, that destruction of the Devil made through the death of Christ is perversely explained. For, not to mention that that abolition is spoken of ambiguously by Crellius, so that it is doubtful whether he understands it to be substantially abolished: the abolition of the former sense of the Devil's powers, which he has for enslaving men to hell, is not explained—namely, how the Devil is restrained, whether so that he may not seduce men, or indeed so that he may not exert power over the same [men], which he himself has over those who have enslaved themselves to him by vices and crimes, or what kind of restraint of the Devil's powers that is; nor does it appear by what reason the same agrees with the mind of the Socinians through the death of Christ. But the other sense, which is approved by Crellius and Schlichtingius, looks to nothing but doctrine and example, because the doctrine concerning the death of CHRIST, and the resurrection following it, draws men to place faith in Christ, and to enslave themselves to Christ, by which pact Christ does not properly abolish the powers of the Devil, or free them from his yoke, but men, who shake off the yoke of the Devil, and him; who has the empire of death, are to be said to destroy, or to abolish his powers, nor should this be ascribed so much to the death of Christ as to his resurrection, or rather to the doctrine concerning his resuscitation from the dead, from which they think faith and the hope of immortality arise, and the same being proposed in the example of Christ, they believe that obedience to Christ and the shaking off of the Devil's yoke follow; but because countless people are certain of the resurrection of Christ, and yet neither have saving faith in Christ, nor obey Christ, nor is it in our power, when we are enslaved to the Devil through vices and crimes, to shake off his yoke, or to believe in Christ, nor do we aspire to immortality after the example of Christ, but the manner of our immortality and entry into glory is far different, all these things as Socinian fictions are deservedly to be rejected, of which not even a faint trace appears here: Where there is no word about the resurrection of Christ, but only about his death, which he tasted for us, and through which he destroyed him who has the empire of death. Now as to the liberation from the fear of death, it is not said that Christ frees us from the fear of it, or from the servitude—which indeed concur in the same subject, yet are different—through resurrection, or resuscitation to immortal life, or even through the attainment of power over the Devil in his exaltation: But here the Apostle treats of the liberation which is and was made through the death of Christ, because by tasting death in our place, and thus undergoing death for us, he destroyed the Devil, insofar as he had power and strength over the human race on account of sin, to enslave them to temporal and eternal death, and freed us from his hand by his death, and redeemed those of us who were subject to the most sad servitude through our whole life by the fear of death, from this fear, and from most miserable servitude, being made obedient to God in the form of a servant, even unto death, even the death of the cross. For he did not only redeem those who enslaved themselves to the Devil by vices and crimes, but the whole world, which was concluded under sin, Rom. XI. v. 33. and ὑπόδικος [liable] to God, Rom. III. 19. and also a servant and subject to the Devil: for by whom anyone is overcome, his servant he has become, 2. Pet. II. v. 19.

v. 19. and thus he freed us from the power of darkness through ἀπολύτρωσιν [redemption], made by his blood, Col. I. v. 13, 14. Nothing here about power obtained over the Devil after the resurrection, but about the λύτρῳ [ransom] of the death of CHRIST, and the victory gained through death endured in our place: by which he despoiled principalities and powers, and led them confidently, openly triumphing over them in himself, Coloss. II. v. 15. We note here I. To be destroyed: who is the διάβολος [devil], not μοναδικῶς [singularly], but εἰδικῶς [specifically] in the whole species, as 1. Pet. V. v. 8, 1. John III. v. 8, John VIII. v. 44, Eph. VI. v. 12. II. The destruction: which is not of the Devil in respect of substance, or inherent malice, but in respect of exercised malice, and by which he has τὸ κράτος τοῦ θανάτου [the power of death] through his tyrannical occupation of the same over men, John VIII. v. 44, not without the just permission of GOD exercising the same power. But that κατάργησις [abolition] of CHRIST is both moral and acquisitory, and real and applicatory. The former was made through the death of CHRIST: the latter is performed on the throne of GOD. The former is treated here: to which the κατάργησις τοῦ νόμου [abolition of the law] Col. II. v. 14, liberation from the curse of the law Gal. III. v. 13, the taking away of the sting of death 1. Cor. XV. v. 55, Rom. V. v. 15, the abolition of sins Heb. IX. v. 25, ch. X. v. 12, looks. For there was need of such a destruction, which would take away the right against us, to which the power of death adhered, and the tyranny of Satan exercised against us: which, as it was most just in respect of GOD decreeing it, on account of the sin of the human race, so in respect of Satan it was unjustly seized: and thus in reason of GOD it required satisfaction, but in reason of Satan it was to be extinguished through κατάργησις: which followed immediately, when the matter was settled before GOD. This (latter) κατάργησις [abolition] looks especially to the Kingly office of Christ, concerning which 1. Cor. XV. v. 24, 25, Rom. XVI. v. 20. III. The mode of the present destruction. The κατάργησις of that power is said to be made through death, insofar as it was satisfactory for sins. For otherwise, unless satisfaction had been rendered to divine justice through the death of Christ, the right of death and Satan over us would not have been abolished, which was held against us by divine judgment on account of sin. Therefore, through his death, Christ is said to have paid what he did not steal, Psalm LXIX. v. 5, 6, and was made an ἀντίλυτρον [ransom] for us 1. Tim. II. v. 6. Which was foreshadowed through the death of victims, as they were given for the soul of men, Lev. XVII. v. 11, to figure the satisfaction of Christ. And what need would there have been for the eternal Son of God Himself both to become a partaker of our flesh and blood and to undergo death, if the Devil could have been destroyed by doctrine and example alone? But concerning these matters in [my work] Socinismus profligatus. Concerning which Chrysostom says: Here he shows what is wonderful, namely that by the very thing through which the Devil conquered, by that he was conquered, and the things which were valid weapons for him against the world, namely death, by that very thing Christ struck him. Here he indicates the great power of Him who conquered. You see how much good death has done. And he might deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage. Why, he says, do you shudder? Why do you fear it, which is abolished, and is plainly both empty and idle? It is no longer terrible, but is trampled underfoot, despised, vile, and abject, and plainly of no value. And furthermore he shows, however, that not only has death ceased, but that through it he also who always wages implacable war against us, the Devil, I say, has been broken and prostrated. For he who does not fear death is outside the tyranny of the Devil.

For if he will give skin for skin, and all that he has for his soul, when he has even dared to despise that very soul, whose servant will he then be? He fears no one, he dreads no one: He is superior to all, and more generous than all. For he who despises his own soul, much more so other things. But when the Devil finds such a soul, he will be able to effect nothing in it of those things which are his. Similarly Theophylact: He explains the cause of the dispensation, namely that through death, which he underwent, who was a partaker of flesh and blood, he might destroy the Devil, who has the power of death. How? Through sin, clearly. For since he made men fall into sins by his own arts from that former disobedience of Adam, he himself soon established death, which he used thereafter as a soldier and stronger weapons against this human nature. Therefore, Christ used this very death to overcome and destroy the Devil. Which is certainly an argument of great power and wisdom, that he should kill the enemy with the same weapons with which he had slain many. But the Apostle does not say that Christ freed us from death, but from the fear of death: For although he freed us both from eternal death, which is the second death, and from temporal death, which is the wages of sin, so that we were no longer subject to the penalty of death, yet the Apostle here dealt specifically with the fear of death; because nothing but the fear of death is set before the eyes outside of Christ, (who is our life, and the ἀρχηγὸς of salvation) and that on account of sin. But since Christ has satisfied for sin by his death, we have been freed from that fear of death through the death of Christ. But throughout our whole life we are said to have been guilty of the fear of death, and subject to slavery, because we were made servants of him who had the power of death, and obtained the power to consign us to death through sin, that is, the Devil, or because we were guilty of slavery, because death ruled over us through sin, as the Apostle taught in Rom. V; from whose tyranny we have been freed through the death of Christ. St. Chrysostom brings forward different explanations: But what is, through fear of death they were all their life subject to slavery? What is this? That he who fears death is a slave, and endures everything, so that he may not die. But that which all were servants of death, and that because it had not yet been abolished, they were held by its dominion. Or that men lived in perpetual fear, always expecting that they would die, and dreading death, they could receive the sense of no pleasure, since this force of fear was always present. For he tacitly signified this, saying throughout the whole life. Osiander explains it concerning the slavery of the Devil, illustrating the whole passage thus: Because therefore the children or sons partook of flesh and blood, that is, because they have flesh and blood; even he himself, the eternal Son of God, similarly partook of the same: he assumed a true human nature from the flesh and blood of the most chaste virgin Mary (Christ therefore (by reason of substance) has the same flesh that we have: but without sin. Which is to be noted against the ravings of the Schwenckfeldians, who assert that Christ's humanity by reason of substance is not the same as our flesh.) But the Son of God assumed human nature for this reason, that in it he might sustain death (the penalty of our sins): that through his death, which he suffered innocent, he might destroy, conquer, and trample upon him who had the power of death, that is, the Devil. (For Satan, on account of sin, had the right of killing men both by bodily and eternal death. But Christ snatched this right from him through his death, which he himself had not deserved. Therefore, the pious are themselves also victors over death, (which has been turned into sleep):

& eternal death has absolutely no right over those who believe in Christ.) And indeed Christ suffered death, that he might free those from the tyranny of the Devil, who through fear of death were all their life subject to slavery, that is, Satan through sin held the human race in most sad slavery under his yoke: so that not only were they in continuous fear of death, but also the most miserable men could expect nothing else, except that they would be precipitated through bodily death into eternal death or damnation. But this fear has now been overcome for all who believe in Christ, and they themselves have been restored into the liberty of the children of GOD. The explanation of B. Hunnius is as follows: That through death he might abolish: The final cause of the incarnation of Christ is shown, which is, that because he could not suffer by his immutable Deity, he might die by having assumed mortal flesh, and through his death abolish the power of him who had the power of death over men, namely the Devil: And thus he might assert men into their pristine liberty, who on account of sin had themselves been subject to death, and had also been tormented throughout their whole life by the fear of death, which is often more terrible than death, because on account of the transgression of the law, damnation after death would also have been to be expected and dreaded by them, had not the Son of GOD incarnate abrogated that most sad slavery for believers by his death. We observe therefore I. The redeemed: ὅσοι φόβῳ θανάτε διὰ παντὸς t̃ zῆν ἔνοχοι ἦσαν δελείας. Where there is an ellipsis of the preposition ἐν, they were servants in the fear of death. For there is fear in impending death, and in fear there is slavery; διὰ παντὸς t̃ zῆν, that is, ἐν πάσῃ τῇ zωῇ. διὰ for ἐν 1. Timothy II. 15. Heb. VII. 9. Rom. IV. 11. Gal. IV. 13. A verb for a noun Luke VII. 21. ὅσοι are all, i.e., individuals of the kinds, not the kinds of individuals Matthew XIV. 36. Mark III. 10. c. VI. 11. 56. Luke IV. 4. c. IX. 5. John I. 12. c. X. 8. Gal. III. 27. II. Ἀπάλλαξιν: which brings about the reconciliation of the human race with God. For after the worst deeds were done by men ἀλλαγὴ, by which they were rendered aliens from the life of God Eph. IV. 18. & on account of which the wrath of God remains upon them, John III. 36. and the curse of the law Gal. III. 13. there was need of ἀπαλλαγῇ which is to be established in God, or in Christ through God, so that Christ, having received our sins into himself, and having destroyed them by a just satisfaction, might propitiate God to the human race, and having bestowed that righteousness upon us, with the fear of punishments driven away, might make a confidence of approaching to God, so that thus men might be led back to God. Whence afterwards he is called ἀρχιερεὺς, εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας t̃ λα̃̃ verse 17. Although therefore that word concerning simple liberation frequently occurs, yet since by reason of its origin it implies reconciliation, and those who are to be liberated must altogether be reconciled to GOD, so that they may be liberated from the fear of death and from servitude, nor can they be immune from the wrath of GOD and the thunderbolt of the law otherwise than through the intervention of the propitiation made through Christ, rightly by the force of the subject matter also underlying it, the liberation which was made by the reconciliation of GOD is understood.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Καὶ ἀπαλλάξῃ τούτους ὅσοι φόβῳ θανάτου διὰ παντὸς τοῦ ζῆν ἔνοχοι ἦσαν δουλείας.

Christus quos à vitiis liberat, eos etiam certos fa- cit vitæ æternæ. Θάνατος φοβερώτατον ait Aristoteles : Homo naturaliter amat sui conservationem; ideo mor- tem maxime metuit. Neque potest eam non metuere, qui aut non putat aliam fore vitam, aut non eo est in statu, ut ejus se debeat sperare futurum participem. Metus autem omnis secum trahit servitutem, id est ser- vilem conditionem. Servorum enim est metuere, Ro- manor. VII. vers. 15.

Οὔποτε δουλεία κεφαλὴ ἐνθεῖα πέφυκεν. ἀπαλλάξῃ nempe τοῦ φόβου, quod ex sequentibus in- telligitur.

Si recte hæc intelligeret Grotius, facile admit- ti possent. Sed quia Socinizat Grotius, in Chri- sti sanctificatione, quam fieri solum doctrina & exemplo vult; vid. v. 11. & in expositione τῆς με- τοχῆς carnis & sanguinis, de communi variorum incommodorum nobiscum sorte; itemque, cum taliter hæc exponit, quod Christus auferendo in suis vitia simul abstulerit Diabolo jus accusandi nos, ac detinendi in morte, quodque quos Christus à vitiis liberat, eos etiam certos faciat vitæ æter- næ, vix alius, quam Socinianus sensus hic subes- se videtur. Nam uti sanctificat nos Christus: Ita etiam nos à vitiis liberat. Id vero tantum fieri doctrina & exemplo statuit Grotius. Conferatur hic Schlichtingio Crellianus commentarius, & apparebit convenientia. Nam vers. 11. ita hic ex- posuit: Quod & populus, qui à Christo sanctifica- tur, id est ab omnibus peccatis penitus expurga- tur, & Christus, qui populum sanctificat, unius sit cum illo, ut sic dicam, generis, ex eodem Pa- tre, nempe de DEO, procreatus. Et advers. 14. Per carnem & sanguinem intelligitur natura & con- ditio infirma, fragilis, caduca, corruptioni & va- riis malis obnoxia. Negat autem incarnationem Christus hinc concludi. Neque CHRISTI meritum hic agnoscit, sed doctrina & exemplo ejus effectus illos solum tribuit sanctificationis & certitudinis immortalis vitæ, quam ex Christi morte, & resurrectione eam consequuta fideles sua resurrectionis seu immortalitatis post mortem, & per mortem consequendæ cupere debere vult, eam- que mentem verborum Apostoli facit, ut per CHRISTI mortem mortis metu liberentur. Dia- boli abolitionem de abolitione virium intelli- gens: quas habet ad homines æterna morti man- cipandos, ceu sibi plane vitiis & flagitiis manci- patos, quod duobus modis explicat 1. quia per mortem adeptus est supremam in eam potestatem, qua omnes inimicos suos, quorum caput est Dia- bolus, coërcet; 2. quia mors Christi, eamque con- secuta resurrectio omnes homines ad CHRISTI fidem amplectendam trahit, iisque immortalitatis spem certam, si Christo obtemperaverint, inserit, ac proinde, ut jugo Diaboli excusso, CHRISTO sese mancipent, facit. Porro liberationem à ti- more mortis hic exponit: Metuere est eorum, qui serviunt. Cogitur autem metuere, quisquis resurrectionis spem non habet. Ab hac servitu- te CHRISTUS homines morte sua liberavit, dum per mortem non tantum ad immortalem vitam evasit, sed etiam potestatem coërcendi & abolendi Diabolum adeptus est. Hæc si cum Gratianis glos- sis componantur, in aprico erit convenientia. Expendamus jam Sociniano-Grotiana, & ve- rum sensum Apostoli profligatis istis commentis subjungamus. Primo autem illa Diaboli destru- ctio per mortem Christi facta perverse explicatur. Nam ne dicam, quod ambigue illa abolitio dica- tur à Crellio, ut dubium sit, anne substantialiter abolendum intelligat: Prioris sensus virium Dia- boli abolitio, quas habet ad mancipandos homines inferno, non explicatur, quomodo nempe coer- ceatur Diabolus, num ne seducat homines, an vero, ne potestatem in eosdem exerat, quam ipse habet in eos, qui sese vitiis & flagitiis ipsi manciparunt, aut qualis illa sit virium Diaboli coërcitio, nec appa- ret, qua ratione Christi morte eadem ex mente Socinianorum conveniat. Alter vero sensus, qui Crellio & Schlichtingio probatur, non nisi doctri- nam & exemplum respicit, quod doctrina de morte CHRISTI, eamque consecuuta resur- rectione homines trahat ad fidem Christo adhi- bendam, Christoque se mancipandos, quo pacto non Christus proprie abolet vires Diaboli, aut jugo ejus liberat, sed homines, qui jugum Dia- boli excutiunt, & eum; qui mortis imperium habet, destruere, aut vires ejus abolere dicen- di sunt, nec tam id morti Christi, quam resurre- ctioni ejus, vel potius doctrinæ de ejusdem à mor- tuis resuscitatione, adscribendum fuerit, è qua fidem oriri putant, & spem immortalitatis, eadem- que in exemplo Christi proposita, obsequium Christi & excussionem jugi Diabolici sequi cre- dunt, sed quia innumeri certi sunt de resurrectio- ne Christi, nec tamen vel fidem salvificam in Christum habent, vel Christo obtemperant, ne- que nostrarum virium est, cum sumus mancipati per vitia & flagitia Diabolo, jugum ejus excu- tere, vel in Christum credere, nec ad exemplum Christi nos ad immortalitatem adspiramus, sed longe disparrima sit nostræ & Christi immorta- litatis & ingressus ad gloriam ratio, hæc omnia ceu commenta Sociniana merito reprobanda, quorum etiam hic ne quidem tenue apparet ve- stigium: Ubi nullo verbo de resurrectione Christi, sed tantum de morte ejus, quam pro nobis gusta- vit, & per quam destruxit eum, qui mortis ha- bet imperium, agitur. Jam quod ad liberationem à metu mortis, non dicitur, Christus nos ab illius metu, aut à servitute, quæ in eodem subjecto qui- dem concurrunt, diversa tamen sunt per resurre- ctionem, vel resuscitationem ad immortalem vi- tam, aut etiam per consequutionem potestatis in Diabolum in exaltatione nos liberare: Sed hic A- postolus de liberatione agit, quæ & quâ facta est per mortem Christi, quia mortem nostri loco gu- stando, & ita pro nobis mortem subeundo Dia- bolum, quatenus propter peccatum in genus hu- manum potestatem & robur habuit, id morti tem- porali & æternæ mancipandi, destruxit, nosque morte sua ab illius manu liberavit, & qui metu mortis per totam vitam rei eramus servitutis tri- stissimæ per mortem, ab hoc metu, & à servitute miserrima redemit, in forma servi obediens fa- ctus Deo,usque ad mortem,mortem autem crucis. Non enim tantum eos redemit, qui vitiis & flagi- tiis sese manciparunt Diabolo, sed totum mun- dum, qui erat sub peccato conclusus, Rom. XI. v. 33. & ὑπόδικος obnoxius Deo, Rom. III. 19. nec non servus & subjectus Diabolo: à quo enim quis devictus, ejus servus factus est 2. Petr. III.

vers. 19. adeoque liberavit nos à potestate tene- brarum per ἀπολύτρωσιν redemptionem, sanguine suo factam, Col. I. vers. 13. 14. Nihil hîc de po- testate in Diabolum post resurrectionem obten- ta, sed de mortis CHRISTI λύτρῳ, & victo- riâ per mortem nostri loco exantlatam parta: qua expoliavit Principatus, & potestates tradu- xit confidenter, palam triumphans eos in semet- ipso, Coloss. II. vers. 15. Notamus hic I. Destru- endum: qui est διάβολος non μοναδικῶς, sed εἰδι- κῶς in totâ specie, ut 1. Petr. V. vers. 8. 1. Johan. III. vers. 8. Johan. IIX. vers. 44. Ephes. VI. vers. 12. II. Destructionem: quæ non est Diaboli ratione substantiæ, vel malitiæ inhærentis, sed ratione malitiæ exercitæ, & qua τὸ κράτος τοῦ θανάτου habet per tyrannicam ejusdem in homines oc- cupationem, Johan. IIX. vers. 44. non absque justâ DEI permissione eandem potestatem ex- ercens. Est autem illa κατάργησις CHRISTI tum moralis & acquisitoria tum realis & applica- toria. Ista facta est per mortem CHRISTI: hæc peragitur in throno DEI. De illa hic agi- tur: ad quam κατάργησις τοῦ νόμου Col. II. v. 14. liberatio à maledictione legis Galat. III. vers. 13. stimuli mortis ademtio 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 55. Romanor. V. vers. 15. peccatorum abolitio Ebr. IX. vers. 25. cap. X. vers. 12. spectat. Opus enim erat tali destructione, quæ tolleret jus adversum nos, cui inhærebat potestas mortis, & tyran- nis Satanæ adversus nos exercita: quod uti re- spectu DEI decernentis fuit justissimum, ob peccatum generis humani, sic respectu Satanæ injuste arreptum: adeoque ratione DEI requi- rebat satisfactionem, ratione Satanæ vero erat extinguendum per κατάργησιν: quæ actutum sequuta, ubi res apud DEUM composita. Hæc (posterior) κατάργησις ad officium Christi Re- gium potissimum spectat, de qua 1. Corinth. XV. vers. 24. 25. Roman. XVI. vers. 20. III. Modum præsentis destructionis. Per mortem dicitur facta κατάργησις istius potestatis, quatenus nempe ea fuit satisfactoria pro peccatis. Nam alias; nisi divinæ justitiæ præstita fuisset per mortem Chri- sti satisfactio, jus mortis & Satanæ in nos abo- litum non foret, quod habebatur ex judicio di- vino ob peccatum adversus nos. Ideo per mor- tem suam Christus dicitur solvisse, quæ non ra- puit Psalm. LXIX. vers. 5. 6. & factus ἀντίλυτρον pro nobis 1. Timoth. II. vers. 6. Quod adumbra- tum fuit per mortem victimarum, utpote quæ datæ sunt pro animâ hominum Levit. XVII. v. 11. ad figurandam satisfactionem Christi. Et quid opus fuisset, ut ipse æternus Dei Filius, & car- nis ac sanguinis nostri particeps fieret, & mor- tem subiret, si tantum doctrinâ, & exemplo de- strui poterat Diabolus. Sed de his in Socinismo pro- fligato. Quo de Chrysostomus: Hic ostendit, quod est mirabile, nempe quod per quam vicit Diabolus, per eam victus fuit, & quæ erant arma ei valida adversus orbem terræ, nempe mors, per eam ipsum Christus feriit. Hic ejus qui vicit, magnam indi- cat potentiam. Vides quantum bonum mors fecerit. Et liberaret eos qui timore mortis per totam vitam obnoxii erant servituti. Cur, inquit, horretis? Quid timetis eam, quæ est abolita, planeque & inanis & otiosa? Non est amplius terribilis, sed est conculca- ta, contempta, vilis, & abjecta, & plane nullius pretii. Et porro ostendit autem, non solum cessasse mortem, sed per eam illum quoque, qui adversum nos semper bellum gerit implacabile, Diabolum, inquam, esse fractum & prostratum. Nam qui mortem non timet, est extra Diaboli tyrannidem.

Si enim pellem pro pelle, & omnia dabit quis pro anima sua, quando etiam ipsam ausus fuerit de- spicere, cujusnam jam erit servus? Nullum timet, nullum formidat: Est omnibus superior, & omni- bus magis liberalis. Qui enim animam suam de- spicit, multo magis alia. Quando autem talem ani- mam invenerit Diabolus, nihil ex iis, quæ sua sunt, in ea poterit efficere. Similiter Theophylactus: Causam dispensationis exponit, ut per mortem vi- delicet, quam ille subivit, qui carnis esset & sangui- nis particeps, Diabolum perdat, qui habet mortis imperium. Quomodo? Per peccatum videlicet. Cum enim ex priori illa Adæ inobedientia homines suis artibus faceret in peccata prolabi, ipse mox condidit mortem, quæ eodem imposterum pro mili- te & fortioribus armis humanam hanc adversus naturam est usa. Morte igitur hac ipsa, ut Dia- bolum expugnaret & perderet, usus est Christus. Quod utique ingentis virtutis & sapientiæ est ar- gumentum, ut hostem iisdem armis occideret, qui- bus ille plurimos enecasset. Non autem dicit Apo- stolus, Christum nos liberasse à morte, sed à me- tu mortis: Nam quamvis tum à morte æterna, quæ est mors secunda, tum à temporali morte, qua est stipendium peccati, liberârit nos, ut non amplius mortis pœna obnoxii essemus, hic tamen peculiariter de metu mortis egit Apostolus; quia nihil nisi mortis metus ob oculos versatur extra Christum, (qui vita nostra, & ἀρχηγὸς salutis) idque ob peccatum. Quum vero Christus morte sua pro peccato satisfecerit, à metu illo mortis liberati per Christi mortem sumus. Per totam autem vitam dicimur metu mortis rei, & obno- xii fuisse servituti, quia servi facti sumus ejus, qui mortis habebat imperium, & per peccatum nos morti mancipandi potestatem obtinebat, hoc est, Diabolo, vel quia rei servitutis eramus, quod mors nobis dominaretur per peccatum, ut Rom. V. docuit Apostolus; à cujus tyrannide liberati sumus per mortem Christi. S. Chrysostomus di- versas affert explicationes: Quid est autem, ti- more mortis per totam vitam obnoxii erant servi- tuti? Quid hoc est? Quod qui mortem timet, est servus, & sustinet omnia, ne moriatur. At illud quod omnes erant servi mortis, & quod ea nondum esset abolita, ejus dominatu tenebantur. Aut quod in perpetuo metu viverent homines, semper expe- ctantes se morituros, & mortem formidantes nul- lius voluptatis sensum poterant accipere, quum hic semper vis adesset metus. Hoc enim tacitè significa- vit, dicens per totam vitam. De servitute Dia- boli Osiander explicat, totum locum ita illustrans: Quia ergo pueri seu filii communicaverunt carni & sanguini, id est, quia carnem & sanguinem ha- bent; etiam ipse æternus Dei Filius similiter partici- pavit iisdem: assumpsit veram naturam humanam ex carne & sanguine pudicissimæ virginis Mariæ (Christus igitur (substantiæ ratione) eandem car- nem habet, quam nos: sed sine peccato. Quod no- tandum est contra Schwenckfeldianorum deliria, qui asseverant, Christi humanitatem ratione sub- stantiæ non esse eandem cum nostra carne.) Ideo autem Filius Dei assumpsit humanam naturam, ut in ea posset mortem (pœnam peccatorum nostro- rum) sustinere: ut per mortem suam, quam inno- cens passus est, destrueret, vinceret atque conculca- ret eum, qui habebat mortis imperium, id est Dia- bolum. (Satan enim propter peccatum jus habuit homines occidendi & corporali & æterna mor- te. Sed hoc jus illi Christus per mortem suam, quam ipse non meruerat, eripuit. Itaque pii & ipsi sunt mortis, (quæ in somnum conversa est) victores:

& mors æterna nihil prorsus juris in eos habet, qui in Christum credunt.) Et quidem mortem Chri- stus passus est, ut liberaret eos è tyrannide Diaboli, qui timore mortis per totam vitam obnoxii erant servituti, id est, Satan per peccatum in tristissima servitute sub jugo suo tenebat genus humanum: ita ut non modo in continuo mortis metu essent, ve- rum etiam nihil aliud expectare possent miserrimi homines, nisi ut per corporalem mortem in æter- nam mortem seu damnationem præcipitarentur. At hic metus omnibus in Christum credentibus jam adeptus est, & ipsi in libertatem filiorum DEI sunt restituti. B. Hunnii explicatio sic habet: Ut per mortem aboleret: Causa finalis incarnationis Christi ostenditur, quæ est, ut quia immutabili Dei- tate sua pati non poterat, assumpta mortali carne moreretur, & per mortem suam aboleret potestatem ejus, qui mortis imperium habebat in homines, nempe Diaboli: Et sic in libertatem pristinam asse- reret homines, qui propter peccatum & ipsi morti fuissent obnoxii, & mortis etiam metu, qui sæpe ter- ribilior est morte, per omnem vitam alias fuissent discruciati, eo quod ob transgressionem legis æternæ quoque damnatio post mortem illis fuisset expectan- da & reformidanda, nisi Filius DEI incarnatus morte sua tristissimam illam servitutem credentibus abro- gasset. Observamus itaque I. Redemtos: ὅσοι φόβῳ θανάτε διὰ παντὸς t̃ zῆν ἔνοχοι ἦσαν δε- λείας. Ubi ellipsis est præpositionis ἐν in metu mor- tis erant servi. Nam in morte impendente timor, & in timore servitus est; διὰ παντὸς τ̃ zῆν, id est, ἐν πάσῃ τῇ zωῇ. διὰ pro ἐν 1. Timoth. II. 15. Ebr. VII. 9. Rom. IV. 11. Gal. IV. 13. Verbum pro nomine Luc. VII. 21. ὅσοι sunt omnes, h. e. singuli generum, non genera singulorum Matth. XIV. 36. Marc. III. 10. c. VI. 11. 56. Luc. IV. 4. c. IX. 5. Johan. I. 12. c. X. 8. Gal. III. 27. II. Ἀπάλλαξιν: quæ reconciliationem infert generis humani cum Deo. Postquam enim pessima facta ab hominibus ἀλλαγὴ, qua redditi sunt alieni à vita Dei Eph. IV. 18. & propter quam ira Dei manet super eos, Joh. III. 36. ac legis ma- ledictio Gal. III. 13. opus fuit ἀπαλλαγῇ quæ in Deo constituenda, vel in Christo per Deum, sic ut Chri- stus receptis nostris peccatis in se, & justa satis- factione peremtis, Deum generi humano propi- tiaret, & nobis justitia ista donata pulso pœnarum metu fiduciam ad Deum accedendi faceret, ut ita reducerentur homines ad Deum. Unde postmo- dum ἀρχιερεὺς dicitur, εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρ- τίας τ̃ λα̃̃ vers. 17. Etsi ergo frequenter ver- bum illud de simplici liberatione occurrat, tamen quum & originis ratione reconciliationem im- portet, & qui liberandi sunt reconciliandi omni- no DEO, ut à mortis metu, & servitute liberari possint, nec ab ira DEI, & fulmine legis aliter quam per interventum placationis per Christum factæ immunes sint, recte vi materiæ etiam sub- stratæ liberatio, quæ reconciliatione DEI facta est, intelligitur.

## 2:16
Vers. 16.

Οὐ γὰρ δήπε Ἀγγέλων ἐπιλαμβάνεται) 'Επιλαμβάνεσθαι among Plato and others is to claim formally. Here, however, it is to be understood from the preceding as to claim or to assert into liberty by casting on the hand. The Hebrews are accustomed to translate אָחַז & חָזַק & שָׁבַת by ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι. All these, however, signify the casting on of the hand: in which way the Greek word is taken in Mark VIII. 23, Luke IX. 47, XIV. 4, XXIII. 26, Acts XXIII. 19. Thus below VIII. 9. Moreover, those who are led out from servitude or chains are accustomed to be apprehended by the hand. Nowhere does he claim Angels into liberty, that is, he is introduced claiming. A similar locution to that which is above I. 6.

Ἀλλὰ σπέρματος Ἀβραὰμ ἐπιλαμβάνεται. That is, he does this, that he may liberate you Hebrews from sins and from the fear of death. For the name of the outcome is often given to the work expended on this. Writing to the Hebrews, he is content to speak about them. There is a place elsewhere to speak about the Gentiles. Christ came to liberate the Hebrews, John 8, verse 36. Matthew 1, verse 21, chapter 15, verse 24. Thus Chrysostom and others of the Greeks truly explain this passage.

The Apostle confirms what he had said about the participation of flesh and blood from the Scriptures or by a comparison of the promise made in the Old Testament and the fulfillment in the New Testament, not having neglected the συγκρίσει (comparison) with the angels, which is solemn to him thus far, to whom he preferred the human nature of CHRIST in the state of exaltation in the preceding sections: Thus he now also prefers it in the assumption of the same into the hypostasis of the Son of GOD. For nowhere did he assume angels, but he assumes the seed of Abraham. The little word δήπε is explained by some as a more vehement assertion, and not unreasonably; but it is more correctly taken as referring to place: nowhere, that is, in the sacred writings, in no place of Scripture is he said to assume angels, but he is said to assume the seed of Abraham; which words are not about vindication, as Grotius wishes, or about assistance, as Johannes Camero in his Myrothecium Evangelicum does with the Jesuit Ribera. wishes, by which method they gratify the Socinians, who similarly deprave the passage. Whence Crellius and Schlichtingius appeal to Ribera: But that they treat of the incarnation, or προσλήψει (assumption) of human nature into the divinity of the Son of God, these things teach: 1. The συνέχεια (continuity) of the text. For by the particle γὰρ (for) a reason is rendered for the preceding: For just as he confirmed all things which the Apostle said by oracles of Scripture or by consequences deduced from Scripture: So also that had to be confirmed from the Scriptures, that the Son of GOD was made a partaker of flesh and blood: and that this is now to be demonstrated, the Apostle teaches by the causal particle γὰρ: As he previously proved the subjection of all things from David, as he proved the συναδελφίαν (brotherhood) from various places of Scripture: So now he also had to prove that μετοχὴν καὶ κοινωνίαν τῆς σάρκος καὶ αἵματος (participation and communion of flesh and blood) after the manner of children: Which therefore is to be believed to be done here. He spoke only of liberation as the end of the ἐνσαρκώσεως (incarnation), being about to act particularly concerning the explanation of the office regarding those things which look to that: But here he is not properly occupied with those things which look to the office, but which look to the person of CHRIST. 2. The σαφήνεια (clarity) of the words. All things are perspicuous if they are taken concerning the assumption into the hypostasis of the Son of GOD: but ambiguous and doubtful if concerning vindication or assistance. For whether we look at that which was assumed, or the one assuming, or the act of assumption, all things are straightforward, according to our explanation: That which was assumed is the seed of Abraham, or that which was procreated from the seed of Abraham. That the one assuming is the Son of GOD begotten from eternity, and consubstantial with the Father, true and eternal God, who, being about to liberate us through his death, had need to assume human nature, so that he might have what he would offer for us, and might be able to undergo death for us: it is evident from chapter 1. The assumption itself also belongs to the Son of God, but not indeed to Christ according to both natures: For the Son of GOD was also said before to participate in flesh and blood. These are predicates of a simple λόγος (word/reason), but not of a composite suppositum, or of Christ the God-man. But the denomination of the seed of Abraham does not fit assistance or vindication; for what, did CHRIST wish to assist only the posterity of Abraham, or to vindicate only it into liberty? Nor does the subject, which is the Son of GOD ἄσαρκος (without flesh), and not God manifested in the flesh, or the whole suppositum after the ἐνσάρκωσιν (incarnation), or the whole Christ. Nor does the word ἐπιλαμβάνεται itself favor the Adversaries more than our opinion, since its force and use are to be sought not from Plato, but from Scripture and the context, as will be said later. 3. The ἀρμονία (harmony) of the promises of the Old Testament. For from that it is evident that nothing was promised concerning the angels, whether regarding their nature or regarding their being raised to dignity: But promises were made concerning the seed of Abraham, that in it all the nations of the earth are to be blessed, concerning that which is to come forth from Abraham, concerning the μοναδικῷ (unique) seed, concerning the individual to arise from his lineage, that it is to be assumed by the Son of God, the eternal God, Creator of heaven and earth, so that through this οἰκονομίαν (economy) that blessing might be obtained by all, the curse having been overthrown, and that seed of the woman, which was promised to Adam himself, might crush the head of the infernal serpent, Genesis 12, verse 3, chapter 22, verse 18, chapter 3, verse 15. Concerning which seed, therefore, the evangelical promises once made treat, concerning the same also the fulfillment is to be understood. But those speak concerning the seed of Abraham understood μοναδικῶς (uniquely) and singularly. He does not say in seeds, as of many, says the Apostle, but in seed, as of one, which is CHRIST, Galatians 3, verse 16. Concerning which unique seed being assumed by the Son of GOD, testimonies of the Holy Spirit exist everywhere, but nowhere concerning angels being assumed. But those speak not of the posterity of Abraham being assumed, but of the individual seed of the woman, the seed of Abraham, the unique seed of Isaac, the seed of Jacob being assumed from the family of Abraham. Concerning the raising up of a branch for David after his death, which was the Son of GOD, concerning the one to come forth from the loins of David, who is both David's Son and Lord, concerning the branch of David, which will be Jehovah; concerning the son of the virgin, who is Immanuel, GOD with us, the future God-man, and Son of the Most High. 4. The ἀκολουθία (sequence) of the preceding words. For the matter of assistance and deliverance had already been treated before, as the final cause of the communication of flesh and blood, which if it be indicated here again in the present words, would not a begging of the question be committed according to the gloss of the dissenters! He delivered the faithful from death. For He delivered them by laying on a hand, as it were, and delivered the seed of Abraham, that is, the faithful. How much more conveniently is the reason rendered here, why παραπλησίως similarly, as τὰ παιδία the faithful, whom GOD gave to His Son, the Son of God κεκοινώνηκε καὶ μετέσχε has communicated in and partaken of our flesh and blood, and has been made a partaker of them, that He might destroy the Devil, and deliver us from the fear of death, because, forsooth, He ἐπιλαμβάνεται takes hold of the seed of Abraham. Imagine it to be said that He delivers the seed of Abraham, and delivers them from the Devil and the fear of death, and neither will that κοινωνία and μετοχὴ, which was to be proved, be taught, and the same will at least be proved by the same. And since in such an illustrious manner in verses 14 and 15. the Apostle has already described the deliverance and liberation of CHRIST, what was the point of inculcating the same thing again, and indeed in a more obscure manner of speaking? σπέρματος Ἀβραὰμ ἐπιλαμβάνεται, that is, He acts so as to deliver you Hebrews from sins and the fear of death. But it was of interest to pursue this more fully, to assert further τὴν κατὰ πάντων ὁμοιότητα, by which there was need of such a High Priest, who ought to be touched by the misery of his brothers and to have mercy on them, because according to Scripture He did not assume Angels, but our nature, and therefore this dignity and grace has uniquely fallen to it, that it enjoys the brotherhood of the Son of God. 5. The proper meaning of the word ἐπιλαμβάνεται. For this word properly denotes to take something by laying hold of it, as even Ostorod the Socinian himself admits. For it is never placed absolutely and nakedly to mean the same as to receive into favor, which from is usually accustomed to be [translated] by the first [meaning] through τὸ ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι, as can be seen in Luke 1, verse 54. For this reason, the Syrian here used the word ܢܣܒ, which properly signifies to apprehend, to join something to oneself. Chrysostom has this to say about this word: He did not, he says, apprehend the nature of Angels, but of man. But what is 'apprehend'? For he did not, he says, apprehend that nature of the Angels, but ours. But why did he not say 'took up', but used this expression 'apprehend'? From a metaphor of those who pursue those who are turning away, and do everything so that they may catch those who are fleeing, and apprehend those who are jumping back. For he pursued and apprehended human nature itself, which was fleeing and fleeing far away; we were far off. Similarly Theophylact: For he did not, he says, accept, but apprehended, to show that this nature of ours, which was fleeing and going further away from him, Christ had pursued, and having finally attained it, had apprehended it, and united it to himself, and having drawn it back from flight, had embraced it. Nor did he say the nature of men, but the seed of Abraham, as much to exalt the Jews and argue that their race was honored, as to assert that they in this respect precede the nations, because the Lord had drawn his origin from them. Nor does Oecumenius say otherwise, so that I have reason to marvel at Grotius, who attributes a completely different opinion to these Fathers, whom he must not have inspected. Naturally, the Greek Doctors explain the emphasis of the word, used by the Apostle with care, because he did not use that word without cause, which would at the same time insinuate again the end already indicated through ἀπάλλαξιν. But that the assumption of our nature is not excluded but included by this word, Chrysostom openly teaches, διὰ τῦτό φησι, τὴν σάρκα ἀνέλαβε τὴν ἡμέτεραν διὰ φιλανθρωπίαν μόνον, ἵνα ἐλεήσῃ ἡμᾶς. Which Chrysostom confirmed both from what preceded and from what followed. From what preceded in this way: Wishing to show the great kindness and charity of GOD, which he had toward the human race, after he said: Since therefore the children have shared in flesh and blood, and he himself likewise participated in the same, he explains and pursues this passage. For do not attend lightly to what has been said, nor think that it is bare, and that it has nothing hidden, that he himself took up our flesh. For he did not grant this to the Angels. For, he says, he did not apprehend the Angels, but the seed of Abraham. Concerning what follows, compared with those things, a little later. Similarly Theophylact: For he never apprehended the Angels, that is, he by no means seized the nature of the Angels, nor did he take this. That indeed argues for an immense charity toward the human race. Since he bestowed upon man what he did not lavish upon the Angelic nature, so that he might assume flesh from him. Therefore, the Blessed Gerhard rightly signifies ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι as to apprehend most firmly, to retain, not to dismiss, not to lay aside. For what ὁ λόγος has once assumed, he never lays aside. 6. The analogy of the whole proposition with other places. For what is it for the Son of God to have assumed the seed of Abraham κατ’ ἀναλογίαν of other places of Scripture? So indeed the Son of God ἐπιλαμβάνεται the seed of Abraham, that he himself is and is called the seed of Abraham, Gen. 22, verse 18, Gal. 3, verse 16. But how can the Son of God, that eternal GOD, be called the seed of Abraham otherwise than through that ἐπίληψιν, by which he assumed human nature from the progeny of Abraham into his own hypostasis, born of the Fathers according to the flesh. Furthermore, this γνώμη is to be accepted concerning that assumption, by which the Son of God was made like us in all things, our brother, and ὁμοιοπαθής to us. Which indeed is not a gracious vindication or acceptance of us, but an assumption of our nature. Moreover, the vindication into liberty was not owed only to the Hebrew people, but to all the nations of the earth. But the assumption of the seed of Abraham, or the taking up of human nature from Abraham, was the proper prerogative and glory of the Hebrews, Rom. 9:15. Nor without cause did the Apostle prefer to say σπέρμα Ἀβραὰμ, rather than human nature. That was done partly so that he might look back at the promises made to Abraham and his descendants concerning the blessed seed, Gen. 12, ch. 22, ch. 22, etc. which he hints are completed in this assumption, partly so that by naming Abraham the Patriarch, he might show honor both to the Father of believers himself, and also to our nature: Concerning which St. Chrysostom: And he did not say only he apprehended men, but wishing to exalt them, and to show that their race is great and honorable, he says, but he apprehended the seed of Abraham. 7. The anomaly of the opposing explanation, which through the seed of Abraham understand either the whole race of the elect or of the faithful from the Jews and Gentiles with Cameron, or with others, whose opinion Estius says is more probable, the carnal posterity of Abraham. For the word seed cannot be understood in this place concerning the human nature species, either collectively, or so that it may be restricted to the spiritual or carnal posterity of Abraham. Crellius and Schlichting fluctuate, and do not know how the word ought to be taken, nay, they say most absurdly and contumeliously that the Apostle, by this ambiguous appellation, which can signify both the spiritual and the corporeal seed of Abraham, gratified the Jews in such a way that he might at the same time signify that they ought to become Christians, who alone are the spiritual seed of Abraham, Gal. 3:29. Whence the spiritual seed ought to be understood here rather than the carnal. It is too manifest that this name must be taken μονάδικῶς and singularly, so much so that even Pareus himself had to admit it, by the force of the collation of Gen. 3:15, ch. 22:18, Gal. 3:16 with Gen. 4:26. In the first promise, he says, the seed of the woman is called Christ singularly, not collectively. It cannot and ought not to be taken otherwise in this place. For the subject is the incarnation of the Son of GOD, and it is explained how and whence He became a partaker of the flesh and blood of the children, because, being the Son of God, He assumed the seed of Abraham, that is, human nature, not only of men in general, but also in particular, the seed of Abraham, that is, the seed of the blessing of Abraham promised, or a certain individual man, from the family of Abraham, by being born of the virgin Mary, a daughter of Abraham according to the flesh, according to the oracles of the Prophets and the history of the Gospel. The Apostle expressed this in 1 Tim. III. 16 by the word σαρκὸς, God appeared IN THE FLESH, that is, in the assumed human nature, which he calls so synecdochically, primarily because it was assumed with the infirmities of the flesh, but without sin, by which indeed not a specific, but an individual nature was endowed. St. John indicated this when he says λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο, The Word was made flesh, chap. I. ver. 14, and the holy Apostle signifies the same again, Romans I. ver. 4, CHRIST is of the seed of David according to the flesh, and Romans IX. ver. 5, Christ is from the Fathers τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, which refers to His human nature, which is indeed singular and individual. And this contributes to the greater majesty of so great a mystery and the more eminent magnitude of supreme love, that the Son of God, true God, 1 John V. ver. 20, the great God, Tit. II. ver. 14, assumed that nature which is from the seed, and which is the seed, which is from the flesh, and is flesh.

God blessed for ever, Rom. IX. 5. Jehovah that immutable God, whose name is I AM THAT I AM, Exod. III. Jerem. XXIII. 5. Which stupendous mystery the highest of the Angels desire to look into, and gaze upon with the greatest appetite and incredible pleasure, 1. Petr. I. verse 12. 8. The connection of the consequences, which do not speak of assistance or vindication, but of the likeness with the brethren, whose nature he assumed, and which pertain to the human nature of the Son of God, because the Son of God could not otherwise be made like his brethren in all things, except that he assumed their same nature. Concerning which Chrysostom: See however with what force and how he shows him to apply great effort, that he might be made like unto us, which indeed was of great care and providence. For when he had said above: Since the children were partakers of flesh and blood, and he himself likewise participated in the same, here also he says he was made like unto his brethren in all things, saying almost, he who is so great, who is the brightness of glory, who is the character of the substance, who made the ages, who sits at the right hand of the Father, he willed and set his effort, that he might become our brother in all things, and therefore he dismissed the Angels and supernal powers, and descended to us, and apprehended us, and did innumerable good things, broke death, snatched us from the tyranny of the Devil, freed us from servitude: he honored us not only with brotherhood, but also with other innumerable things. For he willed to be our High Priest before the Father. So also Theophylact. To the consequences also pertains the Priesthood of Christ, whose work was the assumption of human nature. Concerning which Theodoret on this passage: Because it was human, which he assumed, he paid the debt of men indeed through passion, but through the resurrection of the suffered body he showed his power. But the divine Apostle very wisely placed a proper name for a general one. For he did not say, he apprehended the seed of man, but he apprehended the seed of Abraham, recalling to them also the promise made to Abraham. To those things which follow concerning the Priesthood: He shows, he says, that his saving death was an oblation. For he offered the body which he took for the whole creation. Which Chrysostom more clearly called into account thus: For he subjoins, he says, that he might become a merciful and faithful High Priest before God. Therefore, he says, he took our flesh for the sake of kindness and mercy alone, that he might have mercy on us. For there is no other cause of the dispensation than this alone. For he saw us cast down on the ground perishing, and oppressed by the tyranny of death, and he had mercy. To which Theophylact has similar things on this passage: That he might become merciful &c. For no other cause, he says, did he assume this our flesh, except that through it he might have mercy on us, and lift up those lying on the ground. To which is added 9. the consensus of the Catholic Church, which by approving the Athanasian creed approves this interpretation. For in the same we profess from this Apostolic passage, that the Son of God, God and man, is one Christ by the assumption of humanity into God. 10. Addenda and especially the Grotian [interpretation] in perverting the passage with trickery. He delivers this sense; He acts to free you Hebrews from sins and from the fear of death. But the Apostle does not speak of that which is of the Hebrews, but of that which is of all whom he deigns to call his brethren, of all the free children given by God to the Son of God, with whom he was made a participant of flesh and blood in like manner, to whom he is like in all things, whose High Priest Christ is &c.: Much less does he treat only of those Hebrews to whom he wrote this epistle. Nor indeed does the Apostle give the name of the work to the result, but he discourses about the work itself, and that a notable one, of the assumption of the seed of Abraham, a comparison having been instituted with the Angels, because it is nowhere read that he assumed the Angels, but the seed of Abraham. The Apostle does not say that he acts only to free those Hebrews, but he apprehends, he says, the seed of Abraham, that through death he might free all who were held by the fear of death, and were subject to most miserable servitude, whence that apprehension of our nature was necessary, that he might be able to undergo death and free all mortals.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Οὐ γὰρ δήπε Ἀγγέλων ἐπιλαμβάνεται) Ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι apud Platonem & alios est solenniter vindicare. Hic au- tem ex superioribus intelligendum est vindicare sive asse- rere in libertatem manu injecta. Ebræi אָחַז & חָזַק & שָׁבַת solent verti per ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι. Omnia autem hæc manus injectionem significant: quomodo Græca vox su- mitur Marc. VIII. 23. Luc. IX. 47. XIV. 4. XXIII. 26. Act. XXIII. 19. Sic infra VIII. 9. Solent autem manu appre- hendi, qui e servitute aut vinculis educuntur. Nusquam in libertatem vindicat Angelos, id est, vindicans introdu- citur. Par loquutio ei quæ supra I. 6.

Ἀλλὰ σπέρματος Ἀβραὰμ ἐπιλαμβάνεται. Id est, id agit, ut vos Ebræos liberet à peccatis & à metu mortis. Eventus enim nomen sæpe datur operæ in id impensæ. Ebræis scribens satis habet de illis loqui. De gentibus alibi loquendi locus. Christus ad Ebræos liberandos venit, Johan. VIII. vers. 36. Matth. I. vers. 21. cap. XV. vers. 24. Ita hunc locum vere explicat Chrysosto- mus & Græcorum alii.

Confirmat Apostolus quod dixerat de parti- cipatione carnis & sanguinis è Scripturis vel com- paratione promissi in Veteri Testamento, & com- plementi in Novo Testamento facti, non negle- cta hactenus sibi solemni συγκρίσει cum Ange- lis, quibus uti humanam CHRISTI naturam in exaltationis statu prætulit in superioribus : Ita etiam in assumptione ejusdem in hypostasin Filii DEI jam præfert. Nuspiam enim Ange- los assumpsit, sed assumit semen Abrahæ.
