Vocula & δήπε de asseveratione vehementiori à nonnul- lis explicatur, neque sane; sed rectius de loco acci- pitur: nuspiam, scilicet in sacris literis, nullo in Scripturæ loco Angelos assumere dicitur, dicitur vero assumere semen Abraham; quæ verba non de vindicatione, ut vult Grotius, aut de opitula- tione, ut cum Ribera Jesuita in commentar. Jo- hannes Camero in myroth. Evangel. vult, quo pacto gratificantur Socinianis, similiter locum depravantibus. Unde ad Riberam provocant Crellius & Schlichtingius: Sed de incarnatione, vel προσλήψει humanæ naturæ εἰς θεότητα Filii Dei agere, hæc docent: 1. Textus συνέχεια. Nam per particulam γὰρ ratio redditur superiorum : Ut enim omnia, quæ dixit Apostolus Scripturæ oraculis aut consequentiis è Scriptura deductis, confirmavit: Ita etiam id confirmandum erat è Scripturis, quod Filius DEI particeps factus sit carnis & sanguinis: idque jam demonstratum iri, Apostolus, particula γὰρ causali docet: Ut omnium subjectionem è Davide, ut συναδελφίαν è diversis locis Scripturæ antea probavit : Ita nunc etiam illam μετοχὴν καὶ κοινωνίαν τῆς σάρ- κος καὶ αἵματος adinstar liberorum probare de- buit: Quod proinde hic fieri credendum est. De liberatione tantum dixit ceu fine ἐνσαρκώσεως, peculiariter acturus circa explicationem officii de illis, quæ eo spectant: Hic autem non ver- satur proprie in iis, quæ ad officium, sed quæ ad personam CHRISTI spectant. 2. Verborum σαφήνεια. Perspicua sint omnia, si de assumptio- ne in hypostasin Filii DEI accipiantur: at am- bigua & dubia, si de vindicatione vel opitulatio- ne. Sive enim respiciamus id, quod assumptum est, sive assumentem, sive assumptionis actum, expedita sunt omnia, juxta nostram explicatio- nem: Id quod assumptum est, semen Abrahæ, vel procreatum ex Abrahæ semine. Assumen- tem esse Filium DEI ab æterno genitum, & consubstantialem Patri, verum & æternum Deum, qui per mortem suam nos liberaturus assumere humanam naturam necessum habuit, ut, quod offerret pro nobis, haberet, ac mor- tem pro nobis subire posset : è cap. I. constat. Assumptio etiam ipsa Filio Dei, non vero Chri- sto secundum utramque naturam convenit: Nam Filius DEI etiam antea dictus est participare carnem & sanguinem. Prædicata hæc sunt λόγυ simplicis, non vero suppositi συνθέτε, vel Chri- sti θεανθρώπε. At opitulationi vel vindicationi non convenit denominatio seminis Abrahæ; quid enim, num soli Abrahæ posteritati opitu- lari, aut eam solum in libertatem vindicare vo- luit CHRISTUS? nec subjectum, quod est Filius DEI ἄσαρκος, non autem Deus in carne manifestatus, vel totum suppositum post ἐνσάρ- κωσιν, vel totus Christus. Nec etiam ipsum ver- bum ἐπιλαμβάνεται magis favet Adversariis, quam nostræ sententiæ, utpote cujus vis & usus non è Platone, sed ex Scriptura & contextu petendus, ut deinde dicetur. 3. Promissionum Veteris Testa- menti ἀρμονία. Nam ex illo constat de Angelis nihil promissum esse, sive quoad naturam eo- rum, sive quoad dignitatem evehendis : Promis- sa autem facta de semine Abrahæ, quod in eo- dem benedicenda sint omnes gentes terræ, de eo, quod ex Abrahamo proditurum, de semine μο- ναδικῷ, de individuo è prosapia ejus orituro, quod id assumendum sit à Filio Dei, æterno Deo, Creatore cœli & terræ, ut per hanc οἰκονομίαν benedictio illa maledictione profligata omni- bus obtinget, ac semen illud mulieris, quod A- damo ipsi promissum erat, caput serpenti infer- nali conterat, Genes. XII. vers. 3. cap. XXII. vers. 18. cap. III. vers. 15. De quo ergo semine promis- siones Evangelicæ quondam factæ agunt, de eodem etiam complementum intelligendum. At illæ de semine Abrahæ μοναδικῶς & singula- riter intellecto loquuntur. Non in seminibus, ceu pluribus, inquit Apostolus, sed in semine, tanquam uno, quod est CHRISTUS, Galat. III. vers. 16. De quo unico semine assumendo à Fi- lio DEI passim extant testimonia Spiritus san- cti, nuspiam autem de assumendis Angelis. Illa autem non de assumenda posteritate Abrahæ, sed de assumendo è familia Abrahæ individuo semine mulieris, semine Abrahæ, semine Isaaci, semine Jacobi monadico loquuntur. De exci- tando Davidi germine post fata, quod Filius DEI erat, de prodituro è lumbis Davidis, qui Davidis & Filius & Dominus, de germine Da- vidis, quod erit Jehovah; de filio virginis, quod Immanuel, DEUS nobiscum, θεάνθρωπος futurus, & Filius Altissimi. 4. Verborum præce- dentium ἀκολουθία. Nam de opitulatione ac vin- dicatione jam antea actum erat, ceu causa fina- li communicationis carnis & sanguinis, quæ si hic iterum indicetur verbis præsentibus, annon petitio principii committetur secundum glos- sam dissentientium ! Liberavit fideles à morte. Nam vindicavit manu quasi injecta, & liberavit semen Abrahæ, hoc est fideles. Quanto conve- nientius ratio hic redditur, cur παραπλησίως simi- liter, ut τὰ παιδία fideles, quos DEUS dedit Filio suo, Filius Dei κεκοινώνηκε καὶ μετέσχε com- municavit carni & sanguini nostro, eorumque particeps factus sit, ut destrueret Diabolum, nosque à mortis metu liberaret, quia scilicet semen Abrahæ ἐπιλαμβάνεται. Finge id dici, quia semen Abrahæ liberat, & vindicat à Dia- bolo & metu mortis, nec illa κοινωνία & μετοχὴ, quæ probanda erat, docebitur, & idem saltem per idem probabitur. Et quum tam illustri mo- do vers. 14. & 15. Apostolus jam descripserit vindicationem & liberationem CHRISTI, quid attinebat iterum eandem & quidem obscuriori loquendi ratione inculcare? σπέρματος Ἀβραὰμ ἐπιλαμβάνεται, id est, id agit, ut vos Ebræos libe- ret à peccatis & metu mortis. Hoc vero intererat uberius persequi, ad asserendam porro τὴν κατὰ πάντων ὁμοιότητα, qua opus erat ejusmodi Pontifi- ce, qui fratrum miseria tangi, eorumque misereri debebat, quod secundum Scripturam non Ange- los, sed nostram naturam assumpserit, adeoq; huic unice ea obtigerit dignitas & gratia, ut fruatur Filii Dei fraternitate. 5. Propria verbi ἐπιλαμ- βάνεται σημασία. Nam verbum hoc proprie notat apprehendendo aliquid assumere, fatente ipsomet O- storodo Sociniano. Nunquam a. absolute & nude po- situm idem est, quod in gratiam recipere, quod ex- primi potius solet per τὸ ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι, ut Luc. I vers. 54. videre est. Idcirco Syrus hic usus est voce ܢܣܒ, quæ proprie significat apprehendere, sibi aliquid adjungere. Chrysostomus de hoc ver- bo ita habet: Non Angeli, inquit, apprehendit naturam, sed hominis. Quid est autem apprehen- dit? Non enim apprehendit, inquit, illam Ange- lorum naturam, sed nostram. Cur autem non di- xit, suscepit, sed usus est hac dictione apprehen- dit? A Metaphora eorum, qui persequuntur a- versos, & omnia faciunt, ut fugientes comprehen- dant, & resilientes apprehendant. Ab ipso enim fugientem humanam naturam, & procul fugien- tem, longe eramus, proseqnutus comprehendit. Si- militer Theophylactus: Non enim accepit, inquit, sed apprehendit, ut ostenderet naturam hanc no- stram refugientem, & longius ab se abeuntem, Chri- stum fuisse insectatum, & adeptum tandem appre- bendisse, & sibi univisse, & à fuga retractum com- plexum esse. Nec naturam hominum dixit, sed Abrahæ semen, cum ut Judæos extolleret, & illo- rum genus argueret honoratum, tum ut eosdem in eo affereret anteire gentes, quia ab his Dominus ortum duxisset. Nec aliter Oecumenius, ut mira- ri habeam Grotium, hisce Patribus prorsus aliam sententiam affingentem, quem oportet non in- spexisse eosdem. Nimirum explicant Græci Do- ctores emphasin vocis, ab Apostolo cum cura adhibitæ, quia non citra causam ea usus est vo- ce, quæ finem jam per ἀπάλλαξιν indicatum si- mul iterum insinuaret. Non autem excludi sed comprehendi hac voce naturæ nostræ assumptio- nem, Chrysostomus palam docet, διὰ τῦτό φησι, τὴν σάρκα ἀνέλαβε τὴν ἡμέτεραν διὰ φιλανθρωπίαν μόνον, ἵνα ἐλεήσῃ ἡμᾶς. Quod etiam tum ex an- tecedentibus confirmavit, tum è consequenti- bus Chrysostomus. Ex antecedentibus hoc mo- do: Volens Paulus ostendere multam DEI beni- gnitatem & charitatem, quam habuit in genus humanum, postquam dixit: Quia ergo pueri com- municaverunt carni & sanguini, & ipse simili- ter participavit iisdem, hunc locum explicat & persequitur. Ne enim leviter attendas, quod di- ctum est, neque nudum, & quod nihil habeat la- tens aliquid esse existimes, quod ipse carnem no- stram susceperit. Non enim hoc donavit Angelis. Non enim, inquit, Angelos apprehendit, sed semen Abrahæ. De consequentibus cum illis collatis paulo post. Similiter Theophylactus: Nunquam enim Angelos apprehendit, hoc est, nequaquam Angelorum ille naturam arripuit, neque hanc tulit. Id vero immensam erga genus humanum arguit charitatem. Quandoquidem quod Angelicæ natu- ræ non est elargitus contulerit homini, ut ab hoc carnem assumeret. Ideo recte Beatus Gerhardus ἐπιλαμβάνεσθαι significat firmissime apprehendere, retinere, non dimittere, non deponere. Quod enim ὁ λόγος semel assumpsit, nunquam deponit. 6. Totius propositionis cum aliis locis ἀναλογίαν. Quid enim semen Abrahæ assumpsisse Filium Dei κατ’ ἀναλογίαν aliorum Scripturæ locorum est? Ita sane Filius Dei ἐπιλαμβάνεται semen Abrahæ, ut ipse sit & dicatur semen Abrahæ, Genes. XXII. vers. 18. Gal. III. vers. 16. Qui autem Filius Dei, æternus ille DEUS, Abrahæ semen dici potest aliter, quam per eam ἐπίληψιν, qua ex Abrahæ progenie naturam humanam in suam hypostasin assumpsit ex Patribus, natus secundum carnem. Porro de ea assumptione hæc γνώμη accipienda, qua Filius Dei per omnia nobis factus similis, fra- ter noster, nobisque ὁμοιοπαθής. Quæ vero non est gratiosa nostri vindicatio vel acceptatio, sed naturæ nostræ assumptio. Adhæc vindicatio in libertatem non Ebræo tantum populo debeba- tur, sed omnibus terræ nationibus. At seminis Abrahæ assumptio seu humanæ naturæ ex Abra- hamo susceptio Ebræorum propria erat præro- gativa & gloria, Roman. IX. 15. Nec absque causa Apostolus maluit dicere σπέρμα Ἀβραὰμ, quam naturam humanam. Factum id partim, ut re- spiceret promissiones Abrahæ, ejusque poste- ris, de benedicto semine, factas, Genes. XII. cap. XXII. c. XXII. &c. quas in hac assumptione com- pletas esse innuit, partim ut nominato Abraha- mo Patriarcha illustri honorem tum ipsi Patri credentium, tum etiam naturæ nostræ exhiberet: De quo S. Chrysostomus: Et non dixit solum homi- nes apprehendit, sed volens ipsos extollere, & eo- rum genus esse magnum & honorandum ostende- re, dicit, sed semen Abrahæ apprehendit. 7. Ex- plicationis adversariæ ἀνωμαλία, quæ per semen Abrahæ vel totum genus electorum aut fidelium ex Judæis & gentibus cum Camerone, vel cum aliis, quorum sententiam magis probabilem E- stius dicit, carnalem Abrahæ posteritatem intelli- gunt. Non enim de specie humana natura vel collective intelligi hoc loco potest vox seminis si- ve γενικῶς, sive ut ad spiritualem aut carnalem Abrahæ posteritatem restringatur. Crellius & Schlichtingius fluctuant, & quomodo vox acci- pi debeat, nesciunt, imo perquam absurde ac contumeliose dicunt, Apostolum hac ambigua appellatione, quæ semen Abrahæ tum spirituale tum corporale significare potest, ita Judæis gratificatum esse, ut simul significaret, eos debere Christianos fieri, qui soli spirituale semen Abrahæ sunt, Galat. III. 29. Unde hic spirituale semen intelligendum potius sit, quam carnale. Nimis manifestum est, μονάδικῶς & singulariter hoc nomen accipiendum esse, adeo ut etiam Pareus ipse id fateri necessum habuerit, vi collationis Gen. III. 15. cap. XXII. 18. Galat. III. 16. cum Genes. IV. 26. In prima inquit promissione semen mulieris singulariter, non col- lective, dicitur Christus. Non aliter etiam hoc loco accipi potest & debet. Agitur enim de in- carnatione Filii DEI, & explicatur, quomodo & unde carnis & sanguinis puerorum sit parti- ceps factus, quia, cum Filius Dei esset, assum- psit semen Abrahæ, hoc est naturam humanam, non modo hominum in generali, sed & in sin- gulari, semen Abrahæ, hoc est, semen benedi- ctionis Abrahæ promissum, seu certum hominis individuum, ex Abrahæ familia, nascendo ex vir- gine Maria Abrahæ filia secundum carnem, juxta Prophetarum oracula, & Evangelii historiam. Hoc expressit Apostolus 1. Tim. III. 16. voce σαρκὸς, Deus apparuit IN CARNE, hoc est, in natura humana assumpta, quam Synecdochice ita vocat, imprimis quia cum infirmitatibus carnis, sed abs- que peccato, assumpta est, qua vero non specifica, sed individualis natura donata est. Hoc indica- vit S. Johannes, cum λόγος inquit σὰρξ ἐγένετο, Verbum caro factum est cap. I. vers. 14. atque idem significat iterum S. Apostolus, Roman. I. vers. 4. CHRISTUS est e semine Davidis se- cundum carnem, & Roman. IX. vers. 5. Christus est ex Patribus τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, quod ad naturam ejus humanam, quæ utique singularis est & in- dividua. Atque hoc ad majorem tanti myste- rii majestatem & eminentiorem summi amoris magnitudinem facit, quod eam naturam, quæ ex semine est, quæque semen est, quæ ex carne est, & caro est, assumserit Filius Dei, Deus verus, 1. Johan. V. vers. 20. Deus magnus, Tit. II. vers. 14.

Deus benedictus in secula Roman. IX. 5. Jehovah Deus ille immutabilis, cui nomen SUM QUI SUM, Exod. III. Jerem. XXIII. 5. Quod myste- rium stupendum Angelorum summi quique ἐπι- θυμῶσι παρακύψαι, summo appetitu & incredi- bili voluptate gaudent introspicere, 1. Petr. I. vers. 12. 8. Consequentium συνάφεια, quæ non lo- quuntur de opitulatione vel vindicatione, sed de ὁμοιότητι cum fratribus, quorum naturam assum- psit, & ad humanam Filii DEI naturam spe- ctant, quia aliter non potuit Filius DEI fratri- bus per omnia ὁμοιωθῆναι, nisi quia assumpsit eorundem naturam. Quo de Chrysostomus: Vide autem cum quanta vi & quomodo ipsum osten- dat magnam adhibere studium, ut nobis assimile- tur, quod quidem erat magnæ curæ & providen- tiæ. Nam quum dixisset superius: Quia pueri communicaverunt carni & sanguini, & ipse si- militer participavit eisdem, hic quoque dicit per omnia similatum esse fratribus, propemodum di- cens, qui est adeo magnus, qui est splendor glo- riæ, qui est character substantiæ, qui fecit secula, qui sedet ad dextram Patris, is voluit & studium posuit, ut frater noster fieret in omnibus, & ideo dimifit Angelos & supernas potestates, & ad nos descendit, & nos apprehendit, & bona fecit in- numerabilia, mortem fregit, à Diaboli tyranni- de nos eripuit, à servitute nos liberavit: non so- lum fraternitate honoravit, sed etiam aliis innu- merabilibus. Voluit enim esse noster Pontifex apud Patrem. Sic etiam Theophylactus. Ad conse- quentia etiam pertinet Pontificatus Christi, cujus opus erat assumptione humanæ naturæ. Quo de Theodoretus in hunc locum: Quia humanum erat, quod assumpsit, per passionem quidem homi- num debitum exolvit, per passi autem corporis re- surrectionem vim suam ostendit. Valde autem sa- pienter divinus Apostolus pro generali nomine pro- prium posuit. Non dixit enim, semen hominis ap- prehendit, sed semen Abrahæ apprehendit, eis etiam in memoriam revocans promissum fa- ctum Abrahæ. Ad ea quæ de Pontificatu se- quuntur: Ostendit, inquit, salutarem ejus mor- tem fuisse oblationem. Pro universa enim crea- tura, quod sumpsit corpus, obtulit. Quæ luculen- tius Chrysostomus sic in censum vocavit: Subjun- git enim, inquit, ut misericors fieret, & fidelis Pontifex ad Deum. Propterea inquit carnem no- stram suscepit propter benignitatem solum & cle- mentiam, ut nostri miseretur. Non est enim alia dispensationis causa, quam hæc sola. Vidit enim nos humi abjectos pereuntes, & à mortis op- pressos tyrannide, & misertus est. Quibus gemina habet Theophylactus in hunc locum: Ut miseri- cors fieret &c. Nullam, inquit, aliam ob causam carnem hanc nostram assumpsit, nisi ut per eam nostri miseretur, & humi jacentes attolleret. Quibus accedit 9. Ecclesiæ Catholicæ ὁμοψηφία, quæ approbando symbolum Athanasianum in- terpretationem hanc approbat. In eodem enim profitemur ex hoc loco Apostolico, Filium Dei Deum & hominem unum esse Christum assumptio- ne humanitatis in Deum. 10. Addenda & specia- tim Grotiana in loco pervertendo κυβεία. Sen- sum hunc tradit; Id agit, ut vos Ebræos liberet à peccatis & à metu mortis. At Apostolus non de eo, quod Ebræorum est, sed quod omnium, quos dignatur fratres suos nominare, omnium liberorum Filio DEI à DEO datorum, cum qui- bus consimiliter carnis & sanguinis particeps fa- ctus est, quibus per omnia similis est, quorum Pontifex CHRISTUS est &c. loquitur: Multo minus de istis tantum Ebræis agit, ad quos hanc epistolam perscripsit. Neque vero Apostolus eventus nomen operæ impensæ dat, sed de ope- re ipso, eoque insigni assumptionis seminis A- brahæ disserit, comparatione cum Angelis in- stituta, quod nusquam legatur Angelos assum- psisse, sed semen Abrahæ. Non id agere tan- tum ipsum ait Apostolus, ut liberet Ebræos il- los, sed ἐπιλαμβάνεται, inquit, semen Abrahæ, ut per mortem liberet omnes, qui metu mortis tenebantur, & miserrimæ servitutis rei erant, unde illa ἐπιλήψει naturæ nostræ opus erat, ut mortem subire ac mortales omnes liberare posset.

## 2:17
Verse 17. Wherefore it behooved him to be made like unto his brethren in all things.

Understand 'in all things' from the subject matter; adverse things, torture, hard death. 'It behooved', that is, it was so by usage, in which sense the Latins often use 'ought', not from rigor, but with latitude. Thus 'it was necessary' in Luke XXIV. 26. and here just now 'it was fitting'.

We do not deny that that likeness also extends itself to adverse things, torture and death, but we deny that it is to be understood by those alone, excluding the likeness of human nature, concerning which Romans VIII. verse 3. For not even would he be our brother, much less like us brethren in all things, unless he himself were of the same substance and of the same nature with us. That likeness of the Son of God regarding temptations, concerning which it is explained in Hebrews IV. verse 15, presupposes the very truth of human nature, namely that he was made a participant of our flesh and blood similarly as children, and that he took the seed of Abraham into the unity of his person, and so also that the properties of human nature are not truly to be excluded. For by assuming human nature he was made a participant of its properties also. Directly, however, this likeness does not signify the substantial sameness of substance itself, as it has seemed to some Calvinists: But it is to be referred to the state of emptying, by which 'taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in fashion as a man', Philipp. II. verses 7, 8; which state happened to the substantials of nature, and ceased while the truth of nature remained safe. Therefore, that 'in all things' is not to be extended to those peculiar things which pertain to the person of Christ the God-man, such as to the conception of the human nature of Christ by the Holy Spirit without male seed, to the hypostatic union, to the communication of idioms, or which pertain to his exaltation, to the lifting up to the right hand of God and the universal rule in heaven and on earth. These, as they pertain to the person, not to the state, or not to the state of humiliation: So it is by no means to be said that he was made like to those brethren in them. That all things, whereby he was made like unto his brethren, pertain to human nature as their subject, is not to be doubted. Concerning which Athanasius, Orat. III. contra Arian. p. 379, prays: For when was he made? And when did it happen that he was an Apostle? Was it not when he was likewise, as we are, a partaker of blood and flesh? Or when was he made a merciful and faithful High Priest? Unless when he was in all things assimilated to his brethren. Furthermore, he was made like them when, having put on our flesh, he had begun to be a man. Did not the Apostle, therefore, writing of his human dispensation, speak these things? That he was faithful to his creator, and by no means concerning the substance of the Word. But he had brethren then, when he had put on flesh similar to ours, which, offering it himself through himself, the name of High Priest he obtained. Chrysostom on this passage: Whence was it necessary that he be made like his brothers in all things? What is 'in all things'? He was, he says, brought forth by birth, and nourished, and he grew, and he suffered all things which it was necessary to suffer, and at length he died. This is to be made like the brothers in all things. For since he said many things about his majesty and heavenly glory, from here on he makes words about the dispensation. Following him according to custom, Theophylact: For when, he says, he deigned once to put on this flesh of ours, and to take up human nature, it was altogether consistent that he should be born very similar to us, and have both education and growth equal to ours: And that he should bear all things which were to be borne by him, and finally undergo death. For that is what he intends, when he says 'to be made like in all things.' And Theodoret says no differently: Whence it was necessary that he be made like his brothers in all things. For he was a participant in nourishment just as we are, and he endured labor, and was of an anxious mind, and he wept, and he underwent death. Blessed Hunnius: He shows, he says, the magnitude of the benefit of CHRIST in this, while he shows that he did not only associate with himself human nature from our race, similar to us in all things by reason of substance: But together with that, he also willed to assume and experience all infirmities, sin alone excepted, in soul and body: And thus in respect to both, namely by reason of nature and temptations, he was made similar to us, his brothers. Therefore that κατὰ πάντα is not to be extended to sin, which is expressly excepted, Heb. IV. v. 15, nor to corruption in death, which the Holy One was not to see, Psalm XVI, nor to personal sicknesses, which follow δυσκρασίαν; because he indeed voluntarily assumed our infirmities, but he was not subject to diseases. But why that ὤφειλε is not to be understood properly, that it was necessary for the Son of GOD to be made like his brothers, does not appear; rather, a necessity is evident here: because if he had not been made like his brothers, he could neither have undergone passion and death, nor would he have turned out to be such a merciful and faithful High Priest. Therefore, a certain hypothetical necessity is given here. Which is also observed in Luke XXIV. v. 26.

Ἵνα ἐλεήμων γένηται.

So that he might the more readily succor the wretched, not being ignorant of evil; there are many benefits from the passions and death of Christ. Sacred writers place this one, now that one, before our eyes.

Καὶ πιϲὸς Ἀρχιερεὺς τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν.

מול האלהים, Exod. XVIII. vers. 19. Where similarly in Greek τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν. Often this writer shows here how much Christ excels the legal High Priest. It was his office to act in the place of God before the people, and in the place of the people before God. Christ does both excellently. Now here the latter is considered, as also below V. 1. He is called faithful נאמן here, who performs his duty well, πιϲὸς τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν, that is, κατὰ τὰ in the Greek manner.

It is now explained with what purpose he had to assume both our nature and our harmless infirmities, and to be made like us in all things, namely so that he would not only be our High Priest, and be able to expiate sin in his body, but also that he might condole with the misery of the people, and out of a feeling of commiseration might faithfully conduct our cause before GOD, as one tempted in all things just as we are, and so that he might be a merciful and faithful High Priest. CHRIST felt human misery in the days of his flesh, therefore he is affected toward us with greater συμπαθείᾳ, and for that reason he more readily met death for us, so that he might remove the cause of the same, and more ardently interceded for us before the heavenly Father, so that we might be freed from the same. Faithful, not only on account of the faith of his office, but also on account of the perpetuity of the sacrifice and his firm High Priesthood: As St. Athanasius notes in the cited place: He was made, he says, merciful and faithful: Merciful indeed, because offering himself for us, he had mercy on us: Faithful, however, not because he was a participant in faith, or believed in anyone, as we do, but because he was worthy of faith in those things which he did or said, and because he offered a faithful victim, that is, one enduring and not perishing. For those things which were offered according to the law possessed nothing of faith in themselves: since they were fleeting and passing away daily, and those which needed new purification. On the contrary, the Savior's host, offered once, absolves all things and remains faithful for all time. And successors were indeed given to Aaron, and the legal priesthood altogether received other and different High Priests through the progress of death and time. But the Lord, obtaining a priesthood without transition and without a successor, was made a faithful and firm High Priest by persevering forever. Athanasius also adds faith in promises: And he was faithful in his promises, so that he might hear, and not frustrate the simple: Comparing the passage 1. Peter IV. v. 19. For he is faithful, as one who is not changed, but always remains, and renders those things which he has promised. Just as also in the Hebrews this word 'faithful' is considered to have the meaning of immutability, 2. Timothy II. vers. 13. Chrysostom thinks it implies at the same time both that he is ἀληθὴς, and that he is δυνάμενος, or truthful and powerful. Because the Son is a faithful High Priest, who can free from sins those whose High Priest he is. Therefore, so that he might offer a host which can cleanse and expiate us, for that reason he was made man. He therefore subjoined, to God πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν. We were, he says, enemies of God, condemned, affected with disgrace and ignominy. There was no one who was to offer a sacrifice for us. He saw us to be in this state, and he had mercy, not appointing a High Priest for us, but he himself was made High Priest. Theophylact. For no other reason, he says, did he assume this flesh of ours, except that through it he might both have mercy on us, and lift up those lying on the ground. But in what way was our High Priest made by this very unwashed and sordid flesh, which he had taken from us? Certainly so that he might repurge us from sins, and obtain by his intercession from GOD forgiveness for our errors, by which we were previously attacked. But faithful, that is, truthful and powerful, so that he might fulfill the office of High Priest.

Εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ.

Ἱλάσκεσθαι ἁμαρτίας in this place, as appears from what follows, is to take away sins or to purge from sin, that is, to cause that one does not sin, by supplying strength according to the measure of temptations. It corresponds to the Hebrew words כפר & סלח, which are accustomed to be translated sometimes by καθαρίζειν, Exod. XXIX. 37. XXX. 10. Num. XXX. 9. 13. Ἐκκαθαρίζειν, Deut. XXXII. 44. ἀφαιρεῖν, Exod. XXXIV. 9. Isaiah XXVII. verse 9. Ἐξιλασμὸς ἀποστῆναι ἀπὸ ἁμαρτίας Sirach XXXV. verse 4. And thus perhaps that passage of Sirach III. 3, Ὁ τιμῶν πατέρα ἐξιλάσκεται ἁμαρτίας, can be explained not badly, because reverence for parents keeps many from sin: The Old High Priest only expiated by freeing from the punishments of sins: but Jesus from the sins themselves.

The sense of the Apostle's words is clearly perverted. For where is ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας to cause that one does not sin, by supplying strength according to the measure of temptations? That meaning of the phrase occurs nowhere in the Greek codex, nor in those Hebrew words, nor is it detected in the cited passage of Sirach; therefore Grotius pronounces on this passage only hesitantly. What ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας is, is sufficiently established from an induction of passages: namely, the propitiation of God, who is offended by sins, and expiation of sins to be brought in. Therefore, concerning sacrifices and concerning Priests expiating sins and propitiating GOD through the offering of sacrifices and intercession, it is applied: Nor is there any other sense here, where it is discussed concerning the Pontiff of the New Testament, whom they shadowed forth in the Old Testament, and concerning the one true sacrifice, through which we are all propitiated. That phrase does not sound of preventing future sins, but of expiating committed sins: Not of the supply of strengths by which we ourselves might resist sins or temptations; but of our reconciliation on account of sins, and the propitiation of GOD offended through sins. Nor indeed does the Pontiff supply strengths for resisting temptations: For this was not the work of the Pontiff: Nor is there anything here concerning resistance against temptations, but it treats of συμπαθείᾳ (sympathy) with our infirmity in the preceding words and βοηθείᾳ (help) in our spiritual necessity on account of sins in the following words. Here, however, the very propitiation of God and the expiation of our sins is delivered. Which we have already observed before from Athanasius and Theodoret, and clearly delivered by Theophylact: That he might propitiate the faults of the people: He shows what it is to be faithful to GOD, namely, that he might reconcile the delinquent people to God. For that is the greatest indication of his charity toward us, since he has strenuously done all things so that he might blot out sins. Chrysostom, also recently produced, whose words these are: It was indeed even the very willing to become man, a matter of great care and charity. But now this is not the only thing, but there are also immortal goods, which have been exhibited to us through him. That he might propitiate, he says, the faults of the people. Why did he not say of the world, but of the people? For he carried the sins of all: Because then words were being made by him concerning the Hebrews themselves. These things those Holy Fathers, whom the rest follow ὁμοθυμαδὸν (with one mind). But it pleased Grotius more to gratify the Socinians, whom he had formerly refuted in De Satisfactione Christi c. VII. pag. 91. Let his followers recognize the man's own words: It is most well known that to avert the anger of someone is said in Greek ἱλάσκεσθαι, εἰρηνοποιεῖν, καταλλάσσειν, ὑποκαταλλάσσειν, in Latin to appease, to pacify, to reconcile or to reconcile. Then the act itself, and that by which the act is properly performed, is called ἱλασμὸς by the Greeks and placamen by the Latins. And pag. 93. ἱλάσκειν among all Greek writers, Poets, Historians, others, is to appease, and is accustomed to be constructed with the Accusative designating the person whose anger is averted. Nor is it used otherwise among the LXX Interpreters and Luke XVIII. v. 13. In one place only, which is Heb. II. 17. Christ is said to be the high Priest constituted εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ, where there is an enallage coming from Hebraism, ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας, when it should have been said customarily, ἱλάσκεσθαι θεὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν. It signifies therefore there an expiation, but that which is done by appeasing. Otherwise this use of the word would have nothing in common with the nature of the word and its perpetual signification. Wherefore such an expiation as Socinus imagines, that is, the destruction of sin, which is done without appeasement, this word ἱλάσκεσθαι, and the ἱλασμὸς derived from it, cannot denote. The Socinians themselves confess that it looks not to future, but to committed sins, and their expiation. For thus Schlichtingius with his Crellius on this place: The final cause of the Pontificate is added, and of those things which are to be performed from this office, that he might propitiate, or to expiate the sins of the people εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ. The word ἱλάσκεσθαι which the Author uses here, corresponds to the Hebrew Kipper, whose root caphar, signifies to cover, to smear. For sins are not expiated in any other way than that

HEBREWS CHAP. II. v. 17.

as if they were covered and overlaid, so that they no longer appear in the sight of GOD. To express this Hebrew word, the LXX Interpreters are accustomed to use the word ἱλάσκεσθαι, so that they might not depart entirely from the Greek custom of speaking in this matter of sacrifices. Sometimes, however, they construct this word with the word for sins in the accusative case, just as we see done in this place: but sometimes, and that somewhat more frequently, in the genitive case, and that with the preposition περὶ inserted, following the Hebrew phrase and construction. For the Hebrews are accustomed to construct verbs having the signification of covering with the preposition hal, or bead, to which in the Greek language corresponds περὶ, and other similar particles. But in the same sense exactly it is said ἱλάσκεσθαι ἁμαρτίας, and ἱλάσκεσθαι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν: nor is this word ever referred passively to God himself by the sacred writers. And for that reason the Greek Interpreters were able to use this word, which properly signifies appeasement and propitiation, in this matter, because in every sacrifice the goal is that the Deity be propitiated. What Schlichtingius adds, that it is not always the goal in a sacrifice that the Deity be rendered from angry to appeased and propitious, but often, that he might not cease to be propitious and appeased, and that he might omit causes of anger otherwise just, cannot be proven concerning the ἱλαστικῷ (propitiatory) sacrifice, such as the present one of Christ is. He says that it is not consistent that GOD was angry at the people when he timely procured the expiation of sins. But this is properly asked here, whether propitiatory sacrifices signified both the anger of God against sins, and the appeasement of GOD made by the virtue of the one propitiatory sacrifice of the New Testament, which he offered on the altar of the cross, which they shadowed forth, the application of which those had who offered expiatory sacrifices by faith in the Messiah. Furthermore, the indication of the means of reconciliation does not argue that God is not justly angry, but only this, that divine justice can be satisfied in that way: which arises from the tempering of mercy. Which satisfaction the ἱλαστικὰ (propitiatory) sacrifices shadowed forth. But that Christ purges our sins by no other reason than that, by the power granted to him by God himself, he ensures that we do not suffer the punishments of our sins and perish eternally, is the gloss of Crellius and Schlichtingius, which is contrary to this whole epistle, by which it is taught that Christ, God, propitiated by the sacrifice of his body on the altar of the cross, and made expiation for sins, and having done so, sat down at the right hand of God in the highest. Nor indeed is he ever said to expiate sins in such a way that he ensures by his own power that we do not suffer the punishments of sins, but that by his death he merited for us the forgiveness of sins, so that we might be freed not only from the punishment but also from the guilt of sin. As the High Priest did not offer in the holy of holies: for in it there was no altar: So CHRIST offered himself on the cross, not in heaven, as a sweet-smelling savor. But that, setting aside the Socinians, against whom it was dealt with in 'On the Causes of the Death of CHRIST' and 'Socinianism Overthrown', we may return to Grotius, the distinction between the High Priest of the Old Testament and CHRIST he assigned here only falsely as such, that the former of the old law freed only from the punishments of sins, but CHRIST indeed from sins. For did they not obtain remission of sin in the Old Testament, who offered sacrifices through faith? This epistle teaches the contrary, among other things by the example of Abel, chap. XI. vers. 4. Did CHRIST not free us from the punishment of sins? The Socinians themselves certainly acknowledge this, although they err perversely in this, that they explain it in such a way that, dwelling in the heavens, he may accomplish those things which pertain to freeing us from the punishments of sins.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ὅθεν ὤφειλε κατὰ πάντα τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς ὁμοιωθῆναι.

Κατὰ πάντα intellige ex subjecta materia; rebus ad- versis, cruciatu, morte dura. Ὤφειλε, id est, ita fieri ex usu fuit, quo sensu Latini sæpe usurpant debet, non ex rigore, sed μετὰ πλάτυς. Sic ἔδει Luc. XXIV. 26. & hic modo ἔπρεπε.

Non negamus ὁμοιότητα illam etiam sese ad res adversas, cruciatum & mortem extendere, sed negamus ea sola excluso humanæ naturæ ὁμοιώματι, de quo Roman. IIX. vers. 3. intelligi. Nam ne frater quidem noster esset, nedum κατὰ πάντα per omnia similis nobis fratribus, nisi ipse ὁμοούσιοs & ejusdem nobiscum naturæ es- set. Similitudo illa Filii DEI quoad tentatio- nes, de quibus ea explicatur Ebr. IV. versu 15. præsupponit ipsam humanæ naturæ veritatem, quod nempe similiter ut pueri carnis & sangui- nis nostri particeps factus, quodque semen A- brahæ in unitatem personæ suæ susceperit, adeo- que etiam proprietates humanæ naturæ vere ta- les excludendæ non sint. Assumendo enim hu- manam naturam proprietatum etiam ejusdem particeps factus est. Directe tamen ὁμοιότης hæc non ipsam ὁμοουσίαν substantialem significat, quemadmodum Calviniamis nonnullis visum est: Sed ad statum exinanitionis, quo μορφὴν δούλου λαβὼν ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος, καὶ σχή- ματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος, Philipp. II. vers. 7. 8. referenda; qui status accidit substantialibus na- turæ, ac cessavit salva naturæ veritate. Neque ergo illud κατὰ πάντα extendendum ad illa pecu- liaria, quæ ad personam CHRISTI θεανθρώ- πυ pertinent, utpote ad conceptionem huma- næ CHRISTI naturæ à Spiritu sancto sine vi- rili semine factam, ad unionem hypostaticam, ad communicationem idiomatum, aut quæ ad exaltationem ejus spectant, ad evectionem ad dextram Dei & regimen universale in cœlo & in terra. Hæc ut ad personam, non ad statum, vel non ad statum humiliationis spectant: Ita iis fratribus similem factum esse minime dicendum. Ad humanam autem naturam ceu subjectum il- la πάντα pertinere, quibus fratribus similis fa- ctus est, dubitandum non est. Quo de Atha- nasius orat. III. contra Arian. pag. 379. Quando enim factus est? Et quando eum Apostolum esse contigit? annon quando itidem, ut nos, sanguinis & carnis particeps erat? Aut quando misericors effectus est, & fidelis Pontifex? Nisi quum per omnia fratribus assimilatus fuit. Similis porro tum factus est, cum carnem nostram in- dutus homo inceperat esse. Nonne igitur de ejus humana dispensatione Apostolus scribens ista lo- quutus est? Fidelem eum fuisse conditori suo, ac nequaquam de substantia Verbi. Tunc autem ha- buit fratres, cum similem nostri carnem induerat, quam offerens ipse per seipsum Pontificis nomen obtinuit. Chrysostomus ad hunc locum : Unde debuit per omnia fratribus similari? Quid est per omnia fuit? Fuit, inquit, partu editus, & nu- tritus, & crevit, & passus est omnia, quæ opor- tuit, & tandem est mortuus. Hoc est, per omnia assimilatum esse fratribus. Nam quoniam multa dixit de ejus majestate & superna gloria, de cæte- ro facit verba de dispensatione. Quem sequutus pro more Theophylactus: Cùm enim inquit di- gnatus est semel carnem hanc ille nostram induere, & naturam humanam arripere, consentaneum e- rat omnino, ut & nobis persimilis nasceretur, pa- remque noviscum & educationem haberet & incre- mentum: Ferretque omnia, quæ illi essent ferenda, ac demum mortem obiret. Id namque prætendit, cùm per omnia inquit assimilari. Nec aliter Theodorelus : Unde debuit per omnia fratribus assimilari. Nam & nutrimenti sicut nos fuit par- ticeps, & laborem sustinuit, & anxio animo fuit, & flevit, & mortem subiit. Beat. Hunnius: Ma- gnitudinem, inquit, beneficii CHRISTI in eo mirifice etiam exaggerat, dum ostendit, ipsum non tantum humanam naturam ex nostro genere, no- bis ratione substantiæ per omnia similem, sibi asso- ciare: Sed una cum illa omnes etiam infirmitates, solo peccato excepto, assumere & experiri anima & corpore voluisse : Et sic utriusque respectu, nempe naturæ & tentationum ratione nobis suis fratribus similem esse factum. Non ergo illud κατὰ πάντα extendendum ad peccatum, quod diserte excipi- tur, Ebr. IV. v. 15. non ad corruptionem in mor- te, quam Sanctus videre non debuit, Psal. XVI. non ad personales ægritudines, quæ δυσκρασίαν se- quuntur; quia infirmitates quidem nostras vo- luntarie assumpsit, sed morbis obnoxius non fuit. Cur autem illud ὤφειλε non sit proprie in- telligendum, quod oportuerit Filium DEI fra- tribus assimilari, haud apparet; imo necessitas potius hic patet : quia nisi fratribus similis fa- ctus esset, nec passionem & mortem subire po- tuisset, nec ita misericors & fidelis Pontifex e- vasisset. Datur ergo hic quædam hypothetica solum necessitas. Quæ etiam Luc. XXIV. v. 26. observatur.

Ἵνα ἐλεήμων γένηται.

Ut eo promptius miseris succurrat mali non ignarus; Multæ sunt utilitates ex passionibus & morte Christi. Sacri scriptores nunc hanc, nunc illam nobis ob oculos ponunt.

Καὶ πιϲὸς Ἀρχιερεὺς τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν.

מול האלהים, Exod. XVIII. vers. 19. Ubi similiter in Græco τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν. Sæpe ostendit hic scriptor quantum Christus præstat summo Sacerdoti legali. Erat e- jus officium Dei vice apud populum fungi, & populi vi- ce apud Deum. Utrumque eximie facit Christus. Nunc hic spectatur illud posterius, ut & infra V. 1. fidelis נאמן hic dicitur is, qui munere suo bene fungitur, πιϲὸς τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεόν, id est, κατὰ τὰ more Græco.

Exponitur jam quo consilio & naturam no- stram, & infirmitates nostras innoxias assume- re, ac per omnia similis nobis fieri debuerit, ut scilicet non tantum Pontifex noster esset, ac pec- catum in corpore suo expiare posset, sed etiam ut condoloret populi miseriæ, & ex affectu con- miserationis causam nostram fideliter ageret apud DEUM, utpote tentatus per omnia sicut nos, adeoque ut misericors, & fidelis Pontifex esset. Sensit CHRISTUS humanam mise- riam in diebus carnis, ideo majori συμπαθείᾳ erga nos afficitur, eoque promptius mortem pro nobis oppetiit, ut causam ejusdem tolleret, atque ardentius apud Patrem cœlestem interce- de- dit pro nobis, ut ab eadem liberemur. Fidelem non ob fidem tantum muneris, sed etiam ob perennitatem sacrificii, firmumque Pontificatum: Uti S. Athanasius notat loco citato: Factus est, inquit, misericors & fidelis: Misericors quidem, quia seipsum pro nobis offerens, nostri misertus est: Fidelis autem, non quod fidei particeps fuerit, aut cuipiam crediderit, ut nos facimus, sed quod fide dignus esset in iis, quæ ageret aut diceret, & quia fidelem obtulit victimam perdurantem scilicet & non intercidentem. Quæ enim secundum legem offerebantur, nihil fidei in se possidebant: quippe caduca prætereuntesque quotidie, & quibus nova purgatione opus erat. Contra Salvatoris hostia se- mel oblata absolvit omnia fidaque in omne tempus perdurat. Et Aaroni successores quidem dati sunt, & omnino legale sacerdotium mortis & temporis progressu alios atque alios Pontifices accepit. Domi- nus autem sine transitione & sine successore sacer- dotium obtinens fidus firmusque Pontifex factus est in perpetuum perseverando. Addit Athanasius etiam fidem in promissionibus: Et in suis pro- missis fidelis extitit, ut exaudiret, & non frustra- retur simplices: Conferens locum 1. Petr. IV. v. 19. Fidelis enim est, utpote qui non mutetur, sed semper permaneat, & reddat ea, quæ pollicitus est. Quemadmodum & Ebræis vocabulum hoc fidele significatum habere immutabilitatis, 2. Ti- moth. II. vers. 13. Chrysostomus simul inferre cen- set, & quod ἀληθὴς, & quod δυνάμενος, vel verax & potens sit. Quia Pontifex fidelis est Filius, qui potest liberare à peccatis eos, quorum est Ponti- fex. Ut ergo offerat hostiam, quæ possit nos mun- dare & expiare, propterea factus est homo. Sub- junxit ergo, ad Deum πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν. Eramus in- quit Dei inimici, condemnati, probro & ignomi- nia affecti. Nemo erat, qui pro nobis oblaturus esset sacrificium. Vidit nos in hoc esse statu, & est misertus, non nobis constituens Pontificem, sed ipse factus est Pontifex. Theophylactus. Nullam, in- quit, aliam ob causam carnem hanc nostram as- sumpsit, nisi ut per eam & nostri miseretur, & humi jacentes attolleret. Verum quo pacto Ponti- fex noster effectus est hac ipsa illota & sordida, quam à nobis desumpserat, carne? Certe ut pec- catis nos repurgaret, impetraretque suo intercessu à DEO nostris erratis veniam, quibus antea ipsi op- pugnabamur. Fidelis vero, id est, verax & potens, ut Pontificis adimpleret munus.

Εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ.

Ἱλάσκεσθαι ἁμαρτίας hoc quidem loco, ut ex sequen- tibus apparet, est auferre peccata sive purgare à pecca- to, id est, efficere ne peccetur, vires suppeditando pro modo tentationum. Respondet Ebræis vocibus כפר & סלח, quæ verti solent interdum per καθαρίζειν, Exod. XXIX. 37. XXX. 10. Numer. XXX. 9. 13. Ἐκκαθαρίζειν, Deut. XXXII. 44. ἀφαιρεῖν, Exod. XXXIV. 9. Esaiæ XXVII. vers. 9. Ἐξιλασμὸς ἀποστῆναι ἀπὸ ἁμαρτίας Sirach. XXXV. vers. 4. Et sic forte exponi non male potest, illud Sirach. III. 3. Ὁ τιμῶν πατέρα ἐξιλάσκεται ἁμαρτίας, quia reve- rentia parentum multos custodit à peccato: Vetus Pon- tifex tantum expiabat à peccatorum pœnis liberando: Je- sus vero ab ipsis peccatis.

Plane pervertitur sensus verborum Apostoli. Ubi enim ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας est efficere ne peccetur, vires suppeditando pro modo tentatio- num? Illa phraseos significatio nec in Græco co- dice, nec in Ebræis istis verbis uspiam occur- rit, neque in Siracide deprehenditur loco citato, ideo non nisi titubanter de isto loco pronunciat Grotius. Quid sit ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας ex in- ductione locorum satis constat: Propitiationem nempe Dei, qui peccatis offenditur, & expiationem peccatorum inferri. Ideo de sacrificiis & de Sacerdotibus per oblationem sacrificiorum & intercessionem peccata expiantibus & DEUM propitiantibus adhibetur: Nec alium sensum hic, ubi de Pontifice Novi Testamenti, quem illi in Veteri Testamento adumbrabant, & de unico vero sacrificio, per quod omnes propitiamur, disseritur. Non de peccatis futuris præcavendis, sed de peccatis commissis expiandis phrasis illa sonat: Non de virium subministratione, quibus nos ipsi resistamus peccatis vel tentationibus; sed de nostri ob peccata reconciliatione, Deique per peccata offensi propitiatione. Nec vero ut Pontifex vires suppeditat resistendi tentationibus: Hoc enim non erat Pontificis: Neque quicquam hic de resistentia adversus tentationes, sed de συμπαθείᾳ cum infirmitate nostra in verbis præcedentibus & βοηθείᾳ in spirituali nostra necessitate ob peccata in verbis sequentibus agitur. Hic autem ipsa Dei propitiatio & peccatorum nostrorum expiatio traditur. Quod ex Athanasio & Theodoreto jam ante observavimus, & à Theophylacto luculenter traditum: Ut repropitiaret delicta populi: Ostendit quid præferat ad DEUM esse fidelem, videlicet ut populum delinquentem Deo conciliet. Id enim est maxime suæ in nos charitatis indicium, cum enixe omnia fecerit, ut peccata deleret. Chrysostomus proxime etiam productus, cujus & hæc sunt: Erat quidem ipsum etiam voluisse fieri hominem, magna cura & charitatis. Nunc autem non hoc est solum, sed etiam sunt bona immortalia, quæ per ipsum nobis sunt exhibita. Ut repropitiaret inquit delicta populi. Cur non dixit orbis terræ, sed populi? Nam omnium portavit peccata: Quoniam tunc ab eo de ipsis Ebræis verba fiebant. Hæc illi S. Patres, quos cæteri ὁμοθυμαδὸν sequuntur. Grotio autem magis placuit Socinianis gratificari, quos olim refutarat in De Satisfactione Christi c. VII. pag. 91. Recognoscant ejus sectatores propria viri verba: Notissimum est, iram alicujus avertere, id dici Græce ἱλάσκεσθαι, εἰρηνοποιεῖν, καταλλάσσειν, ὑποκαταλλάσσειν, Latine placare, pacare, conciliare aut reconciliare. Tum actus ipse, tum id, quo proprie actus peragitur, Græcis ἱλασμὸς Latinis placamen dicitur. Et pag. 93. ἱλάσκειν apud Græcos Scriptores omnes, Poetas, Historicos, alios, est placare, soletque construi cum Accusativo designante personam, cujus ira avertitur. Nec aliter apud LXX. Interpretes & Luc. XVIII. v. 13. usurpatur. Uno duntaxat loco, qui est Ebr. II. 17. dicitur Christus summus Sacerdos constitutus εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ, ubi est enallage ex Ebraismo veniens, ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας, cum usitate dici debuerit, ἱλάσκεσθαι θεὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν. Significat ergo ibi expiationem sed eam, quæ fit placando. Alioqui hic vocis usus nihil haberet commune cum natura vocis ac perpetua ejusdem significatione. Quare talem expiationem, qualem Socinus comminiscitur, id est, peccati destructionem, quæ fit sine placamento, ista quidem vox ἱλάσκεσθαι, & inde derivata ἱλασμὸς, denotare non potest. Sociniani ipsi fatentur, non futura, sed commissa peccata, eorumque expiationem respici. Sic enim cum Crellio suo Schlichtingius in hunc locum: Additur finalis causa Pontificatus, & eorum, quæ ex hoc munere peragenda sunt, ut repropitiaret, vel ad expiandum peccata populi εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ. Verbum ἱλάσκεσθαι quo hic utitur Autor, respondet Ebræo Kipper, cujus radix caphar, tegere, oblinere significat. Peccata enim non alia ratione expiantur, quam quod

EBRAEOS CAP. II. v. 17.

veluti tegantur & obducantur, ne amplius in conspectu DEI appareant. Ad hoc verbum E- braicum exprimendum LXX. Interpretes uti solent verbo ἱλάσκεσθαι, ne in hac sacrificiorum materia à Graeca loquendi consuetudine prorsus abeant. A- liquando autem hoc verbum cum voce peccatorum accusandi casu construunt, quemadmodum etiam hoc loco factum videmus: aliquando vero, idque aliquanto frequentius generandi casu, idque inter- jecta Praepositione περὶ, secuti phrasin & constru- ctionem Ebraicam. Ebrai enim verba tegendi si- gnificationem habentia, cum praepositione hal, vel bead construere solent, cui in Graeca lingua respon- det περὶ, & aliae similes particulae. Eodem autem plane sensu dicitur ἱλάσκεσθαι ἁμαρτίας, & ἱλά- σκεσθαι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν: nec unquam haec vox à sa- cris scriptoribus ad Deum ipsum passive refertur. Idcirco autem hac voce, quae proprie placationem & propitiationem significat, Graeci Interpretes in hac materia uti potuerunt, quia in omni sacrificio id agitur, ut Numen propitietur. Quae addit Schlichtingius non semper in sacrificio id agi, ut Numen ex irato placatum, propitiumque redda- tur, sed saepe, ne propitium placatumque esse desi- nat, utque irarum causas alioqui justas omittat, probari de sacrificio ἱλαστικῷ, quale praesens Chri- sti est, non potest. Dicit, DEUM populo ira- tum fuisse, cum is peccatorum expiationem tem- pestive procuravit, non esse consentaneum. At id proprie hic quaeritur, annon sacrificia propitia- toria significarint, tum iram Dei adversus pec- cata, tum placationem DEI virtute unici sacrifi- cii propitiatorii Novi Testamenti, quod in ara crucis obtulit, quod ipsi adumbrabant, factam, cujus applicationem habebant, qui fide in Mes- siam sacrificia expiatoria offerebant. Porro in- dicatio mediorum reconciliationis non arguit Deum jure iratum non esse, sed hoc tantum, ju- ri divino ea ratione satisfieri posse: quod ex tem- peramento misericordiae oritur. Quam satisfactio- nem adumbrabant sacrificia ἱλαστικὰ. Non autem alia ratione Christum peccata nostra purgare, quam quod potestate sibi ab ipso Deo concessa cu- ret, ne peccatorum nostrorum poenas luamus, & in aeternum pereamus, glossa Crellii & Schlichtin- gii est toti huic epistolae adversa, qua Christum Deum sacrificio corporis sui in ara crucis pro- pitiasse, ac peccatorum expiationem fecisse, ea- que facta in excelsis ad dextram DEI consedisse docetur. Nec vero uspiam ita expiare peccata dicitur, quod potestate sua curet, ne peccatorum poenas luamus, sed quod morte sua nobis prome- ruerit condonationem peccatorum, ut non à poe- na solum, sed etiam à culpa peccati liberemur. Ut Pontifex non offerebat in sancto sanctorum: in eo enim nullum erat altare: Ita CHRISTUS in cruce, non in coelo semetipsum in odorem suavitatis obtulit. Ut autem, missis Socinianis, adversus quos in De causis mortis CHRISTI, & Socinismo profligato actum, ad Grotium re- vertamur, discrimen inter Pontificem Veteris Testamenti, & CHRISTUM non nisi falso hic assignavit tale, quod vetus ille à peccatorum poenis tantum liberarit, CHRISTUS vero à peccatis. Num enim in Veteri Testamento non consequuti sunt peccati remissionem, qui per fidem obtulere sacrificia? Contrarium docet haec epistola inter alia exemplo Abelis, cap. XI. vers. 4. Num CHRISTUS non liberavit nos à poena peccatorum? Agnoscunt id utique ipsi- met Sociniani, quamvis in eo perverse errent, quod id eo modo explicent, quod in coelis degens peragat ea, quæ ad nos à pœnis peccatorum liberan- dos pertinent.

## 2:18
Verf. 18.

For in that he himself has suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted) he trusts נענה Isa. LIII. 7. The sense is: For since he himself was tempted through those things which he endured, he is the more able to be moved to bring aid to those who are tempted; ἐν for per is frequent in these writers. And the singular for the plural because of the generality, as just now ὑπὲρ παντός. Ἐν ᾧ באשר. Then there is a Metonymy: he is able to succour for he is able to be moved to succour. For nothing moves us more to pity than the memory of similar evils which have happened to us. Thus we have δύναται συμπαθῆσαι below IV. 15. Where there is also πεπειρασμένοις.

Temptations, therefore, are not understood as those leading to sin—such as Grotius seemed to imply in the previous annotation, which are truly Diabolical—but as those of patience and constancy, which occur divinely through afflictions. For CHRIST was tempted, but without sin, chap. IV. 15. Nor is that aid to be taken as that which supplies strength so that we do not sin; but that which comes to our succour, both by the grace of the Holy Spirit and by the efficacy of his own intercession, so that we do not perish in afflictions and miseries, inasmuch as he himself was subjected to the most grievous temptations of afflictions and passions, and therefore is led by a feeling of commiseration in our temptations and passions. If, however, that πειρασθεὶς is taken more broadly regarding any temptations whatsoever, since the Devil even dared to solicit Christ to sin, and Christ by his temptation merited for us aid in every temptation, it must be especially observed that Christ could only be tempted externally by the Devil proposing temptation, but not internally by concupiscence or any disordered fear of the imagination: inasmuch as this could have no place in Christ. Potens is also explained by Theophylact as prone, prompt, and prepared to succour. But others prefer that to these first two conditions of the mercy and faithfulness of the High Priest, a third is added: the ability which he obtained through his own temptation and passion for our sins; not indeed in the Papistic sense of Cornelius à Lapide, as if he merited for himself dominion over demons and men who inflict passions, but in the Catholic sense, that by the merit of his obedience even unto death, even the death of the cross, and thus by his manifold yet most innocent passion and temptation, he merited and obtained for us, who are guilty, the right and power to succour and assist in our temptations. Cornelius à Lapide attributes that to Chrysostom, but undeservedly. For he handed down the common interpretation: He came, he says, through the very experience of those things which we have suffered. Now he is not ignorant of our sufferings. He not only knows as God, but he has also known as man through that experience by which he suffered. He has suffered many things, he knows how to sympathize and pity, although God is impassible. But here he narrates what pertains to the incarnation. As if he were saying: The very flesh of Christ also suffered many grievous things; he knows what affliction is, he knows what temptation is, no less than we who have suffered. For he himself also has suffered. What then is it? He is able also to succour those who are tempted? As if you were to say, with great alacrity of spirit he will reach out his hand, he will commiserate. Therefore, Cornelius à Lapide rashly builds upon this explanation, as if handed down by Chrysostom, the merits of the saints, that they too by their own passions have merited that they might be able to succour us in those things which they have suffered before God. For the third affection or property of the High Priest is not being brought forward, but a proof of the former mercy and faithfulness is being instituted.

Latin:

Verf. 18.

Ἐν ᾧ γὰρ πέπονθεν αὐτὸς πειρασθεὶς δύναται τοῖς πειραζο- μένοις βοηθῆσαι) πέποιθεν נענה Esa. LIII. 7. sensus est: Cum enim ipse tentatus fuerit per ea quæ pertulit, hoc ma- gis potest moveri ad auxilium ferendum iis qui tentantur, ἐν pro per frequens his scriptoribus. Et singulare pro plu- rali propter generalitatem, ut modo ὑπὲρ παντός. Ἐν ᾧ באשר. Deinde est Μετωνυμία potest auxiliari pro po- test moveri ad auxiliandum. Nihil enim magis ad miseran- dum nos movet, quam malorum similium, quæ nobis eve- nerunt, memoria. Sic δύναται συμπαθῆσαι habemus infra IV. 15. Ubi etiam est πεπειρασμένοις.

Tentationes ergo non ad peccatum, quales in proxima annotatione videbatur innuere Gro- tius, quæ vere Diabolicæ sunt; sed de patientia & constantia, quæ per afflictiones divinitus fiunt, intelliguntur. CHRISTUS enim tentatus est sed absque peccato, cap. IV. 15. Nec illud auxilium eo accipiendum, quod vires suppeditet, ne pec- cemus; Sed quod nobis succurrat tum Spiritus Sancti gratia, tum intercessionis suæ efficacia, ne in afflictionibus & miseriis pereamus, siquidem ipse tentationibus afflictionum & passionum subjectus fuerit gravissimis, ideoque commiserationis affe- ctu ducatur in nostris tentationibus & passioni- bus. Si tamen illud πειρασθεὶς latius accipiatur de quibusvis tentationibus, quum Diabolus Chri- stum etiam ausus sit ad peccatum solicitare, ac Christus tentatione sua meruerit nobis auxilium in omni tentatione, id apprime observandum, Christum tantum exterius à Diabolo tentationem proponente tentari potuisse, non autem interius à concupiscentia, aut metu aliquo phantasiæ inordi- nato: siquidem hic in Christo locum habere non potuerit. Potens exponitur etiam à Theophylacto, pronus, promptus, & paratus ad auxiliandum. Sed alii malunt, his prioribus duabus conditionibus misericordiæ & fidelitatis Pontificis tertiam addi facultatem, quam sua tentatione & passione ob peccata nostra obtinuit, quod non quidem sensu Papistico Cornelii à Lapide, quasi meruerit sibi dominium super Dæmones & homines, passiones infligentes, sed Catholico, quod obedientiæ suæ merito usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, adeoque passione & tentatione sua multivaria, at innocentissima, nobis nocentibus jus & potestatem promeruerit, & impetrarit succurrendi & opitu- landi in tentationibus nostris. Tribuit illud Cor- nelius à Lapide Chrysostomo, ast immerito. Ille enim communem interpretationem tradidit: Ve- nit, inquit, per ipsam experientiam eorum, quæ passi sumus. Nunc non ignorat nostras perpessiones. Non solum scit ut Deus, sed etiam cognovit ut ho- mo per eam, qua passus est, experientiam. Multa passus est, scit compati & misereri, quanquam Deus est impatibilis. Sed hic narrat, quæ sunt incarna- tionis. Quasi diceret: Ipsa quoque caro Christi multa passa est gravia; novit, quid sit afflictio, no- vit quid sit tentatio, non minus quam nos, qui passi sumus. Nam ipse quoque est passus. Quid ergo est? Potens est & iis, qui tentantur auxiliari? Quasi dicas, magna animi alacritate manum porriget, commiserebitur. Temere ergo Cornelius à Lapi- de superstruit isti explicationi ceu à Chrysostomo traditæ sanctorum merita, quod & ipsi passioni- bus suis promeruerint, ut auxiliari in iis, quæ passi sunt, nobis possint apud Deum. Nec enim tertia Pontificis affectio aut proprietas affertur, sed priorum misericordiæ & fidelitatis probatio instituitur.

## 3:1 Argument
OF SECTION II. OF PART I. OF THE EPISTLE, OF MEMBER II. SPECIAL ARTICLE I. CONCERNING THE DOCTORAL OFFICE OF CHRIST. CHAPTER III.

ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He now undertakes to examine the office of Christ more specially, and indeed at the beginning the doctoral [office], in this comparing the Apostle, who is also the High Priest of our confession, with Moses by reason of faith, preferring him to the same, as the Architect of the house to the house, and the Son to the servant: and teaching us that we are his house, if we persevere in confidence. Thence he warns that we should hear his voice (according to the exhortation of the Holy Spirit, Ps. XCV. 8), and not fall away from Christ, as having been made partakers of Christ, lest God be provoked, as formerly toward the Israelites, who were excluded from his rest.

There are two parts: The former is Didactic, concerning Christ as Doctor and Prophet, up to verse 6. The latter is exhortatory, concerning listening to him and not falling away from GOD through apostasy, up to verse 19.

PART I. DIDACTIC, Concerning Christ the Doctor.

Verse 1.

Ὅθεν) Since the things we have said thus far are so.

Ἀδελφοὶ ἅγιοι He addresses them by the more important part, as Paul does in Rom. 1:7, 1 Cor. 1:2, 2 Cor. 1:1, Eph. 1:1, Phil. 1:1, Col. 1:2.

Κλήσεως ἐπουρανίου μέτοχοι) Namely with us: And he calls the calling ἐπουράνιον because it leads us to super-celestial things, not to an earthly possession like the law of Moses.

Κατανοήσατε) Consider well who and how great he was.

From those things which he said about the eminence of the person, he proposes for consideration who and how great Jesus is, both as Apostle or Teacher and as High Priest, whom we confess, namely the Son of God, who, having made purification of sins, sat down at the right hand of God, which he has demonstrated thus far, as regards the truth of his divine nature and the sublimity or majesty of his human nature, to which it has been raised. He calls the calling ἐπουράνιον not only by reason of the end, because it leads to super-celestial things; but also by reason of its origin, since we have been made partakers of that calling from heaven, John 3:27.

Τὸν Ἀπόστολον καὶ Ἀρχιερέα τῆς ὁμολογίας ἡμῶν ἰησοῦν χριστὸν) He calls the Christian faith which we profess ὁμολογίαν, by metonymy, as also below in 4:14 and 10:23. Jesus is called its Ἀπόστολος, that is, sent by God for the sake of publishing it, which he often proclaims about himself. See what we said at John 9:7 and Gen. 49:10. He is called the High Priest of the same faith, who ratified it not with the blood of animals, but with his own blood. He fulfilled the roles of both Moses and Aaron at the same time, but much more sublimely than they.

He names him Apostle rather than Prophet from his teaching office: because the office of an Apostle is more worthy than that of a Prophet, and Christ was sent as a most eminent Teacher, who therefore is deservedly called Apostle, and Prophet, and Evangelist: Yet the denomination is made from the more important, since he who is in the bosom of the Father was sent from heaven into these lands, and he declares to us God, whom no one has ever seen, John 1:18, since no one knows the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him, Matt. 11:27; he compares Christ with Moses, who was a Prophet like unto him, Deut. 18:15, 18. But since Christ makes him more eminent, he calls him an Apostle, concerning whose mission, Isa. 61:1. Nor does he call him only an Apostle, but also a High Priest, because he has determined to speak of both his offices. However, there is no need for us to take the word ὁμολογίας (confession) metonymically for faith itself, nor which in the Old Testament, indeed in the proto-evangelium of Paradise, had already been published, nor anything concerning him, whether Job 9:7 or Gen. 49:10, which passages are entirely alien to this place. But he was sent to preach the coming of the kingdom of God, Mark 1:14, 16. Sent by the Father, just as he himself sent the Apostles, John 20:21. The prophets in the Old Testament foretold the coming of the Messiah, 1 Pet. 1:11. The Apostles announced that he had already arrived, which he himself also testified to both by word and by miracles, that he was the promised Messiah of the world, and especially indeed by the very work of the remission and expiation of sins, of his passion, death, resurrection, and glorious ascension, because all these things were predicted concerning the Messiah. Therefore, he is the Apostle of our ὁμολογίας or confession, because we acknowledge and confess him for that distinguished Apostle formerly promised in Isa. 61:1 ff., ch. 63:1, and the Prophet in Deut. 18:15, 16, 18, who was sent to the lost sheep of Israel, Matt. 15:24. Camerarius explains τῆς ὁμολογίας, that is, of the pledge or promise and agreement: for there is a use of a forensic word. For he who stipulates asks, and he who pledges agrees, and thus it is agreed upon in words. Therefore, the work of the redemption of the human race was a promise from the mercy of the Son of God, freed from its calamity and misery, or it was promised to the demanding divine justice. By the confession of faith, however, an agreement is made that we may be Christians and the peculiar people of God. And this is the promise of Christians in baptism. Similarly, the Priest is not called of faith but of τῆς ὁμολογίας properly accepted, that is, of our confession, or whom we confess as the only High Priest of the New Testament, not because he established the faith with his blood, but because he offered himself for us on the altar of the cross, and having entered the true holy of holies, i.e., heaven, he intercedes and appears before the face of the Lord for us, and for that reason we acknowledge and profess that he fulfilled the parts of both Moses and Aaron, but much more sublimely than they. He determined to speak of both: And first indeed, how he is an Apostle and similar to Moses in faithfulness, but of greater glory on account of the respect both to the house built and to the right of equality. But he compares him to Moses among the Hebrews, who valued Moses most highly, inasmuch as he had led their fathers out of Egyptian slavery, had been famous for many miracles, had himself promulgated the law, and had spoken with God mouth to mouth, whom even the Jews themselves dared to prefer to Christ, John 9:28-29.

Latin:

SECTIONIS II. PARTIS I. EPISTOLÆ, MEMBRI II. SPECIALIS ARTICULUS I. DE OFFICIO CHRISTI DOCTORALI. CAPUT III.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Aggreditur jam officium Christi specialius expendere & quidem principio doctorale, in eo componens Apostolum, qui & Pontifex confessionis nostræ, cum Mose ratione fidei, præferens eidem, ceu Architectum domus domui, & servo filium : nosque docens, esse domum ipsius, qui in fiducia perseveramus. Inde monet, ut vocem ejus (secundum Spiritus Sancti adhortationem Psal. XCV. 8.) audiamus, nec deficiamus à Christo, utpote Christi participes facti, ne Deus exacerbētur, uti quondam erga Israëlitas, à requie ejus exclusos.

Partes duæ sunt: Prior Didactica de Christo Doctore & Propheta, ad vers. 6. Posterior exhortatoria, de ipso audiendo, nec per apostasiam à DEO deficiendo, usque ad v. 19.

PARS I. DIDACTICA, De Christo Doctore.

Vers. 1.

Ὅθεν) Cum ita se habeant ea, quæ diximus hactenus.

Ἀδελφοὶ ἅγιοι Appellat eos à parte potiori, ut Paulus Rom. I. 7. 1. Cor. I. 2. 2. Cor. I. 1. Eph. I. 1. Phil. I. 1. Col. I. 2.

Κλήσεως ἐπουρανίου μέτοχοι) Nempe nobiscum : Et vocationem vocat ἐπουράνιον quia ad supercœlestia nos ducit, non ad terrenam possessionem ut lex Mosis.

Κατανοήσατε) Quis & quantus fuerit, bene attendite.

Ex iis, quæ de eminentia personæ dixit considerandum proponit, quis & quantus sit cum Apostolus vel Doctor, tum Pontifex Jesus, quem confitemur, nimirum Filius Dei, qui peccatorum purificatione facta consedit ad dextram Dei, quod hactenus demonstravit, quantum ad divinæ naturæ veritatem, & humanæ sublimitatem vel majestatem, ad quam evecta est. Vocationem autem ἐπουράνιον dicit non tantum ratione finis, quod ad supercœlestia ducat; sed etiam ratione originis, quum cœlitus vocationis istius facti participes, Johan. III. vers. 27.

Τὸν Ἀπόστολον καὶ Ἀρχιερέα τῆς ὁμολογίας ἡμῶν ἰησοῦν χριστὸν) ὁμολογίαν vocat fidem Christianam quam profitemur, κατὰ μετωνυμίαν ut & infra IV. 14. X. 23. Ejus Ἀπόστολος dicitur Jesus, id est, ejus publicandæ causa à Deo missus, quod ipse de se sæpe prædicat. Vide quæ diximus ad Joh. IX. 7. & Gen. XLIX. 10. Dicitur ejusdem fidei summus Sacerdos, qui sancivit eam non pecudum, sed suo ipsius sanguine. Implevit simul & Mosis & Aaronis partes, at multo, quam illi, sublimius.

Nominat à Doctorali officio Apostolum potius quam Prophetam : quia dignius munus est Apostoli, quam Prophetæ, & missus est Christus ceu Doctor eminentissimus, qui proinde & Apostolus, & Propheta & Evangelista merito nuncupatur: A potiori tamen fit denominatio, quum in has terras missus sit cœlitus, qui in sinu Patris est, & enarrat nobis Deum, quem nemo vidit unquam Johan. I. 18. quum nemo norit Patrem, nisi Filius, & cui Filius vult manifestare, Matth. XI. 27. contendit Christum cum Mose, qui Propheta similis fuit, Deut. XIIX. 15. 18. sed quum eo eminentio- rem faciat Christus, Apostolum dicit, de cujus missione, Ef. LXI. 1. Nec Apostolum tantum, sed etiam Pontificem vocat, quia de utroque ejus offi- cio dicere constituit. Non autem opus est, ut Metonymice accipiamus vocem ὁμολογίας pro ipsa fide, neque missus est Christus fidei publicandæ causa, quæ in Veteri Testamento, imo in Prot- Evangelio Paradisiaco jam publicata erat, nec quicquam de eo sive Job. IX. 7. sive Gen. XLIX. vers. 10. quæ loca prorsus aliena sunt hoc loco. Missus autem est ad prædicandum regni DEI ad- ventum, Marci I. 14. 16. Missus à Patre, sicut ipse misit Apostolos, Joh. XX. 21. Prophetæ in Vete- ri Testamento prænunciarunt adventum Messiæ, 1. Petr. I. 11. Apostoli annunciarunt eum jam ad- venisse, quod & ipse testatus est tum verbo, tum miraculis, se promissum mundi Messiam esse, im- primis vero opere ipso remissionis & expiationis peccatorum, passionis, mortis, resurrectionis & ascensionis gloriosæ, quia hæc omnia de Messia prædicta fuere. Apostolus ergo est τῆς ὁμολογίας vel confessionis nostræ, quia ipsum agnoscimus & confitemur pro illi insigni Apostolo olim pro- misso Es. LXI. 1. seqq. cap. LXIII. 1. & Propheta Deut. XIIX. 15. 16. 18. qui missus est ad oves Israë- lis perditas, Matth. XV. 24. Camerarius τῆς ὁμο- λογίας exponit, id est, sponsionis seu promissi & conventi: Est enim usus forensi verbo. Ἐπερωτᾷ enim is, qui stipulatur, & ὁμολογεῖ, qui spondet, atque ita convenit verbis. Promissum igitur à Filii DEI misericordia fuit opus redemptionis ge- neris humani, expeditum ab hujus calamitate & miseria, vel postulanti justitiæ divinæ illud fuit pro- missum. Confessione autem fidei conventio fit, ut Christiani simus, & populus peculiaris Dei. Et hæc est Christianorum in baptismo promissio. Similiter Sacerdos non dicitur fidei sed τῆς ὁμολογίας pro- prie acceptæ, hoc est confessionis nostræ, vel quem nos unicum Novi Testamenti Pontificem confi- temur, non quod fidem fanciserit suo sanguine, sed quod obtulerit semetipsum pro nobis in ara crucis, & ingressus sanctum sanctorum τὸ ἀληθι- νὸν, h. e. cælum intercedat, & vultui Domini ap- pareat pro nobis, eaque ratione & Mosis, & Aa- ronis partes, sed multo quam illi, sublimius eun- dem implevisse agnoscimus, & profitemur. De utroque dicere constituit: Et primum quidem, quomodo Apostolus & Mosi similis fide, sed major gloria ob respectum tum extructæ domus, tum juris ἰσότητος. Mosi autem confert apud Ebræos, qui Mosen maximi faciebant, utpote qui Patres eorum ex servitute Ægyptiaca duxerat, multis mi- raculis clarus fuerat, legem ipse promulgarat, & cum DEO ab ore ad os loquutus erat, quem et- iam Judæi ipsi CHRISTO præferre ausi sunt Jo- han. IX. vers. 28. 29.

## 3:2
Verse 2.

Being faithful to him who made him) that is, to him who made him both a legate and a Priest: In which sense God is said to have made Moses and Aaron, 1 Sam. 12:6. Thus God made him Lord and Christ. But he says he was faithful because he executed all things commanded to him, however difficult. As also Moses in all his house) From the Greek Num. 12:7. Where 'house' is put in the Greek manner and among other nations frequently for family, as Acts 16:15. But that house is the Israelite people, the house of Israel, Acts 2:36. Moses did not care for parts of it, but the whole of it with the greatest faithfulness. In this comparison, a preeminence also lies hidden, because Moses was faithful to God only in the Israelite people: but Christ in the administration of his office regarding the whole world, partly done directly, partly indirectly through the Apostles, whom he sent into the whole world for the sake of instructing it. But he is not yet compared here with Aaron. The Apostle finally approached that next. Now he stands within the Prophetic office, just as he warns that he should be heard as a Prophet and Apostle of the Lord. Therefore, he is faithful, according to Theophylact, out of a certain special affection, and willingly presides over the first things, nor does he allow them to be corrupted, but considers their salvation as his own, just as Moses looks out for his house, that is, the people. Faithfulness is more fully explained by the blessed Gerhard, that it consisted in three things: 1. That in all things he followed the command handed down to him by the Father, John 12:49. 2. That in all things he sought the glory of the Father, by whom he had been sent, John 8:49. 3. That he revealed every counsel of God concerning our salvation, John 1:18. In which respect he is also called a faithful witness, Rev. 1:6. That Theophylact wishes the pronoun HIS to be either of God himself or of Moses, and some refer it to Moses, does not fit, because it is not the reciprocal 'his own' but the relative 'his': And the Church is not the house of man, but of God, 1 Tim. 3:15, and Num. 12:7, which passage the Apostle respects, Moses is said to be faithful not in his own, but in God's house.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Πιστὸν ὄντα τῷ ποιήσαντι αὐτὸν) id est, ei qui ipsum fecit tum legatum, tum Sacerdotem: Quo sensu Deus dicitur ποιῆσαι Mosen & Aaronem 1. Sam. XII. 6. Sic Κύριον καὶ Χριστὸν αὐτὸν ὁ Θεὸς ἐποίησε. Fidelem autem eum fuisse dicit, quia omnia sibi imperata, quamvis durissima, exe- quutus est. Ὡς καὶ Μωυσῆς ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ οἴκῳ ἀυτῦ) Ex Græco Num. XII. 7. Ubi οἶκος more Græco & aliis gentibus frequen- te ponitur pro familia, ut Actor. XVI. 15. Domus autem illa est populus Israëliticus, οἶκος Ἰσραὴλ, Actor. II. 36. Moses non ejus partes, sed totum eum summa fide cu- rabat. Hac in comparatione occulte latet etiam præ- eminentia, quia Moses in populo Israëlitico tan- tum DEO fidelis fuit: Christus autem in admi- nistratione officii quoad totum orbem, partim ἀμέ- σως factâ, partim ἐμμέσως per Apostolos, quos in universum mundum emisit ejus informandi er- go. Nondum autem hîc cum Aarone compara- tur. Id deinceps demum aggressus est Aposto- lus. Jam sistit intra munus Propheticum, quem admodum monet, ut audiatur tanquam Prophetæ & Apostolus Domini. Fidelis igitur, secundum Theophylactum, est ex affectu quodam præcipuo, & volens rebus præsidet primis, nec eas sinit cor- rumpi, sed illarum salutem pro sua ducit, quemad- modum Moses domui ejus prospicit, id est populo. Plenius fidelitas exponitur à B. Gerhardo, quod in tribus sita fuerit 1. quod in omnibus secutus fue- rit mandatum sibi à Patre traditum Joh. XII. 49. 2. Quod in omnibus gloriam Patris, à quo missus erat, quæsiverit Joh. VIII. 49. 3. Quod omne con- silium DEI de salute nobis patefecerit Johan. I. 18. Quo respectu etiam fidelis testis dicitur Apoc. I. 6. Quod Theophylactus Pronomen EJUS esse vult vel DEI ipsius, vel Mosis, & nonnulli ad Mosen id referunt, non convenit, quia non est recipro- cum ἀυτõ sed relativum ἀυτõ: Nec hominis, sed DEI domus Ecclesia est, 1. Timoth. III. 15. & Num. XII. 7. quem locum respicit Apostolus, Moses non in sua, sed in Dei domo fidelis dicitur.

## 3:3
Verse 3.

For this one has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses) He wants to say this, that what was said about Moses also applies to Christ, and much more excellently. 'Than' here is a comparative particle. It would have been enough to say 'more than' or 'much than'. But comparisons are often accustomed to be expressed twice. The Hebrews would say, he is exalted more than Moses. Inasmuch as he who built the house has more honor than the house) Just as a family is called a house, so he who begets a family is said to build it, from which 'son' comes for the Hebrews. See what we said on Exod. 1:21. Moses is a part of the family, Christ is above the family.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Πλειόνος γὰρ δόξης ὗτος παρὰ Μωϋσῆν ἠξίωται) Hoc vult dicere, quod de Mose dictum est, Christo etiam con- venit, ac multo excellentius. Παρὰ hîc particula compa- rans. Satis fuerat dicere πλείονος ἢ aut πολὺς παρὰ. Sed solent sæpe comparationes bis exprimi. Ebræi dicerent, נשגב הוא יותר ממשה. Καθ᾿ ὅσον πλείονα τιμὴν ἔχει τõ ὀικε ὁ κατασκευάσας ἀυ- τὸν) Sicut familia domus dicitur, ita qui familiam gignit, dicitur eam struere בנה unde בן filius Ebræis. Vide quæ diximus Exod. I. vers. 21. Moses pars familiæ, Christus supra familiam.

## 3:4
Verse 4.

For every house is built by someone) It is begotten by someone, as the Abrahamids by Abraham. But God who built all things) He wants this: God indeed is the Begetter, both of the Israelite people and of the Church, but he begat the Church through the blood of Christ, so that Christ is also rightly said to have begotten it. Which cannot be adapted to Moses regarding the Israelite people. 'The things' for 'these things', as Rom. 11:29.

Strictly speaking, a comparison is no longer being instituted, but the infinite excellence of his glory over Moses is being taught. That this more excellent glory consists in a twofold moment: first, because he is the author of the family, inasmuch as he regenerates all of us, not as a ministerial cause, but as a principal one, seeing that he begat innumerable people through the Apostles and their successors in the New Testament according to Psalm 110:3, and no less also as he who, being one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, begat for himself children in the Old Testament through the Patriarchs and Prophets and other faithful teachers of the Word, because Jesus is the same yesterday, today, and forever, Heb. 13:8, the everlasting Father, Is. 9:6; then because he is the Son, not like Moses, merely a servant in the family or people of the Lord. Regarding the former excellence, Theophylact speaks thus on this passage, following Chrysostom: Moses was indeed in the whole house, that is, the entire people; otherwise, he was one individual of the house, inasmuch as he was a man and mortal, like the others, even if he seemed holier; he was a fellow-servant with the rest. Just as the stewards of a house, even if they seem to preside over others, are nevertheless bound by the same yoke of servitude as the others. Since, therefore, this Moses was also some part of the house, he was nevertheless created by someone. But he who created him must necessarily excel him. Yet the Son of God created the same [Moses], who, having assumed flesh and by his grace exercising the office of High Priest, he excels Moses by a long interval. Observe, however, how he took the comparison from the flesh, and then digressed to the divinity, by which he shows that the Creator incomparably exceeds the created thing: That restriction of Grotius regarding the generation of the family, or rather the construction of the house (for the Apostle remains in the metaphor begun), is contrary to the analogy of faith.
