Because not only the Church of the New Testament was begotten through the blood of Christ, or rather through the word of the cross and the blood of Christ, since the blood of Christ concurs ἱλαστικῶς (propitiatorily) and meritoriously: But the Word of GOD concurs with the blood of Christ ὀργανικῶς (organically) and instrumentally, or as the medium through which we are regenerated, nor are the ancients regenerated or saved in any other way than we are regenerated and saved, as far as the merit and the word of the Gospel are concerned. That the pronoun τὰ is put for ταῦτα is not proven by a convenient parallel. For in Rom. 11:29 its customary meaning prevails, nor does it fit the present passage. For GOD constructed not only ταῦτα those things or certain things, but τὰ πάντα ALL THINGS; not to mention that no noun occurs in the preceding text to which the pronoun ταῦτα could be referred. Therefore, God is said to have prepared all things; where the discourse is specifically about Christ: for he had already demonstrated before that Christ is God and the Creator of all things. He undoubtedly refers to those places in which the work of creation is described as the building of some structure, whose Architect is God, Psalm 127:2, just as it is likewise held concerning Christ in Psalm 102:11. He therefore also established him as the Author of the whole Church, which does not befit Moses, who was only a part or member of the Church, of which the whole Author is Christ, GOD blessed forever over all, Rom. 9:6. Christ is therefore not only a Teacher and Prophet, as Moses, but he is the Author, who constructed all things, and thus also the whole Church, whence he is in infinite ways superior to Moses. The συνέχεια (context) clearly teaches this meaning. For the Apostle proves that Christ is worthy of greater glory than Moses by the argument that he is worthy of greater honor who is the builder of the house; who himself is also the κατασκευασὴς πάντων (builder of all things). Schlichtingius tries in vain to weaken this argument, making a fourfold proportion from the comparison of the two, Moses and Christ, the part of the family or house, and the author of the family or builder of the house, as if Christ were being compared with GOD, and Moses with the Israelite people; whereas no σύγκρισις (comparison) is instituted here of Christ with God, but the preeminence of Christ is demonstrated over Moses in the spiritual house, or Church, which is founded here on the fact that Moses was not the one who had κατασκευάσας τὸν οἶκον (built the house), who in the building of the tabernacle showed ministry only to a superior, and in forming the people with laws; namely, to the Angel speaking before him, and the Rock accompanying the people, that is, Christ, 1 Cor. 10:4, 9, just as the dignity of κατασκευῆς (construction) does not pertain to Moses, but to the inhabitant, Lev. 26:12, 2 Cor. 6:16, by which name Christ is honored in this place, verse 6. Theodoret: As much, he says, as the maker differs from the work, so great is the difference between Moses and Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Πᾶς γὰρ οἶκος κατασκευάζεται ὑπό τινος) Gignitur ab aliquo ut Abrahamidæ ab Abrahamo. Ὁ δὲ τὰ πάντα κατασκευάσας Θεὸς) Hoc vult: Deus quidem Genitor est, & populi Israëlitici & Ecclesiæ, sed Ec- clesiam genuit per Christi sanguinem, ita ut recte & Chri- stus eam genuisse dicatur. Quod Mosi circa populum Israëliticum aptari non potest. Τὰ pro ταῦτα, ut Rom. XI. vers. 29.

Non jam comparatio porro instituitur pro- prie loquendo, sed gloriæ præ Mose excellentia infinita docetur. Quod in duplici momento sita sit illa gloria excellentior, tum quod autor sit fa- miliæ, quippe qui regenerat omnes nos, non tan- quam causa ministerialis, sed principalis, utpote qui per Apostolos eorumque successores in No- vo Testamento genuit innumeros secundum Psal. CX. 3. nec minus etiam qua unus cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto Deus in Veteri Testamento, per Patriarchas & Prophetas, aliosque Doctores Verbi fideles sibi genuit, atque liberos, quia Je- sus heri, hodie, idem & in secula, Ebr. XIII. 3. Pa- ter æternus, Es. IX. 6. tum quod sit Filius, non ut Moses, servus tantum in familia vel populo Do- mini. De priori præstantia ita Theophylactus in hunc locum, præeunte Chrysostomo: Erat sane & Moses ille in tota domo, id est, populo universo, alioqui quidam unus hic erat de domo, quippe qui homo esset & mortalis, ut cæteri, etsi sanctior vi- deretur; conservus & reliquis erat. Sicuti & do- mus dispensatores, etsi præesse aliis videantur, eo- dem tamen servitutis jugo, quo & cæteri adstrin- guntur. Cum itaque & Moses hic pars esset ali- qua domus, est tamen ab aliquo conditus. Qui ve- ro hunc condidit, ei præstet necesse est. Eundem ve- ro Filius DEI creavit, qui carne suscepta & ejus gratia Pontificis munere fungens, quem creaverat, Mofi longo intervallo præcellit. Adverte autem, quemadmodum à carne comparationem defumpfit, & deinceps ad divinitatem digreffus est, qua in- comparabiliter excedere Creatorem re creata often- dit: Illa vero Grotiana generationis familiæ vel potius extructionis domus (manet enim in Me- taphora cœpta Apostolus) restrictio ad Ecclesiam Novi Testam. contrariatur analogiæ fidei. Quia non Ecclesia tantum Novi Testamenti per san- guinem Christi genita est, vel potius per verbum crucis & sanguinis Christi, quum ἱλαστικῶς & me- ritorie concurrat sanguis Christi: Verbum autem DEI de sanguine Christi ὀργανικῶς & instrumen- taliter vel tanquam medium, per quod regenera- mur, nec aliter vel regenerati vel salvati veteres sint, quam nos regeneramur & salvamur, quan- tum ad meritum & verbum Evangelii. Pronomen τὰ pro ταῦτα poni, nec convenienti parallelo pro- batur. Nam Rom. XI. 29. usitata ejus significa- tio obtinet, nec præsenti loco quadrat. Nam DEUS non tantum ταῦτα illa vel quædam con- struxit, sed τὰ πάντα OMNIA; ut taceam, quod non occurrat nomen in præcedentibus, ad quod Pronomen ταῦτα referri queat. Omnia ergo pa- rasse Deus dicitur; ubi de Christo peculiariter sermo est: Christum enim Deum, & Creatorem omnium esse jam antea demonstrarat. Respicit sine dubio illa loca, in quibus creationis opus describitur, tanquam structuræ alicujus ædifica- tio, cujus Architectus Deus est Psal. CXXVII. 2. ut de Christo Psal. CII. 11. pariter habetur. Eun- dem ergo etiam Ecclesiæ totius Autorem consti- tuit, quod Mosi non convenit, qui pars tantum Ecclesiæ, vel membrum fuit, cujus universæ Au- tor Christus est DEUS benedictus in secula super omnia, Rom. IX. 6. Non Doctor itaque tantum & Propheta, ut Moses, sed Autor est Christus, qui omnia construxit, adeoque etiam universam Ecclesiam, unde infinitis modis Mose superior est. Docet hunc sensum evidenter συνέχεια. Pro- bat enim Apostolus, amplioris gloriæ dignum esse Christum Mose eo argumento, quia is ampliori honore dignus, qui fabricator domus est; qui ipse etiam κατασκευασὴς πάντων fabricator omni- um est. Quod argumentum nequicquam ener- vare conatur Schlichtingius, è comparatione duo- rum Mosis, & Christi, partis familiæ vel domus, & autoris familiæ, vel fabricatoris domus, faci- ens proportionem quadripartitam, quasi Christus cum DEO, & Moses cum populo Israëlitico con- feratur; quum nulla hic σύγκρισις instituatur Christi cum Deo, sed præeminentia Christi de- monstretur præ Mose in domo spirituali, vel Ec- clesia, quæ in eo hic fundatur, quod Moses non fuerit κατασκευάσας τὸν οἶκον, qui & in tabernacu- lo extruendo ministerium superiori tantum exhi- buit, & in populo legibus formando; Angelo nem- pe coram loquenti, & Petræ populum comitan- ti, hoc est, Christo, 1. Cor. X. 4. 9. uti dignitas κατασκευῆς non ad Mosen pertinet, sed ad inha- bitatorem, Levit. XXVI. 12. 2. Cor. VI. 6. quo no- mine Christus hoc loco vers. 6. honoratur. Theo- doretus: Quantum, inquit, differt ab opere opifex, tanta est inter Mosen & Christum differentia.

## 3:5
Verse 5. And Moses indeed was faithful in all his house.

In governing the house of GOD. A second comparison preferring Christ to Moses.

As a servant) As he is called in the Greek in the cited passage of Numbers. Philo on the Allegories: Just as Moses is said to have been faithful in all his house.

For a testimony of those things which were to be spoken. That he might announce to the people those things which God commanded him to be said at any time. For he is also said to testify who reports commands, as 1 Cor. 1:6, 2:1, 15:15, 2 Tim. 1:8, Rev. 1:2. Moses did not even move the camp except by the command of GOD.

Vers. 5. Καὶ Μωυσῆς μὲν πισὸς ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ οἴκῳ αὐτῦ.

In domo DEI regenda. Altera comparatio Christum Mosi præferens.

Ὡς θεράπων) Sicut vocatur in Græco dicto Nume- rorum loco. Philo de Allegoriis: Καθάπερ Μωσῆς λέγε- ται πισὸς ἐν παντὶ τῷ οἴκῳ γεγενῆσθαι.

Eis marty/rion tw=n lalhqhsome/nwn. Ut pronuntiaret populo ea quæ Deus ei dicenda quo- que tempore mandabat. Nam testari dicitur etiam qui refert mandata, ut 1. Cor. I. vers. 6. II. vers. 1. XV. vers. 15. 2. Tim. I. vers. 8. Apoc. I. vers. 2. Moses ne castra quidem movebat nisi ex DEI jussu.

## 3:6
Verse 6.

But Christ as a Son over his house. Thus it is read more correctly. Christ is over the family, that is, he commands the family; why? For it is his own family, begotten through him. The Jurisconsults say that even while the father is alive, the son is in a way the master of the paternal property. Whence also in Comedies sons are called by servants the lesser masters, and a daughter 'domnula', that is, little mistress, in inscriptions.

A second preeminence likewise makes Christ our Teacher more eminent than Moses by an infinite reason, namely, that he himself is to be regarded not as a servant, but as a Son in his own house. Moses was faithful in his house of God, but as a servant: Christ was faithful in his house of himself: (For Grotius acknowledges that it is read more correctly thus, and more corrected copies read it so;) not as a servant, but as a Son, who is not only in a way the Master of the paternal property, but is the same Master with the Father because of his divine nature, 1 Cor. 8:6. For he is a Son not by adoption, but by nature, not by regeneration, but by generation, not by grace, but by nature; a Son ὁμοούσιος (consubstantial) of the same essence with the Father. Theodoret meets the heretics here: But Christ is called faithful as a Son. But if heretics think that this title signifies vileness and abjection, let them hear the Apostle, saying of God and the Father: God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, and the Prophet David: The Lord is faithful in all his words. And again: A faithful witness in heaven. Moreover, the divine Moses also says thus: God is faithful, and there is no iniquity in him. He called those who believe the house of God, in accordance with the prophecy which says: I will dwell in them, and walk. Theophylact: Or, he says, he shows that Christ excels Moses in a certain other way, because, namely, that Moses was faithful as a minister and servant, and was appointed to that end, that he might announce to the other servants what belonged to the Lord. Christ, therefore, is faithful, inasmuch as he is the own and heir and son. And he moderates and rules what is paternal, according to the Father's will. The Son of this kind, therefore, differs from Moses the servant by a certain huge and incomparable interval. Blessed Baldwin says the first eminence was by reason of architecture: Moses is a part of the house in which he dwells, that is, the Church. Christ, however, is not a part, but the head, nay, the architect of this mystical house; and the author of any work is worthy of greater glory and honor, nay, dignity and esteem, than the work itself or merely a part of the work. The second is by reason of habitation or the right which each has in the house of GOD, v. 5. Moses was in the Church as a servant, faithfully expediting those things which he had in his commands, in which, however, he had no right. Christ, however, dwells in the Church as a son, and consequently as the Lord of the Church, who acquired it for himself as a possession with his own blood, Acts XX. Moses served only the Son as the Lord of the Church, in testimony of those things which were to be spoken not by Moses, but by the Son, because he himself testified of the Son, how primarily the Son builds, and is to build, the entire Church, Deut. XVIII. v. 19. John I. 46. Therefore Erasmus understands it as from Christ. Moses only proposed prophecies and types concerning Christ: but in CHRIST we have their truth and fulfillment. What Moses pronounced to the people, which God wanted him to know, that now by him was indicated, that he was faithful in the house of God, as a servant. For in this a great part of his service consisted: therefore an antithesis was not to be passed over in this member, which consists in this, that Moses indeed was also faithful, testifying of Christ: For this testimony also was committed to him, just as all the Prophets bore testimony of him, Acts 10:43. But he referred in such a way to the hearing of Christ, and to those things which were to be said by Christ. He testified of them, but less clearly, whereas those things which were to be said by him in the last days were most clearly. Therefore he warned in Deut. 18:18 that Christ was to be heard, and that every soul which did not hear him was to be cut off: By which reasoning he not only testifies of Christ, but also hands the torch to him, that it is not he whom all are bound to hear under the necessity of obtaining salvation, and in whom all are bound to believe, but Christ, that great Prophet to be raised up from the midst of the Israelites. Concerning the hearing of whom God testified from heaven here on Mount Zion, by foretelling, but when he appeared in the flesh, on the holy mount he proclaimed from heaven with a λευκάδι φωνῇ, as if pointing him out with a finger, and surrounding him with a majestic cloud, 'This is my beloved Son, HEAR HIM,' Matt. 17:5. See B. Luther's explanation on Deut. ch. 18, Vol. 5, Old German, p. 1090. Twin to our explanation is the interpretation of B. Balduinus, who locates the third preeminence here: that Moses was a servant in the house of God for a testimony of those things which were to be said, that is, that he might preach of the benefits of Christ which were to follow in the fullness of time by the very act, enlightened by the Spirit of God partly through open promises, and partly also through sacrifices and other Levitical types and shadows. But Christ did not teach concerning future things, but led us into the present reality, and acquired the benefits once promised and shadowed forth by the very act, and exhibited them to us in his word. B. Dorscheus has thus expounded this eminence: Witnesses are accustomed to report things heard elsewhere. Hence Moses is said to have been appointed to testify of those things which he himself had learned from God the best and greatest. But Christ speaks in his house in such a way that he speaks not through a revelation drawn from elsewhere, but from the very bosom of GOD, in which he is as it were the μονογενὴς ὑὸς, John 1:18, so much so that even when the Holy Spirit speaks to us, he speaks things taken from Christ, John 16:14, 15. And so, even if Christ also testifies, and indeed testifies of what he has seen and heard, John 3:11, 32, yet Christ's testimony is far higher and more sublime, and his hearing and vision far broader and deeper. For it is within God himself, in the depths of GOD, which the Spirit of God himself searches, 1. Cor. 2:10. Whence he is a μάρτυς ἐν ὀρανοῖς, 1 John 5:7, in the way that there are only three who testify, whereas Moses belongs to the martyrs ἐκ τῇ γῇ, insofar as he administered the word of the divine Spirit, and also spoke and wrote of Christ, John 5:46. Hence now the Apostle concludes effectively: he who is in the spiritual house by the right of his own Son, and existing in the bosom of his Father, he is superior to him who merely performs the duty of a servant, and can testify nothing beyond what has been communicated from elsewhere. But Christ dwells in the spiritual house of God, that is, the Church, by the right of God's own Son and existing in the bosom of the eternal Father. Therefore he is superior to Moses, who merely performed the duty of a servant and could not testify beyond what was communicated. Whence the Deity of Christ is concluded quite evidently.

Whose house we are.

We Christians are his family and will be, of course. For the present here includes the future.

If indeed we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end) It is a transposition. For the ordinary construction by prozeugma would have been: If we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end. Then indeed by confidence (παῤῥησίαν) is to be understood by metonymy the open profession of Christianity, as also below 10:35. By the rejoicing of hope (καύχημα ἐλπίδος), the joy of hope (for we have shown elsewhere that rejoicing (καύχημα) means the same as exultation (ἀγαλλίαμα)) is understood that joyful hope, namely of eternal life under those laws under which it was promised by Christ. If we have retained this, he says, firm, that is, unshaken even to the end: 'He who endures to the end shall be saved,' Matt. 10:22. A saving birth, not received, but guarded, gives life, says Cyprian.

That eminence of Christ is amplified, that all the faithful are his house and family, and at the same time the glory of the Hebrews converted to Christ is celebrated, that they too have now become the family of Christ, and are to remain so henceforth, provided they have kept a firm faith. That we are the house of God pertains to the gracious presence of God, for nowhere is the universe of creatures called the house of God. Compare Acts 7:48, 49, 50; 17:24 ff. For neither are the Angels, although they are called thrones, Col. 1:16, ever called the house of God. Therefore this is a special dignity (ἀξίωσις) of the faithful and the saints, that they are the house of the most holy Trinity, and especially of Christ, that indeed both by reason of substantial presence, which every indwelling requires, and by reason of gracious approach. This latter, however, both by reason of the admirable illumination from the Prophetic office, for thus Christ is the light in this house, John 1:9, and the Morning Star (Φωσφόρος) 2. Petr. 1:19, and by reason of the priestly dispensation, whence from the Priestly office of Christ this house is called holy (ἱερὰ), etc., 1 Pet. 2:5, and by reason of the saving government from the Kingly office of Christ, whence it is called a Royal priesthood, 1 Pet. 2:9; in general it is a spiritual house (οἶκος πνευματικὸς), whence also the whole economy is spiritual, nor does it exclude substantial presence just because it is spiritual. For it is a spiritual house (οἶκος πνευματικὸς) of the Trinity as well. But the faithful are called a spiritual house (οἶκος πνευματικὸς) with respect to the bodily house (οἴκου σωματικοῦ), Col. 2:9, which pertains to the very hypostasis of the Son, and is joined to him through intimate presence, whereas this house is regarded only by external gracious presence.

Moreover, as B. Dorscheus notes, Grotius wrongly takes οἶκον in this passage as a synecdoche for the family itself: just as the faithful are called οἶκοι τοῦ Θεοῦ, Eph. II. 19. For the force of the word leads us not only to the family, but also to the dwelling itself, which the parallel texts also intend, and Schlichtingius himself acknowledges, being better than Grotius in this part, when he says: Believers are the house of God, whether you understand by house the family or the building. For both can be understood in this passage: They are the family of God and Christ, because Christ and God dwell in them through His Holy Spirit.

Moreover, an excellent description of faith is held here, that it is παῤῥησία or confidence, Eph. III. 12, Heb. IV. 16, and καύχημα τῆς ἐλπίδος, because it has joined to it the boasting of the hope of the heavenly inheritance, Rom. V. 2, and thus does not allow us to doubt either concerning present grace or future glory. There is no need, therefore, that we take παῤῥησία metonymically for an open profession of Christianity (which is not necessary even in Heb. X. v. 35), since saving faith itself can, and indeed must, be understood, which alone is joined with the certain hope of glory and the boasting of hope, which is noted by καύχημα according to its customary meaning rather than joy, even though joy in the Holy Spirit also embraces the very boasting of hope. For we rejoice in the Holy Spirit in such a way that we boast of eternal glory, even in any tribulation and most sad affliction. Concerning which Theophylactus says: He rightly called it confidence and glory. For when the hope of future retribution is more certain to anyone, he will count it as glory, just as if he had obtained everything from hope and prayers. Nor does he betake himself to some retreat, in order to hide and mourn when he is afflicted with evils, but he is more confident, and comes forth into public: and for the sake of CHRIST, whom he uniquely worships, he endures every adversity with an even mind. Rightly, therefore, it is deduced from this passage, both that faith is unmoved and firm, and embracing the promises of the Gospel with confidence without any doubt, which the faithful person applies to himself: and that only believers belong to the house and family of God, the Church, and are true members of the same, and that the faithful can fall from faith.

PART II. PARENETIC, On hearing CHRIST the Teacher.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Xristòs dè w(s ui(òs e)pì tòn oi)=kon au)tou=. Ita rectius legitur. Christus supra familiam, id est, fa- miliæ imperat, quare? Est enim ipsius familia per ipsum genita. Dicunt Jurisconsulti, etiam vivente patre filium quodammodo dominum esse rerum paternarum. Unde & in Comœdiis filii à servis heri minores dicuntur, & filia domnula, id est, dominula in inscriptionibus.

Altera præcellentia itidem infinita ratione eminentiorem Mose Christum Doctorem no- strum facit, qua nempe ipse non ut famulus, sed ut Filius in domo sua spectandus. Moses fidelis in domo au)tou= Dei fuit, sed w(s qera/pwn, ut famu- lus: Christus fidelis fuit in domo au)tou= sui ipsius: (Sic enim rectius legi agnoscit Grotius, & emen- datiora legunt exemplaria;) non ut famulus, sed w(s ui(òs, ut Filius, qui non tantum quodammodo Dominus est rerum paternarum, sed idem cum Patre Dominus est ob divinam naturam, 1. Cor. IIX. 6. Est enim Filius non adoptivus, sed pro- prius, non per regenerationem, sed generationem, non gratiâ, sed naturâ; Filius o(moou/sios ejusdem cum Patre essentiæ. Occurrit hic hæreticis Theo- doretus: Christus autem ut Filius vocatur fidelis. Quod si hæretici existimant, hanc appellationem significare vilitatem & abjectionem, audiant Apo- stolum, de Deo & Patre dicentem: Fidelis Deus, per quem vocati estis in societatem Filii ejus, & David Prophetam: Fidelis Dominus in omnibus verbis suis. Et rursus: Testis in cælo fidelis. Quin etiam Moses divinus sic dicit Deus fidelis, & non est in ipso iniquitas. Domum autem Dei vocavit eos, qui credunt, convenienter prophetiæ quæ dicit: Inhabitabo in ipsis, & ambulabo. Theophylactus: Vel alium, inquit, quendam in modum Mosi Chri- stum præstare ostendit, quia scilicet Moses ille tan- quam minister & servus esset fidelis, & ad id con- stitutus, ut quæ Domini forent, cæteris servis de- nuntiaret. Christus itaque fidelis est, utpote qui proprius sit & hæres & filius. Et quæ paterna sunt, pro Patris arbitrio moderetur & regat. Differt itaque istiusmodi Filius à Mose servo ingenti quo- dam & incomparabili intervallo. B. Balduinus primam eminentiam dicit fuisse ratione archite- cturæ: Moses est pars domus, in qua versatur, hoc est, Ecclesiæ. Christus autem non pars, sed caput est, imo architectus hujus mysticæ domus, majore au- tem gloria & honore, imo dignitate & existimatio- ne dignus est autor alicujus operis, quam opus ipsum aut pars duntaxat operis. Alteram ratione inha- bitationis vel juris, quod quisque habet in domo DEI, v. 5. Moses fuit in Ecclesia, tanquam famu- lus, expediens ea, quæ in mandatis habebat, fideli- ter, in qua tamen nihil juris habebat. Christus au- tem in Ecclesia versatur ut filius, ac proinde ut Dominus Ecclesiæ, qui sibi eam acquisivit in pe- culium sanguine suo Actor. XX. Moses famulaba- tur tantum Filio ceu Domino Ecclesiæ, in testi- monium eorum, quæ dicenda erant non à Mose, sed à Filio, quia testificatus est ipse de Filio, quomo- do imprimis Filius exstruat, & exstructurus sit uni- versam Ecclesiam, Deut. XIIX. v. 19. Joh. I. 46. Ideo Erasmus subintelligit à Christo. Moses tan- tum vaticinia & typos proponebat de Christo: In CHRISTO autem habemus eorum veritatem, & complementum. Quod Moses pronunciavit po- pulo, quæ Deus ipsum scire volebat, id jam eo indicatum, quod fidelis fuerit in domo Dei, ut famulus. Nam in eo magnam partem ejus servi- tium situm erat: Antithesis ergo non tacenda erat in hoc membro, quæ in eo sita est, quod Mo- ses quidem fidelis etiam fuerit testificans de Chri- sto: Nam & hoc testimonium ipsi commissum fuit, quemadmodum omnes Prophetæ testimo- nium de ipso edidere, Actor. X.43. Sed remiserit ita ad Christum audiendum, & ea, quæ dicenda à Christo erant. Testificabatur de illis, sed minus luculenter, quæ dicenda ab ipso novissimis die- bus erant luculentissime. Ideo monebat Deut. XIIX. 18. Christum audiendum esse, animamque omnem, quæ non audierit ipsum, exscindendam: Qua ratione non tantum testificatur de Christo, sed ipsi etiam lampada tradit, non se esse, quem sub necessitate consequendæ salutis audire, in quem credere omnes teneantur, sed Christum, magnum illum Prophetam excitandum è medio Israëlitarium. De quo audiendo Deus de cælo hic testatus est in monte Sion, prænunciando, sed cum in carne apparuit, in monte sancto de cælo λευκάδι φωνῇ pronunciavit, digito quasi ipsum demonstrando, & nube Majestatica ipsum circumdando, hic est Filius meus dilectus, HUNC AUDITE, Matth. XVII. 5. Vid. B. Luther. ex- plicat. in Deut. c. XIIX. T. V. Alt, Germ. p. 1090. Gemella nostræ explicationi B. Balduini interpre- tatio est, qui tertiam hic locat præeminentiam: Mosen fuisse in domo Dei famulum in testimo- nium eorum, quæ dicenda erant, hoc est, ut de bene- ficiis Christi in plenitudine demum temporis ipso actu subsequuturis prædicaret, illuminatus à Spiri- tu Dei partim per apertas promissiones, partim et- iam sacrificia, aliosque typos & umbras Leviticas. Christus vero non de futuris docuit, sed nos in rem præsentem duxit, beneficiaque olim promissa & ad- umbrata ipso actu acquisivit, & in verbo suo nobis exhibuit. B. Dorscheus ita hanc eminentiam edis- serit: Solent testes aliunde audita referre. Hinc Moses dicitur constitutus ut testificaretur, quæ ipse à Deo optimo maximo didicerat. Christus autem ita loquitur in domo sua, ut non per revelationem aliunde haustam, sed ex ipso sinu DEI, in quo est veluti μονογενὴς ὑὸς, Johan. I. 18. loquatur, adeo ut etiam cum Spiritus Sanctus nobis loquitur, τὰ ἐκ τοῦ χριστοῦ sumpta loquatur, Joh. XVI. 14. 15. Itaque etiamsi Christus quoque testificetur, & quidem quæ vidit & audivit testificetur Joh. III. 11.32. Tamen longe altius est & sublimius Christi testimonium, longe amplior atque angustior auditio atque visio. Est enim intra ipsum Deum in profundis DEI, quæ scrutatur ipse Dei Spiritus, 1. Cor. II. 10. Unde est μάρτυς ἐν ὀρανοῖς, 1. Johan. V. 7. quomodo tres tantum sunt, qui testantur, cum Moses pertineat ad martyres ἐκ τῇ γῇ, quatenus verbum divini Spiritus administravit, & de Christo etiam loquu- tus est & scripsit, Joh. V. 46. Hinc jam concludit efficaciter Apostolus, qui est in domo spirituali jure Filii proprii, & in sinu Patris sui existentis, ille eo superior est, qui munere famuli duntaxat fungi- tur, nec ultra aliunde communicata testificari po- test. Atqui Christus jure Filii DEI proprii & in sinu æterni Patris existentis versatur in domo Dei spirituali, id est Ecclesia. Ergo superior est Mose, qui duntaxat munere famuli fungebatur, nec ultra communicata testificari poterat. Unde Christi Deitas satis evidenter concluditur.

Οὗ οἶκός ἐσμεν ἡμεῖς.

Nos Christiani sumus ejus familia & erimus scilicet. Nam præsens hic futurum comprehendit.

Ἐάν περ τὴν παῤῥησίαν καὶ τὸ καύχημα τῆς ἐλπίδος μέ- χρι τέλους βεβαίαν κατάσχωμεν) Est trajectio. Nam ordi- naria constructio per προζευγμα fuerat: Εάν βεβαίαν κα- τάσχωμεν μέχρι τέλες την παῤῥησίαν καὶ τὸ καύχημα τῆς ἐλπίδος. Tum vero per παῤῥησίαν intelligenda est per Metonymiam professio Christianismi aperta, ut & infra X. 35. Per καύχημα ἐλπίδος, lætitiam spei (Nam καύχη- μα idem valere quod ἀγαλλίαμα alibi ostendimus) intel- ligitur spes illa læta, nempe vitæ æternæ sub iis legibus sub quibus à Christo promissa est. Si retinuerimus hanc, inquit, firmam, id est, inconcussam ad finem usque: ὁ ὑπομείνας εἰς τέλος, σωθήσεται Matth. X. 22. Nativitas sa- lutaris non accepta, sed custodita vivificat, ait Cyprianus.

Amplificatur eminentia illa Christi, quod o- mnes fideles ejus sint domus & familia, & celebra- tur simul Ebræorum conversorum ad Christum gloria, quod & ipsi familia Christi jam evaserint, & porro mansuri sint, modo fidem firmam ser- varint. Quod domus simus Dei, pertinet ad præ- sentiam Dei gratiosam, nuspiam enim universitas creaturarum οἶκος Dei appellatur. Conf. Act. VII. vers. 48. 49. 50. XVII. 24. seqq. Neque enim An- geli, quanquam throni appellentur, Col. I. 16. οἶκος Dei uspiam dicuntur. Est itaque specialis hæc fide- lium & sanctorum ἀξίωσις, quod sint οἶκος sacro- sanctæ Trinitatis, & imprimis Christi, illud qui- dem tum ratione substantialis præsentiæ, quam o- mnis inhabitatio requirit: tum ratione gratiosæ ap- propinquationis. Hoc vero tum ratione admiran- dæ illuminationis ex officio Prophetico, sic enim Christus in hac domo est lux Joh. I. 9. & Φωσφό- ρος 2. Petr. I. 19. tum ratione sacerdotalis dispen- sationis, unde ex officio Christi Sacerdotali domus hæc dicitur ἱερὰ &c. 1. Petr. II. 5. tum ratione sal- vifici regiminis ex officio Christi Regio, unde dici- tur Regale sacerdotium 1. Petr. II. 9. in universum est οἶκος πνευματικὸς, unde etiam tota œconomia spiritualis est, nec tantum quia spiritualis, substan- tialem præsentiam excludit. Est enim οἶκος πνευ- ματικὸς etiam Trinitatis. Fideles autem dicuntur οἶκος πνευματικὸς respectu οἴκου σωματικοῦ Col. II. 9. quod ad ipsam hypostasin Filii pertinet, ejusque per præsentiam intimam est conjunctus, cum hic οἶκος præsentia gratiosa extima tantum respiciatur.

Cæterum male, notante B. Dorscheo, Grotius οἶκον hoc loco Synecdoche pro ipsa familia accipit: quomodo fideles dicuntur οἶκοι τοῦ Θεοῦ, Eph. II. 19. Vis enim vocabuli non tantum ad familiam, sed et- iam ad ipsum habitaculum nos deducit, quod & volunt textus paralleli, & agnoscit ipse Schlichtin- gius, Grotio in hac parte melior, cum ait: Sunt credentes domus Dei, sive per domum familiam intelligas, sive ædificium. Utrumque enim hoc loco intelligi potest: Familia Dei & Christi sunt, quia Christus & Deus in iis habitat per Spiritum suum Sanctum.

Habetur autem hic egregia fidei descriptio, quod παῤῥησία sit sive fiducia, Eph. III. 12. Ebr. IV. 16. & καύχημα τῆς ἐλπίδος, quia conjun- ctam habet gloritationem spei hæreditatis cœle- stis, Rom. V. 2. adeoque nos dubitare non sinat vel de præsenti gratia, vel de futura gloria. Non ergo opus est, ut Metonymice παῤῥησίαν accipia- mus de aperta Christianismi professione, (quod nec Ebr. X. v. 35. necessarium est) siquidem ipsa fides salvifica intelligi possit, imo debeat, quæ so- la conjuncta est cum spe certa gloriæ, & gloria- tione spei, quæ per καύχημα secundum usitatum significatum potius notatur, quam lætitia, etsi gaudium in Spiritu Sancto ipsam gloritationem spei etiam complectatur. Nam ita lætamur in Spiritu Sancto, ut gloriemur de æterna gloria, etiam in quavis tribulatione, & afflictione tristis- sima. Quo de Theophylactus: Recte autem fi- duciam dixit & gloriam. Cum enim cuiquam futur ræ retributionis spes certior est, id gloriæ ducet, perinde ac si fit ex spe et votis omnia consequutus. Nec in secessum se aliquem confert, ut deliteat et mareat, cum malis affligitur, sed fidentior est, et in publicum prodit: et CHRISTI ob gratiam, quem unice colit, adversa quaeque aequo tolerat animo. Recte ergo deducitur ex hoc loco, tum quod fides est immota et firma, ac fiducia amplentens promissiones Evangelii citra ullam dubitationem, quas sibi applicat fidelis: tum quod soli credentes ad domum et familiam Dei Ecclesiam pertineant, ejusdemque vera membra sint, tum quod fideles possint fide excidere.

PARS II. PARÆNETICA, De CHRISTO Doctore audiendo.

## 3:7
Ver. 7. Διὸ (Therefore) this must be joined with that which follows after the long testimony of Scripture: Βλέπετε ἀδελφοὶ (Take heed, brethren). It coheres with the aforementioned in this way: Since you have received such great honor, that you are counted as the family of both God and Christ, take heed, lest you fall from such great honor. Καθὼς λέγει τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον (As the Holy Spirit says.) Through David, Psalm

XCV. ver. 8. Σήμερον ἐὰν τῆς φωνῆς αὐτοῦ ἀκούσητε (Today if you will hear his voice) That is, the day of wisdom, for the celebration of which the hymn of Scripture was intended, and at which time that old history was accustomed to be read aloud to the people. This is taken from the Greek LXX. Eà (If), here it is when, where, as often as. Μὴ σκληρύνητε τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν (Do not harden your hearts) אֶל-תַּקְשׁוּ, do not show yourselves intractable.

We have the same word in EXOD. VII. 3. XIII. 15. DEUT. II. 30. X. 16. and it is accustomed to be attributed, as is the word לֵב &amp; similar ones, both to God and to men, but in a sense not entirely the same, as we have said elsewhere. Ὡς ἐν τῷ παραπικρασμῷ (As in the provocation) In the place named מְרִיבָה (Meribah) EXOD. XVII. 7. NUM. XX. 13. 24. That, however, is rendered in those places as λοιδορία (reproach) &amp; ἀντιλογία (contradiction).

But παραπικρασμῷ (provocation) has the same meaning. And note that it is true what we said at GEN. XL. ver. 16. that even proper names of men or places are accustomed to be changed in other languages, not into words of the same sound, but into those signifying the same thing. The Israelites quarreled there with Moses &amp; Aaron, EXOD.

XVII. ver. 2. but God estimates it just as if they had quarreled with Him, as can be seen in NUM. XX. ver. 13. Κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν τοῦ πειρασμοῦ (In the day of temptation) Here also πειρασμὸς (temptation) is for מַסָּה (Massah), which name is likewise of a place in the desert so called from the history. The day of Massah is that time when the people acted around Massah: just as the day of Midian in Isaiah IX.

4. The LXX in EXOD. XVII. 7. &amp; DEUT. VI. 16. translate this proper name as πειρασμὸν (temptation). But נִסָּה (nissah), from which that name comes, is to irritate, which is also πειράζειν &amp; πειράζειν (to tempt/test) for the Greeks. Κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν (In the day), that is, as at that time, as in JOB, XXIX. ver. 2. JER. XLIV. 6. DAN. IX. 15. &amp; elsewhere. Οὗ ἐπείρασόν με οἱ πατέρες ὑμῶν (Where your fathers tempted me) That ὗ (where) shows that the names of the places had preceded.

And it appears here that πειράζειν (to tempt), as we have already said, is the same as πειρασμὸν (temptation). ἐδοκίμασαν με καὶ εἶδον τὰ ἔργα μου (they tested me and saw my works). "Me" is not in the Greek: But it is understood from the former. In the Hebrew it is expressed. The sense, however, is: Although they had seen my great works: yet it pleased them to make a trial of my power by irritating me. κἀγ (and I) for καίπερ (although) (Ps. 95:9), the sense is the same in DEUT. XXIX. 2. 3. 4. The punctuation should be placed after με (me), as in the Hebrew and the Sixtine edition of the Greek. And the things which follow below in 17. and the series of the history itself demand this. Τεσσαράκοντα ἔτη διὸ προσώχθισα τῇ γενεᾷ ἐκείνῃ (Forty years, therefore I was grieved with that generation). Διὸ (Therefore) here signifies on account of these things &amp; similar ones.

Thus we have διὸ (therefore) for διὰ τοῦτο (for this reason) also in 2. COR. IV. ver. 13. Προσώχθισα (I was grieved) I am weary of them. Thus in JOB X. 1. נָקְטָה נַפְשִׁי (my soul is weary) κάμαι τῇ ψυχῇ με (I am weary in my soul), in the Latin: my soul is weary. According to Suidas, προσώχθισα is δυνατισθ (to be indignant), βδελύττομαι (to abhor). And in this Psalm both Aquila and Symmachus have δυσχεραίνω (I am displeased). He calls γενεὰν (generation) the men of that age, and that for the most part, as we shall now see.

And there is a synecdoche in the XL years; for he wishes to say a great part of those years. See NUM. XVI. ver. 22. But he seems to urge that about the XL years because God had predetermined an equal space for the Jews for repentance after Christ was put to death.

For ἐκείνῃ (that) in the Manuscript is ταύτῃ (this). Ver. 10. Καὶ εἶπον ἀεὶ πλανῶνται τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοὶ δὲ ἐν ἔγνωσαν τὰς ὁδούς με (And I said, they always go astray in their heart, and they have not known my ways) In the Greek LXX, καὶ αὐτοί (and they). To know here is (Ps. 95:10) to care for, as in Psalm I. ver. 6. &amp; elsewhere. That people has a wandering heart; it does not please them to persist in the ways prescribed by me. Ver. 11. Ὡς ὤμοσα ἐν τῇ ὀργῇ με (As I swore in my wrath). Ὡς (As) here is worth "therefore," as is the Hebrew אֲשֶׁר (that/as).

And thus the Syrian rightly accepts it: You have this oath in NUM. XIV. ver. 28. The same words will be repeated below. IV. 3. where there is likewise ὡς (as), not οἷς (to whom) as some have read here. Εἰ εἰσελεύσονται εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσίν με (If they shall enter into my rest). Something is understood, as is usual in oaths, 1. SAM. XV. Psalm

CXXXII. 2. 3. MARK VIII. 12. When men swear, it is understood, "may God do so to me," as in 1. SAM. XXV. 22. When God [swears], "may He not have me for God": κατάπαυσις (rest) is called that region where the people rested from long wanderings: as in DEUT. XII. 9. God adds the little word με (my), because God was the Author of that good: partly also because then the Ark, which was called by the name of God, ceased to wander.

David Kimchi also senses that the times of the Messiah are covered under the wrappings. The LXX interpret ἐὰν (if) as "as often as" more correctly than Grotius, who restricts the exhortation to the day of συννοηγίας (assembly). Even if that Psalm were dedicated specifically to this feast, about which, however, it is not certain from the sources, nor even from the version of the LXX: the Apostolic application sufficiently teaches that it pertains to every time when the voice of the Lord sounds "today"; never, when it sounds, are hearts to be hardened.

The word ἀνύειν (to hear) is sometimes understood with affection, when the voice of the Lord is heard not only with the external ears of the body, but with the interior ears of the heart, or is heard in such a way that it is received and kept by a faithful mind and by faith, and hearts are not hardened against it.

But here it is used of external hearing. For we are warned that, hearing the voice from without, we should admit it into us, or not harden our heart, lest we place an obstacle to it or resist it, Acts

VII. 51. It is taught, however, that the voice of Christ was that voice of the Lord, whom the Israelites are also said to have tempted in the desert by their infidelity, 1. Cor. X. 9. We have, therefore, here also that Christ is that Lord, whose voice is to be heard, as this passage teaches. For that pronoun αὐτῷ (him) is to be referred to no other than to Him, whose house and family the faithful are said to be, who is the Son in the house of the Church, and the Lord; and that the Holy Spirit is Jehovah, who said or spoke through David, and whom the Fathers tempted in the desert, whose works they saw for 40 years, and who became hostile to them, cf.

Is. LXIII. ver. 10.

For He who speaks here through David is He who was tempted by the Israelites, whose works they saw, and who became hostile to them, that is, Jehovah the Lord. But the Holy Spirit is He who speaks here, the Apostle being the witness. Therefore. Therefore, a transition here from one person to another is not to be admitted, which some wish, nor is it easily to be granted in the Prophets.

Rather, the person of God tempted by the Israelites, that is, of Christ, and of the Holy Spirit speaking through David is distinctly introduced by the Apostle. However, the Greek copies do not have the word πειρασμῦ (of temptation) in this place, therefore the crisis of Grotius here is superfluous, but [they have] the word πειρασμῦ.

And although the names of the places do not agree with the history described in NUM. XX., we nevertheless easily admit that by synecdoche the others are included under one temptation or irritation. Although there is no need even for that, that the local [term] be referred to a special place, [that] Massah or Meribah, or through παραπικρασμὸν (provocation) a place be understood: since it can be rendered with the Blessed

Luther as an Appellative (not as a significant [term] of a proper name) "in der Verbitterung" (in the bitterness). Therefore, that can be referred to a place in general, or indefinitely, where, namely, the παραπικρασμὸς (provocation) and πειρασμὸς (temptation) took place, whoever that may have been; because for 40 years they had tempted they are said to have tempted God, and to have tested him; however much they may have seen the works of the Lord, by which he testified to his power, truth, and providence with miracles, even very illustrious ones: yet they tempted and tested him more often, and thus provoked the Holy Spirit, and rendered him hostile to themselves. After the word μʊ. a mark is placed without sufficient cause. For although the beginning of a new verse is made at the words τεσσαράκοντα ἔτη in the Hebrew, and the Apostle so arranges v. 17. Yet most Greek Codices refer those words to the preceding: which could also be very well referred to the following v. 17, because there is no discrepancy in the sense. For the Israelites tempted God for forty years: And for 40 years, though not continuous, GOD was hostile to that generation, or to the men in his people in that age, Num. XXXII. v. 4. 13. The Holy Spirit mentions forty years, so that he might compare the time of the destruction of the Apostate Church of the Israelites with the time of the future destruction of the Synagogue after the Messiah was cut off. By the ways of the Lord are understood not the commands which the Lord prescribed to them, but rather the works of divine power, justice, mercy, and truth, in which he himself walks, Psalm XXV. 10. Which concerning the oath

of God is said, Num. XIV. 23. it does not occur: only a simple threat of GOD is held there. But Philo rightly says that each of God's words is an oath. Although it may also be said that David did not have that from Moses, but by immediate revelation from God, namely that God swore that they shall not enter into the rest of the Lord. But concerning anger, because affections do not fall upon God, Augustine rightly in book IX. de civit. DEI chap. 5. The anger of God is the effect of divine vengeance, but not a turbulent affection of God.

In that formula εἰ εἰσελεύσονται, there is no need to understand anything, so that a promissory formula may emerge, since it can be said that in oaths, imprecations, and affirmative obligations the particle אם imports a negation, (as Gen. XXVI. 29. that you may not wish to do evil to us: 1 Kings I. 51. that you may not wish to kill, etc.) in negatives אם לא, if not, an affirmation. Thus therefore, if they shall enter, in this place is, they shall not enter my rest, Conf. Mark VIII. v. 12. Matt. XVI. 4. That rest is the land of Canaan, which he calls his rest, either because it was prepared by him for the Israelites, or because God peculiarly wished to have his rest there, concerning which Psalm CXXXII. 13. 14. For the Apostle is in agreement with David in this, that they propose the example of the ancient Israelites under Moses; Whence the Apostle afterwards most solidly deduces that another rest still remains, into which the faithful are to be led, not hardening their hearts at the voice of the Lord. He is certainly discussing hope here, says Theophylact, namely how there are certain rewards to be expected there for labors, and quietude. And that it will be so, he affirms from the words of the Prophet, just as believers are to enter into rest, so that on the contrary those who have believed less, such as those ancient Jews were, are by no means going to approach this. David therefore, who was later, when he was discussing these matters, said: Today if you will hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, lest you suffer the same things that your ancestors suffered and be deprived of quiet, as if, namely, there is some other quietude which we ourselves are to attain, he says this: For if they had received true quiet, why would he infer that; Today do not harden your hearts, as your Fathers did, and you shall not enter into my rest. What then can be the rest, other than the most pleasant leisure of the heavenly kingdom, whose figure and sabbath he presents, and him, who was typically effected in the entry of the sons of the contradicting generation into Palestine. Where Theophylact observes a triple rest, and discusses it thus: We rest therefore in three ways, either this rest is provided by the sabbath, in which God also rested from his work, concerning which rest David does not seem to be discussing in this place, inasmuch as it was held by those ancients as the true one, and that indeed which was obtained through the entry into the promised land, which the Jews having entered, were to rest from war and battles, and from that error in which they were wandering as vagrants for so long. Of which rest, however, he makes no mention here. For if the region of Palestine was under his and the Hebrews' empire in David's time, how was he to speak of this as if it were deserted? It seems therefore that he is pretending some other state of such rest, into which Joshua had no authority to bring the Jews. We will find such a state only in the heavens. From which, lest you fall away from the example of your ancestors on account of diffidence, you must strive with all zeal. For the reasons of those things which are done by God are not to be demanded from man, but faith is to be rendered to him without doubt. For that is also given as a crime to those ancients, because they tempted the Lord, that is, because they did not hope in him with all doubt entirely removed, inasmuch as all things were most easy for him to do.

Cohæret autem cum antedictis hoc modo: Cum tantum honorem acceperitis, ut et Dei et Christi familia censeamini, videte, ne tanto honore excidatis. Καθὼς λέγει τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον.) Per Davidem Psalm.

XCV. vers. 8. Σήμερον ἐὰν τῆς φωνῆς αὐτοῦ ἀκούσητε) Id est, die sapientiae, cui celebrandæ scripturae hymnus, et quo tempore prælegi populo illa vetus historia solebat. Sumpta haec ex Graeco LXX. Habemus idem verbum EXOD. VII. 3. XIII. 15. DEUT. II. 30. X. 16. tribui que solet, ut et verbum לֵב & similia, cum Deo, tum hominibus, sed sensu non nihil diverso, ut alibi diximus. Ὡς ἐν τῷ παραπικρασμῷ) In loco nominato מְרִיבָה EXOD. XVII. 7. NUM. XX. 13. 24. Id autem redditur illis locis λοιδορία & ἀντιλογία.

XVII. vers. 2. sed Deus id perinde æstimat, quasi secum jurgati essent, ut videre est NUM. XX. vers. 13. Κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν τοῦ πειρασμοῦ) Etiam hic πειρασμὸς est pro מַסָּה quod nomen itidem est loci in deserto ex historia sic dicti. Dies Massæ est tempus illud, quo circa Massam egit populus: sicut dies Madian Esaiae IX.

4. LXX. EXOD. XVII. 7. & DEUT. VI. 16. nomen hoc proprium vertunt πειρασμὸν. Sed נִסָּה unde id nomen, eit irritare, quod et πειράζειν & πειράζειν Graecis. Κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν, id est, quomodo illo tempore, ut JOB, XXIX. vers. 2. JER. XLIV. 6. DAN. IX. 15. & alibi. Οὗ ἐπείρασόν με οἱ πατέρες ὑμῶν) Illud ὗ ostendit locorum praecessisse nomina.

Et apparet hic πειράζειν, ut jam diximus, idem esse quod πειρασμὸν. ἐδοκίμασαν με καὶ εἶδον τὰ ἔργα μου. Me non est in Graeco: Sed subauditur ex priori. In Ebræo exprimitur. Sensus autem est: Quamquam magna mea opera viderant: tamen libuit eis me irritando periculum facere potentiæ meæ. κἀγ pro καίπερ (Ps. 95:9), sensus idem DEUT. XXIX. 2. 3. 4. Ponenda interpunctio post με, ut in Ebræo e editione Sixti Græcæ. Et id exigunt, quæ sequuntur infra 17. & ipsa historiæ series. Τεσσαράκοντα ἔτη διὸ προσώχθισα τῇ γενεᾷ ἐκείνῃ. Suidæ προσώχθισα est δυνατισθ, βδελύττομαι. Et in hoc Psalmo tam Aquila quam Symmachus δυσχεραίνω. Vocat autem γενεὰν homines ætatis istius, idque ex maxima parte, ut jam videbimus.

Et est συνεκδοχὴ in annis XL. vult enim dicere magnam partem illorum annorum. Vide NUM. XVI. vers. 22. Videtur autem ideo urgere illud de XL. annis, quia par spatium Deus Judæis ad pœnitentiam post Christum enectum præfinierat.

Pro ἐκείνῃ in Manuscripto est ταύτῃ. Vers. 10. Καὶ εἶπον ἀεὶ πλανῶνται τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοὶ δὲ ἐν ἔγνωσαν τὰς ὁδούς με) In Graeco LXX. καὶ αὐτοί. Nosse hic est (Ps. 95:10) curare, ut Psal. I. vers. 6. & alibi. Populus iste vagum cor habet, non libet ei insistere viis à me præscriptis. Vers. 11. Ὡς ὤμοσα ἐν τῇ ὀργῇ με. Ὡς hic valet itaque, ut & Ebræum אֲשֶׁר.

Et sic recte accipit Syrus: Juramentum hoc habes NUM. XIV. vers. 28. Repetentur eadem verba infra. IV. 3. ubi itidem est ὡς non ut quidam hic legerunt οἷς. Εἰ εἰσελεύσονται εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσίν με. Subauditur aliquid, ut in juramentis solet, 1. SAM. XV. Psal.

CXXXII. 2. 3. MARC. VIII. 12. Cum homines jurant, subauditur, mile mihi faciat Deus, ut 1. SAM. XXV. 22. Cum Deus, ne pro Deo habeat: κατάπαυσις dicitur regio illa, ubi populus à longis jactationibus quievit: ut DEUT. XII. 9. Addit Deus voculam με, quia ejus boni Autor erat Deus: partim etiam quia tunc Arca, quæ Dei nomine vocabatur, vagari desiit.

Sub involucris obtegi Meffiæ tempora sentit & David Kimchi. Rectius LXX. interpretantur ἐὰν quoties, quam Grotius, restringens adhortationem ad diem συννοηγίας. Esto dicatus fit ille Psalmus peculiari ter huic festo, de quo tamen non constat ex fontibus, neque etiam è versione LXX virali: ad omne tempus, quo sonat vox Domini τὸ σήμερον pertinere, satis docet applicatio Apostolica; nunquam etiam, cum illa sonat, corda obduranda sunt.

Verbum ἀνύειν cum affectu quandoque ἀνύειν intelligitur, cum vox Domini auditur non externis tantum corporis, sed interioribus cordis auribus, vel ita auditur, ut animo fideli, & fide suscipiatur, ac custodiatur, non vero corda ad illam obdurantur.

Sed hic de externo auditu adhibetur. Nam monemur, ut extrinsecus vocem audientes in eam admittamus, vel cor nostrum non obduremus, ne ei obicem ponamus aut resistamus, Act.

VII. 51. Docetur autem ita, vocem Christi fuisse vocem illam, Domini, quem etiam in deserto sua infidelitate tentasse dicuntur Israëlitae, 1. Cor. X. 9. Habemus itaque, hic & Christum esse Dominum illum, cujus vocem audiendam esse docet hoc loco. Nam illud Pronomen αὐτῷ ad nullum alium referendum, quam ad eum, cujus domus & familia esse dicuntur fideles, qui est Filius in domo Ecclesiæ, & Dominus; & Spiritum Sanctum Jehovam esse, qui dixit vel loquutus est per Davidem, & quem tentarunt Patres in deserto, cujus opera viderunt per 40. annos, quique ipsis infensus factus est, conf.

Es. LXIII. vers. 10.

Nam is, qui hic loquitur per Davidem, est ille, qui tentatus fuit ab Israëlitis, cujus opera viderunt, & qui ipsis infensus factus, hoc est, Jehovah Dominus. At Spiritus Sanctus est is, qui loquitur hic, Apostolo teste, Ergo. Non ergo transitus hic admittendus ab una persona ad aliam, quod nonnulli volunt, nec facile is in Prophetis concedendus.

Distincte potius & persona Dei tentati ab Israelitis, hoc est, Christi, & Spiritus Sancti introducitur ab Apostolo loquentis per Davidem. Non autem habent hoc loco exemplaria Græca vocem πειρασμῦ, ideo crisis Grotii hic supervacanea est, sed vocem πειρασμῦ.

Etsi vero nomina locorum non conveniant historiæ NUM. XX. descriptæ, facile tamen admittimus Synecdochice sub una tentatione, vel irritatione cæteras comprehendi. Quanquam ne id quidem opus fit, ut locale ad locum specialem referatur, Massa vel Meriba, vel per παραπικρασμὸν locus intelligatur: cum reddi possit cum B.

Luthera tanquam Appellativum (non tanquam nominis proprii σημαντικὸν) in der Verbitterung. Referri ergo potest illud ad locum in genere, vel indefinite, ubi scilicet factus est παραπικρασμὸς, & πειρασμὸς, quicumque ille fuerit; quia per 40. annos tentasse tentasse Deum dicuntur, & probasse; utut vide- rint opera Domini, quibus potentiam, veritatem & providentiam suam miraculis, etiam valde il- lustribus testabatur: saepius tamen eandem ten- tarunt, & probarunt, adeoque Spiritum Sanctum exacerbarunt, & infensum sibi reddiderunt. Post vocem μʊ. citra sufficientem causam stigma po- nitur. Nam etsi novi versus initium in verbis τεσσαράκοντα ἔτη in Hebraeo fiat, & Apostolus sic ordinet v. 17. Plerique tamen Codices Graeci ver- ba illa ad praecedentia referunt: quae ad sequen- tia v. 17. optime etiam referri poterant, quia in sensu nulla est discrepantia. Quadraginta annis enim tentarunt Israelitae Deum: Et 40. annis, etsi non continuis, DEUS infensus isti generationi fuit, vel hominibus in populo suo isto aevo, Num. XXXII. v. 4. 13. Quadraginta annorum meminit Spiritus Sanctus, ut tempus excidii Ecclesiae Apo- staticae Israëlitarum cum tempore excidii Synago- gae post Messiam excisum futuri conferret. Per vias Domini non mandata, quae praescripsit ipsis Dominus, sed opera potius divinae potentiae, justi- tiae, misericordiae, veritatis, quibus ipse incedit, intelliguntur, Psal. XXV. 10. Quod de juramento

Dei dicitur, Num. XIV. 23. non occurrit: simplex tantum ibi comminatio DEI habetur. Sed recte Philo singula Dei verba ait esse juramenta. Quan- quam etiam dici possit, id Davidem non ex Mo- se, sed immediata Dei revelatione habuisse, quod nempe jurarit id Deus, quod non ingressuri sint in requiem Domini. De ira vero, quia in Deum non cadunt affectus, Augustinus recte libr. IX. de civit. DEI cap. 5. Ira Dei est vindictae divinae effectus, non autem turbulentus Dei affectus.

In formula illa εἰ εἰσελεύσονται, non est opus aliquid subintelligere, ut prodeat formula jura- toria, quum dici possit in juramentis, imprecatio- nibus & obligationibus affirmativis particulam אם importare negationem, (ut Gen. XXVI. 29. quod non velis nobis malefacere: 1. Reg. I. 51. quod non velis interficere &c.) in negativis אם לא, sinon, affirmationem. Ita ergo, si intrabunt, hoc loco est, non introibunt requiem meam, Conf. Marc. IIX. v. 12. Matth. XVI. 4. Requies illa est terra Canaan, quam suam requiem dicit, vel quod abs se parata esset Israëlitis, vel quod ibi peculia- riter requiem suam habere voluit Deus, de quo Psal. CXXXII. 13. 14. In eo enim est Apostolus cum Davide, ut exemplum priscorum Israëlita- rum sub Mose proponant; Unde Apostolus post- modum solidissime deducit, adhuc superesse ali- am requiem, in quam inducendi sint fideles, cor- da sua ad vocem Domini non obdurantes. De spe hic utique disserit, inquit Theophylactus, quem- admodum scilicet ibi sunt pro laboribus certa prae- mia expectanda, & quietudo. Idque sic fore, ex Prophetae dictis affirmat, quemadmodum in requiem sint ingressuri credentes, ut contra qui minus cre- diderint, quales prisci illi fuere Judaei, nequaquam hanc sunt adituri. David itaque qui posterior fuit, cum hisce de rebus dissereret, dixit: Hodie si vocem ejus audiveritis, nolite obdurare corda vestra, ne eadem illa, quae & vestri majores perpessi sunt, pa- tiamini & quiete privemini, tanquam scilicet alia quaedam sit quietudo, quam simus ipsi consequuturi, haec inquit: Nam si veram illi recepissent quietem, cur illud inferret; Hodie nolite obdurare corda ve- stra, sicut & Patres vestri, & non ingrediemini re- quiem. Quae igitur esse alia praeter regni caelestis jucundissimum otium, requies potest, cujus figuram & sabbatum praefert, & eum, qui typice effectus est in Palaestinam filiorum contradicentis generationis introitum. Ubi observat Theophylactus triplicem requiem, & de ea ita differit: Tribus itaque mo- dis quiescimus, aut enim sabbato hæc quies præ- statur, in quo & Deus ab opere conquievit, qua de quiete haudquaquam David videtur hoc loco dis- serere, utpote quæ apud priscos illos pro vera sit ha- bita, & illa quidem quæ per terræ promissionis in- gressum est comparata, quam introgressi Judæi, erant à bello & præliis quieturi, & errore illo, quo tam diuturno devagabantur erratici. De qua ta- men quiete nec ullam hic facit mentionem. Nam si Palæstina regio David temporibus sub ejus erat & Ebræorum imperio, quo pacto de hac erat ille tanquam deserta dicturus? Videtur igitur alium quendam quies hujusmodi statum prætendere, in quem Jesus Nave nullam haberet Judæis inferendi licentiam. Ejusmodi statum in cælis duntaxat re- periemus. A quo ne majorum vestrorum exem- plo ob diffidentiam excidatis, erit vobis omni studio annitendum. Non enim eorum, quæ per Deum ge- runtur, exigendæ sunt ab homine rationes, sed fides illi indubitanter præstanda. Id namque & priscis illis crimini datur, quia Dominum tentaverunt, id est, quia non omni prorsus dubitatione sublata in eum sperarunt, utpote cui omnia essent factu fa- cillima.

## 3:12
Vers. 12. Βλέπετε ἀδελφοὶ) It coheres with those things which were said above at 7.

Lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief.

That there may never be in any of you an evil mind, that is, an unbelieving one. For that genitive takes the place of an adjective.

In departing from the living God.

Unbelief is twofold, from the beginning of the calling, and after the fact. But the latter is worse than the former, because it draws with it the desertion of God. See 2 Tim. IV. 1. Moreover, 'from the living God' is said very effectively, as also below IX. 14 and X. 31. For He who lives, that is, always lives (for so the word is taken here), can also always exact punishment. But it is well said 'from the living God.' For just as he who believes in Christ believes in God, John XII. 4, because God in every way acted to show that Christ was sent by Him, John VI. 27, so he who deserts Christ, at the same time deserts God. 'In the' for 'into the,' which change of particles is frequent in these and other books. Do not return to Judaism, as they did to Egypt, from whence God had led them out.

But why should we not understand Christ by the living God, whose voice the Holy Spirit had warned must be heard? For this is the true God and eternal life, 1 John V. 20. The Apostle warns that they should take heed, lest through unbelief they fall away from Christ, to whom they had given themselves through faith. In verse 6 He was called our inhabitant: therefore He is not to be cast out of the possession of our hearts, in which He wishes to dwell through faith, Eph. III. 17, and we must take heed lest we fall away from Him, as is taught in verse 14, because we have become partakers of Christ. The Fathers tempted Him in the desert, 1 Cor. X. 9, whose apostasy we ought to flee; He is the giver of the promised rest, and therefore we ought not to tempt His severity through apostasy.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Βλέπετε ἀδελφοὶ) Cohæret cum iis, quæ dicta supra 7.

Μήποτε ἔσται ἔν τινι ὑμῶν καρδία πονηρὰ ἀπιστίας.

Ne unquam in quoquam vestrum animus sit malus, id est, incredulus. Nam Genitivus iste vicem habet Ad- jectivi.

Ἐν τῷ ἀποστῆναι ἀπὸ Θεῦ ζῶντος.

Duplex est ἀπιστία, ab initio vocationis, & ex post fa- cto. Hæc autem illa est deterior, quia secum trahit de- sertionem Dei. Vide 2. Tim. IV. 1. Valde autem effica- citer dictum ἀπὸ Θεῦ ζῶντος, ut & infra IX. 14. & X. 31. Nam qui vivit, id est, semper vivit (ita enim hic sumitur id verbum) semper etiam pœnas sumere potest. Bene autem dictum ἀπὸ Θεῦ ζῶντος. Nam sicut qui Christo credit, Deo credit, Joh. XII. 4. quia Deus omni modo id egit, ut Christum a se missum ostenderet Joh. VI. 27. Ita qui Christum deserit, simul Deum deserit. Ἐν τῷ pro εἰς τὸ, quæ particularum mutatio frequens his & aliis libris. Nolite redire ad Judaismum, sicut illi in Ægyptum, unde eos Deus eduxerat.

Cur vero non per Deum vivum intelligamus Christum, cujus vocem audiendam esse monuerat Spiritus Sanctus? Hic enim est verus Deus & vita æterna 1. Joh. V. 20. Monet Apostolus, ut caveant, ne per ἀπιστίαν deficiant à Christo, cui per fidem sese dederant. V. 6. dicebatur habitator noster: non ergo ejiciendus è possessione cordium nostrorum, in quibus habitare vult per fidem, Ephes. III. 17. & cavendum, ne ab eo deficiamus, uti v. 14. doce- tur, quod facti simus μέτοχοι participes Christi. Il- lum tentarunt Patres in deserto, 1. Cor. X. 9. quo- rum apostasiam fugere debemus, ille est dator quietis promissæ, itaque per apostasiam ejus seve- ritatem non debemus tentare.

## 3:13
Verse 13. But exhort one another every day, while it is called today. 'Ourselves' for 'one another,' as 1 Cor. VI. verse 7 and elsewhere. The Feast of Tabernacles of the Jews, indicated by 'today,' was performed once a year. Ours, while this age lasts. For we live in uncertain dwellings, and we await a quiet seat: nor is there need for us to be reminded of what we feel daily.

It is explained what is denoted by 'today,' that David understands that 'today' as long as the voice of the Lord is heard, or the time of grace and of the calling to power lasts. But it is not taught that there is a double sense of that word, one concerning the 'today' of the Feast of Tabernacles, the other concerning the 'today' of the duration of the age. And as that 'today' lasted in its own time, when David used that admonition, so likewise it endured in the time of Paul, and even now it endures. Therefore, Hiero-Pfaltes was rousing the men of his own time, but because the voice of the Lord is still heard, the Apostle warns his Hebrew brethren that they too should be roused by the Holy Spirit, and thus the Holy Spirit continues to rouse us not to harden our heart through unbelief, or to fall away from the faith of CHRIST. Concerning which opportune time of grace, Psalm 32:6, Isaiah 55:6, John 12:35. Theophylact's paraphrase has it thus: Build one another up and strengthen, so that you may not be shaken. Wherefore if anyone has even collapsed, as long as he breathes this air and lives, lift this very person up. For when he says, 'it is named until today,' he designates, that is, as long as he leads his life. For hope accompanies this, and it is possible to hope well of a surviving sinner, that he may repent when admonished. But especially let no one have a wicked heart. But if by chance it should happen, let him by no means fall here into despair and diffidence. Rather, receive him by exhorting, and lift him up soon by helping.

Ἵνα μὴ σκληρυνθῇ τις ἐξ ὑμῶν) May he not be hardened against pious admonitions.

Ἀπάτῃ τῆς ἁμαρτίας) He calls ἁμαρτίαν here by the name of the genus the fear of vexations and hatred, through which many, being seduced at that time, were falling away from the profession of the Gospel.

It is not about the fear of vexations and hatred, which is neither ἁμαρτία nor sin, and can exist without sin, but it is about the seduction of sin, from which at length hardening arises. He wishes σκληροκαρδίαν to be guarded against and to be absent, which he calls καρδίαν πονηρὰν ἀπιστίας. Compare verse 8. Whence the Jews are σκληροτράχηλοι καὶ ἀπερίτμητοι τῇ καρδίᾳ καὶ τοῖς ὠσὶν, Acts 7:51, which consists most especially in ἀποστασίᾳ from the living GOD, and that either formal, when saving truth is denied, or interpretative, when that is done which cannot consist with union and confederation with the true GOD. For that requires ἀγαθὴν συνείδησιν, 1 Peter 3:11, or when offered truth is repelled, as was done by the Jews in Acts 13:46. It is evident, therefore, that the faithful, who have become partakers of Christ, can be seduced by sin or wicked concupiscence, by which each one is tempted, James 1:14, so that they harden their heart against the voice of the Lord, and finally apostasy, or falling away from the Lord, follows. Theophylact seems to understand by ἁμαρτίαν diffidence or despair: He calls it the fallacy of sin, he says, or the suggestions of demons, namely that one hopes for no retribution of good or evil things. Or he calls despair a fallacy. For that there is no hope left for me once I have fallen, this would clearly be the fallacy of sins. But the former explanation is simpler and more suitable. Daily, says Theodoret, it is necessary for those who live to take care of themselves, lest sin, having occupied a place, make an impression in our heart. But he called the present life 'today'.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ἀλλὰ παρακαλεῖτε ἑαυτὸς καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν, ἄχρις ὗ τὸ σήμερον καλεῖται) Ἑαυτὸς pro ἀλλήλες, ut 1. Corinth. VI. vers. 7. & alibi. Σκηνοπηγία Judæorum in- dicata per σήμερον, semel anno peragebatur. Nostra, dum durat hoc seculum. Vivimus enim incertis sedibus, & se- dem quietam expectamus: neque opus est nobis in memo- riam redigi, quod quotidie sentimus.

Explicatur, quid per σήμερον notetur, quod Da- vid illud σήμερον intelligat, quoad usque vox Do- mini auditur, vel tempus gratiæ, & vocationis ad potentiam durat. Non autem docetur, gemi- num esse vocis illius sensum, alterum de hodie τῆς σκηνοπηγίας, alterum de hodie durationis secu- li. Et ut suo tempore illud σήμερον durabat, quum ea commonitione uteretur David, sic pariter id duravit tempore Pauli, atque etiam- num durat. Sui ergo temporis homines exci- tabat Hiero-Pfaltes, sed quia adhuc vox Do- mini auditur, excitari etiam a Spiritu sancto fratres suos Ebræos monet Apostolus, atque ita pergit excitare nos Spiritus Sanctus ad non obdurandum cor per incredulitatem, aut defici- endum a fide CHRISTI. De quo tempore gratiæ opportuno Psal. XXXII. vers. 6. Esa. LV. vers. 6. Johan. XII. v. 35. Theophylacti paraphra- sis ita habet: Ædificate vos mutuo & corrobo- rate, ut non collubamini. Quare si vel quispiam fuerit collapsus, quoad hanc auram spirat, vivit- que, hunc ipsum attollite. Id namque cum inquit, usque hodie nominatur, designat, id est, quousque duxerit vitam. Hanc enim & spes comitatur, & bene sperari de peccatore superstite potest, ut resi- piscat admonitus. Præcipue autem nulli insit cor pravum. Quod si forsan acciderit, nequaquam hic in desperationem & diffidentiam prolabatur. Quin vos illum hortando suscipite, & juvando mox sublevate.

Ἵνα μὴ σκληρυνθῇ τις ἐξ ὑμῶν) Obdurescat contra pia monita.

Ἀπάτῃ τῆς ἁμαρτίας) Ἁμαρτίαν generis nomine hic vocat metum vexationum & odii, per quem multi seducti eo tempore deficiebant ab Evangelii professione.

Non de metu vexationum & odii, qui nec ἁμαρτία vel peccatum est, & sine peccato esse potest, sed de peccati seductione agitur, ex qua tandem oritur induratio. Σκληροκαρδίαν caveri & abesse vult, quam dicit καρδίαν πονηρὰν ἀπι- στίας. Confer. vers. 8. Unde Judæi σκληροτράχη- λοι καὶ ἀπερίτμητοι τῇ καρδίᾳ καὶ τοῖς ὠσὶν, Actor. VII. vers. 51. quæ potissimum consistit in ἀποστασίᾳ a DEO vivente, eaque vel formali, cum abnegatur veritas salvifica, vel interpreta- tiva, quum id agitur, quod cum unione ac con- fœderatione cum vero DEO consistere non potest. Ea enim ἀγαθὴν συνείδησιν requirit, 1. Petr. III. vers. 11. vel cum veritas oblata repel- litur, uti a Judæis factum Actor. XIII. vers. 46. Patet ergo fideles, qui participes facti sunt Chri- sti, per peccatum vel concupiscentiam pravam, a qua unusquisque tentatur, Jac. I. vers. 14. seduci posse, ut cor obdurent adversus vocem Domi- ni, & sequatur denique apostasia, vel defectio a Domino. Theophylactus per ἁμαρτίαν diffiden- tiam videtur intelligere vel desperationem: Falla- ciam vero peccati, inquit, vel Dæmonum sug- gestiones appellat, videlicet quod nullam quis spe- ret bonorum malorumve retributionem. Vel fal- laciam desperationem dicit. Nam quod semel la- benti mihi nihil spei sit reliquum, peccatis plane hæc fuerit fallacia. Sed simplicior & convenien- tior est prior explicatio. Quotidie, inquit Theo- doretus, oportet eos, qui vivunt, sui curam ge- rere, ne peccatum loco occupato in nostro corde faciat impressionem. Hodie autem vocavit vitam præsentem.

## 3:14
Vers. 14.

Μέτοχοι γὰρ γεγόναμεν τοῦ χριστοῦ) We have obtained the right to partake of the glory of CHRIST, but a right that is pending, given under the condition of persevering, as follows. See above 6.

Ἐάν περ τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς ὑποστάσεως μέχρι τέλους βεβαίαν κατάσχωμεν) The same sense as above 6. There it is called ἐλπὶς, which is here ὑπόστασις. For they signify the same thing. Therefore תּוֹחֶלֶת is translated as ἐλπὶς in Lam. 3:18, and ὑπόστασις in Psalm 37:6. See what we shall say below in 11:11. And he said ἀρχὴν τῆς ὑποστάσεως by hypallage, not infrequent in these books of ours, for τὴν ὑπόστασιν τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς, that hope which we had from the beginning. Such are 'silver of the feigned' for 'feigned silver', 'blood in the soul' for 'soul in the blood': 'temple mixed with fire' and similar things noted by David Kimchi and others. But I understand faith joined with a holy profession.

We are called partakers of CHRIST through faith, because through faith we partake of the body and blood of the Lord, John 6:56, through faith He dwells in our hearts, Eph. 3:17, through faith we are united and joined to Christ, and are rendered one spirit with the Lord, 1 Cor. 6:17. Compare Eph. 5:31, 32. We are rendered partakers of His divine nature, 2 Peter 1:4, and of all His benefits, and we become members of His body, concerning which Theophylact says: Through faith we are joined to Him, and thus we are partakers of Him, as the body to the head: and immediately saying this, he consoles them and brings hope. For He who has embraced us with such great love that He has even made us His body, will by no means allow us, if only we are willing, to be torn away from Him. The Apostle speaks not only of the right of partaking of CHRIST in the future, although he does not exclude this; but of the actual μετοχῇ or participation of CHRIST, which the words themselves imply, nor does he teach that the attainment of the μετοχῇ depends on the condition of perseverance: But he says that we have truly been made partakers of CHRIST, and implies that we shall remain partakers of the same, if we persevere in faith: You have been made, says the Blessed Hunnius, through faith partakers of Christ, and in Christ of all His benefits, of the remission of sins, of righteousness, of sanctification and of eternal life. But you should think that both CHRIST and His goods pertain to you to that extent, if you have held the beginning of the substance firm even to the end, that is, if you have persevered with faithful constancy in the profession of the Christian faith (to which you once gave your name) even to the end.

Estius acknowledges the truth of this explanation of the word ὑπόστασις regarding saving faith: 'Most people,' he says, 'interpret it in this place as subsistence or substance, by which we are Christians, that is, a new creature in Christ. The beginning and foundation of this substance is faith, by which we believe in CHRIST. Nevertheless, by substance itself, faith can be understood, and by the beginning of the substance, faith already begun, since in chapter XI the name of substance is also attributed to faith.' Thus the sense will be: If, however, we hold firm and unshaken until the end of life the faith once received, through which we subsist in this spiritual life (or which is the substance, that is, the basis and foundation of our salvation and hope). The Syriac version favors this understanding. For it has it thus: If from the beginning to the end we hold fast this firm substance. Estius also rendered this sense of this conditional: That it will be profitable to us for salvation that we have been made partakers of CHRIST through faith only if we persevere in it until death; and he observes that the argument of the Calvinists vanishes from this, that without perseverance faith is not faith, but a vain opinion. For that is manifestly refuted by the words and the scope of the Apostle at the same time. For he would not exhort the Hebrews to the perseverance of faith, whether they were going to persevere or not, unless he thought they had true faith.

The passage in Psalm 39:5 (even though the word ὑπόστασις is found there) has nothing to do with the explanation of the word ὑπόστασιν which is at hand. But Ezekiel 26:11 is more relevant here, where ὑπόστασις denotes firmness (in Hebrew from מצב, which is accustomed to be rendered by στερεόω, βεβαιόω, στηλόω), and Job 23:20, where it corresponds to the Hebrew קים (which is that which subsists), and Ezekiel 19:5, where תקותה is found in the Hebrew, and the LXX render it ὑπόστασιν, The blessed Luther [translates it as] hope, elsewhere it is rendered ὑπομονὴ [patience], Psalm 39, verse 8; Psalm 62, verse 6. That word descends from ὑφίςασθαι [to stand under/subsist], because faith does not fall or flee, but stands, consists, and rests unmoved and certain in divine promises, like a thing subsisting by itself, 2 Corinthians 9, verse 4; chapter 11, verse 17. Now, some, along with Theodoret, refer the 'beginning of the substance' or 'confidence' to regeneration; who says, 'We were made partakers of Christ’s death through baptism, and were buried with him in the figure of the resurrection, provided we have kept a firm faith.' For he called that the beginning of the substance. For through it we have been renewed and joined to the Lord Christ, and have received the grace of the most holy Spirit. However, the hypallage of Grotius, which others also favor in this passage, does not seem inconvenient to us. The blessed Dorschæus says: Most simply, ἀρχὴ τῆς ὑποσάσεως [the beginning of the substance] is ὑπόσασις ἡ ἐξ ἀρχῆς [the substance from the beginning], the faith communicated to us through divine illumination in our conversion, which is called above in verse 6 'the confidence and the boasting of the hope.' For this is the ὑπόςασις [substance] according to the Apostle below in verse 11, and indeed communicated to us 'from the beginning,' or an 'original substance,' which constitutes the very foundation of salvation while it apprehends CHRIST, John 1, verse 12, and is the 'firstfruits' of the holy Spirit himself. For some codices read τὴν ἀπαρχήν [the firstfruits]. Beza rightly declares 'the firstfruits of the substance' to be that which is established as a fulcrum supporting other things, a metaphor taken from buildings, just as in Plato’s letters 'to cast foundations' signifies to lay the groundwork. For the Apostle is still looking entirely toward the house, of which he made mention in verse 6. He indicates, however, that we do not stand and persevere by any other principle than that which we received in the beginning. Although this in no way depends on our own powers, nor receives any protection or support from good works, it can nevertheless be subverted by our powers. For apostasy can take away the substance. The Apostle, however, opposes the substance itself to the apostasy, of which he made mention in verse 12. Regarding this matter, [he speaks] at greater length below in chapter 6, verse 4 and following, and chapter 10, verse 26 and following. The blessed Gerhard explains: 'If we retain the beginning of the subsistence, or of that which subsists, that is, the faith which we have received, firm until the end.' Chrysostom, with the approval of Camerarius, interprets 'the beginning of the substance' as 'the faith through which we have subsisted, and have been generated and, as one might say, consubstantiated.'

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Μέτοχοι γὰρ γεγόναμεν τοῦ χριστοῦ) Jus nacti sumus, ut participemus de CHRISTI claritate, sed jus pendens, datum sub conditione perseverandi, ut sequitur. Vide supra 6.

Ἐάν περ τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς ὑποστάσεως μέχρι τέλους βε- βαίαν κατάσχωμεν) Idem sensus qui supra 6. Ibi ἐλπὶς dicitur, quæ hic ὑπόστασις. Idem enim significant. Ita- que תּוֹחֶלֶת ἐλπὶς vertitur Lam. III. vers. 18. ὑπόστα- σις Psal. XXXVII. vers. 6. Vide quæ dicemus infra XI. 11. Et dixit ἀρχὴν τῆς ὑποστάσεως per ὑπαλλαγὴν, nostris his libus non infrequentem, pro τὴν ὑπόστασιν τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς spem illam, quam ab initio habuimus. Talia sunt ar- gentum fictorum pro fictis argenteis, sanguis in anima pro anima in sanguine: templum immistum igni & simi- lia à Davide Kimchi & aliis notata. Fidem autem intelli- gocum sancta professione conjunctam.

Participes CHRISTI dicimur per fidem, quia per fidem corpus & sanguinem Domini par- ticipamus, Johan. VI. vers. 56. per fidem habi- tat in cordibus nostris Ephes. III. vers. 17. per fi- dem unimur & conjungimur Christo, & unus cum Domino reddimur spiritus, 1. Corinth. VI. vers. 17. Confer. Ephes. V. vers. 31. 32. reddimur participes divinæ ejus naturæ, 2. Petr. I. vers. 4. & omnium beneficiorum ejus, ac membra eva- dimus corporis ejus, quo de Theophylactus: Per fidem illi sumus conjuncti, & sic ei sumus parti- cipes, ut capiti corpus: & subinde inquiens hos consolatur & spem affert. Qui enim tanta est nos charitate complexus, ut & corpus nos suum effecerit, nequaquam nos, si modo velimus, di- velli à se patietur. Non de jure tantum parti- cipandi CHRISTUM in futurum, etsi hoc non excludat; sed de actuali μετοχῇ vel partici- patione CHRISTI loquitur Apostolus, quam verba ipsa inferunt, nec dependere assecutio- nem μετοχῆς à conditione perseverantiæ docet: Sed nos revera participes factos esse CHRISTI ait, ejusdemque participes mansuros, innuit, si in fide perseveremus: Vos facti estis, inquit Beatus Hunnius, per fidem participes Christi, & in Christo omnium beneficiorum ipsius, remissio- nis peccatorum, justitiæ, sanctificationis & vi- tæ æternæ. Sed eatenus & CHRISTUM & bona ipsius ad vos pertinere cogitetis, si initium substantiæ ad finem usque firmum tenueritis, id est, si in professione fidei Christianæ (cui semel nomen dedistis) usque ad finem fideli constantia perseveraveritis.

Agnoscit hujus explicationis vocis ὑπόστασις de fide salvifica veritatem Estius: Eam vero, inquit, subsistentiam vel substan- tiam plerique interpretantur hoc loco, qua Chri- stiani sumus, id est, nova creatura in Christo. Cujus quidem substantiæ initium & fundamen- tum est fides, qua in CHRISTUM credimus. Potest nihilominus per ipsam substantiam intelli- gi fides, & per initium substantiæ fides jam in- choata, quandoquidem & cap. XI. substantiæ no- men attribuit fidei. Ita sensus erit: Si tamen susceptam semel fidem, per quam in vita hac spi- rituali subsistimus (aut quæ est substantia, id est, basis & fundamentum salutis ac spei nostræ) fir- mam & inconcussam retineamus usque ad exi- tum vitæ. Huic intellectui favet versio Syriaca. Sic enim habet: Si ab initio usque ad finem sub- stantiam hanc firmam rapiamus. Conditiona- lis hujus etiam hunc sensum reddidit Estius; Ita demum nobis profuturum ad salutem, quod CHRISTI effecti sumus participes per fidem, si in ea perseveremus usque ad mortem; & inde argumentum Calvinianorum evanescere obser- vat, sine perseverantia fidem non esse fidem, sed opi- nionem vanam. Id enim ex verbis simul & sco- po Apostoli manifeste redarguitur. Non enim ad fidei perseverantiam Ebræos hortaretur, sive perseveraturos, sive non, nisi veram fidem eos habere existimaret.

Locus Psalm. XXXIX. v. 5. (etsi ibi habeatur vox ὑπόστασις) nihil ad rem facit in explicatione vocis ὑπόστασιν, quæ præ manibus. Magis autem huc faciunt Ezechiel.
