XXVI. vers. 11. ubi ὑπόστασις firmitudinem notat (in Ebræo à מצב, quod per στερεόω, βε- βαιόω, στηλόω reddi solet,) & Jobi XXIII. v. 20. ubi Ebræo קים )quod est quod subsistit) respondet, & Ezechielis XIX. vers. 5. ubi תקותה in Ebræo habetur, & LXX. reddunt ὑπόστασιν, Beat. Lutherus Hoffnung, alibi redditur ὑπο- μονὴ, Psalm. XXXIX. vers. 8. Psalm. LXII. vers. 6. descendit ea vox ab ὑφίςασθαι, quia fides non ca- dit, aut fugit, sed immota & certa in promissis divinis stat, consistit, & acquiescit instar rei per se subsistentis, 2. Corinth. IX. vers. 4. cap. XI. v. 17. Initium autem substantiæ vel fiduciæ referunt nonnulli ad regenerationem cum Theodoreto; qui, cum Christo, inquit, mortis fuimus participes per baptismum, & cum eo consepulti fuimus in figura resurrectionis, siquidem firmam fidem con- servaverimus. Eam enim appellavit initium sub- stantiæ. Per illam enim renovati, & Domino Christo conjuncti sumus, & sanctissimi Spiritus gratiam accepimus. Non incommoda tamen nobis videtur hypallage Grotii, cui etiam alii hoc loco favent. Beatus Dorschæus: Simplicissime, inquit, ἀρχὴ τῆς ὑποσάσεως est ὑπόσασις ἡ ἐξ ἀρχῆς, fides per divinam illuminationem in nostra conversione nobis communicata, quæ supra vers. 6. παῤῥησία καὶ καύχημα τῆς ἐλπίδος vocatur. Hæc enim est ὑπόςασις juxta Apostolum infra vers. 11. & quidem ἐξ ἀρχῆς nobis communicata, sive ἀρχικὴ ὑπόςασις, quæ ipsum fundamentum salutis constituit, dum CHRISTUM appre- hendit Johan. I. vers. 12. & est ἀπαρχὴ ipsius san- cti Spiritus. Nam nonnulli codices legunt τὴν ἀ- παρχήν. Recte Beza ἡ ἀπαρχὴ τῆς ὑποσάσεως declarat id, quod pro fulcro cætera sustinente sta- tuitur, metaphora ab ædificiis sumpta, sicut apud Platonem in epistolis ἀρχὰς βάλλεσθαι fundamenta jacere significat. Nam omnino ad domum, cujus vers. 6. mentionem fecit, Apostolus adhuc respi- cit. Indicat autem non alio principio nos stare & perseverare, quam quod accepimus in principio. Quod quamvis à nostris viribus nequaquam de- pendeat, neque à bonis operibus aliquod præsidium accipiat, aut sustentaculum, subverti tamen à nostris potest viribus. Potest enim ἀποσασία ὑπό- ςασιν tollere. Opponit autem Apostolus aposta- siæ, cujus vers. 12. mentionem fecit, ipsam ὑπόςα- σιν. Qua de re pluribus infra cap. VI. vers. 4. & seqq. & X. vers. 26. seqq. Beat. Gerhardus expo- nit: Si principium subsistentia, sive illius, quod subsistit, hoc est, fidem, quam cepimus, prosi- teri usque ad finem firmam retineamus: Chrysosto- mus, approbante Camerario, ἀρχὴν τῆς ὑποσά- σεως interpretatur τὴν πίςιν, δι᾽ ἧς ὑπέςημεν, καὶ γεγενήμεθα κὴ συνουσιώθημεν ὡς ἄν τις εἴποι.

## 3:15
Verse 15.

Ἐν τῷ λέγεσθαι [While it is said]) Some connect this with the preceding. Chrysostom and the Greeks who follow him connect it with what follows, 'let us fear,' where we have a new section, for no other reason than that it seemed so to the scribes, since the Greeks use different sections. If we follow the Greeks, all those words from 'for some having heard' to 'let us fear' will be a long parenthesis, such as are many in these books: And 'while it is said' will mean, 'when we hear these things being said,' namely, those which pertain to us no less than to those ancients. Σήμερον ἐὰν [Today if]) Repeated from those things which are above in verse 7. It is more correctly connected with the preceding words, for they cohere in that way, as noted by the Syrian, Erasmus, and Estius. 'I exhort you to retain your faith constantly until the end, while, of course, it is still said to you today, if you hear his voice, etc.' Thus, there is also no need for such a long hyperbaton. Thus the rest follows, and they cohere more conveniently.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Ἐν τῷ λέγεσθαι) Hoc quidam connectunt cum præce- dentibus. Chrysostomus & qui eum sequuntur Græci cum iis, quæ sequuntur, φοβηθῶμεν εὖ, ubi nos novam habemus sectionem, non alia de causa, quam quia ita visum est exscriptoribus, cum Græci aliis utantur sectio- nibus. Græcos si sequamur, illa omnia à τινὲς γὰρ ἀκύ- σαντες, ad φοβηθῶμεν εὖ, erunt longa παρενθήκη, quales in his libris multæ: Et ἐν τῷ λέγεσθαι valebit, cum audi- mus hæc dici, nempe quæ ad nos non minus, quam ad ve- teres illos pertinent. Σήμερον ἐὰν) Repetita ex iis, quæ supra 7. Rectius cum verbis præcedentibus connecti- tur, nam ita cohærent illa notante Syro, Era- smo, Estio. Hortor vos, ut fidem constanter reti- neatis usque ad finem, dum scilicet dicitur adhuc vobis hodie, si vocem ejus &c. Ita etiam tam prolixo hyperbato opus non est. Ita cætera se- quuntur, & cohærent commodius.

## 3:16
Verse 16.

Τινὲς γὰρ ἀκύσαντες [For some having heard]) Some who had heard the decalogue pronounced with such Majesty, and other precepts of God given through Moses, and confirmed by very many miracles. Παρεπίκραναν [They provoked]) They provoked, namely, God.

The reason is given why the beginning of the substance must be retained, or the faith preserved which they professed in the beginning: because some of those who heard the voice of the Lord provoked GOD. That voice of the Lord, however, is not so much the decalogue with other precepts as it is the voice of the divine promise, which was despised through unbelief, as is evident from verse 19.

Ἀλλ’ ὀυ πάντες ὁι ἐξελθόντες ἐξ Ἀιγύπτου διὰ Μωυσέως [But not all who came out of Egypt through Moses]) With Moses leading them out. Thus Hosea 12, verse 13, 'by a prophet,' that is, through Moses the Prophet. Not such were Joshua, not Caleb, not the offspring that was born later. Thus also now some have fallen away from Christianity: below in chapter 10, verse 25, do not follow their example: but rather that of Joshua and Caleb, who, terrified by no adversities, always retained a firm hope.

Nor also such as were under 20 years of age in that census, nor the Levites, who were not included in that census made in the second year after the departure from Egypt. It is said, however, that GOD was incensed at them for 40 years, even though the threat was made only in the second year after the departure, because the exacerbation began immediately after the departure at the Red Sea, Exodus 14:11.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Τινὲς γὰρ ἀκύσαντες) Quidam qui audierant decalo- gum tanta cum Majestate pronunciatum, & præcepta Dei alia per Mosen data, & plurimis miraculis confirmata. Παρεπίκραναν) Irritarunt, nempe Deum.

Ratio redditur, cur retinendum initium sub- stantiae, vel fides servanda, quam initio profes- si sunt: quia nonnulli eorum, qui vocem Do- mini audiverunt, irritarunt DEUM. Vox au- tem illa Domini non tam decalogus est cum aliis praeceptis, quam vox promissionis divinae, quae per incredulitatem contempta fuit, ut è vers. 19. constat.

Ἀλλ’ ὀυ πάντες ὁι ἐξελθόντες ἐξ Ἀιγύπτου διὰ Μωυσέως) Mose educente. Sic Osee XII. vers. 13. ἐν προφήτῃ id est, per Mosen Prophetam. Non tales Josue, non Calebus, non quae subnata est soboles. Sic & nunc defecere aliqui à Christianismo: infra X. v. 25. vos nolite illorum exemplum sequi: sed potius Josuae & Calebi, qui nullis adversis territi spem semper firmam retinuere.

Neque etiam tales, qui 20. annis inferiores, in illa recensione erant, neque Levitae, qui in recensione ista anno secundo post egressum ex Ægypto facta non continebantur. Dicitur au- tem annis 40. DEUS infensus ipsis fuisse, etsi secundo anno post exitum demum facta commi- natio, quia exacerbatio statim post exitum coe- pit ad mare rubrum Exod. XIV. 11.

## 3:17
Verse 17.

With whom was he vexed forty years? With all without distinction? Certainly not, he knows how to discern the causes of each one. In the Manuscript τίσι δὲ καὶ.

Was it not with them that had sinned? Understand here ἁμαρτάνειν in that more serious sense, in which it corresponds to the word פשע, as in Job 33:9, Proverbs 29:6, Lamentations 3:4. See what is above at II. 2. This manuscript has ἀπειθήσασιν, perhaps from a gloss.

Blessed Gerhard, regarding the word τοῖς ἁμαρτήσασι, says that the species is understood from the genus, those who sinned by incredulity, disobedience, murmuring (Numbers 14:22), preposterous concupiscence, the idolatrous adoration of the golden calf, despair of occupying the promised land, etc., the head of all which sins was incredulity.

Whose carcasses fell in the wilderness. And this is from the Greek of Numbers 14:29, where in the Hebrew it is פגרים, just as the same word is translated in Leviticus 26:30, Numbers 14:23, 1 Samuel 17:46, Isaiah 66:44. Properly, פגרים are remains, as appears from that place in Leviticus, where the fragments of idols are called by the same name. And to the Chaldeans the verb פגר is to destroy. The desert here corresponds to Gehenna.

The Vulgate rendered κῶλα as carcasses; the Syriac as bones. It signifies members: scattered both members and bones in the desert, when they were struck down.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Τίσι δὲ προσώχθισε τεσσαράκοντα ἔτη) An omnibus sine discrimine? Non sane, novit causas cujusque discernere. In Manuscripto τίσι δὲ καὶ.

Οὐχὶ τοῖς ἁμαρτήσασιν) Intellige hic ἁμαρτάνειν in sensu illo graviore, quo respondet voci פשע, ut Job. XXXIII. vers. 9. Proverb. XXIX. vers. 6. Lam. III. vers. 4. Vide quae supra II. 2. Manuscriptus hic habet ἀπειθήσα- σιν, forte ex Gloffemate.

Beat. Gerhardus ad vocem τοῖς ἁμαρτήσασι, ex genere, inquit, intelligitur species, qui peccabant incredulitate, inobedientia, murmure Num. XIV. vers. 22. concupiscentia praepostera, idololatrica vituli aurei adoratione, desperatione occupandae terrae promissae &c. quorum peccatorum omnium caput erat incredulitas.

Ὧν τὰ κῶλα ἔπεσεν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ) Et hoc ex Graeco Num. XIV. vers. 29. ubi in Ebraeo פגרים, quomodo eadem vox vertitur Levit. XXVI. vers. 30. Numer. XIV. vers. 23. 1. Sam. XVII. vers. 46. Esa. LXVI. vers. 44. Pro- prie פגרים sunt reliquiae, ut apparet ex illo Levitici loco, ubi idolorum fragmina eodem nomine dicuntur. Et Chaldaeis verbum פגר est destruere. Desertum hic ge- hennae respondet.

Κῶλα Vulgatus reddidit cadavera; Syrus ossa. Significat membra: dispersa, & membra, & ossa in deserto, cum prostrati sunt.

## 3:18
Verse 18.

And to whom swore he that they should not enter into his rest? That is, who are they to whom he threatened with an oath that they would not enter.

Except to them that believed not? To those who had stubbornly despised his laws, חמורים, whence the name Mara. For that word is translated by ἀπειθεῖν in Exodus 33:21, Deuteronomy 1:26, chapter 9:7, 23, 24, Joshua 1:8, Isaiah 3:7, 50:5, 63:10.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Τίσι δὲ ὤμοσε, μὴ ἐισελεύσεσθαι εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσιν ἀυ- τοῦ) Id est, qui sunt, quibus cum juramento minatus est, eos non intraturos.

Εἰ μὴ τοῖς ἀπειθήσασι) Iis qui leges ejus contem- pserant praefracte חמורים unde nomen Mara. Id e- nim verbum per ἀπειθεῖν vertitur Exod. XXXIII. vers. 21. Deuteronom. I. vers. 26. cap. IX. vers. 7. 23. 24. Jos. I. v. 8. Ef. III. 7. L. 5. LXIII. 10.

## 3:19
Verse 19. And we see. We know from history.

That they could not enter. Into those quiet seats, because, of course, that peremptory decree of God stood in the way.

Because of unbelief. Because they had not had faith in the divine promises, which was the cause of disobedience then, and is now.

The word ἀπειθήσασι properly denotes the incredulous, and it is also explained in this way in verse 19, which sense is also clear from the scope, namely, the dissuasion from incredulity: To those who would not believe, who after so many and such great signs of divine goodness, justice, and power had been produced, could nevertheless not be persuaded to place faith in the divine promises.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Καὶ βλέπομεν) Ex historia cognoscimus.

Ὅτι ἐκ ἠδυνήθησαν ἐισελθεῖν) In sedes illas quietas, ob- stante nimirum decreto illo Dei peremptorio.

Δὶ ἀπιστίαν) Quia fidem non habuerant promissis divi- nis, quae causa & tunc fuit inobedientiae, & nunc est.

Vox ἀπειθήσασι proprie incredulos notat, at- que ita etiam exponitur vers. 19. qui sensus pa- tet quoque ex scopo, dehortatione nempe ab incredulitate: Illis, qui nolebant credere, qui post tot ac tanta divinae bonitatis, justitiae, & po- tentiae signa edita persuaderi tamen minime po- tuere, ut fidem promissis divinis adhiberent.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He continues to warn, lest we have the promise of entering into rest in vain, by the example of the ancients, to whom the Word without faith profited nothing, since a rest is prepared for us also, of which David speaks, as being not of the Sabbath of creation (Gen. II. verse 2) nor of the rest into which Joshua introduced the people, but of an eternal Sabbath: Whence we must give diligence that we may arrive at the same, and not fall through unbelief; since the Word of God is living and powerful, and nothing is hidden before God. And thus he proceeds to the treatment of Jesus the High Priest, in whose confession we must persist, who sympathizes with our infirmity, so that we may thus approach the throne of grace with confidence, and thereby obtain grace.

There are two parts: I. An admonition concerning the entry into eternal rest, up to verse 13. II. An admonition concerning the confident approach to the throne of grace, up to verse 16. The former pertains to the Doctoral office, that we may embrace the Word of CHRIST with true faith, by which we are introduced into rest: The latter to the Priestly office, for the explanation of which the Apostle thus prepares the way.

PART I. Admonition concerning the entry into eternal rest.

Vers. 1. Φοβηθῶμεν ὖν) We have said, according to the opinion of Chrysostom and others, that these things can not badly be connected with those which are above at III. 15.

We have shown that these are better separated. For it is now concluded from the Davidic admonition what must be avoided, lest they be excluded from the promised rest, by an application made to the Hebrews, whom the Apostle exhorts. Nor does Theophylact disagree, who otherwise perpetually follows Chrysostom. Φοβηθῶμεν is: let us diligently and with the greatest zeal take heed, with all care and solicitude; but it does nothing against confidence, as Estius thinks, since the Apostle strongly urges παῤῥησίαν, and ὑπόστασιν, the consistency of faith: And this fear is not servile, but filial, which properly consists with confidence, and only carnal security is excluded. The blessed Dorscheus embraces the argument of this chapter with this demonstration: That religion which teaches a true, divine, and beatific rest, and applies it to believers through most efficacious causes, is the true religion, drawn from the most ancient principles and monuments of the Jewish religion and solidly established. But such is the Christian religion, which JESUS of Nazareth proposed to the world. Therefore. The major premise is proved by the Apostle, because GOD, when he had finished the creation, commended rest to the human race, when he himself had rested on the seventh day from all his work, and had sanctified it for men for the same rest, and in it had not only shadowed forth, but also promised, an absolute and consummated rest of blessedness, that is, an eternal Sabbath; and afterwards, when he had introduced the Israelitic people into the land of Canaan, which introduction contained an image of the everlasting peace in the land of the living, he spoke of some rest to be communicated to the faithful and beatific, that that religion is true which rightly delivers this rest, and shows its solid and most efficacious causes. The Apostle proves the minor premise throughout this whole chapter and the following ones. And therefore he constitutes two parts of the present chapter: The first, he says, teaches the existence and embrace of divine and beatific rest. The other, its causes and the apprehension of the same. Of the first part, again, this is the special demonstration: In that religion in which a beatific and divine rest is gravely and solidly asserted for miserable souls, and those struggling with various difficulties, in that it behooves men to be solicitous, lest the occasion of obtaining beatific rest slip away from them, and to be attentive and industrious, so that they may be able to enter into it. But this is done in the Christian religion. Therefore. The major is certain. The minor is asserted by the Apostle in verse 9, and proved in verses 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 10. The conclusion is had in verses 1 and 11.

Μήποτε καταλειπομένης ἐπαγγελίας εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσιν αὐτῶ δοκῇ τις ἐξ ὑμῶν ὑςερηκέναι) Lest it should please any of you to be wanting to himself, when the right of entering into his rest has been left to you. Δοκεῖν is not always to seem, but to act according to one's own pleasure, as we said at Matthew III. verse 9. Ὑςερεῖν τινὸς is said in Greek, of one to whom something is lacking for obtaining a thing, as can be seen in Matthew XIX. verse 20, and here below at XII. v. 15. Ἐπαγγελία καταλειπομένη is a left-behind inheritance, which inheritance, because it does not come from the law, but from a promise, as if from a testament, Galatians III. verse 29. Therefore it is called ἐπαγγελία by metonymy, such as we have in the same word in Acts I. verse 14, Ephesians II. v. 12. In a similar way we have κληρονομεῖ ἐπαγγελίαν below at VI. 12. He explains, however, by πρόθεσιν, what that inheritance or promised thing is, namely, to enter into the rest of God, that perpetual and perfect one, which corresponds to the figure already mentioned before, and will be more openly explained in the following; you have καταλείπεσθαι concerning an inheritance not only among writers of Law, but also in Psalm XLIX. 11, and Sirach XI. 18.

Ἐπαγγελία properly is a promise: one must not depart from that propriety of the word. The Apostle does not say that the promise is not to be left behind, that is, that the word of the promise is not to be held in contempt. We do not deny, however, that the object of the promise or the thing promised is the rest of the Lord, which is the heavenly inheritance, but that is not to be confused with the word of the promise, to which the Apostle urges us to be received by faith. Nor was that eternal rest proposed by the Hiero-Psalmist only under a figure, but, as the Apostle demonstrates here, it was predicted: since he proves that David prophesied concerning a rest still to come, and not to be attained except through faith in CHRIST. Therefore, lest anyone be found excluded from that rest because the promise made through David concerning the entry into the heavenly rest was abandoned through unbelief, the Apostle solicitously warns. The particle μήποτε is rendered by the Vulgate as 'lest perhaps': but it should rather be explained as 'lest at any time,' as the Greek word implies. For there is no doubt that unbelief excludes one from the rest. The pronoun αὐτῶ refers to the Lord, who swore to the unbelievers that they would not enter into his rest, which is the Spirit of GOD, as is evident from chapter III, verse 7. Moreover, the unbelief by which the word of the promise is abandoned refers to the voice of the Lord in verse 15, that is, of the Son of God, in whom those who trust are blessed; according to the judgment of the Hiero-Psalmist: But they perish who do not kiss him with true faith, Psalm II, verse 12, whom therefore one must serve with fear, verse 11. The Vulgate rendered τὸ ὑςερηκέναι as 'to be lacking,' others as 'frustrated' or 'not having attained,' in that he is lacking to himself: Theophylact: 'Lest he be passed over.' For he is not passed over, he says, but he is thought to be passed by. Estius renders the sense thus: Since we see that so many from the ancient people were repelled from the promised rest on account of unbelief, we too must fear and take heed, lest at any time, the divine promise having been abandoned or neglected through infidelity and diffidence, by which He promised us an entrance into His rest, any one of us should appear, that is, be found excluded from that rest. The blessed Dorschæus has it thus in this place: The Apostle points his finger to that which he said in Romans 3, verse 23, concerning all men, ὑστερῶνται τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ, and hence also [the lack] of the rest of God. He wishes, therefore, that we should solicitously take care, since we have been redeemed from that ὑστέρησις, raised to the πλήρωμα of CHRIST, and invited to the δόξα and κατάπαυσις, lest through some new ὑστέρησις we lose the promised rest. Thus the negative embrace is described, in which the contrary affirmative is more strongly enjoined, which is also expressed in verse 11, where that embrace is described through the industry of the effort of entering into the beatific rest.

Latin:

CAPUT IV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Pergit monere, ne promissionem ingrediendi re- quiem insuper habeamus exemplo vete- rum, quibus Verbum sine fide nihil pro- fuit, siquidem & nobis requies parata sit, de qua David, utpote non de Sabbato creationis (Genes. II. vers. 2.) nec de re- quie, in quam Josua populum introdu- xit, sed de æterno Sabbatismo agens: Unde opera danda, ut ad eundem perve- niamus, nec per incredulitatem cadamus; quum Verbum Dei vivum & efficax, & coram Deo nihil absconditum sit. Atque ita progreditur ad tractationem de Jesu Pontifice, in cujus confessione persistendum, qui nostræ infirmitati con- dolet, ut ita cum fiducia ad thronum gratiæ accedamus, adeoque gratiam con- sequamur.

PArtes duæ sunt I. Admonitio de ingressu in requiem æternam ad vers. 13. II. Admonitio de accessu fiduciali ad thronum gratiæ ad vers. 16. Illa pertinet ad officium Doctorale, ut Verbum CHRISTI vera fide amplectamur, qua in requiem introducimur: Hæc ad officium Sacer- dotale, ad quod explicandum aditum ita parat Apostolus.

PARS I. Admonitio de ingressu in æternam requiem.

Vers. 1. Φοβηθῶμεν ὖν) Diximus ex Chrysostomi & aliorum sententia non male hæc posse connecti cum iis, quæ supra III. 15.

Ostendimus melius hæc separari. Concludi- tur enim jam ex admonitione Davidica, quid cavendum, ne requie promissa excludantur, ap- plicatione ad Ebræos, quos cohortatur Aposto- lus, facta. Neque abnuit Theophylactus, qui alias perpetuo sequitur Chrysostomum. Φοβηθῶμεν est diligenter & summo studio caveamus, omni cura & solicitudine; non autem quicquam facit con- tra fiduciam, ut Estius arbitratur, siquidem παῤῥησίαν maxime urgeat Apostolus, & ὑπόστα- σιν, consistentiam fidei: Et metus hic sit non ser- vilis, sed filialis, qui probe cum fiducia consi- stit, nec nisi carnalis securitas excludatur. Beat. Dorscheus hujus capitis argumentum hac apo- dixi complectitur: Quæ religio veram divinam ac beatificam requiem docet, & per causas effica- cissimas credentibus applicat, ea est vera, ex an- tiquissimis Judaicæ religionis principiis & monu- mentis educta & solide constituta religio. Atqui talis est Christiana religio, quam JESUS Na- zarenus orbi proposuit. Ergo. Major probatur ab Apostolo, quia DEUS & consummata creatio- ne requiem generi humano commendavit, cum ipse septimo die ab omni opere suo quievisset, & ad eandem quietem hominibus ipsum sanctificas- set, & in eo absolutam consummatamque beati- tudinis quietem, hoc est, Sabbatum æternum non tantum adumbrasset, sed & promisisset, & postea cum introduxisset populum Israeliticum in ter- ram Canaan, quæ introductio sempiternæ pacis in terra viventium tandem aliquando habente imaginem complexa est, de aliqua requie fideli- bus communicanda & beatifica loquutus est, ve- ram esse eam religionem, quæ hanc requiem recte tradit, ejusque solidas, efficacissimasque causas ostendit. Minorem probat Apostolus toto hoc capite & sequentibus. Ideoque capitis præsentis duas partes constituit : Prima, inquit, docet quietis divinæ & beatificæ existentiam & ample- xum. Altera ejusdem causas, earundemque ap- prehensionem. Primæ partis rursus hæc est specia- lis apodixis : In qua religione graviter & solide asseritur beatifica & divina requies animabus mi- seris, & cum variis difficultatibus confligentibus parata, in ea solicitos esse decet homines, ne oc- casio adipiscendi beatificam quietem illis præterla- batur, & attentos atque industrios, ut in illam ipsam ingredi possint. Atqui in Christiana religio- ne hoc fit. Ergo. Major certa est. Minor as- seritur ab Apostolo vers. 9. probatur vers. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. & 10. Conclusio habetur v. 1. & 11.

Μήποτε καταλειπομένης ἐπαγγελίας εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν κα- τάπαυσιν αὐτῶ δοκῇ τις ἐξ ὑμῶν ὑςερηκέναι) Ne cui vestrum libeat sibi deesse, cum relictum sit vobis jus intrandi in ipsius requiem. Δοκεῖν non semper est videri, sed pro lu- bitu agere, ut Matth. III. vers. 9. diximus. Ὑςερεῖν τινὸς Græce dicitur, cui aliquid deest ad rem adipiscendam, ut videre est Matth. XIX. vers. 20. & hic infra XII. v. 15. Ἐπαγγελία καταλειπομένη est hæreditas relicta, quæ hæ- reditas quia non ex lege venit, sed ex promisso, quasi ex testamento, Galat. III. vers. 29. Ideo vocatur ἐπαγγε- λία per μετωνυμίαν, qualem in eadem voce habemus Actor. I. vers. 14. Ephes. II. v. 12. Pari modo κληρονομεῖ ἐπαγγε- λίαν habemus infra VI. 12. Exponit autem per πρόθεσιν, quæ sit illa hæreditas sive res promissa, nempe intrare in requiem Dei, illam perpetuam atque perfectam, quæ respondet figuræ jam ante dictæ, & in sequentibus aper- tius explicabitur, καταλείπεσθαι de hæreditate habes non tantum apud Juris scriptores, sed & Psalm. XLIX. 11. & Si- rac. XI. 18.

Ἐπαγγελία proprie est promissio : ab ea vo- cis proprietate non recedendum. Non dicit Apostolus, non relinquendam promissionem, hoc est, non insuper habendum verbum pro- missionis. Objectum autem promissionis vel rem promissam esse requiem Domini, quæ est hære- ditas cœlestis, non diffitemur, sed id non con- fundendum cum verbo promissionis, ad quod fide suscipiendum excitat Apostolus. Neque requies illa æterna ab Hiero-Psalte tantum sub figura proposita, sed, Apostolo hic demonstrante, prædicta est: quum de requie futura adhuc, nec nisi per fidem in CHRISTUM consequenda Davidem vaticinari evincat. Ne ergo dereli- cta per incredulitatem promissione per Davi- dem facta de ingressu in requiem cœlestem ali- quis ex ea requie inveniatur exclusus, solicite monet Apostolus. Particula μήποτε à Vulgata redditur, ne forte : Sed exponenda potius, ne quando, ut Græca vox infert. Neque enim du- bium est, incredulitatem excludere à requie. Pronomen αὐτῶ respicit Dominum, qui juravit incredulis, non ingressuros in requiem suam, qui est Spiritus DEI, ut è cap. III. vers. 7. con- stat. Incredulitas autem, qua relinquitur ver- bum promissionis, vocem Domini vers. 15. respi- cit, hoc est, Filii Dei, in quo qui confidunt, beati sunt; judicio Hiero-Psaltis: Pereunt autem, qui non osculantur eum vera fide, Psalm. II. vers. 12. cui proinde serviendum cum timore, vers. 11. Tὸ ὑςερηκέναι deesse reddidit Vulgatus, alii frustratus seu non assecuutus, eo, quod sibiipsi desit: Theophylactus: Ne prætereatur. Non enim præ- termissus est, inquit, sed præteritus esse existi- matur. Estius sensum ita tradit: Quum videamus ex veteri populo tam multos à requie promissa fuissse repulsos propter incredulitatem; nobis quoque metuendum est atque cavendum, ne quando dere- licta seu neglecta per infidelitatem ac diffidentiam pollicitatione divina, qua promisit nobis ingres- sum in requiem suam, aliquis nostrum ab requie ea videatur, id est, inveniatur exclusus. Beat. Dorschæus ita habet hoc loco: Apostolus digi- tum intendit ad id, quod Roman. III. vers. 23. de omnibus hominibus dixit, ὑστερῶνται τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ, unde & καταπαύσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ. Vult itaque, ut solicite curemus, quoniam ab ista ὑστερήσει redem- pti, ad πλήρωμα CHRISTI evecti, & ad δόξαν atque κατάπαυσιν invitati sumus, ne per novam quandam ὑστέρησιν requiem promissam amittamus. Sic negative amplexus describitur, in qua con- trarium affirmativum fortius injungitur, quod est & expressum, vers. 11. ubi amplexus iste descri- bitur per industriam conatum ingrediendi in beati- ficam requiem.

## 4:2
Verse 2.

Καὶ γάρ ἐσμεν εὐαγγελισμένοι) A Greek construction, such as in Matthew 1:15, Luke 7:22, which makes the passive of a person even from an active governing the dative: and this proceeds here all the more easily, because the active Εὐαγγελίζω is constructed not only with the dative, as in Luke 1:9, chapter 2:10, and elsewhere, but also with the accusative, as in Luke 3:18. We have received a joyful message, an excellent promise.

The application is now made to the Hebrews converted to the faith of Christ, to whom in these last days GOD had spoken in His Son. For they had been evangelized; to them in the Gospel had been promised rest and eternal beatitude. They are said to be Εὐαγγελίζεσθαι in the passive sense, to whom good and joyful things are announced, Matthew 11:4, Luke 7:21, 2 Samuel 18:19.

Καθάπερ κἀκεῖνοι) In their own way, that is. They had received promises concerning earthly things, we concerning heavenly ones.

Καθάπερ does not mean in their own way, but rather 'just as also,' and the agreement of the promise is taught, that we have received the Gospel similarly just as they did, that is, the ancients under the Old Testament. But not only is a general similarity noted, which Estius wishes, having things in common with the Grotian view: The similarity, he says, consists in the kind of good news. For in species there is a great difference. For to them was announced and promised a certain rest of this age, but to us a rest much happier after this age. But the explanation of the Davidic text and its application teaches that the argument of the Apostle is not taken from a generic similarity. Therefore, by those words, 'just as also they,' either the Fathers in the desert are looked to, to whom Moses spoke, or those to whom David spoke. If we say the latter are looked to, it is manifest that the identity of the promised thing is designated, even if a diversity of the word of promise occurs regarding the mode or degree of evidence. For those promises of the heavenly inheritance are delivered more clearly in the New Testament; nor yet were they silent in the Old Testament, since all the prophets testified concerning Christ, that remission of sins, and thus also eternal life, is had in His name, Acts 10:43, and the Psalmist himself delivered notable promises and oracles concerning salvation and eternal beatitude, Psalm 2:12, Psalm 16:last verse, Psalm 17:last verse, etc., and the Apostle demonstrates that he is not dealing here with any other than heavenly rest. But if the Fathers in the desert are understood, the word of promise made to them indeed concerned the inheritance of the land of Canaan, but not only was the inheritance of eternal life figured through that, but also the Evangelical promises concerning the remission of sins and salvation were available to them, which those who received by faith were saved through the grace of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, just as we also, Acts 15:11. But the Apostle seems to understand these in the present place, verse 2, as those by whose example and loss he warns of the need to avoid unbelief and to receive the Word of CHRIST through faith, to whom the Israelites were also referred for hearing even at the very promulgation of the law, Deuteronomy 18:15 ff., as also in the leading through the desert, Exodus 23:20, 21, as being the Angel who redeemed and saved them, Isaiah 63:9 ff. It appears, therefore, from this place that the Fathers in the desert who fell through unbelief were excluded by that same unbelief not only from temporal but also from eternal rest, who, namely, did not repent, because the word did not profit them, not being mixed with faith. We add what the blessed Dorscheus replied here to Grotius: We are said to be gifted with the Sabbatic Gospel καθάπερ κἀκεῖνοι, that is, those of whom [we spoke] above in chapter 3, verse 19, the Fathers who were spectators of the divine oracles and miracles. But the Apostle does not compare the leaders of the evangelization or two Gospels in this place, as Grotius thinks, who says that the Gospel, comprising only temporal promises, was proposed to the Fathers: but that to us the proclamation of spiritual goods is communicated by the Gospel. This is repugnant to the apostolic scope, which is to show that the promise of rest is open to us no less than to the Israelites, so that we might have certainty of that matter, the Apostle alleges the identity of our preaching and the Israelitic one. Which allegation would be useless if the preaching of only temporal rest had happened to the Fathers of the Israelites. The Petrine assertion in Acts 15:11 also contradicts this.

Ἀλλ’ οὐκ ὠφέλησεν ὁ λόγος τῆς ἀκοῆς ἐκείνως) Λόγος ἀκοῆς, קול שמועה, Jeremiah 10:22. That word heard far and wide profited them nothing.

Ὁ λόγος ἀκοῆς, the word of hearing, which reached only the ears of the people, did not penetrate to their heart, which was stopped up; it is the word τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, because the Apostle exhorted them by this example in verse 1 not to neglect it, and taught that they had been Εὐαγγελισμένως.

Not mixed with faith in those who heard) Many manuscripts have συγκεκραμένως, not συγκεκραμένος: But the reading συγκεκραμένος seems good, so that faith is here compared to the parts of the human body, through which digestion occurs, and food is converted into juice. Thus Luke the physician may have taken terms from the medical art. The sense is not different in the epistle of Demosthenes: The persuasion of words requires the goodwill of the hearers: And in Chrysostom II. against the Jews: For there is no profit in hearing, when the demonstration through works does not accompany what is said. Yet the other can also be borne, in this sense: That the sermon did not profit them, because they had not joined themselves through faith to those who heard, that is, to those who obeyed, namely Joshua and Caleb, but had separated themselves, like Korah and Dathan, and others later: So that by a hidden comparison this writer strikes at those who were deserting the Christian ἐπισυναγωγήν (gathering together). See below X. 25. Chrysostom seems to have conceived this sense.

The reading of the sermon not mixed with faith is more accepted and approved: For there is a reference to the mixture and coupling of faith and the Word in an elegant expression, since the Word ought to be mixed with faith, and united with it, and as it were reduced into one mass, just as seed must be entrusted to good earth and mixed with it, and as it were glued together, Luke VIII. B. Gerhard, not tempered, not aptly joined with the faith of the hearers, just as the soul is coupled to the body by a certain temperature, since faith is as it were the life of hearing, or as in soldering metal is joined to metal. Unless the mixture of faith is added, the medicine of the Word is clearly of no benefit to the hearers. The blessed Luther rendered the sense: 'Those who heard it did not believe.' The blessed Gerhard also notes that several Greek codices and the Syriac version read 'mixed' [with faith], and that this is more congruent with the text. The blessed Dorsch says: 'The received reading being retained, it is said more plainly that there is no comparison here between hearers and hearers, among whom there has not been a *sunkrasis* [mingling] through the unity of faith, but that this is said between the Word itself heard and the hearers themselves, that there has not been a *sunkrasis te pistei* [mingling by faith], and that the preached sermon was not tempered by faith through the medium of faith for those who had heard; for the *akoē tou rhēmatos tou theou* [hearing of the word of God] requires *pistin* [faith], Rom. 10:17, and where it does not find it, it produces it, unless malicious resistance stands in the way.' Thus, therefore, a *sunkrasis tou logou* [mingling of the word] occurs among the hearers when *pistis* [faith] is produced, which immediately apprehends and applies the good *logou* [word]. This, therefore, is the order, namely that through faith a *sunkrasis* [mingling] of the heard Gospel with the hearers may take place. The Apostle compares the Sabbath Gospel to wine, which, in order to benefit us when drunk, heard, and perceived, must be tempered for us through faith, and as it were brought into juice and blood. In short, this *sunkrasis* expresses the union between man and the divine Word through faith, from which also comes the union and communion of all the goods of the Word. Estius criticizes the Vulgate version, which has 'not mixed with faith of those who heard,' although approved by the authority of the Popes and the Council of Trent, in this way: 'It is in no way possible to translate the Greek as "of those who heard."' Whence Ribera not undeservedly suspects that our version has been corrupted by the ignorance of scribes, in whatever way that may have happened. Why, therefore, did the Popes not amend it, if they are infallible in defining?

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Καὶ γάρ ἐσμεν εὐαγγελισμένοι) Constructio Græca, qualis Matth. I. 15. Luc. VII. 22. quæ passivum personæ fa- cit etiam ex Activo Dativum regente: idque hic eo facilius procedit, quod activum Εὐαγγελίζω non tantum cum Da- tivo, ut Luc. I. v. 9. c. II. v. 10. & alibi, sed & cum Accusa- tivo construitur, ut Luc. III. 18. Lætum nuntium accepi- mus, promissionem egregiam.

Applicatio jam fit ad Ebræos conversos ad fi- dem Christi, quibus novissimis diebus DEUS loquutus erat in Filio. Illi enim evangelizati e- rant, illis in Evangelio promissa erat requies, & beatitudo æterna. Εὐαγγελίζεσθαι in significa- tione passiva dicuntur, quibus bona & læta nun- tiantur, Matth. XI. v. 4. Luc. VII. vers. 21. 2. Sam. XIIX. v. 19.

Καθάπερ κἀκεῖνοι) Suo scilicet modo. Illi de rebus ter- renis promissa acceperant, nos de cœlestibus.

Καθάπερ non est suo modo, sed potius sicut & docetur convenientia promissionis, quod simi- liter sicut & illi, hoc est prisci sub Veteri Testa- mento Evangelium acceperimus. Non autem tantum generalis similitudo notatur, quod Estius vult, paria cum Grotianis habens: Similitudo, inquit, consistit in genere boni nuncii. Nam in specie magna est differentia. Illis enim nunciata fuit ac promissa requies quædam hujus seculi, no- bis autem requies multo felicior post hoc seculum. Sed argumentum Apostoli non à similitudine ge- nerica desumptum esse, explicatio textus Davi- dici ejusdemque applicatio docet. Verbis ergo illis, sicut & illi vel respiciuntur Patres in deserto, ad quos Moses, vel illi, ad quos David loquutus est. Si hos respici dicamus, manifestum est, identi- tatem rei promissæ designari, etsi diversitas verbi promissionis occurrat quoad modum vel gradum evidentiæ. Luculentius enim in Novo Testa- mento traditæ sunt illæ promissiones hæreditatis cœlestis; nec tamen in Veteri Testamento tacitæ fuere, quum omnes Prophetæ testificati sint de Chri- sto, remissionem peccatorum, adeoque & vitam æ- ternam in nomine ejus haberi, Act. X. 43. & Hie- ro-Psaltes ipse insignia de salute ac beatitudine æ- terna tradiderit promissa & oracula Psal. II. v. 12. Psal. XVI. v. ult. Psal. XVII. v. ult. &c. nec de alia, quam cœlesti requie hic agat, demonstrante A- postolo. Si vero intelligantur Patres in deserto, verbum promissionis ipsis factæ concernebat qui- dem hæreditatem terræ Canaan, at non solum per illam figurata fuit hæreditas vitæ æternæ, sed pro- missiones etiam Evangelicæ de remissione pec- catorum & salute ipsis prostabant, quas, qui fide suscepere, salvati sunt per gratiam Domini nostri JESU CHRISTI, sicut & nos Actor. XV. vers. 11. Hos autem in præsenti loco vers. 2. intelligere videtur Apostolus, utpote quorum exemplo, & damno monet de cavenda increduli- tate, & suscipiendo Verbo CHRISTI per fi- dem, ad quem audiendum etiam circa ipsam le- gis promulgationem remissi sunt Israëlitæ Deut. XIIX. vers. 15. seqq. ut & in deductione per de- sertum, Exod. XXIII. vers. 20. 21. utpote Ange- lum, qui redemit & salvavit eos Esaiæ LXIII. vers. 9. seqq. Apparet ergo ex hoc loco, Patres in deserto per incredulitatem lapsos per eandem non solum à temporali, sed etiam æterna re- quie exclusos esse, qui scilicet pœnitentiam non egerunt, quia non profuit iis verbum, non ad- mixtum fidei. Addimus quæ hic Grotio repo- suit Beatus Dorscheus: Dicimur Evangelio Sab- batico donati καθάπερ κἀκεῖνοι, illi scilicet, de quibus supra cap. III. vers. 19. Patres oraculorum & miraculorum divinorum spectatores. Non con- fert autem hoc loco Apostolus duces Evangeliza- tionis, aut duo Evangelia, ut Grotius existimat, qui dicit, Patribus Evangelium, temporales dun- taxat promissiones complexum, fuisse propositum: Nobis autem spiritualium bonorum præconium Evangelio communicari. Repugnat hoc scopo Apostolico, qui est, ostendere nobis non minus promissionem quietis patere, quam Israëlitic, ut ejus rei haberemus certitudinem, identitatem prædicationis nostræ & Israëliticæ Apostolus al- legat. Quæ allegatio frustranea esset, si tempora- lis duntaxat quietis prædicatio Patribus Israëli- tarum contigisset. Repugnat etiam assertio Petri- na Actor. XV. 11.

Ἀλλ’ οὐκ ὠφέλησεν ὁ λόγος τῆς ἀκοῆς ἐκείνως) Λόγος ἀκοῆς קול שמועה Jerem. X. 22. Sermo ille longe late- que auditus nihil 'illis profuit.

Ὁ λόγος ἀκοῆς sermo auditionis, qui ad aures tantum populi pervenit, ad cor ipsorum, quod obturatum erat, non penetravit, sermo est τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, quia ad eundem non negligendum hortatus hoc exemplo est Apostolus v. 1. docuit- que eos fuisse Εὐαγγελισμένως.

Μὴ συγκεκραμένως τῇ πίστει τοῖς ἀκούσασιν) Συγκεκρα- μένως non συγκεκραμένος habent manuscripti non pauci: Sed bona videtur lectio συγκεκραμένος, ut fides hic com- paretur partibus humani corporis, per quæ fit digestio, & cibus in succum convertitur. Ita Lucas medicus ex arte medica voces sumpserit. Sensus non dispar in epistola Demosthenis: Ἡ δὲ τῶν λόγων πειθὼ τῆς τῶν ἀκουσάντων εὐ- νοίας προσδεῖται: Et apud Chrysostomum II. adversus Ju- dæos: Οὐδὲν γὰρ ὄφελος ἀκροάσεως, ὅταν ἡ διὰ τῶν ἔργων ἐπίδειξις μὴ συμβαίνῃ τοῖς λεγομένοις. Potest tamen ferri & altera, hoc sensu: Ideo eis sermonem illum non profuisse, quia illi per fidem se non conjunxerant audientibus, id est, obedientibus, nempe Josuæ & Calebo, sed semet separave- rant, ut Core & Dathan, & postea alii: Ita ut occulta com- paratione feriat hic scriptor eos, qui Christianam ἐπισυνα- γωγὴν deserebant. Vide infra X. 25. Hunc sensum videtur concepisse Chrysostomus.

Receptior & probatior est lectio de sermone non commixto fidei: Respicitur enim mixtura & copulatio fidei & Verbi eleganti loquutio- ne, quum Verbum fidei commisceri, & cum eadem uniri, ac veluti in unam massam redigi debeat, ut semen terræ bonæ credendum & cum ea commiscendum, ac veluti conglutinandum est, Luc. IIX. B. Gerhardus, non contemperatus, non apte conjunctus cum fide auditorum, velut anima copulatur corpori quadam temperatura, cum fides veluti vita sit auditus, vel sicut in conferruminatione metallum metallo adjungitur. Nisi fidei mixtura accedat, Verbi pharmacum plane non prodest auditoribus. Beatus Luthe- rus sensum reddidit: Da nicht glåubeten die, so es höreten. Notat & Beatus Gerhardus, complures Græcos Codices, ac Syriacam versionem lege- re commixtus, idque textui magis congruere. Beatus Dorschaeus: Retenta, inquit, lectione visi- tata planius dicitur, non esse comparationem hoc loco inter auditores & auditores, inter quos non sit facta συγκρασία per unitatem fidei, sed hoc di- ci inter ipsum Verbum auditum, & inter ipsos auditores non factam esse συγκρασίαν τῇ πίσει, & sermonem prædicatum non fuisse fide contempera- tum mediante fide illis qui audierant; nimirum ἀκοὴ τῦ ῥήματος τῦ θεῦ requirit πίσιν, Rom. X. vers. 17. & ubi non invenit, efficit, nisi malitio- sa obstet repugnantia. Sic itaque συγκρασία τῦ λόγε fit apud auditores, quando πίσις producitur, quæ statim bona λόγε apprehendit & applicat. Hic est igitur ordo, ut scilicet per fidem fiat συγ- κρασία Evangelii auditi cum auditoribus. Com- parat Apostolus Sabbaticum Evangelium vino, quod ut haustum, auditum & perceptum nobis prosit per fidem nobis sit contemperandum, & quasi in succum sanguinemque deducendum. Pau- cis, ista συγκρασία exprimit unionem inter homi- nem & Verbum divinum per fidem, ex qua etiam unio & communio omnium bonorum Verbi. Vul- gatam versionem, quæ habet, non admixtus fi- dei ex iis, quæ audiverunt, etsi autoritate Pon- tificum, & Concilii Tridentini probatam, sic re- prehendit Estius: Nullo modo Græca verti possunt ex iis quæ audiverunt. Unde non imme- rito suspicatur Ribera, depravatam esse scriba- rum inscitia nostram versionem, quacunque ratio- ne id acciderit. Cur ergo non emendarunt Pon- tifices, si in definiendo infallibiles sunt?

## 4:3
Ver. 3.

For we who have believed enter into the rest) The present tense for all time. And then the believers entered into the rest of GOD, namely by obedient faith, and now they shall enter. A manuscript has *eiserchōmetha* [let us enter], not badly.

By the example of those who were excluded because of unbelief, he joins and opposes the example of those entering into the rest, who are *hoi pisteuontes* [those who believe], who believe and remain constant in faith, joining himself with the converted Hebrews because of the confidence conceived regarding them and the excitation to maintain constancy of faith even in the most grievous afflictions. This second reason for exhortation, therefore, is from utility, as the former was from danger and loss: thus is explained at the same time what had been said in verse 2, 'For indeed to us it was announced.' For this is the Gospel which was announced to us, namely that we shall enter into eternal rest, as many as have perseveringly believed the promise made to us by Christ. Compare chapter 3, verse 14. But it is urged in the present tense because we are here on the way, and in the state of entering, Matt. 7:13-14. Heb. 10:19-20. both to warn tacitly that we should not deviate from the way to the entrance, and to testify to his own certainty concerning the future entrance into eternal rest, or heavenly blessedness: But one manuscript of Grotius is wrongly preferred to all other codices, however approved.

As He has said) GOD, namely, as the cited passage indicates.

As I swore in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest:) He repeats the words which we also had above in 3:11, but in order to adapt them to a more sublime sense: And he urges that 'my,' to show that the rest is understood to be similar to that which GOD enjoys.

This is an exposition of the argument brought from the Psalm, that the Israelites who were unbelieving did not enter, with only those who believed being excepted, and therefore that non-believers are excluded from eternal rest and will not enter it, unless they are those who believe. To *eirēken* [he has said] must be repeated *apo koinou* [in common] from chapter 3, verse 7, the name 'Holy Spirit,' who spoke through David. Nor are these things adapted to a more sublime sense; but David's intention is looked to, which was, with a view to future rest, to warn against hardening the heart to the voice of the Lord.

Although the works were finished from the foundation of the world) This is an *anthupophora* [counter-objection]. For someone, having heard of the rest of GOD, could understand that which followed the creation of things: And of which Adam was in some way a participant, living sweetly without any labor. He says, therefore, the works of GOD were done *apo katabolēs kosmou* [from the foundation of the world], that is, immediately from the time the world was founded. Therefore, GOD was not dealing with that rest when He said so long after that those refractory ones would not enter into His rest: *Apo katabolēs kosmou* here designates that time of the six days described in Genesis. A similarity drawn from a building, as Matt. 13:39, chapter 25:34, Luke 11:50, below 9:26, Rev. 13:8, chapter 17:8. For in these places *katabolē kosmou* is taken in such a way that the final work, that is, the creation of man, is also included.

There is here an ellipsis of a verb to be elicited from the preceding: (See Glassius, Grammat. S. p. 666, 856) from the word *katapauseōs* [rest], in this way: *Kaitoi katēpausen* [Although He rested], and indeed (as the Vulgate rightly has it) God rested, the works of the creation of the world having been finished. It is demonstrated that the Davidic exhortation, which was directed to the end that, when the word of the Lord is heard, hearts should not be hardened, lest those who harden them be excluded from rest, does not look to that rest of the Lord of which [we read] in the history of creation; because it is not about past, but future rest that is being treated here, about the rest to be expected by us, not about the rest celebrated by GOD when the first hexaemeron of the world was finished, and therefore not about the Sabbath of creation, which was GOD's, besides which there occurs in the Scriptures even then the Sabbath of sanctification and the legal weekly one, which was sanctioned in the decalogue in memory of that one, and the spiritual one, which is to be celebrated by us at all times; then the Sabbath of eternal blessedness and glorification. That one was not to be removed here, because it pertains to the precept 'Today, if you will hear His voice,' etc., to which obedience is owed, not to the promise which was made to those who believe and keep the precepts of God concerning the rest to be given to them. Moreover, those words καί τι τῶν ἔργων &c. cohere with the preceding, He spoke of his future rest, although the works had already been done from the foundation of the world, as B. Luther expressed in v. 3: And indeed since the works were made from the beginning of the world.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Εἰσερχόμεθα γὰρ εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσιν οἱ πισεύσαντες) Præ- sens pro omni tempore. Et tunc in requiem DEI intra- runt credentes, fide nempe obediente, & nunc intrabunt. Manuscriptus habet εἰσερχώμεθα, non male.

Exemplo eorum, qui exclusi fuere ob incre- dulitatem, adjungit & opponit exemplum ingre- dientium in requiem, qui sunt οἱ πισέυοντες, qui credunt, & constantes in fide permanent, se cum Ebræis conversis, ob fiduciam de illis conce- ptam, & excitationem ad fidei constantiam in gravissimis etiam afflictionibus servandæ conjun- gens. Altera ergo hæc adhortationis ratio ab utili est, uti prior à periculo & damno: sic expli- catur simul, quod dictum erat vers. 2. Etenim & nobis nunciatum est. Hoc est enim Evange- lium, quod nobis nunciatum, nos scilicet in- gressuros in æternam requiem, quotquot pro- missioni à Christo nobis factæ perseveranter cre- diderimus. Confer. cap. III. v. 14. Uritur autem præsenti, quia hic in via sumus, & in eo, ut in- grediamur, Matth. VII. v. 13. 14. Ebr. X. v. 19. 20. tum ut moneat tacite, ne à via ad ingressum de- viemus, tum ut certitudinem suam de futura in- gressione ad requiem æternam, vel beatitudine cœlesti testetur: Male autem præfertur unum Manuscriptum Grotii omnibus aliis codicibus, utut probatissimis.

Καθὼς εἴρηκεν) DEUS scilicet, ut indicat locus ci- tatus.

Ὡς ὤμοσα ἐν τῇ ὀργῇ μυ, εἰ ἐισελέυσονται εἰς τὴν κα- τάπαυσίν με·) Repetit verba, quæ & supra habuimus III. 11. sed ut ea aptet ad sensum sublimiorem: Et urget illud μυ, ut ostendat quietem intelligi similem ei, qua DEUS fruitur.

Expolitio est argumenti è Psalmo adducto, quod Israëlitæ non ingressi sint, qui increduli erant, illis tantum, qui credidere, exceptis, adeo- que ab æterna requie excludantur non-credentes, nec ingressuri eam sint, nisi qui credunt. Ad e- ρηκεν repetendum ἀπὸ κοινοῦ e cap. III. v. 7. nomen Spiritus Sanctus, qui loquutus est per Davidem. Neque eptantur hæc ad sublimiorem sensum; sed respicitur intentio Davidica, quæ erat intuitu requiei futuræ monere de corde non obduran- do ad vocem Domini.

Καίτοι τῶν ἔργων ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου γενηθέντων) Est ἀνθυποφορά. Poterat enim aliquis audita DEI quie- te intelligere illam, quæ rerum creationem subsequuta est: Et cujus Adamus aliquo modo particeps fuit sine ul- lo labore suaviter vivens. Ait ergo opera DEI ἀπὸ και ταβολῆς κόσμου, id est, statim à mundo condito fuisse fa- cta. Non ergo de illa quiete egit DEUS, cum dixit tan- to post tempore illos refractarios in suam quietem non in- traturos: Ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου hic designat tempus il- lud sex dierum in Genesi descriptum. Similitudo dedu- cta ab ædificio ut Matth. XIII. vers. 39. cap. XXV. v. 34. Luc. XI. vers. 50. infra IX. 26. Apocal. XIII. vers. 8. cap. XVII. vers. 8. Nam istis in locis καταβολὴ κόσμου ita su- mitur, ut & ultimum opus, id est, hominis creatio compre- hendatur.

Est hic ellipsis verbi ex antecedentibus eruen- di: (Vid. Glassias Grammat. S. pag. 666. 856.) è voce καταπαύσεως, hoc modo: Καί τοι κατέπαυ- σεν, & quidem (ut recte Vulgata) quievit Deus, operibus creationis mundi consummatis. De- monstratur, adhortationem Davidicam, quæ eo directa erat, ut, cum auditur verbum Domini, non obturentur corda, ne à requie excludantur, qui obturant, non respicere requiem illam Do- mini, de qua in historia creationis; quia non de præterita, sed futura requie hic agitur, de quie- te nobis expectanda, non de quiete à DEO, primo hexaëmero mundi finito, celebrata, adeo- que non de Sabbato creationis, quod DEI erat, præter quod in Scripturis occurrit, etiam tum Sabbatum sanctificationis & legale hebdoma- dale, quod in decalogo in memoriam istius san- citum est, & spirituale, quod omni tempore à no- bis celebrandum; tum Sabbatum æternæ beatitu- dinis, & glorificationis. Illud removendum hic non erat, quia pertinet ad præceptum hodie, si vocem ejus audieritis &c. cui debetur obedien- tia, non ad promissum, quod credentibus & præ- cepta Dei servantibus factum de quiete illis do- nanda. Cohærent autem illa verba καί τι τῶν ἔρ- γων &c. cum præcedentibus, Dixit de requie sua futura, licet operibus à constitutione mundi jam factis ut v. 3. expressit B. Lutherus: Und zwar da die Werck waren von Anbegin der Welt gemacht.

## 4:4
Vers. 4.

Εἴρηκε γάρ που περὶ τῆς ἑβδόμης ὕτως) The Jews were not accustomed to name the book or chapter of a passage: because from the earliest age they had become so accustomed to those writings that everyone, upon hearing the words, knew the place. Thus he considered it sufficient to say πε. Moreover, elegantly, in the manner of the Alexandrian Jews and certain ones in Syria, he calls the Sabbath τὴν ἑβδόμην, as Philo does in very many places.

Καὶ κατέπαυσεν ὁ Θεὸς τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑβδόμη ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἔργων αὐτῦ) From the Greek of Gen. II. 3. That ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑβδόμῃ is absent in the Manuscript.

Therefore this rest of GOD is the rest of the Lord, who spoke in the Psalm, whom the Israelites provoked, i.e., the Holy Spirit; by which compact the Holy Spirit is established as God the Creator, who rested on the seventh day, not because he was wearied by the work of creation, or even as ceasing from the preservation and sustenance of things, but because he no longer created new species of things, as in the first six-day period of creation. B. Luther, for the sake of greater evidence of the sense, omitted the particle γάρ. But the causal can be retained, and referred to v. 3. Εἰσερχόμεθα we enter into that rest, because some rest still remains. He now undertakes to prove this by first removing the rest of the Lord on the seventh day of creation, then the rest in the land of Canaan. Whence it is left that a third rest still remains in the other life: Otherwise that exhortation, fortified by the example of the Fathers in the desert, would be in vain. Rightly, therefore, did Theophylact observe this: This speech, he says, seems to be less consistent with itself, when yet it is otherwise, but he says thus: For no one will be able to say that David discoursed about the rest of the Sabbath. For how can it be, when that was already accomplished long ago, so that the world was established from the beginning? But rather it is clear that he spoke of some other rest of David, namely of that heavenly entry, which nevertheless is owed in the future, as if some were to enter this rest of heaven hereafter.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Εἴρηκε γάρ που περὶ τῆς ἑβδόμης ὕτως) Non solebant Judæi loci librum aut caput nominare: quia à prima æta- te ita scriptis istis assueverant, ut quisque auditis verbis locum nosset. Adeo satis habuit dicere πε. Eleganter autem more Judæorum Alexandrinorum & quorundam in Syria ἐκπυρίζονταν Sabbatum vocat τὴν ἑβδόμην, ut Philo plurimis in locis.

Καὶ κατέπαυσεν ὁ Θεὸς τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑβδόμη ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἔργων αὐτῦ) Ex Græco Gen. II. 3. Illud ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ ἑβδόμῃ abest in Manuscripto.

Quies ergo hæc DEI est quies Domini, qui in Psalmo loquutus est, quem exacerbarunt Israëlitæ, h. e. Spiritus S. quo pacto Spiritus S. constituitur Deus Creator, qui septima die quievit, non quia defatigatus ab opere creationis, aut etiam ut ces- sans à conservatione & sustentatione rerum, sed quia non amplius novas rerum species, ut in pri- mo creationis hexaëmero, creavit. B. Lutherus ob evidentiam majorem sensus prætermisit par- ticulam γάρ. Sed retineri potest causalis, & re- ferri ad v. 3. Εἰσερχόμεθα ingredimur in requiem illam, illam, quia superest adhuc aliqua requies. Hoc jam probandum sumit primo removendo requiem Domini die septimo creationis, deinde requiem in terra Canaan. Unde relinquitur, tertiam re- quiem adhuc restare in altera vita: Alioquin ea adhortatio adducto exemplo Patrum in deser- to munita frustranea foret. Recte itaque haec observavit Theophylactus: Haec, inquit, minus consentanea sibi videtur esse oratio, cum tamen secus se habeat, sed ita inquit: Neque enim dicere poterit quispiam de Sabbati requie David disse- ruisse. Nam qui fieri potest, quando olim jam illud effectum sit, ut a principio mundus sit consti- tutus? Quin potius perspicuum est, de alia qua- dam David quiete dixisse, de caelesti videlicet illo ingressu, qui tamen in futurum sit debitus, tan- quam imposterum essent nonnulli caeli hanc requiem adituri.

## 4:5
Verse 5.

Καὶ ἐν τούτῳ πάλιν) That is, in this place, which I had already mentioned, he again makes mention of rest, and indeed his own, therefore differing from that first one.

Εἰ εἰσελεύσονται εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσίν μυ) He repeats the words placed above in verse 3, to show that it does not concern that rest immediately after creation.

The sense is: And in the place mentioned a little before (adduced from Psalm 95, verse 11) the Holy Spirit speaks again of his rest, they shall not enter into my rest, signifying, namely, by this threat, that a certain rest still remains to be hoped for by those who are not unbelieving, nor subject to the aforementioned threat.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Καὶ ἐν τούτῳ πάλιν) Id est, in isto, quem jam praedixe- ram loco, iterum quietis & quidem suae mentionem facit, differentis ergo ab illa prima.

Εἰ εἰσελεύσονται εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσίν μυ) Repetit verba supra posita vers. 3. ut ostendat de illa illico post creatio- nem quiete non agi.

Sensus est: Et in dicto paulo ante (ex Psalm. XCV. vers. 11. adducto) loco iterum loquitur Spi- ritus Sanctus de requie sua, non ingredientur in requiem meam, significans scil. hac commina- tione, quandam adhuc quietem restare sperandam iis, qui non sunt increduli, nec comminationi praedictae obnoxii.

## 4:6
Verse 6.

Ἐπεὶ οὖν ἀπολείπεταί τινας εἰσελθεῖν εἰς αὐτὴν) Since, therefore, there is another rest into which men are to be introduced by GOD. Ἀπολείπεται means it remains, or it is to be in the future, as below 9. X. 26. αὐτὴ here signifies the whole genus.

It remains, by consequence, namely deduced from the sense of David's words. For the Apostle continues in his demonstration.

Καὶ οἱ πρότερον εὐαγγελισθέντες) those who had gone out from Egypt, and to whom rest had been promised, but under a condition, above 2.

Οὐκ εἰσῆλθον δι᾿ ἀπείθειαν) Because of disobedience they fell from the promise.

Πάλιν τινὰ ὁρίζει ἡμέραν σήμερον) He says that the times of the Messiah are designated in the Psalm, mystically of course, concerning which mystical sense there was agreement among the Jews. Ὁρίζει means he designates.

There is no trace here of a mystical sense, nor would it be suitable for the Apostle's demonstration among the Hebrews, unless it were assumed by begging the question that that mystical sense underlies the words of the sacred psalmist. But let someone raise a doubt here: how does the Apostle press so strongly, and inculcate again and again the words of David, as if they promised a future rest to the Israelites of his own time and to the faithful who would follow: when David speaks only in the praised Psalm of the rest which he had promised to the Fathers, and from which those who perished in the desert were excluded? Answer: Some of David's words are read explicitly and are expressed κατὰ τὸ γράμμα (according to the letter), others are held there only interpretatively and κατὰ πράγμα (according to the matter). Although, therefore, those things concerning the rest, from which the Fathers were excluded in the desert, were only expressed: Yet since David exhorted the Israelites by their argument, and men in general, as today, when the voice of the Son of God is still heard, not to harden their hearts, lest they too be excluded from the rest of GOD, which is the force of the hortatory argument, although those things are not repeated ἀπὸ κοινοῦ in the Psalm, therefore the Apostle could most rightly use the argument of this exhortation, even if not expressed in so many words by David, yet by understanding it from the mind of the Holy Spirit, which the Apostle declares. If you ask why the Apostle urges this reason for exhortation, which is as it were far-fetched, when there were no lack of other far more expeditious ones? Reply: that this was done for weighty reasons: 1. That Psalm XCV may be rightly understood, namely that it treats of the Son of GOD, that He Himself is the Lord God our salvation v. 1, whose face is to be anticipated in confession, v. 2, the great GOD, the Lord and great King above all gods v. 3, in whose hand are all the ends of the earth, v. 4, who is the Creator of all things v. 5, who made us, and is the Lord our God, whose people we are, and the sheep of his pasture. Which predicates, most of which have already been demonstrated concerning Christ by Paul, are confirmed anew by this allegation of the Psalm, even if as if doing something else. 2. Because this Psalm, and this Apostolic passage likewise, treat of the faith and confession of this our Lord, and of hearing and receiving the voice of our Shepherd. This allegation therefore fits most excellently. 3. Because a comparison was instituted with Moses, whom the Israelites were bound to hear, and regard was had to our Teacher, a Prophet far more excellent than Moses, to whom Moses himself referred his own, Deuteronomy XVIII, to be received by true faith under penalty of exclusion from salvation. To which this oracle of the Holy Spirit concerning the hearing of the Lord's voice, and the same not to be abandoned, but to be kept through faith, unless we wish to be excluded from eternal rest, is most appropriate. 4. Because that rest of the other life promised by so great a Teacher seemed to the Apostle to need illustration, both as to how it corresponds to the rest of GOD Himself, because we are to be participants in the divine rest, and shall be blessed with rest from all the works of this world, and thus from all labors and afflictions; and how much more excellent that rest of the other life is than the rest obtained in the land of Canaan after the labors of battles and pilgrimage. 5. Because the Holy Apostle delighted in comparisons from the Old Testament in this epistle, it pleased him also to introduce this one concerning the Sabbath of creation, compared with the Sabbath of glorification, concerning the rest reconciled by Joshua and the rest by our JESUS.

But that other day designated by David is either the whole span of this life, until it is named 'today' chap. III, v. 13. Because the whole time of life is a day of labor, after which follows a day of rest; or the time of the duration of this age, until its end. The former, which pleased the Blessed Gerhard, seems to us also more convenient with respect to those to whom the exhortation is directed.

Ἐν Δαβὶδ) By David. The Jews cite the Psalms, which do not have another name inscribed, under the name of David: Aben-Ezra in the preface to the Psalms. And in the Greek, that Psalm has inscribed: Αἶνος ᾠδῆς τῷ Δαυΐδ.

Others explain it as 'in David', that is, in a Psalm of David. But the Grotian explanation fits the usual Hebraism better, and is more accepted.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Ἐπεὶ οὖν ἀπολείπεταί τινας εἰσελθεῖν εἰς αὐτὴν) Quan- doquidem igitur alia est quies, in quam homines à DEO sunt introducendi. Ἀπολείπεται restat, sive futurum est, ut infra 9. X. 26. רחךְ αὐτὴ hic totum genus significat.

Restat, per consequentiam, scilicet è verbo- rum Davidis sensu deductam. Pergit enim in demonstratione sua Apostolus.

Καὶ οἱ πρότερον εὐαγγελισθέντες) illi qui ex Aegypto ex- ierant, quibusque promissa fuerat requies, sed sub condi- tione, supra 2.

Οὐκ εἰσῆλθον δι᾿ ἀπείθειαν) Propter inobedientiam ex- cidere promisso.

Πάλιν τινὰ ὁρίζει ἡμέραν σήμερον) Designari ait in Psal- mo, mystice scilicet, tempora Messiae, de quo mystico sensu constabat inter Judaeos. Ὁρίζει designat.

Nullum hic vestigium sensus mystici, neque is conveniret demonstrationi Apostolicae penes Hebraeos, nisi supposito per petitionem principii, quod subsit mysticus ille sensus verbis Hiero- psaltis. Sed dubium hic moveat quis, quomo- do tam fortiter premat, atque iterum, iterum- que inculcet Apostolus verba Davidis, quasi Israelitis sui temporis, & sequuturis fidelibus promittant requiem futuram: quum David tan- tum loquatur in laudato Psalmo de requie, quam Patribus promiserat, & à qua exclusi illi fuere, qui in deserto occubuere? Resp. Verba Davi- dis alia explicite leguntur & expressa sunt κατὰ τὸ γράμμα, alia tantum interpretative ibi habentur & κατὰ πράγμα. Etsi ergo illa de quiete, à qua Patres in deserto exclusi sunt, tantum ex- pressa sint: Tamen quum argumento eorum Da- vid dehortatus Israelitas sit, & quovis omnino homines, ut hodie, quando adhuc vox Filii Dei auditur, non obdurent corda sua, ne & ipsi exclu- dantur à requie DEI, quae vis est argumenti de- hortatorii, licet ἀπὸ κοινοῦ illa in Psalmo non re- petantur, idcirco Apostolus rectissime uti potuit hujus paraeneseos argumento, etsi totidem ver- bis non expresso à Davide, ex mente tamen Spi- ritus Sancti, quam declarat Apostolus, subin- telligendo. Si quæras, cur istam quasi longe pe- titam rationem dehortationis urgeat Apostolus, cum non defuerint aliæ longe expeditiores? Resp. factum id esse gravibus de causis 1. ut Psalmus XCV. recte intelligatur, quod nempe de Filio DEI agat, quod ipse sit Dominus Deus salutare nostrum v. 1. cujus facies præoccupanda in con- fessione, verf. 2. DEUS magnus Dominus & Rex magnus super omnes Deos verf. 3. in cujus manu sunt omnes fines terræ, v. 4. qui est Creator omnium verf. 5. qui fecit nos, & Dominus Deus noster est, cujus pascua populus nos, & oves gregis ejus. Quæ prædicata pleraque de Christo jam demonstrata à Paulo hac allegatione Psalmi de- nuo, etsi quasi aliud agendo, confirmantur. 2. Quia de fide ac confessione Domini hujus nostri, deque audienda & suscipienda voce Pastoris no- stri hoc Psalmo pariter, & hoc loco Apostoli- co agitur. Congruit ergo quam optime hæc al- legatio. 3. Quia instituta fuit comparatio cum Mose, quem audire tenebantur Israelitæ, & respectus habitus ad Doctorem nostrum, Pro- pheta Mose longe excellentiorem, ad quem Mo- ses ipse rejecit suos, Deuteronom. XIIX. sub pœ- na exclusionis à salute vera fide suscipiendum. Cui apprime convenit hoc oraculum Spiritus sancti de vocis Domini auditu, eademque non relinquenda, sed per fidem servanda, nisi ab æ- terna requie excludi velimus. 4. Quia requies illa alterius vitæ à tanto Doctore promissa illu- stranda videbatur Apostolo, tum quomodo re- quiei ipsiusmet DEI respondeat, quia nos di- vinæ requiei futuri sumus participes, & quiete ab omnibus operibus mundi hujus, adeoque o- mnibus laboribus & afflictionibus beabimur; tum quantopere illa quies alterius vitæ præstan- tior sit quiete in terra Canaan post præliorum & peregrinationis labores obtenta. 5. Quia comparationibus è Veteri Testamento gaudebat in hac epistola Sanctus Apostolus, placuit etiam hancce de Sabbato creationis, collato cum sab- bato glorificationis, de quiete à Josua & requie à JESU nostro reconciliata introducere.

Illa autem alia dies designata à Davide est, vel totum hujus vitæ spatium, donec hodie no- minatur cap. III. verf. 13. Quia totum vitæ tem- pus est dies laboris, post quod sequitur dies quietis; vel tempus durationis hujus seculi, us- que ad finem ejusdem. Prius quod Beato Ger- hardo placuit, nobis etiam videtur conveni- entius respectu eorum, ad quos exhortatio di- rigitur.

Ἐν Δαβὶδ) Per Davidem. Judæi Psalmos, qui nomen aliud adscriptum non habent, citant sub Davidis nomine: Aben-Esdra in præfatione ad Psalmos. Et in Græco Psal- mus iste inscriptum habet: Αἶνος ᾠδῆς τῷ Δαυΐδ.

Alii exponunt in Davide, hoc est, in Psalmo Davidis. Sed Grotiana explicatio magis conve- nit usitato Ebraïsmo, & receptior est.

## 4:7
Λέγων μετὰ τοσοῦτον χρόνον, καθὼς εἴρηται) Five hundred years or more after that history which is in Numbers, καθὼς εἴρηται, as we have already touched upon above III. 7. In the Manuscript more clearly, καθὼς προείρηται.

Latin:

Λέγων μετὰ τοσοῦτον χρόνον, καθὼς εἴρηται) Annis quin- gentis aut amplius post illam historiam, quæ est in Numeris, καθὼς εἴρηται, ut jam attigimus supra III. 7. In Manuscri- pto clarius, καθὼς προείρηται.

## 4:8
Verse 8.

Εἰ γὰρ αὐτοὺς Ἰησοῦς κατέπαυσεν) That is, if that had been the full and perfect rest which had come to them through Jesus or Joshua the son of Nun. Joshua and Jesus is the same name. See what was said at Matt. I. 21 and Acts VII. 45.

Theophylact rightly expressed the force of the argument and the sense of the Apostle with these very words: Since therefore David says, again after so many years courses, do not harden your hearts, just as your Fathers did, who because of their unbelief by no means entered into rest, and let it be understood from this by us, that the matter proceeds to the contrary, namely, if we are believing, it will come to pass that we shall enter into it. It is established, therefore, that this rest is to be, and that we are awaited, so that we may approach it. For David was not speaking of such a rest as that of Palestine (since the Jews were in possession of it at that time), nor of the seventh day, as it had been from the very foundation of the world. There is, therefore, a certain third rest, namely the kingdom of the heavens, to which Jesus the Lord also leads us on account of the belief and faith which is held in Him. Blessed Gerhard says more briefly: If Joshua had led them into the true rest, which is in heaven, when he introduced them into the land of Canaan, the Holy Spirit would not have spoken through David after this about another day. However, he wishes the objection concerning those at least introduced by Joshua, namely those under 20 years of age, to be answered in this way, as if he were saying: If Joshua, by the introduction of the Israelite people into the promised land, had provided them with true rest, so that no other rest was to be expected after it, the Holy Spirit would not have promised yet another rest through David after that time.

Οὐκ ἂν περὶ ἄλλης ἐλάλει μετὰ ταῦτα ἡμέρας. Namely, in a more sublime sense. Something greater was lying hidden, he says. This day is time. But we have already said that it was agreed among the Jews that this passage concerns the times of the Messiah.

Nothing here about a more sublime sense. On the contrary, that inference, which is tacitly held in the cited Psalm, introduces the literal sense, demonstrating by the Apostle that a rest will still remain.

Latin:

Verf. 8.

Εἰ γὰρ αὐτοὺς Ἰησοῦς κατέπαυσεν) Id est, si illa plena & perfecta fuisset quies, quæ iis per Jesum sive Josuam filium Nuni evenerat. Josue & Jesus idem est nomen. Vide quæ dicta ad Matth. I. 21. & Act. VII. 45.

Vim argumenti & sensum Apostoli recte his quidem verbis expressit Theophylactus: Quum igitur David inquiat, rursum post tanta annorum curricula, nolite obdurare corda vestra, sicut & Patres vestri, qui ob eorum diffidentiam nequaquam sunt quietem ingressi, deturque ex his nobis intelligi, rem contra procedere, videlicet si creduli fuerimus, futurum esse, ut illam ingrediamur. Constat ergo, requiem istam futuram esse, & nos operiri, ut se ad- eamus. Neque enim David de Palaestina hujusmo- di dictitabat, (quippe qua tunc potirentur Judaei) neque de septimo die, utpote qua ab ipsa mundi fun- datione fuisset. Est igitur requies tertia quaedam, caelorum scilicet regnum, ad quod & Jesus Dominus ob credulitatem & fidem, quae in se habetur, indu- cit. Brevius B. Gerhardus: Si Josua ad requiem veram, quae est in caelo, eos perduxisset, quando scilicet eos in terram Canaan introduxit, non loque- retur Spiritus Sanctus per Davidem post hac de alia die. Responderi autem ita vult objectioni de quibusdam saltem introductis per Josuam, vide- licet minoribus 20. annis, quasi dicat: Si Josua per introductionem populi Israelitici in terram pro- missam veram requiem ipsi praestitisset, ut non fuis- set alia post eam requies expectanda, Spiritus S. per Davidem post illud tempus aliam adhuc requiem non promisiffet.

Οὐκ ἂν περὶ ἄλλης ἐλάλει μετὰ ταῦτα ἡμέρας. Nempe in sensu sublimiore. Majus aliquid latebat, in- quit. Dies hic est tempus. Jam autem diximus, convenisse inter Judaeos agi hic de Messiae temporibus.

Nihil hic de sensu sublimiore. Imo illatio illa, quae tacite in Psalmo laudato habetur, sensu litem- li infert, adhuc reliquam fore requiem, demon- strante Apostolo.

## 4:9
Vers. 9.

Ἄρα ἀπολείπεται Σαββατισμὸς τῷ λαῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ) some greater rest indicated by the sabbath, which signifies rest. From the word σαββάτε comes σαββατίζειν, to celebrate the sabbath, which Justin and others use. Hence σαββατισμὸς is the rest of GOD, as Philo explains concerning Cain: The activity most free from toil, without suffering, with much ease, and he adds, it is most proper to God alone to rest. The day of resurrection will lead us to the participation of this rest. Meanwhile, even in this life there is some taste of it, both in the peace of conscience and in the freedom from Jewish rites: and after this life, before the resurrection, in that state of souls which is described in Revelation XIV, verse 13.

The conclusion is now inferred, that a rest still remains for believers, and that it is not bodily, but spiritual, not temporary, but eternal. For by σαββατισμὸν a heavenly and eternal rest is understood. For, as Theophylact teaches, he did not say rest, but sabbath-keeping, with the proper name explained, and indeed by that name which most delighted them, and they were drawn by the sweetness of that same name. And the heavenly kingdom is no different. For just as the Law itself commanded that one must cease on the sabbath from every carnal and gross work, and that the Priests should perform only those things which seemed to pertain both to the worship of GOD and to the benefit of the soul, so also in the time to come all things will be spiritual and divine, and there will be nothing that is carnal or laborious, where every pain has departed, and sorrow and sighing have gone away. By the word σαββατισμοῦ, says Blessed Dorscheus, the Apostle wished to indicate by analogy what kind of rest awaits the people of God, namely a sabbatic one, that is, a rest similar to the divine rest, and of which the sabbath holidays, the sabbatic year, and the jubilee, and other such institutions were a certain perpetual foreshadowing, by which the life of the Jewish people was distinguished, and he himself, freed from cares and labors, rested in that very rest, that is, the land of Canaan. But the Apostle also altogether wished to hint at the comparison of the typical rest of the land of Canaan, of which Joshua XXIII, verse 1 ff. and XI, verse 23, with that true and eternal one, to which God leads us through the true Joshua, and in which we already have one foot, which we embrace by true faith. Therefore, in this place, it is not a sabbath-keeping of creation, of which Gen. II, verse 2, or ceremonial, or civil (from wars), but spiritual, and that begun in the kingdom of grace, when we, having been made alive together with Christ and raised up together, and placed together with Him in the heavenly places, Eph. II. 5, 6, walk in newness of life, Rom. VI, verse 4, ceasing from the servile works of sin, verse 28, then consummated in the kingdom of glory, in which one lives a sabbath after a sabbath, Is. LXVI, verse 23, and Apoc. XXI, verse 23, and following. But to whom is that rest left? To the people of GOD, that is, to the faithful, who are children of GOD, John I, verse 12, a peculiar people, Tit. II, verse 14, a people for a possession, 1 Pet. II, verse 9, the sanctified Church, Eph. II, verse 26, and following, Acts XX, verse 28, 1 Cor. VI, verse 20, VII, verse 23, as being in the divine order appointed, Acts XIII, 48. and not by internal disposition, but by the removal of the resistance of those fit for the kingdom of God, Luke IX, verse 62. What kind of leaving is it? The Apostle says it remains, not by an absolute decree, by which this beatific sabbath-keeping is preordained for only a few: But 1. by a universal purpose, by which God proposed the mystery of His will, that is, to propose the heavenly sabbath-keeping in such a way that He might gather together all things under one head, Eph. I, verses 9 and 10. Compare 1 Tim. II, 4, 2 Pet. III, 9. 2. By a universal evangelism, by which all are invited to the sabbath of grace and glory, Matt. XI, 28, 29. 3. By a gracious application, which happens to those not rejecting the divine order, John III, 16 and 36.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Ἄρα ἀπολείπεται Σαββατισμὸς τῷ λαῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ) aliqua major quies indicata per sabbatum, quod quietem signifi- cat. A voce σαββάτε est σαββατίζειν, celebrare sabbatum, qua utitur Justinus & alii. Inde σαββατισμὸς DEI quies est, ut Philo explicat de Caino: Ἡ ἄνευ κακοπαθείας μετὰ πολλῆς εὐμαρείας ἀπονώτατος ἐνέργεια, & addit, οἰκειότατον μόνῳ Θεῷ τὸ ἀναπαύεσθαι. Ad hujus quietis participationem perducet nos resurrectionis dies. Interim & in hac vita est ejus gustus aliquis, tum in pace conscientiae, tum in li- bertate a ritibus Judaicis: & post hanc vitam ante resurre- ctionem in statu illo animarum, qui describitur Apocal. XIV. vers. 13.

Infertur nunc conclusio, requiem adhuc su- pereffe credentibus, eamque non corporalem, sed spiritualem, non temporariam, sed aeternam. Per σαββατισμὸν enim caelestis & aeterna requies intelligitur. Non enim, Theophylacto docente, quietem dixit, sed sabbatismum, nomine proprio explicato, & eo quidem, quo maxime hos oble- ctabat, & illecti nominis ejusdem suavitate con- currebant. Nec secus & caeleste regnum se habet. Nam quemadmodum sabbato ab omni opere car- nali & crasso cessandum lex ipsa jubebat, & ea dun- taxat ut peragerent Sacerdotes, quae cum ad DEI cultum, tum ad animae utilitatem facere videren- tur, sic & imposterum illud tempus cuncta spiri- tualia futura sunt, & divina, nihilque, quod car- neum sit aut laboriosum, ubi & dolor omnis exces- sit, & maeror & gemitus abiit.
