Voce σαββατισμοῦ, inquit Beatus Dorscheus, indicare Apostolus voluit per analogiam, qualis requies populum Dei maneat, nempe sabbatica, hoc est, requies, divinae requiei si- milis, & cujus perpetua quaedam adumbratio fue- runt sabbati feriae, anni sabbatici & jubilaei, alia- que talia instituta, quibus vita populi Judaici distinguebatur, & ipse curis atque laboribus solutus in ipsa requie, hoc est, terra Canaan requiescebat. Omnino vero etiam Apostolus innuere voluit colla- tionem typicae quietis terrae Canaan, de qua Josua XXIII. vers. 1. sqq. & XI. vers. 23. cum vera illa & aeterna, ad quam nos Deus per verum Josuam de- ducit, atque adeo in qua jam alterum pedem babe- mus, quam vera fide complectimur. Non est ita- que boc loco sabbatismus vel creationis, de qua Gen. II. vers. 2. vel ceremonialis, vel civilis, (a bellis) sed spiritualis, isque inchoatus in regno gratiæ, quando nos Christo convivificati & conresuscitati, & una cum ipso in cœlestibus collocati sumus, Eph. II. 5. 6. ἐν καινότητι ζωῆς ambulamus, Rom. VI. vers. 4. ces- santes a servilibus peccati operibus, vers. 28. tum consummatus in regno gloriæ, in quo vivitur sab- batum post sabbatum, Es. LXVI. vers. 23. & Apoc. XXI. vers. 23. & seqq. Cui autem requies illa re- linquitur? Τῷ λαῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ, boc est, fidelibus, qui sunt filii DEI, Joh. I. vers. 12. λαὸς περιούσιος, Tit. II. vers. 14. λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν, 1. Petr. II. vers. 9. Ecclesia sanctificata, Eph. II. vers. 26. & sqq. Actor. XX. vers. 28. 1. Cor. VI. vers. 20. VII. vers. 23. ut- pote in ordine divino τεταγμένῳ, Act. XIII. 48. & non dispositione interna, sed remotione repugnantiæ εὐθέτων εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ, Luc. IX. vers. 62. Qualis est relictio? Apostolus inquit ἀπολείπεται, non per absolutum decretum, quo paucis dunta- xat sabbatismus iste beatificus sit præordinatus: Sed 1. per universalem πρόθεσιν, qua proposuit Deus mysterium voluntatis suæ, hoc est, cœlestem sabba- tismum ita proponere, ut omnes ad unum caput re- colligcret, Eph. I. vers. 9. & 10. Conf. 1. Tim. II. 4. 2. Petr. III. 9. 2. Per universalem Evangelismum, quo ad sabbatum gratiæ & gloriæ omnes invitantur, Matth. XI. 28. 29. 3. Per gratiosam applicationem, quæ contingit ordinem divinum non respuentibus, Joh. III. 16. & 36.

## 4:10
Vers. 10.

Ὁ γὰρ εἰσελθὼν εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσιν αὐτοῦ καὶ αὐτὸς κατέπαυσεν ἀπὸ τῶν ἔργων αὑτοῦ, ὥσπερ ἀπὸ τῶν ἰδίων ὁ Θεός) For he who has entered into His rest, he himself also has rested from his works, just as God did from His own.

Philo in the Allegories: 'He rested on the seventh day from all his works which he made,' this is what this means. For God, when fashioning all mortal things, when he begins to make divine things and those akin to the nature of the heptad: But the application to character is as follows: When the holy word, which is after the heptad, comes upon the soul, the hexad is checked, and it seems to finish all the mortal things it is doing. And afterwards: 'The cause by which the rational and holy [man] has become one who leads himself according to the seventh and perfect light, since in this nature the constitution of mortal things ceases.' For it is so, when the light of virtue rises, the bright and truly divine [light], the genesis of the opposite nature is checked. The same [author] on the sacrifices of Cain and Abel: 'For a feast of the soul is the perfect joy in virtues.' And in the book, That God is immutable: 'For he who is appointed to God alone, Samuel, and understanding nothing at all according to the one, has been adorned with the monad, that which truly is.' And this state is the heptad, a rest in God for the soul, and [the soul] no longer busying itself with any of the mortal works, according to the enjoyment of the hexad. Clement, Stromata VI: 'The seventh day, therefore, is proclaimed as rest, an abstinence from evils, preparing the primordial day, our true rest, and the first true genesis of light, in which all things are contemplated together, and all things are inherited. From this day, the fourth, wisdom and knowledge shine upon us.' The book which is called Theologumena Arithmeticae, where it treats of the Heptad: 'One must consecrate the enjoyment of the so-called blessedness.' But this writer uses the aorist tense, not only because that future is most certain, but also because in this very life, as we have already said, a certain taste of that rest is given.

For the explanation of the sabbath-rest, he compares it with the divine sabbath from the work of creation. For as God rested from his works; so also the elect obtain rest from all works and afflictions, Apoc. XIV, verse 13, as if he were saying, according to Theophylact: 'In this life, indeed, there is a most bitter struggle for the righteous, and an immense labor proposed, because one must toil most of all for virtue: But in the heavens they will not be exercised for any immortality, but will enjoy only a certain insatiable sweetness of soul in GOD.' Blessed Dorscheus makes the Apostle's argument here such: What rest is in the divine rest, by which God himself rested from the works of creation, [is] a certain type and foundation of hope which it has, that is the true and consummate rest of the people of GOD. But not a rest of just any tranquility, such as is even the rest of a peaceful habitation in the promised land, which is civil and political, nor the rest of sabbaths, both weekly and others as well, but another which has its type and foundation especially in the rest of creation, etc. Therefore, neither this nor that is the rest ultimately destined for the people of GOD, but another is to be expected. The Apostle proves the minor premise, because although the entry into the holy land was some entry into rest, it was not, however, an entry into a God-like rest. For this is a rest from works. But even for those who had entered into the holy land, there was still always labor to be done, always fighting to be done, always struggling with difficulties, and thus it was a rest mixed with restlessness. Thus, even if the sabbath rest has some principle from the rest of creation, it does not, however, have perfect conformity with the divine rest. For it is indeed a κατάπαυσις ἀπὸ τῶν ἔργων [cessation from works], but not continuous, nor total, but interrupted from time to time by entire six-day periods of labor. But the perfect conformity with the divine rest is that by which one ceases totally and finally from laborious and troublesome works, and in order to be able to arrive at that, one enters into the divine tranquility and serenity itself, that is, one is joined to GOD, and enjoys GOD, and is always with GOD. And this tranquility is not only prefigured and shadowed forth by the sabbath rest, whence it is called the sabbath of sabbaths, of which above; but it is also promised by the divine rest itself after creation, Gen. II. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Ὁ γὰρ εἰσελθὼν εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσιν αὐτοῦ καὶ αὐτὸς κατέ- παυσεν ἀπὸ τῶν ἔργων αὑτοῦ, ὥσπερ ἀπὸ τῶν ἰδίων ὁ Θεός)

Philo allegoriis: Κατέπαυσεν ἐν τῇ ἑβδόμῃ ἡμέρᾳ ἀπὸ τῶν ἔργων αὑτοῦ, ὧν ἐποίησε, τοῦτο δ' ἐσὶ τοῦτο. Τὰ θνητὰ γοῦν πάν- τα πλάττων ὁ Θεὸς, ὅταν ἄρχῃ ποιῶν τὰ θεῖα καὶ ἑβδομάδος φύσει οἰκεῖα· Ἡ δὲ πρὸς τὸ ἦθος ἀπόδοσις τοιαύτη: Ὅταν ἐπι- γίνηται τῇ ψυχῇ, ὁ μετὰ ἑβδομάδα ἅγιος λόγος, ἐπιχείλη ἑξὰς, καὶ ὅσα θνητὰ τελεῖ ποιεῖν δοκεῖ. Et postea: Αἰτία δὲ ᾗι λόγι- μός τε καὶ ἅγιος γέγονεν ὁ κατὰ τὸ ἕβδομον καὶ τέλειον φῶς ἄγων αὐτὸς, ἐπεὶ ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ φύσει παύεται ἡ τῶν θνητῶν σύστα- σις. Καὶ γὰρ ὅτως ἔχει, ὅταν ἀνατείλῃ φέγγος τῆς ἀρετῆς, τὸ λαμπρὸν καὶ θεῖον ὄντως ἐπέχηται δ' ἐναντίας φύσεως ἡ γένεσις. Idem de sacrificiis Caini & Abelis: Ἑορτὴ γὰρ ψυχῆς ἡ ἐν ἀρεταῖς εὐφροσύνη τελεία. Et libro, Deum esse immutabi- lem: Ὁ γὰρ τεταγμένος Θεῷ μόνῳ Σαμουὴλ, ἄξω δὲ τὸ πα- ράπαν συνιὼν μηδενὶ κατὰ τὸ ἓν τὴν μονάδα τὸ ὄντως ὂν κεκόσμη- ται. Αὕτη δὲ ἡ κατάστασις ἐσιν ἑβδομὰς, ἀνάπαυσις ἐν Θεῷ ψυχῆς, καὶ περὶ μηδὲν τῶν θνητῶν ἔργων ἔτι ποιουμένης, κατὰ ἀπόλαυσιν ἑξάδος. Clemens Strom. VI. Ἡ' ἑβδόμη τοί- νυν ἡμέρα ἀνάπαυσις κηρύσσεται, ἀποχὴ κακῶν ἑτοιμάζουσα τὴν ἀρχέγονον ἡμέραν, τὴν τῷ ὄντι ἀνάπαυσιν ἡμῶν, τὴν δὲ καὶ πρώτην τῷ ὄντι φωτὸς γένεσιν, ἐν ᾧ τὰ πάντα συνθεωρεῖται, καὶ πάντα κληρονομεῖται. Ἐκ ταύτης δ' ἡμέρας ἡ τετάρτη σοφία καὶ γνῶσις ἡμῖν ἐπιλάμπεται. Liber qui dicitur Θεολογούμενα τῆς ἀριθμητικῆς, ubi de Heptade agit: Καθοσιωτέον δὲ τ' λεγο- μένης εὐδαιμονίας ἀπόλαυσις. Utitur autem hic scriptor ver- bo ἀορίστῳ, non tantum quia futurum illud certissimum est, verum etiam, quia in hac ipsa vita, ut jam diximus, quidam ejus quietis gustus datur.

Ob explicationem sabbatismi componit eun- dem cum divino sabbato ab opere creationis. Ut enim Deus requievit ab operibus suis; Ita etiam quietem consequuntur electi ab omnibus operi- bus & afflictionibus, Apoc. XIV. vers. 13. quasi dicat juxta Theophylactum: Hac quidem in vita acerrimum est justis certamen, & labor immensus propositus, quia virtuti maxime est insudandum: In cœlis vero neque ad immortalitatem aliquam exercebuntur, sed DEO duntaxat inexplebili qua- dam animi fruentur suavitate. Beatus Dorscheus argumentum Apostoli hic tale facit: Quæ quies in quiete divina, qua ipse Deus quievit ab operibus creationis, typum quemdam & fundamentum spei habet, illa est vera & consummata populi DEI quies. | Atqui non quies qualiscunque tranquillitatis, qualis est vel quies pacatæ habitationis in terra promissa, quæ civilis est & politica, neque quies sabbatorum tum hebdomadariorum, tum aliorum etiam, sed alia potissimum typum & fundamentum in quiete creationis habet, &c. Ergo neque ista, neque illa sunt quies ultimò populo DEI destinata, sed alia expectanda. Minorem probat Apostolus, quia quamvis ingressus in terram sanctam fuerit aliquis ingressus in requiem, non tamen fuit ingressus in re- quiem Deiformem. Hæc enim est requies ab operi- bus. At etiam ingressis in terram sanctam semper tamen laborandum, semper militandum, semper cum difficultatibus luctandum fuerat, adeoque fuit quies inquietudinibus permixta. Sic etiamsi quies sab- batica aliquod ex quiete creationis principium ha- beat, non tamen & ista perfectam conformitatem cum divina quiete habet. Est enim quidem κατά- παυσις ἀπὸ τῶν ἔργων, sed non continua, neque totalis, sed interrupta subinde integris laborandi sextiduis. Perfecta vero conformitas cum divina quiete ista est, quâ quis ab operibus laboriosis mo- lestisque totaliter & finaliter cessat, & ut eo perve- nire possit, ingreditur in ipsam divinam tranquilli- tatem & serenitatem, hoc est, DEO jungitur, Deo- que fruitur, & apud DEUM semper est. Et hanc tranquillitatem non tantum sabbatica quies præfi- gurat & adumbrat, unde sabbatum sabbatorum vo- catur, de quo supra; sed ipsa etiam quies divina post creationem pollicetur, Gen. II. 3.

## 4:11
Vers. 11.

Σπυδάσωμεν οὖν εἰσελθεῖν εἰς ἐκείνην τὴν κατάπαυσιν) Let us devote effort, that we may arrive at that highest tranquility of the future age. Leaving other things aside, let us do this.

Ἲνα μὴ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ τις ὑποδείγματι πέσῃ τ ἀπειθείας) I say this, he says, so that none of you may fall into such disobedience as the example they gave. For that is called an ὑπόδειγμα [example] which shows the way to others, as can be seen in Sirach XLIV. 15, 2 Maccabees VI. 8, 31, John XIII. 15, below VIII. v. 5, IX. v. 23, James V. 10, 2 Peter II. 6. It is therefore an ὑπαλλαγή [hypallage], ὑποδείγματι τ ἀπειθείας for τῇ ἀπειθείᾳ τῇ ἐν ὑποδείγματι. It is a saying of the Hebrews סימן לבנים יאכור.

The blessed Gerhard has correctly conveyed the sense: Let us therefore strive to obey the voice of CHRIST, which is proposed to us in the Gospel, for thus it will come to pass that we enter into that heavenly and eternal rest: Lest if anyone imitates the disobedience of those unbelievers, he falls or perishes, as they did, or lest anyone follows the example of the unbelief of the Israelites, who fell in the desert: or lest anyone falls, namely into eternal destruction, according to the example of Israelite unbelief. He opposes the fall to the straight course, by which he had said one must strive toward that rest. At the same time, he also looks to the punishment of the unbelievers, whose bodies lay prostrate here and there in the desert. Cf. Numbers XIV, Deuteronomy II. The same thing, that is, the example of the Israelites, says Theophylactus; for just as when they had already completed the greater part of the journey, and had suffered very many evils, they nevertheless fell because of unbelief and distrust: So also you must take care, lest after so many struggles which you have already undergone, you collapse, being those who have not shown yourselves strenuous to the very end. For that is a true fall.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Σπυδάσωμεν οὖν εἰσελθεῖν εἰς ἐκείνην τὴν κατάπαυσιν) De- mus operam, ut ad summam illam futuri seculi tranquilli- tatem perveniamus. Rebus aliis omissis hoc agamus.

Ἲνα μὴ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ τις ὑποδείγματι πέσῃ τ ἀπειθείας) Hoc ideo, inquit, dico, ne quis vestrum incidat in inobe- dientiam talem, qualis illi exemplum dedere. Nam ὑπό- δειγμα dicitur illud, quod viam aliis monstrat, ut videre est Sirac. XLIV. 15. 2. Maccab. VI. 8. 31. Joh. XIII. 15. in- fra VIII. v. 5. IX. v. 23. Jacob. V. 10. 2. Petr. II. 6. Est ergo ὑπαλλαγὴ, ὑποδείγματι τ ἀπειθείας pro τῇ ἀπειθείᾳ τῇ ἐν ὑποδείγματι. Dictum est Ebræorum סימן לבנים יאכור.

Sensum recte tradidit Beatus Gerhardus: Stu- deamus igitur obedire voci CHRISTI, quæ in Evangelio nobis proponitur, sic enim fiet, ut ingre- diamur in illam requiem cœlestem & æternam: Ne si quis imitetur incredulorum istorum inobedien- tiam, cadat seu pereat, ut illi, vel ne quis sequatur exemplum incredulitatis Israëlitarum, qui cecide- runt in deserto: vel ne quis cadat, scilicet in æter- num exitium, juxta exemplum incredulitatis Israë- liticæ. Casum opponit recto cursui, quo ad requiem illam dixerat esse contendendum. Simul etiam re- spicit ad pœnam incredulorum, quorum corpora hinc inde prostrata jacùerunt in deserto. Conf. Numer. XIV. Deut. II. Idipsum, id est, Israëlitarum exem- plum, inquit Theophylactus; quemadmodum enim cum majorem itineris partem jam confecissent, & mala plurima essent perpessi, ob incredulitatem ta- men & diffidentiam conciderunt: Sic & vobis ca- vendum, ne post tam multa, quæ jam subiistis, certamina collabamini, utpote qui non ad finem usque strenuos vos præstiteritis. Id enim verus est lapsus.

## 4:12
Vers. 12.

Ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος τῦ Θεῦ κὶ ἐνεργής) That is, acting perpetually, as those things which live. This fits every Word of GOD, but especially the Evangelical. See Psalm CV. 19, CVII. 20, CXLVII. v. 15, 16, Isaiah XL. v. 8, LV. 11, 1 Peter I. v. 23, 24. It is possible that it refers to the fire which was on the altar of victims.

Because he dealt with the word of promise, which, tempered by faith, profits us so that we may enter into eternal rest, he now explains its divine efficacy, so that he may make faith more certain by this argument, and therefore he now presents the Word of GOD, which he warned must be embraced by faith, as a living and efficacious medium, just as, conversely, when it is neglected, it possesses the power of judging the unbelievers. Some understand by λόγον θε̃ [the word of God] the Son of GOD, the hypostatic Word, Aquinas, Lyranus, Cajetanus, both glosses, Stapletonus, Ribera, Menochius, Cornelius à Lapide, Tirinus, Justinianus, as also from the Reformed Gomarus in Anal. p. 622. Oper., Junius in Parall. Tom. I. Oper. c. 1169, Heinsius in Exerc., Jacob. Capell. in Observat. in N. T., Rathmannus in script. Beständige Lehre der Väter, p. 106. Likewise from the Fathers, Cyprianus lib. II. contr. Jud. cap. III. & V. Ambrosius libr. I. de Cain & Abel cap. VIII., libr. IV. de fide cap. III., Hieronymus in Es. LXVI., Cyrillus libr. II. in Joh. c. 37., Augustinus tract. CVIII. in Johan., Theodoretus & Oecumenius, as also Anselmus, in h. l. But others more correctly explain it as the spoken word, and especially the Evangelical, with Cyprianus also not denying this here in de Christi Bapt., as Athanasius orat. III. contra Arian., Augustinus epist. LIIX. & libr. XX. de Civit. DEI cap. 21., Philo Carpathius in Cantic. III. vers. 8., Fulgentius epist. II. ad Gall. de stat. viduit., Andreas Cæsariensis, Aretas, Primasius in cap. I. Apoc., Chrysostomus, Drogo Hostiensis de sacram. Dominicæ passionis serm. I. & Theophylactus in hunc loc., also Ambrosius libr. III. de Virginibus, and also from the Pontificals Bellarminus libr. IV. de Eccles. cap. 12., Stapletonus libr. XI. de Princip. cap. II., Hesselius, Adamus Sasbouth, & Estius in hunc locum. To these agree many of our own, as also Calvin, and others in his school, Beza, Piscator, Pareus, Aretius on this passage. Tossanus in Præl. ad Ebr. Camer. resp. ad quæstion. ad Ebr. page 447. Chamier in Panstrat. Vol. I. book VI. ch. 5. page 77. and Grotius adds his vote. The arguments for this opinion are these: 1. Because ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ according to the most common meaning in the scriptures denotes divine doctrine, nor is it taken otherwise anywhere in this epistle. 2. Because the Apostle has just dealt with the Son of GOD as Teacher, Prophet & Apostle, but not as the Word of GOD, which name properly pertains to his person and eternal generation. 3. He taught that the word of promise, as the voice of the Son of GOD, ought to be received by faith, and promised eternal rest to those who receive it. Therefore he renders the cause, whence this power of faith is placed in the Word of promise; Namely, from the very life and efficacy of the divine Word. 4. It is not the Son of GOD himself, but his Word, which he seemed to carry in his mouth, and which proceeds from his mouth, Apoc. I. verse 16. ch. II. verse 6. ch. XIX. v. 15. that is compared to a two-edged and double-sharpened sword, which is also called the sword of the spirit, Eph. VI. verse 17. Conf. Is. XI. verse 4. ch. XLIX. v. 2. 5. Since the spoken Word of GOD was dealt with in the preceding, not only in ch. II. verse 2. but also in ch. IV. verse 2. & following, therefore these things are to be understood rather of it, since otherwise the mention of the Son of God would be introduced abruptly, which Estius notes here. For he deals with the faith to be had in the Word of promise, and teaches that if we embrace the promises of GOD by faith, we shall enter into his rest: But if not, we shall perish miserably, and that by the example of those to whom the Word of God was once made. He deals with the promise v. 1. with those who have been evangelized, both the Hebrew Christians and the ancient Israelites, with the word of hearing, which ought to be mixed with faith in those who heard it, v. 1. 2. he names v. 6.

those who were previously evangelized, and v. 7. the voice which must be heard, and he warns in the same verse lest any of the converted Hebrews fall into the example of the disobedience of the Israelites. All of which things clearly teach that it is a discourse concerning the spoken word, which must be received by faith, not rejected through unbelief. Add verse 6, which does not so much fit a person, so that it is said to be effective and sharper than any two-edged sword, etc. Here also, says Chrysostom, he shows that the word of GOD itself also did that, and it lives, and is not extinguished. Therefore, do not, because you have heard the word, hear it only. For it is, he says, more penetrable than a sword. See how he humbles himself, and from this consider for what reason it was necessary even for the Prophets to speak of both a sword, and a bow, and a rhomphaea. And afterwards: For the word rushes into their souls more heavily than any sword, inflicting grave wounds, and making certain cuts. Likewise: So here also the sword of the Spirit acts. Then he speaks of the Son. For Chrysostom explains the rest of verse 13 concerning the Son; but these things [he explains] concerning the efficacy of the Word or divine discourse. 7. Let the argument of Theophylact be added from the continuity of the immediately preceding verses. For as then they (the Israelites) perished not by war or sword, but by the Word of GOD: So it will be done with you. For this Word of GOD, as it affected them with punishment, so it will also torment you. For it both lives perpetually, and is never extinguished. Or in another sense, he said it is living, lest perhaps when they had already heard the Word, they might think it inconstant and vain; he called it living, that is, subsisting and effective, so that into whatever soul it rushes, it inflicts a grave wound upon it. 8. Beat. Balduinus proposes the coherence thus: The reasons for the Apostle's exhortation, that they should strive to enter into the rest of eternal life through a true and living faith in Christ, he adds 1. from the inconvenience, lest by our negligence we become an example of unbelief, like those who were killed because of infidelity in the desert, in the same verse. 2. from the efficacy of the Word, which they ought to obey, v. 12. For he names that Word living and effective, in both parts, indeed, whether it is received or rejected. For in those who receive it, it works virtue unto salvation, in the others greater condemnation: It has that virtue in itself, this [it has] by accident, because men place an obstacle to the working Holy Spirit. Similar things are held by Beat. Hunnius, the Weimar Paraphrasts, and others. Beat. Dorscheus: The connection, he says, with the preceding is effective, if we interpret the word of God as the doctrine of Christ. For the Apostle does not look only to v. 11, but to the entire preceding context, when he conceives verse 12 concerning illustrating the word of God: although it also responds most aptly to verse 11. For thus he reasons most powerfully: To which rest the living and effective Word of GOD invites us, and [which is] sharper than any two-edged sword, etc., to that we must strive with all zeal not to neglect but to enter. But the Word of God invites us to the rest of Christ, etc. Therefore, etc. But the rest of Christ is shown and lies open to us in the Gospel. The gloss of the Socinians Crellius and Schlichting, that the decrees of God are understood, by which he destines the incredulous and contumacious to destruction and punishments, hardly deserves refutation. The decrees of GOD are nowhere compared to a two-edged sword, nor do other predicates suit them, nor did such a sense easily come into the mind of anyone before these innovators. And the Apostle dealt here not only with the decrees of GOD, by which the incredulous and contumacious were destined to destruction and punishments, but also with the promises and invitations to embrace Christ. For that voice of Psalm XCV, verse 7, which the Apostle interpreted concerning Christ above in chapter III, verses 6, 7.

not only threatens exclusion, but also invites to entry into rest, as is apparent from Psalm XCV, verses 6 and 7. Moreover, outside the Gospel and the doctrine of Christ there is nowhere rest, or salvation, Acts IV, verse 12, and as many as have arrived at everlasting rest, have arrived through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, Acts XVIII, verse 11. For through Him was made the reconciliation and appeasement or tranquilization of all things, Col. I, verses 20, 21, as B. Dorscheus warned against this gloss.

But the Word of GOD is called living, because it is Spirit and life, John VI, verse 63, and therefore it is also called living by Peter, 1 Epist. I, verse 23, and the word of life, Phil. II, verse 16. Effective, because it is animated by the power of God for illumination, Psalm XIX, v. 11, regeneration, James I, verse 23, salvation, Rom. I, 16, James I, 21, Acts XI, 14. The Word of GOD is not a dead letter, nor idle or ineffective, but living, intrinsically animated by divine efficacy and virtue, which it also exerts in the hearts of men, concerning which we have dealt expressly against various heretics and fanatics in Tom. I, System. Theol. cap. IV, Quæst. XXXIV, page 692, seqq. That the fire which was on the altar of victims is referred to here, there is no evidence; nor does that fire have anything to do with the matter here, even if otherwise the Word of GOD is said to be like fire, Jerem. XXIII, 19.

And sharper) Philo says clearly the same thing concerning the heir of divine things. That you may understand the unteachable God cutting the natures of both incorporeal things and things following, all of which seem to be joined and united, by his own Word, the cutter of all things, which, having been sharpened to the sharpest edge, never ceases to divide all sensible things, until it passes through to the atoms and so-called indivisibles. In the poems which bear the name of Phocylides, we have something not dissimilar: A word is to a man a weapon sharper than iron. The prayers of Moses are equal to a sword cutting all things: in the book Ebæno concerning the death of Moses.

Ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν μάχαιραν δίστομον) The same comparison is found in Philo, whom this writer seems to have read, in his book on Cain: 'Do you not see that even Abraham the wise, when he began to measure all things according to God, and to leave nothing to the created, takes a likeness of the flaming sword, fire and a knife, desiring to divide and burn up the mortal from himself, so that with naked intellect he may fly aloft to God.' It is called μάχαιρα δίστομος or ῥομφαία δίστομος, Apoc. I, 16. II, 12, a sword cutting on both sides: in Hebrew חרב פיפיות as in Psalm CXLIX. 6, or פיות, as in Prov. V. verse 3, or שני סורת, as in Jud. III. verse 16. The Syriac here: וספסרא דתרין פומיה, such as the Levites used in dissecting victims, from which Philo also took that similitude. The Levites used to distinguish which parts in the victims belonged to God, and which to men. And both by fire and by that dissection, the wise even then mystically understood the power of GOD penetrating and judging all things, as some of the ancients have noted.

These things which are brought forward concerning the dissection of the Levites are irrelevant. The efficacy of the word is illustrated by the Apostle by the similitude of a sword of any kind, but a two-edged and most sharp one, on account of its power of cutting and penetrating hearts, not on account of the knowledge that it penetrates all things, as God penetrates all things with the eyes of His knowledge, which pleases Estius, because the power of penetration of a δίστομος or two-edged sword does not tend to that, but that by cutting it may penetrate, affect the hearts of men, strike, wound, and be able to penetrate more sharply than any most penetrating sword, as the added ἐπεξήγησις teaches, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit. 'Observe, however,' says Theophylact, 'how he mentions both a sword and a sharp one, and a penetrating one, so that from things already familiar and better known to us, he may set forth the greatness of divine power.' The origin of this designation, Blessed Dorscheus thinks it is from Psalm XLV. verse 5, where the Messiah is addressed to gird His sword upon His thigh. Whence also in Apoc. I, it appears, brandishing a two-edged sword from His mouth, verse 16, but also Isaiah, chapter XLIX. v. 2, Christ is introduced as saying that GOD has disposed His mouth like a sharp sword. As to the meaning; he says, the spiritual power of affecting and perfecting the mind of men, which belongs to the λόγῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ (Word of God), is described. For just as a two-edged sword penetrates the body, so does the ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ (Word of God) penetrate the soul itself; as a sharp sword separates the parts of the body, so the divine Word separates and divides the faculties and powers of the mind. For this is that μερισμὸς (division) of which the Apostle speaks. For just as a sword separates the soul from the body, draws out the vital spirits, and loosens the joints of the limbs: so the divine Word discusses and examines all the innermost parts. The word δίςομος is said not ἀπὸ τοῦ τέμνειν (from cutting), but ἀπὸ τοῦ ςόματος (from the mouth), as if having two mouths, just as it is customary to say in the Hebrew phrase, to strike with the edge of the sword, such as a two-edged and sharp sword on both sides is most apt for dividing and penetrating, as this very Estius has observed. Blessed [Gerhard]. Hunnius refers it to the Law and to the Gospel: For just as a sword sharp on both sides penetrates and dissects the object much more easily than if it were sharp on only one side, so the Word of GOD is the sword of the Holy Spirit, which Word, as it comprehends two parts, the Law and the Gospel, so it obtains incredible power from both its parts to wound the consciences of mortals by the preaching of the Law, and to refresh, heal, and vivify those same consciences by the voice of the Gospel. Moreover, the power of penetrating and dividing also belongs to the Word of the Gospel, insofar as it reaches all the senses of the mind and heart with its efficacy, so that our minds and hearts are struck and pierced by that divine power which it possesses, just as is said of the hearers of Peter's sermon, Acts II. 37: ἀκύσαντες δὲ κατενύγησαν τῇ καρδίᾳ (and hearing this, they were pricked in their heart).

Καὶ διϊκνέμενος ἄχρι μερισμοῦ ψυχῆς τε καὶ πνεύματος.

Now he explains more clearly where that comparison tends: Πνεῦμα (spirit) here is the appetite for heavenly things, soul [is the appetite] for earthly things. The Word of GOD does not allow these to be confused: it wants the whole man, Matt. VI. 24. Therefore, when applied to the mind, it immediately makes it appear toward which part it inclines. נפש וחר Prov. XX. 27. כל חדרי בטן

Ἁρμῶν τε καὶ μυελῶν.

By metaphor, he applies those things which are of the body to the mind. A sharp knife reaches to the smallest things, such as the nerves in the joints, and to the innermost things, such as the marrow. So also the Word of GOD penetrates both the innermost and the smallest parts of the mind, and acts upon them.

That explanation of some among Theophylact seems to tend that way, which he himself, however, rejects: Some have understood it thus, and in my judgment they feel things not sufficiently consistent with the mind of the Apostle. For they say that the Word of GOD or the Spirit, when it has invaded the soul itself, immediately divides and cuts through the parts of this soul, and for the rest renders it in this manner susceptible and capable of the mystery. And just as a weapon, having first cut through the flesh, is soon accustomed to be immersed in it and to reach to the innermost parts: so also the Word, unless it has separated the more fortified parts of the soul that are enclosed, brings no open entrance for itself into it. However, that [view] does not seem entirely to be despised. Certainly, that which pleased Theophylact appears more convenient: he declares here a truly horrible thing, that it excludes the Holy Spirit from the soul and dissects it, and leaves it completely destitute of the holiness flowing from that same Spirit, which the Lord in the Gospel calls double-minded. For just as some Emperor deposes one of his own, because he has committed some foul crime, and deprives him of his dignity and the office of magistrate, and soon also punishes him with death, and deprives him of life, so in this place, when some spirit has been deprived of dignity, it is then also afflicted with punishment. By πνεῦμα (spirit), however, is not understood here the appetite for heavenly things itself, but that which in man has been made by the renewal of him through the Holy Spirit, just as soul denotes not the appetite for earthly things itself, but, by a received sense, the intellectual soul and its faculties, such as they are by nature, which the Word of GOD itself penetrates, reaches, and divides, and our spirit and soul feel its divine power; nay, it penetrates the innermost and smallest parts of the mind, and acts upon them with an efficacy intrinsic to itself, which it has from the Holy Spirit, proper and perpetual. Whence some think that by the joints of the limbs are metaphorically signified thoughts, and by the marrow, intentions. According to Blessed Gerhard, the scope of the Apostle is, in general, to note any innermost things and those most deeply hidden in the heart of man, because the Word of GOD reaches to them, to the soul, even to the spirit, even to the joints, even to the marrow. For these are the innermost things in man. Similarly, Blessed Hunnius. It is an exposition of the simile, that the Word of GOD is such a sword that it does not strike only the body of man, like an external sword, but reaches even to the division of the soul and at the same time the spirit, and of the joints and marrow. He persists in the metaphor taken from an external sword, and figuratively indicates that there is nothing anywhere in man so abstruse, nothing so recondite, that that Word does not search out and examine by its power. For just as in the human body the innermost parts are the joints and the marrow of the bones: so the Apostle demonstrates that that sword of the Holy Spirit reaches to the joints and marrow, that is, to the innermost penetralia and recesses of human hearts, and ventilates the most abstruse thoughts and intentions of the heart. Thomas and Estius understand by soul the sensitive part of the soul, and by spirit the intellectual part. Therefore, others explain it concerning the searching of the innermost parts, just as GOD is said to search the hearts and reins; others concerning the action upon them, by which it prepares for itself an entrance to all things that are in man, so that it may effectively work in his faculties and innermost recesses. Both can, however, be joined; as regards the power, efficacy, operation, and end of that division even unto penetration, namely that through that division the Word itself may not know the inner parts of man, but that it may make them appear to man: as regards the illumination of the mind, that it may strike, affect, and move the heart of man; as regards his conversion, that it may circumcise our heart, Deut. XXX. verse 6, take away the heart of stone, and make a heart of flesh in us, Ezech. XXXVI. verse 26. Which sense I see also approved by the blessed Dorscheus: Schlichtingius, he says, understands by soul the lower faculty in us, which has desires and affections, or looks only to those things which please the body. By spirit [he understands] the higher power, which discerns the honest from the dishonest, and calls us away from the latter and impels us to the former, which sees better things and approves them, by which we understand, by which we acknowledge GOD and His will and supreme happiness. He adds that spirit can also be taken for that part of us which first vivifies the body, and which remains after death, soul for life or that faculty which flows from the spirit into the whole body. The Weigelians make soul and spirit two constitutive parts of man with the body: Whither? And they abuse the passage 1 Thess. V. verse 23. More correctly, by πνεῦμα are understood the gifts of regeneration communicated by the Holy Spirit Himself dwelling within, among which the divine Word makes a μερισμὸν (division) of the soul itself, not by separating, but by illuminating and of divine grace? Whence under this μερισμῷ (division) arises the struggle between the flesh and the spirit, of which Galat. V. verse 17 and Romans VII. v. 15 and following. And this also is to be understood by πνεῦμα in 1 Thess. V. verse 23: That spirit, namely, which we ought not to extinguish, verse 19, which is our κλῆρος or lot, of which we have been made partakers with the saints in light, Coloss. I. verse 22. Whence it is called the whole spirit (ὁλόκληρον Πνεῦμα). Rightly also the late lamented one here notes Schlichting: In that, however, he by no means exhausts the Apostolic sense, because he refers those words solely to the divine decree concerning the punishing and afflicting of the disobedient. For the virtue of the divine Word unfolds itself not only in punishing, but also in comforting the inner recesses of the soul. For when the arrows of divine wrath are fixed in sinners, when there is no integrity in their flesh, nor peace in their bones, when iniquities pass over their head, when their wounds putrefy and waste away, when they themselves are twisted and bowed down greatly, when their loins are full of vileness; Psalm XXXVIII. verses 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; when like a certain dagger the enemies of the faithful invade them, Psalm XLII. verse 11; when spirit and soul struggle, when the joints and marrow of the miserable man are so struck that his heart withers like grass, and his bone cleaves to his flesh, Psalm CII. verses 5, 6. There the divine Word penetrates all things, insinuates itself into the spirit and soul, probes the joints and marrow, so that it may tranquilize all things, and may restrain that very spiritual enemy everywhere infesting the inner parts of man with divine consolation, so that thus, as far as the Word of the law penetrates, crushing and terrifying, so far also the comfort-flowing Gospel may pervade.

And a judge of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

He attributes to the discourse that which properly belongs to GOD, because GOD judges according to the outcome which the discourse has had, not only concerning the actions, but also concerning the thoughts and counsels of men. See Psalm CXXXIX. 23.

The Word of GOD is said to judge the thoughts and counsels of the heart, insofar as it is manifested through the Word what is to be thought of them, because it is the norm and rule not only of our actions, but also of the thoughts and counsels of the heart, and thus it can also be called a canonical or normal judge, or to judge canonically, because it is the voice of the supreme Judge, God, and the norm of the inferior Judge, the Minister of God. Concerning which the blessed Dorspheus: That which is said 'a judge of thoughts,' etc., can be referred to the fact that by the manifested preaching of Christ the thoughts of many hearts were manifested, Luke II. verse 35. Hence 1 Corinth. XIV. verses 24 and 25 it is said that when the prophecy of Christ sounds, and some unbeliever or unlearned person enters, it happens that he is convinced and judged, etc. And afterwards; 'A judge of the thoughts and intents of the heart,' for the voice of the divine Word is canonical or a canon, and therefore also critical. Hence John III. verse 18, he who does not believe is said to be judged, namely by the Scripture, in which the divine judgment is already set forth and effectively denounced as much to those who believe as to those who reject, cf. Matthew XVI. verse 16, John XII. verse 48. It makes straight for the knowledge of oneself and of the crooked, says Aristotle.

book I of the soul, last chapter, for the Canon is the judge of both; but Scripture is the Canon and is itself divine rectitude, Psalm XIX. verses 5 and 9, Gal. VI. verse 16, Phil. III. verse 16, therefore it is also a judge, cf. 1 Cor. XIV. verses 24 and 25. Cf. Part II. Theol. Zachar. diss. I. at the end. And this indeed pertains to the act, for which it is necessary that Scripture be full and contain all things to be believed; that Scripture be plain to such an extent that it can clearly insinuate all things to be believed; that Scripture be integral, and truncated in no part necessary for belief; that Scripture be pure, not flowing turbid or corrupted, especially in the sources; that Scripture be open to all whose thoughts and desires desire a Judge; that Scripture be able to be spread into the languages of the nations, by which the divine judgment is to be expounded. For if these things are lacking to the Word of God, it cannot be a judge. Cf. 2 Timothy III. verse 15 and following. 1 Peter IV. verse 11, 2 Peter I. verse 19. But the object of the critical word are the thoughts and concepts of the heart, not exclusively. For both the tongue and whatever else there are, by which the senses of men are comprehended, are subject to this judge, Roman. X. verses 9 and 10, and indeed especially insofar as those senses of man are to be informed for salvation. For to this these words most especially look. For thus the Apostle argues: The critical word of the thoughts and concepts of the heart is to be heard and attended to most earnestly by all and each desiring that eternal sabbath. But the Word of GOD and of CHRIST is such a critical word. Therefore. Where it is supposed in the major premise that that beatific judgment, and the one informing for the eternal sabbath, is obtainable from that word sufficiently and fully in the manner of a rule and norm, and as from a principle of knowledge. For unless this were so, the Apostolic exhortation to hear that word would not be sufficiently effective.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος τῦ Θεῦ κὶ ἐνεργής) Id est, agens perpe- tuo, ut ea, quæ vivunt. Convenit hoc omni Verbo DEI, sed præcipue Evangelico. Vide Psalm. CV. 19. CVII. 20. CXLVII. v. 15. 16. Es. XL. v. 8. LV. 11. 1. Petr. I. v. 23. 24. Fieri potest, ut respiciatur ignis, qui erat in altari vi- ctimarum.

Quia de verbo promissionis egit, quod fide con- temperatum nobis prosit, ut ingrediamur ad re- quiem æternam, nunc efficaciam ejus divinam explicat, ut hujus argumento fidem certiorem faciat, ideoque Verbum DEI, quod fide ample- ctendum monuit, jam ceu medium vivum, & effi- cax sistit, quemadmodum id ex adverso, cum negligitur, judicandi incredulos facultate pollet. Nonnulli per λόγον θε̃ Filium DEI, Verbum hypostaticum intelligunt, Aquinas, Lyranus, Ca- jetanus, utraque glossa, Stapletonus, Ribera, Me- nochius, Cornelius à Lapide, Tirinus, Justinianus, ut & è Reformatis Gomarus in Anal. pag. 622. Oper. Junius in Parall. Tom. I. Oper. c. 1169. Heinsius in Exerc. Jacob. Capell. in Observat. in N, T. Rathmannus in script. Beständige Lehre der Väter, p. 106. Item è Patribus, Cyprianus lib. II. contr. Jud. cap. III. & V. Ambrosius libr. I. de Cain & Abel cap. VIII. libr. IV. de fide cap. III. Hieronymus in Es. LXVI. Cyrillus libr. II. in Joh. c. 37. Augustinus tract. CVIII. in Johan. Theodo- retus & Oecumenius, ut & Anshelmus, in h. l. Rectius autem alii explicant de verbo προφορικῷ, & imprimis Evangelico, etiam hic non abnuente Cypriano de Christi Bapt. utpote Athanasius orat. III. contra Arian. Augustinus epist. LIIX. & libr. XX. de Civit. DEI cap. 21. Philo Carpathius in Cantic. III. vers. 8. Fulgentius epist. II. ad Gall. de stat. viduit. Andreas Cæsariensis, Aretas, Pri- masius in cap. I. Apoc. Chrysostomus, Drogo Ho- stiensis de sacram. Dominicæ passionis serm. I. & Theophylactus in hunc loc. etiam Ambrosius libr. III. de Virginibus, nec non è Pontificiis Bellarmi- nus libr. IV. de Eccles. cap. 12. Stapletonus libr. XI. de Princip. cap. II. Hesselius, Adamus Sasbouth, & Estius in hunc locum. Quibus accedunt plerique nostrates, ut & Calvinus, & alii in schola ejus, Beza, Piscator, Pareus, Aretius in hunc loc. Tossanus in Præl. ad Ebr. Camer. resp. ad quæstion. ad Ebr. pag. 447. Chamier in Panstrat. Tom. I. lib. VI. c. 5. pag. 77. calculumque addit Grotius. Argumenta hujus sententiæ hæc sunt: 1. Quia ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ secundum usitatissimam significationem in sacris notat doctrinam divinam, nec uspiam aliter in hac epistola accipitur. 2. Quia de Filio DEI ut Doctore, Propheta & Apostolo proximè egit Apostolus, non verò ut Verbo DEI, quod nomen proprie ad ejus personam, & generationem æter- nam pertinet. 3. Verbum promissionis, ut vocem Filii DEI, fide suscipi debere docuit, & susci- pientibus requiem æternam pollicitus est. Cau- sam ergo reddit, unde hæc vis fidei sit in Verbum promissionis locatæ ; Nimirum ab ipsa Verbi di- vini vita, & efficacia. 4. Gladio ancipiti & bis acuto non ipse Filius DEI, sed Verbum ejus, quod ore suo gerere visus est, quodque ex ore ejus pro- dit, Apoc. I. vers. 16. cap. II. vers. 6. cap. XIX. v. 15. comparatur, quod & gladius spiritus dicitur, Eph. VI. vers. 17. Conf. Es. XI. vers. 4. cap. XLIX. v. 2. 5. De Verbo DEI προφορικῷ in præcedentibus actum, non modo cap. II. vers. 2. sed & cap. IV. vers. 2. & seqq. ideo de eo potius hæc etiam acci- pienda, quum ex abrupto ingereretur alias Filii Dei mentio, quod hic monet Estius. Agit enim de fide habenda Verbo promissionis, docetque, si DEI promissiones fide amplectamur, in requiem ejus ingressuros: Sin minus, male perituros, idque eorum exemplo, ad quos olim Verbum Dei fa- ctum est. Agit de ἐπαγγελίᾳ v. 1. de εὐαγγελισμέ- νοις tùm Ebræis Christianis, tum veteribus Israëli- tis, de λόγῳ τ’ ἀκοῆς, quem συγκεκραμένον τῇ πίστει τοῖς ἀκούσασιν esse oporteat, v. 1. 2. nominat v. 6.

τὺς πρότερον ἐυαγγελισθέντας, & v. 7. τὴν φωνὴν quæ audienda, & monet v. u. ne quis ex Ebræis con- versis cadat ἐν τῷ ὑποδείγματι τῆς ἀπειθείας Israë- litarum. Quæ omnia luculenter docent, de verbo προφορικῷ, quod fide suscipiendum, non per in- credulitatem reprobandum, sermonem esse. Ad- de 6. quod non usque adeò personæ congruat, ut dicatur efficax penetrantior quovis gladio anci- piti, &c. Hic quoque ostendit, inquit Chrysosto- mus, quod illa quoque fecit ipse DEI sermo, & vivit, & non est extinctus. Ne ergo, quoniam audivistis sermonem, id solummodo audias. Est enim, inquit, penetrabilior gladio. Vide quomodo se demittat, & hinc considera, quanam de causa opus fuit etiam Pro- phetis, ut dicerent & gladium, & arcum, & rhom- phæam. Et postea: Quovis enim gladio gravius in eorum animas irruit sermo, graves plagas inferens, certasque dat sectiones. Item: Ita hic quoque facit gladius Spiritus. Deinde loquitur de Filio. Cæte- ra enim vers. 13. de Filio explicat Chrysostomus; sed hæc de efficacia Verbi vel sermonis divini. 7. Addatur Theophylacti argumentum ἐ συνεχείᾳ immediate præcedentium. Ut enim tunc illi (Israëlitæ) non bello aut gladio, sed DEI Verbo in- teriere: Sic & vobiscum agetur. Nam DEI hoc Verbum ut illos affecit supplicio, sic & vos cruciabit. Id namque & vivit perpetuo, & nunquam extin- guitur. Vel in alium sensum vivus est, dixit, ne forte scilicet cum Verbum jam audissent, inconstans esse & vanum existimarent, vivum hoc appellavit, id est, subsistens & efficax, ita ut in quamcunque ir- ruerit animam, grave illi vulnus infligat. 8. Beat. Balduinus sic proponit cohærentiam: Rationes exhortationis Apostoli, ut studeant per veram & vivam fidem in Christum ingredi in requiem vitæ æternæ, addit 1. ab incommodo, ne negligentia no- stra fiamus incredulitatis exemplum, sicut illi, qui occiderunt propter infidelitatem in deserto v. eod. 2. ab efficacia Verbi, cui obedire debent v. 12. Illud enim nominat Verbum vivum & efficax, in utramque ni- mirum partem sive accipiatur sive repudiatur. In iis enim, qui recipiunt, operatur virtutem ad salutem, in cæteris majorem damnationem: Illam virtutem in se habet, hanc per Accidens, obicem nimirum ponentibus hominibus operanti Spiritui Sancto. Si- milia habentur apud Beat. Hunnium, Paraphra- stas Vinarienses & alios. Beat. Dorscheus: Connexio, inquit, cum superioribus efficax est, si de doctrina Christi λόγον τῦ Θεῦ interpretemur. Non enim ad v. 11. duntaxat, sed ad universum contextum an- tecedentem Apostolus respicit, cum de λόγῳ τῦ Θεῦ illustrando versum 12. concipit: quanquam & ver- sui 11. aptissime respondet. Sic enim validissime ra- tiocinatur: Ad quam requiem nos invitat Verbum DEI vivum & efficax, & quovis ancipiti gladio pe- netrantius, &c. ad illam non negligendam sed in- grediendam omni studio contendere debemus. Atqui ad requiem Christi nos invitat Verbum Dei, &c. Ergo &c. Atqui requies Christi nobis in Evangelio ostenditur & patetit. Crellii & Schlichtingii So- cinianorum glossa, quod Dei decreta intelligan- tur, quibus incredulos & contumaces interitui & suppliciis destinat, refutationem vix meretur. De- creta DEI gladio ancipiti nuspiam conferuntur, nec alia prædicata illis conveniunt, neque facile ulli ante hos novatores talis sensus in mentem ve- nit. Et egit Apostolus hic non tantum de decretis DEI, quibus incredulos & contumaces interitui & suppliciis destinati sunt, sed etiam de promissio- nibus & invitationibus ad amplectendum Christum. Illa enim φωνὴ Psal. XCV. vers. 7. quam de Christo interpretatus est Apostolus supra cap. III. vers. 6. 7.

non tantum minatur exclusionem, sed etiam invitat ad ingressum in quietem, sicut ex Psal. XCV. vers. 6. & 7. istud apparet. Extra autem Evangelium & doctrinam Christi nuspiam quies est, aut salus, Act. IV. vers. 12. & quotquot ad quietem sempiternam pervenerunt, per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Chri- sti pervenerunt, Actor. XVIII. vers. 11. Per ipsum enim facta est ἀποκατάλλαξις & placatio seu tran- quillatio omnium, Col. I. vers. 20. 21. ut monuit contra hanc glossam B. Dorsheus.

Vivum autem dicitur DEI Verbum, quia Spi- ritus est & vita, Joh. VI. vers. 63. ideoque vivum à Petro etiam dictum 1. epist. I. vers. 23. & verbum vitæ, Phil. II. vers. 16. Efficax, quia potentia Dei animatum est ad illuminationem, Psal. XIX. v. 11. regenerationem, Jacob. I. vers. 23. salutem, Rom. I. 16. Jac. I. 21. Act. XI. 14. Verbum DEI non est litera mortua, nec otiosum aut inefficax, sed vi- vum efficacia & virtute divina intrinsece anima- tum, quam etiam in cordibus hominum exerit, quo de contra varios hæreticos & fanaticos egi- mus ex professo Tom. I. System. Theol. cap. IV. Quæst. XXXIV. pag. 692. seqq. Ignem hic respici, qui in altari victimarum erat, nullo indicio con- stat; nec ignis ille hic ad rem quicquam facit, etsi alias Verbum DEI instar ignis esse dicatur, Je- rem. XXIII, 19.

Καὶ τομώτερος) Plane idem dicit Philo de hærede rerum divinarum. Ἵνα τὸν ἀδίδακτον ἐννοῇς Θεὸν τέμνοντα τάς τε τῶν ἀσωμάτων καὶ τῶν πραγμάτων ἑξῆς ἁπάσας ἡρμόσθαι καὶ ἡνῶσθαι δοκούσας φύσεις τῷ τομεῖ τῶν συμπάντων ἀυτῶ λόγῳ, ὃς εἰς τὴν ὀξυτάτην ἀκονηθεὶς ἀκμὴν, διαιρῶν ὀυδέποτε λήγει τὰ αἰσθητὰ πάντα, ἐπειδὰν μέχρι τῶν ἀτόμων καὶ λεγομένων ἀμερῶν διε- ξέλθῃ. In Carminibus, qui Phocylidis nomen præferunt, habemus aliquid non dissimile: Ὅπλον τοι λόγος ἀνδρὶ τομώτερόν ἐστι σιδήρου. Mosis preces gladio omnia secanti pares: in libro Ebæno de morte Mosis.

Ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν μάχαιραν δίστομον) Eadem comparatio apud Philonem, quem legisse videtur hic scriptor, libro de Caino Οὐχ ὁρᾷς, ὅτι κἂν Ἀβραὰμ ὁ σοφὸς ἡνίκα ἤρξατο κατὰ Θεὸν με- τρεῖν παντα, καὶ μηδὲν ἀπολείπειν τῷ γεννητῷ, λαμβάνει τῆς φλογίνης ῥομφαίας μίμημα πῦρ καὶ μάχαιραν διελεῖν καὶ κατα- φλέξαι τὸ θνητὸν ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῦ γλιχόμενος, ἵνα γυμνῇ τῇ δια- νοίᾳ μετάρσιος πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν ἀναπτῇ. Dicitur μάχαιρα δί- στομος aut ῥομφαια δίστομος, Apoc. I, 16. II. 12. gladius se- cans in utramque partem: Ebræis חרב פיפיות ut Psal. CXLIX. 6. aut פיות, ut Prov. V. vers. 3. aut שני סורת, ut Jud. III. vers. 16. Syrus hic : וספסרא דתרין פומיה, quali usi Levitæ in victimis dissecandis, unde & similitudi- nem illam sumpsit Philo. Levitæ discernebant, quæ in vi- ctimis partes essent Dei, quæ hominum. Et tum per ignem, tum per illam dissectionem mystice jam tum sapientes intel- ligebant vim DEI omnia penetrantem ac dijudicantem, ut quidam ex veteribus notavere.

Aliena hæc sunt, quæ de dissectione Levitarum afferuntur. Efficacia verbi similitudine gladii cu- juvis, sed ancipitis, & maximè acuti ab Aposto- lo illustratur, ob vim cædendi & penetrandi corda, non ob notitiam, quod omnia penetret, ut Deus oculis suæ cognitionis penetrat omnia, quod Estio placet, quia eò non facit vis penetrandi gladii δι- στόμε, vel ancipitis, sed quod incidendo pene- tret, corda hominum afficiat, percutiat, vulne- ret, & quovis penetrantissimo gladio acrius penetrare valeat, ut addita ἐπεξήγησις docet, per- tingens usque ad divisionem animæ & spiritus. Ad- vertite autem, inquit Theophylactus, quemadmo- dum & gladii meminit & acuti, & penetrantis, ut ex rebus nobis jam consuetis, & notioribus præferat divinæ potentiæ magnitudinem. Origo hujus de- nominationis Beat. Dorscheo videtur esse ex Psal. XLV. vers. 5. ubi Messias compellatur, ut accingat gladium suum super femur suum. Unde etiam A- poc. I. apparet, gladium ancipitem ore exerens, vers. 16. sed & Esaias, cap. XLIX. v. 2. Christum introducit pronunciantem, DEUM os suum ve- luti gladium acutum disposuisse. Quod ad sensum; Describitur, inquit, vis spiritualis afficiendi & perficiendi mentem hominum, quæ λόγῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ competat. Uti enim anceps gladius corpus pene- trat, sic ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ ipsam animam; ut gla- dius acutus separat partes corporis, sic Verbum divinum secernit segregatque facultates & vires animi. Hic enim est iste μερισμὸς, de quo A- postolus loquitur. Quemadmodum enim gladius animam à corpore separat, spiritus vitales ex hau- rit, compages membrorum solvit : Sic verbum divinum intima quæque discutit & excutit. Vox δίςομος non ἀπὸ τοῦ τέμνειν secare, sed ἀπὸ τοῦ ςόματος dicitur, quasi habens duo ora, quem- admodum phrasi Ebræâ dici consuevit, per- cutere in ore gladii, qualis anceps, & utraque parte acutus gladius ad dividendum ac penetran- dum aptissimus est, ut hic ipse Estius observa- vit. Beat. Hunnius refert ad legem, & ad Ev- angelium: Etenim sicut gladius ex utraque parte acutus multo facilius penetrat ac dissecat rem ob- jectam, quàm si ex alterutra duntaxat parte acu- tus foret. Sic Verbum DEI gladius est Spiritus Sancti, quod Verbum ut partes duas, Legem & Evangelium, comprehendit, sic ex utraque sua parte incredibilem vim obtinet ad conscientias mortalium tum Legis prædicatione sauciandas, tum ad easdem conscientias Evangelii voce reficiendas, sanandas & vivificandas. Cæterum penetrandi, & dividendi vis etiam Verbo Evangelii conve- nit, quatenus omnes animi & cordis sensus ita efficacia sua pertingit, ut percutiantur & percel- lantur mentes atque corda nostra divina illa,quam habet, virtute, quemadmodum de concionis Pe- trinæ auditoribus dicitur, Act. II. 37. ἀκύσαντες δὲ κατενύγησαν τῇ καρδίᾳ.

Καὶ διϊκνέμενος ἄχρι μερισμοῦ ψυχῆς τε καὶ πνεύματος.

Jam clarius explicat, quo tendat ista comparatio: Πνεῦ- μα hic est appetitus rerum cœlestium, anima rerum terre- strium. Sermo DEI ista confundi non patitur: totum vult hominem, Matth. VI. 24. Itaque admotus animo statim facit appareat, in utram partem propendeat. נפש וחר Prov. XX. 27. כל חדרי בטן

Ἁρμῶν τε καὶ μυελῶν.

Per translationem ea, quæ sunt corporis, applicat ani- mo. Leviticus culter pervenit ad minima, quales sunt nervi in juncturis, & ad intima, quales sunt medullæ. Sic & sermo DEI & intima & minima animi penetrat, in- que ea agit.

Eo videtur illa nonnullorum apud Theophy- lactum explicatio propendere, quam vero ipse reprobat: Nonnulli ita intellexerunt, & meo ju- dicio haud satis consentanea sentiunt Apostoli ani- mo. Dicunt enim DEI sermonem vel Spiri- tum ubi animam ipsam invaserit, dividere statim & interscindere hujus animæ partes, & eam de cætero hunc in modum susceptibilem reddere & ca- pacem mysterii. Utque & telum carne prius discissa mox in eam immergi, & ad intima ten- dere consuevit: Sic & sermo nisi munitiores animæ partes inclusas sejunxerit, nullum afferunt sibi in eam patere ingressum. Non videtur autem ea omnino contemnenda. Convenientior certe apparet illà, quæ Theophylacto placuit: Rem sane horrendam hic prædicat, quod sanctum Spi- ritum discludat ab anima dissecetque, & eam re- linquat à sanctitate ex Spiritu eodem manante peni- tus destitutam, quam Dominus in Evangelio ancipitem nuncupat. Ut enim Imperator aliquis primatem ex suis quempiam, quia tetrum aliquod commiserit facinus, exautorat, & dignitate, & magistratus munere privat, mox etiam & capite plectat, vita privet, sic hoc loco cum spiritus fuerit aliquis dignitate privatus, deinde & pœna afficitur. Per πνεῦμα tamen non hic ipse cœle- stium rerum appetitus, sed id quod in homine ex renovatione ejus per Spiritum Sanctum facta est, intelligitur, uti anima non appetitum ipsum re- rum terrestrium, sed sensu recepto animam in- tellectualem, & facultates ejus, quales naturâ sunt, denotat, quas ipsas penetrat, pertingit, & dividit Verbum DEI, & vim ejus divinam sen- tiat spiritus noster atque anima, quin & intima & minima animi penetrat, inque ea agit effica- cia sibi intrinseca, quam habet à Spiritu Sancto propriam & perpetuam. Unde nonnulli per compages artuum Metaphorice significari putant cogitationes, per medullas intentiones. Secun- dum Beat. Gerhardum scopus Apostoli est, in genere quævis intima & in corde hominis pro- fundissime abscondita notare, quod ad ea per- tingat Verbum DEI, ad animam, etiam ad spi- ritum, etiam ad compages, etiam ad medullas. Hæc enim in homine intima sunt. Similiter Beat. Hunnius. Expositio est similitudinis, quod hujusmodi sit gladius Verbum DEI, ut non cor- pus hominis feriat tantum, sicut gladius externus, sed usque ad divisionem animi simul atque spiritus pertingat, compagumque & medullarum. Perse- verat in Metaphora sumpta ab externo gladio, & figurate indicat, nihil uspiam in homine tam esse abstrusum, nihil tam reconditum, quod sermo ille vi sua non rimetur atque discutiat. Ut enim in humano corpore intima partes sunt compages & medulla ossium: Sic demonstrat Apostolus, gla- dium illum Spiritus Sancti ad compages & medul- las, hoc est, ad intima cordium humanorum pe- netralia & recessus pertingere, & abstrusissimas ventilare cogitationes & intentiones cordis. Tho- mas & Estius per animam partem animæ sensiti- vam, per spiritum partem intellectualem intel- ligunt. Explicant ergo id alii de scrutatione in- timorum, quemadmodum DEUS corda & renes scrutari dicitur; alii de actione in ea, qua sibi ingressum paret ad omnia, quæ in homine sunt, ut efficaciter in ipsius facultatibus & inti- mis recessibus operetur. Conjungi autem u- trumque potest; quod ad penetrationis usque ad divisionem istam vim, efficaciam, operatio- nem & finem, nimirum ut per eam divisionem non Verbum ipsum intima hominis cognoscat, sed ut apparere ea faciat homini: quod ad men- tis illuminationem pertinet, usque cor hominis feriat, afficiat & commoveat; quod ad ejus conversionem, cor nostrum circumcidat, Deut. XXX. vers. 6. cor lapideum auferat, & cor car- neum efficiat in nobis, Ezech. XXXVI. vers. 26. Quem sensum video etiam probatum Beat. Dor- scheo: Schlichtingius, inquit, per animam in- telligit facultatem in nobis inferiorem, quæ cupi- ditates & affectus habet, seu ea tantum spectat, quæ corpori allubescunt. Per spiritum vim supe- riorem, quæ honesta ab inhonestis discernit, & ab his nos avocat, ad illa impellit, quæ videt melio- ra, probatque, qua intelligimus, qua DEUM ejusque voluntatem & supremam felicitatem agnoscimus. Addit, spiritum etiam sumi posse, pro ea nostri parte, quæ corpus primo vivificat, quæque post mortem remanet, animam pro vita seu ea facultate, quæ à spiritu in universum cor- pus manat. Weigeliani animam & spiritum duas hominis constitutivas partes cum corpore fa- ciunt: Quorsum & abutuntur loco 1. Theffal. V. vers. 23. Rectius per πνεῦμα intelliguntur dona regenerationis ab ipso Spiritu Sancto inhabitante communicata, inter quæ & ipsam animam μερι- σμὸν facit Verbum divinum non separando, sed il- luminando & intimando, quid homo ex propriis viribus sit, quid ex divina gratia? Unde sub isto μερισμῷ oritur pugna inter carnem & spiritum, de qua Galat. V. vers. 17. & Romanor. VII. v. 15. & seqq. Et hoc etiam per πνεῦμα 1. Thessal. V. vers. 23. intelligendum est: Ille nimirum spiritus, quem non debemus extinguere, vers. 19. qui est κλῆρος seu sors nostra, cujus particeps facti sumus cum sanctis in luce, Coloss. I. vers. 22. Unde vo- catur ὁλόκληρον Πνεῦμα. Recte etiam ὁ Μακαρί- της hic notat Schlichtingium: In eo autem sensum Apostolicum nequaquam exhaurit, quod ad decre- tum divinum de puniendis & affligendis inobedien- tibus verba ista duntaxat refert. Etenim non tan- tum in puniendis, sed etiam in consolandis interio- ribus animi recessibus virtus Verbi divini sese expli- cat. Nam cum sagitta iræ divinæ infiguntur peccatoribus, cum non est integritas in carne ipsorum, nec pax in ossibus eorum, cum iniqui- tates transcendunt caput, cum computrescunt & contabescunt sumices eorum, cum ipsi contor- quentur & incurvantur valde, cum ilia ipsorum plena sunt vilitate; Psalm. XXXVIII. vers. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. cum quasi sica quadam hostes fidelium ipso- rum invadunt, Psal. XLII. vers. 11. cum spiritus & anima colluctantur, cum compages & medulla miseri hominis adeo percelluntur, ut tanquam her- ba exarescat cor ejus, & os ejus carni adhærescat, Plal. CII. vers. 5. 6. Ibi verbum divinum penetrat omnia, insinuat se in spiritum & animam, com- pages atque medullas pertentat, ut omnia tranquil- let, & illum ipsum hostem spiritualem ubique in- teriora hominis infestantem solatio divino compe- scat, ut adeo quousque Verbum legis conterens & terrens penetrat, eo usque quoque Evangelium solatifluum pervadat.

Καὶ κριτικὸς ἐνθυμήσεων καὶ ἐννοιῶν καρδίας.

Tribuit sermoni id, quod proprie DEI est, quia DEUS secundum eventum, quem sermo habuit, judicat, non tantum de actionibus, sed & de cogitationibus ac consiliis hominum. Vide Psal. CXXXIX. 23.

Verbum DEI judicare dicitur cogitationes, & consilia cordis, quatenus per Verbum manife- statur, quid de illis habendum sit, quia norma est & regula non tantum actionum nostrarum, sed & cogitationem & consiliorum cordis, adeoque judex etiam κανονικὸς vel normalis dici potest, vel judicare κανονικῶς, quia vox est Judicis supremi, Dei, & norma Judicis inferioris, Ministri Dei. Quo de Beat. Dorspheus: Quod dicitur κριτικὸς ἐνθυμήσεων, &c. eo referri potest, quod manife- stata prædicatione Christi multorum cordium cogi- tationes manifestatæ sunt, Luc. II. vers. 35. Hinc 1. Corinth. XIV. vers. 24. & 25. dicitur sonante Christi prophetia, & ingrediente aliquo infideli aut idiota, fieri, ut ille convincatur & judicetur, &c. Et postmodum; Κριτικὸς ἐνθυμήσεων καὶ ἐν- νοιῶν καρδίας, Est enim Verbi divini vox κανονικὴ sive κανὼν, adeoque etiam κριτική. Hinc Joh. III. vers. 18. qui non credit judicatus esse dicitur, sci- licet per Scripturam, in qua jam judicium divinum expositum est & efficaciter denunciatum tam cre- dentibus, quam respuentibus, conf. Matth. XVI. vers. 16. Johan. XII. vers. 48. Rectum facit ad cognitionem suiipsius & obliqui, inquit Aristot.

libr. I. de anima cap. ult. κριτὴς γὰρ ἀμφοῖν ὁ Κανὼν, Scriptura autem Κανὼν est & ipsa divina rectitudo, Psal. XIX. vers. 5. & 9. Gal. VI. vers. 16. Phil. III. vers. 16. itaque & judex est, conf. 1. Cor. XIV. vers. 24. & 25. Conf. Part. II. Theol. Zachar. diss. I. in fin. Et hoc quidem ad actum pertinet, ad quem necessarium est, Scripturam esse plenam & omnia credenda continere; Scripturam esse planam in tantum, ut omnia credenda perspicue insinuare possit; Scripturam esse integram, & nulla parte ad credendum necessaria truncatam; Scripturam esse puram, non turbidam fluere aut corruptam, inprimis in fontibus; Scripturam omnibus patere, quorum cogitationes & cupiditates Judicem desiderant; Scripturam in linguas gentium diffundi posse, quibus judicium divinum exponendum est. Si enim desint ista τῷ λόγῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ, κριτικὸς esse nequit. Conf. 2. Timoth. III. vers. 15. & seqq. 1. Petr. IV. vers. 11. 2. Petr. I. vers. 19. Objectum vero λόγου κριτικοῦ sunt ἐνθυμήσεις καὶ ἔννοιαι cogitationes & conceptus cordis, non exclusive. Nam & lingua & quaecunque alia sunt, quibus sensus hominum comprehenduntur, huic κριτικῷ subjacent, Roman. X. vers. 9. & 10. & quidem imprimis quatenus isti sensus hominis ad salutem informandi sunt. Nam huc ista verba potissimum spectant. Sic enim argumentatur Apostolus: Λόγος κριτικὸς cogitationum & conceptuum cordis ad aeternum sabbatum consequendum omnibus & singulis illud desiderantibus impensissime audiendus est & attendendus. Atqui Verbum DEI & CHRISTI est istiusmodi λόγος κριτικὸς. Ergo. Ubi supponitur in Majore, κρίσιν illam beatificam, & ad sabbatum aeternum informatricem esse à λόγῳ isto sufficienter & plenarie in genere regula & normae, & tanquam à principio cognitionis impetrabilem. Nisi enim hoc esset, non satis efficax ad istum λόγον audiendum foret Apostolica cohortatio.

## 4:13
Verse 13.

Καὶ οὐκ ἔστι κτίσις ἀφανὴς ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ) It seems to me that in this passage κτίσις signifies the work of man, because that is as it were the creature of man. Thus κτισθῆναι is taken also in Sirach 23:29.

Πάντα δὲ γυμνὰ καὶ τετραχηλισμένα τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς αὐτοῦ) He continues with the comparison of victims, from which not only the wool, which is in the place of a garment, but also the skin is stripped off, so that the interior parts may appear. The Hebrews call that פנק. Moreover, it is a good Greek word τραχηλίζειν, which, according to Phavorinus, signifies to cut the skin of a victim from the neck into two parts and strip it off. And that same grammarian says that it came about from this that, by metaphor, those who are φανεροὶ καὶ ἀνακεκαλυμμένοι (manifest and uncovered) were called τετραχηλισμένοι. Nor did the experts in Greek purity, Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and Theophylact, take it otherwise here. In another sense, ἐξετραχηλίζετο in Josephus, Jewish War 4.21, and in Plutarch, means to seize as if by the twisted neck. And ἐξετραχηλίζετο meant 'was tortured' in Philo, Against Flaccus.

Πρὸς ὃν ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος.

That is, before that word of which we are now speaking, namely, the Evangelical word. Πρὸς is taken here as above in 1:7.

Aperta autem, inquit Chrysostomus, Græce dicitur τετραχηλισμένη, that is, laid open, from the metaphor of skins which are drawn off from victims. For just as when someone, after they have been slaughtered, pulls the skin away from the flesh, he opens everything that is inside and renders it manifest to our eyes: so also are all things set forth clear and manifest to GOD. Phavorinus notes that τράχηλον is the spine of the back, which proceeds from the crown of the head to the rump, whence τραχηλίζειν is to divide an animal through the middle of the spine so that all the intestines lie open. Which explanation of Gagnæus is preferred to others by Estius and Cornelius à Lapide. He admits that the Blessed Dorscheus alludes to the priests: For the priests used to slaughter, skin, split, and dismember the victims, so that they could inspect and discern everything, whether there was nothing in the host that could exclude it from the altar. Whence, through κακοζηλίαν [misplaced zeal], when the Gentile priests either did not know or feigned the true method of inspecting the entrails, they devised another form of divination, from which they would take omens about future events. Therefore, this τραχηλισμὸς [laying bare/exposing] is most correctly referred from the priests of the Old Testament to the supreme Priest of the New Testament. Which, of course, can not only with the sword of the Word, but also with omniscience, denude, dissect, and disembowel every creature to such an extent that it looks into the innermost parts and has nothing at all hidden. Although these things can in some way be referred to the Word of God, which are held in verse 13, and are referred to by some, most, however, more correctly refer them to God or Christ with the Greek pronoun αὐτοῦ: For eyes and omniscience are accustomed to be attributed to God, Prov. 15:3, ch. 16:2, not to the Word of God. Before God, no creature—which sounds not only of man's work, but universally of every created thing—is invisible and hidden; all things, even the most intimate, are naked and laid open before his eyes, not only the substance of each, but also the affections and qualities: since this is especially intended, that hypocrisy lurking deeply in the heart can in no way be hidden from God. Which Chrysostom applies to the scope of the Apostle thus: For he says, if you still stand in the faith, but do not trust with a certain and full persuasion, he himself will judge what is in the heart. For it pervades, both punishing and examining. Nor is the observation of the Blessed Dorscheus inconsistent, that all things are said to be naked and open to his eyes: to the eyes of Christ, that is, to Christ, considered not only according to his divinity, according to which he has no eyes properly so called, but also according to his human nature, according to which his eyes appeared in the Johannine vision ὡς φλὼξ πυρὸς [as a flame of fire], Apoc. 1:14. Which pertains to all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in Christ, that is, communicated to him according to his humanity, Col. 2:3. For it is pious to think that Christ, even with his human eyes, which are akin to ours and endowed with divine and infinite power, not only sees and comprehends the whole most holy Trinity and knows all things. Whence it is said, Φωτίσαι τὰ κρυπτὰ τοῦ σκότους, καὶ φανερῶσαι τὰς βουλὰς τῶν καρδιῶν [To bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and to make manifest the counsels of the hearts], 1 Cor. 4:5, through the judicial power which he received, John 5:27. But also to look upon his faithful ones militant in these lands from the priestly throne of grace, of which v. 16. Which is a huge and inestimable comfort to the faithful. Thus, indeed, the vision of the eyes of Christ is in some way distinguished from the divine vision, in that the former is θεανδρικὴ [theandric], and from the third kind of communication of idioms, thus far a κοινωνίαν ἐνεργειῶν [communion of operations] divine and human, since it is an act of the office of Christ. Chrysostom also proves this sense concerning God or Christ from those words πρὸς ὃν ἡμῖν λόγος [with whom we have to do], to whom, or if you prefer, of whom we have speech. Because he intended to speak of Christ and had spoken thus far, and was about to speak further. Which Theophylact rendered thus: To whom we have λόγος [account/speech], to him, he says, both the account of the deeds done by us must be rendered (because λόγος also signifies an account) and punishments given for what has been committed. Thus also the Syrian and Tossanus explain that an account is to be rendered to the Son of God. But that explanation seems simpler, by which πρὸς ὃν [with whom] is taken as in ch. 1:7, which is expressed thus in ch. 5:11, περὶ οὗ πολὺς ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος [of whom we have much to say]. Whence it is clear that Christ is referred to by the pronoun αὐτοῦ, who is also called God in verse 12, of whose voice or word, when it is heard, the Apostle warned that it should not be neglected. Who that is (so the Blessed Dorscheus) is evident partly from the preceding, partly from the following. He is, of course, Christ, the Son of God and Lord over the holy house of the Church, ch. 3:6. The Apostle and high Priest of our confession, v. 1, faithful to God who appointed him to this holy office, v. 2, not only equal to Moses, but even superior, v. 2, 3, and 5, the creator of all things, and thus also the founder of the Church, v. 4, tempted by the Fathers in the desert, v. 8, 9, 10, 11. and following, of whom we obtain participation through the Gospel, v. 14, whose voice we must hear, inviting us into eternal rest, the Apostle most gravely warned us, ch. 4 from v. 1 to 12, with whom we have business, as with a most severe judge and a most bitter avenger of his word, if we have despised it. The consequences demonstrate the same. The Apostle said that the πρὸς ὃν ὁ λόγος [with whom we have to do] has all things naked and open to his eyes. He infers from this in v. 14 that we have a great Priest, whence he shows that he himself, of whom the Apostle has discoursed thus far from ch. 3:7 and ch. 4:1 and following, is our high Priest. For how else could the Apostle infer: he, of whom we have speech, is the same who was tempted in the desert by the Fathers of the Israelites, from whom they fell away as from the living God, to whom he swore exclusion from eternal rest, who even now after that rebellion invites others to the participation of such blessedness, who, just as he himself rested from his works after the ἑξαήμερον [six days] of creation, so also is about to give his people rest from all the works and labors of this misery, who has a word living, effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword. Therefore we have a great Priest. How, I ask, does that follow, if he of whom the Apostle has spoken thus far is not the same as our high Priest, who is Christ. Therefore, regarding the particle καὶ [and], the Blessed Dorscheus rightly observed: That καὶ does not couple with the previous subject; but with emphasis points out to us that something else is to be understood. For it is evident from the examples of both the Old and New Testament that [the particle] often does not simply connect, but implies a certain emphasis, and is the same as 'And especially,' or 'but chiefly.' Compare John II. verse 1. 2 Sam. II. verse 30. Psalm XVIII. verse 1. Mark I. v. 15. & III. 7. & VIII. verse 16. Acts I. 14. chap. XXVI. v. 22. 1 Cor. IX. 1. etc. Therefore the sense of the Apostle in this place is: But especially the eyes of Him of whom we are speaking, who is the author of the living and efficacious word, who is the promiser of the beatific Sabbath—His eyes, I say, are open to all things, so that in these words there is both a reason why we can most safely believe Him promising us an eternal Sabbath, since He is omniscient and can therefore infallibly foresee whither He can lead His own, whom He invites and entices with such great promises: But also a reason is indicated why we ought to be far from all resistance, since it can by no means escape His omniscient and avenging eyes, even if it lies hidden in the innermost recesses of the soul. Indeed, a reason is also brought forward why the divine word is of such efficacy that it can probe and penetrate the innermost feelings of the soul, namely because it proceeds from the omniscient Majesty, who knows how to temper it so that it is suitable for investigating even the recesses of the mind. Others, with Piscator, refer that αὐτῆ in verse 13, ἐνώπιον αὐτῆ, to the word τῆ Θεῆ in verse 12, Ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος τῆ Θεῆ, and observe, with Chamier (Tom. I. l. VI. cap. V. n. XII.), that the words in verse 14, 'Having therefore a High Priest,' are not a collection deduced from the immediately preceding [matters], but a return to the discourse concerning the Supreme Pontiff, interrupted by a long digression, to which Mr. D. Johann Andr. Quenstädt assented in his Solemn Exercise on the efficacy of the Word of GOD. Yet the relation to Christ seems more suitable to the text, primarily because of the words πρὸς ὃν ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος, concerning whom also Psalm XCV was adduced, ch. IV, verse 3 et seqq., and the warning in ch. III, verse 14, that ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς ὑποστάσεως might be retained, so that we may be and remain μετοχοὶ τοῦ χριστοῦ, and to that end hear his voice, and not harden our heart against the same, which was done by the Israelites, who tempted Christ in the desert, and therefore perished, which the collation of the passage 1 Corinthians X, verse 9 teaches.

PART II. Admonition concerning a confident approach to the throne of grace.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Καὶ οὐκ ἔστι κτίσις ἀφανὴς ἐνώπιον αὐτοῦ) Videtur mihi hoc loco κτίσις significare opus hominis, quia id est velut creatura hominis. Ita κτισθῆναι sumitur & Sirac. XXIII. versu 29.

Πάντα δὲ γυμνὰ καὶ τετραχηλισμένα τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς αὐτοῦ) Pergit in comparatione victimarum, quibus non lana tantum, quæ vestis est loco, sed & pellis detrahitur, ut interiora appareant. Id Ebræi vocant פנק. Est autem vox bene Græca τραχηλίζειν, teste Phavorino significatque à collo pellem victimæ in duas partes dissecare & detrahere. Et ait is ipse Grammaticus, inde factum, ut per μεταφορὰν τετραχηλισμένοι dicerentur φανεροὶ καὶ ἀνακεκαλυμμένοι. Nec aliter hic sumpsere Græcæ puritatis periti Chrysostomus, Oecumenius, Theophylactus. Alio sensu ἐξετραχηλίζετο apud Josephum Belli Judaici IV. 21. & apud Plutarchum est, prehendere quasi obtorto collo. Et ἐξετραχηλίζετο cruciabatur apud Philonem contra Flaccum.

Πρὸς ὃν ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος.

Id est, coram illo verbo, de quo nunc agimus, Evangelico scilicet. Πρὸς hic sumitur, ut supra I. 7.

Aperta autem, inquit Chrysostomus, Græce dicitur τετραχηλισμένη, id est, resupinata, à Metaphorapellium, quæ extrahuntur à victimis. Quomodo enim quando quispiam illis jugulatis pellem à carne abstraxerit, omnia, quæ sunt intus, aperit, & nostris oculis reddit manifesta: ita etiam DEO clara & manifesta proposita sunt omnia. Phavorinus notat, τράχηλον spinam dorsi esse, quæ procedit à vertice usque ad coxendicem, unde τραχηλίζειν est animal mediam per spinam ita dividere, ut intestina omnia pateant. Quæ explicatio Gagnæi aliis præfertur ab Estio & Cornelio à Lapide. Ad sacerdotes alludi admittit Beat. | Dorscheus : Sacerdotes enim victimas mactabant, | excoriabant, diffindebant & dismembrabant, ut | omnia introspicere & discernere potuerint, an nihil | esset in hostia, quod eandem ab ara arcere posset. | Unde per κακοζηλίαν, cum veram rationem inspi- | ciendorum viscerum sacerdotes gentiles aut ignora- | rent aut dissimularent, aliam extispicinam excogi- | tarunt, ex qua de futuris eventibus ominarentur. | A Sacerdotibus itaque Veteris Testamenti, ad sum- | mum Novi Testamenti Sacerdotem iste τραχηλισμὸς | rectissime refertur. Quod nimirum non tantum | gladio Verbi, sed etiam omniscentia omnem crea- | turam denudare, dissecare & exenterare eo usque | queat, ut in intima introspiciat, & nihil plane abscon- | ditum habeat. Haec etsi ad Verbum DEI ali- | qua ratione referri possunt, quae vers. 13. haben- | tur, & à quibusdam referuntur, plerique tamen | ad Deum, vel Christum rectius cum Graecis Pro- | nomen αὐτõ referunt : Nam Deo tribui solent | oculi, & omniscentia, Prov. XV. 3. cap. XVI. v. 2. | non Verbo Dei. Coram Deo nulla creatura, quae | non tantum de hominis opere, sed universim de | re omni creata sonat, est invisibilis & abscondita, | omnia, etiam intima quaeque nuda sunt & re- | supinata coram oculis ejus, non tantum substan- | tia cujusque, sed etiam affectiones & qualitates : | quum hoc praecipue intendatur, quod hypocrisis | intime in corde delitescens Deum minime latere | possit. Quod Chrysostomus sic ad scopum Apo- | stoli applicat: Non enim, si adhuc, inquit, in fide | statis, sed non cum certa & plena persuasione confi- | datis, ipse judicabit quae sunt in corde. Eo enim per- | vadit & puniens & examinans. Nec inconcinna | est Beat. Dorschei observatio, quod omnia dican- | tur oculis ejus nuda & patentia : Oculis Christi, | hoc est Christo, non tantum secundum divinitatem | considerato, secundum quam oculos proprie sic dictos | nullos habet, sed etiam secundum humanam natu- | ram, secundum quam oculi ipsius apparuerunt in | visione Johannea ὡς φλὼξ πυρὸς Apoc. I. vers. 14. | Quod pertinet ad absconditas in Christo, hoc est, | ipsi secundum humanitatem communicatos omnes | thesauros sapientiae & scientiae, Col. II. vers. 3. Pie | enim cogitare licet, Christum etiam humanis suis & | nobis cognatis oculis, divina atque infinita virtute | praeditis, non tantum videre atque comprehende- | re totam sacrosanctam Trinitatem, & cognoscere | omnia. Unde dicitur Φωτίσαι τὰ κρυπτὰ τõ σκό- | τες, καὶ φανερῶσαι τὰς βυλὰς τῶν καρδιῶν, 1. Cor. | IV. vers. 5. per potestatem judiciariam, quam acce- | pit Joh. V. vers. 27. Sed etiam fideles suos in his terris | militantes è sacerdotali gratiae throno, de quo v. 16. | respicere. Quod ingens & inaestimabile fidelibus so- | latium est. Sic sane visio oculorum Christi à vi- | sione divina aliquo modo discernitur, quod illa sit | θεανδρικὴ, & ex tertio genere communicationis | idiomatum, hactenus κοινωνίαν ἐνεργειῶν divinarum | & humanarum, cum sit actus officii Christi. Probat | etiam Chrysostomus hunc de Deo vel Christo sen- | sum ex illis verbis πρὸς ὃν ἡμῖν λόγος, ad quem, | vel si mavis, de quo nobis sermo. Quia de Chri- | sto dicere instituit & dixit hactenus, & porro di- | cturus erat. Quae ita reddidit Theophylactus: Ad | quem nobis est λόγος, illi, inquit, & gestorum per | nos reddenda est ratio (quia λόγος rationem etiam | significat) & pro commissis danda supplicia.
