Sic | etiam Syrus & Tossanus Filio DEI rationem esse | reddendam exponunt. Simplicior autem videtur | illa explicatio, qua πρὸς ὃν accipiatur ut cap. I. v. 7. | quod ita effertur cap. V. v. 11. περὶ ὗ πολὺς ἡμῖν | ὁ λόγος. Unde patet, Christum Pronomine αὐτõ, qui & Deus vers. 12. dictus, respici, de cujus vo- ce vel verbo, cum auditur, ne negligatur, monuit Apostolus. Quis ille sit (ita Beat. Dorscheus) ex antecedentibus partim, partim ex consequentibus constat. Est nimirum χριςὸς Filius DEI & Do- minus super domum sanctam Ecclesiæ cap. III. v. 6. Apostolus & summus Sacerdos ὁμολογίας nostræ, vers. 1. fidelis DEO constituenti ipsum ad hoc sanctum officium, vers. 2. Mosi non tantum par, sed etiam superior, vers. 2. 3. & 5. conditor omnium, adeoque etiam fundator Ecclesiæ, vers. 4. tentatus à Patribus in deserto vers. 8. 9. 10. 11. & sqq. cujus per Evangelium consequimur μετοχὴν vers. 14. cujus vocem audiendam esse in requiem sempiter- nam nos invitantem gravissime, nos monuit Apostol. cap. IV. à vers. 1. ad 12. usque, cum quo nobis nego- tium est, tanquam cum judice severissimo, & vin- dice sermonis sui acerrimo, si eundem spreverimus. Consequentia idem demonstrant. Dixit Apostolus, illam πρὸς ὃν ὁ λόγος ipsi est, omnia habere nuda & aperta oculis suis. Infert exinde vers. 14. quod habeamus Sacerdotem magnum, unde ostendit illum ipsum, de quo hactenus à cap. III. v. 7. & cap. IV. v. 1. atque sqq. disseruit Apostolus, esse summum Sacerdotem nostrum. Qui enim alias inferre posset Apostolus, is, de quo nobis sermo est, est idem qui in deserto à Patribus Israëliturum tentatus fuit, à quo tanquam DEO vivo defecerunt, quibus juravit exclusionem à sempiterna quiete, qui etiamnum post illam rebellionem alios ad participationem tan- tæ beatitudinis invitat, qui uti ipse post ἑξαήμε- ρον creationis ab operibus suis quievit, ita etiam populo suo requiem ab omnibus hujus miseriæ ope- ribus & laboribus daturus est, qui habet sermo- nem viventem, efficacem & penetrantiorem quovis ancipiti gladio. Ergo nos habemus Sacerdotem magnum. Quomodo inquam istud consequitur, si non idem est is, de quo hactenus loquutus est Apostolus cum Sacerdote nostro summo, qui est Christus. Quod ergo ad particulam καὶ recte ob- servavit Beat. Dorscheus: Illud καὶ non cum ante- riori subjecto copulat; sed cum emphasi aliud in- telligendum nobis indigitat. Καὶ enim sæpius non copulare simpliciter, sed emphasin quandam innu- ere, & idem esse, ac Et imprimis, vel præcipue autem, tam Veteris, quam Novi Testamenti ex- emplis constat. Conf. Johan. II. vers. 1. 2. Sam. II. vers. 30. Psal. XVIII. vers. 1. Marc. I. v. 15. & III. 7. & VIII. vers. 16. Act. I. 14. cap. XXVI. v. 22. 1. Cor. IX. 1. &c. Itaque sensus Apostoli hoc loco est: Imprimis autem ejus, de quo nobis sermo est, qui est autor sermonis viventis & efficacis, qui est promissor Sabbatismi beatifici, ejus inquam oculis omnia patent, ut adeo in his verbis & ra- tio sit, cur tutissime credere possimus, sabbati- smum æternum nobis pollicenti, cum sit omniscius, adeoque infallibiliter prospicere queat, quorsum suos, quos invitat & tantis promissionibus lactat, perducere possit: Sed & ratio indicetur, cur ab omni repugnantia alieni esse debeamus, cum illa omni- scios & vindices ejus oculos nequaquam effugere queat, etiamsi in intimis animi recessibus abscon- dita delitescat. Imo & ratio afferatur, cur sermo divinus tantæ sit efficaciæ, ut intima animi sensa per- tentare & penetrare queat, nimirum quia ab omni- scia Majestate promanat, qui illum ita tempera- re novit, ut recessibus etiam mentis pervestigandis idoneus sit. Alii cum Piscatore illud αὐτῆ vers. 13. ἐνώπιον αὐτῆ referunt ad vocem τῆ Θεῆ vers. 12. Ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος τῆ Θεῆ, & verba vers. 14. Haben- tes ergò Pontificem cum Chamiero Tom. I. l. VI. cap. V. n. XII. observant, non esse collectionem ex proximè præcedentibus deductam, sed regres- sionem ad sermonem de Summo Pontifice, longâ digressione interruptum, quibus annuit Dn. D. Johann. Andr. Quenstädt Exerc. Solemni de Verbi DEI efficac. Textui tamen convenientior videtur relatio ad Christum, imprimis ob verba πρὸς ὃν ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος, de quo etiam adductus fuit Psalmus XCV. c. IV. vers. 3. seqq. & monitum cap. III. vers. 14. ut retineantur ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς ὑποσά- σεως, ut simus & maneamus μετοχοὶ τῦ χρισῦ, eâque fini vocem ejus audiamus, nec cor nostrum ad eandem obduremus, quod ab Isräelitis fa- ctum, qui Christum tentarunt in deserto, adeo- que interierunt, quod coll. loc. 1. Corinth. X. vers. 9. docet.

PARS II. Admonitio de fiduciali accessu ad thro- num gratiæ.

## 4:14
Verse 14. Having therefore a great High Priest) Who uses not the ministry of the Levites, but of his own Word, which is so efficacious. Some begin a new chapter here, Blessed Luther especially, following Theodoret, since a new treatment is being undertaken. For the Apostle had dealt up to this point with Christ, his person and his Doctoral office, and the Word, which is to be received by all. Now he proceeds to the Priestly office, concerning which he had intended to treat even primarily, and therefore he takes up a new theme. But because the other Greeks and most other interpreters refer these to chapter IV, and there is at least some approach and preparation for the following treatment in them, with a stimulus of the excitation of confidence and the promise of grace, by which the same is rendered more pleasing, we follow in their footsteps: primarily because this conclusion is still deduced from the preceding, even though the argument of the future treatment, both didactic and parenetic, is simultaneously insinuated in it. For how great a Pontiff we have is already clear from those things which the Apostle has handed down, whose most eminent person he graphically described in chapters I and II, and whom he taught to be, according to his human nature, exalted above all heavens, and according to his divine nature, the very Son of GOD. Whence, just as he shows how great and what kind of Doctor he is, who is to be heard by all: so he now begins to teach how great and what kind of Pontiff he is, in whom we may confide. For the ministries of the Word and of the Levites are not opposed, nor does the Word of the Gospel correspond to the Levites in the New Testament, but rather the Ministry of the Word: just as Christ does not use the Word only as a medium through which he converts us, but also the Ministers of the Word as his legates. Nor does that comparison apply here, where the discourse is about the Pontificate of Christ, which consists not in the preaching or use of the Word, but in the offering of sacrifices and intercession for the people of GOD. Therefore, just as he previously compared CHRIST with Moses as a Doctor: so now he decides to compare the same with Aaron as a Great Pontiff. But our Pontiff is truly great, because he is not a mere man, but true GOD and the Son of GOD: Indeed, he is also great because he did not exercise his Pontificate on earth in the manner of the Priests of the Old Testament, but also penetrated all the heavens and, sitting at the right hand of GOD, exercises it eternally, interceding for us before the Father. Therefore he is also truly great as a man, because he is not a common man, but subsisting in the person of the Son of GOD, and sitting at the right hand

of GOD. Blessed Dorscheus collects several respects from the context here not inelegantly: He is called great, he says, 1. By his eyes, verse 13, to which all things are open. 2. By his Word, verse 12, which is of incomparable efficacy, so much so that the high priest of the Old Testament could not probe and penetrate any victim so much with his sword; just as this Priest with the sword of his Word discerns all the hidden things of men. 3. By the Sabbath-rest, which he promises to his people as the greatest and most perfect of all in verse 9. 4. By his Empire, with which he invites all men of the whole world to the listening of his voice, verse 7. 5. By his Oath, which he issued as the highest and greatest against the refractory, verse 3 and chapter III, verse 11 et seqq. 6. By his Work, both of creation, by which he founded all things, chapter III, verse 4, and rested from all his works on the seventh day, chapter IV, verse 4; and then also of recreation, by which he both built and preserves the house of God, chapter III, v. 4, 6, 7. By his Seat, by which he dwells in all and each of the faithful of the whole world at all times, chapter III, v. 6, and over them from the throne of grace, chapter IV, verse 16, indeed he rules over all enemies from the right hand of God, Psalm CX, v. 2. Therefore he is absolutely great, since he has so many respects of greatness, and thus is truly great God, Tit. II, 13, and a great Pontiff.

Διεληλυθότα τὲς ὐρανὲς.

Who through the air and the ether arrived at that seat of rest. Thus the word heavens is taken below in VII, 16. The legal Pontiff passed through the Atrium and through the Basilica of the temple, of which the Atrium designated the elemental world, the Basilica the starry heaven.

The heaven or seat of rest, to which the Great Pontiff arrived, is not a created or material heaven, situated at an immense distance of space above the air and ether from these lower things, which is evident even from the fact that GOD is in the heavens, who certainly is not in some seat removed from us, and that sitting at the right hand does not demand some certain place, but implies universal rule and the fullness of all things, 1 Corinthians XV, v. 15, Eph. IV, v. 10. The Vulgate rendered it 'penetrated the heavens': because having ascended above all heavens, Eph. IV, verse 10, having become higher than the heavens, Heb. VII, verse 26. A silent opposition is observed here between the Pontiff of the Old Testament, who penetrated the Holy of Holies: and CHRIST, who penetrated into heaven itself, that he might appear now before the face of GOD for us, Heb. IX, verse 24. To penetrate the heavens, therefore, as rightly Blessed Gerhardus concludes, it is not the case that the visible machine of the heavens, varied by distinct orbs of spheres, passes through in such a way that it is held circumscribed in the highest heaven as if in a certain place, in the language of Physics; but that it is made higher than all the heavens, to enter and take possession of the divine glory, in the language of Scripture. Blessed Dorscheus speaks thus of these things from the preceding: He said in chapter III concerning Moses and the high priest of the Old Testament, that they were in the tabernacle, and served there: And yet, which Paul leaves to be thought about, they did not fill the tabernacle, much less the whole Church, which was accustomed to flow together to the tabernacle, far less the desert, in which the Church was then in exile, or afterwards the promised land, to the possession of which the Church was hastening, and least of all the whole earth or the entire world. But the Apostle indicates that the case is far different concerning Christ: That He does not inhabit the whole Church, chapter III. 6, but rather as the living God and author of the eternal sabbath, He pervades and fills the earth and the heavens. Whence he infers in this chapter, verse 14, that διέλευσιν τῶν ὑρανῶν is, of course, constitutive by divine presence. He describes furthermore The Apostle [describes] Christ as dissuading from all hardening, swearing in his wrath destruction to the rebellious, exhorting to the embrace of the offered rest, and thus as such a High Priest who has the right of eternal life, and is moreover able to inflict eternal death upon the contumacious. From this he surely concludes that he, having passed through the heavens, is not contained anywhere, so as to be prevented from receiving the obedient into rest everywhere in the world and excluding the disobedient from the same. Therefore, the passing through is hinted by the Apostle not as a matter of distance but of Majesty and presence. Finally, in verse 12, he spoke of the Word of Christ, how it penetrates all things in men; and of Christ himself in verse 13, how nothing is hidden from him. Whence he infers that this our Priest has even passed through and surpassed the heavens themselves, and has thus arrived at that height from which he can presently behold all things and dispense that efficacy of his Word everywhere, nor is it to be wondered at that the Word of CHRIST penetrates the inmost parts of men, since he has penetrated both those things and the heavens and all things.

Jesus the Son of God) Not a servant but the Son of GOD as above III. 6.

Let us hold fast the profession) Let us retain the profession, that is, let us stand firm in it. Thus to hold fast is used also in Rev. II. verse 25, chap. III. verse 11. חזק. Take profession as above chap. III. v. 1.

From this discourse concerning the eminence of the person of Christ our High Priest, the Apostle deduces this, that we ought to persist in the faith and profession of him, and concludes that the profession of all things which he has treated hitherto concerning Christ is to be retained. Thus the blessed Hunnius: It is a general conclusion of the whole preceding exhortation to retain the confession of JESUS Christ our High Priest. He fortified it indeed on both sides in such a way that he asserts the Majesty of the High Priest JESUS Christ against those who were offended by the observed humility of his flesh: and conversely he so commends his gentleness that he might raise up the weak in faith, lest, terrified by the divine Majesty of Christ, they flee from him as a severe Judge. Theophylact connects these things to the preceding in this way. because the Apostle warned that we should not slip or lose heart: Now therefore, let him teach what kind of High Priest we have obtained, who indeed can bring us aid, if only we will most constantly profess that we are going to trust in him: and that he is not such as Moses, who neither entered that rest, nor introduced the people into it. But this one, passing through the heavens, sat down with the Father, and can provide us access into heaven, and make us heirs of that perpetual rest which he had promised long before.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἔχοντες ἶν Ἀρχιερέα μέγαν) Qui non Levita- rum, sed Verbi sui adeo efficacis ministerio utitur. Inchoant hic nonnulli novum caput, Beat. Lu- therus imprimis, præeunte Theodoreto, quum no- va tractatio suscipiatur. Egerat enim huc usque de Christo Apostolus, ejus persona & officio Do- ctorali ac Verbo, quod suscipiendum ab omnibus. Nunc ad officium Sacerdotale, de quo vel præci- pue agere instituerat, progreditur, ideoque no- vum thema suscipit. Sed quia Græci cæteri & plerique alii Interpretes hæc ad caput IV. refe- runt, iisdemque saltem accessus & parasceve quædam sit ad tractationem sequentem, cum stimulo excitationis fiduciæ & promissionis gra- tiæ, qua eadem gratior redditur, eorum vestigiis insistimus: imprimis quod hoc συμπέράσμα è superioribus adhuc deducitur, etsi eodem etiam argumentum futuræ tractationis cum didacticæ tum paræneticæ simul insinuetur. Quantum e- nim habeamus Pontificem ex iis, quæ tradidit Apostolus, jam liquet, cujus personam eminen- tissimam cap. I. & II. graphice descripsit, quem- que secundum humanam naturam super omnes cœlos evectum, & secundum divinam ipsum- met DEI Filium esse docuit. Unde ut quan- tus & qualis ille Doctor sit, qui audiendus ab omnibus ostendit: Ita porro quantus & qualis Pontifex sit, in quo confidamus jam docere in- stituit. Non enim opposita sunt Verbi & Levi- tarum ministeria, neque Levitis respondet in Novo Testamento Verbum Evangelii, sed po- tius Verbi Ministerium: quemadmodum Chri- stus non utitur tantum Verbo ceu medio, per quod nos convertit, sed etiam Ministris Verbi ceu legatis suis. Neque ea comparatio huc facit, ubi de Pontificatu Christi sermo est, qui non in Verbi præconio vel usu, sed in sacrificiorum oblatione ac intercessione pro populo DEI con- sistit. Ideo ut CHRISTUM ante cum Mo- se contulit ceu Doctorem: Ita jam constituit eundem cum Aarone conferre ceu Pontifice Magno. Magnus autem vere est Pontifex no- ster, quia non ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος, sed verus DEUS & Filius DEI: Imo magnus etiam, quia non in terris Pontificatu functus est more Sacerdotum Veteris Testamenti, sed etiam cœ- los omnes penetravit & confidens ad dextram DEI æternum eo fungitur, interpellans pro nobis apud Patrem. Magnus ergo etiam vere, ut homo, quia non homo communis, sed in persona Filii DEI subsistens, & ad dextram

DEI confidens. Plures respectus è contextu non inconcinne hic colligit Beat. Dorscheus: Magnus, inquit, dicitur 1. Oculis vers. 13. qui- bus omnia patent. 2. Verbo, vers. 12. quod est incomparabilis efficaciæ, adeo ut summus Sacer- dos Veteris Testamenti nullam victimam adeò suo gladio pertentare & penetrare potuerit; sicut hic Sacerdos gladio Verbi sui omnia abscondita hominum discutit. 3. Sabbatismo, quem omnium maximum & perfectissimum populo suo pollicetur versu 9. 4. Imperio, quo omnes totius orbis ho- mines ad auscultationem vocis suæ invitat vers. 7. 5. Juramento, quòd summum & maximum con- tra refractarios edidit vers. 3. & capite III. vers. 11. & seqq. 6. Opere cum creationis, quo condidit omnia cap. III. vers. 4. & septimo die ab omnibus operibus suis quievit, cap. IV. vers. 4; tum etiam recreationis, qua domum Dei & con- struxit & conservat, cap. III. v. 4. 6. 7. Sede, qua in omnibus & singulis totius orbis fidelibus omni tempore habitat cap. III. v. 6. & super illos è throno gratiæ cap. IV. vers. 16. imo super omnes inimicos è dextra Dei dominatur, Psal. CX. v. 2. Itaque absolutè magnus est, cum tot magnitudinis re- spectus habeat, adeoque revera magnus Deus Tit. II. 13. & magnus Pontifex.

Διεληλυθότα τὲς ὐρανὲς.

Qui per aerem ætheremque pervenit ad illam sedem quietis. Sic vox ὐρανῶν sumitur infra VII. 16. Pontifex legalis transibat per Atrium & per Basilicam templi, quo- rum Atrium mundum elementarem designabat, Basilica cœlum sidereum.

Cœlum vel sedes quietis, quo pervenit Ponti- fex Magnus, non est cœlum creatum vel mate- riale, supra aërem & ætherem spatiorum inter- stitio immenso ab hisce inferioribus dissitum, quod vel inde constat, quod DEUS in cælis sit, qui certe non est in sede aliquâ à nobis re- mota, quodque sessio ad dextram non ubi aliquod certum deposcat, sed regimen universale, & πλή- ρωσιν τῶν πάντων importet, 1. Corinth. XV. v. 15. Eph. IV. v. 10. Vulgata reddidit cœlos penetra- vit: quia ἀναβὰς ὑπεράνω πάντων ὀρανῶν, Eph. IV. vers. 10. ὑψηλότερος τῶν ὀρανῶν γενόμενος, Ebr. VII. vers. 26. Tacita hic observatur oppo- sitio inter Pontificem Veteris Testamenti, qui penetravit Sancta Sanctorum : & CHRISTUM, qui in cœlum ipsum penetravit, ut appareat nunc vultui DEI pro nobis, Ebr. IX. vers. 24. Pe- netrare ergo cælos, ut recte Beat. Gerhardus con- cludit, non est visibilem cælorum machinam distinctis sphærarum orbibus variatam eo modo transire, ut in ultimo cælo, tanquam in loco quodam circumscriptus teneatur, phrasi Physica; sed subli- miorem omnibus cælis fieri, divinam gloriam ingre- di & capessere, phrasi Scripturæ. Beat. Dorscheus ita de hisce ex antecedentibus: Dixit cap. III. de Mose & Sacerdote summo Veteris Testamenti, quod illi in tabernaculo fuerint, ibique serviverint: Ne- que tamen, quod cogitandum relinquit Paulus, vel tabernaculum impleverint, multo minus totam Ec- clesiam, quæ ad tabernaculum confluere solita est, longe minus vel desertum, in quo tum Ecclesia exu- labat, vel postea terram promissam, ad cujus posses- sionem Ecclesia properabat, omnium minime totam terram aut universum orbem. Atqui de Christo longe aliam esse rationem Apostolus indicat: Illum non to- tam Ecclesiam habitare cap. III. 6. imo tanquam Deum viventem & autorem æterni sabbatismi terram cælosque pervadere & implere. Unde infert hoc ca- pite, vers. 14. illam διέλευσιν τῶν ὑρανῶν nimirum præsentia divina constitutivam. Describit porro Apostolus Christum dehortantem ab omni indura- tione, jurantem in ira sua rebellibus interitum, ex- hortantem ad amplexum oblatae quietis, adeoque tanquam talem Pontificem, qui jus vitae sempiternae habeat, mortemque insuper aeternam contumacibus infligere valeat. Inde sane concludit, illum διεληλυ- θότα τες ὀρανὲς neque contineri alicubi, quo minus ubique terrarum & in requiem recipere obsequentes & immorigeros ab eadem excludere. Itaque διέ- λευσις non distantiae sed Majestatis & praesentiae ab Apostolo innuitur. Denique proxime vers. 12. de verbo Christi dixit, quomodo omnia penetret in hominibus; & de ipso Christo vers. 13. quomodo ipsi nihil sit absconditum. Unde infert, hunc Sa- cerdotem nostrum ipsos etiam caelos pervafisse & superasse, adeoque ad eam altitudinem pervenisse, ex qua praesenter omnia intueri & ubique istam Verbo suo efficaciam dispensare queat, nec miran- dum esse, Verbum CHRISTI intima hominum penetrare, cum hic & illa & caelos & omnia pe- netraverit.

Ἰησοῦν τὸν ὑὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ) Non famulum sed Filium DEI ut supra III. 6.

Κρατῶμεν τῆς ὁμολογίας) Retineamus professionem, id est, firmi in ea perstemus. Sic κρατεῖν sumitur & Apoc. II. vers. 25. cap. III. vers. 11. חזק. Ὁμολογίαν sume ut supra cap. III. v. 1.

Ex ista de eminentia personae Christi Pontifi- cis nostri διηγήσει hoc deducit Apostolus, nos in fide ac professione ejus persistere debere, omnium- que, quae tractavit hactenus de Christo, τὴν ὁμο- λογίαν retinendam esse concludit. Ita Beat. Hun- nius: Generalis est conclusio totius praecedentis cohortationis ad retinendam confessionem JESU Christi summi nostri Pontificis. Eam vero sic mu- nivit ex utraque parte, ut Majestatem asserat Pontificis JESU Christi contra eos, qui humili- tate conspecta carnis ejus off endebantur: & vicis- sim ejusdem mansuetudinem sic commendet, ut in- firmos in fide erigat, ne divina Majestate Christi territi eundem ceu severum Judicem refugiunt. Theophylactus haec ita connectit superiorib. quod monuerit Apostolus, ne labamur vel anim conci- damus: Jam ergo, qualem Pontificem nacti simus, doceat, qui nempe nobis possit & opem afferre, si mo- do illi confisuros nos constantissime profitebimur: neque talis sit, ut Moses, qui nec requiem illam adivit, nec in eam populum introduxit. Hic vero caelos permeans Patri assedit, potestque nobis adi- tum in caelum praestare, & quietis illius perpetuae, quam longe ante promiserat, haeredes efficere.

## 4:15
Vers. 15.

For we do not have a High Priest not able to sympathize with our weaknesses) Since in the warning he showed severe judgments, now, lest the spirit be despondent, he shows the help prepared by Christ for those wishing to contend lawfully. And to be able here is to be referred to affection, as above II. v. 18. Weaknesses are the adversities to which Christians are subject, as Rom. VIII. verse 26, 1 Cor. II. verse 3, 2 Cor. XI. verse 30, XII. verse 9, 10, Gal. IV. verse 13. To sympathize is a purely Greek word, such as many are in this book. It is found also below X. verse 34, and nowhere else in these books. Isocrates, Aristotle, and others use it. In the Glossary I find to sympathize.

The blessed Dorotheus presents the connection thus: Because the divine Word in verse 12 was compared to a two-edged sword penetrating all things and to a judge, because in verse 15 the principal cause of the eternal sabbath was described as omniscient, because in verse 14 he was depicted as supremely powerful and having surpassed the whole height of the heavens, which we ought to hold with the firmest embrace always, a scruple could arise in the minds of the more tender-conscienced, whether we can be participants of the eternal sabbath, since in that penetration of the inmost recesses of our mind very many imperfections emerge, since in the concupiscences and thoughts of the heart very many failings appear, since those eyes beholding all things detect very many infirmities in us, and thus we lie cast down at a very long interval below that height, nor dare we think to follow our High Priest into the heavens, where he has established the eternal sabbath, and we are often tempted whether we can become participants of our vow and of the perseverance of the trust once conceived, therefore it was necessary for the principal cause of the eternal sabbath to be described by the Apostle also as supremely merciful. Now therefore, with the blessed Hunnius as interpreter, he meets the thoughts of the weak, who could be terrified by the majesty of Christ just mentioned, so that they would not dare to approach him with a certain confidence. And the consolation proposed to the weak is that which teaches that, however great our High Priest may be, he is nevertheless not terrible toward miserable sinners, nor unmerciful, who is not affected by the sense of our infirmities, but that for his immense gentleness he sympathizes with us, healing our contrite hearts and the remaining infirmities in the flesh, and perfecting his power in our weakness, so that we do not fail or despair under the cross and tribulations, but may be able by his grace to persevere even to the end. For, says Theophylact, this is not a High Priest who is ignorant of our condition, such as most high priests are, who, as they have experienced fewer evils, are entirely ignorant of what pressures of bitterness they contain in themselves, and therefore are not the more ready to help the oppressed or sympathize with the miserable. But this our High Priest has undergone all things, and where he has suffered very many evils, he has ascended to heaven, about to grant pardon to human frailty. By weaknesses, therefore, are understood not only, as Estius wishes, the infirmities of the flesh still adhering to the reborn in this life, Heb. V. v. 2, chap. VII. v. 28, but also their consequences, pains, afflictions, persecutions, 2 Cor. XII. 5. Christ is said to sympathize with our infirmities, not as if He still today in the state of glory sustains any passion, but because from the fact that in the days of His flesh He was tempted in all things according to the likeness without sin, He is inclined to have mercy on us, Heb. II. v. 18. as the blessed Gerhard rightly advised.

Πεπειρασμένον δὲ κατὰ πάντα) In all ways from the right and from the left, Matt. IV. Most gravely, however, before death and in death. He repeats what he had said above II. 18.

Καθ᾿ ὁμοιότητα) Just as we are. Thus the Arab rightly here. So the Rabbis would say בדמותנו

Χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας) Yet in such a way that He never succumbed.

That happened especially in the great passion. Concerning which Theophylact says: For the Jews pursued Him and spat upon Him and slandered Him, and always threatened Him with evil and afflicted Him with a shameful death. Therefore the High Priest endured all these things for our likeness, that is to say: He endured all these things no differently than we are accustomed to endure for human frailty, yet they are endured without sin: inasmuch as He was subject to no sin. Therefore, you also, imitating Him, be more constant in faith even in the midst of evils, and alien to all sin. The blessed Hunnius explained these things more fully: The argument, he says, of consolation taken from the example of Christ is in this way: Christ Himself was tempted in all things according to His human nature, therefore He will the more readily succor those who are tempted. Christ was tempted, indeed outwardly experiencing all kinds of miseries, hardships, dangers, snares of enemies, persecutions, and finally death itself. But inwardly and in His soul He was tempted by the terrors of death and the wrath of God on account of the human race's sins, the guilt and punishment of which he had derived upon himself: so much so that in the garden he sweated blood, and during that immense struggle with the terrors of death he said: My soul is sorrowful even unto death. And on the cross he cried out: My GOD, my GOD, why hast thou forsaken me? And thus he was tempted according to the likeness, as the Apostle says, that is, to the likeness of other men, except that he alone was able and had to drink the whole cup of the wrath of GOD, from which the remaining saints draw at least some more bitter drink of tribulations. Not in vain, however, is it added: Without sin: By which appendix the Apostle wished to note the difference between the temptations of CHRIST and other saints. For the temptations of the latter are often joined with impatience and other sins and infirmities: just as they are also very often solicited and tempted to sins themselves by Satan, and by the innate depravity of their own flesh. But the temptations of CHRIST were immune from every stain of sin: otherwise neither could his temptations heal our infirmities, nor could he himself be our High Priest, if he had been subject to sins. For it was fitting that we should have such a High Priest, who was holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, to whom it would not be necessary to offer victims for his own sins, for thus he himself would have needed another High Priest and Savior. To be tempted, therefore, in this place is not to be solicited to sin by corrupt flesh, which kind of temptation was very far from CHRIST, but to be conflicted with various adversities, which are wont to be sent upon men for the sake of temptation, that is, of probation, Luke XXI. verse 18. But CHRIST is said to be tempted κατὰ πάντα, as the Blessed one again warns, Gerhard, because he wished to experience all kinds of temptations voluntarily, which, however, is to be understood concerning the temptations of the Devil and the world, but not concerning the temptations of corrupt flesh, nor concerning personal evils, namely diseases, nor concerning evils which are repugnant to the good of grace, such as ignorance, wicked concupiscence, etc. Whence Cornelius à Lapide rightly concludes: Although there were passions in CHRIST, yet there were not propassions: Which he explains thus: There was in Christ anger, boldness, fear, but in such a way that they could not forestall the reason and will of CHRIST, and arise, be stirred up, and spring forth without his invitation or knowledge, for this is what propassions are: For every movement of anger, boldness, fear, sadness was freely assumed by him, and elicited and commanded by the reason and will of CHRIST: so that CHRIST could not be angry or sad, unless he willed and chose to be angry or sad: For all passions were to CHRIST, as one constituted in an integral and perfect nature (such as was in Adam before sin), entirely subject and subordinate. For such a nature was fitting for a Savior and the Son of GOD. Rightly also observing, that by infirmities are not understood diseases and sicknesses, because these are not of nature, that is, common to all men, but of particular persons, and it was fitting for CHRIST, who had come to heal our nature completely, to be entirely healthy. Wherefore although CHRIST admitted and received stripes and pains: Yet he did not allow the temperament of his body to be so disturbed by them that he would fall into disease, but only permitted his soul to be excluded from his body by their force and bitterness, and a violent death, by which he might redeem us, to be brought upon himself. And it is added χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας, not only because he was devoid of all sin in any temptation, but also so that CHRIST may be distinguished from the High Priest of the Old Testament, as one who, being surrounded by the infirmity of the flesh, needed sacrifices for his own sins, Heb. V. 2. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Οὐ γὰρ ἔχομεν Αρχιερέα μὴ δυνάμενον συμπαθῆσαι ταῖς ἀσθε- νείαις ἡμῶν) Cum in comminatione oftenderit severa judicia, nunc, ne animus despondeatur, oftendit à Christo para- tum auxilium legitime certare volentibus. Et δύνασθαι hic referendum est ad affectum, ut supra II. v. 18. Ἀσθένειαι sunt adversa, quibus subjacent Christiani, ut Rom. VIII. vers. 26. 1. Corinth. II. vers. 3. 2. Cor. XI. vers. 30. XII. vers. 9. 10. Gal. IV. vers. 13. Συμπαθῆσαι vox pure Graeca, quales multae in hoc libro. Reperitur & infra X. vers. 34. nec alibi in his libris. Utuntur Isocrates, Aristoteles, & alii. In Glossario συμπαθῶ misero.

Nexum ita exhibet Beat. Dorstheus: Quia Verbum divinum in vers. 12. gladio ancipiti omnia penetranti & judiciario conferebatur, quia vers. 15. causa principalis sabbatismi aeterni describebatur, tanquam omniscia, quia vers. 14. depingebatur tanquam summe potens, & omnem caelorum alti- tudinem supergressa, quam firmissimo semper am- plexu tenere debeamus, scrupulus conscientia tene- rioribus oboriri poterat, an sabbatismi aeterni participes esse possimus, cum in ista penetratione in- timorum animi nostri recessuum quam plurimæ emergant imperfectiones, cum in concupiscentiis & cogitationibus cordis plurima deliquia appareant, cum oculi illi omnia intuentes plurimas in nobis in- firmitates deprehendant, adeoque nos longissimo in- tervallo infra istam altitudinem abjecti jaceamus, nec in cælos sequi Pontificem nostrum audeamus co- gitare, ubi ille sabbatismum æternum constituit, & multoties tentemur, an voti nostri & fiduciæ semel conceptæ indebita perseverantia participes fieri pos- simus, ideoque necesse fuit, causam principalem sab- batismi æterni ab Apostolo etiam describi, tanquam summe misericordem. Nunc itaque, Beat. Hunnio interprete, infirmorum cogitationibus occurrit, qui Christi majestate modo commemorata terreri pote- rant, quo minus auderent ipsum cum fiducia qua- dam accedere. Estque consolatio proposita infirmis, quæ docet, utcunque magnus sit noster Pontifex: non tamen eum esse terribilem erga miseros peccatores, nec immisericordem, qui non afficiatur sensu infir- mitatum nostrarum, sed quod pro immensa mansue- tudine sua nobis compatiatur, sanans contritiones nostras, & reliquas in carne infirmitates, & virtu- tem suam in nostra infirmitate perficiens, ne defi- ciamus aut desperemus sub cruce & tribulationibus, sed ad finem usque perseverare ipsius gratia valea- mus. Non enim, inquit Theophylactus, est Ponti- fex iste, qui nostræ conditionis ignarus, quales ple- rique Pontificum sunt, qui ut mala minus experti ignorant prorsus quid in se habeant pressuræ acer- bitatis, & ideo nec promptiores sunt, ut oppressis opitulentur vel miseris compatiantur. Atqui cun- cta subivit hic noster Pontifex & ubi mala quam plurima fuit perpessus & cælum conscendit, veniam fragilitati daturus humanæ. Per ἀσθενείας ergo non solum, ut Estius vult, infirmitates carnis renatis adhuc in vita hac adhærentes intelliguntur, Ebr. V. v. 2. cap. VII. v. 28. sed etiam earum conse- quentia dolores, afflictiones, persecutiones, 2. Corinth. XII. 5. Compati autem Christus dicitur nostris infirmitatibus, non quasi adhuc hodie in sta- tu gloriæ passionem aliquam sustineat, sed quia ex eo, quod in diebus carnis suæ per omnia tentatus est se- cundum similitudinem sine peccato, ad miserendum nobis est propensus, Ebr. II. v. 18. ut recte monuit B. Gerhardus.

Πεπειρασμένον δὲ κατὰ πάντα) Omnibus modis à dextra & sinistra, Matth. IV. Gravissime autem ante mortem & in morte. Repetit, quod supra dixerat II. 18.

Καθ᾿ ὁμοιότητα) Perinde ut nos. Ita recte hic Arabs. Sic Rabbini dicerent בדמותנו

Χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας) Ita tamen ut nunquam succubuerit.

Id in passione magna inprimis contigit. Quo de Theophylactus: Hunc enim insectati Judæi & per- conspuerunt & calumniati sunt, & malum sem- per interminati & paribuli morte affecerunt. Per- tulit itaque hæc omnia Pontifex pro similitudine nostra videlicet: hoc est, haud secus hæc omnia tulit, quam ipsi ferre pro humana fragilitate sole- mus, tolerantur tamen & absque peccato: Quippe qui nulli esset peccato obnoxius. Hunc itaque & vos imitati, vel in mediis malis estote in fide constan- tiores, & ab omni peccato alieni. Plenius hæc expo- suit Beat. Hunnius: Argumentum, inquit, consola- tionis ab exemplo Christi sumptum hoc modo: Ipse- met Christus tentatus est per omnia juxta humanam suam naturam, proinde tanto promptius succurret eis, qui tentantur. Tentatus autem est Christus, foris quidem omnis generis miserias, ærumnas, pericula, in- sidias hostium, persecutiones, ac deniq; ipsam mortem expertus. Intus autem & in anima sua tentatus est terroribus mortis & ira Dei propter humani generis peccata, quorum reatum ac pœnam in se deriva- verat: adeo ut in horto sanguinem sudaret, & inter ingentem illam cum mortis pavoribus luctam diceret: Tristis est anima mea usq; ad mortem. Et in cruce clamaret: DEUS meus, DEUS meus, quare me dereliquisti? Atque sic tentatus est juxta similitudinem, ut Apostolus inquit, id est, ad similitudinem aliorum hominum, nisi quod ipse solus totus calicem iræ DEI ebibere debuit ac potuit, è quo reliqui sancti aliquem saltem ama- riorem potum tribulationum hauriunt. Non fru- stra autem subjungitur: Absque peccato: Qua appendice notare voluit Apostolus discrimen in- ter CHRISTI & aliorum sanctorum tentatio- nes. Horum enim tentationes sæpe sunt cum im- patientia & aliis peccatis & infirmitatibus con- junctæ: quemadmodum etiam sæpenumero ad ipsa peccata solicitantur & tentantur à Satana, & propria carnis innata pravitate. At CHRISTI tentationes ab omni labe peccati fuerunt immunes: aliàs nec tentationes ejus nostras infirmitates sa- nare, nec ipse noster Pontifex esse potuisset, si peccatis fuisset obnoxius. Talem enim decebat nobis esse Pontificem, qui esset pius, innocens, impollutus, segregatus à peccatoribus, cui non ne- cesse foret pro propriis peccatis victimas offerre, sic enim ipsemet indiguisset Pontifice & Salvatore alio. Tentari ergo hoc loco non est, ad peccatum à corrupta carne solicitari, qualis tentatio lon- gissime à CHRISTO abfuit, sed cum variis adversitatibus conflictari, quæ tentationis, hoc est, probationis causa hominibus immitti so- lent, Luc. XXI. vers. 18. Tentatus autem dicitur CHRISTUS κατὰ πάντα, iterum monente Beat. Gerhardo, quia omnia tentationum genera spon- te experiri voluit, quod tamen de tentationibus Diaboli & mundi, non autem de tentationibus corruptæ carnis accipiendum, nec de malis per- sonalibus, videlicet morbis, nec de malis, quæ bono gratiæ repugnant, qualia sunt ignorantia, prava concupiscentia, &c. Unde recte colligit Cornelius à Lapide: Licet in CHRISTO pas- siones fuerint, non tamen fuisse propassiones: Quod ita explicat: Fuit in Christo ira, audacia, timor, sed ita ut rationem & voluntatem CHRISTI prævenire, ipsoque invito vel inscio exoriri, con- citari & exurgere non possent, hoc enim est pro- passionum: Omnis enim motus iræ, audaciæ, ti- moris, tristitiæ ab eo libere fuit assumptus, & à ratione & voluntate CHRISTI elicitus & im- peratus: ita ut irasci aut tristari CHRISTUS non posset, nisi irasci aut tristari vellet & eligeret: Erant enim passiones omnes CHRISTO, utpote in natura integra & perfecta (qualis fuit in A- damo ante peccatum) constituto, subditæ prorsus & subjectæ. Talis enim natura decebat Salva- torem & DEI Filium. Recte etiam observans, per infirmitates non intelligi morbos & ægritudi- nes, quia hæ non sunt naturæ, id est, omnibus hominibus communes, sed particularium persona- rum, & CHRISTUM decebat, ut totus esset sanus, qui naturam nostram plane sanaturus ad- venerat. Quare licet verbera & dolores admi- serit & susceperit CHRISTUS: Non tamen iis temperiem sui corporis ita distemperari, ut in mor- bum incideret, sed tantum eorum vi & acerbi- tate animam à corpore excludi, mortemque vio- lentam, quâ nos redimeret, sibi inferri permisit. Et additur χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας, non tantum quod omnis peccati expers in quavis tentatione fue- rit, sed ut etiam CHRISTUS à Pontifice Veteris Testamenti ita distinguatur, utpote qui circumstatus carnis infirmitate indiguit sacrificiis pro peccatis propriis, Ebr. V. 2. 3.

## 4:16
Vers. 16.

Let us therefore come with boldness unto the throne of grace.] Sc. , that is, since we have such a mediator. That throne of grace כסא רחמים is from the Hebrews, who say that GOD, when he sees the whole world to be damnable, rises from the throne of judgment מעל כסא הדין, so that he may sit on the throne of mercy, which appeared most of all after Christ. Μετὰ παῤῥησίας here is with good hope or confidence, see Ephes. III. verse 12. and above III. verse 6. But Christ is conceived as being nearest to the divine throne, as Apoc. VII. 6. and often elsewhere.

That we may obtain mercy, and find grace for timely help.] The word ἐλέος here does not look to sins, but signifies חסד just as χάρις signifies חן, by which the goodness of GOD is signified. But it is explained whither that goodness tends, namely that we may obtain help, namely with CHRIST doing that for us: Εὔκαιρον such as is convenient for the time: Thus the Greeks translate בעתו, Psalm CV. 27. See Mark VI. 21. The Syrian well to the sense in the time of affliction. In the Manuscript for ἔλεος there is ἔλεον. It matters not. For both declensions are found not only in other Greeks, but also in our books. But εὕρωμεν is let us find נמצי. See Luke I. verse 30. and what is said there.

Christ is not only most near to the divine throne, but sits on the very throne of the Father, Apoc. III. verse 21. and by the throne of grace here it is not inappropriately understood by some. Thus the Blessed Gerhard, who thence refutes another reading: The Syrian and certain Latin Codices have the pronoun his added, which occurs also in Bede. But the Greek Codices do not acknowledge it, as neither do the more approved Latin Codices. Nor does it suit the Apostolic context. For by the throne of grace is understood Christ, who reconciled us to his Father through his passion and death, as one who embraces us with his grace on account of CHRIST, and on account of the same hears our prayers, just as he once heard prayers, residing above the ark of the covenant on the mercy seat between the Cherubim. Thus also the Blessed Hunnius on this place: The conclusion of the preceding exhortation, and preparation for the following discussion concerning the sacrifice and priesthood of CHRIST. And the sense of these words is this: because we have Christ as High Priest, therefore, without regard for either our unworthiness or our infirmity, let us approach Him with filial confidence, as that throne of grace which the Father Himself has set before us as a propitiation in His blood. That we may obtain mercy. He subjoins an argument taken from the final cause: therefore let us strive with confidence to approach JESUS CHRIST Himself, so that we who outside of this High Priest are strangers to the grace of GOD, may now through the same obtain mercy and grace, that is, the favor of God and the gratuitous remission of sins, and thus all things pertaining to our eternal salvation, and that at an opportune time, while we are still in the time of grace, and while the door of salvation lies open to us. While His VOICE still sounds, and that TODAY endures, in which we hear His voice, of which [we spoke] above. But why does the word ἐλέες not refer to sins? Do we not also have need of help, when we are crushed and afflicted on account of sins? Is it not necessary that we implore the help of GOD and His mercy, so that, having obtained the gratuitous remission of sins, we may be delivered from temptations, and that we may not have to perish in our sins and their punishments, by the example of David, Psalm XXVII, verse 6 et seqq., Psalm XXXVIII, and Psalm XXXIX, verse 9 et seqq., and of Hezekiah, Isaiah XXXVIII, verses 14, 17. What? That others rather, and not wrongly, distinguish between ἔλεον and χάριν, in that the former refers to for the remission of sins and the warding off of evils: The latter for the salutary bestowing of gifts. Concerning the word παῤῥησίας, the blessed Gerhard says thus: By παῤῥησία is understood full boldness and confidence of mind. The Syrian rendered it with uncovered eye, which is a periphrasis for a confident man, just as that in chapter III, verse 6, concerning the uncovering of faces, to which is opposed the covering of the eyes on account of shame or grief or the consciousness of an offense, which forbids us from being able to bear the sight of him whom we know to be hostile to us, Esth. VII, verse 8. 2 Cor. XIII, verse 12. Tremell. compare Gen. III, verse 8. Heb. X, verses 19, 35. 1 John II, verse 28. chapter III, verse 21. chapter IV, verse 17. Concerning the same, let the points of Cornelius be noted, to be opposed to the Papists regarding diffidence and doubt about grace: For confidence in Greek is παῤῥησία, which (as if πᾶν ῥησία) is the liberty and license of speaking, by which all things are said: or free speech concealing nothing: Then indeed by catachresis παῤῥησία signifies trust or confidence, from which this liberty of speaking arises, and thus Paul often receives this name. Now confidence or trust, says Cicero, is that by which the mind has placed much in itself in great and honorable matters with certain hope, provided that the trust is human. For if it is divine, as it is here, it places its hope not in itself, but in GOD. Moreover, this opportunity does not pertain only to the time of affliction, but to the whole time of the present life: Concerning which Theophylact says: For if, while we live on earth, we shall approach this very one, we shall find both mercy and grace at the same time: as those who have come to him opportunely, and while there is a place for clemency. But he who shall offer himself otherwise will be entirely lacking in these. For hereafter there will not be grace, but a throne of justice.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Προσερχώμεθα ὖν μετὰ παῤῥησίας τῷ θρόνῳ τῆς χάριτος.] Sc. , id est, cum tantum habeamus commendatorem. Illud θρόνῳ τῆς χάριτος כסא רחמים ab Ebræis est, qui dicunt, DEUM ubi videt totum mundum esse damna- bilem, surgere à solio judicii מעל כסא הדין, ut sedeat in solio misericordiæ, quod maxime post Christum ap- paruit. Μετὰ παῤῥησίας hic est cum bona spe sive fiducia, vide Ephes. III. vers. 12. & supra III. vers. 6. Concipitur autem Christus tanquam proximus divino solio, ut Apoc. VII. 6. & alibi sæpe.

Ἵνα λάβωμεν ἔλεον, καὶ χάριν εὕρωμεν εἰς εὔκαιρον βοήθειαν.] Vox ἐλέος hic non peccata respicit, sed significat חסד sic- ut χάρις חן, per quæ bonitas DEI significatur. Expli- catur autem quo tendat ea bonitas, nempe ut auxilium obtineamus, nempe CHRISTO id pro nobis agen- te: Εὔκαιρον quale convenit tempori : Ita Græci vertunt בעתו, Psal. CV. 27. Vide Marc. VI. 21. Syrus ad sensum bene in tempore afflictionis. In Manuscripto pro ἔλεος est ἔλεον. Nihil refert. Est enim utraque declinatio non in aliis tantum Græcis, sed & in nostris libris. Εὕρωμεν vero est consequamur נמצי. Vide Luc. I. vers. 30. & ibi dicta.

Christus non tantum maxime proximus est solio divino, sed sedet in ipso throno Patris, Apoc. III. vers. 21. & per thronum gratiæ hic à nonnullis non incommode intelligitur. Ita Beat. Gerhardus, qui inde refellit aliam lectio- nem : Syrus ac quidam Codices Latini additum habent Pronomen ejus, quod occurrit etiam apud Bedam. Sed Græci Codices illud non agnoscunt, uti nec probatiores Codices Latini. Nec convenit contextui Apostolico. Nam per thronum gratiæ intelligitur Christus, qui Patri suo per passionem & mortem nos reconciliavit, ut qui sua gratia nos complectatur propter CHRISTUM, ac propter eandem exaudiat preces nostras, sicut olim exau- diebat preces, residens super arcam fœderis in propitiatorio inter Cherubim. Ita & Beat. Hun- nius in hunc locum : Conclusio præcedentis ex- hortationis, & præparatio ad sequentem disputa- tionem de sacrificio & sacerdotio CHRISTI. Estque sensus horum verborum hic: quia Christum habemus Pontificem, idcirco non habita ratione vel indignitatis vel infirmitatis nostræ cum fiducia filiali adeamus ipsum, tanquam thronum illum gratiæ, quem Pater nobis ipse proposuit propitia- torium in sanguine illius. Ut consequamur mise- ricordiam. Subnectit argumentum à causa finali sumptum : ideo cum fiducia contendamus accede- re ipsum JESUM CHRISTUM, ut qui ex- tra hunc Pontificem alieni sumus à gratia DEI, nunc per eundem consequamur misericordiam & gratiam, id est, favorem Dei & remissionem peccatorum gra- tuitam, adeoque omnia ad æternam salutem nostram pertinentia, idque tempore opportuno, dum adhuc sumus in tempore gratiæ, & dum patet nobis ja- nua salutis. Dum adhuc sonat VOX ejus, & HODIE illud durat, quo audimus vocem ipsius, de quo supra. Cur vero vox ἐλέες non respiciat peccata? Annon etiam auxilio nobis opus, cum ob peccata conterimur & affligimur? Annon necessum, imploremus auxilium DEI & miseri- cordiam ejus, ut impetrata peccatorum gratuita remissione liberemur à tentationibus, nec in pec- catis eorumque suppliciis pereundum nobis sit exemplo Davidis, Psalm. XXVII. vers. 6. seqq. Psal. XXXIIX. & Psal. XXXIX. vers. 9. seqq. & Hiskiæ Esaiæ XXXIIX. vers. 14. 17. Quid? quod potius alii, nec male, ita distin- guant inter ἔλεον & χάριν, quod prius respiciat ad peccatorum remissionem & malorum depul- sionem: Posterius ad salutarem donorum elar- gitionem. De voce παῤῥησίας ita Beat. Gerhar- dus: Per παῤῥησίαν intelligitur plena animi fiducia & confidentia. Syrus reddidit retecto oculo, quæ periphrasis est hominis confidentis, sicut & illa cap. III. vers. 6. de retectione facierum, cui op- ponitur coopertio oculorum præ pudore aut mœrore vel conscientia offensionis, quæ vetat, quo minus ejus conspectum ferre possimus, quem scimus nobis esse infensum, Esth. VII. vers. 8. 2. Corinth. XIII. vers. 12. Tremell. confer. Gen. III. vers. 8. Ebr. X. vers. 19. 35. 1. Joh. II. vers. 28. cap. III. vers. 21. cap. IV. vers. 17. De eadem notentur & Corne- liana diffidentiæ & dubitationi de gratia Papistis opponenda: Pro fiducia Græce est παῤῥησία, quæ (quasi πᾶν ῥησία) est libertas & licentia loquendi, qua omnia dicuntur: sive oratio libera nihil reti- cens: Inde vero per Catachresin παῤῥησία signi- ficat fiduciam sive confidentiam, ex qua oritur hæc loquendi libertas, & sic sæpe hoc nomen accipit Paulus. Jam confidentia sive fidentia, ait Cice- ro, est, per quam magnis & honestis in rebus mul- tum in se animus fiducia certa cum spe collocavit, nimirum si fidentia sit humana. Nam si sit divina, uti hic est, non in se, sed in DEO, spem suam col- locat. Opportunitas autem hæc non pertinet so- lum ad tempus afflictionis, sed ad totum tempus præsentis vitæ: Quo de Theophylactus: Si enim, dum in terra vivimus, hunc ipsum adibimus, & misericordiam simul inveniemus & gratiam: ut qui opportune ad hunc cesserimus, & dum est cle- mentiæ locus. Qui vero alias se obtulerit, his pror- sus carebit. Neque enim imposterum gratia erit sed justitiæ thronus.

## 5:1 Argument
MEMBER II. ON THE SACERDOTAL OFFICE OF CHRIST. CHAPTER V. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Having premised the description of the High Priest, he teaches the necessity of his vocation by the example of Aaron, and makes God the Father the Author of the vocation of Christ the High Priest from a comparison of the Psalms (II, verse 7, and CX, verse 4), before whom he also offered prayers that he might be saved from death, and by whom, having been appointed, he is named High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek for the sake of the eternal salvation of believers: which he warns is difficult for them to understand on account of their dullness, as they are still in need of milk.

There are two parts: I. It concerns the description and vocation of the High Priest, up to verse 10. II. He kindly reproves the dullness of the Hebrews, up to verse 14. The blessed Dorscheus assigns these parts thus: The first has a comparison between CHRIST and the High Priest of the Old Testament: The second, a preparation for the comparison of CHRIST with Melchizedek.

PART I. Description and vocation of the High Priest.

For every high priest taken from among men) These things cohere with the preceding, and they ought not to have been torn away. For he wishes to show that Christ has all things which are required in a High Priest, and indeed in a most excellent manner. Moreover, he does not only look here to the law, but also to the custom before the law, when either the firstborn of families or kings chosen by the peoples entered into the priesthood. Never did celestial Spirits approach that office. Λαμβάνειν here, as לקח in Numbers XXV, verse 4, is to set apart, as those things which we take from a heap.

Intending to prove that Christ is the unique High Priest of the New Testament by a comparison with the High Priest of the Old Testament, yet so arranged that it is taught at the same time that CHRIST is far more excellent, he first brings forward the description of the High Priest of the Old Testament regarding the subject, that he was a man or taken from among men; regarding the end, that he was appointed for men; regarding the office, which is in general, regarding those things which pertain to God; in particular, that he offered gifts and sacrifices for sins; regarding the requirement, not the least, what kind of affection there ought to have been in the High Priest, namely, of mercy toward sinners; as also regarding the adjunct, that he was encompassed with infirmity. Concerning which the sacrifices testified, which he himself had to offer for his own sins. That he looks to the custom before the law, and that the priesthood was then proper to the kings chosen among the people, is not so clear. It is rather about the Levitical Priests that it is treated, and a comparison is instituted with them. Yet that description is so common that it can easily be applied to them also. Theophylact warns that those things which are common to Christ with the others should be explained first, then those which are proper to him. Therefore, he says, to be taken from among men for the High Priesthood is common to CHRIST with the others. For he himself, while he existed as a man, was made High Priest by God. And to be appointed for men in those things which are toward GOD, that is, to make intercession, that indeed is also common to him with the others.

For men he is appointed in those things which are toward God) A brief expression, such as also above in II, verse 17. He is appointed to perform divine matters for men. The Jews say, according to how the High Priest conducts himself: So is God hostile or propitious to the people. Philo, in his special laws concerning the High Priest, speaks thus: For the law wishes him to be partaker of a greater nature than that of a man, so that through some medium he may appease God for men, and God may reach out and grant graces. Again, concerning rewards and punishments. The high priesthood is ordained, through which, prophesying scientifically, he will serve the Being, and will correct the thanksgivings of the subjects, and he will make prayers and supplications for those who err.

Some take the word καθίσταται in an Active sense, he appoints those things which are toward God. But parallels teach that it must be taken passively, Heb. VIII, verse 3, James III, 6, chapter IV, verse 4. There is no faith here in the tradition of the Jews. For the just shall live by his faith, says Hab. chapter II, 4.

Ἵνα προσφέρῃ δῶρά τε καὶ θυσίας ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν) He explains the generality by certain species. Δῶρα קרבנים is general, but is said especially of burnt offerings, as can be seen in Leviticus 1:2. Θυσίαι is likewise general enough. For it includes also מנחה: But since ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν is added here, it must be understood as חטאת, concerning which see Leviticus 4:3 and following. Ὑπὲρ here, for which elsewhere there is περὶ, signifies on account of. And in the Manuscript below 3, περὶ is written for ὑπὲρ.

Θυσίαι were offered not only on account of sins, but for sins, namely to be expiated. Such phrases are to be explained in a sacrificial sense, concerning which I have written more elsewhere against the Socinians. Theophylact thinks it is explained here what that is, to be appointed for men themselves before God, namely, by sins GOD To render propitious. Which is indeed also Christ's, and if not entirely, common with others: inasmuch as he offered himself for the sake of conciliating the Father. Others, however, offered other things, namely a gift and a sacrifice. But that καθίςασθαι τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν is more general, embracing all the parts of a Priest, to which not only sacrifices pertain, but also intercessions before God.

Latin:

MEMBRUM II. DE OFFICIO CHRISTI SACERDOTALI. CAPUT V. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Præmissa descriptione Pontificis vocationis ejusdem necessitatem exemplo Aaronis do- cet, & Autorem vocationis Christi Pontifi- cis Deum Patrem è collatione Psalmorum (II. vers. 7. & CX vers. 4.) facit, apud quem etiam preces obtulerit, ut à morte sal- varetur, & à quo constitutus causa salutis æternæ credentium nominatus Pontifex se- cundum ordinem Melchisedech: quod ob ru- ditatem ipsis difficile intellectu esse, ceu in- digis adhuc lacte, monet.

Partes duæ sunt I. Pontificis descriptionem & vocationem concernit, ad vers. 10. II. Comiter Ebræorum ruditatem reprehendit, ad vers. 14. Beat. Dorscheus ita has partes assignat: Prima habet collationem inter CHRISTUM & Pon- tificem summum Veteris Testamenti: Secunda præparationem ad collationem CHRISTI, cum Melchisedecho.

PARS I. Pontificis descriptio & vocatio.

Πᾶς γὰρ ἀρχιερεὺς ἐξ ἀνθρώπων λαμβανόμενος) Cohæ- rent hæc cum superioribus, neque divelli debuerant. O- stendere enim vult, Christum omnia habere, quæ in sum- mo Sacerdote requiruntur, & quidem modo excellentis- simo. Non tantum autem legem hic respicit, sed & morem ante legem, cum aut primogeniti familiarum, aut à po- pulis electi Reges inirent sacerdotium. Nunquam cœle- stes Spiritus id munus adiere. Λαμβάνειν hic ut לקח Numer. XXV. vers. 4. est segregare, ut quæ ex acervo de- sumimus.

Probaturus Christum esse Pontificem unicum Novi Testamenti è collatione cum Pontifice Ve- teris Testamenti, sic tamen comparata, ut do- ceatur simul, CHRISTUM longe præstan- tiorem esse, primum affert descriptionem Ponti- ficis Veteris Testamenti quoad subjectum, quod homo vel ex hominibus assumptus fuerit, quoad finem, quod pro hominibus constitutus, quoad officium, quod in genere est, quoad τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, in specie, quod obtulerit dona & sacrifi- cia pro peccatis, quoad requisitum minime po- stremum, qualis in Pontifice affectus esse debu- erit, nimirum misericordiæ erga peccantes, ut & quoad adjunctum, quod circumdatus fuerit infirmitate. Quo de testabantur sacrificia, quæ ipse pro peccatis propriis offerre de- buit. Respici morem ante legem, & tùm in po- pulo electorum Regum proprium fuisse sacer- dotium, non adeo liquet. De Leviticis Sa- cerdotibus potius agitur, & cum iis comparatio instituitur. Descriptio tamen illa adeo com- munis est, ut facile illis etiam applicari possit. Theophylactus explicari primum, quæ Christo cum cæteris sunt communia, deinde quæ ei sunt propria, monet. Ex hominibus igitur, inquit, ad Pontificatum assumi commune est CHRISTO cum cæteris. Ipse namque cum homo existeret, Pon- tifex est à Deo effectus. Et pro hominibus con- stitui, in his quæ ad DEUM sunt, id est, inter- cessionem facere vel id quidem est illi commune cum cæteris.

Ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων καθίσταται τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν) Brevis lo- quutio, qualis & supra II. vers. 17. Constituitur ad rem divinam peragendam pro hominibus. Dicunt Judæi, prout summus Sacerdos se gerit: Ita Deum populo esse infensum aut propitium. Philo de legibus specialibus de summo sa- cerdote sic loquitur: Βούλεται γὰρ αὐτὸν ὁ νόμος μείζονος μεμοιρᾶσθαι φύσεως, ἢ κατ᾿ ἄνθρωπον, ἵνα διὰ μέσου τινὸς ἀνθρώ- ποις μὲν ἱλάσκηται Θεὸν, Θεὸς δὲ τὰς χάριτας ὀρέγῃ καὶ χο- ρηγῇ. Rursus de præmiis & pœnis. Τέτακται δὲ ἀρχιερωσύνη, δι᾽ ἧς προφητεύων ἐπιστημονικῶς θεραπεύσει τὸ ὂν, καὶ τὰς τῶν ὑπηκόων κατορθώσει εὐχαριστίας, οἱ δὲ διαμαρτάνοιεν εὐχὰς καὶ ἱκεσίας ἱλασκόμενος ποιήσεται.

Nonnulli verbum καθίσταται accipiunt sensu Activo, constituit, quæ sunt ad Deum. Sed pas- sive accipiendum esse paraleila docent, Ebr. IIX. vers. 3. Jac. III. 6. cap. IV. vers. 4. Traditioni Judæorum hic nulla est fides. Justus enim sua fide vivet, inquit Hab. cap. II. 4.

Ἵνα προσφέρῃ δῶρά τε καὶ θυσίας ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν) Explicat generalitatem per species quasdam. Δῶρα קרבנים est generale, sed eximie dicitur de holocaustis, ut videre est Levit. I. 2. Θυσίαι item satis generale. Comprehendit enim & מנחה: Sed cum hic addatur ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν, intelligen- dum חטאת, de quo Levit. IV. 3. & sequentibus. Ὑπὲρ hic, pro quo alibi est περὶ, significat ob. Et in Manuscripto infra 3. pro ὑπὲρ scribitur περὶ.

Θυσίαι offerebantur non tantum ob peccata, sed pro peccatis, expiandis scilicet. Sensu sacri- ficiali tales phrases explicandæ sunt, de quibus contra Socinianos alibi pluribus. Theophylactus hic explicari putat, quid illud sit, pro hominibus ipsis ad Deum constitui, peccatis scilicet DEUM Propitium reddere. Quod utique & Christo est, & si non penitus, commune cum aliis : quippe qui Patrem conciliandi gratia seipsum obtulerit. Alii vero alia quædam, donum videlicet & sacrificium. Sed illud καθίςασθαι τὰ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν generalius est, omnes complectens Sacerdotis partes, ad quas non pertinent tantum sacrificia, sed & intercessio- nes apud Deum.

## 5:2
Ver. 2.

Being able to have compassion on the ignorant and erring) Μετριοπαθεῖν is to be not unkindly affected. Thus Appian in his Iberian history said μετριοπαθῶ for to be clement. In the Glosses, μετριοπαθῶ is I moderate. And Aristotle said the wise man is μετριοπαθῆ, not ἀπαθῆ. Μετριοπαθῶν is משכיל אל-דל, Ps. XLI. ver. 1. He rightly adds, however, to the ignorant and erring, because in that place of Leviticus it is added: נפש כי-תחטא בשגגה. In the Greek, If a soul shall sin against the Lord unwittingly, for which Aquila, in ignorance. Both that unwittingly and in ignorance is not taken as it is among the Philosophers, but in such a way that the fault is posited without guile, as in those things which are done through forgetfulness of the law, or by sudden impulse without deliberation. In more serious crimes, if they had become known, the high priest could do nothing, he was unable and there was no remission of punishment, says Josephus against Apion II. Πλανᾶσθαι here is to do something through thoughtlessness. And so פתי is translated both as foolish and as innocent. Moreover, this Dative is placed here for περὶ with the Accusative, just as ל is placed by the Hebrews for על. And δυνάμενος here is again to be referred to the proneness of the affections, as above II. 18. IV. 15.

Some wish the word μετριοπαθεῖν to be to be moved with a certain moderation, so that one does not sin in defect through apathy, nor in excess through excessive sympathy. However, that the high priest could do nothing in more serious crimes is perhaps not a Scriptural, but a Socinian and Jewish opinion. For even the most serious crimes were expiated by the Priests through sacrifices, which is most well-known even from the annual solemn expiation: See also Levit. ch. II. and IV. Theophylact does not understand ignorance specifically, but as it has a place in all sins: Observe, he says, how every kind of wickedness is born from ignorance and error. For even if the mind seems to know what evil it is performing: yet when it exercises it, having darkened the mind, it labors under the disease of insanity and error, and is carried headlong by the allurements of pleasures.

Since he himself also is compassed with infirmity) ἀσθένεια is a general word, which is referred now to the mind, now to the body. Here it signifies that it can happen to the high priest that he either forgets some precept out of so many, or that it does not come to his mind so suddenly. See Rom. IV. 19.

The Pontiff was not only liable to sins of forgetfulness or ignorance, but also to more serious ones, which redound from carnal infirmity, whence he was bound to offer περὶ ἀυτõ for himself, ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν for his own sins, just as for the people. The infirmity of the flesh spreads itself in various ways, just as it is commonly said of original sin, that it has an influence toward sins of every kind. Add that some, as Theophylact observes, understand these things in such a way that the Pontiff differs from the people in only one thing, because he pities and spares others, while in other respects he himself is, like the rest of men, encompassed by infirmity.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Μετριοπαθεῖν δυνάμενος τοῖς ἀγνοῦσι καὶ πλανωμένοις) Μετριοπαθεῖν est non inclementer affici. Sic μετριοπαθῶς pro clementer dixit Appianus Iberico. In Glossis μετριοπαθῶ moderor. Et Aristoteles sapientem dixit esse μετριοπαθῆ, non ἀπαθῆ. Μετριοπαθῶν est משכיל אל-דל, Ps. XLI. vers. 1. Recte autem addit ἀγνοῦσι, καὶ πλανωμένοις, quia in loco illo Levitici additur :נפש כי-תחטא בשגגה In Græco Ψυχὴ ἁμάρτῃ ἐναντίον Κυρίου ἀκουσίως, pro quo Aquila, ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ. Utrumque & illud ἀκουσίως & ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ non sumitur ut apud Philosophos, sed ita, ut culpa ponatur sine dolo, ut in iis, quæ per oblivionem legis fiunt, aut subito motu absque deliberatione. In criminibus gravioribus, si innotuissent, nihil poterat Sacerdos summus, ἀδύνατος ἦν & κολάσεως παραίτησις, ait Josephus contra Appionem II. Πλανᾶσθαι נפחה hic est per incogitantiam aliquid agere. Itaque פתי vertitur & ἄφρων & ἄκακος. Est autem hic Dativus positus pro περὶ cum Accusativo, sicut & ל Ebræis pro על ponitur. Et δυνάμενος hic rursus ad affectus pronitatem referendum est, ut supra II. 18. IV. 15.

Verbum μετριοπαθεῖν nonnulli volunt esse cum moderatione quadam commoveri, ut nec in defectu peccetur per ἀπάθειαν, nec in excessu per nimiam συμπάθειαν. In criminibus autem gravioribus nihil potuisse summum Sacerdotem, non Scripturæ, sed Sociniana forte & Judaica est sententia. Expiabantur enim per sacrificia etiam gravissima crimina à Sacerdotibus, quod vel ex anniversaria solenni expiatione notissimum est: Vid. & Levit. cap. II. & IV. Theophylactus ignorantiam non specialiter intelligit, sed qua in omnibus peccatis locum ea habet : Adverte, inquit, ut ex ignorantia & errore omne facinorum genus gignatur. Nam etsi nosse animo, quod peragit malum, videtur : Tamen cum illud exercet, mentem obtenebratus, insaniæ & erroris morbo laborat, & voluptatum illecebris præceps defertur.

Ἐπεὶ καὶ αὐτὸς περίκειται τὴν ἀσθένειαν) ἀσθένεια vox est generalis, quæ modo ad animum, modo ad corpus refertur. Hic significat accidere summo Sacerdoti posse, ut aut obliviscatur præcepti alicujus de tam multis, aut ut id non ita repente ipsi in mentem veniat. Vide Rom. IV. 19.

Non tantum obnoxius erat Pontifex peccatis oblivionis aut ignorantiæ, sed etiam gravioribus, quæ ex infirmitate carnali redundant, unde æque περὶ ἀυτõ pro seipso, ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν pro peccatis propriis offerre tenebatur, ac pro populo. Ἀσθένεια carnis se diffundit varie, quemadmodum de peccato originis vulgo dicitur, quod influentiam habeat ad omnis generis peccata. Adde, quod nonnulli, observante Theophylacto, hæc ita intelligant, vel una re solum Pontificem differre à populo, quia aliis commiseretur & parcit, cum in cæteris sit & ipse, ut reliqui homines infirmitate præcinctus.

## 5:3
Ver. 3.

And by reason of this he ought, as for the people, so also for himself to offer for sins) Περὶ τõ λαõ is understood in two ways, either distributively for each of the people, of which kind of sacrifice the said chapter Levit. IV. treats, or collectively, such as the sacred rite that was performed once in the turning of the year on the days of כפרים and is described in Levit. XVI. Thus also the Pontiff, if he were conscious that he had committed something through forgetfulness or thoughtlessness, offered a calf, Levit. IV. ver. 2. But if he were not conscious of it to himself, yet because it could happen that he had slipped by not rightly understanding some precept, in that annual sacred rite he offered a calf for himself and his house, as can be seen in Levit. XVI. ver. 6, 11, 17. But since this is said generally of every Priest, it follows that Christ also offered for himself for sins, that is, so that he might be able to be freed from those pains which are wont to be the punishment of sins; and were inflicted upon him on the occasion of our sins: but he offered prayers.

Grotius also drew this opinion from the Socinians, namely that Christ offered for himself for sins. But the argument for that impious opinion is very flimsy. He says it is affirmed generally of every Priest. But Theophylact has already rightly observed before that some things are common to all Priests, others not so. For some things are proper to Christ, inasmuch as he himself had no need to offer for his own sins, seeing that he knew no sin, 2 Cor. V. ver. 21, and was devoid of all sin, Heb. VII. ver. 26. Which distinction the Apostle openly assigned there in ver. 27. Therefore Theophylact most rightly: Christ shares nothing at all of all these things with the others. For he was not liable to such infirmity of sins. Nor did he offer a sacrifice for himself, but for other men. It is not fitting to take the word sins for those pains which are wont to be the punishment of sins, and were inflicted upon CHRIST on the occasion of our sins. For 1. to seek tropes and figures, abandoning the propriety of words, is against the rule of correct interpretation. But the word sins properly denotes sins. 2. That that word is taken somewhere for pains inflicted on the occasion of sins has not yet been proven. 3. If it occurred thus elsewhere, it could not yet be taken so here, because by one and the same word once placed, both his own sins and those of the people are expressed. Therefore, what is denoted by that word when it is referred to the people: the same must also be denoted when it is referred to the Priest. But there it denotes sins properly so called, which were to be expiated through the offering of sacrifices. 4. Concerning the Priest of the Old Testament, Grotius concedes that he offered the same for his own sins properly so called, or for those which he had committed against the law. If, therefore, that general description of a Priest is also to be accepted concerning CHRIST, and CHRIST is to be compared with the Priest of the Old Testament in this, that he likewise offered not only for the people's sins, but also for his own, it is necessary to say that CHRIST committed certain things against the law, which is impious. 5. In that in which Christ is distinguished from the Priest of the Old Testament, in that he cannot be compared with him. And yet in the offering for his own sins Christ is distinguished from the Priest of the Old Testament, Heb. VII. verse 6. 6. It is false that only sorrows, which are wont to be the punishments of sins, were inflicted upon CHRIST. For just as he truly took our sins upon himself and bore them, Is. LIII. verse 6, John I. verse 29, so also he sustained the punishments of our sins and endured them for us. He was afflicted with them not only on the occasion of our sins, but by the merit of the same, because he was wounded for our sins and struck for our iniquities, as Isaiah testifies: delivered for our sins, as the Apostle testifies, Rom. IV. last verse. Which Grotius himself, against Socinus, who asserted that Christ took upon himself our sorrows only on the occasion of our sins, treated at greater length, and proved in his Treatise on the Satisfaction of CHRIST that Christ sustained the punishments of our sins by the merit of our sins, that our sins were the meritorious cause of the afflictions of Christ, and that those afflictions were truly the punishments of sins which CHRIST sustained. 7. It is not a question here of the offering of prayers, but of sacrifices for sins: not only of liberation from sorrows, but of liberation from the penalties and the guilt of sins. Therefore, they are mere false interpretations drawn from the pits of Socinus, which Grotius injects.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Καὶ διὰ ταύτην ὀφείλει, καθὼς περὶ τõ λαõ, ὅτω καὶ περὶ ἑαυτõ προσφέρειν ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν) Περὶ τõ λαõ dupliciter intelligitur, aut distributim pro singulis de populo, de quali sacrificio agitur dicto capite Levit. IV. aut collectim, quale sacrum fiebat semel vertente anno in diebus כפרים & describitur Levit. XVI. Sic & Pontifex si conscius esset se per oblivionem aut incogitantiam aliquid commisisse, offerebat vitulum, Levit. IV. vers. 2. quod si non esset sibi ejus conscius, tamen quia fieri poterat, ut lapsus esset, præceptum aliquod non recte intelligendo, in anniversario illo sacro vitulum pro se ac domo sua offerebat, ut videre est Levit. XVI. vers. 6. 11. 17. Cum autem hoc generaliter dicitur de omni Sacerdote, sequitur Christum quoque obtulisse pro se ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν, id est, ut à doloribus illis, qui peccatorum pœnæ esse solent; & occasione nostrorum peccatorum ipsi infligebantur, posset liberari: obtulit autem preces.

Hanc sententiam hausit etiam à Socinianis Grotius, Christum nempe pro se ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν obtulisse. Argumentum autem impiæ istius opinionis valde leviculum est. Dicit generaliter de omni Sacerdote id affirmari. Sed recte jam observavit antea Theophylactus, quædam communia esse omnibus Sacerdotibus, alia non item. Quædam enim Christo esse propria, utpote quod opus non habuerit ipse pro peccatis suis offerre, quippe qui peccatum non novit, 2. Cor. V. v. 21. omnisque peccati expers fuit, Ebr. VII. vers. 26. Quod discrimen ibi aperte assignavit Apostolus vers. 27. Ideo Theophylactus rectissime: Horum omnium cum cæteris nihil quippiam participat Christus. Non enim erat ejusmodi peccatorum infirmitati obnoxius. Neque pro seipso, sed pro hominibus cæteris sacrificium obtulit. Non convenit vocem ἁμαρτιῶν accipere pro doloribus illis, qui peccatorum pœnæ esse solent, & occasione nostrorum peccatorum CHRISTO inflicti sunt. Nam 1. desertâ proprietate verborum tropos & figuras quærere contra rectæ interpretationis regulam est. Vox autem ἁμαρτιῶν peccata proprie notat. 2. Vocem illam alicubi pro doloribus occasione peccatorum inflictis accipi, nondum probatum est. 3. Si alibi sic occurreret, hic ita tamen accipi non posset, quia una eademque voce semel posita ἁμαρτίαι tum propriæ tum populi exprimuntur. Quod ergo voce ista notatur, cum ad populum refertur: Idem etiam necessum est notari, cum refertur ad Sacerdotem. At ibi peccata proprie dicta notat, quæ per sacrificiorum oblationem expianda erant. 4. De Sacerdote Veteris Testamenti concedit Grotius, obtulisse eundem pro peccatis suis proprie dictis, vel pro iis, quæ contra legem commiserat. Si ergo generalis illa descriptio Sacerdotis de CHRISTO etiam accipienda, & CHRISTUS cum Sacerdote Veteris Testamenti in eo conferendus est, quod pariter non pro populi tantum, sed suis etiam peccatis obtulerit, necessum est dicere, CHRISTUM quædam contra legem commisisse, quod impium est. 5. In quo Christus à Sacerdote Veteris Testamenti distinguitur, in eo cum ipso comparari nequit. Atqui in oblatione pro peccatis propriis distinguitur Christus à Sacerdote Veteris Testamenti, Ebr. VII. vers. 6. 6. Falsum est, CHRISTO tantum dolores, qui peccatorum pœnæ esse solent, inflictos. Nam uti vere peccata nostra in se suscepit, & tulit, Es. LIII. vers. 6. Joh. I. vers. 29. Ita etiam peccatorum nostrorum pœnas sustinuit, & pro nobis exantlavit. Non occasione tantùm peccatorum nostrorum; sed merito eorundem iisdem afflictus fuit, quia vulneratus est propter peccata nostra, & percussus propter iniquitates nostras, teste Esaia: traditus propter peccata nostra, teste Apostolo, Rom. IV. vers. ult. Quæ Grotius ipse contra Socinum, occasione peccatorum nostrorum tantum dolores nostros Christum sucepisse asserentem, prolixius tractavit, ac Christum merito peccatorum nostrorum pœnas sustinuisse, peccata nostra causam meritoriam afflictionum Christi, afflictiones vero illas vere pœnas peccatorum fuisse, quas sustinuit CHRISTUS, Tractatu de Satisfactione CHRISTI evicit. 7. Non hic de oblatione precum, sed sacrificiorum pro peccatis agitur: non de liberatione tantum à doloribus, sed à pœnis & à culpa peccatorum tractatur. Me- ræ ergo ψευδερμηνείαι sunt è Socini lacunis haustæ, quas ingerit Grotius.

## 5:4
Verse 4.

And no one takes the honor to himself) By the law, it is permitted to no one to thrust himself into that office by his own choice.

But he who is called by God, just as Aaron was) He, of course, receives this honor. Now, after the time of Aaron, individuals were not called by God (for in those cases the election of the Senate or the King prevailed, with the Prophets sometimes shining forth), but the whole lineage of Aaron, beyond which the election could not go.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Καὶ ἐκ ἑαυτῷ τις λαμβάνῃ τὴν τιμὴν) Per legem nemi- ni licet se ingerere in id munus, suo arbitratu.

Ἀλλὰ ὁ καλέμενος ὑπὸ τῦ Θεῦ, καθώςπερ καὶ ὁ Ἀαρών) Is scilicet honorem hunc accipit. Vocabantur autem à DEO post Aaronis tempus non singuli, (nam in iis aut Senatus aut Regis electio valebat, prælucentibus interdum Prophetis) sed tota stirps Aaronis, quam egredi electio non poterat.

## 5:5
Verse 5.

So also Christ did not glorify himself to be made high priest) that is, for the being made, which kind of particles are often left unsaid: he did not exalt himself, like Korah and Dathan. See John VIII. 54. In the Manuscript, for 'to be born' (gennethenai) there is 'to be' (genesthai).

But he who spoke to him, You are my son, today I have begotten you) O my son, today I have begotten you, that is, I have bestowed upon you a new dignity, a kingdom joined with the priesthood. See above I. verse 5. Acts XIII. verse 33, and what we have said regarding Psalm II. Jesus had indeed begun his priestly office in some way when he offered himself as a victim to the Father: but that did not sufficiently appear. But then it clearly appeared that he was constituted by God not only King, but also high Priest, when, with the Apostles watching, he was raised to the highest heaven, which all the Hebrews knew was signified by the inner sanctuary of the temple, into which the high Priest alone entered: and we showed this in Matthew XXVII. v. 50. The firstborn of families were priests before the law, but Christ by a better right, as he is the firstborn of God himself, Rom. VIII. 29. Coloss. I. 15. above I. 6.

The Apostle has already shown the necessity of the calling. But the second Psalm is cited, not to prove that it treats of the Priesthood of Christ by design, and much less that those words: 'I have today begotten you,' are to be accepted as: 'I have bestowed upon you a new dignity, a kingdom joined with the priesthood': But for other reasons: First, because God the Father is established there as the fountain and origin of the Son, from whom, just as he received his essence through eternal generation: so he himself possesses everything that he has. Then, because the Anointed of the Lord is spoken of there in verse 1. Now he was anointed to an office not only Prophetic and Royal, but also Priestly: just as Priests and Prophets and Kings were accustomed to be anointed in the Old Testament. Third, because the passion of Christ is treated in that Psalm, according to the interpretation of Peter, or rather the whole choir of the disciples, Acts IV. verse 15. Now these things pertain to the Priesthood of Christ. Therefore, by whose decree Christ endured the passion, by him he was destined and ordained to the Priesthood. But he endured that by the decree of God the Father, by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, Acts II. verse 38. Fourth, the Messiah is commanded to ask and request that the nations be granted to him as an inheritance, and the ends of the earth as a possession, verse 8. But this pertains to the office of the Priesthood, to ask and intercede for men, that they may be and become the inheritance of the Lord and the peculiar people of CHRIST. Fifth, the blessed Dorscheus observes here that from the ancient right of sonship there is a legitimate process to the Priesthood. For the right to that office belonged to the Priests of the Old Testament from him, because they were assumed in place of the firstborn.
