For by ancient right, access to the Priesthood in the Patriarchal family belonged to the firstborn. See Genesis XXVII. verse 21. following, XLIV. verse 3. Whoever, therefore, is a son, and indeed the firstborn and only-begotten, he is a Priest by the most ancient right of birth in the house of his Father. But indeed Christ is the Firstborn and Only-begotten Son of God. Therefore, by the very right of birth, he had access to the Pontificate, no less than the Pontiffs of the Old Testament. Meanwhile, it must be observed that the Apostle intended in this place primarily to designate and describe God the Father, and by this periphrasis, used with singular purpose from Psalm II. verse 7, to teach at the same time that Christ is the Son of God, because it was certain and undoubted to the Hebrews that the same Psalm treats of Christ. For he says nothing else than this: He who said to Christ: 'You are my son, today I have begotten you,' glorified Christ so that he might be Pontiff, but he does not say that by the very fact that he said this, he constituted him Pontiff. He confirms that thesis by the collation of the passage in Psalm CX. verse 1, 'just as' he says in the other place. That 'and' looks back to the antecedent 'to him,' just as it says elsewhere to him, to show that these things were likewise said to CHRIST: 'You are a Priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.' From which place it is manifest that the confirmation of the Priesthood of CHRIST is drawn. Therefore, it is rashly sought by Grotius with the Socinians in Psalm II, which was brought forward primarily for the periphrasis of him who constituted Christ a Priest, which is God the Father, and not for the proof of the Priesthood of CHRIST, or that God the Father professes himself there to be the Author of the Priesthood. Therefore, the passage of Psalm II is signally perverted, which does not treat of a kingdom joined with the priesthood, but of the eternal generation of CHRIST from the Father, as was shown regarding that Psalm: Nor was it brought forward otherwise in Heb. I. verse 5. Regarding the passage in Acts XIII. verse 33, in the annotations. We have argued to the same effect in our own works: That Christ in some way only began his priestly office when he offered himself as a victim to the Father, smells of the Socinian lamp. For CHRIST then finished his priestly office with his former oblation, which consisted in the offering of a sacrifice, and that on the altar of the cross. Moreover, the proof of the priesthood ought not to have been made only regarding the other function, namely intercession, which takes place in the heavens. Add that from the mere sight of his entry into heaven it could not yet clearly appear that CHRIST was entering into the Holy of Holies, so that our High Priest might intercede there for us, since Elisha also saw Elijah taken up into heaven, whom for that reason he neither gathered, nor could or ought to have gathered. If it be asked why the Apostle proves the calling of CHRIST to the High Priesthood so laboriously, the reason is this: because he was not from the family of Aaron, and not even from the tribe of Levi, which alone was priestly, but from the royal family of Judah, whence a scruple could arise for the Hebrews concerning his priesthood.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Οὕτω καὶ ὁ χριστὸς ἐκ ἑαυτὸν ἐδόξασε γεννηθῆναι ἀρχιερέα) id est, εἰς τὸ γεννηθῆναι, quales particulæ sæpe subticentur : non semet extulit, ut Core & Dathan. Vide Joh. VIII. 54. In Manuscripto pro γεννηθῆναι est γενέσθαι.

Ἀλλ' ὁ λαλήσας πρὸς αὐτὸν, ὑός μυ εἶ σὺ, ἐγὼ σήμερον γεγέννηκά σε) O fili mi, ego hodie te genui, id est, novam dignitatem tibi tribui,regnum cum sacerdotio conjunctum. Vide supra I. vers. 5. Actor. XIII. vers. 33. & quæ ad Psalm. II. nobis dicta. Jesus Sacerdotale quidem munus suum aliquo modo erat auspicatus, cum semet Patri victimam offerret: sed id non satis apparebat. Tunc autem plane apparuit, eum non Regem tantum, sed & Sacerdotem summum à DEO constitutum, cum Apostolis spectantibus evectus est ad cœlum supremum, quod per templi adytum, in quod summus Sacerdos solus intrabat, figurari omnes Hebræi noverant : & nos ostendimus Matth. XXVII. v. 50. Primogeniti familiarum ante legem Sacerdotes, Christus autem meliori jure quippe DEI ipsius primogenitus, Rom. VIII. 29. Coloss. I. 15. supra I. 6.

Vocationis necessitatem jam ostendit Apostolus. Psalmus vero secundus affertur, non ut probetur, ibi ex instituto agi de Christi Sacerdotio, mul- to vero minus verba illa: Ego hodie genui te, sic accipienda, novam dignitatem tibi tribui regnum cum sacerdotio conjunctum: Sed ob alias causas: Primo, quod ibi DEUS, Pater fons & origo constituatur Filii, à quo uti essentiam accepit per æternam generationem: ita omnia ipse ha- bet, quæ habet. Deinde quod illic dicatur un- ctus Domini vers. 1. Unctus autem est ad officium non tantum Propheticum & Regium, sed etiam Sacerdotale: quemadmodum ungi Sacerdotes & Prophetæ & Reges solebant in Veteri Testa- mento. Tertio, quod de passione Christi agatur in eo Psalmo, interprete Petro, vel potius toto discipulorum choro, Actor. IV. vers. 15. Hæc autem ad Sacerdotium Christi pertinent. Cujus ergo definitione Christus passionem sustinuit, ab eo ad Sacerdotium destinatus & ordinatus est. At illam sustinuit DEI Patris definitione τῇ ὡρισμένῃ βυλῇ καὶ προγνώσει τῷ Θεῦ, Actor. II. vers. 38.. Quarto petere ac postulare jubetur Mes- sias, ut concedantur sibi gentes in hæreditatem, & fines terræ in peculium, vers. 8. At hoc ad Sacerdotii munus pertinet, petere ac interce- dere pro hominibus, ut sint & evadant hære- ditas Domini & populus CHRISTI περιύσιος. Quinto Beatus Dorscheus hic observat, quod ex antiquo jure ὑότητος ad Sacerdotium legitimus processus sit. Sacerdotibus enim Veteris Testamen- ti jus ad illud munus competebat ex eo, qui in vi- cem primogenitorum assumpti sunt. Primogenitis enim vetusto jure aditus ad Sacerdotium in fami- lia Patriarchali competebat. Vid. Genes. XXVII. vers. 21. seqq. XLIV. vers. 3. Qui itaque filius est, & quidem primogenitus atque unigenitus, is ju- re nativitatis antiquissimo in domo Patris sui Sa- cerdos est. Atqui vero Christus Primogenitus & Unigenitus DEI Filius est. Ipso itaque nativita- tis jure aditum ad Pontificatum habuit, non minus, quam Pontifices Veteris Testamenti. Interim ob- servandum, designare Apostolum hoc loco im- primis voluisse, ac describere DEUM Patrem, atque hac περιφράσει studio singulari è Psalm. II. vers. 7. adhibita simul docere, Christum esse DEI Filium, quia de Christo eundem Psalmum agere Ebræis certum & indubitatum erat. Nec enim quicquam aliud dicit, quam hoc: Is, qui ad Christum dixit: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te, glorificavit Christum, ut esset Pontifex, non vero ait, eo ipso, quo id dixit, constituit eum Pontificem. Illam autem thesin collatione loci Psalm. CX. vers. 1. confirmat, καθὼς sicut & in altero loco dicit. Illud καὶ respicit Antece- dens πρὸς αὐτὸν, quemadmodum & alibi ad ipsum dicit, ut ostendat hæc itidem ad CHRISTUM dicta esse: Tu es Sacerdos in æternum secun- dum ordinem Melchisedech. E quo loco mani- festum est, depromi confirmationem Sacerdo- tii CHRISTI. Temerè ergo ea quæritur à Grotio cum Socinianis in Psalm. II. qui addu- ctus est præcipue ad periphrasin ejus, qui Chri- stum Sacerdotem constituit, quod sit DEUS Pater, non vero ad probationem Sacerdotii CHRISTI, aut quod DEUS Pater ibi sese Autorem Sacerdotii profiteatur. Insigniter er- go pervertitur locus Psalmi II. qui non agit de regno cum sacerdotio conjuncto, sed de æterna generatione CHRISTI à Patre, quemadmodum ad illum Psalmum ostensum: Nec aliter Ebr. I. vers. 5. adductus est. De loco Actor. XIII. vers. 33. in annot. nostris ad eundem egimus: Aliquo modo Christum tantum Sacerdotale munus auspi- catum esse, cum semet Patri victimam offerret, So- cinianam lucernam olet. CHRISTUS enim tum oblatione sua priori defunctus est sacerdotii munere, quod in sacrificii oblatione consistebat, idque in ara crucis. Probatio autem sacerdo- tii non debebat tantum fieri quoad alteram fun- ctionem, nempe intercessionem, quæ in cœlis fit. Adde, quod ex nudo conspectu ingres- sus in cœlum nondum plane apparere potuerit, CHRISTUM in Sanctum Sanctorum ingredi, ut Pontifex noster illic intercederet pro nobis, quum & Elisæus conspexerit Eliam transsum- ptum in cœlum, quem ea de causa transsum- ptum nec colligebat, nec colligere poterat aut debebat. Si quæratur, quomodo tam operose Apostolus probet vocationem CHRISTI ad Pontificatum, causa hæc est, quia non erat ex Aaronis familia, ac ne quidem ex tribu Levi, quæ sola sacerdotalis erat, sed ex Regia Judæ fa- milia, unde scrupulus Ebræis oriri poterat de sa- cerdotio ejus.

## 5:6
Vers. 6.

Καθὼς καὶ ἐν ἑτέρῳ λέγει) Supply τόπῳ. For thus the Greeks call that which the Hebrews call פרשת: the Greeks also call it περιοχὴ, concerning which we have spoken in Acts VIII. 32.

Σὺ Ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα κατὰ τὴν τάξιν τῦ Μελχισεδὲκ) So also below 10. VI. v. 20. VII. v. 11. 17. 21. From the Greek of Psalm CX. In the Hebrew that κατὰ τὴν τάξιν is על־דברתי which below VII. v. 15. is well rendered according to the sense as κατὰ τὴν ὁμοιότητα. In the Syriac ברמותא, that is, after the manner of. דברה is condition or manner, as in Ecclesiastes III. 18. Thus τάξις is used in 2 Maccabees IX. 18. It is a not poorly used Greek word. For the Greeks say, ἐν τάξει ἔχειν γαμετᾶς, ἐν ἰχθυῶν τάξει, τάξιν ἔχειν πολιτῆς, τάξει νόμο, and similar things which signify that this is like another thing. After the manner of Melchizedek, that is, in a most august manner, by which kingdom and priesthood were joined together at the same time, as before the law of Moses. Εἰς αἰῶνα means without a successor.

Concerning Psalm CX, we have treated this in the annotations to the book of Psalms. Even if it were admitted that a likeness is introduced by the word κατὰ τάξιν; yet properly the order or a certain constitution of the priesthood is denoted, that CHRIST had to be a Priest, not according to the law and ordinance of the Levitical priests, but according to the order of Melchizedek, whose priesthood had a different law and ordinance. He was both King and High Priest at the same time, such as the Levitical Priests were not. Nor is there any reason why we should depart from the propriety of the word εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, by which eternity is denoted, and not the lack of a successor, especially because it is openly taught that He remains in the Priesthood eternally, Heb. 7. 24, and lives and intercedes perpetually, and thus performs the priesthood forever, v. 25.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Καθὼς καὶ ἐν ἑτέρῳ λέγει) Supple τόπῳ. Ita enim Græci vocant id, quod Ebræi פרשת: Græci etiam περιοχὴ, qua de re diximus Actor. VIII. 32.

Σὺ Ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα κατὰ τὴν τάξιν τῦ Μελχισεδὲκ) Sic & infra 10. VI. v. 20. VII. v. 11. 17. 21. Ex Græco Psalm. CX. In Ebræo illud κατὰ τὴν τάξιν est על־דברתי quod infra VII. v. 15. benè ad sensum effertur κατὰ τὴν ὁμοιότητα. In Syriaco ברמותא, id est, ad modum. דברה conditio aut modus, ut Ecclesiastæ III. 18. Sic τάξις sumitur 2. Mac- cab. IX. 18. Est vox non male Græca. Dicunt enim Græ- ci, ἐν τάξει ἔχειν γαμετᾶς, ἐν ἰχθυῶν τάξει, τάξιν ἔχειν πολιτῆς, τάξει νόμο, & similia quæ significant, hoc esse instar rei al- terius. Ad modum Melchisedeci, id est, modo augustissi- mo, quo regnum simul & sacerdotium jungebantur, ut ante legem Mosis. Εἰς αἰῶνα valet sine successore.

De Psalm. CX. in annotat. ad librum Psalmo- rum actum. Similitudinem inferri voce κα- τὰ τάξιν etsi admitteretur; proprie tamen ordo notatur vel certa constitutio sacerdotii, quod non secundum legem & ordinationem sa- cerdotum Levitici, sed secundum ordinem Mel- chisedeci, cujus sacerdotii alia lex fuit & ordina- tio, Sacerdos CHRISTUS esse debuerit. Qui fuit & Rex, & Pontifex simul, quales non fuere Sacer- dotes Levitici. Neque est cur à vocis εἰς τὸν αἰῶ- να proprietate discedamus, qua æternitas notatur, non vero carentia successoris, imprimis quia æter- num manere in Pontificatu, Ebr. 7. 24. & perpetuo vivere ac intercedere, adeoque in æternum sacer- dotio fungi, v. 25. palam docetur.

## 5:7
Vers. 7.

ὄς ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τῆς σαρκὸς ἁυτῦ) That is, in the time of His state of being infirm and subject to many evils, which is often accustomed to be signified among the Hebrews by the name בשׂר, that is, σαρκὸς, as in Isaiah XXXI. 3, or even by the words בשׂר ודם σαρκὸς καὶ αἵματος, as above II. 14, because the constitution of the human body, which in the Holy Scriptures is called flesh and blood, makes us subject to those evils.

It is now proved by another document that Christ has His priesthood from God the Father. He whom CHRIST prayed to for His deliverance from death, and from whom He was heard and perfected, and became the cause of eternal salvation to those who obey Him, He, I say, without any controversy called and appointed CHRIST as High Priest. As this consequence radiates with its own light, so the Apostle rightly adds that for that reason CHRIST was named High Priest by GOD according to the order of Melchizedek. For He is the cause of our salvation for this very reason: because He is High Priest, both by the offering of a sacrifice for our sins and by His mediatorial intercession for us. The blessed Gerhard thinks that the Apostle is adapting to Christ here the fact that the High Priest offered prayers not only for the people but also for himself, although not for the same cause. The High Priest in the Old Testament offered prayers to obtain the remission of his own sins, but Christ offered them to obtain deliverance from distress. The days of His flesh are certainly explained as the days of His infirmity. Compare Psalm 56, 5; Psalm 78, 39; Heb. 5, 16. The blessed Dorsheus notes that the days of the flesh are opposed to the days of eternity. Christ had both because of His dual nature. The days of eternity, Micah 5, 2. But the days of the flesh are so called according to His human nature, because they belong to Christ from the property and condition of true flesh. They are the duration of the human nature suitable in these lands. They follow the act of the human nature, and indeed placed in a state of emptying, so that they even include the μορφὴν δύλε, Phil. 2, 7.

Δεήσεις τε καὶ ἱκετηρίας πρὸς τὸν δυνάμενον σώζειν αὐτὸν ἐκ θανάτυ μετὰ κραυγῆς ἰσχυρᾶς καὶ δακρύων προσενέγκας) Δεήσεις is a noun of the genus. Ἱκετηρία signifies something more, prayers that are very submissive, as in 2 Maccabees IX. 18, and תחנון, which signifies great anxiety, is translated by ἱκετεύων, as can be seen in Psalm XXXVII. 7. In the glosses, ἱκετηρία is prayer, supplication, entreaty. ἱκετεύω is I supplicate, I pray. Reference is made here especially to that time when Christ most felt the infirmity of human nature, when, as if forsaken by Divine power, He vehemently dreaded death joined with such great torments, so that there would be nothing human that He had not endured, He who was the Son of GOD, lest we should think ourselves despised by GOD for this reason if such things sometimes happened to us, and not believe nonetheless that we are also in our own way sons of GOD; see Matthew XXVI. 37, 38, 39, 42, 44; Mark XIV. 33; Luke XXII. 42, 43, 44. What in the old law were ignorances and thoughtlessness, those in CHRIST were natural affections, which arise from pain or the fear of pain, which prevailed in CHRIST to such an extent, by the providential permission of GOD, that He was not only λυπῶν, but also ἀδημονῶν, Matthew XXVI. 38. What then did He naturally desire? To be delivered from such a death: If the sole power of GOD is considered, it was not impossible for GOD to grant the effect, Mark XIV. 36. But that this should not happen was for the benefit of the human race, ἐκ θανάτε, that is, ἐκ τύτε τῦ θανάτυ.

How far it was possible for Christ to be delivered from death, so that He would not fall into it, there is no need to dispute here, for the Apostle is not speaking of that deliverance: And it is certain that σώζειν is said not only of one who saves someone from evil so that he does not fall into it, but also of one who raises someone up from the evil into which he has fallen, which has a place here: Because Christ was heard by God in these prayers of His. Nor did the Son of God undergo death because He was made to suffer the most grievous sorrow, anxiety, and even the abandonment of God and the sense of infernal torments, so that we might not doubt that we are sons of God when we fall into the most grievous calamities and afflictions, but so that He might pay the penalty for us, or in our place, and deliver us from the same by the λύτρῳ and ἀντιλύτρῳ of His death, and expiate sins by the sacrifice of His death, appease the wrath of God, and redeem us from the punishments of sin. The sufferings and death of Christ are not to be viewed only as an example, which Pelagius and Abailard and the worst heretics, the Socinians, have wished, but as a merit: Which the Catholic Church has constantly held. However, the prayers understood are not so much those which He offered in the garden during His agony, as those which He is read to have offered on the altar of the cross, because there He did not cry out with a loud voice, and He prayed that the cup might pass, even under the hypothesis, if it were possible and the will of God the Father, where also nothing is expressly read about tears shed there: But here, both in that greatest and truly miserable cry, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me, and in the commendation of His Spirit made with a loud voice, He was heard by the Father, nor did He offer His prayers on the altar of the cross without tears, concerning which Estius says in this place: Although His tears are not read of: Nevertheless, just as He thirsted naturally from the dryness of an exhausted body, so it is credible that tears also naturally burst forth from Him because of His sorrows. For He permitted, according to the famous dictum of Damascenus, the proper actions to each natural faculty. For ἱκετηρία, as B. Dorscheus reminds us, is the prayer of suppliants, such as that of those who cast themselves at the feet, or touch the knees of those whom they entreat, or do something similar, which is to testify to humility. Whence also ἱκετηρία is called an olive branch wrapped in wool, which suppliants carried in their hand, Livy book IV: 'Extending olive branches as the veils of suppliants, they prayed that they might receive them, etc.' The sacrificial phrase προσενέγκας also fits perfectly with the prayers poured out by CHRIST the High Priest, offering Himself on the altar of the cross for His own liberation from death; because then He was substituted in our place, who had taken our guilt upon Himself, and was paying our penalty for us, offering our sins on the tree (ἀνήνεγκεν) in His body, 1. Petr. II. verse 24, whence in Him we have been saved and liberated from death; and therefore, as our vessel and sponsor satisfying for our sins, He had need to offer those prayers and supplications with tears and a loud voice, so that He might not be left in that death, in that desertion by the Father, in those infernal horrors and torments, but being saved from them, He might save us, and become the cause of our salvation.

Καὶ εἰσακουσθεὶς ἀπὸ τῆς εὐλαβειας) It is a contracted expression frequent in both Hebrew and Greek. The sense is: In this He was heard, that He might be liberated from that fear. A similar expression is in Psalm XXII. verse 22, where what is in the Hebrew עניתני is rightly translated 'you heard me,' that is, by hearing you liberated me from those horns of the unicorns, that is, of evil men. Thus Psalm LIV. 17, where in the Hebrew is וישיעני 'He will save me,' the LXX put εἰσήκουσέ με by metonymy. Ἀπὸ τῆς εὐλαβειας, that is, liberated from that fear of torments through an Angel sent to Him, Luke XXII. verse 43, through whom there was placed before His eyes that immense fruit to redound to men from those truly hard sufferings of His, and indeed joined with His own greatest glory, Phil. II. 9. Εὐλάβεια is that which ἀδημονεῖν is called in Matt. XXVI. verse 37. Mark XIV. verse 33. Thus Jos. XXII. verse 24. מִדְּאָגָה the Greeks translate ἕνεκα εὐλαβείας, which very Hebrew word in Proverbs XII. 26. is translated φοβερὸς λόγος. But the word itself דָּאַג is translated εὐλαβεῖσθαι in Isaiah LVII. 11. and φοβεῖσθαι in Jeremiah XVII. 8. chap. XI. v. 6. Thus Josephus concerning the King, the husband of Esther: Εὐλαβείως αὐτὴν ἀπολύων. And Luke himself in Acts XXIII. 10. used Εὐλαβηθεὶς for fearing. From that fear, therefore, Christ was liberated and with a strong spirit prepared himself to bear those sorrows; see what Nazianzen has to say on this passage.

After he had offered prayers, and had been heard, and had been perfected, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him, as the Aorist προσενέγκας has the meaning of the Present, and so also the words εἰσακουσθεὶς καὶ τελειωθείς. He is said to have been heard, however, because he was not only strengthened on the cross, and liberated from infernal horror and torture, and his Spirit received by the Father, but he was also raised from temporal and short-lived death into eternal life. But there is no need here to speak of a brief locution, or even to understand fear by εὐλάβειαν with Calvin, Beza, Toussain, and others: Rather, the reason is openly given why he was heard and saved from death, as Blessed Luther rightly interprets, 'darum daß er GOTT in Ehren hat' [because he holds GOD in honor], where the preposition ἀπὸ is put for διὰ, by which method the meaning of εὐλαβείας accepted in the Holy Scriptures is preserved: For this word nowhere in the Holy Scriptures occurs for fear, but for reverence, Heb. XII. verse 28. Luke II. verse 25. Acts II. verse 5. Which sense verse 8 confirms, and it has been embraced by Photius and Oecumenius, as well as most Latins; among our own, Blessed Hunnius, Blessed Gerhard, and others; among the Papists, Erasmus, Bellarmine, Estius, and most of the rest, Bullinger, Castellio, Pareus, etc. Camerarius: Ἀπὸ τῆς εὐλαβείας, that is, ἐκ τῆς εὐλαβείας, which signifies μετ᾽ εὐλαβείας προσευχόμενος, and what follows indicates the immense humility and submission of the Son of GOD in obeying the Father's will, when, having become man, he sustained the wrath of GOD derived upon himself and appeased GOD reconciled to the human race, Acts XXIII. verse 10. The word εὐλαβηθείς can also be taken for reverence, and although it might denote fear there, it is indubitable that the meaning of reverence is more accepted in the Scriptures. Nor was CHRIST liberated in Luke XXII. verse 43 from the fear of tortures, so that he would no longer fear them. For on the cross he still cried out: My GOD, my GOD, why have you forsaken me? Nor did he offer supplications only that he might be saved from the fear of tortures, but from death, and he was heard. Blessed Dorscheus, Part I. Theolog. Zachar. §. 302, laboriously [proves] the other meaning of Camerarius, as also [does] Franz on the Interpretation of Scripture. proves: He acknowledges, however, that Chrysostom, Theophylact, Anselm, and especially Flacius favor our opinion in arguing for reverence against fear, and he explains his own mind in §. 311, page 272: Those who translate εὐλά- βειαν as fear do not mean this, as if he had been devoid of all horror of sorrows and death, and had hastened to death with an idle and joyful spirit as if to a banquet. For they do not say that CHRIST was heard by the Father and liberated from fear, to the extent that there was never any horror of death, or that it all ceased once and for all before the death of the cross: But that it was mitigated, and began to be more relaxed. Certainly, there are conspicuous intervals of sorrows and horrors in the final times of CHRIST, who was dwelling in the state of humiliation. Nor is it read that fear and anguish overwhelmed CHRIST with such a mass before he descended to the agony in the garden. And after he was strengthened by an Angel, the horror in him was more relaxed, which nevertheless overwhelmed him again on the cross, although from that darkness he was finally placed into a more serene state and expired with a great indication of Divine Majesty, where all fear ceased. But if that fear overwhelmed CHRIST again on the cross, it does not appear how he was then fully liberated from it when he prayed in the garden; and therefore we acquiesce in the explanation of Blessed Luther.

Latin:

Vers. 7..

ὄς ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις τῆς σαρκὸς ἁυτῦ) Id est, in tempo- re sui status infirmis ac multis malis obnoxii, qui sæpe solet apud Ebræos nomine בשׂר, id est, σαρκὸς ut Esaïæ XXXI. 3. aut etiam vocibus בשׂר ודם σαρκὸς καὶ αἵ- ματος ut supra II. 14. significari, quia corporis humani constitutio, quæ in sacris literis vocatur caro & sanguis, nos istis malis subjectos facit.

Alio jam documento probatur, sacerdotium Christum habere à Deo Patre. Is quem pro li- beratione sua à morte precatus, & à quo exauditus & consummatus, ac causa salutis æternæ sibi obe- dientibus factus est CHRISTUS, is, inquam, citra omnem controversiam CHRISTUM vocavit & constituit Pontificem. Quæ consequentia uti sua luce radiat : Ita merito addit Apostolus, ea ratione CHRISTUM nominatum esse à DEO Pontificem secundum ordinem Melchisedech. Nam ea maxime ratione causa salutis nostræ est; quod Pontifex est, cum sacrificii pro peccatis no- stris oblatione, tum mediatoria pro nobis inter- cessione. B. Gerhardus censet Apostolum hisce ad Christum accommodare, quod Pontifex non solum pro populo, sed etiam pro seipso preces obtulerit, quam- vis non ex eadem causa. Pontifex preces obtulit in Veteri Testamento pro impetranda peccatorum suo- rum remissione, Christus vero pro impetranda ex an- gustiis liberatione. Dies carnis certe de diebus in- firmitatis explicantur. Conf. Psal. 56, 5. Psal. 78, 39. Ebr. 5, 16. B. Dorsheus dies carnis notat oppo- ni diebus æternitatis. Utrosque Christus habuit pro- pter geminam naturam. Dies æternitatis Mich. 5, 2. Dies autem carnis juxta Humanam naturam ita vo- cantur, quia ex veræ carnis proprietate & conditione Christo competunt. Sunt duratio Humanæ naturæ in his terris conveniens. Sequuntur actum Huma- næ naturæ, & quidem in statu exinanitionis positæ, adeo ut μορφὴν δύλε Phil. 2, 7. etiam includant.

Δεήσεις τε καὶ ἱκετηρίας πρὸς τὸν δυνάμενον σώζειν αὐτὸν ἐκ θανάτυ μετὰ κραυγῆς ἰσχυρᾶς καὶ δακρύων προσενέγκας) Δεήσεις est nomen generis. Ἱκετηρία plus aliquid signi- ficat, preces valde submissas, ut 2. Maccab. IX. 18. & תחנון quod magnam anxietatem significat, vertitur per ἱκετεύων, ut videre est Psalm. XXXVII. 7. In glossis ins- tηρία oratio, precatio, supplicium. ἱκετεύω supplico, pre- cor. Respicitur autem hic illud præcipue tempus, quo Christus maxime sensit infirmitatem naturæ humanæ, cum à vi Divina quasi destitutus mortem cum tantis cruciati- bus conjunctam vehementer perhorresceret, ne quid es- set humani, quod non pertulisset ille, qui Filius erat DEI, ne nos putaremus ob hoc à DEO despectos, si talia in- terdum & nobis evenirent, ac non eo minus crederemus nos etiam nostro modo Filios DEI esse, vide Matth. XXVI. 37. 38. 39. 42. 44. Marc. XIV. 33. Luc. XXII. 42. 43. 44. Quod in lege veteri erant ignorantiæ & in- cogitantiæ, id in CHRISTO erant affectus naturales, qui ex dolore aut doloris metu oriuntur, qui eo usque in CHRISTO invaluerunt, DEI provido permissu, ut fuerit non tantum λυπῶν, sed & ἀδημονῶν Matth. XXVI. 38. Quid ergo naturaliter appetebat? Liberari à tali mor- te: Quod si sola potentia DEI spectetur, DEO non erat impossibile effectum dare, Marc. XIV. 36. Sed hoc ne fieret, ex re erat humani generis, ἐκ θανάτε, id est, ἐκ τύτε τῦ θανάτυ.

Quo usque possibile fuerit, ut liberaretur à morte Christus, ut ne in illam incideret, hic non opus est disputare, neque enim Apostolus de ea liberatione loquitur: Et constat, σώζειν dici non solum, qui servat aliquem à malo, ne in illud inci- dat, sed etiam qui erigit aliquem ex malo, in quod incidit, quod hic locum habet: Quia Christus in his precibus suis exauditus à Deo est. Nec vero ideo mortem subiit Filius Dei, quod eum gravissi- mo luctu, anxietate, imo derelictione Dei ac sensu cruciatuum infernalium factum, ut nos in gravissi- mas calamitates & afflictiones incidentes ne dubi- temus, filios Dei nos esse, sed ut pro nobis, seu no- stri loco pœnam lueret, nosque ab eadem liberaret mortis suæ λύτρῳ & ἀντιλύτρῳ, ac sacrificio mor- tis expiaret peccata, iram Dei placaret, nosque à pœnis peccati redimeret. Non spectandæ tan- tum passiones, & mors Christi, ut exemplum, quod Pelagius & Abailardus ac Sociniani hæretici pessi- mi voluere, sed ut meritum: Quod constanter tenuit Catholica Ecclesia. Intelliguntur autem preces, non tam quas in horto in agone obtulit, quam quas in ara crucis obtulisse legitur, quia illic nec voce magna clamavit, & deprecatus est calicem, etsi sub hypothesi, si possibile & Dei Patris voluntas sit, ubi etiam de lacrymis ibi fusis nihil expresse legitur: Hic autem tum in clamore illo maximo ac vere miserabili, Deus meus, Deus meus, ut quid me dereliquisti, & in commendatione Spiritus sui voce magna facta exauditus à Patre est, nec sine la- crymis preces suas in ara crucis obtulit, quo de Estius hoc loco: Quamvis lacrymæ ejus non le- gantur: Tamen sicuti sitivit naturaliter præ siccita- te corporis exhausti, sic & lacrymas ei naturaliter præ doloribus erupisse credibile est. Permittebat enim, juxta Damasceni celebre dictum, unicuique facultati naturali proprias actiones. Est enim ἱκετηρία mo- nente B. Dorscheo, supplicum precatio, qualis eorum est, qui se ad pedes abjiciunt, aut genua tangunt eo- rum, quos orant, aut aliquid simile faciunt, quod est humilitatem testari. Unde & ἱκετηρία dicitur ra- mus oleæ lana obvolutus, quem supplicantes in manu ferebant, Livius libr. IV. Ramos oleæ ad velamenta illa supplicum porrigentes orare, ut reciperent se &c. Phrasis etiam sacrificialis προσενέγκας optime con- venit precibus à CHRISTO Pontifice in ara cru- cis sese offerente pro sui liberatione è morte fusis; quia tum nostri loco fuit surrogatus, qui nostram culpam in se susceperat, nostramque pœnam pro nobis luebat, offerens peccata nostra in ligno (ἀνήνεγκεν) in corpore suo, 1. Petr. II. vers. 24. unde in ipso salvati & liberati nos sumus à morte; ideoque ut vas & sponsor noster satisfaciens pro peccatis nostris, preces illas & deprecationes cum lacrymis ac voce magna offerre necessum habuit, ut ne relinqueretur in ista morte, in ista desertio- ne Patris, in istis infernalibus horroribus & cru- ciatibus, sed salvatus ex iisdem nos salvaret, & cau- sa nostræ salutis fieret.

Καὶ εἰσακουσθεὶς ἀπὸ τῆς εὐλαβειας) Est contracta lo- quutio frequens & Ebræis & Græcis. Sensus est: In hoc exauditus fuit ut ab isto metu liberaretur. Par lo- quutio Psalm. XXII. vers. 22. Ubi quod in Ebræo est עניתני recte vertitur exaudisti me, id est, exaudiens li- berasti ab illis cornibus μονοκερώτων, id est, malorum ho- minum. Sic Psalm. LIV. 17. ubi in Ebræo est וישיעני servabit me, LXX. ponunt εἰσήκουσέ με per Μετωνυμίαν. Ἀπὸ τῆς εὐλαβειας, id est, liberatus ab illo metu crucia- tuum per Angelum ad se missum, Luc. XXII. vers. 43. per quem ei ob oculos positus est ingens ille fructus ad homines redundaturus ex illis ipsius duris sane perpessionibus, & quidem conjunctus cum maxima i- psius gloria, Phil. II. 9. Εὐλάβεια est id quod ἀδημονεῖν dicitur Matth. XXVI. vers. 37. Marc. XIV. vers. 33. Sic Jos. XXII. vers. 24. מִדְּאָגָה Graeci vertunt ἕνεκα εὐλαβείας, quae ipsa vox Ebraea Proverb. XII. 26. verti- tur φοβερὸς λόγος. Ipsum autem verbum דָּאַג εὐλα- βεῖσθαι Esa. LVII. 11. φοβεῖσθαι Jerem. XVII. 8. cap. XI. v. 6. Sic Josephus de Rege marito Estherae: Εὐλαβείως αὐ- τὴν ἀπολύων. Et Lucas ipse Actor. XXIII. 10. Εὐλα- βηθεὶς posuit pro timens. Ab illo ergo metu Christus liberatus forti animo se paravit ad ferendos illos dolores, vide ad hunc locum quae habet Nazianzenus.

Postquam preces obtulisset, & exauditus esset, & consummatus, factus est omnibus ipsi obedientibus causa salutis aeternae, ut Aoristus προσενέγκας Praesentis significationem habet, sic etiam verba εἰσακουσθεὶς καὶ τελειωθείς. Exau- ditus autem dicitur, quia non tantum confor- tatus in cruce, ac liberatus ex infernali horro- re & cruciatu, Spiritusque ejus susceptus à Pa- tre, sed etiam è morte temporali & exigui spa- tii in vitam aeternam resuscitatus est. Non au- tem opus hic brevem loquutionem dicere, aut etiam per εὐλάβειαν metum cum Calvino, Beza, Tossano & aliis intelligere: Imo causa aperte redditur, cur exauditus & salvatus sit à morte, ut B. Lutherus recte interpretatur, darum daß er GOTT in Ehren hat, ubi Praepositio ἀπὸ po- nitur pro διὰ, quo pacto εὐλαβείας significatio in sacris literis recepta servatur: Haec enim vox nuspiam in sacris literis pro metu, sed pro reverentia occurrit, Ebr. XII. vers. 28. Luc. II. vers. 25. Actor. II. vers. 5. Quem sensum vers. 8. confirmat, & amplexi sunt Photius & Oecume- nius, necnon Latini plerique; è nostris B. Hun- nius, B. Gerhardus & alii; è Pontificiis Era- smus, Bellarminus, Estius, & plerique reliqui, Bullingerus, Castellio, Pareus, &c. Camerari- us: Ἀπὸ τῆς εὐλαβείας, id est, ἐκ τῆς εὐλαβεί- ας, quod significat μετ᾽ εὐλαβείας προσευχόμε- νος, & quae sequuntur, indicant immensam humi- litatem & submissionem Filii DEI in obediendo vo- luntati Paternae, cum factus homo derivatam in se iram DEI sustinuit & placavit DEUM reconciliatum generi humano, Actor. XXIII. vers. 10. Vox εὐλαβηθείς potest etiam de reverentia acci- pi, & quamvis ibi metum notaret, receptio- rem tamen in Sacris esse reverentiae significatio- nem indubium est. Neque liberatus CHRI- STUS est Luc. XXII. vers. 43. à metu crucia- tuum, ut ne amplius eos metueret. Nam in cruce adhuc exclamavit: DEUS meus, Deus meus, quare deseruisiti me? Nec supplicatio- nes tantum obtulit, ut salvaretur à cruciatuum metu, sed à morte, & exauditus est. B. Dor- scheus part. I. Theolog. Zachar. §. 302. operose alterum significatum Camerarii, ut & Franzii de Interpr. script. probat: Agnoscit tamen nostrae sententiae favere Chrysostomum, Theo- phylactum, Anshelmum, & imprimis Flacium pro reverentia contra metum pugnare, suamque mentem §. 311. ita explicat pag. 272. Qui εὐλά- βειαν metum vertunt, non hoc volunt, quasi o- mni horrore dolorum & mortis caruisset, & tan- tum otioso laetoque animo velut ad convivium ad mortem properasset. Non enim dicunt CHRI- STUM à Patre exauditum & liberatum fuisse à metu, adeo, ut nullus unquam mortis horror fuerit, vel omnis simul & semel ante crucis mor- tem desineret: Sed ut mitigaretur, & remis- fior esse inciperet. Sane dolorum & horrorum in extremis CHRISTI in statu exinanitionis com- morantis temporibus intervalla conspicua sunt. Ne- que tantâ mole metus & angor CHRISTUM obruisse legitur ante, quam ad agoniam in horto descenderet. Et postquam confortatus est ab An- gelo, remissior in eo fuit horror, qui tamen ite- rum in cruce eundem obruit, quanquam ex illâ caligine demum in sereniorem statum positus ma- gna Divinæ Majestatis indicatione expiravit, u- bi omnis metus defiit. Sed si metus ille iterum CHRISTUM in cruce obruit, non apparet, quomodo tum liberatus plene ab eodem fuerit, cum in horto oraret; ideoque in B. Lutheri explicatione acquiescimus.

## 5:8
Verse 8.

Though he was a Son) Much more than Adam, conceived against the order of nature. See Luke 3, 38.

He learned obedience from the things which he suffered) He alludes to the Greek proverb παθήματα, μαθήματα, such sentences and with similar Paronomasia are found in almost all languages. The sense is, He experienced in such great temptations how arduous it is to obey GOD, ἀφ’ ὧν is the same as ἐξ ὧν. A similar locution is in Matthew XXIV. 32. and above verse 7. ἀπὸ τῆς εὐλαβείᾳς.

He is not compared with Adam, nor is he called the Son of GOD by reason of his conception from the Holy Spirit, which the Socinians want, but, as was noted just before from Psalm 2, v. 7, by reason of his eternal generation from the Father. But he is said to have learned obedience through sufferings and in sufferings, because although he underwent suffering out of obedience: Yet the more the sufferings pressed upon him, the more perfect his obedience was rendered, so that Theophylact struggles in vain here as to how he is said to have become obedient only after his sufferings. That is not what is said, but he is said to have learned obedience by the very fact that he suffered. This is a practical and experimental progress, just as in Herodotus, Croesus says to himself γεγονέναι μαθήματα τὰ παθήματα, that is, that he had been made wiser by adverse things. To which Theodoret's explanation leads. Nor does Camerarius speak inelegantly: He gracefully joined ἔμαθεν & ἔπαθεν, in this sense: He learned obedience while suffering, that is, he performed it by suffering. The sense is fuller, however, and more in keeping with the Apostolic scope, which the word itself introduces. Blessed Dorscheus unfolds it thus: This obedience began with the very κενώσει & λήψει μορφῆς δού- λου, and was carried out and produced through obedient actions and sufferings up to the final moment of emptying. It is not, therefore, merely passive obedience, as the Herborn theologians interpret it along with their Piscator. Nor is it taken in this passage, as Schlichtingius invents, only for that part of obedience which is seen in the most arduous matters, such as being afflicted for the sake of Divine justice and truth, and undergoing a dire death. For what the Apostle says, that CHRIST learned obedience from his sufferings, is not to be referred and restricted only to the obedience exhibited in sufferings, but looks to the whole obedience considered in its entire complexity and scope by reason of its most profound intensity and widest extension.

And thus it is said to be known from the passions, because it was increased by the horrible, unusual, and almost incomprehensible accessions of internal and external passions. Some think that ἔμαθεν in this place is clearly redundant, and they do not believe the Apostle intended to say more than that CHRIST performed obedience in his passions, or obeyed the Father in the midst of his passions. But this interpretation is repugnant to the peculiar emphasis which the Apostle intends. Who is especially eager to explain to us this, that although CHRIST, as the Son of GOD and therefore according to his Divine nature the very wisdom of GOD the Father, 1 Corinthians I, verse 24, and Proverbs XII, verse 22, and according to his human nature had all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in himself, Colossians II, verse 2, and had no need to learn anything from elsewhere, John II, verse 25. Nevertheless, in his κένωσις and the bearing of the form of a servant, he laid aside the splendor of the Divine Majesty to such an extent that, among horrible passions, he learned the breadth and depth of the obedience imposed upon him. Others refer that ἔμαθεν to experimental knowledge, so that the sense is: He learned obedience from those things which he experienced. Thus the Papists, who, since they attribute a perpetual clear vision to CHRIST according to his human nature, and therefore the most perfect knowledge of all future events, cannot interpret these words in any other way than as experimental knowledge. Thus Ribera in this place, number 17. The sense in this place is, since he was the Son of GOD, to whom therefore immortality and the glory of his body and the exaltation of his name were due, he willed to suffer, and by experience he knew the power and excellence of obedience, etc. Thus also Beza: He learned, that is, he experienced by the thing itself what it is to have a Father to whom one must be obedient. In this way Judges VIII, verse 16. Gideon made the men of Succoth know, that is, experience, by means of thorny branches. We do not exclude experimental knowledge, yet we believe that it does not by itself satisfy the Apostolic scope. For this is to teach the vocation of CHRIST, and therefore his perpetual ordination and governance under the rule of GOD the Father in his priestly office. But because in a legitimate vocation the designation of labors to be endured is for the most part exhibited, the Apostle indicates that GOD the Father did not spare his own Son, Romans VIII, verse 32, so that he not only insinuated to him in general the vocation to that priestly office, but also specifically and especially, when the sacrifice for the life of the world was now to be brought to completion, he repeatedly intimated to him a catalog of things to be suffered that was arduous, horrible, and clearly most bitter, and in this way taught him the depth and breadth of obedience. Whence ἔμαθε refers not only to the experience itself, but moreover to the communication of the eternal Father, upon whose will the entire dispensation of the passion depends, to whom CHRIST himself also appeals in the agony of the olive grove, Matthew XXVI, verse 39, and following, Luke XXII, verse 42, following. Nor does it agree with the preceding if you refer ἔμαθεν to experimental experience alone. Certainly, when CHRIST offered prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to him who was able to deliver him from death, by this very act he willed μανθάνειν, that is, not only to experience, but also entirely to learn from Divine communication how far GOD the Father would forsake him in temptations and infernal passions, and when GOD the Father would set the limit and measure of his sorrows. This he learned, that is, he perceived from Divine communication, when he was heard. And that communication of angelic strengthening is not the lowest part, concerning which Luke XXII, verse 43, but also the word ἔμαθεν itself is nowhere in the Holy Scriptures taken only for experimental knowledge; compare Matthew IX, verse 13, chapter XI, verse 29, chapter XXIV, verse 32, Mark XIII, verse 28, John VI, verse 45, chapter VII, verse 15, Acts XXIII, verse 27, Philippians IV, verses 9 and 11, etc.; indeed, even the word μανθάνειν in its proper signification denotes the perception of a thing previously either simply or in some way and respect unknown. There is no reason why one should depart from that proper signification in this place.

Nor is it absurd to say that CHRIST did not always, according to his Human nature, and that because of his most profound emptying, think or know all things. It is sufficient if, as often as he willed, and when the reason of his office demanded it, he could know under Divine dispensation what was necessary. Certainly, that non-knowledge of some things did not arise from a defect of communicated Majesty, which the heresy of the Agnoetae maintained; but from a most free emptying. For that nescience of some things and not continuous thought of all things arose from the κένωσις of the form of the omniscient GOD, Philippians II, verse 7. Hence CHRIST also according to his Human nature truly progressed, as in age, so also in wisdom, Luke II, verse 52, and he also truly marveled, Matthew VIII, verse 10, and Luke VII, verse 9, and he truly approached the fig tree to seek fruit, Matthew XXI, verse 19, and Mark XI, verse 13. And although he predicted his passion, and set it forth through almost every circumstance, Luke XVIII, verse 31, and following, it must nevertheless be considered, partly that that prediction was proposed by CHRIST when he was already established in his office; whence it does not follow that CHRIST, according to his Human Nature, had known those passions for himself throughout his entire life from that time, or had used the Majesty of communicated knowledge to know them, and therefore, when he cried in his cradle in the manner of infants, knew, as he is man, that he had to undertake a flight into Egypt from Herod because of his tyranny; or that he had to sweat a bloody sweat on the Mount of Olives, or that he was to be betrayed by Judas his disciple, and what other things there are. Partly also that it does not follow, because CHRIST predicted some moments of his sufferings to his disciples on that last journey to Jerusalem, that he also willed at that time to use his omniscience to such an extent that he looked into the entire breadth and depth of the same. This whole matter certainly depends upon his most free dispensation, which in the state of emptying was clearly so admirable and inscrutable that it is not permitted to conclude one from the other so simply, unless it is sufficiently established concerning the will, upon which the use of Majesty depends. It is therefore enough if CHRIST then knew how great and how exquisite an obedience was to be rendered by him for our redemption, since he had to render it in his own to be rendered in all moments and degrees at all times. But he learned [this] from the passions proposed and imposed upon him by his Father, or from the communicated catalog of things to be suffered. Hence we conclude thus: He who, in rendering priestly and sacrificial acts consisting of most bitter passions and exquisite obedience, learned from the communication of his heavenly Father what was to be rendered by him, he exercised his priesthood only under the calling and ordination of the heavenly Father. CHRIST did this. Therefore.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Καίπερ ὢν υἱὸς) Multo magis, quam Adamus, con- ceptus contra naturæ ordinem. Vide Luc. 3, 38.

Ἔμαθεν ἀφ’ ὧν ἔπαθε τὴν ὑπακοὴν) Alludit ad pro- verbium Græcum παθήματα, μαθήματα, quales sen- tentiæ & cum simili Παρονομασίᾳ sunt ferme in linguis omnibus. Sensus est, Expertus est in tantis tentatio- nibus, quam sit arduum DEO obedire, ἀφ’ ὧν idem est quod ἐξ ὧν. Par loquutio Matth. XXIV. 32. & su- pra vers. 7. ἀπὸ τῆς εὐλαβείᾳς.

Non cum Adamo confertur, nec Filius DEI ratione conceptionis ex Spiritu sancto di- citur, quod Sociniani volunt, sed, ut proxi- me è Psalm. 2. v. 7. monitum, ratione æternæ ge- nerationis à Patre. Didicisse autem per passio- nes & in passionibus obedientiam dicitur, quia etsi ex obedientia passionem subiit: Tamen quo magis ipsum passiones presserunt, eo per- fectior reddita est ejus obedientia, ut frustra hic se torqueat Theophylactus, quomodo post passiones demum obediens factus dicatur. Non id dicitur, sed eo ipso, quo passus est, obe- dientiam didicisse dicitur. Practicus & expe- rimentalis hic est profectus, quomodo apud He- rodotum Cræsus sibi dicit γεγονέναι μαθήματα τὰ παθήματα, id est rebus adversis se reddi- tum esse doctiorem. Quo abit Theodoreti ex- plicatio. Nec inconcinne Camerarius: Ve- nuste junxit ἔμαθεν & ἔπαθεν, hoc sensu: Inter patiendum didicit obedientiam, id est præstitit pa- tiendo. Plenior tamen est sensus, magisque Apostolico scopo convenit, quem vox ipsa infert. Quem sic evolvit B. Dorscheus: Hæc obedientia cum ipsâ κενώσει & λήψει μορφῆς δού- λου cœpit, & actionibus obedientialibus passionibusq; peracta est & producta usque ad ultimum exinani- tionis momentum. Non itaque tantum est obedien- tia passiva, ut Herbornenses cum Piscatore suo interpretantur. Nec hoc loco, uti Schlichtingius comminiscitur, pro ea tantum obedientia parte sumitur, quæ in rebus maxime arduis cernitur, quale est justitiæ & veritatis Divinæ causâ affli- gi, & diram mortem subire. Nam quod Aposto- lus dicit, ex passionibus didicisse CHRISTUM obedientiam, non ad obedientiam in passionibus exhibitam tantum referendam & restringendum est, sed ad totam obedientiam in universo suo complexu & ambitu consideratam ratione profun- dissimæ intensionis & latissimæ extensionis spectat.

Atque ita dicitur ex passionibus cognita, quia horrendis, insolentibus, & fere incomprehensibi- libus internarum & externarum passionum ac- cessionibus aucta fuit. Ἔμαθεν hoc loco nonnul- li plane redundare censent, nec plus Apostolum voluisse dicere existimant, quam quod CHRI- STUS in passionibus præstiterit obedientiam, vel in mediis passionibus Patri obediverit. Sed re- pugnat hæc interpretatio emphası peculiari, quam Apostolus intendit. Qui hoc imprimis nobis ex- plicare satagit, quod quamvis CHRISTUS, utpote DEI Filius adeoque secundum Divinam naturam ipsa sapientia DEI Patris, 1. Corinth. I. vers. 24. & Proverb. XII. vers. 22. & secundum humanam naturam omnes thesauros sapientiæ & scientiæ in se habuerit absconditos Coloss. II. vers. 2. nec opus habuerit, ut aliunde aliquid agnosceret, Johan. II. vers. 25. Nihilominus in κενώσει sua & formæ servilis gestatione eousque splendorem Maje- statis Divinæ deposuerit, ut inter passiones hor- rendas didicerit amplitudinem & profunditatem obedientiæ ipsi impositæ. Alii illud ἔμαθεν ad scientiam experimentalem referunt, ut sensus sit: Expertus est ex iis, quæ didicit obedientiam. Ita Pontificii, qui cum perpetuam claram visionem CHRISTO secundum humanam naturam, adeo- que perfectissimam scientiam omnium eventuro- rum tribuant, non aliter quam de scientia ex- perimentali hæc verba interpretari possunt. Sic Ribera in h. l. num. 17. Sensus hoc loco est, cum esset Filius DEI, cui propterea immortali- tas & gloria corporis & exaltatio nominis sui debebatur, pati voluit, & experimento cogno- vit vim & præstantiam obedientiæ &c. Sic & Beza: Didicit, id est, re ipsa expertus est, quid sit Patrem habere, cui parendum sit. Hoc modo Judic. VIII. vers. 16. Gideon Succotanos per vir- gas spineas scire fecit, id est experiri. Nos scien- tiam experimentalem non excludimus, censemus tamen illam scopo Apostolico per se non satisfa- cere. Hic enim est docere vocationem CHRI- STI, adeoque ejus perpetuam ordinationem & gubernationem sub regimine DEI Patris in officio suo sacerdotali. Quia autem in legitima vocatio- ne ut plurimum laborum exantlandorum designa- tio exhibetur, indicat Apostolus, DEUM Patrem adeo non pepercisse Filio suo Roman. VIII. vers. 32. ut non tantum in genere ipsi vocationem ad offi- cium id sacerdotale insinuaverit, sed etiam sigil- latim & imprimis, eum ad complementum de- ducendum jam erat sacrificium pro mundi vita, ipsi arduum, horrendum & acerbissimum plane patiendorum catalogum subinde intimaverit, & hoc modo profunditatem & amplitudinem obe- dientiæ ipsum docuerit. Unde ἔμαθε non tan- tum respicit ipsam experientiam, sed insuper æ- terni Patris communicationem, à cujus volunta- te tota passionis dispensatio dependet, ad quam CHRISTUS ipse quoque provocat in agone oli- veti Matth. XXVI. vers. 39. & seqq. Luc. XXII. vers. 42. seqq. Neque cum antecedentibus con- gruit, si ἔμαθεν ad solam experimentalem expe- rientiam referas. Certe, cum CHRISTUS preces & supplicationes cum clamore valido & la- chrymis ad eum, qui poterat ipsum ex morte liberare, obtulit, hoc ipso voluit μανθάνειν, hoc est, non tantum experiri, sed omnino etiam ex Divina communicatione discere, quousque ipsum deserturus esset DEUS Pater in tentationibus & passionibus infernalibus, & quando terminum & mensuram dolorum suorum DEUS Pater esset positurus. Hoc didicit, hoc est, ex Divina communicatione percepit, cum fuit exauditus. Est- que ista confortationis Angelicæ communicatio non infima pars, de qua Luc. XXII. vers. 43. sed & ipsum verbum ἔμαθεν nuspiam in Sacris literis tantum de experimentali scientia sumitur, confer. Matth. IX. vers. 13. cap. XI. vers. 29. cap. XXIV. vers. 32. Marc. XIII. vers. 28. Johan. VI. vers. 45. cap. VII. vers. 15. Actor. XXIII. vers. 27. Phil. IV. vers. 9. & 11. &c. imo & verbum μανθάνειν in propria sua significatione denotat perceptionem rei ante vel simpliciter vel aliquo modo & respectu igno- tæ. Ab ista propria significatione cur hoc loco re- cedendum sit, causa nulla est.

Neque absurdum est dicere, CHRISTUM non semper secundum Humanam suam naturam, idque propter profundissimam exanitionem o- mnia cogitasse aut cognovisse. Sufficit si quoties- cunque voluit, & quando ipsius officii ratio po- stulavit, sub Divina dispensatione scire potue- rit, quod necessarium erat. Sane ista non co- gnitio aliquorum non orta est ex defectu commu- nicatæ Majestatis, quod Agnoëtarum hæresis vo- luit; sed ex liberrima exanitione. Est enim ista nescientia aliquorum & non continua omni- um cogitatio orta ex κενώσει formæ DEI omni- scientis, Philipp. II. vers. 7. Hinc CHRISTUS etiam secundum Humanam naturam revera pro- fecit, uti ætate, ita & sapientia Luc. II. vers. 52. & admiratus est etiam vere, Matth. VIII. vers. 10. & Luc. VII. vers. 9. & vere accessit ad ficum fructus quæsiturus Matth. XXI. vers. 19. & Marc. XI. vers. 13. Et quamvis prædixerit passionem suam, & per singulas fere circumstantias expo- suerit, Luc. XVIII. vers. 31. & seqq. Confide- randum tamen est, partim quod ista prædictio à CHRISTO proposita fuerit, cum jam in offi- cio suo consisteret; unde non sequitur, CHRI- STUM secundum Humanam Naturam jam in- de per universam vitam istas passiones sibi habu- isse cognitas, aut ad illas cognoscendas Majesta- te communicatæ scientiæ fuisse usum, adeoque cum in cunis infantum more vagiret cognovisse, qua homo est, sibi ab Herode fugam imminere in Æ- gyptum suscipiendam propter ejus tyrannidem; aut sibi in monte olivarum sudorem sanguineum sudandum esse, aut se à Juda discipulo suo pro- dendum, & quæ sunt alia. Partim & illud non sequi, quia CHRISTUS aliqua patiendorum momenta in ultimo isto Hierosolymitano itinere di- scipulis suis prædixit, illum etiam in tantum tum voluisse omniscientia sua uti, ut omnem earun- dem amplitudinem & profunditatem introspice- ret. Pendet sane hoc totum à liberrima ipsius dispensatione, quæ in statu exanitionis plane fuit admirabilis & inscrutabilis adeo ut non liceat ita simpliciter unum ex altero concludere, nisi de volun- tate, a qua usus Majestatis dependet, sufficienter constet. Satis itaque est, si tum CHRISTUS novit, quantaquamque exquisita ipsi praestanda sit pro redemptione nostra obedientia, cum eam in suam momentis & gradibus praestare debuit, neque enim in omnibus momentis & gradibus omni tem- pore praestanda fuit. Didicit autem propositis & impositis ipsi a Patre suo passionibus seu communi- cato patiendorum catalogo. Hinc ita concludi- mus: Qui in praestandis actibus sacerdotalibus & sacrificialibus constantibus in acerbissimis pas- sionibus & exquisita obedientia ex communicatio- ne Patris sui caelestis didicit, quid praestandum ipsi esset, is non nisi sub vocatione & ordinatione Patris caelestis sacerdotium suum gessit. CHRI- STUS hoc fecit. Ergo.

## 5:9
Ver. 9.

And having been perfected) Persisting to the very end. The work having been completed. See above chapter II. 10. Philippians III. 12. and what was said at Luke XIII. 32.

He became to all those who obey him the author of eternal salvation) That is, to those who have the purpose of obeying, he obtains as high Priest those aids of the Spirit through which they themselves may also be able to overcome temptations, however grave, and thus arrive at that eternal salvation. A huge consolation and exhortation, necessary indeed for all, but especially for those times and men.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Καὶ τελειωθεὶς) Ad ultimum usque perstans. Con- summato opere. Vide supra cap. II. 10. Philipp. III. 12. & quae dicta ad Luc. XIII. 32.

Ἐγένετο τοῖς ὑπακούουσιν αὐτῷ πᾶσιν αἴτιος σωτηρίας αἰωνίου) Id est, iis, qui obediendi propositum habent, obtinet tanquam summus Sacerdos ea Spiritus auxi- lia, per quae possint & ipsi tentationes quamvis gra- vissimas superare, & sic pervenire ad aeternam illam sa- lutem. Ingens & consolatio & exhortatio, omnibus quidem, sed illis maxime temporibus & hominibus ne- cessaria.

## 5:10
Ver. 10.

Having been addressed by God as High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek) Namely in that Psalm 110, of which mention has already been made. Προσαγορευθεὶς [is] נקרא.

Regarding the word τελειωθεὶς, Grotius's explanation is not displeasing. It is explained in two ways: namely, perfected by knowledge and patience, or by experimental discipline, which perfection happened on the cross, John XIX. ver. 30, followed by glory, Heb. II. ver. 10. Then also, in that he became the cause and Author of salvation to all who obey him through faith, Rom. I. ver. 5, chap. XVI. ver. 26. Regarding the former perfection, the blessed Hunnius: And thus he learned to be obedient to GOD the Father for our sake even unto the death of the cross: And by this reason he was rendered perfect not with respect to his own person, but as regards the full, perfect, and exuberant sacrifice which he offered for us, by whose dignity he became the cause, author, and fountain of salvation to all who obey him through faith, and that salvation not temporal but eternal. The blessed Gerhardus accepted the latter sense. That perfection of sufferings seems preferable, because here it is a matter of the humiliation and obedience of Christ, which he rendered so that he might expiate our disobedience and constitute us just by his obedience, and by that pact he is said to have been made the cause of our salvation. Whence Osiander paraphrases thus: Although CHRIST was the Son of GOD, yet in his assumed humanity he emptied himself, assumed the form of a servant, and in it obeyed the heavenly Father most perfectly: and rendered all those things which were to be rendered by reason of the high Priesthood. When he had completed all these things, he obtained eternal salvation (by that most holy merit of his) for all who subject themselves to him by faith and strive to obey him. Therefore, the name of High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek was attributed to him long ago by GOD the Father. For no one else could ward off the curse from us and bring a blessing, except CHRIST (foreshadowed by Melchizedek), the Son of GOD and man in one person, and King of heaven and earth, who made peace between GOD and men.

The fruit therefore of the passion and obedience of Christ is our eternal salvation, because through his obedience even unto the death of the cross he not only merited eternal salvation for us, but is also able to confer the same upon us. He is our Savior both by reason of merit and by reason of efficacy. And that the sacrifice of CHRIST, through which he merited salvation for us, makes for this entirely, the comparison of Psalm 110 teaches: because the Apostle adds that he was surnamed by GOD as Priest according to the order of Melchizedek. Since the chief function of the priesthood is the propitiatory offering and the expiation of sins. Ὑπακούειν does not mean to have the purpose of obeying, but to render obedience, and the discourse is not about legal obedience, but rather about the obedience of faith, even if the pursuit of piety or the observance of moral precepts is a consequence of it, because salvation is obtained not through the obedience of the law but of faith; even if in the subject to whom faith happens, the pursuit of good works also concurs. Whence even if it is admitted that salvation comes to those who obey, that is, to those who observe the precepts prescribed by Divine law as much as they can, nevertheless that observance is not constituted as the cause of salvation. For it is one thing to pertain to the subject to be saved, and another to be the cause of salvation. The Grotian gloss on how CHRIST is the cause of salvation has no place. For there is nothing found here, either according to the letter or according to the meaning, about him having the aids of the Holy Spirit in his hand. Nor is it the duty of the Pontiff, as such, to bestow the aids of the Spirit for overcoming temptations. That belongs to CHRIST rather by reason of his Kingly office. Furthermore, he was made the cause of salvation through his passions, not because he obtained the power of granting the Holy Spirit, but because he obtained salvation by his satisfactory passion, because for that reason he is primarily a Pontiff according to the order of Melchizedek. Finally, not only are grave temptations to be sustained, but above all faith is to be placed in the death and merit of CHRIST and constantly kept, so that we may obtain salvation: Because the just shall live by his faith, Habakkuk II. ver. 4, Hebrews X. ver. 38.

PART II. Rebuke of the Hebrews for their sloth in matters of faith.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Προσαγορευθεὶς ὑπὸ τοῦ Θεοῦ Ἀρχιερεὺς κατὰ τὴν τά- ξιν Μελχισεδὲκ) Nempe in illo Psalmo CX. cujus jam facta mentio. Προσαγορευθεὶς נקרא.

De voce τελειωθεὶς non displicet Grotii ex- plicatio. Bifariam utique explicatur: Consum- matus nempe scientia & patientia, aut disciplina ex- perimentali, quae consummatio in cruce contigit Johan. XIX. vers. 30. subsecuta gloria Ebr. II. vers. 10. Tum etiam, qua omnibus sibi per fidem obedientibus, Rom. I. vers. 5. cap. XVI. vers. 26. causa & Autor salutis factus est. De priori con- summatione B. Hunnius: Atque sic didicit DEO Patri esse obediens nostri causa usque ad mortem crucis: Et hac ratione perfectus est redditus non respectu suae personae, sed quoad plenam, perfectam & exuberantem hostiam, quam pro nobis obtu- lit, cujus dignitate cunctis per fidem sibi obedi- entibus, causa autor & fons salutis factus est, sa- lutis autem non temporaneae sed aeternae. Posterio- ri autem sensu accepit B. Gerhardus. Praeferen- da illa τῶν παθημάτων τελείωσις videtur, quia hic agitur de humiliatione & obedientia Christi, quam praestitit, ut inobedientiam nostram expia- ret, nosque obedientia sua justos constitueret, eoque pacto dicitur causa salutis nostrae factus. Unde ita Osiander παραφράζει: Quanquam CHRISTUS esset Filius DEI, tamen in assum- pta sua humanitate semetipsum exinanivit, for- mam servi assumpsit, & in ea perfectissime obedi- vit Patri caelesti: atque omnia ea praestitit, quae ra- tione summi Pontificatus praestanda erant. Quae cum omnia consummasset, salutem aeternam (san- ctissimo illo suo merito) impetravit omnibus, qui sese illi subjiciunt fide, eique parere student. Ita- que tributum est illi jam olim à DEO Patre no- men summi Pontificis secundum ordinem Melchi- sedech. Nullus enim alius poterat à nobis male- dictionem depellere, & benedictionem afferre, nisi CHRISTUS (per Melchisedecum adumbratus) DEI & hominis Filius in una persona, & Rex cœli & terræ, qui pacem inter DEUM & ho- mines fecit.

Fructus ergo passionis & obedientiæ Christi est nostra æterna salus, quia per obedientiam us- que ad mortem crucis non meruit tantum nobis salutem æternam, sed etiam eandem conferre nobis potest. Salvator noster est tum ratione meriti, tum ratione efficaciæ. Et quod omni- no huc faciat sacrificium CHRISTI, per quod nobis meruit salutem, collatio Psalm. CX. do- cet: quia addit Apostolus, à DEO cognomi- natum esse Sacerdotem secundum ordinem Melchi- sedech. Siquidem sacerdotii præcipua functio sit oblatio ἱλαστικὴ, & expiatio peccatorum. Ὑπακούειν non est obediendi propositum habere, sed obedientiam præstare, non autem de legali obedientia, sed de obsequio fidei potius, etsi e- jus consequens sit studium pietatis vel observa- tionis præceptorum moralium, sermo est, quia salus non per obedientiam legis sed fidei obti- netur; Etsi in subjecto, cui contingit fides, & studium bonorum operum concurrat. Unde etiamsi admittatur obedientibus, hoc est, præ- cepta lege Divina præscripta pro virili obser- vantibus salutem obtingere, non tamen causa salutis ita observatio illa constituitur. Aliud e- nim est pertinere ad subjectum salvandum, aliud causam esse salutis. Glossa Grotiana quomodo CHRISTUS causa salutis sit, locum non ha- bet. Nam de eo, quod Spiritus sancti auxi- lia in manu sua habeat, nihil sive κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν, sive κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν hic reperitur. Nec id Pon- tificis est, qua talis, Spiritus auxilia largiri ad superandas tentationes. Competit id CHRI- STO potius ratione officii Regii. Porro causa salutis per passiones factus est, non quod po- testatem consequutus sit Spiritum sanctum con- cedendi, sed quod salutem passione sua satisfa- ctoria impetrarit, quia ideo imprimis Pontifex est secundum ordinem Melchisedech. Deni- que non tantum tentationes graves sustinendæ, sed ante omnia fides in CHRISTI mortem & meritum collocanda & constanter servanda, ut salutem consequamur: Quia justus fide sua vivet Habac. II. vers. 4. Ebr. X. vers. 38.

PARS II. Correptio Ebræorum ob ignaviam in rebus fidei.

## 5:11
Ver. 11.

Περὶ ὗ πολὺς ἡμῖν λόγος) Supply 'posset esse' [it could be]. We could say many things. περὶ ὗ [concerning which]: Concerning which likeness between Melchizedek and Christ.

Before the Apostle proceeds in explaining the priestly office of CHRIST and the Davidic oracle, namely how he is a Priest according to the order of Melchizedek, using a certain διεξόδῳ [digression] or digression, which seemed necessary so that the slothful Hebrews might be stirred up, he rebukes their ignorance and sloth in matters of faith.

Καὶ δυσερμήνευτος λέγειν) That is, in the speaking, which if I were to utter, you would understand with difficulty. For he who understands what is said to him, interprets it for himself. Thus Jerome rightly accepted this passage in his letter to Evagrius. Cf. John 16:12. He prepares them for that which he defers here, soon to be brought forth in chapter 7.

The Vulgate rendered it, 'and hard to be interpreted in speaking.' Others explain it as difficult to explain in eloquence or in speaking. Which is more conveniently handled by the Grotius interpretation. He does not wish to deter them by the mention of difficulty, but to render them more attentive. For difficulty excites effort, because 'fine things are difficult.' This discourse was not difficult to utter for the Apostle, who was moved by the Holy Spirit: but it was for others. Yet such an interpretation is understood, which might suit the capacity of the Hebrews, as if he were saying: not easily could anyone explain these things concerning the Melchizedekian Priesthood of CHRIST to you, who are still quite unlearned: 'For you have become dull of hearing.' For as it is commonly said, 'it is good to preach to the learned.' This difficulty, therefore, as B. Dorscheus rightly says, is to be understood not absolutely, and by reason of Divine illumination, but relatively, and in respect to the Hebrews themselves, to whom he wished to provide enlightenment and communication concerning that mystery. The Apostle does not, therefore, indicate any obscurity in the Divine revelation itself, which might stand in the way of our being able to perceive as much of it as suffices for salvation, although it is very great and sublime, but he looks primarily at the ineptitude and slowness of those to be instructed, when he calls that word 'hard to interpret.' 'To speak' is added in this place by pleonasm. For to interpret is to speak. Wherefore that discourse concerning Melchizedek is difficult to speak of only insofar as it could hardly be proposed by the Apostle in such a way that it might find assent among the Hebrews, who perceived all other things more than they could discern in Melchizedek the foreshadowed cessation of the Aaronic priesthood and the delineated origin of some more sublime one.

Ἐπεὶ νωθροὶ γεγόνατε ταῖς ἀκοαῖς) That is, 'hard of hearing.' For νωθροὶ are sluggish, as in Prov. 22:27, Sir. 4:32, ch. 11:13. By metaphor, those who do not attend to the things that are said to them are called by this name, just as things that suit bodies are accustomed to be transferred to minds.

Νωθροὶ properly means slow, lazy in walking and in deeds. This disease was not only of those Hebrews; it is common to us all, for we are all slow and lazy to hear Divine things, nor do we hear them with as much attention as we ought. Therefore St. James warns everyone, 'let every man be swift to hear,' ch. 1:19. Yet the Hebrews were peculiarly νωθροὶ, which Oecumenius ascribes to their temptations and afflictions. But that they did not cure this fault, the Apostolic correction sufficiently teaches.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Περὶ ὗ πολὺς ἡμῖν λόγος) Supple posset esse. Mul- ta dicere possemus. περὶ ὗ de qua re: De qua simili- tudine inter Melchisedecum & Christum.

Antequam progrediatur Apostolus in expli- cando officio CHRISTI sacerdotali oraculo- que Davidico, quomodo nempe Sacerdos sit secundum ordinem Melchisedech, aliqua διεξό- δῳ vel digressione usus, quod necessarium vide- batur, ut excitarentur desides Ebræi corripit eo- rum inscitiam atque ignaviam in rebus fidei.

Καὶ δυσερμήνευτος λέγειν) Id est, ἐν τῷ λέγειν, quem si eloquerer, aegre intelligeretis. Nam qui quod sibi di- citur, intelligit, is sibi id interpretatur. Ita recte hunc locum accepit Hieronymus ad Evagrium. Conf. Johan. XVI. 12. Praeparat eos ad id quod hic differt, mox edi- turus cap. VII.

Vulgatus reddidit, & ininterpretabilis ad dicen- dum. Alii explicatu difficilis eloquendo, vel dicen- do exponunt. Quod commodius Grotiana in- terpretatione. Difficultatis autem mentione non absterrere eos vult, sed attentiores reddere. Dif- ficultas enim conatum excitat, quia δύσκολα τὰ καλά. Non Apostolo à Spiritu sancto agitato dif- ficilis erat ad eloquendum hic sermo: Sed aliis. Intelligitur tamen talis ἑρμηνεία, quae Ebraeorum captui conveniat, quasi dicat, non facile quis vo- bis, qui adhuc satis rudes estis, haec de Melchisede- ciano CHRISTI Pontificatu explicaret: Si- quidem segnes facti estis auribus. Nam ut vulgo dicitur, denen Gelehrten ist gut predigen. Diffi- cultas itaque haec, ut recte B. Dorscheus, intelligenda non absolute, & ratione Divinae ἐλλάμψεως, sed rela- te, & in respectu ad ipsos Ebraeos, quibus Φωτισμὸν & communicationem de isto mysterio facere voluit. Non itaque obscuritatem aliquam vel in ipsa Divina revelatione Apostolus indicat, quae obstet, quo minus tantum, quantum ad salutem sufficit, de ea possimus percipere, quanquam maxima sit & sublimis, sed in- eptitudinem & tarditatem informandorum potissi- mum spectat, cum λόγον illum δυσερμήνευτον vocat. Λέγειν hoc loco per Pleonasmum additur. Ἑρμη- νεύειν enim λέγειν est. Quapropter sermo ille de Melchisedecho eatenus dictu difficilis est, quatenus vix ita ab Apostolo poterit proponi, ut assensum apud Ebraeos inveniat, qui omnia alia magis perspiciebant, quam ut in Melchisedecho deprehenderent adum- bratam sacerdotii Aaronici cessationem, & delinea- tam sublimioris alicujus originem.

Ἐπεὶ νωθροὶ γεγόνατε ταῖς ἀκοαῖς) Id est, ὑπόκωφοι. Nam νωθροὶ sunt segnes, ut Prov. XXII. v. 27. Sir. IV. v. 32. c. XI. v. 13. Per μεταφορὰν dicuntur hoc nomine ii qui non attendunt ad ea quae ipsis dicuntur, ut solent quae corpo- ribus conveniunt, ad animos transferri.

Νωθροὶ proprie tardi, pigri in incessu & factis. Morbus hic non tantum Ebraeorum istorum fuit, communis est nobis omnibus, ad audiendas enim res Divinas omnes tardi & pigri sumus, nec tanta attentione illas audimus, quanta oportebat. Ideo omnes monet S. Jacobus, πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ἔστω ταχὺς εἰς τὸ ἀκοῦσαι cap. I. 19. Peculiariter tamen νωθροὶ erant Ebraei, quod Oecumenius tentationibus & afflictionibus eorum adscribit. Sed culpam eam non curasse, correptio Apostolica satis docet.

## 5:12
Verse 12.

Καὶ γὰρ ὀφείλοντες εἶναι διδάσκαλοι διὰ τὸν χρόνον) You have heard the Gospel for so long that you ought now to be fit to teach others. Each of you ought by now to be fit 'for the oversight and for laboring in the word.'

Πάλιν χρείαν ἔχετε τοῦ διδάσκειν ὑμᾶς) Supply 'me.' You have need that I teach you. The same expression is in 1 Thess. 4:9. But it is full in 1 Thess. 1:8.

Τίνα τὰ στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς τῶν λογίων τοῦ Θεοῦ) That is, of the Gospel, in which are the greatest and most necessary oracles of GOD, which are also called such in 1 Pet. 4:11. 'The elements of the beginning' here are not the same as 'the elements of the world,' Gal. 4:3 and Col. 2:8 and 20. But that which is said below in ch. 6:1, 'the word of the beginning' and 'foundation,' the first rudiments, the catechism, concerning which we spoke at Matt. 9:20. And that 'of the beginning' is explanatory. For the principles of all arts are called elements. Thus, to the Hebrews, the principles of the law are called 'the foundations of the law' by Maimonides in the Guide for the Perplexed, ch. 3:35.

By the name of 'the oracles of God,' not only the doctrine of the Gospel is designated, but also that of the law: because the Word of God embraces the doctrine of the law and the Gospel, nor can the doctrine of the law be eliminated from catechesis. In the very initial elements of the Word of God, they still had need to be instructed in Catechetical doctrine; so far were they from being able to grasp those sublime things concerning the Priesthood after the order of Melchizedek, unless they were rendered clear and easier to them by Apostolic, that is, by the Holy Spirit's own instruction.

And you have become such as have need of milk, and not of solid food) He explains the same sense with another similitude. To infants milk is given, to those more adult more solid food, which is βρῶμα 1 Corinthians III. verse 2.

This phrase savors of Paul's style. He calls elementary doctrine milk, to be instilled into the rude and as it were infants in the Christian faith, who are nourished by maternal milk; solid food he calls the more perfect doctrine, to which those more adult ought to progress. For adults both desire solid food and are able to digest it well. Compare 1 Cor. III. 1, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Καὶ γὰρ ὀφείλοντες εἶναι διδάσκαλοι διὰ τὸν χρόνον) Tam- diu Evangelium audistis, ut jam debeatis idonei esse ad docendos alios. Singuli vestrum jam apti esse debebant εἰς τὴν ἐπισκοπὴν καὶ εἰς τὸ κοπιᾷν ἐν τῷ λόγῳ.

Πάλιν χρείαν ἔχετε τοῦ διδάσκειν ὑμᾶς) Supple με. Opus habetis, ut ego vos doceam. Eadem loquutio 1. Thess. IV. 9. Plena autem 1. Thess. I. 8.

Τίνα τὰ στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς τῶν λογίων τοῦ Θεοῦ) Id est, Evangelii, in quo maxima & summe necessaria sunt DEI oracula, quae & sic dicuntur 1. Petr. IV. 11. Στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς non hic id sunt, quod στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου, Gal. IV. 3. & Coloss. II. 8. & 20. Sed id quod infra dicitur c. VI. 1. ὁ τῆς ἀρχῆς λόγος & θεμέλιος, prima rudimenta שמעתא κατήχησις, de qua re diximus ad Matth. XXI IX. 20. Et illud ἀρχῆς est ἐξηγητικὸν. Nam omnium artium principia vo- cantur elementa. Sic Ebraeis legis principia dicuntur יסורי תורה Maimonidae duce dubitantium c. III. v. 35.

Nomine τῶν λογίων τοῦ Θεοῦ non Evangelii tan- tum doctrina designatur, sed etiam legis: quia Ver- bum Dei doctrinam legis & Evangelii complecti- tur, nec è catechesi eliminari potest legis doctrina. In ipsis elementis initialibus Verbi Dei adhuc in- formari opus habebant in doctrina Catechetica; tantum abest, ut sublimia illa de Pontificatu secun- dum ordinem Melchisedeci capere potuerint, nisi Apostolica, hoc est, ipsius Spiritus sancti institu- tione ea ipsis reddantur luculenta & faciliora.

Καὶ γεγόνατε χρείαν ἔχοντες γάλακτος, καὶ ὀυ στερεᾶς τρο- φῆς) Eundem sensum alia similitudine explicat. Infan- tibus lac datur, adultioribus solidior cibus, qui βρῶμα 1. Corinth. III. vers. 2.

Phrasis hæc Pauli stylum resipit. Lac vocat elementarem doctrinam rudibus ac velut infanti- bus in fide Christiana, qui lacte materno nutriun- tur, instillandum, solidum cibum perfectiorem, ad quam adultiores proficere debent. Nam adulti & solidum cibum appetunt, & bene digerere va- lent. Conf. 1. Cor. III. 1. 2.

## 5:13
Verse 13.

For everyone who partakes of milk) Supply, only. Another comparison of milk is 1 Peter III. verse 1, 2.

Unskilled in the word of righteousness) Here he said righteousness for perfection, as appears from what follows. And the genitive is for an adjective. Thus the just stature of a man is called that which has reached its summit. Thus the mammon of righteousness, that is, true riches. And אמת truth, is often translated righteousness. And it is imputed for righteousness, that is, it is held for a great work. He understands, however, that which is called gnosis by Clement of Alexandria and others, the knowledge of the manifold wisdom of God, as Paul speaks Eph. III. 10, wisdom by excellence, 1 Cor. II. 6, which is given through the opening of the scriptures, Luke XXIV. 32. True Cabala.

For he is an infant) He stands in relation to that more profound doctrine as boys do to manly arts. See 1 Corinthians III. verse 1, ch. XIII. verse 11. Infants have neither teeth to chew harder food, nor the power of stomach that might concoct such food. Nourishment convenient for an infant is milk: for a youth, bread, meat, wine. This sentiment has already been adduced by others from Josephus.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Πᾶς γὰρ ὁ μετέχων γάλακτος) Supple, tantum. Alia comparatio lactis est 1. Petr. III. vers. 1. 2.

Ἄπειρος λόγου δικαιοσύνης) Hic δικαιοσύνης dixit pro τελειότητος, ut ex sequentibus apparet. Et Genitivus est pro Adjectivo. Sic justa hominis statura dicitur quæ ad summum pervenit. Sic mammona justitiæ, id est veræ divitiæ. Et אמת veritas, sæpe vertitur δικαιό- σύνη. Et imputatur in justitiam, id est, pro magno o- pere habetur. Intelligit autem id quod Clementi Ale- xandrino & aliis γνῶσις dicitur, cognitio πολυποικίλου σοφίας Θεοῦ, ut loquitur Paulus Eph. III. 10. σοφία per ex- cellentiam, 1. Cor. II. 6. quæ datur per διάνοιξιν τῶν γρα- φῶν, Lucæ XXIV. 32. Vera Cabala.

Νήπιος γὰρ ἐστι) Sic se habet ad illam penitiorem doctrinam, quomodo pueri ad artes viriles. Vide 1. Co- rinth. III. vers. 1. c. XIII. vers. 11. Infantibus nec dentes sunt ad mandendum cibum duriorem, nec ventriculi ea vis, quæ talem cibum concoquat. Alimentum infanti con- veniens est lac: Juveni panis, caro, vinum. Est hæc sententia jam ab aliis adducta ex Josepho.

## 5:14
Verse 14.

But solid food is for the perfect) He understands by perfect, men of perfect age, as 1 Cor. II. 6, ch. XIV. 20, Eph. IV. 13, Phil. III. 15. By these, however, he means those who have progressed much in the meditation of Divine things; those who have received the gnostic faith, as Clement speaks in Strom. VI.

Of those who by reason of habit) Habit is a firm facility, as Quintilian interprets. To the author of the Categories, habit is more chronic and permanent than disposition, or a disposition consolidated by a multitude of time. To Galen, a disposition chronic and difficult to dissolve. To Philo, a bond not unbreakable, but only difficult to dissolve. There are, however, habits in sciences as well as in virtues. Here it is a question of the former kind of habits. Such they have who have been much and attentively occupied in the Scriptures.

Having their senses exercised to discern both good and evil) Just as in the external man the tongue, palate, and nostrils indicate what things are good and what are bad, and the better so, the more they are exercised in them, so also the inner man has his own senses, through which, when some mystical understanding of Scripture is brought forward, he easily judges whether it is correct or not, from the nature both of the Gospel itself and of those dispensations through which GOD figured the Gospel and prepared men to receive it in His own time. Thus also sense is transferred from the body to the mind, Phil. I. 9. I exercise in the glosses. See 1 Timothy IV. verse 7, below ch. XII. 11. Thus Isocrates said to exercise the soul. This discernment, of which there is question here, is not much unlike the discernment of spirits, of which 1 Corinthians XII. verse 10. In the garment of the high priest, alternating golden bells and pomegranates signified his facility to discern good from evil. We have that in Zeror.

We do not disapprove of these Grotian views. By the word of righteousness, however, B. Gerhard and Pareus understand the doctrine concerning CHRIST, who is our righteousness. But if the Hebrews were unskilled in this doctrine, how did they believe in CHRIST? They would not yet have been held in the census and number of the faithful: for he who does not understand CHRIST, that He Himself is our righteousness, cannot apprehend and embrace by faith the righteousness which alone consists before God.
