The symbol of believers, as Jeremiah testifies, is this: The Branch of David is Jehovah our righteousness, chap. XXIII. 6. Wherefore they would have to be called unskilled in the word of righteousness only in a certain respect, if that discourse is to be understood here, namely, regarding the lack of the habit of knowledge, of discerning good and evil, that is, true and false doctrine, just as little children do not know how to discern between food and food, and are often in danger in taking harmful things unless they are prevented by their mothers. Such a habit of doctrine is acquired by frequent reading, hearing, and meditation on Scripture, so that true and false doctrine concerning the word of righteousness are easily discerned, for which there is absolutely a need for exercised senses. Others, just as Grotius, explain it concerning a more perfect doctrine, chap. VI. verse 1, because the name of righteousness is of perfection, so that it may be hinted that whatever is of such a kind in Christian doctrine is appropriate only for the perfect. One partaking of milk is not he who partakes of milk, but he who still has need of it, as is evident from verse 12, who of necessity partakes of milk, still incapable of solid food, who is called unskilled in the word of righteousness, which seems to be understood absolutely, devoid of the doctrine of righteousness; therefore it is better to take it concerning more perfect doctrine. For he is a little child, the Vulgate rendered, for he is a little child. The Greek properly denotes an infant. An infant is spoken of with respect to more sublime doctrine. B. Dorfscheus explains these things more fully as follows: First, men who are infants and adults in age are compared with men who are infants and adults with respect to saving knowledge. Then, food to be proposed to infants and adults is compared with doctrine to be dispensed to beginners and the perfect. The Apostle calls infants infants, and adults perfect. Thus also beginners, the weak, and the slow are infants. In this sense he also calls the Corinthians infants, and carnal, comparatively of course, 1 Cor. III. 1, and he exhorts the Ephesians not to be infants, chap. IV. 14. He compares those who are adults in age to those who are adult and more perfect in doctrine, whom he also calls perfect comparatively, not absolutely, as they are tending toward a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of CHRIST, Eph. IV. 13. And just as adults have exercised senses, especially taste, touch, and smell, by which they can discern good food from bad: so also those who are adult in doctrine have spiritual senses exercised for the discernment of the true from the false, which the Apostle desires for the Philippians, chap. I. 9. The Apostle says the nourishment of infants is milk, that of adults is solid food: so also the instruction of beginners ought to be like milk, simple, easy, and open. But that of the more perfect can be more sublime, more abundant, fuller, and more perfect. But just as an infant who must still be nourished with milk is unfit for solid foods: so also beginners are not suitable to be applied to those more sublime and mystical senses. The Apostle calls them unskilled in the word of righteousness not only because they are not yet exercised in those more sublime senses, but also because they are hardly to be admitted to them before they are more correctly instructed in the elements. Therefore, the word of righteousness in this place is not the discourse of righteousness simply: for that is entirely in spiritual milk as well; but a discourse concerning mysteries explaining saving righteousness that is more sublime, fuller, more perfect, and more solid. For just as blood and spirit for sustaining the body of an infant can be elicited from milk just as well as it is elicited from the solid food of adults: so also the same method of obtaining salvation is to be communicated to beginners through the elements of the oracles, which is communicated to the more perfect through the word of righteousness. The Pauline character appears here again, see 1 Cor. XIII. 11, XIV. 28, Eph. V. 14. Senses are properly the organs of sense, of perception, such as eyes and ears, which, however, are to be understood here entirely spiritually. He therefore calls those perfect who, by long use, as if by a certain habit acquired through frequent actions, have a mind exercised as to what is good or evil in each doctrine, that is, orthodox or heterodox, true or false. For that is called good in doctrine (of which there is discourse here) which is true, and that evil which is false, according to that Apostolic saying 1 Thess. V. 21: Prove all things, hold fast that which is good. How much exercise is needed so that in the doctrine concerning true righteousness, in the article of justification, Apostolic orthodoxy may be distinguished from the heterodoxy of the Papists, Socinians, Arminians, Calixtines, Osiandrians, Weigelians, etc. Note, as Theophylact warns, how there is need of exercise and experience of the Scriptures if those things which savor of heresy and those which do not are to be distinguished by us. Nor are ears to be applied to everyone: for the throat tastes foods, but the soul tests discourses. But Estius wrongly gathers from this that many things are contained in the Holy Scriptures and tradition which it is neither necessary to propose to all, nor expedient, and that it suffices for the rude populace to believe in general that whatever is proposed to it by the Church to be believed is true. The Apostle says nothing of the sort here. He does not teach that such a general implicit faith is sufficient, which is rather mere ignorance of the object to be believed than faith. Indeed, he rebukes those who are unskilled in the word of righteousness, even among the promiscuous common people. He hints at nothing concerning a tradition which contains something different from the Holy Scriptures or the written Word of God. And although there are contained in the Holy Scriptures not a few things which it is not precisely necessary to propose to everyone, yet there is nothing contained in them which is not expedient for everyone. For whatever things were written were written for our learning, Rom. XV. 4. And all Scripture is divinely inspired and is profitable, 2. 1 Tim. 3:16. Neither is one doctrine to be proposed to the perfect, and another to the unlearned, regarding those things which are necessary for faith and salvation, since there is one faith, Eph. 4:5, and one and the same method of salvation, Acts 15:11; yet it is to be proposed in one way here, and in another way there, so that it may serve their capacity: concerning which Augustine in Tract. 98 on John and Thomas in this place warn that in the doctrine of faith the same thing is to be proposed to the perfect and the imperfect, the learned and the more unlearned, but in a different way. The Apostle wished to teach concerning the priesthood of CHRIST according to the order of Melchizedek. Which treatment, unless the necessary Catechetical heads were first repeated and inculcated, was too difficult for the unlearned Hebrews to grasp: nor was it required for the substance of Christian doctrine necessary for all the faithful to know, but for the illustration of those things which were formerly proposed to the Hebrew people in the Old Testament. Therefore the Apostle wished the Hebrews to be carried on to perfection, by repeating through a transition the Catechetical and most necessary heads of doctrine, and diligently warning them not to fall away from those elements of faith, and to slide further into such apostasy that they would finally trample underfoot the means of salvation and the very satisfaction of the Son of God, and expose it to ignominy, as will be taught in the following chapter. The sense is, as Estius admits: Whoever is such in the school of CHRIST, that he is still to be nourished with the milk of simpler doctrine, he is unversed in the doctrine that delivers more perfect things, and is little suited to hear it. He now leaves behind what he had to be taken, which he had said, you have need of milk. Whence he concludes syllogistically: Therefore you are not capable of more solid food. But solid food is for the perfect, that is, it is fitting for the perfect, as if for adults (such as I do not yet see you to be) to be fed with the nourishment of more sublime doctrine. The explanation of Theophylact, who understands by elements and milk the doctrine concerning the humanity of CHRIST, and by the more perfect doctrine and solid food the doctrine concerning the Divinity of Christ, is foreign, nor does it agree with the analogy of faith. For both doctrines, concerning Christ as true man and true God, pertain to τὰ σοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς τῶν λογίων τῦ θεῦ, and are necessary for all: as pertaining to τὴν πίσιν ἐπὶ θεὸν, which the Apostolic and Athanasian Creeds present as necessary for all. He truly does not know his own life, he does not know, as Hilary says in book IX de Trinit. almost at the beginning, who is ignorant of JESUS CHRIST as true God: and so also as true man. This is the true faith of human blessedness, to proclaim God and man, to confess the Word and the flesh: neither to be ignorant of GOD, that He is man, nor to be ignorant of the flesh, that it is the Word, says Vigilius in book III contr. Eutych. Wherefore that confession is utterly useless and impious, which venerates the Lord JESUS CHRIST either as God only and not man, or as man only and not GOD.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Τελείων δέ ἐστιν ἡ στερεὰ τροφή) τελείους intelligit ho- mines perfectæ ætatis, ut 1. Cor. II. 6. c. XIV. 20. Eph. IV. 13. Phil. III. 15. Per hos vero eos qui in rerum Divinarum meditatione multum profecerunt; οἱ τὴν γνωστικὴν πίστιν εἰληφότες, ut Clemens loquitur VI. Strom.

Τῶν διὰ τὴν ἕξιν) Ἕξις est firma facilitas, interpre- te Quintiliano. Κατηγοριῶν Scriptori, ἕξις χρονιώτερον καὶ μονιμώτερον διαθέσεως, sive διάθεσις διὰ χρόνε πλῆθος συμπεφυσιωμένη. Galeno, Διάθεσις χρόνιῳ κὶ δύσλυτος. Philoni, Δεσμὸς ἐκ ἀῤῥηκτος, ἀλλὰ, μόνον δυσδιάλυτος. Sunt autem ἕξεις tum in scientiis tum in virtutibus. Hic de priori genere ἕξεων agitur. Talem habent, qui multum & attente in Scripturis versati sunt.

Τὰ αἰσθητήρια γεγυμνασμένα ἐχόντων πρὸς διάκρισιν κα- λοῦτε καὶ κακοῦ) Sicut in homine externo lingua, pala- tum, nares indicant, quæ res bonæ, quæ malæ sint, eoque melius, quo magis in iis sunt exercitata, sic & homo in- terior sua habet αἰσθητήρια, per quæ allato aliquo mysti- co intellectu Scripturæ facile judicat, an is rectus sit, an non, ex natura tum ipsius Evangelii, tum illarum dispen- sationum, per quas DEUS Evangelium figuravit, & ad id suo tempore recipiendum homines præparavit. Sic & αἴσθησις à corpore ad animum transfertur Phil. I. 9. Γυ- μνάζω exercito in glossis. Vide 1. Timoth. IV. vers. 7. in- fra c. XII. 11. Sic γυμνάζειν τὴν ψυχὴν dixit Isocrates. Hæc διάκρισις, de qua hic agitur, non multum dissimilis est τῇ διακρίσει τῶν πνευμάτων, de qua 1. Corinth. XII. vers. 10. In veste summi Sacerdotis alterna tintinnabu- la aurea & mala Punica significabant facilitatem ejus להבחין בין טוב לרע ad discernenda bona à ma- lis. Habemus id in Zeror.

Non improbamus hæc Grotiana. Per λόγον tamen δικαιοσύνης B. Gerhardus & Pareus intelli- gunt doctrinam de CHRISTO, qui est nostra justi- tia. Sed si ἄπειροι hujus doctrinæ Ebræi fuere, quomodo credidere in CHRISTUM? Non- dum ergo in censu & numero fidelium habendi fuissent: Qui enim CHRISTUM non intelli- git, quod nostra ipse justitia, fide justitiam, quæ so- la coram Deo consistit, apprehendere & amplecti non potest. Symbolum credentium Jeremia te- ste hoc est: Germen Davidis est Jehovah nostra ju- stitia cap. XXIII. 6. Quapropter nonnisi κατά τι di- cendi fuerint ἄπειροι λόγυ δικαιοσύνης, si ille ser- mo hic intelligendus, nimirum quoad defectum habitus cognitionis, discernendi bonum & malum, hoc est, veram & falsam doctrinam, sicut parvuli inter cibum & cibum discernere nesciunt, & sæpe in noxiis sumendis periclitantur, nisi à matribus prohibeantur. Qualis doctrinæ habitus crebra lectione, auditione ac meditatione Scripturæ com- paratur, ut facile veræ & falsæ doctrinæ circa ser- monem justitiæ discernuntur, ad quam opus omni- no est exercitatis sensibus. Alii perinde ut Gro- tius explicant de doctrina perfectiore, cap. VI. vers. 1. quia justitiæ nomen est perfectionis, ut innuatur, quicquid in doctrina Christiana ejusmodi est, ut solis perfectis competat. Ετό μετέχων γάλακτος, non est, qui participat lac, sed qui necesse adhuc habet, ut è vers. 12. constat, qui ex necessitate lac participat, solidioris cibi adhuc incapax, qui dici- tur ἄπειρος λόγυ δικαιοσύνης, quod videtur ab- solute intelligendum, expers doctrinæ justitiæ, ideo præstat de doctrina perfectiori accipere. Νήπιος γάρ ἐςι Vulgatus reddidit, parvulus enim est. Græcum proprie notat infantem. Infans dicitur respectu sublimioris doctrinæ. Plenius hæc ita explicat B. Dorfscheus: Comparantur 1. homines infantes & adulti ætate cum hominibus infantibus & adultis respectu scientiæ salvificæ. Deinde cibus infanti- bus & adultis proponendus cum doctrina incipien- tibus & perfectis dispensanda. Infantes Apostolus vocat νηπίυς, adultos τελείες. Sic & incipientes, imbecilles & tardi νήπιοι sunt. Hoc sensu etiam Co- rinthios νηπίυς vocat, & σαρκικὲς comparate scili- cet, 1. Cor. III. 1. & hortatur Ephesios, ne sint νήπιοι, cap. IV. 14. Adultos ætate comparat adultis & per- fectioribus doctrina, quos τελείες etiam comparate, non absolute vocat, utpote tendentes εἰς ἄνδρα τέλειον ad mensuram staturæ adulti CHRISTI, Eph. IV. 13. Et quemadmodum adulti exercitatos habent sensus, gustus imprimis, tactus, & odoratus, quibus discerne- re possunt bonum cibum à malo: Sic & adulti do- ctrina spirituales sensus ad discretionem veri à falso exercitatos habent, quod optat Philippensibus Aposto- lus cap. I. 9. Nutrimentum infantum Apostolus dicit esse lac, adultorum ςερεὰν τροφήν: Sic & inci- pientium informatio lacti similis, simplex, facilis, aperta esse debet. Perfectiorum vero sublimior, abundantior, plenior, & perfectior esse potest. Quem- admodum autem infans lacte adhuc nutriendus ine- ptus est ad cibos solidos: Sic & incipientes idonei non sunt, qui sublimioribus istis & mysticis adhibe- antur sensibus. Apostolus vocat illos ἀπείρες λόγε δικαιοσύνης non tantum quia nondum exercitati sunt in sensibus istis sublimioribus, sed etiam quia vix antequam in clementis rectius erudiantur, ad illos admittendi. Itaque λόγος δικαιοσύνης hoc loco non est sermo justitiæ simpliciter: Is enim omnino est in lacte etiam spirituali; sed sermo de mysteriis ju- stitiam salvificam explicantibus sublimior, plenior, perfectior, solidior. Quemadmodum enim è lacte sanguis & Spiritus sustentando corpori infantis ac- commodatus æque elici potest, atq; elicitur è solido ad- ultorum cibo : Sic etiam eadem ratio salutis conse- quendæ per στοιχεῖα τῶν λογίων incipientibus commu- nicanda est, quæ per λόγον δικαιοσύνης perfectioribus communicatur. Paulinus hic iterum character comparet, Vid. 1. Corinth. XIII 11. c. XIV. 28. Eph. V. 14. Αἰσθητήρια proprie organa sensuum sunt, αἰσθήσεως ut oculi, aures, quæ vero hic omnino spiritualiter intelligenda. Perfectos ergo vocat, qui longo u- su, velut habitu quodam per crebras actiones com- parato, mentem habent exercitatam, quid in una- quaque doctrina bonum sit vel malum, hoc est, or- thodoxum vel heterodoxum, verum vel falsum. Nam id in doctrina, (de qua hic sermo) bonum dicitur, quod verum, id malum, quod falsum est, juxta illud Apostolicum 1. Thessal. V. 21. Πάντα δοκιμάζετε, τὸ καλὸν κατέχετε. Quanta opus est exercitatione, ut in doctrina de vera justitia in arti- culo de justificatione orthodoxia Apostolica dif- cernatur ab heterodoxia vers. 19. Papistarum, Socinianorum, Arminianorum, Calixtinorum, Osi- andristarum, Weigelianorum, &c. Adverte, mo- nente Theophylacto, quemadmodum exercitatione & experientia Scripturarum sit opus, si nobis, quæ hæresin sapiant, & quæ minus, sunt differenda. Neq; omnibus adhibendæ sunt aures : Guttur enim cibos degustat, anima vero probat sermones. Perperam autem hinc colligit Estius, multa in sacris literis & traditione contineri, quæ nec necesse sit omnibus proponi, nec expediat, sufficere populo rudi, in ge- nere credere, vera esse, quæcunque ei ab Ecclesia credenda proponuntur. Nihil tale hic Aposto- lus. Non sufficere talem fidem generalem impli- citam docet, quæ potius objecti credendi mera est ignorantia quam fides. Imo redarguit, si qui ex- pertes sint sermonis justitiæ, etiam in promiscua ple- be. Nihil de traditione, quæ diversi quid à Sacris literis, vel Verbo Dei scripto contineat, innuit. Et quanquam in Sacris literis contineantur non pauca, quæ non præcise necesse sit proponi omni- bus, nihil tamen in illis continetur, quod non ex- pediat omnibus. Quæcunque enim scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, Rom. XV. 4. Et omnis Scriptura Divinitus inspirata ὠφέλιμος uti- lis est, 2. Timoth. III. 16. neque alia doctrina, quoad ea, quæ ad fidem, & salutem necessaria sunt, perfectis, alia rudibus proponenda, quum una sit fides, Ephes. IV. 5. una & eadem salutis ratio, Actor. XV. 11. alio tamen modo hic, quam illic proponenda est, ut captui eorum inserviat : quo de Augustinus tract. XCVIII. in Joh. & Thomas in h. l. monent, quod in doctrina fidei eadem perfectis & imperfectis eruditis & rudioribus proponenda, sed diverso modo. De sacerdotio CHRISTI secundum or- dinem Melchisedech docere volebat Apostolus. Quæ tractatio, rudioribus Ebræis nisi repeteren- tur & inculcarentur prius capita Catechetica ne- cessaria, perceptu nimis difficilis : nec ad substan- tiam doctrinæ Christianæ omnibus fidelibus cognitu ne- cessaria requirebatur, sed ad illustrationem eorum, quæ in Veteri Testamento populo Ebræo quon- dam proposita. Ideo volebat Apostolus Ebræos ad perfectionem ferri, per transitionem repetens Catechetica, & maxime necessaria doctrinæ capita, & sedulo monens, ne ab illis fidei elementis defi- ciant, eaque apostasia porro ita prolabantur, ut media salutis, ipsamque Filii Dei satisfactionem denique pedibus conculcent, & ignominiæ expo- nant, ut cap. seq. docebitur. Sensus est, fatente Estio : Quicunque in CHRISTI schola talis est, ut adhuc lacte simplicioris doctrinæ fovendus sit, is ru- dis est doctrinæ perfectiora tradentis, & ad eam au- diendum parum idoneus. Jam relinquit affumen- dum, quod dixerat, vos lacte opus habetis. Unde syllogistice concludit: Ergo solidioris cibi non estis capaces. Perfectorum autem est solidus cibus, hoc est, perfectis, tanquam adultis (quales vos nondum esse video) convenit pasci doctrinæ sublimioris ali- mento. Theophylacti explicatio per elementa & lac doctrinam de CHRISTI humanitate; per doctrinam vero perfectiorem & cibum solidum do- ctrinam de Christi Divinitate intelligentis aliena est, nec fidei analogiæ convenit. Nam utraque doctrina, de Christo vero homine & vero Deo ad τὰ σοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς τῶν λογίων τῦ θεῦ per- tinet, omnibusque necessaria est: utpote ad τὴν πίσιν ἐπὶ θεὸν, quam Symbolum Apostolicum, & Athanasianum ceu omnibus necessariam exhibet, pertinens. Nescit profecto vitam suam, nescit, dicente Hilario libr. IX. de Trinit. fere sub ini- tium, qui JESUM CHRISTUM ut ve- rum Deum: Ita & verum hominem ignorat. Hæc humanæ beatitudinis fides vera est Deum & ho- minem prædicare, verbum & carnem confiteri: neque DEUM nescire, quod homo, neque carnem ignorare, quod Verbum sit, ait Vigilius libr. III. contr. Eutych. Quare prorsus inutilis, & im- pia est confessio, quæ Dominum JESUM CHRISTUM aut Deum tantummodo & non hominem aut hominem solum & non DE- UM veneratur.

## 6:1 Argument
CHAPTER VI.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

Having repeated the elements of Christian doctrine, and having declared the supreme danger of those falling away from it by the similitude of unfruitful land, he testifies that he hopes for better things from the Hebrews, leaning upon Divine grace, and warns them to keep a firm hope and not to change, but to imitate those who through faith and patience inherit the promises, by the example of Abraham, to whom God had confirmed the promise with an oath, so that to the heirs He might render His counsel concerning salvation indubitable both by promise and by oath, and that we might have a firm anchor of hope, penetrating into the inner part of the veil, into which Christ has entered as a forerunner for us.

There are three parts. I. A repetition of the chapters of Catechetical doctrine, to verse 3. II. A proposition of the defense of the faith, to v. 8. III. An exhortation to constancy in faith and an immovable hope, to verse 20.

PART I. A repetition of the chapters of Catechetical doctrine.

Verse 1.

Διὸ) That is, lest you always remain such as I have already said you are, looking at the greatest part of your flock; our writers accommodate themselves now to the greater, now to the more advanced.

Ἀφίντες τὸν τῆς ἀρχῆς τῦ Χρισῦ λόγον) The primitive discourse of Christ, that is, concerning Christ and His discipline, which is often comprehended under the name of Christ. These rudiments, you ask, we shall now set aside.

Ἐπὶ τὴν τελειότητα φερώμεθα) He calls τελειότητα the understanding of the figures hidden in the Old Testament and all the dispensations of God tending toward the Gospel. See above c. IV. verse 14. and what is said there.

By rhetorical preterition the Apostle repeats those chapters only, as if he were saying: We shall not speak now of those beginnings, we shall rather be carried to more perfect things; we shall not again lay a foundation, such as you ought not to have been ignorant that you should consist in these chapters, &c. That διὸ is used, not because these things cohere with that ignorance; for thus the contrary would rather have to be inferred, since you are so unversed that you still have need of the elements of the oracles of God, come, I will set them before you, before we are carried to more perfect things, but because they cohere with the duty of teaching, concerning which the Apostle says, καὶ γὰρ ὀφείλοντες εἶναι διδάσκαλοι διὰ τὸν χρόνον, as if he were saying: You ought already to be Teachers, and so to be led from milk to solid food, in proportion to the time that you have spent in Christianity: And it is unworthy of your state that milk should still be instilled into you, as if you were infants; Therefore we too, setting aside the doctrine with which we are accustomed to instruct the unlearned, and not laying a foundation anew, which I present to you at least by bare repetition, will proceed, God willing, to those things which are suitable for adults and the perfect, when we have warned you not to fall away from that faith, but to persist constant in the same, until you penetrate through faith and invincible hope into the interior of the veil of the holy of holies, that is, heaven.

Mὴ πάλιν θεμέλιον καταβαλλόμενοι) Not repeating again those things which you learned long ago, and which are יסודי of Christianity. See above ch. V. verse 13.

Μετανοίας ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἔργων) For repentance precedes baptism, Acts II. 38. Dead works are those which alienate us from God. Just as the soul gives life to the body; so God to the soul. See what was said on this matter at Matt. VIII. verse 21. Repentance תשובה

Καὶ πίστεως ἐπὶ Θεὸν) Which also itself precedes baptism, Acts VIII. verse 37. Faith in Christ is at the same time faith in GOD.

Latin:

CAPUT VI.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Repetitis doctrinæ Christianæ elementis, & declarato supremo periculo deficientium ab eadem, similitudine terræ infrugi- feræ, meliora se de Ebræis sperare testa- tur, innixus Divinæ gratiæ, monetque spem firmam servent nec mutent, sed imitentur eos, qui per fidem & patien- tiam promissiones consequuntur, Abra- hami exemplo, cui juramento Deus pro- missionem firmarat, ut hæredibus con- silium suum de salute indubium redde- ret tum promissione, tum jurejurando, firmamque spei anchoram haberemus, penetrantem in intima veli, quo Chri- stus prodromus ingressus pro nobis.

Partes tres sunt. I. Repetitio capitum doctrinæ Catecheticæ, ad vers. 3. II. Propositio ἀπολογίας fi- dei, ad v. 8. III. Exhortatio ad constantiam in fi- de ac spem immotam, ad vers. 20.

PARS I. Repetitio capitum doctrinæ Catecheticæ.

Vers. 1.

Διὸ) Id est, ne semper tales maneatis, quales jam esse vos dixi, spectans maximam gregis vestri partem; Scriptores nostri modo se majoribus, modo provectiori- bus accommodant.

Ἀφίντες τὸν τῆς ἀρχῆς τῦ Χρισῦ λόγον) Sermonem primitivum Christi, id est, de Christo & ejus disciplina, quæ sæpe Christi nomine comprehenditur. Ista titocinia, inquis, nunc seponemus.

Ἐπὶ τὴν τελειότητα φερώμεθα) Τελειότητα vocat in- tellectum figurarum latentium in Veteri Testamento & dispensationes Dei omnes tendentes ad Evangelium. Vi- de supra c. IV. vers. 14. & ibi dicta.

Per præteritionem Rhetoricam illa capita tantum repetit Apostolus, quasi dicat: Non dicemus jam de initiis illis, feremur potius ad perfectiora; non de- nuo jaciemus fundamentum, quale in hisce capitibus consistere vos ignorare haud debebatis, &c. Illud διὸ adhibetur, non quod hæc cum ista ignorantia cohæreant; sic enim inferendum potius foret contrarium, quum adeo rudes sitis, ut opus habea- tis adhuc elementis eloquiorum Dei, agite ea vo- bis proponam, antequam ad perfectiora feramur, sed quod cohæreant cum debito magisterii, de quo Apostolus, καὶ γὰρ ὀφείλοντες εἶναι διδάσκαλοι διὰ τὸν χρόνον, quasi dicat: Vos jam debebatis Magistri esse, adeoque à lacte ad solidum cibum traduci, pro ratione temporis, quod in Chri- stianismo egistis: Et indignum vestro statui, ut adhuc lac vobis instilletur, tanquam infantibus; idcirco nos quoque, sepositâ doctrinâ, qua rudes instituere solemus, neque jacto de novo funda- mento, quod saltem nuda repetitione vobis fi- sto, ad ea progrediemur, ubi DEUS voluerit, quæ adultis & perfectis conveniunt, ubi monue- rimus, ne ab illa fide deficiatis, sed constantes in eadem persistatis, donec in interiora veli san- cti sanctorum, hoc est, cœli, per fidem & spem invictam penetretis.

Mὴ πάλιν θεμέλιον καταβαλλόμενοι) Non iterum re- petentes ea, quæ pridem didicistis, & quæ sunt יסודי Christianismi. Vide supra c. V. vers. 13.

Μετανοίας ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἔργων) Pœnitentia enim ba- ptismum præcedit, Actor. II. 38. Ἔργα νεκρὰ sunt, quæ à Deo nos alienant. Sicut anima vitam dat corpori; Ita animæ Deus. Vide quæ dicta hac de re ad Matth. VIII. vers. 21. Μετάνοια תשובה

Καὶ πίστεως ἐπὶ Θεὸν) Quæ & ipsa baptismum præce- dit, Actor. VIII. vers. 37. Fides in Christum simul est fi- des in DEUM.

## 6:2
Vers. 2.

Βαπτισμῶν διδαχῆς) That is, the doctrine concerning the double baptism, interior and exterior. See what has been said by us at Matt. III. 6. ch. XXVIII. 19. and John III. 5. The baptized ought always to remember what they have promised, and what they have received.

Ἐπιθέσεώς τε χειρῶν) סמיכת ידים. Under this name are understood all rites outside of baptism and the Eucharist. For hands were laid upon the baptized to obtain the confirming power of the Holy Spirit, and upon those ordained to the Presbyterate, and upon those reconciled after sins, and upon the infirm in body: Indeed, also upon new spouses requesting a blessing from the Church. See what we have said at Matt. XIX. verse 13.

Ἀναστάσεώς τε νεκρῶν) תחית מתים. After he has spoken of our duty, he adds also a mention of the reward. See John V. 25. 1 Cor. XV. 16, 29, 52. It is called resurrection from the dead, and resurrection of the dead, as here and 1 Cor. XV. 12, 13, 42.

Καὶ κρίματος αἰωνίου) דין, namely in both directions, as can be seen in Matt. XXVI. 45. Thus Tertullian in his prescription against the Heretics: He will come with glory to take the saints into the fruit of eternal life and heavenly promises, and to adjudge the profane to perpetual fire, after the resurrection of both parties has been effected with the restoration of the flesh. Hence the opinion of Origen is refuted. There is one judgment, irretractable and valid forever. The foundation of Christian doctrine and the discourse of the beginning of the doctrine of CHRIST or elementary and initial are here interchanged: and to this foundation, upon which gold, silver, and precious stones are to be built—which is likewise a Pauline phrase, 1 Corinthians III, verses 11, 12—the following articles pertain: For that foundation is completed by several articles, joined together among themselves, as for instance

1. concerning repentance from dead works, whence it is necessary that we know what works are dead, that is, sins, which proceed from a man spiritually dead, bring with them eternal death, in which there is nothing of life, mere death, which are destitute of the life of grace, as Thomas explains, which knowledge is drawn from the decalogue, and that it may be clear what that μετάνοια (repentance) is.

2. Concerning faith in GOD the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, such as it is, which is comprised in the Apostolic Creed.

3. Concerning baptism, where the plural is used, not because one baptism is interior and another exterior, since there is not but one baptism, as the Apostle testifies, as there is one faith, Ephesians IV. 5. But either because there were frequent βαπτισμοὶ (baptisms), or by the common Enallage of number, whence the Syrian rendered it in the singular, and Augustine, book on faith and works, chapter XI, [calls it] the washing of doctrine. It is called the foundation of the doctrine of baptisms, so that not the act of baptism itself, but the doctrine concerning baptism, necessarily to be delivered in fundamental or elementary instruction, may be designated. Some, with Oecumenius, Cajetan, Gagney, and Erasmus, divide these, βαπτισμῶν, διδαχῆς, and the blessed Gerhard understands by διδαχὴν (doctrine) the fuller doctrine, which was accustomed to be delivered to Catechumens only after baptism had been received, from Jerome on Matthew XVIII. But the Greek codices are ignorant of the distinction, and most interpreters join the words, nor is a fuller doctrine attended to here, but only the elements of doctrine necessary for all are regarded: Meanwhile, we do not doubt that, by parity of reason and kinship, the doctrine concerning the Lord's Supper is delivered at the same time as another Sacrament. Compare System of Theology, Vol. II, page 5.

4. Concerning the laying on of hands, by which periphrasis [is meant] the doctrine concerning the Holy ministry, to which they were ordained by the laying on of hands, to which the preaching of the word, the administration of the sacraments, and the power of absolving and binding were entrusted, or the use of the keys, Matthew XXVIII, John XX, 1 Corinthians IV, verse 1, 1 Timothy V, verse 22. Grotius, wishing to gratify the Papists, wants seven sacraments to be comprised by this word: But Holy Scripture knows only two sacraments, baptism and the Supper of the Lord, 1 Corinthians XII. 13, and express mention of baptism had already been made, nor is anything commanded in the Holy Scriptures concerning χειροθεσίᾳ (laying on of hands) in confirmation (concerning which, understood in the Papistical sense, there is deep silence in the Scriptures), nor in marriage, and not even in repentance.

5. Concerning the resurrection of the dead. Which article some think is expressed here specifically because of the error of the Sadducees, even though it is comprised in the Apostolic Creed: But it is by no means to be conceded that the Apostolic Creed, such as it is now held, was already known in that age, or was here looked to by the Apostle, concerning which see in the Syncretism of Calixtus, Postulate I. But here is understood not only the blessed resurrection to glory, but in general the resurrection of all, both good and evil.

6. The doctrine concerning eternal judgment, namely the final judgment, which is called eternal because its execution extends itself into eternity. It com-

prises therefore not only the promulgation of the sentence, but also the execution of the promulgated sentence, by which the rewards of the faithful and the punishments of the unfaithful are eternal.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Βαπτισμῶν διδαχῆς) Id est, doctrina de duplice ba- ptismo, interiore & exteriore. Vide quæ à nobis dicta ad Matth. III. 6. c. XXVIII. 19. & Joh. III. 5. Memi- nisse semper debent baptizati quid promiserint, & quid acceperint.

Ἐπιθέσεώς τε χειρῶν) סמיכת ידים. Sub hoc nomine intelliguntur ritus omnes extra baptismum & Eucharistiam. Nam manus imponebantur & baptizatis ad obtinendam vim confirmantem Spiritus sancti, & or- dinatis ad Presbyterium, & post peccata reconciliatis, & corpore in firmis: Imo & novis conjugibus benedictio- nem ab Ecclesia postulantibus. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. XIX. vers. 13.

Ἀναστάσεώς τε νεκρῶν) תחית מתים. Postquam loquutus est de nostro officio, adjicit etiam præmii men- tionem. Vide Johan. V. 25. 1. Corinth. XV. 16. 29. 52. Dicitur ἀνάστασις ἐκ νεκρῶν, & ἀνάστασις νεκρῶν, quomo- do hic & 1. Cor. XV. 12. 13. 42.

Καὶ κρίματος αἰωνίου) דין, nempe in utramque partem, ut videre est Matth. XXVI. 45. Sic Tertullianus in præscriptione contra Hæreticos: Venturum cum clari- tate ad sumendos sanctos in vitæ æternæ & promissorum cælestium fructum, & ad profanos adjudicandos igni per- petuo, facta utriusque partis resuscitatione cum carnis re- stitutione. Hinc refellitur Origenis opinio. Unum est ju- dicium irretractabile valens in perpetuum. Fundamentum doctrinæ Christianæ & sermo initii doctrinæ CHRISTI vel elementaris & initialis hic commutantur: & ad hoc fundamentum, cui superstruendum aurum, argentum & lapides pretiosi, quæ phrasis itidem Paulina, 1. Corinth. III. vers. 11. 12. pertinent sequentes articuli: Absolvitur enim fundamentum illud pluribus articulis, inter se coagmentatis, utpote

1. de pœnitentia à mortuis operibus, unde opus est, ut cognoscamus, quænam opera mortua sint, hoc est, peccata, quæ proficiscuntur ab homine spiritualiter mortuo, æternam secum afferunt mortem, in quibus nihil vitæ est, mera mors, quæ vita gratiæ destituta sunt, ut Thomas explicat, quæ cognitio ex decalogo hauritur, utque quænam illa μετάνοια sit, constet.

2. De fide in DEUM Patrem, Filium & Spiritum sanctum, qualis est, quæ in symbolo Apostolico comprehenditur.

3. De baptismo, ubi pluralis adhibetur, non quod baptismus alius sit interior, alius exterior, siquidem non sit, nisi unus baptismus, teste Apostolo, ut una fides, Ephes. IV. 5. Sed vel quia frequentes βαπτισμοὶ erant, vel per Enallagen numeri usitatam, unde Syrus in singulari reddidit, & Augustinus l. de fid. & oper. cap. XI. lavacri doctrinæ. Fundamentum dicitur doctrinæ baptismi, ut non ipse baptismatis actus, sed doctrina de baptismate necessario tradenda in informatione fundamentali, vel elementaria designetur. Nonnulli cum Oecumenio, Cajetano, Gagneo, Erasmo dividunt hæc, βαπτισμῶν, διδαχῆς, & intelligit B. Gerhardus per διδαχὴν doctrinam pleniorem, quæ demum post perceptum baptismum Catechumenis tradi consueverit ex Hieronym. in Matth. XIIX. Sed codices Græci distinctionem ignorant, & plerique Interpretes voces conjungunt, neque hic attenditur plenior doctrina, sed tantum elementa respiciuntur doctrinæ omnibus necessariæ: Interim non dubitamus, ad paritatem rationis & cognationem, doctrinam de Cœna Dominica, ceu altero Sacramento simul traditam. Conf. System. Theol. Tom. II. pagin. 5.

4. De impositione manuum, qua περιφράσει doctrinam de S. ministerio, ad quod ordinabantur manuum impositione, cui verbi prædicatio, sacramentorum administratio, & potestas absolvendi & ligandi credebatur, vel usus clavium Matth. XXVIII. Johan. XX. 1. Corinth. IV. vers. 1. 1. Timoth. V. vers. 22. Grotius Papistis gratificaturus septem sacramenta hac voce comprehendi vult: Sed Scriptura sacra non novit nisi duo sacramenta, baptismum & cœnam Domini, 1. Corinth. XII. 13. & baptismi jam facta erat diserta mentio, neque in Sacris literis de χειροθεσίᾳ in confirmatione, (qua de Papistico sensu intellecta altum in Scripturis est silentium) neque in copulatione, ac ne quidem in pœnitentia quicquam præcipitur.

5. De mortuorum resurrectione. Quem articulum hic speciatim exprimi propter Sadducæorum errorem nonnulli putant, etsi in Symbolo Apostolico comprehensus sit: Sed Symbolum Apostolicum, quale jam habetur, ætate ista jam cognitum, aut hic ab Apostolo spectatum fuisse minime concedendum, quo de in Syncret. Calixt. Postul. I. Non autem hic tantum resurrectio beata ad gloriam, sed in genere resurrectio omnium tum bonorum tum malorum intelligitur.

6. Doctrina de æterno judicio, judicio nempe novissimo, quod æternum dicitur, quia executio ejus in æternum sese porrigit. Com

plectitur itaque non tantum sententiæ promul- gationem, sed etiam promulgatæ sententiæ exe- quutionem, qua præmia fidelium & supplicia in- fidelium æterna.

## 6:3
Ver. 3.

Καὶ τοῦτο ποιήσομεν, ἐάν περ ἐπιτρέπῃ ὁ Θεὸς) We will do this, if GOD grants life, at another time, for the use of those who are more unlearned. He hoped that he would write other epistles to the Hebrews. And perhaps he did write them, but they have perished. But the Manuscript has ποιήσωμεν, we would do, if GOD were to permit; if there were leisure.

Ribera also refers this to what immediately precedes, namely that he wishes, GOD permitting or granting, to repeat those elementary things at another time. But it is more correctly referred by most others to those more remote words, let us be borne on to perfection, because he did not wish to deal with the Hebrews concerning the things just enumerated, seeing that they ought to have been teachers long ago, and to inform others about such things, not to receive information. However, he undertook that he would now treat of these things which make for perfection, GOD bestowing. For what Grotius suspects concerning another Epistle to the Hebrews is destitute of all authority. But concerning the word ἐπιτρέπειν, Interpreters rightly observe that it does not signify a bare permission, but something more, namely a concession, by which there is authority or power to do something. Compare Acts XVIII. ver. 21. 1 Cor. IV. ver. 19. James IV. ver. 15.

But the Apostle does not here doubt concerning the Divine concession, but teaches that on this condition we should commit all things to the Divine will, without whose nod we can do nothing.

Therefore, as Ribera rightly says, to permit is not here understood in such a way as when GOD is said to permit sins, but so that it is the same as to will, or not to hinder, which is also said in the case of good things. Thus he also said in 1 Cor. XVI. For I do not wish to see you now in passing. For I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits. He indeed wished it, but he saw that it could happen that at that time GOD might command him other things, so that he could not remain with them.

B. Dorscheus indeed refers that ποιήσομεν to the repeated laying of the foundation, but he provides another sense, which we leave in the middle: For there, he says, the Divine permission is properly to be expected. For if anyone becomes a Catechumen so often out of some levity and slipperiness of mind, and has need to be led back to the elements of Christian doctrine, by this very fact he implies that contempt, or a certain inexcusable negligence, dominates the Divine grace in him, and consequently that he also causes the grieving of the Holy Spirit; whether the ministry of the Holy Spirit can always be effective concerning such a man, so often forgetful, so often elementary, so negligent, or whether indeed out of just judgment GOD might sometimes wish to withdraw His grace, and give such contemners of the once-acknowledged truth over to a reprobate mind, that now depends upon the Divine permission. For although GOD offers His grace to all, yet He has not promised, but after so manifold a neglect and contempt of the Divine truth and rejection of the illuminating grace, that He will always restore it. But if that does not happen, then the fall into the sin against the Holy Spirit is easy.

PART II. Proposition of the danger of apostasy from the faith.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Καὶ τοῦτο ποιήσομεν, ἐάν περ ἐπιτρέπῃ ὁ Θεὸς) Fa- ciemus hoc, si DEUS vitam dederit, alio tempore, in u- sum eorum, qui rudiores sunt. Sperabat se & alias ad Ebræos epistolas scripturum. Et forte scripsit, sed in- terierunt. At Manuscriptus ποιήσωμεν faceremus, si DE- US permitteret; si esset otium.

Refert & Ribera id ad proxime præceden- tia, quod nempe alio tempore repetere illa ele- mentaria, DEO permittente, vel concedente, velit. Sed rectius ab aliis plerisque refertur ad remotiora illa ἐπὶ τὴν τελειότητα φερώμεθα, quia de proxime enumeratis nolebat agere pe- nes Ebræos, utpote qui jam pridem Doctores esse debuerant, aliosque de talibus informare, non informationem accipere. De hisce autem, quæ ad perfectionem faciunt, DEO largien- te, sese jam acturum recepit. Quod enim de Epistola alia ad Ebræos suspicatur Grotius, omni destituitur autoritate. De voce ἐπιτρέπειν vero recte observant Interpretes, non nudam signifi- cari permissionem, sed amplius aliquid, videli- cet concessionem, qua autoritas vel potestas sit ali- quid agendi. Confer. Actor. XVIII. vers. 21. 1. Corinth. IV. vers. 19. Jac. IV. vers. 15.

Non autem dubitat hic Apostolus de Divi- na concessione, sed docet eo pacto, nos omnia Divinæ voluntati committere, sine cujus nu- tu nihil valemus.

Ideo, quod recte Ribera, non ita nunc acci- pitur permittere, ut cum DEUS dicitur permit- tere peccata, sed ut idem sit, atque velle, aut non impedire, quod etiam in bonis dicitur. Ita etiam dixit 1. Corinth. XVI. Nolo enim vos mo- do in transitu videre. Spero enim me aliquantu- lum temporis manere apud vos, si Dominus per- miserit. Volebat quidem, sed videbat fieri posse, ut eo tempore DEUS sibi alia præciperet, ut ma- nere apud eos non posset.

B. Dorscheus refert quidem illud ποιήσαμεν ad καταβολὴν τοῦ θεμελίου iteratam, sed alium sen- sum tradit, quem in medio relinquimus: Nam ibi, inquit, proprie permissio Divina ex- pectanda est. Si quis enim toties ex levitate & lubricitate aliqua animi fiat Catechumenus, & ad elementa doctrinæ Christianæ necesse habeat deduci, hoc ipso innuit, gratia Divina apud i- psum dominari contemptum, aut inexcusabilem quandam negligentiam, adeoque etiam causari illum contristationem sancti Spiritus, an circa ejusmodi hominem toties obliviosum, toties ele- mentarium, tam negligentem, ministerium Spi- ritus sancti semper possit esse efficax, annon ve- ro ex justo judicio interdum DEUS gratiam suam subtrahere, & in reprobum sensum contempo- res ejusmodi semel agnitæ veritatis dare velit, id jam à permissione Divina dependet. Quanquam enim omnibus gratiam suam DEUS porrigat, non tamen promisit, sed post totuplicem negle- ctum contemptumque veritatis Divinæ & gratiæ illuminantis rejectionem eam semper redditurum. Quod si non fiat, jam in proclivi est prolapsus in peccatum in Spiritum sanctum.

PARS II. Propositio periculi apostasias à fide.

## 6:3
3. Μετόχυς γενηθέντας Πνέυματος ἁγίυ, who have been made partakers of the HOLY SPIRIT; as of a seal, a pledge, and an earnest of eternal salvation, 1 Cor. 1:22, Eph. 1:14.

Latin:

3. Μετόχυς γενηθέντας Πνέυματος ἁγίυ, qui participes facti sunt SPIRITUS SAN- CTI; ceu sigilli, pignoris, & arrhæ æternæ sa- lutis, 1. Corinth. I. 22. Ephes. I. 14.

## 6:4-5
Vers. 4. 5. 6.

For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, and have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, and have fallen away, to renew them again unto repentance.) He says this, not that those elements or foundations of Christianity are often repeated and inculcated into minds in vain, because there is a huge danger if they are cast aside. This passage was the main reason why the Roman Church hesitated for a long time to receive this book into the canon. It is clear from Tertullian de pudicitia. For it was milder than other Churches in its discipline regarding the lapsed. Most Churches, after baptism, would reconcile some who had lapsed and admit them to communion, but they excepted three most serious crimes: idolatry, homicide, and adultery. Tertullian complains that adulterers were admitted to the peace of the Church by Pope Zephyrinus. But indeed that this was not new but old at Rome, the Shepherd of Hermas II. 4 teaches us, but dealing only with one who had lapsed once, not with one who had lapsed again, which distinction you also have in Clement, Strom. II. In the times of Cyprian, when it was being disputed concerning those who had lapsed into idolatry, whether they could be received to public penance and reconciliation, and the custom had been varied, even in Africa itself, Cyprian sustained his judgment, aiming at this, that with the persecution ceasing, something might be established in common. The Roman Church, being milder than the others, had been the author that after long times of penance the lapsed might be received to communion. This displeased Novatus and Novatian, who for this reason made a schism. But the opinion of the Roman Church concerning those who had lapsed into idolatry, and in like manner concerning those who had lapsed into homicide, pleased the great Nicene Synod, as is to be seen from its canons. Nor, however, should it be thought that those ancients, observers of a more rigid discipline, held for certain that such would perish eternally, but they commended them to Divine mercy, with private, not public prayers, and not in such a way that they promised them anything for certain. And this was also observed in those who, after the first penance publicly performed, would again bind themselves to other crimes, outside those three. Tertullian de pœnitentia: God, therefore, foreseeing these poisons of his, although the gate of forgiveness was closed and the bar of baptism obstructed, still permitted something to lie open. He placed a second penance in the vestibule, which might open to those knocking: But now once, because now a second time, but never more, because the next time in vain. For is not even this once enough? See also the following, where a second penance is spoken of in respect to that which precedes baptism. Below in the same book he calls this penance both second and one, the business of which he says is in a narrow place, and with how severe a discipline it was exercised, Ambrose shows at length; Although it has been cautiously and wholesomely provided that a place for that most humble penance be granted once in the Church, lest a cheap medicine be less useful to the sick, which is the more useful the less contemptible it has been. Yet who would dare to say to GOD: Why do you spare again this man, who after his first penance has again bound himself in the snares of iniquity? And that the gate of penance is sometimes closed even with GOD, the Hebrews felt, as is to be seen in the Chaldean paraphrase of Cant. V. verse 5, and among the Rabbis on Isaiah XXII. verse 14. Philo, however, concerning rewards and punishments says: Ἐνταῦθα δὲ ὅλοι βίοι πίπτουσιν ἐς ἅπαξ διατρα- πέντας μόγις ἐστὶν ἀναγῆψαι. With which those things that Irenæus has in IV. 45 agree well. M. Antonius also in book XI says that a branch once cut off, even if it is grafted again, coalesces with difficulty. How far there has been a departure from that ancient discipline, there is no need to say; the matter is manifest. Nevertheless, the Roman Church, which was milder, as I said, than the others, received this book into Canonical authority afterwards. Whence it follows that this passage was understood by it otherwise than by those others. Wherefore let us also see what sense can be given to this passage that is convenient, which does not fight with those constitutions of the Roman see which I have mentioned. To say what I think, I believe that by παραπεσόντας here are meant those who fall away from the Christian faith. For the Hebrews also use נפל thus, and the word מעל is translated as παραπίπτειν, Ezech. XIV. verse 13, c. XV. verse 8, cap. XVIII. verse 24, c. XX. v. 27, and the noun derived from it מעל is ἀπόστασις, 2. Paral. XXIX. v. 19, c. XXXIII. v. 19, ἀποστασία 2. Paral. XXIX. v. 19. This is the very thing which he signified by παραῤῥυεῖσθαι above c. II. v. 1. By σκληρύνεσθαι c. III. verse 13 and following. The Syrian here, if they have sinned again, namely in a graver sense, as above III. 17. But it is said of them that they cannot be restored to repentance, that is, brought back to a better state, namely through the law of Moses, because they had fallen away from that which is both the best and the most certain, and after Christ was sent, the only one. Justin expressed this sense for us most excellently against Trypho: Τῆς δὲ ὁμολογήσαντας, καὶ ἐπιγνόντας, τοῦτον εἶναι τὸν Χριστὸν, καὶ ἧτινιῶν αἰτίᾳ μεταβάντας ἐπὶ τὴν ἐν- νομον πολιτείαν, ἀρνησαμένους ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ Χριστὸς, καὶ πρὶν τελευτῆς μὴ μεταγνόντας, οὐδόλως σωθήσεσθαι ἀπο- φαίνομαι. He shows, however, that such a falling away from Christianity can happen, not only to Catechumens, or those recently baptized, νεοφύτοις, but even to those who had made much progress, so that no one might think himself immune from such a danger, which Paul himself also teaches us, 1. Corinth. IX. 27. He describes that progress, however, in excellent words. First he says ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας. It is indeed true that baptism had the name of φωτισμοῦ among the ancients, which promises φωτισμὸν, as we said at Matth. XXVIII. verse 19, looking to which the Syrian translates, who have descended to baptism. But it is simpler that those are understood here who have been imbued with the knowledge of Evangelical doctrine, in which sense we have φωτίζειν and φωτισμὸν in John II. verse 9, 2. Corinth. IV. verse 6, and below cap. X. verse 32. The Hebrew הוֹרָה is accustomed to be translated thus. He adds that they have tasted the heavenly gift, that is, the peace of conscience, of which Rom. V. verse 1. Phil. IV. verse 7. which follows the remission of sins granted to the converted. Moreover, here also below γεύσασθαι means to know by experiencing, as in 1 Pet. II. 3, Psalm XXXIV. 9, Prov. XXXI. 18. He also adds that they had been partakers of the Holy Spirit, that is, had obtained the gifts of prophecy, of tongues, of healings, which did not happen at that time except to the justified, that is, the purified. He also says that the good Word of God was tasted by them, that is, those excellent promises. For thus the good Word of God is taken in Jer. XXIX. v. 10 & ch. XXXIII. verse 14, Zech. I. verse 13. δυνάμεις τε μέλλοντος αἰῶνος is an explanation of that good Word, that is, the promise. For this was not the promise of God concerning restoring the people to their lands after 70 years, or concerning the principate of Zerubbabel, but concerning that supreme power which God is about to show concerning us in that other age; see Eph. I. verse 19, where it is called the exceeding greatness of power, which here is plural, powers. These same promises are the precious and very great promises in 2 Pet. I. verse 4. We learn from this that there is no such progress that makes us entirely secure. Ἀνακαινίζειν is חִדֵּשׁ, which often signifies to restore to a former state, as in Psalm CIII. verse 5, Lam. V. 21. No one, he says, is such a Master who can do that, and the word πάλιν is redundant, since ἀνά follows. Such as also elsewhere.

Others report this connection: if anyone is negligent in learning Christian doctrine, it can easily happen that one, by the just judgment of God, may fall headlong into apostasy and into the sin against the Holy Spirit. But the scope of the Apostle appears from verses 9 and 11, where, on the contrary, it is taught that he intended by these things to warn against apostasy, by proposing an extreme danger, which Grotius has hitherto not badly assigned. What he brings forward concerning those who have lapsed after baptism concerns the private interpretation and opinion of some, not the faith of the whole Catholic Church, whether that more ancient one or the less ancient. Since this matter is historical and contributes nothing to the understanding of the present passage, it is not relevant to discuss it in this place. Concerning the canonical authority of this book, we have spoken in the prolegomena and in the special vestibule. As for the sense of the Apostle, Grotius rightly leaves the explanation of those who think it treats of those who have lapsed after baptism, from which the heresy of the Novatians, Cathars, and their followers, as well as of more recent heterodox persons of various kinds, has arisen, denying them repentance and conversion. However, I do not disapprove of interpreting it as apostasy from the faith, provided that repentance is not universally denied to all apostates from the faith, by which method one easily approaches the Novatian heresy. That it treats of the sin against the Holy Spirit is sufficiently evident from the text itself and a comparison with Heb. X. 29, with the addition of the parallels Matt. XII. 32, Mark III. 28, Luke XII. 10, which indeed brings about apostasy, but is a clearly singular species of apostasy: to understand which, one must weigh both the subject and the predicate. Regarding the subject, the blessed Dorscheus notes that those committing the sin against the Holy Spirit in this passage are truly regenerate, having nevertheless attained a sufficient knowledge of Divine truth, and that they can commit it, as the example of the Pharisees teaches, Matt. XII, verse 32: but it is clear that the regenerate are denoted here, both because of the Apostle's purpose and because of the criteria designated. The purpose is to deter from the neglect of Divine truth and from falling away from it, and toward the perfection of Divine knowledge. Therefore, as the object, he takes the truly regenerate, to whom the heavenly doctrine was confirmed, Heb. II, verse 3; who are partakers of the heavenly calling, chap. III, verse 1; who are the house of CHRIST, verse 6; partakers of Him, verse 14; distinguished from the unbelieving, chap. IV, verse 2; called believers, verse 3; illustrious for good works, chap. VI, verse 10. The Apostle warns these people by proposing the dangerous end of such apostates. Now if no such apostates were or could have been regenerate before their fall, the danger of such people is set forth to the regenerate in vain. It appears that the criteria of the regenerate were present in those committing the sin against the Holy Spirit before its commission.

The Apostle altogether implies that he is pointing out 1. ἅπαξ Φωτισθέντας, once enlightened, which some indeed understand of baptism, which he thus called by the name of Φωτισμὸς, from Dionysius on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, Clement of Alexandria, Gregory of Nazianzus, oration II on the holy lights, etc. But it is more correctly explained as those enlightened by the knowledge of Christian doctrine or the guide of heavenly truth, Luke XVI, verse 8; John I, verse 7; chap. XII, v. 10; 2 Corinthians IV, verse 6; Ephesians V, verse 8; 1 Thessalonians V, verse 5; Heb. X, verse 32, just as in the parallel that Φωτισμὸς is explained by τὸ λαβεῖν ἐπίγνωσιν τῆς ἀληθείας, the receiving of the knowledge of the truth, Heb. X, verse 26. True enlightenment is also proved from the word ἅπαξ; which, as the blessed Dorscheus notes, is a mark not only of unity but also of truth; compare 1 Peter IV, verse 10, where the longsuffering in the days of Noah is said to have waited ἅπαξ, which is said to have waited not so much once as seriously and sincerely. Thus Jude, verse 3, says that the faith ἅπαξ delivered to the saints must be contended for, that is, not so much once as perfectly and sincerely delivered; and verse 5, the Apostle wishes that we might ἅπαξ behold the examples of Divine vengeance exercised against the Israelite people in the desert, against the apostate angels, against Sodom and Gomorrah, etc., which he wishes not so much once as plainly and fully to behold; compare Psalm LXXXIX, verse 36, where Jehovah says, I have sworn once by my holiness, that is, altogether and plainly. Now Φωτισμὸς is a criterion of the regenerate. Whence it is opposed to blindness, 2 Corinthians IV, verses 4 and 6, and is joined to vivification, Ephesians V, verse 14. And it is the very opening of the eyes spiritually, Acts XXVI, verse 18, and thus a proper Apostolic duty, and the chief desire of the Apostles for men, Ephesians I, verse 18. Therefore, it is not the enlightenment of the natural intellect, as Beza, Piscator, Marloratus, etc. said regarding the passage John I, verse 9.

For 1. that is nowhere in the Holy Scriptures called Φωτισμὸς, nor is such a thing understood in John I. For there, a Φωτισμὸς is pronounced concerning CHRIST, which properly pertains to the Prophetic office of Christ, in respect of which CHRIST is the light shining in the darkness, verse 5, concerning which light John the Baptist testified, verse 7, by which enlightenment the world could have known CHRIST, had it not loved darkness more than light, John I, verse 10, and chap. III, verse 19. But that there is no discourse here about the light of the natural intellect is evident from this, both because no mention of that light is made anywhere in this epistle, but always of the Evangelical light, and because that enlightenment is understood in verse 4, which contains the word of the beginning of CHRIST, verse 1, and the foundation of repentance, etc., ibid. Nor is there discourse about mental enlightenment only, separated from the change of the will through trust in CHRIST, as Sohnius wishes, Tom. II, Oper., page 776; Robert of Salisbury on grace and perseverance, page 50. For that Φωτισμὸς embraces both, which appears even from this, because the Apostle requires in it both perseverance and increase. But where there is no trust, there perseverance and increase in Φωτισμὸς cannot be required alone. Add that this Φωτισμὸς contains the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith in CHRIST, as is manifest from verse 1.

2. Γευσαμένυς τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς ἐπυρανίυ, who tasted the heavenly gift, such as is the remission of sins according to Chrysostom on this passage, justice, peace, and tranquility of conscience and joy in the Holy Spirit, Romans XIV, verse 17. The blessed Dorscheus understands CHRIST. Simply, he says, CHRIST is understood, who descended from heaven, John III, verse 18, is the one coming from above, verse 31, the gift of God the Father, verse 15. For through Him one goes to eternal life, verse 36, and chap. XIV, verse 6; faith tends especially toward Him, John I, verse 11. Nor do Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius, who interpret it concerning the remission of sins, disagree. For its foundation is Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 4. 5. 6.

Ἀδύνατον γὰρ τοὺς ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας, γευσαμένους τε τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς ἐπουρανίου, καὶ μετόχους γενηθέντας Πνεύμα- τος ἁγίου, καὶ καλὸν γευσαμένους Θεοῦ ῥῆμα, δυνάμεις τε μέλ- λοντος αἰῶνος, καὶ παραπεσόντας πάλιν ἀνακαινίζειν εἰς μετάνοιαν) Hoc dicit, non frustra illa Christianismi ele- menta sive fundamenta sæpe repeti & animis inculcari, quia ex iis abjectis ingens sit periculum. Hic locus ma- xime in causa fuit, cur diu Romana Ecclesia cunctata sit, hunc librum in canonem recipere. Liquet ex Tertullia- no de pudicitia. Erat enim in disciplina circa lapsos mitior cæteris Ecclesiis. Ecclesiæ pleræque post bapti- smum lapsos aliquos reconciliabant & admittebant ad communionem, sed excipiebant tria gravissima crimina: idololatriam, homicidium & adulterium. Queritur Ter- tullianus à Papa Zephyrino admissos ad Ecclesiæ pacem mœchos. At vero id non fuisse novum sed vetus Romæ, docet nos Pastor Hermæ II. 4. sed de semel tantum lapso agens, non de iterum lapso, quam distinctionem etiam habes apud Clement. Strom. II. Temporibus Cypriani, cum de lapsis in idololatriam disputaretur, an recipi ad pœnitentiam publicam & reconciliationem possent, & mos fuisset varius, etiam in ipsa Africa, sustinuit judi- cium suum Cyprianus eo spectans, ut persecutione ces- sante aliquid in commune statueretur. Romana Ecclesia lenior cæteris autor fuerat, ut post longa pœnitentiæ tempora lapsi ad communionem reciperentur. Displicuit id Novato & Novatiano, qui hac de causa schisma fece- re. At sententia Romanæ Ecclesiæ de lapsis in idolola- triam, parique modo de lapsis in homicidium placuit magnæ Synodo Nicænæ, ut ex ejus canonibus videre est. Neque tamen cogitandum est veteres illos rigidio- ris disciplinæ observatores pro certo habuisse tales in æternum perituros, sed commendabant eos Divinæ mi- sericordiæ, privatis, non publicis precibus, neque ita, ut certi quid eis pollicerentur. Et hoc etiam observa- tum in iis, qui post primam pœnitentiam publice actam rursus se aliis, extra illa tria, criminibus obstringerent. Tertullianus de pœnitentia: Hæc igitur venena ejus pro videns Deus, clausa licet ignoscentiæ janua & intinctionis seræ obstructa, aliquid adhuc permisit patere. Collocavit in vestibulo pœnitentiam secundam, quæ pulsantibus pate- faciat: Sed jam semel, quia jam secundo, sed amplius nunquam, quia proxime frustra. Nonne enim & hoc se- mel satis est? Vide & sequentia, ubi pœnitentia secunda dicitur respectu ejus quæ baptismum præcedit. Infra eodem libro hanc pœnitentiam & secundam & unam vocat, cujus in arcto dicit esse negotium, & cum quam severa displina exerceretur; late ostendit Ambrosius; Quamvis caute & salubriter provisum sit, ut locus illius humillimæ pœnitentiæ semel in Ecclesia concedatur, ne me- dicina vilis minus utilis esset ægrotis, quæ tanto magis uti- lis est, quanto minus contemptibilis fuerit. Quis tamen DEO audeat dicere: Quare huic homini, qui post pœ- nitentiam primam rursus se laqueis iniquitatis obstrinxit, iterum parcis? Et portam pœnitentiæ interdum claudi etiam apud DEUM Ebræi sentiebant, ut videre est in paraphrasi Chaldæa Cant. V. vers. 5. apud Rabbinos ad Esaiam XXII. vers. 14. Philo autem de præmiis & pœnis ait: Ἐνταῦθα δὲ ὅλοι βίοι πίπτουσιν ἐς ἅπαξ διατρα- πέντας μόγις ἐστὶν ἀναγῆψαι. Cum quibus bene congruunt ea, quæ habet Irenæus IV. 45. Etiam M. Antonius l. XI. dicit, ægre coalescere ramum semel amputatum, etiamsi rursus inseratur. Quam longe à veteri illa disciplina abitum sit, nihil opus est dici, res manifesta est. Atta- men Romana Ecclesia, quæ lenior, ut dixi, cæteris fuit, hunc librum in autoritatem Canonicam recepit postea. Unde sequitur, hunc locum ab ea aliter, quam ab iis aliis intellectum. Quare & nos videamus, quis huic lo- co sensus dari commodus possit, qui cum Romanæ sedis illis, quas dixi, constitutionibus non pugnet. Ut dicam, quod sentio, existimo παραπεσόντας hic dici eos, qui à fide Christiana deficiunt. Nam & נפל sic usurpant E- bræi, & verbum מעל παραπίπτειν vertitur, Ezech. XIV. vers. 13. c. XV. vers. 8. cap. XVIII. vers. 24. c. XX. v. 27. & nomen inde deductum מעל ἀπόστασις, 2. Paral. XXIX. v. 19. c. XXXIII. v. 19. ἀποστασία 2. Paral. XXIX. v. 19. Hoc ipsum est, quod per παραῤῥυεῖσθαι significavit supra c. II. v. 1. Per σκληρύνεσθαι c. III. vers. 13. & sequentibus. Syrus hic, si ite- rum peccaverint, nempe in sensu graviore, ut supra III. 17. De iis autem dicitur, non posse eos restitui in pœni- tentiam, id est, ad frugem meliorem reduci, nempe per legem Mofis, quia scilicet defecerant ab ilia, quæ & o- ptima est & certissima, & post Christum missum unica. Hunc sensum optime nobis expressit contra Tryphonem Justinus: Τῆς δὲ ὁμολογήσαντας, καὶ ἐπιγνόντας, τοῦτον εἶναι τὸν Χριστὸν, καὶ ἧτινιῶν αἰτίᾳ μεταβάντας ἐπὶ τὴν ἔν- νομον πολιτείαν, ἀρνησαμένους ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ Χριστὸς, καὶ πρὶν τελευτῆς μὴ μεταγνόντας, οὐδόλως σωθήσεσθαι ἀπο- φαίνομαι. Ostendit autem talem defectionem à Christia- nismo posse evenire, non Catechumenis tantum, aut re- cens baptizatis νεοφύτοις, verum etiam iis, qui plurimum profecerant, ne quis se putaret à tali periculo immunem, quod ipsum & Paulus nos docet, 1. Corinth. IX. 27. Pro- fectum autem illum describit verbis egregiis. Primum ait ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας. Verum quidem est, baptismum nomen habuisse apud veteres φωτισμοῦ, qui φωτισμὸν pro- mittit, ut diximus ad Matth. XXVIII. vers. 19. quo spe- ctans Syrus vertit, qui ad baptismum descenderunt. Sed simplicius est, intelligi hic eos, qui cognitione Evange- licæ doctrinæ imbuti fuere, quo sensu φωτίζειν & φωτι- σμὸν habemus Johan. II. vers. 9. 2. Corinth. IV. vers. 6. & infra cap. X. vers. 32. Solet sic verti Ebræum הוֹרָה Addit eos gustasse donum cœleste, id est pacem conscien- tiæ, de qua Rom. V. vers. 1. Phil. IV. vers. 7. quæ conse- quitur peccatorum remissionem conversis indultam. Est autem & hic infra γεύσασθαι experiendo cognoscere, ut 1. Petr. II. 3. Psalm. XXXIV. 9. Prov. XXXI. 18. Subjicit etiam participes fuisse Spiritus sancti, id est, dona conse- cutos prophetiæ, linguarum fanationum, quæ non contin- gebat eo tempore, nisi justificatis, id est, purgatis. Gu- statum etiam ab iis ait bonum DEI Verbum, id est, egre- gia illa promissa. Nam sic bonum DEI Verbum sumitur Jer. XXIX. v. 10. & c. XXXIII. vers. 14. Zachar. I. vers. 13. δυνάμεις τε μέλλοντος αἰῶνος, est ἐξήγησις illius Verbi bo- ni, id est, promissi. Non enim hoc erat promissum DEI de restituendo populo in suas terras post LXX. annos, aut de Zorobabelis principatu, sed de summa illa potentia, quam circa nos ostensurus est Deus in illo altero seculo, vide Ephes. I. vers. 19. ubi ὑπερβάλλον μέγεθος δυνάμεως dicitur, quod hic pluraliter δυνάμεις. Eadem hæc promis- sa τίμια καὶ μέγιστα ἐπαγγέλματα 2. Petr. I. vers. 4. Di- scimus hinc, nullum esse talem profectum, qui nos plane securos faciat. Ἀνακαινίζειν est חִדֵּשׁ, quod sæpe signi- ficat in priorem statum restituere, ut Psalm. CIII. vers. 5. Lam. V. 21. Nemo, inquit, tantus est Magister, qui id facere possit, & πλεονάζει vox πάλιν, cum sequatur ἀνά. Quales & alibi.

Connexionem alii hanc tradunt, si quis in addi- scenda doctrina Christiana negligens sit, facile fie- ri posse, ut quis justo Dei judicio in apostasiam & in peccatum in Spiritum sanctum præceps ruat. Sed scopus Apostoli è v. 9. & 11. apparet, ubià con- trario docetur, quod nimirum hisce intenderit ca- vere de apostasia, proposito periculo extremo, quem hactenus non male assignavit Grotius. Quæ affert de lapsis post baptismum, privatam nonnullo- rum ἐπίλυσιν & sententiam, non totius Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, sive antiquioris illius, sive minus anti- quæ fidem concernunt. Quæ res quum historica sit, & ad præsentis loci intelligentiam nihil faci- at, non attinet, hoc quidem loco eadem discutere. De autoritate vero Canonica hujus libri in prole- gomenis, & in vestibulo peculiari diximus. Quan- tum ad sensum Apostoli, recte illorum explicatio- nem relinquit Grotius, qui de prolapsis post bapti- smum agi censent, è qua Novatianorum, Catharo- rum, & asseclarum, necnon recentiorum diversi generis heterodoxorum orta est hæresis, pœniten- tiam & conversionem ipsis denegans. Quod au- tem de apostasia à fide interpretatur, non improbo: modo non universaliter omnibus à fide apostatis pœnitentia denegetur, quo pacto facile Novatianæ hæresi acceditur. De peccato in Spiritum sanctum agi, è textu ipso, & collatione cum Ebr. X. 29. satis constat, additis parallelis Matth. XII. 32. Marc. III. 28. Luc. XII. 10. quod ἀποστασίαν quidem infert, sed species plane singularis ἀποστασίας est: Ad quam intelligendam cum subjectum, tum predica- tum expendere oportet. Circa subjectum notat B. Dorscheus, committentes peccatum in Spiritum sanctum hoc loco esse vere renatos, sufficientem tamen veritatis Divinæ notitiam consecutos eosque posse id committere exemplum Pharisæorum, Matth. XII. vers. 32. docet: hic autem renatos denotari liquet, tum ob scopum Apostoli, tum ob κριτήρια designata. Scopus est deterrere à neglectu veritatis Divinæ & prolapsu ab eadem, atque ad perfectionem notitiæ Divinæ. Itaque pro objecto vère renatos, quibus doctrina cœlestis fuit confirmata, Ebr. II. vers. 3. qui cœlestis vocationis sunt participes cap. III. vers. 1. qui sunt domus CHRISTI, vers. 6. ejusdem μέτοχοι, vers. 14. incredulis contradistincti, cap. IV. vers. 2. credentes appellati, vers. 3. bonis operibus illustres cap. VI. vers. 10. Hos commonefacit Apostolus proposito periculoso exitu ejusmodi Apostatarum. Jam si nulli apostatæ tales ante suum prolapsum vel fuerunt vel esse potuerunt renati, frustra renatis illorum periculum exponitur. Κριτήρια renatorum in committentibus peccatum in Spiritum sanctum ante ejus commissionem fuisse apparet.

Innuit omnino Apostolus, se indigitare 1. ἅπαξ Φωτισθέντας semel illuminatos, quod de baptismo quidem nonnulli intelligunt, quem ita appellavit nomine Φωτισμῦ, è Dionysio de Hierarch. Eccles. Clemente Alexandrin. Gregor. Nazianzen. orat. II. in sancta lumina &c. Sed rectius de illuminatis doctrinæ Christianæ cognitione vel veritatis cœlestis duce explicatur, Luc. XVI. vers. 8. Johan. I. vers. 7. cap. XII. v. 10. 2. Corinth. IV. vers. 6. Ephes. V. vers. 8. 1. Thessal. V. vers. 5. Ebr. X. vers. 32. quemadmodum in parallelo Φωτισμὸς ille exponitur per τὸ λαβεῖν ἐπίγνωσιν τῆς ἀληθείας Ebr. X. vers. 26. Vera illuminatio etiam ex voce ἅπαξ probatur; quæ, notante B. Dorscheo, non tantum unitatis, sed & veritatis nota est, confer. 1. Petr. IV. vers. 10. ubi longanimitas in diebus Noæ dicitur ἅπαξ expectasse, quæ non tam semel, quam serio expectasse dicitur & sincere. Sic Jud. vers. 3. dicitur propugnandam esse ἅπαξ traditam sanctis fidem, hoc est, non tam semel quam perfecte & sincere traditam, & vers. 5. Apostolus vult, vel ἅπαξ intueamur exempla vindictæ Divinæ adversus populum Israëliticum in deserto, adversus Angelos apostatas: adversus Sodomam & Gomorrham &c. exercitæ, quæ non tam vult semel, quam plane pleneque intueri, confer. Psal. LXXXIX. vers. 36. ubi Jehovah dicit, semel juravi per sanctitatem meam, hoc est, omnino plane. Φωτισμὸς autem est κριτήριον Renatorum. Unde opponitur excæcationi, 2. Corinth. IV. vers. 4. & 6. conjungitur vivificationi, Ephes. V. vers. 14. Estque ipsa apertio spiritualis oculorum, Actor. XXVI. vers. 18. adeoque proprium officium Apostolicum, & præcipuum Apostolorum in hominibus desiderium, Ephes. I. vers. 18. Non est igitur illuminatio naturalis intelligentiæ, uti Beza, Piscator, Marloratus &c. ad locum Johan. I. vers. 9. dixerunt.

Nam 1. illa nuspiam in Sacris literis dicitur Φωτισμὸς, nec Johan. I. talis intelligitur. Est enim ibi de CHRISTO pronuntiatus Φωτισμὸς talis, qui proprie ad officium Christi Propheticum pertinet, cujus respectu CHRISTUS est Φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ Φαῖνον, vers. 5. de qua luce testifi- catus est Johannes Baptista, vers. 7. quâ illumi- natione mundus potuisset cognoscere CHRISTUM, nisi tenebras plus dilexisset, quam lucem Johan. I. vers. 10. & cap. III. vers. 19. Hoc loco autem de luce naturalis intelligentiæ non esse sermonem ex eo patet, tum quia nuspiam in hac epistola ejus lucis mentio fit, semper autem lucis Evangelicæ, tum quia illa illuminatio vers. 4. intelligitur, quæ con- tinet τὸν τῆς ἀρχῆς τῦ Χριστῦ λόγον, vers. 1. & τὸ θεμέλιον μετανοίας &c. ibid. Neque sermo est de illuminatione mentali tantum, separata ab im- mutatione voluntatis per fiduciam in CHRI- STUM, uti vult Sohnius Tom. II. Oper. pagin. 776. Rob. Sarisburiensis de gratia & perseve- rantia pagin. 50. Nam iste Φωτισμὸς utrumque complectitur, quod vel ex eo apparet, quia A- postolus in eo requirit & perseverantiam & au- gmentum. Ubi autem nulla est fiducia ibi perse- verantia & augmentum in Φωτισμῷ tantum re- quiri non potest. Adde quod hic φωτισμὸς con- tineat fundamentum resipiscentiæ ab operibus mor- tuis, & fidei in CHRISTUM, ut è vers. 1. manifestum.

2. Γευσαμένυς τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς ἐπυρανίυ, qui gustarunt donum cœleste, quale est remissio pecca- torum secundum Chrysostomum in hunc locum, stē, justitia, pax, & tranquillitas conscientiæ & gau- dium in Spiritu sancto, Roman. XIV. vers. 17. B. Dorscheus CHRISTUM intelligit. Simpli- citer, inquit, CHRISTUS intelligitur, qui de cœlo descendit, Johan. III. vers. 18. est ἄνωθεν ἐρ- χόμενος vers. 31. δόσις Dei Patris, vers. 15. Per illum enim ad vitam æternam itur, vers. 36. & c. p. XIV. vers. 6. fides in illum potissimum tendit, Johan. I. vers. 11. Nec repugnant Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, & Oecumenius, qui de remissione peccatorum interpretantur. Ejus enim fundamen- tum est Christus.

## 6:4
4. Καλὸν γευσαμένυς Θεῦ ῥῆμα, who have tasted the good Word of God, that is, the sweetness of the Evangelical Word, in which it is perceived how kind the Lord is, Psalm 34:9, 1 Peter 2:3, and whatever is most sweet of GOD'S promises is effectively felt and tasted; which tasting is of saving faith, which makes those promises its own, and in them the truly faithful apply to themselves the grace of GOD and the merit of CHRIST with all the benefits which He has acquired for us, and enjoy them with the greatest delight. To this contributes the perception of the body and blood of CHRIST, concerning which CHRIST preached in the sweetest words in John 6:54, 55. Estius says: They have tasted, he says, the good Word of GOD, who have received with joy and sweetness the doctrine promising heavenly goods. For the Word of GOD is said to be tasted, says St. Thomas, when it not only illuminates the intellect, but also refreshes the affection. That some explain 'to taste' as to perceive slightly, as if to touch with the tips of the lips and to sip, is contrary to the usage of Holy Scripture, in which, whether properly or metaphorically, taste is used even of those things which are drunk in, if I may say so, with full gulps. Cf. chap. 2:9.

Latin:

4. Καλὸν γευσαμένυς Θεῦ ῥῆμα, qui bo- num Dei Verbum gustaverunt, id est, Verbi Ev- angelici suavitatem, in quo percipitur quam benignus sit Dominus, Psalm. XXXIV. vers. 9. 1. Petr. II. vers. 3. & quicquid est dulcissima- rum DEI promissionum efficaciter sentitur ac gustatur; Qui gustus est fidei salvificæ, quæ promissiones illas suas faciunt & in iis gratiam DEI & meritum CHRISTI cum omnibus beneficiis, quæ nobis acquisivit, sibi appli- cant vere fideles, iisque summa cum dele- ctatione fruuntur. Quo facit perceptio corpo- ris & sanguinis CHRISTI, de qua suavissi- mis verbis concionatus est CHRISTUS Jo- han. VI. vers. 54. 55. Estius: Gustaverunt, inquit, bonum DEI Verbum, qui doctrinam cœlestia bona promittentem cum gaudio & sua- vitate perceperunt. Dicitur enim gustari Ver- bum DEI, inquit S. Thomas, quando non so- lum illuminat intellectum, verum etiam reficit affectum. Quod quidam gustare exponunt te- nuiter percipere, quasi labris summis attingere & delibare, præter usum est Scripturæ Sacræ, in qua seu proprie seu Metaphorice gustus est earum etiam rerum, quæ plenis, ut ita dicam, faucibus hauriuntur. Conf. cap. II. 9.

## 6:5
5. Γευσαμένυς δυνάμεις μέλλοντος αἰῶνος, who have tasted the mighty works of the age to come, that is, who have perceived not merely some appearance of heavenly blessedness in the other life, but the very virtues themselves and the heavenly goods themselves, nay, have received them as if into their inmost marrow, as if they had tasted those delights from the tree of life, Apoc. 2. vers. 7. 17. the hidden manna, and the living waters of the crystalline river proceeding from the throne of GOD and the Lamb Lamb, and had refreshed themselves with them, Apoc. 22. v. 7. by feeling and experiencing a foretaste and a pre-drinking of the sweetness of heavenly goods. He speaks of those, says the blessed Hunnius, who had been illuminated by the knowledge of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, who is the true light, so that they understand that this doctrine concerning JESUS CHRIST is an undoubted and heavenly truth. Furthermore, that they had tasted the heavenly gift, that is, CHRIST had already begun to live in them, and through faith the hope of the inheritance of the children of GOD had been established in their hearts. Furthermore, they had been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, by whom they had been converted, regenerated, illuminated, and sanctified. Moreover, they tasted the good Word of GOD and the powers of the world to come, while from the Word of GOD they perceived the riches of Divine goodness and a certain quasi-sense and taste of eternal life and the heavenly kingdom, being sealed, of course, by the Holy Spirit as a pledge of the inheritance of the elect. Flacius explained these things thus: He denotes them by these four properties, that they are those who first had been truly illuminated by the Word and the Holy Spirit, that is, who had had true faith in CHRIST; secondly, who also had tasted the heavenly gift, which I understand concerning justification and the peace of heart following it; thirdly, who had perceived the Holy Spirit, which is the donation of the Holy Spirit with His thanks or gifts, and that whole regeneration; in the fourth place he puts the tasting of the Word of GOD, which is the true knowledge of the Word through the Spirit and the true consolation and governance of our heart, perpetually proceeding to us from the Word of God. The powers of the world to come are that ineffable joy of the pious, proceeding to us from the Word and the Holy Spirit: which is truly a certain taste of the goods and the efficacy of that future life: in which indeed CHRIST Himself also once exulted more joyfully, when sometimes even against themselves once and all the pious feel the pains of hell. In this way he described both the things antecedent to that great sin, and also the persons themselves, who are accustomed to fall so horribly that they cannot clearly rise again. If we weigh these individual things, as is proper (how much less, if all of them), they cannot apply to hypocrites, or to those who have only a certain beginning of faith, or common gifts, as the Calvinists contend, but only to the truly reborn and faithful, who if they are described emphatically anywhere in the sacred scriptures, they are certainly designated here most effectively. To explain these things with Piscator, Toussain, and Pareus—concerning the beginning of illumination certainly without true faith, a light taste without fruition, concerning the non-sanctifying gifts of the Holy Spirit, and common hypocrites, concerning certain miracles perceived of the renewed world or the Church of the New Testament—is to obscure significantly a text that is brighter than the sun. The blessed Dorscheus rightly observes: that 'taste' denotes the true perception of an object, cf. Psalm 34, verse 9; Proverbs 31, verse 18; 1 Peter 2, verse 3; Hebrews 2, verse 9. Hence, when this taste is noted concerning any thing, at the same time perception and true sensation is also noted, Matthew 16, verse 18; Mark 9, verse 1; Luke 9, verse 27; John 8, verse 52, where at the same time, according to the Hebrew form of speaking, the word 'sense' denotes not a bare sensation, but also the annexed motions.

Whence, when those who are falling away are said to have tasted the good Word of God, etc., a true knowledge of the Gospel, a true union with CHRIST, and a true foretaste of the sweetness of eternal life is understood. Therefore, Zanchius in Misc. page 286, Sohnius in the work cited above page 776, and Rob. of Salisbury page 51, distinguish badly between 'tasting' and 'eating.' They tasted, they say, but did not eat, did not swallow, much less retain in the stomach. Whence they conclude that they were not truly reborn, nor had they arrived at spiritual eating. This distinction does not agree with the usage of Scripture. For in sacred matters, to taste is the same as to eat, cf. 1 Samuel 14, verses 24, 27, 28, and 29.
