Requiritur sane μακρο- θυμία, siquidem promissionum complementum hic nondum habeamus, sed non est ea causa hæreditatis, quæ non nisi fide apprehenditur & obtinetur, & monemur saltim, quod fides de- beat esse μακροθυμῦσα καὶ ὑπομένουσα, quo vero sensu non virtus est μακροθυμία, sed fidei con- stantia: Nec dissentientem hic habemus Estium: Hortatur enim Ebræos, ut exemplo majorum, qui Divinis promissis indubitanter credentes, eademque patenter expectantes, ea consecuti sunt & conse- quuntur: In fide & expectatione cælestium pro- missorum, inter hujus tempestatis adversa constan- ter perseverent.

## 6:13
Verse 13.

For when God made promise to Abraham, because he could swear by no greater, he sware by himself. He added an oath to the promise, so that it might be held by two bonds. He uses a saying known among the Hebrews: He who swears, swears by that which is above himself. Likewise: God swears by himself, not by another. Philo on Cain and Abel: Μαρτυρῶ παρότου ὁ μαρτυρῶν κρείττων ἐστὶ τῷ μαρτυρουμένου. The same in the allegories: Ὁρᾷς γὰρ, ὅτι οὐ καθ’ ἑτέρου ὀμνύει Θεὸς, ἀλλὰ καθ’ ἑαυτοῦ, ὅς ἐστι πάντων ἄριστος. The words of Gen. 22, 16 are referred to.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Τῷ γὰρ Ἀβραὰμ ἐπαγγειλάμενος ὁ Θεὸς, ἐπεὶ κατ’ οὐ- δενὸς εἶχε μείζονος ὀμόσαι, ὤμοσε καθ’ ἑαυτῦ) Promis- so addidit jusjurandum, ut duobus vinculis tenere- tur. Utitur dicto noto inter Ebræos: Qui jurat, jurat per id, quod est supra se. Item: Deus jurat per semet- ipsum, non per alium. Philo de Caino & Abele: Μαρ- τυρῶ παρότου ὁ μαρτυρῶν κρείττων ἐστὶ τῷ μαρτυρουμένου. Idem in allegoriis: Ὁρᾷς γὰρ, ὅτι οὐ καθ’ ἑτέρου ὀμνύει Θεὸς, ἀλλὰ καθ’ ἑαυτοῦ, ὅς ἐστι πάντων ἄριστος. Respiciuntur verba Gen. 22, 16.

## 6:14
Verse 14.

Surely blessing I will bless thee, and multiplying I will multiply thee. The same words in the LXX at the cited place in Genesis, except that for πληθυνῶ σε there is πληθυνῶ τὸ σπέρμα σου. But the sense is the same, since it is the custom for Hebrews to name parents for their children, as if they were one person. Those participles joined to their verbs among the Hebrews intensify the meaning. For this is what it means: I will prosper you in a wonderful manner, and I will give you immense prosperity. Ἦ μὴν is a formula of one affirming, most frequent among those swearing. Demosthenes, ὀμνύω ἦ μὴν ἀπολωλέναι Φίλιππον.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Ἦ μὴν εὐλογῶν εὐλογήσω σε, καὶ πληθύνων πληθυνῶ σε) Eadem verba in LXX. dicto Geneseos loco, nisi quod pro πληθυνῶ σε ibi est πληθυνῶ τὸ σπέρμα σου. Sed sensus est idem, cum mos sit Ebræis parentes pro li- beris nominare, quasi una essent persona. Illa vero participia suis verbis adjuncta apud Ebræos intendunt significationem. Hoc enim vult: Mirum in mo- dum & prosperabo te, & ingentem tibi prosperitatem dabo. Ἦ μὴν formula affirmantis maxime frequens jurantibus. Demosthenes, ὀμνύω ἦ μὴν ἀπολωλέναι Φίλιππον.

## 6:15
Verse 15.

And so after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise. Even unto death, amidst very many temptations, he persisted in that hope, which was fulfilled after his own death.

He sets forth Abraham, the Father of believers, most deservedly esteemed by the Hebrews as an example for them to imitate, of a patient and constant faith: relying on the Divine promise, to which GOD had promised blessing and multiplication by an oath: not, however, merely a temporal blessing, but whatever blessing befalls believers in the Messiah, the seed of Abraham, Gen. 22, verse 17. Gal. 3, verse 16. Compare Rom. 4, verse 18 et seqq.

The words 'blessing I will bless' import not only a most certain, but also a most bountiful and most copious blessing. Thus, therefore, he not only excites the Hebrews by this example to preserve the πληροφορίαν ἐλπίδος [full assurance of hope], but also teaches that the promise made to Abraham pertains to them also, as spiritual children of Abraham, and that the promised thing is not obtained except by constant and patient faith, just as Abraham obtained it. Theophylact rightly observed that the oath, of which the Apostle speaks, is contained in those words, 'by myself I have sworn.' For the following words signify the matter concerning which the oath is taken.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Καὶ ὕτω μακροθυμήσας ἐπέτυχε τῆς ἐπαγγελίας) Ad mortem usque inter tentationes plurimas in illa spe per- stitit, quæ post ipsius mortem impleta est.

Abrahamum Patrem credentium, Ebræis meritissimo suo maximi æstimatum in exem- plum, quod ipsi imitentur, fidei patientis, & constantis sistit: innitentes Divinæ promis- sioni, cui DEUS jurejurando benedictionem & multiplicationem promiserat: non autem benedictionem tantum temporalem, sed quic- quid benedictionis in Messia, semine Abrahæ, credentibus obtingit, Genes. 22. vers. 17. Ga- lat. 3. vers. 16. Confer. Rom. 4. vers. 18. seqq.

Verba benedicens benedicam non tantum certissi- mam, sed etiam largissimam, & copiosissimam be- nedictionem important. Sic ergo Ebræos, non tantum hoc exemplo ad πληροφορίαν ἐλπίδος ser- vandam excitat, sed docet quoque, promissio- nem Abrahæ factam ad eos quoque, ceu spiri- tuales Abrahæ filios pertinere, nec nisi fide con- stanti & patienti obtineri rem promissam, quem- admodum Abraham obtinuit. Recte autem Theophylacto observatum, juramentum, de quo loquitur Apostolus, illis verbis contineri, per memetipsum juravi. Nam verba sequentia rem, de qua juratur, significant.

## 6:16
Ver. 16.

For men swear by the greater) By God, who both certainly knows all things and is most powerful to avenge perfidy.

He had said, as Estius notes, that GOD had confirmed His promise with an oath. Why He did this, he now explains from the custom of men, who, wishing to give others certain assurance of those things which they say, interpose an oath. But these indeed, he says, swear by him who is greater, because they hold GOD to be greater than themselves. GOD could not do that, who has no one greater, and therefore He swore by Himself. Since men swear by one greater than they themselves are, it is clear that men borrow the religion or authority of an oath from elsewhere, when faith or authority is lacking to them, as it is necessary to happen in controversies and promises, when either the truth is hidden or the faith is doubtful. But He is truly greater, whose authority and faith no one can despise or call into doubt, God the Best and Greatest, inasmuch as He alone is the first and highest truth, He alone is the καρδιογνώσης [knower of hearts], He alone is infallible in all things, He alone is the avenger of oaths against all, if they break faith, He can punish even the most powerful.

And an oath is the end of all contradiction to them for confirmation) The confirmatory oath of a promise removes all doubt. To the Hebrews, to speak is also to think. Thus ἀντιλογία [contradiction] is a thought to the contrary, namely as if that which is said would not come to pass. The Egyptians called an oath μεγίσην πίσιν [the greatest pledge], as Diodorus Siculus relates. Halicarnassensis called it Τε- λευταίαν πίσιν [the final pledge]. Philo in three places calls it μαρτυρίαν Θεῦ περὶ πράγματος ἀμφισβητημένη [the testimony of God concerning a disputed matter]. Procopius: Ὕπατον κὰι ἐχυρώτατον πίσεως το κὰι ἀληθείας ἐνέ- χυρον [The highest and most secure pledge of faith and truth]. Terence: 'If I knew anything else by which I could confirm my faith to you more holily than an oath, I would promise it to you, Laches.'

He had said that GOD had confirmed the promise with an oath: why He did this he now explains. He renders a twofold reason: First, that there might be no place left for questioning: because an oath is the end of all controversy: 'The religion of an oath has come into use as the greatest remedy for settling lawsuits,' say the Jurisconsults. By an oath, says Theophylact, all ambiguity of altercation is removed. For although many things are said back and forth so that the matter itself may be revealed, yet the oath, finally intervening and confirming, resolves everything about which there is doubt. Secondly, because an oath contributes to the confirmation of truth. An oath is said to be twofold: the one assertory or judicial, when there is doubt about the past or present, whether something was done or not: the other promissory, such as is in treaties, pacts, and homages, when promises are confirmed by oaths. Both seem to some to be noted here: the former when an oath is provided for the sake of ending a controversy: the latter when one swears for the sake of confirming a promise. God had need of neither: But it can be said that He provided an assertory one, so that no controversy would remain which the ἀντίδικος [adversary] could move against us; and a promissory one, so that the Evangelical promise might be firmer and more certain to us, although, speaking properly, the Divine oath should be called promissory rather than assertory.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Ἄνθρωποι γὰρ κατὰ τῦ μείζονος ὀμνύυσι) Per Deum, qui & omnia certo novit, & ad vindicandam perfidiam est potentissimus.

Dixerat, notante Estio, DEUM suam promis- sionem confirmasse juramento. Cur id fecerit, jam explicat à consuetudine hominum, qui volentes aliis certam fidem facere eorum, quæ dicunt, ju- ramentum interponunt. Sed hi quidem, inquit, per eum, qui major sit, jurant, quia se majorem habent DEUM. Id DEUS non potuit, qui ma- jorem non habet, ideoque per semetipsum juravit. Cum homines per majorem, quam sunt ipsi, ju, rent, patet jurisjurandi religionem sive autorita- tem homines aliunde mutuari, quando ipsis fides vel autoritas deest, ut necesse est fieri in con- troversiis & promissionibus, quando vel veritas est occulta vel fides dubia. Is vero major est, cujus autoritatem ac fidem nemo contemnere, vel in du- bium vocare potest, Deus Optimus Maximus, ut- pote qui solus est prima & summa veritas, solus est καρδιογνώσης, solus per omnia infallibilis, solus vindex juramentorum in omnes, si fidem fallant, etiam potentissimos ulcisci potest.

Καὶ πάσης αὐτοῖς ἀντιλογίας πέρας εἰς βεβαίωσιν ὁ ὅρ- κος) Omnem dubitationem tollit juramentum confir- mativum promissi. Ebræis dicere est etiam cogitare. Sic ἀντιλογία cogitatio in contrarium, nempe quasi id, quod dicitur, futurum non esset. Ægyptii jusjurandum vocabant μεγίσην πίσιν, narrante Siculo Diodoro. Τε- λευταίαν πίσιν dixit Halicarnensis. Philo tribus in locis μαρτυρίαν Θεῦ περὶ πράγματος ἀμφισβητημένη: Proco- pio: Ὕπατον κὰι ἐχυρώτατον πίσεως το κὰι ἀληθείας ἐνέ- χυρον. Terentius: Aliud si scirem, qui firmare meam apud vos possem fidem sanctius quam jusjurandum, id pol- licerer tibi Lache..

Dixerat DEUM juramento firmasse pro- missionem: Id cur fecerit jam exponit. Ge- minam autem causam reddit: Primo ut nullus amplius esset quæstioni locus: quia juramen- tum finis est omnis controversiæ: Maximum re- medium expediendarum litium usum venit juris- jurandi religio, ajunt Jurisconsulti. Jurejuran- do, inquit Theophylactus, altercationis omnis am- biguitas tollitur. Nam & ultro citroque multa di- cuntur, ut res ipsa patescat, jus tamen juran- dum postremo invadens confirmansque solvit id o- mne, quo de ambigitur. Deinde quod juramen- tum faciat ad veritatis confirmationem. Du- plex esse dicitur juramentum, alterum asserto- rium vel judiciale, cum de præterito vel præsen- ti, an factum quid sit, vel non, ambigitur: alte- rum promissorium, quale est in fœderibus, pa- ctis, homagiis, cum promissa juramentis con- firmantur. Utrumque hic notari quibusdam videtur: Prius cum controversiæ finiendæ er- go juramentum præstatur: posterius cum pro- l missionis firmandæ causa juratur. Neutro Deus opus habuit: Sed & assertorium præstitisse dici potest, ut nulla superesset controversia, quam movere nobis posset ἀντίδικος; & promissorium, ut eo firmior & certior nobis sit Evangelica promissio, quanquam proprie loquendo juramentum Divinum promissorium potius, quam assertorium dicendum.

## 6:17
Ver. 17.

Ἐν ᾧ, Wherefore, which is otherwise ἐφ' ᾧ. Περισσότερον βυλόμενος ὁ Θεὸς ἐπιδεῖξαι τοῖς κληρονόμοις τῆς ἐπαγγελίας τὸ ἀμετάθετον τῆς βουλῆς ἀυτὸ) God is sometimes accustomed to be said to change His counsel, where a changed situation demands a new plan, as can be seen in Jonah 3:10, Jeremiah 18:11. But this promise, both carnal concerning the multiplying of Abraham's posterity, and spiritual concerning the gathering of the Church to Christ and leading the pious to eternal life, is immutable, ἀμεταμέλητος [irrevocable]. נצב [to stand] to the Rabbis. Understand therefore here the heirs of the promise, both those ancient Fathers and the Christians. See also what is above in chapter 4, 1.

Ἐμεσίτευσεν ὅρκῳ [He mediated with an oath]) From the Latin 'interbenit' [he intervenes]. Those are said in Latin to intervene who support someone's faith. Thus GOD Himself supported His own faith with an oath. In the Glosses, μεσιτεύω [I mediate] is 'I intervene.' Philo on Cain and Abel: 'Men flee to an oath as a pledge to be believed. But God is faithful even in speaking, so that His words differ nothing from oaths for the sake of certainty, and it has happened that our mind is [confirmed] by an oath. But the oath itself is believed by God. For God is not faithful because of an oath, but the oath itself is certain because of Him. Why then did it seem good to the hierophant to introduce Him swearing? That He might expose the weakness of the created, and having exposed it, might at the same time console it.' For we are not able to store up continuously in our own soul the worthy head of the Cause, that God is not as a man, so that we might transcend all things spoken of in human terms, but participating most in the mortal, and being able to conceive nothing without them, nor having the strength to escape our own fates, but entering into the mortal like snails, and being coiled around it, just as they are coiled spherically, and concerning the blessed and incorruptible, just as we think concerning them, we correct the absurdity in the discourse, because they would accept the divine as having human form. And the impiety in the works, because it is subject to human passions. For this reason we attribute to it hands, feet, entrances, exits, enmities, aversions, alienations, angers, parts and passions unsuitable to the Cause, of which there is also an oath; a confirmation of our own weakness. Tertullianus de pœnitentia: O blessed are we, for whose sake God swears! We are miserable if we do not believe Him when He swears.

A doubt occurs, why GOD swore, to whom it is deservedly to be believed without an oath; which indeed He did more abundantly, that He might confirm the immutability of His counsel by two things, namely by promise and by oath: in which there was certainly an immense abundance. For among men, for confirmation, one immutable thing, an oath, suffices. But GOD for confirmation employed not one, but two immutable things: not only an immutable promise, nor only an inviolable oath (since it is impossible for GOD to lie either by promising or by swearing) but both together. Although, however, here the divine oath made to Abraham is properly regarded, Genesis 22, verse 16, there is no doubt, however, since afterwards the Apostle is about to appeal also to the Divine oath concerning the Melchisedecian priesthood, chapter 7, verse 20. By the reason of both, the Apostle so diligently inculcates the immutability of the counsel of God, and so greatly urges the force of the oath, since the sum of both oaths is the reason: of the former, that the blessing may not reach us except in the blessed seed; of the latter, that we have the greatest need of that eternal priesthood of CHRIST, so much so that without it eternal salvation could not exist. The Gospel or sermon concerning the grace of GOD through CHRIST is called βουλὴ or the counsel of God, concerning salvation, Luke 7:30. That the counsel of GOD is indeed immutable is evident from Isa. 46:10, Mal. 3:6. Thus, where it seems that the counsel is changed (μετατίθεσθαι βουλὴν), that is only by reason of us, not by reason of God according to appearance (κατὰ δόξαν), not according to truth (κατ' ἀλήθειαν). But the immutability (τὸ ἀμετάθετον) of God stands entirely firm, inasmuch as He has declared something only with a condition, and that condition not being fulfilled, that which He declared does not come to pass. For thus in God or in the truth of God's sentence no mutability is found, but most truly, according as He declared the matter, whether by threatening or by promising, He performs the same.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Ἐν ᾧ, Quare, quod alias ἐφ' ᾧ. Περισσότερον βυλόμενος ὁ Θεὸς ἐπιδεῖξαι τοῖς κληρονόμοις τῆς ἐπαγγελίας τὸ ἀμετάθετον τῆς βουλῆς ἀυτὸ) Solet DEUS interdum dici μετατίθεσθαι βουλὴν, ubi res mutata novum consilium exigit, ut videre est Jonæ 3, 10. Jerem. 18, 11. Sed hæc promissio tum carnalis de multiplicanda posteritate Abrahami, tum spiritualis, de colligenda Ecclesia Christo, & piis perducendis ad vitam æternam, est immutabilis, ἀμεταμέλητος. נצב Rabbinis. Intellige ergo hic κληρονόμους ἐπαγγελίας & Patres illos veteres & Christianos. Vide & quod supra cap. 4, 1.

Ἐμεσίτευσεν ὅρκῳ) Ex Latino interbenit. Dicuntur autem Latinis intervenire, qui fidem alicujus fulciunt. Sic DEUS suam ipse fidem fulsit jurejurando. In Glossis μεσιτεύω intervenio. Philo de Caino & Abele : Τῷ πιστευθῆναι χάριν ἀπισόμενοι καταφύγουσιν ὡς ὅρκον οἱ ἄνθρωποι. Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς καὶ λέγων πισός ἐστιν, ὥσε καὶ τὺς λόγες ἀυτᾶ βεβαιότητα ἕνεκα μηδὲν ὅρκων διαφέρειν, καὶ συμβέβηκε τὴν μὲν ἡμετέραν γνώμην ὅρκῳ. Τὸν δὲ ὅρκον ἀυτὸν Θεῷ πεπιστεῦσθαι. Οὐ γὰρ δι' ὅρκον πιστὸς ὁ Θεὸς, ἀλλὰ δι' ἀυτὸν καὶ ὁ ὅρκος βέβαιος. Τί οὖν ἔδοξε τῷ ἱεροφάντῃ παρεισαγαγεῖν ἀυτὸν ὀμνύοντα; ἵνα τὴν ἀσθένειαν διελέγξῃ τῶ γενητᾶ, καὶ διελέγξας ἅμα παρηγορήσῃ. Οὐ γὰρ διυνάμεθα διηνεκῶς τὸ ἄξιον τῆ αἰτίε κεφάλαιον ἐν ψυχῇ ταμιέυσαι τῇ ἑαυτῶν, τὸ ὄχ ὡς ἄνθρωπος ὁ Θεὸς, ἵνα ἅπαντα τὰ ἀνθρωπολογύμενα ὑπερκύψωμεν, ἀλλὰ πλεῖσον μετέχοντες τᾶ θνητᾶ, καὶ χωρὶς ἀυτῶν ἐπινοῆσαι μηδὲν δυνάμενοι, μηδὲ ἐκβῆναι τὰς ἰδίας κῆρας ἰσχύοντες, ἀλλ' ὡς τὸ θνητὸν εἰσδυόμενοι καθάπερ οἱ κοχλίαι, καὶ περὶ ἀυτᾶς, ὥσπερ ἐκείνῳ σφαιρηδὸν εἰλούμενοι, καὶ περὶ μακαρίου καὶ ἀφθάρτου, καθάπερ περὶ ἀυτῶν δοξάζομεν, τὴν μὲν ἀτοπίαν τῷ λόγῳ, ὅτι ἀνθρωπόμορφον τὸ θεῖον ἀποδεξασκοιτιες. Τὴν δὲ ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις ἀσέβειαν, ὅτι ἀνθρωποπαθὲς, ἐπανορθώμενοι. Διὰ τοῦτο χεῖρας, πόδας, ὠσόδους, ἐξόδους, ἔχθρας, ἀποτροφὰς, ἀλλοτριώσεις, ὀργὰς προσανταπλάττομεν, ἀνοίκεια μέρη καὶ πάθη τῷ αἰτίῳ, ὧν ἔσι καὶ ὅρκος· τῆς ἡμετέρας ἀσθενείας ἐπικυρά. Tertullianus de pœnitentia : O beatos nos, quorum causa Deus jurat! Miseros sine juranti credimus.

Occurrit dubio, cur DEUS jurarit, cui injurato merito credendum; quod nempe id περισσότερον ex abundanti fecerit, ut immutabilitatem consilii sui duabus rebus promissione nempe ac juramento confirmaret: in quibus utique fuit περισσεῖα ingens. Inter homines enim ad βεβαίωσιν sufficit res una immutabilis jusjurandum. DEUS vero ad βεβαίωσιν adhibuit non unam; sed duas res immutabiles: non solum promissionem immutabilem, nec solum jusjurandum inviolabile (impossibile siquidem, DEUM vel promittendo vel jurando mentiri) sed utrumque simul. Quanquam autem hic proprie respiciatur juramentum divinum Abrahæ factum, Genes. 22. vers. 16. non dubium tamen est, quum postmodum etiam ad juramentum Divinum de Melchisedeciano sacerdotio provocaturus sit Apostolus cap. 7. vers. 20. Utriusque ratione τὸ ἀμετάθετον τῆς βουλῆς θεᾶ tam diligenter inculcare, & vim jurisjurandi tantopere urgere Apostolum, siquidem utriusque juramenti summa sit ratio: illius, quod benedictio non nisi in semine benedicto nobis obtingat; bujus quod æterno illo CHRISTI sacerdotio summopere nobis opus sit, adeo ut sine eo æterna salus constare non potuerit. Ev- angelium vel concio de gratia DEI per CHRI- STUM βουλὴ vel consilium Dei dicitur, de salute, Luc. 7, 30. Immutabile vero DEI consilium es- se, ex Esa. 46, 10. Malach. III, 6. constat. Sic qua μετατίθεσθαι βουλὴν videtur, id ratione no- stri tantum est, non ratione Dei κατὰ δόξαν, non κατ' ἀλήθειαν. τὸ ἀμετάθετον vero Dei omnino sibi constat, siquidem cum conditione solum ali- quid edixerit, qua non præstita, nec id, quod edi- xit, evenit. Sic enim in Deo vel veritate senten- tiæ Dei nihil mutabilitatis invenitur, sed verissi- me prout rem edixit, sive comminando sive pro- mittendo, eandem præstat.

## 6:18
Verse 18.

That by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation) Here, having now dismissed the carnal sense, he seizes upon the mystical or spiritual, which is treated in Matt. 3:9 and Rom. 9:7, Gal. 3:16. The two things of which God does not repent are the promise, when its condition has been fulfilled, and the oath. Furthermore, God acts openly in these, not obscurely, as sometimes in the prophecies of other matters. Open speech is called truth in Dan. 7:16. One is said to lie (ψεύδεσθαι) improperly, by whose words someone is deceived because he does not understand them. Thus Ezekiel deceived Zedekiah, saying that it would not come to pass that he would see Babylon. He thought he would not be deported there, but he was deported, yet blind. Truly, the consolation that rests upon immutable and not at all obscure sayings is firm: such as are, above all, the Evangelical promises.

The promise of GOD did not contain a double sense, carnal and spiritual: but the thing promised was double. For both bodily goods were promised to Abraham, and spiritual and heavenly ones. What is said about Ezekiel, that he deceived Zedekiah, is not said piously enough. For GOD, who spoke through Ezekiel, deceives no one. Nor can that consist with the truth of God. Moreover, nothing alien to the truth was said by him, when the Prophet threatened that it would not come to pass that King Zedekiah would see Babylon. Nor could the speech be ambiguous to the King, if he had weighed the different oracles of God, as was proper. For he ought to have known that for GOD to contradict Himself in them is among the impossibilities (ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων). Since, therefore, both the deportation to Babylon was predicted, and it was predicted that Babylon would not be seen by him: What else could he conclude from that, than that he would be deprived of his eyes and sight, so that, although he was deported there, he would nevertheless not see it. The Apostle applies these things, which he said about Abraham, to himself and the Hebrews, to teach that the heirs of the promise by the immutable counsel of GOD are not only the Patriarchs and other faithful descendants of Abraham in the Old Testament, but also all who walk in the footsteps of Abrahamic faith, Rom. 4, all his children according to the promise, chap. 9, and that for all of them GOD willed, through two immovable things in which it is impossible for God to lie, to render a strong consolation (ἰσχυρὰν παράκλησιν); so that no one may have cause to doubt concerning the blessing to be obtained in CHRIST through faith, and concerning the inheritance of eternal salvation.

Which is to be observed against the Pontifical doubt and the decree of the Council of Trent, that one must doubt concerning the grace of God and salvation: while Pareus attempts to banish this doubt, he involves himself in the same, and cannot but involve himself, by the force of Calvinian hypotheses: For if, he says, salvation is promised to all and each of the believers, how not also to me, to you? For whence can it be certain to a man, adhering to Calvinian principles, that he is of the number of believers? Whence can he believe that God wills to have mercy on him, that Christ has acquired for him the blessing and eternal salvation, if God, by an absolute decree, willed to have mercy on only a very few men, if CHRIST acquired the blessing and eternal salvation for only a very small part of the human race by the immutable counsel of God? Certainly no one can apply that to himself by faith; or make those Divine promises, confirmed with an oath, his own: For how can anyone subsume himself under a particular major proposition, and include himself in the same with firm assurance (πληροφορίᾳ)? What Pareus retorts; even if my faith, yours, is not written in the Bibles: yet it is written in my heart, yours: Namely, the faith by which I believe, by which you believe: It produces only a vain persuasion, not true faith. For if it is written in the heart, not in the Bibles, it must be written in the heart without scripture or the Word of GOD, nor can it have proceeded from the Bibles or the Word of God: For that which is in no way written in the Bibles, neither according to the letter (κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν), nor according to the meaning (κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν), neither in express words, nor according to legitimate consequence, that cannot be said to be the Word of God written in my heart or yours; and therefore I cannot be certain of it by Divine faith, but am only persuaded by human opinion. For there is no Divine faith without the Word of GOD.

Pareus retorts again: Every believer is certain of his own trust: therefore, that I believe, I alone know by the certainty of my faith, that is, by the sense of the trust of my heart. But how can you believe in CHRIST, unless you believe that Christ died for you. But how can you believe that Christ died for you, unless it is certain from the scriptures that Christ died for all. You can be persuaded by human opinion, you cannot believe it by Divine faith, without Divine revelation, which, unless it be feigned as immediate, in the Enthusiastic and Schwenkfeldian manner, is nothing, unless it be that which is contained in the holy scripture. To deny, says Pareus, that the sense of faith can be certain, is in reality to deny that faith is faith, it is to make opinion, a dream, a conjecture, a lie out of faith. But to assert, I say, that the sense of faith, that Christ died for you, can be certain without that Word of God, that Christ died for all, is to give assurance from an opinion, a dream, a conjecture, which can be false. Therefore Estius, adhering to the opinion of absolute predestination, confesses that no one of the faithful can certainly determine that he will arrive at salvation. For, he says, each one is not certain that the promises of God (I speak of absolute ones) pertain to him. For that will of God is very secret to us, concerning which it is written: He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens, Rom. 9. Nevertheless, from the gifts received, by which we draw near to GOD, we are commanded also to hope for those things which will perfectly join us to him. But what is that hope, if not merely conjectural, by which no one can conceive a more certain one from Predestination by the force of οἰκείων principles.

But as for the doubt proper to the Papists concerning the grace of God and salvation, who deny that a man can be certain of it with the certainty of Divine faith, which cannot be subject to falsehood, they can be convinced from their own hypotheses. For they say that from two premises, of which one is revealed and the other evident, that is, from one's own knowledge, a manifest conclusion of Divine certainty is born. And yet this can be done here in this matter. For this proposition is revealed. For to everyone who does not maliciously resist and who hears the consolatory Divine promises, those most certainly are applied. Now someone established in the workshop of the Holy Spirit can subsume: I hear the Divine promises, and I have no malicious resistance against them. Therefore, they are most certainly applied to me. The major premise is revealed, because the whole Scripture speaks this, that no one who hears the Divine promises See John 6:37 and 45. For if God were to constitute any struggle other than a malicious one as an impediment to the application of Divine promises, no human being would be saved or obtain that application. The minor premise, however, is evident and manifest from one's own scrutiny of the mind. For a man can easily explore from that whether there is in him any malicious struggle against Divine truth. For this is not something abstruse or hidden, but open and manifest. There are indeed certain hidden motions by which the flesh sometimes struggles against the Holy Spirit, which are referred to among sins not acknowledged, Psalm 19:3. But those do not impede the operation of the Holy Spirit. Those, however, are manifest which are malicious and oppose the severity of the Divine promises. Nor is there any reason for anyone to say that it is not yet certain that faith is supernatural, and not rather a certain human persuasion which is applied to Divine promises: For where there is no malicious resistance, there the Divine promises not only apply to us the good things contained, but also effect a supernatural faith, nor do they suffer it to be merely a human persuasion; for this is the whole power of the Evangelical promises, that they not only offer the faith which is believed, that is, the good things divinely revealed, but also the faith by which it is believed, that is, the very instrument by which the revealed good things are apprehended. For to both, the Gospel is the power of God, Rom. 1:16, Phil. 2:13. Therefore, now this conclusion of him who is placed in the workshop of the Holy Spirit and says: Therefore the Divine promises are applied to me, is both Divine and of supernatural certainty, as the blessed Dorscheus holds here. One thing we still note: that it is impossible for God to lie, as the Apostle says, does not argue any defect in God, nor a certain impotence of God, as Pliny blasphemously concluded, that God cannot sin, cannot die, and therefore is not omnipotent: But that the highest perfection of God is designated, in that no defect falls into God, nothing that is contrary to Divine immutability, truth, and perfection. Rightly, therefore, did the blessed Dorscheus note the Papists here: Indeed, Tanner, Tom. III. Theol. Scholast. disp. 1. q. 1. dub. 5. p. 43, etc., and Becanus, Tom. I. Oper. p. 384, refer to Gabriel Biel in III. sent. dist. 38. q. 1. and Cardinal Peter of Ailly in I. sent. quest. 12, Robert Holcot in 2. sent. q. 2, and certain others cited by Gregory of Rimini in 1. Sent. dist. 42. q. 2, to have established that God, by absolute power, could have said or testified what is false, both by Himself and through another. Which opinion Tanner thinks is against the faith, Gregory of Valencia calls rash. Arragonius calls it rash and erroneous. Yet no one of them dares to pronounce constantly that it is heretical, since in truth it is more than heretical and subversive of all revealed truth. For if it could even be done by absolute power that God, either by Himself or through another, should testify or say what is false, no certainty could any longer exist in all Divine revelations, because it could not be established that God did not wish to use His absolute power here and now. Whence the Papists, especially the Jesuits, make themselves all the more suspect when it is asked whether it is heretical to say that God, even by ordinary power, can teach or testify what is false. Melchior Canus, lib. 2. Locor. cap. 3, does not dare to pronounce affirmatively with Gregory of Valencia and Dominic Bañez. For if it is not heretical to say that God can teach what is false by ordinary power, it will be much less heretical that God can say that by absolute power. More rightly, Alf. à Castro, lib. 2. adv. hæres. cap. 2, says: It is fair to believe, not only for a Christian but even for a pagan or one moderately pious, and who thinks of God only those things which can be held by natural light, that God is so truthful that He cannot lie.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Ἵνα διὰ δύο πραγμάτων ἀμεταθέτων, ἐν οἷς ἀδύνατον ψεύσασθαι Θεὸν ἰσχυρὰν παράκλησιν ἔχωμεν) Hic jam di- misso sensu carnali mysticum sive spiritualem arripit, de quo agitur Matth. 3, 9. & Romanor. 9, 7. Gal. 3. vers. 16. Duæ res quarum Deum non pœnitet, sunt promissum, ubi impleta est ejus conditio, & juramentum. Præ- terea aperte in his agit Deus, non obscure, ut inter- dum in vaticiniis rerum aliarum. Aperta loquutio vocatur veritas Dan. 7, 16. Ψεύδεσθαι improprie dicitur, cujus verbis aliquis fallitur, ideo quod non ea intelli- gat. Sic Ezechiel decepit Sedeciam, dicens, non futu- rum, ut videret Babylonem. Putabat is se eo non de- portandum, at deportatus est sed jam cæcus. Firma sane est consolatio, quæ nititur dictis immutabilibus, minimeque obscuris: qualis imprimis sunt promissa Evangelica.

Non geminum sensum continebat promissio DEI carnalem & spiritualem: Sed gemina erat res promissa. Nam & corporalia bona Abra- hamo promissa sunt, & spiritualia ac cœlestia. Quod de Ezechiele dicitur, quod Sedeciam de- ceperit, non satis pie dicitur. DEUS enim, qui per Ezechielem loquutus est, neminem de- cipit. Nec id cum veritate Dei consistere potest. Nihil autem in eo à veritate alieni dictum, cum minaretur Propheta, non futurum, ut Rex Se- decias Babylonem videret. Neque ambigua Regi poterat esse loquutio, si diversa Dei ora- cula expendisset, ut par erat. DEUM enim in illis sibi contrariari, ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων esse sci- re debebat. Quum ergo & deportatio in Ba- bylonem prædicta erat, & prædictum, Babylo- nem ab ipso visum non iri: Quid aliud inde concludere poterat, quam oculis & visu se pri- vandum, ut, licet eo deportaretur, eam tamen non videret. Applicat autem Apostolus hæc, quæ dixit de Abrahamo ad se & Ebræos, ut doceat hæredes promissionis ex consilio DEI ἀμεταθέτῳ, non esse tantum Patriarchas, & alios fideles Abrahami nepotes in Veteri Testa- mento, sed etiam omnes, qui in vestigiis fidei Abrahamicæ incedunt, Rom. 4. omnes ejus libe- ros secundum promissionem, cap. 9. omnibus- que illis voluisse DEUM per duas res immobi- les, in quibus mentiri Deum impossibile est, ἰσχυρὰν παράκλησιν consolationem; quam fortis- simam & certissimam reddere, ut ne ullus dubitare habeat de benedictione in CHRISTO per fidem consequenda, deque æternæ salutis hæreditate.

Quod contra Pontificiam dubitationem & decre- tum Conciliabuli Tridentini, quod dubitandum sit de gratia Dei & salute, observandum: quam du- bitationem dum profligare conatur Pareus, semet- ipsum eidem involvit, nec potest non involvere, vi hypothesium Calvinianorum: Si enim, inquit, promittitur salus omnibus, & singulis credentibus, quomodo non etiam mihi, tibi? Nam unde constare potest homini, Calvinianis principiis inhærenti, se esse ex numero credentium? Unde credere potest, Deum sui velle misereri, Christum sibi benedictionem & salutem æternam acquisiuisse, si Deus ex absoluto decreto paucissimorum tantum hominum mise- reri voluit, si CHRISTUS non nisi minimæ parti generis humani benedictionem & salutem æter- nam ex immutabili Dei consilio acquisivit? Non potest certe quisquam id sibi per fidem applicare; vel promissiones illas Divinas cum jurejurando firmatas suas facere: Quomodo enim quis sub- sumere potest sub propositione majori particula- ri, seq; eidem includere firma πληροφορίᾳ. Quod regerit Pareus; etsi fides mea, tua, in Bibliis scripta non sit: scriptam tamen esse in corde meo, tuo: Fidem nempe, qua ego credo, qua tu credis: Prodit tantum vanam persuasionem, non veram fidem. Nam si scripta est in corde, non in Bibliis, sine scriptura vel Verbo DEI in corde scriptam esse oportet, nec è Bibliis vel Verbo Dei profecta esse potest: Quod enim nullatenus in Bibliis scriptum est, neque κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν, neque κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν, ne- que expressis verbis, neque secundum legitimam consequentiam, id è Verbo Dei scriptum in corde meo vel tuo dici non potest; ideoque de eo cer- tus esse nequeo fide Divina, sed tantum persuasus sum opinione humana. Fides enim Divina nul- la est sine Verbo DEI.

Regerit denuo Pareus: Unumquemque fidelem certum de sua fiducia: quod ergo credam, ego solus novi certitudine fidei meæ, hoc est, sensu fiduciæ cor- dis mei. Sed quomodo in CHRISTUM crede- re potes, nisi credas, Christum pro te esse mortuum. Quomodo autem pro te mortuum esse Christum potes credere, nisi constet è scripturis, Christum pro omnibus mortuum esse. Persuasus esse potes opinione humana, credere id non potes fide Di- vina, sine revelatione Divina, quæ nisi immediata fingatur, more Enthusiastico, & Schvenckfeldiano, nulla est, nisi quæ scriptura sacra comprehensa. Negare, inquit Pareus, sensum fidei certum esse posse, revera est negare, fidem esse fidem, est ex fide opinio- nem, somnium, conjecturam, mendacium facere. At asserere, inquam ego, sensum fide, quod Chri- stus pro te mortuus sit, certum esse posse sine illo Verbo Dei, quod Christus mortuus sit pro omni- bus, est ex opinione, somnio, conjectura, quæ mendax esse possit, fidem facere. Ideo Estius in- hærens absolutæ prædestinationis opinioni, fatetur, non posse quenquam fidelium certo statuere, se per- venturum esse ad salutem. Non enim, inquit, certus est unusquisque promissa Dei (de absolutis lo- quor) ad se pertinere. Valde enim secreta nobis est illa Dei voluntas, de qua scriptum est: Cujus vult, miseretur, & quem vult, indurat Rom. 9. Verun- tamen ex donis acceptis, quibus DEO propinqua- mus, jubemur & ea sperare, quæ nos ei perfecte con- jungent. Quænam vero illa spes, nisi conjectura- lis tantum, quâ certiorem nemo è Prædestinatione vi principiorum οἰκείων concipere potest.

Quod vero ad Pontificiis propriam dubitatio- nem de gratia Dei & salute, qui negant, hominem de ea certum esse posse certitudine fidei Divinæ, cui non potest subesse falsum, convinci possunt ex propriis hypothesibus. Dicunt enim ex duabus præmissis, quarum una est revelata, altera evidens, hoc est, ex cognitione propria, manifesta nasci conclu- sionem Divinæ certitudinis. Atqui hic hoc fieri potest in hac materia. Nam hæc propositio revelata est. Omni enim malitiose non repugnanti & audien- ti promissiones Divinas consolatorias, illæ certissime applicantur. Jam potest subsumere aliquis in offi- cina Spiritus sancti constitutus: Ego audio promissio- nes Divinas, & nullam adversus eam habeo malitio- sam repugnantiam. Ergo illæ mihi certissime appli- cantur. Major est revelata, quia tota scriptura hoc loquitur, neminem, qui audit promissiones Divinas, & illis nullam malitiosam repugnantiam opponit, ab applicatione illarum excidere. Vide Joh. 6, 37. & 45. Nam si aliam quamcunque luctam præter malitiosam Deus constitueret impedimentum applicationis pro- missionum Divinarum, nemo hominum salvaretur, aut applicatione ista potiretur. Minor autem evi- dens est, & ex proprio mentis scrutinio manifesta. Potest enim homo ex eo facile explorare, an in ipso sit malitiosa aliqua contra veritatem Divinam lucta. Hæc enim non est abstrusum aut absconditum ali- quid, sed apertum & manifestum. Sunt equidem occulti quidam motus, quibus nonnunquam Spiritui sancto caro reluctatur, qui inter peccata non agnita Psalm. 19, 3. referuntur. Sed illi non impediunt ope- rationem Spiritus sancti. Manifesti autem sunt, qui malitiosi sunt, & severitati promissionum Divi- narum opponunt. Nec est, quod quis dicat, nondum tamen certum esse, fidem esse supernaturalem, & non potius humanam quandam persuasionem, quæ adhi- betur promissionibus Divinis: Nam ubi nulla est ma- litiosa repugnantia, ibi promissiones Divinæ non tan- tum bona contenta nobis applicant, sed & supernatu- ralem fidem efficiunt, nec patiuntur tantum esse per- suasionem humanam; Hæc est enim tota vis promis- sionum Evangelicarum, quod non tantum offerant fidem, quæ creditur, hoc est, bona Divinitus revelata, sed & fidem, qua creditur, hoc est, ipsum organon, quo bona revelata apprehenduntur. Ad utrumque enim Evangelium est potentia DEI, Rom. 1, 16. Phil. 2, 13. Ergo jam ista conclusio ejus, qui in officina Spiritus sancti positus est, & dicit: Ergo mihi applicantur pro- missiones Divinæ, & Divina & supernaturalis cer- titudinis, ut hic habet B. Dorscheus. Unicum ad- huc notamus: Deum mentiri ἀδύνατον cum dicit Apostolus, non aliquem in Deo defectum, non im- potentiam quandam DEI argui, ut blaspheme Pli- nius colligebat, Deum non posse peccare, non posse mori, adeoque non esse omnipotentem: Sed summam Dei perfectionem designari, eo quod in Deum nullus cadat defectus, nihil quod contra- rium sit Divinæ immutabilitati, veritati, perfectio- ni. Merito itaque hic Pontificios notavit B. Dor- scheus: Equidem Tannerus Tom. III. Theol. Scholast. disp. 1. q. 1. dub. 5. pag. 43. &c. Becanus Tom. I. Oper. p. 384. referunt Gabrielem Biel in III. sent. dist. 38. q. 1. & Petrum de Aliaco Cardinalem in I. sent. quæst. 12. Robert. Holcot. in 2. sent. q. 2. & alios quosdam citatos à Gregorio Arminiense in 1. Sent. dist. 42. q. 2. statuisse, Deum de potentia ab- soluta & per se & per alium falsum dicere aut te- stari potuisse. Quam sententiam Tannerus putat esse contra fidem, Gregorius de Valentia vocat te- merariam. Arragonius, temerariam & erro- neam. Nemo tamen ex illis constanter pronun- ciare audet esse hæreticam, quum revera plus quam hæretica sit, & omnis veritatis revelatæ sub- versiva. Si enim etiam de absoluta potentia fie- ri possit, ut DEUS vel per se vel per alium falsum testetur, aut dicat, nulla amplius in omnibus reve- lationibus Divinis certitudo esse potest, quia neque constare poterit, DEUM hic & nunc potentia sua absoluta uti noluisse. Unde tanto magis se suspectos faciunt Pontificii, imprimis Jesuitæ, dum quando quæritur, an hæreticum sit dicere, Deum de potentia etiam ordinaria posse docere seu testari falsum. Melchior Canus lib. 2. Locor. cap. 3. non audet cum Gregorio de Valentia & Dominico Ban- nes pronunciare affirmate. Si enim non est he- reticum dicere Deum de potentia ordinaria posse docere falsum, multo minus hereticum erit, DEUM de potentia absoluta id dicere posse. Re- ctius Alf. à Castro lib. 2. adv. hæres. cap. 2. credi, inquit, par est, non solum à Christiano, verum etiam ab Ethnico vel mediocriter pio, & de Deo ea solum, quæ naturali luce haberi possunt, sen- tienti, DEUM adeo veracem esse, ut mentiri ne- queat.

## 6:18
We, he says, who have fled for refuge, having left behind the vices of the age, to obtain that hope which is proposed to us in the Gospel. We have fled as to an asylum, like those of whom Numbers 35:2 and Joshua 21:27 speak. Hope is said here by metonymy for the thing itself hoped for, that is, eternal life, as in Galatians 5:5 and elsewhere. Κρατῆσαι for εἰς τὸ κρατῆσαι, and κρατᾶν to take possession, as κρατῶν τὸ ποταμῶ. And προκειμένη ἐλπὶς, as below προκείμενον ἀγὼν XII, προκειμένη χαρὰ, XII. 2. Thus προκείμενον σκοπὸς in Galen.

This I refer to the consolation, to the comfort which arises from those promises. It is in place of a firm and tenacious anchor, because among so many waves and tempests of the age, it causes us not to be submerged: namely, if we use it rightly, like those sailors, Acts 27:29. Just as Hecuba in Euripides says of her son: ὦκων ἄγκυρά τ' ἐμῶν.

Latin:

Οι καταφυγόντες κρατῆσαι τῆς προκειμένης ἐλπίδος.] Nos, inquit, qui confugimus, relictis nempe seculi vitiis, ad obtinendam spem illam, quæ nobis in Evan- gelio proponitur. Confugimus tanquam ad asylum, ut illi, de quibus Numeror. 35. vers. 2. & Jos. 21. vers. 27. Spes hic dicitur per Μετωνυμίαν res ipsa sperata, id est, vita æterna, ut Galat. 5, 5. & alibi. Κρατῆσαι pro εἰς τὸ κρατῆσαι, & κρατᾶν potiri, ut κρατῶν τὸ ποταμῶ. Et προκειμένη ἐλπὶς, ut infra προκείμενον ἀγὼν XII. προκειμένη χαρὰ, XII. 2. Sic προκείμενον σκοπὸς apud Galenum.

Ἣν ὡς ἄγκυραν ἔχομεν τῆς ψυχῆς ἀσφαλῆτε καὶ βε- βαίαν] Hanc refero ad παράκλησιν, ad consolationem, quæ ex illis promissis oritur. Ea est vice firmæ ac tenacis anchoræ, quia inter tantos fluctus & tempestates seculi efficit ne mergamur: nempe si ea recte utamur, ut illi nautæ, Actor. 27, 29. Sicut Hecuba apud Euripidem de Filio: ὦκων ἄγκυρά τ' ἐμῶν.

## 6:19
Vers. 19.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

## 6:19
And this I refer to the consolation. That consolation enters, that is, it places us as if present in that highest heaven, which is signified by that inner sanctuary which was within the veil called פַרֹכֶת, which interpreters and Philo call καταπέτασμα for the sake of distinction, when they call the other veil at the doors of the Basilica κάλυμμα. Concerning this whole matter, we have spoken at Matthew 27:51.

Others take the name ἐλπίδος properly, not metonymically, so that those fleeing by faith to CHRIST are said to firmly hold the hope set before them as a kind of sacred anchor, B. Luther: And hold to the offered hope. The metaphor here is not of an asylum, but of an anchor. Theophylact: He says, it is said to be no more on account of Abraham than of us, who flee to him by hoping well. But where do we have that most powerful consolation? Doubtless in holding the hope set before us, that is, from those things which were bestowed upon that Abraham, so that we may be rendered more certain and secure about these things of ours, and not doubt concerning heavenly things, of which the hope ought to be more certain to us, but that we may firmly and securely hold onto that hope, and not allow it to slip away. For the promise was made to us no differently than to Abraham. Nor is consolation the anchor, but hope comes under that name, which is called 'set before' according to the Greek interpreters, because it is set before us by the word of promise and the example of Abraham and others. And here Grotius seems to confuse promise and consolation, which are distinct. For consolation relies on the promise: and therefore the anchor is to be referred not to παράκλησιν and the more remote noun, but to τὴν προκειμένην ἐλπίδα as the nearer noun, of which its ἀσφάλεια or certainty, and βεβαιότης or firmness, is noted. For just as an anchor, which is able to hold a ship tossed among the waves and storms of the sea, ought to be certain, not doubtful; firm, not infirm: So if hope ought to preserve the ship of the heart, tossed by various waves and storms of temptations κάτω καὶ ἄνω, it is necessary that it be both certain and firm. That confusion of Grotius appears from those things which he adds: That consolation enters, that is, it places us as if present in that highest heaven, which seems to be said not so much of consolation as of the Divine promise. Whatever, however, may be the case with that, if such consolation is an anchor, why should hope itself not deserve to be called so? Most interpreters explain it as hope, with Theophylact following Chrysostom: Which hope, of course, we have in place of an anchor. For as that, when a storm has arisen, holds and steadies ships; so also hope itself renders those who are tossed and wavering by temptations stable and patient. And he did not simply say anchor, but added safe and firm. There is, moreover, another kind of anchor, which by no means keeps a ship motionless, if it be either too rotten or too light. Nor does Theodoret say otherwise: The Lord has promised that He will give the kingdom of heaven to those who have believed in Him, those goods, he says, we hope for, we hold this hope as a sacred anchor. For an anchor hidden in the deep does not allow our souls to be shaken. So also the blessed Hunnius, and others: Even the blessed Gerhard, who although he previously accepted the hope proposed concerning eternal life: Afterwards, however, he explains the anchor not as hope taken metonymically, that is, eternal life, but properly so called, and he unfolds that metaphor neatly with Estius thus: Just as an anchor cast into the deep of the sea steadies a ship, and renders it safe from sinking, and preserves the sailors, so that at length, the storm ceasing, they may arrive safely into port: So hope, penetrating into heaven itself and fixed in CHRIST, steadies the hearts of believers, and renders them safe from eternal destruction, and finally preserves them in the storm of persecutions, so that at length they may arrive safely into the port of the heavenly fatherland. As an anchor [is] to a ship against the waves: So hope makes the souls of the faithful immovable against temptations. As an anchor in the midst of the waves holds a ship: lest it perish, carried away by the wind and waves: So hope holds all the saints in the immense ocean of this life, and the stormy waves of labors, in such a way that they remain firm and secure, which anchor the Apostle therefore commands to cast into heaven. There is, however, a dissimilarity in this: 1. That an anchor is sent into the earth, but hope flies up into heaven. 2. That a ship, as long as it is held by an anchor, cannot head into port: Hope so stabilizes and firms souls that it promotes them to the port of the heavenly fatherland. Kρατῆσαι does not signify to hold in any way, but to hold and embrace in such a way that you do not suffer it to be snatched from you, which is likewise observed by Estius. But he who understands hope properly, not metonymically, wishes it to be called proposed by reason of the object, because through it the mind tends toward the promised goods, and those proposed in place of a reward. Johan. Camero in myrothec. pag. 321. He understands, he says, the hope to which we are invited in the Gospel, which is called προκειμένη, because access to it is open to all, unless those who have hardened themselves, but these are the authors of their own destruction, there is no fault of GOD, but rather benevolence, if indeed any obey the Gospel, and therefore hope for what they are commanded to hope for, for them indeed it was not flesh and blood, but the Spirit of GOD that was the author of such a good. In the same sense κοινὴ σωτηρία is called common salvation, that is, salvation as if placed in the middle, Epistle of Jude verse 3. Therefore, hope here is not the thing hoped for, but the virtue itself, which is carried toward the thing hoped for, as if toward an object. Nor indeed is there any reason for anyone to wonder that it is called προκειμένην, since there are many men, and indeed those not entirely profane, who, deluded by the arts of Satan, and dejected in spirit lower than they ought by the force of temptation and the weakness of faith, doubt whether they are of the number of those to whom it is permitted to hope for eternal life. Therefore, the Apostle, in order to stop the mouths of profane men here who cavil that it does not pertain to them to hope in GOD, and on the other hand to confirm those who are doubting, calls this hope προκειμένην. It is, however, a metaphor drawn from contestants, who strive for the βραβεῖα and palms placed in the middle, and that κοινὴν is the same as the προκειμένην of the author of the epistle to the Hebrews is clear from the word ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι, which follows immediately in the same verse in Jude, παρακαλῶν ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι &c. But how is hope said to enter and those to the inner parts of the veil, when hope is to cease in the heavens, 1 Cor. 13, last verse? That can be said far less of eternal life itself. For does eternal life enter into eternal life? Nor could it be explained any more of consolation than of hope. For hope is said to enter there, because it extends itself even into the other life, not by reason of duration, inasmuch as it expires with this life, but by reason of extension. Estius applies the likeness of the anchor thus: Just as a naval anchor does not stick in the waters, but enters the earth hidden under the waters, and is fixed to it: So the anchor of the soul, our hope, is not satisfied to have arrived at the vestibule, that is, it is not content with earthly and visible goods, but penetrates even to those things which are within the veil, namely, it apprehends the holy of holies itself, that is, GOD Himself and heavenly goods, and is fixed in them. He adds: Some explain entering causatively, as making to enter, but they did not attend to the metaphor of the anchor, now explained by us, which the Apostle uses. Which Estian explanation the blessed Gerhard also made his own: But Theophylact seems to have embraced the causal sense: Through hope we already attain those things. For hope, passing through heaven, makes us possessors of the promises and makes us dwell in them clearly: although it seems to consist on earth. For the power of this hope is so great that it renders those who inhabit the earth heavenly.

Moreover, the Apostle adds among the Hebrews, of set purpose, an allegory from the old tabernacle or temple, as he decided to expound it more fully later: in which the inner part, called the holy of holies, was separated by an intervening veil from that part to which the people gathered, and that indeed bore the type of the heavenly dwelling, but this one of present goods. Just as, says Theophylact, in the Old Testament a veil restrained the holier tabernacle and separated it from the rest: So also heaven is stretched out before us, to drive these lower things away from heavenly and Divine things. B. Dorscheus explains ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος otherwise than as heaven. Καταπέτασμα is the very flesh of Christ, Heb. 10, 20. And so ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος will be the very πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος. Hence John 1, 16, it is said that we all receive ἐκ τοῦ πληρώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ grace for grace. Since, therefore, an anchor is otherwise cast downwards, this one is cast upwards εἰς τὰ ἄνω, Col. 3, 2, understood not locally but divinely. For everywhere that God and Christ is, is ἄνω, and when He dwells in our hearts, Eph. 3, 17. Therefore, those who interpret ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος only as the innermost recesses of heaven do not attain the power of the Divine promises. But these are only opposed to the local recesses of the Calvinists, as he explains himself later. For τὸ ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος is not the heaven of glory finite only, which is the dwelling place of the blessed, but the Majesty itself is infinite. And from this it is also manifest, because in it the anchor of our souls must be most firmly and most safely founded and established. But indeed that is not founded and established upon anything finite and created. For that cannot bestow the ultimate and most full foundation of an anchor, but requires infinite virtue and power itself. Furthermore, from that ἐσωτέρῳ τοῦ καταπετάσματος the whole kingdom of our Savior is governed, from that the dominion in the midst of enemies is perfected, from that the hearts of the faithful are inhabited, from that CHRIST is all in all, from that all things are filled. Therefore, the limit cannot be finite. Finally, in that ἐσωτέρῳ τοῦ καταπετάσματος is still perfected that which our Priest JESUS, in his priesthood after the completed expiation of our sins and the full satisfaction rendered, still performs: which is that glorious intercession, which CHRIST is said to perform at the right hand of GOD, Romans 8, verse 34, which is not that humble and meritorious intercession which he performed for us in the days of his flesh, but sublime, and worthy of the right hand of GOD, that is, of infinite glory, exhibited not in the form of a servant, but in the form of GOD. Therefore, the limit of this entry is infinite and immense; namely, the very throne of GOD, the right hand of GOD, the glory of the Father, the glory which CHRIST had before the world was founded, the adorable glory. For to this limit of progress, and to JESUS established therein, every knee ought to bow, Philippians 2, 10, 11. Wherefore furthermore CHRIST entered into that which is within the veil, according to his Human nature, whence below in chapter 10, verse 20, it is said that CHRIST has procured for us the liberty of entering the sanctuary by his blood, that living way which he dedicated for us, fresh and living, through the veil, that is, through his flesh. Therefore, since hitherto in the state of emptying he had as it were veiled his Majesty and glory with flesh, now with majesty and glory revealed he surrounds his flesh, and places it in the Φῶς ἀπρόσιτον, 1 Timothy 6, verse 16. Moreover, this entry is not separative, but conjunctive. For 1. the τὸ ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος is not absent from us, but fills all things, because as I have said, it is the glory of GOD fully dominating, and thus that which fills the whole earth, Isaiah 6, verse 3, Jeremiah 23, verse 24. It is the right hand of GOD, which sustains and carries all things, and the throne of GOD, which extends itself through all things, of which above in chapter 1, 8, 2. This entry tends toward Divine dominion, namely dominion in the midst of enemies, Psalm 110, verse 2, dominion among the saints and in the midst of the faithful, Matthew 28, verse 20, and chapter 28, verse 20. Therefore, it does not constitute an entry distant from those for whom he entered. 3. This entry constitutes CHRIST in the full and most perfect being of a head according to his human nature, Ephesians 1, 22. CHRIST was indeed, even according to his Human nature in the state of emptying, the head of the Church, but humbled and inclined to drink in the way from the brook, Psalm 110, verse 7. But through this entry according to it, he was made a head lifting itself up, and indeed ὑπεράνω πάντων, Ephesians 1, 21, not topically; for this does not contribute to the perfection of the mystical head, but dominically, namely in that height to which all things are subjected, Ephesians 1, 22, and which is not far from each one of us, Acts 17, 27. For it is divine dominion, which is perfected by this head: Therefore, it is not of absence, but of presence, and of the admirable perfection of this head to be in individual members, Ephesians 3, 17, 2 Corinthians 13, 5. 4. This entry constitutes Jesus as fully adorable. For upon him we ought to cast the anchor of our hope most firmly and most safely. But this is nothing other than to adore. For that casting of the anchor is a fiduciary act of adoration. But adoration is not of an absent one, but of a present one. Finally 5. That entry is not so much to be attended to regarding the way, as regarding the limit: Regarding the way it was separative. For that, since CHRIST could have entered into his glory anywhere, he most freely chose, that through some ascent to the heavens, which is the way to the entry, he might separate himself from men regarding his visible presence. Nor is the τὸ ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος situated more toward these visible heavens, or toward that region of heaven to which he strove while ascending, than anywhere else where GOD manifests his infinite and immense glory. Indeed, he had the ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος within himself, as that in which all the fullness of the Deity dwelt bodily, nor did Christ cease to be in the form of GOD regarding his first act and possession, but regarding his second act and full usurpation. Hence that ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος shone forth from Christ on these earths from time to time, when his glory was seen, the glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, John 1, 14. Therefore, he did not need to measure out any spaces of air or heavens in order to reach that ἐσώτερον. Freely, therefore, he made that separation, and primarily to this end, that if CHRIST had departed from them without some such movement (φορᾷ), they might be confirmed in the suspicion of a specter, which they had otherwise conceived through a momentary apparition. But if you consider the limit of this entry, it is most intensely and most deeply conjunctive. Namely, for this reason Christ wished to be separated through his ascent, that through his session at the right hand he might be more closely and more divinely joined to us, and thus might also use that ἐσωτέρῳ which hitherto was veiled under flesh, even according to the flesh, that is, what is said in Acts 2, 36, that JESUS was made Lord and CHRIST, namely an absolute Lord, a Lord dominating with infinite power and Majesty, a Lord filling all things with his Divine presence.

Latin:

Καὶ εἰσερχομένην εἰς τὸ ἐσώτερον τῶ καταπετάσματος.] Et hoc refero ad παράκλησιν. Consolatio ista intrat, id est, velut præsentes nos sistit in cœlo illo summo, quod significatur per adytum illud, quod erat intrà ve- lum dictum פַרֹכֶת, quod discriminis causa interpretes & Philo vocant καταπέτασμα, cum velum alterum in foribus Basilicæ vocent κάλυμμα. De tota hac re dixi- mus ad Matth. 27, 51.

Nomen ἐλπίδος alii proprie accipiunt non Metonymice, ut ad CHRISTUM per fidem confugientes spem propositam firmiter servare velut sacram anchoram quandam dicantur, B. Lutherus: Und halten an der angebothenen Hoffnung. Non hic asyli, sed anchoræ est Me- taphora. Theophylactus: Nec plus quippiam, inquit, Abrahæ ratione, quam nostri id dicitur, qui ad eum bene sperando confugimus. Verum ubinam fortissimum illud habemus solatium? Ni- mirum in tenenda proposita spe, id est, ex his, quæ fuere Abrahæ illi collata, ut de nostris his certio- res reddamur & tuti, nec de cœlestibus ambiga- mus, quorum nobis esse spes certior debet, sed firmi- ter & tuta spem eam detineamus, nec sinamus. hanc ipsam effluere. Non enim secus nobis ac Abrahæ facta pollicitatio est. Neque consolatio est anchora, sed spes eo nomine venit, quæ proposita dicitur juxta Græcos Interpretes, quia verbo promissionis & exemplo Abrahæ & alio- rum proposita nobis est. Et confundere vide- tur hic Grotius promissionem, & consolationem, quæ distincta sunt. Nam consolatio nititur promissione: Ideoque non ad παράκλησιν & no- men remotius, sed ad τὴν προκειμένην ἐλπίδα ceu propinquius nomen ἄγκυρα referenda, cujus no- tatur ἀσφάλεια vel certitudo, & βεβαιότης vel firmitudo. Ut enim certa, non dubia; ut firma non infirma debet esse anchora, quæ navigium retinere queat, inter fluctus maris & procellas agitatum: Ita spes navigium cordis variis tentationum fluctibus & procellis κάτω καὶ ἄνω agitatum servare si debeat, & certa & firma sit oportet. Confusio illa Gro- tiana apparet ex iis, quæ addit: Consolatio illa intrat, id est, velut præsentes nos sistit in cælo illo summo, quod non tam de consolatione quam de promissione Divina dicendum videtur. Quic- quid autem ejus sit, si consolatio talis anchora est, quidni ipsa spes ita dici mereatur? De spe utique explicant plerique Interpretes, Theophylactus præ- eunte Chrysostomo: Quam spem scilicet anchora loco habemus. Nam ut illa, cum tempestas in- gruerit, navigia continet, sistitque; sic & spes ipsa qui tentationibus aguntur & nutant, stabiles reddit & pacientes. Nec simpliciter anchoram dixit, sed tu- tam adjunxit & firmam. Est præterea anchora alia quædam, quæ navim haudquaquam servat immotam, si vel putridior vel levior sit. Nec ali- ter Theodoretus: Regnum cælorum se Dominus daturum est pollicitus iis, qui in ipsum crediderint, illa, inquit, bona speramus, hanc spem tenemus velu- ti sacram anchoram. Anchora enim in profundo absconsa non finit, ut nostræ animæ conquassentur. Sic etiam B. Hunnius, alii: Etiam B. Gerhardus qui etsi spem propositam antea de vita æterna ac- ceperit: Postea tamen non de spe Metonymice accepta, hoc est vita æterna, sed proprie ita di- ctam anchoram explicat, eamque Metaphoram cum Estio concinne ita evolvit: Quemadmodum anchora in profundum maris projecta navim fir- mat, & à submersione tutam reddit, nautasq; con- servat, ut tandem cessante tempestate salvi in por- tum perveniant: Sic spes in ipsum cælum pene- trans atque in CHRISTO fixa firmat corda cre- dentium, & ab æterno exitio eos tutos reddit, deni- que in tempestate persecutionum eos conservat, ut tandem salvi in portum cælestis patriæ perveniant. Sicut anchora navim contra fluctus: Ita spes fide- lium animas contra tentationes facit immobiles. Sicut anchora in medio fluctuum navem retinet: ne à vento & fluctibus abrepta dispereat: Ita spes sanctos omnes in immenso hujus vitæ Oceano, pro- cellosisque laborum fluctibus ita retinet, ut firmi secu- rique permaneant, quam anchoram propterea Apo- stolus in cælum jacere præcipit. Dissimilitudo ta- men in eo est 1. quod anchora mittitur in terram, spes autem in cælum subvolat. 2. Quod navis quamdiu ab anchora retinetur, non potest in por- tum tendere: Spes animas ita stabilit ac firmat, ut eas ad portum cælestis patriæ promoveat. Kρα- τῆσαι non significat quomodocunque tenere, sed ita tenere & complecti, ut non patiaris tibi eri- pi, quod itidem observatum Estio. Qui vero spem proprie intelligit, non Metonymice, sed propositam dici vult objecti ratione, quod per eam tendit animus in bona promissa, & loco præ- mii proposita. Johan, Camero in myrothec. pag. 321. Spem, inquit, intelligit, ad quam invitamur in Evangelio, quæ dicitur προκειμένη, quod ad eam omnibus pateat aditus, nisi qui obduruerunt, hi vero sui sibi exitii autores sunt, culpa DEI nulla est, sed beneficentia potius, si qui vero parent Ev- angelio, ideoque sperant, quæ sperare jubentur, iis profecto non caro & sanguis, sed DEI Spiritus tan- ti boni fuit autor. Eodem sensu κοινὴ σωτηρία di- citur communis salus, hoc est, salus veluti in medio posita, Epist. Judæ vers. 3. Non est ergo hic spes res sperata, sed ipsa virtus, quæ in rem speratam, tanquam in objectum, fertur. Neque vero est, quod quisquam miretur, eam dici προκειμένην, cum mul- ti sunt homines, & quidem ii non prorsus profani, qui delusi Satanæ artibus, & infra, quam decet ani- mo dejecti vi tentationis & imbecillitate fidei, dubi- tant, sintne ex eorum numero, quibus liceat spera- re vitam æternam. Ergo Apostolus ut hinc profa- nis hominibus, cavillantibus, ad se non pertinere, ut sperent in DEUM, os obstruat, inde vero dubi- tantes confirmet, spem hanc dicit προκειμένην. Est autem Metaphora ducta à certantibus, qui ad βραβεῖα & palmas in medio positas contendunt, κοινὴν autem idem esse, quod Autori epistolæ ad E- bræos προκειμένην liquet ex voce ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι, quæ apud Judam eodem versu mox sequitur παρακαλῶν ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι &c. Quomodo autem spes ingre- di dicitur iisque ad interiora velaminis, quum in cœlis cessatura sit spes, 1. Corinth. 13. vers. ult. Id longe minus de vita ipsa æterna dici potest. Vi- ta enim æterna num ingreditur vitam æternam? Nec magis de consolatione, quam spe explicari poterit. Spes enim eo ingredi dicitur, quia porrigit sese usque in alteram vitam non ratio- ne durationis, utpote quæ cum hac vita expirat, sed ratione protensionis. Estius similitudinem anchoræ ita adhibet: Sicut anchora navalis non in aquis hæret, sed terram intrat sub aquis laten- tem, eique infigitur: Ita anchora animæ spes nostra non satis habet in vestibulum pervenisse, id est, non est contenta bonis terrenis & visibilibus, sed pene- trat usque ad ea, quæ sunt intra velum, videlicet in ipsa sancta sanctorum, id est, DEUM ipsum & cælestia bona apprehendit, atque in iis figitur. Ad- dit: Nonnulli incedentem causative exponunt, in- cedere facientem, sed ii non attenderunt ad Me- taphoram anchoræ, nunc à nobis expositam, qua Apostolus utitur. Quam Estianam explicatio- nem suam etiam fecit B. Gerhardus: Causalem autem sensum videtur amplexus Theophylactus: Per spem jam illa consequimur. Spes enim per- means cœlum, promissorum nos compotes & in his ut plane versemur effecit: tametsi videtur in terris consistere. Est namque spei hujusce vis tanta, ut cælestes reddat, qui incolunt terram.

Addit autem Apostolus penes Ebræos de in- dustria allegoriam à veteri tabernaculo seu tem- plo, utpote quam postea uberius exponere con- stituit: in quo pars interior, sanctum sanctorum dicta, interjecto velo separabatur ab ea parte, ad quam populus conveniebat, & illa quidem typum gerebat cœlestis habitaculi, ista vero bonorum præsentium. Quemadmodum, inquit Theophy- lactus, in Veteri Testamento velamen sanctius taber- naculum coërcebat & sejungebabat à cæteris: Sic & cœlum nobis obtenditur, ut inferiora hæc à cælestibus abigat & Divinis. B. Dorscheus aliter ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος, quam de cælo exponit. Καταπέτασμα est ipsa caro Christi, Ebr. 10, 20. I- taque ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος erit ipsum πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος. Hinc Joh. 1, 16. dicitur, nos ἐκ τοῦ πληρώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ omnes sumere gra- tiam pro gratia. Cum itaque anchora alias deorsum jaciatur, hæc sursum jacitur εἰς τὰ ἄνω, Col. 3, 2. non τοπικῶς sed θεϊκῶς intellecta. Ubique enim, ubi Deus & Christus est, ἄνω est, & cum habitat in cordibus nostris, Eph 3, 17. Non itaque assequuntur vim pro- missionum Divinarum, qui per ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπε- τάσματος intimos cæli recessus tantum interpretan- tur. Sed hæc tantum Calvinianis recessibus localibus opposita, ut postea sese explicat. Nam τὸ ἐσώ- τερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος non est cælum gloriæ finita tantum, quod est beatorum domicilium, sed ipsa infinita Majestas. ¶ Et ex eo etiam manifestum est, quia in eo anchora animarum nostrarum firmissime tutissimeque fundanda, & constituenda est. At vero ista non fundatur & constituitur super aliquo finito & creato. Illud enim ultimam plenissimamque anchoræ fundationem largiri non potest, sed ipsam infinitam virtutem potestatemque requirit. Præterea ex illo ἐσωτέρῳ τοῦ καταπετάσματος gubernatur totum regnum Salvatoris nostri, ex illo perficitur dominium in medio inimicorum, ex illo habitantur corda fidelium, ex illo CHRISTUS est omnia in omnibus, ex illo implentur omnia. Itaque terminus finitus esse nequit. Denique in illo ἐσωτέρῳ τοῦ καταπετάσματος perficitur adhuc illud, quod Sacerdos noster JESUS in sacerdotio suo post consummatam peccatorum nostrorum expiationem & satisfactionem plenariam prestitam adhuc perficit: quod est gloriosa illa intercessio, quam ad dextram DEI perficere CHRISTUM dicitur Romanor. 8. vers. 34. quæ non est illa humilis & meritoria intercessio, quam in diebus carnis pro nobis præstitit, sed sublimis, & dextræ DEI, hoc est, infinitæ gloriæ congrua, non in forma servi, sed in forma DEI exhibita. Itaque terminus hujus ingressus infinitus est, & immensus; ipse scilicet thronus DEI, dextra DEI, gloria Patris, gloria quam CHRISTUS habuit, antequam mundus conderetur, gloria adorabilis. Nam ad hunc terminum progressum, in eoque constitutum JESUM omne genu venerari debet, Philip. 2, 10. 11. Quapropter porro ingressus est CHRISTUS in id, quod est intra velum, secundum Humanam naturam, unde infra cap. 10. vers. 20. dicitur, CHRISTUM nobis comparasse libertatem ingrediendi sacrarium sanguine suo, ea viva, quam dedicavit nobis recentem & vivam, per velum, hoc est, per carnem suam. Itaque cum hactenus in statu exinanitionis suam Majestatem & gloriam carne quasi velasset, nunc revelata majestate & gloria carnem circumdat, inque Φῶς ἀπρόσιτον, 1. Timoth. 6. vers. 16. collocat. Adhæc ingressus iste non est separativus, sed conjunctivus. Nam 1. τὸ ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσματος non abest à nobis, sed implet omnia, quia ut dixi gloria DEI est plenarie dominans, adeoque ea, quæ totam terram implet, Esa. 6. vers. 3. Jerem. 23. vers. 24. Est dextra DEI, quæ omnia sustinet & portat, & thronus DEI, qui per omnia se extendit, de quo supra cap. 1, 8. 2. Ingressus iste tendit ad dominium Divinum, nimirum dominium in medio inimicorum Psalm. 110. vers. 2. dominium inter sanctos & in medio fidelium, Matth. 28. vers. 20. & cap. 28. vers. 20. Itaque ingressum non constituit distantem ab iis, pro quibus ingressus est. 3. Ingressus iste constituit CHRISTUM in esse plenario perfectissimoque capitis secundum humanam naturam, Ephes. 1, 22. Fuit equidem CHRISTUS secundum Humanam etiam naturam in statu exinanitionis quoque caput Ecclesiæ, sed humiliatum & inclinatum ad potandum in via è torrente, Psalm. 110. vers. 7. Per ingressum autem hunc secundum eam factus est caput attollens se, & quidem ὑπεράνω πάντων, Ephes. 1, 21. non topice; nam hoc ad perfectionem mystici capitis non facit, sed Dominice, nimirum in eo fastigio, cui subjiciuntur omnia, Ephes. 1, 22. & quod non procul est ab unoquoque nostrum, Actor. 17, 27. Est enim dominium divinum, quod ab hoc capite perficitur: Itaque non absentiæ, sed præsentiæ, & de perfectione admirabili hujus capitis est esse in singulis membris, Ephes. 3, 17. 2. Corinth. 13, 5. 4. Ingressus iste constituit Jesum plenarie adorabilem. Super illum enim anchoram spei nostrae firmissime tutissimeque jacere debemus. Hoc vero nihil aliud est quam adorare. Est enim jactus ille anchorae actus fiducialis adorationis. At- qui adoratio non est absentis sed praesentis. Denique 5. Ingressus ille non tam attendendus est quoad vi- am, quam quoad terminum: Quoad viam separa- tivus fuit. Id enim, cum ubique potuerit in gloriam suam ingredi Christus, liberrime elegit, ut per ascen- sum aliquem ad caelos, qui via est ad ingressum, sese ab hominibus separaret quoad visibilem praesen- tiam. Neque enim τὸ ἐσώτερον τοῦ καταπετάσμα- τος magis versus hos visibiles caelos situm est, aut ver- sus illam caeli plagam, ad quam ascendens contendit, quam ubivis alibi, ubi gloriam suam infinitam & im- mensam patefacit Deus. Imo ἐσώτερον τοῦ κατα- πετάσματος intra se habuit, utpote in quo habita- vit omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter, neque Chri- stus desiit esse in forma Dei quoad actum primum & possessionem, sed quoad actum secundum, & plena- riam usurpationem. Hinc illud ἐσώτερον τοῦ κατα- πετάσματος subinde e Christo in his terris emicuit, cum visa est gloria ejus, gloria tanquam Unigeniti a Patre Johan. 1, 14. Non itaque opus habuit eme- tiri aliqua spatia aëris aut caelorum, ut ad illud ἐσώ- τερον pertingeret. Libere ergo istam separationem fecit, & imprimis eum in finem, ne si sine aliqua ejus- modi φορᾷ ab ipsis discessisset CHRISTUS, in suspi- cione spectri, quam alias conceperant per apparitio- nem momentaneam confirmarentur. At si termi- num hujus ingressus consideres, maxime penatissime- que ille conjunctivus est. Scilicet ideo per ascensum Christus separari voluit, ut per sessionem ad dextram angustius Diviniusque nobis conjungeretur, adeoque eo ἐσωτέρῳ quod hactenus sub carne velatum erat, et- iam secundum carnem uteretur, hoc est, quod Actor. 2, 36. dicitur, JESUM Dominum & CHRISTUM factum esse, Dominum scilicet absolutum, Dominum infinita potestate & Majestate dominantem, Domi- num Divina praesentia omnia complentem.

## 6:20
Verse 20.

Ὅπου πρόδρομος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν εἰσῆλθεν Ἰησοῦς) On the occasion of that veil, he gradually returns to explaining the priesthood of Christ, which matter he had deferred in order to prepare the Hebrews for attention by a reminder of their duty. In the Glossary, πρόδρομος: forerunner, precursor, Isaiah 28, verse 4, בִּכּוּרָה, the early fig, is translated as forerunner. Christ went there first, and for our good, so that he might also summon us there, just as he himself said, John 14, 3. We have, he says, not only a promise, but also an example.

Nay, not only an example, but also a merit. For he is called πρόδρομος not so much by reason of order, because in that way he was not the first to enter into that holy of holies, since both the souls of the Patriarchs and other believers entered before, and Enoch and Elijah in soul and body, as also Moses was seen in glory with Elijah in Matt. 17, as by reason of merit and causality, because as High Priest he entered the holy of holies after the offering of his body had been made and the expiation of sins, and thus he opened for us the way into it, and so he entered ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, for us, that he might prepare a way and a place for us, John 14:2, and that he might intercede for us in the holy of holies in the manner of a High Priest for the obtaining of grace and salvation for us. Theophylact notes that that ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν can be explained either because he is our forerunner, or because he prepared a way for us, or because he entered before us, that he might intercede for us in the heavens, which diverse explanations Estius also adduces. But these can be joined together most excellently.

For they do not introduce different meanings of the same words, but explain how he is a forerunner, how he entered, how as High Priest, how he entered for us, and they exhibit the ends of that entry: that he is a prodromus, not in a ministerial sense, as John was the Prodromus of CHRIST, but in a causal and axiomatic sense, whom we are certainly going to follow, because he earned this for us by his entry, and indeed he entered as the forerunner of all who enter into heaven, and thus even of the High Priests of the Old Testament themselves and the Patriarchs, who did not enter except by the virtue of the entry of this High Priest into the true holy of holies, whom they prefigured as they entered into the typical holy of holies. For JESUS CHRIST, yesterday today the same and forever, Heb. 13:8. CHRIST, says Theophylact, betook himself into heaven, but as a forerunner, that is, he showed himself as a Leader to us who are about to go to the same place. For he who is a forerunner is the leader of some who follow. Cf. Micah 2, last verse. 2. That he entered ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν (for us) partly ἱλαστικῶς (propitiatorily) by earning the entry for us, and partly also εὐκτικῶς (precatorily) by interceding for us in the heavens. For this is the twofold end of CHRIST's entry into heaven: that he might prepare a place for us by entering through his own blood, and that he might intercede with the Father for us, so that we might arrive there. Regarding the former, Theophylact says: For it was not necessary, he says, for him to enter heaven, since heaven was always open to him as GOD, but just as he took on flesh for us, so also for our sake he penetrated the inner parts of the heavens, so that he might open life to us who follow. Therefore we too are necessarily going to go where he has gone. Regarding the latter, he holds thus: For us, that is, so that he might reconcile the Father to us by his intercession, just as the High Priest once every year approached those inner parts of the temple for the sake of reconciling GOD to the people. Chrysostom handed down the connection with the preceding parts thus: He did not say anchor absolutely, but firm and stable, which is not shaken, which enters the inner parts of the veil, that is, which reaches as far as heaven. Then he also added faith, so that it might not only be hope, but also very true. For after the oath he also places another demonstration through the things themselves, namely that JESUS entered as a forerunner for us. Now a forerunner is a forerunner of some, as John was of CHRIST. And he did not say only he entered, but where the forerunner entered for us, as if to say that we too ought to arrive there. But these things are not added only to prepare an approach for the treatment which the Apostle intended concerning the Melchizedekian priesthood of CHRIST, but also to strengthen the proposed hope, and to render us more certain of salvation or entry into heaven, which Guil. Estius acknowledges against his own hypothesis concerning the uncertainty of grace: In this part, therefore, a new argument is contained for the strengthening of our hope. For if CHRIST entered into heaven as a forerunner for us, then surely the hope is certain that we are going to follow him there: either because he runs before us so that we may follow, or because he prepares a place for us, or finally because he intercedes with the Father for us so that we may arrive there. Thus also falls the argument of Mart. Becanus for the limbo of the Fathers, brought forward in the appendix to the disputation on the purgatory of Calvin, chap. I, page 43: CHRIST would not have been the forerunner of the rest if the righteous of the Old Testament had entered before him. For he is not called a forerunner ἁπλῶς (simply) by reason of time or order, but rather by reason of merit and causality, because he entered heaven by his own power, he is the Author of the entry for the rest, Micah 5, last verse, John 3:13, chap. 14:2, just as he is the firstfruits of those who sleep, 1 Cor. 15:20, even though others were raised to eternal life before him, which is evident from the example of Moses.

Κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδὲκ) After the manner of Melchizedek: or by an equal law or condition, as we said above in verse 6. This is because Melchizedek was no less a King than a Priest, and he did not have this from the law of birth, nor did he leave this right to others, in which he differed much from the descendants of Aaron.
