Such similarities do not correspond to a mirror, nor should individual circumstances be pressed: But it must be observed toward what the Divine dispensation of such ancient times tended.

Ἀρχιερεὺς γενόμενος εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) Namely, so that he may make us immune from sins by obtaining for us extraordinary powers, if we have recourse to him. See above chap. 2:17. What follows coheres with these.

We shall discuss the members of the comparison next with the Apostle. Theophylact brings these to the present passage: Or indeed it is valid for comforting them in this way. Since our High Priest dwells in the heavens, and is far superior to the High Priest of the Jews, but in a certain manner and order. For he was not instituted as High Priest according to their rite, but according to that of Melchizedek. Furthermore, he surpasses him both in place and in tabernacle, because it is higher and consists in heaven and in a testament. He also excels because he presides over greater and more perfect things, and stands in a safer place, since he is perpetual and not temporary. Moreover, the person himself is better. For he is the Firstborn from God. But that the priesthood consists in his making us immune from sins by obtaining for us extraordinary powers is akin to the Socinian heresy: since according to scripture our High Priest Christ is not such by obtaining powers for us so that we may desist from sins; but by expiating our sins through the sacrifice of his death, and by reconciling to us the remission of them and our justification through his intercession, which the Apostle is going to explain more fully later. But he is High Priest forever, says Theodoret, not because he offers victims and sacrifices; for he offered his own body once: But as an intercessor, who brings those who believe to the Father. For through him, he says, we both have access to the Father. Now indeed the Lord himself also said in the Gospels: No one comes to the Father except through me. And therefore Estius rightly observes that this part is also compared here for the strengthening of our hope. For to show that Jesus, before he entered into heaven to intercede for us with the Father, was made a High Priest not of the Aaronic order, but such a one as David foretold, and by that name offered a sacrifice of eternal power for us, so that he might have what he could present to the Father for us in heaven, just as the Apostle himself declares in the following chapters 7 and 9. How much this matter avails for the strengthening of our hope is manifest in itself. That this was also observed by Theophylact is clear from his cited commentary.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Ὅπου πρόδρομος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν εἰσῆλθεν Ἰησοῦς) Ex occa- sione veli istius paulatim redit ad explicandum Christi sacerdotium, quam rem distulerat ut Ebraeos officii sui commonitionis ad attentionem praepararet. In Glossa- rio πρόδρομος: antecursor, praecursor, Esa. 28. v. 4. בִּכּוּרָה sicus primitiva vertitur πρόδρομος. Christus eo prior ivit, idque nostro bono, ut & nos eo accerseret, sicut & ipse dixit Joh. 14, 3. Habemus, inquit, non promis- sum tantum, sed & exemplum.

Imo nec exemplum tantum, sed & meritum. Nam dicitur πρόδρομος non tam ratione ordinis, quia sic non primus fuit ingressus in sanctum illud sanctorum, quam & anima ingressi priores sint Pa- triarchae, & alii fideles; & anima & corpore E- noch, & Elias, ut & Moses Matth. 17. in gloria vi- sus cum Elia, quam ratione meriti & causalitatis, quia ut Pontifex ingressus est sanctum sanctorum, post factam oblationem corporis sui & expiatio- nem peccatorum, adeoque nobis patefecit aditum in illud, & ita ingressus est ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, pro nobis, ut aditum ac locum nobis pararet, Joh. 14, 2. utque pro nobis intercederet in sancto sanctorum more Pon- tificis pro gratia & salute nobis impetranda. Theo- phylactus notat, illud ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν explicari posse, vel quia noster praecursor est, vel quia paravit nobis aditum, vel quia ingressus prae nobis, ut intercederet pro nobis in coelis, quas diversas explicationes ad- ducit etiam Estius. Sed conjungi haec possunt optime.

Non enim diversos sensus eorundem verbo- rum inferunt, sed quomodo præcursor, quo- modo ingressus, quomodo ut Pontifex, quo- modo pro nobis ingressus est, explicant, & fines istius ingressus exhibent, quod 1. prodromus sit non sensu ministeriali, quomodo Johannes CHRISTI erat Prodromus, sed causali & axio- matico, quem & sequuturi certe sumus, quia nobis id suo ingressu promeruit, & quidem in- gressus, ut prodromus omnium ingredientium in cœlum, adeoque etiam ipsorum Pontificum Veteris Testamenti & Patriarcharum, qui non nisi virtute ingressus hujus Pontificis in verum sanctum sanctorum ingressi sunt, quem figura- runt ingredientes in sanctum sanctorum typi- cum. Nam JESUS CHRISTUS, heri hodie idem & in secula, Ebr. 13, 8. CHRISTUS in cœlum, inquit Theophylactus, se contulit, sed præcursor, id est, eodem concessuris & nobis Du- cem se præbuit. Qui enim præcursor est, nonnul- lorum est insequentium prævius. Conf. Mich. 2. vers. ult. 2. Quod ingressus ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν partim ἱλαστικῶς nobis promerendo ingressum, partim etiam εὐκτικῶς intercedendo pro nobis in cœlis. Nam hic geminus est ingressus CHRISTI in cœlum finis, ut pararet nobis locum ingredi- endo per sanguinem proprium, & ut Patrem pro nobis, quo illuc perveniamus, interpellaret. De priori Theophylactus: Non enim, inquit, e- rat illi necesse, ut cœlum ingrederetur, quippe cui semper, ut DEO, cœlum pateret, sed quemadmo- dum pro nobis carnem suscepit, sic etiam nostri ob gratiam cæli intima penetravit, ut vitam & no- bis sequentibus aperiret. Sumus ergo & nos ne- cessario, quo ille profectus est, concessuri. De po- steriori ita habet: Pro nobis, id est, ut Patrem suo intercessu nobis conciliet, sicuti & Pontifex se- mel in singulos annos facta illa templi penetralia DEUM populo conciliandi gratia adibat. Con- nexionem cum superioribus ita tradidit Chryso- stomus: Ancoram non dixit absolute, sed firmam & stabilem, quæ non labefactatur, quæ ingredi- tur interiora velaminis, id est, quæ pervadit usque ad cælum. Deinde fidem quoque subjunxit, ut non solum sit spes, sed etiam valde vera. Nam post jusjurandum ponit etiam aliam per res ipsas de- monstrationem, nempe quod præcursor pro nobis in- troüt JESUS. Præcursor autem est aliquorum præcursor, ut Johannes CHRISTI. Et non dixit solum introiit, sed ubi præcursor pro nobis introiit, utpote quod nos quoque debeamus eo pervenire. Non autem hæc adduntur tantum, ut aditum paret sibi ad tractationem, quam intendebat Apostolus de sacerdotio Melchisedeciano CHRISTI, sed et- iam ut spem propositam firmaret, certioresque nos de salute vel ingressu in cœlum redderet, quod agnoscit contra propriam hypothesin de incer- titudine gratiæ Guil. Estius: Hac igitur parte no- vum continetur argumentum spei nostræ confirman- dæ. Si enim CHRISTUS præcursor pro nobis in- troiit in cælum, utique spes certa est, nos eum illuc sequuturos esse: vel quia nos præcurrit, ut sequamur, vel quia locum nobis parat, vel denique quia Patrem pro nobis, ut illuc perveniamus, interpellat. Ruit etiam ita Mart. Becani argumentum pro limbo Patrum append. disput. de purgatorio Calv. cap. I. pag. 43. adductum: CHRISTUS non fuisset præ- cursor reliquorum, si justi Veteris Testamenti ante illum intrassent. Præcursor enim non ἁπλῶς ra- tione temporis vel ordinis dicitur, sed potius ratio- ne meriti & causalitatis, quia propria virtute in- gressus est cœlum, cæteris ingressus est Autor, Mich. 5. v. ult. Johan. 3, 13. cap. 14, 2. sicut & primi- tiæ dormientium, 1. Corinth. 15, 20. etsi alii resusci- tati sint ante ipsum ad vitam æternam, quod exem- plo Mosis constat.

Κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδὲκ) Ad modum Melchi- sedeci: vel pari lege aut conditione, ut diximus supra vers. 6. Hoc ideo, quia Melchisedech non minus Rex fuit quam Sacerdos, neque ex ortus lege id habuit, ne- que alii id jus reliquit, in quo multum differebat ab Aa- ronis posteris. Similitudines tales non ad speculum re- spondent, nec premi debent singulæ circumstantiæ: Sed observandum quo tetenderit Divina tam veterum tempo- rum dispensatio

Ἀρχιερεὺς γενόμενος εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) Nempe ut nos à peccatis immunes faciat, vires nobis eximias impe- trando, si ad ipsum recurramus. Vide supra cap. 2, 17. Cum his cohærent, quæ sequuntur.

De comparationis membris deinceps cum A- postolo dispiciemus. Theophylactus hæc præsen- ti loco affert: Vel id quidem ad hos consolandum ad modum valet. Siquidem Pontifex noster in cælis versatur, & longe præstat Judæorum Pontifici, sed modo quodam & ordine. Non enim pro illorum sed pro Melchisedeci ritu est Pontifex institutus. Hunc præterea & loco & tabernaculo superat, quod & su- perius sit & in cælo & testamento constet. Excellit etiam, quia majoribus rebus & perfectioribus præsit, & loco tutiore consistat, quippe qui perpetuus sit, & non temporarius. Quin & persona ipsa potior est. Est namque à Deo Primogenitus. Sacerdotium au- tem in eo constare, quod nos à peccatis immunes fa- ciat, vires nobis eximias impetrando, Socinianæ hæ- resi affine est: quum juxta scripturam contra non vires nobis impetrando, ut à peccatis desistamus; sed peccata nostra per mortis sacrificium expian- do, & remissionem eorum ac justificationem no- stri intercessione sua nobis conciliando Pontifex noster Christus sit, quod postmodum uberius ex- positurus est Apostolus. Est autem Pontifex in æternum, inquit Theodoretus, non quod hostias & sa- crificia offerat; suum enim corpus semel obtulit: Sed ut intercessor, qui eos, qui credunt, ad Patrem addu- cit. Per eum enim, inquit, accessum habuimus am- bo ad Patrem. Jam vero ipse quoque Dominus dixit in Evangeliis: Nemo venit ad Patrem nisi per me. Ideoque recte observat Estius, conferri hic & istam partem ad spei nostræ firmitatem. Ostendere enim Jesum, priusquam introiret in cælum, pro nobis apud Patrem intercessurus, factum fuisse Pontificem non Aaroncum, sed qualem David prenunciavit, eoque nomine sacrificium æternæ virtutis pro nobis obtulis- se, ut haberet, quod in cælo Patri pro nobis exhiberet, sicut in sequentibus ipse Apostolus declarat cap. 7. & 9. Quæ res quantum ad spem nostram corroboran- dam valeat, per se manifestum est. Quod etiam à Theophylacto observatum esse, ex adducta ejus commentatione patet.

## 7:1 Argument
CHAPTER VII.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

The Apostle now undertakes the treatment of the Priesthood of Christ according to the order of Melchisedech, instituting a brief comparison with the reason for the office, the blessing of Abraham, the tithing, the names, the origin, the beginning, and the end of days: then more prolixly regarding the tithing, from a comparison with the Levites, and his blessing of him who had the promise, proving that perfection was not obtained through the Levitical priesthood, and that being transferred, a translation of the law also took place regarding the Pontiff, who was not sprung from that but from the stock of Judah, since the law was weak, and he was constituted not without an oath, made the sponsor of a better testament, who remains a Pontiff forever, and is able to save forever those who approach God through him, such as it behooved us to have, holy and higher than the heavens, who would have no need to offer for himself, and would be perfect forever.

others were moved by Angelic Spirits, and employed for this work, and having finished it, returned to their accustomed duties, unmindful of those things which they had done under the impulse of a Divine or Angelic Spirit. But what stands in the way of this is that here in verse 2, Melchisedech is clearly distinguished from the Son of God: and thence it is deservedly refuted by Rivetus in Genesis 14, 18. 2. That he was the Holy Spirit, which was the opinion of the Hierocites according to Epiphanius book V, Theodoret book II, Heretical Fables, Augustine on Heresies, chapter 34, the author of the Questions on the Old and New Testament according to Augustine, question 109. These are to be rejected for the reason that a Priest must be taken from among men, Heb. 5, 1. For the Holy Spirit was never made man. Whence neither 3. can it be proven, that he is a certain Virtue of God existing in heavenly places, imagined to be greater than CHRIST himself according to Epiphanius, heresy V, a deprecator for the heavenly Angels according to Tertullian on Prescription, near the end. Nor 4. that he was some Angel, as Origen and Didymus the Alexandrian judged according to Jerome, epistle CXXVI. Nor 5. that he was a heavenly man prior to Adam, indeed to the πρωτοκτίστῳ light, according to Petavius, book I, on the creation of the six days, chapter IV, or a certain holy man produced by God through immediate creation, assimilated to Adam, the Son of God, Luke 3, 36, which fiction Cloppenburg reports without the author's name in his Select Syntagma of Disputations, page 653. To which the scripture Acts 17, 16 and Rom. 5, 12 openly objects. There are two more famous, and not inept, opinions; the other that he was Shem the Patriarch, which most Jews and Samaritans are said to have embraced according to Jerome in the cited place and in the Hebrew Traditions, which pleased Jonathan and the author of the Jerusalem Targum, likewise Lyranus, Tostatus, Eugubinus, Cajetan, Genebrard, Suarez, Torniellus, Vitalpando, Rungius, Pelargus, Peucerus, Brugthonus, and others. The other, that Melchisedech was indeed a man of the first rank, and a Dynast of the race of the Canaanites, proved himself to Philo, Josephus book VII, on the Jewish War, chapter VIII, Hippolytus, Eusebius of Caesarea, Emissenus, Apollinaris, Eustathius according to Jerome in his epistle to Evagrius, Epiphanius heresy LV, Theodoret question XIII on Genesis, Dionysius book I, on the Celestial Hierarchy, chapter 9, B. Hunnius in this place, B. Dorfcheus, Calvin, Pareus, Rivetus, Pererius, Del Rio, Justinianus, Ribera, Cornelius à Lapide, and others. But they leave the matter in the middle with Copres, the Scythian Abbot, B. Polycarp Lyferus, B. Gesner in Genesis 14, B. Balduinus in this place, B. Walther in the Biblical Workshop, Cloppenburg in the School of Sacrifices. That he was a Canaanite rather than Shem, the Apostle's description, that he was ἀπάτωρ καὶ ἀμήτωρ, καὶ ἀγενεαλόγητος, and other things brought forward by us to Genesis 14, 18 in our Commentary on Genesis, page 836, clearly show. Although indeed by Salem here is understood the city of the Sichemites, which occurs in Gen. 33, 18 and Jos. 3, 23, according to Jerome on Hebrew places to Evagrius, Oleastrius, Eugubinus, and Rupert; yet we admit more correctly with the three Targumim, Josephus, Hegesippus, Procopius, Cyril, Isidore, Suidas, and others commonly, that Jerusalem is understood, not being denied by Jerome himself, Vol. I, epistle XVII to Marcellus.

There are three parts: I. The comparison of Melchisedech and Christ to verse 11. II. The demonstration of the necessity of another Pontiff than the Levitical order, v. 19. III. The explanation of his Pontificate by a comparison made with the Levitical priesthood to v. 28.

PART I. The comparison of Melchisedech and Christ.

Οὗτος γὰρ ὁ Μελχισεδέκ βασιλεὺς Σαλήμ) Melchisedech is a proper name in Phoenician or Canaanite in the same form as Adonisedek, Jos. 10, 10. For it is the custom of those nations to interpose a Jod in compound names, which is evident from many examples. King of the same city, which was once called Salem, but more fully Jerusalem in Joshua. I think this Melchisedech is the man famous for justice who was called Συδύκ in Sanchuniathon's history, as Eusebius teaches us from Philo of Byblos, surely in the same way that Jerusalem is Salem. But the name was consecrated by the Phoenicians, who are also Canaanites, to the star of Jupiter, which is צדק to the Phoenicians first, then to the Rabbis; surely because that star is especially benign and peaceful. And in the name of this Prince and Priest lies a mystery, referring itself to CHRIST in an excellent sense. For he is also a King bringing us most exact justice, and the city which he founded, that is, the Church, has peace with God, and seeks peace also among men. And that Salem is Jerusalem, not only Josephus and other Hebrews testify, but also Psalm 76, 2. Nor was it remote from the journey of Abraham returning to Mamre, as learned men have shown. And so that another Salem may be distinguished from this one, it is called the Salem of the Sichemites, Gen. 33, 18.

Regarding the name of Melchisedech, it can be doubtful whether it is a proper name, or whether it is common to Kings in Phoenicia, which Cajetan and Torniellus thought with Grotius: It seems to be brought forward here more as a proper name, since it is appropriated to the person of that King who met Abraham returning from the battle. But it is more doubtful who that Melchisedech was? We dismiss the entirely incongruous opinions.

1. That he himself was the Son of GOD, which is reported by Epiphanius, haer. LXIII., and seems to have been the opinion of Ambrose, lib. I. de Abr. cap. 3; but it was defended above all by Petrus Cunaeus, lib. III. de Rep. Hebraeorum, toward which Petrus Molinaeus also inclines, lib. III. vatic. cap. 14, asserting that Melchizedek and his companions were true men, one of whom [was] by the Spirit of Christ ἱερεὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ ὑψίστου) In the Manuscript τοῦ Θεοῦ ὑψίστου, as it is also in the Greek Gen. 14, 18, where in the Hebrew [it is] כֹּהֵן לְאֵל עֶלְיוֹן. That עֶלְיוֹן, which Plautus and Sisenna rendered Alon, was the name by which the Phoenicians called the highest God. See what we have said at Mark cap. 5, 7. כֹּהֵן when added to God, is always Priest. And in ancient times [that] Kings were also Priests we have shown at the place in Genesis. But how could he be a Priest in Canaan without a people offering sacrifices? Cunaeus and Molin raise this point. Response: He could have performed the priesthood himself in his own household and among the ministers and counselors in his court, even if the people and most of the subjects had not been devoted to the true faith. Regarding what the Papists contend from Genesis about the sacrifice of Melchizedek, in order to obtain their fictitious sacrifice of the Mass, see the Commentaries on Genesis, page 838 et seqq., and in the Biblia Illustrata Veteris Testamenti on Genesis 14.

He who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings) And this is from the Greek of Genesis 14:17, 'after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings with him.' Namely, those four kings who are named in addition to Chedorlaomer at the beginning of the said chapter. 'Meeting' (συναντήσας), when he had come to meet Abraham as a sign of friendship, as in Acts 10:25. Thus, the army met the son of Vitellius in Tacitus, Histories II.

And having blessed him) Namely, by the rite of a Priest, Gen. 14:19. Otherwise, the word εὐλογεῖν (to bless) is of quite broad application, but here it is to be understood as in Numbers 6:22 and Sirach 36:9.

I. epist. XVII. ad Marcell.

Partes tres sunt: I. Comparatio Melchisedeci & Christi ad vers. 11. II. Necessitatis Pontificis alterius quam Levitici ordinis demonstratio, v. 19. III. Pontificatus ejus explicatio collatione cum Levitico sacerdotio facta ad v. 28.

PARS I. Melchisedeci & Christi comparatio.

Οὗτος γὰρ ὁ Μελχισεδέκ βασιλεὺς Σαλήμ) Melchi- sedech nomen proprium in Phœnice sive Cananæa pa- ri forma qua Adonisedek, Jos. 10, 10. Nam inter- ponere Jod nominibus compositis mos est illarum gentium, quod multis exemplis patet. Rex ejus- dem urbis, quæ Salem dicta olim, apud Josuam vero plenius Jerusalem. Puto hunc Melchisedecum virum justitiæ celebrem eum esse, qui in Sanchuniathonis hi- storia dicebatur Συδύκ, ut ex Philone Byblio nos docet Eusebius, nimirum pari modo, quo Jerusalem est Salem. Huic autem nomen à Phœnicibus, qui & Cananæi, con- secratum in Jovis stellam, qui צדק Phœnicibus primum, deinde Rabbinis; nimirum quod id sidus imprimis sit benignum & pacificum. Et in nomine hujus & Princi- pis & Sacerdotis latet mysterium, ad CHRISTUM exi- mio sensu se referens. Nam & is Rex est exactissimam nobis justitiam afferens, & civitas, quam condidit, id est, Ecclesia, pacem habet cum Deo, pacem & inter homines quærit. Salem autem esse Jerusalem, non tan- tum Josephus & Ebræi testantur alii, sed & Psal. 76, 2. Nec ea remota fuit ab itinere Abrahami regredientis Mambrene, ut viri eruditi ostenderunt. Et ut ab hac distinguatur Salem altera, dicitur Salem Sicimorum, Gen. 33, 18.

De Melchisedeci nomine dubium esse potest, an sit proprium, an sit Regibus in Phœnice com- mune, quod cum Grotio Cajetanus & Torniellus putarunt: Ut proprium id magis hic adduci vi- detur, quum personæ Regis istius, qui Abraha- mo obviavit è pugna reduci, approprietur. Ma- gis autem dubium quisnam fuerit ille Melchise- dech? Mittimus opiniones prorsus incongruas

Ebræorum, in quam etiam inclinat Petrus Molineus libr. III. va- tic. cap. 14. asserens Melchisedecum ejusque comites veros fuisse homines, quorum unus à Spiritu Chri- ἱερεὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ ὑψίστου) In Manuscripto τοῦ Θεοῦ ὑψίστου, quomodo est & in Græco Genes. 14, 18. ubi in Ebræo כֹּהֵן לְאֵל עֶלְיוֹן. Illud עֶלְיוֹן, quod Plautus & Sisen- na extulere Alon, erat nomen, quo Phœnices appella- bant summum Deum. Vide quæ diximus ad Marcum cap. 5, 7. כֹּהֵן cum additur Dei, semper est Sacerdos. Sacerdotio ipsum fungi po- tuisse in familia sua & penes Ministros ac Con- siliarios in aula, etiamsi populus & subditi ple- rique haud addicti fidei verae fuissent. Testam. ad Genes. 14.

Ὁ συναντήσας Ἀβραὰμ ὑποστρέφοντι ἀπὸ τῆς κοπῆς τῶν βασιλέων) Et hoc ex Graeco Genes. 14, 17. μετὰ τὸ ὑποστρέψαι αὐ- τὸν ἀπὸ τῆς κοπῆς τῆ Χοδολλαγομὸρ καὶ τῶν βασιλέων μετ' αὐτὂ. Sic exercitus occurrit Vitellii filio apud Tacitum historiarum II.

Καὶ εὐλογήσας αὐτὸν) Ritu nempe Sacerdotis Gen. 14, 19. Est alioqui verbum εὐλογεῖν satis late patens, sed hic intelligendum ut Nu- mer. 6, 22. Sirac. 36, 9.

## 7:2
Verse 2.

To whom also Abraham apportioned a tenth of all) Namely, in honor of the Most High God, whom both Melchizedek and Abraham worshipped, Gen. 14:20. It was a most ancient custom of all nations to give a tenth of the spoils to God. We noted this in Book III of 'On the Law of War and Peace,' VI. 1.

By 'all things' (τὰ πάντα) are understood all the spoils which the Patriarch had taken from the victory reported over those Kings. For here Melchizedek distributed the spoils, he did not offer them against the Patriarch, as the Rabbis maintain; since Abraham professes with an oath that he would accept nothing of the entire spoil from the King of Sodom. How, therefore, would he have accepted it from Melchizedek? Finally, we have here a witness, the Apostle, who is above all exception, that the Patriarch gave tithes to Melchizedek, from which Cloppenburg, in Syntagm. select. exerc. page 663, gathers the kind and material of the sacrifice which Melchizedek offered for Abraham. For if Abraham, and the Levites in his loins, gave Melchizedek tithes of all (מכל מעשר), Gen. 14:20, just as their brothers, the Levites, who once obtained the priesthood by law, were given tithes, Heb. 7:5, it follows from the law, Leviticus 28:32. That Melchizedek also, as Priest of the Most High, received from the hands of Abraham tithes of oxen, sheep, and goats, from which he offered to God a sacrifice both Eucharistic and Propitiatory, in the divine acceptance of which he had the sacrament of the blessing with which he, Melchizedek, Priest of the Most High, blessed him. Thus, Melchizedek, contrary to what the Papists contend, was greater than the Levitical Priests, not in the efficacy, kind, or nature of the blessing of his gifts and sacrifices—because he wished for salvation, he did not confer it, just as they did in Numbers 6:23, 27—but only in the degree of dignity, because, in the office of a Royal Priest, he offered to God for the Patriarch Abraham the gifts brought to him, and by his ministry of blessing, he vowed to the descendants of Abraham, the Levites, that dignity which they obtained when they came forth from the loins of Abraham.

First, being interpreted King of righteousness) An explanation of the name Melchizedek. The genitive, however, stands for an adjective. And so Josephus explains it as 'a just King'.

And then also King of Salem, which is King of peace) An explanation of the name by which the city ruled by him was called. And note that Christ both gave a certain specimen of his kingdom at that time and began his Priesthood at the same city, Matt. 21:3 and 10; Luke 13:33.

It is more emphatic in Greek concerning the King of righteousness, just as also the King of peace, because he brings in, in the antitype, not just a just and peaceful one, but the Author of righteousness and peace. The Lord is our righteousness, Jer. 23:6; our peace, Eph. 2. Therefore, however much Melchizedek is only called King of righteousness and peace, because Christ is a student and lover of righteousness and peace: yet when those names are applied to him, he is implied to be the Author of righteousness and peace. Furthermore, he says 'first' (πρῶτον) because that is the first member of the comparison, consisting in the name, and 'then' (ἔπειτα) follows. A different view was held by Cloppenburg, l.c. page 660, who wishes the Apostle here to begin the interpretation (ἑρμηνείαν) of the figure, that Christ himself is Melchizedek 'being interpreted' (ἑρμηνευόμενος), and 'made like unto the Son of God' (ἀφωμοιωμένος τῷ Υἱῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ), that is, having attained his true interpretation and configuration and solid expression in the person of the incarnate Son of God: in short, Melchizedek 'being allegorized' (ἀλληγορούμενος). To whom, however, the blessed Dorscheus rightly responds: 1. That 'being interpreted' (ἑρμηνευόμενος) cannot be any other subject than that which was established in verse 1 and at the beginning of the second. But that is Melchizedek 'being recorded' (ἱστορούμενος). 2. He is 'being interpreted' who was to be interpreted, from whom the mystery was to be drawn, in whom it was to be shadowed forth. But that is none other than Melchizedek 'being recorded'. 3. If all those things which are said in verses 2 and 3 pertain immediately to Christ, where then are they exhibited in the type, and are these antitypical? 4. How inconvenient, nay, how unskillfully it is said that Christ is 'made like unto the Son of God' (ἀφωμοιωμένον τῷ Υἱῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ). Does that not still remain, that Christ is said to be so assimilated to himself? And how absurdly it sounds if, with Cloppenburg, we say that Christ has attained his configuration and solid expression in the person of the incarnate Son of God. 5. Do not verses 4, 5, et seqq. pertain to Melchizedek 'being recorded'? How, therefore, would verses 2 and 3 not refer to the same?

Vers. 2.

ᾯ καὶ δεκάτην ἀπὸ πάντων ἐμέρισεν Ἀβραὰμ) Nempe in honorem Dei summi, quem & Melchisedech & Abraham colebant, Genes. 14, 20. Vetustissimus mos fuit omnium gentium de praeda decimam Deo dare. Notavimus id in libro III. de jure belli & pacis VI. 1.

Per τὰ πάντα intelliguntur spolia omnia, quae ex victoria ab illis Regibus reportata cepe- rat Patriarcha. Hic enim distribuit spolia non contra Patriarchae Melchisedecus ea obtulit, ut Rabbini statuunt: quum juramento profitea- tur Abraham, se de universa praeda a Rege Sodo- morum nihil accepturum. Quomodo ergo ac- cepisset a Melchisedeco? Denique testem hic habemus, omni exceptione superiorem Aposto- lum,quodPatriarcha decimas dederitMelchisede- cho, unde Cloppenburgius in Syntagm.select.exerc. pag. 663. colligit, sacrificii, quod Melchisedechus pro Abrahamo obtulit, genus & materiam. Nam si Abrahamus & in ipsius lumbis Levitae dederunt Melchisedecho decimas omnium מכל מעשר, Genes. 14, 20. pariter ut ex lege olim Levitis sacerdotium sortitis decimas dederunt fratres ipsorum, Ebr. 7, 5. consequens est ex lege, Levit. 28, 32. Melchisede- chum etiam tanquam Sacerdotem Altissimi acce- pisse ex manibus Abrahami decimas boum, ovium. & caprarum, ex quibus Deo obtulit sacrificium & Eucharisticum simul & Propitiatorium, in cujus acceptatione Divina haberet benedictionis, qua ipse Melchisedechus Sacerdos Altissimi benedixit, sacra- mentum. Sic Melchisedechus secus quam conten- dunt Pontificii, Leviticis Sacerdotibus major fuit donorum & sacrificiorum nec efficacia, nec genere, nec benedictionis natura, quia salutem vovit, non contulit: pariter ut illi Numer. 6, 23.27. sed gradu tantum dignitatis, quod pro munere Sacerdotis Rega- lis pro Abrahamo Patriarcha dona ad se adducta Deo obtulerit, & sua benedictionis ministerio vove- rit Abrahami posteris Levitis, illam, quam egressi ex lumbis Abrahami obtinuerunt, dignitatem.

Πρῶτον μὲν ἑρμηνευόμενος βασιλεὺς δικαιοσύνης) Ex- plicatio nominis Melchisedech. Genitivus autem est pro Adjectivo. Itaque Regem justum explicat Jose- phus.

Ἔπειτα δὲ καὶ βασιλεὺς Σαλὴμ ὅ ἐστι βασιλεὺς εἰρήνης) Explicatio nominis, quo urbs ab ipso regnata vocabatur. Et nota Christum tum regni sui specimen quoddam dedisse, tum Sacerdotium inchoasse apud eandem urbem Matth. 21, 3. & 10. Luc. 13, 33.

Ἐμφατικώτερον est Graecum de Rege justitiae, quemadmodum & Rex pacis, quia non justum tantum & pacificum, in antitypo infert, sed justitiæ & pacis Autorem. Est Dominus justitia nostra, Jerem. 23, 6. pax nostra, Ephes. 2. Utut ergo Mel- chisedech tantum Rex justitiæ & pacis dicatur, quod justitiæ & pacis studiosus & amator Chri- stus: Tamen cum ei applicantur illa nomina, ju- stitiæ & pacis Autor esse innuitur. Porro πρῶ- τον dicit, quod primum id sit comparationis mem- brum, consistens in nomine, ac sequitur ἔπειτα. Aliud visum Cloppenburgio l. c. pag. 660. qui vult Apostolum hic ordiri ἑρμηνείαν seu interpretationem figuræ, quod Christus ipse sit Melchisedech ἑρμηνευό- μενος, & ἀφωμοιωμένος τῷ Υἱῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ, id est, veram interpretationem & effigurationem suam atq; expres- sionem solidam assequutus in persona Filii Dei incar- nati: Breviter Melchisedechus ἀλληγορούμενος. Cui vero recte respondit B. Dorscheus: 1. ἑρμηνευόμε- νος ille non aliud subjectum esse potest, quam quod v. 1. & initio secundi constitutum est. At illud est Mel- chisedecus ἱστορούμενος. 2. Is est ἑρμηνευόμενος, qui erat interpretandus, ex quo mysterium eruendum, in quo illud adumbrandum. At is non est alius, quam Melchisedecus ἱστορούμενος. 3. Si ad Chri- stum ista omnia immediate pertinent, quæ v. 2. 3. di- cuntur, ubi ergo in typo sunt exhibita, hi sunt antity- pica? 4. Quam incommode imo imperite dicitur, Christum esse ἀφωμοιωμένον τῷ Υἱῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ. Nonne manet adhuc illud, Christum sibipsi ita assimilatum dici? Et quam absurde sonat, si cum Cloppenburgio dicimus, Christum effigurationem suam atque expres- sionem solidam assecutum esse in persona Filii Dei in- carnati. 5. Nonne v. 4. 5. seqq. ad Melchisede- cum ἱστορούμενον pertinent? Quomodo itaque 2. & 3. ad eundem non referretur.

## 7:3
Verse 3.

Ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος) This last term explains the former ones. For his lineage is not recounted by Moses, nor indeed his father or mother, from which you may see how far he differs from the Levitical priests, who were required to be of the line of Aaron by their father, and of the tribe of Israel by their mother, Levit. 18, 1. chap. 21, 14. And for this reason, the registers of their lineage were wont to be observed most diligently, as can be seen in Ezra 2, 62. Philo on the Decalogue: 'For the lineage of a priest is examined with all precision, whether it is blameless.' The Syriac translator does not do badly here, whose father and mother are not written in the genealogy. Thus Seneca, epistle 108, when he had said that there were two Roman kings, of whom one had no father, the other no mother, explaining the same thing, says that it is doubted about the mother of Servius: that Ancus is said to have no father. Among very many nations, the maternal lineage was also regarded in priests. Porphyry on the Brahmins: 'They are of one lineage. For they all descend from one father and one mother.' Ion in the tragedy of Euripides: — — 'as one who is motherless and fatherless, I serve the temples of Phoebus that reared me.' Showing that this is contrary to custom. Thus among the Athenians, the King of the sacred rites was required to be from a mother who was a virgin and a citizen, as we showed at the cited passage of Leviticus 21. In the Controversiae of Seneca, the law is: 'Let the priest be chaste from the chaste, pure from the pure.' Where you also have this: 'If your mother had been a prostitute, it would harm you.' It was objected to Hyrcanus that his mother had been captured in war: for suspicion makes it so that such persons are hardly believed to be pure on account of their servile fortune. But Melchizedek is introduced with no lineage, with no mention of parents (which Moses is nevertheless accustomed to employ in very many other cases), no otherwise than as if he had fallen from heaven, in which there is no doubt that a mystery lay hidden. Philo on the Allegories: 'And God has made Melchizedek king of peace, for this is what it is interpreted, a priest of Himself, having prefigured no work of his, but having fashioned such a king and priest as is worthy of His own priesthood first.' He says then that through Melchizedek is figured the true Logos, which has neither the Idea as a father, nor perception as a mother, but draws its origin from God Himself. Thus the ancients often draw an argument from that which is not said in the text. Thus Philo in the book 'The Worse Attacks the Better,' from the fact that the death of Cain is not found written, deduces that folly is an immortal evil.

& on the contrary, that the mind pleases before works, from the fact that Noah is said to have pleased God before the mention of works. Moreover, there is the verb γενεαλογεῖν, whence this name ἀγενεαλόγητος is good Greek, and it is constructed with the Accusative in Herodotus and Plutarch.

These things are rightly explained regarding the type and history, because neither the father nor the mother of Melchizedek is mentioned, nor can a genealogy be brought forward, of which Theophylact also warned. But as for the mystery, in the antitype Christ, Philo's allegory does not deserve approval. Indeed, Christ is called ἀπάτωρ, because he was without a father by reason of his human nature, ἀμήτωρ because he was without a mother by reason of his divine nature: ἀγενεαλόγητος, because Christ's generation cannot be comprehended by the divine mind, nor known by human nature, and neither can be sufficiently expressed or described. Theodoret has rightly executed these points: Divine scripture recounted the genealogy of Abraham and many others, both of those who preceded him and of those who followed afterwards, and his father, and grandfather, and great-grandfather, and his ancestors. Furthermore, it is also added that he was so many years old when he begat: and again when he was so many years old, he died. But divine scripture did not teach either the father or the lineage of Melchizedek: and neither how long he lived, nor when he ever reached the end of his life. For that reason, he is without father, without mother, and without genealogy, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life. For divine scripture taught us none of these things. But the Lord Christ has each of these things by nature and in truth. For he is without mother, as God; for he is begotten from the Father alone. Without father, however, as man, for he was brought forth through birth from a virgin mother alone. He is without genealogy, as God. For he who is begotten from the unbegotten Father has no need of a genealogy. But it is fabulous, what is reported in Epiphanius, Haer. LI, that the father of Melchizedek was Eraclas, and his mother Astharoth or Asteria.

Having neither beginning of days nor end of life) Namely, in the history of Moses. That was done so that he might be more apt for prefiguring Christ. For otherwise, Moses, when dealing with great men, is accustomed to add when they were born and when they died.

The mystery which he prefigured is not that Christ did not have a beginning and an end by reason of his priesthood, as Enjedinus contends, and also Socinus with his followers, but by reason of his person, whose eternity is designated from the side before by the negation of a beginning, and from the side after by the negation of an end, just as Thales called God eternal, ὁ μή τ᾽ἀρχὴν ἔχων, μή τε τέλος. Certainly, to have parents, and lineage, and a beginning, and an end of days belongs to the life of a man or a person, not of an office or priesthood. But see the refuted gloss of the Socinians in the Apodixis on the preexistence of the Son of God. Theodoret says, he did not have a beginning of days, for his generation is eternal, nor does he have an end of life. For he has an immortal nature. And for that reason, he did not liken the Lord Christ to Melchizedek, but Melchizedek to Christ. For the former is the type of the latter. But the latter is the truth of the type. But in the priesthood, Melchizedek did not imitate the Lord Christ; but the Lord Christ is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. For it is the part of a man to perform a priesthood. But it is the part of God to receive those things which are offered. Yet, the only-begotten Son of God, having been made man, also became our Priest according to the order of Melchizedek, not with any accession of Divinity, but with the Divine dignity hidden, and humility assumed for our salvation. Thus he is called a lamb, and sin, and a curse, and the way, and the gate, and many things of that kind.

But made like unto the Son of God, he abideth a priest continually) That is, he comes onto the stage in such a way that his exit does not appear, just as if his priesthood were perpetual, such as Christ's is. Just as things that are narrated are said to be done by the one who narrates, as we saw above in chapter I. 6. So what is not narrated is posited as if it were not. It can be added that Melchizedek was a priest in perpetuity, that is, as long as the worship of the true God remained in Phoenicia.

We do not disapprove of these Grotius-like things. Theodoret has this to say about them: Furthermore, he said of Melchizedek that he remains a priest forever, because he did not transmit the priesthood to his sons, as Aaron, Eleazar, and Phinehas did. For he who transmits this inheritance to another seems in a way to be deprived of the dignity, since another exercises it. It also has another understanding. For just as we call Moses not only a legislator, but also the law itself: So also we name Melchizedek both the person and the thing itself, namely the priesthood. But the Lord Christ possesses it himself, who has life that will never end. But he notably says made like unto the Son of God, and not that Christ was compared to Melchizedek, which we observed a little earlier from Theodoret. For in reality, Melchizedek had a father and mother, a genealogy, and a beginning and end of life. But these things are said about him, both because scripture makes no mention of them, and also and especially because all these things truly belong to Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος) Postremum hoc priora explicat. Neque enim genus ejus à Mose re- censetur, ac ne Pater quidem aut mater, unde videas, quantum hic distet à Leviticis Sacerdotibus, qui Patre debebant esse Aaronide, matre autem Israelitide, Levit. 18, 1. cap. 21, 14. & ob id diligentissime observari solebant census generis ipsorum, ut videre est Esdræ 2, 62. Phi- lo ad Decalogum: Ἱερέως γὰρ τὸ γένος ἐξετάζεται μετὰ πά- σης ἀκριβείας εἰ ἀνεπίληπτον. Syrus hic non male, cujus nec Pater nec mater scripti sunt in genealogia. Sic Seneca epist. CVIII. cum dixisset duos Romanos Reges esse, quo- rum alter Patrem non habeat, alter matrem, idipsum explicans dicit de Servii matre dubitari: Anci Patrem nullum dici. Plurimas apud gentes etiam maternum genus in Sacerdotibus spectabatur. Porphyrius de Brachmantibus: Ἑνός εἰσι γένους. Ἐξ ἑνὸς γὰρ καὶ πατρὸς καὶ μιᾶς μητρὸς πάντες κατάγουσι. Jon. in Tragœdia Euripidis: — — ὡς καὶ ἀμήτωρ Ἀπάτωρ τε γεγὼς τοῖς θρέψαιτας Φοίβου ναοῖς θεραπεύω. Ostendens hoc esse contra morem. Sic apud Atheni- enses Rex sacrorum causa ex matre debebat esse virgi- ne ac cive, ut ad dictum Levitici 21. locum ostendimus. In controversiis Seneca: lex est: Sacerdos casta è castu, pura è puris sit. Ubi & hoc habes: Si mater tua pristi- iisset, tibi noceret. Hircano objectum fuit matrem ejus bello captam fuisse: Suspicio enim facit, ut tales vix puræ credantur ob fortunam servilem. At Melchisedecus nullo genere, nulla parentum mentione (quam tamen in aliis plurimis adhibere solet Moses) non aliter quam quasi de cælo delapsus introducitur, in quo haud du- bium, quin latuerit mysterium. Philo de Allegoriis: Καὶ Μελχισεδὲκ βασιλέα τε τῆς εἰρήνης, τοῦτο γὰρ ἑρμηνεύε- ται, ἱερέα ἑαυτοῦ πεποίηκεν ὁ Θεὸς, οὐδὲν ἔργον αὐτοῦ προδια- τυπώσας, ἀλλὰ τοιοῦτον ἐργασάμενος βασιλέα καὶ ἱερέα οἷον καὶ ἱερασύνης ἄξιον τῆς ἑαυτοῦ πρῶτον. Dicit deinde per Mel- chisedecum figurari τὸν ἀληθῆ λόγον, qui neque ἰδέα ha- beat patrem, neque matrem τὴν αἴσθησιν, sed à Deo ipso trahat originem. Ita sæpe veteres argumentum tra- hunt ab eo, quod in textu non dicitur. Sic Philo libro pejorem insidiari meliori, ex eo, quod Caini mors scripta non inveniatur, deducit κακὸν ἀθάνατον εἶναι ἀφροσύνην,

& contra, animum placere ante opera, ex eo, quod Noe Deo placuisse dicitur ante operum mentionem. Est au- tem verbum γενεαλογεῖν, unde hoc nomen ἀγενεαλόγητος bene Græcum, & construitur cum Accusativo apud Hero- dotum & Plutarchum.

Recte hæc quoad typum & historiam explican- tur, quod MelchisedecinecPaternecmater com- memoratur, nec genealògia afferri potest, quo de Theophylactus etiam monuit. Sed quod ad myste- rium, in antitypo Christo, Philonis allegoria calcu- lum non meretur. Imo ἀπάτωρ dicitur Christus, quia sine Patre fuit ratione Humanæ naturæ, ἀμή- τωρ quia sine matre ratione Divinæ naturæ : Ἀγενεα- λόγητος, quia Christi generatio Divina mente non potest comprehendi, neque humana per naturam cognosci, neutra satis efferri vel describi potest. Recte hæc exequutus est Theodoretus : Abrahæ & multorum aliorum genealogiam Divina recensuit scri- ptura, tam eorum, qui illum præcesserunt, quam eorum, qui postea sequuti sunt, & illius Patrem, & avum, & abavum, & illius majores. Porro autem adjecti etiam, quod tot annos natus genuit: & rur- sus cum tot annos natus esset, mortuus esset. Mel- chisedeci autem nec Patrem nec genus docuit divina scriptura: & neque quanto tempore vixerit, neque quando unquam vitæ finem ceperit. Ea ergo ra- tione est sine patre, sine matre, & sine genealogia, neque initium dierum, neque vitæ finem habens. Di- vina enim scriptura nihil horum nos docuit. Do- minus autem Christus natura & vere habet unum- quodque horum. Est enim sine matre, ut Deus; est enim ex solo Patre genitus. Sine Patre autem, ut homo, ex sola enim matre virgine per partum edi- tus est. Sine genealogia est, ut Deus. Non enim opus habet genealogia, qui est ex ingenito Patre genitus. Fabulosum autem est, quod apud Epiphanium hær. LI. refertur, Patrem Melchisedeci fuisse Era- clam, matrem Astharoth sive Asteriam.

Μή τε ἀρχὴν ἡμερῶν μή τε ζωῆς τέλος ἔχων) Nem- pe in Mosis historia. Id factum, ut eo aptior esset ad fi- gurandum Christum. Solent enim alioqui Moses de viris magnis agens addere, quando nati, quando mor- tui sint.

Mysterium, quod figuravit, est, non quod Chri- stus ratione sacerdotii initium ac finem non habue- rit, ut Enjedinus contendit, nec non Socinus cum assectis, sed ratione personæ, cujus æternitas à par- te ante per negationem initii, à parte post per ne- gationem finis designatur, uti Thales Deum æter- num dixit, ὁ μή τ᾽ἀρχὴν ἔχων, μή τε τέλος. Sa- ne parentes habere, & genus & initium, & finem dierum vitæ non officii vel sacerdotii est, sed ho- minis vel personæ. Sed Socinianorum glossam profligatam vide Apodix. de præexistens. Filii Dei. Non habuit, inquit, Theodoretus, initium dierum, est enim æterna generatio, neque vitæ habet finem. Immortalem enim habet naturam. Eaque de causa non Dominum Christum, sed Melchisedech Christo as- similavit. Ille enim est hujus typus. Hic vero typive- ritas. In sacerdotio autem non Melchisedech Chri- stum Dominum imitatus est; sed Dominus Christus Sacerdos in æternum secundum ordinem Melchise- dech. Est enim hominis fungi sacerdotio. Dei ve- ro ea, quæ offeruntur, suscipere. Sed tamen homo factus unigenitus Dei Filius, Sacerdos etiam noster factus est secundum ordinem Melchisedech, non cum aliqua Divinitatis accessione, sed Divina celata digni- tate, & pro salute nostra suscepta humilitate. Ita agnus vocatus est & peccatum, & maledictum, & via, & porta, & ejusmodi plurima.

Ἀφωμοιωμένος δὲ τῷ Υἱῷ τῦ Θεῦ μένει ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸ διη- rentes) Id est, ita in scenam venit, ut exitus ejus non appareat, plane quasi sacerdotium ejus esset perpetuum, quale est Christi. Sicut quæ narrantur, dicuntur fieri ab eo qui narrat, ut vidimus supra cap. I. 6. Ita quod non narratur ponitur quasi non sit. Addi potest Melchisede- chum fuisse Sacerdotem in perpetuum, id est, quamdiu veri Dei cultus in Phœnice mansit.

Non improbamus hæc Grotiana. Theodore- tus de his ita habet: Porro autem dixit de Mel- chisedech, quod manet Sacerdos in æternum, quo- niam ad filios non transmisit sacerdotium, quemad- modum Aaron, Eleazar & Pinehas. Qui hanc enim hæreditatem ad alium transmittit, videtur quodam- modo privari dignitate, cum eam alius exerceat. A- liam quoque habet intelligentiam. Quemadmodum enim Mosen non solum appellamus legislatorem, sed etiam ipsam legem: Ita etiam Melchisedech nomina- mus & personam, & rem ipsam, nempe sacerdotium. Ipsum autem habet Christus Dominus, qui vitam ha- bet, quæ nunquam desinet. Notanter autem dicit ἀφωμοιωμένῳ τῷ Υἱῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ, non vero quod Christus sit comparatus Melchisedeco, quod pau- lo ante è Theodoreto observavimus. Re ipsa enim habuit Melchisedecus Patrem & matrem, genea- logiam, vitæ principium & finem. Dicuntur au- tem ista de eo, tum quia scriptura non facit eorum mentionem, tum etiam & præcipue quidem, quia Christo hæc omnia revera competunt.

## 7:4
Ver. 4.

But consider how great this man is) of what great dignity.

To whom also Abraham the Patriarch [gave] a tenth from the spoils) And [it is to be] referred to Abraham. Not only others, but that great Abraham, the author of the Jewish race, gave him tithes. And this word ἀκροθινίων is good Greek: but it is a genitive of explanation or in place of apposition. For the very part of the booty which is dedicated to God is called ἀκροθίνια by Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophon, and in the Phoenissae by Euripides. Πατριάρχαι are called both the progenitors of tribes and of families, as can be seen in 1 Chron. 9:9, ch. 22:3, ch. 27:22, 2 Chron. 19:8, ch. 23:20, ch. 26:12, Acts 2:29, ch. 7:8, 9. But with much more justice is Abraham called by that name, from whom all those tribes and families drew their origin. Πατριὰ is most frequently family, but we showed at Matt. 1:16 that it is also taken for a tribe. The writer here rightly understood נתן ἔδωκεν not of Melchizedek, but of Abraham, as also the LXX, Philo, and Josephus. The Syriac for ἔδωκεν has פרש, he separated, which word is proper to sacred things. Thus Num. 8:16, for the Hebrew נתנם, he gave, the Chaldean has אפרשא.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Θεωρεῖτε δὲ πηλίκος οὗτος) quantæ dignitatis.

Ὧ καὶ δεκάτην Ἀβραὰμ ἐκ τῶν ἀκροθινίων ὁ Πατριάρχης) Καὶ referendum ad Ἀβραὰμ. Non alii tantum, sed ma- gnus ille Abraham autor Judaici generis, illi decimas de- dit. Et hæc vox ἀκροθινίων bene Græca est: Sed Geni- tivus est ἐξηγητικὸς sive vice oppositionis. Nam ipsa pars prædæ, quæ Deo dicatur, vocatur ἀκροθίνια Herodoto, Thucydidi, Xenophonti & in Phœnissis Euripidi. Πα- τριάρχαι dicuntur & tribuum progenitores & familiarum, ut videre est 1. Paral. IX. v. 9. cap. XXII. vers. 3. c. XXVII. vers. 22. 2. Paral. XIX. v. 8. cap. XXIII. 20. c. XXVI. v. 12. Actor. II. v. 29. c. VII. v. 8. 9. Multo autem justius eo no- mine vocatur Abraham, undẹ omnes istæ tribus & fami- liæ ortum trahebant. Πατριὰ frequentissime est fami- lia, sed & pro tribu sumi ostendimus ad Matth. I, v. 16. Recte autem hic Scriptor נתן ἔδωκεν intellexit non de Melchisedeco, sed de Abrahamo, ut & LXX. Philo & Jo- sephus. Syrus pro ἔδωκεν habet פרש separavit, quæ vox sacris propria. Sic Num. VIII. v. 16. pro Ebræo נתנם dat Chaldæus habet אפרשא.

## 7:5
Verse 5.

And those indeed from the sons of Levi who receive the priesthood) λαμβάνοντες is placed in such a way as λαμβάνει above in verse 5. 4. All the priests were from Aaron, Aaron from Levi.

They have a commandment) That is, they have this right, משפט, Mark 10:5.

To tithe the people) That is, to exact tithes from their own people: עשר, which is translated as δεκατῶν and ἀποδεκατοῦν, is often referred to things, Gen. 28:22, Deut. 14:22, ch. 26:12, 1 Sam. 8:15, 17. But here it is referred to those whose things they are, as also presently in verse 6. The Latins call ἀποδεκατῶν 'edecumare', as it is in the Glossary.

According to the law) Numbers 18:24 and following, where you see that the Levites received tithes from private individuals, but the priests from the Levites themselves. Therefore, in a double way the Aaronic priests tithed their own people: first, because that very thing which was the Levites' had come from the people, and secondly, because the Levites were also a part of the people.

The comparison in the collation of excellence stands thus: Melchizedek was more excellent than Abraham, to whom as a priest he gave a blessing, and from whom he received tithes. Therefore he is also more excellent than the Levites, who descend from Abraham, and in the loins of Abraham were tithed by Melchizedek. Wherefore CHRIST, who is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, is altogether more worthy than the Levitical priests, from whom also upon Abraham and his spiritual children every blessing descends. When he had accommodated the figure to the truth, says Theophylactus, that is, Melchisedec now finally trusting in Christ, he argues that the figure of Melchisedec himself stood out as more illustrious than the Jewish priests, and not only to them, because he even surpassed the Patriarch Abraham himself. If, therefore, the figure so greatly precedes the others, the High Priest Christ will by far and incomparably precede them in dignity, who is signified through that figure. Nor can it be said (so Theophylactus continues) that Abraham had bestowed these gifts and spoils upon Melchisedec because he had campaigned together with him, and for that reason had paid him the rewards of this military service, but he brought gifts and tithes to him while he was staying at home, and therefore he said above that Melchisedec had gone to meet Abraham. The Vulgate rendered Ἐκ τῶν ἀκροθινίων as 'from the best,' as if it were ἐξ' ἀκροθηνιῶν. The Greek properly signifies from spoils or booty taken from an enemy, in which sense it is also read in Philostratus the Sophist. The Syriac translates it as tithes and first-fruits, Theophylactus as better and more honorable spoils. B. Dorscheus here observes in passing an argument, which he calls evident, that Melchisedec was not Sem. For in respect to him, Abraham could not appear so great, nor be called a Patriarch. For what wonder is it for a great-grandson, if we may say so, to submit himself to the eighth [generation], and to venerate him with the offering of tithes? But it is more to be wondered at that Abraham should offer tithes to a foreign King and Priest, placed outside his own lineage, in which he himself had been the Patriarch.

That is, their brothers, even though they have come out of the loins of Abraham. And this is also of some dignity, to receive tithes not from outsiders, but from one's own countrymen. He prepares this so that he may subsequently infer the greater dignity of Melchisedec. Those who are born from someone's seed are said by the Hebrews to come out of the loins, Gen. 35:11, 2 Chron. 6:9. The cause of this locution is known to those more advanced.

The sense is, just as the Levites are more worthy than other Israelites, who according to the law receive tithes from them: so Melchisedec was more worthy than Abraham and all the Levites descending from him, because as a Priest he received tithes from him. The argument from the brothers, however, holds thus: The Levitical priests receive tithes from the remaining Israelites, the descendants of Abraham, and their right does not extend beyond them. But Melchisedec, although a foreigner, received tithes from the Patriarch Abraham and the author of the entire Levitical race. For in what way, says Theophylactus, would Abraham have brought tithes to a stranger, unless the others had held him in veneration? If Melchisedec, therefore, who presents the figure of Christ, seems to excel in dignity even Abraham, then by a long interval Christ himself, who is the true High Priest, will excel the priests instituted by the law.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Καὶ οἱ μὲν ἐκ τῶν υἱῶν Λευὶ τὴν ἱερατείαν λαμβάνοντες) λαμβάνοντες ita positum, ut λαμβάνει supra v. 5. 4. Omnes Sacerdotes erant ex Aarone, Aaron ex Levi.

Ἐντολὴν ἔχουσι) Id est, jus hoc habent משפט Mar- ci X. vers. 5.

Ἀποδεκατοῦν τὸν λαὸν) Id est, à popularibus suis de- cimas exigendi: עשר quod δεκατῶν & ἀποδεκατοῦν ver- titur, sæpe refertur ad res Gen. XXVIII. v. 22. Deut. XIV. v. 22. c. XXVI. v. 12. 1. Sam. VIII. v. 15. 17. Hic vero ad eos, quorum res sunt, ut & mox vers. 6. ἀποδεκατῶν Latini dicunt edecumare, ut est in Glossario.

Κατὰ τὸν νόμον) Numer. XVIII. vers. 24. & sequenti- bus, ubi vides Levitas accepisse decimas à privatis, Sa- cerdotes vero ab ipsis Levitis. Duplici ergo modo Sacer- dotes Aaronidæ populares suos edecumarunt, primum quia id ipsum, quod Levitarum erat, à populo venerat, deinde quia & Levitæ pars populi.

Comparatio in præstantiæ collatione ita habet: Melchisedech præstantior fuit Abrahamo, cui ut Sacerdos benedixit, & à quo decimas recepit. Præstantior itaque etiam Levitis, qui à Abrahamo descendunt, & in lumbis Abrahami à Melchisede- co decimati sunt. Quare CHRISTUS, qui est Sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedeci, di- gnior omnino est Leviticis Sacerdotibus, à quo etiam in Abrahamum & spirituales ejus filios o- mnis benedictio descendit. Cum figuram veritati inquit Theophylactus, accommodasset, id est, Melchisedec Christo nunc demum fidens, figuram ipsam Melchisedec, Judaeorum Sacerdotibus clariorem argui extitisse, neque his modo, quia vel Abraham Patriarcham ipsum praestare. Si igitur figura tantopere caeteros antecedit, longe magis & Pontifex Christus incomparabiliter istos dignitate anteibit; qui per illam significatur. Nec dici id potest, (ita porro Theophylactus) Abraham dona haec & exuvias fuisse Melchisedeco impertitum, quia secum una hic militasset, & ob id praemia huic dependisset militiae, sed domi se continenti munera & decimas detulit, & ideo dixit superius, obviam Abrahae Melchisedecum processisse. Ἐκ τῶν ἀκροθινίων Vulgata reddidit è praecipuis, quasi esset ἐξ' ἀκροθηνιῶν. Graecum proprie significat ex spoliis sive exuviis ab hoste detractis, quo sensu etiam legitur apud Philostratum Sophistam. Syrus vertit decimas & primitias, Theophylactus meliora & honoratiora spolia. Obiter hic observat B. Dorscheus argumentum, quod evidens vocat, Melchisedecum Semum non fuisse. Nam ejus respectu Abraham tantus videri non poterat, neque Patriarcha dici. Quid enim mirum est, abnepotem fore, ut sic dicamus, Octavo sese submittere, eumque oblatione decimarum venerari? Magis autem mirandum est, Abrahamum Regi & Sacerdoti peregrino & extra genus suum posito, in quo ipse Patriarcha fuerat, decimas offerre.

Τουτέστι τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς ἀυτῶν καίπερ ἐξεληλυθότας ἐκ τῆς ὀσφύος Ἀβραάμ) Et hoc alicujus dignitatis, non ab externis, sed à popularibus accipere decimas. Hoc praestruit, ut majorem deinde Melchisedeci dignitatem inferat. Ex lumbis exire dicuntur Ebraeis, qui ex alicujus semine nascuntur, Genes. XXXV. 11. 2. Paral. VI. 9. Causa ejus loquutionis nota provectioribus.

Sensus est, sicut Levitae sunt digniores aliis Israelitis, qui juxta legem decimas ab illis accipiunt: Sic Melchisedecus Abrahamo & Levitis omnibus ab eo descendentibus dignior fuit, quia ut Sacerdos decimas ab eo accepit. Argumentum autem à fratribus ita habet: Sacerdotes Levitici decimas à reliquis Israelitis accipiunt, Abrahae posteris, nec ultra sese jus eorum extendit. At Melchisedech quamvis alienigena ab Abrahamo Patriarcha ac totius Levitici generis Autore decimas accepit. Nam quo pacto, inquit Theophylactus, alieno homini Abraham decimas detulisset, nisi venerationi hunc caeteri habuissent? Si Melchisedech itaque, qui Christi figuram praetendit, dignitate praestare & Abrahae quidem videtur, longo utique intervallo & Christus ipse, qui verus est Pontifex, Sacerdotibus lege institutis praestabit.

## 7:6
Verse 6.

He whose lineage is derived neither from Levi nor from Abraham. Δεδικάτωκε τὸν Ἀβραὰμ) he tithed Abraham. The construction is as above. The Levitical priests receive tithes by the benefit of the law, and that only if they prove their lineage. But Abraham required neither of these from Melchisedec in order to give him tithes, but offered them voluntarily, revering only the priestly dignity in him, as B. Gerhard says here. Καὶ τὸν ἔχοντα τὰς ἐπαγγελίας ἐυλόγηκε) This also is a great dignity, to bless him who was most dear to God, as appeared from such great and so often repeated promises.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Ὁ δὲ μὴ γενεαλογούμενος ἐξ ἀυτῶν) Cujus genus neque à Levi neque ab Abrahamo deducitur. Δεδικάτωκε τὸν Ἀβραὰμ) edecumavit Abrahamum. Constructio quae supra. Sacerdotes Levitici decimas accipiunt legis beneficio, idque non, nisi probent genus suum. Atqui neutrum horum Abrahamus à Melchisedeco requisivit, ut ei decimas daret, sed ultro obtulit, solam in eo Sacerdotalem dignitatem reveritus, ut hic B. Gerhardus. Καὶ τὸν ἔχοντα τὰς ἐπαγγελίας ἐυλόγηκε) Magna & haec dignitas, ei benedicere, qui Deo erat charissimus, ut ex promissis tantis & toties repetitis apparebat.

## 7:7
Verse 7.

The Latins would say 'beyond controversy'.

Neuter for masculine, as in Eph. 1:10 and elsewhere. Understand εὐλογεῖται as by priestly rite, as above in v. 2. For neither did the people bless the Levites in that way, nor the Levites the priests, nor the priests the High Priest.

Another argument for the dignity of the Melchisedecian priesthood over the Levitical granted to the descendants of Abraham. He who blesses another with a priestly blessing is more worthy than he whom he blesses, by reason of his office. But Melchisedec blessed Abraham with a priestly blessing. Therefore, Melchisedec was greater and more worthy than Abraham, and consequently than the Levites descending from him, by reason of his office. If it be said that Abraham was also a priest, because he offered sacrifices, Gen. 15:10, ch. 22:2. Answer: A priest is blessed by the High Priest as by one of greater dignity of office. Moreover, Melchisedec is called not simply ἱερεὺς but Ἀρχιερεὺς.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Χωρὶς δὲ πάσης ἀντιλογίας) Extra controversiam dicerent Latini.

Τὸ ἔλαττον ὑπὸ τοῦ κρείττονος εὐλογεῖται) Neutrum pro Masculino, ut Ephes. 1, 10. & alibi. Εὐλογεῖται intellige ritu sacerdotali, ut supra v. 2. Nam neque populus eo modo Levitis benedicebat, neque Levitæ Sacerdotibus, neque Sacerdotes summo Sacerdoti.

Aliud argumentum dignitatis sacerdotii Melchisedeciani præ Levitico Abrahæ posteris concesso. Is qui benedicit alteri sacerdotali benedictione, dignior est eo, cui benedicit, officii ratione. At Melchisedech benedixit Abrahamo benedictione Sacerdotali. Major ergo atque dignior Abrahamo, & per consequens Levitis ab eo descendentibus officii ratione fuit Melchisedech. Si dicatur, Abrahamum etiam fuisse Sacerdotem, quia sacrificia obtulit, Gen 15, 10. cap. 22, 2. Resp. Sacerdotem à summo Sacerdote ceu officii dignitate majori benedici. Vocatur autem Melchisedech non simpliciter ἱερεὺς sed Ἀρχιερεὺς.

## 7:8
Verse 8.

Καὶ ὧδε μὲν) here, that is, in the Levitical law. Δεκάτας ἀποθνήσκοντες ἄνθρωποι λαμβάνουσιν) The law itself shows this, which wishes priests to succeed priests, Num. 3 & 18. Ἐκεῖ δὲ) In that place of Genesis. Μαρτυρούμενος ὅτι ζῇ) supply, only. Mention is made of his life: מותא : but no indication of his death.

B. Hunnius adds another sense as well: without rejecting the former and more common one: The words of the Apostle, he says, are to be referred to that silence of the Holy Spirit, by grace of which his death never appears defined or described in Holy Scripture: although, to add this too, it could have happened that Melchizedek, without the intervention of death, was translated into eternal life, just as Enoch and Elijah: so that he might thus more fittingly represent that perpetual priesthood of Christ, which according to the rite and order of this High Priest Melchizedek had to be eternal by the oath of God. But we leave that in its place.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Καὶ ὧδε μὲν) ὧδε, hic, id est, in lege Levitica. Δεκάτας ἀποθνήσκοντες ἄνθρωποι λαμβάνουσιν) Ostendit hoc ipsa lex, quæ Sacerdotibus Sacerdotes vult succedere, Num. 3. & 18. Ἐκεῖ δὲ) In loco illo Geneseos. Μαρτυρούμενος ὅτι ζῇ) supple, tantum. Vitæ ejus fit mentio : מותא : mortis autem nulla significatio.

Addit B. Hunnius & alium sensum : non reprobato priori & usitatiori : Referenda sunt, inquit, verba Apostoli ad silentium illud Spiritus sancti, gratia cujus in sacra scriptura mors ejus definita aut descripta nunquam extat : tametsi, ut hoc quoque addam, fieri potuerit, ut Melchisedech, absque mortis interventu, transferretur in vitam æternam, quemadmodum Enoch & Elias : Ut sic tanto convenientius perpetuum illud Christi sacerdotium repræsentaret, quod secundum ritum atque ordinem hujus Pontificis Melchisedech ex Dei juramento æternum esse debuit. Sed id suo loco relinquimus.

## 7:9
Vers. 9.

Καὶ ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν) This is also a locution of Greek elegance; Aeschylus uses it in the Persians, Thucydides, Plato in the Timaeus and Republic II, Aelian in On Animals IV. 36, and others, especially when they are about to say something bold or exceptional. So also in Euripides' Orestes: ὡς δ᾽ εἰπεῖν ἔπος, because the figure that follows is harsher, he therefore fortified it according to the precept of the learned. Quintilian VIII. 3: And if we seem to have fashioned something more dangerous, it must be fortified with certain remedies: such as 'so to speak': 'if I may say so': 'in a certain way': 'permit me thus'. The Hebrews say על דרך משל. Διὰ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ Λευὶ ὁ δεκάτας λαμβάνων δεδεκάτωται) The goods of parents are also called the goods of descendants in law. And when Abraham gave these tithes, he simultaneously sought that Melchizedek should bless both himself and his posterity. Διὰ Ἀβραὰμ, in the person of Abraham.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Καὶ ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν) Est & hæc loquutio Græcæ elegantiæ; Utuntur Æschylus Persis, Thucydides, Plato Timæo, & de Republ. II. Ælianus de animalibus IV. 36. & alii, præsertim ubi aliquid dicturi sunt παρακεκινδυνευμένον aut eximium. Sic & in Euripidis Oreste : ὡς δ᾽ εἰπεῖν ἔπος, quia durior est figura quæ sequitur, ideo eam præmunivit ex Doctorum præcepto. Quintilianus VIII. 3. Et si quid periculosius finxisse videmur, quibusdam remediis præmuniendum est : ut ita dicam : si licet dicere : quodammodo : permittite mihi sic. Ebræi dicunt על דרך משל. Διὰ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ Λευὶ ὁ δεκάτας λαμβάνων δεδεκάτωται) Bona parentum dicuntur etiam posterorum bona in jure. Et cum Abrahamus has decimas dedit, simul expetivit, ut Melchisedecus & sibi & posteritati suæ benediceret. Διὰ Ἀβραὰμ, in Abrahami persona.

## 7:10
Vers. 10.

Ἔτι γὰρ ἐν τῇ ὀσφύϊ τοῦ Πατρὸς ἦν ὅτε συνήντησεν αὐτῷ ὁ Μελχισεδέκ) Levi was there not in act but in power, namely in him, Abraham.

A new argument for the excellence of the Melchizedekian priesthood. Levi himself also, to whose tribe the priesthood of the Old Testament belongs, in some way gave tithes to Melchizedek, while he offered those tithes to Abraham, in whose loins Levi was. Whence it follows again that Melchizedek stands above the order of the Levites, and therefore Christ with his priesthood stands much more above the Levitical priesthood. Estius is anxious here as to why the Apostle, in such a prolix treatment of the Melchizedekian priesthood, made no mention of the sacrifice of bread and wine, which the Papists invent. But he only betrays the futility of his cause: saying first that it was done because that mention contributed nothing to the Apostle's purpose, the dignity of the priesthood of Christ. Thus, therefore, in that which contributes nothing to the dignity of the priesthood of Christ, he not obscurely confesses that the chief mystery of the priesthood of Christ is sought by the Papists. Furthermore, that that holy thing ought not to have been cast before the Hebrews as if they were dogs. And so, indeed, the faithful and converted Hebrews are to be considered dogs, and unworthy of the mysteries of CHRIST, to whom He proposed things far better than that supposed mystery of the mass.

But if the Levites were tithed in the loins of Abraham, was not Christ also tithed in the loins of Abraham, who was the seed of Abraham? Enjedinus rejects this epistle on this account, as using inept arguments. Pareus replies that Christ was not tithed, even though his mother descends from Abraham, because the census, like the genealogies, was made not in the females, but in the loins of the men; then because He was not conceived and born by natural law, but by a miracle from a virgin mother, and although He was in the loins of Abraham according to the matter of the flesh, yet not according to the seminal reason, since the mother in generation indeed provides the matter, but not the active force, inasmuch as that resides in the male seed. But more accurate physicists will scarcely concede these latter points, to whom we leave those things to be discussed. Augustine, Vol. III, On Genesis literally, Book X, chapter 20. According to that seminal reason, he says, Levi was there, by which reason he was to come into the mother through intercourse, according to which reason Christ was not there, although the flesh of Mary was there according to that same reason. For since there is in the seed both visible corporeality and invisible reason, both ran from Abraham, or even from Adam himself, up to the body of Mary, because it too was conceived and arose in that way: but Christ took the visible substance of flesh from the flesh of the Virgin, but the reason of His conception did not come from male seed, but far otherwise and from above. Nor was He tithed there, whose flesh drew from thence not the heat of the wound, but the matter of the remedy. For since the tithing itself pertained to prefiguring the medicine, that was tithed in the flesh of Abraham which was being cured, not that from which it was being cured. For the same flesh, not only of Abraham, but of the first and earthly man himself, had at once both the wound of transgression and the medicine of the wound. The wound of transgression is in the law of the members resisting the law of the mind, which is, as it were, transcribed through all the flesh propagated thence by seminal reason. But the medicine of the wound is in the fact that it was assumed from the virgin thence without the work of concupiscence in the bodily matter alone by the Divine reason of conception and formation, for the sake of a fellowship of death without iniquity, and an example of resurrection without falsehood. We think it should be replied most simply to the heretic Enjedinus that CHRIST was not in the loins of Abraham according to the plastic force, which was implanted by the virtue of the Divine blessing in the Protoplasts and their descendants before the fall (Gen. 1:28), but according to the virtue of the Evangelical promise, made to Adam after the fall from the most free Economy of Divine grace concerning the seed of the woman (Gen. 3:15). Whence it was a peculiar thing in Mary the Theotokos, that although she herself supplied the matter for the flesh of CHRIST to be formed, yet the flesh of CHRIST could not be procreated thence by the force of the primeval blessing alone, inasmuch as that was granted Divinely not to the mother, but to mother and Father in union and intercourse, but it was procreated and produced from the blood of Mary by the force of the Divine Evangelical promise through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, and thus it came forth from the loins of Abraham not by natural law or mode, as the Levites, but supernaturally.

PART II. The demonstration of the necessity of another Priest than the Levitical order.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Ἔτι γὰρ ἐν τῇ ὀσφύϊ τοῦ Πατρὸς ἦν ὅτε συνήντησεν αὐτῷ ὁ Μελχισεδέκ) Levi illic erat non ἐνεργείᾳ sed δυνάμει, αὐτῷ nempe Abrahamo.

Novum præstantiæ sacerdotii Melchisedeciani argumentum. Ipse quoque Levi, ad cujus tribum pertinet sacerdotium Veteris Testamenti, aliqua ratione decimas dedit Melchisedeco, dum Abrahamo, in cujus lumbis erat Levi, decimas illas obtulit. Unde rursus consequitur, Melchisedecum supra Levitarum ordinem, adeoque multo magis Christum cum suo sacerdotio supra Leviticum sacerdotium eminere. Solicitus hic est Estius, cur nullam mentionem in tam prolixa tractatione Melchisedeciani sacerdotii Apostolus fecerit sacrificii panis & vini, quod fingunt Papistæ. Sed prodit tantum causæ suæ futilitatem: Primo id factum dicens, quia mentio illa nihil faciebat ad Apostoli institutum, dignitatem sacerdotii Christi. Sic ergo in eo, quod nil ad dignitatem sacerdotii Christi facit, præcipu- um mysterium sacerdotii Christi à Pontificiis quæ- rinon obscure fatetur. Deinde quod Ebræis ceu canibus sanctum illud projiciendum non fuerit. Ita- ne vero fideles & conversi Ebræi canes censendi, & indigni mysteriis CHRISTI, quibus longe potiora, quam illud putatitium missæ mysterium proposuit.

Sed si in lumbis Abrahæ Levitæ decimati sunt, annon Christus etiam decimatus in Abrahæ lumbis, qui semen Abrahæ fuit? Rejicit hinc Enjedinus hanc epistolam, ceu ineptis utentem argumenta- tionibus. Pareus respondet, Christum non deci- matum, etsi mater ejus descendat ab Abrahamo, quia census ut genealogiarum, ita decimarum non in fæmi- nis, sed in lumbis virorum fiebat; tum quia non na- turali lege, sed miraculo ex matre virgine est con- ceptus & natus, & quamvis fuerit in lumbis Abra- hæ secundum materiam carnis, non tamen secun- dum rationem seminalem, quum mater in genera- tione materiam quidem præbeat, non autem vim activam, utpote quæ resideat in semine virili. Sed hæc posteriora Physici accuratiores vix conce- dent, quibus illa discutienda relinquimus. Augu- stinus Tom. III. de Genes. ad literam l. X. cap. 20. Secundum rationem illam, inquit, seminalem ibi fuit Levi, qua ratione per concubitum venturus erat in matrem, secundum quam rationem non ibi erat Chri- sticoaro, quamvis secundam ipsam ibi fuerit Mariæ caro. Cum enim sit in semine & visibilis corpulen- tia & invisibilis ratio, utrumque cucurrit ex Abra- ham, vel etiam ex ipso Adam usque ad corpus Mariæ, quia & ipsum eo modo conceptum & exortum est: Christus autem visibilem carnis substantiam de carne Virginis sumpsit, ratio vero conceptionis ejus non à semine virili, sed longe aliter atq; desuper venit. Non autem & ille ibi decimatus est, cujus caro inde non fervorem vulneris, sed materiam medicaminis tra- xit. Nam cum ipsa decimatio ad præfigurandam medicinam pertinuerit, illud in Abrahæ carne deci- mabatur, quod curabatur, non illud, unde curabatur. Eadem namque caro non Abrahæ tantum, sed ipsius primi terreniq; hominis simul habebat & vulnus præ- varicationis, & medicamentum vulneris. Vulnus prævaricationis in lege membrorum repugnante legi mentis, quæ per omnem inde propagatam carnem se- minali ratione quasi transcribitur. Medicamen- tum autem vulneris in eo, quod inde sine opere concu- piscentiali in sola materia corporali per Divinam conceptionis formationisque rationem de virgine as- sumptum est propter mortis sine iniquitate consor- tium, & sine falsitate resurrectionis exemplum. Nos simplicissime id hæretico Enjedino reponen- dum censemus, quod CHRISTUS non fuerit in lumbis Abrahæ secundum vim plasticam, Divinæ benedictionis virtute Protoplastis eorum posteris ante lapsum inditam Genes. 1, 28. sed secundum vir- tutem promissionis Evangelicæ, post lapsum ex li- berrima Oeconomia gratiæ divinæ Adamo factæ de semine mulieris, Genes. 3, 15. unde peculiare id fuit in Maria Θεοτόκῳ, quod etsi ipsa materiam sub- ministrarit formandæ carni CHRISTI, non ta- men vi solius primævæ benedictionis caro CHRI- STI inde procreari potuerit, utpote quæ non ma- tri, sed matri & Patri, in συζυγίᾳ & συνεσίᾳ con- cessa est Divinitus, sed vi promissionis Divinæ Ev- angelicæ per ἐπέλευσιν Spiritus sancti ex sanguini- bus Mariæ procreata & producta est, adeoque non lege aut modo naturali, ut Levitæ, sed supernatu- rali è lumbis Abrahæ prodiit.

PARS II. Necessitatis Pontificis alterius, quam Levitici ordinis demonstratio.

## 7:11
Ver. 11.

If therefore perfection was through the Levitical priesthood) perfection in this place is that which is most perfect in the kind of priesthood. See above II. 10, V. 9, below 19.

For the people were under it given the law) In the Manuscript it is written ἐπ᾿ αὐτῆς. Even then, when that Psalm was written by David, the people had a law concerning the Levitical priesthood: they gave to those priests honor, firstfruits, tithes, and the offering as parts according to the law, ἐπ᾿ αὐτῆς, concerning it. See among the commanding precepts the twenty-third.

What further need that another priest should arise according to the order of Melchizedek) Namely, as that Psalm predicts. He is said to arise who begins some public office, as Exod. 1:8. So also ἐγείρεσθαι, Matt. 11:11, ch. 24:1, Mark 13:22, John 7:52, Acts 9:28, ch. 13:22. The Hebrews say קום, 2 Sam. 23.

And not be called according to the order of Aaron) Namely, in the Psalm. Why that Priest who is to come is said there to be like Melchizedek, and not like Aaron.

It is not the priesthood in itself that mention of τελειώσεως [perfection] speaks of, but it understands τελείωσιν or consummation as the effect of the priesthood, namely that it could not be obtained through the Levitical priesthood, that is, a perfect reconciliation with God; so that it may teach that the Levitical priesthood had to be abrogated, which the Hebrew people, by a certain inveterate persuasion, dreamed would be perpetual. Estius: Consummation in Greek is τελείωσις, that is, perfection. By this name he calls justification or the remission of sins, because it perfects a man before God, that is, constitutes him a friend of God and an heir of His kingdom. Thus, a little later he says: For the law brought nothing to perfection. Therefore, the blessed Hunnius explains the meaning of the argument: If the Levitical priesthood could have rendered men perfected, that is, just and holy before God, and conferred perfection, then there would have been no need for another priesthood, different in kind, to be promised. But God in Psalm 110 promised both a new High Priest and another priesthood, which would not be according to the order of Aaron, but the order of Melchizedek. From which it is concluded that the former one of Aaron, as being imperfect and invalid for conferring justice, had to be abolished: Similarly, the law, under which that sacrifice was established in the Israelite Church, could not justify. If Scripture wished to teach that the Levitical priesthood was so perfect and efficacious for the reconciliation of the human race with God that there was no need for any other sacrifice, what need was there to speak of a new, different Priest, who would be a Priest not according to the order of Aaron, but according to the order of Melchizedek? As Osiander holds. For if the priesthood of the law were perfect, says Theophylact, it would have been necessary for a Priest to arise according to the rite of Aaron. For Aaron, born of the Levitical tribe, is otherwise said to have arisen as a Priest not at all according to Aaron, but according to Melchizedek. Since, therefore, that more imperfect one is refuted, a certain other order is introduced. Regarding the word ἐνομοθέτητο, Flacius says: The people were ordered or constituted by law: Some translate: The people had received the law under it; others, under this the law was sanctioned for the people. I do not doubt that the meaning is that the people were so ordered, formed, and constituted by law in this priesthood that they might worship God through this priesthood, and be sanctified through it, but they could not be sanctified as much as was necessary.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Ei μὲν ὖν τελείωσις διὰ τῆς Λευιτικῆς ἱερωσύνης ἦν) τε- λείωσις hoc loco est id quod in genere sacerdotii perfe- ctissimum est. Vide supra II. 10. V. 9. infra 19.

Ο λαὸς γὰρ ἐπ᾿ αὐτῇ νενομοθέτητο) In Manuscripto ἐπ᾿ αὐτῆς νενομοθέτηται. Jam tum cum à Davide Psal- mus iste scriberetur, populus legem habebat de sacer- dotio Levitico : Illis sacerdotibus honorem, primitias, decimas & oblationem partes dabat ex lege, ἐπ᾿ αὐτῆς, de illa. Vide inter præcepta jubentia tertium & vi- gesimum.

Τὶς ἔτι χρεία κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδὲκ ἕτερον ἀνίστα- σθαι ἱερέα) Nempe, ut prædicit ille Psalmus. Ἀνίστα- σθαι dicitur, qui munus aliquod publicum orditur, ut Exod. 1, 8. Sic & ἐγείρεσθαι Matth. 11, 11. cap. 24, 1. Marc. 13, 22. Johan. 7, 52. Actor. 9, 28. cap. 13, 22. Ebræi dicunt קום, 2. Sam. 23.

Καὶ ἐ κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Ἀαρὼν λέγεσθαι) Nempe in Psal- mo. Cur ille venturus Sacerdos ibi dicitur fore instar Melchisedeci, & non in istar Aaronis.

Non sacerdotium in se perfectissimum mentio- ne τελειώσεως dicit, sed τελείωσιν vel consummatio- nem de effectu sacerdotii, quod nempe ea per sa- cerdotium Leviticum obtineri non potuerit, in- telligit, reconciliationis nempe perfectæ cum Deo; ut Leviticum sacerdotium abrogandum fuisse do- ceat, quod populus Ebræus inveterata quadam persuasione perpetuum fore somniabat. Estius : Consummatio Græce τελείωσις, id est, perfectio. Hoc nomine vocat justificationem seu peccatorum remissio- nem, quod ea hominem perficiat apud Deum, id est, amicum Dei, & regni ejus hæredem constituat. Ita paulo post ait: Nihil enim ad perfectum adduxit lex. Argumenti ergo sententiam explicat B. Hunnius: Si sacerdotium Leviticum consummatos potuisset reddere homines, id est, justos & sanctos coram Deo, & conferre perfectionem, tum non fuisset opus, ut promitteretur sacerdotium aliud specie diversum. Atqui Deus Psal. CX. promisit, & Pontificem no- vum & sacerdotium aliud, quod non secundum ordi- nem Aaronis, sed Melchisedeci ordinem esset. Ex quo conficitur prius illud Aaronis velut imperfe- ctum, & ad conferendam justitiam invalidum fuisse antiquandum : Similiter & legem, sub qua consti- tutum erat illud sacrificium in Ecclesia Israelitica non potuisse justificare. Si scriptura volebat doce- re, Leviticum sacerdotium esse ita perfectum & effi- cax ad reconciliationem generis humani cum Deo, ut nullo alio sacrificio opus esset : quid necesse erat di- cere de novo alio Sacerdote, qui futurus esset Sacer- dos non secundum ordinem Aaron, sed secundum or- dinem Melchisedech? ut habet Osiander. Nam si perfectum, inquit Theophylactus, esset sacerdotium legis, necesse fuisset pro ritu Aaron surgere Sacerdo- tem. Aaron namque de tribu Levitica oriundus, alioqui haudquaquam secundum Aaron, sed secun- dum Melchisedech institutum Sacerdos dicitur sur- rexisse. Cum itaque imperfectius illud coarguatur, alius quidam inducitur ordo.
