De voce ἐνομοθέ- τητο Flacius ita : Populus erat lege ordinatus aut constitutus : Aliqui vertunt : Populus sub eo legem acceperat; alii sub hoc lex sancita est populo. Ego non dubito sensum esse, quod populus in hoc sacer- dotio ita lege erat ordinatus, formatus & constitu- tus, ut per istud sacerdotium coleret Deum, & per id sanctificaretur, sed non potuit, quantum opus fuit, sanctificari.

## 7:12
Ver. 12.

For the priesthood being changed) The priesthood being transferred to someone not of Aaron, which the Psalm predicts will happen. Of necessity and of the law a change takes place) Namely of the priestly [matters], concerning which he had treated above. The Jews wish for the law to be changed in no part. But it appears from the Psalm that it will be changed, and indeed in its most excellent part, namely concerning the priesthood. For while the law stood, no one could be a priest who was not of Aaron. And therefore that sanction of the law also vanished. Cursed is he who does not perform all the words of this law. To be changed is to alter, whence above [we had] the unchangeable. Thus in Plato, let us change, that is, let us change our opinion. Chrysostom in his second [book] against the Jews also notes this, that the greatest part of the law concerns sacred things.

If the priesthood has been transferred to another, it is necessary, says Theophylact, that there be another law also, since a priest cannot exist without a testament and a law. The priesthood has therefore been transferred, not only in mode, i.e., that it by no means consists in the institutions and rite of Melchizedek himself for Aaron, but [also] in tribe. For that priesthood was transferred from the priestly tribe of Aaron to that royal tribe of Judah. Flacius explains these things more fully: From the change of the priesthood he proves also the change of the law. For just as civil laws necessarily cohere with the form of the governors and the whole polity, so that (as Aristotle testifies) when the polity is changed it is necessary that the laws also be changed: so also the form of doctrine and the whole covenant is adjusted to the priesthood and vice versa. Therefore, with the Levitical priesthood changed into the Pontificate of Christ, it is necessary that the laws and the doctrine concerning the form and worship of that priesthood be changed into the laws or doctrine of this Pontiff. Those laws spoke of the person, and the life, and the sacrifices and rites of that [priesthood]: but this law or doctrine of the Gospel prescribes to us a far different form of priesthood and its worship. The Pope hence arrogates to himself the right of establishing new laws, violently applying this saying to himself in his decretals: as if both the priesthood and the right of establishing new laws had been transferred to him: than which impudent sacrilege nothing could be said more impudent and more sacrilegious. For he despoils Christ of his eternal priesthood, and overturns the whole New Testament, just as the Alcoran does to Mahomet. For if the Levitical priesthood had been intended to be perpetual, then it could not have been transferred from the tribe of Levi to another tribe, just as Jeroboam is most gravely rebuked on this account, because he attempted to transfer the priesthood by assuming priests not from the tribe of Levi, but from other tribes of Israel, as we read written in 3 Kings 12. Now indeed the transfer of the priesthood from the tribe of Levi to the tribe of Judah had to take place, according to the undoubted testimonies of the Prophets, who teach and most clearly predict that the Messiah had to arise not from the tribe of Levi, but from the tribe of Judah, and nevertheless they write that an eternal priesthood was decreed and promised to the same [person] thus arisen from the tribe of Judah by God through an oath. Moreover, says Osiander, there was need of a new law, that is, a new kind of doctrine, namely the doctrine of the Gospel. For the priesthood having been transferred or changed, it is necessary that a transfer or change of the law also take place. Therefore there was need for the Gospel to succeed into the place of the law. Those, therefore, who today in Christianity teach nothing but the law, and think that Christ came into the world for the reason that he might promulgate a new and more perfect law, these, as much as in them lies, abrogate the priesthood of CHRIST and restore the Levitical. Because as the Levitical Priesthood and the Mosaic law cohered: so the Priesthood of Christ and the doctrine of the Gospel cohere. And he who takes away or posits the one, also takes away or posits the other.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Μετατιθεμένης γὰρ ἱερωσύνης) Sacerdotio translato in aliquem non Aaroniden, quod futurum prædicit Psal- Ἐξ ἀνάγκης καὶ νόμου μετάθεσις γίνεται) Nempe ἱερα- τικά, de quo supra egerat. Judæi volunt legem nulla in parte mutatum iri. At ex Psalmo apparet, mutatum iri, & quidem in eximia ejus parte, nempe de sacerdotio. Neque enim stante lege, Sacerdos aliquis esse potuit non Aaronides. Ac proinde illa etiam sanctio legis evanuit. Maledictus, qui non fecerit omnia verba legis hujus. Μετατίθεσθαι est mutare, unde supra τὸ ἀμετάθετον. Sic apud Platonem μεταθώμεθα, id est, sententiam mu- temus. Chrysostomus in II. adversus Judæos & hoc no- tat, maximam legis partem circa sacra versari.

Si alio traductum est sacerdotium, necesse est, inquit Theophylactus, & aliam legem esse, quandoquidem nequit, Sacerdos sine testamento & lege constare. Translatum est itaque sacerdotium, non solum pro modo, i. e. quod nequaquam pro Aaron, ipsius Melchisedeci institutis & ritu constet, sed tribu. A sacerdotali namque Aaron tribu in Regiam illam Juda traductum est id sacerdotium. Plenius hæc explicat Flacius: Ex mutatione sacerdotii probat etiam mutationem legis. Sicut enim leges civiles necessario cohærent cum forma gubernatorum to- taque politia, ut (teste Aristotele) mutata politia necesse sit & leges mutari: Sic etiam forma do- ctrinæ, totumque fœdus attemperatum est ad sacer- dotium & contra. Mutato igitur Levitico sacer- dotio in Christi Pontificatum, necesse est, & leges doctrinamque, de forma cultibusque illius sacerdo- tii commutari in leges aut doctrinam hujus Ponti- ficis. Illæ leges loquebantur de persona, vitaque, & sacrificiis ritibusque illius: hæc vero lex aut do- ctrina Evangelii nobis longe aliam formam sacer- dotii cultuumque ejus præscribit. Papa hinc sibi arrogat jus condendi novas leges, violenter hoc dictum in suis decretalibus ad se applicans: quasi ad ipsum sit translatum tum sacerdotium, tum jus condendi novas leges: quo impudenti sacrilegio nihil posset dici impudentius magisq́; sacrilegum. Spoliat enim Chri- stum suo æterno sacerdotio, & totum Novum Testa- mentum evertit, sicut & Alchoranus Mahometi. Si enim Leviticum sacerdotium perpetuum esse debuis- set, tum non potuisset ex tribu Levi in aliam tribum transferri, quemadmodum hoc nomine reprehendi- tur gravissime Jerobeam, quod sacerdotium trans- ferre conatus est, assumendo Sacerdotes non ex tribu Levi, sed ex aliis tribubus Israelis, sicut 3. Regum 12. scriptum legimus. Jam vero fieri debuit translatio sacerdotii ex tribu Levi in tribum Juda, juxta indu- bitata Prophetarum testimonia, qui docent, & claris- sime prædicant, Messiam non de tribu Levi, sed de tribu Juda oriri debuisse, & niholominus eidem sic ex tribu Juda orto sacerdotium æternum à Deo median- te juramento decretum ac promissum scribunt. Quin etiam, inquit Osiander, nova lege, hoc est, novo genere doctrinæ opus erat, doctrina videlicet Evangelii. Translato enim seu mutato sacerdotio, necesse est, ut & legis translatio seu mutatio fiat. Itaq́; opus erat, ut in locum legis Evangelium succederet. Qui igi- tur hodie in Christianismo nihil nisi legem docent, & Christum ideo in mundum venisse putant, ut novam & perfectiorem legem promulgaret, hi quantum in ipsis est, sacerdotium CHRISTI abrogant, & Levi- ticum restituunt. Quia ut Sacerdotium Leviticum & lex Mosaica cohærebant: Sic Sacerdotium Chri- sti & doctrina Evangelii cohærent. Et qui unum tollit aut ponit, etiam alterum tollit aut ponit.

## 7:13
Ver. 13.

For concerning whom these things are said, he has partaken of another tribe, from which no one has devoted effort to the altar) That 'for' pertains to this, that he might now show that the sense of that Psalm, with the things having been premised which were necessary, agrees in all parts to Jesus of Nazareth. 'Concerning whom' [are] those things said which agree. Thus shortly 'to whom'. To partake of a tribe is to be of a tribe, just as to partake of flesh and blood, II. 14, is to have flesh and blood. For 'has devoted effort' a Manuscript has 'has attended'. And it is a good Greek word, and signifies to devote effort. Thus 'to attend to cities, to an action, to works' is frequent among the Greeks. Other books have 'has stood near' [Hebrew word]. It was agreed among the Jews that Christ had to be from the tribe of Judah, namely through David.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Ἐφ’ ὃν γὰρ λέγεται ταῦτα, φυλῆς ἑτέρας μετέσχηκεν, ἀφ’ ἧς οὐδεὶς προσέσχηκε τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ) Illud γὰρ eo per- tinet, ut præstructis, quæ oportebat, jam ostendat sen- sum Psalmi illius omnibus partibus in Jesum Nazarenum competere. Ἐφ᾽ ᾧ in quem dicta ista competunt. Sic mox εἰς ὅν. Μετέχειν φυλῆς est esse de tribu, sicut μετέ- χειν σαρκὸς καὶ αἵματος, II. 14. habere carnem & sangui- nem. Pro προσέσχηκε Manuscriptus habet προσέσχε. Estque vox bene Græca, & significat operam dare. Sic προσέχειν πόλεων, πράξει, ἔργοις frequentia apud Græ- cos. Alii libri habent προσέστηκε קרב. Constabat in- ter Judæos, Christum esse debere ex tribu Judæ, nempe per Davidem.

## 7:14
Ver. 14.

It is evident that our Lord has sprung from Judah) If from David, then from Judah. The kingdom had been promised to the family of Judah. And the Priest predicted in the Psalm had to be no less King than Priest. And the word 'has sprung up' was well chosen, because Christ under the figure of Zerubbabel is called 'branch' [Hebrew word] or 'rising' or 'sprout' or 'offspring'. For in these ways that Hebrew [word] is translated in Jer. 23:5, ch. 33:15, Zech. 3:8, ch. 6:12.

Add also the prophecy of Isa. 11:1, concerning each of which [we speak] in its proper place. But it is clear from these that Mary, the Mother of God, was of the tribe of Judah, and that this was then openly established, and was 'evident' among the Hebrews, which the Socinians today deny, contending that Mary, from whom Christ was born, was not of the tribe of Judah, but of the tribe of Levi. But the exception of Crellius and Schlichtingius in this place is vain and frivolous, that it is said for this reason, because Christ was born from the wife of Joseph, who was of the descendants of David, of Judah, of Abraham. For Christ was not begotten from Joseph, but was born from the virgin Mary through the operation of the Holy Spirit. What they say: Whoever is a son born from someone's wife, who is considered the body of the husband, while he is not born by the work of any other man, although he is not generated from the husband himself, is nevertheless his son; is equally futile. For how can he be called the son of the husband, who is not generated from the husband, [if he is to be called] from the true [father]? Scripture speaks of him far otherwise, namely with the diminutive particle added, ὡς ἐνομίζετο, Luke 3:23. He is not, therefore, said to be the son of Joseph in truth, but was so thought to be. But more on these matters another time.

Of which tribe Moses spoke nothing concerning the priesthood) Concerning which tribe Moses had said nothing pertaining to the priesthood. It follows, therefore, from the Psalm, that the law of Moses is already to be superseded. In the manuscript it is ὀδὲν περὶ ἱερέων. And the Latin reads thus.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Πρόδηλον, ὅτι ἐξ Ἰούδα ἀνατέταλκεν ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν) Si ex Davide, ergo ex Juda. Judæ familiæ promissum fuit regnum. Et Sacerdos in Psalmo prædictus non minus Rex quam Sacerdos esse debuit. Et bene electum est verbum ἀνατέταλκε, quia Christus sub Zorobabelis figura dicitur צמח ἀνατολὴ sive βλαστὸς aut βλάστημα. Nam his modis Ebræum illud vertitur Jerem. 23, 5. cap. 33, 15. Zach. 3, 8. cap. 6, 12.

Adde & vaticinium Esa. 11, 1. de quibus singulis in propria sede. Patet autem ex his Mariam χρισ- τοτόκον ex Judæ fuisse tribu, idque tum palam con- stitisse, & πρόδηλον fuisse penes Ebræos, quod ho- die negant Sociniani, Mariam scilicet, ex qua natus est Christus, non ex tribu Juda, sed ex tribu Levi fuisse contendentes. Vana autem & frivola est Crellii & Schlichtingii in h. l. exceptio, ideo id dici, quia Christus natus ex Josephi uxore, qui fuit ex Davidis, Judæ, Abrahami posteris. Non enim Christus ex Josepho procreatus est, sed è Maria virgine per Spiritus sancti operationem prognatus est. Quod dicunt: Quicunque filius ex alicujus u- xore, quæ corpus censetur mariti, nascitur, dum non nascitur viri alterius ullius opera, quamvis nec ex ipso marito generetur, ipsius tamen est filius; æque futile est. Quomodo enim mariti filius, qui non ex marito generatus, dici potest ex vero? Scriptu- ra longe aliter de eo loquitur, addita nempe parti- cula diminuente, ὡς ἐνομίζετο, Luc. 3, 22. Non er- go ex vero dicitur filius Josephi, sed ita putaba- tur. Sed de his alias.

Εἰς ἣν φυλὴν ὀδὲν περὶ ἱερωσύνης Μωσῆς ἐλάλησεν) In quam tribum competens nihil Moses de sacerdotio di- xerat. Sequitur ergo ex Psalmo, a iam legem legi Mo- sis substitutum iri. In Manuscripto est ὀδὲν περὶ ἱερέων. Et sic legit Latinus.

## 7:15
Vers. 15.

And it is yet more manifest) This very thing which I said about the change of the law is even more evident from elsewhere. Thus the Rabbis are accustomed to say ברור ויותר. Πρόδηλον and κατάδηλον are good Greek words, such as are many in this epistle.

If after the similitude of Melchisedec there ariseth another priest) 'If' here is 'since': as in Rom. 5:10. Take ἀνίσταται as above in verse 11.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Καὶ περισσότερον ἔτι κατάδηλόν ἐστι) Hoc ipsum quod dixi de legis mutatione, amplius etiam aliunde liquet. Sic Rabbini dicere solent ברור ויותר. Πρόδηλον & κατάδηλον voces bene Græcæ, quales multæ in hac epi- stola.

Εἰ κατὰ τὴν ὁμοιότητα Μελχισεδὲκ ἀνίσταται ἱερεὺς ἕτε- ρος) Εἰ hic est quandoquidem: ut Rom. 5, 10. Ἀνίστα- ται sume ut supra 11.

## 7:16
Who not after the law of a carnal commandment) According to that law (for νόμος also signifies 'right' or 'law', as in 1 Cor. 7:39; Exod. 12:49) which comes from a commandment given to the flesh, that is, to mortal men, of whom one succeeds another. Flesh signifies the mortal condition, as above in verse 7.

But after the power of an endless life) By the power of an immortal life. For Christ was brought to immortal life for this reason, that He might be our Priest forever. See above in verses 5 and 6. He calls the life ἀκατάλυτον, because it never departs from that body לא יקרע, Exod. 39, verse 22.

The sense is, who was not constituted a Priest according to the law or norm of the commandment, which was occupied only with carnal and temporary things, as were the external Levitical ceremonies, but according to the power which could work an indissoluble or eternal life. Just as the first comparison concerned the priestly tribe: so this concerns the more intimate reason and nature of the same, that the Levitical Priesthood was made or established according to the law, tenor, rule, and mode of the commandment, which dealt with ceremonial, worldly, and external things:

Moreover, the Melchisedecian priesthood of Christ requires a power and potency of such a kind that it would be occupied with heavenly and eternal things, and by which an indissoluble and eternal life itself could be obtained for us, and be carried out according to the efficacy of the same. There are indeed those who wish the eternity of the priesthood to be considered, and explain with Theodoret that the law of a carnal commandment is so called because of the carnal succession, to which the old priesthood was bound according to the prescription of the law, whereas Christ was not made a Priest in such a way that he would either succeed some prior one or leave another after him, but from a Divine power, which grants him an indissoluble, that is, an immortal life, so that there is no place for a successor. But the Apostle deals with that below, v. 23, 24, 25. Therefore, one should not think that he is treating the same thing here, and peddling or employing it as a different argument, which in reality is one and the same, and has the same nerve of conclusion. Others wish nothing else to be signified than that Christ, the Priest of the New Testament, was not made a Priest according to the Mosaic law, since it admits no others to the priesthood than those who are of the seed of Aaron and the tribe of Levi, but above the law by the power and will of God, who is the author of an indissoluble, that is, an eternal life. But the Apostle had already treated that argument about another tribe in verses 13 and 14. Now he adds something more (περισσότερόν τι). More correctly, therefore, Flacius in his gloss: Another reason, he says, or proof of the change of the priesthood and the law, is from the form of the sanctifications and sacrifices, all of which in the Aaronic are external and perishable and in themselves not at all efficacious: on the contrary, in this Priest they are spiritual, living, and salutary: Where all things consist by the force or power of perpetual life, namely because they consist of true and perpetual justice and peace, whence he is also called the King of justice and peace. Both were indeed ordained by God: But yet the former consists in earthly and perishable things, so as not to endure perpetually: The latter, however, in spiritual and eternal goods. Which explanation is confirmed both from the word Melchisedech, which introduces the King of justice, and from the eternity of the priesthood handed down in the Psalm, which would be nothing if it did not bring eternal goods; and especially from verse 18, because since the priesthood and the covenant with Aaron as a law (in itself) could not truly and fully sanctify anything, and thus it was necessarily required to seek something else, which would absolutely and perfectly sanctify its worshippers. Blessed Gerhard also explained it thus: According to the power of an indissoluble life, that is, that he ought to have a spiritual and efficacious priesthood, through which he would acquire eternal life for us, just as he himself remains forever: adducing Chrysostom and Theophylact to that opinion, because they explain this member of comparison or opposition thus, that he was not created a Priest according to a carnal law, that is, a weak one, in which there were many commandments of bodily ceremonies, but according to the power or potency of an indissoluble life, that is, having received from the Father the power of conferring eternal life upon his own. To which also Osiander in his paraphrase and the German paraphrase of the Vinians tend. John Cameron in his Myrothecium Evangelicum says that the carnal commandment (ἐvτολὴ σαρκικὴ) is the precept of offering a sacrifice, the entire force of which sacrifice is situated in carnal expiation, the entire force, I say, that is productive, as the same Apostle interprets here, chapter 9, 13. The power of an indissoluble life (Δύναμις ἀκαταλύτου ζωῆς) is that perfect force from the Divinity of CHRIST, by which it was brought about that CHRIST not only lives himself forever, but also derives life into us. And this also the Apostle interprets, chapter 9, 14. Certainly the power of an indissoluble life, which is in CHRIST, proceeded from the eternal Spirit, through whom he offered himself to the Father. Which things agree more with the present Apostolic argument than those of Beza and Pareus, that CHRIST was inaugurated into an immortal life by the force of an indissoluble life, that is, by the immediate power of God, so that he does not cease to perform the priesthood forever, as if it were a periphrasis of eternity, opposed to the perishability of the rites and legal Priests, because they would die, while CHRIST, not about to die, enjoys an indissoluble life and priesthood. With whom Crellius and Schlichtingius here have things in common. Whom Grotius also seems to have followed in this place: Blessed Dorscheus says: Life, he says, that is indissoluble (ζωὴ ἀκατάλυτος) is not only that which was given to CHRIST through the resurrection, which being posited, he himself no longer dies, of which he also speaks in Apoc. 1, verse 18, and which will be given to all who are resurrected to the communion of the glory of the kingdom: But it is primarily that which essentially belongs to God, by which he himself lives in supreme perfection, beatitude, power, and wisdom, immense and infinite, and which personally belongs to CHRIST even according to his Human nature. This is evident 1. from the words themselves. For it is called an indissoluble life (ζωὴ ἀκατάλυτος) absolutely and simply. Whence there is no necessity that we restrict it to a created life. 2. The Person himself has this life, in this way indissoluble, according to those things which were treated at length in chapter 1 of this epistle. Therefore, it is also rightly said that he is a Priest in respect to it. 3. This life is said to be so indissoluble (ἀκατάλυτος) that it has neither beginning nor end, above in verse 3 of this chapter. Hence his going forth is said to be from the days of eternity, Micah 5, verse 2, and by reason of this life he is called the beginning and the end, the first and the last, Apoc. 1, verse 8 and 17. 4. Life in the absolute sense of indissoluble (ἀκατάλυτος) pertains greatly to the excellence of this Priest. For in this way an infinite distance is established between this Priest and the Levitical Priests. For thus he differs not only in the degree of beatific life, but in the whole genus. And yet this is the Apostolic institution, to establish the Priest of the Christian religion at the highest degree of perfection, nay, to place the same above every condition of finite perfection. CHRIST is said to have the power of this indissoluble life, for this reason, because not only does He Himself live by an indissoluble life, but He also has the power of communicating life to others, whether in the kingdom of power, or in the kingdom of grace, or in the kingdom of glory, because He has all power in heaven and on earth, Matt. XXVIII. verse 18, and power over all flesh, John XVII. verse 2. Concerning which power, it has been treated at greater length above in chapter 1, verse 3, chapter II, verse 5, following, and chapter III, verse 6. That this power of an indissoluble life was also communicated to CHRIST according to His human nature is evident, partly from the fact that CHRIST, even according to His human nature, is contrasted with the Levitical priests in that He is not a priest according to the law of a carnal commandment, from which it necessarily follows that He is also, according to His human nature, a priest according to the power of an indissoluble life; partly from the fact that, according to that nature, He is a priest according to the power of an indissoluble life, according to which He sprang from Judah, verse 14; partly from the fact that being a priest according to the power of an indissoluble life is an interpretation of that which is said in Psalm CX, verse 4, 'a priest forever'; since he who has the power of an indissoluble life simply and absolutely can most rightly be constituted a priest forever, as being entirely immutable. Wherefore CHRIST also, as man, received a life which is devoid of beginning and end, although He received it in time. This power, the blessed one continues, CHRIST of an indissoluble life according to His human nature truly possessed even in the state of humiliation, because it pertains to the anointing, Acts 10, verse 38.

Now the anointing belongs to CHRIST from the moment of conception, at which time the κατοίκησις (indwelling) of the whole fullness of God took place bodily. Wherefore also Christ is called Lord as soon as he is born, Luke 2:11, nay, even when he still lay in the womb, Luke 1:43; yet he did not use that power of indissoluble life in that state incessantly and indefinitely according to it. For thus he could have received no passions and infirmities into himself, if he had wished to use the power of indissoluble life always and incessantly. For this removes hunger, thirst, fatigue, sleep, fear, sadness, death. Nor can its plenary use stand with the form of a servant, of which Phil. 2:7 seqq. For that requires the ἀδυναμίαν ζωῆς διαλύτη (the inability of a dissoluble life). In the state of exaltation, however, he uses this power of indissoluble life fully and perfectly according to his Human nature also, and he lives not only that life which consists of the union and glorification of soul and body, but that very infinite, Divine, beatifying life which the Father has in himself, John 5:26, and which he gave to the Son to have in himself. And just as our Savior was glorified with that glory which he had with the Father before the world was founded: so also he was quickened with that life which he had with the Father before the world was made, John 17:5.

Latin:

Ὃς ὀ κατὰ νόμον ἐντολῆς σαρκικῆς) Secundum jus il- lud (nam νόμος etiam jus significat, ut 1. Corinth. 7, 39. Exod. 12, 49.) quod venit ex præcepto dato carni, id est, hominibus mortalibus, quorum alter alteri succedit. Caro mortalem conditionem significat, ut supra V. 7.

Ἀλλὰ κατὰ δύναμιν ζωῆς ἀκαταλύτου) Per vim vitæ im- mortalis. Nam ideo Christus ad vitam immortalem perductus est, ut in æternum Sacerdos noster esset. Vi- de supra V. 5. 6. Dicit autem vitam ἀκατάλυτον, quia nunquam ab illo corpore discedit לא יקרע, Exod. 39, vers. 22.

Sensus est, qui non constitutus sit Sacerdos se- cundum legem vel normam mandati, quod in car- nalibus & temporariis tantum occupabatur, ut e- rant ceremoniæ externæ Leviticæ, sed secundum virtutem, quæ vitam insolubilem vel æternam operari posset. Quemadmodum prima comparatio con- cernebat tribum Sacerdotalem: Ita hæc intimio- rem ejusdem rationem & naturam, quod Sacerdo- tium Leviticum secundum legem, tenorem, regulam & modum mandati, quod tractabat cæremonialia, mundana, & externa, factũ vel comparatum fuerit:

Sacerdotium autem Melchisedecianum Christi vir- tutem ac potentiam requirat ejusmodi, quæ cir- ca cælestia & æterna occuparetur, quaque ipsa vita insolubilis & æterna nobis obtineri posset, & se- cundum ejusdem efficaciam peragatur. Sunt qui- dem, qui æternitatem sacerdotii respici velint, cum- que Theodoreto explicent, quod lex carnalis man- dati dicatur propter carnalem successionem, cui jux- ta præscriptum legis alligatum erat vetus sacer- dotium, quum contra Christus ita factus non sit Sa- cerdos, ut vel priori alicui succederet, vel alium post se relinqueret, sed ex virtute Divina, quæ vi- tam ei præstet insolubilem, hoc est, immortalem, ut successori non sit locus. Sed de eo infra agit Apostolus, v. 23. 24. 25. Non ergo idem censendus hic etiam tractare, ac pro diverso argumento ven- ditare vel adhibere, quod revera est unum idem- que, & eundem nervum concludendi habet. Alii nihil aliud significari volunt, quam Novi Testa- menti Sacerdotem Christum non secundum legem Mosaicam factum esse Sacerdotem, quippe quæ non alios ad sacerdotium admittit, quam qui sunt de semine Aaronis & tribu Levi, sed supra legem virtute ac voluntate Dei, qui est autor insolubilis, id est, æternæ vitæ. Sed illud argumentum de alia tribu jam tractarat Apostolus vers. 13. & 14. Nunc περισσότερόν τι addit. Rectius ergo Flacius in glossa: Alia ratio, inquit, aut probatio est muta- tionis sacerdotii & legis, à forma sanctificationum & sacrificiorum, quæ omnia in Aaronico sint externa ac caduca & per se minime efficacia: contra in hoc Sa- cerdote sint spiritualia, viva & salutaria: Ubi o- mnia constent vi aut potentia vitæ perpetuæ, nempe quia constant vera perpetuaq; justitia ac pace, unde quoque Rex justitiæ ac pacis dicitur. Utrumque sane à Deo ordinatum est: Sed tamen illud quidem con- stat in rebus terrenis caducisque, ut non perpetuo du- raturum: Istud vero in spiritualibus & æternis bo- nis. Quæ explicatio tum è voce Melchisedech, quæ Regem justitiæ infert, tum ex æternitate sa- cerdotii in Psalmo tradita, quæ nulla esset, nisi bo- na æterna afferret; tum imprimis è vers. 18. confir- matur, quod Aaroni cum sacerdotium ac fœdus ut lex (per se) nihil vere ac plene sanctificare potue- rit, adeoque necessario quærendum fuerit aliquid aliud, quod absolute perfecteque sanctificaret suos cultores. Sic etiam B. Gerhardus exposuit: Jux- ta virtutem vitæ insolubilis, hoc est, quod debeat habere spirituale ac efficax sacerdotium, per quod vi- tam æternam nobis acquireret, sicut & ipse manet in æternum: adducens in eam sententiam Chrysosto- mum & Theophylactum, quod sic explicent hoc comparationis vel oppositionis membrum, qui non sit creatus Sacerdos secundum legem carna- lem, hoc est, infirmam, in qua multa erant manda- ta ceremoniarum corporalium, sed secundum vir- tutem seu potentiam vitæ indissolubilis, hoc est, acceptâ à Patre potestate conferendi suis vitam æter- nam. Quo etiam abit Osiander in paraphrasi, & paraphrasis Vinariensium Germanica. Johan. Ca- mero in myrothec. Evangel. ἐvτολὴ σαρκικὴ, in- quit, est præceptum offerendi sacrificium, cujus sa- crificii tota vis sita est in expiatione carnali, tota vis, inquam effectrix, ut idem hic Apostolus interpreta- tur, cap. 9, 13. Δύναμις ἀκαταλύτου ζωῆς est vis illa perfecta à Divinitate CHRISTI, qua effectum est, ut CHRISTUS non modo ipse vivat in æternum, sed & vitam in nos derivet. Et hoc item Apostolus interpretatur, cap. 9, 14. Certe δύναμις ἀκαταλύ- του ζωῆς, quæ in CHRISTO est, profecta est à Spi- ritu æterno, per quem sese obtulit Patri. Quæ magis conveniunt præsenti argumento Apostoli- co, quam illa Beza & Paræi, quod CHRISTUS vi indissolubilis vitæ, hoc est immediata Dei virtute ad immortalem vitam inauguratus sit, ut in æternum sacerdotio funginon cesset, quasi periphrasis æter- nitatis sit, opposita caducitati rituum & Sacerdo- tum legalium, quod isti morerentur, CHRI- STUS non moriturus indissolubili vita & sacer- dotio fruatur. Quibus gemina hîchabent Crel- lius & Schlichtingius. Quos etiam sequutus vi- detur Grocius hoc loco : B. Dorscheus : Ζωὴ, in- quit, ἀκατάλυτος non ea tantum est, quæ CHRISTO per resurrectionem data est, quæ posita, ipse non am- plius moritur, de qua etiam loquitur Apoc. 1. vers. 18. quæque omnibus ad regni gloriæ communionem resu- scitatis dabitur: Sed imprimis ea est, quæ essentia- liter Deo competit, qua ipse vivit in summa perfectio- ne, beatitudine, potentia, sapientiaq́, immensa atq́; infinita, quæq́, personaliter CHRISTO etiam secun- dum Humanam naturam competit. Patet id 1. ex verbis ipsis. Dicitur enim ζωὴ ἀκατάλυτος abso- lute & simpliciter. Unde nulla est necessitas, ut ad vitam creatam restringamus. 2. Persona ipsa ha- bet hanc vitam, hoc modo ἀκατάλυτον, juxta ea, quæ prolixe capite I. hujus epistolæ tractata sunt. Ita- que recte etiam ejus respectu dicitur esse Sacerdos. 3. Hæc vita ita ἀκατάλυτος esse dicitur, ut neque principium neq́ finem habeat, supra capitis hujus vers. 3. Hinc egressus ejus dicitur esse è diebus æternitatis, Mich. 5. vers. 2. & ratione vitæ hujus di- citur ἀρχὴ ὴ τέλος, πρῶτος ὴ ἔσχατος, Apoc. 1. vers. 8. & 17. 4. Vita in sensu absoluto ἀκατά- λυτος maximopere ad præcellentiam hujus Sacer- dotis spectat. Hoc enim modo infinita distantia in- ter Sacerdotem hunc & Sacerdotes Leviticos consti- tuitur. Sic enim non gradu tantum ζωῆς beatificæ distat, sed toto genere. Atqui hoc est institutum Apostolicum in summum perfectionis gradum Sa- cerdotem Christianæ religionis constituere, imo su- pra omnem perfectionis finitæ conditionem eandem collocare. Hujus ζωῆς ἀκαταλύτε CHRISTUS dicitur habere δύναμιν, propterea, quia non tan- tum ipse ζωῇ ἀκαταλύτῳ vivit, sed etiam δύναμιν habet aliis communicandi vitam seu in regno poten- tiæ, seu in regno gratiæ, seu in regno gloriæ, quia habet omnem potentiam in cœlo & in terra Matth. XXVIII. vers. 18. & potestatem omnis carnis, Johan. XVII. vers. 2. De qua δυνάμει supra cap. 1. v. 3. cap. II. vers. 5. seqq. cap. III. vers. 6. pluribus actum est. Secundum Humanam naturam CHRISTO eti- am hanc δύναμιν ζωῆς ἀκαταλύτε communica- tam esse, partim ex eo constat, quia CHRISTUS etiam secundum Humanam naturam in eo opponi- tur Sacerdotibus Leviticis, quod non sit secun- dum legem mandati carnalis Sacerdos, unde ne- cessario sequitur, illum etiam secundum Huma- nam naturam etiam Sacerdotem secundum poten- tiam vitæ indissolubilis : partim ex eo, quia se- cundum eam naturam Sacerdos est juxta poten- tiam vitæ indissolubilis, secundum quam ex Juda ortus est vers. 14. partim ex eo, quia esse Sacer- dotem secundum potentiam vitæ indissolubilis, in- terpretatur id, quod Psalm. CX. vers. 4. dicitur Sa- cerdos in æternum; quoniam, qui potentiam vitæ indissolubilis habet simpliciter & absolute, is rectis- sime potest in æternum Sacerdos constitui, utpote plane immutabilis. Quapropter CHRISTUS etiam, qua homo, vitam accepit, quæ initii & fi- nis expers est, licet illam in tempore acceperit. Hanc δύναμιν, pergit postea, ὁ Μακαρίτης ζωῆς ἀκαταλύτε CHRISTUS secundum Humanam naturam in statu exinanitionis etiam revera ha- buit, quia pertinet ad unctionem, Actor. 10. v. 38.

Unctio autem CHRISTO competit a momento con- ceptionis, quo facta est κατοίκησις omnis plenitudinis Dei corporaliter. Quapropter & Christus Domi- nus dicitur statim atque natus est, Luc. 2, 11. imo cum adhuc in utero jacuit, Luc. 1, 43. neque tamen secun- dum eam potentia illa indissolubilis vitæ in isto statu usus fuit incessanter & indefinenter. Sic enim pas- siones & infirmitates nullas in se recipere potuisset, si semper & incessanter vitæ indissolubilis potentia uti voluisset. Hæc enim tollit famem, sitim, fatigatio- nem, somnum, metum, tristitiam, mortem. Neque ejus plenarius usus stare potest cum forma servi, de qua Phil. 2, 7. seqq. Illa enim requirit ἀδυναμίαν ζωῆς διαλύτη. In statu vero exaltationis plenarie perfecteque utitur secundum Humanam naturam eti- am ista potentia vitæ indissolubilis, vivitque non ea tantum vita, quæ ex unione & glorificatione animi & corporis constat, sed ipsa infinita, Divina, beatifi- cavita, quam Pater habet in semetipso, Johan. 5, 26. quamque dedit Filio habere in semetipso. Et quem- admodum glorificatus est ea gloria Salvator noster, quam habuit apud Patrem ante mundum conditum: Ita etiam vivificatus est ea vita, quam apud Patrem habuit, antequam mundus factus est, Joh. 17, 5.

## 7:17
Verse 17.

Μαρτυρεῖ γάρ (For he bears witness) David shows that what he said is true. Μαρτυρεῖν here as in Romans 3:12. In the Manuscript μαρτυρεῖται γάρ, this testimony is rendered to him. Ὅτι σὺ ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδέκ (That you are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek) He presses that word לְעוֹלָם, which elsewhere indeed signifies a long time, but here eternity: For who can be the Lord of King David, unless he who is heavenly, and consequently eternal. Ὅτι here is that of one reciting.

The Davidic testimony is not properly employed in this verse to prove the eternity of the Priesthood: But to prove that efficacy of the priesthood of Christ, of which he had treated in verse 16, which extends itself into eternity, which is derived and overflows from this his eternal priesthood. For how would he be a Priest forever, if the work and effect of his priesthood were terminated by perishable and temporary things, or ended with this age? By consequence, therefore, the Apostle elicits that from the Davidic testimony, which he here so diligently presses, and from which he draws such diverse arguments, but by an invincible reason, concerning both the dignity and the necessity of the Melchizedekian priesthood of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Μαρτυρεῖ γάρ ) David ostendit verum esse quod di- xo. Μαρτυρεῖν hic ut Roman. 3, 12. In Manuscripto μαρτυρεῖται γάρ, redditur illi hoc testimonium. Ὅτι σὺ ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδέκ ) Premit illam vocem לְעוֹלָם, quæ alibi quidem lon- gum tempus significat, at hic æternitatem: Quis enim potest esse Dominus Davidis Regis, nisi qui sit cœlestis, ac proinde æternus. Ὅτι hic est recitantis.

Non adhibetur proprie Davidicum testimo- nium hoc quidem versu ad æternitatem Sacerdo- tii probandam: Sed ad probandam illam efficaci- am sacerdotii Christi, de qua egerat vers. 16. quæ se in æternitatem porrigit, quæ deducitur & re- dundat ex hoc æterno ejus sacerdotio. Nam quomodo in æternum esset Sacerdos, si opus & ef- fectus sacerdotii ejus terminaretur rebus caducis & temporariis, vel cum hoc seculo finiretur? Per consequentiam ergo id elicit Apostolus e testimo- nio Davidico, quod hic tam sedulo premit, & ex quo tam diversa argumenta, sed invicta ratione de- promit cum dignitatis tum necessitatis sacerdotii Christi Melchisedeciani.

## 7:18
Verse 18.

Ἀθέτησις μὲν γὰρ γίνεται προαγούσης ἐντολῆς (For there is a setting aside of the commandment going before) Now he begins to show that it is no wonder that that law of Moses, a part of which was the Levitical law, has been abolished. Ἀθετεῖν here is not to violate, as elsewhere, but to remove by authority, as Galatians 3, verse 15. Ἐντολὴν here he calls the whole collection of commandments. Προάγειν here is to precede, as 1 Tim. 1, verse 18. The law had preceded Christ by many centuries, namely from the times of Moses. Διὰ τὸ ἀυτῆς ἀσθενὲς καὶ ἀνωφελές (Because of its weakness and unprofitableness) Namely, compared relatively. It is no wonder that the more imperfect yield to the more perfect.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Ἀθέτησις μὲν γὰρ γίνεται προαγούσης ἐντολῆς ) Jam in- cipit ostendere, nihil mirum esse, quod lex illa Mosis, cujus pars erat lex Levitica abolita est. Ἀθετεῖν hic non est violare, ut alibi, sed pro imperio tollere, ut Galat. 3, vers. 15. Ἐντολὴν hic vocat totam congeriem ἐντολῶν. Προάγειν hic est præcedere, ut 1. Tim. 1. vers. 18. Præ- cesserat lex Christum multis seculis, a Mosis nempe tem- poribus. Διὰ τὸ ἀυτῆς ἀσθενὲς καὶ ἀνωφελές ) Nempe compa- rata comparate. Non mirum est, imperfectiora perfe- ctioribus cedere.

## 7:19
Verse 19.

Οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐτελείωσεν ὁ νόμος (For the law made nothing perfect) It did not lead men to that true and internal righteousness, but stopped within rites and external deeds. No one in those times was to be compared with Apostolic virtues, because if any approached near, they did not owe that to the law, but to grace, as if borrowed and anticipated from the Gospel. See Rom. 8:3, Gal. 3:2, 21, where see the things said. Οὐδὲν, that is οὐδένα, by a locution such as above v. 7 and John 6:36.

That which he had said concerning the virtue and efficacy of the priesthood of Christ, the Apostle pursues and confirms further from the abolition and the cause of the abolition of the Levitical law, to which the Aaronic priesthood belonged, which namely was eventually to be abolished, as being in itself weak and useless, by its own virtue or αὐτενεργητικῶς (by its own operation) it did not lead men to that true and internal righteousness, but viewed in itself and by itself it stopped within rites and external deeds. But it is not therefore to be concluded that no one in those times of the enduring carnal law was to be compared with Apostolic virtues, as far as the sanctifying gifts, of which he treats here, are concerned. What Grotius adds about those who approached near can be admitted in a sound sense. Although through the ceremonial law no one by itself attained true righteousness. Yet the Evangelical promises were not lacking to the ancients: nay, that which we have fulfilled in the Gospel was figured by that law. Those figures, therefore, were not indeed by their own virtue, but solely in the virtue of the antitype, which they shadowed forth, the unique expiatory sacrifice of the New Testament, which, looked upon or called into use by the ancients through true faith, were useful to them. They are weak in themselves and useless for purging our souls from sins, for reconciling us to God, for justifying us before God, and for obtaining eternal life. The word ἀθέτησις is less correctly rendered by the Vulgate as reprobation, since it signifies abrogation, nor was a reprobation of the law made, as it proceeded from God, but an abrogation as of something temporary and in a certain respect weak and useless, to a succeeding stronger and life-giving one, which that one shadowed forth. The particle γὰρ, however, is not to be considered as redundant with Estius, but rather it should be judged that, although τὸ γὰρ is causal in itself, yet added to the word μὲν, it often signifies not so much something as it ornaments the speech, which Estius himself prefers. B. Dorscheus explains these things more fully on this passage: That which is said to be abrogated is the preceding commandment, that is, the Old Testament on account of its weakness and uselessness, is to be understood of the Old Testament considered in itself, but not insofar as the Gospel was dominated under it, and by Divine ordination its ceremonies and sacrifices were applied to the benefits of the New Testament. For in this respect τὸ ἀσθενὲὲς καὶ ἀνωφελὲς cannot be attributed to them. For in this way, both the moral law, which was comprised under the Old Testament and had been its basis, and the παιδαγωγὸς εἰς Χριστὸν, Gal. 3, 24 [sic], as well as the ceremonial law placed in the sacraments and sacrifices, even if insofar as it served the moral law it profited nothing for salvation, but taught the imputation and slaughter necessary for sinners, nevertheless insofar as God in that same foreshadowing willed the punishments of sins to be borne by Christ, and by a most sweet exchange and substitution to be transferred from the human race onto the one Mediator, insofar as that foreshadowing was as it were a certain visible sermon, which confirmed the pure Gospel to us, to that extent the Old Testament was entirely valid and useful; indeed, by its primary institution it was a rigorous legal covenant, convicting of the debts of Divine justice to be performed from received powers. But by a second Divine ordination it was directed so that it might foreshadow and confirm the benefits of the New Testament. For the matter stands thus: The law had been impressed upon the minds of man in creation, and the same was afterwards repeated in the schools of the Patriarchs. Man having fallen into sin, the Only-begotten Son of GOD brought the Gospel into Paradise, which itself also sounded in the Patriarchal Church to the great consolation of the afflicted. Both doctrines had to be confirmed, and as it pleased Divine wisdom, to be promulgated and corroborated by a solemn Testament. The doctrine concerning the law was promulgated and corroborated by a solemn Testament after the departure of the Israelites from Egypt. Where At Sinai, the law was both moral, repeated, and ceremonial, recollected, and immediately forensic, constituted for the preservation of the Israelite Republic, and the whole covenant between GOD and men was confirmed by sacrifices and the shedding and sprinkling of blood. This rigorous covenant demanded obedience, wherefore, when it fell upon men who, through the fall, were destitute of the powers of obeying, it was called, and of itself was, the διακονία τẽ θανάτε ἐν γράμμασιν &c. 2 Cor. 3:7, and the killing letter, that is, the messenger of death, v. 6, Rom. 8:3. The New Testament was solemnly promulgated and confirmed by Christ, who, the shadows being removed, brought the body, Col. 2:17. Heb. 10:2, and thus he sealed everything with his blood most lavishly poured out, so that even before the solemn promulgation of the New Testament, the Evangelical promises were exhibited in a certain order, as he willed by the ministry of the Old Testament, which of itself was a ministry of the killing letter, and through it he adumbrated and applied that which was contained in the Evangelical promises. Hence, when the law is said to contain a shadow of future goods, that shadow is not vain and ineffectual, but, by Divine ordination, a useful medium for confirming and sealing the Evangelical promises. For it is a shadow, but illuminated by Divine kindness with Evangelical promises. Thus also must it be said concerning circumcision. For even if that act, whether it be considered physically or legally, has no salvific efficacy, because it is nevertheless subordinated to the Evangelical promises by Divine dispensation, and as it were leaning upon them, it has thence become a σφραγὶς τῆς δικαιοσύνης & πίσεως. Moreover, to be a σφραγὶς and of righteousness is an organ of the efficacy of Divine grace, if it be said of the means... For σφραγὶς in Divine matters always denotes the efficacy of either conferring or confirming an Evangelical promise. Conf. John 3:33, ch. 6:27, Eph. 1:13, ch. 4:30, 2 Cor. 1:22, 2 Tim. 2:9, Rev. 7:2, 3, 4, 5 & seqq., ch. 9:4. Furthermore, when the Old Testament is called ἀσθενὲς κὶ ἀνωφελὲς, it is looked at primarily with regard to acquisition. For the Priests of the Old Testament could not recover and acquire salvation and life lost through sins by their sacrifices, nor merit them through all their legal wisdom, for which reason also above, verse 11, and below, verse 19, τελείωσις is denied to the Old Testament and the law: On the contrary, the New Testament had and has an everlasting Priest to whom the finding of eternal redemption belongs, Heb. 9:12, and to him alone must the virtue and efficacy of acquiring be attributed. The Apostle looks to this when he attributes to him an ἐπεισαγωγὴν κρείττονος ἐλπίδος, an introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God.

An introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God) Earthly promises do not work a contempt of death, but a better hope of eternal and heavenly life works it. Hence such frequent martyrdoms: That ἐπὶ in ἐπεισαγωγὴ signifies something later, as in ἐπιδιατάσσεται, Gal. 3:15. And it is a sufficiently frequent expression. After the introduction of a better hope, for a better hope introduced after. For ἐγγίζομεν in the Manuscript is ἐγγίζωμεν, through which we may be able to draw near to God, that is, be rendered truly pious. For this is ἐγγίζειν Θεῷ, Soph. 3:2 & ch. 4:8. Moreover, it is a word properly Priestly, as can be seen in Ezek. 42:13, ch. 43:19. And Christians, through Christ the high Priest, have been made Priests, 1 Pet. 2:5, Rev. 1:6.

This sentence can cohere with the preceding in two ways: 1. In a composite sense, so that the discourse is still about the same law, which, even if it were weak and useless, because it did not suffice for salvation, nor did it confer it by itself, yet it must have been an ἐπεισαγωγὴ of a better hope, which we have in the priesthood of CHRIST: Which sense the blessed Hunnius embraces; so that it may be a mitigation of what he seemed to have said rather harshly about the law: This uselessness, however, is not to be taken as if the ceremonial law were simply and in every respect useless (for it had its uses and ends, on account of which it was commanded by GOD and enjoined to be observed by the Israelite people), but he calls it useless in a certain respect, namely, with regard to eternal salvation, which the priesthood of the Old Testament could not confer by itself, just as those sacrifices were not able to grant justice, sanctification, and salvation to men ex opere operato. Therefore, all that law was, as the Apostle proceeds to explain, a certain introduction, and as it were a χειραγωγία or pedagogical leading by the hand to a better hope: insofar as it adumbrated the Pontiff of the New Testament, CHRIST JESUS, with his priesthood, and by showing him from afar to believers, introduced them to that better hope. Which explanation Pareus acknowledges to be also Calvin's, and not inconvenient. 2. In an opposite sense, so that it is understood not of the law, but of the priesthood of CHRIST, namely, that it perfected men, when the law could not perfect them, so that here the word ἐτελείωσεν is to be repeated from the common: And a better hope is called the Melchisedecian priesthood of CHRIST, which is so named either by its effect, because it makes us hope better concerning God's grace toward us than the old legal one: Or objectively, because it was a hoped-for good already long since far more excellent than the good of the law. Which sense Pareus prefers, and the blessed Gerhardus approves: By ἐπεισαγωγὴν κρείττονος ἐλπίδος, the superinduction of a better hope, he understands the priesthood of Christ, which was superinduced upon the Levitical priesthood, and raised the people of God into a better hope, because through it we are truly sanctified and reconciled to God. Although, however, we admit that the introduction of a better hope renders us perfect, and we judge that this sense is to be preferred here, we do not think that the priesthood itself is described by the introduction of a better hope, but that the same is brought about through it. For a better hope of eternal goods was not introduced by the law or the Levitical priesthood, but by the Gospel and the Melchisedecian priesthood of Christ, since the former had to be abrogated because it could not provide that, but the latter had to succeed, because it procured the same for us. From the fact that a new Priest arises, as from Thomas Estius, who was made not according to the law of a carnal commandment: there follows the abolition of that law. And from the fact that he was made according to the power of an indissoluble life, there follows the introduction of a better hope. That hope is that by which we draw near to God, to the eternal fruition of God in the other life. Nor yet is it to be believed with Grotius, that only earthly promises were made in the Law and the Levitical Priesthood. For sacrifices were offered for the expiation and remission of sins, whence the contempt of death is much less to be denied to the faithful of the Old Testament, who besides those Levitical figures had express oracles concerning the grace of God, the remission of sins, and eternal salvation, nor were they destitute of the hope of a better and eternal life. That is not the point here; but it is taught only that the ceremonial law did not provide or effect that by its own power, or in that it was a law of carnal commandment. Therefore one must come to the unique Priest according to the order of Melchizedek, in whom we solidly possess that which the old Levitical priests with the ceremonial law only prefigured, bringing in themselves no perfection. We add the commentary of the blessed Dorscheus: It is noted: 1. what the better hope is, namely that of the Gospel itself. For the Law indeed provides a hope of salvation, but under the condition of remaining in all its precepts, Deut. 27:26, Gal. 3:10, and without the promise of the powers by which we might be able to render obedience to it, by which the Law is said to be weakened through the flesh, Rom. 8:3, because, of course, after the fall it fell upon a subject that is impotent and destitute of those powers which the Law, as being spiritual, Rom. 7:14—that is, dictating a spiritual and Divine life, such as it ought to have been in the state of integrity, Eph. 4:24—presupposes. Whence also a certain impotence of the Law appeared, insofar as it was made manifest that the Law indeed requires the perfection of obedience, but yet cannot communicate those powers by which it might be effected. And this is what is said in Gal. 3:21, that the Law was not given which is able to give life, that is, to effectively confer upon us that very thing which is required for a Divine and spiritual life. Hence the Law cannot bring it about that we are able to possess the hope given to us by it; nay, on the contrary, it overwhelms us with a curse, insofar as it is considered from its primary institution, Gal. 3:10. Therefore, the better hope is that of the Gospel, as it is without the works of the Law, Acts 15:9, 10, 11, which are intolerable without the curse, without a rigorous condition, and moreover it most liberally confers all good things without any merit or cooperation of ours; because whatever burden and labor there is, the Priest of the New Testament himself bears it, Isa. 43:11.

2. What kind of ἐπαγγελίη (promise) it is, namely of the actual exhibition of Christ. That hope was indeed better, made immediately after the fall, which Abel also looked upon in his sacrifice, Heb. 11:4, and Enoch embraced, v. 5, and Abraham followed, v. 10, and the rest of the Patriarchs, v. 39. And the rays and structure of that hope indeed shone under the Old Testament, yet the ἐπαγγελία itself, that is, the plenary and most perfect exhibition of the promises, was made through CHRIST. Hence Gal.

3:15, it is called ἐλθοῦσα πίστις, the coming faith. Where faith is taken for the thing believed or that which is believed, but not for the act of believing or that by which one believes. For that is said to have come which was believed would come, even before it had come, when CHRIST came. Whence also his very advent is called φανέρωσις (manifestation), 1 Tim. 3:6, and ἐπιφάνεια (appearing), Tit. 2:2, and elsewhere. 3. What is the effect of the better hope, namely τελείωσις (perfection), which the Law could not provide, and the approach to God, of which Rom. 5:2, Heb. 10:19, 20, and above in chapter 4:16.

This third point can be called an argument of the necessity and dignity of a priesthood of a different order than the Levitical. The first was from the Davidic testimony accepted κατὰ γράμμα, or according to the express letter, concerning another and different priesthood, because it was predicted that it would be devolved into another tribe by a certain argument, because perfection was not obtained through it: The second from the consequence built from the same concerning the cause of the abolished ceremonial law through the ordination of another priesthood, namely its infirmity and uselessness. The third, therefore, now flows again from the letter, namely from the eternity of the Melchizedekian priesthood, which he had touched upon in the προτάσει (proposition), v. 8, and now calls into use and applies. But it pleases me, with Flacius, to establish here, from the demonstrated necessity of the Melchizedekian priesthood for the explanation of the same, three illustrious prerogatives of the New Testament, and of this Priest and priesthood over the Levitical, which are commemorated here until the end of the chapter: The first of which is that an oath of God is added to this priesthood, by which both his readiness and kindness in helping us, and also the certainty of this covenant, are indicated. The second, that this Priest is immortal, so that he may be able to help most fully forever. The third, that this Priest is devoid of all sin: Whereas, on the contrary, the other priesthood lacks the firmness of an oath, and the immortality and supreme holiness of the priest. To the word καθ' ὅσον (inasmuch as) in v. 20, corresponds v. 22 κατὰ τοσοῦτον (by so much), whence v. 21 is to be included in a parenthesis. Inasmuch as he was not made Priest without an oath; by so much he was made the sponsor of a better Testament. That Christ was constituted Priest by an oath signified that he has an eternal priesthood, whereas the Levitical priests were made priests without an oath, which signified that their priesthood would cease. Nor indeed is Schlichting's ψευδερμηνεία (false interpretation) to be admitted, which is utterly contrary to the letter of the text and the Apostolic demonstration, as if it is called an eternal priesthood only because it lasts for a very long time, and for as long as there is any place for a priesthood, or as long as the state of things will not be so changed that there is no use at all for a Priest, which he says will happen when the people of Christ are translated into heaven and will no longer need any expiations for sins. To which the blessed Dorscheus responds: There is not only one use of the priesthood of Christ here. Just as, indeed, the Priest of the Old Testament, and the priesthood were enjoyed not only by those to be expiated, but also by those already expiated, who penetrated more and more into the fruit and beauty of the priesthood: So also, much more will it be permitted to enjoy the priesthood of Christ, even when the people of Christ will no longer need the expiation of Christ, namely when we shall contemplate the Priest face to face, when he will exhibit the power and amplitude and infinite dignity of his priesthood by clear vision, when it will be permitted to look into all the secrets and mysteries of the most excellent sacrifice, which will happen in eternity and for eternity; there the fruit of the priesthood of Christ will be most sweet. To these things, the use of the priesthood of Christ is not only for the ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν (recapitulation), Eph. 1:10, and for making εἰρήνην (peace), Col. 1:20, but also for preserving it forever, and the fruit of the priesthood of Christ will be that perennial union and communion with the Most Holy Trinity in supreme blessedness. But those things indeed teach the eternity of the fruit of Christ's priesthood: not the eternity of the priesthood itself. To which the eternal intercession of Christ our Priest contributes entirely, to which that preservation of the elect in eternal glory must be attributed, no less than to the merit of Christ and the expiatory sacrifice made on the altar of the cross. For it is not to be admitted that the intercession at the right hand of God will cease when the kingdom of grace is concluded. Thus, certainly, the Pontificate of CHRIST would not be eternal, which is contrary both to David and to the Apostle.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐτελείωσεν ὁ νόμος ) Non perduxit homi- nes ad justitiam illam veram & internam, sed intra ri- tus & facta externa constitit. Nemo illis temporibus fuit virtutibus Apostolicis conferendus, quod si qui pro- pe accessere, non legi id debebant, sed gratiæ, velut de Evangelio pro mutuo sumptæ atque prærogatæ. Vide Rom. 8, 3. Gal. 3, 2. 21. ubi dicta vide. Οὐδὲν, id est οὐδένα loquutione qualis supra v. 7. & Joh. 6, 36.

Illud, quod dixerat de virtute atque efficacia sa- cerdotii Christi, persequitur & confirmat ulterius Apostolus ex abolitione ac causa abolitionis legis Leviticæ, ad quam pertinebat sacerdotium Aaro- nicum, quod nempe eadem abolenda tandem fue- rit, utpote per se infirma & inutilis, suapte virtute vel αὐτενεργητικῶς non perduxit homines ad ju- stitiam illam veram & internam, sed in se ac per se spectata intra ritus & facta externa constitit. Sed non ideo concludendum, neminem illis temporibus durantis legis carnalis virtutibus Apostolicis, quan- tum ad dona sanctificantia, de quibus hic agitur, conferendum fuisse. Quæ addit Grotius de iis, qui prope accessere, sensu sano admitti possunt. Quanquam per legem ceremonialem per se nemo justitiam veram consequutus sit. Non defuere tamen veteribus promissiones Evangelicæ: imo fi- guratum fuit lege illa, quod in Evangelio habemus impletum. Figuræ ergo illæ non sane propriâ virtute, sed unice in virtute antitypi, quod adum- brarunt, sacrificii unici expiatorii Novi Testa- menti, qua vera fide à veteribus spectatæ vel in u- sum vocatæ iisdem utiles fuere. Infirma per se sunt & inutiles ad animas nostras à peccatis pur- gandas, ad nos Deo reconciliandos, ad nos coram Deo justificandos, & ad vitam æternam obtinen- dam. Vox ἀθέτησις à Vulgato minus recte reddi- tur reprobatio, quum abrogationem significet, nec reprobatio facta sit legis, utpote à Deo profectæ, sed abrogatio ceu temporariæ & certo respectu in- firmæ atque inutilis, succedenti firmiori atque sa- lutiferæ, quam illa adumbrabat. Particula vero γὰρ non pro irreptitia habenda cum Estio, sed po- tius ita censendum, τὸ γὰρ etsi per se causale sit, ad- ditum tamen vocabulo μὲν, sæpe non tam signifi- care aliquid, quam sermonem ornare, quod Estius ipse præfert. Explicat hæc plenius B. Dorscheus in hunc locum: Quod dicitur abrogatum esse man- datum præcedens, hoc est Veteris Testamenti propter ipsius imbecillitatem & inutilitatem, de Veteri Testa- mento in se considerato inteligendum est, non autem quatenus sub eo dominatum est Evangelium, & ex Divina ordinatione ceremoniæ & sacrificia ejus ad- hibita fuerunt ad applicanda bona Novi Testamen- ti. Hoc enim respectu τὸ ἀσθενὲς καὶ ἀνωφελὲς ipsis tribui nequit. Hoc enim modo tum etiam lex mo- ralis, quæ sub Veteri Testamento comprehensa est, & basis ejus fuerat, & παιδαγωγὸς εἰς Χριστὸν, Gal. 2, 23. tum etiam lex ceremonialis in sacramentis & sacrifi- ciis posita, etiamsi quatenus legi morali subserviebat, ad salutem nihil proficeret, sed imputationem, ma- stationemque peccatoribus necessariam doceret, atta- men quatenus Deus in eadem adumbratione voluit pœnas peccatorum à Christo toleratas, & suavissima permutatione atque substitutione à genere humano in unum Mediatorem translatas quatenus insuper ista adumbratio fuit quasi visibilis quædam concio, quæ merum nobis Evangelium confirmaret, eatenus o- mnino Vetus Testamentum validum atque utile fuit, nimirum ex primaria sui institutione fœdus rigoro- sum erat legale, convictivum de debitis justitiæ Di- vinæ ex viribus acceptis præstandis. Secunda au- tem Divina ordinatione eo directum est, ut & ad- um ret & confirmaret beneficia Novi Testa- menti. Sic enim se res habet: Lex in creatione mentibus hominis fuerat impressa, eademque postea in scholis Patriarcharum repetita. Homine in pec- catum prolapso Evangelium in Paradisum attulit Unigenitus DEI Filius, quod ipsum etiam in Ec- clesia Patriarchali magno afflictorum solatio so- nuit. Utrique doctrina confirmanda fuerat, & uti sapientiæ Divinæ placuit, solenni Testamento promulganda & corroboranda. Doctrina de lege promulgata, & solenni Testamento corroborata fuit post exitum Israelitarum ex Ægypto. Ubi è Sinai lex tum moralis repetita, tum ceremonialis recollecta & actutum forensis pro conservanda Israe- litarum Republica constituta, & totum fœdus inter DEUM & homines sacrificiis & sanguinis profu- sione, atque conspersione confirmatum. Hoc fœdus rigorosum postulavit obedientiam, quapropter cum in homines incidisset per lapsum viribus obediendi de- stitutos vocabatur, & ex se διακονία erat τẽ θανάτε ἐν γράμμασιν &c. 2. Corinth. 3, 7. atque litera occi- dens, hoc est mortis nuntia, v. 6. Rom. 8, 3. Novum Testamentum solenniter promulgatum & confirma- tum fuit à Christo, qui umbris sublatis corpus attulit, Coloss. 2, 17. Ebr. 10, 2. atque adeo sanguine suo largis- sime effuso omnia obsignavit, ut tamen etiam ante Novi Testamenti solennem promulgationem promis- siones Evangelicæ certo quodam exhiberentur ordine, uti voluit ministerio Veteris Testamenti, quod ex se ministerium literæ occidentis erat, & per illud adum- brabat & applicabat id, quod promissionibus Evange- licis continebatur. Hinc quando lex dicitur um- bram continere futurorum bonorum, non est ea um- bra vana atque inefficax, sed ex ordinatione Divina medium utile ad confirmandas & obsignandas pro- missiones Evangelicas. Est enim umbra, sed pro- missionibus Evangelicis ex Divina benignitate illu- strata. Sic & de circumcisione dicendum est. Eti- amsi enim actus ille, si vel physice consideretur, vel legaliter, nullam habeat efficaciam salvificam, quia tamen promissionibus Evangelicis ex Divina dis- pensatione subordinatus est, & quasi innixus exinde factus est σφραγὶς τῆς δικαιοσύνης & πίσεως. Esse autem σφραγίδα & δικαιοσύνης est efficacia Divinæ gratiæ organon, si de mediis id dicatur... Σφραγὶς enim in rebus Divinis semper efficaciam seu confe- rendæ seu confirmandæ promissionis Evangelicæ de- notat. Conf. Johan. 3, 33. cap. 6, 27. Ephes. 1. v. 13. cap. 4, 30. 2. Corinth. 1, 22. 2. Timoth. 2, 9. Apoc. 7, 2. 3. 4. 5. & seqq. cap. 9, 4. Præterea cum Vetus Testamentum ἀσθενὲς κὶ ἀνωφελὲς dicitur, ad ac- quisitionem imprimis respicitur. Nimirum Sacer- dotes Veteris Testamenti salutem & vitam per pec- cata deperditam recuperare & acquirere per sacrifi- cia sua, nec promereri per universam legalem sa- pientiam poterant, quo s. etiam supra vers. 11. & infra vers. 19. τελείωσις Veteri Testamento denega- tur & legi: Ex adverso Novum Testamentum Sa- cerdotem habuit & habet sempiternum cui conve- nit inventio æternæ redemptionis Ebr. 9. vers. 12. & unice virtus atque efficacia acquirendi tribuenda est. Huc respicit Apostolus, cum illi tribuit ἐπεισ- αγωγὴν κρείττονος ἐλπίδος introductionem melio- ris spei, per quam appropinquamus Deo.

Ἐπεισαγωγὴ δὲ κρείττονος ἐλπίδος, δι' ἧς ἐγγίζομεν τῷ Θεῷ) Promissa terrestria non operantur mortis con- temptum, sed eum operatur spes melior vitæ æternæ atque cœlestis. Inde tam crebra martyria: Illud ἐπὶ in ἐπεισαγωγὴ significat posterius aliquid, ut in ἐπιδια- τάσσεται, Gal. 3, 15. Et est loquutio satis frequens. Post introductio spei melioris, pro spes melior post intro- ducta. Pro ἐγγίζομεν in Manuscripto est ἐγγίζωμεν, per quam ad Deum prope accedere possimus, id est, vere pii reddi. Hoc enim est ἐγγίζειν Θεῷ, Soph. 3, 2. & cap. 4, 8. Est autem vox proprie Sacerdotalis, ut videre est Ezech. 42, 13. c. 43, 19. Et Christiani per Christum summum Sacerdotem facti Sacerdotes, 1. Petr. 2. vers. 5. Apoc. 1. vers. 6.

Potest bifariam hæc sententia cum præceden- ti cohærere, 1. in sensu composito, ut de eadem lege sermo adhuc sit, quæ etsi infirma & inutilis fuerit, quod non suffecerit ad salutem, nec eam per se contulerit, ἐπεισαγωγὴ tamen esse debuerit spei melioris, quam in CHRISTI sacerdotio ha- bemus: Quem sensum B. Hunnius amplectitur; ut sit mitigatio ejus, quod de lege duriuscule vi- debatur dixisse: Hæc vero inutilitas non ita acci- piatur, quasi simpliciter & omni ex parte inutilis fuerit lex ceremonialis (habuit enim ea suos usus & fines, propter quos à DEO præcepta, & populo Israe- litico observanda injuncta est) sed inutilem appel- lat secundum quid, nempe respectu salutis æternæ, quam Veteris Testamenti Sacerdotium conferre non potuit per se, quemadmodum nec sacrificia illa ex opere operato justitiam, sanctificationem & salutem tribuere hominibus valuerunt. Fuit ergo tota illa lex, ut Apostolus pergit explicare, quædam introdu- ctio, & quasi χειραγωγία seu pædagogica manuductio ad spem potiorem: quatenus Pontificem Novi Te- stamenti CHRISTUM JESUM cum ipsius sacer- dotio adumbravit, eumque credentibus eminus mon- strando ad potiorem illam spem illos introduxit. Quam explicationem etiam Calvini esse, nec in- commodam agnoscit Pareus. 2. In sensu opposito, ut non de lege, sed de CHRISTI sacerdotio intel- ligatur, quod nempe illud perfecerit homines, quum lex perficere non potuerit, ut hic verbum ἐτελείωσεν ἀπὸ κοινοῦ repetendum sit: Et spes melior vocetur sacerdotium CHRISTI Melchisedecia- num, quod ita nuncupetur vel effectione, quia facit nos melius sperare de Dei erga nos gratia, quam vetus legale: Vel objective, quia fuit bonum spe- ratum jam olim longe præstantius, quam bonum legis. Quem sensum Pareus præfert, & appro- bat B. Gerhardus: Per ἐπεισαγωγὴν κρείττονος ἐλ- πίδος superinductionem melioris spei intelligit sa- cerdotium Christi, quod Levitico sacerdotio superin- ductum est, & in spem meliorem populum Dei erexit, quia per illud vere sanctificamur & Deo reconcilia- mur. Quanquam vero admittamus introductio- nem spei melioris nos perfectos reddere, eumque sensum hic præferendum esse censeamus, non ta- men sacerdotium ipsum per introductionem spei me- lioris describi, sed per illud eandem fieri existima- mus. Non enim lege aut sacerdotio Levitico in- troducta est spes melior æternorum bonorum, sed per Evangelium, & sacerdotium Christi Melchi- sedecianum, quum illud abrogandum ideo fuerit, quod præbere illam nequiverit, hoc autem succe- dere debuerit, quod eandem nobis conciliarit. Ex eo, quod surgat novus Sacerdos, ut ex Thoma Estius, qui non secundum legem mandati carnalis factus sit: Sequitur illius legis abolitio. Et ex eo quod factus sit secundum virtutem vitæ insolubilis, sequitur in- troductio spei melioris. Spes illa est, qua proxima- mus ad Deum, ad æternam Dei fruitionem in vita altera. Nec tamen ideo cum Grotio credendum, promissa tantum terrestria in lege & Sacerdotio Le- vitico facta esse. Nam sacrificia offerebantur in expiationem, & remissionem peccatorum, unde multo minus mortis contemptus fidelibus Veteris Testamenti denegandus, qui præter illas Leviticas figuras expressa oracula habebant de gratia DEI, remissione peccatorum, & salute æterna, neque de- stituti fuere spe melioris & æternæ vitæ. Id hic non agitur; sed docetur tantum non eam præstitis- se aut operatam esse legem ceremonialem virtute propria, vel qua erat lex mandati carnalis. Ideo ad Sacerdotem unicum secundum ordinem Mel- chisedech deveniendum, in quo illam solide habe- mus, quam tantum præfigurarunt veteres Sacer- dotes Levitici cum lege ceremoniali, per se nul- lam afferentes perfectionem. Addimus B. Dorschei commentarium: Nota- tur: 1. quæ sit melior spes, nempe Evangelii ipsius. Lex etenim spem facit salutis, sed sub con- ditione manendi in omnibus præceptis suis, Deut. 27, 26. Gal. 3, 10. & sine promissione virium, quibus obe- dientiam illi præstare possimus, qua scilicet infirmata lex dicitur per carnem, Rom. 8, 3. quia nimirum post lapsum incidit in subjectum impotens, iisq; destitutum viribus, quas lex utpote spiritualis, Rom. 7, 14. hoc est, spiritualem & Divinam vitam dictitans, qualis in statu integritatis esse debuit, Eph. 4, 24. præsupponit. Unde impotentia etiam quædam legis apparuit, qua- tenus scilicet, manifestum factum est, legem quidem requirere obedientiæ perfectionem, sed non posse ta- men eas communicare vires, quibus illa efficiatur. Et hoc est, quod Gal. 3, 21. dicitur, non esse datam le- gem, quæ possit vivificare, hoc est, idipsum nobis effi- caciter conferre, quod ad vitam Divinam & spiri- tualem requiritur. Hinc lex non potest efficere, ut spe ab ea nobis facta potiri possimus, imo ex adverso maledictione nos obruit, quatenus ex primaria sua institutione consideratur, Galat. 3, 10. Itaque melior spes est Evangelii, utpote quæ est sine operibus legis, Act. 15, 9. 10. 11. quæ sunt intolerabilia sine maledi- ctione, sine conditione rigorosa, atq; insuper omnia bo- na liberalissime confert sine ullo merito aut coopera- tione nostra; quia quicquid oneris est & laboris, Sa- cerdos Novi Testamenti ipse portat, Esa. 43. vers. 11.

2. Qualis sit ἐπαγγελίη, nimirum actualis exhibi- tionis Christi. Fuit equidem melior ista spes illico post lapsum facta, quam etiam in sacrificio suo intui- tus est Abel, Ebr. 11, 4. & complexus est Henoch, v. 5. & sectatus est Abraham, vers. 10. cæterique Patriar- chæ v. 39. Et radii quidem atque structura illius spei sub Veteri Testamento luxerunt, ipsa tamen ἐπαγ- γωλή, hoc est, plenaria perfectissimaque exhibitio pro- missorum facta est per CHRISTUM. Hinc Galat.

3, 15. dicitur ἐλθοῦσα πίστις veniens fides. Ubi fides sumitur pro re credita seu eo, quod creditur, non au- tem pro actu credendi, seu eo, quo creditur. Dicitur enim id venisse, quod credebatur venturum, etiam an- tequam venisset, cum venit CHRISTUS. Unde etiam ipsius adventus φανέρωσις vocatur, 1. Timoth. 3, 6. & ἐπιφάνεια Tit. 2, 2. & alibi. 3. Quis effe- ctus melioris spei, nimirum τελείωσις, quam lex præ- stare non poterat, & appropinquatio ad Deum, de qua Rom. 5, 2. Ebr. 10, 19. 20. & supra cap. 4, 16.

Tertium hoc dici potest argumentum necessita- tis & dignitatis sacerdotii alterius ordinis quam Levitici. Primum erat à testimonio Davidico κατὰ γεᾶμμα, vel secundum expressam literam ac- cepto, de alio & diverso sacerdotio, quia in aliam tribum devolutum iri prædictum erat certo ar- gumento, quod perfectio per illud non obtige- rit: Secundum à consequentia ex eodem exstru- cta de causa abolitæ legis cæremonialis per ordina- tionem alterius sacerdotii, infirmitate nempe ejus & inutilitate Tertium itaque jam iterum è lite- ra fluit, ex æternitate nempe sacerdotii Melchise- deciani, quam attigerat in προτάσει, v. 8. jam in usum vocat & applicat. Sed placet cum Flacio hic demonstrata necessitate sacerdotii Melchisedecia- ni ad explicationem ejusdem constituere tres præ- rogativas illustres Novi Testamenti, hujusque Sa- cerdotis & sacerdotii præ Levitico, quæ hic com- memorentur usq; ad finem capitis: Quarum pri- ma est, quod huic sacerdotio sit additum juramen- tum Dei, quo tum ipsius promptitudo benignitasq; in nobis juvandis, tum & hujus fœderis certitudo indica- tur. Secunda, quod iste Sacerdos sit immortalis, ut perpetuo juvare plenissime possit. Tertia, quod iste Sa- cerdos careat omni peccato: Cum contra alterum sa- cerdotium careat firmitate juramenti, immortalitate- que & summa sanctitate sacerdotis. Voci καθ' ὅ- σον v. 20. respondet v. 22. κατὰ τοσῦτον, unde v. 21. parenthesi includendus. In quantum non sine jurejurando factus est Sacerdos; in tantum fa- ctus est melioris Testamenti sponsor. Quod Chri- stus jurejurando Sacerdos constitutus est, signifi- cavit ipsum habere æternum sacerdotium, quod Levitici Sacerdotes sine jurejurando facti sunt Sa- cerdotes, significavit ipsorum sacerdotium cessa- turum. Nec vero admittenda Schlichtingii ψευδερ- μηνεία, literæ textus & demonstrationi Aposto- licæ prorsus contraria, quasi æternum sacerdotium dicatur tantum, quod longissimo tempore duret, & tamdiu, quamdiu aliquis sacerdotio sit locus, seu quam- diu rerum status ita non mutabitur, ut Sacerdotis nullus plane sit usus, quod futurum ait, cum Christi populus in cœlum translatus, nullis amplius pecca- torum expiationibus indigebit. Cui respondet B. Dorscheus: Non hic unus sacerdotii Christi usus est. Uti n. Sacerdote Vet. Test. & sacerdotio non tantum fruebantur expiandi, sed etiam expiati, qui magis ma- gisq;, in fructum atq; pulchritudinem sacerdotii pene- trabant: Sic etiam multo magis sacerdotio Christi li- cebit frui, etiam ubi non amplius expiatione Christi populus indigebit, nimirum ubi Sacerdotem de facie ad faciem contemplabimur, ubi ille sacerdotii sui vim atq; amplitudinem, infinitamq;, dignitatem clara vi- fione exhibebit, ubi omnis arcana & mysteria sacrifi- cii præstantissimi introspicere licebit, quod in æternita- te, & in æternum fiet, ibi sacerdotii Christi fructus e- rit dulcissimus. Ad hæc sacerdotii Christi usus non est tantum ad ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν Eph. 1, 10. & εἰρήνην, Col. 1, 20. faciendam, sed etiam in æternum conservan- dam, & fructus sacerdotii Christi erit illa perennis cum Sacrosancta Trinitate in summa beatitudine unio & communio. Sed illa æternitatem quidem fructus sa- cerdotii Christi docent: non a. æternitatem ipsiusmet sacerdotii. Ad quam omnino facit æterna Christi Sacerdotis nostri intercessio, cui illa conservatio in æ- terna gloria electorum accepta ferenda, ut non mi- nus, quam Christi merito & sacrificio expiatorio in ara crucis facto. Non enim admittendum quod intercessio ad dextram Dei cessatura sit, cum regnum gratiæ concludetur. Ita certe æter- nus non foret CHRISTI Pontificatus, quod & contra Davidem & contra Apostolum.

## 7:20
Verse 20.

Καὶ καθ' ὅσον ὐ χωρὶς ὁρκωμοσίας) He adds a third privilege of this priesthood in the Psalm, predicted over the legal one, that this was instituted with an oath, so that it might surely last forever: which is the force of sworn things. The word ὁρκωμοσία, composed of two words signifying the same thing, is found also below in verse 28. Plato in the neuter plural said ὅρκωμόσια, just as a certain place in Attica was called, where Theseus had sworn to the Amazons, as Plutarch records. In the Glossary, ὅρκωμοσία is swearing. Καθ' ὅσον here is 'by how much'. For it corresponds to that which follows, τοσῦτον. To such words, 'by how much' is accustomed to be placed before instead of 'because'. Thus in Tacitus: 'By how much richer, by so much the more unwarlike; by how much more abundant, by so much the greater; by how much more intent, by so much the more hidden; by how much more unknown to the barbarians, by so much the more tolerable.'

Οἱ μὲν γὰρ χωρὶς ὁρκωμοσίας εἰσὶν ἱερεῖς γεγονότες) Aaron and his descendants.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Καὶ καθ' ὅσον ὐ χωρὶς ὁρκωμοσίας) Tertium addit pri- vilegium hujus sacerdotii in Psalmo, prædicti præ legali, quod hoc institutum est cum jurejurando, ut scilicet sem- per duraret: quæ vis est rerum juratarum. Vox ὁρκω- μοσία ex duobus idem significantibus composita reperitur & infra 28. Plato in Neutro plurali dixit ὅρκωμόσια, quomodo & locus quidam dictus in Attica, ubi Theseus Amazonibus juraverat, Plutarcho memorante. In Glos- sario ὅρκωμοσία juratio. Καθ' ὅσον hic est quanto. Re- spondet enim ei, quod sequitur τοσῦτον. Talibus autem vocibus solet præponi quanto pro quia. Sic apud Taci- tum: Quanto dites, tanto magis imbelles; quanto inopi- ma, tanto majora; quanto intentas, tanto occultior; quan- to ignara barbaris, tanto tolernatiora.

Οἱ μὲν γὰρ χωρὶς ὁρκωμοσίας εἰσὶν ἱερεῖς γεγονότες) Aa- ron & posteri ejus.

## 7:21
Verse 21.

Οἱ δὲ μετὰ ὁρκωμοσίας) Namely, Christ, predicted in the Psalm. And it is understood by Zeugma, 'has been constituted' a priest.

Διὰ τῦ λέγοντος πρὸς αὐτόν. Ὤμοσε Κύριος, κὶ ὐ μεταμεληθήσεται· Σὺ ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδέκ) These words, ὤμοσε Κύριος, καὶ ὀ μεταμεληθήσεται, are to be read as a parenthesis. For that 'You are a priest' coheres with 'to him who says to him'. But so that it might be shown that that saying was made with an oath, therefore the preceding words of the Psalm had to be inserted. Οὐ μεταμεληθήσεται, 'he will not change what has been done', see above VI. 17. Repentance in God is nothing other than a change of a prior decision, Tertullian against Marcion II.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Οἱ δὲ μετὰ ὁρκωμοσίας) Nempe Christus in Psalmo præ- dictus. Et subauditur per Zeugma, sacerdotes constitutus est.

Διὰ τῦ λέγοντος πρὸς αὐτόν. Ὤμοσε Κύριος, κὶ ὐ με- ταμεληθήσεται· Σὺ ἱερεὺς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελ- χισεδέκ) Ista ὤμοσε Κύριος, καὶ ὀ μεταμεληθήσεται per παρένθεσιν legenda sunt. Nam illud σὺ ἱερεὺς cohæret cum τῷ λέγοντος πρὸς αὐτόν. Sed ut ostenderetur, di- ctum illud fuisse cum jurejurando, ideo & præcedentia Psalmi verba interjicienda fuere. Οὐ μεταμεληθήσεται non mutabit factum supra VI. 17. Pœnitentia in Deo nihil aliud, quam mutatio sententiæ prioris, Tertullianus ad- versus Marcionem II.

## 7:22
Verse 22.

Verf. 22.

By so much has Jesus become the surety of a better covenant) Jesus has become the sponsor of a better covenant, namely, a covenant that will endure eternally. Ἐγγυητὴς is a fidejussor, a sponsor in the Glossary. Cicero: 'He calls me as a sponsor,' that is, a fidejussor. Moses stood as sponsor for God in the old Law. Jesus for GOD in the new law. Each law and covenant contains: It has, besides the prescription of duty, also promises: Those less known are accustomed to provide a sponsor. And both Moses and JESUS were better known to men than GOD, who is inconspicuous. But CHRIST stood as sponsor, that is, he made us certain of the promise, not by words alone, but by the perpetual holiness of his life, the death endured for that reason, and very many miracles. This pertains to the fact that we should not wonder that the law has been changed.

Grotius received this gloss from the Socinians and gratified them with the same. For thus Schlichting, from the Crellian prelections on this passage: 'JESUS is called the sponsor of the covenant, because he stood as sponsor for us in the name of GOD, that is, he gave assurance that GOD would keep the promises of the covenant.'
