Not, indeed, as if he stood as sponsor for us to God, or took upon himself the payment of our debts. But on the contrary, that CHRIST is called a sponsor here, not because he stood as sponsor for us to God, but because he stood as sponsor to God for us, and took upon himself the payment of our debts, these things confirm: 1. The name ἔγγυος is derived from ἐγγυή, which according to Suidas is ἡ περί τινος ἀποδοχὴ, a taking upon oneself or a promise concerning some matter, by which someone takes something upon himself and promises that it will be performed by him. Which fits better with CHRIST standing as sponsor to God for us, and taking upon himself the payment of our debts. 2. God does not need a sponsor or fidejussor for himself, nor does he ever employ such a one, since he himself is the most truthful promiser and most worthy of all faith, nor could we be made more certain by another fidejussor than by God himself. 3. That Moses stood as sponsor for God in the old law is unwritten, and unworthy of the Divine Majesty, for it is the property of all mortal men to be liars, Romans 3:4, and of the immortal God, whom it is impossible to lie, Hebrews 6:4. That Jesus stood as sponsor for God in the new law is likewise unheard of in Holy Scripture. And the Socinians hold Jesus, as to his nature, to be a mere man. Those less known by reason of their faith, or whose faith is less certain or tested to us, are accustomed to provide a sponsor. But is not the faith of God the most known and most certain of all? 4. God made us as certain as could be, so that he could not have made us more certain, by two immutable things, by promise and by oath, as the Apostle teaches, chapter 6. What need is there, therefore, for a sponsor for God, and how could he make us more certain by his sponsorship than God did by his promise and oath? 5. Since, therefore, the Apostle has taught that God has already employed in the priesthood of Christ and the new covenant those things which cohere, why would he introduce a sponsor here for his sake? Who made us certain of the promise, but by the perpetual holiness of his life, the death endured for that reason, and very many miracles. Do those things stand more certainly, and could they be more certain to the Hebrews, than the Divine oath itself? 6. That JESUS stood as sponsor for God concerning the truth of the Divine promises in those three ways, which Grotius assigns in this place with the heretical Socinians Crellius and Schlichting, is taught nowhere. The passage which they allege from 1 John 5:5 will have to be vindicated in its own place from their distortions. 7. The Apostle does not contend with Moses concerning Christ, but with the Priests, and therefore Grotius wrongly mixes Moses in here. 8. Theophylactus explains that Christ was made a surety through a Mediator and Intercessor. But Christ is not both Mediator and Intercessor for God among us, but for us before God. And for that reason, it is also explained by the Apostle himself in this same epistle, chapter 8:6, chapter 9:15, chapter 12:24, that he is the Mediator of a new and better covenant, just as he is called here the surety of a better covenant. But how he is called the Mediator of God and men, the Apostle explained in 1 Timothy 2:6, because, namely, he gave himself, so that he might reconcile God to us, as a ransom for us, but not so that he might stand as surety for us to God. A ransom is the price by which a debt is paid. To dissolve a debt is to satisfy the creditor for the debt. What? That Grotius himself explains the word Mediator thus in Hebrews 8:6. For he also obtained, he says, that crimes committed before the calling would not exclude men from repentance, or those led by repentance from pardon, and he obtained for us the highest benefits from God pertaining to eternal life, 1 Timothy 2:5. Add Galatians 3:19, 20, below chapter 9:15, chapter 12:24. This office of Christ as sponsor can also be explained from the priesthood of Christ. It is credible, says Crellius on this passage, that in the word 'sponsor' the priesthood of Christ is also understood. For it is the duty of a sponsor not only to promise something in another's name, and to interpose his own faith for another, but also, if the situation requires it, to perform in another's name that which he has promised. But Christ is a Priest, not because he performs something for us on behalf of God, but because he offers a victim to God for us, and intercedes for us before God. What Crellius says, that Christ, insofar as he is a Priest, does nothing more now in heaven than to perform the Divine promises for us, that agrees neither with the description of the priesthood handed down by the Apostle in Hebrews 5:1, nor with the parts or functions of the priestly office of Christ, nor with the office of the High Priest of the Old Testament, nor finally with the scriptures concerning the Priesthood and sacrifice of Christ to the nations: And it is to be referred to the Kingly rather than the Priestly office of Christ. But he preferred to call him a sponsor here, rather than a Mediator, because he is engaged in the explanation of the priesthood. For a surety or sponsor is properly one who promises satisfaction for someone, which he had taken upon himself for us; Christ, by the power of his priesthood, performed the satisfaction, because he offered himself for us as a sacrifice for the expiation of our sins, and for the deletion or abdication of the bond which was against us. The sponsor of the covenant or of the better Testament, because in view of this sponsorship and the satisfaction that followed in its own time, the covenant of grace was initiated and sanctioned through the same. And the covenant or testament and the priesthood cohere. For a priest is a person acting before God on behalf of the people, who has things to perform, offering for the people and interceding for the same, Heb. 5, 1. Christ therefore was made the sponsor of the New Testament, because he erected that covenant for that reason, insofar as Christ, having been made our sponsor, satisfied for our sins as a Priest, a mediator between God and men, by his own blood, which he shed on the altar of the cross, sanctioned and confirmed this new covenant, as the blessed Gerhard rightly says here.

The blessed Dorscheus presents the Apostle's present argument thus: That which contains a more excellent covenant than that which is in the Levitical priesthood, that same thing is also more excellent than the Levitical priesthood. But the Christian priesthood contains a more excellent covenant, etc. Therefore. The Apostle posits the minor premise in v. 27, but he proves it in v. 20 and 21, and that by this argument: That which has a promise through the singular oath of GOD concerning eternity and immutability, that same thing contains a more excellent covenant than that to which no promissory oath intervened. But the Christian priesthood is such. Therefore. The minor is again confirmed from Psalm 110, verse 4, where it is noted, That God has sworn, and indeed with an immutable and irrevocable oath, that the Messiah would be a priest forever, and indeed with such a covenant annexed, in which the Messiah, as the supreme mediator of the covenant, is to sit at the right hand of God, to rule in the midst of his enemies, to subdue peoples to himself far and wide with the heavenly Word as a kind of scepter, and consequently to have a numerous portion, which he has expiated and reconciled to God by a most perfect sacrifice, and finally, having condemned his enemies in the final judgment and broken the heads of his adversaries, has saved them forever. Psalm 110 indicates this summary of the Divine covenant confirmed by oath. The Apostle asserts in verse 21 that no such thing can be brought forward concerning the ancient covenant or Old Testament.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

Verf. 22.

Κατὰ τοσοῦτον κρείττονος διαθήκης γέγονεν ἔγγυος Ἰη- σοῦς) Tanto melioris pacti sponfor factus est Jesus, pacti scilicet æternum valituri. Ἐγγυητὴς fidejussor, sponsor in Glossario. Cicero : Me ut sponsorem appellat, id est, fidejussorem. Moses pro Deo spopondit in Lege veteri. Jesus pro DEO in nova lege. Lex utraque & pactum continet: Habet præter officii præscriptionem etiam promissa: Sponsorem dare solent minus noti. Et Mo- ses & JESUS hominibus melius noti erant, quam DE- US, qui est inconspicuus. Spopondit autem CHRI- STUS, id est, nos certos promissi fecit, non solis ver- bis, sed perpetua vitæ sanctitate, morte ob id tolerata & miraculis plurimis. Hoc eo pertinet, ne miremur muta- tam legem.

Glossam hanc à Socinianis accepit, iisque gra- tificatus eadem est Grotius. Ita enim Schlichtin- gius è prælectionibus Crellianis hoc loco; Spon- sor fœderis appellatur JESUS, quod nomine DEI nobis spoponderit, id est, fidem fecerit, DEUM fœ- deris promissiones servaturum esse. Non vero quasi pro nobis spoponderit Deo, nostrorumve debitorum solutionem in se receperit. At ex adverso CHRI- STUM sponsorem hic dici, non quod nobis pro Deo, sed quod Deo pro nobis spoponderit, no- strorumque debitorum solutionem in se suscepe- rit hæc confirmant 1. Nomen ἔγγυος ab ἐγγυή, quæ secundum Suidam est ἡ περί τινος ἀποδοχὴ, de re aliqua susceptio vel promissio, qua quis aliquid in se recepit, & à se præstitum iri promittit, dicitur. Quod magis convenit CHRISTO pro nobis Deo spondenti, & debitorum nostrorum solutionem in se recipienti. 2. Deus non indiget sponsore vel fidejussore pro sese, nec etiam talem adhibet uspiam, quum ipse sit promissor veracissimus, omnique fide dignissimus, nec per fidejussorem alium possimus certiores reddi, quam ab ipso- met Deo. 3. Mosen pro Deo spopondisse in lege veteri ἄγραφόν est, & Divina Majestate indignum hominem mortalem, quorum omnium proprium est esse mendacem, Roman. 3, 4. & Deo immorta- li, quem impossibile est mentiri, Ebr. 6, 4. Jesum pro Deo in nova lege spopondisse itidem in Scri- ptura sacra inauditum est. Et habent Sociniani Jesum, quantum ad naturam pro ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ. Sponsorem dare solent minus noti ratione fidei, vel quorum fides nobis minus certa aut explorata. Annon vero fides Dei omnium notissima & cer- tissima? 4. Deus nos quam certissimos reddi- dit, ut certiores non potuerit duabus rebus immu- tabilibus promissione & juramento, docente Apo- stolo, cap. 6. Quid opus ergo sponsore pro Deo, & quomodo certiores is sponsione sua nos reddere posset, quam Deus promisso & juramento. 5. Quum ergo jam adhibuisse Deum in Christi sa- cerdotio & novo fœdere, quæ cohærent, Aposto- lus docuerit, cur hic sponsorem ejus causa induce- ret? Qui nos certos promissi fecerit, sed perpetua vitæ sanctitate, morte ob id tolerata & miraculis plurimis. Num illa certius constant, Ebræisque certiora esse poterant, quam ipsummet jusjuran- dum Divinum. 6. Tribus illis modis de pro- missionum Divinarum veritate pro Deo spopon- disse JESUM, quos cum Socinianis hæreticis Crellio & Schlichtingio in h. l. assignat Grotius, nulli- bi locorum docetur. Locus, quem illi allegant è 1. Johan. 5, 5. suo loco vindicandus erit ab eorum detorsionibus. 7. Non cum Mose contendit Apo- stolus Christum, sed cum Sacerdotibus, ideoque perperam hic Grotius Mosen immiscet. 8. Chri- stum ἔγγυον factum esse explicat Theophylactus per Mediatorem & Intercessorem. Non autem Christus & Mediator & Intercessor pro Deo apud nos, sed pro nobis apud Deum. Atque ea ratione etiam explicatur ab Apostolo ipso in hac eadem epistola cap. 8, 6. cap. 9, 15. cap. 12, 24. quod sit νέας καινῆς, & κρείττονος διαθήκης Μεσίτης, ut hic κρείτ- τονος διαθήκης ἔγγυος vocatur. Qui vero Μεσίτης dicatur Dei & hominum, exposuit Apostolus 1. Tim. 2, 6. quia scilicet semetipsum, ut Deum nobis conciliaret, dedit ἀντίλυτρον pro nobis, non autem ut pro Deo nobis fidejuberet. Ἀντίλυτρον pretium est, quo debitum solvitur. Dissolvere debitum est satisfacere creditori pro debito. Quid? quod Grotius ipse vocem Μεσίτης sic explicet Ebr. 8. v. 6. Nam & obtinuit, inquit, ne crimina ante vocationem commissa homines à pœnitentia, aut pœnitentia du- ctos à venia excluderent, & impetravit nobis summa à Deo beneficia ad vitam æternam pertinentia, 1. Ti- moth. 2, 5. Adde Gal. 3, 19. 20. infra c. 9, 15. c. 12, 24. Explicari etiam hoc sponsoris Christi officium è sacerdotio Christi potest. Credibile est, inquit Crellius in hunc locum, in voce sponsuris sacerdotium quoque Christi intelligi. Sponsoris enim est, non tantum alieno nomine quippiam promittere, & fidem suam pro alio interponere, sed etiam si ita res ferat, alterius nomine, id quod spopondit, præstare. At Chri- stus Sacerdos est, non quod pro Deo nobis quid præstet, sed quod pro nobis Deo victimam offerat, & apud Deum pro nobis interpellet. Quod Crel- lius dicit, Christum, quatenus Sacerdos est, nihil ma- gis nunc in cælis facere, quam quod promissa Divina nobis præstet, id nec cum descriptione sacerdotii ab Apostolo tradita Ebr. 5, 1. nec cum partibus vel functionibus officii Christi sacerdotalis, nec cum officio Pontificis Veteris Testamenti, nec denique cum scripturis de Sacerdotio & sacrificio Christi gentibus convenit: Et ad Regium potius, quam Sa- cerdotale munus Christi referendum est. Spon- sorem autem dicere hic maluit, quam Mediatorem, quia in sacerdotii explicatione versatur. Ἔγγυος enim vel sponsor proprie est, qui pro aliquo satisfa- ctionem spondet, quam in se receperat pro nobis Christus, vi sacerdotii sui præstitit satisfactionem, quia semetipsum obtulit pro nobis in sacrificium ad peccatorum nostrorum expiationem, & chiro- graphi, quod adversus nos erat, deletionem vel ab- dicationem. Sponsorem fœderis vel Testamenti melioris, quia hujus sponsionis & subsequutæ suo tempore satisfactionis intuitu fœdus gratiæ initum est, & per eandem sancitum. Et cohærent fœdus vel testamentum & sacerdotium. Sacerdos enim est persona peragens apud Deum pro populo, quæ peragenda habet, offerens pro populo, & interce- dens pro eodem, Ebr. 5, 1. Christus igitur factus est sponsor Novi Testamenti, quia ea ratione fœdus illud erexit, quatenus sponsor noster factus pro peccatis nostris satisfecit Christus tanquam Sacerdos inter Deum & homines medius suo ipsius sanguine, quem fudit in ara crucis fœdus hoc novum sanxit & con- firmavit, ut hic recte B. Gerhardus.

B. Dorscheus argumentum Apostoli præsens ita exhibet: Quod sacerdotium continet præstantius fœdus, quam est in sacerdotio Levitico, idipsum sa- cerdotio Levitico quoque præstantius est. Atqui sacerdotium Christianum continet præstantius fœ- dus &c. Ergo. Minorem ponit Apostolus v. 27. pro- bat vero v. 20. & 21. idque hoc argumento: Quod sacerdotium per juramentum singulare DEI de æternitate & immutabilitate promissionem habet, idipsum præstantius fœdus continet, quam illud, cui nulla intercessit juratoria promissio. At sacer- dotium Christianum tale est. Ergo. Minor rur- sus confirmatur ex Psalm. CX. vers. 4. ubi notatur, Deum jurasse, & quidem immutabili & irrevoca- bili juramento, Messiam futurum Sacerdotem in æ- ternum, & quidem cum annexo tali fœdere, in quo Messias tanquam summus fœderis conciliator sit ad dextram Dei sessurus, dominaturus in medio inimi- corum, Verbo cœlesti longe lateque tanquam sceptro quodam populos sibi subacturus, numerosam proinde habiturus partem, quam expiavit, Deoque conci- liavit sacrificio perfectissimo, & tandem damnatis extremo judicio hostibus suis, fractisque capitibus adversariis in æternum salvavit. Hanc summam fœderis Divini juramento confirmatam Psalmus CX. indicat. Tale vero nullum de fœdere antiquo seu Vetere Testamento proferri posse Apostolus vers. 21. asserit.

## 7:23
Ver. 23.

And they indeed have been made many priests because they were prevented by death from remaining priests, that is, by excellence, high priests, כהנים הגדולים, there were more than seventy from Aaron to the destruction of the temple. They could not remain in the priesthood, death prohibiting it. And the law shows this in Exodus 28:43.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

Καὶ οἱ μὲν πλείονές εἰσι γεγονότες ἱερεῖς διὰ τῷ θανάτῳ κωλύεσθαι παραμένειν) ἱερεῖς, id est, per excellentiam, ἀρχιερεῖς כהנים הגדולים supra septuaginta fuere ab Aarone ad templi excidium. Non poterant per- manere in sacerdotio, morte id prohibente. Et id lex ostendit Exod. 28, 43.

## 7:24
But he, because he remains forever) Because he always remains and does not die.

He has an unchangeable priesthood) In Latin you may translate it best as, he does not transmit the priesthood. A right that comes from a deceased person to a successor is said in Latin to be transmitted, in Greek παραπέμπεσθαι, here παραβαίνειν. Among the ancients, one also succeeded in sacred offices. Servius on Aeneid XI: Ἀπαράβατον. די לא יעדה Dan. 7. Where the Greeks say ὃ παρελεύσεται. The Syrian here says לא עברא.

The Syrian rendered it: His priesthood does not pass by, or does not pass over. Whence the Apostle reasons thus, as Estius notes: That which is eternal is more excellent than that which is transferred from time to time. But the priesthood of CHRIST, by the testimony of David, is eternal, whereas the Levitical is transferable, as the death and succession of the high priests proves; therefore the priesthood of Christ is more excellent than the Levitical. If someone should say that CHRIST also died, and therefore his priesthood was ended by his death, he answers: He did not die in such a way that his priesthood would pass to others, as happened among the priests of the Old Testament, but, as he says a little later, he himself, one and the same, having been raised to life, remained a priest forever, and not only by reason of his person, but also of his office and effect. Which we rightly use against Estius himself. Thus CHRIST remains the same priest perpetually, and if he has a perpetual priesthood, therefore he has no vicars or successors in the priesthood, where it is in vain when Estius repeats that he indeed has no successors, yet has vicars. For, not to mention that some of the Papists even give successors to Christ in the Pontificate, making him the first Pontiff, he cannot even have vicars in the priesthood, since he himself in his own person exercises the priesthood forever. But where someone exercises his office in his own person, he certainly does not use a vicar in that office which he himself exercises. In the administration of the Sacraments, Christ indeed has vicars, because he no longer administers the sacraments in his own person and immediately; but in the priestly office or Pontificate he uses no vicars, because he himself in his own person and immediately exercises the priestly office forever, which the Apostle demonstrates here. The Holy Scripture certainly recognizes no priests of the New Testament other than the one supreme Pontiff, Christ Jesus, whether you call them vicars or by any other name, who truly come under this name, Heb. 5:5, 6; ch. 7:23; ch. 9:15. Concerning whom it testifies that he offered himself once to the Father, Heb. 7:26, 27; ch. 9:28, and does not wish his body and blood to be offered daily by priestly vicars. For he perfected by his one oblation forever all those who are sanctified, ch. 10:10 ff., and opposes the oblation of Christ to the Levitical sacrifices in this, that these were repeated daily, but that one was made once, which is utterly repugnant to the daily Missatic priesthood of the Papists. Finally, Bellarmine himself admits in book VI of the Roman Pontiff, ch. 13, that the ministers of the Church in the New Testament are nowhere called priests, except in those general sayings which designate all Christians by this name because of internal and spiritual sacrifices. Add that nowhere in the New Testament, where the offices of the ministers of the Church are proposed, is there any mention of the duty of sacrificing.

Latin:

Ὁ δὲ διὰ τὸ μένειν αὐτὸν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) Quia semper manet & non moritur.

Ἀπαράβατον ἔχει τὴν ἱερωσύνην) Latine optime vertas, non transmittit sacerdotium. Jus quod à defuncto per- venit ad successorem Latine dicitur transmitti, Græcis παραπέμπεσθαι, hic παραβαίνειν. Apud veteres in sacra quoque succedebatur. Servius ad XI. Æneidos: Ἀπα- ράβατον. די לא יעדה Dan. VII. Ubi Græci ὃ πα- ρελεύσεται. Syrus hic לא עברא.

Syrus reddidit: Sacerdotium ejus non præterit, aut non transit. Unde sic ratiocinatur Aposto- lus, notante Estio: Æternum præstantius est eo, quod subinde transfertur. Atqui CHRISTI sacerdo- tium, Davide teste, æternum est, Leviticum autem translatitium, ut probat Pontificum mors & succes- sio, ergo sacerdotium Christi præstantius est Levitico. Si dicat aliquis, etiam CHRISTUM mortuum esse, & proinde morte ejus finitum sacerdotium, re- spondet: Non ita mortuus est, ut Sacerdotium ejus ad alios transiret, quemadmodum fiebat in Sacerdo- tibus Veteris Testamenti, sed, ut paulo post, ipse unus & idem ad vitam resuscitatus, maneret Sacerdos in æternum, nec id solum ratione personæ, verum etiam officii & effectus. Quod adversus ipsummet Estium merito adhibemus. Sic CHRISTUS idem per- petuo manet Sacerdos, & si perpetuum habet sa- cerdotium, igitur vicarios vel successores in sacer- dotio non habet, ubi frustra est, cum repetit Estius, nullos quidem illum habere successores, habere tamen vicarios. Nam ne dicam, quod nonnulli è Papi- stis etiam successores Christo dent in Pontificatu, ipsum facientes primum Pontificem, ne vicarios quidem habere in sacerdotio potest, quandoqui- dem ipse in propria persona sacerdotio in æter- num fungatur. Ubi autem quis αὐτοπροσώπως of- ficio suo fungitur, vicario utique non utitur in illo officio, quo ipse fungitur. In administratione Sacramentorum Christus quidem vicarios habet, quia ipse jam non in propria persona & ἀμέσως sa- cramenta administrat: sed in sacerdotali officio vel Pontificatu nullis utitur vicariis, quia ipse in propria persona & ἀμέσωσιν æternum fungitur sacerdotali officio, quod hic demonstrat Apostolus. Scriptura certe sacra nullos agnoscit Sacerdotes Novi Test. alios, sive vicarios, sive quocunq; nomine eos di- xeris, qui proprie quidem hoc nomine veniant, præter unicum summum Pontificem, Christum Je- sum, Ebr. 5, 5. 6. c. 7, 23. c. 9, 15. De quo testatur, quod semel scipsum Patri obtulerit, Ebr. 7, 26. 27. c.9, 28. non vero quotidie per Sacerdotes vicarios corpus & sanguinem suum offerri velit. Consum- matum mavit enim unica oblatione sua in æternum omnes, qui sanctificantur, c. X. 10. seqq. ac oblationem Chri- sti Leviticis sacrificiis in ea opponit, quod hæc quotidie repetita, illa vero semel fuerit facta, quæ sacerdotio Missatico Papistarum quotidiano peni- tus repugnant. Denique fatetur Bellarminus ipse libr. VI. de Rom. Pontifice cap. 13. quod ministri Ecclesiæ in Nov. Test. nuspiam vocentur Sacerdotes, nisi in generalibus illis dictis, quæ omnes Christia- nos propter interna & spiritualia sacrificia hoc no- mine indigitant. Adde quod nuspiam in Novo Testamento, ubi officia Ministrorum Ecclesiæ proponuntur, muneris sacrificandi mentio fiat.

## 7:25
Ver. 25.

Whence he is also able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through him, always living to intercede for them.) Who always lives, is also always able to call upon GOD for us, that he may save us, that is, that he may obtain help for us against temptations. We have said that εἰς τὸ παντελὲς means forever, from the words used by Luke in the Gospel, 13:11. And both the Syrian and the Latin have rightly translated it here, just as the Greek Fathers understand this word. In a similar phrase he said above εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς v. 3. In Hebrew לנצח. Those who come to God through him: as below 11:6. Ἐντυγχάνειν is to commend the desires of someone. We had the same word, but in a somewhat deflected sense, Rom. 8:26. Christ does this, however, not with a submissive, but with a powerful intercession, as Gregory the Great speaks. See Rom. 8:34.

The eternity of Christ's priesthood brings forth fruit, so that it may teach at once that such a priesthood is necessary, and therefore the Apostle may render the infinite difference of the same from the Levitical [priesthood] more clearly. Some Latin Codices have, 'approaching through himself to God.' But in the Greek, the article τοὺς requires the accusative προσ- ερχομένους, 'those approaching,' with which the Syriac also agrees. Erasmus and Hentenius render the words εἰς τὸ παντελὲς as 'to the full,' Stapulensis as 'to perfection,' and Estius acknowledges that the Greek properly signifies this: just as the Greek Interpreters also explain it concerning perfect salvation, especially Theodoret, by which Estius interprets both the Vulgate as 'forever' and the Syriac as 'eternally.' For salvation will not be perfect if it does not extend forever. It is better, however, to render it κατὰ πόδα [word for word] as 'to the full': And the sense is more convenient if it is joined with the verb 'to save'; as if he were to say: If Christ has an eternal priesthood, he is certainly able to bring to perfect salvation those who, through him as Mediator, approach God, such as can be expected only from an eternal Priest, because there will not be perfect salvation unless it extends itself into eternity, and for the perfection of salvation, if it is to be true, it must be both intensively perfect and extensively or duratively so. Therefore, the intercession of the saints is neither necessary for this, nor can it be useful, since the saints are not to intercede for others eternally, nor do they perform the priestly office of intercessors in heaven, which is proper to Christ alone. How does Estius grant what is held concerning Jeremiah and Onias (in the Apocryphal book) 2. Macc. 15, that they pray for the people of the Jews, [and] that they did not pray as priests, or in respect of a priesthood which they had once held, or of a sacrifice which they had offered. Although we do not deny in general that the deceased saints pray for the Church, they are not therefore either Mediators, or to be prayed to by us that they may intercede, because they can neither hear our prayers, nor is that enjoined upon us anywhere; nay, they do not even know us, much less do they look into our hearts, so that they could truly distinguish the faithful from hypocrites and assist them with their intercessions. That those who do not have other co-supplicants, whether living in this or in the other world, do not approach legitimately, are Estian trifles, more vain than Sicilian nonsense.

For the just shall live by his faith, Habac. 2, 4. Heb. 10, 38. Furthermore, the Apostle added this cause and reason for the consequence, why He who approaches God through faith by Himself as the only Mediator can save the faithful to the full: Because this High Priest always lives, and that is, so that He may always intercede for us: Which perpetual intercession of His procures for us full and eternal salvation. For His priesthood is neither idle nor useless. Estius, however, explains the intercession of Christ for us in the heavens according to the mind of Gregory, book I, Moral. chap. XXIV, and other Fathers, in such a way that it is not a certain submissive petition, but an eternal commemoration of the passion once undertaken for us. But this is to neglect the literal sense (τὸ ῥητὸν), which ought not to be done without necessity. For there can be a proper intercession, even if not with submissive supplication, such as was made by Christ in the state of humiliation. For even an axiomatic intercession, when an equal intercedes with an equal, which is not done with submission, is an intercession properly so called. Therefore Estius himself asserts a true and properly so-called prayer of Christ for us, even if not without self-contradiction (ἑαυτομαχίᾳ): For, he says, if Christ is our Advocate and Mediator even now, 1 John 2 and 1 Tim. 3, therefore He truly still prays and intercedes for us. For this is the proper office of an Advocate and Mediator. Then the Greek word ἐντυγχάνειν, for which the Interpreter in this place and Rom. 8 translates 'to intercede,' proves this sufficiently by itself. For it signifies an intercession which is made with prayer or petition, as it is easy to show from other places of Scripture. Which Augustine also clearly teaches in epistle 59 to Paul, q. 5, affirming that in the Apostle 'to intercede' is put for that which is 'to petition'. Wherefore if Christ (which cannot be denied) properly intercedes, He certainly properly prays, whether He does this with the mind alone, or also forms and expresses the concept of the mind with a voice. He also twists the opinion of Thomas to this, when he asserted that Christ expressed the desire of His most holy soul, which He had for our salvation. For although the expression of an internal desire is made primarily by voice, here, however, Thomas made mention only of a desire not present, which Christ has in glory, but which He had in the days of His flesh: as if a mere commemoration of it were made, but now such a desire does not properly befit Christ in the state of glory. Which is against this sentiment of the Apostle, and the analogy of the passage in Romans 8, verse 34, and also 1 John 2, verse 2. Therefore Estius is in vain in reconciling the diverse opinions of his own people concerning the intercession of Christ, about which elsewhere.

B. Dorcheus writes thus concerning these matters in this place: Nor do those among the Papists satisfy [the requirements] who do not interpret 'to intercede' (τὸ ἐντυγχάνειν) as a true and properly so-called prayer, but as a mere representation of the merits, stigmata, and passions of Christ. Thus Rupert of Deutz wishes in 'On Divine Offices' chap. III, Claude d'Espence in 'On the Mediator' chap. VIII, Adam Sasbout in his Commentary on Romans VIII. 34, Bartholomew Medina in chap. III of Thomas, q. 21, art. I, Vasquez ibid. disp. 82, chap. 2, and book I 'On Adoration' disp. IV, chap. 3, a. n. 91, who are led by these reasons primarily: 1. because Christ in the heavens asks for nothing new. 2. Because even according to His human nature, now placed on the throne of God, He has the power of effecting all things by Himself. 3. Because in the public prayers of the Church, Christ is never implored to pray for us in the heavens. 4. Because by that prayer Christ would merit something, when yet the merits of Christ were consummated and terminated in the state of humiliation. Thus Tanner lists them in Vol. IV of Scholastic Theology, disp. I, q. 7, dub. II. But they have no efficacy against prayer properly so called.

For 1. Even if Christ asks for nothing new in the heavens, besides that which He asked for in the state of humiliation and on this earth, it is not, however, repugnant that what He, humbly humiliated, asked for on this earth, He, sublimely exalted in the heavens, can ask to be brought into effect, just as He merited.

Then, even if Christ has the power of effecting all things by Himself, nothing, however, prevents Him from exercising that same power with respect to the faithful placed in the Church militant under a certain arrangement, and thus exercising it by petitioning God the Father.

3. The Church could for certain reasons abstain for some time from that form of imploring Christ to pray for us in the heavens, primarily so as not to provide the Arians an occasion for slandering, as if by this very thing Christ were established as inferior to God the Father. Otherwise, it is certain, without prejudice to the analogy of faith, that the Church could have implored Christ in this way, because in truth Christ, adored in this manner, is not established as inferior to God the Father according to His divinity. And in fact, the Church does implore Christ in this way entirely, because it acknowledges Him as the perpetual Mediator before God the Father.

4. It does not follow that because Christ prays, He therefore merits something by that prayer, since not every prayer of Christ, but [only that which was] made in the form of a servant and performed in the state of humiliation, about which see above chap. 5, verse 7, is meritorious. For Christ, as Mediator on the throne of glory and petitioning at the right hand of God, is already placed beyond the condition of meriting.

But he relies on the merits consummated in the state of humiliation. Arriaga, Vol. VI of Theological Disputations, disp. 49, sect. 3, subsect. 1, records that Father Hurtado, disp. LXXIX, sect. 3, also leans toward that opinion, that Christ no longer prays for us in the heavens, because He most ardently desired our salvation while on the way, and all the benefits which have been conferred upon us through Him. Whence He ought not to have deferred any prayer to heaven, but rather to have arranged everything immediately on earth. Hurtado nevertheless concedes that it can be said that CHRIST now retains in heaven the same act of prayer in number which He had on earth, which he thinks can physically remain as long as those benefits are not actually conferred upon us by GOD, and since that act of prayer on the cross was a formal prayer, it even now in heaven obtains the same nature of prayer, although it does not retain the nature of merit, since many circumstances are required for merit which are not in heaven. Furthermore, Hurtado says that there is no reason why that prayer poured forth in the days of His flesh should have changed, since the knowledge from which the prayer arose remains the same in heaven, and the object, as long as it is future, is always apt to terminate prayer, because prayer on the part of the will is a desire that GOD should do something, which desire we explain to Him while we pray. CHRIST could have prayed in various ways in the state of emptying Himself, and primarily He could have sought our salvation immediately, not by saying, 'I ask that in this place You would be willing to save them,' but by saying, 'Save them by the thing itself,' e.g., him who is to live in the seventeenth century after my birth. This prayer or this desire for our salvation could have remained in Christ as long as those for whom CHRIST prayed were not actually saved, even if He already knew that GOD altogether had an efficacious will concerning the conferring of salvation, and knew that that object would exist by the thing itself.

Arriaga rightly refutes this perpetual and physical existence of Christ's prayer, partly because he confuses the desire or love of human salvation with the very act of prayer. For it does not follow: The desire remains. Therefore, the prayer also, which once flowed from that desire and love while Christ was in these lands, remains; partly because that twofold mode of prayer, by which it is said that Christ sought our salvation mediately or immediately, is fictitious and chimerical; partly because prayer in the state of humiliation was a transitory act, not a permanent one, as it is an act, although the memory of the prayer once poured forth may remain in Christ. However, that memory of prayer is not prayer: partly because either Hurtado places that prayer of Christ in an indivisible act, by which he sought all benefits for all, or he places around every man for whom Christ prayed one numerically distinct volition, and indeed even a distinct one, according to the distinction of the things which Christ sought for one and the same man. In neither respect can that perpetual and physical existence of Christ's prayer on the cross be defended: Not in the first, because if that act indivisibly regards all benefits to be granted to all men by desiring them, as soon as he ceases to desire one, which is when that thing is actually exhibited while CHRIST is in heaven, that whole act, which is essentially the desire of all objects, will also cease to exist, and therefore it cannot cease to be the desire of one unless it ceases to be the desire of all. Whence is destroyed that which Hurtado said, that the prayer poured forth by Christ on earth for us endures physically in heaven until we ourselves obtain those benefits. For if it is one indivisible act, it would have lasted only until the first of all benefits for one man. It is highly improbable that the prayer on the cross of Christ should be considered in the second respect. For since we can most conveniently explain the prayer of Christ by one indivisible act, terminated at all the benefits to be provided to the human race, and there is no necessity for continuing those acts until the day of judgment, it seems clearly incredible that Christ had on the cross as many acts distinct in number and species at once as there are men for whom he prayed, and as many distinct benefits as he sought for them, and indeed for no other end than that those acts might afterwards be able to perish successively one after another, in the way in which those sought benefits come to be in reality successively. In vain, therefore, does Hurtado argue that τὸ ἐντυγχάνειν (intercession) ought to be understood not of the conservation and continuation of the prayer made on earth, but of that very act which has already been completed on earth and no longer endures, and that this is the sense of the Apostolic words: That he who had to pray effectively for us on earth had to be πάντοτε ζῶντα (always living), not because he had to pray always, but so that he might pray effectively, because the prayer of a mortal man does not have such efficacy as the prayer of one who is always living and endowed with Divine power. For however plausible Vasquez's interpretation may be, it nevertheless conflicts 1. with the Apostolic scope, which is to teach that CHRIST has an ἀπαράβατον ἱερωσύνην (unchangeable priesthood), and that it is placed ἐν τῷ σῴζειν εἰς τὸ παντελὲς (in saving to the uttermost) and ἐν τῷ ἐντυγχάνειν (in interceding). Therefore, it certainly also requires τὸ πάντοτε ἐντυγχάνειν (always interceding) or ἐντυγχάνειν εἰς τὸ παντελές (interceding to the uttermost). For it is an ἀπαράβατον ἐντυγχάνει (unchangeable intercession). 2. With the words themselves. For it is expressly explained to them why CHRIST is πάντοτε ζῶν (always living), namely so that he may be a perpetual Priest, who, namely, may perform intercession for us. Therefore, πάντοτε (always) is to be referred no less to ἐντυγχάνειν (interceding) than τὸ παντελὲς (the uttermost) is to σῴζειν (saving).

It is therefore most simple if we understand the intercession of CHRIST properly, but yet in such a way that it is appropriate to the state of exaltation, and placed in a certain sublime Divine and glorious petition before God the Father.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

Ὅθεν καὶ σώζειν εἰς τὸ παντελὲς δύναται τοὺς προσερχο- μένους δι’ αὐτοῦ τῷ Θεῷ πάντοτε ζῶν εἰς τὸ ἐντυγχάνειν αὐτοῖς.) Qui semper vivit, semper etiam potest pro nobis DEUM compellare, ut nos servet, id est, ut nobis au- xilia impetret contra tentationes. Εἰς τὸ παντελὲς in per- petuum diximus esse ex Lucæ vocibus usurpatis XIII. 11. in Evangelio. Et recte hic verterunt tum Syrus tum Latinus, quomodo & Græci Patres hanc vocem intelli- gunt. Pari loquutione supra dixit εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς v. 3. Ebraice לנצח τοὺς προσερχομένους δι’ αὐτοῦ τῷ Θεῷ, qui per ipsum DEUM colunt: ut infra XI. 6. Ἐντεύγν- χάνειν est desideria alicujus commendare. Habuimus ean- dem vocem, sed sensu nonnihil deflexo, Rom. 8, 26. Fa- cit autem hoc Christus non submissa ut olim, sed poten- ti interpellatione, quemadmodum loquitur Gregorius Ma- gnus. Vide Rom. 8, 34.

Æternitas sacerdotii Christi fructum affert, ut si- mul necessarium tale sacerdotium esse doceat, ad- eoq; ejusdem à Levitico infinitum discrimen lucu- lentius reddat Apostolus. Nonnulli Codices Lati- ni habent, accedens per semetipsum ad Deum. Sed in Græco articulus τοὺς Accusativum postulat προσ- ερχομένους accedentes, cui etiam Syrus consonat. Verba εἰς τὸ παντελὲς Erasmus & Hentenius red- dunt ad plenum, Stapulensis ad perfectum, idque proprie Græca significare agnoscit Estius: quem- admodum & Græci Interpretes de perfecta salute exponunt, imprimis Theodoretus, quo & Vulgata in perpetuum, & Syri in æternum interpretatur Estius. Non enim erit perfecta salus, si non in per- petuum extendatur. Præstat tamen κατὰ πόδα red- dere ad plenum: Et sensus est convenientior, si jun- gatur cum verbo salvare; quasi dicat: Si Christus æternum habet sacerdotium, potest utique ad per- fectam salutem adducere eos, qui per ipsum, ut Mediatorem, accedunt ad Deum, qualis non nisi ab æterno Sacerdote expectari potest, quia nec perfecta salus erit, nisi in æternum sese porrigat, & perfectio salutis, si vera non sit, oportet eam & in- tensive perfectam esse & extensive vel durativè. Non ergo ad id intercessio sanctorum vel necessaria est, vel utilis esse potest, quum sancti non sint in æter- num intercessuri pro aliis, nec sacerdotali fungan- tur in cœlis intercessorum munere, quod soli Chri- sto proprium est. Quomodo largitur Estius, quod de Jeremia & Onia (in libro Apocrypho) 2. Mac- cab. 15. habetur, eos pro populo Judæorum orare, non orasse eos, ut sacerdotes, aut respectu sacer- dotii, quod aliquando gesserant, aut sacrificii, quod obtulerant. Quanquam vero in genere san- ctos defunctos pro Ecclesia orare non negemus, non tamen ideo vel Mediatores sunt, vel orandi à nobis, ut intercedant, quia nec preces nostras au- dire possunt, nec id nobis uspiam injunctum est, imo ne norunt quidem nos, nedum corda nostra introspiciunt, ut vere fideles ab hypocritis discer- nere, illisq; intercessionibq suis succurrere possint. Non a. legitime accedere, qui non alios compre- catores sive viventes in hoc, sive in altero seculo habeant, nugæ sunt Estianæ, gerris Siculis vaniores.

Justus enim sua fide vivet, Habac. 2, 4. Ebr. 10, 38. Causam porro & rationem consequentiæ, cur salvare possit ad plenum fideles, qui per se unicum Media- torem ad Deum accedunt per fidem, hanc addidit Apostolus : Quia Pontifex hic semper vivit, idque, ut semper pro nobis interpellet: Quæ perpetua ejus in- terpellatio nobis plenam & æternam salutem con- ciliat. Nec enim vel otiosum vel inutile est ejus sacerdotium. Intercessionem autem Christi pro nobis in cœlis ex mente Gregorii libr. I. moral. cap. XXIV. aliorumq; Patrum ita explicat Estius, quod non sit submissa quædam postulatio, sed passionis semel pro nobis susceptæ æterna commemoratio. Verum hoc est τὸ ῥητὸν negligere, quod citra necessitatem fieri non debet. Propria enim potest esse intercessio, etsi non cum submissa supplicatione, qualis in statu exinanitionis à Christo facta est. Nam & interces- sio axiomatica, cum æqualis apud æqualem inter- cedit, quæ non cum submissione fit, intercessio proprie dicta est. Ideo Estius ipse veram ac pro- prie dictam Christi orationem pro nobis asserit, etsi non sine ἑαυτομαχίᾳ : Etenim, inquit, si Chri- stus est Advocatus noster & Mediator etiamnum, 1. Johan. 2. & 1. Tim. 3. vere igitur adhuc orat & in- tercedit pro nobis. Hoc enim proprium est munus Advocati & Mediatoris. Deinde id satis per se pro- bat Græcum verbum ἐντυγχάνειν, pro quo Interpres hoc loco & Rom. 8. vertit interpellare. Significat enim interpellationem, quæ fit cum oratione seu po- stulatione, quemadmodum ex aliis scripturæ locis fa- cile est ostendere. Quod & Augustinus perspicue docet epist. LIX. ad Paul. q. 5. affirmans apud Apo- stolum interpellare positum esse pro eo, quod est postu- lare. Quare si Christus (quod negari non potest) proprie interpellat, utique proprie orat, sive sola mente id faciat, sive etiam voce conceptum mentis efformet atque exprimat. Torquet autem eo etiam Thomæ sententiam, cum Christum animæ suæ sanctissimæ desiderium, quod pro salute nostra habuit, expri- mere asseruit. Nam licet interni desiderii ex- pressio potissimum fiat voce, hic tamen Thomas desiderii non præsentis, quod Christus habet in gloria, sed quod habuit in diebus carnis CHRI- STUS, mentionem tantum fecit: quasi nuda ejus commemoratio fiat, nunc autem proprie tale desi- derium CHRISTO in statu gloriæ non conve- niat. Quod est contra hanc Apostoli senten- tiam, & loci Roman. 8. vers. 34. nec non 1. Johan. 2. vers. 2. analogiam. Frustra ergo est in concilian- dis suorum diversis opinionibus de CHRISTI intercessione Estius, de quibus alias.

B. Dorcheus ita de hisce in h. l. Nec satisfa- ciunt ex Pontificiis illi, qui τὸ ἐντυγχάνειν non de vera & proprie sic dicta oratione interpretantur, sed de nuda repræsentatione meritorum, stigma- tum, & passionum CHRISTI. Ita vult Ruper- tus Tuitiensis de Divinis officiis cap. III. Claudius Espensæus de Mediatore cap. VIII. Adamus Sas- bouth in Comment. Roman. VIII. 34. Bartholo- mæus Medina in cap. III. Thomæ, qu. 21. artic. I. Vasquez ibid. disp. 82. cap. 2. & libr. I. de adorat. disp. IV. cap. 3. a. n. 91. qui his potissimum ducun- tur rationibus 1. quia CHRISTUS in cælis nihil novi postulat. 2. Quia etiam secundum Huma- nam naturam nunc in throno DEI positus pote- statem habet per se efficiendi omnia. 3. Quia in publicis Ecclesiæ precibus nunquam imploratur CHRISTUS, ut in cælis pro nobis oret. 4. Quia illa oratione Christus aliquid promereretur, cum tamen merita CHRISTI statu exinanitionis con- summata & terminata sint. Ita recenset eos Tan- nerus Tom. IV. Theol. Schol. disp. I. q. 7. dub. II. Nullam vero habent efficaciam contra orationem pro- prie sic dictam.

Nam 1. Etiamsi CHRISTUS nihil novi in cœlis postulet, præter id, quod in statu exinanitionis & in his terris postulavit, non tamen repugnat, ut id, quod humiliter exinanitus in his terris postulavit, sublimiter exaltatus in cœlis postulare possit, in effe- ctum deduci, sicut meruit.

Deinde etiamsi CHRISTUS potestatem effici- endi per se omnia habeat, nihil tamen obstat, quo minus illam ipsam respectu fidelium in Ecclesia mili- tanti positorum sub certa taxi usurpet, adeoque postu- lando à Deo Patre eandem exerceat.

3. Potuit ex certis causis Ecclesia aliquandiu ab ista forma implorandi Christum, ut in cœlis pro nobis oret abstinere, imprimis, ne Arianis occasio- nem calumniandi præberet, quasi hoc ipso CHRI- STUS inferior DEO Patre statueretur. Alias certum est, salva analogia fidei, Ecclesiam potuis- se CHRISTUM ita implorare, quia revera Chri- stus hoc modo adoratus inferior Deo Patre secun- dum Divinitatem non statuitur. Et de facto o- mnino ita CHRISTUM Ecclesia implorat, quia perennem ipsum Mediatorem apud DEUM Pa- trem agnoscit.

4. Non sequitur, quia CHRISTUS orat, ideo ipsum aliquid ista oratione mereri, cum non quævis Christi oratio, sed humilis in forma servi facta, & in statu exinanitionis peracta, de qua supra cap. 5. vers. 7. meritoria sit. CHRISTUS enim in throno gloriæ Mediator, & ad Dei dextram po- stulans, ultra merendi conditionem jam positus est.

Nititur autem meritis in statu exinanitionis con- summatiis. Arriaga Tom. VI. dispp. Theol. disp. 49. sect. 3. subsect. 1. commemorat, P. Hurtadum disp. LXXIX. sect. 3. in eam etiam sententiam pro- pendere, CHRISTUM in cœlis pro nobis non amplius orare, quia ardentissime desideravit in via nostram salutem, & omnia beneficia, quæ per ipsum nobis collata sunt. Unde nullam oratio- nem in cœlum differre debuit, sed potius in terris statim omnia componere. Concedere tamen Hur- tadum, posse dici, CHRISTUM in cœlo nunc re- tinere eundem numero actum orationis, quem ha- buit in terris, quem tamdiu manere physice posse existimat, quamdiu illa beneficia non conferun- tur actu nobis à DEO, cumque ille actus oratio- nis in cruce fuerit formalis oratio, etiam nunc in cœlis sortiri eandem rationem orationis, licet non retineat rationem meriti, cum ad meritum mul- ta circumstantiæ requirantur, quæ non sunt in cœlo. Dicere porro Hurtadum, nullam esse ra- tionem, cur illa oratio in diebus carnis fusa de- buerit mutari, cum scientia, à qua oriebatur oratio, eadem maneat in cœlo, & objectum quamdiu est futurum, semper sit aptum, ut ter- minet orationem, quia oratio ex parte voluntatis est desiderium, ut DEUS aliquid faciat, quod desiderium ipsi explicamus, dum oramus. Po- tuisse CHRISTUM variis modis in statu exina- nitionis orare, & imprimis potuisse salutem no- stram petere immediate, non dicendo, peto ut hoc loco illos velis salvare, sed dicendo salva re ipsa, e. g. illum seculo XVII. post nativitatem meam victu- rum. Hanc orationem seu hoc salutis nostræ de- siderium potuisse in Christo manere, quamdiu non actu salvati fuerunt, pro quibus CHRISTUS oravit, etiamsi ille jam sciverit, DEUM omni- no habere voluntatem efficacem de salute confe- renda, & noverit illud objectum re ipsa extiturum.

Recte vero Arriaga hanc existentiam perpetuam & physicam orationis Christi confutat, partim quia con- fundit desiderium seu amorem salutis humanæ cum ipso orationis actu. Non enim sequitur: Desiderium manet. Ergo & oratio, quæ olim Christo in his terris existente ab isto desiderio & amore promanabat, par- tim quia geminus iste orationis modus, qua dicitur Christum salutem nostram mediate vel immediate petiisse, commentitius est & chimericus: partim quia oratio in statu exinanitionis fuit actus transitorius, non permanens, qua actus est, licet permanere possit in Christo memoria orationis olim fusæ. Illa autem orationis memoria non est oratio: partim quia vel Hurtadus eam orationem Christi ponit in actu indi- visibili, quo pro omnibus petierit ille omnia beneficia, vel ponit circa quemlibet hominem, pro quo Christus oravit, unam numero distinctam volitionem, imo et- iam distinctam, juxta distinctionem rerum, quas pro uno eodemque homine Christus petiit. Neutro respe- ctu illa perpetua & physica existentia orationis Chri- sti in cruce defendi potest: Non primo, quia si ille actus indivisibiliter omnia beneficia omnibus hominibus concedenda respicit illa desiderando, cum primum de- sinit unum desiderare, quod sit, cum illud actu ex- hibetur CHRISTO existente in cælis, desinet etiam existere totus ille actus, qui essentialiter est desiderium omnium objectorum, ac proinde non potest desinere esse desiderium unius, nisi desinat esse omnium. Unde destruitur id, quod Hurtadus dixit, durare physice in cælo orationem pro nobis à Christo in terris fusam, quousque ipsi obtineamus ea beneficia. Si e- nim unus indivisibilis est actus, solum usque ad pri- mum omnium beneficium pro uno homine durasset. Secundo respectu considerandam esse orationem in cru- ce Christi valde improbabile est. Cum enim possi- mus commodissime explicare orationem Christi per unum actum indivisibilem, terminatum ad omnia be- neficia generi humano præstanda, nec ulla necessitas sit continuandi illos actus usque ad diem judicii, incre- dibile plane videtur, tot simul & semel actus numero & specie distinctos Christum habuisse in cruce, cum oraret, quot sunt homines, pro quibus oravit, & quot sunt beneficia distincta, quæ pro illis petiit, & quidem ob nullum alium finem, quam ut postea illi actus pos- sint successive perire unus post alterum, eo modo, quo ea beneficia petitæ veniunt re ipsa successive. Fru- stra itaque Hurtadus τὸ ἐντυγχάνειν de conservatione & continuatione orationis in terris factæ intelligi de- bere, sed de illo ipso actu, qui in terris jam peractus est, neque amplius durat, & hunc esse sensum verbo- rum Apostolicorum: Illum, qui in terris efficaciter pro nobis orare debuit, debuisse esse πάντοτε ζῶντα semper viventem, non quia semper debuit orare, sed ut efficaciter oraret, quia oratio mortalis hominis tan- ta efficacia non est, quantæ est oratio semper viventis & Divina potestate præditi. Utut enim plausibilis sit Vasquezii interpretatio, repugnat tamen 1. scopo Apostolico, qui est, docere, CHRISTUM habere ἀπαράβατον ἱερωσύνην, eamque positam ἐν τῷ σώ- ζειν εἰς τὸ παντελὲς & ἐν τῷ ἐντυγχάνειν. Utique ergo etiam requirit τὸ πάντοτε ἐντυγχάνειν seu ἐν- τυγχάνειν εἰς τὸ παντελές. Est enim ἀπαράβα- τον ἐντυγχάνει. 2. Ipsis verbis. Exponitur enim illis diserte, cur CHRISTUS sit πάντοτε ζῶν, scili- cet ut possit perpetuus esse Sacerdos, qui scilicet in- terpellatione pro nobis fungatur. Itaque πάντοτε non minus ad ἐντυγχάνειν etiam referendum est, quam τὸ παντελὲς ad σώζειν.

Simplissimum itaque est, si interpellationem CHRISTI proprie intelligamus, sed ita tamen, ut statui exaltationis sit competens, & in sublimi qua- dam Divina & gloriosa apud Deum Patrem postula- tione posita.

## 7:26
Vers. 26.

Τοιοῦτος γὰρ ἡμῖν ἔπρεπεν Ἀρχιερεὺς) In the Manuscript: Ἡμῖν καὶ ἔπρεπεν. Such also had to be the one whom I shall now describe, much better than those Aaronites, many of whom were evil, others only moderately good. Ἔπρεπεν, that is, it was fitting for us that such a High Priest be given. See above ch. II. vers. 10.

Ὅσιος) חסיד, who has inscribed not on a plate but on his mind קדש ליהוה (Holy to the LORD) Exod. XXXIX. 38.

Ἄκακος) It is necessary that he be removed from every evil thing, not only that he should not take a polluted one, Levit. XXI. 13.

Ἀμίαντος) Who not only has not been polluted by those external contaminations of which Lev. XXII treats, but not even by any vice. See James I. vers. 27. 1. Peter I. vers. 4.

Separated from sinners) Just as no one entered the inner sanctuary except the High Priest, and no one entered the basilica of the temple except the priests: so it was fitting that this far more perfect Priest be placed apart from the contact of evil men, John VII. verse 34.

He shows again the diversity and prerogative of our High Priest, and why he had to be endowed with other qualities, and that this belongs to him alone, that by his own offering he might reconcile us to God the Father, and by the office of his eternal intercession lead us to full and eternal salvation, and be able to save us. By the word ἔπρεπεν, however, not only what is fitting, but also what is necessary is indicated, because he willed that no one else should perform this, which the version of the Blessed Luther rightly hints at: Regarding that holiness, the Blessed Dorscheus warns that it is to be understood eminently and excellently. For our Priest is not holy and undefiled, etc., through the grace of regeneration or glorification, but with respect to the Divine nature indeed through eternal generation, as God blessed forever over all, Rom. IX. 5. and light in whom there is no darkness, 1 John 1, 5. But with respect to the Human nature through the grace of union, by which all the fullness of the Deity, and consequently also the highest holiness, highest purity, and highest justice, was so communicated to him that it dwells in him bodily, Coloss. 2, 19. through which he also was existing in the form of God, to which also belongs the form of highest holiness; how that hypostatic union is the cause of impeccability in Christ according to the Human nature, see in the dissertation on the crucifixion and life of Jesus §. 11. and 12. It is understood also not only regarding the act, but also regarding the power. For he is not only actually innocent and undefiled, and separated from sinners, but he is also unable to be harmful, or to be defiled, or to come into communion with sinners. For the personal union excluded both the act of sins and the very power of sinning and defiling himself, which placed in CHRIST the man the glory of the Only-begotten Son of God, John 1, 14. Whence the disputation of the Papists is rash, whether it could have been in the power of Christ's will, by sinning to reject the personal union, or by not sinning to preserve the same? Concerning which matter Arriaga treats much from Hurtado, Vasquez, Suarez, Lugo, and others, disp. 35. sect. 1. and 2. Rightly also does the Blessed Dorscheus note Salazar, who in his defense for the immaculate conception of the Blessed Virgin, chapter XXI, n. 19, transfers this title to the blessed virgin, when he says: Since the most blessed Virgin enjoys the same office and duty of Mediatrix after CHRIST for the blotting out of the sins of all, it was most fitting for her that she should not only be holy, innocent, and undefiled through the uncleanness of every actual stain, but also separated from sinners, so that although she was a partner of our flesh, yet in that part by which we are all sinners, she had no kinship, and was ignorant of the laws common to others.

So he. Certainly, if the Blessed Virgin enjoys the office and duty of Mediatrix after Christ for the deletion of all sins, and is therefore holy, innocent, undefiled, and separated from sinners, then neither will Christ alone be the High Priest, nor will he alone be the one opposed to the High Priest of the Old Testament. For if the Blessed Virgin performs the same office and duty of Mediatrix in the deletion of all sins as Christ is said to perform in this place; therefore she will be a Mediatrix like the High Priest, and thus she herself will also be opposed to the High Priest of the Old Testament.

And higher than the heavens] Placed above the aerial and ethereal region. So also above in chapter IV, verse 14.

This height is not to be understood locally by reason of site and place, but figuratively by reason of the mode and degree of dignity, just as God is said to sit or dwell in the highest, who is contained by no place. For Christ was made higher than the heavens, that is, all created things; he ascended above all heavens, Eph. 4:10; he occupied the majestic heaven or the heavenly kingdom, Acts 3:21; he sat down at the right hand of Majesty on high, Heb. 1:3; he was exalted above all things, Eph. 1:20; he fills all things, Eph. 4:10; nor is he more enclosed in a place above the aerial and ethereal heaven than God, on whose throne he sits, or the Divine throne and the right hand of God, at which he sits. And that phrase, higher than the heavens, is taken from Job 11:8, where it is applied to God, and so extols God above all things that it posits him as nowhere absent. The scope of the Apostle also proves this sense, who concludes thus: He who is higher than the heavens is most sufficient to save and to intercede for all who desire to approach God. The same sense is also confirmed from Psalm 110, which is established here in the place of a foundation. For it does not speak of a height of place, which might keep one away from the earth, but of a Lordly and Divine height, which constitutes him everywhere present. For it is the height of the right hand of God, which is altogether a Divine height, Psalm 110:1. It is a height ruling in the midst of enemies, and thus constituting him present, verse 2. It is an adorable height, to which voluntary offerings are exhibited by the saints everywhere, and thus an omnipresent height, verse 3. It is a generative height, and like dew, begetting the children of God everywhere in the world, and thus graciously present, in the same verse. It is a height breaking Kings, and exercising judgment among the nations, etc., v. 5. & 7. as here the blessed Dorscheus.

Latin:

Vers. 26.

Τοιοῦτος γὰρ ἡμῖν ἔπρεπεν Ἀρχιερεὺς) In Manuscripto: Ἡμῖν καὶ ἔπρεπεν. Talis etiam esse debebat, qualem jam describam, multo melior istis Aaronidis, quorum mul- ti mali, alii mediocriter tantum boni fuere. Ἔπρεπεν, id est, conveniebat nobis talem Pontificem dari. Vide supra c. II. vers. 10.

Ὅσιος) חסיד, qui non laminæ sed menti inscriptum habeat קדש ליהוה Exod. XXXIX. 38.

Ἄκακος) Oportet sit remotus ab omni re mala, non tantum, ne pollutam ducat, Levit. XXI. 13.

Ἀμίαντος) Qui non tantum pollutus non fuerit illis contaminationibus externis, de quibus agitur Lev. XXII. sed nec ullo vitio. Vide Jacob. I. vers. 27. 1. Petr. I. vers. 4.

Κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν) Sicut in adytum intrabat nullus præter summum Sacerdotem, in Basili- cam templi nemo præter Sacerdotes: Ita oportebat hic Sacerdos perfectior longe sit positus à contactu malorum hominum, Joh. VII. vers. 34.

Ostendit iterum diversitatem & prærogativam nostri Pontificis, & cur aliis qualitatibus instru- ctus esse debuerit, quodque ei soli hoc competat, quod propria sua oblatione nos Deo Patri recon- ciliationis, intercessionis suæ æternæ munere nos ad plenam & æternam salutem perducere, ac salvos facere possit. Per τὸ ἔπρεπεν autem non solum τὸ πρέπον, sed etiam τὸ ἀναγκαῖον indicatur, quod per neminem alium hoc præstare voluit, quod re- cte innuit B. Lutheri versio: De sanctitate illa mo- net B. Dorscheus, quod intelligenda eminenter & ex- cellenter. Non enim Sacerdos noster sanctus est, & impollutus &c. per gratiam regenerationis aut glo- rificationis, sed respectu quidem Divinæ naturæ per æternam generationem, tanquam Deus benedictus in sæcula super omnia, Rom. IX. 5. & lux in qua non sunt tenebræ, 1. Johan. 1, 5. Respectu vero Humanæ naturæ per gratiam unionis, qua omnis plenitudo Dei- tatis, & consequenter etiam summa sanctitatis, sum- mæ puritatis, & summæ justitiæ ita ipsi communicata est, ut in ipso habitet corporaliter Coloss. 2, 19. per quam etiam fuit ἐν μορφῇ Θεῦ ὑπάρχων, ad quam etiam pertinet μορφὴ ὁσιότητος summæ, quomodo unio ista hypostatica impeccabilitatis in Christo secundum Hu- manam naturam causa sit, vide in dissert. de crucif. & vita Jesu §. 11. & 12. Intelligitur etiam non tan- tum de actu, sed etiam de potentia. Non enim tan- tum actu innocens & impollutus est, atque à peccatori- bus segregatus, sed etiam nocens esse, aut pollui, aut in peccatorum communionem venire nequit. Nam & actum peccatorum, & ipsam etiam potentiam peccandi & se polluendi unio personalis exclusit, quæ posuit in CHRISTO homine gloriam Unigeniti Fi- lii Dei, Joh. 1, 14. Unde temeraria est Pontificio- rum disputatio, an potuerit esse in voluntatis Christi potestate, peccando unionem personalem rejicere, aut non peccando eandem conservare? Qua de re mul- ta ex Hurtado, Vasquez, Suarez, Lugo & aliis agit Arriaga disp. 35. sect. 1. & 2. Merito etiam notat B. Dorscheus Salazar, qui in defensione pro imma- cul. concept. B. Virginis cap. XXI, n. 19. ad beatam virginem hunc titulum transfert, cum ait: Cum Virgo beatissima eodem officio ac munere Mediatri- cis post CHRISTUM gaudeat ad omnium peccata delenda, decuit eam maxime, ut non solum sancta, innocens, & impolluta esset per omnis actualis labis immunditiem, sed etiam à peccatoribus segregata, ita, ut quamvis carnis nostræ socia esset, tamen ea ex parte, qua peccatores sumus omnes, nullam cognatio- nem haberet, & leges aliis communes ignoraret.

Hæc ille. Sane si munere & officio Mediatricis post Christum B. Virgo gaudet, ad omnium peccatorum deletionem, atque propterea est sancta, innocens, im- polluta, & à peccatoribus segregata, jam neque solus Christus erit Pontifex summus, neque solus Pontifici Veteris Testamenti oppositus. Nam si B. Virgo eo- dem munere ac officio Mediatricis in deletione peccato- rum omnium fungitur, quo Christus fungi hoc loco di- citur; Ergo Mediatrix erit ut Pontifex, adeoǵ; Pon- tifici Veteris Testamenti & ipsa erit opposita.

Καὶ ὑψηλότερος τῶν ὀρανῶν γενόμενος] Supra aëream & ætheream regionem positus. Sic & supra cap. IV. vers. 14.

Hæc altitudo non τοπικῶς ratione situs & loci, sed τροπικῶς ratione modi & gradus dignitatis in- telligenda, quemadmodum DEUS in excelsis se- dere vel habitare dicitur, qui nullo loco contine- tur. Altior enim factus est CHRISTUS cœ- lis, creatis scilicet omnibus, afcendit supra omnes cœlos, Ephes. 4, 20. occupavit cælum Majestati- cum vel regnum cœleste, Actor. 3, 21. consedit ad dextram Majestatis in excelsis, Ebr. 1, 3. evectus supra omnia, Ephes. 1, 20. implet omnia, Ephes. 4. vers. 10. neque magis loco conclusus supra cœlum aëreum & æthereum, quam Deus, in cujus thro- no sedet, aut thronus Divinus & dextra DEI, ad quam sedet. Et desumpta illa phrasis, altior cælis è Job. 11, 8. ubi de Deo adhibetur, ac Deum ita supra omnia extollit; ut nuspiam absentem statuat. Quem sensum etiam scopus Apostoli probat, qui sic colligit: Qui altior est cœlis, is sufficientissimus est ad salvandum, & ad intercedendum pro omni- bus, qui ad Deum accedere cupiunt. Confirma- tur idem sensus etiam è Psalm. 110. qui hic funda- menti loco constituitur. Ille enim non loquitur de altitudine loci, quæ à terris arceat, sed de altitudine Dominica & Divina, quæ ubique præsentem consti- tuit. Est enim altitudo dextræ DEI, quæ omnino est altitudo Divina, Psalm. CX, 1. Est altitudo domi- nans in medio inimicorum, adeoǵ; præsentem consti- tuens, vers. 2. Est altitudo adorabilis, cui oblationes voluntariæ à sanctis passim exhibentur, adeoǵ; alti- tudo omnipræsens, vers. 3. Est altitudo generatrix, & ad instar roris filios Dei passim in orbe terrarum procreans, adeoǵ; gratiosè præsens, vers. eodem. Est altitudo Reges frangens, & judicium in gentes exer- cens &c. v. 5. & 7. ut hic B. Dorfscheus.

## 7:27
Verse 27.

Who does not have need day by day, as the High Priests formerly, to offer up sacrifices for their own sins, then for those of the people. For this he did once for all, having offered up himself] Day by day, here it is very often, as often as the matter requires, as also below in X, 11. For not only on the sacred anniversary, but also as often as either the High Priest was conscious to himself of some slip, or any other person. Victims were offered for sin, חטאת. However, it seems to be said both here and above in V, 3, that Christ also offered, not indeed very often, but once for the sins not only of the people, but also his own. Which can be defended by that explanation which we brought forward at Matt. 27:50. That the word sins regarding Christ is taken in the same way as the singular sin, Rom. 6:10, for those sorrows which are accustomed to be the punishment of sins, and which Christ endured even on the occasion of the sins of the human race: And from which he was freed by an accelerated death at the time when he offered not a beast, but his own body, as the most perfect victim. And this expression is also taken from the law. For a woman's flow is also called חטאת, Lev. 12:8, ch. 15:30, and leprosy, ch. 14:13. Where in the Greek it is for sin. Just as Christ is said to have offered once here: So he suffered once for sins, 1 Pet. 3:18. For having offered up, in the Manuscript it is having offered, as above ch. 5, 1, 3, 7, and often below.

There is no reason why one should depart from the literal propriety, and explain day by day either as very often, or as every year with the Socinians, since it is daily, and denotes not an anniversary, but a daily sacrifice, which was accustomed to be offered both morning and evening not only for the people's, but also for the Priest's sins, Num. 28:3, Lev. 9:8, 15. Because of Schlichting, the blessed Dorscheus notes this here: It is indeed true that in the anniversary expiation there were different sacrifices, of which the first was slaughtered for the High Priest and his family, the other for the people. But the words of the Apostle are not necessarily to be explained as distinct sacrifices. For it can happen, indeed it has happened in reality, that the morning and evening sacrifice, whether by the High Priest simply, or by him who in his turn was exercising the high priesthood, was offered in the confession of sins first for expiating the Priest himself and his family, then for reconciling the whole people, so that the acts of sacrifice were not distinct, but only the order in confession and prayers was observed, and thus the Priest prayed to God first for himself, then for the people. But that is altogether impious, which Grotius applies to Christ with the Socinians in both members, namely that Christ offered for his own sins as well as for the sins of the people in the manner of the High Priest of the Old Testament. For in this is Christ compared with the High Priest of the Old Testament, or preferred before him, that the former offered sacrifice καθ' ἡμέραν (daily), but Christ indeed only ἐφάπαξ (once for all); that the former had need to offer for his own sins, as being by no means void of sin, but this one only for the sins of the people, as having no sins of his own, being indeed holy, harmless, and undefiled, and separate from sinners, not that he was ever one of them, but because he was most far removed from their life and morals, subject to no sin, he knew no sin 2. Cor. 5, 21. For such a High Priest became us, who did not need to offer himself in sacrifice for his own sins, but only for the sins of the people: God made him sin for us, who knew no sin, and gave the just for the unjust, Isa. 53, 9. 1. Pet. 2, 12. chap. 3, 18. 2. Cor. 5, 21. Nor indeed is it permitted to take sins for infirmities, or for frailty. For not to mention that no passage from the New Testament can be brought forward for this sense (Rom. 6, 10 holds its own proper meaning), sins must be understood in the same sense with ὑπὲρ τῶν ἰδίων ἁμαρτιῶν (for his own sins) as they are taken when it is said he offered ὑπὲρ τῶν τοῦ λαοῦ (for those of the people). But that the sins of the people are properly understood, just as sin is ἀνομία (lawlessness), 1. John 3, 4, is beyond doubt. Therefore, the commentary of Theophylact is far more correct here. For when he had said that this High Priest of ours is separate from sinners, he subsequently amplifies by saying the same thing, and says: He is so much void of all crimes, that even when offering his own body as a victim, he did not offer it for himself (for how could that be done, who had committed no offense?) but he offered it for us. Furthermore, the priests of the Law sacrificed every day, as if they were unable to expiate sins by sacrificing once. But this one offered the victim in such a way, and it was so effective a producer of a great thing, that even in a moment of time it purged the orb of the earth by itself. Whence it happens that even in this, our High Priest CHRIST surpasses the priests of the Law. That interpretation, says B. Dorscheus, which explains verse 26 concerning the state of immortality and happiness, clearly does violence to the words. For holiness is one thing, immortality another. Nor is he primarily ἄκακος (harmless) who suffers no evil, but he who does none. Nowhere, however, are adversities or calamities called μιάσματα (pollutions). Compare 2. Pet. 2, verse 20. Apoc. 14, 4. Schlichtingius clearly does violence to the Apostolic words, when he interprets ἑαυτὸν ἀνενέγκας (having offered up himself) as if he were saying that Christ offered himself once for himself, but now offers himself more often before GOD the Father for us. For he assumes that which

It is contrary to the Apostle's intention, namely that there was a need for Christ to offer for himself, since the Apostle wishes rather that Christ offered himself absolutely only once for all the sins of the human race entirely. Concerning which matter see below Chapter 9, 11, and 12. But also that is false, that death is the antecedent and beginning of Christ's offering, since it is the consummation, John 19, 30, and below C. 9, 27, 28.

Furthermore, that ἐφάπαξ also slays the Papist error, which daily offers Christ in the Mass sacrifice, who ought not to have been offered except once, and thus was offered, as the Apostle testifies: The opposition of which, as the blessed Dorsheus notes, consists in this, that just as the sacrifices of the Old Testament, regardless of whether they were bloody or bloodless, were repeatable, and were to be repeated either yearly, or daily, or more often: So the sacrifice of the Priest of the New Testament is unrepeatable, whatever that may finally be. For if the Priest of the New Testament had one offering only that was unrepeatable, which is bloody, but another, which is bloody, that was repeatable, then the opposition between the two High Priests would have had to be established in such a way that, namely, all the sacrifices of the High Priest of the Old Testament were repeatable, and none unrepeatable. But the sacrifice of the Priest of the New Testament is one, namely bloody and unrepeatable, but the bloodless one is repeatable. Yet the Apostle establishes the opposition otherwise, and indicates that it pertains to the nature of the sacrifice performed according to the order of Melchizedek that it is unrepeatable, or that it must be done ἐφάπαξ.

Latin:

Vers. 27.

Ὃς ἐκ ἔχει καθ᾽ ἡμέραν ἀνάγκην, ὥσπερ οἱ Ἀρχιερεῖς πρό- τερον ὑπὲρ τῶν ἰδίων ἁμαρτιῶν θυσίας ἀναφέρειν, ἔπειτα τῶν τῦ λαῦ. Τῦτο γὰρ ἐποίησεν ἐφάπαξ, ἑαυτὸν ἀνενέγκας] Καθ᾽ ἡμέραν, hic est sæpissime, quoties res fert, ut & infra X, 11. Neque enim tantum in sacro anniversario, sed & quoties aut summus Sacerdos conscius sibi esset subreptio- nis alicujus, aut alius quivis. Offerebantur victimæ περὶ ἁμαρτίας חטאת. Videtur autem & hic & supra V, 3. dici, Christus quoque obtulisse non sæpius quidem, sed semel qui- dem pro peccatis non populi tantum, sed & suis. Quod defendi potest ea explicatione, quam attulimus ad Matth. 27, 50. Ut vox ἁμαρτιῶν de Christo ita sumatur, sicut sin- gulare ἁμαρτία, Rom. 6, 10. pro doloribus illis, qui solent peccatorum pœnæ esse, & quas Christus occasione etiam pec- catorum humani generis toleravit: Et à quibus liberatus est per mortem acceleratam tum cum obtulit non pecudem, sed corpus suum, ut perfectissimam victimam. Et est hæc quoque loquutio de lege sumpta. Nam & profluvium muliebre dicitur תטאת Levit. 12, 8. cap. 15, 30. & lepra, cap. 14, 13. Ubi in Græco περὶ ἁμαρτίας. Sicut hic semel ob- tulisse dicitur Christus: Ita semel pro peccatis passus, 1. Petr. 3, 18. Pro ἀνενέγκας in Manuscripto προσενέγκας, ut supra c. 5, 1. 3. 7. & infra sæpe.

Non est causa, cur à literæ proprietate disceda- tur, & καθ᾽ ἡμέραν vel per sæpissime explicetur, vel quotannis cum Socinianis, quum sit quotidie, nec anniversarium, sed quotidianum sacrificium notet, quod & mane & vesperi offeri solebat non solum pro populi, sed etiam pro Sacerdotis peccatis, Numer. 28, 3. Levit. 9, 8. 15. Ob Schlichtingium id notat hic B. Dorscheus: Verum quidem est, in anniversaria expiatione diversa fuisse sacrificia, quorum prius pro summo sacerdote ejusq́; familia, alterum pro populo jugulabatur. Sed verba Apostolica non necessario de distinctis sacrificiis exponenda sunt. Potest enim fieri, imo re ipsa factum est, ut sacrificium matutinum atq́; vespertinum, seu à summo Sacerdote simpliciter, seu ab eo, qui in vicissitudine sua ἀρχιερωσύνην exercebat, in exomologesi peccatorum primum pro expiando ipso Sacerdote, ejusq́; familia, deinde pro toto populo conciliando offerretur, ita, ut non actus sacrificii fuerint distincti, sed ordo tantum in confessione & precibus observatus, adeoǵ; Sacerdos primum pro se, deinde pro populo apud Deum deprecatus fuerit. Id vero impium prorsus est, quod ad Christum utrumque membrum cum Socinianis applicat Grotius, quod nempe tum pro propriis, tum pro populi peccatis obtulerit Christus more Pontificis V. Testamenti. In eo enim confertur cum Pontifice V. Testamenti, vel præfertur eidem Christus, quod ille καθ' ἡμέραν, Christus vero ἐφάπαξ tantum obtulerit sacrificium, quod ille pro peccatis propriis offerre opus habuerit, utpote peccati minime expers, hic vero non nisi pro populi peccatis, utpote peccata propria non habens, sanctus quippe, innocens & impollutus ac segregatus à peccatoribus, non quod aliquando unus ex illis fuerit, sed quod ab eorum vita & moribus longissime alienus, nulli peccato obnoxius, peccatum non noverit 2. Cor. 5, 21. Talis enim nos decebat Pontifex, qui minime pro suis propriis, sed pro populi peccatis solum sese offerre debuit in sacrificium: Peccatum Deus fecit eum pro nobis, qui peccatum non novit, deditq́; justum pro injustis, Esa. 53, 9. 1. Petr. 2, 12. cap. 3, 18. 2. Cor. 5, 21. Nec vero peccata pro infirmitatibus accipere licet, vel pro fragilitate. Nam ne dicam, quod nullus è Novo Testamento locus pro hoc sensu afferri possit (Rom. 6, 10. propria obtinet significatio) eodem sensu peccata intelligenda cum ὑπὲρ τῶν ἰδίων ἁμαρτιῶν, quo accipiuntur cum ὑπὲρ τῶν τοῦ λαοῦ obtulisse dicitur. Populi autem peccata proprie intelligi, prout peccatum ἀνομία est, 1. Joh. 3, 4. extra dubium est. Longe ergo rectius hic habet commentarius Theophylacti. Cum enim dixisset, nostrum Pontificem hunc esse à peccatoribus segregatum, idipsum dicendo deinceps amplificat, dicitque: Tantopere ille omnium facinorum est expers, ut vel hostiam offerens proprium corpus non illam pro seipso obtulerit (qui enim fieri id poterat, qui nihil deliquisset?) sed pro nobis hanc obtulit. Legis præterea Sacerdotes in dies singulos immolabant, tanquam nequirent semel sacrificando expiare delicta. Hic vero hostiam taliter obtulit, & tam fuit illa rei ingentis effectrix, ut vel temporis momento per se terrarum orbem purgaverit. Quo fit, ut vel in hoc quidem noster Pontifex CHRISTUS superet legis Sacerdotes. Illa interpretatio, inquit B. Dorscheus, quæ vers. 26. de statu immortalitatis & felicitatis explicat, plane vim facit verbis. Aliud enim est sanctitas, aliud immortalitas. Nec primario ἄκακος est, qui nullum malum patitur, sed qui nullum agit. Nuspiam vero adversitates seu calamitates dicuntur μιάσματα. Confer. 2. Petr. 2. vers. 20. Apoc. 14, 4. Plane vero vim facit Schlichtingius verbis Apostolicis, cum ἑαυτὸν ἀνενέγκας ita interpretatur, quasi dicat, Christum semel pro semet seipsum obtulisse, nunc autem offerre apud DEUM Patrem sæpius pro nobis. Sumit enim id, quod

Apostoli intentioni adversatur, scilicet opus fuisse, ut Christus pro se offerret, cum id potius velit Apostolus, absolute tantum semel pro omnibus omnino peccatis humani generis Christum semetipsum obtulisse. Qua de re infra Cap. 9, 11. & 12. Sed & illud falsum est, mortem esse antecedens & initium oblationis Christi, cum sit consummatio, Joh. 19, 30. & infra C. 9, 27. 28.

Porro jugulat etiam illud ἐφάπαξ errorem Papi- sticum, qui quotidie in sacrificio Missatico Chri- stum offerunt, qui non nisi semel offerri debuit, adeoque oblatus est teste Apostolo: Cujus oppo- sitio, ut notat B. Dorsheus, in eo est, quod quem- admodum sacrificia Veteris Testamenti, non atten- to eo, quod vel cruenta vel incruenta fuerint, itera- bilia fuerunt, & seu quotannis, seu quotidie, seu sæpius repetenda: Ita sacrificium Sacerdotis Novi Testamenti sit irreiterabile, quodcunque illud tan- dem sit. Si enim Sacerdos Novi Testamenti babe- ret oblationem unam tantum irreiterabilem, quæ cruenta est, alteram autem, quæ cruenta est, reite- rabilem, tunc ita fuisset constituenda inter utrumq; Pontificem oppositio, quod scilicet sacrificia summi Pontificis Veteris Testamenti omnia fuerint iterabi- lia, nullum irreiterabile. Novi vero Testamenti Pontificis sacrificium unum scilicet cruentum irrei- terabile, incruentum vero reiterabile sit. Atqui aliter oppositionem constituit Apostolus, & ad sacri- ficii secundum ordinem Melchisedechi peragendi na- turam pertinere irreiterabilem, seu quod ἐφάπαξ fieri debeat, indicat.

## 7:28
Verse 28.

For the law appoints men as high priests, having infirmity] The Law of Moses brought forth without an oath. Infirmity here are the adversities to which mortality is subject, as above chapter 4, v. 15.

But the word of the oath] The sworn promise of God in the Psalm.

After the law] Things that are later in laws ought to be more perfect.

A Son perfected forever] Perfected in this place signifies so perfect that he is subject neither to death nor to any adversities. We had that word in a similar sense above chapter 2, 10. And the Son, namely of God, not a man equal to others by the lot of birth.

The reason is given why the Levitical Priests had to offer for their own sins, because, namely, they were not free from infirmities: Why, on the contrary, CHRIST did not have the necessity to offer for his own sins, because he labored under no moral or sinful infirmities. For the word of the oath, which was made after the law, constitutes a High Priest not a man subject to sin, but the very Son of God himself, consummated with all perfections without any defect, who is not only now impeccable, but always remains such: Since he is eternally perfect, not only by reason of his person, as being holy and higher than the heavens, raised to the highest perfection: But also by reason of his priesthood, which alone and uniquely has the perfect power to expiate our sins and to reconcile us to God.
