Pareus takes these as an ἀποδιωκτικὴν (dismissive) conclusion, as if to say: I will say in a word: The legal Priests were infirm and temporary. The Son of God CHRIST is confirmed by the oath of the Father as a perfect High Priest forever; which whole argument could draw the Hebrews to CHRIST. But the reason seems to be given for the preceding sentence. Concerning which Theophylact in this place: Lest perhaps a suspicion should enter your mind, even if he offered a sacrifice here once, that he also offered this for himself, he confirms it now by saying that he offers nothing for his own sins. According to the law, indeed, men devoid of Divinity are appointed Priests, having infirmity, that is, who are less able to resist offenses, but succumb to them as weaklings. But this one, since he is the almighty Son, how could he be subject to sin? Who therefore is conscious of no evil in himself, why would he be about to offer a sacrifice for himself? Since he did not offer often for others, but once. Because since he excels in virtue and power, he could sufficiently accomplish all things by a single and sole offering. And furthermore: Note the disjunction. For there the law is mentioned, here the word of the oath, that is, the most firm and most true. There men and all bound by servitude, here the Son and at the same time Lord. Those were infirm, that is, delinquent and subject to sin, and subject to death. This one is perfect forever, that is, everlasting and powerful. And not only while he lived among men, but he is perpetually devoid of offense. If therefore this one is always, if he never slips, if he leads a life perpetually, why ought he to offer either for himself or for the sake of others a sacrifice more frequently? But Grotius's gloss concerning the adversities to which mortality is subject does not fit. For Christ also performed his priesthood on earth, even though he was subject to death and other adversities. In that, therefore, he is not opposed to the Priests of the Old Testament. B. Dorscheus explains this fuller distinction between the High Priest of the Old and New Testament in these words: The High Priests of the Old Testament are called ἄνθρωποι, that is to say, mere and pure, and therefore subject to all human accidents, both natural and moral. The High Priest of the New Testament is called υἱὸς, and indeed in a proper, most eminent, and most simple sense. Therefore, the natural and substantial Son of God the Father, the Son from eternity. Concerning whom [see] above c. 1, 1. and 3. 6. at greater length. Not that he is not ἄνθρωπος, but that he is not primarily ἄνθρωπος, because he is ἄνθρωπος only in the fullness of time, Gal. 4, 4. seqq. Wherefore, because he is υἱὸς, he is Θεάνθρωπος, whence also Κύριος [see] above v. 14. The Old Testament presented High Priests having ἀσθένειαν, infirmity, not only that which Christ also freely underwent, concerning which it was said above in Chapter 5, v. 2; but also that from which Christ is clearly separated, both of sin, concerning which [see] above v. 26, 27, and of death owed on account of sin, by which title the High Priest of the New Testament did not undergo death, because the just suffered for the unjust, 1 Pet. 3, v. 18, and also such a death, by the intervention of which the ἀξίωμα ἀρχιερωσύνης is lost. The New Testament has a High Priest εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετελειωμένον, and therefore one who does not lose the office of High Priest, even through the intervention of death. For when it is said εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετελειωμένος, it refers not only to the consummated sacrifice for the sins of the whole human race, concerning which it was said above in Chapter 2, 10. Chapter 5, verse 9, but also to the state of glory, in which, after having overcome his emptying and the death he underwent, he was exalted above all things, and therefore also τετελειωμένος to an eternal Priesthood. For even if the immolation and slaughter of the sacrifice was done ἐφάπαξ, v. 27, yet the dispensation of the sacrifice and the preservation of the sanctuary, and the governance of the priestly people, must be continued until the consummation of the age, Matt. 18, 20. For two or three gathered in the name of CHRIST are certainly gathered most especially in the name of the High Priest. For it was the duty of the Priest to make holy congregations. Therefore, the High Priest of the New Testament is the Author of holy congregations. He has τὸ πτῶμα. Therefore, with him occurs the σύναξις τῶν ἀετῶν, Matt. 24, v. 28. He has, however, τὸ πτῶμα of his universal sacrifice, which satisfies all things. There, therefore, in the midst of those gathered, it is necessary that the High Priest be present for the dispensation of the sacrifice, the preservation of the sanctuary, and the custody of those sanctified, cf. Chapter 28, verse 20.

He is, therefore, the high Priest of the New Testament εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετελειωμένος (perfected forever) by his session at the right hand, from which flows an ἐξοχὴ (preeminence) above every principality, power, virtue, and dominion, Eph. 1. v. 20, 21, etc., the πλήρωσις πάντων (fullness of all things) Eph. 4, 10, the ὑποταγὴ πάντων (subjection of all things) Heb. 2, 7, 8. A Παρουσία or gracious presence in the midst of the faithful, of which we spoke before from Matt. 18, 20. Whence it appears how great is the difference between the high Priest of each Testament. The Priest of the Old Testament, after laying aside his ἀσθένειαν (weakness), attained at the same time the τέλος (end) of his office, and if he obtained any τελείωσιν (perfection), it pertained to the state of glory, but not to the prolongation of his duty: the high Priest of the New Testament, after the τελείωσιν (perfection) of his emptying, arrived through his exaltation at a more sublime τελείωσιν (perfection) of his office and priestly dignity. The high Priest of the Old Testament, while he lived, was indeed among his own, although daily among a few, and only in more solemn congregations among the greatest multitude; but after his life, just as his office ceased, so he himself ceased to be present with the gathered assembly. But the Priest of the New Testament is so τετελειωμένος (perfected) that, although in the state of emptying he walked upon these lands (Acts 10, 38) and thus dispensed a beneficent presence under a servile form, he did not, upon attaining the end of bearing the servile form, also put an end to his beneficent presence, but rather is present with a more sublime and divine presence to the whole multitude of holy congregations, wherever in the world they may exist. For the priesthood of the Old Testament is not more perfect than that of the New by reason of the presence of the high Priest. Therefore, since the priesthood of the Old Testament always presented the high Priest as present among the congregations, especially the solemn and greatest ones, unless he were hindered by some chance, it certainly behooves the priesthood of the New Testament also to exhibit the high Priest, who can be hindered by no chance, as always present to the congregations of the faithful. In which respect, in relation to the priesthood of the Old Testament, Christ our Priest was seen (Rev. 1, 13) in the midst of the golden lampstands, clothed with a garment down to the feet, and girt about the paps with a golden girdle. And this also concerning the seventh chapter.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

ὁ νόμος γὰρ ἀνθρώπες καθίστησιν ἀρχιερεῖς, ἔχοντας ἀσθένειαν ] Lex Mosis sine jurejurando prolata. Ἀσθέ- νειαν hic sunt adversa, quibus subjecta est mortalitas, ut supra cap. 4. v. 15.

Ὁ λόγος δὲ τῆς ὁρκωμοσίας ] Promissum Dei juratum in Psalmo.

Μετὰ τὸν νόμον ] Debent posteriora in legibus esse per- fectiora.

Υἱὸν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετελειωμένον ] Τετελειωμένον hoc lo- co significat ita perfectum, ut nec morti, nec ullis adverfi- tatibus subjaceat. Pari sensu id verbum habuimus supra cap. 2, 10. Et Filium nempe Dei, non hominem cæteris parem nascendi sorte.

Causa redditur, cur Levitici Sacerdotes pro pec- catis propriis offerre debuerint, quia nempe infir- mitatibus non destituebantur: Cur ex adverso non offerre necessum habuerit pro peccatis propriis CHRISTUS, quia nullis laborarit infirmitatibus moralibus, vel peccaminosis. Nam sermo jurisju- randi, quod post legem factum, constituit Pontificem non hominem peccato obnoxium, sed ipsummet Fi- lium Dei, omnibus perfectionibus citra ullum de- fectum consummatum, qui non nunc solum im- peccabilis sit, sed talis semper manet: Quum æter- num perfectus sit, non personæ modo ratione, utpote sanctus & excelsior cœlis in summam eve- ctus perfectionem: Sed & ratione sacerdotii, quod solum atque unicum perfectam vim habet peccata nostra expiandi, acDeo nos reconciliandi. Pareus hæc accipit ceu conclusionem ἀποδιωκτι- κὴν, q. d. verbo dicam: Legales Sacerdotes infirmi & temporarii fuerunt. Filius Dei CHRISTUS jurejurando Patris firmatus est Pontifex perfectus in æternum; quæ tota ratio Ebræos ad CHRISTUM trahere potuerit. Sed ratio reddi videtur præce- dentis sententiæ. Quo de Theophylactus in h. l. Ne forsan te suspicio subeat, & si semel hic obtulerit hostiam, pro se etiam hanc obtulisse, confirmat nunc dicens, nihil hunc pro suis peccatis offerre. Secun- dum legem vero homines Divinitatis expertes consti- tuere Sacerdotes, habentes infirmitatem, hoc est, qui minus possint delictis obsistere, sed illis, ut imbecilli succumbunt. Hic autem cum sit filius præpotens, quo pacto quiverit peccato subesse? Qui ergo nullius est sibi conscius mali, cur hostiam esset pro se oblatu- rus? Siquidem nec sæpe pro aliis, sed semel obtulerit. Quia cum virtute is præstet & potestate, vel unica & sola oblatione satis potuit cuncta perficere. Ex porro: Adverte disjunctionem. Ibi enim lex di- citur, hic jurisjurandi sermo, id est, firmissimus ve- rissimusque. Ibi homines & servitute omnes obstri- cti, hic Filius simul & Dominus. Illi infirmi, hoc est, delinquentes & peccato obnoxii, ac morti subje- cti. Hic in æternum perfectus, id est, sempiternus & potens. Nec solum cum inter homines ageret, sed perpetuo delicti est expers. Hic itaq́; si semper est, si labitur nunquam, si vitam perpetuo ducit, quamobrem vel pro se offerre, vel aliorum gratia hostiam frequentiùs debet? Non autem conve- nit Grotii de adversis, quibus subjecta est mortali- tas, glossa. Nam etiam in terris sacerdotio fun- ctus est Christus, etsi morti aliisque adversitatibus subjectus. In eo ergo non opponitur Sacerdoti- bus Veteris Testamenti. Plenius discrimen hoc- ce Pontificis Veteris & Novi Testamenti his verbis indicatum explicat B. Dorscheus: Veteris Testa- menti summi Sacerdotes vocantur ἄνθρωποι, scilicet meri & puri, adeoq́; omnibus humanis Accidentibus obnoxii tum naturalibus tum moralibus. Novi Te- stamenti summus Sacerdos dicitur υἱὸς, & quidem in sensu proprio, eminentissimo, & simplicissimo. Itaq́; naturalis & substantialis Dei Patris Filius, Filius ab æterno. De quo supra c. 1, 1. & 3. 6. pluribus. Non, quod non sit ἄνθρωπος, sed quod non sit primo ἄνθρωπος, quia in plenitudine temporis demum ἄν- θρωπος, Gal. 4, 4. seqq. Quapropter quia υἱὸς est Θεάνθρωπος, unde etiam Κύριος sup. v. 14. Vetus Testamentum stitit summos Sacerdotes habentes ἀσθένειαν infirmitatem, non eam tantum, quam Christus libere quoq́; subiit, de qua supra Cap. 5. v. 2. dictum est; sed & illam, à qua Christus plane est se- paratus tum peccati, de qua sup. v. 26. 27. tum mortis propter peccatum debitæ, quo titulo summus Sacer- dos Novi Testamenti mortem non subiit, quia passus est justus pro injustis, 1. Petr. 3. v. 18. & talis etiam mortis, qua interveniente ἀξίωμα ἀρχιερωσύνης amittitur. Novum Testamentum habet summum Sacerdotem εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετελειωμένον, adeoq́; offi- cium summi Sacerdotis, etiam per interventum mor- tis, non amittentem. Nam cum dicitur εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετελειωμένος, non tantum ad consummatum sacri- ficium pro peccatis totius generis humani respicitur, de quo dictum est supra Cap. 2, 10. Cap. 5. vers. 9. sed etiam ad statum gloriæ, quo post superatam exina- nitionem & mortem subitam exaltatus est super omnia, adeoq́; etiam ad æternum Sacerdotium τετε- λειωμένος. Etiam si enim immolatio & mactatio sacrificii facta sit ἐφάπαξ, v. 27. dispensatio tamen sacrificii & sanctuarii conservatio, & populi Sacer- dotalis gubernatio continuanda est ad consummatio- nem usque seculi, Matth. 18, 20. Nam duo vel tres congregati in nomen CHRISTI, utiq́; potissimum in nomen summi Sacerdotis congregantur. Congre- gationes enim sanctas facere Sacerdotis fuit. Sum- mus ergo Sacerdos Novi Testamenti congregationum sanctarum Autor est. Ille habet τὸ πτῶμα. Ergo apud illum fit σύναξις τῶν ἀετῶν, Matth. 24. v. 28. Habet autem τὸ πτῶμα sacrificii sui universalis, & omnia satiantis. Ibi ergo in medio congregatorum summum Sacerdotem ad sacrificii dispensationem, sanctuarii conservationem, & sanctificatorum custo- diam præstantem esse oportet, conf. Cap. 28. vers. 20.

Est itaq́, summus Sacerdos Novi Testamenti εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τετελειωμένος per sessionem ad dextram, ex qua fluit ἐξοχὴ supra omnem principatum, potesta- tem, virtutem, dominationem, Ephes. 1. v. 20. 21. &c. πλήρωσις πάντων Eph. 4, 10. ὑποταγὴ πάντων Ebr. 2, 7. 8. Παρουσία seu præsentia gratiosa in medio fide- lium, de qua ante ex Matth. 18, 20. Unde apparet, quanta sit differentia inter Sacerdotem summum utriusq́ Testamenti. Veteris Testamenti Sacerdos post depositam ἀσθένειαν adeptus simul est τέλος offi- cii sui, & si quam nactus est τελείωσιν, illa ad statum gloriæ pertinuit, non autem ad prorogationem mune- ris: Summus Sacerdos Novi Testamenti post τελείω- σιν exinanitionis per exaltationem ad sublimiorem τελείωσιν muneris sui dignitatisq́ Sacerdotalis perve- nit. Summus Sacerdos Veteris Testamenti dum vi- xit, apud suos quidem fuit, quamvis quotidie apud paucos, & non nisi in solennioribus congregationibus apud multitudinem maximam, post vitam autem sic- ut munus ipsius desiit, ita & ipse cœtui congregato adeffe desiit. Sacerdos autem Novi Testamenti adeo est τετελειωμένος, ut quamvis in statu exinanitio- nis in his terris circumiverit Actor. 10, 38. adeoque præsentiam beneficam sub servili forma dispensave- rit, non tamen finem formæ servilis circumferendæ consequutus etiam finem fecerit præsentiæ beneficæ, sed potius sublimiori & Divina quadam præsentia toti congregationum sanctarum multitudini, ubicun- que terrarum eæ existant, adsit. Neq́ enim per- fectius est ratione præsentiæ summi Sacerdotis sacer- dotium Veteris Testamenti, quam Novi. Itaq́ cum Veteris Testamenti sacerdotium apud congregationes imprimis solennes & maximas semper præsentem sti- terit Sacerdotem summum, nisi casu aliquo impedire- tur. Utiq́ oportet etiam Sacerdotium Novi Testa- menti Sacerdotem summum, qui nullo casu impediri potest, semper præsentem congregationibus fidelium exhibere. Quo respectu ad Sacerdotium Veteris Te- stamenti Christus Sacerdos noster visus est, Apoc. 1, 13. in medio candelabrorum aureorum, indutus talari veste, & cinctus ad lumbos zona aurea. Atque hæc etiam de septimo capite.

## 8:1 Argument
CHAPTER VIII.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

The principal head of the things said having been repeated, namely, what kind of High Priest we have, who sits at the right hand of God and performs sacred duties, and therefore has brought into the heavens the victim of his own body, which he offered on earth, whereas other priests perform their priesthood only on earth, as they serve only a type, he himself having attained an administration so much more excellent, by which he has become the Mediator of a better Testament. The Apostle now undertakes to prove this, namely, that a better testament has been established by him, adducing a Prophetic passage (Jerem. XXXI. vers 31 seqq.) and arguing that if the former had been blameless, there would have been no place for another, but while a new Testament is introduced, the former must necessarily be antiquated.

There are two parts. I. The supreme eminence of our High Priest is taught, up to v. 5. II. The preeminence of the New Testament is demonstrated, up to v. 13.

PART I. The supreme eminence of our High Priest.

Κεφάλαιον δὲ ἐπὶ τοῖς λεγομένοις] After so many things said, let this be the sum. In the Glossary, κεφάλαιον means sum. ראש Exod. 30, 11. Num. 4, 2. chap. 31, 26. 49. Isocrates, Thucydides, and Plato use it thus. See what was said on Rom. 13, 9. In the Manuscript, ἐν τοῖς λεγομένοις. In the things just said, this is the principal point.

Τοιοῦτον ἔχομεν ἀρχιερέα, ὃς ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ τοῦ θρόνου τῆς μεγαλωσύνης] See above chap. 1. v. 3. Θρόνῳ μεγαλωσύνης (throne of majesty) signifies the very majesty of God. Maimonides correctly explains this in the Guide for the Perplexed, book 9. The sons of Aaron stood by the ark: He sits by the throne of God, as a partner in power.

Ἐν τοῖς ὐρανοῖς] That is, ἐν ὐρανῷ ὐρανῶν (in the heaven of heavens), which he called above ἐν ὑψηλοῖς (in the heights) chap. 1, 3. See what we said on Matthew chap. 3, 2.

Κεφάλαιον denotes not only a sum, but also that which is principal. Grotius himself does not deny this, rendering it thus: In what has been said, this is the principal thing. So also Erasmus: But of those things which we have said, this is the head. The greatest honor, says Theodoret, he left for the last and shows him sitting at the right hand of the Majesty. For the parent of the priesthood, Aaron, who first undertook the office of the Pontificate, entered the Divine tabernacle with fear and trembling. But this one sits at the right hand. Therefore, Pareus rightly noted the translations of others here: The Old [version] obscurely word for word: But the chapter upon the things which are said. Others: But the sum of those things which we say; as if the Apostle were instituting a recapitulation of what has been said, or that he is reducing what has been said thus far into a sum, which indeed I do not disapprove. But because far more things preceded concerning the priesthood of Christ and Aaron than the Apostle repeats here, I do not accept κεφάλαιον as a sum, but properly as a head, but as the principal part of the comparison premised. For the head is always called that which is greatest, says Chrysostom. The sense therefore is ἐπὶ τοῖς λεγομένοις, besides or above those things which have been said thus far concerning the excellencies of Christ, there remains the κεφάλαιον, the head, that is, the principal preeminence. For this must be diligently observed, which these very words of the Apostle sufficiently speak, and it is clear from the whole treatment, that this was especially proposed to him to teach concerning that eminence of our Pontiff, that he himself performs his priesthood in heaven for all eternity. For although he does not omit the former part concerning the offering of the sacrifice of his body on earth, namely on the altar of the cross, in the contention with other priests of the Old Testament, yet he especially urges the other function, as being more eminent, namely the intercession, which he performs as an eternal Priest in the heavens; which clearly teaches how great our Pontiff is, so that by proposing this eminence of his, he may draw the Hebrews from the law to Christ. These words mean this, says the blessed Hunnius, that this is the principal head, and as it were the sum of all those things which can be said concerning Christ the Pontiff, that we have such a Pontiff, who is many times more excellent than the Pontiffs of the Levitical priesthood. First, by reason of his person and Divine majesty, since our Pontiff has sat down at the right hand of God: And thus he is not a terrestrial Priest, who, subject to infirmities, administers his priesthood on earth: But he is a celestial Pontiff, clearly endowed with Divine majesty, and thus to be seen on the very throne of the right hand of God. For although he performed his priesthood on the cross while still existing as mortal, while he offered himself to God as an odor of a sweet fragrance: Yet after the purgation of sins was thus made through him, having laid aside mortality and human infirmities, which, sin excepted, he had taken upon himself for our sake, he sat down at the right hand of God. Furthermore, to sit at the right hand of the throne is to reign by Divine power, which is of the throne or of the Divine empire, of God the Father, τοῦ θρόνου τῆς μεγαλωσύνης, of the empire of Majesty and glory, or glorious. Grotius rightly acknowledges that it signifies the Majesty of God itself. Therefore not to an inferior, than It is divine in power, because the right hand of God denotes the infinite power of God, not by an authority inferior to that of God, because this is the authority of the Divine Majesty itself. Christ reigns with a glory no less than that of the Father. Whence it is manifest what kind of and how great a High Priest we have, who at once excels in such great Royal dignity and Majesty, and is able to powerfully rule, protect, preserve, and save his own eternally; and according to the manner of Melchizedek, he performs both the High Priesthood and the Royal office at once in a most excellent manner. Concerning which Theodoret says: He added that word λειτουργὸς, that is, Minister of the priestly office, because he speaks of the High Priest. For since he performs the priestly office, who offered himself, does he not offer sacrifice any longer? But how can it come to pass that the same one sits and performs the priestly office at the same time? Unless perhaps someone might say that the priestly office is the salvation which the Lord procures. Undoubtedly, he wills that he should procure our salvation both as Priest and as Lord and King, that is, not only by interceding, but also by advancing the same through the Divine authority and power granted to him by his exaltation. Therefore he says in this place, with Theophylact saying, the head is over those things which are spoken, that is, that which I shall say is more excellent, and in brief, we have God himself as our High Priest. But it is most fitting for GOD to sit. Observe, however, that when he had explained many humble things—such as those are when he calls God a High Priest, when he says that he performs intercessions, and as many as are of this kind and human—he soon transcends to higher things, and said that he sits at the right hand of the throne of majesty, which is certainly of the Divine Majesty. But he calls it the seat and throne of the Father's majesty: either because the Father himself has obtained that name of majesty, or simply because that greatest and most sublime throne of GOD is called the seat. Whence most rightly B. Hunnius: But lest anyone should imagine that right hand of God to be local, or some place in the heavens: he adds a certain and evident notation, while he calls it the right hand of the throne of Majesty, implying that Christ, when he ascended into the heavens, occupied the very throne of the Divine Majesty and the omnipotence of God: since the right hand of God, which governs all things, is nothing else but the majesty and omnipotence of God. But what is added, in the heavens, is understood by the name of heaven as eternal life, or the heavenly kingdom, which is described by blessedness and heavenly glory rather than by place. Pareus himself in this place has it thus: The throne of majesty is the empire of God, which he exercises gloriously and with the highest Majesty in the heavens over all creatures. For a throne is a Royal seat; by metalepsis it designates a kingdom, an empire. The right hand of the throne of Majesty is the highest degree of this glorious power. And further: Because CHRIST our High Priest has sat down at this right hand of the throne of Majesty, he is declared to be truly the supreme Monarch of heaven and earth. Indeed, this session argues that he is equal to GOD the Father and the Holy Spirit in nature and power. For no one sits at the right hand of God, reigning with power equal to God, unless he be God, or one with God, that is, God himself. Hence the Fathers always asserted the equality of the Son with the Father against heretics from the session at the right hand. In the first Epistle to the Corinthians XV, this sitting of Christ at the right hand of God is declared by reigning, which is not to be understood absolutely. The Father also reigns: the Holy Spirit reigns: yet the Father or the Holy Spirit is not said to sit at the right hand of God: But this honor is claimed in the Scriptures as proper to Christ the exalted Mediator. Christ therefore reigns more strictly by sitting at the right hand of God: because, namely, the expiation of our sins having been made by himself in his flesh, he was exalted in priesthood and kingdom above all Angels and men, declared the head of all, through whom the Father governs all things in heaven and on earth. That exaltation was, first, the laying aside of all humility and infirmity, and the all-manner of perfection of the assumed flesh, and glory above all heavenly powers. Next, the declaration and usurpation of the Pontifical power and Royal power, which is supreme, in the assumed flesh. Finally, divine honor and worship is to be attributed to this exalted High Priest and King by all creatures of heaven, earth, and the underworld. In these parts, if you observe well, the glory of the session of Christ at the right hand of God is described, Eph. 1, Phil. 2, 1 Cor. 15, and elsewhere. These are the words of Pareus; who, however, contradicts himself no less than the Divine truth when he explains the right hand in terms of the honor which monarchs communicate to ambassadors coming to them. For that is not the supreme honor absolutely so called, fitting for the supreme Monarch of heaven and earth himself, which pertains to the Father and the Holy Spirit, and which implies power, rule, and Divine worship equal to God; just as the glory, power of reigning, and authority of an ambassador or some lieutenant is not the same in all respects as that of the King or Prince himself. The sophisms which he opposes to the Majesty of the flesh of Christ with notable self-contradiction are discussed elsewhere. But that he calls the Hunian explanation of the words in the heavens a twisted gloss, and strives to prove with arguments that the name of heavens properly denotes here the heavenly place where our High Priest lives and reigns gloriously as if on a throne and in a heavenly Palace, does not seem to be passed over in silence. And therefore we must briefly examine those things. By the session, he says, at the right hand, glory and kingdom are signified. We agree: But are the words in the heavens therefore to be understood properly of a place? The right hand of the Divine Majesty and the throne of God is also in the heavens: But is God properly in a place, and does he dwell in the heavens as if in his Royal palace, namely a heavenly one? Is not the heavenly glory, in which he is established, and that unapproachable light in which God dwells, rather denoted by the name of heavens, than a place and some Royal or heavenly region? Concerning the word in the heights, chapter 1, 3, it was dealt with around that place. But when in chapter 4, 14, it is said that he has penetrated the heavens, and c. 7, 26, that he was made higher than the heavens, the Calvinist gloss concerning the sublimity of place is openly refuted. For what material place is there above the created heavens? What will remain above the created heavens when they are consumed by fire and substantially destroyed? We do not see what stands in the way of Hunnius's explanation. But he has not been made higher than the heavenly kingdom, nor can he be said to have penetrated glory. Resp. But who has ever said that? And what is the consequence, when he is said to be above the heavens, to be higher than the heavens, and to have penetrated the heavens, material heavens are understood. Therefore, also when he is said to be in the heavens, the material heaven is to be understood, in which he is established as if in his proper place. Should these not rather be reconciled in such a way that Christ is also said to be in heaven, because he reigns in glory or in the Divine Majestic heaven, just as the Father, who is contained by no place, whom the heaven of heavens do not contain, is in the heavens. And furthermore, he is higher than the heavens, because he transcends the heavens in glory, and Christ has been made higher than them. In which way also, on account of the eminence of glory and Majesty, we say διεληλυθότα τῆς ὐρανὸς, Heb. 4, 14, not because we understand by that heavenly glory, but material heavens, which by passing through he penetrated into the holy of holies, the glorious and Majestic heaven of God. But that it is material, as a certain local or corporeal and material palace, not even the Calvinists themselves would say: Just as they cannot conclude from the antithesis of earth that heavens and earths are locally opposed, since God himself is in the heavens and on the earth, to whom indeed no place is suitable, and it is said of the Son of man that he both ascended into the heavens and is on earth, John 3, 13. He who ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things Eph. 4, 10. See what we have argued against the Calvinists in Vol. III. System. page 997. et seqq. B. Dorscheus wishes to imply here by the word throne the seat in the holy of holies, and thus he discourses concerning these things:

The Apostle, when he speaks of the session at the right hand of the throne of Majesty, alludes to the holy of holies itself, in which also a throne was placed, namely on the cover of the ark, which, covered by the outstretched wings of the Cherubim, was called the throne of God. Whence God is frequently said to sit between the Cherubim, or to rest upon them. But this inner sanctuary, this retreat, this seat was of such dignity, and was observed with such religion, that no priest of the Old Testament ever dared to sit upon it. That session was reserved for God alone; as many as entered the holy of holies were compelled to stand before that seat. Hence the excellence of the Priest of the New Testament shines forth exceedingly. For since as GOD blessed for ever Rom. 9, 5. & as the rock, which was always at hand for the Israelites, 1. Corinth. 10, 4. he had hitherto always sat even above the Cherubim in the holy of holies, now he has surpassed all those things by a very great distance. The cover of the ark, which was called the mercy seat, was by no means the right hand of God. The high priest of the New Testament sat at the very right hand of GOD. The cover of the ark was called a certain throne of Divine glory, but finite and shadowy. The high priest of the New Testament sat not only above those carved Cherubim, but above the spiritual Cherubim or thrones, as they are called Coloss. 1, 16. and occupied the very highest and everlasting throne of Divine glory. The cover of the ark pertained to the priesthood, but it did not have a peculiar greatness. The high priest of the New Testament has attained the very infinite and Divine greatness. The cover of the ark was on earth, where the tabernacle itself was fixed. The seat of the high priest of the New Testament is in the heavens, not finite but infinite, as being the right hand of GOD, consistent with his throne and majesty. Therefore in this way the Apostle wishes to argue: He who is a Priest who sat not only on the throne of the sanctuary, and above the mercy seat, which was never granted to any priest of the Old Testament, but also sat above the throne of immense Majesty in the heavens at the right hand of God, he is incomparably more excellent than the priests of the Old Testament, and thus is the true Priest according to the Davidic prediction. But such is the Priest of the Christian religion. Therefore Capellus in this place, page 127, says ineptly: It is one thing to sit at the right hand, another to be co-extended with the right hand or to be equal to the right hand of the Father. The former is attributed to the body of CHRIST, or if you prefer, to CHRIST considered according to his Human nature, not the latter, and thus the sublimity of the seat granted to the body of Christ does not infer infinity, it does not infer, I say, immensity, any more than eternity. For who has inferred the infinity or immensity of the body of CHRIST from that session? The orthodox have inferred from thence that this session bestows a Divine presence, which Scripture calls now the filling of all things, now a presence in the midst of the faithful until the end of the age, now a dwelling in the body of the faithful, now a walking in the midst of the golden lampstands. For he who sits at the right hand of God, so that he may rule in the midst of his enemies, and everywhere reign in the faithful, although he may not have all the attributes in which the Divine right hand excels, nevertheless he is there where the right hand of GOD is. Otherwise he would not sit at the right hand of God, but would be below the right hand of God, and thus subject to the right hand, not Lord at the right hand, as is said in Psalm CX, 5. concerning Christ. But he sits at the right hand in such a way, and indeed according to his Human nature. Therefore he is there where the right hand of GOD is.

Therefore he is in all things such as the right hand of God is. Wherefore infinity and immensity must be distinguished from the Divine presence. For those are absolute attributes. But the Divine presence has a relation to the outside and to creatures, and does not exist except when creatures exist. Whence with the world about to pass away, the presence to the world will cease, although the Majesty of being present to the world and to all creatures existing or about to exist is immutable and perpetual. Who also has claimed co-extension or equalization with the right hand of the Father for the Human nature by this session? For the right hand of God the Father is not something extended. Therefore, so that the Human nature may be everywhere through the right hand of God, there is no need for co-extension. The Majesty and power of the right hand suffice, from which Christ can also present his Human nature present to the objects of his dominion.

Latin:

CAPUT VIII.

ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Præcipuo dictorum capite repetito, qualem habeamus Pontificem, qui nempe ad dex- tram Dei considet, sacrisq́ operatur, atque ideo victimam corporis sui, quam obtulit in terris in cælos intulit, quum Sacerdotes alii non nisi in terris sacerdotio suo defungan- tur, utpote typo tantum inservientes, ipse administrationem tanto excellentiorem adeptus, quo melioris Testamenti Mediator factus est. Id jam probandum sumit Apo- stolus, quod nempe testamentum melius ab ipso sancitum sit, adducens locum Propheti- cum (Jerem. XXXI. vers 31. seqq.) arguens- que, si prius inculpabile foret, alteri locus non fuisset, dum vero novum Testamentum introducitur, prius antiquari oporteat.

Partes duæ sunt. I. Pontificis nostri summa eminentia docetur, ad v. 5. II. Novi Testamenti præcellentia demonstratur, ad v. 13.

PARS I. Pontificis nostri summa eminentia.

Κεφάλαιον δὲ ἐπὶ τοῖς λεγομένοις] Post tot dicta hæc esto summa. In Glossario κεφάλαιον, summa. ראש Exod. 30, 11. Num. 4, 2. cap. 31, 26. 49. Utuntur sic Iso- crates, Thucydides, Plato. Vide quæ dicta ad Rom. 13, 9. In Manuscripto, ἐν τοῖς λεγομένοις. In jam dictis hoc est præcipuum.

Τοιοῦτον ἔχομεν ἀρχιερέα, ὃς ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ τοῦ θρόνου τῆς μεγαλωσύνης] Vide supra cap. 1. v. 3. Θρόνῳ μεγαλω- σύνης כסא כבוד significat ipsam Dei majestatem. Ex- plicat id recte Maimonides Ducis dubitantium l. 9. Aaro- nidæ apud arcam stabant: Hic apud thronum Dei consi- det, ut potestatis consors.

Ἐν τοῖς ὐρανοῖς] Id est, ἐν ὐρανῷ ὐρανῶν, quod supra di- xit ἐν ὑψηλοῖς c. 1, 3. Vide quæ diximus ad Matthæum c.3, 2.

Κεφάλαιον non summam tantum notat, sed et- iam id, quod præcipuum est. Id Grotius ipse non dif- fitetur, ita reddens: In jam dictis hoc est præci- puum. Sic etiam Erasmus: Cæterum eorum, quæ diximus, illud est caput. Maximum hono- rem, inquit Theodoretus, postremum reliquit & ostendit eum sedere in dextra Majestatis. Sacerdo- tem enim Parens Aaron, qui Pontificatus munus su- scepit primus, cum timore & horrore Divinum in- troibat tabernaculum. Hic autem sedet à dextris. Ideo recte aliorum translationes notavit hic Pa- reus: Vetus obscure ad verbum: Capitulum autem super ea, quæ dicuntur. Alii: Cæterum eorum, quæ dicimus, summa est; quasi Apostolus ἀνακεφαλαίω- σιν instituat dictorum, seu quod hactenus dicta redi- gat in summam, quod quidem non improbo. Sed quia longe plura præcesserunt de Christi & Aaronis sa- cerdotio, quam Apostolus hic repetat, κεφάλαιον non accipio pro summa, se proprie pro capite, sed principa- li parte comparationis præmissæ. Caput enim semper, quod maximum est, dicitur, inquit Chrysostomus. Est ergo sensus ἐπὶ τοῖς λεγομένοις præter vel super ea, quæ dicta sunt hactenus de Christi præcellentiis, restat κε- φάλαιον caput, h. e. principalis præexcellentia. Nam id sedulo observandum, quod hæc ipsa etiam Apo- stoli verba satis loquiuntur, & è tota tractatione li- quet, hoc præcipue eidem propositum fuisse doce- re de eminentia illa Pontificis nostri, quod in cælo ipse sacerdotio suo fungatur in omnem æternitatem. Etsi enim priorem partem de sacrificii corporis obla- tione in terris, in ara nempe crucis, facta non præ- termittat in contentione cum aliis Sacerdotibus Veteris Testamenti, maxime tamen alteram fun- ctionem, ceu eminentiorem, nempe intercessionem, quam ceu Sacerdos æternus in cælis peragit, urget; quæ quantus sit noster Pontifex, luculenter docet, ut à lege ad Christum, illâ hujus eminentiâ propo- sita Ebræos trahat. Hæc verba hoc volunt, inquit B. Hunnius, esse hoc caput principale, & quasi summam omnium eorum, quæ de Christo Pontifice dici possunt, quod Pontificem habemus talem, qui multis vicibus excellentior sit Pontificibus Sacerdotii Levitici. Pri- mo ratione suæ personæ & Divinæ majestatis, quan- doquidem noster Pontifex consedit ad dextram Dei: Atq; sic non terrenus Sacerdos est, qui infirmitatibus subjectus suum in terris Sacerdotium administret: Sed cœlestis est Pontifex, Divina plane majestate præditus, adeoq́; in ipso throno Dei dextra conspiciendus. Quan- quam enim Sacerdotium suum præstitit in cruce mor- talis adhuc existens, dum seipsum Deo in odorem bonæ fragrantiæ obtulit: Tamen postquam sic purgatio peccatorum per ipsum facta est, deposita mortalitate & humanis infirmitatibus, quas dempto peccato nostri causa in se receperat, consedit ad dextram Dei. Por- ro in dextra throni sedere est regnare virtute divina, quæ throni vel imperii est Divini, Dei Patris, τοῦ θρόνου τῆς μεγαλωσύνης, imperii Majestatis & glo- riæ, vel gloriosi. Ipsam Dei Majestatem significare recte agnoscit Grotius. Non ergo inferiori, quam Divina, est virtute, quia dextra Dei infinitam Dei virtutem notat, non inferiori, quam Dei est, impe- rio, quia ipsius Majestatis Divinæ imperium hoc est. Non inferiori gloria, quam Patris est, regnat Christus. Unde qualem & quantum Pontificem habeamus, qui simul tanta Regia dignitate ac Ma- jestate præemineat, suosq; potenter regere, tueri, servare ac salvare æternum queat, manifestum est; & juxta Melchisedechi morem & Pontificatu & Re- gali munere simul fungatur excellentissima ratio- ne. Quo de Theodoretus: Adjecit autem illud λει- τυργὸς, hoc est, Sacerdotalis muneris Minister, quoni- am de Pontifice loquitur. Quoniam enim munere sa- cerdotali fungitur, qui seipsum obtulit, & non offert amplius sacrificium? Quomodo autem fieri potest, ut idem simul sedeat, & sacerdotali officio fungatur? Nisi dixerit forte quispiam, esse munus sacerdotale sa- lutem, quam ut Dominus procuret. Nimirum & ut Sacerdotem, & ut Dominum ac Regem salutem no- stram procurare ipsum vult, hoc est, non interpel- lando tantum, sed etiam autoritate ac potestate Divina sibi per exaltationem concessa provehen- do eandem. Ait itaq́, hoc loco, Theophylacto dicen- te, caput est super ea, quæ dicuntur, id est, quod præ- stantius dicam & brevibus Deum ipsi habemus Pon- tificem. Considere autem maxime congruit DEO. Adverte autem, quod cum humilia pleraq; explicasset, cujusmodi illa sunt, cum Pontificem Deum appellat, cum intercessiones dicit hunc facere, & quotquot istiusmodi sunt & humana, mox ad celsiora transcen- dit, dixitque hunc in dextra sedis magnitudinis consi- dere, quod utiq́ Divinæ est Majestatis. Sedem au- tem & magnitudinis thronum Paternum dicit: Vel quia Pater ipse magnitudinis sit id nomen sortitus, vel simpliciter, quia maximus ille & sublimior DEI thronus, dicitur sedes. Unde rectissime B. Hunnius: Caterum ne quis sibi dextram illam Dei localem fin- geret, aut locum quempiam in cœlis: Certam & evi- dentem notationem addit, dum dextram throni Ma- jestatis appellat, subinnuens, Christum, cum in cœlos adscenderet, ipsum thronum Divinæ Majestatis & omnipotentiæ Dei occupasse: quandoquidem omnium rerum gubernatrix dextræ Dei nihil aliud est, nisi majestas Dei & omnipotentia. Quod autem addi- tur in cœlis, intelligitur cœli appellatione vita æter- na, vel regnum cœleste, quod beatitudine potius & gloria cœlesti, quam loco describitur. Pareus ipse in h. l. ita habet: Thronus majestatis est imperium Dei, quod gloriose & summa cum Majestate in cœlis exercet in omnes creaturas. Thronus enim est se- des Regia, metalepsi regnum, imperium designat. Dex- tra throni Majestatis est gloriosa hujus potestatis summus gradus. Et porro: Ad hanc dextram throni Majestatis, quia consedit CHRISTUS Pon- tifex noster, summus sane Monarcha cœli & terræ esse declaratur. Imo DEUM Patri & Spiritui sancto æqualem natura & potentia sessio hæc arguit. Nemo enim sedet ad dextram Dei, æquali cum Deo potentia regnans, nisi Deus sit, seu unus cum Deo, hoc est, Deus ipse. Hinc Patres æqualitatem Filii cum Patre ex sessione ad dextram adversus hæreticos sem- per adstruxerunt. Epistola priore ad Corinth. XV. hoc Christi sedere ad dextram Dei declaratur per regnare, quod non est absolute intelligendum. Re- gnat etiam Pater: regnat Spiritus sanctus: nec ta- men dicitur sedere ad dextram Dei Pater vel Spiri- tus sanctus: Sed hic honos in Scripturis Christo Me- diatori exaltato vendicatur proprius. Adstrictius igitur regnat Christus sedendo ad dextram Dei: quia nempe expiatione peccatorum nostrorum per semet- ipsum facta in carne sua exaltatus est in sacerdotio & regno supra omnes Angelos & homines, declaratus ca- put omnium, per quod Pater omnia in cælo & in ter- ra gubernat. Ea vero exaltatio primum fuit humilita- tis & infirmitatis omnis depositio, & carnis assumptæ omnimoda perfectio, & gloria supra omnes potestates cælestes. Deinde potestatis Pontificalis & potestatis Regiæ, quæ summa est, declaratio & usurpatio in car- ne assumpta. Deniq; honor & cultus divinus huic Pontifici & Regi exaltato ab omnibus creaturis cæli, terræ, & inferorum tribuendus. His fere partibus, si bene advertas, gloria sessionis Christi ad dextram Dei describitur, Eph. 1. Phil. 2. 1. Cor. 15. & alibi. Hæc Pareus; qui vero sibi ipsi adversatur, non minus, quam veritati Divinæ, cum dextram de honore, quem monarchæ legatis ad se venientibus commu- nicant, explicat. Nam is non est summus honor ab- solute ita dictus ipsi summo Monarchæ cæli & ter- ræ conveniens, qui Patri & Spiritui sancto compe- tat, & æqualem cum Deo potentiam, regimen & cultum Divinum inferat; Uti non eadẽ per omnia gloria potentia regnandi, potestas est legati aut lo- cumtenentis alicujus, quæ ipsiusmet Regis vel Principis. Sophismata, quæ insigni ἑαυτομαχίᾳ Majestati carnis Christi opponit, alibi discutiun- tur. Quod autem Hunianam verborum in cælis explicationem contortam glossam dicit, argumen- tisq; probare satagit, cælorum nomine proprie hic notari locum cælestem, ubi Pontifex noster gloriose vivit & regnat tanquam in throno & Regia cæle- sti, silentio transmittendum non videtur. Ideoque de illis breviter dispiciendum. Sessione, inquit, ad dextram gloria & regnum significatur. Annuimus: Sed num ideo verba ἐν τοῖς ὐρανοῖς de loco proprie intelligenda? Dextra Majestatis Divina, & thronus Dei etiam in cælis est: Num vero Deus in loco proprie est, & in cælis, tanquam in Regio suo pala- tio, nempe cælesti, moratur? Annon potius cæ- li appellatione gloria cælestis, in qua constitutus est, & lux illa inaccessa, in qua habitat Deus, nota- tur, quam locus & Regia quædam aut regio cæle- stis? De voce ἐν ὑψηλοῖς cap. 1, 3. actum est circa il- lum locum. Cum vero cap. 4, 14. dicitur cælos pene- trasse, & c. 7, 26. sublimior cælis factus, Calviniana glossa de loci sublimitate palam profligatur. Nam quis super cælos creatos locus est materialis? Quis supererit cælis creatis igne consumtis & substan- tialiter destructis? Hunnii a. explicationi quid ob- stet, non videmus. At non est sublimior factus cælesti regno, nec gloriam penetrasse dici potest. Resp. Ec- quis vero id unquam dixit? Et quæ consequentia, cum supra cælos esse, sublimior cælis esse, ac pene- trasse cælos dicitur, materiales cæli intelliguntur. Ergo etiam cum in cælis dicitur esse, cælum mate- riale intelligendum, in quo tanquam loco proprio constitutus sit. Annon ita potius hæc concilianda, ut Christus & in cælo dicatur esse, quia in gloria vel cælo Majestatico Divino regnat, quemadmodum Pater, qui nullo loco continetur, quem cæli cælo- rum non capiunt, in cælis est. Et porro sublimior cælis sit, quia gloria transcendit cælos, illisq; sub- limior Christus factus est. Quo pacto etiam ob gloriæ & Majestatis eminentiam διεληλυθότα τῆς ὐρανὸς, Ebr. 4, 14. dicimus non quod illic per τῆς ὐρανὸς cælestem gloriam intelligamus, sed cælos materiales, quos pertranseundo in sancta sanctorum cælum Dei gloriosum & Majestaticum penetravit. Quod vero materiale, ut Regiam quandam locale vel corporea & materialem esse nec ipsi Calviniani dixerint: Quemadmodum nec ex antithesi terræ concludere possunt, cælos & terras localiter oppo- ni, quum Deus ipse in cælis & in terris sit, cui vero nullus locus convenit, & de Filio hominis dicatur, quod & ascenderit in cælos, & in terra sit Joh. 3, 13. ἀναβὰς ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν ὀυρανῶν, ἵνα πληρώσῃ τὰ πάντα Eph. 4, 10. Vide quæ disputavimus contra Calvinianos Tom. III. System. pag. 997. seqq. B. Dorscheus hic alludi vult voce throni ad solium in sancto sanctorum, atque ita de hisce differit:

Alludit Apostolus, cum de sessione in dextra throni Majestatis loquitur, ad ipsum sanctum sanctorum, in quo etiam positus erat thronus, nimirum in operculo arcæ, quod expansis Cherubinorum alis contectum, thronus Dei dicebatur. Unde frequenter Deus inter Cherubinos considere, vel iisdem insistere dicitur. Hoc vero adytum, hic secessus, hæc sedes tanta erat dignitatis, tantæq́; religione observabatur, ut nullus unquam Sacerdotum Veteris Testamenti isti insidere ausus fuerit. Soli nimirum Deo servabatur ista sessio, quotquot sanctum sanctorum ingressi erant, coram ista sede stare cogebantur. Hinc præstantia Sacerdotis Novi Testamenti maximopere elucescit. Cum enim ut DEUS benedictus in secula Rom. 9, 5. & ut petra, quæ semper Israëlitis præsto fuit, 1. Corinth. 10, 4. etiam super Cherubinos in sancto sanctorum hactenus semper consedisset, nunc longissime ista omnia superavit. Operculum arcæ, quod propitiatorium dicebatur, dextra Dei nequaquam fuit. Sacerdos Novi Testamenti summus in ipsa DEI dextra consedit. Operculum arcæ thronus quidam gloriæ Divinæ, sed finitus & umbratilis dicebatur. Sacerdos summus Novi Testamenti non tantum supra Cherubinos illos sculptiles, sed supra spirituales Cherubinos sive thronos, ut vocantur Coloss. 1, 16. consedit, & ipsum thronum summum & sempiternum Divinæ gloriæ occupavit. Operculum arcæ ad ἱερωσύνην pertinuit, μεγαλωσύνην autem peculiarem non habuit. Sacerdos summus Novi Testamenti ipsam infinitam Divinitamq́; μεγαλωσύνην consequutus est. Operculum arcæ fuit in terris, ubi & ipsum tabernaculum fixum fuit. Summi Sacerdotis Novi Testamenti sedes est ἐν τοῖς ὀυρανοῖς non finitis sed infinitis, utpote dextræ DEI, throno & majestati consentaneis. Itaque hoc modo argumentari vult Apostolus: Qui Sacerdos non tantum in throno sanctuarii, & super propitiatorium consedit, quod nulli unquam Sacerdoti Veteris Testamenti concessum fuit, sed etiam super thronum immensæ Majestatis in cælestibus ad dextram Dei consedit, is est incomparabiliter præstantior Sacerdotibus Veteris Testamenti, adeoque verus secundum prædictionem Davidicam Sacerdos. Atqui talis est Sacerdos Christianæ religionis. Ergo inepte Capellus h. l. pag. 127. dicit: Aliud est assidere dextræ, aliud coëxtendi dextræ vel æquari dextræ Patris. Corpori CHRISTI, s. mavis CHRISTO secundum Humanam naturam considerato tribuitur prius, non posterius, eoq́; solii sublimitas corpori Christi concessa non infert infinitudinem, non infert inquam immensitatem, non magis quam æternitatem. Quis enim infinitudinem aut immensitatem corporis CHRISTI ex ista sessione intulit? Præsentiam Divinam istam sessionem largiri, quam Scriptura nunc πλήρωσιν πάντων, nunc παροσίαν in medio fidelium ad consummationem usq́; seculi, nunc habitationem in corpus fidelium, nunc ambulationem in medio candelabrorum aureorum appellat, exinde orthodoxi intulerunt. Qui enim sedet ad dextram Dei, ut dominetur in medio inimicorum suorum, & passim regnet in fidelibus, is quamvis non omnia attributa habeat, quibus pollet Divina dextra, tamen ibi est, ubi est dextra DEI. Alias non sederet ad dextram Dei, sed esset infra dextram Dei, adeocq́; subditus dextræ, non Dominus ad dextram, ut dicitur Psalm. CX, 5. de Christo. Atqui is ita sedet ad dextram, & quidem secundum Humanam naturam. Itaq́; ibi est, ubi est dextra DEI.

Ergo per omnia talis est, qualis est dextra Dei. Qua- propter infinitudo & immensitas à praesentia Divina sunt discernenda. Illa enim sunt attributa absoluta. Praesentia vero Divina respectum ad extra & ad crea- turas habet, nec est nisi creaturis existentibus. Unde mundo transituro desinet praesentia ad mundum, quanquam Majestas adessendi mundo & omnibus creaturis existentibus aut extituris sit immutabilis & perpetua. Quis etiam coëxtensionem aut aequa- tionem dextrae Patris ista sessione Humana naturae vindicavit? Dextra enim Dei Patris non est quid- dam extensum. Itaq; ut Humana natura ubiq; per dextram Dei adsit, coëxtensione opus non est. Suffi- cit Majestas & virtus dextrae, ex qua Christus etiam suam Humanam naturam objectis dominii sui prae- sentem sistere potest.

## 8:2
Vers. 2.

Minister of the holy things] He calls the whole temple holy things, which is the sanctuary to Moses and the Prophets, sometimes the holy, as in Psalm CII, 26. He understands, however, as the following things indicate, this whole universe, including also the region above the ether. Minister signifies him who performs something by the command of another, a servant, as can be seen above in chapter 1, 7. and Rom. 13, 6. And it is wont to be said especially of the Priests, Nehem. 10, 39. because they bring those things which God requires, which is called to minister, Exod. 18, 35. 43. ch. 29, 30. ch. 35, 18. ch. 39, 25. 43. and elsewhere. Christ performed his ministry partly on earth, and partly performs it in the highest heaven.

By the holy things Grotius understands the whole temple in type, this whole universe, including also the region above the ether, which he understands as the antitype. Others wish the Church serving God in these lands, which we call militant, to be designated by the holy things, in which way it will correspond not to the holy of holies, but to the holy place in the tabernacle or temple: Or they also think that the name of the holy things is taken in the masculine gender, and that holy men are understood, that Christ is the minister of sanctified men. Which explanation is brought forward by Theophylact, but is not approved. No one, he says, understands λειτυργὸς τῶν ἁγίων as that which makes men holier, since he is our High Priest, but because there is an allusion to τὰ ἅγια in the tabernacle and temple, without doubt that noun is used in the neuter gender: And therefore by τὰ ἅγια, without doubt, the holy things are referred to, which are called so κατ᾿ ἐξοχὴν, chapter 9, 3. and also absolutely τὰ ἅγια in the same chapter v. 12. which passage, compared to this one, brings light to the true understanding. Add also v. 24, 25, and chapter 10, v. 19. Which sense not only Theodoret embraced: He called the tabernacle heaven, of which he himself is the maker, whom the Apostle said functions as a priest as a man: But also Theophylact: For just as those earthly and inferior High Priests, having entered the holy of holies and those inner sanctuaries, performed their ministry: So Christ is the λειτουργὸς of those supercelestial sanctuaries, which are truly holy. For here there is a tacit opposition between the typical τὰ ἅγια, in which the Levitical High Priests performed their priesthood, and the τὰ ἅγια ἀληθινὰ, in which Christ performs his priestly office, which are heaven. And therefore heaven is entirely understood here, but as I said with an allusion and comparison to the holy of holies in the tabernacle and the Solomonic temple so named: which the word τῶν ἁγίων hints at; and that word τῆς ἀληθινῆς, with which the word τῆς σκηνῆς is constructed, as regards the sense is also to be referred to the preceding noun τῶν ἁγίων, so that indeed that holy thing ἀληθινὸν or true, not typical, is understood here. Although indeed Christ has power over this whole universe, and administers it: That, however, is not the issue here, since the Apostle is now treating of the priesthood of Christ, not of the kingdom of Christ's power. Although it is also certain that Christ performs his λειτουργίαν partly on earth, partly in heaven:

Yet this is not said in these words, when he is called τῶν ἁγίων λειτουργὸς. But the Apostle understands the true holy of holies, i.e., the heavens, and discourses concerning the priestly function which he now administers, after he has sat down at the right hand of the throne of majesty. B. Hunnius, with Lyra and Dionysius, wishes that by the appellation of the saints those gifts and heavenly goods should come, which Christ procured by the sacrifice of his death, and now at the right hand of God dispenses to the faithful: while by the ministry of the Word and Sacraments he excites faith in them, and through the same faith effectively applies and gives to them all heavenly goods, the remission of sins, the grace of God, righteousness, and eternal life. But since the Apostle himself subsequently explains τὰ ἅγια as heaven, those gifts also pertain rather to the effect of the priesthood of Christ, so that the bestowal of those gifts is more correctly referred to the Kingly office than to the priestly, concerning which it is discoursed here; the explanation already given, to which B. Gerhard also adds his vote, is better. How, however, does he call the Minister of the saints sitting on the throne of Majesty? Theophylact answers: The Apostle does this so that he may condescend somewhat to humanity, whence he has also mixed the lowest with the highest. We add, however, that the word λειτουργὸς does not precisely imply a minister, or λειτουργίαν a ministry. For it is said concerning the priesthood, and him who performs sacred rites: just as Grotius admits that that word notably denotes a Priest. Priesthood, however, is not a ministry which imports anything abject or humble; and as λειτουργία is one thing, and διακονία another, so also it is one thing to be a λειτουργὸν, and another to be a διάκονον. Therefore B. Luther aptly rendered it: He is a caretaker of heavenly goods. Rightly B. Gerhard: Λειτουργεῖν is to perform sacred rites, in general, to discharge a public office, whether Ecclesiastical or Political. Λειτουργὸς therefore is one who performs sacred rites, or in general, one who discharges a public Ecclesiastical or Political office. By this λειτουργία is understood the intercession of Christ, which he performs by virtue of the sacrifice offered on the altar of the cross. Λειτουργὸς therefore of the sanctuary he is, because he administers his priestly office in heaven, which in the Old Testament was prefigured by the holy of holies. Λειτουργὸς is a curator of a public office, just as specifically to perform sacred rites, Acts 13:2, λειτουργεῖν signifies. B. Dorscheus says of these things: That we should translate λειτουργὸν as a servant or Minister perpetually, neither does the word itself considered in its origin require, nor does the Apostolic Text demand, nor does the Kingly office of Christ, when fully exercised, permit. As far as the origin of the word pertains, λειτουργὸς is deduced by Plutarch and Hesychius from the name λεῖτος, that is, δημόσιος, public, and ἔργον, that is, work. It denotes, therefore, him who does and procures a public work, whom he calls an agent, which Pareus himself observes in this place. When Scripture speaks of the λειτουργίᾳ of a mere man, it is rightly rendered ministry, as Luke 1:23, Acts 13:2, 2 Cor. 9:12, Heb. 10:11. Just as also either a created Angel, or a mere man, when he is called λειτουργὸς, can rightly be called a minister, Heb. 1:7 and 14, Rom. 13:6, ch. 15:16. Although λειτουργῆσαι is also used of men, where the inclusion of servitude is not necessary, Rom. 15:27, where λειτουργῆσαι is the same as κοινωνεῖν. As concerns the text itself, it by no means has as its purpose the servitude and ministry of Christ, but rather his dominion and glory. Whence he considers Christ as λειτουργὸν at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens, and calls this λειτουργίαν more excellent, by which very thing he indicates that it is to be separated from the state of servitude. Therefore the Apostle wishes by this vocabulary to describe the office of Christ, but placed outside the state of servitude and emptying, and shining in supreme majesty. Finally, that the Kingly office of Christ does not allow that, while he is fully exercising it, he should be called a minister or servant, is evident from the fact that this office, considered in this way, has universal kingdom, dominion, and the rule of full Majesty and glory, by which very thing one is placed above all servitude, Eph. 1:21. Hence the Apostle, Heb. 1:13-14, intending to prove that the glory of the session at the right hand, which is attributed to Christ, is incommunicable to the Angels, relies on that foundation, because the Angels are λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα. Whence if Christ were called λειτουργὸς in that respect in which the Angels are λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα, the session at the right hand would not be a glory incommunicable to the Angels. Although, however, the Son has been constituted λειτουργὸς by GOD the Father, it does not, however, properly imply any dependence and inferiority, but only an ordination. For an equal can be ordained to some office by an equal without regard to ministry or inferiority, indeed one Divine person by another, just as the Son has been ordained and constituted High Priest by the Father, which in itself does not detract from the Divine dignity of the equality of the Son with the Father.

. Καὶ τῆς σκηνῆς τῆς ἀληθινῆς] Those things are called true which are the principal things, of which lesser things are figures. Thus also below ch. 9:24. See what we have said at Matt. 26:29, Luke 22:16, John 1:9, ch. 6:32, ch. 15:1, below ch. 9:24. Add 1 John 2:8. Not less did that tabernacle, which served as a temple, than the temple itself built by Solomon, bear the figure of the universe. See what we have said at Matt. 27:5. Add the excellent passage of Clement of Alexandria, Strom. V. Albelda and Abarbanel say that great wisdom is hidden in the whole structure of the tabernacle. Philo, in his work on the creation of the world, calls the heaven a most pure temple.

. Ἣν ἔπηξεν ὁ Κύριος] The maker of the world. Πήγνυσθαι is properly said of tents, which were fastened with pegs, the mention of which is in Isa. 33:20 and ch. 54:2. The word πήγνυσθαι is נטה Gen. 26:25, ch. 35:21, Exod. 33:7, Judg. 4:11, 2 Sam. 6:17, 1 Chron. 16:1, 2 Chron. 1:4. But by translation it is also used of the universe, Job 38:6, Isa. 42:5.

Καὶ ὐκ ἄνθρωπος] Not Bezalel or the Levites. You have a similar opposition of Divine and human structure below ch. 9:11, 24, and ch. 11:10.

By the tabernacle, Grotius likewise understands the whole universe: But the tabernacle is distinguished by the Apostolic phrase from the holy place, since he himself explains these things thus in ch. 9, 11. 12. that Christ διὰ τῆς μείζονος καὶ τελειοτέρας σκηνῆς ὐ χειροποιήτε, τῧτ’ ἔσιν ὐ ταύτης τῆς κτίσεως, entered once εἰς τὰ ἅγια, where it is most manifest that the tabernacle through which he entered into the holy place is one thing, and the holy place itself, into which he entered through the tabernacle, is another, the Apostle himself being the interpreter. And who can doubt that the same thing is denoted by the expression τῆς σκηνῆς τῆς ἀληθινῆς, ἣν ἔπηξεν ὁ κύριος, καὶ ἐκ ἄνθρωπος, which the Apostle later expressed by the expression τῆς μείζονος καὶ τελειοτέρας σκηνῆς ὐ χειροποιήτε, τῧτ’ἔσιν, ὐ ταύτης τῆς κτίσεως. Therefore, through that true tabernacle, others prefer to understand something different from the true sanctuary. Blessed Gerhard wishes the body of Christ to be understood by σκηνὴν ἀληθινὴν, in which as a tabernacle and temple the whole fullness of the Divinity dwells, Col. 2, 19. He is said, therefore, by his own interpretation, to be Christ λειτουργὸς τῶν ἁγίων κὴ τῆς σκηνῆς ἀληθινῆς, because through the sacrifice of his body he administered the first part of his priestly office, so that later in the heavens he might be able to perform the other part of his office, that is, by the power of his merit and sacrifice to intercede for us in the heavens. Blessed Hunnius, just as he understands by τὰ ἅγια heavenly goods: So he understands by τὴν σκηνὴν τὴν ἀληθινὴν heaven as the eternal tabernacle. But just as by τὰ ἅγια he did not understand heavenly goods, which he rather encompassed under the name of τῶν μελλόντων ἀγαθῶν, and designated heaven by τὰ ἅγια, expressly distinguishing those from τοῖς ἁγίοις Heb. 9, 11. 12. So by the tabernacle, through which Christ, our High Priest, entered, it seems rather that the Church is to be understood, which is the tabernacle of the Lord, Ps. 15, 2. and the house of the living God, 1 Tim. 3, 15. formerly foreshadowed by the tabernacle and temple, since the body of Christ, because he did not enter into heaven through his body, but brought his own body into heaven: he entered, however, through the tabernacle of the Church, which is most rightly called both the outer holy place and the first tabernacle from chapter 9. 2, (as far as the antitype represented by that figure) into heaven, through the kingdom of grace into the kingdom of glory, through the Church militant into the Church triumphant. On earth he acted in the tabernacle of the Church, but through it he entered into the holy of holies, that is, into heaven itself through the ascension into heaven. The body of Christ is indicated rather by the victim, which our Priest ought to offer, and did offer on earth, of which the Apostle says in the following verse. For every High Priest is appointed to offer gifts and victims, whence it was necessary for this one also to have something to offer, which he did through the σκηνὴν, in which the offering was made, before he entered into the holy of holies, Heb. 1, 3. Thus, therefore, he is a λειτουργὸς and administrator, a caretaker, both of the Church of the blessed, or of those who are comprehended, as they call them, in the heavens, and of the Church of the wayfarers on earth, τῶν ἁγίων κὴ τῆς σκηνῆς τῆς ἀληθινῆς, of which the former was foreshadowed in the temple by the holy of holies and that tabernacle of which the Apostle speaks in chapter 9, verse 2, Μετὰ δὲ τὸ δεύτερον καταπέτασμα σκηνὴ ἡ λεγομένη ἁγία ἁγίων: but the latter is understood by τὴν σκηνὴν τὴν πρώτην, ἥτις λέγεται ἁγία, v. 2, since he has care of both Churches, and is a λειτουργὸς in the heavens both of the wayfarers and of the blessed through his intercession, which he performs at the right hand of God, as the eternal High Priest. For we have already warned that the Apostle is occupied with this argument. Paræus, with Calvin, explains the body of Christ in such a way that Christ is a λειτουργὸς, that is, a sacrificer of the true tabernacle, that is, of his own body. But since he is called a λειτουργὸς of the true tabernacle in the same sense in which he is called a λειτουργὸς of the holy things, and the particle καὶ is exegetical according to Paræus: How then will it denote sacrificing here? For he is also a sacrificer of the holy things, and of the holy of holies, or even of heavenly gifts? But here it is not opposed to false, for the tabernacle of Moses was not false, or rashly constructed; but to shadowy and typical. That periphrasis also, ἣν ἔπηξεν ὁ Κύριος κὴ ὀυκ ἄνθρωπος, fits the Church most excellently. For by the word ἔπηξεν allusion is made to the Mosaic tabernacle, in which the Aaronic Priests performed their λειτουργίᾳ, which was fixed on earth by the hands of men, since the Church of the Lord is also fixed on earth. Compare especially the notable passage Isa. 54, 2. But this word brings in two things, both fabrication and construction, and firmness and solidity, because πήγνυμι means to join together, to fabricate, to construct, as well as to fix, and to establish as fixed. By τὸν κύριον the Son of God himself can be understood, who is usually called ὁ Κύριος with the article in the New Testament, who built the temple of his Church, 2 Sam. 7, 13. Matt. 16, 18.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Τῶν ἁγίων λειτουργὸς] Ἅγια vocat totum templum, quod מִקְדָשׁ Mosi & Prophetis, interdum קֹדֶשׁ, ut Psal. CII, 26. Intelligit autem, ut sequentia indicant, universum hoc, com- prehensa etiam regione superætherea. Λειτουργὸς eum signi- ficat, qui aliquid peragit alterius imperio מְשָׁרֵת ut vide- re est supra c. 1, 7. & Rom. 13, 6. Soletque eximie dici de Sa- cerdotibus, Nehem. 10, 39. quia afferunt ea, quæ Deus exigit, quod dicitur λειτουργεῖν, Exod. 18, 35. 43. c. 29, 30. c. 35, 18. c. 39, 25. 43. & alibi. Christus ministerium suum partim in terris peregit, partim in summo cœlo peragit.

Per τὰ ἅγια totum templum in typo, totum hoc universum, inclusa etiam regione superætherea, quod ad antitypum intelligit Grotius. Alii per τὰ ἅγια Ecclesiam in his terris Deo servientem, quam militantem vocamus, designari volunt, quo pacto non sancto sanctorum, sed sancto respondebit id in tabernaculo vel templo: Vel etiam τῶν ἁγίων nomen in genere Masculino accipi, hominesq; san- ctos intelligi, quod Christus hominum sanctifica- torum λειτουργὸς sit, existimant. Quæ explicatio à Theophylacto adducitur, non approbatur. Non- ulli vero, inquit, λειτυργὸς τῶν ἁγίων intelligunt, quod perinde homines faciat sanctiores, quippe qui noster sit Pontifex, sed quia allusio est ad τὰ ἅγια in tabernaculo & templo, fine dubio neutro genere nomen istud adhibetur : Ideoque per τὰ ἅγια sine dubio respiciuntur sancta, quæ κατ᾿ ἐξοχὴν ita dicuntur, cap. 9, 3. nec non absolute τὰ ἅγια Cap. eodem v. 12. qui locus huic collatus lucem affert ve- ræ intelligentiæ. Adde & v. 24. 25. & cap. 10. v. 19. Quem sensum non tantum Theodoretius amplexus est: Tabernaculum autem vocavit cælum, cujus est ipse opifex, quem ut hominem Apostolus dixit fungi Sacerdotio: Sed etiam Theophylactus: Quemad- modum enim terreni & inferiores Pontifices hi, san- cta sanctorum & penetralia illa ingressi eorum mini- sterio fungebantur: Sic Christus supercœlestium il- lorum penetralium, quæ vere sunt sancta, λειτουργὸς est. Habetur enim hic tacite oppositio inter τὰ ἅγια typica, in quibus Levitici Pontifices sacerdo- tio functi sunt, & τὰ ἅγια ἀληθινὰ, in quibus Chri- stus officio suo sacerdotali fungitur, quæ sunt cæ- lum. Ideoq; cœlum omnino hic intelligitur, sed ut dixi cum allusione, & comparatione ad sanctum sanctorum in tabernaculo & templo Salomonæo ita nuncupatum: quam vox τῶν ἁγίων subinnuit; & vox illa τῆς ἀληθινῆς, cum qua vox τῆς σκηνῆς construitur, quoad sensum etiam referenda adpræ- cedens nomen τῶν ἁγίων, quod nempe sanctum il- lud ἀληθινὸν seu verum, non typicum hic intelliga- tur. Quanquam vero Christus potestatem habeat super totum hoc universum, idq; administret: Id ta- men hic non agitur, quum de sacerdotio Christi jam tractet Apostolus, non de regno potentiæ Christi. Quanquam etiam certum sit, Christum λειτουργίαν suam partim in terris, partim in cœlis peragere:

non tamen id his verbis dicitur, cum τῶν ἁγίων λειτουργὸς vocatur. Sed sancta sanctorum vera, h. e. cœlos intelligit Apostolus, & de sacerdotali fun- ctione, quam jam, postquam consedit ad dextram throni majestatis, administrat, disserit. B. Hunnius cum Lyra & Dionysio vult, sanctorum appellatione venire dona & bona illa cœlestia, quæ Christus sacrifi- cio mortis suæ peperit, & nunc ad dextram Dei fide- libus dispensat: dum ministerio Verbi & Sacramen- torum fidem in illis excitat, & per eandem fidem omnia bona cœlestia, remissionem peccatorum, gratiam Dei, justitiam & vitam æternam efficaciter illis ap- plicat & donat. Sed quum Apostolus ipse τὰ ἅγια deinceps de cœlo explicet, illa etiam dona potius ad effectum sacerdotii Christi pertineant, ut donorum illorum collatio ad Regium munus rectius refe- ratur, quam ad sacerdotale, de quo hic disseritur, præstat jam tradita explicatio, cui etiam calculum addit B. Gerhardus. Quomodo autem sanctorum Ministrum dicit sedentem in throno Majestatis? Theophylactus respondet: Id facit Apostolus, ut condescendat aliquantisper humanitati, unde & summis admiscuit infima. Addimus autem, vocem λειτουργὸς non præcise ministrum, aut λειτουργίαν ministerium inferre. Nam de sacerdotio dicitur, & eo, qui sacris operatur: quemadmodum fatetur Grotius illam vocem eximie Sacerdotem notare. Sa- cerdotium autem non est ministerium, quod abje- ctum aut humile quid importet; & ut aliud est λει- τουργία, aliud διακονία, ita etiam aliud esse λειτουρ- γὸν, aliud διάκονον esse. Ideo B. Lutherus concinne reddidit: Er ist ein Pfleger der himmlischen Güter. Recte B. Gerhardus: Λειτουργεῖν est sacris operari, in genere, publico officio fungi vel Ecclesiastico, vel Po- litico. Λειτουργὸς ergo est, qui sacris operatur, vel in genere, qui publico officio Ecclesiastico vel Politico fun- gitur. Per hanc λειτουργίαν intelligitur Christi inter- cessio, quam vi sacrificii in ara crucis oblati præstat. Λειτουργὸς ergo sanctuarii est, quia sacerdotale su- um officium administrat in cœlo, quod in Vet. Te- stamento præfiguratum fuit per sanctum sanctorum. Λειτουργὸς est publici muneris curator, uti specia- tim sacra peragere, Act. 13, 2. λειτουργεῖν significat. B. Dorscheus de his ita: Ut servum seu Ministrum perpetuo λειτουργὸν vertamus, nec requirit vox ipsa in origine sua considerata, nec Textus Apostolicus postu- lat, nec officium Christi Regium plenarie usurpatum permittit. Originem vocis quod attinet, λειτουργὸς à Plutarcho & Hesychio deducitur ex nomine λεῖ- τος, hoc est, δημόσιος, publicus, & ἔργον, hoc est, opus, Notat ergo eum, qui publicum opus facit & procurat, quem agentem vocat, quod Pareus ipse hoc loco obser- vat. Quando de hominis nudi λειτουργίᾳ Scriptura loquitur, recte ministerium redditur, ut Luc. 1, v. 23. Act. 13, 2. 2. Cor. 9, 12. Ebr. 10, 11. Sicut & vel An- gelus creatus, vel homo nudus, cum λειτουργὸς dicitur, recte minister dici potest, Ebr. 1, 7. & 14. Rom. 13, 16. c. 15, 16. Quamvis & λειτουργῆσαι de hominibus usurpetur, ubi servitutis inclusio non est necessaria, Rom. 15, 27. ubi λειτουργῆσαι idem est, quod κοινωνεῖν. Textum ipsum quod concernit, nequaquam sibi pro- positum habet Christi famulatum & ministerium, sed potius dominium & gloriam. Unde considerat Christum ut λειτουργὸν in dextra throni Majestatis in cœlestibus, & hanc λειτουργίαν vocat διαφορωτέραν, quo ipso indicat, eam à statu servitutis esse secernen- dam. Itaq; vult Apostolus hoc vocabulo describere officium Christi, sed extra statum servitutis & exina- nitionis positum, & in summa majestate refulgens. Officium Christi Regium denique non pati, ut cum eo ipse plenarie fungitur, minister aut servus appelletur, ex eo patet, quia hoc modo consideratum illud officium habet universale regnum, dominium, & plenæ Maje- statis gloriæque dominatum, quo ipso quis supra omnem servitutem ponitur, Eph. 1, 21. Hinc Apostolus Ebr. 1, 13. 14. probaturus, Angelis incommunicabilem esse illam gloriam sessionis ad dextram, quæ Christo tri- buitur, eo fundamento nititur, quia Angeli sunt λει- τουργικὰ πνεύματα. Unde si Christus eo respectu λει- τουργὸς diceretur, quo Angeli sunt λειτουργικὰ πνεύ- ματα, sessio ad dextram non esset Angelis incommu- nicabilis gloria. Etsi autem constitutus sit à DEO Patre Filius λειτουργὸς, non tamen id aliquam de- pendentiam & inferioritatem proprie infert, sed or- dinationem solum. Potest enim ad aliquod munus ordinari æqualis ab æquali citra respectum mini- sterii vel inferioritatis, imo una persona Divina ab altera, uti Filius à Patre ordinatus est & constitutus Ἀρχιερεὺς, quod per se non derogat dignitati Di- vinæ τῇ ἰσοτιμίᾳ Filii cum Patre.

. Καὶ τῆς σκηνῆς τῆς ἀληθινῆς] Ἀληθινὰ vocantur res præ- cipuæ, quarum res minores figuræ sunt. Sic & infra cap. 9, 24. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. 26, 29. Luc. 22, 16. Joh. 1, 9. cap. 6, 32. cap. 15, 1. infra cap. 9, 24. Adde 1. Joh. 2, 8. Non minus tabernaculum illud, quod pro templo fuit, quam ipsum templum à Salomone structum figuram gerebat uni- versi. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. 27, 5. Adde egregium locum Clementis Alexandrini Strom. V. In tota structura tabernaculi magnam abscondi sapientiam ajunt Albelda & Abarbanel. Philo de mundi creatione cœlum vocat ἱερὸν καθαρώτατον.

. Ἣν ἔπηξεν ὁ Κύριος] Mundi opifex. Πήγνυσθαι proprie de tentoriis dicitur, quæ clavis attinebantur, quorum men- tio Esa. 33, 20. & c. 54, 2. Vox autem πήγνυσθαι נטה Gen. 26, 25. c. 35, 21. Exod. 33, 7. Jud. 4, 11. 2. Sam. 6, 17. 1. Paral. 16, 1. 2. Paral. 1, 4. Sed per translationem etiam de universo usurpatur Job. 38, 6. Esa. 42, 5.

Καὶ ὐκ ἄνθρωπος] Non Beseleel aut Levitæ. Similem oppositionem structuræ Divinæ & humanæ habes infra cap. 9, 11. 24. & cap. 11, 10.

Per tabernaculum itidem intelligit Grotius totum universum: Sed tabernaculum distinguitur phrasi Apostolica à sancto, quum ipse hæc ita explicet c. 9, 11. 12. quod Christus διὰ τῆς μείζονος καὶ τελει- οτέρας σκηνῆς ὐ χειροποιήτε, τῧτ’ ἔσιν ὐ ταύτης τῆς κτίσεως, ingressus sit semel εἰς τὰ ἅγια, ubi mani- festissimum est, aliud esse tabernaculum, per quod in- gressus est in sanctum, aliud esse ipsum sanctum, in quod per tabernaculum est ingressus, interprete ipfomet Apostolo. Et quis dubitare potest, idem notari voce τῆς σκηνῆς τῆς ἀληθινῆς, ἣν ἔπηξεν ὁ κύ- ριος, καὶ ἐκ ἄνθρωπος, quod postea expressit A- postolus voce τῆς μείζονος καὶ τελειοτέρας σκηνῆς ὐ χειροποιήτε, τῧτ’ἔσιν, ὐ ταύτης τῆς κτίσεως. Proinde per tabernaculum illud verum alii aliquid diver- sum à sanctuario vero intelligere malunt. B. Ger- hardus per σκηνὴν ἀληθινὴν intelligi vult corpus Christi, in quo tanquã tabernaculo ac templo tota plenitudo Divinitatis habitat, Col. 2, 19. Dicitur er- go, ipso interprete, Christus λειτουργὸς τῶν ἁγίων κὴ τῆς σκηνῆς ἀληθινῆς, quia per sacrificium corporis sui primam sacerdotalis officii partem administravit, ut postea in cœlis alteram officii partem perficere, hoc est, vi meriti & sacrificii sui in cœlis pro nobis intercedere posset. B. Hunnius uti per τὰ ἅγια bona cœlestia: Ita per τὴν σκηνὴν τὴν ἀληθινὴν cœlum ceu æternum tabernaculum intelligit. Sed uti per τὰ ἅγια non bona cœlestia, quæ nomine τῶν μελλόντων ἀγαθῶν potius complexus est, & cœlum per τὰ ἅγια desi- gnavit, illa à τοῖς ἁγίοις expresse distinguens Ebr. 9, 11. 12. Ita per tabernaculum, per quod ingressus est Christus, Pontifex noster, intelligenda potius vi- detur Ecclesia, quæ est tabernaculum Domini, Ps. 15, 2. & domus Dei viventis, 1. Tim. 3, 15. per ta- bernaculum & templum olim adumbrata, quum corpus Christi, quia non per corpus suum ingressus est in cœlum, sed corpus suum in cœlum intulit: ingressus autem est per tabernaculum Ecclesiæ, quæ & sanctum exterius, & tabernaculum primum è cap. 9. 2. dicitur rectissime, (quantum ad antity- pum figura illa repræsentatum) in cœlum, per re- gnum gratiæ in regnum gloriæ, per Ecclesiam mi- litantem in Ecclesiam triumphantem. In terris egit in tabernaculo Ecclesiæ, sed per illud ingressus est in sanctum sanctorum, hoc est, in cœlum ipsum per ascensionem in cœlum. Corpus Christi indi- gitatur potius per victimam, quam offerre debuit Sacerdos noster, & in terris obtulit, de quo Apo- stolus v. seq. Omnis enim Pontifex ad offerenda do- na & victimas constituitur, unde necesse fuit, hunc quoq́; habere quod offerret, quam per σκηνὴν, in qua facta est oblatio, antequam in sanctum sanctorum ingressus est, Ebr. 1, 3. Ita ergo λειτουργὸς & admi- nistrator est, ein Pfleger, tum Ecclesiæ beatorum, vel comprehensorum, quos vocant, in cœlis, tum Ec- clesiæ viatorum in terris, τῶν ἁγίων κὴ τῆς σκηνῆς τῆς ἀληθινῆς, quarum illa per sanctum sanctorum & ta- bernaculum illud, de quo Apostolus cap. 9. vers. 2. Μετὰ δὲ τὸ δεύτερον καταπέτασμα σκηνὴ ἡ λεγο- μένη ἁγία ἁγίων adumbrata fuit in templo: hæc ve- ro per τὴν σκηνὴν τὴν πρώτην, ἥτις λέγεται ἁγία, v. 2. intelligitur, quum utriusque Ecclesiæ curam ge- rat, & λειτουργὸς sit in cœlis & viatorum & beato- rum intercessione sua, quam ad dextram Dei per- agit, ceu æternus Pontifex. In hoc argumento e- nim Apostolum occupari jam monuimus. Paræus cum Calvino corpus Christi ita exponit, Christum esse λειτουργὸν, h. e. sacrificatorem tabernaculi veri, h. e. sui ipsius corporis. Sed quum λειτουργὸς eodem sensu dicatur τῆς σκηνῆς τῆς ἀληθινῆς, quo sensu λειτουργὸς τῶν ἁγίων dicitur, & particula καὶ exege- tica sit secundum Paræum: Quomodo ergo sacrifi- care hic notabit? Nam sacrificator etiam est τῶν ἁ- γίων, & sancti sanctorum, vel etiam donorum cœ- lestium? Verum hic non opponitur falso, neque enim Mosis tabernaculum fuit falsum, aut temere constructum; sed umbratili & typico. Periphrasis etiam illa ἣν ἔπηξεν ὁ Κύριος κὴ ὀυκ ἄνθρωπος opti- me convenit Ecclesiæ. Nam voce ἔπηξεν alluditur ad tabernaculum Mosaicum, in quo Aaronici Sa- cerdotes λειτουργίᾳ fungebantur, quod opera ho- minum clavis in terra figebatur, quum in terris et- iam fixa sit Ecclesia Domini. Confer. imprimis lo- cus insignis Esa. 54, 2. Duo autem infert hoc ver- bum, tum fabricam & constructionem, tum firmi- tatem & soliditatem, quia πήγνυμι est compinge- re, fabricari, construere, ut & figere, ac fixum sta- tuere. Per τὸν κύριον ipse Filius Dei intelligi pot- est, qui ὁ Κύριος plerumque cum articulo dicitur in Novo Testamento, qui extruxit templum Ec- clesiæ suæ, 2. Sam. 7, 13. Matth. 16, 18.

## 8:3
Vers. 3.

Πᾶς γὰρ ἀρχιερεὺς εἰς τὸ προσφέρειν δῶρά τε καὶ θυσίας καθίσταται] He shows why he said λειτουργὸς, because every High Priest is such. What δῶρα καὶ θυσίαι are, we said in v. 1. Ὅθεν ἀναγκαῖον ἔχειν τι κᾀκεῖ τοῦτον ὃ προσενέγκῃ] Wherefore it is necessary that Christ, whom the Psalm calls a Priest, and indeed an eminent one above the Aaronids, should offer something. What that is, he will say below in chapter 9, 12.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Πᾶς γὰρ ἀρχιερεὺς εἰς τὸ προσφέρειν δῶρά τε καὶ θυσίας καθίσταται] Ostendit, cur dixerit λειτουργὸς, quia talis est omnis Sacerdos summus. Quid sint δῶρα καὶ θυσίαι dixi- mus v. 1. Ὅθεν ἀναγκαῖον ἔχειν τι κᾀκεῖ τοῦτον ὃ προσενέγκῃ] Quare necesse est Christus, quem Psalmus Sacerdotem vocat, & quidem eximium supra Aaronidas, aliquid offerat. Id quid sit, dicet infra cap. 9, 12.

## 8:4
Vers. 4.

Εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἐπὶ γῆς, ὀυδ’ ἂν ἦν ἱερεὺς] In the Manuscript: Εἰ μὲν ἦν.
