Id quod significare voluit Deus procul dubio, palam etiam exposuit Mosi tam fideli servo in tota domo sua : Quod hic nunc Ebræis aperitur per Apostolorum coryphæum. Quod autem cælum per ea, quæ in monte Mosi monstrata, & per tabernaculum ad il- lud instar adornatum significatum sit, non nisi quantum ad sanctum sanctorum, quod ejusdem ὑπόδειγμα fuit, concedimus : Nec ea, quæ de vir- tutibus è Philone adducta, huc quadrare censemus. Notæ sunt Philonis & Ebræorum allegoriæ, raro è Scripturis elatæ, frequentissimè Scripturis illatæ. Nec solum tabernaculi forma, sed ea etiam, quæ in illo expianda, videntur Mosi monstrata. Quomodo Theophylactus : Cum enim quæ oculis intuemur, acrius ipsi perspicimus, quam ea, quæ audiendo addiscimus, propterea Mosi Deus universa aperuit. Nec solum tabernaculi formam, sed quemadmodum esset etiam immolandum, & cul- tus alii peragendi & ritus.

## 8:6
Verse 6.

Νυνὶ δὲ διαφορωτέρας τετύχηκε λειτουργίας] He is a minister, as he said above in verse 2. But his ministry is much more excellent than that Levitical one. We had the word διαφορωτέρᾳ also above at 1:4. Νυνὶ δὲ is not a note of time, but of opposition. See what was said at Rom. 7:17, 1 Cor. 5:11, chapter 7:15. τυγχάνειν means to obtain, as in Luke 20:35, 2 Tim. 2:10, below in chapter 11:35. קָנָה. For τετύχηκε other books have τέτευχε.

Ὅσῳ κρείττονός ἐστι διαθήκης Μεσίτης] What he had begun to say in chapter 7:12, that the law was changed, he now shows was predicted by the Prophets. And he uses the word διαθήκης, בְּרִית, because every Divine law promises certain things under a condition, and therefore it also takes on the nature of a covenant, as we said in the preface to the New Testament. CHRIST, not Moses, is the Mediator of this covenant. For He both obtained that crimes committed before calling would not exclude men from repentance, or those led by repentance from pardon, and He won for us the highest benefits from GOD pertaining to eternal life, 1 Tim. 2:5. Add Gal. 3:19, 20, below chapter 9:15, chapter 13:24.

Now is gathered both the diversity or rather the excellence of the ministry of Christ over the ministry of the Aaronic priests, which is more excellent, more superior, and more worthy (see Heb. 8:6) from a better Testament, of which Christ is the Mediator. For where a Testament is more worthy, there also is a more worthy priesthood. By so much, he says, is the priesthood of Christ more excellent, by how much better is the Testament of which he himself is the Mediator. The reason for the consequence is: Because it was the duty of the Priest both to offer sacrifices for the expiation of sins, and to intercede for the people. But the duties of a Mediator are, by reason of the covenant, to bring those who disagree among themselves into favor, or to reconcile them, and to plead the cause of the party which has offended before the other party, namely, the one offended, which is to be reconciled. Whence it is evident that these things are most closely related to one another, and that from a more worthy covenant or Testament one may rightly conclude to a more worthy priesthood. The things which Estius introduces concerning the office of the Priest for the sake of this inference, that it is required for covenants agreed upon between God and men to confirm them with the ceremony of an offered sacrifice, and to take pains that men may obtain the Divine promises, do not deserve approval; because the priestly office was completed by those two functions which we have mentioned. A more excellent ministry, says the blessed Dorscheus, is the most excellent ministry of those of whom Christ has hitherto been constituted the minister through his session at the right hand. And so it is called a more excellent ministry not by reason of distance of place, as if that were performed only in heaven, which it was indicated above that it is wrongly elicited from v. 4, but by reason of the excellence of the act, because clearly, as is evident from v. 5, the latreia or leitourgia of the Old Testament was occupied and involved in the pattern and shadow of heavenly things. This itself provides heavenly things. That was performed by a decaying and fragile priesthood, this consists in an eternal priesthood. That was performed visibly only on earth; this, after it was administered for some time on earth for the acquisition of the price of our redemption, finally, with the Priest taken up into the heavens and having entered into his glory, is performed in the heavens in a certain invisible manner and by divine presence, in such a way that it does not fail on earth. For 1. this leitourgia is most necessary on earth. Therefore, it must also be performed on earth, but in an infinite and divine manner, so that it may suffice for the whole militant Church. 2. The Testament, and indeed that new and better one, is not circumscribed only by the heavens, but extends itself also to the earth. Therefore, the leitourgia of the Testament must also be referred to the same. 3. The power and efficacy of the better promises extends itself also to the earth, so that they might attain recapitulation with heavenly things, Eph. 1:10, for which reason the leitourgia also pertains to the same. 4. The Mediator himself, after he acquired the price of redemption, makes its application not only in the heavens, but also and especially on earth. The leitourgia is also more excellent in that which is performed wherever two or three are gathered in the name of the minister, and he provides his gracious presence to them themselves, whereas the faithful themselves had need to approach the leitourgia of the Old Testament celebrated in the tabernacle or the Jerusalem temple, nor did the high priest with his leitourgia thrust himself into the midst of the Jews here and there throughout Palestine; this leitourgia, with its true tabernacle, which for that reason has been placed at the right hand of God into the heavenly throne, approaches the faithful themselves, thrusts and penetrates itself into their midst, and causes true latreia to be performed there. Finally, this leitourgia is also more excellent in that it is performed in the very hearts of the faithful through gracious indwelling. For this leitourgia is not terminated in the assumed hypostatic sanctuary, but proceeds so far that it makes the hearts of the faithful a tent or temple of the whole most holy Trinity, concerning which [see] above from 1 Cor. 1:11, 12, ch. 6:19, 2 Cor. 6:16, Eph. 3:17. Therefore, it is so far from the case that we say this leitourgia is more excellent because it is performed far from these lands in a certain circumscribed place of the heavens, that all other things are manifest from its consideration. But the argument of the Apostle here is such: That priesthood must be most excellent and incomparably perfect, in respect of which the first Testament and its priesthood was not amempton and without defect. But in respect of the priesthood of the New Testament, the Old Testament with its priesthood was not amempton, nor without defect. Therefore, the priesthood of the New Testament must be most excellent and incomparably perfect. The major proposition is clear in itself. For that by whose intuition and comparison a defect and imperfection appears in another, that must be far more excellent and perfect. Add that David greatly admires and delights when he sets the worship of the Old Testament before his eyes, and therefore explains his perpetual conversation with the same among his desires to Jehovah, v. 27. He posits the minor in v. 7 and confirms it thus: If the first Testament with its priesthood had been amempton, and no defect had appeared in it in the comparison of the second or New Testament, then a place would not have been sought for the second or New Testament. The reason for the consequence is because it is superfluous and not consistent with divine wisdom to establish two Testaments, of which one is not more imperfect than the other, nor brings forth greater fruits. But a place was sought for the second or New Testament. Therefore the first or Old Testament was not amempton, nor was it lacking in defect in the comparison of the other.

Which has been established by law upon better promises) [Hebrew word]. It would have been enough to say tithetai, but he preferred to say nenomothetetai, to show that this covenant is at the same time a law. Thus law and covenant are joined in Ps. 78:10. Epi with the dative in this place, as often among the more elegant Greeks, signifies the basis of a contract. But the promises are better because to believers is promised righteousness not external but internal, forgiveness not of errors but of any preceding sins, gifts of the Spirit not to a few, as under the law, but to all, and life not earthly and temporary, but heavenly and eternal.

The Old Testament is viewed either by reason of the moral law, or also by reason of the ceremonial. In respect of the former, the Old Testament did not have such good or excellent promises, because although it also promised eternal life, than which nothing is more worthy or eminent, 'he who shall do these things shall live in them,' Lev. 18:5, Gal. 3:12. Yet that promise was made under the condition of perfect obedience to the law, which after the fall is impossible for us, Rom. 8:3. And therefore the promises of the New Testament are altogether more excellent, by which eternal life is promised freely on account of the merit of Christ, to be conferred provided we apprehend it by faith, Rom. 7:last v., Gal. 3:11. They are more excellent, I say, not by reason of the good promised, but by reason of the condition required. Add that they are more excellent by reason of efficacy: because the law only promises life to those who obey, but does not confer upon us the strength to obey. But the Gospel not only promises life to believers, but also brings the strength to believe, since the Holy Spirit and faith are obtained through the Gospel,

If the Old Testament is viewed with respect to the ceremonial law, although promises of the remission of sins, and consequently of eternal life and salvation, are also exhibited, those ceremonies nevertheless seem to be referred not so much to the substance of the Old Testament as to the figure and shadow of the New Testament, just as they are not to be referred to the law, insofar as it is distinguished from the Gospel: but they belonged properly to the Gospel: And those promises, although they do not differ from the promises of the New Testament by reason of the thing and the good promised; yet by reason of the manner of proposing them, these are to be judged κρείττονες [better], because there they were presented under wrappings, types, and figures; here, however, they are presented most brightly and clearly: There only shadows and ὑποδείγματα [examples] were held, but here the heavenly goods are expressed in living outlines. Blessed Gerhard adds that the New Testament has better promises than the Old, insofar as the promises of the Old Testament are considered outside of Christ and outside of their spiritual significance.

What Grotius says, that the new covenant is at the same time a law, can be admitted in a certain respect, provided that a moral condition is not included in the promises of the New Covenant: as if the observation of the moral law were necessary for salvation, when it is by faith alone that we obtain both the remission of sins and eternal salvation. But the reasons which he brings forward, as to why the promises of the New Testament are better, in no way agree with the analogy of faith: 1. that righteousness is promised to believers, not external but internal: For where is this difference taught, that in the Old Covenant external righteousness was promised to believers, but in the New Testament internal righteousness is promised? In the Old Covenant, under this notion which is now being considered, not faith, by which one must believe in Christ the Savior, was contained, but the law requiring observance of the commandments of both tables; in the new covenant, not internal righteousness, but imputed righteousness is regarded, which is apprehended by faith. 2. That forgiveness is promised not from errors, but from any preceding sins whatsoever. But how is forgiveness promised in the decalogue or moral law from errors? And is forgiveness from errors not promised in the Evangelical covenant? 3. That the gifts of the Spirit are promised not to a few, as under the law, but to all. But indeed, no one received the Holy Spirit through the law, or by the force of the legal covenant. I want to know this, says the Apostle Gal. III. 2, did you receive the Holy Spirit from the works of the law, or from the hearing of faith. 4. That life is promised not terrestrial and temporary, but celestial and eternal. That this is false, it has already been noted quite often, that the legal covenant promises only terrestrial and temporary life. For Christ himself explains the promise of the same regarding eternal life, Luke X. 28, as does Paul Gal. III. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Νυνὶ δὲ διαφορωτέρας τετύχηκε λειτουργίας] Est λειτουρ- γὸς, ut supra dixit vers. 2. Sed λειτουργία illius multo ex- cellentior est illa Levitica. Nomen διαφορωτέρᾳ ha- buimus & supra 1, 4. Νυνὶ δὲ non temporis est nota, sed oppositionis. Vide quæ dicta Rom. 7, 17. 1. Corinth. 5, 11. cap. 7, 15. τυγχάνειν nancisci ut Luc. 20, 35. 2. Tim. 2, 10. infra cap. 11, 35. קָנָה. Pro τετύχηκε alii libri habent τέτευχε.

Ὅσῳ κρείττονός ἐστι διαθήκης Μεσίτης] Quod cœperat dicere cap. 7, 12. legem esse mutatam, id nunc à Pro- phetis prædictum ostendit. Et utitur voce διαθήκης בְּרִית, quia omnis lex Divina sub conditione quædam promittit, ideoque & pacti induit naturam, ut diximus in anteloquio ad Novum Testamentum. CHRISTUS, non Moses, hujus pacti est Μεσίτης. Nam & obtinuit, ne crimina ante vocationem commissa homines à pœni- tentia, aut pœnitentia ductos à venia excluderent, & impetravit nobis summa à DEO beneficia ad vitam æter- nam pertinentia, 1. Tim. 2, 5. Adde Galat. 3, 19. 20. infra cap. 9, 15. cap. 13, 24.

Colligitur jam & diversitas vel præstantia potius λειτουργίας Christi præ sacerdotum Aaronicorum λειτουργίᾳ, qui διαφορωτέρα est, præstantior & di- gnior (vid. Ebr. 1, 4.) è meliori Testamento, cujus Mediator Christus est. Ubi enim dignius est Te- stamentum, ibi etiam dignius sacerdotium. Tan- to, inquit, excellentius est Christi sacerdotium, quan- to melius est Testamentum, cujus ipse est Mediator. Ratio consequentiæ est: Quia Sacerdotis erat & offerre sacrificia in expiationem peccatorum, & intercedere pro populo. Mediatoris autem par- tes sunt ratione fœderis eos, qui inter se dissident, in gratiam redigere, vel conciliare, ac partis, quæ offendit, causam agere penes alteram partem, of- fensam scilicet, quæ reconcilianda est. Unde pa- tet, hæc maxime inter se cognata esse, & à digniori fœdere vel Testamento ad dignius sacerdotium recte concludi. Quæ Estius de Sacerdotis officio hujus illationis gratia ingerit, quod requiratur ad pacta inter Deum & homines conventa, oblati sa- crificii ceremonia confirmare, operamque dare, ut Divinis promissis homines potiantur, calculum non merentur; Quia illis duabus, quas dixi- mus, functionibus officium sacerdotale absolve- batur. Διαφορωτέρα λειτουργία, inquit B. Dor- scheus, est præstantissima eorum λειτουργία, quorum Christus λειτουργὸς hactenus per sessionem ad dextram constitutus est. Itaque διαφορωτέρα λειτουργία vocatur non ratione distantiæ loci, quasi illa in cælo duntaxat perageretur, quod ex v. 4. male elici supra indicatum est, sed ratione præstantiæ actus, quia scilicet, ut ex vers. 5. patet, λατρεία sive λειτουργία Veteris Testamenti ὑπο- δείγματι καὶ σκιᾷ τῶν ἐπουρανίων occupatur & invol- vebatur. Hæc ipsa ἐπουράνια præstat. Illa Sacerdo- tio caduco & fragili peracta est, hæc Sacerdotio æter- no constat. Illa tantum in terris visibiliter perficie- batur, hæc postquam aliquandiu in terris propter acquisitionem pretii redemptionis nostræ admini- strata fuit, tandem Sacerdote in cælos evecto, & glo- riam suam ingresso, invisibili quadam ratione, di- vinaq́; præsentia ita in cælis perficitur, ut in terris non deficiat. Nam 1. hæc λειτουργία in terris maximo- pere necessaria est. Itaq́; in terris etiam perficienda est, sed infinita divinaq́; ratione, ut universæ Ec- clesiæ militanti sufficere queat. 2. Testamentum & quidem novum illud atq́; melius non cælis dunta- xat circumscribitur, sed in terras etiam sese ex- tendit. Itaq́; Testamenti λειτουργία eodem etiam re- ferenda est. 3. Meliorum promissionum vis atq́; effi- cacia in terras quoq́; sese extendit, ut illæ cum cæ- lestibus adipiscerentur ἀνακεφαλαίωσιν, Ephes. I, 10. quapropter & λειτουργία eodem pertinet. 4. Ipse Me- diator postquam pretium redemptionis acquisivit, ejus applicationem non in cælis duntaxat facit, sed & in terris potissimum. Est etiam præstantior λει- τουργία in eo, quod perficitur, ubicunq́; duo vel tres in nomine λειτουργῦ congregati sunt, ipsisq́; gratio- sam ejus præstas præsentiam, cum ad λειτουργίαν Ve- teris Testamenti in tabernaculo aut templo Hiero- solymitano celebratam ipsi fideles accedere necesse habuerint, neq́; summus Sacerdos cum sua λειτουργίᾳ se passim per Palæstinam in medium Judæorum in- gesserit, hæc λειτουργία cum vero suo tabernaculo, quod propterea ad dextram Dei in thronum cæle- stem collocatum est, ipsis fidelibus appropinquat, in eorundem medium sese ingerit & penetrat, utque ibidem vera λατρεία perficatur, efficit. Deniq́; in eo etiam hæc præstantior λειτουργία posita est, quod in ipsis cordibus fidelium per inhabitationem gra- tiosam perficitur. Neq́; enim hæc λειτουργία in as- sumpto hypostatico sanctuario terminatur, sed eo usq́; progreditur, ut corda fidelium faciat σκηνὴν seu ναὸν totius sacrosanctæ Trinitatis, de quo supra ex 1. Cor. I, 11. 12. cap. VI, 19. 2. Corinth. VI. vers. 16. Ephes. III, 17. Tantum itaque abest, ut propterea dicamus διαφορωτέραν hanc λειτουργίαν, quod scili- cet procul ab his terris, in circumscripto quodam cælorum loco perficiatur, ut omnia alia ex ejus consideratione manifesta sint. Argumentum autem Apostoli hic tale est: Illud Sacerdotium oportet esse præstantissimum, atq́; incomparabiliter perfectum, cujus respectu primum Testamentum & Sacerdo- tium illius non fuit ἄμεμπτον & sine defectu. At respectu Sacerdotii Novi Testamenti Vetus Testa- mentum cum Sacerdotio non fuit ἄμεμπτον, nec sine defectu. Ergo oportet Sacerdotium Novi Te- stamenti esse præstantissimum & incomparabiliter perfectum. Major propositio per se clara est. Cu- jus enim intuitu & collatione in altero defectus ap- paret atq́; imperfectio, illud oportet esse longe præ- stantius atq́; perfectius. Adde quod David sum- mopere admiretur & delectetur, cum cultum Ve- teris Testamenti sibi ob oculos ponit, ideoque peren- nem apud eundem conversationem inter desideria sua Jehove exponit v. 27. Minorem ponit vers. 7. & ita confirmat: Si primum Testamentum cum Sacerdotio suo fuisset ἄμεμπτον, neque in collatio- nec secundi seu Novi Testamenti apparuisset in illo defectus, tunc secundo seu Novo Testamento non fuisset quæsitus locus. Ratio consequentiæ est, quia duo Testamenta, quorum unum altero non est im- perfectius, neque majores affert fructus, constitue- re, supervacaneum, neque divina sapientiæ con- sentaneum est. Atqui secundo seu Novo Testamen- to quæsitus locus est. Ergo primum seu Vetus Testa- mentum non fuit ἄμεμπτον, neque defectu in colla- tione alterius caruit.

Ἥτις ἐπὶ κρείττοσιν ἐπαγγελίαις νενομοθέτηται) נסמכה. Satis fuerat dicere τίθηται, sed maluit dicere νενομοθέτη- ται, ut ostenderet pactum hoc simul & legem esse. Sic jun- guntur lex & pactum Psal. LXXVIII, 10. Ἐπὶ vero cum Dativo hoc loco, ut sæpe apud elegantiores Græcos, signi- ficat contractus partem. Sunt autem promissa meliora, quia credentibus promittitur justitia non externa sed inter- na, venia non ab erroribus, sed a peccatis quibusvis ante- cedentibus, Spiritus dona non paucis, ut sub lege, sed omnibus, & vita non terrestris & temporaria, sed cœlestis & æterna.

Vetus Testamentum spectatur vel ratione legis moralis, vel simul ratione cæremonialis. Respe- ctu illius non tam bonas vel eximias promissio- nes habuit Vetus Testamentum, quia etsi vitam æternam, qua nihil dignius, vel eminentius, etiam promiserit, qui fecerit hæc, vivet in eis, Lev. XIIX. 5. Gal. III. 12. Promissio tamen illa fa- cta est sub conditione perfectæ obedientiæ legis, quæ post lapsum nobis impossibilis est, Rom. VIII. v. 3. Ideoque præstant omnino promissiones Novi Testamenti, quibus vita æterna promittitur gra- tis propter meritum Christi, modo fide id appre- hendamus, conferenda, Rom. VII. v. ult. Gal. III. v. 11. Præstant, inquam, non ratione boni promis- si, sed ratione conditionis requisitæ. Adde quod præstent ratione efficaciæ: quia lex solum promit- tit obedientibus vitam, non autem confert no- bis vires obsequendi. Evangelium vero non so- lum credentibus pollicetur vitam, sed etiam vi- res credendi affert, quum Spiritus Sanctus & fi- des per Evangelium obtineatur,

Si respectu legis cæremonialis Testamentum vetus spectetur, etsi promissiones etiam exhibeantur remissionis peccatorum, & consequenter vitæ & salutis æter- næ, illæ tamen cæremoniæ non tam ad Testamen- ti Veteris substantiam, quam ad Testamenti Novi figuram & umbram referendæ videntur, uti nec ad legem, quatenus ab Evangelio distinguitur: sed ad Evangelium proprie spectabant: Illæque promissiones, etsi ratione rei & boni promissi non differant a promissionibus Novi Testamenti; tamen ratione modi proponendi hæ κρείττονες cen- sendæ, quia ibi sub involucris, typis & figuris si- stebantur; hic vero maxime luculenter & perspi- cue sistuntur: Ibi umbræ tantum habebantur & ὑποδείγματα, hic vero vivis lineamentis expressa sunt bona cœlestia. Addit B. Gerhardus, Novum Testamentum meliores habere promissiones, quam Vetus, quatenus scilicet promissiones Ve- teris Testamenti considerantur extra Christum, & extra spiritualem significationem.

Quod Grotius dicit, pactum novum simul & legem esse, certo respectu admitti potest, modo non conditio moralis includatur promissis Novi fœderis: quasi observatio legis moralis ad salu- tem sit necessaria, quum fide tantum; ut remis- sionem peccatorum, ita & salutem æternam con- sequamur. Quas autem affert rationes, quod meliora Novi Testamenti sint promissa, analo- giæ fidei nullatenus conveniunt: 1. promitti cre- dentibus justitiam non externam sed internam: Ubi enim hæc differentia tradita, quod in Vete- ri fœdere credentibus promissa sit externa, in Novo Testamento promittatur interna justitia? In veteri fœdere sub hac notione, quæ jam atten- ditur, non fides, qua credendum in Christum Salvatorem, continebatur, sed lex requirens ob- fervantiam mandatorum utriusque tabulæ in no- vo fœdere, non justitia interna, sed imputata respicitur, quæ fide apprehenditur. 2. Veniam non ab erroribus, sed à peccatis quibusvis ante- cedentibus promitti. Quomodo vero venia in decalogo vel lege morali promittitur ab errori- bus? Et num in Evangelico fœdere promissa non est ab erroribus venia? 3. Promitti Spiritus dona non paucis, ut sub lege, sed omnibus. At vero per legem nemo Spiritum Sanctum accepit, vel vi fœderis legalis. Id volo scire, inquit Apostolus Gal. III. 2. anne ex operibus legis Spiritum San- ctum accepistis, an ex auditu fidei. 4. Promitti vitam non terrestrem & temporariam, sed cæle- stem & æternam. Falsum id esse, jam sæpius mo- nitum, fœdus legale tantum vitam terrestrem & temporariam promittere. Nam explicat ipse Christus promissionem ejusdem de æterna vita, Luc. X. 28. ut & Paulus Gal. III. 2.

## 8:7
Vers. 7. (For if that first was faultless) πρώτη for προτέρα. See what we said on John I. 16. Ἄμεμπτος is taken here comparatively, and somewhat improperly, in the sense that it is to be understood that the Sinaitic covenant was not such that another could not be more perfect. See above VII. 18. 19. In almost the same way κατεγνωσμένος is taken, Gal. II. 11, as we said on that passage. And in this very matter ἀνωφελὲς above VII. 18. See also what was said Acts XIII. 38.

There would not have been sought a place for a second) That is, that ancient one would not have been, for this to succeed it. For he who seeks a place for one thing often removes another thing for its sake.

The Apostle proves that the legal covenant does not contain such good promises. For if that first legal covenant were faultless, that is, such that nothing could be desired in it, as far as the effect is concerned, there would be no place for another, namely the Evangelical. However, he does not deny that it was faultless in itself, as the Manichaeans abused this passage to teach that the Old Testament proceeded from an evil God and is reprehensible, because the law is from GOD the best, and the Author of all good, Deut. XXXII. 4, from whom nothing can arise that is reprehensible, James I. 17, but [he denies it] in relation to us and as regards the effect, in this state of man after the fall: because it is able neither to be performed by man, nor to confer perfection upon man. If nothing had been lacking to the old covenant, what was the point of substituting another? But another was substituted: therefore that one must not have been perfect.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Εἰ γὰρ ἡ πρώτη ἐκείνη ἦν ἄμεμπτος) πρώτη pro προτέρα. Vide quæ diximus Joh. I. 16. Ἄμεμπτος hic comparate sumitur, & nonnihil improprie, eo sensu, ut intelligatur fœdus Sinaiticum non tale fuisse, quo non al- terum posset esse perfectius. Vide supra VII. 18. 19. Pari ferme modo sumi κατεγνωσμένος, Gal. II. 11. ad illum lo. cum diximus. Et in hac ipsa re ἀνωφελὲς supra VII. 18. Vi- de & quæ dicta Act. XIII. 38.

Οὐκ ἂν δευτέρας ἐζητεῖτο τόπος) Id est, non fuisset illud antiquum, ut hoc fuccederet. Nam qui locum alicui rei quærit, sæpe ejus causa rem alteram amovet.

Probat Apostolus fœdus legale promissiones tàm bonas non continere. Nam si ἄμεμπτον, hoc est tale, in quo nihil desiderari possit, quan- tum ad effectum, esset primum illud legale fœdus, alteri locus non esset, Evangelico nempe, Non autem negat, ἄμεμπτον fuisse in se, quemadmo- dum Manichæi abusi hoc loco docuere, quod Vetus Testamentum à malo Deo profectum, & reprehensibile sit, quia lex à DEO optimo, omnisque boni Autore est, Deut. XXXII. 4. à quo nihil oriri potest, quod reprehensibile sit, Jac. I. 17. sed ratione nostri & quoad effectum, in hoc statu hominis post lapsum: quia nec ab ho- mine præstari, nec perfectionem homini confer- re valet. Si nihil defuisset veteri fœderi, quid at- tinebat surrogari aliud? Atqui aliud surrogatum est: Ideoque illud oportet non fuisse perfectum.

## 8:8
Vers. 8. (For finding fault with them he says) μεμφόμενος, that is, thinking less of the former covenant, he says to them, who indeed were living under the former covenant.

He opposes the word μεμφόμενος to τῷ ἀμέμπτῳ. The Vulgate renders it 'incusans' (accusing). That which God himself accuses is by no means so perfect that nothing can be desired in it. It is said ambiguously that the ancients lived under the former covenant, either because they only had the legal covenant and were destitute of the Evangelical; or because they lived while only the promises and types concerning the Messiah were still in force, before the fulfillment and the body itself succeeded, where Moses seemed to reign more with his covenant, which he ratified with the people in God's name. The former sense seems to be Grotius's: But it is false: For the Fathers likewise obtained salvation by the grace of Christ the Savior, as the decree of the Council of Jerusalem teaches us, Acts XV. 11. The latter is admitted. Cajetan and Stapulensis refer the little word ἑαυτοῖς to the word λέγει, because the fault of those to whom the law was given cannot be referred to the law itself. But Chrysostom, Theophylact, and others refer it to the word μεμφόμενος with the Syrian Interpreter. For although the law is perfect in itself, Ps. XIX. 8, and holy, Rom. VII. 12, it is nevertheless weakened as regards the effect through the flesh in respect to us, Rom. VIII. 3, and so its promises are useless to us for salvation, because there is no one who keeps the law, whence there was need for the New Testament. (Behold the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will accomplish upon the house of Israel, and upon the house of Judah a new covenant) From the Greek of the chapter Jer. XXXI. 31, and following. But that chapter in many Greek editions is XXXVIII. because of the transposition made there. Ἔρχονται (are coming) is present in sound, often future in sense, as 1 Thess. I. 10, and elsewhere, καὶ συντελέσω, that is, when I shall effect, by a frequent idiom of the Hebrews. Ἐπὶ (upon) with or towards. Justin against Trypho and Tertullian IV against Marcion use this same passage in this same sense. In Justin these things precede: 'For the old law in Horeb is already old, and yours alone. But that [new one] is for all simply. But a law set against a law caused the one before it to cease. And a covenant made afterwards extinguished the former in the same way, and Christ was given to us as an eternal and final law, and a faithful covenant, after which there is no law, no ordinance, no commandment.' There is mention of a new covenant, and indeed an eternal one also Jer. XXXII. 40, Ezech. XVI. 60, XXXIV. 25. And the sense indeed of those passages more openly regards that time in which the Jews, almost all of them, and those from the ten tribes who wished, having been restored to their ancestral seats, had restored the worship of God, which was corrupted by no idolatry afterwards, which had often happened before. Compare what is said about that time Is. II. 3, Jer. XXXI. 1, XXXIII. 8, Ezech. XI. 17, XX. 41, XXXVI. 24. And the solemn renewal of the covenant itself on the part of the people with God approving, which we have Nehem. XI. 12. And certainly that benefit was so great that it could induce forgetfulness of all old things, and therefore the individuals of the people would acknowledge the supreme goodness of God not from the teaching of masters, but from their own sense: which sense, and after it the very recent memory both of this good and of the evils which they had suffered from idolaters, was most effective for long retaining the worship of God in that people. But since that dispensation of God, through which He gathered a people for Himself from all lands, figures the times of the Messiah more manifestly than any others, as the Rabbis also acknowledge, therefore words from the places of the Prophets looking to that are often brought forward by the Apostles and their helpers in a more sublime sense, as can be seen in very many places of the Gospels and Acts and the epistles of Paul. And certainly the words were so directed by God that they fit the times of Christ more exactly. For through this one, the covenant was truly not renewed, but a clearly new one was made: and indeed not a lasting one, but clearly an eternal one. Moreover, the names of Judah and Israel are referred to the Church of Christ by an excellent mystery, not only because this is now the people of God by a better right than they were: but also because the meaning of the names demands it: for Judah is ἐξομολογούμενος, and Philo rightly interprets it, which Christians did even at the price of their lives, but Israel, who overcomes God, that is, obtains anything from God, just as Christians obtain all things that lead to eternal life. See Rom. II. 28. 29. & IX. 6. & what is said there. Add now that in those times the people restored to their fatherland were not only a figure, but also a certain taste of the Gospel. For Christ, as now approaching, was more openly indicated by the Prophets; certain words of the Prophets explained mystically by Ezra and others created a certain hope of a better life, and a Spirit much stronger than of old fell to the lot of the believers. That double sense is a Grotius invention. The Apostle knows no other than a single sense, which he urges. Nor does one sense after another occur in the Prophet, but only that one which flows from the letter and is urged by the Apostle is to be admitted. If by a more open sense the time after the Babylonian captivity is regarded, how then can it be conceded that those same things which regard that time pertain to the fullness of times, and that the same words treat both of the times of the released captivity and of the times of the New Testament. If it treats of the restoration of the worship of God in Judea, how is it to be thought to discourse of the remission of sins in the very same words? And what does the restoration of worship in Judea, with idolatry abrogated, have to do with the new covenant? The passages which are brought forward as parallels are each weighed in their own place. The true sense of the oracle of Jeremiah has also been treated in its proper seat. We assume that through Christ the old covenant was not renewed, but a clearly new one was made, and indeed not a lasting one, but clearly an eternal one: whose benefits are enjoyed not by those who are Jews or Israelites according to the flesh, but by those who are such according to the Spirit, true ἐξομολογούμενοι or confessors, overcoming God by faith, and obtaining all things which lead to eternal life. It must not be denied, however, that such were the ancients before Christ. For the Patriarchs, Prophets, and other righteous men are celebrated for their faith and confession in ch. XI of this epistle, and elsewhere throughout: who had not merely some taste of the Evangelical promises, but rejoiced because of the day of the Lord, which they saw in the Spirit, with Abraham, the Father of believers, John VIII. 56. That hope of a better life was made to them, long before the times of Ezra, from Moses, Job, the Psalms of David, and other earlier Canonical writings, is certain; to whom, finally, that the Principal Spirit was granted, their heroic deeds and other works and testimonies of the Holy Spirit are a most clear indication. But those words, 'the days are coming, and I will perfect a new covenant,' signify nothing other than that God is about to enter into a new covenant, or a new arrangement or testament, with men; where, in the word συντελέσω used by the Apostle, for which the word διαθήσομαι is found among the LXX Interpreters, Augustine, in his book De Spiritu et Littera, ch. XVIII, observes an emphasis, namely, that it is noted that this new testament will by no means be frustrated, as the old one was, but will have its effect in the children of the promise, who are comprehended under the name of the house of Israel and the house of Judah, although this house denotes both the ten tribes of the Israelite people and the two remaining tribes of the Jewish, not excluding proselytes or Gentiles gathered to them, Eph. II. 14, and thus extends itself to all the families of the earth, Gen. XII. 3. For God establishes the covenant of grace with all, even if its fruit redounds only to those who believe from among all these. Thus Augustine, l. XXII. contra Faust. c. 84. and l. XVIII. De Civitate Dei, c. 28. by Israel he understands the Church to be gathered from the Gentiles; by the house of Judah, the remnant to be gathered from the Jews.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Μεμφόμενος γὰρ αὐτοῖς λέγει) μεμφόμενος, id est, minoris faciens pactum prius, dicit illis, qui nempe sub pacto priore vivebant.

Verbum μεμφόμενος opponit τῷ ἀμέμπτῳ. Vulgatus reddit incusans. Quod Deus ipse incu- sat, illud minime ita perfectum, ut nihil in eo de- siderari possit. Sub priori pacto vixisse veteres am- bigue dicitur, vel quod tantum legale pactum ha- buerint, Evangelico verò destituti fuerint; vel quod vigentibus adhuc solum promissis & typis de Messia, antequam complementum & corpus ipsum succederet, ubi Moses regnare magis vi- debatur cum fœdere suo, quod sancivit cum po- pulo Dei nomine, vixerint. Prior sensus Grotii videtur: Sed falsus est: Nam Patres itidem gratia Christi Salvatoris salutem adeptos esse, ut nos concilii Hierosolymitani decretum docet, Act. XV. 11. Posterior admittitur. Voculam ἑαυτοῖς ad verbum λέγει referunt Cajetanus & Stapulensis, quod non possit culpa eorum, quibus lex data, in ipsam legem referri. Sed Chrysostomus, Theophyla- ctus & alii referunt illud ad verbum μεμφόμενος cum Syro Interprete. Quamvis enim lex in se per- fecta sit, Ps. XIX. 8. & sancta, Rom. VII. 12. infir- mata tamen est quoad effectum per carnem respe- ctu nostri, Rom. VIII. 3. adeoq; promissiones ejus nobis ad salutem sunt inutiles, quia nemo est, qui legem servat, unde Novo Test. opus fuit. Ἰδοὺ ἡμέραι ἔρχονται, λέγει Κύριος, καὶ συντελέσω ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον Ἰσραὴλ, καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον Ἰούδα διαθήκην καινήν ) Ex Græco capitis Jer. XXXI. 31. & seqq. Sed id caput in Græ- cis editionibus multis est XXXVIII. ob transpositionem ibi factam. Ἔρχονται באים sono est præsens, sensu sæpe fu- turum, ut 1. Thessal. I. 10. & alibi, καὶ συντελέσω, id est, cum efficiam, locutione frequenti Ebræis. Ἐπὶ את cum vel erga. Utuntur hoc eodem loco in hunc eundem sensum Justinus contra Tryphonem, & Tertullianus IV. adversus Marcionem. In Justino hæc præcedunt: Ὁ γὰρ ἐν Χωρὴβ παλαιὸς ἤδη νόμος, καὶ ὑμῶν μόνον. Ὁ δὲ πάντων ἁπλῶς. Νόμος δὲ κατὰ νόμον τεθεὶς τὸν πρὸ αὐτοῦ ἔπαυσε. Καὶ δια- θήκη μετέπειτα γενομένη τὴν προτέραν ὁμοίως ἔσβυσεν αἰώ- νιός τε ἡμῖν νόμος καὶ τελευταῖος ὁ Χριστὸς ἐδόθη, καὶ ἡ δια- θήκη πιστὴ, μεθ᾽ ἣν οὐ νόμος, οὐ πρόσταγμα, οὐκ ἐντολή. Men- tio est novi pacti, & quidem αἰωνίου etiam Jer. XXXII. 40. Ezech. XVI. 60. XXXIV. 25. Et sensus quidem apertior lo- corum illorum respicit tempus illud, quo Judæi prope omnes, & ex decem tribubus, qui vellent, restituti in pa- trias sedes, cultum Dei restituerant, qui nulla postea ido- lolatria corruptus fuit, quod ante sæpe evenerat. Conf. di- cta de eo tempore Es. II. 3. Jer. XXXI. 1. XXXIII. 8. Ezech. XI. 17. XX. 41. XXXVI. 24. Et ipsam solemnem pacti re- novationem ex parte populi Deo approbante, quam ha- bemus Nehem. XI. 12. Et certe tantum erat illud benefi- cium, ut omnium veterum possit oblivionem inducere, ac proinde singuli de populo non ex doctrina magistrorum, sed proprio sensu Dei bonitatem summam agnoscerent: qui sensus & post eum recens admodum memoria tum hujus boni, tum malorum, quæ ab idololatris pertulerant, efficacissima erat ad Dei cultum in illo populo diu reti- nendum. Sed quum illa dispensatio Dei, per quam sibi ex omnibus terris collegit populum, manifestus, quam ullæ aliæ, figuret Messiæ tempora, ut & Rabbini agnoscunt, ideo sæpius ex Prophetarum locis eo spectantibus verba in sensu sublimiore ab Apostolis & eorum adjutoribus producuntur, ut in plurimis locis Evangeliorum & Actuum & Pauli epistolarum videre est. Et certe ita à Deo directæ sunt verba, ut in Christi tempora quadrent exactius. Per hunc enim vere non antiquum fœdus renovatum est, sed factum plane novum: & quidem non diuturnum, sed plane æternum. Judæ autem & Israelis nomen egregio mysterio ad Christi Ecclesiam referuntur, non tantum quia hæc nunc populus Dei est meliore jure, quam illi fuere: verum etiam quia nominum significatio id postulat: nam Judas est ἐξομολογούμενος, & Philo recte interpretatur, quod Christiani faciebant etiam vitæ suæ pretio, Israel vero, qui Deum superat, id est, quidvis à Deo obtinet, sicut Chris- tiani obtinent omnia, quæ ad vitam ducunt æternam. Vi- de Rom. II. 28. 29. & IX. 6. & ibi dicta. Adde jam quod in illis temporibus populi in patriam restituti non figura tan- tum, sed & gustus quidam Evangelii fuit. Nam Christus, ut jam appropinquans, apertius à Prophetis indicatus est; verba quædam Prophetarum per Esdram & alios mystice explicata spem quandam fecere vitæ melioris, & creden- tibus contigit Spiritus multo quam olim fortior. Sensus ille geminus commentum est Grotia- num. Apostolus non novit nisi unicum sensum, quem urget. Nec apud Prophetam alius atq; alius sensus occurrit, sed unice ille, qui tum ex litera fluit, tum ab Apostolo urgetur, admittendus est. Si apertiori sensu tempus respicitur post Babylo- nicam captivitatem, quomodo ergo concedi po- test, quod eadem illa, quæ eo respiciant, ad pleni- tudinem temporum pertineant, iisdemq; verbis & de temporibus solutæ captivitatis, & de tempo- ribus Novi Test. agatur. Si de restauratione cul- tus Dei in Judæa agit, quomodo de peccatorum remissione iisdem omnino verbis censendus est disserere? Et quid restitutio cultus in Judæa, ab- rogata idololatria, ad pactum novum? Dicta, quæ pro parallelis adducuntur, suo quæque loco ex- penduntur. De vero etiam sensu oraculi Jeremiæ in propria sede actum. Assumimus, per Christum non antiquum fœdus renovatum esse, sed factum plane novum, & quidem non diuturnum, sed pla- ne æternum: Cujus beneficiis, non qui Judæi aut Israëlitæ secundum carnem, sed qui tales secundum Spiritum sunt, fruantur, veri ἐξομολογούμενοι vel confessores, fide Deum vincentes, & obtinentes omnia, quæ ad vitam ducunt æternam. Non ta- men negandum, tales fuisse veteres ante Christum. Nam Patriarchæ, Prophetæ, aliiq; justi à fide cele- brantur & confessione c. XI. hujus epistolæ, & ali- bi passim : qui non gustum tantum aliquem Evan- gelicarum promissionum habuere, sed gavisi sunt ob diem Domini, quem viderunt in Spiritu, cum Abrahamo, Patre credentium, Joh. VIII. 56. qui- bus spem fuisse factam melioris vitæ, longe ante Esdræ tempora ex Mose, Jobo, Davidis Psalmis, aliisq; anterioribus scriptis Canonicis constat, quibus deniq; Spiritum Principalem contigisse Heroica eorum facta, & alia Spir. S. opera ac te- stimonia indicio sunt luculentissimo. Verba au- tem illa, veniunt dies, & perficiam novum fœdus nihil aliud innuunt, quam quod Deus initurus sit cum hominibus novum fœdus, vel novam dispo- sitionem aut testamentum ; ubi in voce συντελέσω ab Apostolo adhibita, pro qua apud LXX. Inter- pretes habetur verbum διαθήσομαι, Augustin. libr. de Sp. & lit. c. XIIX. emphasin observat, notari nempe, novum hoc testamentum minime fru- stratum iri, ut vetus, sed effectum in filiis promis- sionis habiturum, qui nomine domus Israel, & domus Juda comprehenduntur, quamvis hæc do- mus tum decem tribus populi Israelitici, tum duas reliquas Judaici notet, non exclusis proselytis, vel gentibus ad illas aggregatis, Eph. II. 14. adeoque ad omnes familias terræ se extendat, Genes. XII, 3. Cum omnibus enim sancit Deus fœdus gratiæ, etsi fructus ejus ad solos eos, qui ex omnibus istis credunt, redundet. Ita Augustin. l. XXII. contra Faust. c. 84. & l. XIIX. de Civ. Dei c. 28. per Israel Ecclesiam colligendam ex gentibus; per domum Judæ reliquias colligendas ex Judæis intelligit.

## 8:9
Vers. 9. 'Not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers') That is, with better success. κατὰ is accustomed to signify likeness. But this likeness in this place is viewed in the outcome. 'In the day when I took them by the hand') 'In the day,' that is, about that time. In the Hebrew, 'in the day of my taking their hand,' that is, when I had taken, which is expressed here not inelegantly by a participle. Those who lead someone out of prison are accustomed to take his hand. See what we said above II, 6. 'In the day,' for 'about that time,' you have in the same matter Ezech. XX, 5. 'To lead them out of the land of Egypt') That is, εἰς τὸ ἐξαγαγεῖν, which is clearer in the Hebrew להוציאם. 'Because they did not remain in my covenant') They did not stand by the agreements. Thus 'to remain' is used with words in Virgil. We have ἐμμένειν in this sense in Deut. XXVII. 26, Jer. XXIV. 25, Acts XVI, 22, Gal. III, 10. In the Hebrew it is, 'they themselves violated my covenant,' namely, in the worship of the calf, in Massah and Meribah, in the Midianite affair, and again shortly after the times of Joshua, to omit now more recent ones. 'And I neglected them, says the Lord') For 'says the Lord,' both here and below in the Greek, it is φησὶ Κύριος in the same sense. It appears, however, that the LXX Interpreters read בחלתי instead of בעלתי, for that is what ἠμέλησα is. I neglected them in turn, I did not defend them against the serpents, I armed the Levites for their slaughter: I suffered them to come under the yoke of the Midianites, the Philistines, and other nations.

The legal covenant was indeed established with the Fathers of the Israelites and their Jews, who were living in the time of Jeremiah, for whose sake the Lord speaks thus: But not excluding the Gentiles, to whom access to the people of the Lord was open, and the moral law inscribed by nature sufficed for the obligation due to the precepts of both tables. But here, neglect and observation of the divine law is reproached to the Israelites and Jews, as those with whom the Prophet had business, even though it is certain that it is kept by no one, and that the whole world is therefore made ὑπόδικον (accountable) to God, Rom. III. 19. Therefore it is also said peculiarly to them that God neglected them, as the Apostle has it from the LXX Interpreters. But in the Hebrew there is the word בעלתי בם, not that it was read differently in the past, but because they looked to the sense, as Thomas explains: because they made my covenant void, therefore I became their Lord, i.e. I showed that I was their Lord, not suffering my law to be despised with impunity; I punished them according to their deserts, as their Lord. More lenient are the interpretations of Tremellius, who rendered it interrogatively, 'And I, would I have remained joined to them?' and of Piscator, who explained it, 'And yet I was joined in marriage.' For by the examples of the Jewish and Israelite people, the Prophet, and with him the Apostle, wishes to teach what follows when the divine law is not kept, as it is certain that the same is kept and fulfilled by no one: namely, punishment and rejection by the Lord, because He casts off the care of those who violate His law by the force of the legal covenant. This is what the Apostle teaches elsewhere, that we are concluded under sin by the law, Gal. III. 22, under unbelief, Rom. XI. 32, and that we are accountable to God, Rom. III. 19. Which is the reason why, unless we were to perish eternally, we had need of a new covenant, a covenant of grace, which was to be established in Christ, of which it follows further. Furthermore, the accusation of the Israelites, in that they did not remain in the covenant entered into with God, is to be explained, as the blessed Dorscheus rightly advises, as meaning that they violated it most gravely and most enormously. For thus negative words are very often placed for affirmative ones with singular emphasis, Is. XLII. 3, Zech. VIII. 17, Job XIV. 18, Matt. XII. 32. This non-continuance in the covenant is not only placed in the fact that they did not perform those things which the covenant in its rigor had demanded of them, since that very thing was ἀδύνατον, Rom. VIII. 3, inasmuch as the law was spiritual, i.e., demanding a spiritual and most perfect idea of charity and justice; but they themselves were σαρκικοῖς, neither apt nor able to conform their life to that idea, Roman. VII. 14; but also that they did not attend to the secondary end and use of that covenant, which was pedagogical and leading to the Messiah, Gal. III. 24; nay, they even clearly corrupted that covenant, partly by interpreting the law of that covenant as if salvation and justice could be had solely from it, concerning which Acts XV. 10, Rom. III. & IV. & Gal. II. III. & IV., and partly by depraving the most holy and most perfect law of the covenant with various additions and impertinent comments, concerning which Matth. V. 21. & seqq. & XV. 2. seqq. Whence the covenant is not to be accused, as Schlichting does in his Commentary on this passage, p. 345, when he says: This is the reason why God wishes to strike a New Testament different from that Old one with the people, because that ancient covenant was not of such strength that it could keep the people in their duty. For hence it happened that the people fell away from it and transgressed it. Therefore, the consequent is posited, so that from it the antecedent, a certain defect and impotence of that covenant, may be understood. For if there had been no defect in the covenant, no vice, but only in the people, the covenant itself ought not to have been abolished on account of the vice of the people alone. And therefore it appears that it happened by the vice of the people, and thus also by the defect of the covenant itself, that it was not observed. Thus Schlichting against the holiness of the old covenant. For although it did not supply the powers by which the people could be reconciled with God, it nevertheless led them through various institutions to Him who would offer those powers. Hence it should not be ascribed to the covenant that the people fell away from it and transgressed it; for even if there was a certain defect and impotence in the covenant, there was nevertheless under the covenant, if it had been rightly estimated and according to the divine intention, that by which that defect and impotence might be succored. Whence that defect is in no way to be called a vice. And although also on account of a certain defect and imperfection the ancient covenant was temporary, and to be finished at a certain period of ages, Gen. XLIX. 10, yet the vice, on account of which the covenant was finally abolished, was to be ascribed to the people, just as it is also ascribed throughout Scripture. Compare Matthew 23:4 up to the end of the chapter. Again, in the punishment of the Israelites, the word, 'I have been their Lord,' namely by punishing, by casting away, and by showing that I am the Lord, and that I can do toward them what I wish, which is the right of Lords, implies the rejection of the Israelite people, and it agrees well with the Greek ἠμέλησα ἀυτῶν, insofar as a certain negation of divine ἐπιμελείας (care) is contained in it, and thus an opposite act is hinted at, that is, not only the omission and intermission of preserving custody, but also the imposition and sending in of curses and manifold punishments.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Οὐ κατὰ τὴν διαθήκην, ἣν ἐποίησα τοῖς πατράσιν ἀυτῶν) Id est, meliore successu. κατὰ similitudinem significa- re solet. Similitudo autem ista h. l. in eventu spectatur. Ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἐπιλαβομένου με τῆς χειρὸς ἀυτῶν ) Ἐν ἡμέρᾳ, id est, circa illud tempus. In Ebræo, in die apprehendere me manum eorum, id est, cum apprehendissem, quod hic per participium exprimitur non ineleganter. Solent, qui ali- quem è carcere educunt, manum ejus prehendere. Vide quæ diximus supra II, 6. In die, pro circa illud tempus, ha- bes in re eadem Ezech. XX, 5. Ἐξαγαγεῖν ἀυτὸς ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπ]ε) Id est εἰς τὸ ἐξαγαγεῖν, quod clarius in Ebræo להוציאם. Ὅτι ἀυτοὶ ἐκ ἐνέμειναν ἐν τῇ διαθήκῃ με) Non stete- runt pactis. Sic dictis manere apud Virgilium. Ἐμμένειν hoc sensu habemus Deut. XXVII. 26. Jer. XXIV. 25. Act. XVI, 22. Gal. III, 10. In Ebræo est, ipsi violarunt pactum meum, nempe in cultu vituli, in Massa & Meriba, in Madianiide, & rursum paulo post Josuæ tempora, ut jam seriora omittam. Κἀγὼ ἠμέλησα ἀυτῶν, λέγει Κύριος) Pro λέγει κύριος tum hic tum infra in Græco est φησὶ Κύριος sensu eodem. Ap- paret autem LXX. Interpretes pro בעלתי legisse בחלתי, id enim est ἠμέλησα. Neglexi eos vicissim, non defendi eos contra serpentes, Levitas in eorum occisionem arma- vi : Passus sum eos venire sub jugum Madianitarum, Phi- listinorum & aliarum gentium.

Pactum legale sancitum quidem est cum Patri- bus Israelitarum & Judæorum eorum, qui tempo- re Jeremiæ vivebant, quorum causa ita loquitur Dominus : Sed non exclusis gentibus, quibus pate- bat aditus ad populum Domini, & lex moralis na- tura insculpta ad obligationem præceptis utrius- que tabulæ debitam sufficiebat. Exprobratur au- tem hic Israelitis & Judæis, utpote quibuscum ne- gotium erat Prophetæ, neglectus & observatio legis divinæ, etsi ea à nemine servari, totumque mundum ideo ὑπόδικον Deo fieri certum sit, Rom. III. 19. Idcirco etiam peculiariter istis dicitur, quod neglexerit eos Deus, ut è LXX. Interpreti- bus habet Apostolus. In Ebræo autem est verbum בעלתי בם, non quod olim aliter lectum sit, sed quod sensum respexerint, quomodo Thomas expo- nit: quia pactum meum fecerunt irritum, ideo domi- natus sum iis, i.e. Dominum me esse ostendi, non pas- sus impune legem meam contemni, punivi eos pro meritis, tanquam ipsorum Dominus. Alle- niores sunt interpretationes Tremellii, qui red- didit interrogative, & ego conjunctus mansissem eis? & Piscatoris, qui exposuit, & tamen conjugio junctus eram. Exemplis enim populi Judaici, & Israelitici docere vult Propheta, & cum eo Apo- stolus, quid consequatur, cum lex divina non ser- vatur, uti à nemine eandem servari, & impleri cer- tum est: Pœna nempe, & abjectio à Domino, quod curam eorum abjiciat, qui legem suam violant vi fœderis legalis. Hoc est, quod alias docet Apo- stolus, per legem nos conclusos esse sub peccato, Gal. III. 22. sub incredulitate Rom. XI. 32. & obnoxios esse nos Deo, Rom. III. 19. Quæ causa est, cur, nisi æternum nobis pereundum, fœdere novo opus nobis fuerit, fœdere gratiæ, quod in Christo pan- gendum erat, de quo porro sequitur. Cæterum accusatio Israelitarum in eo posita, quod non per- manserint in fœdere cum Deo inito, sic explicanda, ut recte monet B. Dorscheus, quod gravissime illud & enormissime violaverint. Sic enim verba negan- tia pro affirmantibus cum singulari emphasise pissi- me ponuntur, Es.XLII. 3. Zach. VIII. 17. Job. XIV. 18. Matth. XII. 32. Quæ non-permansio in fœdere, inito non tantum in eo posita est, quod non præstite- rint ea, quæ in rigore fœdus ab ipsis postulaverat, cum idipsum ἀδύνα]ον esset, Rom. VIII. 3. quippe lege exsistente spirituali, h. e. exigente spiritualem per- fectissimamq; ideam charitatis & justitiæ; ipsis au- tem σαρκικοῖς, nec aptis, aut valentibus ad istam ideam vitam suam componere, Roman. VII. 14. sed etiam secundarium finem usumq; fœderis istius non attenderint, qui fuit pædagogicus & ad Messiam adductivus, Gal. III. 24. imo etiam fœdus illud pla- ne corruperint, partim legem fœderis istius eo inter- pretando, quasi ex ea unice salus & justitia haberi posset, de quo Act. XV. 10. Rom. III. & IV. & Gal. II. III. & IV. partim vero sanctissimam perfectissimam- que fœderis legem additamentis variis & commen- tis impertinentibus depravarint, de quo Matth. V. 21. & seqq. & XV. 2. seqq. Unde non est accusandum fœdus, quemadmodum facit Schlichting. in Comm. ad h. l. p. 345. cum ait: Hæc est causa, cur N. T. à Ve- teri illo diversum percutere cum populo Deus velit, quod antiquum illud fœdus tantarum virium non fuerit, ut populum in officio continere posset. Hinc e- nim factum est, ut populus ab eo descisceret, illudq; transgrederetur. Itaq; consequens ponitur, ut ex eo antecedens, fœderis illius defectus & impotentia quædam intelligatur. Si enim in fœdere fuisset defe- ctus nullus, vitium nullum, sed tantum in populo, propter solius populi vitium fœdus ipsum tolli non debuisset. Ideoq; apparet, ut populi vitio, sic ipsius quoq; fœderis defectu factum esse, quod observatum non fuerit. Sic Schlichtingius contra sanctitatem veteris fœderis. Etsi enim vires illud non suppedita- verit, quibus cum Deo populus reconciliari posset, ad eum tamen per varia instituta deduxit, qui vires istas porrigeret. Hinc fœderi adscribi non debet, quod populus ab eo desciverit, illudq; transgressus sit; etiamsi enim in fœdere defectus & impotentia quæ- dam fuerit, fuit tamen sub fœdere, si recte illud & ex divina intentione æstimatum esset, quo defectui isti atque impotentiæ succurreretur. Unde defectus iste nullo modo vitium appellandus est. Et quamvis etiam propter defectum & imperfectionem quandam fœ- dus antiquum fuerit temporarium, & certa seculo- rum periodo finiendum, Gen. XLIX. 10. Vitium ta- men, propter quod fœdus tandem sublatum est, soli populo adscribendum fuit, sicut & passim in Scriptu- ra adscribitur. Conf. Matth. XXIII. 4. usq; ad fin. cap. Rursus in punitione Israëlitarum verbum, ego sum dominatus eorum, scilicet puniendo, abji- ciendo, & ostendendo, me esse Dominum, ac posse erga eos facere, quod vellem, quod Dominorum est, reprobationem populi Israëlitiçi, infert, & probe convenit cum Græco ἠμέλησα ἀυτῶν, qua- tenus negatio quædam divinæ ἐπιμελείας eodem continetur, adeoque actus oppositus innuitur, hoc est, non tantum omissio & intermissio custo- diæ conservatricis, sed etiam impositio & immissio maledictionum & pœnarum multiplicium.

## 8:10
V. 10. 'For this is the covenant which I will make with the house of Israel, after those days, says the Lord.' Ὅτι is for the Hebrew כִּי, which here means 'but,' as Jerome correctly translates in Jeremiah. For διαθήσομαι, in the Hebrew is אֶכְרֹת, 'I will cut,' because covenants were made by a slaughtered animal. Μετὰ τὰς ἡμέρας ἐκείνας in the primary sense means 'after the exile': In a more sublime sense, 'after those evils which the Jews endured through civil wars among themselves, and the external ones of Pompey and Sosius.' In the manuscript it is διαθήκη μου. Here Israel is put for all the posterity of Israel, where it is opposed to Judah, it signifies the ten tribes, as we have said elsewhere.

The Syriac rendered the particle ὅτι as 'but also'; it is doubtful of which days they speak in 'after those days.' Oecumenius and Thomas Aquinas understand it as the time of the giving of the Mosaic law; but those days are far distant from that time. Theophylact explains it as those days of which the Prophet had spoken: 'Behold, the days are coming.' But this is not that the testament is given after those days, but in those very days. Estius also praises another opinion, as if the days were being referred to of which the Lord had spoken: 'And I neglected them,' so that the sense is, after I shall have cast away the Jews, I will give a new law to the sons of Israel, that is, to the elect from the Gentiles: But Estius opposes this: that the times of the rejection of the Israelites and the calling of the Gentiles were not different, and that the New Testament is promised to the same people to whom the old was given. Therefore, he himself renders this sense. After those days, that is, after some space of time, since not only those 'after many days' (Isa. 19, Ezek. 38, Dan. 8), but also these, which are frequent among the Prophets, 'in that time,' 'in that day,' 'in those days,' are often put without the designation of a certain time, so that it may be signified in general that some future time will come, uncertain indeed to men, but certain and defined to God, after which has passed, or while it is running, that which is predicted may happen: With which explanation the other easily agrees, which Estius nevertheless disapproves, because the time is designated in which the Prophet lived, i.e., 'hereafter,' 'henceforth,' or 'after these days,' 'after my times.' We do not deny it. But we think it must be observed that, although that promise began to be fulfilled in a peculiar way in the days future after the Prophet, partly by the release from the Babylonian captivity, partly in the time of the New Testament, or after the coming of Christ: yet that a double sense of the same words is not to be inferred, nor is it to be referred exclusively to those times which were finally to follow: since this covenant of grace pertains to all times, but yet those things which pertain to that covenant were bestowed in a more solemn manner after the coming of Christ. The times therefore that were to come are introduced for the sake of example only, or also by reason of a more solemn promulgation, reserved for the last times, because as in former times, as far as the Israelites are concerned, from the time the law was promulgated, their transgressions—how they did not keep, but made void the covenant of God, even though they had solemnly received it, 'all that the Lord has spoken we will do' (Exod. 24:3)—were most notorious, and their rejection followed therefrom; so there were to follow thereafter times in which the grace of the new covenant, as if it were then finally to be cut, would be manifested most clearly, and would be conspicuous throughout the whole world, even though that new covenant, consisting in the remission of sins, reception into the people and children of God, and the inscription of the law in hearts, had not only flourished with Abraham, and been sanctioned by the peculiar sacrament of circumcision (Gen. 17). But it had obtained from the Paradisiacal Proto-Evangelium, when God forgave the sins of the protoplasts in the blessed seed of the woman, received them as children, and having granted them the Holy Spirit, inscribed His law in their hearts. For what? Shall we deprive the protoplasts, the patriarchs, and other faithful ones before Christ of these benefits obtained through that blessed seed, that is, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ? Who were saved by the same grace of His, just as we are (Acts 15:11), of which the Apostle himself testifies (ch. 13:9), 'Jesus Christ yesterday, today, the same also forever.' Concerning which Estius says in this place: 'All the just, as many as preceded the coming of Christ in any age, were participants of the New Testament, and could not be justified otherwise than by participation in the same New Testament: However, Christians do not pertain to the New Testament, except insofar as the promise of the grace of the New Testament is fulfilled in them.' And furthermore: The New Testament, if we trace its first origin, received its beginning immediately from the fall of the first man, when the seed was promised which would crush the head of the serpent (Gen. 3). For this seed is Christ the Savior, through whom, although it was to be long after, liberation from the power of the Devil, the observance of the divine law, and eternal life were promised to men of all times: To which pertain other similar promises about the coming Christ, whether made to Abraham and David, or announced through the Prophets, or even shadowed forth through the very ceremonies of the ancient law. For that the promise made to Abraham pertains to the New Testament, Zacharias, the father of John the Baptist, teaches us in his Canticle in Luke 1, where he says that God remembers His holy covenant, and explaining that, he adds: The oath which He swore to our father Abraham, that He would grant unto us, that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve Him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before Him, all the days of our life. These are indeed the promises of the New Testament. It is clear, therefore, that the New Testament, if the thing itself is considered, that is, the covenant and promise proper to the New Testament, is prior in time to the Old Testament, which was given through Moses. Yet it is rightly and deservedly called new by the Prophet, not only because it makes a man spiritually new from an old one, which is proper to grace, but also by reason of time: for it was both ratified at a later time, namely in the death of Christ the Redeemer, and then revealed to the world through the preaching of the Apostles. Finally, during that same time and thereafter, the promised thing was bestowed more broadly and copiously. Which is therefore called the time of the New Testament.

But that these things are comprehended under the name of covenant and pact, the Socinians, Arminians, Papists, and Calixtines wrongly conclude that the covenant of grace has the condition of good works annexed to it, inasmuch as the nature of a covenant or pact is such that it is entered into upon certain conditions from both sides. For against the Papists, one can oppose what Estius has here: that the little word ברית, for which Latin interpreters render now 'covenant' and now 'pact', is of broad signification, so that it comprehends not only those things which are properly called covenants or pacts; but also gratuitous promises free from every condition, and indeed even stable ordinances of God concerning inanimate things, from which nothing can be understood to be performed in return. For the promise of the land

Canaan was clearly gratuitous, as Moses himself testifies in Deut. IX. Which, however, is called a covenant throughout Scripture: and indeed most openly in that place where the first express and distinct promise of that land was made, Gen. XV. Then, says Moses, the Lord made a covenant with Abraham saying: To your seed I will give this land from the river of Egypt, &c. So also the Lord, Gen. IX., as a type of the New Testament, established a covenant with the human race, that He would by no means destroy them again by the waters of the flood, and He places the rainbow in the clouds as a sign of that covenant or treaty. Nor is any condition read there. Again, Jer. XXXIII. He says thus: If my covenant with the day can be made void, and my covenant with the night, so that there be not day and night in their time: Then my covenant with David my servant can be made void, so that there be not a son from him who shall reign on his throne. Where certainly in the former place a condition to be performed by the other party cannot even be imagined. Such, therefore, is this covenant which is called the New Testament, namely, a promise of God that is entirely absolute and gratuitous, by which He deigned to promise a Savior to man who had fallen into sin and destruction, and through Him the remission of sins. All these things Estius. It is to be noted, however, with the blessed Gerhard, that there are twofold promises of the New Testament: Some are entirely absolute, such as the promise concerning the sending of the Messiah and the work of redemption to be performed through Him; but some are conditional, having attached a condition not of our works or merits, but of faith, such as the promise concerning the remission of sins, the gift of the Holy Spirit, and righteousness and eternal life to be conferred upon those who believe in Christ: which condition, however, added to the promise, is so constituted that it depends not on the powers of man, but on the grace and operation of God. For He promised that He is willing not only to offer the benefits of the Messiah to men in the Word of the Gospel, but also through that very Word of the Gospel to work faith in their hearts, through which they may embrace the benefits offered in the Gospel and apply them to themselves. Unless the New Testament had been known to the Fathers also (the words are of the blessed Chemnitz, part III. LL. CC. p. 90), whence I ask would Abraham and the rest of the faithful have had the Spirit and life? Since the ministration of the New Testament is Spirit and life. Therefore, although both kinds existed from the beginning of the world; yet there was a difference by reason of the promulgation and the time.

Διδὺς νόμους με εἰς τὴν διάνοιαν αὐτῶν, καὶ ἐπὶ καρδίας αὐτῶν ἐπιγράψω αὐτές.) A comma should be placed after the second αὐτῶν. In the Greek LXX it is διδὺς δώσω & γράψω αὐτές. In the Hebrew it is I will give. The sense is: I will cause that all may hold my law in memory: namely, in the first sense, through the multitude of synagogues which were built at that time, where the law was taught three times in the week: in the more sublime sense: I will give the Holy Spirit to Christians, who may teach and exhort them, John XIV. 17. 26. XV. 26. XVI. 13. 1 John II. 27. Both senses are in Ezech. XXXVI. 16.

This is the first promise of the New covenant, not according to the order of nature but of doctrine, as they say: since those things which the Prophet placed in the first place are those which are later, which therefore proceed in the order of nature as causes. For thus those things follow one another: 1. The knowledge of the Lord or faith, which is the cause of the other benefits. 2. The remission of sins or justification. 3. The inscription of the law upon the hearts. 4. The preservation of paternal benevolence and the peculiar appropriation of the faithful. But the inscription of the law is placed first, because mention had been made of the legal covenant, not kept by the Israelites; and also that gracious appropriation, and the promise of paternal benevolence; and I will be to them for a God, and they shall be to me for a people, because the commemoration of their rejection had preceded, κἀγὼ ἠμέλησα αὐτῶν. Then the cause of both that benefit is subjoined, namely faith, or the saving knowledge of God, and the remission of sins obtained through the same. For those who are gifted with faith, and obtain the remission of sins through faith in Christ, to them the Holy Spirit is conferred, who will write the law of God upon their hearts, and furthermore God embraces them with paternal benevolence, and wills to be to them for a God forever, and to claim them for His own perpetual treasure, so that they may be His people not only in this age, but forever, Apoc. XXI. 3. & 7. These follow one another: Regeneration, justification, renovation or sanctification, and preservation unto the heavenly inheritance. Because Christ has been made for us by God wisdom, for the knowledge of God in regeneration, righteousness in justification, sanctification in renovation, and redemption in the full ἀπολυτρώσει of the sons of God, and the collation of the heavenly inheritance, 1 Cor. I. 30. It is said therefore to give His laws εἰς τὴν διάνοιαν, into the mind: In the Hebrew בקרבם, in their interior or middle, in their bowels, καὶ ἐπὶ καρδίας and to write upon the hearts; He gives into the mind, as regards the intellect: He writes upon the hearts, as regards the affection: so that they may both understand the laws of the Lord, and render obedience to them with a ready mind, conf. 2 Cor. III. 3. But there is no need for a new point. For the customary punctuation is correct: And upon their hearts ἐπιγράψω αὐτὰς, namely laws, I will inscribe them, namely my laws. By a Hebrew phrase the law is said to be written upon the heart, when it is inscribed upon the heart, which is to be understood not only of the daily memory of the law, as the Jews wish, but also of the collation of new and spiritual powers, through which not only exterior, but also interior and spiritual obedience to the law is begun by the regenerate. This phrase alludes to the promulgation of the moral law. For the sense is: I will not again write my law on tables of stone, as I did formerly, but I will write it in the hearts of men, on the fleshy tables of the heart, 2 Cor. III. 3. by giving them the Holy Spirit, through whom true obedience to the law may be begun in them; as here the blessed Gerhard.

The law was written on external tablets, nor could it penetrate to the heart, therefore its covenant was void. The Gospel, however, penetrates hearts, whence it is said to be written on hearts. Therefore, there is nothing here for the immediate inspirations of fanatics: since it is rather a matter of the inscription of the divine law, which is done through the word; not that which is done through immediate revelations. Nor does the phrase 'to be written in the hearts' imply an internal afflatus, but any impression whatsoever, whether made through nature, Rom. II. 14, or through doctrine, 2 Cor. III. 2, Prov. III. 3, chap. VII. 3. Moreover, Grotius's sense, both the primary and the more sublime, is to be rejected for the reason that it is not permitted to attribute a double sense to the same words, and because that primary sense—that the people held the law of God in their memory—is too jejune, since God promised not only to put it into their minds but also to write it on their hearts; nor did the law stick in the memory of the faithful of those times only, but it was also observed holily in practice itself; nor can the operation of the Holy Spirit, both of information and of renewal, be denied to them, Neh. IX. 20, Ps. CXLIII. 10, Ps. LI. 13, 14. The more sublime sense also, by which Grotius wishes only the doctrine and exhortation of the Holy Spirit to be implied, is by no means sufficient for the present benefit of the new covenant, inasmuch as it is certain that the grace of internal renewal and sanctification is claimed for it, not merely external information, 2 Cor. IV. 3, 1 Cor. VI. 11, 1 Pet. I. 2, Tit. III. 5, etc. The sense is, as interpreted by the blessed Hunnius: 'I will put my laws into their mind and write them on their hearts': so that they may not, according to the oldness of the letter, obey me unwillingly with a certain servile compliance, but according to the newness of the mind, may approve their obedience to me spontaneously by the Spirit (insofar as they are reborn). For those justified by faith will be gifted with the Holy Spirit, who will excite their minds to spontaneous and prompt obedience. The blessed Dorscheus does not refer the inscription of the law to renewal, but to the communication of saving doctrine. Νόμος, he says, denotes the entire saving doctrine. Thus it is used throughout the Old and New Testaments. See what has been said in Pentad. dissert. 1. on the passage of Isa. VIII. 20. and compare Ps. I. 2. XIX. 8. and following. It is called the law of faith, Rom. III. 27. It is not, therefore, that law which is inscribed on stone tablets. For that, too, is partly inscribed by nature on the hearts of men, and partly is inscribed more and more through teaching and instruction. Nor are there certain more perfect commands and additions to the moral law, such as the New Testament recognizes none. Nor are they of perfection, which are both nothing, and would not pertain to the whole multitude of the confederated, even if they were at all. But they are the Evangelical promises themselves, which are the proper good of the new covenant. But the exposition already handed down seems more elegant, on account of the opposition of the Old and New Testaments, by which the inscription of the law.

Concerning this inscription, however, Estius wrongly notes that, to commend the grace of the New Testament, Christ did not wish to leave us anything written on membranes or papers, lest he seem to have need of these aids for impressing his law upon our minds. For the inscription on the hearts is not done immediately, but through the Word of God, contained in Holy Scripture, which Christ willed to be the medium of our renewal and sanctification, just as it is the canon of faith: who, even if he himself left nothing written by his own hands, nevertheless commanded whatever he wished us to know of his sayings or deeds to be written by the Apostles, as if by his own hands, as Augustine says in his book on the Consensus of the Evangelists and the cult.

And I will be to them a God, and they shall be to me a people) They will worship me, I will protect them; A locution equal to that which we had above I. 5.

Here is a parallelism of passages which are anything but parallel. For chapter I. 5 deals with the eternal Son of God and the Fatherhood of God κατ᾿ ἔσω (internally); here there is not even talk of adoption properly, nor is the Fatherhood of God κατ᾽ ἔξω (externally) expressed according to the letter: But God promises that he will be to believers εἰς Θεὸν (as a God), by cherishing them with his grace, protecting them, and preserving them for eternal salvation, just as it is promised to every believer concerning the other life in Rev. XXI. 7. And I will be to him a God, and v. 3. and God himself shall be with them, their God. He promises that believers will be to him as a people: which likewise extends itself to the tabernacle of the other life, Rev. XXI. 3. and they shall be his peoples. But we are the people of the Lord when he appropriates us to himself as his own treasure, and ensures that we remain as the chosen people of God, his Royal priesthood; this is what is not situated in our own powers, but we obtain it by the virtue and grace of the Holy Spirit, nor is it done by worship, but by faith, because we are kept by the power of God through faith 1 Pet. I. 5. It is his to perfect us, to establish, to strengthen, to ground us, 1 Pet. V. 10. We have here Estius not denying: To me, he says, it is more likely that by both members the affection of God toward men is signified, to whom the promise is made, so that the sense here is briefly: I will show myself to be God to them, and I will have them for my people. That is, with both terms joined, and because I will be their God, and because they will be my people, I will do good to them. Compare Gen. XVII. 7. Lev. XXVI. 12. 2 Cor. VI. 16. Matt. XXII. 31. Blessed Dorscheus interprets this benefit as concerning the spiritual union with God, and discourses about it thus: He establishes that God, who is to be united to us, or the Lord, Jer. XXXI. 31, 32, is not God absolutely, but primarily also as mediator v. 6. For thus, he says, the foundation of the gracious union is established. Whence the Apostle, with that respect to the appointed Mediator of the New Testament, which is sanctioned by better promises, alleges the Prophetic text. For he must prove that a more sublime dispensation in divine goods belongs to the Messiah, that he is the Mediator of a better Testament, and has proposed better promises. He says that God at Jeremiah prophesied concerning this constitution of a better Testament, that it would contain those things which were said in v. 6. Therefore these Prophetic words speak entirely of the Messiah as of the appointed Mediator of a more sublime liturgy and a better Testament. Therefore, through that Lord who speaks in Jeremiah, the Messiah, the Mediator of the New Testament, is also to be understood. Hence that 'finding fault' in v. 8 cannot have a more convenient subject than the 'mediator' in v. 6. For the Apostle, about to render a reason why Christ is the Mediator of the New Testament, brings this forward, because if he were not the Mediator of a better and New Testament, or if that Testament which he himself is about to bring were not more perfect and fuller, he would have prophesied in vain concerning its introduction at the Prophet. If you ask, how did the Mediator prophesy concerning his own New Testament? The Apostle answers, he prophesied by 'finding fault'. Therefore 'finding fault' and the Mediator in this place are one and the same. Therefore the Son of God comes into this gracious union under a double respect, first absolutely, insofar as he is one supreme God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, John X. 30 and 1 John V. 7. In which way he also accomplishes all things with one and undivided name with the Father and the Holy Spirit, Matt. XXVIII. 19, and thus also consummates this holy union, as God blessed over all forever, Rom. IX. 5. Secondly relatively, by reason of the office undertaken, in which he acts not only divinely, but theandrically 1 Tim. II. 5, and indeed acts to effect this union according to his Prophetic, Priestly, and Kingly office. From which those results of the inscription of the law and of the union necessarily flow. For neither is pacification and gracious union accomplished without the Messiah, Col. I. 20. Hence the persons of the Holy Trinity come to this union, not only as those to be united, but also as those uniting, or the principal Efficient cause of this holy and saving union. Which the word συντελέσω indicates, by which not only the end and consummation of the new covenant, but also the perfection deduced from the very beginning itself and owed to God is indicated, and it is manifest in itself, since the union on the part of God depends solely upon the divine will; but on the part of man there is no power for that, it being impossible for that union to be perfected unless God unites, which is among the things of the Spirit of God, which man does not grasp of himself, much less effect, 1 Cor.
