II. 14. Therefore God is here the one who works, Phil. II. 13, and in a peculiar way Christ is the author and finisher of it, Heb. XII. 2. Concerning the union itself, the blessed one has it thus: The union itself is to be noted, of which there is a twofold result: By the former it is effected that God is God to those united to Him, which is not perfected by universal presence. For thus God is God to all creatures, and for this relationship there is no need of any new covenant; nor even of a certain deification, such as the fanatics have imagined, which Scripture also ignores; but by a gracious approach, the foundation of which is the incarnation, or the assumption of our nature into the divine person, concerning which see above chapter II. 14 et seq. For by that very fact He was most especially made God to us when He was made Immanuel, Is. VII. 14, when the Son of God was made the Son of man, John I. 14, when all the fullness of the Godhead began to dwell in human nature bodily, Col. II. verse 9. From this foundation II. a gracious approach is made (a) through justification, by which God, being angry with us on account of sin, but reconciled through Christ, is united by the remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ apprehended through faith, so that Christ may be to us a propitiation, Rom. III. 25, and a ransom, 1. Tim. VI. insofar as He was made sin 2 Cor. V. 21, He bore our sins in His body upon the tree 1 Pet. II. 24, and thus God is to us as a God justifying the ungodly

Romans IV. 5. when we approach with confidence to the throne of grace, etc. Hebrews VI. 13. in which justification Christ again undergoes the twofold respect which we have mentioned. For since neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit is the propitiation, he is that in justification which the Father and the Holy Spirit are, and furthermore is the propitiation, for which reason he is also called the mediator in this very chapter v. 6, without whom our God did not wish to be God. Thus, by being united to God, he becomes (β) for us into God by regeneration, insofar as he makes us, who were dead in sins, alive together with Christ, raises us up, and seats us in the heavenly places in Christ, * regenerating us, namely, by a seed not corruptible, but incorruptible, namely, by the Word of the living and eternally abiding God, 1 Peter II. 23, and to us who receive him he gives the power to become children of God, John I. 12, as being born of God, v. 13. Thus God becomes for us into God the Father, giving us the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry Abba Father. Following this is III. gracious indwelling, by which God becomes for us into God indwelling. Concerning which indwelling it has been treated at length above in chapter III. 6. Following this is IV. gracious renewal, by which God becomes for us into God renewing, Eph. IV. 23, and making new, Col. III. 10, concerning which it has been treated above in chapter V. 12 and VI. 7 ff. For God, after he has become our Father and Guest, is not idle in us, but strives for this, that the works of the Devil being more and more destroyed, the inner man may be renewed day by day, 2 Cor. IV. 16, so that we may be transformed from glory to glory, 2 Cor. III. 18. But in all these things God becomes for us into God 1. sanctifying, by reason of holiness both imputed, by which Christ becomes for us sanctification, 1 Cor. I. 30, and VI. 11, and also begun, in regeneration indeed by reason of the powers or sanctifying gifts through illumination or translation from the kingdom of darkness into the kingdom of light, where we receive a portion of the lot of the saints in light, Acts XXVI. 18 and Col. I. 12, and that through Christ who has abolished death and brought life and immortality to light, 2 Tim. I. 12. In renewal, however, by reason of daily promotion to greater holiness, insofar as we more and more put on the new man, created according to God in righteousness and true holiness, Eph. IV. 24. 2. God becomes for us into God washing away, and that both by the washing of baptism, Tit. III. 5, Matt. XXVIII. 20, where again purification through the washing of water in the Word pertains peculiarly, insofar as we are purified through his own blood, 1 John I. 7, the sprinkling of which comes to us, 1. Peter I. 2, and also in daily renewal through repentance, by which we are washed and purified, Is. I. 16. 3. God becomes for us into God satisfying or feeding, and that again both in justification and regeneration, by which he himself is for us that bread descending from heaven, concerning which John VI. 33 and following at length: and in renewal, or daily spiritual communion, by which we taste more and more the sweetness of the Lord, and are strengthened in him: and in sacramental participation, by which the communion of the body and blood of Christ comes to us, 1 Cor. X. 16, XI. 24, 25, XII. 13. 4. God becomes for us into God joining together, and summing up, insofar as he inserts us into the mystical body through faith, and unites us to Christ the head, Eph. I. 10 and 22, and that both in justification and in regeneration. And thus, being inserted and united, and joined and compacted to the mystical body, he promotes us to spiritual growth, Eph. IV. 16. Where again Christ, just as in nutrition he is food and the one feeding in a peculiar way, so also here he is both the author and the end of that joining together and summing up. For we are rendered members not of the Father or the Holy Spirit, if we speak immediately and formally: for finally they also pertain here, Rom. VI. 19, 1 Cor. XII. 14 and following, but of Christ, just as he, not the Father or the Holy Spirit, is our head, Eph. IV. 15. 5. God becomes for us into God betrothing, insofar as he causes us to be betrothed, as a chaste virgin, to one husband, 2 Cor. XI. 2. 2 Cor. II. 20, insofar as he himself is the bridegroom, John III. 29, who loved the Church with this affection, and betrothed her to himself, Eph. V. 25, where although the betrothal, which happened in justification, is the work of the most holy Trinity, the marriage however is between Christ and the Church, and her members. Whom the heavenly bridegroom also watches over in such a way that the cherishing and nourishment of the Church is ascribed peculiarly to him, Eph. V. 29. The Holy Spirit, however, provides the earnest in our hearts, 2 Cor. I. 22. In general 6. God is for us into God subjecting, not only by that general subjection, concerning which it was treated above in chapter II. 8, but by that special one, in respect to which man is naturally insubordinate, nor is he subject to the law of God, Rom. VIII. 7, and thus through faith by reason of lordship is subjected to God. Nor does he allow sin to reign in his mortal body, Rom. VI. 12, which subjection, since it is joined with rebellion, is not perfect, but is a struggle arising in our members, Rom. VII. 23, Gal. V. 17. And therefore Christ through the Holy Spirit more and more makes alive our mortal bodies, Rom. VIII. 11, so that through daily subjection we may perfect that 'we more than conquer' in the midst of adversities, concerning which Rom. VIII. 37, and that through faith, which is the victory, overcoming the world, 1 John V. 4. And in this course, being ordered and fitted for the kingdom of God, God then becomes for us into God 7. glorifying, when the union will take place in glory according to the order of Rom. VIII. 30. And this, if we may so say, Deification, by which God is for us God from this federal sanction, and which is the result of this union, is followed by the other, by which we are made the people of God, a peculiar people, Tit. II. 14. Which it is right to call a divine λαοποίησις [making of a people], by which again there is not that general subjection, by which all peoples are held to serve Him, but a special one, and that placed (α) upon the foundation of the flesh assumed from us into the divine person, in respect of which we can say, it is flesh of our flesh (β) in the gracious reception of the divine union Joh. I. 12. and of the other acts, of which it was spoken in the first apotelesma, until the glorious reception follows in the meeting of the Lord, 1. Thess. IV. 17. where, whereas in this life we might see what θεοποίησις [making of a god] is, by which God has been made God to us, and λαοποίησις, by which we have been made the people of God, only δι᾽ ἐσόπτρε ἐν αἰνίγματι [through a glass in a riddle], at length we may know that face to face. Whence that ἔσομαι καὶ ἔσονται [I shall be and they shall be] does not deny the past, as if hitherto He had not been the God of the saints and the faithful. For that is repugnant to those things which He has expressly stated below in chapter XI throughout and XII, especially v. 22, 23. But 1. it indicates a beginning, that this by no means happened to the saints and faithful under the Old Testament, by the force of that [covenant] it came to pass, but redounded to them from the benefits of the New Testament through the Messiah, who was yesterday, and is today, and will be forever, Heb. XIII. 9. 2. A continuation, that is to say, that He will continue to dispense and diffuse those very benefits and effects, a taste of which He has hitherto provided to the saints and faithful. (γ) A solemn confirmation to be made in the N. T. confirmed by the shedding of divine blood. (δ) An increase, and that both by reason of the clarity, which will follow the renewal of the shadows, under which He has hitherto shown Himself as God to His people, and made a people for Himself: and by reason of the goods hitherto μελλόντων [about to be], Heb. X. 1. now to be really exhibited, among which excels, as has been said, the ἐνσάρκωσις [incarnation], and by reason of the means, which are to be very few and most simple. (ε) A complement, which the Old Testament, as has been said above, could not bring, this New one will perform. Most imperfectly therefore and most generally does Schlichtingius explain this benefit on page 347, from whom Ribera does not depart much on page 359, when they render this sense of these words: I shall be their highest protector, and will heap them with benefits, and they will act with me, as befits my people. Both of us will perform our parts, I by doing good, they by acting rightly and worshipping me. This certainly touches only very lightly upon the inexplicable depth of the divine benefit.

Latin:

V. 10. Ὅτι ἄυτη ἡ διαθήκη, ἣν διαθήσομαι τῷ οἴκῳ ἰσραὴλ, μετὰ τὰς ἐκείνας ἡμέρας λέγει Κύριος.) Ὅτι est pro Ebræo כִּי, quod hic valet, sed, quomodo Hieronymus recte vertit in Jeremia. Pro διαθήσομαι in Ebræo est אֶכְרֹת scindam, quia fœdera scissa pecude fiebant. Μετὰ τὰς ἡμέρας ἐκείνας in sensu primo valet post exilium: In sensu sublimiore post mala illa, quæ Judæi pertulere per arma civilia inter se, & externa Pompeji & Sossii. In manuscripto est διαθήκη μου. Hic Ἰσραὴλ ponitur pro omni posteritate Israelis, ubi op- ponitur Judæ, significat decem tribus, ut alibi diximus.

Particulam ὅτι per sed etiam Syrus reddidit; De quibusnam diebus loquantur μετὰ τὰς ἡμέρας ἐκείνας dubium est. Oecumenius & Thomas de A- quino de tempore datæ legis Mosaicæ intelligunt; sed isti dies longe distant ab isto tempore. Theo- phylactus explicat de illis diebus, de quibus dixerat Propheta: Ecce dies veniunt. Verum hoc non est testamentum dari post illos dies, sed illis ipsis die- bus. Laudat & aliam sententiam Estius, quasi re- spiciantur dies, de quibus dixerat Dominus: Et ego neglexi eos, ut sensus sit, postquam Judæos abje- cero, dabo novam legem filiis Israël, id est electis ex gentibus: Cui verò hæc opponit Estius: quod non fuerint diversa tempora rejectionis Israëlita- rum & vocationis gentium, quodque Testamen- tum novum promittatur eidem populo, cui da- tum erat vetus. Hunc ergo ipse reddit sensum. Post dies illos, id est, post aliquantum temporis spa- tium, quum non tantum illa post multos dies, Es. XIXV. Ezech. XXXIIX. Dan. IIX: Sed & hæc apud Prophetas frequentata in illo tempore, in illa die, in illis diebus sæpe ponantur, absque designa- tione certi temporis, ut significetur in gene- re futurum aliquod tempus, hominibus qui- dem incertum, sed DEO certum ac defini- tum, quo transacto, vel quo currente fiat, quod prædicitur: Cum qua explicatione facile consen- tit altera, quam tamen Estius improbat, quod tem- pus designetur, quo vixit Propheta, q. d. posthac, deinceps, vel post hosce dies, post tempora mea. Non abnuimus. Sed id observandum censemus, quod etsi promissum illud peculiari ratione futu- ris post Prophetam diebus compleri cœperit par- tim soluta captivitate Babylonica, partim tempo- re Novi Testamenti, vel post Christi adventum: non tamen vel geminum sensum eorundem ver- borum inferendum esse, vel exclusivè ad ea tem- pora, quæ demum post sequutura erant, referen- dum:Siquidem ad omnia tempora hoc fœdus gra- tiæ pertineat, sed solenniori tamen ratione post adventum Christi ea, quæ ad illud fœdus perti- nent, donata sint. Tempora ergo post futura ex- empli causa tantum inducuntur, vel etiam ratione solemnioris promulgationis, novissimis temporibus reservatæ, quia ut prioribus temporibus, quod ad Israëlitas attinet, inde à promulgata lege eorun- dem transgressiones, quomodo non servarint, sed irritum fecerint Dei fœdus, etsi receperint solen- niter, omnia, quæ loquutus est Dominus, faciemus, Exod. XXIV. 3. maxime notoriæ fuere, & sequuta inde eorum abjectio; ita sequutura erant dein- ceps tempora, quibus novi fœderis gratia, quasi tum demum id scindendum sit, manifestabitur lu- culentissime, ac per totum orbem conspicua futura est, utut novum illud fœdus, in remissione pecca- torum, receptione in populum & filios Dei, & in- scriptione legis in corda consistens, non cum Ab- rahamo tantum viguerit, sancitumq; sit peculiari sacramento τῆς περιτομῆς, Gen. XVII. Sed inde à Prot-Evangelio Paradisiaco obtinuerit, quando protoplastis in semine mulieris benedicto Deus peccata condonavit, eos in liberos recepit, iisque concesso Spiritu Sancto legem suam in corda in- scripsit. Quid enim? num hisce beneficiis per semen illud benedictum partis, hoc est, gratia Do- mini nostri Jesu Christi privabimus Protoplastos, Patriarchas & fideles alios ante Christum: qui ea- dem ipsius gratia salvati sunt, quemadmodum & nos, Act. XV. 11. de quo testatur Apostolus ipse, cap. XIII. 9. Jesus Christus heri, hodie, idem & in secula. Quo de Estius hunc in locum: Omnes, ait, justos, quotquot adventum Christi quacunq; ætate præcesserunt, participes fuisse novi Testamenti, nec aliter justificari potuisse, quam ejusdem novi Testa- menti participatione: Cæterum Christianos ad novum Testamentum non pertinere, nisi quatenus in eis promissio gratiæ novi Testamenti impletur. Et por- ro: Testamentum novum, si primam ejus originem re- petamus, initium accepisse statim à lapsu primi homi- nis, quando promissum est semen, quod contriturum esset caput serpentis, Gen. III. Hoc enim semen est Chri- stus Salvator, per quem, etsi longe post futurum, pro- missa fuit omnium temporum hominibus è potestate Diaboli liberatio, divina legis observatio, & vita æter- na: Quo pertinent aliæ similes de Christo venturo promissiones, sive ad Abraham & Davidem factæ, sive per Prophetas annunciatæ, sive etiam per ipsas anti- quæ legis ceremonias adumbratæ. Quod enim pro- missio facta Abrahæ pertineat ad Test. novum, do- cet nos Zacharias Johannis Baptistæ Pater in Canti- co Luc. I, ubi dicit Deum memorari Testamenti sui sancti, idque explicans subjungit: Jusjurandum, quod juravit ad Abraham Patrem nostrum, datu- rum se nobis, ut sine timore de manu inimicorum no- strorum liberati serviamus illi in sanctitate & ju- stitia coram ipso omnibus diebus nostris. Quæ pro- fecto novi Testamenti promissiones sunt. Liquet er- go novum Testamentum, si res ipsa spectetur, id est, pactum & promissio, novo Testamento propria, tem- pore prius esse veteri Testamento, quod datum est per Mosen. Rectè tamen ac merito novum dicitur à Propheta, non solum quia hominem spiritualiter ex veteri facit novum, id quod gratiæ proprium est, ve- rum etiam ratione temporis: Nam & sancitum est posteriori tempore, scilicet in morte Christi Redem- ptoris, & deinde mundo patefactum per Apostolorum prædicationem. Deniq; per idem tempus, ac dein- ceps res promissa largius & copiosius præstita. Quod proinde Novi Testamenti tempus appellatur.

Cæterum quod fœderis & pacti nomine ista comprehenduntur, perperam Sociniani, Arminia- ni, Papistæ, Calixtini colligunt, pactum gratiæ an- nexam habere conditionem bonorum operum, siqui- dem fœderis vel pacti ea sit natura, ut certis ex utraq; parte conditionibus ineatur, Nam Papistis opponi potest, quod Estius hic habet: Voculam ברית pro quo nunc fœdus, nunc pactum Latini red- dunt interpretes, esse latæ significationis, ut non solum ea comprehendat, quæ propriè fœdera seu pacta di- cuntur; verum etiam promissiones gratuitas & ab omni liberas conditione, imo & ordinationes Dei stabiles circa res inanimatas, à quibus nihil vicissim præstandum intelligi potest. Etenim promissio terræ

Canaan plane gratuita fuit, ipso Mose teste Deut. IX. Quæ tamen passim in Scriptura pactum vocatur : & quidem apertissime eo loco, ubi primum expres- sa ac distincta illius terræ facta est promissio, Gen. XV. Tunc, inquit Moses, pepigit Dominus fœdus cum Abraham dicens : Semini tuo dabo terram hanc à flumine Ægypti, &c. Ita quoque Dominus Gen. IX. in typum Novi Test. statuit pactum cum genere humano, se nequaquam ultra deleturum eos aquis diluvii, ejusque pacti seu fœderis signum ponit in nubibus arcum cælestem. Nec ulla ibi conditio le- gitur. Rursum Jer. XXXIII. sic ait : Si irritum potest fieri pactum meum cum die, & pactum meum cum nocte, ut non sit dies & nox in tempore suo: Et pa- ctum meum irritum esse poterit cum David servo meo, ut non sit ex eo filius, qui regnet in throno ejus. Ubi sane priori loco ne fingi quidem potest conditio ex altera parte præstanda. Tale igitur pactum est hoc, quod vocatur Novum Test. videlicet promissio Dei prorsus absoluta & gratuita, qua dignatus est homini in peccatum & interitum prolapso, promit- tere Salvatorem, ac per eum peccatorum remissio- nem. Quæ omnia Estius. Notandum tamen cum B. Gerhardo, duplices esse Novi Testam. promissiones: Quædam sunt prorsus absolutæ, qualis est promissio de mittendo Messia ac opere redemptionis per ipsum præstando; Quædam vero conditionales, habentes adjectam conditionem non operum vel meritorum nostrorum, sed fidei, qualis est promissio de peccato- rum remissione, Spir. S. donatione, justitia & vita æterna credentibus in Christum conferenda: quæ ta- men conditio promissioni adjecta ita comparata est, ut non ab hominis viribus, sed Dei gratia & opera- tione pendeat. Is enim promisit, quod non solum in Verbo Evangelii beneficia Messiæ hominibus offerre velit, sed etiam per illud ipsum Evangelii Verbum fidem in ipsorum cordibus operari, per quam oblata in Evangelio beneficia amplectantur, sibique appli- cent. Nisi Novum Test. Patribus quoque notum fuisset (verba sunt B. Chemnitii part. III. LL. CC. p. 90. unde quæso Abraham & reliqui fideles Spiritum & vitam habuissent? Cum N. T. ministratio sit Spiri- tus & vita. Ergo licet utrumque genus fuerit ab ini- tio mundi; tamen ratione promulgationis & tem- poris fuit discrimen.

Διδὺς νόμους με εἰς τὴν διάνοιαν αὐτῶν, καὶ ἐπὶ καρδίας αὐτῶν ἐπιγράψω αὐτές.) Ponendum comma post alterum αὐτῶν, In Græco LXX. est διδὺς δώσω & γράψω αὐτές. In Ebræo est dabo. Sensus est : Efficiam, ut omnes legem meam memoriter teneant : nempe in sensu primo, per multitudinem synagogarum, quæ structæ sunt illo tempo- re, ubi lex ter in hebdomade docebatur : in sublimiore sensu : Spiritum Sanctum dabo Christianis, qui eos do- ceat atque hortetur, Joh. XIV. 17. 26. XV. 26. XVI. 13. 1. Joh. II. 27. Uterque sensus est in Ezech. XXXVI. 16.

Hoc primum est Novi pacti promissum, non se- cundum ordinem naturæ sed doctrinæ, ut loquun- tur: quum eorum, quæ priori loco Propheta po- suit, ut sint posteriora, quæ causæ proinde ordine naturæ procedunt. Ita enim sese illa consequuntur 1. Domini cognitio vel fides, quæ causa est cætero- rum beneficiorum. 2. Peccatorum remissio vel justi- ficatio. 3. Legis in corda inscriptio. 4. Paterna bene- volentia conservatio & peculiaris fidelium appro- priatio. Præmittitur autem inscriptio legis, quia le- galis pacti, ab Israelitis non servati, mentio facta e- rat; nec non appropriatio illa gratiosa, & paternæ benevolentiæ promissio; & ero ipsis in Deum, & ipsi erunt mihi in populum, quia præcesserat comme- moratio abjectionis eorum, κἀγὼ ἠμέλησα αὐτῶν. Subjungitur deinde causa utriusque beneficii istius, nimirum fides, vel salvifica Dei cognitio, & per eandem obtenta peccatorum remissio. Qui enim fi- de donantur, & peccatorum remissionem conse- quuntur per fidem in Christum, illis Spiritus S. confertur, qui legem Dei in corda eorum inferi- bit, eosq; porro Deus paterna benevolentia am- plectitur, & in æternum ipsis esse vult in Deum, eosq; sibi in peculium suum perpetuum asserere, ut sint non in hoc tantum seculo, sed in æternum in populum suum, Apoc. XXI. 3. & 7. Sequuntur hæc invicem: Regeneratio, justificatio, renovatio, vel sanctificatio, & ad hæreditatem cælestem conservatio. Quia Chri- stus nobis factus est à Deo sapientia, ob Dei cognitio- nem in regeneratione, justitia in justificatione, sanctificatio in renovatione, & redemptio in plena filiorum Dei ἀπολυτρώσει, hæreditatisq; cælestis collatione, 1. Cor. I. 30. Dicitur ergo dare leges suas εἰς τὴν διάνοιαν, in mentem: In Ebræo בקרבם, in interiori vel medio eorum, in visceribus eorum, καὶ ἐπὶ καρδίας & in corda scribere; in mentem dat, quo- ad intellectum: in corda scribit, quoad affectum: ut & intelligant leges Domini, & prompto animo illis obedientiam præstent, conf. 2. Cor. III. 3. Non autem opus est novo puncto. Nam recte se habet consueta interpunctio: Et in corda ipsorum ἐπι- γράψω αὐτὰς, scilicet νόμους, inscribam illas, videli- cet leges meas. Super cor phrasi Ebræa lex dicitur scribi, quando cordi inscribitur, quod non solum de quotidiana legis memoria, ut Judæi volunt, accipi- endum, sed etiam de collatione novarum & spiritua- lium virium, per quas non solum exterior, sed etiam interior, & spiritualis legis obedientia à renatis in- choetur. Alluditur hac phrasi ad promulgationem le- gis moralis. Sensus enim est: Non iterum scribam legem meam in tabulis lapideis, ut olim feci, sed scribam eam in cordibus hominum, in tabulis cordis carneis, 2. Cor. III. 3. dando ipsis S. S. per quem vera legis obe- dientia in ipsis inchoëtur; ut hic B. Gerhardus.

Lex scripta fuit in tabulis externis, nec ad cor penetrare potuit, ideo pactum ejus fuit irritum. Evangelium verò corda penetrat, unde cordibus inscriptum dicitur. Non ergo hic quicquam pro fanaticorum immediatis inspirationibus: siquidem potius de inscriptione legis divinæ, quæ per verbum fit, agatur; non quæ per immediatas revelationes. Neq; phrasis scribi in corda infert internum affla- tum, sed impressionem quãcunq; sive per naturam, Rom. II. 14. sive per doctrinam factam, 2. Cor. III. 2. Prov. III. 3. cap. VII. 3. Sensus autem Grotii tum pri- mus, tum sublimior ideo rejiciendus, quod dupli- cem sensum iisdem verbis tribuere non liceat, quodq; sensus ille primus, quod legem Dei memo- ria tenuerit populus, nimis jejunus sit, quum non in mentem tantum dare, sed etiam in corda scribere promiserit Deus, neq; fidelibus istorum temporum tantum in memoria lex hæserit, sed etiam sancte in ipsa praxi observata sit, neq; Spiritus S. operatio cum informationis, tum renovationis denegari iisdem possit, Neh. IX. 20. Ps. CXLIII. 10. Ps. LI. 13. 14. Sensus etiam sublimior, quo tantum doctrinam atq; exhortationem Sp. S. inferri vult Grotius, minime sufficiat fœderis novi præsenti beneficio, utpote quo internæ renovationis & sanctificationis gra- tiam eidem vindicari certum est, non tantum ex- ternam informationem designari, 2. Cor. IV, 3. 1. Cor. VI. 11. 1. Pet. I. 2. Tit. III. 5. &c. Sensus est, inter- prete B. Hunnio: Leges meas dabo in mentem illorum & cordibus illorum inscribam: ut non juxta vetusta- tem literæ inviti mihi obtemperent servili quodam obsequio, sed juxta novitatem mentis spontaneo Spiri- tus (quatenus renati sunt) mihi obsequia sua appro- bent. Justificati enim fide donabuntur Sp. S. qui ani- mos illorum ad spontaneum & promptum obsequium excitabit. B. Dorscheus inscriptionem legis non ad renovationem refert, sed ad doctrina salvifica com- municationem. Νόμος, inquit, notat totam salvifi- cam doctrinam. Sic passim in Veteri & Novo Test. su- mitur. Vide quæ dicta sunt in Pentad. dissert. 1. ad lo- cum Es. VIII. 20. & confer. Psal. I. 2. XIX. 8. & seqq. Vocatur νόμος πίσεως, Rom. III. 27. Non est itaq; lex illa, quæ tabulis lapideis est exarata. Nam & illa par- tim per naturam inscripta est hominum cordibus, par- tim etiam per doctrinam & informationem inscribi- tur magis magisq;. Neq; sunt perfectiora quædam mandata & additamenta legis moralis, qualia Novum Test. nulla agnoscit. Neq; sunt perfectionis, quæ & nulla sunt, & ad universam confæderandorum multi- tudinem, si vel maxime essent, non pertinerent. Sed sunt ipsæ promissiones Evangelicæ, quæ proprium sunt novi fœderis bonum. Sed concinnior videtur expo- sitio jam tradita, ob oppositionem Veteris & Novi Testamenti, qua legis inscriptionem.

Circa hanc autem inscriptionem Estius perpe- ram advertit, ad gratiam Novi Test. commendandam, Christi nihil in membranis aut chartis scriptum nobis relinquere voluisse, ne his adminiculis ad imprimen- dam animis nostris legem suam opus habere videretur. Nam inscriptio in corda non fit immediate, sed mediante Verbo Dei, Scripturâ sacrâ compre- henso, quod ut canonem fidei, sic medium nostræ renovationis & sanctificationis esse voluit Chri- stus: qui etsi ipse nihil manibus suis scriptum relique- rit: tamen quicquid de suis dictis vel factis nos scire voluit, scribendum Apostolis, tanquam suis manibus imperavit dicente Aug. l. de Cons. Evang. & cult.

Καὶ ἔσομαι αὐτοῖς εἰς Θεὸν, καὶ αὐτοὶ ἔσονταί μοι εἰς λαὸν) Illi me colent, ego eos protegam; Loquutio par ei, quam su- pra habuimus I. 5.

Hic parallelismus est locorum, quæ nihil mi- nus, quam parallela sunt. Nam cap. I. 5. de æterno Dei Filio, & Paternitate Dei κατ᾿ έσω agitur; hic ne quidem de ipsa υἱοθεσία proprie sermo est, nec Paternitas Dei κατ᾽ ἔξω κατὰ γράμμα exprimitur: Sed promittit Deus, se futurum credentibus εἰς Θεὸν in Deum, eosdem gratia sua fovendo, prote- gendo, ad salutem æternam conservando, uti cre- denti cuivis de altera vita promissum Apoc. XXI. 7. Καὶ ἔσομαι αὐτῷ Θεὸς, & v. 3. καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἔσται μετ᾽ αὐτῶν, Θεὸς αὐτῶν. Promittit credentes sibi fu- turos in populum: quod itidem ad tabernaculum alterius vitæ sese extendit, Apoc. XXI. 3. καὶ αὐτοὶ λαοὶ αὐτοῦ ἔσονται. Populus autem Domini sumus, cum nos sibi ut peculium suum appropriat, & ut electus Dei populus, Regale ejus sacerdotium ma- neamus, præstat, quod in nostris viribus situm non est, sed virtute ac gratia Spiritus S. obtinemus, nec cultu fit, sed fide, quia in virtute Dei custodimur per fidem 1. Pet. I. 5. Hujus est καταρτίσαι ἡμᾶς, στη- ρίξαι, σθενῶσαι, θεμελιῶσαι, 1. Petr. V. 10. Habemus hic Estium non abnuentem: Mihi, inquit, verisi- milius est, utroq; membro significari affectum Dei in homines, quibus sit promissio, ut breviter hic sit sen- sus: Ego me eis præstabo Deum, & habebo eos pro po- pulo meo. Id est, utroq; nomine conjuncto, & quoniam ego Deus eorum ero, & quoniam ipsi populus meus e- runt, benefaciam eis. Conf. Gen. XVII. 7. Levit. XXVI. 12. 2, Cor. VI. 16. Matth. XXII. 31. B. Dor- scheus beneficium hoc de spirituali cum Deo unio- ne interpretatur, & ita de eo disserit: Deum, qui nobis uniendus est, seu Κύριον, Jer. XXXI. 31. 32. non esse Deum absolute, sed imprimis etiam ut mediato- rem constituit v. 6. Ita enim, inquit, unionis gratiosæ fundamentum constituitur. Unde Apostolus cum isto respectu ad constitutum Mediatorem Novi Test. quod melioribus promissionibus sancitum est, textum Pro- pheticum allegat. Debet enim probare, Messiæ com- petere sublimiorem in bonis divinis dispensationem, eum esse Mediatorem melioris Testamenti, & pro- mis- posuisse promissiones meliores. Dicit Deum apud Je- remiam vaticinatum esse de ista melioris Testamenti constitutione, quod ista contineret, de quibus v. 6. dictum est. Ergo ista verba Prophetica omnino de Messia loquuntur tanquam de constituto Media- tore sublimioris liturgiæ & melioris Testamenti. Ita- que per istum Dominum, qui apud Jeremiam loqui- tur, etiam Messias Mediator Novi Test. intelligen- dus est. Hinc illud μεμφόμενος v. 8. commodius sub- jectum habere non potest, quam μεσίτην in v. 6. Red- diturus enim rationem Apostolus, cur Christus Novi Test. sit Mediator, hanc affert, quia si non melioris & Novi Test. esset Mediator, aut si id Testamentum, quod ipse allaturus est, nec esset perfectius pleniusq́;, frustra de ejus introductione ipse apud Prophetam vaticinatus esset. Si quæras, quomodo de suo Novo Test. vaticinatus sit Mediator? respondet Apostolus, μεμφόμενον vaticinatum fuisse. Itaq́; μεμφόμενος & Mediator hoc loco unum sunt. Itaq́; Filius Dei duplici respectu in hanc unionem gratiosam venit, primum absolute, quatenus est cum Patre & Sp. S. unus summus Deus, Joh. X. 30. & 1. Joh. V. 7. Quo- modo etiam uno indivisoq́; nomine cum Patre & Spiritu S. perficit omnia, Matth. XXVIII. 19. atq́; ita etiam consummat hanc sanctam unionem, tanquam Deus benedictus super omnia in secula, Rom. IX. 5. Secundo relative, ratione suscepti officii, in quo non agit tantum θεϊκῶς, sed θεανδρικῶς 1. Tim. II. 5. & a- git quidem ad unionem hanc efficiendam juxta offici- um suum Propheticum, Sacerdotale, & Regium. Ex quibus ἀποτελέσματα illa inscriptionis legis & unio- nis necessario fluunt. Neq́; enim pacificatio & unio gratiosa sine Messia perficitur, Col. I. 20. Hinc per- sonæ SS. Trinitatis ad hanc unionem veniunt, non tantum ut uniendæ, sed etiam ut unientes, sive princi- palis causa Efficiens istius sanctæ & salvificæ unio- nis. Quod indicat verbum συντελέσω, quo non tan- tum finis & consummatio novi fœderis, sed jam inde ab ipso etiam principio deducta, Deoq́; debita per- fectio indicatur, & per se manifestum est, quoniam unitio ex parte Dei unicè à voluntate divina depen- det; ex parte autem hominis nulla est ad istam po- testas, non posse nisi Deo uniente istam unitionem perfici, quæ est inter τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ θεοῦ, quæ homo ex se non capit, multo minus efficit, 1. Cor. II. 14. Itaq́; Deus est hic ὁ ἐνεργῶν, Phil. II. 13. pecu- liariter vero Christus est ἀρχηγὸς καὶ τελειωτὴς ejus, Ebr. XII. 2. De unitione ipsa ita habet ὁ Μακαρί- της: Notanda unitio ipsa, cujus geminum est ἀπο- τέλεσμα: Priori efficitur, ut Deus sibi unitis sit De- us, quod non perficitur præsentia universali. Nam sic omnibus creaturis DEUS est DEUS, & ad hanc relationem opus non est aliqua nova con- fœderatione; nec etiam Deificatione quadam, qualem fanatici finxerunt, illam etiam Scriptura ignorat; sed gratiosa appropinquatione, cujus 1. fun- damentum est ἐνσάρκωσις, sive nostra natura in per- sonam divinam assumptio, de qua supra cap. II. 14. seq. Eo enim ipso maxime Deus factus est nobis De- us cum factus est Immanuel, Es. VII. 14. cum Filius Dei factus est Filius hominis, Joh. I. 14. cum omnis plenitudo Deitatis in Humana natura habitare cœ- pit corporaliter, Col. II. vers. 9. Ex hoc funda- mento II. fit gratiosa appropinquatio (a) per ju- stificationem, qua Deus propter peccatum nobis iratus, per Christum autem reconciliatus unitur remissione peccatorum, & imputatione justitiæ Christi per fidem apprehensa, ita ut Christus nobis sit ἱλαστήριον, Rom. III. 25. & ἀντίλυτρον, 1. Tim. VI. quatenus factum peccatum 2. Cor. V. 21. tulit pecca- ta nostra in corpore suo super lignum 1. Pet. II. 24. & sic Deus nobis est εἰς θεὸν δικαίοντα ἀσεβεῖς

Roman. IV. 5. cum nos accedimus μετὰ παῤῥησίας ad thronum gratiæ &c. Ebr. VI. 13. in qua justificatio- ne Christus rursus geminum, quem diximus, respe- ctum subit. Cum enim neq; Pater neque Spiritus S. ἱλαστήριον sit, ille id est in justificatione, quod Pater & Spiritus S. & insuper ἱλαστήριον est, quapropter & μεσίτης dicitur hoc ipso capite v. 6. sine quo Deus noster Deus esse noluit. Sic unitis Deo fit ille (β) nobis in Deum regeneratione, quatenus nos in peccatis mortuos cum Christo revivificat, resuscitat, & col- locat in cælestibus in Christo, * regenerans scil. semi- ne non corruptibili, sed incorruptibili Verbo scil. Dei viventis & in æternum permanentis 1. Petr. II. 23. & nobis recipientibus ipsum dat ἐξουσίαν τέκνα Θεoῦ γί- νεσθαι Joh. I. 12. utpote ex Deo genitis, v. 13. Sic Deus nobis fit εἰς Θεὸν Πατέρα, dans nobis Spiritum ad- optionis, in quo clamamus Abba Pater. Hanc sequi- tur III. gratiosa inhabitatio, qua fit nobis Deus εἰς Θεὸν ἐνοικῶντα. De qua ἐνοικήσει prolixe actum est supra c. III. 6. Hanc sequitur IV. gratiosa renova- tio, qua fit nobis Deus εἰς Θεὸν ἀνανεῶντα, Eph. IV. 23. & ἀνακαινῶντα, Col. III. 10. de qua supra cap. V. 12. & VI. 7. seqq. actum est. Neq; enim Deus postquam nobis Pater & Hospes factus est, in nobis otiosus est, sed eo contendit, ut magis magisq́; destructis operi- bus Diaboli, interior homo ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ἡμέρᾳ renove- tur, 2. Cor. IV. 16. ut nos transformemur ἀπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν 2. Cor. III. 18. Atqui in his omnibus fit no- bis Deus εἰς Θεὸν 1. ἁγιάζοντα ratione sanctitatis tum imputatæ, qua Christus nobis fit ἁγιασμὸς, 1. Cor. I. 30. & VI. 11. tum inchoatæ, in regeneratione qui- dem ratione virium sive donorum sanctificantium per illuminationem sive translationem è regno tene- brarum in regnum lucis, ubi accipimus partem sortis sanctorum in luce Act. XXVI. 18. & Col. I. 12. idq́; per Christum καταργήσαντα τὸν θάνατον, κὴ φωτίσαντα ζωὴν καὶ ἀφθαρσίαν, 2. Tim. I. 12. In renovatione ve- ro ratione quotidianæ promotionis ad majorem san- ctitaten, quatenus magis magisq́; induimus novum hominem secundum Deum creatum in justitia & sanctitate vera, Eph. IV. 24. 2. Fit nobis Deus εἰς Θεὸν ἀπολέσαντα abluentem, idque tum lavacro ba- ptismi, Tit. III. 5. Matth. XXVIII. 20. ubi rursus pu- rificatio per lavacrum aquæ in Verbo peculiari- ter competit, quatenus purificamur per ipsius sangui- nem, 1. Johan. I. 7. cujus ῥαντισμὸς nobis contingit, 1. Petr. I. 2. tum in quotidiana per pœnitentiam re- novatione, qua nos lavamur & purificamur, Es. I. 16. 3. Fit nobis Deus εἰς Θεὸν χορτάζοντα saturantem sive cibantem, idq́; rursus tum in justificatione & regene- ratione, qua ipse nobis est panis iste de cælo descen- dens, de quo Joh. VI. 33. & seqq. prolixe: tum in reno- vatione, sive quotidiana spirituali communione, qua magis magisq́; gustamus suavitatem Domini, & cor- roboramur in eo: tum in sacramentali participatio- ne, qua nobis contigit κοινωνία σώμα[τος] κὴ αἵμα[τος] τοῦ Χριστοῦ 1. Cor. X. 16. XI. 24. 25. XII. 13. 4. Fit nobis Deus εἰς Θεὸν συναρτίζοντα, καὶ ἀνακεφαλαιῶντα, quatenus nos inserit corpori mystico per fidem, & Christo capiti unit, Eph. I. 10. & 22. idq́; tum in ju- stificatione, tum in regeneratione. Atq́; sic infertos & unitos, atq́; corpori mystico συναρμολογουμένως, καὶ συμβιβαζομένως promovet ad spiritualem auctio- nem Eph. IV. 16. Ubi rursus Christus, quemadmodum in nutritione cibus est & cibans peculiari ratione, sic etiam hic illius συναρτισμοῦ & ἀνακεφαλαιώσεως & autor est & terminus. Reddimur enim membra non Patris aut Spiritus S. si immediate & formaliter loquamur: finaliter enim etiam huc pertinent, Rom. VI. 19. 1. Cor. XII. 14. & seqq. sed Christi, sicut & ille, non Pater aut Sp. S. caput nostrum est, Eph. IV. 15. 5. Fit nobis Deus εἰς Θεὸν γαμίζοντα, quatenus nos de- spondere facit, tanquam virginem sanctam, uni vi- ro, 2. Cor. XI. 2. Of. II. 20. quatenus ipse est νύμφιος Joh. III. 29. qui hoc affectu dilexit Ecclesiam, eamque sibi despondit, Eph. V. 25. ubi licet desponsatio, quæ in justificatione contigit, sit sacrosanctæ Trinitatis opus, γάμος tamen inter Christum est & Ecclesiam, ejusque membra. Cui etiam ita advigilat cælestis sponsus, ut ipsi peculiariter adscribatur fomentum & nutrimentum Ecclesiæ, Eph. V. 29. Spir. S. autem arrhabonem præbet in cordibus nostris, 2. Cor. I. 22. In universum 6. Deus nobis est εἰς Θεὸν ὑποτάσ- σοντα, non tantum illa generali ὑποταγῇ, de qua su- pra c. II. 8. actum est, sed illa speciali, cujus respectu homo naturaliter est ἀνυπότακτος, nec legi Dei sub- jicitur, Rom. VIII. 7. adeoque per fidem ratione do- minii Deo subjicitur. Nec τὸ βασιλεύειν concedit peccato in mortali suo corpore, Rom. VI. 12. quæ ὑπο- ταγὴ, cum conjuncta sit cum rebellione, non perfe- cta, sed tentata in membris nostris oriunda, Rom. VII. 23. Gal. V. 17. Ideoq́ue Christus per Spir. S. magis magisque vivificat mortalia nostra corpora, Rom. VIII. 11. ut adeo per quotidianam ὑποταγὴν perfici- amus illud ὑπερνικῶμεν in mediis adversitatibus, de quo Rom. VIII. 37. idque per fidem, quæ est victoria, vincens mundum, 1. Joh. V. 4. Atque in hoc decursu τεταγμένοις καὶ εὐθέτοις εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῦ Θεῦ, fit deinde Deus εἰς Θεόν. 7. δοξάζοντα, cum fiet unio in gloria juxta ordinem Rom. VIII. 30. Atque hanc, ut sic dicamus, Deificationem, qua nobis Deus sit Deus ex hac sanctione fœderali, quæque prius est hujus unionis ἀποτέλεσμα, sequitur alterum, qua nos populus Dei efficimur, λαὸς περιύσιος, Tit. II. 14. Quam divinam λαοποίησιν vocare fas est, qua rur- sus non est ista subjectio generalis, qua omnes populi ipsi servire tenentur, sed specialis, eaque posita (α) su- per fundamento carnis è nobis in divinam personam assumptæ, cujus respectu dicere possumus, eam esse carnem de carne nostra (β) in gratiosa receptione uni- tionis divinæ Joh. I. 12. cæterorumque actuum, de qui- bus in primo apotelesmate dictum est, donec sequa- tur gloriosa receptio in occursum Domini, 1. Thess. IV. 17. ubi cum in hac vita, quid sit θεοποίησις, qua Deus nobis Deus factus est, & λαοποίησις, qua nos Dei populus effecti sumus δι᾽ ἐσόπτρε ἐν αἰνίγματι tantum videremus, tandem de facie ad faciem illud cogno- scamus. Unde illud ἔσομαι καὶ ἔσονται non negat præ- teritum, quasi hactenus non fuerit Deus sanctorum & fidelium Deus. Id enim iis repugnat, quæ infra cap. XI. toto & XII. imprimis v. 22. 23. professus est. Sed 1. indicat principium, quod id nequaquam con- tigerit sub Veteri Testamento sanctis & fidelibus, vi illius evenerit, sed ex Novi Testamenti bene- ficiis per Messiam, qui fuit heri, & est hodie, ac erit in æternum, Ebr. XIII. 9. ad ipsos usque redundarit. 2. Continuationem, quod scil. ea ipsa beneficia & apo- telesmata, quorum gustum hactenus præbuit sanctis & fidelibus, porro quoque sit dispensaturus & diffusu- rus. (γ) Solennem confirmationem faciendam N. T. per sanguinis divini effusionem confirmatam. (δ) Au- gmentum, idque tum ratione claritatis, quæ sequetur renovationem umbrarum, sub quibus hactenus se Deum populo suo ostendit, & sibi populum fecit: tum ratione bonorum hactenus μελλόντων, Ebr. X. 1. nunc realiter exhibendorum, inter quæ excellit, ut dictum est, ἐνσάρκωσις, tum ratione mediorum, quæ paucissi- ma futura sunt & simplicissima. (ε) Complementum, quod Vetus Test. uti supra dictum est, afferre non po- terat, id hoc Novum præstabit. Imperfectissime itaque & generalissime hoc beneficium explicat Schlich- tingius pag. 347. à quo non multum abit Ribera pag. 359. cum hunc sensum horum verborum red- dunt: Ero ipsorum summus protector, omnibusque eos beneficiis cumulabo & illi mecum agent, quemad- modum meum populum decet. Vtrique fungemur nostris partibus, ego benefaciendo, illi recte agendo, meg, colendo. Hoc sane profunditatem divini be- neficii inexplicabilem vix levissime attingit.

## 8:11
Vers. 11. And they shall not teach every man his citizen, and every man his brother, saying, Know the Lord, for all shall know me from the least of them to the greatest of them. The Greek interpreters stated 'they shall not teach' in the potential mood, that is, there will be no need for them to teach. He said 'citizen' here for 'fellow-citizen'. In the Hebrew here it is רעהו; but in Leviticus 19:18 it is בן עמו. Thus also the Latins say, 'my fellow-citizen', that is, a participant of the same municipality as me. Formerly, those who were in doubt about some matter used to consult the prophets and were taught their duty by them, 1 Sam. 9:9. To know the Lord, that is, the will of the Lord. After the return from Babylon, all who were not forced to seek a living by perpetual labor learned the law. And thus all Christians easily learn the precepts of Christ, which is the new law. See 1 Cor. 1:5, John 6:45. From the least to the greatest: that is, adolescents and the elderly. The same expression is in Gen. 19:11, 1 Sam. 5:9, 30:2, 19, 2 Kings 24:46, 2 Chron. 31:15, 34:30, Isa. 22:24. 'Of them' [greatest of them], that is, among themselves.

To know the Lord is not only to know the will of the Lord, but primarily also to know the Lord regarding his nature, which knowledge and faith is proper to the Church of God, in which we are taught that eternal life consists, John 17:3. Nor is it now a matter of the legal will, which was already comprehended in verse 10, when the promise was made concerning the inscription of the law, but of the Evangelical will, concerning which 1 Tim. 2:4, 2 Pet. 3:9. The law was not unknown either to those returning from Babylon, or to other Jews, and not even to the Gentiles, since it is inscribed by nature on their hearts, Rom. 2:14. Therefore, it is a matter here of another knowledge of the will, namely, that which is revealed in the Gospel: which Grotius rashly and perversely transforms into the law, when the law and the Gospel are opposed as contraries. Nor is it understood as merely a bare knowledge of God, but one with a fiducial apprehension of divine grace, i.e., true faith. Cf. Jer. 9:23, 1 Cor. 1:31, Isa. 53:11. This benefit is promised to all by the power of the new covenant from the least to the greatest, because no one is excluded from it by God, even if most people exclude themselves from it by their own fault, 1 Tim. 2:4, Isa. 54:13, John 6:45. However, this passage provides no support for the Schwenkfeldians, who teach that God works the knowledge and conversion in the hearts of men without the ministry of His Word. Since, according to the blessed Hunnius, the Prophet here deals with the benefit of the New Testament, not only as it is begun in this life, but also as it is perfected in the future life: where certainly there will no longer be any need for the ministry of teaching, but all things will be exposed in the clearest light. In this life, however, the Lord works grace in us not immediately, but through the Word and the sacraments of regeneration. Since faith is from the hearing of the Word of God, Rom. 10. This is from the blessed Hunnius. Theodoret, Augustine in his book 'On the Spirit and the Letter' ch. 24, 25, Primasius, and Anselm also refer this to the state of the future age, which, however, along with the other promises, pertains to the state of the present age. And therefore Jerome, as Estius notes, interprets it as being promised to the sons of Israel that they would by no means seek Jewish teachers, and the mandates and traditions of men, but would be taught by the Holy Spirit. Chrysostom explains it as the manifestation of the Evangelical law through all nations. Theophylact and Oecumenius think that laborious instruction is denied, because the faith of Christ is persuaded to men with little effort. St. Thomas believes this promise was fulfilled only in the first founders of the New Testament, that is, the Apostles perfectly taught by Christ, provided it pertains to the present age; otherwise, he is more inclined to the opinion that refers it to the state of the blessed. Some explain it more generally, as if it were said of the faithful of the primitive Church. Again, another exposition refers it to the whole time of grace, yet not to the whole multitude of the faithful, but to the greater and better part, whose number is known to God. Finally, another, which is that of Francisco Ribera, extends it to all the faithful without exception. Since, he says, it is true of all and singular of Christ's faithful that they know God and His Christ through faith. To which Estius seems to add his vote, asserting that these things pertain to all and only the sons of the New Testament who are the sons of the promise, whence he names a citizen and a brother, that is, a man of the same city and family, which is none other than the Church of believers, and comparing the passage 1 John 2:27, 'You do not have need that anyone should teach you, but as His anointing teaches you concerning all things.' He seeks the reason from the preceding; because ALL will have the law of God inscribed in their hearts. But we have already warned that this is not a matter of the legal will. Others, as the blessed Gerhard notes, respond that these words, 'A man shall no longer teach his neighbor, etc.', are to be taken comparatively, namely, with respect had, first, to the preaching of the Gospel throughout the whole world. Only the Jews had known that old legal covenant, Ps. 147:19, Rom. 9:4, whence the Gentiles had need to learn it from the Jews: But in the New Testament, the covenant of grace was to be preached not only to the Jews, but to all nations. Second, to the amplitude of the Church in the New Testament, because in the New Testament there will be a greater number of those who are imbued with the saving knowledge of God than in the Old Testament, since the solemn and public preaching of the Word is no longer restricted to one nation, but is common to all peoples. Then Chrysostom explains concerning the manifestation of the Evangelical law through all nations. Thirdly, concerning the more perfect and fuller knowledge of God that would follow in the time of the New Testament than was in the Old, since today a little boy, rightly instructed in the Catechism, understands the mystery of the Gospel concerning Christ more explicitly than once in the Old Testament did any of the chief Priests, Is. XI. v. 9. the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, chap. XXX. 26. the light of the Moon shall be as the light of the Sun, Jer. XXIV. 7. I will give them a heart to know me. Fourthly, concerning an instruction less laborious and difficult, because on account of the spiritual worship of the New Testament and the more abundant grace of God there will be no need for great labor and trouble in teaching the pious: for it precedes, I will write my law in their hearts, so that thus in these words of the Prophetic prediction a tacit opposition is established between the old and new Testament, between the doctrine of the Law and the Gospel: the former is the ministry of the letter; the latter, however, of the Spirit: The former is inscribed on tablets of stone; the latter, however, on the hearts of men by the Holy Spirit, and has the grace of the Spirit joined to it, 2. Cor. III. v. 3. and 6. The simplest answer is, because it is not the difference of time before Christ and after Christ, but of the old and new covenant that is being handed down, and the benefits under the New Testament, which are certainly not to be denied to the time of the Old Testament, are explained, that nothing else is taught than that that saving knowledge of GOD is so constituted, which is revealed in the Gospel, that flesh and blood does not reveal it by human information, but it consists solely in the manifestation of the divine Word, Matth. XI. vers. 27. chap. XVI. vers. 17. that by the force of the covenant of grace it is to be granted to all by God, and all are to be taught by GOD, yet not immediately, but through the Word, and the ministry of the Word. Concerning the law a man can [teach] his neighbor to instruct, Deut. 6:7, which even those endowed with the light of nature know, and one more accurately than another looks into it by its benefit: But concerning the Gospel, all must be θεοδιδάκτης (taught by God), Is. 54:13. The universal preaching of the Gospel after the coming of Christ, and the amplitude of the Church in the New Testament, as well as a fuller knowledge, pertain to the distinction of the time of the Old and New Testament, but not indeed of the old and new covenant, of which the Apostle treats here from the Prophet. That opposition, however, between the Old and New Testament, between the doctrine of the law and the Gospel, that the former is the ministry of the letter, but the latter of the Spirit, etc., only makes for this, but not precisely to the present benefit concerning the saving knowledge and faith to be divinely granted, and to explaining those words, 'all shall know me,' since the force and nature of the Spirit extends itself also to other benefits recounted here.

Blessed Dorscheus compares more fully and [discusses] diverse opinions concerning this passage, and explains the mind of the Apostle: Some, he says, because they do not find how this will not be in the militant Church, refer it to the triumphant one. Thus Augustine on the Spirit and the Letter, ch. 24 and 28. Theodoret and Cajetan in their commentary on this place. Theophylact and Oecumenius interpret it not of instruction simply, but of laborious education, viz., that it will not be joined with such great labor in the New Testament, that men are led to the knowledge of the true GOD, both because all things in the N.T. are going to be far clearer than they had been in the Old, where most things were wrapped in types and shadows; and thus the doctrine of that [Old Testament] consisted in the observation of very many ceremonies: and also because new revelations are going to arrive, which will make all things more expeditious and easier. Jerome refers this to the doctrine of the Jewish Masters, who long ago burdened their own people with human mandates and traditions, namely that in the New Testament there will be a destruction and refutation of traditions πατροπαραδότων (handed down from the fathers). Thomas on this place restricts these words to the Apostles. Ribera refers these words to knowledge with affection: At that time, he says, when the Apostles and their disciples were living, Christians for the most part were fervent in charity, and all were called saints, as we see everywhere in the epistles of Paul, Heb. 3, 2 Cor. 1. For such were the Christians then, that if we hear the testimonies of the Apostles concerning them, we do not doubt that this prophecy of Jeremiah rightly applies to them, although there were some wicked ones, who ought not to harm the multitude of whom these things are said. Therefore at that time one did not teach his neighbor, saying, know the Lord, that is, love the Lord. For to know or to understand the Lord is accustomed to be said in Scripture in this way, as 1 Chron. 28:9, 1 John 2:3. Wherefore the Chaldean rightly translates: And they shall no longer teach a man his neighbor, and a man his brother, saying, know the fear of the Lord, because all shall learn so that they may know the fear of God. For the new believers, seeing themselves liberated by the grace of Christ from so many sins and such terrible damnation, gave thanks to God, and loved Him with their whole heart. Wherefore it is not contrary to this prophecy if someone were to exhort a brother to love God more ardently than he was loving, or if the Apostles write to the Church, or to disciples, that they should love Christ. For they wish to excite many to a more ardent love, nor were they writing to that age [only], but also to future ones, in which many are in need of admonition. But even in that age there were some Christians who did not love God, and to whom it could rightly be said that they should know the Lord. For the prophecy is not about all Christians of that age, but about the churches themselves, since a great part of each church loved God then.

For what is said about any church, it is enough that it be true in its greater and lesser part. Thus Ribera, who, because he sees that the first two benefits, namely the inscription of saving truth into the hearts of men, and spiritual gracious union, are universal, and do not pertain only to the time of the primitive Church, and thus that this very thing must likewise be extended, finally proceeds to the point of asserting that nothing prevents it from being explained of us also and all Christ's faithful, what is said in v. 11. Cf. Is. 54:13, where it is promised in the New Testament that all will be θεοδιδάκτους (taught by God), and yet John 6:44, 45 refers it to the ordinary and perpetual way of coming to God. Therefore, he says, the Prophets only mean this, that all human diligence in teaching the sacred mysteries of faith will be useless, unless God assists inwardly, illuminating the mind and persuading that the things which are taught are true: because we can neither know by faith, much less adhere to the known truth out of the affection of charity, unless God teaches us inwardly by His special help and aid. And afterwards: As far as our passage is concerned, then this is said by the Prophet, which Ribera has already indicated after others, and that from the nature of the New Testament. For the Old Testament indeed inculcated the doctrine of the law by itself and through itself, and thus everyone led his neighbor and his brother to its knowledge, but there was not present any peculiar vivifying and saving power in that doctrine of the law, so that from it one might be illuminated and excited to the knowledge and embrace of Jehovah. It was indeed said in the doctrine of the law, 'know the Lord,' and 'you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul,' Deut. 6:5. But saying this did not provide the doing; it will not be so in the New Testament, says the Prophet; the Gospel of the New Testament will not be taught ineffectively and without powers infused from heaven, as the law was taught, upon which the Old Testament relies. Moreover, another thing is also included in this benefit, which pertains greatly to the excellence of the New Testament, namely the universality of the preaching of the heavenly doctrine, so that this will not be the case, namely that the ordinary ministry of the New Testament will not be restricted to some certain nation, in which one would ordinarily inform only his neighbor, fellow citizen, and brother, and lead him to the knowledge of the beatific truth, as happened among the Israelite people, where although even those from the nations were admitted, who embraced τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ entrusted to the Israelites, and for the sake of religion associated themselves with them according to the prayers of Solomon, 1 Kings 8:41. Although furthermore then through pilgrimages, negotiations, and indeed even deportations and exiles of the Israelites the saving truth became known to the nations; nevertheless, the ordinary ministry remained only among the Israelite nation. This, says the Prophet, will not be the case in the New Testament when it is solemnly promulgated. For the ministry will be extended to all nations, which the fulfillment itself taught, Matt. 28:19, Mark 16:15, by reason of the command; but by reason of the fulfillment, Eph. 4:11, Rom. 15:19, Col. 1:23. Therefore, that negative expression, ὀυ μὴ διδάξωσιν, is to be supplemented by μόνον, as sacred philology warns that an expression conceived negatively is to be supplemented in very many places of both the Old and New Testament; so that the sense may be concerning the New Testament solemnly promulgated through Christ, no one taught only his brother, his fellow citizen, his neighbor, and will preach to him alone the knowledge of the Lord: cf. Gen. 32:28, 1 Sam. 8:7. After he argues laboriously against Cloppenburg, who contends that there was no calling to salvation among other nations under the old Mosaic economy; whose exception concerning the Ninevites, and that Jonah was not sent for the calling of the uncircumcised nation and extraordinary conversion, but he refutes at length those who were sent to the circumcised, if not Jews, at least Abrahamites and other associates of the Jewish religion, and he responds to the place in Psalm 147:19-20: He speaks not of the act of the communication of divine rights, but of the manner. For the divine Φανερώσεις (manifestations) which occurred among the Israelites concerning the communication of divine rights did not happen at all to other nations, although it is manifest that the rights themselves were to be communicated to the nations, from Deuteronomy 4:6, where it is said that these very rights are to be diligently observed by the Israelites for this reason, because they are their wisdom and prudence before the eyes of the peoples, who, hearing these statutes, will say, 'Surely this great nation is a wise and prudent people.' Hence, Acts 17:30, the times of gentilism are called times of ignorance, but not arising from a lack of salvific will. For this fights against the preceding disputation of the Apostle, v. 24, 25, 26, 27. Where it is asserted that God for this reason both created man, and after the fall even dispersed him across the surface of the earth, so that he might seek God, who presents Himself everywhere; but [he seeks] out of an affection of malicious ignorance. Afterward, having returned to this place of ours, he adds: The Prophet says, he says, that it will come to pass under the revelation of the New Testament that all shall know the Lord from the least even to the greatest. The active verb is to be explained not so much concerning the act as the faculty and the duty in this way: That in the New Testament, access to divine salvific knowledge is not only to be shown to all remotely, but proximately and intimately through the mission of an army of Evangelists, so that each one can almost have the Word of salvation in his own bosom, Romans 10:8. and that by a certain most easy and most plain reason, heavenly wisdom is not to be communicated as it was in the Old Testament under shadows and types, so that all, provided they are willing, can easily be enlightened. Indeed, and by a new and immediate calling, all are obligated to know the Lord, Acts 17:30, through the actual exhibition of faith, v. 31, to which divine purpose, granting the faculty and facility and imposing the duty upon all, if the outcome does not respond so that individuals obey, it is nevertheless brought about that from that gracious divine συγκαταβάσει (condescension) infinite numbers among the nations are converted, who would not have been converted without such a dilatation of the New Testament.

And this is what the Apostle says in Romans 11:25, that the fullness of the nations enters into the Church. Verse 12. (Ὅτι ἵλεως ἔσομαι ταῖς ἀδικίαις αὐτῶν καὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν καὶ τῶν ἀνομιῶν αὐτῶν ὀὐ μὴ μνησθῶ ἔτι) That which is here in the Hebrew כִּי and in the Greek ὅτι is best translated by 'indeed.' Ἵλεων εἶναι, just as ἱλάσκεσθαι above II. 17, in the common sense is to be unwilling to exact the punishments of crimes: in the mystical sense it is to heal the mind in such a way that crimes do not return. Thus also God is said not to remember them in a more sublime sense, where there is nothing new that might bring the old things back to memory. For ἀδικίαις in the Hebrew is עֲוֹנָם. That word signifies all deeds against what is right. For the two Greek words τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν, καὶ τῶν ἀνομιῶν αὐτῶν, there is one in the Hebrew לְחַטָּאתָם, which is so general that it includes all other sins which are not accustomed to come under the name of ἀδικία. The Syriac and Latin read only one word in this place, and certain Greeks as well, so that one of these might seem to have crept in from a gloss. There is no reason why its own proper and more accepted meaning should not be left to the particle. For the cause of the former benefits, namely the inscription of the law and the gracious divine preservation, and indeed also the more abundant illustration and confirmation of faith, is the gratuitous remission of sins. Rightly

Paraeus: This is the promise of the Gospel concerning the gratuitous remission of sins and justification through faith in Christ, in which the chief difference of both covenants is situated. For the Old promised life to those performing the law, and threatened death to those transgressing. The New proposes the forgiveness of sins to transgressors in Christ: ἵλεως ἔσομαι, I will be propitious: This promise includes the satisfaction of Christ, because God is not propitious to sinners except on account of Christ the Mediator, who is therefore called ἱλασμὸς, the propitiation or propitiator for the sins of the whole world. Where again the text is perverted by Grotius through a commentary of a double sense. For the remission of sins is the pardon of both guilt and punishment, but to say that in the mystical sense it is that healing of the mind so that crimes do not return is to confuse sanctification with justification. Finally, why should we bring all other things into suspicion of corruption from a few copies? Grotius is too prone to such suspicions: which, however, produce nothing but uncertainty of the canon. B. Dorscheus has this to say about them: The word ἀδικίας is neither found among the LXX Interpreters, nor does it have a peculiar word in the sources in Jeremiah corresponding to it. Nor does the Syriac translation have either ἀδικίαν or ἀνομίαν; it certainly judged one or the other superfluous, because it expressed only one. Nor did Chrysostom, Theophylact, or Oecumenius place both. Yet we do not think it should be said that it was added badly in the Greek Codices of the New Testament, as Franc. Ribera judged in this place. Grotius produces a manuscript where there is no mention of ἀνομιῶν. For those words express nothing except one object, namely, whatever in man is opposed to the divine law, whether originally or actually. Schlichtingius in this place, p. 348. & seqq. he thinks that the Apostle intended to indicate the difference between the mercy and the remission dispensed in the New Testament and that which was under the Old Testament. Hence he notes that the words for unrighteousnesses, iniquities, and transgressions, by which sins are designated here, teach that the subject here is the remission of the sins of any persons, even the most grievous, and that such is the proper promise of the New Testament, and that here shines forth that which was said above: that the New Testament is established upon better promises than the Old. But Schlichtingius in reality confuses that which was under the Old Testament and by the power of the Old Testament. For by the power of the Old Testament, a gracious remission of sins, even the smallest, had no place, which the Apostle expressly proved from Deut. XXVII. 26 in Gal. III. 10. Under the Old Testament, however, although not by the power of that, but of this New one, not only lesser sins but also the most grievous were remitted, which is clear even from the example of David in Psalm LI. 3 & seqq. Schlichtingius also wrongly notes in this place that the literal sense of these words was that God, being about to liberate the Jewish people from the Babylonian captivity, and thus being about to obliterate their past most grievous sins, would remove their temporal punishments, by which great benefit the people ought to have been wonderfully bound to God and led to worship Him constantly thereafter. For certainly this promise can in no way be accepted as concerning the liberation from the Babylonian captivity, as has also been noted above. Whence Schlichtingius himself is forced to admit that the interpretation concerning the liberation from the Babylonian captivity is far too meager to respond fully and solidly to such august words. For neither did God, through it, then enter into any New covenant, properly speaking, and one different from the former with the people: nor was that benefit of such great power that it could perpetually keep the people in their duty, and therefore it appears that the Holy Spirit designates some other sense far more august than this. These are his words.

But since God remits sins in such a way that He wills to remember them no more, it is manifest that they will not be brought into judgment, and are fully remitted, so that no temporal punishment is reserved, by which the Papists distress and terrify consciences. are said to be blotted out, Isa. XLIV. 22, and cast into the depths of the sea, Mic. VII. 19, and their guilt is so pardoned that the punishment is also remitted, Matt. XVIII. v. 27. The blessed Dorscheus says this about these words: Οὐ μὴ μνησθῶ ἔτι, I will not remember anymore; these negative words most strongly affirm. For non-remembrance implies the suspension of all punishments and a completely whole and unfailing restoration of divine friendship or charity. These things are explained in more words in Mic. VII. 18, 19, and 20. Therefore, it does not have only guilt and eternal punishment as its object, but also temporal punishment. For if this were still remaining, then he would still remember the sins by reason of temporal punishments. However, this non-remembrance is not by reason of omniscience, by which he is infallible and immutable, but by reason of vindictive justice. I will not remember iniquities, says Jehovah, namely to the effect of vindictive and punishing justice: by which, of course, sins are also said to be covered, not in the act of omniscience, by which all things are γυμνὰ κὶ τετραχηλισμένα (naked and laid bare) to divine eyes, Heb. IV. v. 13, but in the court of justification, and that through the intervening justice of Christ. Whence the Papists ineptly conclude from that covering in Ps. XXXII. 1, Rom. IV. 7, that a total deletion of sins, even by reason of their root, occurs in baptism. For this ἐπικάλυψις (covering) does not only regard original sin and inherent vices, which are to be covered through justification, but also actual sins placed in transient acts, all of which come under the name of ἁμαρτιῶν (sins). But those transient acts, by the very fact that they are such, do not have, as they say, physical entity or real existence in man, except insofar as some memory of them still remains in the conscience, but they only survive morally in the divine memory, just as the crimes of a thief are in the knowledge of a Judge. Whence we cannot establish such a real covering or even extinction with respect to them, unless we wish to say that a justified man causes the memory of past sins to be emitted through justification, or even that the knowledge of sins is blotted out from the divine mind itself, which is impossible. The blessed Hunnius here noted a triple difference between the Old and New Testament: First, that the old one was violated by the people; but this new one, inscribed on the hearts of the faithful, is not violated. Then that the transgression of the old covenant rendered the Israelites hateful to God; but the new covenant makes believers grateful and acceptable to GOD, by conferring the remission of sins so effectively that the Lord does not wish to remember them anymore. Third, that the former covenant left men imperfect; but this latter one makes them perfect, bestowing a full and consummated knowledge of God, so that it would give the effect of the N. Testament forever, with the old one vanishing in turn. From all of which he gathers that the dignity of the New Testament is greater, and therefore also that of the annexed Priesthood of Christ, than the Old Testament and its Priesthood was of old.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Καὶ ὀυ μὴ διδάξωσιν ἕκαστος τὸν πολίτην ἀυτο͂υ, καὶ ἕκαστος τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἀυτο͂υ, λέγων, γνῶθι τὸν Κύριον, ὅτι πάντες εἰδήσουσί με ἀπὸ μικρο͂υ ἕως μεγάλου ἀυτῶν) Dixere Graeci Interpretes ὀυ μὴ διδάξωσιν in potentiali, id est, non opus erit ut doceant. Πολίτην hic dixit pro συμπολίτην. In Ebraeo hic רעהו; at Levitici XIX. 18. בן עמו. Sic & Latini dicunt, meus municeps, id est, ejusdem mecum mu- nicipii particeps. Olim qui aliqua de re dubitabant, con- sulebant Prophetas, & ab iis officium suum edocebantur, 1. Sam. IX. 9. Cognoscere Dominum, id est, Domini vo- luntatem. Post reditum a Babylone omnes, qui non per- petuo labore victum cogerentur quaerere, legem edisce- bant. Et sic Christi praecepta, quae lex est nova, facile edi- scunt omnes Christiani. Vide 1. Cor. I, 5. Joh. VI. 45. A minimo ad maximum: id est, adolescentes & senes. Eadem loquutio Genes. XIX. 11. 1. Sam. V. 9. XXX. 2. 19. 2. Reg. XXIV. 46. 2. Paral. XXXI. 15. XXXIV. 30. Esa. XXII. 24. Μεγάλου ἀυτῶν, id est, inter ipsos.

Cognoscere Dominum, non est tantum Do- mini voluntatem, sed imprimis etiam Dominum quoad naturam cognoscere, quae cognitio & fides Ecclesiae DEI est propria, in qua consistere ater- nam vitam docemur, Joh. XVII. 3. Neque de vo- luntate legali jam agitur, quaev. 10. jam compre- hensa, cum de inscriptione legis facta promissio, sed de voluntate Evangelica, de qua 1. Tim. II. 4. 2. Petr. III. 9. lege non ignota fuit sive reducibus e Babylone, sive aliis Judaeis, ac ne gentibus qui- dem, cum natura cordibus inscripta sit, Rom. II. vers. 14. De alia itaq; cognitione hic agitur vo- luntatis, nempe in Evangelio patefactae: Quod te- mere & perverse in legem transformat Grotius, quum lex & Evangelium ἀντιδιηρημένως opposita sint. Nec vero nuda tantum cognitio DEI, sed cum fiduciali gratiae divinae apprehensione intel- ligitur, h. e. vera fides. Conf. Jer. IX. 23. 1. Cor. I. 31. Esa. LIII. 11. Quod beneficium vi foederis novi omnibus promittitur a minimo ad maximum, quia nemo ab eodem a Deo excluditur, etsi culpa propria plerique sese ab eodem excludant, 1. Tim. II. 4. Esa. LIV. 13. Joh. VI. 45. Nihil autem hic lo- cus patrocinatur Schvvenckfeldianis, docentibus, Deum absque ministerio Verbi sui agnitionem & conversionem in corde hominum operari fi- naliter. Quandoquidem, juxta B. Hunnium, Pro- pheta hic agit de beneficio Novi Testamenti, non tantum, ut in hac vita inchoatur, sed etiam quem- admodum in futura vita perficitur: ubi certe non amplius opus erit ministerio docendi, sed omnia erunt in clarissima luce exposita. In hac autem vi- ta non immediate, sed per Verbum & sacramenta regenerationis gratiam in nobis operatur Dominus. Siquidem fides ex auditu Verbi Dei est, Roman. X. Haec B. Hunnius. Ad statum futuri seculi refe- runt etiam Theodoretus, Augustinus l. de Spiritu & lit. cap. 24. 25. Primasius, Anshelmus, quae ta- men cum caeteris promissionibus ad statum prae- sentis seculi pertinent. Ideoque Hieronymus, no- tante Estio, interpretatur, promitti filiis Israel fu- turum, ut nequaquam Judaicos quaerant magistros, & mandata & traditiones hominum, sed doceantur a Spiritu Sancto. Chrysostomus exponit de mani- festatione legis Evangelicae per omnes gentes. Theo- phylactus & Oecumenius negari putant laboriosam institutionem, eo quod facili negotio persuadeatur hominibus fides Christi. S. Thomas in solis primis novi Testamenti fundatoribus, id est, Apostolis a Christo perfecte edoctis, censet impletam esse hanc promissionem, siquidem pertineat ad praesens secu- lum; alioqui propensior in eam sententiam, quæ re- fert ad statum beatorum. Nonnulli generalius ex- ponunt, tanquam dictum de fidelibus Ecclesiæ pri- mitivæ. Rursus alia quædam expositio refert ad to- tum tempus gratiæ, non tamen ad totam fidelium multitudinem, sed ad majorem & meliorem par- tem, cujus numerus Deo cognitus sit. Alia denique, quæ est Francisci Riveræ, extendit ad omnes omni- no fideles. Quoniam, inquit, de omnibus & singu- lis Christi fidelibus verum est, eos per fidem scire Deum & Christum ejus. Cui videtur Estius cal- culum adjicere, pertinere hæc asserens ad omnes & solos filios Novi Testam. qui sunt filii promis- sionis, unde civem ac fratrem nominet, id est, hominem ejusdem civitatis ac familiæ, quæ alia non est, quam Ecclesia credentium, & conferens locum 1. Joh. II. 27. Non necesse habetis, ut ali- quis doceat vos, sed sicut unctio ejus docet vos de omnibus. Rationem ex præcedentibus petit; quia legem DEI OMNES habebunt inscriptam in cordibus suis. Sed hic non agi de voluntate legali jam monuimus. Alii, notante B. Gerhardo, respondent, verba hæc, Non docebit ultra vir proxi- mum suum &c. accipienda esse comparate, videli- cet respectu habito Primò, ad Evangelii per totum orbem prædicationem. Vetus illud legææ pactum co- gnoverant soli Judæi Psal. CXLVII. 19. Rom. IX. 4. unde gentiles illud cognituri opus habebant discere à Judæis: Sed in Novo Testamento, non solis Judæis, sed omnibus gentibus fœdus gratiæ erat prædican- dum. Secundo ad Ecclesiæ in Novo Testamento am- plitudinem, quod in Novo Testamento major nume- rus futurus sit eorum, qui salutari Dei cognitione sunt imbuti, quam in Veteri Testamento, cum solen- nis & publica Verbi prædicatio non amplius ad unam gentem sit adstricta, sed omnibus populis com- munis. Inde Chrysostomus exponit de manifesta- tione legis Evangelicæ per omnes gentes. Tertio ad perfectiorem & pleniorem Dei notitiam tempore Novi Testamenti sequuturam, quam fuit in Vete- ri, cum hodie puerulus, in Catechesi rectè institu- tus, explicatius intelligat mysterium Evangelii de Christo, quam olim in Veteri Testamento aliquis ex præcipuis Sacerdotibus, Es. XI. v. 9. terra repleta est scientia Domini, cap. XXX. 26. lux Lunæ erit, sicut lux Solis, Jer. XXIV. 7. dabo eis cor ad scien- dum me. Quarto ad institutionem minus laborio- sam ac difficilem, quod propter spiritualem Novi Testamenti cultum & uberiorem Dei gratiam non sit opus futurum magno labore & molestia in do- cendis piis: præcedit enim, Ego scribam legem meam in cordibus ipsorum, ut sic in bisce Prophetici va- ticinii verbis statuatur tacita oppositio inter vetus ac novum Testamentum, inter Legis & Evangelii doctrinam: illa est ministerium literæ; hæc verò Spiritus: Illa tabulis lapideis; hæc vero cordibus hominum per Spiritum Sanctum inscribitur, & gratiam Spiritus conjunctam habet, 2. Cor. III. v. 3. & 6. Simpliciffima responsio est, quia non differentia temporis ante Christum & post Christum, sed veteris & novi fœderis traditur, ac beneficia sub Novo Testamento, quæ tempori Veteris Te- stamenti deneganda certe non sunt, explicantur, nihil aliud doceri, quam quod illa salvifica DEI notitia sic comparata sit, quæ in Evangelio reve- lata, ut non humana informatione caro & san- guis revelet, sed sola Verbi divini patefactione constet, Matth. XI. vers. 27. cap. XVI. vers. 17. vi fœderis gratiæ omnibus divinitus conceden- da sit, omnesque à DEO, non tamen immedia- te, sed mediante Verbo, Verbique ministerio edocendi sint. De lege potest vir proximum suum informare, Deut. VI. 7. quam etiam lumine natu- ræ præditi norunt, & unus præ alio accuratius ejusdem beneficio introspicit: Sed de Evangelio omnes oportet esse θεοδιδάκτης, Es. LIV. 13. Uni- versalis Evangelii prædicatio post Christi adven- tum, & Ecclesiæ in Novo Testamento amplitudo, necnon plenior notitia, pertinent ad distinctio- nem temporis Veteris & Novi Testamenti, non ve- ro fœderis veteris & novi, de qua hic è Propheta agit Apostolus. Oppositio vero illa inter Vetus & Novum Testamentum, inter legis & Evangelii doctrinam, quod illa sit ministerium literæ, hæc vero Spiritus, &c. sola huc facit, sed non præcise ad præsens beneficium de cognitione & fide sal- vifica divinitus concedenda, & ad verba illa ex- plicanda, omnes cognoscent me, quum vis & na- tura Spiritus etiam ad alia beneficia hic recensita se extendat.

Plenius & diversas sententias de hoc loco con- fert, & mentem Apostoli explicat B. Dorscheus: Nonnulli, inquit, quia non inveniunt, quomodo in Ecclesia militante hoc non futurum sit, ad trium- phantem istud referunt. Ita Augustinus de Spir. & lit. cap. 24. & 28. Theodor. & Cajet. in comment. h. l. Theophylactus & Oecumenius non de informa- tione simpliciter, sed de laboriosa institutione id in- terpretantur, scil. non tanto cum labore conjunctum fore in Novo Testamento, ut ad cognitionem DEI veri deducantur homines, tum quia omnia in N. T. longe futura sunt clariora, quam fuerant in Veteri, ubi typis & umbris involuta erant pleraq;,; adeoque plurimarum ceremoniarum observatio il- lius doctrina constabat : tum etiam quia accessuræ sunt novæ revelationes, quæ expeditiora & facilio- ra factura sint omnia. Hieronymus ad doctrinam Judæorum Magistrorum, qui jam olim mandatis & traditionibus humanis gentiles suos oneraverunt, istud refert, nimirum in Novo Test. futuram de- structionem & confutationem traditionum πατρο- παραδότων. Thomas h. l. verba hæc ad Apostolos re- stringit. Ribera ista verba ad cognitionem cum af- fectu refert : Eo, inquit, tempore, quo Apostoli eorum discipuli vivebant, Christiani magna ex parte cha- ritate fervebant, & sancti omnes appellabantur, ut passim videmus in epistolis Pauli Ebr. III. 2. Cor. I. Tales enim erant tum Christiani, ut si Apostolorum de illis præconia audiamus, recte in illos convenire hanc Jeremiæ prophetiam non dubitemus, quamvis nonnulli fuerint improbi, qui multitudini, de qua hæc dicuntur, nocere non debent. Itaque eo tempore non docebat unusquisque proximum suum, dicens, cognosce Dominum, id est, ama Dominum. Nam cognoscere aut scire Dominum, ita solet dici in Scri- ptura, ut 1. Paral. XXVIII. 9. 1. Job. II. 3. Quare recte Chaldæus vertit : Et non docebunt ultra vir proximum suum, & vir fratrem suum, dicendo, scitote timere Dominum, quia omnes discent, ut sci- ant timorem Dei. Etenim videntes novi fideles, se per gratiam Christi tot peccatis & tam terribili damna- tione liberatos, Deo gratias agebant, & illum toto corde diligebant. Quare non est huic Prophetiæ con- trarium, si quis fratrem hortaretur, ut ardentius Deum amet, quam amabat, aut si Apostoli scribant ad Ecclesiam, aut ad discipulos, ut Christum ament. Volunt enim multos ad amorem ardentiorem excita- re, nec illi seculo scribebant, sed futuris etiam, in quibus multi admonitione indigent. Sed & illo seculo erant nonnulli Christiani, qui Deum non amabant, & quibus jure diceretur, ut cognoscerent Dominum. Etenim Prophetia non est de omnibus Christianis illius seculi, sed de ipsis Ecclesiis, quoniam magna pars uniuscujusque Ecclesiæ tunc Deum amabant.

Quod enim de aliqua Ecclesia dicitur, id in majori & minori ejus parte verùm esse satis est. Sic Ribe- ra, qui, quoniam videt, priora duo beneficia, nimi- rum inscriptionem veritatis salvifica in corda ho- minum, & spiritualem gratiosam unionem, univer- salia esse, nec ad tempus primitiva Ecclesia dunta- xat pertinere, adeoq́; hoc ipsum pariter esse exten- dendum, tandem eo progreditur, ut asserat, nihil ve- tare, quo minus de nobis quoq́; & omnibus Christi fidelibus, quod v. 11. dicitur, explicetur. Conf. Esa. LIV. 13. ubi promittitur in Novo Testam. omnes fore θεοδιδάκτως & tamen Joh. VI. 44. 45. ad ordi- narium perpetuumq́; ad Deum perveniendi modum refertur. Itaq́;, inquit, id tantum volunt Prophetæ, inutilem fore omnem humanam in docendo sacra fidei mysteria diligentiam, nisi Deus interius assi- stat, mentem illustrans & vera esse persuadens, quæ docentur: quia neque fide cognoscere, multo minus ex affectu charitatis veritati cognita adhærere pos- sumus, nisi Deus speciali sua ope & auxilio nos do- ceat interius. Et postea: Nostrum locum quod con- cernit, tum hoc dicitur à Propheta, quod jam in- dicavit post alios Ribera, idq́; ex natura Novi Te- stamenti. Nam Vetus Test. doctrinam quidem legis ex se & per se inculcabat, adeoq́; unusquisque pro- ximum suum fratremque suum ad ejus cognitio- nem deducebat, sed non aderat peculiaris aliqua vis vivifica & salvifica in ista doctrina legis, ut exinde ad cognitionem & amplexum Jehova illuminaretur & excitaretur. Dicebatur quidem in doctrina legis, γνῶθι τὸν Κύριον, & diliges Dominum Deum tuum in toto corde tuo & in tota anima tua Deut. VI. 5.
