Sed hoc dicere non suppeditabat facere; non ita futurum est in Novo Test. inquit Propheta, non inefficaciter & sine viribus cœlitus infusis docebitur Novi Test. Evangelium, sicut docebat lex, qua Vetus Testamen- tum nititur. Cæterum aliud etiam in hoc beneficio comprehenditur, quod ad Novi Testamenti excel- lentiam maximopere pertinet, nimirum universa- litas prædicationis doctrinæ cœlestis, ut non futurum sit hoc, quod scilicet ministerium ordinarium Novi Test. non sit substiturum in certa aliqua gente, in qua quis proximum, concivem, & fratrem suum ordinarie tantum informet, & ad agnitionem veri- tatis beatifica deducat, sicut in populo Israëlítico con- tigit, ubi quanquam ex gentibus etiam admissi fue- runt, qui τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ Israëlitis concredita am- plexi sunt, & religionis causa iisdem sese sociarunt juxta preces Salomoneas, 1. Reg. VIII. 41. Quan- quam insuper tum per peregrinationes, negotiatio- nes, imo etiam deportationes & exilia Israëlitarum veritas salvifica gentibus innotuerit; ordinarium tamen ministerium inter gentem Israëliti-cam tan- tum substitit. Hoc, inquit Propheta, non futurum est in Novo Test. cum solenniter promulgabitur. Exten- detur enim ministerium in omnes gentes, id quod complementum ipsum docuit, Matth. XXVIII. 19. Marc. XVI. 15. ratione mandati; ratione comple- menti vero Eph. IV. 11. Rom. XV. 19. Col. I. 23. Itaq́; negativa ista loquutio, ὀυ μὴ διδάξωσιν supplenda est per μόνον, uti plurimis in locis tum Veteris tum Novi Testamenti, supplendum esse loquutionem negative conceptam Philologia sacra monet; Ut sensus sit de Novo Testam. solenniter per Christum promulgato, non docuit unusquisque tantum suum fratrem, su- um concivem, suum proximum, & illi tantum præ- dicabit cognitionem Domini: conf. Gen. XXXII. 28. 1. Sam. VIII. 7. Post operose contra Cloppenburgium, contendentem, nullam fuisse sub veteri œconomia Mosaica in gentibus aliis vocationem ad salutem disputat; cujus exceptionein de Ninevitis, & quod Jonas non ad gentis præputiatæ vocationem & conversionem extraordinariam missus fuerit, sed ad circumcisos, si non Judæos, saltim Abrahami- tas, aliosq; socios religionis Judaicæ prolixe re- fellit, & ad locum Pfal. CXLVII. 19. 20. respondet: De communicationis jurium divinorum non actu, sed modo loquitur. Nam quæ inter Israëlitas circa jurium divinorum communicationem factæ sunt di- vinæ Φανερώσεις, gentibus aliis nequaquam conti- gerunt, quanquam jura ipsa gentibus communicanda esse manifestum sit, ex Deut. IV. 6. ubi hæc ipsa jura propterea ab Israëlitis diligenter observanda esse, di- citur, quia sint sapientia & prudentia eorum ante oculos populorum, qui audientes ista statuta dicent, tantum gens ista maxima populus sapiens est & pru- dens. Hinc Act. XVII. 30. tempora gentilismi vocan- tur tempora ignorantiæ, sed non ex defectu volunta- tis salvificæ orta. Nam hoc contra disputationem Apostoli antecedentem pugnat, v. 24. 25. 26. 27. Ubi asseritur, Deum propterea & creasse hominem, & post lapsum etiam per superficiem orbis terrarum dispersisse, ut quærat Deum, ubiq; sese ingerentem; verum ex affectu malitiosæ imperitiæ. Postmodum reversus ad hunc nostrum locum ita subjicit: Fu- turum, inquit Propheta, sub Novi Testamenti pate- factione, ut omnes sciant Dominum à minimo usq; ad maximum. Verbum activum non tam de actu, quam facultate & debito hoc modo explicandum est: Quod in N. T. non tantum remote omnibus osten- dendus sit aditus ad cognitionem salvificam divi- nam, sed proxime atque intime per missionem exer- citus Evangelistarum, ita ut in sinu fere quisq; suo Verbum salutis habere possit, Rom. X. 8. & quod fa- cillima quadam, planissimaq; ratione non sic in Ve- teri Testamento sub umbris & typis sapientia cæle- stis communicanda, adeo, ut facile, modo velint, omnes illuminari queant. Imo & nova atq; imme- diata vocatione omnes obligati sint ad cognoscen- dum Dominum Actor. XVII. 30. per actualem fidei exhibitionem, v. 31. cui proposito divino facultatem facilitatemque largienti, & debitum universis im- ponenti, si eventus non respondeat, ut singuli pa- reant, id tamen efficitur, ut ex illa gratiosa divina συγκαταβάσει infiniti inter gentes convertantur, qui conversi non fuissent sine tali Novi Test. dilatatione.

Et hoc est, quod Apostolus Rom. XI. 25. dicit, pleni- tudinem gentium in Ecclesiam ingredi. Vers. 12. Ὅτι ἵλεως ἔσομαι ταῖς ἀδικίαις αὐτῶν καὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν καὶ τῶν ἀνομιῶν αὐτῶν ὀὐ μὴ μνησθῶ ἔτι) Quod hic in Ebræo est כִּי & in Græco ὅτι optime vertitur per profecto. Ἵλεων εἶναι sicut ἱλάσκεσθαι supra II. 17. in sen- su vulgari est pœnas exigere nolle criminum: in sensu mystico est ita sanare animum ut crimina non redeant. Sic & non meminisse eorum sublimiori sensu Deus dicitur, ubi nihil est novi quod vetera in memoriam reducat. Pro ἀδικίαις in Ebræo est עֲוֹנָם. Ea vox significat facta omnia contra æquum. Pro duabus vocibus Græcis τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν, καὶ τῶν ἀνομιῶν αὐτῶν una est in Ebræo לְחַטָּאתָם, quæ ita generalis est, ut omnia alia peccata quæ sub nomine ἀδικίας non solent venire, comprehen- dat. Syrus & Latinus unam tantum vocem legerunt hoc loco & Græci quidam, ita ut altera harum videri possit irrepsisse ex glossemate. Nulla est causa, cur non relinquatur particu- læ sua propria & receptior significatio. Causa enim superiorum beneficiorum, nempe inscri- ptionis legis, & gratiosæ conservationis divinæ, imo etiam uberioris illustrationis & confirmatio- nis fidei est gratuita peccatorum remissio. Recte

Paræus : Hæc est promissio Evangelii de gratuita peccatorum remissione & justificatione per fidem in Christum, in qua præcipua differentia utriusq; fœ- deris sita est. Vetus enim promittebat vitam præ- stantibus legem, mortem minabatur transgredien- tibus. Novum veniam peccatorum transgressori- bus proponit in Christo: ἵλεως ἔσομαι propitius ero: Hæc promissio satisfactionem Christi inclydit, quia Deus non est propitius peccatoribus, nisi propter Christum Mediatorem, qui ideo dicitur ἱλασμὸς propitiatio seu propitiator pro peccatis totius mun- di. Ubi iterum à Grotio pervertitur textus gemi- ni sensus commento. Nam remissio peccatorum est & culpæ & pœnæ condonatio, quam vero sen- su mystico esse animi eam sanationem, ut crimi- na non redeant, est confundere sanctificationem cum justificatione. Denique cur è paucis exem- plaribus cætera omnia in suspicionem corruptio- nis adducamus? Nimis pronus est ad tales suspi- ciones Grotius: quæ vero nihil nisi incertitudi- nem canonis pariunt. B. Dorscheus de his ita ha- bet: Vox ἀδικίας neq; apud LXX. Interpretes repe- ritur, neque etiam peculiarem vocem in fontibus apud Jeremiam sibi respondentem habet. Nec Sy- riaca translatio vel ἀδικίαν vel ἀνομίαν habet, al- terutrum sane superfluum censuit, quia unum tan- tum expressit. Neq; Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius utrumq; posuerunt. Neque tamen male additum esse in Codicibus Græcis Novi Testamenti dicendum existimamus, quemadmodum Franc. Ri- bera h. l. censuit. Grotius producit MS. ubi ἀνομιῶν præterita sit mentio. Nihil enim exprimunt ista vo- cabula, nisi unum aliquod objectum, scil. quicquid legi divinæ adversatur in homine sive originaliter sive actualiter. Schlichtingius h. l. p. 348. & seqq. existimat, Apostolum voluisse indicare differentiam misericordiæ & remissionis in Novo Test. dispensan- dæ ab ea, qua sub V. T. fuit. Hinc notat voces inju- stitiarum, iniquitatum, transgressionum, quibus hic peccata designantur, docere, agi hic de quorumvis etiam gravissimorum peccatorum remissione, & ta- lem propriam esse Novo Testam. promissionem, & hic elucere id, quod supra dictum fuit: Novum Test. esse in præstantioribus promissionibus sancitum, quam Vetus. Sed confundit Schlichtingius revera id, quod subat sub Veteri Test. & vi Veteris Test. Vi enim V. T. gratiosa peccatorum remissio, etiam minimo- rum, nulla locum habuit, quod diferte ex Deut. XXVII. 26. Apostolus evicit Gal. III. 7. Sub V. au- tem Testamento, quanquam non vi illius, sed hujus Novi, non tantum minora peccata, sed & gravissi- ma remittebantur, quod vel exemplo Davidis Psal. LI, 3. & seqq. liquet. Male etiam Schlichtingius hoc loco annotat, literalem horum verborum sen- sum fuisse, quod Deus Judaicum populum ex capti- vitate Babylonica liberaturus, & sic præterita illo- rum gravissima peccata obliteraturus esset, sublatis nimirum pœnis eorum temporariis, quo tanto be- neficio populus Deo mirifice obstringi, & ad ipsum imposterum constanter colendum adduci debuit. Sa- ne enim de liberatione ex captivitate Babylonica hæc quidem promissio accipi nullo modo potest, ut supra quoque annotatum est. Unde fateri cogitur ipse Schlichtingius, interpretationem de liberatione ex captivitate Babylonica longe exiliorem esse, quam ut verbis tam augustis plene & in solidum respon- deat. Neque enim per eam tunc ullum fœdus No- vum & à priori diversum proprie loquendo Deum cum populo inivisse: neque illud beneficium tanta- rum prorsus fuisse virium, ut populum in officio continere perpetuo posset, atque ideo apparere, Spi- ritum Sanctum alium quendam hoc longe augustio- rem designare sensum. Hæc ille.

Cum vero Deus ita remittat peccata, ut eorum non amplius recordari velit, eadem nec addu- cum iri in judicium, & plene remitti, ut non reservetur pœna temporalis, qua conscientias an- gunt & terrent Papistæ, manifestum est. deleri dicuntur Ef. XLIV. 22. & in profundum ma- ris projici, Mich. VII. 19. & culpa eorum sic con- donatur, ut pœna etiam remittatur, Matth. XIIX. v. 27. B. Dorscheus ita de hisce : Οὐ μὴ μνησθῶ ἔτι non recordabor amplius, verba negantia fortiffime affirmant. Etenim non-recordatio suspensionem omnium pœnarum, & integram plane indeficien- temque restitutionem amicitia divinæ sive chari- tatis innuit. Pluribus verbis ista exposita est Mich. VII. 18. 19. & 20. Non itaque pro objecto tantum habet culpam & pœnam æternam, sed & tempora- riam. Si enim hæc adhuc esset residua, tunc adhuc peccatorum recordaretur ratione pœnarum tempo- ralium. Est autem hæc non-recordatio non ratio- ne omniscientiæ, quo infallibilis est & immutabilis, sed ratione vindicativæ justitiæ. Non recordabor iniquitatum, inquit Jehovah, nimirum ad effectum justitiæ vindicatricis & punitricis : Quo scilicet etiam peccata dicuntur tegi, non in actu omniscien- tiæ, quo omnia sunt γυμνὰ κὶ τετραχηλισμένα ocu- lis divinis, Ebr. IV. v. 13. sed in foro justificationis, idque per justitiam Christi intervenientem. Unde inepte Pontificii ex tectione illa Psal. XXXII. 1. Rom. IV. 7. concludunt, totalem peccatorum etiam ratio- ne radicis in baptismo fieri deletionem. Nam hæc ἐπικάλυψις non tantum originale peccatum respicit & inhærentia vitia, quæ per justificationem tegen- da sint, sed etiam actualia peccata in actibus trans- euntibus posita, quæ omnia veniunt nomine ἁμαρ- τιῶν. Isti vero actus transeuntes eo ipso, quod tales sint, non habent entitatem, ut loquuntur, physicam, sive existentiam realem in homine, nisi quatenus in conscientia adhuc aliqua superest illorum memo- ria, sed moraliter tantum supersunt in memoria di- vina, quemadmodum latronis scelera in notitia sunt Judicis. Unde ejusmodi realem tectionem aut etiam extinctionem respectu eorum statuere non possumus, nisi velimus dicere, hominem justificatum esse peccatorum præteritorum per justificationem emittere memoriam, aut etiam ex ipsa mente divi- na peccatorum notitiam expungi, quod impossibile est. B. Hunnius hic triplicem differentiam nota- vit Veteris & Novi Testamenti : Primo quod ve- tus illud violatum sit à populo; hoc vero novum cordibus fidelium inscriptum non violetur. Deinde quod transgressio veteris pacti exoson Israelitas red- diderit Deo; pactum vero novum DEO gratos & acceptos efficiat credentes, conferendo remissionem peccatorum tam efficaciter, ut Dominus non velit eorum recordari amplius. Tertio quod prius pactum homines reliquit imperfectos; hoc vero posterius per- fectos illos efficit, plenam & consummatam Dei co- gnitionem tribuens, adeo ut effectus N. Test. daret in æternum, vicissim evanescente veteri. Ex qui- bus omnibus colligit, majorem esse dignitatem No- vi Test. & proinde quoq́. adjuncti Sacerdotii Christi, quàm olim fuerit Veteris Test. ejusq́; Sacerdotii.

## 8:13
V. 13. Ἐν τῷ λέγειν καινὴν πεπαλάιωκε τὴν πρώτην (In that he says a new, he has made the first old) that is, he shows it to be useless, such as decrepit old men are. For this is a similar figure to the one above at I. 6.

What the passage in chap. I. 6 has to do with this, I do not grasp. Nevertheless, the sense of Grotius can be admitted if those things which the Apostle added in the following words are joined: Τὸ παλαιόμενον κὶ γηράσκον (that which is becoming old and aging), which things are indeed more rightly unfolded distinctly by Theophylact: He interprets, he says, the Prophetic saying, when he calls this new testament of ours old, he clearly argues that the former one is seen to be old. But that which is becoming ancient and aging is near to destruction. The revenue, Theophylact further saying, through the Prophet more confidently attacks the law, arguing that ours now has germinated and flourishes more day by day. Therefore, from the Prophet's words it receives the name of antiquity, but from itself it added old age, and finally, it added destruction as being owed to the law, as if to say: for it is not that this new one of ours did not opportunely remove the old, but by reason of old age and antiquity it compelled it to cease, because it was weak and clearly useless, just as he says elsewhere; For the weakness of the law, in which it is weaker, through the flesh, Rom. VIII. 3. The blessed Hunnius succinctly encompasses everything, so that he applies them to the scope of the Apostle, thus: Hence the Apostle now subsumes, and from the Prophetic testimony infers that God, by promising a New Testament, simultaneously indicates the abrogation of the old, whence it is a consequence that together with the old covenant, the old Priesthood also had to vanish and be abrogated.

Τὸ δὲ παλαιούμενον καὶ γηράσκον ἐγγὺς ἀφανισμοῦ (Now that which is becoming old and aging is near to destruction). He secretly prophesies that both the temple and the commonwealth of the Jews will soon perish. That happened almost ten years after this epistle was written. Death follows old age. Luke could have learned this both from Dan. IX. 22 and from those things which he himself placed in the words of Christ in the Gospel XXI. 20.

He assumes that Luke is the author of the epistle, which we refuted above. But whether a prophecy about the destruction of the temple and the Commonwealth is held here is doubtful. Nothing else is said than that because the legal covenant as an old one has been antiqued and has grown old, in that another new one was introduced by the Prophet, that one is ἐγγὺς ἀφανισμοῦ (near to destruction). But it would have been such, even if neither the temple nor the Commonwealth of the Jews had perished. If you listen to Estius, such is the reasoning of the Apostle: This is a new testament; Therefore that is old: furthermore, that which is old grows older day by day, and (as in men) ages: but that which grows old and ages hastens to destruction and death. From which he leaves it to be concluded that the former testament finally had to be finished; and in the fullness of time, that is, with the New Testament revealed and confirmed through Christ, it received an end. Experience proves the force of the argument. The Scriptures also agree, Levit. XXVI. you shall cast out the old from the coming of the new, and 2 Cor. V. Old things have passed away, behold all things have become new. Briefly: From the antiquation of the former Testament it infers the abrogation or ἀφανισμὸν of the same. The Vulgate renders it destruction. But it is from ἀφανίζομαι, I disappear, I vanish from sight. By it, therefore, it is noted that upon the appearing of the new, the old disappears, and vanishes from the sight both of God, who wishes to deal with the faithful not according to the rigor of the old, but the grace of the new, and of man, because the faithful do not look upon the law with its precepts and rigorous and intolerable threats; but have their eyes fixed solely on Christ, who is τέλος νόμου, Rom. X. 4. and performed obedience to the law for us, and bore the curse of the law, and they embrace him by faith; whence the κατάκριμα of the law vanishes, Rom. VIII. 1. Beautifully the blessed Winckelmann discusses these things in disp. XVIII. Tom. IV. Giessenf. thes. 84. & following, discusses these things: And indeed since the Fathers would have made the old covenant void, unless the Lord had antiquated and abrogated it for us, διὰ τὸ αὐτῆς ἀνωφελὲς καὶ ἀσθενὲς (inasmuch as it could not lead us to perfection) by instituting the New Testament and by giving and sending a new mediator and Redeemer, we would have had to perish eternally. Therefore, just as the Old T. condemns and mortifies the old man corrupted by sin: so it vivifies the new man by the abolition of the old man, namely by the remission of sins through faith in Christ, and makes him new. For we are a new creature in Christ Jesus: Old things have passed away, behold all things have become new, 2 Cor. V. 17. Furthermore, the law also restrains and bridles the old man by external discipline: But the New Testament not only vivifies and consoles, but also makes him so new that he begins to serve God in newness of Spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter,

Rom. VII. 6. And thus that old man, who is on the outside, is corrupted, and he who is on the inside is renewed from day to day. And this is the benefit of renewal, which the Lord promised through the Prophet that He would give a new heart and a new Spirit, etc. Ezech. XI. 19. XVIII. 26. 27. Augustine also noted this reason for the naming: The Old Testament, he says, pertains to the old man, from whom it is necessary for man to begin: but the new pertains to the new man, to whom man ought to pass from oldness. The blessed Chemnitius had preceded him, and had handed down these distinctions of the Old and New Testament in almost the same way, part III. LL. Theol. de discrim. V. & N. T. p. 91. and had deduced the same from the property of the word בלה, he is consumed, he is grown old, he is consumed by old age, Ps. XXXII. 3. Deut. VIII. 4. XXIX. 5. Jos. IX. 4. Es. XXXIIX. 27. Psal. CII. 26.

Pareus discourses concerning the present passage of the Apostle, how the two Testaments, old and new, are spoken of, when nevertheless there is one eternal covenant? And he observes that ברית, a covenant or Testament established by GOD, and entered into with men from the beginning of the world to the end, is in reality one, perpetual, eternal, and immutable, namely, a spiritual doctrine offering to men in the name of GOD blessing and eternal salvation, obliging men in turn to render obedience and gratitude to GOD, which doctrine is called a covenant from the form of the agreement between God and men, and a Testament from the manner of its sanction, because it is sealed by the death of the Testator, Christ. But because, he says, it seemed good to God to inform that doctrine in one way formerly, and in another way in the latter times, and to dispense His benefits, therefore Scripture often speaks of one covenant and testament as if of two, and expressly names two testaments, old and new, Jerem. XXXI. Gal. IV. and in this place. He followed Bucer and Calvin, Inst. book II, chap. 10, and others (such as Peter Martyr, class I, Loc. Theol. loc. XVI, § 2, seqq.; Ursinus, part II, Catech. p. 130; Grynæus, vol. II, disp. Theol. p. 125, 260; Bucanus, loc. XXII, p. 200). Whose opinion the blessed Chemnitius, in the cited place, explained thus: that by the word of covenant or Testament they understand only the doctrine concerning the person and benefits of Christ the Mediator, and just as that doctrine was revealed and handed down in the time of the Patriarchs, Moses, and the Prophets, clothed or wrapped in various shadows of ceremonies, this they call the Old Testament. But just as, with that veil of figures removed by Christ and the Apostles, the doctrine of the Gospel was handed down, this they call the New Testament; and thus in reality, regarding the matter or substance, they maintain that the Old and New Testament are not two different things, but one and the same, but that they differ only regarding the form or mode of revelation, and regarding the measure of the gifts. However, the blessed Chemnitius judges that the thing itself of this opinion (namely, that Christ the Savior is the same, the Gospel is the same, as we commonly say, the faith is the same, the justification of the saints in the Old and in the New Testament is the same) is true: but that the question in this place is, what does Scripture properly understand when it distinguishes between the Old and New Testament? Wherefore it is to be observed: I. That the names of covenant, pact, and testament are indeed not rarely used indiscriminately in this matter; just as the word ברית is general, and is rendered by Greek and Latin interpreters now as Testament, now as covenant, now as pact, and what the LXX Interpreters and the Apostle here explained by διαθήκην, Aquila interpreted by συνθήκην; yet, speaking accurately, these are different things. For a pact is commonly called the agreement of two or more concerning any matter to be either given or done, conceived in express words. A covenant or συνθήκη, according to Suidas, is such an obligation by which dissenting parties agree on certain conditions to be mutually performed concerning society, commerce, peace, and truces, and other things of that kind. But a Testament is the expression of our will concerning that which one wished to be done after his death, or a disposition concerning the last will of one about to die, by which he distributes his goods among his heirs, whence the difference is clear, both because a Testament proceeds from one who has the disposition in his own power, whereas for covenants and pacts the consent of many is required; and because a Testament concerns inheritance and other wills of those who are dying, while covenants and pacts do not precisely concern the disposition of one who is not dying nor an inheritance; and because a Testament can be changed before death, and has no strength unless it is confirmed by death, Heb. IX. 16, whereas pacts and covenants can neither be changed by one party, nor do they have need of confirmation by death; and because these are sometimes strengthened by an oath, Heb. VI. 16, whereas in a testamentary action an oath is not used at all; and finally, because covenants consist of a natural obligation, where there is a certain analogy and proportion between the contracting parties, which is not required for testaments, such as it would be absurd to imagine between God and men, Creator and creatures. That there is, however, some tempering of covenant and Testament here, and that it can be called a federal testament and a testamentary covenant in a certain respect when one deals with the divine covenant and testament, was already observed in the preface to the New Testament. The blessed Dorscheus: That sanction of our Mediator participates in the nature of both covenant and Testament. For it is also a Testament on account of the most ample bequeathed goods and the necessity of intervening death: which two are not necessarily required in a covenant. For there is no need that one of the covenanters should transcribe and destine all his goods to another, or even devote himself to death for the other of the covenanters. But the sanction of our Mediator from the covenant has a certain immutability and personal obligation. For from a testament, if the death of the testator follows, the person is no longer obligated, but the inheritance itself and the goods defined by the testament. In the sanction of our Mediator, however, both the goods and the inheritance are obligated, and the very person of the Mediator, and those who enter into that covenant with the Mediator, of which 1 Peter 3:21 speaks; whence Matthias Flacius, in his preface to the Gloss. compend. on the N.T., judged that it should be called not a covenant nor a testament separately, but a testament-covenant. Concerning which matter, it has been treated more prolixly in Theol. Zachar. part I: Where in chapter V, § 42, from Flacius's preface to the gloss on the N.T., he has these words: The sacred covenant of God with men has a most sweet mixture and tempering of covenant and testament, and has a participation of both, otherwise of a different kind. For in a covenant, he says, 1. two parties are joined more closely, 2. the consent of each party is required, 3. a mediator and a herald intervene, 4. reciprocal obligations and promises are sanctioned, 5. certain benefits proceeding therefrom are designated, 6. ceremonies and even external seals are used, 7. only the living are obligated, the dead party is no longer held, 8. once consummated, it is not permitted for either party to withdraw, 9. witnesses and confirmations are added. All these things appear in a certain manner in our sacred covenant. Furthermore, in a testament 1. the parties are for the most part already most closely joined; but God consecrated his goods to us who were most alien to him. 2. For a Testament there is no need for a mediating Mediator: who nevertheless appears in the divine Testament. 3. For the confirmation and execution of a testament, the death of the Testator is necessary. Christ, the Testator, underwent that. 4. In a Testament, the Testator is primarily obligated, although conditions annexed to the Testament must also be performed by the heir, and the name of the Testator must be defended and held sacred. The divine Testament exhibits the same. 5. In a Testament, primarily, indeed almost solely, the advantage of the heir is sought. The same happens here. 6. A Testament can be made void by the surviving Testator as often as he pleases. The Testament of N. is immutable and confirmed by a heavenly oath, Ps. 89; the old was changed and made obsolete, Jer. 31, Ezek. 20, Heb. 8 and 9. 7. In a Testament, the consent of both parties is not necessary for its making; it is permitted, however, for the instituted heir to enter upon the inheritance or to renounce it. The Testament of God requires the highest consent of both parties, which is founded on the promise offering and the faith receiving, although God ordained the tablets and goods of the testament without our consent. Yet it is not permitted with impunity to neglect or spurn such a great inheritance. 8. A Testament has its solemn requirements, writing and witnesses; yet so that it does not need peculiar ceremonies, as the divine one, etc. Therefore, a covenant is rightly called a covenant and a divine Testament. Moreover, that it is quite solemn for the Calvinists, as often as the two Testaments of the Church are discussed, to use the terms of covenants and pacts, not Testaments, so that they may persuade the more imprudent, just as there is only one covenant of grace, which God entered into with us concerning salvation; so each also that each Testament must be properly defined by this very covenant of grace, and that the substance of both Testaments is one and the same, though the mode of dispensation is different and diverse on both sides, was not rashly noted by the blessed Hutter, even if he concedes that the word Testament can also be referred to the covenant of GOD in some respect; because the covenant of GOD has some agreement with a testament; then because the people of GOD, on account of this covenant, are adorned with the title of sons, and the promised goods with the title of inheritance: But let us not be heirs intestate, being by nature children of wrath, Eph. 2:3. Then because that eternal covenant was confirmed in no other way than by the destination and intervention of the death of Christ, Heb. 9:16. Therefore the question is not: Can the covenant of grace come under the name of Testament improperly, and because of some analogy; But can it properly? Is it called a testament by the phrase of Scripture, and not rather, is it asked by the Ecclesiastical phrase? And in particular, whether in this sense, which is in Jeremiah and the Apostle in this place?

II. We do not deny that the word Testament is also referred to those three requirements which concur in every gracious covenant between God and men, namely 1. to the divine promise, and that merely gratuitous, in which way in Gal. 3:17 the promise made to Abraham comes under the name of διαθήκης. 2. to the obedience of reciprocal faith, Ps. 67:10, they did not keep my Testament. 3. to an external sign, or instrument, or testimony of the tablets: in which way the sign of circumcision is called a testament, Acts 7:8, and the federal tablets come under the name of the Prophetic and Apostolic testament, 2 Cor. 3:6, 14. Therefore these also are alien to the state of the question: Namely, it is not asked whether a federal promise, or the requirement or stipulation of the obedience of faith, or federal instruments or tablets sometimes obtain the name of Testament, which we admit are called so improperly: But what by the name

of Testament, when the Old and New Testament, taken in their proper sense, are opposed to each other and distinguished from one another, as is the case in this place, do they note?

III. Although the covenant of grace after the fall is one and the same: yet it cannot be denied by any means that the divine covenant before the fall was of a different kind, because in it there was no place for Christ the Mediator, nor for the remission of sins, where there was as yet no sin, and therefore it cannot be said simply that the covenant of grace was established from the beginning of the world, as it only began after the fall.

IV. The covenant of grace is one and the same, not one old, another new: but the Testaments are diverse, one is called Old, the other New, according to these testimonies of the Prophets and Apostles. The covenant of grace is absolutely immutable, devoid of all abrogation and innovation, as far as the substantials are concerned. The Old Testament is not immutable, but has been innovated or rather abrogated and made obsolete, and finally vanished as the new succeeded.

V. Although the doctrine of the Gospel was delivered otherwise formerly, and otherwise in the most recent times, yet the nature of the Old and New Testament, as Testament is taken properly, does not consist in the diverse tradition of Evangelical doctrine. The Prophetic and Apostolic Scripture are indeed called by the name of Old and New Testament, but metonymically, not properly. The instruments or tablets of the Old and New Testament are properly those writings, not the Testaments themselves. Nor did the Prophetic Scriptures hand down only about the Old Testament, but also about the New, as appears even from this place of Jeremiah.

VI. Nor is the Old Testament properly the doctrine of the law, or the New Testament the doctrine of the Gospel. The doctrine of the law is indeed sanctioned by the Old Testament, but not alone: yet the doctrine of the law itself is by no means the O. Testament. Similarly, the doctrine of the Gospel is sanctioned by the N. Testament, but not alone; so far is it from being the case that the doctrine of the Gospel itself is properly the N. Testament.

VII. A testament is not religion or the doctrine itself, but something concerning its legitimate dispensation. A testament does not deliver or inform the doctrine of salvation itself, but rather instructs the ecclesiastical polity among the people of GOD with a certain form of constitutions.

VIII. Just as the Jewish people and the Christian people are different peoples: so the most wise God willed that there be a different ecclesiastical polity for each, and prescribed the same to them; which arrangement, because He sanctioned it with death, He distinguished by the name of Testament. He sanctioned it, however, among the Jewish people by the death of brute animals, which He willed to be a type of the death of Christ, so that this might always be before the eyes of the same, and might be apprehended by faith even in those figures. But among the Christian people He sanctioned His arrangement by the death of His own only-begotten Son, when He willed those types to be fulfilled, and, the figures ceasing, to exhibit the body itself in the fullness of time. Whence a twofold Testament arose, not indeed as if there were a twofold religion, or a different way of salvation or saving faith; but because it pleased divine wisdom to apply a different arrangement concerning religion and faith according to the reason of the different people and time before Christ was exhibited, and after the exhibition of the same: Inasmuch as He had enclosed the Israelite people, whom He had once chosen before all others, Deut. VII. 6., in a certain ecclesiastical as well as civil or forensic polity, which would endure as long as a new face of the ages should approach, namely that by which the Messiah, there prefigured, exhibited in the flesh, having abrogated that polity, he might introduce another form and polity of living and acting.

IX. Although in both Testaments the benefits are the same, as regards the thing itself; yet as regards the manner of dispensation on the part of GOD and as regards the means and organs which it pleased divine wisdom to employ for the dispensing of the same, there is a diversity: since He established different means for generating and preserving faith, that is, of regeneration and confirmation: for the Israelite people indeed before Christ was exhibited, the Sacrament of Circumcision and the Passover, which were appropriate to the time and state of figures; but for the Christian people, after Christ was exhibited, the Sacrament of Baptism and the Lord's Supper, which were appropriate to the time of the fullness, 1 Cor. XII. 13.

X. But because the nature of a Testament consists properly in a disposition and confirmation, and not only the variety of the disposition is to be attended to in the diversity of the testaments, but primarily the confirmation, which is made by the intervention of death, and here there is only one Testator, nor could any but his only death intervene: For in that Christ died to sin, he died once, Rom. VI. 10. by the death indeed of the Testator, the Son of GOD, in the fullness of time, that other disposition, which the Holy Spirit calls by the name of the New Testament, is properly sanctioned; yet some analogy intervened in the prior disposition by the death of the Testator, when it was sanctioned with the blood of cattle, which God willed to be representatively like the blood of the Testator before the Son was exhibited in the flesh. Hence, therefore, the appellation of the Old Testament.

XI. Wherefore the form and substance of the Old and New Testament are different, if indeed the Old and New Testament are distinguished both by the disposition concerning the attainment of the bequeathed goods by the old and new people, as regards the means of participation, as also as regards the order and polity, which the Testator constituted in a diverse manner, and willed to be different in each people to whom those goods were to be dispensed, and by the reason of the sanction and confirmation: since the former or Old Testament was sanctioned with the blood of cattle, Exod. XXIV. 8. Heb. IX. 18, 19, 20. But the New with the blood of the Son of GOD, Matt. XXVI. 28. Mark XIV. 24. Luke XXII. 10. 1 Cor. XI. 25. Whence the blood of cattle pertains to the substance of the Old Testament, as that was to be sanctioned under the nature of a Testament, but the blood of Christ pertains to the substance of the New Testament, and for that reason, by a double respect, an essential difference emerges between the Old and New Testament, both by reason of the matter, because there other ordinances and requirements are prescribed concerning the religion and polity of the Israelite people than here by reason of the Christian people, even if the same principal inheritance of goods was bequeathed to both; and by reason of the form and manner by which each Testament was sanctioned. For there Moses, by the command of GOD, having taken the blood of calves and goats with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, sprinkled both the volume of the law itself or the ordinances, and the people themselves with this solemn formula: This is the blood of the Testament which God has commanded to us: But here Christ, about to execute the sanction of the New Testament by his death, willed to use this formula, when he sealed and confirmed it with a peculiar sacrament, and for that cause distributed the Eucharistic cup: This is my blood of the New Testament, and this cup is the new Testament in my blood.

XII. Therefore, the name of Testament fits here more correctly than that of covenant, and in the definition of the Old and New Testament, the word disposition is more conveniently used in place of genus than covenant or league. The former is evident: because the Holy Spirit himself urges the notion of a Testament, especially since it both designates an inheritance and requires the intervention of the death of the Testator: The latter, because to attain that inheritance, God did not properly make any covenant by which He assigned the same to us under a condition situated in our own powers: For that inheritance is merely gratuitous: and the principal goods which are promised to us, of whose promise and fruition the ancients were not destitute, were ordained and conferred not otherwise than by grace, without any condition on the part of the receivers, provided they are received by true faith as if by a hand from the Lord offering and providing the same.

XIII. Whence the Old Testament is most correctly defined as being a solemn disposition by which the Son of GOD, without flesh, delivered to the Israelite people, led out of Egypt, the entire administration of both religion and polity, described by a certain form of constitutions and primarily concerning the sacraments of circumcision and the Paschal lamb, and sanctioned it with the blood of cattle, bequeathing to them both the land of Canaan with temporal happiness, and primarily the heavenly inheritance and spiritual goods. But the New Testament is a solemn disposition by which the Son of GOD, in the flesh, willed the Gospel to be announced to his people, to be gathered from the whole world in the fullness of time, the Old Testament having been abrogated, from Zion and from Jerusalem, with new sacraments, Baptism and the Eucharist, having been ordained, with goods bequeathed to them, both temporal and primarily spiritual and heavenly, sanctioned by his death and his own blood.

XIV. From which the agreement and difference of both Testaments now easily appear. First, they agree 1. by reason of the Author, the Testator, the Son of GOD, by whom both were founded. 2. By reason of the legacies, both as regards spiritual and heavenly goods, and also in general, as regards temporal goods. For that those were promised to the Fathers, the remission of sins, righteousness, the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, and eternal life, is evident from Gen. XVII. 7. Exod. III. verse 6. Lev. XXVI. verse 12. Matt. XXII. verse 32. Heb. XI. verses 9, 10. 3. By reason of the quality of the inheritance, because in both cases the inheritance bequeathed by the Testament is merely gratuitous. 4. By reason of the heirs, who in both cases are so by right of adoption, not of birth, who are the people of GOD, or pertain to the people of GOD, and thus observe the prescribed ordinances. 5. By reason of confirmation, because both were sanctioned by blood. 6. By reason of the right of binding, which belongs to Christ the Testator with respect to both peoples by virtue of the obedience rendered to GOD the Father, both active and passive. 7. By reason of the covenant which God struck with men, of unity, if we consider its reciprocal stipulation, but not the mode of dispensation. For God bound Himself to the Fathers of the Old Testament, that He would be their God, and they in turn were bound to GOD, that they would observe His statutes. 8. By reason of the same doctrine, because in both places the same method of justification and salvation is proposed, Acts XV. verse 11. 9. By reason of the communion of saints, because the Church of the Old and New Testament is one. 10. By reason of the laws, because in both places moral laws are prescribed, and those perfect, Deut. IV. verse 12. chap. XII. v. 32. Psal. XIX. verses 8, 9. 11. By reason of the means of application, which are contained in both Testaments, such as the observation of the Scriptures of the Holy Testament and the use of the sacraments.

12. By reason of solemn promulgation, because both were promulgated in a public assembly not without solemnity: The former indeed in the presence of the people of Israel, Exod. XX. The latter truly in the congregation of the Apostles and brethren of more than five hundred, Matth. XXIX. 1. Cor. XV.

XV. The difference between both Testaments consists in these things. 1. As to the Author, that the Old was founded, sanctioned, and promulgated through the Son of God ἄσαρκον (without flesh), Exod. XX. Acts VII. v. 38. The New, however, through the Son of God ἔνσαρκον (in the flesh). 2. As to the legacies, that in the Old Testament the inheritance of the land of Canaan was bequeathed, and the preservation of the Israelite polity promised: in the New Testament such special promises were not made. 3. As to the heirs, who there are the Israelite people, but here the Christian people, or those who believe in Christ exhibited, in Jesus of Nazareth. 4. As to confirmation. For the Old was confirmed by the blood of cattle, but the New by the blood of the Son of God himself, Zech. IX. 11. Heb. IX. 15. 5. As to the means of application, which there are the observation of the tables of the Old Testament or the Prophetic Scripture: Here, however, of the tables of the New Testament or the Apostolic Scripture. There, faith was required in Christ to be exhibited: here, however, faith in Christ exhibited: There, the use of the sacraments of Circumcision and the Paschal lamb; here, of the sacrament of Baptism and the Lord's Supper. 6. By reason of the manner, place, and time of promulgation, that the Old Testament was promulgated with terror among lightnings and thunders, Exod. XIX. ver. 16. the New with sweet invitation, Matth. XXIX. 19. seqq. that the former was published on Mount Sinai: the latter, however, in Zion and Jerusalem: that the former was after the exodus from Egypt, Jer. XXXI. 32. the latter, however, in the last days of the Jewish polity, or in the fullness of times, Jer. XXXI. 33. Is. II. 2. Mic. IV. 1. 7. By reason of the constitutions, because in the Old Testament there were various ordinances of law, not only moral, but also ceremonial or Ecclesiastical, and forensic or Political: In the New Testament, however, ceremonial laws ceased, nor does the observance of the Political law lie upon Christians. 8. Mode of exhibiting the promises: The Old Testament had the shadow: The New has the body itself and the complement, Col. II. 17. Heb. IX. 1. There, spiritual and heavenly goods were promised less openly, covered for the most part by the shadows and figures of types: Here, however, those things are promised more openly, and the wrappings of the types are unfolded. 9. As to the term of the pedagogy of the law: In the Old Testament, the law was a pedagogue to Christ to be exhibited: In the New Testament, to Christ exhibited. 10. As to the adjuncts: The Old Testament, with respect to those things which it contained openly and more clearly, was of fear and servitude: The New, however, is in all things of joy and liberty, Gal. IV. ver. 24. seq. The Old Testament, because of the variety of laws, was more burdensome, and because of the manner of exaction, more rigorous: The New is immune from those burdens, and exhibits more manifestly the remission of that rigor, 2. Cor. III. 14. 11. As to the principal προσκείμενον (addition) of the Old Testament: because the law properly pertains to the Old Testament, whose end is Christ, and in order that that end might be shown, therefore certain things pertaining to the Gospel were also included in the O.T.; yet so that the principal and main ministry of Moses is legal, which he does not truly execute rightly, unless he also rightly shows Christ, the end of the law, as the blessed Chemnitius warns here. Deut. XVIII. 15. John I. 17. 12. As to tradition and effect. Because the Old Testament, by reason of the moral law, whose solemn promulgation was the principal part of the Old Testament, was inscribed on tables of stone: The New, however, by reason of the Gospel, whose universal preaching is likewise a primary part of the New Testament, is written in the hearts of men. Jer. XXXI. ver. 24. 2. Cor. III. ver. 6. 12. As to the Mediator of the sanction. Because the Old Testament was sanctioned with respect to the people through Moses, who is indeed nowhere called Μεσιτης (Mediator), but the servant of the Lord, Num. XII. ver. 7. Heb. III. ver. 4. so that that honor might be reserved for Christ alone, yet he sprinkled the tables of the Testament, namely the volume of the law, and the people with sacrificial blood, so that the Old Testament might be sanctioned on the part of the people in that manner: The New Testament, however, which was sanctioned on the altar of the cross, is confirmed on the part of God by the blood and death of Christ the Mediator, and on our part in the Holy Supper by the same blood of Christ, with which we are not sprinkled, but are given to drink by Christ, the Mediator of the new covenant. For this cup is the new testament in my blood, testifies CHRIST, Luke XXII. ver. 20. 1. Cor. XI. v. 25. 14. As to the circumstances of faith required from the heirs. For although the same faith as to substance is in both Testaments: In the Old, however, faith was required in the obedience to be rendered by the Messiah, in the New Testament in the obedience rendered: In the Old Testament in the ransom to be paid, in the New Testament in the ransom paid, Romans III. ver. 25. 26. Heb. IX. v. 15. 15. As to duration: The Old Testament was to be made old, Heb. VIII. ver. 13. The New, however, lasts until the consummation of the age, 1. Cor. XV. ver. 24. 16. As to breadth and scope: The Old Testament was stayed within the narrow borders of Judea: The New, however, extends itself to the ends of the whole earth, Zech. IX. ver. 10. Matth. XXIX. ver. 19.

XVI. Therefore, the definition of Pareus is not to be simply approved: That the Old Testament in its primary and proper signification is the doctrine of spiritual grace, formerly promising eternal salvation through Moses and the Prophets to the Fathers and the gross people of the Jews, openly indeed under the condition of perfect obedience to the moral law, and the commination of eternal curse, unless they performed it, together with the intolerable burden of legal rites, and the yoke of the most strict Mosaic polity, but covertly under the condition of repentance and faith in the Messiah to come, prefigured by the shadows and figures of ceremonies. For 1. the legal covenant or pact and the Old Testament are thus openly confounded. 2. the spiritual doctrine of grace, which had a place in both Testaments when the Testament is taken in its proper signification. 3. The Old Testament was promulgated through Moses after the exodus from Egypt to the people, as Jeremiah testifies: Therefore, other Prophets do not belong here. 4. Although the moral law pertained principally to the Old Testament regarding the ministry proper to Moses, which was that of the letter that kills and of condemnation and death, 2 Cor. III. verses 6 et seq., just as for that reason the Old Testament is also said to have generated unto bondage, Gal. IV. verse 24, nevertheless the Old Testament was not lacking in oracles concerning Christ and His benefits, beyond the types: although through the παιδαγωγίαν of the moral law the ancients were led to Christ, and through the figure of the ceremonial law they were informed as by a visible sermon concerning Christ: yet open sermons concerning Christ were also added, such as that one in Deut. XVIII, and those which had already been made to the Patriarchs, without doubt repeated by Moses, and confirmed by the aforementioned prophecy and His other Evangelical sermons. Furthermore, it is not without reason noted here by the blessed Chemnitz that the Levitical ceremonies are considered in two ways, 1. as carnal and external observations, or pedagogical works, by which the members of that assembly were preserved in some external and carnal cleanliness: And thus he says that they pertain to the law. For the end of that polity was that the promise might be preserved in it, that from it the Messiah was to come, who would reign over the whole world professions concerning sin, concerning the wrath of God and divine punishments, and to that extent they also pertain to the law. But because the end of the law is Christ, therefore 2. they are also considered as types of Christ, and to that extent they pertain to the Gospel, where furthermore this is also to be observed, that insofar as those ceremonial types look to Christ, they were not first delivered at Sinai. For those ceremonies were known and used by the Patriarchs before the flood. And 2 Cor. III. 14. Paul teaches that this scope is the true use of the whole law: But when that end is not considered, but opinions are added only concerning external observation, and that the work performed justifies, then he calls it a veil. Of which the latter is proper to Moses, the former is proper to CHRIST.

which were, namely, proper to it, which were not to be defined by the doctrine of the decalogue itself, but by those things which pertained to the state of the Church and the polity of the Israelite people. And these things concerning the present matter, to which can be compared what the blessed Chemnitius, the blessed Hutterus, and the blessed Winckelmannus have handed down in the cited places, and which we have observed in the preface to the Illustrious Bible of the Old Testament, as well as in the Grotian prolegomena to the New Testament.

Latin:

V. 13. Ἐν τῷ λέγειν καινὴν πεπαλάιωκε τὴν πρώτην) id est, ostendit esse inutilem, quales sunt senes decrepiti. Est enim hic similis figura, qualis supra I. 6.

Quid huc faciat locus cap. I. 6. non capio. Ad- mitti tamen potest sensus Grotii, si conjungantur, quæ verbis sequentibus subjunxit Apostolus : Τὸ παλαιόμενον κὶ γηράσκον, quæ vero distincte recti- us à Theophylacto evolvuntur : Interpretatur, in- quit, Propheticum dictum, cum testamentum hoc nostrum novum prorsus appellat, arguit plane prius illud vetus videri. Quod autem antiquatur & se- nescit prope interitum est. Redditus, dicente por- ro Theophylacto, per Prophetam fidentior legem carpit, arguens nostram nunc germinasse & flore- scere magis indies.. Ex Prophetæ utaque dictis vetu- statis nomen accipit, à se autem ipso senectutis ad- jecit, & legi demum deberi, adjunxit interitum, q. d. non enim non opportune novum hoc nostrum su- stulit vetus, sed senectutis & vetustatis gratia cessa- re coëgit, quia infirmum esset & plane inutile, sicuti & alibi dicit; Nam impotentia legis, in qua infir- mior est, per carnem, Roman. VIII. 3. Succincte omnia, ita ut ad scopum Apostoli ea applicet, sic complectitur B. Hunnius: Hinc nunc subsumit A- postolus, & ex testimonio Prophetico infert, Deum promittendo Testamentum novum simul veteris ab- rogationem indicere, unde consequens sit una cum pacto veteri Sacerdotium quoque vetus evanescere & abrogari debuisse.

Τὸ δὲ παλαιούμενον καὶ γηράσκον ἐγγὺς ἀφανισμοῦ) Occulte vaticinatur & templum & rempublicam Judæorum brevi perituram. Id evenit decem ferme annis post scriptam hanc epistolam. Senectutem mors excipit. Didicisse hoc potuit Lucas tum ex Dan, IX. 22. tum ex iis, quæ ipse Chri- sti verbis posuit in Evangelio XXI. 20.

Assumit Lucam Autorem epistolæ esse, quod supra diluimus. An vero hic vaticinium de inte- ritu templi & Reipublicæ habeatur, dubium est. Nihil aliud dicitur, quam quia pactum legale ceu vetus antiquatum est & senuit, eo quod aliud no- vum introductum à Propheta, illud ἐγγὺς ἀφανι- σμοῦ sit. Fuisset autem id tale, etiamsi nec templum, nec Respublica Judæorum interiisset. Estium si audias, talis est ratiocinatio Apostoli: Hoc testa- mentum novum est; Ergo illud vetus: porro quod vetus est, indies magis magisq́; veterascit, & (ut in hominibus) senescit: quod autem veterascit & senescit, ad interitum properat & mortem. Ex quo concludendum relinquit, prius testamentum tan- dem debuisse finiri; atq́; in plenitudine temporis, id est, revelato firmatoq́; per Christum Novo Testam. finem accepisse. Vim argumenti probat experientia. Consonant etiam Scripturæ, Levit. XXVI. vetera novis advenientibus projicietis, & 2. Cor. V. Vetera transierunt, ecce facta sunt omnia nova. Breviter: Ex antiquatione prioris Testamenti abrogatio- nem ejusdem infert vel ἀφανισμὸν. Vulgatus red- dit interitum. Sed est ab ἀφανίζομαι dispareo, è conspectu evanesco. Eo igitur notatur, quod novo comparente vetus dispareat, è conspectu tum Dei, qui non secundum rigorem veteris, sed gratiam novi agere vult cum fidelibus, tum homi- nis evanescat, quod fideles non intueantur legem cum suis præceptis & comminationibus rigorosis & intolerabilibus; sed oculos unice defixos ha- beant in Christum, qui est τέλος νόμου, Rom. X. 4. & pro nobis obedientiam legi præstitit, ac male- dictionem legis tulit, eumq; fide amplectantur; unde evanescit legis κατάκριμα, Rom. VIII. 1. Pul- chre B. Winckelmannus disp. XIIX. Tom. IV. Giessenf. thes. 84. & seqq. de his disserit: Et sane cum Patres vetus pactum irritum fecerint, nisi Do- minus illud nobis antiquasset & abrogasset, διὰ τὸ αὐτῆς ἀνωφελὲς καὶ ἀσθενὲς (siquidem ad perfectio- nem adducere nos non possit) instituto Novo Testa- mento & dando & mittendo novo mediatore ac Re- demptore, in æternum nobis pereundum fuisset. Sicut ergo vetus T. veterem hominem corruptum peccato damnat & mortificat: Ita novum abolito vetere homine, remissis scilicet peccatis vivificat per fidem in Christum & novum reddit. Sumus enim in Christo Jesu nova creatura: Vetera præter- ierunt, ecce nova facta sunt omnia, 2. Cor. V. 17. Adhæc etiam lex veterem hominem coërcet & fre- nat externa disciplina: Novum autem Testa- mentum non solum vivificat, & consolatur, sed etiam ita novum reddit, ut incipiat servire Deo in novitate Spiritus, & non vetustate literæ,

Rom. VII. 6. Atque ita vetus ille homo, qui foris est, corrumpitur, & is, qui intus est, de die in diem re- novatur. Atque hoc est beneficium renovationis, quod per Prophetam Dominus promisit se daturum cor novum & Spiritum novum &c. Ezech. XI. 19. XVIII. 26. 27. Hanc appellationis rationem etiam notavit Augustinus : Testamentum, inquiens, ve- tus pertinet ad veterem hominem, a quo necesse est, hominem incipere: novum autem ad hominem no- vum, quo debet homo ex vetustate transire. Præive- rat B. Chemnitius, & eadem fere ratione hæc dif- crimina Veteris & Novi Testamenti tradiderat part. III. LL. Theol. de discrim. V. & N. T. p. 91. eademq; deduxerat ex proprietate vocabuli בלה consummatus est, inveteratus est, vetustate consumptus est, Ps. XXXII. 3. Deut. VIII. 4. XXIX. 5. Jos. IX. 4. Es. XXXIIX. 27. Psal. CII. 26.

Disserit circa præsentem Apostoli locum Pa- ræus, quomodo duo Testamenta vetus & novum dicantur, cum tamen sit unum fœdus æternum? Et observat ברית fœdus seu Testamentum a DEO conditum, & cum hominibus initum ab initio mundi ad finem revera unum esse, perpe- tuum, æternum, & immutabile, nempe doctri- nam spiritualem gratiæ offerentem hominibus DEI nomine benedictionem & salutem æternam, homines vicissim obligantem ad obedientiam & gratitudinem DEO præstandam, quæ doctrina a forma conventionis inter Deum & homines di- catur fœdus, a modo sanctionis Testamentum, quia morte Testatoris Christi est obsignata. Quia vero, inquit, Deo visum fuit aliter olim, aliter po- stremis temporibus doctrinam illam informare, & beneficia sua dispensare, ideo Scriptura de uno fœ- dere & testamento sæpe loquitur, ut de duobus, & diserte nominat duo testamenta, vetus & novum, Jerem. XXXI. Gal. IV. & hoc loco. Sequutus est Bucerum & Calvinum libr. II. instit. cap. 10. ali- osque (ceu sunt Petrus Martyr classe I. Loc. Theol. loc. XVI. §. 2. seqq. Ursinus part. II. Catech. pag. 130. Grynæus vol. II. disp. Theol. p. 125. 260. Bucanus loco XXII. pag. 200.) Quorum senten- tiam B. Chemnitius loco cit. sic exposuit: quod vocabulo pacti seu Testamenti intelligant tantum doctrinam de persona & beneficiis Christi Media- toris, & sicut doctrina illa patefacta & tradita fuit tempore Patriarcharum, Mosis, & Prophetarum, variis ceremoniarum umbris vestita seu involuta, hoc vocent Testamentum vetus. Sicut autem re- moto illo velamento figurarum a Christo & Apo- stolis doctrina Evangelii tradita est, hoc vocent novum Testamentum; Atque ita reipsa quoad materiam seu substantiam statuant, non esse duo diversa, sed unum & idem esse Vetus & Novum Testamentum, sed tantum quoad formam seu modum revelationis, & quoad mensuram dono- rum differre. Judicat autem B. Chemnitius, rem quidem ipsam hujus opinionis (quod scilicet idem sit Salvator Christus, idem Evangelium, ut vulgo loquimur, eadem fides, eadem justificatio sanctorum in Veteri & in Novo Testamento) veram esse: sed quæstionem hoc loco esse, quid Scriptura proprie intelligat, quando inter Vetus & Novum Testamentum distinguit? Ubi proin- de observandum I. fœderis, pacti, & testamenti no- mina promiscue quidem non raro in hac mate- ria usurpari; quemadmodum vox ברית gene- ralis est, & Græcis ac Latinis Interpretibus modo Testamentum, modo fœdus, modo pactum red- ditur, & quod hic LXX. Interpp. & Apostolus per διαθήκην exposuere, Aquila per συνθήκην inter- pretatus est; accurate tamen loquendo diversa hæc esse. Nam pactum vulgo dicitur consensus duorum aut plurium de re quacunque vel danda vel facienda expressis verbis conceptus. Fœdus vel συνθήκη secundum Suidam est talis obligatio, quâ partes dissidentes certis conditionibus mu- tuo præstandis conveniunt de societate, de com- merciis, de pace, deque induciis, deque id genus rebus aliis. Testamentum vero est voluntatis no- stræ sententia de eo, quod quis post mortem su- am fieri voluit, vel dispositio de extrema mori- turi voluntate, qua bona sua inter hæredes dis- pensat, unde differentia in aprico est, tum quod Testamentum ab uno proficiscatur, qui disposi- tionem habet in potestate sua, quum ad fœdera & pacta plurium requiratur consensus; tum quod Testamentum de hæreditate & aliis moriturorum voluntatem concernat, fœdera & pacta non mo- rituri dispositionem nec hæreditatem præcise at- tineant; tum quod Testamentum mutari possit ante mortem, nec nisi robur habeat, postquam morte confirmatum est, Ebr. IX. 16. quum pacta & fœdera nec mutari possint ab una parte, nec opus habeant confirmatione per mortem; tum quod hæc quandoq; juramento roborentur, Ebr. VI. 16. in testamentaria vero actione juramentum minime adhibeatur; tum denique quod fœdera constant naturali obligatione, ubi inter pacifcen- tes quædam est analogia, & proportio, quæ ad testamenta non requiritur, qualem & inter Deum & homines, Creatorem & creaturas comminisci absurdum foret. Esse autem hic aliquod tempe- ramentum fœderis & Testamenti, & testamentum fœderale, ac fœdus testamentarium, certo respectu dici posse, cum de divino fœdere ac testamento agitur, in præloquio ad Nov. Testamentum jam observatum fuit. B. Dorscheus: De utriusq; fœde- ris & Testamenti natura sanctio illa Mediatoris no- stri participat. Nam & Testamentum est propter legata bona amplissima, & mortis intervenientis ne- cessitatem: qua duo in fœdere non necessario requi- runtur. Non enim opus est, ut fœderatorum unus alteri omnia sua bona transcribat, destinetq́;, aut etiam morti pro confœderatorum altero sese devo- veat. A fœdere vero sanctio Mediatoris nostri ha- bet quandam immutabilitatem & personalem obli- gationem. Nam ex Testamento si mors Testatoris subsequatur, persona non amplius obligata est, sed ipsa hæreditas & bona Testamento definita. In san- ctione vero Mediatoris nostri & bona atque hære- ditas obligata sunt, & ipsa etiam Mediatoris perso- na, & quæ cum Mediatore in fœdus illud descen- dunt, de quo 1. Petr. III. 21. unde nec fœdus nec Testamentum seorsim, sed Testamento-fœdus appel- landum censuit Matthias Flacius in præfat. ad Gloss. compend. super N. T. Qua de re in Theol. Zachar. part. I. prolixius actum est: Ubi cap. V. §. 42. è Flacii præfat. glossæ in N. T. hæc habet: Sacrum Dei cum hominibus fœdus habere suavis- simam fœderis & Testamenti mixturam atque tem- peraturam, & habere utriusque alias diversi generis participationem. In fœdere enim, inquit, 1. duæ partes arctius conjunguntur, 2. utriusq́; partis con- sensus requiritur, 3. mediator atque fecialis inter- venit, 4. obligationes & promissiones reciprocæ san- ciuntur, 5. certa commoda exinde provenientia de- signantur, 6. ceremoniæ & externa etiam signacula usurpantur, 7. vivi solum obligantur, alterutra pars mortua non amplius tenetur, 8. semel consummato resilire neutri parti licet, 9. testes & confirmatio- nes adduntur. Ista omnia certa ratione in fœdere nostro sacro comparent. Porro in testamento 1. par- tes plerumque ante sunt conjunctissimæ; Deus vero nobis à se alienissimis bona sua consecravit. 2. Ad Testamentum opus non est Mediatore conciliante: qui tamen in divino Testamento comparet. 3. Ad testamenti confirmationem & executionem opus est morte Testatoris. Illam Christus Testator, subiit. 4. In Testamento potissimum obligatur Testator, quamvis & hæredi sint præstandæ conditiones Testamento an- nexæ, & Testatoris nomen defendendum & sanctè habendum. Idem divinum Testamentum exhibet. 5. Testamento potissimum, imo ferè solum commo- dum hæredis quæritur. Idem & hic fit. 6. Testa- mentum à superstite Testatore, quoties placet, irri- tum fieri potest. Testamentum N. immutabile est & juramento cælesti firmatum Psal. LXXXIX. ve- tus mutatum est & antiquatum, Jer. XXXI. Ezech. XX. Ebr. VIII. & IX. 7. In Testamento non est ne- cessarius utriusque partis consensus ad illius confe- ctionem; licet tamen instituto hæredi adire hære- ditatem, vel eidem renunciare. Testamentum Dei requirit summam utriusque partis consensionem, quæ fundatur in promissione offerente & fide recipiente, quamvis Deus sine nostro consensu testamenti tabu- las & bona ordinaverit. Nec tamen impunè licet tantam hæreditatem negligere aut aspernari. 8. Te- stamentum habet sua solennia requisita, scriptum & testes; ita tamen ut peculiaribus ceremoniis non egeat, sicut divinum &c. Itaque Testamento fœdus rectè fœdus & Testamentum divinum appellatur. Cæterum Calvinianis solenne admodum esse, quoties de duobus Testamentis Ecclesiæ agitur, non Testamentorum, sed fœderum & pactorum uti terminis, quo imprudentioribus persuadeant, quemadmodum unum tantum est fœdus gratiæ, quod Deus de salute nobiscum iniit; Ita utrumq; etiam Testamentum proprie definiendum esse per hoc ipsum fœdus gratiæ, & unam eandemq; esse utriusque Testamenti substantiam, modum tamen dispensationis utrinque alium & diversum, haud temere notavit B. Hutterus, etsi concedat vocem Testamenti etiam ad fœdus DEI aliquo respectu referri posse; quia fœdus DEI aliquam convenientiam habet cum testamento; tum quod populus DEI propter hoc fœdus filiorum elo- gio, bona promissa hæreditatis titulo ornentur: Hæredes autem ab intestato non simus, utpote natura filii iræ, Eph. II. 3. tum quod fœdus illud æternum non aliter quam destinatione & inter- ventu mortis Christi confirmatum fuerit, Ebr. IX. 16. Non ergo quæritur: Anne fœdus gratiæ Testamenti nomine venire possit improprie, & ob aliquam analogiam; Sed an proprie? An phrasi Scripturæ testamentum vocetur, non vero an phrasi Ecclesiastica quæritur? Et in specie, num hoc sensu, qui apud Jeremiam & Apostolum hoc loco?

II. Testamenti vocem etiam ad tria illa requi- sita, quæ in omni fœdere gratioso inter Deum & homines concurrunt, referri, non diffitemur, ut- pote 1. ad promissionem divinam, eamque mere gratuitam, quomodo Gal. III. 17. διαθήκης nomi- ne venit promissio Abrahæ facta. 2. ad fidei re- ciprocæ obedientiam, Psal. LXVII. 10. non cu- stodierunt Testamentum meum. 3. ad externum vel signum, vel instrumentum, seu testimonium ta- bularum: quomodo signum circumcisionis testa- mentum dicitur, Act. VII. 8. & tabulæ fœderales li- bri Prophetici & Apostolici testamenti nomine ve- niunt, 2. Cor. III, 6. 14. Idcirco & hæc à statu quæ- stionis aliena sunt: Nimirum non quæritur, num promissio fœderalis, aut obedientia fidei postulatio vel stipulatio, aut instrumenta vel tabulæ fœderales no- men Testamenti nonnunquam sortiantur, quæ improprie ita dici admittimus: Sed quid nomine

Testamenti, cum Vetus & novum Testamentum proprio sensu accepta sibi opponuntur, & à se invicem discriminantur, quemadmodum hoc lo- co sit, notent?

III. Etsi fœdus gratiæ post lapsum unum sit idemque: Fœdus tamen divinum ante lapsum di- versi generis fuisse, nullo pacto negari potest, quia in eo Christo Mediatori locus nullus erat, nec remissioni peccatorum, ubi nullum adhuc erat peccatum, ideoque fœdus gratiæ ab initio mundi conditum fuisse, simpliciter dici non po- test, utpote quod demum post lapsum cœpit.

IV. Fœdus gratiæ, unum est idemque, non aliud vetus, aliud novum: Testamenta vero diversa sunt, alterum Vetus dicitur, alterum Novum, se- cundum hæc Propheticæ & Apostoli testimonia. Fœdus gratiæ immutabile prorsus est, omnis ab- rogationis & innovationis, quantum ad substan- tialia, expers. Testam. vetus non est immutabile, sed innovatum vel potius abrogatum & antiqua- tum est, atque succedente novo tandem evanuit.

V. Doctrina Evangelii etsi aliter olim, aliter novissimis temporibus tradita sit, non tamen in diversa Evangelicæ doctrinæ traditione consistit natura Veteris & Novi Testamenti, prout Testa- mentum proprie accipitur. Scriptura sane Pro- phetica & Apostolica Veteris & Novi Testamenti nomine nuncupantur, sed Metonymice, non pro- prie. Veteris & Novi Testamenti instrumenta vel tabulæ proprie sunt illa scripta, non vero ipsa Te- stamenta. Neque tantum de Veteri Testamento tradebant Scripturæ Propheticæ, sed etiam de No- vo, ut vel ex hoc loco Jeremiæ apparet.

VI. Neque vetus Testamentum proprie est do- ctrina legis, aut novum Testamentum doctrina Evangelii. Sancita quidem Testamento Veteri est doctrina legis, sed non sola: Neutiquam ve- ro ipsa legis doctrina Testamentum V. est. Si- militer sancita est doctrina Evangelii Testamen- to N. sed non sola, tantum abest, ut ipsa Evange- lii doctrina proprie sit N. Testamentum.

VII. Testamentum non est religio sive doctri- na ipsa, sed aliquid circa legitimam ejus dispen- sationem. Testamentum non tradit vel informat ipsam salutis doctrinam, sed instruit potius poli- tiam Ecclesiasticam in populo DEI certa consti- tutionum forma.

VIII. Ut alius atque alius populus est populus Judaicus & populus Christianus: Ita aliam atque aliam politiam Ecclesiasticam Deus Sapientissimus esse utriusque voluit, eidemq; præscripsit, quam dispositionem, quia morte sancivit, Testamenti nomine insignivit. Sancivit autem penes popu- lum Judaicum morte brutorum, quæ typum esse voluit mortis Christi, ut hæc ante oculos ejusdem semper versaretur, atque in illis etiam figuris fide apprehenderetur. Penes populum vero Christia- num sancivit dispositionem suam, morte ipsius- met Filii sui Unigeniti, quando typos illos imple- ri voluit, & cessantibus figuris corpus ipsum ex- hibere in temporis plenitudine. Unde duplex Te- stamentum ortum, non quidem quasi duplex re- ligio, vel alia atque alia salutis ratio aut fides sal- vifica sit; sed quia dispositionem aliam circa reli- gionem & fidem pro diversi populi & temporis ra- tione ante Christum exhibitum, & post ejusdem exhibitionem adhibere divinæ sapientiæ placuit: Siquidem populum Israëliticum, quem olim præ cunctis aliis elegerat, Deut. VII. 6. certæ tum Ec- clesiasticæ, tum civili sive forensi politiæ inclufe- rit, quæ tamdiu duraret, donec nova seculorum facies ingrueret, ea nempe, qua Messias, ibi præ- figuratus, in carne exhibitus, abrogata illa poli- tia, aliam vivendi agendique formam & politiam introduceret.

IX. Quanquam in utroque Testamento eadem beneficia sint, quod ad rem ipsam; tamen quoad dispensationis modum ex parte DEI & quoad me- dia atque organa, quæ iisdem dispensandis adhi- beri divinæ placuit sapientiæ diversitas: quum alia atque alia media generandæ & conservandæ fidei, id est, regenerationis, & confirmationis con- stituerit: penes populum quidem Israëliticum an- te Christum exhibitum Sacramentum Circumci- sionis & Paschatos, quæ conveniebant tempori & statui figurarum; penes vero populum Christia- num, post exhibitum Christum, Sacramentum Baptismi & Cœnæ Dominicæ, quæ conveniebant τῷ καιρῷ τῶ πληρώματος, 1. Cor. XII. 13.

X. Quia vero ratio Testamenti proprie con- sistit in dispositione, ac confirmatione, nec sola dis- positionis varietas attendenda est in diversitate te- stamentorum, sed imprimis confirmatio, quæ mor- tis interventu fit, hic vero non nisi unicus est te- stator, nec nisi unica mors ejus intervenire po- tuit: Quod enim Christus mortuus est peccato, mortuus est semel Rom. VI. 10. morte quidem Te- statoris Filii DEI in plenitudine temporis san- cita proprie tantum est dispositio illa altera, quam Novi Testamenti nomine vocat Spiritus Sanctus, analogon tamen aliquid in priori dispositione in- tervenit morte Testatoris, cum sanguine pecuino illa sancita est, quem instar sanguinis Testatoris repræsentative esse voluit Deus ante exhibitum in carne Filium. Inde ergo Veteris T. appellatio.

XI. Quapropter forma ac substantia est alia atque alia Veteris & Novi Testam. siquidem di- stinguatur Vetus & Novum Testam. tum disposi- tione circa consequutionem bonorum legatorum penes veterem & novum populum, quoad media participationis, ut & quoad ordinem & politiam, quam Testator diversimodam constituit, ac di- versum in utroque populo esse voluit, cui dispen- sanda illa bona erant, tum sanctionis & confirma- tionis ratione: quum prius vel Vetus Testamen- tum sancitum fuerit sanguine pecuino, Exod. XXIV. 8. Ebr. IX. 18. 19. 20. Novum vero sanguine Filii DEI, Matth. XXVI. 28. Marc. XIV. 24. Luc. XXII. 10. 1. Cor. XI. 25. Unde sanguis pecuinus ad substantiam Veteris Testamenti, ut illud sub ra- tione Testamenti sanciendum fuit, sanguis vero Christi ad substantiam Novi Test. pertinet, atque ea ratione duplici respectu differentia essentialis inter Vetus ac Novum Testamentum emergit, tum ratione materiæ, quia ibi aliæ ordinationes & requisita præscribuntur circa religionem & po- litiam populi Israëlitici, quam hic ratione Chri- stiani populi, etsi eadem utrique quoad bona præ- cipua hæreditas legata sit; tum ratione formæ & modi, quo sancitum est Testamentum utrumque. Ibi enim Moses ex mandato DEI sumpto sangui- ne vitulorum & hircorum cum aqua, lana cocci- nea & hyssopo tum volumen ipsum legis vel or- dinationes, tum populum ipsum aspersit hac so- lenni formula: Hic est sanguis Testamenti, quod mandavit nobis Deus: Hic vero Christus Testa- menti Novi sanctionem expediturus morte sua hac uti voluit formula, cum id obsignaret & con- firmaret peculiari sacramento, ejusque causa ca- licem Eucharisticum distribueret: Hic est sanguis meus Novi Testamenti, & hic calix est novum Te- stamentum in meo sanguine.

XII. Rectius itaque hic convenit Testamenti, quam pacti nomen, & generis loco in definitio- ne Veteris ac Novi Testamenti convenientius adhibetur dispositio, quam pactum vel fœdus. Prius patet: quia Spiritus Sanctus ipse notionem Testamenti urget, præcipue quum & hæredita- tem designet, & mortis Testatoris interventum requirat : Posterius, quia ad hæreditatem illam consequendam proprie non pactum aliquod fe- cit, quo sub conditione in nostris viribus sita eandem nobis assignavit Deus : Est enim hære- ditas illa mere gratuita : & bona præcipua, quæ nobis promissa sunt, quorum etiam promissione ac fruitione veteres non destituti, non nisi ex gratia citra ullam ex parte percipientium condi- tionem, dummodo vera fide ceu manu â Domi- no eadem offerente ac præbente recipiantur, or- dinata sint ac conferantur.

XIII. Unde Vetus Testamentum rectissime de- finitur, quod sit solennis dispositio, qua Filius DEI ἄσαρκος populo Israëlitico ex Ægypto edu- cto universam tum religionis, tum politiæ admi- nistrationem certa constitutionum forma & im- primis de sacramentis circumcisionis & agni Pa- schalis, descriptam, tradidit, & sanguine pecuino sancivit, legans eidem tum terram Canaan cum felicitate temporali, tum imprimis hæreditatem cœlestem & bona spiritualia. Novum vero Te- stamentum est solennis dispositio, qua Filius DEI ἔνσαρκος populo suo in plenitudine temporis è toto terrarum orbe colligendo, abrogato Veteri Testamento, Evangelium ex Sion ex Jerusalem annunciari voluit, sacramentis novis, Baptismo & Eucharistia, ordinatis, legatis eidem bonis cum temporalibus, tum imprimis spiritualibus & cœ- lestibus, morte sua & sanguine proprio sancita.

XIV. E quibus jam convenientia & differen- tia utriusque Testamenti facile constat. Primum conveniunt 1. ratione Autoris, Testatoris Filii DEI, à quo utrumque conditum est. 2. Ratio- ne legatorum, tum quoad bona spiritualia & cœ- lestia, tum etiam in genere, quoad bona tempo- ralia. Nam & Patribus illa promissa fuisse, remif- sionem peccatorum, justitiam, inhabitationem Spiritus Sancti, & vitam æternam, constat è Gen. XVII. 7. Exod. III. vers. 6. Levit. XXVI. vers. 12. Matth. XXII. vers. 32. Ebr. XI. vers. 9. 10. 3. Ra- tione qualitatis hæreditatis, quia utrobique hæ- reditas Testamento legata mere est gratuita. 4. Ratione hæredum, qui utrobique sunt ad- optionis non nativitatis jure, qui populus DEI sunt, vel ad populum DEI pertinent, adeoque ordinationes præscriptas observant. 5. Ratione confirmationis, quia utrumque sancitum est san- guine. 6. Ratione juris legandi, quod Christo Testatori utriusque populi respectu convenit vi obedientiæ DEO Patri præstitæ cum activæ tum passivæ. 7. Ratione fœderis, quod Deus cum ho- minibus pepigit, unitatis, si reciprocam ejus sti- pulationem, non vero dispensationis modum re- spiciamus. Nam & Patribus Veteris Testamenti Deus se obstrinxit, quod velit Deus ipsorum esse, & iidem DEO obstricti fuere, quod velint ejus statuata observare. 8. Ratione doctrinæ ejusdem quia utrobique eadem proposita est justificatio- nis & salutis ratio, Actor. XV. vers. 11. 9. Ratio- ne communionis sanctorum, quia una est Ecclesia Veteris & Novi Testamenti. 10. Ratione legum, quia utrobique præscriptæ sunt leges morales, eæque perfectæ, Deut. IV. vers. 12. cap. XII. v. 32. Psal. XIX. vers. 8. 9. 11. Ratione mediorum appli- cationis, quæ in utroque Testamento comprehen- sa sunt, qualia sunt, tabularum Testamenti Scri- pturæ S. observatio & sacramentorum usurpatio.

12. Ratione solennis promulgationis, quia utrumq; in publica panegyri non absque solennitate promulgatum est: Prius quidem in præsentia populi Israëlitici, Exod. XX. Posterius vero in congregatione Apostolorum & fratrum plus quam quingentorum, Matth. XXIX. 1. Cor. XV.

XV. Differentia vero utriusque Testamenti in his consistit. 1. Quod ad Autorem, quod Vetus per Filium DEI ἄσαρκον conditum, sancitum, & promulgatum fuerit, Exod. XX. Actor. VII. v. 38. Novum autem per Filium DEI ἔνσαρκον. 2. Quod ad legata, quod in V. Testamento hæreditas terræ Canaan legata sit, & conservatio politiæ Israëliticæ promissa: in Novo Testam. tales speciales promissiones factæ non sint. 3. Quod ad hæredes, qui illic sunt populus Israëliticus, hic vero populus Christianus, vel qui in Christum exhibitum, in Jesum Nazarenum credunt. 4. Quod ad confirmationem. Vetus enim sanguine pecuino, novum vero ipsius Filii DEI sanguine confirmatum est, Zach. IX. 11. Ebr. IX. 15. 5. Quoad media applicationis, quæ illic sunt tabularum Veteris Testam. vel Scripturæ Propheticæ observatio: Hic vero tabularum Novi Testamenti vel Scripturæ Apostolicæ. Illic requirebatur fides in Christum exhibendum: hic verò fides in Christum exhibitum: Illic sacramentorum Circumcisionis & agni Paschalis usurpatio; hic sacramenti Baptismi & Cœnæ Dominicæ. 6. Ratione modi, loci, & temporis promulgationis, quod Vetus Test. cum terrore inter fulgura & tonitrua Exod. XIX. vers. 16. novum cum suavi compellatione promulgatum sit, Matth. XXIX. 19. seqq. quod illud in monte Sinai publicatum: hoc vero in Sion & Jerusalem: quod illud post exitum ex Ægypto, Jer. XXXI. 32. hoc vero novissimis politiæ Judaicæ diebus, vel in plenitudine temporum Jerem. XXXI. 33. Es. II. 2. Mich. IV. 1. 7. Ratione constitutionum, quia in Veteri Testam. variæ fuere ordinationes legis non moralis tantum, sed etiam ceremonialis vel Ecclesiasticæ, & forensis seu Politicæ: In Novo Test. vero desiere leges ceremoniales, nec Christianis Politicæ legis observantia incumbit. 8. Modo exhibendi promissa: Vetus Testam. habebat umbram: Novum habet ipsum corpus & complementum, Col. II. 17. Ebr. IX. 1. Ibi minus aperte promittebantur bona spiritualia & cœlestia, tecta magnam partem typorum umbris & figuris: Hic vero apertius illa promissa sunt, & involucra typorum evoluta. 9. Quoad terminum pædagogiæ legis: In Veteri Test. lex erat pædagogus ad Christum exhibendum: In Novo Test. ad exhibitum. 10. Quoad adjuncta: Vetus Testam. respectu eorum, quæ palam & apertius continebat, timoris erat & servitutis: Novum autem per omnia est gaudii & libertatis, Gal. IV. vers. 24. seq. Vetus Test. ob legum varietatem erat onerosius, & ob modum exactionis rigorosius: Novum ab istis oneribus immune est, & manifestius istius vigoris remissionem exhibet, 2. Cor. III. 14. 11. Quoad præcipuum Veteris Testamenti προσκείμενον: quia lex proprie pertinet ad Vetus Testamentum, cujus finis est Christus, & ut finis ille monstraretur, ideo quædam ad Evangelium pertinentia etiam V. T. comprehensa sunt; ita tamen, ut præcipuum & principale ministerium Mosis sit legale, quod ipsum vero non recte exequitur, nisi finem legis Christum simul recte monstret, ut monet hic B. Chemnitius. Deut. XIIX. 15. Joh. I. 17. 12. Quoad traditionem & effectum. Quia Vetus Testam. ratione legis moralis, cujus promulgatio solennis præcipua fuit Veteris Testam. pars, tabulis lapideis inscri- ptum fuit: Novum vero ratione Evangelii, cujus universalis prædicatio itidem pars est Novi Te- stamenti primaria, in cordibus hominum scri- bitur. Jerem. XXXI. vers. 24. 2. Cor. III. vers. 6. 12. Quoad sanctionis Mediatorem. Quia Vetus Testamentum sancitum est respectu populi per Mosen, qui non quidem Μεσιτης uspiam vocatur, sed servus Domini, Num. XII. vers. 7. Ebr. III. vers. 4. ut honor ille Christo soli servetur, sanguine tamen sacrificiali tabulas Testamenti, volumen nempe legis, & populum conspersit, ut à parte populi Testamentum Vetus ea ratione sanciretur: Novum vero Testam. quod in ara crucis sancitum est, ex parte DEI, sanguine & morte Christi Mediatoris, ex parte nostri confir- matur in S. cœna eodem Christi sanguine, quo non aspergimur, sed potamur à Christo, Media- tore novi fœderis. Hic enim calix est novum Te- stamentum in meo sanguine, testatur CHRISTUS, Luc. XXII. vers. 20. 1. Cor. XI. v. 25. 14. Quoad circumstantias fidei ab hæredibus requisitæ. Nam utut eadem fides quoad substantiam sit in utro- que Testamento: In Veteri tamen fides require- batur in obedientiam Messiæ præstandam, in No- vo Testam. præstitam: In Veteri Testam. in ly- trum folvendum, in Novo Testam. in lytrum solutum, Roman.
