III. vers. 25. 26. Ebr. IX. v. 15. 15. Quoad durationem: Vetus Testam. antiquan- dum erat, Ebr. VIII. vers. 13. Novum autem du- rat usque ad consummationem seculi, 1. Cor. XV. vers. 24. 16. Quoad latitudinem & complexum: Vetus Testamentum sistebatur intra angustos Ju- dææ terminos: Novum autem porrigit sese ad fines universæ terræ, Zachar. IX. vers. 10. Matth. XXIX. vers. 19.

XVI. Non ergo simpliciter probanda defini- tio Parei: Quod Vetus Testamentum prima & propria significatione sit doctrina gratiæ spiritualis, olim per Mosen & Prophetas Patribus & crasso Judæorum populo salutem æternam promittens, pa- lam quidem sub conditione perfectæ obedientiæ legis moralis, & comminatione maledictionis æternæ, nisi eam præstarent, una cum onere intolerabili rituum legalium, atque jugo arctissimæ politiæ Mosaicæ, tecte vero sub conditione pœnitentiæ & fidei in Messiam futurum, ceremoniarum umbris & figu- ris præfiguratum. Nam 1. confunditur ita aperte fœdus vel pactum legale & Vetus Testamentum. 2. doctrina spiritualis gratiæ, quæ in utroque Te- stamento locum habuit cum Testamento propria significatione accepto. 3. Vetus Test. per Mo- sen post egressum ex Ægypto promulgatum est populo, teste Jeremia: Huc ergo non faciunt alii Prophetæ. 4. Etsi principaliter lex moralis per- tinebat ad Vetus Test. quoad ministerium Mosi proprium, quod erat literæ occidentis ac con- demnationis & mortis, 2. Cor. III. vers. 6. seqq. quemadmodum etiam ideo Vetus Testamentum ad servitutem generasse dicitur, Gal. IV. vers. 24. non tamen Veteri Testamento præter typos dee- rant oracula de Christo, ejusque beneficiis: li- cet per legis moralis παιδαγωγίαν veteres ad Chri stum adducti sunt per ceremonialis figuram, ceu concionem visibilem de Christo informati: Ad- ditæ tamen etiam apertæ conciones de Christo fue- re, qualis illa est Deut. XIIX. & quæ Patriarchis jam factæ, sine dubio à Mose repetitæ, ac præ- dicto vaticinio, aliisque Evangelicis ejus concio- nibus sunt confirmatæ. Id præterea non abs re hic monetur à B. Chemnitio, quod Leviticæ ce- remoniæ dupliciter considerentur, 1. tanquam observationes carnales & externæ, seu opera pæ- dagogica, quibus membra illius cœtus in exter- na aliqua & carnali munditie conservata: Et ita ad legem eas pertinere ait. Nam finis illius politiæ fuit, ut in ea promissio conservaretur, quod inde venturus sit Messias, qui super universum orbem regnaturus esset: Item ceremoniæ illæ conside- rantur tanquam conciones & professiones de pecca- to, de ira Dei & pænis divinis, & eactenus quoque ad legem pertinent. Quia vero finis legis est Chri- stus, ideo 2. etiam considerantur ut typi Christi, & eactenus pertinent ad Evangelium, ubi præterea & hoc observandum, quod quatenus typi illi ce- remoniales Christum respiciunt, non primum in Sina traditi fuerunt. Nam & Patriarchis ante di- luvium illæ ceremoniæ notæ & usitatæ fuerunt. Et 2. Cor. III. 14. Paulus docet, hunc scopum in- tellectum verum esse usum totius legis: Sed quan- do finis ille non consideratur, sed opiniones ac- cedunt tantum de externa observatione, & quod opus operatum justificet, tunc vocat velamen. Quorum hoc proprium est Mosis, illud propri- um est CHRISTI.

quæ scilicet ipsi propria fuere, quæ vero non de- finienda per ipsam doctrinam decalogi, sed per ea, quæ pertinebant ad statum Ecclesiæ & politiæ Israëlitici populi proprium. Atque hæc de præ- senti materia, quibus conferri poterunt, quæ B. Chemnitius, B. Hutterus, B. Winckelmannus loc. cit. tradidere, quæque in proœmio ad Bibl. Illustr. V. Test. nec non ad præloquium Grotianum in Novum Testamentum observavimus.

## 9:1 Argument
CHAPTER IX. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle explains both the ministry (λειτουργίαν) of Christ, comparing the Old Testament, whose laws, worship, and worldly sanctuary he designates, and especially the annual entry into the sanctuary, which he teaches to be typical of Christ, the true High Priest, and his entry into the holy of holies: and also the mediation (μεσιτείαν), that he was made the Mediator of the New Testament, so that through his death we might obtain the inheritance, which was confirmed by the Testament, just as formerly the old one was by the blood of the sacrifice (Exod. XXIV. 8.), as well as the fruit of both, namely regarding the Priesthood, that the entry of our High Priest into heaven was made for the sake of intercession for us, and that not often, but only once, and that through his sacrifice sins were taken away, as well as regarding the mediation of the New Testament, that by the power of the same he is to appear again for the salvation of the faithful.

XVII. The reason why the Calvinists contend that the Old and New Testaments are of the same substance is to maintain that the sacraments of the Old and New Testaments do not differ in substance, and therefore, just as the body and blood of Christ were only typically in the Old Testament, so also in the Holy Eucharist, which is the sacrament of the New Testament, they are not substantially present, but only the figure and symbol of the same are exhibited there. But it has been shown that the Old and New Testaments differ in substance, in the former only the shadow of the body and blood of Christ: But in the latter the very body and blood of Christ are had, and it is evident from the sacrament of the Eucharist itself that the blood of Christ shed for us for the remission of sins, and provided there for drinking, pertains to the substance of the New Testament, Luke XXII. 20, 1 Cor. XI. 25.

There are three parts: I. The explanation of the ministry (Λειτουργίας) of Christ, to verse 14. II. The elucidation of the mediation (Μεσιτείας) of the New Testament, to verse 22. III. The account of both, to verse 28.

PART I. The explanation of the ministry (Λειτουργίας) of Christ.

XVIII. When it is asked concerning the abrogation of the Old Testament, whether it is abrogated in whole or in part? Pareus responds that it is not abrogated regarding the substance of the spiritual doctrine of grace through Christ; but this did not pertain to the proper substance of the Old Testament, by which it is opposed to the New Testament: nor regarding the doctrine of the moral law, which likewise did not pertain to the Old Testament, as it is distinguished (ἀντιδιηρημένως) from the New. Then Pareus responds that the Old Testament is abrogated 1. as to the circumstance of the spiritual doctrine of grace concerning the future, that salvation is no longer promised on account of the Christ who is to come: concerning which it has already been warned; one must take care not to confuse the doctrine of the Gospel with the Testament. 2. As to the impossible condition of perfect obedience, under which eternal salvation was promised to the Fathers. But this is to be understood only regarding the pedagogy, which did not vanish even under the New Testament, as far as the moral law is concerned. 3. As to the curse: because we are no longer under the curse. But neither were the faithful in the Old Testament under the curse. 4. As to the burden of the rites and the Levitical Priesthood, and the shadows, which vanished when Christ was exhibited. 5. As to the yoke of the Mosaic polity imposed upon the necks of the Jewish people. We indeed admit these last two: But why did Pareus omit the Sacraments of the Old Testament? Are they not likewise abrogated? Therefore the blessed Hutterus responds more correctly: that the Old Testament is not abrogated only in part, but entirely, regarding its substantials,

Vers. 1. Εἶχε μὲν ὖν ἡ πρώτη σκηνὴ δικαιώματα λατρείας] In the Manuscript that word σκηνὴ is absent, as also in the Syriac and in the Latin: and rightly so. For it was born from a gloss, nor did Chrysostom and the Greeks who followed him read it. And ἡ πρώτη is to be understood from the preceding διαθήκη. That had δικαιώματα, many precepts, by no means to be compared with the precepts of Christ. Δικαιώματα are חקים, Num. XXX. 17. Deut. IV. 14. 40. 45. Psal. CXIX. 12. Luc. I. 6. It also had λατρείας. For you may rightly take this noun also in the Accusative. For a third Accusative will also follow. That covenant had its own forms of worship, namely external ones, concerning which [we read] in Leviticus.

Erasmus indeed reads σκηνὴν, and rendered it first tabernacle, and Beza confesses that most copies have long had it so, but that from Photius, the most acute of all Greek Interpreters, whose words are cited in the Greek scholia, it appears that the name of the tabernacle has crept in, and that erroneously, since from the series of the argument, and the last verse of the previous chapter, it easily appears that the noun διαθήκης is to be understood, and therefore he did not hesitate to expunge σκηνὴν, following the authority of the Claromontane Codex, the Syriac Interpreter, and the received Latin edition. Grotius also asserts the consensus of his MS: We add also that of B. Luther, as well as the Arabic, and Chrysostom, and other Interpreters. B. Dorscheus rejects it from the context: The antecedents, he says, manifestly refute it. For that is ἡ πρώτη, verse 1, which in chapter VIII. 13 God made old, which is opposed to the new, concerning whose abolition the Prophet prophesied; but the consequences also reject it. For as is clear from v. 2 & following, σκηνὴ is the content, and that which ἡ πρώτη had. Just as also δικαιώματα λατρείας are that which was had and exercised ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ. Therefore it is not the thing itself containing. Therefore ἡ πρώτη [the first], that is to say, the covenant, is to be understood; for it comprised both τὰ δικαιώματα λατρείας [the ordinances of divine service] and τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικόν [the worldly sanctuary]. Indeed, before this, no mention had been made of the old tabernacle under the name πρώτη: but the Old Testament was named in the last verse of the preceding chapter: and here in verse 2 follows immediately ἡ πρώτη concerning the tabernacle, but the outer part of the same, not the old tabernacle, where Camero in myrothecio notes that σκηνὴν is an interpretation of that which he had called ἅγιον κοσμικὸν. And he urges that σκηνὴ did not have σκηνὴν. If, however, for the sake of the faith of many codices one wishes to retain it, the sense of the particle πρώτη will be: The first or Old tabernacle had a worldly sanctuary. For the tabernacle was then built, and indeed the first, in which were the candlestick, etc., which was called the holy place, and the second, which was called the holy of holies. Which sense has nothing absurd in it. But the matter comes to almost the same thing, whether it is said that the λατρεία [divine service] of the tabernacle is explained, or that of the former Testament, because the tabernacle belonged to the former Testament. The particle καὶ

also, Beza thinks should be expunged, but Camero rightly notes that καὶ is here ἐμφατικὸν [emphatic], as in Phil. II. 9. Furthermore, Chrysostom explained the connection thus: He has shown hitherto from the Priesthood, and from the testament, that it would have an end. Next, he shows the same from the plan of the tabernacle. Others connect it thus: that the Apostle, having spoken generally before about the abrogation of the Old Testament, now adapts it specifically to the ceremonies, to show that there was nothing in the Levitical worship so minute to which Christ did not put an end by His coming. But it seems to be a concessive anticipation from the preceding verse, to which it could be objected: But the Old Testament also had its magnificent worships, venerable rites, useful justifications, salutary expiations, purifications, and legal justifications. Therefore it does not seem that there was so little that it had to be entirely abolished. The Apostle concedes that it indeed had its δικαιώματα [ordinances], its λατρείας [divine services], and its ἅγια [holy things] which were magnificent, yet all were merely shadowy and ineffectual: but that the truth and completion of all things are finally obtained in Christ. And the particles μὲν and καὶ indicate this sense not obscurely. It indeed had also, etc. He concedes, I say, that it also had its sacred things: but that Christ abolished them all by His coming. Therefore the suspended particle μὲν in v. 1 will correspond to the adversative δὲ in v. 11, so that the antithesis may be established, as Pareus holds here.

But as for δικαιώματα and λατρείας, which words Beza rashly reads in the construct state, since what follows, τὸ ἅγιον, stands in the way—for that notes that an asyndeton preceded, otherwise it should have been said καὶ ἅγιον—he observes that one should not anxiously seek a difference, and that by the name of δικαιώματα the precepts of the ceremonial law are noted in general, since a δικαίωμα is whatever God has ordained [ἐδικαίωσεν], and that is called so peculiarly because it is just for no other reason than that God commanded it, so that one should not seek the reason for a precept which God has ordained; (which name, however, also occurs concerning the law of nature in Rom. I. verse 32.) but by the name of λατρείας that worship of GOD is peculiarly designated which consisted in sacrifices, besides which there were other δικαιώματα which concerned men, verse 10, such as ablutions, sprinklings, abstinence from a certain kind of food, fasts, etc., provided that λατρέυειν properly signifies external worship according to the LXX Interpreters. Whence the worship of the New Testament is not simply called λατρεία, but λογικὴ λατρεία [reasonable service], Rom. XII. 1, and λατρέυειν ἐν πνεύματι [to serve in spirit], Rom. I. 9, so that in this way the Apostle designated the external and carnal or typical Aaronic worship by the name of λατρειῶν. But others more correctly distinguish in this place between δικαιώματα or justifications, and λατρείας or worships, since the Apostle both enumerates these three—justifications, worship, and sanctuary—distinctly in the type, and unfolds them in the antitype, as Pareus taught in his analysis. He enumerates them distinctly, though in reverse order: First the tabernacle, v. 2 seqq., then the worship in the same, v. 6, 7, finally τὰ δικαιώματα, verse 9, 10. Thus, therefore, he would have called δικαιώματα not rites, but the effects of rites, namely, ceremonial justices or justifications. Here the blessed Dorscheus unfolds the homonymy of the word: Δικαιώματα are taken in various ways in the Scriptures. For they either denote the righteous acts themselves, and are opposed to transgressions. Thus Rom. V. 18, VIII. 32, where the δικαίωμα of God is that which is agreeable to the divine law, which is right, which pleases God, which is opposed to all those wickednesses which are wont to flow from a reprobate mind, which are called τὰ μὴ καθήκοντα [things not fitting], verse 28, and are enumerated in v. 19, 20, 21. Thus Aristotle, book I. Rhetoric, chapter 13, opposes δικαιώματα and ἀδικήματα [injustices]: Or it denotes the same as δικαίωσις, that is, the very act of absolution opposed to condemnation. Thus it is taken in Rom. V. 16, where δικαίωμα is opposed to κατακρίματι [condemnation]. Or it denotes a judgment, whether it be of absolution or of condemnation, which is exercised divinely, in which way in Rev. XV. 4, the divine δικαιώματα are celebrated in the Song, which is called of Moses and of the Lamb. Or it denotes the law or divine constitution, Luke I. 6, where δικαιώματα are joined with ἐντολαῖς [commandments], and seem properly to designate the ceremonial laws themselves, in the accurate observation of which Zacharias and Elizabeth exercised themselves. Thus also Rom. II. 26, τὰ δικαιώματα τοῦ νόμου are the law itself, as is evident from Psalm LV. 25, 32, 22, and 18. Thus Rom. VIII. 4, τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ νόμου is nothing else than the rigor of the law, which, since men could not perform it, Christ Himself took upon Himself. Among the later Greeks, δικαιώματα are called proofs, documents, and instruments which litigants use to claim something for themselves. Thus in the Oriental law, book 1, page 109, the title is περὶ δικαιωμάτων, concerning proofs or instruments. In this place, δικαιώματα are the institutes or sanctions which pertain to divine worship.

Τότε ἅγιον κοσμικὸν] And this is an accusative. That sanctuary had its own worldly [sanctuary], that is, an image of the whole world. See above VIII. 2.

It is wrongly called a worldly sanctuary, because it was an image of the world. For neither does that adjective κοσμικὸν imply that it is an image of the world from the manner of speaking, nor does the thing itself fit: for the sanctuary was not a figure of the world, but of the Church and of heaven: nor was it the Apostle's purpose here to explain figures of the world. To the Apostle's scope, says B. Dorscheus, that explanation in no way squares. For neither in the fact that the tabernacle had some form of a worldly system is there anything that contributes to the Apostle's purpose, who rather intends this, to indicate its perishability and aptitude for παλαίωσιν, concerning which see above chapter VIII. 13. Whence he looks more to this quality than to the form. Most have called it worldly, because it consisted of worldly and earthly matter, to which something divine, spiritual, and heavenly corresponded. Τὸ ἅγιον, says B. Dorscheus, the tabernacle itself is called κοσμικὸν, which is called worldly partly materially, because it consisted of worldly things, and partly also in opposition. For it is opposed to the τῷ ἁγίῳ ὑπερκοσμίῳ or ὑπερουρανίῳ, such as the sanctuary of Christ is. Thomas, as Ribera reports, interprets it in this place as the very sanctification of the old law, which was called secular, because it was temporal and not perpetual, or worldly, because it did not contain the grace of the Old Testament. He attributes the same to Cajetan, that he called the secular sanctuary a worldly holiness, which was seen by the eyes of men, as if it were not spiritual, inasmuch as it is seen only by the eyes of God. But in the holiness of the Old Testament, which has already been expressed clearly enough by δικαιώματα λατρείας. Nor is the Apostle accustomed to place something more obscure, such as what the ἅγιον κοσμικὸν would be if it were taken for the holiness of the Old Testament itself, after placing something clearer, but the whole enumeration of the τὸ ἁγίου κοσμικοῦ made in v. 2 and following explains nothing other than the tabernacle itself. The Vulgate rendered worldly as secular. It was external, typical, to which heavenly truth did not yet underlie. Those who say it is called secular because it was to last for many centuries are ignorant of the authentic text. Whence they are also deservedly rejected by Thomas, who explain secular, that is, temporal, not perpetual, because in Greek it is worldly, not secular. But that Chrysostom, whom Theophylact, Oecumenius, and Haymo follow, understands by the τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν the outer place of the tabernacle, or the atrium, to which access was open not only to Jews but to men of the whole world, does not fit for the reason that the Apostle does not explain three parts of the tabernacle, but only two, inasmuch as those in which the λατρείαι were performed, and to which the τὰ δικαιώματα, the effects of the λατρειῶν, belonged. Meanwhile, if an application of that atrium were also desired in the antitype, so that the Priest comes through it into the holy place, and through the holy place into the holy of holies: thus it will not be irrelevant to say that Christ came into the world, and from there into the Church, and finally entered into heaven through the Church. Furthermore, it is certain that that atrium never comes under the name of the holy place, and therefore cannot be understood here. Blessed Dorscheus weighs the diverse opinions here thus: Chrysostom, whom Theophylact follows, judges that the tabernacle was called κοσμικὸν because the outer tabernacle was open not only to the Jews, but also to the Gentiles, and therefore to all the nations of the world. But besides the fact that this appellation is also against the Apostolic scope, since he does not now intend to explain how widely and to which nations the tabernacle was open, the τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν in this place comprises not only the first tabernacle, but also the second. For the whole of that which is explained in v. 2, 3, 4, and 5 is comprised by these words, and is distinguished from the δικαιώματα λατρείας. Others wish the τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν to be called the temple, which is called secular because it was thought that it would last for many centuries. However, they are stuck on the fact that κοσμικὸν is rendered secular by the Vulgate, when it is more fully called worldly. Furthermore, they do not observe that the Apostle is dwelling on the times of Moses, and therefore is always speaking of the tabernacle, not even mentioning the temple in this passage. He clearly wished to lead back to the very beginnings of the sanction and constitution of the Jewish religion, and to elicit from them the excellence of the new covenant. Whence also, when he had called it the ἅγιον κοσμικὸν, which he is about to explain afterwards, he commemorates not the parts and contents of the temple, but especially those of the tabernacle. Franc. Ribera stops at this, that the τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν is nothing other than the first tabernacle, which is explained in verse 2: That it is called secular because it signified the life and worship of God, which the saints offered to God in this age, until they should enter through the blood of Christ into the second tabernacle, that is, heaven. It is also said to be worldly, because it represented the life which the saints had in this world before the coming of Christ. Thus in Tit. II. 12, those desires which are in the men of the age, and such as worldly men have, are called κοσμικὰς ἐπιθυμίας. Whence he concludes that this appellation can neither properly belong to the holy of holies, nor to the whole tabernacle, because it bore the figure of both the age and eternity. But (1) in this place there is another meaning of this word than in Tit. II, where the discourse is about that world which ὅλως ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ κεῖται, 1 John V. 19. Then (2) the τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν extends as widely as the δικαιώματα λατρείας. And these extend themselves into the holy of holies itself. For there are δικαιώματα outside, and there are also inside the veil, verse 7. Therefore, the τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν is also contended to extend that far. (3) That it is called κοσμικὸν from the representation of the worship and state of this age is by no means gathered from the Apostolic intention. For there is no opposition between the first and second tabernacle in that the former is κοσμικὴ and the latter is not: But that all that apparatus of the Old Testament, if it is compared with the institutions of the new, is κοσμικὸς, fashioned from worldly, perishable, and dying things, and therefore to be abolished and consumed by old age. (4) If the τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν did not comprise the whole tabernacle, external and internal, the enumeration in v. 1 of those things which the first covenant had would be insufficient. For a third thing would have had to be added, which was behind the veil, the holy of holies. Therefore, it is more simply said that the τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν is so called because it is opposed to the super-worldly and super-heavenly, which is the tabernacle of the body of Christ, of which above in chapter VIII. 2.

Latin:

CAPUT IX. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Explicat Apostolus tum λειτουργίαν Christi, con- ferens Vetus Testamentum, cujus jura, cultum, & sanctum mundanum designat, imprimis vero annuum ingressum in san- ctum, quæ typica esse docet Christi, veri Pontificis, & ingressus ejusdem in sanctum sanctorum: tum μεσιτείαν, quod NoviTe- stamenti Mediator factus sit, ut per mor- tem ejus hereditatem consequamur, quæ confirmata est Testament. uti quondam vet9 sanguine pecunio(Exod.XXIV.8.) necnon fructum utriusque, utpote quoad Sacerdotium, quod ingressus Pontificis no- stri in cælum ob interpellationem pro no- bis factus, idque non sæpius, sed semel tan- tum, quodque per sacrificium ejus peccata sublata sint, necnon quoad mediationem Novi Testamenti, quod vi ejusdem iterum appariturus sit ad salutem fidelium.

XVII. Causa, cur Calviniani Vetus & Novum Testamentum ejusdem substantiæ esse conten- dunt, est, ut sacramenta Veteris & Novi Testam. substantia haud differre obtineant, ac proinde, quemadmodum Christi corpus & sanguis non nisi typice in Veteri Test. fuit, ita etiam in S. Eucha- ristia, quæ Novi Test. sacramentum est, non sub- stantialiter præsto esse, sed figuram solum & sym- bolum ejusdem ibi exhiberi. Sed ostensum est Vetus & Novum Test. substantia differre, in illo umbram tantum corporis & sanguinis Christi: Hic vero ipsum corpus & sanguinem Christi ha- beri, & ex ipso sacramento Euchariftiæ constat, sanguinem Christi effusum pro nobis in remis- sionem peccatorum, ibique præbitum ad biben- dum ad substantiam Novi Testamenti pertinere, Luc. XXII. 20. 1. Cor. XI. 25.

PArtes tres sunt: I. Λειτουργίας Christi explica- tio, ad v. 14. II. Μεσιτείας Novi Testam. dilu- cidatio, ad v. 22. III. Utriusque ratio ad v. 28.

PARS I. Λειτουργίας Christi explicatio.

XVIII. De abrogatione Veteris Test. cum quæ- ritur, an ex toto, an ex parte id abrogatum sit? Resp. Pareus, non esse abrogatum quoad substan- tiam doctrinæ spiritualis gratiæ per Christum; Sed hæc non pertinebat ad substantiam propriam Ve- teris Testamenti, qua opponitur id Testamento novo: neque quoad doctrinam legis moralis, quæ itidem non pertinebat ab Vetus Testamentum, prout ἀντιδιηρημένως contradiftinguitur Novo. Deinde respondet Pareus abrogatum esse Vetus Testam. 1. quantum ad doctrinæ spiritualis gratiæ circumstantiam de futuro, quod non amplius fa- lus promittatur propter Christum venturum: de quo jam monitum; cavendum esse, ne doctrina Evangelii cum Testamento confundatur. 2. Quan- tum ad conditionem impossibilem perfectæ obedien- tiæ, sub qua Patribus æterna salus promissa. Quod vero non nisi quoad pædagogiam intelligendum, quæ nec sub Novo Testamento, quod ad legem moralem, evanuit. 3. Quantum ad maledictionem: quia nos non sumus amplius sub maledictione. At- qui nec fideles in Veteri Testamento sub male- dictione fuerunt. 4. Quantum ad onus rituum & Sacerdotii Levitici, & quod umbras, quæ Christo exhibito evanuerunt. 5. Quantum ad jugum politiæ Mosaicæ populi Judaici cervicibus impositum. Quæ duo posteriora admittimus qui- dem: Sed cur prætermisit Pareus Sacramenta Ve- teris Test. annon eadem itidem quoque abrogata sunt? Rectius itaque respondet B. Hutterus: Ve- tus Testamentum non ex parte tantum, sed to- tum abrogatum esse, quoad substantialia ejus,

Vers. 1. Εἶχε μὲν ὖν ἡ πρώτη σκηνὴ δικαιώματα λατρείας] in Manuscripto abest illud σκηνὴ, ut & in Syro & in Lati- no: & recte. Est enim natum ex glossemate, nec lege- runt id Chrysostomus, & sequuti eum Græci. Et ἡ πρώτη intelligendum ex prioribus διαθήκη. Ea habuit δικαιώματα præcepta multa, neutiquam conferenda cum Christi præ- ceptis. Δικαιώματα חקים, Num. XXX. 17. Deut. IV. 14. 40. 45. Psal. CXIX. 12. Luc. I. 6. Habuit & λατρείας. Recte enim & hoc nomen sumas in Accusativo. Nam & tertius Accusativus sequetur. Habuit illud pactum cultus suos, nempe externos, de quibus in Levitico.

Erasmus legit quidem σκηνὴν, & reddidit prius tabernaculum, & fatetur Beza, pleraque exempla- ria jam pridem ita habere, sed ex Photio omnium Græcorum Interpretum acutissimo, cujus verba in scholiis Græcis citantur, apparere, irrepsisse taber- naculi nomen, idque perperam, quum ex argu- menti serie, & ultimo superioris capitis versicu- lo facile appareat, subaudiendum esse διαθήκης nomen, ideoque non dubitasse se σκηνὴν expun- gere Claromontani Codicis, Syri Interpr. & Latinæ receptæ editionis autoritatem seqvutum. Assert & Grotius MS. sui consensum: Addimus & B. Lu- theri, ut & Arabis, & Chrysostomi, aliorumque In- terpretum. B. Dorscheus eam ex contextu repro- bat: Antecedentia, inquit, manifeste refellunt. Ea enim est ἡ πρώτη, vers. 1. quæ cap. VIII 13. quam Deus antiquavit, quæ opponitur καινῇ, de cujus abo- litione Propheta vaticinatus est; sed & conseqq. respuunt. Nam uti ex v. 2. & seqq. liquet, σκηνὴ est contentum, & id, quod habebat ἡ πρώτη. Sicut & δικαιώματα λατρείας sunt id, quod habebatur & exercebatur ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ. Ergo non est ipsum continens. Ergo ἡ πρώτη scil. διαθήκη intelligenda est; ea enim complectebatur & τὰ δικαιώματα λα- τρείας, & τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικόν. Sane antea facta non erat tabernaculi veteris sub nomine πρώτη men- tio: Testamentum autem Vetus vers. ult. capitis præc. nominatum est: & sequitur hic vers. 2. sta- tim ἡ πρώτη de tabernaculo, sed parte exteriori ejusdem, non de veteri tabernaculo, ubi σκηνὴν interpretamentum esse illius, quod dixerat ἅγιον κοσμικὸν notat Camero in nἱyroth. idque urget, quod σκηνὴ non habebat σκηνὴν. Si tamen ob plu- rimorum Codicum fidem retinere quis velit, par- ticulæ πρώτη sensus erit: Primum vel Vetus ta- bernaculum habuit sanctum mundanum. Ta- bernaculum enim extructum tum fuit, & pri- mum quidem, in quo erant candelabrum &c. quod dicebatur sanctum, & alterum, quod dice- batur sanctum sanctorum. Qui sensus nihil absurdi habet. Res autem eodem fere reci- dit, sive dicatur λατρεία tabernaculi, sive Te- stamenti prioris explicari, quia tabernaculum pertinebat ad prius Testamentum. Particulam καὶ

etiam expungendam censet Beza, sed recte no- tat Camero, καὶ esse hic ἐμφατικὸν, ut Phil. II. 9. Cæterum nexum ita exposuit Chrysostomus: O- stendit hactenus ex Sacerdotio, & ex testamento, quod finem habiturum illud esset. Deinceps idem ostendit ex tabernaculi schemate. Alii sic conne- ctunt, Apostolum quod prius de abrogatione Vete- ris Testamenti generatim dixerat, nunc speciatim ad ceremonias accommodare, ut ostendat, nihil in cultu Levitico fuisse tam minutum, cui finem non imposuerit adventu suo Christus. Videtur ve- ro occupatio esse concessoria ex præcedente versu, ad quem excipi poterat: Atqui Vetus quoque Te- stamentum suos habuit magnificos cultus, venera- biles ritus, utiles justificationes, salutares expiatio- nes, purgationes & justificationes legales. Non igi- tur videtur adeo nihil fuisse, ut antiquari in to- tum debuerit. Concedit Apostolus, habuisse id qui- dem sua δικαιώματα, suas λατρείας & sua ἅγια magnifica, omnia tamen umbratilia duntaxat & inefficacia: Veritatem vero & complementum o- mnium in Christo demum obtineri. Atque hunc sensum non obscure indicant particulæ μὲν & καὶ. Habuit quidem etiam &c. Concedit, inquam, ha- buisse & illud sua sacra: sed quæ omnia Christus suo adventu aboleverit. Particulæ igitur suspensi væ μὲν v. 1. respondebit adversaria δὲ, v. 11. ut con- stet antithesis, ut hic habet Pareus.

Δικαιώματα vero & λατρείας, quas voces in sta- tu constructionis temere legit Beza, quum ob- stet, quod sequitur τότε ἅγιον, id enim notat præ- cessisse ἀσύνδετον, alioquin dicendum fuisset καὶ ἅγιον, non anxie quærendam esse differentiam observat, & δικαιωμάτων nomine in genere præ- cepta legis ceremonialis notari, quum δικαίωμα sit, quicquid ἐδικαίωσεν ὁ Θεὸς, & peculiariter il- lud dicatur ita, quod non aliam ob causam justum, quam quia Deus jussit, ut non quærenda sit ra- tio præcepti, quod Deus ἐδικαίωσε; (Quod no- men tamen etiam de jure naturæ occurrit Rom. I. vers. 32.) λατρείας autem nomine peculiariter ille cultus DEI designetur, qui in sacrificiis po- situs erat, præter quem alia erant δικαιώματα, quæ homines respiciebant vers. 10. ut ablutiones, aspersiones, abstinentia à certo ciborum genere, jejunia &c. siquidem λατρέυειν cultum externum proprie significet LXX. Interpp. Unde cultus N. Testamenti non simpliciter λατρεία, sed λο γικὴ λατρεία dicatur, Rom. XII. 1. & λατρέυειν ἐν πνεύματι, Rom I. 9. ut hoc pacto Apostolus cul- tum Aaroniscum externum & carnalem seu typi- cum nomine λατρειῶν designarit. Sed rectius alii hoc loco distinguunt δικαιώματα seu justificatio- nes, & λατρείας seu cultus, quum hæc tria justi- ficationes, cultus, & sanctuarium distincte Apo- stolus & recenseat in typo, & evolvat in antity- po, ut Pareus in analysi docuit. Recenset distin- cte, licet ordine inverso: Primum quidem taber- naculum, v. 2. seqq. post cultus in eodem, v. 6. 7. denique τὰ δικαιώματα vers. 9. 10. Sic ergo di- καιώματα non ritus, sed rituum effecta justitias vel justificationes ceremoniales dixerit. Evolvit hic B. Dorscheus ὁμωνυμίαν vocis: Δικαιώματα varie in Scripturis accipiuntur. Vel enim notant ipsa κατορθώματα, & opponuntur παραπτώμασι. Sic Rom. V. 18. VIII. 32. ubi δικαίωμα τοῦ Θεοῦ est illud, quod legi divinæ consentaneum, quod rectum est, quod Deo placet, quod opponitur omnibus istis sceleribus, quæ fluere solent ex reproba mente, quæ vocantur τὰ μὴ καθήκοντα, vers. 28. & enumeran- tur v. 19. 20. 21. Sic Arist. lib. I. Rhet. cap. 13. δι- καίωματα & ἀδικήματα opponit: Vel notat idem, quod δικαίωσις, hoc est, ipsum actum absolutionis condemnationi oppositum. Sic sumitur Rom. V. 16. ubi δικαίωμα opponitur κατακρίματι. Vel notat ju- dicium, sive jam sit absolutionis sive damnationis, quod divinitus exercetur, quomodo Apoc. XV. 4. δικαιώματα divina in Cantico, quod Mosis vocatur & Agni, celebrantur. Vel notat legem sive consti- tutionem divinam Luc. I. 6. ubi δικαιώματα con- junguntur ἐντολαῖς, & videntur proprie ipsas leges ceremoniales designare, in quarum accurata ob- servatione sese exercuerunt Zacharias & Elisabe- tha. Sic & Rom. II. 26. τὰ δικαιώματα τοῦ νόμου sunt ipse νόμος, ut patet ex Psal. LV. 25. 32. 22. & 18. Sic Rom. VIII. 4. τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ νόμου nihil est aliud, quam rigor legis, quem cum homines prestare non potuerint, Christus ipse in se recepit. Apud recentiores Græcos δικαιώματα vocantur probationes, documenta & instrumenta, quibus utuntur litigantes, ut aliquid sibi vindicent. Sic in jure Orientali l. 1. pag. 109. titulus est περὶ δικαι- ωμάτων de probationibus sive instrumentis. Hoc loco δικαιώματα sunt instituta sive sanctiones, quæ ad cultum divinum pertinent.

Τότε ἅγιον κοσμικὸν] Et hic accusativus est. Habuit pactum illud sanctuarium suum mnduanum, id est, mun- di totius imaginem. Vide supra VIII. 2.

Perperam sanctuarium mundanum dicitur, quod mundi imago fuerit. Nam nec id adjecti- vum κοσμικὸν infert imaginem mundi esse ex mo- do loquendi, nec res ipsa convenit: non enim sanctuarium figura erat mundi, sed Ecclesiæ & cœli: neque propositum Apostolo hic fuit, figu- ras mundi exponere. Ad scopum Apostoli, inqui- B. Dorscheus, ista explicatio nulla ratione quadrat. Neque enim in eo, quod tabernaculum aliquam Sy- stematis mundani formam habuerit, quicquam est, quod ad propositum Apostoli faciat, qui potius hoc intendit, ut caducitatem & aptitudinem ad παλαί- wσιν, de qua supra cap. VIII. 13. indigitet. Unde ad qualitatem hanc magis, quam ad formam respicit. Mundanum pleriq; dixere, quod è materia mun- dana & terrena constiterit, cui respondebat ali- quid divini, spiritualis, & cœlestis. Τὸ ἅγιον, in- quit B. Dorscheus, κοσμικὸν appellatur ipsum ta- bernaculum, quod κοσμικὸν vocatur partim mate- rialiter, quia ex rebus mundanis constabat, par- tim etiam in oppositione. Opponitur enim τῶ ἁγίῳ ὑπερκοσμίῳ sive ὑπερουρανίῳ, quale est sanctuari- um Christi. Thomas referente Ribera hoc loco in- terpretatur pro ipsa sanctificatione veteris legis, quæ secularis dicebatur, quia temporalis erat & non perpetua, aut mundana, quia Veteris Test. gra- tiam non continebat. Idem tribuit Cajatano, quod sanctum seculare vocaverit mundanam sanctita- tem, quæ oculis hominum cernebatur, quasi non sit spiritualis, utpote quæ solis Dei oculis cernitur. At inusitatum est & insolitum, τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν san- ctitatem Veteris Testamenti appellare, quæ jam satis clare per δικαιώματα λατρείας expressa est. Neque solet Apostolus obscurius, quale esset ἅγιον κοσμι- κὸν, si pro ipsa sanctitate Veteris Testam. accipere- tur, post clarius ponere, sed & tota enumeratio τοῦ ἁγίου κοσμικοῦ v. 2. & seqq. facta, nihil aliud, quam ipsum tabernaculum explicat. Mundanum Vulga- tus reddidit seculare. Erat externum, typicum, cui cœlestis veritas nondum suberat. Qui secu- lare dictum ajunt, quod multis secularis duraturum, textum authenticum ignorent. Unde rejiciuntur etiam merito à Thoma, qui seculare explicant, id est, temporale, non perpetuum, quod in Græ- co mundanum sit, non seculare. Quod vero Chry- sostomus, quem Theophylactus, Oecumenius & Hay- mo sequuntur, per τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν tabernaculi locum exteriorem, vel atrium, in quod non Judæis tantum, sed totius mundi hominibus aditus pa- tebat, intelligit, non convenit ideo, quia Apo- stolus non tres tabernaculi partes explicat, sed tantum duas, utpote illas, in quibus λατρείαι pera- gebantur, & ad quas pertinebant τὰ δικαιώματα, effectus λατρειῶν. Interim si applicatio desidere- tur etiam atrii istius in antitypo, ut Sacerdos per illud venit in sanctum, & per sanctum in sanctum sanctorum: Ita Christum venisse in mundum, & inde in Ecclesiam, denique per Ecclesiam in cœlum ingressum esse haud abs re dicetur. De cætero cer- tum est, atrium illud nunquam venire τοῦ ἁγίου nomine, adeoque hic intelligi non posse. B. Dor- scheus ita hic diversas sententias ponderat: Chry- sostomus, quem sequitur Theophylactus, κοσμικὸν propterea vocatum esse censet tabernaculum, quia exterius tabernaculum, non solum Judæis, sed & gentibus, adeoque omnibus mundi nationi- bus patuit. Sed præterquam, quod & hæc appel- latio contra scopum Apostolicum sit, eum nunc non intendat explicare, quam late, & quibus nationibus tabernaculum patuerit, τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν hoc loco non tantum σκηνὴν πρώτην, sed & δευτέραν complectitur. Est enim totum id his ver- bis comprehensum, quod v. 2. 3. 4. & 5. explicatur, & à δικαιώμασι λατρείας distinguitur. Alii volunt τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν dici templum, quod seculare dica- tur, quia multis seculis duraturum existimabatur. Hærent autem illi in eo, quod κοσμικὸν à Vulgato seculare redditur, cum amplius mundanum dica- tur. Præterea non observant, Apostolum in tempo- ribus Mosis morari, adeoque de tabernaculo semper loqui, ne verbo quidem de templo in hoc facto. Vo- luit scilicet ad ipsa primordia sanctionis & constitu- tionis religionis Judaicæ deducere, & ex illis novi fœderis excellentiam elicere. Unde etiam cum ἅγιον κοσμικὸν appellasset, quod postmodum explicaturus est, non templi sed tabernaculi partes & contenta præcipue commemorat. Franc. Ribera in eo subsi- stit, τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν nihil aliud esse, quam pri- mum tabernaculum, quod vers. 2. explicatur: Il- lud seculare vocari, quia significabat vitam & cul- tum Dei, quem in hoc seculo sancti Deo offerebant, donec per sanguinem Christi introirent in secundum tabernaculum, id est, cœlum. Idem etiam dici mun- danum, quia repræsentabat vitam, quam in hoc mundo habebant sancti ante adventum Christi. Sic Tit. II. 12. vocari κοσμικὰς ἐπιθυμίας desideria illa, quæ sunt in hominibus seculi, & qualia habent ho- mines mundani. Unde concludit, hanc appellatio- nem neq́ue, sancto sanctorum proprie convenire posse, neque toti tabernaculo, quia totum & seculi & æter- nitatis figuram gerebat. Sed (1) hoc loco alia est hu- jus vocabuli significatio, quam Tit. II. ubi de eo xó- σμῳ sermo est, qui ὅλως ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ κεῖται, 1. Joh. V. 19. Deinde (2) τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν tam late se extendit, quam δικαιώματα λατρείας. Atq́; hæc in ipsum sese sanctum sanctorum extendunt. Sunt enim δικαιώματα extra, sunt etiam intra velum vers. 7. Itaq́; eo usque etiam τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν contenditur. (3) Quod à repræsentatione cultus & status hujus seculi κοσμικὸν appelletur, rursus ex intentione Apo- stolica nequaquam colligitur. Non enim est oppo- sitio inter σκηνὴν πρώτην καὶ δευτέραν in eo, quod illa sit κοσμικὴ, hæc non: Sed quod omnis iste appa- ratus Veteris Testamenti, si conferatur cum institu- tis novi, κοσμικὸς sit, ex mundanis, caducis & pe- rituris concinnatus, adeoque antiquandus & senio conficiendus. (4) Si τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν totum ta- bernaculum exterius & interius non complecteretur, insufficiens esset enumeratio in v. 1. eorum, quæ ἡ πρώτη διαθήκη habuit. Fuisset enim adjiciendum tertium, quod post velum erat, sanctum sanctorum. Simplicius itaque τὸ ἅγιον κοσμικὸν dicitur ita ap- pellatum esse, quia oppositum est τῷ ὑπερκοσμίῳ καὶ ὑπερουρανίῳ quod est tabernaculum corporis Christi, de quo supra cap. VIII. 2.

## 9:2
Vers. 2.

Σκηνὴ γὰρ κατεσκευάσθη ἡ πρώτη] He explains the form of that sanctuary, such as it was in the times of Moses, when the law was given. Σκηνὴ, that is, משכן, is often called that whole tabernacle or rather tent, of which there were two most important parts, but which themselves are also rightly called σκηναὶ, because they each had their own covering, as it were. And learned men have noted that the Hebrews also speak in this way. And note here again πρώτη for προτέρα as above VIII. 7. 13. But he calls that the first which was entered first, and was called the holy place, to which in the temple corresponds the היכל, the vestibule to Philo. But the second is that which, because of its greater holiness, was called the holy of holies, to which in the temple corresponded the דביר, the place of the oracle. The former was an image of the celestial ether and of those things which are governed by the ether, the latter was an image of that which is above the ether, as we have said elsewhere.

Commonly the punctuation is made at the word κατεσκευάσθη. And not wrongly. For the tabernacle was constructed: And indeed that first one, in which were the lampstands etc., which was called the holy place. It is certain that those two parts of the tabernacle are noted. But that the former part was an image of the ethereal heaven and of those things which are governed by the ether, neither did the Apostle teach here, nor did it easily come into the mind of any interpreters: but that the latter part was an image of heaven, is evident from the Apostle. But that there is a heaven above the firmament, into which Christ has entered, is ἐκ ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως, and is asserted ἄτερ γραφῆς. Piscator, through the ignorance of a copyist, thinks that the plural has been put for the singular, and therefore that ἅγιον ought to be read. But more correctly, with the usual reading retained, it is said to be a plural of excellence.

Ἐν ᾗτε ἥ λυχνία] מנורה, an image of the planets. For there were six branches and one shaft in the middle, as Philo explains in his Life of Moses, and in On the Heir of Divine Things. Nor does Josephus say otherwise, Ant. III. 7.

Καὶ ἡ τράπεζα κὴ ἡ πρόθεσις τῶν ἄρτων] The table שלחן and the twelve loaves placed upon it. Ἡ πρόθεσις τῶν ἄρτων for οἱ προτεθέντες ἄρτοι, by a frequent idiom in both Hebrew and Greek. They are the לחמי פנים in Exodus 25:30, so called because they were always in the sight of the priests. These signified that food is indeed born from the earth, but by the power of the stars vegetating it. Thus Philo in On the Heir of Divine Things and in the Life of Moses.

Ἥτις λέγεται ἁγία] It should not be written ἁγία, but ἅγια, as appears from what follows, and above in 8:2. קדש in Exodus 26:33, where the Greeks have ἅγιον. Ἥτις, namely, the first tabernacle.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Σκηνὴ γὰρ κατεσκευάσθη ἡ πρώτη] Explicat formam illius sanctuarii, qualis fuit Mosis temporibus, cum lex lata est. Σκηνὴ, id est, משכן, sæpe vocatur totum illud taberna- culum sive tentorium potius, cujus duæ erant potissimæ partes, sed quæ & ipsæ recte σκηναὶ dicuntur, quia habe- bant quæq; suum velut tectum. Et sic loqui etiam Ebræos notarunt eruditi. Et nota hic rursum πρώτη pro προτέρα ut supra VIII. 7. 13. Πρώτην autem vocat eam, quæ prior intrabatur, & vocabatur ἅγιον, cui in templo respondit היכל πρόναον Philoni. Δευτέραν vero eam, quæ ob ma- jorem sanctimoniam vocabatur ἅγια ἁγίων, cui in templo respondebat דביר locus oraculi. Illud cæli ætheri & eo- rum quæ ab æthere reguntur, hoc super ætherei imago erat, ut alibi diximus.

Communiter interpunctio fit ad verbum κα- τεσκευάσθη. Nec male. Tabernaculum enim con- structum : Et quidem primum illud, in quo erant candelabra &c. quod dicebatur sanctum. Certum est, notari duas illas partes tabernaculi. Sed prio- rem partem cæli ætherei, & eorum, quæ ab æthere reguntur, imaginem fuisse, nec Apostolus hic do- cuit, nec ulli interpp. facilè in mentem venit: po- steriorem vero imaginem fuisse cæli, ex Aposto- lo constat. Sed supra firmamentum cælum esse, in quod ingressus Christus est, ἐκ ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως est, & ἄτερ γραφῆς asseritur. Piscator per imperi- tiam Librarii pluralem pro singulari positum esse, adeoque debere legi ἅγιον putat. Rectius autem retenta usitata lectione dicitur esse pluralem ex- cellentiæ.

Ἐν ᾗτε ἥ λυχνία] מנורה imago planetarum. Erant enim rami sex & unus in medio scapus, ut Philo explicat de Vita Mosis, & de hærede rerum divinarum. Nec ali- ter Josephus Ant. III. 7.

Καὶ ἡ τράπεζα κὴ ἡ πρόθεσις τῶν ἄρτων] Mensa שלחן & panes duodecim in ea positi. Ἡ πρόθεσις τῶν ἄρτων pro οἱ προτεθέντες ἄρτοι loquutione frequenti & Ebræis & Græ- cis. Ii sunt לחמי פנים Exod. XXV. 13. ita dicti, quia in conspectu semper erant Sacerdotibus. Significabant hæc alimenta ex terra quidem nasci, sed vi siderum eam vege- tante. Ita Philo de hærede rerum divinarum & de vita Mosis.

Ἥτις λέγεται ἁγία] Non ἁγία scribendum, sed ἅγια, ut ex sequentibus apparet, & supra VIII. 2. קדש Exodi XXVI. 33. ubi Græci ἅγιον. Ἥτις nempe σκηνὴ πρώτη.

## 9:3
Vers. 3. Μετὰ δὲ τὸ δεύτερον καταπέτασμα] Within the פרכת, which is properly καταπέτασμα to the Greeks, since that veil, through which one first entered into the tent is accustomed to be called by the Greeks κάλυμμα or ἐπίσπαστον, by the Hebrews מסך, as we have said at Matt. XXVII. 51.

The tabernacle which is called the holy of holies] קדשׁ הקדשׁים, Exod. XXVI. 33. The Greek interpreters call it singularly the holy of holies. This writer hereafter calls it the holy [things], namely, with the word understood which had once been expressed, of the holies. This signifies that that place was holier than the other. For the Hebrews often express comparatives or the superlative by added genitives.

It is not permitted to gather from the Apostle that the lampstands were an image of the planets. For what do the planets have to do with the present Apostolic treatment? Far less, indeed, are the foods born from the earth, but quickened by the power of the faithful, figured by the table and the showbread. God did not wish such philosophical things to be set before the people in the tabernacle or temple, and they were established more plainly elsewhere. For what commerce had the Mosaic tabernacle and the Solomonic temple with such worldly things? They were figures of heavenly things, as the Apostle testifies, not of worldly ones. By the holy, therefore, the Church is rather understood, which is the house of the living God, 1 Tim. III. 15, and the sanctuary of the Lord, in which the lampstands shining with seven lights (the number of perfection) represent the Churches, or the chairs in which the light of the divine Word shines, Apoc. I. 20, chap. II. 5. By the table with the showbread, the Eucharistic table is figured with the blessed bread, 1 Cor. X. 17, 21. Pareus says that this πρόθεσις signified that Christ, who is the bread of life, continually feeds His Church. B. Dorscheus handed down this spiritual meaning: It is most pleasing to us to have light and life. Both are communicated to us most fully in the new covenant through Him who is τὸ φῶς, καὶ ἡ ζωὴ, John I. 4 and following. That was shadowed forth in this tabernacle. Light indeed in the lampstand, but life in the food placed upon the table. But what Primasius and Haymo gather from the fact that the lampstands are spoken of here in the plural is that it does not refer to the tabernacle of Moses, in which there was only one lampstand, but to the temple of Solomon, in which there were ten lampstands, 1 Kings VII. 2. Par. IV is invalid, because, as Anselm, Thomas, and Lyranus [say], even if there was only one lampstand as far as the stem is concerned, there were nevertheless many as far as the branches or reeds rising from the stem are concerned: Indeed, what Estius acknowledges to the prejudice of the Vulgate version, in the Greek text it is read in the singular number, ἡ λυχνία, the same word which the LXX interpreters used in Exodus, who also observes that the Syriac interpreter agrees with the Greeks, but that Erasmus and Hentenius are mistaken, who think that a lamp is signified by the Greek word in this place. With these things observed, the fabrication of Grotius concerning the seven planets clearly collapses. For what analogy is there of the lampstand with the planets? Not to mention that more than seven planets have been observed by more recent and more accurate astronomers. Some place a hypallage in the words ἡ πρόθεσις τῶν ἄρτων, as if the proposition of the loaves were said for the loaves of the proposition: But the proper sense can be retained: For in the tabernacle the proposition of the loaves was performed by the priests, who had to set them before the faces of the Lord: Although I am not unaware that the Hebrew text said the loaves of the faces, which the Syriac also has here, and the LXX interpreters rendered as the loaves of the proposition, ἄρτους τῆς προθέσεως. Furthermore, in the words μετὰ δὲ τὸ δεύτερον καταπέτασμα, it is manifest that the second is not to be referred to the tabernacle, which differ in gender, but to the veil, so that it is a wonder to Estius that the interpreter wished to make the sense ambiguous by a metathesis of the word; who prefers the Syriac translation, which has it thus: The inner habitation, however, which was within the second veil, was called the holy of holies. For two veils were ordered to be made, Exod. XXVI, one inner, which would divide the holy from the holy of holies, the other outer, which would separate the holy from the atrium placed outside, which therefore was the first for those entering.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Μετὰ δὲ τὸ δεύτερον καταπέτασμα] Intra פרכת, quod proprie Græcis καταπέτασμα, cum illud velum, per quod primum in tentorium intrabatur, dici Græcis soleat κάλυμμα vel ἐπίσπαστον, Ebræis מסך, ut diximus ad Matth. XXVII. 51.

Σκηνὴ ἡ λεγομένη ἅγια ἁγίων] קדשׁ הקדשׁים, Exod. XXVI. 33. Græci Interpretes singulariter ἅγιον ἁγίων vocant. Hic scriptor posthac ἅγια, nempe subaudito, quod semel expressum fuerat τῶν ἁγίων. Id significat, eum lo- cum altero fuisse sanctiorem. Nam comparativos aut su- perlativo Ebræi per Genitivos additos sæpe exprimunt.

Candelabra imaginem planetarum fuisse ex A- postolo colligere non licet. Quid enim planetæ ad præsentem tractationem Apostolicam? Lon- ge vero minus figurata per mensam & panes pro- positionis alimenta ex terra nascentia, sed vi fide- rum vegetata. Talia Philosophica neque populo sistere in tabernaculo aut templo Deus voluit, & constabant ea aliunde planius. Ecquid enim com- mercii tabernaculo Mosaico ac templo Salomo- nico cum ejusmodi mundanis? Figuræ erant re- rum cœlestium teste Apostolo, non mundana- rum. Per sanctum ergo Ecclesia potius, quæ est domus Dei viventis, 1. Tim. III. 15. & sanctuarium Domini intelligitur, in quo candelabra septem luminibus lucentia (numero perfectionis) re- præsentant Ecclesias, vel cathedras, in quibus lu- cet Verbi divini lumen, Apoc. I. 20. cap. II. 5. Per mensam cum panibus propositis figurata mensa Eucharistica cum pane benedicto, 1. Cor. X. 17. 21. Significabat ea πρόθεσις, Christum, qui panis est vitæ, jugiter pascere suam Ecclesiam ait Pareus. B. Dorscheus hanc spiritualem significationem tradidit: Gratissimum nobis est, lucem & vitam habere. Utrumque plenissime in novo fœdere nobis communicatur per eum, qui τὸ φῶς est, καὶ ἡ ζωὴ, Joh. I. 4. & seq. Id adumbrabatur in hoc taberna- culo. Lux quidem in candelabro, vita autem in victu mensæ imposito. Quod vero Primasius & Haymo, ex eo, quod candelabra hic in Plurali di- cantur, colligunt, non tabernaculum Mosis, in quo unum tantum erat candelabrum, sed tem- plum Salomonis respici, in quo decem erant can- delabra 1. Reg. VII. 2. Par. IV. invalidum est, quia, ut Anshelmus, Thomas & Lyranus, etsi unum tantum fuerit candelabrum, quantum ad stipitem, plura tamen fuere, quantum ad ramos seu calamos e stipite surgentes: Imo quod in præjudicium Vulgatæ versionis agnoscit Estius, in textu Græco legitur singulari numero, ἡ λυχνία eadem voce, qua LXX. Interpp. usi sunt in Exodo, qui obser- vat etiam, Græcis consonare Syrum Interpretem, falli vero Erasmum & Hentenium, qui Græca vo- ce lucernam putant hoc loco significari. Quibus observatis plane corruit commentum Grotii de septem Planetis. Quæ enim analogiæ candela- bri cum Planetis? Ut non dicam, plures quam se- ptem Planetas dari observatos recentioribus, iisq; accuratioribus Astronomis. In verbis ἡ πρόθεσις τῶν ἄρτων hypallagen ponunt nonnulli, quasi pro- positio panum dicatur, pro panes propositionis: Sed retineri potest sensus proprius: In tabernacu- lo enim fiebat propositio panum a Sacerdotibus, qui eos proponere debebant ad facies Domi- ni: Etsi non ignorem, quod textus Ebræus pa- nes facierum dixit, quod etiam hic Syrus habet, LXX. Interpretes reddidisse panes propo- sitionis ἄρτους τῆς προθέσεως. Porro in verbis μετὰ δὲ τὸ δεύτερον καταπέτασμα manifestum est, secundum non esse ad σκηνὴν refe- rendum, quæ genere differunt, sed ad κατα- πέτασμα, ut mirum sit Estio, interpretem metathesi dictionis sensum ambiguum facere voluisse; qui Syriacam translationem præfert, quæ sic habet: Habitaculum autem interius, quod erat intra velum secundum, vocabatur sanctum sanctorum. Duo enim vela fieri jussa sunt, Exod. XXVI. alterum interius, quod sanctum divideret à sancto sanctorum, alterum exterius, quod sanctum separaret ab atrio foris posito, quod proinde in- gredientibus erat primum.

## 9:4
V. 4. Having a golden censer, and the ark of the covenant covered round about with gold, in which was a golden pot having the manna, and Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant] This is the passage which made the epistle suspect to very many learned men: but it has greatly tormented others: because it is sufficiently established from Moses, Philo, Josephus, and the Rabbis that the censer was in the outer tabernacle. But then 1 Kings VIII. 9, 2 Chron. V. 10, Josephus VIII. 2, it is said quite openly that there was nothing in the ark except the two tables of the covenant, that is, the decalogue, which is the beginning of the covenant. I, who value this epistle most highly, will never be brought to abandon its authority. But I think the objections are best answered in this way: the censer here is not the table, but the pan placed upon the table: Josephus calls it ἐσχάραν III. 8, the LXX call it πυρεῖον, Levit. XVI. 12, where in the Hebrew it is המחתה, which word Saadias Gaon translates as מנמרה. which signifies a fire-pan or coal-pan, by which name that star in the sky is called by the Arabs, as noted by Scaliger. This fire-pan was easily carried, as that same Josephus teaches us. But where that rite of the annual expiation is described in Leviticus XVI, verse 12, it is said in the Hebrew concerning the high priest: And he shall take a full censer of burning coals of fire from off the altar before the Lord, and his hands full of sweet incense beaten small, and bring it within the veil: And he shall put the incense upon the fire before the Lord: Which the LXX translate thus: And he shall take the fire-pan full of coals of fire from the altar that is before the Lord, and shall fill his hands with incense of fine composition. And he shall bring it within the veil. And he shall put the incense upon the fire before the Lord. The sense of these words, as I judge, is this: The high priest shall take the pan with coals from that table which faces the ark, and he shall fill his hands with the best-made incense: then with these, [namely, first moving the pan within the veil, then entering himself with the handfuls of incense] he shall enter within the inner veil: and he shall put of that incense upon the coals of the pan by the ark. The fire-pan is said to have been before God in that passage of Leviticus, because it faced the ark, as is openly said Exod. XXV. 5. Known, however, is the custom of the Hebrews, who by synecdoche of the sign for the thing signified call the ark by the name of God. Thus Exod. XXX. 6, 8, what had been said to be before the mercy seat is soon said to be before the Lord. Now it is not difficult to understand why this writer says that that inner tent had a censer, not because it was always there, but because it always looked toward the ark, which was in the inner sanctuary, and on that most solemn day of atonement it was transferred into the inner tent, that is, into the inner sanctuary. For we are said to have that which is in our use. But as for what is objected concerning the urn and the rod from the book of Kings and elsewhere, I think it is best resolved thus. In the time of Moses, that urn with the Manna and Aaron's rod were in the ark. And where better than in the ark, since it is clear from the passage in Exodus 16:33 that the Manna was placed inside the inner sanctuary? It is clear from Numbers 17:10 that the rod was placed beside the law itself, which is also called the testimony. And Gorionides says that the rod was placed in the ark. And with the passage of time, when there was a fear that the rod might suffer decay and the Manna might suffer mold, they were taken out of the ark and kept in a place free from winds and suns. And when Solomon's temple was being built, for the same reason those things were not replaced in the ark, but in an underground crypt, as the ancient Rabbis write. However, all these things are not set down in vain by this writer. For that censer brought from the outer tent into the inner sanctuary signifies the body of Christ, which, after the most grievous sufferings, which are wont to be compared to fire in the sacred scriptures, passed from the earth into the highest heaven. The incense signifies the prayers of Christ, which he always makes for us, Revelation 5:8. But Aaron's rod, which brought forth fruit, [for that is what ἐβλάστησε means, concerning which there is the history in Numbers 17], signifies the ever-enduring priesthood of Christ: the Manna indeed signifies the heavenly food which he gives us in his Word: but the tables of the covenant signify the better precepts of Christ, to love God above all things, and our neighbor as ourselves. Furthermore, this divine writer says that the censer was of gold, which is also mentioned by Josephus in the aforementioned place, Antiquities 3.7. The ark ארון הברית served no other purpose than to preserve those things which were in the ark, as Philo notes concerning the life of Moses, just as the sacred chests of many nations were stored away, as Clement teaches us in his Exhortation to the Greeks concerning the Eleusinian mysteries: and concerning the Theban mysteries, Seneca in Hercules Oetaeus: Not accustomed to carry the Orgia of Cadmus in baskets hidden away.

He says that this ark or chest also was covered with gold, which we also read in Exodus 25:11, 33:3. He adds also that there was a golden urn, which we have in Exodus 16:33. Στάμνος is a pitcher, an urn in the glossary. Among Hesychius, κάμνος, a water-pot, a jar. Gold, because it does not feel rust, as Philo notes in 'On the Heir of Divine Things', signifies the perpetual duration of those goods which are signified by these golden or gilded things. Πλάκες לחת Exodus 31:18. Hence the writer of the Orphics said διπλακα θεσμὸν. Understand the tablets as whole and new: although some also hand down that the remains of the broken ones were stored in the ark.

As for the golden θυμιατήριον, Theophylact, Anselm, Thomas, Lyranus, and among the Reformed, Ludovicus de Dieu, also understand it as a censer, whose arguments this blessed Dorscheus also brings forward and approves: It is clear from the fact that, in the Holy of Holies, besides the ark, there was also a censer among the instruments of the sanctuary: and that this same censer, even if it had been carried out of the Holy of Holies immediately after the cloud was raised, could be said much more correctly to be held by the Holy of Holies than that the altar of incense could be held by the same. For that which never appeared between the veil, how could it be said more correctly to have been held by the Holy of Holies than that sacred instrument which was at least for some time every year between the veil: furthermore, it is nowhere said that that censer was carried out of the Holy of Holies immediately after that annual use. It is more likely that it was kept there until it was to be used again. And for that reason it was golden, as being used only by the High Priest in that solemn entry, whereas a golden censer could hardly sustain the daily fumigations to be raised by the priests in the sanctuary. Therefore, Paul teaches nothing that does not manifestly shine forth from the circumstances of the fact. Nor does the authority of Josephus stand in the way, who only describes the contents of the outer tabernacle. With this golden censer, therefore, the High Priest entered the Holy of Holies, burning incense, so that the Holy of Holies might be covered by its smoke and cloud, lest they could be seen by those who were in the outer tabernacle. Tostatus opposes such an argument to this opinion: If it was kept in the Holy of Holies, it follows that the High Priest entered it at least three times on the one day of atonement, namely, first, to take away the censer; second, when he returned with it filled with incense and fire, to burn the incense and fumigate in the Holy of Holies; third, when he had to go out again to set aside the ashes and fire, and return to replace the censer, although it was permitted for him to enter the Holy of Holies only once. Which argument moved Villalpandus so much that in Ezekiel 1, chapter 4, verse 25, he determined that the High Priest always left a censer of this kind in the Holy of Holies after his entry, by which the incense would be completely consumed there, and that he brought in another the following year, and then carried back the former one left there before the year. Others urge that, although censers are indeed read to have been made in Exodus 25:29 and chapter 27:16, it is not read that one of these censers was in the Holy of Holies. But Grotius's explanation is cold, that that inner tent is said to have had a fire-pan, not because it was always there, but because it always looked toward the ark, which was in the sanctuary: and on that day of atonement it was brought into the sanctuary: For in this latter sense it would also be said that the High Priest had it, because the High Priest entered that inner tent or the Holy of Holies. Origen in Homily 9 on Leviticus, Augustine in Questions 133 and 174 on Exodus, Alphonsus Tostatus on Exodus 25, question 6, and

in 1 Kings 6, question 16, Francis Ribera in this place, Estius, Cornelius à Lapide, Jacob Capellus, Francis Junius, B. Gerhardus, and others, namely that by that θυμιατήριον is to be understood the golden altar of incense, Exodus 30, verse 1, chapter 37, verse 25, which is said to have had the Holy of Holies, which altar, as some of them declare, had that [the Holy of Holies] turned toward it, and erected for its worship, whence it was also called the altar of the oracle, Leviticus 16, verse 12, or that the Holy of Holies did not indeed have it in itself, but before itself, yet in such a way that it was nearest and clearly turned toward it, so that from this altar the smoke would enter from above into the very τὰ ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων, so that in that daily fumigation God residing in them might be honored. Schlichting, along with Crell, agrees with this opinion: that the Altar is signified, upon which incense was burned to God, which was indeed in reality in the first tabernacle, but because it adhered to the second veil, by which the latter tabernacle was divided from the former, and because it was so near to the tabernacle, for that reason the Author attributes it to the second tabernacle. But how could it be so attributed to the second tabernacle, which was in reality established in the first, as in that enumeration, in which those things which were in the first, and which were in the second, which were established before the veil, and which after the veil, are distinctly enumerated?

Junius notes that the sanctuary had certain instruments outside, but within the veil, namely the altar of incense, which it had in the very entrance before the sight of Jehovah before the ark of the testimony, opposite the mercy seat, which was upon the ark of the covenant. But if it had been within the veil, how then not within the holy of holies? Add that θυμιατήριον, or censer, is one thing, and θυσιαστήριον θυμιάματος, or altar of incense, is another, concerning which Luke 1, verse 11, which were distinct is evident from Leviticus 16, verse 12, and Numbers 16, verse 46: and that the former is here called χρυσᾶν, golden, in an accurate sense, just as it is distinguished from περιεκαλυμμένῳ πάντοθεν χρυσίῳ, overlaid with gold on every side, whereas this altar of incense was not entirely golden, but only overlaid with gold. However, the observations of the blessed Gerhard support this opinion somewhat, namely: 1. That the Apostle did not say that that golden censer was in the posterior part of the tabernacle, or the holy of holies, but that the tabernacle HAD a censer, σκηνὴ ἔχουσα, namely, placed very near to itself, so that it might serve its uses. Add that it had it as regards use, as Cornelius à Lapide says, namely that the smoke from it ascended into the holy of holies and penetrated it, and the Lord on the mercy seat of the ark smelled its fragrance there, and willed to be honored by it daily, Lev. 16, verse 13. That altar, says the blessed Gerhard, was made to serve the holy of holies. For since it was lawful only for the High Priest to enter there, and that only once a year, lest that part of the tabernacle which was more sacred should lack the honor of incense, the Lord commanded an altar to be set up nearby, on which incense was to be burned, the smoke of which would cloud the holy of holies from nearby. 2. That that altar was nothing other than a large censer, yet no larger than having a cubit of length and a cubit of breadth, since it had no other use than that fire should be placed upon it and fragrances burned: And that θυμιατήριον signifies not only a censer, but also a place or altar on which there is incense, according to Josephus, Book 3, Antiquities, ch. 7, and Book 6, Jewish War, ch. 6. And what perhaps moves one most, that Moses made no mention of any golden censer, which was distinct from the altar of incense: while the Apostle does not introduce the altar of incense by another name when describing the things that were in the tabernacle, which nevertheless was one of the principal things in the tabernacle. 3. That it is called the golden altar by the Mosaic voice, Exod. XXXIX. 38. chap. XL. 26. although it was not cast from solid gold, because, namely, it was entirely covered with gold, Exod. XXX. 3. chap. XXXVII. 26. In which sense also the table, on which the showbread was, is called golden, 1 Kings VII. 48. not because it was made of gold (for both the altar of incense and the table were made of Shittim wood) but because it was entirely covered with gold. Aug. last question on Exodus. Scripture sometimes called the altar of incense golden, sometimes gilded: Calling it golden, at any rate, which was gilded. It is added that it is called golden to distinguish it from the altar of burnt offerings, which was of bronze, Exod. XXVII. verse 2. B. Dorscheus, thus in this place. Why did Paul say that the holy of holies had a golden censer, when Scripture taught in the last chapter of Exodus that the altar of incense was outside the veil, that is, outside the holy of holies. This altar was made to serve the holy of holies. For since the priests could not enter into that, except the High Priest, and that only once every year, lest that part of the tabernacle which was more sacred, and in which were the ark and the mercy seat and the Cherubim, should lack the honor of incense, the altar of incense was made and moved to the holy of holies, in which aromatics were to be burned, the smoke of which would enter into the holy of holies. Therefore, the altar of incense was not in the holy of holies, as Oecumenius and Aug. question 133 on Exodus think, but joined near to it. Hence it is called the altar of the oracle Reg. VI. vers. 22. but also he overlaid the altar of the oracle with gold, and Levit. XVI. vers. 23. it is called the altar, which was before the Lord, because it was before the holy of holies, and where we have the altar of the oracle, in the Hebrew it is the altar, which was to the oracle, or next to the oracle, which the LXX translate more clearly, and he made the altar before the face of the oracle. It can also be translated, as Jerome translates it, the altar of the oracle, or the altar, which belonged to the oracle, i.e., which the holy of holies had for its own uses.

Of these two opinions, which one should be preferred might seem ambiguous. However, that one seems more likely which wishes to designate not the altar of incense covered with gold, but a golden censer, upon which coals with incense were to be placed. For since the High Priest was commanded to do this, Lev. XVI. 12, having taken the censer (the LXX interpreters have λήψεται τὸ πυρεῖον: in the Hebrew it is מַחְתָּה a receptacle, B. Luther renders it Nåpffen, likewise Kohlpfannen Exod. XXVII. 3. chap. XXXIIX. 3. which is otherwise called θυμιατήριον Exod. XXVI. verse 19. Ezek. XIIX. verse 11. Heb. מִקְטֶרֶת) which he had filled with coals from the altar, and taking the incense prepared by hand to enter beyond the veil into the holy place, so that with the aromatics placed upon the fire, their cloud and vapor might cover the oracle, which was above the testimony, it was necessary that a censer be prepared. Which without doubt was golden: indeed, we are taught that it was even in this place, just as also 2 Chron. XV. verse 22. golden censers are commemorated. Therefore, the High Priest could not bring in the incense to make the offering without a censer, and he was commanded to bring it in thus. Although, therefore, it was not rendered by the name θυμιατήριον in the list of utensils making up the tabernacle, and not even other censers than bronze ones are mentioned there; yet for the entry of the High Priest into the holy of holies, a special censer was needed, fitting for the holy of holies, which shone entirely with gold: that it was golden, the Apostle indicates by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and for that purpose it was kept in the holy of holies. That there was some special golden censer destined for that end and use, so that with it the High Priest might enter into the holy of holies annually on the day of atonement, does not displease Buxtorf, even though he denies that it was kept in it. But because the Apostle says the same thing about the golden censer, that the holy of holies had it, as he affirms about the ark of the covenant, which was certainly kept in it, and that when he is occupied in explaining distinctly what things were in the holy place and what were in the holy of holies; either with Villalpando, two such golden censers are to be posited, used alternately, so that the High Priest would not have need to enter into the holy of holies except once annually: Or with B. D. Georg König in Vindic. sacr. loc. CXIV. page 708, it must be said: It is one thing to enter to burn incense and to offer blood, another to repair, if anything had been broken or cut, or if the camp was to be set up or moved, or if anything was to be put back or taken out. That the former was for the High Priest alone to perform once a year, the latter was permitted, as often as necessity demanded, not to the High Priest alone, but also to other priests; which he proves from Num. IV. verse 5, where it is enjoined not only upon Aaron, but also upon his sons, what the duty should be in repairing the holy of holies. Which seems to be favored especially by the fact that only one golden censer is named here, nor is anything easily found in Hebrew antiquity, as Buxtorf observes, concerning a twin golden censer used alternately: But he who added this to the history of the ark of the covenant, ch. V. page 68, from the Talmudic additions in Bava Bathra fol. 14: We read in Erurim fol. 118 that when necessity demanded that something be repaired in it, it was permitted to enter the holy of holies. Nay, on page 75 he observed that, according to the mind of the Hebrews, the High Priest entered the Holy of Holies four times on the Day of Atonement: 1. When he brought the censer with coals and aromatics into it, leaving it there until he had performed the other rites as well. 2. With the blood of the bullock, sprinkling it eight times between the staves of the ark. 3. With the blood of the slaughtered goat, etc. 4. Toward evening he enters and brings out from there the incense shovel and the censer. See Maimonides and Talmud Joma, chapter VII; Abarbanel on Lev. XVI. He who enters, he says, a fourth time, is to remove from there the censer and the incense shovel, which remained there from the time when he made the incense offering. R. Levi ben Gerson is also praised there, giving the reason: 1. Why these were left there for so long? Because, forsooth, it was not fitting that he should remove those vessels from there before the incense and the fire in the censer had been completely consumed. 2. Why does Scripture make no explicit mention of the removal of these vessels? Because this was not the primary purpose of this day, nor a necessity of the atonement. 3. Why were they to be removed? Because this pertained to the honor of that place, so that the ashes might not be left there for the whole year until the following Day of Atonement, on which the High Priest would finally remove them. These matters we leave to their own place. B. Dorsecheus gathers that he had to enter four times from Lev. XVI as follows: 1. When the incense was to be kindled between the veil, v. 12. 2. When the blood of the bullock was to be sprinkled toward the mercy seat. 3. When the same was to be done with the blood of the goat, v. 14, 15. 4. Finally, when the whole sanctuary was to be atoned for, v. 32. But whether in absolutely no case the High Priest could have betaken himself within the veil outside of this day, may be inquired into, partly because there could be a case where the mouth of the Lord had to be consulted, who promised that he would speak with the High Priest from the upper part of the mercy seat, from the midst of the two Cherubim, which are above that ark of the testimony, Exod. XV. [sic] verse 22. where it seems that nothing could have stood in the way of the High Priest entering within the veil and receiving divine responses. For urgent necessity itself did not permit that this consultation with the Lord be deferred until the 10th of Tishri. The other case is that in which those things had to be referred to the book of the sanctuary which pertained to its completion as a divine canon, concerning which it was treated above from Deut. and other sayings of Scripture. For it is by no means manifest that this inscription had to be restricted or postponed to the 10th of Tishri. Therefore, what is said in Lev. XVI, 2, that the High Priest should not enter at any time into the holy place within the veil before that mercy seat which is upon the ark, lest he die, is to be understood of promiscuous and arbitrary access, but not to be extended to necessity and divine office. Sometimes such access, namely expiatory and conciliatory, ἅπαξ τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ, was permitted on that one day of the year. But that is clearly illicit, and would have been attempted against the divine command, if it were true what is said, that the B. Virgin in the very years of her childhood was hidden and educated by the High Priest in the holy of holies, which Baronius in his apparatus to the annals did not blush to assert after some of the Ancients, refuted by Casaubon, Montagu, Jacob Capellus, Rivet concerning the B. Virgin, and others. Conf. Anti-Conr. cap. XXVI. 377.

As for those things which are said to have been in the ark of the covenant, namely the golden urn containing Manna, and the budding rod of Aaron, as also the tables of the Testament, the difficulty which is moved from the collation of 1 Kings 8, verse 9, is certainly more successfully resolved by Grotius than by Ribera in this place, John Scanno in Symph. Proph., Stapul., and Jacob Capellus in his book on the power of the Roman see, book I, cap. III, page 10, who resolve it in vain by the relation of the words ἐν ᾗ to the more remote, namely the tabernacle, because the collation of verse 5 teaches that it is not what was in the tabernacle, but what was in the ark that is being explained, by which it is certain that that, ὑπεράνω δὲ αὐτῆς Χερυβὶμ, is to be understood not of the tabernacle, as if the Cherubim were above it, but of the ark. Others, however, prefer to consider the ark of the covenant distinctly, either determinately and properly regarding the body itself or the middle cavity, which was covered by the mercy seat, or broadly, as it denotes the whole structure, comprehending not only the body of the ark itself, but also the lateral receptacles, such as they gather it had from Deut. XXXI, verse 26, and 1 Sam. VI, verse 8, in which the urn and the rod were, which was the explanation of Lyranus and Bellarmine, lib. I, de Verbo Dei cap. 17, approved by B. Glassius, part III, Phil. S. p. 179. But since in the accurate description of the construction of the ark no mention is made of such a lateral receptacle, Exod. XXV, nor is it said in those places what was stored in such a receptacle or appendage added to the ark, which pertained to the ark and made a certain whole called by the name of the ark with it, but only מצד, from the side of the ark or from the region of the ark, near the ark, next to the ark, the book of the law is said to be stored, no one would easily say that Deuteronomy was in the ark of the covenant itself: this reconciliation is rejected by Ribera in his commentary on this place and by B. D. König in vind. sacr. page 711.

B. Dorscheus answers Ribera: That the structure of the ark is described generally in Exod. XXV, but not the figure and constitution itself delineated, by which it was adorned and composed by the hand of the craftsman: nor does it abhor from that delineation which Exodus has, if it be said that the ark had sinuous sides, in which something could be stored: The ark was certainly two and a half cubits in length and a cubit and a half in width, and likewise a cubit and a half in height. And so for the sake of greater ornament it could have those sinuses. Add that in some sinus of the ark of this kind the book of the sanctuary was also stored, into which was written successively what God wished to transmit to posterity as the Canon of the Church of the Old Testament, Deut. III, 26. Concerning its preservation see Theol. Zachar. part II, θ. 84. Certainly in Exod. XVI, 34, before the tables of the law were exhibited or the ark of the covenant constructed, it is commanded concerning the golden urn that it be stored and placed before the sight of Jehovah to be preserved through the ages, and it is said that Aaron placed it before the testimony itself, which testimony is Exod.
