XXIII, 34. 1. Petr. I. vers. 14. Quo de Scholastici disputant præeunte Thoma, nullum esse peccatum, quod non ab er- rore judicii practici procedat. Non autem com- mode hic transtulit Vulgatus, quam offert pro sua & populi ignorantia: Siquidem Græce non ha- beatur : ὑπὲρ τῶν ἑαυτῦ καὶ τῶ λαῶ ἀγνοημά- των, sed ὑπὲρ ἑαυτῦ, καὶ τῶν τῦ λαῶ &c. quem offert pro seipso, & populi ignorantiis, ut reddidit Syrus Interpres.

## 9:8
Verse 8.

The Holy Spirit signifying this] Namely, God commanding these things to Moses through His inspiration. See Levit. XVI, 1. For the Lord spoke sometimes indeed, where that is expressed, is understood of a voice: but for the most part of inspiration.

That the way of the holy places had not yet been made manifest] That is, into the holy places. When the writer says holy places hereafter, he uses a shorthand. For he wishes the holy of holies to be understood, just as heavens are often called heavens of heavens. But in this place understand true holy places, from those things which are above VIII, 2, the thing itself which was signified by that sanctuary, that is, the super-ethereal seats. The way leading there is the Gospel, having truly heavenly precepts. Christ first opened that way, and made access for all to the highest heaven. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob will indeed arrive there, as can be seen

Matt. VIII, 11, and other excellent men, as we shall see below XI, 34 and 40. But they will arrive there, as it were, by a machine, not by a way, by a certain extraordinary and rare dispensation of God. Therefore the veil of the sanctuary was torn when Christ was dying.

While the first tabernacle still had a standing] That is, as long as the worship of that temple was performing its duty. For standing signifies duty, as Kimchi explains on Isaiah XXII, 19. So also 2 Chron. IX, 4, XXX, 16, XXXV, 10, 15, Dan. X, 11. But it ceased to perform its duty before God indeed when Christ died, was raised from the dead, was taken up into heaven, and the Holy Spirit was sent. But before all men, then when the temple fell. For then at the same time that worship (which is understood here by tabernacle metonymically) collapsed.

What the Holy Spirit is in Holy Scripture is sufficiently clear. If Grotius wishes it to be an inspiration, not a divine person, he sides with Crellius and Schlichtingius. Whom, however, the Socinian himself preferred to be a power in God, rather than an inspiration outside of God. But concerning these in Socinismus Profligatus. But the Apostle now begins to explain the mysteries which lay hidden in those figures, namely, what the Holy Spirit wished to signify by them, and first indeed, what by that, that the High Priest entered into the holy of holies only once annually, that namely, while this typical tabernacle was still standing, the way to the true holy of holies had not yet been made manifest. Since the true High Priest had, by his entry into the holy of holies, that is, into heaven, to open the way for us, so that free access might be open to us, Heb. X, 19, 20. Whence, when he was entering into glory through his passion and death, the veil of the temple was torn, Matt. XXVII, 51. By the first tabernacle the former part of the tabernacle is understood, as before. But Becanus wrongly gathers from this passage that heaven was closed to the righteous until the death of Christ, and that it was opened by his death, so that entrance might be open to holy souls introduced into it from the limbo of the Fathers, append. disp. de purg. Calvin. c. I. p. 43. Because these things are to be understood by reason of merit, not by reason of the actual opening of heaven, or as Stephen is said to have seen heaven opened, Acts VII, 56. He opened the way to heaven as a moral cause, because he merited for us that what was closed by sins might in turn be open to us once sins were expiated, not as a physical cause. Moreover, the merit of Christ was valid at all times, forward and backward, Heb. XIII, v. 8. Through it also the ancients were saved, Acts XV, 11. Concerning which Theophylact: Since it is agreed that Christ was sacrificed once, how can it be that he endowed all with holiness in this one sacrifice? Because this sacrifice was destined for Christ from the former ages, which was to be for the salvation of all. There was no need, therefore, that they should be led out of limbo only then, when Christ suffered and died. To say nothing of the fact that Thomas and Dionysius understand Christ by the way of the saints, John XIV, 6, who at that time had not yet been so revealed, but lay hidden, shadowed under figures. Estius, however, understands grace, through which access to heaven is open to us, which way in the time of the Old Testament was not yet revealed or manifested, that is, openly known and preached, but lay hidden under the shadows of ceremonies, etc., to which also the interpretation of Origen tr. XXXV. in Matth., Cyril of Alexandria l. XII. in Joh. cap. 37, Theodoret in Dan. IX, Ambrose l. VI. in Luc., Jerome in Matth. XXVII, Augustine in Ps. LXVII tends. and LXX. Leo, sermon X. on the passion, etc. Grotius also teaches here that the Gospel is the way leading to heaven, but he perverts it with that addition of his, that it has heavenly precepts, very badly confusing the legal way, through which no access to heaven is open to anyone after the fall, and the evangelical way, in which alone is salvation through the grace of Christ, who revealed it to all, not only by proclamation but by his own merit; for he is not Redeemer and Mediator only by reason of the announcement, but by reason of the acquisition of eternal salvation; nor did he himself first announce the same in the New Testament, but already in Paradise itself to the Protoplasts, and in them to the whole human race: just as not only the Patriarchs and other eminent men, but all the faithful of the Old Testament even before Christ arrived in heaven by the grace of Christ, and through Christ as the only way, John XIV, 6. Acts XV, 11. That they were saved as if by a machine, and only by an extraordinary and rare dispensation of God, is taught contrary to and against Scripture, since Abraham is rather set forth by Paul as an example for all believers of obtaining salvation through faith in Christ. But these portents of the Socinian heresy we have already expressly refuted elsewhere. B. Dorscheus, in his refutation of Schlichting, here proved that opinion which explains the passage concerning the revelation of the doctrine as being more clear. Schlichting, he says, clearly indicates that no one of the saints came or will come into possession of heavenly joys not only before the first advent of Christ, but even before the second. But this is against both the words and the scope of the Apostle. For as far as the words themselves are concerned, the revelation of the way to eternal life itself is nowhere in the Holy Scriptures called φανέρωσις τῆς τῶν ἁγίων ὁδοῦ, and the way of the saints in Holy Scripture is very often called the doctrine of salvation delivered in the New Testament. Thus Acts XVI, 17, it is ὁδὸς σωτηρίας, and Chapter XVIII, 25, it is ὁδὸς τοῦ Κυρίου. verse 26, it is ὁδὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ, and Chapter XIX, 33, it is called ὁδὸς simply, and Chapter XXII, 4, similarly 2. Peter II, 2, it is ὁδὸς τῆς ἀληθείας. v. 15, ὁδὸς εὐθεῖα, and v. 21, ὁδὸς τῆς δικαιοσύνης. Hence also below Chapter X, v. 20, it is ὁδὸς πρόσφατος καὶ ζῶσα, which in v. 19 is called εἴσοδος τῶν ἁγίων ἐν τῷ αἵματι Ἰησοῦ, which is also above Chapter IV, 16, προσέλευσις τῷ θρόνῳ τῆς χάριτος μετὰ παρρησίας. Whence it is not necessary in this place to understand the actual entry itself or the passage from the kingdom of grace into the kingdom of glory, since for the most part it designates the kingdom of grace itself or its doctrine in the Holy Scriptures. Nor does φανέρωσις in this place denote the opening of the kingdom of glory, but rather the open manifestation of that which had hitherto been wrapped in types and shadows. Thus also the word φανερόω is taken in Romans XVI, verse 26, where the mystery silent for eternal times is said in the New Testament to have been φανερωθὲν through the Prophetic Scriptures, that is, fulfilled, which is to say, exhibited in reality after the shadows and types were removed. In which sense also 2. Tim. I, 10, grace given in Christ before secular times is said to be φανερωθεῖσα through the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ, not that before this appearing no grace exerted itself anywhere, but that in the appearing of the Savior it presented itself most clearly and without shadows. For the same reason, Tit. I, 2, it is said of the hope of eternal life that God, who cannot lie, promised it before secular times, ἐφανέρωσε δὲ, but appeared, καιροῖς ἰδίοις, that is, in the time of the New Testament, without shadows. Thus also 1. Peter I, 10, the φανέρωσις of the immaculate lamb is his actual exhibition and representation outside of shadows. Compare 1. John I, 2, and III, 8, and 1. Tim. III, 16, just as ἐπιφαίνειν, Tit. II, 11, is taken. Therefore the sense is that the promises concerning the Messiah, and the whole doctrine of salvation, were still wrapped in shadows and types, and to some extent obscured, as long as the old tabernacle and the temple that succeeded it stood in its vigor. But with that removed or profaned, it is an indication that that long-desired φανέρωσις and exhibition of the Messiah, and of the whole new covenant, has taken place. The prefiguration is placed in this, that just as the outer sanctuary as it were surrounded and overshadowed the holy of holies itself, so that access was open to no one except the High Priest, and one had to enter through the outer sanctuary into the inner one. Thus the entire Old Testament shadowed and overshadowed the promises of grace, which as it were encompassed the holy of holies itself. But with the Old Testament removed, the mystery of the New Testament is now manifest. Whence what the Apostle implies is that the Jews, as long as they cling tenaciously to their rites and shadowy institutions, for so long do they shut off for themselves access to the kingdom of grace, and make shadows for themselves, when they could be enjoying the light. Πρώτη σκηνὴ, which is said to have στάσιν, is that very one of which we spoke above in verse 2, which surrounded τὴν μετὰ τὸ δεύτερον καταπέτασμα σκηνὴν, whence the Apostle wishes to say that he himself was placed τῷ κόσμῳ ἁγίῳ, by which the outer tabernacle was ordered toward the inner, and one had to pass through the outer to the inner, and yet the inner was open to no one except the High Priest. This very arrangement of the sanctuary, I say, commanded by the Holy Spirit, reminds us that the true throne of grace has not yet been so exhibited and manifested that access to it is given most freely with παρρησία. The same is required by the Apostolic scope, which is to show that the condition of the Old Testament is transitory, that the New is altogether to be expected, and that in it a clear, apt, and most plain way will be revealed. This the Apostle has already done both many times above, and especially in Chapter VIII, where he mentions the true sanctuary, v. 2, and the λειτουργίας διαφορωτέρας of a better Testament, of better promises, all of which contribute to τὴν τῶν ἁγίων ὁδόν; this he is doing now, and this he does in the following Chapter X. The εὕρημα αἰωνίας λυτρώσεως, of which below in verse 12, pertains to this way of the saints. Therefore, ὁδὸς τῶν ἁγίων φανερωθεῖσα is opposed to the way of the Old Testament, which was among shadows, of which below in Chapter X, 1, and above in Chapter VIII, 5, Col. II, 17. It is therefore not the kingdom of glory itself, but of grace, which is the way to that.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Τῦτο δηλῶντος τῦ πνεύματος ἁγίε] Nempe Deo per af- flatum suum Mosi hæc præcipiente. Vide Levit. XVI, 1. Nam וידבר יהוה interdum quidem ubi id exprimitur, de voce intelligitur: sed plerumque de afflatu.

Μήπωτε πεφανερῶσθαι τὴν τῶν ἁγίων ὁδὸν] Id est, εἰς τὰ ἅγια. Ἅγια posthac cum dicit scriptor, compendio uti- tur. Vult enim intelligi ἅγια ἁγίων, quomodo ὐρανοὶ sæpe dicuntur ὐρανοὶ ὐρανῶν. Hoc autem loco ἅγια intel- lige ἀληθινά, ex iis, quæ supra VIII, 2. rem ipsam, quæ per adytum illud significabatur, id est, superæthereas sedes. Via eo ducens est Evangelium, præcepta habens vere cœlestia. Eam viam Christus primus patefecit, aditum- que fecit omnibus ad summum cœlum. Pervenient qui- dem eo etiam Abrahamus, Isaacus, Jacobus, ut videre est

Matth. VIII, 11. & alii viri eximii, ut videbimus infra XI, 34. & 40. Sed hic eo pervenient, quasi per machinam, non per viam, extraordinaria quadam ac rara Dei dispensatione. Ideo velum adyti disruptum fuit Christo moriente.

Ἔτι τῆς πρώτης σκηνῆς ἐχούσης στάσιν] Id est quamdiu cultus templi illius officium suum faciebat. Nam מעמד officium significat, explicante Kimchi ad Esaiam XXII, 19. Sic & 2. Paral. IX, 4. XXX, 16. XXXV, 10. 15. Dan. X, 11. Of- ficium autem suum facere desiit apud Deum quidem Chri- sto mortuo, a morte excitato, in cœlum evecto, & misso Spiritu S. Apud homines vero omnes tunc cum corruit tem- plum. Nam tunc simul & cultus ille (qui hic per σκηνὴν in- telligitur μετωνυμικῶς) concidit.

Quid πνεῦμα ἅγιον in Scriptura S. sit, satis con- stat. Afflatum esse, non personam divinam si Gro- tius velit, cum Crellio & Schlichtingio facit. Quem vero ipsummet Socinianum potius, virtutem in DEO, quam afflatum extra Deum esse voluit. Sed de his in Socinismo profligato. Explicare autem jam incipit Apostolus mysteria, quæ in figuris istis latebant, quid nempe Spiritus Sanctus iis- dem significare voluerit, & primum quidem, quid per illud, quod non nisi semel annuatim in sanctum sanctorum ingressus est Pontifex, quod nempe stante adhuc tabernaculo isto typico via ad san- ctum sanctorum τὸ ἀληθινὸν nondum fuerit pate- facta. Siquidem verus Pontifex habuerit ingressu suo in sanctum sanctorum, hoc est, in cœlum no- bis viam patefacere, ut liber nobis aditus pateat, Ebr. X, 19. 20. Unde cum per passionem & mor- tem suam in gloriam ingrederetur, velum templi scissum fuit, Matth. XXVII, 51. Per πρώτην σκηνὴν prior intelligitur, ut antea, tabernaculi pars. Per- peram autem ex hoc loco colligit Becanus, cœ- lum usque ad mortem Christi justis fuisse clau- sum, ejus vero morte reclusum fuisse, ut ingres- sus pateret animabus sanctis è limbo Patrum in illud introductis, append. disp. de purg. Calvin. c. I. p. 43. Quia intelligenda hæc sunt ratione me- riti, non ratione apertionis cæli actualis, aut prout Stephanus cœlum apertum vidisse dicitur, Actor. VII, 56. Patefecit viam ad cœlum, ut causa mora- lis, quia promeruit nobis, ut, quod clausum erat per peccata, vicissim pateret nobis expiatis pec- catis, non ut causa Physica. Meritum autem Chri- sti valuit omni tempore antrorsum & retrorsum, Ebr. XIII, v. 8. Per id etiam veteres salvati sunt, Act. XV, 11. Quo de Theophylactus: Cum semel constet, Christum sacrificatum, qui fieri potest, ut cunctos in uno hoc sacrificio sanctitate dona- verit? Quia a prioribus seculis Christo hoc sa- crificium destinatum, quod omnibus esset saluti futurum. Non opus ergo fuit, ut tum demum e limbo educerentur, cum Christus passus est & mortuus. Ut taceam, quod Thomas & Dionysius per viam sanctorum intelligant Christum, Joh. XIV, 6. qui tum nondum ita patefactus fuerit, sed sub figuris adumbratus latuerit. Estius vero gra- tiam, per quam nobis aditus patet ad cœlum, quæ via tempore Veteris Testamenti nondum erat propalata vel manifestata, id est, palam cognita & prædicata, sed latebat sub umbris ceremonia- rum &c. quo etiam abit interpretatio Origenis tr. XXXV. in Matth. Cyrilli Alexandr. l. XII. in Joh. cap. 37. Theodoreti in Dan. IX. Ambrosii l. VI. in Luc. Hieronymi in Matth. XXVII. Augustini in Pf. LXVII. & LXX. Leonis serm. X. de passion. &c. Viam in cælum ducentem Evangelium esse, etiam Grotius hic tradit, sed id pervertit additamento illo suo, quod præcepta habeat cœlestia, pessime confundens viam legalem, per quam nulli post lapsum aditus patet ad cœlum & viam Evangeli- cam, in qua sola est salus per gratiam Christi, qui eam patefecit omnibus non præconio tantum sed merito suo, non enim est Redemptor & Me- diator tantum ratione annuntiationis, sed ratione acquisitionis salutis æternæ, nec primus ipse ean- dem annuntiavit in Novo Testam. sed eam jam in ipso Paradiso Protoplastis, & in iis toti generi hu- mano: quemadmodum non Patriarchæ solum & alii viri eximii, sed omnes fideles Veteris Testa- menti vel ante Christum gratia Christi in cœlum pervenere, ac per Christum ceu unicam viam, Joh. XIV, 6. Act. XV, 11. Quos per machinam quasi, & extraordinaria solum ac rara quadam Dei dis- pensatione salvatos esse citra & contra Scriptu- ram docetur, quum Abraham potius à Paulo in exemplum consequendæ per fidem in Christum salutis omnibus credentibus fistatur. Sed hæc portenta hæreseos Socinianæ alias ex professo jam profligavimus. B. Dorscheus in Schlichtingii con- futatione hic probavit illam sententiam, quæ de patefactione doctrinæ luculentori locum explicat. Schlichtingius, inquit, non tantum ante Christi ad- ventum primum, sed etiam ante secundum nemi- nem sanctorum in possessionem cœlestium gaudio- rum venisse aut venturum esse manifeste indicat. Sed tum contra verba, tum contra scopum Apostoli. Nam quod ad ipsa verba attinet, patefactio aditus ad ipsam vitam æternam in sacris literis nuspiam voca- tur Φανέρωσις τῆς τῶν ἁγίων ὁδῦ, & via sancto- rum in S. literis ipsa doctrina salutis Novo Testam. tradita sæpissime nominatur. Sic Act. XVI, 17. est ὁδὸς σωτηρίας, & Cap. XVIII, 25. est ὁδὸς τῦ Κυ- ρίε. vers. 26. est ὁδὸς τῦ Θεῦ, & Cap. XIX, 33. dici- tur ὁδὸς simpliciter, & Cap. XXII, 4. similiter 2. Petr. II, 2. est ὁδὸς τῆς ἀληθείας. v. 15. ὁδὸς εὐθεῖα, & v. 21. ὁδὸς τῆς δικαιοσύνης. Hinc & infra Cap. X. v. 20. est ὁδὸς πρόσφατος καὶ ζῶσα, quæ v. 19. dicitur εἴσοδος τῶν ἁγίων ἐν τῷ ἕιματι Ἰησῦ, quæ & su- pra Cap. IV, 16. προσέλευσις τῷ θρόνῳ τῆς χάριτος μετὰ παῥῥησίας. Unde necesse non est hoc loco actua- lem ingressum ipsum seu transitum ex regno gratiæ in regnum gloriæ intelligere, cum ut plurimum ipsum regnum gratiæ seu doctrinam ejus in S. lite- ris designet. Nec Φανέρωσις hoc loco notat apertio- nem regni gloriæ, sed potius ejus, quod typis & um- bris hactenus involutum fuerat, apertam manife- stationem. Sic & verbum Φανερόω sumitur Rom. XVI, vers. 26. ubi mysterium æternis temporibus tacitum in Novo Testamento dicitur per Scripturas Propheticas scilicet impletas Φανερωθὲν, hoc est, post umbras & typos remotos reapse exhibitum. Quo sensu etiam 2. Tim. I, 10. gratia ante tempora secu- laria in Christo data dicitur Φανερωθεῖσα per appa- ritionem Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi, non quod ante apparitionem hanc nulla uspiam sese exerue- rit gratia, sed quod in apparitione Salvatoris luci- dissime & extra umbras sese stiterit. Eadem ra- tione Tit. I, 2. de spe vitæ æternæ dicitur, quod eam promiserit fallere nescius Deus ante tempora secula- ria, ἐφανέρωσε δὲ apparuerit autem καιροῖς ἰδίοις scil. tempore Novi Testam. sine umbris. Sic & 1. Petr. I, 10. Φανέρωσις agni immaculati est ipsa actualis ejus exhibitio & repræsentatio extra umbras. Conf. 1. Joh. I, 2. & III, 8. & 1. Tim. III, 16. quomodo & ἐπιφαίνειν, Tit. II, 11. accipitur. Itaq; sensus est, promissiones de Messia, & totam doctrinam salutis umbris adhuc & typis fuisse involutam, & quadan- tenus obscuratam, quamdiu vetus tabernaculum & illi succedaneum consistebat in suo vigore tem- plum. Eo vero sublato aut profanato manifestum esse indicium, factam esse illam diu desideratam Φανέρωσιν & exhibitionem Messiæ, totiusque novi fœderis. Præfiguratio in eo posita est, quod quem- admodum sanctuarium exterius ipsum sanctum sanctorum quasi obvallabat & obumbrabat, ut ne- mini præter summum Sacerdotem in illud patuerit aditus, & per sanctuarium exterius in interius fuit ingrediendum. Sic V. Testamentum universum ad- umbrabat & obumbrabat promissiones gratiæ, quæ ipsum sanctum sanctorum quasi complectebantur. Veteri vero Testamento sublato jam manifestum est mysterium Novi Test. Unde quod innuit Apostolus, Judæi quamdiu suis ritibus & umbraticis institu- tis mordicus inhærent, tamdiu sibi ipsis aditum ad regnum gratiæ intercludunt, & umbras faciunt, cum luce frui possent. Πρώτη σκηνὴ, quæ dicitur στάσιν ἔχουσα, est ea ipsa, de qua supra vers. 2. quæ circumdabat τὴν μετὰ τὸ δεύτερον καταπέτασμα σκηνὴν, unde dicere vult Apostolus, ipse positus τῶ κό- σμῳ ἁγίῳ, quo exterius tabernaculum ordinabatur ad interius, & per exterius ad interius fuerat transeun- dum, nec tamen interius nisi summo Sacerdoti patuit. Ipsa inquam ista dispositio sanctuarii à Spiritu Sancto præcepta commonefacit nondum verum gratiæ thro- num ita exhibitum esse & manifestatum, ut μετὰ παῤῥησίας ad eum liberrimus detur accessus. Idem requirit & scopus Apostolicus, qui est, ostendere, tran- sitoriam esse Veteris Test. conditionem, Novum omni- no expectandum esse, & in eo viam lucidam, aptam, planissimam patefactum iri. Hoc jam egit Apostolus tum supra multoties, tum imprimis Cap. IIX, ubi me- minit sanctuarii veri, v. 2. & λειτουργίας διαφορω- τέρας melioris Testamenti, meliorum promissionum, quæ omnia faciunt ad τὴν τῶν ἁγίων ὁδόν, hoc ipsum jam agit, hoc & seq. Cap. X. Pertinet ad hanc san- ctorum viam εὕρημα αἰωνίς λυτρώσεως, de quo in- fra vers. 12. Itaque ὁδὸς τῶν ἁγίων φανερωθεῖσα op- ponitur viæ Veteris Testamenti, quæ erat inter um- bras, de qua infra Cap. X, 1. & supra Cap. IIX, 5. Col. II, 17. Est itaq́; non ipsum regnum gloriæ sed gratiæ, quod est ad illud via.

## 9:9
Vers. 9.

Ἥτις παραβολὴ εἰς τοῦτον καιρὸν τὸν ἐνεστηκότα] Other books have τὸν καιρὸν. The sense is the same. For ἐνεστηκὼς καιρὸς is the present time. Thus also ἐνεστῶτα Rom. VIII, 35, 1. Cor. III, 22, VII, 26, Gal. I, 4. Nor does it matter that this Participle is of the past tense. For thus also ἐνέστηκε is said for ἐνίσταται, 2. Thess. II, 2. This says: This mystical explanation, מָשָׁל, even now has a place among those in whose opinion that worship still stands and has force. Concerning the word παραβολῆς, see what is said at Matthew XIII, 3.

Καθ᾿ ὃν δῶρά τε καὶ θυσίαι προσφέρονται] This epistle was written while the temple was standing, while that worship still remained, and while the opinion prevailed among most Jews that that worship was still most pleasing to God. He says this, however, so that the Hebrews to whom he writes would not allow themselves to be drawn back to Judaism. What δῶρα and what θυσίαι are, we have stated above at V, 1. In the manuscript [it is] καθ᾿ ἣν, namely παραβολὴν, just as it appears some Greeks also read.

Rectius ad tempus refertur, as Chrysostom and Theophylact and others read, and as the Syriac rendered it, in this sense: at which time gifts and sacrifices were offered, that is, were accustomed to be offered. Thus, indeed, the Apostle also spoke in verse 6 in the present tense εἰσίασιν καὶ προσφέρουσι, not as if the discourse were about the entry of the High Priest into Solomon's temple while it was still enduring, seeing that in it there was neither the ark, nor the manna, nor the rod, but to signify the custom, that they were accustomed to enter into that part of the tabernacle every day. For it is not properly about the παραβολῇ of the Solomonic temple that is treated here, but of the Mosaic tabernacle, and of the gifts and sacrifices accustomed to be offered in it. By τὸν λατρεύοντα some understand the Priest, others indifferently both the Priest offering and the people and anyone for whom the offering was made, which is more correct.

Μὴ δυνάμεναι κατὰ συνείδησιν τελειῶσαι τὸν λατρεύοντα] By the word συνείδησις he understands the soul synecdochically, the inner man, as here, and below [says] Theophylact. Those forms of worship cannot purge the minds of their followers from vices, which the Gospel does. See above VII, 19.

Grotius very badly confuses the soul and the inner man (τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον), by which name the soul is nowhere found in the Scriptures, but rather man, in that part in which he is reborn and renewed, or according to the spirit, just as the spirit is opposed to the flesh, and the inner man to the outer in a reborn man, as one in whom both the oldness of the flesh and the renewal of the spirit are detected, as the Apostle testifies, Rom. VII, 14. seqq. Gal. V, 17. The soul is one thing, and the conscience is another: because the conscience is in the soul as in a subject, which is named here, because God looks upon the conscience, and just as it accuses us of sins, so it has need of cleansing from sins, which even if it is done organically through the Gospel, which is a medium on the part of GOD perfecting or cleansing us: yet that is not what is being treated here, where it is manifest from those things which he claims for Christ, as Priest, that the Apostle is rather discoursing about the meritorious cause: Which is sufficiently taught in verse 15 concerning the justification of the conscience through the offering of Christ: For the Apostle explains not how that is done through the Gospel, but how it has been done through the offering of Christ. It is said, however, as the blessed Dorscheus rightly advises here, that the gifts and sacrifices of the Old Testament could not purify and perfect the consciences of those offering them, not because the Holy Spirit did not use those gifts and sacrifices of the Old Testament as certain instruments by which justifying and sanctifying grace was applied. For they were nothing other than a certain visible sermon and proposition of those mysteries which were to be represented in the New Testament. And so they had that power to that extent, which the audible word also had, and were a power unto salvation Rom. I, 16. For even if by reason of the act they pertained to the law: Yet by reason of the image or the image in act, or, as above c. VIII, 5. Paul speaks, by reason of the example (ὑποδείγματος) they looked toward the Gospel, and from it received certain justifying streaks, but for the reason that in this very apparatus and body of sacrifices and gifts, so to speak, there was not that virtue by which wounded consciences could be helped. Whence the argument is evident, and a manifest confirmation of expecting another more perfect worship. For whoever has a worship that has sacrifices and other institutions, which are not the body itself and as it were the seat and dwelling of that virtue which suffices for perfecting the conscience, that is abrogable, and indicates that another is to be substituted, in which is the body itself, the seat and dwelling of perfection and divine virtue. Such, however, is the worship of the Old Testament; it is therefore abrogable, etc. By this very thing, indeed, by which the worship of the Old Testament, although it was founded upon the law, was nevertheless an evangelical parable, or a real sermon of saving mysteries, but under a shadow it was certainly accommodated, so that for the time then present until the time of the New Testament it dispensed the grace of eternal salvation. Therefore the sacrifices (θυσίαι) are said to be unable to perfect (μὴ δυνάμεναι τελειῶσαι), namely of themselves, and as a body in which all the fullness of the divinity might dwell, just as the sacrifice of the New Testament contained in itself the power of perfection (δύναμιν τελειώσεως), as it contained in itself all power in heaven and on earth Matth. XXVIII, 18.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Ἥτις παραβολὴ εἰς τῦτον καιρὸν τὸν ἐνεστηκότα] Alii libri habent τὸν καιρὸν. Idem est sensus. Nam ἐνεστηκὼς καιρὸς est tempus præsens. Sic & ἐνεστῶτα Rom. VIII, 35. 1. Cor. III, 22. VII, 26. Gal. I, 4. Nec refert, quod hoc Participium sit Præ- teriti temporis. Nam sic & ἐνέστηκε dicitur pro ἐνίσταται, 2. Thess. II, 2. Hoc dicit: Hæc mystica explicatio, מָשָׁל, et- iam nunc locum habet in iis, quorum opinione stat adhuc il- le cultus & vim habet. De voce παραβολῆς vide quæ ad Matth. XIII, 3.

Καθ᾿ ὃν δῶρά τε καὶ θυσίαι προσφέρονται] Scripta est hæc epistola stante templo, manente adhuc cultu illo, & apud Ju- dæos plerosque opinione illum adhuc cultum Deo esse gratis- simum. Hoc autem ideo dicit, ne Ebræi, ad quos scribit, pa- terentur se retrahi ad Judaismum. Quid δῶρα, quid θυσίαι, diximus supra V, 1. In Manuscripto καθ᾿ ἣν nempe παραβολὴν, quomodo & Græcos quosdam apparet legisse.

Rectius ad tempus refertur, quemadmodum Chrysostomus & Theophylactus aliique legere, ac Syrus reddidit, hoc sensu, quo tempore munera & hostiæ offerebantur, id est, offerri consueverunt. Sic vero & vers. 6. loquutus est Apostolus in præsenti εἰσίασιν καὶ προσφέρες, non quasi sermo sit de in- gressu Pontificis in templum Salomonis eo tem- pore adhuc durante, utpote in quo nec arca, nec manna, nec virga erat, sed ad significandam con- suetudinem, quod singulis diebus in illum taber- naculi partem ingredi fuerunt soliti. Non enim de παραβολῇ templi Salomonici, sed tabernaculi Mosaica proprie hic agitur, & de donis & sacrifi- ciis in eo offerri solitis. Per τὸν λατρεύοντα non- nulli Sacerdotem, alii indifferenter & Sacerdotem offerentem, & populum ac quemlibet pro quo fie- bat oblatio, rectius intelligunt.

Μὴ δυνάμεναι κατὰ συνείδησιν τελειῶσαι τὸν λατρεύοντα] συνειδήσεως voce animam intelligit συνεκδοχικῶς, τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον, ut hic, & infra Theophylactus. Isti cultus non possunt sectatorum suorum animos purgare a vitiis, quod facit Evangelium. Vide supra VII, 19.

Pessime confundit Grotius animam & τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον, quo nomine nuspiam in Scripturis ani- ma venit, sed homo, qua ex parte renatus & reno- vatus est, vel secundum spiritum, prout spiritus carni, & homo interior exteriori in homine re- nato opponuntur, utpote in quo & vetustas car- nis & renovatio spiritus deprehenditur, Aposto- lo teste, Rom. VII, 14. seqq. Gal. V, 17. Aliud etiam est anima, aliud conscientia: quia conscientia est in anima tanquam in subjecto, quæ hic nomina- tur, quia Deus conscientiam intuetur, eademque uti nos accusat ob peccata, ita mundatione a pec- catis opus habet, quæ etsi fiat per Evangelium ὀργανικῶς, quod medium est ex parte DEI nos perficientis vel mundantis: non tamen id hic agi- tur, ubi potius de causa meritoria Apostolum dis- serere, ex iis, quæ Christo, ceu Sacerdoti vindi- cat, manifestum est: Quod vers. 15. de justifica- tione conscientiæ per oblationem Christi satis doce- tur: Illa enim non quomodo per Evangelium fiat, sed quomodo facta sit per oblationem Chri- sti, Apostolus explicat. Dicitur autem, quod re- cte hic monet B. Dorscheus, dona & victimas Ve- teris Test. non potuisse conscientias offerentium pu- rificare & consummare, non quod non usus sit Spi- ritus Sanctus istis donis victimisque Veteris Testam. tanquam instrumentis quibusdam, quibus gratia justificans & sanctificans applicaretur. Fuerunt enim nihil aliud, quam visibilis quædam concio & propositio eorum mysteriorum, quæ in Novo Testam. repræsentanda fuerunt. Itaque catenus habebant vim illam, quam & verbum audibile, erantque potentia ad salutem Rom. I, 16. Etiamsi enim ratione actus pertinuerint ad legem: Tamen ratione imaginis sive imaginis in actu, sive, ut supra c. VIII, 5. Pau- lus loquitur, ratione ὑποδείγματος ad Evangelium respiciebant, ab eoque stricturas quasdam accipie- bant justificas, sed propterea, quod in ipso hoc sacri- ficiorum & donariorum apparatu & corpore, ut sic dicam, non fuerit ista virtus, qua conscientiis sau- ciis succurri poterat. Unde evidens est argumen- tum, & manifesta confirmatio expectandi cultus alterius perfectioris. Qui enim cultus habet sa- crificia & cætera instituta, quæ non sunt ipsum corpus & quasi sedes atque domicilium illius vir- tutis, quæ conscientiæ consummandæ sufficit, is abrogabilis est, & indicat surrogandum alium, in quo sit ipsum corpus, sedes atque domicilium per- fectionis & virtutis divinæ. Talis autem est cultus Veteris Test. est itaque abrogabilis &c. Hoc ipso vero, quo cultus Vet. Testam. licet fundatus super legem erat, tamen parabola Evangelica, sive rea- lis concio mysteriorum salvificorum, sed sub um- bra accommodatus utique fuit, ut pro tempore tunc instante usq; ad tempus N. Test. dispensaret gratiam æternæ salutis. Ergo θυσίαι dicuntur μὴ δυνάμεναι τελειῶσαι, scil. ex se, & tanquam corpus, in quo habitaret omnis plenitudo divinitatis sicut sacrificium N. Test. δύναμιν τελειώσεως in se com- plectebatur, utpote omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra in se complexum Matth. XXVIII, 18.

## 9:10
Vers. 10.

Only with meats, and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed until the time of reformation (Μόνον ἐπὶ βρώμασι, καὶ πόμασι, καὶ διαφόροις βαπτισμοῖς, καὶ δικαιώμασι σαρκὸς μέχρι καιρῶ διορθώσεως ἐπικείμενα)] That law, in its greatest part ritual, was imposed upon the Jews, so that by that bridle they might be restrained both from impiety and from idolatry, and thus be more prepared to receive the Gospel. See what is said Gal. III, 23. 24. The time of reformation is the time of the law and of the better covenant. See above VIII, 6. Moreover, ἐπὶ in this place is for besides or over. For those gifts and sacrifices were only imposed upon the Hebrews, just as other parts of the Law, which he now adds, for that use which he will state. He says meats (βρώματα) because of the laws concerning forbidden foods. Drinks (πώματα) because of the abstinence from wine in the Priests, at the time when they performed their duty, Levit. X, 9. He names various washings: because one washing was of the Priests, Exod. XXIX, 4, another of the Levites, Num. VIII, 7, another of the Israelites after some impurity was contracted, Levitic. XV, 8. 16. 18. 27. XVII, 15. XXII, 6. Num. XIX, 16. Carnal ordinances (Δικαιώματα σαρκὸς) are the other precepts, the observation of which either freed a man from punishment, or admitted him to the fellowship of others and access into the basilica of the temple as regards the Priests, or into the atrium of the temple as regards others. All of which pertain to the flesh, that is, the present life. But in the Manuscript it is not carnal ordinances (δικαιώμασι σαρκὸς), but ordinances (δικαιώματα), so that the sense refers to the former, as if he were saying which are ordinances (ἅτινά ἐσι δικαιώματα), nor does the Syrian read otherwise. Ordinances (Δικαιώματα) are statutes (חקים) as above l. And the construction imposed (ἐπικείμενα) is good, just as unable (μὴ δυνάμενα), because where the Feminine and Neuter have preceded concerning things, not persons, as here gifts and sacrifices (δῶρα καὶ θυσίαι), the Adjective is added in the Neuter, sometimes also in the Feminine, as just now unable (δυνάμεναι). Laws and the forced decrees of the people in Lucan.

The Apostle meets a tacit objection: For it could be asked why God instituted them if they could not perfect (τελειῶσαι)? He answers that they were not instituted to be kept perpetually, but were only imposed until the time of reformation. In the words truly only with meats (μόνον ἐπὶ βρώμασιν) others prefer to understand something, i.e., those sacrifices cannot make perfect, but consist only in meats and drinks. Others refer it to him who ministers (λατρεύοντα), that he could not make him perfect who ministers only in meats and drinks. But because neither did the sacrifices consist properly in meats and drinks, but were distinguished from them, nor are the Priests alone understood in v. 9, nor were they alone occupied in meats, drinks, and washings. Wherefore it does not displease that ἐπὶ should be besides, that only besides meats, drinks, and divers washings were the gifts and sacrifices and carnal ordinances imposed until the time of reformation. Where, as B. Dorscheus says, it is certain that verse 10 is to be interpreted concerning that which was joined with the sacrifices of the Old Testament in the Levitical worship: But that we should refer it to the sacrifices of verse 10, is not necessary. It is simpler to refer it to the δῶρα of verse 10, which even the participle ἐπικείμενα insinuates, which cannot be referred to θυσίας: Otherwise it would have to be said ἐπικείμεναι, just as δυνάμεναι is said in v. 9. The Vulgate seems to have read ἐπικειμένοις, whence it renders it as 'impositis' [imposed]. But the trustworthiness of the Greek codices protests against this. It fits best, however, and also completes the sentence, if we refer it to the δῶρα, so that the Apostle says something about the θυσίαι and something about the δῶρα: About the θυσίαι, indeed, that they were of themselves powerless to perfect the conscience of the worshipper. But concerning the δῶρα, that they were ἐπικείμενα, added, or super-imposed, until the time of reformation, so that they might be presented to God according to those things which are prescribed concerning the distinctions of foods and drinks, and also concerning various washings, and other justifications of the flesh: so that if anything here is either to be understood or supplied at the beginning of verse 10, δῶρά τε is to be repeated from v. 9, so that this may be the complete sentence: The first tabernacle has an adumbrative image of future goods for the instant and current time, insofar as in it gifts and sacrifices are offered: Sacrifices, indeed, which cannot perfect the worshipper in conscience: But gifts, (which likewise cannot provide that) which were imposed according to foods and drinks and various washings and justifications of the flesh, until the time of reformation, so that they might be presented. Therefore, the gifts which had to be brought into the temple besides the sacrifices, such as first-fruits, tithes, spontaneous offerings, showbread, libations, and other similar things, are distinguished from the other ceremonies to which a man had to devote effort even outside the tabernacle and temple. Moreover, they are called gifts 1. imposed according to or besides foods and drinks, etc., because, namely, they could not be offered or presented except by those who consisted in the observation of those ceremonial distinctions, which some who were converted from Judaism to Christianity in the beginning did not sufficiently notice, whence a dispute was stirred up in the Churches, concerning which both elsewhere and especially in Rom. XIV, where the Apostle finally seals the dispute in v. 17, when he says that the kingdom of God is not βρῶσιν καὶ πόσιν, but righteousness and peace, etc., where by the kingdom of God he does not understand the kingdom of grace simply. For this was promoted even under the shadows of the ceremonies, indeed it was governed in a certain way through the shadows, but the kingdom of grace was consecrated by the promulgation of the new covenant: by which also in the beginning of the new covenant it was proclaimed as if by solemn words, ἤγγικεν ἡ βασιλεία τῶν ὀρανῶν by John the forerunner, Matt. III, 2, and by Christ himself, Matt. IV, 17. The first head, therefore, which had to be observed by the one serving and offering the gifts lying upon him, was the distinction of foods and drinks. For this, not being observed, brought legal uncleanness upon a man and made him unfit for the gifts. Concerning the distinction of foods, the matter is clear and especially explained at length in Lev. XI, the traces of which are detected even before the flood in Gen. VII, 2, and it is repeated after the flood in Chapter VIII, 20. Concerning drinks, Chrysostom and Theophylact assert that nothing is written in the law, and therefore what is written here concerning them refers either to the Priests, who abstained from wine when they were about to minister in the tabernacle, or to the Nazarites, who made a vow of abstinence. But in truth, although both Priests and Nazarites had to abstain from wine, wine nevertheless did not become unclean: the Apostle is indeed speaking of the distinction of drinks, namely, of clean from unclean. Therefore, there is no need for us to flee to this. It is clear in itself, however, that drink could also have become unclean among the Israelites in many ways, although they are not all set forth in the sacred rites. For by all those ways in which other things could become unclean, drink also could in its own way contract uncleanness. A general rule stands in Lev. XI, 32, where it is commanded that whatever has been touched by an unclean thing is to be held as unclean, whence easily very many

distinctions could arise. The second are διάφοροι βαπτισμοὶ: The old Interpreter translates it more obscurely as various baptisms. For in general, these are the diverse washings commanded in Lev. XI and XV and Num. XIX, concerning which also in Matt. XXIII, 25 and Mark VII, 3, 4. Indeed, baptism was also in the custom of the Hebrews, as often as someone approached Judaism from idolatry. The third head is placed in δικαιώμασι σαρκὸς. Beza notes that he found δικαιώματα in an ancient codex, so that this pertains to what follows and looks back as a third to the gifts and sacrifices, concerning which in v. 9. But there is no need to abandon the received reading. For after the Apostle had commemorated the differences of food and drink, and likewise of washings, he rightly adds δικαιώματα σαρκὸς as a general term, which embraces the remaining Mosaic constitutions added to the gifts and sacrifices: i.e., and other ordinances of the flesh. For thus the noun δικαίωμα was already used above in v. 8. The Vulgate renders it as justices of the flesh, Erasmus as justifications of the flesh. But Castellio clearly departs from the text when he translates it as human institutions. For he is not speaking here of the commandments of men, concerning which in Matt. XVIII, 9, but of those which belonged to the old covenant by divine sanction and which taught that they performed the duty of a parable in v. 9. Nor, because mention is made of reformation, are those institutions therefore reproved as if they were fabricated. For here reformation is not to be taken in such a way that it is opposed to those things which are repugnant to divine law and must be recalled to the rule. Therefore, the word flesh does not denote the efficient cause, but the subject, that is, that about which those ordinances, considered in themselves, were for the most part occupied. For although, when considered in the category of relation, that is, insofar as they were a type and a parable of the good things to come, they also touched the soul itself and contributed their effort to the perfection of the Spirit, yet in the category of action they were terminated at the flesh. The blessed Hunnius says: He mentions Mosaic justifications, not only insofar as they were reputed to be cleansed again from Levitical uncleanness, but also insofar as they were said to be expiated before the Lord through the mediation of sacrifices, not indeed because of the merit and dignity of those sacrifices, but because those victims pointed the finger toward Christ, who justifies the faithful by his own truly propitiatory sacrifice. Therefore, what the Apostle affirms here, that these victims were invalid for the purification of the conscience and heart: it must be known that he is speaking of the sacrifices as they are considered in themselves. For otherwise, by reason of their end and spiritual signification, they certainly did not lack their effect, since they led the people to the consideration of future good things in Christ. The time of reformation, however, is said by some to be by reason of correction; not so much of those Levitical rites, which were not corrected but abolished, as by reason of the correction of those things which were corrupted by sin: because Christ came for this purpose, that he might destroy the works of the devil, 1 John III, 8, and restore all things and bring them back to their pristine integrity. The blessed Hunnius: The time of correction, where the figures were to be made old, with the truth and substance of the thing substituted, that is, with Christ exhibited, manifested in the flesh, having suffered and been exalted. Estius observes that the Greek term διόρθωσιν properly signifies rectification; but that what the Latins call correction is more commonly called ἐπανόρθωσιν by the Greeks: According to B. Dorscheus, καιρὸς διορθώσεως is most simply the time of fulfillment and improvement, insofar as things are brought from the state of shadows and types to the state of completion and antitype. Διορθῶσαι among the LXX now corresponds to the root ישר Jer. VII, 2. & 4. and now to the root כון Es. XVI, 5. & LXI, 7. It is therefore the time of the N.T. in which, with the shadow appearing, it was necessary for it to cease, and for the whole divine worship to be established most rightly and most perfectly. For not only do things that are evil require διόρθωσιν, but also those that are less good and perfect: He also corrects who adds what is lacking, Tit. I, 5. Budaeus thinks that this word properly signifies a certain raising up, when someone who is about to fall grasps something by which he can raise himself. But that such was Christ, without whom the Jews tottered. But here the Apostle's discourse is not so much about the διόρθωσις of the Jews as of the old covenant itself. Theophylact notes an emphasis in the word ἐπικείμενα: Since the law was a very heavy yoke, he said it was rightly imposed, just as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: Why do you tempt to impose a yoke upon the disciples, which neither your fathers bore?

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Μόνον ἐπὶ βρώμασι, καὶ πόμασι, καὶ διαφόροις βαπτισμοῖς, καὶ δικαιώμασι σαρκὸς μέχρι καιρῶ διορθώσεως ἐπικείμενα] Lex illa maxima sui parte ritualis imposita erat Judæis, ut eo freno retinerentur tum ab impietate, tum ab idololatria, & sic paratiores essent ad recipiendum Evangelium. Vide quæ dicta Gal. III, 23. 24. Tempus correctionis est tempus legis ac fœderis melioris. Vide supra VIII, 6. Est autem ἐπὶ hoc lo- co pro præter sive super. Nam dona illa & victimæ imposi- tæ tantum erant Ebræis, sicut & aliæ partes Legis, quas jam addit, ei usui, quem dicet. Βρώματα dicit propter leges de cibis vetitis. Πώματα propter vini abstinentiam in Sacer- dotibus, quo tempore munus suum fungebantur, Levit. X, 9. Varias lotiones nominat: quia lotio alia erat Sacerdotum, Exod. XXIX, 4. alia Levitarum, Num. VIII, 7, alia Israëli- tarum post impuritatem aliquam contractam, Levitic. XV, 8. 16. 18. 27. XVII, 15. XXII, 6. Num. XIX, 16. Δικαιώμα- τα σαρκὸς sunt cætera præcepta, quorum observatio homi- nem aut à pœna liberabat, aut admittebat ad consortium aliorum & aditum in templi basilicam quoad Sacerdotes aut in templi atrium quoad alios. Quæ omnia ad carnem, id est, vitam præsentem pertinent. At in Manuscripto non est δικαιώμασι σαρκὸς, sed δικαιώματα, ut sit sensus ad priora se referens, quasi dicat ἅτινά ἐσι δικαιώματα, neque aliter legit Syrus. Δικαιώματα חקים ut supra l. Et bona est constructio ἐπικείμενα, sicut & μὴ δυνάμενα, quia ubi præcessit Fœmininum & Neutrum de rebus, non de per- sonis, ut hic δῶρα καὶ θυσίαι, additur Adjectivum in Neutro, interdum & in Fœminino, ut modo δυνάμεναι. Leges & ple- bis scita coacta apud Lucanum.

Occurrit Apostolus tacitæ objectioni: Quæri enim posset, cur Deus ea instituerit, si non pote- rant τελειῶσαι? Respondet non esse instituta, ut perpetuo ferventur, sed imposita tantum usque ad tempus correctionis. In verbis vere μόνον ἐπὶ βρώμασιν alii malunt aliquid subintelligere, q.d. sacrificia illa non possunt perfectum reddere, sed consistunt solummodo in cibis & potibus. Alii ad λατρεύοντα referunt, quod non perfectum fa- cere eum potuerint, qui ministrat solum in cibis & potibus. Sed quia nec sacrificia in cibis & po- tibus proprie consistebant, sed ab iisdem distin- guebantur, nec Sacerdotes soli intelliguntur v. 9. neque illi solum in cibis, potibus, & baptismis occupati fuere. Quapropter non displicet, ut ἐπὶ sit præter, quod solum præter cibos, potus, & baptismos diversos dona & victimæ & justifica- tiones carnis ad tempus usque correctionis im- posita erant. Ubi, B. Dorscheo dicente, illud cer- tum est vers. 10. de eo interpretandum esse, quod cum sacrificiis Veteris Testam. in cultu Levitico con- junctum est: Sed ut ad sacrificia vers. 10. refera- mus, necesse non est. Simplicius est ad δῶρα vers. 10. referre, quod vel participium ἐπικείμενα insinuat, quod ad θυσίας referri non potest: Alias ἐπικεί- μεναι dicendum foret, sicut δυνάμεναι in v. 9. dicitur. Vulgatus legisse videtur ἐπικειμένοις, unde reddit im- positis. Sed reclamat Græcorum Codd. fides. Opti- me autem quadrat & absolvit etiam sententiam, si ad δῶρα referamus, ut ita aliquid de θυσίαις, ali- quid de δώροις dicat Apostolus: De θυσίαις quidem, quod ex se fuerint impotentes ad consummandam cultoris conscientiam. De δώροις vero, quod fuerint ἐπικείμενα, adjecta, sive superimposita, usque ad tempus correctionis, ut præstarentur Deo juxta ea, quæ de discriminibus ciborum & potuum, de diver- sis etiam lotionibus, cæterisque carnis justificationi- bus præcipiuntur: adeo ut si quicquam hic vel sub- audiendum, vel supplendum est ad initium vers. 10. δῶρά τε ex v. 9. repetendum sit, ut sententia inte- gra hæc sit: Prius tabernaculum imaginem adum- brativam futurorum bonorum pro instanti & cur- rente tempore habet, quatenus in eodem dona & sacrificia offeruntur: Sacrificia quidem, quæ non possunt in conscientia perficere cultorem: Dona ve- ro, (quæ itidem illud præstare nequeunt) quæ juxta cibos & potus & diversas lotiones & justificationes carnis, usque ad tempus correctionis imposita sunt, ut præstarentur. Itaque distinguuntur dona, quæ præter sacrificia templo inferenda fuerunt, qualia sunt primitiæ, decimæ, oblationes spontaneæ, panes pro- positionis, libamina & similia alia à ceremoniis cæ- teris, quibus etiam extra tabernaculum & templum operam dare homo debuit. Dicuntur autem dona 1. imposita juxta vel præter cibos & potus &c. quia scil. non poterant offerri aut præstari nisi ab illis, qui in observatione istorum discriminum ceremonia- lium consistebant, quod in principio ex Judaismo ad Christianismum conversi nonnulli non satis animad- verterunt, unde disputatio mota in Ecclesiis, de qua tum alibi, tum imprimis Rom. XIV. ubi Apostolus denique disputationem obsignat v. 17. cum inquit, re- gnum Dei non esse βρῶσιν καὶ πόσιν, ἀλλὰ δικαιοσύ- νην κ, εἰρήνην &c. ubi per regnum Dei non intelligit re- gnum gratiæ simpliciter. Hoc enim sub umbris cere- moniarum etiam promovebatur, imo per umbras gubernabatur certo modo, sed regnum gratiæ pro- mulgatione novi fœderis consecratum: quo etiam in principio novi fœderis tanquam per verba solennia exclamatum fuit, ἤγγικεν ἡ βασιλεία τῶν ὀρανῶν ἀ Johanne prodromo, Matth. III, 2. & ipso Christo Matth. IV, 17. Primum itaque caput, quod τῷ λα- τρεύοντι, & dona ἐπικείμενα offerenti observandum fuit, erat discrimen ciborum & potuum. Nam hoc non observatum conciliabat homini immundi- tiem legalem, eumque ad dona inhabilem faciebat. De discrimine ciborum res clara est, & imprimis prolixe explicata Lev. XI. cujus etiam vestigia jam ante diluvium deprehenduntur Gen. VII, 2. & Cap. VIII, 20. post diluvium repetitur. De potibus Chry- sostomus & Theophylactus asserunt, nihil esse scri- ptum in lege, ideoque hic quod de illis scriptum est, vel ad Sacerdotes refert, qui ministraturi in taber- naculo à vino abstinebant, vel ad Nazaræos, qui votum faciebant de abstinentia. Sed revera licet & Sacerdotibus & Nazaræis abstinendum fuerit à vi- no, vinum tamen immundum non fiebat: Loquitur vero Apostolus de discrimine πομάτων, mundorum utique ab immundis. Itaque non opus est, ut huc con- fugiamus. Per se vero patet multis modis potum et- iam apud Israelites immundum fieri potuisse, quam- vis illi omnes in sacris non sint expositi. Omnibus enim istis modis, quibus res aliæ immundæ fieri po- terant, etiam potus suo modo immunditiem contra- here potuit. Generalis regula extat Lev. XI, 32. ubi immundum jubetur haberi, quicquid ab immundo contactum est, unde facile quam plurima πομάτων

discrimina nasci potuerunt. Alterum sunt διάφοροι βαπτισμοὶ: Obscurius vertit vetus Interpres varia baptismata. Nam in genere hic diversæ lotiones Lev. XI. & XV. & Num. XIX. præceptæ, de quibus & Matth. XXIII, 25. & Marci VII, 3. 4. Imo & ba- ptismus in more erat Ebræorum, quoties aliquis ab idololatria ad Judaismum accederet. Tertium caput positum est in δικαιώμασι σαρκὸς. Beza notat, se in Veteri codice reperisse δικαιώματα, ita, ut ad se- quentia istud pertineat, & respiciat tanquam tertium δῶρα καὶ θυσίας, de quibus v. 9. Sed non opus est de- serere receptam lectionem. Postquam enim Aposto- lus differentias cibi & potus, itemque lotionum com- memorâsset, adjicit recte δικαιώματα σαρκὸς tan- quam generale, quod reliquas constitutiones Mosaicas donis & sacrificiis adjectas complectitur: q. d. καὶ δι- καιώμασι σαρκὸς ἄλλοις. Sic enim nomen δικαίωμα- τῶ jam supra v. 8. usurpatum est. Vulgatus red- dit justitiis carnis, Erasmus justificationibus carnis. Plane autem recedit à textu Castellio, cum vertit institutis humanis. Neque enim de ἐντάλμασιν ἀν- θρώπων hic loquitur, de quibus Matth. XVIII. 9. sed de iis, quæ divina sanctione ad antiquum fœdus pertinuerunt, & officio παραβολῆς v. 9. fungi docue- runt. Neque enim quia διορθώσεως mentio fit, propter- ea instituta ista tanquam commentitia reprobantur. Non enim h. l. διόρθωσις hic accipienda est, ut oppo- natur iis, quæ legi divinæ repugnant, & revocanda sunt ad regulam. Itaque vocabulum σαρκὸς non no- tat causam Efficientem, sed subjectum, hoc est, id, circa quod ista δικαιώματα per se considerata ma- xima ex parte occupabantur. Quanquam enim in prædicamento relationis considerata, hoc est, quate- nus erant typus & παραϐολὴ τῶν μελλόντων ἀγα- θῶν, ipsam etiam attigerint animam, & perfectioni Spiritus suam contulerint operam, tamen in prædi- camento actionis ad σάρκα terminabantur. Justifi- cationum, inquit B. Hunnius, meminit Mosaica- rum, non tantum quatenus à Levitica immunditie rursum mundati reputabantur, sed etiam, quatenus mediantibus sacrificiis dicebantur expiari coram Domino, non quidem propter meritum atque dignita- tem eorum sacrificiorum, sed quia victimæ illa digi- tum intendebant ad Christum, sacrificio suo vere pro- pitiatorio justificantem fideles. Quod igitur Aposto- lus hic affirmat, hasce victimas invalidas extitisse ad conscientiæ & cordis purificationem: Sciendum est, loqui illum de sacrificiis, prout in sese consideran- tur. Nam alias ratione finis & spiritualis significa- tionis suo effectu certe non caruerunt, quoniam dedu- cebant populum ad considerationem futurorum bono- rum in Christo. Tempus autem διορθώσεως quibus- dam dicitur ratione correctionis; non tam rituum illorum Leviticorum, qui non correcti, sed sublati sunt, quam ratione correctionis eorum, quæ per peccatum corrupta sunt: quia ideo venit Christus, ut opera diaboli destrueret, 1. Joh. III, 8. & omnia repararet, atque integritati pristinæ restitueret. B. Hunnius: Tempus correctionis, ubi figuræ antiquan- dæ essent, substituta rei veritate atque substantia, id est, Christo exhibito, carne manifestato, passo & ex- altato. Estius observat Græcam dictionem διόρθω- σιν proprie significare rectificationem; quod vero Latini correctionem dicunt, Græcis usitatius ἐπα- νόρθωσιν appellari: Secundum B. Dorscheum simpli- cissime καιρὸς διορθώσεως est tempus impletionis & meliorationis, quatenus scilicet ex umbrarum atque typorum statu ad statum complementi & antitypi res perducitur. Διορθῶσαι apud LXX. nunc respondet Radici ישר Jer. VII, 2. & 4. nunc radici כון Es. XVI, 5. & LXI, 7. Est itaq; tempus N. T. quo apparente um- bræ cessare, & totus cultus divinus rectissime perfe- ctissimeque constitui debuit. Non enim διόρθωσιν tan- tum requirunt, quæ mala sunt, sed quæ minus bona & perfecta: Etiam corrigit, qui, quæ desunt, addit, Tit. I, 5. Budæus existimat hoc vocabulo proprie signi- ficari quandam erectionem, cum quis lapsabundus aliquid apprehendit, quo se possit erigere. Talem au- tem fuisse Christum, sine quo nutarunt Judæi. At hic Apostolo non tam de διορθώσει Judæorum, quam ipsius fœderis antiqui sermo est. In voce ἐπικείμενα em- phasin notat Theophylactus: Cum esset autem lex grave admodum jugum, jure imposita dixit, sicut & in Apostolorum actis est scriptum: Quid tentatis imponere jugum discipulis, quod neque Patres vestri portaverunt?

## 9:11
Vers. 11. Χριστὸς δὲ παραγενόμενος.] That is, Christ after he arrived; after he manifested himself. The word is frequent in Luke in the Gospel and in the Acts.

Now it is explained what that διόρθωσις is which we have from Christ, and how those things which were prefigured there in the entry of the Priests into the holy place have been fulfilled in Christ the High Priest of the N.T. The Vulgate has 'assistens' (standing by): but the Greek properly signifies 'accedens' (approaching), or when he had approached or arrived, as Estius admits with Hentenius. For it is, he says, an Aorist having the signification of the Preterite: So that the sense may be: Christ, by his arrival and incarnation, became High Priest. For he did not, like others, first become a High Priest after being born and grown and instructed in disciplines, but to arrive, that is, to be incarnate, was for him to become High Priest. Thus generally the Greek commentators. The Syriac reading agrees with the Greek. Therefore, this is signified, which is said in the following chapter in other words: Therefore, coming into the world, he says: Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me. What follows also agrees with this sense.

High Priest of the good things to come.] To obtain for us internal righteousness, the Holy Spirit, and eternal life. See below XI, where you likewise have 'of the good things to come.' Therefore the Syrian adds, 'which he made,' that is, which he performed for us.

How those gifts of the High Priest of the New Testament are called μέλλοντα, our blessed Dorsheus explains thus: The priest of the Old Testament had his gifts, the anointed one of the New Testament likewise. But those gifts are called μέλλοντα; above v. 9, 'gifts and sacrifices' are attributed to the Priest, which the Priest offered immediately. But because they had a shadow of the good things to come, and indeed a confirmatory and sealing shadow, not an idle one, therefore they also led mediately to the good things to come. But the Priest of the New Testament has the good things to come themselves immediately without shadows and types. They are called good things to come, however, not so much because they were future, and were regarded as future under the Old Testament, but primarily because they are the best, most perfect, and of themselves effect that which our salvation requires. For thus μέλλων in the Holy Scriptures is often taken for the best, most perfect, most sufficient, invisible, and heavenly. In this way the 'world to come' is spoken of above in Chapter II, 5, and C. VI, 5, the 'age to come,' which already is; but it is invisible to us, heavenly and most perfect, Eph. I, 21, where it is opposed to 'this age,' that is, the transient and perishing one. Just as also the 'life to come' is not so much called so because it is future, but because it is better, nay, the best and most perfect, and is still hidden with Christ in God, Coloss. III, 4. Thus also Isaac is said to have blessed Jacob 'concerning things to come' Heb. XI, 20, because he gave him power over the chief goods, that is, the primacy in the priesthood and kingdom, as it is called Gen. XLIX, 3. Thus also C. XIII, 14, the 'city to come and abiding' is that very heavenly Jerusalem, of which C. XII, 22, which is called 'to come,' both because it is to come to us through faith, and truly primarily because it is the best and most perfect, invisible and heavenly. Simpler is the explanation of blessed Hunnius and blessed Balduinus, that the goods of the other age, which Christ acquired for us and distributes in the word, are designated: which will be revealed to us in the future, as Theophylact has it, because, as blessed Gerhard says, he appeared for this reason, that he might acquire for us eternal and heavenly goods, which we shall possess in eternal life. Whether the word μέλλων formally signifies the best and most perfect is doubtful, even if those future things are the best and most perfect. If the passage C. X, 1 is compared, where the 'good things to come' are opposed to the Levitical shadows, the High Priest can be called the High Priest of future goods, because the High Priest of the New Testament is occupied not with shadows, as the Aaronic ones were, but with things that were truly good and then still future. To which those Hunnian points seem to look: he also contends regarding the goods of both priesthoods, that formerly the High Priests handled a shadow; but Christ is the High Priest of future goods, not handling shadows, but the prefigured truth of them, while by assuming flesh, and immolating himself in the flesh, he acquired the future eternal goods stored up in the heavens.

Through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is, not of this creation.] Wishing to say that Christ entered into the highest heaven through sufferings and death, in order to pursue more closely the similarity begun with the legal Priest, he wished to say that he entered through his body and through his blood: because 'body' can rightly be put metonymically for the pains of the body, and it is common to all nations to take 'blood' for death, for the reason that death follows from a copious shedding of blood. Truly he did not express 'body' by its own word, but by a certain mystical circumlocution apt for pursuing, as I said, the similarity. It is the custom of the Hebrews to call the body סוּכָּה, whence the Pythagoreans also drew it, as we said at Sap. IX, 15, and 2 Cor. V, 14. Then indeed Christ's body, because of the indwelling divine power, is called a temple, John II, 21. But this body is said not to be 'made with hands,' and he explains what he signifies by that word by adding, i.e., 'of this creation,' understanding by creation the order established in nature, which is בְּרִיאָה to the Hebrews. For that body was conceived in a supernatural way. He well usurped in this sense that 'not made with hands,' because it is customary for the Hebrews by a certain abuse of language to call everything that is done by a natural mode 'made with hands.' Thus also below IX, 24, and Mark XIV, 58, Acts VII, 58, XVII, 24, Eph. II, 11, 2 Cor. V, 1. The Prophets also often call idols 'made with hands,' because there is nothing divine in them. It is to be noted, however, that often the same thing of the Old Testament is referred to several meanings: as the outer tent to signify the starry heaven and its effects, to signify the whole legal cult, to signify the body of Christ, because of the diverse accidents of that tent, which could conveniently be referred here and there.

The same explanation of the greater and more perfect tabernacle concerning the body of Christ has been followed also by not a few others along with Primasius, Theophylact, and Haymo, namely Ribera, Piscator, Capellus, and blessed Gerhard. B. Dorscheus; but because the analogy and correspondence of the type and antitype demand that, just as the high priest truly entered with soul and body through the court into the holy place, and from there from the holy place into the holy of holies; so Christ, the High Priest of the New Testament, insofar as He is our God-man Priest, entered through the court into the holy place, and finally into the inner sanctuary: where, therefore, it does not appear how the entry of Christ the High Priest, after He arrived, can be explained as the very advent of the Son of God into the flesh, and how furthermore He entered from the tabernacle of His flesh or body into heaven itself, since He brought His very body into heaven, whereas the outer tabernacle in the type could not be brought into the inner one, nor did it contribute to the constitution of the Priest, but is only the way through which He Himself entered into the holy of holies. However, therefore, the body of a man may otherwise be called a tabernacle with respect to the soul dwelling in the body as in a tabernacle, yet this does not fit the body of Christ here, insofar as it is distinguished from His soul; for the Son of God did not come into the flesh by assuming only a body, but when He was made man, consisting of a true soul and a true body, and it is one thing to enter into glory through the sufferings of the body, that is, with the sufferings intervening, and quite another to proceed through the tabernacle of the body, as if it were some intermediate πῆ, or something analogous to an intermediate place into the inner tabernacle itself. Nor does it appear how the outer and inner holy place can be conveniently spoken of regarding the body of Christ and heaven, since the body of Christ itself penetrated into heaven. Nor, when it is said that Christ entered through His own blood, is the blood of Christ thereby constituted as the outer tabernacle through which Christ entered into the inner sanctuary or into heaven. But it is hinted, as Estius admits, that He entered by His shed blood. And that metonymy is foreign here, by which the body is said to be taken for the pains of the body. For thus it would have to be said that Christ entered into heaven through the pains of the body as an outer tabernacle. But where is the analogy of the type and antitype here? Add that, without doubt, the holy of holies was more excellent than the holy place through which the High Priest entered into the holy of holies. But that heaven, which is the holy of holies, is a more excellent tabernacle than the very body of the Son of God, in which the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily (Col. 2:9), which was assumed into the hypostasis of the Son of God, and with Him constitutes one subsistent being, which has been raised into the fellowship of the most holy Trinity, which has been made co-throned with the divine nature, which has been exalted to the right hand of the Majesty on high, one would not easily say; or if for that reason it must be said at all, that the heaven of infinite glory is to be understood, it will have to be explained how those things agree: Christ entered through the tabernacle of human nature into the heaven of infinite glory? For Christ entered or according to the divine, or according to the human nature. Not according to the divine nature, for in respect of the same he neither ascended into heaven, nor sat down at the right hand of God. But if according to the human nature: Therefore that which entered is the very Human nature of Christ. In what way then shall it be said that the Human nature of Christ entered through the outer tabernacle, that is, through the Human nature, into the inner, that is, into the heaven of infinite glory? There remains therefore, according to that explanation, this inconsistency entirely, and so to avoid it, it seems rather to be asserted that through the outer tabernacle, the Church militant, or the kingdom of grace, Christ entered into the Church triumphant, into the kingdom of glory, and the eternal tabernacles, Luke 16:9. Wherefore it is better, with Cajetan, to understand the Church by the greater and more perfect tabernacle. For Christ the God-man, the High Priest, came through the atrium of the world into that tabernacle not made with hands, the Church; he was not only in the world, which was made through him, but he also came εἰς τὰ ἴδια into his own, John 1:10, 11, and ἐσκήνωσεν and dwelt, as in a tabernacle among his own, v. 14. And through the tabernacle of the Church he entered into the holy of holies, having left his own (as regards his bodily visible presence), he went to prepare a seat for them, John 14:2, 28; 15:16, 28, and penetrated into heaven itself. For the outer tabernacle was an image and figure of the Church, just as the inner was a figure of heaven. The Church is a greater tabernacle than that Mosaic one, extending itself everywhere through the world; it is more perfect, because it is furnished with divine gifts; the tabernacle of the Church is not made with hands, like that of Bezalel, it is not of this worldly condition: it was built by Christ through the Spirit. upon the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, Matt. 16:16; Eph. 2:20. Theophylact says this about the Mosaic tabernacle: There were three places of the tabernacle: The outer was destined for all, as for the Jews, so also for the Gentiles; next, a veil was stretched out in the second place, which the Priests entered daily to attend to sacrifices and divine worship. This place is called the holy, which would present the form of the old Testament, because there the immolations were performed. There was also the holy of holies, the inner place, which we now call the holy of holies, and they prefigured the mystery. Which fit very well (1) the world, in which are Jews and Gentiles, (2) the Church, in which is the candlestick together with the lamps, that is, the Sun of righteousness, who through the Apostles of the word illuminates those sitting in darkness: And the table of the banquet of the grace of God instructed in the Gospel, Isa. 35. Luke 14, the showbread, by which Christ the bread of life is shadowed forth, feeding and nourishing us to eternal life, as the blessed Hunnius explains this: According to the blessed Osiander, the candlestick with seven lamps signified the Ministers of the Church, shining with the Word of truth and the innocence of life, and showing the way to the heavenly fatherland, with Christ as leader, who is the true light. The table designated the ministry of the Word, in which the bread of life, Christ, revealed and proposed to the world by the work of the twelve Apostles, is set forth. But where are those antitypes found, if not in the Church? (3) Heaven, which is prefigured by the sanctuary, in which is the mercy seat, the throne of grace, the ark of the covenant, Christ, consisting of a twofold nature, as once the ark of wood and gold, and the Cherubim or Angels, and also the golden censer, shadowing forth the most pleasing odor of the perpetual intercession of Christ, according to the same interpreter. Ambrose, Anselm, the ordinary interlinear Gloss, Thomas, Lyranus understand heaven by the greater tabernacle from Isa. 33:20, cf. Luke 16:9, Rev. 21:3. Nor does the blessed Hunnius deny this, judging that by the holy of holies the most holy part of the heavenly tabernacle, the throne of the right hand and of the divine Majesty, is designated. But since the Apostle himself explains the holy of holies in heaven, insofar as it is distinguished from that tabernacle through which he entered into heaven, the former explanation is to be preferred. The blessed Glassius indeed thinks that the particle διὰ can be taken either ἐνυπαρκτικῶς, so that it refers to the good things to come in the heavenly tabernacle, or αἰτιολογικῶς, so that it is said that Christ approached on account of the greater and more perfect tabernacle (heaven), namely, that he might enter into it. But in that way there will be no application of the former tabernacle, and the particle διὰ in v. 12, if it is likewise rendered 'on account of', the sense will be less suitable, as if Christ entered into the holy places on account of his own blood. Therefore the blessed Gerhard rightly says: Because the Apostle says that Christ entered into the holy places, that is, into heaven, through this greater and more perfect tabernacle. Therefore, by that greater tabernacle, something else is necessarily understood than heaven. And Wilhelm Estius rightly observed: Those words 'through the greater and more perfect tabernacle' ought not to be connected to the preceding, but to the following, so that the sentence is completed in the word 'he entered' placed below. Which latter construction is more accepted, and the same is more congruent to the text because of the following particle 'neither by the blood etc.', which connects the following to the preceding. Which is favored by what the blessed Dorscheus has on chapter 9, v. 8. Which two kingdoms (of grace and glory) the arrangement of the old sanctuary also shadowed forth. For thus access was opened through the outer into the inner sanctuary. Thus one must pass through the kingdom of grace to the kingdom of glory. The former is the way, the latter is the destination. What could be more fitting than this: It is said, however, that he entered through the assumed Human nature as through a tabernacle into the very holy of holies by reason of the offering. For just as the High Priest, about to enter the holy of holies, walked through the first tabernacle that had been trodden: so Christ, about to enter the holy of holies, in a way trod upon the assumed Human nature, when he delivered it to be tortured by the hands of the wicked. Or these: We say that through the first tabernacle, that is, His human nature trampled and exposed to sufferings, our Priest has entered into the inner, that is, into His glory: yet the first tabernacle is of a different state, when Christ entered through it, than the inner and more sublime one into which He entered. Nor indeed, just as the High Priest of the Old Testament, when he entered through the first tabernacle into the inner, abandoned the former: so also our Priest laid aside His tabernacle, through which He entered. Nay, rather, He entered through the tabernacle in such a way that even when He had entered the tabernacle, He also placed that very tabernacle into the inner and more sublime tabernacle. Catharinus's exposition, that the Virgin Mother of God is that tabernacle, is clearly foreign to the mind of the Apostle and does not require refutation. The things which Grotius says about the outer tent to signify the starry heaven and its effect, as also to signify the legal worship, are destitute of scriptural examples.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Χριστὸς δὲ παραγενόμενος.] Id est, Christus post- quam advenit; postquam se patefecit. Vox est frequens Lu- cæ in Evangelio & in Actis.

Jam explicatur, quænam illa διόρθωσις sit, quam à Christo habemus, & quomodo in Christo Ponti- fice N. T. impleta sint, quæ ibi figurata fuere in ingressu Sacerdotum in sanctum. Vulgatus habet assistens: Græcum autem proprie significat ac- cedens, vel cum accessisset sive advenisset, fatente Estio cum Hentenio. Est enim, inquit, Aoristus ha- bens significationem Præteriti: Ut sensus sit: Chri- stus adventu & incarnatione sua factus Pontifex. Non enim aliorum more prius natus & adultus & disciplinis instructus Pontifex factus est, sed advenire, id est, incarnari, fuit ei Pontificem fieri. Ita fere Græ- ci commentatores. Græca lectioni Syriaca consonat. Igitur hoc significatur, quod sequenti capite dicitur aliis verbis: Ideo mundum ingrediens dicit: Hostiam & oblationem noluisti, corpus autem aptasti mihi. Conveniunt etiam huic sensui, quæ sequuntur.

Ἀρχιερεὺς τῶν μελλόντων ἀγαθῶν.] Ad obtinendam nobis justitiam interiorem, Spiritum S. & vitam æternam. Vide infra XI. ubi itidem habes τῶν μελλόντων ἀγαθῶν. Ideo Syrus addit, quæ fecit, id est, quæ nobis præstitit.

Dona illa Pontificis Novi Testamenti quomo- do μέλλοντα dicantur, ita explicat B. Dorsheus no- ster: Sacerdos Veteris Testamenti sua dona habuit, unctus Novi Test. pariter. Vocantur autem illa dona μέλλοντα; supra v. 9. tribuuntur Sacerdoti δῶρα, καὶ θυσίαι, quæ immediate Sacerdos offerebat. Sed quia umbram habebant τῶν μελλόντων ἀγαθῶν, & qui- dem umbram confirmativam & obsignativam, non otiosam, ideo mediate ad μέλλοντα ἀγαθὰ etiam de- ducebant. Sacerdos autem Novi Test. habet ipsa μέλ- λοντα ἀγαθὰ immediate sine umbris & typis. Dicun- tur autem μέλλοντα ἀγαθὰ, non tam quia futura erant, & ut futura sub V. T. respiciebantur, sed impri- mis, quia optima, perfectissima, & per se id efficientia, quod salus nostra requirit. Sic enim μέλλων in sacris literis sæpius sumitur pro optimo, perfectissimo, suffi- cientissimo, invisibili, cælesti. Hoc modo μέλλουσα οἰ- κουμένη supra Cap. II, 5. dicitur, & C. VI, 5. μέλλων αἰὼν, qui jam est; invisibilis autem nobis est, cælestis & perfectissimus, Eph. I, 21. ubi opponitur τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, hoc est, caduco & perituro. Quemadmodum & ζωὴ μέλλουσα non tam dicitur, quia futura est, sed quia melior est, imo optima & perfectissima, & adhuc cum Christo in Deo abscondita, Coloss. III, 4. Sic & Isaac dicitur benedixisse Jacob περὶ μελλόν- των Ebr. XI, 20. quia præcipuorum bonorum, hoc est primatus in sacerdotio & regno, uti appellatur Gen. XLIX, 3. ipsi potestatem dedit. Sic & C. XIII, 14. μέλλουσα πόλις καὶ μένουσα, est illa ipsa cælestis Hie- rosolyma, de qua C. XII, 22. quæ μέλλουσα dicitur, tum quia nobis per fidem obventura est, tum vero impri- mis, quia optima est & perfectissima, invisibilis & cæ- lestis. Simplicior est B. Hunnii & B. Balduini ex- plicatio, alterius seculi bona, quæ nobis acquisi- vit, & in verbo distribuit Christus, designari: quæ in futurum nobis revelabuntur, ut habet Theophyl. quia B. Gerhardo dicente, ideo apparuit, ut nobis æterna ac cælestia bona acquireret, quæ in æterna vi- ta possidebimus. An formaliter vox μέλλων signi- ficet optimum & perfectissimum, dubium est, etsi futura illa optima sint, & perfectissima. Si con- feratur locus C. X, 1. ubi τὰ μέλλοντα ἀγαθὰ op- ponuntur umbris Leviticis, Pontifex bonorum futurorum dici poterit, quod non circa umbras, ut Aaronici, sed circa vere bona tum adhuc futu- ra occupetur Pontifex N. T. Quo respicere vi- dentur illa Hunniana: Bona quoque utriusque Sacer- dotii contendit, quod olim Pontifices umbram tracta- rint; Christus autem sit futurorum bonorum Ponti- fex non tractans umbras, sed earum præfiguratam ve- ritatem, dum carne assumendo, & seipsum carne immo- lando, futura æterna bona in cælis reposita acquisivit.

Διὰ τῆς μείζονος καὶ τελειοτέρας σκηνῆς, ὀ χειροποιήτε, του τέστιν ὀ ταύτης τῆς κτίσεως.] Volens dicere Christum ingres- sum esse in summum cælum per passiones & mortem, ut ma- gis persequeretur cœptam cum Sacerdote legali similitudi- nem, dicere voluit intrasfe eum per corpus suum & per san- guinem suum: quia corpus μετωνυμικῶς recte poni poterit pro doloribus corporis, & sanguinem pro morte sumere frequens est omnibus gentibus, ideo quod ex copiosa sanguinis effu- sione mors sequatur. Verum corpus non sua voce expressit, sed circumloquutione quadam mystica apta ad persequen- dam, ut dixi, similitudinem. Ebræorum mos est, corpus vo- care סוּכָּה, unde id & Pythagorici hausere, ut diximus ad Sap. IX, 15. & 2. Cor. V, 14. Tum vero Christi corpus ob in- habitantem vim divinam, templum dicitur Joh. II, 21. Dicitur autem hoc corpus non esse χειροποίητον, & quid ea voce signi- ficet exponit addens, i. e. hujus creationis per creationem in- telligens constitutum in natura ordinem, qui בְּרִיאָה Ebræis. Fuit enim corpus illud conceptum supernaturali mo- do. Bene autem usurpavit hoc sensu illud ὀ χειροποίητον, quia solet Ebræis per abusionem quandam χειροποίητον dici omne id, quod fit per modum naturalem. Sic & infra IX, 24. & Marc. XIV, 58. Act. VII, 58. XVII, 24. Eph. II, 11. 2. Cor. V, 1. Idola quoque χειροποίητα sæpe vocant Prophetæ, quia nihil est in illis divini. Notandum autem sæpe eandem rem V. T. ad plu- res significatus referri: ut tentorium exterius ad significan- dum cælum astriferum, ejusque effectus, ad significandum totum cultum legalem, ad significandum corpus Christi, pro- pter diversa tentorii illius accidentia, quæ commode & huc & illuc referri poterant.

Eandem explicationem majoris & perfectioris tabernaculi de corpore Christi sequuti etiam alii non pauci cum Primasio, Theophylacto & Haymone sunt Ribera, Piscator, Capellus, B. Gerh. B.
