Dorscheus; sed quia analogia & convenientia typi & antitypi poscit, ut quemadmodum summus Sacerdos anima & corpore revera ingressus est per atrium in sanctum, & exinde è sancto in sanctum sanctorum; Ita Chri- stus Pontifex N. T. prout θεάνθρωπος Sacerdos noster est, ingressus sit per atrium in sanctum, & deniq; in adytum: Ubi proinde non apparet, quo- modo ingressus Christi Pontificis, postquam ad- venit, explicari possit de adventu ipsomet Filii Dei in carnem, & quomodo porro è tabernaculo car- nis vel corporis sui ingressus sit in cælum ipsum, quum ipsum corpus suum in cælum attulerit, ta- bernaculum autem exterius in typo in interius in- ferri nequiverit, neq; ad constitutionem Sacerdotis fecerit, sed tantum via sit, per quam ingressus ipse est in sanctum sanctorum. Utut ergo corpus homi- nis alias vocetur tabernaculum respectu animæ habitantis in corpore ceu tabernaculo, non tamen id hic convenit corpori Christi, qua animæ ejus contradistinguitur, non enim Filius Dei in carnem venit, corpus solum assumendo, sed cum homo factus est, vera anima & vero corpore constans, & longe aliud est per passiones corporis, id est, inter- venientibus passionibus, ingredi in gloriam, aliud vero per corporis tabernaculum incedere, ceu in- termedium quoddam πῆ, seu analogum quid in- termedio loco in ipsum interius tabernaculum. Nec apparet, quomodo exterius, & interius san- ctum de corpore Christi & cælo commode dicantur: quum corpus ipsummet Christi in cælum pene- trârit. Neque, cum dicitur per sanguinem proprium ingressum esse Christum, constituitur eo ipso sanguis Christi tabernaculum exterius, per quod ingressus Christus est in interius adytum vel in cælum. Sed innuitur, fatente Estio, sanguine suo fuso ingressum esse. Et aliena est hic illa μετωνυμία, qua corpus dicitur sumi pro doloribus corporis. Sic enim di- cendum Christum ingressum esse per dolores cor- poris tanquam tabernaculum exterius in cælum. Ubi vero hic analogia typi & antitypi? Adde, quod sine dubio sanctum sanctorum præstantius fuerit sancto, per quod Pontifex ingressus est in sanctum sanctorum. At cælum, quod est sanctum sancto- rum, præstantius esse tabernaculum, quam ipsum- met corpus Filii Dei, in quo tota plenitudo divini- tatis habitat σωματικῶς, Col. II, 9. quod assumptum est in hypostasin Filii Dei, & cum eo constituit unum ὑφισάμενον, quod in consortium sacrosan- ctæ Trinitatis evectum est, quod σύνθρονον factum est divinæ naturæ, quod exaltatum est ad dex- tram Majestatis in excelsis, non facile quis dixe- rit, aut si ideo omnino id dicendum, quod cæ- lum infinitæ gloriæ intelligendum, explicandum erit, quomodo illa conveniant, Christus ingressus est per tabernaculum humanæ naturæ in cælum infinitæ gloriæ? Christus enim ingressus est vel secundum divinam, vel secundum humanam natu- ram. Non secundum divinam naturam, nam quoad eandem nec in coelum ascendit, nec ad dextram Dei consedit. Si autem secundum humanam naturam: Ergo quod ingressum est, est ipsa Humana Christi natura. Quo pacto ergo dicetur, Humanam Chri- sti naturam per tabernaculum exterius, hoc est, per Humanam naturam ingressam esse in interius, hoc est, in coelum infinitae gloriae? Manet ergo juxta illam explicationem omnino ista inconvenientia, adeoque ad eam declinandam videtur id potius asserendum, quod per exterius tabernaculum Ec- clesiam militantem, vel regnum gratiae ingressus sit Christus in Ecclesiam triumphantem, in regnum gloriae, & aeterna tabernacula, Luc. XVI, 9. Qua- propter praestat, cum Cajetano per tabernaculum majus & perfectius intelligere Ecclesiam. Venit enim Christus θεάνθρωπος Pontifex per atrium mundi in tabernaculum illud non manu factum, Ecclesiam; non in mundo tantum erat, qui per ipsum factus est, sed etiam εἰς τὰ ἴδια in propria ve- nit, Joh. I, 10. 11. & ἐσκήνωσεν & habitavit, velut in ta- bernaculo inter suos, v. 14. Et per Ecclesiae tabernacu- lum ingressus est in sanctum sanctorum, relictis suis, (quod ad corporalem visibilem praesentiam) ivit sedem illis paraturus, Joh. XIV, 2. 28. c. XV, 16. 28. & in coelum ipsum penetravit. Imago enim & figura Ecclesiae fuit tabernaculum exterius, quemadmo- dum interius figura coeli. Majus est tabernaculum Ecclesia prae illo Mosaico, passim sese extendens per orbem; perfectius est, quia donis divinis in- structum; non manufactum tabernaculum Eccle- siae, ut illud Bezaleelis, non est istius mundanae conditionis: A Christo exstructum est per Spir. S. super fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolo- rum, Matth. XVI, 16. Eph. II, 20. De tabernaculo Mosaico ita Theophylactus: Tria erant tabernacu- li loca: Exterior quidem omnibus, ut Judaeis, ita & gentilibus destinatus; deinceps & velum secundo in lo- co obtendebatur, quod Sacerdotes ingressi sacrificiis & divino cultui quotidie intendebant. Hic locus san- cta appellatur, quae formam veteris praeferrent Testa- menti, quia ibi immolationes perficerentur. Erat & sancta, interior locus, quae nos sanctorum sancta nunc dicimus, & praefigurabant mysterium. Quae optime conveniunt (1.) mundo, in quo Judaei & gentiles, (2.) Ecclesiae, in qua candelabrum una cum lucernis, id est, Sol justitiae, qui per Apostolos verbi illuminat sedentes in tenebris: Et mensa convivii gratiae Dei in Evangelio instructi, Esa. XXXV. Luc. XIV. panes propositionis, quibus Christus panis vitae adumbratus pascens & alens nos ad vitam aeter- nam, ut haec explicat B. Hunnius: Juxta B. Osian- drum Candelabrum cum septem lampadibus significa- bat Ministros Ecclesiae, lucentes Verbo veritatis, & vi- tae innocentia, & ostendentes viam ad caelestem pa- triam, duce Christo, qui est vera lux. Mensa designa- bat ministerium Verbi, in quo proponitur panis vitae, Christus, opera duodecim Apostolorum mundo reve- latus & propositus. Ubi vero illa antitypa inve- niuntur, nisi in Ecclesia? (3.) Caelo, quod praefigu- ratum est per sanctuarium, in quo propitiatori- um, thronus gratiae, arca foederis Christus, gemi- na natura constans, ut olim arca ex ligno & auro, & Cherubim seu Angeli, nec non aureum thuri- bulum gratissimum odorem perpetuae interces- sionis Christi adumbrans, eodem interprete. Am- brosius, Anselmus, Glossa ordinaria interlin. Tho- mas, Lyranus per tabernaculum majus intelligunt caelum ex Esa. XXXIII, 20. conf. Luc. XVI, 9. Apoc. XXI, 3. Nec abnuit B. Hunnius, per sanctum san- ctorum deinde sanctissimam caelestis tabernaculi partem, thronum dextrae & Majestatis divinae de- signatum censens. Sed quum Apostolus ipse san- ctum sanctorum in coelo explicet, quatenus illud a tabernaculo isto, per quod ingressus est in coe- lum, distinguitur, prior explicatio praeferenda. B. Glassius quidem putat, particulam διὰ posse ac- cipi vel ἐνυπαρκτικῶς, ut referatur ad bona futura in tabernaculo caelesti, v. αἰτιολογικῶς, ut dicatur ac- cessisse Christus propter majus & perfectius taber- naculum (coelum) nimirum, ut in illud ingredia- tur. Sed ita nulla erit applicatio prioris taberna- culi, & particula διὰ v. 12. si pariter reddatur pro- pter, sensus minus conveniet, quasi propter san- guinem proprium in sancta ingressus sit Christus. Ideo recte B. Gerhardus: Quia Apostolus dicit, Christum per hoc majus & perfectius tabernaculum introiisse in sancta, hoc est, in caelum. Ergo per ta- bernaculum illud majus necessario aliud quid intelli- gitur, quam caelum. Et observavit probe VVilhel- mus Estius: Verba illa per amplius & perfectius taber- naculum non praecedentibus annecti debere, sed se- quentibus, ut sententia compleatur in verbo introivit infra posito. Quae posterior constructio magis rece- pta est, eademque textui congruentior propter sequen- tem particulam neque per sanguinem &c. quae se- quentia praecedentibus copulat. Cui favent, quae B. Dorscheus habet ad cap. IX. v. 8. Quae duo regna (gratiae & gloriae) etiam adumbravit dispositio vete- ris sanctuarii. Sic enim per exterius in interius san- ctuarium patuit aditus. Sic per regnum gratiae ad regnum gloriae transcendum. Illud via est, hoc terminus. Quae concinniora sunt, quam haec: Dicitur autem per assumptam Humanam naturam ingressus esse tanquam per tabernaculum in ipsum sanctum sanctorum ratione oblationis. Sicut enim Pontifex sanctum sanctorum ingressurus per prius tabernaculum calcatum incessit: Sic Christus sanctum sanctorum ingressurus assumptam Humanam natu- ram quodammodo calcavit, cum manibus impiorum excarnificandam tradidit. Aut ista: Dicimus per prius tabernaculum, hoc est, Humanam suam natu- ram conculcatam & passionibus objectam introivisse Sacerdotem nostrum in interius, hoc est, in gloriam suam: Alterius tamen status prius tabernaculum est, cum Christus per illud introivit, quam interius & sublimius, in quod introivit. Neq; vero, quemadmo- dum Pontifex Veteris Testamenti, cum per prius ta- bernaculum in interius introivit, prius deseruit: Ita etiam Sacerdos noster suum tabernaculum, per quod ingressus est, deposuit. Imo potius ita per tabernacu- lum ingressus est, ut etiam cum tabernaculum ingres- sus fuerit, & illud in ipsum interius & sublimius ta- bernaculum collocaverit. Catharini expositio, quod Virgo Deipara tabernaculum illud sit, a mente Apo- stoli plane aliena, refutatione non indiget. Quae de tentorio exteriori ad significandum coelum astriforum ejusque effectum, ut & ad significan- dum cultum legalem Grotius, exemplis scriptu- rae destituuntur.

## 9:12
V. 12. Οὐδὲ δὶ αἵματος τράγων κὶ μόσχων. That which does not happen without something is said to be done through something. Thus the legal High Priest did not enter into the sanctuary, namely in the final entry, unless he carried with him the blood of goats for the people, and of calves for himself.

The Vulgate version must therefore be corrected, which has: Or of calves; which Estius likewise observed: The true reading is and of calves, which is not only that of the Greek and Syriac Codices, but is also in many MSS. and in the text of the Ambrosian Commentary. Furthermore, the matter demands that reading. For the High Priest brought the blood of both, both of the calf and of the goat, inside the veil into the holy of holies, as is commanded in Lev. XVI. But why does the Apostle use the plural of goats and of calves, Estius rightly notes that this was done, not because more were offered at the same time, but because in different years.

Διὰ δὲ τοῦ ἰδίου ἅιματος.] By his own blood shed, which blood is of the new covenant, Matt. XXVI, 28. Luke XXII, 20. Rom. III, 25. ch. V, 9. 1 Cor. X, 16. ch. XI, 25. Eph. I, 7. ch. II, 13. Col. I, 14. 20. here below XIII, 12. 20.

Εἰσῆλθεν ἐφάπαξ εἰς τὰ ἅγια.] Into the highest heaven Mark XVI, 19. Luke XXIV, 51. Acts I, 10. and ch. II, 34. Eph. IV, 10. Col. II, 1. Once, not in a year, but in all time until its end.

There is a threefold difference here between the Priesthood of Christ and that of Aaron. The Aaronic priest entered with the blood of goats and calves; Christ entered through his own blood: The former once a year, the latter once for all: The former into the holy places made by hands, the latter into the heavenly holy places. That ἐφάπαξ, once for all, is rightly observed by the blessed Dorscheus, as being also against the dogma of the Socinians, by which they maintain that Christ, before the beginning of his Prophetic office, was caught up into heaven and there, as it were, invested and inaugurated. To which they drag all the sayings that declare Christ went forth from the Father, came into the world, and whatever others there are. Likewise that in John III, 13, where Christ is said to be ἄνωθεν ἐν τῷ ὐρανῷ, which they render in the imperfect tense, so that it is, who was in heaven. And v. 31, where Christ is said to be ἄνωθεν ἐρχόμενος. For if Christ once entered into the holy of holies, that is, heaven, and that indeed through and after death; how can he be said to have entered into heaven through that translation at the beginning of his office, before he had solemnly begun it? Then also against the dogma of the Pontificians, by which they maintain that Christ, through transubstantiation, is set present in these lands on the altars as to his body indeed immediately, but as to his whole self concomitantly, and is as it were brought down from heaven, and when the act of communion is finished, when the species are consumed, he returns to heaven, and by a notable miracle is snatched away even from the closed mouth of the communicant. For thus he would have to be said to enter into the holy places, and indeed through his own blood (for he never returns without blood), not only once, but infinitely and as many times as he is brought onto the earthly altar through transubstantiation, and afterwards, when the species are consumed, returns to the heavens. The blessed one also notes that, just as the passage of the High Priest of the New Testament through the outer tabernacle was not a momentary act, but consisted of its own steps and progressions. For it lasted during the whole time of his emptying, during which he was in a fragile tabernacle, and covered by a skin as if it were servile. So also his entry into the holy of holies had, as it were, its own steps. For Christ entered into the holy of holies immediately after his death according to his soul, according to which he had the converted thief with him in Paradise and his kingdom, Luke XXIII, 42, 43, in which entry he undoubtedly showed his heavenly Father his body slaughtered and mortified lying in the sepulcher, as a most precious sacrifice; he also showed his blood, but scattered on the earth, on stones, on wood, on linens, and on other instruments of his passion, then clinging outside the vessels, but scattered from the altar of the cross toward the most holy place. Afterwards, also, with the ἀναζωοποιήσει (making alive) having taken place, and the subsequent ascension to the heavens, another step of the entry into the most holy place was completed, and thus the entry itself was consummated, when he had fully migrated into his glory according to both body and soul.

Αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν εὑράμενος.] Having found a way by which he might liberate us from sins forever, namely through his death and resurrection, Rom. IV, 25. In this sense we have λύτρωσιν in 1 Pet. I, 18. See what we said above II, 18, ch. VII, 19. He will now say the same thing, καθαρίζειν ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἔργων (to cleanse from dead works). And this liberation is perpetual, whereas that legal one was valid only for a year. For it had to be repeated.

It is not that a way by which he might liberate us henceforth was found, but the liberation itself has already been found, or rather redemption has been accomplished at a certain price, which the word λύτρωσις implies. For we have already been redeemed by his precious blood, 1 Pet. I, 19. But it is said to be found, partly because this counsel is to be credited to the hypostatic divine wisdom, because, as Chrysostom notes, it was a difficult matter, which no one else could have found; partly because that finding was not made without care and labor regarding the act of redemption itself and the execution of the counsel, just as things are wont to be sought with care that are lost, until they are found, Luke XIX, 10, ch. XV, 4 ff. Compare Is. XLIII, 24. Having found redemption, says the Apostle, that is, after he had acquired redemption for us, who were subject to the servitude of death on account of sins, by giving his blood as the price, as Estius rightly says. The blessed Dorscheus notes that by this participle εὑράμενος it is implied that Christ obtained this redemption both judicially and also laboriously. The verb εὑρίσκω is often taken for judicial conviction. Thus in Gal. II, 17, the Apostle says, if we seek to be justified through Christ, we ourselves will also be found sinners, that is, we will be convicted. Thus in 2 Cor. V, 3, the Apostle says that we ought to strive for spiritual garments, lest we be found naked, namely in the divine judgment, to which one must proceed after laying aside the slough of the body. Thus in Acts XIII, 28, Paul says that the Jews found no cause of death in Christ, namely judicially, or which could stand in judgment. And Chapter XXIII, 9, those who pronounced judgment on Paul in the Sanhedrin, on the part of the Pharisees, confess that they found nothing evil in him, namely of which he could be judicially convicted. Thus, therefore, and in this place, this λύτρωσις (redemption) is a judicial acquisition and such a redemption as has been established and proven in the rigorous divine judgment. The same word also denotes at times a laborious and painstaking attainment. Thus below, Chapter XII, 17, it is said of Esau that he sought with tears to have his father revoke the blessing which he had bestowed upon Jacob, yet he did not find it, that is, he did not attain it by those poured-out prayers and laborious tears. Thus, Rom. IV, 1, it is said that Abraham did not find anything by working according to the flesh. Thus, the εὕρησις (finding) of the parents of Christ was laborious, Luke II, 46, by which they found Christ in the temple. For it is said in v. 48, 'we have been seeking you in sorrow.' Thus also the εὕρησις (finding) of Christ, by which he obtained eternal life, is laborious and painstaking. For it contains within itself the 'pains of death,' Acts II, 24, the bearing of the curse of the law, Gal. III, 13, and it was accomplished through prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears, Heb. V, 7. Whence Christ complains that he was pressed and fatigued by servitude on account of sins and iniquities, Isa. XLIII, 11, which he bore in his body upon the tree, 1 Pet. II, 24. Schlichting, in order to evade the term redemption properly so called in this place, says that the word redemption is taken for expiation, which he says is a certain species of liberation, both on account of the effect of liberation itself, which is contained in expiation, and on account of a certain expenditure which is accustomed to be made in expiation. But in reality, redemption in this place restricts and limits the very condition and nature of expiation. For it is a redemption made according to the ἀντίλυτρον (ransom) provided, 1 Tim. II, 6. Therefore, not just a certain expenditure, but the whole and adequate and satisfactory [price] is contained in it. In the expiations of the Old Testament, whether anniversary or otherwise, certain expenditures had to be made. But those were valid only by the covenant of GOD for procuring a perishable and fleeting victim. These expenditures Peter, in his first epistle, Chapter I, 18, calls corruptible, namely, gold or silver or something of that kind. In this redemption, the Redeemer himself is the expenditure, so that he might satisfy, with infinite justice procured for us, 2 Cor. V, 21; 1 Cor. I, 30. Whence the expiation, which is contained in this redemption, is clearly of a different species than that which was in use in the Old Testament. Furthermore, Estius explains eternal redemption in two ways: either true and solid and always remaining, so that there is no need for another passion or redemption, or because it is an eternal inheritance, which he acquired for us. But the latter sense is undoubtedly more suitable, because the inheritance of redemption is contained in the very word λυτρώσεως, and is subsequently deduced further. A double distinction of the Aaronic priesthood is again hinted at here, as Estius notes: One, that Christ did not offer a sacrifice for his own sins, like the legal High Priest, but only for the sins of others. The other, that Christ's sacrifice availed for eternal redemption, whereas the Aaronic sacrifice did not. For that is left to be understood from the antithesis. And indeed, by that one sacrifice he obtained for us eternal redemption and liberation from sins, the devil, and hell. Whence Osiander concludes: If therefore Christ entered the holy of holies ONCE and found ETERNAL redemption? Why do the little sacrificers offer Christ so often in the Mass (as a propitiatory sacrifice)? And if Christ obtained eternal redemption for us, why do we tremble because of sins committed, if we believe in this Priest and redeemer? But it must be observed first of all that αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν is said here absolutely. Concerning which B. Dorscheus says beautifully: An αἰωνία expiation followed, valid for all years, beyond all years, before all years, vigorous and operative at all moments of time, precious beyond the moments of all time. For αἰωνία λύτρωσις is said absolutely, and therefore estimated and to be estimated as much from the part before as from the part after. Hence, in view of this eternal redemption, we were chosen in Christ πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμυ, Eph. I, 4. and grace is said to have been given to us in Christ πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων, 2. Tim. I, 9. and to that extent Christ, as a lamb without blemish and without spot, shedding his precious blood, is said to be προεγνωσμένος πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμε, 1. Petr. I, 20. And as that expiation or redemption performed by Christ is called eternal by reason of moral estimation, because it was held precious by God the Father from eternity to eternity; so it is also infinite, that is, infinitely estimated, or held to be infinitely precious, and thus not only equaling the infinite malice of the sins of the human race, so estimated by the infinite divine justice wounded by merit, but also surpassing it by its perfection, Rom. V, 20. And it is also most simple, admitting little composition with any other redemption, whatever it may be, or be imagined to be. For it is so estimated by God, that nothing can be added to it, just as nothing can be added to the infinite. It is also omnipotent, morally speaking, and in obtaining, because it can obtain everything from God the Father, Rom. VIII, 37.

Latin:

V. 12. Οὐδὲ δὶ αἵματος τράγων κὶ μόσχων.] Dicitur per ali- quid fieri id quod sine eo non fit. Sic summus Sacerdos legalis non intrabat in adytum, nempe postremo introitu, nisi se- cum ferens sanguinem hircinum pro populo, vitulinum pro se.

Corrigenda ergo versio Vulgata, quae habet: Aut vitulorum; quod observavit itidem Estius: Vera lectio & vitulorum, quae non modo Graecorum & Syrorum Codicum est, verum etiam in multis est MSS. atq; in textu Commentarii Ambrosiani. De- inde eam lectionem res postulat. Nam utriusq; san- guinem, & vituli & hirci, Pontifex inferebat intra velum in sancta sanctorum, ut praecipitur Lev. XVI. Cur autem plurali utatur Apostolus hircorum & vitulorum, id factum recte notat Estius, non quod plures offerrentur eodem tempore, sed quod di- versis annis.

Διὰ δὲ τοῦ ἰδίου ἅιματος.] Suo sanguine fuso, qui sanguis novi pacti, Matth. XXVI, 28. Luc. XXII, 20. Rom. III, 25. c. V, 9. 1. Cor. X, 16. c. XI, 25. Eph. I, 7. c. II, 13. Coloff. I, 14. 20. hic infra XIII, 12. 20.

Εἰσῆλθεν ἐφάπαξ εἰς τὰ ἅγια.] In summum coelum Marc. XVI, 19. Luc. XXIV, 51. Act. I, 10. u. c. II, 34. Eph. IV, 10. Col. II, 1. Semel non in anno, sed in omni ævo ad ejus finem.

Triplex hîc differentia Sacerdotii Christi & Aa- ronici. Aaronicus intrabat cum sanguine hircino & vitulino, Christus intravit per proprium sangui- nem: Ille semel in anno, hic semel omnino: Ille in sancta, manu facta, hic in sancta cœlestia. Illud ἐφάπαξ semel recte observat B. Dorscheus, tum contra dogma Socinianorum, quo statuunt, Christum ante aditum officii sui Prophetici raptum fuisse in cœ- lum, atq; ibi quasi investitum atq; inauguratum fuisse. Quorsum trahunt omnia dicta, quæ tradunt Christum à Patre exivisse, venisse in mundum, & quæ alia sunt. Item illud Joh. III, 13. ubi Christus dicitur ἄνωθεν ἐν τῷ ὐρανῷ quod illi imperfecto tempore reddunt, ut sit, qui erat in cælo. Et v. 31. ubi Christus dicitur ἄνωθεν ἐρχόμενος. Si enim Christus semel ingres- sus est in sanctum sanctorum, hoc est cælum, & id quidem per & pòst mortem; quomodo per istam trans- lationem in principio officii sui, antequam illud solen- niter inciperet, in cælum ingressus dici poterit: tum etiam contra Pontificiorum dogma, quo statuant Chri- stum per transsubstantiationem quoad corpus quidem immediate, concomitanter autem totum in altaribus in his terris præsentem sisti, & e cælo quasi adduci, finito vero communionis actu, cum species consumma- tæ sunt, ad cælum redire, & insigni miraculo commu- nicanti etiam ex ore clauso eripi. Sic enim non se- mel tantum, sed infinities & toties, quoties per trans- substantiationem in altare terrenum adducitur, & postea consumptis speciebus in cælos revertitur εἰς τὰ ἅγια εἰσέρχεσθαι, & quidem per proprium sangui- nem (nunquam enim sine sanguine revertitur) dicen- dus esset. Notat & illud ὁ Μακαρίτης, quod quem- admodum transitus Pontificis Novi Testamenti per tabernaculum exterius non fuit actus momentaneus, sed suis constans gradibus & progressibus. Duravit enim toto tempore exinanitionis, quo fuit in taberna- culo fragili, & pelle quasi servili tecto. Sic etiam in- gressus in sanctum sanctorum suos quasi habuit gra- dus. Nam Christus ingressus est in sanctum sancto- rum statim post mortem suam secundum animam, secundum quam in Paradiso & regno suo latronem conversum secum habuit, Luc. XXIII, 42. 43. quo in aditu procul dubio Patri suo cælesti ostendit corpus suum mactatum & mortificatum in sepulchro jacens, tanquam pretiosissimum sacrificium, ostendit etiam suum sanguinem, sed sparsum in terris, lapidibus, lignis linteis, & aliis passionis instrumentis extra vasa tum hærentem, sparsum vero ex ara crucis versus san- ctissimum. Postmodum etiam facta ἀναζωοποιήσει, & subsecuta ascensione ad cælos, alter gradus aditus in sanctissimum perfectus est, & ita ipse ingressus con- summatus, cum plene secundum corpus & animam in gloriam suam migrasset.

Αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν εὑράμενος.] Reperta ratione, qua nos in perpetuum liberaret à peccatis, per mortem nempe suam & resurrectionem, Rom. IV, 25. Hoc sensu λύτρωσιν habemus 1. Petr. I, 18. Vide quæ diximus supra II, 18. c. VII, 19. Idem jam nunc dicet, καθαρίζειν ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἔργων. Et est hæc li- beratio perpetua, cum illa legalis non nisi in annum value- rit. Erat enim repetenda.

Non ratio, qua nos deinceps liberaret, inventa est, sed inventa jam est ipsa liberatio, vel potius redemptio certo pretio facta, quod vox λύτρωσεως importat. Jam enim redempti sumus pretioso san- guine ejus, 1. Pet. I, 19. Inventa autem dicitur, par- tim quia sapientiæ divinæ hypostaticæ consilium hoc accepto ferendum, quia notante Chrysostomo res erat difficilis, quam nemo alius reperire potue- rit; partim quia non sine cura & labore inventio illa quoad actum ipsum redemptionis & exequu- tionem consilii facta, uti solent res cum cura quæ- ri, quæ deperditæ sunt, donec inveniantur, Luc. XIX, 10. c. XV, 4. seqq. Conf. Es. XLIII, 24. Inven- ta redemptione, inquit Apostolus, id est, postquam dato in pretium sanguine suo nobis, ob peccata servituti mortis obnoxios, acquisivisset redemptio- nem, ut recte Estius. B. Dorscheus notat hoc parti- cipio εὑράμενος innui, Christum tum judicialiter, tum etiam laboriose hanc redemptionem consequu- tum. Verbum εὑρίσκω pro judiciali convictione sæpe sumitur. Sic Gal. II, 17. dicit Apostolus, si per Chri- stum quæramus justificari, inveniemur & nos pecca- tores, hoc est, convincemur. Sic 2. Cor. V, 3. Apo- stolus dicit, nos studere debere spiritualibus indumen- tis, ne nudi inveniamur, scil. in judicio divino, ad quod depositis corporis exuviis proficiscendum est. Sic Act. XIII, 28. Paulus dicit, Judæos nullam cau- sam mortis in Christo invenisse scilicet judicialiter, vel quæ in judicio posset subsistere. Et Cap. XXIII, 9. qui in synedrio de Paulo pronunciarunt, ex parte Pharisæorum fatentur, nihil mali in ipso se invenisse, scil. cujus judicialiter convinci possit. Sic itaque & hoc loco hæc λύτρωσις est judiciale obtentum & re- demptio talis, quæ in rigoroso divino judicio evicta est & comprobata. Idem verbum notat etiam labo- riosam & operosam interdum consecutionem. Sic infra Cap. XII, 17. de Esavo dicitur, quod cum lacry- mis quæsiverit, ut parens revocaret, quam Jacobo impertitus fuerat benedictionem, nec tamen invene- rit, hoc est, fusis illis precibus & operosis lacrymis consequutus fuerit. Sic Rom. IV, 1. dicitur Abraha- mum operando non invenisse aliquid secundum car- nem. Sic laboriosa fuit εὕρησις parentum Christi, Luc. II, 46. qua Christum in templo repererunt. Dicitur enim v. 48. ὠδινώμενοι ἐζητῶμέν σε. Sic & Christi εὕρησις, qua obtinuit vitam æternam, operosa & labo- riosa est. Continet enim in se τὰς ὠδῖνας τοῦ θανάτου, Act. II, 24. portationem maledictionis legis, Gal. III, 13. factaque est per preces & supplicationes cum cla- more magno & lacrymis, Ebr. V, 7. Unde conqueri- tur Christus, se servitute pressum & fatigatum esse propter peccata & iniquitates, Esa. XLIII, 11. quas portavit in corpore suo super lignum, 1. Petr. II, 24. Schlichtingius ut hoc loco redemptionem proprie sic dictam subterfugiat, dicit, redemptionis vocem sumi pro expiatione, quam dicit esse speciem quandam liberationis, tum propter ipsum liberationis, qui in expiatione continetur, effectum, tum propter impen- sam quandam, quæ in expiatione fieri solet. Sed reve- ra redemptio hoc loco ipsam expiationis conditio- nem atq; naturam restringit & limitat. Est enim re- demptio ad præstitum ἀντίλυτρον facta, 1. Tim. II, 6. Itaque non quædam tantum impensa, sed tota & ad- æquata & satisfactoria in ea continetur. In expiatio- nes Veteris Testamenti seu anniversarias seu alias impensæ quædam fuerant faciendæ. Sed illæ ex pacto duntaxat DEI ad comparandam victimam caducam & perituram valuerunt. Quas impensas Petrus priori epistola Cap. I, 18. corruptibiles vocat, aurum scil. vel argentum vel tale quid. In hac re- demtione impensus est Redemptor ipse, ut fatisface- ret, infinita justitia nobis parta, 2. Corinth. V, 21. 1. Cor. I, 30. Unde expiatio, quæ hac redemtione continetur, plane alterius speciei est, quam illa, quæ in Veteri Test. in usu fuit. Redemptionem porro æternam explicat Estius bifariam: vel veram & folidam semperque mansuram, ut altera passione vel redemptione non sit opus, vel quod sit æterna hæreditas, quam nobis acquisivit. Convenientior autem sine dubio est posterior sensus, quia hære- ditas redemptionis in ipsa voce λυτρώσεως con- tinetur, & postea ulterius deducitur. Duplex au- tem hic iterum innuitur discrimen Aaronici sacer- dotii, notante Eslio: Unum Christum non pro suis, ficut legalis Pontifex, sed tantum alienis peccatis sa- crificium obtulisse. Alterum Christi sacrificium va- luisse ad æternam redemptionem, non item sacrificium Aaronicum. Id enim intelligendum relinquitur ex antithesi. Et sane unico illo sacrificio æternam re- demptionem & liberationem à peccatis, diabolo & inferno nobis impetravit. Unde Osiander con- cludit: Si ergo Christus SEMEL in sanctum san- ctorum ingressus ÆTERNAM redemptionem invenit? Cur sacrificuli Christum toties in Missa (ut propitiatorium sacrificium) offerunt? Et si Christus æternam redemptionem nobis impetravit, cur pro- pter peccata admissa trepidamus, si in hunc Sacerdotem & redemptorem credimus? Sed observandum im- primis αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν hic absolute dici. Quo de pulchre B. Dorscheus: Expiatio αἰωνία sequuta est pro omnibus annis, ultra omnes annos, ante omnes annos valida, omnibus temporum momentis vigoro- sa & operosa, ultra omnium temporum momenta pretiosa. Dicitur enim αἰωνία λύτρωσις absolute, adeoq́, tam à parte ante, quam à parte post æstimata & æstimanda. Hinc hujus æternæ redemptionis intuitu electi sumus in Christo πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμυ, Eph. I, 4. & dicitur nobis gratia in Christo data πρὸ χρό- νων αἰωνίων, 2. Tim. I, 9. atq́, eactenus Christus tanquam agnus immaculatus & irreprehensibilis pretiosum suum sanguinem fundens dicitur προεγνωσμένος πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμε, 1. Petr. I, 20. Et ut ista expia- tio seu redemptio à Christo præstita æterna dicitur ra- tione æstimationis moralis, quia ab æterno in æternum à Deo Patre pretiose habita fuit; ita etiam est in- finita, hocest, infinite æstimata, seu infinite pretiosa habita, adeoque non tantum exæquans infinitam ma- litiam peccatorum humani generis, ita à justitia divina infinita læsa merito æstimatam, sed etiam sua perfectione superans, Rom. V, 20. Et est etiam simpli- cissima, multam compositionem admittens cum alia, quæcunque tandem sit, aut esse singatur, redemptione. Ita enim à Deo æstimata est, ut illi nihil addi possit, sic- ut infinito nihil potest addi. Est etiam omnipotens, moraliter scilicet, & impetrando, quia impetrare à Deo Patre potest omnia, Rom. VIII, 37.

## 9:13
Vers. 13. Εἰ γὰρ τὸ αἷμα τάυρων καὶ τράγων.] He said τάυρων, for which above [he said] μόσχων. So also below X, 4. Rightly. For μόσχος is a younger bull. And Josephus III, 1, where he describes the sacred ἱλασμῦ, said ταύρον, where the LXX [said] μόσχον. The whole passage of Josephus is worthy of being read.

Καὶ σποδὸς δαμάλεως.] From Num. XIX. In the Glossary δάμαλις is a heifer, a young cow. Thus Myron's heifer is called δάμαλις by the Greeks. From this ash water was made, the sprinkling of which purified, that is, admitted to the fellowship of men and to the atrium of the temple those who had touched a human corpse or a sepulcher.

ῢαντίζουσα τὺς κεκοινωμένυς] טמאים which the LXX are accustomed to translate as ἀκαθάρτους. The word itself טמא [means] μιαίνειν, ἀκαθαίρειν, βεβηλῦν, which is κοινῦν in Matthew 15, 11. 18. 20. Mark 15, 18. 20. 23. Acts 10, 15. c. 11, 9. c. 21, 28. Ap. 21, 27. The locution comes from the fact that things which are holy are separated for God, [and] things which are not such remain in profane use, which is common use. Hence, by an extended meaning, those who cannot approach the sanctuary are called κεκοινωμένοι, and foods which not the people of God, but other nations used, are called κοινά, Acts X, 14. Rom. XIV, 14. Therefore, also below, κοινὸν is opposed to ἐν ᾧ τις ἡγιάσθη, X, 29. Mention of the sprinkling, which was done by blood, is also found in the Scholiast on the Acharnians of Aristophanes.

Ἁγιάζει πρὸς τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς καθαρότητα.] Ἁγιάζειν is the same as καθαρίζειν, below טהר, whence the adjective טהור is translated sometimes as καθαρὸς, sometimes as ἅγιος. That purification or sanctification pertains only to the uses of this mortal life. See the example in Num. XIX.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Εἰ γὰρ τὸ αἷμα τάυρων καὶ τράγων.] Τάυρων dixit, pro quo supra μόσχων. Sic & infra X, 4. Recte. Est enim μό- σχος, τᾶυρος νεώτερος. Et Josephus III, 1. ubi describit sacrum ἱλασμῦ ταύρον dixit, ubi LXX. μόσχον. Totus Josephi locus dignus, qui legatur.

Καὶ σποδὸς δαμάλεως.] Ex Num. XIX. In Glossario δάμα- λις vitula, juvenca. Sic bucula Myronis Græcis δάμαλις. Ex hoc cinere fiebat aqua, cujus aspersio purgabat, id est, ad ho- minum consortium & ad atrium templi admittebat eos, qui attigissent cadaver hominis aut sepulchrum.

ῢαντίζουσα τὺς κεκοινωμένυς] טמאים quod ἀκαθάρ- τυς solent vertere LXX. Ipsum autem verbum טמא μιαίνειν, ἀκαθαίρειν, βεβηλῦν, quod κοινῦν Matth. 15, 11. 18. 20. Marc. 15, 18. 20. 23. Act. 10, 15. c. 11, 9. c. 21, 28. Ap. 21, 27. Loquutio in- de, quod quæ sancta sunt, ea Deo sunt separata, quæ non sunt talia, manent in usu profano, qui est usus communis. Hinc prolata significatione, qui ad sanctuarium accedere non pos- sunt, dicuntur κεκοινωμένοι, & alimenta, quibus non Dei po- pulus, sed aliæ gentes utebantur, κοινά Act. X, 14. Rom.XIV, 14. Itaq; & infra opponitur κοινὸν, & ἐν ᾧ τις ἡγιάσθη, X, 29. Aspersionis, quæ per sanguinem fiebat, mentio etiam apud Scholiasten ad Acharnenses Aristophanis.

Ἁγιάζει πρὸς τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς καθαρότητα.] Ἁγιάζειν idem quod καθαρίζειν, infra טהר, unde Adjectivum טהור mo- do καθαρὸς, modo ἅγιος vertitur. Illa purgatio sive sancti- ficatio tantum ad vitæ hujus mortalis usus pertinet. Exem- plum vide Num. XIX.

## 9:14
Vers. 14.

Πόσῳ μᾶλλον τὸ αἷμα Χριστῦ, ὃς διὰ Πνεύματος αἰωνίε ἑαυτὸν προσήνεγκεν ἄμωμον τῷ Θεῷ, καθαριεῖ τὴν συνείδησιν ἡμῶν ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἔργων εἰς τὸ λατρεύειν Θεῷ ζῶντι] By how much the blood of Christ, the Son of God and innocent, excels the blood of animals by reason of the living creatures, by so much the purification ought to be greater. Both are for worshipping God, the blood of beasts ritually, the blood of Christ especially in the mind, which is called συνείδησις here by synecdoche, as also above in 9. The blood of beasts purifies through ash from contact with a dead body, the blood of Christ from sins, which are called dead works here, as also above VI, 1. And excellently, the worship of the living God is opposed to dead works, who, just as he always lives, so he can also always benefit us. But the offering of Christ here is understood as that which corresponds to the legal offering made in the inner sanctuary. That, however, is not the offering made on the altar of the cross, but that made in the heavenly inner sanctuary. But it was made there through the eternal Spirit, or, as he said before in VIII, 17, through the power of an indissoluble life, because his Spirit was no longer merely living, as in this earthly life, but vivifying the body joined to itself for eternity, 1. Cor. XV, 45. Διὰ Πνεύματος αἰωνίε is in the best Codices, and Theophylact reads it so, as does the Syriac. Other Greeks and Latins [read] διὰ Πνεύματος ἁγίε, for which sense it can receive, see Rom. I, 3. and 1. Petr. III, 18. Take Διὰ here as above in 12 for the preposition 'with', in which way the Hebrew is also accustomed to be placed. The dignity of the offering is understood here, that he who was already immortal in Spirit and body made it. But this purification is attributed to the blood, because through the blood, that is, the death of Christ, followed by his excitation and elevation, faith is generated in us, Rom. III, 25, which faith then purifies the hearts, Acts XV, 9. Rom. III, 22. and passim in the same epistle. The similarity, however, between the legal and the Evangelical purification is not in the mode of purifying, but in the effect. The former rendered men fit for entry into the earthly sanctuary: the latter for entry into the heavenly sanctuary. When he says ἄμωμον, he refers to the law of victims, Lev. XXII, 20, Num. XIX, 2, Deut. XV, 21. In legal victims there was to be no bodily defect: in the life of Christ there was nothing defective: and therefore He was immediately endowed with that eternal Spirit. Certain books have ὑμῶν here instead of ἡμῶν: but ἡμῶν is in the Manuscript, and the Syriac reads it so, and some Latin Codices have the verse thus. The Manuscript indeed has καθαρίσει, that is, it has the force of to purify. For we are accustomed to use the future in this way. It also has καὶ ἀληθινῷ after ζῶντι. See Joh. XVII, 3, 1. Thessal. I, 9, 1. Joh. V, 20, and Theophylact also reads it thus.

It was the person of the Holy Spirit, and although he admits that it should not be read 'Spiritum Sanctum' with the Vulgate, as Ribera contends, but with the most approved Greek codices, as the Aldine, Vatablus, Pagninus, Stephanus, Ariusmontanus, etc., have expressed and hold; Athanasius in his epistle to Serapion, Theodoret, Theophylact, Oecumenius, Πνεῦμα αἰώνιον, as also Cajetan, Jac. Faber, Mariana, Saa have explained, which reading the opposition also requires, for the spirit which was in bulls and goats and heifers, when they were slaughtered and shed their blood, was extinguished. Therefore, the Apostle wished to oppose to that fallen and extinguished spirit the eternal Spirit in the sacrifices of the New Testament. Whence the mention of eternity was more appropriate than that of holiness. He prefers, however, to understand the Holy Spirit here by 'eternal Spirit,' both because the Holy Spirit also brought the greatest momentum to the oblation of Christ, as an ointment given without measure to this sacrifice, John 3:34, from which an ὀσμὴ εὐωδίας, Eph. 5:2, redounded to God the Father, and because the Greek Fathers explain it thus: Athanasius, Chrysostom, Cyril, Theodoret, Theophylact, Oecumenius. He acknowledges, however, that the Deity of Christ contributed the greatest momentum to constituting the sacrifice of Christ, and is solidly opposed to the perishability which was in the sacrifices of the Old Testament, concerning which, therefore, not only Beza, Franc. Junius in Parall. lib. III, c. 9, Tossanus, Pareus, Capellus, Bisterfeld, but also among our own B. Gerh., B. Hunnius, and others have interpreted 'eternal Spirit'. Nor is it indeed inconveniently explained as the Divinity of Christ, as it is from this that the efficacy of Christ's expiatory sacrifice comes, just as the word 'Spirit' is taken when it concerns the person of Christ in the ἀντιθέσει of the flesh or human nature, Rom. 1:4, 1 Tim. 3:16, 1 Pet. 3:18. B. Hunnius paraphrases thus: 'Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, offered himself as an immaculate sacrifice to God, not kindled by fire, but offered by the eternal Spirit, while this flesh and blood, which were offered by the virtue of the Holy Spirit in the conception of Christ, were freed from all filth of sin and sanctified for an immaculate sacrifice: which were also personally united to the eternal Spirit himself, namely God, who is Spirit, John 4. From which union they obtain this divine efficacy and power of purging from sins before God and vivifying consciences, by a true and real κοινωνίᾳ.' B. Glassius in Exegesis Epist. Dom. Judica: neither of these explanations displeased him. He offered himself, he says, through the eternal Spirit, by which is denoted either the Holy Spirit, the third person of the Holy Trinity, by whom he was impelled and led into this most bitter struggle with Satan during his passion, just as had happened in the pre-agony and first struggle with the devil in the desert, Matt. 4:1. Or the very true Deity of Christ is understood, which sustained the human nature in passion and death, and conferred upon the sacrifice of Christ that salutary force, and granted that weight of efficacy, so that it could be an ἰσόῤῥοπον λύτρον, an equivalent price of redemption for the sins of the whole world, just as the word Πνεύματος, Spirit, is taken, 1 Tim. 3:16, 1 Pet. 3:18. This, therefore, is the immovable foundation of the efficacy of the blood of Christ. B. Hieronymus Wellerus explains it concerning the Holy Spirit, so that it may be shown that Christ offered himself as a victim for the human race not only of his own accord and highest will, but also by the common consent and decree of the Trinity, that is, of the Father and the Holy Spirit. B. Osiander: 'If the Levitical sacrifices could bring carnal and external cleanliness, much more does the sacrifice of Christ, which is far more excellent, which he offered by the impulse of the Holy Spirit (who is most ardent charity), cleanse us from our sins, so that hereafter through faith we may have a good conscience, and from that faith serve GOD in true piety.' B. Hutter and others, who prove the eternal Deity of the Holy Spirit from this passage, the Weimar Paraphrasts, and others. Neither interpretation, therefore, is to be rejected, yet that concerning the Divinity of Christ seems to contribute more to the Apostolic inference, because the fact that the sacrifice of Christ's body was of such divine virtue and efficacy that it made for our eternal redemption, that the blood of Christ has the power of cleansing our consciences from sins, the cause of which is that it is not the body and blood of a ψιλῶ ἀνθρώπυ, but of a Θε-ανθρώπυ, that it has the divine nature personally united and communicated to it, that in Christ himself dwells all the fullness of the Deity bodily, for which reason also the Apostle laid that foundation in this πρoθέσει, chapter 1:3, namely that Christ is the eternal and consubstantial Son of GOD, ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτῦ, who therefore made purification of sins by himself. Through the Holy Spirit the faithful priests of the Old Testament offered sacrifices, and we offer ourselves to God as a true, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God, not otherwise than through the Holy Spirit, Rom. 12:1. But this is proper to Christ alone, that he offered himself through the eternal Spirit, through the eternal Deity personally united to himself, and thus the divine virtue communicated to him, just as πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς Θεότητος ἐν ἀυτῶ σωματικῶς κατοικεῖ, Col. 2:9.

Piscator indeed understands here the immortal soul; διὰ πνεύματος αἰωνίε, that is, by an immortal soul, he says; by which words it is signified that Christ offered himself knowingly and willingly, and thus his obedience toward the command of the Father is commended. But although it is certain that Christ offered himself willingly, John 10:14, yet the words 'through the eternal Spirit,' even if you explain them as the immortal soul, do not infer this, since it is expressed more clearly by other words that he offered himself, nor does it contribute to the divine power of this eternal redemption and expiation of sins. The reason which Piscator opposes to the previous explanation is null. The reason, he says, why the Deity, or the Holy Spirit, does not seem to be understood by these words is because it is not the role of the Deity to offer a sacrifice, but it is the very one to whom a sacrifice is offered by man insofar as he is man. For Christ is a Priest not only as man, but also as God, since the names of Christ's office apply according to both natures: And in a different respect Christ is God, the one to whom we have been reconciled, and he is also the one who reconciled us; because God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, 2 Cor. 5:19, and thus he can also be said to have offered himself to himself in a different respect: To himself, namely, insofar as he is that one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, offended by our sins and to be reconciled to us: Himself as a sacrifice or victim to be offered to God for the sins of the world, which victim is not a mere man, but Christ himself the God-man, who nevertheless is also the same Priest himself, who offered himself through his eternal Deity, which is personally united to him and indwelling. For in these mysteries there are diverse significations, and the same thing is even presented under diverse types and figures; nor is it foreign to the sacred scriptures that the same one is both God, who is to be reconciled to the human race, and the Mediator and Priest, through whom the reconciliation and the sacrifice, which is offered for the sake of expiation, is made. But the Grotian gloss is in no way to be admitted, because the eternal Spirit is not a soul vivifying a body into eternal life, much less an immortal soul and an immortal body, nor did Christ offer himself through a soul, or if you say 'through' is the same as 'with', it is understood here that he offered himself with a soul. For what is this: Christ offered himself with a soul? Who could doubt that when Christ is named, the soul is included, or that Christ entered into the heavens not destitute of a soul? And what does the vivification of the body of Christ to eternal life have to do with the power of expiating sins through the offering of Christ, or when he offered himself to GOD? Are our bodies also to be vivified to eternal life? Does the power of expiating sins belong to them as well? Since Christ 1 Corinthians XV is said to have been made into a life-giving Spirit, not that it is taught how the body of Christ was vivified by his soul, but a truly divine life-giving power (δύναμις ζωοποιητικὴ) communicated to Christ according to his human nature is understood, by the power of which communion (κοινωνίας) the body of Christ could also be offered as a sacrifice for the sins of the whole world.

Socinus in his Response to Bellarmine and Wujek, ch. X, p. 496, thinks that in this passage it is not signified that the Holy Spirit also exercised his power in the sacrifice of Christ, but only that the manner according to which Christ offered himself was not legal and temporary, but spiritual and eternal, which is also said above in Chapter VII, 16, 28.

Socinus drew this explanation from Faber Stapulensis, but it is certainly not immediate. For 1. the words themselves do not speak of a spiritual and eternal manner, but of the eternal Spirit itself. But the eternal Spirit is never the spiritual manner itself. Furthermore, in this place, the substance of the things offered in the Old Testament is immediately opposed, and indeed a corruptible one, which is the blood of bulls and goats together with the ashes of a heifer, to the very substance of the thing offered in the New Testament, which is Christ and his blood; namely, just as in those Old Testament offerings the spirit was also natural and vital, but that one was perishable and corruptible: so in the New Testament the victim to Christ is the eternal and incorruptible Spirit, as here Blessed Dorscheus.

If you say with Crellius and Schlichting that the cause is explained here why the blood of Christ has such power that it cleanses our consciences; namely, from the fact that, having shed it, Christ offered himself unblemished to God through the eternal Spirit in that heavenly sanctuary: I respond that the cause of that matter is indeed explained, but it is not that he offered himself in the heavens unblemished, that is, as they explain it, immortal, or freed from every stain of infirmity: for there exists no word here, nor anywhere else in the Scriptures, concerning an offering made in the heavens: But that he offered himself on the altar of the cross, where he shed his own blood, through a divine power personally proper to himself, as an expiatory sacrifice for the sins of the whole world to God for a sweet-smelling savor, Eph. V, 2, and that unblemished (ἄμωμον), i.e., not immortal, or freed from every stain of infirmity, but immaculate, pure from every stain of sin. For GOD made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, 2 Cor. V, 21, which sense of the word Schlichting could not deny, having interpreted this epistle from the mind of Crellius, namely that he notes here that he himself was pure from every stain with respect to the most innocent life, which he passed without the least stain of sin, although he tries to attach another sense to it very absurdly (since there cannot be a double and disparate meaning for one and the same word placed in one and the same place), that he is also called unblemished (ἄμωμος) in this place with regard to the immortal nature which he obtained, freed from every stain of infirmity, when he was about to enter into those heavenly sanctuaries, and was inspired and imbued with that eternal Spirit. And where, I ask, is unblemished (ἄμωμος) the same as immortal, or freed from every infirmity? What kind of stain does infirmity bring? Was Christ not infirm in the days of his flesh, and was he not unblemished (ἄμωμος) without stain, who was and had to be holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, Heb. VII, 26? Did he not receive an immortal nature when, after his passion, he entered into glory, Luke XXIII, 26? Did he have a mortal body in his resurrection, as we are to have in the resurrection, and when did he receive an immortal one? What, furthermore, is that eternal Spirit with which he is inspired and imbued, and where or when was he inspired and imbued with it? Neither Crellius nor Schlichting explained these mysteries of Socinian vanity. What, finally, does the immortality of the body of Christ have to do with the expiatory or purificatory power of the sacrifice of Christ? The Socinians cannot explain that. For what Schlichting says here with Crellius, that the blood of Christ, insofar as it is the blood of a victim, takes its power and efficacy of expiation from the offering Christ accomplished in the heavens, he asserts both without and against Scripture. For Christ made purification by himself before he sat down at the right hand of God in the heavens, Heb. I, v. 3. He perfected us by the offering of his body on earth, having offered one sacrifice for sins (μίαν ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν προσενέγκας θυσίαν), by one sacrifice having been performed (μιᾷ προσφορᾷ), Heb. X, verses 12, 14, since through the death of Christ redemption and deliverance (λύτρωσις & ἀπολύτρωσις) were made for us, verses 12, 15, the offering of his body having been made once, v. 10, which was done by his passion, Ch. IX, 21, 26, and by the shedding of his own blood, through which he entered into heaven, and thus before he entered into the holy of holies, Ch. IX, 12, 14, since through the death of Christ redemption and deliverance (λύτρωσις & ἀπολύτρωσις) were made for us, v. 12, 15. As the high priest did not sacrifice in the holy of holies, but offered sacrifices outside of it, yet entered into the holy of holies with the blood of the victim, so that he might appear before the ark of the covenant: So Christ, the Priest of the New Testament, did not offer himself as a sacrifice in the sanctuary of heaven, but on the altar of the cross, when he was slaughtered for us, as a victim for the sins of the whole world, and shed his own blood for us for the remission of sins. But afterwards, having made purification for our sins, he entered into that holy of holies, the heavenly tabernacle, through his own blood or not without it, so that he himself might appear before the face of God for us, Heb. IX, 24. The Apostle does not say that the Aaronic high priest offered a sacrifice in the holy of holies, but he says only this, that entering into the holy of holies he brought with him the blood of the animals slaughtered for sacrifice: Thus also Christ brought his own blood, shed as a sacrifice on the altar of the cross, into the heavenly sanctuary; indeed, the Apostle testifies that eternal redemption had already been found by Christ when he entered into the heavenly holy places; therefore, certainly, the sacrifice was also completed. And how did the blood of Christ, insofar as it was shed on earth, insofar as it is the blood of the victim, take on the power of expiation from the oblation of Christ that followed in heaven, when that blood had already been shed on earth for the remission of sins, Matt. XXVI, verse 28, and by that blood shed on the earth, we have been redeemed as by the precious blood of that lamb ἀμώμου καὶ ἀσπίλου, 1 Pet. I, 18, 19. And from the earth it cried out, the blood of sprinkling for the remission of our sins, Heb. XII, v. 24. When he himself was wounded for our sins, we are healed by his stripes, Isa. 53:5, 6. In him we have τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ, τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν, Col. 1:24. because ἐκατάλλαξεν ἐν τῷ σώματι τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ διὰ τοῦ θανάτου, v. 22. Therefore, the blood of Christ did not finally take on the power of expiation from some offering or other in the heavens, since that power is attributed to it in the very shedding, in the passion of Christ, and in his death.

When Schlichting, along with his Crell, saw this, he feigns that what is said in this passage about the offering of Christ is not said properly of Christ, but on account of the comparison of Christ with that ancient High Priest, and an allusion to him: Namely, that it signifies the singular and unique care of CHRIST for our salvation and the expiation of our sins, but a care worthy of and congruent with such a High Priest, who, unlike that ancient one, is not destitute of the power to confer salvation by his own authority, such that he needs to truly obtain it from another: But one who, having himself obtained all authority in heaven and on earth, and having received all judgment handed over to him by the Father, releases his own from all guilt of sins by his own authority, exempts them from all punishments, and finally makes them possessors of eternal life. But in truth, this is how one first departs from the literal meaning of words to figures, which is against the sound rule of Theology, as we have observed elsewhere from Smalcius. Next, those things which are attributed to the shedding of the blood of Christ, to the blood, the passion, and the death of Christ, are denied to the same, and are snatched away to the ascension into heaven. Thirdly, from the offering on the altar of the cross, an offering in the heavens is feigned, nor yet, fourthly, can it be explained by any words of Scripture what offering is made or has been made there, and fifthly, according to Socinian hypotheses, not even blood is left to Christ in the heavens, so far is it from being the case that he can or could offer blood there for our sins. Smalcius in exam. 157. errorum err. 68. page 21. Christ, he says, when he offered himself through the eternal Spirit to GOD, offered himself blameless. Now if he had offered himself with blood, he would not have been free from all imperfection, since it is no less an imperfection in respect of immortality to have blood than it is in respect of holiness to have sin, which paradox is deservedly opposed by another, even if it is most false, and collapses by its own vanity, since ἄμωμον in the whole of Holy Scripture neither signifies him who lacks blood, nor an immortal one, nor does blood detract anything from immortality, or bring about imperfection by itself, which is evident from the example of our first Parents in the state of integrity, and of the perfect just in the heavens: and it is too manifest that Christ is called ἄμωμον with respect had to the qualities of the goats and calves in the Old Testament sacrifices offered, which had to lack every blemish, which Grotius acknowledges here, and it was altogether necessary to teach that, not because Christ lacks blood, which he still offers to us in the Eucharist, but because he offered himself for us without the stain of sin, since otherwise, if he himself had been stained by sin, he could not have offered himself for us as the just for the unjust 1 Pet. 3:18, 1:19. Sixthly, the expiation of sins is converted into care for salvation. But yet, even those who make no expiation can exercise care for the salvation of another: And if the offering of Christ, by which he offered himself into expiation of sins as a sacrifice, is itself the care for salvation and the expiation of sins, why is that not also attributed to the Father, who certainly exercises care for the salvation and expiation of our sins? If it brings in nothing other than releasing his own from all guilt of sins by his own authority, exempting them from all punishments, and finally making them possessors of eternal life, does not all that most especially befit God the Father? But it is too manifest that it is a far different thing to offer oneself to God as a sacrifice for the sins of men, and to exercise care for the salvation of men. The former pertains to the Priestly office of Christ, the latter to the Kingly. That offering and expiation has already been made, and made ἐφάπαξ once for all, by which one offering all who are sanctified are perfected. This care for the salvation of men, and their release from the guilt of sin, exemption from all punishments, and the gift of eternal life is perpetual. Therefore, these are only most poorly confused with one another, and indeed with a completely heretical intention to overturn the satisfaction for our sins made through the blood and death of Christ, which is invincibly asserted in the refuted Socinianism.

3. Therefore, that Socinian hypothesis of Grotius also collapses, that purification is attributed to the blood; because through the blood, that is, the death of Christ, followed by his resurrection and ascension, faith is generated in us, which purifies hearts. For in that way, purification would have to be attributed not to the blood and death of Christ, but to his exaltation: Which, however, is otherwise in the Scriptures, and indeed perpetually. For the purification of sins is never attributed to the exaltation of Christ; it is always attributed to the passion, death, and blood of Christ. But it would be strange if it were not even once attributed to that to which it most especially befits, but was always ascribed to the other, to which it does not properly befit. Furthermore, Grotius confuses the expiation or purification already made, which is attributed to the death and blood of Christ, namely, regarding the merit and satisfaction for sins, and the enjoyment of the satisfaction of Christ and the purification of sins, namely, the remission of sins, justification, and salvation. Nor can Grotius explain by his Socinian hypotheses how the blood of Christ makes us fit to worship God, or even purifies us for the entry into the heavenly sanctuary, since he attributes these rather to the resurrection and ascension of Christ, and to the obedience to the commands of Christ performed by us because Christ was raised and ascended. Concerning which most perverse Pelagian and more than Pelagian hypotheses we have dealt elsewhere.

Furthermore, regarding the ἕιρμον τῆς ἀκολυθείας, the Apostle had said that Christ, having obtained eternal redemption, entered into the holy of holies through his own blood as the High Priest of heavenly goods, such as righteousness and eternal salvation, which he also acquired for us by his blood, or by the merit of his passion and death, and applies to us by his intercession at the right hand of God, which is fitting for him as High Priest, Rom. VIII, 37. He now confirms this by making a comparison with ceremonial cleansing. For if the blood of bulls and goats, as well as the ashes of a heifer sprinkled, sanctified and cleansed the defiled for carnal and external Levitical purity, how much more shall the blood of Christ cleanse for the internal purity of consciences. The reason for the major proposition is that there is a far smaller proportion between the blood of bulls and goats, and likewise the ashes of a heifer, and that external and ceremonial cleanliness and holiness, than there is between the blood of Christ and that effect by which he is said to confer internal cleanliness, penetrating consciences and destroying sins. Whence it ought to seem far more likely that this effect flows from the blood of Christ than that the former flows from the blood of bulls and goats and the ashes of a heifer, as it might seem to someone if he were to follow reason and not rather weigh divine institutions. For the Apostle proposes for consideration both the blood itself and its effect. Whence it may be evident how great is the aptitude and sufficiency of this blood for that effect. The blood itself is commended 1. That it is the blood of Christ. Yet how great the force and power of Christ is toward all effects, but especially toward the effect of our liberation, shines forth most sufficiently from the previous praises by which he has already rendered Christ commended to us. Whence the Apostle argues, extending his finger to the things that are before: Who is the blood of the very Son of God the Only-begotten, the Creator of all things, the brightness of glory, and the express image of the Father's substance, he who upholds all things by the word of his power, who has the right of sitting at the right hand of Majesty in the highest, etc., that blood is most apt and most sufficient for those effects. But this blood is his blood. Therefore. 2. That it is the blood ἄμωμος [unblemished], by which name Christ himself also was commended above in chapter VII. 26 and 1 Peter I. 19. This name is noted, however, when the highest purity and infinite holiness are attributed to Christ, which pertains to the μορφὴν τῦ Θεῦ [form of God], Philippians II. 6. For that irreproachability is understood in this place, which can stand in the rigorous divine judgment, in which not even God himself can desire any perfection, and which could produce the most perfect obedience. In the blood of bulls and goats, as also in the ashes of a heifer, the τὸ ἄμωμον [unblemished state] cannot be established. And so it does not appear so much how that blood of the unclean can constitute [people] ἀμώμους [unblemished] through sprinkling. But this blood is ἀμώμος [unblemished], and indeed not merely comparatively, but absolutely ἀμώμος and infinitely holy. Whence it easily appears how that blood can make us clean. For the blood that is absolutely ἀμώμος and infinitely holy, that can also make [one] ἄμωμον and holy. But the blood of Christ is such. For Christ is the Holy of holies, Daniel IX, to whom also pertains the trisagion in Isaiah VI and John XII. 41. 3. That it is the blood of him who offers himself to God. The priest of the Old Testament did not offer his own blood, but another's, when he offered the blood of bulls and goats, and indeed so much another's that it was even constituted outside the species of those whom he ought to sanctify to the purity of the flesh. Whence again it does not appear so much what the proportion is of the blood of another, placed outside the human species, to the legal holiness and purity to be conferred upon men. The priest of the New Testament offered himself and his own blood, the blood of our race, Hebrews II. 14, whence the proportion between this blood and the redemption to be obtained for us through the same easily appears. For there must be supreme efficacy for our sanctification in the blood of our high Priest. 4. That it is blood poured out. For it is the blood of him who offers himself into bloody death. Indeed, the blood of bulls and goats was also poured out, but that pouring out contains nothing singular in itself. Whence the proportion of the poured-out blood to sanctification might be detected. But this blood was poured out unjustly. For Christ was not obligated to that pouring out by his nature, but of his own accord he bound himself to the same; men obtain right and dominion over bulls and goats and other animals, so that they can slaughter them and pour out their blood when necessity demands it. But no creature has any right or dominion over the blood of Christ, by which it could have poured it out. Whence its pouring out is said to have been done διὰ χειρῶν ἀνόμων [by the hands of lawless men], Acts II. 23. Whence appears the proportion which this blood has, if it be poured out, to the purification of our consciences. For the blood which is poured out by its own motion and altogether unjustly and from no natural obligation for the salvation of our race, that has the greatest proportion or aptitude for sanctifying our consciences, as [says] this blessed Dorscheus. Where it is manifest that the argument of confirmation looks not to the bare entry into the holy of holies, but as that was done in the type with the victim's blood being presented to God for actual expiation, in the antitype it is done with the blood of Christ, the one expiatory victim of the New Testament, being presented to God in the heavens for the justification and the actual fruition of the eternal redemption found, which comes to us through Christ the Pontiff of future goods, and his entry into heaven by virtue of his oblation made on the altar of the cross. Moreover, it is a proof from the lesser to the greater, in which the sprinkling of the blood of the victim, with which the defiled used to be sprinkled, Leviticus XVI. 14, and also of the ashes of the red heifer, which was likewise ordained for the τοῖς κεκοινωμένοις [those who were defiled], Numbers XIX. 9 ff., corresponds to the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, 1 Peter I. 2, and of his ashes, when he himself was placed into the dust of death, Psalm XXII. 16, and furthermore to the Levitical sanctification or purification, which was for carnal purification (although this is not to be taken exclusively, but as that which was a type of interior purification), corresponds the purification of consciences from dead works, that is, from sins. For the blood of goats and bulls, as also the sprinkled ashes of the heifer, sanctified, as the blessed Hunnius rightly noted, in a twofold manner: First, it cleansed those polluted by external uncleanness, so that it was permitted to be present in the assemblies of the Israelites. Then, spiritual internal uncleanness was not imputed to them before God either, who sacrificed from faith. And the blood of brutes accomplished that, not for its own sake, but for the sake of a certain other ἀντίτυπον [antitype], that is, the blood of Christ, of which it was a type. If, therefore, the blood of brutes could accomplish this, how much more does the blood of Christ not only take away external uncleanness, nor cleanse consciences in respect of another antitype, but is valid by itself for cleansing consciences from dead works, that is, from sins, to serve the living God in true justice and holiness? Since indeed that is the proper blood of God. To these corresponds the oblation or sacrifice of bulls and goats, whose blood, as also that of the red heifer, whose ashes were used for sprinkling, corresponds to the oblation and sacrifice of Christ made in his bloody passion and death.

Schlichtingius thinks it is not necessary for the conclusion of the Author's argument that the ashes of the heifer here be posited as a type of the blood of Christ, for he says that an argument is not drawn here from type to antitype, unless perhaps accidentally and from unequal things. He says he gives this warning so that no one might think it is to be gathered from this that the author is comparing the expiatory offering of Christ with other sacrifices besides that anniversary one in which the high priest entered into the holy of holies; he admits, however, that those ashes were a type of the blood of Christ, and an excellent one, insofar as these ashes had the power at any time to cleanse anyone who was sprinkled with them from certain stains of the flesh, and indeed it was perpetual by the decree of God alone, not depending on the will of any man. For it was necessary that those ashes always be at hand; for thus also the blood of Christ has the power to cleanse from their guilt any men at any time, provided they are sprinkled with it or washed from the filth of their sins, and it is a certain perpetual remedy for purging the conscience, instituted by the counsel of God himself. But Schlichtingius opposes things that are not opposed. For the Apostle expressly forms an argument from type to antitype, between which there is a great disparity, and thus he also argues from unequal things. Whence he accommodates to Christ not only the bulls and goats, as well as the heifers to be burned, of which he makes mention here, but also the gifts and sacrifices in general as a type, e.g. What he adds concerning the blood of Christ having a type in the perpetually present ashes is usefully accepted for our cause. And so, just as the ash was always at hand, so that by its sprinkling men could be cleansed; thus it is also necessary that the blood of Christ, surviving and always present, be for the purging of consciences. Which, however, is denied in the school of Socinus, as B. Dorscheus rightly observed here, who brought Schlichtingius into the open here, speaking with us but thinking heretically; which was done by us elsewhere, especially in [the work] on the causes of the death of Christ: Whom he finally betrays when he says: That the purging of our conscience obtained by the blood of Christ is to be understood in this place in such a way that it depends in its very effect upon our duty in turn, that is, that it begins in its very effect when the beginning is made by us toward God and the faith and obedience of Christ, and is continued by it: until it is finally completed at the end in constancy in faith and piety, and consists in a full and immutable right to eternal life, the effect of which is certainly to follow in its own time. For unless the very effect and complement of the expiation depended in turn upon our duty, and our duty, or the will addicted to divine service, remained from the expiation of us in a continuous flow. For how many will there be who will want to serve God on account of the expiation of sins, if they know that they can be expiated without this very effect, and, freed from all guilt of sins, enjoy that eternal life by full right; because therefore the expiation of Christ draws us back from sins, and brings it about that we serve the living God hereafter, hence it is that Christ expiates us by a single offering, or that the expiation proceeding from the offering and sacrifice of Christ is eternal, or would give an eternal one. For what need is there to repeat the offering, if men once expiated do not sin anymore. For although sometimes true worshippers of Christ can slip through some error and infirmity, yet because the offering of Christ does not look so properly to such lighter sins as it does to the expiating of all grave ones; as is evident from the proper nature of the new covenant, for the sake of executing which Christ offered himself to God, by which it is distinguished from the old. Therefore, on account of infirmities or lighter lapses, the offering of our Pontiff Christ ought not to be repeated. For to remove the guilt of those, the perpetual dwelling of our Pontiff in that heavenly sanctuary and his intercession for us before the Father is sufficient, so that it is by no means necessary to shed blood again on their account, and through the shedding of it to enter into the sanctuary. Thus Schlichtingius. From which it appears that that purging of our conscience is nothing other than the zeal and endeavor of obeying God; hence he establishes it in the continuation of faith and obedience and constancy in faith and piety to the very end, whence to Schlichtingius it is nothing other than that that very way of salvation, which Christ taught and illustrated by his example, has been sealed also by blood, so that we might be the more incited in treading the footsteps of the life of Christ, and in this way also it is to be understood what Schlichtingius says, that the offering of Christ draws men back from sin. For he wants this to be done by the example of Christ, by which we are warned that we should resist sin even to blood, and adhere to God. And what he says, that Christ expiated us by a single offering, Schlichtingius understands it in the same way as the obedience of Christ was not repeated, but persisted in one continuous course even to death; so also those converted to Christ ought not or cannot interrupt that obedience which they have begun, but must continue it to the end of life. But in this way he plainly takes away the proper and most genuine end of the offering of Christ, by which he gave himself to men not only as a τύπον and ὑπόγραμμον, 1 Pet. 2:21, but especially also as an ἀντίλυτρον, 1 Tim. 2:6, and in this also the office of the Pontiff is placed, that he might offer some sacrifice as a price for man to God, which, since it was only typical in the Old Testament, and not proportionate to that which was to be redeemed, therefore it was necessary that Christ be both Mediator and the price, which would fulfill all types, and consummate the redemptions already made. In this also Schlichtingius hallucinates, in that he asserts that the offering of Christ does not look so properly to lighter sins and those proceeding from weakness as to the expiating of all grave ones. For the offering of Christ extends itself to all sins properly, because he is the ἱλασμὸς for the sins of the whole world, 1 John 2:2. Nor is that consistent with the truth, which Schlichtingius says, that the perpetual dwelling of our Pontiff in that heavenly sanctuary and the intercession for us before the Father is sufficient to remove the guilt of lighter sins and those proceeding from weakness. For the intercession of Christ for us before the Father, performed at the right hand of God, founds itself upon the bloody offering, as will be taught below from verse 24. Therefore sins are not to be divided, so that some are to be expiated by the offering of Christ, others by his intercession at the right hand of the Father; nay rather, for those for whom he intercedes, when they are accused before the Father, their sins must be compensated by the offering of Christ. Hence also the Apostle, Rom. 8, joins the intercession of Christ for us, of which he speaks in verse 34, with the handing over of the same for all, of which he speaks in verse 32. And this is the reason why it is by no means necessary for blood to be shed by Christ on account of lighter sins, not because they can be satisfied for in any other way than by the shedding of blood. For this would be against verse 32. But because satisfaction has been made by Christ for lighter sins and those proceeding from weakness just as much as for graver ones.

Furthermore, to return to the Apostle, works are called dead because they neither have any life in themselves, nor do they bring anything but death. And here the Greeks note a reference to the contact with the dead. Theophylact: In the same place, (in the Old Testament) he who had touched anything dead and cadaverous is purified. But here the purification is from dead works, which can undoubtedly defile a man and render him liable to death. To serve the living and true God. He, therefore, who has devoted himself to dead works, by no means serves the living and true God, but rather will hold and worship as God the very works which he has chosen to be looked upon by himself. For thus, those who are given to gluttony will establish their belly as their God. Thus, I say, the covetous man also serves idols. Such works are therefore to be called dead. And not only because they are alien to eternal life, but because when these are practiced, they are rendered abominable and indeed deceptive, because when they have enticed us, they capture us, and they seem sweet, when they are less so. That end also, the admission to the tabernacle and the worship of God, such as was prescribed there, corresponds to the communion of saints and the worship by which we serve the living God with a pure heart: Conf. Tit. II. 14. indeed to the admission into the heavenly sanctuary, but not except through the blood of Christ. For redemption, purification, and salvation are handed down by the Apostle in order. Concerning which we must now speak in the second part of the chapter.

We add, moreover, the exegesis of the blessed Dorscheus: Consider 1. the subject, which is our conscience. It is placed in this passage for the whole man. For he is the adequate subject of purification and sanctification, although especially with respect to the conscience, as being impure and defiled, in which are λογισμοὶ καθῃγοροῦντες, Rom. II. 25, which is otherwise called a condemning heart in 1 John III, 20. 2. Then the object, which is νεκρὰ ἔργα. For the blood of Christ is said to purify us from dead works. Dead works are sins themselves, as being perpetrated by a man dead in sins, Eph. II. 5, who is in the body of death, Rom. VII. 24, which work death, Rom. VIII. 13, conf. above chap. I. 3. The act is purification, both of regeneration and of justification. Both are a benefit of the sacrifice of Christ, conf. above chap. I. 3. 4. The end is to serve the living God, or to worship the living God. Just as in the Old Testament, those who touched a dead body were unclean, and could not enter the sanctuary to perform solemn worship to God, and therefore had to be freed from pollution by blood and ashes: So in the New Testament and by its power there is a liberation from that pollution which man has contracted from the commerce of dead works, on account of which man is otherwise excluded from the worship and presence of the living God. Whence again the amplitude and preeminence of the sacrifice of the New Testament over the sacrifices of the Old Testament appears.

PART II.

Clarification of the Mediation of the New Testament.

Latin:

Vers. 14.
