Πόσῳ μᾶλλον τὸ αἷμα Χριστῦ, ὃς διὰ Πνεύματος αἰωνίε ἑαυτὸν προσήνεγκεν ἄμωμον τῷ Θεῷ, καθαριεῖ τὴν συνείδησιν ἡμῶν ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἔργων εἰς τὸ λατρεύειν Θεῷ ζῶντι] Quanto Christi Filii Dei & innocentis sanguis præstat saguini caren- tium ratione animantium, tanto purgatio debet esse major. Uterque ad colendum Deum, sanguis pecudum ritualiter san- guis Christi præcipue animo, qui κατὰ συνεκδοχὴν hic ut & supra 9. συνείδησις dicitur. Sanguis pecudum per cinerem purgat à contactu mortui corporis, sanguis Christi à pecca- tis, quæ hic vocantur opera mortua, ut & supra VI, 1. Et egregie operibus mortuis opponitur cultus Dei vivi, qui sic- ut semper vivit, ita & semper prodesse nobis potest. Oblatio autem Christi hic intelligitur illa, quæ oblationi legali in ady- to factæ respondet. Ea autem est non oblatio in altari crucis facta, sed facta in adyto cælesti. Facta autem ibi est per Spi- ritum æternum, aut, ut ante dixit VIII, 17. per vim vitæ in- dissolubilis, quia Spiritus ejus jam non erat vivens tantum, ut in vita hac terrena, sed in æternum corpus sibi adjunctum vivificans, 1. Cor. XV, 45. Διὰ Πνεύματος αἰωνίε habent optimi Codices, & ita legit Theophylactus, ut & Syrus. Græ- ci alii & Latini διὰ Πνεύματος ἁγίε, quod quem sensum re- cipere possit, vide Rom. I, 3. & 1. Petr. III, 18. Διὰ hic sume ut supra 12. pro præpositione cum, quomodo & Ebræum poni solet. Intelligitur hic dignitas oblationis, quod eam fecit is, qui jam Spiritu & corpore erat immortalis. Sangui- ni autem purgatio. ista tribuitur, quia per sanguinem, id est, mortem Christi, secuta ejus excitatione & evectione, gigni- tur in nobis fides, Rom. III, 25. quæ deinde fides corda pur- gat, Act. XV, 9. Rom. III, 22. & passim in eadem epistola. Similitudo autem purgationis legalis & Evangelicæ non est in modo purgandi, sed in effectu. Illa idoneos homines red- debat ad ingressum sanctuarii terrestris: Hæc ad ingressum sanctuarii cælestis. Cum dicit ἄμωμον respicit legem victi- marum, Lev. XXII, 20. Num. XIX, 2. Deut. XV, 21. In vi- ctimis legalibus nullum debebat esse corporis vitium: InChri- sti vita nihil fuit vitiosum: Et ideo Spiritu illo æterno statim donatus est. Quidam libri pro ἡμῶν hic habent ὑμῶν: Sed ἡμῶν est in Manuscripto, & sic Syrus legit, & ita versum ha- bent quidam Codices Latini. Manuscriptus vero καθαρίσει, id est, purgare valet. Solemus enim futuro sic uti. Etiam post ζῶντι habet καὶ ἀληθινῷ. Vide Joh. XVII, 3. 1. Thessal. I, 9. 1. Joh. V, 20. & ita legit etiam Theophylactus.

Spiritus Sancti persona fuit, etsi autem admittat, non esse cum Vulgata, ut Ribera contendit, legen- dum Spiritum Sanctum, sed cum probatissimis codicibus Græcis, ut expressit Aldina, Vatablus, Pagninus, Stephanus, Ariusmontanus, &c. est, ha- betq; Athanasius in epist. ad Serap. Theodoretus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius, Πνεῦμα αἰώνιον, uti et- iam exposuere Cajetanus, Jac. Faber, Mariana, Saa, quam lectionem etiam oppositionem requirere spiritus fatetur, qui in tauris & hircis & juvenca fuit, cum interficerentur & sanguinem effunderent, extinctus fuit. Illi itaq; caduco & extincto spiritui Apostolus opponere voluit in sacrificiis Novi Te- stamenti Spiritum æternum. Unde convenientior erat mentio æternitatis quam sanctitatis. Mavult ta- men per æternum Spiritum hic intelligere Spiritum Sanctum, tum quia Spiritus sanctus maximum etiam momentum ad oblationem Christi attulit, tanquam unguentum huic sacrificio sine mensura datum Joh. III, 34. Ex quo ὀσμὴ εὐωδίας, Eph. V, 2. ad Deum Patrem redundavit, tum quia Græci Patres ita expli- cant, Athanasius, Chrysostomus, Cyrillus, Theodore- tus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius. Agnoscit tamen Deitatem Christi maximum momentum ad sacri- ficium Christi constituendum contulisse, ac solide opponi caducitati, quæ erat in sacrificiis Veteris Test. de qua proinde interpretati sunt Spiritum æternum non Beza tantum, Franc. Junius in pa- ral. l. III, c. 9. Tossanus, Pareus, Capellus, Bisterfel- dius, sed & è nostris B. Gerh. B. Hunnius, & alii. Nec sane incommode explicatur de Divinitate Chri- sti, utpote à qua efficacia est sacrificii Christi ex- piatorii, quemadmodum vox Spiritus accipitur, cum de persona Christi agitur in ἀντιθέσει carnis seu naturæ humanæ, Rom. I, 4. 1. Tim. III, 16. 1. Petr. III, 18. B. Hunnius sic παραφράζει: Christus uni- genitus Dei Filius seipsum obtulit Deum immacu- latum sacrificium, non igne accensum, sed Spiritu æterno oblatum, dum hæc caro & sanguis, quæ offerebantur virtute Spiritus Sancti in conceptione Christi ab omni immunditie peccati liberata, & ad immaculatum sacrificium sanctificata fuerunt: Quæ etiam personaliter unita fuere ipsi æterno Spi- ritui, Deo scilicet, qui Spiritus est, Joh. IV. Ex qua unione hanc divinam efficaciam & potentiam, à peccatis coram Deo purgandi & vivificandi consci- entias, vera & reali κοινωνίᾳ obtinent. B. Glassio in exegesi epist. Dom. Judica neutra harum ex- plicationum displicuit. Obtulit se, inquit, per Spiritum æternum, quo vel Spiritus Sanctus, ter- tia SS. Trinitatis persona denotatur, à quo in acerrimum hoc certamen cum satana in passione fuit impulsus & perductus, sicut in proagonia & primo certamine cum diabolo in deserto factum fuerat, Matth. IV, 1. Vel ipsa vera Christi Deitas intelligitur, quæ humanam naturam in passione & morte sustentavit, & sacrificio Christi vim illam salutarem contulit, & pondus illud efficaciæ conces- sit, ut ἰσόῤῥοπον λύτρον æquivalens redemptionis pretium pro peccatis totius mundi esse potuerit, uti Πνεύματος Spiritus vox accipitur, 1. Timoth. III, 16. 1. Petr. III, 18. Hoc igitur efficaciæ san- guinis Christi immotum fundamentum est. De Spiritu Sancto explicat B. Hieronymus VVellerus, ut ostendatur Christum non modo sua spon- te & summa voluntate, verum etiam de com- muni consensu & decreto Trinitatis, hoc est, Patris & Spiritus Sancti, se obtulisse hosti- am pro genere humano. B. Osiander: Si sacrificia Levitica potuerunt afferre munditiem carnalem & externam: multo magis sacrificium Christi, quod longe præstantius est, quod ille impulsu Spiri- tus Sanctus (qui est charitas ardentissima) obtulit, nos à peccatis nostris emundat, ut posthac per fidem bonam conscientiam habeamus, & ex fide illa DEO in vera pietate serviamus: B. Hutterus & alii, qui Spiritus Sancti Deitatem æternam ex hoc loco probant, Vinarienses Paraphrastæ & alii. Neutra ergo interpretatio reprobanda, illa tamen de Di- vinitate Christi magis videtur ad illationem Apo- stolicam facere, quia quod corporis Christi sa- crificium tam divinæ virtutis & efficaciæ fuerit, ut ad æternam redemptionem nostram fecerit, quod sanguis Christi vim emundandi à peccatis conscientias nostras habeat, cujus causa est, quod non sit ψιλῶ ἀνθρώπυ corpus & sanguis, sed Θε- avθρώπυ, quod divinam naturam sibi personali- ter unitam & communicatam habeat, quod in ipso Christo habitet tota plenitudo Deitatis corpora- liter, cujus rei causa etiam in πρoθέσει hac funda- mentum illud jecit Apostolus cap. I, 3. quod nem- pe Christus sit æternus & consubstantialis DEI Filius, ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτῦ, qui proinde per semetipsum pu- rificationem peccatorum fecit. Per Spiritum Sanctum obtulere & fideles Veteris Testamenti Sacerdotes sacrificia, & nos offerimus nos ipsos Deo in sacrificium verum sanctum & Deo placens, non nisi per Spiritum Sanctum, Rom. XII, 1. At Christi unius hoc proprium est, quod semetipsum obtulerit per æternum Spiritum, per æternam Deitatem sibi personaliter unitam, adeoque di- vinam virtutem sibi communicatam, uti πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς Θεότητος ἐν ἀυτῶ σωματικῶς κα- τοικεῖ, Coloff. II, 9.

Piscator intelligit quidem hic animam immor- talem; διὰ πνεύματος αἰωνίε, id est, per animam, inquit, immortalem; quibus verbis significatur, quod Christus obtulerit se sciens & volens, atque ita commendatur ejus erga mandatum Patris obe- dientia. Sed quanquam id certum sit, Christum vo- lentem sese obtulisse, Joh. X, 14. id tamen nec ver- ba per Spiritum æternum, etiamsi explices de ani- ma immortali, inferunt, cum aliis verbis, quod se- metipsum obtulerit, clarius exprimatur, neque ad vim divinam hujus æternæ redemptionis & expia- tionis peccatorum facit. Ratio, quam opponit su- periori explicationi Piscator, nulla est. Quo minus, inquit, per hæc verba videatur intelligenda Deitas, vel Spiritus Sancti, ratio est, quia Deitatis non est, offer- re sacrificium, sed ipsa est, cui offertur sacrificium ab homine quatenus homo. Nam Christus non tan- tum qua homo, sed etiam qua Deus Sacerdos est, quum nomina officii Christi conveniant secun- dum utramque naturam: Et pro diverso respectu Christus Deus est is, cui reconciliati nos sumus, est & is, qui nos reconciliavit; quia Deus erat in Chri- sto mundum reconcilians sibi ipsi, 2. Cor. V, 19. adeo- que idem etiam sibi ipsi obtulisse dici potest se- metipsum diverso respectu: Sibi nempe, prout est unus ille Deus cum Patre & Spiritu S. per pec- cata nostra offensus & reconciliandus nobis: Se- metipsum ut sacrificium vel hostiam pro pecca- tis mundi Deo offerendam, quæ hostia est non nudus homo, sed Christus ipse θεάνθρωπος, qui tamen idem etiam est ipse Sacerdos, qui fele per suam sibi personaliter unitam, & inhabitantem æternam Deitatem obtulit. In his enim myste- riis diversæ significationes sunt, & res eadem et- iam sub diversis typis & figuris sistitur; nec alie- num est à sacris literis, eundem & Deum esse, qui reconciliandus est humano generi, & Mediatorem ac Sacerdotem, per quem fit reconciliatio & sacri- ficium, quod offertur expiationis causa. Grotiana vero glossa nullo prorsus modo ad- mittenda, quia Spiritus æternus non est anima cor- pus vivificans in æternam vitam, nedum anima im- mortalis & corpus immortale, nec per animam sese obtulit Christus, aut si per dicas idem esse quod cum, obtulisse hic sese intelligitur cum ani- ma. Quid enim hoc: Christus se obtulit cum anima? Ecquis ambigere possit, Christo nomi- nato animam comprehendi, aut Christum in cœlos ingressum esse anima haud destitutum? Et quid vivificatio corporis Christi ad vitam æ- ternam facit ad vim expiandi peccata per obla- tionem Christi, vel cum seipsum obtulit DEO? Anne etiam corpora nostra vivificanda ad vi- tam æternam sunt? Num & illis vis expiandi pec- cata convenit? Cum Christus 1. Corinth. XV. fa- ctus dicitur in Spiritum vivificantem, non quo- modo corpus Christi ab anima ejus vivificatum sit docetur, sed δύναμις ζωοποιητικὴ vere divina Christo secundum humanam naturam commu- nicata intelligitur, vi cujus κοινωνίας etiam cor- pus Christi offerri potuit in sacrificium pro pec- catis totius mundi.

Socinus in Resp. ad Bell. & VVuieck. c. X. p. 496. existimat h. l. non significari in sacrificio Christi, Spi- ritus S. etiam virtutem sese exercuisse, sed illud tantum rationem, secundum quam Christus seipsum obtulit, non esse legalem & temporariam, sed spiritualem atq́; æternam, quod & dicitur supra Cap. VII, 16. 28.

Hausit Socinus hanc explicationem ex Fabro Stapulensi, sed certe immediata non est. Nam 1. ver- ba ipsa non loquuntur de ratione spirituali & æter- na, sed de ipso Spiritu æterno. Nunquam autem Spi- ritus æternus est ipsa spiritualis ratio. Deinde imme- diate hoc loco opponitur rerum in Vet. Testam. oblata- rum substantia, & quidem corruptibilis, quæ est tau- rorum & hircorum sanguis una cum cinere juvencæ, ipsi substantiæ rei in Novo Testamento oblatæ, quæ est Christus & sanguis ejus, nimirum sicut in illis Vet. Testam. oblationibus Spiritus fuit etiam naturalis & vitalis, verum ille caducus & corruptibilis: Ita in Novo Testamento hostia Christo est Spiritus æternus & cor- ruptibilis, ut hic B. Dorscheus.

Si dicas cum Crellio & Schlichtingio, hic cau- sam explicari, cur Christi sanguis tantam vim ha- beat, ut conscientias nostras emundet; inde nimi- rum, quod eo fuso Christus in cælesti illo sacrario per Spiritum æternum semetipsum immaculatum obtu- lerit Deo: Resp. Omnino causam ejus rei expli- cari, sed eam non esse, quod se in cœlis immacu- latum, hoc est, ut illi exponunt, immortalem, vel omni infirmitatis labe solutum obtulerit: nam de oblatione in cœlis facta neque hic, neque uspiam alibi in Scripturis ullum extat verbum: Sed quod sese in ara crucis, ubi fudit sanguinem proprium, per divinam sibique personaliter propriam virtu- tem obtulerit in sacrificium expiatorium pro pec- catis totius mundi Deo in odorem suavitatis Eph. V, 2. idque ἄμωμον, h. e. non immortalem, vel ab omni infirmitatis labe solutum, sed immacula- tum, ab omni labe peccati purum. DEUS enim eum, qui non novit peccatum, pro nobis fecit peccatum, 2. Cor. V, 21. quem sensum vocis non po- tuit diffiteri Schlichtingius, è mente Crellii hanc epistolam interpretatus, quod nempe hic notet, ipsum ab omni labe purum fuisse respectu vitæ in- nocentissimæ, quam sine minima peccati macula transegit, quanquam perabsurde (quum unius vo- cis uno eodemque loco semel positæ non possit esse gemina ac disparata significatio) alium adhuc sensum affricare conetur, quod ἄμωμος etiam dicatur hoc loco habitæ ratione immortalis natu- re, quam omni infirmitatis labe solutus, in cœle- stia illa adyta ingressurus, æternoque illo Spiritu afflatus & imbutus adeptus est. Et ubi obsecro ἄμωμος idem est, quod immortalis, vel ab omni infirmitate solutus? Quamnam affert infirmitas labem? Annon Christus infirmus erat in diebus carnis, ἄμωμος fine labe erat, qui ὅσιος, ἄκακος, ἀμίαντος, κεχωρισμένος ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν & esse debuit, & omnino fuit, Ebr. VII, 26.? Annon immortalem naturam accepit, quando post passio- nem ingressus in gloriam, Luc. XXIII, 26.? Num corpus mortale in resurrectione sua habuit, uti nos in resurrectione habituri sumus, & quando immortale accepit? Quid porro est Spiritus ille æternus, quo afflatus & imbutus est, & ubi vel quando eodem est afflatus & imbutus? Non ex- posuit hæc Socinianæ matæologiæ mysteria vel Crellius vel Schlichtingius. Quid denique immor- talitas corporis Christi facit ad sacrificii Christi vim expiatoriam vel purificatoriam? Id vero edisserere nequeunt Sociniani. Quod enim ait hic cum Crellio Schlichtingius, quod Christi san- guis, quatenus victimæ sanguis est, expiandi vim & efficaciam sumat à Christo in cœlis consecuta oblatione, id & citra & contra Scripturam assexi- tur. Nam purificationem Christus per semet- ipsum fecit, antequam consederit ad dextram Dei in cœlis, Ebr. I. v. 3. consummavit nos oblatione corporis sui in terris μίαν ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν προσενέγ- κας θυσίαν unico facto sacrificio pro peccatis, μιᾷ προσφορᾷ unica peracta oblatione, Ebr. X. vers. 12. 14. cum per mortem Christi nobis λύτρωσις & ἀπολύτρωσις facta sit, vers. 12. 15. facta se- mel oblatione corporis sui, v. 10. quod passione ipsius factum est, Cap. IX, 21. 26. & fuso sanguine proprio, per quem ingressus est in cœlum, adeoque antequam in sanctum sanctorum ingre- deretur, Cap. IX, 12. 14. cum per mortem Christi nobis λύτρωσις & ἀπολύτρωσις facta sit, v. 12. 15. Ut summus Sacerdos non sacrificabat in sancto san- ctorum, sed extra illud sacrificia offerebat, cum sanguine autem victimali ingrediebatur in sanctum sanctorum, ut coram arca fœderis com- pareret: Ita Christus Sacerdos N. T. non obtulit sese in Sacrificium in adyto cœli, sed in ara crucis, cum mactatus est pro nobis, tanquam victima pro peccatis totius mundi, & sanguinem suum pro nobis effudit in remissionem peccatorum. Postea autem facta purificatione peccatorum nostrorum in sanctum illud sanctorum cœleste tabernacu- lum ingressus est per sanguinem proprium vel non sine illo, ut ipse compareret coram vultu Dei pro nobis, Ebr. IX, 24. Apostolus non dicit, Ponti- ficem Aaronicum in sancto sanctorum sacrificium obtulisse, sed hoc tantum dicit, quod ingrediens in sanctum sanctorum sanguinem animalium in sa- crificium mactatorum secum intulerit: Sic etiam Christus sanguinem suum in ara crucis in sacrifi- cium effusum in cœleste sanctuarium intulit; imo testatur Apostolus, æternam redemptionem jam dum à Christo fuisse inventam, quando in sancta cœlestia est ingressus, utiq; ergo etiam sacrificium peractum. Et quomodo à consequuta in cœlis ob- latione Christi sanguis, quatenus in terris effusus est, quatenus victimæ sanguis est, expiandi vim sumpsit, quum in terra jam sanguis ille fusus sue- rit in remissionem peccatorum, Matth. XXVI. vers. 28. eoque in terra fuso, ceu agni illius ἀμώμου καὶ ἀσπίλου pretioso sanguine redempti simus, 1. Petr. I, 18. 19. Et è terra clamarit αἷμα ῥαντισμοῦ pro remissione peccatorum nostrorum, Ebr. XII, v. 24. Cum vulneratus ipse est propter peccata nostra, sanati nos sumus vicibus ejus, Esa. LIII, v. 5. 6. In ipso habemus τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ, τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν, Col. I, 24. quia ἐκατάλλαξεν ἐν τῷ σώματι τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ διὰ τοῦ θανάτου, v. 22. Non ergo demum ab oblatio- ne, nescio qua, in coelis, sanguis Christi expiandi vim sumpsit, siquidem in ipsa effusione, in passio- ne Christi & morte ejus vis illa ipsi tribuitur.

Quod quum viderit Schlichtingius cum Crellio suo, quae de oblatione Christi hoc loco dicuntur, fingit non proprie de Christo dici, sed propter Christi cum antiquo illo Pontifice comparationem, & ad eum allusionem: Significari nempe CHRI- STI pro salute nostra peccatorumque nostrorum expiatione singularem & unicam curam, sed cu- ram tanto Pontifice dignam eique congruam, qui non ut antiquus ille, propria potestate confe- rendae salutis destitutus ab alio eam vere impe- trare necesse habeat: Sed qui ipse omni in coelo & in terra imperio potitus, omneque judicium à Patre sibi traditum, adeptus, propria potestate su- os omni peccatorum reatu solvat, omnibus poenis eximat, & vitae sempiternae compotes tandem effi- ciat. Verum enim vero ita primum à proprietate verborum ad figuras disceditur, quod est contra sanam Theologiae regulam, ut alias è Smalcio ob- servavimus. Deinde quae sanguinis Christi effu- sioni, sanguini, passioni & morti Christi tribuun- tur, eidem denegantur, & ad evectionem in coe- lum abripiuntur. Tertio ex oblatione in ara crucis fingitur oblatio in coelis, nec tamen quarto quae- nam illic oblatio fiat aut facta sit, explicari potest ullis Scripturae verbis, & hac quinto juxta Soci- nianas hypotheses ne relinquitur quidem Christo in coelis sanguis, tantum abest, ut ibi sanguinem offerre possit aut potuerit pro peccatis nostris. Smalcius in exam. 157. errorum err. 68. pag. 21. Christus, inquit, cum se obtulit per Spiritum aeter- num DEO, inculpatum sese obtulit. Jam si se cum sanguine obtulisset, omni imperfectione non caruisset, cum non minor sit imperfectio ra- tione immortalitatis sanguinem habere, quam est respectu sanctitatis peccatum habere, quod para- doxon merito alteri opponitur, etsi falsissimum sit, propriaque vanitate concidat, quum ἄμωμον in tota Scriptura S. nec significet eum, qui san- guine caret, nec immortalem, neque sanguis im- mortalitati quicquam deroget, aut imperfectio- nem per se afferat, quod exemplo primorum Pa- rentum in statu integritatis, & justorum perfe- ctorum in coelis constat: & nimis manifestum sit, Christum ἄμωμον dici respectu habito ad qualita- tes hircorum & vitulorum in Vet. Testam. sacrifi- ciis oblatorum, qui omni macula debuerunt ca- rere, quod agnoscit hic Grotius, ac necessarium omnino id fuerit docere, non quod Christus san- guine careat, quem nobis adhuc in Eucharistia praebet, sed quod sine labe peccati sese obtulerit pro nobis, quum alias si ipse peccato maculatus fuisset, se pro nobis offerre non potuisset ceu ju- stus pro injustis 1. Petr. III, 18, c. I, 19. Sexto expia- tio peccatorum convertitur in curam pro salute. Atqui curam pro salute alterius gerere possunt etiam qui nullam expiationem faciunt: Et si obla- tio Christi, qua semetipsum in expiationem pec- catorum obtulit in sacrificium, est ipsa cura pro salute & peccatorum expiatione, cur non illa Pa- tri etiam tribuitur, qui utique curam pro salute & expiatione peccatorum nostrorum gerit? Si ni- hil aliud infert illa, quam propria potestate suos omni peccatorum reatu solvere, omnibus poenis eximere, & vitae sempiternae tandem compotes efficere, annon id omne maxime Deo Patri con- venit? Sed nimis manifestum est, longe aliud esse, offerre sese Deo in sacrificium pro peccatis homi- num, & curam gerere salutis hominum. Illud ad Sacerdotale Christi officium pertinet, hoc ad Re- gium. Illa oblatio & expiatio jam facta est, & facta ἐφάπαξ semel, qua una oblatione consummantur omnes, qui sanctificantur. Hæc cura pro salute hominum, & solutio eorum à peccati reatu, exem- ptio à pœnis omnibus & vitæ æternæ donatio per- petua est. Non ergo nisi pessime hæc inter se con- funduntur, & quidem intentione prorsus hæretica ad evertendam satisfactionem pro peccatis no- stris per sanguinem & mortem Christi factam, in- victe in Socinismo profligato assertum.

3. Corruit ergo sic hypothesis etiam illa Socinia- na Grotii, quod sanguini purgatio tribuatur; quia per sanguinem, id est, mortem Christi, sequuta ejus excitacione & evectione gignitur in nobis fides, quæ corda purgat. Nam ita non sanguini & morti Chri- sti, sed ejus exaltationi esset tribuenda purgatio: Quod tamen secus sit in Scripturis, & quidem per- petuo. Nunquam enim purgatio peccatorum tri- buitur exaltationi Christi, semper tribuitur eadem passioni, morti & sanguini Christi. Mirum au- tem foret, ne semel quidem illi eam tribui, cui maxime ea conveniat, alteri autem, cui proprie non convenit, semper adscribi. Adhæc confundit Grotius expiationem vel purificationem jam factam, quæ tribuitur morti & sanguini Christi, scil. quoad meritum & satisfactionem pro peccatis, & satisfa- ctionis Christi & purificationis peccatorum frui- tionem, remissionem nempe peccatorum, justifi- cationem & salutem. Neque explicare potest Gro- tius per hypotheses suas Socinianas, quomodo sanguis Christi ad colendum Deum faciat, aut et- iam ad ingressum sanctuarii cœlestis nos purget, quum hæc potius tribuat excitationi & evectioni Christi, & obedientiæ mandatis Christi ob excita- tum & evectum Christum à nobis præstitæ. De quibus perversissimis hypothesibus Pelagianis & plus quam Pelagianis alias egimus.

Cæterum quod ad ἕιρμον τῆς ἀκολυθείας, dixe- rat Apostolus, parta æterna redemptione Chri- stum per sanguinem proprium ingressum esse in sanctum sanctorum ceu Pontificem bonorum cœ- lestium, ceu sunt justitia & salus æterna, quæ & ac- quisivit nobis sanguine suo, vel merito passionis & mortis suæ, & applicat nobis intercessione sua ad dextram Dei, ipsi, ut Pontifici, convenienti, Rom. VIII, 37. Id ergo jam confirmat, collatione facta mundationis ceremonialis. Nam sitaurorum & hircorum sanguis, ut & cinis juvencæ aspersus sanctificavit & purgavit inquinatos ad carnalem & externam Leviticam puritatem, quanto magis purgabit sanguis Christi ad internam conscientiarum puritatem. Ratio majoris Propositionis est, quia longe minor proportio & inter sanguinem taurorum & hircorum, itemque cinerem juvencæ, & inter istam exteriorem atque ceremonialem munditiem & san- ctitatem, quam est inter sanguinem Christi & illum effectum, quo scilicet dicitur conferre munditiem in- ternam conscientias penetrantem & peccata perimen- tem. Unde longe verisimilius videri debet, hunc effectum à sanguine Christi promanare, quam illum à sanguine taurorum & hircorum atque cinere ju- vencæ promanare, alicui videri possit, si rationem sequeretur, & non potius instituta divina perpende- ret. Considerandum enim Apostolus proponit tum sanguinem ipsum, tum ejus effectum. Unde patere possit, quanta sit sanguinis hujus ad effectum istum aptitudo & sufficientia. Sanguis ipse commendatur 1. quod sit sanguis Christi. Atqui quanta sit Christi ad omnes effectus, imprimis vero ad effectum libera- tionis nostrae vis atque potestas, ex superioribus elo- giis, quibus Christum jam nobis commendatum red- didit, sufficientissimè elucescit. Unde argumentatur Apostolus, digitum ad anteriora extendendo: Qui est sanguis ipsius Filii Dei Unigeniti, Conditoris rerum omnium, splendoris gloriae, & characteris hypostaseos Patris, ejus qui fert omnia verbo potentiae suae, qui jus sessionis ad dextram Majestatis in altissimis ha- bet &c. is sanguis ad istos effectus aptissimus, & suffi- cientissimus est. At hic sanguis est sanguis ejus. Ergo. 2. Quod sit sanguis ἄμωμος, quo nomine ipse Christus quoque commendatus est supra cap. VII. 26. & 1. Petr. I. 19. Notatur autem hoc nomine, quando Christo tribuitur summa puritas, & sanctitas infi- nita, quae ad μορφὴν τῦ Θεῦ, Philipp. II. 6. pertinet. Ista enim irreprehensibilitas hoc loco intelligitur, quae in judicio divino rigoroso consistere potest, in qua ne Deus ipse quidem aliquid perfectionis desiderare potest, quaeque perfectissimam obedientiam parere potuit. In sanguine taurorum & hircorum, ut & in cinere juvencae τὸ ἄμωμον constitui non potest. Itaque non adeo apparet, quomodo iste sanguis im- mundorum per aspersionem possit constituere ἀμώ- μυς. Hic verò sanguis est ἀμώμος, & quidem non comparate duntaxat, sed absolute ἀμώμος & infini- te sancti. Unde facile apparet, quomodo ille sanguis nos possit mundos constituere. Qui enim sanguis est absolute ἀμώμος & infinite sancti, ille potest etiam ἄμωμον & sanctum efficere. Atqui sanguis Christi talis est. Est enim Christus Sanctus sanctorum, Dan. IX. ad quem pertinet etiam trisagion Esa. VI. & Johan. XII. 41. 3. Quod sit sanguis, semetipsum Deo offerentis. Sacerdos Veteris Testamenti non suum sanguinem, sed alienum obtulit, cum sangui- nem taurorum & hircorum obtulit, & quidem ita alienum, ut etiam fuerit extra speciem eorum constitutus, quos debebat sanctificare ad carnis puri- tatem. Unde iterum non adeo apparet, quae sit pro- portio sanguinis alieni & extra speciem humanam po- siti, ad sanctitatem & puritatem legalem hominibus conferendam. Sacerdos Novi Testamenti obtulit semetipsum & suum sanguinem, sanguinem generis nostri Ebr. II. 14. unde facile apparet proportio inter sanguinem hunc & inter redemptionem nostram per eundem comparandam. Oportet enim summam efficaciam esse ad sanctificationem nostram in sangui- ne summi Sacerdotis nostri. 4. Quod sit sanguis effu- sus. Est enim sanguis offerentis sese in mortem cru- entam. Equidem taurorum & hircorum sanguis ef- fusum est etiam, sed illa effusio singulare nihil in se com- plectitur. Unde proportio effusi sanguinis ad sancti- ficationem deprehendi possit. Hic verò sanguis effu- sus est indebite. Christus enim ad illam effusionem ex natura sua non erat obligatus, sed sponte sua ad eandem sese obstrinxit, homines in tauros hircosque & caetera animalia jus ac dominium obtinent, ut possint ista obtruncare, eorundemque effundere san- guinem, ubi id necessitas flagitat. In sanguinem au- tem Christi nulla creatura juris aliquid aut dominii habet, quo eundem potuerit effundere. Unde ejus effusio dicitur facta διὰ χειρῶν ἀνόμων, Act. II. 23. Unde apparet proportio, quam hic sanguis habet, si effundatur, ad purificationem conscientiarum no- strarum. Qui enim sanguis proprio motu & omnino indebite atque ex nulla naturali obligatione pro salute generis nostri effunditur, ille maximam habet propor- tionem sive aptitudinem ad conscientias nostras san- ctificandas, ut hic B. Dorscheus. Ubi manifestum est, argumentum confirmationis respicere non nu- dum ingressum in sancta sanctorum, sed prout ille in typo fiebat cum sanguine victimali Deo sistendo ad actualem expiationem, in antitypo facto est cum sanguine Christi, victimæ unicæ Novi Testam. ex- piatoriæ, Deo præsentando in cælis ad justificatio- nem & æternæ redemptionis inventæ actualem fruitionem, quæ per Christum Pontificem futuro- rum bonorum, ejusque ingressum in cælum vir- tute oblationis ejus in ara crucis factæ nobis obtin- git. Est autem probatio à minori ad majus, in qua respondet aspersioni sanguinis victimalis, quo in- quinata solebant conspergi Levit. XVI. 14. etiam ci- neris vaccæ ruffæ, quæ τοῖς κεκοινωμένοις ordinata itidem erat Num. XIX. 9. seqq. aspersio sanguinis Christi, 1. Petr. I. 2. & cineris ejus, quum positus sit ipse in pulverem mortis Psal. XXII. 16. ac porrò sanctificationi vel purgationi Leviticæ, quæ erat ad carnalem purificationem (quamquam non exclu- sive hæc accipienda sit, sed quæ typus erat interio- ris purificationis) respondet purgatio conscien- tiarum operibus mortuis, hoc est, à peccatis. Nam sanctificabat, ut recte notavit B. Hunnius, hircorum & taurorum sanguis, ut & juvencæ cinis aspersus duplici ratione: Primo enim externa immunditie pollutos mundabat, ut interesse Israelitarum cœti- bus liceret. Deinde spiritualis interna immunditia non imputabatur iis coram Deo quoque, qui ex fide sacrificabant. Idque præstabat sanguis brutorum, non propter se, sed propter aliud quoddam ἀντίτυ- πον, hoc est, Christi sanguinem, cujus typus erat. Si ergo hoc præstare brutorum sanguis potuit, quanto magis sanguis Christi non externam tantum tollit immunditiam, nec alterius antitypi respectu emun- dat conscientias, sed per se valet ad purgandas con- scientias ab operibus mortuis, hoc est, à peccatis, ad serviendum Deo viventi in justitia & sanctitate ve- ra? Siquidem is proprius est Dei sanguis. Ad hæc respondet oblationi vel sacrificio taurorum & hir- corum, quorum sanguis, ut & vaccæ ruffæ, cujus cinis adhibebatur ad aspersionem, oblationi & sa- crificio Christi in passione & morte ejus cruenta factæ.

Schlichtingius existimat, non necesse esse ad argu- mentum Autoris concludendum, ut hic vitulæ cinis ponatur fuisse typus sanguinis Christi, non enim hic duci argumentum à typis ad antitypum, nisi forte per accidens & ab imparibus. Quod ideò dicit se monere, ne quis hinc colligendum putet autorem oblationem Christi expiatoriam cum aliis sacrificiis conferre præterquam cum anniversario illo, in quo summus Pontifex in sanctum sanctorum intrabat, fatetur ta- men, cinerem istum fuisse sanguinis Christi typum, eumque egregium, quatenus nimirum hic cinis quo- vis tempore quemvis, qui eo conspersus esset, à carnis quibusdam maculis emundandi vim habuit, & qui- dem fuit perpetuum ex Dei solius decreto, non verò hominis cujusquam arbitrio pendens. Semper enim cinerem illum in promptu esse oportuit; sic namque & sanguis Christi quovis tempore quosvis homines, dummodo eo conspersi sive à peccatorum sordibus abluti sint, vim emundandi ab eorum reatu habet, perpetuumque quoddam expurgandæ conscientiæ remedium ipsius Dei consilio institutum. Sed Schlich- tingius opponit, quæ non sunt opposita. Apostolus enim disertè argumentum format à typo ad antity- pum, inter quæ magna est imparitas, & sic etiam ab imparibus argumentatur. Unde non tantum tauri & hirci, ut & juvencæ comburendæ, quorum hic facit mentionem, sed & donorum atque sacrificio- rum in universum typum ad Christum accommo- dat, v. g. Quod de sanguine Christi typum in perpe- tuo præsente cinere habente addit, utiliter pro causâ nostra acceptatur. Sicut itaque cinis semper in prom- ptu fuit, ut ejus aspersione homines emundari potue- rint; sic & superstitem, semperque præsentem san- guinem Christi esse necesse est ad expurgandas con- scientias. Quod tamen in schola Socini negatur, ut hic recte observavit B. Dorscheus, qui hic Schlich- tingium nobiscum loquentem, sed hæretice sen- tientem in apricum produxit; quod a nobis alibi, imprimis in de causis mortis Christi, factum: Quem tandem prodit, cum dicit: Purgationem conscien- tiæ nostræ Christi sanguine partam ita hoc loco acci- piendam esse, ut effectu ipso a nostro vicissim pen- deat officio, id est, eam effectu ipso incipere, cum a no- bis initium sit in Deum ac Christi fidei & obedientiæ, & ipsam continuari: usque ad extremum in fide at- que pietate constantia tandem compleri, ac in pleno & immutabili vitæ sempiternæ jure consistere, cujus effectus suo tempore certe sit sequuturus. Nisi enim ex nostro vicissim penderet officio ipse expiationis effe- ctus & complementum usque ex nostri expiatione continuo fluxu maneret nostrum officium, seu divino servitio addicta voluntas. Quotusquisque enim erit, qui Deo propter expiationem peccatorum servire vo- let, si sciat, se absq; hoc effectu ipso expiari posse, omni- que peccatorum reatu solutum vitæ illius sempiternæ pleno jure gaudere; quia ergo Christi expiatio a pec- catis nos retrahit, & ut Deo viventi imposterum ser- viamus efficit, hinc sit, ut Christus unica oblatione nos expiet, seu ut expiatio a Christi oblatione & sacrifi- cio proficiscens æterna sit, æternumve daret. Quid enim opus est, oblationem repetere, si homines semel expiati amplius non peccent. Nam licet interdum errore & infirmitate aliqua veri Christi cultores la- bi possint, quia tamen Christi oblatio non ita proprie ad talia peccata leviora, quam ad gravia quæque expianda spectat; quemadmodum ex fœderis novi, cujus exequendi causa Christus seipsum Deo obtu- lit, natura propria, qua ab antiquo distinguitur, pa- tet. Propterea infirmitatum aut lapsuum leviorum causa Christi Pontificis nostri oblatio repeti non de- bet. Ad istorum enim reatum tollendum sufficit no- stri Pontificis in illo cælesti sacrario perpetua man- sio, & pro nobis apud Patrem interpellatio, ita ut minime necesse sit eorum causa sanguinem denuo fundere, perque illius fusionem in sacrarium ingre- di. Sic Schlichtingius. Ex quo apparet, illam pur- gationem conscientiæ nostræ nihil aliud esse, quam studium & conatum Deo obediendi, hinc constituit illum in continuatione fidei ac obedientiæ & constan- tia in fide ac pietate ad extremum usque, unde san- guine Christi partam esse Schlichtingio nihil aliud est, quam illam ipsam viam salutis, quam Christus docuit, & exemplo suo illustravit, sanguine quo- que obsignatam esse, ut tanto incitatiores essemus in calcandis vestigiis vitæ Christi, & hoc modo etiam intelligendum est, quod Schlichtingius dicit, obla- tionem Christinos a peccato retrahere. Vult enim hoc fieri exemplo Christi, quo monemur, ut ad san- guinem usque peccato resistamus, & Deo adhærea- mus. Quodque dicit, Christum unica oblatione nos expiasse, id ita intelligit Schlichtingius, quem- admodum non fuit repetita Christi obedientia, sed uno continuo ductu ad mortem usque perseveravit; Ita & conversos ad Christum non interrumpere de- bere aut posse illam, quam cæperunt obedientiam, sed ad finem usque vitæ continuare. Hoc vero modo proprium & maxime genuinum finem oblationis Christi plane tollit, quo se non tantum τύπον & ὑπό- γραμμον, 1. Petr. II. 21. sed imprimis etiã ἀντίλυτρον dedit hominib9, 1. Tim. II. 6. & in hoc etiam Pontifi- cis officium positum est, ut sacrificium aliquod tan- quam pretium pro homine Deo offerat, quod cum in Veteri Testamento typicum duntaxat fuerit, neque proportionatum ei, quod redimendum erat, ideoque oportebat Christum & Mediatorem esse & pretium, quod omnes typos impleret, & redemptiones jam fa- ctas consummaret. In eo etiam hallucinatur Schlich- tingius, quod asserit, Christo oblationem non ita pro- prie ad peccata leviora & ex imbecillitate profecta, quam ad gravia quaque expianda spectare. Extendit enim sese oblatio Christi ad omnia peccata proprie, quia pro totius mundi peccatis ἱλασμὸς est, 1. Joh. II. 2. Nec istud veritati consentaneum est, quod Schlich- tingius ait, ad leviorem & ex imbecillitate profecto- rum peccatorum reatum tollendum suffi.ere Pontifi- cis nostri in illo cælesti sacrario perpetuam mansionem & pro nobis apud Patrem interpellationem. Nam interpellatio Christi apud Patrem pro nobis ad dex- tram Dei peracta fundat se in oblatione cruenta, ut infra ex v. 24. docebitur. Itaque non sunt dividenda peccata, ut alia sint oblatione Christi expianda, alia interpellatione ejusdem ad dextram Patris, quin imo potius, pro quibus interpellat, cum accusantur apud Patrem, Christus, eorum peccata oblatione Christi oportet esse compensata. Hinc & Apostolus Rom. VIII. interpellationem Christi pro nobis, de qua v. 34. con- jungit cum traditione ejusdem pro omnibus, de qua v. 32. Atque hac causa est, cur leviorum peccatorum causa minimè necesse sit à Christo sanguinem fundi, non quia alia ratione, quam sanguinis fusione pro iis satisfieri queat. Hoc enim esset contra v. 32. Sed quia pro levioribus & ex imbecillitate profectis peccatis æque atque pro gravioribus à Christo satisfactum est.

Porrò, ut ad Apostolum redeamus, opera mor- tua dicuntur, quod nec in se quicquam vitæ habe- ant, nec nisi mortem afferant. Et respectum hic ad contactum mortuorum notant Græci. Theophyla- ctus: Ibidem, (in Veteri Testamento) qui morti- cinum aliquid & cadaverosum attigerat, purgatur. Hic verò mortuorum operum purgatio fit, quæ pos- sunt haud dubie hominem inquinare & morti obno- xium reddere. Ad serviendum Deo viventi & vero. Qui ergo operibus mortuis incubuerit, haudqua- quam Deo vivo & vero inserviat, quin opera ipsa, quæ sibi spectanda elegerit, pro Deo habebit & colet. Sic enim, qui gulæ sunt dediti, pro Deo ventrem con- stituent. Sic inquam & cupidus idolis servit. Sunt ita- que istiusmodi opera mortua appellanda. Nec solum quia sint à vita perpetua aliena, sed quia cum hæc exercentur, abominanda redduntur & fallacia qui- dem, quia nos, ubi illexerint, capiunt, & videantur suavia, cum minus sint. Finis etiam ille admissio ad tabernaculum & cultus Dei, qualis ibi præscriptus erat, respondet communioni sanctorum & cultui, quo corde puro servimus Deo viventi: Conf. Tit. II. 14. imò admissioni in adytum cœleste, sed non nisi per sanguinem Christi. Nam ordine traduntur ab Apostolo redemptio, mundatio, salvatio. De qua nunc altera parte capitis dicendum.

Addimus autem exegesin B. Dorschei: Confi- dera 1. subjectum, quod est conscientia nostra. Poni- tur hoc loco pro toto homine. Is enim purificationis & sanctificationis subjectum adæquatum est, quan- quam maximè respectu conscientiæ, utpote impu- ratæ & coinquinatæ, in qua sunt λογισμοὶ καθῃ- γορῶντες, Rom. II. 25. qua alias 1. Joh. III, 20. voca- tur cor damnans. 2. Deinde objectum, quod est νεκρὰ ἔργα. Dicitur enim sanguis Christi nos purificare ab operibus mortuis. Opera mortua sunt ipsa peccata, utpote ab homine mortuo in peccatis, Eph. II. 5. perpetrata, qui est in corpore mortis, Rom. VII. 24. quæ operantur mortem, Rom. VIII. 13. conf. supra cap. I. 3. Actus est καθαρισμὸς tum regenerationis tum justificationis. Uterque est beneficium sacri- ficii Christi, conf. supra cap. I. 3. 4. Finem, qui est servire Deo viventi, vel colere Deum viven- tem. Sicut in Veteri Testamento, qui tetigerunt mor- tuum, immundi fuerunt, neque ingredi potuerunt in sanctuarium, ut solennem Deo cultum præstarent, ideoque per sanguinem & cinerem à pollutione fue- runt liberandi: Ita in Novo Testamento ejusque vir- tute sit liberatio ab isto pollutione, quam ex mortuo- rum operum commercio contraxit homo, propter quæ alias à cultu & facie Dei viventis homo excluditur. Unde rursus sacrificii Novi Testamenti amplitudo & præcellentia supra Vet. Testamenti sacrificia apparet.

PARS II.

Μεσιτείας Novi Testamenti dilucidatio.

## 9:15
Ver. 15. And for this cause he is the Mediator of the new testament] בְּרִית, which signifies a pact or covenant (now a covenant is not every pact, but a public one) the Greek Interpreters translate as διαθήκην, the Latins as testament, not in that special sense of civil law, but in a more general one, because it is a declaration of will, concerning which matter we have spoken in the Prolegomena to the Gospels: But also that testament, as it is taken in civil law, where a condition is added to the institution of an heir, as is wont to be done, or the burdens of legacies or trusts, is a certain pact and indeed a more noble one, because once the testator's death has followed, it admits of no change. And therefore this writer wishes the new pact of God, which ought to be more perfect than the former, to be also a Testament in that more potent or civil law signification. Therefore, he says, Christ was made Mediator not of the old, but of the new pact, because this new pact was to be repaired not by the blood of animals, but by the blood of the Mediator himself. A Mediator is one who brings about peace between parties, as we explained in Gal. III. 19. Now peace is often wont to be made under certain laws to be fulfilled before the peace is valid. Such a peace is also a διαθήκη.

That death having occurred] Of himself, not of the victims. For that is easily understood from what was said above.

For the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament] His death intervened to this end, that men might be freed from those sins which had prevailed ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον [for the most part] among the people of God before Christ. The same sense as Acts XIII. 38, where see what is said. Redemption, which above is λύτρωσις, redemption of transgressions, that is, from transgressions, just as in Cicero, liberation of guilt for from guilt. In the first testament, that is, in the time of the former pact. The multitude of that time could not in any part be compared with the Christian multitude of the Apostolic times. Everywhere there was so much filth, not only lurking in the mind, but also appearing outwardly. We have noted in their places that redemption is taken in another sense elsewhere. But what we have said fits this place very well. For he who ceases to sin is already in peace with God by the law of the new pact, Rom. V. 1.

That they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance] To those who are thus freed from sins, the thing promised in the new pact will happen, which is eternal life, 1 Tim. IV. 8, 2 Tim. I. 1, above VIII. 6. Understand 'called' with effect, as 1 Cor. I. 24, Jude v. 1. And see the things said in Gal. III. 18, Eph. I. 14, 18, Col. III. 24, as to why eternal life is called by the name of inheritance. Moreover, you have 'promise' for the thing promised also in Luke XXIV. 49, Acts I. 4, II. 33, Rom. IV. 13, and elsewhere.

He passes from the office of Priest to that of Mediator, which are related here. Why Christ is the Mediator of the New Testament: Namely, for the sake of our salvation, as one who not only made himself a medium between God the Father and the human race, so that he might bring us back into favor with the Father, which are the parts of a Mediator; but also ratified the new Testament, so that with his death intervening in the redemption of those things which remained in the first Testament, and were pressing upon men, those who are called might obtain the promise, the eternal inheritance. Theophylact thus exhibits the connection: What seemed to deter very many of the weaker ones, because they often and much usurped that, if Christ died a death, by what pact is he going to give what he had promised? Paul, now soothing that very thing, argues that Christ's Testament is valid and firmer for that reason, because he died. For the name of Testament does not acquire that force while we are still alive, which we institute by testifying. Therefore (he says)

he underwent death to render us purer; and by his testament he remitted our sins, and left us the enjoyment of heavenly goods, having been made Mediator between us and the Father, when it was by no means in the Father's mind to leave us an inheritance, as he was bitterly angry with those whom he was more wrathful toward, as if they were children alien to him; Christ therefore intervened, and reconciled the Father to us. In what way? For that which was to be borne by us as stubborn ones, he has now borne, and the death which was to be undergone by us, he underwent for us, and made us worthy of this inheritance.

The Apostle calls it a testament, not a covenant, which is entered into mutually between parties, and that to be confirmed by death. Therefore, he calls it so in a proper sense, or certainly in a special rather than a general signification of a covenant or league. Concerning the Mediator, see what is in 1 Tim. II. 5, 6. Concerning which, Theophylact is likewise to be heard: It is therefore, he continues, also this testament already confirmed through the death of the Son, which by no means transmitted the inheritance as to the unworthy. Furthermore, a testament also has heirs. For thus Christ testified, saying: I will, Father, that where I am, there my ministers may also be: Whom, however, he disinherited, he expresses thus: I do not pray for all, but for those who have both professed me and believed. Moreover, a testament has witnesses, as is evident from these: the Father who sent me bears witness of me, and the Paraclete will bear witness of me, and you will bear witness.

But he is called the Mediator of the New Testament because by his mediation he brought it about that a new testament or one of grace could be established, which is distinguished from the Old Testament in this, that under the former, as far as the legal covenant which obtained in that prior one, transgressions remained, and were not expiated by its force or virtue, even if they were entirely pardoned in the time of the Old Testament, but by the force of the covenant of grace, of which Christ is the Mediator, who is also called the Angel of the covenant of grace, Mal. III. 1. Therefore, through the Mediator of the New Testament and by the force of that very covenant of grace, with the death of the Mediator and Testator intervening, it was brought about that those transgressions which remained in the old, their heirs might obtain the redemption or liberation from the same for the eternal inheritance, but through the λύτρῳ of the blood of Christ, as heirs instituted in this testament, and sons of adoption, of the promises, or those things which were promised. Now the things promised were the remission of sins, salvation, and eternal life by the new covenant of grace, and the same were sanctioned by a special testament, and bequeathed to the heirs out of mere grace. You see, says Theophylact, how Christ underwent death so that he might redeem us; by what covenant, therefore, or out of weakness and impotence do you think that was brought about? Since the death of Christ was so efficacious and valid that through it every transgression of the law returned to health. Why, therefore, do you flee to the law, which is so impotent and weak that it cannot correct how many transgressions may have been in it? Nor, however, is it done because that is more iniquitous, but because it is weaker. Let them receive the promise to the words: For unless, he says, the death of Christ had exempted us from the sins and crimes by which we had already rendered the Father an enemy, by what covenant would we have obtained this divine inheritance. Blessed Hunnius assigns here a new part of the comparison, by which he compares covenant with covenant, the new with the old, as truth with shadows and types. And in this part also the Apostle places a huge distinction, that those priests indeed were ministers of the Old Testament: but Christ is not a minister of the New Testament, but High Priest and Mediator. The Apostle introduces this member of the comparison from the former ones in this sense: Because Christ entered into the holy places not with the blood of another but with his own, and because this blood was effective for the removal of transgression, not, like the blood of brute animals, typically, but truly and in reality: It follows from this that Christ is not the Mediator of the Old Testament (which was ratified by shadows, that is, by the blood of brute animals, which was indeed true, but which shadowed forth the blood of Christ, and was not of itself sufficient for the removal of sins) but of the New Testament: Where, by his own death interceding, he conferred that redemption which could not be truly obtained by any Levitical sacrifices: freeing, namely, from the transgressions which were under the Old Testament, that is, which could not be removed by the Old Testament and its priesthood and sacrifices, except insofar as believers from the Old Testament looked toward this reconciler of the New Testament. He therefore assigns the supreme end of the New Testament, which is the perpetual salvation of souls, and the attainment of the eternal inheritance, which was once promised on account of the coming Messiah, and is now acquired through the same for those who believe in him. The force of the argument, therefore, as Estius notes, is this: Because Christ, shedding his blood on the altar of the cross, offered himself to God, and through this acquired for us eternal redemption, which are the effects of the New Testament, he is indeed the Mediator of that New Testament which was promised through the prophet Jeremiah, for he is the one who ratified the promises of that Testament with his own blood. Nor does Piscator inappropriately present the connection of the text thus: Since he affirmed that Christ, by the offering of himself, that is, by his death, acquired the remission of sins and eternal life, he now subsequently explains the reason why it had to be done so: and he brings forward these two reasons in total: One is that in this way it was necessary for the Testament of God, of which he had been constituted the Mediator, to be ratified. He explains this reason in verses 15, 16, and 17. The other reason is that in this way it was necessary for him to perform in reality what had been prefigured by the rite of the Old Testament: for it was ratified by the blood of animals poured out and sprinkled. He explains this reason from verse 18 to verse 24. The exposition of the former reason is comprehended by this syllogism: He who is constituted the Mediator of any Testament, it is necessary for his death to intervene, so that the testament may be ratified and be valid, v. 16 and 17. But Christ was constituted the Mediator of a certain Testament, namely the New Testament, at the beginning of v. 15. Therefore, it was necessary for the death of Christ to intervene for the ratification of that testament, namely to acquire for the called (or believers) the remission of sins and eternal life, in the remaining part of v. 15. The exposition of the latter reason is comprehended by this syllogism: If the Old Testament was dedicated and ratified by the blood of animals: It was necessary for the New Testament to be ratified by the blood of Christ himself, as if prefigured by those animals. But the Old Testament was ratified by the blood of animals, v. 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, and the first part of v. 23. Therefore, the New Testament had to be ratified by the blood of Christ himself, in the latter part of v. 23.

Blessed Dorotheus notes here 1. The Testator, who in this place is called Mediator, and indeed between God and men, as one who received from the side of God the fullest power of testifying, since in him all the fullness of the Godhead dwelt, and all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge were hidden, and all power in heaven and on earth was given to him, nay, all things were given into his hands. He does not, therefore, concur in this testament as a witness, or counselor, or notary, or intercessor, who would pray for legacies from someone, which were in no way placed in his own power, but as Lord, Dictator, and Author of the covenant. 2. The nature of the Testament. It is called by the Apostle the New Testament, concerning which it was treated most extensively above in chapter VIII, at verse 6 and following. The newness consists in this, that with types and shadows removed, it exhibits all things most clearly, and having been fulfilled

, first, since the Old Testament had been so ratified that death was accomplished not in the Testator or Mediator himself, but in some adjunct or substitute, and thus the promise was ratified: this showed death in the Testator himself. Whence we note 3. The consummation of the Testament, which was done by death having occurred. The will of the heavenly Testator was not indeed ambulatory until death, as is said of any other Testator. For whatever has been given to us by this Testament was given before eternal times, 2 Tim. I. 9, and thus stands by an immutable will, nevertheless it was sealed by death, because it was so decreed from eternity. For death also pertains to the determined counsel, Acts II. 23, and because natural death was repugnant to the condition of Christ, and indeed also to the condition of a sacrifice. For there was such perfection in the human nature of Christ that causes bringing about natural death could never fall upon it, and those things which have perished by natural death are never held to be fit for sacrifice, and therefore by an admirable emptying and the counsel of God it was so glorious that it admitted a violent death. Whence he could also have blood, with which he might enter into the sanctuary. 4. The effect of the Testament: It is twofold, the first is the remission of sins or transgressions repugnant to the first covenant: The second is the promise of the eternal inheritance. For after the curse of the Old Testament following the transgressions expired through the redemption made by the death of Christ, the promise of the eternal inheritance follows of itself, as the Apostle speaks. Which also Gal. III. 13. 14. explains more fully, where he says that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, when he himself was made a curse for us, that the blessing of Abraham might come upon the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, and that we might receive the promise of the Spirit. 5. Heirs. They are called κεκλημένοι, called or named. For heirs must be named and called in Testaments. But in this place οἱ κεκλημένοι are not those called by an absolute decree through irresistible grace. For the Holy Scripture knows nothing of such. Nor are they only men of the New Testament, as Schlichtingius thinks, when he says: That those are called to whom in the time of the New Testament the eternal inheritance is offered through the Gospel of Christ, and who embrace such grace of God by faith. For Christ indicates in illustrious parables, Matt. XX. and XXII., that a calling to the eternal inheritance occurred even before the time of the New Testament. and elsewhere: But they are all men by the intention of God, who by the ordinance of God do not maliciously resist the grace offered, and thus are receiving the same. Paul explains the intention in 2 Tim. II. 4, and the ordinance partly in Acts XIII. 46. and following, and partly in XVII. 30. and following.

Furthermore, he is said to redeem transgressions remaining under the former testament, from which we could not be freed under it, that is, to redeem us from those transgressions through the intervention of his death, because he took upon himself the penalty due to us for them, and endured it for us. Not those which were committed in the time of the Old Testament; for he did not free us only from those, but those which remained unremitted under the rigor of the Old Testament, or from which they could not be justified in the law of Moses, Acts XIII. 39, under which we had been shut up, by virtue of the legal covenant, which only worked wrath, and shut up all under sin, Rom. III. 9. 19. 20. chap. IV. 15. chap. XI. 32. Gal. III. 22.

Others understand the sins committed in the Old Testament, which are particularly commemorated here, because it could be doubted concerning them whether they were expiated by the death of Christ, and on account of it were formerly remitted to believers, since they preceded the time of the Messiah being exhibited, so that the sense may be: The Fathers were not freed in the Old Old Testament through its carnal and external sacrifices, but only through faith and the expiation of the future sacrifice of the Messiah, which was prefigured by them, Acts XV. 11. Heb. XIII. 8. Rev. XIII. 8. But the former explanation is more solid; which the blessed Dartheus asserts at length, teaching that the particle ἐπὶ here is εἰς in or against the first testament: The Covenant, he says, or the first Testament was sanctioned with the condition of the strictest observance owed to the law. Against this, sin has been committed infinitely ever since the foundation of the world, and will be committed until the consummation of the age. When, therefore, mention is made of transgressions ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ committed, nothing else can be understood than those which run against the law, which alone in the Old Testament was that which suffered παραϐάσεις and violations. Therefore these words are not to be referred to the time of the said Old Testament, but to the covenant and the condition adhering to the ancient covenant, which is imposed upon us by the very bond of nature. Indeed, those very κεκλημένοι or municipal heirs of eternal happiness enjoy that ἀπολυτρώσει τῶν παραϐάσεων ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ. Therefore, also, the transgressions or sins which are committed under the New Testament are παραϐάσεις ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ not by reason of time, but by reason of the object, because they strike at the base and foundation τῆς πρώτης διαθήκης, that is, the moral law. Nor is it permitted to restrict ἀπολύτρωσιν only to transgressions committed in the time of the Old Testament. For where would be the ἀπολύτρωσις of transgressions perpetrated in the time of the New Testament? For thus also λῆψις ἐπαγγελίας would be restricted only to the New Testament, if the discourse here were about time, and not rather about the object. But an absurd opinion would also be given if we were to explain it in this way. For the sense would be: Therefore Christ is the Mediator of the New Testament, so that by His death having taken place, they might receive the redemption of their transgressions who lived in the time of the Old Testament. Conversely, those who are called to the eternal inheritance in the New Testament would receive the promise of eternal blessedness. Which sense is most inconvenient and inept. For what does the remission of transgressions made to men living in the time of the Old Testament pertain to those called in the New Testament? Can men of the New Testament receive the promise without the remission of transgressions? Or have men in the Old Testament, having obtained the remission of their transgressions, been excluded from the promise? The simplest sense is thus, that this is the fruit of the death of Christ, that He redeems and frees by His infinite preciousness from the transgressions of which the human race could be convicted by the force of the ancient and rigorous covenant, in which the law was concreated in man, but later, with malice increasing, was oppressed, restored, and solemnly repeated. Ἐπὶ therefore is rightly said to be placed for εἰς in this place.

Therefore, Ribera is in vain after others, when he says in this place, n. 74: That it is the Apostle's mind to say that the passion of Christ was of such virtue that not even the saints who were in the Old Testament could obtain salvation without it, since their sins could not be remitted except through the blood of Christ, which was to be shed as the price of redemption, the shedding of which they prefigured by their sacrifices, and professed that by it they were to be blotted out. Whence sins were so remitted then, that they seemed to be sustained by God, because the price of them had not yet been paid, but was expected to be paid. The opinion is indeed true, but it does not square with the Apostolic scope, since it restricts the first fruit of the death of Christ to the time rather than to the object of the Old Testament: For which cause the same man inquires in vain, when he says: But why did he not speak also of the sins of those who lived under the law of nature, since neither were those remitted, except because of the future passion of Christ? And he answers: He was writing to the Hebrews, for whom he feared, lest perhaps, attributing more than was right to the law, they might return to it, and therefore he always demonstrates the infirmity of the law. Then there was no need to speak of them. For if the Hebrews, who had received from God through Moses the law and the rites of sacrifices for sins, could not be cleansed by those sacrifices, but were sanctified through the blood of Christ, much less could those who were under the law of nature have been cleansed by their sacrifices, which were not given by God. The response is partly false, partly superfluous. False, when he says: That it should be said that there was nothing of the fruit redounding from the death of Christ to those who lived before the promulgation of the Old Testament, for fear of the Hebrews' relapse into the veneration of the law. For what would this have pertained to the exaggeration of the law, if the Apostle had said that as many as lived from the origin of the world were freed from sin by the power of the death of Christ. Then, that also is false, that men who lived before the New Testament was solemnly promulgated did not have sacrifices given by God. This is the error of those who refer sacrifices to the dictate of nature, and think that, with natural reason itself suggesting it, sacrifices ought to have been continued at all times among all men, against whom it has been argued in Mys. Mist. c. 1. Abel offered by true faith, Heb. XI. 4. Therefore from revelation. For faith without revelation is not faith. But that response is superfluous, because the Apostle speaks of transgressions against the law, which that law argues, which was confirmed under the Old Testament. But it existed before, and from the origin of men. Just as Gal. III. 17, the New Testament is said to have been κεκυρωμένον in Abraham, which was afterwards solemnly promulgated through Moses. Ribera also adds in vain in this place: There was no need to say anything about the new law or that of Christ, which has no sacrifice except that of the body and blood of Christ, and sacraments, which have the power of sanctifying from the passion and blood of Christ. As if, indeed, the Apostle were saying nothing in this place about the new law, as they call it, when he proposes its supreme and inexplicable power. Schlichtingius makes the same error when he interprets this passage concerning time, and says: The Apostle uses the word παραϐάσεων, that is, of transgressions, by which grave sins are wont to be denoted, in order to show what kind of sins are especially remitted in the New Testament, namely, grave ones, for which in the Old Testament no expiation, but only the penalty of death, was established. Therefore he adds: Which under the former Testament, understand, remained, or could not be expiated, for which no remission was then granted. He seems, however, to have wished to indicate at the same time that those grave sins had a place under the Old Testament, or were accustomed to be committed, while the New Testament, together with their guilt, takes them away entirely in those who believe in its promises from the heart. Thus Schlichtingius, who afterwards proceeds to give a reason why the Apostle mentioned only the graver sins. But as for the fact, he says, that only the expiation of transgressions or graver crimes is mentioned, that is not done as if all lighter sins are not also expiated under the New Testament: But it is just as if it had been said, even of those transgressions, etc. For Scripture is sometimes accustomed to speak simply, so that it does not exclude others, but teaches that those are also included about which there could be greater doubt, and which, if they are considered to be included, it must be established much more so concerning the rest. Thus, among other things, David in Psalm 25:8 pronounces concerning God, as the Hebrew text has it, the Lord is good and upright, therefore he will teach sinners in the way, that is, even sinners, not only righteous men, or, as he immediately adds, the meek and humble, of whom he affirms this. Thus also Paul says that the impious is justified by God, not that he justifies this one alone, but that he justifies this one also, Romans IV. Or the author mentions grave sins only for this reason, that he may show that they are especially expiated under the New Testament, and that this is the proper fruit of the New Testament and of the expiation of Christ. But if the guilt of grave sins is taken away under the New Testament, it must be judged that this is done much more in lighter ones. Add that those grave sins could have disturbed the conscience much more than lighter offenses, since for the latter some expiation was then granted in the law, from which it was at least permitted to suspect that God, for His immense goodness, would also wash away the penalty of eternal death, but for the former, clearly none. Thus he, who 1. hallucinates in this, that he says grave sins only are noted by παραβάσεων, when neither the force of the word nor usage demands it. For above in chapter II. 2. παράβασις and παρακοὴ are joined, and they designate any disobedience, not just grave and enormous. 2. He errs when he thinks that the Apostle understands not the very things which were ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ, but such sins for which redemption happens through the death of Christ, when the Apostle speaks expressly of transgressions ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ. Therefore, he by no means pronounces that they have redemption from Christ only of such, but rather of them themselves. 3. He sins in this, that he says grave sins had a place under the Old Testament, or were accustomed to be committed, when the New Testament together with their guilt takes them away entirely. For if the discourse is about time, grave sins are committed in the time of both the New and the Old Testament: But if we speak of the institution of either Testament, neither grants a place to grave sins, both wish them to be taken away entirely: But if we understand it concerning the virtue prevailing against sins, it is most true that it is the same in the New Testament, but not in the Old: Yet it is also certain that that virtue was dispensed backwards under the Old Testament. Whence 4. he also slips in this, that he says that under the Old Testament grave offenses remained, or could not be expiated, and that no remission of them was then granted, that for lighter offenses only some expiation was granted in the law, from which it was permitted to suspect that God, for His immense goodness, would also wash away the penalty of eternal death. For even if by the force of the Old Testament no remission of sins was made, but the whole was drawn from the goods of the New Testament prefigured, nevertheless remission happened under the Old Testament; indeed the Old Testament was ordered so that it might serve to shadow forth those mysteries, whence remission of sins could be received through faith. It remains, therefore, that the redemption (ἀπολύτρωσιν) or liberation made by a paid price from the transgressions ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ is universal, and of all times, and not to be restricted only to either the Old or the New Testament. For every transgression of all men is ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ, because in it is the tribunal of divine justice, that is, the moral law, which concludes all men under sin by divine authority, so that mercy may happen to all, Romans XI. 32. Galatians III. 22. And to that extent also the law is a pedagogue to Christ, insofar as it so argues transgressions that it nevertheless promises no redemption (ἀπολύτρωσιν) in itself, but rather drives us to seek elsewhere, Galatians III. 24. Whence it is also said to be added and imposed because of transgressions (παραβάσεων χάρις), Galatians III. 19. The Syrian clearly translates it thus: Therefore he himself became the Mediator of the new covenant, who through his death became the same Redeemer for those who had transgressed the former covenant. Calvin in this place commemorates the force and effect of the death of Christ, when he says that the price was paid for sins which could not be washed away under the former Testament by the blood of animals, by which words he wished to lead the Jews from the law to Christ. For if the weakness of the law is so great that whatever remedies it applies for expiating sins, they do not at all perform what they figure: Who would rest in it as in a harbor? This, I say, one thing ought to have abundantly stimulated them to seek the correction of the law, because it could not be but that they were perpetually anxious. On the contrary, when one has come to Christ, because in Him we obtain full redemption, there is nothing that can trouble us any longer, etc. Nor does Osiander deny it: As certain as it is that Christ died for our sins, so firm also is the covenant of grace, or the New Testament: In which the remission of sins and eternal life are offered and given to all who believe in Christ. For the first Testament argues our sins: the second Testament forgives them. For it is not the account of the former time, but rather of the former pact, that is held, as we observed at the preceding chapter.

In vain, therefore, is Grotius, comparing the filth of the times of the Old Testament and the people of Israel with the time of the New Testament and the Christian people. Salvation, however, is called an inheritance, because believers are gratuitously adopted into it as children of God in regeneration, and it is given to them not by merit, but by the grace of Him who, because of Christ, has become the Father of believers, Revelation 21, 6. 7. We easily admit Grotius's observation that the redemption of transgressions (ἀπολύτρωσις παραβάσεων) is from transgressions (ἀπὸ παραβάσεων). But he does not rightly explain the redemption from transgressions as concerning those being perpetrated, since it must be understood of those already perpetrated, not that we cease to sin, but that we have been liberated from the guilt and penalty of sins to which we were liable, which those who enjoy through faith, namely justified by God and having obtained the remission of sins, are in peace with God, Romans V. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Καὶ διὰ τῦτο διαθήκης καινῆς Μεσίτης ἐστὶν ] בְּרִית, quod pactum significat aut fœdus (Est autem fœdus non omne pactum, sed publicum) Græci Inter- pretes vertunt διαθήκην, Latini testamentum, non illo spe- ciali sensu juris civilis, sed generaliori, quia testatio est voluntatis, de qua re diximus in Prolegomenis ad Evan- gelia: Sed & testamentum illud, ut in jure civili sumi- tur, ubi hæredis institutioni, ut fieri solet, conditio addi- tur, aut legatorum fideive commissorum onera, est pa- ctum quoddam & quidem eo nobilius, quia testatoris morte secuta nullam jam mutationem recipit. Et pro- pterea scriptor hic pactum Dei novum, quod perfectius esse debuit priore, vult esse etiam Testamentum in illo significatu potiore sive juris civilis. Propterea, inquit, fa- ctus Christus Μεσίτης non veteris, sed novi pacti, quia hoc pactum novum non pecudum sanguine, sed ipsius Μεσίτε fuit sarciendum. Μεσίτης est, qui pacem inter par- tes efficit, ut explicavimus Gal. III. 19. Solet autem sæpe pax fieri sub certis legibus prius implendis, quam pax va- leat. Talis pax etiam διαθήκη est.

Ὅπως θανάτε γενομένε] Ipsius, non victimarum. Id enim facile intelligitur ex dictis supra.

Εἰς ἀπολύτρωσιν τῶν ἐπὶ τῇ πρώτῃ διαθήκῃ παραβάσεων] Mors ejus intercessit eum in finem, ut liberarentur homi- nes ab illis peccatis, quæ in populo Dei dicto ante Chri- stum ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον valuerant. Idem sensus qui Act. XIII. 38. ubi dicta vide. Ἀπολύτρωσις quod supra 12. λύτρωσις, ἀπολύτρωσις προβάσεων, id est, ἀπὸ παραβάσεων, quomodo apud Ciceronein liberatio culpæ pro à culpa. Ἐν τῇ πρώ- τῃ διαθήκῃ, id est, prioris pacti tempore. Non poterat il- lius temporis multitudo cum multitudine Christiana Apostolicorum temporum ulla ex parte comparari. Tantum ubique erat sordium non tantum in animo la- tentium, sed & foris apparentium. Alibi ἀπολύτρωσιν alio sensu sumi suis locis annotavimus. Sed huic loco id, quod diximus, optimè convenit. Nam qui cessat peccare, is jam ex lege novi pacti in pace est cum Deo Rom. V. 1.

Τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν λάβωσιν οἱ κεκλημένοι τῆς αἰωνία κληρονο- μίας] Qui sic liberati sunt à peccatis, eis continget res in pacto novo promissa, quæ est vita æterna 1. Tim. IV. 8. 2. Tim. I. 1. supra VIII. 6. Κεκλημένοι intellige cum effe- ctu, ut 1. Cor. I. 24. Judæ v. 1. Et cur vita æterna κληρονο- μίας appelletur nomine vide dicta Gal. III. 18. Eph. I. 14. 18. Col. III. 24. Ἐπαγγελίαν autem pro re promissa ha- bes & Luc. XXIV. 49. Act. I. 4. II. 33. Rom. IV. 13. & alibi.

A Sacerdotis munere transit ad Mediatoris, quæ hic cognata sunt, officium. Cur Christus Novi Te- stamenti Mediator sit: Nostræ nempe salutis gra- tia, utpote qui non tantum medium sese inter Deum Patrem & humanum genus fecerit, ut in gratiam nos reduceret apud Patrem, quæMediato- ris partes sunt;sed etiam Testamentum novum san- xiverit, ut morte ipsius interveniente in redempti- one eorum, quæ in primo Testamento manebant, hominesq; premebant, promissionem conseque- rentur, qui vocati sunt, æternam hæreditatem. Ne- xum ita exhibet Theophylactus: Quod deterrere quamplurimos videbatur infirmiores, quia illud sæpe ac multum usurporent, si Christus obiit mortem, quo pacto daturus est, quod promiserat? Id ipsum nunc Paulus leniens, ob id arguit Christi ratum esse & firmius Testamentum, quia mortuus sit. Neque enim dum superstites sumus, Testamenti nomen illud forti- tur, quod testando nos instituimus. Ut igitur (inquit)

puriores nos redderet, mortem subivit; & testamento nobis peccata remisit, & cælestium reliquit bono- rum fruitionem, nos inter & Patrem Mediator ef- fectus, cum Patri baudquaquam in animo esset, no- bis hereditatem relinquere, ut quibus acriter succen- sebat, & erat iratior, tanquam liberis à se alienis, Christus itaque intercessit, & Patrem nobis concilia- vit. Quo modo? Id namque quod erat nobis feren- dum ut contumacibus, ille jam tulit, & mortem quæ fuerit per nos subeunda, pro nobis subivit, effecitque hæreditate hac dignos.

Testamentum, non pactum, quod mutuo in- ter partes initur, vocat Apostolus, idque morte firmandum. Proprio ergo sensu, vel certè speciali potius quam generali pacti aut fœderis significati- one ita vocat. De Mediatore vid. quæ 1. Tim. II. 5. 6. Quo de itidem audiendus Theophylactus: Est igitur, pergit, & testamentum hoc per Filii mortem jam con- firmatum, quod minimè, ut ad indignos, hæredita- tem transmisit. Habet præterea & Testamentum hæ- redes. Sic enim inquiens testatus est Christus: Volo Pater, ut ubi sum ego, illic & ministros meos esse: Quos vero exhæredaverit ille, sic exprimit: Non pro omni- bus peto, sed pro his, qui me & professi sunt & credi- derunt. Habet insuper testamentum & testes, ut pa- tet ex his, testimonium autem perhibet de me, qui mi- sit me Pater, & Paracletus testimonium perhibebit de me, & vos testimonium perhibebitis.

Mediator autem Novi Testamenti dicitur, quia mediatione sua id effecit, ut Testamentum novum vel gratiæ condi possit, quod à Veteri Testam. in eo distinguitur, quod sub illo, quantum ad pactum legale, quod in ipso priori obtinebat, transgressio- nes manserint, non expiatæ illius vigore aut virtu- te fuerint, etiamfi tempore Veteris Testamenti o- mnino condonatæ sint, sed vigore fœderis gra- tiæ, cujus Mediator est Christus, qui & Angelus fœ- deris gratiæ dicitur, Mal. III. 1. Per Mediatorem er- go Novi Testam. & vi fœderis ipsius gratiæ, inter- veniente morte Mediatoris, & Testatoris effectum est, ut quæ in veteri mansere, prævaricationes, eo- rum hæredes æternæ hæreditatis redemptionem, vel liberationem ab iisdem, sed mediante λύτρῳ san- guinis Christi, ceu hæredes in hoc Testamento in- stituti, filiique adoptionis, promissionũ, vel ea quæ promissa sunt, consequantur. Promissa autem erant remissio peccatorum, salus & æterna vita novo gra- tiæ fœdere, eademque per Testamentum peculia- re sancita, & hæredibus ex mera gratia legata. Vi- des, inquit Theophylactus, quemadmodum ut nos re- dimeret Christus, mortem obierit, quo ergo pacto vel ex imbecillitate & impotentia effectum id esse existi- mas? Quandoquidem Christi mors tam efficax fuerit & valida, ut per eam legis prævaricatio omnis ad sani- tatem redierit. Cur igitur ad legem confugis, quæ tam impotens sit & imbecilla, ut quot vel in se fue- rit prævaricatum, corrigere nequeat? Nec tamen ideo fit, quia illa iniquior, sed quia infirmior sit. Ad verba repromissionem accipiant: Nisi enim, inquit, Christi nos obitus à peccatis & facinoribus exemis- set, quibus Patrem jam hostem reddideramus, quo pacto effemus divinam hanc hæreditatem adepti. Novam hic collationis partem assignat B. Hun- nius, qua fœdus cum fœdere, novum cum antiqno tanquam veritatem cum umbris ac typis comparat. Et hac quoque in parte ingens ponit discrimen A- postolus, quod illi quidem Pontifices ministri erant Testamenti Veteris: Christus autem Novi Testamen- ti non minister, sed Pontifex & Mediator est. Infert autem Apostolus hoc membrum comparationis ex prioribus hoc sensu: Quia Christus sanguine non alieno sed proprio ingressus est in sancta, & quia is sanguis ad tollendam prævaricationem efficax fuit, non, ut brutorum sanguis, typice, sed vere & re ipsa: Consequitur hinc, Christum non Veteris Testamenti Mediatorem esse (quod umbris sanciebatur, id est, sanguine brutorum, vero quidem, sed qui Christi san- guinem adumbraret, nec tollendis peccatis per se suf- ficeret) sed Novi Testamenti: Ubi sua propria morte intercedente redemptionem contulit eam, quæ nullis Leviticis sacrificiis vere impetrari poterat: liberans scilicet à prævaricationibus, quæ sub Veteri Testamen- to erant, id est, quæ per Testamentum Vetus ejusq; sacerdotium & sacrificia tolli non poterant, nisi qua- tenus credentes ex Veteri Testamento respicerent ad hunc Novi Testamenti reconciliatorem. Novi ergo Testamenti supremum finem assignat, qui est salus animarum perpetua, & consequutio hæreditatis æternæ, quæ olim propter venturum Messiam promis- sa, & nunc per eundem acquisita est credentibus in ipsum. Vis argumenti ergo, notante Estio, hæc est: Quia Christus in ara crucis sanguinem suum fun- dens semetipsum obtulit Deo, & per hoc æternam redemptionem nobis acquisivit, qui sunt Novi Te- stamenti effectus, utique est Novi illius Testam. quod per Prophetam Jeremiam promissum est, Mediator quippe, qui sanguine suo Testamenti illius promissa sancivit. Nec incommode συνέχειαν textus sic exhibet Piscator: Quoniam affirmavit, Christum oblatione sui ipsius, hoc est, sua morte ac- quisivisse remissionem peccatorum & vitam æternam, nunc deinceps causam exponit, cur ita fieri oportue- rit: ac omnino has duas causas affert: Una est, quod hoc modo necesse erat, ratum fieri Testamentum Dei, cujus Mediator ipse fuerat constitutus. Hanc cau- sam exponit v. 15. 16. 17. Altera causa est, quod hoc modo præstare eum re ipsa oportebat, quod per Veteris Testamenti ritum fuerat præfiguratum: quippe quod sanguine pecudum effuso & asperso sanciebatur. Hanc causam exponit à v. 18. ad v. 24. usque. Prioris causæ expositio comprehenditur hoc syllogismo: Qui constitutus est Mediator alicujus Testamenti, ejus mortem intercedere necesse est, ut ratum fiat testa- mentum ac valeat, v. 16. & 17. Atqui Christus consti tutus est Mediator alicujus Testamenti, videlicet Novi Testamenti, in principio v. 15. Ergo Christi mor- tem intercedere necesse fuit ad testamenti illius rati- ficationem, videlicet ad acquirendum vocatis (seu credentibus) remissionem peccatorum & vitam æter- nam, reliqua parte v. 15. Posterioris causæ expositio comprehenditur syllogismo isto: Si Vetus Testamen- tum sanguine pecudum dedicatum atque sancitum fuit: Oportuit Novum Testamentum sanciri sangui- ne ipsius Christi, tanquam per pecudes illas præfigu- rati. Atqui Vetus Testamentum sanguine pecudum sancitum fuit, v. 18. 19. 20. 21. 22. & priore parte v. 23. Ergo Novum Testamentum oportuit ipsius Christi sanguine sanciri, posteriori parte v. 23.

B. Dorotheus notat hic 1.
