That appearance in the heavens, which Grotius makes the oblation itself against the mind of the Apostle, Crellius and Schlichtingius explain thus: that Christ is similar to one appearing and interceding for others only insofar as, being desirous of our salvation and bearing the greatest care for it, he nevertheless does not have the power of saving from himself, but received all of it from God, so much so that, having regard for this matter, Christ may indeed be said to care solicitously that we be saved, but God himself is to be said to confer salvation upon us according to his mercy. But who does not see how forced this interpretation is? To intercede for for our salvation, namely, is nothing else than to care anxiously for our salvation, and to bear the greatest care for it? But what kind of power, and whence, Christ has regarding our salvation, it is not the place of this passage to explain. The Socinians themselves are certainly bound to acknowledge that in the legal Pontiff there was an appearance distinct from the oblation, although both were joined, and the Pontiff did indeed appear; but the victim or the blood of the victim was offered. Why, therefore, when the Apostle distinguishes these things so exquisitely even in Christ the antitype, do the Socinians confuse them? But, they say, both the oblation and the appearance of our Pontiff, just as also the intercession, are in reality the same thing, namely, if the appearance and intercession are taken not for the bare arrival of Christ to the Father, but, as it ought to be done here, joined with the care of our salvation. For while Christ appears, he offers himself, and while he offers himself, he appears: but while he both offers and appears, he intercedes. Is this not a most wretched confusion? Who, therefore, would the Apostle infer an iteration of the passion from an iteration of the oblation, if the oblation were only an appearance? Could it not be said that he appears more often, even if he did not suffer more often? Since an oblation of a living thing cannot be made without slaughter and suffering, as Schlichting and Crell have admitted, can an appearance, however joined with the care of our salvation, not be made without slaughter and suffering? Since in the victim offered by Christ his bloody death or the shedding of blood is included at the same time, as the same men admitted at verse 23, is the shedding of blood also included in the appearance of Christ? But we dismiss these portents, abundantly refuted elsewhere.

Schlichting attempts to overturn the very satisfaction of Christ from that ἐμφανισμῷ [appearance], when he says, where it has been satisfied for another, there the matter does not need an oblation, an appearance, and an intercession. His syllogism is this: For whom it is necessary that Christ should also after his session at the right hand before God the Father ἐμφανίζεσθαι [appear], for them a satisfaction in every way rendered to God the Father has not been made. The reason is that there is no need for intercession where one acts by right. But for the human race there is need even after the session of Christ at the right hand for an ἐμφανισμῷ [appearance]: Therefore for it a satisfaction rendered to God has not been made. Resp. to the major proposition by denying it. For one thing is satisfaction without the tempering of mercy, and another with such a tempering. Satisfaction of the former kind does not require perpetual intercession. With satisfaction of the latter kind, intercession can very well consist. But such is the satisfaction of Christ for us. For even if that, speaking absolutely, is most precious and of infinite efficacy, yet from the tempering of mercy with justice it has come about that it profits and is applied to us. For that the satisfaction of Christ for us is accepted before God, that is, that the punishment which we deserved has been transferred to the Mediator, and that justice does not inhere in the Divine debtor, which is most fitting in punishments that are by no means wont to be exacted from the innocent, proceeds from mere mercy. And so, by intercession before God the Father, that which was acquired by satisfaction is most rightly applied to us. We add to the major also this, that once satisfaction has been rendered, intercession for him for whom satisfaction has been made is not necessary. Yet it can be done out of superabundance of love toward him for whom satisfaction was made, and therefore it is not impossible. Thus, therefore, the satisfaction of Christ, because of his superabundant love toward the human race, admits of intercession, although it is not absolutely necessary, as here B. Dorscheus.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Οὐ γὰρ εἰς χειροποίητα ἅγια εἰσῆλθεν ὁ χριστὸς, ἀντίτυπα τῶν ἀληθινῶν] Χειροποίητα intellige, quæ facta sunt arte hominum, ac proinde non vi Divina. Vide supra IX, 11. 24. Ἀντίτυπος vox est anceps, nam & de figu- ra dicitur, ut hic; & de re per figuram significata, ut 1. Petr. III. 21. In Glossario ἀντίτυπον exemplum, exemplar. Idem sensus Sap. IX. 8. Εἶπας οἰκοδομῆσαι ναὸν ἐν ὄρει ἁγίῳ σου καὶ ἐν πόλει κατασκηνώσεώς σου, θυσιαστήριον μίμημα σκη- νῆς ἁγίας, ἣν προητοίμασας ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς. Philo de Mosis vita: Τὰ ἄδυτα τῆς σκηνῆς, ἅπερ ἐστὶ συμβολικῶς νοητά. Sic & Rabbi Israël de anima inferius sanctuarium ait fa- ctum ad similitudinem superioris. Ergo hic ἀντίτυπα idem, quod Sapienti Ebræo μιμήματα, τύποι Rom. V. 14. 1. Cor. X. 11. Et ἀληθινὰ hic ut supra VIII. 2. quæ νοητά Philoni.

Ἀλλʼ εἰς αὐτὸν τὸν οὐρανὸν] Nempe ἐρανο͂ν, id est, sum- mum cœlum. Sic ἅγια aliquoties dixit, & dicet pro ἅγια ἁγίων. Id enim ex rei natura satis intelligitur.

Νῦν ἐμφανισθῆναι τῷ προσώπῳ τῦ Θεοῦ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν] Id est εἰς τὸ ἐμφανισθῆναι, quale loquendi compendium & supra habuimus. Ἐμφανίζεσθαι apparere, conspiciendum se dare, ut Matth. XXVII. 53. Φανερῶσθαι infra 26. Syrus hic דְנִתְחֲזֵא ut conspici se faceret. Persitat in similitudine. Nam & summus Sacerdos dicitur apud Deum apparere, ubi stat apud arcam. Sic Christus apparet coram solio Majestatis, ut nostras res Deo commendet, supra VII. 25.

De voce ἀντίτυπος B. Dorstheus: Quod taberna- culum manufactum ἀντίτυπον dicitur, non in respe- ctu ad typum, sed ad πρωτότυπον sive ἀρχήτυπον dictum est. Sunt enim ἀντίτυπα idem, quod vers. 23. ὑποδείγματα. Ὑπόδειγμα autem & σκιὰ Ebr. V. conjunguntur. Sunt igitur ἀντίτυπα hoc loco ima- gines ex prototypo expresse. Non igitur quasi sint ἀντὶ τῦ τύπυ ex adverso typi seu imaginis, sicut res ipsa sua imagini opponitur, quomodo alias typum & antitypum solemus opponere, sed quasi sint τύποι ἀντὶ τῦ πράγματος typi seu imagines ex adverso ipsius rei positæ. Quare perinde est, acsi typi sim- pliciter fuissent dicta χειροποίητα ἅγια, sicut 1. Cor. X. 6. & 11. res Veteris Testamenti typi vocantur: Ita & 1. Tim. II. v, 6. ἀντίλυτρον pro λύτρῳ posi- tum est.

Porro meliori hostia, & sanguine victimali Pon- tifici Novi Testamenti Christo opus fuisse, docet Apostolus; quia non ingredi debuit in sanctum sanctorum manu factum, in quod Pontifices Vete- ris Testamenti sanguine pecuino ingressi sunt; sed in cœlum ipsum, ut nunc compareat coram facie Dei pro nobis. At non ea ratione, ut sæpius sese offerret in hostiam, quo iteraretur sæpius ingres- sus cum sanguine proprio: sed ut Pontifex ingre- ditur in sanctum sanctorum quotannis in san- guine alieno; alioqui oportebat eum sæpius pa- ti & mortem subire ab origine mundi, quo posset hominum peccata inde à conditu mundi expiare, qui non minus eorum expiatione opus habuerunt, quam qui Veter. Testamenti tempore vixere, aut sub Novo Testamento, iisque sanguine & morte sua expiatis cum sangine proprio in cœlum in- gredi.

Ex quo patet luculentissime, quod προσφέ- ρειν v. 25. non sit ἐμφανίζειν ostendere se in sanctua- rio cœli, ut Grotius Socinianos sequutus perver- tit, quia accurate hæc distinguit Apostolus v. 24. 25. apparere vultui Dei pro nobis, & semetipsum offerre. Non ergo hæc inter sese confundenda. Et oblationem, ac passionem commutat, vers. 25. 26. ut & mortem v. 27. & oblationem vers. 28. ubi Socini- sta illi, Crellius & Schlichtingius ita ad vers. 26. Pu- tat Christum non debere sæpe seipsum offerre. Nam alioquin & sæpe pati eum oportebat, cum oblatio rei vivæ fieri nequeat, sine cæde & perses- sione. Confundit etiam Grotius tò ἐμφανισθῆναι vers. 24. Φανερῶσθαι, vers. 26. Nam ibi de ap- paritione Christi in cœlis coram vultu Dei, vel intercessione pro nobis: Hic vero de apparitione in terris ad oblationem, ut victima fieret pro no- bis εἰς ἀθέτησιν ἁμαρτίας, agitur. Illa in cœlis apparitio, quam Grotius ipsam oblationem contra mentem Apostoli facit, Crellius & Schlichtingius sic explicant, quod Christus hactenus pro aliis appa- renti & interpellanti sit similis, quatenus salutis no- stræ cupidus ejusque maximam curam gerens, ser- vandi tamen potestatem ex seipso non habet, sed eam omnem à Deo accepit, adeo ut hujus rei habita ra- tione Christus quidem, ut fervemur, solicite cura- re, Deus vero ipse salutem nobis pro sua miseri- cordia conferre dicendus sit. Sed quis non videt, quam coacta hæc sit interpretatio? Interpellare pro pro salute nostra nempe esse nihil aliud, quam so- licite curare nostram salutem, ejusque maximam curam gerere? Qualem autem, & unde potesta- tem habeat Christus quoad salutem nostram, huj9 loci non est explicare. Agnoscere utique tenen- tur illi ipsi Sociniani in Pontifice legali apparitio- nem distinctam fuisse ab oblatione, licet utraque esset conjuncta, & appareret quidem Pontifex; ob- lata autem fuerit victima seu sanguis victimæ. Cur ergo quum Apostolus hæc etiam tam exquisite in Christo antitypo distinguat, confundunt ea Soci- niani? At nostri Pontificis, inquiunt, & oblatio & apparitio, quemadmodum & interpellatio, nempe si apparitio & interpellatio non pro nudo Christi ad Patrem adventu, sed ut hic fieri debet, cum salutis nostræ cura conjuncto accipiatur, re ipsa idem sunt. Dum enim apparet Christus, seipsum offert, & dum seipsum offert, apparet: dum autem & offert & ap- paret, interpellat. Nonne hæc pessima est confu- sio? Qui ergo Apostolus ex oblationis iteratione iterationem passionis inferret, si oblatio tantum esset apparitio? Annon sæpius apparere dici pos- set, etiamsi non sæpius pateretur. Quum oblatio rei vivæ fieri nequeat sine cæde & perpessione, ut fassi sunt Schlichtingius & Crellius, an etiam appari- tio, utut cum salutis nostræ cura conjuncta, sine cæde & perpessione fieri nequit? Quum in Christi oblati victima includatur simul mors illius cruenta seu effusio sanguinis, ut iidem fassi ad vers. 23. num etiam in apparitione Christi includitur effusio san- guinis? Sed hæc portenta mittimus, alibi abunde profligata.

Schlichtingius ex illo ἐμφανισμῷ evertere cona- tur ipsam Christi satisfactionem, cum dicit, ubi al- teripiane satisfactum est, ibi oblatione, apparitione & interpellatione res non indiget. Syllogismus ejus hic est: Pro quibus necesse est, Christum etiam post sessionem ad dextram apud Deum Patrem ἐμφανί- ζεσθαι, pro illis satisfactio omnimoda Deo Patri præ- stita non est. Ratio, quia non est opus interpellatio- ne, ubi jure agitur. Atqui pro genere humano opus est etiam post sessionem Christi ad dexteram ἐμφανισμῷ: Ergo pro illo satisfactio Deo præstita non est. Resp. ad majorem propositionem negando. Alia enim est satisfactio sine temperamento misericordiæ, & alia cum temperamento tali. Prioris generis satisfactio interpellationem perpetuam non re- quirit. Cum posterioris generis satisfactione in- terpellatio optime potest consistere. Talis au- tem est satisfactio Christi pro nobis. Etiamsi enim illa absolute loquendo pretiosissima sit, & infinitæ effi- caciæ, ex temperamento tamen misericordiæ cum ju- stitia factum est ut nobis prosit & applicetur. Quod enim Christi satisfactio pro nobis apud Deum acce- ptetur, hoc est pœna, quam nos meruimus, in Media- torem translata sit, nec justitia Divino reo inhæreat, quod in pœnis, quæ ab innocente exigi nequaquam solent, maxime conveniens est, ex mera misericordia promanat. Itaque interpellatione apud Deum Pa- trem rectissime nobis applicatur, quod satisfactione acquisitum est. Addimus ad majorem & illud, sa- tisfactione præstita interpellationem pro eo, pro quo satisfactum est, necessariam non esse. Posse tamen fieri ex superabundantia amoris erga illum, pro qua satisfactus est, adeoque non esse incompossibilem. Sic itaque satisfactio Christi propter superabundan- tem erga genus humanum amorem interpellatio- nem admittit, licet absolute non sit necessaria, ut hic B. Dorscheus.

## 9:25
Vers. 25. ῾Ουδ᾽ ἵνα πολλάκις προσφέρῃ ἑαυτὸν [Nor that he should offer himself often] ὐδὲ here means: But not. After the proposed similarities, he also shows certain disparities. The High Priest entered into the ark of God every year: Christ to the throne of God once; never to depart from there: The High Priest carried with him the blood of the victim in place of the victim. Christ himself, who had been made a victim. Truly this one oblation performed immensely more than those so often repeated. Understand προσφέρεσιν [to offer] here as ἐμφανίζειν [to appear], to show himself in the heavenly sanctuary.

Ὥσπερ ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς εἰσέρχεται εἰς τὰ ἅγια κατ᾽ ἐνιαυ- τὸν ἐν αἵματι ἀλλοτρίῳ [As the High Priest enters into the holy places year by year with the blood of others] εἰς τὰ ἅγια [into the holy places] is said briefly, as we have already warned, for εἰς τὰ ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων [into the holy of holies]. And ἐν [in/with] for with, as διὰ [through] above 12. A similar manner of speaking 1 John 5:6, Gen. 32:10, Hosea 4:3, and elsewhere. He uses the present tense, as also above 13 and 22, because that temple and worship still remained.

Latin:

Vers. 25. ῾Ουδ᾽ ἵνα πολλάκις προσφέρῃ ἑαυτὸν] ὐδὲ hic valet: At non. Post propositas similitudines etiam dispa- ritates quasdam ostendit. Summus Sacerdos quotan- nis ad arcam Dei intrabat: Christus ad solium Dei se- r mel; nunquam inde abiturus: Summus Sacerdos san- guinem victimæ vice victimæ secum ferebat. Christus semet, qui factus victima fuerat. Nimirum hæc una ob- latio immensum præstabat illis toties repetitis. Προσφέρεσιν hic intellige ἐμφανίζειν, ostendere se in sanctuario cœlesti.

Ὥσπερ ὁ Ἀρχιερεὺς εἰσέρχεται εἰς τὰ ἅγια κατ᾽ ἐνιαυ- τὸν ἐν αἵματι ἀλλοτρίῳ] Εἰς τὰ ἅγια breviter dictum, ut jam monuimus pro εἰς τὰ ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων. Et ἐν pro cum, ut διὰ supra 12. Simile loquendi genus 1. Joh. 5, 6. Gen. 32, 10. Oseæ 4, 3. & alibi. Utitur præsenti tempore, ut & su- pra 13. & 22. quia templum & cultus ille adhuc manebant.

## 9:26
Vers. 26. Ἐπεὶ ἔδει αὐτὸν πολλάκις παθεῖν ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου [Since he would have needed to suffer often from the foundation of the world] If there had been any greater efficacy in a repeated oblation, it would have been expedient that Christ not be promised for so long, but be sent immediately after the world was founded, so that he could suffer and offer in every century or at least every jubilee. Ἔδει [it would have been necessary] often does not signify a precise necessity, but that which is better or more useful; see Luke 2:44, ch. 13:16, ch. 19:5. So above ἀνάγκη [necessity] v. 23. From the foundation of the world, i.e., long ago, as Luke 11:50.

This distortion of the words from the foundation of the world is found likewise from Luke 11:50 in the Crellius-Schlichting commentary on this passage. But the Apostle does not conclude thus: If there had been any greater efficacy in a repeated oblation, it would have been expedient that Christ be sent immediately after the world was founded. But as the context and the words themselves demand, if he had been obliged to offer himself more often, it would have been necessary for him to suffer right from the origin of the world. That, furthermore, the property of the word ἔδει [it would have been necessary] and the received meaning of the phrase ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου [from the foundation of the world], from which even Luke 11:50 has not departed, demand: which, when Grotius sees that they do not suit his glosses, he has not feared to twist even that so that ἔδει [it would have been necessary] is only that which is better or more useful, and from the foundation of the world is long ago. Is this not an unworthy method of treating scripture? Theophylact expresses the meaning thus: For if, he says, he were about to offer himself more often and to undergo death, it would have been necessary more frequently; since he was about to make an offering through his own blood. Estius approves our meaning: That which he had said, that Christ did not enter into heaven in order to offer himself often, he proves by a reduction to the absurd. For since that offering is not made without blood and death, it would behoove him to suffer and die often, which clearly contradicts the ordinance of God and the glory of Christ, as one who once overcame death by his own death, and rose again to immortal life, is demanded again and more often for death. We know, says the Apostle in Rom. VI, that Christ rising from the dead dies no more, death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that he died, he died unto sin once. He adds, however, 'from the foundation of the world,' both because sin began right from the beginning in our first parents, and because if he were to suffer often, it would be no less necessary in the first ages than in the following ones, since the reason for all times is the same, assuming the necessity of repeating the sacrifice.

But now once at the end of the ages for the putting away of sin by his sacrifice he has been manifested] 'Now' here is not of time but of opposition, as above II. 8, VIII. 6. That it is not true, what one might imagine, that a repeated offering is of more value, appears from this, that Christ neither suffered often (which Paul also said in Rom. VI. 9, 10) nor showed himself often in the heavenly sanctuary, but once, and that while the world was so approaching its destruction that it seems not even time remains in which Christ could be sent again and suffer again. Just as Paul, so also this writer inclined to the belief that the ruin of the world was imminent. Thus the 'ends of the ages' are called the times of the Apostles, 1 Cor. X. 11. That it would stand somewhat longer than they thought was revealed first to Peter, then to John, as appears from the second epistle of Peter, ch. III, v. 3, and from the Apocalypse. What 'end of the age' or 'ages' is, is easily understood from Matt. XIII. 39, 40, 49, XXIV. 3, XXVIII. 20. There are, however, learned men who understand 'end of the ages' with respect to the temple and the Jewish commonwealth. Christ 'has been manifested,' that is, 'appeared,' as he has already spoken, offered himself, and showed himself to God the Father in the heavenly sanctuary. Moreover, both are passive used for the Hithpahel in the Hebrew manner. For 'has been manifested' here is equivalent to נתגלה, and

of the sacrifice itself, that is, after he himself was made a victim. But both of this εἰς ἀθέτησιν ἁμαρτίας, so that sin might be extinguished in us. Thus we had ἀθέτησιν ἐντολῆς above. This is done, however, first through the passion of Christ, which generates faith in us, which purifies hearts: Then through the appearance of Christ before God, because there Christ obtains for us those aids which are necessary by reason of the times.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Ἐπεὶ ἔδει αὐτὸν πολλάκις παθεῖν ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου] Si aliqua major efficacia fuisset in oblatione re- petita, expediisset, Christum non tam diu promitti, sed mitti illico post mundum conditum, ut posset singulis seculis aut certe jubilæis pati & offerre. Ἔδει sæpe non præcisam significat necessitatem, sed id, quod melius aut utilius est; vid. Luc. 2, 44. c. 13, 16. c. 19, 5. Sic supra ἀνάγκη v. 23. A fundatione mundi, i. e. jam olim, ut Luc. 11, 50.

Hæc verborum à fundatione mundi detorsio è Luc. XI. 50. habetur itidem in Crellio Schlichtingia- no commentario ad hunc locum. Non autem ita concludit Apostolus: Si aliqua major efficacia fuis- set in oblatione repetita, expediisset Christum illico mitti post mundum conditum. Sed uti contextus, & verba ipsa poscunt, si sæpius seipsum offerre de- buisset, necessum fuisset ipsum jam inde ab origine mundi pati. Id porro & verbi ἔδει proprietas & si- gnificatio recepta phraseos ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, à qua nec Luc. XI. 50. recessum est, postulant: quas quum suæ glossæ non convenire videat Grotius, il- la etiam ita torquere veritus non est, ut ἔδει tantu sit id, quod melius aut utilus est, & à fundatione mundi sit jam olim. Annon hæc indigna scriptu- ram tractandi ratio? Theophylactus ita sensum ex- primit: Si enim, inquit, seipsum esset sæpius oblatu- rus & ut mortem subiret, frequentius fuisset necesse; quandoquidem per proprium sanguinem oblatio- nem esset facturus. Approbat sensum nostrum Esti- us: Quod dixerat, Christum non ideo introiisse in cœlum, ut sæpe seipsum offerat, id probat deductione ad absurdum. Cum enim oblatio illa non fiat sine sanguine & morte, oporteret eum sæpe pati ac mori, quod ordinationi DEI & gloriæ Christi plane repu- gnat, ut qui semel mortem morte sua superavit, & ad vitam immortalem resurrexit, iterum atque sæ- pius reposcatur ad mortem. Scimus, inquit Apo- stolus Rom. VI. quod Christus resurgens ex mortuis jam non moritur amplius, mors illa ultra non domi- nabitur. Quod enim mortuus est, peccato mortu- us est semel. Addit autem ab origine mundi, tum quia peccatum cœpit jam inde ab initio in primis pa- rentibus, tum quia si sæpe passurus erat, non minus id oportebat primis seculis, quam sequentibus, cum sit omnium temporum eadem ratio, supposita necessitate iterandi sacrificii.

Νῦν δὲ ἅπαξ ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ τῶν αἰώνων εἰς ἀθέτησιν ἁμαρ- τίας μιὰ τῆς θυσίας ἀυτῦ πεφανέρωται] Νῦν hic non est temporis sed oppositionis, ut supra II. 8. VIII. 6. Non esse verum id, quod quis imaginari possit, oblationem repeti- tam sæpe plus valere, inde apparet, quod Christus nec sæpe passus est, (quod & Paulus dixit Rom. VI. 9. 10.) nec sæpe se ostendit in sanctuario cœlesti, sed semel, idque mundo adeo ad interitum suum appropinquante, ut ne tempus quidem superesse, videatur, quo Christus denuo mitti & denuo pati possit. Sicut Paulus ita & hic scriptor in id propendebant, ut crederent de propinquo immine- re mundi ruinam. Sic τέλη αἰώνων dicuntur Aposto- lorum tempora, 1. Cor. I. 11. Aliquanto diutius quam illi putarunt, staturum Petro primum, deinde Johanni pa- tefactum est, ut ex epistola II. c. III. v. 3. Petri & ex Apo- calypsi apparet. Συντέλεια αἰῶνος vel αἰώνων quid sit, intelligi facile est, ex Matth. XIII. 39. 40. 49. XXIV. 3. XXVIII. 20. Sunt tamen viri eruditi, qui συντέλειαν αἰώ- νων intelligunt respectu templi & reipublicæ Judaicæ. Christus πεφανέρωται, id est ἐνεφανίσθη, ut jam loquutus est, obtulit se, & ostendit Deo Patri in sanctuario cœle- sti. Est autem utrumque passivum pro Hithpahel mo- re Ebræo. Nam πεφανέρωται hic valet נתגלה, δὲ

τῆς θυσίας αὑτῆς, id est, postquam ipse victima fuit factus. Utrumque autem hoc εἰς ἀθέτησιν ἁμαρτίας, ut peccatum in nobis extingueretur. Sic ἀθέτησιν ἐντολῆς habuimus supra. Fit autem hoc per passionem primum Christi, quæ fidem nobis ingenerat, quæ corda purificat: Dein- de per apparitionem Christi apud Deum, quia ibi Christus nobis ea impetrat auxilia, quæ temporum ratione sunt ne- cessaria.

## 9:27
Vers. 27. And inasmuch as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment.] Ἀπόκειται is reserved: It remains to die after this life is finished. Thus we have ἀπόκειται in Deut. XXXII. 34. 2 Tim. IV. 8. It is a general law laid upon men, that they should die. If it happens otherwise to some, as to Enoch and Elijah, they are nothing compared to such a great multitude of dying men. Afterwards the judgment, that is, afterwards they shall be set before God. For this is given to be understood from the name of judgment in Rom. XIV. 10. For καθ’ ὅσον other codices have καθ’ ὁ. Perhaps it had been written καθὼς. For a certain similarity of Christ with other men is brought forward. The Syriac is איכנא. The Latin is quemadmodum.

Grotius understands the oblation of Christ sometimes of the passion, sometimes of the offering of himself in the heavenly sanctuary, indeed of both. But why τὸ πεφανέρωται should be taken in the Hitpahel sense does not appear, except that Grotius judges it more convenient for his gloss: Which, however, we deny is to be understood of the appearance in heaven. The Apostle treats here of the φα- νερώσει ἐν σαρκὶ, of which 1 Tim. III. 16, which happened in the fullness of time Gal. IV. 4. For he appeared that he might destroy sins διὰ τῆς θυσίας through the sacrifice of his body, which was to be offered in death on the altar of the cross, just as for that reason he is said to have been offered once εἰς τὸ πολλῶν ἀνε- νεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας, v. 28. He appeared, that he might destroy the works of the Devil, 1 John III. 8. The words διὰ τῆς θυσίας ἁυτῦ are perversely rendered, after he himself was made a victim, because he did not appear after he was made a victim, but so that he might be made a victim; for he wished to be manifested in the flesh, and to be made a partaker of flesh and blood, as the Apostle testifies, Heb. II. 14, so that through his death he might destroy him who had the power of death; Grotius says that both, the oblation in passion and death, and the appearance in heaven, were done εἰς ἀθέτησιν ἁμαρτίας; which, although it can be said, is nevertheless not expressed by these words, but now once in the consummation of the age he appeared for the destruction of sin through his sacrifice. For the end of the appearance in the flesh is expressed, and it was the oblation of the body of Christ as a victim for the destruction of sin, which is done through expiation, when the reason of its powers and guilt is destroyed, and the remission of sins, when they are not imputed to us, but are pardoned to us by reason of fault and punishment. In the very consummation and end of the ages, says Theophylact, when the time had already arrived in which the sayings of the Prophets were to be fulfilled, and the lost wickedness of men had already reached its height, so that he might ἀθετήσῃ, that is, so that he might overcome sin, and take away all its confidence in itself by his oblation and sacrifice, that is, through the destruction of his flesh. Thomas, in Estius, interprets the consummation of the age as the last age of the world: The last age is the present state, after which there is no other state, just as there is no other age after old age. But just as in other ages there is a determined number of years, but not in old age: So it is not determined how long this state of the world ought to last, yet it is the consummation of the ages, because no other state remains. Thus he, citing also that of the Apostle 1 Cor. X. We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come. The same, says Estius, is the opinion of the ordinary gloss, and of Lyranus, and of others generally. What Grotius trifles about Paul's opinion concerning the end of the world has been touched upon elsewhere. St. Paul was led into all truth by the Holy Spirit no less here than was

St. Peter and St. John. But what is that truth, that the end of the world was imminent, when it was not imminent? Gregory of Nyssa, as Theophylact observes, asks here, why did the Son of God assume flesh in the consummation of the age? And he says: Just as the most skilled physicians, while the fever still remains in the vitals, and more sharply vexes the body of the sick man, and the heat of the sickness is increased and inflamed, bring no remedy to the languishing man that removes the causes of the languor, but wait for the disease to increase: So also does that Physician of souls deal with us. For he waits until all wickedness is completely uncovered, so that nothing remains of those things which are hidden, uncured; thus at last he will heal the uncovered and manifest evils. Estius renders the sense thus: Christ did not enter into heaven to offer himself often, for there was no need, since he who appeared once, and that at the time of the consummation of the ages, and was manifested to the world through his sacrifice, then indeed, when he openly offered himself on the cross, so, I say, he appeared, that by that oblation of his he might abolish and crush sin once and for all. But the force of the argument, and the scope and connection of the Apostolic treatment, was rightly expressed thus by the Blessed Dorschæus: The Apostle proves the difference between the sacrifice of the Old and New Testament, namely that the former is iterable: and to be continued through the succession of many sacrifices, but the latter is unrepeatable and to be performed once, and that by this argument: He who as Priest offers himself by his own blood and death for the sins of the whole world, he offers only once, and therefore does not offer himself reiterably. For if he had to offer himself repeatedly, and indeed for the sins of all ages, then it would be necessary for him to die many times from the very beginning of the world and onwards to the very end of the world. For from the very beginning of the world men have sinned, and have desired the remission of sins from the sacrifice of this prefigured priest. But this is repugnant to the Divine law, and to the ordinary course of Divine providence, that a man should die more than once, since it has been appointed even for sinful men to die only once, and afterwards to undergo the Divine judgment of either damnation or salvation. This proposition and its proof are found in verses 26 and 27. But Christ offered himself as a sacrifice to GOD by his own blood and death. The minor proposition is found partly in the second part of verse 26 and verse 25, as well as verse 28. A resolution of this proof can also be made, so that it contains two foundations of non-repeatability, the first of which is: He who has a sacrifice that is repeatable and to be renewed every year, he ought not to have offered it finally at the end of the ages, but rather immediately after the beginning of sin. But Christ, the Priest of the New Testament, had to offer his sacrifice finally at the end of the ages. Therefore, Christ did not have a repeatable sacrifice. The major is proved, because where the cause of a sacrifice is present, there the sacrifice itself ought to be present as a remedy to remove that cause, unless that sacrifice is of such a nature that it is valid for all times. For in this respect, if indeed it diffuses its expiatory power into all times and ages, it is the same at whatever time it is performed, provided it is performed, whether it is done at the beginning of the ages or at their consummation. However, on the contrary, if it is valid only for some time, it would have had to be repeated many times from the very beginning of the world, and must be continued until the end of the world, because the cause of the sacrifice has existed from the very beginning of the world. Whence also the Patriarchs began their typical sacrifices immediately from the beginning of the world after the fall, whom the High Priests who led the people out of Egypt succeeded. The minor is proven in verse 26, where it is asserted that he appeared once at the end of the ages for the putting away of sin through his sacrifice; and it is asserted indeed with respect to the prophecy of Daniel 9:25-26, where it is expressly said that after the end of the 62 weeks Christ will be cut off, and an end will be put to the legal sacrifices, verse 27. Now the 62 weeks contain a certain period of ages, to the completion (συντέλειαν) of which reference is made in this place. Therefore Christ did not offer his sacrifice many times (πολλάκις) but once (ἅπαξ).

Latin:

Vers. 27. Καὶ καθ’ ὅσον ἀπόκειται τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἅπαξ ἀποθανεῖν, μετὰ δὲ τῦτο κρίσις.] Ἀπόκειται reservatur: Re- stat post exactam hanc vitam mori. Sic habemus ἀπό- κειται Deut. XXXII. 34. 2. Tim. IV. 8. Est lex generalis in homines lata, ut moriantur, Si quibus aliter evenit, ut Enocho & Eliæ, ii nihil sunt ad tantam hominum mo- rientium multitudinem. Postea judicium, id est, postea sistentur Deo. Nam hoc ex nomine judicii intelligi da- tur Rom. XIV. 10. Pro καθ’ ὅσον alii Codices habent καθ’ ὁ Forte scriptum fuerat καθὼς. Affertur enim si- militudo quædam Christi cum hominibus cæteris. Syrus איכנא. Latinus quemadmodum.

Oblationem Christi modo de passione, modo de offensione sui in cælesti sanctuario, imò de utraque intelligit Grotius. Cur autem τὸ πεφανέρωται in sensu Hitpahelico accipiendum sit, non appa- ret, nisi quod id suæ glossæ convenientius judicet Grotius: Quod vero de apparitione in cælis intelli- gendum esse negamus. Agit hic Apostolus de φα- νερώσει ἐν σαρκὶ, de qua 1. Tim. III. 16. quæ in ple- nitudine temporis contigit Gal. IV. 4. Apparuit enim ut destrueret peccata διὰ τῆς θυσίας per sa- crificium corporis sui, quod offerendum erat in morte in ara crucis, quemadmodum ideo semel προσενεχθεὶς oblatus dicitur εἰς τὸ πολλῶν ἀνε- νεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας, v. 28. apparuit, ut opera Diaboli destrueret, 1. Joh. III 8. Verba διὰ τῆς θυσίας ἁυτῦ perverse redduntur, postquam ipse victima fuit factus, quia non apparuit, postquam factus est victima, sed ut victima fieri possit; nam ideo in carne manifestari, & carnis & sanguinis parti- ceps fieri voluit teste Apostolo, Ebr. II. 14. ut per mortem suam destrueret eum, qui habebat mortis imperium; Utrumque, & oblationem in passione & morte, atque apparationem in cælis, factum dicit Grotius εἰς ἀθέτησιν ἁμαρτίας; quod quamvis dici possit, his tamen verbis non expri- mitur, nunc autem semel in consummatione secu- li ad destructionem peccati per hostiam suam ap- paruit. Finis enim exprimitur apparitionis in carne, fuitq; corporis Christi in victimam oblatio ad destructionem peccati, quæ fit per expiatio- nem, cum destructa ratione virium suarum & rea- tus, & remissionem peccatorum, cum ea nobis non imputantur, sed ratione culpæ & pœnæ nobis condonantur. In ipsa seculorum, inquit Theo- phylactus, consummatione & fine, cum tempus jam adventasset, quo Prophetarum dicta complerentur, & perdita hominum nequitia ad summum jam evasisset, ut ἀθετήσῃ id est ut peccatum devincat, & omnem illi demat fiduciam sui ipsius oblatio- ne & hostia, hoc est, per suæ carnis interitum. Thomas apud Estium consummationem seculi in- terpretatur de ultima mundi ætate: Ultima ætas est status præsens, post quem non est alius status, sicut nec post senium alia ætas. Sicut autem in aliis ætatibus est numerus annorum determinatus, non autem in senio: Ita non est determinatum, quantum iste sta- tus mundi debeat durare, tamen est consummatio seculorum, quia non restat alius status. Sic ille, citans etiam illud Apostoli 1. Corinth. X. Nos su- mus, in quos fines seculorum devenerunt. Ea- dem, dicente Estio, est sententia glossæ ordinariæ, & Lyrani, & aliorum fere communis. Quæ nugatur Grotius de Pauli opinione circa finem mundi, ali- bi tacta sunt. Non minus in omnem veritatem & hic à Spiritu sancto ductus est S. Paulus, quam ab

S. Petrus & S. Johannes. Quæ autem veritas il- la, de propinquo imminuisse finem mundi, quum non imminuerit? Quærit hic, observante Theo- phylacto, Gregorius Nyssenus, cur in seculi con- summatione carnem assumpserit Filius DEI? Aitque: Quemadmodum peritissimi medici, febri adhuc in præcordiis manente, & ægroti corpus acrius divexante, & ægritudinis foventis adaucta magis incensaque, nullam afferunt languenti me- delam, quæ languoris causas tollat, sed ut mor- bus increscat, opperiuntur: Sic & nobiscum agit animarum Medicus ille. Expectat enim, ut pror- sus omnis retegatur nequitia, ut nihil maneat ex his, quæ recondita sunt, incuratum; sic demum retectis ille & patentibus malis medebitur. Sen- sum vero sic reddit Estius: Christus non est ingres- sus in cælum, ut sæpius offerat seipsum, nihil enim opus erat, ut qui semel, idque tempore consum- mationis seculorum apparuit, ac manifestatus est mundo per hostiam suam, tunc scilicet, quando palam semetipsum obtulit in cruce, sic, inquam, apparuit, ut illa sua oblatione peccatum semel ac prorsus aboleverit atque contriverit. Vim autem argumenti, & scopum atque συνέχειαν Apostoli- cæ tractationis recte ita expressit B. Dorschæus: Apostolus probat differentiam inter sacrificium Veteris & Novi Testamenti, quod nempe illud ite- rabile sit: & per successionem plurimorum sacri- ficiorum continuandum, hoc vero irreiterabile & semel perficiendum, idque hoc argumento: Qui Sacerdos sanguine & morte propria pro totius or- bis peccatis sese offert, is non nisi semel offert, adeoque non offert se reiterabiliter. Nam si reite- rabiliter sese offerre deberet, & quidem pro pec- catis omnium seculorum, tunc oporteret ipsum jam inde ab origine mundi, & porro ad finem usque mundi multoties mori. Nam jam inde ab origine mundi homines peccarunt, & ab hujq sacerdotis præ- figurati sacrificio remissionem peccatorum desidera- runt. At hoc repugnat legi Divinæ, & cursui providentiæ Divinæ ordinario, ut homo sæpius mo- riatur, cum etiam peccatoribus hominibus semel tantum impositum sit mori, & postea subire Divi- num judicium sive damnationis sive salvationis. Hæc propositio ejusque probatio habetur vers. 26. & 27. Atqui Christus sanguine & morte propria se sacrificium DEO obtulit. Minor propositio ha- betur partim altera parte versûs 26. & v. 25. ut & v. 28. Potest etiam fieri resolutio hujus proba- tionis, ut duo contineat fundamenta irreiterabili tatis, quorum primum est: Qui habet sacrificium reiterabile & quotannis renovandum, ille non debu- it demum in fine seculorum illud offerre, sed potius statim post initium peccati. At Christus Sacerdos Novi Testamenti in fine seculorum demum sacri- ficium suum offerre debuit. Ergo Christus non ha- buit sacrificium reiterabile. Major probatur, quia ubi adest causa sacrificii, ibi ipsum sacrificium ad- esse oportet tanquam remedium ad tollendam istam causam, nisi sacrificium illud ita se habeat, ut per omnia tempora valeat. Hoc enim respectu, si sci- licet in omnia tempora & secula vim suam expiatri- cem diffundat, perinde est, quocunque tempore illud præstetur, dummodo præstetur, sive in principio secu- lorum, sive in consummatione istud fiat. Attamen ex adverso, si pro aliquo tantum tempore valet, multo- ties jam inde ab origine mundi repetendum fuerat, & ad finem usque mundi continuandum est, quia causa sacrificii jam inde ab origine mundi extitit. Unde etiam sua sacrificia typica statim ab origine mundi post lapsum inchoarunt Patriarchæ, quibus populo ex Aegypto educto successerunt summi Sa- cerdotes. Minor probatur vers. 26. ubi asseritur, semel in fine seculorum ad sublationem peccati per suum sacrificium apparuit; & asseritur quidem cum respectu ad vaticinium Danielis IX. 25. 26. ubi ex- presse dicitur, post finem LXII. septimanarum exci- sum iri Christum, & finem impositum sacrificiis lega- libus, vers. 27. Continent autem LXII. septimanae certam seculorum periodum, ad quorum συντέλειαν hoc loco respicitur. Ergo Christus non πολλάκις sed ἅπαξ suum obtulit sacrificium.

## 9:28
Verse 28. So also Christ having been offered once (Οὕτω καὶ ὁ χριστὸς ἅπαξ προσενεχθεὶς). This word 'offered' (προσενεχθεὶς) also has the meaning of the Hithpahel: that is, after he once offered himself to God, he presented himself to God: one must understand 'through his sacrifice,' which preceded a little before. Just as men die once, and from that point will be presented once to God: so Christ, having died once, also presented himself once to God. And this was the judgment which God rendered to Christ, his elevation without delay into supreme glory.

But he offered himself to God, not when he had entered into heaven did he present himself to Him, but when he was sacrificed for us on the altar of the cross: which is that unique oblation of which the Apostle speaks so frequently here, which shines forth more clearly than the midday sun from chapter 10:1, 2, 5, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13. Most ineptly, however, is it compared by Grotius, that we are to be presented to God once on the last day, concerning which standing before God there is not even a jot here, and that Christ also presented himself once in the oblation, as he calls it: Which standing or appearing of Christ before God the Apostle does not touch upon with even a single word in this place, dealing only with the oblation which was made on the altar of the cross, as we have already warned. Nor indeed did God render any judgment to Christ through his elevation into glory: But He gave to Christ judicial (δικαστικὴν) power and all judgment, John 5, inasmuch as He has appointed him to judge the world through one Man, Acts 17. There is also nothing here about the judgment of God upon Christ, but about the final judgment upon the human race, and especially upon the faithful of Christ. The argumentation of Paul, with Estius as interpreter, is as follows: Christ, having been made man, underwent the human condition, but it is necessary for men to die, yet only once: Therefore Christ also had to die only once, and consequently to be offered only once, because this oblation does not take place without death. But as for the words: 'After this, however, judgment,' Estius rightly observes that the final words correspond to them: 'He will appear a second time without sin to those who wait for him for salvation.' For this judgment is also accommodated to Christ, not as one being judged, but as one about to judge, and about to render rewards to the redeemed and the elect.

To bear the sins of many (Εἰς τὸ πολλῶν ἀνενεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας). This is the same as what he just said, 'for the putting away of sin.' For 'to bear' (ἀναφέρειν) is used for the simple 'to carry' (φέρειν, נשׂא) in Numbers 14:33, Deuteronomy 15:24, Isaiah 53:12. Now 'to carry,' that is, נשׂא, is often 'to take away' and is translated by 'to remove' (ἀφαιρεῖν) in Leviticus 10:17, Numbers 14:8, and elsewhere. Thus also 'to take up' (ἀνάγειν) is taken in Joshua 24:32, 2 Samuel 21:13, Ezra 1:11. The Latin here says 'to exhaust the sins of many.' And he said 'of many,' looking to the outcome, as in Matthew 26:28.

The comparison of those phrases 'to bear sins' (εἰς τὸ ἀνενεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας) and 'for the putting away of sin' (εἰς ἀθέτησιν ἁμαρτίας) is correct. But this was done 'through the sacrifice' of the death of Christ, and therefore this synonymy and the context itself convince us that that also was done in such a way. But what kind of circulation of words is that, that 'to bear up' (ἀναφέρειν) should first be taken for the simple 'to carry' (φέρειν), and then 'to carry' (φέρειν) for 'to take away'? The word 'to bear up' (ἀναφέρω), whose infinitive is 'to bear up' (ἀνενεγκεῖν), is 'to carry upwards,' because he carried our sins upwards onto the wood of the cross. 1 Peter 2:24: 'He bore up (ἀνήνεγκεν) in his body onto the tree.' Chrysostom and other Greeks interpret it in this way regarding the oblation: He offered them to the Father to be remitted, just as we offer our sins to God, saying, 'forgive us our debts.' Thus this word occurs with the meaning of offering, Hebrews 7:27, chapter 13:15, James

2:21, 1 Peter 2:5. And thus also the Syriac rendered it: 'And in himself he offered the sins of many.' But because it is foreign to the language of Scripture to say that sins are offered to God, and the speech of the Apostle seems inconsistent—'Christ was offered, that he might offer sins'—our former explanation is more convenient: Christ was offered once on the altar of the cross, that he might carry upwards the sins of many for their 'putting away.' For when he carried them in his body, and carried them upwards onto the wood of the cross, by suffering for them in it, they were destroyed, so that they cannot be imputed to us either by reason of guilt or by reason of punishment, since Christ has satisfied for them, and has borne the guilt and punishment of our sins, John 1:29. Estius approves this sense, having dismissed the Vulgate version, 'to exhaust the sins of many': 'I think it should rather be said that the Greek word is placed here for that which is to carry upwards, to lift up, to raise above oneself; this, however, is to carry, so that the sense is: that Christ was offered so that he might carry the sins of many, that is, that he might receive into himself the punishment due to their sins, and through this might take them away and blot them out.' In this manner, he continues, Scripture is accustomed to speak about Christ, as in Isaiah 53: 'Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he himself carried our sorrows.' And again: 'GOD laid on him the iniquity of us all.' Finally, at the end of the same chapter: 'He himself bore the sins of many'; where, according to the LXX, the same word is read as in this place; so that it is almost certain that Paul, writing these things, looked to that passage of Isaiah, just as it is likely that Peter did when he said in his first epistle, chapter 2: 'Who himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree.' For in that place also the word in the Greek is the same. That which John the Baptist said about Christ pertains to the same: 'Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.' Takes away, that is, carries.

As for the fact that he said 'the sins of many,' whereas elsewhere Christ is said to have borne the sins of many, Estius interprets it in the Calvinist sense: that Christ, as far as the sufficiency of his passion is concerned, bore the sins of all men, because it was valid for the redemption of all. But as far as efficiency is concerned, not of all, but of many. This is very bad. For he understands the sufficiency of value as merely possible, if God had ordained this satisfaction for all, not actual, whereas in truth he satisfied for all, even if not all enjoy this satisfaction and λύτρῳ paid for them on account of their ἀπισίαν. This universal satisfaction, even for those who perish by their own fault, is clearly evident from the Scriptures: Is. 53:6 ff., John 1:29, ch. 3:16, 2 Cor. 5:19, 1 Tim. 2:6, 1 John 2:1, 2 Pet. 2:1. He therefore bore the sins of many, because he bore the sins of all; because the universality which is expressed in other passages is not to be restricted by the designation of 'many,' but rather this multitude is to be extended to all men or the whole human race by the force of the Catholic statements, since all are many, and many are accustomed to be spoken of for all, Rom. 5:19. As for the Synod of Valence in Gaul, in the year 855, to which Estius appeals, it was only a particular one of fourteen bishops, nor do they seem to have sufficiently understood the opinion of Hincmar and others, as Hildebrand declares in his 'Orthodox Declaration of the Three Articles'. judge: For those bishops did not wish to say that Christ on the cross proposed to himself to rescue from hell those who had departed from this life as infidels and impenitent, but they thought that Christ had been destined from eternity as a λύτρον for the redemption of all, but that it would profit only those who had not despised the saving grace, and that therefore not all are redeemed, insofar as the captivity is not paid for all, but all are redeemed, insofar as the necessity of captivity is paid, and that this is also true of those who had died in their sins before the passion of Christ, insofar as by these, while they lived, the necessity of perishing was removed, so that those who did not perish, not because Christ was unwilling to die for them, but because, although they could by the grace of God, they were unwilling to follow the way of salvation by the example of the saints of their own time, without which it would have been that even they would have been saved on account of the sacrifice of Jesus Christ, whose power extends no less to the time of the Old Testament than to the new. What? That that Synod of Valence in canon V defined that Christ also died for those who are temporary, who fall away again by the grace of regeneration, and thus are not in the number of the elect. Rightly, therefore, Theophylact here: But why did he say 'of many,' not 'of all'? Because by no means did all mortals believe. But the death of Christ equalized the perdition of all, that is, it was strong enough that not all would be lost, and it was paid for the salvation of all, and as far as it lay in him, he died for all. Yet he did not exhaust the sins of all, because they resisted. Whence these rendered this death of Christ entirely useless to themselves. Which is truly horrible to say, and greatly to be deplored, since it brought salvation to many. In this sense Basil himself also concedes. We find, however, in the Gospel that he would deliver his soul as a ransom for many, interpreted as for all. For 'many' often designates all.

He shall appear a second time without sin to those who wait for him for salvation) The Manuscript adds 'through faith,' not badly. Concerning this expectation, see 1 Thess. 1:9-10, 2 Tim. 4:8. He shall appear is constructed with 'for salvation': The Syriac: 'therefore he shall appear, so that he may bring eternal salvation to those who wait for him through faith.' To the same must be referred 'without sin,' that is, when they shall already be out of the danger of sinning; so that they no longer have need of an intercessor for themselves, when they shall already be sinless. Often the names of acts are wont to be put for the names of power. Thus 'immortal,' one who cannot die.

That 'without sin' is preposterously snatched to 'those who wait for him.' For it coheres with the verb 'he shall appear.' Christ in his first advent appeared bearing the sins of the whole world (Isa. 53:6, John 1:29, 2 Cor. 5:21). For in his second advent he shall be seen without any sin, or no longer bearing the sin of the world, with which he was burdened in his first advent. He will not, however, come to make satisfaction for sins, but to transfer believing sinners into heaven, and to admit them into the full possession of salvation, which pertains to the Mediator of the New Testament himself. The Apostle speaks, however, not only of those who will be alive and desiring the advent at the end of the world, but of all the elect who have ever lived and desired the final advent of Christ, just as the faithful are described by this mark in 2 Tim. 4:8 and Tit. 2:13. He died, says Theophylact, burdened with our crimes, and offering the same to God the Father, that he might delete and blot out those for whose sake he himself had suffered death. For the Father made him who had committed no sin a fountain, as one who had taken our misdeeds upon himself. He shall appear, however, a second time, carrying nothing further of sins, for which he will not have to die again, who died once, but he shall arrive as Judge, to be for the salvation of those waiting for him, that is, of those having both hope and faith in him, waiting for his advent, for whose dignity he considered his life. And he is to come not only for salvation, but for punishment to those who believe less and are subject to sins. Salvation, therefore, is understood not of souls, but of men, and that perfect, so that nothing of blessedness is lacking to either soul or body.

Which salvation, by ordinary law, happens to no one before the second advent of CHRIST.

The Apostle proves that the law had only a shadow of good things to come from the fact that sacrifices were repeated every year, and that it was impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of animals, and therefore a body was adapted to the Son of God, as David (Ps. 40 and following) testifies, that he was not delighted by offerings in themselves, but by the fulfillment of the Divine will, made through the offering of the body of Christ, and that the priests offered the same sacrifices daily, which could not take away sins; but Christ, having offered one sacrifice, sits forever at the right hand of God, and by that one sacrifice he has perfected those who are sanctified, concerning which the New Testament testifies in Jeremiah (ch. 31:31 ff.), with the remission of sins promised. He warns, therefore, that we should approach with confidence, and retain an immovable hope, and not desert the communion, lest we fall into that transgression for which no victim is available, with the horrible Divine judgment proposed, and the moment of that transgression, and the most certain punishment (Deut. 17:6, 19:15, ch. 30:32, 35, 36). Finally, he exhorts that, mindful of their former patience in various afflictions, they should not cast away their confidence, since the Lord is about to come shortly, and the just man, according to Habakkuk (ch. 2:3-4), shall live by his faith.

There are two parts: The former is the confirmation of the unique satisfactory sacrifice of Christ, up to verse 18. The latter is an exhortation to confidence in Christ and perseverance, up to verse 39. The former pertains to the completion of the treatment of the first didactic part of the epistle concerning Christ: The latter pertains to the beginning of the other principal part of the epistle, namely, the paraenetic part concerning faith in Christ.

PART I. Confirmation of the unique satisfactory sacrifice for sins.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Οὕτω καὶ ὁ χριστὸς ἅπαξ προσενεχθεὶς) Hoc quoque προσενεχθεὶς significationem habet Hithpahel: id est, postquam semel se Deo obtulit, Deo se stitit: Sub- intelligendum διὰ τῆς θυσίας ἀυτοῦ, quod paulo ante praecessit. Sicut homines semel moriuntur, inde semel sistentur Deo: Sic Christus semel mortuus semel quoque Deo se stitit. Et hoc fuit judicium, quod Deus Christo reddidit, evectio ejus sine mora in summam gloriam.

Deo autem sese obtulit, non dum in coelum in- gressus se ipsi stitit, sed cum in ara crucis pro no- bis immolatus est: quae est unica illa oblatio, de qua hic tam frequenter Apostolus, quod è cap. X. 1. 2. 5. 8. 9. 11. 12. 13. luce meridiana clarius effulget. In- eptissime vero confertur à Grotio, quod nos semel Deo sistendi simus in die novissimo, de qua coram Deo statione ne gry quidem hic habetur, & quod Christus semel quoque se stitit in oblatione, quam vocat: Quam Christi coram Deo stationem vel ap- paritionem nullo quidem verbo hoc loco tangit Apostolus, de oblatione solum, quae in ara crucis facta est, agens, uti jam monuimus. Nec vero ju- dicium aliquod Deus Christo reddidit per evectio- nem ejus in gloriam: Sed Christo potestatem δικα- στικὴν & omne judicium dedit Joh. V. utpote qui per unum Virum orbem terrae judicare constituit, Act. XVII. Nihil etiam hic de judicio Dei in Chri- stum, sed de judicio novissimo in genus humanum, imprimis vero in fideles Christi. Argumentatio Pauli, Estio interprete, talis est: Christus factus ho- mo subiit conditionem humanam, atqui homines mo- ri necesse est, sed non nisi semel: Igitur & Christus se- mel tantum mori debuit, & consequenter semel tan- tum offerri, quia oblatio haec non fit sine morte. Quod vero ad verba: Post hoc autem judicium, recte ob- servat Estius, illis respondere verba ultima: Secundo sine peccato apparebit expectantibus se in salutem. Hoc enim judicium etiam accommodatur Chri- sto, non ut judicando, sed ut judicaturo, & praemia redemptis atque electis reddituro.

Εἰς τὸ πολλῶν ἀνενεγκεῖν ἁμαρτίας) Idem hoc est, quod modo dixit εἰς ἀθέτησιν ἁμαρτίας. Nam ἀναφέρειν pro simplici φέρειν נשׂא ponitur Num. XIV. 33. Deut. XV. 24. Es. LIII. 12. Ferre autem, id est נשׂא saepe est auferre & per ἀφαιρεῖν vertitur Levit. X. 17. Num. XIV. 8. & alibi. Sic & ἀνάγειν sumitur Josuae XXIV. 32. 2. Sam. XXI. 13. Esdr. I. 11. Latinus hic ad multorum exhaurienda pec- cata. Et multorum dixit, eventum respiciens, ut Matth. XXVI. 28.

Recte phrasium illarum εἰς τὸ ἀνενεγκεῖν ἁμαρτί- ας & εἰς ἀθέτησιν ἁμαρτίας collatio habet. Haec au- tem facta est διὰ τῆς θυσίας per sacrificium mortis Christi, ideoque & illud ita factum esse haec syno- nymia & contextus ipse convincit. Quaenam ve- ro illa circulatio est vocum, ut ἀναφέρειν pro sim- plici φέρειν primum accipiatur, deinde vero φέρειν pro auferre? Vox ἀναφέρω, cujus infinitivus est ἀνενεγκεῖν est sursum ferre, quia peccata nostra sursum tulit in lignum crucis. 1. Petr. II. 24. ἀνήνεγ- κεν ἐν τῷ σώματι ἀυτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον. Chrysostomus & alii Graeci de oblatione interpretantur hoc mo- do: Obtulit ea Patri remittenda, quomodo nos peccata nostra Deo offerimus, dicentes, dimit- te nobis debita nostra. Ita significatu offerendi oc- currit hoc verbum, Ebr. VII. 27. cap. XIII. 15. Jac.

II. 21. 1. Petr. II. 5. Atque ita etiam reddidit Sy- rus: Et in seipso obtulit peccata multorum. Sed quia à lingua Scripturæ alienum est dicere, quod peccata Deo offerantur, & sermo Apostoli incon- cinus videtur, Christus oblatus est, ut offerret pec- cata, prior explicatio nostra convenientior est, Christus semel oblatus est in ara crucis, ut sursum ferret multorum peccata εἰς ἀθέτησιν eorum. Nam cum in corpore suo ea tulerit, & sursum super li- gnum crucis tulerit, in eo pro iisdem patiendo, de- structa eadem sunt, ut nobis sive ratione culpæ, sive ratione pœnæ imputari non possint, quandoqui- dem pro iisdem Christus satisfecerit, ac culpam pœnamque nostrorum peccatorum tulerit, Joh. I. I. 39. Quem sensum dimissa Vulgata versione, ad multorum peccata exhaurienda, approbat Estius: Dicendum potius arbitror Græcam vocem hic posi- tam pro eo, quod est sursum ferre, sustollere, supra se levare, hoc autem est portare, ut sensus sit: Christum oblatum fuisse, ut peccata multorum portaret, id est, pœnam peccatis eorum debitam in se reciperet, & per hoc ea tolleret atque deleret. Ad hunc modum, per- git, Scriptura loqui solet de Christo, ut Es. LIII. Vere languores nostros ipse tulit, & dolores nostros ipse por- tavit. Et iterum: Posuit DEUS in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum. Denique in fine ejusdem capi- tis: Ipse peccata multorum tulit; ubi secundum LXX. legitur idem verbum, quod hoc loco; ut pene certum sit, Paulum hæc scribentem ad illum Esaia locum respexisse, quemadmodum & Petrum veri simile, quando dixit 1. epist. II. Qui peccata nostra ipse pertulit in corpore suo super lignum. Nam & eo loco idem est in Græco verbum. Pertinet eodem, quod Johannes Baptista de Christo dixit: Ecce Agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi. Tollit, id est, portat.

Quod autem multorum peccata dixit, cum alias multorum peccata Christus tulisse dicatur, sensu Calviniano interpretatur Estius, Christum quantum ad sufficientiam passionis attinet, omnium hominum peccata tulisse, quia valebat ad omnium redemptio- nem. Quantum vero ad efficientiam, non omnium, sed multorum. Pessimè. Nam intelligit sufficienti- am valoris passibilem, si Deus ordinasset hujus sa- tisfactionem omnibus, non actualem, quod revera pro omnibus satisfecerit, etsi non omnes hac satis- factione & λύτρῳ pro se soluta propter ἀπισίαν fruantur. Quæ universalis satisfactio etiam pro iis, qui culpa sua pereunt, è Scripturis luculenter constat, Es. LIII. 6. seqq. Joh. I. 29. cap. III. 16. 2. Cor. V. 19. 1. Tim. II. 16. 1. Joh. II. 1. 2. Petr. II. 1. Multorum ergo peccata tulit, quia omnium, quia universalitas, quæ in aliis locis exprimitur, non per multorum designationem restringenda, sed hæc potius multitudo ad omnes homines vel to- tum genus humanum vi Catholicorum dictorum extendenda, quum & omnes multi sint, & multi pro omnibus dici soleant, Rom. V. 19. Quod ad Syno- dum Valentinam in Gallia, An. 855. ad quam provo- cat Estius, particularis tantum illa fuit XIV. Episco- porum, nec satis Hincmari & aliorum sententiam intellexisse videntur, Hildebrando in orthod. trium artic. declarat. judice: Nec enim Episcopi illi volue- runt, Christum in cruce sibi proposuisse, ut gehenna eximeret eos, qui infideles & impœnitentes de hac vita discessissent, sed putarunt, Christum ab æterno destinatum fuisse λύτρον pro omnium redemptione, sed solis profuturum, qui gratiam salutarem non con- tempserint, eoque non redimi omnes, quatenus non solvitur omnibus captivitas, at redimi omnes, quate- nus solvitur captivitatis necessitas, atque id quoque de his, qui ante passionem Christi in peccatis suis mor- tui essent hactenus verum esse, quatenus ab his, dum viverent, sublata fuit pereundi necessitas, ut qui non perierint, quia Christus pro iis noluerit mori, sed quia, cum per Dei gratiam possent, exemplo sancto- rum sui temporis, salutis viam insistere noluerunt, absque quo esset, etiam illos fuisse salvandos propter sacrificium Jesu Christi, cujus virtus non minus ad Veteris Testamenti tempus, quam ad novi se exten- dat. Quid? quod synodus illa Valentina can. V. definiverit, quod Christus etiam mortuus sit pro προσκαίροις qui regenerationis gratia iterum exci- dunt, adeoque in numero electorum non sunt. Re- cte itaque hic Theophylactus: Verum cur multorum dixit, non omnium? Quia nequaquam cuncti credi- dere mortales. At Christi mors omnium aequavit perditionem, id est, sat valuit, ne omnes perderentur, & pro cunctorum salute depensa est, & quantum in eo fuit, pro cunctis est mortuus. Nec tamen omnium, quia illi reluctarentur, peccata exhausit. Unde inu- tilem prorsus sibi hi mortem hanc Christi reddide- re. Quod sane horrendum est dictu, & admodum deplorandum, cum multis illa salutem attulerit. In hunc sensum & Basilius ipse concedit. Reperimus tamen in Evangelio, quod traderet animam suam in redemptionem pro multis, pro omnibus interpreta- tum. Multi enim plerumque universos designant.

Ἐκ δευτέρου χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας ὀφθήσεται τοῖς αὐτὸν ἀπεκ- δεχομένοις εἰς σωτηρίαν) Addit Manuscriptus διὰ πίστεως, non male. De hac expectatione vide 1. Thess. I. 9. 10. 2. Tim. IV. 8. Ὀφθήσεται cum εἰς σωτηρίαν construit: Syrus: ideo apparebit, ut illis salutem afferat æternam, qui ipsum expectant per fidem. Eodem referri de- bet χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας, id est, cum jam erunt extra periculum peccandi; ita ut amplius interpellatore pro se opus non habeant, cum jam erunt ἀναμάρτητοι. Sæpe solent actuum nomina poni pro potentiæ nominibus. Sic ἀθάνατος, qui mori nequit.

Illud χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας præpostere rapitur ad τοῖς αὐτὸν ἀπεκδεχομένοις. Cohæret enim cum verbo ὀφθήσεται. Christus in primo suo adventu appa- ruit peccata totius mundi ferens Es. LIII. 6. Joh. I. 29. 2. Cor. V. 21. In secundo enim adventu vide- bitur sine ullo peccato, vel non amplius portans peccatum mundi, quo onustus erat in primo ad- ventu. Non vero veniet ad satisfaciendum pro peccatis, sed ad transferendos in cœlum peccato- res credentes, eosque in plenam salutis possessio- nem immittendos, quod ipsi Mediatori Novi Testa- menti competit. Loquitur autem Apostolus non de iis tantum, qui vivi desiderabunt adventum sub finem mundi, sed de omnibus electis, qui unquam vixerunt, ac desiderarunt adventum Christi novis- simum, quemadmodum fideles 2. Tim. IV. 8. Tit. II. 13. ab hoc γνωρίσματι describuntur. Mortuus est, inquit Theophylactus, nostris onustus criminibus, & eadem Deo offerens Patri, ut deleat, obliteretque, quorum gratia mortem sit ipse perpessus. Eum namq; qui peccatum nullum patrarit, fontem effecit Pater, tanquam qui nostra in se conscivisset facinora. Appa- rebit tamen secundo, nihil ultra deferens peccato- rum, pro quibus non iterato erit huic moriendum, qui semel obivit, sed ut Judex adveniet, saluti futu- rus se expectantibus, id est, in se cum spem tum fidem habentibus operientibus illis adventum, pro cujus di- gnitate duxerit & vitam. Nec solum in salutem venturus est ille, sed in supplicium minus credentibus & peccatis obnoxiis. Salus itaque intelligitur non animarum, sed hominum, eaque perfecta, ut nec animæ quicquam beatitudinis desit, nec corpori.

Quæ salus ordinaria lege nemini contingit ante secundum CHRISTI ad- ventum.

Umbram tantum habuisse legem bonorum futu- rorum Apostolus ex eo convincit, quod quot- annis repetita fuerint sacrificia, quodque impossibile fuerit, sanguine pecuino tolli pec- cata, ideoque corpus adaptatum Filio Dei sit, Davide (Psal. XL. & seqq.) teste, quod non hostiis per se delectatus fuerit, sed impletio- ne voluntatis Divinae, per oblationem cor- poris Christi facta, & quod quotidie easdem hostias obtulerint Sacerdotes, quae non pote- rant tollere peccata; Christus vero, una oblata hostia, in perpetuum sedeat in dextra Dei, unaque illa hostia consummavit eos, qui sanctificantur, de quo Novum Testamentum apud Jeremiam (cap. XXXI. 31. seqq. testa- tur, remissione peccatorum promissa. Monet itaque, ut cum fiducia accedamus, & spem immotam retineamus, nec deseramus com- munionem, ne in delictum illud, pro quo non suppetit victima, incidamus, proposito horri- bili judicio Divino, & momento illius deli- cti, certissimoque supplicio, (Deut. XVII. 6. XIX. 15. c. XXX. 32. 35. 36.) Hortatur deni- que ut prioris patientiae in variis afflictionibus memores, ne abjiciant fiduciam, quum brevi venturus sit Dominus, justusque secun- dum Aabacucum (cap. II. 3. 4.) fide sua vi- cturus sit.

Partes duae sunt: Prior confirmatio unicae satis- factoriae Christi hostiae, ad v. 18. Posterior exhorta- tio ad fiduciam in Christum & perseverantiam ad v. 39. Illa pertinet ad complementum tractationis prio- ris partis epistolae Didacticae de Christo: Haec ad ini- tium partis alterius principalis epistolae, Paraeneti- cae nempe ad fidem in Christum spectat.

PARS I. Confirmatio unicae hostiae satisfactoriae pro peccatis.

## 10:1 Argument
Verse 1. For the law having a shadow of good things to come) Of those goods of which we spoke in 9:11. Concerning the word 'shadow,' see above 8:5, Col. 2:17.

Not the very image of the things) Not the substance itself of the things, as the Syriac translates here. Thus 'image' is used in 2 Cor. 5:7. Thus also Pliny the Elder uses 'effigy' concerning the thing itself, which is fully viewed.

The Apostle confirms what he had said concerning the difference between the Levitical sacrifices and the propitiatory sacrifice of Christ with various arguments: 1. From the repetition of those sacrifices, v. 1, 2, 3, 4. 2. From the testimony of Christ himself, the Son of God, v. 4, seqq., Ps. XL. 7, seqq. 3. From the eternal value of Christ's sacrifice, v. 11, seqq. 4. From the promise of the New Testament, v. 15, 16, 17. All of which also tend to this, that the Hebrews might be convinced of the cessation of ceremonial sacrifices, because the shadow ceases when the body arrives; and the fulfillment of types brings an end to the types. What need is there for sacrifices, which in themselves were of no value, when that which was prefigured by them, a sacrifice of eternal value, has already been accomplished? Finally, since by the power of the New Testament, as now confirmed by the death of the Testator, the remission of sins is obtained, of what use will sacrifices for sins according to the Old Testament be? Above he taught that Christ, having been offered once, abolished sin and prepared eternal redemption. Now, on the contrary, he shows that the law, through its sacrifices, nothing of the kind could provide, having taken the argument from the annual repetition of the sacrifices themselves. For the causal conjunction assumes this or a similar inference from those things which have been said immediately before. Therefore, salvation is to be expected from Christ, not from the law, as Estius says here. By the law, therefore, he understands not the moral or judicial law, but the ceremonial, which he says had a shadow or adumbration and figuration of good things to come, not of justice, the Holy Spirit, and eternal life, as Grotius wishes, as if those goods did not exist under the Old Testament, or before the Son of God came into the world, which certainly cannot be denied to the faithful in the Old Testament, who believed equally in the Messiah to come as we do in the one exhibited, Apoc. 13.8. Heb. 13.8. Acts 15.11. but of those things to which those ceremonies were applied to adumbrate, such as were those mysteries which were fulfilled in Christ, such as the incarnation of the Son of God, obedience, passion, and death, the sacrifice and priesthood of Christ, and things pertaining thereto: Which are called μέλλοντα ἀγαθὰ, because at that time they were future, and πράγματα, in respect of the figures and shadows by which those things so significant were adumbrated. Nor indeed with Calvin, Beza, Cajetan, Arias Montanus, and others are heavenly and eternal goods understood, but because those are future goods not only for the ancients but also for us, not present, and for the same reason were hoped for by them, it does not appear how in their respect any diversity can be established here. Estius himself refutes this opinion of Cajetan: If the Apostle meant nothing else than that the old law obscurely represented the goods of the future age which the new law represents openly: he therefore teaches nothing other than that both laws are typical and figurative, with this difference, that the old law is an obscure type, the new an express type. But that fact does nothing for the weakness of the old law compared to the new. For whether a ceremony represents heavenly glory openly or obscurely: it will not for that reason be more or less effectively valid for providing it, as Ribera well declares. Furthermore, it does not appear true that all the ceremonies of the law were instituted to prefigure the goods of the heavenly fatherland; but their institution has this, that they all be referred to Christ as a shadow to the body, as is said Col. II. Which are a shadow of things to come: but the body is of Christ. This, therefore, is what the Apostle means: If an image has already been fashioned in vivid and natural colors, what need is there to seek the σκιαν and new outlines? For it is not understood as a natural shadow, such as a body opposite the sun casts from itself; but an artificial shadow, a metaphor taken from painters, as noted elsewhere, so that σκια is σκιαγραφια, an adumbration or rough delineation, such as painters are accustomed to make first with charcoal when they are about to paint some image. Concerning which Cyril of Alexandria, in the last volume, book IX, against Julian, page 309. Just as skilled bronze-smiths, and among them the most famous, first exhibit the forms of the images they are about to make in liquefied wax, not so that their art progresses only that far, but so that in them, as I said, the beauty of those things which are soon to be made may first shine forth: yet after the work has been brought to completion, we shall no longer rightly blame the craftsman because he neglects the types: In a similar way, I think, after Christ has shone forth, who is the truth, and the Christian cult has been introduced, we shall rightly establish that the types are vain, for they were images of spiritual things. Εἰκὼν therefore here does not signify a figure or type, because it is opposed to τῇ σκιᾷ: But image denotes the very substance of the thing adumbrated, if indeed substantial images are also given, just as the Son of God is the image of God the Father, Col. I. 14. Therefore the Syrian rendered it substance. B. Luther, das Wesen selbst. The image, therefore, is not an express representation of some thing, but the thing itself exhibited and represented, which sense Grotius confirms from 2 Cor. V. 7, and for it Estius brings forward Chrysostom, Theophylact, Gagnaeus, Arias Montanus, and Ribera: Estius prefers to understand a natural shadow with Anselm, Thomas, Cajetan, and Arias Montanus, because the shadow of a body, from which it is projected, is a most imperfect likeness, from Col. II. 17. But B. Gerhard warns that the reason for that passage is different. For there, he says, τῇ σκιᾷ is opposed to σῶμα, but here, indeed, ἡ εἰκών.

Κατ' ἐνιαυτὸν ταῖς αὐταῖς θυσίαις, ἃς προσφέρουσιν εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς, ὐδέποτε δύναται τοὺς προσερχομένους τελειῶσαι) There is also a transposition here, for the natural construction would have been: Ταῖς αὐταῖς θυσίαις, ἃς προσφέρουσιν εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς κατ' ἐνιαυτὸν, that is, not every year, not for ten or a hundred years, but perpetually, while the temple stands. And he calls them the same victims, that is, of the same kind, calves and goats. Προσφέρουσι, namely, the High Priests, which is easily understood from what precedes. Προσερχομένοις, namely, to God, as above VII. 25, below XI. 6, those who worship God in such a way, whom he will presently call λατρεύοντας עבדי. For the High Priest in that sacred rite represented the person of the people themselves. Take τελειῶσαι as above IX. 9. If the High Priest could not do this, and in such a solemn sacred rite, how much less the other priests?

Latin:

Vers. 1. Σκιὰν γὰρ ἔχων ὁ νόμος τῶν μελλόντων ἀγαθῶν) Illorum bonorum, de quibus diximus IX. 11. De voce umbræ vide supra VIII. 5. Coloss. II. 17.

Οὐκ αὐτὴν τὴν εἰκόνα τῶν πραγμάτων) Non ipsam re- rum substantiam, ut hic vertit Syrus. Sic εἰκὼν usurpa- tur 2. Cor. V. 7. Sic & effigiem Plinius major usurpat de re ipsa, quae plene spectatur.

Quae dixerat de differentia sacrificiorum Leviti- corum, & sacrificii Christi propitiatorii, confirmat variis argumentis Apostolus 1. è sacrificiorum illo- rum repetitione, v. 1. 2. 3. 4. 2. è Christi ipsius Filii Dei testificatione, v. 4. seqq. Ps. XL. 7. seqq. 3. Ex aeterno sacrificii Christi valore, v. 11. seqq. 4. è Te- stamenti novi promissione, v. 15. 16. 17. Quae omnia eo etiam tendunt, ut Ebraei de cessatione sacrificio- rum ceremonialium convincantur, quia umbra cessat adveniente corpore; & complementum ty- porum finem adfert typis. Quid opus est sacrifi- ciis, quae per se nihil valebant, quum peractum jam sit, quod eis figuratum fuit, aeterni valoris sacrifici- um? Denique cum vi Novi Testamenti, ceu jam confirmati Testatoris morte, obtineatur remissio peccatorum, cui usui erunt sacrificia pro peccatis secundum Vetus Testamentum? Supra docuit, Christum semel oblatum abolevisse peccatum, & aeternam parasse redemptionem. Nunc ex adver- so ostendit, legem per sua sacrificia nihil ejusmodi præstare potuisse, sumpto argumento ex ipsorum sa- crificiorum annua repetitione. Conjunctio causa- lis enim supponit hanc aut similem illationem ex iis, quæ proxime dicta sunt. Ergo salus est à Christo expectanda non ex lege, ut hîc Estius. Per legem ergo intelligit non legem moralem aut judicialem, sed ceremonialem, quam umbram dicit habuisse vel adumbrationem & figurationem bonorum fu- turorum, non justitiæ, Spiritus sancti, & vitæ æternæ, ut Grotius vult, quasi illa bona non fuerint sub Veteri Testamento, vel antequam Filius DEI in mundum veniret, quæ utique fidelibus in Veteri Testamento denegari non possunt, qui æque in Messiam futurum, ut nos in exhibitum credidere, Apoc. 13.8. Ebr. 13.8. Act. 15,11. sed eorum ad quæ ad- umbranda ceremoniæ istæ adhibitæ sunt, qualia erant illa mysteria, quæ in Christo impleta sunt, ut- pote incarnatio Filii Dei, obedientia, passio, & mors, sacrificium & sacerdotium Christi, & eò pertinen- tia: Quæ dicuntur μέλλοντα ἀγαθὰ, quia illo tem- pore erant futura, & πράγματα, respectu figura- rum & umbrarum, quibus adumbratæ sunt res illæ tam insignes. Neque vero cum Calvino, Beza, Caje- tano, Ariamontano, & aliis cælestia & æterna bona intelliguntur, sed quia illa non tantum Veteribus, sed etiam nobis futura sunt bona, non præsentia, & eadem ratione ab illis sperata sunt, non apparet, quomodo eorum respectu aliqua hic diversitas constitui possit. Refellit hanc Cajetani sententi- am Estius ipse: Si nihil aliud voluit Apostolus, quam legem veterem obscure novam aperte repræsentare futuri seculi bona: non aliud ergo docet, quam utramque legem esse typicam & figurativam, hoc discrimine, quod vetus lex sit typus obscurus, nova typus expressus. At ea res nihil facit ad veteris le- gis præ nova imbecillitatem. Sive enim aperte sive obscure ceremonia quæpiam repræsentet gloriam cæ- lestem: non ideo plus aut minus efficaciter valebit ad eam præstandam, ut bene declarat Ribera. Deinde nec verum apparet, omnes legis ceremonias institu- tas fuisse ad præfiguranda cælestis patriæ bona; sed earum institutio id habet, ut omnes referantur ad Christum velut umbra ad corpus, sicut dicitur Col. II. Quæ sunt umbra futurorum: Corpus autem Christi. Id ergo vult Apostolus: Si quæ imago vivis & nativis coloribus effigiata jam est, quid opus est σκιαν & nova lineamenta requirere? Non e- nim umbra intelligitur naturalis, qualem corpus soli oppositum de se spargit; sed umbra artificialis, metaphora à pictoribus sumpta, ut alias moni- tum, ut σκια sit σκιαγραφια adumbratio seu ru- dis delineatio, qualem primum carbone solent fa- cere pictores, imaginem aliquam picturi. De quo Cyrillus Alexandr. tom. ultim. libr. IX. contra Ju- lianum pag. 309. Quemadmodum periti fabri æra- rii, & inter eos celeberrimi quique formas imagi- num, quas facturi sunt in cera liquefacta prius exhibent, non ut eatenus tantum illorum ars pro- grediatur, sed ut in ipsis, uti dixi, eorum, quæ mox facienda sunt, decus prius eluceat: postquam tamen ad exitum perductum opus erit, non jam ar- tificem jure incusabimus, quod typos negligat: Simi- li, opinor, modo, posteaquam Christus illuxit, qui est veritas, & Christianus cultus introductus est vanos esse typos jure statuemus, spiritualium quippe imagi- nes erant. Εἰκὼν itaque hic non significat figuram vel typum, quia opponitur τῇ σκιᾷ: Sed imago no- tat ipsam rei adumbratæ substantiam, siquidem eti- am imagines substantiales dentur, uti Filius DEI imago est Dei Patris, Col. I. 14. Ideo Syrus reddi- dit substantiam. B. Lutherus, das Wesen selbst. Imago ergo non est expressa rei alicujus repræ- sentatio, sed ipsa res exhibita & repræsentata, quem sensum confirmat Grotius è 2. Cor. V. 7. & pro eo adducit Estius Chrysostomum, Theophylactum, Ga- gnæum, Ariamontanum & Riberam: Estius ma- vult umbram naturalem cum Anshelmo, Thoma, Cajetano, Ariamontano intelligere, quia umbra corporis, à quo projicitur, imperfectissima simi- litudo est, è Col. II. 17. Sed B. Gerhardus monet, disparem esse illius loci rationem. Ibi enim, in- quit, τῇ σκιᾷ opponitur σῶμα, hic vero ἡ εἰκών.

Κατ' ἐνιαυτὸν ταῖς αὐταῖς θυσίαις, ἃς προσφέρουσιν εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς, ὐδέποτε δύναται τοὺς προσερχομένους τελειῶσαι) Est & hic trajectio, nam nativa constructio fuerat: Ταῖς αὐταῖς θυσίαις, ἃς προσφέρουσιν εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς κατ' ἐνιαυτὸν, id est, non quotannis, non per annos decem aut centum, sed perpetuo, dum stat templum. Et easdem dicit victi- mas, id est, ejusdem generis vitulinas & hircinas. Προσ- φέρουσι nempe Ἀρχιερεῖς, quod ex antecedentibus faci- le intelligitur. Προσερχομένοις, nempe τῷ Θεῷ, ut supra VII. 25. infra XI. 6. eos, qui tali modo Deum colunt, quos jamjam dicet λατρεύοντας עבדי. Nam summus Sacerdos in illo sacro personam referebat populi ipsius. Τελειῶσαι sume, ut supra IX. 9. Si summus Sacerdos hoc non potuit, & in tam solenni sacro, quanto minus alii Sacerdotes?

## 10:2
Vers. 2.

Ἐπεὶ ἂν ἐπαύσαντο προσφερόμεναι) A well-Greek locution, and familiar to Luke V. 4, Acts V. 42, VI. 13, XIII. 16, XXI. 32. Ἐπεὶ ἂν here is 'otherwise', the manuscript has ἐκ ἂν ἐπαύσαντο. Just as Greek expositors also read it, and they warn that it should be pronounced with a question mark.

Διὰ τὸ μηδεμίαν ἔχειν ἔτι συνείδησιν ἁμαρτιῶν τοὺς λατρεύοντας ἅπαξ κεκαθαρμένους) If they had been purged once (as true Christians are 1 Pet. I. 22, above IX. 14, 16, 18) they would no longer be conscious to themselves of new sins every year, which would require expiation. The disease having been removed, there would have been no need for new medicines. The manuscript has κεκαθαρισμένους, not badly. Thus Acts XV. 9, 2 Cor. VII. 1, Eph. V. 29, Tit. II. 14, 1 John I. 7.
