Estius had also explained it thus: The whole discourse is to be ordered and explained as follows: The Law, by those sacrifices which the priests offer every year, the same ones incessantly (or as it is in Greek, assiduously and continually), can never make those who approach or offer, that is, the priests themselves, perfect, that is, justified and sanctified. Some understand those who approach generally, both the priests and others for whom the sacrifices were offered. But even if only the priests are understood, whom he also names below as worshippers, that is, ministers of sacred things (for thus he said in the preceding chapter: Which cannot make the one serving, that is, the worshipper or his minister, perfect according to the conscience), the same judgment is nevertheless left for the others. For if the law could not perfect the offerers themselves, certainly it could not perfect others for whom something was offered. And if it could not perfect the priests, therefore neither could it the inferior priests. For the Apostle looks, as Cajetan well advises after Thomas, to those sacrifices which were offered every year by the High Priest on the day of atonement, which was the tenth day of the seventh month, concerning which matter see Leviticus 16 and 23. But infer the same regarding the rest. For if a sacrifice instituted specifically for atonement could not atone, how much less could other sacrifices which were offered throughout the whole year? It is to be noted, however, that the reason for the latter part of this sentence is contained in the former part. For from the fact that those sacrifices had to be offered every year, the same ones, and never ceased to be offered as the years recurred, he wishes to infer that they could not make their worshippers perfect. Theophylact has it thus: Such, he says, is the meaning of the context of this discourse. For if the immolations and sacrifices of such a law had acquired any strength, they would by no means be offered so continually, since once offered they would have been of some benefit, and would have ceased to be offered thereafter. But now, since that offering was made every year and very often, it is clear that the sacrifices intended to bring those wishing for perfection were weaker, and therefore after the first offering, both a second and then others, and likewise still others, followed. For even among remedies, that which is applied or taken only once is said to be both strong and more effective in curing and healing. But that which is applied changed frequently and in various ways is argued to have no power of healing, nor does it benefit the sick. This, therefore, is the Apostle's first argument from the repetition of the sacrifices of the Old Testament.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Ἐπεὶ ἂν ἐπαύσαντο προσφερόμεναι) Loquutio bene Græ- ca, & Lucæ familiaris V. 4. Act. V. 42. VI. 13. XIII. 16. XXI. 32. Ἐπεὶ ἂν hic est cæteroquin, Manuscriptus ἐκ ἂν ἐπαύσαντο. Quomodo & Græci expositores legerunt, & monent id pronunciandum cum interrogationis nota.

Διὰ τὸ μηδεμίαν ἔχειν ἔτι συνείδησιν ἁμαρτιῶν τοὺς λατρεύον- τας ἅπαξ κεκαθαρμένους) Si semel purgati fuissent (quem- admodum sunt veri Christiani 1. Petr. I. 22. supra IX. 14. 16. 18.) non ultra conscii sibi essent novorum quot- annis peccatorum, quæ expiatione egerent. Morbo ab- lato nihil opus fuisset novis medicaminibus. Manu- scriptus habet κεκαθαρισμένους, non male. Sic Act. XV. 9. 2. Cor. VII. 1. Eph. V. 29. Tit. II. 14. 1. Joh. I. 7.

Ita etiam Estius exposuerat: Sermo totus sic ordi- nandus & exponendus est: Lex iis hostiis, quas sin- gulis annis easdem indesinenter (vel ut Græce est, as- sidue & jugiter) offerunt sacerdotes, nunquam pot- est accedentes sive offerentes, hoc est, eos ipsos Sacer- dotes, reddere perfectos, id est, justificatos & sanctifi- catos. Quidam accedentes generaliter intelligunt, tum Sacerdotes, tum alios, pro quibus hostiæ offere- bantur. Sed etsi soli intelligantur Sacerdotes, quos & infra nominat cultores, id est, sacrorum ministros, (Sic enim capite præcedenti dixit: Quæ non possunt juxta conscientiam perfectum facere servientem, id est, cultorem, seu ministrum suum) De aliis tamen idem relinquitur judicium. Nam si lex non poterat perficere ipsos offerentes, certe nec alios, pro qui- bus aliquid offerebatur. Et si non poterat per- ficere Sacerdotes, ergo nec inferiores Sacerdotes. Respicit enim Apostolus, ut bene post Tho- mam Cajetanus admonet, ad ea sacrificia, quæ singulis annis offerebantur à Pontifice in die ex- piationis, qui erat decimus dies mensis septimi, de qua re Levit. XVI. & XXIII. Sed idem de cæte- ris collige. Nam si sacrificium peculiariter ad ex- piationem institutum expiare non poterat, quanto minus alia sacrificia, quæ toto anno offerebantur? No- tandum autem in priori parte hujus sententiæ conti- neri rationem posterioris. Ex eo namque quod ea sacrificia singulis annis eadem offerenda erant, nec unquam recurrentibus annis offerri desinebant: in- ferri vult, ea non potuisse cultores suos perficere. Theophylactus ita habet: Talis, inquit, est hujusce orationis contextus sententia. Si enim hujusmodi legis immolationes & hostiæ aliquid essent virium na- ctæ, nequaquam continenter adeo offerrentur, quip- pe cum semel oblatæ aliquid profuissent, & offerri præterea desiissent. Nunc vero cum singulis annis & persæpe illæ fieret oblatio, perspicuum est, hostias basce ad perfectionem volentibus afferendam, fuisse infirmiores,eoq; post primam oblationem, & secunda deinceps & alia item atque alia sequebatur. Nam & inter medelas ea dicitur & valida esse & efficacior, quam semel vel imposita vel hausta, curat & sanat. Quod vero sæpius & varie immutatum imponitur, vim medendi nullam habere arguitur, nec prodest languenti. Hoc ergò primum est Apostoli argu- mentum à sacrificiorum V. T. repetitione.

## 10:3
Vers. 3. But in them) namely, in the sacrifices: on the days of atonement. A remembrance of sins year by year) Mention is made in the prayers of the High Priest of the new crimes committed in that year, with the people assenting. See Levit. XVI, 20, and following.

After he taught that the sacrifices of the Old Testament could not make the offerers perfect; he now teaches for what purpose they were useful, namely, that annually, on the day of atonement, a commemoration of sins might be made, which is evident from the ceremony of the scapegoat, upon which all the sins of the people were placed, Lev. XVI. Which memory, repeated every single year, is an argument that that ceremony was not indeed useless, but was accustomed to be performed for the confession of sins and repentance; yet it brought perfection, justification, and salvation to no one by itself. This is the Apostolic argument: Whatever sacrifice had to be repeated frequently, by its offering those by whom it was offered could not be perfected or expiated by themselves. But the expiatory sacrifice on the day of atonement was repeated frequently for the people, namely, every year. Therefore, by the expiatory sacrifice on the day of atonement, the people for whom it was offered could not be perfected or expiated. Which form of argumentation, when observed, can be effectively concluded against the Papistic mass-sacrifice, that through it the expiation of sins cannot be accomplished, because it must be repeated frequently.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Ἀλλ’ ἐν αὐταῖς) nempe θυσίαις: diebus ἱλασμῶ. Ἀνάμνησις ἁμαρτιῶν κατ’ ἐνιαυτὸν) Mentio fit in preci- bus summi Sacerdotis novorum criminum illo anno commissorum, adstipulante populo. Vide Levit. XVI, 20. & sequentibus.

Postquam docuit sacrificia Veteris Testamenti non potuisse perfectos reddere offerentes; jam ad quid ea profuerint,docet,nimirum ut annuatim in die scil. expiationis commemoratio peccatorum fieret, quod ex hirci emissarii ceremonia constat, utpote super quem omnia peccata populi posita sunt,Lev. XVI. Quæ memoria singulis annis repetita argu- mento est, non quidem inutilem fuisse illam cere- moniam, sed ad confessionem peccatorum & pœ- nitentiam fieri consuevisse; nemini tamen per se attulisse perfectionem, justificationem ac salutem. Argumentum Apostolicum hoc est: Quodcunque sacrificium iterandum fuit sæpius, ejus oblatione non per se potuere illi, à quibus id oblatum est, perfici vel expiari. At sacrificium expiatorium in die expiationis populi sæpius, quotannis nempe iteratum fuit. Ergo per sacrificium expiatorium in die expiationis populi non potuit populus, pro quo id oblatum est, perfici vel expiari. Quæ argu- mentandi forma observata pariter adversus missi- ticum sacrificium Papisticum efficaciter concludi potest, per illud non posse fieri expiationem pec- catorum, quia id sæpius iterandum est.

## 10:4
Vers. 4. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins) See above IX. 13. To take away sins, which above is to annul and to offer up, is to extinguish sins, or to cause that one does not sin anymore. The blood of Christ does this, both because it produces faith in us, and because it gives Christ the right to obtain necessary aids for us. The blood of cattle accomplishes nothing of the sort.

He confirms what the Apostle had said, that the law concerning sacrifices could make no one perfect: because it is impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of bulls and goats: whose offering took place on the day of atonement: which anniversary sacrifices on the day of the great atonement are not brought forward by the Apostle without cause above others, but partly because they were both universal for all the sins of the whole people, and most solemn; and partly and primarily for the reason of the antitype, because they set before the eyes in a more illustrious way the expiation of the sins of the whole world to be accomplished through Christ, who had to take away the sins of the whole world in one day, Zach. III. 9, and was excellently foreshadowed regarding the placing of all sins upon the scapegoat. Is. LIII. 6. If you object, Levit. XVI. 3, it is expressly said: On this day there shall be your atonement, and cleansing, you shall be cleansed from all your sins before the Lord. Estius replies: That that remission was not true, but legal and figurative, just as were the other remissions of sins, about which there is mention in Leviticus; legal indeed, because it was only valid for averting the threats of the law, but figurative, because it signified the true remission to be given through Christ. But the response is not sufficient; namely, those ceremonies were viewed either nakedly according to the law or by themselves; or with respect to the antitype, for the representing of which they were employed. Furthermore, they are considered to have contributed to expiation either by the work performed, or insofar as those sacrifices were offered through faith. In the former way, by themselves and from the work performed alone, as they call it, they had no power of expiating, as if that immolation by itself were so pleasing to God that on account of it He would remit the sins for which they were offered, which Estius rightly denies from Jerem. XI. Will holy flesh take away your malice from you, in which you have boasted? And Mich. VI. Can the Lord be appeased with thousands of rams, or with many thousands of fat goats? But in the latter sense, it is clear from the words of the Lord brought forward that the sacrifices contributed to the remission of sins, insofar as they foreshadowed the one true expiatory sacrifice of the New Testament, and those who offered the sacrifices, or had them offered, apprehended that with true faith, Ebr. XI. 4. Which not even Estius himself could deny: For if some Jew, he says, spiritually wise, offered those sacrifices of the law with faith in the Mediator, he certainly perceived the fruit of the remission of sins. And further: The sacraments of the old law as such, that is, insofar as they pertained to the Old Testament, conferred nothing of spiritual grace: But if anyone, as I said, approached them as a Son of the New Testament, looking to the Mediator, he obtained grace. That to take away is to extinguish sins, we are nowhere taught in the sacred writings, let alone that it is to cause that one does not sin anymore. Which not even the blood of Christ does in this life, indeed, where the flesh always lusts against the Spirit, let alone the blood of cattle. Nor is the blood of Christ said to take away sins because it causes that one does not sin, but because Christ by His blood has merited and obtained that our sins might be forgiven us, and we might be cleansed by His blood from all sin, 1. Joh. I. 7, and our consciences might be purged from dead works, Ebr. IX. 15. If the blood of the sacrifices typically expiated sins, as often as minds were stirred by it to contemplate the blood of Christ by faith, and the sacrifices were offered through faith, Ebr. XI. 4. Therefore it is certain that sins were truly expiated through the blood of Christ, of which the type was there, Lev. XVII. 11. The blood of Christ does not produce faith, but faith, which is from the hearing of the Word, and through the regeneration of the Spirit, apprehends the blood of Christ, or the expiation made by the blood of Christ, so that hearts may be cleansed by it, Acts 15:9. Nor did Christ obtain for himself by his passion or the shedding of blood a certain right of obtaining necessary aids for us, but he acquired for us the grace of God, by which the gift and aid of the Holy Spirit and faith are granted to us, so that we may believe in Christ, whom no one can call Lord, except in the Holy Spirit, 1 Cor. 12:3.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ἀδύνατον γὰρ αἷμα ταύρων καὶ τράγων ἀφαιρεῖν τὰς ἁμαρτίας) Vide supra IX. 13. Ἀφαιρεῖν ἁμαρτίας quod supra ἀθετεῖν & ἀναφέρειν, est extinguere peccata, sive fa- cere, ne ultra peccetur. Id sanguis Christi facit, tum quia fidem in nobis parit, tum quia Christo jus dat nobis au- xilia necessaria impetrandi. Pecudum sanguis nihil effi- cit tale.

Confirmat, quod dixerat Apostolus, legem de sacrificiis neminem potuisse perfectum reddere: quia impossibile sanguine taurorum & hircorum auferri peccata: Quorum oblatio fiebat in die expiatio- nis: Quæ sacrificia anniversaria in die magnæ ex- piationis non citra causam præ aliis adducuntur ab Apostolo, sed partim ideo, quod fuerint & univer- salia pro peccatis omnibus totius populi, & maxi- me solennia; partim & imprimis ob rationem anti- typi, quia illustriori modo expiationem peccato- rum totius mundi per Christum perficiendam ob oculos ponebant, qui in una die peccata totius mundi auferre debuit, Zach. III. 9. & quoad impo- sitionem omnium peccatorum in hirco ἀποπομ- παίῳ eximie adumbratus fuit. Es. LIII. 6. Si obver- tas, Levit. XVI. 3. diserte dici: In hac die erit expia- tio vestra, atque mundatio, ab omnibus peccatis co- ram Domino mundabimini. Respondet Estius: Re- missionem illam non veram fuisse, sed legalem ac figu- rativam, sicut & cæteras peccatorum remissiones, de quibus in Levitico, legalem quidem, quia tantum valebat ad avertendas legis minas, figurativam ve- ro, quia significabat veram remissionem dandam per Christum. Sed non sufficit responsio; nimirum ceremoniæ istæ vel spectabantur nude secundum legem seu per se; vel respectu antitypi,cui repræsen- tando adhibitæ sunt. Adhæc vel ex opere operato ad expiationem fecisse censentur,vel quatenus per fidem offerebantur illa sacrificia. Priori modo per se, & ex solo opere operato,quod vocant, nul- lam vim expiandi habebant, quasi immolatio illa per se ita fuerit grata Deo, ut propter eam peccata remitteret illis, pro quibus offerebantur, quod re- cte negat Estius e Jerem. XI. Numquid carnes san- ctæ auferent à te malitias tuas, in quibus gloriata es? Et Mich. VI. Numquid placari potest Dominus in millibus arietum, aut in multis millibus hircorum pinguium? Posteriori autem sensu sacrificia fecisse ad remissionem peccatorum, ex verbis Domini ad- ductis patet, quatenus adumbrabant unicum ve- rum sacrificium expiatorium Novi Testamenti, idque vera fide apprehendebant, qui sacrificia of- ferebant, vel offerri curabant, Ebr. XI. 4. Quod nec ipse Estius diffiteri potuit: Quod si Judæus, in- quit, aliquis spiritualiter sapiens, cum fide Media- toris illa legis sacrificia offerret, utique fructum re- missionis peccatorum percipiebat. Et porro: Sacra- menta veteris legis ut talia, id est, quatenus ad Vetus Testamentum pertinebant, nihil conferebant gratiæ spiritualis: Sed si quis, ut dixi, ad ea accederet ut Fi- lius Novi Testamenti, respiciens in Mediatorem, gra- tiam consequebatur. Quod ἀφαιρεῖν sit extingue- re peccata, nuspiam in sacris docemur, nedum, quod sit facere, ne ultra peccetur. Quod nec san- guis Christi facit in hac quidem vita, ubi caro sem- per concupiscit adversus Spiritum, nedum pecu- dum sanguis. Nec ἀφαιρεῖν ἁμαρτίας dicitur Chri- sti sanguis, quod efficiat, ne peccetur, sed quod san- guine suo Christus promeruerit, & impetraverit, ut nobis condonentur peccata, nosque sanguine ejus mundemur ab omni peccato, 1. Joh. I. 7. & con- scientiæ nostræ purgentur ab operibus mortuis, Ebr. IX. 15. Si sanguis sacrificiorum typice expia- bat peccata, quoties eodem excitabantur animi ad fide contemplandum sanguinem Christi, & sacrifi- cia per fidem offerebantur, Ebr. XI. 4. Ergo certum est, vere expiata esse peccata per Christi sangui- nem, cujus typus illic erat, Lev. XVII. 11. Non facit sanguis Christi fidem, sed fides, quæ ex auditu Ver- bi est, & per regenerationem Spiritus, apprehendit sanguinem Christi, vel expiationem sanguine Chri- sti factam, ut ea mundentur corda Act. XV. 19. Neq; sibi impetravit Christus passione vel sanguinis ef- fusione jus quoddam nobis auxilia necessaria im- petrandi, sed nobis acquisivit gratiam Dei, qua conceditur nobis donum & auxilium Spiritus san- cti & fides, ut in Christum credamus, quem nemo potest Dominum vocare, nisi in Spiritu sancto, 1. Cor. XII. 3.

## 10:5
Verse 5. Wherefore, when coming into the world, he says) Psalm 40. David came into the world when, coming out of the caves and from exile, he showed himself to the people in Hebron, 2 Sam. 2. Christ came into the world when, departing from private life, he began to deal with the people in the name of God. For Christ himself understands this by 'coming into the world,' as we showed at John 1:9. He says, he is introduced speaking these things, David in the literal sense, Christ in the mystical.

He proves a second argument from the testimony of David, that the expiation of sins was made not through Levitical sacrifices, but solely through the sacrifice of Christ, and that those were then only types of the unique expiatory sacrifice. To attribute that double sense to the Psalm is to make the oracles of the Holy Spirit into the equivocations of the Delphic Apollo. We have refuted that double sense in the annotations to the book of Psalms, and we showed that the Psalm treats of nothing but Christ. Indeed, the Apostle assumes this here as a teaching, and as certain among the Hebrews, to whom it ought to have been acknowledged. He interprets the words of the Psalmist concerning the coming into the world not of David, but solely of Christ: which Bartholomew Petrus acknowledges against Estius: 'It seems much more straightforward if we take Psalm 40 as the voice of Christ himself, in the literal sense.' And that [interpretation] is inept concerning A gloss on David coming out of the caves and from exile. For did he then finally come into the world? That application to a mystical sense is rather inept. For who will say that the Son of God, when He came from the Father out of heaven, for He testifies that He then came into the world, John 16:28, ch. 3:19, ch. 6:14, is to be compared with the departure of David from the caves and from exile? Finally, the assertion of both senses in the same place is most inept, as is the Grotian explanation, that the words of the Psalter speak both of the departure of David from the caves and from exile, when he showed himself to the people in Hebron, of which neither in Paul nor in the book of Psalms is there any word here, and of the departure of Christ from private life, when He began to act in the name of God with the people, since nothing of such a departure occurs in the present words of the Psalter, nor does the Apostle speak of it; but rather of the adaptation of the body, which the Son of God assumed, not when He began His office having left private life, but when He was made a partaker of our flesh and blood, Heb. 2:14, and assumed the seed of Abraham, ver. 16, when He was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, Rom. 1:4, when the Word was made flesh, John 1:14. The Socinian gloss concerning the entry into the future world, which they have from their infamous Preceptor in his defens. animadv. p. 82, is unworthy of being refuted. For it is established from the perpetual usage of Holy Scripture that ἔρχεσθαι εἰς κόσμον is nowhere taken for an entry into the future world, but for the arrival into this earthly orb, John 1:9, ch. 3:19, ch. 6:14, 9:39, ch. 11:27, ch. 12:46, ch. 16:28, ch. 13:37, 1 Tim. 1:16.

Θυσίαν καὶ προσφορὰν οὐκ ἠθέλησας) In the common sense: You do not value these highly, you prefer obedience to them, 1 Sam. 15:21, 22, Hos. 6:6. In the mystical sense, you wish to put an end to the ancient sacrifices. We have said above what θυσία is, V. 1, VIII. 3. I take προσφορὰν here to refer to voluntarily offered sacrifices, נדבות. For the name קרבן, that is, προσφορὰς, is also given to them, as can be seen in Levit. 7:16.

Σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι) Jerome, in the version he made from the LXX, put 'but ears you have perfected for me.' Whence it is clear that in the Greek books there was ὦτία, which is also noted in the scholia on the Psalms by many. And Cyril among the Greeks and Arnobius the Younger among the Latins read it thus in the Psalm, as others have also advised. And this indeed agrees with the Hebrew. But for κατηρτίσω in the Hebrew is כרית, which some of the ancients translated as ὠτία δὲ διεσκαψάς μοι, with an allusion not obscure to that custom by which, after seven years had passed, those who had been in servile status, wishing to remain, enslaved themselves to their masters, Deut. 15:17. David therefore wished to say to God: You have so bound me with benefits that I wish to be yours forever by use and by servitude. But κατηρτίσω is not badly placed here either, that is, you have fitted me to the doorpost, which that law of Deuteronomy indicates was the custom. But our writer, for ὠτία, put σῶμα, according to which example a change was also made in the codices of the version of the LXX Interpreters, such as we have observed in other places. He did this, however, to express the mystical sense more clearly, for in Christ it was not the ear to the doorpost, but the whole body that was fitted to the cross in testimony of obedience. And that ear in the law was a part and at the same time a sign of the whole body, which was assigned to the master.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Διὸ εἰσερχόμενος εἰς τὸν κόσμον λέγει) Psal. XL. Venit in mundum David, cum ex speluncis & ab exilio egrediens ostendit sese populo in Hebrone, 2. Sam. II. Venit in mundum Christus, cum è vita privata egre- diens nomine Dei agere cœpit cum populo. Id enim Christus ipse intelligit per ἐρχεσθαι εἰς τὸν κοσμον, ut osten- dimus ad Joh. I. 9. Λέγει, introducitur hæc loquens, David sensu vulgari, Christus mystico.

Argumentum alterum è testimonio Davidis pro- bat, non per sacrificia Levitica, sed unice per sacrifi- cium Christi peccatorum expiationem factam, & tum typos illa saltem fuisse sacrificii unici expiatorii. Geminuin illum sensum Psalmo tribuere, est è Spirit9 sancti oraculis æquivocationes Apollinis Delphici facere. Profligavimus illum geminum sensum in annot. ad librum Psalmorum, & ostendimus non nisi de Christo Psalmum agere. Imo id hic docet, ac pro certo penes Ebræos, quibus id oportet fuisse ὁμολογούμενον, Apostolus assumit. De adventu in mundum non Davidis, sed Christi unice inter- pretatur verba Hierophaltis: Quod contra Estium agnoscit Bartholomæus Petrus: Videtur multo ex- peditius, si Psal. XXXIX. accipiamus tanquam vo- cem ipsius Christi, sensu literali. Et inepta est illa de David è speluncis & ab exilio egresso glossa. Num enim tum demum in mundum venit? Ineptior illa ad sensum mysticum applicatio. Nam quis dicet, Filium Dei, cum à Patre egressus de cœlo venit, tum enim in mundum se venisse testatur, Joh. XVI. 28. cap. III. 19. cap. VI. 14. comparandum esse cum egressu Davidis è speluncis & ab exilio? Ine- ptissima denique utriusque sensus in eodem loco assertio, & Grotiana explicatio, quod verba Psalterii & de egressu Davidis ex speluncis & ab exilio, cum sese populo in Hebrone ostendit, de quo nec apud Paulum, nec in libro Psalmorum ullum hic verbum habetur, & de egressu Christi è vita privata, cum nomine Dei agere cœpit, cum populo, loquantur, quum de tali egressu nihil in Psalterii præsentibus verbis occurrat, nec Apostolus de eo sermonem fa- ciat; sed potius de adaptatione corporis, quod Fi- lius Dei assumpsit, non eum officium suum relicta vita privata aggressus est, sed cum carnis & sangui- nis nostri particeps factus est, Ebr. II. 14. & semen Abrahæ assumpsit, vers. 16, cum natus est ex semine Davidis secundum carnem, Rom. I. 4. cum Ver- bum caro factum est, Joh. I. 14. Socinianorum glos- sa de ingressu in mundum futurum, quam ab infau- sto suo Præceptore in defens. animadv. p. 82. ha- bent, indigna est, quæ confutetur. Nam ex per- petuo S. Scripturæ usu constat, ἔρχεσθαι εἰς κόσμον nuspiam de ingressu in mundum futurum, sed de adventu in hunc terrenum orbem accipi, Joh. I. 9. cap. III. 19. cap. VI. 14. IX. 39. cap. XI. 27. cap. XII. 46. cap. XVI. 28. cap. XIII. 37. 1. Tim. I. 16.

Θυσίαν καὶ προσφορὰν οὐκ ἠθέλησας) In sensu vulgari : Hæc non magni facis, obedientiam istis præfers, 1. Sam. XV. 21. 22. Os. VI. 6. In sensu mystico, finem vis face- re sacrificiis veteribus. Quid sit θυσία diximus supra V. 1. VIII. 3. Προσφορὰν hic accipio de sacrificiis sponte ob- latis נדבות. Nam & iis datur nomen קרבן, id est, προσφορὰς, ut videre est Levit. VII. 16.

Σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι) Hieronymus in versione, quam fecit ex LXX. posuit aures autem perfecisti mihi. Un- de liquet, in Græcis libris fuisse ὦτία, quod & in scholiis ad Psalmos multis annotatum est. Et sic legere in Psal- mo Cyrillus inter Græcos, Arnobius minor inter Lati- nos, ut & alii monuere. Et hoc quidem cum Ebræo con- venit. Sed pro κατηρτίσω in Ebræo est כרית, quod ve- terum quidam verterunt, ὠτία δὲ διεσκαψάς μοι, allusio- ne non obscura ad morem illum, quo septennio exacto, qui in servili fortuna fuerant, imposterum se volentes heris suis mancipabant, Deut. XV. 17. Voluit ergo Da- vid dicere Deo: Ita me devinxisti beneficiis, ut impo- sterum semper tuus esse velim usu ac mancipio. Sed nec κατηρτίσω male hic positum, id est, aptasti me posti, quod fieri solitum lex illa Deuteronomii indicat. At scriptor noster pro ὠτία posuit σῶμα, ad quod exem- plum etiam in codicibus versionis LXX. Interpretum facta est mutatio, qualem & aliis locis observavimus. Fecit autem hoc, ut sensum mysticum magis expri- meret, non enim in Christo auricula posti, sed corpus totum cruci aptatum est in obedientiæ testimonium. Et auricuta illa in lege pars erat simulque signum totius cor- poris, quod hero addicebatur.

## 10:6
Vers. 6. Ὁλοκαυτώματα καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας οὐκ ἐυδόκησας) In the LXX it is οὐκ ᾔτησας, as also in the Hebrew לא שאלת. But our writer did not wish to show the force of disgust. And therefore he chose a word most effective for that purpose. Περὶ ἁμαρτίας, supply θυσίαν חטאת.

But what is the reason here for the different senses, common and mystical, when one flows from the other spontaneously without a mystery? For if God does not magnify the victim and the oblation, why would He have required them either by Himself or in perpetuity? Nor did these burnt offerings, which are indeed consumed by fire (so Theophylact has it), please you as sacrifices, that is, you did not want them, nor did you accept these, nor those which were offered for sin. There was indeed, as there were diverse causes, a diverse name imposed upon the sacrifices. For some were offered for transgressions, some for negligence, some were even called salutary, and some conciliatory, others moreover precatory, and finally others were offered for the sake of purification. Which are nevertheless entirely abolished, because you did not want sacrifice and oblation. These kinds of sacrifices are distinguished otherwise, so that by θυσίαν זבח is designated the peace or Eucharistic victim, by προσφορὰν מנחה any oblation of inanimate things, such as fine flour, incense, firstfruits, etc., by ὁλοκαυτώματα the sacrifices which were entirely burned, called by the Hebrews עֹלָה and אִשָׁה from being elevated upon the altar, and by τὰς περὶ ἁμαρτίας any propitiatory sacrifices for sin. As for the words of the Psalmist, σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι, Grotius hallucinates most gravely regarding both their integrity and their interpretation, by calling the former into doubt, and by devising the latter as a twin, and one most diverse, and, which is the head of the cause, entirely alien.

The words brought from the version of the LXX Interpreters are rashly called into doubt. For although in the Hebrew it is, 'ears you have dug for me,' and the Septuagint interpretation already has σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι, it is not to be presumed that this reading is vicious, or that it crept in from this text of ours: Because it is not new for the LXX not to render according to the letter, but according to the sense, which they also observed here; because they noticed that in the verse immediately following, David opposes the arrival of the Messiah to the sacrifices, whence they gathered that the same sense obtains here also, and so the adaptation of the body is opposed to the sacrifices, which the arrival of the Son of God into the world for the oblation of the body through the offering of sacrifices requires and imports: Which cannot be doubtful to us from the Apostolic interpretation, unless we wish to say that the same was distorted by the Apostle beyond the mind of that version. The Son of God would certainly not have had ears in the human manner, nor would they have been pierced for him, had he not had a body; and that piercing or boring of the ears, which is attributed to God, whether to pierce is understood simply as to open, as the Messiah says in Isaiah 50:4, 'The Lord God has opened my ear,' or whether regard is had to the ceremony employed for servants in Exodus 21:5, or whether, as others prefer, that physical opening of the ears is understood, because by nature ears in the human body are not closed but open, does it not presuppose the adaptation of a human body made by God? The Chaldean also expounded on the formation of the ears, which indeed requires a human body, in which the ears are understood to be formed for listening to the precepts of the Lord. For he rendered it thus: 'But ears for listening to your precepts you have formed for me.' That suspicion regarding the Greek Codices of the LXX Interpreters corrected from the present passage by substituting the word σῶμα for ὠτία is vain. For it is by no means likely that the Apostle, when citing the received version of the LXX Interpreters, changed it. For when he cites passages differently than the LXX Interpreters have them, he cites the words from the Hebrew text; but that he should cite a word from the text of the LXX Interpreters and substitute another word, which is found neither in the LXX Interpreters nor in the Hebrew text, you will nowhere easily find. That he says Jerome, in the version he made from the LXX Interpreters, used 'ears you have perfected for me' is false. In the Basel edition it is read: 'But a body you have perfected for me,' and thus the version of the LXX is also cited: Σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι. Regarding the commentaries attributed to Jerome on the Psalms, in which the Latin translation is inserted, the judgment of learned men, that they were falsely inscribed to Jerome, was not unknown to Grotius. And although the text of the Psalm has 'ears,' yet in the commentary no mention is made of ears, but only of a body; although also the Vulgate edition of the Psalms, which is from the Greek, has 'ears,' not 'body,' yet Estius rightly says that this was taken from the Hebrew, or from some other Greek translation. For the Greek codices that exist today consistently read σῶμα, that is, body, and the ancients, both Greek and Latin, explain it as such; Ambrose, Augustine, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Euthymius, and Apollinarius the Paraphrast, which reading the old and Roman Latin Psalters also exhibit. Now, a certain 'old Psalter' is spoken of, different from the Roman and Gallican, the use of which was among the Latins, among others, before the age of Jerome, as Estius notes here. But Cyril of Alexandria, in book IX against Julian, page 309 in my edition, does not read ὠτία, but σῶμα, thus repeating the text of the Psalm: Σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω, and who would believe that he falsely alleged the same against Julian?

How Crellius and Schlichtingius sweat to argue that the Hebrew text is corrupt. Let their commentary on this passage teach us. It seems, they say, that one must say either that there was once some Hebrew reading other than that which now exists, especially if there is some similarity of the names by which ears and body are signified in Hebrew: or that the Greek version in this place, as in many others, was changed. The former is more approved by us, especially because, although not necessary, it is highly probable that the author, when he mentions the offering of the body of Christ a little later, which he does nowhere else, had regard for these words. But it is hardly credible that he would have done so if they departed entirely from the Hebrew truth. Although we willingly leave it to those who are more skilled in the Hebrew language to think about what Hebrew reading they might suspect to be close to this one which now exists, and which might have induced the Greek interpreters to this version: yet we ought not to cast this labor onto others in such a way that we do not also attempt something in this matter ourselves, and submit our conjecture to the judgment of others. Therefore, as far as the word καταρτίζεσθαι is concerned, there seems to be less need to labor over it, since the Hebrew word carab can also signify to strike or to cut out, and by metaphor to form, to adapt, to make complete with its members and parts, by a likeness taken from statuaries or sculptors, who by striking, sculpting, and, if I may say so, digging, form and fashion statues, which in Greek you would rightly call καταρτίζεσθαι. And if a noun that denotes a body were joined to this verb, there would hardly be anything more fitting in meaning. Wherefore one must think primarily about the word σῶμα or body. In the Hebrew, it now reads oznaim, ears: one must find some word similar to this, or close as far as the shapes of the letters are concerned (for the similarity of vowel points, which in ancient times were hardly ever written, as is the case today in the books of the Rabbis, is not to be sought here) which signifies body. Such a word seems to be geviah, which occurs very often in the sacred writings. For take away from the word oznaim the first letter aleph, which could have fallen out without difficulty, the remaining letters are not unlike those which constitute the word geviah, which has the meaning of body, which those who wish to write both in Hebrew letters will easily recognize; but let those who are more skilled think further about this matter. Nor does anything stand in the way of both readings having been agreeable to the mind of the Holy Spirit and once accepted. But what, I pray, is the analogy of the words גויה and אזנים, even if you set aside the points? What necessity is there to establish that the Hebrew text is corrupt? How great also is this rashness, to invent at will some word that could be substituted by mere whim, without the testimony of any codex or author? Thus, forsooth, those sectarians play with the Holy Scriptures as boys do with knucklebones. We have discussed another word substituted by Grotius in the annotations to the Psalms in the 'Biblia Illustrata V. T.', and another by Morin in 'Critica Sacra Biblica', second edition, page 296, and the first edition, page 529 ff., where this passage, especially regarding the reading, has been treated more fully.

As for the sense handed down by Grotius. It is doubled without cause in the Psalm; as it treats not of David, but solely of Christ: nor can it have the sense at the same time: You adapted me to the post, and you adapted my body to the cross. For these are very different things. Nor does the Psalmist treat of a body adapted to the cross or the crucifixion of Christ, but of the coming of Christ into the world, as does the Apostle. Finally, that gloss of the words of the sacred psalmist is also foreign: you have bound me so with benefits, that I wish to be yours forever by use and ownership. For how will this sense be extorted from the words: But you have pierced my ears or completed them for me? But enough has already been said about these Grotian inventions regarding the book of Psalms, where we have also pursued the true sense more extensively. The sense of the Apostolic allegation is obvious: In the coming of the Son of God into the world, which happened in the incarnation, a human body was adapted to him, and his ears were perfected by piercing to the point of rendering obedience even to the death of the cross, so that by the offering of the body he might fulfill that which was prefigured through the offering of sacrifices. Estius thus reconciles (not unsuitably) the version of the Psalm cited by the Apostle and the Hebrew text: That which is referred to the opening of the ears as obedience is not entirely different from what the LXX wrote, 'you adapted a body to me'. But just as it most perfectly befits Christ to have been taught by the Father, and to have rendered obedience to the Father: So it applies to him singularly above all others, that he can say to God, 'you adapted a body to me', namely through the incarnation: insofar as in the womb of the most pure Virgin a most perfect body was formed for him, and free from every stain of corruption, and clearly such that, with the useless multitude of sacrifices of the Old Testament removed, the one offered to God the Father on the cross would be pleasing and valid for the salvation of all men. Nor is Theophylact obscure on the sense of these words: 'But you adapted a body to me': As if he were to say, 'Since you have already destined from eternity that this body of mine would be a finished and perfect sacrifice.' And to the following: 'Then I said: Behold I come': You see how, even before the Lord assumed flesh, the sacrifices were cast out and repudiated. For even after the former rites of sacrificing were abolished, then Christ himself said, I have professed, behold I come, to perform thy will. But the Father's will is of this kind, that the Son be immolated for the world, and men be justified not in sacrifices, but in his death. For I have announced, he says, righteousness in the great assembly. In the addition of the Censor Estianus it is thus held: It is known that by a certain metalepsis these three readings come to the same sense, thou hast dug ears, thou hast prepared a body, thou hast perfected ears, and that each of them announces the incarnation of the Son of God, and the magnitude of the grace which was to be conferred upon him made man; specifically of the obedience, to be undergone even unto death for the redemption of men. B. Gerhard advises that the LXX expressed the sense, and therefore their version can be joined with the sense which the Hebrew text expresses, in this way: Because thou hast prepared a body for me in the incarnation, therefore thou hast also made me an obedient servant, that I may offer that same body to thee in true obedience as a sacrifice for the sins of the human race. Certainly the gloss concerning the incorruptible and immortal body of CHRIST prepared, that he might offer himself in heaven, agrees neither with the words of David concerning ears pierced, nor with the intention of the Apostle, who speaks of his coming into this world that he might do the will of God, nor with the truth of the matter, because the offering of Christ was made on the altar of the cross, and not in the heavens.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Ὁλοκαυτώματα καὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας οὐκ ἐυδόκησας) In LXX. est, οὐκ ᾔτησας, ut & in Ebræo לא שאלת. Sed noluit noster Scriptor vim fastidii ostendere. Ideoque verbum ad id quam maxime efficax delegit. Περὶ ἁμαρ- τίας, supple θυσίαν חטאת.

Quænam vero hic ratio diversorum sensuum, vulgaris & mystici, quum unum ex altero sponte citra mysterium fluat. Nam si non magnificat De- us hostiam & oblationem, cur vel per sese, vel in perpetuum illa requisivisset? Nec holocaustomata hæc, quæ scilicet igne conficiuntur (ita habet Theo- phylactus) sacrificia tibi placuerunt, id est noluisti ea, nec in acceptum hæc retulisti, neque quæ essent de peccato oblatæ. Erat quidem ut diversis de causis, ita & diversum sacrificiis nomen impositum. Nam alia quidem pro commissis offerebantur, nonnulla pro negligentia, quædam etiam salutaria diceban- tur, & conciliatoria quædam, alia insuper preca- toria, alia demum purgationis gratia offerebantur. Quæ tamen eo sunt prorsus sublata, quia sacrificium & oblationem noluisti. Genera hæc sacrificiorum ita alias discernuntur, ut per θυσίαν זבח victima pacifica seu Eucharistica, per προσφορὰν מנחה, vel quævis inanimatarum rerum oblatio, ut similæ, thuris, primitiarum, &c. per ὁλοκαυτώματα sacrifi- cia, quæ tota cremabantur, Ebræis עֹלָה & אִשָׁה ab elevando super altare dicta, per τὰς περὶ ἁμαρτίας sacrificia quævis propitiatoria pro peccato desi- gnentur. Quod ad verba Psaltis, σῶμα δὲ κατηρ- τίσω μοι circà eorum tum integritatem tum inter- pretationem gravissime hallucinatur Grotius illam in dubium vocando, hanc verò geminam, eamque maxime diversam, & quod caput causæ est, prorsus alienam excogitando.

Temere in dubium vocantur verba adducta è versione LXX. Interpretum. Nam etsi in Ebræo sit, aures perfodisti mihi, ac septuaginta-viralis in- terpretatio jam habet σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι, non tamen præsumendum, vitiosam esse hanc lectio- nem, vel ex hoc nostro textu irrepsisse: Quia non novum est LXX. non reddere κατὰ γράμμα, sed κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν, quod hic etiam observarunt; quia animadvertebant, versu proxime sequente Davidem sacrificiis opponere adventum Messiæ, unde colli- gebant, eundem sensum hic etiam obtinere, adeoq; sacrificiis opponi corporis adaptationem, quam adventus Filii Dei in mundum ad oblationem cor- poris per sacrificiorum oblationem figuratam re- quirit, & importat: Quod ex Apostolica interpre- tatione nobis dubium esse nequit, nisi præter men- tem versionis istius ab Apostolo eandem detortam esse, dicere velimus. Aures certe nec habuisset Filius Dei humano more, nec eidem perfossæ fuissent, nisi habuisset corpus; Et aurium illa per- fossio sive perforatio, quæ Deo tribuitur, sive per- fodere simpliciter intelligatur aperire, ut Messias Es. L. 4. Dominus Deus, inquit, aperuit mihi aurem, sive ad ceremoniam penes servos adhibi- tam, Exod. XXI. 5. respectus habeatur, sive, quod alii malunt, physica illa aurium apertio, quod na- tura non clausæ, sed apertæ sint aures in humano corpore, intelligatur, annon præsupponit corpo- ris humani adaptationem à Deo factam? De for- matione aurium etiam Chaldæus exposuit, qua vero requirit corpus humanum, in quo formandæ in- telligantur aures ad auscultanda præcepta Domi- ni. Sic enim reddidit: Aures autem ad auscultanda præcepta tua formasti mihi. Suspicio illa de corre- ctis è præsenti loco Codicibus Græcis LXX. Inter- pret. posita voce σῶμα pro ὠτία, vana est. Nam mutasse Apostolum allegantem LXX. Interpret. receptam versionem, nullatenus est verisimile. Cum enim aliter adducit loca, quam LXX. Inter- pret. habent, è textu Ebræo adducit verba, at addu- cere eum verbum è textu LXX. Interp. & aliud ver- bum substituere, quod neque in LXX. Interpreti- bus invenitur, nec in Ebræo textu, nuspiam facile reperies. Quod Hieronymum dicit in versione, quam fecit ex LXX. Interpret. posuisse, aures per- fecisti mihi, falsum est. In editione Basileensi legi- tur: Corpus autem perfecisti mihi, atq; ita etiam ad- ducitur versio τῶν LXX. Σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω μοι. De commentariis vero Hieronymo tributis, in Psal- mis, quibus inserta est Latina translatio, non igno- tum fuit Grotio eruditorum judicium, quod falso Hieronymo inscripti sint. Et licet textus Psalmi ha- beat aures, in commentario tamen nulla fit aurium mentio, sed corporis tantum; licet etiam Vulgatæ Psalmorum editio, quæ ex Græco est, aures habeat, non corpus, recte tamen id ex Ebræo sumptum dicit Estius, vel ex alia quapiam Græca translatione. Nam qui hodie extant Codices Græci, constanter le- gunt σῶμα, id est, corpus, idque exponunt veteres, tam Græci, quam Latini; Ambrosius, Augustinus, Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, Euthymius, & Apolli- narius Paraphrastes, quam lectionem etiam exhi- bent Latina Psalteria vetus & Romanum. Dicitur autem Psalterium vetus certum quoddam, diversum à Romano & Gallicano, cujus usus inter alia erat apud Latinos, ante ætatem Hieronymi, ut hic Estius. Cyrillus vero Alexandrinus libr. IX. contra Julian. pag. mihi 309. non ὠτία legit, sed σῶμα, ita repe- tens textum Psalmi : Σῶμα δὲ κατηρτίσω, quem falfo eundem contra Julianum allegasse quis cre- diderit?

Quomodo Crellius & Schlichtingius sudent, ut textum Ebræum corruptionis arguant. Commen- tarius eorum h. l. edoceat. Videtur, inquiunt, dicendum esse, aut aliquam etiam olim fuisse lectionem Ebraicam, quam ista, quæ nunc extat, præsertim si aliqua sit vicinitas nominum, quibus aures & corpus in Ebræo significantur: aut versionem Græcam hoc lo- co, quemadmodum & aliis in multis fuisse mutatam. Prius nobis magis probatur, præsertim quia, utut non necessarium, maxime tamen verisimile est, au- torem, cum paulo post oblationem corporis Christi commemorat, quod alibi nuspiam facit, ad hæc ver- ba respexisse. Vix autem credibile est, id eum factu- rum fuisse, si à veritate Ebræa penitus recederent. Et- si vera iis, qui Ebraicæ linguæ peritiores sunt, cogi- tandum libenter relinquimus, quam suspicentur fuisse Ebraicam lectionem, quæ huic, quæ nunc extat, vicina, Græcos Interpretes ad hanc versionem induxerit: non debemus tamen in alios hunc labo- rem ita rejicere, quin ipsi quoque aliquid ea in re conemur, & conjecturam nostram aliorum judi- cio subjiciamus. Quod igitur ad verbum καταρτί- ζεσθαι attinet, de illo minus laborandum videtur, cum verbum Ebræum carab possit etiam cædere vel exci- dere significare, & per Metaphoram formare, apta- re, suis membris ac partibus integram efficere, simili- tudine à statuariis aut sculptoribus sumpta, qui cæ- dendo, sculpendo, atque, ut ita dicam, fodiendo sta- tuas efformant, atque effingunt, quod Græce recte di- xeris καταρτίζεσθαι. Quod si huic verbo adjunctum fuerit nomen, quod corpus denotet, significatione illa vix quid erit concinnius. Quare de voce σῶμα sive corporis potissimum cogitandum est. In Ebræo nunc legitur oznaim aures: Huic voci reperienda est aliqua similis, seu quod ad literarum figuras attinet vicina, (nam similitudo punctorum vocalium, quæ antiquitus vix unquam scribebantur, ut hodieque in Rabbinorum sit libris, non est hic requirenda) quæ corpus significet. Talis autem videtur esse vox geviah, quæ sæpissime in sacris occurrit. Tolle enim ex voce oznaim primam literam aleph, quæ excidere haud difficulter potuit, reliquæ literæ non sunt absimiles illis, quæ vocem geviah, corporis significationem ha- bentem, constituunt, quod facile agnoscent, qui literis Ebraicis utramque pingere voluerint; sed peritiores ea de re amplius cogitent. Neque vero quicquam repugnat, utramque lectionem fuisse Spiritus sancti menti consentaneam & olim receptam. Sed quænam obsecro est analogia vocum גויה & אזנים, etiamsi puncta seponas? Quæ necessitas textum E- bræum corruptum esse statuendi? Quanta etiam hæc temeritas, excogitare pro lubitu aliquam vo- cem, quæ substitui possit ex mero arbitrio, sine ul- lius codicis vel autoris testimonio? Ita scilicet lu- dunt sectarii illi sacris literis veluti pueri astragalis. Aliam vocem à Grotio substitutam discussimus in annot. ad Psal. in Bibl. Illustr. V. T. aliam Morini in Crit. S. Bibl. edit. poster. pag. 296. prioris pag. 529. seqq. ubi de hoc loco, quod ad lectionem im- primis, plenius actum.

Quod ad sensum è Grotio traditum. Geminatur ille citra causam in Psalmo; utpote qui non de Da- vide, sed unice de Christo agit: neque simul sen- sum habere potest: Aptasti me posti, ac corpus me- um cruci aptasti. Sunt enim hæc diversissima. Neq; de corpore cruci aptato vel crucifixione Christi, sed de adventu Christi in mundum agit Psaltes, ut & Apostolus. Denique aliena etiam est glossa illa verborum Hieropsaltis: ita me devinxisti beneficiis, ut imposterum semper tuus esse velim usu & mancipio. Quomodo enim hic sensus è verbis: Aures autem perforasti mihi vel perfecisti mihi, extorquebitur? Sed de hisce commentis Grotianis jam dictum ad librum Psalmi, ubi etiam fusius verum sensum prosecuti sumus. Sensus Apostolicæ allegationis in proclivi est: In adventu Filii Dei in mundum, qui in incarnatione accidit, corpus humanum ipsi adaptatum, auresque perforando perfectas esse ad obedientiam usq; ad mortem crucis præstandam, ut oblatione corporis id impleret, quod per sacri- ficiorum oblationem præfiguratum fuit. Estius ita conciliat (non absimiliter) versionem Psalmi lau- datam ab Apostolo; & textum Ebræum: Ab hoc sensu quod obedientiam refertur aurium apertio, non omnino diversum est, quod scripserunt LXX. corpus aptasti mihi. Sicut autem Christo perfectis- sime convenit doctum esse à Patre, & obedientiam Patri præstitisse: Ita præ omnibus singulariter in eum competit, ut Deo dicere possit, corpus aptasti mihi, sci- licet per incarnationem: quatenus in utero purissima Virginis formatum est ei corpus integerrimum, & ab omni labe corruptionis liberum, ac plane tale, quod remota inutili multitudine sacrificiorum Vete- ris Testamenti, unum Deo Patri in cruce oblatum placeret ad omnium hominum salutem valiturum. Nec obscure sensum Theophylactus ad hæc verba: Corpus autem aptasti mihi: Perinde, inquit, ac si dicat: Cum enim corpus hoc meum consummatam perfectamque hostiam fore jam à seculo destinasti. Et ad sequentia: Tunc dixi: Ecce venio: Vides, quem- admodum vel antequam Dominus carnem assume- ret, ejecta sacrificia fuerunt & repudiata. Nam & post sublatos sacrificandi pristinos ritus, tunc Christus ipse professus sum inquit, ecce venio, tuæ exequendæ voluntatis. Patris vero voluntas hujus- modi est, ut Filius immoletur pro mundo, & homi- nes justificentur non in sacrificiis, sed hujus in mor- te. Annuntiavi enim, inquit, justitiam in Eccle- sia magna. In additione Censoris Estiani sic habe- tur: Notum est, quadam metalepsi has tres lectio- nes in eundem sensum venire, aures fodisti, corpus aptasti, aures perfecisti, & quamlibet earum præ- nunciare Filii Dei incarnationem, & gratiæ, quæ ipsi homini facto esset conferenda, magnitudinem; obe- dientiæ speciatim, usque ad mortem pro redem- ptione hominum subeundam. B. Gerhardus mo- net LXX. sensum expressisse, ac proinde versio- nem ipsorum cum sensu, quem textus Ebræus expri- mit, conjungi posse, hoc modo: Quia corpus mihi in incarnatione aptasti, ideo etiam obsequentem servum me fecisti, ut idem illud corpus pro pecca- tis humani generis in vera obedientia tibi in sacrifi- cium offeram. Sane glossa de corpore incorru- ptibili & immortali CHRISTI concinnato, ut in cælis sese offerret, nec Davidis verbis de au- ribus perforatis, nec Apostoli, qui de adven- tu in hunc mundum, ut faceret voluntatem Dei, loquitur, intentioni, nec rei veritati con- venit, quia oblatio Christi in ara crucis facta, non autem in cœlis est.

## 10:7
Ver. 7.

Τότε εἶπον) These are also words of the Psalm, and אז, which is translated τότε, signifies therefore.

Ἰδὺ ἥκω, ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίου γέγραπται περὶ ἐμῦ, τῦ ποιῆσαι ὁ Θεὸς τὸ θέλημά συ) So also the LXX, among whom ὁ Θεὸς is usually the vocative. ספר, which is translated βιβλίον, is called by the Hebrews any writing whatsoever. Thus a bill of divorce is called ספר כריתת, βιβλίον ἀποσασίας, Deut. XXIV. 1. And the Syrian well placed ܛܬܒܝ here. But here is understood an instrument drawn up concerning perpetual mancipation into slavery, of which it has now begun to be treated. Moreover, all the papers of the Hebrews were not accustomed to be divided into pages, but to be rolled into a little circle, as can be seen in Jerem. XXXVI. 27; wherefore מגלת—ספר here in the Hebrew is nothing else than a rollable paper, which Aquila and Symmachus called ἕλημα. They called that very thing κεφαλίδα from the round shape of the head, whence also in buildings that are round, they are called κεφαλίδες, as in Exod. XXVI. 32, XXVII. 17, XXXVI. 34, XXXVIII. 27, 28, Num. III. 36, 1 Kings VIII. 30, 2 Chron. III. 5, and in other places. Suidas: Κεφαλὶς βιβλίυ ὅπερ τινὲς ἕλημά φασιν. Esdræ VI. 2. In the Hebrew מגלה, in the Greek κεφαλὶς, nor does the same Hebrew name translate it otherwise in Ezech. II. 9, III. 1, 2, for which in Jerem. XXXVI. 23 is placed χάρτης and χαρτίον, but in Isaiah VIII. 1 is another Hebrew name, but of the same origin and meaning, גליון, where Eusebius says that among certain interpreters κεφαλίδας is placed. In the instrument, he says, made between us, it is written that I will do whatever you wish. Thus gladiators made an auctoratio to be burned, to be bound, to be beaten with rods, and to be killed with the sword.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Τότε εἶπον) Sunt & hęc verba Psalmi & אז, quod ver- titur τότε, significat propterea.

Ἰδὺ ἥκω, ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίου γέγραπται περὶ ἐμῦ, τῦ ποιῆσαι ὁ Θεὸς τὸ θέλημά συ) Sic & LXX. apud quos, ὁ Θεὸς, solet esse Vocativus. ספר quod vertitur βιβλίον Ebræis dici- tur quodvis scriptum. Ita scriptura divortii vocatur ספר כריתת βιβλίον ἀποσασίας, Deut. XXIV. 1. Et bene Syrus hic posuit ܛܬܒܝ. Hic verò intelligitur instru- mentum confectum de mancipatione perpetua in servi- tutem, de qua jam agi cœpit. Omnes autem chartæ E- bræorum non in paginas distingui, sed in orbiculum convolvi solebant, ut videre est Jerem. XXXVI. 27. quare מגלת—ספר hic in Ebræo nihil est aliud, quam charta volubilis, quod Aquila & Symmachus dixere ἕλημα. Id ipsum vocabant κεφαλίδα à rotunda capitis forma, unde & in ædificiis, quæ rotunda sunt, κεφαλίδες dicuntur, ut Exod. XXVI. 32. XXVII. 17. XXXVI. 34. XXXVIII. 27. 28. Num. III. 36. 1. Reg. VIII. 30. 2. Paral. III. 5. & aliis in locis. Suidas: Κεφαλὶς βιβλίυ ὅπερ τινὲς ἕλημά φασιν. Esdræ VI. 2. In Ebræo מגלה in Græco κεφαλὶς, nec aliter idipsum nomen Ebræum vertit Ezech. II. 9. III. 1. 2. pro quo Jerem. XXXVI. 23. ponitur χάρτης & χαρτίον, Esaiæ verò VIII. 1. est nomen alterum Ebræum, sed ejusdem originis & significatus גליון ubi Eusebius apud quosdam Interpretes ait positum κεφαλίδας. In instrumento, inquit, inter nos facto scriptum est, me facturum, quicquid vis. Sic gladiatores auctorationem faciebant uri, scindi, ferro necari.

## 10:8
Ver. 8.

Ἀνώτερον λέγων) that is, having said: the present for the past tense.

ὅτι θυσίαν, κὶ προσφορὰν, κὶ ὁλοκαυτώματα, κὶ περὶ ἁμαρτίας ὐκ ἠθέλησας, ὐδὲ εὐδόκησας) ὅτι here, as often, is the word of one reciting. And he contracted two members of the Psalm, dissected because of the parity of sense, into one.

Αἵτινες κατὰ τὸν νόμον προσφέρονται) It is apparent that all those things were prescribed by the law. There was impending, therefore, a change of the law, namely, with those words ὐκ ἠθέλησας and ὐκ εὐδόκησας taken in a more sublime sense.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Ἀνώτερον λέγων) id est λέξας: Præsens pro modo exacto.

ὅτι θυσίαν, κὶ προσφορὰν, κὶ ὁλοκαυτώματα, κὶ περὶ ἁμαρ- τίας ὐκ ἠθέλησας, ὐδὲ εὐδόκησας) ὅτι hic, ut sæpe, est reci- tantis verbum. Et duo membra Psalmi dissecta ob sensus paritatem in unum contraxit.

Αἵτινες κατὰ τὸν νόμον προσφέρονται) Apparet illa omnia lege præscripta. Imminebat ergo legis mutatio nempe verbis illis ὐκ ἠθέλησας & ὐκ εὐδόκησας sumptis in sensu sublimiore.

## 10:9
Ver. 9.

Τότε εἴρηκεν) For that reason he subjoined. The words of our writer. In the Latin also it ought to be read dixit, as not a few codices have.

Ἰδὺ ἥκω τῦ ποιῆσαι ὁ Θεὸς τὸ θέλημά συ) He omitted that ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίε γέγραπται περὶ ἐμῦ, because it is figurative and was employed only for the sake of ornament.

A new and hitherto unheard-of sense of the word book again: That by it is understood an instrument concerning perpetual manumission into slavery, and that it is added here only for the sake of ornament. Most interpreters understand a volume of Holy Scripture, although differences of opinion occur regarding the word ἐν κεφαλίδι, and what exactly the Apostle may be referring to in the book of scripture is explained in various ways. For some, as Estius reports, take it concerning Genesis, as Jerome does concerning the beginning of Genesis, Theophylact concerning the words of Gen. I. 26: let us make man in our image: Others more recent, among whom is Ribera, concerning the passage Gen. II. 23, because of the comparison with Eph. V. 30. (But because in these there is nothing at all of that which Christ says here: I do your will, therefore) some others explain it concerning the Proto-Evangelium, Gen. III. 15, some indeed concerning any promises whatsoever about the Messiah existing in Genesis, others concerning the promises in Moses, or specifically concerning that which is held in Deut. XVIII, as Estius does, with Junius leading the way, thinking that the volume of the book is noted, and understands the scriptures of the Old Testament, which abound in prophecies about the Messiah. Alien are the interpretations in Estius of Thomas concerning the book of life, of Augustine concerning the book of Psalms, as being not yet compiled at that time, of others concerning the passage Exod. XXI. 5, concerning the piercing of the servant's ear, and of Crellius, concerning that part of the law in which the offices of the King are described, Deut. XVII, and also of those who interpret it concerning Christ according to his human nature, of which God is the head. Concerning an instrument established between God and David, or between God and Christ, it is neither to be found in Holy Scripture, nor does it appear how one could have appealed to such an instrument here. It is also rashly asserted that this particle was added only for the sake of ornament, since Christ could truly testify in במגלת, in the volume of the book, and ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίε, which has been rendered most simply by the blessed Luther, im Buch, κατ' ἐξοχὴν, just as the Holy Bible comes under this name κατ' ἀν´ονομασίαν, that it was written about himself, which is written about him in Moses and the Prophets, namely concerning all the prophecies which deal with Christ, just as Christ explained most things about himself, Luke XXIV and elsewhere in the Evangelical history. That word also occurs in Ezech. II and III, where by κεφαλίδα it cannot be understood as head or chapter, and Zach. V, where the Hebrew word the LXX. δρέπανον, a sickle; Aquila and Theodotion placed διφθέραν, which in ancient times was the skin of the Amalthean goat, on which they used to fable that Jupiter wrote human affairs, whence it began to be used for parchment on which something is written: Symmachus translated κεφαλίδα, and Jerem. XXXVIII, where the LXX interpreters rendered χαρτίον, that is, paper. In the volume, therefore, and κεφαλίδι of the book is not in the head or chapter, but in the book. For because books were accustomed to be rolled up in the manner of the ancients, it came about that a book and a volume of a book were considered the same. By book, says Crellius, κατ' ἐξοχὴν, the book of the law is understood. But it is called a volume, because formerly the law was accustomed to be described on membranes joined to one another with glue in a continuous series, which were rolled up and unrolled into the form of a cylinder. Hence volumes were named from books. Concerning the words [τοῦ ποιῆσαι ὁ Θεὸς τὸ θέλημά σꙋ, how they correspond to the Hebrew text, Estius at length: The sum is that they are to be referred to the words, Behold I come, and those intermediate words (in the volume of the book it is written of me) are to be enclosed in a parenthesis: since afterwards they are repeated thus, behold I come, that I may do your will. Theophylact: In all scripture mention has been made of my coming, and how I myself was to be offered for the world.

Ἀναιρεῖ τὸ πρῶτον, ἵνα τὸ δεύτερον στήσῃ) Just as is accustomed to be done in disjunctive syllogisms. Ἰστάνειν, העמיד, is to set, to fix, to establish. Deservedly the lesser things vanish, when such great things are provided.

With the Apostolic intention more rightly considered, by τὸ πρῶτον are understood the Levitical sacrifices, and by τὸ δεύτερον, the fulfillment of the paternal will, which Christ performed when he became obedient to him even unto death, and offered the sacrifice of his own body on the cross to expiate the sins of the whole world. For he shows that Christ, by his one sacrifice offered on the altar of the cross, has abolished all the sacrifices of the Old Testament as being typical. Indeed, he concludes that which, among other things, he instituted as the abrogation of the sacrifices of the Old Law, both because they were not of themselves pleasing to God, and because they are taken away by the sacrifice of Christ. Therefore he says, he takes away, which refers to the thing signified by those words before, or the old sacrifices, in order to establish the latter, which was signified by the remaining words, the voluntary sacrifice of Christ, by which he offered himself, willingly executing the will of the Father. For in these words, when the Son of God was saying and professing that those things which are offered according to the prescription of the Mosaic law do not at all please his Father by themselves, then he added and inferred that he was prepared to do the will of God, which is most pleasing, that is, that he would offer the sacrifice of his own body which would be pleasing to him. Theophylact: What is that first? Sacrifices and immolations. But what is the second? The will of the Father, that is, the immolation of Christ's body through the cross. Those former things are therefore cast out, so that the oblation which is made through the death of Christ may be confirmed, which the Father indeed willed and accepted.

It follows, therefore, that these sacrifices were by no means rejected and cast out because of any crime of those offering them, but because of their own imperfection.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Τότε εἴρηκεν) Ob id subintulit. Verba scriptoris nostri. In Latino quoque legi debet dixit, ut habent Codices non pauci.

Ἰδὺ ἥκω τῦ ποιῆσαι ὁ Θεὸς τὸ θέλημά συ) Omisit illud ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίε γέγραπται περὶ ἐμῦ, quia est figuratum & ornatus tantum causa adhibitum.

Sensus iterum novus & inauditus hactenus vo- cis libri: Per eum intelligi instrumentum de man- cipatione perpetua in servitutē, & id ornatus tan- tum causa hic addi. Pleriq; interpretes intelligunt volumen Scripturæ sacræ, etsi de voce ἐν κεφαλίδι divortia sententiarum occurrant, & quidnam in li- bro scripturæ specialiter respiciat Apostol9, diver- simodè explicetur. Quidam enim, Estio referente, de Genesi accipiunt, ut Hieronymus de initio Ge- neseos, Theophylactus de verbis Gen. I. 26. faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram: Alii recentiores, è quibus Ribera est, de loco Gen. II. 23. ob collatio- nem Eph. V. 30. (Sed quia in iis nihil habetur quic- quam de eo, quod hic ait Christus: Voluntatem tuam facio, idcirco) alii nonnulli de Prot-Evange- lio, Gen. III. 15. quidam vero de promissionib9 qui- busvis de Messia in genere in Genesi extantibus, alii de promissionibus in Mose, vel nominatim de ea, quæ Deut. XIIX. habetur, explicat, uti Estius, præ- eunte Junio, volumen libri notari existimans, scri- pturas Veteris Testamenti intelligit, quæ vaticiniis de Messia abundant. Alienæ sunt interpretationes apud Estium Thomæ de libro vitæ, Augustini de li- bro Psalmorum, utpote tum nondum digesto, alio- rum de loco Exod. XXI. 5. de servi auri perfodien- da, & Crellii, de parte illa legis, in qua officia Regis describuntur, Deut. XVII. nec non eorum, qui de Christo secundum Humanam naturam, cujus ca- put est Deus, interpretantur. De instrumento inter Deum & Davidem, vel inter Deum & Christum erecto, neque in Scriptura sacra reperire est, neque quomodo ad tale instrumentum hic provocari potuerit, apparet. Ornatus etiam causa tantum ad- jectam hanc particulam temere statuitur, quum ex vero Christus testari potuerit במגלת, in volu- mine libri, & ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίε quod simplicissime redditum à B. Luthero, im Buch, κατ' ἐξοχὴν, uti Bi- blia sacra, κατ' ἀν´ονομασίαν hoc nomine veniunt, de sese scriptum esse, quod de ipso in Mose & Pro- phetis scriptum sit, de vaticiniis nempe omnibus, quæ de Christo agunt, quemadmodum pleraque de sese exposuit Christus, Luc. XXIV. & alias in hi- storia Evangelica. Occurrit etiam ea vox Ezech. II. & III. ubi per κεφαλίδα non potest intelligi ca- put aut capitulum, & Zach. V. ubi vocem Ebræam LXX. δρέπανον falcem, Aquila & Theodotio διφθέ- ραν posuerunt, quæ antiquis pellis erat Amaltheæ capræ, in qua res humanas Jovem scribere fabula- bantur, unde cœpit usurpari pro membrana, in qua aliquid scribitur : Symmachus κεφαλίδα ver- tit, & Jerem. XXXIIX. ubi χαρτίον LXX. Interpre- tes reddidere, id est, chartam. In volumine ergo & κεφαλίδι libri non est in capite aut capitulo, sed in libro. Quod enim libri more Veterum convol- vi soleant, inde factum, ut liber & volumen libri pro eodem haberentur. Per librum, inquit, Crel- lius, κατ' ἐξοχὴν liber legis intelligitur. Volumen au- tem appellatur, quia olim lex in membranis sibi invi- cem glutine junctis, continua serie describi fuit solita, qua in cylindri formam convolvcbantur & evolve- bantur. Hinc de libris volumina dicta. De verbis [τοῦ ποιῆσαι ὁ Θεὸς τὸ θέλημά σꙋ, quomodo respon- deant Ebræo textui prolixe Estius : Summa est, ea referenda esse ad verba, Ecce venio, & interme- dia illa (in volumine scriptum est de me) paren- thesi includenda : siquidem postea ita repetan- tur, ecce venio, ut faciam voluntatem tuam. Theophylactus : In omni scriptura de meo adventu facta est mentio, & quemadmodum ipse essem offe- rendus pro mundo.

Ἀναιρεῖ τὸ πρῶτον, ἵνα τὸ δεύτερον στήσῃ) Sicut solet fieri in syllogismis disjunctivis. Ἰστάνειן העמיד est statuere, fige- re, firmare. Merito minora evanescunt, ubi tam magna præstantur.

Rectius pensi habita Apostolica intentione per τὸ πρῶτον intelliguntur sacrificia Levitica per τὸ τ' ἐκπρώτω δεύτερον, impletio voluntatis paternæ, quam Chri- stus præstitit, cum obediens ei factus est usque ad mortem, & sacrificium corporis sui ad expianda totius mundi peccata in cruce obtulit. Ostendit enim Christum unico suo sacrificio in ara crucis oblato omnia Veteris Testamenti sacrificia utpote typica sustulisse. Nimirum concludit id, quod inter alia instituit sacrificiorum Veteris legis abrogatio- nem, tum quia per se non erant Deo placida, tum quia per sacrificium Christi illa tolluntur. Ideò ait, tollit, quod ad rem verbis istis significatam prius, vel sacrificia vetera, ut statuat posterius, quod reli- quis verbis significabatur, sacrificium Christi vo- luntarium, quo sese obtulit, voluntatem Patris li- benter exequens. In his enim verbis cum prius di- ceret, ac profiteretur Filius Dei ea, quæ secundum legis Mosaicæ præscriptum offeruntur, Patri suo per sese nequaquam placere, tunc adjecit & intulit, se paratum esse, facere Dei voluntatem maxime gratam, id est, corporis sui sacrificium ipsi placitu- rum oblaturum. Theophylactus : Quod est illud primum? Sacrificia & immolationes. Quod verò secundum? Patris voluntas, id est, Christi corpo- ris per crucem immolatio. Ejiciuntur itaque priora illa, ut confirmetur, quæ fit per mortem Christi, obla- tio, quam voluit quidem & acceptam habuit Pater.

Fit igitur, ut nequaquam ullo offerentium crimine, sed sua imperfectione repudiata sint & ejecta haec sa- crificia.

## 10:10
Ver. 10.

Ἐν ᾧ θελήματί ἠγιασμένοι ἐσμὲν οἱ διὰ τῆς προσφορᾶς τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐφάπαξ ) One must silently repeat from the previous ἁγιασμένοι, and take εἰς ὃ θέλημα in ᾧ θελήματι. We who are sanctified through the offering of Christ once made in the highest heaven, are sanctified in this, that we fulfill the same will of God which prefers obedience to victims, that is, that we ourselves also, if the situation should so require, adapt our body to sufferings and death, in this, that God may be obeyed. Compare what is above II. 11. and following.

He has that [notion] about the offering in the highest heaven from Socinus, which, however, not even Crellius and Schlichtingius dared to embrace without hesitation. They certainly waver greatly about it, whether it is a matter here of the arrival into this world, or indeed of the entry into heaven? For that opinion they bring forward: 1. that it seems to be a matter here of such a thing in which Christ showed himself obedient to God in a certain singular and excellent manner, and executed his will. Whence it follows that here one must understand not only the offering of Christ itself made in the heavens, which, as far as the entry into heaven pertains, was more properly the work of God himself than of Christ; but also his obedience and bloody death, which was the necessary antecedent of the offering. 2. That that signification of 'world,' when it is taken for the future world, is rare and less customary. However, one should not easily depart from the customary significations of words. Add that from the words of the Psalm, according to the Authors themselves, it seems to be evident that Christ mystically sang this whole Psalm before his death, and that they render this sense (although they also waver in it): Because legal victims and sacrifices do not please you, therefore behold I am present, that I may do your will, that is, that I may offer you such a sacrifice as is plainly according to your pleasure and will.

In this, however, Grotius is far worse than Socinus and his associates, that he wishes it to be said here that we fulfill that will of God, and are sanctified in it, when we ourselves also, if the situation should so require, adapt our body to pain and death in this, that God may be obeyed; for the sake of which distortion he even perverts those words ἐν ᾧ θελήματι so that they sound εἰς τὸ θέλημα, as if we were sanctified in this through the offering of Christ according to the Apostle's sense, that we might fulfill the same will of God which prefers obedience to victims. There is nothing here about our obedience, but about the obedience of Christ: nothing about the will of God preferring the obedience of men to victims, but about the will of God, which Christ had to fulfill, and willed, so that victims might cease, since they did not please God in themselves, but were only types of the victims of Christ. There is nothing about our body being adapted by us to sufferings and death, but about the body formed or adapted for the Son of God, so that by offering the sacrifice of his body on the altar of the cross he could expiate our sins. Let the Socinians themselves now refute Grotius: It could, they say, be considered, what this has to do with us or the expiation of our sins, that Christ says he will do the will of God in place of legal offerings, or has performed it? The Author shows, namely, that this will of God, or its execution, consists in the sacrifice and offering of Christ made for us, whence it is also tacitly compared with sacrifices and offerings, and at the same time opposed to them as being far more excellent and more acceptable to God. Therefore he says that we have been sanctified in it, we, I say, as he immediately adds, who have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Christ, by which words he at the same time taught what that will of God is, namely that it is the offering of the body of Christ once made, or at least that it is entirely joined with this offering. For in what way otherwise could we be said to be sanctified or expiated in this will, we who have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Christ? But it seems that thus far this will of God is also opposed to legal victims, insofar as in this [will] at last men are truly sanctified. For while sanctification is attributed to the divine will, opposed to legal victims; it is tacitly taken away from them, as if he were saying, in which will we have been truly sanctified, but not in those ancient victims and offerings. They add besides: In which, that is, through which, will. Will is placed here not for the act of willing itself, but for that thing which God wills, which he approves, and in which he delights. For it is opposed to offerings, which he does not will, nor approve. Therefore it signifies the sacrifice and offering of Christ, as the following also teach. We have been sanctified, that is, expiated, cleansed, see the chapter above, verse 13. Finally, regarding the words οἱ διὰ τῆς προσφορᾶς, who through the offering, they are thus: Either the article οἱ in these words is to be expunged, as some copies do, and these words are to be read by apposition, or, which is more certain, the word sanctified is to be repeated from the common. Once, that is, once made. Therefore the offering is not of legal victims often made, and repeated every year, and therefore ineffective and imperfect: But that offering is of the body of Jesus Christ once made, which is vehemently pleasing to God, and is plainly conformable to his will, and truly sanctifies. These things are far more suitable for them than for Grotius. Theophylactus: In which, namely the Father's will, we have been sanctified through the offering of Christ's body, which was done once. For we, believing and faithful, having been sanctified from the offering of the Only-Begotten, have obtained this very sanctification by the Father's will. We also add the commentary of Estius: When therefore the Apostle says that those who are sanctified through the offering of the body of Christ are sanctified in the will of God, he gives us to understand that this was the will of God, that Christ should offer his body for us to be sanctified, that is, to be justified. Moreover, he expressly mentions the body, when otherwise it would have been enough to say through the offering of Jesus Christ, because in the words cited from the Psalm this name is expressed, where he says: But a body you have prepared for me. For he undoubtedly looks to these words. Whence it is further gathered that this epistle was written in Greek, not in Hebrew. For in the Hebrew it is not body, but ear.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Ἐν ᾧ θελήματί ἠγιασμένοι ἐσμὲν οἱ διὰ τῆς προσφορᾶς τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐφάπαξ ) Repetendum tacite ex priori ἁγιασμένοι, & ἐν ᾧ θελήματι sume εἰς ὃ θέλημα. Nos qui per oblationem Christi semel in summo cœlo fa- ctam sanctificamur, in hoc sanctificamur, ut eandem vo- luntatem Dei impleamus, quæ obedientiam præfert vi- ctimis, id est, ut & ipsi corpus nostrum, si res ita ferat, aptemus doloribus & morti, in hoc ut Deo obediatur. Confer quæ supra II. 11. & sequentibus.

Illud de oblatione in summo cœlo a Socino habet, quod tamen ne quidem Crellius & Schlichtingius citra titubationem amplecti ausi sunt. Fluctuant utique valde de eo, an de adventu in hunc mun- dum, an verò de ingressu in cælum hic agatur? Pro ista sententia hæc adducunt 1. quod hic de tali re agi videatur, in qua Christus singulari quadam & exi- mia ratione Deo sese obedientem præbuerit, ejusque voluntatem executus fuerit. Unde consequitur, hic non tantum ipsam oblationem Christi in cœlis fa- ctam, quæ, quod ad ingressum in cœlum attinet, magis propriè ipsius Dei opus fuit, quam Christi; sed etiam ejus obedientiam & mortem cruentam, quæ oblatio- nis necessarium fuit antecedens, intelligendam esse. 2. Quod significatio illa mundi, cum pro futuro mun- do accipitur, rara sit & minus usitata. Non est au- tem ab usitatis vocum significationibus facile disce- dendum. Adde quod è verbis Psalmi, ipsis Autori- bus, patere videatur, Christum totum istum Psal- mum mystice ante suam mortem cecinisse, quod- que hunc sensum, (quamvis & in eo fluctuent) reddant: Quia victima & sacrificia legalia tibi non placent, propterea ecce ego adsum, ut voluntatem tuam faciam, id est, tale tibi sacrificium offeram, quod plane est secundum placitum ac velle tuum.

In eo vero longe deterior est Socino & sociis ejus Grotius, quod voluntatem illam Dei nos implere hic dici velit, inque eo sanctificari, cum & ipsi, si res ita ferat, corpus nostrum aptamus dolori & morti in hoc, ut Deo obediatur, cujus detorsionis causa verba etiam illa ἐν ᾧ θελήματι sic pervertit, ut so- nent εἰς τὸ θέλημα, quasi in hoc sanctificemur per oblationem Christi secundum Apostoli sensum, ut eandem voluntatem Dei impleamus, quæ obedi- entiam præfert victimis. Nihil hic de obedientia nostra, sed de obedientia Christi: Nihil de voluntate Dei obedientiam hominum præferente victimis, sed de voluntate Dei, quam implere Christus de- buit, voluit, ut victimæ cessarent, quum eæ per se Deo non placuerint, sed victimæ Christi typi so- lum fuerint. Nihil de corpore nostro à nobis dolori- bus & morti aptando, sed de corpore Filio Dei for- mato vel aptato, ut sacrificio corporis sui in ara cru- cis offerendo expiare posset peccata nostra. Resel- lant nunc Grotium ipsimet Sociniani: Poterat, in- quiunt, cogitari, quid hoc ad nos peccatorumve no- strorum expiationem pertineat, quod Christus obla- tionum legalium loco Dei voluntatem sese facturum dicat, eamve perfecerit? Ostendit nempe Autor Dei hanc voluntatem, ejusve executionem in sacrificio & oblatione Christi pro nobis facta consistere, unde etiam tacitè cum sacrificiis & oblationibus confer- tur, iisdemque simul tanquam longè præstantior ac Deo acceptior opponitur. Itaq; ait, nos in ea sanctifi- catos esse, nos inquam, ut statim addit, qui per obla- tionem corporis Christi, sanctificati scilicet sumus, quibus verbis simul, quæ sit Dei ista voluntas do- cuit, nempe quod sit oblatio corporis Christi semel facta, vel saltem quod sit cum hac oblatione omnino conjuncta. Quo pacto enim aliter in hac voluntate sanctificati seu expiati esse diceremur, nos qui per oblationem corporis Christi sanctificati sumus? Vide- tur vero hactenus etiam voluntas ista Dei opponi vi- ctimis legalibus, quatenus in hac demum homines vere sanctificantur. Dum enim voluntati divinæ, victimis legalibus oppositæ, sanctificatio tribuitur; illis tacitè adimitur, quasi dicat, in qua voluntate vere sanctificati sumus, non vero in victimis illis & oblationibus antiquis. Addunt præterea: In qua, id est, per quam, voluntate. Voluntas hic ponitur non pro ipso volendi actu, sed pro ea re, quam Deus velit, quam approbet, & qua delectetur. Opponitur enim oblationibus, quas non vult, nec probat. Itaque signi- ficat sacrificium & oblationem Christi, ut & sequen- tia docent. Sanctificati sumus, id est, expiati, emun- dati, vid. cap. sup. vers. 13. Denique ad verba oi dià τῆς προσφορᾶς, qui per oblationem ita habent; Vel articulus oi in his verbis expungendus est, ut faciunt nonnulla exemplaria, verbaque hæc per appositio- nem legenda, vel quod certius est, verbum sanctifica- ti, ἀπὸ κοινῦ repetendum. Semel, id est, semel factam.
