Itaque oblatio non victimarum legalium sæpe facta, & quotannis repetita, ideoque inefficax & imperfe- cta: Sed corporis Jesu Christi semel facta est illa ob- latio, quæ Deo vehementer placet, ejusque voluntati plane conformis est, & vere sanctificat. Hæc illi lon- ge convenientius, quam Grotius. Theophylactus: In qua Patris scilicet voluntate per Christi corporis oblationem sumus sanctificati, quæ semel effecta sit. Credentes namque nos & fideles ex Unigeniti obla- tione sanctificati, hanc ipsam sumus Patre volente sanctificationem adepti. Addimus etiam Estii com- mentarium: Cum ergo dicit Apostolus eos, qui per oblationem corporis Christi sanctificantur, in Dei voluntate sanctificari, intelligendum præbet, hanc fuiffe Dei voluntatem, ut Christus corpus suum of- ferret pro nobis sanctificandis, id est, justificandis. Corporis autem expresse meminit, cum alioqui satis esset dicere per oblationem Jesu Christi, quia in ver- bis è Psalmo citatis hoc nomen expressum est, ubi ait: Corpus autem aptasti mihi. Ad hæc enim verba sine dubio respicit. Unde præterea colligitur, hanc episto- lam Græce scriptam esse, non Ebraice. Nam in Ebræo non est corpus, sed auris.

## 10:11
Vers. 11.

Καὶ πᾶς μὲν Ἀρχιερεὺς) Namely, the legal one. In other books it is ἱερεύς. But the Manuscript has Ἀρχιερεὺς, which is clearer.

Ἕστηκε καθ' ἡμέραν λειτυργῶν) In lighting the lampstand, in performing the incense offering, the primary roles were those of the high priest. The others were his assistants. Ἕστηκε is used for standing at all times.

Καὶ τὰς ἀυτὰς πολλάκις προσφέρων θυσίας) take τὰς ἀυτὰς as above 1. Πολλάκις that is, as often as the situation requires. See above VII. 27.

Αἵτινες ὀυδέποτε δύνανται περιελεῖν τὰς ἁμαρτίας) περιελεῖν which is ἀφαιρεῖν above 4. We have περιαιρεῖν in this sense in Gen. XXXVIII. 14, 19, XLI. 42, Exod. VIII. 8, 11, 31, X. 17, Psal. CXIX. 22, & 43, Exod. XXXIII. 6, & often elsewhere. Thus also Luke uses this word, Acts XXVII. 20, and good Greek writers. Paul also often inculcates this sense, as being of great importance.

The received text is rashly corrected by Grotius. For it is not Ἀρχιερεὺς that is read, but ἱερεὺς in most Codices and commentaries of the Ancients. And this is a new argument, third in order, from the eternal value of Christ's sacrifice: by reason of which it is now compared not only with the high priest's offering, but with the daily sacrifices of any priests whatsoever, nor is it a repetition of the same argument, but a new confirmation, as noted by Thomas, Cajetan, and Estius. For it is not κατ' ἐνιαυτὸν yearly, he says, as above, but καθ' ἡμέραν, daily. Since the Socinians interchange these, is this not an open corruption of the text? Namely, to interchange among themselves those things which the text openly distinguishes. For the daily καθ' ἡμέραν sacrifices are pointed out. sacrifices, since the Levitical priests offered the same victims often, as being twice daily, not different ones, but they offered the same, namely the lamb, both morning and evening. Which can never take away sins: which are said in an illative sense: Which therefore never etc. For that the same victims are offered daily is an argument of their weakness to expiate sins. Not concerning the office of the high priest in lighting the lampstand, and in making the incense, but concerning the sacrifices, which were offered not only as often as the occasion might arise, but daily. Estius rightly notes here, because of the force of the Apostolic argument, that the legal sacrifices were of no value, except for legal and external sanctification, that is, in themselves, not as they looked toward Christ and were offered by faith. Wherefore, he says, they erred gravely, the Jews against whom the Apostle disputes, writing both in this epistle and to the Galatians, who from the sacrifices and other ceremonies of their law, considered thus separately and in themselves, expected internal sanctification and true justice. For they wished to retain the law and its ceremonies, as if salvation were from them, without respect to the oblation and merit of Christ. Whom they indeed received as the Son of God sent for this purpose, that he might teach the way of justice by precept and example, that is, that he might exhibit himself as a legislator and master with notable holiness of life, but not as a Redeemer. Whence also in his death and cross, as being by no means necessary for the salvation of men, most of them suffered scandal.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Καὶ πᾶς μὲν Ἀρχιερεὺς) Nempe legalis. In aliis libris est ἱερεύς. Sed Manuscriptus habet Ἀρχιερεὺς, quod cla- rius.

Ἕστηκε καθ' ἡμέραν λειτυργῶν) In accendendo candela- bro, in suffitu faciendo, primæ erant partes summi Sacer- dotis. Cæteri erant ei adjutores. Ἕστηκε pro omni tempore solet stare.

Καὶ τὰς ἀυτὰς πολλάκις προσφέρων θυσίας) τὰς ἀυτὰς sume ut supra 1. Πολλάκις id est, quoties res fert. Vide su- pra VII. 27.

Αἵτινες ὀυδέποτε δύνανται περιελεῖν τὰς ἁμαρτίας) περιελεῖν quod ἀφαιρεῖν supra 4. Hoc sensu περιαιρεῖν habemus Gen. XXXVIII. 14. 19. XLI. 42. Exod. VIII. 8. 11. 31. X. 17. Psal. CXIX. 22. & 43. Exod. XXXIII. 6. & alibi sæpe. Sic & Lucas hac voce utitur, Act. XXVII. 20. & Scriptores bene Græci. Sæpe hunc sensum inculcat & Paulus, ut magní momenti.

Temere corrigitur à Grotio textus receptus. Non enim Ἀρχιερεὺς legitur, sed ἱερεὺς in pleris- que Codicibus & Veterum commentariis. Estque hic novum argumentum in ordine tertium, ab æter- no sacrificii Christi valore: Cujus ratione jam non confertur solum cum summi Sacerdotis oblatione, sed cum Sacerdotum quorumvis quotidianis sacri- ficiis, nec ejusdem argumenti est repetitio, sed no- va confirmatio, notante Thoma, Cajetano, Estio. Non enim κατ' ἐνιαυτὸν quotannis, inquit, ut su- pra, sed καθ' ἡμέραν, quotidie. Quæ cum commu- tant Sociniani, annon hæc est aperta textus corru- ptela? Ea scilicet inter se commutare, quæ textus aperte discriminat. Indigitantur enim quotidiana καθ' ἡμέ- sacri- sacrificia, siquidem Sacerdotes Levitici easdem hostias offerebant sæpe, utpote bis quotidie, non diversas, sed easdem offerebant, agnum nempe, & mane & vesperi. Quæ nunquam possunt auferre pec- cata: quæ dicuntur sensu illativo: Quæ proinde nun- quam &c. Nam easdem quotidie offerri hostias ar- gumentum est imbecillitatis earum ad expianda peccata. Non de officio summi Sacerdotis in accen- dendo candelabro, & in suffitu faciendo, sed de sa- crificiis, quæ non quoties res ferat tantum, sed quo- tidie offerebantur. Recte hic ob vim argumenti Apostolici notat Estius, sacrificia legalia non va- luisse, nisi ad sanctificationem legalem atque ex- ternam, per se scilicet, non qua respiciebant Chri- stum, & fide offerebantur. Quocirca graviter, in- quit; errabant Judæi, contra quos Apostolus tum in hac epistola, tum ad Galatas scribens, disputat, qui ex sacrificiis, aliisque suæ legis ceremoniis, ita scorsim ac per se consideratis internam sanctificationem & ve- ram justitiam expectabant. Volebant enim legem & ceremonias ejus retinere, tanquam ex illis esset salus, absque respectu ad oblationem & meritum Christi. Quam recipiebant quidem ut Filium Dei ad hoc mis- sum, ut præcepto & exemplo viam justitiæ doceret, id est, ut cum insigni sanctitate vitæ legislatorem se ac magistrum exhiberet, non autem ut Redemptorem. Unde & in morte ejus & cruce, velut ad salutem ho- minum minime necessaria plurimi eorum scandalum passi sunt.

## 10:12
Verse 12.

Αὐτὸς δὲ ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν προσηνέγκας θυσίαν) Namely in heaven, as high priest in the sanctuary. For αὐτὸς δὲ in the Manuscript: Οὗτος δὲ. Εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς ἐκάθισεν ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ τοῦ Θεοῦ) Because that oblation suffices, therefore he will not return to offer: he will remain there, until he returns, not to offer again but to judge and to triumph. Εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς we have had concerning the same matter also above VII. 3. Ἐν δεξιᾷ we have had also above I. 3. VIII. 1. below XII. 2. Rom. VIII. 34. Eph. I. 20. Col. III. 1. Elsewhere ἐκ δεξιῶν, as the Manuscript also has here, or ἐν τοῖς δεξίοις. Δεξιὰν κατάχρησις we have cited elsewhere from Pindar.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Αὐτὸς δὲ ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν προσηνέγκας θυσίαν) Nempe in cœlo, ut summus Sacerdos in sanctuario. Pro αὐτὸς δὲ in Manuscripto: Οὗτος δὲ. Εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς ἐκάθισεν ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ τοῦ Θεοῦ) Quia illa oblatio sufficit, ideo non redibit ut offerat: manebit ibi, donec redeat, non iterum oblaturus sed judicaturus & triumphaturus. Εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς de eadem re habuimus & supra VII. 3. Ἐν δεξιᾷ habuimus & supra I. 3. VIII. 1. infra XII. 2. Rom. VIII. 34. Eph. I. 20. Col. III. 1. Alibi ἐκ δε- ξιῶν, quomodo & hic habet Manuscriptus, aut ἐν τοῖς δε- ξίοις. Δεξιὰν κατάχρησις ex Pindaro citavimus alibi.

## 10:13
Verse 13.

Τὸ λοιπὸν ἐκδεχόμενος ἕως τεθῶσιν οἱ ἐχθροὶ αὐτοῦ ὑποπό- διον τῶν ποδῶν αὐτοῦ) Expecting, he says, that which remains, that all enemies may be subjected to him, not only empires opposing Christ, but also death itself, as Paul explains 1 Cor. XV. 26. And this excludes a new oblation.

The Apostle is ignorant of any oblation being made in the heavens. He affirms more often that it was made only once, and that on earth. Nor is the comparison here instituted concerning the high priest, to whom alone the entry into the holy of holies belonged, but with any Levitical priests whatsoever. Nor is 'offering' rightly explained in the Vulgate, since the Greek προσενέγκας has the meaning of the past tense, 'when he had offered.' For it is not signified that he is presently offering a victim for sins, as it is explained by some, but that having once offered one victim for the remission of sins, he now rests. Which the antithesis confirms. For the priests offered more often daily, Christ offered himself only once. They remained on earth: He, the oblation having been made on earth, is forever at the right hand of God. They stood and standing ministered, he sits at the right hand of God, and thus reigns forever, after he once offered himself, or he is even said to have offered himself forever, because the oblation of Christ is valid forever, as Bartholomew Petrus explains with Thomas I. sec. q. 102. art. 3. at the end. For the rest, expecting, until etc. that is to say, he is not to return from there at any time, to offer a victim for sins again.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Τὸ λοιπὸν ἐκδεχόμενος ἕως τεθῶσιν οἱ ἐχθροὶ αὐτοῦ ὑποπό- διον τῶν ποδῶν αὐτοῦ) Expectans, inquit, id, quod restat, ut omnes inimici ipsi subjiciantur, non imperia tantum Christo adversantia, sed & mors ipsa, ut explicat Paulus 1 Cor. XV. 26. Et hoc excludit oblationem novam.

Oblationem quandam in cœlis fieri ignorat A- postolus. Semel tantum factam esse, idque in terris, sæpius affirmat. Neque de summo Sacerdote, cui soli competebat ingressus in sanctum sanctorum, sed cum quibusvis Sacerdotibus Leviticis collatio hic instituitur. Nec recte offerens exponitur in Vul- gata, cum Græcum προσενέγκας Præteriti significa- tionem habeat, cum obtulisset. Non enim significa- tur in præsenti pro peccatis hostiam offerre, sicutia nonnullis exponitur, sed una hostia quondam se- mel in peccatorum remissionem oblata nunc quie- scere. Quod antithesis confirmat. Sacerdotes enim sæpius quotidie offerebant, Christus semel tantum sese obtulit. Illi in terris manebant: Hic oblatione in terris facta in sempiternum est in dextra Dei. Illi stabant & stantes ministrabant, hic sedet in dextra Dei, adeoque regnat in æternum, postquam semel sese obtulit, vel etiam in sempiternum sese obtulisse dicitur, quod oblatio Christi in sempiternum va- leat, ut Bartholomæus Petrus cum Thoma I. sec. q. 102. art. 3. in fine explicat. De cætero expectans, do- nec &c. q. d. non inde rediturus est aliquando, ut ite- rum pro peccatis hostiam offerat.

## 10:14
Verse 14.

Μιᾷ γὰρ προσφορᾷ τετελείωκεν εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς τοὺς ἁγιαζο- μένους). By oblation he understands also that which is joined to it, the impetration of the Holy Spirit: By whom those who are sanctified have that by which they may keep themselves holy forever, if they do not desert the help of God. Nothing will be lacking to them on the part of God. This he calls τελειῶσαι. See above IX. 19. and in this chapter, v. 2.

He gives the reason why he performed only a single oblation on the altar of the cross, because by that single oblation he perfected forever those who are sanctified. Estius notes the Vulgate here again, because ἁγιαζομένους is a participle of the Present tense, but taken broadly, so that it may extend to the elect of all times, as many as ever have been or are to be. The sense is, he says, that Christ perfects, renders perfect, and sanctifies all, as many as are ever sanctified by any means, by one oblation, nor does it happen to any who are to be sanctified otherwise than through this one oblation. For the discourse is similar to that by which he said above: In which will we are sanctified, who are sanctified once through the oblation of Jesus Christ. Thus that εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς is not to be referred to those who are sanctified, but to the word consummavit, in this way: He has perfected and sanctified forever all those who are to be sanctified, i.e., his offering made once has infinite power, so that it can both always sanctify and confer a holiness that will last forever. Thus in the previous chapter he said: Having obtained eternal redemption: And chap. VII. Whence also he is able to save forever, as Estius uses here again: Whence the nerve of the daily mass sacrifice is cut. The Estian distinction between a primary and secondary offering, dependent and independent, is unwritten, nay, it is a counter-writing, and contrary to the unity of the offering of Christ, which was made only once, and that on the altar of the cross. But from where will it be taught that the impetration of the Holy Spirit is included in the offering of Christ? Christ certainly merited, as other spiritual goods; so also the gift of the Holy Spirit by his offering made on the altar of the cross. Yet these differ greatly: the offering of Christ, and the impetration of the Holy Spirit.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Μιᾷ γὰρ προσφορᾷ τετελείωκεν εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς τοὺς ἁγιαζο- μένως). Per oblationem intelligit & id, quod ei conjun- ctum est, impetrationem Spiritus sancti: Per quem qui sanctificati sunt, habent, quo in perpetuum sanctos se ser- vent, si Dei opem non deserant. Nihil illis ex parte Dei deerit. Hoc dicit τελειῶσαι. Vide supra IX. 19. & hoc capite, v. 2.

Causam reddit, cur unicam tantum oblationem peregerit in ara crucis, quia illa unica oblatione consummavit in perpetuum eos, qui sanctifican- tur. Vulgatam hic iterum notat Estius, quia ἁγια- ζομένους est temporis Præsentis participium, sed ample acceptum, ut ad omnium temporum ele- ctos, quotquot unquam fuerunt aut futuri sunt, extendatur. Sensus est, inquit, Christum omnes, quotquot ullo unquam sanctificantur, una oblatione consummare, perfectos reddere, sanctificare, nec ullis sanctificandis aliter quam per hanc unam oblatio- nem contingere, ut sanctificentur. Est enim sermo similis illi, quo superius dixit: In qua voluntate san- ctificati sumus, qui per oblationem Jesu Christi semel sanctificati sumus. Ita illud εἰς τὸ διηνεκὲς non ad eos, qui sanctificantur, sed ad verbum consumma- vit, referendum, hoc modo: Omnes eos, qui sanctifi- candi sunt, consummavit & sanctificavit in perpe- tuum q. d. oblatio ejus semel facta vim habet infini- tam, ut & semper sanctificare possit, & sanctitatem conferre semper duraturam. Sic capite superiori dixit: Æterna redemptione inventa: Et cap. VII. Unde & salvare in perpetuum potest, uti iterum hic Estius: Unde nervus inciditur quotidiano sacri- ficio missatico. Distinctio Estiana inter oblatio- nem primariam & secundariam, dependentem & independentem, ἄγραφός est, imò ἀντίγραφος, & unitati oblationis Christi, quæ semel facta tantum est, idque in ara crucis, contraria. Impetrationem autem Spiritus sancti includi oblationem Christi, unde docebitur? Promeruit sane Christus, ut alia spiri- tualia bona; ita & donum Spiritus sancti oblatio- ne sua in ara crucis facta. Differunt tamen hæc maxime Christi oblatio, & Spiritus sancti impe- tratio.

## 10:15
Verse 15.

Μαρτυρεῖ δὲ ἡμῖν καὶ τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον) Through Jeremiah, to whom the Holy Spirit dictated what was to be spoken. Μετὰ γὰρ τὸ προειρηκέναι) The manuscript has Eipηκέναι. But it makes no difference.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Μαρτυρεῖ δὲ ἡμῖν καὶ τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον) Per Jeremiam, cui Spiritus sanctus loquenda dictavit. Μετὰ γὰρ τὸ προειρηκέναι) Eipηκέναι habet Manuscriptus. Sed nihil refert.

## 10:16-17
Verses 16. 17.

Αὕτη ἡ διαθήκη ἣν διαθήσομαι πρὸς ἀυτὸς μετὰ τὰς ἡμέρας ἐκείνας, λέγει ὁ Κύριος, διδὺς νόμους με ἐπὶ τὰς καρδίας ἀυτῶν, καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν διανοιῶν ἀυτῶν ἐπιγράψω ἀυτοὺς; καὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἀυτῶν καὶ τῶν ἀνομιῶν ἀυτῶν ὐ μὴ μνησθῶ ἔτι) Even here he omitted certain things placed in the middle, as can be seen both in the passage of Jeremiah XXXI. 30. and following, and above VIII. 8. and thereafter. Doubtless he repeats here those things which serve most for that which he wishes to infer. The Syriac translates that ὐ μὴ μνησθῶ as I will not commemorate, that is, I will not reproach. And ἔφηκε is understood before those words καὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν. Some codices also have τότε ἔιρηκεν added.

The fourth argument for the distinction between the sacrifices of the Old Testament and the sacrifice of the death of Christ, which is the only expiatory or propitiatory sacrifice of the New Testament, taken from the efficacy of this sacrifice from the reason of the New Testament, is adduced from Jerem. XXXI. 23. seqq. However, the particle γὰρ seems to be redundant, which it is better to say than to make the Apostle's speech imperfect or to seek some supplement without the faith of approved codices. He had adduced the same passage also in chapter VIII, but especially because of those words New Testament, so that he might teach that the old had been abrogated, and might set forth the nature of the New Testament: But here he alleges that promise because of the last part concerning the remission of sins, so that he may teach that the same is not to be attributed in itself by the sacrifices of the O.T. κατ' ἀυτὸ, but that it uniquely belongs to the sacrifice of Christ, which pertains to the New Testament in respect of its completion, whereas the shadows of the same properly looked toward the Old Testament.

Latin:

Vers. 16. 17.

Nimirum ea hic repetit, quæ maxime ad id servi- unt, quod vult inferre. Syrus illud ὐ μὴ μνησθῶ vertit non commemorabo, id est, non exprobrabo. Et ἔφηκε subaudi- tur ante illa καὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν. Quidam Codices etiam ad- scriptum habent τότε ἔιρηκεν.

Argumentum quartum pro discrimine sacrifi- ciorum Veteris Testamenti, & sacrificii mortis Christi, quod unicum est Novi Testamenti expia- torium vel propitiatorium sacrificium, ab effi- cacia hujusce sacrificii è Testamenti Novi ratione desumptum è Jerem. XXXI. 23. seqq. adducitur. Particula autem γὰρ abundare videtur, quod bræstat dicere quam vel orationem Apostoli im- perfectam facere vel aliquod supplementum citra probatiorum Codicum fidem quærere. Adduxe- rat eundem locum & cap. IIX. sed imprimis ob verba illa Novum Testamentum, ut vetus abroga- tum esse doceret, & naturam Novi Testamenti sisteret: Hic autem allegat eam promissionem ob postremam partem de remissione peccatorum, ut doceat eandem non sacrificiis V. T. κατ' ἀυτὸ per se tribuendam, sed ita unice convenire sacrifi- cio Christi, quod ad Novum Testamentum perti- net respectu complementi, quum ad Vetus Testa- mentum umbræ ejusdem proprie spectarint.

## 10:18
Verse 18.

“Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer an offering for sin.” He takes ἄφεσις here as the healing of the soul from sins, just as ἱλάσκετο in 11, 19 and ἵλεων εἶναι in VIII, 12. And this sense is more sublime and mystical. For then sins are truly forgiven (ἀφίενται), when they are sent away in such a way that they do not return. For if the penalty only has been removed, but the sins truly return, it is no wonder that an offering for sin is repeated. He speaks of Christians, not as all are, but as they ought to be, and as most were at that time. They were taught that to fall away after baptism was fatal, or joined with the greatest danger of destruction. And so, very many reached the goal with an unhindered course.

That ἄφεσις τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν (forgiveness of sins) is the healing of the soul from sins cannot be taught from the Scriptures. That passage concerning the word ἱλάσκετο, although it is different, Heb. II. 17. (not 19.), does not prove that meaning; the discourse there is not about the healing of the soul from sins, but about the propitiation and reconciliation of God. That the other passage, Heb. VIII. 12., from the Prophetic text which the Apostle has here again adduced, ἵλεων εἶναι, deals not with the healing of the soul but with the remission of sins, is evident from the appended explanation, that He will no longer remember iniquities, which phrase is repeated here also, v. 17, and thus sufficiently teaches that such a remission is understood, by which God, speaking in an anthropopathic manner, wills that our sins be as it were obliterated in His divine memory, and that He wills to forget them, or to remember them no more, to the oblivion of both guilt and punishment. But where there is such a remission of sins, there is no longer need for an offering for sins. The Apostle's argument is: By whatever sacrifice a full remission of sins is obtained, by that we are so perfected that there is no need for an offering for sins. But by the sacrifice offered on the altar of the cross, a full remission of sins is obtained by virtue of the New Testament, Jer. XXXI. 31. Therefore, by the same we are so perfected that there is no longer need for an offering for sins. For if, says Theophylact, the remission of sins has been granted by one offering, what further need is there for a second? It is clear, therefore, that by one offering of Christ alone we have been made more perfect, having received the remission of wicked deeds, and we have need of no other sacrifice. Therefore, those things which are attached to the text under the title of a more sublime sense are foreign to it. The copies (ἀντίγραφα) are first, that sins are then truly remitted when they are sent away, because the remission of sins is prior to the sanctification by which it comes about that they are sent away: Secondly, that sins are so sent away that they never return. For since that evil εὐπερίσατον (easily besetting) remains, Jer. XII. 1. and ἡ οἰκῶσα ἐν ἡμῖν ἁμαρτία (the sin dwelling in us), Rom. VII. 17. 20. τὸ κακὸν παρακείμενον (the evil lying near), v. 21. it always bubbles up and breaks forth, Jas. I. 14. and from there various sins proceed, Matt. XV. 19. Thirdly, that if the penalty is removed while sins return, an offering for sin must be repeated: Which is completely contrary to the most perfect satisfaction of Christ and the present Apostolic tradition. For is there therefore need for a new or other offering of Christ for sins if anyone sins after justification? It is our work to have repentance and faith in the merit and victim of Christ once offered for sins, not a new offering of Christ, a new sacrifice. Fourthly, although all sins, even those which are committed after baptism, are in themselves fatal and joined with danger, they are not therefore to be excluded from repentance and the fruit of the unique expiatory sacrifice of Christ: Indeed, as often as anyone has sinned, if he has repented, he will be able to be received into favor again by that victim once offered and apprehended by faith, Ezek. XVIII. XXXIII. Matt. XVIII.

PART II OF CHAPTER X. THE EXHORTATORY PART, AND THE SAME IS THE SECOND PART OF THE EPISTLE CONCERNING FAITH IN CHRIST.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Ὅπου δὲ ἄφεσις αὐτῶν, ὀυκ ἔτι προσφορὰ περὶ ἁμαρτίας) Sumit hic ἄφεσιν pro sanatione animi à peccatis, quo- modo ἱλάσκετο 11, 19. & ἵλεων εἶναι, VIII, 12. Et est hic sen- sus sublimior & μυστικώτερος. Tunc enim verè ἀφίενται peccata, cum ita missa fiunt, ut non redeant. Nam si pœ- na tantum ablata sit, peccata vero redeant, non mirum est repeti προσφορὰν περὶ ἁμαρτίας. Loquitur de Christia- nis, non quales sunt omnes, sed quales esse debent, & ple- rique tunc erant. Docebantur omnes post baptismum prolabi esse exitiale, aut cum maximo exitii periculo conjunctum. Itaque plurimi inoffenso cursu ad metam pertingebant.

Ubi ἄφεσις τῶν ἁμαρτίων sit sanatio animi à pec- catis, è scripturis doceri non potest. Locus ille de voce ἱλάσκετο, quamvis illa diversa sit, Ebr. II. 17. (non 19.) significatum istud non probat; non de sanatione animi à peccatis, sed de propitiatione & reconciliatione Dei illic sermo est: Locum alte- rum Ebr. VIII. 12. è textu Prophetico, quem hic ite- rum adduxit Apostolus, ἵλεων εἶναι, non de sanatio- ne animi, sed de peccatorum remissione agere, è subjuncta ἐξηγήσει constat, quod iniquitatum non amplius recordari velit, quæ phrasis hic etiam re- petitur, v. 17. adeoque satis docet, eam remissionem intelligi, qua Deus ἀνθρωποπαθῶς loquendo pec- cata nostra quasi in memoria sua divina obliterari, eorumque dememinisse, vel non amplius recorda- ri velit ad culpæ & pœnæ oblivionem. Ubi autem talis est peccatorum remissio, ibi non amplius ob- latione opus est pro peccatis. Argumentum A- postoli est: Per quamcunque hostiam plena remis- sio peccatorum obtinetur, ea ita perficimur, ut opus oblatione pro peccatis non sit. At per hosti- am in crucis ara oblatam plena remissio peccato- rum obtinetur vi Testamenti Novi, Jer. XXXI. 31. Ergo per eandem ita perficimur, ut amplius opus non sit oblatione pro peccatis. Si enim, inquit Theophylactus, peccatorum remissio, una oblatione permissa est, quod ultra opus est secunda? Liquet itaque una duntaxat Christi oblatione perfectiores nos esse effectos, accepta pravorum facinorum re- missione, nec alio sacrificio indigemus. Aliena ergo sunt, quæ sub titulo sublimioris sensus affinguntur textui. Ἀντίγραφα sunt primum, peccata tunc vere remitti, cum missa fiunt, quia remissio peccatorum prior est sanctificatione, qua fit, ut missa fiant: De- inde peccata ita missa fieri, ut nunquam redeant. Quum enim maneat malum illud εὐπερίσατον, Jerem. XII. 1. & ἡ οἰκῶσα ἐν ἡμῖν ἁμαρτία, Rom. VII. 17. 20. τὸ κακὸν παρακείμενον. v. 21. semper id ebullit & prorumpit, Jac. I. 14. prodeuntque inde peccata varia, Matth. XV. 19. Tertio pœna ablata peccatis redeuntibus προσφορὰν περὶ ἁμαρτίας repetendam esse: Quod satisfactioni Christi perfectissimæ, tra- dationique præsenti Apostolicæ contrarium pe- nitus est. Num enim ideo nova Christi aut alia ob- latione peccatis opus est, si quis post justificatio- nem peccet? Pœnitentia ac fide in meritum ac vi- ctimam Christi semel oblatam pro peccatis, no- strum opus est, non nova Christi oblatione, novo sacrificio. Quarto etsi peccata omnia etiam illa, quæ post baptismum committantur, per se exitialia sint, & cum periculo conjuncta, non tamen ideo tales à pœnitentia & fructu unici Christi expiatorii sacri- ficii excludendi: Imò quoties peccaverit quis, si pœ- nitentiam egerit, hostia illa semel oblata fide appre- hensa in gratiam recipi denuo poterit, Ezech. XIIX. XXXIII. Matth. XVIII.

PARS II. CAPITIS X. PARÆNETICA EADEMQUE PARS ALTERA EPISTOLÆ DE FIDE IN CHRISTUM.

## 10:19
Verse 19. “Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus.” Having now well established the dignity of Christ over the Levitical Priests, and the excellence of the offering made by Him over their offerings, he infers from this exhortations to persevere in the profession of Christianity and in piety. Παῤῥησία (boldness) here signifies the right of entering into the highest heaven; by a similar figure, as ἐνλογεῖν (to bless) is to do good. See 2 Cor. VII. 4. Christ entered there through His own blood: and we shall enter the same through the blood of Christ, that is, by faith, and by keeping, and by showing in deeds, that which has its origin from His blood.

Theophylact speaks beautifully concerning the continuity: Having then set forth the greatness by which both our High Priest Christ excelled those ancient High Priests of the law, and how much this new testament of ours exceeds that old one, and how much the offering of Christ excels the immolations and sacrifices of the law, through which we ourselves have been freed from the yoke and weight of sins, he now ceases to dispute about dogma and very opportunely passes over to morality, and provides space for the hearers to collect themselves. For when he had discoursed about remission, he finally reminds them not to relapse again into crimes once committed: “Having,” he says, “brethren, confidence,” because, namely, our sins have been remitted. For just as sin brings shame, and forces one who is bound by it not to dare to go out in public: so the remission itself makes spirits bold and provides confidence. Exhortations therefore are instituted not only for perseverance in the profession of Christianity, and in piety; but primarily for faith in Christ, and for perseverance in the same. Παῤῥησία denotes not a right of entering into heaven, but the confidence which we conceive in the merit of Christ, of entering the heaven which He opened with His blood: just as Grotius confesses, that through the blood of Christ, that is, faith in it, we enter. But this faith does not have its origin from the blood of Christ, except by reason of merit and procurement, but from the word of salvation, insofar as we apprehend it, that Christ by entering heaven through His own blood has prepared an entrance for us, and therefore we trust that we also shall enter. Estius himself also observes against Erasmus that the name of confidence fits better here: In which meaning, he says, the Apostle often uses παῤῥησία elsewhere, and indeed in this very chapter, where we have: Do not cast away your confidence: in which place Erasmus also translates it as confidence. Certainly the commentaries of the Greeks make more for confidence than for liberty. Finally, Erasmus corrected himself in his paraphrase, and substituted confidence for liberty. Therefore the sense is: Since confidence has been given to us to enter into heaven through the blood, therefore let us approach the throne of grace. Which observation is to be noted against the Papists, when they deny that faith is confidence. Theophylact has it thus: Since therefore our crimes have been forgiven us, we trust that we shall always approach those holy things, that is, heaven. In the blood of Christ, that is, through the blood. For through the cross, and the blood of Christ, having merited pardon, we are made more confident. Estius also adds this, that there was a representation of this matter in a type. For although the High Priest alone entered into those holy places, yet he carried in there with him the names of the twelve tribes inscribed on stones, which he wore on his shoulders and before his breast. By which it was signified, that Christ through His entrance with his own blood into heaven, opened for us the way into the heavenly sanctuary.

it, so that it itself may be both living and perpetual, because it offers everlasting life. Or understand a living and flourishing new way, in contrast to that old and now obsolete one, by which one went into the holy places, which without doubt is dead.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Ἔχοντες ὖν ἀδελφοὶ παῤῥησίαν εἰς τὴν εἴσοδον τῶν ἁγίων ἐν τῷ αἵματι Ἰησοῦ) Bene jam fundata dignitate Christi præ Le- viticis Sacerdotibus, & oblationis ab illo factæ præ illo- rum oblationibus egregia hinc infert monita ad perse- verandum in professione Christianismi & in pietate. Παῤῥησία hic significat jus intrandi in summum cœlum ; pari figura, qua ἐνλογεῖν est benefacere. Vide 2. Cor. VII. 4. Christus per sanguinem suum eo intravit : & nos per sanguinem Christi, id est, fidem & servando, & factis monstrando, quæ ex sanguine ipsius ortum habet, eo- dem intrabimus.

De συνεχεία pulchre Theophylactus : Tum ma- gnitudinem prætulisset, qua & Pontifex noster Chri- stus legis veteres illos Pontifices præstaret, & quan- tum testamentum hoc nostrum novum vetustum il- lud excedat, quamve legis immolationibus & sacri- ficiis præstet Christi oblatio, per quam sumus & ipsi peccatorum jugo & pondere liberati, desinit jam de dogmate disputare & perpportune ad moralita- tem pertransit, & spatium præbet auditoribus sese colligendi. Nam cum de remissione disseruisset, commonefacit demum, ne rursum in commissa olim facinora relabantur : Habentes, inquiens, fratres, fiduciam, quia nobis scilicet sint peccata remissa. Quemadmodum enim pudorem affert peccatum, co- gitque ne quis audeat, qui eo obstringitur, prodire in publicum : Sic remissio ipsa animos facit, & fiduciam præstat. Hortamenta itaque instituuntur non tan- tum ad perseverantiam in professione Christianismi, & in pietate; sed imprimis ad fidem in Christum, inque eadem perseverantiam. Παῤῥησία non jus intrandi in cœlum, sed fiduciam notat, quam in Christi meritum concipimus, cœlum, quod san- guine suo aperuit, ingrediendi : quemadmodum fatetur Grotius, per sanguinem Christi, id est, fidem eo nos intrare. Quæ vero fides non ex sanguine Christi ortum habet, nisi ratione meriti & impetra- tionis, sed ex verbo salutis, quatenus id apprehendi- mus, Christum per sanguinem suum in cœlum in- grediendo nobis ingressum parasse, adeoque con- fidimus nos etiam ingressuros. Observat & Estius ipse contra Erasmum, fiduciæ nomen hic magis quadrare : Qua significatione, inquit, sæpe etiam ali- bi παῤῥησίαν usurpat Apostolus, & quidem hoc ipso capite, ubi nos habemus : Nolite amittere confiden- tiam vestram : Quo loco etiam Erasmus fiduciam vertit. Certe Græcorum commentarii magis pro fi- ducia faciunt quam pro libertate. Denique Erasmus in paraphrasi se correxit, & pro libertate fiduciam reposuit. Igitur sensus est : Quum data nobis sit fi- ducia ingrediendi in cœlum per sanguinem, itaque accedamus ad thronum gratiæ. Quæ observatio contra Pontificios, cum negant fidem esse fiduciam, notanda. Theophylactus ita habet : Cum itaque no- bis remissa sint scelera, confidimus semper sancta illa nos adituros, id est, cœlum. In sanguine Chri- sti, id est, per sanguinem. Per crucem namque, & Christi sanguinem, veniam meriti, fidentiores effici- mur. Addit & Estius hoc, hujus rei in typo re- præsentationem fuisse. Nam etsi Pontifex so- lus in illa sancta intraret, nomina tamen duodecim tribuum lapidibus insculpta, quæ in humeris & ante pectus gestabat, illuc secum inferebat. Quo significatum fuit, Christum per ingressum suum cum sanguine proprio in cœlum, aditum nobis in cœleste adytum patefecisse.

cit, ut & ipsum vivens & perpetuum sit, quia vitam præbeat sempiternam. Vel viventem novam viam intellige & florentem, ad veteris illius & obsoletæ jam differentiam, qua in sancta ibatur, quæ procul dubio mortua est.

## 10:20
Vers. 20.

Ἣν ἐνεκαίνισεν ἡμῖν) of which, namely, the entrance, which he will now also call a way. Ἐνεκαίνισεν he initiated, he dedicated. See above IX. 8.

Ὁδὸν πρόσφατον) It is an addition. For he explains that which he called an entrance. And he rightly calls it new, which you may interpret as above IX. 8. Πρόσφατος חָדָשׁ in Ecclesiastes I. 9. A way trodden by no one's sole before.

Καὶ ζῶσαν) that is, life-giving. Which expression we noted at John VI. 50. That way seems hard and rough, because it often draws us even into death; but it truly leads to life, and that eternal.

They note that the word πρόσφατον is said to be πρὸ τοῦ σφατόμενον, so that it is not used without emphasis by the Apostle: if indeed one looks to the body of Christ slaughtered on the cross. For Christ is the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through him, John XIV. 6. Christ is said to have initiated or innovated or rather dedicated, as Erasmus rendered it, the entrance for us: For the pronoun ἣν is rightly referred to εἴσοδον, with Theophylact, Oecumenius, and Cajetan preceding, namely by his own entry preparing for us a new way to the holy places: because that old way through the law, in that it could not be fulfilled by us, did not lead us to heaven, but excluded us from heaven. But this new way is the obedience of Christ, by which alone we are justified and saved: Which is called living, because it is the cause of life. The entrance, therefore, is initiated or dedicated through Christ into a new way and a way not for Christ's sake but for ours. For Christ is both the dedicator by his entry, and has been made for us a way to life. Jacobus Arminius, in response to the 1st article, page 256, regarding his epoch concerning the believers of the Old Testament not having entered into heaven before Christ's ascension, refers πρόσφατον to the verb ἐνεκαίνισε, as if to say: Christ made the inaccessible way of death passable; which ought to be referred to the veil in this way: Christ initiated that way as recently slaughtered and living through his flesh, so that it is thus alluded to the passion of the flesh, by means of which that way was not so long ago, not indeed according to the promise at least as of old, but in the very act rendered slaughtered and living for believers. Hence it is called πρόσφατος, newly slaughtered, from Φάομαι, I am struck, according to Suidas: Which construction is thus proven by the blessed Georg König in his vindication of sacred things, page 293. Διὰ καταπετάσματος either modifies ἐνεκαίνισεν, or πρόσφατον καὶ ζῶσαν. Not the former, because through the veil or the passion of the flesh that way is not initiated and newly trodden, but through his ascension in HIS OWN POWER: in consideration of which he is to have neither predecessor nor successor, Micah II. 13. Therefore the latter. That which we intend. And further: Ἐγκαινίζειν τινὶ ὁδὸν does not properly signify to tread newly, but to open a way for someone, to open the pass to someone. Because, therefore, the gate of grace was closed, and no one without the blood of Christ, as the High Priest of the New Testament either to be exhibited or already exhibited, yet apprehended by faith, would dare to appear before the face of God; and indeed Christ through his blood obtained for all the liberty of entering, he is rightly said ἐγκαινίζειν ἡμῖν τὴν ὁδὸν, to open for us the house of the omnipotent Olympus. There is contained, therefore, in the word ἐνεκαίνισεν an exaggeration and prerogative of the Priest of the New Testament, as is hinted in verse 19: The High Priest of the Old Testament entering into the holy of holies. He did not open a way of entering to others, but to himself alone; he excluded the rest by the veil placed in the way. But Christ, by entering the heavenly holy places, dedicated an accessible way not for himself, but for others, both those who once fell asleep in the Lord, and those who do so now. I add the commentary of Theophylact: For that former path does not hold any place of salvation, but rather it even draws those approaching it into destruction. But this one of ours thus leads to life

Through the veil, that is, his flesh) We said just now at IX. 11 that the whole body of Christ is called a tabernacle. But its outer part is the flesh, just like the veil of the tabernacle. One could not penetrate into the inner sanctuary unless that veil were opened, that is, the flesh torn asunder. Through the veil מבית לפרכת, Levit. XVI. 2.

By the flesh of Christ is not understood the outer part of the body of Christ, just as we do not think the body of Christ is to be understood by 'tabernacle' in this place: And although some think the tabernacle of the body of Christ is shadowed forth by 'tabernacle': they nevertheless, according to the Apostle, wish to denote not his body, but the human nature of Christ. Furthermore, how is the entrance into the heavenly sanctuary open through the outer part of the body of Christ as a veil? Estius established this comparison: Just as the Aaronic High Priest entered into the holy places through the veil: So Christ entered into heaven through his flesh, so that through such an entrance he might initiate a way for us, by which we might follow him. But the issue here is not the way by which Christ entered into the sanctuary, but the way which has been prepared for us for entrance. Nor can we enter by the same way by which Christ did; rather, we enter through the merit of Christ: but Christ did not enter in that way. Nor can it be said that Christ entered into the heavenly sanctuary through his flesh as a veil. For the flesh pertains to the substance of Christ himself, the High Priest, who entered; it is not, however, outside of Christ. If it be said that the Son of God came into the flesh, and entered through the flesh: I reply that the subject entering is not the Son of God without flesh, but with flesh, not when he came into the flesh, but after he was incarnate and performed his office, and entered into glory through his passion. Nor is the flesh of Christ either the way through which, or the veil by which, Christ entered. And therefore the comparison of others is to be preferred: As entrance into the holy of holies was open to the priests taken from among men through the veil: So the flesh, that is, the human nature of Christ, in which he endured passion and death, when the veil was rent, is the medium through which we enter heaven. For the issue here, as we have said, is the way by which we must enter: Nor is the High Priest now being compared with Christ, but it is being taught how Christ, who is the same High Priest of the New Testament, has opened for us the way into heaven through the veil of his flesh. He renewed this way for us into heaven, says Theophylact, through his flesh, which, when it was indeed taken away on the cross, and subsequently carried up to the heavens, then certainly opened the heavenly things to us as well. Whence he also aptly called this flesh a veil. For when the veil has been drawn back, that which had lain hidden within is revealed.

Vers. 20.

Ἣν ἐνεκαίνισεν ἡμῖν) ἧς nempe εἱσόδου, quam & ὁδὸν jam vocabit. Ἐνεκαίνισεν initiavit, dedicavit. Vide supra IX. 8.

Ὁδὸν πρόσφατον) Est πρόσθεσις. Explicat enim illud quod εἴσοδον dixit. Et bene appellat novam, quod inter- pretare ut supra IX. 8. Πρόσφατος חָדָשׁ Ecclesiastæ I. 9. Via nullius ante trita solo.

Καὶ ζῶσαν) id est, ζωοποιοῦσαν. Quam loquutionem observavimus ad Joh. VI. 50. Via ista dura & aspera vide- tur, quia sæpe etiam in mortem nos trahit; sed vere ad vitam ducit, eamque æternam.

Vocem πρόσφατον notant dici πρὸ τοῦ σφατόμε- νον, ut non absque emphasi adhibita sit ab Aposto- lo: Siquidem respiciatur corpus Christi in cruce mactatum. Christus enim est via, veritas & vita. Nemo ad Patrem venit, nisi per ipsum, Johan. XIV. 6. Christus nobis initiasse vel innovasse aut potius dedicasse, ut Erasmus reddidit, dicitur introitum: Nam ad εἴσοδον recte refertur pronomen ἣν, præ- eunte Theophylacto, Oecumenio, Cajetano, ingressu scilicet suo nobis parans viam novam ad sancta: quia vetus illa via per legem, eo quod illa à nobis impleri non possit, non ad cœlum nos adducebat, sed à cœlo excludebat. Via autem hæc nova est obe- dientia Christi, qua sola justificamur & salvamur: Quæ viva dicitur, quia causa vitæ est. Ingressus ergo initiatus vel dedicatus est per Christum in viam novam & viam non Christi sed nostri causa. Nam Christus & ingressu suo dedicator est, & via nobis factus est ad vitam. Jacobus Arminius pro ἐποχῇ sua de fidelibus Veteris Testamenti non in- gressis in cœlum ante Christi ascensum resp. ad 1. artic. pag. 256. πρόσφατον refert ad verbum ἐνεκαίνι- σε, q. d. Christus inaccessam viam mortis fecit permea- bilem; quam referri debeat ad καταπέτασμα hoc modo: Christus viam istam initiavit recenter jugu- latam & vivam per carnem suam, ut sic alludatur ad passionem carnis, qua mediante via ista non ita pri- dem, non quidem secundum promissionem saltim ut olim, sed ipso actu jugulata & viva reddita est cre- dentibus. Hinc dicitur πρόσφατος noviter jugulata, à Φάομαι cædor, teste Suida: Quam constructio- nem sic probat B. Georg. König in vindic. sacr. pag. 293. Διὰ καταπετάσματος aut modificat τὸ ἐνεκαίνι- σεν, aut τὸ πρόσφατον καὶ ζῶσαν. Non prius, quia per velum sive passionem carnis via ista non initiata est, noviterque calcata, sed per ascensionem suam in PROPRIA VIRTUTE: consideratione cujus neque Antecessorem neque successorem habiturus est, Mich. II. 13. Ergo posterius. Id quod volumus. Et porro: Ἐγκαινίζειν τινὶ ὁδὸν non significat proprie noviter calcare, sed pandere alicui viam, einem den Paß öffnen. Quia itaque porta gratiæ erat occlu- sa, nec quisquam sine sanguine Christi, ceu Pontifi- cis magni Novi Testamenti sive exhibendi sive ex- hibiti, attamen fide apprehensi, coram facie Dei com- parere auderet; & verò Christus per sanguinem suum omnibus ingrediendi libertatem impetravit, rectè dicitur ἐγκαινίζειν ἡμῖν τὴν ὁδὸν, pandere no- bis domum omnipotentis Olympi. Continetur ita- que verbo ἐνεκαίνισεν exaggeratio & prerogativa Sacerdotis Novi Testamenti, uti v. 19. innuitur: Pontifex Veteris Testamenti in sancta sanctorum introiens. Aliis viam ingrediendi non aperuit, sed sibi soli, reliquos opposito velo exclusit. At Chri- stus sancta cœlestia ingrediendo non sibi, sed aliis, & qui olim in Domino obdormiverunt, & qui nunc, viam dedicavit acceffibilem. Addo Theophylacti commentarium: Neque enim illud pristinum iter locum habet ullum salutis, quin & in exitium tra- hit se adeuntes. At nostrum hoc ita ad vitam dedu

Διὰ τοῦ καταπετάσματος, τουτέστι, τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ) Dixi- mus modo ad IX. 11. Corpus Christi totum vocari σκη- νὴν. Ejus autem pars extima est caro, sicut velum σκηνῆς. In sanctuarium interius pervadi non poterat, nisi velo isto adaperto, id est, carne perrupta. Διὰ τοῦ καταπετά- σματος מבית לפרכת, Levit. XVI. 2.

Per carnem Christi non intelligitur pars extima corporis Christi, uti neque per σκηνὴν corpus Christi hoc loco intelligendum censemus: Et quanquam nonnulli tabernaculum corporis Chri- sti per σκηνὴν adumbratum censeant: Illi tamen pe- nes Apostolum, non corpus ejus, sed humanam Christi naturam denotari volunt. Porrò quomo- do per extimam partem corporis Christi ceu ve- lum ingressus patet in cœleste sanctuarium? Estius hanc instituit comparationem: Quemadmodum Pontifex Aaronicos per velum intrabat in sancta: Ita Christus per carnem suam intravit in cœlum, ut per hujusmodi ingressum viam nobis initiaret, quæ nos eum sequeremur. Sed non agitur hic de via, qua Christus ingressus est in sanctum, sed quæ no- bis parata est ad ingressum. Neque nos eadem via, qua Christus, ingredi possumus, imò ingredi- mur per Christi meritum: ita verò Christus ingres- sus non est. Nec dici potest, Christum per suam carnem ceu velamen ingressum esse in sanctuarium cœleste. Caro enim pertinet ad substantiam Christi ipfius Pontificis, qui ingressus est; non verò extra Christum est. Si dicatur, Filium Dei in carnem ve- nisse, & per carnem ingressum esse: Resp. Subje- ctum ingrediens non esse Filium Dei ἄσαρκον, sed ἔνσαρκον, non cum venit in carnem, sed postquam incarnatus officium suum obiit, & per passionem suam ingressus est in gloriam. Neque caro Chri- sti vel via est, per quam, vel velamen, per quod Christus ingressus est. Ideoque præferenda alio- rum comparatio: Ut per velum patebat Sacerdo- tibus ex hominibus assumptis ingressus in sanctum sanctorum: Sic caro, id est, Humana Christi natu- ra, in qua passionem ac mortem sustinuit, ubivelum scissum fuit, est medium, per quod cœlum ingredi- mur. De via enim, ut diximus, qua nobis ingredi- endum, hic agitur: Neque jam confertur Pontifex Summus cum Christo, sed docetur, quomodo Christus, qui idem Pontifex est Novi Testamenti nobis per carnis suæ velum patefecerit viam in cœ- lum. Innovavit hanc ille, inquit Theophylactus, no- bis in cœlum viam per carnem suam, quæ utique cum esset in cruce sublata, & deinceps ad cælos evecta, tunc sane & nobis cœlestia reseravit. Unde & apte velamen carnem hanc dixit. Cum enim velamen fue- rit detractum, cum intus latuerat, reseratur.

## 10:21
Verse 21.

And a great priest over the house of God) Namely, 'having'. We have not only received that right, but we also have a perpetual intercessor for our affairs. He takes care of the Church, which is called the house of God. 'Over' with the accusative often has the same value among the Greeks as 'because of', just as the Hebrew 'al.

Now a second argument for boldness and confident entrance is brought forward. For not only, as the Apostle had just said, do we have a new and living way, but since entrance is open to us through the rent veil, that is, through the passion and death of the human nature of Christ into heaven, we also have a great High Priest over the house of God, the Church, who himself entered into that sanctuary the heavenly [place] of the saints, and he takes care in the heavens of the Church, established over the house of God, interceding for the same and all its household, which is the proper role of the High Priest; and since he himself is a great High Priest, being exalted to the right hand of God, he also reigns with infinite power, preserving, protecting, defending the Church, and advancing and exalting it to blessed immortality and eternal life. Theophylact brings forward a twofold interpretation: Having, namely, both a Priest, Christ indeed, over the house of God, that is, the faithful, who are the temple and dwelling place of God, as that is: And I will walk and dwell in them: Or, which I would say is truer, heaven itself. For that, it calls holy, and teaches that he performs his office as High Priest in it, and intercedes for us. But the former explanation seems more convenient. See Heb. III. 5. 1. Tim. III. 15. unless perhaps both the Church, as much the triumphant as the militant, is joined, of which both the High Priest and the head is Christ, indeed which is truly one, and the same Church Heb. XII. 22.

sins, he says, cause and bring shame, so it brings and makes confidence, that all things have been remitted to us, and that we have been made co-heirs, and have attained such great love. There is added μετὰ ἀληθινῆς καρδίας, so that it may be designated as corrected and open, sincere and ἀνυπόκριτον, by which indeed with the whole heart, with the whole soul, with the whole mind we may pant after, embrace, and receive divine grace, and apply it to ourselves and make it our own through faith. But whence to us such a true and sincere heart, which is uniquely fixed upon God, whence that faith and confidence embracing divine grace in Christ, and confirming it by the expiation and merit of Christ, and relying upon it entirely. (I.) From the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, which is through the sprinkling of the word, 1 Pet. I. 2. John XV. 3. Whence it is said ἐῤῥαντισμένοι τὰς καρδίας ἀπὸ συνειδή- σεως πονηρᾶς, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, that is, from sins, from which an evil conscience arises, because through the blood of Christ, as the Apostle testifies Heb. IX. 14, our consciences are purified from dead works, which, since it is to be apprehended through faith, our hearts are said to be cleansed through faith,

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Καὶ ἱερέα μέγαν ἐπὶ τὸν οἶκον τοῦ Θεοῦ) Nempe ἔχοντες. Non jus tantum illud accepimus, sed & perpetuum habemus commendatorem rerum nostrarum. Is curam gerit Ec- clesiæ, quæ domus Dei dicitur. Ἐπὶ cum Accusativo sæpe apud Græcos idem valet quod propter, sicut & עַל Ebræum.

Jam alterum argumentum fiduciæ & confiden- tis introitus affertur. Non enim tantum, ut modo dixerat Apostolus, viam habemus novam & vi- vam, sed quum pateat nobis introitus per vela- men scissum, id est, per Humanæ Christi naturæ passionem & mortem in cœlum. Sed etiam Pontificem magnum habemus super domum Dei Ecclesiam, qui ingressus ipse est in sanctum illud sanctorum cœleste, & curam gerit in cœlis Eccle- siæ super Dei domum constitutus, interpellans pro eadem & omnibus ejus domesticis, quod Pontificis proprium est, & quum magnus ipse Pontifex sit, utpote exaltatus ad dextram Dei, regnat idem quo- que infinita virtute, Ecclesiam conservans, prote- gens, defendens, & ad beatam immortalitatem ac vitam æternam provehens & exaltans. Theophyla- ctus geminam affert interpretationem: Habentes scilicet & Sacerdotem Christum quidem super Dei domum, id est, fideles, qui Dei sunt templum & ha- bitaculum, ut illud est: Et inambulabo & inhabita- bo eis: Vel quod verius dixerim, cœlum ipsum. Illud namque sancta appellat, & in eo suo perfungi mune- re Pontificem docet, pro nobisque intercedere. Sed prior explicatio commodior videtur. Vid. Ebr. III. 5. 1. Tim. III. 15. nisi forte utraque Ecclesia tam triumphans quam militans conjungatur, cujus utriusque & Pontifex & caput est Christus, imò quæ vere una est, eademque Ecclesia Ebr.XII.22.

peccata, inquit, efficiunt & afferunt pudorem, ita fi- duciam affert & facit, quod omnia nobis sint re- missa, & quod simus cohæredes facti, & tantam simus assequuti charitatem. Additur μετὰ ἀληθινῆς καρ- δίας, ut designetur correctum & apertum, sincerum & ἀνυπόκριτον, quo nempe toto corde, tota anima, tota mente anhelemus, amplectamur & suscipia- mus divinam gratiam, eamque nobis applicemus ac nostram faciamus per fidem. Unde autem no- bis cor ejusmodi verum & sincerum, quod unice in Deum defixum est, unde fides & fiducia illa divinam gratiam in Christo amplectens, & expia- tione ac merito Christi firmans, ac in solidum in- nitens. (I.) Ex aspersione sanguinis Christi, quæ sit per aspergillum verbi, 1. Petr. I. 2. Johan. XV. 3. Un- de dicitur ἐῤῥαντισμένοι τὰς καρδίας ἀπὸ συνειδή- σεως πονηρᾶς aspersi corda & purgati à mala consci- entia, id est, à peccatis, à quibus mala conscientia oritur, quia per sanguinem Christi, teste Apostolo Ebr. IX. 14. purificantur conscientiæ nostræ ab ope- ribus mortuis, qui cum per fidem apprehenden- dus sit, per fidem dicuntur mundari corda nostra,

## 10:22
Vers. 22.

Προσερχώμεθα) Let us worship, namely, God.

Acts XV. 9. (II.) A true heart is also obtained through washing, which is in baptism, as a means and sacrament of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, Tit. III. 5. by which we are washed from sins, Acts XXII. 16. and which is dispensed for the remission of sins Luke III. 3. Acts II. 38. whence it is said λελυμένοι τὸ σῶμα ὕδατι καθαρῷ, washed as to the body with clean water; mention of the body having been made, both because the body is sprinkled with the water of baptism according to the institution of Christ, and lest, the heart having been named before as sprinkled and purged from sins, it be believed that the body is excluded; since we are purged both in soul and body no less by the sacrament of baptism than by the word of the Gospel from the filth of sin, 1 Pet. III. 21. By which name baptism is called clean water from the effect, because by it we are cleansed and washed from our spiritual uncleanness, from all our iniquities, Zech. XIII. 1. just as also the word of God, by which it is sprinkled, is called clean water, Ezek. XXXVI. 25. on account of the Holy Spirit, who is united both to the water of baptism, John III. 6. and to the word of the Gospel, John VI. 63. by which our hearts are sanctified, when it is poured out through the word into us Isa. XLIV. 3. Joel II. 28. and the washing of water in the word for our purification, Eph. V. 26. Tit. III. 5. 1 Cor. VI. 11. Nor is there any doubt that there is an allusion to the offering of the Priests, when they entered into the holy place, which was a type of our spiritual washing, who approach God into the holy place of the Church, and the inner sanctuary of the heavens, being made Priests by Christ, and washed from sins by his blood, Rev. I. 5. 6. ch. V. 9. 10. ch. VII. 14. ch. XX. 6. Compare what is read in Exod. XXX. 18. concerning the washings of the Priests, and what is read elsewhere here and there concerning Levitical washings. Some wish for the former words, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, to allude to the water of lustration, by which those who had defiled themselves were to be sprinkled according to the law: but for the latter, washed with clean water, to that washing which is required of those about to enter for the worship of God into the tabernacle. Chrysostom explains the clean water of baptism by the name of Φωτισμὸς, and Theophylact, who says, the water of baptism. Clean, indeed, because it makes [them] pure, and wipes away stains. Likewise: or clean, he says, because in the washing the grace of the Spirit cleanses souls and renders them bright. And before these, Theodoret: He placed these also by way of comparison. For in the law they used sprinklings, and frequently washed the body. But those who institute their life from the New Testament, purge the soul through most holy baptism, and from

Μετὰ ἀληθινῆς καρδίας) With unfeigned piety. The same is said ἐν ἁπλότητι καρδίας, in singleness of heart, Eph. VI. 5. Col. III. 22. not an evil heart, of which above III. 12.

In the full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience) For by faith hearts are purified, 1 Pet. 1:22. The full assurance of faith is called here such a faith as fills the whole man, which leaves nothing empty. See Col. 2:2, 1 Thess. 1:5, above 6:11.

An evil conscience is called here a mind conscious to itself of evil, just as on the contrary a good conscience, Acts 23:1, 1 Tim. 1:5, 19, 1 Pet. 3:16. By an evil or bad conscience, however, the sins themselves are understood, the word for the effect being taken for the cause. For ἐῤῥαντισμένοι in the manuscript there is ῥεραντισμένοι from some dialect, as I suppose.

Let us draw near, he says, to God, that is, or to the throne of grace, in that true and heavenly holy of holies: in which was seen that true ark of the Testament, Rev. 11:19, in the heavenly temple: just as the Apostle had advised in Heb. 4:16, let us draw near with boldness to the throne of grace. But for boldness, the term full assurance of faith is now used, because boldness had preceded, so that with greater emphasis the confidence might be expressed which is necessary for the enjoyment of the expiation of sins obtained by the sacrifice of Christ, and it might be taught that faith is not a bare assent, but joined with trust and confidence, which is the soul of faith, through which, being certain of obtaining the grace of God the Father, and relying on the merit of Christ, we may draw near with full hope, so that we may obtain mercy and grace, and apprehend and appropriate to ourselves by faith with boldness and full assurance those spiritual and heavenly goods which are offered to us in the word. Which confidence is deservedly opposed to Popish doubt and the doctrine concerning the uncertainty of divine grace. Therefore, says Chrysostom, it is added in the fullness of faith. But it cannot be that one who doubts also believes. It is as necessary to believe as it is concerning those things which are seen, and much more so. For here indeed one can be mistaken in those things which are seen: there, however, by no means. Here indeed we allow for sense, there however for the Spirit. And a little before: Having therefore, brethren, confidence. Confidence from where, pray? Just as they render the conscience free from former stains. Therefore, he called divine baptism the sprinkling and clean water. Estius observes that this is the common exposition of both the Greeks and the Latins. What then? Since even the Calvinists Pareus, Tossanus, and others explain it concerning baptism.

We do not dwell on Crellius and Schlichting, those Socinian chicks. For what they say, that the baptism of water is only an external sign and a certain shadowing forth of this washing, is contradicted by the most manifest testimonies of Scripture, which attribute to baptism the remission of sins, washing from sins, purification, regeneration, renewal, and salvation. For the rest, they seem to speak correctly enough about the washing, provided they understood it in an orthodox sense, and that saying of Irenaeus did not apply to them: Ὅμοια μὲν λαλοῦσιν, ἀνόμοια δὲ φρονοῦσι. They say the Author transfers that cleansing of the flesh to the mind and Spirit, or understands by it a spiritual cleansing, by which the mind is purged from the stain of conscience and the body from the filth of sins. But it seems that having been sprinkled, that is, having the heart cleansed from an evil conscience, can be taken in two ways: either as signifying that cleansing by which, having obtained full forgiveness of sins through the blood and sacrifice of Christ, we have been freed from an evil conscience and the fear of divine punishment, in which manner he said above that our conscience is cleansed by the blood of Christ from dead works: Or because our mind is purged from internal and hidden sins. For by the name of an evil conscience, by a metonymy of the effect, in this place, specifically hidden and latent vices of the mind seem to be designated; being opposed to the filth of the body, which the Author also teaches immediately ought to be washed. For what else can those stains of the body signify than external sins, and those which are committed by the body itself? Not indeed as if these also do not wound the conscience, but because open crimes are exposed even to the eyes and censures of others: whereas the hidden and internal stains of the mind, although they have no one aware of them, nevertheless weary and exercise the conscience.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

Προσερχώμεθα) Colamus nempe Deum.

Acttor. XV. 9. (II.) Obtinetur etiam καρδία ἀλη- θινὴ per ablutionem, quæ sit in baptismo, ceu me- dio & sacramento regenerationis & renovationis Spiritus sancti, Tit. III. 5. quo abluimur à peccatis, Actor. XXII. 16. quique dispensatur in remissionem peccatorum Luc. III. 3. Actor. II. 38. unde dicitur λελυμένοι τὸ σῶμα ὕδατι καθαρῷ abluti quoad cor- pus aqua munda; corporis mentione facta, tum quod corpus aqua baptismi conspergatur secun- dum institutionem Christi, tum ne denominato prius corde asperso & purgato à peccatis ex- cludi credatur corpus; siquidem & anima & corpo- re purgemur non minus baptismos sacramen- to, quam Evangelii verbo à sordibus peccati, 1. Petr. III. 21. Quo nomine baptismus aqua munda dicitur ab effectu, quia eadem mundamur & ab- luimur ab immunditia nostra spirituali, ab omnibus inquitatibus nostris, Zach. XIII. 1. quemadmo- dum & verbum Dei, quo aspergitur, aqua munda dicitur, Ezech. XXXVI. 25. ob Spiritum sanctum, qui & aqua baptismatos unitur, Johan. III. 6. & verbo Evangelii, Johan. VI. 63. quo sanctificantur corda nostra, quum effunditur per verbum in nos Esa.XLIV.3. Joël. II. 8. & lavacrum aquæ in verbo ad nostri purificationem, Eph. V. 26. Tit. III.2. Cor. VI. 2. 6. Neque dubium est alludi ad oblationem Sacerdotum, cum in sanctum ingrediebantur, quæ typus erat spiritualis nostræ ablutionis, qui accedimus ad Deum in sanctum Ecclesiæ, & ady- tum cœlorum, utpote Sacerdotes à Christo facti, ejusque sanguine à peccatis abluti, Apoc. I. 5. 6. cap. V.9.10.cap. VII. 14. cap. XX. 6. Conf. quæ Exod. XXX. 18. de ablutionibus Sacerdotum, & quæ passim alias de lotionibus Leviticis leguntur. Non- nulli prioribus verbis, coaspersi corda à conscientia mala alludi volunt ad lustralem aquam, qua, qui se polluerant, conspergendi erant secundum le- gem: Posterioribus verò abluti aqua munda ad ab- lutionem illam, quæ requiritur ab ingressuris ad cultum Dei in tabernaculum. De aqua munda baptismatis exponunt Chrysostomus nomine Φω- τισμᾶς, & Theophylactus, qui baptismi aqua, inquit. Munda verò quia puros efficiat, abstergit- que à labibus. Item: vel munda, dicit, quia in la- vacro Spiritus gratia animas mundet & nitidas reddat. Et ante hos Theodoretus: Hæc quoque posuit per comparationem. In lege enim utebantur asparsionibus, & corpus frequenter lavabant. Qui autem ex Novo Testamento vitam instituunt, per sanctissimum baptismum animam expurgant, & à

Μετὰ ἀληθινῆς καρδίας) Pietate non ficta. Idem dicitur ἐν ἁπλότητι καρδίας, Eph. VI. 5. Col. III. 22. non καρδία πονηρὰ de qua supra III. 12.

Ἐν πληροφορίᾳ πίςεως ἐῤῥαντισμένοι τὰς καρδίας ἀπὸ συνει- δήσεως πονηρᾶς) Per fidem enim purgantur corda, 1. Petr. I. 22. Πληροφορία πίςεως plenitudo fidei hic dicitur fides talis, quæ hominem totum impleat, quæ nihil relin- quat vacui. Vide Coloss. II. 2. 1. Thessal. I. 5. supra VI. 11.

Συνείδησις πονηρὰ hic dicitur animus mali sibi conscius, sicut contra συνείδησις ἀγαθὴ, Act. XXIII. 1. Tim. I. 5. 19. 1. Petr. III. 16. Per conscientiam autem malam sive mali intelliguntur ipsa peccata, vocabulo effecti sumpto pro causa. Pro ἐῤῥαντισμένοι in Manuscripto est ῥεραντισμένοι ex dialecto, ut puto, aliqua.

Accedamus, inquit, ad Deum scilicet, vel thro- num gratiæ, in sancto illo sanctorum vero, & cœle- sti: in quo visa est vera illa arca Testamenti, Apoc. XI.19. in templo cœlesti: quemadmodum Ebr. IV. 16. monuerat Apostolus, προσερχώμεθα μετὰ παῤῥησίας τῷ θρόνῳ f χάριτος. Pro παῤῥησίᾳ au- tem adhibetur jam vox πληροφορίας πίςεως, quia παῤῥησία præcesserat, ut majori emphasi exprima- tur fiducia, qua opus est ad fruitionem expiatio- nis peccatorum sacrificio Christi partæ, ac docea- tur, fidem non esse nudum assensum, sed cum fi- ducia & confidentia, quæ anima est fidei, conjun- ctam, per quam certi de gratia Dei Patris impe- tranda, nitentes Christi merito plena spe acceda- mus, ut misericordiam & gratiam consequamur, & ea, quæ in verbo nobis offeruntur, bona spiri- tualia & cœlestia per fidem μετὰ παῤῥησίας κὴ πλη- ροφορίας apprehendamus, nobisque approprie- mus. Quæ fiducia merito opponitur Pontificiæ dubitationi, & doctrinæ de gratiæ divinæ incertitu- dine. Propterea, inquit Chrysostomus, in pleni- tudine fidei additur. Fieri autem non potest, ut etiam credat dubitans. Æque oportet credere at- que de his, quæ videntur, & multo amplius. Nam hic quidem errari potest in iis, quæ videntur: illic autem nequaquam. Hic quidem sensui permitti- mus, illic verò Spiritui. Et paulò ante: Habentes ita- que fratres fiduciam. Fiduciam unde nam? Sicut prioribus maculis liberam reddunt conscientiam. Aspersionem ergo & aquam mundam divinum baptismum appellavit. Communem esse & Graecorum & Latinorum expositionem observat Estius. Quid? quod Calviniani etiam Pareus, Tossanus alii de baptismo explicent.

Crellium & Schlichtingium, Socinianos pullos, non moramur. Quod enim ajunt, baptismum aquae externum signum tantum, & adumbrationem quandam esse hujus ablutionis, apertissimis Scripturae testimoniis, quae remissionem peccatorum, ablutionem a peccatis, purificationem, regenerationem, renovationem, salutem baptismo tribuunt, contrariantur. De caetero de ablutione videntur satis recte loqui, modo sensu orthodoxo intelligerent, nec illud Irenaei in eos quadraret: Ὅμοια μὲν λαλοῦσιν, ἀνόμοια δὲ φρονοῦσι. Carnis illam emundationem, inquiunt, ad animum & Spiritum transfert Autor, seu spiritualem, qua animus a conscientiae labe, corpus a peccatorum sordibus purgatur, intelligit emundationem. Videtur vero conspersum, id est, emundatum cor a conscientia mala, dupliciter accipi posse, vel ut significet eam emundationem, qua plenam peccatorum veniam per Christi sanguinem sacrificiumque adepti, mala conscientia ac poenae divinae formidine soluti sumus, quo pacto supra dixit, conscientiam nostram Christi sanguine ab operibus mortuis emundari: Vel quia animus noster ab internis & occultis peccatis purgatur. Mala enim conscientia nomine per Metonymiam Effecti, hoc loco, speciatim occulta & latentia animi vitia designari videntur; quippe corporis, quod & ipsum statim ablutum esse debere docet Autor, sordibus opposita. Quid enim aliud corporis istae sordes significare possunt; quam externa, &, quae corpore ipso peragantur, peccata? Non quidem quasi haec quoque conscientiam non laedant, sed quod aperta crimina aliorum etiam oculis ac censuris sint exposita: Operta autem & interna animi labes, quamvis neminem habeant conscium, conscientiam tamen fatigent & exerceant.

## 10:23
Ver. 23.

Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering.] He says this because some had already fallen away from the profession through fear of evils. See also above III, 1. IV, 14. And he excellently commended the profession by adding the name of hope, as also Peter does in 1 Pet. III, 15. That profession has the hope of eternal life as its companion. Ἀκλινῆ means not inclined, not wavering. He adds this also not in vain, because there were also those who had not deserted the profession, but were wavering in it.

He calls the confession of hope the confession of faith itself; either because he who confesses the faith simultaneously confesses the hope of eternal life; or because believing and hoping are interchanged in a phrase accepted in the Old Testament. For by believing we hope, and by hoping we believe and trust concerning the grace of God, at the same time both certainly expecting the same as regards its continuation, and embracing it through a fiduciary reception. Theophylact: Let us hold the confession of our hope, that is, the hope which we have professed, stable and immovable. For we hoped in the beginnings of our reception of the faith that we would enter into heaven, and subsequently we also confessed that we believed the resurrection would come to pass, and that we would have that perpetual life. That indeed is what was agreed upon with us in the faith, and thus it was permitted to covenant, wherefore this confession is to be held by us. But this both faith and our hope relies upon the divine faith, namely, the certainty and truth of the divine promises and the constancy of God who promises, 1 Cor. I, 9. Chap. X, 13. 2 Tim. I, 12. Theophylact explains it concerning Christ: He, namely, supplies the strength, insofar as we keep this hope unshaken and firm. Which indeed will come to pass if we know the faithfulness of the one promising. For Christ is faithful and truthful, and his promises are more certain. For he says: Where I am, there also will my minister be.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

Κατέχωμεν τὴν ὁμολογίαν τῆς ἐλπίδος ἀκλινῆ.] Hoc ideo dicit, quia quidam jam malorum metu a professione defecerant. Vide & supra III, 1. IV, 14. Et egregie commendavit professionem addito spei nomine, ut & Petrus 1. III, 15. Illa professio spem vitae aeternae habet comitem. Ἀκλινῆ nihil inclinatam, nihil nutantem. Hoc quoque non frustra addit, quia erant & qui non deseruerant professionem, sed in ea vacillabant.

Confessionem spei dicit ipsam fidei confessionem; sive quia, qui fidem confitetur, simul spem vitae aeternae confitetur; sive quia credere & sperare phrasi in Veteri Testamento recepta permutatur. Credendo enim speramus, & sperando credimus ac confidimus de gratia Dei, eandem simul & certo expectantes quoad continuationem, & complectantes per fiducialem susceptionem. Theophylactus: Spei nostrae confessionem, hoc est, quam professi nos sumus, spem teneamus stabilem & immotam. Speravimus namque in fidei suscepta primordiis, ingressuros nos in coelum, deinceps & illud sumus confessi, resurrectionem nos credituros futuram, & vitam illam perpetuam habituros. Id quidem est nobis cum fide conventum, & sic licuit depacisci, quocirca haec nobis tenenda confessio est. Haec autem & fides & spes nostra nititur divinae fidei promissionum nempe divinarum certitudini ac veritati & constantiae Dei promittentis, 1. Corinth. I, 9. Cap. X, 13. 2. Tim. I, 12. De Christo explicat Theophylactus: Vires scilicet ille suppeditat, quatenus spem hanc inconcussam servemus & firmam. Quod sane futurum est, si fidem noverimus pollicentis. Ei- dem delis est enim & veridicus Christus, & certiora sunt ejus promissa. Ait namque: Ubi ego sum, illic & erit meus minister.

## 10:23
For he is faithful that promised.] Thus also in the cited place 2 Cor. VII, 1, the admonition is founded on the promises. If we do not deceive God, God will not deceive. Thus also 1 Thess. V, 24. 2 Thess. III, 3. But these things are to be written and read as a parenthesis. For the discourse is continued afterwards.

Latin:

Πιστὸς γὰρ ὁ ἐπαγγειλάμενος.] Sic & dicto loco 2. Cor. VII, 1. admonitio fundatur in promissis. Si nos Deum non fallimus, Deus non fallet. Sic & 1.Thessal. V, 24. 2. Thessal. III, 3. Hæc autem scribenda & legenda κατὰ παρένθεσιν. Nam continuatur deinde sermo.

## 10:24
Ver. 24.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

## 10:24
And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works.] Let us observe one another's acts, so that, if any are languishing, we may excite them to love and pious deeds. Κατανοεῖν means to observe, Ps. XXII, 19. Παροξύνειν is a middle word, which from the things added here is taken in a good sense, as also Prov. VI, 3. One may translate with the Glossary: To sharpen, to stimulate. Thus παροξύνειν ἐπὶ μάχην is found in Plutarch.

Since faith and good works cohere, where he has exhorted to faith and the perseverance of faith, the Apostle now warns that they should mutually excite one another to charity and good works. Others thus: First he exhorts to the fullness of faith, then to the firmness of hope, thirdly to the works of charity. The Vulgate rendered the word κατανοῶμεν: Let us consider one another: Let us direct all our thoughts toward that, so that one may invite another by good example to charity. B. Luther: Let us take heed of ourselves among one another. The Vulgate renders εἰς παροξυσμὸν as unto provocation, B. Luther as with irritation. That word otherwise signifies irritation, exasperation, such as is in the onset of fevers, but here it is taken in a good sense, and we are warned that one should irritate and excite another both by word and by example to virtue, with a certain ardor of holy contention. Which kind of provocation, according to Theophylact, is an argument of charity, not of envy. For as iron is sharpened by iron: so also the mind, which struggles with a well-instructed mind, is more and more kindled toward the good.

Latin:

Καὶ κατανοῶμεν ἀλλήλους εἰς παροξυσμὸν ἀγάπης καὶ καλῶν ἔργων.] Observemus alii aliorum actus, ut, si qui languescant, eos excitemus ad dilectionem & pia facta. Κατανοεῖν obser- vare, Psal. XXII, 19. Παροξύνειν vox est media, quæ ex adjectis hic in bonam partem sumitur, ut & Prov. VI, 3. Vertere licet cum Glossario: Exacuere, stimulare. Sic παροξύνειν ἐπὶ μάχην est apud Plutarchum.

Quum fides & bona opera cohæreant, ubi ad fidem & perseverantiam fidei hortatus est, jam mutuo se excitent ad charitatem & opera bona, mo- net Apostolus. Alii ita: Primo hortatur ad fidei plenitudinem, deinde ad spei firmitatem, tertio ad opera charitatis. Verbum κατανοῶμεν Vulgata red- didit: Consideremus invicem: In illud omnes co- gitationes nostras dirigamus, ut alter alterum bo- no exemplo ad charitatem invitet. B. Lutherus: Lasset uns untereinander unser selbst warnehmen. Εἰς παροξυσμὸν Vulgata reddit in provocationem, B. Lutherus mit Reitzen. Significat alias ea vox ir- ritationem, exasperationem, qualis est in invasio- nibus febrium, sed hic in bonam partem accipitur, monemurque ut alter alterum tum verbo tum ex- emplo irritet atque excitet ad virtutem, cum quo- dam sanctæ contentionis ardore. Cujusmodi pro- vocatio, secundum Theophylactum, charitatis est non invidiæ argumentum. Nam ut ferro acuitur ferrum: Sic & animus, qui cum animo conflictatur bene instructo, magis ac magis ad bonum accendi- tur.

## 10:25
Verse 25.

Μὴ ἐγκαταλείποντες τὴν ἐπισυναγωγὴν ἑαυτῶν.] That is, of one another, as 1 Cor. VI, 7, and elsewhere. Ἐπισυναγωγὴ is a gathering into one place, 2 Maccab. II, 7. So also συναγωγὴ, James II, 2. To desert the assemblies is a certain beginning of defection. On the contrary, in the Churches God increases his gifts. Therefore, in the letters of Ignatius we have similar warnings: To Polycarp: Πυκνότερον συναγωγαὶ γινέσθωσαν. To the Ephesians: Σπουδάζετε οὖν πυκνότερον συνέρχεσθαι εἰς εὐχαριστίαν Θεοῦ καὶ δόξαν. For when you are frequently in the same place, the powers of Satan are destroyed, and his fiery darts against sin will stand ineffective. For your concord and harmonious faith is his destruction, and a torment to his shield-bearers.

Καθὼς ἔθος τισίν.] He had learned that some had already done this, therefore he fears lest the example spread more widely.

Some understand this of apostasy, or the defection of the Church through schism before the apostasy, to which some Jews, once converted to the faith, were prone, as the Latins generally do, as Estius notes; he, however, prefers the sense of the Greeks, that they should not withdraw themselves from Ecclesiastical assemblies. Such, indeed, as either out of fear of persecution, or out of a persuasion of perfection, or out of damnable negligence, neglect the assemblies of others, by which we are confirmed and stirred up in faith and in the pursuit of good works through both the communion of prayers and mutual examples of piety and charity, are near to a more grievous ruin, by which they either beget their own sects, or through apostasy relapse into the former darkness of unbelief. The fact that what follows, 'as is the custom of some,' favors this exposition of the Greeks. For custom designates a frequency of acts: but apostasy is completed by a single act.

Ἀλλὰ παρακαλοῦντες.] Namely, one another, which is to be repeated from the preceding. Also in this, exhort one another, that the assemblies may not be deserted.

The Vulgate rendered it 'consoling,' B. Luther, as also Erasmus, 'exhorting': It can be rendered 'exhorting' with consolation: because in order that those who are constrained by distresses and pressures, from which the faithful are never destitute, may persevere in the faith, such an exhortation is required as may be made with the consolation of the divine word, so that those exhorting to patience may at the same time be consoled by the hope of future retribution.

And so much the more, as you see the day approaching.] See what was said above IX, 26.

Concerning the day of the final coming of the Lord, which is called the day by way of eminence, most understand it as that which is said to be approaching, that is, drawing nearer and nearer every day; or also in the sense that this last time after the coming of Christ is the age of the world, 1 John II, 18. Others, however, explain it as the day of judgment concerning the Jewish nation, or the destruction of Jerusalem, like Crellius and Schlichtingius; some explain it as the day of death approaching for each person, which is less approved by Estius, both because the Apostle is not dealing with individuals, but with the assembly or community of the faithful, in which as some die others succeed them; and truly because the word 'day' placed alone, especially with the article added, as in this place (τὴν ἡμέραν), is almost never understood in the Apostolic scriptures as anything other than the day of universal judgment and retribution. Examples are 1 Thess. II, 2 Thess. I, 2 Tim. I & IV. But that Crellius and Schlichtingius say that the last day of the Lord is imminent for everyone through death, can be admitted, both because after death there will be no change in the state of our salvation or damnation, and because when we are dead, and thus destitute of all sense of time, the last moment of one rightly departing and the first moment of one returning (in the last judgment) will seem to those about to live again to be one and the same: But under this caution, that soul-sleep and an absolute cessation of the life and sense of the mind not be introduced. Therefore, we can grant that this is the reason why the sacred scriptures speak sometimes as if we were to live until the coming of Christ, but not that this is also the reason why they speak as if we were to migrate immediately from death to heavenly joys. For that is to be believed to happen immediately, 2 Cor. V, 8, Phil. I, 23.

Latin:

Vers. 25.
