Μὴ ἐγκαταλείποντες τὴν ἐπισυναγωγὴν ἑαυτῶν.] Id est, ἀλ- λήλων, ut 1. Cor. VI, 7. & alibi. Ἐπισυναγωγὴ congregatio in unum locum, 2. Maccab. II, 7. Sic & συναγωγὴ Jac. II, 2. De- serere conventus est initium quoddam defectionis. Contra in Ecclesiis Deus auget sua dona. Ideo in literis Ignatii pa- ria habemus monita: Ad Polycarpum: Πυκνότερον συναγω- γαὶ γινέσθωσαν. Ad Ephesios: Σπουδάζετε οὖν πυκνότερον συν- έρχεσθαι εἰς εὐχαριστίαν Θεοῦ καὶ δόξαν. Ὅταν γὰρ συνεχῶς ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ γένησθε, καθαιροῦνται αἱ δυνάμεις τοῦ Σατανᾶ, καὶ ἄπρα- κτα αὐτοῦ ἑστήξεται τὰ πεπυρωμένα βέλη πρὸς ἁμαρτίαν. Ἡ γὰρ ὑμετέρα ὁμόνοια καὶ σύμφωνος πίστις αὐτοῦ μέν ἐστιν ὄλε- θρος, τῶν ὑπασπιστῶν αὐτοῦ βάσανος.

Καθὼς ἔθος τισίν.] Didicerat, jam aliquos id fecisse, ideo metuit, ne exemplum latius serpat.

Alii de apostasia, vel defectione Ecclesiæ per schisma ante apostasiam, ad quam Judæi nonnul- li, semel ad fidem conversi, proclives erant, in- telligunt, ut Latini fere, notante Estio; qui vero Græcorum sensum, ne conventibus Ecclesiasticis sese subducant, præfert. Quales utique, qui sive ex metu persecutionis, sive ex persuasione perfectionis, sive ex damnabili negligentia conventus alios ne- gligunt, quibus & per precum communionem, & mutua pietatis & charitatis exempla in fide ac studio bonorum operum confirmamur, & exci- tamur, ruinæ graviori proximi sunt, qua vel se- ctas proprias pariant, vel per apostasiam in pri- stinas incredulitatis tenebras relabantur. Cui expositioni Græcorum favet, quod sequitur, sic- ut consuetudinis est quibusdam. Nam consue- tudo frequentiam actuum designat: Apostasia vero uno actu completur.

Ἀλλὰ παρακαλοῦντες.] Nempe ἑαυτοὺς, quod ex præcedenti repetendum. Etiam in hoc alii alios hortamini, ne con- ventus deserantur.

Vulgata reddidit consolantes, B. Lutherus, ut & Erasmus exhortantes: Potest reddi exhortantes cum consolatione: quia ut perseverent in fide ii, qui angustiis & pressuris coarctantur, quibus fide- les nunquam destituuntur, exhortatio talis requi- ritur, quæ cum consolatione verbi divini fiat, ut adhortantes ad patientiam simul consolentur spe futuræ retributionis.,

Καὶ τοσούτῳ μᾶλλον, ὅσῳ βλέπετε ἐγγίζουσαν τὴν ἡμέραν.] Vide quæ dicta supra IX, 26.

De die adventus Domini novissimi, qui κατ' ἐξο- χὴν ἡ ἡμέρα dicitur, plerique intelligunt, qui ap- propinquare dicitur, id est, accedere magis ac ma- gis quotidie; vel etiam eo sensu, quod ultima hæc post Christi adventum tempus sit mundi ætas, 1. Joh. II, 18. Alii tamen de die judicii de gente Ju- daica, seu excidii Hierosolymitani, ceu Crellius & Schlichtingius; nonnulli de appropinquante cuivis die mortis explicant, quod minus probatur Estio, tum quia non de singulis agit Apostolus, sed de con- ventu seu communitate fidelium, in qua aliis morien- tibus alii succedunt; tum vero quia dies solitarie po- situs, præsertim addito articulo, ut hoc loco (τὴν ἡμέ- ραν) non alius fere solet intelligi in scripturis Apo- stolicis, quam dies universalis judicii ac retributio- nis. Exempla sunt 1. Thessal. II. 2. Thessal. I. 2. Tim. I. & IV. Quod autem per mortem instare cuique ultimum Domini diem Crellius & Schlichtin- gius ajunt, tum quia post mortem nulla futura sit ra- tione salutis vel damnationis nostræ mutatio, tum quia mortuis nobis, & sic omni temporis sensu desti- tutis, momentum ultimum rite abeuntis & momen- tum primum redeuntis (in ultimo judicio) unum idemque revicturis videbitur, admitti potest: Sed sub hac cautione, ne ψυχοπαννυχία, & omnimo- da vitæ sensusque animi cessatio inferatur. Idcirco hanc causam esse, cur sacræ literæ ita loquantur nonnunquam, ac si ad Christi adventum victuri omnino essemus, largiri possumus, non item hanc causam etiam esse, cur ita loquantur, atque si statim à morte ad cœlestia gaudia migraremus. Id enim omnino statim fieri credendum est, 2. Cor. V, 8. Phil. I, 23.

## 10:26-27
Vers. 26. 27.

For if we sin willfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins. But a certain fearful expectation of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries.] Clement of Alexandria cites this passage in Strom. II to prove that only one repentance is admitted after baptism, and he says, 'But continuous and successive repentances for sins differ nothing from those who have not believed at all, except only in the feeling that they are sinning. And I do not know which is worse for them, either to sin knowingly, or after repenting of what they have sinned, to offend again.' Theodoret produces this passage in a not dissimilar sense in Book XII against the Greeks. I acknowledge that these things are usefully said to deter men from the repetition of crimes and sufficiently agree with the discipline of the ancient Church. Moreover, the things that precede here concerning holding fast to the profession lead me to interpret these in the same way as those we had above VI, 4, and I take 'to sin' as rejecting Christianity, just as those who were rejecting the law are called 'having sinned' above III, 17, as in 2 Peter II, 4, the apostate angels. 'Willfully' is added, because such persons cannot plead ignorance of their guilt. But those who thus fall away from Christianity, and hold the blood of Christ as profane blood, as is said presently, will not be recalled to a good way of life by any other victims, so that they might obtain pardon. 'To receive the knowledge of the truth' is the same as 'to have been enlightened' above VI, 4. 'Knowledge' (ἐπίγνωσις) is not just any knowledge, but a certain experimental knowledge. See Eph. I, 17, IV, 13, Phil. I, 9, Col. I, 10, II, 2, III, 10, 1 Tim. II, 4, 2 Tim. II, 25, III, 7, Tit. I, 1, Philem. v. 6. 'Expectation of judgment' (ἐκδοχὴ κρίσεως) is a Hebrew idiom for judgment to be expected. The punishment remains horrible for that reason. 'Fiery indignation' (πυρὸς ζῆλος) is the wrath of God, exerting itself through fire. Conversely, he said 'fire of zeal' in Ezek. XXXVI, 3, Zeph. I, 10, III, 8. Thus we say for the same 'flame of fire' and

fire of flame. Fire is said to 'eat' (אכל), as in Isa. XXX, 27, Jer. V, 14, and elsewhere. 'The adversaries' (τοὺς ὑπεναντίους), namely of GOD, as in Isa. LIX, 18, Nahum I, 2. The history which is in Num. XVI, 35, Lev. X, 2 seems to be looked back upon. Among those who understand this of those who have fallen after baptism is also Augustine in his unfinished exposition of the Epistle to the Romans, who indeed explains the passage as concerning the non-repetition of baptism. The Apostle signifies that he who has sinned cannot thereafter be purged by being baptized again. But it is not a question here of any who have fallen after baptism, nor of the denial of purgation through baptism, but of the sacrifice not being left. Nowhere, however, is baptism called a sacrifice.

The Novatians denied repentance after baptism to such as had fallen, by the force of this passage: which knot, since they could not untie, they dared to cut, who therefore denied canonical authority to the present Epistle to the Hebrews. But it is too manifest that it does not treat of just any who have fallen into sins, even more grievous ones, after baptism, if their description exhibited here and in Chapter VI in the parallel passage is fully weighed, to whom return to repentance and a sacrifice for sin is denied.

Estius therefore teaches that the present passage is not to be understood of any mortal sin whatsoever, but of the sin of apostasy, by which the Christian faith and religion, once embraced, is utterly cast off. Which also seemed so to Grotius here. Estius says, however, that the Apostle speaks of this kind of sin as an irreparable fall, not because a place for pardon is not open to a true penitent through the blood of Christ, but to signify that those who sin in this way are hardly ever brought to true repentance. And thus Estius observes that Titelmann, Catharinus, Hassellanus, Arias Montanus, Fr. Rieber, and also Erasmus interpret the passage as concerning the sin of apostasy, as well as Hugo of Saint Victor among the ancients, and indeed even Thomas. Add also Gregory of Valencia, Vasquez, Tirinus, Cornelius à Lapide, Bellarmine, book I de Verbo Dei, chapter XVII, in response to the 5th argument.

But in the Estian explanation we find this lacking, that he takes this sin only as apostasy from the Christian faith, whereas those can also sin ἑκεσίως (willfully) in the aforementioned manner who do not defect from the faith of Christ, whether to Judaism, or to Mahometanism, or Paganism. Although in that part Estius is hardly consistent with himself, inasmuch as he later denies against Calvin, as he thinks, that only the sin of universal apostasy from the Church is designated. Furthermore, that he says those of whom the Apostle treats are hardly ever brought to repentance, when on the contrary the Apostle simply wishes it to be ἀδύνατον (impossible) for such to be renewed to repentance, chapter VI, the cause of which is that such persons utterly repudiate the means through which they might be renewed by the voluntary rejection of the acknowledged truth, the sacrifice of Christ, the blood of the Testament, and the word of truth, and that they trample underfoot the Son of God himself, and do despite to the Spirit of grace; concerning which we have spoken more fully at chapter VI, 4.

Whence it is clear that it is not any apostasy, much less any voluntary sin, but a special apostasy and sin, to which is attributed the name of the sin against the Holy Spirit, and which is said to be simply irremissible, that is treated here: just as is clear from the collation of Matthew XII, 31 and 1 John V, 16 with these passages.

Episcopius, in response to Question LXIV, q. 14, wishes it to be treated not as the sin against the Holy Spirit, but as apostasy from the Gospel, and the dissolute life proceeding therefrom:

And Maresius, on the sin against the Holy Spirit, thesis 12, refers these passages of Hebrews VI and X to all apostates: But the letter contradicts this: For it treats only of those to whom no pardon remains, nor return to repentance, whereas other sins of apostasy from the faith and dissolution of life can obtain remission, except for the sole sin against the Holy Spirit. For to whom no sacrifice is left any longer for sins, how can he have hope of remission? The limitation of Episcopius, unless he renounces the sin, contradicts the text: Because the punishment of hell is inevitably joined with this sin, v. 27, and it is ἀδύνατον to be renewed by it to repentance, Heb. VI, 4.

Crellius and Schlichting, treading in the footsteps of the Novatians, wish for sin not to be understood strictly, or as ἀποστασία, or defection from the Christian religion, or incredulity, or infidelity in general, but broadly, as it extends to various sins which are committed against the precepts of Christ, both because the word for sinning has a general signification, and because the exhortation is broadly open and is and ought to be opposed to all kinds of sin. But if for all those who sin in any way after conversion no sacrifice is left for sins, what hope of pardon will remain for miserable sinners? Whence we have expressly refuted that Novatianism of the Socinians in exeg. Aug. Conf. art. XII. Although the word for sin is indeed general, and a general dissuasion from sins ought to be made, here, however, a danger is proposed, or rather a punishment, which awaits those who sin ἑκουσίως, which kind of sin easily follows if exhortations are neglected or held in contempt: And it is explained by those very Socinians themselves, that to sin voluntarily is to sin with a high hand, Num. XV, 30.31, and thus through contempt of the divine majesty, by which the law is fortified, or through contumacy and pride of spirit. Ἀθετεῖν τὸν νόμον is to despise the word of the Lord and to make his commandment void. Add that the Apostle speaks of those who trample underfoot the Son of God, who treat him with extreme ignominy, such as is that of those who do not fear to trample someone under their feet, who count the blood of the Testament common and profane, who treat the Spirit of grace with contumely and blaspheme: And by force of the comparison Heb. VI, 6. They crucify the Son of God to themselves again, and hold him up to reproach, which things no one would say are spoken of any and all who sin after conversion. What? That Crellius and Schlichting admit that in Heb. VI the discourse is properly about apostasy. Therefore, these things are not to be taken as applying to all sins which are committed by one who is knowing, prudent, and acting with set purpose, and which altogether argue for malice of spirit, nor to any vicious habit, to every custom of sinning, and perseverance in evil, and all grave and enormous crimes committed voluntarily after the reception of the knowledge of the truth, as Crellius and Schlichting contend, who affirm here that there is one reason for voluntary sins admitted before the knowledge of the truth, and another for those which follow it, so that they argue that the sacrifice of Christ was established for the expiation of the former, but that for the expiation of the latter no other victim is to be expected. What, therefore, is to be held concerning this passage? As we have said, it speaks openly of the sin against the Holy Spirit. For the sin which 1. after the reception of the knowledge of the truth, not theoretical but practical, not of bare notice, but of illumination and true conversion (conf. Heb. VI, 4.5.) 2. Ἑκουσίως, with a full and high hand, with a resisting conscience, through contempt of the Divine majesty, out of mere pride and contumacy, is knowingly and prudently committed. 3. Is joined with the extreme contempt and reprobation of the means of salvation. 4. And with the ignominious trampling of the Son of God himself, a new crucifixion, and the profane rejection of his blood and merit, and the shameful ignominy and profanation of the same. 5. Consists in the contumely and contumelious blasphemy of the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of grace, nay, in the malicious denial, hostile impugnation, and persistent and incorrigible blasphemy of the divine truth itself, once known and approved, and thus brings with it both induration, and incorrigibility, and final impenitence. 6. It is simply irremissible, so much so that to be converted from it to repentance is ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνάτων, for which no application of a sacrifice remains, that is nothing other than the sin against the Holy Spirit. Which proposition shines with its own light if all the subject members are taken together. That such is the sin here, which is presently being dealt with, is manifest: And therefore it is invincibly concluded that no other sin is being dealt with here than the sin against the Holy Spirit.

Some take the words οὐκ ἔτι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἀπολείπεται θυσία as referring to the non-repetition of baptism, but beyond the letter of the text. Others, with Chrysostom, as referring to the non-repetition of the crucifixion of Christ, which indeed is truly repeated for no sin, but it is expressly said that Christ is crucified anew by those who commit this sin of which the Apostle speaks: Others as referring to the fact that no other expiatory sacrifice remains, which, even if it be true, since there is no truly expiatory sacrifice other than that one of Christ, yet it does not apply here; since for no sin at all does another sacrifice remain: Others understand a different sacrifice from the former, but of the same Christ, which sense is explained by Estius in such a way that it almost coincides with the interpretation of Chrysostom: If any of us shall have sinned voluntarily after having cast away the knowledge of the truth: Since these, by their apostasy, have thoroughly and altogether frustrated in themselves the sacrifice of Christ once offered, there is no reason for them to expect the sacrifice of Christ to be repeated for their sins, that is, that the Son of God be crucified again, which the gravity and magnitude of their fall, if it were to be repaired, seemed to demand. For Christ dies no more, Romans VI. But rather let them know that a terrible judgment is to be expected by them. But thus it can be applied to every voluntary sin, it is not proper to the sin against the Holy Spirit, although Estius professes that this sin, of which the Apostle speaks, is akin to the sin against the Holy Spirit. Nor does this sense square with the words of the Apostle, THERE REMAINS NO LONGER a sacrifice: For he does not say that the sacrifice or the crucifixion of Christ is not to be repeated, which he has already warned of quite often, that no other than the unique offering of Christ ought to have been made, and that by that one all who are sanctified are perfected: But this is not relevant here, where the discourse is no longer about the expiation of Christ's sacrifice, but about the application of the same through faith; and sanctification and renewal are denied to him who sins ἑκουσίως according to the prescribed manner: nor what the gloss of Estius intends, that such repentance is rare, and forgiveness difficult; (which does not harmonize with that of the same gloss: For what, does Christ indeed rarely, yet sometimes again undergo death? but he says none, and clearly impossible.

Crellius and Schlichtingius pervert it thus: that, since the victim and offering of Christ does not profit them, there remains no longer any [sacrifice] by which their sins can be expiated, because they are not washed away otherwise than if they are utterly renounced by the very effect, and in their place all Christian virtues, and the Spirit, and the fruits of faith are introduced. But are those not for the penitent? But it is ἀδύνατον (impossible) for these to be renewed to repentance. Does the sacrifice of Christ not profit the penitent, who was made a propitiation for all sins, just as the atonement on the great day of atonement profited all the penitent and those looking to Christ by faith for the remission of sins, even those committed ἑκουσίως (willfully)? Why then would the Apostle say ἐκ ἔτι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἀπολείπεται θυσία (there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins). That Crellio-Schlichtingian gloss certainly contradicts the Apostle's assertion entirely: For they say, the Author does not seem to teach in this place that for those who sin willfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth there remains no hope of pardon and salvation in any way, but that it does not remain as long as they do not strip off their vices by their very deeds, nor put on new morals worthy of Christians. But where is that limitation found in the text? Is the expiatory sacrifice, and thus atonement and pardon, not precisely denied to such people? Is there not introduced against them simply ἐνδοχὴ κρίσεως καὶ πυρὸς ζῆλος χωρὶς οἰκτιρμῶν (a fearful expectation of judgment and a zeal of fire without mercies), v. 27, 28? Is their renewal to repentance not said to be impossible? Heb. VI, 5. That they wish to say Paul is speaking of some other victim besides that unique one of Christ is false: He denies that a victim remains for them any longer: He does not, however, imply that ANOTHER victim is not left for them. Which differ greatly. And how those glosses harmonize with the Novatian heresy of the Socinians does not appear. We certainly cannot reconcile them. See just now what was said in the cited place of the Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession expressly.

David Pareus interprets it thus: You ask, why does no sacrifice remain? Because there is no sacrifice for the expiation of sins except the unique one, namely of the High Priest Christ. But apostates reject this. Therefore, no other remains for them. Thus: He who repudiates the sacrifice of Christ through the voluntary denial of the acknowledged truth hopes in vain for another sacrifice for sins. For as Christ dies no more: So neither is He offered again as a sacrifice. But what we might desire in those explanations, we have already indicated. The point here is not for the Apostle to inquire whether there is only one expiatory sacrifice, namely of the High Priest Christ, or whether besides the sacrifice of Christ some other truly expiatory sacrifice is given: Or whether Christ offered Himself only once, or whether He offers Himself more often? Which discussion has already been solidly settled and completed in the preceding Didactic part concerning Christ. Now he is occupied in the exhortation to faith in Christ, or the fiducial apprehension of that unique expiatory sacrifice, by which, having been cast off through voluntary, contumacious, and ignominious rejection out of infidelity, he teaches that no sacrifice remains any longer; that is therefore to be understood not simply concerning the sacrifice of Christ, but as it is applicable, or is applied through faith, that is, that no application of the sacrifice of Christ can be made any longer; it is taught. For those who trample under foot the sacrifice of Christ, and pollute the blood of the Testament by which they were sanctified, and count it profane, and insult the Spirit of grace, who shows that conversion is worked in them through the word and sacraments, and thus that that expiatory sacrifice is applied to them through the ministry of the word for the remission of sins, how could the expiatory sacrifice of Christ be applied to them in turn, how can they apprehend that unique expiatory sacrifice again through faith, which they so traduce, or admit the operation of the Holy Spirit, whom they ἑκουσίως (willfully) and stubbornly blaspheme? Whence it is altogether impossible for such to be renewed to repentance.

What else remains, therefore, when the application of the expiatory sacrifice of Christ no longer remains, except φοβερὰ ἐκδοχὴ κρίσεως (a fearful expectation of judgment), or a terrible expectation of judgment, or a terrible judgment and zeal of fire (the Vulgate wrongly [translates] 'emulation of fire') which is about to consume the adversaries, as the Syrian also rendered it: Which the Papists perversely take concerning purgatorial fire, rashly leaning on the word 'emulation,' that purgatorial fire is an emulation, or a certain representation of that fire which will consume the adversaries. For in the authentic text, 'zeal of fire' designates the fervor and ardor of that fire which is unquenchable, and which consumes utterly τοὺς ὑπεναντίους (the adversaries), nor is it threatened to the faithful not yet fully expiated, but still having the punishment of purgatorial fire for forgiven guilt (which are Papist inventions entirely unknown to Scripture, nay, entirely contrary to it), but to sinners against the Holy Spirit, who are adversaries ἐξοχικῶς (preeminently) of God, Christ, and the Holy Spirit, whom a horrible judgment certainly awaits, not those who are one day to be admitted into celestial joy. Add that the name ζῆλος (zeal) never denotes a likeness or representation, which Erasmus himself explained concerning the vehemence of fire: Concerning fire, which consumes not sins, but sinners, not by purging, but by devouring: yet so that it is never satisfied, never ceases to consume, never is extinguished, since this judgment is eternal, an ἄσβεστος (unquenchable) fire. In which the Greek Interpreters note an emphasis in the words ἐσθίειν μέλλοντος (about to devour), because the Apostle has as it were animated the fire, and attributed life and strength to it, because it apprehends and devours enemies like an irritated wild beast: Which is the observation of Hentenius and Estius, so that there is in the words of the Apostle a certain Prosopopoeia with a latent Hebraism. For he is said to be zealous among the Hebrews who is moved by grief and a just desire for vengeance for the good against the bad. Examples are frequent in the scriptures. Whence also God is called jealous (Exod. XX and XXIV). Thus, therefore, the Apostle fashions the fire as if it were zealous for the glory of God, and as if grieving and avenging His injuries. Elsewhere, however, we read the opposite, the fire of divine zeal, as in Ezech. XXXVI. & Zeph. 1.3. as Estius here; who acknowledges that this explanation concerning the fire of Gehenna seems more accommodated to the phrase of Scripture than that concerning the fire of purgatory, and finally that it is supported by the mention of judgment, which in ch. 5 is called eternal, and by the threat of combustion, which awaits the reprobate. To which corresponds in the parallel passage Heb. 6.8, a curse and combustion, which does not happen through some representation or likeness of fire, but through the fire itself. It is the fervor of fire, by Hebraism a most fervent fire, which he says will devour the adversaries, not that they are to be utterly consumed by fire (as to substance), so that they might at length cease to feel torments: But it is a metaphor taken from a fire raging in a horrible manner, into which those falling are tortured with horrible torments. Because he does not say, a horrible judgment of God awaits them, but a certain horrible expectation of judgment, this, as Pareus warns, has a tacit objection: Lest they dare to trifle, that this judgment is for a day, to be late or never, as scoffers are wont to do, he says: Daily with a horrible expectation, that is, that they are inwardly horribly tortured by the trepidation and fear of the future judgment, and are tormented by the stings of an evil conscience, although outwardly they feign hope with their countenance. This expectation of judgment of the impious is opposed to the peace and tranquility of conscience of the pious, by which, justified by faith, and certain of the forgiveness of sins and of a reconciled God, they peacefully enjoy themselves.

Latin:

Vers. 26. 27.

Ἑκουσίως γὰρ ἁμαρτανόντων ἡμῶν μετὰ τὸ λαβεῖν τὴν ἐπίγνω- σιν τῆς ἀληθείας, οὐκ ἔτι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἀπολείπεται θυσία. Φο- βερὰ δέ τις ἐκδοχὴ κρίσεως καὶ πυρὸς ζῆλος, ἐσθίειν μέλλοντος τοὺς ὑπεναντίους.] Citat hunc locum Clemens Alexandrinus Strom. II. ut probet post baptismum unam tantum pœni- tentiam admitti, aitque, αἱ δὲ συνεχεῖς καὶ ἐπάλληλοι ἐπὶ τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασι μετάνοιαι οὐδὲν τῶν καθάπαξ μὴ πεπιστευκό- των διαφέρουσιν, ἢ μόνῳ τῷ συναισθέσθαι ὅτι ἁμαρτάνουσι. Καὶ οὐκ οἶδ' ὁπότερον αὐτοῖς χεῖρον, ἢ τὸ εἰδότα ἁμαρτάνειν, ἢ μετανοήσαντα ἐφ' οἷς ἥμαρτεν, πλημμελεῖν αὖθις. Non dispari sensu hunc locum producit Theodoretius Libr. XII. contra Græcos. Quæ utiliter dici ad homines absterren- dos ab iteratione criminum & disciplinæ veteris Eccle- siæ satis congruere agnosco. Cæterum quæ hic ante- cedunt de proffessione retinenda, me eo ducunt, ut hæc eodem modo interpreter, quomodo ea, quæ supra ha- buimus VI, 4. & ἁμαρτάνειν accipiam pro rejicere Chri- stianismum, sicut ἁμαρτήσαντες dicuntur supra III, 17. ii, qui legem rejiciebant, ut 2. Petr. II, 4. Angeli defectores. Additum autem ἑκουσίως, quia tales ignorantiam culpæ suæ obtendere nequeunt. Illi autem, qui sic à Chri- stianismo deficiunt, & Christi sanguinem pro profano sanguine habent, ut mox dicitur, per nullas victimas alias ad bonam frugem revocabuntur, ut veniam conse- qui possint. Λαβεῖν ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας idem quod φω- τισθῆναι supra VI, 4. Ἐπίγνωσις non est qualiscunque, sed experimentalis quædam cognitio. Vide Ephes. I, 17. IV, 13. Phil. I, 9, Coloss. I, 10. II, 2. III, 10. 1. Timoth. II, 4. 2. Tim. II, 25. III, 7. Tit. I, 1. Philem. v. 6. Ἐκδοχὴ κρίσεως loquutione Ebræa judicium expectandum. Pœna eo manet horribilis. Πυρὸς ζῆλος est ira Dei, per ignem se exerens. Vice versa πῦρ ζήλες dixit Ezech. XXXVI, 3. So- phon. I, 10. III, 8. Sic dicimus pro eodem φλὸξ πυρός &

πῦρ φλογὸς. Ignis dicitur comedere אכל, ut Esa. XXX, 27. Jerem. V, 14. & alibi. Τὲς ὑπεναντίες nempe DEI, ut Esa. LIX, 18. Nahum. I, 2. Respici videtur historia, quæ est Num. XVI, 35. Levit. X, 2. - Ex iis, qui de lapsis post baptismum intelligunt, etiam Augustinus est in inchoat. exposit. epist. ad Rom. qui vero de non iterando baptismo locum explicat. Significat Apostolus, non posse deinceps eum, qui peccaverit, iterum baptizando purgari. Sed nec de quibusvis post baptismum prolapsis, nec de denegatione purgationis per baptismum hic agitur, sed de non relicta hostia. Nuspiam autem baptismus hostia vocatur.

Novatiani ta- libus prolapsis post baptismum pœnitentiam de- negabant vi hujus loci: Quem nodum cum sol- vere non potuerint, scindere ausi sunt, qui inde præsenti Epistolæ ad Ebræos autoritatem Canoni- cam denegarunt. At nimis manifestum est, non agi de quibusvis in peccata etsi graviora post baptismum prolapsis, si plene eorum descriptio hic & Cap. VI. in loco parallelo exhibita perpen- datur, quibus reditus ad pœnitentiam & hostiam pro peccato derogatur.

Estius itaque non de quo- cunque peccato mortifero præsentem locum ac- cipiendum esse docet, sed de peccato apostasiæ, qua fides & religio Christiana semel suscepta prorsus abjicitur. Quod hic etiam Grotio visum. Loqui autem Apostolum Estius ait de hujusmodi peccato de lapsu irreparabili, non quia vere pœnitenti non pateat locus veniæ per sanguinem Christi, sed ut significet, eos, qui hoc modo peccant, vix unquam ad veram pœnitentiam adduci. Atque ita de pec- cato apostasiæ etiam interpretari locum Titelman- num, Catharinum, Hassellanum, Ariasmontanum, Fr. Rieberam, nec non Erasmum observat Estius, Hugonem etiam Victorinum è Veteribus, imo & Thomam. Adde & Gregorium de Valentia, Vas- quezium, Tirinum, Cornelium à Lapide, Bellarmi- num libr. I. de Verbo Dei cap. XVII. resp. ad V. argum.

Sed in explicatione Estiana id desidera- mus, quod solum de apostasia à fide Christiana hoc peccatum accipiat, quum ἑκεσίως ad prædi- ctum modum peccare etiam possint, qui non de- ficiunt à fide Christi sive ad Judaismum, sive ad Ma- hometanismum aut Paganismum. Quanquam ea in parte vix sibi constet Estius, utpote qui postea negat contra Calvinum, ut putat solum apostasiæ universalis ab Ecclesia peccatum designari. De- inde quod dicat, vix unquam eos, de quibus agit Apostolus, ad pœnitentiam adduci, quum ex ad- verso Apostolus simpliciter id ἀδύνατον esse velit, tales renovari ad pœnitentiam, cap. VI. cujus cau- sa est, quod tales media, per quæ renovari queant, prorsus repudient per voluntariam agnitæ verita- tis agnitionem hostiam Christi, sanguinem Testa- menti & verbum veritatis, quodque ipsummet Fi- lium Dei conculcent, & Spiritui gratiæ contume- liam faciant; quo de plenius ad cap. VI, 4. diximus.

Unde liquet, non de quavis apostasia, ne dum de quovis voluntario peccato, sed de apostasia & peccato speciali, cui tribuitur nomen peccati in Spiritum san- ctum, quodque simpliciter irremissibile dicitur, hic agi: quemadmodum è collatione Matth. XII, 31. 1. Joh. V, 16. cum hisce locis liquet.

Episcopius resp. ad Quæst. LXIV. q. 14. non de peccato in Spiritum sanctum, sed de apostasia ab Evangelio, & inde profecta dissoluta vita agi vult:

Et Maresius de peccat. in Spiritum sanctum th. 12. ad omnes apostatas loca hæc Ebr. VI. & X. refert: Sed repugnat litera: Nam de illis tantum, quibus venia non restat, nec reditus ad pœnitentiam, agi- tur, at alia peccata apostasiæ à fide & dissolu- vitæ remissionem consequi possunt, excepto s- lo peccato in Spiritum sanctum. Cui enim nu la amplius hostia relicta est pro peccatis, quome do is spem habere potest remissionis? Limitati Episcopii, nisi peccatum abdicet, contrariatur tex tui: Quia pœna inferni inevitabilis conjuncta e cum hoc peccato v. 27. & ab eo renovari ad pœ nitentiam ἀδύνατον est, Ebr. VI, 4.

Crellius & Schlichtingius Novatianorum calcan tes vestigia non peccatum stricte sive ἀποστασία vel defectionis à Christiana religione vel incredu- litatis sive infidelitatis, in genere, sed late intelligi volunt, prout extenditur ad varia peccata, quæ committuntur adversus Christi præcepta, tum quia vox peccandi generalem significationem ha- bet, tum quia adhortatio late patet, & omnibus peccati generibus opponi solet & debet. Sed si illis omnibus, qui quomodocunque peccant, post conversionem nulla relinquitur hostia pro pecca- tis, quænam spes veniæ remanebit miseris pecca- toribus? Unde Novatianismum illum Sociniano- rum ex professo profligavimus in exeg. Aug. Conf. art. XII. Etsi vero vox peccati generalis sit, & ge- neralis dehortatio à peccatis fieri debeat, hic ta- men periculum proponitur, vel potius supplicium, quod ἑκουσίως peccantes manet, cujusmodi pec- catum facile sequitur, si adhortationes negligan- tur, vel contemptui habeantur: Et explicatur ab ipsis illis Socinianis, quod voluntarie peccare sit elata manu peccare, Num. XV, 30.31. atque adeo per contemptum divinæ majestatis, qua lex com- munita est, seu per animi contumaciam & super- biam. Ἀθετεῖν τὸν νόμον est spernere verbum Domini, & mandatum illius irritum facere. Adde quod Apostolus de iis loquatur, qui Filium Dei concul- cant, extrema ignominia afficiunt, qualis est eo- rum, qui aliquem pedibus conculcare non veren- tur, qui sanguinem Testamenti communem & pro- fanum ducunt, qui Spiritum gratiæ contumelia afficiunt & blasphemant: Et vi collationis Ebr. VI, 6. Filium Dei sibimetipsis iterum crucifigunt, ac pro opprobrio habent, quæ omnia de quibusvis etsi post conversionem peccantibus & peccatis di- ci, nemo dixerit. Quid? quod fateantur Crellius & Schlichtingius Ebr. VI. de apostasia proprie ser- monem esse. Non ergo de omnibus peccatis, quæ à sciente, prudente ac dedita opera committuntur, ac malitiam animi omnino arguunt, non de quo- vis vitioso habitu, de omni peccandi consuetudine, inque malo perseverantia, omnibusque gravibus ac enormibus sceleribus voluntarie post acceptam veritatis notitiam commissis, quemadmodum Crellius & Schlichtingius contendunt, hæc acci- pienda, qui hic aliam esse rationem peccatorum voluntariorum ante veritatis notitiam admisso- rum, aliam eorum, quæ hanc sequuntur, affir- mant, ut illorum quidem expiandorum causa sa- crificium Christi esse constitutum, his vero expian- dis nullam aliam expectandam esse victimam di- micent. Quid ergo de hoc loco habendum? De peccato in Spiritum sanctum, ut diximus, is aperte loquitur. Nam quod peccatum 1. post acceptam veritatis cognitionem non theoreticam, sed practi- cam, non nudæ notitiæ, sed illuminationis & conversionis veræ (conf. Ebr. VI,4.5.) 2. Ἑκουσίως plena & elata manu, reluctante conscientia per contemptum Divinæ majestatis, ex mera superbia atque contumacia scienter ac prudenter committi- tur. 3. Conjunctum est cum mediorum salutis extremo contemptu ac reprobatione. 4. Ipsiusque Filii Dei ignominiosa conculcatione, nova cru- cifixione, ac sanguinis & meriti ejus profana re- jectione, & probrosa ejusdem ignominia, & pro- fanatione. 5. Spiritus sancti, qui Spiritus gra- tiæ est, contumelia & contumeliosa blasphematio- ne, imo in ipsa veritatis divinæ cognitæ & appro- batæ malitiosa abnegatione, hostili impugnatione, & pertinaci atque incorrigibili blasphematione consistit, adeoque tum indurationem, tum incor- rigibilitatem, tum finalem impænitentiam secum trahit. 6. Simpliciter irremissibile est, adeo, ut ab eo ad pœnitentiam converti sit ἐκ τῶν ἀδυνά- των, pro quo nulla superest hostiæ applicatio, id nullum aliud est, nisi peccatum in Spiritum san- ctum. Quæ propositio luce sua radiat, si omnia membra subjecta conjunctim accipiantur. Tale autem hic esse peccatum, de quo in præsenti agi- tur, manifestum est: Ideoque invicte concludi- tur, de nullo alio, quam de peccato in Spiritum sanctum hic agi.

Verba οὐκ ἔτι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἀπολείπεται θυσία nonnulli de non iterando baptismo accipiunt, sed citra literam textus. Alii de non iteranda cruci- fixione Christi cum Chrysostomo, quæ utique ob nullum peccatum iteratur vere, sed ab his, qui hoc peccatum, de quo Apostoli sermo, committunt, de novo crucifigi Christum diserte dicitur: Alii de non restante alia hostia expiatoria, quod etsi ve- rum sit, quum non nisi unica illa Christi hostia vere expiatoria sit, huc tamen non facit; siquidem nulli omnino peccato alia hostia restat: Alii aliam quidem hostiam intelligunt à priori, sed ejusdem Christi, qui sensus ab Estio sic explicatur, ut eum Chrysostomi interpretatione fere coincidat: Si qui nostrum voluntarie peccaverint abjecta veritatis notitia: Hi quoniam Christi hostiam semel oblatam sua apostasia penitus & omnino in se frustraverunt, non est, quod expectent hostiam Christi pro suis peccatis iterandam, id est, ut iterum crucifigatur Filius DEI, quod gravitas & magnitudo lapsus eorum, si reparandus sit, videbatur exposcere. Non enim amplius moritur Christus, Roman. VI. Quin potius sciant, expectandum sibi esse terribile judicium. Sed sic applicari potest omni peccato voluntario, non est proprium peccato in Spiritum sanctum, quum tamen Estius profiteatur, hoc pec- catum, de quo Apostolus, affine esse peccato in Spiritum sanctum. Neque hic sensus quadrat verbis Apostoli, NON AMPLIUS relinquitur hostia: Non enim ait, non iterandam hostiam, vel crucifixionem Christi, quod sæpius jam monuit, non nisi unicam Christi oblationem fieri debuisse, eaque unica omnes consummari, qui sanctifican- tur: Sed huc non facit, ubi non amplius de hostiæ Christi expiatione, sed ejusdem per fidem applica- tione sermo est; ac sanctificatio, & renovatio dene- gatur illi, qui juxta præscriptum modum ἑκουσίως peccat: neque quod glossa Estii vult, raram esse ta- lem pænitentiam, ac difficilem veniam; (quod non consonat illi ejusdem glossæ: Quid enim, an raro quidem, aliquando tamen iterum mortem subit Christus? sed nullam dicit, atque plane impossi- bilem.

Crellius & Schlichtingius sic pervertunt: quod, cum Christi victima & oblatio illis non profit, nulla amplius restet, qua peccata ipsorum expiari possint, quia non aliter eluantur, quam si effectu ipso penitus abdicentur, eorumque loco Christiana virtutes omnes, ac Spiritus, fideique fructus inducantur. At annon illa poenitentium sunt? Hos vero ἀδύνατον est renovari ad poenitentiam. Annon poeniten- tibus prodest hostia Christi, qui factus est propi- tiatio pro omnibus peccatis, quemadmodum omnibus poenitentibus, & fide Christum respi- cientibus expiatio in die magnae expiationis pro- derat ad remissionem peccatorum, etsi ἑκουσίως commissorum? Qui ergo diceret Apostolus ἐκ ἔτι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἀπολείπεται θυσία. Glossa certe illa Crellio-Schlichtingiana prorsus contrariatur asser- tioni Apostolicae: Neque enim, inquiunt, in hoc loco docere videtur Autor, quod voluntarie post acceptam veritatis notitiam peccantibus nulla omni- no ratione spes veniae salutisque supersit, sed quod non supersit, quamdiu vitia opere ipso non exuunt, nec mores novos Christianis dignos induunt. Ubi vero illa limitatio in textu habetur? Annon prae- cise talibus denegatur hostia expiatoria, adeoque expiatio & venia? Annon inducitur contra ipsis simpliciter ἐνδοχὴ κρίσεως καὶ πυρὸς ζῆλος χωρὶς οἰκτιρμῶν, v. 27. 28. Annon impossibilis dicitur eorum ad poenitentiam renovatio? Ebr. VI, 5. Pau- lum de alia aliqua praeter illam Christi unicam vi- ctimam loqui, quod illi volunt, falsum est: Am- plius illis victimam superesse negat: Non autem innuit, ALIAM victimam non reliquam ipsis esse. Quae maxime differunt. Et quomodo illae glossae consonent Novatianae haeresi Socinianorum, non apparet. Nos certe conciliare non possumus. Vid. modo, quae dicta sunt loco citato Exeg. Aug. Conf. ex professo.

David Pareus sic interpretatur: Quaeris, cur nulla supersit hostia? Quia non est nisi unica hostia peccatorum expiatrix, nempe Pontificis Christi. Hanc vero abjiciunt Apostatae. Nulla igitur alia eis est reliqua. Sic: Qui Christi sacrificium per vo- luntariam agnitae veritatis abnegationem repu- diat, frustra aliud pro peccatis sacrificium sperat. Christus enim ut non amplius moritur: Ita nec de- nuo in sacrificium offertur. Sed quid in illis ex- plicationibus desideremus, jam indicavimus. Non hic in eo est, ut disquirat Apostolus, anne unica tantum sit hostia expiatoria, Christi nempe Pon- tificis, an vero praeter Christi hostiam alia quaedam vere expiatoria hostia detur: Aut anne semel tan- tum se obtulerit Christus, an vero saepius se offe- rat? Quae tractatio solide expedita & absoluta jam est in praecedenti parte Didactica de Christo. Jam in paraenesi ad fidem in Christum, vel fiducialem apprehensionem unicae illius hostiae expiatoriae occupatur, qua per voluntariam, contumacem & ignominiosam reprobationem ex infidelitate ab- jecta, nullam superesse amplius docet hostiam; id ergo de hostia Christi non simpliciter, sed qua ap- plicabilis est, vel applicatur per fidem intelligen- dum, hoc est, nullam amplius fieri posse hostiae Christi applicationem; docetur. Qui enim pe- dibus conculcant Christi hostiam, & sanguinem Testamenti, quo sanctificati sunt, polluunt & profanum ducunt, & contumelia afficiunt Spiri- tum gratiae, qui per verbum & sacramenta conver- sionem in ipsis operari, adeoque hostiam illam ex- piatoriam ipsis per verbi ministerium ad remissio- nem peccatorum applicari ostendit, quomodo posset illis hostia Christi expiatoria vicissim appli- cari, quomodo possunt illi hostiam illam unicam expiatoriam denuo per fidem apprehendere, quam ita traducunt, aut Spiritus sancti operatio- nem admittere, quem ἑκουσίως & praefracte blas- phemant? Unde impossibile omnino est, tales re- novari ad poenitentiam.

Quid ergo restat aliud, quum non amplius su- persit hostiæ Christi expiatoriæ applicatio, nisi φοβερὰ ἐκδοχὴ κρίσεως terribilis seu formidabilis ex- pectatio judicii, seu terribile judicium & zelus ignis (Vulgata perperam ignis æmulatio) qui consum- pturus est adversarios, ut etiam Syrus reddidit: Quod de igne purgatorio perverse accipiunt Pa- pistæ, temere innitentes voci æmulationis, quod ignis purgatorius sit æmulatio, seu repræsentatio quædam illius ignis, qui consumet adversarios. In textu enim authentico zelus ignis fervorem & ar- dorem ejus ignis, qui inextinguibilis est, quiq; con- sumit penitus τοὺς ὑπεναντίους, designatur, nec ille fidelibus nondum plane expiatis, sed adhuc dimissa culpa pœnam ignis purgatorii (quæ commenta Pa- pistica Scripturæ penitus ignota, imo prorsus con- traria sunt) indicitur, sed peccatoribus in Spiritum sanctum, qui adversarii sunt ἐξοχικῶς Dei, Christi, & Spiritus sancti, quos certe manet horribile ju- dicium, non qui admittendi olim sunt in cœleste gaudium. Adde quod nomen ζῆλος nunquam similitudinem vel repræsentationem notet, quod de ignis vehementia Erasmus ipse exposuit: De igne, qui consumit non peccata, sed peccatores non purgando, sed devorando: ita tamen, ut nunquam satietur, nunquam consumere desistat, nunquam extinguatur, quum judicium hoc æternum, ignis ἄσβεστος sit. In quo Græci Interpretes emphasin notant in verbis ἐσθίειν μέλλοντος, quod Apostolus ignem veluti animaverit, vitamque & vires ei tri- buerit, quod instar irritatæ feræ apprehendat & de- voret inimicos: Quæ Hentenii & Estii est observa- tio, ut sit in verbis Apostoli Prosopopœia quædam cum Ebraismo latente. Nam Ebræis zelare dicitur, qui dolore & justa ultionis desiderio commovetur pro bonis adversus malos. Exempla frequentia sunt in scripturis. Unde & Deus zelotes vocatur Exod. XX. & XXIV. Sic igitur ignem veluti fingit Apostolus zelantem pro gloria Dei, & quasi dolentem ac vindicantem ejus injurias. Alibi vero è con- verso legimus ignem zeli divini, ut Ezech. XXXVI. & Sophon. I. 3. ut hic Estius; qui hanc explicatio- nem de igne gehennæ ad Scripturæ phrasin magis vi- deri accommodatam, quam illam de igne purgatorii agnoscit, eam deniq; adjuvari mentionem judicii, quod c. 5. æternum vocatur, & comminatione com- bustionis, quæ reprobos maneat. Cui respondet in loco parallelo Ebr. VI, 8. maledictio & combu- stio, quæ non fit per repræsentationem aliquam sive similitudinem ignis, sed per ipsum ignem. Fer- vor ignis est, per Ebraismum ignis ferventissimus, quem dicit devoraturum adversarios, non quod igne penitus sint (quod ad substantiam) absumendi, ut tandem cruciatus sentire cessent: Sed meta- phora desumpta ab incendio horrendum in mo- dum sæviente, in quod incidentes horribilibus cruciatibus torquentur. Quod non dicit, manet eos horrendum Dei judicium, sed horribilis quædam & expectatio judicii, id, monente Pareo, tacitam oc- cupationem habet: Ne ludere ausint, in diem esse hoc judicium, sero vel nunquam futurum, ut solent ἐμπαῖκται, dicit: Indies expectatione horrenda, hoc est, trepidatione & metu judicii futuri eos intus hor- ribiliter torqueri, & stimulis male conscientiæ cru- ciari, licet foris spem vultu simulent. Hæc impiorum expectatio judicii opposita est piorum paci & tran- quillitati conscientiæ, qua justificati fide, deque venia peccatorum, & Deo placato certo confisi placide per- fruuntur.

## 10:28
Verse 28.

But anyone who has set aside the law of Moses.] To set aside here is to violate law, as in Ezekiel 22:26 and elsewhere. Understand this, however, concerning crimes for which the penalty of death was established in the law. Χωρὶς οἰκτιρμῶν.] Punishment is inevitable, as we have brought forward elsewhere from Josephus. Neither the King nor the Senate had the power of pardoning. Ἐπὶ δυσὶν ἢ τρίσι μάρτυσιν.] That is, if the matter comes to the cognizance of the Judges, Deut. 17:6. But no one escapes the cognizance of God. Ἀποθνήσκει.] By the sword, stoning, strangulation, or fire.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

Ἀθετήσας δὲ τίς νόμον Μωϋσέως.] Ἀθετεῖν hic est violare legem, ut Ezechiel. XXII, 26. & alibi. Intellige autem hoc de criminibus, quibus mortis poena in lege con- stituta est. Χωρὶς οἰκτιρμῶν.] Ἀπαραίτητος ἡ κόλασις, ut ex Josepho alibi attulimus. Neque Rex neque Senatus ignoscendi ha- bebant potestatem. Ἐπὶ δυσὶν ἢ τρίσι μάρτυσιν.] Id est, si res ad cognitionem Judicum perveniat Deut. XVII, 6. Dei autem cognitionem nemo effugit. Ἀποθνήσκει.] Gladio, lapidatione, strangulatione aut igne.

## 10:29
Ver. 29.

How much worse punishment do you think he will be deemed worthy of? For the crime is both graver, as he will now say, and God holds the punishments in His own hand, to which no human power can reach. And that word δοκεῖτε is elegantly interjected. What do you yourselves think about that matter? Just as ἄξιος, so the word ἀξίοις is a middle term, and refers as much to punishments as to rewards.

This is not to be understood concerning the violation or petulant transgression of the law, but rather concerning apostasy from the law, by which one thoroughly repudiates and casts off the law, departing through apostasy from the law and religion toward the worship of foreign Gods, or declining into idolatry; since the word ἀθετεῖν is not simply to transgress, but to make void, to cast off, to repudiate, Galatians 2:21. And the Apostle is treating of apostasy conjoined with the sin against the Holy Spirit, and the passage Deut. 17:3 is being looked to, where it is decreed concerning those who fall away to foreign Gods, concerning whom it is ordained in verse 6 that they be cut off at the mouth of two or three witnesses; as also to Deut. 13:8, where it concerns the penalty to be inflicted without mercy upon seducers, whose sin is undoubtedly graver than the sin against the Holy Spirit. If the penalty of death was justly inflicted upon apostates in the Jewish religion, and likewise upon seducers, when will he be judged worthy of a graver punishment who has trampled the Son of God underfoot and treated the Spirit of grace with contumely?

Ὁ τὸν Υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ καταπατήσας.] Trampling as useless, בעט, 1 Sam. 2:29.

He who repudiates the Son of God offered in word and sacraments, treats Him with ignominy, and perversely contemns Him, whether regarding His person, or His office, or both, and that ἑκουσίως (voluntarily), which is to be repeated from the common context. For to trample someone underfoot is a sign of extreme contempt, or to trample as useless, as Grotius says. Just as we trample underfoot things which we detest and consider most vile, and, as Ambrose says, weigh as of no moment: so those who sin voluntarily without fear and without repentance consider Christ of no value, nor do they fear Him as the future Judge. Trampling also occurs with arrogance and pride. Just as it was answered to Socrates, who was trampling on the rugs of Diogenes and saying that he was trampling on the pride of Diogenes, that he was doing so with greater pride.

Καὶ τὸ αἷμα τῆς διαθήκης κοινὸν ἡγησάμενος.] That blood in which the covenant was sanctioned, holding it for profane blood: pronouncing Christ worthy of death, as if He had abused the name of God. This is what was said above in 6:6, to crucify again and to defame. Ἐν ᾧ ἡγιάσθη.] This aorist is put for the pluperfect: By which blood they themselves had been purged from vices and made holy.

Κοινὸν ἡγησάμενος, he considers common, that is, he holds it in no other place than the blood of an unclean animal, and that not only in external appearance, as Tofsanus perverts it, but in the truth of the matter. The phrase is of the law, says Pareus, to consider common, for to hold as not sacred, but profane and impure, as can be seen in Acts 15:15. Apostates do this while they estimate the blood of Christ shed on the cross for our redemption as if it were the blood of a common man, or indeed of some thief: and they distinguish the blood of Christ in nothing from the blood of the two thieves crucified together with Him: whereas it is the blood of the Testament, by which indeed the Testator, the Son of God, made valid and sealed the new testament, as he taught in Chapter 9. What he adds, by which they had been sanctified, exaggerates the crime (so Pareus continues) from ingratitude, because apostates exchange the sanctification they obtained through the blood of Christ with most shameful impurity. Not bad. But the things added by Pareus do not fit. The sanctification of the apostates, he says, was not internal but external, consisting in the profession of faith and the external participation of the sacraments. They were sanctified, that is, separated from Jews and Pagans by profession, and held as true Christians. For what? Are those truly apostates from the faith who never truly believed? Are those only sanctified by external sanctification who were truly enlightened, who tasted the heavenly gift, who were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, who tasted and perceived how good the word of GOD is, who tasted and perceived the mighty works of the age to come, which is said of them in Heb. 6:4, 5?

Καὶ τὸ Πνεῦμα τῆς χάριτος ἐνυβρίσας.] Treating with contumely that Spirit whom they had received by the highest benefit of God: estimating as of no value such a gift, by which he himself is deprived. You see here also that those who had received the Spirit, which was not given except to the justified, can become deserters. See 1 Thess. 5:19.

Which Grotius rightly notes against the Calvinists and Anabaptists, and which is to be duly noted. For it provides an invincible argument against the apostasy of the saints, which Pareus perverts, and the claim that we, by denying the πληροφορίαν of perseverance, are imprudently reverting to the ἐποχὴν of the Papists, is an impudent calumny. For we do not deny the certainty of perseverance, except for the absolute kind, which the Calvinists deduce from an absolute decree; but we do not deny the hypothetical kind, which includes the condition of prayers and the means of salvation and the avoidance of sins against conscience. And therefore we have no commerce with the Papistical ἐποχῇ, which is a mere fluctuation and uncertainty not only concerning perseverance, but even concerning present grace; which, however, the Calvinists incur no less, since they can be certain of their absolute election neither a priori nor a posteriori, but must necessarily conclude with Piscator: God wills that some be saved, Christ redeemed some, therefore it is possible that I also am in their number. But the absolute certainty which they pretend is only a phantom of opinion, and not a faith arising from the word of divine promise, unless perhaps they prefer to betake themselves to immediate revelation with the Enthusiasts and fanatics.

The Spirit of grace, although grace is given by God, is not so called by reason of origin, because it is conferred by the benefit of God, but by reason of causality, because it exhibits grace and supplies the gifts of grace, just as it is also called the Spirit of prayers because it is the Author of prayers, Zech. 12:10. For the conferring of grace and the sealing of the same, as well as the communication of the gifts of grace, is attributed peculiarly to the Holy Spirit, by virtue of the third article, 2 Cor. 13:14. Ἐνυβρίσας means to treat with contumely and to blaspheme, whence the blasphemy of the Spirit is spoken of, Matt. 12:31. That contumely, therefore, is joined with blasphemy. Concerning which supreme ingratitude Theophylact says: He made the Son of God, but you, indeed, are subject to the slavery of vices: He had come to stay with you, but you, for his sake, admitted the devil. This, therefore, is to offer an injury to the grace of the Spirit. The Holy Spirit is also affected by insult in the ministry of the word, which is the ministry of the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:8), when it is wantonly despised, and the means of salvation, through which the Holy Spirit wishes to work, the word and the Sacraments, are rejected and treated with blasphemy, inasmuch as it redounds upon the Holy Spirit himself.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

Πόσῳ δοκεῖτε χείρονος ἀξιωθήσεται τιμωρίας.] Nam & crimen est gravius, ut jam dicet, & Deus in sua manu poe- nas habet, ad quas nulla potentia humana potest pertinge- re. Et eleganter interjicitur illud δοκεῖτε. Quid ipsi puta- tis ea de re? Sicut ἄξιος, ita ἀξίοις vox est media, & tam ad poenas quam ad praemia refertur.

Non de violatione vel transgressione legis pe- tulanti, sed potius de apostasia a lege hoc intelli- gendum, qua penitus quis legem repudiat, & ab- jicit, per apostasiam a lege & religione discedens ad cultum alienorum Deorum, sive idololatriam declinando; siquidem verbum ἀθετεῖν non sit sim- pliciter transgredi, sed irritum facere, abjicere, re- pudiare, Galat. II, 21. & de apostasia cum peccato in Spiritum sanctum conjuncta tractet Apostolus, atque respiciatur locus Deut. XVII, 3. ubi de iis, qui deficiunt ad Deos alienos, de quibus vers. 6. sanci- tum est, ut in ore duorum aut trium testium ex- scindatur; ut & ad Deut. XIII, 8. ubi de poena se- ductoribus absque misericordia infligenda, quo- rum peccatis gravius proculdubio est peccatum in Spiritum sanctum. Si Apostatis in religione Ju- daica supplicium mortis juste irrogabatur, nec non seductoribus, quando graviori dignus ju- dicabitur supplicio, qui Filium Dei pedibus conculcaverit, Spiritum gratiae contumelia affe cerit?

Ὁ τὸν Υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ καταπατήσας.] Proculcans tanquam inutilem בעט, 1. Sam. II, 29.

Qui Filium Dei in verbo & sacramentis obla- tum repudiat, ignominia afficit, proterve con- temnit sive quoad personam, sive quoad officium, seu quoad utrumque, idque ἑκουσίως, quod ἀπὸ κοινοῦ repetendum. Nam pedibus aliquem con- culcare, est extremi contemptus indicium, vel proculcare tanquam inutilem, ut Grotius. Sic- ut pedibus conculcamus, quae detestamur & vi- lissima ducimus, nullius, ut Ambrosius ait, mo- menti pendimus: Sic qui voluntarie peccant abs- que timore & absque poenitentia, Christum nul- lius pretii existimant, nec eum Judicem futurum formidant. Fit etiam conculcatio cum fastu & superbia. Sicut Socrati, calcanti stragula Dio- genis & dicenti, se conculcare fastum Diogenis; respondebatur, sed majore fastu.

Καὶ τὸ αἷμα τῆς διαθήκης κοινὸν ἡγησάμενος.] Sanguinem illum, in quo sancitum est foedus, habens pro sanguine pro- fano: morte dignum Christum pronuntians, tanquam Dei nomine abusum. Hoc est, quod supra VI, 6. dictum est, ite- rum crucifigere & infamare. Ἐν ᾧ ἡγιάσθη.] Aoristus hic pro plusquamperfecto poni- tur: Per quem sanguinem ipsi a vitiis purgati, sanctique facti fuerant.

Κοινὸν ἡγησάμενος, communem ducit, id est, non alio loco habet, quam sanguinem immundi anima- lis, idque non ad externam tantum speciem, ut Tof- sanus pervertit, sed in rei veritate. Phrasis est legis, inquit, Pareus, communem ducere, pro, non sacrum, sed profanum, impurum habere, ut videre est Actor. XV, 15. Id faciunt Apostatae, dum sanguinem Christi in cruce pro nostri redemptione fusum, quasi com- munis hominis, imo quasi latronis alicujus sangui- nem æstimant: nihilque Christi sanguinem à sangui- ne duorum latronum una crucifixorum dissiernunt: cum sit sanguis Testamenti, quo nempe Testator Filius Dei testamentum novum ratum fecit & obsignavit, ut docuit Cap. IX. Quod addit, quo fuerant sancti- ficati, crimen, (ita pergit Pareus) ab ingratitudine exaggerat, quod apostatæ sanctificationem per san- guinem Christi assequuti cum turpissima impuritate eam commutent. Non male. Sed quæ adduntur à Pareo, haud congruunt. Erat autem, inquit, san- ctificatio Apostatarum non interna sed externa in professiione fidei & participatione sacramentorum externa consistens. Erant sanctificati, hoc est, à Ju- dæis & Paganis professione segregati, & pro veris Christianis habiti. Quid enim? An illi vere A- postatæ sunt à fide, qui nunquam vere crediderunt? An illi tantum externa sanctificatione sanctificati, qui vere illuminati, qui gustaverunt donum cœle- ste, qui participes facti Spiritus sancti, qui gustarunt ac perceperunt, quam bonum sit DEI verbum, qui gustarunt ac perceperunt virtu- tes seculi venturi, quod de ipsis dicitur, Ebr. VI, 4. 5.

Καὶ τὸ Πνεῦμα τῆς χάριτος ἐνυβρίσας.] Spiritum illum, quem summo Dei beneficio acceperant, contumelia affi- ciens: nullius pretii æstimans tantum donum, quo se ipse it privatum. Vides hic etiam eos, qui Spiritum acce- perant, qui nisi justificatis non dabatur, defectores fieri posse. Vide 1. Thess. V. 19.

Quod recte notat Grotius contra Calvinianos & Anabaptistas, probeque notandum est. Invi- ctum enim pro apostasia sanctorum præbet argu- mentum, quod pervertit Pareus, nos negando per- severantiæ πληροφορίαν ad Papistarum ἐποχὴν im- prudentes revolvi, calumnia impudens est. Nam neque perseverantiæ certitudinem negamus, nisi absolutam, quam ex absoluto decreto Calviniani deducunt, hypotheticam vero, quæ conditionem precum & mediorum salutis ac fugæ peccatorum contra conscientiam includit, non negamus: Ideo- que nihil nobis commercii cum Papistica ἐποχῇ, quæ mera est fluctuatio & incertitudo non tantum de perseverantia, sed de præsente etiam gratia; quam vero Calviniani non minus incurrunt, cum de absoluta sui electione nec à priori nec à poste- riori certi esse possint, sed cum Piscatore conclu- dere necesse habeant: Deus vult quosdam salvos fieri, Christus quosdam redemit, Ergo fieri potest, ut & ego sim in eorum numero. Quam vero præ- tendunt absolutam certitudinem, ea spectrum tan- tum opinionis est, non vero è verbo divinæ pro- missionis oriunda fides, nisi ad immediatam reve- lationem forte cum Enthusiastis & fanaticis se re- cipere malint.

Spiritus autem gratiæ, etsi gratia Dei detur, non tamen ratione originis, quod Dei beneficio confe- ratur, ita dicitur, sed ratione causalitatis, quod gra- tiam exhibeat, & gratiæ dona sufficiat, quemadmo- dum & precum Spiritus idem dicitur, quod Autor sit precum, Zach. XII, 10. Tribuitur enim peculiari- ter Spiritui sancto, vi tertii articuli gratiæ collatio, ejusdemque obsignatio, nec non donorum gratiæ communicatio, 2. Cor. XIII. v. ult. Ἐνυβρίσας est contumelia afficere & blasphemare, unde blasphemia Spiritus dicitur, Matth. XII, 3. Contumelia ergo illa cum blasphemia conjuncta est. De qua summa ingratitudine Theophylactus: Deite Filium ille ef- fecit, tu vero es, prob, vitiorum servituti obnoxius: Venerat ille apud te mansurus, tu vero pro eo diabo- lum admisisti. Est ergo hoc Spiritui gratia injuriam inferre. Afficitur etiam Spiritus sanctus contume- lia in verbi ministerio, quod est Spiritus sancti mini- sterium 2. Corinth. III, 8. cum id proterve conte- mnitur, & media salutis, per quæ operari vult Spi- ritus S. verbum & Sacramenta reprobantur, & blasphemia afficiuntur, utpote, quæ in ipsummet Spiritum sanctum redundat.

## 10:30
Verse 30.

For we know him who said.] Let us consider who and how great (Deuteronomy 32:35).

Vengeance is mine, I will repay,] For there, too, it concerns those who desert God. The words are taken from the Hebrew, as also by Paul in Romans 12:19, who himself also adapts other words of that chapter to the times of Christ (Romans 10:19).

Latin:

Vers. 30.

Οἴδαμεν γὰρ τὸν εἰπόντα.] Cogitemus quis & quantus Deut. XXXII, 35.

Ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις, ἐγὼ ἀποδώσω,] Nam & ibi de Dei deser- toribus agitur. Verba ex Ebræo sumpta, ut & à Paulo Ro- man. XII, 19. qui & ipse alia ejus capitis verba aptat Christi temporibus, Rom. X, 19.

## 10:30
And again. The Lord shall judge his people.] And this is from the LXX, Psalm 135:14 in the Hebrew. To judge there means to vindicate. Thus also God will take vengeance on those who have despised the Church.

He says 'we know,' because, of course, he is writing to Hebrews who were instructed in the Law and were knowledgeable of Mosaic scripture. The latter statement is likewise held in the Mosaic passage, Deuteronomy 32, in the verse immediately following, 36, and is repeated by the Holy Psalmist: which deals with the judgment and vengeance of God against his enemies, the impious deserters, and the attackers of his people, as interpreted by the holy Apostle: such as are, above others, sinners against the Holy Spirit; however, something must be understood: And again, i.e., it is written. For these are not, like the former, words of God, but of Moses concerning God.

Latin:

Καὶ πάλιν. Κύριος κρινεῖ τὸν λαὸν ἀυτοῦ.] Et hoc ex LXX. Psalmo, qui apud Ebræos CXXXV. 14. Κρίνειν ibi est vindi- care. Sic etiam ultionem Deus sumet de iis, qui Ecclesiam contempsere.

Οἴδαμεν dicit, quia scilicet ad Ebræos, qui in le- ge instituti & scripturæ Mosaicæ gnari erant. Po- sterius dictum itidem in loco Mosaico Deuter. XXXII. versu proxime sequenti 36. habetur, & ab Hiero-Psalte repetitur: quod de judicio & vindi- cta Dei adversus hostes suos, impios desertores, & populi sui impugnatores agit, interprete S. Apo- stolo: quales præ aliis sunt peccatores in Spiritum sanctum, subintelligendum autem aliquid est: Et iterum, scil. scriptum est. Non enim hæc, ut priora, sunt Dei, sed Mosis de Deo dicta.

## 10:31
Verse 31.

Latin:

Vers. 31.

## 10:31
It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.] For since he lives forever, he can also punish forever. See above 9:14. To fall into the hands is to pay the penalty (2 Samuel 24:14; Sirach 2:22).

To fall into the hands of God is not only to rush into the hands of an angry Judge and pay the penalty; but sometimes it is also to fall into the hands of God as a placated Father to undergo fatherly chastisement, which is sufficiently clear from the cited passages 2 Samuel 24:14 and Sirach 2:22; because with God, as is added in the same place, there is much mercy, and the mercy of God is as great as he himself is. And therefore it is said not only in a bad sense, but also in a good one. But that it is to be taken here in a bad sense, both the text teaches and that word 'fearful' sufficiently testifies, because the Apostle terrifies the Apostates with that epiphonema, and deters us from apostasy. He designates God as living, however, because the affliction of mortal men cannot extend beyond death. But the punishment of the living God can be extended into eternity (Matthew 10:28). The pious ancients, as the blessed Gerhard observes, warn that it is a horrible thing for the impenitent to fall into the hands of the living God, but it is salutary to fall into the hands of Christ dying on the cross, and through true faith to hide oneself in his wounds.

Latin:

Φοβερὸν τὸ ἐμπεσεῖν εἰς χεῖρα Θεοῦ ζῶντος.] Nam cum in æternum vivat, in æternum etiam potest punire. Vide supra IX. 14. Incidere in manus est pœnas dare, 2. Sam. XXIV. 14. Sir. II, 22.

Incidere in manus Dei non est tantum in manus irati Judicis irruere, ac pœnas dare; sed quando- que etiam est in manus Dei placati Patris incidere ad castigationem paternam subeundam, quod ex laudatis locis 2. Sam. XXIV, 14. Sir. II, 22. satis li- quet; quia apud Deum, ut ibidem additur, est mi- seratio multa, & Dei misericordia tanta est, quantus ipse est. Ideoque non tantum in malam partem di- citur, sed etiam in bonam. Sed hic in malam partem accipi, & textus docet, & illud φοβερὸν satis testa- tur, quia terret Apostolus isto epiphonemate Apo- statas, nosque deterret ab apostasia. Deum autem viventem indigitat, quia hominum mortalium af- flictio ultra mortem extendi non potest. Dei autem viventis pœna porrigi potest in æternum Matth. X. 28. Pii veteres, observante B. Gerhardo, monent, quod horrendum sit impœnitentibus, incidere in ma- nus Dei viventis, sed salutare est incidere in manus Christi in cruce morientis, & per veram fidem in ipsius vulnera se abscondere.

## 10:32
Verse 32. But call to remembrance the former days.] He stirs them up to fortitude by their own example.

Ἐν αἷς φωτισθέντες.] Having first received the light of the Gospel. See above VI, 4.

Πολλὴν ἄθλησιν ὑπεμείνατε παθημάτων.] Thus ἀγωνίζεσθαι is used in Col. I, 29. And here the Syrian has placed the Greek word ἀγῶνα. A struggle with adverse circumstances. For παθήματα are called adversities of every kind, Rom. VIII, 18. 2. Cor. I, 6. 7. Col. I, 24. Phil. III, 10. above II, 9. 10.

To the incitement to faith and perseverance, with a dehortation from the desertion of the Church and apostasy from the faith, lest they finally fall into the sin against the Holy Spirit, since the Hebrews could easily have been tempted by dangers, he subjoins an admonition to their former fortitude in undergoing afflictions for the faith. Since, as Theophylact says, he had secretly consoled them before, now he both addresses them openly and exhorts them not to fail in the tolerance of faith, and says: Do not imitate others whoever they may be, but imitate yourselves, who from the very beginnings of the faith have struggled. I would like you to turn this struggle you have accepted over in your mind and thought, lest through sloth and indolence you lose the labors which you once endured. Observe how prudently and spiritually Paul has said these things. For when he had previously disturbed their minds with the memory of hell, now he soothes and consoles them. Not even flattering them, but from those things which they had previously endured, he makes them more confident, and exhorts them. For he undoubtedly claims credibility for himself, who advises anyone, and urges him to imitate himself in what he had previously done.

Latin:

Vers. 32. Ἀναμιμνήσκετε δὲ τὰς προτέρας ἡμέρας.] Excitat ipsos ad fortitudinem suo ipsorum exemplo.

Ἐν αἷς φωτισθέντες.] Accepta primum Evangelii luce. Vi- de supra VI, 4.

Πολλὴν ἄθλησιν ὑπεμείνατε παθημάτων.] Sic ἀγωνίζεσθαι usurpatur Col. I, 29. Et hic ἀγῶνα Græcam vocem posuit Sy- rus. Luctam cum rebus adversis. Nam παθήματα dicuntur omnis generis adversa, Rom. VIII, 18. 2. Cor. I, 6. 7. Col. I, 24. Phil. III, 10. supra II, 9. 10.

Excitationi ad fidem & perseverantiam, cum de- hortatione à desertione Ecclesiæ & apostasia à fide, ne incidant denique in peccatum in Spiritum san- ctum, quum periculis tentari facile potuerint E- bræi, subjungit commonitionem ad pristinam forti- tudinem, in subeundis pro fide afflictionibus. Cum latenter, ut Theophylactus esset hos antea consolatus, nunc eos & alloquitur palam & cohortatur, ne à fidei deficiant tolerantia, aitque: Nolite alios imitari quoscunque, sed ipsi vos imitemini, qui ab ipsis fidei suscepta primordiis decertastis. Velim tum vestrum hoc acceptum certamen animo & cogitatione verse- tis, ne per ignaviam atque socordiam labores, quos olim tuleritis, amittatis. Adverte quam prudenter & spiritualiter hæc dixerit Paulus. Cum enim prius eorum animos gehennæ memoria obturbasset, nunc lenit & consolatur. Nec blandiens quidem, sed ex his, quæ antea tolerassent, facit fidentiores, hortatur- que. Vendicat enim sibi proculdubio fidem, qui cui- quam consulit, impellitque ut seipsum, quæ antea ges- serit, imitetur.

## 10:33
Vers. 33.

Τοῦτο μὲν.] Partly. For thus Demosthenes and other Greeks, through τοῦτο μὲν and τοῦτο δὲ, express what the Latins express through the double 'partly'.

Ὀνειδισμοῖς τε καὶ θλίψεσι θεατριζόμενοι, that is, having become a theater, as Paul speaks in 1. Cor. IV, 19. You were a spectacle to all through the reproaches and losses heaped upon you. Thus the Syrian rightly here.

Theophylact: Contemplate therefore what men of great and excellent spirit were here, who for the sake of Christ despised both glory and wealth at the same time. Then, having been affected by insults, when they were a spectacle and a laughingstock, and no differently than those who are hissed and mocked in the theater, they endured injuries inflicted even by the lower and abject classes.

Τοῦτο δὲ κοινωνοὶ τῶν ὅτως ἀναστρεφομένων γενηθέντες.] That is, as he will soon explain, having sympathized. He signifies that they were both touched by grief from the evils of their brothers, and that they helped those who were laboring as much as they could, by praying for them and supplying what was necessary. Τῶν ὅτως ἀναστρεφομένων, of those who were living in such evils. Thus κακὴ ἀναστροφὴ, 2. Maccab. V, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 33.

Τοῦτο μὲν.] Partim. Nam sic Demosthenes & Græci alii, per τοῦτο μὲν & τοῦτο δὲ exprimunt, quod Latini per gemi- num partim.

Ὀνειδισμοῖς τε καὶ θλίψεσι θεατριζόμενοι,] id est, θέατρον γενόμενοι, ut loquitur Paulus 1. Cor. IV, 19. Spectaculum fuistis omnibus per ingesta vobis probra & damna. Ita re- cte hic Syrus.

Theophylactus: Contemplare itaque quam essent hic magno & præstanti animo viri, qui Christi ob gra- tiam & gloriam simul & opes contempserint. Contu- meliis deinde affecti, cum spectaculo & derisui essent, nec secus quam qui in theatro exsibilantur & illu- duntur vel à tenuioribus & abjectis illatas injurias tolerabant.

Τοῦτο δὲ κοινωνοὶ τῶν ὅτως ἀναστρεφομένων γενηθέντες.] Id est, ut mox exponet συμπαθήσαντες. Significat eos & do- lore tactos ex fratrum malis, & succurrisse eos, quantum pote- rant laborantibus, deprecando pro iis & necessaria submini- strando. Τῶν ὅτως ἀναστρεφομένων, eorum, qui in malis talibus versabantur. Sic κακὴ ἀναστροφὴ, 2. Maccab. V, 8.

## 10:34
Vers. 34.

Καὶ γὰρ τοῖς δεσμοῖς με συνεπαθήσατε.] He proves the two members he had posited, but in reverse order. It should be read, as it is in the Manuscript, τοῖς δεσμίοις συνεπαθήσατε, just as below XIII. 3. remember those in bonds. And it appears that the Syrian and Latin read it this way here. After the death of Stephen, those Christians in Judea were vehemently harassed, as can be seen in Acts XI, 19. 1. Thess. II, 14.

The text is rashly corrected from the Manuscript, the Latin, and the Syriac version. For most Greek codices have, ὴ γὰρ τοῖς δεσμοῖς με συνεπαθήσατε: For you also sympathized with my bonds, in which way the Greek interpreters also read it. The Apostle had already dealt with compassion with others in the preceding words: Partly indeed you endured such great insults and tribulations that you were a spectacle to the world, which although it opposed your religion: Nevertheless it admired your supreme patience and constancy in afflictions: Partly indeed you shared in the miseries of those who sustained grave persecutions, and not without danger you strove to soothe their miseries, as Osiander explained it paraphrastically. Now this latter member of the distribution, as B. Hunnius rightly advises, he confirms by his own example, you became partakers of my afflictions, while those things which I suffered in my bonds for the Gospel, you received no otherwise than if they had happened to you yourselves. And as you were not ashamed of my bonds, so also you bore your own calamity, namely the plundering of your goods, with a most calm mind and with a certain joy: under this undoubted hope, that a better, and indeed in infinite parts more noble inheritance of substance was laid up for you in heaven, which would not be so perishable as the goods of this age, the loss of which you suffered for Christ's sake, but remaining and lasting for all eternity, as now follows further. Not only, he says with Theophylact as interpreter, did you lack anyone to console you in your evils, but you were also a consolation to others, and to me cast into bonds. What is to be thought of the citation of the passages Acts XX, 19. 1. Thess. II, 14, has been said in its own place.

And you accepted the plundering of your possessions with joy.] Namely, through the seditions of the populace, which are wont to arise often from hatred of religion. With joy, namely because they considered it the highest honor to suffer for Christ, Acts 5:41, Matt. 5:21, James 1:2.

He had said, says Theophylact, how they were joined in fellowship with others in enduring evils. But now, that they also bore with an even mind the things that had been inflicted upon themselves. And that the plundering of goods of this kind was a great argument for the magnitude of their faith. For, he says, your things all went into plunder for this reason, because you stood firm in the faith you had received. For it was permitted to you also, if you had wished, to accept it less; but when you did accept this, it indicates without doubt a voluntary tolerance, and that you prefer Christ to the goods of fortune, not unwillingly. And with joy, he says, they accepted this plundering. He makes them equal to the Apostles, who returned rejoicing that they had been affected by insults for the name of Christ.

Knowing that you have for yourselves a better possession in heaven and an abiding one.] In the glossary, ὕπαρξις is substance, wealth. Polybius and others use it, as do the Greek Interpreters of the Old Testament, such as Prov. 13:11, 18:11, 19:14, Jer. 9:10, 2 Chron. 35:7, Ezra 10:8, Dan. 11:13, 24, 28. He understands, however, the goods of eternal life, which are also called by the name of treasures, Matt. 6:20, 19:21, Mark 10:21, Luke 12:33. Thus also wisdom is said to have הון עתק, a durable substance, Prov. 8:18. They are said to have a thing to which they have a right, in a manner of speaking also used by Jurisconsults. In the Manuscript it is ἔχειν ἑαυτοὺς in the same sense, and ἐν ὀυρανοῖς is missing, as it is also in the Latin. Ἑαυτοὶ among the Greeks is of every person. See above 25.

To some it seems to be understood as public plunder made by the authority of the Magistrate, by which the goods of Christians were adjudged to the treasury. Not all, therefore, had goods in common, but some even possessed their own among the Jews, whose plundering they could suffer, which is to be noted against the Anabaptists. Or that, he says, with Theophylact interpreting again, you act with a certain more sure judgment and faith. For you know that you are going to obtain a better substance in heaven, and one that will last longer than that was, the loss of which you have now made. For that is both more certain, and cannot be lost by any insults of men. They are said to have ὕπαρξιν ἑαυτοῖς, which is ἐν ὀυρανοῖς (which Ribera and Estius rashly suspect to have crept in here from chapter 11:16, for it is also read in the Syriac version) because they had in their heart a certain faith and firm hope that that better possession was laid up for them in heaven.

Latin:

Vers. 34.

Καὶ γὰρ τοῖς δεσμοῖς με συνεπαθήσατε.] Probat duo, quæ posuerat membra, sed inverso ordine. Legendum, ut in Ma- nuscripto est, τοῖς δεσμίοις συνεπαθήσατε, quomodo infra XIII. 3. μιμνήσκετε τῶν δεσμίων. Et apparet hic ita legisse Syrum & Latinum. Post Stephani mortem vehementer ve- xati fuere illi in Judæa Christiani, ut videre est Act. XI, 19. 1. Thess. II, 14.

Temere corrigitur textus è Manuscripto, Latina, & Syriaca versione. Plerique enim Græci Codd. habent, ὴ γὰρ τοῖς δεσμοῖς με συνεπαθήσατε: Nam & vinculis meis compassi estis, quo pacto etiam le- gerunt Græci Interpretes. De compassione cum aliis verbis jam præcedentibus egerat Apostolus: Partim quidem tantas contumelias & tribulationes perpessi estis, ut mundo fueritis spectaculum, qui licet religionem vestram adversatus est: Tamen admira- tus est vestram summam in afflictionibus patientiam & constantiam: Partim vero communicastis eorum miseriis, qui persecutiones graves sustinuerunt, & non sine periculo ipsorum miserias lenire studuistis, ut ea paraphrastice exposuit Osiander. Jam hoc posterius membrum distributionis, quod recte monet B. Hun- nius, confirmat à suo exemplo, vos participes facti estis mearum afflictionum, dum ea, quæ in meis vin- culis ob Evangelium perpessus sum, non aliter acce- pistis, ac si vobis ipsis accidissent. Et ut de vinculis meis non erubivistis, sic & propriam vestram calami- tatem, direptionem scilicet facultatum vestrarum, æquissimo animo & cum gaudio quodam tulistis: sub indubia hac spe, quod substantiæ potior, atque adeo infinitis partibus nobilior hæreditas in cælis vobis es- set reposita, quæ non ita caduca foret, ut hujus seculi bona, quorum jacturam propter Christum estis per- pessi, sed permanens ac durans in omnem æternita- tem, ut jam porro sequitur. Non modo, inquit Theophylacto interprete, vestris in malis consolan- te nemine indiguistis, sed & aliis consolationi fuistis, & mihi conjecto in vincula. Quid de alle- gatione locorum Act. XX, 19. 1. Thess. II, 14. haben- dum, suo loco dictum.

Καὶ τὴν ἁρπαγὴν τῶν ὑπαρχόντων ὑμῶν μετὰ χαρᾶς προσε- δέξασθε.] Nempe per plebis seditiones, quæ sæpe ex odio religionis oriri solent. Cum gaudio, nempe quod summum honorem existimarent ob Christum pati Act. V, 41. Matth. V, 21. Jac. I, 2.

Dixerat, inquit Theophylactus, quemadmodum aliis essent in malis perpetiendis societate conjuncti. Nunc vero & quæ in sese fuissent ingesta, æquo animo tulerint. Atque bonorum direptionem hujusmodi magnum fuisse eorum fidei magnitudinis argumen- tum. Nam eo inquit vestra omnia in prædam cessere, quia in fide suscepta stabiles perstitistis. Licebat enim & vobis, si libuisset, minus illam suscipere; ubi vero hanc suscepistis, voluntariam procul dubio indicat tolerantiam, & quod bonis fortunæ Christum non in- viti præponitis. Et cum gaudio, inquit, eos dire- ptionem hanc suscepisse. Reddit utique Apostolis pares, qui gaudentes redirent, quod pro Christi no- mine contumeliis essent affecti.

Γινώσκοντες ἔχειν ἑαυτοῖς κρείττονα ὕπαρξιν ἐν ὀυρανοῖς καὶ μένουσαν.] In glossario ὕπαρξις substantia, opes. Usurpat Po- lybius & alii, etiam Græci Interpretes Veteris Testamenti, ut Prov. XIII, 11. XVIII, 11. XIX, 14. Jerem. IX, 10. 2. Paral. XXXV, 7. Esd. X, 8. Dan. XI, 13. 24. 28. Intelligit autem bona vitæ æternæ, quæ & thesauri nomine vocantur, Matth. VI, 20. XIX, 21. Marci X, 21. Luc. XII, 33. Sic & sapientiæ adesse di- citur הון עתק substantia durabilis. Prov. VIII, 18. Dicun- tur autem rem habere, ad quam jus habent, loquendi gene- re etiam Jurisconsultis usitato. In Manuscripto est, ἔχειν ἑαυτοὺς pari sensu, & deest ἐν ὀυρανοῖς, ut & in Latino. Ἑαυτοὶ apud Græcos omnis personæ est. Vide supra 25.

Nonnullis videtur intelligi rapina publica Ma- gistratus autoritate facta, qua bona Christianorum fisco adjudicata fuerint. Non omnes ergo habue- re bona communia, sed quidam etiam propria possederunt inter Judæos, quorum rapinam pati possent, quod contra Anabaptistas notandum. Vel id, inquit, iterum interpretante Theophylacto, certi- ori quodam judicio ac fide vos agitis. Nostis enim meliorem vos esse in cælis adepturos substantiam, & diutius permansuram, quam ea fuerit, cujus nunc ja- cturam feceritis. Illa namq;, & certior est, nec amitti ullis hominum insultibus potest. Ἑαυτοῖς dicuntur habere ὕπαρξιν, quæ ἐν ὀυρανοῖς (quod temere Ri- bera & Estius huc è cap.
