XI, 16. irrepsisse suspican- tur, nam in Syriaca versione id etiam legitur) quia in corde fidem certam & spem firmam habuerunt, possessionem illam meliorem sibi in cælo deposi- tam esse.

## 10:35
Verse 35. Do not therefore cast away your confidence.] Thus he calls here the free profession of Christianity: as in Mark 8:32, Acts 4:13, 29, 31, and elsewhere.

Which has a great reward.] It has a right to great rewards. This writer also used the word μισθαποδοσίας above in 2:2, and is about to use it below in 11:26. In the glossary, μισθαποδοσία is the retribution of a reward.

The Apostle has treated of confidence thus far, and he has been accustomed to designate it by the name of παῤῥησία. Why should not that meaning of trust or confidence in Christ be retained here also: to which the promise of a great reward is made, not from merit or the debt of justice, but from grace. Compare Matt. 5:46, ch. 6:1, with Luke 6:32, see also Gen. 15:1, Psalm 127:4, Rom. 4:4. Heavenly glory is rendered to faith, therefore not from our merit, but because of the merit of Christ, which faith apprehends. It is rendered to the faithful just as an inheritance to children, therefore the reason of a due reward has no place: But just as a large inheritance is at the same time a reward of filial obedience, so also the heavenly inheritance takes on the notion of a reward at the same time. Whence Lyranus: Heavenly glory is not properly called a reward, but only broadly, in so far as everything that is rendered as a recompense for labor is called a reward. Therefore the rewards of good works, Col. 3:24, are called ἀνταπόδοσις τῆς κληρονομίας, the retribution of the inheritance. But an inheritance is distinguished from a reward properly so called, just as a son, to whom an inheritance is due, is distinguished from a hired laborer, to whom a reward is due. Add that μισθαποδοσία, what kind it is, is declared in verse 36 and following, with mention made of τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, of the promise. But the Divine promise is gratuitous and proceeds from grace, which is received only by faith, and is by no means obtained by our merits, Gal. 3:21, 22. If those who are heirs by the law are such, faith is made void, and the promise is destroyed, Rom. 4:14.

Latin:

Vers. 35. Μὴ ἀποβάλητε ὖν τὴν παῤῥησίαν ὑμῶν.] Ita hic ap- pellat liberam Christianismi professionem: ut Marci IIX, 32. Act. IV, 13. 29. 31. & alibi.

Ἣ τις ἔχει μισθαποδοσίαν μεγάλην.] Jus habet ad magna præmia. Vocem μισθαποδοσίας & supra usurpavit hic Scriptor II, 2. & usurpaturus est infra XI, 26. In glossario μισθαποδο- σία mercedis retributio.

De fiducia hactenus egit Apostolus, eamque nomine παῤῥησίας designare consuevit. Cur non & hic retineatur ea significatio fiduciæ vel confi- dentiæ in Christum: cui magnæ mercedis promissa est retributio, non ex merito, aut debito justitiæ, sed ex gratia. Conf. Matth. V. v. 46. cap. VI. v. 1. cum Luc. VI, 32. vid. & Gen. XV, 1. Psalm. CXXVII, 4. Rom. IV, 4. gloria cœlestis redditur fidei, non ergo ex nostro merito, sed propter Christi meritum, quod fides apprehendit. Redditur fidelibq; sicut hæredi- tas liberis, ideo mercedis debitæ ratio locum non habet: Sed sicut larga hæreditas simul est præmium filialis obedientiæ, ita & hæreditas cœlestis præmii simul notionem subit. Unde Lyranus: Gloria cæle- stis non proprie dicitur merces, sed tantummodo lar- ge, in quantum omne quod redditur in præmium la- boris dicitur merces. Ideo præmia bonorum ope- rum Col. III, 24. vocantur ἀνταπόδοσις τῆς κληρονο- μίας, retributio hæreditatis. Hæreditas autem di- stinguitur à mercede proprie dicta, sicut filius, cui debetur hæreditas, distinguitur ab operario con- ductitio, cui debetur merces. Addę quod μισθα- ποδοσία, qualis illa sit v. 36. seq. declaretur, men- tione facta τῆς ἐπαγγελίας, promissionis. At pro- missio Divina gratuita est & ex gratia profecta, quæ non nisi fide recipitur, neutiquam autem meritis nostris obtinetur, Gal. III, 21. 22. Si illi, qui ex lege hæredes sunt, fides evacuatur, & destruitur promis- sio, Rom. IV, 14.

## 10:36
Verse 36. For you have need of patience.] It is not enough to have begun, one must persevere, Matt. 10:22, 24:13, Mark 13:13, Luke 21:19, Rom. 2:7.

That having done the will of God, you may receive the promise.] Having done, namely, even to the end. Κομίζειν is a word very proper for signifying the receiving of good or evil from a preceding promise or threatening, 2 Cor. 5:10, Eph. 6:8, Col. 3:25, below 11:19, 39, 1 Pet. 1:9, 5:2, 2 Pet. 2:13. And ἐπαγγελίαν here again for the thing which has been promised, as Luke 24:49, Acts 1:4, Gal. 3:22, above here 6:15, 9:15.

The Vulgate renders it patience. Because, therefore, it is necessary for us, from this the Papists, Majorists, and Calixtines strive to prove the necessity of good works from this passage. But ὑπομονὴ, as Guil. Estius warns, properly signifies patient expectation: Generally it denotes perseverance in confidence of both faith and hope. Thus the LXX translate the word חכה, which signifies the confidence of one desiring to obtain a desirable thing for which he has panted, by ὑπομένειν, Hab. 2:3, and Luke 8:15, those who are compared to seed falling into good ground retain the good seed through faith, and bear fruit ἐν ὑπομονῇ, in perseverance of faith. To these things the Apostle calls the ὑπομονὴ, which brings back the promise, immediately in verse 35, παῤῥησίαν, having a great remuneration. Furthermore, in verse 39 he declares his mind more expressly, explicitly calling the same πίστιν, faith. The Apostle therefore speaks properly of faith persevering in confidence, which by reason of its primary operation continues spiritual life on account of the apprehended merit of Christ received, but by reason of its secondary operation exercises itself in hope and patience, sustaining tribulation, verse 32. Therefore this ὑπομονὴ of faith, as the blessed Höpfner rightly says in disp. XI. de justif. §. 15. page 1024, or perseverance, is necessary for us, both by reason of its primary operation, for obtaining justification, spiritual life, and salvation promised by God, and because by reason of its secondary operation it is a consequence of justification and spiritual salvation already obtained, but an antecedent sign and testimony of eternal salvation. For insofar as it is required for justification, to that extent it is an instrument of apprehending the justifying thing, namely the obedience of Christ performed for us. But insofar as it exercises itself in sustaining calamities, and lightens its losses by the hope of future liberation, to that extent it is necessary only for the demonstration of preceding justification and salvation, and also by reason of the order by which these fruits of it either follow justification and spiritual salvation, or precede the attainment of eternal life. Thus also the blessed Hülsemann in Brev. instruct. de resuscit. & excusat: Phraseos Majorist. page 81: It is of extreme impudence to wish to restrict either the etymology or the use of the word ὑπομένειν and ὑπομονῆς among sacred and profane authors to only perseverance in adversities, or the sustaining of a painful affection, when by name and common usage it denotes perseverance in any affection or quality, whether concupiscible or irascible, as much concerning objects hoped for as concerning those desired and sought after, as much concerning things believed as concerning adverse things. The latter meaning is indeed more frequent in usage and predominant, but by no means is it, nor is the true meaning derived from the force of the word alone, which Suidas and his interpreter in the Lexicon, which Erasmus, Budaeus, and others in their notes not only show with many examples, but have also proposed as its native sense the indefinite and abstract meaning of perseverance, apart from the objects in which one persists 41:8, Jeremiah 14:8, 17:13, Ezra 10:2. Here, however, the connection and the comparison of the opposite sufficiently show that perseverance in faith and confidence in it is urged, and that ὑποστολήν, or withdrawal and falling back from faith, is discouraged; and thus Chrysostom, Oecumenius, and Theophylact explain it regarding persistence in παῤῥησίᾳ (boldness). Chrysostom: Since, he says, you have all your confidence fixed on God and eternity, furthermore you need no other thing, and no addition, except perseverance alone, so that you may remain in that state, and not lose the good things already grasped, but that you may persist in that course, so that having attained the end you may carry off the promised things. Oecumenius and Theophylact repeat the words of Chrysostom, and here likewise make the immediate and adequate object of ὑπομονῆς (patience) τὸ πιστεύειν εἰλικρινῶς εἰς αὐτόν (to believe sincerely in Him). Therefore, the Apostle is not speaking properly of patience, but of faith, persevering in confidence, and not withdrawing itself from GOD even in the midst of tribulations, in the enduring of which they exercise themselves, verse 32. For faith does not only justify, but is also effective through charity, hope, and patience. For the Apostle is still discussing faith here by design, and exhorts them to keep it constantly, intending to exhort them to endure afflictions subsequently, especially in chapter 12. Add that it is not said that ὑπομονή (patience) is necessary for attaining eternal life, but that doing the will of God we may carry off the promise. If, therefore, ὑπομονή were mostly patience, yet the necessity for salvation is not predicated of that, but it is required so that we may do the will of God and carry off the promise. Now, they do the will of God who believe in Christ and constantly persevere in that faith, John 6:27, 29, 39; 1 John 3:23. Furthermore, if the will of God is also said to be performed by love and the pursuit of holiness, it is only a description of those who carry off the promise, not a cause or means of salvation designated, or at least only an event and consequence; and thus it is hinted that the performance of the Divine will precedes the attainment of the promise in order alone, but not in respect of influence. Theophylact: It is certainly clear, he says, that God wills this above all, that this patience be perpetually performed in all things: For he says: He who shall have persevered to the end, he shall be saved. The Apostle warns us no differently than if someone, having seen a contestant, with adversaries defeated and overcome, who can bear neither heat nor thirst any longer, and as if impatient of delay, and not waiting for the earned crown, is departing immediately from the arena, were to urge him by pursuing him with these words: You have already performed your duty and have decided excellently, and in such a way that you have carried off the palm; I beg you, wait a little, so that you may carry off the crowns as a reward. Strive, so that as far as the rewards are carried off, you may overcome yourself, and patiently bear that delay. Finally, the reference here is of patience not to salvation itself, as if it were the cause of it; but to faith, for which we need patience, lest we suffer shipwreck in such storms of adversities and persecutions.

Latin:

Vers. 36. Ὑπομονῆς γὰρ ἔχετε χρείαν.] Non sufficit cœpisse, perstandum est, Matth. X, 22. XXIV, 13. Marc. XIII, 13. Luc. XXI, 19. Rom. II, 7.

Ἵνα τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ ποιήσαντες, κομίσησθε τὴν ἐπαγγε- λίαν.] Ποιήσαντες nempe ad finem usque. Κομίζειν verbum valde proprium ad significandam boni aut mali perceptionem ex præcedente promisso aut comminatione, 2. Cor. V, 10. Eph. VI, 8. Col. III, 25. infra XI, 19. 39. 1. Petr. I, 9. V, 2. 2. Petr. II, 13. Et ἐπαγγελίαν hic rursum pro re quæ promissa est, ut Luc. XXIV, 49. Act. I, 4. Gal. III, 22. supra hic VI, 15. IX, 15.

Vulgata reddit patientia. Quia ergo ea nobis necessaria est, unde Papistæ, Majoristæ, Calixtini ne- cessitatem bonorum operum ex hoc loco probare satagunt. Sed ὑπομονὴ monente Guil. Estio pro- prie significat patientem expectationem: Generali- ter notat perseverantiam in fiducia cum fidei tum spei. Ita LXX. verbum חכה, quod fiduciam signi- ficat re desiderabili, cui inhiaverat, potiri cupien- tis, exponunt per ὑπομένειν, Hab. II, 3. & Luc. VIII, 15. ii, qui semini, in bonam terram cadenti, com- parantur bonum semen retinent per fidem, & fe- runt fructum ἐν ὑπομονῇ, in perseverantia fidei. Ad hæc Apostolus ὑπομονὴν, quæ reportat promissio- nem, vocat proxime v. 35. παῤῥησίαν magnam ha- bentem remunerationem. Præterea vers. 39. expres- sius mentem suam declarat, eandem diserte πίσιν fidem appellans. Loquitur ergo Apostolus pro- prie de fide perseverante in fiducia, quæ ratione pri- mariæ suæ operationis continuat vitam spiritualem propter apprehensum Christi meritum acceptam, ratione vero secundariæ suæ operationis exercet se in spe, & patientia, sustinente tribulationem vers. 32. Itaque hæc fidei ὑπομονὴ, ut recte B. Höpfnerus disp. XI. de justif. §. 15. pag. 1024. seu perseverantia est nobis necessaria, tum ratione primariæ operationis, ad obtinendam justificationem, vitam spiritualem, & salvationem Divinitus promissam, tum quia ra- tione secundariæ operationis est obtentæ justificationis & salutis spiritualis consequens, salutis vero æternæ antecedens signum & testimonium. Nam prout re- quiritur ad justificationem, eatenus est organum ap- prehendendi rem justificantem, nempe obedientiam Christi pro nobis præstitam. Prout autem se exer- cet in sustinendis calamitatibus, & spe futuræ libera- tionis sua damna levat, eatenus necessaria est tan- tum ad ostensionem præcedaneæ justificationis & sa- lutis, nec non ratione ordinis, quo hi fructus ejus vel consequuntur justificationem & salutem spiritualem, vel antecedunt vitæ æternæ consecutionem. Sic et- iam B. Hülsemannus Brev. instruct. de resuscit. & excusat: Phraseos Majorist. pag. 81. Extremæ im- pudentiæ est, velle sive etymologiam sive usum vocabuli ὑπομένειν & ὑπομονῆς apud sacros & profanos Autores restringere ad solam perseve- rantiam in adversis, seu sustinentiam affectus do- lorifici, quum nomine & usu vulgari notet per- severantiam in quovis affectu sive qualitate tum concupiscibili, tum irascibili, tam circa objecta spe- rata, quam circa desiderata & expetibilia, tam circa credita, quam circa adversa. Posterior significa- tio frequentior quidem usu & prædominans est, sed nequaquam, nec ex vi vocis sola vera significatio est, quod Suidas & ejus Interpres in Lexico, quod Eras- mus, Budæus, aliique in notis non solum multis exemplis ostendunt, sed perseverantiæ quoque inde- finitum significatum & abstractum ab objectis, in quibus persistitur, tanquam nativum proposuerunt, sicuti clara ipsorum verba testantur. Adducit Si- riac. XI, 16. Cap. XLI, 8. Jerem. XIV, 8. XVII, 13. Esdr. X, 2. Hic vero connexio & oppositi col- latio satis ostendit, suaderi perseverantiam in fide, ejusque fiducia, dissuaderi ὑποστολὴν seu subductio- nem & resultum à fide, atque ita Chrysostomus, Oe- cumenius, Theophylactus de persistentia in παῤῥησίᾳ exponunt. Chrysostomus: Quandoquidem, in- quit, omnem fiduciam in Deum & æternitatem de- fixam habetis, porro nulla alia re, nulloque addi- tamento, nisi solo perseverantia indigetis, ut manea- tis in illo statu, & bona jam apprehensa non amitta- tis, sed ut in illo cursu persistatis, ut finem assecuti re- portetis res promissas. Oecumenius & Theophyla- ctus verba Chrysostomi repetunt, & proximum ac adæquatum objectum ὑπομονῆς hic itidem faciunt τὸ πιστεύειν εἰλικρινῶς εἰς αὐτόν. Non ergo proprie de patientia loquitur Apostolus, sed de fide, perse- verante in fiducia, neque se subtrahente à DEO in mediis etiam tribulationibus, in quibus tolerandis se exercent, vers. 32. Nam fides non justificat tan- tum, sed etiam efficax per charitatem, spem & patientiam. De fide enim ex instituto adhuc dis- serit hic, & ad eandem constanter servandam hor- tatur Apostolus, ad tolerandas afflictiones horta- turus deinceps imprimis cap. XII. Adde quod non ὑπομονὴ necessaria dicatur ad consequendam æter- nam vitam, sed ut voluntatem Dei facientes repor- temus promissionem. Si ergo maxime ὑπομονὴ fo- ret patientia, non tamen de ista prædicatur neces- sitas ad salutem, sed requiritur ea, ut voluntatem Dei faciamus, & promissionem reportemus. Vo- luntatem autem Dei faciunt, qui in Christum cre- dunt, & in illa fide constanter perseverant, Joh. VI, 27. 29. 39. 1. Joh. III, 23. Porro si præstari etiam voluntas Dei dicatur dilectione & studio sanctitatis, descriptio tantum eorum, qui promissione repor- tant, non causa vel medium salutis designatur, aut certe eventus tantum & consequens, adeoque id in- nuitur, quod præstatio voluntatis Divinæ antece- dat solo ordinis, non vero influxus respectu, pro- missionis adeptionem. Theophylactus: Constat sa- ne, inquit, Deum id apprime velle, ut omnibus in rebus perpetuo præstetur hæc patientia: Ait namque: Qui ad finem usque perseveraverit, hic salvus erit. Nec secus nos monet Apostolus, ac faceret quispiam certatorem aliquem conspicatus, devictis superatisque adversariis, qui nil ultra nec æstum ferat, nec sitim, & ut mora impatiens, nec emeritam expectet coro- nam è medio protinus abeuntem, his dictis prose- quendo hortetur: Perfunctus jam tuo munere es & egregie decrevisti, & ita, ut palmam retuleris, pau- lulum obsecro opperire, ut coronas in præmium refe- ras. Contende, ut quoad præmia referantur, te- ipsum vincas, & patienter id moræ feras. Denique relatio hic est patientia non ad ipsam salutem, qua- si causa illius sit; sed ad fidem, cujus naufragium ne in tantis adversitatum & persecutionum pro- cellis faciamus, patientia nobis opus est.

## 10:37
Verse 37.

For yet a little while, he who is coming will come and will not delay.] The former words are of our Writer, the following are from the LXX, Habakkuk 2:3. Μικρὸν ὅσον, ὀλίγον ὅσον (a little while, a little while) are frequent among the Greeks. Moreover, to repeat that ὅσον twice is according to the custom of the Hebrews. A similar expression is in Jeremiah 23:3. He who is to come will come, and will not delay: Namely, fire in the common sense, in the more sublime sense Christ about to judge the world. He says the same thing as above, 25. Thus also Peter comforts the faithful, that their evils last for a short time, 1 Peter 1:6, 5:10.

Because the former words are the Apostle's, the latter the Prophet's, it is not necessary that the sense of that time and advent, of which the Prophet speaks, should hold here, since it was permissible to apply the words of the Prophet in a similar way, so that what he said about the first advent of Christ might be accommodated to the last advent of Christ. The words, therefore, are indeed the same, but not the same advent. That custom regarding ὅσον ὅσον is observed in Isaiah 23:20, hide yourself for a little while. However, I do not find a similar expression, 'he who is to come will come and will not delay,' in Jeremiah 23:3, but in Isaiah 13, at the end, where there is no talk of fire or of Christ. That fire is also somewhere in the common sense, and in the more sublime sense is Christ, will be taught by no example.

Latin:

Vers. 37.

Ἔτι γὰρ μικρὸν ὅσον ὅσον ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἥξει καὶ οὐ χρονιεῖ.] Priora verba sunt Scriptoris nostri, sequentia ex LXX. Habac. II, 3. Μικρὸν ὅσον, ὀλίγον ὅσον, frequentia apud Græcos. Repetere autem bis illud ὅσον ex more est Ebræorum. Similis loquutio Jerem. XXIII, 3. Is qui venturus est veniet, nec tardabit: Nempe ignis in sensu vulgari, in sensu sublimiori Christus mundum judicaturus. Idem dicit quod supra 25. Sic & Petrus fideles solatur, quod mala illorum ad breve tempus durent, 1. Petr. I, 6. V, 10.

Quia verba priora Apostoli sunt, posteriora Prophetæ, necessum non est, ut sensus illius tempo- ris & adventus, de quo Propheta, hic obtineat, quum in simili applicare licuerit verba Prophetæ, ut quæ de adventu Christi primo dixit, accommo- darentur ad adventum Christi novissimum. Verba ergo eadem quidem sunt, non autem idem adven- tus. Mos ille quoad ὅσον ὅσον observatur Es. XXIII, 20. ἀποκρύβηθι μικρὸν ὅσον ὅσον. Loquutionem autem similem, is, qui venturus est, veniet & non tardabit, non invenio Jer. XXIII, 3. sed Esa. XIII. ult. ubi nec de igne nec de Christo sermo est. Ignem etiam alicubi in sese vulgari, in sensu sublimiori esse Christum, nullo exemplo docebitur.

## 10:38
Verse 38.

The just man shall live by faith.] He who is good and upright, he shall live, that is, he shall remain in his faith: as it is in the Hebrew, or ἐκ πίστεώς μου (by my faith), as it is in the Greek, and the Syrian reads here, that is, he shall live by faith in me, that is, he shall sustain himself, he shall breathe through faith, through the expectation of the promises. See what we have said regarding Habakkuk and Romans 1:17. In the Manuscript, ὁ δὲ δίκαιός μου, and so it is written in many Greek Codices of Habakkuk. And Eusebius follows this reading both in Habakkuk and in this place, Demonstratio 6:14. Therefore the LXX read צַדִּיקִי.

This is the promise, on account of which we ought not to cast away our confidence: Namely, that the just man shall live by faith at the coming of the Lord, which will be shortly. But the matter comes to the same thing whether it is said simply ἐκ πίστεως (by faith), or ἐκ πίστεώς μου (by my faith). For faith looks to God or the divine promise, as Grotius admits: Although in the Hebrew it is 'by his faith,' not 'by my faith,' through which we are not only sustained or breathe, but live: nor is 'to live' here to remain in faith, but rather to remain in the life of grace, or to attain the life of glory, or both; because when we continue to live the life of grace, we attain the life of glory. The Holy Spirit judged this oracle worthy, which is also in Romans 1:17. & Gal. III, 14. The Apostle might bring [this] forward to assert the justification of faith, and he might inculcate it here, where the matter concerns the promise of salvation and glory; since we are both justified and saved only through faith, and the exhortation is to the perseverance of faith, εἰς περιποίησιν τῆς ψυχῆς. Therefore, 1. regarding the subject, he is called just, not who is justified before God by his own righteousness, but by imputed righteousness, who, apprehending Christ and His expiatory sacrifice through faith, has obtained the remission of sins and has attained true spiritual life in Christ. For since the just is denominated from righteousness, and that is either of works and legal, Eph. IV, v. 24, 1 John III, 7, or of faith or Evangelical, Rom. X, v. 3, Phil. III, 9, which is the very righteousness of Christ, but becomes ours through faith, Is. XLV, 24, Rom. V, 19. Phil. III, 9. That it is not the former but the latter that is referred to is evident, first, from the determination of the Prophet, that the just shall live by his faith: for the righteousness of faith is imputative righteousness: secondly, from the antithesis, for the just by faith is opposed to the soul that exalts itself or is unfaithful: thirdly, from the preceding chapter, in which the prayer of the Prophet, proceeding from true confidence, is presented, ver. 12. Art thou not my God, my holy one, our rock, that we die not? The Lord therefore answers: The just shall not die by his faith, but shall live. He does not seek righteousness in himself, but in Christ. Jehovah my holy one. For this is the symbol of the faithful concerning Christ: He himself is Jehovah our righteousness, Jer. 23, 6. Fourthly, from the Apostolic citation, Rom. I, 17, where the Apostle proposes to discourse concerning imputative or the righteousness of faith, with these words of prophecy adduced, concerning the righteousness of God, which is revealed by the Gospel from faith unto faith, concerning the righteousness of God revealed without the law, Chap. III, 21. concerning the righteousness not of works, because by this no one is justified before God, but of faith, by which we are justified without works ver. 20, 28. just as Abraham was justified without the law through faith, so that faith was imputed to him for righteousness Chap. IV, 3. seqq. allegation Gal. III, 11. by which it is proved from this Prophetic passage, that no one is justified in the law or through the observation of the law before God, for he says that it is δῆλον manifest from thence, ὅτι ὁ δίκαιος ἐκ πίσεως ζήσεται, because the just shall live by faith.

As to the second point, regarding the predicate, the life of both grace and glory is signified, but he shall live in the future, says the Prophet, to intimate the continuation of the life which the just shall enjoy in the time of grace, as also the blessed transition of the life of grace into the life of glory, but the life of grace is both spiritual and bodily. The former, as it consists in freedom from sin, Eph. II, 5. and the right of obtaining eternal life, Joh. VI, 51. So it does not arise from the law or from works, Rom. VII, 10. chap. VIII, 2. but from the Gospel and faith, Gal. II, 20. Phil. I, 21. 1. Joh. V, 12. The latter, however, embraces the enjoyment of the goods of this life, Psal. XXXIV. ver. 14. which is likewise obtained through faith, as can be seen in illustrious examples, Matth. IX, 12. Act.

III, 16. Finally, the life of glory is nothing other than the enjoyment of heavenly blessedness, which we attain only through faith, Joh. III, 15. chap. V, 29. chap. VI, 54. All of which the Prophetic voice embraces with the word shall live used generally, both the happiness of bodily life and also spiritual life, which coheres immediately with justification, Rom. VII. by way of comparison chap. I, 12. 13. where he prays against destruction by enemies, as also the death of the soul, and not least the Apostolic explanation concerning the spiritual life of grace, Rom. I, 17. then finally the life of glory and the heavenly, as is clear from this passage ver. 39. this not from the comparison of Galat. III, 11. 12. For just as the Apostle teaches that we are justified by faith alone Rom. I, 17. So he also hands down here that we are saved by faith alone: nor are the causes of salvation other than those of justification, since the causes of salvation are equally the grace of God, because it is a χάρισμα, Rom. VI, 23. and it is given τῇ χάριτι, Act. XV, 11. Rom. IV, 3. the merit of Christ, Ebr. X, 14. Act. IV, 12. and faith without works, Eph. II, 8. 2. Tim. I, 9.

In vain therefore does Piscator object vol. II. p. 132. that it is not a consequence, if we are justified by faith alone, that we also obtain salvation by faith alone: For nothing forbids that the consequent thing should have more causes than the antecedent: Just as parents indeed alone beget children, but do not alone educate those begotten, but rather employ nurses and tutors to educate them. For in this analogy there is a great dissimilarity. The consequent thing, I say, if it follows immediately, does not have other causes than the antecedent. But the remission of sins and eternal salvation cohere immediately, not so education and generation. To these, regeneration corresponds to our generation, by which faith is given to us, and we are adopted as children of God: But the life consequent to this adoption as children does not correspond to nutrition or education, but to the inheritance of children. But to education, renewal is more correctly compared, by which we successively grow in the knowledge of God, Col. I, 9. 10. until we grow into a perfect man, Eph. IV, 13. But eternal life is the end not of renewal, but of justification and faith, Rom. VI, 22. 1. Petr. I. 9. to which alone on our part both the beginning is attributed, because through faith we have access to grace and the medium, because by faith we stand in grace, and the term of righteousness is salvation, because by faith we glory in the hope of the glory of the children

of God, Rom. V. ver. 1. and are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation, 1. Petr. I, 5.

But it is mere trickery, when Cardinal Bellarmine explains in Book II on the efficacy of the Sacraments, chapter 9, concerning patience and long-suffering, which Grotius imitates here, that it will sustain itself, just as Bellarmine explains himself in Book II on justification, chapter 15; that sentence, 'the just shall live by faith,' seems literally to signify that the just man sustains himself and endures through a desire for the heavenly fatherland by faith. Coster the Jesuit in this place interprets life as concerning tolerance and the life of honest constancy: Coster in Enchiridion, chapter IV, interprets it as the formation of life according to the norm of faith or the doctrine of faith. But thus from the promise of life is fashioned a precept of sustaining oneself through patience, or of continuing an honest life, and of living according to the norm of God's commandments: From the faith by which we believe, is fashioned the faith by which it is believed, and this is again transformed by a remarkable metamorphosis into the doctrine of the law, prescribing a mode of living: From life, which is opposed by the Prophet to death and destruction, and is called by the Apostle the acquisition or salvation of the soul opposed to perdition (verse 39), and a reward (verse 36), an inheritance (Gal. III, 18), the salvation to which the Gospel is effective (Rom. I, 16-17), is fashioned the formation of life according to the norm of the law or the constancy and continuation of an honest life. The Apostle distinguished life both from ὑπομονῇ, through which these men understand patience, and from the performance of the Divine will. Why, therefore, do these Sophists confuse them? By the mention of life, neither the Prophet nor the Apostle denotes an object to be directed by faith, nor a moral action or habit resulting from faith, much less from the doctrine of virtues, but they note the event of justification and the gratuitous reward, which the Apostle teaches is given by God to those justified through faith, just as Jerome rightly explains: 'he shall live,' that is, he shall receive the reward, eternal life. Therefore, Francis Ribera here deserts his own in his Commentary on the XII Minor Prophets and explains life as the beginning of life, which he trifles is had from the first justification, which Bellarmine also finally embraces, not without hesitation and self-contradiction, in Book II on justification, chapter 4. The Holy Spirit preferred to say: 'The just shall live by faith,' either because He was speaking not of the life of justice but of the life of hope, which makes the just man hope patiently, or because He wished to commend that from which the life of the just takes its beginning. But both these glosses are contrary to the text; it indeed exhorts to the hope of the Messiah, or the expectation of His advent, but which is joined with faith in the Messiah, for whom they eagerly panted, because they believed in Him as their Redeemer and Savior. To this faith, however, in which they were confirmed by the promise of a certain and swift advent, that eulogy is attributed by the Prophet, that the just man is to live by faith. That word חכה denotes not only hope, but also the full assurance of faith, and is taken in general for the confidence both of faith (Heb. X, 22) and of hope (C. VI, 11), just as faith also apprehends future things, although in a different way: For hope apprehends things to be hoped for by reason of the complement, which is to be in the future. Faith, however, apprehends them as present on account of the present promise of fulfillment. Therefore the word חכה, which denotes confidence panting for a desirable thing, is [translated] by the LXX Interpreters Hab. III, 3, is rendered by ὑπομένειν, and Isa. XXX, 18, by ἐμμένειν, whence comes the ὑπομονὴ of Heb. X, 30, which we said is taken concerning faith. Nor indeed is the beginning of the life of the just attributed only to faith, but life itself, and the acquisition of the soul, and the obtaining of the promise of life, or the attainment of eternal salvation. And it is a Popish fiction that faith is a disposition antecedent to justification, which they pretend consists in the infusion of justice: because faith is not said to justify dispositively, but organically by apprehending the righteousness of CHRIST, nor is justification a certain physical act, situated in the infusion of charity, but a judicial act, by which we are absolved from sins and declared righteous, not through or because of inherent righteousness, which follows justification, does not precede it, but through the righteousness of Christ imputed to faith, as the Apostle demonstrated in Rom. IV and V.

III. As to the determination which is made by the mention of πίστεως: by אמונה is not denoted the faith or faithfulness of God in promises, as the Chaldean rendered it: In truth the just shall live, which Divine promise had already been made before, verse 2. For here what is required on our part is expressed, which is also evident from the pronoun, the just shall live by his faith, not by the faith of GOD. By which, therefore, is designated the confidence or παῤῥησία, by which the promise of GOD is apprehended, so that the mind may acquiesce in it, as it is the Amen, and most certain, 2 Cor. I, 20. What kind of confidence, however, the Prophet required with the word חִכָּה in verse 3, which is to pant for some thing with open mouth, and to apprehend and hold it, as the hungry are accustomed to pant for food with their throats, and to hold it: For חֵךְ denotes the palate or throat, and is used to express the πληροφορία of faith, Psalm XXXIII, verse 20, Isa. XXX, verse 18. Such was the confidence

of the Prophet Habakkuk I, 12. Jehovah my God, my holy one, my rock: Whence it is also clear that this faith, by which we live the life of grace and glory, has for its object the righteousness of Christ, because it apprehends the Lord as his Holy One, as our righteousness, Jer. XXIII, verses 5, 6; XXXIII, verse 16, made unto us for righteousness and sanctification, 1 Cor. I, verse 30, whose coming the Israelites are therefore commanded to await with true confidence, Hab. II, verse 3, and to faith is attributed by the Prophet rectitude or righteousness, verse 4, which, since no one has that from which or through which he can live, there is need of the righteousness and obedience of Christ, Rom. V, verse 19, so that he may be justified through faith in CHRIST, Rom. V, verse 1. For that is finally the object of justifying faith, which a sinful man, about to be condemned before the tribunal of GOD for sin, apprehends, so that he may not be condemned, but justified. But this is solely the perfect obedience, which we have only in Christ, Rom. VIII, verse 3; Chap. X, verse 3; 2 Cor. V, verse 21.

IV. As to the connection THE JUST SHALL LIVE BY FAITH, whether he is said to live by faith, or rather to be a just man by faith, that is, whether that ἐκ πίστεως pertains to the subject or to the predicate? I answer: it is referred to the subject in the Venetian edition of the Bibles in Quarto, that of Felix Pratensis in folio, and other editions, which add the simple Merca accent to the word צַדִּיק (just) and the syntactic Tiphcha accent to the word בֶּאֱמוּנָתוֹ, so that the sense is: the just, who is by faith, shall live, so that it is implied that he will live by faith. For the former reading and opinion these things can be urged: 1. That the just and the infidel are opposed, whence the determination is to be referred to the just, by which he himself is opposed to the infidel, that is, to faith. 2. That that just man, to whom life is promised, professes through faith, Chap. I, verse 12, that GOD is his GOD, that He is his rock; 3. That he is opposed to the perfidious, whom God does not regard, Chap. I, verse 13; 4. That the Apostle in Rom. I, verse 17, proposes the state of the case thus: Righteousness is obtained from faith unto faith: Cf. Rom. III, verses 21, 22. 5. That in this place, Chap. X, verse 39, the just are called οἱ τῆς πίστεως, and are opposed to τοῖς ὑποστολῆς, namely, the children, and those are said to live, but these to perish: Now the children of withdrawal are called those who are the infidel soul to the Prophet: And therefore they will be the children of faith, who are called by the Prophet just ἐκ πίστεως. 6. Add the collation of the similar passage Rom. V, verse 1. Furthermore, even if that determination ἐκ πίστεως pertains to the subject, because of the individual connection of the extremes, it is not undeservedly also referred to the predicate, which the blessed Luther expressed: which is confirmed both by the immediate connection of righteousness before God and life. For as through faith we obtain justification and are righteous: So through the same faith we obtain life, 1 John III, v. 3, 36; 1 John V, verse 12; and from the parallel passage, Rom. I, verse 17, where, after mention has been made of life or salvation and righteousness, promised through faith in the Gospel, as the cause of both the antecedent and the consequent, he brings forward this Prophetic saying, which ascribes both righteousness and life to faith; and from the collation of the passage Gal. III, verse 12, where the Apostle concludes thus: From that from which the just lives, by that he is justified, proceeding from the effect to the cause: The just lives by faith, the Prophet testifies. Therefore he is justified by faith: finally, from the purpose of the Apostle in the present passage, who teaches both that we please God through faith in justification, and that we obtain the περιποίησιν τῆς ψυχῆς through faith in salvation or the attainment of eternal life, and he executes both of these more fully in chapter XI. One may therefore conclude from this that the Holy Spirit placed these words ἐκ πίστεως in the middle of the statement so that the word of faith could be referred to both extremes of the statement.

V. As to the word of application, silent indeed in the Apostle, but expressed by the Prophet, BY HIS FAITH, Grotius in his annotations on Hab. II, 3, rashly troubles the same by the force of the affixed pronoun. For it is read constantly in the Hebrew Codices, nor does Jerome testify that the LXX Interpreters read it otherwise, and all the other Greek Interpreters rendered it so, Symmachus even with emphasis δίκαιος τῇ ἑαυτῦ πίςει ζήσει. That the LXX read ὁ δὲ δίκαιός μꝸ, seems certain to Grotius: that the Apostle also had it so in this place. But although the Aldine edition has it so, ὁ δίκαιός μꝸ ἐκ πίςεως ζήσεται, other Codices nevertheless read it with that pronoun omitted, or placed it after the word πίςεως, or according to the Hebrew text and other Greek Codices referred the pronoun to the faith of the just, the just shall live by his faith. In this Apostolic passage, however, the pronoun μꝸ is not observed in most Greek Codices, just as it is not in Rom. I, verse 17. Galatians 3:11. That is found in no one. Therefore, according to the Prophet, the just man is said to live by HIS OWN faith, and by that it is intimated that he is both justified and saved by his own faith, not another's. For just as no one lives by another's soul in natural life, so no one lives by another's faith in spiritual and heavenly life. Concerning which the Apostle says in Romans 4:5: To him who believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, HIS OWN faith is imputed for righteousness. As for the words of St. Augustine, Sermon 14 on the words of the Apostle: How do infants believe? By the faith of their parents: those are to be understood as referring to the faithful intercession of parents and godparents, by which faith is obtained for children from God, so that they may attain the same through baptism. Therefore, they believe by the faith of their parents, by obtaining faith, but they do not live by the faith of their parents, by attaining salvation, not by their own, but by another's faith. Nor is there any reason for Beza to say, Vol. 3, fol. 346, that infants are saved by the faith of their parents, but as if it were made their own and proper. For how does it become their own, whether by generation or imputation? But they beget children, not as believers are, but by what generative faculty they are endowed through Divine blessing, nor is faith obtained through generation, but through regeneration: Or through imputation: But faith as a gift of God is conferred through the Word and Sacraments, but it is not attributed through imputation to anyone in whom it does not exist.

VI. Finally, the mode of concurrence or causality of faith in the act of justification and salvation is designated by the particle ב ἐξ, which indeed has the nature of a medium or instrument. For this is accustomed to be expressed and explained either by ἐκ, Deut. VI, 5, Mark XII, 30, or by ἐν, Matt. III, 11, Gal. III, 11, or by διὰ with the Genitive, Deut. XXXII, 21, Psalm LXXVIII, 2, or simply by the Ablative of the instrument, and therefore in the matter of justification these modes of speaking are equivalent: ἐκ πίςεως, διὰ πίςεως, ἐν πίσει, πίσει, Rom. III, 30, Gal. II, 20, Rom. IV, 20, Chap. V, 2. But nowhere is διὰ πίςιν found, meaning to be saved on account of faith, as we are said to obtain the remission of sins and to be saved through and on account of Christ, Acts X, 43, John VI, 27. For the proper business of faith in justification is to receive Christ and his righteousness, John I, 12, Rom. III, 22, Chap. IX, 30. Galat. III, 21. which fiduciary apprehension is followed also by the apprehension of other promised things after justification, Mark XI, 24, Galat. III, 14, Heb. IV, 16. A novel interpretation is that of Cocceius, in the last of Moses: The just in his faith (of the witness who knows not how to lie) whose soul is upright in him, shall live. To the witness who is to be sent after the Prophecy, faith is due unto righteousness and life. And this is the uprightness of the soul; and it is the duty of man, if he wishes to live, that his soul be upright in him. To which exegesis one will not easily add his vote.

And if he draws back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him.] He inverts the order of the words. For in the Prophet these things precede, and it appears that to that, if he draws back, one must understand 'anyone'. But the LXX Interpreters, whom this Writer loves to follow, read not his soul, but his soul, but 'aphlah' and not 'aphlah' with a very good sense indeed. 'Aral', as we said regarding Habakkuk, is accustomed to be translated by 'to fail' and 'to be faint-hearted', and 'hypostellesthai' has the same sense, for it is to do less than is right, Acts XX, 20. God says this: if anyone grows weary in waiting, and on that account ceases to wait for those promised good things, he will greatly displease me.

It is in vain that a different reading is imagined in the authentic text, and without the authority of the codices the noun 'aphel' according to Kircher signifies a place between cliffs or narrow mountains, according to others a more elevated or fortified place, a citadel and tower, and it is attributed to the Jerusalem tower, 2 Chron. XXIII, 14, where the LXX render it 'adyton', an inaccessible place. The verb 'aphal' is therefore explained by some as to be set in a narrow place, by some as to be exalted, to be lifted up into a high place and strengthened, which is used metaphorically of the proud and fierce man, who extols himself through arrogance. Avenarius interprets the verb 'aphal' as: he built a high fortification within narrow cliffs or mountains, through which it is necessary to contend, and in this place he explained it in the passive conjugation: 'aphal', behold his soul is compacted into a ball, proud and arrogant like a ball or a swelling hill. Forster in his lexicon rendered it: He is in a narrow strait, who likewise thinks that Num. XIV, 44 is being referred to, where by the LXX it is rendered by the interpreters 'diabainomai', I use force in ascending, they ascended by using force: Luther: They were stubborn to go up; and it seems to denote a balling up or constriction into narrow straits, even though a rash and proud daring was joined to it, as is explained in Deut. I, 43, where the LXX expressed it: 'you rebelled and forcing your way you went up into the mountain', because in the ascent they showed themselves to be rebels not without contention, and therefore Forster in his explanations and Blessed Luther in his Commentary believe that the Prophet also looked to the passage Rom. II, 9, 'to those who are of contentiousness'. From which collation it appears that the LXX translation of the Interpreters, 'if he draws back', corresponds to the Hebrew verb, whether it is translated as concerning constriction or retraction, or concerning pride and elation, or concerning the contention which arises from balling up and elation, or if one prefers to take those meanings together according to parallel passages, as Blessed Hoepfner explained from Forster, to withdraw oneself with a certain contention, and to dare and attempt something with a certain impatience of mind without faith. Who also compares Habakkuk I, verse 12, where the Prophet called God a Rock. For he who does not place his trust in God, he makes other things, or even himself, a rock, a fortified citadel, and a safe refuge, and Rabbi Moses brings forward one who explains it thus from Sante Pagnino: The soul of the impious, which is not upright in itself, that is, which has no trust, nor faith in God, which sets itself up as a tower and citadel, to flee thither from the face of the enemy, and does not turn to GOD, nor seeks from him that he might rescue him. But the just, who trusts in the Lord, and believes, shall live, and there will be no need that he set himself in a citadel and fortification. He says therefore that the sense of the version of the LXX, retained by the Apostle, is the same: 'If he draws back', if anyone shall withdraw himself. For 'hypostellesthai' is to be cast down in spirit, to fear, to withdraw oneself out of fear and diffidence, and to betake oneself elsewhere as if into a place safe from all things. Munster explains it concerning pride: The soul thinks that it is sufficiently fortified: So also Vatablus. Certainly it is accustomed to be brought out: And Tremellius and Junius: Behold it bubbles up, that is, the unjust man laboring from infidelity and wickedness, although in appearance he may seem to rise up into a slope and become a very great mountain, yet he bubbles up, that is, he bursts no more than a bubble, and is broken by his own weakness, which sense Blessed Joh. Tarnovius approves in his commentary on this passage, but in the reconciliation with the LXX Interpreters and the translation of the Apostle he seems to join pride and fear, for thus the Greek renders it: He who out of infidelity, security or fear shall withdraw himself from my promise. But the Vulgate, which rendered it 'he who is incredulous', refutes, as does Ribera, who defends the same, that he ignorantly confuses that word with the word 'ophal', whose heart is not illuminated, although the LXX Interpreters also [translated] 'aphal' 2. 2 Kings, verse 24. Where B. Luther took it as a proper name, Pagninus and Arias Montanus rendered it as a built-up and fortified place, having interpreted it as σκοτεινὸν, dark. Whence B. Gerhard here: In the Hebrew it is: Behold, he who is unbelieving עפלה, obscure, nebulous, a shunner of light, tenebricose. They can be reconciled, he says, the Hebrew text and the Greek version in this way: He who withdraws himself either through unbelief or through impatience, he also is proud, because as to believe is of humility: so to be unwilling to believe is of an elated mind. Ludovicus de Dieu, from the usage of the Arabic word עפל, explains it as, if this promise is neglected, or the mind is turned away from it, which excellently agrees with ὑποστείληται. Joh. Coccejus from Polybius brings forward the meaning of this Greek word as applying oneself to a fortification for security, if anyone has applied himself to another than the Messiah, as his fortification and protection. All of which teach that there is no necessity that we should posit that the Hebrew text is corrupt; but it seems to be more fitting, if the Dievian [interpretation] does not please, that explanation concerning withdrawal out of fear or anguish of heart, not disapproved neither to B. Höpffner, nor to B. Tarnovius, nor is it alien to the meaning of the Hebrew word, and it is by no means incongruous with the Prophetic text, nor with the present passage. For that the people were in distress on account of the monstrous and bloodthirsty invasion of the Chaldeans, the complaining voice of the Prophet, resounding in his name, testifies: but you, O Lord my God, my holy one, who are from eternity, lest we die, why are you silent, because the wicked devours the righteous? etc. And the Apostle in this place raises up the Hebrews with the Prophetic oracle in their distresses and afflictions, and animates them to constancy in faith and perseverance in confidence, because the Lord is about to come quickly for the liberation of the pious, whether this is understood of the final advent of glory, or the timely advent of grace, just as there is discourse concerning the advent of prophecy or promise, or even of him who was promised (for the matter comes to the same thing), and to those who withdraw themselves out of fear and distress and diffidence, and do not firmly lean upon the Divine promise, the displeasure of the Lord, and thus certain destruction, is intimated; but to those who through faith lean upon him and await the Lord, life is promised. In the Hebrew it is, coming he will come, that is, he will most certainly and infallibly come. In the Greek, he who is to come, will come. In the Hebrew, Habakkuk speaks of prophecy, and testifies that it will most certainly come. Luther. See, the promise will certainly come. But because the Messiah is accustomed to be called ὁ ἐρχόμενος [the one who is coming], Matt. 11:3, John 11:27, from there, with the article ὁ prefixed (which is not held in the version of the LXX Interpreters), he refers this part of the prophecy to Christ, especially since in the Greek a transition is made from the feminine to the masculine, and the nucleus of all Prophetic promises is Christ, as here B. Gerhard. He adds: Nothing prevents the Prophetic saying from being referred to the first and second advent of Christ, since the first advent is the foundation of the second, and the second is the consequence of the first.

These things concerning the subject: That B. Tarnovius indeed, with Vatablus, Münster, Junius, and Tremellius, constitutes it as the predicate, but according to the interpretation of the LXX Interpreters approved by the Holy Spirit himself in this place, it is manifest that it occupies the place of the subject, which the Latin Vulgate and Luther also observed. Therefore, as for the predicate, 'his soul is not upright in him,' by that is properly denied to him who recedes or withdraws himself through infidelity and fear the uprightness of soul, or even the Divine good pleasure, and thus consequently the rest and tranquility of the soul. For the word יָשַׁר signifies 'is upright,' as יָשַׁר 1 Sam. 18:20, 26 is rendered εὐθύνω 'I am upright.' It is also expounded by ἀρέσκω 'I please,' Num. 23:27, Jud. 14:3, 7, 1 Kings 9:7, Dan. 4:24, and by εὐδοκέω 'I am well pleased,' as it is rendered in this place: οὐκ εὐδοκεῖ ἡ ψυχή με ἐν ἀυτῷ [my soul is not well pleased in him]. B. Luther, having disregarded the pronoun, took it concerning the εὐδοκίᾳ [good pleasure] of the soul, 'in itself there will not be the good pleasure of his soul in it': He will have no rest in his heart. However, there is no reason why we should admit that the LXX Interpreters read otherwise, namely the letter Vav for Jod in the word עפלא, or even with B. Tarnovius maintain that the Holy Spirit made good use of the slip of the Greek Interpreters, since the sense remains the same, even if the text was not rendered word for word. For in whom the soul is not upright, in him God cannot have good pleasure: just as the consequent is often put for the antecedent, nor is force brought upon the text; for the seventy elders did not always render word for word, but not rarely looked to the sense, which was approved here by the Holy Spirit. For also above, chapter 1:3, the Prophet had said: Will you look upon the treacherous, or will you have good pleasure in them? Will you delight in the unfaithful? And the Apostolic axiom makes for this, Heb. 11:6, 'without faith it is impossible to please God.' Thus those opposite members explain each other: 'The just shall live by his faith,' he is about to have an upright nature, and God will have good pleasure in him, and on the contrary, the unfaithful, or those who withdraw themselves out of fear and infidelity, will not live, but of ὑποστολῆς [withdrawal], his end will be ἀπώλεια [destruction], there is not in him uprightness of mind (which is the life of the faithful, for they live in the faith of Christ, and his righteousness and uprightness, who himself is our righteousness, Jer. 23:6, Gal. 2:20), God does not have good pleasure in him, whence neither does he himself have rest and tranquility of soul, or εὐδοκίαν [good pleasure] in himself. Osiander expressed the sense: He who is justified by faith in Christ, he will have a tranquil conscience, being refreshed indeed by the Word of the Gospel, and will live with Christ for all eternity. Therefore, there is no reason why a man should shudder at the mention of the advent of Christ. But if anyone shall withdraw himself, withdrawing himself from the confession of the Gospel, lest he fall into dangers and persecutions, he, says the Lord, will not please my soul: Just as a captain is not pleased with a soldier who (having neglected the military oath) withdraws himself from the army on account of imminent danger. For whoever shall have denied me before men (says Christ), I also will deny him before my Father who is in heaven, Matt. 10. Likewise B. Hunnius: If a man, failing from the faith, shall withdraw himself, and on account of afflictions shall cast away the profession of faith, he will not be approved by my soul. B. Gerhard: In the Hebrew, he says, in the Prophet it is: 'His soul is not upright in him.' The LXX refer the mind to God. The Hebrew text to man. They can be reconciled in this way: Whose mind is not upright, but perverse, he also does not please God. See concerning this place two learned disputations of B. Höpfner in the Theological disputations. Num. 12, 13, and the trumpet of the Lutheran Jubilee of B. Johann Tarnovius.

Latin:

Vers. 38.

Ὁ δὲ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται.] Qui bonus rectusque est, is vivet, id est, manebit in fide sua: ut est in Ebræo, aut ἐκ πίστεώς με, ut est in Græco, & hic legit Syrus, id est, per fidem in me vivet, id est, semet sustentabit, respirabit per fidem, per expectationem promissorum. Vide quæ diximus ad Ha- bacucum & Rom. I, 17. In Manuscripto ὁ δὲ δίκαιός με, & ita scriptum in Codicibus multis Græcis Abacuci. Et hanc le- ctionem tum in Abacuco, tum hoc loco sequitur Eusebius demonst. VI, 14. Legerunt ergo LXX. צַדִּיקִי.

Hæc est promissio, ob quam παῤῥησίαν abjicere non debemus: Quod nempe justus ex fide sub ad- ventum Domini brevi futurum victurus sit. Res autem eodem redit sive simpliciter dicatur ἐκ πί- στεως ex fide, seu ἐκ πίστεώς με. Respicit enim fides in Deum vel promissionem divinam, fatente Gro- tio: Quanquam in Ebræo sit, fide sua, non fide mea, per quam non sustentamur tantum aut respi- ramus, sed vivimus: nec vivere hic est manere in fide, sed potius manere in vita gratiæ, vel conse- qui vitam gloriæ, vel utrumque; quia cum pergi- mus vivere vitam gratiæ, consequimur vitam glo- riæ. Oraculum hoc dignum judicavit Spiritus san- ctus, quod & Rom. I, 17. & Gal. III, 14. ad asseren- dam justificationem fidei afferret Apostolus, & hic inculcaret, ubi de promissione salutis & gloriæ res est; siquidem & justificemur & salvemur non nisi per fidem, & ad fidei perseverantiam exhorta- tio sit, εἰς περιποίησιν τῆς ψυχῆς. Quod itaque 1. ad subjectum justus dicitur, non qui propria, sed im- putata justitia coram Deo justificatus, qui Chri- stum ejusque sacrificium expiatorium per fidem apprehendens remissionem peccatorum conse- quutus & in Christo veram vitam spiritualem ad- eptus est. Nam cum justus à justitia denomine- tur, eaque vel operum sit & legalis, Ephes. IV. v. 24. Job. III, 7. vel fidei seu Evangelica, Rom. X. v. 3. Phil. III, 9. quæ est ipsa Christi justitia, nostra au- tem fit per fidem Es. XLV, 24. Rom. V, 19. Phil. III, 9. non illam sed hanc respici, primum è determina- tione Prophetæ constat, quod justus ex fide sua vi- vat: Justitia enim fidei est justitia imputativa: Dein- de ex antithesi, animæ enim extollenti sese seu infide- li opponitur justus ex fide: tertio ex capite præce- denti, quo exhibetur precatio Prophetæ è vera fi- ducia profecta, vers. 12. Attu Deus meus, sanctus meus, rupes nostra, ne moriamur: Respondet itaque Dominus: Justus ex fide sua non morietur, sed vivet. Non quærit justitiam in seipso, sed in Christo. Jeho- vah sanctus meus. Hoc enim symbolum est fide- lium de Christo: Ipse Jehovah justitia nostra, Jer. 23, 6. Quarto ex allegatione Apostolica, Rom. I, 17. ubi de imputativa vel fidei justitia disserere proponit Apostolus, verbis hisce Prophetiæ adductis, de ju- stitia Dei, quæ per Evangelium revelatur ex fide in fidem, de justitia Dei absque lege patefacta, Cap III, 21. de justitia non operum, quia hac nemo justificatur coram Deo, sed fidei, qua justificamu absque operibus vers. 20, 28. quemadmodum Abraham justificatus est sine lege per fidem, ita ut fide ipsi imputata sit ad justitiam Cap. IV, 3. seqq. Quinto ex iterata allegatione Gal. III, 11. qua probatur loco hocce Prophetico, quod nemo in lege vel per legis observationem justificetur coram Deo, id enim inde δῆλον manifestum esse dicit, ὅτι ὁ δίκαιος ἐκ πίσεως ζήσεται, quia justus ex fide vivet.

Quod II. ad prædicatum, vita tum gratiæ tum gloriæ significatur, sed vivet in futuro, inquit Propheta, ad innuendam vitæ, qua justus fruetur, in tempore gratiæ, continuationem, ut & vitæ gratiæ cum vita gloriæ beatam commutationem, Vita autem gratiæ tum spiritualis est, tum corporalis. Illa uti consistit in libertate à peccato, Eph. II, 5. & jure adipiscendi vitam æternam, Joh. VI, 51. Ita non ex lege aut ex operibus oritur, Rom. VII, 10. cap. VIII, 2. sed ex Evangelio & fide, Gal. II, 20. Phil. I, 21. 1. Joh. V, 12. Hæc autem fruitionem bonorum hujus vitæ complectitur, Psal. XXXIV. vers. 14. quæ pariter per fidem obtinetur, uti in illustribus exemplis videre est, Matth. IX, 12. Act.

III, 16. Denique vita gloriæ nihil aliud est, quam fruitio beatitudinis cœlestis, quam non nisi per fidem consequimur, Joh. III, 15. cap. V, 29. cap. VI, 54. Quæ omnia complectitur Prophetica voce vivet generaliter adhibita, tum felicitatem vitæ corporalis, tum etiam vitam spiritualem, quæ cum justificatione immediate cohæret, Rom. VII. vi collationis cap. I, 12. 13. ubi deletionem per hostes deprecatur, ut & mortem animæ, nec non explicationis Apostolicæ de vita gratiæ spirituali, Rom. I, 17. tum denique vitam gloriæ & cœlestem, ut ex hoc loco vers. 39. liquet, hec non è collatione Galat. III, 11. 12. Nam uti fide sola nos justificari docet Apostolus Rom. I, 17. Sic etiam sola fide nos salvari hic tradit: neque aliæ sunt salvationis quam justificationis causæ, quum æque causæ salutis sint gratia Dei, quia χάρισμα est, Rom. VI, 23. & τῇ χάριτι donatur, Act. XV, 11. Rom. IV, 3. meritum Christi, Ebr. X, 14. Act. IV, 12. & fides absque operibus, Eph. II, 8. 2. Tim. I, 9.

Frustra ergo obvertit Piscator vol. II. p. 132. non esse consequens, si sola fide justificemur, sola etiam fide nos salutem adipisci: Nihil enim vetare, quin rei consequentis plures causæ sint, quam antecedentis: Sicut parentes soli quidem liberos procreent, procreatos autem non soli educent, verum ad illos educandos nutrices & pædagogos adhibeant. In hoc enim simili magna est dissimilitudo. Rei consequentis, inquam, si immediate consequatur, non sunt aliæ causæ quam antecedentis. At immediate cohæret remissio peccatorum & salus æterna, non idem educatio & generatio. Ad hæc generationi nostræ respondet regeneratio, qua nobis fides donatur, & adoptamur in filios Dei: Hujus autem adoptionis in filios consequens vita non nutritioni vel educationi respondet, sed hæreditati filiorum. Educationi autem rectius conferetur renovatio, qua successive crescimus in agnitione Dei, Col. I, 9. 10. donec evadamus in virum perfectum, Eph. IV, 13. Vita autem æterna est finis non renovationis, sed justificationis & fidei, Rom. VI, 22. 1. Petr. I. 9. cui soli ex parte nostra & initium tribuitur, quia per fidem habemus accessum ad gratiam & medium, quia fide stamus in gratia, & terminus justitiæ salus, quia fide gloriamur in spe gloriæ filiorum

Dei, Rom. V. vers. 1. & virtute Dei custodimur per fidem ad salutem, 1. Petr. I, 5.

Mera autem κυβεία est, cum exponit Cardinalis Bellarmin. libr. II. de effic. Sacr. cap. 9. de patientia & longanimitate, quem hic imitatur Grotius, semet sustentabit, uti Bellarminus sese explicat l. II. de ju- stif. cap. 15. ad literam videtur sententia illa, justus ex fide vivet, significare justum sustentare se, ac to- lerare desiderio cælestis patriæ ex fide. Castrius Je- suita in h. l. vitam de tolerantia & vita honestæ con- stantia: Costerus in Enchirid. cap. IV. de vita for- matione ad normam fidei vel doctrinæ fidei inter- pretatur. Sed ita è promissione vitæ fingitur præ- ceptum, per patientiam sese sustentandi, vel vitam honestam continuandi, & ad normam præceptorum Dei vivendi: E fide qua credimus, fingitur fides, qua creditur, & hæc iterum insigni metamorphosi transformatur in doctrinam legis, modum vivendi prescribentem: E vita quæ à Propheta opponitur morti, & interitui, & ab Apostolo acquisitio vel sa- lus animæ opposita exitio vers. 39. dicitur, & remu- neratio vers. 36. hæreditas Gal. III, 18. salus ad quam Evangelium efficax est, Rom. I, 16.17. effingitur for- matio vitæ ad normam legis vel constantia & conti- nuatio vitæ honestæ. Vitam distinxit Apostolus & ab ὑπομονῇ, per quam patientiam isti intelligunt, & à præstatione voluntatis Divinæ. Cur ergo ista confundunt Sophistæ? Vitæ mentione nec Prophe- ta nec Apostolus objectum à fide dirigendum, nec moralem actionem vel habitum ex fide resultantem, nedum è doctrina virtutum, sed eventum justifica- tionis notant, & præmium gratuitum, quod justifi- catis per fidem à Deo dari Apostolus docet, uti Hie- ronymus recte explicat, vivet, id est, accipiet præ- mium, vitam æternam. Ideo Franc. Ribera hic de- serit suos in Comment. in XII. Prophetas Min. & vitam explicat de initio vitæ, quod ex prima justifi- catione haberi nugatur, quod etiam non citra titu- bationem & ἑαυτομαχίαν tandem amplectitur Bel- larminus libr. II. de justif. cap. 4. Maluit Spiri- tus sanctus dicere: Ex fide vivet justus, vel quia lo- quebatur non de vita justitiæ sed de vita spei, quæ ju- stum patienter sperare facit, vel quia commendare voluit id, unde initium ducit vita justorum. Sed utraque hæc glossa textui contraria est; ad spem Messiæ, vel expectationem adventus ejusdem hor- tatur quidem, sed quæ cum fide conjuncta in Mef- siam, quem avide inhiabant, quia in eum ceu Re- demptorem & Salvatorem suum credebant. Huic autem fidei, in qua promissione certi, celerisque adventus confirmabantur, à Propheta elogium il- lud tribuitur, quod justus ex fide victurus sit. Ver- bum illud חכה non spem tantum, sed & πληροφο- ρίαν fidei notat, & in genere de fiducia tum fidei Ebr.X, 22. tum spei C.VI, 11. accipitur, quemadmo- dum & fides apprehendit res futuras, etsi diversa ra- tione: Spes enim apprehendit res sperandas ratione complementi, quod futurum est. Fides autem ap- prehendit illas ut præsentes propter præsentem im- pletionis promissionem. Ideo verbum חכה, quod fiduciam rei desiderabili inhiantem notat à LXX. Interpr. Hab. III, 3. redditur per ὑπομένειν, & Esa. XXX, 18. per ἐμμένειν, unde ὑπομονὴ Ebr. X, 30. quam de fide accipi diximus. Neque vero fidei tantum initium vitæ justorum tribuitur, sed vita ipsa, & περιποίησις τῆς ψυχῆς, & reportatio promissionis vitæ, vel adeptio salutis æternæ. Et commentum est Papisticum, fidem dispositionem esse antecedaneam justificationis, quam in justi- tiæ infusione consistere fingunt: quia non dispositi- ve justificare dicitur fides, sed organice appre- hendendo justitiam CHRISTI, neque justifi- catio est actus quidam Physicus, in infusione charitatis situs, sed actus judicialis, quo absolvi- mur a peccatis & justi declaramur, non per vel ob inhærentem justitiam, quæ justificationem sequi- tur, non antecedit, sed per justitiam Christi fidei imputatam, Rom. IV. & V. demonstravit Apo- stolus.

III. Quod ad determinationem, quæ mentio- ne πίστεως fit: per אמונה non notatur fides vel fidelitas Dei in promissis, ut Chaldæus reddi- dit: In veritate justus vivet, quæ promissio Divi- na jam ante facta erat, vers. 2. Hic enim quid ex parte nostri requiratur, exprimitur, quod ex pronomine etiam constat, justus ex fide sua, non fide DEI vivet. Qua proinde fiducia vel παῤ- ῥησία designatur, qua promissio DEI apprehen- ditur, ut mens in eadem acquiescat, utpote quæ Amen est, & certissima, 2. Cor. I, 20. Qualem fiduciam autem verbo חִכָּה requisivit Propheta vers. 3. quod est aperto ore inhiare rei alicui, eam- que apprehendere ac tenere, ut famelici solent fau- cibus inhiare cibo, eumque tenere: Nam חֵךְ notat palatum vel fauces, & ad exprimendam fidei πληροφορίαν adhibetur Psalm. XXXIII. vers. 20. Eja. XXX. vers. 18. Qualis fiducia erat

Prophetæ Habac. I, 12. Jehovah Deus meus, sanctus meus, rupes mea: Unde etiam liquet, fidem hanc, qua vivimus vita gratiæ & gloriæ, pro objecto ha- bere justitiam Christi, quia apprehendit Domi- num ut Sanctum suum, ut justitiam nostram, Je- rem. XXIII. vers. 5. 6. XXXIII. vers. 16. factum no- bis in justitiam & sanctificationem, 1. Cor. I. vers. 30. cujus adventum ideo vera fiducia expectare jubentur Israëlitæ, Habac. II. vers. 3. & fidei tri- buitur a Propheta rectitudo vel justitia vers. 4. quam cum nemo habeat eam, ex qua vel per quam vivere queat, opus est Christi justitia & obedientia, Rom. V. vers. 19. ut justificetur per fi- dem in CHRISTUM, Rom. V. vers. 1. Illud enim demum est objectum fidei justifick, quod homo peccator coram DEI tribunali ob pec- catum condemnandus apprehendit, ut ne con- demnetur, sed justificetur. Hoc autem unice est perfecta obedientia, quam non nisi in Christo habemus, Rom. VIII. vers. 3. Cap. X. vers. 3. 2. Cor. V. vers. 21.

IV. Quod ad vinculum JUSTUS EX FI- DE vivet, anne vivere dicatur ex fide, an ve- ro justus ex fide esse hoc est, an illud ἐκ πίστεως ad subjectum, an vero ad prædicatum pertineat? Resp. ad subjectum referri in editione Biblio- rum Veneta in Quarto, Felicis Pratensis in fo- lio aliisque editionibus, quæ ad vocem צַדִּיק ju- stus accentum Etymologicum Merca simplex, ad vocem autem בֶּאֱמוּנָתוֹ accentum syntacticum Tiphcha adjiciunt, ut sensus sit justus, qui est ex fide, vivet, ut scilicet victurus innuatur ex fide. Pro priori lectione & sententia hæc urgeri possunt 1. quod justus, & infidelis, opponantur, unde ad justum referenda determinatio, per quam ipse opponitur infideli, hoc est fidei. 2. Quod justus ille, cui vita promittitur, per fi- dem profiteatur, Cap. I. vers. 12. DEUM esse DEUM suum, esse rupem suam; 3. Quod op- ponatur perfidis, quos Deus non respicit, Cap. I. vers. 13. 4. Quod Apostolus Rom. I. vers. 17. sta- tum causæ ita proponat: Justitia ex fide in fidem obtinetur: Conf. Rom. III. vers. 21. 22. 5. Quod hoc loco Cap. X. vers. 39. justi vocentur οἱ τῆς πίστεως, & opponantur τοῖς ὑποστολῆς scilicet τέκ- νοις, atque illi dicantur vivere, hi autem perire: Jam filii subductionis dicuntur illi, qui Prophe- tæ sunt anima infidelis: Ideoque filii fidei erunt, qui à Propheta vocantur justi ἐκ πίςεως. 6. Ad- de collationem similis loci Rom. V. vers. 1. Cæ- terum etsi ad subjectum pertineat illa determina- tio ἐκ πίςεως, propter individuum tamen extre- morum nexum, non immerito etiam ad prædica- tum refertur, quod expressit B. Lutherus: quod confirmatur tum ab immediato justitiæ coram Deo & vitæ nexu. Ut enim per fidem conse- quimur justificationem ac justi sumus: Ita per eandem fidem vitam consequimur, 1. Joh. III. v. 3. 36. 1. Joh. V. vers. 12. tum à loco parallelo, Rom. I. vers. 17. ubi à vitæ vel salutis & justitiæ mentione facta, per fidem in Evangelium pro- missa, utriusque & antecedentis & consequentis causa, dictum hoc Propheticum affert, quod & justitiam & vitam fidei adscribat; tum è colla- tione loci Gal. III. vers. 12. ubi sic colligit Apo- stolus: Ex quo vivit justus, eo justificatur, ab effectu ad causam procedens: Ex fide vivit ju- stus, teste Propheta. Ergo ex fide justificatur: tandem ex scopo Apostoli in præsenti loco, qui & per fidem nos Deo placere in justificatione, & per fidem nos περιποίησιν τῆς ψυχῆς consequi in salvatione vel vitæ æternæ consecutione docet, idque utrumque cap. XI. uberius exequitur. Col- ligere ergo hinc licet, Spiritum sanctum hæc verba ἐκ πίςεως in medio enunciationis propter- ea collocasse, ut ad utrumque extremum enun- ciationis vox fidei referri posset.

V. Quod ad vocem applicationis ab Apostolo quidem tacitam, sed à Propheta expressam FI- DE SUA, vi pronominis affixi temere solici- tat eandem Grotius in annotat. ad Hab. II, 3. Nam & in Codd. Ebræis constanter legitur, nec aliter LXX. Interpretes legisse testatur Hieronymus, & cæteri Græci Interpretes omnes ita reddidere, Symmachus etiam cum emphasi δίκαιος τῇ ἑαυτῦ πίςει ζήσει. Contra LXX. legisse ὁ δὲ δίκαιός μꝸ, Grotio certum videtur: ita etiam habuisse hoc loco Apostolum. Sed quamvis Aldina editio ita habeat, ὁ δίκαιός μꝸ ἐκ πίςεως ζήσεται alii tamen Codices legerunt prætermisso illo pronomine, vel post vocem πίςεως id posuere, vel secundum Ebræum textum & alios Græcos Codices prono- men ad fidem justi retulerunt, justus fide sua vi- vet. In hoc vero Apostolico loco Pronomen μꝸ in plerisque Codicibus Græcis observatum non est, quemadmodum nec Rom. I. vers. 17. Galat. III. vers. 11. id repertum in ullo. Juxta Prophe- tam ergo justus fide SUA vivere dicitur, eoque propria fide, non aliena & justificari & salvari in- nuitur. Ut enim nemo anima aliena vivit, natu- rali vita: Ita nemo aliena fide vivit vita spiritua- li & cœlesti. Quo de Apostolus Rom. IV. vers. 5. Credenti in eum, qui justificat impium, fides SUA imputatur ad justitiam. Quod ad verba S. Augustini serm. XIV. de verb. Apost. Quo- modo credunt infantes? fide parentum: Intelligen- da illa sunt de fideli intercessione parentum & pa- trinorum, qua filiis impetratur à Deo fides, ut eandem per baptismum consequantur. Paren- tum ergo fide credunt, fidem obtinendo, non au- tem parentum fide vivunt, salutem consequendo, non propria, sed aliena fide. Nec est, quod dicat Beza Volum. III. fol. 346. infantes salvari fide pa- rentum, sed ut sua, & propria facta. Quomodo enim propria ipsorum fit, num per generationem vel im- putationem. At procreant liberos, non ut fideles- sunt, sed qua facultate generatrice per Divinam be- nedictionem sunt præditi, nec fides per generatio- nem obtinetur, sed per regenerationem: Num per imputationem: At fides ceu donum Dei per Ver- bum & Sacramenta confertur, non autem per im- putationem ulli, cui non inest, tribuitur.

VI. Denique modus concursus vel causalitas fi- dei in actu justificationis & salvationis particula ב ἐξ designatur, quod nempe medii vel instrumenti rationem habeat. Hoc enim ita exprimi solet & explicari vel per ἐκ, Deut. VI, 5. Marc. XII, 30. vel per ἐν, Matth. III, 11. Gal. III, 11. vel per διὰ cum Genitivo, Deut. XXXII, 21. Psalm. LXXVIII, 2. modo simpliciter per Ablativum instrumenti in- dicem, ideo & in materia justificationis æquipol- lent hi loquendi modi ἐκ πίςεως, διὰ πίςεως, ἐν πί- σει, πίσει, Rom. III, 30. Gal. II, 20. Rom. IV, 20. Cap. V, 2. Nuspiam autem reperitur διὰ πίςιν propter fidem servari, uti per & propter Christum remif- sionem peccatorum consequi & salvari dicimur, Act. X, 43. Joh. VI, 27. Fidei enim proprium negotium est in justificatione accipere Christum, ejusque justitiam, Joh. I, 12. Rom. III, 22. Cap. IX, 30. Galat. III, 21. quam fiducialem apprehensio- nem sequitur etiam aliarum rerum promissarum apprehensio post justificationem, Marc. XI, 24. Galat. III, 14. Ebr. IV, 16. Novella est interpre- tatio Cocceji, in ultim. Mosis, Justus in fide illius (testis mentiri nescii) cujus anima recta est in ipso, vivet. Testi post Prophetiam mittendo debetur fides ad justitiam & vitam. Et hæc est rectitudo animæ; & officium hominis est, si velit vivere, ut anima ejus sit recta in ipso. Cui ἐξηγήσει non fa- cile quis adjiciet calculum.

Καὶ ἐὰν ὑποσείληται, ἐκ ἐυδοκεῖ ἡ ψυχή με ἐν ἀυτῷ.] In- vertit verborum ordinem. Nam in Propheta hæc præce- dunt, & apparet ad illud, ἐὰν ὑποσείληται subaudiri τις. Le- gerunt autem LXX. Interpretes, quos hic Scriptor sequi amat, non נֶפֶשׁוֹ, sed נפשו sed עַפְלָה & non עפלה sen- su sane optimo. ערל, ut ad Habacucum diximus, verti so- let per ἐκλείπειν & ὀλιγοψυχεῖν, eundem sensum habet ὑποσείλεσθαι, est enim minus facere, quam rectum est, Act. XX, 20. Hoc dicit Deus, si quis expectando defatigetur, & propterea expectare bona illa promissa desinat, is mihi sum- mopere displicebit.

Frustra fingitur diversa lectio in textu authenti- co, & sine codicum fide nomen עפל juxta Kirche- rum locum inter scopulos seu montes angustum, juxta alios editiorem vel munitum, arcem & turrim signi- ficat, & tribuitur turri Hierosolymitanæ, 2. Chron. XXIII, 14. ubi LXX. reddunt ἄδυτον inaccessum locum. Verbum proinde עפל exponitur à quibus- dam in arctum constitui, à nonnullis exaltari, in locum excelsum attolli & corroborari, quod Me- taphorice de superbo & effero adhibeatur, qui se extollit per fastum. Avenarius interpretatur ver- bum עפל extruxit munitionem altam intra scopu- los seu montes angustos, per quos contendere oportet, & hoc in loco in conjugatione passiva ex- posuit עפל ecce compacta in pilam est anima ejus fastuosa & arrogans instar pilæ aut collis tumescen- tis. Forsterus in lexico reddidit: In angustia arcta est, qui itidem putat Num. XIV, 44. respici, ubi à LXX. Interpretibus redditur διαβαίνομαι, vim fa- cio in ascendendo, vim faciendo ascenderunt: Lu- therus: Sie waren störrig hinauf zuziehen; & vi- detur notaricon globatio vel coarctatio in angusti- as, tametsi conjunctus fuerit ausus temerarius & su- perbus, ut exponitur Deut. I, 43. ubi LXX. expref- serunt ὑπερεβιήσατε καὶ παραβιασάμενοι ἀνέβη- τε εἰς τὸ ὄρος, quod in ascensione rebelles sese de- monstrarunt non absque contentione, ideoque locum Rom. II, 9. τοῖς ἐξ ἐριθείας etiam respexisse Prophetam Forsterus in explicat. & B. Lutherus in Comment. censent. E qua collatione apparet, LXX. Interpretum translationem, ἐὰν ὑποστείληται, verbo Ebræo respondere, sive vertatur de coarcta- tione vel retractatione, sive de superbia & elatione, sive de contentione, quæ oritur è conglobatione ac elatione, sive juxta loca parallela malit quis ea significata conjunctim accipere, ut è Forstero B. Hœpfnerus exposuit, contentione quadam sese subducere, atque aliquid audere & aggredi qua- dam animi impatientia sine fide. Qui etiam con- fert Habac. I, vers. 12. ubi Propheta Deum Pe- tram appellavit. Qui enim non in Deum fidu- ciam suam collocat, ille alias res, vel etiam se- metipsum facit, petram, arcem munitam, & tu- tum receptum, atque ita exponentem ex Sante Pagnino adducit R. Mosen: Anima impii, quæ non est recta in semetipso, id est, cui non est fi- ducia, nec fides in Deo, quæ ponit seipsam, ut turrim & arcem, ad confugiendum illuc à facie inimici, & non convertitur ad DEUM, nec ab illo quærit, ut eripiat eum. At justus, qui fidit Domino, & credit, vivet, & non opus erit, ut ponat seipsum in arce & munitione. Eun- dem ergo sensum esse versionis LXX. ab Apo- stolo retentæ ait: Ἐὰν ὑποστείληται si quis se sub- duxerit. Ὑποστέλλεσθαι enim est animo demitti, metuere, ex metu & diffidentia se subducere, atque aliorsum se recipere tanquam in locum omnibus tutum. Münsterus de superbia expo- nit: Anima putat, se satis munitam esse: Sic & Vatablus. Certe efferri solet: Et Tremellius ac Ju- nius: Ecce ebullat, id est, injustus ex infidelitate & improbitate laborans, etsi in clivum specie vi- deatur, assurgere & permagnus mons effici, tamen ebullat, id est, non magis quam bulla crepat, & sua imbecillitate rumpitur, quem sensum ap- probat B. Joh. Tarnovius in comment. ad. h. l. sed in conciliatione cum LXX. Interpp. & Apo- stoli translatione superbiam & metum conjunge- re videtur, ita enim reddit Græca: Qui se ex infidelitate, securitate aut metu subduxerit à pro- missione mea. Vulgatum autem, qui reddidit incredulum redarguit, ut & Riberam, eundem defendentem, quod verbum illud cum voce עופל imperite confundat, cujus cor non est illu- minatum, quanquam & עפל LXX. Interpretes 2. Reg. IV. vers. 24. ubi B. Lutherus id accepit, ut nomen proprium, Pagninus & Ariamonta- nus locum editum & munitextensionem reddiderunt, interpretati sint σκοτεινὸν tenebrosum. Unde B. Gerhardus hic: In Ebræo est: Ecce, qui incredu- lus est עפלה, obscurus, nebulosus, lucifuga, te- nebricosus. Conciliari possunt, inquit, textus Ebræus & versio Græca hoc modo: Qui se subtra- hit vel per incredulitatem vel per impatientiam ille etiam superbit, quia ut credere est humilitatis: Ita nolle credere est animi elati. Ludovicus de Dieu ex usu vocis עפל Arabico eam explicat, si negligatur hæc promissio, vel animus ab ea averta- tur, quod eximie convenit cum ὑποστείληται. Joh. Coccejus è Polybio adducit significationem hujus Græcæ vocis applicare sese munimento ob securitatem, si quis applicarit sese alteri, quam Messiæ, ceu munimento & præsidio suo. Quæ omnia docent, nullam necessitatem esse, ut textum Ebræum corruptum statua- mus; Magis autem convenire videtur, si Die- viana non placeat, illa de subductione è me- tu vel angustia cordis explicatio, non improbata B. Höpffnero, nec B. Tarnovio, nec aliena à vocis Ebrææ fignificatu, & cum Prophetico textui, tum præfenti loco haud incongrua. In angustia enim fuiffe populum ob Chaldæorum immanem ac tru- culentam invafionem, querula vox Prophetæ no- mine ejusdem refonans testatur, sed tu Domine Deus meus, sanctus meus, qui ab æterno es, ne moria- mur, cur taces, quod impius devorat probos? &c. Et erigit Apostolus hoc loco Ebræos oraculo Pro- phetico in angustiis, & afflictionibus ipforum, animatque ad constantiam in fide ac perfeveran- tiam in fiducia, quod celeriter venturus fit Do- minus ad piorum liberationem, five id de adven- tu novissimo gloriæ, five adventu tempestivo gratiæ intelligatur, quemadmodum de adventu prophe- tiæ vel promiffionis, aut etiam ejus, qui promiffus erat (res enim eodem recidit) sermo est, & illis, qui se subducunt præ metu & angustia ac diffiden- tia, nec firmiter promiffioni Divinæ innituntur, displicentia Domini; adeoque certus interitus inti- matur, illis vero qui per fidem ei innituntur ac dominum expectant, vita promittitur. In Ebræo est, veniens veniet, hoc est, certiffime veniet & infallibi- liter. In Græco, qui venturus est, veniet. In Ebræo lo- quitur Habacuc de prophetia, ac testatur eam certiffi- me venturam. Lutherus. Sie, die Verheissung wird gewißlich kommen. Quia vero Messias dici folet, ὁ ἐρχόμενος Matth. XI, 3. Joh. XI, 27. inde præmisso articulo ὁ (qui non habetur in LXX. Interpretum versione) hanc vaticinii partem refert ad Christum, presertim cum in Græco transitus fiat à fœminino ad masculinum, ac nucleus omnium promissionum Pro- pheticarum sit Christus, ut hic B.
