Gerhardus. Addit: Nihil impedire, quo minus dictum Propheticum ad primum & secundum Christi adventum referatur, cum adventus primus fit fundamentum secundi, & secundus fit consequens primi.

Hæc de subjecto: Quod B. Tarnovius quidem, cum Vatablo, Münstero, Junio, Tremellio prædica- tum constituit, sed juxta interpretationem LXX. Interpretum approbatam ipfimet Spiritui sancto in hoc loco manifestum est, subjecti locum id obti- nere, quod etiam obfervavit Vulgata Latina & Lu- therus. Quod itaque ad prædicatum, non est recta anima ejus in eo, eo proprie denegatur per infide- litatem & metum recedenti vel sese subducenti re- ctitudo animæ, vel etiam beneplacitum Divinum, adeoq; consequenter quies & tranquillitas animæ. Nam vox יָשַׁר fignificat recta est, uti יָשַׁר 1. Sam. XIIX, 20. 26. redditur εὐθύνω rectus sum. Expo- nitur etiam per ἀρέσκω placeo, Num. XXIII, 27. Jud. XIV, 3. 7. 1. Reg. IX, 7. Dan. IV, 24. & per εὐδοκέω complaceo, uti hoc loco redditur οὐκ εὐδοκεῖ ἡ ψυ- χή με ἐν ἀυτῷ. B. Lutherus pensihabito pronomi- ne accepit de εὐδοκίᾳ animæ, in feipfa non erit be- neplacitum animæ ejus in ipsa: Er wird keine Ruhe in seinem Herzen haben. Non est autem, cur aliter LXX. Interpretes legisse admittamus, literam nem- pe Vav pro Jod in voce עפלא aut etiam cum B. Tarnovio statuamus, lapfu Græcorum Interpretum bene ufum effe Spiritum sanctum, quum sensus idem maneat, etfi non κατὰ πόδα redditus fit textus. Nam in quo non est recta anima, in eo non potest habe- re beneplacitum Deus: quemadmodum fæpe conse- quens pro antecedenti ponitur, nec tamen textui vis infertur; neque enim verbum verbo reddidere femper LXX. senes, sed διάνοιαν non raro respexe- re, quæ hic probata fuit Spiritui sancto. Nam & su- pra, cap. I, 3. Propheta dixerat: Num ad perfidos respicies, vel in iis habebis beneplacitum? Num dele- ctaberis infidelibus? Et facit eo axioma Apostoli- cum, Ebr. XI, 6. fine fide impossibile est Deo placere. Ita membra illa opposita sese mutuo explicant: Justus ex fide sua vivet, naturam rectam habiturus est, & beneplacitum Deus in eo habebit, & ex adverso infidelis, vel qui ex metu & infidelitate sese subducunt, non vivet, sed ὑποστολῆς, ejus finis erit ἀπώλεια in- teritus, non est ei animi rectitudo (quæ vita est fide- lium, vivunt enim in fide Christi, ejusque justitia & rectitudine, qui ipse est justitia nostra, Jerem. XXIII, 6. Gal. II, 20.) non habet in eo Deus bene- placitum, unde nec ipse quietem & tranquillitatem habet animæ, vel εὐδοκίαν in semetipso. Sensum Osiander expressit: Qui fide in Christum justificatus est, is tranquillam habebit conscientiam, recreatus quippe Verbo Evangelii, & vivet cum Christo in omnem æternitatem. Itaque non est, quod ad men- tionem adventus Christi homo cohorrescat. Quod si quis subtraxerit se, subducens se à confessione Evan- gelii, ne in pericula & persecutiones incidat, is, in- quit Dominus, non placebit animæ meæ: Quemad- modum capitaneo non placet miles, qui (neglecto sa- cramento militari) propter periculum imminens sese ab exercitu subducit. Qui enim negaverit me coram hominibus (inquit Christus) negabo & ego eum co- ram Patre meo, qui in cælis est, Matth. X. Cap. Nec absimiliter B. Hunnius: Si deficiens à fide sese sub- duxerit homo, & propter afflictiones fidei professio- nem abjecerit, non probabitur animæ meæ. B. Ger- hardus: In Ebræo, inquit, apud Prophetam est: Non est recta anima ejus in ipso. LXX. referunt animum ad Deum. Ebræus textus ad hominem. Conciliari possunt hoc modo: Cujus animus non est rectus, sed perversus, ille etiam Deo non placet. Vid. de hoc loco duæ eruditæ disputationes B. Höpfneri in di- sputat. Theol. Num. XII. XIII. & tuba Jubilæi Lu- therani B. Johann. Tarnovii.

## 10:39
Verse 39. 'But we are not of withdrawal unto destruction, but of faith unto the preservation of the soul.' 'Children' is understood, which we also find expressed in certain Latin codices by the added word 'sons.' 'Children of withdrawal' are those who fail, 'children of faith' are those who believe and continue to believe. And 'unto' in both places signifies the outcome of the matter, like the Hebrew לְ. 'Preservation of the soul' is that which is called 'to gain the soul,' Luke 21:19, 'to find,' Matt. 16:25. Concerning the word 'preservation,' see what we have said on Eph. 1:14, 1 Thess. 5:9, 2 Thess. 2:14.

In the expression 'to the acquisition of the soul,' some note a metaphor drawn from negation, by which one either gains something more, or loses what he had, Mark 10:39. The application, says B. Hunnius, is a general sentence to the person of the Hebrews, whose faith the Apostle commends, so that he may more excite them to the zeal of persevering, to whom he also proposes a fruit, the acquisition of the soul, that is, the perpetual salvation of souls, to which by antithesis he opposes the perdition which certainly awaits apostates.

Latin:

Vers. 39. Ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐκ ἐσμὲν ὑποστολῆς εἰς ἀπώλειαν, ἀλλὰ πίστεως εἰς περιποίησιν ψυχῆς.] Subauditur τέκνα, quod & in Latinis codicibus quibusdam addita voce filii expressum re- perimus. Τέκνα ὑποστολῆς ii, qui deficiunt, τέκνα πίστεως, ii qui credunt & pergunt credere. Et εἰς utrobique exitum rei significat, ut לְ Ebræum. Περιποίησις ψυχῆς est id, quod κτᾶσθαι ψυχὴν dicitur Luc. XXI, 19. εὑρίσκειν, Matth. XVI, 25. De voce περιποιήσεως vide, quæ diximus ad Ephes. I, 14. 1. Thess. V, 9. 2. Thess. II, 14.

In voce ad animæ acquisitionem notant non- nulli metaphoram à negatione ductam, qua quis vel lucratur amplius quid, vel perdit, quod habebat, Marci X, 39. Applicatio, inquit B. Hunnius, gene- ralis sententiæ ad personam Ebræorum, quorum fi- dem commendat Apostolus, ut ad perseverandi stu- dium magis exuscitet, quibus etiam fructum propo- nit, acquisitionem animæ, hoc est, salutem animarum perpetuam, cui per antithesin opponit perditionem quæ certo maneat apostatas.

## 11:1 Argument
CHAPTER XI.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

He explains what faith is, and by the examples of the ancients, especially Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, the parents of Moses, Moses himself, the Israelites, Joshua, Rahab, and others, he declares the nature and exercises of justifying faith, who received a testimony, even though they did not obtain the promise.

There are two parts: 1. The definition of faith, verse 1. 2. The catalog and review of the faithful of the Old Testament, up to verse 40.

PART I. The definition of faith.

Verse 1.

Ἔστι δὲ πίστις] Since mention of faith had occurred through the passage of Habakkuk, this writer wished to heap up its great praises; not that faith alone suffices for obtaining salvation, but because from faith are born both that justice and holiness to which eternal life is promised. And therefore he shows that faith has always been held in the highest regard by God and pious men. Faith is the root of the law, say the Rabbis Bacchai and Channanael. But he understands by faith that by which one believes and trusts in the words of God. For he is not dealing with faith in Christ when he brings forward examples from ancient times, but with faith in God, of which that Evangelical faith is the most excellent species, which is faith in Christ in such a way that it is simultaneously faith in GOD, because what Christ said, he said in the name of GOD. See John XIV. 1. He describes faith partly through its effects, partly through its causes, and that by metonymy.

Various errors of Grotius are contained here: 1. That he denies, against the constant opinion of the Apostle, that faith alone suffices for obtaining salvation, than which the holy Apostle urges nothing more against the pseudo-Apostles than that we are justified by faith alone: Nor has he taught anything else here, but for that purpose he dealt with the unique expiatory sacrifice of Christ, so that he might teach that salvation consists for us by that alone, apprehended through faith, for the sake of which he began an exhortation to faith and perseverance in faith in the next chapter: which he now pursues for that same reason, having brought in the definition of justifying faith and a catalog of the examples of the ancient faithful, who were justified and saved through faith in Christ. 2. Grotius therefore significantly perverts the scope of the present chapter when he wishes it to be shown only that faith has always been held in the highest regard by God and pious men. He does not do this alone or primarily, but he describes above all the nature and exercises of faith; he does not present the estimation of faith before God and pious men, but the duties and acts of faith. 3. Grotius asserts in an Arminian sense that justice and holiness, to which eternal life is promised, are born from faith; but Scripture does not promise eternal life to our justice or inherent holiness, but teaches that the justice of Christ is apprehended by faith, and that we are both justified and saved by a justice not our own but imputed. 4. Grotius wishes to designate faith as legal, not Evangelical, in the manner of the Socinians, which is to say, that which pertains to the commandment of the first table, by which one believes and trusts in the words of God, not that by which the justice of Christ is apprehended, or which is said to be imputed for justice. 5. And therefore he very badly denies that it is dealing with faith in Christ when the examples of ancient times are produced: when nevertheless the Apostle is dealing with that faith and trust which is not to be cast away, lest they fall into apostasy from faith in Christ, and which has a great reward: Of ὑπομονῇ (patience) in faith, by which the promise is obtained: Of the faith by which the just man lives, of the faith which has περιποίησιν τῆς ψυχῆς (the preservation of the soul) and eternal salvation as its end, which is faith in Christ, 1 Pet. I. verse 9. 6. He makes Evangelical faith a species of legal faith, sophistically, indeed with a heretical spirit, confusing the law and the Gospel, which are most distinct in justification: All of which will be more abundantly clear from what follows.

Ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις] A certain firm expectation of things hoped for. For we have also had the word ὑποστάσεως above at III. 14, and there we said that the Hebrew word תוחלת is translated sometimes by the word ἐλπίδα (hope), sometimes more effectively by the word ὑποστάσεως (substance/assurance). See also 2 Cor. IX. verse 4. Thus Polybius calls the fortitude of Cocles ὑπόστασιν.

The whole substance of faith, says Tertullian in 'On the Apparel of Women' II. Πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος ὀ βλεπομένων) That is, faith is born from a diligent examination of those things which are said about matters that do not fall under the senses. Such as offspring from a barren wife, those future riches of which we spoke above at X. 35, and other similar things. In the glossary, ἔλεγχος is judgment, proof. Thus Herodotus, Thucydides, Plato, and Isocrates often use this word. Thus in Xenophon, ἐλέγχεσθαι γελοῖον ὢν, he is convicted of being ridiculous. And hence in dialectics, ἔλεγχοι are methods of testing arguments. This is a certain delineation of faith from its effects and from its causes, as we have said. Let us see others as well. For Sirach, πίστις ἀρχὴ κολλήσεως Θεῶ (faith is the beginning of cleaving to God), XXV. 17. For Epicurus, πίστις is πρόληψις τῆς διανοίας (a preconception of the mind). For Strabo, περὶ τὸ ὂν σάσις (a standing regarding being). For Basilides, ψυχῆς συγκατάθεσις τῶν μὴ κινόντων τὴν αἴσθησιν διὰ τὸ μὴ παρεῖναι (the soul's assent to things that do not move the senses because they are not present). For Clement of Alexandria, Strom. II. Συγκατάθεσις ἰσχυρά τινι (a strong assent to something): Also ὑπόληψις ἑκούσιος (a voluntary assumption), καὶ πρόληψις εὐγνώμονος προκαταλήψεως (and a preconception of a favorable anticipation). Then ἰσχὺς εἰς σωτηρίαν καὶ δύναμις εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον (strength for salvation and power for eternal life). And because hope is placed here as an effect of faith, I will not wrongly bring in here the passage of Philo concerning rewards and punishments: 'One must look at the most necessary seed, which the poet sowed in the virtuous land of the rational soul. The first seed of this is hope, the source of lives; for by hope the merchant strips himself for the manifold ways of gain. By hope the shipmaster attempts the long seas; by hope of glory the ambitious man chooses citizenship and the care of public affairs. Through hope of prizes and crowns, even the athletes of the body have contended in the gymnastic games.' Hope of happiness also raises the zealots of virtue to philosophize, as those who will be able by this both to see the nature of things that are, and to do what follows for the theoretical and practical perfection of the best lives, of which he who attains it is immediately happy.' And soon: 'But only that which is worthy of acceptance: to which one has entrusted hope in God, both as the cause of its generation, and as the only one sufficient to preserve it, unchangeable and incorruptible.' To the same Philo, in 'On the Confusion of Tongues,' πίστις is called ὀχυρωτάτη καὶ βεβαιοτάτη διάθεσις (a most fortified and most certain disposition). The same, in 'On the Heir of Divine Things': 'The work of one who has believed is to no longer seek.' In the same place, for ἐπίστευσε (he believed) he put βεβαίως κατείληφε (he has firmly grasped). In the same author's book on Abraham: Μόνον ἦν ἀψευδὲς καὶ βέβαιον ἀγαθὸν πίστις, ἡ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν πίστις παρηγόρημα βίου, πλήρωμα χρηστῶν ἐλπίδων, ἀφορία μὲν κακῶν, ἀγαθῶν δὲ φορὰ, κακοδαιμονίας ἀπόγνωσις, εὐσεβείας γνῶσις, εὐδαιμονίας κλῆρος., ἓν ἅπασι βελτίωσις ἐπερηρεισμένη τῷ πάντων αἰτίῳ, καὶ δυναμένῳ μὲν πάντα, βουλομένῳ δὲ τὰ ἄριστα. In the same place he soon calls faith towards the Existent One the queen of virtues. The words which Josephus, Antiquities II. 6, attributes to Moses during the crossing of the Red Sea pertain to this matter: Οὐδὲ ἀνθρώποις καλῶς τὰ παρόντα πεπολιτευμένοις πρὸς ὑμᾶς δίκαιον ἀπιστεῖν, ὡς οὐχ ὁμοίοις ἐσομένοις πρὸς τὰ μέλλοντα. Τῆς δὲ τοῦ Θεοῦ τὸν ἀπογνώσεσθαι ὑμᾶς προνοίας μανίας ἔργον ἂν εἴη παρ᾽ ᾧ πάντα ὑμῖν ἀπήντηκεν, ὅσα δι᾿ ἐμοῦ σωτηρίαν, καὶ τὴν ἀπαλλαγὴν τῆς δουλείας οὐδὲ προσδοκῶσιν ὑπέσχετο, μᾶλλον δὲ χρῆν ἐν ἀπόροις γεγενημένους βοηθὸν ἐλπίζειν τὸν Θεόν. Then: Οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ μικροῖς τὸ θεῖον τὴν ἑαυτοῦ συμμαχίαν ἵστησιν ἵνα δίδωσιν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐφ᾽ οἷς ἀνθρωπίνῃ ἐλπίδι μὴ βλέποι πρὸς τὸ κρεῖττον παρέσται. Ὅθεν τοιαῦτα βοηθήσειν πιστεύοντες, ᾧ δύναμις καὶ τὰ μικρὰ ποιῆσαι μέγαλα, καὶ τῶν τηλικούτων ἀσθένειαν καταψηφίσασθαι, μὴ καταπεπλήχθαι τὴν Αἰγυπτίων παρασκευήν. Μηδὲ ὅτι θάλασσα κωλύει ὑμῖν, ὄρη τε φυγῆς ὁδὸν οὐ παρέχοντα διὰ τοῦτο ἀπογινώσκετε τῆς σωτηρίας. Γένοιτο γὰρ ἂν καὶ ταῦθ᾽ ὑμῖν πεδία τῷ Θεῷ θελήσαντι, κἂν γῆ τὸ πέλαγος. Faith is sometimes taken in such a way that it includes the obedience which faith produces. Salvian, On the Government of God, III: What then is credulity or faith? I think it is for a man to believe Christ faithfully, that is, to be faithful to God, which is to keep the commands of God faithfully.

Just as the first member in this definition of faith, ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, is not badly explained as a certain firm expectation of things hoped for; so the sense of the latter, πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων, is rendered less appropriately, that is, faith is born from a diligent examination of those things which are said about matters that do not fall under the senses. Also, that whole description is wrongly taken as a certain delineation of faith from effects and causes, as if a firm expectation were the effect of faith: and as if the ἔλεγχος, which he interprets as an examination of those things which are said, were the cause of faith. Others more correctly think that the form of faith is expressed as the consistency of the mind in assent, and of the will in firm and immovable trust in the things exhibited in the Divine promise, which without doubt we hope for, because we are convinced in our mind of the truth of things which do not appear, but are exhibited by the word of promise, which conviction of mind is brought about not by the weight of arguments, but by the authority of God promising and of the Word of promise. For faith is formally a ὑπόστασις of this kind, both of the mind and of the will regarding the assent of the mind, but also regarding the trust of the will, leaning upon the Word of promise concerning things hoped for, together with the ἐλέγχῳ and conviction of the mind concerning those things which we do not see, but perceive and understand with the mind, and therefore embrace; that consistency of mind and will is rendered certain, firm, and immovable, and is as it were substantiated. But these things are to be explained a little more fully. 1. The word ὑπόστασις does not denote substance properly so called, or a person, as it is taken in Heb. 1:2: for who would call faith a substance? Wherefore there is no reason why we should laboriously inquire with the Scholastics how faith is called a substance, as is done by Ludovicus Terra on this passage. 2. Nor is faith called a ὑπόστασις because it makes absent things present and sets them forth, as the Calvinists trifle, that the body of CHRIST, although absent and confined in heaven, is nevertheless set forth as present on earth through faith in the holy supper, truly and really, which is to play and to delude oneself, when we imagine that something is really present to us which is as far distant as the highest heaven is from the earth, and we ascribe to faith that power, that it really sets forth things that are really absent, that is, that it performs those things which are truly ἀνύπαρκτά, and cannot be done even by GOD. 3. Nor is faith called a substance by analogy, because as a substance is the foundation of accidents, which proceed from the substance, which is the cause of the existence of accidents, without which they cannot exist: so faith might be a substance through similarity or agreement with a substance, as the foundation and first Being of the whole spiritual edifice, from which all virtues proceed, and the cause of their existence, as the Scholastics and the sententiaries foolishly imagine. For the Apostle did not say that faith is the ὑπόστασιν of virtues, but of things hoped for, nor does the Holy Spirit ever philosophize about faith in this way. See concerning these things the Philosophia sobria of Meisner, part II, section I, question XI. 4. Nor is Thomas's analogy that faith is a substance through similarity, because it embraces in itself things hoped for, as a substance is said to support accidents by its power: But it apprehends them in act in the promises, and therefore embraces and appropriates them to itself. 5. Bellarmino approaches closer to the truth, book 1 de justif. chap. V, when he renders ὑπόστασιν as base and foundation. For also the blessed Hunnius on this passage says: The word ὑποστάσεως, he says, is metaphorical, by which the Apostle intimates that faith is like a base and column or foundation of those things which are hoped for, so that it is permitted to hope for the goods of the future age without doubt, since that hope leans upon the immutable promise of God, of which faith is the correlate.

So that the genuine sense of the Apostle may be clearly established, the other word τῶν ἐλπιζομένων must be joined at the same time: which Augustine almost everywhere understood actively, of those hoping, as in epist. 112 to Paul, book II de peccat. merit. & remiss. chap. 31, tract. 79 in John, hom. 32 in book 2 of the Homilies, etc. But it is without doubt more correctly rendered passively, of things hoped for, just as is evident from the other member, τῶν μὴ βλεπομένων, which cannot be understood actively of seeing men, but must be taken passively of things not appearing. Whence all the Greeks, Basil in his explanation of Psalm 115, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Theophylact, Oecumenius understand the word τῶν ἐλπιζομένων passively, as the Vulgate Interpreter rendered it, of things hoped for. But by things hoped for are understood either strictly future things, about which faith is concerned, not indeed as they are future: for thus they are the object of hope: But by reason of the present promise, or in a more general sense, those things which are hoped for, that is, about which we are confident, in which way hope often occurs also concerning present goods. In the former sense faith is the ὑπόστασις of things hoped for, insofar as faith, looking at the promise concerning future things, sets them before not only the intellect, but also the affection as if they were present, on account of the infallible truth of GOD, namely the word ὑπόστασις is taken in the sense of setting forth and establishing and confirming, in which way the Apostle called the ὑπόστασις καυχήσεως, 2 Cor. 9:4, the alacrity in providing for alms, and chapter 11:17, the labors of his apostleship, because they confirmed and established his boasting. To this pertains what Galen said, that the foot is an ὄργανον βάσεως ἢ ἕδρας, that is, such a thing as provides the use of a base or foundation for the body, book III de usu part. chap. 5 and 6, and what Aristotle teaches, book II de part. animal. chap. 16, that animals have feet also ἕνεχ' ὑποστάσεως τῦ βάρους, so that they may carry or support the mass of the human body; thus faith sets forth and confirms things hoped for to the mind and affection, and bestows consistency upon them. In which way Chrysostom explains in this place that faith is the ὑπόστασιν of things hoped for, since those things which are in hope ἀνυπόστατα εἶναι δοκεῖ, seem not to have subsistence; but faith grants them ὑπόστασιν, bestows consistency, nay, it is the essence of things hoped for. And Oecumenius: For since those things which are in hope do not have subsistence, as things which are not yet present, faith is a certain essence of them and a subsistence, making them in a certain way to be and to be present, by this very fact, that it believes them to be. It is therefore said to be so not only because it establishes the one hoping, but because it also sets forth and represents to him the thing hoped for, as Chrysostom declared by the example of the resurrection on this passage. By this reasoning, therefore, that definition will be causal, because the name of the proper effect is attributed to its cause. To which contributes what Bellarmino himself has, book 1 de justif. chap. V, col. 821: For faith being the substance of things hoped for is nothing else than that those things which are hoped for, because they are future, have no subsistence or foundation, except in the intellect through faith. Therefore faith is as it were the life and soul of things which are hoped for, since by apprehending them and representing them to the mind, it makes them in a certain way to be present, and to live, although in reality they are not, except as future.

In the latter sense, however, faith is τῶν ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, because in those things concerning which we are confident, and thus which are exhibited to us by Divine promise, we stand and remain unmoved and firm. And thus the consistency, or subsistence, of faith is defined in those things concerning which confidence can be had. Which subsistence includes the confidence itself, which we constitute as the form of faith. Since such ὑπόστασις and consistency occurs not only in the intellect, but also in the will or appetite, and that especially, and not only regarding future goods, but also regarding present ones. Which can easily be proved 1. because the faith, concerning which from Habac.

II. verse 3. the Apostle discoursed, was nothing other than a firm assent held to the Divine promise concerning the Messiah, and trust in Him, as our righteousness and our rock, as was shown before. Therefore, when the Apostle now wishes to define it, saying, 'but faith is the ὑπόςασις of things hoped for,' it is necessary that the Apostolic description should agree with the Prophetic explanation of faith. 2. Because that faith, by which the just man lives and obtains the promise, the περιποίησιν τῆς ψυχῆς, by which he is justified and saved, is a trust concerning present and future goods, which he describes by παῤῥησίαν, and for which he requires ὑπομονὴν. 3. Because he designated the trust of hope, by which he designated future things, and of faith, by which he designated present things, by the general name ὑπόςασις in Heb. III. 14, which he also named παῤῥησίαν in verse 6; where Bellarmine is absurd in book 1 on justification chapter XI. contending that Heb. III. verse 14, 'the beginning of the ὑποσάσεως' is to be explained as the beginning of the new creature, which is faith; and furthermore the beginning of the new substance of CHRIST, through which He himself is formed in us, rather than it being explained by the Apostle himself as παῤῥησίᾳ and trust. 4. Ὑπόςασις is said from ὑφίςασθαι, to stand firmly, not to yield, not to flee; as Plutarch says: those who surrendered were spared, but those who stood their ground (ὑφισαμένους) were slaughtered. Polybius in the description of Horatius Cocles (which passage Grotius points out): 'the enemies were struck not so much by his strength as by his ὑπόςασιν and daring': The enemies did not fear his strength so much as his trust, and that undaunted subsistence of his spirit, not yielding to terrors or dangers. And therefore ὑπόςασις denotes a firm subsistence of mind and heart, when it conceives an immovable trust, and firmly subsists and persists in it. 5. Thus also ὑπόςασις is taken among the LXX. Interpreters of Ruth I. verse 12. 'I have no ὑπόςασις, that I should have a husband' (תִּקְוָה), Psalm XXXIX. verse 8. 'And now what is my ὑπομονὴ expectation?' 'My ὑπόςασίς is from you'; where in the Hebrew it is קוֹוִי and תּוֹחַלְתִּי, Ezech. XIX. 5. 'your ὑπόςασίς perished' (תִקְוָתָהּ) Mich. V. verse 6. 'that he may not stand (ὑποσῇ) among the sons of men', that he waits for no one nor expects any man, as B. Luther translates. In the Hebrew the words יִקַוֶּה and יְיַחֵל explain each other, which word יִחֵל is otherwise rendered by προσμένειν, ἐλπίζειν, ἐπελπίζειν, to expect, to hope, to fix hope, whence the noun תּוֹחֶלֶת is explained by the LXX as ἐλπὶς, Thren. III. 18. 'boasting', Prov. XI. verse 7. 'ὑπόςασις', Psalm XX. verse 7, XXXIII. verse 5. To which 6. B. Gerhard refers in this place, Is. XXVI. 3. Faith is יֵצֶר סָמוּךְ, a supported figment, which supports itself and leans upon Christ the Savior and His Word. 7. Flacius illustrates this explanation from the German language, with the approval of B. Meisner in Phil. Sobr., where the word 'unterstehen' comprises not only some great endeavor, but also great trust or boldness in carrying out a matter rightly, because the Greek word ὑφίστημι and the German 'unterstehen' agree in etymology. Concerning which B. Höpfner in disputation VI. on justification, p. 357, has this: How faith is a subsistence in things of trust or things about which trust can be had: Namely, faith is like a foot, by which we move and approach GOD, Heb. XI. verse 6, and we insist upon His promise offering grace, Rom. V. verse 2, and we dare to desire and ask from Him the promised goods, Rom. IV. verse 2. The Germans would express this meaning thus: 'Since one rests upon GOD'S promise, and stands upon it, and therefore also dares to desire and ask for the benefits promised by Him.' And in this meaning it is taken in Eph. III. verse 12. Where it is helpful to observe from the same B. Höpfner the metaphor taken from the nature of the foot, disp. II. page 110. For the body cannot be moved from place to place unless one foot is resting while the other is moved forward in walking: So also through faith we walk in the perfect obedience of Christ, and have access into grace, and through the same faith we stand, Rom. V. verse 2. Thus we walk as if with a foot upon the Evangelical promises showing Christ's righteousness, so that we may fix the steps of our trust in and upon it, and come to GOD, John XIV. verse 6, and enter into eternal life, John V. verse 24. Hence to come to Christ is the same as to believe in Him, John V. verse 40, chapter VI. verse 44, 65, chapter VII. verse 35, 36, 37. In such a way Abraham walked before GOD, Gen. XVII. verse 1, and all who are justified are said in Rom. IV. verse 12 to 'στοιχεῖν τοῖς ἴχνεσι πίςεως', to walk with a straight foot in the footsteps of Abraham, that is, by such faith, as if in his footsteps, according to whose example they believe in Christ. This B. Höpfner learnedly states, because the appellation of trust, which is named ὑπόστασις, looks to the metaphor taken from the office of the foot: Inasmuch as the foot is an ὄργανον not only βασιτικὸν, an ambulatory instrument, as Galen teaches in book III. de usu part. cap. IV., but also of a base or support, such that it provides the use of a base or prop to the body. 8. Philipp Melanchthon in consiliis Theolog. page 138. concerning these things: Some say it is an encomium rather than a definition, which I do not disapprove, but yet encomia, if they are apt and proper, are taken from definitions: Certainly they ought not to dissent from them. I affirm, therefore, that it is a true and convenient definition. For faith, of which mention is made here, comprises two things: Knowledge or assent, and trust or the motion of the heart, which accompanies assent. First, therefore, faith is certain knowledge of things not appearing. He calls that ἔλεγχον, that is, by faith we certainly establish that GOD is, that Christ is the Son of GOD, the Redeemer of the human race, that He is going to judge the whole human race. Then it is not only knowledge, but also the expectation of promises, that is, trust, by which we establish that the promises of GOD happen to us, namely that on account of Christ GOD forgives our sins, hears us, cares for us, helps us, and is about to deliver us from eternal death. This confidence, by which we determine that God is propitious to us, and that we are an object of care to GOD, he embraces when he says it is an expectation. Since, therefore, the nature of faith is rightly declared, the definition is to be approved, and if one must speak dialectically, certain knowledge rightly holds the place of the genus, and then expectation. For faith is first knowledge, then also a movement of the heart, by which we expect the things promised, and truly determine that we are an object of care to GOD. The differences are taken from the objects: Because faith is occupied with the word of GOD, by which heavenly goods are promised, not yet subject to sense, namely the remission of sins, because God hears us, cares for us, and is about to grant us eternal life.

As regards, therefore, the other member, ἔλεγχον μὴ βλεπομένων, as it is certain that ἔλεγχον denotes argumentation and conviction, in the way it occurs in John VIII. verse 16: Who ἐλέγχει convinces me, or can convince me of sin? and John XVI. The Holy Spirit ἐλέγξει will convince the world of sin: Add Tit. I. verse 13. 1. Tim. III. verse 16. Which signification is also accepted by secular writers, e.g., Lucian: Socrates walks about there, διελέγχων [convincing] all: Thus, by metalepsis, the assent of the mind is signified as elicited through the conviction of the Word. Nor does Bellarmine deny this in the place cited. Those words, the argument of things not appearing, do not refer to the things themselves, but explain another virtue of faith, which is to convince the intellect and lead it to assent to those things which it neither grasps nor understands.

Where, however, two things are to be observed: First, that he explains τὰ μὴ βλεπόμενα [things not seen] as things that are not understood, when they are rather those things which are not seen, as is evident even from verse 3: For there a twofold argument is held: then that faith cannot be defined by ignorance, because it is said πίστει νοοῦμεν [by faith we understand]. But where νόησις [understanding] is, there is no ignorance: then that τὰ βλεπόμενα [things seen] and τὰ μὴ ἐκφαινόμενα [things not manifest] are opposed: therefore they are not those things which are not understood, but those which are not seen. This, however, must be understood reduplicatively, namely, that they are not seen in that they are believed, even if other things that are believed could otherwise be seen; just as, for example, it was said to Thomas in John 20:29: because you have seen, you have believed. He had seen that it was not a ghost, but Jesus himself who was appearing; yet he did not see in the way he believed: For to see belongs to the eyes of the body, to believe belongs to the eyes of the mind, whence it is added that they are blessed who are μὴ ἰδόντες [not having seen], not seeing with the eyes of the body, καὶ πιστεύσαντες [and having believed]. B. Selneccer distinguishes in Part II, Paedag., p. 438, between the complex or whole statements, and the incomplex, or parts of a statement. The complex itself is not seen, but believed; the incomplex, however, and that which has the nature of a part, can sometimes be seen: where he says: That canon, that articles of faith are not visible, must be understood concerning propositions, or the complex; which is not visible, even if the subjects in many propositions are invisible. But because faith, as it is knowledge and assent, is concerned only with Divine statements, and thus mere complexes, hence everything that is believed, insofar as it is believed, does not fall into the senses, although in part, and according to another respect, it may be seen.

Secondly, that Bellarmine gathers from this description that faith does not pertain to the will, but to the intellect, because ἔλεγχος [conviction], that is, demonstration and conviction, pertains to the intellect: For it belongs to the intellect to be convinced by arguments, to assent, and to judge. But in vain. For the fallacy of composition and division is committed, since the Apostle calls faith not only ἔλεγχον μὴ βλεπομένων [the conviction of things not seen], but also ὑπόστασιν τῶν ἐλπιζομένων [the substance of things hoped for], and both are joined in the description of faith. That this indeed brings in trust has already been shown. Bellarmine replies that faith is called the substance of a future thing, but to represent is not of the will, where there is trust, but of the intellect. For the latter, apprehending the thing through an impressed species, makes the thing to be ancient. Resp. 1. Faith as ὑπόστασις [substance] is not only of a future thing, but is also occupied with present goods, insofar as it is a subsistence in those things about which trust can be had, as we have already said: just as hope can also be taken from trust concerning present goods. 2. Nor does the representation of a hoped-for thing occur only in the intellect, but also, and indeed especially, in the appetite. For even those things which are feared are represented to the intellect, yet they are not the object of trust. 3. Even if τὰ ἐλπιζόμενα [things hoped for] were taken as future things, they are not presented to faith as future, but by reason of the present promise: And thus faith, looking at the promise concerning future things, presents the things to be hoped for not only to the intellect but also to the affection, as if they were present: and bestows upon them subsistence in the mind and will. 4. Bellarmine is mistaken in that he thinks future things subsist in the mind through the impression of a species. For how can a species be abstracted from unknown things, such as he wishes those things to be which are believed or hoped for? How will anyone imagine for himself a species of that life which the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard? 5. Faith cannot cause those things which are hoped for to subsist in the mind unless there is at the same time firm and immovable trust. For since they do not subsist in the mind because of the impression of a species, but because of the highest πληροφορίαν [full assurance] and infallible certainty, trust is needed, by which faith embraces the things hoped for as certainly as if they were already present in actual fact: Just as it is said of Abraham, that he did not consider his own body now dead; but having embraced the Word of God, he acquiesced in the promise of GOD alone with such certain and full παῤῥησίᾳ [boldness] as if he had already obtained the promised thing, Rom. 4:19-20. Thus, when someone is persuaded of the Evangelical promises, he conceives trust from the grace of God and the merit of CHRIST, and firmly trusts in God, so much so that no one will assent to Divine promises with full persuasion in whose heart an immovable trust does not arise. Whence Jansenius, Bishop of Ghent, in Harmon. Evang. ch. 32, most correctly says: the name of faith is used in the Gospels, when salvation is attributed to it, or the attainment of all things which we wish to embrace, to mean both: namely, both that firm assent in believing things about God and Christ, and the trust conceived from His omnipotent goodness.

Bellarmine objects against this that special mercy is not something to be hoped for, but a present or past gift, since we ourselves say that it pertains to faith that everyone should believe that his sins have been forgiven him, and that he is acceptable to GOD through Christ, and is reputed as just. But although the mercy of GOD is viewed as present, yet it can be comprehended under the name of τὰ ἐλπιζομένων [things hoped for], by which all things about which trust can be had are comprehended. Nor indeed is justifying faith to believe that sins have already been forgiven, but this is a consequence of justification, and pertains to a reflex act; it is not, however, an antecedent of justification, but it looks at the Divine promise, that GOD wills to forgive sins, and it apprehends the grace which is offered, and trustfully embraces the merit of Christ, the Word of promise, and in the same the things hoped for offered therein, the remission of sins and eternal life. As for the objection which the Papists raise, that in this definition of faith no mention is made of CHRIST or of His merit, which is also the objection of the Socinians and Arminians: whence Grotius also gathers that the Apostle is not here treating of faith in CHRIST, but of faith in GOD: to this we reply: that the Papists, as may be seen in Bellarmine at the cited passage, acknowledge that justifying faith is here described. Now, that faith in CHRIST is required for justifying faith is placed beyond all hazard of controversy between us and the Papists. For that the Apostle in this place defines justifying faith (so Bellarmine has it in chapter V.), since in the final part of the previous chapter he had said: The just shall live by faith; but if he withdraw himself, my soul shall have no pleasure in him. But we are not the children of withdrawal unto perdition, but of faith unto the acquisition of the soul: he immediately subjoins, with no word intervening: Now faith is the substance of things to be hoped for, etc., where you see defined that faith by which the just man lives, and by which we please God, and whose children we are unto the acquisition of the soul, and from which he who withdraws himself rushes into extreme perdition. Then, in the rest of the chapter, the Apostle repeats more than once that this is the faith without which it is impossible to please God, and through which all the saints have pleased God. Justifying faith is therefore defined. Furthermore, concerning faith in Christ, Bellarmine says thus in chapter VIII: This faith, he says, which regards the Divinity of Christ, is itself that which grants to itself both justice and eternal life, when he had brought forward the passage from Rom. X: This is the word of faith which we preach, that if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved, Bellarmine added: Here also we see most openly that the object of justifying and saving faith is the resurrection of the Son of God. And then, when he had proposed the words of the Apostle from 1 Corinthians XV: I make known to you the Gospel which I preached, in which you stand, by which also you are saved, if you have not believed in vain. For I delivered to you first of all, which I also received, that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the Scriptures, etc., he adds: Where without doubt the object of saving faith is explained, and it is not only said, I delivered to you, that each one should certainly believe that he himself is justified through Christ, but I delivered to you to be believed the passion, burial, and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ: These therefore undoubtedly pertain to the object of faith: but that it pertains to it, that each one should believe that he is justified through Christ, is not our opinion, but Bellarmine's calumny: For this is a consequence of justification. Yet justifying faith has for its object the remission of sins as something to be obtained, not as already obtained, which not even Bellarmine himself could deny: Since in the Apostolic Creed, by which he wishes the objects of faith to be contained, we profess that we believe in the remission of sins. But he objects in vain that the meaning of that article is, I believe and confess that in the Catholic Church there is the gift of the remission of sins. For just as each one must believe in God the Father, and the Son of God, and in the Holy Spirit: Just as also the passion, burial, and resurrection of Christ must be believed, as Bellarmine admits: So also the remission of sins must be believed by each one: but those things are believed, not because they are in the Church, or because they are to be delivered, but because each one ought to believe in God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as his own God, and that Christ suffered for him, was buried, and rose again, just as 1 Corinthians XV has it, for his sins. Therefore each one ought also to believe that the remission of sins is obtained by him, that he will rise again, that he will obtain eternal life, because the just man shall live by his faith. Although, however, in that Pauline description of faith no mention is made explicitly of faith in Christ, yet elsewhere, when the object of faith is explained, which is expressed here only in general, Christ and his merit and satisfaction are not passed over in silence: and when mention is made of things to be hoped for or to be believed, and of τῶν μὴ βλεπομένων, which we do not see but believe, it ought to be considered that under these words are comprehended those things which he taught elsewhere are to be believed, and indeed which the Apostle has already proposed expressly in this epistle for that reason, and which he is now about to illustrate with examples. For he exhorts both by precepts and by examples to πληροφορίαν πίστεως, and παῤῥησίαν καὶ ὑπομονήν, so that they may not become children of ὑποστολῆς εἰς ἀπώλειαν, but remain children of πίστεως εἰς περιποίησιν ψυχῆς by the example of the faithful of old, as having παῤῥησίαν for the entrance of the Saints IN THE BLOOD OF JESUS, and a great priest, concerning whose expiatory sacrifice and intercession in heaven he had treated at length. Since therefore the Apostle advises and exhorts by design that we should embrace this Priest and his sacrifice and intercession by faith, so that we may live by that faith and obtain the redemption of the soul, who can doubt that these pertain to the object of justifying and saving faith according to the mind of the Apostle? But that faith is taken, whether here or elsewhere, when there is talk of justifying faith, in such a way that it comprehends the obedience which faith produces, which Grotius wishes, cannot be demonstrated from the scriptures, and is in reality ἀντιφαλικόν: For the effect is not the cause itself, therefore neither should faith as a cause be confused with the obedience which it itself produces, much less can it be comprehended together in one word.

PART II. A catalog or review of the faithful of the Old Testament.

Latin:

CAPUT XI.

ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Explicat, quid sit fides & exemplis veterum imprimis, utpote Abelie, Enochi, Noæ, Abra- hami, Saræ, Isaaci, Jacobi, Josephi, Paren- tum Mosis, Mosis ipsius, Israëlltarum, Jo- suæ, Rahab, & aliorum fidei justificantis na- turam & exercitia declarat, qui testimo- nium acceperunt, etsi non adepti sint pro- missionem.

Partes duæ sunt 1. Fidei definitio vers. 1. 2. Fi- delium Veteris Testamenti catalogus & recensio, ad vers. 40.

PARS I. Fidei definitio.

Vers. 1.

Ἔστι δὲ πίστις] Cum per Habacuci locum fidei inci- disset mentio, voluit Scriptor hic magna ejus præco- nia congerere; non quod sola fides sufficiat ad conse- quendam salutem, sed quod ex fide nascatur & justi- tia & sanctitas illa, cui vita æterna promittitur. Ideoq; ostendit, fidem semper à Deo & piis hominibus factam maximi. Fides radix legis ajunt Rabbini Bacchai [& Channanael. Fidem autem intelligit eam, qua Dei dictis creditur atque fiditur. Neque enim de fide in Christum agit, cum veterum temporum exempla pro- fert, sed de fide in Deum, cujus species excellentissima est fides illa Evangelica, quæ ita est fides in Christum, ut simul sit fides in DEUM, quia quæ dixit Christus, ea dixit DEI nomine. Vide Joh. XIV. 1. Describit autem fidem partim per effectus, partim per causas, idque per Μετωνυμίαν.

Diversi hic continentur Grotii errores, 1. Quod negat contra Apostoli constantem sententiam so- lam fidem sufficere ad consequendam salutem, quàm nihil magis contra Pseudo-Apostolos urgeat S. Apostolus, quam quod sola fide justificemur: Nec aliud hic tradiderit, sed eo fine de unico sa- crificio Christi expiatorio egerit, ut eo solo per fi- dem apprehenso salutem nobis constare doceret, cujus gratia parænesin ad fidem & perseverantiam in fide, proximo capite cœpit: quam nunc idea etiam, adducta fidei justificantis definitione & exemplorum fidelium veterum, qui per fidem in Christum justificati & salvati sunt, catalogo, per- sequitur. 2. Scopum ergo capitis præsentis insi- gniter pervertit Grotius, cum id solum ostendi vult fidem semper à Deo & piis hominibus factam ma- ximi. Non id solum aut potissimum agit, sed im- primis naturam & exercitia fidei describit, non æstimationem fidei apud Deum & pios homines, sed officia & actus fidei exhibet. 3. Ex fide nasci ju- stitiam & sanctitatem, cui vita æterna promittatur, Grotius Arminiano sensu asserit; Scriptura vero nõ justitiæ nostræ aut sanctitati inhærenti vitam pro- mittit æternam, sed fide apprehendi justitiam Chri- sti, nosque & justificari & salvari justitia non pro- pria sed imputata docet. 4. Fidem cum Socinianis legalem, non Evangelicam designari vult Grotius, quæ scilicet ad tabulæ primæ pertineat præceptum qua Dei dictis creditur, ac confiditur, non qua justi- tia Christi apprehenditur, aut quæ imputari dicitur ad justitiam. 5. Ideoque pessime negat de fide in Christum agi, cum veterum temporum exempla pro- ducuntur: quum tamen Apostolus de ea fide ac fi- ducia agat, quæ abjicienda non sit, ne in apostasiam à fide in Christum ruant, quæque magnam remune- rationem habet: De ὑπομονῇ in fide, qua promissio obtinetur: De fide, qua justus vivit, de fide quæ περιποίησιν τῆς ψυχῆς & salutem æternam pro fine habeat, quæ est fides in Christum, 1. Petr. I. vers. 9. 6. Fidem Evangelicam facit speciem fidei legalis, So- phistice, imò hæretico Spiritu, confundens legem & Evangelium, quæ in justificatione distinctissima sunt: Quæ omnia è sequentibus uberius con- stabunt.

Ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις] Rerum sperandarum firma quædam expectatio. Nam & sic supra habuimus vo- cem ὑποστάσεως III. 14. & ibi diximus vocem Ebræam תוחלת modo verti per vocem ἐλπίδα, modo effica- cius per vocem ὑποστάσεως. Vide & 2. Cor. IX. vers. 4. Sic fortitudinem Coclitis vocat Polybius ὑπόστασιν,

Tota fidei substantia ait Tertullianus de cultu fœmina- rum II. Πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος ὀ βλεπομένων) Id est nascitur fi- des ex diligenti examine eorum, quæ dicuntur de rebus, quæ sub sensum non cadunt. Qualia sunt proles ex uxo- re sterili divitiæ illæ futuræ, de quibus supra X. 35. & alia similia. In glossario ἔλεγχος judicium, probatio. Ita Herodotus, Thucydides, Plato, Isocrates sæpe vocem hanc usurpant. Sic apud Xenophontem ἐλέγχεσθαι γε- λοῖον ὢν, convincitur esse ridiculus. Et hinc in Diale- cticis ἔλεγχοι rationes explorandi argumenta. Est hæc quædam delineatio fidei ex effectis & ex causis, ut dixi- mus. Videamus & alias. Siracidæ πίστις ἀρχὴ κολλή- σεως Θεῶ. XXV. 17. Epicuro πίστις πρόληψις τῆς δια- νοίας. Straboni περὶ τὸ ὂν σάσις. Basilidi ψυχῆς συγκα- τάθεσις τῶν μὴ κινόντων τὴν αἴσθησιν διὰ τὸ μὴ παρεῖναι· Clementi Alexandrino Strom. II. Συγκατάθεσις ἰσχυρά τινι: Item ὑπόληψις ἑκούσιος, καὶ πρόληψις εὐγνώμονος προκαταλήψεως. Deinde ἰσχὺς εἰς σωτηρίαν καὶ δύναμις εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον. Et quia spes hic ponitur, ut fidei effe- ctus, non male huc afferam & Philonis locum de præ- miis & pœnis: Τὴν δὲ ἀναγκαιοτάτην σπορὰν ἐπισκεπτέον, ἣν ὁ ποιητὴς ἐν ἀρετώσῃ χώρᾳ καλέσπειρε λογικῇ ψυχῇ. Ταύτης δὲ ὁ πρῶτος σπόρος ἐστὶν ἐλπὶς ἡ πηγὴ τῶν βίων; Ἐλπίδι γὰρ κέρδος ὁ χρηματιστὴς ἐπαποδύεται πολυτρόποις ἰδίαις πορισμῶν. Ἐλπίδι δὲ ὁ ναύκληρος, ἐνπλοίας πειρᾶται τὰ μακρὰ πελάγη· Ἐλπίδι δόξης καὶ ὁ Φιλότιμος αἱρεῖται πολιτείαν, καὶ κοινῶν πραγμάτων ἐπιμέλειαν. Δι ἐλπίδα βραβείων καὶ στεφάνων, καὶ οἱ τῶν σωμάτων ἀθληταὶ τοὺς γυμνικοὺς ἀγῶνας ἤθλησαν. Ἐλπὶς εὐδαιμονίας καὶ τοὺς ἀρε- τῆς ζηλώτας ἐπαίρει φιλοσοφεῖν, ὡς ταύτῃ δυνησομένους καὶ τὴν τῶν ὄντων Φύσιν ἰδεῖν, καὶ δρᾶσαι τὰ ἀκόλουθα πρὸς τὴν τῶν ἀρίστων βίων θεωρητικᾶ τε καὶ πρακτικὴ τελείωσιν, ὧν ὁ τυχὼν ἐστιν εὐθὺς εὐδαίμων. Et mox: Μόνη δὲ ἀποδοχῆς ἀξία· ἡ ἀναθεὶς τὴν ἐλπίδα Θεῷ, καὶ ὡς αἰτίῳ τῆς γενέσεως αὐτῆς, καὶ ὡς ἀτιπῇ καὶ ἀδιαφθόρῳ ἱκανῷ μόνῳ διαφυλάξαι. Eidem Philoni de confusis linguis πίστις dicitur ὀχυρω- τάτη καὶ βεβαιοτάτη διάθεσις. Idem de hærede rerum Divinarum: Τὸ μηκέτι ζητεῖν πεπιστευκότος ἔργον. Ibi- dem pro ἐπίστευσε posuit βεβαίως κατείληφε. Apud eundem libro de Abrahamo: Μόνον ἦν ἀψευδὲς καὶ βέ- βαιον ἀγαθὸν πίστις, ἡ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν πίστις παρηγόρημα βίου, πλήρωμα χρηστῶν ἐλπίδων, ἀφορία μὲν κακῶν, ἀγαθῶν δὲ φο- ρὰ, κακοδαιμονίας ἀπόγνωσις, εὐσεβείας γνῶσις, εὐδαιμο- νίας κλῆρος., ἓν ἅπασι βελτίωσις ἐπερηρεισμένη τῷ πάντων αἰτίῳ, καὶ δυναμένῳ μὲν πάντα, βουλομένῳ δὲ τὰ ἄριστα. Ibi- dem mox τὴν πίστιν πρὸς τὸ ὂν vocat τὴν βασιλίδα τῶν ἀρε- τῶν. Pertinent ad hanc rem verba, quæ Josephus Antiq. IL. 6. tribuit Mosi in transitu maris Erythræi: Οὐδὲ ἀν- θρώποις καλῶς τὰ παρόντα πεπολιτευμένοις πρὸς ὑμᾶς δί- καιον ἀπιστεῖν, ὡς ὀχ ὁμοίοις ἐσομένοις πρὸς τὰ μέλλοντα. Τῆς δὲ τοῦ Θεοῦ τὸν ἀπογνώσεσθαι ὑμᾶς προνοίας μανίας ἔργον ἂν εἴης παρ᾽ ὦ πάντα ὑμῖν ἀπήντηκεν, ὅσα δι᾿ ἐμοῦ σωτηρίαν, καὶ τὴν ἀπαλλαγὴν τῆς δουλείας οὐδὲ προσδοκῶσιν ὑπέσχετο, μᾶλλον δὲ χρῆν ἐν ἀπόροις γεγενημένους βοηθὸν ἐλπίζειν τὸν Θεόν. Deinde: Οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ μικροῖς τὸ θεῖον τὴν ἑαυτοῦ συμ- μαχίαν ἵστησιν ἱνικι δίδωσιν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐφ᾽ οἷς ἀνθρωπίνῃ ἐλπίδα μὴ βλέποι πρὸς τὸ κρεῖττον παρέσται. Ὅθεν τοιαῦτα βοηθήσειν πιστεύοντες, ᾧ δύναμις καὶ τὰ μικρὰ ποιῆσαι μέγαλα, καὶ τῶν τηλικούτων ἀσθένειαν καταψηφίσασθαι, μὴ καταπεπλήχθαι τὴν Αἰγυπτίων παρασκευήν. Μηδὲ ὅτι θάλασσα κωλύει ὑμῖν, ὄρη τε φυγῆς ὁδὸν ὦ παρέχοντα διὰ τοῦτο ἀπογινώσκετε τῆς σωτηρίας. Γένοιτο γὰρ ἂν καὶ ταῦθ᾽ ὑμῖν πεδία τῷ Θεῷ θελή- σαντι, κὰν γῆ τὸ πέλαγος. Sumitur autem interdum fides ita, ut obedientiam comprehendat, quam efficit fides. Salvianus de gubernatione Dei III. Quid igitur credulitas vel fides? Opinor fideliter hominem Christo crede- re, id est fidelem DEO esse, boc est, fideliter DEI mandata servare.

Ut prius membrum in hac definitione fidei ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις non male explicatur re- rum sperandarum firma quædam expectatio; Ita po- sterioris, πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος ὀ βλεπομένων sensus minus conveniens traditur, id est, nascitur fi- des ex diligenti examine eorum, quæ dicuntur de rebus, quæ sub sensum non cadunt. Tota etiam il- la descriptio male habetur pro delineatione qua- dam fidei ex effectis & causis, quasi expectatio firma effectus fidei sit: ἔλεγχος vero, quem in- terpretatur, examen eorum, quæ dicuntur, cau- sa fidei sit. Rectius alii formam fidei exprimi censent, quod sit consistentia mentis in assensu, & voluntatis in fiducia firma atque immota rerum in promissione Divina exhibitarum, quas indubitato speramus, eo quod de veritate rerum, quæ non ap- parent, sed verbo promissionis exhibentur, in ani- mo nostro convincamur, quæ animi convictio non argumentorum pondere, sed Dei promitten- tis & Verbi promissionis autoritate fit. Nam fi- des formaliter est ejusmodi ὑπόστασις cum mentis tum voluntatis: Consistentia, & firmitudo non so- lum quoad assensum mentis, sed etiam quoad fidu- ciam voluntatis, innitentem Verbo promissio- nis de rebus speratis cum ἐλέγχῳ & convictione animi de his, quæ non videmus, sed mente per- cipimus, intelligimus, adeoque amplectimur, consistentia illa mentis & voluntatis certa, fir- ma, atque immota redditur, & veluti substantifica- tur. Sed hæc explicanda paulo plenius. 1. Vox ὑπόστασις non notat substantiam proprie dictam, aut personam, uti Ebr. I. vers. 2. accipitur: quis enim fidem dixerit substantiam? Quo de pro inde non est, quod operose cum Scholasticis disquiramus, quomodo substantia dicatur fides, ut à Ludovico Terra fit, in hunc locum. 2. Nec etiam ὑπόστασις dicitur fides, quod res absentes præsentes faciat ac sistat, uti Calviniani nu- gantur, corpus CHRISTI, etsi absens, & in cœlo conclusum, in terris tamen per fidem præsens sisti in sacra cœna, verè & realiter, quod est ludere ac sibiipsi illudere, cum imaginamur aliquid nobis realiter præsens est, quod tanto intervallo abest, quanto supremum cœlum à ter- ra distat, eamque virtutem fidei adscribimus, quod præsentia realiter sistat realiter absentia, hoc est, quod præstet ea, quæ vere ἀνύπαρκτά sunt, ac ne à DEO quidem fieri possunt. 3. Nec substantia dicitur fides per ἀναλογίαν, quod ut substantia est fundamentum Accidentium, quæ à substantia procedunt, quæ causa est existentiæ Accidentium, sine qua ea esse non possint: Ita fides substantia sit per similitudinem vel conveni- entiam cum substantia, ceu totius spiritualis ædi- ficii fundamentum & primum Ens, à quo pro- cedunt virtutes omnes, & causa existentiæ ea- rum, ut Scholastici & sententiarii ineptiunt. Non enim virtutum sed rerum sperandarum ὑπό- στασιν dixit Apostolus, nec uspiam ita philoso- phatur de fide Spiritus sanctus. Vid. de his Phi- los. sobr. Meisneri part. II. sect. I. quæst. XI. 4. Neque Thomæ analogia quod fides substantia sit per similitudinem, quia complectitur in se res sperandas, ut substantia virtute accidentia dici- tur sustinere: Sed actu eas apprehendit in promis- sionibus, adeoque amplectitur & sibi appropriat. 5. Propius accedit ad veritatem Bellarminus l. 1. de justif. cap. V. cum ὑπόστασιν reddit basin & fundamentum. Nam & B. Hunnius in hunc lo- cum: Vox ὑποστάσεως, inquit, Metaphorica est, qua subinnuit Apostolus, esse fidem instar basis, & columnæ seu fundamenti earum rerum, quæ sperantur, adeo ut indubitato futuri seculi bona sperare liceat, quandoquidem spes illa innititur Divinæ immutabili promissioni, cujus correlatum fi- des est.

Ut de genuino sensu Apostoli planè constet, altera vox τῶν ἐλπιζομένων simul conjungenda: Quam Augustinus fere ubique activè intellexit, sperantium, utpote epist. CXII. ad Paul. libr. II. de peccat. merit. & remiss. cap. 31. tract. LXXIX. in Johann. hom. XXXII. in libr. 2. Homil. &c. Rectius autem sine dubio passivè redditur, rerum sperandarum, quemadmodum ex altero membro constat, τῶν μὴ βλεπομένων, quod non potest Active intelligi de videntibu hominibus, sed passive accipiendum est de rebus non apparentibus. Unde Græci omnes, Basili- us in explic. Psal. CXV, Chrysostomus, Theo- doretus, Theophylactus, Oecumenius vocem τῶν ἐλπιζομένων passive intelligunt, uti Vulgatus Inter- pres reddidit, rerum sperandarum. Per res au- tem sperandas vel stricte intelliguntur res futuræ, circa quas fides versatur, non quidem ut futuræ sunt: Sic enim objectum spei sunt: Sed ratione præsentis promissionis, vel generaliori sensu, ea quæ sperantur, hoc est, de quibus confidimus, quomodo spes sæpe etiam de fiducia circa bona præsentia occurrit. Priori sensu fides est ὑπό- στασις rerum sperandarum, quatenus fides intu- ens promissionem de rebus futuris eas non tan- tum intellectui, sed etiam affectui sistit quasi præ- sentes, ob infallibilem DEI veritatem, nem- pe vox ὑπόστασις sistendi & statuminandi ac fir- mandi sensu accipitur, quomodo ὑπόστασις καυ- χήσεως, 2. Cor. IX. vers. 4. alacritatem in eleemo- synis curandis, & cap. X I. vers. 17. Apostolatus sui labores dixit Apostolus, quia firmabant & statuminabant gloriationem. Quo pertinet, quod Galenus pedem ὄργανον βάσεως ἢ ἕδρας, hoc est, tale quod basis aut fundamenti usum præ- stat corpori libr. III. de usu part. cap. 5. & 6. dixit, quodque Aristoteles l. II. de part. animal. cap. 16. docet, animalia habere pedes etiam ἕνεχ' ὑποστάσεως τῦ βάρους, ut gestent seu susten- tent molem corporis humani; Ita sistit & firmat res sperandas animo, & affectui fides, iisque largitur consistentiam. Quo pacto explicat Chry- sostomus hoc loco fidem ὑπόστασιν esse τῶν ἐλπιζο- μένων, quandoquidem, quæ in spe sunt, ἀνυ- πόστατα εἶναι δοκεῖ, videntur non habere subsi- stentiam; fides autem eis ὑπόστασιν χαρίζεται lar- gitur consistentiam, imo essentia est rerum spe- randarum. Et Oecumenius: Cum enim quæ in spe sunt, subsistentiam non habeant, ut quæ nondum adsint, fides est eorum quædam essen- tia & subsistentia efficens quodammodo, ut ea sint & adsint, per hoc ipsum, quod ea credat es- se. Dicitur ergo ita non tantum quod statumi- net sperantem, sed quod ei etiam sistat ac repræsen- tet rem speratam, ut exemplo resurrectionis de- claravit Chrysostomus in hunc locum. Hac ratio- ne ergo definitio illa causalis erit, quod nomen proprii effectus tribuatur causæ suæ. Quo fa- cit, quod Bellarminus ipse libr. 1. de justif. cap. V. col. 821. habet: Nihil enim aliud est fidem esse substantiam rerum sperandarum, nisi quæ speran- tur, quoniam futura sunt, non habere ullam sub- sistentiam vel fundamentum, nisi in intellectu per fidem. Itaque fides est quasi vita & anima rerum, quæ sperantur, quoniam eas apprehendens ac menti repræsentans, facit eas quodammodo esse præ- sentes, ac vivere, quamvis revera non sint, nisi futuræ.

Posteriori autem sensu fides est τῶν ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, quod in iis, de quibus confidimus, adeoque quæ nobis promissione Divina exhiben- tur, stemus & consistamus immoti & firmi. Atque ita definitur fidei consistentia, vel subsi- stentia in iis, de quibus fiducia haberi potest. Quæ subsistentia ipsam fiduciam includit, quam fidei formam constituimus. Quandoquidem non modo in intellectu ὑπόστασις & consistentia ejusmodi fit, sed etiam in voluntate vel appeti- tu, idque maxime, nec tantum quoad bona fu- tura, sed etiam quoad præsentia. Quod pro- bari facile potest 1. quia fides, de qua ex Habac.

II. verf. 3. disseruit Apostolus, non alia fuit, quam assensus firmus promissioni Divinæ de Mef- sia habitus, & fiducia in ipsum, ceu justitiam nostram, & rupem nostram, ut ostensum an- tea. Eam ergo, quum definire jam voluerit Apostolus, est autem, inquit, fides ὑπόςασις rerum sperandarum, convenire descriptionem Apostolicam Propheticæ fidei explicationi opor- tet. 2. Quia fides illa, qua justus vivit, & promissio- nem consequitur, περιποίησιν τῆς ψυχῆς, qua ju- stificatur & salvatur, fiducia est de bonis præsenti- bus & futuris, quam per παῤῥησίαν describit, & ad quam ὑπομονὴν requirit. 3. Quia fiduciam spei, qua futura, & fidei, qua præsentia generali no- mine ita designavit ὑπόςασιν Ebr. III. 14. quam etiam παῤῥησίαν vers. 6. nominavit; ubi absur- dus est Bellarminus libr. 1. de justif. cap. XI. con- tendens Ebr. III. vers. 14. initium ὑποσάσεως ex- ponendum initium novæ creaturæ, quod est fides; & porro initium novæ substantiæ CHRISTI, per quam formatus est ipse in nobis, quàm de παῤῥησίᾳ & fiducia ab ipso Apostolo explicetur. 4. Ὑπόςασις dicitur ab ὑφίςασθαι firmiter stare, non cedere, non fugere; quomodo Plutarchus: il- lis, qui se dedebant, parcebatur, ὑφισαμένυς autem trucidabant. Polybius in descriptione Horatii Coclitis (quem locum indigitat Grotius) ἐχ ὅ- τω τὴν δύναμιν, ὡς τὴν ὑπόςασιν ἀυτῦ καὶ τόλ- μαν καταπεπλημένον τῶν ἐναντίων: Hostes non tam metuebant robur ipsius, quam fiduciam, & imperterritam animi illius subsistentiam, non ce- dentem terroribus aut periculis. Ideoque ὑπόςα- σις firmam notat mentis & cordis subsistentiam, quando immotam fiduciam concipit, in eaque firmiter subsistit & persistit. 5. Sic etiam accipi- tur ὑπόςασις apud LXX. Interpretes Ruth. I. vers. 12. Non est mihi ὑπόςασις, ut ducam virum תִּקְוָה, Psal. XXXIX. vers. 8. Et nunc quæ ὑπο- μονὴ expectatio mea est? τ’ ὑπόςασίς με παρά σύ ἐςιν, spes mea à te est; ubi in Ebræo קוֹוִי & תּוֹחַלְתִּי, Ezech. XIX. 5. ἀπώλετο ἡ ὑπόςασίς σκ & periit expectatio tua תִקְוָתָהּ Mich. V. vers. 6. μηδὲ ὑποσῇ ἐν ὑοῖς ἀνθρώπων, non subsistit in fi- liis hominum, das auf niemand harret noch auf Menschen wartet, ut vertit B. Lutherus. In Ebræo explicant sese mutuo verba יִקַוֶּה & יְיַחֵל, quod verbum יִחֵל per προσμένειν ἐλπίζειν ἐπελ- πίζειν expectare, sperare, spem figere alias reddi- tur, unde nomen תּוֹחֶלֶת à LXX. expositum ἐλ- πὶς Thren. III. 18. καύχημα, Prov. XI. vers. 7. ὑπόςασις Psal. XX. vers. 7. XXXIII. vers. 5. Quo refert 6. B. Gerhardus in h. l. Es. XXVI. 3. Fides est יֵצֶר סָמוּךְ figmentum fultum, quod ful- cit se ac nititur in Christo Salvatore & illius Ver- bo. 7. Flacius illustrat hanc explicationem è Ger- manica lingua, approbante B. Meisnero in Phil. Sobr. ubi verbum unterstehen non tantummodo magnum aliquem conatum, sed magnam quoq; fiduciam sive audaciam rem recte peragendi com- plectitur, quia verbum ὑφίστημι Græcum & Ger- manicum unterstehen Etymologia conveniunt. Quo de B. Höpfner. disput. VI. de justificat. p. 357. ita habet: Quomodo fides subsistentia sit in rebus fiducialibus vel de quibus fiducia potest ha- beri: Nimirum fides est veluti pes, quo movemur & accedimus ad DEUM, Ebr. XI. vers. 6. & ejus promissioni gratiam offerenti insistimus Rom. V. vers. 2. & audemus ab eo desiderare ac petere promissa bona Rom. IV. vers. 2. Germani sic ef- ferrent hanc significationem: Da man auf GOTTES Zusage fusset, und darauf be- stehet, auch daher sich unterstehet, die von ihm verheissene Wolthaten zu begehren und zu bit- ten. Et in hoc significatu accipitur Eph. III. vers. 12. Ubi juvat observare ex eodem B. Höpf- nero metaphoram à natura pedis desumptam disp. II. pag. 110. Corpus namque non potest de loco in locum moveri, nisi pede altero quiescente, alte- ro per incessum promoto: Ita & per fidem ince- dimus in perfecta Christi obedientia, ac habemus aditum in gratiam, & per eandem fidem stamus, Rom. V. vers. 2. Ita incedimus veluti pede in promissionibus Evangelicis monstrantibus Christi justitiam, ut in & super ea gressus fiduciæ figa- mus, atque ad DEUM veniamus, Johan. XIV. vers. 6. & ingrediamur in vitam æternam, Joh. V. vers. 24. Hinc venire ad Christum idem est, quod in eundem credere Joh. V. vers. 40. cap. VI. vers. 44. 65. cap. VII. vers. 35. 36. 37. Tali modo Abraham coram DEO ambulavit, Gen. XVII. vers. 1. & qui justificantur, omnes dicun- tur Rom. IV. vers. 12. στοιχεῖν τοῖς ἴχνεσι πίςεως recto pede incedere vestigiis Abrahami, hoc est, fi- de tali, quasi vestigiis ejus, ad cujus exemplum credunt in Christum. Hæc erudite B. Höpfnerus, quia appellatio fiduciæ, quæ nominatur ὑπόστα- σις, respicit metaphoram à pedis officio sumptam: Siquidem pes sit ὄργανον non tantum βασιτικὸν, in- strumentum ambulatorium, ut Galenus libr. III. de usu part. cap. IV. docet, sed etiam βάσεως ἤ ἕδρας, tale, quod basis aut fulcimenti usum præ- stat corpori. 8. Philippus Melanchthon in consi- liis Theolog. pag. 138. de hisce ita: Quidam ajunt, encomium potius esse, quam definitionem, quod non improbo, sed tamen encomia, si sunt apta & propria, sumuntur ex definitionibus: Certe ab his dissentire non debent. Affirmo igi- tur, esse veram & commodam definitionem. Nam fides, de qua hic sit mentio, duo complectitur: Notitiam seu assensum, & fiduciam seu motum cordis, qui comitatur assensum. Primum igitur fides est notitia certa non apparentium. Id vocat ἔλεγχον, id est fide certo statuimus, DEUM es- se, Christum esse Filium DEI, generis humani Redemptorem, judicaturum esse totum genus hu- manum. Deinde non solum notitia est, sed etiam expectatio promissionum, id est, fiducia, qua sta- tuimus nobis contingere promissa Dei, scilicet quod propter Christum DEUS nobis ignoscat peccata, exaudiat, curet, juvet nos, & sit nos ab æterna morte liberaturus. Hanc fiduciam, qua statui- mus, nobis Deum propitium esse, nosque DEO curæ esse, complectitur, cum ait, esse expectationem. Cum igitur fidei natura recte declaretur, compro- banda est definitio, & si dialecticè loquendum est, recte locum generis obtinet notitia certa, & dein- de expectatio. Est enim fides primum notitia, de- inde & motus cordis, quo expectamus promissa, & vere nos DEO curæ esse statuimus. Differentiæ sumptæ sunt ab objectis: Quia fides versatur circa verbum DEI, quo promittuntur bona cælestia, nondum subjecta sensui, scilicet remissio peccato- rum, quia Deus nos exaudiat, curet, & sit dona- turus nobis vitam æternam.

Quod ergo ad alterum membrum, ἔλεγχον μὴ βλεπομένων, uti certum est, ἔλεγχον argumen- tationem & convictionem notare, quomodo Joh. VIII. vers. 16. occurrit: Quis me ἐλέγχει con- vincit, vel convincere potest de peccato? & Joh. XVI. Spiritus sanctus ἐλέγξει convincet mundum de peccato: Adde Tit. I. vers. 13. 1. Tim. III. vers. 16. Quæ significatio etiam exotericis scripto- ribus recepta est, e. g. Luciano: Socrates illic de- ambulat, διελέγχων convincens omnes: Ita Me- taleptice assensus mentis significatur per convictio- nem Verbi elicitus. Nec diffitetur id Bellarminus l. c. Verba illa argumentum non apparentium non referuntur ad res operatur, sed explicant aliam fi- dei virtutem, quae est convincere intellectum, atque eum adducere, ut assentiatur iis, quae non capit neq; intelligit.

Ubi tamen duo observanda sunt: Primo quod τὰ μὴ βλεπόμενα explicet, quae non intelliguntur, quum potius ea sint, quae non videntur, quemad- modum vel e v. 3. constat: Ibi enim geminum ar- gumentum habetur: tum quod fides non possit definiri per ignorantiam, quia dicitur πίστει νοῦ- μεν. Ubi autem νόησις cognitio, ibi non est igno- rantia: tum quod τὰ βλεπόμενα, & τὰ μὴ ἐκφαινό- μενα opponantur: non ergo sunt ea, quae non intelliguntur, sed quae non videntur. Id tamen intelligendum reduplicative, quod nempe non videantur, quà creduntur, etsi alias videri pos- sint nonnulla, quae creduntur; quomodo e. g. Thomae dicebatur Joh. XX. vers. 29. quia vidi- sti, credidisti. Viderat, non spectrum esse, sed ipsummet Jesum qui apparebat; non tamen qua credebat, videbat: Nam videre est oculo- rum corporis, credere est oculorum animi, un- de additur beatos esse μὴ ἰδόντες, non videntes oculis corporis, καὶ πιστεύσαντες, & credentes. B. Selneccerus distinguit part. II. paedag. pag. 438. inter complexum vel enuntiationes integras, & in- complexum, vel partes enuntiationis. Comple- xum ipsum non videtur, sed creditur, incom- plexum tamen, & quod partis rationem haberi, nonnunquam videri potest: ubi ait: Canonem istum, articuli fidei non sunt visibiles, intelligen- dum esse de propositionibus, sive de complexo; quod non est visibile, etiamsi subjecta in mul- tis propositionibus invisibilia sint. Quia vero fi- des, ut notitia & assensus est, non nisi circa Divi- nas enunciationes, adeoque mera complexa versa- tur, hinc omne id, quod creditur, quatenus cre- ditur, in sensus non incurrit, licet ex parte, & se- cundum alium respectum videri possit.

Secundo quod Bellarminus ex hac descriptione colligat, fidem non pertinere ad voluntatem, sed ad intellectum, quia ἔλεγχος, id est, demonstra- tio & convictio ad intellectum pertinet: Ejus enim est convinci argumentis, cujus est assentiri & ju- dicare. Sed frustra. Committitur enim fallacia compositionis & divisionis, quum Apostolus fidem non solum ἔλεγχον μὴ βλεπομένων, sed etiam ὑπό- στασιν τῶν ἐλπιζομένων dicat, & utrumq; in descri- ptione fidei conjungatur. Hanc vero fiduciam inferre jam ostensum. Regerit Bellarminus, fi- dem dici substantiam rei futurae, at repraesentare non est voluntatis, ubi est fiducia, sed intellectus. Ille enim rem apprehendens per speciem sibi impressam facit rem esse antiquam. Resp. 1. Fides ut ὑπό- στασις non est rei tantum futurae, sed etiam circa bona praesentia occupatur, quatenus est subsisten- tia in rebus illis, de quibus fiducia haberi potest, jam diximus: quemadmodum spes etiam de fidu- cia circa bona praesentia sumi potest. 2. Neque repraesentatio rei speratae tantum fit in intellectu sed etiam, & maxime quidem in appetitu. Nam & ea, quae timentur, intellectui repraesentantur, non tamen fiduciae sunt objectum. 3. Etsi acciperentur τὰ ἐλπιζόμενα de rebus futuris, non tamen fidei ut futuræ sistuntur, sed ratione præ- sentis promissionis: Et ita fides intuens promissio- nem: de rebus futuris, res sperandas non tantum intellectui sed etiam affectui sistit, quasi præsentes: iisq; largitur in mente & voluntate subsistentiam. 4. Fallitur in eo Bellarminus, quod censet res futu- ras in animo subsistere per impressionem speciei. Nam quomodo à rebus incognitis, quales vult es- se eas, quæ creduntur aut sperantur, abstrahi pot- est species? Quomodo quis speciem sibi imagi- nabitur ejus vitæ, quam oculus non vidit, auris non audivit? 5. Fides non potest facere, ut in ani- mo subsistant ea, quæ sperantur, nisi sit simul firma & immota fiducia. Quum enim non subsi- stant in animo ob impressionem speciei, sed ob summam πληροφορίαν & infallibilem certitudi- nem, fiducia opus est, qua fides tã certo res speran- das amplectitur, ac si jam ipso actu essent præsen- tes: Sicut de Abrahamo dicitur, quod non consi- derarit corpus suum jam emortuum; sed Verbum Dei amplexus in sola DEI promissione tam certo acquieverit plena παῤῥησίᾳ, ac si jam rem promis- sam obtinuerit Rom. IV. vers. 19. 20. Ita quando quis persuasus est de promissionibus Evangelicis, gratia Dei & merito CHRISTI fiduciam conci- pit, Deoque firmiter confidit, adeo ut nemo persuasione plena promissis Divinis assentietur, in cujus corde non fiducia immota oriatur. Un- de Jansenius Episcopus Gandavensis in Harmon. Evang. cap. 32. rectissime, inquit, dicitur nomen fi- dei in Evangeliis, cum ei tribuitur salus, aut con- sequutio omnium, quæ volumus complecti, utrumq; nempe & assensum illum firmum in credendis de Deo & Christo, & fiduciam ex illius omnipotente bonitate conceptam.

Objicit contra Bellarminus specialem miseri- cordiam non esse rem aliquam sperandam, sed do- num præsens aut præteritum, quum ad fidem per- tinere ipsimet dicamus, ut unusquisque credat, sibi esse remissa peccata, seque per Christum gratum es- se DEO, & pro justo reputari. Sed quanquam misericordia DEI ut præsens spectetur, tamen nomine τῶν ἐλπιζομένων comprehendi potest, quo omnia, de quibus fiducia haberi potest, compre- henduntur. Neque vero fides justificans est, cre- dere, quod jam remissa sint peccata, sed hæc est consequens justificationis, & ad actum reflexum pertinet; non vero antecedens justificationis, sed intuetur promissionem Divinam, quod DEUS velit peccata remittere, & apprehendit gratiam, quæ offertur, ac meritum Christi amplectitur fidu- cialiter, Verbum promissionis, & in eodem obla- tas res sperandas, remissionem peccatorum & vi- tam eternam. Quod autem Pontificii obvertunt, in hac definitione fidei nullam fieri mentionem CHRISTI aut meriti ejus, quæ etiam Sociniano- rum & Arminianorum est objectio: Unde Grotius quoque colligit, non de fide in CHRISTUM, sed de fide in DEUM hic agere Apostolum: Ad id respondemus: Pontificios, ut apud Bellarminum loco citato videre est, agnoscere fidem justificantem hic describi. Ad fidem autem justificantem re- quiri fidem in CHRISTUM, inter nos & Ponti- ficios extra omnem controversiæ aleam positum est. Nam quod Apostolus hoc loco definiat fidem justificantem (ita habet Bellarminus cap. V.) cum enim in capite superiori extremo dixisset: Justus ex fide vivit, quod si subtraxerit se, non placebit animæ meæ Nos autem non sumus subtractionis filii in perditionem, sed fidei in acquisitionem animæ: conti- nuo subjungit nullo interposito verbo: Est autem fides fperandarum subftantia rerum &c. ubi vides defi- niri eam fidem, ex qua justus vivit, & ex qua pla- cemus Deo, & cujus filii sumus in acquifitionem a- nimæ, & à qua, qui se subtrahit, in extremam perditionem ruit. Deinde in reliquo capite non femel Apostolus repetit, hanc esse fidem, fine qua impossibile est, Deo placere, & per quam sancti omnes Deo placuerunt. Definitur igitur fides ju- stificans. Porrò de fide in Christum ita Bellarmi- nus cap. VIII. Hæc igitur fides, inquit, qui re- spicit Christi Divinitatem, ipsa est, quæ & justi- tiam & vitam æternam sibi tribuit, cum addu- xiffet locum Rom. X. Hoc est verbum fidei quod prædicamus, quia si confitearis in ore tuo Dominum Jesum, & in corde tuo credi- deris, quia Deus eum suscitavit à mortuis, sal- vus eris, addidit Bellarminus: Hic quoque a- pertissime videmus, objectum fidei justificantis & salvantis esse resurrectionem Filii Dei. Et deinde, cum è 1. Corinth. XV. verba Apostoli proposuisset: Notum vobis facio Evangelium, quod prædica- vi, in quo statis, per quod & salvamini, nisi forte frustra credidistis. Tradidi enim vobis impri- mis, quod & accepi, quoniam Christus mortuus est pro peccatis secundum Scripturas, & quia se- pultus est, & quia resurrexit tertia die secundum scripturas &c. subjicit: Ubi sine dubio fidei salvan- tis objectum explicatur, nec tantum dicitur, tradidi vobis, ut unusquisque certo credat: se per Christum esse justificatum, sed tradidi vobis credendum pas- sionem, sepulturam, & resurrectionem Domini nostri Jesu Christi: Hæc proinde indubie ad ob- jectum fidei pertinent: eo autem pertinere, quod credat quisque, se per Christum esse justificatum, non nostra est sententia, sed Bellarmini calumnia: Hoc enim consequens est justificationis: Pro ob- jecto tamen habet fides justificans remissionem pec- catorum ut obtinendam, non ut jam obtentam, quod nec Bellarminus ipse negare potuit: Siqui- dem in symbolo Apostolico, quo objecta fidei contineri vult, profiteamur, nos credere remissio- nem peccatorum. Frustra verò obvertit, sensum illius articuli esse, credo & confiteor in Ecclesia Ca- tholica esse donum remissionis peccatorum. Nam uti unicuique credendum est in Deum Patrem, & Filium Dei, & in Spiritum sanctum: Uti etiam cre- denda est passio, sepultura & resurrectio Christi, fatente Bellarmino: Sic credenda etiam ab uno- quoque remissio peccatorum: at illa creduntur, non quod ea in Ecclesia sint, aut quod tradenda sint, sed quod in Deum Patrem, Filium & Spiritum Sanctum ceu Deum suum credere quisque de- beat, & quod Christus pro se passus, sepultus sit, & resurrexit, velut 1. Corinth. XV. habet, pro pec- catis suis. Proinde credere etiam quisque de- bet, sibi remissionem peccatorum obtingere, se resurrecturum esse, se vitam æternam consequu- turum esse, quia justus fide sua vivet. Quamvis verò in ista Paulina fidei descriptione nulla fidei in Christum mentio fiat explicite, alibi tamen, cum objectum fidei explicatur, quod hic in genere tantum exprimitur, Christi, ejusque meritum & satisfactio non tacetur: & cum rerum speranda- rum vel credendarum, & τῶν μὴ βλεπομένων, quæ non videmus, sed credimus, mentio fit, sub istis vocibus comprehendi, quæ credenda & esse, alias docuit, imo quæ jam ex professo in hac epistola ideo proposuit Apostolus, quæque exemplis il- lustraturus nunc est, censeri debet. Hortatur enim tum præceptis, tum exemplis ad πληροφορί- αν πίσεως, &παῥῥησίαν καὶ ὑπομονὴν ne evadam9 fi- lii ὑποστολῆς εἰς ἀπώλειαν, sed maneant filii πίστεως εἰς περιποίησιν ψυχῆς exemplo veterum fideli- um, utpote habentes παῤῥησίαν in ingressum Sanctorum IN SANGUINE JESU, & Sa- cerdotem magnum, de cujus sacrificio expia- torio & intercessione in cælis prolixe tractarat. Cum ergo ex instituto, ut hunc Sacerdotem e- jusque sacrificium & intercessionem fide am- plectamur moneat atque hortetur Apostolus, ut ea fide vivamus, & animæ redemptionem consequamur, ecquis ambigere potest, hæc ad objectum fidei justicæ & salvificæ pertinere ex mente Apostoli? Sumi autem fidem sive hic sive alibi, cum de fide justificante sermo est, ita, ut obedientiam comprehendat, quam effi- cit fides, quod Grotius vult, è scripturis de- monstrari non potest, & ἀντιφαλικὸν revera est: Nam effectus non est ipsa causa, ideò nec fides ceu causa cum obedientia, quam efficit ipsa, con- fundi debet, nedum una voce comprehendi si- mul potest.

PARS II. Fidelium Veteris Testamenti catalogus vel recensio.

## 11:2
Verse 2.

Ἐν ταύτῃ γὰρ ἐμαρτυρήθησαν οἱ πρεσβύτεροι] πρεσβύτεροι here are those who are the הקדמני in 1 Sam. XXIII. 14. Those ancient, excellent men: οἱ πρότεροι καὶ ἀπίκολι, says Simonides. Just as here the elders are the ancients: So in Tacitus, vetus is often an old man or one more advanced in age than others. For these are of similar meaning, except that senex is more frequently referred to the span of one man's life, vetus to the times of the world. Ἐν ταύτῃ, that is, through this faith. Ἐμαρτυρήθησαν, they obtained a testimony, namely from God, a good and honorable one. In like manner Acts VI. 3, ἄνδρας ἐξ ὑμῶν μαρτυρουμένους, men of whom all bear good witness. So also Acts X. 22, XVI. 2, XXII. 2.

The description of faith is now illustrated and confirmed by the examples of the faithful of the Old Testament, who lived, that is, before Christ was exhibited. For all these come under the name of τῶν πρεσβυτέρων. For the Apostle teaches that the ancients received the testimony of faith not only after the Old Testament was sanctioned by Moses, but also before the times of Moses: and not only after the flood, but also before the flood, since he weaves the catalog of the faithful starting from Abel, the son of the Protoplast. And that they received it in that faith to which he exhorts, and in which he warns that one must persevere, from which he teaches that the just man lives and is justified and obtains salvation, and which he described through the ὑπόστασιν of things to be hoped for, or about which confidence can be had, and the ἔλεγχον and conviction of those things which are not seen by the eyes of the body, but are to be looked upon by the eyes of the mind; The ancients, he says, are a testimony, not only because they had that faith which both the Prophet requires, that a man may be just and live by faith, and which the Apostle here demonstrates to be necessary for justification and salvation: But also because they obtained justice and salvation in that very faith: Which he is now about to prove by special examples, in which, although the act of justification and salvation is not always expressly treated: yet it is evident from the Apostolic treatment that justifying faith is pointed out, and it has been proven by Bellarmine himself, and the conclusion clearly shows this scope, that the faith ἐπαγγελίας in the promise concerning the Messiah is intended, p. 39. which Habakkuk chap. II. 4. intended, and that surrounded by a cloud of witnesses we ought to run δι' ὑπομονὴν, looking, gazing with the eyes of the mind ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν πίστεως Ἰησοῦν, ὃς ἀντὶ τῆς προ-

for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross. Heb.
