XII. 1. 2. because we have come to Jesus the Mediator of the New Testament, and to the blood of sprinkling that speaks better than the blood of Abel, ver. 24. that is, demanding not vengeance, but the remission of sin, for which it was shed for us, in whom the examples of the ancients are set before us to be imitated: Since Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever Heb. XIII. 8. For we are not saved by any other reason than they, but we believe that we shall be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, in the same way as they, Acts XV. 11.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Ἐν ταύτῃ γὰρ ἐμαρτυρήθησαν οἱ πρεσβύτεροι] πρεσ- βύτεροι hic sunt, qui הקדמני 1. Sam. XXIII. 14. Veteres illi egregii viri: οἱ πρότεροι καὶ ἀπίκολι, ait Simonides. Sic- ut hic seniores sunt veteres: Ita Tacito vetus sæpe est senex aut ætate provectior aliis. Sunt enim ista vicini si- gnificatus, nisi quod frequentius senex ad spatium vitæ hominis unius, vetus ad mundi tempora refertur. Ἐν ταύ- τῃ, id est, per hanc fidem. Ἐμαρτυρήθησαν testimonium adepti sunt, à Deo scilicet, bonum atque honorificum. Pa- ri modo Act. VI. 3. ἄνδρας ἐξ ὑμῶν μαρτυρουμένους viros, de quibus omnes bene testantur. Sic & Actor. X. 22. XVI. 2. XXII. 2.

Illustratur jam, & confirmatur fidei descri- ptio exemplis fidelium Veteris Testamenti, qui scilicet ante Christum exhibitum vixerunt. Hi enim omnes nomine τῶν πρεσβυτέρων veniunt. Nam non tantum postquam à Mose sancitum est Vetus Testamentum, sed etiam ante tempora Mosis fidei accepisse testimonium veteres docet Apostolus: nec solum post diluvium, sed eti- am ante diluvium, quum inde ab Abele, Pro- toplastων filio pertexat fidelium catalogum. Ac- cepisse autem in illa fide, ad quam hortatur, & in qua perseverandum esse monet, è qua ju- stumper vivere & justificari ac salutem consequi do- cet, quamque per rerum sperandarum, vel de quibus fiducia haberi potest, ὑπόστασιν, & eorum, quæ non oculis corporis cernuntur, sed oculis mentis aspicienda sunt, ἔλεγχον & con- victionem descripsit; testimonium veteres ait, non tantum, quod eam fidem habuerint, quam & Propheta, ut quis per fidem justus sit & vi- vat, requirit, & Apostolus ad justificationem & salutem necessariam esse hic demonstrat: Sed quod etiam in ista fide justitiam & salutem adepti sint: Quod jam probaturus est specialibus exem- plis, in quibus etsi non de actu justificationis & sa- lutis semper expresse agatur: Fidem tamen ju- stificantem indigitari è tractatione Apostolica con- stat, & a Bellarmino ipso probatum est, & conclusio hunc scopum luculenter ostendit, quod inten- datur fides ἐπαγγελίας in promissionem de Messia, p. 39. quam Habacuc cap. II. 4. intendebat, quod- que nube testium circumdati δι' ὑπομονὴν currere debeamus, ἀφορῶντες, intuentes oculis mentis ἀρχηγὸν καὶ τελειωτὴν πίστεως Ἰησοῦν, ὃς ἀντὶ τῆς προ-

κειμένης αὐτῷ χαρᾶς ὑπέμεινε σταυρόν. Ebr. XII. 1. 2. quia pervenimus ad Novi Testamenti Media- torem Jesum, & sanguinem aspersionis melius lo- quentem, quam sanguis Abel, vers. 24. id est, po- stulantem non vindictam, sed remissionem pecca- ti, ob quam pro nobis effusus est, in quo e- xempla veterum nobis imitanda sistuntur : Si- quidem Jesus Christus heri, hodie, idem & in se- cula Ebr. XIII. 8. Neque enim alia ratione nos salvamur quam illi, sed credimus διὰ τῆς χά- ριτος κυρίου Ἰησοῦ χριστῦ σωθῆναι, καθ' ὃν τρό- πον κἀκεῖνοι, Act. XV. 11.

## 11:3
Ver. 3.

By faith we understand that the worlds were framed] By worlds here, as above, he understands this whole universe, such as it is now distinguished into its members, heaven, earth, sea, stars, rocks, plants, living creatures, men. He says they were framed, that is, arranged into order and a certain form. In the same sense we have καταρτίζειν for the Hebrew כּוּן in Ps. LXXIV. 16. & LXXXIX. 30. He says this, that by faith we comprehend, that is, through the revelation of God made to Adam, Abraham, and others, and then handed down by hand, and written by Moses and the Prophets Gen. I. the whole chapter, XIV. 19. XX. 11. XXXI. 16. Neh. IX. 6. Job XII. 9. Psalm LXXXIX. 12. CII. 26. CXV. 16. CXXXV. 6. CXXXVI. 4. Isa. XXXVII. 16. XL. 16. XLII. 5. XLV. 7. 12. XLVIII. 13. LXVI. 2. Jer. X. 16. XXVII. 5. XXXII. 17. LI. 15. Zech. XII. 1. Specious arguments are produced by philosophers on both sides, and it is not for everyone to judge of their force. Justin to Diognetus, treating of God: He showed Himself, and He showed Himself through faith, by which alone it is permitted to see God.

By the word of God] By the command of God. For we have shown that ῥῆμα is taken thus in Heb. I. 3. Ps. XXXIII. 9.

So that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear] A similar expression is in 2 Macc. VII. 28. I beseech you, my son, look upon the heaven and the earth, and all that is in them, and see that God made them out of things that were not, and the race of men likewise. We now see trees born from trees, living creatures from living creatures, men from men. But those first trees, the first living creatures, the first men did not have their origin from such things as now exist and are seen. He says this so that we may more easily believe that God can exhibit things which we do not see. See below 7. In the manuscript it is τὸ βλεπόμενον ἐποίησε, namely, the whole. But then εἰς τὸ here means so that.

He does not only premise these things so that we may more easily believe that God can exhibit things which are not seen; but also because he had determined to illustrate and confirm from Moses and the Prophets, starting immediately from Abel, what he had said about faith, and especially because he wished to set forth the first act of faith, which is understanding or knowledge, and the first article, which is about creation, lest faith be believed to be a blind assent, or the article about creation be excluded from the system of things to be believed. For that is why God so frequently describes Himself as the Creator of heaven and earth, because He wishes to be acknowledged, believed, and celebrated as such, and invoked with true confidence of heart. From the creation of all things we learn that all things are under the power of the Lord, that all things can be directed to our good, indeed that all things serve the Divine glory, and we understand that the Creator is the only true God who is to be worshipped by us. Thence His invisible things from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even His eternal power and Godhead, Rom. I. 20. Therefore, note here 1. cognition, which is expressed by the word νοῦμεν, νοέω is I understand, I turn my mind to, Matt. XV. 17. ch. XVI. 9. 11. ch. XXIV. 16. John XII. 41. Eph. III. 4. 2 Tim. II. 7. which is the first act of faith, embracing the knowledge of things to be believed. Therefore, cognition cannot be excluded from saving faith. For how shall we place confidence in Him whom we do not acknowledge? How shall we worship what we do not know? John IV. 22. Cf. Rom. X. 14. Whence Job's faith is described by the word ידע, οἶδα I know, ch. XIX. 25. & the faith by which we are justified, Isa. LIII. ver. 11. is expressed by the same word. The LXX render it σύνεσιν understanding, Jer. IX. 24. The words συνιεῖν καὶ γινώσκειν are joined, and וידע & משכיר &c. Whence Bellarmine is refuted in book I. de justific. ch. 7. contending that faith is more correctly defined by ignorance than by knowledge.

II. The object of cognition, which is creation. But creation is described (1.) as to the act, but partly κατηρτίσθαι which is I construct, I join together, I adapt, I perfect, Heb. X. 5. Eph. IV. 12. by which both the perfection of the work and its apt arrangement are hinted at, namely, that the world was constructed with parts joined together among themselves by a wonderful workmanship. Which is evident from the history of creation, describing in what order all works were founded and perfected.

Partly by the words 'so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear,' which refer particularly to visible creatures, which were made from things that did not appear, though others are not excluded. For all things were created by God, whether visible or invisible, Colossians 1:16. Some read 'ἐκ φαι- νομένων,' as if to say that those things which were adapted by the word became spectacles of things not appearing, in which the invisible things of God might be seen, Romans 1:20. But 'τὰ βλεπόμενα' is not a noun, but a participle, denoting 'things which are seen,' not 'sights' or 'spectacles,' and in the more approved codices there are two words 'ἐκ φαινομένων.' And therefore, a transposition should rather be noted here, made for the sake of the euphony of the words 'μὴ' and 'ἐκ,' when it should have been said, 'εἰς τὰ ἐκ μὴ φαινομένων,' so that from things not appearing, that is, invisible things, as the Vulgate rendered it, visible things might be made. The term from which are 'the things which do not appear,' by which Thomas and Ribera understand ideas or reasons in the mind of God, but those are the formal cause rather than the term from which creation proceeds: others wish to indicate that rude and undigested mass, which is called by the LXX 'invisible and unformed,' Genesis 1:2, just as Moses designated the darkness upon the face of the deep before 'the things which are seen' were adapted by the word: But it is more convenient that 'the things which are not' are noted, as in 2 Maccabees 7:28, God is said to have made heaven and earth 'out of things which were not,' and Romans 4:17, 'to call those things which be not as though they were': because even if all things were made from that unformed matter, yet this very matter was made from absolutely nothing, as Augustine says in book 1 against the Manichaeans, chapter 6. Proverbs 8:24, 'when there were no depths, I was brought forth.'

2. Regarding the medium, 'by the word of God,' by which the imperative word of command is understood, concerning which Psalm 33:9 speaks, not the hypostatic Word, which never comes under the name of 'rhema,' but is called 'Logos,' and is included here in the word 'God,' because that name is taken essentially in this place for God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, by whose word and command all things were created, 'for he spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast,' as the sacred Psalmist speaks. Compare Genesis 1. Yet the hypostatic Word was in the word of command, when GOD the Father said: 'Let there be light,' etc. He said it by commanding, not without the Word, but through the hypostatic Word, through whom all things were made, Gen. I. 3. John I. 3. not without, but in the Spirit of the mouth of the Lord, Ps. XXXIII. 6. that is, in the Holy Spirit. 3. Regarding the Author or Principal cause, which he expresses by the word Θεῦ, which placed absolutely here and in the whole chapter and throughout the entire Code, denotes the true God, whom Moses designates by the plural name Elohim, joined to a verb of creation in the singular number, and who is that one God in essence, three in persons. All of which the Apostle implies pertains to the understanding of faith. 4.

Regarding the object, the ages, by which are comprehended both times and secular things, which were founded in time, as Theophylact says here that the ages, times, and all temporal things are called: Or rather the whole world, because it is secular, by Metonymy, just as the ages are said to be founded through the Son, Heb. I. 2. because all things were created through him, John I. 3. to which secular things also pertain the invisible things, Angels, powers, thrones, etc., it is evident from Col. I. 16. What therefore the Apostle said here afterwards, the things which are seen, is to be understood either inclusively, not exclusively, or rather as the things which are not seen denote those things which, because they were absolutely not, could not appear, or the things which are not, so the things which are seen must be understood generally as all things which are.

III. The mode or act of cognition. By faith we understand, says the Apostle. It is not therefore ocular or sensual cognition, but mental; not cognition of science or evident, but of faith, which the Scholastics call non-evident. But can creation not be known by the light of nature? How then is it claimed for faith? Both are certain, both that we gather and acknowledge God as the Author of creatures through nature and the discourse of reason from the very works of creation, as the Apostle testifies, Rom. I. 20. Acts XIV. 17. ch. XVII. 27. Concerning which in Theology of nature and Revelation expressly, and that we conceive faith concerning the work of creation through scripture and the grace of revelation. There is general knowledge, here special, as to who that Creator God is, namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, how he created? by word alone? in what order he joined and perfected all things? Let us understand within the hexaemeron, according to the Mosaic revelation. There is knowledge of science through demonstration, by which we gather a posteriori and from effect to cause: Here of faith, by which we embrace with faith the word of God, by which it is revealed. Nor is it inconvenient that there are certain things which are objects of faith, which become known through demonstration either a priori or a posteriori: nor is it repugnant that an article of faith, which namely is handed down in Holy Scripture to be received by faith, can also be known by nature, which becomes known through the discourse of reason by the benefit of the light of nature. By which name some articles of faith are simple, of mere revelation, others however mixed, which also consist in reason. Which the Calixtines will not be able to deny, if they wish to defend the hypothesis concerning the Apostolic symbol as a perfect compendium of things to be believed, and not deny the first article of faith, by which we believe in God the Father, almighty Creator of heaven and earth.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Πίστει νοῦμεν κατηρτίσθαι τὲς αἰῶνας ] Per αἰῶνας hic ut su- pra intelligit totum hoc universum, ita ut nunc distin- ctum in sua membra, cœlum, terram, mare, sidera, saxa, plantas, animantia, homines. Eos ait κατηρτίσθαι, id est, in ordinem certamque speciem digesto. Eodem sensu καταρτίζειν pro Ebræo כּוּן habemus Psal. LXXIV. 16. & LXXXIX. 30. Hoc dicit fide nos comprehendere, id est, per Dei revelationem factam Adamo, Abrahamo, & aliis, ac deinde per manus traditam, & à Mose Prophe- tisque conscriptam Gen. I. toto capite, XIV. 19. XX. 11. XXXI. 16. Nehem. IX. 6. Job. XII. 9. Psalmo LXXXIX. 12. CII. 26. CXV. 16. CXXXV. 6. CXXXVI. 4. Esa. XXXVII. 16. XL. 16. XLII. 5. XLV. 7. 12. XLVIII. 13. LXVI. 2. Jerem. X. 16. XXVII. 5. XXXII. 17. LI. 15. Zach. XII. 1. Argumenta à Philosophis producuntur speciosa in utramque partem, nec omnium est de eorum vi dijudicare. Justinus ad Diognetum de Deo agens : ᾿Αυτὸς ἑαυτὸν ἐπέδειξεν, ἐπέδειξε δὲ διὰ πίστεως, ᾗ μόνῃ ἰδεῖν Θεὸν συγκεχώρηται.

Ῥήματι Θεῦ ] Jussu Dei. Ita enim sumi ῥῆμα ostendimus Ebr. I. 3. Psal. XXXIII. 9.

Εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐκφαινομένων τὰ βλεπόμενα γεγονέναι ] Similis loquutio 2. Macc. VII. 28. ᾿Αξιῶ σε τέκνον, ἀναβλέψαντα εἰς τὸν ὀρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν, καὶ τὰ ἐν ἀυτοῖς πάντα ἰδόντα γνῶναι, ὅτι ἐκ ἐξ ὄντων ἐποίησεν ἀυτὰ ὁ Θεὸς κὶ τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένος. Nos nunc videmus arbores ex arboribus gigni, animantia ex animantibus, homines ex hominibus. At pri- mæ illæ arbores, prima animantia, primi homines non ha- buere ortum ex talibus, qualia nunc existunt atque conspi- ciuntur. Hoc ideo dicit, ut eo facilius credamus, Deum ex- hibere posse quæ non conspicimus. Vide infra 7. In Ma- nuscripto est τὸ βλεπόμενον ἐποίησε, nempe τὸ πᾶν. Tum verò εἰς τὸ hic valet ita ut.

Non tantum ideò hæc præmittit, ut eo facilius credamus, Deum exhibere posse, quæ non conspiciuntur; sed etiam, quia è Mose & Prophetis illustrare ac confirmare, initio facto statim ab Abele, constituerat, quæ de fide dixe- rat, & imprimis quia fidei primum actum, qui est νόησις vel notitia, primumque articulum, qui est de creatione sistere voluit, ne vel fides cæ- cus assensus credatur, vel articulus de creatio- ne ex systemate credendorum excludatur. Nam ideò tam frequenter Deus se tanquam Creato- rem cœli & terræ describit, quod talis agnosci, credi ac celebrari, & vera cordis fiducia invo- cari velit. E creatione rerum omnium omnia sub potestate Domini esse, omnia ad nostrum bonum dirigi posse, imò omnia Divinæ gloriæ inservire discimus, ac Creatorem solum verum esse illum Deum, qui à nobis colen- dus sit, intelligimus. Inde invisibilia ejus ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμυ τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθορᾶται, ἥτε ἀΐδιος ἀυτῦ δύναμις καὶ θειότης, Rom. I. 20. Notanda ergo hic 1. cognitio, quæ verbo νοῦ- μεν exprimitur, νοέω est intelligo, animum ad- verto, Matth. XV. 17. cap. XVI. 9. 11. cap. XXIV. 16. Johan. XII. 41. Ephes. III. 4. 2. Tim. II. 7. qui primus fidei actus est, rerum cre- dendarum notitiam complectens. Ideo co- gnitio à fide salvifica excludi non potest. Quo- modo enim fiduciam collocabimus in eum, quem non agnoscimus? Quomodo adorabimus, quod non novimus? Johan. IV. 22. Conf. Roman. X. 14. Unde Jobi fides verbo ידע, οἶδα novi scio de- scribitur cap. XIX. 25. & fides, qua justifica- mur, Es. LIII. vers. 11. eodem verbo expri- mitur. LXX. reddunt σύνεσιν intelligentiam, Jerem. IX. 24. Conjunguntur verba συνιεῖν καὶ γινώσκειν וידע & משכיר &c. Unde refelli- tur Bellarminus libr. I. de justific. cap. 7. fidem rectius per ignorantiam quam per notitiam defini- ri, contendens.

II. Cognitionis objectum, quod est creatio. Describitur autem creatio (1.) quoad actum, par- tim verò κατηρτίσθαι quod est construo, coagmen- to, adapto, perficio, Ebr. X. 5. Ephes. IV. 12. quo operis tum perfectio, tum apta concinnatio in- nuitur, quod nempe mundus partibus inter se mirabili opificio coaptatis constructus sit. Quæ ex historia creationis, quo ordine opera omnia condita & perfecta sint, describente con- stant.

Partim verbis εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐκφαινομένων τὰ βλεπόμενα γεγονέναι, quæ respiciunt peculia- riter creaturas visibiles, quæ ex iis, quæ non apparebant, factæ, non exclusis tamen aliis. Nam omnia condita sunt à Deo sive visibilia, sive invisibilia, Coloss. I. 16. Nonnulli ἐκ φαι- νομένων legunt, q. d. ut non apparentium spe- ctacula fierent ea, quæ verbo adaptata sunt, in quibus invisibilia Dei conspicerentur, Roman. I. 20. Sed τὰ βλεπόμενα non nomen est, sed participium, quæ videntur, notans, non vi- sa vel spectacula, & in probatioribus codici- bus duæ sunt voces ἐκ φαινομένων. Ideoque potius hic notanda trajectio, euphoniæ causa facta vocis μὴ & ἐκ, quum dici deberet, εἰς τὰ ἐκ μὴ φαινομένων, ut ex non apparentibus, hoc est, invisibilibus, ut Vulgatus reddidit, visibilia fierent. Terminus à quo sunt τὰ μὴ φαινόμενα, per quæ Thomas & Ribera intelli- gunt ideas seu rationes in mente Dei, sed illæ causa exemplaris potius, quam terminus à quo creationis sunt: alii rudem illam & indigestam molem, quæ à LXX. ἀόρατος, καὶ ἀκατα- σκεύαστος dicitur, Gen. I. 2. indigitari volunt, quomodo & tenebras super faciem abyssi Mo- ses designavit, antequam τὰ βλεπόμενα apta- rentur verbo: Sed convenientius est, τὰ μὴ ὄντα notari, ut 2. Maccab. VII. 4. ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων Deus cœlum & terram fecisse dicitur, & Ro- man. IV. 17. τὰ μὴ ὄντα vocare ὡς ὄντα: quia etsi omnia formata de materia illa informi fa- cta sint: tamen hæc ipsa materia de omnino ni- hilo est facta, dicente Augustino libr. I. contra Ma- nich. cap. 6. Proverb. IIX. 24. cum abyssi essent nihil, genita sum.

2. Quoad medium, ῥήματι Θεῦ, quo verbum mandati προστακτικὸν, de quo Psal. XXXIII. 9. intelligitur, non verbum ὑποστα- τικὸν, quod nunquam nomine ῥήματος venit, sed λόγος vocatur, & comprehenditur hic voce Θεῦ, quia nomen illud essentialiter sumitur hoc loco pro Deo Patre, Filio & Spiritu Sancto, cujus ver- bo & jussu condita sunt omnia, ὅτι αὐτὸς εἶπεν, αὐτὸς ἀνετείλατο; ipse dixit, & facta sunt, ipse mandavit, & creata sunt, ut Hiero-Psaltes loqui- tur. Conf. Genes. I. Fuit tamen in verbo man- dati verbum hypostaticum, cum DEUS Pater dixit: Fiat lux &c. Dixit id jubendo non sine verbo, sed per verbum hypostaticum, per quod quod facta sunt omnia, Gen. I. 3. Johan. I. 3. non sine, sed in Spiritu oris Domini Psal. XXXIII. 6. hoc est, in Spiritu sancto. 3. Quoad Au- torem seu causam Principalem, quam voce Θεῦ exprimit, quæ absolute posita hic & in toto ca- pite ac per universum Codicem, verum Deum notat, quem Moses nomine Elohim plurali, juncto verbo creationis numero singulari desi- gnat, quique unus ille in essentia, trinus in personis Deus est. Quæ omnia proinde ad fi- dei νόησιν pertinere Apostolus innuit. 4.

Quoad objectum τὺς αἰῶνας secula, quibus com- prehenduntur & tempora & res seculares, quæ in tempore conditæ sunt, uti Theophylactus ait hic vocari secula, tempora, & omnia temporaria: Vel potius mundus universus, quia secularis est, per Metonymiam, quomodo per Filium secula condita dicuntur, Ebr. I. 2. quia omnia per ipsum creata sunt, Johan. I. 3. ad quæ secularia etiam pertinere τὰ ἀόρατα, Angelos, potestates, thronos &c. è Col.I. 16. constat. Quod ergo post- ea τὰ βλεπόμενα hic dixit Apostolus, vel inclusi- ve, non exclusive intelligendum, vel potius ut τὰ μὴ φαινόμενα notant ea, quæ ideo, quod plane non erant, apparere non poterant, seu τὰ μὴ ὄντα, ita τὰ βλεπόμενα generatim intelligenda erunt omnia τὰ ὄντα.

III. Cognitionis modum vel actum. Πίστει νοῦμεν, inquit Apostolus. Non ergo est cognitio ocula- ris vel sensualis, sed mentalis, non cognitio scien- tiæ vel evidens, sed fidei, quam inevidentem di- cunt Scholastici. Sed annon creatio lumine na- turæ cognosci potest? Quomodo ergò fidei vindi- catur? Utrumque certum est, & quod per naturam & discursum rationis ex ipsis operibus creationis Deum Autore creaturarum colligamus & agno- scamus, teste Apostolo, Rom. I. 20. Actor. XIV. 17. cap. XVII. 27. Quo de in Theol. natur. & Re- vel. ex professo, & quod per scripturam & gratiam revelationis fidem concipiamus de opere creati- onis. Ibi generalis est notitia, hic specialis, ut quis Deus ille Creator sit, Pater nempe Filius, & Spiri- tus sanctus, quomodo crearit? per solum ver- bum? quo ordine omnia coagmentarit & perfe- cerit? Intra hexaëmeron, juxta revelationem Mo- saicam, intelligamus. Ibi est notitia τῆς ἐπιστήμης per demonstrationem, quà à posteriori & ab effe- ctu ad causam colligimus: Hic τῆς πίστεως, qua verbum Dei, quo id revelatum est, fide amplecti- mur. Neque enim inconveniens est, quædam esse & πιστὰ, quæ per demonstrationem sive à pri- ori, sive à posteriori innotescunt: nec repugnat ar- ticulum fidei esse, quæ nempe in Scriptura sacra fide suscipienda traditur, & natura cognosci posse, quæ per discursum rationis beneficio luminis na- turæ innotescit. Quo nomine alii articulē fidei simplices sunt meræ revelationis, alii verò mi- xti, qui etiam ratione constant. Quod negare non poterunt Calixtini, si ὑπόθεσιν de symbolo Apostolico credendorum perfecto compendio tueri ve- lint, nec primum articulum fidei, quo credimus in Deum Patrem, omnipotentem Creatorem cœli & terræ abnegare.

## 11:4
Verse 4.

By faith Abel offered a more excellent sacrifice to God than Cain.] Note that sacrifice is said here as much of fruits as of cattle, concerning which we spoke at Lev. II. at Mark IX. 49. and here above VIII. 3. More here means more acceptable, in the way that the Hebrews also take יתר. Thus almost Matt. VI. 25. XII. 41. 42. Mark XII. 33. Luke XI. 31. 32. XII. 23. And than Cain is to be understood as than that of Cain, as the Syriac accepted it here. Such is that of Pliny: Having obtained a greater laurel of all triumphs. For laurel is understood. And therefore he says the offering of Abel was more acceptable, because he had faith. He believed that God repays good and evil deeds, which the Jerusalem Paraphrast also added explicitly to the history. Similar is what Bacchai says, that God in the exodus from Egypt did not look at the blood sprinkled on the doorposts, but at the faith of the Israelites.

Through which he was testified to be righteous] Through faith he was made righteous, and his righteousness received testimony, namely from God, as follows. There is here the same word to be testified of which we spoke above 2.

God testifying of his gifts] Namely, by fire sent from heaven upon those gifts, God showed that Abel, and because of Abel his offering, was acceptable to him, as we said at Gen. IV. 4. And so here all the Greek interpreters, Gen. IV. 4. where in the Hebrew it is אל־מנחתו: whence it appears that formerly minchah was a name of a genus, which in the law is a name of a species. Thus also under the Gospel God holds as acceptable works proceeding from faith.

And through it, though dead, he still speaks] Manuscript: He still speaks: namely in Genesis. Because of faith, having died, he still speaks there, that is, his blood cries out to God, Gen. IV. 10. For here is the Present for the Past, which is so vividly shown as if it were present. The murder of Abel demanded vengeance from God. It must be read, as I said, it shows that which is below XII. 24. to the blood of sprinkling that speaks better than that of Abel, where the same place of Genesis is looked back upon. Through it here means the same as through him. See what we said above I 2. The common sense of the Genesis passage is clear: but the mystical sense, that the pious live after death, because they also speak. Philo, after having treated this history in the book: The worse plots against the better: for he who has died lives, since he is found to be a suppliant of God and using a voice. The Targum almost has Jonathan at the said place of Genesis.

1. As to the connection and scope: The Apostle proves by this example that we obtain the grace of God and are justified by faith in Christ; which he had deduced from Habakkuk 2:4, because by faith in the promised seed of the woman Abel offered a sacrifice pleasing to God, and obtained the testimony that he was righteous. For what other object of Abel's faith was there than that seed of the woman, concerning whom it had been announced to the Protoplasts, that he ought to be wounded in the heel by the infernal serpent in his passion and death, but truly ought to crush its head and all its power, Gen. 3:15; which Eve, the mother of Cain and Abel, had proclaimed, designating that she possessed in her heart and embraced by faith, by the symbolic name of Cain, as איש את־יהוה, that man, the crusher of the serpent, the Lord: Gen. 4:1; whose slaughter, as of an unblemished lamb, God prefigured when he had clothed the Protoplasts with the skins taken from slaughtered lambs or sheep, whose flesh was offered in sacrifice, as a type of the death of the Messiah, by whose justice and obedience to be performed even unto death we, to whom nakedness was ignominious on account of sin, were to be clothed. Nor indeed did Abel offer sacrifice out of his own will-worship, or with reason and nature as a guide, as the Papists wish, because faith, through which he offered, presupposes the word of God, or divine revelation, which without doubt was made to the Protoplasts in that slaughter and typical stripping of skins, and was preached to the sons by the Patriarch, the first Doctor of the first domestic Church: without which faith it is impossible to please God, Heb. 11:6, through which also he alone obtained righteousness, because the righteousness of God is through faith in JESUS CHRIST εἰς πάντα, καὶ ἐπὶ πάντας τοὺς πιστεύοντας, Romans 3:22.

2. If it be asked what kind of sacrifice it was, the Apostle in general calls it πλείονα, which the Vulgate barbarously rendered 'plurimam', others with the Syriac and Theophylact have interpreted as 'more excellent' or 'better'. But whence that excellence? Some seek it in the matter offered, because from the flock Abel offered the firstborn, while Cain offered sacrifices only from the fruits of the earth. Estius says that Abel was taught, admonished, and incited by faith to choose the fatter and better things from his goods, which he might offer to God, otherwise than Cain was doing, whom Scripture indicates, by the very fact that it does not commend him, to have offered either worse things or without selection as a carnal and greedy man. Ribera warns that the Apostle's words can be understood in two ways: (1.) By faith Abel was induced to offer a more precious sacrifice to God. (2.) His faith caused it to be more precious and more pleasing to God than the offering of his brother. He says that in both ways these things seem to him to be understood from Gen. IV, because Abel's sacrifice was better, since Abel is said to have offered the best things he had, namely the firstborn of his flock and their fat. But concerning Cain, it is only said that he offered gifts to the Lord from the fruits of the earth: which he confirms from Chrysostom, Homily XVIII on Genesis. Ambrose in Book I of 'On Cain and Abel', chapters VII and X, noting a double fault: one, that he offered after the days, and the other, that he offered from the fruits, not the first fruits. Ribera adds: And although neither of them offered without faith, yet a greater faith is understood to have been in Abel, who offered better things; and the same greater faith also rendered the sacrifice more pleasing to God. But it is not gathered from either Moses or Paul that Cain offered by faith, even if Abel's faith was greater; indeed, faith is attributed to Abel alone, and righteousness, and divine complacency: faith is denied to Cain, and furthermore righteousness as well; and it is said that God did not look upon his gifts, which is divine displeasure. A more excellent sacrifice is indeed said to have been offered by Abel compared to Cain, but his faith is not said to be greater than his: That one was more excellent or better, and pleasing to God, because it was offered by faith: This one was not pleasing to God, because it was not offered through faith, without which it is impossible to please God. The latter sense of Ribera is therefore granted, but in such a way that this—that Abel's sacrifice was pleasing—is attributed to faith simply, but not to a greater faith. For true faith can exist, and be pleasing to God, even if it is weak, Is. XLII. 1. Nor does the Apostle deal with degrees of faith, or a comparison of greater and lesser faith, but he contrasts faith and unbelief, attributing righteousness and life to the former, and divine displeasure and destruction to the latter, ch. X. 38, 39. The former sense is also opposed by the Papists, whereby Abel is said to be induced by faith to offer a more excellent sacrifice; because if he offered it through faith: therefore he was not induced by reason and the light of nature: And it can be admitted thus far, that Abel, taught by divine revelation through the instruction of his parents concerning the garments prepared by God, recognized that sacrifices of firstborn cattle ought to be offered to God, and offered the same through faith in the seed of the woman: but that Cain departed from the word of the institution, and offered fruits as a sacrifice from private intention, and that without faith: whereas sacrifices ought to have been offered to God from the firstborn of cattle: and indeed with true faith in the Messiah, whose types were sacrifices of such a kind as propitiatory sacrifices.

Whence the 3rd proclamation of Abel's sacrifice shines forth: (1.) That through faith he received testimony that he was righteous. 'Through which' is referred not to the sacrifice, as it seemed to some, but to faith, because the Apostle had begun to deal with faith; he had spoken of faith in general in v. 2, 'they were testified of', and the Apostle would continue to discourse about faith. He is therefore called righteous by the righteousness not of works, but of faith, because through faith he offered a better sacrifice, through faith he received testimony that he is righteous, and thus through faith he was justified: concerning which the gracious acceptance of Abel's sacrifice and the Lord's address to Cain also teaches how one is accepted by God. See what we said on Gen. IV. 4 and 7 in our commentary on Genesis. This is the theme which the Apostle here primarily sets out to prove through the examples of the ancients, even though he has interspersed other predicates and praises of faith.

(2.) That God himself testified concerning the gifts of Abel: which is evident from Gen. IV. 5. The manner of the testimony, however, is expressed by Theodotion, as witnessed by Jerome in 'Hebrew Questions', interpreting the Mosaic words thus: 'and he inflamed', and God inflamed [the sacrifice] upon the sacrifice of Abel: for this was a sign of testimony and a symbol of divine gracious acceptance: prefiguring typically how God, with the fire of justice and wrath tempered by the flame of divine love, would ignite the unique propitiatory victim of the New Testament 'for a sweet-smelling savor', Eph. V. 2.

(3.) That through faith he is still preached, even though Abel is now dead. Chrysostom, Theophylact, and also Scaliger explain the word 'is spoken of' as 'is preached', 'is praised', it is in the mouth of all, so that the sense is: That he lives even today in the memory of men with the praise of righteousness. Others prefer to explain it actively, that Abel's blood spoke even after death, from a comparison of Gen. IV. 10 and Heb. XII. 24. But the former explanation seems more suitable, α because the Apostle has no word here concerning the blood of Abel and the fratricide of Cain, whence those parallel passages can by no means be held. β The speech or cry of blood contributes nothing to this, as only the faith of Abel is commended. γ 'Through it', the Apostle says, 'he being dead still is spoken of'. For what does this cry and voice of the slain Abel's blood have to do with faith and the proclamation of faith? Did the voice of Abel's blood cry out through faith? Then even if you refer those words 'through it' to the nearest participle 'having died', 'through faith having died', although it is certain that for most it is referred to the verb 'is spoken of', what does Abel's faith have to do with the fact that his blood cries to God for vengeance? δ The particle 'still' is more correctly referred to the times of the Apostle than to the past. For there is greater emphasis in the fact that through faith STILL, even now in the Apostle's time, indeed even in the present time, although he was destroyed long ago, 'he is spoken of'. It is customary for Scripture that a continuous act is denoted by a present verb, and when the word 'still' is added besides, the continuation is indicated all the more. And we have no reason why we should not leave that in its full extent. ε It was most fitting that the memory of that first just man, who is mentioned after the Protoplasts, the first martyr, who underwent death for the justice of faith, because by offering a sacrifice in faith he was declared just by God, the first Candidate for eternity, and a guest of heaven as to his soul, be celebrated, because through faith he obtained justice and life: whom Christ himself also celebrated as just, and designated as the first martyr, Matt. XXIII. 35. ζ Even if you render it actively, as some Codices have had it, λαλεῖ: Yet that λαλιὰ of Abel is made διὰ πίστεως, and therefore what else does Abel still speak through faith, than what the Apostle had preached concerning his faith, namely that through faith ἐμαρτυρήθη εἶναι δίκαιος. Not so much did his voice cry out by demanding vengeance upon Cain the fratricide, as his faith cries out, confirmed by divine testimony, by celebrating the divine grace exhibited in Christ to him, as the first, not only justified by faith, but also saved. Which λαλιὰ is to be properly observed by the Hebrews, if they wish to be justified and saved in the same way, and to be children of πίστεως εἰς

the preservation of the soul, chap. X. 39, There is therefore no need for a mystical sense, for since Abel still speaks though dead, if, as Grotius prefers, an active sense must be admitted, it is necessary that he be alive at all. For he is introduced as if speaking from heaven, in what way he was received into heaven, namely solely through faith in the seed of the woman, just as Abraham also ordered from heaven to hear Moses and the Prophets, as those who testify of Christ, and eternal life, to be obtained in Christ through faith John V. 39. 40. Luke XXIV. 26. seqq. as also v. 45. 46. 47. Acts X. 43. chap. XV. 11. Ribera explains it thus: As if he were to say: He lives, and this is the evidence that he lives, that he is on the lips of all, that all admire him and proclaim him blessed: For he who admonishes others to be just, speaks. For the discourse does not profit as much as his passion. For just as the sky, merely by appearing, speaks, so also does he when he comes to mind. For he would never be in such admiration, if he had a thousand tongues, if he were living, as he is now in admiration &c. In the same way Theophylact, Oecumenius, Theodoret explain it. He speaks, says Theophylact, and exalted by glory, and having attained the celebrity of the fame of his name.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Πίστει πλείονα θυσίαν ᾿Αβὲλ παρὰ Κάϊν προσήνεγκε Θεῷ.] Nota θυσίαν hic dici tam de frugibus quam de pecudi- bus, qua de re diximus ad Levit. II. ad Marc. IX. 49. & hic supra VIII. 3. Πλείονα hic valet acceptiorem, quo- modo & Ebræi sumunt יותר. Sic ferme Matth. VI. 25. XII. 41. 42. Marc. XII. 33. Luc. XI. 31. 32. XII. 23. Et παρὰ Κάϊν intelligendum παρὰ τῆς τῦ Κάϊν quomodo hic accepit Syrus. Tale est illud Plinii: Omnium tri- umphorum lauream adepte majorem. Subauditur enim laurets. Ideo autem acceptiorem dicit fuisse oblatio- nem Abelis, quia fidem habuit. Credidit Deum re- pensare bona & mala facta, quod & differte ad histo- riam addidit Paraphrastes Hierosolymitanus. Simile est quod Bacchai ait, Deum in exitu ex Ægypto non sanguinem respexisse aspersum postibus, sed Israëlitarum fidem.

Δι' ἧς ἐμαρτυρήθη δίκαιος εἶναι] Per fidem factus est ju- stus, & ejus justitia accepit testimonium, à Deo nempe, ut sequitur. Est hic idem verbum μαρτυρεῖσθαι de quo dixi- mus supra 2.

Μαρτυροῦντος ἐπὶ τοῖς δώροις αὐτοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ] Nempe igne cœlitus misso super ea dona Deus ostendit Abelem, & propter Abelem ejus oblationem sibi gratam esse, ut di- ximus ad Gen. IV. 4. Et ita hic Græci interpretes omnes, Gen. IV. 4. ubi in Ebræo est אל־מנחתו: unde appa- ret olim מנחה fuisse nomen Generis, quod in lege est nomen speciei. Sic & sub Evangelio opera ex fide profi- ciscentia grata habet Deus.

Καὶ δ' αὐτῆς ἀποθανὼν ἔτι λαλεῖται] Manuscriptus: Ετι λαλεῖ: nempe in Genesi. Ob fidem mortuus adhuc ibi loquitur, id est, sanguis ejus ad Deum clamat, Gen. IV. 10. Est enim hic Præsens pro Præterito, quod ita vivide ostenditur quasi præsens sit. Cædes Abelis à Deo vin- dictam exegit. Legendum, ut dixi, ostendit id quod infra est XII. 24. αἵματι ῥαντισμοῦ κρεῖττον λαλοῦντι παρὰ τὸν 'Aβὲλ, ubi idem locus Geneseos respicitur. Δι' αὐτῆς hic valet idem quod δι' αὐτήν. Vide quæ diximus supra L 2. Sensus vulgaris loci Geneseos apertus est: at sensus mysti- cus, pios post mortem vivere, quia & loquuntur. Philo post tractatam hanc historiam libro: pejorem insidiari me- liori: ζῇ γὰρ ὁ τεθνᾶαι, ὥγε καὶ ἱκέτης ὢν Θεοῦ καὶ φωνῇ χρώμενος εὑρίσκεται. Patria ferme habet Jonathan ad di- ctum Geneseos locum.

Quod 1. ad συνέχειαν & scopum: Probat hoc exemplo Apostolus, fide in Christum nos gra- tiam Dei consequi, ac justificari; quod ex Ha- bac. II. 4. deduxerat, quia fide in semen muli- eris promissum obtulit Abel sacrificium Deo gratum, & testimonium, quod justus esset, ob- tinuit. Quodnam enim aliud fidei Abelis ob- jectum erat, quam semen illud mulieris, de quo Protoplastis anunciatum erat, quod à ser- pente infernali calcaneo lædi in passione ac mor- te, eidem verò caput & omnem potestatem ita conterere debeat, Gen. III. 15. quod prædica- rat Eva, mater Caini & Abelis, se corde possi- dere ac fide amplecti nomine symbolico Caini designans tanquam איש את־יהוה, virum il- lum, conculcatorem serpentis, Dominum: Gen. IV. 1. cujus mactationem ceu agni immaculati præfiguratat Deus, cum è pellibus occisis agnis vel ovibus detractis, quarum carnes in sacrifi- cium oblatæ sunt, vestiverat Protoplastos in ty- pum mortis Messiæ, cujus justitia & obedientia usque ad mortem præstanda nos, quibus ob peccatum nuditas ignominiosa erat, vestiendi eramus. Nec verò è propria ἐθελοθρησκεία, vel ratione ac natura Duce, quod Papistæ vo- lunt, obrulit Abel sacrificium, quia fides, per quam obtulit, verbum Dei præsupponit, vel re- velationem divinam, quæ sine dubio facta Pro- toplastis in illa mactatione, & pellium detractio- ne typica, & filiis à Patriarcha primæ domesticæ Ecclesiæ primo Doctore prædicata fuit: Sine qua- li fide impossibile est placere Deo, Ebr. XI. 6. per quam etiam unice justitiam consequutus est, quia justitia Dei per fidem JESU CHRISTI εἰς πάντα, καὶ ἐπὶ πάντας τοὺς πιστεύοντας, Ro- man. III. 22.

2. Qualis hostia fuerit, si quæratur, Aposto- lus in genere πλείονα vocat, quod Vulgatus pluri- mam barbare reddidit, alii cum Syro & Theo- phylacto præstantiorem vel meliorem interpreta- ti sunt. Unde autem præstantia illa? Nonnul- li quærunt eam in materia oblata, quod de pecudi- bus primogenita Abel, Cain solum de frugibus terræ sacrificia obtulerint. Estius Abelem fide edoctum, admonitum atque incitatum fuisse ait, ut de bonis suis pinguiora ac meliora, quæ Deo of- ferret, eligeret, secus quam faciebat Cain, quem ut hominem carnalem & avarum vel deteriora vel sine delectu obtulisse Scriptura indicat, eo ipso, quod non commendat. Ribera duobus modis in- telligi posse Apostoli verba monet: (1.) Fide Abel inductus est ad offerendum Deo hostiam preti- osiorem (2) fides ejus effecit, ut pretiosior, Deoque gratior esset oblatione fratris. Utroque modo sibi ea intelligenda videri ait è Gen. IV. quod me- lior hostia Abelis fuerit, quoniam Abel dicitur obtulisse optima, quæ habebat, primogenitos sci- licet gregis sui & adipes eorum. De Cain autem tantum dicitur, obtulisse eum de fructibus terræ munera Domino: Quæ firmat è Chrysostomo homil. XIIX. in Genes. Ambrosio libr. I. de Cain & Abel cap. VII. & X. duplicem culpam notante, uuam quod post dies obtulit, alteram quod ex fructibus non primis fructibus. Addit Ribera: Et quamvis neuter eorum sine fide obtulerit, tamen major fides intelligitur fuisse in Abele, qui meliora obtulit; atque eadem fides major gratiorem etiam Deo reddidit hostiam. Sed nec à Mose, nec à Pau- lo colligitur, Cainum fide obtulisse, etsi Abelis fides major fuerit; imò Abeli soli fides tribuitur, & justitia, & complacentia divina: Caino denega- tur fides, ac porrò etiam justitia; diciturque non respexisse Deum munera ejus, quæ est divina dis- plicentia. Præstantior quidem hostia ab Abele oblata dicitur præ Caino, sed non major illius, quam hujus fides dicitur: Illa præstantior vel me- lior erat, & Deo grata, quia ex fide offerebatur: Hæc Deo grata non erat, quia non offerebatur per fidem, sine qua Deo placere ἀδύνατον. Poste- rior ergo Riberæ sensus conceditur, sed ita, quod fidei simpliciter, non autem fidei majori tribuatur hoc, quod grata esset hostia Abelis. Fides enim vera esse potest, Deoque placens, etiamsi imbe- cillis sit, Es. XLII. 1. Neque de gradibus fidei, aut comparatione majoris & minoris fidei agit Apo- stolus, sed fidem & ἀπιστίαν componit, illi justi- tiam & vitam tribuens, huic divinam displicen- tiam & ἀπώλειαν, cap. X. 38. 39. Prior sensus & Papistis adversatur, qua Abel inductus fide dici- tur ad offerendam πλείονα θυσίαν; quia si per fi- dem obtulit eam: Ergo non inductus ratione & lumine naturæ: Et admitti hactenus potest, quod è revelatione divina per informationem Paren- tum de vestibus à Deo paratis edoctus Abel agno- verit, sacrificia de pecudibus primogenitis Deo offerenda, eademque per fidem in semen mulieris obtulerit: Cain autem à verbo institutionis dis- cesserit, & ex privata intentione fruges, idque sine fide, in sacrificium obtulerit: quum in pri- mogenitis pecudum sacrificia Deo offerri de- buerit: & quidem vera fide in Messiam, cujus sacrificii propitiatorii typi erant sacrificia ejusmodi.

Unde 3. præconium sacrificii Abelis elucescit (1.) quod per fidem testimonium acceperit, quod justus esset δι' ἧς refertur non ad hostiam, quod nonnullis visum, sed ad fidem, quia de fide agere cœperat Apostolus; De fide dixerat in genere v. 2. ἐμαρτυρήθησαν, de fide etiam deinceps disse- ret Apostolus. Δίκαιος ergo dicitur justitia, non operum, sed fidei, quia per fidem obtulit hostiam potiorem, per fidem testimonium accepit, quod justus sit, adeoque per fidem justificatus est: De quo etiam gratiosa sacrificii Abelis acceptatio & concio Domini ad Cainum quomodo acceptus quis Deo sit, docet. Vid. quæ ad Gen. IV. 4. & 7. in comment. ad Genesin diximus. Quod thema Apostolus hic per exempla veterum probare im- primis instituit, etsi alia prædicata & elogia fidei intermisit.

(2.) Quod Deus ipse testificatus sit super donis Abelis: quod è Gen. IV. 5. constat. Modus autem testificationis à Theodotione, teste Hieronymo in Quæst. Ebraic. expressus est, verba Mosaica sic in- terpretante, καὶ ἐνεπύρωσεν, & inflammavit Deus super sacrificium Abelis: Hoc enim erat signum testificationis & symbolum gratiosæ acceptatio- nis divinæ: præfigurans typice, quomodo Deus igne justitiæ & iræ temperato flamma amoris divi- ni incensurus sit victimam unicam propitiatoriam Novi Testamenti εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας, Eph. V. 2.

(3.) Quod per fidem adhuc prædicetur, etsi jam mortuus Abel. Verbum λαλεῖται Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, ut & Scaliger exponunt prædica- tur, laudatur, est in ore omnium, ut sit sensus: Eum adhuc hodie vivere in hominum memoria cum laude justitiæ. Alii active malunt explicare, quod Abelis sanguis adhuc post mortem loquu- tus fuerit, è collatione Gen. IV. 10. & Ebr. XII. 24. Sed prior explicatio convenientior videtur, α quia de sanguine Abelis & fratricidio Caini hic nul- lum verbum Apostolus, unde loca illa parallela minimè haberi possunt. β Nihil huc facit loque- la vel clamor sanguinis, uti unice commendatur fi- des Abelis. γ Δι' αὐτῆς per fidem mortuus adhuc λαλεῖται, inquit Apostolus. Quid enim hic cla- mor & vox sanguinis occisi Abelis ad fidem fidei- que præconium? Num per fidem clamavit vox sanguinis Abelis? Tum etiamsi referas illa δι' αὐτῆς ad participium proximum ἀποθανὼν, per fi- dem mortuus, etsi plerisque ad verbum λαλεῖται referri certum sit, quid eo facit fides Abelis, quod sanguis ejus clamet ad Deum pro vindicta? δ Par- ticula ἔτι rectius ad tempora Apostoli refertur, quam ad Præterita. Major enim est in eo empha- sis, quod per fidem ADHUC, etiamnum Apo- stoli tempore, imò hodierno etiam tempore, etsi jam pridem destructus, λαλεῖται. Præsenti verbo continuum actum notari, Scripturæ solenne est, & quum vox ἔτι insuper addatur, eo magis conti- nuatio indicatur. Quam cur in sua amplitudine non relinquamus, causam nullam habemus. ε Pri- mi illius justi, qui post Protoplastos commemo- ratur, primi martyris, qui pro justitia fidei mor- tem subiit, quod sacrificium fide offerens justus declaratus fuerit à Deo, primi æternitatis Candi- dati, & cæli quoad animam hospitis memoriam, quod per fidem justitiam & vitam consequutus sit, celebrari par erat vel maxime: quem justum etiam celebravit, ac martyrem primum designavit Christus ipse, Matth. XXIII. 35. ζ Etiamsi acti- ve reddas, ut nonnulli Codices habuerunt, λαλεῖ: Ea tamen Abelis λαλιὰ fit διὰ πίστεως, ideoque quid aliud adhuc loquitur Abel per fidem, quam quod de fide ejus prædicarat Apostolus, quod nempe per fidem ἐμαρτυρήθη εἶναι δίκαιος. Non tam vox ejus clamavit poscendo vindictam de Cai- no fratricida, quam fides ejus clamat, testimo- nio divino comprobata, celebrando divinam gra- tiam in Christo, sibi, ceu primo, per fidem non justificato tantum, sed & salvato, exhibitam. Quæ λαλιὰ Ebræis propriè observanda, si justificari itidem ac salvari velint, & filii esse πίστεως εἰς

περιποίησιν ψυχῆς, cap. X. 39, Non ergo sensu opus est mystico, nam cum adhuc loquatur Abel etsi mortuus, si, quod mavult Grotius, sensus Activus admittendus, vivere omnino eum oportet. Intro- ducitur enim quasi de cœlo loquens, quomodo in cœlum receptus sit, nimirum unice per fidem in se- men mulieris, quemadmodum & Abraham de cœ- lo jussit Mosen & Prophetas audire, utpote qui de Christo testificantur, & vita æterna, in Christo per fidem obtinenda Johan. V. 39. 40. Luc. XXIV. 26. seqq. ut & v. 45. 46.47. Actor. X. 43. cap. XV. 11. Ri- bera ita exponit: Quasi dicat: Vivit ille, & hoc in- dicium est, quod vivat, quod in ore omnium versa- tur, quod omnes eum admirantur & beatum prædi- cant: Qui enim admonet alios, ut justi sint, loqui- tur. Non enim tantum proficit sermo, quantum passio illius. Sicut enim cœlum tantum apparens loquitur, sic & ille dum in memoriam venit. Nun- quam enim in tanta esset admiratione, si mille lin- guas haberet, si viveret, in quanta nunc est admira- tione &c. Eodem modo exponunt Theophylactus, Oecumenius, Theodorets. Loquitur, inquit, The- ophylactus, & gloria evectus, & fama nominis ade- ptus celebritatem.

## 11:5
Ver. 5.

By faith Enoch was translated so as not to see death, and was not found, because God had translated him] Sir. XLIV. 16 also has translated concerning Enoch. Those words 'and was not found' with the following are a proof of what he said, from the Greek text Gen. V. 24. But that text was understood by the wise in such a way that it was believed Enoch was preserved immune from death by a special privilege. The Samaritan in that place: His Angel took him. Onkelos: God did not kill him, that is, did not suffer him to die, to which locution 1 Kings XVII. 20 is similar. Jonathan: He was taken up and ascended into heaven by command before the Lord: Josephus: Ἀνεχώρησε πρὸς τὸ θεῖον. He was translated into Paradise, the Arab in this place. That was a great argument that this better life could be given.

For before his translation he was testified to have pleased God] What is said in Hebrew, Enoch walked before God, the Greeks translate in Gen. V. 22 & 24: Εὐηρέστησεν Ἐνὼχ τῷ Θεῷ. Nor does the Syrian interpreter of Genesis translate it otherwise. Properly, walked before God signifies, he was at leisure for God, he devoted effort to God. The Chaldean, as much of Enoch as of Noah, walked in the fear of God, and those who are such, please God. Neither can be without faith. Therefore it follows here.

From Abel, the first just man received into heaven as to his soul through faith in the Messiah, the Apostle proceeds to Enoch, not that other Patriarchs were not worthy of commemoration, but because he was the first of those who, having been received into heaven both in soul and body, attained eternal salvation through faith in the Messiah, not that he was exhibited only as an argument that this better life could be given, but because it was also taught by him that this life is obtained in no other way than through faith in Christ. For the Apostle here collected faith a posteriori, namely from the divine complacency, the testimony of which he also praises here from Gen. V. 22. 24. from the version of the LXX Interpreters, who rendered what is said in Hebrew, 'walked before God', in this way: By which therefore not only the pursuit of holiness is noted, or that he was at leisure for God, but according to that interpretation approved by the Holy Spirit, that divine complacency is expressed. Therefore he walked before God in such a way that reciprocally God also walked with him, and dwelt in him, Levit. XXVI. 12. 2 Corinth. VI. 15. He walked with God, in God, and God walked with him, and in him: Just as God is the temple of the elect, in whom they are and dwell, and the elect and faithful are the temple of God, in whom God is and deigns to dwell. Conf. 1 Corinth. III. 16. Apoc. XXI. 22. they have complacency in God, to whom they devote effort, and God has εὐδοκίαν in them, and cares for them paternally. Whence the faith of Enoch is clearly collected, because neither does God have complacency in man, unless he believes, nor can anyone have solid complacency and unmoved acquiescence in God and the divine will, except through faith. Therefore here, especially in such an illustrious example, the Apostle added: Without faith it is impossible to please God. Blessed Luther says that Enoch, as some one above all the Doctors or Patriarchs of the original world, is celebrated by the phrase 'walked with God', because to walk with God is to go forth according to one's calling and to oppose oneself to the iniquity and malice of Satan and the world, and to profess the seed of the woman; not to love the religion of the world, and to preach with zeal that there is another life after this life through Christ &c. Which can also be said to express the appearances of God by the phrase, so frequent to him, that he could seem to walk with God. His faith in the Messiah as the Lord who would judge the unfaithful is also testified to by the sermon of Enoch observed by St. Jude v. 14. Nor can there be any doubt that he entered into heaven through faith in the blood of Jesus and through the veil, that is, his flesh, because there is no access to the holy places except by that reason, the Apostle testifying, Heb. X. 19. 20.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Πίστει Ἐνὼχ μετετέθη τοῦ μὴ ἰδεῖν θάνατον, καὶ οὐχ εὑρίσκετο, διότι μετέθηκεν αὐτὸν ὁ Θεὸς] Μετετέθη de Enocho habet & Sir. XLIV. 16. Illa καὶ οὐχ εὑρίσκετο cum sequentibus sunt ejus, quod dixit probatio, ex textu Græco Gen. V. 24. Ita autem à sapientibus intellectus fuit textus ille, ut crede- retur Enochus à morte immunis servatus speciali privile- gio. Samaritanus eo loco: Accepit eum Angelus ejus. Onkelos: Non occidit eum Deus, id est, non passus est mori, cui loquutioni similis 1. Reg. XVII. 20. Jonathan: Sublatus fuit & ascendit in cœlum ex mandato coram Do- mino: Josephus: Ἀνεχώρησε πρὸς τὸ θεῖον. Translatus est in Paradisum, Arabs hoc loco. Id magnum argumentum erat posse dari vitam hanc meliorem.

Πρὸ γὰρ τῆς μεταθέσεως αὐτῷ μεμαρτύρηται εὐηρεστηκέ- ναι τῷ Θεῷ] Quod in Ebræo dicitur, ambulavit Enoch coram Deo, id Græci Gen. V. 22. & 24. vertunt: Εὐηρέστη- σεν Ἐνὼχ τῷ Θεῷ. Nec aliter Syrus Geneseos Interpres. Proprie ambulavit coram Deo significat, vacavit Deo, Deo operam dedit. Chaldæus tam de Enocho quam de Noa ambulavit in timore Dei, qui autem tales sunt, Deo placent. Neutrum esse potest fine fide. Ideo sequitur hic.

Ab Abele primo justo per fidem in Messiam in cœlum quoad animam recepto ad Enochum pro- greditur Apostolus, non quod alii Patriarchæ non digni fuerint commemoratione, sed quod ille pri- mus fuerit eorum, qui & anima & corpore recepti in cœlum æternam salutem adepti per fidem in Messiam, non ut argumentu tantum exhiberetur, posse dari vitam hac meliorem, sed quod etiam eo doceretur, non aliter, quam per fidem in Christum hanc vitam obtingere. Collegit enim Apostolus hic fidem à posteriori, nempe à complacentia divina, cujus etiam testimonium hic laudat è Gen. V. 22. 24. è LXX. Interpr. versione, qui sic reddidere, quod in Ebræo dicitur, ambulavit coram Deo: Quo pro- inde non tantum studium sanctitatis notatur, vel quod vocarit Deo, sed juxta interpretationem illã Spiritui sancto probatam exprimitur illa compla- centia divina. Proinde ita ambulavit coram Deo, ut reciproce etiam Deus ambulavit cum ipso, & in ipso habitavit, Levit XXVI. 12. 2. Corinth. VI. 15. Ambulavit cum Deo, in Deo, & Deus ambulavit cum ipso, & in ipso: Uti Deus est electorum tem- plum, in quo illi sunt & habitant, & electi ac fideles sunt templum Dei, in quo Deus est & habitare di- gnatur. Conf. 1. Corinth. III. 16. Apoc. XXI. 22. ipsi habent complacentiam in Deo, cui operam dant, & Deus habet εὐδοκίαν in ipsis, eosque paterne cu- rat. Unde fides Enochi liquido colligitur, quia nec Deus complacentiam habet in homine, nisi credat, nec quisquam in Deo & voluntate divina potest habere complacentiam solidam, & acquie- scentiam immotam, nisi per fidem. Idcirco hic imprimis in tam illustri exemplo addidit Aposto- lus: Sine fide impossibile est placere Deo. B. Lu- therus Enochum ait, tanquam solum aliquem præ omnibus mundi originalis Doctoribus, seu Patriar- chis phrasi ambulavit cum Deo celebrari,quod am- bulare cum Deo sit prodire secundum vocationem & se opponere iniquitati & malitiæ Satanæ, & mundi, ac profiteri, semen mulieris; non amare mundi religionem, & studio prædicare per Christum aliam vitam post hanc vitam esse &c. Quæ etiam phrasi apparitiones Dei exprimi dici potest, adeo ipsi frequentes, ut cum Deo ambulare videri pos- set. Fidem ejus in Messiam ceu Dominum judi- caturum infideles, testatur etiam concio Enochi S. Judæ observata v. 14. Neque dubium esse potest, quin per fidem ἐν τῷ ἅιματι Ἰησοῦ & διὰ τοῦ κατα- πετάσματος, τοῦτ᾽ ἔστι τῆς σαρκὸς ἀυτοῦ in cœlum ingressus est, quia non patet aditus in sancta, nisi ea ratione teste Apostolo, Ebr. X. 19. 20.

## 11:6
Ver. 6.

But without faith it is impossible to please] Namely God, which must be repeated from the preceding. He will now give the reason for this saying.

Ribera gathers that the word God was added in some copies from the Vulgate and Syriac translation. But that collection is weak. It is not found in the Greek, nor in Chrysostom, Theophylact, Theodoret, Oecumenius. That it must be understood, however, is manifest from the preceding words. Which aphorism must be properly fixed in the mind. For it not only confirms the faith of all who pleased God before the flood, but also of any others at any time, from which it is invincibly concluded that no one ever pleased or pleases God, or could attain eternal life without faith: But faith in Christ: For this is the whole of this treatment. For he who does not believe in him is already judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God, John III. 18. He was therefore translated by faith, says Theophylact, that is, faith itself translated this man to another place, who also was seen to have pleased. From this aphorism it is also evident that nothing pleases God without faith, and that not only are persons not acceptable without faith, but neither do virtues or works please God without faith, Rom. XIV. last. No virtue is true before God without faith, says Augustine, book XIX de Civitate Dei, ch. 25. Just as nothing is delightful to men without light, so nothing is delightful and acceptable to God without the light of faith, says Origen, book I on John.

For he who comes to God must believe that He is, and that He becomes a rewarder to those who seek Him] That is, no one will have any religion unless he believes both that there is some eternal and omnipotent divinity, and that He takes care of human affairs, in such a way that He is willing to render good things to those who obey Him. To approach God is to worship God, as we said above VII. 25. XI. 1. 22. To seek God, בִּקֵּשׁ or דָּרַשׁ, is to enter upon those ways by which the favor of God can be obtained, as can be seen in Deut. IV. 29. Jer. XXIX. 13. Zach. VIII. 21. 22. Amos V. 4. Ps. X. 4. XL. 17. Cicero also said in De Natura Deorum that there is no religion if the gods have no care for human affairs. And Epictetus requires two things for piety which we have here, except that he names gods instead of God: To have right opinions about the gods, as existing and governing all things well and justly. Seneca: The first worship of the gods is to believe in the gods: then to render to them their majesty, to render their goodness, without which there is no majesty. Thus also Aelian says that it is affirmed even by the barbarians, both that there is a Divinity and that He takes care of us. Plutarch very well: For one ought to conceive of God not only as immortal and blessed, but also as philanthropic, caring, and beneficial in such a way. But Lactantius: Neither can any honor be owed to God if He provides nothing to the worshiper, nor any fear, if He is not angry at the one who does not worship.

See more, if you have time, in our second book on the law of war and peace XX. 46. in the text and in the annotations. Just as this writer uses the word μισθαποδότης here, so he uses the word μισθαποδοσίας elsewhere, as II. 2. X. 35. below 26.

Προσερχόμενον τῷ Θεῷ, approaching or about to approach God, like Enoch, that is, who even wishes to be transferred to God, although not by that μεταθέσει, by translation, without the intervention of death, but by a blessed ἀνάλυσιν, so that he may nevertheless arrive at God, he must believe that God is, namely that true God, who is none other than the one we profess in Baptism, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in the knowledge of whom consists eternal life, John XVII. 3. and that to those who seek Him through faith, who seek His grace, which can be obtained only through faith in Christ, without which it is impossible to please God, because no one comes to the Father except through the Son, John XIV. 6. nor is there salvation in any other name, Is. XLV. 24. Acts IV. 12. μισθαποδότης γίνεται, He becomes a rewarder, not out of debt, but out of grace. For the reward is unmerited and of pure grace, because it is a χάρισμα, a gift of God in Christ Jesus, Romans VI. last verse, just as it was promised to the Patriarch Abraham, who believed, out of grace: I will be your great reward, Gen. XV. 1. who believed God, and this was credited to him for righteousness, v. 6. For here μισθαποδοσία and κληρονομία are interchanged, as is clear from the comparison of v. 6 and 7. In vain, therefore, do either Papists or Socinians try to extract from this merit or retribution owed to our works. For there is no mention here of works, but only of faith; no mention of merit or of retribution owed, but of that which is obtained through faith, and therefore out of grace. For both faith and grace are opposed to debt, Romans IV. 4. ch. XI. 6. Eph. II. 8. 9. μισθαποδότης therefore is the giver of the reward, that is, of the prize, as is also μισθαποδοσία, ch. X. 35. and in this chapter XI. 26. it is taken from a gratuitous and unmerited reward, by which God is said to reward believers, which is not done except gratuitously, and Coloss. III. 24. eternal life, which is a gratuitous reward, is called ἀνταπόδοσις τῆς κληρονομίας, where the name of retribution or reward is used improperly, but inheritance is used properly; because heirs and sons through gratuitous adoption deserve nothing, whence Ambrose, l. Lep. I. says: One reward, he says, is of liberality and grace, another is the stipend of virtue, the remuneration of labor.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Χωρὶς δὲ πίστεως ἀδύνατον ἐυαρεστῆσαι] Nempe Θεῷ, quod ex præcedentibus repetendum. Hujus dicti jam reddet ra- tionem.

In nonnullis exemplaribus additam fuisse vo- cem Θεῷ è translatione Vulgata & Syriaca colligit Ribera. Sed infirma est ea collectio. In Græcis non reperitur, nec apud Chrysostomum, Theophy- lactum, Theodorectum, Oecumenium. Id tamen subaudiendum esse, ex verbis præcedentibus est manifestum. Qui aphorismus probe animo in- figendus est. Nam non modo firmat fidem omni- um, qui ante diluvium Deo placuerunt, sed etiam quorumvis aliorum quovis tempore, ex eo invicte concluditur, neminem unquam Deo placuisse aut placere, vel vitam æternam consequi posse sine fide= Fide autem inChristum: De hac enim tota hæc est tractatio. Nam qui non credit in ipsum, jam judi- catus est, eo quod non credat in nomen Unigeniti Filii Dei, Johan. III. 18. Est ergo fide translatus,in- quit Theophylactus, hoc est, fides ipsa hunc alio transtulit, qui & placuisse est visus. Ex hoc apho- rismo etiam constat, nihil Deo placere absque fi- de, non personas tantum gratas sine fide non esse, sed nec virtutes, vel opera placere Deo, sine fide, Rom. XIV. ult. Nulla virtus vera apud Deum sine fide, ait Augustinus l. XIX. de D. Dei c.25. Sicut ni- hil est delectabile hominibus sine luce; sic nihil est de- lectabile & acceptum Deo absque fidei lumine, ait Origenes l. I. in Joh.

Πιστεῦσαι γὰρ δεῖ τὸν προσερχόμενον τῷ Θεῷ ὅτι ἐστὶ, καὶ τοῖς ἐκζητοῦσιν ἀυτὸν μισθαποδότης γίνεται] Id est, nemo reli- gionem habebit ullam nisi credat & esse numen aliquod æternum atque omnipotens, & curam agere rerum huma- narum, ita ut obedientibus sibi bona reddere velit. Ac- cedere ad Deum, est Deum colere, ut diximus supra VII. 25. XI. 1. 22. Quærere vero Deum בִּקֵּשׁ aut דָּרַשׁ est eas inire vias, per quas Dei favor obtineri possit, ut vide- re est Deut. IV. 29. Jer. XXIX. 13. Zach. VIII. 21. 22. Amos V. 4. Ps. X. 4. XL. 17. Etiam Cicero de natura Deorum dixit nullam esse religionem, si nullam rerum humana- rum procurationem habeant Dii. Et Epictetus ad pieta- tem requirit duo quæ hic habemus, nisi quod pro Deo Deos nominat: Ὀρθὰς ὑπολήψεις περὶ Θεῶν ἔχειν ὡς ὄν- των καὶ διοικούντων τὰ ὅλα καλῶς καὶ δικαίως. Seneca: Pri- mus est Deorum cultus, Deos credere: Deinde reddere illis ma- jestatem suam, reddere bonitatem, sine qua nulla Majestas est. Sic & Ælianus ait etiam à Barbaris affirmari, & esse Numen & nostri curam gerere. Plutarchus optime: Οὐ γὰρ ἀθάνατον καὶ μακάριον μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ φιλάνθρωπον καὶ κη- δεμονικὸν,καὶ ὠφέλιμον προλαμβάνεσθαι τῇ τοιάυτῃ χρὴ τὸν Θε- όν. At Lactantius: Neque honor ullus deberi potest Deo sinibil præstat colenti, nec ullus metus, si non irascitur non colenti.

Vide plura, si vacat, in libro nostro secundo de jure belli & pacis XX. 46. in textu & in annotatis. Sicut hic voce μισθαποδότης, ita & voce μισθαποδοσίας alibi utitur hic Scri- ptor, ut II. 2. X. 35. infra 26.

Προσερχόμενον τῷ Θεῷ accedens vel accessurus ad Deum, ut Enoch, hoc est, qui etiam velit trans- ferri ad Deum, etsi non illa μεταθέσει per transla- tionem, sine mortis interventu, sed per beatam ἀνάλυσιν, ut ad Deum tamen perveniat,eum opor- tet credere, quod Deus sit, nempe verus ille Deus, qui nullus alius est, quam quem in Baptismo pro- fitemur, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus, in cujus cognitione consistit vita æterna, Johan. XVII. 3. & quod illis, qui requirunt ipsum per fidem, qui gratiam ejus requirunt, quod non nisi per fidem in Christum obtineri potest, sine qua impossibile est Deo placere, quia nemo venit ad Patrem nisi per Filium, Johan. XIV. 6. nec est in alio nomine sals, Es. XLV. 24. Actor. IV. 12. μισθαποδότης γίνεται, remunerator fit, non ex debito, sed ex gratia. Mer- ces enim est indebita & gratiæ meræ, quia χάρισμα donum Dei in Christo Jesu, Roman. VI. v. ult. quemadmodum Abrahamo Patriarchæ creden- tium ex gratia promissum est: Ero merces tua ma- gna, Gen. XV. 1. qui credidit Deo, & hoc imputa- tium est ei ad justitiam, v. 6. Commutatur enim hic μισθαποδοσία & κληρονομία, ut è v. 6. & 7. collati- one liquet. Frustra ergo hinc vel Papistæ vel Socini- ani exsculpere conantur meritum aut retributio- nem operibus nostris debitam. Nulla enim hic operum mentio facta, sed solius fidei, nulla meriti vel retributionis debitæ, sed quæ per fidem, adeo- que ex gratia obtinetur. Nam & fides & gratia opponitur debito, Roman. IV. 4. cap. XI. 6. Eph. II. 8. 9. Μισθαποδότης ergo est largitor mercedis, id est, præmii, uti & μισθαποδοσία, cap. X. 35. & hoc cap. XI. 26. de gratuita & indebita mercede abripi- tur, qua Deus dicitur credentes præmiare, quod non sit nisi gratis, & Coloss. III. 24. vita æterna, quæ præmium est gratuitum, ἀνταπόδοσις τῆς κληρονο- μίας dicitur, ubi retributionis seu mercedis nomen improprie, hæreditas autem proprie adhibetur; quia hæredes & filii per gratuitam adoptionem ni- hil merentur, unde Ambrosius l. Lep. I. Alia, in- quit, merces est liberalitatis, & gratiæ, alia virtutis stipendium, laboris remuneratio.

## 11:7
Vers. 7.

Πίστει χρηματισθεὶς Νῶε περὶ τῶν μηδέπω βλεπομένων εὐλα- βηθεὶς κατεσκεύασε κιβωτὸν εἰς σωτηρίαν τοῦ οἴκου αὑτοῦ] Χρηματισθεὶς, warned by an oracle, as Matt. II. 12. 22. Acts X. 22. above VIII. 5. That πίστει refers to κατεσκεύασε, he built the ark by faith, that is, because he had faith in the oracle. But you will rightly construe περὶ τῶν μηδέπω βλεπομένων with εὐλαβηθεὶς, for we read εὐλαβεῖσθαι περὶ τούτου even in Plato, and in Latin we say no less, I fear about this matter, than I fear this matter. Concerning the word εὐλαβηθεὶς, in what sense it is taken by this writer, we spoke above V. 7. By the warning of the oracle he feared the universal flood, such as had never been seen. And this example is well brought forward, because in the Holy Scripture the faith of Noah is evident: of works, which nevertheless accompanied faith, there is no mention, as that passage aptly says; where Noah is said to have pleased God, as Philo well notes in his allegories. That κιβωτὸν or λάρνακα is for the Hebrews תבה a decked ship, such as arks are, we said at Matt. XXIV. 36. and at Gen. VI. 14. Let him who has time see what is said there. But it is said that Noah did this for the salvation of his house, that is, of himself, and his wife, and his three sons and daughters-in-law, Gen. VI. 18. 1 Pet. III. 20. So also we ought to fear the punishments which we do not see, and to enter the ark to avoid them, that is, to embrace baptism, with the doctrine of baptism as Peter explains 1 Pet. III. 21. and thus to save ourselves, and as many others as we can.

Δὶ ἧς κατέκρινε τὸν κόσμον] He is said to condemn some even who by his own deed shows what others ought to have done, and from that convicts those not doing the same of guilt, as can be seen in Matt. XII. 41. 42, where let him who wishes see what we have said. Δι ἧς, through which, namely the ark, for the mention of faith will follow. When Noah was building the ark, he was at the same time telling everyone the reason why he was building it. But they believed nothing, Matt. XXIV. 38. 1 Pet. III. 28. Τὸν κόσμον, that is, the whole human race, outside his family. In the same sense the word κόσμος is used 2 Pet. II. 5.

Καὶ τῆς κατὰ πίσιν δικαιοσύνης ἐγένετο κληρονόμος.] He calls righteousness here the reward of righteousness, just as sin among the Hebrews is the punishment of sin. The reward of righteousness was the possession of the whole world. But he had arrived at that righteousness through faith. And the possession of a better world will come to us likewise through righteousness from faith.

After the Apostle asserted the justification of faith by the very illustrious examples of the faith of the antediluvians, from which it is evident that the saints of the former world were justified by no other reason than through faith in Christ, concerning which our special Diatribe on the faith of the ancients before the flood may be consulted, he now brings forward Noah, who lived partly before the flood, partly after the flood, and was a herald of the righteousness of faith to both worlds, whose faith he commends both from the object of the divine oracle, which was about his being preserved in the flood through faith in the ark, while the whole world was to perish through the waters of the flood, περὶ τῶν μηδέπω βλεπομένων: because faith is ἔλεγχος of things not seen, v. 1. Noah, says Theophylact, received an answer from God by faith, that is, he was instructed by God concerning uncertain things, and yet he did not distrust the words of God, even though all things were proceeding in tranquility, and all men were devoting their efforts to delights and pleasures, and nothing serious was expected. For nothing of that kind had been seen before, nor did it come into anyone's mind that the world would be destroyed by waters. Otherwise, believing God in this, he was struck by the fear of the future flood and prepared and built an ark; which was a salvation for all whom he had in his house, and for the other living creatures. Since he received this oracle ἐυλαβηθεὶς with reverence and therefore with true faith; then by his work, because by faith κα]εσκεύασε τὸν κιβω]ὸν εἰς σωτηρίαν τῆ οἴκυ ἀυτῦ. For he believed that he would be saved in that ark with his household, and there is no doubt that the great Patriarch knew that this ark was a type of the Church, outside of which there is no salvation. It is entirely certain that, believing that the seed of the woman would arise from his own seed, and that eternal salvation would be obtained and secured in him, he undertook this construction of the ark according to the divine oracle: because the noun πίςε- tiã extends itself to these words ἐυλαβηθεὶς κα]εσκεύασε: then by the condemnation of the unbelief of the world, because δι ἧς, by that faith he condemned the unbelieving world both by his work and by his preaching, denouncing not only temporal but also eternal judgment upon their incredulity. For that relative pronoun δι ἧς is conveniently referred to faith, as the principal object, concerning which the Apostle here treats expressly, that the world was convicted of infidelity toward God and His grace through the faith of Noah. If anyone should say that it must be referred to the nearest noun, thus it will pertain not to the ark, but to salvation, in this sense: that Noah by his salvation or rescue from the flood convicted the first world of infidelity, or because it had held this method of escaping as ridiculous, and had rejected the whole Noachic proclamation through infidelity, as the blessed Hülsemann noted in his annotations to Genesis 7:1: then finally from the inheritance τῆς κατὰ πίσιν δικαιοσύνης, of that righteousness which is by faith, which is a most brilliant argument, and that he possessed that faith of which Paul here treats, which faith is justifying and saving, faith in the Messiah, by which alone the just man lives and obtains the preservation of his soul, and through faith he obtained that true righteousness, which is κατὰ πίσιν, obtained only through faith, may have attained, Rom. III. 22. and may have been made an heir of righteousness; an heir, because through adoption he is a son of God; but an heir of righteousness, because it happens that one is an heir not through the law but through the righteousness of faith, Rom. IV. 3. Where Chrysostom and Theophylact observe that, by a Hebraism, 'heir' is used generally for 'possessor'; and 'to be made an heir' for that which is to obtain or attain something. To which is added also the proclamation of righteousness, because Noah was made a herald of righteousness to both worlds, 1 Pet. II. 5. and especially for 120 years before the flood, so that he might be able to free the souls of men in the former world from eternal destruction by the proclamation of true righteousness, because the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, Rom. I. 16. For he was a herald of that righteousness which false prophets and false teachers, denying the Lord who bought them with His own blood, reject, v. 1. because of which, being neglected and not apprehended by true faith when it was preached by Noah, God did not spare the ancient world, v. 15. to whom, being disobedient at one time, when they neglected the longsuffering of God, Christ presented Himself alive, having been delivered for our sins and raised for our righteousness, but [it was] spurned by the unbelievers, who held Noah, the herald of that righteousness, in contempt. On which account Blessed Luther says that Noah is preached by Moses as having walked with God, that is, as Peter interprets, as having conducted the cause of God in public. For that, he says, Peter beautifully explains in 2 Epist. II, when he calls him a herald not of human righteousness but of God's, that is, of faith in the promised seed. Blessed Hülsemann also observes in the same place that when Noah is said to have walked before God, that particle 'before God,' when it is said of a righteous man or of righteousness, is understood to apply only to imputed righteousness, as the Apostle warns in Rom. IV. 2, where he attributes boasting before men to works, but Abraham's boasting before God to imputed righteousness. This faith of Noah relied not only on the Proto-Evangelium, Gen. III. 15, but also on the COVENANT which God established with him, Gen. VI. 18, which, as Megalandrus teaches, God confirmed to him so that Noah might certainly conclude that Christ would be born from his posterity, and that God would preserve a seed-plot of the Church in the midst of such great wrath. But Grotius wrongly says that the reward of Noah's righteousness was the possession of the whole world: for the present world is not possessed through the righteousness of faith, but the inheritance of eternal life is obtained; nor is anything held here concerning the present world, which Noah might have attained through inheritance or through faith.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Πίστει χρηματισθεὶς Νῶε περὶ τῶν μηδέπω βλεπομένων εὐλα- βηθεὶς κατεσκεύασε κιβωτὸν εἰς σωτηρίαν τοῦ οἴκου αὑτοῦ] Χρημα- τισθεὶς oraculo monitus, ut Matth. II. 12. 22. Actor. X. 22. supra VIII. 5. Illud πίστει refertur ad κατεσκεύασε fide stru- xit arcam, id est, quia oraculo fidem habebat. Illa autem περὶ τῶν μηδέπω βλεπομένων recte construes cum εὐλαβηθεὶς, nam εὐλαβεῖσθαι περὶ τότου etiam apud Platonem legimus, & Latine non minus dicimus, metuo de hac re, quam metuo hanc rem. De verbo εὐλαβηθεὶς, quo sensu ab hoc Scri- ptore sumatur, diximus supra V. 7. Ex oraculi monitu me- tuit diluvium universale, quale quid nunquam visum fuerat. Et bene hoc exemplum profertur, quia in sacra Scriptura fi- des Noë patet: Operum, quæ tamen fidem comitata sunt, nulla mentio apte eum locum; quo Noë Deo placuisse dici- tur, ut bene notat Philo in allegoriis. Κιβωτὸν aut λάρνα- κα Ebræis תבה esse navem constratam, quales sunt arcæ, diximus ad Matth. XXIV. 36. & ad Gen. VI. 14. Videat ibi dicta, si cui vacat. Dicitur autem hoc fecisse Noah ad salu- tem domus suæ, id est, suam, & uxoris, & trium filiorum ac nuruum, Gen. VI. 18. 1. Petr. III. 20. Sic & nos debemus metuere pœnas, quas non videmus, & ad eas vitandas in- trare arcam, id est, amplecti baptismum, cum doctrina bap- tismi explicante Petro 1. III. 21. atque ita servare nos ipsos, & quot possumus, alios.

Δὶ ἧς κατέκρινε τὸν κόσμον] Condemnare dicitur aliquos etiam, qui suo facto ostendit, quid alii facere debuerint, atque inde eos non idem facientes culpæ convincit, ut q videre est Matth. XII. 41. 42 ubi à nobis dicta videat, qui vo- let. Δι ἧς per quam, arcam scilicet, nam fidei mentio se- quetur. Cum arcam strueret Noah, simul causam omnibus dicebat, cur strueret. Illi autem nihil credidere, Matth. XXIV. 38. 1. Petr. III. 28. Τὸν κόσμον, id est, totum, extra familiam suam, genus humanum. Eodem sensu vox κόσμος usurpatur 2. Petr. II. 5.

Καὶ τῆς κατὰ πίσιν δικαιοσύνης ἐγένετο κληρονόμος.] Justiti- am hic vocat præmium justitiæ, sicut peccatum apud Ebræos est pœna peccati. Præmium justitiæ erat totius mundi pos- sessio. Ad eam autem justitiam per fidem pervenerat. Et nobis obveniet possessio mundi melioris itidem per justitiam ex fide.

Postquam exemplis fidei antediluvianorum perquam illustribus justificationem fidei asseruit Apostolus, unde constat non alia ratione, quam per fidem in Christum justificatos esse sanctos prioris mundi, quo de peculiaris nostra Diatribe de fide veterum ante diluvium conferatur, jam No- am, qui partim ante diluvium vixit, partim post di- luvium, & utrique mundo præco fuit justitiæ fidei, producit, cujus fidem commendat tum ab oraculi divini objecto, quod erat de ipso in diluvio per fi- dem in arca conservando, mundo universo per aquas diluvii perituro, περὶ τῶν μηδέπω βλεπομέ- νων : quia fides ἔλεγχος est πραγμάτων ὐ βλεπο- μένων, v. 1. Accepit, inquit Theophylactus, Noë à Deo ex fide responsum, hoc est, instructus à Deo fuit de rebus incertis, nec tamen ille Dei verbis diffisus est, ta- metfi in tranquillo omnia agerent, & cuncti homines deliciis & voluptatibus operam darent, & nihil grave expectaretur. Neque enim fuerat istiusmodi aliquid ante conspectum, nec in mentem cuiquam veniebat, ut mundus aquis deperderetur.
