Alioqui credens hic Deo, futuri diluvii formidine percitus paravit arcam & extruxit; quæ universis, quos domi habe- ret, & animantibus cæteris saluti fuit. Quandoqui- dem hoc oraculum ἐυλαβηθεὶς cum reverentia ade- oque vera fide suscepit; tum ab opere, quia ex fide κα]εσκεύασε τὸν κιβω]ὸν εἰς σωτηρίαν τῆ οἴκυ ἀυτῦ. Credidit enim in illa arca se cum domo sua ser- vatum iri, neque dubium est, tantum Patriarcham, typum hanc arcam fuisse Ecclesiæ, extra quam non est salus, novisse. Id certum omnino, quod ex se- mine suo benedictum mulieris semẽ oriturum, in- que eo salutem æternam impetratum atque obten- tum iri, credens, hanc arcæ extructionem juxta oraculum divinum susceperit: quia nomen πίςε- tiã ad hæc ἐυλαβηθεὶς κα]εσκεύασε sese extendit: tum ab ἀπισίας mundi condemnatione, quod δι ἧς, illam fidem mundum incredulum & opere & con- cione sua condemnarit, incredulitati non tempo- rale tantum, sed & æternum judicium denuncians. Nam relativum illud δι ἧς ad fidem commode re- fertur, utpote principale objectum, de quo hic agit Apostolus ex professo, quod mundus infideli- tatis in Deum ejusque gratiam convictus fuerit per fidem Noæ. Si dicat quis, referendum esse ad proximum nomen, ita non ad κιβω]ὸν, sed ad σω]η- ρίαν pertinebit, hoc sensu: Noam salute seu ere- ptione sua ex diluvio convicisse primum mundum infidelitatis, seu quod hunc elabendi modum pro ridiculo habuisset, totumque præconium Noachicum per infidelitatem reprobasset, ut B. Hülsemannus in annot. ad Genes. VII. 1. mo- nuit: tum denique ab hæreditate τῆς κατὰ πίσιν δικαιοσύνης, ejus quæ per fidem justitiæ, quæ lu- culentissimo argumento est, & quod fidem illam, de qua Paulus hic agit, quæ fides est justificans & salvifica, fides in Messiam, qua sola justus vivit, & animæ περιποίησιν consequitur, ha- buerit, & per fidem eam justitiam veram, quæ est κατὰ πίσιν, non nisi per fidem obtinetur, consequutus sit, Rom. III. 22. & κληρονόμος justi- tiæ factus sit; hæres, quia per adoptionem Dei fili- us; hæres autem justitiæ, quia hæredem esse non διὰ νόμο contingit ἀλλὰ διὰ δικαιοσύνης πίςεως, Rom. IV. 3. Ubi Chrysostomus & Theophylact. obser- vant, per Ebraïsmum hæredem generaliter dici pro possessore; & hæredem fieri pro eo, quod est adipisci seu consequi aliquid. Quib9 accedit etiam præconium justitiæ, quia Noah utriq; mundo factus est κῆρυξ τῆς δικαιοσύνης, 1. Petr. II. 5. & imprimis per 120. annos ante diluvium, ut animas hominum in priori mundo ab æterno interitu liberare justi- tiæ veræ præconio posset, quia Evangelium est poten- tia Dei ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. I. 16. Ejus e- nim justitiæ præco fuit, quam Pseudo-Prophetæ & falsi Doctores abnegantes herum, qui ipsos sanguine suo mercatus est, reprobant, v. 1. ob quam neglectam nec apprehensam vera fide, cum à Noah prædica- retur, Deus non pepercit ἀρχαίῳ κόσμῳ, v. 15. qui- bus ἀπειθήσασί ποτε, cum μακροθυμίαν Dei ne- gligerent Christus sese inferno stitit redivivum, qui tradit9 erat propter peccata, & resuscitat9 propter justitiam nostram, sed spretam ab incredulis, No- am præconem istius justitiæ despicatui habentib9. Quo nomine B. Lutherus Noam dicit prædicari à Mose, quod ambularit cum Deo, hoc est, interpre- te Petro, causam Dei egerit in publico. Id enim, inquit, pulchre exponit Petrus 2. epist. II. cum vo- cat ipsum Præconem justitiæ non humanæ sed Dei, hoc est, fidei in promissum semen. Observat etiam B. Hülsemannus l. c. quum Noah dicatur ambulasse coram Deo, particulam illam coram Deo, quando de justo vel justitiâ dicitur soli justitiæ imputatæ convenire, monente Apostolo Rom. IV. 2. ubi glo- riationem coram hominibus operibus, Abrahami gloriationem coram Deo justitiæ imputatæ tribuit. Fides hæc Noæ nitebatur non Prot-Evangelio tan- tum, Gen. III. 15. sed etiam PACTO, quod cum ipso erigebat Deus, Gen. VI. 18. quod ipsi, Megalan- dro docente, confirmavit Deus, ut certo statueret Noah, Christum ex sua posteritate nasciturum, & Deum in tanta ira retenturum esse seminarium Ec- clesiæ. Perperam autem Grotius præmium justitiæ dicit Noæ fuisse totius mundi possessionem : non enim per justitiam fidei præsens mundus posside- tur, sed hereditas vitæ æternæ obtinetur; neque hic quicquam habetur de mundo præsenti, quem per hæreditatem consequutus sit Noah, aut per fi- dem.

## 11:8
Verse 8.

By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed] That is, Abraham, when called, obeyed by faith, Gen. XII. 5, Acts VII. 3. Clement of Alexandria, and Ambrose after him, illustrate the saying of Pythagoras, 'follow God,' with this example. But in the Manuscript: 'By faith he who is called Abraham,' he to whom God made a name, so that it is a prolepsis. 'To go out into the place which he was about to receive for an inheritance'] From the Chaldean land and Mesopotamia into Canaan, which he himself, that is, his posterity, was to possess. 'And he went out, not knowing whither he goeth'] That is, he did not know what and of what kind that land of Canaan was. This agrees with the words of Gen. XII. 1 and 7. Thus 'whither' (ᾗ) among the Greeks also signifies 'to where,' as in 'the entry of the land' (ᾗ γῆς εἰσόδυ) in Euripides. Regarding the matter, see Gen. XII. 1, Acts VII. 3, where it is said: 'Go into the land which I will show thee.'

Vers. 8.

Πίςει καλέμεν© ᾿Αβραὰμ ὑπήκυσε] Id est, Ἀβραὰμ κα- λέμεν© πίςει ὑπήκυσε vocatus per fidem obedivit Gen. XII. 5. Act. VII. 3. Dictum Pythagoræ ἕπε Θεῷ hoc exem- plo illustrat Clemens Alexandrinus, & post eum Ambro- sius. At in Manuscripto: Πίςει ὁ καλέμεν© ᾿Αβραὰμ, îs cui Deus Abrahamo fecit nomen, ut sit πρόληψις. Ἐξελθεῖν εἰς τὸν τόπον ὃν ἔμελλε λαμβάνειν εἰς κληρονομίαν] Ex Chaldaica terra & Mesopotamia in Cananæam, quam ipse, id est, posteri ipsius erant possessuri. Καὶ ἐξῆλθε μὴ ἐπιςάμεν©, πῦ ἔρχεται] Id est nesciebat, quæ & qualis erat illa terra Canaan. Congruit hoc cum verbis Gen. XII. 1. & 7. Sic ᾗ apud Græcos etiam quo, significat, ut ᾗ γῆς εἰσόδυ apud Euripidem. De re vide Gen. XII. 1. Act. VII. 3. ubi dicitur: I in terram, quam monstrabo tibi.

## 11:9
Verse 9.

By faith Abraham sojourned in the land of promise as in a strange country] 'Into the land' (εἰς τὴν γῆν) for 'in the land' (ἐν τῇ γῇ), in which way 'to sojourn' (παροικεῖν), which corresponds to the Hebrew (גּוּר), is constructed, Gen. XX. 1, XXI. 34, XXVI. 3. In the same way you have 'to dwell in the land' (κατοικεῖν εἰς τὴν γῆν) for 'in the land' (ἐν τῇ γῇ) in Acts VII. 4. He lived there as an inhabitant. See what we have said on Luke XXIV. 18, Eph. II. 19, and 1 Pet. II. 11. The land promised to him, that is, to his race, was to him as if it were foreign. For he did not possess even a clod of earth there, except for the tiny bit which he bought for himself to bury Sarah, Acts VII. 5. By that example we are taught not to be offended by delay, but to wait patiently for the fulfillment of divine promises.

Dwelling in tents] Like those whose wagons draw their wandering homes in the proper manner. For those who possess soil build there, and remain there.

With Isaac and Jacob, the fellow-heirs of the same promise] 'With' (μετὰ) here does not signify the same time, but the parity of the matter; for the same promises were made also to Isaac, Gen. XXII. 17, XXVI. 24, and to Jacob, Gen. XXVIII. 13. Isaac, the Hebrews say, found the water necessary for himself with difficulty, Jacob found the place in which to pitch his tent with difficulty. See Gen. XXVI and XXXIII. Nevertheless, they did not doubt the fulfillment of the promises. Thus, long expectation ought not to weary us.

For he looked for the city which has foundations] They hoped that their posterity would not have wandering homes in those places, but a city well-placed on good foundations, that is, Jerusalem. But by 'metropolis' (μητρόπολιν) is signified the possession of the whole land. Tents do not have foundations, because they are moved. The city of Jerusalem is called an immovable tent by catachresis, Isa. XXXIII. 20.

Vers. 9.

Πίςει παρῴκησεν ᾿Αβραὰμ εἰς τὴν γῆν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας ὡς ἀλλοτρίαν] Εἰς τὴν γῆν pro ἐν τῇ γῇ quomodo παροικεῖν, quod respondet Ebræo גּוּר construitur, Gen. XX. 1. XXI. 34. XXVI. 3. Pari modo κατοικεῖν εἰς τὴν γῆν pro ἐν τῇ γῇ habes Act. VII. 4. Vixit ibi ut incola. Vide quæ diximus ad Luc. XXIV. 18. & Eph. II. 19. 1. Petr. II. 11. Terra illi, id est, generi ejus, promissa, ipsi fuit tanquam aliena. Nam ne glebam quidem terræ ibi possedit, præter tantillum quod sibi comparavit ad Saram sepeliendam Actor. VII. 5. Eo exemplo docemur non offendi morâ, sed patienter exspectare implementa divinarum promissi- onum.

Ἐν σκηναῖς κατοικήσας] Ut illi, quorum rite vagas plau- stra trahunt domos. Nam qui solum possident, ibi ædifi- cant, ibi manent.

Μετὰ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ Ἰακὼβ συγκληρονόμων τῆς ἐπαγγελίας τῆς ἀυτῆς] Μετὰ hic non significat idem tempus, sed parita- tem rei; nam & Isaaco eædem factæ sunt promissiones, Gen. XXII. 17. XXVI. 24. & Jacobo, Gen. XXVIII. 13. Isaa- cus, ajunt Ebræi, ægre aquas sibi necessarias reperit, Ja- cobus ægre locum, in quo tentorium figeret. Vide Gen. XXVI, & XXXIII. Tamen de implemento promissionum non dubitarunt. Sic & nos longa exspectatio lassare non debet.

Ἐξεδέχετο γὰρ τὴν τὰς θεμελίως ἔχεσαν πόλιν] Spera- bant aliquando posteros suos illis in locis non vagas do- mos habituros, sed urbem in bonis fundamentis bene loca- tam, id est, Hierosolyma. Per μητρόπολιν verò signifi- catur terræ totius possessio. Tentoria non habent θεμελίως, quia transmoventur. Urbs Hierosolyma per κατάχρησιν vocatur tentorium immobile, Esa: XXXIII. 20.

## 11:10
Whose builder and maker is God] That is, which city God was about to prepare for them in wondrous ways. See 1 Sam. V, Ps. CXXII. Therefore it is called the holy city, the city of God. 'Technites' (τεχνίτης) is the architect, 'demiourgos' (δημιουργὸς) the craftsman; God both found the reasons for preparing this city for them and executed them. This city is an image of the heavenly city.

From Noah, the herald of righteousness, the Apostle proceeds to the faith of Abraham, whom he establishes as the Father of believers in Romans IV. 11. From whose justification he demonstrated in the same place that we are justified by no other means than through faith in Christ: He teaches, therefore, 1. that his calling was undertaken through faith and the obedience of faith, when he was commanded to go into that place which he was to receive as an inheritance, which faith shines forth, partly from the cause of that assigned place and inheritance, for this was the reason, that in that land that blessed seed was to come forth: partly from the name of inheritance, because under that earthly inheritance lay hidden a heavenly one: which Abraham expected through faith as if under a type and figure: But his constancy in the obedience of faith shines forth from the fact that Abraham went, relying on the divine word, not knowing whither he went; nor did he allow himself to be called away from the obedience of the divine calling by that ignorance. For always and everywhere, through faith in his heart, the Father of believers held and carried with him the seed of the woman, by which faith he was able to overcome all difficulties. 2. The pilgrimage in the land of promise, and his dwelling there, which is likewise ascribed to the Abrahamic faith in verse 9. Which, although it was still foreign, he nevertheless inhabited, fixing his dwelling there in tents with Isaac and Jacob, the co-heirs of that same promise. Because he was expecting (through faith) the city which has foundations, that is, heaven, whose architect and builder is God, which city is not merely an image of the heavenly city, as Grotius, against the common faith of interpreters, perverts the meaning of the Apostle, but was the heavenly fatherland itself: the Apostle himself interpreted this below in verse 16 and chapter XIII. 14. For the earthly city of Jerusalem is not such a city as would have immovable foundations, since it has been overturned and leveled to the ground again and again: Nor is its architect and builder properly and immediately God, but of that city of which the Apostle speaks in verse 16, 'for he has prepared a city for them.' Compare chapter XII. 22. The earthly city, because it was built by the hands of men, can also be destroyed by the hands of men: but this city has God himself as its Architect and builder, and therefore it persists firm and fixed forever. Therefore, says Theophylact, they dwelt in tabernacles, which were less substantial, because they were awaiting the heavenly city, which was established with true and valid and perpetual foundations, and was firmer, and would never collapse from any decay or desire to collapse. Whence also God, having observed that these men considered earthly promises of little value, in order to prepare greater ones for them, deferred this for the future, and would not bestow upon them things worthy of these very goods of the earth. For they, a long time after, having received these earthly promises, by no means valued them highly, but were held by a desire for heavenly things; whereas you, having already received the faith of Christ, while receiving the promise of eternal goods, both imprudently and so eagerly desire these earthly ones, and yet you are not ashamed. Nor, finally, did Abraham so greatly expect any earthly city, but a heavenly one, which the Apostle demonstrates below regarding him and his co-heirs, v. 13, 14, 15, 16. To whom, therefore, Grotius contradicted to his face with this new and unheard-of gloss of his. But how he lived in tents, not in fixed houses, Gen. XII 8, ch. XIII 3, ch. XVIII 1, and received nothing of his own in that land by promise, Acts VII 5, is to be read, even if he bought a field for himself, not for dwelling, but for the use of a sepulcher, Gen. XXIII 17. Similar things are commemorated about Isaac, Gen. XXIV 67, as also about the tents of Jacob, ch. XXXIII 17, ch. XXXV 21. But the error of Socinus is refuted by this faith and expectation, who detracts from the Patriarchs the hope of a heavenly inheritance, in vain in epistle VI to Smalcius, p. 527, translating the word ἐξεδέχετο as 'he was receiving,' that is, 'he was about to receive'; when he himself cannot deny that it has the meaning of 'expecting' in the New Testament. See John V 3, Acts XVII 1, 2 Cor. XI 33, ch. XVI 11, 1 Pet. III 20, and regarding the noun ἐκδοχῆς, 'expectation,' Heb. X 27. Which expectation is later explained in this place, v. 16, as κρείττονος πατρίδος ὀρέγεσθαι, that he sought and desired a better country, and thus expected it with desire. But this expectation of a heavenly city rested upon a trust placed in the divine promise, not concerning the land of Canaan, but concerning eternal life, which had been prefigured through the same, as the Apostle taught in ch. III, which Abraham, the Father of believers, was certain he would obtain through faith in the Messiah. For the promise was not made to him through the law, τὸ κληρονόμον ἀυτὸν εἶναι τῷ κόσμῳ, but through the righteousness of faith, Rom. IV 13.

Latin:

Ἧς τεχνίτης καὶ δημιουργὸς ὁ Θεός] Id est, quam urbem Deus illis erat miris modis paraturus. Vide 1. Sam. V. Psal. CXXII. Ideo urbs sancta, urbs Dei vocatur. Τεχνί- της est Architectus, δημιουργὸς faber Deus rationes ad paran- dam ipsis hanc urbem & invenit & exequutus est. Hæc urbs imago est civitatis cœlestis.

A Noæ Præconis justitiæ fide ad Abrahamum progreditur Apostolus, quem Patrem credentium constituit Roman. IV. 11. è cujus justificatione de- monstravit ibidem non alia ratione, quam per fi- dem in Christum, nos justificari: Ejus ergo 1. vo- cationem per fidem & obedientiam fidei susceptâ esse docet, cum jussus est ire in illum locum, quem accipere debebat in hæreditatem, quæ fides eluce- scit, partim è causâ assignati illius loci & hæredita- tis, hæc enim erat, quod in ista terra semen illud benedictum prodire debuerit: partim ex hæredi- tatis nomine, quia sub illa terrena hæreditate la- tebat cœlestis: quam per fidem expectabat Abra- ham ceu sub typo & figura: Constantiâ autem in o- bedientia fidei effulget inde, quod iverit verbo di- vino fretus Abraham μὴ ἐπισάμενος πᾶ ἔρχεται; nec ea ignorantia sere vocari passus sit ab obsequio divinæ vocationis. Semper enim, & ubique per fi- dem in corde habuit, secumq; gessit Pater creden- tium semen mulieris, qua fide omnes difficultates superare potuit. 2. Peregrinationem in terra promif- sionis, ejusque inhabitationem, quæ itidem τῇ πίςει fidei Abrahamicæ adscribitur v. 9. Quam etsi ad- huc alienam tamen inhabitavit, in tentoriis cum Isaaco & Jacobo cohæredibus promissionis istius ibi habitaculum sibi figens. Quia expectabat (per fidem) civitatem, quæ fundamentum habet, hoc est, cœlum, cujus τεχνίτης καὶ δημιουργὸς ὁ Θεὸς, quæ urbs non imago tantum est civitatis cœlestis, ut Grotius contra communem Interpretum fidem pervertit sententiam Apostoli, sed ipsa cœlestis pa- tria fuerit: Apostolus ipse interpretatus est infra v. 16 cap. XIII.14. Non enim Hierosolyma terrena urbs talis est, quæ fundamenta haberet immota, quum iterum iterumque eversa & solo æquata fue- rit: Neque ejus τεχνίτης καὶ δημιουργὸς proprie & immediate est Deus, sed ilius, de qua v. 16. Apo- stolus, ἡτοίμασε γὰρ ἀυτοῖς πόλιν. Conf. c. XII. 22. civitas terrena, quia manibus hominum ex- tructa, manibus etiam hominum destrui potest: at hæc civitas Deum ipsum habet Architectum & extructorem, ideoque in æternum firma & fixa persistit. Eo, inquit Theophylactus, in tabernaculis habitabant, quæ minus subsisterent, quià cœlestem civitatem opperiebantur, quæ veris esset fundamentis & validis ac perpetuis stabi- lita & firmior, & nullo unquam situ vel putre- dine collapsura. Unde & Deus hos conspicatus parvi ducere terrena promissa, ut majora illis pararet, hac imposterum distulit, & his ipsis condigna non his terræ bonis elargiretur. Illi namque longo post tempore, terrenis hisce acceptis promissionibus, haud- quaquam magni has faciebant, sed cælestium cupi- dine tenebantur; cum vos Christi jam fide suscepta, æternorum bonorum accipientes promissionem ter- rena hac & imprudenter adeo enixeque concupi- scitis, nec pudet tamen. Nec denique Abraham tantopere expectavit terrenam aliqua civitatem, sed cælestem, quod de ipso & de cohæredibo ejus demonstrat infra Apostolus v. 13. 14. 15. 16. Cui proinde in os contradixit Grotius hac glossa sua novella & inaudita. Quomodo autem in taber- naculis non in fixis domibus habitaverit, Gen. XII 8. cap. XIII. 3. cap. XIIX. 1. nihilque proprii in ista terra ex promissione acceperit, Actor. VII. 5. legere est, etsi agrum sibi emerit non ad habitandum, sed ad sepulchri usum Gen. XXIII. 17. De Isaaco simi- lia commemorantur, Gen. XXIV. 67. ut & de Ja- cobi tabernaculis cap. XXXIII. 17. cap. XXXV. 21. Refellitur autem ex hac fide & expectatione Socini error, qui derogat Patriarchis spem cælestis hæredi- tatis, nequicquam epist. VI. ab Smalc. pag. 527. vo- cem ἐξεδέχετο vertens excipiebat, hoc est, exceptu- rus erat; quum diffiteri nequeat ipse in Novo Te- stamento expectandi significationem eam habere. Vid. Johan. V. 3. Actor. XVII. 1. 2. Cor. XI. 33. cap. XVI. 11. 1. Petr. III. 20. & de nomine ἐκδοχῆς ex- pectationis, Ebr. X. 27. Quæ expectatio postea v. 16. hoc loco ita explicatur, κρείττονος πατρίδος ὀρέ- γεσθαι, quod meliorem patriam expetierit ac desi- derarit, adeoque cum desiderio expectarit. Hæc verò expectatio civitatis cælestis fiducia niteba- tur in promissionem divinam collocata, non de terra Canaan, sed de æterna vita, quæ per ean- dem præfigurata fuerat, ut cap. III. docuit Aposto- lus, quam per fidem in Messiam se consequuturum certus erat Abraham Pater credentium. Non enim per legem ipsi promissio facta erat τὸ κληρο- νόμον ἀυτὸν εἶναι τῷ κόσμῳ ἀλλὰ διὰ δικαιοσύνης πίστεως Rom. IV. 13.

## 11:11
Verse 11.

By faith Sarah herself also, being barren] Both by nature and by years. By faith she received, as follows. Thus above IV, V, VII. He comes from the examples of men to women, so that he may stir up both sexes. She received power for the casting of seed] There are those who think that the ejaculation of female seed into its places is understood here. But I do not think that those who feel this way err in natural matters. Nevertheless, I do not think the Hebrews spoke so subtly, nor this writer; but that he meant this, that Sarah obtained the power for the casting of seed, namely, to receive the male seed; just as Chrysostom accepted it, 'for the retaining of seed.' To cast down is to throw down from a higher place. And so, as I said, the Syrian accepted it. And she gave birth beyond the time of age] Gen. XVIII 11. In the manuscript it is only 'beyond the time of age,' so that it coheres with that 'she received.' Good. For 'beyond the time of age' is אַחַר בְּלֹתִי Gen. XVIII 12, nor does the Latin read it otherwise. Since she considered Him faithful who promised] Namely, after she had been taught by the Angel that it was not a joke, but a serious matter, Gen. XVIII 12, 13, 14. See above X 23. See a similar one in Luke I 45.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Πίστει καὶ ἀυτὴ Σάῤῥα στεῖρα ὖσα] Et natura & annis. Πίστει ἔλαβεν, ut sequitur. Sic supra IV. V. VII. A virorum exemplis venit ad fœminas, ut sexum utrumque ex- citet. Δύναμιν εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος ἔλαβε] Sunt qui hic intelligi putant muliebris seminis ejaculationem in locos suos. Sed ego eos, qui ita sentiunt, non puto ἐν τοῖς φυσικοῖς errare. Attamen Hebræos non ita subtiliter lo- quutos arbitror, neque hunc Scriptorem; Sed hoc vo- luisse, consequutam Saram vim εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος, nempe virilis recipiendam; quomodo accepit Chrysosto- mus εἰς τὸ κατασχεῖν σπέρμα. Καταβάλλειν est dejice- re de loco superiore. Et ita, ut dixi, accepit Syrus. Καὶ παρὰ καιρὸν ἡλικίας ἔτεκε] Gen. XVIII. 11. In Ma- nuscripto est tantum παρὰ καιρὸν ἡλικίας, ut cohæreat cum illo ἔλαβε. Bene. Nam παρὰ καιρὸν ἡλικίας est אַחַר בְּלֹתִי Genef. XVIII. 12. nec aliter legit Latinus. Ἐπεὶ πιστὸν ἡγήσατο τὸν ἐπαγγειλάμενον] Nempe post- quam ab Angelo edocta esset, non esse jocum, sed rem seri- am, Gen. XVIII. 12. 13. 14. Vide supra X. 23. Simile vide Luc. I. 45.

## 11:12
Verse 12.

Therefore also from one they were born, and that too as one dead, as the stars in the sky in multitude and as the sand by the lip of the sea, the innumerable] Those promises which are in Gen. XV 5, XXII 17, XXIV 4 were fulfilled in their time, and Moses openly signifies this very thing in Deut. I 10. Add 2 Sam. XXIV 9. Refer 'Therefore' to the faith of both Abraham and Sarah. He spoke excellently 'from one,' for so the Hebrews were accustomed to call Abraham, as can be seen in Mal. II 15. 'And that too' is a Greek idiom, which you may correctly express in Latin: 'And indeed.' He calls Abraham 'dead' with respect to procreation: because through long age those powers were dead in him. Thus Paul said 'the deadness of Sarah's womb' in Rom. IV 19, where see the remarks. You have 'dead lion' also in Martial. The Hebrews say that the powers given to Abraham out of the ordinary on account of Sarah remained even until the time of Keturah. By this argument we also believe that the power to raise the dead to life is not lacking to God, especially since that is not only promised, but an admirable specimen of it was given in Christ. When we indicate innumerable things, we use either the name of the stars, of which there are many that escape sight, or of the sands. See what has been said by us and others regarding Genesis.

Lest anyone think that there was a different reason for faith and salvation for the female sex, the Apostle sets forth certain illustrious women as an example, and here he joins Sarah to Abraham, who might seem incredulous, if indeed at the announcement that the Messiah was to come forth from her seed she testified to her unbelief by laughing, Gen. XVIII 12. Therefore he asserts her faith. By faith, he says, even Sarah herself, about whom one might perhaps doubt, received power for the casting of seed, which faith does not so much look to her immediate offspring about to come forth from her dead body, as to that seed of the woman promised to the first-formed in Gen. III 15. The seed of Abraham announced beforehand, in whom all the families of the earth were to be blessed, Gen. XII 3, and that through the mediation of Isaac who was to be born from Sarah, Gen. XVII, with whom the Lord wished to establish the covenant, v. 19, 21. Which faith of Sarah, although it may not be expressly designated by Moses before the conception; yet here, being proclaimed by the Apostle as divinely inspired, it was placed beyond doubt among the Hebrews, since the promise concerning all peoples being blessed in him, that is, in the seed of his Messiah, was repeated to Abraham for the third time, Gen. XVIII 18, and was not unknown to Sarah, nor did it leave her doubtful any longer, but produced faith in her heart; whence the Lord visited her, just as He had promised her, Gen. XXI 1, whence Abraham himself was ordered to obey the word of Sarah, and the blessed seed was promised to her for the fourth time, v. 12. Indeed, even concerning the attempted offering, for the fifth time, Gen. XXII 18, 'In your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed.' Whence Sarah is celebrated, because she considered him faithful who had promised, that is, she deemed him trustworthy, or believed him who had made the promise, and thus beyond the time of age brought forth a son through this faith in the Messiah, and of all those it is said v. 13. these all, including Sarah, died in faith. By which agreement it is not obscurely taught that the same ones obtained eternal salvation through this faith in the Messiah, because they fell asleep sweetly in the same, even if they did not see the fulfillment of the promise near, but only from afar, which is then more expressly handed down in their confession, that by professing themselves to be pilgrims in the world they manifested that they were seeking a fatherland, not that earthly one from which they went out, but a better one, that is, the heavenly. It must be considered here whether that blessed seed is also looked to by the phrase for the foundation of seed, which some otherwise render as for the casting out of seed, because the seed of women is also required for generation, as Theophylact observes. Others have more correctly explained it as for the foundation of seed. Some also place here a metaphor from architects who lay a foundation. For since the Holy Spirit does not so much hand down physical matters here, or even the propagation of a numerous family from one stem, of which v. 12 treats, as he celebrates the faith of Sarah, who especially looked upon the foundation of the blessed seed in this Isaac of hers, because the Lord had made a covenant with him, and through him, and in his family the promised Messiah was to arise, this was to be founded in the sterile and worn-out Sarah, which she, having embraced by faith itself, received such power through faith, that she might found the blessed seed. There is therefore no reason why we should here understand Abraham with Lyranus and Estius: By faith (he himself, namely Abraham)

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Διὸ καὶ ἀφ' ἑνὸς ἐγεννήθησαν, καὶ ταῦτα νενεκρωμένε, καθὼς τὰ ἄστρα τῷ ἐρανε τῷ πλήθει καὶ ὡσεὶ ἄμμος, ἡ παρὰ τὸ χεῖλος τῆς θαλάσσης ἡ ἀναρίθμητος] Sunt impleta suo tempore pro- missa illa, quæ sunt Gen. XV. 5. XXII. 17. XXIV. 4. idque ipsum aperte significat Moses Deut. I. 10. Adde 2. Sam. XXIV. 9. Διὸ refer ad fidem & Abrahami & Saræ. Egre- gie dixit ab uno, nam sic Abrahamum vocare solebant E- bræi, ut videre est Mal. II. 15. Καὶ ταῦτα Græca loquutio, quam Latine rectè exprimas: Et quidem. Νενεκρωμένου vocat Abrahamum, respectu genituræ: quia per longam æta- tem eæ vires in eo erant emortuæ. Sic τὴν νέκρωσιν τῆς μή- τρὸς Σάῤῥας dixit Paulus Rom. IV. 19. ubi dicta vide. Si- mortuum leonem habes & apud Martialem. Ajunt Ebræi vires extra ordinem Abrahamo propter Saram datas man- sisse etiam ad tempus Cethuræ. Hoc argumento & nos credimus, non deeffe Deo vires mortuos excitandi ad vi- tam, præsertim cum id non promissum tantum sit, sed & specimen ejus admirabile datum in Christo. Cum innu- mera indicamus, usurpamus aut stellarum nomen, quarum multæ sunt, quæ visum effugiunt, aut arenarum. Vide quæ ad Genesin à nobis & aliis dicta.

Ne aliam rationem fidei ac salutis quis fuisse sexus fœminei putet, Apostolus in exemplum illu- stres quasdam fœminas sistit, & hic Abrahamo jungit Saram, quæ videri posset incredula, siqui- dem ad annunciationem prodituri è semine suo Messiaæ ridendo ἀπιστίαν suam testata fuerit, Gen. XIIX. 12. Ejus ergo fidem asserit. Fide ET IPSA inquit Sara, de qua fortè quis dubitaret, δύναμιν εἰς κα]αβολὴν σπέσμα]G- ἔλαβε, quæ fides non tam respicit immediatam ejus prolem è corpore suo emortuo prodituram, quam semen illud mulieris Protoplastis promissum Gen. III. 15. Semen Abra- hæ prænunciatum, in quo benedicendæ erant omnes familiæ terræ, Gen. XII. 3. idque mediante Isaaco è Sara nascituro, Gen. XVII. cum quo pa- ctum erigere voluit Dominus, v. 19. 21. Quæ fides Sara etsi ante conceptionem non expresse designe- tur à Mose; hic tamen ab Apostolo θεοπνεύςῳ de- prædicata penes Ebræos extra dubium posita erat, quandoquidem Abrahamo tertia vice promissio de omnibus populis in ipso, hoc est, in semine ipsius Messiæ benedicendis, repetita, Gen. XIIX. 18. Saræ non incognita fuerit, neque amplius eam du- biam reliquerit, sed fidem in ejusdem corde pepe- rerit; unde Dominus eam visitavit, quemadmo- dum ipsi promiserat, Gen. XXI. 1. unde Abraham ipse jussus est, verbo Saræ obsequi, eique quarta vice semen benedictum promissum, v. 12. Imò etiam circa tentatam oblationem quinta vice, Gen. XXII. 18. In semine tuo benedicentur omnes po- puli terræ. Unde celebratur Sara, quod πιστὸν ἡγή- σατο τὸν ἐπαγγειλάμενον, quod fidum duxerit, vel crediderit eum, qui promissionem fecerat, adeo- que præter temp9 ætatis filium pepererit per hanc fidem in Messiam, ac de omnibus illis dicitur v. 13. ὗτοι πάν[ες inclusa etiam Sara, κα]ὰ πίσιν ἀπέθα- νον. Quo pacto non obscure docetur, eosdem per hanc fidem in Messiam salutem æternam adeptos esse, quod in eadem suaviter obdormierint, etsi promissionis complementum non prope, sed πόῤῥωθεν tantum id viderint, quod expressius de- inde traditur in confessione eorundem, quod pro- fessi sese peregrinos esse in mundo manifestarint, se patriam quærere, non illam terrenam, unde exi- erunt, sed meliorem, hoc est, cælestem. Cogitan- dum hic, anne semen illud benedictum etiam re- spiciatur phrasi εἰς κα]αβολὴν σπέσμα]G-, alias reddunt quidam ad ejiciendum semen, quod fœmi- narum semen etiam requiratur ad generationem, observante Theophylacto. Rectius alii explicarunt ad fundationem seminis. Nonnulli etiam Meta- phoram ab architectis, qui fundamentum jaciunt, hic collocant. Nam quum Spiritus sanct9 non tam physica hic tradat, vel etiam propagationem fami- liæ numerosæ ab uno stemate, de qua v. 12. agi- tur, quam fidem Saræ celebret, quæ fundationem feminis benedicti in hoc Isaaco suo intuita maxime est, quod cum ipso pactum fecerit Dominus, & per ipsum, inque ejus familia ortus Messia pro- missus, hic fundandus in sterili & effœta Sara fue- rit, quod fide ipsa complexa per fidem ejusmodi δύναμιν accepit, ut semen benedictum fundaret. Non ergo est, quod cum Lyrano & Estio hic Abra- hamum subaudiamus: Πίσει (ἀυτὲ, scil. τὲ Ἀβραὰμ)

## 11:13
Ver. 13. By faith these died, all not having received the promises, but having seen them from afar and having greeted them) Even here that 'by faith' ought to be construed not with the nearest words, but with that 'having seen'. And understand 'these all' from Abraham onwards. Through faith those about to die saw, and with a certain hope embraced the promises which they had not received, that is, the promised things, the possession of the land, the kingdom, the most famous city, the temple. This is what is said, that the name YHWH, that is, of him who executes the promises, was not known to them, Exod. VI. 3. 'Having seen from afar' namely as those sailing see land. Abraham had learned that four hundred years were to be awaited. So also to us, those things which seem to be far off are to be hoped for even in the very time of death. That some codices have 'and being persuaded' here after 'having seen', that is absent in the Manuscript.

And having confessed that they are strangers and sojourners on the earth) They confessed that they lived in that very land not as possessors, but as guests and foreigners. The words of Abraham in Gen. XXIII. 4. and of Jacob in Gen. XLVII. 9. are referred to. The same sense as above in 9. except that here it is also adapted to Isaac and Jacob, which had been said of Abraham, as also in Gen. XXVIII. 4. The mystical sense is sufficiently clear. Philo in his book on agriculture explains those same words of Jacob thus: We came to dwell as foreigners, not to settle. For in truth every soul of the wise has obtained heaven as its fatherland, and the earth as a foreign land. And on the confusion of tongues: For this reason all the wise according to Moses are introduced as dwelling as foreigners; for the souls of these are sent as a colony from heaven. But they are accustomed, as lovers of sight and lovers of learning, to travel to the earthly nature. When they have spent time in bodies and have seen through them all things that are sensible and mortal, they return there again from whence they first set out, considering the heavenly region, in which they are citizens, as their fatherland, and the earthly, in which they have dwelt as foreigners, as foreign. He is called a stranger who passes through places foreign to him. A sojourner is one who spends time there. Plato in the Axiochus: This common thing, and one bruited about by all, is that life is a kind of sojourning.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Κατὰ πίσιν ἀπέθανον ὗτοι, πάντες μὴ λαβόντες τὰς ἐπαγγελίας, ἀλλὰ πόῤῥωθεν ἀυτὰς ἰδόντες κᾀ ἀσπασάμενοι) Etiam hic illud κατὰ πίσιν construi debet non cum pro- ximis vocibus, sed cum illo ἰδόντες. Et ὗτοι πάντες intelli- ge ab Abrahamo deinceps. Per fidem illi morituri vide- bant, & spe quadam amplexabantur promissa quæ non acceperant, id est, res promissas, possessionem terræ, regnum, urbem famosissimam, templum. Hoc est quod dicitur nomen יהוה, id est, promissa exequentis illis non fuisse cognitum, Exod. VI. 3. Πόῤῥωθεν ἰδόντες nempe sicut navigantes terram. Abraham didicerat expectan- dos annos quadringentos. Sic & nobis, quæ longe ab- esse videntur speranda sunt etiam in ipso mortis tempo- re. Quod hic post ἰδόντες quidam codices habent καὶ πειθέντες, id abest in Manuscripto.

Καὶ ὁμολογήσαντες, ὅτι ξένοι καὶ παρεπίδημοί εἰσιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς) Fatebantur se in ipsa illa terra non ut possessores vivere, sed ut hospites & peregrinos. Respiciuntur verba Abrahami Gen. XXIII. 4. & Jacobi Gen. XLVII. 9. Idem sensus qui supra 9. nisi quod hic etiam ad Isaacum & Jacobum aptatur, quod de Abrahamo dictum fuerat, ut & Gen. XXVIII. 4. Sensus mysticus satis patet. Philo libro de agricultura eadem illa Jacobi verba sic explicat: Παροικεῖν ὀ κατοικεῖν ἤλθομεν. Τῷ γὰρ ὄντι πᾶσα μὲν ψυχὴ σο- φῦ πατρὶδα μὲν ὀρανὸν, γῆν δὲ ξένην ἔλαχεν. Et de confusione linguarum: Διὰ τῦτο οἱ κατὰ Μωυσῆν σοφοὶ πάντες εἰσάγον- ται παροικῦντες· Αἱ γὰρ τῶν των ψυχαὶ στέλλονται μὲν ἀποικίαν δήποτε τὴν ἐξ ὀρανῦ. Εἰώθασι δὲ, ἅτεκα τῦ Φιλοθεάμονθ, καὶ φι- λομαθᾶς εἰς τὴν περίγειον Φύσιν ἀποδημᾶι. Ἐπειδὰν ἐν ἐνδια- τρίψωσαι σώμασι τὰ αἰσθητὰ καὶ θνητὰ δι' αυτῶν πάντα κατίδω- σιν, ἐπανέρχονται ἐκεῖσε πάλιν ὅται ὡρμήθησαν τὸ πρῶτον, πα- τρὶδα μὲν τὸν ὀράνιον χῶρον, ἐν ᾧ πολιτεύονται, ξένον δὲ τὸν πε- ρίγειον ἐν ᾧ παρῴκησαν, νομίζεσαι. Dicitur ξένος, qui per loca sibi externa transit. Παρεπίδημος qui moram ibi ducit. Plato Axiocho: Τὸ κοινὸν δὴ τῦτο καὶ πρὸς πάντων θρυλλύμε- νον, παρεπιδημία τίς ἐστιν ὁ βίθ.

## 11:14
Ver. 14. For those who say such things make it manifest that they seek a fatherland.) They desire to have a fatherland. For he who is in his fatherland is not a guest, or a sojourner, in Latin an inhabitant. 'Make manifest' they signify. Thus Acts XXIII. 15. Esth. II. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Οἱ γὰρ τοιαῦτα λέγοντες ἐμφανίζεσιν, ὅτι πατρὶδα ἐπιζητῦσιν.) Desiderant habere patriam. Nam qui in pa- tria est, non est aut hospes, aut παρεπίδημος, Latine in- cola. Ἐμφανίζεσι significant. Sic Act. XXIII. 15. Esth. II. 2.

## 11:15
Ver. 15. And if indeed they were mindful of that from which they went out, they would have had opportunity to return) If they called themselves foreigners for the reason that they had Chaldea as their fatherland, it was permitted to return there. Within the more than two hundred years which intervened between Abraham's departure from Chaldea and Jacob's death, there was enough time for Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to return to Chaldea, if they had loved it as their fatherland. We have the verb 'to return' also in Matt. II. 12. Luke X. 6. Acts XVIII. 21. For 'they went out' in the Manuscript is 'they went forth'. Abraham and Sarah had gone out from there, but the children as if the same with their parents.

But now they reach for a better one) namely a fatherland, not which they had had, but which their descendants were to have from the promise of God. 'Now' here, as elsewhere, is for opposition, meaning 'But truly', as above IX. 26. And the Present is for the Past, as also above 14. and below 16.

That is heavenly) that is, that fatherland in a mystical sense signifies the highest heaven. Maimonides teaches this very thing in the title on Repentance, chap. VIII. §. 1. & 2. A similar expression in II. Cor. III. 13 where likewise the figure and the thing figured are mixed, as also above XI. 26. Anaxagoras, to someone saying to him, 'You have no care for your fatherland', said, 'Speak better things, for my fatherland is of the greatest care to me', pointing to heaven with his finger. Philo in his book on dreams says that in that history of the wanderings of Abraham and his children an excellent doctrine is hidden, and explaining it a little later, he says: It is recorded that the dogma concerning the immortality of the soul is hinted at through these things. For having left the region above heaven, as was said a little before, it came into the body as if into a foreign land. And he says that even until the end, when it has grown old, the one who begat it and the Father will not overlook it, but taking pity will loose the bonds, and will safely send it free as far as the mother-city. And again: But let a long age and life be stored up for it in the intelligible city. He names it the intelligible city also in the book on the creation of the world. And Jerusalem is called the holy city, the city of God, which names in a much fuller sense befit that highest heaven.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Καὶ εἰ μὲν ἐκείνης ἐμνημόνευον, ἀφ' ἧς ἐξῆλθον, εἶχον ἂν καιρὸν ἀνακάμψαι) Si ideo se peregrinos vocabant, quod Chaldæam haberent pro patria, licebat illuc redire. In- tra annos plus ducentos, qui intercesserunt inter Abra- hami exitum è Chaldæa & Jacobi mortem satis tempo- ris fuit Abrahamo, Isaaco, Jacobo redeundi in Chal- dæam, si illam amassent ut patriam suam. Verbum ἀνα- κάμψαι habemus & Matth. II. 12. Luc. X. 6. Act. XVIII. 21. Pro ἐξῆλθον in Manuscripto est ἐξέβησαν Abrahamus & Sara inde exierant, liberi autem quasi iidem cum pa- rentibus.

Νυνὶ δὲ κρείττονος ὀρέγονται) nempe patriæ, non quam habuerant, sed quam habituri erant eorum posteri ex promisso Dei. Νῦν hic, ut alibi, est oppositionis pro At vero, ut supra IX. 26. Et Præsens est pro Præterito, ut & supra 14. & infra 16.

Τῦτ' ἔστι ἐπουρανίυ) id est, illa patria sensu mystico cœ- lum summum significat. Docet hoc ipsum Maimonides in יד titulo de Pœnitentia cap. VIII. §. 1. & 2. Similis lo- quutio II. Cor. III. 13 ubi itidem miscentur figura & res figurata, ut & supra XI. 26. Anaxagoras dicenti cuipiam, nulla tibi patriæ cura est; meliora loquere, inquit, maxi- mæ enim mihi curæ patria est, cœlum digito mon- strans. Philo libro de somniis dicit in historia ista pere- grinantium Abrahami & liberorum ejus egregium oc- cultari doctrinam, & aliquanto post eam explicans, ait: Ἱστορεῖται τὸ περὶ ἀφθαρσίας ψυχῆς ὑπαινίττεσαι δόγμα διὰ τύ- των' Απολιπῦσα μὲν γὰρ τὸν ὑπεράνιον τόπον, ὡς κὴ μικρὸν πρό- τερον ἐλέχθη, καθάπερ εἰς ξένην χώραν ἦλθε τὸ σῶμα. Φησὶ δὲ κὴ μέχρι τᾶ παντὸς καταγηραμένη αὐτὴ ὁ γενήσας περιόψεται κὴ πατὴρ, ἀλλ' οἶκτον λαβὼν λύσει τὰ δεσμὰ, καὶ ἐλευθέραν ἄχρι τῆς μητροπόλεως ἀσφαλῶς παραπέμψει. Et rursum: Ο' δὲ μακρὸς αἰὼν αὐτῷ κἀμβίος ἐν τῇ νοητῇ πόλῃ ταμιευέσθω. Idem & in libro de mundi opificio nominat νοητὴν πόλιν. Et voca- tur Jerusalem urbs sancta, urbs Dei, quæ nomina sensu multo pleniore summo illi cœlo conveniunt.

## 11:16
Ver. 16. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God. For he has prepared for them a city) The sense is: God himself is not ashamed, that is, God is not ashamed to be called their God. The verb 'to be ashamed' is constructed either with the Accusative of the person, as Mark VIII. 38. Luke IX. 26. or with the Infinitive of the thing, as above II. 11. When God is specifically called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Exod. III. 15. by that very fact it is understood that he is their benefactor in the highest degree, and a benefactor, as we have said, and have confirmed from Aben-Ezra at the passage Matt. XXII. 32. But our Writer shows that this name is rightly attributed to God, because he had prepared, that is, had destined for them an excellent city, namely Jerusalem, as we have already said: By which 'city', or rather 'mother-city', is signified mystically the highest heaven, as we have already learned from this Writer and Philo. 'To prepare' is to destine, as Tob. VI. 22. in the Greek, Matt. XX. 23. XXV. 34. Mark X. 40. So also 'to prepare beforehand' Wisd. IX. 8.

Why do those things which cohere as to letter and sound not cohere as to sense? Κατὰ πίσιν, whether you render it 'according to faith,' or as the preposition κατὰ is sometimes taken for ἐν, as in Rom. VIII. 4, 8, and chapter XIV. 15, 'in faith,' it fits perfectly. For both 'according to faith,' that is, in the Lord, as their faith allowed, and 'in faith they died,' because they kept the faith even unto death and departed in it, is appropriate. See concerning Abraham, John VIII. 56, Gen. XXV. 8, where it is said that in death he was gathered to his people as to his soul, which triumphs in the heavens; 'the spirits of just men made perfect,' Heb. XII. 23. The same is held concerning Isaac, Gen. XXXV. 29, and concerning Jacob, who, near the time of his death, invoked the Angel the Redeemer, Gen. XLVIII. 16, sighing for Jesus the salvation of the Lord, Gen. XLIX. 18, and having Shiloh and his blood in his mind and mouth, v. 11, 12. And commanding his sons concerning his burial in the promised land, in which the Messiah was to come forth, and awaiting the gathering to his people through a blessed analysis in the faith of Shiloh and the blessed seed, chapter XLIX. 29 and 33, is to be read. By τὰς ἐπαγγελίας are designated not only the promise of the land of Canaan, and of the kingdom and temple therein, but especially the promise of the blessed seed, in whom all promises are yea and amen, 2 Cor. I. 20, in whom and through whom every blessing was promised to all the promises of the earth. Which they saw only πόῤῥωθεν, where that κατὰ πίσιν can be repeated ἀπὸ κοινᾶ, concerning which John VIII. 56, 'Abraham,' says Christ, 'your father rejoiced to see my day, and he saw it (in the Spirit and πόῤῥωθεν) and was glad.' Whither does that πεισθέντες go? For he was persuaded of it with great παῤῥησίᾳ, Rom. IV. 21. And ἀσπασάμενοι, greeting and as it were kissing the Lord now approaching with their mouth, whom they so greatly panted for in their heart. In this place, says Theophylact, he shows that they held from heaven, and from the heavenly kingdom, the mysteries and knowledge of the resurrection and of invisible goods, and had greeted them, that is, being joyful and cheerful, having imparted a greeting, they called out, in the manner of sailors, or of those looking out from a distance at most desired cities, which, before they reach them, they greet in anticipation and claim for themselves. Theophylact indeed adds another explanation, which pleased Grotius; but he rejects it: Or he calls those now, who were with Abraham, as having by no means received the promises by which the land was to be destined. Yet they looked forward to this from further off, that is, before the fourth generation should follow them. For they knew it would come to pass that their descendants, when they withdrew from Egypt, would inherit this very land. This latter exposition, however, is in no way consistent with the former ones, which, as Paul says, does not apply to all these, but seems to correspond more to those who existed in the times of Moses. By which confidence, therefore, relying on the promised Savior of the world, they professed themselves to be only guests and strangers in these lands, not by reason of earthly habitation: For thus they were not seeking an earthly fatherland, nor did they desire to return to Chaldea, whence Abraham had gone out, which was the fatherland of him alone, not of the rest, but the matter here concerns a common fatherland. Nor, if you wish to call Canaan by the name of fatherland, did they have need to seek and desire the same with such ὀρέξει or such desire, because they were already living in it. But the Apostle’s discourse here is about such a fatherland as was desired by those Ancients, which he himself also defines: That it was not that from which they had gone out, but one much BETTER, that is, ἐπουράνιος, heavenly. What, therefore, is more clear than that the heavenly fatherland is that which they desired, since he himself interprets the desire to the Apostle in this way? For what Grotius objects, that the Apostle is already departing to a mystical sense, is futile and ἀσύστατον. For he speaks according to the letter about that fatherland which they themselves desired. But concerning that very one, he testifies that it is the heavenly fatherland. He also calls the same ἐπουράνιον, which he designates with the epithet κρείττον. But it cannot be imagined that one comes by this name and another by that: that by the former heaven is designated, but by the latter the land of Canaan. He indicates the same one, for the possession of which even after death God was not ashamed to call Himself their God. But not for the possession of the land of Canaan, which is nothing to the dead, but of the heavenly life, He called Himself the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, as Christ teaches in Matt. XXII. 32. Whence he concluded that they live even after death as regards the blessed life of the soul, cf. Luke XX. 37. & Exod. III. 15. 16. He indicates that fatherland and city which God ἡτοίμασε, prepared for them, v. 16, which is altogether that fatherland which is prepared for all the Elect, to which they are to be admitted with the men who shall be set at the right hand of God by the voice of the same, Mat. XXV. 34, of which city God is the τεχνίτης κὴ δημιουργὸς, which has immovable and eternally stable foundations v. 10. Whence Theophylactus paraphrases thus: They profess themselves not only strangers and guests of the promised land, but strangers of the lands. Wherefore they prayed to receive this very one. For they were not of this, but worthy of heaven. For when they call themselves strangers, they clearly argue that they are seeking their own. But where he did not of his own accord betake himself to it, it is clear that he neither remembered this land, nor was that one his fatherland, but he desired another and a more ample one, that is, the heavenly, to approach which the time had not yet arrived. And to the words: For He prepared a city for them: So, he says, God is not ashamed of these men, that He has both admitted them as intimates and prepared a city in the heavens, by the desire of which they were held. If you ask where the Patriarchs confessed themselves to be strangers, I answer, Gen. XXIII. 4, that it is read concerning Abraham, and Gen. XLVII. 9, concerning Jacob, and that their whole life sufficiently testifies to this concerning all of them, which was nothing other than a perpetual pilgrimage. Certainly, Abraham was so far from desiring an earthly fatherland that he even bound Eleazar by an oath not to bring his son back there, Gen. XXIV. 6.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Διὸ ἐκ ἐπαισχύνεται αὐτὲς ὁ Θεὸς. Θεὸς ἐπικα- λεῖσθαι αὐτῶν. Ητοίμασε γὰρ αὐτοῖς πόλιν) Sensus est: Οὐκ ἐπαι- σχύνεται ἀυτὸς ὁ Θεὸς, τετέστιν ἐκ ἐπαισχύνεται Θεὸς ἐπικα- λεῖσθαι αὐτῶν. Verbum ἐπαισχύνυμαι, aut cum Accusativo personæ construitur, ut Marc. VIII. 38. Luc. IX. 26. aut cum Infinitivo rei, ut supra II. 11. Deus cum specialiter dicitur Deus Abrahami, Isaaci & Jacobi Exod. III. 15. eo ipso intelligitur eorum esse fautor summe, atque ἐνεργέτης, ut diximus, & ex Aben-Esdra firmavimus ad locum Matth. XXII. 32. Ostendit autem noster Scriptor, jure Deo hoc nomen tribui, quia illis paraverat, id est, desti- naverat egregiam urbem, nempe Hierosolyma, ut jam diximus: Per quam πόλιν imò μητρόπολιν significatur μυσικῶς summum cœlum, ut ex hoc Scriptore & Philo- ne jam didicimus. Ετοιμάζειν est destinare, ut Tob. VI. 22. in Græco, Matth. XX. 23. XXV. 34. Marc. X. 40. Sic & προετοιμάζειν Sap. IX. 8.

Cur non quoad sensum cohæreant, quæ cohæ- rent quoad literam & sonum? Κατὰ πίσιν sive red- das secundum fidem, sive ut alias quandoque Præ- positio κατὰ pro ἐν accipitur Rom. VIII. 4. 8. cap. XIV. 15. in fide, optime convenit. Nam & secundum fidem, id est, in Domino, uti fides eorum ferebat, & in fide mortui sunt, quia fidem usque ad mortem servarunt, & in ea decesserunt. Vide de Abrahamo Joh. IIX. 56. Gen. XXV. 8. ubi dicitur in morte ad populum suum congregatus quoad animam qui in cœlis triumphat; πνεύματα δικαίων τετελειωμένων, Ebr. XII. 23. De Isaaco idem habetur Gen. XXXV. 29. de Jacobo sub mortis viciniam Angelum Goë- lem invocante. Gen. XLVIII. 16. suspirante Jesum salutare Domini, Gen. XLIX. 18. inque animo & ore habente Schilo & sanguinem ejus v. 11. 12. & man- dante filiis suis sepulturam in terra promissa, in qua proditurus erat Messias, & expectante collectio- nem ad populum suum per beatam analysin in fide Schilo & benedicti seminis, cap. XLIX. 29. & 33. le- gere est. Per τὰς ἐπαγγελίας non tantum promissio terra Canaan, regnique & templi in eodem, sed in- primis promissio benedicti seminis, in quo omnes promissiones sunt næ & amen, 2. Cor. I. 20. in quo & per quem omnis benedictio promissa erat omni- bus terræ promissionibus, designantur. Quam ποῤ- ῥωθεν tantum viderunt, ubi ἀπὸ κοινᾶ illud κατὰ πί- σιν repeti potest, quo de Joh. IIX. 58. Abraham, in- quit Christus, Pater vester optavit videre diem meum, & vidit eum (in Spiritu & πόῤῥωθεν) & exultavit. Quo abit illud πεισθέντες: Nam de eo magna cum παῤῥησίᾳ persuasus fuit, Rom. IV. 21. & ἀσπασαμέ- νοι salutantes & veluti basiantes jam Dominum ad- ventantem ore, quem tantopere anhelabant cor- de. Hoc loco, inquit Theophylactus, ostendit eos de cœ- lo, deque cœlesti imperio resurrectionem & invisibili- um bonorum accepta mysteria & cognitione tenere, & consalutasse, hoc est latiores & hilares, impertita sa- lute, appellasse, navigantium more, vel è conspectu de- sideratissimas urbes prospicientium, quas priusquam adeant, anticipantes appellant lepidius & sibi adsci- scunt. Addit quidem & aliam explicationem, quæ Grotio placuit, Theophylactus; sed eam reprobat: Vel eos nunc dicit, qui apud Abrahamum essent, ne- quaquam accepisse promissa, quibus terra destinare- tur. Longiùs tamen hanc prospexerunt, id est ante- quam quarta hos subsequeretur generatio. Futurum quippe sciebant, ut eorum nepotes, ubi se ex Ægypto reciperent, hanc ipsam hereditarent. Hæc tamen po- sterior expositio nihil est superioribus consentanea, cum isti omnes Paulus inquit, sed his, qui Mosis tem- poribus extitere, videtur magis congruere. Qua pro- inde fiducia in promissum mundi servatorem freti, professi se sunt his in terris hospites tantum esse & peregrinos non ratione terrenæ habitationis: Sic enim patriam non quærebant terrenam, neque de- siderabant in Chaldæam, unde Abraham egressus erat, reverti, quæ ipsius unius, non reliquorum pa- tria erat, agitur autem hìc de communi patria. Neq; si Canaanæam patriæ nomine vocare velis, eandem quærere ac desiderare opus habebant tanta ὀρέξει vel tanto desiderio, quia in illa jam agebant. Apo- stolo verò hic sermo est de tali patria, quæ Veteri- bus istis desiderata fuerit, quam etiam ipse definit: Quod non illa fuerit è quà egressi erant, sed MELIOR multò, hoc est ἐπουράνιος cœlestis. Quid ergo lucu- lentius, quam quod patria cœlestis ea sit, quam desi- derarunt, quum ipse Apostolo desiderium ita inter- pretetur? Nam quod Grotius obvertit, Apostolum jam ad sensum mysticum abire, futile est, atq; ἀσύ- στατον. De ea enim patria, quam ipsi desiderabant, secundum literam loquitur. At de illa ipsa testatur, quod ea sit cœlestis patria. Eandem etiam ἐπουρά- νιον vocat, quam κρείττον elogio designat. Non verò fingi potest, aliam hoc, aliam isto nomine ve- nire: Illo cœlum designari, hoc vero terram Ca- naan. Eandem indicat, ob cujus possessionem etiam post mortem Deus veritus non est, se Deum ipso- rum vocare. At non ob possessionem terræ Canaan, quæ nihil ad mortuos, sed vitæ cœlestis, Deum A- brahæ, Deum Isaac, Deum Jacob se vocavit, docen- te Christo Matth. XXII. 32. Unde conclusit, eos post mortem etiam vivere quoad vitam animæ beatam, conf. Luc. XX. 37. & Exod. III. 15. 16. Eam indicat pa- triam & civitatem, quam ipsis ἡτοίμασε præparavit Deus, v. 16. quæ omnino est illa patria, quæ omnibus Electis parata, ad quam cum hominibus, qui ad dextram Dei statuentur, intromittendi voce ejus- dem sunt, Mat. XXV. 34. cujus civitatis Deus τεχνί- της κὴ δημιουργὸς est, quæ immota & æternum stabilia habet fundamenta v. 10. Unde Theophylactus ita παραφράζει: Nec solum peregrinos & hospites terræ promissæ, sed terrarum hospites se profitentur. Quo circa hanc ipsam accipere precabantur. Non enim hac erant, sed cælo digni. Cum enim se peregrinos appel- lant, arguunt plane propriam quærere. Advertamus autem, qualem hi patriam quærant, num terrenam, quam reliquissent, ut Abraham Mesopotamiam? At patebat illi in eam reditus. Ubi verò non ultro in eam se contulit, perspicuum est, nec terræ hujus hunc memi- nisse, nec illam sibi fuisse in patriam, sed aliam deside- rasse & ampliorem, id est, cœlestem, quam ut adiret, haud dum advenerat tempus. Et ad verba: Paravit e- nim illis civitatem: Adeo, inquit, istorum nihil Deum hunc pudet, ut eos & in familiares adsciverit, & civi- tatem in cælis, cujus desiderio tenerentur, paraverit. Ubi Patriarchæ peregrinos se confessi sint, si quæ- ras, respondeo, Gen. XXIII. 4. id de Abrahamo le- gi, & Gen. XLVII. 9. de Jacobo, deque omnibus illis totam ipsorum vitam id satis testari, quæ nihil aliud erat, quam perpetua peregrinatio. Patriam certè terrenam tantum abest, ut desiderarit Abraham, ut Eléazarum etiam jurejurando adstrinxerit de filio suo eò non reducendo, Gen. XXIV. 6.

## 11:17
Abraham) if indeed the faith not of Abraham but of Sarah herself is now celebrated, and the same which obtained the mighty work; into the conception of seed) let him be honored with that eulogy, that he deemed him faithful who had promised, which is a clear testimony of Sarah's faith. And not only, says Theophylact, did her faith cause Sarah to bring forth, but so much and so abundant, such as not even the most fruitful woman would have brought forth. Those things which are added in v. 12 serve to amplify the mighty work of Abraham's faith, by which it is taught that from that one man such a multitude of descendants, which may be compared with the stars of heaven and the sands of the sea, has proceeded, even though he was already dead, and his wife barren, Rom. IV: 9. where they judge that the comparison with the stars of heaven refers to the elect and the good, and with the sands of the sea, which is hyperbolic, to the bad and the reprobate.

Latin:

Ἀβραάμ) siquidem non Abrahami sed Saræ ipsius fides jam celebretur, eademque quæ virtutem ad- epta est; εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος) eo elogio ma- ctetur, quod fidum duxerit eum, qui promiserat, quod est illustre fidei Saræ testimonium. Nec solùm, inquit Theophylactus, ut partum ederet Sara, ejus fi- des effecit, sed multum adeo & abundantem, qualem nec fœcundissima mulier edidisset. Quæ v. 12. addun- tur, faciunt ad amplificandam virtutem fidei Abra- hæ, qua factum docetur, ut ex uno illo homine tanta posterorum copia, quæ cum stellis cœli & a- renis maris comparetur, prodierit, etiamsi ille jam emortuus esset, & uxor ejus sterilis, Rom. IV: 9. ubi comparationem cum stellis cœli respicere electos & bonos, cum arenis maris, quæ hyperbolica est, malos & reprobos censent.

## 11:17
Vers. 17. Πίστει προσενήνοχεν Ἀβραὰμ τὸν Ἰσαὰκ) Thus also James II. 24. ἀνενέγκας τὸν ἰσαὰκ τὸν υἱὸν αὐτῶ. For he fulfilled the father of the offering also in effect, placing the son on the altar: Part in mind, prepared even to slaughter him. Salvianus on the government of God, book I. God ordered the son to be sacrificed to Him: The father offered, and as far as the completion of the heart is concerned, sacrificed. Philo on the same matter in the book on Abraham: τῷ δ' ἡ πράξεις, εἰ μὲ τὸ τέλ@ ἐπηκολούθησεν ὁλόκληρ@ κὰν παντελὴς ὐ μόνον ταῖς ἱεραῖς βίβλοις, ἀλλὰ κὰν

in the minds of the readers, may be left inscribed. And so he received from God Himself as if it were a reward for a completed deed: You have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake Gen. XXII. 12. And he indeed did not spare the Son: but Christ and His martyrs did not spare themselves.

Πειραζόμεν@) With God exploring his faith, and that the last time. For after that he was not explored further, Gen. XXII. 1. in this history: God tempted Abraham. Sirachides on the same matter: Ἐν πειρασμῷ εὑρέθη πιστὸς. XLIV. 22.

Καὶ τὸν μονογενῆ προσέφερεν) The only one, namely, from the legitimate mistress יחיד Gen. XXII. 16.

Ὁ τὰς ἐπαγγελίας ἀναδεξάμεν@) Which promises made to him by God he had admitted into his mind, namely, to be fulfilled in the posterity of Isaac, which he will now add. Ἀναδέχεσθαι is more than δέχεσθαι. And so the Latin does not translate it badly as to undertake.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Πίστει προσενήνοχεν Ἀβραὰμ τὸν Ἰσαὰκ) Sic & Jacobus II. 24. ἀνενέγκας τὸν ἰσαὰκ τὸν υἱὸν αὐτῶ. Patrem enim oblationis etiam effectu implevit, imponens filium al- tari: Partem animo, paratus eum etiam mactare. Sal- vianus de gubernatione Dei libr. I. Immolari sibi Deus filium jussit: Pater obtulit, & quantum ad aefunctionem cordis attinet, immolavit. Philo de eadem re in libro de Abrahamo: τῷ δ' ἡ πράξεις, εἰ μὲ τὸ τέλ@ ἐπηκολούθησεν ὁλόκληρ@ κὰν παντελὴς ὐ μόνον ταῖς ἱεραῖς βίβλοις, ἀλλὰ κὰν

ἐν ταῖς τῶν ἀναγινωσκόντων διανοίαις ἀνάγραπθ' ἐγκαλίπῃ- ται. Itaque & à Deo ipso tanquàm rei perfectæ præ- mium accepit: Non pepercisti unigenito filio tuo propter me Gen. XXII. 12. Et ille quidem Filio non pepercit: Chri- stus autem & ejus martyres nec sibi.

Πειραζόμεν@) Deo explorante ipsius fidem, idque po- stremum. Nam post id ultra exploratus non est, Gen. XXII. 1. in hac historia: Tentavit Deus Abraham. Sirachides dere eadem: Ἐν πειρασμῷ εὑρέθη πιστὸς. XLIV. 22.

Καὶ τὸν μονογενῆ προσέφερεν) Unicum nempe ex justa matrefamilias יחיד Gen. XXII. XXII. 16.

Ὁ τὰς ἐπαγγελίας ἀναδεξάμεν@) Quæ promissa à Deo sibi facta in animum admiserat, nempe in Isaaci posteri- tate implenda, quod jam addet. Ἀναδέχεσθαι plus est quam δέχεσθαι. Itaque suscipere non male vertit Latinus.

## 11:18
Vers. 18. Πρὸς ὃν ἐλαλήθη· ὅτι ἐν Ἰσαὰκ κληθήσεταί σοι σπέρμα) Gen. XXI. 12. that is, that posterity will be by far the most illustrious, and will propagate your name, and will possess that notable land which will fall to you through Isaac, Gen. XXI. 12. where in the Greek of Genesis it is similarly κληθήσεταί σοι σπέρμα, just as also Rom. IX. 17. It is to be noted, however, that Isaac, when he was destined for death, was childless. Ὅτι here is redundant, as in Matth. XVI. 18. Luc. I. 6. VIII. 4. and elsewhere.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Πρὸς ὃν ἐλαλήθη· ὅτι ἐν Ἰσαὰκ κληθήσεταί σοι σπέρμα) Gen. XXI. 12. id est, ea posteritas erit longè cla- rissima, tuumque nomen propagabit, & terram illam in- signem possidebit, quæ per Isaacum tibi obveniet, Gen. XXI. 12. ubi in Græco Geneseos similiter κληθήσεταί σοι σπέρμα quomodo & Rom. IX. 17. Notandum autem Isaa- cum, cum morti destinabatur, fuisse improlem. Ὅτι hic abundat, ut Matth. XVI. 18. Luc. I. 6. VIII. 4. & alibi.

## 11:19
Vers. 19. Λογισάμεν@) That λογισάμεν@ is to be referred to the more remote, namely, to προσενήνοχε. λογισάμεν@ חשב reckoning in his mind.

Ὅτι καὶ ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐγείρειν δύναται ὁ Θεὸς) This was the faith, truly equal to the Evangelical. He believed that he would have descendants from Isaac. He believed that the same was to be killed. These could not be reconciled except through the admirable power of God to effect that which at that time lacked an example.

Whence he also received him in a parable) whence in a parable, that is, ἐν νεκρῶν ἐν παραβολῇ כמשל by a certain image of a resurrection from the dead. For he was already dead in his own opinion and that of his Father. He was returned to him from the jaws of the underworld. Thus, a resurrection from death and a deliverance from the most imminent dangers are compared, 2 Cor. 1:9, 10.

The Apostle brought forward a new proof of Abraham's faith for these matters, in whom, as the father of believers, a great deal was situated, namely the offering of Isaac, when his faith in the promised seed was tested, in which all the nations of the earth were to be blessed, inasmuch as it could not be propagated otherwise than through Isaac. Moreover, Isaac is called the μονογενὴς (only-begotten) son, either because Ishmael was no longer reckoned as a son, Gen. 21:12, or because he alone was to be Abraham's heir, or because he was the only one begotten of Sarah, his primary wife. It is added concerning Abraham, to whom it had been said, 'In Isaac shall your seed be called.' The particle ὅτι is merely expletive, accustomed to be added when some saying of the Old Testament is recited. The passage is Gen. 21:12, which the Apostle also cited in Rom. 9:7, in which the nerve [of the argument] consists. For just as Abraham's faith was fixed upon that promise concerning the Messiah, whom the Lord had promised him repeatedly would come forth from Isaac's family: so a more grievous temptation could not have happened to the faith of the Patriarch than when he was ordered to sacrifice Isaac, in whom he had received the promise. For thus it would have been all over with that seed through which the curse was to be removed and the blessing was to reach all the nations of the earth: thus it would have been all over with faith, all over with the salvation of men. But he overcame this temptation, leaning upon the Divine promise by faith, not showing himself sluggish toward the command of the Lord concerning offering his only son Isaac, but, without prejudice to the Divine command, believing that the promise would be fulfilled concerning the blessed seed to come forth through Isaac, even if Isaac, in whom the promise had been made to him, were offered and reduced to ashes. This is truly to believe in hope against hope, which the Apostle said concerning Abraham, who had faith regarding the birth of Isaac from his own worn-out body and Sarah, who was decrepit and barren, Rom. 4:18. That is truly wonderful, says Theophylact, that when he had no other son here through whom he might think the promises of God would have an outcome, he offered this only one whom he had received. If you ask why this was done? I would say, because of the greatness of his faith. For he held it as indubitable, and trusting, he had thus fortified his mind, that it was for God very easy to raise his son, slain at the altars, from the dead, so that he might fulfill the promises in that manner, and through Isaac restored to life, his seed also might increase. But the Apostle, from the infallible revelation of the Holy Spirit, sets before us the reasoning (λογισμὸν) not of human reason but of Abrahamic faith, even though reason resisted, which he brought into subjection to the obedience of faith, saying: 'reasoning (λογισάμενος) that God is able to raise even from the dead.' By which very reasoning (λογισμῷ) not only was Abraham's full assurance (πληροφορία) concerning the Messiah supported in this most grievous temptation, but also his faith concerning the resurrection of the dead was declared: without which the justifying and beatifying faith of the Patriarch could not even consist, as its object was God raising Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was to be delivered up for our sins, and to be raised for our justification, as the Apostle testifies, Rom. IV. 24. 28. 'Reasoning' (λογισάμενος) is rendered by the Vulgate as 'thinking' (arbitrans). But in the Greek it is an Aorist, when he had reasoned with himself, a collection having been instituted: 'whence also he received him' (ὅθεν αὐτὸνἐκομίσατο), he brought him back. He was already as if dead in the heart of Abraham during those three days from which he had received the command concerning sacrificing him. He received him, therefore, as if brought back to life, when God inhibited the immolation of the same. Therefore, some explain the words 'in a parable' (ἐν παραβολῇ) as 'in a similitude,' because it was just as if he had been raised from the dead: But it is better to explain them concerning the type and figure of Christ, whom Isaac bore in the demanded immolation, because the immolation figured the passion and death of Christ, which, even if it was only attempted in Isaac, was nevertheless completed in the ram, sticking within the thickets, substituted in his place, into a type of the passion and death of Christ, entangled in the thickets of sins, and delivered to death in our place. Moreover, the reception of Isaac alive was a parable and figure of Christ to be delivered from death, in which he remained for three days. Which Oecumenius explains thus: See what he says 'by a parable': Abraham was a type of God and the Father, but Isaac of the Son of God: Since because God was about to bestow something great upon us, namely the immolation of His Son, since He was vehemently 'loving to mankind' (φιλάνθρωπος), lest He should seem to save us by grace alone, He made it a debt, that Christ should be delivered, and a debt in this manner: 'Just as,' he says, 'Abraham endured to deliver his only-begotten to death for me: So also I ought to deliver the Only-begotten to death for men.' The same Oecumenius, adapting the parable to the person of Isaac, unfolds it thus: 'Isaac received, and made him to be a parable, a type and example of Christ, so that just as Isaac was slaughtered, as far as concerns the prompt will of Abraham, so also Christ should be slaughtered, but here according to the truth itself.' Which explanation Theophylact had also handed down: 'Abraham indeed had presented the figure of God and the Father, but Isaac indeed of the Son of God. When therefore God was about to dispense this great mystery, and one above the minds of men, and it was to be that for our sake, since He was affected with huge charity toward the human race, that He would even deliver His Son to be immolated, nor did it please Him, as if He seemed to bestow grace from Himself, but as to pay a debt, God then says these things: I would have granted nothing new to human nature for its sake by grace, by immolating my son.' For Abraham, that he might obey me, offered his son as a victim. Whence it happens that I myself pay a debt, I do not do a favor. But it fits the commendation of Abraham's faith very well, as it looked to Christ to be delivered for our sins, and to be raised for our justification, and by that reason it was vehemently strengthened by this figure, just as also Christ was to be immolated on that mountain on which the immolation of Isaac was undertaken, concerning which Augustine writes in book XVI of the City of God, chapter 32. Jerome the Presbyter wrote that he had learned most certainly from the elders of the Jews that Isaac was immolated there where Christ was afterwards crucified. Add that the parable is thus accepted by Paul in Heb. IX. 19 for a type, and that it is not unsuitably established here that Abraham saw the day of the Lord in this offering of sacrifice, concerning which Theophylact in John VIII. With great zeal he sought and desired that day. But he says the day of the cross was pre-signified by the figure of the offering and the slaughtered ram. Blessed Gerhard also refers to this the explanation of the Angel in Gen. XXII, 10, when Abraham snatched the sword that he might immolate his son, v. 12, behold the Angel, who was the Son of God Himself, cried from heaven, saying: 'Do not extend your hand over the boy,' i.e., there is no person to be slaughtered in sacrifice for the sins of the world, but in your seed, that is, in the Messiah, who is to come forth from your seed, all nations shall be blessed, v. 18, i.e., when the promised Messiah shall take away the curse brought upon the human race through sin, when He is about to bring back the blessing and grace, then in that manner that work of redemption will be performed, which I wished to prefigure to you in this history or parable, He Himself will stand in blood, will be bound, will be killed, will become a curse on the wood of the cross, but on the third day He will revive. Thus Tertullian expounded it, book against the Jews, chapter IV. Clem. Alex. book I. Strom. Origen homily XVIII on Genesis, Ephrem Syrus book on Abraham and Isaac, Augustine sermon LXXII on the time, and others both ancient and recent. Compare the twin homilies of Blessed Gerhard in part I, sacred homilies on the day of Preparation, concerning this parable.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Λογισάμεν@) Istud λογισάμεν@ referendum ad remotius, nempe ad προσενήνοχε. λογισάμεν@ חשב animo reputans.

Ὅτι καὶ ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐγείρειν δύναται ὁ Θεὸς) Hæc erat fides, Evangelicæ sane suppar. Credebat ex Isaaco se habiturum posteros. Credebat eundem interficiendum. Hæc conci- liari non poterant, nisi per admirandam Dei potentiam ad id efficiendum, quod eo tempore exemplo carebat.

Ὅθεν αὐτὸν καὶ ἐν παραβολῇ ἐκομίσατο) ὅθεν ἐν παραβολῇ, id est, ἐν νεκρῶν ἐν παραβολῇ כמשל per imaginem quan- dam resuscitationis ex mortuis. Jam enim mortuus erat in sua & Patris opinione. Redditus ei est ex orci faucibus. Sic resuscitatio à morte & liberatio à præsentissimis pericu- lis comparantur 2. Cor. I. 9. 10.

Novum ad hæc documentum fidei Abrahami, in quo ceu Patre credentium plurimum erat situm, adduxit Apostolus Isaaci oblationem, cum fides ejus in promissum semen tentaretur, in quo benedicen- dæ erant omnes nationes terræ, utpote quod non aliter quam per Isaacum debebat propagari. Dici- tur autem Isaac filius μονογενὴς, sive quod Ismael pro filio amplius non reputaretur, Gen. XXI. 12. sive quod solus Abrahæ hæres ipse futurus esset, sive quod ex Sara conjuge primaria unicus ille susce- ptus. Additur de Abrahamo, ad quem dictum erat, in Isaaco vocabitur tibi semen. Particula ὅτι exple- tiva tantùm est, addi solita, cum dictum aliquod V. Test. recitatur. Locus est Gen. XXI. 12. quem etiam adduxit Apostolus Rom. IV. 7. in quo nervus consistit. Nam ut in eam promissionem fixa fuit fides Abrahami de Messia, quem ex Isaaci familia proditurum Dominus iterata vice pollicitus ei fuerat: Sic tentatio gravior accidere non poterat fidei Patriarchæ, quam cum immolare juberetur Isaacum, in quo promissionem acceperat. Ita enim actum fore de semine illo, per quod maledi- ctio tolli, & benedictio in omnes nationes terræ obtingere debebat: Sic actum de fide, actum de sa- lute hominum. Quam verò tentationem innixus promissioni Divinæ fide superavit, non immorig rum se præbens mandato Domini de offerendo unico filio Isaaco, sed salvo Divino mandato cre- dens, impletum iri promissionem, de prodituro per Isaacum benedicto semine, etiamsi offerretur, & in cineres redigeretur Isaac, in quo ipsi facta erat promissio. Hoc verè est in spem contra spem cre- dere, quod de Abrahamo fidem habenti de nasci- turo Isaaco ex effœto suo corpore Saraq; decrepita & sterili dicebat Apostolus, Rom. IV. 18. Id sanè mi- rum, inquit Theophylactus, ut cum alium nullum ha- beret hic filium, per quem Dei promissiones habituras eventum existimaret, unicum hunc, quem suscepisset, obtulerit. Quamobrem id factum si quæras? Præ fidei nimirum magnitudine dixerim. Pro indubitato enim habebat, & fidens sic animum obfirmarat, Deo id esse perfacile, filium ad aras occisum ex mortuis excitare, ut eum in modum promissa perficeret, & per Isaac vi- ta redditum ejus etiam semen incresceret. Λογισμὸν autem non rationis sed fidei Abrahamicæ, etsi ob- nitente ratione, quam sub obsequium fidei redegit ita proponit nobis Apostolus ex Spiritus sancti re- velatione infallibili, λογισάμενος ὅτι κὴ ἐκ νεκρῶν ἐγείρειν δυνατὸς ὁ θεός. Quo ipso λογισμῷ non tan- tum πληροφορία Abrahami de Messia in hac gra- vissima tentatione fulcita, sed etiam fides ejusdem de resuscitatione mortuorum declarata est: Sine qua ne constare quidem poterat fides justifica & beati- fica Patriarchæ, utpote cujus objectum erat Deus excitans Jesum Dominum nostrum à mortuis, qui tra- dendus erat propter peccata nostra, & resuscitandus ob justitiam nostram, teste Apostolo, Rom. IV. 24. 28. Λογισάμενος, redditur à Vulgata arbitrans. Sed in Græco est Aoristus, cum secum reputasset, collectio- ne instituta: ὅθεν αὐτὸν, unde eum, cum ἐν παραβολῇ ἐκομίσατο recepit, reportavit. Mortuus veluti jam erat in corde Abrahami per triduum illud, ex quo mandatum de ipso immolando acceperat. Recepit ergo eundem, quasi redivivum, cum immolationem ejusdem Deus inhibebat. Ideo verba ἐν παραβολῇ in similitudine explicant nonnulli, quod perinde fuerit, ac si ex mortuis excitatus fuisset: Sed præstat ea de typo & figura Christi explicare, quem gere- bat Isaacus in immolatione demandata, quia immo- latio figurabat passionem & mortem Christi, quæ etsi in Isaaco tantum tentata fuit, in ariete tamen, intra vepreta hærente, ejusdem loco surrogata, comple- ta est, in typum passionis & mortis Christi, vepretis peccatorum impliciti, & nostri loco in mortem traditi. Receptio autem Isaaci vivi erat parabola & figura Christi à morte, inqua per triduum hærebat, liberandi. Quod Oecumenius ita explicat: Vide quod ait per parabolam: Abraham erat typus Dei & Patris, Isaac verò filii Dei: Siquidem quia magnum quoddam erat nobis Deus præstiturus, nempe immolationem Filii sui, cum esset vehementer φιλάνθρωπος, ne sola gra- tia nos salvare videretur, fecit esse debitum, ut trade- retur Christus, debitum autem hoc modo: Quemad- modum, inquit, Abraham sustinuit, ut unigenitum suum in mortem traderet propter me: Ita & ego de- beo in mortem tradere Unigenitum pro hominibus. Idem Oecumenius parabolam in persona Isaaci aptans, ita evolvit eandem: Recepit Isaac, & fecit eum parabolam esse, typum & exemplum Christi, ut quemadmodum Isaac jugulatus est, ὅσον πρὸς τὴν προαίρεσιν, quantum est ex prompta voluntate Abrahæ, ita & Christus trucidetur, sed hic secun- dum veritatem ipsam. Quam explicationem tra- diderat etiam Theophylactus: Abraham quidem Dei & Patris figuram prætulerat, Isaac vero Filii Dei. Cum itaque magnum hoc Deus & supra hominum mentem mysterium esset dispensaturus, futurumque, ut nostri ob gratiam, quandoquidem erga genus hu- manum charitate ingenti afficeretur, ut vel Filium traderet immolandum, nec id placuit, tanquam de se videretur gratiam elargiri, sed ut debitum solvere, subinde hæc inquiat Deus: Nihil novum humanæ na- turæ ejus ob gratiam ipse concesserim, filium meum immolando. Abraham siquidem ut mihi obtempera- ret, filium in victimam obtulit. Quo fit, ut debitum ipse dependam, non gratiam faciam. Optime autem ea convenit Abrahæ fidei commendationi, utpo- te quæ respexit Christum propter peccata nostra tradendum, & propter justitiam nostram resusci- tandum, & ea ratione per hanc figuram vehemen- tet roborata fuit, quemadmodum etiam in illo monte immolandus erat Christus, quo Isaaci im- molatio suscipiebatur, de quo Augustinus libr. XVI. de Civ. Dei cap. 32. Hieronymus Presbyter scri- pfit, se certissime à seniorib9 Judæorum cognovisse, quod ibi immolatus sit Isaac, ubi postea Christus est crucifi- xus. Adde quod ita parabola à Paulo accipiatur Ebr. IX. 19. pro typo, quodq; non inconcinne hic sta- tuitur, Abraham vidisse diem Domini in hac sacri- ficii oblatione, quo de Theophylactus in Joh. VIII. Magno studio expetitam atq; optatam habuit diem istam. Dicit autem diem crucis præsignificatam figura oblationis & mactati arietis. Eò etiam refert B. Ger- hardus explicationem Angeli Gen. XXII, 10. cum Abraham gladium arriperet, ut filium suum imo- laret v. 12. ecce Angelus, qui fuit ipse Dei Filius, de cœlo clamavit, dicens: Non extendas manum tuam super puerum, q. d. non est persona pro peccatis mundi in sacrificio mactanda, sed in semine tuo, id est, in Messia, ex semine tuo prodituro, benedicentur omnes gentes, v. 18. i. e. quando promissus Messias maledictionem, per peccatum in genus humanam illatam, auferet, quando benedictionem & gratiam iterum adducturus est, tunc eo modo opus illud re- demtionis peragetur, quem in hac historia vel pa- rabola præfigurare tibi volui, constabit ipse san- guine, ligabitur, occidetur, fiet maledictum in li- gno crucis, sed tertia die reviviscet. Sic exposuere Tertull. l. adv. Jud. cap. IV. Clem. Alex. l. I. Strom. Origenes hom. XIIX. in Gen. Ephren Syrus lib. de Abrahamo & Isaaco, Augustinus ser. LXXII. de tempore, aliiq; cum veteres tum recentiores. Conf. gemina B. Gerhardi hom. in part. I. hom. sacr. in die Parasc. de hac parabola.

## 11:20
Verse 20. 'By faith concerning things to come Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau.' He had believed God that great things would happen to his descendants, Gen. XXVI. 24. But as if about to make a will solemnly, God directing, he divided them in such a way that he assigned the better ones to Jacob, namely concerning that land promised to Abraham. And therefore Jacob is preferred here although younger by birth: just as also Abraham to Nahor, Gen. XI. 26. In this matter also a figure of the Jewish and Christian people lies hidden, which Paul unfolds in Rom. IX.

The Apostle had previously treated of the trio of Patriarchs in general: then also specifically of Abraham: Now concerning Isaac, he observes from Gen. 27, 29. 30. that through faith in the Messiah, in whom every blessing is obtained, Isaac blessed his sons Jacob and Esau concerning things to come. For no blessing can be made with effect, unless in Christ and through Christ, whom the Apostle testifies Isaac looked upon by faith in bestowing this blessing. For the blessing of the Messiah had been promised as that blessed seed in the posterity of Isaac, Gen. 21, 12. chap. 22, 18. and especially v. 26. 4. which promise Isaac, having embraced by faith, always had in his heart, nor did he institute this blessing of his sons except through faith in that blessed seed. Theophylact, in the words περὶ μελλόντων, weighs not only the certainty of faith concerning the promised land: For in what way, he says, would he who had settled in a foreign land promise and wish for so many good things for his sons, unless he had hoped with indubitable faith that God would give what was promised? But he also weighs the future heavenly goods, of which those were a figure. When he says 'concerning things to come,' he demonstrates either the goods which do not remain into the future.
