Vers. 36. Ἕτεροι δὲ ἐμπαιγμῶν καὶ μαστίγων πεῖραν ἔλαβον) - Scourged, Micaiah 1 Kings XXII. 24. Jeremiah

XXVII. 14. In the times of Antiochus, very many, Josephus Antiq. lib. XII. 7. 1 Macc. I. 34. 2 Macc. V. 24. Elisha mocked 2 Kings II. 23. & others Luke XX. 11. Πείραν λαμβάνειν is to experience.

Ἔτι δὲ δεσμῶν καὶ φυλακῆς) As Josephus & Jeremiah & those of whom 1 Macc. I. 34.

Latin:

Vers. 36. Ἕτεροι δὲ ἐμπαιγμῶν καὶ μαστίγων πεῖραν ἔλα- βον)- Verberati, Michaeas 1. Reg. XXII. 24. Jeremias

XXVII. 14. Antiochi temporibus plurimi, Josephus Antiq. lib. XII. 7. 1. Macc. I. 34. 2. Macc. V. 24. Irrisus Elisæus 2. Reg. II. 23. & alii Luc. XX. II. Πείραν λαμβάνειν est sentire.

Ἔτι δὲ δεσμῶν καὶ φυλακῆς) Ut Josephus & Jeremias & illi de quibus 1. Macc. I. 34.

## 11:37
Vers. 37. Ἐλιθάσθησαν) As Naboth 1 Kings XXI. 13. Zechariah the Priest 2 Chron. XXIV. 21. Others. See Matt. XXI. 35. XXIII. 37. Mark XII. 4. Luke XIII. 34. Some count Jeremiah among the stoned, but the author is uncertain.

Ἐπρίσθησαν, ἐπειράσθησαν) This latter word crept into the text from a dittography. It has no place here among the kinds of deaths. The Syriac does not read that ἐπειράσθησαν, nor does Chrysostom, nor Theophylact. Ἐπρίσθησαν, however, refers to Isaiah, whom Scripture does not say was sawn asunder by Manasseh, but Jewish tradition does, which both Jerome and Epiphanius follow. And that this punishment was not unknown to the places neighboring Judea appears from Amos I. 3. 2 Sam. XII. 31. 1 Chron. XX. 3.

Ἐν φόνῳ μαχαίρας ἀπέθανον) In the times of Ahab. 1 Kings 19. v. 10. Many also in the times of Manasseh. Both are treated in Matt. 23, 30. Acts 7, 52. Many also in the times of Antiochus, 1 Macc. 1. v. 35. 52. 61. 2 Macc. 5. v. 13. c. 6. v. 9.

Περιῆλθον ἐν μηλωταῖς ἐν αἰγείοις δέρμασιν) To whom this pertains, Clement explains to the Corinthians by transcribing part of the words: 'Let us become imitators also of those who walked about in skins, goat-skins and sheepskins, preaching the coming of Christ. We speak of Elijah and Elisha, and also Ezekiel and the other prophets.' The prophets used vile clothing, such as is made from sheep or goat skins, about which matter we spoke at Matt. 3. v. 4. You have the name μηλωταῖς at 1 Kings 19. v. 13. 19. 2 Kings 2. v. 8. 13. 14. Μηλωταὶ in the Glossary means skins; the Chaldean Paraphrasts and Rabbis use this Greek word, and write מילא or מילת or מילתא. When he says περιῆλθον, he shows them to be ἀστατῆσαι, as Paul speaks in 1 Cor. 4. v. 11.

Ὑστερέμενοι) Destitute of things, חסרים or אביונים, as Deut. 15. v. 8, for which Ps. 34, 11 uses ἐλαττῦσθαι. Hence ὑσέρημα means a poor fortune, Jud. 19. v. 19. Luke 21. v. 4. See concerning Elijah 1 Kings 17. 4.

Θλιβόμενοι, κακυχύμενοι) These and the following pertain partly to the Prophets, of whom we have treated, partly to the times of Manasseh, but especially to the times of Antiochus. They were involved in great dangers, vexed by great hardships.

Latin:

Vers. 37. Ἐλιθάσθησαν) Ut Nabothes 1. Reg. XXI. 13. Zacharias Sacerdos 2. Paral. XXIV. 21. Alii. Vide Matth. XXI. 35. XXXIII. 37. Marc. XII. 4. Luc. XIII. 34. Qui- dam lapidatis accensent Jeremiam, sed incerto autore.

Ἐπρίσθησαν, ἐπειράσθησαν) Posterior hæc vox in textum irrepsit ἐκ διπλογραφίας. Locum autem hic non habet inter mortium genera. Syrus illud ἐπειράσθησαν non le- git, sed nec Chrysostomus, nec Theophylactus. Ἐπρίσθη- σαν vero ad Esaiam refertur, quem serra sectum à Manasse scriptura non dicit, sed Judæorum traditio, quam sequun- tur & Hieronymus & Epiphanius. Et fuisse hoc supplicium non incognitum vicinis Judææ locis apparet Amos I. 3. 2. Sam. XII. 31. 1. Paral. XX. 3.

Ἐν φόνῳ μαχαίρας ἀπέθανον) Achabi temporibus. 1. Reg. 19. v. 10. Multi & Manassis temporibus. De utrisq; agitur Matth. 23, 30. Act. 7, 52. Multi etiam temporibus Antiochi, 1. Macc. 1. v. 35. 52. 61. 2. Macc. 5. v. 13. c. 6. v. 9.

Περιῆλθον ἐν μηλωταῖς ἐν αἰγείοις δέρμασιν) Ad quos hoc pertineat, explicat Clemens ad Corinthios partem ver- borum transcribens: Μιμηταὶ γενώμεθα καὶ κἀκείνων, οἵτινες ἐν δέρμασιν, αἰγείοις καὶ μηλωταῖς περιεπάτησαν κηρύσσοντες τὴν ἔλευσιν τῦ χρισῦ. Λέγομεν δὲ Ἠλίαν καὶ Ἐλισαῖον, ἔτι δὲ καὶ Ἰεζεκιὴλ καὶ τὰς ἄλλες προφήτας. Prophetæ vili ha- bitu utebatur, qualis est ex ovium aut caprarum pelli- bus de qua re diximus ad Matth. 3. v. 4. Nomen μηλω- τῆς habes 1. Reg. 19. v. 13. 19. 2. Reg. 2. v. 8. 13. 14. Μηλω- ταὶ in Glossario pelles, Paraphrastæ Chaldæi & Rabbini Græcam hanc vocem usurpant, scribuntque מילא aut מילת aut מילתא, cum dicit περιῆλθον, ostendit eos ἀστα- τῆσαι ut Paulus loquitur 1. Cor. 4. v. 11.

Ὑστερέμενοι) rerum inopes חסרים aut אביונים, ut Deut. 15. v. 8. pro quo Psal. 34, 11. ponitur ἐλαττῦσθαι. Hinc ὑσέρημα fortuna pauper, Jud. 19. v. 19. Luc. 21. v. 4. Vide de Elia 1. Reg. 17. 4.

Θλιβόμενοι, κακυχύμενοι) Hæc & sequentia partim ad Prophetas pertinent, de quibus egimus, partim ad Ma- nassis, maxime vero ad Antiochi tempora. Magnis in periculis versati sunt, magnis vexati incommodis.

## 11:38
Vers. 38. Ὧν ἐκ ἦν ἄξιος ὁ κόσμος, ἐν ἐρημίαις πλανώμενοι καὶ ὄρεσι καὶ σπηλαίοις, καὶ ταῖς ὀπαῖς τῆς γῆς) See examples in the cited place, 1 Kings 17. 3. c. 18. v. 13. 2 Kings 6, 1. 1 Macc. 1. v. 56. c. 2. v. 29. 30. 2 Macc. 5. v. 27. c. 10. v. 6. And it is effectively said: Those of whose daily company other men were not worthy, driven from cities and villages, could find no reception except in inaccessible and rough places, and in caves and caverns. See also concerning David 1 Sam. 22. v. 1. c. 23. v. 19. c. 24. v. 2. Understand caves as from rock נקיקי הסלעים, Isa. 7. v. 16, caverns under the earth.

These works and deeds of saving faith, though not occupied with its own proper object, yet exerted and celebrated by notable exercises of piety, love, constancy, and heroic fortitude, have been digested in a summary manner; which, indeed, without faith in the Messiah, could neither be performed, nor be adorned with such praise by the Holy Spirit himself; and by his divine testimony they were judged worthy of the eulogy of faith. Although, however, these are only exercises and works of faith outside the act of justification, they are nevertheless referred to justifying faith, inasmuch as with respect to them, the faithful and the saints are enrolled in the catalogue by the Holy Spirit, who searches the hearts and reins, and knows who are his. In which also, as sacred history testifies, saving faith peculiarly shone forth. Moreover, as to 1. those who through faith subdued kingdoms, Joshua does not belong here, because he had already been treated of specifically; but the judges, and David, in whose victories also a type of Christ's victory over spiritual enemies and the Satanic kingdom shone forth, but primarily faith in the Messiah shines. 2. They are said to have wrought righteousness through faith, not in general, by keeping God's commandments, living piously and justly, but specifically by promoting justice and piety in their kingdoms and lands, so that the kingdom of Christ, which consists of justice, Isa. IX. 6, Jer. XXIII. 6, might be advanced and flourish. Of the more sublime precepts of the Gospel he knows nothing scripture. 3. Through faith they obtained the promises, not the land of Canaan which they occupied, promised to the Patriarchs, because the Apostle had already dealt with those, but those who embraced special promises by faith and actually attained them; from the times of the Judges, whom the Apostle did not wish to recount one by one for the sake of brevity, just as, for example, the victory to be won over the Midianites promised to Gideon, Judg. 7:7. The addition of 15 years to Hezekiah, etc. The acceptance of these promises was founded on the fiducial acceptance of the promise concerning the Messiah, which is the basis of all, which alone is justifying and saving. 4. Through faith Daniel stopped the mouths of lions, chap. 6:22, because through faith he possessed Christ, who overcame even the infernal lion himself, by the power of whose victory Daniel also trampled upon Satan and all his scales. Cf. Gen. 3:16, Ps. 91:13, Rom. 16:20. 5. Through faith they obtained that the fire should not exercise its power, as did the companions of Daniel, because they had present with them Him who deigned to experience the flames of divine wrath for our sake, so that He might deliver us from any flames whatsoever. 6. Through faith they escaped sharp swords, because by faith they apprehended Him who for our sake willed to undergo the swords of enemies, Ps. 22:21. 7. Through faith they recovered from diseases, which is evident from the example of Job the confessor, chap. 19:25, and of Hezekiah imploring Jesus the Savior. 8. Through faith they were strong in war, by the example of David in the duel with Goliath, relying on circumcision as the seal of righteousness, 1 Sam. 17, and confirmed concerning the Messiah of the God of Jacob, 2 Sam. 23:1, and of the mighty men of David, of Jehoshaphat, 2 Chron. 20:20, and of others, it is clear. 9. Through faith they scattered the camps of foreigners, as Jonathan was an example, 1 Sam. 14, or put armies to flight, which can be read everywhere also in the history of the Maccabees. For they relied on the power of Him who defeated the infernal camps and led principalities and powers in triumph, Col. 2:15. 10. Through faith women received their dead, who had embraced the resurrection from the dead of the Messiah. 11. Through faith others sustained most grievous afflictions, which the Apostle now subjoins to the heroic and singular deeds, who by faith received the most grievous passions of Christ endured for us, and by His power patiently sustained all things; inasmuch as they were stretched, like leather on a drum, although others understand by τύμπανον not the instrument which is beaten, but that by which it is beaten, the cudgel, with which executioners beat the bodies of the guilty stretched by a rack; and to this they refer the example of Eleazar, 2 Macc. 6:30. 12. Who did not accept deliverance, that a better resurrection might be obtained by them, which is an evident demonstration of faith in the Messiah, in whom alone resurrection to eternal life is obtained by us. Grotius rashly perverts this, as if it were a matter of the restoration of Judea to a better lot, when it clearly treats of the blessed resurrection, both in 2 Macc. 7:9 seqq. and Dan. 12:1. 13. Others received the experience of mockings and scourgings, furthermore also of bonds and imprisonment, by which four kinds of afflictions are comprehended, to which others and still others were exposed, either separately or conjunctively, for the sake of Christ, who sustained all these things for us, apprehended by faith. Josephus does not belong here, because these concern later times. But the others recounted by Grotius are well taken. Also Samson, Judg. 15:26, 27. 14. Others were stoned, which the Hebrews also report concerning Jeremiah. 15. Others ἐπρίσθησαν, which Jerome renders 'they were sawn asunder,' which Justin in Dial. with Trypho, and Tertullian in the book against the Gnostics, chap. 8, and the book on patience, chap. 14, and Origen in hom. 1 on Ps. 37, and Dorotheus in the Synopsis report concerning Isaiah. 16. Others were afflicted by other kinds of temptations, ἐπειράσθησαν, which Grotius rashly suspects to be an interpolation, even though the Syriac does not have it. For all Greek codices have it consistently. Piscator, without the authority of codices, thinks ἐπυράσθησαν should be read. 17. Others died by the edge of the sword, ἐν φόνῳ μαχαίρας ἀπέθανον. To which also pertain the priests in Nob killed by Saul, 1 Sam. 22:18. Urijah the prophet struck by the sword by King Jehoiakim, Jer. 26:23. 18. Now he also commemorates poverty and exiles and dangers endured through faith in Christ, who for our sake also had to become, and willed to become, needy and an exile, and to be exposed to various dangers.

Latin:

Vers. 38. Ὧν ἐκ ἦν ἄξιος ὁ κόσμος, ἐν ἐρημίαις πλανώμε- νοι καὶ ὄρεσι καὶ σπηλαίοις, καὶ ταῖς ὀπαῖς τῆς γῆς) Exempla vide dicto loco, 1. Reg. 17. 3. c. 18. v. 13. 2. Reg. 6, 1. 1. Macc. 1. v. 56. c. 2. v. 29. 30. 2. Macc. 5. v. 27. c. 10. v. 6. Et effica- citer dictum: Illi quorum quotidiana consuetudine ho- mines cæteri digni non erant, ex urbibus vicisque exacti, receptum nullum nisi in locis inviis & asperis, specubusq; & cavernis invenire potuerunt. Vide & de Davide 1. Sam, 22. v. 1. c. 23. v. 19. c. 24. v. 2. Specus intellige è saxo נקיקי הסלעים, Efa. 7. v. 16. cavernas sub humum.

Fidei hæc salvificæ, non in proprio quidem ob- jecto occupatæ, insignibus tamen exercitiis pieta- tis, amoris, constantiæ & fortitudinis heroicæ exer- tæ ac celebratæ, opera & facta sunt per saturam digesta, quæ vero sine fide in Messiam nec effici, nec ea laude ab ipso Spiritu sancto mactari potue- runt; ejusque divino testimonio fidei elogio digna judicata sunt. Quanquam vero hæc tantum exer- citia & opera fidei sint extra justificationis actum: ad fidem tamen justificantem referuntur, utpote quorum respectu fidelium & sanctorum catalogo, qui ab iisdem celebrati sunt, à Spiritu sancto, qui corda & renes scrutatur, & novit, qui sint sui, re- feruntur. In quibus etiam, teste sacra historia, fides salvifica peculiariter eluxit. Cæterum quod 1. ad eos, qui per fidem regna vicerunt, Josua huc non pertinet, quia de eo peculiariter jam actum erat; sed judices, ac David, in quorum victoriis etiam typus victoriæ Christi de hostibus spiritua- libus, & regno Satanico emicuit, sed imprimis fides in Messiam effulget. 2. per fidem Justitiam operati dicuntur non in genere, servando Dei præ- cepta, piè ac juste vivendo, sed speciatim in regnis & terris suis justitiam & pietatem promovendo, ut regnum Christi, quod justitia constat, Esa. IX. 6. Jer. XXIII. 6. proveheretur ac floreret. De sublimioribus Evangelii præceptis nihil novit scriptura. 3. Per fidem consequuti promissiones, non qua terram Canaan occuparunt, Patriarchis pro- missam, quia de illis antea egerat Apostolus, sed qui specialia promissa fide amplexi & reapse adepti sunt; inde à Judicum temporibus, quos sigillatim recensere brevitatis causa noluit Apostolus, quo- modo Gideoni, e. g. promissa victoria à Midianitis reportanda, Jud. VII. 7. Hiskiæ προσθήκη 15. anno- rum, &c. Quarum promissionum acceptatio fun- data fuit in fiduciali promissionis de Messia, quæ omnium basis est, acceptatione, quæ sola est justifi- ca & salvifica. 4. Per fidem obturavit leonum ora Daniel cap. VI. 22. quia per fidem Christum possi- debat, qui ipsum etiam infernalem leonem supe- ravit, cujus victoriæ virtute Satanam, & omnes ejus squamas calcabat quoque Daniel. Conf. Gen. III. 16. Psal. XCI. 13. Rom. XVI. 20. 5. Per fidem obti- nuere, ut ignis vim suam non exerceret, ut Socii Da- nielis, quod habuerint eum præsentem, qui flammas iræ divinæ pro nobis experiri dignatus est, ut nos à flammis quibusvis liberaret. 6. Per fidem effuge- runt enses acutos, quia fide apprehenderunt eum, qui nostri causa hostium gladios subire voluit, Psal. XXII. 21. 7. Per fidem convalvere à morbis, quod exemplo Jobi confessoris cap. XIX. 25. & Hiskiæ Jesum Salvatorem implorantis constat. 8. Per fidem in bello fortes fuere, exemplo Davidis in duello cum Goliath, circumcisione sigillo justitiæ freti, 1. Sam. XVII. & confirmati de Messia Dei Ja- cob 2. Sam. XXIII, 1. fortiumque Davidis, Josa- phati 2. Chron. XX. 20. & aliorum liquet. 9. Per fi- dem castra exterorum dissiparunt, ut exemplo fuit Jonathan, 1. Sam. XIV. vel exercitus in fugam ege- runt, quod passim etiam in historia Maccabæorum legere est. Nixi enim fuere virtute ejus, qui castra infernalia debellavit, & principatus ac potestates in triumphum egit, Col. II. 15. 10. Per fidem rece- perunt mulieres defunctos suos, quæ Messiæ resu- scitationem è mortuis complexæ erant. 11. Per fi- dem alii afflictiones gravissimas sustinuere, quas nunc factis heroicis & singularibus subjungit Apo- stolus, qui passiones Christi gravissimas pro nobis exantlatas fide suscepere, ejusque virtute patienter omnia sustinuere; utpote qui distenti sunt, veluti corium in tympano, quanquam alii per τύμπανον non instrumentum, quod pulsatur, sed quo pulsatur, fustuarium, quo carnifices corpora reorum per machinam tractariam distenta pulsarunt, intelli- gant; eoque exemplum Eleazari 2. Macc. VI. 30. referant. 12. Qui non suscepere redemptionem, ut melior eis obtingeret resurrectio, quæ est evidens fidei in Messiam, in quo solo nobis resurrectio obtingit ad æternam vitam, demonstratio. Perver- tit ista temere Grotius, ac si de restitutione Judææ in meliorem sortem ageretur, quum luculenter de beata resurrectione, & 2. Macc. VII. 9. seqq. & Dan. XII. 1. agatur. 13. Alii ludibriorum & flagro- rum experientiam ceperunt, adhæc & vinculorum & carceris, quo comprehenduntur quatuor genera afflictionum, quibus alii atque alii vel seorsim, vel conjunctim expositi fuere, ob Christum, qui omnia ista pro nobis sustinuit, fide apprehensum. Jose- phus huc non pertinet, quia concernunt hæc po- steriora tempora. Bene autem cæteri à Grotio re- censiti. Etiam Samson Judic. XV. 26. 27. 14. Alii lapidibus obruti, quod de Jeremia etiam tradunt Ebræi. 15. Alii ἐπρίσθησαν, quod Hieronymus red- dit serrati sunt, quod de Esaia etiam Justinus in Dial. cum Tryph. & Tertullianus libr. adversus Gnost. cap. VIII. libr. de patient. cap. XIV. Orige- nes hom. I. in Psal. XXXVII. Doroth. in Synopsi tra- dunt. 16. Alii aliis tentationum generibus afflicti sunt, ἐπειράσθησαν, quod temere suspicatur Grotius irreptitium esse, etsi nec Syrus habeat. Habent e- nim omnes Græci Codices constanter. Piscator ci- tra Codicum fidem putat ἐπυράσθησαν legendum. 17. Alii ἐν φόνῳ μαχαίρας ἀπέθανον. Quo etiam pertinent Sacerdotes in Nobe à Saule occisi, 1. Sam. XXII. 28. Vrias Propheta gladio à Rege Jojakim percussus Jer. XVI. 23. 18. Jam egestatem & exilia atque pericula etiam commemorat per fidem exan- tlata in Christo, qui nostri causa egenus & exul eti- am fieri debuit, voluit, ac periculis variis exponi.

## 11:39
Vers. 39. And all these having obtained a good report through faith) See above 11:2, 4, 5.

They did not receive the promise) Others, of whom it was said above in 33, received the promises: but these did not receive: it was not permitted for them to remain safely in the promised land: they succumbed to hostile wrath. Κομίζεσθαι here and above in 10:36 is the same as ἐπιτυγχάνειν. In the manuscript it is not 'the promise' but 'the promises,' as this writer usually speaks here, where he deals with the ancient promises.

All these having obtained a testimony through faith, not as the Vulgate says, 'approved by the testimony of faith,' that is, that they were justified by faith, cf. v. 5, but not having attained that promise, for which they most greatly panted, concerning the mission of the Son of God into the flesh. What Grotius rendered, that it was not permitted for them to remain safely in the promised land, is foreign to the phrase and to the divine promises, which are to be understood with the exception of the cross, or that they succumbed to hostile wrath, which is not true of all of them. Did David succumb in the duel with Goliath? Or Jonathan in the visitation of the enemy's camps? Or Daniel in the lions' den? etc. Nor is it a matter of the consummated blessedness of soul and body. For no one of us in the New Testament attains that before the consummation of the age. It is a matter of faith in the promised Messiah, whom they indeed awaited with boldness, but they were not made partakers of that promise: whence those are pronounced more blessed who lived in the time of the New Testament, Matt. 13:16, 17, Luke 10:23.

Latin:

Vers. 39. Καὶ ὗτοι πάντες μαρτυρηθέντες διὰ τῆς πίστεως) Vide supra XI. 2. 4. 5.

Οὐκ ἐκομίσαντο τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν) Alii, de quibus dictum supra 33. accepere promissa: hi vero non accepere: non licuit illis in terra promissa tuto consistere: succubuere iræ hostili. Κομίζεσθαι hic & supra X. 36. idem quod ἐπι- τυγχάνειν. In manuscripto non est τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν sed τὰς ἐπαγγελίας, quomodo plerumque hic Scriptor loqui- tur, ubi de veteribus promissis agit.

Omnes istos testimonium consequutos per fi- dem, non ut Vulgatus, testimonio fidei probatos ait, quod nempe fide justificati fuerint, conf. v. 5. non vero adeptos promissionem illam, quam maxime anhelarunt, de missione Filii Dei in carnem. Quod Grotius reddidit, non licuisse illis in terra promissa tuto consistere, alienum est à phrasi & divinis pro- missionibus, quæ cum exceptione crucis intelli- gendæ, vel quod succubuerint iræ hostili, quod non de omnibus illis vero consonat. Num suc- cubuit David in duello cum Goliatho? Vel Jona- than in castrorum hostilium visitatione? Vel Da- niel in spelunca leonum? &c. Nec de animæ & cor- poris consummata beatitudine agitur. Nam eam nec nostrum quisquam in Novo Testamento con- sequitur ante seculi consummationem. De fide in Messiam promissum agitur, quem illi quidem ex- pectarunt μετὰ παῤῥησίας, sed promissionis istius compotes redditi non fuere: Unde beatiores præ- dicantur, qui Novi Testamenti tempore vixerunt, Matth. XII. 16. 17. Luc. X. 23.

## 11:40
Vers. 40. God having provided some better thing for us) He had decreed to reveal that truly heavenly and eternal promise to us at last openly. See above 7:19, 8:6, where you have the word 'better' in a similar sense.

Ἵνα μὴ χωρὶς ἡμῶν τελειωθῶσιν) They too, the ancients, will be partakers of those eternal goods, but in such a way that they are an accession to us: for those promises were made to us, not to them. Take τελειοῦσθαι here as above II. 10. V. 9. Thus God did those ancients no injury. For He will provide for them greater things than He had promised.

These glosses proceed from a false hypothesis, as if heavenly goods had not been promised in the Old Testament. Furthermore, they are inconsistent, in that the ancients were not perfected without us, but that they are only an accession to us, and that this concerns the promise of eternal beatitude, when the discourse is about the promise of the Messiah, on account of whom God foresaw κρεῖττόν τι for the Hebrews. But what of that ἵνα μὴ χωρὶς ἡμῶν τελειωθῶσι? The Apostle speaks by κοινωνία with the Hebrews, to whom that τελείωσις befell, because they knew the Lord in the days of His flesh, which beatitude Christ proclaimed in Luke X. 23. But if those whom he enumerated had obtained the promise, this beatitude or perfection would not have come to those descendants of theirs, but they themselves would have been perfected without them. Which sense is without doubt simpler, and more convenient than the explanation of Tossanus and Piscator, although approved by Blasius de Viega in Ap. page 28: If Christ had been exhibited to those Fathers, and had even then expiated their sins by His sacrifice, then by hypothesis, namely by the force of the divine decree, we would have been neglected, because with Christ exhibited, nothing else can be expected than the end of the world, and thus the end of the world would have come before we were born: or also the interpretation of Theophylact: Lest the saints of the O.T. seem to us more excellent, if they are crowned first, He established one time for the crowns of all; for He did not say that they should not be crowned, but that they might not be perfected. Therefore, those will seem perfect then, who already have the earnest and pledge of honor, but they will receive a more perfect one then. Thus, there is no refuge here in the limbo of the Fathers; to which that exposition of Theophylact also leaves no room, as is clear from Estius: But most others, both Greeks and Latins, explain the Apostle thus: They did not receive the promise, i.e., perfectly or consummately. For the promise will be received perfectly when, with their bodies raised to immortality, holy men will reign with Christ in the heavens. For before that time, only souls reign and are blessed, not men, unless synecdochically. But the Apostle speaks of men. This sense, as it is more common than others, so it is also much more probable, which Augustine also hands down in epistle 99 to Evodius and tract 49 on John, and Chrysostom explains beautifully in his commentary: And Erasmus, having changed his opinion for the better, follows it in his paraphrase. More probable, I say, first, because the final part intends this, which does not say, that they might not be rewarded without us, but that they might not be perfected without us, i.e., that they might receive the perfected and whole remuneration which was promised. Then, because a little before he said of certain ones: That they might find a better resurrection. He treats, therefore, of the consummation which ought to come about through the resurrection. Finally, the exhortation of the preceding chapter demands this sense, from which he passes to the commendation of faith and to exciting the imitation of those who pleased God through faith. For that exhortation was to bear afflictions patiently, in contemplation of the remuneration to be received at the end of the age. Which those sentences prove: So much the more, as you see the day approaching. That the promise which those saints received is to be understood concerning the Messiah to be exhibited, the comparison of v. 13 clearly teaches. Κατὰ πίσιν ἀπέθανον ὗτοι πάντες μὴ λαβόντες τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν. Which sense B. Gerh. himself approved at v. 33: Lower down, he says, in v. 39, the discourse is about the general promise, and common to all, namely, of Christ, who was not exhibited to them. And B. Hun. favors it, rendering this opinion: Since those Fathers of the O.T., by doing noble things and suffering adverse things, gave so many and such great proofs of their faith, however much they had not yet received the promise concerning the exhibition of the Messiah: How much more does it behoove us to be constant in faith, and to do and suffer anything for its propagation? Since God has provided a better condition for us, by exhibiting, indeed, the Messiah, whom they were expecting to come.

Therefore, it is not for us to establish with Cameron in Myroth. either the τελείωσιν in knowledge, which is much more illustrious in the N.T. For that would have happened to us also, if Christ had been exhibited earlier. Or let us say with the same: That the spirits of the perfect just also finally attained with us a greater mystery of redemption, but that they were not perfected without us, concerning which he says thus on page 336: Although this may seem a paradox to some, it is nevertheless true that the mystery of our redemption was not as well known even to the Angels before Christ was exhibited as it is now known to the Church. And therefore, not even to the blessed spirits of the pious received into heaven. Therefore, if anyone asks whether they have been enriched with new glory now that Christ has been exhibited, we can affirm that without any suspicion of excessive curiosity, since it is certain that that mystery was rendered much better known to them. Which paradox we leave in its own place: It certainly does not fit this place, where the comparison of τελειώσεως is instituted not with the spirits of the perfect just, but with the just of the O.T. when they were living. Concerning which Camero himself previously, when he was arguing against limbo: This perfection was situated in the exhibition of the promise, for they were not perfect in that they had not attained the promise; we, therefore, are perfect compared to them, in that we have attained the promise. But the promise was of a thing to be performed in this life. Therefore, the difference between our perfection and that of the Fathers is situated in that which is exhibited in this life. Therefore, this does not treat of the state of the soul after this life. If you say that many wished to enjoy that blessedness, and did not attain it, that τελειώσει, or τοῖς κρείτ]οσι. Resp. That they could nevertheless enjoy and attain them, because they fell into their own times. If they did not attain it, that is not to be attributed to God, who provided something better (κρεῖτ]όν τι) for those Hebrews in those times.

Latin:

Vers. 40. Τῦ Θεῦ περὶ ἡμῶν κρεῖττόν τι προβλεψαμένε) Promissum illud vere cœleste & æternum nobis demum aperte revelare decreverat. Vide supra VII. 19. VIII. 6. ubi simili sensu habes vocem κρεῖττον.

Ἵνα μὴ χωρὶς ἡμῶν τελειωθῶσιν) Erunt & illi veteres istorum æternorum bonorum participes, sed ita, ut nostri sint acces- sio: Nobis enim non illis facta sunt illa promissa. Τελειοῦσθαι hic sume ut supra II. 10. V. 9. Ita Deus illis veteribus nullam fecit injuriam. Præstabit enim illis majora, quam promiserat.

Hæ glossæ è falsa hypothesi procedunt, quasi in Veteri Testamento non promissa fuerint bona cœ- lestia. Adhæc inconvenientes sunt, quod non sine nobis veteres perfecti, sed eos tantùm nostri esse ac- cessionem, & quod hic de promissione agatur beati- tudinis æternæ, quum de promissione Messiæ ser- mo sit, cujus ratione Ebræis κρεῖττόν τι prospexit Deus. Quid vero illa ἵνα μὴ χωρὶς ἡμῶν τελειωθῶ- σι? Loquitur Apostolus per κοινωνίαν cum Ebræis, quibus illa τελείωσις obtigit, quod Dominum in diebus carnis noverint, quam beatitudinem præ- dicavit Christus Luc. X. 23. Si autem illi, quos re- censuit, promissionem consequuti fuissent, non ve- nisset hæc beatitudo aut perfectio ad posteros illos eorum, sed perfecti ipsi fuissent sine iisdem. Qui sen- sus sine dubio simplicior est, & convenientior Tos- sani & Piscatoris explicatione, etsi Blasio de Viega in Ap. pag. 28. probata: Si Christus Patribus illis fuiffet exhibitus, & jam tùm à sacrificio suo pec- cata ipsorum expiasset, tùm ex hypothesi, nimi- rum vi decreti divini nos fuissemus negleci, quia Christo exhibito, nihil aliud, quam finis mun- di expectari potest, atque sic finis mundi venisset antequam essemus nati: vel etiam interpretatio- ne Theophylacti: Ne nobis videantur præstantio- res V.T. sancti, si primi coronentur, unum omnibus coronarum tempus statuit; nec enim dixit ut non coronentur, sed utne consummentur. Proinde tum perfecti videbuntur, qui jam arrhabonem & pignus honoris habent, perfectiorem autem tunc accipi- ent. Ita nullum limbo Patrum hic præsidium; Cui et- iam locum non relinquit illa Theophylacti ἔκθεσις, ut ex Eftio liquet: Alii vero pleriq́; tam Græci, quam Latini sic exponunt Apostolum: Non acceperunt pro- missionem, scil. perfecte seu consummate. Perfecte enim accipietur promissio, quando resuscitatis ad immorta- litatem corporibus sancti homines cum Christo regna- bunt in cælis. Nam ante id temp9 animæ solæ regnant, & beatæ sunt, non homines, nisi synecdochice. Loquitur autem Apostolus de hominibus. Hic sensus ut commu- nior est aliis; ita & multo probabilior, quem & Augu- stinus tradit in epist. 99. ad Evodium & tr. 49. in Joh. & Chrys. in Com. pulchrè explicat: Et Erasmus sen- tentia in meliùs mutata sequitur in paraphrasi. Pro- babilior inquam primo, quia id vult extrema pars, quæ non dicit, ne sine nobis remunerarentur, sed ut non sine nobis consummarentur, i. e. consummatam ac to- tam, quæ promissa est, acciperent remunerationem. Deinde quia paulo ante de quibusdam dixit: Ut me- liorem invenirent resurrectionem. Agit ergo de con- summatione, quæ per resurrectionem fieri debeat. De- niq́; sensum hunc postulat exhortatio capitis præce- dentis, à qua transit ad fidei commendationem, & ad excitandam imitationem eorum, qui per fidem Deo placuerunt. Erat enim illa exhortatio ad ferendas pa- tienter afflictiones, contemplatione remunerationis in fine seculi recipiendæ. Quod probant illæ sententiæ: Tanto magis, quanto videritis appropinquantem di- em. Promissionem, quam sancti illi acceperint, de Messia exhibendo intelligendam esse luculenter docet collatio v. 13. Κατὰ πίσιν ἀπέθανον ὗτοι πάντες μὴ λαβόντες τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν. Quem sensum ad v. 33. B. Gerh. ipse approbavit: Inferius, inquit, in v. 39. sermo est de promissione generali, & omnibus commu- ni, videl. Christi, qui illis non fuit exhibitus. Eiq; fa- vet B. Hun. hanc reddens sententiam: Cum illi Pa- tres V. T. præclara faciendo & adversa patiendo tot tantaq́; documenta fidei suæ ediderint, quantumvis promissionem de exhibitione Messiæ nondum accepis- sent: Quanto magis decet nos esse in fide constantes, & ad propagationem ejus facere quævis & perpeti? Cum de meliori conditione Deus nobis providerit, exhibendo nimirum Messiam, quem illi venturum expectabant.

Non ergo est ut cum Camerone in Myroth. vel τελείωσιν in cognitione constituamus, quæ multo il- lustrior in N. T. est. Nam ea etiam nobis obtigisset, si prius Christus exhibitus fuisset. Vel dicamus cum eodem: Spiritus etiam perfectorum justorum ade- ptos tandem nobiscum majorem mysterii redem- ptionem, sine nobis, verò non fuisse perfectos, de quo ita pag. 336. Etsi Paradoxum id nonnullis videa- tur, verum tamen est, mysterium redemptionis nostræ, ne Angelis quidem ante exhibitum Christum fuisse perinde notum, atque jam Ecclesiæ notum est. E. nec beatis Spiritibus piorum receptis cælo. Itaq́; si quis quæ- rat, an nova gloria locupletati sint Christo exhibito, possumus id affirmare citra ullam nimiæ curiositatis suspicionem, cum certum sit mysterium illud redditum iis fuisse multo notius. Quod paradoxum nos suo re- linquimus loco: Huic certe non convenit loco, ubi non cum Spiritibus justorum perfectorum, sed cum justis V. T. cùm viverent, instituitur τελειώσε- ως comparatio. Quo de ipse Camero antea, cum ad- versus limbum ageret: Hæc perfectio fuit sita in exhi- bitione promissionis, nam eo non fuerunt perfecti, quod non erant consequuti promissionem, nos ergo præ illis perfecti sumus, eo quod adepti sumus promissio- nem. Promissio autem erat rei præstandæ in hac vita. Ergo discrimen nostræ perfectionis & Patrum situm est in eo, quod in hac vita exhibetur. Non ergo hic agitur de statu animæ post hanc vitam. Si dicas, mul- tos voluisse frui ea beatitudine, nec potitos, τελειώσει illâ, aut τοῖς κρείτ]οσι. Resp. Frui tamen ac potiri il- lis potuisse, quia in tempora ipsorum inciderunt. Si non potiti sint, Deo id non tribuendum, qui Ebræis istis temporibus κρεῖτ]όν τι omnino pro- spexit.

## 12:1 Argument
CHAPTER XII. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The Apostle exhorts to perseverance in faith by the example of the ancient faithful, with the proper object of faith proposed, Christ, his cross and reproach, and his sitting at the right hand of God, and the fruit of paternal chastisements; he commands them to pursue peace and holiness, and not to neglect the grace of God, by the example of Esau. Since they have not approached the mountain smoking with fire and terrible, but to Mount Zion and the city of God, and to the Mediator of the New Testament, and they hear him speaking from heaven, and again according to the Prophet, moving not only the earth but also the heaven, and they may obtain an immovable kingdom, and so God is to be served with fear, as one who is an unquenchable fire.

There are two parts: I. An exhortation to perseverance in the proposed struggle up to v. 11. II. An incitement to holiness and to hearing the voice of the Lord up to v. 29.

PART I. Exhortation to perseverance in the proposed struggle.

Vers. 1. Τοιγαροῦν καὶ ἡμεῖς τοσοῦτον ἔχοντες περικείμενον ἡμῖν νέφος μαρτύρων) Since we have such a host of witnesses concerning the utility of faith. Thus Virgil, what he had said: Clouds of deeds press upon them. He soon explains: In dense crowds. Thus in Livy it is: The King throws clouds of infantry and cavalry against them. A cloud of arms is in Statius. Clouds are accustomed to follow one another in a long train. A similar comparison is in Isaiah 60:8. And the Hebrews want עב, which signifies a cloud, to be said from עבה, which is to thicken.

The Apostle now presents the proper object of justifying faith, to which both the faithful of the Old Testament, whose cloud he had set forth, looked, and to which the Hebrews ought to look by their example, so that, having laid aside sin as much as possible in the race set before us, we may run with persevering faith, relying on the help of him who is ἀρχηγὸς, καὶ τελειωτὴς τῆς πίσεως. That object of faith is Jesus himself, insofar as for the joy he chose the cross and reproach, and sat down at the right hand on the throne of God. He sets him forth not only as an example, but primarily for his merit, because he endured those things for our sake, and the ancients looked to him through faith, whose examples he had brought forward. Which is to be carefully observed here. This is taught by 1. The scope and proposition of the Apostle, who has been concerned with this since chapter X. 19, that we may hold fast the confession of our hope ἐν πληροφορίᾳ πίσεως. 2. The repeated exhortation in chapter X. 35, μὴ ἀποβάλητε τὴν παῤῥησίαν. 3. The confirmation of the same, both by the oracle of Habakkuk in verses 37, 38, 39, and by the examples of the ancients in chapter XI. 4. The description of justifying faith in chapter XI. verse 1, which he illustrated with examples, both in terms of the act and its proper duty, and in terms of its varied exercise. 5. The analogous inference or conclusion, which as it is instituted here: so it ought to correspond to the previous discussion on faith. Wherefore it was necessary that, first of all, the proper object of saving faith be set forth: And that Christ, who is our Jesus, and whose passion was especially meritorious, be proposed in that manner in which He was apprehended by faith by the ancient believers, and is to be apprehended by all for salvation. 6. Mention of ὑπομονῆς [patience/endurance], which, as is evident from comparison with chapter X. 36, denotes not mere patience, but perseverance in faith that is patient or suffering all things, or the constancy of faith with patience: Without which faith and constancy there is also no running in the proposed race, 2 Tim. IV. 7, no complacency of God, Heb. XI. 6. 7. The naming of Jesus, whom we ought to look upon by faith. For He is called ἀρχηγὸς καὶ τελειωτὴς πίσεως [the author and finisher of faith] both by reason of merit and of efficacy. By reason of merit indeed, because unless Christ had been delivered for our sins, and raised again for our justification, or as the Apostle here says, unless for our sake He had chosen the cross and reproaches for joy, and had sat down at the right hand of God, our faith in Christ would be nothing, as it is manifest from Rom. IV, 1 Cor. XV. 3, Is. LIII. 11, compared with these, that this is its proper object. Add that He also merited faith for us, that is, by His merit He obtained both regeneration and the gift of the Holy Spirit, by whose power we attain faith, Phil. I. 29. But by reason of efficacy, Christ is also the ἀρχηγὸς καὶ τελειωτὴς [author and finisher] of faith, because He works in us both to will and to do, He begins, increases, and completes our faith, Mark IX. 24, Luke XVII. 5. 8. The designation of the end of that looking and remembering, so that ὑπομονὴ [endurance] or perseverance in faith may be obtained, v. 1, by which they are ἀφορῶντες [looking away/fixing their eyes], and with the eyes of the mind look upon Jesus in His passion, and the glory that followed it, v. 2, because from thence faith has life, and its ὑπόςασιν [substance/assurance] Gal. II. 20, and thus, diligently looking upon Jesus in the Word of faith, they do not become τέκνα ὑποσο- λῆς εἰς ἀπώλειαν [children of drawing back unto perdition], but πίσεως εἰς περιποίησιν ψυ- χῆς [of faith to the saving of the soul] Heb. X. 39. Just as the Hebrews are also commanded to ἀναλογίσασθαι [consider] τὸν τοιαύτην ὑπομεμενηκότα ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν εἰς ἀυτὸν ἀντιλογίαν [Him who endured such contradiction of sinners against Himself], to the end that they may be comforted in that faith in Christ, and patiently persevere in it, ἵνα μὴ κάμητε ταῖς ψυ- χαῖς ὑμῶν ἐκλυόμενοι [lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds] chapter XII. 3. 9. The communion of believers militant on earth with those triumphant. For that faith, by which the ancient believers and others now triumph in heaven, must be constantly retained in any tribulations whatsoever, which indeed was the faith of those on earth who are now designated by πνέυματα δικαίων τετελειωμένων [the spirits of just men made perfect], v. 23, who were justified by faith in the blood of Christ, Rom. III. 25, and were perfected forever by the one expiatory offering of Christ, Heb. X. 14, and now live forever by faith, v. 38, through which they had approached the Mediator of the New Testament, Jesus, and the blood of cleansing and expiation, chapter XII. 24, to whom because the Hebrews also approached, they are gravely warned here, so that they do not neglect that grace, and thus constantly and patiently persevere in that faith, so that they do not lose the kingdom which they received, ἀσάλευτον [unshakable]. Everything therefore aims at faith in Christ, not just any faith, but that by which every just man lives, to be retained, and not to be lost or cast away either through ἀποsασίαν [apostasy], because of persecutions and afflictions, or through sins that burden the conscience. 10. The denomination of witnesses. For these holy and faithful ones are called martyrs because of the testimony which they gave concerning faith in Christ, both by doctrine and life and martyrdom or their own blood, each in his own time and manner, through which faith they were justified, approved by God, and eternally saved, which is no other faith than that which received testimony from all the Prophets,

Acts X. 43, by which we also are saved, and they themselves were saved, Acts XV. 11. Whom the blessed Gerhard observes are compared to clouds 1. because of the sublimity of their conversation, Is. LX. 8, Phil. III. 20. 2. Because of the fruitfulness of their doctrine, Job XXXVI. 37. 3. Because of the utility of spiritual consolation. For as clouds provide cooling: so also do the examples of the saints. 4. Because of the quality of their effects. As rain, lightnings, and thunderbolts proceed from clouds: so from the saints proceed doctrine, miracles, and warnings. As lightnings are generated from the collision of clouds: so rational clouds, if they speak with themselves, emit the fire of divine love and the lightnings of spiritual warnings. Origen on Jeremiah. Theophylact: He did not even say a multitude, he says, but a cloud, which is more appropriate to the present subject. For since these have burned with the heat of pressures, this multitude of witnesses, by which we are surrounded on every side, will cool us, he says, like some dewy cloud surrounding those who are burning.

O̓́γκον ἀποθέμενοι πάντα [Laying aside every weight]) A simile taken from the stadium. There, those who are about to run lay aside everything that can be a burden. So also do we [lay aside] the love of this world, and indeed even of ourselves, Matt. XVI. 24, ὄγκος [weight/bulk], as the Syrian took it here. Thus Aristotle spoke of ὄγκος μείζυς [greater bulk] regarding hail.

Καὶ τὴν ἀπερίστατον ἀμαρτίαν [And the sin which doth so easily beset us]) Most codices have Εὐπερίστατον [easily besetting], and the Syrian and Latin read it thus. And here, as often elsewhere, is ἐξηγητικόν [explanatory]. For it explains what he understands by the burden in this matter, namely sin, by which we are so surrounded that we cannot run. Perhaps he refers to the place in Lam. I. 14, where sins are compared to the thongs of a yoke entangling a man and often casting him down. For Εὐπερίστατον seems to correspond to the Hebrew ישתרגו, where in the Greek it is συνεπλάκησαν [they were intertwined].

By ὄγκον, therefore, one must understand not so much the burden of earthly affairs with Theophylact, but primarily that heavy weight of sins, as the Apostle adds by way of explanation εὐπερίστατον ἀμαρτίαν [the sin which doth so easily beset us], where Grotius rashly placed the word ἀπερίστατον in the text, abandoning the genuine reading, which is approved by most and the most excellent Codices, and is most appropriate, because we are commanded to put off the old Adam, and to lay him aside more and more, even if he is not fully or entirely put off or laid aside until life ends. For this sin is truly εὐπερίστατον, both firmly adhering to us, and surrounding us on every side, and thus never ceasing to weary and solicit us, checking our course, and perpetually provoking us to battle, Gal. V. 17. Jac. I. 14. concerning which the Apostle complains primarily, Rom. VII. ἠ οἰκου̃σα ἐν ἡμι̃ν ἀμαρτία [the sin that dwelleth in us] v. 17. 20. τὸ κακὸν ὑποκείμενον [the evil that is present], v. 21. ὁ νόμος ἐν τοι̃ς μέλεσιν ἡμω̃ν ἀντιστρατευόμενον [the law in our members warring against] the law of our mind, and bringing us into captivity to the law of sin, v. 23. [sic], that depraved concupiscence innate in us, Job. III. 5. which surrounds and encompasses us on all sides like a garment, which hinders the runner, but which can never be completely laid aside in this life. Blessed Chemnitius, Part II, Loc. De peccato Orig. cap. I. περίσασις signifies θλίψιν πανταχόθεν εἰς ἀδυναμίαν εἰσάγυσαν [affliction from every side leading into helplessness], according to Varino, that is, it signifies evils which rush in from every side: therefore εὐπερίσατος ἀμαρτία is the sin which occupies all powers, all members, and the whole man from every side. That ἀποθέμενοι [laying aside], therefore, is to be understood in a certain respect, namely, as regards zeal and effort, and also as regards the dominion of sin, so that we may shake it off and resist its temptations, putting off the old man with his actual concupiscences, lest they break out into action and hinder our course toward the proposed prize; even though we cannot fully lay aside that habitual evil until life itself ends. The Syriac rendered it: The sin which at all times sinks us, as a most heavy weight, unless, of course, we resist it.

Δἰ ὑπομονη̃ς [With patience]) Constantly.

We have previously warned that the constancy or perseverance of faith is noted, and it is clear from the comparison of chapter X. 36, where there is more on this.

Let us run the race that is set before us) ἀγὼν is a noun of genus, under which a course is also included. And it is beautifully said, to run an ἀγὼν, just as to run a labor in Cicero. Not dissimilar: to run a course, to fight a fight.

Estius here criticizes the Vulgate, which rendered it, 'let us run to the contest set before us,' since in the Greek the preposition πρὸς is not present, nor in the Syriac, and he notes with both calculations that it overturns the genuine sense of the Apostle. For the Apostle exhorts, not that they should run to the contest, but that in the stadium which they have entered, they should run through, and fight the contest undertaken through faith, so that they may arrive at the promised prize. See 1 Cor. IX. 21, 26; chapter 4, 7.

Latin:

CAPUT XII. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Ad exemplum veterum fidelium, ad perseve- rantiam in fide hortatur Apostolus, proposito objecto fidei proprio, Christo, ejus cruce & opprobrio, ac consensu ad dextram Dei, & castigationum Paternarum fructu; sectari jubet pacem & sanctimoniam, nec gratiam Dei posthabere, exemplo Esavi. Siquidem non ad montem igne fumantem & terribi- lem, sed ad montem Zion & civitatem Dei, & ad Mediatorem Novi Testamenti accesse- rint, eumq; cælitus loquentem, ac iterum secundum Prophetam, non tantum terram, sed & cælum moventem audiant, & regnum immobile consequantur, adeoque Deo cum timore serviendum sit, utpote qui ignis est inextinguibilis.

Partes duæ sunt: I. Ad perseverantiam in agone proposito exhortatio ad v. 11. II. Ad sanctimoniam & audiendam vocem Domini excitatio ad v. 29.

PARS I. Exhortatio ad perseverantiam in agone proposito.

Vers. 1. Τοιγαροῦν καὶ ἡμεῖς τοσοῦτον ἔχοντες περικείμενον ἡμῖν νέφος μαρτύρων) Cum habeamus tantum agmen te- stium de fidei utilitate. Sic Virgilius, quod dixerat: Facta nube premunt . Mox explicat: Densis catervis. Sic apud Livium est: Rex contra peditum equitumq; nubes jactat. Armorum nu- bes est apud Statium. Solent nubes longo tractu aliæ alias sequi. Par similitudo apud Esaiam LX, 8. Et Ebræi עב, quod nubem significat, dictum volunt ab עבה, quod est densare.

Exhibet jam Apostolus proprium fidei justificæ objectum, quod & respexerint fideles Vet. Testa- menti, quorum nubem proposuerat, & exemplo eorum respicere debeant Ebræi, ut peccato, quoad fieri potest, deposito in agone proposito, fide per- severante decurramus, freti auxilio ejus, qui est ἀρχηγὸς, καὶ τελειωτὴς τῆς πίσεως. Objectum il- lud fidei est idem Jesus, quatenus pro gaudio cru- cem & opprobrium elegit, ac consedit ad dextram in throno Dei. Quem non tantùm ut exemplum sistit, sed imprimis ob meritum, quia nostri causa illa su- stinuit, eumque per fidem veteres respexere, quo- rum exempla adduxerat. Quod hic probe obser- vandum. Docet id 1. Apostoli scopus & propositio, qui in eo fuit inde à cap. X. 19. ut ἐν πληροφορίᾳ πίσεως κατέχωμεν τὴν ὁμολογίαν τῆς ἐλπίδος. 2. Repetita cohortatio cap. Χ. 35. μὴ ἀποβάλητε τὴν παῤῥησίαν. 3. Ejusdem confirmatio, tùm per Haba- cuci oraculum vers. 37. 38. 39. tùm per exempla ve- terum cap. XI. 4. Fidei justificantis descriptio cap. XI. vers. 1. quam exemplis illustravit, cum ra- tione actus & officii proprii, tùm ratione va- rii exercitii. 5. Analoga illatio vel conclusio, quæ uti hic instituitur: ita respondere debet superiori de fide tractationi. Quapropter neces- fum erat, ut inprimis objectum proprium fidei fal- vificæ sistatur: Et Christus, qui Jesus noster, & cu- jus passio præcipuè meritoria fuit, ea ratione pro- ponatur, quemadmodum per fidem & apprehen- sus fuit ab antiquis fidelibus, & apprehendendus est ab omnibus ad salutem. 6. Ὑπομονῆς mentio, quæ ut è collatione cum cap. X. 36. constat, non nudam patientiam, sed patientem vel omnia suffe- rentem in fide perseverantiam, vel fidei constan- tiam cum patientia importat: Sine qua fide ac con- stantia etiam nullus est cursus in agone proposito, 2. Tim. IV. 7. nulla Dei complacentia Ebr. XI. 6. 7. Jesu, quem fide respicere debemus nuncupatio. Vo- catur enim ἀρχηγὸς καὶ τελειωτὴς πίσεως tûm me- riti, tùm efficaciæ ratione. Meriti quidem, quia nisi Christus traditus esset propter peccata nostra, & resuscitatus propter justitiam nostram, vel ut hic Apostolus, nisi nostri causa præ gaudio elegisset crucem & opprobria, & ad dextram Dei consedis- set, nulla esset fides nostra in Christum, utpote cujus hoc proprium esse objectum è Rom. IV. 1. Cor. XV. 3. Es. LIII. 11. cum hisce collatis mani- festum est. Adde quod etiam fidem nobis merue- rit, hoc est merito suo impetrarit & regeneratio- nem & Spiritus sancti donationem, cujus virtute fidem consequimur, Phil. I. 29. Efficaciæ autenî ra- tione Christus etiam ἀρχηγὸς κὴ τελειωτὴς est fidei, quia in nobis & velle & perficere operatur, in- choat, adauget, & consumat fidem nostram, Marc. IX. 24. Luc. XVII. 5. 8. Finis istius intuitus & re- miniscentiæ designatio, ut ὑπομονὴ perseverantia in fide obtineatur, v. 1. qua illi ἀφορῶντες sunt, & ocu- lis mentis intuentur Jesum in passione, eaque con- sequuta gloria v. 2. quia inde fides vitam habet, & ὑπόςασιν suam Gal. II. 20. atque ita in Verbo fidei Jesum sedulo intuentes non evadunt τέκνα ὑποσο- λῆς εἰς ἀπώλειαν, ἀλλὰ πίσεως εἰς περιποίησιν ψυ- χῆς Ebr. X. 39. Quemadmodum & ἀναλογίσασθαι jubentur Ebræi τὸν τοιαύτην ὑπομεμενηκότα ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν εἰς ἀυτὸν ἀντιλογίαν, eo fine, ut confortentur in fide illa in Christum, inque ea patienter perseverent, ἵνα μὴ κάμητε ταῖς ψυ- χαῖς ὑμῶν ἐκλυόμενοι cap. XII. 3. 9. Fidelium militantium in terris cum triumphantibus commu- nio. Ea enim fides, qua prisci fideles aliique in cœlis jam triumphant, constanter in quibusvis tribulationibus retinenda est, quæ scilicet eorum fuit in terris, qui jam per πνέυματα δικαίων τετελειωμένων designantur, v. 23. qui justificati per fidem in sanguine Christi, Rom. III. 25. & consum- mati sunt in æternum unica oblatione Christi ex- piatoria, Ebr. X. 14. ac per fidem in æternum jam vivunt, v. 38. per quam accesserant ad Testamenti Novi Mediatorem Jesum, & sanguinem munda- tionis & expiationis cap. XII. 24. ad quem quia Ebræi etiam accessere, ut ne gratiam illam post- habeant, adeoque in fide illa constanter & pa- tienter perseverent, graviter hic monentur, ut re- gnum, quod acceperunt ἀσάλευτον, non amittant. Omnia ergo collineant ad fidem in Christum, non qualemcunque, sed eam, qua justus quisque vivit, retinendam, nec vel per ἀποsασίαν, ob persecu- tiones & affiictiones, vel per peccata conscientiam onerantia, deperdendam vel amittendam. 10. Te- stium denominatio. Hi enim sancti & fideles mar- tyres dicuntur ob testimonium, quod de fide in Christum & doctrina & vita & martyrio vel sangui- ne suo deposuere quisq; suo tempore ac modo, per quam fidem justificati, Deo probati, & æter- num salvati sunt, quæ non est alia fides, quam quæ ab omnibus Prophetis testimonium accepit,

Act. X. 43. quoque & nos salvamur, & salvati sunt ipsi, Act. XV. 11. Quos nubibus comparari obser- vat B. Gerhardus 1. propter conversationis subli- mitatem, Esa. LX. 8. Phil. III. 20. 2. Propter doctrina foecunditatem, Job. XXXVI. 37. 3. Propter spiritualis consolationis utilitatem. Ut enim nubes refrigerium praestant : Ita etiam exempla sanctorum. 4. Propter effectus qualitatem. Ut à nubibus procedunt pluvia, coruscationes, fulgura : Sic à sanctis doctrina, mira- cula, comminationes. Ut fulgura generantur ex nubium collisione : Sic nubes rationales, si secum lo- quantur, ignem amoris divini & fulgura commina- tionum spiritualium emittunt. Origenes in Jere- miam. Theophylactus : Ne quidem, inquit, multitu- dinem dixit, sed nubem, quod magis est praesenti ma- teria accommodatum. Nam cum hi pressurarum aestu flagrarint, refrigerabit nos, inquit, haec testium multi- tudo, qua undequaque obducimur, tanquam nube- cula aliqua roscida aestuantibus circumfusa.

O̓́γκον ἀποθέμενοι πάντα ) A stadio sumpta similitudo. Ibi qui cursuri sunt, omnia quae oneri esse possunt, depo- nunt. Sic & nos amorem hujus seculi, imò & nostri, Matth. XVI. 24. ὄγκος pondus, ut hic sumpsit Syrus. Sic ὄγκος μείζυς de grandine dixit Aristoteles.

Καὶ τὴν ἀπερίστατον ἀμαρτίαν ) Εὐπερίστατον habent plu- rimi Codices, & sic legerunt Syrus & Latinus. Kαὶ hic ut alibi saepe est ἐξηγητικόν. Explicat enim, quid in hac re per onus intelligat, nempe peccatum, quo ita circumdamur, ut currere non possimus. Respicit forte locum Lam. I. 14. ubi peccata comparantur jugi loris implicantibus homi- nem ac saepe dejicientibus. Videtur enim εὐπερίστατον re- spondere Ebræo ישתרגו, ubi in Graeco συνεπλάκησαν.

Per ὄγκον itaque non tam terrestrium negotiorum sarcinam cum Theophylacto, sed imprimis grave il- lud peccationus intelligere oportet, ut κατ̓ ἐπεξή- γησιν addit Apostolus εὐπερίστατον ἀμαρτίαν, ubi temere in textu Grotius vocem ἀπερίστατον posuit, relicta genuina lectione, plerisque ac pro- batissimis Codicibus probata, maximeque conve- nienti, quia peccatum originale veterem Adamum subinde exuere, ac magis magisque deponere, etsi plene totus non exuatur aut deponatur, nisi cum vita jubemur. Hoc enim peccatum vere est εὐπε- ρίσατον & firmiter nobis adhaerens, & undiquaque nos cingens, & ita nunquam non fatigans nos & so- licitans, cursum nostrum sufflaminans, nosque ad pugnam perpetuo provocans, Gal. V. 17. Jac. I. 14. de quo conqueritur imprimis Apostolus, Rom. VII. ἠ οἰκου̃σα ἐν ἡμι̃ν ἀμαρτία v. 17. 20. τὸ κακὸν ὑποκεί- μενον, v. 21. ὁ νόμος ἐν τοι̃ς μέλεσιν ἡμω̃ν ἀντισρα- τευόμενον τω̃̃ νόμω του̃ νοός ἡμω̃ν, καὶ αἰχμαλωτίζων ἡμα̃ς τω̃ νόμω τη̃ς ἀμαρτίας v. 29. prava illa nobis congenita concupiscentia, Job. III. 5. quae nos un- dique circumcingit & complectitur instar vestis, quae cursorem remoratur, sed quae nunquam peni- tus in hac vita deponi potest. B. Chemnitius par- te II. Loc. De peccato Orig. cap. I. περίσασις significat θλίψιν πανταχόθεν εἰς ἀδυναμίαν εἰ- σάγυσαν, juxta Varinum, hoc est, mala, quae un- dique ingruunt, significat: ergo εὐπερίσατος ἀμαρτία peccatum, quod undique omnes vires, omnia membra, & totum hominem occupat. Illud ergo ἀποθέμενοι secundum quid intelligendum, nimirùm quoad studium & conatum, nec non quoad peccati dominium, ut illud excutiamus, ejusque tentationibus resistamus, deponentes ve- terem hominem cum suis concupiscentiis actua- libus, in nervum ne erumpant & remorentur cur- sum nostrum ad propositum brabejum; etsi ha- bituale illud malum plenarie deponere non possi- mus, nisi cùm ipsa vita. Syrus reddidit: Peccatum quod omni tempore nos demergit, ceu pondus gra- vissimum, nisi scilicet eidem resistamus.

Δἰ ὑπομονη̃ς) Constanter.

fidei constantiam vel perseverantiam notari antea monuimus, & e collatione cap. X. 36. ubi de eo plura, patet.

Τρέχωμεν τὸν προκείμενον ἡμῖν ἀγῶνα) Ἀγὼν nomen Ge- neris, sub quo & cursus comprehenditur. Et pulchre di- ctum, currere ἀγῶνα, sicut decurrere laborem apud Cice- ronem. Non dissimilia : Cursum currere, certare certa- men.

Vulgatam, quæ reddidit, curramus ad proposi- tum nobis certamen, quum in Græco non habea- tur præpositio πρὸς, nec in Syriaco, castigat hic Estius, utroque notat calculo, quod genuinum Apostoli sensum evertat. Hortatur enim Apo- stolus, non ut currant ad certamen, sed ut in stadio, quod ingressi sunt, decurrant, ac certamen susce- ptum per fidem decertent, ut ad brabæum promis- sum perveniant. Vide 1. Cor. IX. 21. 26. cap. 4, 7.

## 12:2
who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross) ἀντὶ τῆς προκειμένης ἀυτῷ χαρᾶς, that is, because of the joy which was present to his mind. ἀντὶ for ἕνεκα. Thus what is ἕνεκα τέτε in Matt. XIX. 5 is the same as ἀντὶ τέτε in Eph. V. 31. Concerning the word προκειμένης see what was said above VI. 18. χαρὰ here is immortal life and supreme power, the reward of Christ's sufferings, John XII. 28; XVIII. 1, 2, 3, 4; Phil. II. 9. That angel seems to have vividly recalled this to Christ's mind, Luke XXII. 4.

Despising the shame) He endured two evils: pains, which are understood under the name of the cross, and the ignominy joined to such a punishment; καταφρονήσας here is to be taken comparatively, not valuing that ignominy so highly that he would wish to withdraw himself from it.

We have already observed that Christ is the author and finisher of faith not only by example, but also by merit. Theophylact says: For if we wish to learn thoroughly how to run through this world through patience, let us look at Jesus no differently than those who become more skilled in some craft are accustomed to look more attentively at the craftsman himself or the worker. Some, as B. Gerhard notes, take the name τελειωτὴς as placed absolutely, and not related to faith, since the verb τελειῶσαι is used several times in this epistle referring to persons, not to things. But Christ is our consummator, because through the offering of the cross he does not consummate and perfect in this life by justifying and sanctifying, but by leading us to consummated blessedness in the future life. But why should we not take the word ἀντὶ in its proper sense, in which it is 'in place of' or 'in stead of'? For Christ did not choose the cross for the sake of his own joy or reward, but since both were προκείμενον, the joy which he had in his hand, and the cross and reproach to which he was to be subjected, he chose ἀυτεξυσίως and by free will, as if by option, to sustain the cross and reproach instead of the joy. B. Luther therefore correctly expressed the sense: 'Who, when he could well have had joy, endured the cross, and did not regard the shame.' The preposition ἀντὶ does not serve the final cause among the Greeks, as 'pro' does among the Latins, but has its proper use in exchange, as in this chapter v. 16, Matt. XX. 28, 1 Tim. II. 6. Compare 1 Cor. II. 9. Theophylact says: He could, he says, neither suffer what he suffered, nor undergo the cross. Seeing that he was entirely immune from sin. Whence he was not liable to death, which he himself also testifies. The Prince of this world comes, he says, and has nothing in me. For he would not have been fastened to the gallows if it had pleased him, which he himself certainly also confessed: saying, I have power to lay down my life, yet he himself sustained the cross. And not death simply, but ignominious and foul, and having despised the confusion and ignominy of this death.

And is set down at the right hand of the throne of God) See above VIII, 5.

We learn from Rom. IV. 25, chapter X. 9, 1 Cor. XV. 3, 4, Heb. V. 8, 9, that it is required for the object of faith not only that Christ was delivered for our sins, but also that he was raised and exalted. Furthermore, the verb ἐκάθισεν has the meaning of the past tense in such a way that it connotes an act still present.

Latin:

ὃς ἀντὶ προκειμένης ἀυτῷ χαρᾶς ὑπέμεινε τὸν σταυρὸν) ἀντὶ τῇς προκειμένης ἀυτῷ χαρᾶς, id est, ob gaudium, quod ipsi animo obversabatur. Ἀντὶ pro ἕνεκα. Sic quod Matth. XIX. 5. est ἕνεκα τέτε idipsum est, ἀντὶ τέτε, Eph. V. 31. De voce προκειμένης vide quæ dicta supra VI. 18. χαρὰ hic est vita immortalis & summa potestas, præ- mium passionum Christi, Joh. XII. 28. XVIII. 1. 2. 3. 4. Phil. II. 9. Hanc videtur Christo vivide in animum re- vocasse Angelus ille, Luc. XXII. 4.

Αἰσχύνης καταφρονήσας) Duo mala toleravit: dolores, qui sub crucis nomine intelliguntur, & ignominiam tali supplicio conjuncta; καταφρονήσας hic comparate sumen- dum, non tanti faciens eam ignominiam, ut ei se vellet subducere.

Non exemplo tantum, sed merito etiam Chri- stum esse ἀρχηγὸν κὰι τελειωτὴν πίστεως jam observa- vimus. Theophylactus: Si enim, inquit, perdiscere volumus per patientiam decurrendi hunc mundum, Jesum haud secus spectemus, ac solent, qui opificii alicujus fiunt peritiores, opificem ipsum vel operan- tem attentius intuentur. Quidam, notante B. Ger- hardo, nomen τελειωτὴς accipiunt ut absolute posi- tum, & non relatum ad fidem, cum verbum τελειῶ- σαι in hac epistola aliquoties usurpatum ad personas non ad res referatur. Est autem Christus noster con- summator, quia per oblationem crucis non consum- mat & perficit in hac vita justificando, & sanctifi- cat, in futura vita ad consummatam beatitudinem nos perducendo. Vocem ἀντὶ autem cur non acci- piamus sensu proprio, quo est loco vel vice? Nam non sui gaudii vel præmii ergo Christus elegit cru- cem, sed quum utrumque esset προκείμενον, gaudi- um, quod habebat in manu sua, & crux atque op- probrium, quibus subjiciendus erat, ἀυτεξυσίως & libera voluntate, veluti per optionem, elegit loco gaudii sustinere crucem & opprobrium. B. Luthe- rus itaque sensum recte expressit: Welcher, da er wohl hätte mögen Freude haben, erduldet er das Creutz, und achtet der Schande nicht. Præposi- tio ἀντὶ non servit causæ finali apud Græcos, ut pro apud Latinos, sed proprium usum habet in com- mutatione, ut hoc capite v. 16. Matth. XX. 28. 1. Tim. II. 6. Conf. 1. Cor. II. 9. Theophylactus: Po- terat, inquit, nec perpeti, quod passus est, nec crucem subire. Quippe qui peccati prorsus esset immunis. Unde nec morti erat obnoxius, quod & ipse testatur. Venit, inquiens, Princeps mundi hujus, & in me non habet quippiam. Non enim si libuisset, patibu- lo fuisset ille suffixus, quod utique & ipsemet fateba- tur: Potestatem habeo, dicens, ponendi animam me- am, crucem tamen ipse sustinuit. Nec mortem sim- pliciter, sed ignominiosam & fœdam, contemptaque mortis hujusce confusione & ignominiam.

Ἐν δεξιᾷ τε τῦ Θρόνυ Θεῦ κεκάθικε) Vide supra VIII, 5.

Ad objectum fidei requiri non modo, quod Christus propter peccata nostra traditus sit, sed quod etiam resuscitatus & exaltatus sit e Rom. IV. 25. cap. X. 9. 1. Cor. XV. 3. 4. Ebr. V. 8. 9. discimus. Cæterum verbum ἐκάθισεν ita habet significatio- nem Præteriti, ut actum adhuc præsentem con- notet.

## 12:3
Vers. 3. Consider now) Ἀναλογίζεσθαι [to consider] is for Xenophon also to weigh in the mind. The same as λογίζεσθαι above XI. 19. The such contradiction endured by sinners against himself) Ἀντιλογίαν [contradiction] is ריב [strife]. For just as εὐλογεῖν [to bless] is also to do good; so ἀντιλέγειν [to contradict] is also to do evil to someone, concerning which we spoke at Luke II. 34. And the word τοιαύτην [such] comprehends the whole history of Christ's passion. That you may not grow weary in your souls, fainting) Κάμνειν [to grow weary] here is to be affected by the weariness of labor. בוקט [to be weary], Job X. 1. Ἐκλύεσθαι [to faint] indeed is רפה [to be slack/weary], Jud. VIII. 15. 1 Sam. XIV. 26. 2 Sam. XVI. 2. 14. XVII. 29. XXI. 16. Isa. XLVI. 2. Weariness brings about tedium.

As if he were saying, with Theophylact as interpreter, such was the vehemence of that kind of contradiction, that it led even to death, which, having been brought upon him by sinners, that is, Jews and Gentiles, he bore along with the harmful and the robbers, being affected by such a foul kind of death. The word ἐκλυόμενοι [fainting] has greater emphasis, lest they fail in spirit, as if dissolved.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Ἀναλογίσασθε νῦν) Ἀναλογίζεσθαι etiam Xeno- phonti est expendere animo. Idem quod λογίζεσθαι su- pra XI. 19. Τὴν τοιαύτην ὑπομενηκότα ὑπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτωλῶν εἰς αὐ- τὸν ἀντιλογίαν) Ἀντιλογίαν ריב. Nam sicut εὐλογεῖν est etiam benefacere; ita ἀντιλέγειν etiam est male cuiquam facere, de quo diximus ad Luc. II. 34. & vox τοιαύτην to- tam passionis Christi historiam comprehendit. Ἵνα μὴ κάμητε ταῖς ψυχαῖς ὑμῶν ἐκλυόμενοι) Κάμνειν hic est tædio laboris affici. בוקט, Job. X. 1. Ἐκλύεσθαι ve- ro est רפה lassari, Jud. VIII. 15. 1. Sam. XIV. 26. 2. Sam. XVI. 2. 14. XVII. 29. XXI. 16. Esa. XLVI. 2. Lassitudo affert tædium.

Quasi dicat, interprete Theophylacto, tam vehe- mens erat istiusmodi contradictio, ut ad mortem usq; traduxerit, quam à peccatoribus, hoc est, Judæis & gentilibus illatam, cum noxiis & latronibus tulit, tam fœdo mortis genere affectus. Verbum ἐκλυόμε- νοι majorem habet emphasin, ne animo deficiant, quasi resoluti.

## 12:4
Vers. 4. You have not yet resisted unto blood) Let it shame you to be exhausted by lighter evils. Those prophets, and then others of the Maccabean times, whom I mentioned above, were dragged partly to capital punishments, partly to tortures. Christ himself suffered death, and indeed that of the cross, you have incurred only losses or dangers to liberty and property. See above X. 33, 34. Struggling against sin) Understand ἁμαρτίαν [sin] here κατ' ἐξοχὴν [by way of eminence] as defection from the Gospel, in which sense we had ἁμαρτάνειν [to sin] above III. 17, X. 26.

It is explained more correctly concerning indwelling sin, and that which solicits to defection, than concerning the sin of the enemies of the Gospel soliciting to defection. For it is introduced, as Blessed Gerhard warns, by prosopopoeia, as an enemy, waging war against us, and soliciting us to defection, to which we ought to resist with all our strength. Sin ἀγωνίζεται [struggles] against us, but we ought to ἀνταγωνίζεσθαι [struggle against] it. Compare Rom. VII. 14 seqq.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Οὔπω μέχρις ἅιματος ἀντικατέστητε) Pudeat vos defatigari levioribus malis. Illi Prophetæ, deinde & alii Maccabaicorum temporum, quorum supra me- minimus, partim ad capitalia supplicia, partim ad tor- menta rapti fuere. Christus ipse mortem, & quidem crucis perpessus est, vos libertatis tantùm & facultatum damna aut pericula incurristis. Vide supra X. 33. 34. Πρὸς τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἀνταγωνιζόμενοι) ἁμαρτίαν hic intel- lige κατ' ἐξοχὴν defectionem ab Evangelio, quo sensu ἁμαρτάνειν habuimus supra III. 17. X. 26.

Rectius de peccato inhabitante, & ad defectio- nem solicitante, quam de peccato hostium Evange- lii ad defectionem solicitantium explicatur. In- troducitur enim, B. Gerhardo monente, per proso- popœiam, tanquam hostis, bellum adversus nos mo- vens, & ad defectionem nos solicitans, cui totis viri- bus resistere debeamus. Peccatum contra nos ἀγω- νίζεται, sed nos debemus ei ἀνταγωνίζεσθαι. Conf. Rom. VII. 14. seqq.

## 12:5
Vers. 5. And have you forgotten the exhortation, which speaks to you as to sons) These things are to be read interrogatively: And that is an excellent admonition, which is Prov. III. 11, it personifies. See a similar one Eph. V. 14.

It can also be taken enunciatively: You act as if you had forgotten the consolation. So much, he says, with Theophylact as interpreter, have you been dissolved into sloth and torpor, that even the forgetfulness of the words has taken hold of you, which exhort to preserve greatness of soul, even though you have not yet suffered any grave and urgent evil. For immense tortures, by reason of excessive bitterness and intolerable pain, are wont to take away even the memory of those things which would contribute in a great way. The word διαλέγεσθαι [to speak] does not signify so much to speak, as to address someone, to converse with someone, which Blessed Gerhard observes against the Papists, who deny that Scripture can be a judge, since it is mute, and does not deliver a sentence between dissenting parties.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Καὶ ἐκλέλησθε τῆς παρακλήσεως, ἥτις ὑμῖν ὡς υἱοῖς διαλέγεται) Legenda hæc interrogative: Et egregie monitum illud, quod est Prov. III, 11. προσωποποιεῖ. Si- mile vide Eph. V. 14.

Potest etiam accipi enunciative: Ita agitis, ac si obliti essetis consolationis. Adeo, inquit, Theophy- lacto interprete, estis in segnitiem & torpedinem re- soluti, ut vel verborum vos oblivio ceperit, ad animi servandam magnitudinem cohortantium, tametsi nondum grave aliquod sitis & urgens malum per- pessi. Solent enim cruciatus immensi præ acerbita- te nimia & dolore intolerabili, vel earum rerum me- moriam tollere, quæ magnum in modum conduce- rent. Verbum διαλέγεσθαι non tam loqui signifi- cat, quam alloqui aliquem, sermocinari cum aliquo, quod observat B. Gerhardus contra Pontificios, qui scripturam negant posse esse judicem, cum sit mu- ta, nec proferat inter partes dissidentes senten- tiam.

## 12:6
Vers. 6. My son, do not despise the discipline of the Lord, nor faint when you are reproved by him; for whom the Lord loves, he disciplines, and scourges every son whom he receives) So it is also in the Greek version of Proverbs, except that for παιδεύει [he disciplines] in some codices there is ἐλέγχει [he reproves]. It appears the interpreters read ויכאב [and he will cause pain] for וכאב [and as a father], which is, and he will cause to be affected by pain. Ἀλγεῖν ποιεῖ [he causes to feel pain], as Job V. 18. For μὴ ὀλιγώρει [do not despise] Aquila put μὴ ἀποδοκίμασον [do not reject], others μὴ ἀπαθὴς [do not be indifferent] אל תמאס [do not despise]. For μηδ' ἐκλύε [nor faint] Theodotion [put] μηδὲ ἐγκακήσῃς [nor be weary] אל תקץ [do not be impatient], some in adversities kick back: others despond in spirit; neither should be done by Christians, to whom the name of sons of God eminently belongs. For if they are truly Christians, such adversities will not happen to them, except by a certain decree of God, and indeed one benevolent toward them, namely that if there is any filth adheres, may be refined, or that they themselves may be rendered better through the exercises of patience. Such castigations are called by the Hebrews יסורי אהבה, the chastisements of love, as has been noted by the learned. Παιδεία, מוסר from יסר, by which word is usually signified the instruction which is done by deeds, for example, by bonds, laws, punishments. Ελέγχειν, הוכים is to rebuke; but they are accustomed, as we have just now said, to transfer those things which are said properly of words to deeds as well. Thus also the word μαστιγοῦν is transferred from the species to the genus. Concerning the noun μασίγων we have spoken at Mark III, 10. Ὅν παραδέχεται: In the Hebrew ירצה, with באשר understood, whom he loves. Παραδέχεσθαι is properly to acknowledge as one's own. Parents are not accustomed to care for those who are disowned, ἀποκηρυχθέντας. That δὲ after μαστιγοῖ is an explanatory conjunction, in which way the Syrian and others have accepted it.

Estius has here those things which confound the Papists themselves. From these and similar sentiments, first conclude that no just man or Son of GOD, of the kind understood here, is or has been in this life without sin. For one is not properly chastised unless sin is found in him. Which collection will be fuller if you understand the chastisement not as one, but frequent and, as it were, assiduous; which other scriptures similar to these declare, as Prov. XIII: He who loves his son, constantly instructs him, in Hebrew, chastises. And Ecclesiasticus XXX: He who loves his son, makes the scourges frequent for him. For why does he make the scourges frequent for him, unless because he makes sins frequent, and offends daily in many things, so that he always has need to say to God: Forgive us our debts. It is to be noted, however, that although chastisements are sent upon the faithful on account of the remnants of sins, they are nevertheless not properly τιμωρίαι or punishments, but παιδείαι or δοκιμασίαι, because they proceed not from an angry, but from a placated and benevolent mind, so that sins are not punished, but that the flesh may be crucified with its lusts, and the faith of the elect may be tested and rendered approved, 1 Pet. I, 7; whence these are by no means drawn by Estius to satisfactory punishments. The Apostle has demonstrated even in this epistle that sins are freely forgiven on account of the expiation or satisfaction performed for us solely by Christ. Nor are calamities of this kind always or to all people sent, but when and where God judges this to be useful and salutary, Rom. VIII, 28. Therefore, as Theophylact says, temptations are brought in by the Lord, but so that they may profit us, not harm us. For for that reason he generally allows us to be tempted, so that our endurance may be tested, and he may finally reward us with crowns.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Ὑἱέ με μὴ ὀλιγώρει παιδείας Κυρίε, μηδ' ἐκλύε ὑπ' ἀυτᾶ ἐλεγχόμενος, ὃν γὰρ ἀγαπᾷ Κύριος, παιδεύει, μασι- γοῖ δὲ πάντα υἱὸν ὃν παραδέχεται) Sic est & in Græca ver- sione Proverbiorum, nisi quod pro παιδεύει in quibusdam codicibus est ἐλέγχει. Apparet Interpretes pro וכאב, quod est tanquam Pater legisse ויכאב quod est, & dolore afficiet. Ἀλγεῖν ποιεῖ, ut Job. V. 18. Pro μὴ ὀλιγώρει Aquila posuit μὴ ἀποδοκίμασον, alii μὴ ἀπαθὴς אל תמאס. Pro μηδ' ἐκλύε Theodotion, μηδὲ ἐγκακήσῃς אל תקץ, qui- dam in adversis recalcitrant: alii animum despondent; neutrum faciendum Christianis, quibus eximie compe- tit nomen filiorum Dei. Nam si vere sunt Christiani, adversa talia illis non evenient, nisi ex decreto quodam Dei, & quidem in ipsos benevoli, nempe ut si quid sordis adhæret, excoquatur, aut ut ipsi per patientiæ exercitia red- dantur meliores. Tales castigationes vocantur ab Ebræis יסורי אהבה amoris, ut notatum eruditis. Παιδεία מוסר à יסר, quo verbo significari solet institutio, quæ factis fit, puta vinculis, legibus, pœnis. Ελέγχειν הוכים est objurga- re; sed solent, ut jam modo diximus, ea quæ de verbis pro- prie dicuntur, ad facta quoque transferri. Sic & verbum μα- στιγοῦν à specie transfertur ad genus. De nomine μασίγων di- ximus ad Marc. III, 10. Ὅν παραδέχεται: In Ebræo ירצה, subaudito באשר, quem diligit. Παραδέχεσθαι est proprie pro suo agnoscere. Abdicatos ἀποκηρυχθέντας parentes cu- rare non solent. Illud δὲ post μαστιγοῖ est copula ἐξηγητικὴ, quo modo accepit Syrus & alii.

Estius hic ea habet, quæ Papistas ipsos conficiunt. Ex his & ejusmodi sententiis primum collige, nullum justum seu Filium DEI, cujusmodi hic intelligitur, in hac vita esse aut fuisse fine peccato. Non enim pro- prie castigatur, nisi in quo peccatum invenitur. Quæ collectio plenior erit, si castigationem intelligas non unam sed frequentem, & quasi assiduam; quod de- clarant aliæ scripturæ his consimiles, ut Prov. XIII. Qui diligit filium suum, constanter erudit eum, Ebraice castigat. Et Ecclesiastici XXX. Qui di- ligit filium suum, assiduat illi flagella. Cur enim assiduat illi flagella, nisi quia ille assiduat peccata, & in multis offendit quotidie, ut semper opus habeat di- cere Deo: Dimitte nobis debita nostra. Notandum tamen, quod etsi ob peccatorum reliquias immittan- tur fidelibus castigationes: non tamen proprie sunt τιμωρίαι vel pœnæ, sed παιδείαι vel δοκιμασίαι, quia non ab irato, sed placato & benevolo animo profi- ciscuntur, ut non puniantur peccata, sed ut crucifi- gatur caro cum concupiscentiis suis, fidesque ele- ctorum probetur, & probata reddatur, 1. Petr. I, 7. unde nequaquam hæc ab Estio ad pœnas satisfacto- rias trahuntur. Peccata gratis remitti propter ex- piationem vel satisfactionem unice à Christo, pro nobis præstitam, etiam hac epistola demonstravit Apostolus. Neque semper aut omnibus etiam calamitates ejusmodi immittuntur, sed quando & ubi Deus hoc utile ac salutare judicat, Rom. VIII, 28. Ingeruntur ergo, Theophylacto dicente, & à Domino tentationes, sed nobis ut prosint, non ut offi- ciant. Nam idcirco tentari plerumque nos sinit, ut & nostram toleramiam periclitetur, & coronis tan- dem condonet.

## 12:7
Vers. 7. Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith) Who went before us in this course by His own example, and will also be its βραβευτὴς (umpire). We have had the word ἀρχηγὸς concerning Christ also above II. 10. Take τελειωτὴς here in the same way as τελειωθῶσι at the end of the preceding chapter.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἀφορῶντες εἰς τὸν τῆς πίστεως ἀρχηγὸν κὰι τε- λειωτὴν Ἰησῦν) Qui nobis exemplo suo hunc cursum præ- iit, idemque ejus erit βραβευτὴς, Ἀρχηγῦ vocem de Chri- sto habuimus & supra II. 10. Τελειωτὴς hic sume, quo- modo fine capitis præcedentis τελειωθῶσι.

## 12:7
Vers. 7. Εἰ παιδείαν ὑπομένετε.] If adversities happen to you. For ὑπομένειν sometimes is nothing other than to endure, as in James I, 12. Thus ὑπομένειν κρίσεως is to plead a case.

Ὡς υἱοῖς ὑμῖν προσφέρεται Θεὸς.] God will treat you in this very matter as a father. Thus προσφέρεται ταχέως ἀυτοῖς, they treat them harshly, in Plutarch's Lycurgus. Our writer drew this word, like many others, from the purer Greeks.

Estius rashly suspects here, in favor of the Vulgate, that the Greek reading is faulty, with εἰ placed for εἰς. For he admits that Theodoret and Theophylact read as the Greek Codices now have it, and the sense is excellent: If you endure discipline, God offers himself as a Father. Nor has Estius himself rarely observed elsewhere the faulty translation of the Vulgate; who, therefore, dares here to amend the authentic text from it? Since it cannot be said conveniently enough εἰς παιδείαν ὑπομένειν, it is more correct to say παιδείαν ὑπομένειν. Or even from these things, says Theophylact, which they thought were an argument that they had been abandoned by God, he shows that these people are a care to God.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Εἰ παιδείαν ὑπομένετε.] Si adversa vobis eveniunt. Nam ὑπομένειν interdum nihil aliud est, quam perpeti, ut Jac. I, 12. Sic ὑπομένειν κρίσεως causam dicere.

Ὡς υἱοῖς ὑμῖν προσφέρεται Θεὸς.] Deus vos in hoc ipso pa- terne tractabit. Sic προσφέρεται ταχέως ἀυτοῖς aspero eos tractant apud Plutarchum Lycurgo. Hanc vocem ut multas alias Scriptor noster hausit è Græcis purioribus.

Temere hic suspicatur in gratiam Vulgatæ Estius Græcam lectionem esse mendosam εἰ pro εἰς posito. Theodoretum enim & Theophylactum fatetur legis- se, uti nunc habent Græci Codices, & sensus est optimus: Si disciplinam sustinetis, offert se Deus ut Patrem. Neque raro observavit alias Estius ipse Vulgatæ vitiosam translationem, qui ergo hic ex ea textum authenticum emendare audet? Quum nec convenienter satis dicatur εἰς παιδείαν ὑπομέ- νειν, rectius παιδείαν ὑπομένειν.
