Vel ex his quidem, inquit Theophylactus, qua illi argumento esse existi- mabant, sese fuisse à Deo idem destitutos, ostendit cu- ra hos Deo esse.

## 12:7
Τὶς γάρ ἐστιν ὑὸς, ὅν ὐ παιδεύει πατὴρ.] A response to a tacit objection. But he allows us to suffer such hard things. Thus the Hebrews interpret the sentiment which is in Prov. XIII, v. 1.

Latin:

Τὶς γάρ ἐστιν ὑὸς, ὅν ὐ παιδεύει πατὴρ.] Responsio ad taci- tam objectionem. Atqui finit nos pati tam dura. Sic inter- pretantur Ebræi sententiam, quæ est Prov. XIII. v. 1.

## 12:8
Vers. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

## 12:8
Εἰ δὲ χωρὶς ἐστε παιδείας, ἧς μέτοχοι γεγόνασι πάντες, ἄρα νόθοι ἐστὲ καὶ ὀυχ' ὑοὶ.] Πάντες, understand, those of whom it was treated in the preceding chapter. But do not take νόθος as born from an unequal mother, but those whom a mother has begotten from adultery and wishes to foist upon her husband, but he rejects them. Philo, in his book on the confusion of tongues, speaking of those who make pleasure the end of life, adds: Τῶν ἐκ πόρνης ἀποκυηθέντων ὀδὲν ὡς ὅι- μη διαφέροντες.

Theophylact's paraphrase has correctly expressed the sense: If, he says, you were devoid of pressures, you would undoubtedly appear adulterine and illegitimate, not sons. For what parent is concerned with instructing or adorning illegitimate sons? You, therefore, since you are oppressed by these evils, this gain certainly comes from them, that you do not spend this life in excess and in luxury, nor indeed otherwise than those more just and most holy men whom we mentioned a little before, who were both called sons of God and were approved. That, therefore, will be clear, and it will not be able to be refuted in any way, that God has offered himself to you as to sons, and likewise has you in his care and mind, lest you turn out depraved and not at all instructed, and that he would disinherit them and cast them out as adulterine. Fathers, says Theodoret as interpreter, are accustomed to instruct true and legitimate sons; and if they see them being whipped by teachers, they do not take it ill. For they see the fruit which is born from correction and discipline. But they despise base-born and illegitimate sons, nor do they deem them worthy of such great care. If, therefore, you also avoid discipline, you are in the number of the spurious.

Latin:

Εἰ δὲ χωρὶς ἐστε παιδείας, ἧς μέτοχοι γεγόνασι πάντες, ἄρα νόθοι ἐστὲ καὶ ὀυχ' ὑοὶ.] Πάντες, intellige, illi, de quibus actum capite præcedenti. Νόθος autem non sume na- tos ex matre impare, sed eos quos mater ex adulterio genuit, & marito vult obtrudere, ille autem rejicit. Philo libro de confusione linguarum loquutus de iis, qui finem vitæ faciunt voluptatem, adjicit: Τῶν ἐκ πόρνης ἀποκυηθέντων ὀδὲν ὡς ὅι- μη διαφέροντες.

Sensum recte expressit paraphrasis Theophyla- cti: Si enim, inquiens, essetis pressurarum expertes, videremini haud dubie adulterini & nothi, non filii. Quis enim parens illegitimis filiis erudiendis ornan- disve studet? Vos itaque, cum his estis malis oppressi, id sane ex his lucri obvenit, ut vitam hanc non effuse & in decore degatis, nec secus quidem, quam justio- res illi & sanctissimi viri, quos paulo ante memoravi- mus, qui & Dei dicti sunt filii & comprobati. Illud igitur perspicuum erit, nec poterit quoquam pacto re- felli, Deum & vobis sese ut filiis obtulisse, habereque item vos curæ & menti, ne pravi evadatis & nihil eru- diti, eosque & exhæredet, & tanquam adulterinos ejiciat. Patres, inquit, Theodoreto interprete, solent veros ac legitimos filios instituere; & si eos videant flagellari à magistris, non ægre ferunt. Vident enim fructum, qui ex castigatione & disciplina nascitur. Nothos autem & illegitimos filios contemnunt, nec tanta eos cura dignos censent. Si ergo vos quoque di- sciplinam vitatis, estis in numero spuriorum.

## 12:9
Vers. 9. Εἶτα, then indeed. Τὺς μὲν τῆς σαρκὸς ἡμῶν πατέρας ἕιχομεν παιδευτὰς, καὶ ἐνεπρεπόμεθα.] Namely, in the first years. Ἐντρέπεσθαι means to revere, Matt. XX, 37. Mark XII, 6. Luke XX, 13. Wisd. II, 10, and elsewhere. Πατέρας τῆς σαρκὸς, that is, those who themselves, being mortal, had begotten us to a mortal life. Καὶ ἐνεπρεπόμεθα, that is, so that we might the more revere them. A Hebraism, such as the other that follows. Οὐ πολλῷ μᾶλλον.] Much more justly. Ὑποταγησόμεθα.] Niphal for Hithpahel, that is, we shall subject ourselves, namely to bearing adversities, he himself so willing it. Τῷ Πατρὶ τῶν Πνευμάτων.] If he who gives spiritual gifts to every Christian, in such a way that he makes us certain of the future life, which will be plainly πνευματικὴ, 1 Cor. XV, 46: he uses the speech of the Hebrews. For they oppose האב הנשמי and האב הרוחני. Otherwise, if you understand the souls of men by Spirits, God is the maker of the flesh as well as of these, Num. XVI, 23, where in the Greek: God, the God of the Spirits and of all flesh.

If, he says, we had chastisers of our flesh, and we readily accepted them (chastising us), shall we not much more be subject to the spiritual Father who chastises us, being altogether certain that his chastisement proceeds from a mind desirous of our salvation, and that it will be profitable to us for a spiritual and heavenly life? However, let not the Calvinists, Estius, or Drejerus impugn traducianism from this passage, nor defend the immediate creation of souls. For he is also the Father of our souls, not only the God of the body, even if he does not create souls immediately, just as the body is not created by him immediately. Nor is there anything here except an opposition between the carnal and the spiritual Father, the one begetting us to this natural life, and the other regenerating us to a spiritual and heavenly life: of whom the former is called the Father of the flesh, the latter the Father of the Spirit, and by the name of flesh is understood the whole man corrupted by sin, and by the name of Spirit the whole man regenerated and renewed by the Spirit, John III, 7. Therefore, the plural noun πνευμάτων is placed either by Enallage for the singular, or it respects the number of spiritual sons, because there are many. Thus Theodoret: He calls them fathers of the flesh who begat us according to the flesh, that is, the authors of our carnal generation, by which we are men prone to the desires of the flesh, and the Father of Spirits is he who regenerated us according to the Spirit, that is, he is the Author of our spiritual generation, by which we are sons of GOD.

And we shall live.] That is, that we may live, namely forever. It is a Hebraism, such as we have just now observed.

There is no need for the particle καὶ to be taken as expressing a purpose. Much less is patience to be established as the cause of life in this way, with Toussain: It is said simply that those who submit themselves to the spiritual Father by enduring chastisements will live, namely through the faith by which they overcome the same, and which is rendered approved through them, 1 Pet. 1:7, the end of which is salvation, as St. Peter says there, v. 9.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Εἶτα tum vero. Τὺς μὲν τῆς σαρκὸς ἡμῶν πατέρας ἕιχομεν παιδευτὰς, καὶ ἐνεπρεπόμεθα.] Nempe in primis annis. Ἐντρέπεσθαι est revereri, Matth. XX, 37. Marc. XII, 6. Luc. XX, 13. Sap. II, 10. & alibi. Πατέρας τῆς σαρκὸς, id est, qui nos mortales ipsi ad mortalem vitam generaverant. Καὶ ἐνεπρεπόμεθα, id est, ut eos hoc magis revereremur. Ebraismus, qualis alter sequetur. Οὐ πολλῷ μᾶλλον.] Multo justius. Ὑποταγησόμεθα.] Niphal pro Hithpahel, id est, sub- jiciemus nos ipsos, nimirum ad ferenda adversa, ipso ita vo- lente. Τῷ Πατρὶ τῶν Πνευμάτων.] Si qui Christiano cuique dat Spiritus dona, ita, ut nos certos faciat vitæ futuræ, quæ erit plane πνευματικὴ, 1. Cor. XV, 46: Ebræorum loquutione utitur. Nam ii opponunt האב הנשמי & האב הרוחני. Alioqui si per Spiritus hominum animos intelligas, Deus tam carnis, quam horum est opifex, Num. XVI, 23. ubi in Græco: Θεὸς, Θεὸς τῶν Πνευμάτων καὶ πάσης σαρκός.

Si Patres, inquit, carnis nostræ habuimus casti- gatores, & prompte suscepimus eos (castigantes) annon multo magis subjiciemur Patri spirituali nos castiganti, certi omnino, quod ab animo salu- tis nostræ cupido ejus proficiscatur castigatio, & ad vitam spiritualem ac cœlestem nobis profutura sit. Ne quicquam autem ex hoc loco Calviniani, Estius, Drejerus impugnant traducem, & propu- gnant immediatam animarum creationem. Nam Pater etiam animarum nostrarum, est, non tantum corporis Deus, etsi animas non immediate creet, uti nec corpus ab ipso creatur immediate. Nec hic quicquam habetur, nisi oppositio Patris carnalis & spiritualis, nos generantis ad hanc vitam natura- lem, & regenerantis ad vitam spiritualem & cœle- stem: quorum ille dicitur carnis, hic Spiritus Pater, & carnis nomine intelligitur totus homo per pec- catum corruptus, nomine Spiritus totus homo per Spiritum regeneratus & renovatus, Joh. III. 7. No- men ergo plurale πνευμάτων vel per Enallagen pro singulari ponitur, vel respicit numerum filio- rum spiritualium, quod plures sint. Ita Theodo- retus: Patres carnis vocat eos, qui nos secundum car- nem genuerunt, id est, autores generationis no- stræ carnalis, qua homines sumus ad desideria carnis propensi, & Patrem Spirituum eum, qui nos regeneravit secundum Spiritum, id est, Autor est generationis nostræ spiritualis, qua sumus filii DEI.

Καὶ ζήσομεν.] Id est, ut vivamus, nempe in perpetuum. Est Ebraismus, qualem jam jam observavimus.

Non opus est, ut particula καὶ τελικω̃ς acci- piatur. Neque multo minus patientia ita vitæ causa constituenda cum Tossano: Simpliciter dici- tur, qui subjiciunt se Patri spirituali castigatio- nes sustinendo, eos victuros scilicet per fidem qua easdem superant, quæque per easdem pro- bata redditur, 1. Petr. I, 7. cujus finis est salus, ut ibi S. Petrus v. 9.

## 12:10
Verse 10.

For they indeed for a few days.] For a short time, of childhood, as we have already said: Their power and care is only temporary, ימים being used by the Hebrews for time, as in Luke 1:5, 7, and often elsewhere. According to what seemed good to them they disciplined.] According to their own judgment, often out of error, sometimes even instilling their own vices as virtues, such as avarice or ambition, of which kind of parents Horace writes in Satire 6 and Juvenal in chapter 5, verse 14. But He for what is profitable.] For our uses. For He neither errs nor is carried away by depraved affections. The same expression is in 1 Cor. 7:35. To partake of His holiness.] That we may become holier day by day after His example. Taken from Lev. 11:44, 19:2. Whence also Peter took it, 1 Epist. 1:16. But that happens chiefly through the gifts of the Spirit, of which mention has already been made.

We add Theophylact's not inconvenient paraphrase: For parents of the flesh cannot discipline us unto perfection, since either the death of these, or the more advanced age of the son, or the stubbornness and perversity of character of the same will often put an end to the chastisement. But God, because He is eternal, can make us more perfect by chastising. And further: For not everything that is the Father's will is profitable to the children. For parents often train them in evil arts. For God brings chastisement upon us so that He may confer something. And not so that He may claim anything for Himself from us, but rather so that He may impart His own holiness, that is, purity, so that we may be rendered more fit to receive His good things. This Divine discipline is therefore nothing else but a certain participation in holiness: which, whoever has attained, benefits not only himself but others. For He turns their souls back to God by deeds and words, not allowing them to be submerged in earthly things. There is therefore a comparison: 1. By reason of imperfection, as to time; 2. By reason of arbitrary chastisement, there less useful, here always useful; 3. By reason of the end, while that looks to a perishable utility in this life, this one looks to the other life, so that we may be prepared for it, or so that we may not be abstracted from it by being devoid of the cross.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Οἱ μὲν γὰρ πρὸς ὀλίγας ἡμέρας.] Ad tempus exiguum, puerilis ætatis, ut jam diximus: Potestas illorum & cura non est nisi temporaria ימים pro tempore usitatum Ebræis, ut Luc. I, 5. 7. & alibi sæpe. Κατὰ τὸ δοκου̃ν αὐτοι̃ς ἐπαίδευσαν.] Pro arbitratu, sæpe ex errore, interdum etiam sua vitia pro virtutibus instillantes, ut avaritiam, ut ambitionem, de qualibus parentibus agit Ho- ratius. Sat. VI. & Juvenalis cap. V. vers. 14. Ὁ δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ συμφέρον.] Ad nostros usus. Nam nec errat, nec pravis affectibus abripitur. Eadem loquutio 1. Cor. 7, 35. Εἰς τὸ μεταλαβει̃ν τη̃ς ἁγιότητος αὐτου̃.] Ut indies san- ctiores fiamus ad ipsius exemplum. Sumptum ex Levit. XI, 44. XIX, 2. Unde & Petrus sumpsit 1. epist. I, 16. Id autem sit præcipue per Spiritus dona, quorum jam facta mentio.

Addimus Theophylacti paraphrasin non incom- modam: Non enim carnis parentes ad perfectionem usque erudire nos possunt, quandoquidem vel ho- rum interitus, vel filii ætas provectior, vel eorundem contumacia sæpe & morum perversitas castigationi factura sunt finem. At Deus quia est sempiternus, perfectiores potest castigando efficere. Et porro: Non enim quodcunque Patris arbitrium conducit & liberis. Nam & ad malas artes hos plerumque erudiunt genitores. Deus namque nobis, ut con- ferat, castigationem inducit. Nec à nobis sibi ut aliquid vendicet, sed potius suam ut impertiat san- ctitatem, hoc est, puritatem, ut ad ejus bona exci- pienda aptiores reddamur. Est igitur nihil aliud Divina hæc eruditio, nisi sanctitatis participatio quæ- dam: quam qui fuerit adeptus, non solum sibi, sed aliis prodest. Animas namque factis dictisque ad Deum retorquet, nihil has sinens terrenis in rebus demergi. Est ergo comparatio 1. Ratione imper- fectionis, quo ad tempus, 2. Ratione arbitrariæ castigationis, illic minus utilis, hic semper utilis, 3. Ratione finis, dum ista in hac vita caducam uti- litatem spectat, hæc vero alteram vitam, ut ad ean- dem præparemur, vel ne ab ea abstrahamur exper- tes crucis.

## 12:11
Verse 11.

And all discipline for the present does not seem to be of joy but of grief.] Bitter roots; sweet fruits, that is, if we have consulted the external senses and the opinions arising from them.

These things are about chastisements, insofar as they are viewed in themselves and from themselves, and according to the judgment of the flesh. But if they are considered with respect to the fruit that will follow, and that the judgment of the Spirit is that they ought to be reckoned not as sorrow, but as joy, we are admonished in James 1:2.

But afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.] For exercise strengthens the habit and adds increments to it. Righteousness is taken more broadly here, not as it is the beginning of sanctification, but in such a way that it embraces all parts of our duty. See what was said at 11:33. Peaceful fruit, that is, grateful. For this is opposed to grief. In this sense we have peaceful in Deut. 2:26, Jer. 12:6, Micah 7:3. And deservedly is the fruit grateful, which brings tranquility to the conscience, Rom. 5:1. You have the verb to exercise also in 1 Tim. 4:7 and above in verse 14.

What does it mean, asks Theophylact, when he says most peaceful? Surely not turbulent, but sweet and gentle. For he who is affected by sorrow,

and is disturbed in mind, it is necessary: But he who is in joy both attains gentleness and is more tranquil. The fruit of righteousness is understood either as Divine, as Theophylact explained. For God, since He is undoubtedly more righteous than those who are affected by sorrow and evils in this life, is going to bring rest in the future. Compare 2 Thess. 1:6. Or it is understood of our righteousness, and indeed either of imputed righteousness; because works of piety or holiness overflow from it as fruits: or of begun righteousness, because chastisement produces righteousness or holiness as a fruit. But the explanation concerning our righteousness is without doubt more convenient, or concerning the fruit of chastisement, which is the pursuit of holiness, so that it may be understood as a genitive of the object, or the fruit of imputed righteousness may be designated, such as are all the fruits of the Spirit, Gal. 5:22, because faith turns out more approved through chastisements, so much so that we even glory in them, Rom. 5:2. Whence Chrysostom and Theophylact observe that chastisement is called γυμνασίαν, because it renders the faithful, like certain athletes, more robust and invincible through the very exercise of patience. Blessed Gerhard wishes the peaceful fruit to be spoken of in comparison to the previous time in which a man is chastised. For while he is afflicted, he is troubled and restless, but afterwards follows the peaceful fruit of righteousness, so that with a composed mind he may congratulate himself on that which was previously troublesome and bitter. But it can be referred primarily to the tranquility of conscience, when we persevere in tribulation in faith, Rom. V, 1. seqq.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Πα̃σα δὲ παιδεία πρὸς μὲν τὸ παρὸν οὐ δοκει̃ χαρα̃ς εἶναι ἀλλὰ λύπης.] Radices amaræ; fructus dulces, videlicet si sen- sus externos & inde nascentes ὑπολήψεις consuluimus.

Hæc de castigationibus, quatenus in se & ex se spectantur, & quoad judicium carnis. Sed si re- spectu sequuturi fructus considerentur, & quod judicium Spiritus non mœrorem, sed gaudium easdem reputari debere, monemur Jac. I, 2.

Ὕστερον δὲ καρπὸν εἰρηνικὸν τοι̃ς δι αὐτη̃ς γεγυμνασμένοις ἀποδίδωσι δικαιοσύνης.] Nam ἄσκησις firmat τὴν ἕξιν, eique incrementa adjicit. Δικαιοσύνη hic latius sumitur, non ut est initium ἁγιασύνης, sed ita, ut omnes officii nostri par- tes complectatur. Vide quæ dicta XI, 33. Καρπὸν εἰρηνικὸν id est gratum. Opponitur enim hoc λύπῃ. Hoc sensu εἰρη- νικὸν habemus Deut. II, 26 Jerem. XII, 6. Michææ VII, 3. Et merito gratus est fructus, qui tranquillitatem affert conscien- tiæ, Rom. V, 1. Verbum γυμνάζειν habes & 1. Tim. IV, 7. & supra V, 14.

Quidnam sibi vult, quærit Theophylactus, cum pacatissimum dicit? Nimirum non turbulentum, sed suavem & lenem. Nam qui mœrore afficitur,

& animo obturbetur necesse est: Qui vero gaudio, & lenitatem assequitur & tranquillior est. Fructus justitia vel de Divina intelligitur, ut Theophylactus exposuit. Deus enim cum justior sit his procul dubio, qui in hac vita mœrore & malis afficiuntur, in futura quietem est allaturus. Cons. 2. Thess. I, 6. Vel de nostra justitia, & quidem vel de imputa- ta; quia ex illa redundant ceu fructus opera pie- tatis vel sanctitatis: vel de inchoata, quia castigatio pariat justitiam vel sanctitatem ceu fructum. Con- venientior autem sine dubio est explicatio de no- stra justitia, sive de fructu castigationis, qui est stu- dium sanctitatis, ut sit genitivus objecti, intelliga- tur, sive fructus justitiæ imputatæ designetur, qua- les sunt omnes fructus Spiritus Gal. V. vers. 22. quia fides probatior evadit per castigationes, adeo, ut in illis etiam gloriemur, Rom. V. vers. 2. Unde Chrysostomus & Theophylactus observant, castiga- tionem vocari γυμνασίαν, quia fideles tanquam athletas quosdam ipso patientiæ exercitio robu- stiores & invictos reddat. Pacatum vero fructum B. Gerhardus dici vult, comparatione prioris tempo- ris, in quo homo castigatur. Dum enim affligitur, turbatur, & irrequietus est, sed postea sequitur pa- catus justitiæ fructus, ut mente composita sibi gra- tuletur de eo, quod antea molestia erat & acerbum. Sed referri potest imprimis ad tranquillitatem conscientiæ, cum perseveramus in tribulatione in fide, Rom. V, 1. seqq.

## 12:12
Vers. 12.

Διὸ τὰς παρειμένας χεῖρας καὶ τὰ παραλελυμένα γόνατα ἀνορθώσατε.] Holy men, addressing the people or the Church, turn themselves now to the best, now to those who are far removed from the best. And there were many of this kind among those Hebrews, as we have already seen. The simile of the hands is taken from laborers, that of the knees from runners. The life and labor of Christians is both a race. The expression is taken from Isaiah 35, verse 3, where the Greeks have: ἰσχύσατε χεῖρες ἀνειμένας, καὶ γόνατα παραλελυμένα. But the Hebrew can be rightly translated as we have it here: Ἀνορθώσατε τὰς χεῖρας ἀνειμένας, καὶ τὰ παραλελυμένα γόνατα. For חזק, to strengthen, often governs the Accusative, as Jud. IX, verse 24, XVI, verse 29, Ezech. XXX, verse 25, XXXIV, v. 4, 16, Dan. X, verse 18. That your hands may not be slack, you have also 2 Paral. XV, verse 6. Οὐαὶ καρδίαις δειλαῖς, καὶ χερσὶ παρειμέναις, Sirach II, verse 14. Ὑπόλυσις γονάτων is found in Nahum II, 10.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Διὸ τὰς παρειμένας χεῖρας καὶ τὰ παραλελυμένα γόνατα ἀνορθώσατε.] Viri sancti populum aut Ecclesiam alloquen- tes modo ad optimos, modo ad eos, qui multum ab optimis distant, se vertunt. Et hujus generis multi erant inter illos Ebræos, ut jam vidimus. Manuum similitudo sumpta à labo- rantibus, genuum à currentibus. Christiani vita & labor est & cursus. Sumpta autem loquutio de Esaia 35. vers. 3. ubi Græci habent: ἰσχύσατε χεῖρες ἀνειμένας, καὶ γόνατα πα- ραλελυμένα. Sed Ebræa recte verti possunt, ut hic habemus : Ἀνορθώσατε τὰς χεῖρας ἀνειμένας, καὶ τὰ παραλελυμένα γό- νατα. Nam חזק roborare sæpe Accusativum regit, ut Jud. IX. vers. 24. XVI. vers. 29. Ezech. XXX. vers. 25. XXXIV. v. 4. 16. Dan. X. vers. 18. Ne remittantur manus vestræ, habes & 2. Paral. XV. vers. 6. Οὐαὶ καρδίαις δειλαῖς, καὶ χερσὶ πα- ρειμέναις, Sirach. II, vers. 14. Ὑπόλυσις γονάτων est apud Na- humium II, 10.

## 12:13
Vers. 13.

Καὶ τροχιὰς ὀρθὰς ποιήσατε τοῖς ποσὶν ὑμῶν.] From the Greek of Prov. IV, near the end, you have τροχιὰς for way in the same book of Proverbs II, verse 15, IV, verse 11, V, verse 6, 21. Make the ways straight for yourselves, through which you are to go: פלס, as in Matt. III, 3, that is, take away all impediments to piety. See the remarks on that place in Matthew.

Ἵνα μὴ τὸ χωλὸν ἐκτραπῇ.] He calls the lame part here a member of the body where the nerves have lost some of their vigor, צלע Gen. 32, v. 31, Mich. 4, v. 16, which members, if a journey is made through uneven places, easily slip from their place or are dislocated, which here is ἐκτρέπεσθαι. And the Syrian understood it in this way.

Ἰαθῇ δὲ μᾶλλον.] Which happens sometimes by the very act of walking comfortably, through which heat returns to the nerves. Thus those to whom this epistle is written ought to avoid uneven paths, that is, doctrines mixed from Judaism and Christianity, lest the mind, beginning to grow weary, should fail completely.

These things pertain primarily to the mind to be confirmed in faith, expressed metaphorically, because he does not want the hands of faith to be slack, nor the knees loosened, when one must approach the throne of grace in a time when there is need of help. For the Holy Spirit imposes such strengthening upon the Evangelists of the New Testament, just as he teaches in the subjoined explanation: Say to every faint-hearted one: Be strengthened, do not fear; Behold God will come, Isa. XXXV, 3. Whence Theophylact not incorrectly: Just as if he were haranguing some athletes and contestants, he writes these things to the faithful Jews. And in these he certainly imitates Isaiah here, arguing from the former members that these are resolved in spirit. For hands indeed bear the proof of actions, feet of movement. Therefore, those who are despairing, first the organs of the mind are dissolved, then those of the body, which he exhorts them to lift up, and that they should not despair at all. The things which are subjoined, Theophylact wishes to be said as if to runners, just as the former were to athletes, because he had ordered them to run δι' ὑπομονῆς (through endurance). Καὶ τροχιὰς ὀρθὰς ποιήσατε τοῖς ποσὶν ὑμῶν (And make straight paths for your feet), which is a just measure. From the LXX, Prov. XV, 26. Erasmus rendered: And make, that the steps may be straight for your feet, that is, make straight the steps of your actions, from which indeed Estius rashly concludes the powers of free will, since the discourse is about the reborn and the faithful, for whom it is ἐξαγώνιον (a struggle) to cooperate with the Holy Spirit not by natural but by supernatural powers granted by the Holy Spirit: Ἴνα μὴ τὸ χωλὸν ἐκτραπῇ (Lest that which is lame be turned out of the way): Vulgate: That no one who is lame may wander, which Erasmus refers to morals. But Blessed Gerhard judges this sense to be more congruent; lest those who are weak among you fall away entirely from the faith, and deny Christ, which explanation properly accords with the scope of the Apostle. The discourse, therefore, is not about any kind of limping of steps, but about that which wavers in the path of truth and faith: since the exhortation is directed toward perseverance in the faith. Thus also Theophylact: Lest anyone limping should wander, that is, let no one of you be of a small and intolerant spirit, since you trace your origin from the Jews, who are of this kind. Or lest, forsooth, anyone among you be more inconstant regarding the hope of goods and faith, and walk with oblique and distorted feet. But rather, he says, apply yourselves, so that whatever was maimed and limping in you may return to health, that is, correct it, if there was any diffidence in you at that time. For incredulity cannot reside in one who bears adversities tolerantly.

PART II. Excitation to holiness.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Καὶ τροχιὰς ὀρθὰς ποιήσατε τοῖς ποσὶν ὑμῶν.] Ex Græco Prov. IV. circa finem τροχιὰς pro via habes in eodem Prover- biorum libro II. vers. 15. IV. vers. 11. V. vers. 6. 21. Facite com- planari vobis vias, per quas ituri estis : פלס, ut Matth. III, 3. id est, auferte omnia pietatis impedimenta. Vide dicta ad illum Matthæi locum.

Ἵνα μὴ τὸ χωλὸν ἐκτραπῇ.] Τὸ χωλὸν hic vocat membrum corporis, ubi nervi aliquid de vigore suo perdidere צלע Gen. 32. v. 31. Mich. 4. v. 16. qualia membra, si iter fiat per lo- ca inæqualia facile loco suo excidunt sive luxantur, quod hic est ἐκτρέπεσθαι. Et ita accepit Syrus.

Ἰαθῇ δὲ μᾶλλον.] Quod sit interdum ipsa ambulatione commoda, per quam calor nervis redit. Sic illi, ad quos hæc epistola scribitur, vitare debebant vias inæquales, id est, do- ctrinas ex Judaismo & Christianismo mixtas, ne animus fa- tigari incipiens plane deficiat.

Hæc imprimis ad animum in fide confirmandũ pertinent Metaphorice expressa, quia manus fidei non vult esse remissas, nec soluta genua, cum ac- cedendum ad thronum gratiæ in tempore, quo opus est auxilio. Talem enim confortationem Evangelistis Nov. Test. imponit Spiritus sanctus, quemadmodum explicatione subjuncta docet: Di- cite pusillanimi cuique: Confortamini, nolite timere; Ecce Deus veniet Esa. XXXV, 3. Unde Theophyla- ctus non inrecte: Haud secus ac apud Athletas ali- quos concionaretur & certatores, & Judæis fidelibus ista perscribit. Et in his sane Esaiam hic imi- tatur, arguens à prioribus membris esse hos animo resolutos. Manus siquidem actionum præ- ferunt argumentum, pedes motus. Desperantes itaque, inprimis animi organa dissolvuntur, dein- ceps & corporis, quæ ut attollant, hortatur, & nil prorsus desperent. Quæ subjunguntur, tan- quam ad cursores, ut priora ad athletas dici vult Theophylactus, quia jusserat, δι' ὑπομονῆς currant. Καὶ τροχιὰς ὀρθὰς ποιήσατε τοῖς ποσὶν ὑμῶν, quod metrum justum est. Ex LXX. Prov. XV, 26. Erasmus reddidit: Et facite, ut recti sint gressus pedibus vestris, id est, rectos facite gressus actionum vestrarum, unde vero temere Estius concludit liberi arbitrii vires, quum de renatis & fidelibus sermo sit, quos cooperari Spiritui san- cto non naturalibus sed supernaturalibus viribus à Spiritu sancto donatis ἐξαγώνιον est: Ἴνα μὴ τὸ χωλὸν ἐκτραπῇ: Vulgatus: Ut non claudicans quis erret, quod ad mores refert Erasmus. Sed B. Gerhardus hunc sensum magis congruere cen- set; ne illi, qui inter vos infirmi sunt, à fide penitus excidant, & Christum abnegent, quæ explicatio scopo Apostoli proprie consonat. Sermo igi- tur est non de quacunque gressuum claudicatio- ne, sed de ea, quæ ambigit in semita veritatis, & fidei: Siquidem adhortatio directa sit ad perse- verantiam in fide. Sic & Theophylactus: Ne quis claudicans erret, id est, nemo vestrum fuerit ani- mo pusillo & intoleranti, cum à Judæis ducatis originem, qui istiusmodi sunt. Vel ne scilicet circa bonorum spem & fidem è vobis quispiam sit incon- stantior & obliquis distortisque incedat pedibus. Quin potius itaque incumbite inquit, ut ad sanita- tem redeat quodcunque in vobis mancum fuerit & claudicans, id est, corrigite, si qua inerat vobis ad id temporis diffidentia. Non enim potest in eo, qui toleranter ferat adversa, incredulitas residere.

PARS II. Extitatio ad sanctimoniam.

## 12:14
Ver. 14.

Εἰρήνην διώκετε μετὰ πάντων (Pursue peace with all men).] A softening of the previous statement. You ought indeed to beware of Judaism: yet not to hate the Jews, but to show them all duties of humanity. See Rom. XII, 18. c. XIV, 19. 1. Petr. III, 13. Καὶ τὸν ἁγιασμὸν (And holiness).] A life holy in all things. See Eph. II, 26. This is so, lest those who had absolved them from the law of Moses might believe that a license for living more loosely was granted to them, when on the contrary the discipline of Christ is much holier than the law. Liberty in Christ did not do injury to innocence; the whole law of piety, holiness, humanity, truth, chastity, justice, mercy, benevolence, prudence remains, says Tertullian concerning modesty, who also shortly after: Do we therefore evacuate the law through faith? Far be it, but we establish the law, namely in those things which, although now forbidden by the New Testament, are prohibited by an even more cumulative precept: which he also explains there with many examples.

Οὗ χωρὶς οὐδεὶς ὄψεται τὸν Κύριον (Without whom no one shall see the Lord).] That is, Christ, by the proper locution of the New Testament; but to see Christ presupposes coming to where Christ is, that is, into the highest heaven, namely after the judgment itself, 1. Joh. III, 3. Let those who think it sufficient for our salvation that Christ was holy for us well observe this place.

Now therefore, to the exhortation to perseverance in the faith, according to the custom solemn to the Apostle, are subjoined the precepts of the Christian life, and first indeed in general to holiness in peace with the faithful and mutual excitation to be pursued with diligent zeal, which the word διώκειν (pursue) implies. When you follow, he says, he prescribes that, or if that peace should be far off, that you should grasp it, strive earnestly, says Theophylact. Conf. Rom. XII, 18. 2. Corinth. VII, 1. Therefore, it does not appear that a softening of the sentence is held here, just as no such thing occurs in the parallel passages. Even if the Apostle had ordered the avoidance of the mixture of Jewish and Christian doctrine, it could not be concluded that all conversation with the Jews was therefore to be avoided. A distinction must therefore be made here rather between political and external peace, and ecclesiastical and internal, worldly or civil communion and mystical and spiritual. The former can be cultivated μετὰ πάντων (with all men), yet so that we do not communicate in the sins of others; but the latter ought not to be cultivated with those who dissent in the foundation of the faith, so that I may thus be rendered a participant in their doctrine through such μετοχὴν (participation) or κοινωνίαν (communion), 2. Cor. VI. ver. 16. 2. Joh. ver. 10. Also alien is that admonition of Grotius, that those who think it sufficient for our salvation that Christ was holy for us, or the justice and obedience of Christ, ought to observe this place well. For this is the very sentiment of the Apostle, that by the obedience of one Christ we are constituted just, Rom. V, 18. That Christ is made unto us justice and sanctification, 1. Cor. I, 30. that by the grace of God we are saved through faith without works, Ephef. II. ver. 8. that the just shall live by faith, Ebr. X. ver. 38. To which indeed this aphorism does not in the least conflict. For although no one will see Christ without holiness by the blessed vision, yet holiness does nothing for justification or salvation, nor is it required for obtaining the same besides faith. Which sentiment of the Pseudo-Apostles the Apostles condemned in the Jerusalem council, and concluded that we are saved solely by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, Act. XV, 11. To the Calixtines, who with the Papists, from the words of the Apostle, οὗ χωρὶς οὐδεὶς ὄψεται τὸν κύριον (without whom no one shall see the Lord), without whom no one shall see not God, as the Vulgate, but the Lord according to the authentic text, by which name Christ is accustomed to be understood, gather that good works are necessary for salvation, in the Calixtine-Heretical Harmony the answer is given: Here we only subjoin the solution of Blessed Gerhard, whose authority they are accustomed to abuse in this cause: The quality of those who are to see God is described in this place, but not the merit of the beatific vision. In those who are to see God beatifically, holiness is absolutely required. For where there is no holiness, there is no true faith either. We add for the same reason the declaration of the blessed Höpfner, although somewhat lengthy, so that the Innovators may no longer appeal to his consent; the place is disp. L. de Justif. pages 16, 17. In the third pair (we are saved without works, & works are necessary for the salvation of souls) we acknowledge the former statement as our own: We are justified and saved by faith alone without works, because both the salvation of grace and the salvation of glory is the end of justification. But as regards the other statement; it is said ambiguously that good works are necessary for salvation, either improperly regarding the mere precedence of order, by which works are required in those who are to be saved: or properly regarding a certain manner of causing in the act of salvation. The former sense notes that works indeed necessarily cohere with saving faith, which is shown through them: Yet they do not pertain to the essence of salvation, but describe the subject of salvation by a sign preceding salvation. And thus works are necessary not for salvation, but before salvation in those who are saved. For that is properly necessary for salvation which is a cause, effecting salvation, or an instrument through which the saving righteousness of CHRIST is apprehended, so that salvation may exist and be obtained. Neither applies to works, because faith alone is the medium ἀντιληπτικὸν, but those works are the fruits of saving faith: Much less, however, are they a cause either effecting, or meriting, or applying and assisting salvation, which the Papists wish to signify by the use of this statement, but only an antecedent mark of those to be saved, and they describe the subject of salvation, according to the saying Heb. XII. verse 14. Without holiness no one will see God, that is, no one through faith in Christ will be saved without the fruits of faith, because where there are no fruits of faith, there is not faith itself, through which we are saved. And in this But the Papists and Anabaptists accept the same properly, while they wish to insinuate their error concerning the efficiency of salvation through works into the minds of men. Wherefore blessed Luther, to avoid the danger of seduction, expressly rejects that proposition in Chapter XXII of Genesis, as also in the disputation held in the year 38, and Chapter I of Galatians. And when the Münsterites were refuting that proposition: Faith saves without good works, and were substituting this one: Faith saves, but not without good works, Urbanus Regius adorned their refutation, which exists in Volume II. Wittenberg, page 443. In the same place is also held the writing of Dr. Manius, with the preface of blessed Luther, in which this statement is discussed at length. After the death of Luther, this proposition began to be used in the formula of religion, where, to avoid the Samaritan confusion of our religion, there was a caution, lest by its use Papist errors should gradually creep into our Churches. Therefore also the Formula of Concord, article IV, first antithesis, demonstrated the suspicious and damnable use of this proposition with clear reasons. Furthermore, Philip himself in his Response to the Bavarian and Worms Articles, and in the Formula of Concord, confesses that he indeed teaches that good works are necessary, because they are owed by Divine order, but that he does not wish them to be called necessary for salvation or eternal life, lest by this addition merit be understood. What? That Dr. Georgius Major himself, who had sharply defended that proposition in his historical admonition annexed to the first volume of his works, page 1203, constantly denies that he accepted it in the sense which the Papists wish to force upon us, as if good works were the cause or merit of salvation, and furthermore promises that he will no longer use them because of their ambiguity.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Εἰρήνην διώκετε μετὰ πάντων.] Emollitio prioris dicti. Debetis quidem vobis à Judaismo cavere: attamen non odis- se Judæos, sed omnia illis exhibere humanitatis officia. Vide Rom. XII, 18. c. XIV, 19. 1. Petr. III, 13. Καὶ τὸν ἁγιασμὸν.] Vitam per omnia sanctam. Vide Eph. II, 26. Hoc ideo, ne, qui à lege Mosis eos absolverat, ide.. laxius vivendi licentiam sibi fieri crederent, cum contra mul- to sanctior lege sit Christi disciplina. Libertas in Christo non fecit innocentiæ injuriam, manet lex tota pietatis, sanctitatis, humanitatis, veritatis, castitatis, justitiæ, misericordiæ, benevo- lentiæ, prudentiæ, ait Tertullianus de pudicitia, qui & mox: Legem ergo evacuamus per fidem? Absit, sed legem sistimus, scilicet in his, quæ etsi nunc novo testamento interdicta etiam cumulatiore præcepto prohibentur: quod & multis exemplis ibm explicat.

Οὗ χωρὶς οὐδεὶς ὄψεται τὸν Κύριον.] Id est, Christum lo- quutione propria Novi Testamenti, Christum autem videre præsupponit eo venire, ubi Christus est, id est, in cœlum sum- mum, nempe post judicium ipsum, 1. Joh. III, 3. Bene obser- vent hunc locum, qui putant sufficere nobis ad salutem, quod Christus pro nobis sanctus fuit.

Jam ergo exhortationi ad perseverantiam in fide, pro more Apostolo solenni, subjunguntur præcepta vitæ Christianæ, & primum quidem in ge- nere ad sanctimoniam in pace cum fidelibus mu- tuaque excitatione studio sedulo sectandam, quod verbum διώκειν infert. Cum sequimini, in- quit, illud præscribit, vel si longe pax illa abfuerit, ut hanc comprehendatis, enixe contendite, ait Theo- phylactus. Conf. Rom. XII, 18. 2. Corinth. VII, 1. Emollitionem ergo sententiæ hic haberi, non ap- paret, sicut nec in locis parallelis tale quid occur- rit. Etsiamsi vitare jussisset Apostolus doctrinæ Ju- daicæ & Christianæ mixturam, non tamen ideo vitandam omnem cum Judæis conversationem præcipi, poterat concludi. Distinguendum ergo hic potius inter pacem politicam & externam, & Ecclesiasticam & internam, communionem mun- danam vel civilem & mysticam ac spiritualem. Illa coli potest μετὰ πάντων, ita tamen, ut aliorum pec- cata non communicemus, hæc autem coli non de- bet cum iis, qui in fidei fundamento dissentiunt, quod ita doctrinæ ipsorum participes reddamur per talem μετοχὴν vel κοινωνίαν, 2. Cor. VI. vers. 16. 2. Joh. vers. 10. Aliena etiam est illa commonitio Grotii, quod hunc locum observare bene debeant, qui putant sufficere nobis ad salutem, quod Christus pro nobis sanctus fuit, vel justitiam & obedientiam Christi. Hæc enim est ipsius Apostoli sententia, per unius Christi obedientiam nos justos constitui, Rom. V, 18. Christum nobis factum esse justitiam & sanctificationem, 1. Cor. I, 30. gratia Dei nos sal- vari per fidem sine operibus Ephef. II. verf. 8. justum fide vivere, Ebr. X. vers. 38. Cui vero hic apho- rismus minime refragatur. Nam etsi sine sancti- monia Christum nemo visurus sit beata visione, non tamen ad justificationem vel salutem quic- quam facit, aut ad impetrandam eandem requi- ritur præter fidem sanctimonia. Quam Pseudo- Apostolorum sententiam damnarunt Apostoli in concilio Hierosolymitano, & concluserunt, per gratiam Domini nostri Jesu Christi unice nos sal- vari, Act. XV, 11. Calixtinis, qui cum Pontificiis e verbis Apostoli, ὗ χωρὶς ὐδεὶς ὄψεται τὸν κύριον, sine qua nemo videbit non Deum, ut Vulgata, sed Dominum juxta textum authenticum, quo nomi- ne Christus solet intelligi, colligunt, bona ope- ra ad salutem esse necessaria, in Harmonia Calixti- no-Hæretica responsum est: Hic tantum subjici- mus B. Gerhardi, cujus autoritate abuti in hac causa consuevere, solutionem: Describitur hoc loco qualitas eorum, qui Deum sunt visuri non autem meritum beatificæ visionis. In illis, qui De- um beatifice sunt visuri, requiritur omnino sancti- monia. Ubi enim non est sanctimonia, ibi nec vera fides. Addimus ex eadem causa B. Höpfneri de- clarationem, etsi prolixiusculam, ne amplius ad ejusdem consensum provocent Novatores, locus est disp. L. de Justif. pag. 16. 17. In tertio pari (nos salvamur absque operibus, & opera necessaria sunt ad animarum salutem) priorem enuntiationem agnoscimus pro nostra: Sola fide absque operibus justificamur & salvamur, quia & salus gratia & salus gloriæ finis est justificationis. Quod vero al- teram enuntiationem attinet; ambigue dicitur, bo- na opera esse necessaria ad salutem, vel improprie quoad nudum antecessum ordinis, quo requirun- tur opera in salvandis: vel proprie quoad causandi rationem quandam in actu salvationis. Prior sen- sus notat opera necessario quidem cohærere cum fide salvifica, quæ per illa ostenditur: Non tamen ad sa- lutis essentiam pertinere, sed subjectum salutis describere à signo salvationem antecedente. Atque ita opera non ad salutem, sed ante salutem sunt necessaria in iis, qui salvantur. Ad salutem enim id proprie necessarium est, quod est causa, salutem efficiens, vel organum, per quod salu- tifera CHRISTI justitia apprehenditur, ut salus existat & obtingat. Neutrum operibus conve- nit, quia fides sola est medium ἀντιληπτικὸν, opera vero ista sunt fructus fidei salvificæ: Multo mi- nus autem sunt causa salutem vel efficiens vel promerens, vel applicans & adjuvans, quod Pon- tificii hujus enunciationis usu significare volunt, sed tantum salvandorum antecedens nota, & describunt subjectum salvationis, juxta dictum Ebr. XII. vers. 14. Sine sanctimonia nemo videbit Deum, id est, nemo per fidem in Christum salvus erit sine fructibus fidei, quia ubi non sunt fidei fructus, ibi non est fi- des ipsa, per quam salvamur. Atque hoc impro- prio sensu Philippus eam enuntiationem usurpavit. Pontificii autem & Anabaptistæ eandem accipiunt proprie, dum suum de salutis efficientia per opera errorem volunt animis hominum insinuare. Qua- propter B. Lutherus ad declinandam seductionis pe- riculum ex professo istam propositionem rejicit Cap. XXII. in Gen. ut & in disp. ann. 38. habita & Cap. I. Galat. Cumque Monasterienses, propositionem istam: Fides salvat absque bonis operibus, redargue- rent, & substituerent illam: Fides salvat, sed non absque bonis operibus, refutationem illorum ador- navit Urbanus Regius, quæ extat Tom. II. Witteb. pag. 443. Ibidem & habetur D. Manii scriptum, cum B. Lutheri præfatione, in quo prolixe hæc enuntiatio perstringitur. Post mortem Lutheri promulgata in religionis formula frequentari cœ- pit hæc propositio, ubi ad vitandam Samaritican confusionem nostræ religionis cautio fuit, ne illius usu sensim in nostras Ecclesias serperent errores Pon- tificii. Ideo & Form. Conc. art. IV. antith. pri- ma hujus propositionis suspectum & damnabilem usum luculentis rationibus demonstravit. Quin etiam Philippus in Respons. ad Artic. Bavar. & Wormatiens. Formula Concordia ipse fatetur, se docere quidem, bona opera esse necessaria, quia debita sint ordine Divino, sed nolle ea dici ne- cessaria ad salutem seu vitam æternam, ne hac additione intelligatur meritum. Quid? quod ipse D. Georgius Major, qui propositionem istam acriter propugnaverat in commonefact. histor. to- mo primo operum suorum annexa pag. 1203. con- stanter neget, se illam accepisse eo sensu, quem Pontificii nobis obtrudere volunt, quasi bona opera sint causa vel meritum salutis, & insuper pro- mittat, se propter ambiguitatem illa non amplius usurum.

## 12:15
Verse 15.

Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God.] Supply ᾖ, which particles are often left unsaid, and now it will be left unsaid in 16. Lest there be anyone to whom something is lacking, by which he might be less able to attain grace (that is, eternal life, Rom. VI, 13). Concerning the meaning of the word ὑστερεῖν חסר we spoke above IV, 1. Ἐπισκοπεῖν here is to attend diligently, as 1 Pet. V, 2, and so also Esther II, 11. Isocrates and Xenophon also use it thus.

Not only, he says, with Theodoret as interpreter, take care of your own, but also of one another's, and do not despise him who is weak, and help him who is in need of the assistance of your hands. As he not only commanded each one for himself to pursue holiness, but in communion and Ecclesiastical peace mutually preserved, just as he had commanded in chapter X, verse 14, that they should provoke one another to love and good works, not forsaking the communion: So now he commands the ἐπισκοπὴν, by which not only should each one have regard for himself, but also for his neighbor, lest either he himself, or anyone else, should fail of the grace of God, as the Vulgate says, or as others, lest anyone fall away from the grace of GOD. He said that without holiness we shall not see the Lord. He explains that in this way, not that we seek blessedness through holiness, but that by neglecting the pursuit of holiness, or not having care for ourselves, we fall away from the grace of GOD and perish. That one must take care, lest anyone either lose saving grace by sinning, or neglect good inspirations, or place an obstacle to the grace of GOD. He does not say, lest grace of GOD be lacking to anyone, but lest anyone be lacking to the grace of GOD, because the grace of GOD is ready for all, but it is we who repel the grace of GOD or place a barrier to it.

Lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled.] It appears from Deut. XXIX, 18, that one should read here not ἐνοχλῇ but ἐν χολῇ, and it is necessary to understand ᾖ as in the preceding and following member, and to understand καρπόν after φύουσα. Thus also we have χολὴν πικρίας in Acts IX, 23. It is the custom of the Hebrews to call all poison gall ראש, and everything bitter, which is evil. Lest an evil root produce poison, so that many contract leprosy or another disease. For that is what μιαίνεσθαι means in Leviticus XIII. Thus almost σπιλοῦν in James III, 6. The meaning: Lest an evil thought produce foul works (for thus the Chaldean explains that place in Deuteronomy) by whose example many are corrupted, which in the said place of Deuteronomy is explained proverbially: To add the drunken to the thirsty, concerning which proverb we spoke in the same place. But the writer here understands especially certain harmful dogmas of the Jews. Antiochus 1. Maccabees I, verse 11, is called a root of sin, because he brought forth the worst actions from his own nature. Hermas II, 5, uses the name of bitterness specifically for anger. In the Manuscript in this place it is μιανθῶσιν οἱ πολλοὶ, that is, the common people, who are easily corrupted by the Doctors. See Gal. V, 19.

There is no cause for suspecting corruption of the text, since all the Codices agree, even if in Deut. XXIX, verse 18, ἐν χολῇ is read, provided that the sense of the Apostle remains perfectly consistent for him: Provide, lest anyone as a bitter root germinate upward by bringing forth bitter fruits of false doctrine or of vices, ἐνοχλῇ the Vulgate rendered as hinder, but Augustine more correctly in Sermon XVI on the Words of the Apostle, as molest, others as disturb, or interrupt peace and the pursuit of holiness. That it is not a matter of sin or vices, but of a man disturbing others with bitter and harmful or poisonous fruits, is evident from the Mosaic passage, as also from the reason added: And thereby many be defiled, because by the example and contagion of one, many can be infected both in doctrine and in life, and also from the subjoined example, lest there be any fornicator or profane person, like Esau. Compare 1 Cor. XV, 33.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Ἐπισκοποῦντες μή τις ὑστερῶν ἀπὸ τῆς χάριτος τοῦ Θεοῦ.] Sup- ple ᾖ, quales particulæ sæpe subticentur, & jam nunc retice- bitur 16. Ne quis sit, cui aliquid desit, quo minus gratiam (id est, vitam æternam, Rom. VI, 13.) consequi possit. De signifi- catu verbi ὑστερεῖν חסר diximus supra IV, 1. Ἐπισκοπεῖν hic est diligenter attendere, ut 1. Petr. V, 2. sic & Esther II, 11. Utuntur sic & Isocrates & Xenophon.

Non solum, inquit, Theodoreto interprete, vestrum, sed etiam alter alterius curam gerite, nec eum, qui est infirmus despicite, & ei qui vestræ ma- nus auxilio indiget, subvenite. Ut non solum quemque pro se jussit sanctimoniam sectari, sed in communione ac pace Ecclesiastica mutuo ser- vata, quemadmodum cap. X. vers. 14. præcepe- rat, ut sese invicem provocarent ad charitatem, & opera bona non deserentes communionem: Ita nunc ἐπισκοπὴν præcipit, qua non tantum quisque suiipsius rationem habeat, sed & proxi- mi sui, ne vel ipse, vel quisquam alius gratiæ Dei desit, ut Vulgata, vel ut alii, ne quis ex gra- tia DEI excidat. Sine sanctimonia nos non visuros Dominum dixit. Id explicat ea ratio- ne, non quod per sanctimoniam conquiramus beatitudinem, sed quod negligentes studium sanctimoniæ, vel curam nostri non habentes gra- tia DEI excidamus ac pereamus. Cavendum esse, ne quis vel gratiam salutiferam peccando amittat, vel bonas inspirationes negligat, aut gratiæ DEI obstaculum ponat. Non dicit, ne cui desit gratia DEI, sed ne quis desit gra- tiæ DEI, quia DEI gratia præsto est omnibus, nos autem sumus, qui gratiam DEI repellimus vel obi- cem eidem ponimus.

Μή τις ῥίζα πικρίας ἄνω φύουσα ἐνοχλῇ, καὶ διὰ ταύτης μι- ανθῶσι πολλοὶ.] Apparet ex Deut. XXIX, 18. legendum hic non ἐνοχλῇ sed ἐν χολῇ, & oportet subaudire ut in antece- dente & sequente membro ᾖ, & ad φύουσα subaudire καρπόν. Sic & χολὴν πικρίας habemus Act. IX, 23. Mos est Ebræis, omne venenum fel vocare ראש, & amarum omne, quod malum est. Ne mala radix producat venenum, quod multi lepram aut morbum alium contrahant. Id enim est μιαίνεσ- θαι Levit. XIII. Sic ferme σπιλοῦν Jac. III, 6. Sensus: Ne mala cogitatio producat fœda opera (ita enim illum Deute- ronomii locum Chaldæus explicat) quorum exemplo cor- rumpantur multi, quod in dicto Deuteronomii loco sic ex- plicatur proverbialiter: Ut addat ebrium sitienti, de quo pro- verbio ibidem diximus. Intelligit autem hic scriptor præci- pue noxia quædam Judæorum dogmata. Antiochus 1. Macc. I vers. 11. vocatur ῥίζα ἁμαρτωλός, quia pessimas de suo inge- nio actiones protulit. Amaritiæ nomen specialiter de ira usurpat Hermas II, 5. In Manuscripto hoc loco est μιανθῶσιν οἱ πολλοὶ, id est, plebs, quæ à Doctoribus facile corrumpitur. Vide Gal. V, 19.

Non est causa suspicandi de textus corruptio- ne, quum Codices omnes consentiant, etsi Deut. XXIX. vers. 18. ἐν χολῇ legatur, siquidem sen- sus Apostoli sibi optime constet: Providete, ne quis ceu radix amaricans sursum germinet fru- ctus amarulentos falsæ doctrinæ aut vitiorum proferendo, ἐνοχλῇ Vulgata impediat reddidit, sed rectius Augustinus Serm. XVI. de Verb. Apostol. molestet, alii obturbet, vel interturbet pacem & sanctimoniæ studium. Non de pecca- to vel vitiis agi, sed de homine alios turbante fructibus amarulentis & noxiis vel venenatis è loco Mosaico constat, ut & è ratione addita: Καὶ διὰ ταύτης μιανθῶσιν οἱ πολλοὶ, quia unius exemplo & contagio multi possunt infici tum in doctrina, tum in vita, nec non è subjuncto exem- plo, ne quis sit fornicator aut prophanus, sicut Esau. Conf. 1. Cor. XV, 33.

## 12:16
Verse 16.

Μή τις πόρνος [Lest there be any fornicator]. Supply ᾖ [let there be]. Holy writers are accustomed to add special warnings to general ones, which place and time demanded: and to meet the diseases which they saw arising. Many of the Jewish Masters did not think it a sin if a Jew had relations with a woman who was not an Israelite: because the law of Moses forbids only Israelite women to prostitute themselves. We have shown at 1 Cor. V, 9, 10, 11, chap. VI, 9, Eph. V, 5, 1 Tim. I, 10, that by the word Πόρνος among our writers is signified one who engages in sexual intercourse outside of marriage. That is manifest also here below in chapter XIII, verse 4.

Ἢ βέβηλος ὡς Ἡσαῦ, ὃς ἀντὶ βρώσεως μιᾶς ἀπέδοτο τὰ πρωτοτόκια αὑτοῦ [Or profane like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright]. In which the right of primogeniture was included, and the right of the priesthood. He touches upon those who, for the sake of avoiding loss, were deserting Christian assemblies, in which Christians as priests offer prayers to GOD. See above X, 25. An exchange is also called ἀπόδοσις.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Μή τις πόρνος.] Supple ᾖ. Solent sancti Scriptores gene- ralibus addere monita specialia, quæ locus & tempus exige- bant: & iis, quos surgere videbant, morbis occurrere. Ju- dæorum Magistrorum multi non putabant delinqui, si quis Judæus cum fœmina non Israëlitide rem haberet: quia lex Mosis tantum Israëlitidas prostare vetat. Πόρνος voce apud nostros scriptores significari eum, qui Venere extra conjugi- um utitur, ostendimus ad 1. Cor. V, 9. 10. 11. cap. VI, 9. Eph. V, 5. 1. Tim. I, 10. Manifestum id & hic infra cap. XIII. vers. 4.

Ἢ βέβηλος ὡς Ἡσαῦ, ὃς ἀντὶ βρώσεως μιᾶς ἀπέδοτο τὰ πρωτοτόκια αὑτοῦ.] In quo jure primogenituræ comprehen- debatur & jus sacerdotii. Tangit eos, qui damni vitandi cau- sa conventus Christianos deserebant, in quibus Christiani tanquam Sacerdotes preces DEO offerunt. Vide supra X, 25. Etiam permutatio dicitur ἀπόδοσις.

## 12:17
Vers. 17.

Ἴστε γὰρ ὅτι καὶ μετέπειτα θέλων κληρονομῆσαι τὴν εὐλογίαν [For you know that even afterwards, when he wanted to inherit the blessing]. Namely, that portion of the promised land of the Fathers. Κληρονομῆσαι [to inherit] is to obtain by right of possession. Ἴστε [you know], the history is known to you.

Ἀπεδοκιμάσθη [He was rejected]. He was rejected by his Father, Gen. XXVII, 35, 37, 40. Ἀποδοκιμάζεσθαι [to be rejected] is not to obtain what we wish. The epistle to the Romans, which is attributed to Ignatius, uses it thus.

Μετανοίας γὰρ τόπον οὐχ εὗρεν [For he found no place for repentance]. To find a place for repentance is said by the Hebrews of one who attains that, or at least can attain that, toward which repentance tends. This appears in Job XXVII, 23, and in the Latin Wisdom XII, 10, when compared with what is there in 19, 20. Thus also the Roman jurists say that there is no place for repentance where it is no longer in our power to rescind what has been done. Philo reveals the mystical sense in his allegories: Πολλαῖς γὰρ ψυχαῖς [For to many souls]

wishing to use repentance, God did not permit, but just as if from a back-flow they retreated to the opposite. Although having sought it with tears.] It itself, repentance, that is, its effect, metonymically. See Gen. 28, 39.

Therefore, this reprobation of Esau has nothing to do with the temporal blessing, which he sought from his Father with tears, regarding Esau's eternal reprobation, as Beza himself acknowledges those to be foolish who gather the same from this passage; so far is it from favoring an absolute decree: nor is there any discourse about the repentance of Esau, as if he did not find a place for repentance, even though he shed tears, regarding the fruit before God. But it is about the repentance of Isaac, that even though Esau sought it with tears, he did not find a place for repentance, so that, namely, the parent might repent of the blessing conferred upon Jacob and revoke it. Therefore, this passage provides no support for the Novatians.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Ἴστε γὰρ ὅτι καὶ μετέπειτα θέλων κληρονομῆσαι τὴν εὐλογία αν.] Nempe illam portionem de terra promissa Patribus. Κληρονομῆσαι obtinere jure mancipii. Ἴστε scitis, nota vo- bis historia.

Ἀπεδοκιμάσθη.] Rejectus fuit à Patre Gen. XXVII, 35, 37. 40. Ἀποδοκιμάζεσθαι est non obtinere quod volumus. Uti- tur sic epistola ad Romanos, quæ dicitur Ignatii.

Μετανοίας γὰρ τόπον οὐχ εὗρεν.] Ebræis dicitur pœni- tentiæ locum invenire is, qui id consequitur, aut certe consequi potest, quo tendit pœnitentia. Appa- ret id Job. XXVII, 23. in Latino Sap. XII, 10. collatis, quæ ibidem 19, 20. Sic & Jurisconsulti Romani dicunt, non esse locum pœnitentiæ, ubi non amplius in nostra potestate est id, quod actum est, rescindere. Sensum mysticum in allegoriis aperit Philo: Πολλαῖς γὰρ ψυχαῖς

μετανοίᾳ χρῆσθαι βουληθείσαις, οὐκ ἐπέτρεψεν ὁ Θεὸς, ἀλλ᾽ ὥσπερ ἀπὸ παλιῤῥοίας εἰς τὔμπαλιν ἀνεχώρησαν. Καίπερ μετὰ δακρύων ἐπιζητήσας αὐτὴν.] Αὐτὴν τὴν με- τάνοιαν, id est, effectum ejus, Μετωνυμικῶς. Vide Gen. 28, 39.

Non ergo quicquam hæc reprobatio Esavi quo- ad benedictionem temporalem, quam cum lacry- mis à Patre expetebat pro Esavi æterna reproba- tione fecit, ut Beza ipse eos ineptos esse agnoscit, qui eandem ex hoc loco colligunt; tantum ab- est, ut absoluto decreto faveat: neque de pœni- tentia Esavi sermo est, quasi locum pœnitentiæ, etiamsi lacrymas effuderit, non invenerit quoad fructum penes Deum. Sed de pœnitentia Isaaci, quod etiamsi eam cum lacrymis quæsiverit Esavus, pœnitentiæ tamen locum non invenerit, ut nempe parentem benedictionis in Jacobum collatæ pœni- teret, eamque revocaret. Nihil itaque patroci- natur hic locus Novatianis.

## 12:18
Verse 18. For you have not approached a mountain that can be touched.] He repeats the admonition which we also had above at II, 2. For by how much the Evangelical law with its promises excels the law of Moses, by so much more damnable is its contempt. A mountain that can be touched is here a sensible mountain, which is opposed to an intelligible or heavenly mountain, as will follow shortly. See what we said at Matthew XXVI, 29. The Hebrews approached a corporeal mountain with their bodies, we approach a spiritual one with our spirit. 'That can be touched' for 'touchable' after the manner of the Hebrews, see Gal. II, 11.

The Apostle now renders the reasons for his admonition to be observed, both from the gracious calling of the Hebrews, which he magnificently extols by a comparison instituted with the state of the Israelites when they were called to Mount Sinai: and from the gravity of the punishment if GOD, who spoke to them and who is truly a consuming fire to the ungodly, is spurned. However, that comparison with Chapter II is not to be admitted, because it does not appear at all that a comparison of the promulgation of the law was instituted there: which, however, is in the open here. Rather, it refers to the premonition proposed in verses 15 and 16: that no one ought to repudiate the grace of GOD offered in the Gospel. For he commends this grace to the law, which was proposed in a very severe and terrible manner, opposing the same to it, and by that reason explaining the nature of the Evangelical doctrine concerning the grace of GOD, so that they may be rendered more eager to pursue Christian virtues, since they are no longer under the law, so that their obedience might be servile, but under grace, so that they may henceforth serve GOD with a spontaneous Spirit. Whence the blessed Hunnius makes this inference of the Apostle: The Gospel is a doctrine in all ways more pleasant and lovable than the law. Therefore, it is not to be despised with a profane mind, but piously regarded, and one must live holily according to it. Thus, therefore, the Apostle continues his exhortation, so that he does not cease to illustrate the doctrine which he had delivered concerning Christ, nor does he depart from his custom, which he had observed hitherto in this epistle to the Hebrews, rendering all things sweeter to the Hebrews constituted under the grace of the New Testament by comparison and collation with the Old Testament. The principal members of the collation are these: 1. By reason of place, that the law was promulgated on the earthly and tangible Mount Sinai: the Gospel was delivered on Mount Sion and the spiritual one, in the city of God, the heavenly Jerusalem. 2. By reason of manner, that the law was given in a terrible manner, with fire kindled in darkness and gloom, and a storm, and the sound of a trumpet and the voice of words, which those who heard begged off, because of which Moses himself trembled and was terrified. Whereas, on the contrary, there is nothing of the sort in the Gospel, but all things are sweet and pleasant, with the very blood of Christ, even if it had to be shed, speaking better things, not demanding vengeance, as the blood of Abel once did, but reconciliation with GOD, grace, and life. 3. By reason of the festive assembly, which was at Mount Sinai, of the whole Israelite people and the angelic retinue, but here the Hebrews are said to have approached not only to the assembly of the Church militant on earth, but also of that triumphant in heaven, to myriads of holy Angels, as also to the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, indeed to the Mediator of the New Testament himself.

And with burning fire, and with gloom and darkness, and with a storm, and with the sound of a trumpet and the voice of words.] From the passage in Exodus XIX, where you have in the Greek 'lightnings,' which are here 'storm' and 'cloudy darkness,' and then 'smoke,' which are here 'gloom and darkness,' and 'the voice of a trumpet' and 'fire,' which is here 'burning fire.' Then 'the Lord spoke,' for which here is 'the voice of words,' as also in Deut. IV, 11, where it is also said that the fire was 'up to heaven,' and in the same place is 'gloom,' as also in Deut. V, 22, for which there are 'lightnings' in Exodus. Great storms, which are called 'storms,' are not without lightning. See the descriptions of storms among the poets, as in Virgil: The ether flashes with frequent fires. In the Manuscript, for 'darkness' there is 'gloom' with the same sense.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Οὐ γὰρ προσεληλύθατε ψηλαφωμένῳ ὄρει.] Re- petit admonitionem, quam & supra habuimus II, 2. Quanto enim lex Evangelica cum suis promissis præstat legi Mosis, tanto damnabilior est ejus contemptus. ὄρει ψηλαφωμένῳ est hic ὄρει αἰσθητῷ, quod opponitur ὄρει νοητῷ sive ἐπουρα- νίῳ, ut mox sequetur. Vide quæ diximus ad Matth. XXVI, 29. Accesserunt Ebræi ad montem corporeum corpore, nos ad spiritualem spiritu. ψηλαφωμένῳ pro ψηλαφητῷ more E- bræorum, Vide Gal. II, 11.

Causas jam reddit Apostolus observandæ suæ commonitionis, tum ab Ebræorum gratiosa voca- tione, quam comparatione cum Israëlitarum sta- tu, cum ad montem Sinai vocarentur, instituta, magnifice extollit: tum à pœnæ gravitate, si sper- natur DEUS ad ipsos loquutus, qui vere ignis consumens est impiis. Non autem admitten- da illa cum Cap. II. collatio, quia illic σύγκρισις promulgationis legis institutam esse, minime ap- paret: quæ vero hic in aprico est. Respicitur potius ad præmonitionem vers. 15. & 16. proposi- tam: quod nemo DEI gratiam in Evangelio ob- latam repudiare debeat. Hanc enim gratiam commendat legi, quæ perquam severa, ac ter- ribili modo proposita fuit, eandem opponens, eaque ratione naturam doctrinæ Evangelicæ de gratia DEI explicans, ut eadem alacriores red- dantur ad sectandas virtutes Christianas, si- quidem non amplius sub lege sint, ut servile ipsorum sit obsequium, sed sub gratia, ut spon- taneo Spiritu DEO deinceps serviant. Unde hanc illationem Apostoli facit B. Hunnius: Ev- angelium est doctrina, modis omnibus jucundior & amabilior quam lex. Ergo non profano ani- mo contemnenda, sed pie suspicienda, & san- cte juxta illam vivendum. Ita ergo parænesin suam pergit Apostolus, ut doctrinam, quam tra- diderat de Christo, illustrare non intermittat, nec morem suum migret, quem observaverat hacte- nus in ista ad Ebræos epistola, omnia è συγκρίσει & collatione Veteris Testamenti suaviora Ebræis sub gratia Novi Testamenti constitutis red- dendo. Præcipua autem collationis membra hæc sunt 1. ratione loci, quod lex in monte Sinai ter- reno & contrectabili promulgata: Evangelium in monte Sion & spirituali traditum sit, in civi- tate Dei Hierosolyma cœlesti. 2. Ratione mo- di, quod lex terribili ratione, igne accenso in tenebris & caligine, & procella, & tubæ sono & voce verborum, quam qui audivere, depreca- ti sunt, data sit, ob quam Moses ipse tremuit & perterritus fuit. Quum ex adverso nihil tale in Evangelio, sed omnia suavia & grata sint, san- guine ipso Christi, etsi effundi debuerit, κρείτ- τονa loquente, non vindictam, ut Abelis san- guis quondam, sed reconciliationem cum DEO gratiam & vitam postulante. 3. Ratione conventus Panegyrici, qui ad montem Sinai erat, totius populi Israelitici, & comitatus Angelici, hic vero accessisse dicuntur Ebræi non ad cœtum tan- tum Ecclesiæ in terris militantis, sed etiam in cœ- lis triumphantis, ad myriadas sanctorum Ange- lorum, ut & ad Ecclesiam primogenitorum in cælis consignatorum, imo ad ipsum Mediatorem Novi Testamenti.

Καὶ κεκαυμένῳ πυρὶ, καὶ γνόφῳ καὶ σκότῳ, καὶ θυέλλῃ, καὶ σάλπιγγος ἤχῳ καὶ φωνῇ ῥημάτων.] Ex loco Exod. XIX. ubi habes in Græco ἀστραπὰς, quæ hic θυέλλα & νεφέλην γνοφώδη, & deinde καπνὸς, quæ hic γνόφῳ καὶ σκότῳ, & φωνὴν σάλ- πιγγος & πῦρ, quod hic πῦρ κεκαυμένον. Deinde ἐλάλησε Κύριος, pro quo hic φωνὴ ῥημάτων, ut & Deut. IV, 11. ubi & πῦρ dicitur fuisse ἕως τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, & ibidem est γνόφος, ut & Deut. V, 22. pro quo ἀστραπαὶ in Exodo. Magnæ tempesta- tes, quæ θύελλαι dicuntur, non sunt sine fulgure. Vide descriptiones tempestatum apud Poëtas, ut apud Virgi- lium: Crebris micat ignibus æther. In Manuscripto pro σκότῳ est ζόφῳ sensu eodem.

## 12:19
Verse 19.

Which those who heard begged that the word should not be added to them.] In the Manuscript, 'that it should not be added.' They prayed that God would not add a word further, that is, that He would not henceforth address them with such a terrible sound, Exodus XX, verse 19, Deut. V, 25, 26, 27. So also the Latins: 'Do not add a word any more.' 'To beg off' here is to pray against, soon it is taken otherwise.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Ης οἱ ἀκούσαντες παρῃτήσαντο μὴ προστεθῆναι αὐτοῖς λόγον.] In Manuscripto μὴ προσθεῖναι. Orabant, ne ultra Deus ver- bum adderet, id est, ne posthac eos tam terribili sono allo- queretur Exod. XX. vers. 19. Deut. V, 25. 26. 27. Sic & Lati- ni: Verbum non amplius addas. Παραιτεῖσθαι hic est depre- cari, mox aliter sumitur.

## 12:20
Verse 20.

For they could not endure that which was commanded.] זהר For וזר διαστέλλει is translated, and signifies to command strictly and severely. Κἂν θηρίον θίγῃ τοῦ ὄρους, λιθοβοληθήσεται.] Exod. XIX. verse 13. Everyone who touches the mountain shall die by death, no hand shall touch him. For he shall be stoned with stones, or shot through with a dart, whether it be beast, or man, he shall not live. Where it is to be noted that that λιθοβοληθήσεται is referred by zeugma also to κτῆνος. For even mute animals were accustomed to be stoned. For Deut. XX, 16, where it is about a woman and an animal: Their blood is upon them, by the interpretation of the Sages, stoning is understood. And note where here is θηρίον in the LXX κτῆνος, in the Hebrew it is בְהֵמָה, by which name all animals walking upon the earth are comprehended. This was not the only cause of fear for the Israelites: But truly a huge one from such great severity, which would not spare even beasts.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Οὐκ ἔφερον γὰρ τὸ διαστελλόμενον.] זהר Nam וזר δια- στέλλει vertitur, & significat districte severeque præcipere. Κἂν θηρίον θίγῃ τοῦ ὄρους, λιθοβοληθήσεται.] Exod. XIX. vers. 13. Πᾶς ὁ ἁψάμενος τοῦ ὄρους θανάτῳ τελευτήσει, οὐχ ἅ- ψεται αὐτοῦ χεὶρ. Ἐν γὰρ λίθοις λιθοβοληθήσεται, ἢ βόλι- δι κατατοξευθήσεται, ἐάν τε κτῆνος, ἐάν τε ἄνθρωπος οὐ ζήσε- ται. Ubi notandum illud λιθοβοληθήσεται per πρόζευγμα etiam ad κτῆνος referri. Solebant enim & muta animantia lapidari. Nam Deut. XX, 16. ubi est de muliere & animan- ti: Sanguis eorum super eos, ex interpretatione Sapientium lapidatio intelligitur. Et nota ubi hic est θηρίον in LXX. κτῆνος, in Ebræo esse בְהֵמָה, quo nomine comprehendun- tur omnia animantia super terram gradientia. Non erat hæc sola Israëlitis metus causa: Sed ingens sane ex tanta severita- te, quæ nec bestiis parceret.

## 12:21
Verse 21.

And so terrible was that which was seen.] Τὸ φανταζόμενον is also for Plato the appearance of things presented to the mind. Μωυσῆς εἶπεν, ἔκφοβός εἰμι καὶ ἔντρομος.] It is credible that Moses himself said things similar to what he said in Job IV. 14, where in the Greek: Fear met me and trembling.

That edict indeed had been given three days before the promulgation of the law, yet it contributed very much to the terror of the people, who could easily infer, if even brute animals were to be crushed with stones or pierced with javelins for the mere contact of the mountain, how much heavier a punishment will await men who are about to transgress the words of the law, or even about to approach the mountain without due reverence: If not even the beasts themselves shall touch the mountain with impunity, how will the Israelites themselves endure the voice of the thundering God so terrible; especially because that which was presented was also so terrible—fire, darkness, storm, the sound of the trumpet, the voice of words—that Moses himself, who had been accustomed to converse familiarly with God, was vehemently terrified. Which some gather from the coherence of the sentences in Chapter XIX, verse 19, even if they are not expressly written, nor is there need to admit a tradition. But it had those things, as the Apostle had all things from divine inspiration and Divine inspiration, and by the same he consigned them to letters, and therefore there is by no means a necessity to admit a tradition here. And even if this should be especially admitted in certain things comprehended by the Apostles in the sacred writings, it is of no help to the Papists, or even to the Roman Pontiff himself, because the Apostles were infallible through the immediate illumination of the Holy Spirit in discerning traditions, which the Roman Pontiffs are not, and with the canon of scripture completed by men left no further place for traditions, but commanded the Church with the most grave adjuration to acquiesce in the same as perfect and sufficient. Apoc. XXII, 18. 19. Concerning those symbols external in the promulgation of the law, Theophylact says thus: The fire, he says, was offered there so that the lawgiver might set forth the threatened punishments and immediately strike terror. But the cloud and the darkness prefigured that old testament, that it still remained covered and had not yet been revealed at that time. But the storm stirred up the Hebrews, who were rather slow, so that they might turn their minds to the words of God and the wondrous things. But the trumpet signified that the King and God was present, which same thing will also be in the future at the second coming of Christ. Furthermore: God speaking was heard, so that assurance might be given to the laws already laid down, and they might not believe that they were the words of Moses and of a mortal man. For in God there was a voice that was horrible, sonorous, and thundering, but in Moses it was slender and thin. Whence also, fearing a voice of this kind, they confessed that they did not wish to hear God speaking, and kept saying to Moses, speak thou to us, and let not GOD speak to us. For they could not bear what was being said: That is, what proceeded from the mouth of God, which was terrifying, they could not sustain with their ears. Therefore they offered a cause; that God might appear in the flesh, so that he could be perceived and understood by them. And if a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned: So terrible was that which was seen. This place demonstrates the excellence of the New Testament. For although the Old had nothing which excelled in its own magnitude, nor anything similar by which it might possess this new one, yet it was a source of fear and terror, and so much so that it was not lawful even for beasts to touch the mountain, that is, the brute animals which the people possessed. But since the New contains perfection, it sets forth nothing that is horrible, but in it all things are mild and most pleasant.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Καὶ οὕτω φοβερὸν ἦν τὸ φανταζόμενον.] Τὸ φανταζόμενον etiam Platoni est species rerum objecta animo. Μωυσῆς εἶπεν, ἔκφοβός εἰμι καὶ ἔντρομος.] Credibile est, ipsum Mosen dixisse similia, qualia dixit Job. IV. 14. ubi in Græco: Φρίκη μοι συνήντησε καὶ τρόμος.

Edictum quidem illud triduo ante legis pro- mulgationem datum erat, ad terrorem tamen populi plurimum faciebat, qui facile colligere poterat, si & animantia bruta ob solum montis contactum lapidibus opprimenda aut jaculis con- fodienda, quanto gravior pœna manebit homi- nes verba legis transgressuros, vel etiam citra de- bitam reverentiam monti appropinquaturos: Si nec bestiæ ipsæ impune montem contingent, quo- modo ipsi Israëlitæ vocem Dei tonantis tam terri- bilem sustinebunt; imprimis quia ita terribile erat etiam quod objiciebatur ignis, caligo, procella, tubæ sonitus, vox verborum, ut Moses ipse, qui fa- miliaris cum Deo colloqui consueverat, vehe- menter perterrefactus fuerit. Quod e cohæren- tia sententiarum Cap. XIX. vers. 19. colligunt nonnulli, etsi expresse scripta non sint, neque opus habeant traditionem admittere. Sed habuis- t illa, ut omnia Apostolus e θεοπνευσίᾳ & Di- vina inspiratione, & per eandem consignavit literis, ideoque nullatenus necessum est, hic admittere traditionem. Quæ si etiam maxime ad- mittatur in quibusdam ab Apostolis sacris literis comprehensis, nihil juvat Papistas, aut etiam ipsum Romanum Pontificem, quia Apostoli in- fallibiles erant per immediatam Spiritus sancti ἐλ- λαμψιν in discernendis traditionibus, quales non sunt Pontifices Romani, & absoluto scripturæ ca- none à viris θεοπνεύσοις Ecclesiæ tradito nullum amplius traditionibus locum reliquerunt, sed eo- dem ceu perfecto & sufficiente acquiescere Eccle- siam cum obtestatione gravissima jusserunt. Apoc. XXII, 18. 19. De symbolis istis in legis pro- mulgatione externis Theophylactus ita: Ignis, in- quit, eo offerebatur, ut legum lator indictas præferret pœnas, & terrorem statim incuteret. Nebula vero & caligo testamentum vetus illud præfigurabat, opertum adhuc permanere, necdum fuisse tum tem- poris revelatum. Atqui procella excitabat Ebræ- os, qui tardiores essent, ut Dei dictis & rebus miran- dis intenderent animos. Tuba vero adesse Regem & Deum significabant, quod ipsum erit & in secun- do Christi adventu futurum. Porro: Deus lo- quens exaudiebatur, ut fides latis jam legibus fieret, nec crederent Mosi verba esse & viri mortalis. Deo namque vox inerat horribilis quædam sonora & tonans, Mosi vero gracilis & exilis. Unde & vocem illi hujusmodi reformidantes, Deum se nolle loquentem audire fatebantur, & Mosi dictitabant, loquere tu ad nos, & non DEUS nobis loquatur. Non enim portabant; quod dicebatur: Hoc est, quod à Dei ore prodibat, quod esset horrifonum, ne- quibant auribus sustinere. Causam ergo hi obtule- re; ut Deus appareret in carne, ut percipi posset ab his & intelligi. Et si bestia tetigerit montem, la- pidabitur: Ita terribile erat quod videbatur. De- monstrat hoc loco N. T. excellentiam. Vetus namque etsi nihil haberet, quod sui præcelleret magnitu- dine, nec simile quicquam, quo novum hoc potire- tur, formidini tamen erat & terrori, & adeo, ut nec belluas fas esset montem attingere, id est, bruta animantia, quæ populus possideret. Novum vero cum perfectione contineat, nihil præfert quod horridum sit, sed in eo cuncta sunt mitia & per- jucunda.

## 12:22
Vers. 22.

But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.] You have present in your mind that super-celestial city, of which Jerusalem and Mount Zion within it bore the figure. See what was said above XI, 15. and below XIII, 14. Apoc. III, 2. XXI, 2. 10. And rightly naming Jerusalem, he added the city of the living God. For Jerusalem was also accustomed to be called so. By Zion are to be understood the most eminent places in that heavenly city. See John XIV, 2. and what is said there.

And to the myriads of angels in festive assembly.] It is a preposition, such as in Luke II, 14. A festive assembly is called the gathering of the Israelite people to praise God, Hosea II, 11. ch. IX, 5. Amos V, 21. Ezekiel XLVI, 12. But how much more narrow was that festive assembly than the myriads of thousands of angels praising God, Dan. VII, 10. Apoc. VII, 11. ch. XIX. v. 1. 3. 4. 6.

How did the Hebrews approach Mount Zion? Because through the preaching of the Gospel begun at Jerusalem they were called and gathered to the fellowship of the Church of the New Testament, Luke XXIV, 47, which was also prefigured by Mount Zion and the city of Jerusalem, and was frequently designated by that name in the Old Testament. Theophylact also notes an emphasis in the word you have approached: They indeed approached nothing of the mountain, but stood far off. But you have now approached to this one. You see, therefore, by how great an interval you surpass them. However, there is no reason why we should here exquisitely distinguish which things pertain to the Church militant and which to the triumphant, or believe that they were delivered in that order. For it is viewed as one body and one assembly, so that the excellence of the faithful may be the more declared, because they constitute one assembly with those who triumph in the heavens and with the myriads of holy angels, even if they still war on earth. And therefore both Mount Zion and the city of the living God and the heavenly Jerusalem can be taken collectively and in the aggregate: or if it pleases to refer those things separately to the spiritual assembly of the faithful on earth, and the rest which follow to the heavenly, it is called the heavenly Jerusalem because of its origin and end, because it both descends from heaven and seeks the things that are above; its citizens dwell on earth, but their conversation is in heaven, Phil. II. verse 20. But because in the latter parts mention is made of both the Mediator of the New Testament and the sprinkling of blood, which pertain entirely to the Church in these lands, and the whole description is more pleasant if both the names and those outward appearances are referred to the whole aggregate, we prefer that sense; yet concerning the word you have approached, we observe that the Hebrews did not immediately arrive at the triumphant assembly, but in such a way that they have communion with it, and ought to set for themselves an actual blessed association as their goal, and furthermore that this approach and gathering is not to be understood as irrevocable, as the Calvinists contend—against the most open testimonies and examples of scripture—that the faithful can in no way be excluded from heaven and the heavenly society, but that by the very fact that they are and remain faithful, they belong to the heavenly society, whence the dignity of the calling, conversion, and state of the faithful sufficiently shines forth, which the Apostle wished to place before the eyes of the Hebrews with this illustrious description, lest they themselves be wanting to the divine grace and their own happiness.
