Whence it is clear that it cannot be proven from this place that angels belong to the Church of Christ, which Estius wishes in this place, even if they constitute one city of God with us according to Augustine, book X of The City of God, ch. 7, or even the Apostle himself. For angels are not members of the visible Church, even if they are present in its assembly, 1 Cor. XI, 10, because their external communion consists in the profession of the same faith and the use of the same sacraments; but the internal consists in true and living faith. That Estius says Christ merited by his passion that he himself, as head of all, should be set over both angels and men gathered into one Church, is asserted without scripture; Christ merited nothing for himself, all things for us. Nor did he finally become the head of the Angels after death, but by reason of his Deity he always was, while by reason of his human nature he possessed power over them as to supreme κτῆσιν [possession] in the very moment of his extreme emptying, even though by reason of χρήσεως [use] he emptied himself of the same, nor is Christ called the head of Angels and men for the same reason, since he is head as to us both by reason of ὁμουσίας [consubstantiality] and by reason of the influx of spiritual gifts of grace, by virtue of the redemption and his merit obtained for us: but he can only be called the head of the Angels by reason of plenary dominion and their worship and obedience, Ephes. I. vers. 22. Phil. II. vers. 10. Coloss. II. vers. 10. 1. Petr. III. vers. 22. But that Grotius understands these things solely of the supercelestial Jerusalem, and imagines in the same a certain most eminent place indicated by the name of Sion, drawing Job. IV. vers. 2 to this, that has no foundation in the sacred writings: nor can it be proven from the mansions in the house of the Father, by which only different degrees of glory are designated. Furthermore, the word πανηγύρει [festal assembly] is not to be referred to the preceding things, as by the Vulgate and Ambrose, Book II, on Abel and Cain

Cain chap. 2. done, by the Syrian; likewise also in our German version, but it must be joined according to the received Greek Codices to the following verse, that is, not to the festal assembly of Angels, but to the Church of the firstborn: Since the Greek Codices begin a new verse from there.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

Ἀλλὰ προσεληλύθατε Σιὼν ὄρει καὶ πόλει Θεῦ ζῶντος, Ἱερου- σαλὴμ ἐπουρανίῳ.] Animo præsentem habetis civitatem illam supercœlestem, cujus Jerusalem & in ea mons Sion figuram gessere. Vide quæ dicta supra XI, 15. & infra XIII, 14. Apoc. III, 2. XXI, 2. 10. Et recte Jerusalem nominans addidit urbem Dei viventis. Nam & Jerusalem sic vocari solebat. Per Sio- nem intelligendi loci eminentissimi in cœlesti illa urbe. Vide Joh. XIV, 2. & ibi dicta.

Καὶ μυρίασιν Ἀγγέλων πανηγύρει.] Est πρόθεσις, qualis Luc. II, 14. Πανήγυρις dicitur conventus populi Israëlitici ad Deum laudandum, Osea. II, 11. c. IX, 5. Amos V, 21. Ezech. XLVI, 12. At quanto angustior illa πανήγυρις toties milleno- rum Angelorum Deum laudantium, Dan. VII, 10. Apoc. VII, 11. c. XIX. v. 1. 3. 4. 6.

Quomodo accesserunt Ebræi monti Sion? Quia per prædicationem Evangelii Hierosolymis cœptam vocati & congregati sunt ad consortium Ecclesiæ Novi Testamenti Luc. XXIV, 47. quæ etiam per montem Sion ac civitatem Hierusalem præfigurata, & in Veteri Testamento eo nomine frequenter designata fuit. Etiam in verbo acces- sistis emphasin notat Theophylactus: Illi quidem monti nihil appropinquarunt, sed procul adsta- bant. Vos vero ad hunc jam accessistis. Videtis ergo, quanto hos intervallo præstetis. Non autem est, quod hic exquisitè discernamus, quænam ad Ecclesiam militantem, quæ ad triumphantem per- tineant, aut ordine ea tradita esse credamus. Spe- ctatur enim tanquam unum corpus & unus cœtus, ut eo magis præstantia fidelium declaretur, quod unum cœtum cum illis, qui in cælis triumphant, & myriadibus sanctorum Angelorum universis constituant, etsi adhuc in terris militent. Ideoque & mons Sion & civitas Dei viventis & Hierso- lyma ἐπυράνι@ συνόλως & complexim accipi possunt pro toto illo aggregato: aut si illa placeat ad spiritualem fidelium in terris cœtum seor- sim referre, cætera vero, quæ sequuntur ad cœlestem, ἐπυράνι@ dicitur Hierosolyma pro- pter originem & finem, quia & de cœlo descendit, & quæ sursum sunt, quærit, cives ejus habitant in terris, sed conversatio eorum est in cælis, Phil. II. vers. 20. Sed quia in posterioribus & Mediatoris Novi Testamenti & sanguinis conspersionis mentio fit, quæ ad Ecclesiam in hisce terris omnino spectant, & jucundior est tota descriptio, si ad totum aggregatum, & nomina & προσχήμενα illa referantur, sensum illum præferimus, de voce tamen accessistis ob- servamus, quod Ebræi non immediate jam ad cœtum triumphantem pervenerint, sed ita, ut communionem habeant cum eadem, & actua- lem beatam associationem pro termino sibi fi- gere debeant, quodque præterea accessus ille ac conventus non sit intelligendus irrevocabilis, quemadmodum Calviniani fideles cœlo ac cœ- lesti societate nullatenus excludi posse, contra apertissima scripturæ testimonia & exempla con- tendunt, sed quod eo ipso, qua fideles sunt & manent, ad cœlestem societatem pertineant, unde vocationis, conversionis & status fidelium digni- tas satis elucescat, quam Ebræis, ne gratiæ divi- næ suæque felicitati ipsimet desint ob oculos hac illustri descriptione ponere voluit Apostolus. Unde liquet, non probari posse ex hoc loco, quod Angeli pertineant ad Ecclesiam Christi, quod vult hoc loco Estius, etiamsi unam nobis- cum Dei civitatem constituant secundum Augu- stinum libr. X. de Civ. Dei cap. 7. imo ipsummet Apostolum. Nec enim Angeli Ecclesiæ visibi- lis membra sunt, etsi in cœtu ejusdem præsto sint, 1. Cor. XI, 10. quia illorum externa commu- nio in professione ejusdem fidei, & usu eorun- dem sacramentorum; interna vero in vera ac viva fide consistit. Quod Christum passione sua promeruisse dicit Estius, ut tam Angelis quam ho- minibus in unam Ecclesiam collectis ipse tan- quam caput omnium præficeretur, ἄτεξ γραφῆς asseritur Christus nihil sibi promeruit, omnia nobis. Neque caput Angelorum demum factus est post mortem, sed ratione Deitatis semper fuit, ratione vero humanæ naturæ potestatem in eosdem quoad κτῆσιν supremam, in ipsa exinani- tionis extremæ habuit, etsi ratione χρήσεως eadem sese evacuarit, nec eadem ratione caput dicitur Christus Angelorum & hominum respectu, quum quoad nos caput sit, & ratione ὁμου- σίας & ratione influxus donorum spiritualium gratiæ, virtute redemptionis & meriti sui nobis partorum: Angelorum autem caput tantum dici queat ratione dominii plenarii & cultus ac obse- quii ipsorum Ephes. I. vers. 22. Phil. II. vers. 10. Coloss. II. vers. 10. 1. Petr. III. vers. 22. Quod au- tem Grotius de Hierosolyma supercælesti hæc uni- ce intelligit, inque eadem fingit locum quendam eminentissimum nomine Sionis indicatum, eo trahens Job. IV. vers. 2. id in sacris nullum habet fundamentum: nec à mansionibus in do- mo Patris, quibus diversi gradus gloriæ tan- tum designantur, probari potest. Porro vox πανηγύρει non ad præcedentia referenda est, ut à Vulgata & Ambrosio Libr. II. de Abel & Cain

Cain cap. 2. factum, à Syro; itidem & in Germanica nostra versione, sed conjungenda est juxta rece- ptos Codices Græcos ad sequentem versum, hoc est, non ad Angelorum panegyrin, sed ad Ecclesiam primogenitorum: Quum Græci Codices novum inde versum oriantur.

## 12:23
Vers. 23.

And to the Church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven.] By faith you are united with the Apostles, who are rightly called firstborn here, just as having the firstfruits of the Spirit, Rom. 8:23. Namely, because those were the first regenerated through Christ. But the names of these, even when they were living, were written in the highest heaven, Luke 10:20. that is, even then God held them for heavenly citizens by right, although not yet by possession. See what we have said at Luke 10:20 and Phil. 3:20. The firstborn of the Israelites were written in the earthly register, Num. 1:15, 16, 17. These, however, in the heavenly roll. For ἀπογράφεσθαι is a census word, as we see in Luke 2:1. Ἀπογεγραμμένοι here is the same as נהבו ανακληθέντες ἐξ ὀνόματος, Num. 1:17, and הפקדים, Num. 2:9, 16, the visited. And they are rightly called Church, that is, קהל, not because they were joined in place, as that word is accustomed to be taken in the Old Testament, but because in spirit, which is much greater and worthy of the New Testament.

That the Apostles alone are understood by the Church of the firstborn, who it is rashly asserted are also the only ones designated in Rom. 8:23, is refuted even by the fact that a full description of the universal Church is held here, and that the names of the Apostles were not written in the heavens only, but of all the Elect, and finally that they are not the only firstborn, but all the faithful, inasmuch as they have been made both Kings and Priests by Christ, Apoc. 1:6, chap. 5:10. Nor indeed would the word πανήγυρις, by which a crowd is signified, since that name is derived from a market, befit the assembly of a few Apostles who were still acting on earth. Nor did God hold only the Apostles for heavenly citizens by right, even if not yet by possession, but He holds all the elect also, just as the discourse is not about the Apostles in Luke 10:20, but about the 70 disciples: whose names are said there to be written in the heavens: Theophylact says, he calls the primitive faithful, who as already dedicated to God, became even holier, whose names are written in the book of life; just as the Lord also said to the disciples: Your names are written in the heavens. And since God is the parent of all, of Him also all men universally are children, of whom the primitive (that is, the firstborn, which is held in Greek) will be the faithful, worthy indeed according to predestination to be taken into the children. He does indeed add another interpretation: Or also all believers can be called children: but the firstborn, who have obeyed God and the Father, and are with the same both in word and life, having merited huge gifts: Which is the interpretation of Oecumenius: But that does not deserve approval: just as neither that explanation of some, who understand by the firstborn the saints already reigning in heaven, let alone the holy Angels. Therefore the elect can be called the firstborn of God, because they are the most beloved children of God, and have the right of royal primogeniture and priestly dignity, just as the Israelite people, because of the elect in that people, is called the firstborn Son of God collectively, Exod. 4:22, because we are all one in Christ, Gal. 3:end, all of them also are inscribed in the heavens, in the book of life, Apoc. 13:8, chap. 17:8, chap. 21:28, Dan. 12:1.

And to God the judge of all.] That is, who knows and judges not only acts, but also thoughts, not only of the Jews, but of all the gentiles, as those whom He now embraces with equal care.

And to the spirits of just men made perfect.] Τελειοῦσθαι when it is treated concerning rewards, and that word is referred to the whole man, signifies that life which happens to us after the end of the age. But here it is restricted to the Spirits, namely separated from the body, in the way that word is taken in Luke 23:46, Acts 7:59, in this sense, namely, that the best state is indicated, to which spirits separated from the body can arrive. And this is what he wants, that true Christians are joined by faith and love, not only with the Apostles who live, but also with the Apostles and their coadjutors who have finished this life, such as were James, the son of Zebedee, Stephen, and those of whom he treats below in 13:7. The Hebrews called that best state being put under the leaf of glory, and they thought it happened to Spirits sooner or later, the more or less purified they had departed from this life. And they called the Spirits brought to that degree ἁγίους τετελειωμένους. You have that in Midrash Aneoholam in the section Bereshith, in the Gemara of Hagigah, in Moses Bar-Shemtob in the book of the soul of wisdom (where you have the very words of the perfected just.) And in Moses Maimonides in many places. But it is credible, just as the word עץ or paradise was used by Christ, so these words ἁγίων τετελειωμένων קדושים נכלים were used by this writer in the sense in which they were accustomed to be understood by the Hebrews. The Greek Fathers also understood that it is treated here concerning the spirits of the deceased.

Chrysostom and Theophylact indeed explained this concerning Christ, to whom the Father has given all judgment, John 5:22; but because Christ is dealt with specifically afterwards in verse 24, it is more correctly understood of God the Father, or of the Most Holy Trinity. From the city and the people, he ascends to God, the President of the city, and a just Judge both of those who belong to the city, whom he protects, and of the enemies, whom he strikes down, 2 Thess. 1:5, 6, 7. But so that it may be established more certainly that the church is taken collectively, and that those Elect triumphing in heaven are also included, by whose reception into heavenly glory God proved himself a just judge even then, and by whose example the Hebrews, still struggling with various persecutions, could be greatly encouraged, therefore the mention of the spirits of just men made perfect is added, whom Grotius rashly restricts to the Apostles, who were already triumphing in heaven at that time; nor does he any less prepare some support for the Popish purgatory from the pits of the Jews, whom we willingly leave to the Papists as blind leaders; since the Papal apostasy has long since been demonstrated both to Jewish traditions and to the fables of the Gentiles, which effort the blessed Nicolaus Hunnius made his own especially in his specific treatise on the Apostasy of the Roman Church. However, it is presumed without foundation that the ancient Hebrews in the time of the Apostles thought such things, nor is it consistent with any reason. Rather, that fictitious purgatory and the related error of the Greeks, who deprived the souls of the faithful after death of τελειώσει [perfection] and the vision of God, are refuted by this nomenclature; since it is said indefinitely of the spirits of the just that they are perfected, and not that any still stand in need of purgation. For the just after death (or the spirits of the just) and the perfected are joined and reciprocated: nor can τελείωσις [perfection] be imagined without the blessed vision and fruition of God.

Latin:

Vers. 23.

Καὶ Ἐκκλησίᾳ πρωτοτόκων ἐν ὀυρανοῖς ἀπογεγραμμένων.] Fi- de uniti estis cum Apostolis, qui recte πρωτότοκοι hic di- cuntur, sicut ἀπαρχὴν τῦ Πνεύματος ἔχοντες, Rom. IIX, 23. Nempe quia primi illi per Christum regeniti sunt. Horum au- tem nomina, etiam cum viverent, erant in summo cœlo scri- pta, Luc. X, 20. id est, jam tum illos Deus habebat pro civi- bus cœlestibus jure, etsi nondum possessione. Vide quæ dixi- mus ad Luc. X, 20. & Phil. III, 20. Primogeniti IsraëExpressionitarum scripti erant in matricula terrestri, Num. I, 15. 16. 17. Hi vero in albo cœlesti. Nam ἀπογράφεσθαι vox est censualis, ut vi- demus Luc. II, 1. Ἀπογεγραμμένοι hic idem quod נהבו ανα- κληθέντες ἐξ ὀνόματος, Num. I, 17. & הפקדים, Num. II, 9. 16. οἱ ἐπεσκεμμένοι. Et recte vocantur Ἐκκλησία, id est, קהל, non quod loco juncti essent, sicut illa vox in Veteri Testam. solet accipi, sed quod animo, quod multo majus & dignum Novo Testamento.

Per Ἐκκλησίαν πρωτοτόκων Apostolos tantum intelligi, quos Rom. IIX, 23. etiam solos designari te- mere asseritur, vel inde convellitur, quod hic ple- na habeatur descriptio Ecclesiæ universæ, quodq; Apostolorum nomina non in cœlis tantum descri- pta sint, sed omnium Electorum, nec deniq; illi soli πρωτότοκοι sint, sed omnes fideles, utpote qui & Reges & Sacerdotes facti sunt à Christo Apocal. I, 6. cap. V, 10. Neque conveniat sane Apostolorum pau- corum, qui in terris agebat adhuc, cœtus voci πανή- γυρις, qua frequentia significatur, quum à mercatu nomen illud deducatur. Neque Apostolos tantum Deus pro civibus cœlestibus habebat jure, etiamsi nondum possessione, sed habet etiam electos omnes, quemadmodum nec de Apostolis, Luc. X, 20. sed de LXX. discipulis sermo est: quorum no- mina in cœlis scripta ibi dicuntur: Primitivos, in- quit, Theophylactus, fideles appellat, qui ut Deo jam dedicati, sanctiores etiam evasere, quorum nomina in libro vitæ conscripta sunt; sicut & Dominus dicebat discipulis. Nomina vestra scripta sunt in cælis. Et quoniam Deus est omnium parens, hujus & homines communiter universi sunt filii, cujus & primitivi (id est primogeniti, quod Græce habetur) erunt fideles, digni quidem secundum prædestinationem adsciri in filios. Addit quidem & aliam interpretationem: Vel etiam credentes omnes filii dici poterunt: primo- geniti vero, qui Deo & Patri gesserint morem, & apud eundem sunt cum verbo, tum vita, ingentia dona promeriti: Quæ Oecumenii est interpretatio: Sed ea calculum non meretur: quemadmodum nec illa quorundam explicatio, qui sanctos in cælis jam re- gnantes, nedum Angelos sanctos intelligunt per pri- mogenitos. Electi ergo primogeniti Dei dici pos- sunt, quia maxime dilecti Dei sunt filii, & jus pri- mogenituræ Regiæ & dignitatis Sacerdotalis ha- bent, quemadmodum & populus Israëliticus pro- pter electos in illo populo dicitur Filius Dei pri- mogenitus collective, Exod. IV, 22. quia omnes unum sumus in Christo, Gal. III. ult. omnes etiam illi inscripti sunt in cælis, in libro vitæ, Apoc. XIII, 8. cap. XVII, 8. cap. XXI, 28. Dan. XII, 1.

Καὶ κριτῇ Θεῷ πάντων.] Id est, qui non actus tantum, sed & cogitationes & novit & judicat, non Judæorum tantum, sed gentilium omnium, ut quas pari jam cura complectitur.

Καὶ Πνεύμασι δικαίων τετελειωμένων.] Τελειοῦσθαι cum de præmiis agitur, & ad hominem totum ea vox refertur, si- gnificat vitam illam, quæ nobis post seculi finem contin- get. At hic restringitur ad Spiritus, nempe à corpore sepa- ratos, quomodo ea vox sumitur Luc. XXIII, 36. Actor. VII, 59. hoc scilicet sensu, ut indicetur status optimus, ad quem spiritus à corpore separati pervenire possunt. Et hoc vult, Christianos veros conjunctos esse fide & dilectio- ne, non modo cum Apostolis, qui vivunt, verum etiam cum Apostolis, eorumque coadjutoribus hac vita functis, quales erant Jacobus, Zebedæides, Stephanus & illi, de quibus agit infra XIII, 7. Statum illum optimum Ebræi vocabant ponī sub folio gloriæ, eumque putabant Spiritibus contingere ci- tius aut tardius, quo magis minusque purgati ex hac vita abiissent. Et ad illum gradum perductos Spiritus vocabant ἁγίυς τετελειωμένυς. Habes id in Midrasch Aneoholam in sectione Bereschith, in Gemara Hagigæ, apud Mosen Bar- schemtob in libro animæ sapientiæ (ubi ipsas voces habes ju- storum τετελειωμένων.) Et apud Mosen Maimonidem plu- ribus in locis. Credibile est autem, sicut vocem עץ sive παράδεισον Christo ita has voces ἁγίων τετελειωμένων קדושים נכלים ab hoc Scriptore usurpatas eô sensu, quo ab Ebræis intelligi solebant. De spiritibus defunctorum hic agi intellexere & Græci Patres.

Explicavit quidem hoc de Christo Chrysostomus & Theophylactus, cui Pater dedit omne judicium Joh. V, 22. sed quia de Christo postea v. 24. agitur specialiter, rectius de Deo Patre intelligitur, vel de Sacrosancta Trinitate. A civitate & populo ascendit ad Deum, Præsidem civitatis, & justum Judicem tum eorum, qui ad civitatem pertinent, quos tue- tur : tum hostium, quos prosternit, 2. Thess. I, 5. 6. 7. Ut autem eo certius constet, ecclesiam complexim sumi, & ipsam quoque Electorum in cœlis trium- phantium comprehendi, quorum in gloriam cœ- lestem susceptione Deus sese judicem justum jam tum probavit, & quorum exemplo erigi maxime poterant Ebræi cum variis persecutionibus adhuc conflictantes, ideo subjungitur mentio Spirituum justorum perfectorum, quos temere Grotius restrin- git ad Apostolos, qui tum jam triumphabant in cœ- lis; nec minus purgatorio Papistico aliquod præsi- dium parans à lacunis Judæorum, quos cæcos du- ctores lubenter Papistis relinquimus; cum jam pri- dem demonstrata sit apostasia Papalis cum ad Ju- daicas traditiones, tum ad Ethnicorum fabellas, quam operam imprimis suam fecit B. Nicol. Hun- nius in pecul. de Apostasia Rom. Eccl. tractatu. Ve- teres autem Ebræos Apostoli tempore talia sapuis- se, citra fundamentum præsumitur, nec ulla ratione consentaneum est. Profligatur potius ex hac no- menclatura & purgatorium illud commentitium & error affinis Græcorum, qui animas fidelium post excessum τελειώσει & visione Dei privarunt: quum indefinite de Spiritibus justorum dicatur, quod consummati sint, non autem aliqui adhuc purga- tione egeant. Conjunguntur enim & reciprocan- tur justi post fata (vel justorum spiritus) & consum- mati: nec fingi possit τελείωσις sine beata Dei vi- sione & fruitione.

## 12:24
Vers. 24.

Καὶ διαθήκης νεάς Μεσίτῃ Ἰησοῦ.] Διαθήκης νεάς, that is, eternal, since Moses was the mediator of only a temporary covenant. See above 8:6, 9:15.

Καὶ αἵματι ῥαντισμοῦ κρεῖττον λαλοῦντι παρὰ τὸν Ἀβέλ.] It should be read παρὰ τὸ Ἀβὲλ, as the ancient Greeks and the Syrian read it. Thus we had παρὰ Καῦν for παρὰ τὴν Καῦν above 11:4, and there indeed 'sacrifice' is understood, but here 'blood'. See Gen. 4:10 and above 11:4. The blood of Abel demanded vengeance: but the blood of Christ, that is, his death, through which he entered into eternal life, gives us also the participation of eternal life and eternal goods. This is what Ezekiel 18:32, 33:11 pre-signifies. Moreover, the blood of Christ is called αἷμα ῥαντισμοῦ [blood of sprinkling], because just as those ancients were sprinkled with the blood of victims for carnal holiness, namely so that they could enter into the earthly sanctuary, Num. 19, above 9:13, 19, 21. So we are led to eternal life by the blood of Christ, that is, by the imitation of his sufferings. See what is to be said on 1 Pet. 1:2.

After the Apostle designated the Church as the city of God, its citizens as myriads of angels, the elect inscribed in the register of heaven, and God as the President of the city and people, a just Judge, and specifically to the same also the spirits of just men made perfect he referred, lest he should pass over him, by whose merit the Elect are inscribed in the roll of heaven, and the spirits or souls brought to perfection in heaven after justification on earth, he named the Mediator of the New Testament, and his blood, by which the new Testament of grace was sanctioned, and by which the faithful are sprinkled through faith book of life, Apoc. XIII, 8. by which he also taught that the justified, Rom. III, 25. and the eternally perfected, Ebr. X, 14. To which Mediator the Hebrews approached through faith: through which they were also justified: in which they also expected the most ample promises of the New Testament: and that by the merit of the sprinkling of blood, which was shed for us all for the remission of sins, and with which they were sprinkled through faith, 1. Pet. I, 2. just as the people were sprinkled with typical blood in the Old Testament, Exod. XXIV, 8. Ebr. IX, 18. Grotius empties the power of this blood, having followed the heresy of Socinus, when he says that we are brought to eternal life by the blood of Christ, that is, by the imitation of his sufferings. For the passion of Christ is not only exemplary, but meritorious, by which he was made a ransom for us, Matth. XX, 28. Marc. X, 45. 1. Tim. II, 6. nor can we so imitate his actions or passions, that we may aspire to eternal life by our actions or passions; because we are constituted righteous by his obedience alone, and we obtain salvation only through his passion and death, Rom. IV, 25. cap. V, 18. cap. VI. ult. Gal. III, 20. Eph. II, 8. Ebr. II, 14. Our passions, however, are not worthy of the future glory Rom. IIX, 18. Therefore his blood is introduced as asking for the grace of God, because, namely, we have been reconciled by that blood, Rom. V, 1. For the blood of Christ is said to be better, or adverbially, to speak better, than the blood of Abel: not that the example of Abel is set before us, but that the expiatory power of the blood of Christ is proposed; since Abel the righteous was commemorated in the first place in the catalogue of holy believers, who shed his blood, as the first martyr, to seal the righteousness of faith: now when the Hebrews are said to approach the blood of Christ the Mediator of the New Testament likewise through faith, so that the distinction between the blood of martyrdom and the blood of merit may be clearer, and the passions of martyrs may not be mixed with the satisfactions of Christ, reconciliation is attributed to his blood, and therefore it spoke better than the blood of Abel, which demanded vengeance with its cry, whereas on the contrary the blood of Christ seeks grace, not as that one for a time, but crying out forever in the ears of God.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

Καὶ διαθήκης νεάς Μεσίτῃ Ἰησοῦ.] Διαθήκης νεάς, id est, αἰω- νίας, cum Moses temporarii tantum pacti μεσίτης fuerit. Vi- de supra IIX, 6. IX, 15.

Καὶ αἵματι ῥαντισμοῦ κρεῖττον λαλοῦντι παρὰ τὸν Ἀβέλ.] Le- gendum est παρὰ τὸ Ἀβὲλ quomodo legerunt Græci Veteres & Syrus. Sic παρὰ Καῦν pro παρὰ τὴν Καῦν habuimus supra XI, 4. & ibi quidem subauditur θυσίαν, hic vero αἷμα. Vide Gen. IV, 10. & supra XI, 4. Sanguis Abelis vindictam posce- bat: Sanguis vero Christi, id est, mors ejus, per quam intra- vit ad vitam æternam, dat nobis quoque vitæ æternæ, & æter- norum bonorum participationem. Hoc est, quod præsignifi- cat Ezechiel XVIII, 32. XXXIII, 11. Vocatur autem Christi sanguis αἷμα ῥαντισμῦ, quia sicut veteres illi victimarum san- guine aspergebantur ad carnalem sanctitatem, nempe ut in- gredi possent in sanctuarium terrestre, Num. XIX. supra IX, 13. 19. 21. Ita nos sanguine Christi, id est, imitatione perspef- fionum ipsius perducimur ad vitam æternam. Vide quæ di- cenda 1. Petr. I, 2.

Postquam Ecclesiam ceu civitatem Dei, ejus ci- ves myriadas Angelorum, electos in cœli matricula inscriptos, & civitatis ac populi Præsidem Deum, ju- stum Judicem designavit Apostolus, & peculiariter ad eandem Spiritus justorum perfectorum quoque retulit, ne præteriret eum, cujus merito Electi in cœli album inscripti, & Spiritus vel animæ ad con- summationem in cœlis post justificationem in ter- ris perductæ, Mediatorem Novi Testamenti nomi- navit, ejusque sanguinem, quo novum gratiæ Testa- mentum sancitum, quoque per fidem conspersi fi- deles sunt, quo inscripti in librum vitæ dicuntur, Apoc. XIII, 8. quo & justificatos docuit, Rom. III, 25. & æternum consummatos, Ebr. X, 14. Ad quem Mediatorem accesserunt Ebræi per fidem : per quam etiam justificati erant: in qua Novi Testa- menti promissa amplissima quoque expectabant: idque merito sanguinis aspersionis, qui pro nobis omnibus in remissionem peccatorum effusus, & quo per fidem aspersi erant, 1. Pet. I, 2. quemadmo- dum sanguine typico in Veteri Testamento popu- lus aspersus est, Exod. XXIV, 8. Ebr. IX, 18. Cujus sanguinis vim evacuat Grotius, Socini hæresin se- quutus, cum nos sanguine Christi, id est, imitatione perpessionum ipsius perduci ad æternam vitam ait. Non enim passio Christi exemplaris tantum est, sed meritoria, qua ἀντίλυτρον pro nobis factus est, Matth. XX, 28. Marc. X, 45. 1. Tim. II, 6. neque nos actiones vel passiones ipsius imitari sic possumus, ut sive actionibus sive passionibus nostris ad æternam vitam adspiremus; quia solius ipsius obedientia ju- sti constituimur, &salutem non nisi ejus passione ac morte consequimur, Rom. IV, 25. cap. V, 18. cap. VI. ult. Gal. III, 20. Eph. II, 8. Ebr. II, 14. Nostræ passio- nes vero dignæ non sunt futura gloria Rom. IIX, 18. Idcirco sanguis ejus, ut gratiam Dei postulans, in- troducitur, quia scilicet sanguine illo reconciliati sumus, Rom. V, 1. Dicitur enim sanguis Christi me- lior, vel adverbialiter, melius loqui, quam sanguis Abel: non quod exemplum Abelis nobis sistatur, sed quod sanguinis Christi vis expiatoria propona- tur; siquidem in catalogo sanctorum fidelium prio- ri loco commemoratus sit Abel justus, qui sangui- nem profudit, ceu martyr primus, ad obsignandam justitiam fidei: nunc cum Ebræi ad sanguinem Christi Mediatoris Novi Testamenti itidem per fi- dem dicantur, ut discrimen luculentius sit sangui- nis martyrii, & sanguinis meritorii, nec martyrum passiones Christi satisfactionibus admisceantur, sanguini ejus tribuitur reconciliatio, & propterea melius loquebatur, quam sanguis Abelis, qui vin- dictam poscebat clamore suo, quum contra Christi sanguis gratiam expetat, non ut ille ad tempus, sed in perpetuum clamans in auribus Dei.

## 12:25
Ver. 25. See that you do not refuse him who speaks. ] To refuse is to oppose, as 1. Tim. IV, 7. and elsewhere what he will now say, to turn away from him who speaks, namely God, who commanded us to obey Christ, as he will now say. Speaking for having spoken by a frequent mode of speech.

For if they did not escape.] In the Manuscript they escaped, as Luc. XXI, 36. Rom. II, 3. 1. Thess. V, 3. Namely the punishment. A just recompense, Ebr. II, 2. where the sense is equal.

Him who spoke on earth.] In the Manuscript on earth having refused him who spoke. In whichever way you read him, which is placed here, and which will follow, it does not distinguish him, whom one must obey, but the manner in which he revealed himself. And thus we often speak of one, considered in different ways, as if of two ways, as - - - - How changed from that Hector - - - - And speaking for having spoken Present for Past. Those, who turned away from God speaking from the earth, that is, from Mount Sinai, namely through an Angel Act. VII, 38. Deut. XXXIII, 2. We have already spoken about the word to refuse. The histories are looked back upon, which are Exod. 32. Num. 14, 20. Actor. 7, 29. above 3, 6.

Much more we.] Supply we shall not escape as above 2, 3.

Those who turn away from him from heaven.] Him from heaven namely speaking for having spoken. If we turn away from the same God, who gave us oracles from heaven, wishing his son to be obeyed, Matth. 3, 17. Marc. 1, 11. Matth. 17, 5. Marc. 9, 7.

in Luc. 9, 35. Joh. 12, 28. From heaven, namely the highest. For the region of the lower heaven was also opened for that reason.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Βλέπετε μὴ παραιτήσησθε τὸν λαλῦντα. ] Παραι- τεῖν est adversari, ut 1. Tim. IV, 7. & alibi quod jamjam dicet, ἀποστρέφεσθαι τὸν λαλῦντα Deum nempe, quiChristo nos obe- dire jussit, ut jam dicet. Λαλῦντα pro λαλήσαντα frequenti locutione.

Εἰ γὰρ ἐκεῖνοι ὐκ ἔφυγον.] In Manuscripto ἐξέφυγον, ut Luc. XXI, 36. Rom. II, 3. 1. Thess. V, 3. Nempe pœnam. ἔν- δικον μισθαποδοσίαν, Ebr. II, 2. ubi par sensus.

Τὸν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς παραιτησάμενοι χρηματίζοντα.] In Manu- scripto ἐπὶ γῆς παραιτησάμενοι τὸν χρηματίζοντα. Utrovis modo legas τὸν, quod hic ponitur, & quod sequetur, non di- stinguit eum, cui parendum est, sed modum, in quo is se re- velavit. Et sic sæpe de uno, diversis modis considerato, tan- quam de duobus modis loquimur, ut - - - - Quantum mutatus ab illo Hectore - - - - Et χρηματίζοντα pro χρηματίσαντα Præsens pro Præterito. Illi, qui aversati sunt Deum de terris loquentem, id est, de monte Sinai, per Angelum nempe Act. VII, 38. Deut. XXXIII, 2. De verbo παραιτεῖσθαι jam diximus. Respiciuntur historiæ, quæ sunt Exod. 32. Num. 14, 20. Actor. 7, 29. supra 3, 6.

Πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἡμεῖς.] Supple ἐκ ἐκφευξόμεθα quomodo supra 2, 3.

Οἱ τὸν ἀπ᾿ ὀρανῶ ἀποστρεφόμενοι.] Τὸν ἀπ᾿ ὀρανῶ nempe χρηματίζοντα pro χρηματίσαντα. Si aversamur eundem Deum, qui de cœlo nobis oracula dedit, filio suo pareri volens, Matth. 3, 17. Marc. 1, 11. Matth. 17, 5. Marc. 9, 7.

in Luc. 9, 35. Joh. 12, 28. Ex cælo, nempe summo. Nam & ideo aperta est regio cæli inferior.

## 12:26
Ver. 26. Whose voice shook the earth then.] Namely when the law was given on Mount Sinai Psalm. 104, 4.

But now he has promised saying.] He promised concerning our times in Haggai 2, 17. which we said there pertain directly to Christ.

Yet once more I will shake not only the earth, but also the heaven.] In the Manuscript I will shake, well. In the Greek version of Haggai: Yet once more I will shake the heaven and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land. Nothing is lost to the sense. For sea and dry land are nothing other than distributions of the word earth, that is, the terrestrial globe into its parts, which we said were fulfilled to some extent by the coming of Christ to the earth at Haggai. But they will be fulfilled much more perfectly at the coming of the same Christ to judgment. That once more, however, is not referred to heaven specifically, but to the whole matter. I have made great changes of things before this. But a far greater one remains.

A second argument for not neglecting grace, from the gravity of the punishment that will follow from it, is set forth again by way of comparison, on the occasion of the λαλιᾶς (speech) of the blood of Christ: by which the Hebrews are now warned to take heed, lest they despise Christ speaking, or the Gospel of Christ. The Israelites did not want to hear God, because they could not endure his voice, v. 19. Therefore God, out of his immense mercy, promised another whom they should hear, namely Christ, to whom the Mosaic law was a tutor, whom he was about to raise up in place of Moses from among their brothers, Exod. XIX, 19. 20. Deut. XVIII, 16. 17. 18. 19. The Apostle now presents this one to the Hebrews as the one to be heard. If those who refused to hear God speaking on earth could not escape punishment, when indeed they became disobedient to his word, as history testifies, how much more will the most grave punishments await you, who do not hear him speaking from heaven, or turn yourselves away from him. It is not said that he spoke through an Angel formerly, which Grotius did not find in sacred history, but added of his own: but he spoke on earth then on Mount Sinai. Here, however, he is said to speak from heaven to the Hebrews, because he sits at the right hand of majesty on the throne of God. Therefore, Constantinus Presbyter and Oecumenius do not rightly understand Moses by τὸν χρηματίζοντα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς (the one warning on earth), since God spoke immediately, and Moses himself even trembled. His voice is also said to have moved the earth at that time. For it is evident from a comparison of this passage with Exod. XIX. XX. and Acts VII, and we have taught more than once, that the Son of God descended onto Mount Sinai, and the earth was moved then by his voice. For the whole mountain trembled greatly then, Exod. XIX, 18, and therefore the earth was truly shaken, which the Psalmist also says in Ps. LXVIII, 8, so that one need not resort to a figure here with Estius. But now, with the Apostle as witness, he foretold the same, saying: Yet once more I will shake not the earth only, but also heaven. The Apostle says, as interpreted by the blessed Dorscheus in Exeg. of the passage Heb. XIII, 8. §. 21, if those who rejected Christ as the leader of the Israelites in the desert, ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς (on earth) on Mount Sinai, that is, warning and publishing heavenly revelations, did not escape his avenging right hand, by no means will those in the New Testament escape the most just distributor of punishments, who have violated him warning from heaven with an averted mind. Who is that ἀπ᾽ ὀυρανῶν χρηματίζων (warning from heaven)? Jesus, the Mediator of the new covenant, who τῷ ἅιματι ῥαντισμῷ κρείττονα λαλεῖ παρὰ τὸν Ἀβὴλ (speaks better things by the blood of sprinkling than Abel), v. 24. For Paul says, the voice sounded from Mount Zion, but it was terrible and threatened vengeance, just as the voice of the blood of Abel. In the New Testament the voice resounds from heavenly Zion and Jerusalem, but it is lovable, conciliatory, and supported by the sweet-sounding cymbals of the propitiatory blood, which is the Mediator's. This is not to be despised. Why? 1. Because his voice then moved the earth, when indeed everything was shaken on all sides by lightnings, flames, and thunders. Whence he shows how much he can do against the disobedient. 2. Because his voice, according to the declaration uttered in Hagg. II, 7, with the resonant sound of the Gospel is yet once more to shake not only the earth, but also the heaven. Whence it is manifest that it was one and the same person who was τὸν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [the one on earth] and the one speaking ἀπ' ὀυρανῶν [from the heavens]; for it is of one and the same person that it is said: ἡ φωνὴ, ἡ τὴν γῆν τότε σαλεύσα, καὶ ἔτι ἅπαξ ὀυ μόνον τὴν γῆν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸν ὀυρανὸν σαλεύσα [the voice that then shook the earth, and yet once more not only the earth, but also the heaven]. v. 26. The Apostle teaches that this ought to have been fulfilled, and has already been fulfilled. The sense is, says the blessed Gerhard, that Christ denounced this which follows in the Prophet, or in a passive sense ἐπήγγελται [it has been promised]. But now, that is, as regards the present time, or the time of the New Testament, he is denounced by the Prophet to say. As it is certain that these things in the Prophet speak of the first advent of Christ, as we have clearly proved there: so they could not be brought forward otherwise here, nor were they: because we are commanded to hear him who by his advent shook both heaven and earth, speaking, for whom there will no longer be place or time under the second advent: for then the punishment will follow only of those who did not hear, which the Apostle urges here. And it is entirely inconvenient, nay, absurd, to explain these things at present concerning the first and then the second advent, as if that prophecy, understood according to its inception and metaphorically, had been fulfilled in the first advent of Christ, then especially when the Gospel began to be preached to every creature: but was to be fulfilled completely and in a proper sense in the second advent of Christ, and the Apostle applies to the second advent of Christ what was said by the Prophet concerning the first advent of Christ; and those words: I will shake heaven and earth, pertain generally to the whole time which runs from the beginning of the kingdom of Christ on earth until its completion. Which interpretation of Estius, taken in part from Gagnaeus, is in no way to be approved. For thus, in the first place, a double interpretation of the same passage, both proper and improper, is admitted, both concerning the first and the second advent of Christ: Then the prophecy, which deals with the first advent, since Estius confesses that it is plain, is drawn by the Apostle to the second advent of Christ. For what he himself says with Gagnaeus, that nothing prevents some prophetic testimony from being referred by the Apostle, either by extension, or by accommodation, or even by concession, to that of which the Prophet did not properly speak, that in our judgment is very inconvenient and contrary to the simplicity of Scripture. Thirdly, that it began to be fulfilled metaphorically in the first, and is to be consummated properly in the second advent, according to the sense of the same oracle and the same words, is equally absurd, even if an abstract and general sense is feigned which extends itself to both. Finally, it is false that the Apostle here looks to the second advent of Christ, of which there is no indication in his words. Whence also the Grotius gloss collapses. He acknowledges that the promise in Haggai is about our times, and yet he snatches it to the second advent of Christ. Theophylact does not dissent from our opinion: Christ, he says, speaking to us from heaven, that is, who when he was taken up, gave us the law through the Spirit. Nor does Paul say these things because he brought a discrepant or different law, as if he had established some other law for us when he was taken up into heaven, but the very mode of establishing this seems to differ. For he introduced that one when he was on earth, and this one when he was carried up into heaven, as we have said. Whence it is that he is to be feared the more. But that the former law was not less different from the following one, hear what follows: Whose voice then shook the earth: Do you see that it was the same who was speaking then, and who now speaks to us from heaven? For his voice at that time, when the law was being given, shook the earth. But now he promises, saying: Yet once more I will shake the earth, not only the earth, but also the heaven. We read in the sacred writings that the earth was shaken twice. First, when the law was being given on Mount Sinai. For David testifies that the earth also trembled, when he says: The earth shook: Secondly, when Christ assumed flesh and came into the world. For all Jerusalem was moved (he says), and the foundations of Egypt were shaken, that is, they were removed, lest they deceive their worshippers, and their power was cast down. What he adds about a third shaking, he has neither from the Prophet nor from the Apostle. Therefore we dismiss those. Nor is the blessed Hunnius alien: Whose (Christ's) voice formerly in the promulgation of the law shook the earth, so that the foundations of the mountains trembled, and the orb of the earth, according to Psalm 115, was shaken by the voice of the thundering and lightning God. But now by the voice of his Gospel, according to the prophecy of Haggai, he has again shaken not only the earth, but also the heaven, or the heavenly kingdom, which by this voice of evangelical doctrine has been opened to those who believe. Furthermore, what the Prophet says, yet once more, etc., signifies the removal of those things which are shaken. For by those crashes which were heard in the promulgation of the law, the earth, which passes away, had been shaken. But now the voice of the Gospel has penetrated even to the unlocking of the inner chambers of heaven, which heaven, or heavenly kingdom, remains and endures forever, and cannot be so shaken that it is destroyed. And page 321, in the Locis Communibus, no. 18, concerning the power of the Gospel, whose voice, as the Apostle testifies, shook the kingdoms of the heavens: so that it is as if the very gate were opened, and the hinges of the heavenly kingdom were moved by Christ in the Gospel, and an entrance into the tabernacles of God and the holy of holies was opened to us through faith.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Οὗ ἡ φωνὴ τὴν γῆν ἐσάλευσε τότε.] Nempe cum in monte Sinai lex daretur Psalm. 104, 4.

Νῦν δὲ ἐπήγγελται λέγων.] Promisit de nostris temporibus apud Haggæum 2, 17. quæ ad Christum directe pertinere ibi diximus.

Ἔτι ἅπαξ ἐγὼ σείσω ὀυ μόνον τὴν γῆν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸν ὀυρανὸν.] In Manuscripto σείσω, bene. In Græca versione Aggæi: Ἔτι ἅπαξ ἐγὼ σείσω τὸν ὀυρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν, καὶ τὴν θάλασσαν, καὶ τὴν ξηράν. Nihil sensui deperit. Nam θάλασσα & ξηρά nihil aliud quam distributiones vocis γῆς, id est, orbis terrestris in suas partes, quæ Christi adventu in terras aliquatenus imple- ta diximus ad Haggæum. Multo autem perfectius implebun- tur in adventu ejusdem Christi ad judicium. Illud autem ἅπαξ non ad cælum speciatim refertur, sed ad rem totam. Ma- gnas antehac feci rerum mutationes. Sed restat longe major.

Alterum argumentum non negligendæ gratiæ, à gravitate pœnæ inde sequuturæ,iterum comparatio- ne instituta, ex occasione λαλιᾶς sanguinis Christi expeditur: quo jam monentur Ebræi, videant, ne contemnant Christum loquentem, vel Evangelium Christi. Audire noluerunt Israëlitæ Deum, quia vocem ejus sustinere non poterant, v. 19. Idcirco Deus ex immensa misericordia alium ipsis audiendum promittebat, Christum nempe, ad quem pædago- gus erat lex Mosaica, quem loco Mosis excitaturus erat è fratribus ipsorum, Exod. XIX, 19. 20. Deut. XVIII, 16. 17. 18. 19. Hunc ergo audiendum Ebræis jam sistit Apostolus. Si illi non potuere pœnas effu- gere, qui recusarunt Deum audire in terris loquen- tem, cum nempe verbo ejus immorigeri facti sunt, teste historia, quanto magis vos pœnæ manebunt gravissimæ, qui ipsum de cælo loquentem non audi- tis, vel ab eo vos avertitis. Non per Angelum quon- dam loquutus dicitur, quod in historia sacra non invenit, sed de suo addidit Grotius: In terris autem tum loquutus in monte Sinai. Hic vero de cælo lo- qui dicitur Ebræis, quia ad dextram majestatis in throno Dei sedet. Non ergo per τὸν χρηματίζοντα ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς recte Mosen intelligunt Constant. Presbyter & Oecumenius, quum Deus immediate loquutus sit, adeoque Moses ipse tremuerit. Ejus etiam vox terram tunc movisse dicitur. Filium enim Dei in montem Sinai descendisse, & terram tunc voce ejus motam fuisse, è collatione hujus loci, cum Exod. XIX. XX. & Act. VII. constat, ac plus vice simplici docuimus. Tremuit enim tunc totus mons valde, Exod. XIX, 18. ideoque concussa vere fuit terra, quod etiam ait Psaltes Psal. LXIIX, 8. ut non ad fi- guram hic recurrendum sit cum Estio. Jam vero, Apostolo teste, prænunciavit idem dicens: Iterum semel adhuc ego movebo non terram tantum, sed & cælum. Ait Apostolus, interprete B. Dorscheo in Exeg. loci Ebr. XIII, 8. §. 21. si illi, qui Christum utpo- te in deserto Israëlitis ducem ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς in monte sci- licet Sinai χρηματίζοντα, & revelationes cælestes pu- blicantem respuerunt, vindicem illius dextram non effugerunt, nequaquam eos in Novo Testamento effu- gituros pœnarum justissimum distributorem, qui è cæ- lis scilicet χρηματίζοντα averso violaverint animo. Quis est ille ἀπ᾽ ὀυρανῶν χρηματίζων? Μεσίτης διαθή- κης νέας Ἰησᾶς, qui τῷ ἅιματι ῥαντισμῷ κρείττονα λαλεῖ παρὰ τὸν Ἀβὴλ, v. 24. Ait enim Paulus, vox so- nuit è monte Sion, sed terribilis & vindictam minita- ta, sicut & vox sanguinis Abelis. Novo Testamento vox resonat è cælesti Sione & Jerusalem, sed amabilis, conciliatrix, & sanguinis propitiatorii dulcisonanti- bus cymbalis suffulta, quæ Mediatoris est. Hæc non est aspernanda. Cur? 1. quia vox ejus tunc terram commovit, cum scilicet fulguribus, flammis atque tonitrubus omnia undique concuterentur. Unde ostendit, quanta possit contra immorigeros. 2. Quia vox ejus juxta denuntiationem apud Hagg. II, 7. ja- ctam sonora Evangelii turba adhuc semel non ter- ram solum, sed & cælum commotura est. Unde ma- nifestum est, unum & eundem fuisse τὸν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, & τὸν ἀπ' ὀυρανῶν χρηματίζοντα, unius enim ejus- demque est ἡ φωνὴ, ἡ τὴν γῆν τότε σαλεύσα, καὶ ἔτι ἅπαξ ὀυ μόνον τὴν γῆν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸν ὀυρανὸν σαλεύσα. v. 26. Quod impleri debuisse, & impletum jam esse docet Apostolus. Sensus est, inquit B. Gerhardus, Christum apud Prophetam hoc, quod sequitur, de- nunciasse, vel in sensu passivo ἐπήγγελται. Nunc au- tem, id est, quod attinet tempus instans, seu tempus Novi Testamenti, per Prophetam denunciatus est dicere. Quæ uti certum est in Propheta loqui de primo Christi adventu, quemadmodum illic luculen- ter probavimus : Ita nec aliter hic adduci potuere, nec adducta sunt: quia jubemur eum, qui adventu suo & cælum & terram movit, loquentem audire, cui locus aut tempus non amplius erit, sub adven- tum secundum : Tum enim pœna sequetur tantum eorum, qui non audierunt, quam hic urget Apo- stolus. Et inconveniens prorsus, imo absurdum est hæc exponere in præsentitum de primo, tum de se- cundo adventu, quasi prophetia illa secundum in- choationem, & metaphorice intellecta, impleta fuerit in primo Christi adventu, tunc maxime, quando Evangelium prædicari cœpit universæ creaturæ:consummate vero ac sensu proprio implen- da sit in Christi adventu secundo, & Apostolus ad secundum Christi adventum applicet, quæ à Pro- pheta de primo Christi adventu dicta; ac verba illa: Ego commovebo cœlum & terram, generatim per- tineant ad totum tempus, quod decurrit ab initio regni Christi in terris usque ad ejus complemen- tum. Quæ interpretatio Estiana ex parte à Gagnao petita, nullo modo probanda. Sic enim primo ejus- dem loci gemina interpretatio & propria & impro- pria admittitur, & de primo, & de secundo Christi adventu : Deinde Prophetia, quæ de primo adven- tu agit, quum fateatur Estius planum id esse, ab A- postolo trahitur ad secundum Christi adventum. Quod enim ait ipse cum Gagneo, nihil vetare, quo minus testimonium aliquod Propheticum sive per extensionem, sive per accommodationem, sive etiam per concessionem ab Apostolo referatur ad id, de quo proprie loquutus non est Propheta, id nostro judicio per quam inconveniens, & simplicitati scri- pturæ adversum est. Tertio metaphorice impleri cœptum in primo, & proprie consummari in secun- do adventu, secundum ejusdem oraculi & eorun- dem verborum sensum æque absurdum est, etiamsi abstractus & generalis sensus fingatur, qui se ad utrumque extendat. Denique falsum est, Aposto- lum hic respicere secundum adventum Christi, de quo nullum in verbis ejusdem indicium. Unde et- iam glossa Grotiana concidit. Promissionem de nostris temporibus esse apud Aggæum agnoscit, & rapit ta- men eam ad secundum Christi adventum. Nostræ sententiæ non abnuit Theophylactus : Christum, in- quiens, de cælo nobis loquentem, id est, qui ubi fuit assumptus, legem nobis per Spiritum dedit. Nec quia discrepantem aut diversam tulerit legem, hæc Pau- lus dicit, perinde aliam quandam nobis, ubi est in cœ- lum sublatus, statuerit legem, sed modus ipse hanc sta- tuendi videtur differre. Illam siquidem cum esset in terris, induxit hanc in cælum subvectus, ut diximus. Quo sit, ut magis sit ille extimescendus. Quod autem minus fuerit prior lex illa ab insequenti diversa, audi quæ insequuntur : Cujus vox mox movit terram tunc : Videsne, eundem fuisse, qui tunc loquebatur, & qui nunc nobis è cælo profatur ? Vox enim ejus tunc tem- poris, cum lex ferebatur, terram concussit. Nunc au- tem pollicetur dicens : Adhuc semel & ego movebo terram, non solum terram, sed & cælum, Bis terram apud sacras literas legimus fuisse succussam. Primum cum in monte Sinai lex ferebatur. Nam & terram contremuisse David testificatur, cum inquit: Terra tremuit: Secundo, cum carnem Christus assumpsit & venit in mundum. Commota est enim (inquit) omnis Hierosalem, & quatiebantur mansacta Ægypti, id est, sublata sunt, ne suos fallant cultores, & dejecta est illorum potentia. Quæ addit de tertia commotione, nec à Propheta habet, nec ab Apostolo. Ea ergo mittimus. Nec alienus est B. Hunnius: Cujus (Chri- sti) vox olim in promulgatione legis concussit terram, ita, ut montium fundamenta contremiscerent, & or- bis terrarum juxta Psal. CXV. voce tonantis & ful- minantis Dei concuteretur. At nunc voce Evangelii sui juxta Prophetiam Haggæi, denuo concussit non terram tantum, sed & cælum, sive regnum cæleste, quod hac voce doctrinæ Evangelicæ credentibus aper- tum est. Porro, quod Propheta inquit, adhuc semel &c. significat eorum, quæ concutiuntur, translationem. Nam fragoribus illis, qui in promulgatione legis ex- audiebantur, concussa erat terra, quæ transit. At nunc vox Evangelii ad usque cæli penetralia reseranda pe- netravit, quod cælum, sive regnum cæleste manet & du- rat in æternum, neque ita concuti valet, ut destruatur. Et pag. 321. in LL. CC. n. XIIX. de potentia Evan- gelii, cujus vox regna cælorum, teste Apostolo, concus- sit: adeo, ut ipsa quasi porta aperta, & cardines regni cælestis per Christum in Evangelio moti sint, nobisq; per fidem ingressus in tabernacula Dei & sancta san- ctorum patefactus.

## 12:27
Vers. 27. Τὸ δὲ, ἔτι ἅπαξ [But the, yet once more]. In the Hebrew it is אַחַת מְעַט [yet a little while]. But the Greeks seem to have read אַחַד מַעַל [once after this]. We are accustomed to speak thus when we attempt something great and hitherto unheard of.

Δηλοῖ τῶν σαλευομένων τὴν μετάθεσιν [It signifies the removal of those things that are shaken]. Not a shaking of any kind, as in Sinai, but an overturning and a mutation of every kind, concerning which 2 Peter 3:13. See concerning the word μετατίθεσθαι [to be removed/changed] above 7:12.

As of things that have been made, that those things which are not shaken may remain.] It is no wonder, he says: For this machine, which we see, was made for this purpose, that it might one day make room for another better and unchangeable one. See the said passage 2 Pet. III, 13. and Rev. XXI, 1. But since godly men will then be in that region in which the Angels now are, for what good the new heaven, that is, the ether and air, and the new earth are to serve, is difficult to say: but perhaps something can be conjectured from Rev. II, 22. and similar passages.

Latin:

Vers. 27. Τὸ δὲ, ἔτι ἅπαξ.] In Ebræo est אַחַת מְעַט. Sed videntur Græci legisse אַחַד מַעַל semel posthac. Solemus ita loqui cum magnum aliquid & ante hac inaudi- tum molimur.

Δηλοῖ τῶν σαλευομένων τὴν μετάθεσιν.] Non concussionem qualemcunque, ut in Sinai, sed eversionem, mutationemque omnimodam, de qua 2. Petr. III, 13. Vide de voce μετατίθε- σθαι supra VII, 12.

Ὡς πεποιημένων, ἵνα μείνη τὰ μὴ σαλευόμενα.] Non mirum hoc, inquit: Nam in id facta est hæc, quam videmus machi- na, ut olim alteri meliori & non immutandæ locum faciat. Vide dictum locum 2. Petr. III, 13. & Apoc. XXI, 1. Cum au- tem pii homines futuri tunc sint in illa regione, in qua nunc sunt Angeli, cui bono novum cælum, id est, æther & aër & nova terra servitura sint, difficile est dictu: sed aliquid forte conjici potest ex Apoc. II, 22. & similibus locis.

## 12:28
Vers. 28. Wherefore receiving an unshakable kingdom.] That is, about to receive. An unshakable kingdom is that which is the eternal kingdom 2 Pet. I, 11.

let us have grace.] Let us retain grace. Ἔχωμεν for κατέχωμεν. And the Syrian understood it thus, in the same way as ἔχομεν is taken also in Rom. XV, 4.

By which let us serve God acceptably.] By which grace, that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit given to us by grace, we may be able to serve God, so that we may please Him. In the glossary εὐαρέστως complacito, it should be read complacito. Adverbs coming from Adjective nouns govern the case which the Adjective is accustomed to govern.

With reverence and godly fear.] Αἰδὼς here signifies reverence for God. For the Greeks take αἰδεῖσθαι in this way. And thus we had εὐπείπειαν above in 9. Εὐλαβεία, however, signifies in addition the fear of punishment, as the following words show. In the Manuscript it is μετὰ ἐνλαβείας κὶ δέως, Ps. II, 12. ביראה וברעדה in Greek ἐν φόβῳ καὶ ἐν τρόμῳ. This is what Micah c. VI, 8 means.

But that 'yet once more' signifies (it signified at that time) the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that have been made, that those things which are not shaken may remain, and thus we admit that sense, that participles are placed for verbal nouns, so that σαλευόμενα are things that can be moved, and μὴ σαλευόμενα are things that cannot be moved, in this way: He who says, 'yet once more,' signifies that something has already passed away, and another thing is to come, which may remain, and not be changed any further into anything else. By which name this is referred to the times of the Prophet, in which that 'yet once more' was predicted to be about to happen, which had already been done, according to the interpretation of the Apostle, at the time of the promulgation of the law. For the Prophet prophesies concerning the time of the New Testament, or the coming of the Messiah to his temple. There, therefore, he assigns a notable commotion that is still to happen once, and that not only of the earth, but also of the heaven, and the Apostle teaches that this was signified, that the translation of the things that are moved, as having been made, has been promised; to this end, that the things that are immovable may remain thereafter, so that neither another commotion nor translation may follow. For in the consummation of the world, a new commotion of heaven and earth is not so much to be expected, with a certain innovation, as the destruction of the whole universe. And we already have τὰ μὴ σαλευόμενα through Christ, namely his immovable kingdom, which began here and will be consummated in the other life. By the μετάθεσιν τῶν σαλευομένων of the instruments serving the legal ceremonies, and indeed the translation of the legal ceremonies themselves, the blessed Gerhard, along with others, understood it, nor do we deny that it was signified, as the Apostle interprets: ὡς πεποιημένων as if made, namely by the hands of men from perishable materials, so that the tabernacle of the Levitical cult, the ἐργαστήριον, is looked upon in this way, and the discourse is about the Levitical cult sanctioned in the promulgation of the law, which had to be changed because it was only a type of the future, Heb. 10:1, namely of the good things, the τῶν μὴ σαλευόμενα, which cannot be shaken, that is, which are eternal, prepared through Christ the Mediator of the New Testament, and offered in the Gospel; to which the kingdom of Christ belongs, which he acquired for us, and is truly immovable: Since, therefore, we receive this in the present, let us reverently have thanks, or as Grotius says, let us retain it, it is right, that is, let us receive that immovable kingdom of Christ with true obedience of faith, and let us apprehend the grace which comes to us in Christ, through which we may so worship God that we serve GOD with fear and reverence: Since God is a consuming fire. Thus all things cohere optimally and are most rightly consistent with themselves.

It is most alien that Grotius snatches the μετάθεσιν toward an all-encompassing destruction in 2 Pet. 3:13, and those words ὡς πεποιημένων toward this machine of the world which we see; concerning which translation and change I know not what Grotius dreamed, and in what Elysian field, namely that pious men, even in that region in which the angels are to be, would then be at the consummation of the age, and yet a new heaven (which he himself does not know for what purpose it is to be created), that is, ether and air, and a new earth. What he wanted to be divined from Rev. 2 or 22, I cannot augur, nor did he himself dare to express it, and therefore we deservedly dismiss such trifles. To Estius, who snatches the words about fear and reverence against the confidence of grace, it is easy to answer. For filial fear does not exclude the confidence of present grace; indeed, he who fears and is solicitous lest he lose some treasure is certain that he possesses the same, otherwise he would be solicitous about it in vain.

Latin:

Vers. 28. Διὸ βασιλείαν ἀσάλευτον παραλαμβάνοντες.] Id est, παραληψόμενοι. Βασιλεία ἀσάλευτος est quæ βασιλεία αἰ- ώνιος 2. Petr. I, 11.

ἔχωμεν χάριν.] Retineamus gratiam. Ἔχωμεν pro κατέ- χωμεν. Et ita accepit Syrus, quomodo ἔχομεν sumitur etiam Rom. XV, 4.

Δι ἧς λατρεύωμεν εὐαρέστως τῷ Θεῷ.] Per quam gratiam, id est, dona Spiritus S. ex gratia nobis data, servire possimus Deo, ita, ut ipsi placeamus. In glossario εὐαρέστως complacito, le- gendum complacito. Adverbia à nominibus Adjectivis ve- nientia regunt casum, quem regere solet Adjectivum.

Μετὰ αἰδοῦς κὶ ἐνλαβείας.] Αἰδὼς hic reverentiam Dei si- gnificat. Nam αἰδεῖσθαι sic sumunt Græci. Et ita εὐπείπειαν habuimus supra 9. Εὐλαβεία vero insuper pœnæ metum, ut ostendunt sequentia. In Manuscripto est μετὰ ἐνλαβείας κὶ δέως, Psal. II, 12. ביראה וברעדה Græce ἐν φόβῳ καὶ ἐν τρόμῳ. Hoc est, quod vult Michæas c. VI, 8.

Illud autem adhuc semel significat (significabat eo tempore) eorum quæ concutiuntur, translatio- nem, velut jam factorum, ut maneant ea, quæ non con- cutiuntur, & ita sensum illum admittimus, partici- pia poni pro nominibus verbalibus, ut σαλευόμενα sint mobilia, μὴ σαλευόμενα immobilia, hoc modo: Qui dicit, adhuc semel, significat, aliquid jam præ- teriisse, & aliud futurum, quod permaneat, nec am- plius in aliud quicquã commutetur. Quo nomine hoc refertur ad tempora Prophetæ, quibus illud adhuc semel futurum esse prædicebatur, quod jam factum erat, interprete Apostolo, tempore promul- gatæ legis. Nam vaticinatur Propheta de tempore Novi Testamenti, aut adventus Meffiæ ad templum fuum. Illic ergo tum ἅπαξ adhuc futuram commo- tionem infignem, eamque non terræ tantum, sed & cœli affignat, eaque fignificatum fuiffe docet Apo- stolus, quod translatio mobilium jam factorum promissa sit; eo fine, ut maneant deinceps immobi- lia, ne alia vel commotio sequatur, vel translatio. Neque enim in consummatione mundi tam com- motio nova cœli & terræ expectanda, cum quadam innovatione, quam interitus totius universi. Et τὰ μὴ σαλευόμενα habemus jam per Christum, regnum nempe ejus immotum, quod hic cœpit, in altera vita consummabitur. Per μετάθεσιν τῶν σαλευομένων in- stramentorum inservientium ceremoniis legalib9, atq; adeo ipsarum ceremoniarum legalium trans- lationem intellexit cum aliis B. Gerhardus, nec ab- nuimus, eam significatam esse, interprete Aposto- lo: ὡς πεποιημένων tanquam effectorum, scilicet manibus hominum ex caducis materiis, quo ita re- spiciatur tabernaculum cultus Levitici ἐργαστήριον, & sermo sit de cultu Levitico in promulgatione le- gis sancito, quem mutari oportuit, quia fuit dunta- xat typus futuri, Ebr. X, 1. bonorum scilicet τῶν μὴ σαλευομένων, quæ concuti non possunt, hoc est, quæ æterna sunt per Christum Mediatorem Novi Testamenti parata, & in Evangelio oblata; ad quæ regnum Christi pertinet, quod nobis acquisivit, ve- reque immobile est: Quum ergo id accipiamus in præsenti, gratiam reverenter habeamus, vel ut Gro- tius, retineamus, par est, hoc est, suscipiamus re- gnum illud Christi immobile vera fidei obedientia, & apprehendamus gratiam, quæ in Christo nobis obtingit, per quam ita colamus Deum, ut DEO serviamus cum timore & reverentia: Siquidem Deus ignis consumens sit. Ita omnia cohærent opti- me, sibique constant rectissime.

Alienissimum est, quod Grotius τὴν μετάθεσιν abripit ad eversionem omnimodam 2. Pet. III, 13. & illa ὡς πεποιημένων ad hanc, quam videmus, mundi machinam; de qua μεταθέσει & immutatione ne- scio quæ & in quo campo Elysio somniavit Grotius, quod nempe pii homines & in illa regione, in qua nunc Angeli sunt futuri, tunc in consummatione secu- li sint, & novum tamen cælum (quod ipse nescit, cui bono? creandum sit, id est, æther & aër, & nova ter- ra. Quid divinatum voluerit ex Apoc. II. vel XXII. non augurari possum, nec ipse ausus est ex- primere, ideoque tales nænias merito missas faci- mus. Estio, qui verba de timore & reverentia abri- pit adversus fiduciam gratiæ, facile est respondere. Nam timor filialis non excludit fiduciam præsen- tis gratiæ; imo qui timet ac solicitus est, ne amit- tat thesaurum aliquem, certus est, se eundem possi- dere, alioquin de eo frustra solicitus foret.

## 12:29
Vers. 29. For our God is a consuming fire. It appears to be taken from the Greek, Deut. 4:24. The sense is: that God is no less gravely angry with sinning Christians than He was once angry with sinning Israelites, and that it is very easy for Him, no less than for a most blazing fire, to destroy most miserably those whom He has seized. Compare what we had above at 10:27. Add Deut. 9:3 and 32:22.

By this saying he confirms what the Apostle had said, that we shall not escape if we have turned away from Him who speaks from the heavens. Cf. Deut. 18:19. Concerning which Theophylact says here: For when he had said that all things of the Old Testament were full of dread and terror, but those of the new were far otherwise, lest they neglect gentleness, he says that thanks are to be given to God through us with fear and reverence. Since the soul that is afflicted by pressures and evils, if it should despair entirely, will seem to act impudently. Or, it is necessary that your worship toward God be exhibited modestly and reverently. For this God of ours, since He is a consuming fire, is to be feared by us entirely, lest, as despisers and having no regard for Him, we be taken from the midst, consumed by this fire.

Latin:

Vers. 29. Καὶ γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν πῦρ καταναλίσκον.] Sumptum apparet ex Græco, Deut. IV, 24. Sensus est: Deum non minus graviter Christianis peccantibus irasci, quam olim Israëlitus peccantibus iratus fuit, facillimumq; ei esse non minus, quàm igni flagrantissimo, eos, quos arripuit, pessime perdere. Con- fer quod habuimus supra X, 27. Adde Deut. IX, 3. & XXXII, 22.

Hoc dicto confirmat, quod dixerat Apostolus, nos non effugituros, si de cœlis loquentem aver- sati fuerimus. Conf. Deut. XIIX, 19. Quo de Theo- phylactus hic: Cum enim Vet. Test. universa dixiffet formidinis esse & terroris plena, novi vero longe se- cus, ne mansuetudinem negligant, cum metu & reve- rentia, Deo inquit per nos agendæ gratiæ sunt. Siqui- dem qui pressuris & malis afflictatur animus, si pror- sus desperet, facere impudenter videbitur. Vel vester in Deum cultus, ut verecunde & reverenter exhibea- tur, necesse est. Deus namque hic noster, cum ignis sit confumens, erit à nobis omnino verendus, ne veluti contemptores, & fui nullam habentes rationem, tolla- mur è medio, hoc igne absumpti.

## 13:1 Argument
CHAPTER XIII. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

The Apostle now exhorts specifically to brotherly love and hospitality and compassion, to reverence for marriage, to freedom from the love of money, and confidence in God, and grateful memory of those in charge; and with the perennial grace of Christ proposed, he wishes to guard against strange doctrines, and he recalls to their memory again our spiritual altar and the satisfactory passion of Christ, and commands them to bear His reproach, having suffered outside the gate, even in exile, and to offer to Him a sacrifice of praise. Finally, he requires obedience toward Teachers, and prayers: And having testified to the faith of his own conscience, and promised a return, he subjoins both a vow to the God of peace and a doxology: and in place of a colophon, he exhorts them to receive the word of exhortation, makes them certain about the liberation of Timothy, and having made a salutation in the name of the brothers, he concludes the epistle with a vow of grace.

There are two parts: The former is Paraenetic, up to verse 9. The latter is votive with the closing of the epistle.

PART I. Special exhortations to various virtues and duties of piety.

Vers. 1. Let brotherly love continue. Rom. 12:10, 1 Thess. 4:9, 1 Pet. 1:22, 2 Pet. 1:7. May that love which is proper among Christians, and which you have shown heretofore, never depart from us. See above 6:10. Let not the fact that some are foreigners or some other cause draw you away from it.

Do not forget hospitality. In Pirke Aboth, let your house be open toward the street. See Rom. 12:13, 1 Pet. 4:9.

Blessed Gerhard establishes four chapters of the Apostolic exhortation: 1. to works of charity and piety, v. 7. 2. to constancy of doctrine in the Gospel, to v. 15. 3. to spiritual sacrifices to be offered to God through Christ, v. 15, 16. 4. to obedience to be rendered to the leaders of the Churches, v. 17, and to pour out prayers for them, v. 18, 19. The beginning of the special exhortation is made from charity, which is the mother of other Christian virtues. Let the charity of the brotherhood remain in you, as the Vulgate version has it: But the author added that 'in you' of his own, for it is not held in the original text. He assumes Φιλαδελφίαν from the judgment of charity, and therefore warns them to remain in it. Concerning which Theophylactus says: For he did not say, acquire these for yourselves, for they already possessed them, as it appears. But since they were being urged by more frequent pressures, they were coming almost into danger, lest they should henceforth exercise virtues of this kind more negligently. He says therefore, let the charity of the brotherhood remain, and let it be stable, and do not allow this to depart from you.

Latin:

CAPUT XIII. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Adhortatur jam Apostolus in specie ad φιλα- δελφίαν & φιλοξενίαν ac compassionem, ad con- jugii reverentiam, ἀφιλαργυρίαν, & confiden- tiam in Deum, ac gratam præpositorum me- moriam; & proposita Christi perenni gratia caveri vult alienas doctrinas, & spirituale nostrum altare, ac passionem Christi satisfa- ctoriam ipsis denuo in memoriam revocat, ejusque extra portam passi opprobrium porta- re jubet, etiam in exilio, ipsique sacrificium laudum offerre. Postremo requirit obedien- tiam erga Doctores, ac preces: Et de conscien- tiæ suæ fide testatus, & reditum pollicitus vo- tum ad Deum pacis, tum δοξολογία subjungit: & colosphonis loco hortatur, ut suscipiant ser- monem παρακλήσεως, de liberatione Timothei eosdem certos reddit, ac facta nomine fra- trum salutatione gratiæ voto concludit episto- lam.

Partes duæ sunt: Prior Parænetica est, ad v. 9. Posterior votiva cum clausula epistolæ.

PARS I. Speciales adhortationes ad varias virtutes & pietatis officia.

Vers. 1. Ἡ φιλαδελφία μενέτω.] Rom. XII, 10. 1. Thessal. IV, 9. 1. Petr. I, 22. 2. Petr. I, 7. Nunquam à nobis disce- dat ea dilectio, quæ Christianorum inter se propria est, & quam ostendistis ante hac. Vide supra VI, 10. Ne vos inde dutrahat, aut quod quidam sint alienigenæ aut alia causa.

Τῆς φιλοξενίας μὴ ἐπιλανθάνεσθε.] In Pirke Aboth יהי ביתך פתוח לרוחה, pateant fores tuæ plateam versus. Vide Rom. XII, 13. 1. Petr. IV, 9.

Exhortationis Apostolicæ quatuor capita con- stituit B. Gerhardus, 1. ad opera charitatis & pietatis v. 7. 2. ad constantiam doctrinæ in Evangelio, ad vers. 15. 3. ad spiritualia sacrificia Deo per Christum of- ferenda, v. 15. 16. 4. ad obedientiam præpositis Eccle- siarum præstandam v. 17. ac preces pro illis funden- das, v. 18. 19. Initium specialis exhortationis fit à charitate, quæ aliarum Christianarum virtutum mater est. Charitas fraternitatis maneat in vobis, ut habet Vulgata versio: Sed illud in vobis autor de suo adjecit, non habetur enim in textu originali, Sup- ponit ex judicio charitatis Φιλαδελφίαν, ideoque ut in ea maneant, monet. Quo de Theophylactus: Non enim hæc vobis, dixit, comparate, his namque, ut apparet, potiti jam erant. Sed quùm frequentioribus urgerentur pressuris, in discrimen propemodum venie- bant, ne de cætero virtutes bujusmodi negligentius ex- ercerent. Inquit igitur, maneat fraternitatis chari- tas, & stabilis sit, nec abscedere à vobis hanc sinite.

## 13:2
Vers. 2. Διὰ ταύτης γὰρ ἔλαθόν τινες ξενίσαντες ἀγγέλους.] The histories of Gen. XVIII. and XIX. are referred to, where we also brought forward those verses of Homer. Καί τε Θεοὶ ξείνοισιν ἐοικότες ἀλλοδαποῖσι Παντοῖοι τελέθοντες ἐπιστρωφῶσι πόληας Ἀνθρώπων ὕβριντε, καὶ εὐνομίην ἐφορῶντες.

But this is referred to, so that it may appear how great are the rewards of φιλοξενίας before God. And note the well-Greek expression, ἔλαθον ξενίσαντες, they received them unknowingly. For thus also Aristophanes speaks, and Plato, and Xenophon, with ἑαυτοὺς understood, which is sometimes expressed. And Abraham and Lot, when they first received the Angels, thought they were Arabs, whom although they were strangers, they received with great honor. Afterwards, from the message which they brought, they knew them to be Angels. Add what is said in 1 Tim. III, 2.

The Vulgate version, therefore, arising from ignorance of the Greek language, must be corrected here: ἔλαθόν τινες, rendering it 'some have pleased'. Theophylact brings forward this special reason for the exhortation: It could happen that these people, since they were deprived of the goods of fortune, might perhaps receive guests and strangers sparingly and rarely. And he urges them to continue this hospitality, as they had begun before.

But why did he make mention only of Angels, if, as we said regarding Gen. XVIII, Abraham unknowingly received the Son of God Himself into his hospitality? Resp. Either that history is not precisely referred to, but the one which follows in chapter XIX with others, where perhaps Angels were received: Or, which is more pleasing, that more sublime matter concerning the Son of God is not commemorated, but only the accompanying Angels, who were properly received at the banquet. For the Son of God, a more honorable guest, was recognized from Abraham's conversation and honored with greater reverence than the others. For the Apostle, speaking here not of religious but only of civil honor, had enough in naming the Angels: And because he wished to join both histories, because he commemorates not one, but several who thus received Angels into hospitality: therefore he makes mention only of the Angels. For the Son of God was not present as a guest in visible form at the house of Lot. We have treated this passage elsewhere more copiously against the Socinians and Calixtines who deny that the Son of God appeared to Abraham, and who rashly urge this passage. Here we observe that the blessed Dorscheus, l. c. §. 21, takes the name of Angels here generally, so that it includes the uncreated: He says, if Christ was the same regarding His Deity in the Old Testament, who appeared to the Patriarchs with the Angels, why is it not commemorated in chapter XIII, 2, in the incitement to hospitality, because some thus received Angels into hospitality. Resp. Paul does not posit only created Angels. He understands, therefore, those who, from the heavens, in the assumed appearance of travelers, wished to dwell among men and lodge with them. The Apostle points his finger to the histories of the Old Testament, as if he were saying: You know what apparitions were made, and who and how great the Angels were who once lodged with the saints. Imitate the virtue which God deemed worthy of such great display. But it is better that this doubt be resolved by the reason I have already proposed, that this discourse is not about religious worship or the honor of the first table, but about the civil honor of the second table, such as was exhibited unexpectedly not to the Son of God, but to the Angels.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Διὰ ταύτης γὰρ ἔλαθόν τινες ξενίσαντες ἀγγέλους.] Respiciuntur historiæ Gen. XVIII. & XIX. ubi & illos Ho- meri versus attulimus. Καί τε Θεοὶ ξείνοισιν ἐοικότες ἀλλοδαποῖσι Παντοῖοι τελέθοντες ἐπιστρωφῶσι πόληας Ἀνθρώπων ὕβριντε, καὶ εὐνομίην ἐφορῶντες.

Refertur autem hoc, ut appareat, quanta sint apud Deum præmia φιλοξενίας. Et nota loquutionem bene Græcam, ἔλαθον ξενίσαντες excepere inscii. Nam sic & Aristophanes loquitur, & Plato, & Xenophon, subaudito ἑαυτοὺς, quod interdum exprimitur. Et Abraham & Loth, cum pri- mum Angelos exciperent, putarunt eos Arabes, quos, quanquam ignotos, multo cum honore exceperunt. Postea ex nuncio, quem afferebant, cognoverunt esse Angelos. Ad- de, quæ dicta 1. Tim. III, 2.

Vulgata ergo versio, ex ignorantia Græcæ linguæ oriunda, hic castiganda: ἔλαθόν τινες, reddens pla- cuerant quidam. Causam adhortationis specialem hanc affert Theophylactus: Fieri poterat, ut hi, cum bonis fortunæ essent privati, parcius forsan & raro hospites & peregrinos exciperent. Et eos hortatur, ut prius cæperant, hospitalitatem hanc persequantur.

Cur autem Angelorum tantum mentionem fecit, si, quod ad Gen. XIIX. diximus, ipsummet Filium Dei nescius hospitio excepit Abraham? Resp. Vel non respicitur præcise illa historia, sed quæ cap. XIX. sequitur cum aliis, ubi forte Angeli excepti: Vel, quod magis placet, sublimius illud de Filio Dei non commemoratur, sed solum de comitibus Angelis, qui proprie excepti sunt convivio. Filius Dei enim hospes ἐντιμιώτερος, agnitus fuit ex colloquio Ab- rahami, majorique cultu, quam cæteri, honoratus. Hic enim de honore non religioso sed civili tantum loquens Apostolus satis habebat nominare Ange- los: Et quia conjungere volebat utramque histo- riam, quia non unum, sed plures, qui hospitio ita Angelos excepere commemorat: ideo Angelorum solum mentionem facit. Non enim Lothodomi suæ aderat hospes in forma visibili Filius Dei. Egi- mus de hoc loco alias copiosius contra Socinianos, & Calixtinos negantes Filium Dei Abrahamo appa- ruisse, & temere hunc locum urgentes. Hic obser- vamus B. Dorscheum l. c. §. 21. Angelorum nomen hic generatim accipere, ut increatum comprehen- dat: Dicit, si idem fuit Christus quoad Deitatem in Veteri Testamento, qui cum Angelis apparuit Patri- archis, cur non commemoratur cap. XIII, 2. in excita- tione ad φιλοξενίαν, quia ita nonnulli hospitio Angelos exceperunt. Resp. Paulus non ponit Angelos creatos duntaxat. Intelligit ergo eos, qui è cælestibus in assum- pta viatorum specie inter homines versari, & apud hos hospitare voluerunt. Apostolus digitum ad histo- rias Veteris Testamenti intendit, quasi dicat: Nostis, quæ apparitiones factæ, qui quantique Angeli olim apud sanctos hospitaverint. Imitamini virtutem, quam tanto apparatu dignatus est Deus. Sed præstat ea, quam jam proposui ratione dubium hoc expe- diri, quod non de religioso cultu, vel honore tabulæ prima, sed de civili tabulæ secundæ hic sermo sit, qualis non Filio Dei, sed Angelis ἀπροσδοκήτως exhibitus est.

## 13:3
Vers. 3. Remember those in bonds, as bound with them.] Do not care for them lightly, but in such a way as if you yourselves were feeling the same evils: 'Perhaps thinking the event to be one's own,' says Menander. See above X, 34.

Of those who are ill-treated, as being yourselves also in the body.] In a body subject to the same evils: 'I am a man, I consider nothing human alien to me.' In the body, namely, mortal, which is added in Rom. VIII, 11; earthly in 1 Cor. XV, 40; corruptible in 1 Cor. XV, 53. We had the participle 'ill-treated' also above in XI, 37.

He speaks of those bound for the confession of Christ, and with that affection of sympathy he wishes them to assist them with help and consolation, as if they themselves were equally bound. For true charity looks upon the misery of others as its own. Ribera's gloss, that you yourselves are also bound and captive in the body of death, as not fitting the word 'bound with them,' which implies the same bonds, is deservedly rejected by Estius.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Μιμνήσκεσθε τῶν δεσμίων, ὡς συνδεδεμένοι.] Non leviter eos curate, sed ita, quasi ipsi eadem mala sentiretis: Ἴσως νομίζων ἴδιον εἶναι τὸ γεγονός. ait Menander. Vide supra X, 34.

Τῶν κακουχουμένων, ὡς καὶ αὐτοὶ ὄντες ἐν σώματι.] In cor- pore iisdem malis obnoxio: Homo sum, humani nihil à me alienum puto. Ἐν σώματι nempe θνητῷ, quod additur Rom. IIX, 11. ἐπιγείῳ 1. Cor. XV, 40. φθαρτῷ 1. Cor. XV, 53. Participium κακουχού- μενοι habuimus & supra XI, 37.

Loquitur de vinctis ob confessionem Christi, eo- que συμπαθείας affectu vult subveniant iisdem au- xilio & solatio, ac si ipsi pariter vincti essent. Vera enim charitas aliorum miseriam aspicit, ut suam. Riberæ glossa, quod & ipsi vincti & captivi sitis in corpore mortis, ceu nō congrua voci συνδεδεμένοι, quæ eadem vincula innuit, ab Estio merito rejicitur.

## 13:4
Vers. 4. Marriage is honorable in all, and the bed undefiled.] That is, among all civilized nations there is honor for marriage, and that bed is not displeasing even to GOD. 'Undefiled' is that which lacks vice, Wisd. III, 13; IV, 2; above VII, 26; Jas. I, 22. This is treated quite well in the book of Musaeus. And many Essenes abstained from marriage, yet 'not abolishing marriage and the succession from it.'

These things are said not assertively, but as the blessed Luther rendered it, preceptively. For exhortations are held here. 'In all' refers to all states, whence marriage is to be honored by no state whatsoever, and to be held in value: which is not done in the Papacy; since it is less honored by the clergy, and is a contemner, as if unworthy of that order. Indeed, by the Pope, marriage is forbidden to ecclesiastical persons, as a carnal state, in which those who live cannot please God, as noted elsewhere: Which doctrine of demons the Apostle called, 1 Tim. IV, 2. Ignatius in his epistle to the Philadelphians: If anyone calls lawful intercourse and the procreation of children pollution, such an apostate fosters that Dragon dwelling within him.
