Grotius, in order to help the Papists, perverts the Apostle's sentiment, as if it were only an assertion that marriage is honorable among all nations; but the remaining exhortations teach that it is a precept, and the added threat of judgment or Divine punishment. And if it is honorable among all nations, why then is it less honorable among the Papists, or why is it afflicted with ignominy? Are the Papists not thus worse than the Gentiles? Siricius and Innocent certainly did not hesitate to condemn the marriages of priests for the reason that those who are in the flesh cannot please God. C. Proposuisti dist. 82 and many others. Distinction of the same, that Bellarmine excuses in vain that there is some baseness and impurity in the act of marriage by reason of concupiscence and the rebellion of the members: For he confuses the substance of marriage and the conjugal act with that which adheres to it only by accident: Since marriage and the conjugal act are in themselves a holy ordinance of God, to which depraved concupiscence and ἀταξια (disorder) adhere only συμβεβηκότως (accidentally). The good of marriage, says Augustine in book II de peccat. merit. & remiss., is not the fervor of concupiscence, but a certain lawful and honest manner of using that fervor, adapted for propagating offspring, not for satisfying lust. Therefore, from this Apostolic passage, Paphnutius in the Council of Nicaea proved that intercourse with one's own wife in marriage is chastity, σωφροσύνην εἶναι την της νομίμου γυναικος συνελευστη (that the union with a lawful wife is temperance): See Socrates, book I, history, chapter 8; Sozomen, book I, chapter 22; C. Nicena, distinction 31. He calls not only the γάμον (marriage) or nuptial contract honorable in all things, but he also calls the κοίτην (bed), the use of marriage, undefiled. For it is evident that κοίτην is spoken of in this way in Romans 8:10 and chapter 13:13. Therefore, the Holy Spirit designates ἀγνείαν (purity) as chastity in the very conjugal intercourse, Titus 2:14, 1 Peter 3:2, and ἁγιασμὸν (sanctification) in 1 Corinthians 7:14, 1 Thessalonians 4:4, 1 Timothy 2:15. Whence Peraldus in his treatise on temperance says the use of marriage is called the undefiled bed. Ribera on this passage: The bed is called undefiled and unpolluted when it is not defiled by any adultery.

Πόρνες δὲ και μοιχὲς κρινεῖ ὁ Θεὸς (But fornicators and adulterers God will judge). God will punish not only adulterers, who, if they are caught, are accustomed to be punished even by human laws, but also πόρνες (fornicators), that is, those using Venus outside of marriage. He opposes this to the opinion of those Jews, of whom we treated above at 12:16. We have taken κρινει (will judge) for κατακρινεῖν (will condemn), often in the epistle to the Romans. Moreover, κατακρινειν by metonymy is to punish, as in Mark 16:16, 1 Corinthians 11:32, and elsewhere. And thus κρινειν is to punish in John 3:17. And rightly he reserves for God's judgment those crimes which are accustomed to be hidden from other men.

He will therefore judge and punish, not only with temporal but also with eternal torments, unless they have repented: See Leviticus 20:10, Job 24:19, chapter 31:9, 12, Proverbs 6:23, 1 Corinthians 6:9, Galatians 5:21, Ephesians 5:5, Colossians 3:6, Revelation 21:8, chapter 22:15. Theophylact: Or in this passage marriage attains honor, inasmuch as it interrupts and prohibits adulteries. But God will judge, that is, he will condemn, and deservedly so. For if marriage is permitted, no fornicator or adulterer will be able to excuse the allurements of the flesh, but he will be justly tormented.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσι, καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος.] Id est, apud omnes gentes moratas honos est conjugio, ac ne DEO quidem is thorus displicet. Ἀμίαντος est, quod vitio caret, Sap. III, 13. IV, 2. supra VII, 26. Jac. I, 22. Tractatur hoc in libro Mu- sæ fatis bene. Et Esseni multi abstinebant à matrimonio, at- tamen τὸν γάμον, καὶ τὴν ἐξ αὐτῶ διαδοχὴν ὐκ ἀναιρῶντες.

Dicta hæc non assertive, sed ut B. Lutherus red- didit, præceptive. Habentur enim hic exhortatio- nes. Ἐν πᾶσι respicit omnes status, unde à nullo non statu honorandum conjugium, & in pretio haben- dum: quod in Papatu non fit; quum à clero minus honoretur, & contemnator, quasi ordine illo indi- gnum. Imo à Papa personis Ecclesiasticis interdi- citur conjugium, ceu status carnalis, in quo, qui vi- vunt, Deo placere non possint, ut alias notatum: Quam doctrinam Dæmoniorum dixit Apostolus, 1. Tim. IV, 2. Ignatius in epist. ad Philad. Si quis την νομιμον μίξιν legitimam commixtionem, & libero- rum procreationem pollutionem appellat, talis apo- stata illum Draconem in se habitantem fovet. Gro- tius, ut juvet Papistas, pervertit Apostoli senten- tiam, ac si assertio tantum sit, inter omnes gentes ho- norabile esse conjugium; sed præceptum esse, reliquæ cohortationes docent, & addita judicii vel pœnæ Divinæ comminatio. Et si inter omnes gentes ho- norabile est, cur ergo inter Papistas minus honora- bile est, vel ignominia afficitur? Annon ita Papistæ deteriores sunt gentilibus? Siricius certe & Innocen- tius non dubitarunt, Sacerdotum conjugia ea de causa damnare, quod, qui in carne sunt, Deo placere non possunt. C. Proposuisti dist. 82 eo plurim. dist. ead. quod frustra sic excusat Bellarminus, in actu matrimonii turpitudinem & immunditiem aliquam esse ratione concupiscentiæ & rebellionis membro- rum: Confundit enim substantiam conjugii & actum conjugalem, cum eo, quod ipsi per accidens adhæret: Siquidem conjugium, & actus conjugalis per se sit sancta Dei ordinatio, cui prava concupi- scentia & ἀταξια non nisi συμβεβηκότως adhæret. Bonum conjugii, inquit Augustinus libr. II. de pec- cat. merit. & remiss. non est fervor concupiscentiæ, sed quidam licitus & honestus illo fervore utendi modus, propagandæ proli, non explendæ libidini accommoda- tus. Ideo ex hoc Apostolico loco Paphnutius in Conci- lio Niceno probavit, quod consuetudo cum pro- pria uxore in conjugio sit castitas, σωφροσύνην εἶναι την της νομίμου γυναικος συνελευστη: Vide Socrat. l. I. histor. cap. 8. Sozom. l. I. cap. 22. C. Nicena dist. 31. Non solum γάμον sive contractum nuptialem in omnibus vocat honorabilem, sed etiam κοίτην, usum conjugii impollutum vocat. Nam ita κοίτην di- ci è Rom. IIX, 10. cap. XIII, 13. constat. Ideo Spiritus sanctus in ipsa consuetudine conjugali ἀγνείαν ca- stitatem designat, Tit. II, 14. 1. Petr. III, 2. ἁγιασμὸν sanctificationem 1. Cor. VII, 14. 1. Thess. IV, 4. 1. Tim. II, 15. Unde Peraldus tract. de temperantia, conju- gii usus dicitur torus immaculatus. Ribera in hunc locum: Torus immaculatus dicitur & impollutus, cum nullo adulterio fœdatur.

Πόρνες δὲ και μοιχὲς κρινεῖ ὁ Θεὸς.] Non adulteros tantum, qui si deprehendantur, etiam humanis legibus puniri solent, puniet Deus, sed & πόρνες, id est, Venere utentes extra con- jugium. Opponit hoc Judæorum illorum sententiæ, de qui- bus egimus supra XII, 16. Κρινει pro κατακρινεῖν habuimus, sæ- pe epistola ad Romanos. Κατακρινειν autem per Μετωνυμίαν est punire, ut Marc. XVI, 16. 1. Cor. XI, 32. & alibi. Et sic κρινειν punire Joh. III, 17. Et recte Dei judicio reservat illa flagitia, quæ solent hominibus aliis esse abscondita.

Judicabit ergo & puniet, non solum temporali- bus, sed etiam æternis suppliciis, nisi pœnitentiam egerint: Vid. Lev. XX, 10. Job. XXIV, 19. cap. XXXI, 9. 12. Prov. VI, 23. 1. Cor. VI, 9. Gal. V, 21. Eph. V, 5. Col. III, 6. Apoc. XXI, 8. cap. XXII, 15. Theophylactus: Vel hoc loco connubium honorem assequitur, quippe quod adulteria interpellet prohibeatque. Judicabit autem Deus, id est, condemnabit, & merito quidem. Nam si permissæ sunt nuptiæ, nil poterit fornicarius aliquis vel adulter carnis illecebras excusare, sed jure excruciabitur.

## 13:5
Verse 5. Ἀφιλάργυρος ὁ τρόπος (Let your manner of life be without covetousness).] The word ἦ (let be) is understood here as above XII, 13. 16. Let your ways be free from the love of money. To use τρόπος in the singular number for that which we in Latin call by the plural 'sermores' is frequent in Plato and Demosthenes. Thus Χρηστὸς τρόπος, τρόπος δίκαιος, τρόπος βέλτιστος also among Aristophanes and Plutarch. What φιλαργυρία is, see 1 Tim. VI, 10. Polycarp also in his epistle to the Philippians: 'Being far from all love of money'.

Ἀρκούμενοι τοῖς παροῦσιν.] Supply ἦτε, that is, having for the present what is necessary for nature, be content with these. See 2 Cor. 9, 8. Phil. 4, 11. 12. 1 Tim. 6, 6. 8. Do not be anxious about the future. See Matt. 6, 34, and what is said there.

To avarice is opposed ἀυτάρκεια, 1 Tim. VI, 6. 10. Τὰ παρόντα are called those goods which are present, that is, which are possessed and are at hand, in distinction to those which are not possessed. Isocrates to Demonicus: 'be content with what is present'.

Αὐτὸς γὰρ εἴρηκε.] GOD, of course. Thus we have הוא sometimes among the Prophets.

Οὐ μή σε ἀνῶ, οὐδ᾽ οὐ μή σε ἐγκαταλίπω.] Jos. I. verse 5. לא ארפך ולא אעזבך, where the Greeks: Οὐκ ἐγκαταλείψω σε, οὐδ᾽ ὑπερόψομαί σε.] Our writer uses the potential mode: as if he were saying: it is impossible that I should cast you off entirely, or even desert you for a time. What was said to Joshua was said to him for the sake of the whole people. But that people is a figure of the Christian people. There is here in the latter member a triple negation, which among the Greeks denies vehemently. A similar sentiment in Isa. XLI, 13.

Latin:

Vers. V. Ἀφιλάργυρος ὁ τρόπος.] Subauditur & hic ἦ ut supra XII, 13. 16. Mores vestri absint a studio pecuniae quae- rendae. Τρόπος in numero singulari dicere pro eo, quod Lati- ne plurali sermores dicimus, frequens Platoni & Demosthe- ni. Sic Χρηστὸς τρόπος, τρόπος δίκαιος, τρόπος βέλτιστος et- iam apud Aristophanem & Plutarchum. Quid sit φιλαργυρία vide 1. Tim. VI, 10. Polycarpus quoque epistola ad Philippen- ses: Μακρὰν ὄντες πάσης φιλαργυρίας.

Ἀρκούμενοι τοῖς παροῦσιν.] Supple ἦτε, id est, habentes in praesens, quae naturae sunt necessaria, iis contenti estote. Vide 2. Cor. 9, 8. Phil. 4, 11. 12. 1. Tim. 6, 6. 8. Nolite anxii esse de fu- turo. Vide Matth. 6, 34. & ibi dicta.

Avaritiae opponitur ἀυτάρκεια, 1. Tim. VI, 6. 10. Τὰ παρόντα vocantur ea bona, quae adsunt, id est, quae habentur, & in promptu sunt, ad differentiam eorum, quae non habentur. Isocrates ad Demoni- cum: στέργε τὰ παρόντα.

Αὐτὸς γὰρ εἴρηκε.] DEUS scilicet. Sic הוא aliquoties ha- bemus apud Prophetas.

Οὐ μή σε ἀνῶ, οὐδ᾽ οὐ μή σε ἐγκαταλίπω.] Jos. I. vers. 5. לא ארפך ולא אעזבך, ubi Graeci: Οὐκ ἐγκαταλείψω σε, οὐδ᾽ ὑπερόψομαί σε.] Utitur autem Scriptor noster modo potentiali: quasi dicat: fieri non potest, ut te abjiciam plane, aut etiam ad tempus deseram. Quod Josuae dictum fuit, dictum ei fuit populi totius causa. Populus autem iste populi Christiani figura. Est hic in posteriore membro tri- plex negatio, quae apud Graecos vehementer negat. Similis sententia Esa. XLI, 13.

## 13:6
᭄στε θαῤῥοῦντας ἡμᾶς λέγειν.] θαῤῥοῦντας, בטוחים with confidence in God. The LXX, where in the Hebrew there is אל־תירא, are accustomed to put θαῤῥει, as Gen. 35, 17. Exod. 13, 13. 20, 20. 1 Kings 17, 13. Joel 2, 2. 22. Zeph. 3, 17. Hag. 2, 6. Zech. 8, 13. 15. See also Matt. 9, 2. 22. 14, 27. Mark 6, 50. 10, 49. Luke 8, 48. John 16, 33. Acts 23, 11. 2 Cor. 6, 8. 7, 16. 10, 1. 2.

Look at the passage Jos. I, 5. because his words are brought forward, there is no doubt: But because that is singular, pertaining to Joshua, as such it also occurs in 1 Chron. XXVIII, 20, without doubt a general parallel passage is looked at at the same time, Deut. XXXI, 6. 8. where the same promise was made to the whole Israelite people, under which as a general one each person can subsume himself, and apply it to himself singularly, just as David applies the same to Solomon, and God himself to Joshua. That the negations are doubled is for the sake of emphasis, so that the assertion may be more vehement, as if he were saying, in no way will it happen that I shall desert or abandon you.

Vers. 6. Κύριος ἐμοὶ βοηθὸς, καὶ οὐ φοβηθήσομαι, τί ποιήσει μοι ἄνθρωπος;] It is the LXX in the Psalm, which is CXVIII, 6 to the Hebrews. In the Hebrew it is יהוה לי literally, The Lord is to me, that is, for me. The LXX expressed the sense very well by adding the word βοηθὸς. A similar sentiment in Psalm LVI, 5, where for man is said flesh, so that his infirmity may be better signified. Nor does that which we have in Psalm XXVII, 1 depart far from this. Our writer adapts this well to those Hebrew Christians who, because of religion, were often stripped of their faculties by the wicked, above I, 34. Ἄνθρωπος here is ἄνθρωπων τις.

By the example of Christ himself, who speaks in the Psalm, he teaches that one must trust in God not only in indigence, but also in every adversity. Which Christ therefore wished to experience without example, so that he might acquire for us Divine assistance, abandoned for a short time by the Lord, so that we might not be abandoned, and helped in every necessity by the Lord, as he trusted, so that we might learn to trust in the Lord. Conf. Matt. IV, 4. chap. XXVII, 46. Heb. II, 13. where there is also added that which, joined with the faithful given to him in confidence, is from Isa. VIII, 18. Add Heb. II, 17. chap. IV, 15. chap. V, 8. 9.

Latin:

Ὥστε θαῤῥοῦντας ἡμᾶς λέγειν.] θαῤῥοῦντας, בטוחים cum fidu- cia in Deum. LXX. ubi in Ebraeo est אל־תירא ne time so- lent ponere θαῤῥει, ut Gen. 35, 17. Exod. 13, 13. 20, 20. 1. Reg. 17, 13. Joel. 2, 2. 22. Soph. 3, 17. Hagg. 2, 6. Zach. 8, 13. 15. Vide & Matth. 9, 2. 22. 14, 27. Marc. 6, 50. 10, 49. Luc. 8, 48. Joh. 16, 33. Act. 23, 11. 2. Cor. 6, 8. 7, 16. 10, 1. 2.

Respice locum Jos. I, 5. quia verba ejus adducun- tur, non est dubium: Sed quia is singularis est, ad Josuam pertinens, uti talis etiam 1. Par. XXIIX, 20. occurrit, sine dubio generalis parallelus locus simul respicitur, Deut. XXXI, 6. 8. ubi toti populo Israeli- tico facta est eadem promissio, sub qua ceu gene- rali subsumere quisque potest, & sibi singulariter eam applicare, quemadmodum David eandem ap- plicat Salomoni, & Deus ipse Josuae. Quod nega- tiones conduplicantur, sit emphaseos causa, ut asser- tio sit vehementior, quasi dicat, nulla ratione futu- rum est, ut te deseram vel derelinquam.

Vers. 6. Κύριος ἐμοὶ βοηθὸς, καὶ οὐ φοβηθήσομαι, τί ποιήσει μοι ἄνθρωπος;] Est LXX. in Psalmo, qui Ebraeis CXVIII, 6. In Ebraeo est יהוה לי ad verbum, Dominus mihi, id est, pro me. Sensum addito vocabulo βοηθὸς optime expressere LXX. Par sententia Psalm. LVI, 5. ubi pro homine dicitur caro, ut melius significetur ejus infirmitas. Nec longe abit id, quod habemus Psalm. XXVII, 1. Bene autem aptat hoc Scriptor noster Ebraeis illis Christianis, qui ob religionem saepe ab im- probis exuebantur suis facultatibus supra I, 34. Ἄνθρωπος hic ἄνθρωπων τις.

Exemplo ipsius Christi, qui in Psalmo loquitur, Deo confidendum esse docet non tantum in indi- gentia, sed etiam in omni adversitate. Quam ideo sine exemplo Christus experiri voluit, ut nobis ac- quireret Divinam assistentiam, derelictus ad modi- cum temporis a Domino, ut ne nos derelinquere- mur, & adjutus in omni necessitate a Domino, ut confidebat, ut nos confidere Domino disceremus. Conf. Matth. IV, 4. cap. XXVII, 46. Ebr. II, 13. ubi etiam addita est, quae cum fidelibus sibi datis in fi- ducia conjunctus ex Esa. VIII, 18. Adde Ebr. II, 17. cap. IV, 15. cap. V, 8. 9.

## 13:7
Vers. 7. Μνημονεύετε τῶν ἡγουμένων ὑμῶν] ἡγύμενοι אלוהים in the Old Testament are the leaders and princes of peoples or armies, which name is here with the best right adapted to those who among Christians are called κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν both προεστῶτες and ἐπίσκοποι, whose duty it is not only to preside over the Presbytery, but also to κοπιᾶν ἐν τῷ λόγῳ, 1 Tim. V. v. 17. such as was among the Jews, and now is the duty of τῶν ἀρχισυναγώγων. Thus also in the epistle of Clement to the Corinthians ἡγύμενοι are placed twice, then πρεσβύτεροι. He speaks, however, of those who had already died, as the following shows.

Again the Apostle exhorts to constancy of faith, because this is the whole in these exhortations, and first indeed by the word and example τῶν ἡγεμένων, especially of those who persevered constant in faith until the end of life v. 7. Then of the word and intercession, or rather generally of the office of Christ in perpetual vigor, v. 8. because Jesus Christ, as he is eternal regarding existence; so he performs a perpetual and eternal office for our sake, and is Jesus, that is, eternal Savior, and Christ, that is, Priest, who from eternity intervenes with his λύτρῳ interposed, and will intercede eternally by its presentation as a Priest forever, who has neither beginning nor end of days, who was yesterday, and is today, and remains the same immutable forever, as essence, by which he is true God: so also by grace of μεσιτείας; whence we can place in him perennial confidence μετὰ παῤῥησίας; whose word as our supreme Teacher is the eternal Gospel Rev. XIV, 6. and who also bears care for us, as our eternal King, forever, here in the kingdom of grace, so that we may be defended and preserved, and one day in the kingdom of glory, so that we may enjoy eternal beatitude; then the eternal grace of this intercession of our Priest; then also the power and eternal efficacy of the eternal Word, then the glory of the eternal dominion over us, by which he will gloriously illuminate us, so that we also may reign forever, triumphing over our enemies without end, Rev. XXI, 24. Chap. XXII, 5.

Furthermore, thirdly, concerning the fruit and merit of the satisfactory passion of Christ, v. 10, 11, 12. Finally, fourthly, by the example of the very passion of Christ, who willed to go out of the city and bear reproach outside the gate in a notorious place, so that we too might not fear to endure departures and bear his reproaches; primarily because he adds, most importantly for the sake of the exiles, that we have no permanent city here, but we seek the one to come, v. 13, 14.

Οἵτινες ἐλάλησαν ὑμῖν τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ.] Namely, in different towns, perhaps even at different times, when others had succeeded the dead.

Ὧν ἀναθεωροῦντες τὴν ἔκβασιν τῆς ἀναστροφῆς μιμεῖσθε τὴν πίστιν.] Recall to your minds their ἀναστροφή, that is, their manner and way of living. You have this word in Gal. I, 13; Eph. IV, 22; 1 Tim. IV, 12; Jas. III, 13; and often in the epistles of Peter. They exhibited holiness in their whole life and persisted in it even unto death, which is the ἔκβασις or καταστροφή of this life, and is called 'excessus' by the Latins. To the Hebrews, אחרית דרכיהם. They had received and kept this holiness through faith; therefore, see that you retain the same faith, so that your end may be equal.

By leaders can be understood not only the Apostles and Apostolic men, but also the Patriarchs, Prophets, and Priests of the Old Testament, since they were indeed also the ἡγούμενοι of the Hebrews, who spoke the Word of God to them, whom they could still hear speaking in the Word, Luke 16:29, whose ἔκβασις ἀναστροφῆς is also to be considered and imitated by constant ἀναθεωρίᾳ, as he had set forth their example at length above in chapter XI, when he introduced their νέφος μαρτύρων, because they were all μαρτυρηθέντες διὰ τῆς πίστεως, C. XI, 39, having commemorated primarily their ἐκβάσει ἀναστροφῆς, which is truly ἀξιομνημόνευτος. Whence Constantine of Antioch, according to the mind of Chrysostom, homily XXXIII, says regarding this exhortation to the memory of the leaders: τοῦτο ἄνωθεν ὠδινεν εἰπεῖν, 'he was already laboring to say this above,' cf. Jas. V, 10. The Apostle proposes to the Hebrews of the leaders 1. & primarily τὸν λόγον, the word, as the foundation of faith and perseverance, and he wishes them to be mindful of it, because faith is from the Word, and faith is to be fostered through the Word, which is the principle and nourishment or support of faith. 2. Τὴν ἀναστροφὴν, the manner of living, not only regarding holiness, but primarily regarding faith; as he expressly and clearly presents it to them to be imitated, so that, just as he had previously proposed to them the examples of the faith of the ancients, so now also he brings to their memory the same Let him recall the example of his teachers, who no less by their whole manner of life than by the doctrine of the Gospel, shone forth to them as heralds of the faith, according to the admonition of Christ, Matt. 5:16. 3. Τὴν ἔκβασιν or καταστροφὴν τῆς ἀναστροφῆς, the end and outcome of a faithful and holy manner of life, and consequently of the whole life, because they persevered in the true faith until the very end of life, and consequently obtained the end of faith, the salvation of souls, 1 Pet. 1:9. Which, therefore, he commands them to ἀναθεωρεῖν, that is, to contemplate with the greatest zeal. 4. He names specifically Τὴν πίστιν, the faith, which he commands them not only to contemplate accurately in those leaders who have died piously, remaining constant and persevering in certain adversities and persecutions, and even sealed by martyrdom, but also to imitate holily: Because he who is faithful even unto death, to him is given the crown of life, Rev. 2:10. He who shall have conquered through faith (1 John 5:10) shall not be harmed by the second death, Rev. 2:11. He who shall have believed and persevered in the faith shall be saved, Matt. 24:13, Mark 16:16. Theophylact: 'Looking upon,' that is, contemplating more intently. And just as the student of a painter directs the keenness of his eyes and mind toward some model proposed to him, so you too, diligently considering the outcome, that is, the manner of life and the end of life of those who instruct you in the faith, because it will be excellent, imitate their faith as well. For from faith flows an upright mode of living. For unless they had placed their faith in future goods, they would never have lived so uprightly and without blame, never hesitating.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Μνημονεύετε τῶν ἡγουμένων ὑμῶν] ἡγύμενοι אלוהים in Veteri Testamento sunt populorum aut exercituum Duces atque Principes, quod nomen hic optimo jure aptatur iis, qui apud Christianos κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν tum προεστῶτες tum ἐπίσκοποι dicuntur, quorum munus est non tantum praeesse Presbyterio, sed & κοπιᾶν ἐν τῷ λόγῳ, 1. Tim. V. v. 17. quale apud Judaeos fuit, & nunc est munus τῶν ἀρχισυναγώγων. Sic & in episto- la Clementis ad Corinthios bis ponuntur ἡγύμενοι, deinde πρεσβύτεροι. Loquitur autem de iis, qui jam obierant, ut ostendunt sequentia.

Iterum ad fidei constantiam hortatur Apostolus, quia haec in hisce exhortationibus τὸ πᾶν, & primo quidem verbo & exemplo τῶν ἡγεμένων, imprimis eorum, qui ad finem usque vitæ in fide constantes per- severarunt v. 7. Deinde verbi atque intercessionis, vel potius generatim officii Christi perpetuo vigo- re, v. 8. quod Jesus Christus, uti quoad existentiam æternus est; ita perpetuum & æternum munus no- stri causa gerat, & Jesus, id est, Salvator æternus sit, & Christus, hoc est, Sacerdos, qui ab æterno inter- venit λύτρῳ suo interposito, & in æternum ejus præsentatione interpellabit ceu Sacerdos in æter- num, qui nec principium nec finem dierum habet, qui heri fuit, & hodie est, & in æternum manet idem immutabilis, ut essentia, qua verus Deus : ita etiam μεσιτείας gratia; unde in eum perennem fiduciam collocare possumus μετὰ παῤῥησίας; cujus supremi Doctoris nostri verbum æternum est Evangelium æternum Apoc. XIV, 6. quique nostri curam etiam, ceu Rex noster æternus, in æternum gerit, hic in re- gno gratiæ, ut defendamur & conservemur, & olim in regno gloriæ, ut æterna beatitudine fruamur; tum intercessionis hujus Sacerdotis nostri æterna gratia; tum etiam æterni Verbi potentia & efficacia æterna, tum æterni in nos dominii gloria, qua nos gloriose illustrabit, ut & nos regnemus in æternum, de hostibus nostris triumphantes sine fine, Apoc. XXI, 24. Cap. XXII, 5.

Porro tertio passionis Christi satisfactoriæ fructu & merito v. 10. 11. 12. Quarto deniq; exemplo etiam ipsius passionis Christi, qui urbe exire, & extra por- tam in loco famoso opprobrium ferre voluit, ut & nos ne vereamur exitia sustinere, & opprobria ejus ferre; imprimis quod exulum causa potissimum addit, quia nullam hic habemus permanentem ci- vitatem, sed futuram quærimus v. 13. 14.

Οἵτινες ἐλάλησαν ὑμῖν τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ.] Nempe in diver- sis oppidis, forte etiam diversis temporibus, cum mortuis alii successissent.

Ὧν ἀναθεωροῦντες τὴν ἔκβασιν τῆς ἀναστροφῆς μιμεῖσθε τὴν πίστιν.] In animum vobis revocate ipsorum ἀναστροφὴν, id est, vivendi rationem ac modum. Habes hanc vocem Gal. I, 13. Eph. IV, 22. 1. Tim. IV, 12. Jac. III, 13. & in Petri epistolis sæ- pe. Sanctitatem in omni vita exhibuerunt, & in ea perstite- runt ad mortem usque, quæ est vitæ hujus ἔκβασις sive κατα- στροφὴ, & Latinis excessus dicitur. Ebræis אחרית דרכיהם. Hanc sanctitatem per fidem acceperant atque servaverant, quare videte eandem fidem retineatis, ut par sit & vester exi- tus.

Per præpositos intelligi possunt non solum Apo- stoli & viri Apostolici; sed etiam Patriarchæ, Pro- phetæ ac Sacerdotes Veteris Testamenti, quando- quidem illi revera quoque fuerint Ebræorum ἡγού- μενοι, qui ipsis Verbum Dei loquuti sunt, quos in verbo adhuc audire poterant loquentes, Luc. 16, 29. quorum etiam ἔκβασις ἀναστροφῆς perpetuæ ἀνα- θεωρίᾳ consideranda & imitanda, utpote quorum exemplum supra cap. XI. ipsis prolixe stiterat, cum eorũ νέφος μαρτύρων induxit, quod fuerint omnes μαρτυρηθέντες διὰ τῆς πίστεως, C. XI, 39. commemo- rata imprimis eorum ἐκβάσει ἀναστροφῆς, quæ vere ἀξιομνημόνευτος. Unde Constantinus Antiochenus ex mente Chrysostomi homil. XXXIII. de hac ad μνήμην τῶν ἡγεμένων cohortatione ait τοῦτο ἄνωθεν ὠδινεν εἰπεῖν hoc jam superius dicere parturiebat, conf. Jac. V, 10. Proponit autem Apostolus Ebræis præpositorum 1. & imprimis τὸν λόγον verbum, ceu fundamentum fidei & perseverantiæ, ejusque me- mores esse vult, quia è Verbo est fides, & per Ver- bum fovenda est fides, quod est principium ac nu- trimentum vel fulcimentũ fidei. 2. Τὴν ἀναστροφὴν, vivendi rationem, non quoad sanctitatem tantum, sed imprimis quoad fidem; utpote quam expresse ac diserte iisdem imitandam exhibet, ut, quemadmo- dum ipsis veterum fidelium exempla fidei antea proposuerat, ita nunc etiam in memoriam iisdem Doctorum suorum exemplum revocet, qui nõ mi- nus tota sua conversatione, quam doctrinã Evan- gelicæ præconis fide ipsis præluxere juxta Christi monitum, Matth.V.16. 3. Tὴν ě̄κβασιν vel κατασρο- φὴν τη̃ς άνασροφη̃ς, finem & exitũ conversationis fidelis & sanctæ, adeoq; vitæ totius, quod ad finem usque vitæ in vera fide perseverarint, adeoq; finẽ fidei salutem animarũ reportarint, 1.Pet.I.19. Quam proinde άναθεωρει̃ν, h.e. sum̃o studio intueri jubet. 4. Tὴν πίσιν peculiariter nominat Apostolω, quam in præpositis piè defunctis constantẽ & perseverantẽ in quibusdam adversitatibus & persecutionib9 mar- tyrio quoq; obsignatam, non intueri tantum accu- ratè, sed & imitari etiã sancte jubet: Quia qui fidelis est usq; ad mortem, ei datur corona vitæ, Ap. II. 10. Qui vicerit per fidem (1. Joh. V. 10.) non lædetur à morte secunda Ap.II.11. Qui crediderit & perseve- raverit in fide, salvus erit, Matth.XXIV.13. Marc. XVI.16. Theophylactus: Intuentes, hoc est, enixius contemplantes. Utq́ & pictoris discipulus in exemplar aliquod sibi propositum oculorum & ingenii intendit aciem, sic & vos se- dulo exitum considerantes, id est, eorum conversationem & vitæ finem, qui ad fidem vos instruunt, quod optimus sit futurus, imi- tamini illorum & fidem. A fide namque integer vivendi modus emanat. Nisi enim futuris bonis fidem hi præstitissent, & nihil hesitantem unquam tam integre & sine culpa vixissent.

## 13:8
Verse 8. Jesus Christ yesterday and today, the same also for the ages] He is the same, that is, like unto himself; just as we say, King Jupiter is the same to all. As he was yesterday, that is, in the time of those leaders of yours, so he is now and will be forever. For 'yesterday' signifies past time, as in Exod. 5, 7, 14; Isa. 30:33; Sir. 28:23. Just as he supported them with his Spirit even unto death, so he will support you, if you do what is yours to do.

Some interpret the subject 'Jesus Christ' metonymically as the knowledge of Christ, like Calvin, to whom Enjedinus appeals on p. 413. Or as the doctrine of Christ, like the Tigurines in their biblical notes, Bullinger, and Hyperius: But there is no reason why one should depart from the literal meaning of the word: Nor does the term 'Jesus Christ' occur anywhere for the doctrine or knowledge of Christ. Furthermore, the doctrine and knowledge that we have here of Christ is enigmatic, ἔσοπτρον, specular, and partial, which does not extend itself into the ages, but when that which is perfect shall have come, then that which is in part shall be done away, then we shall see face to face, 1 Cor. 13:9. Add that this periphrasis 'yesterday, today, the same, and for the ages' implies eternity, and consequently does not suit the doctrine and knowledge of Christ as it is now. That opposition also holds up very well between Christ, the Author of the saving doctrine, and the ἀρχηγὸν τῶν ἡγουμένων, through whom the word of God was delivered, who were always like themselves, and between strange doctrines, which are various, and their authors, v. 7, 8, 9.

As for the predicate, Christ is designated both by reason of his person and by reason of his office as being yesterday, today, the same, and for the ages, and his immutability in both respects is especially indicated. He had commended faith by the example of the leaders in Hebrews. Now he exhorts them from the proper object of faith to perseverance in the faith, because Jesus Christ is viewed both by reason of his person and his office. But he expresses the immutability and eternity of his person: Because the foundation of the eternal and immutable Mediatorial office is situated in it, because he could not be believed to be our Mediator and Jesus from eternity to eternity, nor anointed for the office with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, unless he were himself eternal and immutable by reason of his person. And therefore he is called ὁ αὐτὸς by way of excellence in an immutable sense, just as he is with that word from Ps. 102:26, above in ch. 1:10. divine immutability is expressed, regarding the divine nature of Christ, according to which he is Jehovah, that is, αὐτοταὐτόν, and through those differences of time taken together, 'yesterday and today, and for the ages,' his eternity is designated, embracing all differences of time without time, θειῶς καὶ ἀμέτρως, as we have shown in the Apodixis of the pre-existence of the Son of God, book 2, ch. 26. For Scripture everywhere establishes this as the foundation of redemption and the office of Christ the Mediator, his eternal Deity, Eph. 4:23 ff., Jer. 23:6, Acts 20:28. Because as Jesus our Savior is ὁ αὐτὸς, immutable, and 'yesterday and today, and for the ages,' that is, he is eternal, from the part before and from the part after, as they say. For in him we were chosen from eternity, and grace was given to us in Christ Jesus πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων, Eph. 1:4, 2. 2 Tim. 1:9, similarly as Christ, that anointed one of the Lord, is the same and immutable and eternal, because that anointing was decreed from eternity, even if it happened in time, and by the power of the eternal decree Christ was defined as our Priest, King, and Teacher: Who by an eternal decree, Ps. 2:7, 8, and the covenant of the Father, Gal. 3:9. John 17:1, 2, 3, was constituted our Mediator and Redeemer: who, as far as the priestly office is concerned regarding intercession, and the satisfaction of himself, present even then to the eyes of God and of the bride, to be performed once in the fullness of time, Heb. 9:26, ch. 10:12, is the cause of the virtue and efficacy both of the predestination of believers from eternity, and of the justification not only of us, but also of the Fathers in the Old Testament, because of the infinity of his person, whence he is also called the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world, Rev. 13:8, because of the eternal intuition of the future slaughter of Christ, and its eternal efficacy in predestination, the meritorious cause of which is the slaughter of the Lamb or the whole obedience of Christ. Furthermore, the Apostle also teaches with the Psalmist that the Priesthood of Christ endures forever, when he asserts that he is the same priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

But the kingly office of the Son of God, which it concerns, did not begin only in the fullness of time, except as regards human nature, as is clear from v. 5 preceding here, where ὁ αὐτὸς is introduced promising to Joshua: Οὐ μή σε ἀνῶ, ὐδ᾽ ὐ μή σε ἐγκαταλίπω, c. I. 5. which was done by the Son of God himself, as Leader of the army of the Lord, afterwards presenting himself in reality for aid, Jos. V. 14: Who was the Leader of the Israelite people, Exod. III. 2. seqq. cap. XXIII. 20. Is. LXIII. 1. Therefore the procession of this Leader is from the days of eternity and from of old, Mich. V. 2. Wherefore to this eternal King, the Son of the eternal King of God, Ps. LXXII. 1. Is. 7. 8. this eulogy best applies, that he is ὁ αὐτὸς χθὲς, καὶ σήμερον καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, inasmuch as of his kingdom there shall be no end, Is. IX. 6. Luke I. 33. Rev. XXII. 5. Whither the interpretation of Anselm of Canterbury goes. But lest you doubt that the Lord is a help to you, which was present to them, know that Jesus Christ was yesterday, and is today, the same also will be forever; as if it were said that the same Christ, who was with them, is with you, and will be with those who are to come even to the consummation of the age. He was yesterday with the Fathers, today he is with us, he himself also will be with our descendants forever. Lombard, in h. l. He says, this pertains to the previous sentence, where he testified that God had said, I will not desert you, nor will I abandon you. However, it might have seemed to them that this promise only concerned Joshua: To which the Apostle, speaking, replied: That it will also help us, just as it helped him. Wherefore there is no reason to doubt the promise, that Jesus Christ, who yesterday, i.e., in the past, helped Joshua, he himself today, that is, in the present, helps us and other believers, and will help in the future forever, that is, without end.

The same is to be held concerning the doctoral office of Christ: which the eternal λόγος exercised from the foundation of the world, but in the last times manifested in the flesh, he administered by ordinarily undertaking the duties of teaching, and even now speaks to us from heaven, not indeed immediately, but through his Ministers, and he will be our Teacher for all eternity, whose Word is also eternal, Is. XL. 7. Rev. XIV. 16. since through it all who are to believe perseveringly and to be saved in Christ are predestined. The Apostle had spoken of those set over them, whose most constant faith in Christ they ought to imitate. Now Jesus Christ, in whom not only they believed, and whom they professed: But from whom also they had doctrine and office, he sets before them, who was also the author and finisher of their faith. He calls the same one always and immutable, because His Word is immutable and eternal, and thus in respect of doctrine 'yesterday and today the same and for ever.' Whence the blessed Henricus Hopfnerus, in his dissertation for the Licentiate, which is the first in his Theological Disputations, Aph. IV, teaches that this aphorism, when compared with what precedes and follows, means this: Jesus Christ is the unique and invariable foundation of the doctrine of faith and of Christian confession and constancy, because 'the same' is opposed to plurality and to otherness, signifying the same as 'one' in Apoc. XVII. 10, just as Christ is called 'the same Lord,' 1 Cor. XII. 6, 'one Lord,' 1 Cor. VIII. 6, Eph. IV. 5; and it is opposed by David and the Apostle to mutability, as in Heb. I. 12, where the heavens 'shall be changed' and grow old, but 'the same' is opposed to them. He proves this sense from v. 7 of this passage, namely that identity is considered in respect of the doctrine, faith, and constancy of the Fathers: and from v. 9, what is opposed to that identity, 'to be carried about with diverse and strange doctrines,' i.e., to be carried about by various and foreign doctrines. For because Christ is the unique foundation of doctrine, Christian doctrine cannot be 'diverse': that is, according to Chrysostom, multiform and multimode. Because, likewise, Christ is the invariable foundation of doctrine, Christian doctrine cannot be 'strange,' i.e., nowhere consistent like wandering pilgrims, and, as Theophylact adds, straying from the path and as it were the dwelling-place of truth, by which men are carried about here and there, agitated by any wind of doctrine, Eph. IV. 14. Finally, the blessed Hopfnerus judges that it is indicated here that identity and immutability are attributed to Christ in respect of his office, when it is said that the heart, i.e., faith and constancy, is established by grace, and he makes the Apostle conclude thus: 'He who is the same yesterday, today, and for ever, the discourse of the Leaders concerning him is not to be consigned to oblivion: the faith of the Leaders placed in him is to be imitated: finally, the constancy of the Leaders in enduring his reproach is to be imitated: But Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and for ever. Therefore.' He teaches that the Apostle afterwards executes this general reason specifically by parts: 1. Regarding the memory of the doctrine of the Fathers: 'To whom it is good (salutary) that the heart be established with grace, that they be not carried about with diverse and strange doctrines.' 2. Regarding the imitation of the faith and confession of the Leaders. They who have an altar, whereof they have no power to eat, serving the tabernacle, let them offer to God through Christ (as through a Pontiff, Theophylact) the sacrifice of praise and of lips to his name (of divine power, justice, and mercy), the fruit of those confessing. We have an altar (i.e., a victim, by synecdoche of the container for the contained, such as is also 1 Cor. IX. 13, X. 10, which victim is Christ) whereof they have no power to eat who serve the tabernacle (followers of Judaism, who after Christ was exhibited denied his victim, while they wished to offer typical ones). Therefore 3. Concerning looking to the end of the conversation or life, by which the leaders testified to their constancy in bearing the cross of Christ. Whose Savior suffered outside the gate, let them go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach, v. 13. Item: They who have no abiding city, but seek one to come, they ought to go out to Christ, that is, to follow Christ, and to take up his cross, and to contradict all other things in the world, v. 14. These are the words of the blessed Hopfnerus.

But in this opinion two things are to be observed: first, that it does not favor the interpretation of Socinus against Bellarmine, c. VII, or of the Calvinists against Franz, p. 98, or of Schlichtingius on this passage: as if Christ, by metonymy of the cause, were the doctrine of Christ. Since indeed the prophetic office of Christ is one thing, and the doctrine proceeding from it is another: and the Apostle considers Christ insofar as he is the same foundation of doctrine, i.e., unique and immutable, 1 Cor. III. 9, Acts IV. 12, and from this identity of his concludes the identity of Christian doctrine as an effect, and opposes it to the variety of doctrines, and to being carried about here and there by them. Rightly, therefore, do the Genevans, Piscator, Tossanus, Polanus, etc., understand Christ with us properly as the person of Christ. Next, that by this explanation the demonstration of the eternal and immutable Deity of Christ is not denied. But although the words of the Apostle are not understood immediately of Christ as he is God, yet by consequence it is evinced from this. For the person whose efficacy is the same from eternity, that very person is invariable and eternal. But the efficacy of the person of Christ was the same from eternity.

We do not see, however, why it should not be believed that the immutability and eternity of Christ are immediately hinted at by these words, both in regard to his existence and hypostasis or Divine person, and in regard to his office of Mediator, and the eternal Gospel which he brought from the bosom of the eternal Father, John I. 18, just as the Fathers with great consensus accepted this aphorism concerning the very immutable and eternal Deity of Christ, concerning which more has been said at length in the cited Apodixis, and treated expressly and particularly by the blessed Dorscheus in his exegesis on this passage: who in § 46 notes: That this supreme and most perfect identity, which is the immovable basis of all human salvation, is to be understood in this place primarily. Every other thing falls where this does not subsist. For our finite salvation is not built upon 'selfhood' § 22. From the preceding he thus proves that 'to be the same' in this place infers a most excellent and clearly superior excellence placed above all the rules of creatures. The more remote antecedents, among which stands out the testimony of Jerome the Psalmist, c. I. 12, we do not repeat, but concerning the proximate ones he argues thus: The Apostle, he says, recalls the Hebrews to the assembly of the saints as an exemplar, μνημονεύετε τω̃ν ἡγυμένων ὑμω̃ν &c. of the Patriarchs, of the Prophets, and of all the heralds of heavenly truth universally. He recalls them, however, at the same time to the cause of the μνήμης. Jesus Christ ὁ αὐτὸς, is the same today, who was the author of the faith absolutely, who was the object, light, mover, and leader of the Patriarchs: The same whose Φωνὴ on Mount Sinai, speaking, shook the earth: The same whose Φω- νὴ now in the heavenly Jerusalem speaks from heaven better things than Abel; the same whose voice causes a shaking not only on earth, but also in heaven; The same: who is Jehovah of hosts proclaiming such things, Hag. II. 7. From the consequences, however, he meditates upon the sublimity of this identity thus: Do not be carried about by various and strange doctrines, v. 9. Why? Christ Jesus is ὁ αὐτὸς, and therefore he turns away from Vertumni and Eccboli; establish your heart with grace, not with foods, v. 9. Why? Jesus Christ ὁ αὐτὸς, has never loved the sons of the earth, he has always kissed those desirous of grace. Worship and embrace the altar of Jesus. Why? Jesus Christ ὁ αὐτὸς, opens his altar to all, he wishes to be worshipped by all, and so on. This, therefore, he says, is that greatness and amplitude attributed to the ἀὐτότης of Jesus, from which he concludes that Christ is called τὸν αὐτὸν with respect to supreme immutability, perfect eternity, perpetual immortality, and essential life, infinite power, who by infinite virtue has hitherto performed all things, immense goodness, who was first and unceasingly the fountain of every good, from whom are all the gifts and goods of mediation and satisfaction eternal. For he is ὁ αὐτὸς who from eternity found redemption by counsel and in time by aid, Heb. IX. 14. For just as when the holy scripture speaks of the Divine presence, it never represents the same to us in such a way that it depicts only a bare presence and lack of distance, but everywhere commends the same both by the nearness of ἀδιαστασίας and by the active συνδρομη̃ of various other Divine attributes, whence it is called the presence of power, of grace, and of glory, as has been shown elsewhere; So when that supreme αὐ- τότης, identity and immutability, is spoken of to us concerning God and the person of Christ, we must conceive of the same with the inclusion and combination of the other Divine perfections. Moreover, the words χθὲς καὶ σήμε- ρον καὶ εἰς αἰῶνας imply an infinite duration extending from eternity to eternity, a place concerning which we have already treated in the cited passage. The passage Heb. VII. 3 is to be compared primarily, where Christ is said to have μήτε ἀρχὴν ἡμερῶν, μή- τε τέλος ζωῆς ἔχων; as also the similar… parallel in Apoc. I. 8, Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α, καὶ τὸ Ω, ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος, λέγει Κύρι- ος, ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος. Regarding the antecedents in this passage, the blessed Dorscheus §. 35 connects them with the eternity of Christ in this way: Those who have been sent as heralds of the Divine Word by Jesus Christ as the ἀρχηγο͂ of the heavenly mission, who also was yesterday, and is now, and is to be in eternity, are to be followed in both memory and imitation. To this also pertains the corollary, since it is validly concluded thus: Those who have a doctrine flowing from that source which was from eternity, is now, and is to be in eternity, they ought by no means to be carried away to foreign and new doctrines. To this opinion Athanasius adds in his letter to Serapion: Υἱὸς ἀτρεπτός ἐστι καὶ ἀναλλοίωτος, ὡς ὁ Πατὴρ. Ἰησοῦς γὰρ Χριστὸς &c. Chrysostom on this passage: That word 'yesterday' signifies all past time, and 'today' the present age, but 'unto the ages' the future and infinite [time]. Johannes Cassianus, a disciple of Chrysostom: The same Jesus yesterday and today, that is, the same before the beginning of the world, who [is] in the flesh, the same in the past, who [is] in the present, the same also unto the ages, because he is the same through all things, who [is] before all things. Compare also Ambrose, book V de fide, ch. 2. Maximus, hom. III de Pasch. The blessed Gerhard on this passage: The full sense, he says, is this: Christ's nature, will, and power is immutable. Therefore, just as he made constant the confessors of his word safe: so he will also make you safe. And he brings forward the explanation of Haymo: That although Christ sustained his passion at a certain and appointed time, yet since he is an infinite person, the virtue of that passion itself extends to all times. And he adds: Which exposition likewise presupposes that the Divinity of Christ is proven in this saying. Osiander: But lest we think that the Gospel of Christ will be destroyed by the cruelty of tyrants, the Apostle sprinkles consolation, saying: Jesus Christ was yesterday and today, he himself is and will remain unto the ages, that is, Christ the Son of God, who according to his divinity was before all ages, who today (even as man) lives and reigns at the right hand of God, who is about to live and rule into all eternity, he will not allow the law of the Gospel to be extinguished at all: even if all tyrants rage and burst. For Christ remains with his Gospel. But tyrants descend to the underworld. The paraphrase of the Weimar theologians also agrees. Jesus Christ (the eternal Son of God, in whom you believe, is the very same) yesterday and today (as he is immutable according to his eternal Godhead, so he is also immutable according to his counsel and will, Matth. 3. v. 6. Therefore, just as he has made those who believed in him in the Old Testament, and steadfastly confessed him, blessed, so he also wishes now in the New Testament to make you and all who persevere in the confession of his name until the end, blessed. Act. 15. v. 11.) and the same (remains, the one eternal God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, immutable until) also in eternity. And Theodorus Zwinger acknowledges in his diatribe on this saying, that Christ is said to be the same with respect to himself, and to us: With respect to himself, both regarding his person and his office. Regarding his person, because, as Athanasius teaches concerning the one Christ: Ὁ αὐτὸς Θεὸς, ὁ αὐτὸς ἄνθρωπος, τὸ συ- ναμφότερον, ὢν ἂν ἑκάτερον ὡς μόνον: The same regarding his office as Mediator: with respect to us, that Christ is the same both by the communion of himself and his benefits, and by the knowledge of himself to the Fathers in the Old Testament and to us in the New Testament. To which latter respect our own blessed Hunnius tends: because it is shown that this doctrine concerning

Christ is not new, but that this Christ is the scope of the doctrine of all times. Jesus Christ yesterday, that is, in the past time of the Old [Testament], and today, that is, under the rise of the New Testament, and remains the sum and head of our salvation. And Guilielmus Estius exhibits the connection with the antecedents and consequents in such a way that it does not exclude that respect: namely, Your faith is in Jesus Christ, just as it was also that of your leaders. But Jesus Christ is always the same, therefore your faith also ought to be the same as the faith of those: and therefore it is necessary that you imitate their faith. If, however, Christ is always the same, and consequently the faith is the same: therefore you ought not to change the faith once received, nor lend your ears to those bringing other doctrines.

However, Horneius rashly opposes subordinate explanations here: St. Ambrose l. V de fide c. XI, Cyril de Fide ad Reginas, Nazianzen, Theodoret, and other ancients interpret these things concerning the eternal divinity of the Son of God, so that it becomes the same as that in Apoc. I. 4, 'Who is, who was, and who is to come.' Oecumenius accepted it concerning the doctrine of Christ, remaining always the same. But these expositions do not agree with the preceding ones. Therefore, Thomas more correctly and aptly to the purpose explains them thus: Do not wonder that I order you to imitate the faith and constancy of the Apostles: for he who instructed and confirmed them yesterday and today, that is, so recently by his grace, the same one will also be present with us by his Spirit: for he still lives and will live unto the ages.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ἰησου̃ς Χριστός χθὲς καὶ σήμερον, ὁ αὐτός καὶ εἰς τὺς αἰ ω̃νας] Idem est, id est, sibi similis; sicut dicimus, Rex Iupiter omnibus idem. Qualis heri, id est, tempore illorum præposi- torum vestrorum, talis & nunc est & erit semper. Nam heri præteritum tempus significat, ut Exod. 5, 7. 14. Es. 30, 33. Sir. 28, 23. Sicut illos ad mortem usque Spiritu suo fulsit, sic & vos fulciet, si faciatis, quod vestrum est.

Subjectum Jesus Christus nonnulli Metonymice interpretantur de agnitione Christi, ut Calvinus, ad quem provocat Enjedinus p. 413. Vel de doctrina Christi, ut Tigurini in not. Bibl. Bullingerus & Hy- perius: Sed nulla est causa, cur à proprietate vocis recedendũ sit: Nec uspiam vox Jesus Christus oc- currit pro doctrina vel cognitione Christi. Ad hæc doctrina & cognitio, quam hic habem9 de Christo ænigmatica est, ě̄σοπīρικὴ, specularis, & partialis, quæ nõ porrigit sese in secula, sed cum τὸ τέλειον venerit, tunc id, quod ex parte est, consummabitur, tunc à fa- cie ad faciem videbimus, 1. Cor. XIII. 9. Adde quod περίφρασις illa heri, hodie, idẽ & in secula æternitatẽ inferat, adeoq; doctrinæ, & cognitioni Christi, qua- lis nunc est, nõ conveniat. Optimè etiam sibi con- stat oppositio illa inter Christum Autorem doctrinæ salutiferæ, & ἀρχηγὸν τω̃ν ἡγυμένων, per quos tra- ditum est verbum Dei, qui semper sibi similes fue- re, & inter doctrinas peregrinas, quæ variæ earum- que autores v. 7. 8. 9.

Quod ad prædicatum designatur Christus & ra- tione personæ, & ratione officii esse heri, hodie, idem & in secula, ejusque imprimis immutabilitas utrius- que respectu indicatur. Fidem exemplo τω̃ν ἡγυμέ- νων Ebr. com̃endarat. Jam ab objecto fidei proprio eos ad perseverantiam in fide exhortatur, quod Jesus Christus est tũ personæ tum officii ratione spectatus. Personæ autem exprimit immutabilitatem & æterni- tatem: Quia in ea situm est fundamentum officii Me- diatorii æterni & immutabilis, quia nec ab æterno in æternum Mediator & Jesus noster, nec ad offici- um unctus credi posset isnensis SpiritusS. donis, nisi æternus ipse ac immutabilis esset personæ ratione. Ideoq; ὁ αὐτὸς dicitur κατ̓ ἐξοχὴν immutabili rati- one, quemadmodum ea voce è Psal. CII. 26. supra c.I.10. immutabilitas divina expressa, quoad naturā Christi divinam, juxta quam Jehovah est, hoc est, αὐτοτα[υ]τόν, & per illas differentias temporis simul acceptas, χθὲς καὶ σήμερον, καὶ εἰς τὺς αἰω̃νας designa- ta est ejusdē æternitas, omnes temporis differentias sine tempore, θει̰κω̃ς καὶ ἀμέτρως complectens, ut in Apodixi præxist. Filii Dei libr. II. c. XXVI. ostendi- mus. Nam hoc fundamentum redemptionis & of- ficii Mediatoris Christi constituit scriptura passim æternam ejusDeitatem, Ef.XLV. 23. seq. Jer. XXIII. 6. Act. XX. 28. Quia ut Jesus Salvator noster ὁ αὐτὸς immutabilis, & χθὲς καὶ σήμερον, καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, hoc est, ætern9 est, à parte ante & à parte post, ut loquun- tur. Nam in ipso ab æterno sumus electi, & data no- bis est χάρις inChristo Jesu πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων Eph. I. 4. 2. Tim. I. 9. similiter ut χρισὸς unct9 ille Domini est idem, & immutabilis atque æternus, quod ab æ- terno decreta sit illa unctio, etsi in tempore conti- gerit, & vi decreti æterni Christus definitus fuerit Sacerdos, Rex & Doctor noster : Qui æterno decre- to, Pfal. II. 7. 8. & pactoPatris, Gal. III. 9. Joh. XVII. 1. 2. 3. constitutus est Mediator & Redemptor noster: qui quantum ad Sacerdotale officium quoad inter- cessionem, & sponsæ, atque oculis Dei jam tum præsentis satisfactionis ipsius in plenitudine tem- poris semel peragendæ, Ebr. IX. 26. c. X. 12. virtutem, atque efficaciam, causa est tum Prædestinationis cre- diturorum ab æterno, tum justificationis non nostræ tantum, sed etiamPatrum in V. Test. propter personæ infinitatē, unde & Agnus dicitur mactatus ab origine mundi, Apoc. XIII. 8. ob æternum intuitum macta- tionis Christi futuræ, æternamq; efficaciam in præ- destinatione, cujus causa meritoria est mactatio A- gni vel tota obedientia Christi. Porrò etiam in æ- ternum durareSacerdotiumChristi docet cum Hi- ero- PsalteApostol. cum eundem Sacerdotem esse in æternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech adstruit.

Regium veròFiliiDei officium quod concernit, non id demum cœpisse in plenitudine temporis, nisi quoad naturam humanam, vel è v. 5. hic præce- dente liquet, ubi ὁ αὐτὸς introducitur Josuæ pro- mittens: Οὐ μή σε ἀνῶ, ὐδ᾽ ὐ μή σε ἐγκαταλίπω, c. I. 5. quod à FilioDei ipsi, ceuDuce exercitusDomi- ni, postea in auxilium sese reapse sistente, Jos. V. 14. factum: QuiDuctor populi Israëliti ci fuit, Exod. III. 2. seqq. cap. XXIII. 20. Ef. LXIII. 1. Ideo Ducis ejus proceffus inde à diebus æternitatis & à seculo est, Mich. V. 2. Quapropter huic Regi æterno, Dei æ- terni Regis Filio, Pf. LXXII. 1. Il. 7. 8. hoc elogium optime convenit, quod sit ὁ αὐτὸς χθὲς, καὶ σήμερον καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, utpote cujus regni non erit finis, Esa. IX. 6. Luc. I. 33. Apoc. XXII. 5. Quo abit interpre- tatio Anshelmi Cantuar. Ne autem dubitetis, Domi- num vobis adjutorium esse, quod illis adfuit, scitote, quia Jesus Christus heri fuit, & hodie est, ipse & in secula erit; ac si dica- tur idem Christus, qui cum illis fuit, vobiscum est, & erit cum eis,qui futuri sunt usque ad consummationem seculi. Heri fu- it cumPatribus, hodie est nobiscum, ipse etiam erit cum posteris nostris in secula. Lombardus, in h. l. Hoc inquit, pertinet ad superiorem sententiam, ubi testatus est, Deum dixisse, non deseram te, neque de relinquam te. Poterat autem illis videri,quod hæc promissio tantum ad Josuam specta- ret: Ad quod Apostolus dicens respondit: Quod & nos juva- bit, sicut & illum juvit. Quare non est dubitandum de promis- sione, quod JesusChristus, qui heri, i. e. in præterito adjuvit Jo- suæ, ipse hodie, id est, in præsenti adjuvet nos, & alios fideles, & adjuvabit in futuro in secula, id est, sine fine.

Quod de officioChristiDoctorali pariter haben- dum : quod λόγος æternus inde à condito mundi gessit, novissimis verò temporib9 in carne manife- status ordinariè susceptis docendi partibus admi- nistravit, atque etiamnum de cœlo nobis loquitur non ἀμέσως quidem, sed per Ministros suos, ac Doctor noster erit in omnem æternitatem, cujus etiam Verbum æternum est, Ef. XL. 7. Apoc. XIV. 16. siquide per illud omnes perseveranter credituri, ac salvandi inChristo sint prædestinati. DixeratA- postolus de præpositis, quorum fidem in Christum imitari debeant constantissimam. Jam Christum Je- sum, in quem non tantú illi credidere, quemq; pro- fessi sunt: Sed à quo etiam doctrinā & officium ha- buere, ipsis sistit, qui & ἀρχηγὸς κὴ τελειωτὴς fidei ipsorum fuit. Quem eundem semper, & immutabilem dicit, quod Verbum ejus immutabile, & æternum sit, adeoque doctrinæ ratione χθὲς κὴ σήμερον τὸν αὐ- τὸν κὴ εἰς τὴς αἰῶνας. Unde sensum hujus aphorismi B. Henr. Hopfnerus in disp. pro Licentia, quæ prima est in disp. Theol. Aph. IV. cum antecedentib9 & consequentibus collati huncce docet: Jesus Christus est doctrinæ fidei & confessionis ac constantiæ Christia- næ unicum & invariabile fundamentum, quia ὁ αὐτὸς & pluralitati & ἀλλότητι opponitur, significans ide, quod εἷς unus Apoc. XVII. 10. uti Christus ὁ αὐτὸς κύ- ριος, 1. Cor. XII. 6. εἷς κύριος, 1. Cor. VIII. 6. Eph. IV. 5. vocatur; & mutabilitati, ut Ebr. I. 12. cœlis ἀλ- λαγησομένοις mutãdis ac veteraturis ὁ αὐτὸς oppo- nitur à Davide & Apostolo. Quem sensum è v. 7. hu- jus loci probat, quod nempe identitas consideretur ratione doctrinæ, & fidei, ac constantiæ Patrum: & è v. 9. quid identitati illi opponatur τὸ περιφέρε- σθαι ποικίλαις κὴ ξέναις διδαχαῖς i. e. circumferri variis & peregrinis doctrinis. Quia enim Christus est fun- damentum doctrinæ unicum, doctrina Christiana non potest esse ποικίλη: hoc est juxta Chrysostomum mul- tiformis & multimoda: Quia item Christus invaria- bile est doctrinæ fundamentum, doctrina Christia- na non potest esse ξένη peregrina, i. e. nusquã con- sistens instar oberrantium peregrinatorum, atque, ut Theophyl. addit, à semita & quasi domicilio veri- tatis aberrans, qua homines circumferuntur huc & illuc, quolibet doctrinæ vento agitati, Eph. IV. 14. Deniq; quod hic identitas & immutabilitas ratione officii Christo tribuatur, indicari censet B. Hopf- nerus, cum cor, h. e. fides & constantia gratia stabiliri dicitur & Apostolum ita concludente facit: Qui ho- die, heri, & in secula idẽ, de illo sermo Ductorũ non est oblivioni tradenda: in illum posita fides Ductorum est imitanda: in illius deniq; opprobrio sustinendo con- stantia Ductorum est imitanda: Sed Jesus Christus est heri, hodie, & in secula idem. Ergo. Quam generalem ratione postea per partes speciatim exequi docet Apostolum 1. Quoad memoriam doctrinæ Patrum: Quibus bonũ (salutare) est, gratia stabiliri cor, illi ne circumferantur variis & peregrinis doctrinis. 2. Quoad imitationem fidei & confessionis Ductorum. Qui habent altare, de quo non habent potestatem edendi, tabernaculo inservientes, illi per Christum (tanquam per Pontificem Theophyl.) offerant Deo sacrificium laudis & labiorum nomini ejus (poten- tiæ, justitiæ, ac misericordiæ divinæ) fructum con- fitentium. Nos habemus altare (i. e. victimam, per Sy- necdochen continentis pro contento, qualis etiam est 1. Cor. IX. 13. X. 10. quæ victima est Christ9) de quo non habent potestatem edendi deservientes tabernacu- lo, (sectatores Judaismi, qui post exhibitum Chri- stum victimam ejus abnegarunt, dum typicas vo- luerunt offerre). Ergo 3. De intuendo exitu conver- sationis vel vitæ, qua ductores suam in tollenda cru- ce Christi constantiam testati sunt. Quorum Salva- tor passus est extra portam, illi exeant ad eum extra castra, opprobrium ejus portantes, v. 13. Item: Qui non habent manentem civitatem, sed futuram inquirunt, illi debent ad Christum exire, id est, sequi Christum, ejusque crucem tollere, & cæteris ominibus in mun- do contradicere, v. 14. Hæc B. Hopfnerus.

In qua vero sententia duo observãda, primo quod non faveat Socin. contr. Bellarm. c. VII. vel Calvi- niarum contra Franz. p. 98. Schlichtingii in h. l. in- terpretationi: quasi Christus per Metonymiã causæ doctrinam Christi: Siquidẽ aliud sit officium Christi Propheticũ, & aliud inde proveniens, nempe doctri- na: Et Apostolus consideret Christum, quatenus est fundamentum doctrinæ idem, h. e. unicum & immu- tabile, 1. Cor. III. 9. Act. IV. 12. & ex hac ejus identita- te concludat identitatem doctrina Christiana, tan quam effectus, eamque opponat doctrinarum va- rietati, perque illas nobilitati, & huc illuc agitatio- ni. Rectè itaque nobiscum Christum intelligunt proprie de persona Christi Genevenses, Piscator, Tos- sanus, Polanus &c. Deinde quod non negetur hac explicatione apodixis æternæ & immutabilis Deitatis Christi: Sed quamvis ἀμέσως non intelligantur verba Apostoli de Christo, qua Deus est, per con- sequentiam tamen illa hinc evincatur. Cuj9 enim personæ efficacia est eadem ab æterno, illa ipsa persona est invariabilis & æterna. Sed personæ Christi efficacia fuit ab æterno eadem.

Non videmus tamen, cur non immediatè hisce verbis Christi immutabilitas & æternitas, & quoad existentiam ac hypostasin vel personam ejus Divinam & quoad officium Mediatorii, ac Evangelium æter- num, quod è sinu æterni Patris protulit, Joh. I. 18. in- nui credenda sit, quamadmodum magno cō sensu Patres hunc aphorismũ de ipsa immutabili & æter- na Deitate Christi accepere, quo de in Apodixi ci- tata fusius dictum, & ex professo imprimis à B. Dor- scheo in exeg. h. l. peculiariter actum: Qui §. 46. no- tat: Πρώτως identitatem illam summam ac perfectis- simam, qua basis est immobilis totius salutis humanæ, hoc loco intelligendam. Cadit omnis alia, ubi hæc non subsistit. Neq́ enim salus nostra finita ἀὐτότητι super- struictur §. 22. ex Antecedentibus ita probat αὐτὸν εἶ- ναι hoc loco præstantissimam, & plane supra omnes creaturarum regulas positam excellantiã inferre. Remotiora antecedentia, in quib9 eminet testimo- nium Hiero Psal̃tis, c. I. 12. adductũ non repetimus, de proximis ita discurrit: Ad cœtum, inquit, sancto- rum exemplarẽ revocat Ebræos Apostolus μνημονεύ- ετε τω̃ν ἡγυμένων ὑμω̃ν &c. Patriarcharum, Prophe- tarum, & uiuniversũ omnium cœlestis veritatis præ- conum. Revocat autem simul ad causam μνήμης. Je- sus Christus ὁ αὐτὸς, idem hodie est, qui fuit ἀρχηγὸς γῆς πίσεως absolutè, qui fuit Patriarcharum obje- ctũ, lumen, motor, dux: Idẽ cujus Φωνὴ in monte Sinai χρηματίζυσα τὴν γῆν ἐσάλευσεν: Idẽ cuj9 nunc Φω- νὴ in Ἱερυσαλὴμ ἐπυρανίῳ ἀπ’ ὐρανω̃ κρείττονα λα- λει̃ παρὰ τὸν Ἄβελ; idem cuj9 vox σεισμὸν facit non solum in terra, sed etiam in cœlo; Idem: qui est Jeho- vah exercituum talia ἀπαγγέλλων Agg. II. 7 Ex con- sequentib9 autem identiatis sublimitatem ita me- ditatur: Doctrinis variis & peregrinis ne circũferimi- ni, v. 9. Cur? Christus Jesus est ὁ αὐτὸς, itaque Ver- tumnos & Eccbolos aversatur, gratia, non cibis stabi- lite cor, v. 9. Cur? Jesus Christus ὁ αὐτὸς, nunquam terra filios amavit, gratia cupidos semper est osculatus. Altare Jesu colite & complectimini. Cur? Jesus Chri- stus ὁ αὐτὸς, altare suum patefacit omnibus, vult ab omnibus coli, & sic deinceps. Hæc ergo, inquit, est illa ἀὐτότης Jesu tributa magnitudo & amplitudo, un- de concludit Christum dici τὸν αὐτὸν respectu summæ immutabilitatis, perfectæ æternitatis, perpetuæ im- mortalitatis, & vitæ essentialis, infinitæ potentiæ, qui infinitæ virtute hucusque omnia præstitit, immensæ bo- nitatis, qui primum & indefinenter fuit fons omnis bo- ni, à quo omnia dona & bona mediationis & satisfa- ctionis æternæ. Est enim ὁ αὐτὸς qui ab æterno re- demptionē invenit consilio & in tempore auxilio, Ebr. IX. 14. Quemadmodum namque quando de præsentia Divina sacrosancta scriptura loquitur, nunquam ita eandem nobis repræsentat, ut nudam adessentiam & indistantiam tantum depingat, sed ubique eandem & ἀδιαστασίας propinquitate, & variorum aliorũ attributorum Divinorum operosa συνδρομη̃ commen- dat, unde præsentia potentiæ, gratiæ & gloriæ dicitur, ut alibi ostensum est; Ita cum summa illa αὐ- τότης identitas & immutabilitas nobis de Deo & Christi persona dicitur, eandem cum inclusione & complexione cæterarum Divinarum perfectionum con- cipere necesse habemus. Verba autem χθὲς καὶ σήμε- ρον καὶ εἰς αἰῶνας inferunt durationem infinitam ab æterno in æternum se extendentem, quo de loco laudato egimus. Conferendus imprimis locus Ebr. VII. 3. ubi Christus dicitur μήτε ἀρχὴν ἡμερῶν, μή- τε τέλος ζωῆς ἔχων; ut & similis parallelus Apoc. I. 8. Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α, καὶ τὸ Ω, ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος, λέγει Κύρι- ος, ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος. Quod ad anteceden- tia in hoc loco ita ea connestit cum æternitate Chri- sti B. Dorscheus §. 35. Qui Verbi Divini præcones à Jesu Christo tanquam cælestis missionis ἀρχηγο͂ missi sunt, qui & heri fuit, & nunc est, & in æternum futu- rus est, illi & memoria & imitatione prosequendi sunt. Eo etiam pertinet πόρισμα, quum valide ita con- cludatur: Qui habent doctrinam ab eo fonte proma- nantem, qui ab æterno fuit, nunc est, & in æternum fu- turus est, illi ad peregrinas novasq́; doctrinas nequa- quam ferri debent. Sententiæ huic accedit Athana- sius ad Serapium: Υἱὸς ἀτρεπτός ἐστι καὶ ἀναλλοίωτος, ὡς ὁ Πατὴρ. Ἰησοῦς γὰρ Χριστὸς &c. Chrysostomus in hunc locum: Illud heri dicit omne tempus præteritum, & hodie præsens sæculum, in sæcula autem futurum & infinitum. Johannes Cassianus Chrysostomi discipu- lus: Idem Jesus heri & hodie, id est, idem ante exor- dium mundi, qui in carne, idem in præterito, qui in præsenti, idem quoque etiam in secula, quia idem per omnia, qui ante omnia. Conf. & Am- brosius libr. V. de fide cap. 2. Maximus hom. III. de Pasch. B. Gerhardus in h. l. Plenus sensus, inquit, hic est: Christi natura voluntas & potentia est immuta- bilis. Vt ergo salvos fecit constantes verbi sui con- fessores: ita & vos salvos faciet. Et adducit Hay- monis explicationem: Quod Christus, quamvis certo & constituto tempore passionem sustinuerit, tamen cum sit infinita persona, virtutem passionis ipsius se extendere ad omnia tempora: Additque: Quæ expo- sitio itidem Divinitatem Christi in hoc dicto probari præsupponit. Osiander: Ne autem putemus, Christi Evangelium sævitia Tyrannorum deletum iri, asper- git Apostolus consolationem, dicens: Jesus Christus fuit heri & hodie, ipse est & manebit in sæcula, id est, Christus Filius Dei, qui juxta divinitatem suam fuit ante omnia sæcula, qui hodie, (etiam ut homo) vivit & regnat ad dextram Dei, qui victurus & domina- turus est in omnem æternitatem, is non patietur pror- sus extingui legem Evangelii: etiamsi omnes tyranni insaniant & rumpantur. Christus enim cum Evan- gelio suo manet. Tyranni verò ad tartara descendunt. Consonat & paraphrasis Vinariensium. Jesus Chri- stus (der ewige Sohn GOttes, an welchen ihr glau- bet, ist eben derselbe) gestern und heute (wie er sei- ner ewigen Gottheit nach ist unwandelbar, also ist er auch nach seinem Rath und Willen unwandel- bar, Matth. 3. v. 6. Demnach wie er diejenigen so im Alten Testament an ihn geglaubet, und standhaff- tig ihn bekennet, selig gemacht hat, also will er auch jetzo im N. Testament euch und alle, so in Bekänt- niß seines Namens bis ans Ende verharren, selig machen. Act. 15. v. 11.) und derselbe(bleibet, der einis ge ewige GOtt m't Vater und dem Heiligen Geis ste unwandelbar bis) auch in Ewigkeit. Et agno- scit Theod. Zwingerus in diatribe de hoc dicto, Christum eundem dici respectu sui, & nostri: Sui re- spectu tum quoad personam, tum quoad officium. Quoad personam, quia, ut Athanasius docet de uuo Christo: Ὁ αὐτὸς Θεὸς, ὁ αὐτὸς ἄνθρωπος, τὸ συ- ναμφότερον, ὢν ἂν ἑκάτερον ὡς μόνον: Eundem quo- ad officium Mediatorem: nostri respectu, Christum eundem esse tum communione sui & beneficiorũ suo- rum, tum cognitione sui & Patribus in V. Test. & no- bis in N. Test. Ad quem posteriorem respectum ten- dit è nostris B. Hunnius: quod monstretur, hanc de

Christo doctrinam non esse novam, sed hunc Christum scopum esse doctrinæ omnium temporum. Jesus Chri- stus heri, id est, in præterito tempore veteris, & hodie, id est, sub exortu N. Test. & manet summa, atque caput salutis nostræ. Et Guilb. Estius connexionem cum antecedentibus & consequentibus eam exhi- bet, quæ illum respectum non excludat: h. m. Fides vestra est in Jesum Christum, sicut & fuit vestrorum præpositorum. Atqui Jesus Christus semper idem est, ergo & fides vestra eadem esse debet cum fide illorum: ideoque necesse est, ut fidem illorum imitemini. Si a. Christus semper idem est, ac proinde fides eadem: non ergo debetis mutare fidem, semel acceptam, nec aures præbere alias doctrinas adferentibus.

Temerè a. hic subordinatas explicationes op- ponit Horneius: S. Ambrosius l. V. de fide c. XI. Cyril- lus de Fide ad Reginas, Nazianzenus, Theodoretius & veteres alii de æterna divinitate Filii Dei hæc inter- pretantur, ut idem fiat cum illo Apoc. I. 4. Qui est, qui erat, & qui venturus est. Oecumenius de doctrina Christi accepit, eadem semper permanente. Sed hæ ex- positiones cum præcedentibus non conveniunt. Rectius ergo & apte ad propositum Thomas ea sic explicat: Ne miremini, quod imitari vos fidem & constantiam Apostolorum jubeam: nam qui illos heri & hodie, id est, tam nuper gratia sua instruxit & confirmavit, idem ille & nobis aderit Spiritu suo: adhuc enim vi- vit & in secula vivet.

## 13:9
Vers. 9. Διδαχαῖς ποικίλαις κὴ ξέναις μὴ περιφέρεσθαι] Πε- ριφέρεσθαι is to be agitated, as Eph. IV. 14, Jude 12, Prov. 10, 25, Eccl. VII. 8, ὅτι ἡ συκοφαντία περιφέρει σοφὸν. Hesychius: περιφορά, πλάνη, that is, aberration. But the Manuscript [reads] μὴ παραφέρεσθε, that is, do not be insane, in which way that word is taken in 1 Sam. XXI. 13. To Plato, παραφέρεσθαι is to err: truly to be carried past. And thus the Latin seems to have read, when it translates 'to be led away,' as also the Syriac. He touches upon Jewish doctrines, which were first various, from Shammai and Hillel, not concordant, such as those of the Apostles: then foreign, that is, new, recently discovered, not from the very words of the law or perpetual use. See Mat. XV. 9 and what is said there. Thus ξένα δαιμόνια Act. XVII. 8, new, hitherto unknown.

If these things are referred to Jewish doctrines, there will be an opposition between the ancient Jews, adhering to the faith most ancient from Abel onwards, and the newcomers, who had introduced foreign doctrines, such as the Pharisees were, and the Pseudo-Apostles who followed them, and other Judaizers. Yet any new and foreign doctrine can in general be considered as having diverged from that ancient faith τῶν ἡγεμένων, which is not one, just as truth is, but ποικίλη, various and manifold, as Thomas says here: Since truth consists in the middle, therefore many false things can be opposed to one true thing; just as many extremes to one mean. The doctrine of faith is one, because it is not fitting to draw from point to point except one straight line. But all other doctrines are many, because it happens to deviate from the straight in many ways. This is the Apostolic inference according to Blessed Dorscheus, l. c. §. 37. Whose doctrine was defined from all eternity in the secret counsel of the most holy Trinity, afterwards handed down from the origin of the world by most holy men. Finally, it is to be forever, and to obtain victory against all other doctrines; that is by no means to be exchanged with various and foreign doctrines. But the doctrine of Christ concerning salvation to be obtained only through Him was defined from all eternity in the secret counsel of the most holy Trinity, afterwards handed down from the origin of the world by most holy men, finally it is to be forever, and to obtain victory over all other doctrines. Therefore.

Καλὸν γὰρ χάριτι βεβαιοῦσθαι τὴν καρδίαν ὐ βρώμασι] He commends, as above, τὴν ἀυτάρκειαν. For many were being led away from Christianity, because they could not bear narrow circumstances. Feasts, which easily arise from an abundance of riches, are said to support the heart, that is, the strength of the body, Gen. XVIII. 5. In the Hebrew Ps. CV. 16, where in the Greek it is στήριγμα ἄρτου. So also Ez. IV. 16. V. 16. VII. 11. XIV. 13. But indeed grace, that is, the gifts of the Spirit given through the goodness of God, is that which supports the heart, that is, the mind against temptations, 1. Cor. I. 6. 8. 2. Cor. I. 21. Coloss. II. 7. Rom. I. 11. XVI. 25. 1. Thessal. III. 2. 13. 2. Thess. II. 17. III. 3. 2. Petr. I. 12.

In which they were not profited who walked] In the manuscript περιπατῶντες; so that ὠφελήθησαν is an Aorist used for the present tense. They never profit unto piety who, not content with necessary food, are eager for similar delicacies. He notes those teachers of Judaism, whom their very works betrayed, Rom. XVI. 18. Phil. III. 19. Tit. I. 12.

These things are rashly snatched by Grotius to refer to banquets: which gloss he seems to have from Crellius and Schlichtingius, whereas the Apostle descends from the genus to the species, from the thesis to the hypothesis, bringing forward one example from the various doctrines which the teachers of error were preaching, and that one adapted to those to whom he writes. For the Jews converted to Christ were clinging too superstitiously to the observation of legal ceremonies, especially to the distinction of foods prescribed by Moses, Num. XIV. 2. Deut. II. 16. He argues against them, says Theophylactus, who had introduced the Jewish abstinence from foods and their observation. For he says, you are to be established by grace (that is, by faith), and rendered more certain that nothing is absolutely unclean, and that all things are pure to the believer. Therefore, this faith, not the observation of foods, is necessary. For as for those who have taken heed from foods, that is, who are always intent upon such observation of foods, it is clear that these have profited nothing: as those who wander outside the true bounds of faith, and serve a law that is entirely useless. For what advantage were they obtaining from that observation? Blessed Höpfner takes these things in the antithesis of the doctrine of the Law and the Gospel, and wishes to be proved here what had been said, it is good for you to have the heart established by grace, from the opposition of the ἀντιδιηρημένων (contrasted) species, either by grace or by foods it is good for the heart to be established. But not by foods (that is, by legal observations, as Chrysostom, Theophylactus, Theodoret, and Anselm explain by synecdoche), 1 Tim. IV. 8. E.g., the doctrine of the Gospel offering and giving grace. Furthermore, he thinks the epilogism of this minor premise is also added from the experience of the contrary effect: Those who have not been helped (justified and saved) by walking in it (the observers of it), it is not good for the heart to be established in it. But the observers of foods have not been helped by foods. Therefore, it is not good for the heart to be established by foods. The verb βεβαιῶσθαι is opposed to the fluctuation signified by the verb περιφέρεσθαι, In which they were not profited who walked. Vulgate: Which (foods) did not profit those walking in them. In the Greek it is properly: In which, those who walked, obtained no utility, that is, which contributed nothing to those who placed much effort and importance in such observations.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Διδαχαῖς ποικίλαις κὴ ξέναις μὴ περιφέρεσθαι] Πε- ριφέρεσθαι est agitari, ut Eph. IV. 14. Judæ 12. Prov. 10, 25. Eccl. VII. 8. ὅτι ἡ συκοφαντία περιφέρει σοφὸν Hesychius περιφορά, πλάνη id est, aberratio. At Manuscriptus, μὴ παραφέρεσθε, id est, ne insanite, quomodo ea vox sumitur 1. Sam. XXI. 13. Platoni παραφέρεσθαι est, errare: verum prætervehi. Et ita videtur legisse Latinus, cum vertit abduci, ut & Syrus. Tangit Judaicas doctrinas, quæ erant primum variæ à Saimea & Hillele, non concordes, quales illæ Apostolorum: deinde peregrinæ, id est, novæ, nuper repertæ, non ex ipsis verbis legis aut perpetuo usu. Vide Mat. XV. 9. & ibi di- cta. Sic ξένα δαιμόνια Act. XVII. 8. nova, antehac incognita.

Si ad Judaicas doctrinas hæc referantur, opposi- tio erit inter veteres Judæos, antiquissimæ inde ab Abele fidei inhærentes, & novellos, qui peregrinas doctrinas invexerant, quales Pharisæi erant, & eos sequuti Pseudo Apostoli, aliiq; Judaizantes. Potest tamen in genere quævis doctrina nova & peregri- na ab illa antiqua fide τῶν ἡγεμένων divaricata, quæ nõ una est, quemadmodum veritas, sed ποικίλη varia & multiplex, ut hic Thomas: Cum veritas in medio consistat, ideo uni vero multa falsa opponi possunt; sic ut uni medio multa extrema. Doctri- na fidei una est, quia à puncto in punctum non con- venit ducere, nisi unam lineam rectam. Omnes au- tem aliæ doctrinæ multæ sunt, quia à recto multis modis cõtingit deviare. Apostolica illatio hæc est secundum B. Dorsheum l. c. §. 37. Cujus doctrina fuit ab omni æternitate in arcano satrosanctæ Trinitatis consilio definita, postea ab origine mundi à sanctissimis viris tradita. Deniq; futura est in perpetuum, & obten- tura contra omnes alias doctrinas victoriam, illa nequa- quam cum variis & peregrinis doctrinis commutanda est. At doctrina Christi de salute non nisi per ipsum im- petranda fuit ab omni æternitate in arcano SS. Trini- tatis consilio definita, postea ab origine mundi à san- ctissimis viris tradita, deniq; futura est in perpetuum, & obtentura omnes alias doctrinas victoriam. Ergo.

Καλὸν γὰρ χάριτι βεβαιοῦσθαι τὴν καρδίαν ὐ βρώμασι] Com- mendat, ut supra, τὴν ἀυτάρκειαν. Nam multi à Christiani- smo abducebantur, eò quod res angustas ferre nequibant. Epulæ, quæ ex divitiarum affluentia facile nascuntur, di- cuntur cor fulcire, id est, vires corporis Gen. XVIII. 5. In Ebræo Ps. CV. 16. ubi in Græco στήριγμα ἄρτου. Sic & Ez. IV. 16. V. 16. VII. 11. XIV. 13. At vero gratia, id est, dona Spiritus per Dei bonitatem data ea est, quæ fulcit cor, idest, animum contra tentationes, 1. Cor. I. 6. 8. 2. Cor. I. 21. Co- loss. II. 7. Rom. I. 11. XVI. 25. 1. Thessal. III. 2. 13. 2. Thess. II. 17. III. 3. 2. Petr. I. 12.

Ἐν οἷς οὐκ ὠφελήθησαν οἱ περιπατήσαντες] In Manuscripto περιπατῶντες; ita ut ὠφελήθησαν sit Aoristus pro præsenti tempore positus. Nunquam ad pietatem proficiunt, qui necessariis non contenti epulis & similibus deliciis student. Notat illos Judaismi magistros, quos ipsa opera prodebant, Rom. XVI. 18. Phil. III. 19. Tit. I. 12.

Temere hæc ad convivia abripiuntur à Grotio: Quam glossam à Crellio & Schlichtingio habere videtur, quum Apostolus à genere descendat ad speciẽ, à thesi ad hypothesin, ex variis doctrinis, quas prædicabant errorum magistri, unum afferens exemplum, idq; iis, ad quos scribit, accommodatum. Siquidẽ Judæi ad Christum conversi superstitiosius inhærebant observationi ceremoniarum legalium, cumprimis discrimini ciborum à Mose præscripto Num. XIV. 2. Deut. II. 16. Arguit eos, inquit Theophylactus, qui Judaicam ciborum abstinentiam & observationẽ induxerant. Estis enim inquiens vos gratia (hoc est, fide) stabiliendi, reddendique certiores, nihil esse prorsus immundũ, & perpura esse credenti omnia. Est itaque fides hac, non escarum observatio, necessaria. Qui enim à cibis præcaverint, id est, qui in ejusmodi escarum observationem semper intendunt, perspicuum est, nihil hos profecisse: ut qui extra veros fidei terminos divagentur, & legi inserviant prorsus inutili. Quid enim commodi ex ea observatione assequebantur? B. Höpfnerus hæc in antithesi doctrinæ legis & Evangelii accipit, & probari hic vult, quod dictum erat, vobis bonum est, gratia stabiliri cor à specierum ἀντιδιηρημένων oppositione, aut gratia aut cibis bonum est cor stabiliri. At non cibis, (id est, legalibus observationibus, uti per Synecdochen Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, Theodoretius & Anshelmus explicant) 1 Tim. IV. 8. E. g. doctrina Evangelii gratiam offerente & dante.
