Porrò hujus etiam minoris Epilogismum addi putat à cõtrarii effectus experientia: Qui non sunt adjuti (justificati & salvati) in eo ambulantes (observatores illius) in eo stabiliri cor, non est bonum. Sed ciborum observatores non sunt adjuti cibis. Ergo cibis stabiliri cor non est bonum. Verbum βεβαιῶσθαι opponitur fluctuationi significatæ per verbum περιφέρεσθαι, Ἐν οἷς οὐκ ὠφελήθησαν οἱ περιπατήσαντες. Vulgata: Quæ (escæ) non profuerunt ambulantibus in eis. In Græco proprie est: In quibus, qui ambulaverunt, nihil utilitatis consequuti sunt, hoc est, quæ nihil contulerunt iis, qui in hujusmodi observationibus plurimum operæ & momenti posuerunt.

## 13:10
Vers. 10. We have an altar, from which they have no authority to eat who serve the tabernacle] Excellently said. We also serve a tabernacle, that is, the Church figured by the tabernacle: But those who served the old tabernacle were eating, that is, were feasting sumptuously from the altar, or from the victims, Lev. VII. Our worship does not provide us with such feasts and delicacies. To eat often signifies the use of such things beyond necessity, as 1 Cor. X. 7. XV. 32. Although it is permitted for Christian pastors to live from the Gospel, IX. 14. But to live, not to feast. See 1 Tim. VI. 8. By the word θυσιαστηρίῳ, worship is signified metonymically. See 1 Cor. IX. 3. For in the Jewish worship, that was the principal part which concerned the altar of victims.

By the altar, not the Jewish worship, but rather the victim is understood by synecdoche of the container for the contained, as from the comparison of 1 Cor. IX. 13. chap. X. 14. with Blessed Höpfner and Blessed Gerhard, which victim is Christ, who offered himself to God as a sacrifice on the altar of the cross. That those who served the old tabernacle feasted sumptuously, has nothing to do with the present matter; where the Apostle denies that they have the authority to feed from our altar or spiritual victim. And how do these things cohere, if the Grotian sense is admitted: They feast sumptuously; Therefore they do not have the authority to live sparingly, as we are sustained in the N.T.: But our sense is plain: Those who still wish to cling to those typical and ceremonial things under the opinion of necessity, cannot become participants of the true altar, or of the true sacrifice of Christ, and the benefits obtained by the same.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ἔχομεν θυσιαστήριον, ἐξ ἧ φαγεῖν οὐκ ἔχουσιν ἐξουσίαν οἱ τῇ σκηνῇ λατρεύοντες] Egregie dictum. Servimus nos quoque tabernaculo, id est, Ecclesiæ per tabernaculum figuratæ: Sed illi qui veteri tabernaculo serviebant, edebant, id est, opipare epulabantur de altari, sive de victimis Lev. VII. Noster cultus nobis tales epulas & delicias non suppeditat. Edere sæpe significat usum talium rerum supra necessitatem, ut 1. Cor. X. 7. XV. 32. Licet & Christianis pastoribus vivere ex Evangelio IX. 14. Sed vivere, non deliciari. Vide 1. Tim. VI. 8. Θυσιαστηρίῳ voce μετωνυμικῶς cultus significatur. Vide 1. Cor. IX. 3. Erat enim in cultu Judaico præcipua pars illa, quæ circa altare victimarum versabatur.

Per altare non cultus Judaicus, sed potiꝫ victima intelligitur per Synecdochen continentis pro contento, ut è collatione 1. Cor. IX. 13. cap. X. 14. cum B. Höpfnero B. Gerhardus, quæ victima est Christus, qui in ara crucis seipsũ Deo in sacrificium obtulit. Quo illi, qui veteri tabernaculo deservierunt, opipare epulati sint, nihil ad rem præsentem facit; ubi negat Apostolus, eos potestatẽ habere de altari vel victima nostra spirituali vescẽdi. Et quomodo hæc cohærent, si sensꝰ Grotianus admittatur: Illi opipare epulantur; Ergo non habent potestatem parce, uti nos in N. T. sustentamur, vivendi: Sensus autem noster planus est: Qui adhuc volunt inhærere typicis illis & ceremon. sub opinione necessitatis, par- par- ticipes non possunt fieri veri altaris, vel veri sacri- ficii Christi, & beneficiorum eodem partorum.

## 13:11
Vers. 11. Ὧν γὰρ εἰσφέρεται ζώων τὸ αἷμα περὶ ἁμαρτίας εἰς τὰ ἅγια ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἀρχιερέως, τούτων τὰ σώματα καίεται ἔξω τῆς παρεμβολῆς] This, he says, which I state, was prefigured on that solemn day of the purification, on which the high priest especially acted the part of Christ, as was shown above. For of the victims offered on that day, that is, the calf and the goat, no one partook: for the bodies of those victims were carried outside the camp, and were burned there. From this he infers two things mystically: that Christians ought not to be surprised, not only if they lack an abundance of things, but even if they are destitute of necessary things for some time, which not rarely happened to the Apostles, as can be seen in 1 Cor. 4:11, 2 Cor. 11:27. Furthermore, if sometimes they are even expelled from cities, which likewise happened to the Apostles, Acts 16:37, 13:50, and elsewhere, although the Apostles truly expiated sins more than that goat and calf. These things are very apt for consoling the Christian Hebrews in the evils which they were then bearing. Understand Περὶ ἁμαρτίας as of the people: although, so that I omit nothing, these words are absent in the manuscript. And understand τὰ ἅγια by brevity of speech as τὰ ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων. The camps were formerly in place of the city, and whatever was then not permitted to be done inside the camps, that was afterwards not permitted inside the city. Thus Moses Maimonides. Compare 24, 12. Jos. 5, 24. with Acts 7, 50.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Ὧν γὰρ εἰσφέρεται ζώων τὸ αἷμα περὶ ἁμαρτί- ας εἰς τὰ ἅγια τῦ Ἀρχιερέως, τύτων τὰ σώματα καίεται ἔξω τῆς παρεμβολῆς] Hoc, ait, quod dico, figuratum fu- it in die illo solenni τῦ καθαρισμῦ, in quo summus Sacer- dos eximie personam gessit Christi, ut supra fuit ostensum. Nam de victimis illo die oblatis, id est, vitulo & hirco nemo epulabatur: Corpora enim illarum victimarum por- tabantur extra castra, & ibi urebantur. Duo hinc infert μυσικῶς: Non mirari debere Christianos, non modo, si rerum affluentia careant, verum etiam si rebus necessariis ad tempus aliquod destituantur, quod Apostolis non ra- ro evenit, ut videre est 1. Cor. 4, 11. 2. Cor. 11, 27. De- inde si interdum etiam expellantur ex urbibus, quod iti- dem Apostolis evenit Act. 16, 37. 13, 50. & alibi, cum tamen Apostoli verius peccata expiarent, quam hircus ille & vitulus. Hæc valde apta sunt ad consolandos Christia- nos Ebræos in malis, quæ tum ferebant. Περὶ ἁμαρτίας intellige populi: quanquam, ne quid omittam, absunt hæ voces in Manuscripto. Et τὰ ἅγια intellige per bre- viloquentiam τὰ ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων. Castra olim erant pro urbe, & quicquid tunc non licebat fieri intra castra, id post- ea non licuit intra urbem. Sic Moses Maimonides. Confer 24, 12. Jos. 5, 24. cum Act. 7, 50.

## 13:12
Vers. 12. Wherefore also Jesus, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate] Just as you are being cast out of the cities, so also he himself, before he underwent death, was cast out of the city. You have also in this evil that leader. Ἁγιάζειν is taken here as above 10, 29. Ἔξω πύλης, that is, outside the city, as Tertullian correctly explains according to the sense against the Jews.

This explanation is too jejune, as if those things referred only to a lack of necessary things and exile, and pertained to moral precepts; whereas the Apostle had rather exhorted them to keep faith in Christ steadfastly by the example of τῶν ἡγουμένων [the leaders], nor are they being led away by Judaizers from the sincerity of the same under the opinion of the necessity of observing legal ceremonies in the distinction of foods: And the Apostle may exhibit to them the virtue of the merit of Christ through the illustration of this type, so that they may steadfastly persist in that faith. For as the bodies of those sacrifices, whose blood was brought into the holy of holies, were to be burned outside the camp. Thus Christ, the unique propitiatory sacrifice, who had to enter not indeed by the shedding of calves or goats, but by his own blood into the holy of holies, that is, into heaven itself, was to be burned by the fire of divine wrath and offered outside the city, so that he might sanctify, or cleanse from sins, the people through his own blood, which he shed for us on the altar of the cross. Some think that mention is made here of the burning of the bodies, so that it might be indicated that not even the high priest, much less the remaining priests, could eat of those expiatory sacrifices, and hence it is concluded that those who still wish to serve the shadowy tabernacle can much less eat of our expiatory victim of the New Testament. But if the reason of the type is to be observed in that part, not even any could eat of the same, just as, because the whole bodies were burned, no one could partake of their flesh, whereas on the contrary our Christ, our victim, willed to be burned outside the gate and offered to God so that all might spiritually eat of his sacrifice. Wherefore it is not to be thought that that act of burning is brought forward because of the non-participation of the flesh; but so that the figure of the expiatory passion of Christ, which was to be outside the city, might be unfolded, which God willed to shadow forth in the type in this way: just as the Apostle also made the application only in that part: Which in these things is situated in general: 1. Those anniversary sacrifices were expiatory for the sins of the whole people: Thus the death of Christ is an expiatory sacrifice for our sins, 1 John 2:2. 2. Those sacrifices had to be slaughtered and shed blood: Thus Christ also was slaughtered for us, and willed to shed his blood, 1 Cor. 5:7, Matt. 26:26. 3. The high priest of the Old Testament with the blood of the sacrifices entered the holy of holies: The High Priest of the New Testament, Christ, had to enter with his own blood into the true sanctuary, into heaven. 4. The shedding of blood in sacrifices served for atonement, for it was given for the life of the people, Lev. XVII. 11. The blood of Christ was shed, that he might sanctify or cleanse the people with the same. 5. The bodies of those sacrifices were burned outside the camp: Thus Christ also had to suffer not in the city, which the camp represented, but outside the gate. But why the Apostle wished to make special mention of this circumstance, he taught in the following words. 6. If, however, these things are also to be referred to the preceding matters concerning foods, the explanation of Socinus in Loc. expl. p. 111, judged not alien by B. Gerhard, may be admitted: The Apostle, he says, in order to confirm by a certain allegory that worship is not to be placed in foods, says that this appears from the fact that in the sacrifice performed for us, the high priest entered into the holy places for us. For under the law, whenever the High Priest entered into the holy places, namely to bring in the blood of the slaughtered animal, then it was not permitted to eat anything from that slaughtered animal, but it was necessary to burn it all with fire, since otherwise it would have been necessary to eat it. It is further to be observed that the Apostle makes no application, either in the fact that the blood of Christ was offered in the holy of holies, or that the slaughter and burning of Christ were distinct in place in the antitype, both of which Schlichting acknowledges here. For it is not necessary that the type and antitype should agree in everything. Concerning the former, he says: The Author, although he has the occasion, by inviting a comparison and similarity of Christ with the legal High Priest, to speak of the blood of Christ brought into that heavenly tabernacle, nevertheless deliberately avoids that, and uses only those words from which it appears that sins were indeed atoned for by the blood of Christ, but not insofar as it was brought into the heavenly tabernacle and offered to God, but only insofar as it was shed. Concerning the latter: The particle AND (v. 12. & Jesus) in this place has the force of comparison, as if he were saying, not only were the bodies of animals burned outside the camp, but Jesus himself also suffered outside the gate. He suffered, namely, the death of the cross. He used the genus for the species. But the death of Jesus corresponds not only to the slaughter of animals, which took place within the camp and the city and the circuit of the temple, but also to the burning of the bodies, which was carried out outside the camp and the city and the circuit of the temple: The former indeed, insofar as Christ himself was put to death. And those things which were as if dispersed in shadow and type, these were collected into one in the body itself and the antitype, just as one death in Christ corresponds to both the shedding of blood and the burning of bodies. Theodoret thinks the type of the red heifer is being referred to in Num. XIX. But it is manifest that these things pertain to the sacrifices on the day of atonement, Lev. XVI.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Διὸ καὶ Ἰησῦς, ἵνα ἁγιάσῃ διὰ τῦ ἰδίε αἵματος τὸν λαὸν, ἔξω τῆς πύλης ἔπαθε] Sicut vos ex urbibus eji- cimini, sic & ipse, priusquam mortem obiret, ex urbe eje- ctus est. Habetis etiam in hoc malo illum ἀρχηγόν. Ἁγιά- ζειν hic sumitur, ut supra 10, 29. Ἔξω πύλης, id est, extra ci- vitatem, quomodo recte quoad sensum explicat Tertullianus adversus Judæos.

Nimis jejuna est hæc explicatio, quasi tantum ca- rentiam rerum necessariarum & exilium illa respici- ant, & ad moralia præcepta pertineant; quum poti9 ad fidem in Christum constanter servandam ex- emplo τῶν ἡγουμένων hortatus fuerit Apostolus, nec à Judaizantibus ab ejusdem sinceritate sub opinione necessitatis observationis legalium ceremoniarum in ciborum discrimine abducuntur: Et meriti Chri- sti virtutem ipsis per illustrationem hujus typi ex- hibeat Apostol9, ut in illa fide cõstanter persistant. Nam ut sacrificiorum illorũ, quorum sanguis in san- ctum sanctorũ inferebatur, corpora cremanda erant extra castra. Ita Christus unicum sacrificium pro- pitiatorium, qui non quidé fuso vitulorum aut hir- corum, sed proprio sanguine suo in sanctum san- ctorum ingredi debuit, hoc est, in cœlum ipsum, extra civitatem igne iræ divinæ ustulandus & offe- rend9 erat, ut sanctificaret, vel à peccatis mundaret populum per proprium sanguiné, quem in ara cru- cis pro nobis effudit. Nonnulli putant cremationis corporũ hic mentionem fieri, ut indicetur, ne qui- dem Pontificem summum, nedum Sacerdotes re- liquos vesci potuisse de illis sacrificiis expiatoriis, & hinc cõcludatur, qui adhuc deservire taberna- culo umbratili volunt, multo minus vesci posse de victima nostra expiatoria N. T. Sed si typi ratio in ista parte observanda, ne quidem ulli vesci pote- runt eadem, quemadmodum ideo, quod tota cre- marentur corpora, nemo de carnibus ipsorum par- ticipare poterat, quum ex adverso Christi9 victima nostra cremari extra portam & offerri Deo ideo voluerit, ut vesci sacrificio ejus spiritualiter omnes possent. Quapropter non est existimandum, illum cremationis actum adduci ob non participatam car- nem; sed ut figura evolveretur passionis Christi expiato- riæ extra urbẽ futuræ, quam in typo sic adumbrare voluit Deus: quemadmodum etiam Apostolus ea parte applicationẽ tantum fecit: Quæ in hisce in u- niversum sita est: 1. Sacrificia illa anniversaria expi- atoria erãt pro peccatis totius populi: Ita Christi mors sacrificium est expiatorium pro peccatis nostris, 1. Job. II. 2. 2. Sacrificia illa mactari & sanguinẽ profun- dere debuere: Ita Christus etiã pro nobis mactatus est, & sanguinem suum effundere voluit, 1. Cor. V. 7. Matth. XXVI. 26. 3. Pontifex V. T. cum sanguine sacrificiorum ingresso est sanctum sanctorum: Pon- tifex Novi Test.Christus ingredi cum proprio san- guine debuit in verum sanctuarium in cœlum. 4. Sanguinis fusio in sacrificiis faciebat ad expiationẽ, dabatur enim pro vita populi, Lev. XVII. 11. Sanguis Christi fusus est, ut sanctificaret vel mundaret eo- dem populum. 5. Corpora sacrificiorum illorum cremabantur extra castra: Sic Christus etiam pati debuit non in urbe, quam referebant castra, sed ex- tra portam. Cur autem hujus circumstantiæ pecu- liariter mentionẽ facere voluerit Apostol9, sequen- tibus verbis docuit. 6. Si tamẽ ad præcedentia de ci- bis hæc etiã referenda, Socini explicatio in Loc. ex- plic. p. 111. à B. Gerhardo non aliena judicata, admitti poterit: Apostolus, inquit, ut Allegoria quadem ra- tione confirmet, non esse ponendum cultum in cibis, ait hoc ex eis apparere, quod in sacrificio pro nobis peracto pontifex pro nobis ingressus est in sancta. Nam sub lege, quandocunque Pontifex ingredieba- tur in sancta, ut scilicet eo inferret sanguinem macta- tæ pecudis, tunc non licebat quicquam comedere ex pecude illa mactata, sed necesse erat, eam totam igne comburere, cum oporteret alioquin illa comedere. Id autem observandum porrò, Apostolum nullam fa- cere applicationem, vel in eo, quod sanguis Christi in sancto sanctorum oblatus fuerit, vel quod Chri- sti mactatio & crematio loco distincta fuerint in antitypo, quod utrumque agnoscit hic Schlichtin- gius. Non enim necessum est, ut in omni cõveniant typus & antitypus. De illo ait. D. Autorem, licet oc- casionem habeat, invitante Christi cum Pontifice lega- gali comparatione ac similitudine, de Christi in cæle- ste illud tabernaculum illato sanguine dicendi, istud tamen de industria defugere, & iis tantum uti verbis, ex quibus appareat Christi quidem sanguine expiata fuisse peccata, verum non quatenus in cæleste taber- naculum illatus, ac Deo oblatus sit, sed tantum qua- tenus fusus fuit. De hoc: Particula ET (v. 12. & Je- sus) hoc loco comparandi vim habet, quasi dicat, non tantum animalium corpora extra castra cremata sunt, sed etiam Jesus ipse extra portam passus est. Pas- sus est, nempe crucis mortem. Genus posuũ pro specie. Mors vero Jesu non solum animalium mactationi, quæ intra castra & urbem templiq́; ambitum fiebat, sed etiam cremationi corporum, quæ extra castra ur- bemque & templi ambitum peragebatur, respondet: Illi quidem, quatenus ipse Christus extinctus fuit. Et quæ in umbra & typo veluti dispersa erant, hæc in ipso corpore & antitypo in unum collecta sunt, sicut una mors in Christo & sanguinis fusioni & corporum cremationi respondeat. Theodorets vaccæ ruffæ typum respici censet Num. XIX. Sed mani- festum est, hæc pertinere ad sacrificia in die expi- ationis, Lev. XVI.

## 13:13
Vers. 13. Let us therefore go forth to him outside the camp.] Let us not be ashamed of being cast out of cities. He said, however, camp, because in the time of Moses, when that solemn rite was instituted, the camps were in the place of a city, or rather a temporary city. And many cities now also began from camps, and have the name of camps.

Bearing his reproach] Willingly bearing these insults, which we bear after his example. We had a similar expression above VI. 26, except that there it is about the figure of a future thing, here about the imitation of an accomplished thing.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Τοίνυν ἐξερχώμεθα πρὸς ἀυτὸν ἔξω τῆς παρεμ- βολῆς.] Ne nos pudeat ex urbibus ejici. Dixit autem πα- ρεμβολῆς, quia Mosis tempore, cum illud sacrum solenne institutum est, castra erant urbis vice, imò urbs tempora- ria. Et multæ nunc quoque urbes à castris cœpere, & castro- rum habent nomen.

Τὸν ὀνειδισμὸν ἀυτῦ φέροντες] Libenter ferentes has con- tumelias, quas ad ipsius exemplum ferimus. Similem loquu- tionem habuimus supra VI. 26. nisi quod ibi de figura rei fu- turæ, hic de imitatione rei exactæ agitur.

## 13:14
Vers. 14. For we have here no abiding city] If those ancient Patriarchs said this, above XI. 53, much more does this befit us, for whom nothing is certain. We are always wandering, 1 Cor. IV. 11.

But we seek the one to come] Not the earthly Jerusalem, as they did, but the super-celestial one, which was signified by the earthly, Heb. XI. 15. XII. 22. Phil. III. 20.

The sense is incomplete: Let us not be ashamed of being cast out of cities. For we are commanded to go forth to him, to Christ, outside the gate, both by the contemplation of faith, so that by considering his satisfactory sufferings we may be confirmed in confidence, and be sustained by them until the blessed outcome: To which outcome pertains what the blessed Hunnius's paraphrase implies: Let us go forth with Christ, leaving the shadows and types to the unbelieving Jews: but in turn apprehending the truth signified by the types: then by the imitation of his example, by which, insisting on his footsteps, we may patiently endure even exiles, nay, bear his reproach, who did not hesitate to undergo the cross in an ignominious place, Mount Calvary. B. Hunnius understands the reproaches as if they were deserting the Levitical sacred rites through apostasy, so that they may bear this reproach with equanimity, and not allow themselves to be carried away from the doctrine of the Gospel into foreign doctrines. The reproach of Christ is understood either of the reproaches of Christ himself, or of those which we sustain for the sake of Christ. The matter comes to the same thing. For because we are afflicted with reproaches for the imitation of the patience and constancy of Christ, we undergo the reproach of Christ himself, that is, what Christ underwent. But the following clause shows that exile is being referred to; because we do not have (in this age) an abiding city, but we seek the one to come: which refers itself to the example outside of Christ. Concerning which heavenly city, chap. XI. 10, 14, 16, chap. XII. 22. Therefore Theophylact rightly: Since Christ suffered death outside the city, let us also go to him outside the camp, that is: outside the world, bearing his reproach, that is, let us tolerate those same things which he himself sustained. He is outside, as some harmful person and a robber, nailed to the cross. And so let us not be ashamed to depart from this world, and to abandon the honors and glory that are of the world: Or if that seems to us to result in ignominy: He also exhorts them to bear more tolerantly the things that are inflicted upon them by the Jews, whether they bring insults or plunder their goods. Theodoret refers these things to the abandonment of legal shadows: Outside the camp: For that which is, let us withdraw from legal institutions: bearing reproaches for him who saved. Thus also B. Baldwin: Those who still served in the Levitical tabernacle could not eat from our altar, which we have in the cross of Christ; therefore one must go out outside the camp of the Levitical priesthood. Therefore they must go out of Jerusalem, and bid farewell to all Levitical rites and types, if we wish to use and enjoy the benefits of Christ. For those Levitical sacred rites cannot endure forever, since indeed not even this worldly conversation is perpetual, but another fatherland must be sought by us in the heavens, which Christ has acquired for us with his blood.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Οὐ γὰρ ἔχομεν ὧδε μένουσαν πόλιν] Si hoc ve- teres illi Patriarchæ dixere, supra XI. 53. multo magis hoc nobis convenit, quibus nihil certi est. Semper ἀστατῦμεν, 1. Cor. IV. 11.

᾿Αλλὰ τήν μέλλουσαν ἐπιζητῦμεν] Non terrenam Jerusalem, ut illi, sed supercœlestem, quæ per terrenam significabatur, Ebr. XI. 15. XII. 22. Phil. III. 20.

Sensus est incompletus: Ne nos pudeat ex urbibus ejici. Nam exire jubemur πρὸς ἀυτὸν ad Christum extra portã, tum contemplatione fidei, ut passiones ejus satisfactorias considerando in fiducia confir- memur, & ad beatam usque ἔκβασιν iisdem susten- temur: Ad quem exitum pertinet, quod B. Hunnius paraphrasis importat: Exeamus cum Christo, relin- quentes umbras & typos Judæis incredulis: vicissim autem veritatem typis significatam apprehendentes: tum imitatione exempli, quo ejusdem vestigiis in- sistentes patienter etiam exilia sustineamus, imò opprobrium ejus feramus, qui in loco ignominio- so, monte Calvariæ, crucem subire non dubitavit. De opprobriis, quasi per ἀποsασίαν deserant sacra Levitica intelligit B. Hunnius, ut hoc opprobrium æquis animis perferant, nec propterea à doctrina Evangelii sese in peregrinas doctrinas abripi pati- antur. Improperium Christi vel de ipsius Christi op- probriis, vel de iis, quæ nos Christi causa sustinemus, intelligitur. Res eodem redit. Nam quod ad imita- tionem patientiæ & constantiæ Christi cum oppro- briis afficimur, ipsius Christi improperium subi- mus, hoc est, quod Christus subiit. Exilium autem respici sequens comma docet; quia non habemus (in hoc seculo) manentem civitatem, sed futuram quærimus: quod sese refert ad exemplum extra Christum. De qua civitate cœlesti cap. XI. 10.14.16. cap. XII.22. Ideo Theophylactus recte: Cum mortem Christus sit extra urbem perpessus, concedamus & ipsi ad hunc extra castra, hoc est: extra mundum, im- properium ejus portantes, id est, eadem illa, qua ipse sustinuit, toleremus. Foris ille, ut noxius quidam & la- tro cruci affigitur. Nec nos itaque pudeat, ex hoc mundo excedere, & honores & gloriam, quæ mundi sunt, destituere: Vel si ad ignominiam id nobis cedere videatur: Simuletiam hos adhortatur, ut tolerantius ferant, quæ ab ipsis ingeruntur Judæis, sive contume- lias inferant, sive bona diripiant. Theodoretus hæc refert ad derelictionē umbrarum legalium: Extra castra: Pro eo quod est, recedamus ab institutis lega- libus: ferentes probra pro eo qui servavit. Sic & B. Balduinus: De altari nostro, quod habemus in cruce Christi, edere non poterant, qui Levitico tabernaculo adhuc serviebant, egrediendum igitur est extra castra sacerdotii Levitici. Exeundem igitur iis est Hie- rosolyma, & valedicendum omnibus sacris & typis Leviticis, si beneficiis Christi uti frui volumus. Neque enim sacra illa Levitica perpetuo durare possunt, si- quidem ne quidem conversatio hæc mundana est per- petua, sed alia nobis patria quærenda est in cœlis, quam acquisivit nobis Christus sanguine suo.

## 13:15
Vers. 15. Δι᾿ αὐτᾶ ὖν ἀναφέρωμεν θυσίαν αἰνέσεως διαπαντὸς τῷ Θεῷ] Δι᾿ αὐτᾶ, that is, according to the precepts of Christ, as below 21. Θυσία αἰνέσεως זבח תודה, Levit. VII. 2. 3. 5. 2. Par. XXIX. 31. XXXIII. 16. Esdr. X. 12. Nehem. XII. 31. 39. 45. Psal. L. 15. 23. Everything that is offered to God is rightly called θυσία, as can be seen in Levit. II. Ἀναφέρωμεν is קרב and תרומה.

Τελέσι καρπὸν χειλέων ὁμολογόντων τῷ ὀνόματι ἀυτᾶ] From the Greek of Hos. XIV. 3, where the interpreters took פרי הדר from פרה and not from פר, as we noted regarding Hosea. The Israelites also offered words giving thanks in the tabernacle and temple. But those Israelites deported by Tiglath-Pileser to distant places, since they could not offer victims, offered words alone, and therefore more purely than formerly with victims. That was not only a figure, but also a certain preparation for the Gospel. See Dan. IX. 27. Mich. VI. 7. 8. Joh. IV. 24. 1. Petr. II. 5. Rom. XII. 1. And rightly ὁμολογόντων, for ידד is translated no less as ἐξομολογεῖν than as αἰνεῖν: and תודה, no less as ἐξομολόγησις than as αἴνεσις. See above XIII. 15. Matth. XI. 25. Luc. X. 21. Rom. XIV. 11. XV. 9. Phil. II, 11. Apoc. III. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Δι᾿ αὐτᾶ ὖν ἀναφέρωμεν θυσίαν αἰνέσεως διαπαντὸς τῷ Θεῷ] Δι᾿ ἀυτᾶ, id est, secundum Christi præcepta, ut infra 21. Θυσία αἰνέσεως זבח תודה, Levit. VII. 2. 3. 5. 2. Par. XXIX. 31. XXXIII. 16. Esdr. X. 12. Nehem. XII. 31. 39. 45. Psal. L. 15. 23. Omne quod Deo offertur, recte θυσία di- citur, ut Levit. II. videre est. Ἀναφέρωμεν est קרב un- תרומה

Τελέσι καρπὸν χειλέων ὁμολογόντων τῷ ὀνόματι ἀυτᾶ] Ex Græco Os. XIV. 3. ubi Interpretes פרי הדר sumpsere à פרה non à פר, ut ad Oseam notavimus. Offerebant verba gratias agentia etiam Israëlitæ in tabernaculo & templo. At Israëlitæ illi deportati à Thiglathpelasffaro in loca lon- ginqua, cum victimas offerre non possent, offerebant sola verba, ideoque parius quam olim cum victimis. Id non figura tantum, sed & præparatio quædam fuit ad Evangelium. Vide Dan. IX. 27. Mich. VI. 7. 8. Joh. IV. 24. 1. Petr. II. 5. Rom. XII. 1. Et bene ὁμολογόντων, nam ידד non minus ἐξομολογεῖν transfertur quam αἰ- νεῖν: & תודה, non minus ἐξομολόγησις quam αἴνεσις. Vide supra XIII. 15. Matth. XI. 25. Luc. X. 21. Rom. XIV. 11. XV. 9. Phil. II, 11. Apoc. III. 5.

## 13:16
Vers. 16. Τῆς δὲ ἐνποιΐας καὶ κοινωνίας μὴ ἐπιλανθάνεσθε] μὴ ἐπιλανθάνεσθε as above 1. Εὐποιΐας here refers to deeds. In the Glossary ἐνποιΐα is merit, benefit. Pollux says the word is less common. But it corresponds well to the Rabbinic סכות. Κοινωνίας refers to money and those things which are acquired with money. See Act. II. 42. Rom. XV. 26. 2. Cor. VIII. 4. IX. 13. The duties of love which he names here relate to the Hebrew victims σωτηρίως שלמים. Lest the Hebrews appear to be destitute of sacrifices; indeed, that they may be moved more toward the confession of the faith of the name of the Lord, the Apostle proposes their duty in such a way that he recalls them from the corporal sacrifices of the Judaizers to spiritual ones, through Christ himself as a propitiatory sacrifice, or as the Priest of the New Testament, he commands them to offer both of praise and evangelical confession, and of charity and beneficence. These are called the fruit of lips with an allusion to the offerings of the fruits of the earth, as in Hosea 14:3, the fruit of lips among the LXX interpreters, who in the sources are called the calves of our lips. Compare Leviticus 7:12, Psalm 116:17, Romans 12:1. Concerning these, Romans 12:13, Philippians 4:15. There is a twofold sacrifice, says Thomas in this place, which we ought to offer upon the altar of Christ, namely, devotion toward God and compassion toward our neighbor. Theophylact exclaims here: Where in the world are those who excuse their poverty and impart nothing at all to others? Let them understand that even to those laboring in extreme want and stripped of all goods, Paul urges that they do not forget to do good to others, and that they bestow alms and charity upon the needy. Δι' αὐτῶ is not according to his precepts, but through him, as our Priest. See 1 Peter 2:5, Revelation 8:3-4. For nothing, as Theodoret says, helps us in the song of praise which is offered to God without faith in the Son. What is said about persecution in relation to the Gospel comes from an erroneous hypothesis, as if spiritual sacrifices were not offered in the Old Testament. The contrary is evident everywhere in Psalm 50, 51, 141, Hosea 14.

For with such sacrifices God is well pleased] By such victims (namely, more than by those legal ones) God is pleased. In the active voice it is said εὐαρεστεῖν τῷ Θεῷ, as above 11:5, Genesis 22:24, 39:4. But it is the custom of the Greeks to form the passive and construct it with the nominative, no less than those governing the dative or accusative from the active. The Latin 'promeretur Deus' is not bad. For I am surprised that delicate men say this is barbaric. Is Pliny a barbarian, who said: 'Quæ Cannis corona merita?' 7:28. Nor are there almost any words which are called deponents that cannot be used in a passive sense, and have been used by good writers. Secondly, because they say this interpretation is false, in that they are egregiously mistaken. The offering of Christ was made for this, that we might receive both knowledge and the Spirit, through whom we might offer to God pious deeds according to his example. The honor returns to the Author.

Grotius rightly departs from the Vulgate version, which falsely rendered: 'Talibus hostiis promeretur Deus.' However, nothing excuses the Vulgate: since Estius himself admits that it is translated more correctly as 'God is delighted,' since the Greek verb does not signify to be appeased, but to be delighted, and we cannot merit anything before God by our works. For one is not said to merit well of someone who does a pleasing thing for someone, but it is necessary that he also confer some duties or benefits upon him, such as no man can do toward God. Add that Estius does not deny the barbarism here: the Interpreter said 'promeretur' in the passive, even if it is poor Latin.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Τῆς δὲ ἐνποιΐας καὶ κοινωνίας μὴ ἐπιλανθάνεσθε] μὴ ἐπιλανθάνεσθε ut supra 1. Εὐποιΐας hic ad facta refertur. In Glossario ἐνποιΐα meritum, beneficium. Pollux vocem esse dicit minus usitatam. Sed bene respondet Rabbinico סכות. Κοινωνίας refertur ad pecunias & ea, quæ pecuniis comparantur. Vide Act. II. 42. Rom. XV. 26. 2. Cor. VIII. 4. IX. 13. Quæ hic nominat dilectionis officia respiciunt E- bræorum victimas σωτηρίως שלמים. Ne sacrificiis Ebræi destitui videantur; imò ut ad confessionem fidei nominis Domini magis moveantur, officium ipsorum ita proponit Apo- stolus, ut à sacrificiis corporalib9 Judaizantium ad spiritualia eos revocet, per ipsum Christum ceu sa- crificium propitiatorium, vel Sacerdotem N. Test. offerre jubet tum laudum & confessionis Evangelicæ, tum charitatis & beneficentiæ. Illa fructus labio- rum dicuntur cum allusione ad oblationes fructuum terræ, uti Os. XIV. 3. fructus labiorum apud LXX. interpretes, qui in fontibus vituli labiorum nostro- rum dicuntur. Conf. Levit. VII. 12. Psalm. CXVI. 17. Roman. XII. 1. De his Roman. XII. 13. Philip. IV. 15. Duplex, inquit, Thomas hoc loco, est sacrificium, quod super altare Christum offerre debemus, scilicet devotionem erga Deum, ac misera- tionem erga proximum. Exclamat hic Theophyla- ctus: Ubinam gentium sunt, qui paupertatem excu- sant, & nihil quicquam aliis impertiuntur? Intelli- gant vel summa inopia laborantibus & bonis omni- bus exstriatis, Paulum suadere, ne aliis benefacere obliviscantur, & eleemosynam stipemque indigenti- bus tribuant. Δι' αὐτῶ non est secundum ipsius præce- pta, sed per ipsum, tanquam Sacerdotem nostrum. Vid. 1. Petr. II. 5. Apoc. VIII. 3. 4. Nihil enim, Theodo- reto dicente, nos juvat laudis canticum, quod Deo offertur absque fide in Filium. Quod de persecuti- one ad Evangelium dicitur, ex erronea hypothe- si, quasi in Veteri Testamento non oblata fuerint spiritualia sacrificia. Contrarium passim patet Psal. L, LI, CXLI. Os. XIV.

Τοιαύταις γὰρ θυσίαις εὐαρεστεῖται Θεὸς] Per ejusmodi vi- ctimas (magis nempe, quam per illas legales) Deo placetur. In Activo dicitur εὐαρεστεῖν τῷ Θεῷ, ut supra XI. 5. Genes. XXII. 24. XXXIX. 4. Sed Græcorum mos est passiva forma- re & cum Nominativo construere, non minus ab Activis Dativum, quam Accusativum regentibus. Non male La- tinus promeretur Deus. Nam primum quod barbarum hoc esse ajunt homines delicati miror. Estne Plinius barbarus, qui dixit: Quæ Cannis corona merita? VII. 28. Nec ulla fer- me sunt verba, quæ vocantur deponentia, quæ non & in sensu παθητικῷ & usurpari possint, & usurpata sint à probis Scriptoribus: Deinde quod falsam ajunt hanc interpretatio- nem, in eo egregie falluntur. Oblatio Christi in hoc facta est, ut nos acciperemus & cognitionem & Spiritum, per quem offeramus Deo pia facta ad ipsius exemplum. Honos ad Autorem redit.

Rectè à Vulgata versione discedit Grotius, quæ falso reddidit: Talibus hostiis promeretur Deus. Ne quicquam autem excusat Vulgatam: Siquidẽ Estius ipse fateatur, rectius verti, delectatur Deus, cum Græcum verbum non significet placari, sed delecta- ri, neque nostris operibus mereri quicquam apud Deum possumus. Non enim bene mereri de aliquo dicitur, qui rem gratam alicui facit, sed oportet, ut præterea aliqua officia aut beneficia in eum confe- rat, quale quid null9 hominum in Deum facere po- test. Adde quod etiam barbarismum hic non diffi- teatur Estius: Promeretur passive dixit Interpres, etsi parum Latine.

## 13:17
Verse 17. Obey those who lead you, and submit] We have already seen above in verse 7 who these leaders are. He says that these are both to be obeyed and yielded to, that is, honor is to be shown, such as inferiors show to superiors. For the Greeks often signify this by ὑπείκειν. Understand obedience, however, not only in those things which are of evangelical doctrine, but also in those which are of governance, namely, that they may bear such a heavy burden with a joyful spirit, as follows.

For they watch over your souls, as those who will give an account] In the Manuscript, not badly: For they watch, as those who will give an account for your souls. These are to be read as a parenthesis. For what follows coheres directly with what precedes. It is right that they be obeyed and held in honor. For they are anxious for you night and day, as those who must render an account to God if you sin through their negligence. See Jeremiah 13:20, Ezekiel 3:17 and following, 33:2 and following. We have 'ἀποδιδόναι λόγον' also below in 1 Peter 4:5. That expression signifies either to bring back a reward or a punishment, according to how one has behaved. Soldiers obey their leaders because the leaders are anxious for the temporary safety of the soldiers. How much more justly will they be obeyed who keep watch for our eternal salvation?

That they may do this with joy and not with groaning] Soothe that labor with all duties and obsequies, so that they may perform a sufficiently heavy duty with alacrity rather than with sorrow, even if nothing sad comes from you. By metonymy, understand joy as the alacrity which arises from joy. But 'groaning' signifies the sorrow which is accustomed to be indicated by a sigh. See concerning the word 'groaning' Romans 8:23, 2 Corinthians 5:2, 4. We have examples of such sorrow in 2 Corinthians 2:3 and 12:21.

However, that obedience to be shown to superiors or Bishops ought not to be blind; Estius himself warns: If a Bishop perverts the doctrine of the faith with beautiful preaching, there is no longer any reason why we should obey him. For thus he strips himself of power, as one who declares himself an enemy of the Church. We add the exhortation of Theophylact, to be well weighed by Papal Bishops, who for the most part are Bishops only in title and calf: Let them understand, who are leaders of others and preside over the rest: because just as it is necessary that the people show themselves obedient and compliant to the leaders themselves: so also it behooves the Priest to care for the souls of others, or to spend sleepless nights, to watch over the salvation of the people, as one who is to render an account for the crimes of the people.

For this is unprofitable for you] For they do not perform their duty as well who are sad as those who are of a joyful spirit. And if they owe an account of their negligence to God, you also owe an account for your ungrateful spirit toward them.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Πείθεσθε τοῖς ἡγουμένοις ὑμῶν, καὶ ὑπείκετε] Qui sint ἡγούμενοι jamjam vidimus supra 7. 1 His & obediendum dicit, & concedendum, id est, honorem exhibendum, qua- lem minores majoribus exhibent. Nam & hoc pet ὑπείκειν sæpe significant Græci. Obediendum autem intellige, non tantum in iis, quæ sunt doctrinæ Evangelicæ, sed etiam in iis, quæ sunt regiminis, nempe ut onus tam grave læto ani- mo sustineant, ut sequitur.

Ἀυτοὶ γὰρ ἀγρυπνοῦσιν ὑπὲρ τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν, ὡς λόγον ἀ- ποδώσοντες] In Manuscripto non malè: Ἀυτοὶ γὰρ ἀγρυ- πνῦσιν, ὡς λόγον ἀποδώσοντες ὑπὲρ τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν. Hæc per παρένθεσιν legenda. Nam quæ sequuntur, directè cum an- tecedentibus cohærent. Æquum est illis pareri & honorem haberi. Nocte enim dieque soliciti sunt vestri causa, ut qui Deo rationem reddere debeant, si quid vos per ipsorum negligentiam peccetis. Vide Jer. XIII. 20. Ezech. III. 17. & seqq. XXXIII. 2. & seqq. Ἀποδιδόναι λόγον habemus & infra 1. Petr. IV. 5. Significat autem ea loquutio aut præ- mium referre aut pœnam, prout quis se gesserit. Obediunt milites Ducibus suis, quia Duces pro militum temporaria sa- lute soliciti sunt. Quanto justius eis parebitur, qui pro æ- terna nostra salute excubant?

Ἵνα μετὰ χαρᾶς τῦτο καὶ μὴ ςενάζοντες] Mulcete eum labo- rem omnibus officiis & obsequiis, ut cum alacritate potius, quam cum dolore fungantur munere satis gravi, etiamsi à vobis nihil triste accedat. Per Μετωνυμίαν gaudium intellige, alacritatem, quæ ex gaudio oritur. ςενάζειν vero dolorem, qui per gemitum indicari solet, significat. Vide de verbo ςενά- ζειν Rom. VIII. 23. 2. Cor. V. 2. 4. Doloris talis exempla ha- bemus 2. Cor. II.3. & XII. 21.

Obedientia autem illa præpositis vel Episcopis præstanda non debet esse cæca; monet ipse Estius: Si Episcopus doctrinam fidei pulchra prædicatione per- vertat, jam non est, cur ei amplius pareamus. Sic enim potestate seipsum exspoliat, ut qui Ecclesiæ hostem se declaret: Addimus Theophylacti parænesin, Pontifi- ciis Episcopis probe ponderandam, qui pleriq; ti- tulo tantum & vitulo suntEpiscopi: Intelligant, qui aliorum sunt Duces & cæteris præsunt: quia quemad- modum necesse est, ut populus obsequentem se præbeat & præsidibus ipsis morigerum: Ita & Sacerdotē opor- tet, ut aliorum animas curet, vel noctes ducat inso- mnes, ut populi saluti invigilet, ut qui rationem pro populi facinoribus sit redditurus.

᾿Αλυσιτελὲς γὰρ ὑμῖν τῦτο] Neque enim tam bene obeunt munus suum, qui mœsto, ut qui læto sunt animo. Et si il- li rationem suæ negligentiæ debent Deo, etiam vos ingrati in ipsos animi.

## 13:18
Vers. 18. Pray for us] So also Col. 4.3. For we are persuaded that we have a good conscience, in all things willing to live honestly] Paul gives a similar reason for a similar request in 2 Cor. 1.11, 12. They deserve to be helped by the prayers of others, who do everything they can to benefit others. In all things, namely, in matters, as the Syriac interprets it. For we are persuaded, in the manuscript it is we are persuaded [peithometha], with the same meaning. It is certain, he says, to you. Paul declares similar things about himself in Acts 24.16.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Προσεύχεσθε περὶ ἡμῶν] Sic & Col. I. 3. IV. 3. Πεποιθαμεν γὰρ ὅτι καλὴν συνείδησιν ἔχομεν, ἐν πᾶσι καλῶς θέλοντες ἀναςρέφεσθαι] Similem similis petitionis causam reddit Paulus 2. Cor. I. 11. 12. Merentur aliorum precibus adjuvari, qui nihil non faciunt, ut aliis prosint. Ἐν πᾶσι nempe πράγμασι, quomodo interpretatur Syrus. Pro πε- ποίθαμεν in Manuscripto est πειθόμεθα, pari sensu. Constat, inquit, hoc vobis. Paria Paulus de se prædicat Actor. XXIV. vers. 16.

## 13:19
Vers. 19. But I beseech you the more abundantly to do this, that I may be restored to you the sooner] And this fits well with Luke, who was a Syrian by birth, from where an excursion into Judea was easy. Moreover, he was thinking of returning there, where he had sown the seed of the Gospel through Italy. But I beseech you the more abundantly, I pray you this the more.

Useless, that is, pernicious, harmful. It is a meiosis. For he says less, and understands more. For God will hear the groaning of them, and will avenge for them. Therefore, the Apostle, weighing how grave this duty is, asks them to render an account of their hearers, that they may pray to God for him, and for his fellow-workers, and he is confident of this, relying on the good conscience of his conduct carried out among them; Yet he asks for it from an abundance, especially also that by their prayers he might be more quickly restored to them, having been freed from prison and bonds, ch. 10.34, or simply returned: Since it is not sufficiently certain that this epistle was written from bonds. The invention about Luke rests on no suitable document. Theodoret: He was ill-spoken of in this place among them, he says, as one who preached things contrary to the law. Therefore he teaches them that he does this for no other reason than to obey the Divine word. For which reason he also called his conscience to witness. Theophylact: Since most of the faithful from among the Jews were disparaging Paul, because he taught that the former law was to be abandoned, for this reason some held him in hatred, on account of which hatred the Apostle had not added his name at the beginning of this epistle, especially since he had discovered that they would not even bear the hearing of his name. Therefore, excusing and as it were purging the hatred: First he prays them to pray for him (which we ourselves are accustomed to ask of those who are well-disposed and joined by faith). Then he argues that he is innocent, and has not committed any offense. In all things indeed, that is, not only among the Gentiles themselves, but in all other things. He says furthermore that he has a good conscience, that is, pure and clean, and that he is not conscious of having advised anything evil to them, nor of having brought any harm.

PART II. Votive [prayers] with the conclusion of the Epistle.

Latin:

Vers.19. Περισσοτέρως δὲ παρακαλῶ τῦτο ποιῆσαι, ἵνα τά- χιον ἀποκαταςαθῶ ὑμῖν] Et hoc Lucæ bene convenit, qui Syrus erat patria, unde facilis in Judæam excursus. Eo autem reverti cogitabat, ubi per Italiam jecisset semen- tem Evangelii. περισσοτέρως δὲ παρακαλῶ, hoc magis id vos precor.

Inutile, hoc est, pernitiosum, noxium. Μείωσις est. Minus enim dicit, & plus intelligit. Deus enim i- psorū gemit9 exaudiet, & pro illis ulciscetur. Ideo pensitans Apostolus, quam grave hoc mun9 sit, ra- tionem reddere de auditoribus petit, ut Deum pro se precentur, & pro coadjutoribus suis, & de eo confidit, fret9 bona conscientia conversationis in- ter ipsos gestæ; Ex abundanti tamen id petit impri- mis etiam, ut ipsorum precibus celerius ipsis suis li- beratus ex carcere & vinculis cap.X.34. restituatur, seu simpliciter reddatur: Quum non satis constet, è vinculis exaratam esse hanc epistolam. Commen- tum de Luca nullo nititur idoneo documento. Theodoretus: Male, inquit, hoc loco audiebat apud eos, ut qui legi contraria prædicaret. Eos ergo docet, se nulla alia causa id facere, quam ut pareat verbo Divino. Quapropter etiam conscientiam vocavit in testimonium. Theophylactus: Cum ex Judæis fidelibus plerique Paulum obtrectarent, quia destituendam pristinam legem esse doceret, eo hunc & invisum ha- bebant nonnulli, cujus odii gratia, nec ejus nomen A- postolus initio epistolæ hujus adjecerat, præsertim cum compertum haberet, hos ipso nec auditu quidem no- men ejus laturos. Excusans itaque & quasi odium purgans: Primum illos precatur, pro se orent (quod utique & ipsi solemus à benevolis & fide conjunctis deposcere.) Deinde arguit, se esse insontem, nec quid- piam deliquisse. In omnibus vero, hoc est, non solum in gentibus ipsis, sed aliis universis. Ait præterea, con- scientiam se bonam habere, hoc est, puram & niti- dam, nec se conscium esse pravi his quidpiam consulu- isse, nec malum aliquod attulisse.

PARS II. Votiva cum clausula Epistolae.

## 13:20
Verse 20. Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης ] He who loves peace. Thus Rom. 15:33, 1 Cor. 14:33, 2 Cor. 13:11, Phil. 4:9, 1 Thess. 5:23. He adds this because he saw seeds of discord arising among them. Ὁ ἀναγαγὼν ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν τὸν ποιμένα τῶν προβάτων τὸν μέγαν, ἐν αἵματι τῆς διαθήκης αἰωνίε, τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν χριστόν. Often when something great is requested from God, mention is made of His being raised from the dead, so that we may trust the more in His power. But incidentally, when he calls Christians the sheep of one Shepherd, he commends the concord of the flock. Moreover, Christ is our Shepherd, as in John 10:11, and in a mystical sense in Ezekiel 34:23, or as here, the great Shepherd, 1 Pet. 5:4, both for other reasons and because He shed His blood for us, John 10:15. And this is what is said here, ἐν αἵματι: He fed us with such affection that He even shed His blood: This was done so that a covenant might be ratified, not a temporal one, but an eternal one, which would last forever; just as he spoke above of His Priesthood and eternal redemption. But when it is said here that He was raised by God, it is simultaneously understood that He was also exalted to supreme power, through which He can protect His own, and in this respect also perform the office of Shepherd.

The vow is in conformity with the treatment of the Epistle. In it, the Apostle dealt primarily with the Priesthood of Christ, to which belongs the shedding of His blood for the remission of our sins. He dealt with the New Testament, ratified through the same: He dealt with the Doctoral office, as well as the Regal; by the name of both of which He is called the great Shepherd of the sheep: Indeed, also with the state of humiliation and exaltation; both of which are indicated by His being led out from the dead, and the appellation of our Lord, just as the names Jesus Christ and His office of Savior in general, and specifically, because He is anointed as Prophet, Priest, and King, designate those three offices. But what Grotius says, that He fed us with such affection that He even shed His blood: If it is understood in such a way that He shed His blood merely for the sake of the doctrine by which He feeds us, one must be careful lest from the λύτρον of Christ only a μαρτύριον be formed. For in that way, the Prophets and Apostles also fed the people with doctrine, so that they did not hesitate to shed their own blood. Cf. Zech. 9:11. He is called the great Shepherd not only in respect to other shepherds, but also because He is absolutely great, by reason of His person and office, Ezek. 34, where He is described as the true God; and it is not only in a mystical, but in a literal sense that it treats of Him, as we showed there. That προσδιορισμὸς ἐν αἵματι is wrongly attributed by Thomas to the participle ὁ ἀναγαγὼν in this sense, as if Christ were led out by the power and merit of the blood, since the merit of Christ does not pertain to Himself, but to us solely τελικῶς, or viewed by reason of the end: It should be referred to the nearest ποιμένα τὸν μέγαν, the great Shepherd. For by that He was made the great Shepherd, that He shed His blood for us: Great by acquiring for Himself a great flock as a possession: Great by establishing an eternal Testament. Which was done through His blood, Acts 20:28, Zech. 9:11. But it is called an eternal Testament because it was established by the eternal good pleasure of God the Father, by Christ the eternal God, the eternal Mediator, it embraces eternal goods, and extends from eternity to eternity by its own power and efficacy. Lest anyone should also think that it would come to pass that this too would cease through another Testament, he rightly shows that it will never cease. Osiander also rightly infers here: If the Testament of Christ, which offers the remission of sins to all who repent, is eternal: Therefore, as often as we truly repent, by the vigor of that Testament, we shall obtain the remission of sins. Therefore, he calls Him the God of peace primarily because He has been reconciled to us through the blood of the Testament, Rom. 5:9. Secondly, because He instructs us with the Spirit of peace and concord, 2 Tim. 1:7.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Ὁ δὲ Θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης ] Qui pacem amat. Sic Rom. XV. 33. 1. Cor. XIV. 33. 2. Cor. XIII. 1. Phil. IV. 9. 1. Thess. V. 23. Hoc ideo addit, quia videbat inter eos nasci discor- diae semina. Ὁ ἀναγαγὼν ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν τὸν ποιμένα τῶν προβάτων τὸν μέγαν, ἐν αἵματι τῆς διαθήκης αἰωνίε, τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν χριστόν. Saepe cum magni aliquid a Deo optatur, fit mentio e mortuis excitati, ut eo magis ejus potentiae confida- mus. Sed obiter cum Christianos oves vocat unius Pa- storis, commendat gregis concordiam. Est autem Chri- stus Pastor noster, ut Joh. X. 11. & in mystico sensu E- zech. XXXIV. 23. aut ut hic, magnus Pastor, 1. Petr. V. 4. tum aliis rebus, tum eo, quod sanguinem pro nobis fudit, Joh. X. 15. & hoc est, quod hic dicitur, ἐν αἵματι: pavit nos tanto affectu, ut & sanguinem funderet: Quod factum est, ut sanciretur foedus non temporale, sed ae- ternum, semper duraturum; quomodo & Sacerdotium ejus & redemptionem aeternam supra dixit. Cum autem di- citur hic a Deo suscitatus, simul intelligitur & evectus in sum- mam potentiam, per quam suos tueri potest, & in hac quo- que parte Pastoris officio fungi.

Votum conforme est tractationi Epistolae. Egit in ea Apostolus imprimis de Christi Sacerdotio, ad quod pertinet sanguinis ejus in remissionem pecca- torum nostrorum effusio. Egit de Testamento novo, per eundem sancito: Egit de Doctorali officio, ut & Regio; cujus utriusque nomine Pastor ovium magnus dicitur: Imo & de statu exinanitionis & ex- altationis; quem utrumque indicat ejus ex mortuis eductio, & Domini nostri appellatio, quemadmo- dum nomina Jesu Christi & Salvatorium ejus mu- nus in genere, & speciatim, quia unctus est ut Pro pheta, Sacerdos & Rex, trina ista officia designant. Quod autem Grotius ait, passive nos tanto affectu Christum, ut & sanguinem funderet: Si ita intelli- gatur, quod sanguinem doctrinae causa, qua nos pa- scit, tantum effuderit, cavendum, ne è λύτρῳ Chri- sti μαρτύριον tantum efformetur. Nam ea ratio- ne & Prophetae atque Apostoli paverunt doctrina populum, ut non dubitarint, sanguinem suum pro- fundere. Conf. Zach. IX. 11. Pastor magnus vocatur non respectu aliorum tantum pastorum, sed eti- am; quia absolute magnus est, ratione personae, & officij, Ezech. XXXIV. ubi ut verus Deus describi- tur; nec tantum mystico, sed literali sensu de ipso agitur, ut illic ostendimus. προσδιορισμὸς ille ἐν αἵματι perperam a Thoma trahitur ad Participiũ ὁ ἀναγαγὼν hoc sensu, quasi Christus virtute ac merito sanguinis sit eductus, quum meritum Chri- sti nõ ad ipsum pertineat, sed ad nos unice τελικῶς, vel ratione finis spectatum: Referendus ad proxi- mum ποιμένα τὸν μέγαν, Pastorem magnum. Nam per id magnus Pastor effectus est, quod sanguinem suum effuderit pro nobis: Magnus acquirendo sibi gregem magnum in peculium: Magnus condendo aeternum Testamentum. Quod factum est per san- guinem ipsius, Act. XX. 28. Zach. IX. 11. Aeternum autem dicitur Testamentum, quia aeterno Dei Pa- tris beneplacito conditum est à Christo aeterno Deo, aeterno Mediatore, aeterna bona complecti- tur, & ab aeterno in aeternum sese porrigit virtute & efficacia sua. Ne quis etiam existimaret, fore, ut hoc quoque per aliud Testamentum cessaret, merito ostendit, id nunquam esse desiturum. Re- cte etiam hic infert Osiander: Si Testamentum Chri- sti, quod remissionem peccatorum omnibus poeniten- tibus offert, aeternum est: Ergo quoties vere poeniten- tiam agimus, vigore illius Testamenti, remissionem peccatorum consequemur. Deum ergo pacis πρώ- τως ideo vocat, quod nobis reconciliatus sit per sanguinem Testamenti, Rom. V. 9. Deinde quod Spiritu pacis & concordiae nos instruat, 2. Tim. I. vers. 7.

## 13:21
Verse 21. Καταρτίσαι ὑμᾶς ἐν παντὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ] In the Manuscript: Ἐν παντὶ λόγῳ καὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ. May He make you fit for every good word and good work, in which category concord is chief, to which the participle καταρτισμένοι also refers, 1 Cor. 1:10. Ἐν is taken for ad, just as the Hebrew ל. You have καταρτίσαι in a similar sense in 1 Pet. 5:10. It corresponds to the Hebrew כּוּן. Εἰς τὸ ποιῆσαι τὸ θέλημα ἀυτᾶ] See Eph. 6:6, 1 John 2:17. It is an explanation of what precedes. Ποιῶν ἐν ὑμῖν τὸ ἐυάρεστον ἐνώπιον ἀυτὲ] God is said to work in us both to will and to do, Phil. 2:13. He does this, both by giving us knowledge of His promises, and by exciting and strengthening us by the Spirit. For he is also said to do rightly who gives the causes for doing. And the whole honor of the effects returns εἰς τὸ πρῶτον αἴτιον. Moreover, ἐυάρεστον ἐνώπιον ἀυτᾶ is the same as the shorter ἐυάρεστον τῷ Θεῷ, Rom. 12:1, ch. 14:18, Eph. 5:10, Phil. 4:18. And ποιῶν is construed with καταρτίσαι.

Because the Apostle has already excited the Hebrews to the pursuit of good works, he now prays that the Lord may make them fit for every good work, and perfect them, so that they may do the will of God according to the prescription of His Word: and he attributes this to Divine operation, who not only makes them fit, but also works it in them, in their will and heart by the efficacious ἐνέργεια of grace; which therefore happens not only through moral action, the propensity of the promises, and excitement through the Spirit, but through the concession of supernatural powers, regeneration, and the renewal of the Holy Spirit: lest by chance the powers of nature be believed to be helped by the external propensity of the Divine promises, or the Holy Spirit be thought to concur with natural powers by exciting them as if they were only dormant or hindered, and rendering them freer, and a συνέργεια be attributed to the powers of nature themselves. Therefore, all things here are attributed to Divine grace. In two ways, says Thomas, is a man adapted to doing good: in one way by working outwardly, and thus one man adapts another by persuading or threatening; in another way by exhibiting something inwardly, and thus God alone adapts the will, who alone can change it. Whence Estius himself concludes: Let us not therefore say that God moves the will of men as He knows it to be adapted, so that they may follow, as if the efficacy of grace were in that, but let us confess that God makes men adapted by a good succession of the will. Who also, regarding that ποιῶν ἐν ὑμῖν, far more rightly [opposes] Grotius, inasmuch as he, through the trope of Metonymy, perverts it, [saying] that God is said to do it only because He gives the causes of doing. That is, by His grace effecting, effectively working in us works pleasing to Himself. This passage manifestly teaches that the grace of God is not considered efficacious because our will accommodates itself by its assent to God calling or persuading, but that it is efficacious by itself and from itself, while God by His powerful operation adapts us, and effects in us every good thing by which we please Him. Under which good the very assent and cooperation of our will is also contained, no one who is sound in the faith would doubt; for it is God who works in us both to will and to perform, Phil. II, and who works all our works in us, Is. XXVI.

Διὰ Ἰησοῦ χριστῦ] This is rightly construed with that ἐυάρεστον. For those things finally please God now which are done according to the precepts of Christ. Thus Peter uses διὰ in 1 Pet. II. 5.

It is not according to the precepts of Christ, but through Jesus Christ. For the name of Christ nowhere denotes the precepts of Christ. Nor does that sense obtain in 1 Pet. II. 5: But rather, spiritual sacrifices offered through Christ, the Priest of the New Testament, are said to be acceptable to God. Cf. Rev. VIII. 4, 5; Heb. XIII. 8. Theophylact refers these not to τὸ ἐυάρεστον, but to the word ποιῶν; that God does those things through Christ the Mediator: Nor is it a wonder, he says, if He, who from the beginning has worked for us salvation, in the very action of the mighty works the Mediator is made, and he executes the will of the Father, with strengths bestowed upon us, so that we may perform what is right. ᾧ ἡ δόξα εἰς τὼς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰῶνων ἀμήν] Such a doxology in other places is to be referred to God the Father of Christ, but here it seems to be referred to Christ himself, as in Apoc. V. 12. Here the epistle was finished. ’Εις τὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰῶνων עד עולם עולמים. A Hebrew locution, which you have also in Philipp. IV. 20, 1. Tim. I. 17. 2. Tim. IV. 18. ἀμήν. See Rom. XVI. 27.

Although some refer this doxology to the Father, we prefer to refer it to Christ, whose mention was made, according to the more customary usage of pronouns. We do not at all think it should be admitted that the epistle was finished here. For Paul to append some things where he already wished to conclude his epistles is both lacking in precedent and does not sufficiently agree with τῇ θεοπνευσίᾳ. Add that the final wish in v. 25 follows at last.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Καταρτίσαι ὑμᾶς ἐν παντὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ] In Ma- nuscripto: Ἐν παντὶ λόγῳ καὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ. Aptos vos red- dat ad omnem sermonem bonum & opus bonum, in quo ge- nere præcipuum est concordia, ad quam & participium κα- ταρτισμένοι refertur, 1. Cor. I. 10. Ἐν pro ad quomodo ל Ebræum sumitur. Καταρτίσαι habes pari sensu 1. Petr. V. 10. Respondet Ebræo כּוּן. Εἰς τὸ ποιῆσαι τὸ θέλημα ἀυτᾶ] Vide Eph. VI. 6. 1. Joh. II. 17. Est explicatio ejus quod præcedit. Ποιῶν ἐν ὑμῖν τὸ ἐυάρεστον ἐνώπιον ἀυτὲ] Deus dicitur in nobis operari velle & perficere Phil. II. 13. Facit autem hoc, tum notitiam nobis dando promissionum su- arum, tum Spiritu nos excitando & roborando. Face- re enim recte & is dicitur, qui faciendi causas dat. Et ho- nos omnis effectuum redit εἰς τὸ πρῶτον αἴτιον. Est autem idem ἐυάρεστον ἐνώπιον ἀυτᾶ, quod brevius ἐυάρεστον τῷ Θεῷ Rom. XII. 1. cap. XIV. 18. Eph. V. 10. Phil. IV. 18. Et ποιῶν construitur cum καταρτίσαι.

Quia ad studium bonorum operum excitavit Ebræos Apostolus, jam precatur, ut ad omne opus bonum aptos reddat, ac perficiat eos dē Dominus, ut voluntatem Dei juxta præscriptum Verbi ipsius faciant: idque Divinæ operationi tribuit, qui non modo aptos reddat, sed etiam operetur id in ipsis, in voluntate ac corde ipsorum gratiæ efficaci ἐνερ- γείᾳ; quæ proinde non tantum per moralem actio- nem propensionem promissionum, & excitatio- nem per Spiritum, sed per virium supernaturali- um concessionem, regenerationem & renovationem Spiritus sancti fit: ne forte credantur vires naturæ externa propensione Divinarum promissionum juvari, aut Spiritus S. cum naturalibus viribus eas- dem ceu tantum sopitas aut præpeditas excitando, & liberiores reddendo concurrere, ac συνέργειαν ipsis viribus naturæ tribuatur. Omnia ergo hic gratiæ divinæ tribuuntur. Dupliciter, inquit Tho- mas, aptatur homo ad benefaciendum, uno modo ex- terius operando, & sic unus homo aptat alium per- suadendo vel comminando: Alio modo aliquid inte- rius exhibendo, & sic solus Deus aptat voluntatem, qui solus eam potest immutare. Unde Estius ipse concludit: Non ergo dicamus Deum movere vo- luntatem hominum, sicut aptum novit, ut sequantur, tanquam in eo sit efficacia gratiæ, sed fateamur, De- um facere homines aptos bona voluntatis successio- ne. Qui etiam ad illud ποιῶν ἐν ὑμῖν longe recti- us Grotio, utpote qui per tropum Metonymiæ id pervertit, facere Deum id dici tantum, quia faci- endi causas dat. Hoc est, per gratiam suam effici- ens, efficaciter operans in nobis opera sibi placentia. Manifeste docet hic locus, gratiam Dei non ex eo ef- ficacem censeri, quod voluntas nostra per suum as- sensum sese accommodeet vocanti aut suadenti Deo, sed efficacem esse per seipsam & à seipsa, dum Deus potenti sua operatione nos aptat, & in nobis efficit omne bonum, per quod ei placemus. Sub quo bono ipsum etiam assensum & cooperationem voluntatis nostræ contineri, nemo qui sanus sit in fide, dubita- verit; Deus est enim, qui operatur in nobis & velle & perficere, Phil. II. & qui omnia opera in nobis operatur Es. XXVI.

Διὰ Ἰησοῦ χριστῦ] Recte hoc construitur cum illo ἐυά- ρεστον. Ea enim demum nunc Deo placent, quæ fiunt secundum Christi præcepta. Sic διὰ usurpat & Petrus 1. II. 5.

Non est secundum Christi præcepta, sed per Je- sum Christum. Nomen enim Christi nuspiam notat præcepta Christi. Nec 1. Petr. II. 5. sensus ille se- cundum Christi præcepta obtinet: Sed potius per Christum teu Sacerdotem Novi Testamenti oblatâ spiritualia sacrificia Deo grata esse dicuntur. Conf. Apoc. IIX. 4. 5. Ebr. XIII. 8. Theophylactus non ad τὸ ἐυάρεστον, sed ad verbum ποιῶν hæc refert; Quod faciat illa Deus per Christum Mediatorem: Nec mirum, inquit, si is, qui ab initio nobis operatus est salutem, in actione ipsa virtutum Mediator effici- tur, & Patris exequitur voluntatem, collatis nobis, ut, quæ recta sunt, peragamus, viribus. ᾧ ἡ δόξα εἰς τὼς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰῶνων ἀμήν] Talis δοξολο- γία aliis locis ad Deum Patrem Christi, sed hic ad Christum ipsum referenda videtur, ut Apoc. V. 12. Hic finita fuit epi- stola. ’Εις τὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰῶνων עד עולם עולמים. Lo- quutio Ebræa, quam habes & Philipp. IV. 20, 1. Tim. I. 17. 2. Tim. IV. 18. ἀμήν. Vide Rom. XVI. 27.

Quanquam nonnulli ad Patrem reférant hanc δοξολογίαν, ad Christum tamen, cujus mentio facta, referre ex usitatiori Pronominum ratione malu- mus. Hic autem finitam fuisse epistolam minime admittendum censemus. Nam subtexere Pau- lum nonnulla, ubi jam concludere volebat episto- las, & exemplo caret, nec satis τῇ θεοπνευσίᾳ con- venit. Adde quod finale votum v. 25. demum se- quatur.

## 13:22
Vers. 22. Παρακαλῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοὶ] What follows are things appended to an already finished epistle, as is often the case with Paul. Παρακαλῶ here is 'I beseech', as in Rom. XII. and elsewhere. ᾿Ανέχεσθε τῦ λόγε τῆς παρακλήσεως] Take in good part the admonitions which I have added to this epistle in chapters X. XI. XII. XIII. Ἀνέχεσθαι סבלו. Καὶ γὰρ διὰ βραχέων ἐπέστειλαὴμῖν] I have instructed you, as in Acts XV. 20. A large subject was offering itself: But I, so that I might be less burdensome to you, have contracted into a few words what could have been said in many. Διὰ βραχέων is a good Greek locution, existing also in Lucian. ῥημάτων is understood, which Demosthenes adds.

Chrysostom, Theophylact, and Oecumenius understand παράκλησιν as consolation. But Blessed Gerhard thinks exhortation is more fitting; because he exhorts that they should bear with, or calmly receive, the word of παρακλήσεως. But the word of consolation is always welcome. The Apostle had exhorted the Hebrews not without the stings of reproofs, which was done especially in chapters V. and XII: therefore he adds a mitigation here: He also alleges brevity, because an exhortation is more willingly admitted which does not blunt the mind with a multitude of words, as Estius says here. For these things do not pertain to the whole epistle, but to those things which the Apostle had commanded the Hebrews. The state of the epistle also, if you depart from the Didascalia, is more exhortatory than consolatory. For the Hebrews are stimulated both concerning all doctrines, and especially in the latter part, which is almost entirely Paraenetic, to the perseverance of faith and the pursuit of piety. Finally, the Apostle himself explains it thus through the word ἐπέστειλα, I have instructed you. There is no need, therefore, to inquire how the Apostle says that he has written in few words, when the epistle is quite prolix, provided that these things do not look to the whole epistle.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Παρακαλῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοὶ] Quæ sequuntur e- pistolæ jam finitæ subtexta sunt, ut apud Paulum sæpe. Πα- ρακαλῶ hic est rogo, ut Rom. XII. & alibi. ᾿Ανέχεσθε τῦ λόγε τῆς παρακλήσεως] Boni consulite mo- nita, quæ huic epistolæ adjeci cap. X. XI. XII. XIII. Ἀνέ- χεσθαι סבלו. Καὶ γὰρ διὰ βραχέων ἐπέστειλαὴμῖν] Præcipi vobis, ut Act. XV. 20. Larga se dabat materia: Sed ego, quo mi- nus gravis vobis essem, quæ multis dici poterant, in pau- ca contraxi. Διὰ βραχέων, est bene Græca loquutio, eti- am apud Lucianum extans. Subauditur ῥημάτων, quod adji- cit Demosthenes.

Chrysostomus, Theophylactus, & Oecumenius παράκλησιν de consolatione intelligunt. Magis au- tem congruere exhortationem censet B. Gerhar- dus; quia hortatur, ut sufferant, vel placide suspici- ant verbum παρακλήσεως. Consolationis autem ver- bum semper gratum est. Ex exhortatus erat Apo- stolus Ebræos non sine reprehensionum aculeis, quod imprimis cap. V. & XII. factum: ideo hic mi- tigationem addit: Brevitatem quoque allegat, quia exhortatio libentius admittitur, quæ non obtundit verborum multitudine, ut hic Estius. Non enim ad totam epistolam hæc pertinent, sed ad ea, quæ præ- ceperat Ebræis Apostolus. Status etiam episto- læ, si à Didascalia abeas, magis est exhortatorius, quam consolatorius. Extimulantur enim Ebræi & circa quasque doctrinas, & imprimis parte postre- ma, quæ tota fere est Parænetica, ad perseverantiam fidei & studium pietatis. Denique explicat ita ipse Apostolus per verbum ἐπέστειλα, præcepi vo- bis. Non ergo opus est disquirere, quomodo di- cat Apostolus, se paucis scripsisse, quum epistola satis prolixa sit, siquidem hæc non spectent ad to- tam epistolam.

## 13:23
Vers. 23. Γινώσκετε τὸν ἀδελφὸν Τιμόθεον ἀπολελυμένον] who had been with Paul in Rome, and upon his departure had remained in Italy, and having been given into chains, and then liberated, had undertaken some journey, perhaps into Gaul, intending to return from there into Italy. In the Manuscript there were some letters worn away: He saw that it had certainly been written ἀδελφὸν ὑμῶν, as it was also in the copies which the Syriac and Latin used. Some understand the word γινώσκετε assertively. But it is more correctly taken Imperatively: Know ye: As it is in the Syriac version: For he makes manifest to the Hebrews across the sea what they did not yet know. ᾿Απολελυμένον, which is, not freed from the business by which he was detained, but released from the chains by which Timothy had been confined. He announces that, however, as a joyful thing to the Hebrews. For he was in good estimation among the Hebrews, for whose sake he even wished to be circumcised, Acts XVI. Μεθ’ ὗ ἐὰν τάχιον ἔρχηται, ὄψομαι ὑμᾶς] Thus he will have returned quickly from his journey. Thus he asserts at once his affection and his immense desire to see them: With him, he says, as a companion, if he returns to me in time, I will visit you: otherwise I will go to you without him, impatient of a longer delay: Whence it also seems to be gathered that Paul was not in chains when he sent these things. For otherwise he would not have promised it so absolutely: I will see you, but I hope that I will see you; or as in the epistle to Philemon: I hope through your prayers that I am granted to you. But it seems likely to Estius that he did not visit them, hindered either by more serious business of the Church or by some persecution, because no history records that Paul, after the Roman departure, about which the last chapter of Acts speaks, had ever returned into Judea, and therefore the words of the Apostle are assertive of an intention, not an event, as in 1 Cor. XVI. Theophylact, however, says: Perhaps it could even happen that he might go from the city into Judea, since it is certain that he was dismissed as soon as he was captured by Nero. We leave that in the middle.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Γινώσκετε τὸν ἀδελφὸν Τιμόθεον ἀπολελυμένον] qui cum Paulo Romæ fuerat, & eo digresso remanserat in Italia, datusque in vincula, ac deinde liberatus iter aliquo instituerat, in Galliam forte, inde redire in Itali- am cogitans. In Manuscripto erant literæ aliquæ detritæ: Videbat utique scriptum fuisse ἀδελφὸν ὑμῶν, quomodo fuit & in exemplaribus, quibus usi sunt Syrus & Latinus. Verbum γινώσκετε nonnulli assertive intelligunt. Sed rectius Imperative accipitur: Scitote: Ut est in Syriaca versione: Transmarinis enim Ebræis ma- nifestat, quod nondum sciebant. ᾿Απολελυμένον, quod est, non expeditum à negotiis, quibus deten- tus fuit, sed solutum à vinculis, quibus conclu- sus fuerat Timotheus. Id autem ceu rem lætam nunciat Ebræis. Nam is apud Ebræos in bona existimatione erat, in quorum gratiam etiam cir- cumcidi voluit, Act. XVI. Μεθ’ ὗ ἐὰν τάχιον ἔρχηται, ὄψομαι ὑμᾶς] Sic cito ab iti- nere suo redierit. Ita simul affectum suum, & desiderium ingens ipsos videndi asserit: Cum illo, inquiens, comite, si mature ad me redierit, vos invisam: alioqui sine eo ad vos iturus, mora longioris impatiens: Unde etiā colligi videtur, Paulum non fuisse vinctum, cum hæc mitteret. Nam alias ita absolute id non pro- misisset: Videbo vos, sed spero, me vos visurum; vel ut in epist. ad Philem. Spero per orationes vestras me donari vobis. Verisimile autem videtur Estio, quod eos non inviserit, sive gravioribus Ecclesiæ negotiis, sive persecutione quadam impeditus, quia nulla historia prodat, Paulum post Romanam profectionem, de qua Act. ult. reversum aliquando fuisse in Judæam, adeoque verba Apostoli esse as- sertiva propositi non eventus, ut 1. Cor. XVI. Theo- phylactus vero Forte, inquit, etiam fieri id poterat, ut ab urbe in Judæam concederet, cum constet hunc fuisse dimissum, ut primum fuit à Nerone compre- hensus. Nos id in medio relinquimus.

## 13:24
Vers. 24. Ἀσπάσασθε πάντας τὺς ἡγυμένυς ὑμῶν] Namely those who were Princes of the Churches in individual towns, as we said above 7 and 17.

Καὶ πάντας τὺς ἁγίυς] as in Rom. XVI. 15.

The overseers of the Churches especially through Judea and Syria, and all the saints, that is, all the faithful who are among you. He commands, therefore, to greet the whole Church in those places where the Hebrews perhaps were.

Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς ὁι ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰταλίας] For there were many Christians already, not only at Rome, but also at Puteoli, and throughout all Italy, partly from those times in which the Acts end, and partly from the labor of the helpers of Paul, Luke, Timothy, Titus, Crescens, Tychicus, Onesimus, and Epaphroditus.

In the Vulgate, 'brethren' is added: But Estius warns that it is contained neither in the Syriac nor in many Latin manuscripts. Moreover, this manner of greeting among Christians is not merely a bare custom, but a pious vow, and not an empty one, if it is received with true faith.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Ἀσπάσασθε πάντας τὺς ἡγυμένυς ὑμῶν] Nempe eos, qui in singulis oppidis Ecclesiarum erant Principes, ut di- ximus supra 7. & 17.

Καὶ πάντας τὺς ἁγίυς] ut Rom. XVI. 15.

Præpositos Ecclesiarum maxime per Judæam & Syriam, & omnes sanctos, id est, fideles omnes, qui apud vos sunt. Totam ergo Ecclesiam salutare ju- bet istis locis, ubi Ebræi forte agebant.

Ἀσπάζονται ὑμᾶς ὁι ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰταλίας] Erant enim non Romæ tantum, sed & Puteolis, & per omnem Ita- liam multi jam Christiani, partim ab illis temporibus, in quibus acta desinunt, partim ex labore adjutorum Pauli, Lucæ, Timothæi, Titi, Crescentis, Tychici, Onesimi, E- paphroditi.

In Vulgata additur fratres: Sed Estius monet, nec in Syriaco, nec in compluribus MS. Latinis id habe- ri. Hæc autem ratio salutandi inter Christianos, non nuda tantum quædam consuetudo est, sed pi- um votum, nec inane, si vera fide suscipiatur.

## 13:25
Vers. 25. Ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν, ᾿Αμήν] And this is after the example of Paul, Eph. VI. 24, Col. IV. 18, 1 Tim. VI. 21, 2 Tim. IV. 22, Tit. III. 15. Who elsewhere explains what that grace is, namely, of Christ.

The final vow of Paul himself, not Luke, after the example of Paul: by which, in one word of grace, he embraces all things that flow from this fountain, both bodily and especially spiritual, insofar as these are salutary and agreeable to the Divine will. Theophylact, however, understands this particularly of spiritual goods: 'By grace,' he says, 'he means both the remission of sins, and purity of mind, and the participation of the Holy Spirit itself.' He prays for these for ALL without distinction, since this kind of grace is common, says Theophylact; Paul prays for this commonly for both those presiding and those subject, with a necessary reminder added: by what means will it remain with them? Namely, if you have done injury to no one, if you lead a life worthy of this grace. For this grace remains with us as long as we apply ourselves to good works. But it flies away immediately and departs far off, when we desert its institutions and laws by living wickedly, he who bestowed this upon us. I would therefore wish you to lead a life not unworthy of such grace. And not to live to the injury of him who endowed us with so many goods: but rather to praise him by doing right: so that it may finally be evident from our best actions, and our tolerance of the evils brought upon us, that he did not bestow this grace upon the ungrateful. Amen!

Glory be to GOD THE FATHER, and to THE SON, and to THE HOLY SPIRIT, as it was in the Beginning, and now and always, and for ever and ever, Amen!

* * *

Latin:

Vers. 25. Ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν, ᾿Αμήν] Et hoc ad Exemplum Pauli Eph. VI. 24. Col. IV. 18. 1. Tim. VI. 21. 2. Tim. IV. 22. Tit. III. 15. Qui alibi explicat, quæ sit illa gratia, nempe Christi.

Votum finale ipsius Pauli, non Lucæ, ad exem- plum Pauli: quo una gratiæ voce omnia, quæ ab hoc fonte promanant bona, cum corporalia, tum imprimis spiritualia, simul complectitur, quatenus ista salutaria sunt & Divinæ voluntati congrua. De spiritualibus tamen bonis peculiariter hæc intelli- git Theophylactus: Gratiam autem, inquit, cum pec- catorum dicit remissionem, tum animi puritatem, tum ipsam Spiritus sancti participationem. Ea au- tem OMNIBUS sine discrimine precatur, cum communis sit hujusmodi gratia, inquit Theophyla- ctus, communiter etiam tam præsidentibus, quam subjectis Paulus hanc comprecatur, addita com- monefactione necessaria; quo pacto illa perman- sura cum ipsis sit? Nimirum si nulli injuriam intule- ritis, si dignam hac gratia ducetis & vitam. Tamdiu enim hæc apud nos gratia manet, quamdiu operibus bonis incumbimus. Evolat autem statim & procul abscessit, ubi ejus instituta & leges male vivendo de- serimus, qui nobis hanc contulit. Velim itaque vos istiusmodi gratia vitam ducere non indignam. Nec ad illius injuriam vivere, qui nos tot bonis donavit: quin recta potius operando eundem collaudare: ut pateat tandem ex nostris optimis actionibus, & illa- torum malorum in nos tolerantia, non ingratis hunc gratiam hanc contulisse. Amen!

Gloria sit DEO PATRI, & FILIO, & SPIRITUI SANCTO, sicut erat in Principio, & nunc & semper, & in secula seculorum, Amen!

* * *

# James

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N. I. ANNOTATIONS ON THE EPISTLE OF ST. JAMES.

Latin:

I. N. I. ANNOTATA AD EPISTOLAM S. JACOBI.

## 1:1 Introduction: Prolegomena
PROLEGOMENA.

Grotius deals first with the inscription of the Epistle: which, however, is not a canonical part of the epistle, because it did not proceed from the Author himself, but from some other person: just as Grotius for that reason dismissed the inscriptions or titles of other epistles without commentary. Let us nevertheless hear the same man: Ἡ τῶ ἁγίε Ἰακώβε ἐπισολὴ καθολικὴ) that is, ἐγκύκλιος, not destined for one Church, as those of Paul, but sent in many copies to many places, so that from there other copies might be made, and sent elsewhere.

Why these and the following Epistles are called Catholic, there is not the same opinion among all. B. Brochman cites the cause that they were sent to many churches, and that Oecumenius brought this forward: and he reports that Salmeron and Justinian reject it for that reason, and adds his own vote; because among the seven epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude, which are called Catholic by Origen in Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. bk. VI, ch. 25, and Athanasius in the Synopsis, the two later Johannine ones are also included, of which one, however, is inscribed to the elect lady, the other to the distinguished man Gaius, not to many churches. Moreover, the words of Origen brought forward by Eusebius have nothing about the seven epistles being called Catholic, nor do they state anything about the Johannine ones, that they obtained that name in the Church. Eusebius, however, in bk. II, ch. 23, makes mention of τῶν ἑπτὰ λεγομένων καθολικῶν. And Athanasius names them the same way in the Synopsis: Καθολικαὶ ἐπισολαὶ διαφόρων Ἀποςόλων αἱ πᾶσαι ἑπτὰ εἰς ἓν ἀριθμώμεναι βιβλίον. It is added that the Epistle to the Hebrews should equally have been called ἐγκύκλιος, as the Jacobean one was sent ταῖς δώδεκα φυλαῖς ταῖς ἐν διασπορᾷ. But no better reason for the appellation is brought forward by Salmeron, even though he obtained the suffrage of Tirinus and Cornelius à Lapide; namely, that the epistles are called Catholic because they contain universal doctrine and are by universal authors. For thus all the Pauline ones would likewise have to be called Catholic. Therefore, this cause for the appellation is deservedly rejected by Estius and Justinian. But the latter thinks this is the genuine reason for that name, that the ancients wished by it to distinguish these genuine Apostolic ones from other adulterine epistles. But for the same reason the Pauline epistles should also have been called Catholic. However, all the causes can be joined: namely, that the epistles are called Catholic 1.
