By reason of the object, because they were sent to many, in many copies, so that they might be communicated everywhere with other Churches: which can also be said to have been done for the second and third of John, because they were believed to be joined to the first, because they are very short, even if they pertained particularly to certain persons: Whence in the ἐπιγραφῇ the name of ἐπισολῆς καθολικῆς was attributed to all these three Johannine ones: Which I see is also approved by Estius: We do not grudgingly concede that there are only five Catholic epistles: Yet it has prevailed that those two also were so called, for the reason that they were included in one volume with others which are properly such. He says, however, that the Epistle to the Hebrews was written particularly to those who were living in Jerusalem and in Judea, of whom he says that they sustained the plundering of their goods with joy, Heb. X, although the intention of the writer was that it should also be communicated to the others placed in the dispersion. Although it can also be said that they are not numbered among the Catholic ones because they should have been reckoned among the other epistles of Paul, which are not Catholic: 2. By reason of authority, because all seven were accepted as Divine by the universal or Catholic Church at that time when they obtained that name, even if at the beginning some were doubted by some. 3. But above all it seems to be said that these epistles were called particularly Catholic so that, because they were comprised in one volume, they might be distinguished from the Pauline ones, likewise contained in one volume, by that distinguishing name. Dionysius in Proem. Cathol. on the Canonical name: Although, he says, the epistles of Paul could also be called Canonical; yet this name is imposed more on these epistles, because they were written by diverse Authors, and thus could not obtain some peculiar name from one of them, but some common name had to be attributed to them, and that a worthy and venerable one. The same must be said of the name Catholic.

As regards the order of these epistles, even if in the Canon of the Apostles, as also in Augustine, bk. on faith and works ch. 14, which B. Luther followed, it is placed in this series, so that the epistles of Peter obtain the first place, the Johannine the second, the Jacobean the third, and the Judean the last: and the epistle of James is placed in the last position in the Council of Carthage III, can. 47, and in Augustine, bk. II, on Christian doctrine, ch. 8: and Innocent I, in ep. 4 to Exuperius, puts the epistles of John before the rest; and the Council of Florence and Trent make the epistles of Peter the first: Most, however, follow Jerome, who, even if he confesses that Peter obtained the first place among the Greeks, as also in Latin Codices, yet says in his Epist. to Paulinus, which he calls this, that he restored those epistles to their own order: For the first of them is one of James, two of Peter, three of John, and one of Jude. Just as also in the Council of Laodicea, can. ult., the Epistle of James is placed in the first position, and likewise by Gelasius, C. Sancta Romana, dist. XV. Indeed, also in Latin editions of the Bibles fortified by the diplomas of the Roman Pontiffs. Lyranus gives this reason, that it was written in the first place: others, that that James presided over the Bishopric of the Jerusalem Church, which was held as the mother of the remaining Churches. Which we leave in its own place.

Furthermore, at v. 1, ch. 1, concerning the name and office of James, Grotius inquires about the Author, who is that James? I find three opinions, just as three are believed to be enumerated in the sacred writings, or at least among ecclesiastical writers called by that name, in the age of the Apostles the first attributes this epistle to James the son of Zebedee, who is called the Greater, who is in the Chronicles of Lucius Dexter and in Tom. V of the Bibliotheca Patrum of Pope Sixtus III, it is attributed in the epistle concerning the evils of the Doctors (which, however, the Parisians and Bellarmine in his Catalogus ascribe not to Sixtus, but to some Pelagian), which is also assigned to Isidore, as well as to the Author of the Mozarabic liturgy, and also of the Arabic and Syriac version, nor is it judged improbable by Gaspar Sanchez, tr. III on the journey of St. James to Spain, ch. 12. But it is disapproved by most others, primarily by the authority of the ancient Doctors of the Church. Wherefore the greatest part of Interpreters and Doctors vindicate this epistle for the second James, the son of Alphaeus, who is called the Less. Origen on ch. V to the Romans, Ephraem Syrus in the tract that one must abstain from judgments, Chrysostom in the admonitory sermon on the Eucharist at the dedication of the church of Leontius in the life of John the Almsgiver, Theophylact on ch. VI. Matthew. Simeon Metaphrastes in the life of John the Almsgiver from the Greeks: Jerome, book 1, against Jovinian, ch. 24. Augustine on ch. II to the Galatians. Ambrose, book VII, on Luke, ch. IX, are praised by B. Brochmand, because they call James, the author of the epistle, the brother of the Lord. To these Latins, Cornelius à Lapide also appeals for this opinion, adding for James the son of Alphaeus, Clem. Alex. book VI, Stromata; Eusebius, book II, Ecclesiastical History, ch. 23; Epiphanius, heresy XXIX; as also Chrysostom, homily XXXIII and XLIV on Matthew, with whom let those settle the matter who do not fear to allege most others to the contrary, as if they make someone other than James the son of Alphaeus the author of this epistle. For some name a third James here, called the Just, on account of the remarkable holiness of his life, Bishop of Jerusalem, distinct from that one, such as Erasmus in his annotations, Turrianus on book VI of the Apostolic Constitutions of Clement, ch. 12 and 14, Carolus Bovius in his scholia. on book II of the constitutions of Clement, ch. 59, who in support of that opinion praises Epiphanius, heresy LXXIX, Dorotheus in his synopsis, and Nicephorus, book III, Ecclesiastical History, ch. 40, and others: to which Estius admits that even Jerome in Isaiah XVII accedes. But it cannot be solidly taught that there were three of that name in the age of the Apostles who were established in authority over the universal Churches, or at least over the twelve tribes, or that a third flourished besides the two aforementioned Apostles, namely James, to whom the Catholic epistle can be vindicated. Sufficient documents of that matter from antiquity do not exist. Furthermore, it is better for a Canonical writing to be referred to an Apostle who is θεόπνευστον (divinely inspired) than to another, concerning whose θεοπνευσίᾳ (divine inspiration) it is not certain. Thirdly, if some such remarkable Bishop had been established in the Jerusalem Church in the time of the Apostles, St. Luke, the writer of the Acts of the Apostles, would by no means have kept silent about it. Fourthly, Paul clearly teaches in Gal. I. 19 that James the brother of the Lord was from the college of the XII Apostles: 'But other of the apostles saw I none, save James the Lord's brother.' Fifthly, when Paul enumerates those three Doctors who were seen to be pillars in the Church, James and Cephas and John, it is in no way likely that James, mentioned in the first place, was someone other than one from the same college of the XII Apostles, to which Cephas and John belonged: who indeed, since he cannot be James the son of Zebedee, as he was already taken from the living at that time, it is necessary that we understand James the son of Alphaeus, whom the Apostle had previously called the brother of the Lord. Moreover, that the author of this epistle is the brother of the Lord is confessed by most: nor does Grotius deny it. Sixthly, the designation of Mark agrees, when in ch. XV. 40. he names Mary the mother of James the Less and of Joses; who was the wife of Alphaeus, and is held to be the sister of Mary the Θεοτόκῳ (Mother of God), whence James is called the brother, that is, the kinsman of the Lord, by the customary manner of scripture, Matt. XII. XIII. 55, Mark VI. 2, Luke VIII, John VII. 5, Acts I, 1 Cor. IX. Seventhly, the designation of Jude agrees, who in the epistle v. 1 calls himself the brother of James, where there is no doubt that James the son of Alphaeus is designated from the collation of Matt. XIII. 55, Mark VI. 3. For James and Joses and Simon and Jude are called the brothers of the Lord. Who then, therefore, could doubt that James the brother of the Lord is James the Less, the son of Alphaeus? Eighthly, Christ deigned to appear to this James particularly after his resurrection, as to his brother or kinsman, by the common calculation of Interpreters, 1 Cor. XV. 7. Ninthly, James, to whom the liberation of Peter was to be announced, after James the son of Zebedee had already been beheaded, according to the almost unanimous opinion of the Doctors, was James the son of Alphaeus from the college of the Apostles, Acts XII. 17. Tenthly, nor is any other believed to have been present and to have delivered the opinion in the council of the Apostles, Acts XV. For it is not likely that, after Peter, he defined the controversy with such authority: 'Wherefore I judge' v. 19, who was outside the Apostolic college. Eleventhly, the authority of the ancient Doctors stands most for this opinion, as well as those who admit that there were no more than two famous men by this name in the time of the Apostles: just as the Martyrologies of all the Western Churches recount only those two from the college of the Apostles. But concerning the third, where, how, and when he suffered, no history exists: as well as those who acknowledge James, who is said to have performed the office of Bishop by some at Jerusalem, to be the son of Alphaeus: as well as those who acknowledge James the brother of the Lord to be none other than James the son of Alphaeus: and finally those who expressly make him the author of this epistle: which, so that they may be more fully established, it is helpful here to weigh the Grotian notes, even though they are annotated on ch. I. 1, so that we may not have need to say the same things twice. But he says it thus:

Chap. I. v. 1. James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ] The Apostle does not say so, as Paul and Peter are accustomed to do, who did not do that without cause. For it added great authority to them, that they had been chosen by Christ himself into a position which stood out above all others in the Church. The Syrian who wrote the inscription to these and the following epistles thinks this James was the son of Zebedee. But that is less credible, because he, as we learn in Acts 12, was killed by Herod before the word of the Gospel had spread much outside of Judea. But it does not seem probable to me that this James is the son of Alphaeus either. For he too would have added the name of Apostle. He is, therefore, the one who was appointed by the Apostles as Prince of the Jerusalem presbytery, so that while the Apostles were running here and there, as was happening, that assembly might have an outstanding man, and one to whom, because of his exceptional virtues, the name 'the Just' adhered, by whom it might be governed. Many have believed that this James is called an Apostle in Galatians 1:19. But we have shown from that passage that it by no means follows from it. But that he was not an Apostle is clearly indicated by those cited by Eusebius in book II, Hegesippus and Clement of Alexandria in his book of Outlines. The epistle to Hero among the Ignatian letters, Cyril of Jerusalem, and Jerome in his 'On Ecclesiastical Writers', and on Galatians, and in Acts, and likewise in his First to the Corinthians and on Galatians, Chrysostom, agree with these. The same is in the Constitutions which are called those of Clement of Rome, a very ancient book, II. 59, VIII. at the end. And Eusebius follows this opinion in I. 12. This James, however, is called the brother of the Lord, because he was the son of Joseph the carpenter by a former wife, as some think, Eusebius, Jerome, Epiphanius, and certain others; there are those who think he was a kinsman of Christ according to the flesh in another way. There are those who doubt whether this opinion or that one is truer. Servants of Jesus Christ are called not only the Apostles, but also all the faithful, Acts 2:18, but especially those who are placed in an eminent position, Phil. 1:1.

This is Grotius. Concerning which I would wish it to be observed: 1. That the argument is of no moment, that James called himself not an Apostle, but a servant of Christ. Which is evident even from this, that neither did Jude call himself an Apostle, but a servant of the Lord: who nevertheless was an Apostle, the brother of James, by unanimous confession of all. Nor do the later epistles of John, the second and third, prefix the name of Apostle, and yet they are received by the Church as Apostolic. What of the fact that Paul himself does not always call himself an Apostle in the inscription of his letters, but sometimes a servant of God, as in Phil. 1:1, and sometimes a prisoner of Jesus Christ, Philem. v. 1? an Apostle in the frontispiece of the second epistle, Grotius nevertheless did not fear to call into doubt whether Peter the Apostle was the author of that epistle. But there is no reason to doubt that the name servant of Jesus Christ is used not only in the sense that denotes those who are placed in an eminent position, but also as Paul and Jude call themselves servants of Christ, since this is the more eminent meaning, and there is no reason that would exclude the present James from the college of the Apostles. Cornelius à Lapide brings forward reasons why Saint James calls himself a servant of Christ, not an Apostle: Of which the first is a zeal for humility and modesty, which can be admitted: The second, that he is properly called an Apostle who, sent by Christ, runs about the world to preach the Gospel; but James was fixed to Judea and Jerusalem, which proceeds from the false hypothesis about James being created Bishop of Jerusalem by Christ and the Apostles: which is destitute of solid documents of antiquity. The third, that it is a huge dignity to be a servant of Christ, and that the Apostles preferred it to all the kingdoms of the world, boasting more of it, as Didymus and Oecumenius testify, that they were servants of Christ, than if they had been Kings of the whole world: Which we do not disapprove. The fourth, that Peter and Paul occupied the title of Apostle antonomastically, and it does not suit their truth or modesty. The fifth, that a servant of Christ is the same as an Apostle, insofar as it does not signify here just any servant, but one most faithful, most beloved, closest, and most intimate to Christ the master, who takes care of all his affairs, and is thus sent to any nations to convert them, who is none other than an Apostle, is joined with a begging of the question, unless it is proposed as we have already rendered it above: that one should not depart from the more eminent meaning, especially because the parallel inscription, Jude v. 1, persuades it. The final reason, that Sixtus of Siena in book VII of his Bibliotheca and Fevardentius here say the name of Apostle was evaded by some forger, so that by removing the author he might remove the authority of the Church, cannot be proven. For the fact that some Latin, Syriac, and Arabic codices have the name of Apostle is by no means sufficient, unless the same is found in the original codices, such as the Greek ones: But that it is found in those cannot be taught by proven exemplars. Observe also the 2nd Syriac title concerning James the son of Zebedee, although it is read in the Viennese edition of Johann Albrecht Widmanstadius, it is nevertheless not found in other codices, and thus was even omitted by the Londoners. Nothing is found about it in the Syriac version of the text either; James is only called an Apostle, just as the London Arabic and Ethiopic versions also name him 3. To the argument brought against James the son of Zebedee as author, that he was killed by Herod earlier, when the word of the Gospel was spreading much outside of Judea, Estius replies that this fails due to the calculation of times: Since according to a true computation it is found that ten years more or less had passed between the death of Christ and the martyrdom of this James, within which time the Epistle could have been written to the brothers dispersed after the death of Stephen, which dispersion happened in the first year after the death of the Savior. But there is no need to labor over the son of Zebedee, whom we acknowledge is not the author. 4. The opinion of Grotius concerning the author of the epistle labors under many hypotheses, which are neither sufficiently proven nor can they be proven. First, that he was constituted by the Apostles as Prince of the Jerusalem Presbytery is said precariously. For that is by no means evident from the scriptures: nor would Saint Luke, the diligent writer of the Acts of the Apostles, have passed it over in silence, who did not even remain silent about the election of the Deacons, Acts VI. Nor did Grotius teach that from Ecclesiastical history either. And why, sitting at Jerusalem and appointed Bishop over an eminent assembly, would he write to Jerusalem to the XII tribes in the dispersion? If those tribes were in the dispersion, how was an eminent Church with an entire presbytery and Bishop found in Jerusalem from the same? Add that there were no bishops superior to presbyters in the Apostolic age, nor did such bishops have their origin from the Apostles, which has been shown elsewhere. Walo Messalinus on Bishops and Presbyters, p. 201. He says, that figment of Clement of Alexandria is absurd, who thought to transmute James the Apostle, and consequently a universal Bishop, into a special and local one, and thus force him into an order. For a local and special Bishop destined for a church would not have had greater authority in the Jerusalem Church than if he had remained an Apostle, and from his Apostleship bearing the care of the universal Church. Indeed, even less, insofar as special bishops were accustomed to be constituted and ordained by the Apostles, and were subject to their authors and ordainers. But James, if he had received power ordained by the Apostles, would have received it as if delegated by those by whom he had been ordained. But an equal has no authority over an equal. He has it from himself and through himself, and uses it by his own right in the same way as his colleague. Nothing, therefore, is more inept and unlearned than that fable which feigned that James was ordained by the Apostles as a special Bishop of Jerusalem, who was himself an Apostle. Therefore, in the Jerusalem Church, in that first council which was celebrated there, gathered from the Apostles and Presbyters and others from the faithful laity to decide the controversy which had arisen in the Church among the disciples, in that council, after the embassy of Paul and Barnabas had been heard, who had been sent by the brethren of the Antiochene Church to consult the Apostles and Presbyters residing in Jerusalem, Peter spoke his opinion first concerning that dispute. After him spoke James, the brother of the Lord. Finally, from his opinion, the decree of the council was formed and pronounced: Τότε ἔδοξε τοῖς Ἀποστόλοις καὶ Πρεσβυτέροις σὺν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ. Where is the bishopric of James? When it was a matter of sending Paul and Barnabas to inquire the opinion of the Jerusalem Presbytery among the Antiochenes, they decided simply that Paul and Barnabas, and certain others from among them, should go up to Jerusalem to the Apostles and Presbyters. He did not, therefore, preside there alone as Bishop. But the other Apostles were with him. This is what Hegesippus had said, that James διαδέχεσθαι τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν μετὰ τῶν Ἀποστόλων. If he had been the proper Bishop of the Jerusalem Church at that time, ordained by the Apostles, there was an opportunity in that council to address him by that title. Peter spoke first in it, after him James. Then, by the common opinion of all, the decree was made, in which the consensus of the Apostles and Presbyters with the whole Church, that is, with the people of the faithful, was expressed. The Apostles were greater and general Bishops; the Presbyters were special and ἀφωρισμένοι. If the Apostles were not present, the Presbyters alone held the first and supreme authority in the Church and alone exercised the ἐπισκοπικὴν ὀικονομίαν. And indeed, when Presbyters were created Bishops by the Apostles with that supreme authority and full right of the Church, so that in their absence—because they themselves were not attached to any certain place and were often away—by the Presbyters everything might be administered. It is therefore false what Clemens writes about James being ordained by the Apostles as the proper Bishop of Jerusalem. Nor is it any more true, what he had placed in the same spot, that the three primary Apostles, Peter, John, and James, had received τὴν γνῶσιν from the Lord after his resurrection, that they had given it to the other Apostles, and the Apostles furthermore to the remaining LXX disciples. These things Claudius Salmasius against Dionysius Petavius.

Then, that James, who was surnamed the Just, was different from James the son of Alphaeus was not only to be said, but to be taught. For most, both of the ancients and of the moderns, do not admit this. Thirdly, Grotius did not express who they were that believed that third James, about whom there is controversy, to be called an Apostle in Galatians 1:19. But he could not have been ignorant that most people believed this concerning James the son of Alphaeus. Grotius perverts this Apostolic passage in vain, making an adversative out of an exceptive word. For it is too clear that the James of whom Paul speaks there, the brother of the Lord, is one of the XII, which all interpreters hitherto, with no one, so far as I know, dissenting, have acknowledged. For all have admitted the exceptive force of the particle εἰ μὴ. Grotius himself also acknowledged this in his annotations on the book. of the Gospel on Matthew 13:54, writing thus concerning James the son of Alphaeus: This therefore is the James, whom not only Paul but also Josephus in his Jewish annals calls the brother of Jesus, that is, his cousin, by a manner of speaking known even to the Greeks and Romans.

But the things which he now brings forward against his former opinion are easily disposed of. 1. He says that those cited by Eusebius in Book II, Hegesippus and Clement of Alexandria, clearly indicate that he was not an Apostle. But concerning Clement of Alexandria, that is clearly false. He holds the contrary in Chapter I, namely that there were only two Jameses, not three: 'Otherwise,' he says, 'there were two Jameses, one by the surname of Justus, who was cast down from the pinnacle of the temple and died struck by a fuller's club: the other who was beheaded.' Since this one is the son of Zebedee, it is manifest that the other is the son of Alphaeus: since there were only two Jameses. Therefore, James the son of Alphaeus is the same as James the Just. But from Hegesippus in Eusebius, Book II, Chapter 23, nothing else is held than that James the brother of the Lord was surnamed the Just. Whom Eusebius says agrees entirely with Clement. Whence, if those things which Eusebius has in Chapter I are compared, it is permitted to conclude that no other than the son of Alphaeus is designated. And yet Eusebius observes that the first of those epistles which are called Catholic is ascribed to this James. But Hegesippus does not indicate by any word that James the Just was not an Apostle; he only asserts that many were called by the name of James. But concerning this Just one, he recounts that he was cast down from the pinnacle of the temple and killed by a fuller's club. Which Eusebius taught from Clement happened to the son of Alphaeus. Nor did Grotius understand Hegesippus to be speaking of any other than the son of Alphaeus in his notes on Matthew 13:55. But Hegesippus mixed many fables into his account, for which reason he was noted by Scaliger, Estius, and others; indeed, even by Grotius himself in the same place. Concerning whom (James the son of Alphaeus, he says) the things which Hegesippus fabled are not worth the effort to recite or refute. Josephus teaches us that he was stoned by the people, under the High Priest Ananus.

2. Grotius appeals to the epistle to Hero among the Ignatian ones, but it is agreed among the learned that it is spurious: nor is anything read in it other than that Stephen ministered to James and the Presbyters at Jerusalem; but it is not hinted at by any jot that that James was different from the Apostles.

3. He alleges Cyril of Jerusalem, but without mention of the place. Others bring forward Catechesis XIV, Illuminat. But in it there is nothing else held than that Christ was seen by James his brother after the resurrection, whom he calls the first pastor of the Church of Jerusalem. But how is it to be gathered from there that James the brother of the Lord was not an Apostle? Is it because Cyril named him specifically, after he had said that the Lord had appeared to the twelve Apostles? But the same was done by Paul, 1 Corinthians 15, who also named Cephas specifically. But did Paul or Cyril for that reason exclude Peter from the number of the XII? Furthermore, others do not hesitate to gather from Catechesis XVII that Cyril counts James, who acted at Jerusalem, among the Apostles after the son of Zebedee was killed; he certainly said 'Apostles,' who by a written epistle liberated the whole world at Jerusalem from all legal and typical things, among whom James was easily the Prince.

4. Jerome on Ecclesiastical writers is contrary to, and does not favor, the opinion of Grotius. For he makes James the brother of the Lord, surnamed the Just, whom he says wrote one of the seven Canonical epistles, the son of Mary the sister of the mother of the Lord, whom John mentions, and adds concerning the same: 'This is he, of whom the Apostle Paul writes to the Galatians saying: But I saw none of the other Apostles, except James the brother of the Lord, and an Apostle, besides these the frequent acts teach.' Which characters sufficiently testify that the son of Alphaeus is understood as the Apostle. Although indeed Jerome in Chapter I to the Galatians inclines to the view that the James named there and in 1 Corinthians 15 by Paul was not one of the XII Apostles: yet he acknowledges in Chapter II that James, named with Peter and John, was an Apostle from that venerable college. 'They are therefore columns of the Church,' he says, 'the Apostles and especially Peter, James, and John.' And elsewhere, namely in Epistle 103 to Paulinus. Vol. III, p. 9 of the previous edition, expressly reckons James, the author of the epistle, among the Apostles. James, he says, Peter, John, and Jude, the Apostles, published seven epistles, as mystical as they are succinct, and equally short and long: short in words, long in meanings, so that there is rarely anyone who does not go blind in the reading of them. Which epistle is prefixed to all Vulgate editions of the Bibles with the Galeated Prologue. And in Book 1 against the Pelagians, Vol. II of his works, p. 268 of the previous edition: I beseech you, does not the Apostle James write, that he who offends in one point is guilty of all? And also in Book II against the Pelagians, page 282: The Apostle James writes: If you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law, but a judge. Whence Cornelius a Lapide rightly gathers that Jerome retracted his opinion about James, that he was not one of the Twelve. Add that in the epistle of Epiphanius to John of Jerusalem, which Jerome translated from Greek into Latin, ch. IV. James, the author of this epistle, is called both an Apostle and, jointly, an Apostle and brother of the Lord.

5. Chrysostom has nothing in Acts 12 and 15, nothing in 1 Cor. 15, in favor of Grotius; but on Galatians ch. 1, he openly opposes Grotius. For he calls James the brother of the Lord, James of Cleophas.

6. The Clementine Constitutions (to which Henr. Valesius on Book 1, chapter 12 of Eusebius, along with others, adds Baronius) are here rejected by the Papists themselves, especially Cardinal Baronius in his Annals for the year of Christ 44, no. 36, who here answers Grotius, Turrianus, and Valesius: Those who handed these down, imprudently indeed, place the third James, whom we mentioned, outside the number of the twelve Apostles. But it seems sufficient for the refutation of his opinion if the origin from which it is derived is repeated. For from those rejected books of Recognitions written under the name of Clement concerning the three Jameses, the authority once assumed has been most inconsiderately [spread] among some. propagated. Some have thought the same opinion to be strengthened by the constitutions of the same Clement, but apocryphal ones; while these things are held there as recited from the person of the Apostles: We therefore, who have been made worthy to be witnesses of his coming, with James the brother of the Lord, and the other seventy-two and seven Deacons, etc. by which words they wish James the brother of the Lord to be established outside the number of the Apostles. But in that opinion the same words rather show James included: For since James is recited there as placed outside the number of the seventy-two, it is clearly evident that he was numbered among the twelve: otherwise, (which it is absurd to say) James the brother of the Lord would have a place not only not among the Apostles, but not even among the disciples. Whence (as is evident from these things) the fact that he is named there singularly as James, was not done so that he might be excluded from the number of the twelve, but rather according to a certain emphasis, because he was the brother of the Lord, he is named.

7. Eusebius, book I, chapter 12, speaks according to the mind of others, when he says that James, of whom 1 Cor. XV, is reported to have been one of the number of the LXX disciples, and besides that one of the brothers of the Lord, if we admit this codex which Robert Stephanus published. Henry Valesius, however, observes that the words μαθητῶν ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ are missing in the remaining Maz. Sc. Med. Frik. & Savil. codices, but neither does Rufinus acknowledge them. For he translates thus: After he also says that he was seen by James, who was one of those who were called brothers of the Savior. But what does this help Grotius? It is evident, therefore, that Grotius could not bring forward any patron from antiquity for his opinion. Valesius indeed, in the place cited, standing for that opinion, alleges Gregory of Nyssa, orat. II on the resurrection of Christ, & Cyril of Jerusalem, Catech. Illumin. IV. But falsely. For nothing is held there to that effect.

As to the fourth point, that Grotius says James was called the brother of the Lord because he was the son of Joseph the carpenter from a former wife, and that Eusebius, Jerome, Epiphanius, and certain others think so; in that which pertains to Jerome, he is mistaken. For this man makes James the son of Mary, the sister of the mother of the Lord. James, he says in De Script. Ecclesiast., who is called the brother of the Lord, surnamed the Just, as some think, the son of Joseph from another wife, (but as it seems to me) the son of Mary, the sister of the mother of the Lord, whom John mentions in his book. Valesius, in his annotations to book II of Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History, chapter 1, acknowledges that Chrysostom and Theodoret in the epistle to the Galatians and many others agree with Jerome, even though he departs from them and Baronius, who argues for that opinion at length. What of the fact that not even Eusebius hands down that opinion assertively but only reportively; Καὶ ὗτος τᾶ Ἰωσὴφ ὠνόμαςο παῖς. Origen, however, traces the origin of this fiction in Matt. XIII to the Gospel which has the title according to Peter, or to the book of James; but Jerome refutes this in Matt. XII. Some suspect the brothers of the Lord to be sons of Joseph from another wife, following the ravings of the apocrypha and inventing them from a certain woman named Esta. We, however (as is contained in the book which we wrote against Helvidius), understand the brothers of the Lord not as sons of Joseph, but as cousins of the Savior, the children of Mary, the maternal aunt of the Lord: who, even though she is called the mother of James the Less and Joseph and Jude, whom we read in another place were called brothers of the Lord; yet all scripture demonstrates that cousins are called brothers. And Baronius, in his apparatus to the Ecclesiastical Annals, no. 63, affirms that not only Theodoret but all the other orthodox writers of the Latins who lived afterwards agree with this opinion. And Grotius himself, at Matt. XIII. 55, acknowledged that one should agree with Jerome rather than Epiphanius, whose words and reasons it is pleasing to repeat here: Epiphanius, whom the Greeks follow, posits for certain that all these were sons of Joseph from a former marriage. But Origen teaches us that this rumor took its beginning from books which falsely bore the name of Peter and James. Wherefore we shall more rightly accede to Jerome, who thinks that all these were cousins of our Lord. For it seems impossible to deny that the same Mary who is called below in Matthew and similarly in Mark the mother of James and Joses, is called in John the sister of the mother of the Lord, as one who stood with the mother of the Lord and with Magdalene at the cross of CHRIST. But if she is the mother of James and Joses, she will certainly also be the mother of Simon and Jude, namely of him who in his epistle names himself the brother of James, and who in the list of the Apostles makes a pair with the same Jude. But that James, to distinguish him from the other, who had John as a brother and Zebedee as a father, is called the Less, by reason of age, I think, and the son of Alphaeus: Whence it may be gathered that Clopas or Cleopas, from whom this Mary is denominated, was the father of the same Mary, and Alphaeus the husband. This, therefore, is the James whom not only Paul, but also Josephus in his Jewish annals, calls the brother of Jesus, that is, his cousin, by a manner of speaking known also to the Greeks and Romans. And these things for the present concerning the Author of the Epistle.

It must now be inquired into, fourthly, concerning its Canonical authority: Which Grotius seems scarcely to concede, for no other reason, as it appears, than that he adjudges it away from the Apostle, and attributes it to an excellent man indeed, but not one inspired by God. The Papists also most gravely attack the blessed Luther on this account, because he derogates from its Canonical authority, nay, even calls it truly straw-like, and also, as Lorinus and Tirinus reproach him along with Cornelius, contentious, swollen, and arid. But as these latter could not yet be shown from the writings of the blessed Luther: So the former was said only in comparison with the Gospel of John and the Pauline epistles in the preface of the year 1528. Which preface, however, was no longer repeated in other editions of the bibles, but rather he testified that he held the epistle as useful and not to be despised, because it brings forward nothing of human doctrine, and strongly urges the law of GOD. Although he indeed judges it to be of no Apostle even in his more recent preface, he nevertheless professes that he establishes this outside of all prejudice: yet he forces no one to believe it. In which manner also some of ours have followed B. Luther: B. Bugenhagen on chapter IV of Romans and on chapter III of Jonah, Vitus Theodorus in his summary of Luke, Osiander in the Magdeburg Centuries, century I, book 2, chapter 54, Flacius in his gloss; which is not surprising, since even in antiquity itself there was doubt concerning the canonical authority of the epistle: when Eusebius himself in book II, chapter 23, openly says ἴστεον, ὡς νοθεύεται, which passage Rufinus and Valesius also translated as if this were the opinion of some. But afterwards Valesius in his annotations judged that Eusebius absolutely pronounces this epistle of James to be spurious: which, when B. Hunnius judged it, he was vehemently traduced by Gretser in Tom. I, Def. Bellarm. book I, chapter 10, he was vehemently traduced, although it cannot be denied that the words of Eusebius can be taken in both ways, as is evident even from the life of Thucydides. λέγουσι δέ τινες τὴν ὀγδόην ἱστορίαν νοθεύεσθαι, which is explained, καὶ μὴ εἶναι Θυκυδίδου. Meanwhile, from the collation of Eusebius, book III, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 25, we easily admit that, according to the opinion of Eusebius, it is not reckoned among spurious writings, but among those things which were placed in controversy, which can also be called θεύεσθαι, by reason of the author, though not by reason of authority, according to the account of Eusebius, and that according to some only, not according to all. Which Jerome also observed in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers: James, who is called the brother of the Lord, wrote only one epistle, which is of the seven Catholic ones, which is itself asserted by some other person to have been published under his name: although gradually as time went on it obtained authority. But are those, among whom it did not formerly obtain authority, or by whom it was itself contradicted, therefore to be accused of heresy immediately, just as some of the Papists, the Luther-scourgers, accuse B. Luther? Thus Erasmus, the beloved son of Leo X, and Cardinal Cajetan would also have to be accused, because by the judgment of Estius they likewise disparaged and rendered doubtful the authority of this epistle, which however is the case regarding Erasmus from his annotations. it does not appear where he bids us kiss the Holy Spirit as Author. But regarding the Cardinal, Estius says thus: Cajetan takes an argument from the salutation to overthrow the authority of the epistle. Since, he says, the salutation is so pure that it is not conformable to the salutation of any other Apostolic epistle. For it sounds nothing of God, nothing of Jesus Christ, nothing of grace, nothing of peace, but, in the profane manner, greetings. These are his words, (which is truly strange) in words borrowed from Luther. For Sixtus in his Bibliotheca sacra attributes almost the same things to Luther. But Cajetan is rightly answered that the Apostles used a similar salutation in the synodical epistle in Acts 15:25. And from that it could be gathered that no other author is to be sought for James than the one with whom, as the mentioned epistle suggests, it was to be sent. But the reasons by which B. Luther and others called the canonical authority into doubt, even if they are altogether so constituted that they could have moved him and others, yet they could not thoroughly convince them, but it will be established in their proper places, especially around chapter 2, verses 21 and 23, that they can be solidly resolved by accurately observing the scope and analysis of the text. Whence in our churches afterwards, all things having been more rightly weighed, this present epistle was easily held by unanimous consent as canonical, both because of the arguments and intrinsic criteria, and also because of the extrinsic documents, namely the testimonies of antiquity, because it was recognized as such by almost all the Fathers, Clement of Alexandria, Athanasius, Gregory Nazianzen, Jerome, Augustine and others, a good long catalogue of whom is exhibited by Jodocus Coccius in his Thesaurus Theologicus, Vol. I, Book VI, art. 23, and from our own side by B. Brochmand, sect. I, Proleg. page 10. But also by the Councils, the Council of Laodicea c. 59. the Council of Milevis cap. 7, the Third Council of Carthage cap. 47, the Second Council of Orange cap. 25, the Second Council of Chalon cap. 33, the Eighth Council of Toledo c. 2. Eusebius certainly in book II, cap. 23, professes himself: That this epistle with the others (Catholic) is publicly read in very many churches, and in book III, cap. 25, he designates the epistle of James, Jude, the second of Peter, and the second and third of John by the name of those things which are spoken against, yet are known to the many. Jerome, however, reports that it not only obtained authority as time went on (when the doubt about the Apostle as author ceased), but in his Epistle to Paulinus he counts it without hesitation among the other canonical books received in the Church.

Fifthly, the occasion, scope, and argument of the epistle must be examined. Grotius touched upon this at verse 14 of chapter II, that Simon Magus and other carnal men, when the Apostles preached the efficacy of faith, received it in such a way as if they could be saved without just works, that it can be obtained through faith: which he judges James is refuting here. We do not deny this, provided that the scope is rightly explained. Namely, that it was the Apostle's purpose to teach that that faith is nothing, nor is it justifying, which is destitute of works, but not that he requires works for justification and salvation. For thus he would be entirely contradicting Paul, who excludes the same from justification and salvation, even though he makes them a necessary consequence of justifying faith. Concerning which Augustine writes in his book on faith and works, chapter 14. Wherefore let us now see that which must be shaken out of religious hearts, lest they lose their salvation through a false security, if they think that faith alone is sufficient to obtain it, but have NEGLECTED to live well and to keep the way of GOD by good works. For even in the times of the Apostles, because certain obscure sentences were not understood, some thought to conduct themselves thus: Let us do evil, that good may come; because he had said the law entered in, that the offense might abound: but where the offense abounded, grace did much more abound. Since therefore this opinion had then arisen, other Apostolic epistles of Peter, John, and Jude direct their intention especially against it, so that they vehemently assert that faith without works profits nothing, but he defined it as wholesome and plainly evangelical, whose works proceed from love. Faith, he says, which works through love. But James is vehemently hostile to those who think that faith without works is valid for salvation, so that he even compares them to demons, etc. And in his book of 83 Questions, q. 76, Vol. IV of his Works, p. 598: Because the Apostle Paul, preaching that a man is justified by faith without works, was not well understood by those who received the saying in such a way that they thought, once they had believed in Christ, even if they worked evil and lived wickedly and flagitiously, they could be saved through faith. This passage of this epistle (of St. James) explains the same meaning of the Apostle Paul, how it is to be understood, etc. Grotius judges this opinion of Augustine to be contrary to the doctrine of the reformed (our churches), and he is himself deceived, and deceives others most wretchedly. But more on that at chapter II of the Epistle. However, this was not the only occasion for the Apostle, nor the sole purpose, as was believed by Baillie and Estius, since that treatment is almost concluded in chapter II. An occasion was also given to the Apostle by the persecutions of the converted Hebrews. Therefore, he consoles them against these both at the beginning of chapter I and also in chapter V, verses 10 and 11. No less dangerous were certain dogmas of heretics concerning God as the cause of sin, which gave cause for the encyclical letter; these he counters in chapter I. To these were added, finally, corrupt morals, especially in judging one's neighbor, whence he suggested necessary admonitions concerning them in chapters III, IV, and V. The argument is thus presented by the blessed Brochmand. The summary comprehension of the epistle is that adversities must be borne with an even mind, that the cause of sins must not be ascribed to GOD, and that the boasting of religion and faith is vain when it is separated from the pursuit of good works; for it becomes those who have professed the Christian religion to flee vices and pursue virtues, having enumerated one by one both the vices which they were to turn away from and the virtues in which they would exercise themselves.

The epistle may be distributed into three parts: the first is Paracletic, concerning the cross and afflictions in chapter I up to verse 12 inclusive: the second is Didactic, concerning both the cause of sin up to verse 21, and the true θρησκείᾳ of the reborn up to verse 27 of chapter II, and concerning the vain boasting of faith to the end of chapter II.

The third is Parenetic, partly general, both concerning the bridling of the tongue, ch. III, and concerning the avoiding of the base desire for contention, ch. IV, to v. 12, and concerning the avoiding of the presumption regarding the future, to v. 17; partly special, ch. V, concerning the wicked rich, to v. 6; the afflicted, to v. 11; those swearing rashly, v. 11; the sick, to v. 18; and those straying from the truth, v. 19, 20.

Those who have illustrated this epistle with commentaries are enumerated chiefly as follows: Of the ancients, there survive Didymus of Alexandria, Tom. IX of the Library of the Fathers, Bede, and Oecumenius. Of the Papists: Dionysius the Carthusian, Lyranus, Hugo Cardinalis, Thomas Anglicus, Cajetanus, Augustinus de Quiro, Augustinus de Ancona, Petrus Aureolus, Erasmus of Rotterdam, Jacobus Faber, Nicolaus Gorranus, Alphonsus Salmero, Mariana, Emanuel Saa, Arias Montanus, Nicolaus Serarius, Fevardentius, Adam Sasbouth, Johannes Gagneius, Benedictus Justinianus, Balthasar Paëz, Johannes Lorinus, Cornelius à Lapide, Guilhelmus Estius, Tirinus, Menochius, Haraus, Johannes Baptista Foleneus, Libertus Fromondus, Pricæus. Of the Reformed: Zwingli, Bullinger, Calvin, Beza, Rudolph Gualther, Aretius, Junius, Piscator, Marloratus, Simler, Paulus Tossanus, Pareus, the Belgian Interpreters, Thomas Thukus, Franciscus Gomarus, Drusius, Heinsius. Of our own: Andr. Althammer, Petrus Palladius, Lucas Osiander, Andreas Osiander, Casparus Erasmus Brochmand, the Weimar Paraphrasts. To whom, from the Schismatics, Victor Strigelius, Matth. Flacius, and from the Calixtines, Horneius are to be added.

PART I. OF THE EPISTLE, PARENETIC.

Latin:

PROLEGOMENA.

DE Epistolæ inscriptione primum agit Grotius: Quæ vero non est pars Cano- nica epistolæ: quia non profecta ab Autore ipso, sed ab alio quopiam: quemadmodum ideo inscriptiones vel titulos aliarum epistolarum sine commentatio- ne dimisit Grotius? Audiamus tamen eundem: Ἡ τῶ ἁγίε Ἰακώβε ἐπισολὴ καθολικὴ) id est, ἐγκύκλιος, non uni Ecclesiæ destinata, ut illæ Pauli, sed multis exem- plis missa in plures locos, ut inde & alia fierent exempla, & alio mitterentur.

Cur Catholica hæc, & sequentes Epistolæ dican- tur, non eadem omnium est sententia. Causam il- lam, quod ad plures missæ sint Ecclessias, & Oecu- menius adduxit: Quam vero ea ratione reprobare Salmeronem & Justinianum B. Brochman. refert, additq; calculum suum; quia inter septem epistolas Jacobi, Petri, Johannis, & Judæ, quæ Catholicæ ab Origene apud Eusebium l. VI. Hist. Eccl. c. 25. & Athanas. in Synopsi dicta, etiam referantur duæ posteriores Johanneæ, quarum altera tamen ἐκλε- κτῇ κυρίᾳ, altera insigni viro Cajo inscripta, non pluribus Ecclesiis. Cæterum verba Origenis ab Eusebio adducta, nihil de septem epistolis habent, quod Catholicæ dictæ sint, nec de Johanneis quic- quam perhibent, quod id nominis obtinuerint in Ecclesia. Eusebius tamen l. II. cap. 23. τῶν ἑπτὰ λεγομένων καθολικῶν mentionem facit. Atque ita nominat easdem Athanasius in synopsi: Καθολι- καὶ ἐπισολαὶ διαφόρων Ἀποςόλων αἱ πᾶσαι ἑπτὰ εἰς ἓν ἀριθμώμεναι βιβλίον. Accedit, quod Epi- stola adEbræos æque ita dicẽda fuerit ἐγκύκλιος, ut Jacobæa missa ταῖς δώδεκα φυλαῖς ταῖς ἐν διασπο- ρᾷ. Non autem melior appellationis affertur à Salmerone ratio, etsi suffragium Tirini & Cornelii à Lapide impetrarit; Catholicas nempe epistolas di- ci, quia & universalem continent doctrinam, & uni- versalium sunt autorum. Ita enim omnes Pauli- næ pariter Catholicæ dicendæ forent. Merito itaq; causa hæc appellationis ab Estio & Justiniano rejici- tur. Qui posterior vero hanc censet nominis isti- us genuinam rationẽ esse, quod eodem discernere voluerint veteres istas genuinasApostolicas ab ali- is adulterinis epistolis. Sed eadam ratione vocan- dæ etiam erantPaulinæ epistolæ Catholicæ. Con- jungi autem possunt omnes causæ : quod nempe Catholicæ nuncupatæ epistolæ sint1.Ratione objecti, quod ad plures missæ, exemplis pluribus, ut passim cum aliis Ecclesiis communicarentur: quod etiam factum dici potest secundæ, & tertiæ Johannis, quod primæ conjunctæ creditæ fuerint, quia per- breves sunt, etsi peculiariter ad certas personas spe- ctarint: Unde in ἐπιγραφῇ omnibus istis tribus Jo- hanneis nomen ἐπισολῆς καθολικῆς tributum: Quod video etiam Estio probatum: Non gravatim concedimus quinq; tantum esse Catholicas epistolas: Obtinuisse tamen, ut & illæ duæ sic vocarentur, eo quod in unum volumen, cum aliis, quæ proprie ta- les, essent inclusæ. Epistolam autem ad Ebræos pe- culiariter illis scriptam dicit, qui Hierosolymis & in Judæa versabantur, de quibus dicit, quod rapinam bonorum suorum cum gaudio sustinuerint Ebr. X. licet intentio scribentis fuerit ut & cæteris in disper- sione positis communicaretur. Tametsi etiam dici potest, ideo non numerari inter Catholicas, quod ali- is epistolis Pauli, quæ non sint Catholicæ, debuerint accenseri: 2. Ratione autoritatis, quod ab Ecclesia universa vel Catholica isto tempore, quo nomen illud adeptæ sunt, omnes septem, ceu Divinæ acce- ptæ sint, etiamsi initio de quibusdam dubitatum à nõnullis fuerit 3. Sed imprimis dicendum videtur, hasce epistolas peculiariter Catholicas esse nuncu- patas, ut, quia uno volumine comprehensæ, àPau- linis, uno itidem volumine contentis, nomine isto διακριτικῷ distinguerentur. Dionysius in Procem. Cathol. de nomine Canonico: Quamvis, inquit, etiam Pauli epistolæ possent dici Canonicæ; magis ta- men hoc nomen his est impositum epistolis, quod à di- versis Autoribus sint conscriptæ, & ita ab uno eo- rum peculiare aliquod nomen sortiri nequirent, sed commune eis aliquod nomen tribuendum erat, idque condignum & venerabile.' Idem de nomine Ca- tholico dicendum.

Ordinem quod attinet harum epistolarum, etsi in Canon. Apostolorum ultimo, ut & apud Augusti- num l. libr. de fide & operibus cap. 14. quem se- quutus est B. Lutherus hac serie collocatur, ut epi- stolæ Petri primum Johanneæ alterum, tertium Ja- cobi, ultimum Judæ obtineant locum: Jacobi eti- am epistola in concilio Carthag. III. can. 47. & apud Augustinum libr. II. de doctr. Christ. cap. 8. postremo loco posita sit: Innocentius autem I. in epist. 4. ad Exuperium Johannis epistolas reliquis anteponat; Concilium vero Florentinum & Tri- dentinum Petri epistolas primas faciat: Pleriq; ta- men Hieronymum sequuntur, qui etsi Petrum pri- mas apud Græcos obtinuisse, ut & in Latinis Codici- bus fateatur, proprio ordini tamen epistolas illas se reddidisse, ait in Epist. ad Paulin. quam hanc dicit: Est enim prima earum una Jacobi, duæ Petri, tres Johannis & una Judæ. Quemadmodum etiam in Concilio Laodiceno can. ult. primo loco posita est epistola Jacobi, nec non à Gelasio C. Sancta Ro- mana dist. XV. Imo in Latinis quoque Bibliorum editionibus Pontificum Romanorum diplomati- bus munitis. Causam reddit hanc Lyranus, quod primo loco fuerit scripta: Alii quod Jacobus ille Hierosolymitanæ Ecclesiæ Episcopatui præfuerit, quæ ceu reliquarum Ecclesiarum mater habita. Quæ nos suo loco relinquimus.

Porro ad v. 1. cap. 1. circa nomen & officium Ja- cobi disquirit Grotius de Autore, quisnam ille Ja- cobus sit? Tres invenio sententias, quemadmodum tres recenseri creduntur in sacris, vel apudEcclesi- astic. solum scriptores eo appellati, Apostolorum ætate, nomine. Prima tribuit hanc epistolam Ja- cobo Zebedæi filio, qui Major dictus est, qui Lucii dexteri fuit in Chronic. & Sixto III. Pontif. Tom. V. Biblioth. Patr. tribuitur in epist. de malis Do- ctor. (quam tamen Parisienses, & Bellarminus in Catal. non Sixto, sed Pelagiano cuipiam adscri- bunt) quæ etiam Isidoro assignatur, ut & Auctori li- turgia Mozarabum, nec non versionis Arabicæ, & Syriacæ, neque improbabilis judicatur Caspari San- ctio tr. III. de profect. S. Jacob. in Hispan. cap. 12. Sed ea à plerisque aliis improbatur, autoritate im- primis veterum Ecclesiæ Doctorum. Quapropter secundo Jacobo Alphæi filio, qui minor dictus est, maxima Interpretum & Doctorum pars hanc epi- stolam vindicat. Origenes in cap. V. ad Rom. Ephræm Syrus tract. quod judiciis abstinendum sit, Chrysost. admonit. serm. de Euchar. in Encæniis Le- ontii in vita Joh. Eleemosyn. Theophyl. in cap. VI. Matth. Simeon Metaphrastes in vita Joh. Elee- mos. è Græcis: Hieronymus l. 1. contra Jovin. cap. 24. Augustinus in cap. II. ad Gal. Ambrosius l. VII. in Luc. cap. IX. laudantur à B. Brochmando, quod Jacobum Autorem epistolæ fratrem Domini nun- cupent. Ad quos Latinos pro hac sententia etiam provocat Cornelius à Lapide, addens pro Jacobo Alphæi Clem. Alex. l. VI. Strom. Euseb. l. II. Hi- stor. Eccl. cap. 23. Epiphan. hær. XXIX. ut & Chry- sostomum homil. XXXIII. & XLIV. in Matth. cum quo transigant, qui plerosque in contrarium alle- gare non verentur, quasi alium, quam Jacobum Al- phæi filium autorem hujus epistolæ faciant. Terti- um enim nonnulli Jacobum hic nominant, Justum vocatum, ob insignem vitæ sanctitatem, Hierosoly- morum Episcopum, ab illo diversum, utpote Era- smus in annot. Turrianus super lib. VI. Const. Apo- stol. Clement. cap. 12. & 14. Carolus Bovius in schol. ad l. II. constitut. Clem. cap. 59. qui in eam senten- tiam laudat Epiphanium hæres. LXXIX. Doroth. in synopsi & Nicephorum lib. III. Histor. Eccl. cap. 40, & alios: Cui accedere fatetur Estius etiam Hie- ronymum in Es. XVII. Sed doceri solidè non pot- est, tres esse nominis istius, ætate Apostolorum, qui in autoritate penes Ecclesias universas, vel saltem penes duodecim tribus constituti, fuerint, vel terti- um præter duos prædictos Apostolos floruisse tum Jacobum, cui vindicari queat epistola Catholica. Non prostant ejus rei documenta sufficientia ex antiquitate. Porro scriptum Canonicum præstat ad Apostolum θεόπνευστον referri, quam ad alium, de cujus θεοπνευσίᾳ non constat. Tertio si tam in- signis aliquis in Hierosolymitana Ecclesia consti- tutus fuisset Episcopus tempore Apostolorum, S. Lucas Actuum Apostolicorum Scriptor id mini- me subticuisset. Quarto Jacobum fratrem Domi- ni Paulus Gal. I. 19. è XII. Apostolorum collegio fuisse luculenter docet: Ἕτερον δὲ τῶν Ἀποστόλων οὐκ εἶδον, εἰ μὴ Ἰάκωβον τὸν Ἀδελφὸν τοῦ κυρίου. Quin- to cum tres illos Doctores, qui columnæ visi sunt in Ecclesia, Paulus recenset Jacobum & Cepham & Jo- hannem nullo modo verisimile est, Jacobum pri- mo loco nuncupatum alium quemdam fuisse, quàm è collegio eodem XII. Apostolorum, ad quod Ce- phas & Johannes pertinebant: Qui vero, quum Ja- cobus Zebedæi esse non possit, utpote tum jam è vi- vis sublatus, necessum est intelligamus Jacobum Alphæi filium, quem antea fratrem Domini dixerat Apostolus. Autorem autem hujus epistolæ fra- trem Domini esse, penes plerosque in confesso est: nec diffitetur Grotius. Sexto congruit Marci de- nominatio, cum cap. XV. 40. Mariam Jacobi mi- noris & Jose matrem nominat; quæ Alphæi conjux fuit, & Mariæ Θεοτόκῳ soror habetur, unde frater, id est, consanguineus Domini vocatur Jacobus, usi- tato more scripturæ, Matth. XII. XIII. 55. Marc. VI. 2. Luc. VIII. Joh. VII. 5. Act. I. 1. Cor. IX. Se- ptimo congruit Judæ nuncupatio, qui in epist. v. 1. se vocat Jacobi fratrem, ubi Jacobum Alphæi desi- gnari dubium nullum est è collatione Matth. XIII. 55. Marc. VI. 3. Dicuntur enim fratres Domini Ja- cobus & Joses, & Simon & Juda. Ecquis ergo por- ro ambigat, Jacobum fratrem Domini esse Jaco- bum minorem Alphæi filium? Octavo huic Jacobo peculiariter post resurrectionẽ suam apparere di- gnatus est Christus, ceu fratri vel consanguineo suo communi Interpretum calculo, 1. Cor. XV. 7. Nono Jacobus, cui Petri liberatio nuncianda erat, post- quam decollatus jam esset Jacobus Zebedæides, jux- ta unanimen fere sententiam Doctorum, è colle- gio Apostolorum fuit Alphæi filius, Act. XII. 17. Decimo nec alius creditur interfuisse, ac sententiam tulisse, in concilio Apostolorum, Act. XV. Non enim verisimile est, post Petrum eum tanta autori- tate controversiam definiisse: Διὸ ἐγὼ κρίνω v. 9. qui extra collegium Apostolicum fuerit: Unde- cimo autoritas veterum Doctorum maxime stat pro hac sententia, tum qui non nisi duos tempore Apostolorum fuisse hoc nomine celebres admit- tunt: quemadmodum Martyrologia omnium Ec- clesiarum Occidentalium solum illos duos è colle- gio Apostolorum recensent. De tertio autem, ubi, quomodo, & quando passus sit, historia nulla pro- stat: tum qui Jacobum, qui Hierosolymis à qui- busdam Episcopatu functus dicitur, Alphæi filium agnoscunt: tum qui fratrem Domini Jacobum Al- phæi non alium agnoscunt: tum deniq; eorum, qui diserte illum hujus epistolæ autorem faciunt: Quæ ut uberius constent, juvat hic expendere Grotiana, etiamsi ad cap. I. 1. annnotata, ne eadem bis dicere opus habeamus. Ita autem ille:

Cap. I. v. 1. Ἰάκωβος Θεῦ καὶ Κυρίυ Ἰησῦ χρισῦ δῦλος] Non dicit Apostolus, ut solent Paulus & Petrus, qui id non sine causa fecerunt. Magnam enim autoritatem ad- debat illis, quod à Christo ipso in locum, qui supra omnes in Ecclesia emineret, essent electi. Jacobum hunc Syrus qui inscriptionem fecit ad has & sequentes episto- las, putat fuisse Zebedæidem. At id minus credibile est, quia is, ut Act. XII. discimus, prius ab Herode fuit in- terfectus, quam se multum extra Judæam promoveret Evangelii sermo. At nec Jacobum hunc esse Alphæi mihi sit probabile. Adscripsisset enim & is Apostoli no- men. Est ergo is, qui ab Apostolis constitutus fuit Prin- ceps presbyterii Hierosolymitani, ut Apostolus huc illuc, ut fiebat, excurrentibus, haberet cœtus ille virum egre- gium, & cui ob eximias virtutes nomen δίκαιος adhæsit, à quo regeretur. Eum Jacobum multi credidere Aposto- lum dici, Gal. I. 19. Sed minime id inde sequi ex eo loco ostendimus. Sed non fuisse Apostolum apertè indi- cant citati ab Eusebio libro II. Hegesippus & Clemens Alexandrinus libro ὑποτυπώσεων indicant. His adstipu- latur epistola ad Heronem inter Ignatianas, Cyrillus Hie- rosolmiytanus & Hieronymus de Scriptoribus Ecclesia- sticis, & ad Galatas, & in Acta itemque in Priorem ad Corinthios & ad Galatas Chrysostomus. Idem est in Constitutionibus quæ dicuntur Clementis Romani, li- bro perantiquo II. 59. VIII. in fine. Et sequitur hanc sententiam Eusebius I. 12. Dictus autem hic Jacobus fra- ter Domini, quod filius esset Josephi τῦ τέκτονος ex prio- ri uxore, ut quidam sentiunt Eusebius, Hieronymus, Epiphanius & alii quidam; Sunt qui alio modo propin- quum eum κατὰ σάρκα Christo fuisse sentiunt. Sunt qui dubitant, hæc ne sententia, an illa sit verior. Δῦλοι Ἰη- σῦ χρισῦ vocantur non Apostoli soli, sed & fideles omnes, Act. II. 18. maxime vero qui in loco eminente sunt posi- ti, Phil. I. 1.

Hæc Grotius. De quibus observari velim 1. Nullius momenti esse argumentum, quod Jaco- bus non Apostolum, sed servum Christi sese dixerit. Quod vel ex eo constat, quod nec Judas sese Apo- stolum, sed servum Domini nominarit: Qui tamen Apostolus fuit frater Jacobi, unanimi confessione omnium. Neque Johannis posteriores, secunda & tertia, Apostoli nomen præmittunt, & pro Apo- stolicis tamen ab Ecclesiâ recipiuntur. Quid, quod nec Paulus se semper nominet Apostolum in ἐπι- γραφῇ literarum suarum, sed quandoque δοῦλον Θεοῦ, ut Phil. I. 1. quandoque δέσμιον Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, Phi- lem. v. 1. Et quanquam Petrus Apostolus in fron- tispicio secundæ epistolæ diserte dicatur, Grotius tamen non veritus est in dubium id vocare, anne Petrus Apostolus ejus epistolæ Autor fuerit. No- men autem δοῦλος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ non solum eo sensu adhiberi, quo eos, qui in loco eminenti positi sunt, notat, sed prout Paulus & Judas sese servos Christi vocant, dubitandum non est, quum hæc eminenti- or significatio sit, nec ulla ratio sit, quæ Jaco- bum præsentem ex Apostolorum collegio exclu- dat. Causas affert Cornelius à Lapide, cur sanctus Ja- cobus servum Christi sese dicat, non Apostolum: E quibus prima studium humilitatis & modestiæ est, quæ admitti potest: Secunda, quod Apostolus proprie vocetur is, qui missus à Christo per orbem Evangelizatum discurrit; Jacobus autem affixus fuerit Judææ & Hierosolymæ, quod è falsa hypo- thesi procedit de Jacobo Episcopo Hierosolymæ creato à Christo & Apostolis: quæ solidis antiqui- tatis documentis destituitur. Tertia quod ingens dignitas sit esse servum Christi, quodque Apostoli omnibus mundi regnis eam prætulerint, magis de eo, teste Didymo & Oecumenio gloriati, quod servi Christi essent, quam si fuissent Reges totius orbis: Quam non improbamus. Quarta quod Petrus & Paulus Autonomastice Apostoli titulum occupa- rint, nec veritati nec modestiæ ipsorum convenit. Quinta quod servus Christi idem sit, quod Aposto- lus, siquidem non significet hic qualem qualem servum, sed Christo hero fidelissimum, dilectissi- mum, proximum, & intimum, qui ejus res omnes curat, adeoque ad quasvis gentium ad eas con- vertendas mittitur, qui alius non sit, quam Apo- stolus, cum principii petitione conjuncta est, nisi ita, ut superius à nobis jam reddita est, propona- tur: quod ab eminentiori significatu discedendum nõ sit, imprimis quia id suadet parallela ἐπιγραφὴ, Jud. v. 1. Ultima ratio, quod Sixtus Senensis libr. VII. Biblioth. & Fevardentius hic nomen Aposto- li à falsario aliquo evasum dicant, ut sublato Auto- re tolleret autoritatem Ecclesiæ, probari non pot- est. Quod enim Codices nonnulli Latini Syria- ci, & Arabici nomen Apostoli habeant; minime sufficit, nisi in Codicibus originalibus, quales Græ- ci sunt, idem inveniatur: In illis autem id inventum esse, probatis doceri exemplaribus nequit. Ob- serva etiam 2. titulum Syriacum de Jacobo Zebe- dæide, etsi in Viennensi Joh. Alberti Widmansta- dii legatur, in aliis tamen Codicibus non reperiri, adeoque à Londinensibus etiam omissum esse. Nihil etiam in Syriaca textus versione de eo invenitur, so- lum Apostolus dicitur Jacobus, uti eundem etiam Arabica & Ethiopica Londinensis nuncupat 3. Ad argumentum, quod contra Jacobum Zebedæi- dem autorem affertur, quod is prius ab Herode in- terfectus fuerit, quum se multum extra Judæã pro- moveret Evangelii sermo, respondet Estius, quod id fallat temporum ratione: Siquidem juxta veram supputationem reperiantur intercessisse decem anni plus minus inter mortem Christi, & martyrium hu- jus Jacobi, intra quod tempus scribi potuerit Episto- la ad fratres post Stephani mortem dispersos, quæ di- sperstio anno primo post mortem Salvatoris conti- gerit. Sed non laborandum de Zebedaide, quem agnoscimus autorem non esse. 4. Sententia Grotii de autore epistolæ multis laborat hypothesibus, quæ sufficienter neque probatæ sunt, neq; proba- ri possunt. Primo ab Apostolis constitutum fuisse Principem Presbyterii Hierosolymitani, precario dicitur. Id enim è scripturis minime constat: non autem silentio præteriisset id sanctus Lucas, dili- gens Apostolicorum actuum Scriptor, qui ne qui- dem Diaconorum electionem tacuit, Act. VI. Ne- que etiã ex historia Ecclesiastica illud docuit Gro- tius. Et cur Hierosolyma sedens, & eximio cœtui E- piscopus præfectus Hierosolymam ad XII. tri- bus ἐν διασπορᾷ scriberet? Si tribꝫ illę ἐν διασπορᾷ fuere, quomodo Hierosolymis insignis Ecclesia cum integro presbyterio & Episcopo ex iisdem in- venta? Adde quod Episcopi superiores Presbyteris ætate Apostolica nulli fuerint, nec tales Episcopi ab Apostolis ortum habuerint, quod alias osten- sum. Walo Messalinus de Episc. & Presbyt. p. 201. Absurdum, inquit, illud Clementis Alexandrini com- mentum, qui Jacobum Apostolum ac proinde univer- salem Episcopum in specialem & localem transmu- tare, & sic in ordinem cogere cogitavit. Nec enim majorem in Ecclesia Hierosolymitana autoritatem habuisset localis & specialis & Ecclesiæ destinatus Episcopus, quam si mansisset Apostolus, & ex A- postolatu universalis Ecclesiæ solicitudinem gerens. Imo & minorem, quatenus speciales Episcopi ab Apostolis constitui & ordinari soliti, autoribus suis & ordinatoribus suberant. Jacobus autem ab A- postolis ordinatus potestatem accepisset, ab illis, à quibus ordinatus fuerat, quasi delegatam. At par à pari non habet imperium. Eam habet ex se ac per se, ac suo jure utitur eodem modo quo & collega suo. Nihil igitur ineptius & indoctius illa fabula, quæ Jacobum finxit ab Apostolis ordinatum fuisse specialem Hierosolymorum Episcopum, qui & ipse fuit Apostolus. Ideo in Ecclesia Hierosolymitana primo illo concilio, quod ibi celebratum est, ex Apo- stolis & Presbyteris & aliis è plebe fidelibus congre- gato ad decidendam controversiam, quæ in Ecclesia inter discipulos orta fuerat in eo concilio audita le- gatione Pauli & Barnabæ, qui missi fuerant ab An- tiochenæ Ecclesiæ fratribus ad consulendos Apostolos & Presbyteros Hierosolymis consistentes, super ea di- sceptatione primus sententiam Petrus dixit. Post eum loquutus est Jacobus frater Domini. Ex ejus demum sententia formatum est & pronunciatum concilii decretum: Τότε ἔδοξε τοῖς Ἀποστόλοις καὶ Πρεσβυτέροις σὺν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ. Ubi Episcopatus Jacobi? Cum de mittendis Paulo & Barnaba ad sci- scitandam sententiam Hierosolymitani Presbyterii apud Antiochenos ageretur, statuerunt simpliciter, ut Paulus & Barnabas, & quidam alii ex illis ascen- derent Hierosolyma ad Apostolos & Presbyteros. Non solus igitur ibi præsedit ut Episcopus. Sed cæ- teri Apostoli cum eo. Hoc est, quod dixerat Hege- sippus, Jacobum διαδέχεσθαι τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν μετὰ τῶν Ἀποστόλων. Si proprius tunc fuisset Hicroso- lymitanæ Ecclesiæ Episcopus ab Apostolis ordinatus, lo- cus erat in eo concilio isto titulo eum appellandi. Pri- mus in eo loquutus est Petrus, post eum Jacobus. Tunc ex communi omnium sententia factum est decretum, in quo expressus est consensus Apostolorum & Pres- byterorum cum tota Ecclesia, id est, cum populo fide- lium. Apostoli majores erant & generales Episco- pi; Presbyterispeciales & ἀφωρισμένοι. Sinon ad- essent Apostoli, soli Presbyteri primam & summam in Ecclesia obtinebant autoritatem & ἐπισκοπικὴν ὀικονομίαν soli gerebant. Et sane cum summa illa autoritate ac pleno jure Ecclesiæ Presbyteri ab Apo- stolis creabantur Episcopi, ut iis absentibus, quia ipsi nulli certo loco addicti, sæpius aberant, a Presbyteris omnia administrarentur. Falsum itaque quod Cle- mens scribit de Iacobo Hierosolymorum proprio Epi- scopo ab Apostolis ordinato. Nec magis verum, quod ibidem posuerat, tres primarios Apostolos, Petrum, Iohannem, & Jacobum τὴν γνῶσιν à Domino post ejus resurrectionem accepisse, cæteris Apostolis eam illos dedisse, Apostolos porro reliquis LXX. discipu- lis. Hæc Claudius Salmasius contra Dionysium Petavium.

Deinde Jacobum, qui Justus cognominatus, di- versum fuisse à Jacobo Alphæi non dicendum tan- tum, sed docendum erat. Plerique enim tum ve- terum tum recentiorum id non admittunt. Tertiò Jacobum illum tertium, de quo controversia est, quinam crediderint Apostolum dici Gal. I. 19. non expressit Grotius. De Jacobo autem Alphæi filio id plerosq; credidisse ignorare nõ potuit. Quem Apo- stolicum locum nequicquã pervertit Grotius è vo- ce exceptiva adversativam faciens. Nimis enim lu- culentum est, Jacobum, de quo ibi Paulus loqui- tur, fratrem Domini unum esse è XII. quod omnes hactenus Interpretes, nemine, quod sciam, dissen- tiente, agnovere. Omnes enim vim particulæ εἰ μὴ exceptivam admiserunt. Agnovit & Grotius ipse annot. in libr. Evang. ad Matth. XIII. 54. de Jacobo Alphæi filio ita scribens: Hic ergo est Ja- cobus, quem Jesu fratrem, id est consobrinum, lo- quendi genere etiam Græcis & Romanis notò vocat non Paulus tantum sed & Josephus in Judaicis an- nalibus.

Quæ vero jam adversus pristinam suam senten- tiã profert, facile expediuntur. 1. Non fuisse Apo- stolum aperte indicare citatos ab Eusebio L. II. Hege- sippum & Clementem Alexandrinum ait. At de Cle- mente Alexandrino id aperte falsum. Contrari- um is habet cap. I. nimirum duos tantum fuisse Ja- cobos, non tres: Cæterum, inquit, duo fuern Jacobi, alter cognomento Justus, qui ex templi fastigio præci- pitatus, & à fullone fuste percussus interiit: alter qui capite truncatus est. Hic quia Zebedæides est, illum alium, quum Alphæi filium non esse manifestum est: quam non nisi duo Jacobi fuerint. Idem ergo est Jacobus Alphæi, qui Jacobus Justus. Ex Ægesip- po vero apud Eusebium l. II. cap. 23. nihil aliud ha- betur, quam quod Jacobus frater Domini Justus cognominatus sit. Quem Eusebius prorsus cum Cle- mente consentire, ait. Unde, si conferantur, quæ cap. I. habet Eusebius, non alium quam Alphæi fi- lium designari concludere licet. Atqui huic Jaco- bo etiam Epistolam primam earum, quæ Catholicæ dicuntur, adscribi, observat Eusebius. Non autem Apostolum fuisse Jacobum Justum, nullo verbo indicat Hegesippus; solum plures nomine Jacobi appellatos asserit. De hoc Justo autem, quod è fa- stigio templi præcipitatos & à fullonis fuste interfe- ctus sit, recenset. Quod Alphæi filio contigisse è Cle- mente docuit Eusebius. Nec de alio quam Alphæi filio Hegesippum intellexit Grotius ad Mat. XIII. 55. Multas autem fabulas relationi admisscuit He- gesippus, eo nomine à Scaligero, Estio, & aliis nota- tus; imò etiam ab ipso Grotio l. c. De quo (Jacobo Alphæi, inquit) quæ fabulatus est Hegesippus, neq́; recitare neque refutare est operæ pretium. Lapida- tum à populo fuisse, Anano Pontifice, Josephus nos docet.

2. Provocat Grotius ad epistolam ad Heronem inter Ignatianas, sed eam νοθεύεσθαι inter eruditos constat: neque in ea quicquam aliud legitur, quam quod Stephanus Jacobo, & Presbyteris Hierosoly- mis ministravit; Jacobum autem illum diversum fuisse ab Apostolis, nullo apice innuitur.

3. Cyrillum Hierosolymitanum allegat, sed sine mentione loci. Alii Catechesin XIV. Illuminat: adducunt. Sed in ea nihil aliud habetur, quam quod a Jacobo fratre suo Christus visus sit post resurrectionem, quem primum Ecclesiae Hierosolymitanae vocat parochum. Quomodo vero inde colligetur, Jacobum fratrem Domini non fuisse Apostolum? Num quod peculiariter illum nominavit Cyrillus, postquam apparuisse Dominum duodecim Apostolis dixerat. At idem factum a Paulo, 1. Cor. XV. qui cum & Cepham peculiariter nominavit Cyrillus: An vero ideo Paulus, vel Cyrillus Petrum exclusit e numero XII. Caeterum alii Jacobum, qui Hierosolymis egit, post Zebedaeidem trucidatum Apostolis accensere Cyrillum e Catech. XVII. colligere non dubitant; Apostolos utique dixit, qui Hierosolymis omnibus legalibus & typicis rebus per scriptam epistolam universum orbem liberarunt, inter quos facile Princeps erat Jacobus.

4. Hieronymus de scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis contrariatur, non favet opinioni Grotii. Jacobum enim fratrem Domini, cognomento Justum, quem unam de septem Canonicis scripsisse ait, Mariae sororis matris Domini, cujus Johannes meminit, filium facit, deque eodem addit: Hic est, de quo Apostolus Paulus ad Galatas scribit dicens: Alium autem Apostolorum vidi neminem, nisi Jacobum fratrem Domini, & Apostolum, super haec crebri9 acta docent. Qui characteres satis testantur Apostolum intelligi Alphaei filium. Quanquam vero Hieronymus in cap. I. ad Gal. eo inclinet, quod Jacobus illic & 1. Cor. XV. a Paulo nominatus non fuerit e XII. Apostolis: Agnoscit tamen cap. II. Jacobum cum Petro & Johanne nominatum Apostolum e venerando illo collegio fuisse. Columnae igitur sunt, inquiens, Ecclesiae Apostoli & maxime Petrus, Jacobus, & Johannes. Et alibi nempe in Epistola CIII. ad Paulin. Tom. III. p. m. 9. diferte accenset Jacobum, epistolae autorem Apostolis. Jacobus, inquit, Petrus, Johannes & Judas Apostoli septem epistolas ediderunt, tam mysticas, quam succinctas & breves pariter, & longas: Breves in verbis, longas in sententiis, ut rarus sit, qui non in lectione earum caecutiat. Quae epistola omnibus Vulgtis Bibliorum editionibus cum prologo Galeato praefigitur. Et libr. 1. adversus Pelag. Tom. II. oper. p. m. 268. Obsecro te, nonne Jacobus Apostolus scribit, qui in uno offenderit, eum esse omnium reum. Nec non in lib. II. contra Pelag. pag. 282. Jacobus Apostolus scribit: Si judicas legem, non es factor legis, sed Judex. Unde recte colligit Cornelius a Lapide, Hieronymum sententiam suam de Jacobo, quod non fuerit e XII. retractasse. Adde quod in epistola Epiphanii ad Joh. Hierosolym. quam Hieronymus e Graeca Latinam fecit c. IV. Jacobus hujus epistolae autor tam Apostolus vocetur, quam conjunctim Apostolus & frater Domini.

5. Chrysostomus nihil ad Act. XII. & XV. nihil ad 1. Cor. XV. pro Grotio habet; ad Galatas vero cap. 1. Grotio palam adversatur. Nam Jacobum fratrem Domini dicit Jacobum Cleophae.

6. Constitutiones Clementinas (quibus Henr. Vales. ad l. 1. cap. 12. Euseb. cum aliis l. 1. Baronius addit) hic reprobant ipsimet Papistae, imprimis Card. Baronius in ann. ad ann. Christ. 44. n. 36. qui hic Grotio, Turriano, & Valesio respondeat: Qui haec tradiderunt, tertium, quem diximus Jacobum extra numerum duodenarium Apostolorum imprudenter quidem nimis constituunt. Sed satis ad ejus sententiae confutationem esse videtur, si unde est deducta, repetatur origo. Ex rejectis enim illis Clementis nomine scriptis recognitionum libris de tribus Jacobis, autoritas semel sumpta, in nonnullos est inconsultissime propagata. Putarunt aliqui eandem sententiam ex ejusdem Clementis constitutionibus, sed apocryphis, roborari; dum hæc ibi ex persona Apostolorum reci- tata habentur: Nos ergo, qui digni facti sumus, ut essemus testes adventus ejus, cum Jacobo fra- tre Domini, & aliis septuaginta duobus & septem Diaconis, &c. quibus verbis volunt Jacobum fratrem Domini extra numerum Apostolorum constitutum Sed in ea sententia magis eadem ver- ba Jacobum monstrant inclusum: Nam cum ex- tra numerum septuaginta duorum Jacobus illic positus recenseatur, plane constat inter duodecim an- numeratum: alioqui, (quod absurdum est dicere) non tantum non inter Apostolos, sed neque inter discipulos Jacobus frater Domini locum haberet. Unde (ut ex his patet) quod ibi Jacobi singu- lariter nominetur, non est factum, ut è numero duodenario excluderetur, sed potius secundum energiam quandam, quod frater esset Domini, no- minatur.

7. Eusebius libr. I. cap. 12. ex mente aliorum loquitur, quum Jacobum, de quo 1. Cor. XV. unum ex LXX. discipulorum numero, ac præ- terea ex fratribus Domini fuisse perhiberi ait, si istum codicem, quem Robertus Stephanus ex- pressit, admittamus. Observat autem Henr. Va- lesius, verba μαθητῶν ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ in reliquis Co- dicibus Maz. Sc. Med. Frik. & Savil. deesse, sed neque Ruffinum illa agnoscere. Sic enim vertit: Post etiam dicit eum visum esse Jacobo, qui erat unus ex his, qui fratres Salvatoris appellabantur. Quid vero hoc juvat Grotium. Patet ergo, nullum adducere ipsum pro opinione sua potuisse Gro- tium ex antiquitate Patronum. Valesius quidem l. c. pro ea stans sententia Gregorium Nyssenum allegat orat. II. de resurr. Christi, & Cyrill. Hie- rosol. Catech. Illumin. IV. Sed falso. Nihil enim illic eam in rem habetur.

Quod quarto Grotius Jacobum fratrem Do- mini dictum, quod filius essé Josephi τῦ τέκτονος ex priori uxore, atque ita sentire ait Eusebium, Hieronymum, Epiphanium, & alios quosdam; In eo, quod ad Hieronymum attinet, fallitur. Hic enim Jacobum filium facit Mariæ sororis matris Domini. Jacobus, inquit de Script. Ecclesiast. qui appellatur frater Domini, cognomento Justus, ut nonnulli existimant, Josephi ex alia uxore (ut au- tem mihi videtur) Mariæ, sororis matris Domini, cujus Johannes in libro suo meminit, filius. Cum Hieronymo consentire Chrysostomum & Theodore- tum in epist. ad Galatas aliosque plures agnoscit Valesius in annot. ad l. II. Hist. Eccles. Eusebii cap. 1. etsi ab his pariter & Baronio, prolixe illam sententiam adserente discedat. Quid? quod nec Eusebius assertivè sed recitative tantum illam sententiam tradat; Καὶ ὗτος τᾶ Ἰωσὴφ ὠνόμαςο παῖς. Originem autem hujus commenti refert Origenes in Matth. XIII. ad Evangelium quod ti- tulum habet juxta Petrum, aut ad librum Jacobi; Refellit vero id Hieronymus in Matth. XII. Qui- dam fratres Domini de alia uxore Josephi filios suspicantur, sequentes deliramenta apocryphorum & à quadam Esta muliere confingentes. Nos au- tem (sicut in libro, quem contra Helvid. scripsi- mus, continetur) fratres Domini, non filios Josephi, sed consobrinos Salvatoris Mariæ liberos intelligi- mus, materteros Domini: quæ etsi dicitur mater Ja- cobi Minoris & Josephi, & Judæ, quos in alio lo- co fratres Domini legimus appellatos; fratres au- tem consobrinos dici omnis scriptura demonstrat. Atque huic sententiæ non Theodoretum modo sed cæteros omnes, qui post vixerunt, Latinorum orthodoxos scriptores consentire, Baronius in appar. ad ann. Eccles. n. 63. affirmat. Et Hiero- nymo potius, quam Epiphanio annuendum hic es- se agnovit Grotius ipse ad Matth. XIII. 55. cujus verba & rationes hic repetere placet: Pro certo po- nit Epiphanius, quem Græci sequuntur, fuisse hos omnes filios Josephi ex priori matrimonio. Sed do- cet nos Origenes, famam hanc initium sumpsisse ex libris, qui falso Petri & Jacobi nomen præferebant. Quare rectius Hieronymo accedemus arbitranti, hos omnes Domini nostri fuisse consobrinos. Ne- gari enim videtur non posse, quin eadem, quæ infra Matthæo & similiter Marco dicitur Maria mater Jacobi & Jose, Johanni dicatur Maria, soror matris Domini, ut quæ cum Domini matre, & cum Magda- lena cruci CHRISTI adstiterit. Quod si ea est mater Jacobi & Jose, erit sane & Simonis & Ju- dæ, ejus nempe, qui in epistola se fratrem Jacobi nominat, quique in Apostolorum recensu cum eo- dem Juda par unum facit. Is autem Jacobus ad discrimen alterius, qui fratrem Johannem, Patrem habebat Zebedæum, minor vocatur, ætatis, ut pu- to, ratione, & Alphæi filius: Unde colligere liceat Clopan sive Cleopan, à quo Maria ista denomina- tur, Patrem ejusdem Mariæ fuisse, Alphæum au- tem conjugem. Hic ergo est Jacobus, quem Jesu fratrem, id est consobrinum, loquendi genere etiam Græcis & Romanis noto, vocat non Paulus tantum, sed & Josephus in Judaicis annalibus. Atq; hæc in præsenti de Epistolæ Autore.

Disquirendum jam quarto de Canonica ejus- dem autoritate: Quam vix concedere videtur Grotius, non alia, ut apparet, de causa, Apostolo eandem abjudicans, ac viro quidem egregio, non autem Θεοπνεύστῳ tribuens. Gravissime etiam exa- gitant Pontificii eo nomine B. Lutherum passim, quod autoritatem Canonicam eidem deroget, imò vere stramineam dicat, ut &, quod cum Cornelio, Lorinus & Tirinus, eidem exprobrant, contentio- sam, tumidam, & aridam. Sed ut hæc poste- riora è scriptis B. Lutheri ostendi nondum potue- re: Ita prius in συγκρίσει tantum dictum cum Ev- angelio Johannis, & epistolis Paulinis in præfat. de Anno 1528. Quæ vero præfatio in aliis bi- bliorum editionibus non amplius repetita, quin potius epistolam pro utili & non contemnenda se habere testatus est, quod plane nihil humanæ doctrinæ afferat, & legem DEI fortiter urgeat.
