Quamvis vero nullius Apostoli eam esse censeat etiam in recentiori præfatione, id tamen extra omne præjudicium se statuere profitetur: nemi- ni autem credendum obtrudit. Quo pacto etiam nonnulli è nostris B. Lutherum sequuti sunt B. Bugenbagius ad cap. IV. ad Rom. & ad cap. III. Jonæ, Vitus Theodorus in summar. Luc. Osiander Centuriat. Magdeb. cent. I. l. 2. c. 54. Flacius in glossa; quod non mirum, siquidem in ipsa etiam antiquitate de autoritate Canonica epistolæ dubi- tatum fuerit: quum Eusebius ipse l. II. cap. 23. aperte ἴστεον, inquiat, ὡς νοθεύεται, quem locum Rufinus & Valesius etiam ita verterunt, quasi hæc quorundam opinio esset. Sed postea Valesius in annot. cen- suit, Eusebium absolute hanc Jacobi epistolam spuriam pronunciare: Quod cum judicaret B. Hunnius à Gretsero Tom. I. Def. Bellarm. l. I. cap. 10. vehementer traducebatur, tametsi negari haud possit, utroque modo verba Eusebii accipi posse, ut vel è vita Thucyd. constat. λέγουσι δέ τινες τὴν ὀγδόην ἱστορίαν νοθεύεσθαι, quod explicatur, καὶ μὴ εἶναι Θυκυδίδου. Interea è collatione Eusebii l. III. Hist. Eccl. cap. 25. faciles admittimus, ex sen- tentia Eusebii, non nothis scriptis eam accenseri, sed iis, quæ in controversia posita fuere, quæ vo- θεύεσθαι, etiam dici potest,ratione autoris, etsi non ratione autoritatis, juxta relationem Eusebii,idque secundum quosdam tantùm, non secundum omnes. Quod etiam Hieronymus in cat. script. Eccl. ob- servavit: Jacobus, qui appellatur frater Domini, unam tantum scripsit epistolam, quæ de septem Ca- tholicis est, quæ & ipsa ab alio quodam sub ejus nomine edita asseritur: licet paulatim tempore proce- dente obtinuerit autoritatem. Num vero illi, penes quos olim non obtinuit autoritatem, vel à quibus ipsi contradictum fuit,ideo statim hæreseos arguen- di, quemadmodum Luthero-mastiges nonnulli è Pontificiis B. Lutherum arguunt? Sic redarguen- dus quoque esset Erasmus, Leonis X. dilectus filius, & Cardinalis Cajetanus, quod judicio Estii elevarint itidem, dubiamque reddiderint episto- læ hujus autoritatem, quod tamen de Erasmo ex annot. non apparet, ubi Spiritum sanctum Auto- rem exosculari jubet. De Cardinali vero ita Esti- us: Cajetanus ex salutatione sumit argumentum, ad convellendam autoritatem epistolæ. Quoniam, inquit, salutatio tam pura est, ut nulli salutatio- ni cujusquam alterius epistolæ Apostolicæ confor- mis sit. Nam nihil Dei, nihil Jesu Christi, ni- hil gratiæ, nihil pacis sonat, sed, profano mo- re, salutem. Hæc ille, (quod sane mirum est) verbis à Luthero mutuatis. Nam eadem pene Lu- thero Sixtus in Bibliotheca sacra attribuit. Recte autem respondet Cajetano, quod Apostoli simi- lem salutationem adhibuerint in epistola Synodi- ca Act. XV. 25. Atque inde colligi possit, non ali- um Jacobum quærendum autorem, quam cum quo, suggerente memorata epistola, mitten- da fuerit. Rationes autem, quibus B. Lutherus aliique Canonicam autoritatem in dubium voca- runt, etsi omnino ita comparatæ sint, ut ipsum, aliosque potuerint movere, non tamen penitus convincere, sed accurate observata scopi & ana- lyseos textus ratione solide expediri posse, suis locis constabit, imprimis circa caput II. vers. 21. & 23. Unde in Ecclesiis nostris postea, omnibus rectius pensitatis, facile unanimi con- sensu pro Canonica habita præsens epistola tum ob argumenta & κριτήρια intrinseca, tum etiam ob documenta extrinseca, testimonia nempe antiqui- tatis, quod non tantum à Patribus fere omnibus talis agnita sit, Clemente Alexandrino, Athanasio, Gregorio Nazianzeno, Hieronymo, Augustino ali- isque, quorum catalogum bene longum exhibet Jodocus Coccius thesaur. Theol. T. I. l. VI. art. 23. & è nostris B. Brochmand. sect. I. Proleg. pag. 10. Sed etiam à Conciliis, Laodiceno c. 59. Milevitano cap. 7. Concilio Carthaginensi III. cap. 47, Arau- sicano II. cap. 25. Cabilonensi II. cap. 33. Toletano VIII. c. 2. Eusebius certe libr. II. cap. 23. profite- tur ipse: Hanc epistolam cum cæteris (Catholicis) in plurimis Ecclesiis publice lectitari, & l. III. cap. 25. Jacobi, Judæ, secundum Petri, Johannis alte- ram & tertiam designat nomine τῶν δ' ἀντιλεγο- μένων γνωρίμων δ' ἐχ ὅμως τοῖς πολλοῖς. Hiero- nymus vero non modo tempore procedente, (cum dubium de autore Apostolo cessaret) autoritatem obtinuisse tradit, sed Canonicis cæteris in Ecclesia receptis eam in Epist. ad Paulin. citra cunctatio- nem accenset.

Quinto de occasione, scopo, & argumento epi- stolæ dispiciendum. Attigit ea Grotius ad v. 14. cap. II. quod Simon magus, aliique homines carna- les, cum Apostoli efficaciam fidei prædicarent, id ita acceperint, quasi sine operibus justis salvi aser- varentur na obtineri possit per fidem: quod hic refellere Ja- cobum censet. Non abnuimus, si modo recte scopus ille explicetur. Quod nempe docere pro- positum Apostolo sit, fidem illam nullam esse, nectum justificam, quæ operibus destituta sit, non autem opera ad justificationem & salutem re- quirere. Ita enim omnino contrariaretur Paulo, qui eadem à justificatione & salute excludit, etsi necessariam fidei justificantis consequentiam fa- ciat. Quo de Augustinus l. de fid. operibus cap. 14. Quare jam illud videamus, quod excutiendum est à cordibus religiosis, ne mala securitate salutem suam perdant, si ad eam obtinendam sufficere so- lam fidem putaverint, bene autem vivere & bonis operibus viam DEI tenere NEGLEXE- RINT. Nam etiam temporibus Apostolorum, non intellectis quibusdan subobscuris sententiis, sic eum quidam arbitrati sunt ducere: Faciamus mala, ut eveniant bona; quia dixerat lex sub- intravit, ut abundaret delictum: ubi autem abun- davit delictum, superabundavit gratia. Quo- niam ergo hæc opinio tunc fuerat exorta; aliæ epistolæ Apostolicæ Petri, Johannis, Judæ contra eam maxime dirigunt intentionem, ut vehe- menter adstruant, fidem sine operibus nihil prod- esse, sed eam salubrem planeque Evangelicam definivit, cujus opera ex dilectione procedunt. Fides, inquit, quæ per dilectionem operatur. Jacobus autem vehementer infestus est eis, qui sa- piunt, fidem sine operibus valere ad salutem, ut illos etiam Dæmonibus comparet, &c. Et in l. qq. 83. q. 76. Tom. IV. Oper. p. 598. Quo- niam Paulus Apostolus prædicans justificari per fi- dem hominem, sine operibus, non bene intelle- ctus est ab eis, qui sic acceperunt dictum, ut pu- tarent, cum semel in Christum credidissent, etiam- si male operarentur & facinorose flagitioseque viverent salvos se esse posse per fidem. Locus iste hujus epistolæ (S. Jacobi) eundem sensum Pauli Apostoli, quomodo sit intelligendus, exponit, &c. Hanc sententiam Augustini, cum doctrinæ repur- gatæ (Ecclesiarum nostrarum) adversari censet Grotius, & fallitur ipse, & alios fallit pessime. Sed de eo ad caput II. Epistolæ. Non autem hæc sola occasio fuit Apostolo, neque sco- pus unicus, uti à Bailio & Eslio creditum, si- quidem ea tractatio fere cap. II. expediatur. Data & à persecutionibus conversorum Ebræo- rum Apostolo occasio. Ideo adversus eas conso- latur ipsos tum sub initium cap. I. tum etiam cap. V. vers. 10. 11. Nec minus periculosa quæ- dam hæreticorum dogmata, de Deo, causa pec- cati, causam literis encyclicis dedere; quibus cap. I. occurrit. His accessere denique corru- pti mores, imprimis in judicando proxime, unde de illis necessaria monita suggessit cap. III. IV. & V. Argumentum itaque sic exhibet B. Broch- mand. Comprehensio summaria epistolæ est, adver- sitates æquo animo ferendas esse, causam peccato- rum in DEUM non transscribendam esse, va- nam esse religionis & fidei gloriationem, quæ à studio bonorum operum abjuncta est; decere enim homines Christianam professos religionem, ut vitia fugiant, & virtutes sectentur, enume- ratis sigillatim tum vitiis, quæ aversabantur, tum virtutibus, in quibus se exercebunt.

Distribuere licet epistolam in tres partes: Prima est Paracletica, qua crucem & afflictio- nes cap. I. ad vers. 12. inclusive: Altera est Di- dactica tum de causa peccati ad vers. 21. tum de vera renatorum θρησκείᾳ ad vers. 27. cap. II. tum de fidei vana jactantia ad finem cap. II.

Tertia est Pænetica partim generalis tum de frenanda lingua cap. III. tum de fugienda pra- va contendendi libidine cap. IV. ad v. 12. tum de cavenda præsumptione qua futurą ad v. 17. partim specialis cap. V. concernens divites iniquos ad v. 6. afflictos, ad v. 11. temerarie jurantes, v. 11. ægrotos, ad v. 18. & à veritate devios, v. 19. 20.

Qui commentariis illustrarunt hanc epistolam, hi præcipuè recensentur: Ex antiquis supersunt Di- dymus Alexandrinus Tom. IX. Bibl. Patrum, Be- da, & Oecumenius. E Pontificiis Dionysius Carthn- sianus, Lyranus, Hugo Cardinalis, Thomas Angli- cus, Cajetanus Augustinus de Quiro, Augustinus de Ancona, Petrus Aureolus, Erasm. Roterodamus, Jacobus Faber, Nicolaus Gorranus, Alphonsus Sal- mero, Mariana, Emanuel Saa, Ariasmontanus, Nicolaus Serarius, Fevardentius, Adam Sasbouth, Johannes Gagneius, Benedictus Justinianus, Bal- thasar Paëz, Johannes Lorinus, Cornelius à Lapi- de, Guilhelmus Estius, Tirinus, Menochius, Haraus, Johannes Baptista Foleneus, Libertus Fromondus, Pricæus. E Reformatis Zwinglius, Bullingerus, Calvinus, Beza, Rudolphus Gualtherus, Aretius, Junius, Piscator, Marloratus, Simlerus, Paulus Tossanus, Pareus, Interpretes Belgici, Thomas Thukus, Franciscus Gomarus, Drusius, Heinsius. E nostris: Andr. Althammer, Petrus Palladius, Lucas Osiander, Andreas Osiander, Casparus Erasmus Brochmand, Paraphrasta Vinarienses. Quibus è Schismaticis Victor. Strigelius, Matth. Flacius, & è Calixtinis Horneius addendi.

PARS I. EPISTOLÆ PARACLETICA.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

The inscription and salutation having been premised, he admonishes that afflictions are to be held for joy, and to stir up patience and prayers with true confidence, as also to the contempt of this fleeting life, and that they are blessed who sustain afflictions. He teaches that God tempts no one to evil, but that this is done by the concupiscence of each person, but that good things proceed from GOD, who therefore regenerates us through the Word: which is to be received with meekness, and in such a way that we are not only hearers but also doers of the Word, and serve God without hypocrisy.

The parts of the chapter after the salutation are two: The former is consolatory regarding divine temptation, to v. 12. The latter is informative, both concerning the temptation of sin and its cause, and concerning true θρησκεία and religiosity, to v. 27.

PART I. Consolatory in the temptation of the cross.

Vers. 1. James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ.)

In the inscription, first the Writer is designated. Then those to whom the epistle is directed, thirdly the salutation. What Grotius had noted here concerning the Writer has already been presented in the Prolegomena and subjected to censure. The Apostle calls himself a servant of God and of Christ, not in a general sense, as we are all servants of GOD by right of creation and redemption, as Justinianus wishes, but by a special reason of office, by which being a servant of Christ and an Apostle of CHRIST are interchanged or joined together exegetically. Cf. Rom. I. 1, Eph. I. 1, Phil. I. 1, Tit. I. 1, 2 Pet. I. 1. James is called Θεῦ καὶ Κυρίε Ἰησῦ Χριςῦ δῦλος, which are to be read in one Spirit, just as the Greek Codices interpose no distinction here, so that James professes himself a servant of JESUS CHRIST, whom he acknowledges as both his God and his Lord with Thomas, John XX. 28. For if he understood the Father by the name of God, which seemed to be the case to Oecumenius, who gathers from it that the Son is equal in honor to the Father in essence and in operation, because James is a servant of the Father and the Son equally, he would without doubt have interjected the name of the Father, just as was done in 1 Cor. I. v. 3, Gal. I. v. 3, Eph. I. v. 2, Col. I. v. 2, 1 Thess. I. v. 1, 1 Tim. I. v. 2, 2 Tim. II. v. 2, Tit. I. v. 4, Philem. v. 3.

Ταῖς δώδεκα φυλαῖς, ταῖς ἐν τῇ διασπορᾷ) That is, the Israelite people who were outside Judea. For every place outside Judea is in Hebrew נדח, and in Greek διασπορὰ, Deut. XXX. 4, Neh. I. 9, Psal. XLVII. 2. The Syriac here [uses a word meaning] scattered among the nations. In the same sense the verb זָרָה is used, and is translated διασπείρειν, Levit. XXVI. 33, Psal. XLIV. 12, Jerem. XV. 7, chap. XLIX. 35, Ezech. XII. 14, 15, XX. 23, XXII. 15. You have Τὰς τῶν ἐν τῇ διασπορᾷ εὐχὰς in Justin, Colloq. cum Tryphon. It is called Τὰῖς δώδεκα φυλαῖς in the same way as τὸ δωδεκάφυλον in Acts XXVI. verse 7. Doubtless because there were twelve sons of Jacob, Gen. XXXV. verse 22, and the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, although they received a double portion, yet were from one stock. Hence the number twelve is always sacred to the Hebrews, Exod. XV. 27, XXIV. 4, XXVIII. 21, XXIX. 12, Levit. XXIV. 5, and often elsewhere. There are in this epistle certain admonitions common to all Israelites, and certain ones pertaining properly to those who had already believed in CHRIST.

The word διασπορᾶς itself teaches, and all interpreters acknowledge, that not only a seat outside Judea, but a certain dispersion is designated: although they vary concerning the dispersion. That the Assyrian dispersion of the ten tribes, or the Babylonian of the two, is not meant—which Lorinus in Acts VIII and Estius here desire—is apparent from the fact that from both those dispersions, but especially from the latter, the Israelite tribes were gathered back. Therefore, Beda, Gagneius, Fevardentius, Bellarminus, Bannes, and Paëz understand it as the dispersion which occurred after the death of Stephen, Acts VIII. 3. Although some might prefer to join both dispersions, which opinion our Brochmand says is approved by Salmeron, Cornelius à Lapide, Menochius, Tirinus, Calvin, Pareus, and the Belgian Interpreters. However, it seems to render it doubtful, both because several centuries had already elapsed since the Babylonian captivity was resolved, and because those converted to Christ, who by chance were survivors from the tribes deported by Shalmaneser, had remained in Judea at the time of the New Testament, and at the feast of Pentecost, with the Holy Spirit poured out, and in the subsequent time, had adhered to the Apostles until, a persecution having arisen, they were dispersed, Acts VIII. It is likely that the rest had for the most part coalesced with the Gentiles, who, having been deported into Assyria, were not made returnees into Judea. Moreover, to that first dispersion of Acts VIII was added another, Acts XVIII. 2, to which Grotius himself later seems to refer these things around verse 2. That James and Peter (1 Epist. I. 1) speak of a recent rather than that obsolete one is also very credible to Pareus. We add, however, here the opinion of our blessed Gerhard from his commentary on 1 Peter, page 22. It must be known, he says, as Scaliger advises in his notes on the N. T., that for the Jews there was one metropolis of religion and worship, Jerusalem, but three metropolises of citizenship: Jerusalem, Babylon, and Alexandria.

For there are two dispersions: the Asian, to which Peter writes; and the European, mention of which is made in John 7:35. The head of the Asian dispersion was Babylon, and those Jews used, and still use today in their synagogues, the Chaldean paraphrase of Onkelos. And so Peter writes from the very metropolis of Babylon. The metropolis of the European dispersion was Alexandria. Those Jews had a temple almost as great as the Jerusalemites, and they used the Greek paraphrase of the 70 Interpreters, for which reason they were called Hellenists (Acts 6:1, 11:20). For ἑλληνίζειν does not mean to dwell in Greece, as a certain interpreter annotated, but to use the Greek language. The third kind of citizenship were the Jews assigned to the Jerusalemite metropolis, as in the same chapter 6, Hebrews are distinguished from those who were Hellenists; they used the Jerusalemite paraphrase, which exists today. Those whom James calls those in the dispersion, namely, being (ch. 1:1), Peter calls them sojourners of the dispersion, strangers scattered throughout Hebraism.

James gave his epistle to the Israelite tribes rather than to the nations, not because he was the Bishop of Jerusalem, but because the Jews were especially entrusted to him, as can be gathered from Acts 12, 15, and 21. But that the epistle was also directed to those who were not converted to Christ does not appear from the scope and argument of the writing. For they would undoubtedly have needed to be more informed about the knowledge of Christ. And the Apostle calls those to whom he writes brothers, not by reason of blood, but primarily by reason of the communion of faith: 'My brothers,' he says. Concerning which Pareus: 'He calls them his brothers by the unity of race and faith.' Thirteen times he captures benevolence with this insinuation, adding 'beloved' several times, so that his exhortations, tempered with brotherly affection, might penetrate more deeply into the minds of the faithful. Nor does he himself observe beside the point: that those three Apostles, Peter, James, and Paul, wrote this consolatory exhortation at nearly the same time to the same faithful Hebrews wandering in dispersion through the regions of Asia and Europe for the sake of the Gospel. And I place Peter first in this order, James second, because James follows Peter's words, phrases, and doctrine in large part; Paul third, because what Peter and James warn the Hebrews to do, Paul praises the same ones for having done. Finally, what warnings common to all Israelites, even those not converted to Christ, occur in this epistle, does not appear.

Χαίρειν (Greetings): a custom of greeting, Acts 15:23, ch. 23:25, 2 John v. 11. Thus שלמא in Ezra 5:7. But joy is not to be understood as of this world (Luke 12:19), but spiritual, concerning which John 16:22, Galatians 5:22, which consists in the grace of God, the righteousness of Christ, and the communion of the Holy Spirit, not only in joyful things, but also in adverse ones (Romans 14:17).

Latin:

CAPUT I. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Præmissa inscriptione, ac salutatione, affli- ctiones pro gaudio habendas, & ad patien- tiam, & preces cum vera fiducia excitare, ut & ad contemptum vitæ caducæ, ac beatos esse, qui afflictiones sustinent, monet. Deum vero neminem ad malum tentare, sed id à concupiscentia cujusvis fieri, à DEO vero bona proficisci docet, nos ideo regene- rante per Verbum: quod cum mansuetudi- ne suscipiendum, & ita, ut non simus tan- tum auditores sed & factores Verbi, Deoq, sine fuco serviamus.

Partes capitis post salutationem, duæ sunt: Prior consolatoria in divina tentatione: ad v. 12. Altera informatoria, tum de tentatione peccati, ejusq; causâ, tum de vera θρησκεία & religiositate, ad v. 27.

PARS I. In tentatione crucis consolatoria.

Vers. 1. Ἰάκωβος Θεῦ καὶ Κυρίκ Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ δῦ- λος.)

In ἐπιγραφῇ primo Scriptor designatur. Dein- de illi ad quos directa est epistola, tertio salutatio. Quæ de Scriptore hic annotarat Grotius, jam in Prolegomenis exhibita, & sub censuram revo- cata sunt. Vocat autem Apostolus sese servum Dei & Christi, non generali sensu, prout DEI servi sumus omnes jure creationis, & redemptio- nis, ut Justinianus vult, sed speciali ratione muneris, quo servum esse Christi, & Aposto- lum CHRISTI inter se permutantur aut ἐξη- γητικῶς conjunguntur. Conf. Rom. I. 1. Eph. I. 1. Phil. I. 1. Tit. I. 1. 2. Petr. I. 1. Dicitur au- tem Jacobus Θεῦ καὶ Κυρίε Ἰησῦ Χριςῦ δῦλος, quæ uno Spiritu legenda, quemadmodum nullam hic distinctionem interponunt Græci Codices, ut se servum profiteatur Jacobus JESU CHRI- STI, quem & Deum & Dominum suum agno- scit cum Thoma, Joh. XX. 28. Si enim Patrem nomine Θεῦ intelligeret, quod Oecumenio vi- sum, qui ex eo colligit, Filium Patri esse ἰσό- τιμον κατ' ὀσίαν καὶ κατ' ἐνέργειαν, quod ex æquo Patris & Filii servus Jacobus sit, nomen Patris si- ne dubio interjecisset, quemadmodum factum 1. Cor. I. vers. 3. Gal. I. vers. 3. Eph. I. vers. 2. Col. I. vers. 2. 1. Thess. I. vers. 1. 1. Tim. I. vers. 2. 2. Tim. II. vers. 2. Tit. I. vers. 4. Philem. v. 3.

Ταῖς δώδεκα φυλαῖς, ταῖς ἐν τῇ διασπορᾷ) Id est, gen- te Israëlitica, qui erant extra Judæam. Omnis enim lo- cus extra Judæam est Ebraice נדח, Græcis διασπορὰ Deut. XXX. 4. Neh. I. 9. Psal. XLVII. 2. Syrus hic spar- sis inter gentes. In eodem sensu usurpatur verbum זָרָה, & vertitur διασπείρειν, Levit. XXVI. 33. Psal. XLIV. 12. Jerem. XV. 7. cap. XLIX. 35. Ezech. XII. 14. 15. XX. 23. XXII. 15. Τὰς τῶν ἐν τῇ διασπορᾷ εὐχὰς habes apud Justin. Colloq. cum Tryphon. Ταῖς δώδεκα φυλαῖς sic di- tur, quomodo τὸ δωδεκάφυλον Act. XXVI. vers. 7. Ni- mirum quia duodecim filii fuere Jacobo Gen. XXXV. vers. 22. & duæ tribus Ephraimi & Manassis, quan- quam duplam sortem cepere; tamen ex una erant stir- pe. Hinc sacer semper Ebræis numerus duodenarius, Exod. XV. 27. XXIV. 4. XXVIII. 21. XXIX. 12. Levit. XXIV. 5. & alibi sæpe. Sunt in hac epistola quædam monita omnibus Israëlitic communia, quædam pro- prie pertinentia ad eos, qui jam in CHRISTUM cre- diderant.

Non tantum sedem extra Judæam, sed disper- sionem certam designari vox ipsa διασπορᾶς docet, & agnoscunt Interpretes omnes: quanquam de di- sspersione varient. Non autem intelligi vel Assy- riacam decem, vel Babylonicam duarum tribuum, quod Lorinus in Act. VIII. & Estius hic volunt, vel inde apparet, quod ex illa utraque διασπο- ρᾷ, imprimis autem è posteriori recollectæ fue- rint tribus Israëliticæ. De dispersione ergo, quæ post mortem Stephani facta, Act. VIII. 3. Beda, Gagneius, Fevardentius, Bellarminus Bannes, Paëz intelligunt. Quanquam nonnulli utramque διασπορὰν conjungere malint, quam sententiam Salmeronis, Cornelii à Lapide, Menochii, Tirini, Calvini, Parei, Interpretum Belgicorum sibi pro- bari ait Brochmandus noster. Dubiam tamen eam reddere videtur, tum quod soluta Babylonica ca- ptivitate secula jam aliquot erant lapsa, tum quod ad Christum conversi, qui forte superstites erant è tribubus à Salmanassere deportatis in Judæa tem- pore Novi Testamenti hæserint, & in festo Pente- costes effuso Spiritu sancto, ac subsequenti tempo- re Apostolis adhæserint, donec oborta persecu- tione dispergerentur Act. IIX. Cæteros magnam partem cum gentilibus coaluisse verisimile est, qui in Assyriam deportati reduces facti non sunt in Judæam. Accessit autem ad primam illam disper- sionem Act. VIII. alia Act. XIIX. 2. ad quam Gro- tius ipse postmodum hæc referre videtur circa v. 2. De recenti potius quam de illa obsoleta Jacobum & Petrum 1. epist. I. 1. loqui, etiam Pareo valde credibile est. Addimus tamen hic B. Gerhardi nostri sententiam è comment. in 1. Petr. pag. 22. Sciendum, inquit, ut monet Scaliger in notis ad N. T. Judæis unam religionis καὶ θρησκείας metropolin fuisse Hierosolymam, tres autem πολιτείας metro- poles, Hierosolymam, Babylonem, Alexandriam.

Duæ enim διασποραὶ, Asiana, ad quam scribit Pe- trus; Europæa, cujus mentio sit Joh. VII. 35. Asianæ διασπορᾶς caput erat Babylon, iíq́; Judæi uteban- tur, utunturq́; adhuc in Synagogis paraphrasi Chal- daica Onkelos. Adeoque scribit Petrus ex ipsa metro- poli Babylone. Διαsπορᾶς Europææ metropolis erat Alexandria. Ii Judæi habebant templum quasi quantum Hierosolymitani, & Græca paraphrasi LXX. Interpretum utebantur, ob id dicti Hellenistæ Act. VI. 1, cap. XI. 20. Nam ἑλληνίζειν non est habitare in Græcia, ut quidam Interpres annotavit, sed Græca lingua uti. Tertium genus πολιτείας erant Judæi at- tributi metropoli Hierosolymitanæ, ut eodem cap. VI. Ebræi distinguuntur ab iis, qui ἑλληνισαὶ, ii para- phrasi Hierosolymitana, quæ hodie extat, utebantur. Quos Jacobus vocat τὲς ἐν τῇ διασπορᾷ scilicet ὄντας, cap. I. 1. eos Petrus vocat παρεπιδήμυς διασπορᾶς, advenas dispersos per Ebraismum.

Ad tribus vero Israëliticas potius, quam ad gen- tes Jacobus epistolam dedit, non quod Hierosoly- morum Episcopus fuerit, sed quia Judæi maxime ipsi crediti, ut ex Act. XII. c. XV. & XXI. colligere est. Quod autem epistola etiam directa ad illos, qui non conversi ad Christum fuere, non apparet à scri- ptionis scopo, & argumento. Illi enim sine du- bio magis de Christi notitia informandi fuissent. Et vocat illos Apostolus fratres, ad quos scribit, non ratione sanguinis, sed imprimis ratione com̃unio- nis fidei: Ἀδελφοί μs, inquit. Quo de Pareus: Fratres suos vocat gentis & fidei unitate. Decies ter insinuatione hac benevolentiam captat, addito ali- quoties ἀγαπητοὶ dilecti, út hortationes fraterno af- fectu temperata altius penetrent fidelium animos. Nec præter rem ipse observat: Tres illos Apostolos, Petrum, Jacobum & Paulum ad eosdem fideles Ebræ- os Evangelii causa per Asiæ & Europæ regiones in di- spersione errantes, eodem prope tempore hanc conso- latoriam parænesin perscripsisse. Et Petrum quidem in hoc ordine primum colloco, Jacobum secundum, quia Petri verba, phrases, & doctrinam Jacobus ma- gna parte sequitur: Paulum vero tertium: quia quod Petrus & Jacobus Ebræos monent, ut faciant, Paulus collaudat eosdem, quod fecerint, Denique quænam monita omnibus Israëlitis communia, etiam non conversis ad Christum in hac occur- rant epistola, non apparet.

Χαίρειν) mos salutandi, Act. 15, 23. cap. 23, 25. 2. Joh. v. 11. Sic שלמא Esdr. V. 7. Gaudium autem non hujus seculi, Luc. XII. 19. sed spirituale intelligi, de quo Joh. XVI. 22. Gal. V. 22. quod in gratia Dei, justitia Christi, & commu- nione Spiritus sancti consistit, non in lætis tantum, sed etiam in adversis Rom. XIV. 17.

## 1:2
Verse 2. 'Count it all joy, my brothers.' 'All joy,' that is, the matter of highest joy, namely spiritual. For both the cause is wont to be named for the effect, and 'all' is said for that which is highest, as in 1 Timothy 1:15. Concerning such joy, see what is said in Hebrews 10:34, Acts 5:41, and elsewhere; add Job 5:16, where in the Greek is 'do not reject the chastening of the Almighty.' There is also in the book Musar: 'Rejoice in chastisements.' 'When you fall into various temptations.' 'To fall into' is neuter in sound, passive in sense, and signifies to be surrounded, Luke 10:30, 2 Samuel 1:6. Various temptations (נסיונות) are such as those of exile, confiscation, and hatred, to which the pious are wont to be subject, Sirach 2:1, 1 Peter 1:6, 2 Peter 2:9. I would think this epistle was written at the time of that Claudian edict, mention of which is made in Acts 18:2, at which time Jews, and Christians among them, were ejected from Rome, and following that example from other great cities, as John from Ephesus, as we said in our commentary on certain places of the Apocalypse. He begins the epistle with that part by which the faithful Hebrews were most grieved and needed to be helped by consolation, namely, from the cross and their afflicted state. For they were not only greatly hated by the pagans on account of the name of Christ, but they also had their own fellow Jews as most hostile, from whom, what kind of things they were forced to suffer, Paul explained in Hebrews 10:34, as Pareus does here. With the optative 'greetings' (τῷ χαίρειν), the consolatory admonition coheres very well, that the faithful ought to count multivarious temptations as 'all joy.' Which conforms to the exhortation of Christ, Matthew 5:12, 'rejoice and be glad,' and of St. Peter 1. Peter 4:13, as also the joy and boasting of St. Paul in afflictions, Romans 5:3, and of the faithful, 1 Peter 1:3.

But since temptation is twofold—of the cross or of probation, which temptation is in itself good, from a good God, and directed toward good (Genesis 22:1, Exodus 16:4, Deuteronomy 8:22, Romans 8:28, Hebrews 12:5 ff.), or of seduction, which is an evil temptation from evil, the devil being the author of sin, and in itself brings nothing but evil. James deals with the former here, but he is about to deal with the latter in verse 13. He brings forth a fivefold fruit of the former: 1. The testing of faith. 2. Patience in the cross. 3. Spiritual perfection (v. 4). 4. Fiduciary prayer for necessary wisdom and Divine grace (v. 5 ff.), and thus 5. Joy and singular boasting from the cross and opposition (v. 9), where the rich are also warned not to boast in riches, but in their humility, by which they submit themselves to God, since they easily wither like grass with their riches (v. 10, 11). From which the Apostle infers that they are blessed who suffer temptation (v. 12). Which is to be understood of external temptations: one would not rashly say that internal ones, by which either the mind is solicited to dissent or the will to various concupiscences, produce such fruits, since they are not sent by God, but are forbidden. Concerning the word 'fall into' (περιπέσητε), Pareus does not speak badly, that by its composition it amplifies a heap of calamities, that the pious are wont to be overwhelmed by them as if from all sides.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Πᾶσαν χαρὰν ἡγήσασθε ἀδελφοί με) Πᾶσαν χα- ρὰν, id est, materiam summi gaudii, nempe spiritualis. Nam & causa pro effectu nominari solet, & πᾶσα dici pro eo, quod summum est, ut 1. Tim. I. 15. De tali gaudio vide quæ dicta Ebr. X. 34. Act. V. 41. & alibi, adde Job. V. 16. ubi in Græco 18θήτημα τὲ παντοκράτορος μὴ ἀπαναί- νs. Est & in libr. Musar. Gaude in castigationibus. Ὅταν πειρασμοῖς περιπέσητε ποικίλοις) Περιπίπτειν est so- no neutrum, sensu passivum, & significat circumveniri, Luc. X. 30. 2. Sam. I. 6. Variæ tentationes נסיונות sunt quales exilii, confiscationis, odii, quibus subjaccere so- lent pii, Sirach. II. 1. 1. Petr. I. 6. 2. Petr. II. 9. Putem epistolam hanc scriptam tempore edicti illi Claudiani, cujus mentio Act. XVIII. 2. quo tempore Judæi & in il- lis Christiani Roma, & ad id exemplum ex aliis magnis urbibus ejecti sunt, ut Johannes ex Epheso, ut diximus in nostro ad loca quædam Apocalypseos commentario. Ordietur epistolam ea parte, qua maxime dole- bant, & solatio juvari indigebant Ebræi fideles, à cruce nimirum & afflicto eorum statu. Erant enim pa- ganis non modo exosi valde propter Christi nomen, sed & gentiles suos Judæos habebant infestissimos, à quibus, qualia perpeti cogerentur, Paulus Ebr. X. 34. explicavit, ut hic Pareus. Cum tῷ χαίρειν autem votivo cohæret optime admonitio consolatoria, quod πᾶσαν χαρὰν ducere debeant fideles multivarias tentationes. Quæ consonant adhortationi Christi, Matth. V. 12. χαίρετε κὶ ἀγαλλιᾶσθε, & S. Petri 1. Petr. IV. 13. ut & gaudio & gloriationi S. Pauli in afflictionibus, Rom. V. 3. ac fidelium, 1. Petr. I. 3.

Πειρασμὸς vero quum geminus sit, crucis vel probationis, quæ tentatio in se bona est, à bono Deo, & in bonum directa, Gen. XXII, 1. Exod. XVI. 4. Deut. VIII, 22. Rom. VIII. 28. Ebr. XII. 5. seqq. vel seductionis, quæ est tentatio mala à malo, diabolo peccati Autore, & per se nihil nisi malum affert. De priori hic agit Jacobus, de posteriori verò v. 13. acturus est. Affert autem illius quintuplicem fructum, 1. τὸ δοκίμιον τῆς πίσεως explorationem fidei. 2. ὑπομονὴν seu patientiam in cruce. τελειότητα perfectio-nem spiritualem v. 4. 4. Precationem fiducialem pro sapientia necessaria, gratiaque Divina v. 5. seqq. adeoque 5. Lætitiam & gloriationem singularem ex cruce & objectione, v. 9. ubi & divites monentur, ne in divitiis, sed in sua humilitate, qua se submittunt Deo, gaudeant, siquidem instar herbæ facile cum divitiis suis marcescant, v. 10. 11. E quibus infert Apostolus, beatos esse, qui tentationem sufferunt, v. 12. Quæ de tentationibus externis intelligenda: Internas, quibus vel mens ad dissidentiam, vel voluntas ad varias concupiscentias solicitatur, non temere quis dixerit, easdem tales fructus parere, quum à Deo non immittantur, sed prohibeantur; De verbo περιπέσητε non male Pareus, quod sua compositione cumulum calamitatum amplificet, quod undiq́, quasi circumcirca illis pii obrui soleant.

## 1:3
Vers. 3. Know that the testing of your faith produces endurance. Δοκίμιον is that by which an examination is made. Plato uses it thus when speaking of the papillae, through which we judge flavors; the Rabbis say בְּחִינָה. Therefore, δοκίμιον is taken differently here than δοκιμὴ in Rom. V. 4, where see the remarks. It produces ὑπομονήν, that is, it produces in us a firmer habit of endurance.

To others, τὸ δοκίμιον is properly an experiment, which is taken from superior metals, so that it may be known whether they are genuine. The cross, therefore, and affliction is such an experiment of faith. And by δοκιμασίᾳ faith is explored, so that it may be evident both to ourselves and to others whether it is δόκιμος or indeed ἀδόκιμος, 1 Pet. I. 7. By which word also the reason is given why he called afflictions πειρασμὺς, because, namely, through them faith is explored, just as gold is through the fire of testing. And this is the first fruit of affliction. The second is ὑπομονὴ, patience, which overflows from the former. For when faith has been tested through affliction and found genuine, it patiently sustains whatever is imposed, and commits itself to the Divine grace, nor does it allow itself to be torn away from its God by any thing, Rom. VIII. 35, Job XIII. 15. But as for what Paul says to the contrary in Rom. V. 4, patience, he says, produces experience, but James says, the testing of your faith produces endurance, that is easily reconciled if we understand Paul to be speaking of the experience which we acquire in the promises and Divine acts or ways of the Lord through patience, Ps. 69, 9. seqq., Is. 43, 1. seqq., 1 Cor. X, 13, Jas. V. 11. James, however, speaks of the exploration of faith through afflictions, which works in us patience, by which we cling to God in adversities, being inseparable, by the example of Job ch. 13, 15, David Ps. 66, 10, Paul, Rom. 8, 35. Pareus agrees in his Commentary on Romans, page 142. It is not a conflict of the Apostles, but an ambiguity of terms. For δοκιμὴ and δοκίμιον are not the same. Δοκιμὴ signifies testing passively, that is, the experience which is generated in the pious through patience as our Apostle says. But Δοκίμιον signifies probation actively, that is, exploration, by which name the very oppression is called by its effect, says Beza, because affliction tests faith, just as fire explores gold. And this testing of faith produces patience according to James, who does not call afflictions δοκιμὴν, but δοκίμιον τῆς πίστεως ἡμῶν, the exploration of our faith. Just as also Peter 1 Pet. 1:17. Nor is there a disagreement in the fact that Paul writes that ὑπομονὴν, patience, is produced by oppression, and James by the testing of faith. For Paul considers oppression, not as it is oppression, but as it is the exploration of faith.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Γνώσκετε ὅτι τὸ δοκίμιον ὑμῶν τῆς πίσεως κατεργάζεται ὑπομονὴν ) Δοκίμιον est id, per quod fit exploratio. Utitur sic Plato de Venulis loquens, per quas sapores dijudicamus, Rabbini dicunt בְּחִינָה. Itaque aliter hic sumitur δοκίμιον, quam δοκιμὴ Rom. V. v. 4. ubi dicta vide. Efficit ὑπομονήν, id est, firmiorem in nobis ἕξιν producit tolerantiæ.

Aliis τὸ δοκίμιον proprie est experimentum, quod sumitur de metallis præstantioribus, ut cognoscatur, annè proba sint. Crux ergò, & afflictio tale est experimentum fidei. Et δοκιμασίᾳ exploratur fides, ut tum nobis ipsis constet, tum aliis, sitne δόκιμος, an vero ἀδόκιμος, 1. Petr. I. 7. Qua voce etiam causa redditur, cur afflictiones πειρασμὺς dixerit, quia nempe per easdem fides exploratur, uti aurum per ignem probationis. Atque hic primus fructus afflictionis. Alter ὑπομονὴ patientia est redundans è priori. Nam cum per afflictionem probata est fides, & proba inventa, patienter sustinet, quæcunque imponuntur, ac se Divinæ committit gratiæ, nec sese à Deo suo avelli ulla re patitur, Rom. VIII. 35. Job. XIII. 15. Quod autem contra Paulus Rom. V. 4. ἡ ὑπομονὴ, inquit, κατεργάζεται δοκιμὴν, Jacobus vero, τὸ δοκίμιον ὑμῶν τῆς πίσεως κατεργάζεται ὑπομονὴν, id facile conciliatur, si Paulum loqui de experientia, quam in promissionibus & actibus Divinis vel viis Domini acquirimus per patientiam, Ps. 69, 9. seqq. Es. 43, 1. seqq. 1. Cor. X, 13. Jac. V. 11. Jacobum vero de exploratione fidei per afflictiones, quæ operatur in nobis patientiam, qua Deo in adversitatibus divulse adhæremus exemplo Jobi cap. 13, 15. Davidis Ps. 66, 10. Pauli, Rom. 8, 35. Consonat Pareus in Comment. ad Rom. pag. 142. Non est pugna Apostolorum, sed ὁμωνυμία vocabulorum. Neque enim idem sunt δοκιμὴ & δοκίμιον. Δοκιμὴ significat probationem passivè, hoc est, experientiam, quam per patientiam generari in piis dicit noster Apostolus. Δοκίμιον vero probationem si- gnificat active, hoc est explorationem, quo nomine ipsa oppressio vocatur à suo effectu ait Beza, quia afflictio probat fidem, sicut ignis explorat aurum. Et hac pro- batio fidei efficit patientiam secundum Jacobum, qui afflictiones non vocat δοκιμὴν, sed δοκίμιον τῆς πίστεως ἡμῶν explorationem fidei nostræ. Sicut & Petrus 1. Petr. I. 17. nec est dissidium in eo, quod ὑπομονὴν patientiam Paulus oppressione, Jacobus probatione fidei effici scribit. Paulus enim oppressionem, non ut est oppressio, sed ut est exploratio fidei, considerat.

## 1:4
Ver. 4. And let patience have a perfect work) Let the mind be such that it neither kicks back nor collapses, but plainly submits itself to the Divine will.

That you may be perfect and entire) One Hebrew word שלם is translated sometimes by perfect, sometimes by entire, as can be seen in Deut. 27:6, Josh. 8:31, 1 Kings 8:62, 11:4, 15:3, 14, 1 Chron. 28:9, Jer. 13:19. Otherwise these can be distinguished, so that perfect, to the Rabbis גמיר, which word the Syriac also uses here, is that which lacks a blemish, and entire is that which has all its parts.

Lacking in nothing) The Syriac translates λειπόμενος here as חסרן. He is called חסר who has less in some matter than he ought. In a similar sense we have λείπεσθαι twice below, here just now, and in 2:15.

We assign here a third fruit, spiritual perfection, which, because it ought to be joined with faith and patience, the Apostle submits this by way of a precept. But a perfect work requires that we become perfect and entire in virtues, Matt. 5:48, and that we lack nothing, 1 Cor. 1:7. The Papists assert that the perfect stand here in patience before the tribunal of God, especially Alph. Salmero: But this is not a matter of justification, and these things are prescribed to the reborn and justified, not to those to be justified, nor is there any perfection of ours so great that it could stand before the Divine tribunal, Job 9:23, 1 Cor. 4:4, since not even the patience of the just is perfect, but labors under much imperfection, as the examples of Job, Wis. 3:1, Elijah 1 Kings 19:4, Jeremiah ch. 20:7, and others testify. Pareus understands by a perfect work not the legal perfection of moral works, as if this were situated in patience, but a sincere and final constancy in faith, overcoming all temptations. By the words also, be you yourselves perfect, he does not wish to designate the legal perfection of the person, but the sincerity of patience, so that he may beware of hypocrisy, by a phrase customary in Scripture. And they are said to be entire not only by the goodness of the cause, but also by the innocence of life, lest patience be for a misdeed, 1 Pet. 4:15. According to which explanation this passage does nothing for the perfection of works. Daniel Heinsius, however, observes that perfect is not only said of one who is perfect, but is also referred to effort, and to a certain degree, or to the 'how much' in progress, if it is compared especially with others, just as Epictetus joined the perfect and the one who is progressing. And Simplicius: Whoever you are who have already progressed by any reason, never cease to progress, never stop having progressed. Phil. 3:13, 14, he called him perfect who has not yet reached the end of his progress, but who tends toward the goal. B. Brochmand thinks that tolerance is required, which is not momentary, but which is continued until the end, so that we may be perfect, that is, conformed to the example of Christ in the same, Eph. 4:13, Rom. 8:17, who explains entire as heirs in full, comparing Matt. 5:10, but because perfect and entire are either joined exegetically, or at least in such a way that they cohere here, where we are said to be lacking in nothing, it is better to refer these to explaining the fruit of patience, which a perfect work can produce with that perfection which falls to travelers, and by Divine intention ought to. Therefore the Apostle commands it: And let patience have a perfect work. But the things which follow are to be understood as final, not that we are perfect and entire in all ways, but that we must strive toward that.

But the rule is known that a consequence does not hold from a precept to the ability or the being. Meanwhile, patience is naturally apt to produce, that is, not simple patience, but patient perseverance in faith, a perfect work, and it would produce it, if our imperfection in this life did not stand in the way, because all things are possible to faith. But since we do not attain perfection here on the way, they will obtain it eventually at the end and the goal, who remain constant in faith, and strive toward perfection, Phil. 3:3 seqq.

Therefore, to be lacking here is not to be overcome, or to succumb in the fight, as Lorinus and Cornelius à Lapide wish, but as is evident from the following verse, to be deficient and to be in need. Although we are deficient in many things through our own poverty and imperfection, yet through Divine sufficiency it can be provided for us that we are not destitute of any gift of grace necessary for us, 1 Cor. 1:7; we ought also to strive for that, so that we may become perfect and entire, and lack nothing that is desired for perfection and integrity, relying on a certain hope, if we are lacking in anything, that it will be given to us by God through faithful prayer and the gift of Divine grace, as much as He knows to be sufficient. Pareus prefers that 'in nothing' not be taken generally, but specifically, as lacking or succumbing in no temptation. But for the reason stated, the given explanation is to be preferred. It is most manifest, says B. Brochmand, from the verse which is added next, that to be lacking here denotes a defect and need. But he refers that to the promise of God, who wishes to be present to the afflicted, lest anything be lacking to them which could be necessary for a joyful victory in temptations, Ps. 91:15, 1 Cor. 10:13, Jas. 5:11.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ἡ δὲ ὑπομονὴ ἔργον τέλειον ἐχέτω) Talis sit ani- mus, ut nec recalcitret nec concidat, sed plane se subjiciat Divinæ voluntati.

Ἴνα ἦτε τέλειοι καὶ ὁλόκληροι) Vox una Ebræa שלם modo per τέλειον, modo per ὁλόκληρον vertitur, ut videre est Deut. XXVII. 6. Jos. IIX. 31. 1. Reg. VIII. 62. XI. 4. XV. 3. 14. 1. Paralip. XXVIII. 9. Jerem. XIII. 19. Possunt alioquin ista distingui, ut τέλειόν. Rabbinis גמיר, qua voce & hic Syrus utitur, sit quod labe caret ὁλόκληρον quod omnes suas habet partes.

Ἐν μηδενὶ λειπόμενοι) Λειπόμενος חסרן hie vertit Syrus. Dicitur חסר qui aliqua in re minus habet, quam oportet. Pari sensu λείπεσθαι habemus bis infra, hic jam mox, & II. 15.

Tertium hic assignamus fructum, perfectionem spiritualem, quæ quia conjuncta cum fide & pati- entia esse debet, per modum præcepti hoc subjicit Apostolus. Ἔργον autem τέλειον requirit, ut nos in virtutibus evadamus τέλειοι & ὁλόκληροι, Matth. V. v. ult. nec in ullo deficiamus, 1. Cor. I. 7. Pontifi- cii sistere patientiam hic perfectos coram tribunali Dei adserunt, imprimis Alph. Salmero: Sed hic non agitur de justificatione, & præscribuntur hæc renatis & justificatis, non justificandis, neque ulla nostra est tanta perfectio, quæ coram tribunali Di- vino consistat, Job. IX. 23. 1. Cor. IV. 4. quum ne pa- tientia quidem justorum perfecta sit, sed multa im- perfectione laboret, ut exempla Jobi, sap. III. 1. Eliæ 1. Reg. XIX. 4. Jeremiæ cap. XX. 7. aliorum testantur. Pareus per opus perfectum intelligit non operum moralium perfectionem legalem, quasi hæc in pa- tientia sita sit, sed sinceram & finalem, tentationes omnes superantem, in fide constantiam. Per verba etiam, sitis ipsi perfecti non designari vult perfectio- nem legalem personæ, sed sinceritatem patientiæ, ut caveat hypocrisi, phrasi scripturæ usitata. Inte- gros autem dici non solum bonitate causæ, sed etiam innocentiæ vitæ, ne patientia sit pro maleficio, 1. Petr. IV. 15. Juxta quam explicationem nihil hic locus facit pro perfectione operum. Daniel Hein- sius vero observat τέλειον non tantum dici qui perfe- ctus est, sed referri etiam ad conatum, & ad certum gradum, sive ad τὸ πόσον in profectu, si cum aliis præsertim conferatur, ut Epictetus τὸν τέλειον καὶ τὸν προκόπτοντα profectum & proficientem adhuc conjunxit. Et Simplicius: Qui quavis ratione progres- sus jam profectus sis, qui nunquam progredi desistat, nunquam progressus sistas. Phil. III. 13. 14. τέλειον di- xit, qui nondum terminum profectionis attigit, sed qui ad metam tendit. B. Brochmand. tolerantiam requiri censet, quæ non sit momentanea, sed quæ ad finem usque continuetur, ut perfecti simus, id est, exemplari Christi conformemur in eadem, Eph. IV. 13. Rom. IIX. 17. qui ὁλοκλήρυς exponit hære- des ex asse, conferens Matth. V. 10. sed quia τέλειοι & ὁλόκληροι vel exegetice conjunguntur, vel ita tamen, ut hic cohæreant, ubi ἐν μηδενὶ λειπόμενοι dicimur, præstat hæc ad explicandum patientiæ fructum referre, quæ opus perfectum ea perfectio- ne, quæ in viatores cadit, gignere potest, & ex in- tentione Divina debet. Ideo id præcipit Apo- stolus: Ἡ δὲ ὑπομονὴ ἔργον τέλειον ἐχέτω. Quæ vero sequuntur, τελικῶς, ut sonant, intelligenda, non quod omnibus modis perfecti & ὁλόκληροι simus, sed quod eo contendendum nobis sit.

præcepto autem ad posse vel esse non valere conse- quentiam nota est regula. Gignere interim apta nata est ὑπομονὴ, hoc est, non simplex patientia, sed patiens in fide permanentia, ἔργον τέλειον, gigneretque, nisi obstaret nostra in hac vita im- perfectio, quia fidei omnia possibilia. Quum vero hic in via non assequimur perfectionem, olim in termino & meta eam obtinebunt, qui constantes in fide permanent, & ad perfectionem contendunt, Phil. 3, 3. seqq.

Λείπεσθαι ergo hic non est superari, vel succum- bere in pugna, ut Lorinus & Cornelius à Lapide vo- lunt, sed ut è v. sequenti constat, deficere, ac indige- re. Quamvis vero in multis deficiamus per nostram inopiam, & imperfectionem, per Divinam tamen sufficientiam præstari nobis potest, ut nullo dono gratiæ nobis necessario destituamur, 1. Cor. I. 7. ad id etiam eniti debemus, ut perfecti, atque integri eva- damus, nec in ullo deficiamus, quod ad perfectio- nem atq; integritatem desideratur, certa spe freti, si qua deficiamus, oratione fideli, & gratiæ Divinæ munere nobis donatum iri à Deo, quantum suffi- cere novit. Pareus mavult ἐν μηδενὶ non γενικῶς accipi, sed εἰδικῶς in nullo πειρασμῷ deficientes, vel succumbenses. Sed ob causam dictam præferenda est data explicatio. Maxime manifestum est, inquit B. Brochmand, è versu, qui proxime adjungitur, quod λείπεσθαι hic defectum & indigentiant notet. Id autem refert ad promissionem Dei, qui adesse vult afflictis, ne quid ipsis desit, quod ad lætam in tentationibus victoriam necessarium esse possit, Psal. XCI. 15. 1. Cor. X. 13. Jac. V. 11.

## 1:5
Vers. 5. If any of you lacks wisdom) If he feels that he does not have enough prudence to judge what must be done in individual circumstances.

Let him ask of God who gives to all liberally, and does not reproach) More clearly in the Manuscript: From God who gives. But that matters little. God gives to all (namely, to those who ask piously) liberally, or as the Latin correctly translates here, abundantly. (For that is what ἁπλῶς is, as can be seen in Rom. 12:8, 2 Cor. 8:2, ch. 9:13.) And He does not give haughtily, like those who by their words or expression impute, and as it were reproach, their gifts, such as what Seneca calls stony bread. For ἁπλῶς the Syrian here has פשיטאית, that is, profusely. For ὀνειδίζοντος, מחסד.

And it shall be given to him) According to the conditions which we have set forth, Matt. 18:19.

Since for the purpose that we may sustain afflictions in faith and constancy, there is need primarily of heavenly wisdom and divine grace of strengthening, St. James teaches that the cross also contributes to the fervor of the prayers by which that is obtained, and this is the fourth fruit of afflictions, Is. 26:16. Necessity is the best teacher of prayer. But there is need of heavenly wisdom so that we may sustain the cross of Christ, and the cross ensures that we pray fervently for true patience, see Heb. 12:5 ff., Ps. 119:21, Lam. 3:27. The conditional 'if any' does not mean this, as if this wisdom were not lacking to all by nature, but he proposes the counsel to individuals specifically, as if he were saying, it is not that it is lacking to all, but whoever desires it, let him ask for it from God. For that wisdom, why God wills the Church to be under the cross, and variously chastises the children whom He receives, is foolishness or injustice to the flesh, nor can the flesh submit itself to the Divine will, Rom. 8:6. And the Apostle teaches that we obtain by prayers from God not only the wisdom of bearing adversities patiently, but also Divine assistance and the grace of strengthening (concerning which see 1 Kings 8:19, Col. 1:9 ff.), inasmuch as He gives to all liberally, which the Old [Version] rendered abundantly, not because he read 'suddenly' as Gagnejus imagines, but because he did not grasp the sense of the word, which the places cited by Grotius do not prove ought to be translated 'abundantly' or 'liberally'; indeed, 2 Cor. 8:2, those are clearly distinguished, wealth and simplicity. ἁπλότης [simplicity], & Rom. XII. 2. 'distributing in simplicity' are called those who do not hunt for vainglory or gain, Matth. VI. 2. 3. Luc. XIV. 12. nor is the sense otherwise, 2. Cor. IX. 11. 13. It is noted here therefore rather, that God gives to all with a simple and candid mind, & without superstitious selection, Matth. V. 45. Which sense the word adduced confirms, μὴ ὀνειδίζων [not upbraiding], because God does not reproach, as the avaricious & envious are wont to do, Sirac. XX. 13. 14. but the more He has given, the more prompt He is to give, if one uses the gifts rightly, Matth. XIII. 12. XXV. 14. sqq. An argument therefore is contained here for a prayer of confidence; for if God is so liberal, that He even gives to those who do not ask, why should He not be about to give necessary things to those who seek them with ardent prayers, Matth. VII. 7. 8. Luc. XI. 13. XIIX. 17. Joh. XVI. 23.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Εἰ δέ τις ὑμῶν λείπεται σοφίας) Si sentiat se non satis habere prudentiæ ad dijudicandum quid in singulis circumstantiis agendum sit.

Αἰτείτω παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ διδόντος πᾶσιν ἁπλῶς, καὶ μὴ ὀνειδί- ζοντος) Clarius in Manuscripto: Παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ διδόντος. Sed parum id refert. Deus omnibus (nempe pie petentibus) dat liberaliter, aut ut Latinus recte hic vertit, affluenter. (Id enim est ἁπλῶς, ut videre est Rom. 12, 8. 2. Cor. 8, 2. cap. 9, 13.) Et non dat superbe, ut qui verbis aut vultu im- putant, ac velut exprobrant data, qualia panem lapidosum vocat Seneca. Pro ἁπλῶς Syrus hic habet פשיטאית, id est, effuse. Pro ὀνειδίζοντος מחסד.

Καὶ δοθήσεται αὐτῷ) Secundùm conditiones, quas ex- posuimus, Matth. 18, 19.

Quum ad id, ut afflictiones sustineamus in fide ac constantia, opus imprimis sit sapientia cælesti, gratiæq; divinæ confortationis, crucem etiam ad pre- cum, quibus ea impetratur, ardorem facere docet S. Jacobus, atque hic quartus est fructus afflictio- num Es. XXVI. 16. Optimus orandi magister ne- cessitas. Sapientia autem opus est cælesti, ut cru- cem Christi sustineamus, & crux præstat, ut arden- ter pro vera patientia precemur, vid. Eb. XII. 5. sqq. Ps. CXIX, 21. Thren. III. 27. Conditionalis εἰ δέ τις non hoc vult, quasi non omnibus desit natura hæc sapientia, sed singulis speciatim proponit consi- lium, quasi dicat, non eam omnibus deesse, quis- quis vero eam expetit, à Deo eam postulet. Est enim ea sapientia, cur Deus Ecclesiam velit esse sub cruce, & filios, quos suscipit, varie castiget, carni stultitia, vel injustitia, nec potest caro Divinæ vo- luntati se submittere, Rom. VIII. 6. Nec tantum sapientiam patienter ferendi adversa, sed etiam Di- vinam assistentiam, & confortationis gratiam pre- cibus à Deo obtinere docet Apostolus (de quo vid. 1. Reg. VIII. 19. Col. I. 9. seqq.) utpote qui dat omnibus ἁπλῶς, quod Vetus reddidit affluenter, non quod ἀθρόως, uti fingit Gagnejus, legerit, sed quod sensum vocis non assequutus sit, quam affluenter vel liberaliter verti debere, lo- ca à Grotio adducta non probant, imo 2. Cor. VIII. 2. aperte illa distinguuntur πλῶτος & ἁπλό- ἁπλότης, & Rom. XII. 2. ἐν ἁπλότητι μεταδιδόντες dicuntur, qui non venantur gloriolam vel lucrum, Matth. VI. 2. 3. Luc. XIV. 12. nec alius sensus est, 2. Cor. IX. 11. 13. Notatur hic ergo potius, Deum dare omnibus simplici ac candido animo, & sine super- stitioso delectu, Matth. V. 45. Quem sensum con- firmat verbum adductum μὴ ὀνειδίζων, quod Deus non exprobret, ut avari, & invidi solent, Sirac. XX. 13. 14. sed quo plura dedit, eo promptior ad dan- dum sit, si datis recte quis utatur, Matth. XIII. 12. XXV. 14. sqq. Argumentum ergo hic continetur fi- ducialis orationis; si enim Deus adeo liberalis est, ut etiam det non petentibus, quidni hic daturus necessaria est, qui ea ardentibus precibus expetunt Matth. VII. 7. 8. Luc. XI. 13. XIIX. 17. Joh. XVI. 23.

## 1:6
Vers. 6. 'But let him ask in faith') With confidence of obtaining.

Μηδὲν διακρινόμενος [Nothing wavering]) לא מתפלג [not divided], doubting nothing either concerning the power of God, or His will. Διακρίνεσθαι is what the Chaldeans call הרהור [reflection/doubt], the Rabbis הסתפק [to doubt], others ἐνδοιάζειν & διστάζειν & ἐπαμφοτερίζεσθαι [to hesitate & to waver & to be of two minds]; we have spoken of this at Matth. XIV. 31. XXI. 21. Mark XI. 23. & Acts X. 20. Rom. IV. 20. See also below II. 4. where the word is the same as here. Hermas II. 9. Again he said to me: Take away from yourself doubt, & do not doubt at all when asking from the Lord, &c.

Ὁ γὰρ διακρινόμενος ἔοικε κλύδωνι θαλάσσης ἀνεμιζομένῳ κὰι ῥιπιζομένῳ [For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed]) Just as a sea wave is driven by the winds, & is tossed now here now there; so his mind now hopes, now casts away hope. In the Glossary ἀνεμίζω [to drive with wind] is to ventilate, likewise ῥιπίζω [to toss/fan] is to fan. Philo on the world, 'the water is fanned by the wind.' The Rabbis would say כשגש [like a storm]. Isaiah LIV. 11. Jerem. XXII. 14. מרוח [from the wind] is translated by some interpreters as ῥιπίζω. Κλύδων [surge] is a whirlpool, a wave in the glossary, גל [wave] to the Hebrews. A similar comparison in Is. LVII. 25. as the driven sea, where the Greeks use κλυδωνισθήσονται [shall be tossed];

The principal condition of prayer, which is to be heard by God, is that it be made with confidence, and thus that hesitation be absent, Matth. XXI. 22. But that we may ask in faith, it is necessary to ask in the name of Jesus, upon whose merit faith uniquely relies, Joh. XVI. 23. Rom. IIX. 32. 1. Joh. V. 14. Those are said to be διακρινόμενοι [wavering] who fluctuate in mind and heart, and are thus doubtful about being heard: Which is opposed to the confidence adhering immovably to the Divine promise, and in no way wavering, Matth. XXI. 21. just as disceptatio [disputation/wavering] signifies not only the doubt of the mind, but also the anxiety of the heart: Conf. Acts X. 20. c. XI. 12. Rom. IV. 20. Such διακρινόμενοι are therefore compared to sea waves tossed hither and thither by a stronger wind, on account of the instability of mind & affections. Conf. also Matth. XIV. 31. Luc. XII. 29. Which are therefore deservedly opposed to the doubt of the Papists. If the one who wavers fluctuates so dangerously, how much more miserably is the one who doubts swallowed up. For the doubtful man, whether God is truthful in His promises or not, merciful to him or not, wanders in soul and heart between the two, until he is swallowed up by the waves of doubt. But Estius objects in vain that the promise has this condition, if we ask as we ought, Jac. IV. 13. Of which no one can be certain. For why should we not be certain, when we are made certain from the Word how we ought to pray, and the pious do not doubt that they pray according to His prescription. But that it is impossible for anyone to be heard without faith, the Apostle teaches further on.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Αἰτείτω δὲ ἐν πίσει) Cum fiducia impetrandi.

Μηδὲν διακρινόμενος) לא מתפלג, nihil addubitans aut de potentia Dei, aut de voluntate. Διακρίνεσθαι est, quod Chaldaei dicunt הרהור, Rabbini הסתפק, alii ἐνδοιάζειν & διστάζειν & ἐπαμφοτερίζεσθαι diximus ad Matth. XIV. 31. XXI. 21. Marci XI. 23. & Act. X. 20. Rom. IV. 20. Vide & infra II. 4. ubi vox eadem, quae hic. Hermas II. 9. Ite- rum dixit mihi: Tolle a te dubitationem, & nihil omnino dubites petens a Domino, &c.

Ὁ γὰρ διακρινόμενος ἔοικε κλύδωνι θαλάσσης ἀνεμιζομένῳ κὰι ῥιπιζομένῳ) Sicut marina unda a ventis impellitur, & nunc huc nunc illuc jactatur; ita ipsius animus modo spe- rat, modo spem abjicit. In Glossario ἀνεμίζω ventilo, ibi- dem ῥιπίζω flabello. Philo de mundo, πρὸς ἀνέμω ῥιπίζε- ται τὸ ὕδωρ. Rabbini dicerent כשגש. Esaias ער LIV. 11. Jerem. XXII. 14. מרוח ab interpretibus nonnullis ver- titur ῥιπίζω. Κλύδων gurges, unda in glossario, גל Hebraeis. Par similitudo Es. LVII. 25. ut mare impulsum, ubi Graeci κλυδωνισθήσονται;

Orationis, quae a Deo exaudienda est, praecipua conditio est, ut fiat cum fiducia, adeoque absit haesi- tatio, Matth. XXI. 22. In fide autem ut petamus, in nomine Jesu petere oportet, cujus merito unice in- nititur fides, Joh. XVI. 23. Rom. IIX. 32. 1. Joh. V. 14. Διακρίνεσθαι vero dicuntur, qui mente ac corde fluctuant, adeoq; dubii sunt de exauditione: Quod opponitur fiduciae immote promissioni Divinae in- haerenti, nec ullatenus vacillanti, Matth. XXI. 21. uti disceptatio non modo mentis dubitationem, sed & cordis anxietatem significat: Conf. Act. X. 20. c. XI. 12. Rom. IV. 20. Tales διακρινόμενοι ergo conferun- tur fluctibus marinis a validiori vento hinc inde jactatis, ob mentis & affectuum instabilitatem. Conf. & Matth. XIV. 31. Luc. XII. 29. Quae pro- inde dubitationi Pontificiorum merito opponun- tur. Si disceptans ita periculose fluctuat, quanto miserius dubitans absorbetur. Dubius enim, sit- ne Deus in promissis sibi verax an non, sibi miseri- cors, annon, anima & corde inter utrumq; vagatur, donec dubitationum fluctibus absorbeatur. Ne- quicquam autem obvertit Estius, promissionem habere hanc conditionem, si petamus, ut oportet, Jac. IV. 13. De qua nemo certo sit. Quidni enim cer- ti simus, cum, quomodo orare oporteat, e verbo certi reddamur, & juxta ejus praescriptum orare se- se pii non ambigant. Fieri autem non posse, ut quis exaudiatur sine fide, jam porro docet Apostolus.

## 1:7
Vers. 7. Μὴ γὰρ ὀίέσθω ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνος) Such a one. Μὴ ὀίέσθω [Let not think] לא יסבור [let him not suppose].

Ὁτι λήψετάι τι παρὰ τῦ Κυρίου [That he shall receive any thing of the Lord] Of those things which he asks. Παρὰ τῦ Κυρίυ [of the Lord], from Christ, that is through Christ, who commends our prayers to God. Λαμβάνειν [to receive] here is to obtain, נסכ [to receive] to the Rabbis.

But why should παρὰ τῦ Κυρίυ [of the Lord], that is, from Christ, be explained as through Christ? Is not Christ, who commends our prayers to God, also the Author of the gifts which are bestowed upon us, for example, of wisdom, & of the grace of persevering? Whatever you shall ask in my name, says Christ Joh. XIV. 13. I will do it. But that such a one should in no way persuade himself that he will receive anything, who hesitates, and prays without faith. The cause is this, that it is impossible to please God without faith, Heb. XI. 6. and that such prayer is a sin, which is not of faith Rom. XIV. 23. Nor indeed is faith necessary only in obtaining spiritual things, but also in corporal ones, Matth. IX. 28. Mark VI. 5. 6. cap. IX. 23. Whence the Carthusian, & Lyranus in vain restrict the sentiment of James to spiritual things. It is general, let not that man think, ὅτι λήψεταί τι [that he shall receive any thing] that he is about to receive anything. Although indeed faith may sometimes be languid, it does not therefore suffer a repulse, Matth. XVII. 20. which we are taught by the example of the Nobleman, Joh. IV. 47. For even weak faith is faith. A begging hand can grasp a gift, even if it be sick & weak: how much more the weak hand of faith, which God wishes to strengthen, Mark IX. 24. not breaking the bruised reed, but graciously stabilizing it, Is. XLII. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Μὴ γὰρ ὀίέσθω ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνος) Talis ali- quis. Μὴ ὀίέσθω לא יסבור.

Ὁτι λήψετάι τι παρὰ τῦ Κυρίου Eorum quae petit. Παρὰ τῦ Κυρίυ, a Christo, id est per Christum, qui preces nostras Deo commendat. Λαμβάνειν hic est obtinere נסכ Rabbinis.

Cur autem παρὰ τῦ Κυρίυ a Domino, id est, Chri- sto exponendum per Christum? Annon Christus, qui preces nostras Deo commendat, etiam Autor est donorum, quae nobis tribuuntur, verbi gratia, sapientiae, & gratiae perseverandi? Quicquid petie- ritis in nomine meo, inquit Christus Joh. XIV. 13. illud faciam. Quod autem talis nullatenus sibi persuadere debeat, se quicquam accepturum, qui haesitat, ac sine fide orat. Causa haec est, quod impossibile sit Deo sine fide placere, Ebr. XI. 6. quodque peccatum sit talis oratio, quæ non est ex fide Rom. XIV. 23. Nec vero tantum in rebus spiritualibus impetrandis opus est fide, sed etiam in corporalibus, Matth. IX. 28. Marci VI. 5. 6. cap. IX. 23. Unde Carthusianus, & Lyranus frustra sen- tentiam Jacobi ad spiritualia restringunt. Genera- lis ea est, non existimet homo ille, ὅτι λήψεταί τι quod quicquam accepturus sit. Quanquam vero fi- des quandoq; languida sit, non tamen ea repul- sam patitur, Matth. XVII. 20. quod exemplo Re- guli docemur, Joh. IV. 47. Nam & infirma fides fi- des est. Apprehendere munus potest manus men- dica, etiamsi ægra, & infirma sit: quanto magis fi- dei infirma manus, quam Deus firmare vult, Marc. IX. 24. arundinem quassatam non confrin- gens, sed gratiose stabiliens, Es. XLII. 3.

## 1:8
Vers. 8. Ἀνὴρ δίψυχος [A double-minded man].) That is, διτάζων [wavering] as we have already said. You have this noun also below IV. 8. Adamantius also has it in his Physiognomonics. But they are said to be of a double mind, who διάνδιχα θυμὸν ἔχουσι [have a mind divided in two], or in whom δίχα θυμὸς ὀρώρηται [the mind is stirred in two ways], as Homer speaks.

Bede, Salmero, Cornelius à Lapide, Piscator, the Belgian Interpreters, and B. Brochmand explain it otherwise, for whom ἀνὴρ δίψυχος is a double-minded man, who has a divided heart, so that he serves partly God, partly the world, Matt. VI. 24. But we easily agree with Grotius: since not only does Hesychius explain διψυχίαν as perplexity, doubt, but also for the Greeks ἀνὴρ δίψυχος is a man unsupported and unsteady, driven and tossed here and there, an unstable and not firm man, as Heinsius explains this passage: who alternates, who wavers, who doubts, who inclines his mind now to this, now to that side, which the Greeks call μερμηρίζειν, and Maro called alternating. The Greek poet says, Δίχα θυμὸς ὀρώρεται ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα: He is moved as it were into two parts. Wherefore, to avoid ambiguity, I shall call διακρινόμενον a doubter rather than one who disagrees; and likewise I shall call one who disagrees, one who inclines his mind now here now there, rather than one of double mind. For such are both deceitful and for the most part indeed. The preceding words demand this sense.

Unstable in all his ways) Wavering in all his acts. It is the custom of the Hebrews to call an act ὁδὸς. He who wavers in faith, it is necessary that he produce various actions, and ones that differ much among themselves. This is that constant change of purpose, and the tossing of a mind that nowhere settles, and a hanging life, as Seneca speaks in his book on tranquility. The same in his work on the happy life: A certain whirlwind rotates and involves our minds, fleeing and seeking the same things, and snatches them now lifted on high, now dashed into the depths. And in his work on leisure: We fluctuate, and we grasp one thing after another, we abandon what we sought, we seek again what we abandoned. Epistle XX: This diversity is a vice, and a sign of a wavering mind, as one not yet having its own tenor.

Thus Plutarch called him ἀκατάστατον, who is full of disturbance and tumult, and ἀκαταστασία, Luke XXI. 19, 1 Cor. XIV. 33, 2 Cor. XII. 20, is tumult and agitation, which hinders a thing from being able to consist in quiet.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Ἀνὴρ δίψυχος.) Id est διτάζων ut jam diximus. Habes hoc nomen & infra IV. 8. Habet & in Physiogno- monicis Adamantius. Dicuntur autem duplici esse animo, qui διάνδιχα θυμὸν ἔχουσι, aut quibus δίχα θυμὸς ὀρώρηται, ut Homerus loquitur.

Aliter explicant Beda, Salmero, Cornelius à Lapi- de, Piscator, Interpretes Belgici, & B. Brochmand. quibus ἀνὴρ δίψυχος vir bianimis est, cui cor di- visum est, ita ut partim Deo, partim mundo serviat, Matth. VI. 24. Sed facile annuimus Grotio: siqui- dem non Hesychius tantum διψυχίαν explicet ἀπορίαν, dubitationem, sed & Græcis ἀνὴρ δίψυχος sit ἀνὴρ ἀνεπέρειστος, καὶ ἀστήρικτος, τῇδε κἀκεῖσε ἀγόμενος καὶ περιφερόμενος, vir instabilis & non firmus, ut Heinsius hunc locum explicat: qui alter- nat, qui vacillat, qui dubitat, qui nunc in hanc, nunc in illam partem animum inclinat, quem Græci μερμηρίζειν, Maro alternare dixit. Poëta Græcus, Δίχα θυμὸς ὀρώρεται ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα: In duas quasi movetur partes. Quare ut διακρινόμενον dubitantem potius quam discrepantem; Ita discrepantem nunc huc nunc illuc animo inclinantem potius, quam ani- mo duplici, vitandæ ambiguitatis causa dicam. Ta- les enim & dolosi & plerumq; quidem. Postulant hunc sensum antecedentia.

Ἀκατάστατος ἐν πάσαις ταῖς ὁδοῖς αὐτοῦ) Fluctuans in omnibus suis actibus. Non actus ὁδὸς dicere mos est Ebræo- rum. Qui fide vacillat, is necesse est actiones edat varias, atque inter se multum discrepantes. Hæc est illa assidua mu- tatio propositi, & nusquam residentis animi volutatio, ac vita pendens, ut Seneca loquitur libro de tranquillitate. Idem de vita beata: Turbo quidam animos nostros rotat & involvit, fugientes petentesque eadem, & nunc in sublime allevatos, nunc in intima allisos rapit. Et de otio: Fluctua- mus, aliudque ex alio, comprehendimus, petita relinquimus, relicta repetimus. Epistola XX: Vitium hæc diversitas, & si- gnum vacillantis animi, ut nondum habentis tenorem suum.

Ita Plutarchus ἀκατάστατον dixit, qui perturba- tionis ac tumultus plenus est, & ἀκαταστασία, Luc. XXI. 19. 1. Cor. XIV. 33. 2. Cor. XII. 20. est tumul- tuatio & agitatio, quæ impedit, quo minus res quæ- piam in quiete consistere possit.

## 1:9
V. 9. But let the brother of low degree glory in his exaltation) Καυχάσθω, that is, ἀγαλλιάσθω, let him rejoice, as we have explained elsewhere. Ὁ ταπεινὸς, he who is of abject lot. The Hebrew עני is translated thus, Ps. LXXXII. 3, Prov. III. 34, Is. XI. 4, XIV. 32, XXXII. 7, XLIX. 13, LIV. 11, LXVI. 2, Jer. XXII. 16, Amos II. 7, Zeph. II. 3. See Luke I. 48. Because of his sublimity ברוממתו, i.e., because of the honor placed in him in that he is considered the Son of God.

Latin:

V. 9. Καυχάσθω δὲ ὁ ἀδελφὸς ὁ ταπεινὸς ἐν τῷ ὕψει αὐτοῦ) Καυχάσθω, id est, ἀγαλλιάσθω lætetur, ut alibi exposuimus. Ὁ ταπεινὸς, qui abjectæ est sortis. Vertitur sic Ebræum עני Psal. LXXXII. 3. Prov. III. 34. Es. XI. 4. XIV. 32. XXXII. 7. XLIX. 13. LIV. 11. LXVI. 2. Jerem. XXII. 16. Amos II. 7. Soph. II. 3. Vid. Luc. I. 48. Ob sublimitatem suam ברוממתו, i. e. ob honorem in eo positum quod Dei Fi- lius censetur.

## 1:10
Vers. 10. But the rich in his humiliation) Supply ταπεινούσθω, which is sufficiently understood partly from the preceding opposite (just as 1 Tim. IV. 3 and elsewhere), partly from the following noun. Let the rich man bear a submissive mind, considering his own vileness, that is, the instability of his lot. The same sense is in 1 Tim. VI. 17.

For as the flower of the grass he shall pass away) Χόρτου for the Hebrews is every herb עשב, as we said Gen. I. 11. Ἄνθος, however, is greenness. The same similitude is in Ps. XXXVII. 2, Is. XL. 6 and 7, 1 Pet. I. 24. Nor does that which is in Sirach XIV. 17 differ much. Παρελεύσεται יעבור.

This is the fifth fruit of afflictions, that they produce glorying and joy, Rom. 5:3. Now the humble man is said to glory in his high estate, not because he is proud, but because he trusts in the same; which, since he does not have it in himself, being as he is ταπεινὸς (humble), and acknowledging his humility all the more the more he is depressed by affliction (Ps. 119:71), he seeks through faith in Christ, in whom alone there is solid joy (Phil. 4:4). Whence the rich man also is warned not to trust or glory in his riches, and to rejoice, but in his ταπεινώσει (humiliation) to acknowledge his humility, or even from his very fragility, which passes easily like the flower of the grass, and in this his humility to glory likewise solely in the Lord, according to the warning of Jeremiah, ch. 9:24. For even the rich man, when he acknowledges from the Word of God how he is ταπεινὸς (humble), nay rather ταλαίπωρος, καὶ ἐλεεινὸς, κᾐ πλωχὸς, κᾐ γυμνὸς (wretched, and miserable, and poor, and naked) (Rev. 3:17), in that recognition of himself, humbling himself, he seeks high estate and true riches in another, that is, in Christ, if he be endowed with faith: such as the word ἀδελφὸς (brother) implies. Thus there is no need for Grotius's supplement: for which Oecumenius has another word, αἰσχυνέστω (let him be ashamed). Nor must it be determined, either with Salmeron and Justinian, that a new doctrine is being taught here, or with Pareus and Cornelius, that the Apostle is passing from the thesis of various temptations to the hypothesis of humble poverty. For all things cohere most excellently, and the conclusion subjoined in v. 12 convinces us that the Apostle is persevering in the same general consolation. Now, the connection (συνέχειαν) of the blessed Brochmand regarding these verses consists well with this analysis of ours: After the Apostle has taught that men who fluctuate in mind when praying are διψύχες (double-minded) and ἀκαταστάτους (unstable) in all their ways, he now warns and shows what must be done, both for the poor and for the rich, lest this ἀκαταστασία (instability), or the restlessness that disturbs and perturbs the mind and will, should invade them: Namely, that everyone ought to acquiesce willingly in the condition of his life; so that neither the poorer man should lose heart because of his afflicted state, nor he who is richer be puffed up in mind because of his riches, mindful of the instability and momentary duration of riches. From which opinion Arias Montanus also does not seem to be alienated in his commentary on this passage. I do not approve of the explanation of Cornelius à Lapide: 'Let the humble man glory in his exaltation, which he certainly expects,' for a twofold reason: because it follows only in the conclusion regarding blessedness or exaltation in v. 12: nor does that sense fit the following verse concerning the rich man's glorying in his humiliation. The interpretation of Vatablus, Cajetan, Salmeron, Aretius, Piscator, Pareus, and the Belgian Interpreters also seems insufficient, because James urges that he who is eminent in this world, abounding in wealth and raised to the greatest honors, should think submissively and humbly of himself, mindful of the mutability of human affairs. For that humbler sense is indeed required, and not only in the rich man, but also in the ταπεινῷ (humble man) (concerning which the patrons of that opinion deny, however, that ταπεινὸν here signifies a man of lowly mind, and who thinks submissively of himself, even though they themselves admit that ταπείνωσιν does not denote a state here, but an affection of the mind, and is referred to morals, as can be seen in Piscator), but it does not bring about καύχησιν (glorying) or joy; but in order for there to be a place for it, it is necessary that both the ταπεινὸς (humble man) and the πλούσιος (rich man) should seek outside of themselves, through true faith, that in which they may glory, and for that reason the humble man, by the sense of his misery, or as πτωχὸς τῷ Πνεύματι (poor in spirit), as Christ calls him in Matt. 5:3, has material for glorying in his true high estate, which he possesses in Christ. But the πλούσιος (rich man) is first sent back to that ταπείνωσιν (humiliation), so that he may acknowledge his spiritual poverty, and arrive at that high estate in which alone one must glory. The Apostle does not say Ἐν ταπεινότητι (in humility), as the Vulgate translates, but ἐν ταπεινώσει (in his humiliation), or lowliness of mind: Cf. Luke 12:14. But the ironic sense, which Thomas Anglicus, Hugo, and Lyranus hand down from Jerome along with Bede, is most to be reprobated. For a consolatory instruction, not an ironic agitation, occurs here. The passage which James produced from Isa. 40:6-7, cited by Sixtus Senensis in Bib. S. Haeres. lib. 8, and by Coccius in Thesaur. Tom. 1, lib. 6, art. 17, p. 180, seems to be produced from Sir. 14, and they approve the canonical authority of the book from that. But Claud. Guillaud on Isa. 40:25, Lorinus on 1 Pet., Salmeron, Dominicus à Soto, and Justinian judge it to be produced from Isaiah: nor does Grotius deny it. Nor is the citation alone an argument for the canonical authority of the cited book.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ὁ δὲ πλούσιος ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει αὐτοῦ) Supple ταπεινούσθω, quod partim ex contrario præcedente (sicut 1. Tim. IV. 3. & alibi) partim ex nomine sequente satis intelligitur. Dives submissum gerat animum, conside- rans suam vilitatem, id est, sortis suæ instabilitatem. Idem sensus 1. Tim. VI. 17.

Ὅτι ὡς ἄνθος χόρτου παρελεύσεται) Χόρτου Ebræis est omnis herba עשב, ut diximus Gen. I. 11. Ἄνθος vero viror. Eadem similitudo Ps. XXXVII. 2. Es. XL. 6. & 7. 1. Petr. I. 24. Nec multum dissidet illa, quæ est Sirach. XIV. 17. Παρελεύσεται יעבור.

Quintus hic fructus est afflictionum, quod glo- riationem & gaudium pariant, Rom. V. 3. Humilis autem in sublimitate sua gloriari dicitur, non quod superbiat, sed quod confidat eadem, quam cum non habeat in sese, utpote ταπεινὸς humilis, & hu- militatem suam eò magis agnoscens, quo magis per afflictionem deprimitur Psal. CXIX. 71. per fidem in Christo quærit, in quo uno solidum est gaudi- um, Phil. IV. 4. Unde dives etiam monetur, ut non in divitiis suis confidat aut glorietur, atque gau- deat, sed ἐν τῇ ταπεινώσει αὐτẽ agnoscat humilita- tem suam vel ex ipsa fragilitate, quam facilè veluti flos fœni transeat, & in hac humilitate sua glorie- tur pariter unice in Domino, juxta Jeremiæ moni- tum c. IX. 24. Nam & dives cum è verbo Dei sese agnoscit, quam sit ταπεινὸς imò ταλαίπωρος, καὶ ἐλεεινὸς, κᾐ πλωχὸς, κᾐ γυμνὸς Ap. III. 17. in illa sui agnitione sese humilians quærit in alio, hoc est, in Christo unice sublimitatem, & divitias veras, si fide præditus sit: Qualem vox ἀδελφὸς insinuat. Ita opus non est supplemento Grotiano: Pro quo Oe- cumenius aliud habet αἰσχυνέστω pudeat. Neq; vel cum Salmerone & Justiniano novam hic doctrinam tradi, vel cum Pareo & Cornelio Apostolum à thesi variarum tentationum ad hypothesin bumilis pau- pertatis transire statuendum. Cohærent enim omnia optime, & perseverare in eadem generali consolatione Apostolum conclusio v. 12. subjuncta convincit. Bene autem cum hac nostra ἀναλύσει consistit B. Brochmandi quoad hosce versus συνέ- χεια: Postquam docuit Apostolus, homines, qui flu- ctuant animo precaturi, διψύχες esse, & ἀκαταστά- τους in omnibus viis suis: monet jam & monstrat, quid facto sit opus, tum pauperibus, tum divitibus, ne ipsos hæc ἀκαταστασία seu mentis & voluntatis tumultuans & perturbans inquietudo invadat: Ni- mirum unumquemque in vitæ suæ conditione libenter acquiescere debere; ita ut neque pauperior ob affli- ctiorem statum animum despondeat, neque, qui ditior est, ob divitias animo efferatur, memor instabilitatis ac momentaneæ durationis divitiarum. A qua sen- tentia etiam Ariasmontanus in suo ad hunc locum commentario non videtur alienus esse. Cornelii à La- pide explicationem: Humilis glorietur in sua exal- tatione, quam certo expectat; gemina de causa non probo: quia de beatitudine vel exaltatione v. 12. in conclusione demum sequitur: nec congruit ille sensus versui sequenti de divitis gloriatione in sua humiliatione. Insufficiens etiam videtur interpre- tatio Vatabli, Cajetani, Salmeronis, Aretii, Piscato- ris, Parei, Interpretum Belgicorum, quod urgeat Ja- cobus, ut qui eminet in hoc mundo, affluens opi- bus, & ad maximos evectus honores, submisse & humiliter de sese sentiat, memor mutabilitatis re- rum humanarum. Ille enim humilior sensus qui- dem requiritur, nec solum in divite, sed etiam in ταπεινῷ, (de quo id istius sententiæ Patroni tamen negant, ταπεινὸν nempe hic significare hominem de- missi animi, & qui de se submisse sentit, etsi fateantur ipsi, ταπείνωσιν non statum hic, sed animi affectum notare, & ad mores referri, ut apud Piscatorem vide- re est) non autem καύχησιν gloriationem, vel gau- dium infert; sed ut illi locus sit, opus est, ut & ὁ τα- πεινὸς & πλύσιο vera fide extra se quærat, quo glorietur, eaque de causa humilis sensu miseriæ, vel πτωχὸς τῷ Πνεύματι, ut Christus eum vocat Matth. V. 3. de vera sua sublimitate, quam in Christo possidet, gloriandi materiam habet. Ὁ δὲ πλύσιο prius ad illam ταπείνωσιν remittitur, ut paupertatem suam spiritualem agnoscat, & ad sublimitatem illam, in qua sola gloriandum est, perveniat. Non dicit Apostolus, Ἐν ταπεινότητι in humilitate, ut Vulga- tus vertit, sed ἐν ταπεινώσει in humiliatione sua, seu animi demissione: Conf. Luc. XII. 14. Maxime au- tem reprobandus sensus Ironicus, quem ex Hiero- nymo cum Beda Thomas Anglicus, Hugo, Lyranus tra- dunt. Nam consolatoria informatio, non ironica exagitatio hic occurrit. Locus quem ex Ef. XL. 6. 7. produxit Jacobus, Sixto Senensi l. IIX. Bib. S. Hæ- res. 3. & Coccio Tom. I. Thesaur. Libr. VI. art. 17. p. 180. productus videtur è Sir. XIV. qui inde autori- tatem libri Canonicam approbant. Sed Claud. Guil- laud. in Ef. XL. 25. Lorinus in 1. Petr. Salmero, Do- minicus à Soto, Justinianus ex Esaia productum censent: nec abnuit Grotius. Neque sola citatio ar- gumentum est autoritatis Canonicæ libri citati.

## 1:11
Verse 11. 'For the sun is risen with the burning heat, and it hath dried the grass, and the flower thereof hath fallen, and the grace of the fashion of it hath perished.' They are aorists for the present or any time. And besides, it is a Hebraism: 'The sun rises, and has dried,' for 'the sun, when it has risen, has dried.' A wind was accustomed to accompany the rising of the sun, which is called burning heat (καύων) in Jonah 4:8, where there is רוח in the Greek, 'east wind.' Now it is the property of the burning heat to dry, as you see in Ezek. 18:10, as also of the sun in Matt. 13:6. 'Hath fallen' (ἐξέπεσε) is נפל in the Syriac, that is, it has departed. 'The grace of the fashion' (ἡ εὐπρέπεια τῶ προσώπυ) is after the manner of the Hebrews, who call that which comes into view of any thing פנים. The Syriac here has 'the beauty of its appearance,' that is, that which was beautiful to the sight.

So also the rich man in his ways shall fade away. The future for the potential. If he proceeds for a long time, namely by living, he will easily wither, that is, he will be deprived of his riches.
