He pursues the comparison. For those things are properly said to wither (μαραίνεσθαι) which lose their greenness or flourishing appearance. נבל in Hebrew. 'In his ways' (ἐν ταῖς πορείαις ἀυτῶ) is בהלכותו. To be compared with this passage is that of Philo in his book on those who sacrifice: 'Let God alone, he says, be your glory and greatest renown, and do not be puffed up by wealth, nor by glory, nor by rule, nor by the beauty of the body, nor by strength, or by similar things on which those void of sense are accustomed to be puffed up, having considered it a miserable thing, that first of all these things are devoid of the good nature, and then that they also have a swift change, withering in a certain way before they have bloomed securely.'

This may be understood concerning the rich man, unless he glories solely in the Lord by humbling himself, or he who trusts in his riches, which are the ways of the rich of this age, as the Apostle teaches, that the condition of herbs, which, deprived of natural moisture, the heat of the sun scorches and cooks, is equal to that of the rich, upon whom God casts the rays of His justice and wrath more ardently when they are deprived of the life-giving irrigation of the Holy Spirit, see Ps. XLIX. 18, Luke XVI. 19. Although indeed the life of all men is compared to the momentary greenness of flowers: yet the rich cling most to worldly things that quickly perish, 1 Tim. VI. 17. But there is no reason why we should read πορίας (riches) instead of πορείαις (ways) with Erasmus and Calvin: for no approved Greek codex has that reading, and the word itself πορίας is entirely unknown to the Greeks, as Beza admits with Stephanus. And the metaphor of the way is most appropriate, both because of the parallel passages Ps. I. v. last, Job XXX. 13. Prov. XII. 26. 28. as well as because of the intention of the Apostle. For he wishes to indicate that not only the rich man himself and the riches themselves, but also whatever the rich man either designs in his mind or does, withers and is consumed as if by a slow wasting disease. For μαραίνομαι is to waste away, to grow faint, and μαρασμὸς is a wasting disease, or an immoderate dryness and consumption of the whole body, as the blessed Brochmand has it here.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Ἀνέτειλε γὰρ ὁ ἥλιος σὺν τῷ καύσωνι κὶ ἐξήρανε τὸν χόρτον καὶ τὸ ἄνθος αὐτῶ ἐξέπεσε, κὶ ἡ εὐπρέπεια τῶ προσώπυ αὐτῶ ἀπώλετο) Sunt ἀόριστοι pro præsenti aut quovis tem- pore. Et præterea Ebraismus: Sol oritur, & arefecit, pro sol ubi ortus est, arefecit. Solebat solis ortum comitari ventus, qui καύσων dicitur Jonæ IV. 8. ubi est רוח in Græ- co ἀνατολικος. Est autem καύσων proprium ξηραίνειν, ut vides Ezech. XVIII. 10. ut & solis Matth. XIII. 6. Ἐξέπεσε נפל Syrus, id est, abiit. Ἡ εὐπρέπεια τῶ προσώπυ more E- bræorum, qui cujusvis rei quod in aspectum venit, vocant פנים. Syrus hic habet שופרא דחזוה pulchri- tudo visionis ejus, id est, id quod aspectu erat pulchrum.

Οὕτω καὶ ὁ πλούσιος ἐν ταῖς πορείαις αὐτῶ μαρανθήσεται) Fu- turum pro potentiali. Si diu procedit, nempe vivendo, fa- cile marcescet, id est, opibus suis destituetur. Persequitur comparationem. Nam μαραίνεσθαι dicuntur proprie, quæ virorem speciemve floridam amittunt. נבל Ebraice. ἐν ταῖς πορείαις ἀυτῶ בהלכותו. Conferendus cum hoc loco ille Philonis libro de sacrificantibus: Ἔςω δὲ, φησὶ, μόνος Θεὸς καύχημά σε κὶ μέγιστον κλέος, κὶ μήτ' ἐπὶ πλούτῳ, μήτ' ἐπὶ δόξῃ, μήθ' ἡγεμονίᾳ, μήτε σώματος εὐμορφίᾳ, μήτε ῥώμῃ, ἢ τοῖς παραπλησίοις ἐφ' οἷς εἰώθασιν οἱ κενοὶ φρεσῶν ἐπαίρεσθαι, συμπε- θὲς λογισάμενος, ὅτι πρῶτον μὲν ἀμέτοχα ταῦτ' ἐςὶ τῆς ἀγαθῆς φύσεως, ἔπειτα δὲ ὅτι κὶ ὀξεῖαν ἔχει τὴν μεταβολὴν μαραινόμενα τρόπον τινὰ πρὶν ἀνθῆσαι βεβαίως.

Hoc de divite, nisi sese humiliando in Domino unice glorietur, vel qui confidit in opibus suis, quæ via divitum hujus seculi sunt, accipi potest, ut do- ceat Apostolus, parem esse rationem herbarum, quas humore naturali destitutas æstus solis adurit & coquit, & divitum, in quos justitiæ & iræ suæ ra- dios Deus ardentius spargit, ubi destituuntur vivi- fica Spiritus sancti irrigatione, vid. Psal. XLIX. 18. Luc. XVI. 19. Quanquam vero omnium hominum vita momentaneæ florum viriditati comparetur: Rebus tamen mundanis cito pereuntibus maximè adhærent divites 1. Tim. VI. 17. Non autem est, quod cum Erasmo & Calvino pro πορείαις viis legamus πορίας divitias: nam nec ullus probatus codex Græcus eam lectionem habet, & vox ipsa πορίας Græcis prorsus ignota est, Beza cum Stephano fa- tente. Et convenientissima est Metaphora viæ, tum ob locos parallelos Pf. I. v. ult. Job. XXX. 13. Prov. XII. 26. 28. tum ob intentionem Apostoli. Vult enim indicare, non tantum ipsum divitem & ipsas divitias, sed etiam quicquid dives aut animo designat, aut facit, marcescere, & velut lenta tabe consumi. Nam μαραίνομαι est tabefio, elangueo, & μαρασμὸς est ta- bes, seu immodica totius corporis ariditas & consum- ptio, ut hic habet B. Brochmandus.

## 1:12
Vers. 12. Blessed is the man who endures temptation) That is, who is tested by adversities. For ὑπομένειν is to be taken here as in Heb. XII. 7. The following words show this. It seems that the passage in Job V. 17 is being referred to, where it is: Blessed is the man whom the Lord corrects. And in this place the Manuscript has not ἀνὴρ but ἄνθρωπος.

He does not say that we are blessed through the tolerance of temptations, but blessed are those who tolerate them. Which is to be noted on account of the Papists. For patience is not the cause of blessedness, but it is required for the subject which is declared blessed. But if the translation of Grotius prevails, blessed is he who is tested by adversities, will being tested by adversities be called the cause of blessedness? Paul certainly denies that the sufferings are worthy of the future glory, Rom. VIII. 18.

But we admit that τὸ ὑπομένειν (to endure) signifies not being tested. For it is by the force of the word to remain underneath, and to wait, and it is used of those who manfully sustain the rushing attack of an enemy, as is evident from Plutarch, Thucydides, and Herodian; and therefore he is said to ὑπομένειν πειρασμὸν (endure temptation) who does not yield to adversities, but receives and sustains whatever attacks of adversities. However, blessedness is not attributed to that endurance, because the one enduring is proclaimed blessed. For one is not blessed except through faith, Hab. II. 4, Heb. X. 38, which alone is the victory that overcomes the world, 1 John V. 4.

Ὅτι δόκιμος γενόμενος) When he has become (that is, has appeared) approved or constant שׁוֹחַד 2 Chron. IX. 17. See Rom. XIV. 18, XVI. 10, 1 Cor. XI. 19, 2 Cor. X. 8, XII. 7, 2 Tim. II. 15.

δóκιμος is not the same as constant. For there are also πρόσκαιροι (temporary ones), who are found to be δόκιμοι for a time. As δοκιμασία is testing: so δόκιμος is approved, who through testing not only appears approved, but also becomes so, not indeed by himself, because the cross and temptation do not by themselves make one approved: but the Holy Spirit works that in us through the cross. This metaphor is not so much taken from coins, which are tested by a touchstone, as from metals, which are tested by fire, 1 Pet. I. 7, Jer. V. 27, seqq.

Λήψεται στέφανον τῆς ζωῆς) For στέφανον in Arabic there is אִנְרָא, which the Chaldeans pronounce אַנְרָא, it is properly a crown of a kingdom. Thus the Paraphrast has it in Esth. I. 3, II. 17, Cant. V. 7. It is called, however, the crown of life, because it is given in that eternal life, as in Apoc. II. 10. This is the mystical sense of that which follows in Job V. 19. Beautifully, the blessed Brochmand: Where in the arena of temptations you have fought manfully until the end of life, a crown will fall to you, not woven from parsley or wild olive, or some similar fleeting thing, but you will be gifted with a ςεφάνῳ ἀφθάρτῳ καὶ ἀμαράντῳ (an incorruptible and unfading crown), 1 Pet. I. 4, which will so ςέψει (crown), gird, surround, and encompass you with life, Apoc. II. 10, righteousness, 2 Tim. IV. 5, and glory, 1 Pet. V. 4, that there will no longer be any place for sin, dangers, sickness, or death, 2 Cor. XV. 54, 55, 56, seq.

Ὃν ἐπηγγείλατο ὁ Κύριος τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν ἀυτὸν) And therefore it is called τῆς δικαιοσύνης ςέφανος (the crown of righteousness), 2 Tim. IV. 8. See Luke XXII. 19. In the Manuscript, ὁ Κύριος is not present. And so Θεὸς is understood, as in Heb. XIII. 15 and elsewhere. Nor did the Syriac and Latin read and accept it otherwise here.

The Vulgate rendered it 'which He promised,' from which Cornelius tries to carve out merit, but in the Greek it is ἐπηγγείλατο (He promised). Moreover, ἐπαγγελία is a promise not meritorious, but merely gratuitous, Acts II. 39, Gal. III. 14, nor is the crown rendered because of love, but to those who love. For how could our love merit anything, since it is owed in many ways, and is altogether imperfect: nor does it have any proportion to the crown of life?

PART II. DIDACTIC EPISTLE CONCERNING INTERNAL TEMPTATIONS OF SEDUCTION, WHICH IS THE SECOND PART OF CHAPTER I.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Μακάριος ἀνὴρ ὃς ὑπομένει πειρασμὸν) Id est, qui adversis exploratur. Nam ὑπομένειν hic sumendum, ut Ebr. XII. 7. Ostendunt id sequentia. Videtur respici locus Job. V. 17. ubi est: Μακάριος ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ὃν ἐλέγξεξ ὁ Κύριος. Et hoc loco Manuscriptus habet non ἀνὴρ sed ἄνθρωπος.

Non dicit beatos nos esse per tolerantiam tentatio- num, sed beatos, qui tolerant. Quod ob Pontificios notandum. Non enim patientia causa est beatitudi- nis, sed ad subjectum, quod beatum prædicatur, re- quiritur. Quod si Grotii translatio obtineat, beatus, qui adversis exploratur, num explorari adversis causa dicetur beatitudinis? Negat utique Paulus, digna esse τὰ παθήματα gloria futura, Rom. IIX. 18.

Sed admittimus τὸ ὑπομένειν sustinere & tolerare non explorari significare. Est enim vi vocis subtus manere, & expectare, ac usurpatur de illis, qui irru- entem hostis impetum viriliter sustinent, ut à Plu- tarcho, Thucydide, Herodiano constat, ideoque ὑπομένειν πειρασμὸν dicitur, qui adversis non ce- dit, sed impetus adversitatum quosvis excipit ac sustinet. Non autem illi sustinentiæ beatitudo tri- buitur, quod sustinens beatus prædicetur. Beatus enim est non nisi per fidem, Hab. II. 4. Ebr. X. 38. quæ sola est victoria, quæ mundum vincit, 1. Job. V. 4.

Ὅτι δόκιμος γενόμενος) Cum factus sit, (id est, apparu- erit) probus sive constans שׁוֹחַד 2. Paral. IX. 17. Vide Rom. XIV. 18. XVI. 10. 1. Cor. XI. 19. 2. Cor. X. 8. XII. 7. 2. Tim. II. 15.

Non idem est δόκιμος, qui constans. Sunt enim etiam πρόσκαιροι, qui ad tempus δόκιμοι inveniun- tur. Ut δοκιμασία est probatio: Ita δόκιμος probus, qui per explorationem non apparet tantum pro- bus, sed etiam fit, non quidem per se, quia crux & tentatio per se non faciunt, ut probus quis sit: Sed Spiritus sanctus in nobis id operatur per crucem. Metaphora hæc non tam à numismatis, quæ explo- rantur per lapidem lydium, desumpta, quam à me- tallis, quæ per ignem explorantur, 1. Petr. I. 7. Jer. V. 27. seqq.

Λήψεται στέφανον τῆς ζωῆς) Pro στέφανον in Arabico est אִנְרָא, quod Chaldæi efferunt אַנְרָא proprie est corona re- gni. Sic habet Paraphrastes Esth. I. 3. II. 17. Cant. V. 7. Vocatur autem corona vitæ, quia datur in vita illa æter- na, sicut Apoc. II. 10. Hic est sensus mysticus ejus, quod sequitur apud Jobum V. 19. Pulchre B. Brochmandus: Ubi in arena tentatio- num ad finem usque vita viriliter pugnaveris, cedet tibi corona non ex apio aut oleastro, aut simili re eva- vida contexta, sed donaberis ςεφάνῳ ἀφθάρτῳ καὶ ἀμαράντῳ, 1. Petr. I. 4. qui te vita Apoc. II. 10. justitia, 2. Tim. IV. 5. & gloria, 1. Pet. V. 4. ita ςέψει cinget, cir- cumdabit & circumfundet, ut nullus amplius pecca- to, periculis, morbo, morti futurus sit locus 2. Cor. XV. 54. 55. 56. seq.

Ὃν ἐπηγγείλατο ὁ Κύριος τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν ἀυτὸν) Atque ideo dicitur τῆς δικαιοσύνης ςέφανος, 2. Tim. IV. 8. Vide Luc. XXII. 19. In Manuscripto non est ὁ Κύριος. Itaque subauditur Θεὸς, ut Ebr. XIII. 15. & alibi. Nec aliter hic legerunt & acceperunt Syrus & Latinus.

Vulgatus reddidit, quam repromisit, unde Corne- lius meritum exsculpere conatur, sed in Græco est ἐπηγγείλατο promisit. Est autem ἐπαγγελία pro- missio non meritoria, sed mere gratuita, Act. II. 39. Gal. III. 14. nec corona redditur ob dilectionem, sed iis, qui diligunt. Nostra enim dilectio mereri quomodo posset, quum debita multis modis sit, & admodum imperfecta: nec proportionem ullam habeat ad vitæ coronam?

PARS II. EPISTOLÆ DIDACTICA DE TENTATIONIBUS INTERNIS SEDUCTIONIS QUÆ PARS ALTERA EST CAPITIS I.

## 1:13
Vers. 13. Μηδεὶς πειραζόμενος λεγέτω, ὅτι ἀπὸ Θεῦ πειράζομαι) Let no one of you, when he falls into evils, think that they are so directed by God that through them any of you is impelled into sin, πρὸς τὸ τίϰτειν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν (to bring forth sin), as follows immediately, as if God were casting upon us unavoidable necessities for sinning. He says this so that those pressed by many evils might not succumb. For this exhortation coheres with those things which follow below in 16, 17. The sense of this passage is clearly the same as 1 Cor. X. 13. God does not send adversities upon you to make you worse, but better. Do not lose heart. God will be present to those who wish well. Note ἀπὸ for παρὰ, which we have also observed elsewhere. Tertullian on prayer: The devil tempts, God tests. Hence the devil is called ὁ πειράζων (the tempter) Matt. 4, 3.

Ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς ἀπείρασός ἐςι ϰαϰῶν) Just as He Himself cannot be seduced to wicked actions. ἀπείρατος is more frequent among the Greeks. But neither is that other one against analogy. And in the glossary I find ἀπείρατος (untemptable). Πειράζει δὲ ἀυτὸς ἐδένα) So neither does He Himself love to seduce others. He wishes men to be such as He Himself is.

The Apostle proceeds to overthrow impious and false dogmas, and to fortify the Hebrews against the same with solid instruction. Such were then the dogmas concerning the cause of sin, concerning θρησκεία (religion) and the worship of God, and concerning the nature of faith. Concerning the cause of sin, heretics were spreading blasphemous dogmas even in the time of the Apostles: Simon Magus, as witnessed by Vincent of Lérins in his Commonitorium, ch. XXXIV, taught that God the Creator is the author of evils, that is, of our crimes, impieties, and shameful deeds: whom the Valentinians followed, asserting that malice exists in things from their primeval origin and creation, whose impious dogmas their successors have revived, both the Zwinglians, constituting God as the cause of sin, and the Scholastics, and the more recent Papists and Calixtines seduced by them, seeking the origin of sin in the condition of matter, concerning which [see] the solid discussion in the preface and dedication of the tract of Dreier on the cause of sin. James then removes the false cause and the impious dogma, and then designates the true cause of sin. And first he teaches concerning its origin; then, indeed, he also overthrows the blasphemy with arguments, both from the holy and immutable nature of God, and from the grace of regeneration, and from θρησκεία or true religion. Now, therefore, he removes the ἀντίθεσιν. Let no one who is tempted say that he is tempted by God. In which words the word πειράζειν is not taken in different ways—that is, of the temptation of affliction and of seduction, as Grotius wishes—but in the same sense. Let no one who is tempted by sins say: I am tempted by God. This requires συνέχειαν. For he instructs those tempted by sins, lest they impute the temptation to God. What is that coherence: Let one tempted by afflictions not say: I am tempted by sins by God? The Apostle adds the reason: Ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς ἀπείρα- ςός ἐςι ϰαϰῶν, where it is in the open that the discourse is likewise about the evils of fault, which do not fall upon God, and he explains this further: But he himself tempts no one: which likewise look toward the temptation of sin. The things which follow in verses 16 and 17 are opposed entirely to the same error, concerning God as the cause of sin: whom he confirms to be the author of no evil, because from him, as the Father of lights, good things indeed, but not evil things or sins, can proceed, since in that Father of lights there cannot be a παραλλαγὴ, ἢ τροπῆς ἀπο- σκίασμα of light or darkness. But the passage 1 Cor. X. 13 is here entirely ἀλλότριος. Everything here teaches that πειράζειν is to incite and πειράζεσθαι is to be incited to sin, as the Devil is called ὁ πειράζων in Matt. IV. 13, 1 Thess. III. Therefore, the Apostle desires that this be entirely removed from God.

Those are called internal temptations, not because the Devil does not also tempt with external afflictions, as we know was done to Job, ch. I. 11, ch. II. 5. But because those external ones are also referred to God, Am. III. 6, whereas here the discourse is about temptations which can in no way proceed from God; and because the Devil never infests the pious with external temptations without at the same time soliciting them to sin with internal ones, and directing the external ones toward that; whereas God renders them a proof of faith to himself, exercises patience, perfects virtues, and promotes blessedness.

The Vulgate barbarously rendered the word ἀπείραςος as 'intentator' [untempter]: which Lorinus tries in vain to defend, because God provokes no one to sin. For the Greek word carries not an active but a passive meaning. And what kind of assertion would that be: God does not provoke to sin, but he tempts no one to sin? Finally, if the active sense prevails, would not God be called the untempter of sinners, because he tempts sins, that is, may incite to evils! Which is diametrically opposed to the opinion of the Apostle. It would therefore be more correctly rendered, is untemptable by evils. Clement also ineptly, Constit. b. II. ch. 8, explained it as untempted by evils, because God does not tempt the evil but only the good, because James asserts that God simply οὐδένα, no one, tempts with that temptation of which there is speech here. Therefore, he is rightly called Ἀπείραστος, according to Grotius's interpretation, because he cannot be seduced to sin, and cannot be affected or solicited by any evil thing: Who is supremely good, Matt. XIX. 17. He does not will impiety, nor can he will it, because of his immutable and infinite goodness, Ps. V. 5. Deut. XXXII. 4. Zeph. III. 5.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Μηδεὶς πειραζόμενος λεγέτω, ὅτι ἀπὸ Θεῦ πει- ράζομαι) Nemo vestrum, ubi in mala incidit, putet à Deo ea sic dirigi, ut per ea vestrum aliquis in peccatum impel- latur, πρὸς τὸ τίϰτειν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, ut mox sequitur, quasi Deus inevitabiles nobis ad peccandum injiciat necessitates. Hoc ideo dicit, ne multis malis pressi succumberent. Co- hæret enim hæc adhortatio cum iis, quæ sequuntur infra 16. 17. Plane idem hujus loci sensus est qui 1. Cor. X. 13. Non ideo adversa vobis immittit Deus, ut vos pejores faciat, sed meliores. Ne despondete animum. Deus bene volentibus aderit. Nota ἀπὸ pro παρὰ, quod & alibi observavimus. Tertulliano de oratione: Diabolus tentat, Deus probat. Hinc Diabolus vocatur ὁ πειράζων Matth. 4, 3.

Ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς ἀπείρασός ἐςι ϰαϰῶν) Sicut ipse ad actiones pravas seduci nequit. Frequentius apud Græcos est ἀπεί- ρατος. Sed nec alterum illud contra analogiam est. Et in glossario reperio ἀπείρατος Intentabilis. Πειράζει δὲ ἀυτὸς ἐδένα) Sic nec ipse amat alios seducere. Qualis ipse est, tales ut homines sint optat.

Progreditur Apostolus ad impia & falsa dogma- ta profliganda, & adversus eadem Ebræos, solida in- formatione muniendos. Talia erant tum de causa peccati, tum de θρησκεία & cultu Dei, tum de natu- ra fidei. De causa peccati blasphema dogmata spar- gebant hæretici jam Apostolorum tempore: Simon Magus, teste Vincent. Lirin. in commonit. cap. XXXIV. Deum Creatorem docuit autorem malo- rum, id est, scelerum, impietatum, flagitiorumque no- strorum esse: Quem sequuti Valentiniani, malitiam rebus inesse à primæva earum origine & creatione asseruere, quorum & successorum impia dogmata resuscitarunt cum Zwingliani, Deum causam pec- cati constituentes, tum Schoslastici, & ab iis seducti Pontificii recentiores & Calixtini, originem peccati in conditione materiæ quærentes, de quibus in so- lida discuss. scandal. tract. Dreieri de causa peccati prafat. dedicat. actum. S. Jacobus tum falsam re- movet causam & dogma impium tum veram pecca- ti causam designat. Et de origine ejus primum do- cet; Deinde verò etiam argumentis profligat bla- sphemiam, tum à sancta & immutabili Dei natura, tum à regenerationis gratia, tum à θρησκεία vel reli- gione vera. Jam ergò ἀντίθεσιν removet. Nemo ten- tatus dicat, quod à Deo tentetur. In quibus verbis vox πειράζειν non diversimodè, hoc est, de tentatio- ne tum afflictionis, tum seductionis, ut Grotius vult, sed eodem sensu accipitur. Nemo qui peccatis tentatus est dicat: A Deo tentor. Requirit id συνέ- χεια. Nam tentatos peccatis instruit, ne tentatio- nem Deo imputent. Quænam illa cohærentia: Ten- tatus afflictionibus ne dicat: Ego peccatis tentor à Deo? Addit rationem Apostolus: Ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς ἀπείρα- ςός ἐςι ϰαϰῶν, ubi de malis culpæ itidem sermonem esse, quod non cadant in Deum, in aprico est, & explicat id porrò: Πειράζει δὲ ἀυτὸς ἐδένα: quæ pariter ad tentationem peccati spectant. Quæ v. 16. 17. sequuntur, eidem omnino errori, de Deo causa peccati, opponuntur: Quem nullius mali autorem esse confirmat, quia ab ipso ceu Patre luminum bo- na quidem, non vero mala vel peccata provenire possunt, quum in illo luminum Patre non possit es- se lucis vel tenebrarum παραλλαγὴ, ἢ τροπῆς ἀπο- σκίασμα. Locus vero 1. Cor. X. 13. hic prorsus est ἀλλότριος. Omnia hic docent πειράζειν esse inci- tare & πειράζεσθαι incitare ad peccandum, ut Dia- bolus ὁ πειράζων dicitur Matth. IV. 13. 1. Thess. III. Id ergo à Deo prorsus removeri cupit Apostolus.

Interna illæ dicuntur tentationes, non quod Diabolus non externis etiam afflictionibus tentet, quemadmodum Jobo factum novimus, cap. I. 11. c. II. 5. Sed quod illæ externæ ad Deum etiam refe- rantur Am. III. 6. hic vero de tentationibus agatur, quæ nullatenus à Deo proficisci possunt; quodque Diabolus nunquam externis tentationibus pios in- festet, quin simul internis ad peccatum solicitet, eoque externas dirigat; quibus vero Deus fidem sibi probationem reddit, patientiam exercet, vir- tutes perficit, & beatitudinem promovet.

Vocem ἀπείραςος Vulgata barbare reddidit in- tentator: quam Lorinus tueri frustra conatur, quod Deus neminem ad peccandum provocet. Vox enim Græca non activam sed passivam significationem infert. Et quænam foret illa assertio: Deus non pro- vocat ad peccatum, neminem autem tentat ad pecca- tum? Denique si activus sensus obtinet, annon Deus intentator peccatorum dicetur, quod intentet peccata, hoc est, ad mala incitet! Quod e diametro sententiae Apostoli contrariatur. Rectius ergo red- deretur, est intentabilis malorum. Inepte etiam Cle- ment. Constit. l. II. cap. 8. intentatorum malorum exposuit, quod Deus non malos sed duntaxat bonos tentet, quia simpliciter οὐδένα neminem ea tentatio- ne, de qua hic sermo, tentare Deum asserit Jacobus. Ἀπείραστος ergo recte dicitur, interprete Grotio, quod ad peccatum seduci nequeat, & a nulla re mala affici ac solicitari: Qui summe bonus est Matth. XIX. 17. Impietatem non vult, nec velle potest, ob bonitatem immutabilem & infinitam, Psal. V. 5. Deut. XXXII. 4. Soph. III. 5.

## 1:14
Vers. 14. But each one is tempted by his own desire) מיצר הרע, as the Hebrews say. If we are led away from God by adversities, God is not the cause: But that we love the goods of this life and this life itself more than we ought. Eve signified this ἐπιθυμίαν, as Philo explains both in his allegories and elsewhere.

Ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος) Ἐξελκόμενος משיכא, so that he is led away from the right path. Δελεαζόμενος, so that he is drawn toward evils, namely, like fish by bait. A frequent simile. Thus the best Greek writers say to be enticed by the belly and by words. In the glossary, δελεάζω is to entice, to allure, to attract, to inveigle. In Syriac, מתרגרג ומתנגד.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας) מיצר הרע, ut loquuntur Ebraei. Si per adversa a Deo abducimur, non Deus in causa est: Sed quod bona hujus vitae vitamque hanc ipsam plus amamus quam fieri oporte- ret. Hanc ἐπιθυμίαν significabat Eva, ut & in allegoriis & alibi explicat Philo.

Ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος) Ἐξελκόμενος משיכא ita ut abducatur a recto. Δελεαζόμενος ita ut pertrahatur ad mala scilicet, ut pisces esca. Frequens similitudo. Sic Grae- ci scriptores optimi dicunt γαστρὶ & λόγοις δελεάζεσθαι. In glossario δελεάζω illecebro, pellicio, allicio, illicio. In Sy- riaco מתרגרג ומתנגד.

## 1:15
Ἡ δὲ ἁμαρτία ἀποτελεσθεῖσα ἀποκύει θάνατον) Ἀποκύει תכליד. Eve would not have brought forth those destined to die, had Adam not sinned by the act itself. Thus also, an affection will not condemn us to death, if it miscarries, but only if it brings forth deliberate and evil actions. Not only to die, but also to remain in death is the punishment of sin, that is, the end of a life not Christian, 1 Cor. XV. 55, 56. Ἀποκύω or ἀποκυέω is a good Greek word, which we shall also have shortly in verse 18. Plutarch uses it several times. In the glossary, ἀποκυήσασα is having brought forth. Ἀποκύω is to bring forth.

The Apostle now presents the true cause of sin, and that not an external one, which is Satan, but an internal one, which is the depraved concupiscence in us. But it is not only about that temptation by which we are led away from God through adversities: But it concerns any irritation to sin, whatever the occasion may be. For it is a general assertion, ἕκαστος, each one. And ἐπιθυμία is common to all, which is not considered here absolutely. For the faculty of desire is from God, and desire in itself is good. Therefore, it is not as it was in man before the fall, but as it began to be through the fall. For it is thus prone to evil all the days, Gen. VI. 5, ch. VIII. 21, of which depraved concupiscence Rom. VII. 7, Gal. V. 17. And therefore it deals with concupiscence while it is abstracted and baited. As therefore he previously taught against the Simonians that God is not the author of sin: So now he teaches that sin is not from the condition of matter or creation. (For thus it would entirely be from God, because the cause of the cause is the cause of the caused,) but from ἰδίᾳ ἐπιθυμίᾳ, from one's own desire, he argues against other heretics, just as Christ says of the Devil in John VIII. 44, when he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own. Desire, not as it is from God, tempts us, but as it is our own, as it turns itself away from God: Which depraved concupiscence, when after the first aversion of the first-created it is propagated through carnal generation, and is inherent in us by nature, is called original sin. Ἐξέλκειν is to drag out of the way, to lead away from the right path. Δελεάζειν is to circumvent by some blandishment under the guise of utility, just as wild beasts are wont to be baited. For δέλεαρ is bait, which is used for catching brutes. Cf. Gen. III. 5, Matt. IV. 8, 9. Through the former, abstraction from the good is brought about; through the latter, the appetite for evil is brought about by depraved concupiscence. By which the first motion of depraved desire is established.

There follows the other, the conceived assent of the will, or the deliberate will of sin, the twofold effect of which James expresses, namely, prohairetic sin, and death. Nor yet is it to be denied that the first motions are sins, or deserve death, toward which Grotius seems to incline here with the Scholastics and Papists. For every lawlessness is sin; but lawlessness is without doubt concupiscence, because the law said, you shall not covet; and the wages of any sin is death, John III. 4, Rom. VI. last verse. But here the speech is particularly about voluntary and prohairetic sins, because not only is whatever has the nature of sin removed from God, but also the degrees of sins are set forth, because the first sin has its origin from ἰδίᾳ ἐπιθυμίᾳ, by which the first-created were seduced, and because it is propagated to us, each one of us is seduced by it to sin: namely, we are seduced from original sin to actual; which furthermore is viewed either in the first motions of evil concupiscence, or as the deliberate assent of the will is added, which the Apostle calls συλλαβεῖν, the Scholastics call second motions, when desire after the pleasurable baiting conceives sin with the will and heart. That, therefore, is thus far internal. There follows the external when it breaks forth and is brought out abroad, which had been conceived in the heart. This is τίκτειν, just as a woman who had conceived brings forth a birth, when sin is perpetrated with an external work. James therefore does not distinguish sin into different species, as if one were mortal by its nature and another venial: But he makes conceived and brought-forth sin merely different degrees of sin. For concupiscence does not conceive one sin and bring forth another, but the same in species, though distinguished by degree, just as a woman does not conceive one offspring and bring forth another, but the same, though different in perfection. Death also reigned over those who did not sin after the likeness of Adam's sin, by committing external actual sin, as the Apostle testifies in Rom. 5:13. James attributes death rather to sin brought to completion than to τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐπιθυμίᾳ, because sin brought to completion evidently and manifestly, even by the testimony of men, deserves death according to the law, Ezek. 18:4. James uses these words, not without emphasis, implying that men who indulge in carnal concupiscences, as it were, consort with Satan, the impure spirit, and the malignant world, Lev. 16:7, Apoc. 17:2, ch. 18:3. Cf. Gen. 3:1 seqq., 2 Sam. 11:2, 3. And he notably designates ἁμαρτίαν ἀποτελεσθεῖσαν, not τελεσθεῖσαν: because by that word is noted a freely chosen act, since ἀνὴρ ἀποτετελεσμένος to Xenophon is a man perfect in all respects: but by this latter, any sin designated by deed, even if noted, even if extorted, Rom. 7:17. Which, although by its nature it deserves death, Deut. 27:26, is nevertheless not actually deadly, since he who is held captive against his will under the law of sin is immediately led to repentance, and raises himself by the merit of Christ, Rom. 7:24, 25. For thus in act no κατάκριμα finds a place in him, ch. 8:1. But that other brings forth death, which is the mature fetus of sin admitted with full assent. Because, as Estius says here, after someone has once, having cast off the fear of God by which he was deterred, rushed into the work of sin, he is not content to have done it once, but having become bolder, he repeats it again and again, whence he comes into the frequency and habit of sinning, whereby it happens that he is finally led to death. And afterwards: For sin brought to completion is not said to beget death, because it makes a man worthy of death, but because it leads a man in very deed to death: That this is not equally true of sin not yet consummated, has already been declared.

Latin:

Ἡ δὲ ἁμαρτία ἀποτελεσθεῖσα ἀποκύει θάνατον) Ἀποκύει תכליד. Eva non peperisset morturos, nisi Adam actu ipso peccasset. Sic & nos non damnabit morti affectus, si abortiat, sed ita demum si deliberatas easque malas actio- nes pariat. Non mori tantum, sed & in morte manere poena est peccati, id est exitus vitae non Christianae, 1. Cor. XV. 55. 56. Ἀποκύω vel ἀποκυέω est vox bene Graeca, quam & mox habebimus 18. Utitur Plutarchus aliquoties. In glossario ἀποκυήσασα enixa. Ἀποκύω enitor.

Veram peccati causam jam exhibet Apostolus, eamque non externam, quae Satanas est, sed inter- nam, quae prava in nobis concupiscentia. Non au- tem tantum de illa tentatione, qua per adversa a Deo abducimur: Sed de quavis irritatione ad pec- candum, quacunque occasione fiat, agitur. Nam generalis assertio est, ἕκαστος quisque. Et ἐπιθυμία omnibus communis est, quae hic non absolute con- sideratur. Nam facultas ἐπιθυμητικὴ a Deo est, & ἐπιθυμία per se bona. Non ergo qualis erat in ho- mine ante lapsum, sed qualis esse coepit per lapsum. Ita enim prona est ad malum omnibus diebus, Gen. VI. 5. cap. IIX. 21. de qua prava concupiscentia Rom. VII. 7. Gal. V. 17. Ideoque de concupiscentia, dum ab- strahitur & inescatur, agit. Ut ergo prius, Deum non esse peccati autorem contra Simonianos do- cuit: Ita nunc a conditione materia, vel creatione peccatum non esse. (Sic enim omnino foret a Deo, quia causa causae est causa causati,) sed ab ἰδίᾳ ἐπι- θυμίᾳ a propria cupiditate, contra alios haereticos adstruit, quemadmodum de Diabolo Christus Joh. VIII. 44. cum mendacium loquitur, ἐκ τῶν ἰδίων λαλεῖ. Cupiditas, non qua a Deo est, tentat nos, sed qua idia propria nostrum, qua se avertit a Deo: Quae prava concupiscentia, cum post primam aversionem τῶν πρωτοπλάστων per carnalem gene- rationem propagetur, & natura nobis insit, origi- nale peccatum vocatur. Ἐξέλκειν est extra viam rapere, a recto tramite abducere. Δελεάζειν est blandimento aliquo sub specie utilitatis circumveni- re,uti feræ inescari solent. Nam δέλεαρ esca est, quæ brutis capiendis adhibetur. Conf. Gen. III. 5. Matth.IV.8.9. Per illud abstractio à bono, per hoc appetitio mali conciliatur à prava concupiscentia. Quibus constat primus motus cupiditatis pravæ.

Sequitur alter, conceptus voluntatis assensus, seu deliberata voluntas peccati, cujus effectum gemi- num exprimit Jacobus, peccatum scilicet proareti- cum, & mortem. Nec tamen eo negandum, primos motus peccata esse, vel mortem mereri, qua cum Scholasticis, & Papistis hic inclinare videtur Grotius. Nam omnis ἀνομία peccatum; ἀνομία autem citra dubium est concupiscentia, quia lex dixit, non con- cupisces; & cujusvis peccati stipendium mors est, Joh.III.4. Rom.VI.v.ult. Sed hic de peccatis volun- tariis, & proæreticis peculiariter sermo est, quia non tantum quicquid peccati rationem habet, à Deo removetur, sed etiam gradus peccatorum expo- nuntur, quod primum ab ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἰδίᾳ peccatum ortum habeat, qua seducti sunt Protoplasti, & quia ea ad nos propagatur, unusquisque nostrum ab ea seducitur ad peccatum : nimirum à peccato origina- li seducimur ad ætuale; quod porrò vel in primis concupiscentiæ malæ motibus spectatur, vel prout af- sensus voluntatis deliberatus accedit, quod συλλα- βῆν vocat Apostolus, Scholastici secundos motus, cum cupiditas post delectabilem inescationem vo- luntate & corde concipit peccatum. Id ergo ha- ctenus internum est. Sequitur externum cum pro- rumpit & foris editur, quod corde conceptum erat. Hoc est τίκτειν, sicut fœmina, quæ concepe- rat, partum edit, cum externo opere peccatum perpetratur. Non ergo Jacobus peccatum in di- versas species distinguit, quasi aliud natura sua mor- tale sit, aliud veniale: Sed peccatum conceptum & genitum diversos tantum peccati gradus facit. Ne- que enim concupiscentia aliud peccatum concipit, aliud gignit, sed idem specie, licet gradu distinctum, uti fœmina non alium concipit partum, alium edit, sed eundem, licet perfectione diversum. Mors ętiam dominata est in eos, qui non peccarunt ad si- militudinem peccati Adami,peccatum actuale ex- ternum committendo, teste Apostolo Rom. V.13. Mortem autem potius peccato consummato, quam τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐπιθυμίᾳ tribuit Jacobus, quia peccatum consummatum evidenter & manifeste, etiam homi- num testimonio, meretur mortem secundum le- gem, Ezech.XIIX.4. Utitur autem his vocibus Ja- cobus, non sine emphasi, innuens, quod homines carnalibus concupiscentiis indulgentes cum Sata- na, impuro spiritu, & mundo maligno, veluti con- suescant, Levit. XVI.7. Apoc.XVII.2.cap. XIIX.3. Conf. Gen.III.1.seqq. 2.Sam.XI.2.3. Et notanter de- signat ἁμαρτίαν ἀποτελεσθεῖσαν, non τελεσθεῖσαν : quod illa voce notetur libere proareticum, quia ἀνὴρ ἀποτετελεσμένος Xenophonti est vir omnibus numeris perfectus: hac vero quodvis peccatum opere designatum, etiam notent, etiam extortum, Rom. VII.17. Quod etsi natura sua mortem mereatur, Deut. XXVII. 26. non tamen actu mortiferam est, cum qui invitus sub legem peccati captivatur, pœnitentia statim ducitur, meritoque Christi sese erigit, Rom.VII.24.25. Sic enim actu nullum in ipso locum invenit κατάκριμα, cap.VIII.1. Illud vero mortem ἀποκύει, quæ peccati pleno assensu ad- missi maturus est fœtus. Quia, ut hic Estius, postea- quam semel quis abjecto Dei timore, quo deterreba- tur, in opus peccati proruperit, non contentus est illud semel fecisse, sed audacior factus subinde repetit, unde in frequentationem & consuetudinem peccandi ve- nit, quo fit ut tandem ducatur ad mortem. Et postea: Non enim dicitur peccatum consummatum gene- rare mortem, quia facit hominem dignum morte, sed quia hominem re ipsa ducit ad mortem: Quod de peccato nondum consummato non perinde verum esse, jam declaratum est.

## 1:16
Vers. 16. Then desire having conceived brings forth sin) συλλαβοῦσα τίκτει הרה ותלד. The first birth of Eve was Cain, the earthly man thinking, figured through Adam, and the desire adhering to him signified through Eve, by itself (that is, with no higher Spirit of God intervening) what can it produce of itself, except the depraved? Philo in his allegories: Folly is the proper name of injustices, because the fool is always in injustices with unbridled works. When he desires money unjustly, when glory, when pleasure, when anything else. And later: For of vice, one part is considered in relation, the other is considered in motion. For it inclines toward the fulfillment of results, or something by being moved, etc. Plotinus cited by Theodoret, book VI against the Greeks: A small turning having happened at the beginning, proceeding, it always makes the thing sinned more and greater, and the body is constituted of necessity by desire.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Εἶτα ἡ ἐπιθυμία συλλαβοῦσα τίκτει ἁμαρτίαν) συλλαβοῦσα τίκτει הרה ותלד. Primus Evae partus Cain, Homo terrestris cogitans per Adamum figuratus, & adhae- rens ei cupiditas per Evam significata, per se, (id est, nullo Dei Spiritu sublimiore interveniente) quid producere de se potest, nisi pravum? Philo in allegoriis: Ἀφροσύνη δέ ἐστι κύ- ριον ὄνομα ἀδικημάτων, ὅτι ὁ ἄφρων τοῖς ἀνυποίκλοις ἔργων ἑκάστοτε ἐν ἀδικήμασί ἐστιν. Ὅταν χρημάτων ἐρᾷ ἀδίκως, ὅτε δόξης, ὅτε ἡδο- νῆς, ὅτε ἄλλου τινός. Et postea: Τῆς γὰρ κακίας ἡ μὲν ἐν σχέσει θεωρεῖται, ἡ δὲ ἐν κινήσει θεωρεῖται. Νεύει γὰρ πρὸς τὰς τῶν ἀποτελεσμάτων ἐκπληρώσεις, ἤ τι τῷ κινεῖσθαι &c. Plotinus citatus Theodoreto libr. VI. contra Graecos: Ὀλίγη κατ᾿ ἀρχὰς τροπὴ γενομένη προϊοῦσα αὐτὴ πλέον καὶ μεῖζον τὸ ἀμαρ- τανόμενον ἀεὶ ποιεῖ, καὶ σῶμα δὲ συνέστηκεν ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἐπιθυμία.

## 1:17
Vers. 17. Μὴ πλανᾶσθε (Do not be deceived) A manner of speaking, where we wish to remove false opinions which have either crept into the minds of some, or could creep in. Thus 1 Cor. VI. 9, XV. 33, Gal. VI. 7, 1 John III. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Μὴ πλανᾶσθε) Mos loquendi, ubi falsas opi- niones, quæ aut irrepsere in quorundam animos, aut ir- repere possent, amoliri volumus. Sic 1. Cor. VI. 9. XV. 33. Gal. VI. 7. 1. Joh. III. 7.

## 1:17
Vers. 17. Πᾶσα δόσις ἀγαθὴ (Every good gift) A truly good bestowing, that is, one which makes us good. Matt. VII. 11. Cicero and Seneca also use 'datum' for the Greek δόσις.

Καὶ πᾶν δώρημα τέλειον (And every perfect gift) that is, which perfects us or leads us to eternal life. Thus we have τελειωθῆναι in Heb. II. 10, X. 40.

Ἄνωθέν ἐστι (is from above) See John III. 31, IX. 11. Thus also below III. 15, 17. Philo on the confusion of tongues: And indeed, since those things which are within us regarding the criterion of sense are mistaken, it is necessary to agree as a consequence that God rains down some things upon the senses, and there are some things of our parts which are grace, but not by that by which we were born. All gifts.

Rightly δόσις and δώρημα are distinguished thus far, that the former denotes the giving and bestowing itself, the latter the effect of the giving. But it is not a giving that makes us good, but a gift that perfects us for eternal life. In general, every good giving and every good work, because ἀγαθὸν and τέλειον are interchanged here and taken exegetically, is ascribed to God, who as He is good in working and bestowing, so also in the work and the gift itself, but is never and nowhere, neither by action nor by any work, evil; the author of all good, but in no way the author of evil. For it can happen that what is given is good, but the donation is not good. Thus the origin of good is referred to God, but not to man: The origin of evil, however, is ascribed to man, and is removed from God. Those who understand δόσις as gifts of nature, and δώρημα as gifts of grace, or the former with Thomas Aquinas as gifts of this life, and the latter as gifts of the other life, do not attain the sense of James. Salmero also touches upon the same less accurately, when he wishes δόσις to be supernatural grace given freely, and δώρημα to be the perfect, gratuitous justification, adoption, and salvation from the beneficence of God; to whom, however, Beza, Lorinus, Cornelius à Lapide, and Estius approach more closely, when they wish these to be spoken exegetically.

Καταβαῖνον ἀπὸ τοῦ Πατρὸς τῶν φώτων (Coming down from the Father of lights) A similar expression to that in Heb. XII. 9, to the Father of spirits. God as the author of spirits or spiritual gifts; so specifically also of those illuminations which are more correctly called אורים than those splendors in the breastplate of the High Priest. Father to the Hebrews is the author of a thing, Gen. IV. 19, 20. To come down is said to be מן שמיא, which comes from God, John I. 33.

Those expressions are different: for the Father of Spirits is a spiritual Father: but this Father of lights is the source and author of light and of the gifts of light. Nor is it established that there is a reference to Urim, as even Heinsius thought. Certainly, God is never called the Father of Urim in the scriptures. The nature of God is rather being referred to, because God is light, and there is no darkness in Him, 1 John 1:6, 7, that is, He is entirely most holy light, and most lucid holiness; and of those things which are from God, that they are not from Him, except those which conform to His holiness and goodness. However, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not called lights, as seemed to Cyril of Jerusalem, Catech. VII, because the name of Father is taken here essentially, not personally, nor are the Son and the Holy Spirit different lights from the Father, but these three are one, 1 John 5:7, that one light 1. John 1:5, although the Son is light from light, that must nevertheless be accepted in such a way that two lights are not thereby constituted, but there is one light, just as God is from God, and yet there is one God according to the Athanasian creed. Lights are viewed here as created, so that the appellation of the lights, with the mention of the Father or author of the lights from whom they descend, may agree with the divine gift and donation, of which James speaks. Whence it appears that it is in vain to inquire among the interpreters whether spiritual or corporeal lights, or both, are to be understood—namely, revelations, as Lorinus, or the sun and stars, as some others—because it is taught that they do not pertain to spiritual illuminations and to these stars, but that whatever is holy, whatever is good, its origin is from God, as He who is supremely good and holy by nature and causality, and by that name is deservedly called the Father of lights. God is no less the author of the darkness which is opposed to corporeal light than of corporeal light, as the scripture testifies, Gen. 1:2, 3, 4, 5; Isa. 45:7. Because the Apostle is discoursing here about sins, which he desires to be removed from God, the lights to be understood are those which are opposed to sins and conveniently serve to dispel them, that is, all those gifts which are in any way suitable for illuminating the mind and bending the will for the better. And so, just as in the Hebrew phrase he is called a Father who is the author and effector of some thing, Gen. 4:20, 21, so God is the Father, the author and effector of lights, because He illuminates all men who come into this world, John 1:9, and gives the eyes of the heart illuminated, Eph. 1:18, and in His light we see light, Ps. 36:10, so that he who follows this light may not walk in darkness, John 8:12, not even fearing the darkness of death and hell itself with this light going before, Ps. 23:4. If, therefore, God is the Father of lights, that is, the effector of any holy, most joyful, and sacred things, those who wish God to be the author of evil temptations, which are dense darkness, certainly depart most dangerously from the truth. For as it is alien to the sun, the source of all light, to pour forth darkness from itself, so it is absurd for God, the sole author of all holiness, to impel anyone to evil, as here the blessed Brochmand.

With whom there is no variation or shadow of turning. All these words are astronomical. For God is compared to the sun, and it is shown that His light is much more perfect than the light of the sun. The sun has variations or parallaxes, as Plato also says in the Timaeus; it is seen differently at sunrise, differently at midday, differently at sunset. Furthermore, it has annual turnings, our departures from it, which we call solstices; the Greeks call them turnings, Avienus translates them as pulses. Because of these departures, it casts other shadows for us, which is to cast a shadow. And for the word shadow, which signifies a shadow, the Syriac and Arabic translators have placed it here. God neither rises, nor sets, nor departs, but is always near to those who call upon Him. He casts the same lights without any mixture of shadow. Malachi 3:6, 'I am the Lord and I have not changed.'

The discourse here is not about the answering of prayers, an explanation which does not easily come to the mind of any of the interpreters. But it is about the immutable divine goodness and holiness, through which there can be no evil in Him, nor from Him. Therefore, that sun of holiness is unlike the sun. For it is a light which does not suffer any defect of light, no change of splendor, a light without variation, admitting no alternation ever, in which there is not only no turning, or the slightest change or conversion of light and darkness, but not even a shadow of turning, any trace. nay, not even any shadow of any change. That the Apostle had regard to those philosophical and mathematical παραλλάξεις (variations) and τροπὰς (turnings) or annual solstices, is hardly credible. The emphasis of the Apostle's words is greater, as we have said.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Πᾶσα δόσις ἀγαθὴ) Largitio vere bona, id est, quæ nos bonos faciat. Matth. VII. 11. Datum pro Græco δόσις etiam Cicero & Seneca usurpant.

Καὶ πᾶν δώρημα τέλειον) id est, quod nos perficiat sive perducat ad vitam æternam. Sic τελειωθῆναι habemus Ebr. II, 10. X. 40.

Ἄνωθέν ἐστι) Vide Joh. III. 31. IX. 11. Sic & infra III. 15. 17. Philo de confusis linguis: Καὶ μὴν σφαλλομένων γε τῶν καθ' ἡμᾶς αὐτοὺς περὶ τὸ τῶν κἀμ αἴσθησιν κριτήριον, ἀνάγκη πα- κόλουθον ὁμολογεῖν, ὅτι ὁ Θεὸς τὰ μὲν τὰς ὁποίας, τῇ δὲ τὰς αἰ- σθήσεως ἐπομβρεῖ, καὶ ἔστιν ὧν τῶν καθ' ἡμᾶς μερῶν χάρις τὰ γι- νόμενα, ἀλλὰ τῷ δὲ ᾗ καὶ ἡμεῖς γεγόναμεν. Δωρεαὶ πᾶσαι.

Recte δόσις, & δώρημα hactenus distinguuntur, quod illa datio & largitio ipsa, hoc vero dationis effectus notetur. Non autem datio est, quæ nos bo- nos faciat, donum, quod nos perficiat ad æternam vitam. In genere omnis bona datio, & omne bo- num opus, quia ἀγαθὸν & τέλειον hic permutantur, & exegeticè accipiuntur, Deo transcribitur, qui ut in operando & largiendo, ita & in opere & dono ipso bonus, nunquam autem & nuspiam neque actione neque opere ullo malus est, autor omnis boni, nullatenus vero autor mali. Fieri enim potest, ut, quod donatur, bonum sit, donatio autem non bona. Sic origo boni ad Deum refertur, non vero ad hominem : Origo autem mali homini transcri- bitur, à Deo vero removetur. Qui δόσιν de donis naturæ, δώρημα de donis gratiæ, vel illam cum Tho- ma Angelico de donis hujus, hoc de donis alterius vitæ intelligunt, Jacobi sensum non assequuntur. Attingit etiam eundem minus Salmero, cum δόσιν vult esse supernaturalem gratiam gratis datam, δώ- ρημα vero perfectum, gratuitam ex Dei beneficentia justificationem, adoptionem, salvationem; ad quem verò propius accedunt Beza, Lorinus, Cornelius à Lapide, Estius, cum ista ἐξηγητικῶς dicta volunt.

Καταβαῖνον ἀπὸ τοῦ Πατρὸς τῶν φώτων) Par locutio cum illa Ebr. XII. 9. τῷ Πατρὶ τῶν πνευμάτων. Deus sicut Spiri- tuum sive spiritualium donorum autor; ita specialiter etiam illarum illuminationum, quæ rectius אורים dicuntur, quam fulgores illi in pectorali summi Sacerdo- tis. Pater Ebræis autor rei, Gen. IV. 19. 20. Καταβαίνειν מן שמיא dicitur, quod à Deo venit, Joh. I. 33.

Diversæ sunt illæ loquutiones: Pater enim Spi- rituum est Pater spiritualis: hic verò Pater lumi- num est fons & autor lucis & donorum lucis. Neque ad Urim respici, quod Heinsio etiam visum, constat. Nunquam certè Deus in scripturis Pater Urim di- citur. Natura potius Dei respicitur, quia Deus lux est, & non sunt in ipso tenebræ, 1. Joh. I. 6. 7. hoc est, totus sanctissima lux est, & lucidissima sanctitas; & eorum, quæ à Deo sunt, quod non sint ab ipso, nisi quæ sanctitati & bonitati ejus congruunt. Non au- tem lumina dicuntur Filius, & Spiritus sanctus, ut Cyrillo Hierosolymitano Catech. VII. visum, quia Pa- tris nomen essentialiter hic sumitur, non verò per- sonaliter, nec Filius & Spiritus S. sunt diversa lu- mina à Patre, sed hi tres unum sunt 1. Job. V. 7. una il- la lux 1. Joh. I. 5. etsi Filius lumen sit de lumine, id ta- men ita accipiendum, ut non duo inde lumina con- stituantur, sed lumen unum sit, quemadmodum & Deus est à Deo, & unus tamen est Deus secundum symbolum Athanasii. Lumina hic spectantur crea- ta, ut δόσις & δωρήματι Divino, de quo Jacobus, conveniat appellatio τῶν Φώτων, mentione Patris, vel autoris luminum, à quo illa descendunt. Unde apparet, frustra disquiri apud Interpretes, an hic spiritualia, an corporalia lumina, an utraque, reve- lationes nempe, ut Lorinus, sol & astra, ut alii non- nulli, intelligantur, quia non ad illuminationes spi- rituales, & ad astra hæc pertinent, sed quicquid est sancti, quicquid boni, ejus originem esse à Deo, do- cetur, utpote qui summe bonus & sanctus natura & causalitate est, eoque nomine Pater luminum meritò appellatur. Deus non minus tenebrarum, quæ lumini corporeo opponuntur, quam luminis cor- porei autor est teste scriptura Gen. I. 2. 3. 4. 5. Es. XLV. 7. De peccatis quia hic disserit Apostolus, quæ à Deo remota cupit, lumina intelligenda sunt, quæ peccatis opponuntur, & illis pellendis commodè serviunt, hoc est, omnia illa dona, quæ menti illustrandæ & volun- tati in melius flectendæ ullo modo accommoda sunt. Veluti itaque is phrasi Ebræa dicitur Pater, qui rei alicujus autor & effector est Gen. IV. 20. 21. Ita Deus Pater autor & effector luminum est, quia omnes, qui in hunc mundum veniunt homines, illuminat Joh. I. 9. & dat illuminatos cordis oculos, Eph. I. 18. & in ejus lumine videmus lumen, Psal. XXXVI, 10. ut, qui hanc sequitur lucem, in tenebris non ambulet, Johan. VIII. 12. ne ipsius quidem mortis & inferni tenebras horrens hac luce prævia Ps. XXIII. 4. Si itaque Deus est Pater luminum, hoc est, quarumvis rerum san- ctarum, lætissimarum & sanctarum effector, à veri- tate certè quam periculosissime recedunt, qui Deum tentationum malarum, quæ densæ sunt tenebræ, vo- lunt autorem esse. Quam enim alienum est à sole, omnis lucis fonte, tenebras de se fundere: tam abso- num est, Deum, sanctitatis omnis unicum autorem, ad mala quemquam impellere, ut hic B. Broch- mand.

Παρ᾿ ᾧ ὑκ ἔνι παραλλαγὴ ἢ τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα) Omnes hæ voces sunt astronomicæ. Nam Deus soli compara- tur, ostenditurque multo ejus lux solis perfectior. Sol παραλλαγὰς sive παραλλάξεις habet, ut & Plato dicit in Timæo, aliter conspicitur in ortu, aliter in meridie, ali- ter in occasu. Præterea habet τροπὰς annuos à nobis ab- scessus, quos solstitia dicimus, Græci τροπὰς Avienus vertit pulsus. Pro iis abscessibus alias nobis umbras jacit, quod est ἀποσκιάζειν. Et pro ἀποσκίασμα vocem, quæ um- bram significat, posuere hic Syrus & Arabs. Deus nec ori- tur, nec occidit, nec abscedit, sed semper propinquus est se invocantibus. Easdem luces jacit sine umbræ mixtura. Malachiæ III, 6. Ἐγὼ Κύριος & ὐκ ἠλλοίωμαι.

Non de precum exauditione sermo hic est, quæ ex- plicatio nulli Interpretum in mentem facile venit. Sed de incommutabili Divina bonitate ac sanctitate, per quam nec in ipso, nec ab ipso esse potest malum. Dissimilis ergo soli est sol ille sanctitatis. Lux enim est, quæ non patitur ullum luminis defectum, nullam splendoris immutationem, lux ἀπαράλ- λακτος, nullam unquam alternationem admit- tens, in qua non modo nulla est τροπὴ, vel minima mutatio aut conversio lucis & tenebrarum, sed ne quidem ἀποσκίασμα τροπῆς, ullum vestigium, imò nec ulla adumbratio mutationis ullius. Ad Philofophica illa & Mathematica παραλλάξεις & τροπὰς annuas vel folstitia Apostolum respexisse, vix credibile est. Major emphasis est verborum Apostoli, uti diximus.

## 1:18
Vers. 18. Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth) God is said of old to have begotten the Israelites, when he delivered them from Egypt, Deut. XXXII. 18. But now he has begotten them much more excellently unto eternal life through the Gospel, 1 Pet. I. 23. and that for the reason that he willed it, being moved to it by no works of ours, Eph. I. 4, 5. בחפצו.

Most connect these things thus with the preceding, because by a singular example of regeneration it is taught that every good work is from the Father of lights, but the Apostle proceeds in his principal design, and renders a new reason for his thesis, that God is so far from being the cause of sin, or that evil is from God, that he therefore regenerates us, that we may be delivered from evil, and renewed unto true holiness and righteousness: the Apostle gravely warns that we should not despise this counsel of God, nor indulge in depraved desire, but admit the word of truth as the medium of regeneration and renovation. Therefore, by the word βουληθεὶς (having willed), the cause is noted by which God is impelled to our regeneration, namely, the benefits and the gracious will of God, Eph. I. 9, Phil. II. 13, 2 Tim. I. 9, 1 Pet. I. 3. Which regeneration is not to be restricted to the Hebrews under the New Testament: for thus the ancient believers would be excluded not only from the benefit of divine regeneration, but also from the title of children of God, and consequently also from the right of heavenly inheritance. Nor indeed are the Israelites said to be begotten in Deut. XXXII. 18 because they were delivered from Egypt, but because God willed to regenerate them through His Word, and to adopt them as sons, and into a Royal priesthood. That Socinian error of Grotius has been refuted elsewhere. Oecumenius understands creation in this place, but that is not attributed to the Word of Truth, that is, the Gospel, which is so called in Eph. I. 13, Col. I. 5, because the righteousness which it promises, it also truly confers: Therefore most others more correctly explain it as spiritual regeneration, which is effected both by the uncreated Word, 1 Pet. I. 19, and by Baptism, the visible word, Eph. V. 23, 1 John III. 5.

That we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures) ראשית דרכו. Understand κτισμάτων (creatures) as καινῶν (new) or νέων (new), which is not always expressed, but is understood from the nature of the thing, as Eph. II. 10, III. 9. Those are called ἀπαρχαὶ (firstfruits) who were called before others, Rom. XVI. 5, 1 Cor. XVI. 15. Therefore that name is attributed to the Jews, Rom. XI. 16, who are also called προηλπικότες (those who first hoped), Eph. I. 12, chosen ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς (from the beginning), 2 Thess. II. 13.

Not only Hebrews are designated by that title here, nor can that be proved from Eph. I. 12, 2 Thess. II. 13, concerning which places see in their proper seat, but it is common to all the reborn, and especially the elect, Jer. II. 13, Apoc. XIV. 4, designating their excellent and singular dignity, just as the ἀπαρχὴ (firstfruits) was more worthy, and was peculiarly consecrated to God. For they are separated from the world and consecrated to God, John XV. 19, 1 Pet. II. 9. If only the Jews were the firstfruits, the Apostle's argument would be diminished, whose scope is to teach that God solicits no one to evil, as one who wills all to be regenerated for this reason, that they may be consecrated to Him, and not remain polluted by sin, such as they are by nature, Ps. LI. 7, John III. 6. All the causes of regeneration indeed absolve God from sin, as they are delivered here by the Apostle. The principal cause is the Father of lights, the fountain and origin of all good, of all holiness, in whom, and from whom, there can be no darkness of sins. The internal impulsive cause is the gracious will of God, which does not will that we remain in sin and perish, but that we be converted to repentance and be saved, Ezek. XVIII, 1 Pet. II. 4. Who then would be the cause of evil? The efficient medium cause is the Word, which is the good Word of God, Heb. VI. 5.

by which we are sanctified, John XVII. 17. The material cause is man, who is corrupted by depraved concupiscence, which is in us by nature after the fall, as an evil adhering to us, sin dwelling in us, the law of our members, Rom. VII, from which God frees us through the grace of regeneration. Therefore, that which belongs to nature, which is turned away from God, can in no way be imputed to God. The formal cause consists in this, that God bestows upon man, who is dead in sins by his own fault, the strength to rise from spiritual death and the life of faith. He who does this, how can he be considered the cause of sin? The end is that we may be the firstfruits of his creatures, a new creature in Christ, 2 Cor. V. 17. Gal. VI. 15. 17. κτίσμα created in Christ, Eph. II. 10. created according to God, Eph. IV. 24. according to the image of God, Col. III. 10. and that we be consecrated to God, just as the firstfruits were consecrated to God, Lev. XXIII. 4. Num. XV. 20. 21. Deut. XXVI. 3. seqq. All of which teach that God is neither physically nor morally the cause of sin.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Βουληθεὶς ἀπεκύησεν ἡμᾶς λόγῳ ἀληθείας) Deus olim Israëlitas genuisse dicitur, cum eos ex Ægypto libe- ravit, Deut. XXXII. 18. At nunc multo excellentius eos genuit ad vitam æternam per Evangelium, 1. Petr. I. 23. idque ideo quia voluit, nullis nostris operibus ad id excita- tus Eph. I. 4. 5. בחפצו.

Connectunt hæc ita plerique præcedentibus, quod singulari regenerationis exemplo doceatur à Patre luminum omne opus bonum esse, sed pergi in suo principe instituto, novamque reddit ratio- nem theseos suæ Apostolus, Deum tantum abesse, ut causa peccati sit, vel ut à Deo malum sit, qt ideò nos regeneret, ut à malo liberemur, ac ad veram sanctitatem & justitiam renovemur: quod consi- lium Dei ne aspernemur, nec cupiditati pravæ in- dulgeamus, sed verbum veritatis, ceu medium rege- nerationis & renovationis admittamus, graviter monet Apostolus. Voce ergo βουληθεὶς causa nota- tur, qua Deus impellitur ad nostri regenerationem, beneficia nempe & gratiosa Dei voluntas, Eph. I. 9. Phil. II. 13. 2. Tim. I. 9. 1. Petr. I. 3. Quæ regeneratio non restringenda ad Hebræos sub Novo Testamento: Nam ita excluderentur antiqui fideles non à rege- nerationis tantum divinæ beneficio, sed etiam à fi- liorum Dei titulo, adeoque etiam ab hæreditatis cælestis jure. Neque verò Deut. XXXII. 18. geniti Israëlitæ dicuntur, quod ex Ægypto liberati, sed quod Deus per Verbum suum ipsos regenerare voluerit, & in filios adoptare, inque Regale sacerdo- tium. Error ille Grotii Socinianus alias profligatus est. Oecumenius hoc loco creationem intelligit, sed ea non tribuitur Verbo Veritatis, hoc est, Evangelio, quod ita vocatur Eph. I. 13. Col. I. 5. quia quam pro- mittit justitiam, eam etiam revera confert: Ideo de spirituali regeneratione plerique alii rectius expli- cant, quæ & per Verbum ἄκτιστον fit, 1. Petr. I. 19. & per Baptismum, verbum ὁρατὸν Eph. V. 23. 1. Joh. III. 5.

Εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἡμᾶς ἀπαρχήν τινα τῶν αὐτοῦ κτισμάτων) ראשית דרכו. Κτισμάτων intellige καινῶν sive νέων quod non semper exprimitur, sed ex rei natura intelligitur, ut Eph. II. 10. III. 9. Ἀπαρχαὶ dicuntur qui ante alios voca- ti sunt, Rom. XVI. 5. 1. Cor. XVI. 15. Ideo Judæis id no- men tribuitur, Rom. XI. 16. qui etiam dicuntur προηλπι- κότες, Eph. I. 12. electi ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς 2. Thess. II. 13.

Non Ebræi tantum illo titulo hic designantur, nec id ex Eph. I. 12. 2. Thess. II. 13. probari potest, de quibus locis vid. in propria sede, sed communis est omnibus renatis, & imprimis electis Jer. II. 13. Apoc. XIV. 4. designans ipsorum dignitatem eximiam & singularem, quemadmodum ἀπαρχὴ dignior erat, & peculiariter Deo consecrabatur. Sunt enim à mundo separati & consecrati Deo, Johan. XV. 19. 1. Petr. II. 9. Si soli Judæi essent primitiæ, imminueretur argumentum Apostoli, cujus sco- pus est, docere, neminem Deum ad malum solicita- re, utpote qui ideo omnes velit regenitos, ut sibi consecrentur, nec maneant polluti peccato, quales per naturam sunt, Psal. LI. 7. Joh. III. 6. Omnes uti- que regenerationis causæ Deum à peccato absol- vunt, prout hic ab Apostolo traditæ. Causa prin- ceps est Pater luminum fons & origo omnis boni, omnis sanctitatis, in quo, & è quo nullæ peccato- rum tenebræ esse possunt. Causa impulsiva interna est Dei gratiosa voluntas, quæ non vult in pec- cato nos manere & perire, sed ad pœnitentiam converti & salvari, Ezech. XIIX. 1. Petr. II. 4. Qui ergo causa mali esset? Causa efficiens media est Verbum, quod bonum Dei Verbum est, Ebr. VI. 5.

per quod sanctificamur, Joh. XVII. 17. Materialis causa homo est, qua concupiscentia prava corru- ptus, quæ post lapsum natura nobis inest, ceu ma- lum nobis adjacens, peccatum in nobis habitans, lex membrorum nostrorum, Rom. VII, à qua per gra- tiam regenerationis liberat nos Deus. Quod ergo naturæ est à Deo aversæ, id Deo imputari nullo modo potest. Formalis causa in eo sita est, quod Deus homini in peccatis culpa sua mortuo vires surgendi è morte spirituali & vitam fidei largitur. Qui id agit, quomodo peccati causa haberi potest? Finis est, ut simus primitiæ creaturæ ejus, nova crea- tura in Christo, 2. Cor. V. 17. Gal. VI. 15. 17. κτίσμα conditum in Christo, Eph. II. 10. conditum secun- dum Deum, Eph. IV. 24. secundum imaginem Dei, Col. III. 10. & Deo consecremur, veluti primitiæ Deo consecratæ erant, Lev. XXIII. 4. Num. XV. 20. 21. Deut. XXVI. 3. seqq. Quæ omnia docent, Deum nec physice, nec moraliter causam peccati esse.

## 1:19
Ἀδελφοί μου ἀγαπητοὶ (My beloved brethren) A kind address, such as also 1 Cor. XV. 59, Eph. VI. 21, Col. IV. 9, 14, Philem. 16. Thus also below 19 and II. 5. He means this: Do not think your zeal suffices without prayers, as not a few Jews imagine. There is need of prayers, and indeed of unwearied ones. See Luke XVIII. 1. Ἀγαπητοὶ the Syriac translates חביבי, which in that language is a very endearing term.

He is no longer dealing with prayers, which he says the Jews believed were not necessary, he does not teach Grotius: But he continues the subject begun. He dissuades from that impious error, and more fully refutes the same, both because God is the Author of every good, and indeed of good alone, as the Father of lights, in whom there is no evil, from whom none can arise, because that work is of darkness, which has no place in Him, in whom there is no vicissitude of light and darkness, and also because He regenerates us for this reason, that being freed from sin we may strive for holiness. How then could He be considered the author of sin in us? This continuation is plain and open.

Latin:

Ἀδελφοί μου ἀγαπητοὶ) Benigna alloquutio, qualis & 1. Cor. XV. 59. Eph. VI. 21. Col. IV. 9. 14. Philem. 16. Sic & infra 19. & II. 5. Hoc vult: Ne putate vestrum studium sufficere fine precibus, ut Judæi non pauci existimant. Precibus opus est, & quidem indefeffis. Vide Luc. XVIII. 1. Ἀγαπητοὶ Syrus vertit חביבי, quod illa lingua blan- dum admodum vocabulum est.

Non jam de precibus agit, quibus opus non esse Judæos credidisse, dicit, non docet Grotius: Sed ma- teriam cœptam pertexit. Dehortatur ab errore illo impio, eundemque uberius profligat, tum quia Deus Autor omnis boni est, & quidem solius bo- ni, ut Pater luminum, in quo esse malum nullum, à quo nullum oriri potest, quia opus illud tenebra- rum est, quæ in eo locum non habent, in quo non est vicissitudo lucis & tenebrarum, tum quia ideo nos regenerat, ut à peccato liberati sanctitati stu- deamus. Quomodo ergo autor peccati in nobis censeri posset? Hæc συνέχεια plana est & aperta.

## 1:19
Vers. 19. Wherefore, my beloved brethren) Since the adversities which are sent upon us tend toward this, that we may become better, as was said above in 4, and furthermore God has deemed us worthy of such a great calling, as has just been said. For ὥστε the Manuscript has ἴστε and the Latin reads thus.

Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak) Therefore philosophers say that we have been given two ears, one tongue, and ears that are open, but a tongue walled in by the fence of the teeth. But there are many to whom that Sophoclean saying can be applied: 'To speak with counsel, and even if one says nothing, it is better.' See Prov. X. 19. and XIII. 3. and XVII. 28.

Slow to wrath) ארך רוח or ארך אפים.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Ὥστε ἀδελφοί μου ἀγαπητοὶ) Cum in id tendant adversa, quæ nobis immittuntur, ut fiamus meliores, ut dictum supra 4. ac præterea Deus nos tanta vocatione di- gnatus sit, ut jamjam dictum. Pro ὥστε Manuscriptus habet ἴστε & sic legit Latinus.

Ἔστω πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ταχὺς εἰς τὸ ἀκοῦσαι, βραδὺς εἰς τὸ λα- λῆσαι) Ideo Philosophi ajunt nobis datas aures duas: lin- guam unam, & aures patulas, linguam septo dentium obval- latam. At multi sunt, quibus dici potest Sophocleum illud: Βουλῇ λέγειν τι, κᾀν λέγειν μηδὲν πλέον· Vide Prov. X. 19. & XIII. 3. & XVII. 28.

Βραδὺς εἰς ὀργὴν) ארך רוח vel ארך אפים.

## 1:20
Vers. 20. For the wrath of man worketh the righteousness of God) If anyone becomes accustomed to being angry quickly and often, he will not attain the righteousness of God (that is, the internal righteousness which God requires), or if he has attained it, he will lose it. Concerning that righteousness of God or internal righteousness, see Matt. V. 20. Rom. III. 21. 22. X. 3. 2 Cor. V. 21.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Ὀργὴ γὰρ ἀνδρὸς δικαιοσύνην Θεῦ κατεργάζε- ται) Si quis cito & sæpe irasci affuescat, is justitiam Dei, (id est, internam, quam Deus requirit) non adipiscetur, aut si adeptus est, amittet. De justitia illa Dei sive interna vide Matth. V. 20. Rom. III. 21. 22. X. 3. 2. Cor. V. 21.

## 1:21
Vers. 21. Wherefore) refer this also to those things to which those things above in 19 refer.

Laying aside all filthiness) ῥύπος and ῥυπαρία signify filth, as the Glossary interprets. And it is usually said of bodily filth, 1 Pet. III. 21. Thence it is transferred to the soul: and it signifies everything by which the soul is defiled, as can be seen in Is. IV. 4. and Job XIV. 4. צוא is translated as ῥύπος. The Syriac here has שומהא from the Syriac verb סנא, which means to defile, and is also found in Cant. V. 4.

And superfluity of naughtiness) He seems to have wished to express the force of the Hebrew word ערלה, which properly signifies foreskin, but is transferred to all those things which, as useless, ought to be rejected. In the Manuscript there is περίσσευμα.

In meekness receive) In meekness here means with a teachable mind, in which way πραότης seems to be taken also in Ps. XLV. 5.

The engrafted word) That word which, through the work of the Apostles, is inserted into your souls. What the Latins call grafting, Theophrastus and other Greeks call ἐμφυτείας. In the Glossary, ἔμφυτον is 'engrafted'. See Matt. XIII. 3. and what is said there, and 1 Cor. III. 6. The Syriac here has רכיצב, that is, well planted.

Which is able to save your souls) For the Gospel is the power of God unto salvation, Rom. I. 16.

The Apostle discourses not about the end of afflictions, but about regeneration, intended by divine kindness so that we might be freed from sins, while absolving God from all causality of sin. Since this happens through the word of truth, the Apostle instructs us as to how we ought to conduct ourselves, lest the βουλὴ, and counsel of God be made void in us, whom our own concupiscence continually solicits to sin. For a new exhortation is not being instituted here, which Cornelius à Lapide maintains, but the Apostle continues the doctrine concerning regeneration, which he had begun, for the sake of refuting blasphemy against God, which Justinianus and Estius also, along with Pareus, acknowledge. Both the Apostolic συνέχεια and the word ὥστε favor this opinion. Moreover, those things pertain to the reborn, to which effort must be devoted, so that, not being ensnared by depraved desires, they may not fall from the grace of regeneration, but be preserved in it unto salvation. He requires, moreover, 1. a readiness to hear the word of God, that we may be quick εἰς τὸ ἀκοῦσαι: What? but τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας, by which them he had called them reborn. He who is of God hears the word of God, John VIII.47. As we are regenerated through the word of truth: So by its power we are also preserved unto salvation, Rom. I, 16. 1 Tim. IV. 16. 1. The avoidance of rash judgment concerning divine matters. Let one be slow to speak, namely, concerning the word of truth. For every thought must be taken captive (every height that is raised up against the knowledge of God) unto the obedience of Christ, 2 Cor. X, 4.

3. The bridling of anger also, when we are corrected by our own desires: That every concupiscence, thus especially the irascible, which is most common and is brought forward by way of example, must be restrained: Even if we are corrected or chastised, we must not murmur or kick against the goad. But as anger is to be restrained and bridled at all times, so it is especially then, cf. Ps. CXLI, 5, inasmuch as it easily precipitates us into grave sins, if the anger be illicit. See 1 Sam. XXV. 13. Luke IX. 54, 55. For it does not work the righteousness of God, that is, that which is just before God. The discourse here is not about the righteousness of evangelical faith, but about righteousness according to the law of God. For although that righteousness is consequently lost when those things which are opposed to the law are committed: yet that righteousness is not immediately understood here, because the subject is not justification, but renewal. 4. The putting away of all filthiness. Now therefore in general he commands that we strive to put away everything by which the mind is defiled, and all the abundance of malice as a heavy burden, Ps. XXXVIII. 5, which presses by night and by day. By filthiness is meant not only the vices of the flesh, which the Papists call so, as Salmero wishes, nor only avarice and a sordid mind, which was the view of Cornelius, but any sins whatsoever, inasmuch as they arise from an impure Spirit, Luke XI. 24, defile the heart, 2 Pet. II. 22, are fostered in an impure heart, and bring in the stench of the eternal prison, Is. LXVI. 24. By the abundance of malice, some wish a certain excess of malice to be noted, and under it they also comprehend the remnants of sin. To put these away, we must devote every effort. However, in the explanation of the phrase, we judge that one should not depart from Grotius, unless perhaps the Glassian view is to be preferred, that the abundance of malice is by Hebraism an abundant malice, and one that corrupts a man abundantly, with all the powers of soul and body, just as the sin which easily besets is said in the same sense, Heb. XII. 1.

5. The meek reception of the divine word. The word of God is called the implanted word, not because it is a native, ingenuous speech, unadulterated by any paint—which sense Heinsius indeed brings forward, but proves by no example—but as Grotius rightly says, because it has been implanted through the work of the Apostles. Blessed Brochmand indeed prefers, with Oecumenius, Vatablus, and Heinsius, to explain it as innate rather than implanted: But how it can be called innate, I confess I cannot perceive, and therefore we acquiesce in the common interpretation approved by Beza, Piscator, Pareus, the Belgian Interpreters, Lorinus, Cornelius à Lapide, Estius, and others. The Heinsian distinction, that the implanted word is one thing and the word that is implanted is another, the former being that which is born in, the latter that which is implanted, is more subtle than solid. The explanation of Blessed Glassius, part III, Exeg. Evang. & Epist. page 146, is more fitting. A shoot applied externally to a tree does not bear much fruit, but when it is intimately implanted in it and rendered one with it: Thus the word of God brings the fruit of eternal salvation to a man, not if it remains externally, but if it is as it were implanted and inserted into the heart and becomes one with it. If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, you will bear fruit, etc., says Christ, John XV. 5, 7, 8, while he speaks of the spiritual grafting of the branches of believers into himself, as the true heavenly vine. But the gloss of Oecumenius, that the reason by which we discern good from evil is the innate word, is clearly alien.

For is regeneration, or salvation, brought about through reason? And what is it to receive the word with meekness? Ἐν πραότητι, it is not only with a teachable mind, but primarily with a meek one. Rightly B. Brochmand. The doctrine concerning Christ is hostile both to the mind and to the will. It is indeed hostile to the mind, because to the natural man (ψυχικῷ) it is mere foolishness, 1 Cor. II. 14. Moreover, this doctrine is opposed to the will and the affections, because it prescribes things that are harsh and difficult and burdensome to the flesh, such as to hate parents, brothers, sisters, to leave all things, to hate one's own soul, Matt. X. 37, 38, 39. Wherefore there is need of meekness, so that you neither recoil from this doctrine because it is opposed to blind reason, John VI. 60, 66, nor admit it unwillingly, because its bitterness is burdensome to the ulcerous nature and malignant flesh, Matt. V. 13. The Apostle emphatically expresses the power of the word of truth when he says, 'who is able to save our souls,' by which act the efficacy of saving us is attributed to the word primarily, as if intrinsic to it, Rom. I. 6, and it is implied that it exerts itself in the same way by a secondary act, when that word is implanted in us through the ministry of the word, and is received by us with meekness. For it is the word of salvation, Acts XIII. 26, Eph. I. 13. The word of life, Phil. II. 16. Spirit and life, John VI. 63, through which we are saved, 1 Tim. IV. 16. Although the whole man, both soul and body, is to be saved, yet mention is made particularly of the soul, which is the primary recipient of sin and of depraved concupiscence, as well as of regeneration and renewal, and which is properly restored here through the ministry of the word, with the restoration of the bodies, which remain here in their natural state, being deferred to the universal day of judgment, Rom. VIII. 11, 23, Phil. III. 21. And thus St. James instructed the reborn man: 1. His ears, that he be quick to hear, not about filthy and rotten things, Is. XXXIII. 15, but about divine things, what is pious, what is true, what is honest, what is just, etc., Phil. IV. 8, to hear the word of truth. 2. His tongue, that he be slow to speak, Prov. XVII. 27, Ps. XXXIX. 2. 3. His heart and affection, that he be slow to wrath, Eccl. VII. 9, 10, Col. III. 8. 4. His spirit: That he may more and more put off the foreskin of the flesh, and be renewed according to the Spirit, v. 21, 1 Pet. 2, 15. 5. His whole life, that nothing be more of a care and concern to him than the implanted word, which he may not only hear with pleasure, but also fulfill with all readiness. What is added concerning the salvation of the soul is to be referred to the implanted word, when it is received with true faith. For to that alone is the salvation of the soul attributed; not to the putting away of malice, although this is joined with the faithful reception of the word in the reborn.

Latin:

Vers. 21. Διὸ) hoc quoque refer ad ea, ad quæ referunt illa supra 19.

Ἀποθέμενοι πᾶσαν ῥυπαρίαν) ῥύπος & ῥυπαρία sordes significat, interpretante Glossario. Et solet de corporis sordibus dici 1. Petr. III. 21. Inde ad animum transfertur: significatque omne id, quo inquinatur animus, ut videre est Es. IV. 4. & Job. XIV. 4. צוא vertitur ῥύπος. Syrus hic habet שומהא à verbo סנא Syriaco, quod inqui- nare significat, & reperitur etiam Cant. V. 4.

Καὶ περισσείαν κακίας) Videtur exprimere voluisse vivo vocis Ebrææ ערלה quæ proprie præputium significat, sed transfertur ad omnia ea, quæ ut inutilia rejici debent. In Manuscripto est περίσσευμα.

Ἐν πραότητι δέξασθε) Ἐν πραότητι hic est animo docili, quomodo πραότης sumi videtur & Ps. XLV. 5.

Τὸν ἔμφυτον λόγον) Verbum illud, quod Apostolorum ope- ra vestris animis inseritur. Quod Latini insitionem vocant, id Theophrastus Græcique alii ἐμφυτείας. In Glossario ἔμφυτον insitum. Vide Matth. XIII. 3. & ibi dicta, & 1. Cor. III. 6. Syrus hic רכיצב, id est, plantatum bene.

Τὸν δυνάμενον σῶσαι τὰς ψυχὰς ὑμῶν) Est enim Evange- lium potentia Dei ad salutem Rom. I. 16.

Non de fine afflictionum, sed de regeneratio- ne, divina benignitate, intenta, ut à peccatis li- beremur, Deum absolvente ab omni peccati cau- salitate, disserit Apostolus. Quæ cum per ver- bum veritatis fiat, ne in nobis βουλὴ, & consilium Dei irritetur, quos concupiscentia propria subinde ad peccatum solicitat, quales nos gerere debea- mus, instruit Apostolus. Non enim novam hic adhortationem institui, quod Cornelius à Lapide vult, sed doctrinam de regeneratione, quam cœ- perat, profligandæ blasphemiæ in Deum causa, Apostolus continuat, quod Justinianus etiam & Estius cum Pareo agnoscunt. Cui sententiæ tum συνέχεια Apostolica, tum verbum ὥστε favet. Ad renatos autem ea pertinent, quibus opera danda, ut ne cupiditatibus pravis inescati rege- nerationis gratia excidant, sed in ea conserven- tur ad salutem. Requirit autem 1. audiendi verbi Dei promptitudinem, ut celeres simus εἰς τὸ ἀκοῦ- σαι: Quid? nisi τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας, quo eos regenitos dixerat. Qui ex Deo est, verbum Dei au- dit, Joh.VIII.47. Uti per verbum veritatis regene- ramur: Ita ejusdem virtute etiam ad salutem con- servamur, Rom.I,16. 1.Tim.IV.16. 2. Temerarii de re- bus divinis judicii vitationem. Βραδὺς sit εἰς τὸ λαλῆ- σαι de λόγῳ scilicet ἀληθείας. Nam captivandum πᾶν νόημα, (πᾶν ὕψωμα ἐπαιρόμενον κατὰ τῆς γνώ- σεως Θεõ) εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τẽ Χριστẽ, 2. Cor. X, 4.

3. Iræ etiam, cum corripimur ἀπ' ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας, refrenationem: Ut omnis concupiscentia sic impri- mis irascibilis, quæ maxime communis est, & exem- pli loco adducitur, compescenda est: Etiamsi cor- ripiamur, vel castigemur, non obmurmurandum, vel contra stimulum calcitrandum. Sed uti perpe- tuo, ita tum imprimis etiam ira est refrænanda & compescenda, conf. Psal. CXLI, 5. utpote quæ in gravia peccata facile, si ira sit illicita, nos præcipi- tat. Vid. 1.Sam. XXV.13. Luc. IX.54.55. Non enim operatur justitiam Dei, hoc est, id, quod coram Deo justum est. Non hic de justitia fidei Evangelica, sed de justitia secundum legem Dei sermo est.
