Etsi enim illa justitia consequenter amittatur, cum ea, quæ legi adversantur, designantur: non tamen imme- diatè illa justitia hic intelligitur, quia non de justi- ficatione, sed renovatione agitur. 4. Omnis immun- ditiæ depositionem. Jam ergo in genere jubet, omne id, quo inquinatur animus, deponere studeamus, omnemque malitiæ abundantiam ceu onus grave, Psal. XXXVIII. 5. quod noctu diuque urget. Per immunditiam non tantum vitia carnis, quæ Pontifi- cii vocant, ut Salmero vult, neque avaritia solum & animus sordidus, quod visum Cornelio, sed peccata quævis, utpote quæ ab impuro Spiritu oriuntur, Luc. XI. 24. cor inquinant, 2. Petr. II. 22. in corde impuro foventur, & fœtorem æterni carceris in- ducunt Es. LXVI. 24. Per περισσείαν κακίας ni- mium quiddam malitiæ notari quidam volunt, & sub illa etiam reliquias peccati comprehendunt. Quos ut deponamus, omnino opera danda. In phraseos autem explicatione Grotio non abuen- dum censemus, nisi forte præferenda Glassiana, quod περισσεία κακίας per Ebraismum sit malitia abundans, & hominem abunde corrumpens, cum omnibus animæ & corporis viribus, uti εὐπερίστα- τος ἁμαρτία eodem sensu dicitur Ebr. XII. 1.

5. Mansuetam verbi divini susceptionem. Verbum Dei λόγος ἔμφυτος dicitur, non quod sermo na- tivus, ingenuus, nullo fuco adulteratus sit, quem sen- sum adfert quidem Heinsius, nullo autem exemplo probat, sed ut recte Grotius, quod Apostolorum ope- ra insitus sit. Mavult quidem B. Brochmand. cum Oecumenio, Vatablo, & Heinsio explicare innatum, quam implantatum: Sed quomodo innatus dici possit, fateor, me percipere non posse, ideoq; com- muni interpretationi, Bezæ, Piscatori, Pareo, Inter- pretibus Belgicis, Lorino, Cornelio à Lapide, Estio aliisque probatæ acquiescimus. Heinsiana distin- ctio, quod aliud sit ὁ ἔμφυτος, aliud ὁ ἐμφυτευθεὶς λόγος, ille qui innascitur, hic verò qui implanta- tur, subtilior est, quam solidior. Magis convenit B. Glassii explicatio part. III. Exeg. Evang. & Epist. pag. 146. Surculus exterius arbori admotus tantum fructum non fert, sed eidem intime insitus, & unum cum ea redditus: Sic verbum Dei fructum salutis æternæ homini affert, non si exterius maneat, sed si cordi quasi implantetur, inseratur, & unum cum eo fiat. Si manseritis in me, & verba mea in vobis man- serint, fructum feretis &c. inquit Christus Joh. XV. 5. 7. 8. dum de spirituali institione palmitum creden- tium in seipso, ut vera vite cælesti, loquitur. Oecu- menii verò glossa, quod ratio, qua bonum à malo discernimus, verbum innatum sit, plane aliena est.

Num enim per rationem fit regeneratio, aut falva- tio? Et quid est rationem cum mansuetudine sufci- pere? Ἐν πραότητι, non est tantum animo docili, sed imprimis mansueto. Recte B. Brochmand. Inimica est doctrina de Christo tum menti, tum voluntati. Menti quidem est inimica, quia homini ψυχικῷ mera stultitia est 1. Cor. II. 14. Voluntati autem & affectibus adversatur haec doctrina, quia ea praescribit, quae car- ni dura & difficilia & molesta praestitu sunt, qualia sunt, odisse parentes, fratres, sorores, relinquere omnia, odisse suammet animam, Matth. X. 37. 38. 39. Quo- circa mansuetudine opus est, ita ut nec resilias ab hac doctrina, quia caeca rationi adversatur, Joh. VI. 60. 66. nec eam illibenter admittas, quia atrimonia sua ulcerosa natura & maligna carni molesta est, Matth. V. 13. Virtutem autem λόγυ τῆς ἀληθείας emphaticè exprimit Apostolus, cum dicit τὸν δυνάμενον σῶσαι τὰς ψυχὰς ἡμῶν, quo actu primo verbo efficacia tribuitur nos salvandi, ceu ipsi intrinseca, Rom. I. 6. & actu secundo eandem sese exerere innuitur, cum λόγῳ ille nobis per verbi ministerium implanta- tur, & à nobis cum mansuetudine recipitur. Est enim verbum salutis, Act. XIII. 26. Eph. I. 13. Verbum vi- ta, Phil. II. 16. Spiritus & vita, Joh. VI. 63. per quod salvamur, 1. Tim. IV. 16. Quanquam verò totus ho- mo, & anima & corpore salvandus sit, anima tamen peculiaris sit mentio, quae πρῶτον δεκτικὸν est pec- cati, & prava concupiscentiae, nec non regeneratio- nis, & renovationis, quaeque hic propriè restituitur per verbi ministerium, corporum restitutione, quae hic manent in statu suo naturali, in universalem ju- dicii diem dilata, Rom. VIII. 11. 23. Phil. III. 21. Atque ita informavit S. Jacobus hominis renati 1. Aures, ut velox sit ad audiendum, non de rebus spurcis & putridis, Es. XXXIII. 15. sed de rebus divinis, quae pia, quae vera, quae honesta, quae justa &c. Phil. IV. 8. ad audiendum verbum veritatis. 2. Linguam, ut tardus sit ad loquendum, Prov. XVII. 27. Psal. XXXIX. 2. 3. Cor & affectum, tardus sit ad iram, Eccl. VII. 9. 10. Col. III. 8. 4. Spiritum: Ut magis ma- gisque deponat carnis praeputium, & renovetur se- cundum Spiritum v. 21. 1. Petr. 2, 15. 5. Vitam uni- versam, ut nihil magis ipsi curae sit cordique, quam verbum ἔμφυτον, quod neque audiat tantum cum voluptate, sed impleat etiam cum omni prompti- tudine. Quod additur de salute animae, ad λόγον ἔμφυτον, cum vera fide suscipitur, referendum. Illi enim unice tribuitur salus animae; non deposi- tioni malitiae, etsi haec cum susceptione verbi fideli conjuncta sit, in renatis.

## 1:22
Ver. 22. But be doers of the word and not hearers only) A similar admonition to that which is in Matt. VII. 21, 24, 26, where see the remarks. The Rabbis say there are two crowns, one of hearing, the other of doing. See Exod. XIX. 15. And the Hebrews say of the pious man, he learns so that he may do.

Deceiving yourselves) Those who hope that they can be saved by merely hearing the word of God and professing themselves to be Christians without pious deeds, deceive themselves. We have παραλογίζεσθαι for πλανᾷν also in Col. 2, 4, Judg. 13, 16, Gen. 29, 25, and elsewhere. Thus we deceive ourselves, 1 John 1, 8.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Γίνεσθε δὲ ποιηταὶ λόγυ καὶ μὴ μόνον ἀκροαταὶ) Par admonitio ei, quae est apud Matth. VII. 21. 24. 26. ubi dicta vide. Rabbini dicunt, duas esse coronas, alteram שמיעה auditionis, alteram מעשה operis. Vide Exod. XIX. 15. Et Ebraei de pio, discit ut faciat.

Παραλογιζόμενοι ἑαυτοὺς) Qui tantum audiendo ver- bum Dei & profitendo Christianos se esse sine factis piis servari se posse sperant, semet fallunt. Παραλογίζεσθαι pro πλανᾷν habemus & Col. 2, 4. Judic. 13, 16. Gen. 29, 25. & alibi. Sic ἑαυτὺς πλανῶμεν, 1. Joh. 1, 8.

## 1:23
Ver. 23. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man observing the face of his birth in a mirror) ὅτι is missing in the Manuscript, as also in the Syriac. Ἔοικε is similar to the Syriac דמי. Κατανοῶν here is to behold. It corresponds to the Hebrew נבט and ראה and the Syriac חזא. Thus also Matt. 7, 3, Luke 6, 43, Acts 7, 31, 32, 11, 6, 27, 37. Γένεσις indeed here and below 3, 6, as also in Wisd. 1, 14 and 14, 27, signifies that which is natural to someone, the face of his birth. Proclus said the archetype. It is the same as if he were seeing his own face: because that which is in the mirror corresponds to it exactly. Thus we say: -- I recently saw myself on the shore.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Ὄτι εἴτις ἀκροατὴς τῦ λόγυ ἐσὶ, κὴ ὐ ποιητὴς, ὗτος ἔοικεν ἀνδρὶ κατανοῦντι τὸ πρόσωπον τῆς γενέσεως αὑτῦ ἐν ἐσό- πτρῳ) ὅτι deest in Manuscripto, ut & apud Syrum. Ἔοικε si- milis est דמי Syro. Κατανοῶν hic est conspicere. Re- spondet Ebraeo נבט & ראה & Syriaco חזא. Sic & Matth. 7, 3. Luc. 6, 43. Act. 7, 31. 32. 11, 6. 27, 37. Γένεσις vero hic & infra 3, 6. ut & Sap. 1, 14. & 14, 27. id quod alicui natu- rale est, significat, τὸ πρόσωπον τῆς γενέσεως. Proclus dixit τὸ ἀρχέτυπον. Perinde est, atque suam ipse faciem videret: quia ei planè respondet id, quod est in speculo. Sic dicimus: -- Nuper me in littore vidi.

## 1:24
Ver. 24. For he observed himself, and went away) Women are accustomed to linger long at the mirror, so that they may form themselves according to it. Men, having scarcely looked at the mirror, are accustomed to go away, and not care what they are like.

And immediately he forgot what kind he was) For we easily forget those things which we do not care much about. Εὐθέως in a moment the Arab translates.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Κατενόησε γὰρ ἑαυτὸν, καὶ ἀπελήλυθε) Mulieres solent diu inhaerere speculo, ut ad id se forment. Viri vix conspecto speculo solent abire, nec curare, quales sint.

Καὶ εὐθέως ἐπελάθετο ὁ ποῖος ἦν) Facile enim oblivisci- mur, quæ non multum curamus. Εὐθέως in momento vertit Arabs.

## 1:25
Vers. 25.

Ὁ δὲ παρακύψας εἰς νόμον τέλειον τὸν τῆς ἐλευθερίας καὶ παρα- μείνας.] He calls the Gospel the perfect law, compared to the less perfect law of Moses, Heb. VII, 19. 2. Cor. III, 6. He compares that same Gospel to a mirror. And rightly so. For it shows us what we are like. But it is not enough to παρακύπτειν, that is, to look into it in any way, (for thus that word is taken in 1. Pet. I, 12. & Ps. XXXIII, 14. & the Syrian here correctly placed חזא, although it is properly said of those who look out through a window, as Gen. XXVI, 8. 1. Chron. XV, 29. Prov. VII, 6. Cant. II, 9.) One must adhere to it as women do, who take counsel from a mirror to arrange each individual hair well.

Οὗτος οὐκ ἀκροατὴς ἐπιλησμονῆς γενόμενος.] A hearer of forgetfulness in Hebrew idiom, that is, forgetful. The word ἐπιλησμονῆς was used by Cratinus, according to the Scholiast on the Clouds of Aristophanes & Suidas.

Ἀλλὰ ποιητὴς ἔργου.] Singular for Plural, a doer of those works which the Evangelical law demands.

Οὗτος μακάριος ἐν τῇ ποιήσει αὑτοῦ ἔσται.] There is a beautiful anaphora in the pronoun οὗτος. Ἐν τῇ ποιήσει αὑτοῦ here signifies by the action, that is, his own actions. Thus περὶ τῆς ποιήσεως, Exod. 32, 34. In which place in some others מעשה is translated ποίησις.

The discourse here is not about pious deeds, but on the occasion of the doctrine concerning regeneration, it concerns the duty of the reborn, and thus the rationale of the whole of Christianity, or ϑρησκείας & the Christian religion, is explained, namely the true one, not rashly boasted of, or changed or corrupted: which is evident from v. 27. But it consists both in faith and in piety. Therefore the Apostle requires both from the reborn. For it must be observed that this instruction is directed to the reborn, to those who were the firstfruits of the creatures of the Lord, to spiritual brothers, concerning whose regeneration and duty he had discoursed. Wherefore those things are not to be snatched away to the powers of free will. By λόγον, of which the reborn are commanded to be doers, by the force of the context, is understood the λόγος τῆς ἀληθείας, through which God, βουληθεὶς ἀπεκύησεν, out of his gracious will, regenerated them, v. 18. λόγος ἔμφυτος, which through the ministry of the word was implanted and engrafted in them, ὁ δυνάμενος σῶσαι, which was powerful and effective to save them, v. 21. which word is nothing other than the word of the Gospel, Rom. I, 6. For we are not regenerated through the law, nor can the law save us, Galat. II, 21. And since it is immediately subjoined, γίνεσθε δὲ ποιηταὶ λό- γου, but be ye doers of the word, how can it be understood of any other word than that of which he had treated?

Therefore the reborn are commanded to be not only hearers, but ποιηταὶ, doers, of the word of the Gospel: which is not done by works or pious deeds, for these pertain to the law, not to the Gospel, but by faith, by which alone the word of the Gospel is received. For works and the Gospel are not related: But faith and the word of the Gospel, through which, just as we are regenerated and conceive faith, so we do not retain and preserve faith through the law and its observation, but through the keeping of the word of the Gospel, Luke XI, 28. It is therefore a mere paralogism when someone is persuaded that he can be saved merely by hearing the word of God and professing Christianity: But it is no less a mere paralogism when he hopes that he can obtain salvation through the observation of the law. For that

The Apostle testifies that it is ἀδύνατον [impossible], Rom. VIII, 6. The passage in Matth. VII, 24, 25 is not entirely parallel to ours. For there, it is not precisely a matter of the word of the Gospel: but that whole discourse is regarded, which Christ held to the people on the mountain, chap. V, VI, VII, in which he expounded the law no less than the doctrine of the Gospel. And whoever shall hear these my sayings, says Christ, and shall do them. Which certainly look to all the discourses held there. It is added that in this place St. James compares him who is an ἀκροατὴς [hearer] only and not a ποιητὴς [doer] of the word, with a man contemplating only his own face in a mirror, and immediately forgetting what kind he is, v. 23, 24, who is so far from being able to cleanse his face or wipe away spots, that it escapes his memory immediately how his face appears. Whoever, therefore, from the mirror of the divine word [sees] the natural face defiled by the stain of his own concupiscence, how variously he is solicited by it, how foul the offspring he both conceives in his heart and sometimes brings forth into the light, when he is captivated under the law of sin, which is in the members themselves, Rom. VII, 23, since indeed the divine law is spiritual, but he himself is still σαρκικὸς [fleshly] πεπραμένος ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν [sold under sin], v. 14, even if he is reborn, and with Paul indeed delights in the law of God according to the inner man, but sees in his members a contrary law, v. 22, 23, he certainly ought not only to observe the μολυσμὸς σαρκὸς καὶ πνεύματος [defilement of flesh and spirit], but also to be purified from the same, as one possessing through faith the excellent promises of GOD, 2 Cor. VII, 1. But that purification of the heart is through the blood of Christ, 1 John I, 7, Heb. IX, 14, apprehended in the word of the Gospel through faith, by which our hearts are purified, Acts XV, 9. And just as we are justified through redemption in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as ἱλαστήριον [propitiation] through faith in his blood, Rom. III, 25. So, since the just man is still commanded to be justified, Apoc. XXII, 11, the reborn have need of daily repentance and faith in Christ on account of the sins of daily incursion, so that they may be further justified, and preserved in that state of righteousness, and thus through faith be guarded by the power of God unto salvation, 1 Pet. I, 5, and attain the end of faith, the salvation of souls, v. 19. But how are the reborn ποιηταὶ λόγου [doers of the word], καὶ μὴ μόνον ἀκροαταὶ [and not hearers only], when they do not resist the operation of God, who strengthens them through the word of the Gospel, but also never cease to receive with meekness the λόγον ἔμφυτον [implanted word], by which faith is to be fostered and strengthened from time to time, and yield obedience to it, and destroying any contrary reasonings, 2 Cor. X, 4, keep that holy deposit in themselves, 2 Tim. I, 14. For what else does Christ mean when he says in John VIII, 47: If anyone shall keep my saying, he shall not see death forever, and when in Luke VIII, 15 he deals with those who ἐν καρδίᾳ καλῇ κ᾿ ἀγαθῇ ἀκούσαντες τὸν λόγον κατέχουσι [having heard the word in an honest and good heart, keep it], or when in Luke XI, 28, he says, μακάριοι [blessed are] those who hear the word of God and keep it. To which pertains what Christ commands in John VI, 27: Ἐργάζεσθαι τὴν βρῶσιν τὴν μένουσαν εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον [Work for the food which endures unto eternal life]; they are commanded to work for that food, and yet it is added that it will be given to them by the Son of man: And when they ask what they ought to do so that they may work the works of God; it is explained by Christ in v. 29: This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent. Why may not ποιεῖν τὸν λόγον Θεοῦ [to do the word of God], to perform the word of God through faith, be said of those who are said ἐργάζεσθαι ἔργον τοῦ Θεοῦ [to work the work of God], to work the work of God, when they believe in him?

Furthermore, who is not a forgetful hearer, but a ποιητὴς ἔργου [doer of the work], the Apostle illustrates thus: ὁ παρακύψας εἰς νόμον τέλειον τὸν τῆς ἐλευθερίας, καὶ παραμείνας [he who has looked into the perfect law of liberty, and continued in it]. But what is that perfect law of liberty, ὁ νόμος τέλειος τῆς ἐλευθερίας [the perfect law of liberty]? The doctrine of the Gospel. For it is beyond doubt that the name of law is not rarely taken for doctrine in general: But the doctrine of the Gospel is both perfect, and of the true liberty which we have through Christ, John VIII, 36. The doctrine and cause is called the perfect Law, not so much because it is perfect in itself, for in that way the Mosaic law is also perfect, namely as an adequate norm of things to be done and things to be avoided: which Grotius rashly argues of imperfection with the Socinians and Papists; but because it renders man perfect, Rom. VIII, 2, Heb. X, 14, Col. I, 26, seqq. The law of liberty, of which the Apostle speaks in Rom. VIII, 2, according to the interpretation of Ambrose and others, and even Grotius himself: Ὁ νόμος τῆς πνεύματος τῆς ζωῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ ἠλευθέρωσέ με ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου τῆς ἁμαρτίας κ.

to death. Those who understand the Mosaic law cannot explain how that law is called the perfect law of liberty. It is inconsistent, what Piscator brings forward, that it freely and without respect of persons condemns any transgressors whatsoever. For thus it would rather have to be called a law of servitude. It is not a law of liberty which freely condemns transgressors, but one which asserts its worshippers into liberty, Gal. IV, 24, 25, 26. Hemmingius reports that it is called the law of liberty because, the more one has been addicted to the moral law, provided he believes in Christ, the more he declares himself to be free; or as others say, because it does not force, terrify, and curse any longer the man constituted under the grace of Christ (whose heart has been inscribed by the Holy Spirit, Jerem. XXXI, 33), but leads him spontaneously in the way of righteousness. But these are not properly of the law, but of grace, which was made through Christ, John VIII, 36, chap. I, 17. and of the Gospel, Rom. VIII, 2, and are openly taken away from the law of works, Roman. III, 27. But that the Papists wish the evangelical law to be noted, and say that it confers evangelical grace, by which precepts are easily and freely fulfilled, is frivolous. The Gospel, as it contains laws, does not confer that grace, but the Gospel, as it is the law or doctrine of faith, and not of works, Roman. I, 16, 17, chap. X, 4, Galat. III, 12, chap. II, 12, Coloss. II, 12, seqq. That the law of works makes a man free is repugnant to Paul, Galat. IV, 24. Conf. Luke XVII, 10, Roman. VII, 10, seqq. The law, therefore, that is, the doctrine of perfect liberty, is the very doctrine of the Gospel. Into it we look with the eyes of the mind illuminated, Eph. I, 18. Therefore, we ought indeed to look into the mirror of the moral law, when we contemplate our native face, our connate malice, and the stains that are accustomed to be in us from thence, since even the reborn are accustomed to be defiled and stained by the impurity of depraved concupiscence, and we desire to know them: Yet not only to look into that mirror in any way whatsoever, but

to stoop down, to look into it thoroughly, which is the emphasis of the word (as the Angels, 1 Pet. I, 12, and as the eyes of God himself most thoroughly look into and perceive all things) so that we may attain through that mirror to Christ, the very end of the law, with the eyes of the mind, and cling to him with fixed eyes, which the word 'remaining' implies: which he who does, this man is not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, not of moral works, which the evangelical law might demand, as Grotius says, confusing the law and the Gospel, and derogating from the perfection of the law, but of the work which the perfect law of liberty uniquely requires for salvation, which it behooves everyone to do, that he may be saved, which is to believe in Christ Jesus, Act. XVI, 30, 31. For the Apostle distinguishes 'the beholding of the face of his birth in a mirror,' which must be repeated in the apodosis from the common, and is required for the knowledge of our defilement and stains, and is the contemplation of our face in the mirror of the moral law, from which is the acknowledgment of sin, Rom. 3, 20, and 'the stooping down into the perfect law of liberty,' when we penetrate through the moral mirror with illuminated eyes, even to the end of the law, Christ, and so we look with pleasure into the law of liberty itself, that is, the evangelical doctrine, in which shines the face of Jesus Christ as in a most lucid mirror, opposed, or contraposed to the mirror of the moral law; 'for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God,' 2 Cor. IV, 6, and we all, who are reborn, 'with open face beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord,' 2. Cor. III, 18. Through which catoptric power liberty comes to us, v. 17, so that we may be freed from sin through faith in Christ, and be transformed from glory to glory, Rom. VIII, 2.

This, therefore, is that work which must be done by the reborn, not perfunctorily, but with the greatest zeal, because there is need for a perpetual 'beholding' in the mirror of the law, a 'stooping down' into the perfect law of liberty, and 'remaining,' since we are constantly defiled, and are variously solicited and tempted on account of those stains of sin, lest we should not be pleasing in the eyes of the Lord. Wherefore there is need of faith, which the eyes of the Lord look upon, Jer. V, 3, and without which it is impossible to please God, Heb. XI, 16, which is fostered by the constant and accurate consideration of the evangelical doctrine, and by the most constant intuition of the face of Christ crucified and resurrected for us in the word, by which 'Jesus Christ was evidently set forth before your eyes,' Gal. III, 1, and is strengthened against any temptations whatsoever. Of such a doer of the work, therefore, St. James testifies in the present, 'that he shall be blessed in his doing': Which by the force of the context, as has been shown, is to be understood of the doing of faith, of the intuition of Christ exalted for us on the cross, John III, 15. There is indeed, says the blessed Höpfner in his disputation XII on justification, a twofold doing, as it is called by a general name in Scripture; one is faith in Christ, that is, the fiducial apprehension of the merit of Christ, John VI, 41; the other is the performance of good works, James I. And both are opposed to a bare hearing, Matthew VII, verses 24, 26, and to a mere profession of faith, Matthew VII, 21; they differ, however, as the signified and the sign. The former doing, or faith in Christ, which makes a Christian, is the thing to be acknowledged. The latter doing, however, are good works, which do not make, but only show a good Christian, and have themselves like a certain mark, so that from their defect, when they ought to be performed, it can be infallibly concluded that he who is given to sins is not a true Christian or a truly faithful one.

Although indeed some interpret this passage concerning the performance of good works, and understand the blessed one SIGNOTENUS [by the sign], who in the doing, in the exercise of the law of liberty, effectively delivers what he has heard must be done, is infallibly recognized and judged: nor is it unknown that a thing is said in the scriptures to be done or to be, when it is manifested or known: It is better, however, to adhere to the letter and the context for the stated reason: and that name νόμος τελείας ἐλευθερίας [law of perfect liberty] is too sublime to befit the moral law: Furthermore, the effect of a deeper inspection into that law of liberty, and of remaining in the same, is not our knowledge of blessedness, but is μακαριότης [blessedness] itself, nor do we, through the introspection of the moral law, even if we should remain in it to the greatest degree, become ποιηταὶ τῶν ἔργων νόμου [doers of the works of the law], so that we can be infallibly recognized as righteous and blessed; but by the law is the knowledge of sin, and the inspection of it only works wrath, unless we penetrate εἰς τὸ τέλος νόμου [into the end of the law], into the end of the law, which is Christ, for righteousness to every one that believeth, Rom. X. 4. or we are blessed only by a sign; so that this sign may be infallible: since the execution of the moral law labors under much imperfection in this imperfection of travelers. For we know in part only, and therefore we also love in part, 1 Cor. XIII, 9. The law of liberty is perfect, says the blessed Glassius, Part III. Exeg. Evang. Epist. p. 209. It is the word of God itself, which in v. 21 he called the engrafted word, which is able to save souls. It is called law, as in Rom. III, 27. c. IIX, 2. and elsewhere, in imitation of the Hebrew word תּוֹרָה, which is translated as law, and yet in general signifies doctrine, Ps. I, 2. c. XIX, 8. etc. It is called perfect, because it is a full and perfect medium and instrument for exciting faith, forming life, and conferring eternal salvation, 2. Tim. III, 16. 17. It is called the law of liberty, because this word of life is ordained by God, so that through it we may be freed from sin, Satan, and hell, and be brought into the liberty of the children of God on account of Christ the Savior, Joh. IIX, 32. c. XVII, 17. Rom. VI, 17. c. VII, 6. IIX, 2. With which can be compared the excellent words of Paul, by which the Gospel of Christ is [distinguished] both by the effect of liberty describes, then compares it to a mirror in a pleasant way, 2 Cor. 3:17. Now the Lord is the Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is (acting among men through his word, as the preceding parts show), there is liberty. v. 18. But we all with open face beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord. Into this mirror, therefore (according to the admonition of James), one must look continually; in it our filthiness, and on the contrary the goodness of Christ, must be recognized, and we must strive earnestly for the washing and cleansing of the former, and for the living application and faithful reception of the latter: In this (as James further speaks) one must remain, and all negligence and forgetfulness must be shaken off: Thus the blessedness of the soul and eternal salvation follows. Which explanation easily harmonizes with our own already delivered one and is its foster-sibling. Nor does the blessed Brochmand’s ἔκθεσις (exposition) deny this: Now παρακύπτειν (to look into) is to look into some matter with head bowed and neck and body bent, as is clear from a comparison of the passages Luke 24:12, John 20:5, 1 Pet. 1:12. Therefore, by the single word παρακύψεως (looking into), both singular humility and intent study in contemplating Christ, proposed in the Evangelical doctrine, are commended to us. For since Christ, God blessed forever, Rom. 9:5, and made man in the fullness of time, Gal. 4:4, John 1:14, is proposed to be seen in the Gospel as in a mirror, it is right and just that, besides the fervent study of learning which one ought to bring, we should bow our heads, submit our necks, and remove as far as possible that pride which is hostile to God. One must say with Paul, 1 Tim. 3:16, great is the mystery of godliness, that God was manifest in the flesh. It is fitting to imitate the angels, who desire to look into the doctrine which is proposed concerning Christ in the Gospel with a most humble mind and an affection prone to devotion, 1 Pet. 1:12. Furthermore, it is not enough to have looked into the perfect law of liberty, but the Apostle further requires that we remain in this very thing. But he remains in this law of liberty who constantly adheres to the Evangelical doctrine both in adversity and in prosperity: he always delights himself in the meditation of it, he prefers it to all things, so that he would rather undergo the hardest death and leave the dearest things in the world than depart even a little from the profession and obedience of the Evangelical doctrine. These things [says] the blessed Brochmand, even if he later turns to ποίησιν (doing), which is a sign of blessedness: Truly blessed are they who look into the perfect law of liberty in such a way, and so remain in it, that they express by deed what they say they believe, not that that work is the cause of blessedness, Rom. 6:23, Eph. 2:10, Rom. 9:11, but because it is a document and certain evidence of blessedness: For as many as are of the number of the blessed, these testify to their faith in Christ by their deeds. In which sense, however, he does not fix his foot, nor does he testify that he is alien to our opinion: If anyone presses more closely, that blessedness is ascribed by James to the work itself as a cause in this way: Just as by the law of liberty the Gospel is understood: So nothing prevents the faith from being understood by the work, and the doer of the work being the man believing the Gospel. For Christ sometimes used this formula of speaking. For when the Jews asked: What shall we do, that we might work the works of God? He answers: This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent, John 6:29. Lucas Osiander indicates in this place that this is the most convenient exposition of this passage: whose paraphrase can be compared here with our twofold explanation. I hope, however, that the piously learned reader, about to weigh these things ἄνω προκρίματος (without prejudice), will recognize that a fuller unfolding of the whole text has been exhibited here.

This Jacobean sentence explains itself mutually,

ἔσται μακάριος ἐν τῇ ποιήσει αὐτõ ἔσται (he shall be blessed in his doing); and that of Christ in Luke 11:28. Μακάριοι οἱ ἀκούοντες τὸν λόγον τõ θεõ, καὶ φυλάσσοντες αὐτόν (Blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it). Cf. also Matt. 12:49 with John 6:40. I judge, however, while I conceived these things, regarding the explanation of the blessed Walther, as far as v. 25 in the harmony, which I approve of as entirely consonant with our own (except that I do not think the Royal law in v. 14 is to be taken as the Gospel): he says, James is most simply to be believed to be speaking not of the Decalogue, which Paul does, but of the Gospel, which he had hitherto called the word of truth, the engrafted word, and the Royal law; he now calls it by the name of law in a broad signification, that is, the doctrine of liberty, from the effect, of course, since it vindicates believers into the true liberty of the sons of God, of which Christ said in John 8:36: If the Son shall make you free, you are free indeed. In the same sense Paul calls the Gospel the law of faith, Rom. 3:27, and the law of the Spirit, by which he says he was freed from sin and death, Rom. 8:2. To understand the words of James concerning the Mosaic law, certainly neither the scope nor the epithet allows, because that law in the New Testament is everywhere one of servitude, not of liberty. And further: In the same chapter, same verse, the doer of the work is declared blessed in his deed. Since we are saved by the grace of God, not by our works, Eph. 2:8, 9. Resp. 1. In this place there is no talk of the law, but of the Gospel. For in the preceding parts the Apostle wishes to say this: He who looks into the doctrine of the Gospel, which brings true peace and liberty to consciences, and has constantly persevered in that doctrine apprehended by faith, so that he accommodates himself entirely to it, he shall obtain salvation, not because he was a hearer of the word of GOD, but because he believed and obeyed it. On the contrary, they ought not to promise themselves salvation who think it is enough if they can speak splendidly and magnificently about the Gospel, and meanwhile the Gospel takes no roots in their hearts, nor is any godliness found in it. 2. Therefore, the doer of the work is the believer, who has drawn faith from the Gospel, which Christ himself testifies, for he not only said to the Jews in John 6:29: This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent, but also in Matt. 7:21 and ch. 12:50 he broke forth into these words: Whosoever SHALL DO the will of my Father, he shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, and is my brother, etc. Where he certainly speaks primarily of the faith by which we ought to embrace his Gospel. And hence 3. it is not said here of such a doer of the work or believer, that he is blessed ἐν τῷ ἔργῳ in the work, lest anyone take this concerning the law, but ἐν ποιήσει in his operation, or in his deed, as the Vulgate translates, and Luther in seiner That, that is, in the obedience of the word, which presupposes faith, in which alone the believer shall be saved, and blessed according to that of Habakkuk II. v. 4. The just shall live by his faith. I, with Osiander, judge this to be the most convenient exposition of this passage. Otherwise this text would simply conflict with the doctrine of Paul. That of Calvin on v. 25 also contributes to this. After, he says, he has spoken of vain speculation, he now descends to that penetrable intuition, which transforms us into the likeness of God. The opposition in the protasis between a man and a woman, that any man might glance at a mirror in passing, whereas a woman looks at a mirror attentively and for a long time, in order to comb and adorn herself, is [such] that it can be founded on the word ἀνήρ.

Latin:

Vers. 25.

Ὁ δὲ παρακύψας εἰς νόμον τέλειον τὸν τῆς ἐλευθερίας καὶ παρα- μείνας.] Νόμον τέλειον vocat Evangelium, comparatum legi Mosis minus perfectæ, Ebr. VII, 19. 2. Cor. III, 6. Id ipsum Evangelium comparat speculo. Et bene. Ostendit enim no- bis nos quales sumus. Sed non satis est παρακύπτειν, id est, quovis modo inspectare, (ita enim id verbum sumitur 1. Petr. I, 12. & Psal. XXXIII, 14. & Syrus hic recte posuit חזא, quan- quam proprie de iis dicitur, qui per fenestram prospectant, ut Gen. XXVI, 8. 1. Paral. XV, 29. Prov. VII, 6. Cant. II, 9.) In- hærendum est sicut fœminæ faciunt, quæ ad singulos capillos bene ponendos de speculo consilium sumunt.

Οὗτος οὐκ ἀκροατὴς ἐπιλησμονῆς γενόμενος.] Auditor obli- vionis loquutione Ebræa, id est obliviosus. Ἐπιλησμονῆς voce usus est Cratin9 teste Scholiaste ad nubes Aristophanis & Suida.

Ἀλλὰ ποιητὴς ἔργου.] Singulare pro Plurali Effector eorum operum, quæ Evangelica lex exigit.

Οὗτος μακάριος ἐν τῇ ποιήσει αὑτοῦ ἔσται.] Est pulchra ἀνα- φορὰ in Pronomine ὗτος. Ἐν τῇ ποιήσει αὑτοῦ hic valet ob acti- onem, id est, actiones ipsius. Sic περὶ τῆς ποιήσεως, Exod. 32, 34. Quo loco in aliis nonnullis מעשה vertitur ποίησις.

Non de factis piis hic sermo est, sed occasione doctrinæ de regeneratione de officio renatorum, agi- tur, adeoque ratio explicatur totius Christianismi, vel ϑρησκείας & religionis Christianæ, veræ nempe, non temere jactatæ, vel mutatæ aut corruptæ: quod è v. 27. constat. Ea vero consistit tum in fide, tum in pietate. Utramque ergo requirit Apostolus à rena- tis. Observandum enim, quod hæc informatio ad renatos, ad eos, qui primitiæ erant creaturarum Do- mini, ad fratres spirituales directa sit, de quorum regeneratione, atque officio disseruerat. Quapro- pter illa abripienda non sunt ad vires liberi arbitrii. Per λόγον, cujus ποιηταὶ esse jubentur renati, vi con- textus, intelligitur λόγος τῆς ἀληθείας, per quem eos Deus βουληθεὶς ἀπεκύησεν, ex gratiosa voluntate regenuit, v. 18. λόγος ἔμφυτος, qui per ministeriu verbi implantatus & insitus ipsis fuit, ὁ δυνάμενος σῶσαι, qui potens erat & efficax ipsos salvare, v. 21. quod verbum nullum aliud est, quam verbum Ev- angelii, Rom. I, 6. Non enim per legem regenera- mur, neque lex potest nos salvare, Galat. II, 21. Et quum immediate subjiciatur, γίνεσθε δὲ ποιηταὶ λό- γου, sitis autem factores verbi, quomodo de alio verbo, quam de quo egerat, intelligi id potest?

Verbi ergo evangelii non auditores solum, sed ποι- ηταὶ factores esse jubentur renati: quod non sit operi- bus vel factis piis, hæc enim ad legem pertinent, non ad Evangelium, sed fide, qua sola Evangelii verbum suscipitur. Non enim relata sunt opera, & Evange- lium: Sed fides & verbum Evangelii, per quod uti regeneramur, & fidem concipimus, ita non per le- gem ejusque observationem retinemus ac conser- vamus fidem, sed per verbi Evangelii custodiam, Luc. XI, 28. Paralogismus ergo merus est, cum tan- tum audiendo verbum Dei, & profitendo Chri- stianismum quis se servari posse persuasus est : Sed nec minus paralogismus merus est, cum se salutem per legis observationem consequi posse sperat. Nam id

ἀδύνατον esse testatur Apostolus, Roman. VIII, 6. Locus Matth. VII, 24. 25. non est ex asse nostro pa- rallelus. Ibi enim non de verbo Evangelii præcise agitur : Sed respicitur illa concio tota, quam Chri- stus ad populum in monte habuit, cap. V. VI. VII. qua non minus legem exposuit, quam doctrinam Evangelii. Et qui audierit hoste sermones meos, in- quit Christus, & fecerit eos. Quæ spectant utique ad omnes illic habitos sermones. Accedit, quod hoc loco S. Jacobus eum, qui ἀκροατὴς tantum & ποιητὴς auditor, non factor est verbi, comparet cum viro, contemplante solum faciem suam in speculo, & ob- liviscente statim, qualis sit, v. 23. 24. qui tantum ab- est, ut purgare faciem, vel maculas abstergere pos- fit, ut memoria excidat illico, quomodo sese ha- beat facies. Qui ergo è speculo verbi divini nati- vam faciem propriæ concupiscentiæ labe commacu- latam, quam varie ab eadem sollicitetur, quam fœ- dos & in corde concipiat, & quandoque in lucem progignat fœtus, cum captivatur sub legem pecca- ti, quæ in membris ipsis est, Rom. VII, 23. siquidem lex divina spiritualis, ipse autem σαρκικὸς adhuc sit πεπραμένος ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, v. 14. etiamsi re- natus sit, & cum Paulo delectetur quidem lege Dei secundum interiorem hominem, sed videat in membris suis legem contrariam, v. 22. 23. is utique non observare tantum μολυσμὸς σαρκὸς καὶ πνεύ- ματος debet, sed etiam purificari ab iisdem, utpote per fidem possidens eximias DEI promissiones, 2. Cor. VII, 1. Illa autem cordis purificatio per san- guinem Christi sit, 1. Joh. I, 7. Ebr. IX, 14. in verbo Evangelii apprehensum per fidem, qua purificantur corda nostra, Act. XV, 9. Et quemadmodum justifi- camur per redemptionem in Christo Jesu, quem pro- posuit Deus ἱλαστήριον per fidem in sanguine ipsius, Rom. III, 25. Ita quum justus adhuc justificari jubea- tur, Apoc. XXII, 11. renatis propter peccata quoti- dianæ incursionis opus est pœnitentia quotidia- na, & fide in Christum, ut porro justificentur, & in illo justitiæ statu conserventur, adeoque per fidem in virtute Dei ad salutem custodiantur, 1. Petr. I, 5. & finem fidei, animarum salutem consequantur, v. 19. Quomodo autem ποιηταὶ λόγου sunt renati, καὶ μὴ μόνον ἀκροαταὶ, cum operatione Dei, per verbum Evangelii ipsos confortantis, non resistunt, sed & nunquam non cum mansuetudine λόγον ἔμφυτον, quo subinde fides fovenda est, & roboranda, susci- piunt, eique obsequium præstant, ac quasvis ratio- cinationes contrarias destruentes 2. Cor. X, 4. in sese sanctum illud depositum custodiant, 2. Tim. I, 14. Quid enim aliud vult Christus, cum Joh. VIII, 47. ait: Si quis sermonem meum servarit, mortem non videbit in æternum, & cum Luc. VIII, 15. de iis agit, qui ἐν καρδίᾳ καλῇ κ᾿ ἀγαθῇ ἀκούσαντες τὸν λόγον κατέχουσι, aut cum Luc. XI, 28. μακάριοι, inquit οἱ ἀκούσαντες τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ φυλάσσοντες αὐτὸν. Quo pertinet, quod jubet Christus Joh. VI, 27. Ἐρ- γάζεσθαι τὴν βρῶσιν τὴν μένουσαν εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον ; operari jubentur cibum illum, & additur tamen, eum datum iri ipsis à Filio hominis : Et cum id quæ- rentibus, quid facere debeant, ut opera Dei operentur; exponitur id à Christo v. 29. Hoc est opus Dei, ut cre- datis in eum, quem ipse misit. Quid ni ποιεῖν τὸν λό- γον Θεοῦ, præstare verbum Dei per fidem dici pos- sunt, qui dicuntur ἐργάζεσθαι ἔργον τοῦ Θεοῦ, operari opus Dei, cum credunt in eum?

Porro quisnam sit non obliviosus auditor, sed ποιητὴς ἔργου, ita illustrat Apostolus, ὁ παρακύψας εἰς νόμον τέλειον τὸν τῆς ἐλευθερίας, καὶ παραμείνας, qui perspexerit in legem perfectam libertatis, & per- manserit in ea. Quæ vero est lex illa perfecta liber- tatis, ὁ νόμος τέλειος τῆς ἐλευθερίας ; Doctrina Evangelii. Nomen enim legis non raro pro doctri- na generatim accipi, extra dubium est: Doctrina autem Evangelii & perfecta est, & veræ libertatis, quam per Christum habemus, Joh. IIX, 36. Doctri- na & causa Lex perfecta dicitur, non tam quia in se perfecta est, nam ita & lex Mosaica perfecta est, norma nempe faciendorum & fugiendorum adæ- quata: Quam temere cum Sociniis & Pontificiis imperfectionis arguit Grotius; quam quia homi- nem perfectum reddit, Rom. IIX, 2. Ebr. X. 14. Col. I, 26. seqq. Lex libertatis, de qua Apostolus Rom. VIII, 2. interprete, Ambrosio, aliisque, ipso etiam Groto : Ὁ νόμος τῆς πνεύματος τῆς ζωῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ ἠλευθέρωσέ με ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου τῆς ἁμαρτίας κ.

τῆ θανάτε. Qui legem intelligunt Mofaicam, ex- plicare non poffunt, quomodo lex ea perfecta liber- tatis dicatur. Ἀσύςα]ον est, quod adfert Piscator, quod ea libere, & absque respectu personarum damnet quosvis transgressores. Ita enim potius lex servitutis dicenda foret. Non ea est lex libertatis, quæ libere transgressores damnat, sed quæ cultores in liberta- tem asserit, Gal. IV, 24. 25. 26. Hemmingius tradit, legem libertatis dici, quia, quo magis legi morali addictus fuerit, modo in Christum credat, eo magis se liberum esse declarat; vel quod alii, quia sub gra- tia Christi constitutum hominem, (cujus cordi in- scripta est per Spiritum sanctum Jerem XXXI, 33.) non cogit, terret, & maledicit amplius, sed sponta- neum ducit in via justitiæ. Atqui hæc non legis proprie sunt, sed gratiæ, quæ per Christum facta est, Johan. VIII, 36. cap. I, 17. & Evangelii, Rom. VIII, 2. legique operum palam adimuntur, Roman. III, 27. Quod vero Pontificii legem Evangelicam no- tari volunt, eamque Evangelicam conferre gra- tiam dicunt, qua præcepta facile ac libere imple antur, frivolum est. Non Evangelium, qua leges continet, eam confert gratiam, sed Evangelium, qua est lex seu doctrina fidei, & non operum, Roman. I, 16. 17. cap. X, 4. Galat. III, 12. cap. II, 12. Coloss. II, 12. seqq. Legem operum hominem liberum præstare, repugnat Paulo, Galat. IV, 24. Conf. Luc. XVII, 10. Roman. VII, 10. seqq. Lex ergo, id est, doctrina per- fecta libertatis est ipsa Evangelii doctrina. In illam perspicimus oculis mentis illuminatis, Eph. I, 18. Ergo speculum quidem legis moralis intueri debemus, cum nativam faciem nostram, connatam malitiam, & quæ inde nobis maculæ inesse solent, quum pra- væ concupiscentiæ impuritate inquinari & com- maculari etiam renati subinde soleant, contempla- mur, & cognoscere cupimus: Non tamen in spe- culum illud tantum quovis modo inspectare, sed

παρακύψαι, penitus id perspicere, quæ verbi empha- sis est, (uti Angeli, 1. Petr. I, 12. & uti oculi ipsi DEI penitissime omnia introspiciunt, & perspiciunt) ut ipsum τὸ τέλος νόμο, Christum per illud speculum, oculis mentis assequamur, eique fixis oculis inhæ- reamus, quod verbum παραμείνας importat: quod qui facit, ὗτος ἐκ ἀκροατὴς ἐπιλησμονῆς est, ἀλλὰ ποιητὴς ἔργε, effector non operum moralium, quæ Evangelica lex exigat, ut Grotius, confundens le- gem & Evangelium, legisque perfectioni derogans, sed operis, quod unice νόμθ τέλειος τῆς ἐλευθε- ρίας ad salutem requirit, quod quemque ποιεῖν δεῖ, facere oportet, ut salvetur, quod est τὸ credere in Christum Jesum, Act. XVI, 30. 31. Nam distinguit Apostolus τὸ κατανοεῖν τὸ πρόσωπον τῆς γενέσεως ἐν ἐσόπτρῳ, quod in ἀποδόσει ἀπὸ κοινᾶ repetendum est, & iuquinationis ac macularum nostrarum co- gnitionem requiritur, estque contemplatio faciei nostræ in speculo legis moralis, ex qua est agnitio peccati, Rom. 3, 20. & τὸ παρακύψαι εἰς νόμον τέλει- ον τῆς ἐλευθερίας, cum per speculum morale pene- tramus oculis illuminatis, usq; εἰς τὸ τέλος νόμο in finem legis Christum, adeoq; ita cum voluptate in- trospicimus in ipsam etiam legem libertatis hoc est, Evangelicam doctrinam, in qua effulget πρόσωπον Ἰησῦ Χριςᾶ velut in speculo lucidissimo, opposito, vel contraposito speculo legis moralis; πρὸς Φωτισμὸν τῆς γνώσεως τῆς δόξης τᾶ Θεᾶ, 2. Cor. IV, 6. nosque omnes, qui renati sumus. ἀνακεκαλυμμένῳ προσώ- πῳ τὴν δόξαν τᾶ Κυρίε κα]οπριζόμενοι τὴν ἀυ]ὴν εἰ- κόνα με]αμορΦύμεθα ἀπὸ δόξης εἰς δόξαν, καθά- περ ἀπὸ Κυρίε Πνεύματος, 2. Cor. III, 18. Per quam catoptricam vim nobis ἐλευθερία obtingit, v. 17. ut à peccato per fidem in Christum liberemur, ac de gloria in gloriam transformemur, Rom. VIII, 2.

Hoc ergo illud ἔργον est, quod agendum renatis non perfunctorie est, sed summo studio, quia perpe- tuo τὸ κατανοεῖν in speculo legis, τὸ παρακύψαι εἰς νόμον τέλειον τῆς ἐλευθερίας, καὶ παραμένειν opus est, quum subinde inquinemur, varieque ob illas peccati maculas solicitemur ac tentemur, ne non placeamus in oculis Domini. Quapropter fide opus est, quam respiciunt oculi Domini, Jer. V, 3. & sine qua impossibile est Deo placere, Ebr. XI, 16. quæ ex evangelicæ doctrinæ jugi, & accurata consideratio- ne, & τῷ προσώπῳ Christi pro nobis crucifixi & re- suscitati in verbo, quo κατ᾿ ὀφθαλμοὺς προεγρά- φη ὑμῖν Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς, Gal. III. 1. intuitu constantis- simo fovetur, & adversus tentationes quasvis fir- matur. De tali ergo operis factore S. Jacobus in præsenti testatur, ὅτι μακάριος ἐν τῇ ποιήσει αὐ- τοῦ ἔσται: Quod vi contextus, ut ostensum, de ποιή- σει fidei, de intuitu Christi pro nobis in cruce exaltati, Joh. III, 15. intelligendum. Est sane, inquit B. Höpf- nerus disp. XII. de justificatione, duplex ποίησις, ut generali nomine appellatur in scriptura, una est fides in Christum, id est, fiducialis apprehensio meriti Chri- sti Joh. VI, 41. altera vero præstatio bonorum ope- rum, Jac. I. & utraque opponitur nudo auditui Mat- thæi VII. vers. 24. 26. & soli professioni fidei, Mat- thæi VII, 21. differunt tamen, ut signatum & signum. Prior ποίησις seu fides in Christum, quæ facit Christia- num, est res agnoscenda. Posterior autem ποίησις sunt bona opera, quæ non faciunt, sed duntaxat ostendunt bonum Christianum, & habent se instar certæ notæ, ita ut ex eorum, cum præstari deberent, defectu fallibi- liter concludi possit, illum, qui peccatis deditus est, non esse verum Christianum seu vere fidelem.

Quanquam vero hunc locum de præstatione bo- norum operum accipiant nonnulli, & beatum in- telligant SIGNOTENUS, qui ἐν ποιήσει in exercitio le- gis libertatis, cum effectu tradit, quæ audivit facien- da esse, infallibiliter agnoscatur & censeatur: neq; ignotum sit, tum rem dici in scripturis fieri, vel esse, cum manifestatur vel cognoscitur: Præstat tamen in- hærere literæ & contextui dicta ratione: & sublimius est nomen illud νόμος τελείας ἐλευθερίας, quam ut legi morali conveniat: Ad hæc effecto penitioris inspe- ctionis in illam legem libertatis, & permansionis in eadem non cognitio nostra beatitudinis, sed ipsa μα- καριότης est, neque per introspectionem legis moralis, si in eadē maxime permaneamus, vel evadimus nos ποιηταὶ τῶν ἔργων νόμου, ita ut infallibiliter possumus agnosci justi & beati; sed ex lege est cognitio pec- cati, & ejus inspectio tantum iram operatur, nisi pe- netremus εἰς τὸ τέλος νόμου, in finem legis, qui est Christus, ad justitia omni credenti, Rom. X. 4. vel beati sumus signotenus; ita ut signum hoc infallibile sit: quum multa imperfectione laboret legis moralis exequutio in hac viatorũ imperfectione. Ex parte enim cognoscimus tantum, ideoq; & ex parte diligi- mus, 1. Cor. XIII, 9. Lex libertatis perfecta, inquit B. Glassius Part. III. Exeg. Evang. Epist. p. 209. est ipsum verbum Dei, quod v. 21. sermonem insititium vocavit, qui potest salvare animas. Lex vocatur, uti Rom. III, 27. c. IIX, 2. & alibi, ad imitationem vocis Ebrææ תּוֹרָה, quæ per legem vertitur, & in genere tamen doctri- nam significat, Ps. I, 2. c. XIX, 8. &c. Perfecta dicitur, quia plenum & perfectum fidei excitandæ, vitæ infor- mandæ, & salutis æternæ conferendæ medium est & organon, 2. Tim. III, 16. 17. Libertatis lex nuncupatur, quia à Deo ordinatum est hoc vitæ verbum, ut per id à peccato, satana, inferno liberemur, & in filiorum Dei libertatem traducamur propter Christum Salva- torem, Joh. IIX, 32. c. XVII, 17. Rom. VI, 17. c. VII, 6. IIX, 2. Quo cum conferri possunt præclara Pauli verba, quibus Evangelium Christi tum à libertatis effectu describit, tum speculo jucunda ratione comparat, 2. Corinth. III, 17. Dominus autem Spiritus est: por- ro ubi Domini Spiritus (per verbum suum cum ho- minibus agens, ut præcedentia ostendunt) ibi libertas v. 18. Nos autem omnes retecta facie, gloriam Do- mini in speculo contemplantes ad eandem imaginem transformamur à gloria in gloriam, tanquam à Domini Spiritu. In hoc igitur speculum (secundum monitum Jacobi) jugiter prospiciendum, in illo no- stra fœditas, & contra Christi bonitas cognoscenda, deque illius ablutione & emundatione, hujus vero viva applicatione atque receptione fideli enixe la- borandum: In hoc (ut porro Jacobus loquitur) per- manendum, & omnis negligentia ac oblivio excu- tienda: Sic beatitudo animæ & salus æterna sequi- tur. Quæ explicatio facile nostræ jam traditæ con- sonat & collactea est. Nec abnuit B. Brochmandi ἔκθεσις: Est autem παρακύπτειν prono capite, ac inflexo collo & corpore in rem quampiam introspi- cere, uti liquet è collatione locorum Luc. XXIV, 12. Joh. XX, 5. 1. Petr. I, 12. Una igitur παρακύψεως voce commendatur nobis tum singularis humili- tas, tum intentum studium in contemplando Chri- stum, in Evangelica doctrina propositum. Nam cum in Evangelio, tanquam in speculo proponatur videndus Christus, Deus in secula benedictus, Rom. IX, 5. & in plenitudine temporis factus homo, Galat. IV, 4. Joh. I, 14. fas & æquum est, ut præter stu- dium discendi fervidum, quod afferre oportet, ca- put inflectamus, collum submittamus, & inimicam Deo superbiam quam longissime removeamus. Di- cere oportet cum Paulo 1. Timoth. III, 16. magnum pietatis mysterium, Deum in carne manifestatum esse. Imitari convenit Angelos, qui doctrinam, quæ de Christo proponitur in Evangelio, humillimo animo, & in devotionem prono affectu introspicere gestiunt, 1. Petr. I, 12. Cæterum non sufficit introspe- xisse in perfectam legem libertatis, sed porro requirit Apostolus, ut in hac ipsa permaneamus. Perma- net vero in hac libertatis lege, qui doctrina Evange- lica tam in adversis, quam secundis constanter ad- hæret: hujus meditatione se semper oblectat, hanc rebus omnibus præfert, ita ut malit & durissimam mortem subire, & charissima in mundo relinquere, quam à doctrina Evangelica professione & obedien- tia vel tantillum recedere. Hæc B. Brochmandus, etsi postea abeat ad ποίησιν, quæ signum beatitudi- nis: Vere beati sunt, qui in perfectam libertatis legem ita introspiciunt, atque ita in ea manent, ut quod se credere dicunt, facto exprimant, non quod illud opus sit causa beatitudinis, Rom. VI, 23. Eph. II, 10. Rom. IX, 11. sed quod documentum & certum indi- cium sit beatitudinis: Nam quotquot è numero beatorum sunt, hi fidem in Christum factis testantur. In quo vero sensu non figit pedem, nec à nostra se- se alienum esse sententia testatur: Siquis pressius ur- gerit, operi ipsi, tanquam causæ, à Jacobo adscribi bea- titudinem hoc modo: Veluti per legem libertatis intel- ligitur Evangelium: Ita nihil impedit, quo minus per opus intelligatur fides, & factor operis sit homo cre- dens Evangelio. Etenim Christus interdum usus est hac loquendi formula. Nam cum quærerent Judæi: Quid faciemus, ut operemur operibus Dei? Respondet: Hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in eum, quem ille misit, Jo- han. VI, 29. Quam esse commodissimam hujus loci ex- positionem, indicat hoc loco Lucas Osiander: cujus pa- raphrasis hic conferri poterit nostræ explicationi geminæ. Pleniorem tamen textus totius evo- lutionem hic exhibitam esse, lector pie erudi- tus, ἄνω προκρίματος hæc expensurus, spero, agnoscet.

Explicat sese mutuo Jacobea hæc sententia,

ἔσται μακάριος ἐν τῇ ποιήσει αὐτõ ἔσται; & illa Christi Luc. XI. 28. Μακάριοι οἱ ἀκούοντες τὸν λόγον τõ θεõ, καὶ φυλάσσοντες αὐτόν. Conf. & Matth. 12, 49. cum Joh. VI, 40. Judico autem, dum hæc concepi, in B. Waltheri explicationem, quoad v. 25. in harmonia, quam totam nostræ consonam probo (nisi quod legem Regiam v. 14. non arbitrer de Evangelio accipi:) simplicissime, inquit, Jacobus credendus est, non de Decalogo, quod Paulus facit, sed de Evangelio loqui, quod hactenus appellaverat sermonem veritatis, sermonem insitum & legem Re- giam, illud jam in lata significatione cognominat le- gem, id est, doctrinam libertatis, ab effectu nimirum, quoniam credentes vindicat in veram filiorum Dei libertatem, de qua Christus Joh. VIII, 36. dixit: Si Filius vos liberaverit, vère liberi estis. Eodem sensu Paulus Evangelium vocat legem fidei, Rom. III, 27. & legem Spiritus, quo se liberatum esse ait à peccato & morte, Roman. VIII, 2. De lege Mosaica Jacobi verba intelligere, certe nec scopus sinit, nec epitheton, quia lex illa in Novo Testamento ubique est servitu- tis, non libertatis. Et porro: Cap. eodem, vers. eo- dem, factor operis beatus prædicatur in facto suo. Quum gratia Dei salvemur, non operibus nostris, Eph. II, 8. 9. Resp. 1. Hoc loco non de lege sermo est, sed de Evangelio. In antecedentibus enim Aposto- lus hoc vult dicere: Qui intuetur in doctrinam Ev- angelii, quæ conscientiis veram affert pacem & li- bertatem, & in ea doctrina fide apprehensa constanter perseveraverit, ita ut totus se ad eam accommodet, is salutem consequetur, non quia auditor fuit verbi DEI, sed quia huic credidit & paruit. Econtra sa- lutem sibi polliceri non debent, qui satis esse putant, si de Evangelio splendide & magnifice loqui possint, & interim Evangelium in ipsorum cordibus nullas agat radices, neque quicquam pietatis in ipso depre- hendatur. 2. Factor itaque operis credens est, qui fidem hausit ex Evangelio, quod Christus ipse testa- tur, quippe qui non solum Joh. VI, 29. Judæis di- xit: Hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in eum, qui misit me, verum etiam Matth. VII, 21. & cap. XII, 50. in hæc erupit verba: Quicunque FECERIT volun- tatem Patris mei, intrabit in regnum cælorum, & meus frater est, &c. Ubi certe primario de fide lo- quitur, qua Evangelium ipsius debemus amplecti. At- que hinc 3. de ejusmodi factore operis seu credente hic non dicitur, quod beatus sit ἐν τῷ ἔργῳ in opere, ne quis hoc de lege accipiat, sed ἐν ποιήσει in operatio- ne sua, sive in facto suo, ut Vulgatus vertit, & Lu- therus in seiner That, hoc est in obedientia verbi, quæ supponit fidem, in qua sola credens salvus erit, & beatus juxta illud Habacucci II. v. 4. Justus fide sua vivet. Hanc ego cum Osiandro commodiffimam loci hujus expositionem esse judico. Alias hic textus simpliciter pugnaret cum doctrina Pauli. Facit etiam huc illud Calvini ad v. 25. Postquam, inquit, de inani speculatione loquutus est, nunc ad penetra- bilem illum intuitum descendit, qui nos in Dei simi- litudinem transformat. Oppositio in προτάσει in- ter virum & mulierem quodvis speculum obiter in- tueatur, fœmina contra attente & diu speculum aspi- cie, ut se comat atque ornet, est, quam ut fundari possit in voce ἀνήρ.

## 1:26
Vers. 26.

Εἴ τις δοκεῖ θρῆσκος εἶναι ἐν ὑμῖν.] More frequently θρησκεύτης, which is explained in the glossary as religious. But Hesychius also finds θρῆσκος elsewhere. The Syriac and Arabic translate it as serving God. And δοκεῖ is סבר in the Syriac, he thinks.

Μὴ χαλιναγωγῶν γλῶσσαν αὐτοῦ.] He often reproves evil-speaking, because he saw that this vice reigned widely among the Hebrews. And the comparison taken from a bridle is frequent in this matter. For thus Euripides said, ἀχαλίνων στομάτων τέλος δυστυχίαν (the end of unbridled mouths is misfortune). Such is also Psalm XXXIX, 2. The Greeks say γλώσσης κρατεῖν (to control the tongue). After the Apostle has dealt with faith as the first part of θρησκείας [religion]; now he deals with the second part of true θρησκείας or the Christian religion, namely piety, and primarily that which touches upon our own duties and those which touch our neighbor, as these fall more into the senses and are certain marks of the love of God, with which the love of neighbor coheres in an inseparable bond, 1 John 4:20, 21. He brings forward three special works of piety, which seemed most to need urging among the Hebrews living ἐν διασπορᾷ [in the dispersion], as fruits and exercises of true faith: 1. The bridling of the tongue, v. 26. 2. Sincere conversation, and 3. Separation from the world. Which last, however, is so constituted that it also comprehends the immediate worship of God, as that by which we separate ourselves entirely from the world. As to the bridling of the tongue, because we sin not only by evil-speaking against our neighbor, but primarily by blasphemy against God, and indeed also by filthy and idle talk, therefore in all these things there is need of a bridle, concerning which James is about to treat as if of set purpose in chapter III. Cf. Eph. 4:29, 31; ch. 5:4; Ps. 39:2; Prov. 12:14; ch. 21:23.

Ἀλλὰ ἀπατῶν καρδίαν αὑτῶ [But deceiving his own heart]. A Hebrew idiom, as can be seen in Job 31:27. He deludes himself with a vain hope. The Syrian [translates] מטעיא לה לבה [he leads his heart astray], with כרקא in the Syrian, and באטלה in the Arabic.

Τότε μάταιος ἡ θρησκεία [Then his religion is vain]. Such an imaginary religion will profit him nothing. Μάταιος, which lacks effect, Acts 15:17; Tit. 3:9. And θρησκεία is used here as a general term, so that it may comprehend both good and bad religion. See Wisd. 14:18, 27. That is apparent from what follows. This saying is especially to be considered in this century.

Because very many think little of sins concerning the abuse of the tongue, the Apostle teaches that such people not only deceive their own heart, but that all their θρησκεία [religion] is vain. It is clear, however, from this and the following verse, that the word θρησκεία in general denotes the worship of God, or religion, and ought not, with Salmeron, to be restricted to the worship and vows by which the religious in the Papacy, so called falsely, strive. Salmeron wished to designate those who have followed the perfection of Christ by a stricter bond of counsels. Which Justinian and Corn. à Lapide rightly reject. The name θρῆσκος, which originated from the Thracians, as Plutarch, Suidas, and others observe, whom Orpheus taught the rites and ceremonies by which he thought God wished to be worshipped, is general, denoting the worship and veneration of GOD, Wisd. 14:18, 27; Acts 16:5; Col. 2:18, 23. And any faithful man is θρῆσκος [religious], worshipping God decently: To these things James directs his speech universally to those to whom he writes, not specifically to I know not what religious [orders].

Latin:

Vers. 26.

Εἴ τις δοκεῖ θρῆσκος εἶναι ἐν ὑμῖν.] Frequentius θρησκεύτης, quod in glossario exponitur religiosus. Sed θρῆσκος etiam Hesychius alibi reperit. Syrus & Arabs vertunt ministrans Deo. Et δοκεῖ סבר Syro existimat.

Μὴ χαλιναγωγῶν γλῶσσαν αὐτõ.] Sæpe reprehendit male- dicentiam, quod videret id vitium late regnare apud Ebræos. Et frequens in hac re comparatio à fræno desumta. Nam sic ἀχαλίνων στομάτων τέλος δυστυχίαν dixit Euripides. Talis & Psalm. XXXIX, 2. Græci dicunt γλώσσης κρατεῖν. Postquam de fide ceu prima parte θρησκείας egit Apostolus; jam de altera veræ θρησκείας vel religionis Christianæ parte, pietate agit, & imprimis ea, quæ nos ipsos, & quæ proximum attingunt, mu- nia attingit, utpote, quæ magis in sensus incurrunt, & notæ certæ sunt dilectionis Dei, cum qua nexu in- divulso cohæret proximi dilectio, 1. Joh. 4, 20. 21. Tria autem affert specialia pietatis opera, quæ maxime videbantur penes Ebræos ἐν διασπορᾷ agentes, ur- genda, ceu veræ fidei fructus & exercitia, 1. linguæ refrenatio v. 26. 2. Sincera conversatio, & 3. à mundo separatio. Quod postremum tamen ita compara- tum est, ut comprehendat quoque cultum Dei im- mediatum, utpote quo nos omnino à mundo sepa- ramus. Quod ad refrenationem linguæ, quia non ma- ledicentia tantum adversus proximum, sed imprimis blasphemia adversus Deum, imo spurcis quoque, & otiosis sermonibus peccamus, ideo in hisce omni- bus fræno opus est, quo de velut ex professo actu- rus Jacobus cap. III. Conf. Eph. IV, 29. 31. c. V, 4. Ps. XXXIX, 2. Prov. XII, 14. cap. XXI, 23.

Ἀλλὰ ἀπατῶν καρδίαν αὑτῶ.] Loquutio Ebræa, ut videre est Job. 31, 27. Lactat se vana spe. Syrus מטעיא לה לבה seducit sibi cor suum, כרקא Syro, Arabi באטלה.

Τότε μάταιος ἡ θρησκεία.] Nihil illi proderit talis imagi- naria religio. Μάταιος, quod effectu caret, Act. XV, 17. Tit. III, 9. Et dicitur hic θρησκεία voce ista generali, ut & bonam & malam religionem comprehendat. Vide Sap. XIV. 18. 27. Apparet id ex sequentibus. Dictum maxime hoc seculo co- gitandum.

Quia plurimi peccata, linguæ abusum concer- nentia parvi æstimant, tales non tantum cor suum seducere, sed omnem eorum θρησκείαν vanam es- se, docet Apostolus. Patet autem ex hoc, & sequenti versu, θρησκείας vocem in genere cultum Dei, vel re- ligionem notare, non autem cum Salmerone restrin- gi debere ad cultum, & vota, quibus religiosi in Papatu ψευδωνύμως ita dicti, nituntur. Salmero de- signari eos voluit, qui arctiori nexu consiliorum Christi perfectionem sequuti sint. Quod merito reprobant Justinianus & Corn. à Lapide. Nomen θρῆσκος, quod à Thracibus ortum, Plutarcho, Sui- dæ, aliisque observantibus, quos ritus & ceremo- nias, quibus Deum coli velle censuerit, Orpheus docuit, generale est, cultum ac venerationem DEI notans, Sap. XIV, 18. 27. Act. XVI, 5. Col. II, 18. 23. & θρῆσκος quivis homo fidelis est, Deum decenter colens: Ad hæc Jacobus sermonem universe diri- git ad eos, quibus scribit, non speciatim ad, nescio quos, religiosos.

## 1:27
Vers. 27. Θρησκεία καθαρὰ κὴ ἀμίαντος [Pure and undefiled religion]. True and unadulterated religion. A simile taken from gems, in which it is required that they be both sincere and not ulcerated. In the Manuscript this is connected not badly with the preceding in this way: Θρησκεία γάρ [For religion]. And thus the Syrian reads. Καθαρὰ [pure] is דכיו [pure], as also the Arab here. Ἀμίαντος [undefiled] is קדישתא [holy] in the Syrian, and טהרה [pure] in the Arabic.

Παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ κὴ Πατρὶ [Before God and the Father]. That is, in the estimation of God, who is also our Father. Καὶ [and] is placed here, as in 2 Cor. 1:3; Eph. 1:3, 4:6, 5:20; Phil. 4:20; Col. 1:3, 2:2; 1 Thess. 1:3, 3:11, 2:16.

Estius provides this coherence with the preceding doctrine: It is not enough that your religion is not vain, because you moderate your tongue. For it is not enough, to testify to the truth of religion, not to harm your neighbor by deeds or words; you must be of use to your neighbor, and keep yourself unspotted from the world.

Αὕτη ἐστὶν, ἐπισκέπτεσθαι ὀρφανὸς καὶ χήρας ἐν τῇ θλίψει αὐτῶν [This is, to visit the orphans and widows in their affliction]. The genus is understood from the species, as in Matt. 25:3. Thus, judge for the fatherless, defend the widow, in Isa. 1:16. True religion indeed requires faith, but it is perfected by two things especially, beneficence and purity of life. Ἐπισκέπτεσθαι [to visit] is taken here as in Matt. 25:36, 43. The Syrian here has מסעד [to support]. Ἐν τῇ θλίψει αὐτῶν [in their affliction], the Arab translates in their straits.

That it requires purity of life is certain; but that it is perfected primarily by these two things, I deny. For faith is the chief thing in it; which is followed next by love as its fruit, and purity of life, Gal. 5:6. However, we admit that by the species of the mentioned love, beneficence toward miserable persons, such as orphans and widows are in the highest degree—whence the care for them is so often commended to us in the sacred writings—is included as a genus.

Moreover, it requires beneficence above all, and does not hesitate to call it θρησκεία, lest they think that the worship of the first table alone suffices for θρησκεία and religion, and imitate the ways of the Pharisees, who under the pretext of religion consumed the houses of widows, Matt. 18:13, and because of Corban and sacrifices neglected beneficence and mercy, Matt. 7:11, 9:13. He teaches, therefore, that those who do not care for their neighbor do not sincerely worship God, 1 John 3:17, ch. 4:20.

By ἐπίσκεψις, therefore, are understood both the affection with effect, or both sincere commiseration proceeding from the heart, and the works of the same ἐυεργεσίας, so that those who are in need may be relieved by comfort, by counsel, and by help, Luke 7:16, Heb. 2:6. Concerning this visitation of widows and orphans, see Exod. 22:12, Deut. 24:17, 18, Isa. 1:16, for whose sake God calls Himself the Father of the fatherless and the defender of widows, Ps. 68:6. Cornelius à Lapide thinks that mention is made of them here particularly because, in the persecution of the Hebrews, many converted to the Christian faith were partly killed, partly cast into exile, partly shut up in prison, and stripped of all their goods, Acts 8:1, who left behind orphaned children and widowed wives.

To keep oneself unspotted from the world.] That is, from the evil examples of the world. See John 17:14, 1 John 2:15, ch. 5:19. We have had ἄσπιλοι also in 1 Tim. 6:14 and 2 Pet. 3:14. In Hebrew, one might translate it דלא מום. The Syriac here translates it דלא מומ, without spot. The same well translates τηρεῖν as למטר, to guard.

Ἄσπιλος, according to Suidas, is he who does not have a spot. Now, spots are called those splashes which are on garments, whence Jude v. 23 mentions a χιτῶνος ἐσπιλομένης, a spotted garment. But sins are those spots by which the garment of righteousness and holiness, with which both the reborn are adorned, Isa. 61, Col. 3:12, is defiled, Jas. 1:21, 2 Pet. 2:20, Rev. 3:4. By the world, however, are not understood here the impure men in the world, but impure desires, 1 John 2:15, 16; both meanings cannot hold at the same time. For it is not enough to avoid the company of the wicked, Wis. 13:1, Rom. 12:2, but one must also keep oneself ἄσπιλον from impure thoughts and desires, Matt. 15:19.

Latin:

Vers. 27. Θρησκεία καθαρὰ κὴ ἀμίαντος.] Religio vera & non adulterina. Similitudo sumpta à gemmis, in quibus re- quiritur, ut & sinceræ sint, & non ulceratæ. In Manuscripto hoc connectitur non male cum præcedentibus hoc modo: Θρησκεία γάρ. Et sic legit Syrus. Καθαρὰ דכיו quomodo & hic Arabs. Ἀμίαντος קדישתא sancta Syro, Arabi טהרה pura.

Παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ κὴ Πατρὶ.] Id est, ex existimatione Dei, qui & Pater est noster. Καὶ hic ponitur, ut 2. Cor. 1, 3. Eph. 1, 3. IV, 6. V, 20. Phil. 4, 20. Col. 1, 3. 2, 2. 1. Thess. 1, 3. 3, 11. 1. Thess. 2, 16.

Cohærentiam cum præcedenti doctrina hanc tradit Estius: Non sufficit, ut religio tua non sit va- na, quod linguæ tuæ moderaris. Nec enim satis est, ad testandum veritatem religionis, proximo nec factis, nec verbis nocere, prodesse oportet te proximo, & à mundo te ipsum custodire imma- culatum.

Αὕτη ἐστὶν, ἐπισκέπτεσθαι ὀρφανὸς καὶ χήρας ἐν τῇ θλίψει αὐτῶν.] Ex specie genus intelligitur, ut Matth. 25, 3. Sic jus dicite pupillo, defendite viduam, apud Esa. I, 16. Religio vera fidem quidem requirit, sed perficitur duabus maxime rebus, beneficentia & vitæ puritate. Ἐπισκέπτεσθαι hic sumitur, ut Matth. 25, 36. 43. מסעד Syrus hic. Ἐν τῇ θλίψει αὐτῶν, in angustiis earum vertit Arabs.

vitæ puritatem requirere, certum est; sed quod his- ce duabus rebus maxime perficiatur, nego. Nam præcipuum est in ea fides; quam sequitur deinceps ceu fructus dilectio, & vitæ puritas, Gal. V, 6. Spe- cie autem nominatæ dilectionis beneficentia erga miserabiles personas, quales maxime sunt orphani, & viduæ, unde toties in sacris cura ipsorum nobis commendata, genus comprehendi admittimus.

Beneficentiam autem imprimis requirit, & θρησκεί- av vocare non dubitat, ne ad θρησκείαν, & religio- nem solam primæ tabulæ cultum sufficere arbi- trentur, & Pharisæorum mores, qui prætextu reli- gionis viduarum domus absumebant, Matth. 18, 13. & ob Corban, & sacrificia negligebant beneficen- tiam & misericordiam, Matth. VII, 11. IX, 13. imi- tentur. Docet ergo, quod Deum sincere non co- lant, qui proximi curam non gerunt, 1. Joh. III, 17. c. IV, 20.

Per ἐπίσκεψιν ergo affectus cum effectu, seu tum sincera & ex corde profecta commiseratio, tum ejusdem opera ἐυεργεσίας quæcunque intelli- guntur, ut quibus opus est subveniatur tum solatio, tum consilio, tum auxilio, Luc. VII, 16. Ebr. II, 6. De hac viduarum & orphanorum visitatione vid. Exod. XXII, 12. Deut. XXIV, 17. 18. Es. I, 16. quorum causa Deus se Patrem pupillorum, & defensorem viduarum nominat, Psal. LXIIX, 6. Peculiariter autem hic de iis mentionem fieri putat Cornelius à Lapide, quod in Ebræorum persecutione multi con- versi ad fidem Christianam partim occisi, partim in exilium ejecti, partim in carcerem compacti, omnibusque bonis exuti fuerint, Act. IIX, 1. qui li- beros orphanos & uxores viduas reliquerint.

Ἄσπιλον ἑαυτὸν τηρεῖν ἀπὸ τῦ κόσμυ.] Id est, à malis mun- di exemplis. Vide Joh. 17, 14. 1. Joh. 2, 15. c. 5, 19. Ἄσπιλοι ha- buimus & 1. Tim. 6, 14, & 2. Petr. 3, 14. Ebraice vertere liceat דלא מוםש. Syrus hic דלא מומש sine macula. Idem τηρεῖν bene vertit למטר custodire.

Ἄσπιλος secundum Suidam est, ὁ μὴ ἔχων σπῖ- λον. Dicuntur autem σπῖλοι, quæ in vestitus ma- culosæ sunt aspergines, unde Jud. v. 23. mentio χι- τῶνος ἐσπιλομένης tunicæ maculatæ. Peccata au- tem sunt maculæ illæ, quibus vestis justitiæ & san- ctitatis, qua utraque ornantur renati, Esa. LXI. Col. III, 12. fœdatur, Jac. I, 21. 2. Petr. II, 20. Apoc. III, 4. Per mundum autem hic non intelliguntur impuri in mundo homines, sed impuræ cupiditates, 1. Joh. II, 15. 16. utraque significatio simul locum habere non potest. Neque enim sufficit vitare conversa- tionem malorum, Sap. XIII, 1. Rom. XII, 2. sed ab impuris etiam cogitationibus & desideriis sese ἄσπιλον servare, Matth. XV, 19.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

He continues to warn about religion, that in it there is no respect of persons, because God chose the rich in faith, and the law of love regards the neighbor equally, and he teaches that those who boast of faith but do not have works cannot be saved by such faith: But as a profession of charity without the exhibition of charity is of no use, so faith destitute of works is dead in itself; but true faith must be demonstrated by works, otherwise it would be no better than the faith of demons, and truly dead, which is confirmed by the example of Abraham demonstrating justifying faith by the offering of Isaac, and also of Rahab receiving the messengers, and so he concludes, that as the body without breath is dead: So also faith without works.

There are therefore two parts: The former is information concerning προσωποληψίᾳ [respect of persons] up to v. 15. The latter concerning vain boasting of faith up to v. 26.

PART I. Information concerning προσωποληψίᾳ [respect of persons].

Vers. 1. Ἀδελφοί με [My brethren].] as above I, 2. 16. Μὴ ἐν προσωποληψίαις ἔχετε τὴν πίσιν τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χρισῦ τῆς δόξης [Do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory with respect of persons].] The Syrian rightly constructed these in this way: The faith of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. And ἔχετε [hold] is the same as κατέχετε [hold fast], Rom. I, 18. The faith of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. And it is called faith of glory just as faith of Jesus Christ, Gal. III, 22. Phil. III, 9. faith of the Son of God Gal. II, 20. for which elsewhere faith in Christ, as 1. Timoth. I, 13. 2. Tim. III, 15. This, therefore, is what he means: do not hold that faith which you have concerning the glory of Christ, or concerning Christ raised to the highest brightness, namely because of obedience, as if it were captive and ineffective, because of those considerations of qualities, which pertain nothing to the matter of Christ. Just as in judgments there is προσωποληψία [respect of persons], where the judge looks to something other than what is in the merits of the case, as we touched upon in Matth. XXII, 16. so in the Evangelical matter προσωποληψία is to prefer some over others on account of those things which pertain nothing to the Gospel. You would not easily find προσωποληψίαι in the plural number among the more elegant Greek writers. But our writers often make unusual plurals from usual singulars.

Because he had dealt with the showing of the offices of charity toward the forsaken, and had taught that this is true θρησκείαν [religion], but this προσωποληψία [respect of persons] was very common among the Hebrews and stood in the way, the Apostle warns specifically about the same. Estius's συνέχεια [connection] with v. 9, where he bids the poor to glory in their high estate, neither coheres because of other things interjected, nor does it fit the design. Therefore Lorinus more rightly joins it with those things which had been said about visiting widows and orphans. For one is warned that he is by no means to be considered religious who prefers a poor but pious man to a rich but impious man in false causes. Moreover, προσωποληψία is vicious where we favor one over another, not on account of the matter, but out of respect for the person. Pareus thinks the plural is used because of its many species, because one is judicial, which is condemned in Lev. XIX, 15. Deut. XVI. 9. Prov. XVIII, 5. another is extra-judicial: such as this one; which again arises from various considerations. Moreover, the faith of Christ, or in Christ, is understood concerning saving faith, which is the more famous acceptation, who is by no means called the Lord of glory because he was raised to the highest brightness on account of obedience, since he was in the form of God, which is the highest glory, before he emptied himself, which was done for our sake. Therefore his spontaneous obedience earned brightness for us, not for himself. But he is the Lord of glory, or, if you prefer, glorious, by Hebraism, so that there is no need for transposition. (Conf. Eph. I, 12. not only by reason of his divine nature, because as he is ὁμούσιος [consubstantial], so he is ἰσότιμος [equal in honor] to God the Father of the same essence and glory: But also by reason of his human nature, which was admitted into the κοινωνίαν [communion] of the divine Majesty, by which he emptied himself in the state of ταπεινώσεως [humiliation] for the sake of our redemption, which pertains to the full use, but having finished that, in the state of ὑπερυψώσεως [exaltation] he uses the same most fully, governing all things gloriously in heaven and on earth. Conf. 1. Cor. II, 8. Matth. XXIX, 18. Marc. XVI, 19. Eph. I, 20. To which full use of Majesty because Christ did not arrive until after his sufferings were endured, Luc. XXIV, 26. Ebr. I, 3. we are warned not to despise the poor, since the Lord of glory himself, when he was rich, willed to be poor, that he might make us rich, 2. Cor. IIX, 6. whence faith in Christ does not suffer the rejection of the poor, to whom they are to be conformed in poverty, one day also to be glorified with him Rom. IX, 17. 29.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Pergit de religione monere, quod in ea non sit respectus personarum, quia Deus divites in fide elegit, & lex dilectionis proximum ex æquo respicit, docetque eos, qui fidem ja- ctant, opera autem non habent, fide tali servari non posse: Sed uti nulli usui est professio charitatis sine charitatis exhibi- tione, ita fidem operibus destitutam mor- tuam esse in se ipsa; fidem autem veram demonstrandam operibus, alioquin non meliorem fore fide Dæmonum, vereque mortuam, quod exemplo Abrahæ oblatio- ne Isaaci fidem justificantem demonstran- tis, nec non Rahabe, nuncios suscipienti confirmatur, adeoque concludit, ut corpus sine respiratione mortuum est : Ita & fides sine operibus.

Partes itaque duæ sunt: Prior est informatio de προσωποληψίᾳ ad v. 15. Posterior de vana fide jactantia ad v. 26.

PARS I. Informatio de προσωποληψίᾳ.

Vers. 1. Ἀδελφοί με.] ut supra I, 2. 16. Μὴ ἐν προσωποληψίαις ἔχετε τὴν πίσιν τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χρισῦ τῆς δόξης.] Recte hæc construxit Syrus hoc modo : Τὴν πίσιν τῆς δόξης τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χρισῦ. Et ἔχετε idem est, quod κατέχετε, Rom. I, 18. Τὴν πίσιν τῆς δόξης τῦ Κυ- ρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χρισῦ. Et dicitur πίσις δόξης sicut πίσις Ἰησοῦ Χρισῦ, Gal. III, 22. Phil. III, 9. πίσις τῦ ὑῦ τῦ Θεῦ Gal. II, 20. pro quo alibi πίσις ἐν Χρισῷ, ut 1. Timoth. I, 13. 2. Tim. III, 15. Hoc ergo vult, ne fidem illam, quam habetis de Christi glo- ria, sive de Christo in summam claritatem evecto, nempe pro- pter obedientiam, detinete velut captivam & inefficacem, propter respectus illos qualitatum, nihil ad rem Christi per- tinentium. Sicut in judiciis est προσωποληψία, ubi alia re- spicit judex, quam quæ sunt in causæ meritis, ut attigimus Matth. XXII, 16. ita in Evangelica re προσωποληψία est alios aliis præferre ob ea, quæ ad Evangelium nihil pertinent. Προσωποληψίαι in numero multitudinis haud facile reperias apud elegantiores Scriptores Græcos. Sed nostri scriptores pluralia inusitata sæpe faciunt de singularibus usitatis.

Quia de exhibendis charitatis officiis adversus derelictos egerat, eamq; veram θρησκείαν esse do- cuerat, huic autem προσωποληψία valde communis inter Hebræos obstabat, peculiariter de eadem mo- net Apostolus. Estii συνέχεια cum v. 9. quo paupe- res in sublimitate sua gloriari jubet, neq; cohæret propter alia interjecta, neque instituto congruit. Ideo Lorinus rectius conjungit cum iis, quæ de vi- sitandis viduis, & pupillis dicta erant. Moneri enim, neutiquam religiosum censendum, qui pau- perem, sed pium, diviti sed impio in falsis causis præfert. Προσωποληψία autem vitiosa est, ubi uni favemus præ altero, non ob rei, sed personæ respe- ctum. Pluralem adhiberi censet Pareus ob plures ejus species, quod alia sit judicialis, quæ damnatur Lev. XIX, 15. Deut. XVI. 9. Prov. XVIII, 5. alia ex- tra judicium : qualis hic; quæ iterum è variis respe- ctibus oritur. Fides autem Christi, vel in Christum de fide salvifica, quæ famosior est acceptio, intelli- gitur, qui neutiquam Dominus gloriæ dicitur, quod ad claritatem summam propter obedientiam eve- ctus, siquidem in forma Dei erat, quæ gloria sum- ma est, antequam sese exinaniret, quod nostri cau- sa factum. Obedientia ergo sua spontanea nobis claritatem meruit, non sibi. Dominus autem gloriæ est, vel, si mavis, gloriosus, per Ebraismum, ut opus non sit trajectione. (Conf. Eph. I, 12. non tantum ratione divinæ naturæ, quia ut ὁμούσιος, ita ἰσότι- μος Deo Patri ejusdem essentiæ & gloriæ: Sed et- iam ratione humanæ, quæ in κοινωνίαν divinæ Maje- statis admissa, qua se in statu ταπεινώσεως redem- ptionis nostræ gratia ἐκένωσε, quod ad usum plena- rium, sed peracta illa in statu ὑπερυψώσεως utitur eadem plenissime, gloriose omnia in cœlo, & in terra gubernans. Conf. 1. Cor. II, 8. Matth. XXIX, 18. Marc. XVI, 19. Eph. I, 20. Ad quam Majestatis plenariam χρῆσιν quia Christus non provenit nisi post exantlatas passiones, Luc. XXIV, 26. Ebr. I, 3. pauperes ne contemnamus monemur, quum ipse Dominus gloriæ, cum dives esset, pauper esse vo- luerit, ut divites nos redderet, 2. Cor. IIX, 6. unde fides inChristum non patitur reprobationem pau- perum, cui conformentur in paupertate olim cum ipso etiam glorificandi Rom. IX, 17. 29.

## 2:2
