Ἐὰν γὰρ εἰσέλθῃ εἰς τὴν συναγωγὴν ὑμῶν ἀνὴρ [For if there come into your assembly a man].] Although later usage has received that synagogue is said of the assembly of the Jews, but Church is said of the assembly of Christians, nevertheless we have shown that Ἐκκλησίαν [Church] is very often said of the assembly of the Jews at Matth. XVI, 18. and conversely Synagogue of Christian assemblies, Acts XV, 21. And the preceding words show that this word is to be taken in this way entirely. Ἀνὴρ [a man] שִׁיש, that is, someone.

Χρυσοδακτύλιος [Gold-ringed].] Not inelegantly he made a compound name after the likeness of others which were accepted in Greek. A gold ring, no less among the ancient Hebrews than among other nations, was the adornment of the honored and the wealthy, Gen. 38, 18. 25. chap. 41, v. 42. Isa. 3. v. 19.

Ἐν ἐσθῆτι λαμπρᾷ.] Splendidly dressed כבגדי החמודת, Gen. 27, 15. See Luke 16, 19. Rev. 15, 6. where the Hebrew word ההום, which the Arab uses here, ch. 18, 14. ch. 19, 8. ch. 22, 16. Menander: Λαμπρῶς τε πλᾶτῳ κἂν γένει καυχώμενον. The following opposition also shows this meaning. The Syrian translates λαμπρᾷ as שפירא beautiful. The Arab in the same sense.

Εἰσέλθῃ δὲ πτωχός.] That is, a poor man. For the word πτωχὸς is not rarely used in this way by writers, as can be seen in Mark 12, 41. Luke 14, 13. In Arabic it is משכן, just as מסכן, Eccles. 4, 12. Hence the Italian Mesquino.

Ἐν ῥυπαρᾷ ἐσθῆτι.] A garment neither neat nor elegant לבוש צואים, בגדים צואים, Zech. III, 3. 4. Thus Cicero from Caecilius: Often there is wisdom even under a shabby cloak. Virgil: The sordid garment hangs from the shoulders in a knot. Thus Zech. 3, 3. & 4. בגדים צואים is translated ἱμάτια ῥυπαρά.

Latin:

Ἐὰν γὰρ εἰσέλθῃ εἰς τὴν συναγωγὴν ὑμῶν ἀνὴρ.] Quanquam usus posterior recepit, ut synagoga de cœtu Judæorum, de cœtu vero Christianorum Ecclesia dicatur, tamen & Ἐκκλησίαν sæpissime dici de cœtu Judæorum ostendimus ad Matth. XVI, 18. & contra Synagogam de cœtibus Christianis, Acton XV, 21. Et ita omnino sumendam hanc vocem ostendunt verba præcedentia. Ἀνὴρ שִׁיש, id est, aliquis.

Χρυσοδακτύλιος.] Non ineleganter fecit nomen compositum ad instar aliorum, quæ in Græco erant recepta. Annulus aureus, non minus apud veteres Ebræos, quam apud alias gentes gestamen honoratorum ac ditiorum, Gen. 38, 18. 25. cap. 41, v. 42. Esa. 3. v. 19.

Ἐν ἐσθῆτι λαμπρᾷ.] Vestitum splendide כבגדי החמודת, Gen. 27, 15. Vide Luc. 16, 19. Apocal. 15, 6. ubi vox Ebræa ההום, quam hic usurpat Arabs, cap. 18, 14. c. 19, 8. c. 22, 16. Menander : Λαμπρῶς τε πλᾶτῳ κἂν γένει καυχώμενον. Ostendit hunc sensum & sequens oppositio. Syrus λαμπρᾷ vertit שפירא pulchra. Arabs eodem sensu.

Εἰσέλθῃ δὲ πτωχός.] Id est, homo pauper. Nam sic vox πτωχὸς non raro apud Scriptores sumitur, ut videre est Marc. 12, 41. Luc. 14, 13. Arabi est משכן, sicut מסכן, Eccles. 4, 12. Hinc Italicum Mesquino.

Ἐν ῥυπαρᾷ ἐσθῆτι.] Veste nec nitida nec elegante לבוש צואים, בגדים צואים, Zach. III, 3. 4. Sic Cicero ex Cæcilio : Sæpe est etiam sub palliolo sordido sapientia. Virgilius : Sordiduo ex humeris nodo dependet amictus. Sic Zach. 3, 3. & 4. בגדים צואים vertitur ἱμάτια ῥυπαρά.

## 2:3
Vers. 3.

Καὶ ἐπιβλέψητε τὸν φορῦντα τὴν ἐσθῆτα τὴν λαμπρὰν.] Ἐπιβλέπειν in this place is indeed what the Latins call to look up to.

Καὶ εἴπητε ἀυτῷ.] You, namely, who have the care of these matters, that is, the deacons. See the Constitutions of Clement II, 57. 58. The passage is significant. In the manuscript, αὐτῷ is missing here, so that the σὺ which follows may be demonstrative.

Σὺ κάθου ὧδε καλῶς.] That is, decorously, honorably, the Arab. In the Church there are also their own orders of seats, but based on virtues, not on wealth. Tertullian in his Apology: The approved elders preside, having obtained this honor not by price but by testimony. Thus among women the first place belongs to widows who have had one husband, the next to virgins, then to matrons. James, however, rightly, when he had understood that the custom had prevailed of giving precedence based on wealth rather than virtues, opposes this evil which would draw many evils after it. Also in the republic, that excellent saying of Sallust, or another, who gives advice to C. Caesar: Therefore, first of all, take away the authority of money: let no one judge more or less regarding status or honor based on resources: let neither praetor nor consul be created from opulence, but from dignity.

Καὶ τῷ πτωχῷ εἴπητε, σὺ στῆθι ἐκεῖ.] Young men were accustomed to stand a great deal. Philo on the contemplative life: The young men standing by. Clement in the cited place of the constitutions II, 57. Let the younger ones sit separately, if there is room, but if not, let them stand upright.

Ἢ κάθου ὧδε ὑπὸ τὸ ὑποπόδιόν με.] At my feet, which is the place of learners. See what we said on Acts 22, 3. That ὧδε is absent here in the manuscript.

Nomen synagogæ Act. XV, 21. is not understood of the assemblies of Christians, but of Jews: in which from ancient times Moses was read. Ἐπισυναγωγή, however, occurs regarding Christian assemblies, Heb. X, 22. and the word συναγωγῆς is used for any collection by the LXX, Job VIII, 17. Jer. XXXI, 4. 13. Ezech. XXXVII, 10. Zeph. III, 9. Which we understand not of any assembly generally, whether public, or private, or civil or Ecclesiastical, with Thomas the Englishman, Salmeron, Gagneius, Serarius, Lorinus, Cornelius, but rather specifically of a sacred or Ecclesiastical assembly, with Justinianus and other interpreters, in which he who prefers a rich but impious man to a pious poor man, with contempt for the latter, commits a scandal. Conf. 1 Cor. XI, 20. seqq. That there were different seats in sacred assemblies, some more exalted than others, can be gathered from verse 3. For he does not write that he says this to those who render due honor to honorable men, Rom. XIII, 7. 1. Petr. II, 17. but to those who, having no regard for piety and probity, honor rich men and those proud in splendid attire, while the poor, however pious, are superciliously despised, Eccl. X, 5. 6. For by that word ἐπιβλέψητε is indicated the affection of men admiring and valuing external splendor. For what we admire and magnify, that we look upon intently, and regard with reverence and veneration. The signs of contempt for the extremely poor are here, both because they are ordered to stand in sacred assemblies, which is the task of servants, and because they are told to sit in the most despised places.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Καὶ ἐπιβλέψητε τὸν φορῦντα τὴν ἐσθῆτα τὴν λαμπρὰν.] Ἐπιβλέπειν hoc quidem loco est, quod Latini dicunt suspicere.

Καὶ εἴπητε ἀυτῷ.] Vos nempe, qui curam habetis rerum istarum, id est, diaconi. Vide Clementis constitutiones II, 57. 58. Locus est insignis. In Manuscripto hic deest αὐτῷ, ut nimirum quod sequitur σὺ sit δεικτικόν.

Σὺ κάθου ὧδε καλῶς.] Id est, decore, honorate, Arabs. In Ecclesia sunt & sui sedilium ordines, sed ex virtutibus, non ex opibus. Tertullianus Apologetico : Præsident probati quique seniores, honorem istum non pretio sed testimonio adepti. Sic inter fœminas primus locus viduis univiris, proximus virginibus, deinde matronis. Recte vero Jacobus, cum intellexisset, morem invaluisse dandi προεδρίαν ex opibus non ex virtutibus, huic malo multa post se mala tracturo occurrit. Etiam in republica egregium illud Salustii, sive alterius, qui. C. Cæsari dat consilium : Ergo imprimis autoritatem pecuniæ demito : neque de capite, neque de honore ex copiis quisquam magis aut minus judicaverit : neque prætor neqs consul ex opulentia, verum ex dignitate creetur.

Καὶ τῷ πτωχῷ εἴπητε, σὺ στῆθι ἐκεῖ.] Juvenes multum stare solebant. Philo de vita contemplativa : Οἱ παρεστῶτες νέοι. Clemens constitutionum dicto loco II, 57. Οἱ μὲν νεώτεροι ἰδίᾳ καθιζέσθωσαν, ἐὰν ᾖ τόπος, εἰ δὲ μὴ, στηκέτωσαν ὀρθοί.

Ἢ κάθου ὧδε ὑπὸ τὸ ὑποπόδιόν με.] Ad pedes meos, qui locus discentium. Vide quæ diximus ad Act. 22, 3. Illud ὧδε hic abest in Manuscripto.

Nomen synagogæ Act. XV, 21. non de cœtibus Christianorum, sed Judæorum accipitur: in quibus à temporibus antiquis Moses legebatur. Ἐπισυναγωγή autem occurrit de Christianis conventibus, Ebr. X, 22. & de quavis collectione vox συναγωγῆς apud LXX. adhibetur Job. IIX, 17. Jer. XXXI, 4.13. Ezech. XXXVII, 10. Soph. III 9. Quam non de cœtu quovis generatim sive publico, sive privato, sive civili seu Ecclesiastico cum Thoma Anglico, Salmerone, Gagnejo, Serario, Lorino, Cornelio, sed potius specialiter de cœtu sacro, vel Ecclesiastico, cum Justiniano aliisque Interpretibus intelligimus, in quo qui divitem, sed impium pauperi pio cum hujus contemptu præfert, scandalum committit. Conf. 1. Cor. XI, 20. seqq. In cœtibus sacris fuisse diversa sedilia, alia aliis sublimiora, è vers. 3. colligere est. Non enim illis dicam scribit, qui viris honoratis debitum honorem deferunt, Rom. XIII, 7. 1. Petr. II, 17. sed qui nulla habita pietatis & probitatis ratione homines divites & cultu splendido superbos honorant, pauperibus, quantumvis piis superciliose spretis, Eccl. X, 5. 6. Nam voce illa ἐπιβλέψητε indicatur affectus homi- num admirantium, & æstimantium splendorem ex- ternum. Quod enim admiramur & magnificamus, id intente aspicimus, & cum reverentia atque vene- ratione respicimus. Contemptus extremi paupe- rum indicia hic sunt, tum quod stare in cœtibus sa- cris jubeantur, quod ministrorum est, tum quod sessuri remandentur ad despectissima loca.

## 2:4
Ver. 4. Καὶ ὐ διεκρίθητε ἐν ἑαυτοῖς.] Have you not made a distinction among yourselves, that is, out of carnal affection? For these things are to be read interrogatively, as the Syrian reads. Διακρίνεσθαι is the same as the active διακρίνειν, Acts XI, 2. XV, 9. Jude v. 22.

Καὶ ἐγένεσθε κριταὶ διαλογισμῶν πονηρῶν.] The genitive here is not of the object, but of the attribute. You judge according to evil thoughts. For you prefer fleeting things to those that endure. We have διαλογισμὺς πονηρὺς also in Matthew XV, 9; κακοὺς in Mark VII, 2.

Others render it passively with Erasmus and the Tigurines: And you have not been judged among yourselves, that is, not convicted by your own judgment of respect of persons. Simpler is the active exposition of Grotius, which the Syrian and Vulgate, Vatablus, Beza, Pareus, Piscator, and Cornelius also hold. Similarly, most of those interpret κριτὰς διαλογισμῶν πονηρῶν not as judges of thoughts, but as judges of evil affections, not badly.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Καὶ ὐ διεκρίθητε ἐν ἑαυτοῖς.] Annon discrimen fecistis apud vos ipsos, id est, ex carnali affectu. Interrogative enim hæc legenda, quomodo legit Syrus. Διακρίνεσθαι idem, quod Activum διακρίνειν, Act. XI, 2. XV, 9. Judæ v. 22.

Καὶ ἐγένεσθε κριταὶ διαλογισμῶν πονηρῶν.] Genitivus hic est non objecti, sed attributi. Judicatis secundum malas co- gitationes. Præfertis enim caduca duraturis. Διαλογισμὺς πο- νηροὺς habemus & Matth. XV, 9. κακοὺς Marc. VII, 2.

Alii reddunt Passive cum Erasmo & Tigurinis: Et non dijudicati estis in vobismet ipsis, hoc est, non convicti proprio judicio acceptionis personarum. Simplicior est Grotii expositio activa, quam etiam tenent Syrus & Vulgatus, Vatablus, Beza, Pareus, Piscator & Cornelius. Similiter κριτὰς διαλογισμῶν πονηρῶν judices non certe affectus interpretantur plerique illi, non male.

## 2:5
Ver. 5. ᾿Ακούσατε.] That is, pay attention: as in Matthew XI, 13.

᾿Αδελφοί μυ ἀγαπητοὶ.] Thus 1 Cor. XV, 58. Eph. VI, 21. Col. IV, 7, 9. above I, 16, 19.

Οὐχὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἐξελέξατο τὺς πτωχὺς τῦ κόσμυ.] He set apart for Himself the very poor as His own possession. See Matthew XX, 16. 1 Thess. I, 4, and what was said at Eph. I, 4. And he said πλωχὺς τῦ κόσ- μυ, who seem poor to the world, so that he might better introduce the antithesis which follows.

Πλυσίυς ἐν πίσει.] Lest anyone should think that all the poor are set apart by God as His own possession, he adds, but rich in faith. For thus the word πλέτυ and πλυσίυ is taken in Rom. II, 4, Eph. II, 4, and elsewhere. Such people, however, are always found more in the flock of the poor than in that of the rich, for the reasons which we have brought forward at Matthew V, 3, and 1 Cor. I, 26.

Why should πλύσιοι ἐν πίσει be rendered as 'abundant in faith,' when it properly sounds as 'rich in faith'? Nor may one infer from abundance in God to the abundance of men, from the abundance of divine grace, Rom. I, 4, Eph. II, 4, to the abundance of our faith. Our faith never abounds. They are called rich in faith, just as they are rich in good works, 1 Tim. VI, 18, in which there is certainly no abundance. Furthermore, those who are rich in faith are called rich in God in Christ, Luke XII, 21, because they possess the highest treasure, God Himself, by true faith: who gives Himself entirely to us. Through faith we apprehend divine grace: because we apprehend Christ, from whose fullness we have grace for grace, John I, 17. Christ acquired for us, when He became poor for our sake, true riches 2 Cor. IIX, 9, which those who apprehend through faith are rendered rich in God, and are called πλέσιοι ἐν πίσει, not because their faith is rich, because even a very poor and languid faith is true faith, and apprehends heavenly riches in Christ, Matthew XVII, 20, Luke XVII, 6, but because faith enriches them, and renders them rich in Christ, in God, however poor they may be in the world, who are enriched with the treasure of divine grace and the merits of Christ, when they apprehend the same offered in the word through faith, 2 Cor. IV, 7. This is a periphrasis for believers, so that the opposition of the poor in the world and the rich in God through faith may be consistent. Which Piscator perverts by injecting the infinitive εἶναι or γί- νεσθαι, so that the accusative πλυσίυς is governed by the verb ἐξε- λέξατο, not by itself, but through that understood infinitive, lest he be forced to admit that the elect believe before they are elected, or are elected because they believe, namely, because of foreseen faith. But this is to add something of one's own to Scripture, so that James, even if unwilling, teaches that the poor are not elected as rich in faith; but that the poor are elected so that they may become rich in faith. But woe to him who adds! Woe to him who takes away! according to Tertullian. We are elected in Christ, as the Apostle testifies, Eph. I, 4. But we are not in Christ except through faith. Therefore, only those are finally elected who are in Christ through faith, or whose faith in Christ God foresaw. As without faith it is impossible to please God, Heb. XI, 6, so without faith no one could be elected. As they are not saved unless they believe, and because they believe: so neither were they elected from eternity to salvation unless those who were to believe, and because they were to believe. James teaches here who and what kind of people are those who are elected, namely, rich in faith, or those who apprehend the riches of divine grace and the merit of Christ through faith, and are enriched by them, but he does not teach to what end they are elected. He teaches that we should not show partiality in the faith of the Lord or in the Lord of glory: because God, in that very eternal election, looked to nothing but faith in Christ: in whom, he teaches, there is no partiality of persons, whether one be poor or rich in the world, and whatever other external partialities there may be, Acts 10:34, whose eyes look only to faith, Jeremiah 5:3. But just as faith alone makes us rich in God: so also faith alone saves us, and thus faith alone is what God looked to from eternity when He chose us for eternal salvation. And therefore, when James says that He has chosen the rich in faith, but not the rich in good works, he excludes both the absolute election of the Calvinists, by which the foresight of faith is excluded in those being chosen, and the Papistic election from the merits of works: because before we had done anything good or evil, God chose us in Christ, whom He foresaw would believe in Christ and be rich in faith, ἵνα ἦ καθ᾽ ἐκλογὴν τῶ Θεῶ πρόθεσις μένῃ ἐκ ἐξ ἔργων, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ τῶ καλῶντος, Romans 9:11, Ephesians 1:4. But if it pleases one to understand 'rich in faith' not effectively, as those who are rich through faith, even if they are poor in the world: but attributively, as those whose faith is rich; one must nevertheless take care that those whose faith is needy, who are less rich in faith in συγκρίσει (comparison) with others, are not excluded from election. For our salvation does not depend on the richness or poverty, the intensity or remission of faith; nor is faith viewed by God in the category of quality, and in divine election, but in the category of relation. Properly, therefore, faith in Christ is not needy, but most rich, because it apprehends the most rich riches of Christ, and thus it is objectively rich, whatever and however great it may be subjectively. For we must not boast of our own riches, whether of faith or of works, but solely in the Lord, 1 Corinthians 1:31.

And heir of the kingdom which He promised to those who love Him.] That 'and' is more correctly absent in the Manuscript: And it is understood that they were to be heirs, which the Syriac supplied. Thus after 'He chose' follows 'to be' in Ephesians 1:4. But such words are often understood. That eternal kingdom is promised to those who love God, 1 Corinthians 2:9, 2 Timothy 4:8. Add Titus 1:2.

The inheritance is promised to those who love God, not because they love or on account of love, for it is purely gratuitous, the grace of God in Christ Jesus, Romans 6, last verse; nor is it acquired by love or good works, but it is obtained by the grace of God, who adopts us as heirs; the promise of the inheritance is not obtained διὰ νόμυ (through the law) or by the observance of the law, ἀλλὰ διὰ δικαιοσύνης πίςεως (but through the righteousness of faith), Romans 4:13. But if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is vain, the promise is made void, verse 14. If it is by grace, it is not by works, otherwise grace is not grace: If it is by works, it is not by grace, otherwise works are not works, Romans 11:6. Moreover, this description of the subject is added, that the inheritance is promised to those who love God, so that it may be taught that those who are rich in faith are the same ones who truly love God, and that love cannot be separated from faith, and that faith is boasted of in vain if charity is not present, 1 Corinthians 13:2, 3. Which the Apostle is subsequently about to confirm more fully.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ᾿Ακούσατε.] Id est, animum attendite : ut Matth. XI, 13.

᾿Αδελφοί μυ ἀγαπητοὶ.] Sic 1. Cor. XV, 58. Ephes. VI, 21. Col. IV, 7. 9. supra I, 16. 19.

Οὐχὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἐξελέξατο τὺς πτωχὺς τῦ κόσμυ.] Pauperes plurimos sibi in peculium secrevit. Vide Matth. XX, 16. 1. Thess. I, 4. & quæ dicta ad Eph. I, 4. Et dixit πλωχὺς τῦ κόσ- μυ, qui mundo videntur pauperes, ut melius inferret ἀντίθε- τον, quod sequitur.

Πλυσίυς ἐν πίσει.] Ne quis putaret, pauperes omnes esse à Deo tanquam peculium ipsius sepositos, addit, sed ab- undantes fide. Nam ita vocem πλέτυ & πλυσίυ sumi Rom. II, 4. Eph. II, 4. & alibi. Tales autem plures semper reperti in pauperum, quam in divitum grege, ob causas, quas attuli- mus ad Matth. V, 3. & 1. Cor. I, 26.

Cur πλύσιοι ἐν πίσει reddendi abundantes in fi- de, quum proprie sonet divites in fide? Neque ab abundantia in Deo ad abundantiam hominum, ab abundantia gratiæ divinæ, Rom. I, 4. Eph. II, 4. ad abundantiam fidei nostræ colligere liceat. Nun- quam fides nostra abundat. Divites in fide dicun- tur, ut divites in bonis operibus 1. Tim. VI, 18, in qui- bus sane non est abundantia. Porro qui in fide divi- tes sunt, divites in Deo dicuntur Christo, Luc. XII, 21. quia thesaurum summum, Deum ipsum, vera fi- de possident: qui se totum nobis donat. Per fidem apprehendimus divinam gratiam: quia apprehen- dimus Christum, è cujus plenitudine habemus gra- tiam pro gratia, Joh. I, 17. Christus acquisivit nobis, cum pauper factus est propter nos, veras divitias 2. Cor. IIX, 9. quas qui per fidem apprehendunt, divites in Deo redduntur, & dicuntur πλέσιοι ἐν πίσει, non quorum fides dives est, quia fides etiam paupercula & languidula vera fides est, ac divitias cœlestes apprehendit in Christo, Matth. XVII, 20. Luc. XVII, 6. sed quos fides ditat, ac divites in Chri- sto, in Deo reddit, utut in mundo illi pauperrimi sint, qui thesauro gratiæ divinæ, & meritorum Christi ditantur, cum eundem in verbo oblatum per fidem apprehendunt, 2. Cor. IV, 7. Est hæc περί- φρασις credentium, ut oppositio pauperum in mun- do, & divitum in Deo per fidem constet. Quam Pi- scator pervertit, ingerendo infinitivum εἶναι seu γί- νεσθαι, ut Accusativus πλυσίυς regatur à verbo ἐξε- λέξατο, non per se, sed mediante illo Infinitivo subintellecto, ne admittere cogatur, electos credere, antequam eligantur, vel eligi, quia credant, ob præ- visam nempe fidem. Sed hoc est de suo aliquid scri- pturæ addere, ut Jacobus vel invitus doceat, non eligi pauperes, divites fide; sed eligi pauperes, ut divi- tes fide fiant. Væ autem addenti! Væ detrahenti! se- cundum Tertullianum. Electi sumus in Christo, teste Apostolo, Eph. I, 4. At in Christo non sumus, nisi per fidem. Illi ergo demum electi, qui per fidem in Christo sunt, vel quorum fidem in Christum prævi- dit Deus. Ut sine fide impossibile est Deo placere, Ebr. XI, 6. ita sine fide eligi nemo potuit. Ut non salvan- tur, nisi qui credunt, & quia credunt : Ita nec electi sunt ab æterno ad salutem, nisi qui credituri, & quia credituri erant. Docet hic Jacobus, qui, & quales sunt, qui eliguntur, divites nempe in fide, vel qui di- vitias gratiæ divinæ & meriti Christi per fidem appre- hendunt, & iisdem ditantur, non autem docet, in quem finem eligantur. Respectum personarum non attendere fidem Domini vel in Dominum gloriæ do- cet: quia Deus non respexit in ipsa æterna electione ad gloriam, nisi fidem in Christum: penes quem do- cet, nullus est personarum respectus, sive pauper quis sit, sive opulentus in mundo, & qui alii sint re- spectus externi, Act. X, 34. cujus oculi solum fidem respiciunt, Jerem. V, 3. Quemadmodum autem sola fides nos divites reddit in Deo : Ita etiam sola fides nos salvat, adeoque sola fides est, quam Deus ab æterno respexit, cum nos ad salutem æternam ele- git. Ideoque cum Jacobus divites in fide, non vero divites in operibus bonis elegisse dicit, & absolutam Calvinianorum electionem, per quam prævisio fi- dei in eligendis excluditur, & Papisticam electio- nem ex meritis operum excludit: quia antequam boni vel mali quicquam fecissemus, elegit nos Deus in Christo, quos credituros in Christum prævidit divi- tes in fide, ἵνα ἦ καθ᾽ ἐκλογὴν τῶ Θεῶ πρόθεσις μένῃ ἐκ ἐξ ἔργων, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ τῶ καλῶντος, Rom. IX, 11. Eph. I, 4. Si autem placeat divites in fide non effective in- telligere, qui per fidem divites sunt, etsi pauperes sint in mundo: Sed attributive, quorum fides dives est; id tamen cavendum, ne ab electione excludantur, quorum fides egena est, qui minus opulenti sint fide in συγκρίσει cum aliis. Non enim à fidei vel opulenta, vel paupertate, intensione vel remissione sa- lus nostra dependet; nec fides in prædicamento qualitatis spectatur à Deo, & in electione divina, sed in prædicamento relationis. Proprie ergo fides in Christum egena non est, sed opulentissima, quia di- vitias Christi opulentissimas apprehendit, & ita objective dives est, qualiscunque & quantulacun- que ea subjective sit. Non enim de nostris divitiis sive fidei, sive operum, sed unice in Domino nobis gloriandum est, 1. Cor. I, 31..

Καὶ κληρονόμως τῆς βασιλείας ἧς ἐπαγγείλατο τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν ἀυτόν.] Illud κἀι rectius abest in Manuscripto : Et intelligi- tur, ut essent hæredes, quod supplevit Syrus. Sic post ἐξελέ- ξατο sequitur εἶναι Eph. I, 4. Talia autem verba sæpe subau- diuntur. Promissum est regnum illud æternum Deum diligen- tibus, 1. Cor. II, 9. 2. Tim. IV, 8. Adde Tit. I, 2.

Promissa est hæreditas illis, qui diligunt Deum, non quia diligunt vel ob dilectionem, mere enim gratuita est, χάρισμα Θεῶ ἐν Χρισῷ Ἰησῶ, Rom. VI. v. ult. nec acquiritur dilectione, vel operibus bo- nis, sed obtinetur gratia Dei, nos hæredes adoptan- tis, non διὰ νόμυ per legem, aut observationē legis obtingit promissio hæreditatis, ἀλλὰ διὰ δικαιοσύ- νης πίςεως, Rom. IV, 13. Si autem illi, qui ex lege sunt, hæredes sunt, vana est fides, evacuata est promissio. v. 14. Si ex gratia, non ex operibus, alioquin gratia non est gratia : Si ex operibus, non ex gratia, alioquin opera non sunt opera, Rom. XI, 6. Additur autem hæc subjecti descriptio, quod diligentibus Deum promissa hæreditas sit, ut doceatur, qui divites in fi- de sunt, eosdem Deum vere diligere, nec separari posse dilectionem à fide, ac frustra jactari fidem, si non adsit charitas. 1. Cor. XIII, 2. 3. Quod dein- ceps uberius confirmaturus est Apostolus.

## 2:6
Verse 6.

But you have dishonored the poor man.] Aorist for any time. Ἠτιμάσατε means you have held in contempt, as the Syriac here שׁוֹטֵ לְעַנְיָא, he who mocks the poor, Prov. XVII, 5. בּוֹשׁ כֹּחַ עַל־דַּל Amos V, 11. compare also Psalm X.

Do not the rich oppress you?] See, he says, with what pride, what insolence riches are wont for the most part to be accompanied, so that you may value them the less. In the manuscript ὑμᾶς by construction according to the sense. For καταδυναστεύειν is to oppress, as can be seen in Wisdom II, 10. XVII, 7. I answer with the Hebrew רָדָה, as we said at Matthew XX, 25, and מָשַׁל, as in Prov. XXII, 7, where the same words as here occur, but also with other words. It is the custom of the rich to act imperiously against the poor, to devote little effort to them. Finally—The liberty of the poor is this: The bruised man asks, and beaten with fists, he prays. Euripides says, Wealth begets insolence. Compare Ps. X, 2, 8, 9. There is also an excellent passage on this matter in the Aulularia of Plautus, Act II, Scene 2.

And they drag you into courts.] They drag into law, as Plautus speaks in the Curculio. Moreover, even in a just cause, the struggle in court is hard for a poor man against a rich one. Not only because judges often add to the rich man for the sake of favor, but also because the expenses of the lawsuit and the time spent on it burden the poor man. Therefore, it is wont to be said in contempt, 'Go, read,' as Donatus noted. He speaks, however, of the rich in general, not specifically of those who frequented the Church. You have an example in Acts XIII, 50.

Latin:

Verf. 6.

Ὑμεῖς δὲ ἠτιμάσατε τὸν πτωχὸν.] Ἀόριστος pro quovis tempore. Ἠτιμάσατε despicatui habuistis, ut hic Syrus שׁוֹטֵ לְעַנְיָא, ὁ καταγελῶν πτωχῷ, Prov. XVII, 5. בּוֹשׁ כֹּחַ עַל־דַּל Amofi V, 11. confer & Pfalm. X.

Οὐχὶ οἱ πλούσιοι καταδυναστεύουσιν ὑμῶν.] Videte, inquit, qua fastus, quæ infolentia divitias plerumque comitari foleat, quo eas minoris faciatis. In Manuscripto ὑμᾶς constructione πρὸς τὸ σημαινόμενον. Nam καταδυναστεύειν est opprimere, ut videre est Sap. II, 10. XVII, 7. Respondeo Ebræo רָדָה, ut diximus ad Matth. XX, 25. & מָשַׁל, ut Prov. XXII, 7. ubi eadem, quæ hic verba, sed & verbis aliis. Divitum mos est imperiofe agere adversus pauperes, operam, eorum parvi ducere. Denique - - - Libertas pauperis hæc est Contufus rogat, & pugnis concisus adorat. Ὕβριν τοι τίκτει πλοῦτος ait Euripides. Conf. Pf. X, 2. 8. 9. Est & in hanc rem egregius locus in Aulularia Plauti Act. II. Scen. 2.

Καὶ ἀυτοὶ ἕλκουσιν ὑμᾶς εἰς κριτήρια.] In jus rapiunt, ut Plautus loquitur Curculione. Est autem etiam in re æqua durum in judicio certamen pauperi cum divite. Non modo, quia fæpe judices ob gratiam addunt diviti, verum etiam quia & fumptus litis & temporis, quod in eam impenditur, gravat pauperem. Itaque per contemptum folet dici, age, lege, ut Donatus notavit. Agit autem de divibus in genere, non speciatim de iis, qui frequentabant Ecclesiam. Exemplum habes Act. XIII, 50.

## 2:7
Verse 7.

Do they not blaspheme the good name that was called upon you?] Among those rich men, many are found who so hate Christianity that they even curse Christ, by whose name you are called. It is a Hebrew idiom. My name is called upon him, that is, he is named from my name, Gen. 48:16, Isa. 4:1. Just as children are said to be named after their parents, and wives after their husbands; so Christians are named after Christ. A good name, that is, an honorable name. See concerning the word καλῶς above, 3.

The Apostle had said that the poor, rich in faith, were so highly valued by God that they were appointed by Him as heirs of the heavenly kingdom. He now commands that they themselves judge how great a crime it is to treat with insult him whom GOD has deemed worthy of such honor; this insult certainly redounds upon God, Prov. XXII, 2, Matth. XXV, 45. However, there does not seem to be a need for the verb to be taken in the Aorist for any time, or for it to indicate only what is wont to accompany riches: but it is likely that such things also prevailed among the Hebrews, and therefore such vices are noted at the same time as being contrary to the Royal Law of love, even if they are brought forward as an argument for avoiding partiality, so that the rich are not preferred in sacred assemblies, since experience has taught them that the rich oppress them through tyranny, καταδυναστεύουσι, which occurs concerning diabolical oppression itself, Acts X, 38, compare Sir. XIII, 24, and that they drag them to the tribunals without cause, so that they may be oppressed under the guise of right, Eccles. V, 7. That those who frequented the Church are being referred to, the scope of the Apostle teaches, because he warns about sacred assemblies: that the rich, through partiality, should not be preferred in them while the poor are despised. Such vices, found even among the Corinthians who had converted to the faith of Christ, are rebuked by Paul, 1 Cor. VI, 1. Therefore, such are said to blaspheme the name of the Lord, because they cause the name of the Lord to be blasphemed, both among the Gentiles and also among weak Christians, just as among the Hebrews the Kal is wont to be used for the Hiphil: which sense Piscator, Gagneius, Lorinus, Estius, Cornelius à Lapide, and Justinianus approve, and similar passages favor it, Rom. II, 24, 1 Tim. VI, 1, Tit. II, 5, 2 Pet. II, 2. For although they may not violently oppress other believers or drag them to tribunals without cause; yet who would deny that there are hypocrites among those who frequent the Church or are in the assembly of Christians, professing the faith of Christ but denying it by unjust deeds? Thus Blessed Höpfnerus, disp. XII, on justification, page 1072. Certain rich Christians abuse their wealth for pride and the oppression of other Christians, and

give occasion by these and other sins to the Gentiles to blaspheme the Christian religion. There is no need, therefore, for these things to be understood of those who hate Christianity and curse Christ, since through a common Hebraism it can be taken of those who cause Christ to be cursed, who blaspheme Christ not as physical but as moral causes of blasphemies, not from hatred of Christianity, but from opulence through pride and injustice. But the Apostle does not say that that good name, that is, the illustrious and glorious one, was 'called' upon them, but 'invoked' upon them, which difference Blessed Brochmandus notes here: Who indeed does not know that it is one thing for a name to be called upon someone, but another for a name to be invoked upon someone. The name of parents is certainly called upon children, Gen. XLVIII, 16, and of a husband upon a wife, Isa. IV, 1. But the name of God alone is invoked; as the entire New Testament Scripture testifies, Rom. X, 12, 13, 14, 1. Cor. I, 2. 2 Cor. I, 23. 2 Tim. II, 22. 1 Pet. I, 17. I consider, therefore, with Pareus and the Belgian interpreters not dissenting, that the Apostle here looks to baptism, in which the name of Christ is invoked upon him who is washed in that sacred bath, Matth. XXVIII, 19, Acts II, 38.

Latin:

Verf. 7.

Οὐκ ἀυτοὶ βλασφημοῦσι τὸ καλὸν ὄνομα τὸ ἐπικληθὲν ἐφ' ὑμᾶς.] Ex divitibus illis multi reperiuntur, qui ita odere Christianifmum, ut & Christo maledicant, ex cujus nomine vos vocamini. Locutio est Ebræa. Vocatur nomen meum super eum, id est, ille dicitur de meo nomine, Gen. 48, 16. Efa. 4, 1. Sicut filii de parentum, fœminæ de maritorum dicuntur nominibus; ita à Christo Christiani ὄνομα καλὸν, id est, nomen honorificum. Vide de voce καλῶς fupra 3.

Dixerat Apostolus tanti à Deo æstimavi pauperes divites fide, ut ab ipso constituantur hæredes regni cœlestis. Jubet jam, ut ipsi judicent, quantum sit scelus, eum contumelia afficere, quem DEUS tanto dignatus est honore; in Deum certe redundat hæc contumelia, Prov. XXII, 2. Matth. XXV, 45. Non autem videtur opus esse, ut Ἀορίστως de quovis tempore Verbum accipiatur, aut indicetur tantum, quidnam comitari soleat divitias : Sed verisimile est, ea etiam inter Ebræos obtinuisse, eoque talia vitia simul notari, ceu legi Regiæ dilectionis contraria, etsi in argumentum adducantur fugiendæ προσωποληψίας, ne præferantur divites in sacris cœtibus, quum experientia ipsos docuerit, quod divites per tyrannidem ipsos opprimant, καταδυναστεύουσι, quod de oppreffione ipsa diabolica, Act. X, 38. occurrit, conf. Sir. XIII, 24. quodque trahant citra causam ipsos ad tribunalia, ut sub specie recti opprimantur, Eccles. V, 7. Eos autem respici, qui frequentabant Ecclesiam scopus Apostoli docet, quia de conventibus sacris monet: ne divites per προσωποληψίαν, contemptis pauperibus, in iisdem præferantur. Qualia vitia etiam inter Corinthios, ad fidem Christi conversos, reperta à Paulo reprehenduntur, 1. Cor. VI, 1. Ideo blasphemare tales dicuntur nomen Domini, quod faciant, ut nomen Domini blasphemetur, tum penes gentiles, tum etiam penes infirmos Christianos, uti apud Ebræos Cal pro Hiphil adhiberi solet: quem sensum Piscator, Gagneius, Lorinus, Estius, Cornelius à Lapide, Justinianus probant, eique favent similia loca, Rom. II, 24. 1. Tim. VI, 1. Tit. II, 5. 2. Petr. II, 2. Quamvis enim fideles alios non opprimant violenter, aut ad tribunalia trahant immerito; tamen inter eos, qui frequentant Ecclesiam, vel in cœtu Christianorum sunt, hypocritas esse, fidem Christi profitentes, sed factis injustis abnegantes, quis neget? Ita B. Höpfnerus disp. XII. de justif. pag. 1072. Quidam Christiani divites opulentia sua abutuntur ad fastum & oppressionem reliquorum Christianorum, &

bis aliisque peccatis ansam præbent gentibus ad blas- phemandum religionem Christianam. Non ergo opus est, ut de iis hæc intelligantur, qui Christia- nismum odere, & Christo maledicunt, quum per usitatum Ebraismum de illis accipi possit, qui fa- ciunt, ut Christo maledicatur, qui blasphemant Christum non ut causæ physicæ sed morales blas- phemiarum, non ex Christianismi odio, sed ex opulentia per fastum & injustitiam. Nomen au- tem illud καλὸν, id est, præclarum & gloriosum non dicit Apostolus κληθὲν vocatum super ipsos, sed ἐπικληθὲν, invocatum, quam differentiam hic notat B. Brochmandus: Quis vero nescit, aliud esse, nomen aliquod super quempiam vocari, aliud au- tem, nomen super aliquem invocari. Parentum certe nomen vocatur super liberos, Gen. XLVIII, 16. & mariti super uxorem, Esa. IV, 1. At non nisi solius Dei nomen invocatur; teste universa N. T. Scriptu- ra, Rom. X, 12.13.14. 1. Cor. I, 2. 2. Cor. I, 23. 2. Tim., II, 22. 1. Petr. I, 17. Confidero itaque non dissentien- tibus Pareo, & interpretibus Belgicis, Apostolum hic respicere ad baptismum, in quo nomen Christi super eum invocatur, qui sacro illo lavacro tingitur, Matth. XXVIII, 19. Act. II, 38.

## 2:8
Vers. 8. If indeed you fulfill the royal law.] Of Christ, who is our King, John XVIII, 37. Heb. VII, 2. Rev. I, 5. XV, 3. Calvin, Beza, Piscator, Pareus, and the Dutch interpreters prefer that the royal law be called such in the sense in which, by a proverbial figure, a road is called royal, Num. XXI, 22. 'we will go by the king's highway,' בדרך המלך. For just as everyone walks on this, so that law is the same for all, commanding equally the love of the poor and the rich. This explanation, along with Heinsius, is approved by the blessed Brochmand as being suited to the purpose: and for that reason we also judge it to be preferred.

According to the scripture.] Namely Lev. XIX, 18. 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' These are words from the LXX version of the said passage, but which are to be understood here mystically, so that the neighbor is not only an Israelite, but any human being: and love is to be understood as that which the Gospel prescribes. The law is to be accepted not in a mystical, but in a literal sense regarding any human being, nor does Christ in the New Testament prescribe a different love than Moses did in the law: which is clearer than the midday sun from Matt. XXII, 39 and Luke X, 25: however, with respect to both the object, which are neighbors, whoever they may be without distinction whether they are poor or wealthy, and the manner, that it behooves us to love our neighbor as ourselves, partiality is excluded, since there is no one who does not desire the best for himself, even if he is very poor.

You do well.] Thus Phil. IV, 14. Vers. 9. But if you show partiality.] He coined the verb analogously from the noun 'partiality' (προσωπολήπτης) and 'you shall not respect the person of the great' (ולא תהדרו פני גדול) 'you shall not show partiality to the person of the mighty' (θαυμάσατε πρόσωπον δυνάς) Lev. XIX, 15. 'You commit sin.] Thus 'you who practice lawlessness.' Matt. VII, 23. 'Being convicted by the law as transgressors.] (כמעול). See Rom. II, 25, 27. Gal. II, 8. below 11. He understands the law which is Deut. XVI, 19, where in the Greek, 'nor shall they recognize a person.' But these things also must be taken from this place, namely, that it pertains not only to judgments, but also to signs of honor in the assembly of the Church. For there is also a certain species of judgment in this. That the law regarding partiality is not specifically looked at, which Cajetan wants, and Grotius here, but the royal law of love, which is general, the context teaches, and Estius admits. Since in it that commandment concerning avoiding the respect of persons is also comprehended; so that there is no need to proceed from judgments to signs of honor.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Εἰ μὲν τοι νόμον τελεῖτε βασιλικὸν.] Christi, qui Rex noster, Joh. XVIII, 37. Ebr. VII, 2. Apoc. I, 5. XV, 3. Legem Regiam Calvinus, Beza, Piscator, Pa- reus, Interpretes Belgici malunt dici eo sensu, quo via proverbiali figura dicitur Regia, Num. XXI, 22. ὁδῷ βασιλικῇ πορευσόμεθα, בדרך המלך. Nam veluti hac omnes ambulant, ita illa est omnibus eadem, mandans ex æquo pauperum & divitum dilectionem. Quam explicationem cum Heinsio, probat B. Brochmandus, tanquam instituto accom- modam: eoque nomine præferendam & nos cen- semus.

Κατὰ τὴν γραφὴν.] Nempe Levit. XIX, 18. ᾿Αγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτόν.] Verba sunt ex ver- sione LXX. dicti loci, sed quæ hic intelligenda μυστικῶς, ut proximus sit non solus Israelita, sed homo quivis: et dilectio intelligatur, qualem præscribit Evangelium. Non mystico, sed literali sensu lex accipienda de quovis homine, neque aliam dilectionem Christus in Novo Testamento præscribit, quam Moses in lege: quod è Matth. XXII, 39. & Luc. X, 25. luce meridiana clarius: utriusque autem respectu tum objecti, quod sunt proximi, quique sine distinctio- ne pauperes an opulenti sint, tum modi, quod dili- gere nos oporteat proximum, sicut nos ipsos προ- σωποληψία excluditur, siquidem nemo non sibi- metipsi etiam pauperrimo optime consultum cu- piant.

Καλῶς ποιεῖτε.] Sic Phil. IV, 14. Vers. 9. Εἰ δὲ προσωποληπτεῖτε.] Verbum fecit ἀναλογι- xῶς ex nomine προσωπολήπτης ולא תהדרו פני גדול θαυμά- σατε πρόσωπον δυνάς Levit. XIX, 15. ῾Αμαρτίαν ἐργάζεσθε.] Sic ἐργαζόμενοι ἀνομίαν. Matth. VII, 23. Ελεγχόμενοι ὑπὸ τοῦ νόμου, ὡς παραβάται.] כמעול. Vide Rom. II, 25. 27. Gal. II, 8. infra 11. Legem intelligit, quæ est Deu- ter. XVI, 19. ubi in Græco, ἐδὲ ἐπιγνώσονται πρόσωπον. Sed hæc quoque ex hoc loco sumenda, nempe, ut non tantum ad judicia pertineat, sed & ad honorum signa in cœtu Ecclesiæ. Est enim & in hoc quædam judicii species. Non legem de προσωποληψίᾳ speciatim respi- ci, quod Cajetanus vult, & hic Grotius, sed legem Regiam dilectionis, quæ generalis est, contextus docet, atque admittit Estius. Siquidem in ea illud præceptum de fugiendo personarum respectu et- iam comprehendatur; ut opus non sit à judiciis ad honorum signa procedere.

## 2:10
Vers. 10. For whoever shall keep the whole law.) In the manuscript 'shall fulfill,' which is the expression in Rom. XIII, 8. & (Gcc ccc) 4 Psalm.

Psalm 20:5, 6. He takes up the argument again from the law of Moses to the law of the Gospel, as Paul and the writer to the Hebrews often do. If anyone should keep the other precepts of the law, namely those which carry the threat of capital punishment, such as those forbidding many things, and commanding that one regarding circumcision and the Passover. Πταίσει δὲ ἐν ἑνὶ.] Namely of those for whom capital punishment has been established, as we have already said, and the following will make clear, Deut. 7:25. תוקש you shall ensnare yourself. It is translated in Greek as πταίσῃς. Γέγονε πάντων ἔνοχος.] That is, as guilty of all. He is punished with death no less than if he had violated all the precepts. Thus the Rabbis say: He who transgresses one precept, it is as if he transgressed all. Regarding such precepts, that statement in the book to the Maccabees, which is attributed to Josephus, must be understood: For to transgress in small and great matters is equal. For ἔνοχος the Syrian has אתחיב, the Arab פראנא, namely, a debtor to punishment.

He does not argue from the Mosaic law to the Evangelical law, but urges the force of the Mosaic law. For the Gospel does not prescribe laws, but is opposed to the law. Nor is the discourse only about precepts for which capital punishment has been established; but generally about any whatever: which the letter testifies. For there is no restriction in the text. The thing itself also testifies: because he is pronounced cursed by Moses who does not remain in all things which are written in the law, Deut. 27:26. Although those examples seem to be brought forward in which capital punishment is mentioned, yet with Christ as interpreter, Matt. 5:21, 22, 27, 28, both laws—concerning not killing and not committing adultery—deserve Divine condemnatory judgment not only for external acts, but also for thoughts and words contrary to the same. And even the application, which is present here to partiality, teaches that it is not only the transgression of laws that brings capital punishment that is regarded: and that every transgression of the law is said to be so constituted that through it one is considered guilty of the whole law: which is also clear from the context: since, lest that partiality be perhaps considered a small sin, the Apostle teaches that they render themselves guilty of the whole law, as Augustine observes in Epistle 29 and Bede in this place. And it is gathered not obscurely from the condition of the law: For the law requires an all-encompassing and consummate observation of Divine precepts, which he who does not perform is condemned by the law just as much as he who has violated the whole law, even if he has transgressed only a single precept, if it were possible that one might sin only against a single precept and keep all the others. Compare Matt. 5:19. Yet sins are not therefore rendered equal, if indeed there is a disparity of curse and punishments in the condemnation itself, Matt. 5:22, ch. 10:15, Luke 12:47, 2 Pet. 2:20, 21.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ὅστις γὰρ ὅλον τὸν νόμον τηρήσει.) In Manu- scripto πληρώσει, quæ loquutio est Rom. XIII, 8. & (Gcc ccc) 4 Psalin.

Psalm. XX, 5. 6. Argumentum iterum sumit à lege Mosis ad legem Evangelicam, ut sæpe Paulus & Scriptor ad Ebræos. Si quis cætera legis præcepta servet, nempe quæ comminatio- nem habent pœnæ capitalis, qualia sunt vetantium multa, ju- bentium illud de circumcisione & de Paschate. Πταίσει δὲ ἐν ἑνὶ.] Nempe eorum, quibus pœna capitalis constituta est, ut jam diximus, & sequentia apertum facient, Deut. VII, 25. תוקש illaquees te. Græce vertitur πταίσῃς. Γέγονε πάντων ἔνοχος.] Id est, ὡς πάντων ἔνοχος. Non minus morte punitur, quam si omnia præcepta violasset. Sic Rabbini dicunt : Qui transgreditur unum præceptum, ac si transgrederetur omnia. De talibus præceptis intelligendum & illud in libro εἰς τοὺς Μακκαβαίους, qui Josepho attribuitur : Τὸ γὰρ ἐπὶ μικροῖς καὶ μεγάλοις παρανομεῖν ἶσόν ἐστι. Pro ἔνοχος Syrus habet אתחיב Arabs פראנא, debitor nempe pœnæ.

Non à lege Mosaica ad legem Evangelicam ar- guit, sed vim legis Mosaicæ urget. Neque enim Evangelium leges præscribit, sed legi opponitur. Nec de præceptis tantum, quibus constituta est pœ- na capitalis sermo est; sed generatim de quibusvis: quod litera testatur. Nulla enim in textu est re- strictio. Testatur & res ipsa : quia maledictus à Mose pronunciatur, qui non permanet in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in lege, Deuter. XXVII, 26. Etsi vero exempla ea afferri videantur, quibus pœna capitalis dicta est, Christo tamen interprete, Matth. V, 21. 22. 27. 28. lege utraque de non occidendo & de non mœchando non externa tantum facta, sed cogitata etiam, & dicta eidem adversa judicium Di- vinum condemnatorium merentur, Et vel applica- tio, quæ in præsenti sit ad προσωποληψίαν, docet, non respici tantum legum transgressionem, quæ pœnam capitalem infert : omnemque legis trans- gressionem ita comparatam dici, ut per eandem quis totius legis reus censeatur: quod & ἐ συνέχειᾳ patet : quum ne forte ceu exiguum peccatum illa προσωποληψία habeatur, Apostolus doceat totius legis reos sese illos reddere, observante Augustino epist. XXIX. & Beda in h. l. & à legis conditione haud obscure colligitur : Lex enim omnimodam & consummatam præceptorum Divinorum obser- vationem requirit, quam qui non præstat, per le- gem æque ac is, qui totam violavit legem, conde- mnatur, etiamsi vel unicum præceptum transgres- sus sit, si fieri possit, ut quis non nisi contra unicum præceptum peccet, cætera omnia servet. Conf. Matth. V, 19. Nec tamen ideo peccata omnia paria redduntur, siquidem maledictionis & pœnarum in ipsa condemnatione disparitas detur Matth. V, 22. c. X, 15. Luc. XII, 47. 2. Petr. II, 20. 21.

## 2:11
Verse 11. For he who said, Do not commit adultery. God, who forbade adultery with the added penalty of death, Deut. 22:22. He said, and do not kill. Likewise with the added penalty of death, Exod. 21:12, Lev. 24:17, 21, Deut. 19:13. But if you do not commit adultery, but do kill, you have become a transgressor of the law. To transgress, מעל, is said not of any act against the law, but of those more serious ones. In the Manuscript it is, you have become an apostate of the law, מרד, Num. 14:9, Josh. 22:19. Verse 12. So speak, and so do, as those who are about to be judged by the law of liberty. He shows that what he had said about the law of Moses must now be adapted to the Evangelical law. The law of Moses threatens capital punishment for certain acts: the law of the Gospel threatens Gehenna, not only for acts, but also for words, Matt. 5:22. And it is called the law of liberty, because those who follow it ought to be free even from those vices which were not punished by the law of Moses, above 1:25, 2 Cor. 3:17. It is not for us to choose which precepts we wish to obey and which not. It is not sufficient for salvation if, having spurned the greater, we do the lesser, he says, and to confirm this, he cites this passage, Salvianus, Book 3, On the Governance of God.

Grotius rightly understands the law of liberty as the doctrine of the Gospel, which brings true liberty, but he transforms it very poorly into a more rigid Mosaic law. For nothing can be more rigid than the Mosaic law, Deut. 27:26, even in the New Testament, Gal. 3:10, and the doctrine of the Gospel is opposed to the law diametrically: who then would deliver laws with greater rigor? Who would condemn, since it is not the office of the ministry of reconciliation and righteousness, but of the ministry of the law and death, which is opposed to it, 2 Cor. 3:7 ff. It is called the law of liberty because it brings true liberty, because it brings the Spirit of liberty, 2 Cor. 3:17, not because those who follow it ought to be free even from those vices which were not punished by the law of Moses. For all vices are forbidden by the law of Moses, all vices are punished by the law of Moses, if not in the forum of the earth, at least in the forum of heaven and of the Divine curse. For as every sin is lawlessness, 1 John 3:4. So every lawlessness draws a curse with it no less according to Paul than according to Moses, Deut. 27:25, Gal. 3:10, and Christ, Matt. 5:19. But that is what James wants here: let us so speak, let us so act, as those who are to be judged by the Gospel, which admits no discrimination of persons, Acts 10:31, according to which the rich are chosen in faith by God without any external respect, according to which we shall also be judged, John 12:48. He who wishes to speak so, to act so, as befits sincere followers of liberty or the doctrine of the Gospel, cannot and ought not to honor the rich and despise the poor: for thus he will admit a discrimination of persons, which does not befit the law of liberty, Gal. 3:28, Luke 4:18, 1 Cor. 1:26, 27. But those who are his followers, and yet show partiality, and honor the rich to the prejudice of the poor, they, being dragged to the tribunal of God, are to be judged not by the law of liberty, but by the law of Moses: according to the rigor of the Mosaic law, according to which they are guilty of all the laws, verse 10.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Ὁ γὰρ εἰπὼν μὴ μοιχεύσῃς.] Deus, qui mœchari vetuit addita mortis pœna Deut. 22. v. 22. Εἶπε, καὶ μὴ φονεύσῃς.] Itidem addita mortis pœna, Exod. 21, 12. Levit. 24, 17. 21. Deut. 19, 13. Εἰ δὲ ὐ μοιχεύσεις, φονεύσεις δὲ, γέγονας παραβάτης νόμου.] Παραβαίνειν מעל non de quovis facto contra legem, sed de gravioribus illis dicitur. In Manuscripto est ἐγένου ἀποστά- της νόμου מרד, Num. 14, 9. Jos. 22, 19. Vers. 12. Οὕτω λαλεῖτε, καὶ ὅυτω ποιεῖτε, ὡς διὰ νόμου ἐλευ- θερίας μέλλοντες κρίνεσθαι.] Ostendit jam ad Evangelicam legem aptanda, quæ de Mosis lege dixerat. Lex Mosis factis quibusdam capitale supplicium minatur : Lex Evangelii Ge- hennam, ne factis tantum, sed & dictis, Matth. V, 22. Et di- citur lex libertatis, quia qui eam sequuntur, liberi esse debent etiam ab illis vitiis, quæ lege Mosis non puniebantur, supra I, 25. 2. Cor. III, 17. Non est nostrum seligere, quibus præ- ceptis obsequi velimus, quibus non. Non sufficit ad salutem, si majoribus spretis, minora faciamus, ait, & ut id firmet, lo- cum hunc adducit Salvianus III. de gubernatione Dei.

Legem libertatis de Evangelii doctrina, quæ ve- ram libertatem affert, recte intelligit Grotius, sed pessime eam in legem Mosaica rigidiorem trans- format. Nec enim rigidius quid esse potest lege Mosaica, Deut. XXVII, 26. etiam in Novo Testa- mento, Gal. III, 10. & κατ’διάμετρον opposita est le- gi Evangelii doctrina: qui ergo traderet leges cum majori rigore? Qui condemnaret, quod non mini- sterii reconciliationis & justitiæ, sed ministerii le- gis & mortis, quæ illi opponitur, munus est, 2. Cor. III, 7. seqq. Libertatis lex dicitur, quod veram li- bertatem afferat, quia affert Spiritum libertatis, 2. Cor. III, 17. non quod qui eam sequuntur, liberi es- se etiam ab illis vitiis debeant, quæ lege Mosis non puniebantur. Omnia enim vitia lege Mosis pro- hibita sunt, omnia vitia puniuntur lege Mosis, si non in foro soli, saltem in foro poli & maledictio- nis Divinæ. Ut enim omnis ἁμαρτία ἀνομία est, 1. Joh. III, 4. Ita omnis ἀνομία maledictionem se- cum trahit non minus secundum Paulum, quam secundum Mosen Deut. XXVII, 25. Gal. III, 10. & Christum, Matth. V, 19. Id autem est, quod hic vult Jacobus: ita loquamur, ita agamus, ut qui per Evangelium judicandi simus, quod nullum admit- tit personarum discrimen, Act. X, 31. secundum quod divites in fide electi sunt à Deo sine ullo exter- no respectu, secundum quod etiam judicabimur, Joh. XII, 48. Qui ita vult loqui, ita agere, uti de- cet sinceros libertatis seu doctrinæ Evangelii secta- tores, non potest nec debet honorare divitem, & contemnere pauperem: Sic enim personarum di- gcrimen admittet, quod legi libertatis non conve- nit, Gal. III, 28. Luc. IV, 18. 1. Cor. I, 26. 27. Qui autem sectatores ejus sunt, & tamen personas acci- piunt, & divites honorant in præjudicium paupe- rum, illi ad tribunal Dei tracti, non è lege liber- tatis, sed è lege Mosis judicandi sunt: juxta rigo- rem legis Mosaicæ, secundum quem omnium legum rei sunt, vers. 10.

## 2:13
Verse 13. For judgment is without mercy to him who has not shown mercy. Mercy, to our writers, signifies not only leniency in exacting punishments, but also every kind of beneficence, corresponding to the Hebrew חסד, as can be seen in Gen. 19:19, Num. 11:15, and elsewhere. Thus also Matt. 9:13, ch. 12:17, ch. 23:23. The law of the Gospel is that we should do good to all; he who does not do this will be treated harshly, Matt. 7:1 ff., ch. 25:42.

Κατακαυχᾶται ἔλεος κρίσεως.] On the contrary, beneficence has this property, that it frees us from condemnation, Matt. 5, 7. c. 25, 37. When salvation is promised to one virtue, it is not to be understood that others are excluded, but that the power of that virtue is exceptional. See Luke 11, 41. & Matt. 5, 3. 4. 5. chap. 6, 14. Luke 6, 37. Κατακαυχᾶται ἔλεος κρίσεως signifies: beneficence triumphs over damnation: it does not fear it. God cannot condemn the imitators of His goodness. For the Hebrews also say that among the מדות or properties of God, clemency is the chief. See Jarchi on Dan. 9, 45. Claudian: Clemency, the guardian of the great world at its beginning. Seneca the Elder: The tortured world would have perished, had not mercy put an end to wrath. In the manuscript, κατακαυχάσθω is not bad. Bring it about that through beneficence you may triumph over damnation. And the Syrian follows this sense.

Now, He not only does not wish the poor to be despised, but He also commands that mercy be shown to them according to the law of love previously cited, unless they wish to expect judgment without mercy, that is, tempered by no leniency, no grace, Luke VI, 37. 38. Matt. XVIII, 28. He who exercises no mercy toward the poor, neither in judgment, nor in the marketplace, nor in the choir, nor deigns to show them beneficence, to him in the judgment of God will come in turn judgment without mercy. But divine mercy will prevail over all judgment, and will glory against judgment; therefore, by God's example, let it also prevail and triumph in us, Luke VI, 36. As Augustine says in Ps. CXLIII, mercy is placed above judgment, in which a work of mercy has been found: Even if he has perhaps had something in judgment for which he might be punished, the fire of sin is extinguished as if by a wave of mercy. Grotius is therefore in vain, intending to bring aid to the Papists, as if the matter here were about the merit of our mercy or beneficence, by which its power we are freed from condemnation. For even if these things were understood concerning the benevolence of men, yet it cannot be set against the judgment of God, I will not say alone, but not even joined with other virtues, Ps. CXLIII, 1. Rom. III, 27. Therefore, others understand it concerning the judgment of the devil, of sin, and of death accusing, against which a man can raise himself not by the merit of his own mercy, but by the promise of Divine grace made from mercy to the merciful, Matt. V, 7. Blessed are the merciful, for mercy shall be attributed to them. Others agree. Bede: As he who has not shown mercy will grieve in judgment: So he who has shown it will be rewarded, exult, and rejoice. Thomas Aquinas: 1. p. q. 21. art. 3. ad 2. Mercy superexalts judgment, because God acts mercifully not against his own justice of punishing, but by working something above justice. But Augustine more correctly understands Divine mercy here; who presents an elegant figure of this matter in q. CV. in Exod. In the ark, he says, the law, and the manna, and the rod of Aaron were commanded to be placed: In the law are precepts, the rod signifies power; the manna grace: because there is no power to perform the precepts except with grace: Nevertheless, because the law is not completed in every part by any one performing it, the mercy seat is above. For this reason, there is need that God be propitious, and therefore it is placed above, because mercy superexalts judgment. Two Cherubim indeed overshadow the mercy seat with their wings, that is, they honor it by covering it. And their faces are toward the mercy seat, because they highly commend the mercy of the Lord, in which alone is hope. Fulgentius agrees with Augustine in book 1 to Monimus, chapter 25. For he (the Prophet) knew that all were to be held by an equal bond of punishment, unless God had made mercy to superexalt judgment in those whom He willed. For thus Estius corrects the faulty passage of Fulgentius in this place. Gregory the Great also agrees: After James said that mercy superexalts judgment, he rightly added that he who has not imitated this ineffable mercy will undergo strict judgment. Thomas Anglicus: Mercy exalts judgment, because it is as it were a greater court of mercy than of justice; just as it is permitted to appeal from a lesser court to a greater: So from the court of justice to the court of mercy. Add also Erasmus on this passage. Clichtoveus, book V, on John, chapter 14, in the works of Cyril: Mercy, he says, is exalted above judgment, just as oil above water. Mariana: as if he were saying: Mercy is superior to judgment. Eman. Saa. Some read, he says, superexaltat judicio, that is, prevails over judgment, namely, freeing man from condemnation. The explanation of Cornelius à Lapide himself also contributes to this: It is a prosopopoeia. For judgment and mercy are imagined as two persons litigating before God concerning a sinful and guilty man: Judgment as the plaintiff accuses the defendant and sues for his condemnation; mercy defends and excuses, and obtains and causes that he be absolved and depart free. This is Cornelius, not at all disapproving of our explanation: although he may subsequently bring forward another opinion concerning the mercy of our own, serving his hypothesis concerning the merits of good works. Similarly, Estius observes: This passage is to be explained concerning the mercy of God, so that the sense may be that in the judgment of God His mercy will prevail over justice, and will be superior to it: Which understand concerning the elect, who are all to be judged with mercy. Although he indeed judges the sense concerning the mercy of a man to be judged as more genuine; he adds, however: No one will be saved without mercy. But indeed our whole salvation is the mercy of God. Estius, along with Erasmus, notes here a fault in the Vulgate version: Nor does Erasmus rashly suspect that the codices are corrupted, and that it should be read superexultat. For it is so read and repeated for the third time in Augustine, epistle 29 to Jerome, and again in epistle 89 to Hilary, question 4. And a passage in the same author in his enarrations on Psalm CXLIII also argues for that reading. For he explains the sentiment of James in this way: Mercy is placed above judgment. In the same way, it is read in good copies in the same author, De peccatorum meritis et remissione, book II, chapters 3 and 7, and Contra Julianum, book IV, chapter 8, and Confessions, book IX, chapter 13. Let it be that Bede also read it in his commentary, etc. The word κατακαυχᾶται properly means to boast against someone, Rom. XI, 8. Jas. III, 14. and according to the etymology, because the root is ἀυχὴν (neck), to lift up the neck, and to carry one's head as if the matter were well done. Whence Cornelius à Lapide: It boasts against judgment unto condemnation, as if superior to condemnation, and victorious, it insults: it raises its neck against judgment; that is, it lifts its neck above judgment, as if to say: mercy is the victor of judgment: For it has a higher tribunal, so that it can invalidate or change the sentence of judgment.

According to this explanation, by which mercy is accepted here as Divine mercy, as in the former clause, so also in the latter, just as in both κρίσις is also understood as Divine judgment, a twofold reason for exercising mercy toward the poor and not inflicting injury upon them is brought forward: The first is from the Divine judgment against the unmerciful, which he who has not performed will experience mercy without mercy, and much more he who has done injury to the poor: The second is from the example of Divine mercy, which in God Himself, whom we are bound to imitate, mercy seems as it were to boast and exalt itself above judgment and condemnation, which He exercises toward the poor who are spiritually wretched sinners according to the Gospel, whom Divine justice condemns according to the Mosaic law, provided they flee to the tribunal of mercy and betake themselves with true faith, Heb. IV, 16.

PART II. Concerning the vain boasting of faith, void of works.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ἡ γὰρ κρίσις ἀνίλεως τῷ μὴ ποιήσαντι ἔλεος.] Ἔ- λεος Scriptoribus nostris non solum lenitatem in pœnis exi- gendis, sed & omne genus beneficentiæ significat, respondens Ebræo חסד, ut videre est Gen. 19, 19. Num. 11, 15. & alibi. Sic & Matth. 9, 13. cap. 12, 17. cap. 23, 23. Lex Evangelii est, ut benefaciamus omnibus, qui id non facit, dure tractabitur, Matth. 7, 1. & seqq. cap. 25, 42.

Κατακαυχᾶται ἔλεος κρίσεως.] Contra vero beneficentia hoc habet, ut nos à condemnatione liberet, Matth. 5, 7. c. 25, 37. Cum uni virtuti salus promittitur, non intelligendum excludi alias, sed illius virtutis vim esse eximiam. Vide Luc. 11, 41. & Matth. 5, 3. 4. 5. cap. 6, 14. Luc. 6, 37. Κατακαυχᾶ- ται ἔλεος κρίσεως fignificat: beneficentia de damnatione tri- umphat: eam non metuit. Non potest Deus damnare suæ bonitatis imitatores. Nam & inter Dei מדות sive proprie- tates præcipuam esse clementiam dicunt Ebræi. Vide Jarchi ad Dan. 9, 45. Claudianus: Principio magni custos clementia mundi. Seneca Pater: Perierat tortus orbis, nisi iram finiret mise- ricordia. In manuscripto non male est κατακαυχάσθω. Effi- cite, ut per beneficentiam triumphetis de damnatione. Et hunc sensum sequitur Syrus.

Jam pauperes non tantum haud vult contemni, sed etiam iisdem misericordiam exhiberi jubet ex lege dilectionis antea allata, nisi judicium absque misericordia expectare velint, hoc est, nulla lenita- te, nulla gratia temperatum, Luc. VI, 37. 38. Matth. XVIII, 28. Qui nec in judicio, vel in foro, vel in choro, misericordiam erga pauperes exercet, nec beneficentiam ipsis exhibere dignatur, illi in judicio Dei vicissim judicium eveniet sine misericordia. Di- vina autem misericordia prævalebit omni judicio, & gloriabitur adversus judicium, idcirco Dei ex- emplo etiam in nobis prævaleat & triumphet, Luc. VI, 36. Quomodo Augustinus in Ps. CXLIII. su- perponitur misericordiæ judicio, in quo inventum fuerit opus misericordiæ: Etsi habuerit aliquid forte in judicio, quo puniatur, tanquam unda misericor- diæ peccati ignis extinguitur. Frustra ergo est Gro- tius, suppetias laturus Papistis, quasi hic de miseri- cordiæ, vel beneficentiæ nostræ merito agatur, quod ejus vi à condemnatione liberemur. Nam etiam- si de beneficentia hominum hæc acciperentur, ea tamen judicio Dei opponi non potest, non dicam sola, sed ne quidem cum aliis virtutibus conjuncta, Pfal. CXLIII, 1. Rom. III, 27. ideo de judicio dia- boli, peccati, mortis accusantis, alii accipiunt, ad- versus quod sese erigere potest homo non merito suæ misericordiæ, sed promisso Divinæ gratiæ è mi- sericordia facto misericordibus, Matth. V, 7. Beati misericordes, quia ipsis tribuetur misericordia. Con- sonant alii. Beda: Sicut in judicio dolebit, qui non fecit misericordiam : Ita, qui fecit remuneratus exultabit, atque gaudebit. Thomas de Aquino : 1. p. q. 21. art. 3. ad 2. Misericordia superexaltat ju- dicium, quia Deus misericorditer agit non contra su- am justitiam fatiendi, sed aliquid super justitiam operandi. Sed rectius hic intelligit Divinam mi- sericordiam Augustinus ; qui ejus rei figuram ele- gantem exhibet q. CV. in Exod. In arca, inquit, jussa sunt poni lex, & manna, & virga Aaronis : In lege præcepta sunt, virga potestatem significat ; man- na gratiam : quia nisi cum gratia non est potestas fa- ciendi præcepta : Veruntamen quia lex à quovis per- ficiente non ex omni parte completur, propitiatorium est desuper. Adhæc enim opus est, ut propitius sit Deus, & ideo desuper ponitur, quia superexaltat misericordia judicio. Duo vero Cherubim pennis suis obumbrant propitiatorium, id est, honorant ve- lando. Et vultus eorum sunt in propitiatorium, quia misericordiam Domini, in qua una spes est, valde commendant. Augustino consonat Fulgentius libr. 1. ad Monim. cap. 25. Sciebat enim (Propheta) cun- ctos pari retinendos punitionis vinculo, nisi Deus, in quibus vellet, misericordiam fecisset superexaltare ju- dicio. Sic enim locum Fulgentii mendosum emen- dat Estius hoc loco. Consonat & Gregorius Magnus: Postquam Jacobus dixit, misericordiam superexalta- re judicium, recte addidit, judicium districtum subi- turum eum, qui hanc ineffabilem misericordiam non fuerit imitatus. Thomas Anglicus : Misericordia exaltat judicium, quia major est veluti curia miseri- cordiæ, quam justitiæ ; sicut licet à minori curia ap- pellare ad majorem : Ita à curia justitiæ ad curiam mi- sericordiæ. Adde & Erasmum in h. l. Clichtoveus l. V. in Joh. cap. 14. in operibus Cyrilli : Supra judicium, inquit, exaltatur misericordia, sicut oleum super aquam. Mariana: quasi dicat : Misericor- dia judicio superior est. Eman. Saa. Aliqui legunt, inquit, superexaltat judicio, id est, prævalet ju- dicio, scilicet liberans hominem à condemnatione. Facit etiam huc ipsius Cornelii à Lapide explica- tio: Est Prosopopœia. Judicium enim & misericordia finguntur quasi duæ personæ litigantes apud Deum de homine peccatore & reo : Judicium quasi actor, reum accusat, reumque damnationis agit ; defendit & excusat misericordia, impetratque & facit, ut absolvatur, liberque abeat. Hæc Cornelius, haud reprobans nostram explicationem : tametsi alte- ram sententiam de misericordia nostravi, ὑποθέσει suæ de meritis bonorum operum δυλεύων, dein- ceps adducat. Similiter Estius observat: Exponi hunc locum de misericordia Dei, ut sensus sit, in judi- cio Dei misericordiam ejus prævalituram esse justitiæ, atque ea superiorem fore : Quod intellige de electis, qui omnes cum misericordia judicandi sunt. Quam- vis vero sensum de misericordia hominis judi- candi magis germanum arbitretur ; addit tamen : Nullus sine misericordia salvabitur. Quin vero to- ta salus nostra Dei misericordia est. Notat hic vi- tium in Vulgata versione Estius cum Erasmo : Nec temere suspicatur Erasmus, vitiatos esse codices, ac legendum superexultat. Nam ita legitur ac tertio re- petitur apud Augustinum epist. 29. ad Hieron. & ite- rum epist. 89. ad Hilarium quæst. 4. Eamque lectio- nem arguit etiam locus apud eundem in enarrat. ad Psal. CXLIII. Nam Jacobi sententiam exponit hoc modo: Superponitur misericordia judicio. Eodem modo in bonis exemplaribus legitur apud eundem de pecc. mer. & rem. libr. II. cap. 3. & 7. & contr. Ju- lian. libr. IV. cap. 8. & conf. l. IX. c. 13. Sit quoque Bedam in commentario legisse, &c. Verbum κατα- καυχᾶται proprie est gloriari adversus aliquem,, Rom. XI, 8. Jac. III, 14. & juxta etymon, -quia radix est ἀυχὴν cervix, attollere cervices, & caput velut re bene gesta exercere. Unde Cornelius à La- pide: Gloriatur contra judicium ad condemnatio- nem, damnationi quasi superior, & victrix, insultat: cervicem erigit contra judicium; id est, super judici- um cervicem attollit, q. d. misericordia est judicii vi- ctrix: Habet enim altius tribunal, ut judicii senten- tiam irritare, aut mutare possit.

Juxta hanc explicationem, qua misericordia hic de Divina misericordia, ut in priori commate, ita & in altero accipitur, quemadmodum in utroq; etiam κρίσις de judicio Divino intelligitur, gemina ratio exercendæ misericordiæ erga pauperes, nec inferendæ iisdem injuriæ affertur: Prior est à Di- vino contra immisericordes judicio, quod qui non præstiterit, misericordiam sine misericordia expe- rietur, ac multo magis, qui fecerit pauperi inju- riam: Posterior à misericordia Divina exemplo, quod in Deo ipso, quem imitari tenemur, quasi gloriari, & sese exaltare videatur misericordia supra judici- um, & condemnationem, quam erga pauperes Spi- ritu miseros peccatores secundum Evangelium exercet, quos justitia Divina secundum legem Mo- saicam condemnat, modo ad misericordiæ tribu- nal confugiant, veraq; fide se recipiant, Ebr. IV, 16.

PARS II. De vana fidei, operibus cassa, jactantia.

## 2:14
Vers. 14. What is the profit, my brethren,] On this passage, up to the end of the chapter, we have published a sufficiently rich commentary, which we have appended to our annotations on the Gospels. From there and elsewhere we shall take here those things which are suitable for the manner of this treatise. Since the Apostles everywhere preached much about the efficacy of faith, it came about that many carnal men, among whom was Simon Magus, seized upon this as a defense for a faulty life, as if eternal salvation could be obtained without just works, as Irenaeus speaks, namely through faith. Whereas, on the contrary, the doctrine of the Apostles was that faith is fit to cleanse us, and to those cleansed to give the Holy Spirit, and thus faith is made effective through love, Gal. V, 6. And therefore love, which arises from faith and the hope accompanying it, is worth more than both faith and hope 1. Cor. XIII, 13. Τί τὸ ὄφελος, מַה בֶּצַע, as Gen. XXXVII, 25. Psalm. XXX, 10. Malach. III, 14. what profit, namely for eternal salvation, as 1. Cor. XV, 32. For the same, Paul said οὐδὲν ὠφελῶ 1. Cor. XIII, 2.

If any man say he has faith, but have not works.] Λέγῃ, that is, think, in the same way as λεγέτω above I, 13. If anyone thinks within himself; my works indeed are not right, but my faith is right: and therefore I am not in danger regarding salvation. This opinion was once very frequent among the Jews, who thought that every Israelite, provided he had not cast off the profession of Judaism, would eventually have a part in the other world, that is, in eternal life. Augustine, in his book on faith and works, shows that the same opinion has prevailed among many Christians, and he refutes them sharply, as he certainly ought to have. In this unhappy century that opinion has been reborn, and indeed under the name of purified doctrine, to which all who love piety and the salvation of their neighbor ought to oppose themselves.

On this passage, against that commentary of Grotius, the blessed Lord my father-in-law, Dr. Joh. Hülsemann, prepared an accurate defense in the year 1643 under the title Apostolic Harmony of SS. Paul and James concerning JUSTIFICATION, vindicated from the corruptions of HUGO GROTIUS. It will therefore be permitted for us to be more brief. Yet, lest that treatise of Grotius be missed, since we have brought forward the rest complete to the end, though distributed otherwise, with annotations added to the Gospels, and have determined to bring them forward subsequently, it is helpful to add this commentary here as well, and thus to refute it at the same time, and with the same fidelity to kill two birds with one stone. Now Grotius has it thus at v. 14 in the same place:

Vers. 14. What is the profit, my brethren, if anyone says he has faith, but does not have works?] (What will it profit, my brethren, if anyone says he has faith, but does not have works?) When James had spoken at length, having exhorted to beneficial works toward one's neighbor, he shows the necessity of such works from the danger of not obtaining salvation without them. If anyone says, namely from the heart, as the expression was just taken similarly at 14. James concedes that this is truly said by some, that they have faith, even if works do not follow, not in the sense in which faith signifies the whole Christian piety metonymically or synecdochically through transnomination or inclusion, as Rom. X, 16, Tit. I, 1, but in that sense in which it indicates assent given to the truth revealed by God, and is distinguished from repentance, Mark I, 15, likewise from love, 1 Cor. XIII, 2, Gal. V, 6, Eph. VI, 23, 1 Tim. I, 14, 2 Tim. I, 13, & II, 22, and purity, Acts XV, 9. & a good conscience, 1 Tim. I, 19, such an assent as can exist without profession and therefore also without pious works, from which it is distinguished here, as we are also taught at Tit. III, 8, John XII, 42. Nor is that a wonder, since that which the Spartans said about the Athenians often has a place: that they knew what was right, but did not want to do it. Thus Medea in Ovid: --- I see the better things and approve them, I follow the worse. The same in the Greek Tragedy: And I learn indeed what evils I am about to do, but passion is stronger than my counsels. Nor does it escape me now what bloody things I contemplate, but anger overcomes the health of the heart.

Therefore it happens that the will acts with right of dominion over the ministering faculties, and indeed even over the intellect itself in some part, namely, that it should consider this or that, and apply itself to it, and makes itself be obeyed entirely. But the intellect, like orators in a free Republic, acts upon the will with persuasions, and does not always obtain obedience, because of that liberty which is innate and proper to the will. Hence it happens that the clearer the knowledge is, the heavier the punishment is if the will does not follow, Luke XII, 47, 48, Rom. II, 21. Tertullian: This will be the power of Divine grace, more potent certainly than nature, having within us the power of free will subject to it, which is called autexousion, which, since it is itself both natural and mutable, is converted to whatever nature it is turned. That the autexousion is in us naturally, we have already shown both to Marcion and to Hermogenes. The writer of the responses to the orthodox: That we are good or evil, God did not place in the knowledge of the things known, but in the choice of the things chosen: Which agree very well with those things which Justin himself discourses upon piously in his Apology, both the former and the latter, concerning proairesis, and what Irenaeus says in book IV, chap. 29. Therefore James does not deny that such a faith is given, but he denies that there is utility from it, which is hoped for, contrary to what the Simonians taught. See Irenaeus book I, chap. 20.

Regarding the occasion of this treatment, it was said in the Prolegomena: But the doctrine of the Apostles was not this, that faith is apt to cleanse us, that to the cleansed the Holy Spirit is given, and thus faith is made effective through love. They do indeed ascribe the purification of the heart to faith, Acts XV, 9, but not from some aptitude of faith, or because it behaves itself toward purification or the remission of sins by way of a disposition, which the Papists imagine as primary justification, contending that faith justifies only dispositively, which they affirm indeed of the unformed faith which they have invented: But from the mere grace of God, because God imputes faith for righteousness, and by the blood of Christ, by which alone our consciences are purified from all sin, 1 John I, 7. Heb. IX, 14, apprehended through faith, He washes away our sins, and remits the same to us, and imputes to us the righteousness or obedience of Christ through faith, so that we may be constituted righteous before the Divine tribunal, Rom. V, 18. Faith therefore does not justify us by disposing us, but by apprehending the satisfaction and merit of Christ, whom God set forth for us as a propitiation through faith in his blood, Rom. III, 25. By faith our justification before God is not only begun, but perfected, and indeed without our works, concerning which the Apostle says in the same place v. 27, we reckon that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law. We admit that to those cleansed in this way, that is, justified, the Holy Spirit is given, and thus the faith by which we are justified is made effective through love; not that unformed faith works, that is, is formed, as the Papists barbarously say: But its form is the very apprehension of the righteousness or obedience of Christ, both active and passive: Love, however, is its consequent, through which faith is energetic, laborious, and effective, not for justification, seeing that it is without the works of the law, such as love is, but for exercising itself, or because saving faith is not idle, but active in love and through the works of love, which do not precede the one to be justified, but follow the one justified. But the Scripture is utterly ignorant of the two diverse species of justification which the Papists have devised. For where, I beseech you, is the first justification taught, in which faith is imputed for righteousness begun, and is a way and disposition toward righteousness; so that on account of this faith God remits sins to the believer, and infuses complete righteousness? Where is the second justification read of in the scriptures, and the same such that faith completed by works is imputed for righteousness, so that works merit it, insofar as they are done from faith and the grace of Christ? Where is it taught in the sacred writings that by the first justification a man is made just from being not just: and by the second, more just from being just? On the contrary, however, since no inherent righteousness contributes to our justification before God; how can the distinction of justification into first and second be admitted, seeing that it is built upon the diversity of inherent righteousness? Where is it taught that a man is justified by the first justification, when grace, that is, habitual righteousness or charity, is infused? By the second justification, when works of righteousness are performed from the habit of charity, and habitual righteousness is increased and perfected by actual righteousness? Such empty sounds and cacophonies we leave to the Scholastics, with their little distinctions, both unknown to scripture and adverse to scripture, perverting and overturning the opinion of Paul, against which enough has been done elsewhere.

Furthermore, we have spoken at 1 Cor. XIII, 3, of how love is greater than faith and hope. That faith is of more value for eternal life is a blasphemy against the satisfaction and merit of Christ, by whose trustful reception we alone obtain salvation. For the rest, if anyone boasts of faith, but is destitute of works, we readily admit that such faith is worth nothing, and that such a boaster of faith is worthless and vain, whether he thinks it within himself or boasts of it with his voice, and we acknowledge that such boasting has been refuted not only by Augustine in his book On Faith and Works, but by other ancient Doctors, and not only by them, but here also by St. James, and indeed even by the Apostle Paul.

But it is a cruel calumny that, under the name of the reformed doctrine, that Jewish persuasion—that he who does not cast off the profession of Judaism has a part in the next world—and the heretical one—that those who merely profess Christianity obtain eternal salvation—have been reborn in this unhappy age, to which all who love piety and the salvation of their neighbor ought to oppose themselves.
