In the Papacy let such things be sought. In the doctrine purified by the ministry of Blessed Luther, they will be sought in vain. They admit, nay, they contend, that those are saved who profess to believe what the Catholic Church believes, even if they are ignorant of what she believes or what ought to be believed. They, on the contrary, contend against Scripture and antiquity that true faith can exist even if it is without just works: both of which St. James rejects here, teaching that a bare profession of faith is vain, and that faith which is void of good works is not true faith; much less does a bare profession of faith, and faith of such a kind falsely boasted of, save anyone. But what has this to do with the purified doctrine, by which we believe that we are justified solely through faith in Christ, that is, through the obedience of Christ apprehended by faith, so that the grace of God and the merit of Christ may be asserted against the Anti-Christian tramplers of the same: but that faith in Christ cannot be separated from love and good works, which, although they contribute nothing to our justification before God, yet cohere with justifying and saving faith in an inseparable bond, nor can they ever be absent from it. The former of these Paul taught especially in his treatment of the fundamental article concerning justification: the latter James has executed here: the purified doctrine defends both, neither of which was kept safe and sound in the Papacy, the purification of which is therefore to be attributed not to the misfortune of the age, but to the happiness and inestimable grace of God, unless we wish to be ungrateful to God, equally injurious to ourselves, and harmful to the salvation of our neighbor.

It is no wonder concerning the Papists that they feign that it was the heresy of Simon Magus that a man is justified by faith alone, which Lorinus, Estius, and Cornelius a Lapide slanderously claim is refuted here by James. But that Grotius, a glutton of antiquity, should wander on the same string is more to be detested than wondered at. For nothing of the sort is read anywhere, whether in Irenaeus, or Epiphanius, or Eusebius, or Theodoret, or Augustine, but all that was devised by the Papists out of hatred against Blessed Luther: Which Augustine teaches concerning faith and works, chapter XIV. That certain Pseudo-Apostles asserted that faith alone suffices to obtain salvation, and that this is refuted here by James, which likewise most Popish interpreters contend, is refuted by Augustine himself, who teaches only this, that it is not true faith which is not joined with a zeal for holiness: nor was that the doctrine of the Pseudo-Apostles, but of the Apostles, that true and living faith, which Augustine calls a wholesome and plainly Evangelical faith, suffices for salvation, Eph. II, 8, 9. And it is apparent that James is not so much refuting the opinion of heretics as of hypocrites, who, while they lived impiously, nevertheless boasted of faith: Which cause of this treatment is confirmed by the persuasion that had already arisen in the Apostle's age from the abuse of Evangelical doctrine; Rom. III, chap. VI, 1. seqq. conf. 2. Pet. II, 10. chap. III, 5. seqq.

As to the connection with what precedes, it is not to be sought so remotely where a closer one is given. He had exhorted to beneficial works toward one's neighbor, not to teach their necessity for salvation, which the Apostle does not establish even now, but he taught that true religion is when we show beneficence to widows and orphans, and keep ourselves unspotted from the world, tacitly exhorting to that: But for salvation he required only this, that having recognized our impurity from the mirror of the law, we should look into the Evangelical mirror or the perfect doctrine of liberty with the eyes of the mind, and be cleansed from sins through faith. Meanwhile, he shows the connection of such faith in the glorious Christ with the zeal of piety and charity to be exercised without partiality, which the Royal law of charity does not admit at all, and he asserts it to be so necessary against vain boasters of faith that faith cannot even be true where it does not exert itself through charity and works. Rightly, therefore, Blessed Hülsemann: The Apostle indeed exhorted to beneficial works toward one's neighbor in chapter I, verse last. But the manner of connecting this argument concerning imaginary faith with the immediately preceding argument is not hortatory but dehortatory from partiality, as a vice contrary to Christian charity and beneficence, which is evident from the comparison of the preceding verses with this verse. And the means of proving the baseness and harm of this vice is its incompatibility, if I may so say, with the nature of true faith. The means, therefore, of dehorting from partiality is not the necessity of beneficence for obtaining salvation, but a physical necessity, that true faith cannot consist with partiality, or the deliberate preference of the rich over the poor, or the deliberate desertion and injury or contempt of the poor. Which is proved from the continuation and application of the same humble example in verse 2. & 15. as faith in the glorious Christ cannot consist with the preference of a man splendidly dressed over a poor and naked one, verse 2. So much the less with the desertion and illusion of a naked and poor brother, verses 15, 16, 17.

There is a still more specific connection with verse 5, that God has chosen the rich in faith to be heirs of the kingdom which He promised to those who love Him: where he intimates that love is not to be torn away from faith, because although faith alone is looked upon in election to salvation, it nevertheless necessarily has love joined with it, as that which is inseparable from faith in the heirs of the heavenly kingdom; and from verse 13, that although in the Divine absolutory judgment Divine mercy alone dominates, triumphing against the condemnation of the law which lies upon miserable sinners, Rom. XI, 32, yet faith in the glorious Christ, the reconciler of Divine mercy, is by no means destitute of the works of charity and mercy; and that the unmerciful have judgment without mercy to expect, as being destitute of faith, which is nothing without mercy.

Now as to the proposition in this latter part, in the words ἐὰν πίςιν λέγῃ τις ἔχειν, it is manifest that the discourse is by no means about true faith in the glorious Christ, but about the boasting of faith: nor does James concede that this is truly said by some, that they have faith, even if works do not follow; for this is what James proves, that that faith is not true but vain, not living but dead, which is destitute of works: nor does that phrase import anything else, if anyone says that he has faith, but does not have works, than a boasting of faith: just as it is established in James that to say is opposed to the truth of the matter, chap. I, 13. chap. II, 16. and denotes a hypocritical or false discourse, not a true one. It is indeed certain that true faith is understood by the word πίςεως, just as James describes faith in chap. I, 3. 6. chap. II, 1. 5. chap. V, 15. and the boasting itself demands that; for who would boast of a faith that is not true? But that λέγειν is only a vain saying, it does not accord with the truth. Such a one boasts of true faith; but in reality it is not true faith. The boasting of true faith is vain. The Papists indeed explain the faith which, being separated from works, cannot save a man, as true but unformed faith, Cornelius à Lapide, Estius, and others: But James. If anyone says, he says, that he has faith, and does not have works, can this faith, which does not have works, save him? He does not say: If anyone has faith, but if anyone says that he has faith, that is, boasts of faith; for true faith cannot exist without works, Gal. V, 6. John XI, 1. seqq. Luke VII, 42. 43. Unformed faith is not true faith, but an unformed monster of faith. Which has been shown in the Exegesis of the A. C. Faith without works is dead by itself, as James testifies, v. 17. Nor is true faith any more than a dead body a true body. A person can indeed have assent to revealed truth, but that is not faith in Christ, for which trust is required. Nor do those cited passages speak of bare assent, Mark I. Faith is indeed distinguished from repentance, yet it is true trust in Christ, when we believe the Gospel, which Christ preached along with repentance: for this was the sum of his sermons, who required not bare assent, but trust; nor is bare assent understood in Galatians V, 6, but trust, which is active through love: and thus it is indeed distinguished from love; but it necessarily has the same as a companion. And 1 Cor. XIII, 2, nor Eph. VI, 23. Faith is to be taken otherwise than as trust in Christ, (in which latter passage the discourse is not of our love, but of God's towards us) nor 1 Tim. I, 14, or 2. Tim. I, 13, or chap. II, 22, or even Acts XV, 11, 1 Tim. I, 19. Although, therefore, assent can exist without profession, yet trust in Christ cannot exist without profession or works. We deny, however, that faith signifies the whole of Christian piety, Rom. X, 16, Tit. I, 1: nor do we allow faith to be confused with works, which the Apostles accurately distinguish. Paul certainly opposes faith in Christ and righteousness to works, Rom. X, 3, seqq., when he teaches that we are justified by faith, not by works, and asserts that the Jews, who, trying to establish their own righteousness, destroy the righteousness of faith: Tit. I, 1, he understands the faith of the elect as faith in the object hidden from the ages, v. 2, which certainly cannot be said of the pursuit of piety. Moreover, the blessed Hülsemann learnedly argues here that the reason why not all who assent to things to be believed live well is not a natural inability of the intellect to persuade the will, but a corruption of the appetite and affections, and a defect, absence, or withdrawal of renewing grace, Lev. VIII, 15, seqq., Deut. XXIX, 4; nor that the intellect naturally knows from the command of the will, or that every application of the intellect is from the dominion of the will; but just as the eye sees a colored object spontaneously, so the intellect by a natural and spontaneous motion desires the knowledge of knowable things. But we do not pursue these matters here, as they contribute little to the opinion of St. James.

Can faith save him?] He concedes that some faith can be such: but he denies that eternal salvation belongs to it. For 'save' the Arab has 'deliver', the Syrian 'quicken'. Holy men do indeed sometimes say that some are saved by faith before works, but they understand before a perpetual series and course of good works, because, forsooth, life was not granted to them for that purpose. Otherwise, no faith has profited anyone without such work as time permitted, as appears from the example of him crucified with Christ. Salvianus IV, On the Government of God: 'Since the Holy Spirit says that not even faith can profit Christian men without good works.' Cyprian, On the Dress of Virgins: 'A reward is given to the believer: if what is believed is also performed.' Add Jerome, Dialogue I against the Pelagians.

No such concession is found here, that true faith can exist which is destitute of works. But the contrary: since St. James says that that boast of faith is vain, if works are not present: and concerning such faith he pronounces that that faith, which is void of works, cannot save a man, however much he may boast that he has true faith: Just as Augustine teaches in chapter XIV of On Faith and Good Works, by this restriction, 'if it has not works', it is shown not that any faith, by which one believes in God, justifies, but that healthy and plainly Evangelical faith, whose works proceed from love: And this against those who asserted that faith alone suffices for obtaining salvation, even if one has neglected to live well and to keep the way of God by good works. James therefore denies here by this interrogation that faith not having works saves; yet he does not assert that works are necessary for salvation along with faith: Just as it is rightly said from Gal. V, 6 that faith, which is effective through love, saves, but not likewise faith, insofar as it is effective through love. It is certain that love must necessarily coexist with faith, and that the faith by which we are saved is not without works, but that love or works cooperate with faith so that we may be saved, or that they contribute to salvation, James does not assert this in the least, and he openly opposes St. Paul, who concludes in Rom. III, 25 that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law: And Rom. IV, 6 that the blessedness is of the man to whom God imputes righteousness (of Christ) without the works of the law. Nor do holy men, the ancient Fathers, teach that some are saved by faith alone before works in such a way that they are saved before a perpetual series and course of good works, to whom life was not granted for that purpose, but they assert with Paul that they are saved by faith, not by works; nor that works are excluded from justification and salvation regarding the course and perpetual series, but it is established simply from Paul and the Catholic Doctors, and confirmed by the example of the converted thief, who obtained salvation not through works, but through faith in CHRIST. We admit, indeed, what Salvianus said in Book IV of On the Government of GOD, that faith does not profit without good works because it is not, nor can it be, faith in Christ without good works; and if a faith is posited which is without good works, James proclaims here with a resounding voice that it does not profit, nor can it save anyone. St. Cyprian likewise acts against the vain boasters of faith: 'But if the liberated owes obedience to the liberator, we who desire to be Christians ought to imitate what Christ did and taught. Then the follower of truth responds to the faith of the name, and a reward is given to the believer, if what is believed is also performed.' He does not teach that we are saved by works, but affirms that faith is true, and obtains a reward, when what we believe, we also perform. Nor is Jerome's opinion any different. But let us hear Grotius more fully, executing this in his own special commentary:

Can faith save him? This question denies most effectively. That σῶσαι, to save, is as it is for the most part in the New Testament, to lead someone to eternal life. Here that which Chrysostom said in his oration on faith and natural law and the Holy Spirit can be opposed: 'Without works I can show a believer both having lived and having been deemed worthy of the kingdom. No one has lived without faith. But the thief, having only believed, was justified, and do not tell me he did not have time to live uprightly, for I am not arguing this, but I have demonstrated that, that faith by itself saved. For if he had lived on after his faith and neglected works, he would have fallen from salvation': I can show a believer without works both gifted with life and the kingdom. No one has lived without faith. But the thief, having only believed, was justified. And do not tell me he did not have time to live rightly; for that is not what I am arguing about, but I have made this clear, that faith even by itself saves. For certainly if he had survived his faith, and had neglected to work well, he would have fallen from salvation. And Tertullian on baptism: 'Faith that is whole is secure regarding salvation.' Irenaeus had said: 'The householder is the Lord, who rules over the entire paternal house, giving to servants and those still undisciplined a fitting law: but giving to the free and those justified by faith suitable precepts.' And Augustine, Vol. IV, Book of 83 Questions, question 76: 'But if he has believed it, and soon departed this life, the justification of faith remains with him: not by preceding good works, because he arrived at it not by merit but by grace: nor by following ones, because he is not allowed to be in this life.' Then: It is not, however, to be understood in such a way that, if he has lived after receiving faith, we call him righteous, even if he has lived wickedly. Zosimus the pagan says this is the promise of the Christian faith, τὸ τὺς ἐνσεβῶς ἀναλαμβάνοντας αὐτὴν πάσης ἁμαρτίας ἔξω παραχρῆμα καθίσασθαι, that those who have piously embraced it are immediately placed outside of all sin. Philo also said of Noah before works was pronounced righteous. But it must be noted that faith is understood by these writers and others as that which includes a purpose of obeying God, and now the Gospel, kindled by love of God and neighbor, if not yet most exact, certainly sincere, which is called believing with the whole heart, Acts 8:37. Jerome, in his dialogue between an orthodox believer and a Luciferian, interprets such faith in the Gospel passages concerning the centurion and the woman as a soul devoted to God. Such faith, however, which is immediately followed by death, is said to be without works, not because it does not have pious thoughts as companions, and often some pious words and deeds as well, but because it has not produced a series and course of conspicuous deeds (for that is what τὰ ἔργα, spoken in the plural, signifies, which Christian Greek writers often call πολιτείαν, and Chrysostom very often) having been cut short by time: To this pertains that of Jerome on Matthew 12. Matthew: In the Law, works are required: he who does them shall live in them. In the Gospel, the will is sought, which even if it has not had effect, nevertheless does not lose its reward. Chrysostom on Romans 9:10: ψυχῆς ἀρετὴν δεῖ ζητεῖν, ἣν κὰι πρὸ τῶν ἔργων ὁ Θεὸς οἶδεν. The virtue of the soul must be sought, which God knows even before the works. Why, therefore, does this faith, which could produce salvation without works, not also lead those living longer to salvation? The cause is this: that the indulgence of God given to such believers has in itself a condition, provided that given time and opportunity, pious works follow. But those things which are given under the condition of future time do not remain if the condition is not fulfilled. Sons are called lords of their father's property; yet they can be disinherited for grave reasons. For similar reasons, donations are revoked: liberties are revoked, and a forfeiture clause is usually added to sales, and it is inherent in the very nature of fiefs. Legacies are also considered tacitly taken away if enmities have arisen afterwards. Thus Kings grant an indulgence for crimes to many, but under a certain law, which unless they fulfill, they fall from the promises, as Solomon did to Shimei. In the same manner, Christ shows that unless we forgive others, the remission of sins already obtained from God (which the right of eternal life follows) is rendered void, Matthew 18:34. And those who are again entangled in those vices which they had escaped through the acquired knowledge of Christ, their final lot is said to be worse than that which preceded the knowledge, 2 Peter 2:21, to which places can be added that of Hebrews 10:38. Tertullian in Scorpiace: God had foreseen that even after the washing, after a more advanced faith, many would perish again after salvation. On Repentance: For do not many fall away afterwards? Is not that gift taken away from many? Cyprian, Epistle 7: With the departure of the discipline of the Lord, one has departed from grace. The same on the truth of the Church: Which indeed the Lord would not wonder that the crown of justice could be taken away, except that with the departure of justice, the crown must necessarily depart also. On the Exhortation to Martyrdom: That those snatched from the jaws of the Devil and freed from the snares of the world ought not to return to the world again, lest they lose what they have escaped. Chrysostom on Ephesians 5:14: Ἔπαινός ἐστι τῆς δόξης ἀυτῶ, τὸ τὸς ἐχθρὺς σῶσαι, ἄλλο τὺς ἐκείνως τὺς με- τὰ τὸ γενέσθαι φίλες μείναντας φίλες, ὡς εἰ πάλιν ἐπὶ τὴν προτέραν ἔχθραν ἐπανέλθοιεν, πάντα εἰκῆ κὰι μάτην. It is the praise of His glory to save enemies, but others are those who, after having become friends, remain friends, so that if they should return to their former enmity, all those things become void and vain; where he also adds many excellent things to that matter. Augustine, in his book On Corruption and Grace, says: That some begin to live in the faith which works through love, and live faithfully and justly for some time, and afterwards fall: In the same place: If one already regenerated and justified relapses into an evil life by his own will, certainly he cannot say, 'I did not receive,' because he lost the grace of God he had received by his own free choice for evil. Prosper: That some, from among those regenerated in Christ, having abandoned the faith and pious morals, apostatize from God and end an impious life in their turning away, is proven by many examples, which is to be lamented. It may be asked here, is every such fault of such a kind that it takes away from a man the received right of pardon and that state of grace before God? Not every one; but those which Paul describes in 1 Corinthians 6:9-10, and Galatians 5:19-21, 1 Timothy 1:9-10. Grave, as Tertullian speaks in On Modesty, and destructive, which he who has been born of God will not admit at all, not being about to be a son of God if he should admit them. Ambrose gives an example, 1 Corinthians 6:15: members adhering to a harlot cease to be members of Christ. See also Augustine, Vol. 10, Sermon 41 on the Saints, where he says some are capital by the very act, some if they are held for a long time; some if they are habitual. For there are also faults of another kind, sins (as Tertullian speaks in the aforementioned place) of daily incursion, to which we are all subject. Augustine, Sermon 29 on the words of the Apostle: I do not say, however, that we cannot be here without sin, because we ought therefore to commit homicides or adulteries, or other deadly sins, which kill with a single blow. The same, Book 11 of The City of God, Chapter 12. Since today we not imprudently call those blessed whom we see leading this life justly and piously with the hope of future immortality, without a crime devastating the conscience, easily obtaining Divine mercy for the sins of this infirmity. The same on Faith and Works: Unless there were some things without which this life is not led, He would not have proposed the daily remedy in the prayer which He taught; so that we may say: Forgive us our debts: which can be seen to be taken from Cyprian. For he says thus concerning prayer: Lest anyone please himself as if innocent, when no one is innocent, and perish more by exalting himself, he is instructed and taught that he sins daily, while he is ordered to pray daily for his sins. But this prayer also wants a companion of diligence in working. The same Cyprian on Work and Almsgiving: And because the remission of sins is given once in baptism, constant and continual work, imitating the likeness of baptism, will again bestow the indulgence of God. James himself teaches us to think so below when he says: Πολλὰ πταίομεν ἅπαντες: In many things we all offend; that is, even the best, especially through ignorance, chap. III. 1. Chrysostom on Rom. XI. Πολλὰ καθ᾽ ἑκά- στην πλημμελῶμεν τὴν ἡμέραν, διὸ κᫀν πολλῶ ἡμῖν δεῖ τῶ ἐλέυς, in many things we offend daily, therefore we have need of much mercy. And on chapter XII. Ἐπειδὴ ἄνθρωπος ὄντας εἰκὸς καθ᾽ ἑκάστην ἁμαρτά- νειν τὴν ἡμέραν, since we are human, it is no wonder if we offend in something daily. The same on 1 Cor. XIII. Οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ὃς ἔξω ἐστὶν ἁμαρτίας χωρίς. For there is not, there is not anyone who does not fail. And chap. XVI. Οὐδεὶς ἁμαρτίας ἐκτός. The same in his oration on the earthquake and the rich man and Lazarus: For if anyone is righteous, even if he were righteous a thousand times, and even if he ascended to the very summit, so as to be rid of sins, he cannot be clean of a stain. Even if he were righteous a thousand times, yet he is a man, for who shall boast that his heart is pure? Or who shall be bold enough to say he is clean from sin? For this reason we are commanded in prayer to say, forgive us our debts; so that by the custom of prayer we may be reminded there that we are liable to punishments. Even if someone is righteous, even if he is righteous a thousand times, and has reached the highest summit, so that he is freed from sin, yet no one is pure from every blemish. Even if he is righteous a thousand times, he is a man. For who will boast that his heart is entirely clean; who will glory that he is immune from every fault? Therefore we are commanded to say in prayer, forgive us our debts, so that by that custom of praying we may be reminded that we can be punished. A little later: He is righteous, he is merciful, he is a lover of the poor: But he has some defect: He is righteous, he is merciful, he is a lover of the poor: But he has something in which he still falls short. For the Evangelical covenant is full of equity, and it does not condemn those who walk according to the Spirit, Rom. VIII. 1. that is, it acknowledges as its own those in whose body sin does not reign, Rom. VI. 12. Clement of Alexandria, Strom. II. says that for the elect in CHRIST, those sins are not imputed which μὴ κατὰ προαίρεσιν συνί- στανται, which are not committed by a choice of the will. Furthermore, it must be known that even those who by those graver crimes had fallen from the right of pardon can be restored to their former condition, but through sorrowful repentance, as Augustine speaks, adding that no salvation is to be hoped for them unless they have offered to God a sacrifice, a spirit broken through repentance, Tom. IV. book 83. questions, question 25. But repentance undoubtedly also contains the most diligent amendment of life. And for that reason Irenaeus, when he recites the rule of faith, says: Τοῖς δὲ δικαίοις κᫀμ ὁσίοις, καὶ τὰς ἐντολὰς ἀυτῦ τετηρηκό- σι, καὶ ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ ἀυτῦ διαμεμενηκόσι, τοῖς ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς τῆς δὲ ἐκ μετανοίας ζωὴν χαρισάμενος, ἀφθαρ- σίαν δωρήσηται, καὶ δόξαν αἰωνιον περιποιήσῃ. To the righteous and holy, and those who have kept his commandments, and have remained in his love, some from the beginning, some through repentance, he grants life, and bestows incorruptibility, and procures eternal glory. Salvian paraphrases this passage of James thus in book IV. de Gubernat. Dei: What reason is there that we should deceive ourselves with a false opinion, thinking, namely, because we are called Christians, that a good name can be of help to us among the evils we do, when the Holy Spirit says that not even faith can profit Christian men without good works: and certainly it is much more to have faith than a name: because a name is a word for a man; but faith is the fruit of the mind: and yet the Apostle testifies that this very fruit of faith is unfruitful without good works. The chorus of ancient martyrs and saints agrees with this. Justin, Apology II. 'For he said that not only those who speak, but those who also perform the works, will be saved.' For he said that not those who only speak, but those who also perform the works, will be saved. Irenaeus, book II, chapter LVI. 'But the just will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. But the unjust and those who do not perform the works of justice he will send into eternal fire, where their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished.' Book IV, chapter XXIX. That which was always free and in his own power in man, God has preserved, and his own exhortation, so that he who does not obey him may be justly condemned, because they did not obey, and those who obeyed and believed in him may be honored in incorruptibility, and in the same book, chapter XXXII. 'For God, who is in need of nothing, takes upon himself good and just operations, to the end that he may grant us the retribution of his good things.' Clement, Stromata V. 'We are saved by grace, yet not without good works.' And book VI. 'So that when we hear, "your faith has saved you," we do not expect him to say that those who have believed in any way at all will be saved, unless works also follow.' As often, therefore, as we hear, 'your faith has saved you,' let us not believe it is said that those who believe in any way are saved; but only if works also follow. Cyprian on the precepts of the Church: His precepts and warnings must be obeyed, so that our merits may receive a reward: in which place the word 'merit' of others among the ancients is to be taken in the same way as the word 'reward' is not only among them, but also in the Holy Scriptures, Matt. V. 12, X. 42, Luke VI. 35, 1 Cor. III. 14, certainly not from an equality of work and retribution, which here is certainly none, Rom. VIII. 18, looking back to which Chrysostom said 'greater rewards than the labors' on Rom. VIII and elsewhere: 'Greater indeed than your worth, but worthy of his own kindness,' greater indeed than your merit is worth, but worthy of his own goodness toward men, which Cyprian teaches us is to be understood even of martyrdom itself, the most excellent of works, in his exhortation to martyrdom: 'We have received more in the reward of the passion than we sustain in the passion itself.' But from a most generous promise, which gives a right to us who labor: so that this matter approaches more closely to a donation under condition than to a properly called hiring and letting, to which contract the words of reward and meriting are related; in which sense Paul also says that God will render to the pious according to their works, Rom. II. 6, the explanation of which works is synecdochical through a complex, Matt. XXV, near the end, namely that he will render by a judgment not rigid, but tempered by a certain wonderful clemency and directed to the nature of a most benign covenant made through and because of Christ. Ambrose on Eph. I: 'The redeemed are designated as heirs, if they persevere in regeneration, so that the first faith may merit pardon, but holy conduct persevering with faith may merit the crown.' Jerome against Pelagius, Dial. I: 'To the believer a reward is given, if what is believed is also carried out.' And soon after: Baptism cuts away old sins, it does not bestow new virtues, it releases from prison, and to the one released, if he labors, it promises rewards. Those, therefore, who through faith have obtained the forgiveness of sins, and consequently a right to eternal life, if they desire to retain those good things, ought to take care of two things, having implored the help of God for this with earnest prayer, that they may guard themselves against those crimes that exclude one from the kingdom of God, 1 Pet. III. 10, 2 John V. 14, Rom. VI. 12, 13, 1 John II. 1, where, as in other places of his epistles, the word 'sin' is taken not in a broader sense, which also includes 'offenses' or stumbles, but in a stricter and more serious sense: Then, indeed, that when the opportunity is given, they may produce actions honorable to God and useful to their neighbor, 1 Pet. III. 10, 11. Rom. VI. 13, as if they should progress more and more in piety, but they ought to believe that both are so necessary that, unless they are performed, it will come to pass that a man falls from what he has already obtained. Chrysostom toward the end of chapter IV to the Ephesians: 'It is not enough to be freed from malice, if we are to attain the kingdom of heaven, but there is need also of much working of virtues.' He adds soon after: 'For me to do good is a part of malice,' even not to do good is a part of malice, which Ambrose illustrates with many comparisons in Eph. IV: 'Forgive one another: otherwise God takes back what he has forgiven.' Augustine: 'Forgiven sins return where there is no charity, as the Lord most clearly teaches in the Gospel in the case of that servant from whom the Lord demanded the debt that had been forgiven, because he was unwilling to forgive the debt to his fellow servant.' Elsewhere: 'He who is ungrateful, like a dog, has returned to his vomit, has mortified his past good deeds, and has revoked the sin that was forgiven.' Gregory the Great: 'It is evident from the evangelical sayings that if we do not forgive from the whole heart what is committed against us, that which we were already rejoicing had been forgiven us through repentance is demanded back again.'

Grotius in the same place, in order to refute these testimonies of Chrysostom, Tertullian, Irenaeus, and others, so that they may not testify that faith alone saves without works; he says that by them faith is understood as that which includes the purpose of obeying God, and now the Gospel (by which he understands, in the Socinian manner, a law more perfect than the Mosaic) kindled by the love of God and neighbor: But does this purpose kindled by love not pertain to the works of the law, which are not only external, but also the interior movements of the soul, without which those Doctors, with Paul, deny that we are either justified or saved? Nor does it appear by any indication from those testimonies that they require that purpose to the same end by which faith saves us. But this is rather clear, that faith by itself alone καθ’ ἑαυτὴν saves: that whole faith is secure concerning salvation, that we are justified by faith, and become children of God, and thus heirs of life, that the justification of faith remains with him who departs from life, immediately when he has believed, and thus that salvation is attained neither by preceding nor by consequent good works, and therefore by faith alone. Nor does Acts 8:37, to believe with the whole heart, mean to have faith and a purpose of obeying Divine precepts, kindled by the love of God and neighbor, if not yet most exact, certainly sincere: But to place trust in Jesus with a sincere heart. Nor do the sayings of Jerome on Matthew 12 or of Chrysostom on Romans 9:10 teach that they themselves, by faith, which alone suffices for salvation, understand a faith which includes a purpose of obeying God and the love of God and neighbor, or that a virtue of the soul pertains to the definition of justifying faith, or even that it possesses the faculty of justifying and saving men, which Chrysostom only intimates to be of the duty of a Christian man.

But Grotius himself admits: That faith produces salvation without works: However, he raises a doubt, why does it not also lead those living longer to salvation? He gives this cause, that the indulgence of God given to believers has in itself a condition, provided that given time and opportunity, pious works follow. But where does Scripture teach that faith, when it has produced salvation without works for those living longer, cannot lead to salvation without works? Where does it teach that the remission of sins and the indulgence given to believers has in itself a condition, provided that given time and opportunity, pious works follow? If faith can produce salvation without works, and the condition of works is not included so that it may produce it, why can salvation not also be retained through faith, without the cooperation of our works? For there is not one reason for acquiring justification and salvation, and another for retaining and possessing the same. By faith we acquire salvation, by faith we are also guarded in the acquired salvation and possession of the right to salvation 1 Peter 1:5; nor is justification and the acquisition of salvation only, but also the highest degrees, namely the possession of eternal salvation, so called an effect of faith, that it is denied to works, Romans 4:6. Which Canus teaches against Bannes his preceptor, part 2, rel. de sacr. concl. 3, that justification is the final disposition, and salvation follows without doubt, that salvation is acquired by the same means as justification; which opinion he says is that of Soto, and others in 2, q. 1, a. 8, concl. ult., which also the brothers Walenb. say is in exeg. A. C. We have shown; Grotius’s analogy regarding the manner in which children are called lords of their paternal property, or acquire a paternal inheritance, is opposed to, and does not favor, the Grotian opinion. For just as it is not necessary that children do anything positive of good to obtain possession of an inheritance, but legitimate birth alone suffices as a positive cause: whereas the fact that they do nothing of evil privatively is not something positively influencing the acquisition of the inheritance, but at least something not hindering it, or the absence of a thing harmful to the inheritance: So, for entering into the inheritance of the kingdom of grace and glory, positive works are not required, but regeneration alone suffices, Rom. VIII. 17. The omission of offenses, however, is not a co-influencing cause in the acquisition or taking of the inheritance; but only a requirement on the part of the heir, so that the inheritance may not be hindered, or the sole positive cause, which is faith, through which we are adopted as children, may not be removed. The same is the reasoning for other similar cases. That faith and grace are lost through proaretic (deliberate) sins, Grotius indeed rightly proves against the Calvinists, who contend that faith in the regenerate is unlosable: But this in no way helps the Papists, as if good works were necessary for salvation, or were a condition of obtaining the heavenly inheritance: and it does not even prove this, that abstinence from proaretic offenses contributes to obtaining salvation. For it does not follow that whatever privation hinders an agent principle in its activity, its opposite habit co-influences the actions of the agent principle. Thus, the admission of poison kills natural life, yet abstinence from poison does not preserve natural life: Theft and adultery meritoriously take away a man's life, yet abstinence from theft and adultery does not preserve life. Evil motions, both internal and external, are like poisons to faith; yet the opposite virtues or good works neither preserve faith nor co-influence the proper effect of faith, which is salvation. That not every fault takes away the right to pardon received, and the state of grace, is not from the nature of sin, as if one were venial by itself and by its own nature, and another mortal, as Grotius seems to hint with the Papists: But because proaretic sins do not have repentance as a companion, but have it connected with them among the regenerate, inasmuch as when they are assailed by them, they seriously groan with Paul: Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death? Roman. VII. 20.

Nor indeed do the testimonies from Salvian brought forward regarding this passage of James help Grotius at all, whether he wishes to prove that James understands faith, not as it is merely assent, but also trust, when he says that faith which is without works does not save, or that true faith not destitute of works does not save without works, but that works are required along with faith to obtain salvation, and co-influence this effect, which is the salvation and blessedness of man. He certainly proved neither by any of these testimonies. Regarding the passage of Salvian, it has already been spoken of in part, who does not say that trust in Christ is the saving faith which is destitute of good works, but asserts the contrary, that faith without good works is of no profit: not that good works co-influence salvation, but that without good works there is not even true faith. He does not teach that James, under the word of non-saving faith, includes faith according to its essential definition, as it simultaneously embraces trust in Christ. Our churches deny that mere assent, offered to Divine revelation, is that justifying faith. Salvian also denies this. He testifies that it is also denied by James. He distinguishes the usurpation of the Christian name, or of a faithful man, from faith itself: and faith, as it is a fruit of the mind (assent), from living faith producing works. Nor does he explain that 'faith without works is dead' otherwise than our Church does. By which, he says, he (James) indicates that good acts are witnesses of Christian faith: because a Christian, unless he has done good works, cannot fully prove his faith: and by this, because he is unable to prove that it exists, it must be held entirely as if it did not exist.

Justin, however, describes the subject to be saved, he does not exhibit the definition of saving faith or the manner of obtaining salvation, when he says: He said that not those who merely say, but those who simultaneously do works, will be saved. But he does not say that James understands non-saving faith as trust in Christ; rather, he pronounces with James that the faith which one merely boasts of is not true faith.

Irenaeus also deals with the subject in the earlier passages: finally, he asserts that retribution is provided for good operations; he does not say that good works are the cause of salvation. But he ascribes salvation to faith alone in Book IV, ch. 5. The Law exhorted them, saying, men are not otherwise saved from the ancient plague of the serpent, unless they believe in Him who is exalted in martyrdom according to the likeness of the flesh of sin.

Clement, Strom. V., says we are saved by grace, but not without good works: not that good works save us, for thus we would not be saved by grace, Rom. XI. 6, but that without works there are none who are saved: which he explains in ch. VI, that those who believe in any way whatsoever, even if works do not follow, are not saved. For the 'unless' (ἐὰν μὴ) in the Greek is not an exceptive condition, or to be rendered adversatively; but it is a periphrasis for those who do not truly believe, so that supposititious faith may be refuted, which is also done by James: although even so those things are correctly held, that those who believe in any way whatsoever are not saved, unless works follow faith, so that they are twin Jamesian opinions, that no one is saved by that faith which good works do not follow. In which book Clement says, The Lord says, he who believes has eternal life; blessed therefore are all who trust in Him. But to have trust is something more than faith, which is, namely, bare assent.

The passage of Cyprian does not exist in the book on the precepts of the Church, such a title is not found in Cyprian, but in the book on the unity of the Church. He says, however, that our merits receive a reward; but he does not pronounce them to be the cause of salvation: And Grotius himself acknowledges, in that place, as also in others, that the word merit is to be taken improperly, just as the word reward is not only among them, but also in the Holy Scriptures, Matt. V. 12, chap. X. 42, Luke VI. 35, 1 Cor. III. 14, namely, not from the equality of the work, but from a most liberal promise: which word is accustomed to be taken concerning any acquisition whatsoever, even that which happens through a purely gratuitous gift: as Cyprian said to Fidus that infants merit from Divine mercy. But what Grotius adds, that the most liberal promise of GOD gives us a right; so that this business approaches more closely to a donation under a condition than to a properly so-called contract of letting and hiring, to which contract the words reward and meriting are related: is not to be approved. For the right of eternal life is not given to us as we labor, as such, but as we believe, John I. 12, and those things are inconsistent with the former. For no comparison has a place here with a contract of letting and hiring, where those names find a place not from the equality of work and retribution, but solely from a most liberal promise. For if they do approach here, even if not so closely, yet in some way to a properly so-called hiring, merit will not depend solely on the liberal promise of God and His benign acceptance, but also on the aptitude of the work for such a reward, both of which reasons for merit Grotius has brought forward elsewhere, not without significant self-contradiction, if you compare them with these words; namely, in his annotations to Art. IV of the consultation of Cassander, openly siding with the Papists, nay, worse than the Papists, since they themselves even

The state of the Roman Empire at the Diet of Augsburg in the year 1530, in response to Article IV, and the Council of Siena held two years earlier, c. XXI, ascribe the acceptance of merit entirely to the liberality of the Divine promise: which opinion Vasquez, disp. CCXIV, in I. 2. c. 1, teaches is also that of Scotus, Gregory of Rimini, Biel, Ockham, William of Paris, the Canons of Cologne, Alfonso à Castro, Vega, Bunderius, etc.

But what Grotius inserts here concerning the nature of the new covenant, that it is this, that GOD has accepted that He would accept our works, by their intrinsic goodness and equality, as sufficient for retribution or reward, though they are less than just, is diametrically opposed to Scripture: according to which the nature of the covenant is this, that God, in place of our merits and satisfactions, because we are destitute of them, since they are required by the law, wills to substitute His Son who will perform those things, Rom. VIII. 6, so that through faith in Him we may have eternal life.

As for the remaining testimonies, it is not Ambrose but Ambrosiaster who is cited in chapter 1 to the Ephesians, having used the word merit improperly, because a holy life continuing with faith obtains a crown, which, because he called it an inheritance, he acknowledges by that very fact that it comes to us not by our works, but from the grace of God who adopts us. Jerome, however, adv. Pelag. dial. I, designates the subject to whom the rewards may come, namely that he has labored, not the cause or merit of the rewards, which must also be said of Chrysostom on chapter IV of Ephesians. In the others, the issue is not a positive cause contributing to the acquisition or possession of eternal salvation, but only the impediments to salvation.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Τί τὸ ὄφελος, ἀδελφοί μυ,] In hunc locum ad finem usque capitis commentationem edidimus satis uberem, quam adjunximus nostris ad Evangelia annotatis. Inde & aliunde sumemus hic ea, quæ hujus tractationis modo conve- niunt. Cum Apostoli multam ubique prædicarent fidei ef- ficaciam, inde factum est, ut multi homines carnales, in qui- bus fuit Simon Magus, id arripuerint in vitæ mendosæ patro- cinium, quasi sine operis justis, ut Irenæus loquitur, salus æ- terna possit obtineri, nempe per fidem. Cum contra Apo- stolorum esset doctrina, fidem aptam esse, ut nos purget, pur- gatis dare Spiritum sanctum, & sic fidem fieri efficacem per dilectionem, Gal. V, 6. Ac proinde dilectionem, quæ ex fi- de & spe eam comitante exurgat, plus valere & fide & spe 1. Cor. XIII, 13. Τί τὸ ὄφελος, מַה בֶּצַע, ut Gen. XXXVII, 25. Psalm. XXX, 10. Malach. III, 14. quæ utilitas nempe ad salutem æternam, ut 1.Cor. XV, 32. Pro eodem ὀδὲν ὠφελῶ dixit Paulus 1. Cor. XIII, 2.

Ἐὰν πίστιν λέγῃ τις ἔχειν, ἔργα δὲ μὴ ἔχῃ.] Λέγῃ, id est, cogitet, quomodo λεγέτω supra I, 13. Si quis intra se cogi- tet; opera quidem mea non recta sunt, sed fides recta est: ac propterea de salute non periclitor. Hæc opinio olim valde fuit frequens apud Judæos, qui existimabant, omnem Israëlitam, qui modo professionem Judaismi non abjecisset, partem tandem habiturum in altero seculo, id est, in vita æterna. Eandem sententiam apud multos Christianos in- valuisse ostendit, & eos acriter, ut certe debuit, refellit Au- gustinus libro de fide & operibus. Renata est hoc infelici seculo ea sententia, & quidem sub nomine repurgatæ doctri- næ, cui omnes, qui pietatem & salutem proximi amant, se debent opponere.

In hunc locum adversus comentationem illam Grotii accuratas vindicias An. 1643. adornavit B. Dn. Socer D. Joh. Hülsemannus sub titulo Harmo- nia Apostolica SS. Pauli & Jacobi de JUSTIFI- CATIONE, ab HUGONIS GROTII cor- ruptelis vindicata. Licebit ergo nobis esse brevio- ribus. Ne tamen ille tractatus Grotii desideretur, quum reliquos integros in finem aliter tamen di- stributos, annotatis ad Evangelia adjunctos addu- xerimus, & deinceps adducere constituerimus, ju- vat istam commentationem & hic addere, adeoque; simul confutare, ac eadem fidelia duos dealbare parietes. Ita autem habet ad v.14. ibidem Grotius:

Vers. 14. Τί τὸ ὄφελος, ἀδελφοί μυ, ἐὰν πίςιν λέγῃ τις ἔχειν, ἔργα δὲ μὴ ἔχῃ;] Quid proderit, fratres mei, si fidem quis di- cat se habere, opera autem non habeat?) Cum hortatus ad opera benefica in proximum late exequutus esset Ja- cobus, necessitatem talium operum ostendit ex periculo absque eis non obtinendæ salutis. Si quis dicat, ex ani- mo scilicet, ut modo sumpta est loquutio similis 14. Con- cedit Jacobus hoc ab aliquibus vere dici, fidem se habe- re, etsi opera non accedant, non eo sensu, quo fides to- tam pietatem Christianam μετωνυμικῶς aut συνεκδοχι- κῶς per transnominationem aut complexionem signifi- cat, ut Rom. X, 16. Tit. I, 1. sed illo, quo assensum veri- tati à Deo revelatæ præbitum indicat, & à pœnitentia di- sttinguitur, Marc. I, 15. item à dilectione, 1. Cor. XIII, 2. Galat. V. 6. Eph. VI, 23. 1. Tim. I, 14. 2. Tim. I, 13. & II, 22. & puritate Act. XV, 9. & bona conscientia, 1. Tim. I, 19. qualem assensum esse posse sine professione ac proinde & sine piis operibus, à quibus hic distinguitur, ut & Tit. III, 8. docemur Joh. XII, 42. Neque id mirum, quum sæpe locum habeat illud, quod de Atheniensibus dicebant Spartani, scire eos, quid rectum esset, sed facere nolle. Sic Medea apud Ovidium: - - - Video meliora proboque Deteriora sequor. Eadem in Græca Tragoedia: Καὶ μανθάνω μὲν οἷα δρᾶν μέλλω κακὰ, Θυμὸς δὲ κρείσσων τῶν ἐμῶν βουλευμάτων. Nec me latet, nunc quam cruenta cogitem, Sed vincit ira sanitatem pectoris.

Ideo evenit, quod voluntas in facultates ministras, imo & in ipsum intellectum ex parte aliqua, nempe, ut hoc vel illud consideret, atque in id se intendat, agit do- minatus jure, & obtemperari sibi omnino facit. At in- tellectus, ut in libera Republica oratores, persuasionibus agit in voluntatem, neque semper impetrat obsequium, ob eam libertatem, quæ agnata ac propria est voluntati. Hinc fit, ut quo cognitio est lucidior, eo, si voluntas non sequatur, pœna est gravior, Luc. XII, 47. 48. Rom. II, 21. Tertullianus: Hæc erit vis Divinæ gratiæ potentior utique natura, habens in nobis subjacentem sibi liberam arbitrii potestatem, quod ἀυτεξύσιον dicitur, quæ cum ipsa sit & naturalis atque mutabilis, quoquo vertitur, na- tura convertitur. Inesse autem nobis τὸ ἀυτεξύσιον na- turaliter jam & Marcioni ostendimus & Hermogeni. Scriptor responsionum ad orthodoxos: Τὸ ἀγαθὺς ἢ μᾶς εἶναι κακὺς, ὁ Θεὸς ἐκ ἐν τῇ γνώσει ἔθηκε τῶν γινω- σκομένων, ἀλλ' ἐν τῇ ἁιρέσει τῶν ἁιρεμένων, ut boni aut ma- li simus, Deus non in cognitione posuit eorum, quæ co- gnoscuntur, sed in electione eorum quæ eliguntur: Qui cum optime conveniunt ea, quæ Justinus ipse Apologe- tico tum priore tum posteriore περὶ προαιρέσεως pie dis- serit, & quæ Irenæus libr. IV. cap. 29. Non ergo talem fidem dari negat Jacobus, sed utilitatem negat esse ab ea, quæ speratur, contra quam docebant Simoniani. Vide Irenæum libr. I. cap. 20.

De occasione hujus tractationis dictum in Prole- gomenis: Apostolorum autem doctrina non hæc erat, fidem aptam esse, ut nos purget, purgatis dari Spiritum sanctum, & sic fidem fieri efficacem per di- lectionem. Adscribunt quidem fidei purificatio- nem cordis, Act. XV, 9. non autem ex fidei quadam aptitudine, aut quod per modum dispositionis sese habeat ad purificationem, vel peccatorum remissio- nem, quam justificationem primam fingunt Papi- stæ, fidem dispositive tantum justificare contenden- tes, quod vero de informi fide, quam commenti sunt, affirmant: Sed ex mera Dei gratia, quia Deus fidem imputat ad justitiam, & sanguine Christi, quo unice purificantur conscientiæ nostræ ab omni pecca- to, 1. Joh. I, 7. Ebr. IX, 14. per fidem apprehenso peccata nostra eluit, eademque nobis remittit, ac justitiam vel obedientiam Christi nobis per fidem imputat, ut eadem justi coram tribunali Divino constituamur, Rom. V, 18. Fides ergo non dispo- nendo nos justificat, sed apprehendendo Christi sa- tisfactionem & meritum, quem Deus nobis in pro- pitiatorium proposuit per fidem in sanguine ipsius, Rom. III, 25. Fide non inchoatur tantum, sed per- ficitur nostri coram Deo justificatio, & quidem si- ne operibus nostris, quo de Apostolus ibidem v. 27. λογιζόμεθα ἐν πίςει δικαιῶσθαι ἄνθρωπον χωρὶς ἔργων νόμꙋ. Purgatis hoc modo, id est, justificatis dari Spiritum sanctum, & sic fidem, qua justificati sumus, efficacem fieri per dilectionem admittimus; non quod fides informis operetur, id est, formetur, ut barbare Papistæ: Sed forma ejus est ipsa appre- hensio justitiæ vel obedientiæ Christi tam activæ quam passivæ: Dilectio autem consequens ejus est, per quam ἐνεργυμένη operosa & efficax est fides, non ad justificationem, utpote quæ sine operibus le- gis, quale est dilectio, sit, sed ad exercendum sese, vel quod fides salvifica non otiosa sit, sed in dile- ctione, & per opera dilectionis actuosa, quæ non antecedunt justificandum, sed sequuntur justifica- tum. Duas autem diversas justificationis species, quas excogitarunt Papistæ, ignorat penitus scri- ptura. Ubi enim, obsecro, docetur prima justifica- tio, in qua fides imputetur pro justitia inchoata, & via sit ac dispositio ad justitiam; ita, ut propter hanc fidem Deus credenti peccata remittat, & justitiam completam infundat? Ubi secunda justificatio legi- tur in scripturis, eademque talis, qua fides completa per opera imputetur ad justitiam, ita, ut opera illam mereantur, quatenus fiunt ex fide & gratia Christi? Ubi docetur in sacris literis, justificatione prima hominem ex non injusto fieri justum: Secunda ex justo fieri justiorem? Ex adverso vero quum nulla inhæ- rens justitia ad justificationem nostri coram Deo faciat; quomodo admitti potest justificationis in primam & secundam distinctio, utpote quæ ex- truitur ex inhærentis justitiæ diversitate? Ubi doce- tur hominem prima justificatione justificari, cum infunditur gratia, hoc est, habitualis justitia, seu charitas? Secunda justificatione cum ex habitu charitatis præstantur opera justitiæ, & per justitiam actualem augetur, ac perficitur habitualis? Kενοφω- νίας, & κακοφωνίας ejusmodi Scholasticis relin- quimus, distinctionculis suis tum in scriptura ignotis, tum scripturæ adversis, sententiam Pauli pervertentibus, & evertentibus, adversus quas alias satis actum.

Porro quomodo dilecti major fide & spe sit ad 1. Cor. XIII, 3. diximus. Plus valere fide ad vitam æternam, blasphemia est in satisfactionem, & me- ritum Christi, cujus fiduciali receptione unice sa- lutem consequimur. De cætero si fidem quis jactet, operibus autem destituatur, talem fidem nihil vale- re, illumque fidei jactatorem nihili ac vanum esse, sive intra se cogitet, sive voce se jactet, ultro ad- mittimus, eamque jactantiam non ab Augustino so- lum l. de fide & oper. sed ab aliis antiquis Doctori- bus, nec ab illis tantum, sed hic etiam à S. Jacobo, imo etiam ab Apostolo Paulo profligatam esse agnoscimus.

Calumnia vero atrox est, sub nomine repurgatæ doctrinæ Judaicam illam persuasionem, quod par- tem habeat in altero seculo, qui modo professio- nem Judaismi non abjiciat, atque hæreticam, quod salutem æternam consequantur, qui modo Chri- stianismum profitentur, hoc infelici seculo rena- tam esse, cui omnes, qui pietatem & salutem proxi- mi amant, se debeant opponere. In Papatu quæ- rantur talia. In doctrina repurgata ministerio B. Lutheri frustra quaerentur. Illi salvari admittunt, imo propugnant, qui credere se profitentur, quod Catholica credit Ecclesia, etiamsi quid illa credat, aut quid credendum sit, ignorent. Illi contra scri- pturam & antiquitatem contendunt fidem veram esse posse, etiamsi sine operibus justis sit:quod utrumq; hic reprobat S. Jacobus, docens, vanam esse profes- sionem nudam fidei, neque veram esse fidem, quae cas- sa sit bonis operibus; multo minus nudam professio- nem fidei, fidemque ejusmodi falso jactatam quen- quam salvare. Sed quid hoc ad repurgatam do- ctrinam, qua per fidem in Christum, hoc est, per obe- dientiam Christi fide apprehensam unice nos justi- ficari credimus, ut gratia Dei & meritum Christi contra ejusdem conculcatores Anti-Christianos ad- seratur: fidem autem in Christum non separari posse a dilectione & bonis operibus, quae etsi ad nostram coram Deo justificationem nihil conducant, cum justifica tamen & salvifica fide indivulso nexu co- haerent, nec ab eadem unquam abesse possunt. Quorum prius imprimis Paulus in tractatione ar- ticuli fundamentalis de justificatione docuit: posteri- us hic exequutus est Jacobus: utrumque repurgata doctrina tuetur, neutrum in Papatu sartum tectum custoditum, cujus proinderepurgatio non infelici- tati seculi, sed felicitati & gratiae Divinae inaestima- bili tribuenda, nisi in Deum ingrati, in nos ipsos aeque, & in proximi salutem injurii esse velimus.

De Papistis non mirum, quod fingant, eam fuis- se Simonis Magi haeresin, quod homo fide sola justifi- cetur, quam hic profligari a Jacobo calumniantur Lorinus, Estius, Cornelius a Lapide. Sed eadem chorda oberrare Grotium, antiquitatis heluonem detestandam magis, quam mirandum. Nihil enim tale uspiam sive apud Irenaeum, sive Epiphanium,si- ve Eusebium, sive Theodoreturn, sive Augustinum legitur, sed ex odio adversus B. Lutherum id omne a Papistis excogitatum est: Quod Augustinus docet de fide & operibus cap. XIV. Pseudo-Apostolorum quosdam asseruisse, ad salutem obtinendam solam fidem sufficere, idque hic refelli a Jacobo, quod iti- dem plerique Pontificii Interpretes contendunt, ex ipso Augustino refellitur, qui id solum docet, non esse veram fidem, quae cum studio sanctitatis conjun- cta non est: nec Pseudo-Apostolorum, sed Apo- stolorum ea fuit doctrina, veram & vivam fidem, quam Augustinus vocat fidem salubrem ac plane Evangelicam sufficere ad salutem Eph.II, 8. 9. Neque tam haereticorum, quam hypocritarum, qui cum impie viverent, fidem tamen jactabant, opinionem hic profligare Jacobum, apparet: Quam causam hujus tractationis confirmat persuasio ex abusu doctrinae Evangelicae Apostoli aetate jam exorta; Rom. III, cap. VI, 1. seqq. conf. 2. Petr. II, 10. cap. III, 5. seqq.

Quod ad συνέχειαν cum superioribus, non tam remote quaerenda, ubi propior datur. Hortatus ad opera benefica in proximum fuit, non ut ne- cessitatem eorum ad salutem doceret, quam neq; nunc adstruit Apostolus, sed veram θρησκείαν esse docuit, cum viduis & orphanis beneficentiam ex- hibemus, & nos immaculatos a mundo servamus, ad id tacite exhortans: Ad salutem autem id unice requisivit, ut agnita e speculo legis nostra impuritate, speculum Evangelicum vel doctrinam libertatis per- fectam oculis mentis introspiciamus, ac per fidem a peccatis mundemur. Nexum interim fidei talis in Christum gloriosum ostendit cum studio pietatis & charitatis sine προσωποληψία exercendae, quam lex Regia charitatis minime admittit, eumque contra vanos fidei jactatores adeo necessarium asserit, ut ne quidem fides vera esse possit, ubi non exerit sese per charitatem & opera. Recte itaque B. Hülse- mannus: Hortatus est quidem ad opera benefica adversus proximum Apostolus cap. I. v. ult. At mo- dus connectendi hoc argumentum de fide imagina- ria cum argumento antecedente immediate, non est hortatorius sed dehortatorius à προσωποληψίᾳ, tan- quam vitio charitati & beneficentiae Christianae con- trario, quod patet ex versuum antecedentium colla- tione cum hoc versu. Et medium probandi turpi- tudinem & noxam hujus vitii est incompatibilitas ejus, ut sic dicam, cum natura vera fidei. Dehortan- di ergo à προσωποληψίᾳ medium non est necessitas beneficentiae ad obtinendam salutem, sed necessitas physica, quod vera fides consistere non possit cum προσωποληψίᾳ, seu deliberata prælatione divi- tis præ paupere, aut deliberata desertione & injuria vel contemptu pauperis. Quod probatur ex con- tinuatione & applicatione ejusdem inopis exem- pli vers. 2. & 15. ut fides in Christum gloriosum consistere non potest cum prælatione viri splen- dide vestiti præ paupere & nudo, vers. 2. Ita multo minus cum desertione & illusione fratris nudi & pauperis vers. 15. 16. 17.

Specialior adhuc nexus est cum v. 5. quod Deus legerit divites in fide hæredes regni, quod promisit diligentibus ipsum: ubi dilectionem iterum à fide divellendam non esse innuit, quod sola quidem fi- des in electione ad salutem spectata sit, ea tamen necessario conjunctam habeat dilectionem, utpo- te quæ in hæredibus regni cœlestis à fide insepara- bilis sit; & è v. 13. quod in judicio quidem Divino absolutorio unice misericordia Divina dominetur, triumphans adversus condemnationem legis, quæ miseris peccatoribus incumbit, Rom. XI, 32. operi- bus tamen charitatis & misericordiæ minime desti- tuta sit fides in Christum gloriosum, misericordiæ Divinæ conciliatorem; ac immisericordes judici- um sine misericordia expectare habeant, utpote fi- de destituti, quæ sine misericordia nulla est.

Jam quod ad propositionem in hac posteriori parte, in verbis ἐὰν πίςιν λέγῃ τις ἔχειν, manifestum est, nequaquam de fide vera in Christum glorio- sum, sed de fidei jactantia, sermo est: neq; concedit Jacobus, vere hoc ab aliquibus dici, quod fidem ha- beant, etiamsi opera non accedant; Nam hoc est, quod probat Jacobus, fidem illam non veram esse sed vanam, non vivam, sed mortuam, quæ operibus destituta est: nec aliud phrasis illa importat, si quis dicat, fidem se habere, opera autem non habeat, quam gloriationem de fide: quomodo constat apud Jacobum dicere opponi veritati rei, cap. I, 13. cap. II, 16. ac sermonem hypocriticum vel falsum, non verum notare. Id quidem certum, quod fi- des vera per vocem πίςεως intelligatur, prout fi- dem Jacobus cap. I, 3. 6. cap. II, 1. 5. cap. V, 15. describit, idque postulat gloriatio ipsa; nam quis de fide non vera gloriaretur? Sed illud λέγειν va- num tantum est dicere, non congruit veritati. Ja- ctat talis veram fidē; sed revera non est vera fides. Vana est veræ fidei jactantia. Papistæ quidem fi- dem, quæ abjuncta ab operibus non possit homi- nem servare, de vera fide, sed informi explicant, Cornelius à Lapide, Estius, alii: Sed Jacobus. Si quis dicat, inquiens, fidem habere se, & opera non habeat, num potest hæc fides, quæ opera non habet, eum servare? Non ait: Si quis fidem habeat, sed si quis dicat, se habere fidem, hoc est, jactet fidem; Vera enim fides sine operibus esse nequit, Gal. V, 6. Joh. XI, 1. seqq. Luc. VII, 42. 43. Fides informis non est fides vera, sed informe monstrum fidei. Quod in Exegemate A. C. ostensum. Fides sine operibus καθ' ἑαυτὴν mortua est, teste Jacobo, v. 17. nec aliter fides vera quam corpus mortuum corpus verum. Assensum quidem habere quis veritati revelatæ potest, sed is non est fides in Christum, ad quam fidu- cia requiritur. Neque dicta illa adducta de nudo assensu loquuntur, Marc. I. Fides à resipiscentia quidem distinguitur, vera tamen in Christum fidu- cia est, cum Evangelio credimus, quam cum resi- piscentia Christus prædicavit: hæc enim summa con- cionum ejus fuit, qui non nudum assensum, sed fi- duciam requisivit; neque nudus assensus Galat. V, 6. sed fiducia intelligitur, quæ per dilectionem operosa est: adeoque distinguitur quidem à dilectione; sed necessario eandem habet comitem. Et 1. Cor. XIII, 2. nec Eph. VI, 23. Fides aliter accipienda, quam de fiducia in Christum, (quo posteriori loco de dile- ctione non nostra, sed Dei erga nos sermo) nec 1. Tim. I, 14. vel 2. Tim. I, 13. aut cap. II, 22. vel etiam Act. XV, 11. 1. Tim. I, 19. Licet ergo assensus esse possit, sine professione; non tamen fiducia in Chri- stum sine professione aut operibus esse potest. Fi- dem autem totam pietatem Christianam, Rom. X, 16. Tit. I, 1. significare negamus: neque fidem cum operibus confundi permittimus, quæ accura- te Apostoli distinguunt. Paulus certe fidem in Christum ac justitiam, operibus opponit, Rom. X, 3. seqq. cum per fidem nos justificari, non per ope- ra docet, Judæos qui propriam justitiam erigere conantes justitiam fidei destruere, adstruit: Tit. I, 1. fidem electorum de fide in objectum à seculo ab- sconditum intelligit v. 2. quæ utique non potest di- ci de studio pietatis. Cæterum causam, quod non omnes assentientes rebus credendis bene vivant non esse naturalem impotentiam intellectus ad per- suadendam voluntatem, sed corruptionem appetitus & affectuum, & defectum, absentiam vel subtra- ctionem renovantis gratiæ, Lev. VIII, 15. seqq. Deut. XXIX, 4. neq; naturaliter cognoscere intellectum ex mandato voluntatis, aut omnem applicationem intellectus esse ex dominatu voluntatis; sed uti ocu- lus sponte videt rem coloratam; ita intellectum motu naturali & spontaneo appetere cognitionem rerum cognoscibilium, erudite hic disserit B. Hül- semannus. Sed illa ceu ad S. Jacobi sententiam pa- rum facientia hic non prosequimur.

Μὴ δύναται ἡ πίστις σῶσαι αὐτόν.] Concedit aliquam fidem talem esse posse: sed salutem æternam ei competere negat. Pro σῶσαι Arabs habet eruere, Syrus לתח יוני vivificare. Dicunt quidem interdum viri sancti, aliquos servari fide an- te opera, sed intelligunt ante perpetuam seriem tractumque bonorum operum, quia scilicet vita illis ad id indulta non est. Cæterum nulla cuiquam fides profuit sine tali opere, quale tempus permittebat, ut illius cum Christo crucifixi exemplo apparet. Salvianus IV. de gubernatione Dei: Cum Spiritus sanctus nec fidem quidem dicat hominibus Christianis sine operibus bonis posse prodesse. Cyprianus de habitu virgi- num: Credenti præmium datur: si quod creditur & geratur. Adde Hieronymum dialogo I. adversus Pelagium.

Non hic talis concessio deprehenditur, quod fi- des vera esse possit, quæ operibus destituta est. Sed contrarium: siquidem eam jactantiam vanam esse dicat S. Jacobus fidei, si opera non adsint: ac de ta- li fide pronunciat, eam fidem, qua cassa est operibus, hominem, utut maxime jactitet, se veram habere fidem, salvare non posse: Quomodo Augustinus cap. XIV. de fide & bonis operibus docet, per hanc restrictionem, si opera non habeat, osten- di non quamlibet fidem, qua in Deum creditur, sed eam salubrem, planeque Evangelicam, cujus opera ex dilectione procedunt, justificare: Idque adversus eos, qui asserebant, quod ad salutem ob- tinendam sufficiat sola fides, etsi bene vivere, & bonis operibus viam Dei tenere quis neglexerit. Negat hic ergo hac interrogatione Jacobus, fidem opera non habentem salvare; non tamen adferit opera ad sa- lutem necessaria esse cum fide: Uti fidem, quæ per charitatem efficax est, salvare, è Gal. V, 6. recte di- citur, non item fidem, quatenus efficax est per chari- tatem. Fidei necessario coëxistere charitatem, ac fidem, qua salvamur, non esse sine operibus, cer- tum est, sed fidei cooperari charitatem vel opera, ut salvemur, aut coinfluere illa ad salutem, id minime adserit Jacobus, & aperte S. Paulo repugnat, qui concludit Rom. III, 25. hominem justificari per fi- dem sine operibus legis: Et Rom. IV, 6. beatitudi- nem esse hominis cui Deus imputat justitiam (Chri- sti) sine operibus legis. Neque sancti viri, Patres antiqui aliquos servari fide ante opera solum ita docent, quod ante perpetuam seriem tractumque bonorum operum serventur, quibus ad id vita in- dulta non est, sed fide non operibus servari cum Paulo adserunt; neque opera excludi à justificatio- ne & salvatione quoad tractum & perpetuam se- riem, sed simpliciter è Paulo, & Doctoribus Ca- tholicis constat, & exemplo conversi latronis con- firmatur, qui salutem non per opera, sed per fidem in CHRISTUM consequutus est. Admittimus utique, quod Salvianus Libr. IV. de gubernatio- ne DEI dixit, nec fidem sine operibus bonis prodesse quia ne quidem est fides in Christum, aut esse potest sine bonis operibus; ac si statuatur fides, quæ sine bonis operibus sit, eam haud prodesse, nec quen- quam servare posse sonora voce hic proclamat Ja- cobus. S. Cyprianus adversus vanos fidei jactatores itidem agit: Quod si liberatori debet obsequium li- beratus, qui esse cupimus Christiani debemus, quod Christus fecit & docuit, imitari. Tunc respondet ad fidem nominis sectator veritatis, & credenti præmium datur, si quod creditur, & geratur. Non per ope ra nos servari docet, sed fidem veram esse, ac præ mium consequi, cum quod credimus, etiam geri mus, affirmat. Nec alia Hieronymi est sententia Sed audiamus Grotium fusius, sua in commenta tione peculiari exequentem:

Mὴ δύναται ἡ πίσις σῶσαι αὐτὸν.] Nunquid pote- rit salvare eum? Interrogatio hæc efficacissi- me negat. Illud σῶσαι salvare, ut plerumque in No- vo Testamento est ad vitam æternam aliquem per- ducere. Opponi hic potest id, quod dixit Chryso- stomus oratione de fide & lege naturali & Spiritu sancto: Ἄνευ ἔργων τὸν πισὸν δύναμαι δεῖξαι καὶ ζήσαν- τα καὶ βασιλείας ἀξιωθέντα. Οὐδεὶς ἄνευ πίστεως ἔζησεν. Ὁ δὲ λῃστὴς πιστεύσας μόνον ἐδικαιώθη, καὶ μή μοι λέγε, οὐκ ἔσχε καιρὸν πολιτεύεσθαι, οὐδὲ γὰρ ἐγὼ τῦτο φιλονει- κῶ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκεῖνο παρέστησα, ὅτι ἡ πίστις καθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν ἔσωσεν. Εἰ γὰρ ἐπέζησε τῇ πίστει καὶ ἔργων ἠμέλησεν, ἐξέπεσε τῆς σωτηρίας: Sine operibus fidelem possum ostendere & vita & regno donatum. Nemo sine fide vixit. At latro tantum credens justificatus est. Nec mihi di- cas tempus recte vivendi non habuit; neque enim id est, de quo disputo, sed hoc apertum feci, fidem etiam per se solam salvare. Nam certe si supervixisset fidei, & operari bene neglexisset, excidisset a salute. Et Tertullianus de baptismo: Fides integra secura est de salute. Irenæus dixerat: Paterfamilias dominus est, qui universæ domui paternæ dominatur, servis quidem & adhuc indisciplinatis condignam tradens legem: liberis antem & fide justificatis congrua dans præcepta. Et Augustinus Tom. IV. Libr. LXXXIII. quæstionum, quæstione LXXVI. quod si eam credi- derit, mox hac vita decesserit, justificatio fidei ma- net cum illo: nec præcedentibus bonis operibus, quia non merito ad illam sed gratia pervenit: nec conse- quentibus, quia in hac vita esse non sinitur. Dein- de: Non tamen ita intelligendum est, ut accepta fi- de si vixcrit, dicamus eum justum, etiamsi male vixe- rit Zosimus paganus Christianæ fidei hanc dicit esse pollicitationem, τὸ τὺς ἐνσεβῶς ἀναλαμβάνοντας αὐτὴν πάσης ἁμαρτίας ἔξω παραχρῆμα καθίσασθαι, eos qui pie eam sunt amplexi statim extra peccatum omne poni. Philo quoque Noam ante opera dixit justum pronunciatum. Sed notandum fidem ab his scriptoribus & aliis eam intelligi, quæ propositum o- bediendiDeo, & nunc Evangelio, accensum Dei & pro- ximi dilectione, si nondum exactissima; certe sincera, includat, quod dicitur toto corde credere, Actor. VIII. 37. Talem fidem Hieronymus in dialogo orthodoxi & Luciferiani in Evangelii locis de centurione & mu- liercula interpretatur devotam in DEUM animam. Ta- lis autem fides, quam statim mors subsequitur, sine operibus esse dicitur, non quod non pias cogitationes habeat comites, sæpe & dicta & facta aliqua pia, sed quod seriem tractumque factorum conspicuorum (id enim τὰ ἔργα pluraliter dicta significant, quod πολιτεί- αν vocant Græci scriptores Christiani sæpe, sæpissime autem Chrysostomus) tempore interclusa non ediderit: Huc illud pertinet Hieronymi ad XII. Matthæi: In le- ge opera requiruntur: quæ qui fecerit, vivet in eis: In Evangelio voluntas quæritur, quæ etiam si effectum non habuerit, tamen præmium non amittit. Chrysosto- mus ad Rom. IX. 10. ψυχῆς ἀρετὴν δεῖ ζητεῖν, ἣν κὰι πρὸ τῶν ἔργων ὁ Θεὸς οἶδεν. Animi virtus quærenda est, quam & ante opera Deus novit. Cur ergo ista fi- des, quæ sine operibus salutem parere potuit, non e- tiam diutius viventes perducit ad salutem? Causa hæc est, quod indulgentia Dei data sic credentibus habet in se conditionem, dummodo dato tempore & occasione pia opera sequantur. Quæ autem sub conditione futuri temporis dantur, ea non permanent, si non præstetur conditio. Filii Domini dicuntur rerum paternarum; tamen exhæredari gravibus de causis possunt. Ex cau- sis similibus revocantur donationes: revocantur liber- tates, & venditionibus adjici solet lex commissoria, & feudis suapte inest natura. Tacite quoque adempta censentur legata ortis post inimicitiis. Sic Reges mul- tis dant criminum indulgentiam, sed sub certa lege, quam nisi impleverint, cadant promissis, ut Salomo Semei. Eundem in modum nisi nos remittamus aliis, impetratam jam a Deo peccatorum remissionem (quam jus vitæ æternæ consequitur) irritam fieri ostendit Christus, Matth. XVIII. 34. Et qui iterum impli- cantur iis vitiis, quæ per adeptam Christi cognitio- nem effugerant, eorum fors postrema pejor ea, quæ cognitionem præcesserat, dicitur futura, 2. Petr. II. 21. quibus locis addi potest ille Ebr. X. 38. Tertul- lianus Scorpiaco: Prospexerat Deus, etiam post la- vacrum, post editiorem fidem perituros plerosque rursum post salutem. De pœnitentia: Non enim multi postea excidunt? Non à multis donum illud au- fertur? Cyprianus epistola VII. Recedente disciplina Dominicæ recessit à gratia. Idem de veritate Ecclesiæ: Quod utique Dominus non miraretur, auferri posse coronam justitiæ, nisi quia recedente justitia recedat necesse est & corona. De exhortatione martyrii: Ere- ptos de faucibus Diaboli, & de laqueis seculi liberatos non debere denuo ad seculum reverti, ne perdant, quod evaserint. Chrysostomus in Eph. V. 14. Ἔπαινός ἐστι τῆς δόξης ἀυτῶ, τὸ τὸς ἐχθρὺς σῶσαι, ἄλλο τὺς ἐκείνως τὺς με- τὰ τὸ γενέσθαι φίλες μείναντας φίλες, ὡς εἰ πάλιν ἐπὶ τὴν προτέραν ἔχθραν ἐπανέλθοιεν, πάντα εἰκῆ κὰι μάτην. Laus est gloriæ ipsius servare inimicos, sed eos, qui, postquam facti sunt amici, amici manent, ita ut si ad inimicitias priores redeant, irrita ac vana fiant illa omnia; ubi & multa ad eam rem subnectit egregia. Augustinus libro de corruptione & gratia ait: Quos- dam in fide, quæ per dilectionem operatur, incipe- re vivere, & aliquandiu fideliter ac juste vivere, & postea cadere: Ibidem: Si jam regeneratus & justifica- tus in malam vitam sua voluntate relabitur, certe iste non potest dicere, non accepi, quia acceptam grati- am Dei suo in malum libero amisit arbitrio. Prosper. Ex regeneratis in Christo quosdam relicta fide & piis moribus apostatare à Deo, & impiam vitam in sua aversione finire, multis, quod dolendum est, proba- tur exemplis. Quæri hic potest, an igitur omnis cul- pa talis sit, ut homini adimat acceptum jus veniæ, sta- tumque illum gratiæ apud Deum? Non omnis; Sed il- læ, quos describit Paulus 1. Cor. VI. 9. 10. & Gal. V. 19. 20. 21. 1. Tim. I. 9. 10. Gravia, ut loquitur Tertul- lianus de pudicitia, & exitiosa, quæ non admittet o- mnino, qui natus ex Deo fuerit, non futurus Dei fili- us, si admiserit. Exemplum dat Ambrosius, 1. Cor. VI. 15. membra adhærentia meretrici desinunt esse membra Christi. Vide & Augustinum Tom. X. de San- ctis serm. XLI. ubi quædam capitalia dicit actu ipso, quædam si longo tempore teneantur; quæ- dam si assidua sint. Sunt enim & alterius generis culpæ, delicta (ut dicto loco Tertullianus loqui- tur) quotidianæ incursionis, quibus omnes sumus subjecti. Augustinus serm. XXIX: de verbis Aposto- li. Non autem dico, quia non possumus hic esse sine peccato, quod ideo homicidia facere debemus aut adul- teria, aut cætera mortifera peccata, quæ uno ictu per rimunt. Idem libr. XI. de civit. DEI cap. XII. Cum hodie non imprudenter beatos vocemus, quos videmus juste ac pie cum spe futuræ immortalitatis hanc vitam ducere, sine crimine vastante conscientiam, facile im- petrantes peccatis hujus infirmitatis Divinam misericor- diam. Idem de fide & operibus: Nisi essent quædam, sine quibus hæc vita non agitur, non quotidianam me- delam proponeret in oratione, quam docuit; ut dica- mus: Dimitte nobis debita nostra: quæ ex Cypriano sumpta videri possunt. Is enim sic de oratione: Ne quis sibi quasi innocens placeat, cum innocens nemo sit, & se extollendo plus pereat, instruitur & doce- tur peccare se quotidie, dum quotidie pro peccatis ju- betur orare. Sed & hæc oratio comitem sibi vult ope- randi diligentiam. Idem Cyprianus de opere & Elee- mosyna: Et quia semel in baptismo remissio pecca- torum datur, assidua & jugis operatio, baptismi in- star imitata, Dei rursus indulgentiam largietur. Ita sentire nos docet ipse Jacobus infra cum ait: Πολλὰ πταίομεν ἅπαντες: In multis offendimus omnes; id est, etiam optimi, per ignorantiam præsertim, cap. III. 1. Chrysostomus in Rom. XI. Πολλὰ καθ᾽ ἑκά- στην πλημμελῶμεν τὴν ἡμέραν, διὸ κᾀν πολλῶ ἡμῖν δεῖ τῶ ἐλέυς, in multis quotidie offendimus, ideo & multæ nobis opus misericordia. Et in caput XII. Ἐπειδὴ ἄνθρωπος ὄντας εἰκὸς καθ᾽ ἑκάστην ἁμαρτά- νειν τὴν ἡμέραν, homines cum simus, nihil mirum, si quotidie in aliquo offendimus. Idem in 1. Cor. XIII. Οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ὃς ἔξω ἐστὶν ἁμαρτίας χωρίς. Non est enim, non est quispiam, qui non delinquat. Et cap. XVI. Οὐδεὶς ἁμαρτίας ἐκτός. Idem oratione de terræ motu & divite & Lazaro: Εἰ γὰρ δίκαιος ἦ τις, κἄν μυριάκις ἦ δίκαιος, κᾂν πρὸς ἀυτὴν ἀναβῇ τὴν κορυ- φὴν, ὥστε ἀπηλλάχθαι τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων, ἐ δύναται και θαρὸς εἶναι κηλῖδος. Κἄν μυριάκις ἦ δίκαιος, ἀλλ᾽ ἄν- θρωπός ἐσι, τίς γὰρ καυχήσεται ἁγνὴν εἶναι τὴν καρ- δίαν; ἢ τίς παῤῥησιάσεται καθαρὸς εἶναι ἀπὸ ἁμαρτίας; Διὰ τῦτο κελευόμεθα εἰς τὴν εὐχὴν λέγειν, ἄφες ἡμῖν τὰ ὀφειλήματα ἡμῶν; ἵνα τῇ συνηθείᾳ τῆς εὐχης ἀνα- μνησθῶμεν ἐκεῖ, ὅτι ὑπεύθυνοι ἐσμεν κολάσεσιν. Eti- amsi justus quis sit, etiamsi millies sit justus, & ad sum- mum pervenerit culmen, ut liberatus sit a peccato, non tamen quis ab omni nævo est purus. Etiamsi millies justus sit, homo est. Quis enim jactabit, mundum sibi omnio esse cor; Quis gloriabitur, ab omni culpa se esse inmunem? Ideo jubemur in precatione dicere, dimitte nobis debita nostra, ut ista precandi consue- tudine admoneamur nos puniri posse. Paulo post: Δίκαιός ἐστιν, ἐλεήμων ἐστι, φιλόπτωχός ἐστιν, ἀλλ᾽ ἔχει τι ἐλάττωμα: Justus est, misericors est, amans est pauperum: Sed habet aliquid, in quo adhuc deficit. Est enim plenum æquitatis fœdus Evangelicum, & eos, qui secundum Spiritum ambulant, non damnat, Rom. VIII. 1. id est, pro suis agnoscit eos, in quorum cor- pore non regnat peccatum, Rom. VI. 12. Clemens A- lexandrinus Strom. II. ait, electis in CHRISTO non imputari peccata illa, quæ μὴ κατὰ προαίρεσιν συνί- στανται, quæ non consilii electione fiunt. Præterea vero sciendum est, etiam eos, qui per crimina illa gra- viora jure veniæ exciderant, restitui in priorem condi- tionem posse, sed per pœnitentiam luctuosam, ut lo- quitur Augustinus, addens nullam illis sperandam sa- lutem, nisi sacrificium obtulerint Deo, spiritum con- tribulatum per pœnitentiam Tom. IV. libr. 83. quæst. quæstione 25. Pœnitentiam autem seria haud dubie eti- am diligentissimam vitæ emendationem continet. Et propterea Irenæus, ubi regulam fidei recitat, ait: Τοῖς δὲ δικαίοις κᾀμ ὁσίοις, καὶ τὰς ἐντολὰς ἀυτῦ τετηρηκό- σι, καὶ ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ ἀυτῦ διαμεμενηκόσι, τοῖς ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς τῆς δὲ ἐκ μετανοίας ζωὴν χαρισάμενος, ἀφθαρ- σίαν δωρήσηται, καὶ δόξαν αἰωνιον περιποιήσῃ. Justis contra & pietate præditis, quique ipsius præcepta ser- vaverunt, atque in ipsius charitate partim jam inde ab initio, partim ex pœnitentia perstiterunt, vitam do- net, atque incorruptibilitatem largiatur, gloriamque sempiternam afferat. Salvianus hunc Jacobi locum sic παραφράζει libr. IV. de Gubernat.
