Dei: Quæ ratio est, ut ipsi nos falsa opinione fallamus, existimantes scilicet quia Christiani esse dicamur, quod optuhtari nobis in- ter mala quæ agimus, nomen bonum possit, cum Spi- ritus sanctus nec fidem quidem dicat hominibus Chri- stianis sive bonis operibus posse prodesse: Et utique multo plus est, fidem habere, quam nomen: quia nomen est vocabulum hominis; fides autem fructus est mentis: Et tamen hunc ipsum fidei fructum in- fructuosum Apostolus sine operibus bonis esse testa- tur. His consonat veterum martyrum & sancto- rum chorus. Justinus Apologia II. Οὐ γὰρ τοὺς μό- νον λέγοντάς, ἀλλὰ τοὺς καὶ τὰ ἔργα πράττοντας σω- θήσεσθαι ἔφη. Non enim eos, qui dicunt tantum, sed qui simul & opera faciunt, salvos dixit fore. Ire- næus libr. II. cap. LVI. Justi autem fulgebunt sicut sol in regno Patris eorum. Injustos autem & qui non faciunt opera justitiæ mittet in ignem æternum, ubi ver- mis ipsorum non morietur, & ignis eorum non extin- guetur. Libr. IV. cap. XXIX. Id quod erat semper li- berum & suæ potestatis in homine servasse Deum & su- am exhortationem, ut juste damnetur, qui non obe- diunt ei, quoniam non obedierunt, & qui obedierunt & crediderunt ei, honorentur in corruptibilitate, & libro eodem cap. XXXII. Qui enim nullius indigens est Deus, in se assumit bonas operationes justas, ad hoc ut præstet nobis retributionem bonorum suorum. Clemens Strom. V. Χάριτι μέντοι σωζόμεθα ἐξ αἰτιῶν μέν τοι τῶν καλῶν ἔργων, servamur sane gratia, at non sine bonis operibus. Et libr. VI. Ὥστε ὅτʼ ἂν ἀκούσω- μεν, ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέ σε, οὐχ ἁπλῶς τοὺς ὁπωσοῦν πιστεύσαντας σωθήσεσθαι λέγειν αὐτὸν ἐκδεχόμεθα, ἐὰν μὴ καὶ τὰ ἔργα ἐπακολουθήσῃ : Quoties ergo audimus, fides tua te salvavit, ne credamus dici, credentes quovis modo salvari; sed ita demum, si & opera sequantur. Cyprianus de præceptis Ecclesiæ: Præceptis ejus & mo- nitis obtemperandum est, ut accipiant merita nostra mercedem: quo in loco & veterum aliis vox meriti sic su- menda est, sicut vox mercedis non apud ipsos tantum, sed & in sacris literis, Matth. V. 12. X. 42. Luc. VI. 35. 1. Cor. III. 14. nimirum non ex æqualitate operis & re- tributionis, quæ hic certe nulla est, Rom. VIII. 18. quo respiciens μείζονα ἔπαθλα τῶν πόνων majora la- boribus præmia dixit Chrysostomus Rom. IIX. & ali- bi: Μείζονα μὲν τῆς ὑμετέρας ἀξίας, ἄξια δὲ τῆς ἑαυ- τοῦ φιλανθρωπίας majora quidem, quam quanti sit me- ritum vestrum, sed condigna sua in homines bonitate, quod de ipso etiam martyrio operum excellentissimo in- telligendum Cyprianus exhortatione ad martyrium nos fic docet: Plus accepimus in passionis mercede, quam sustinemus in ipsa passione. Sed ex liberalis- sima promissione, quæ laborantibus nobis jus dat: ita ut hoc negotium ad donationem sub conditione, quam ad proprie dictam locationem & conductio- nem, cui contractui agnatæ mercedis & merendi vo- ces, propius accedat; quo sensu etiam Paulus dicit, redditurum Deum piis secundum ipsorum opera, Rom. II. 6. quorum operum explicatio συνεκδοχικῶς per com- plexionem est, Matth. XXV. circa finem, redditu- rum scil. judicio non rigido, sed mira quadam cle- mentia temperato & directo ad naturam benignissimi fœderis per & propter Christum facti Ambrosius in Eph. I. Redempti hæredes designati sunt, fi in regenera- tione perdurent, ut fides prima veniam, sancta ve- ro conversatio perdurans cum fide coronam merea- tur. Hieronymus adversus Pelagium Dial. I. Creden- ti præmium datur, si quod creditur, & geratur. Et mox: Baptismus vetera peccata conscindit, novas vir- tutes non tribuit, dimittit e carcere, & dimisso, fi laboraverit, præmia pollicetur. Qui ergo per fidem consequuti indulgentiam peccatorum, ac proinde jus ad vitam æternam, ea bona retinere cupiunt, curare duo debent, implorato in id seria prece Dei auxilio, ut sibi ab illis criminibus à regno Dei excludenti- bus, caveant, 1. Petr. III. 10. 2. Joh. V. 14. Rom. VI. 12. 13. 1. Joh. II. 1. ubi, ut & in aliis epistolis ejus locis peccandi vox non in latiore significatu, qui & πταίσματα offen- dicula comprehendit, sumitur, sed in strictiore & gravio- re sensu: Deinde vero, ut occasione data actiones edant in Deum honorificas, & in proximum utiles, 1. Petr. III. 10. 11. Rom. VI. 13. ac si in pietate magis magisque proficiant, utrumque autem debent credere ita esse ne- cessarium, ut, nisi præstetur, futurum sit ut excidat homo jam impetratis. Chrysostomus sub finem capitis IV. ad Ephesios: Οὐκ ἀρκεῖ κακίας ἀπαλλαγῆναι, εἰ δὲ τῆς βασιλείας τῶν ὀυρανῶν ἐπιτυχεῖν, ἀλλὰ δεῖ κᾀ πολλῆς τῆς τῶν ἀρετῶν ἐργασίας: Non fatis à malitia liberatum esse, ut regnum cœleste consequamur: Sed accedere debent multæ virtutis actiones. Addit mox: Τὸ δʼ ἀγαθόν με ποιῆσαι, κακίας μέρος, etiam non facere bonum, pars malitiæ, quod multis comparationibus illustrat Am- brosius in Eph. IV. Donate invicem: alioquin Deus repetit remissa. Augustinus: Redire dimissa peccata, ubi charitas non est, apertissime Dominus in Evan- gelio docet in illo servo, a quo dimissum Dominus de- bitum petiit, eo, quod ille conservo suo noluit debi- tum dimittere. Alibi: Qui ingratus, sicut canis, ad vomitum rediit, anteacta bona mortificavit, & pec- catum dimissum revocavit. Gregorius Magnus: Ex dictis Evangelicis constat, quia si ex toto corde non dimittimus, quod in nos delinquitur, & hoc rursus exigitur, quod jam nobis dimissum per pœnitentiam gaudebamus.

Hæc ibidem Grotius Testimonia Chrysostomi, Tertulliani, Irenæi & alia ut elidat, ne fidem solam servare, sine operibus testentur; fidem ab illis intelli- gi ait, quæ propositum obediendi Deo, & nunc Evan- gelio (per quod intelligit, more Sociniano, legem perfectiorem Mosaica) accensum Dei & proximi dilectione includat: Sed hoc propositum accensum dilectione annon ad opera legis, quæ non externa tantum sunt, sed etiam interiores animi motus, per- tinet, sine quibus vero & justificari nos, & servari, cum Paulo Doctores illi negant. Neque illud pro- positum ad finem requirere eosdem, qua fides nos servat, ullo indicio ex istis testimoniis apparet. Sed hoc potius luculentum est, fidem per se solam καθ’ ἑαυτὴν servare: fidem integram de salute securam es- se, fide justificari nos, & liberos Dei, adeoque hære- des vitæ fieri, justificationem fidei manere cum illo, qui vita discedit, mox cum crediderit, adeoque salu- tem nec præcedentibus nec consequentibus bonis operi- bus contingere, ac proinde sola fide. Neque Act. VIII. 37. toto corde credere, est fidem & propositum obediendi præceptis Divinis, accensum Dei, & pro- ximi dilectione, sinondum exactissima, certe sincera habere: Sed sincero corde fiduciam in Jesum col- locare. Nec Hieronymi ad Matth. XII. aut Chry- sostomi ad Rom. IX. 10. dicta docent ipsos per fidē, quæ sola ad salutem sufficit, intelligere fidem, quæ propositum obediendi Deo, & dilectionem Dei ac proximi includere, aut virtutem animi pertinere ad definitionem fidei justificantis, aut etiam polle- re facultate justificandi & salvandi homines, quam solum de officio hominis Christiani esse innituit Chry- sostomus.

Sed admittit Grotius ipse: Fidem sine operibus sa- lutem parere: Dubium autem movet, cur non e- tiam diutius viventes ea ad salutem perducat? Cau- sam hanc dat, quod indulgentia Dei data sit creden- tibus in se conditionem habeat, dummodo dato tempo- re & occasione pia opera sequantur. Sed ubi scriptu- ra docet, fidem diutius viventes, quando sine ope- ribus peperit salutem, sine operib9 ad salutem per- ducere non posse? Ubi docet, remissionem pecca- torū, & indulgentiam datam credentibus conditi- onem in se habere, dummodo dato tempore & occasione pia opera sequantur? Si parere potest fi- des salutem sine operibus, nec ut pariat conditio operum includitur, quidni & retineri salus per fidē possit, sine cooperatione nostrorum operum? non enim alia est ratio acquirendi justificationem & sa- lutem, alia eandem retinendi & possidendi. Fide acquirimus salutem, fide etiam custodimur in ac- quisita salute & possessione juris ad salutem 1. Petr. I. 5. nec justificatio solum & salutis acquisitio, sed supremi etiam gradus, nempe æternæ salu- tis possessio sic dicitur effectus fidei, ut operi- bus ea denegetur, Rom. IV. 6. Quod Canus docet contra Bannem Præceptorem part. II. rel. de sacr. concl. 3. quod justificatio sit ultima dispositio, ac sal- vatio sequatur haud dubie, quod iisdē mediis ac- quiratur salus, quibus justificatio; quam sententi- am dicit Soti esse, aliorumque in 2. q. 1. a. 8. concl. ult. quam etiam Fratr. Walenb. esse in exeg. A. C. Ostendimus; Simile Grotii de modo, quo filii dicun- tur Domini rerum paternarum, vel acquirere heredi- tatem paternam, Grotianæ adversatur, non favet sententiæ. Ut enim necessum nõ est, ut filii positive aliquid agant boni ad consequendam hæreditatis possessionem, sed sufficit, ceu causa positiva, sola nativitas legitima: Quod vero privative nihil mali agant, non est aliquid positive influens in acquisi- tionem hæreditatis, sed aliquid saltem non impedi- ens, seu absentia rei noxiæ hereditati: Sic ad adeundã hæreditatem regni gratiæ & gloriæ non requirun- tur opera positive sed sufficit sola regeneratio, Rom. VIII. 17. Omissio autem delictorum non est causa co- influens in acquisitionem, vel captionem hæreditatis; sed tantum requisitum ex parte hæredis, ne impe- diatur hæreditas, vel tollatur causa unica positiva, quæ est fides, per quã adoptamur in filios. Eadem est aliorum similium ratio. Per peccata autem pro- aretica amitti fidem & gratiam recte quidem pro- bat Grotius contra Calvinianos, qui fidem in renatis esse inamissibilem contendunt: Neutiquam vero id juvat Pontificios, quasi bona opera ad salutem ne- cessaria sint, vel conditio sint consequendi heredita- tem cælestem: ac ne quidem hoc evincit, quod ab- stinentia à proareticis delictis faciat ad consequendã salutem. Non enim sequitur, quæcunque priva- tio accidens principio agenti ejus activitatem im- pedit, illius oppositus habitus coinfluit, in actio- nes principii agentis. Ita admissio toxici enecat vitam naturalem, nec tamen abstinentia à toxico conservat vitam naturalem: Furtum & adulteri- um meritorie adimunt homini vitam, nec tamẽ ab- stinentia à furto, ab adulterio conservat vitam. Ma- li motus tam interni, quã externi sunt veluti toxica fidei; nec tamen oppositæ virtutes vel opera bona vel conservant fidem, vel coinfluunt in effectum fi dei proprium, salutem. Quod autem non omnis culpa adimat jus acceptum veniæ, statumque gra- tiæ, non sit ex natura peccati, quasi aliud per se & natura sua veniale, aliud mortale, ut cum Papistis innuere videtur Grotius: Sed quod peccata proæ- retica nõ habeant comitem pœnitentiam, sed ean- dem connexam habeant penes renatos, utpote qui cum incursantur ab iisdem, serio cum Paulo inge- miscunt: Miser ego homo, quis me liberabit à corpore mortis hujus? Roman. VII. 20.

Neq; vero quicquam juvant Grotium testimo- nia è Salviano quoad hunc Jacobi locum adducta, sive id probare velit, Jacobum fidẽ intelligere, nõ prouti tantum assensus est, sed etiam fiducia, cum fidem, quæ sine operibus est, dicit non salvare, sive fidam veram & operibus non destitutã non serva- re sine operib9, sed opera cum fide correquiri ad consequendam salutem, & confluere in hunc effe- ctum, qui est salus & beatitudo hominis. Neu- trum certe ullo istorum testimoniorum probavit. De Salviani loco jam ex parte dictum, qui non ait, fiduciam in Christum fidem salvificam esse, quæ bonis operibus destituitur, sed contrarium adstruit, fidem sine bonis operibus non prodesse: non quod coinflu- ant bona opera in salutem, sed quod sine bonis o- peribus ne quidem fides vera sit. Non docet Jaco- bum sub voce fidei non salvantis fidem compre- hendere secundum essentialem definitionem, pro- ut fiduciam in Christum simul complectitur. Ne- gant Ecclesiæ nostræ, solum assensum, revelationi Divinæ præbitum, esse fidem illam justificantem. Negat id quoque Salvianus. Testatur idem quoq; à Jacobo negatum. Distinguit usurpationem no- minis Christiani, seu hominis fidelis à fide ipsa: ac fidem, ut est fructus mentis (assensus) à fide viva producente opera. Nec aliter explicat illud fides fine operibus est mortua, quam Ecclesia nostra. Quo utique, inquit, hoc indicat (Jacobus) actus bonos Christiana fidei testes esse : quia Christianus nisi bona opera fecerit, fidem suam penitus comprobare non possit: ac per hoc, quod probare non valeat, quia sit, sic omnino habendum esse, quasi non sit.

Justinus vero subjectum salvandu describit, non fidei salvifica definitionem, vel salutis consequendæ rationem exhibet, cum ait: Non eos, qui dicunt tan- tum, sed simul & opera faciunt, salvos dixit fore. Ja- cobum autem fidem non salvantem intelligere de fiducia in Christum non dicit, imo cum Jacobo pro- nunciat fidem, quam quis tantum jactitat, non es- se veram fidem.

De subjecto etiam agit Irenæus prioribus locis: postremo retributionem præstari bonis operationibus asserit, bona opera causam esse salutis, non ait. Fidei autem soli salutem adscribit I. IV. c. 5. Lex adhortabatur eos dicens, non aliter servari homines ab antiqua serpentis plaga, nisi cre- dant in eum, qui secundum similitudinem carnis peccati in martyrio exaltatur.

Clemens Strom. V. gratia nos salvari ait, at non sine operibus bonis: non quod opera bona nos servent, ita enim non serva- remur gratia, Rom. XI. 6. sed quod sine operibus non sint qui serventur: quod cap. VI. explicat, non quovis modo credentes, tametsi opera non sequan- tur, servari. Non enim ἐὰν μὴ in Græco est exce- ptiva conditio, vel adversative reddendu; sed pe- riphrasis est no vere credentium, ut profligetur fi- des supposititia, quod à Jacobo etiam fit: quan- quam & ita recte sese illa habeant, non salvari quovis modo credentes, nisi fidem opera consequan- tur, ut gemina sint sententiæ Jacobeæ, neminem sal- vari ea fide, quam non consequuntur bona opera. Quo libro Clemens, dicit Dominus, qui credit, ha- bet vitam æternam, Beati ergo sunt omnes, qui con- fidunt in ipso. Fiduciam autem habere est quid am- plius fide, quæ scilicet nudus assensus sit.

Cypriani locus non extat libro de præceptis Ecclesiæ, qualis titulus nullus invenitur in Cypriano, sed de unita- te Ecclesiæ. Merita autem nostra mercedem accipere ait; non autem causam salutis esse pronunciat: Et agnoscit Grotius ipse, eo loco, ut & in aliis veterum vocem meriti impropriè accipiendam esse, sicut & vocem mercedis non apud ipsos tantum, sed & in sacris literis Matth. V. 12. cap. X. 42. Luc. VI. 35. 1. Cor. III. 14. nimirum non ex æqualitate operis, sed ex liberalissima promissione: quæ vox de acquisitione quavis, etiam quæ per donationem mere gratui- tam contingit, accipi solet: uti Cyprianus ad Fidum infantes de Divina misericordia mereri dixit. Quod autem addit Grotius promissionem DEI liberalissi- mam nobis jus dare; ita ut hoc negotium ad donatio- nem sub conditione, quam ad proprie dictam locatio- nem & conductionem, cui contractui agnata merce- dis & merendi voces, propius accedat: non proban- dum. Nam neque nobis laborantibus, qua talibus, datur jus vitæ æternæ, sed qua credentibus, Joh. I. 12. & ἀσύςατα illa sunt cum prioribus. Nulla enim hic comparatio locum habet cum contractu Loca- tionis & conductionis, ubi non ex æqualitate operis & retributionis, sed ex liberalissima solum promis- fione nomina illa locum inveniunt. Si enim acce- dant ea hic, etsi non tam prope, aliquo modo ta- men ad proprie dictam conductionem non pendebit meritum à liberali Dei promissione & benigna acce- ptatione sola, sed etiam ex aptitudine operis ad talem mercedem, quam utramque meriti rationem alibi, non absque insigni ἑαυτομαχίᾳ, si cum hisce ver- bis conferas, attulit Grotius; nimirum annotat. ad Art. I V. consult. Cass. aperte cum Papistis faciens, imo deterior Papistis, quum ipsi etiam

Status Rom. Imperii in Comitiis Augustanis An- no 1530. resp. ad art. IV. & Concilium Senense bien- nio ante celebratum c. XXI. meriti acceptationem promissionis Divinæ liberalitati in solidum adscri- bant: quam etiam sententiam esse Scoti, Gregorii Arim. Bielis, Occam, Guilhelmi Parisiensis, Ca- nonicorum Coloniens. Alphonsi à Castro, Vegæ Bun- derii, &c. docet Vasquez disp.CCXIV. in I. 2. c.1.

Quod vero Grotius de natura fœderis novi hic inserit, eam hanc esse, quod DEUS receperit, se opera nostra intrinseca bonitate sua, & æqualitate ad retributionem vel mercedem justo minora acce- ptaturum pro sufficientibus, καδδιάμετρον adver- satur scripturæ: juxta quam natura fœderis hæc est, quod Deus in locum meritorum & satisfactionum nostrarum, quia illis destituimur, quum à lege re- quirantur, velit surrogare Filium suum illa præsti- turum, Rom. VIII. 6. ut per fidem in ipsum vitam æternam habeamus.

Quod ad reliqua testimonia, non Ambrosius sed Ambrosiaster est, qui in cap.1. ad Ephes. adduci- tur, voce meriti improprie usus, quod sancta con- versatio perdurans cum fide coronam consequatur, qui quia hereditatem eam dixit, non nostris ope- ribus, sed ex gratia Dei nos adoptantis eam cõ- tingere, eo ipso agnoscit. Hieronymus vero adv. Pelag. dial. I. subjectum designat, cui præmia obtin- gant, quod nempe laboraverit, non causam, vel meritum præmiorum, quod etiam de Chrysostomo ad cap. IV. Eph. dicendum. In cæteris non agi- tur de causa positiva coinfluente in acquisitionem aut possessionem salutis æternæ, sed tantum de im- pedimentis salutis.

## 2:15
Vers. 15. If a brother or sister be naked] He illustrates the matter with an excellent comparison taken from the deeds of those whom he opposes, naked, how the word naked is taken in Job XXII. 6, Matt. XXV. 36, 38, 43, 44, Mark XIV. 52, John XXI. 7, 1 Cor. IV. 10, and nakedness in Rom. VIII. 35, 2 Cor. XI. 27.

And be destitute of daily food] Destitute, see above I. 4. 5. If they are not only destitute of a moderate supply of things, but do not even have wherewith to live from day to day. What is here daily food, is food for the day to Alexis and Aristophanes. Those who have nothing more are daily-livers to the Greeks. See what we have said on Matt. VI. 14. For and in the Manuscript there is or.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Ἐὰν δὲ ἀδελφὸς ἢ ἀδελφὴ γυμνοὶ ὑπάρχωσιν] Egregia similitudine ab illorum, quos oppugnat, factis sum- pta rem illustrat, γυμνοὶ quomodo vox γυμνὸς sumitur Job. XXII. 6. Matth. XXV. 36. 38. 43. 44. Marci XIV. 52. Joh. XXI. 7. 1. Cor. IV. 10. & γυμνότης Rom. VIII. 35. 2.Cor. XI. 27.

Καὶ λειπόμενοι ὦσι τῆς ἐφημέρου τροφῆς] Λειπόμενοι חסרו, vide supra I. 4. 5. Si non modo destituantur re- rum mediocri copia, sed nec habeant unde in diem vi- vant. Quod hic τροφὴ ἐφήμερος, id τροφὴ καθ’ ἡμέραν Alexidi & Aristophani. Qui nihil habent amplius καθημε- ρόβιοι Græcis. Vide quæ dicta nobis ad Matth. VI. 14. Pro καὶ in Manuscripto est ἤ.

## 2:15
Vers. 15. 'But if a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food'] If, however, a brother and sister are naked, and are in need of daily sustenance, James illustrates the proposed matter with similar examples. Well said, however, by Tertullian concerning modesty. Although, even if all things can correspond to a mirror, there is a peculiar danger of interpretations, lest the happiness of the comparison of others be tempered otherwise than the matter of each parable has commanded: And soon he adds: we do not invent matters from parables, but we interpret parables from matters. Agreeing with whom is Chrysostom in Rom. IX. 'And this must be observed everywhere, that examples must not always be taken universally. But having gathered the useful part of them, and that which has been adopted, one must leave all the rest.' And this must be observed entirely, that comparisons are not to be taken from every part, but one must use what is useful, and that for the sake of which the comparison is instituted. The rest is to be omitted. It must be seen, therefore, what the comparison has set before itself. That, however, is as follows. Just as good words do not profit the needy person to whom they are spoken, even if perhaps there is present a mind wishing good things for the needy: So neither does faith destitute of works profit the believer. In this similarity, however, there is also a demonstration of equity. He did not wish to profit another; it is equitable that it should not profit him either. Hunger and nakedness by synecdoche through inclusion signify all calamities to which human life is exposed, and which can easily be relieved by the help of another, as in the already mentioned place of Matthew, Matt. XXV. The verses of Menander do not differ from this.

The lightest of all evils bites you, Poverty. For what is this, which one friend having helped as a physician could easily fix? Does poverty, which is the lightest of all evils, so torment you? For how little is it, for which one friend suffices by healing?

Ἐφήμερος τροφὴ daily sustenance] It is not a heap of things, but a daily ration. The comic poets Alexis and Antiphanes called this τροφὴν καθ’ ἡμέραν. The Greek interpreters Dan. I. 5. 'That of the day for the day.' And Philo in the allegories: 'That of the day for the day.' Those who have this, and live content with it, are called καθήμερόβιοι by the Greeks.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Ἐὰν δὲ ἀδελφὸς ἢ ἀδελφὴ γυμνοὶ ὑπάρχω- σι, καὶ λειπόμενοι ὦσι τῆς ἐφημέρου τροφῆς] si autem frater & soror nudi sint, & indigeant victu quoti- diano, Rem propositam Jacobus similibus illustrat. Be- ne autem dictum à Tertulliano de pudicitia. Quan- quam etsi omnia ad speculum respondere possint, uncam sit proprium periculum interpretationum, ne aliorum temperetur felicitas comparationis, quam quo parabolæ cujusque materia mandavit: Et mox addit: non ex parabolis materias commentamur, sed ex materiis parabolas interpretamur. Cui con- sentiens Chrysostomus in Rom. IX. Καὶ τῦτο παν- ταχῦ δεῖ παρατηρεῖν, ὅτι τὰ παραδείγματα ὀυ πάντα κα- θόλυ δεῖ λαμβάνειν. Ἀλλὰ τὸ χρήσιμον ἀυτῶν ἀναλεξα- μένες, κᾀγ ὡς ὅπερ παρειλήπται, τὸ λοιπὸν ἅπαν ἐᾷν. Et hoc omnino servandum est, comparationes non ex omni parte sumendas, sed utendum & quod utile est, & cujus causa instituitur comparatio. Omittenda cæ- tera. Videndum ergo, quid propositum sibi habeat comparatio. Id autem sic se habet. Sicut bona di- cta non prosunt egenti, cui dicuntur, etiamsi adsit forte animus optans egenti bona: Ita nec fides destituta operibus prodest credenti. In hoc autem simili in- est & æquitatis demonstratio. Noluit ille prodesse alteri, æquum est, ut nec sibi prosit. Fames & nu- ditas κατὰ συνεκδοχὴν per complexionem omnes ca- lamitates, ad quas vita humana patet, & quæ alie- na ope sublevari facile possunt, significat, ut dicto jam Matthæi loco Matth. XXV. Menandri versus hinc non abludunt.

Τὸ κυφότατόν σε κακῶν πάντων δάκνει Πενία. Τί γάρ τῦτ’ ἐςιν, ἧς γίνοιτ’ ἂν εἷς Φίλος βοηθήσας ἰατρὸς ῥᾳδίως; Adeon’ te excruciat quod malorum est omnium Levissimum paupertas? quantillum est enim, Amicus unus cui medendo sufficit?

Ἐφήμερος τροφὴ victus quotidianus] Est non a- cervus rerum, sed dimensum quotidianum. Hoc τρο- φὴν καθ’ ἡμέραν dixere Comici Alexis & Antiphanes. Græci Interpretes Dan. I. 5. Τὸ τῆς ἡμέρας καθ’ ἡμέ- ραν. Et Philo in allegoriis: τὸ τῆς ἡμέρας εἰςἡμέ- ραν. Qui id habent, eoque contenti vivunt, καθήμε- ρόβιοι dicuntur Græcis.

## 2:16
Vers. 16. And one of you say to them] Of you who believe that faith is sufficient for salvation.

Go in peace] May it be well with you. For it is the expression of one praying for good. Go in peace or into peace, as Mark V. 34, Go into peace, Luke VII. 50, VIII. 48, 1 Sam. I. 17.

Be warmed, a metonymy for be clothed. Thus they were warmed for they were clothed, Job XXXI. 20.

And be filled] May you be well fed, may you have wherewith to be satisfied. See Matt. XIV. 20, and XV. 31, 33, Mark VI. 42, VII. 27, VIII. 4, 42, Luke VI. 21, IX. 17, XVI. 21, John XVI. 21, John XVI. 26, Phil. IV. 12.

But you do not give them the things necessary for the body] Namely, when it is easy for you to do so. Good wishes are not to be despised, but they are of no value if they proceed from one who can bring about what he wishes, but does not will to do so.

Things necessary for the body are not badly called those things which are expedient for the body. For that adjective among the Greeks governs now the Genitive, now the Dative. Xenophon said to procure necessities and to have and to give a necessity. In the Glossary, necessities are the things needed. The Arabic, the necessary things, just as the Latin here.

What is the profit?] What do these good wishes profit them?

Grotius had thus set forth these things in a commentary previously and separately published,

Latin:

Vers. 16. Εἴπῃ δέ τις αὐτοῖς ἐξ ὑμῶν] Ex vobis qui fidem creditis sufficere ad salutem.

Ὑπάγετε ἐν εἰρήνῃ] Bene vobis sit. Est enim bene pre- cantis. Ὑπαγε ἐν εἰρήνῃ vel εἰς εἰρήνην, ut Marci V. 34. Πορεύου εἰς εἰρήνην, Luc. VII. 50. VIII. 48. לכי לשלום 1.Sam. I. 17.

Θερμαίνεσθε Metonymia pro estote vestiti. Sic ἐθερμάν- θησαν pro vestiti sunt, Jobi XXXI. 20.

Καὶ χορτάζεσθε] Bene pascimimor, sit vobis unde satu- remini. Vide Matth. XIV. 20. & XV. 31. 33. Marci VI. 42. VII. 27. IIX. 4. 42. Luc. VI. 21. IX. 17. XVI, 21. Joh.XVI. 21. Joh. XVI. 26. Phil. IV. 12. שבען

Μὴ δῶτε δὲ αὐτοῖς τὰ ἐπιτήδεια τῶ σώματος] Nempe cum id facere vobis in proclivi sit. Bona vota non sunt spernen- da, sed nullius pretii, si ab eo proficiscantur, qui quod o- ptat, effectum dare potest, & non vult.

Ἐπιτήδεια τῶ σώματος non male dicuntur, quæ cor- pori expediunt. Nam adjectivum istud apud Græcos modo Genitivum, modo Dativum regit. Ἐπιτήδεια πορίζεσθαι & ἔχειν & διδόναι ἐπιτηδείαν dixit Xenophon. In Glossario ἐπιτήδεια τὰ ἀναγκαῖα copiæ. Arabs תאגו necessaria, quomodo etiam Latinus hic.

Τί τὸ ὄφελος;] Quid hæc bona vota illis prosunt?

Hæc in commentatione prius & seorsim edita ita tradiderat Grotius,

## 2:16
Vers. 16.

And if one of you say to them, 'Go in peace, be warmed and be filled'] But let someone of you say to them: Go in peace, be warmed and be filled. That 'go in peace' shows that what are uttered here in the imperative mood are precative or optative. 'Peace' from the Hebrew שָׁלוֹם signifies prosperous things. And so 'go in peace,' as here, or 'go into peace,' as it is enunciated in Mark V. 34, or 'go into peace,' as in Luke VII. 50, VIII. 48, signifies: May it be well with you: which is then specially accommodated here by the following words and adapted to the present necessity of that man who is seen: May you have wherewith to clothe yourself; may you have wherewith to satisfy yourself. For 'to be warmed' here is to be clothed, as in Job XXXI. 20. Good wishes and all things from one who cannot provide more are not to be spurned: Even if strength is lacking, the will is to be praised. But when they proceed from one in whose power it is to give effect to what he wishes, they are reckoned as nothing.

But do not give them the things necessary for the body] Namely, those things by the denial of which nature suffers, coverings and food. See 1 Tim. VI. 8. Do not give, that is, when you have an abundance of that thing. See 2 Cor. VIII. 13.

What is the profit?] Such a will did not have the effect which it ought to have had; it vanished.

In vain does Grotius presume in him a mind wishing good things for the needy, whom the Apostle openly argues against as a hypocrite: so that he might fashion faith in the application of the similitude as indeed true, but not useful for salvation, because it is destitute of works. For the Apostle concludes that faith is therefore dead in itself, and thus is nothing, because it is boasted of by the tongue or by external profession, but is mere hypocrisy, and therefore can in no way be a salvific faith: Just as that charity is hypocritical and feigned, which is declared by words indeed, but is not rooted in the mind, 1 John III. 17. For to say and not to do is a periphrasis of deceit and hypocrisy, Matt. XXIII. 3, 4, 13, 14, James I. 22, chap. II. 4, 1 John I. 6, chap. II. 4, 8, 9, chap. III. 17, 18, chap. IV. 20, Rev. II. 9, 20, 24, chap. III. 9, 17. Nor does Lorinus deny at v. 15, as B. Hülsemann observes in the cited harmony page 54, in view of this comparison, namely that dogmatic faith, or ratification of credible dogmas, being destitute of the sequence of good works, is compared by the Apostle to naked words given to the needy. That the faith which is called dead has been termed by the Fathers fictitious, hypocritical, feigned, shadowed, deceitful, painted, and masked, to believe by Word and tongue only, to confess God with words, but to deny Him with deeds act of believing (insofar as faith denotes only assent) is fictitious or feigned, but that the moral act of faith, namely to proceed into charity toward one's neighbor, is fictitious and null, due to the absence of which inseparable adjunct it is rightly judged that the form is also absent, of which the adjunct charity is an individual attribute. Lorinus says that ἀνυπόκριτον (unfeigned) faith is opposed to this hypocritical faith, 2 Tim. 1:5. And at the end of the commentary on verse 16, after he had brought forward the suffrage of Valerian of Cimiez, he adds: He cites our present passage against the pursuits of certain people, who, although they show no fruit of mercy, nevertheless LIE about the affection of mercy. How, therefore, such mercy LIES about the affection, so the boaster of true and integral faith also LIES about the affection. Blessed Hülsemann adds: No one attending to the cohesion of the words will deny that this is the third point of comparison intended by the Apostle. And having posited that he who consoles the needy with mere words does not lie about every effect of compassion, but has some sense of sincere mercy while he utters those words: Go in peace, be filled, etc. nevertheless the force of the comparison persists, namely in a similar way that he who boasts of a naked assent provided to dogmas proposed by GOD as if it were integral faith, indeed has something of faith, and does not lie entirely in that, but yet lies in this, that he puts forward a true and integral faith (of which an inseparable attribute is to flourish in works of charity), which it is clear is not present from the defect of the individual effect, which is charity.

What? That Grotius himself is forced to acknowledge that the mind and will to help are not present in this person who puts forward charity in James: because he says that vows proceeding from him who has the power to give effect to what he wishes are reputed AS NOTHING. Furthermore: He DID NOT WANT, he says, to benefit the other. Therefore there was no will of his. Likewise, good vows are not to be spurned, but are OF NO VALUE if they proceed from him who can give effect to what he wishes, and DOES NOT WANT TO. Therefore, true charity is not compared with true faith: but a comparison is instituted between the vain boasting of faith and charity, of which neither has any use.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Εἴπῃ δὲ τις ἀυτοῖς ἐξ ὑμῶν, ὑπάγετε ἐν εἰρήνῃ θερ- μαίνεσθε καὶ χορτάζεσθε] Dicat autem aliquis ex vo- bis illis: Ite in pace, calefacimini & saturamini. Il- lud ὕπαγε ἐν εἰρήνῃ vade in pace ostendit, quæ hic efferuntur modo Imperativo, esse precativa sive opta- tiva. Ἐιρήνη pax ex Ebræo שָׁלוֹם res prosperas significat. Itaque ὕπαγε ἐν εἰρήνῃ, ut hic, aut ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην, ut enunciatur Marc. V. 34. aut πορεύε εἰς εἰρήνην, ut Luc. VII. 50. VIII. 48. significat: Bene tibi sit: quod deinde hic sequentibus verbis specialiter & accommodate ad præsentem ejus hominis, qui con- spicitur, necessitatem accommodtaur: Habeas unde te vestias; habeas, unde te saties. Nam θερμαίνεσθαι ca- lefieri, hic est vestiri, ut Job. XXXI. 20. Bona vota atque omnia ab eo, qui plus præstare non potest, sper- nenda non sunt: Ut desint vires tamen est laudanda voluntas. At ab eo profecta, cujus in potestate est, quod optat, effectum dare, pro nihil reputantur.

Μὴ δῶτε δὲ ἀυτοῖς τὰ ἐπιτήδεια τῶ σώματος] Non dederitis autem eis, quæ necessaria sunt corpori: Ea nimirum, quibus doleat natura negatis, tegumen- ta & alimenta. Vide 1. Tim. VI. 8. Non detis, cum ejus rei vobis copia suppetat scilicet. Vide 2. Cor. VIII. 13.

Τί τὸ ὄφελος; Quid proderit?] Non habuit talis voluntas effectum, quem debuit, evanuit.

Frustra Grotius in eo animum optantis egenti bo- na præsumit, quem Apostolus ceu hypocritam aperte arguit: ut fidem in ἀποδόσει similitudinis quidem veram, non autem utilem ad salutem, quia operibus destituitur, effingat. Apostolus enim fidem inde in semetipsa mortuam, adeoque nullam esse concludit, quod lingua quidem, aut professio- ne externa jactetur, sed mera sit hypocrisis, ideoque nullatenus salvifica fides esse possit: Quemadmo- dum charitas illa hypocritica sit, & ementita, quæ verbis quidem declaratur, sed in animo radicata non est, 1. Joh. III. 17. Nam dicere, & non fa- cere periphrasis doli est, & hypocriseos, Matth. XXIII. 3. 4. 13. 14. Jac. I. 22. cap. II. 4. 1. Joh. I. 6. cap. II. 4. 8. 9. cap. III. 17. 18. cap. IV. 20. Ap.II. 9. 20. 24. cap. III. 9. 17. Nec diffitetur Lorinus ad v. 15. observante B. Hülsemanno in harmonia laudata pag. 54. hujus comparationis intuitu, vi- delicet quod fides dogmatica, aut ratihabitio dogmatum credibilium destituta bonorum operum sequela comparetur ab Apostolo nudis verbis egeno datis. Fidem, quæ mortua dicitur, Patribus dictam esse fictam, hypocriticam, simulatam, adumbra- tam, dolosam, fucatam ac personatam, credere Verbo & lingua tantum, confiteri verbis Deum, factis autem negare. Non quod assensus seu actus formalis & proprius credendi, (in quantum fides solum assensum notat, sit fictitius aut simulatus, sed quod actus moralis fidei, scilicet prodire in charita- tem erga proximum, sit fictitius & nullus, ob cujus inseparabilis adjuncti absentiam recte judicetur eti- am abesse illa forma, cujus individuum attributum est adjuncta charitas. Huic hypocriticæ fidei ait opponi Lorinus ἀνυπόκριτον fidem 2. Tim. I. 5. Et in fine commentarii ad v. 16. postquam Valeriani Cemelensis suffragium attulerat, addit: Citat præsentem locum nostrum adversus quorundam stu- dia, quæ cum nullum exhibeant misericordiæ fru- ctum, misericordia tamen MENTIANTUR affectum. Quomodo igitur talis misericordia MENTITUR affectum, sic jactator etiam fidei veræ atque integræ MENTITUR affectum. Addit B. Hülsemannus: Hoc esse tertium compa- rationis ab Apostolo intentum nemo cohæsionem verborum attendens diffitebitur. Et posito, eum qui meris verbis solatur egentem, non mentiri omnem miserationis effectum, sed habere aliquem misericordiæ sinceræ sensum, dum profert illa ver- ba: Ite in pace, saturamini, &c. perstat tamen vis comparationis, nempe simili modo eum, qui nu- dum assensum præbitum dogmatibus à DEO pro- positis jactat pro fide integra, habere quidem ali- quid fidei, nec prorsus mentiri in eo, sed mentiri tamen in hoc, quod veram atque integram fi- dem, (cujus inseparabile attributum est, efflo- rescere in charitatis opera) præ se fert, quam non inesse patcat ex defectu effectus individui, qui est charitas.

Quid? quod Grotius ipse agnoscere id coga- tur, animum, & voluntatem non adesse juvandi huic, qui charitatem præ se fert apud Jacobum: quia vota ab eo profecta, cujus in potestate est, quod optat effectum dare, PRO NIHILO reputari ait. Adhæc: NOLUIT ille, inquit, prodesse alteri. Nulla ergo ejus voluntas fuit. Item Bona vota non sunt spernenda, sed NULLI- US PRETII, si ab eo proficiscantur, qui, quod optat, effectum dare potest, & NON VULT. Non ergo confertur vera charitas cum vera fide: Sed collatio instituitur, inter vanam fidei & charitatis jactantiam, cujus utriusque nullus est usus.

## 2:17
Verse 17. Οὕτω καὶ ἡ πίσις, ἐὰν μὴ ἔργα ἔχῃ, νεκρά ἐσι καθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν] Just as that faith of yours joined with good words does not benefit your neighbors, so it will not benefit you. God will measure you by your own standard. Whatever does not attain its effect is said to be dead: as can be seen in Rom. 4:19, Heb. 11:12, Rom. 7:8. The effect toward which faith tends is eternal life, but it only attains its effect if there is present a purging from vices, love, and the works of love. Καθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν means by itself, or in its entirety. Thus ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῦ in John 15:4. Thus καθ᾽ ἑαυτῆς and ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτὸν abound in Matt. 12:25, 26, and ἐν ἑαυτοῖς in Rom. 1:24. Below, for the same thing, it is said without such an addition, νεκρά ἐσι, 20, 25.

We add what the prior Grotian commentary has concerning these things:

Verse 17. Οὕτω καὶ ἡ πίσις, ἐὰν μὴ ἔργα ἔχῃ, νε- κρά ἐσι καθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν] So also faith, if it does not have works, is dead in itself. Everything that is not active is said to be dead. For whatever departs from its own boundaries is immediately the death of that which it was before; says Lucretius. See Rom. 4:19, Heb. 11:12. Thus sin without the law is said to be lifeless in Rom. 7:8, because it had lost the force it ought to have had of moving the conscience through evil habit. The act is not indeed natural to faith nor owed to it, but it is freely granted by God to save. It is destitute of that act unless the condition of works prescribed after faith is fulfilled. That καθ' ἑαυτὴν in itself is redundant here, as ἐφ' ἑαυτῶν, Matt. 12:25, 26, 13:21, and ἀφ' ἑ- αυτᾶ, John 15:4, ἐν ἑαυτοῖς Rom. 1:24, and many similar things throughout. And so soon after, for the same thing, it is simply said: Νεκρά ἐςι it is dead.

From these things it is manifest that Grotius understands true and justifying faith, which, however, cannot save unless the condition of works prescribed after faith is fulfilled. For no one doubts that that faith which tends toward eternal life is saving faith. But he professes that it only attains its effect if there is present a purging from vices, love, and the works of love. But who will admit to calling it true and justifying faith, to which there is not present a purging from vices, love, and the works of love, nay, which is dead in itself? All antiquity testifies that love is necessarily connected to true and justifying faith, along with St. James, who taught this most clearly here and refuted the contrary dogma in heretics: from which, besides Cyprian who was brought forward earlier; Jerome on Gal. 5, Augustine in his tractate 10 on the Epistle of John, on faith and works ch. 16, ch. 23, in Psalms 77, 130, 138, book of 83 Questions, q. 76. Prosper on the calling of the Gentiles, book 1, ch. 8, book 3 on the contemplative life, ch. 21. Fulgentius on the incarnation, ch. 22, epistle 3 to Proba, Gregory of Rome, Homily 29 on the Gospel. Bede on this passage. Anselm in the Monologion, ch. 25, on Rom. 1 and Gal. 5. Bernard, sermon 2 on the Resurrection and sermon 1 on the Octave of Easter, from the Latins: But from the Greeks, besides Justin, Irenaeus, Clement, and Chrysostom, Didymus on this passage in the Library of the Fathers, Vol. 4. Origen on chapter 4 of Romans, Athanasius on virginity, Ephrem the Syrian on the spiritual life, Diadochus Bishop of Photice in on spiritual perfection, ch. 21. Basil the Great on Ps. 62, Gregory Nazianzen, oration 13, Chrysostom, homily 2 on the epistle to the Philippians and homily 2 on Genesis. Cyril of Alexandria on Malachi 4 and John 9, Isidore of Pelusium, book 3, ep. 73. Proclus of Constantinople, Epistle to the Armenians, John Damascene, book 4 on the Orthodox Faith, ch. 10, were brought forward by Blessed Hülsemann in his Harmony, page 40 et seqq. To these are added those who are thought to adhere to the Romanist sect: Lombard, Thomas, Brulifer, Tauler, Cusanus, Cassander, Georgius Wicelius, Gropper, Sadolet, Rivius, Nausea, Schopper, Franciscus Lucas, etc., cited by B. Gerb. in the last part of the Confessio catholica, art. XXIII, for this opinion: that they do not acknowledge faith as faith in the true sense of the word if it lacks charity, whether internal only or external as well. Add that Lorinus also acknowledges that Gregory the Great, Cyprian, and Bede, as well as Eucherius, Maximus the Abbot, and Philo of Carpathos, join faith and love in such a way that they cannot be separated, so that faith without works is true faith, [but] faith lacking works is blind faith; however, faith, however small, provided it is true faith and not dead, begins to work, and faith and works are connected by an indissoluble bond, so that where one is missing, the other does not exist at all: and that Cornelius à Lapide teaches at this place that many Fathers argue that faith lacking good works is not true faith. The present comparison of James absolutely demands this sense: just as naked and smooth words, to which the things themselves do not correspond due to the zeal and malice of the speaker, are intrinsically and by their own nature empty and futile: so also faith not producing good works is intrinsically and by its nature empty and nothing.

Τὸ νεκρὸν καθ' ἑαυτὸν is to be destitute of the first act and the form that ought to be present; that form of beneficence, pity, and liberality was absent from the Jamesian hypocrite saying to the needy: Go in peace, be warmed. For καθ’ ἑαυ- τὴν is in itself, intrinsically, as Heb. VI. 13. (Gen. XXII. 16.) Matt. XXII. 25. 26. Which example Grotius rashly alleges for his own pleonasm, and against the faith of all the Codices wishes ἐφ’ ἑαυτῆν to be read instead of καθ’ ἑαυτῆς: just as the other examples of pleonasm have been rashly adduced, when it is rather evident from an inspection of the passages that that word was not added without a peculiar emphasis. And since in the last verse it is taught that the body is dead from the absence of the Spirit, and faith is dead from the absence of works, that 'dead' is to be understood not only of a suspension of animal or natural acts, while the vital faculty remains safe; but of a lack of life as regards the first act, as even Grotius himself could not deny by his interpretation. Didymus of Alexandria on this passage: It is to be noted, he says, that since faith is dead apart from works, it is no longer even faith. For neither is a dead man a man. Ephrem Syrus on the life of the spirit, §. 91, explains this saying, 'faith without works is dead,' concerning those who say they know God but deny Him by their deeds, whom he denies to be faithful and affirms to be truly dead: and §. 88 (which passage the Douay Great Bible cites) when you dispute about faith, he says, consider whether you have works congruent with faith: For if you are studious only of learning and hearing, that will be cast at you: Faith without works is dead. For truly dead are all who profess that they know God, but deny Him by their deeds, since they are, as the Apostle says, unbelieving and reprobate to every good work. Therefore, to be dead is to be unbelieving. Therefore, a dead faith cannot have the essence or nature of faith. Chrysostom, Homily II on Genesis: Faith, he says, without works is dead, and works without faith are dead. As therefore works done outside of faith are not truly good: so, in the mind of Chrysostom, neither is faith lacking works truly good. Cyril of Alexandria on ch. IV of Malachi: If anyone after justification returns to those things which are of the flesh and of the world, he kills faith as if in himself. Damascene, book IV de orthod. fide, ch. 10: For it is necessary to keep ourselves pure from the works of iniquity by virtue. For faith without works is dead, and likewise works without faith. For true faith is proven through works. Isidore of Pelusium, book III, ep. 73: You seem to be ignorant of things which are known and clear even to CHILDREN. Nor should you think this, that faith (if indeed it is permitted to call that faith which is refuted by its own works) can bring you salvation. For that faith which first justified demands actions consistent with itself. And ep. 403. One must join piety with sound dogmas: Since that is true, as it is certain, that faith without works is dead. Simeon the Younger, T. XII. Bibl. Patr. part. I. f. 749: To confess Christ, he says, and to obey Christ, although they seem to be two: yet they are not two, but one thing. For neither does one consist without the other: Although some IGNORANT people may think otherwise. Hear the Apostle: Faith without works is dead, and with evil works it is not even faith. For a dead thing, if it is recent, is said to be dead as if just expired. But if it is already of many days, it is called not dead, but rotten, corrupt, and foul. Since therefore there are two kinds of works, those pleasing to God and those hateful: if faith without works is dead, as we read written, by what name will that faith be affected which not only lacks works acceptable to God, but also has works invisible to God? Dead? Nay, it ought to be called more rotten and corrupt, or to speak more truly, unbelief and impiety. From which it is abundantly evident that faith is not said to be dead on account of the mere absence of external works, but on account of the extinction or absence of the vital principle, not merely through a syncope or swoon of motion hindering it from the outside, but through a lack of life, and thus truly dead in itself: and that it designates not only a faith destitute of the second act of saving, but one which has no intrinsic faculty of saving, as is also clear from the examples adduced by Grotius, Rom. IV. 19, Heb. XI. 12. The body of Abraham νενεκρωμένον and the νέκρωσις of the womb of Sarah, are to be understood not only as regards the suspension of the second act in the generative faculty, but as regards the extinction of this faculty on account of a body now effete, and sterility on account of the cessation of the menses (Gen. XVIII. 11.), when they received new δύναμιν εἰς καταβο- λὴν σπέρματος, Heb. XI. 11. 12. But let the properly parallel passages, which explain how faith is said to be truly dead without works, which were here passed over by Grotius, be seen: Mat. VIII. 22, Luc. XV. 24. 32, Eph. II. 15, Col. II. 13, Eph. V. 14, Apoc. III. 1, Jude v. 13.

It pleases some to refer that determination καθ' ἑαυτὴν to faith, not to the word νεκρὰν, as the Syriac rendered it, 'alone,' or that which is solitary, without hope, without charity, as Augustine speaks, book I, sent. 8. But a periphrasis for solitary faith was already expressed by the words, ἐὰν μὴ ἔργα ἔχῃ; it is better therefore to refer it to the predicate, that such faith is dead in itself.

As for what B. Hülsemannus suspected here concerning the act of faith—not indeed a natural one, nor one owed to it, but one liberally granted by GOD for our SALVATION—the later writings, especially those of Grotius, have shown these things to be only too true: namely, that he did not wish to patronize the Papists, Socinians, and disciples of Arminius, [by separating] the act of faith from its merit and moral value, which the liberality and ἐπιείκεια of God, and indeed moral congruity attributes it to him, in the estimation of some, although according to Scripture faith saves only instrumentally, insofar as it receives the offered good, not because of any dignity of its own, nor can a natural act be distinguished from a supernatural one in faith, but faith in its whole essence is a supernatural gift, and has the faculty of saving only from a supernatural principle, which nature because God implanted it in faith, thence that act is not undeservedly called natural faith, after it pleased GOD to save us through faith, and to make faith justifying and salvific. For it pertains to the nature of faith from the Divine economy, that it can save, Gal. III. 11. 1. Petr. I. 9. just as it is natural for the Word of the Gospel to be living and effective Ebr. IV. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Οὕτω καὶ ἡ πίσις, ἐὰν μὴ ἔργα ἔχῃ, νεκρά ἐσι καθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν] Sicut vestra illa fides cum bonis verbis con- juncta proximis vestris non prodest, ita nec vobis pro- derit. Deus vestro vos modulo metietur. Mortuum esse dicitur, quicquid effectum suum non consequitur: ut videre est Rom. IV. 19. Ebr. XI. 12. Rom. VII. 8. Ef- fectus, ad quem tendit fides, est vita æterna, sed ita de- mum effectum suum consequitur, si adsit purgatio à vi- tiis, dilectio, & dilectionis opera. Καθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν per se, sive tota quanta est. Sic ἀφ᾽ ἑαυτῦ Joh. XV. 4. Sic abun- dat καθ᾽ ἑαυτῆς & ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτὸν Matth. XII. 25. 26. & ἐν ἑαυ- τοῖς Rom. I. 24. Infra pro eodem dicitur sine tali additamen- to, νεκρά ἐσι, 20. 25.

Addimus quæ de his habet prior commenta- tio Grotiana:

Vers. 17. Οὕτω καὶ ἡ πίσις, ἐὰν μὴ ἔργα ἔχῃ, νε- κρά ἐσι καθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν] Sic & fides, si non habeat ope- ra, mortua est in semetipsa. Mortuum dicitur omne quod actuosum non est. Nam quodcunque suis mu- tatum finibus exit continuo hoc mors est illius, quod fuit ante; ait Lucretius. Vide Rom. IV. 19. Ebr. XI. 12. Sic sine lege peccatum exanime dicitur Rom. VII. 8. quia vim, quam habere debebat, commovendi conscientiam, eam prava consuetudine perdiderat. Actus non quidem naturalis fidei neque ei debitus, sed à Deo liberaliter concessus est servare. Eo actu de- stituitur, nisi conditio operum post fidem præscripta impleatur. Illud καθ' ἑαυτὴν in semetipsa hic πλεονά- ζει ut ἐφ' ἑαυτῶν, Matth. XII. 25. 26. XIII. 21. & ἀφ' ἑ- αυτᾶ, Joh. XV. 4. ἐν ἑαυτοῖς Rom. I. 24. & multa pas- sim similia. Itaque mox pro eodem simpliciter dicitur: Νεκρά ἐςι mortua est.

Ex hisce manifestum est, Grotium fidem intelli- gere veram & justificantem, quæ vero servare ne- queat, nisi conditio operum post fidem præscripta im- pleatur. Ea enim fides, quæ tendit ad vitam æter- nam, quin fides salvificans sit, nemo ambigit. Quam vero effectum suum ita demum consequi profitetur, si adsit purgatio à vitiis, dilectio cum di- lectionis operibus. At fidem veram & justificantem dicere, cui non adsit purgatio à vitiis, dilectio, cum dilectionis operibus, imo quæ mortua sit in semetipsa, ecquis admittet? Fidei veræ & justifice necessario connexam esse dilectionem, cum S. Ja- cobo, qui id luculentissime hic docuit, & contra- rium in hæreticis dogma profligavit, tota antiqui- tas testatur: è qua præter Cyprianum antea addu- ctum; Hieron. in Gal. V. Augustinum in epist. Joh. tract. X. de fide & B. O. cap. XVI. cap. XXIII. in Psal. LXXVII. CXXX. CXXXVIII. libr. 83. Qq. q. 76. Prosperum de vocat. gent. l. 1. c. 8. libr. III. de vit. contempl. cap. 21. Fulgentium de incarnat. cap. XXII. epist. III. ad Probam, Gregor. Rom. Hom. XXIX. in Evangel. Bedam in h. l. Anshel- mum in Monol. cap. XXV. in Rom. I. & Gal. V. Bernhardum serm. II. de Resurr. & serm. I. in Octav. Paschat, è Latinis: E Græcis vero præ- ter Justin. Iren. Clement. & Chrysostomum Didy- mum in h. l. in Bibl: Patr. T. IV. Origenem ad cap. IV. Rom. Athanasium περὶ παρθενείας Ephren. Sy- rum de vit. Spirit. Diadochum Episcopum Photices in de perfect. spiritual. cap. XXI. Basilium M. in Ps. LXII. Gregor. Nazianz. orat. XIII. Chrysost. ho- mil. II. in epist. ad Phil. & homil. II. in Gen. Cy- rillum Alexandrinum in IV. Malach. & IX. in Joh. cap. Isid. Pelusiotam l. III. ep. 73. Proclum Constan- tinop. Epist. ad Armen. Joh Damascenum l. IV. de O. Fide cap. X. adduxit B. Hülsemannus in Harm. pag. 40. seqq. Quibus ii, qui sectæ Romanensium adhærere putantur accedunt, Lombardus, Tho- mas, Brulifer, Taulerus, Cusanus, Cassander, Te- rus Wicelius, Gropperus, Sadoletus, Rivius, Nau- sea, Schopperus, Franciscus Lucas, &c. à B. Gerb. Conf. cathol. parte ult. art. XXIII. adducti in hanc sententiam quod non agnoscant fidem illâ pro ve- ri nominis fide, quæ charitate sive interna solum, seu externa simul careat. Adde quod etiam Lo- rinus agnoscat, Gregorium M. ac Cyprianum & Be- dam, Eucherium item, Maximum Abbatem, ac Philonem Carpathium fidem & dilectionem ita co- pulare, ut separari non possint, ut fides sine operi- bus vera, fides operibus carens sit cæca fides; Fides autem quantulacunque, modo vera fides sit, & non mortua, incipiat operari, fides & opera indissolu- bili vinculo connectantur, ut ubi alterum desit, al- terum penitus non stet: quodque Cornelius à Lapi- de ad h. l. doceat, multos Patres disserere, fidem ca- rentem bonis operibus non esse veram fidem. Quem sensum poscit omnino præsens comparatio Jacobi: quemadmodum nuda & blanda verba, quibus stu- dio & malitia dicentis res ipsæ non respondent, in- trinsece & suapte natura sunt inania & futilia: ita etiam fides non pariens bona opera intrinsece & na- tura sua inanis, & nulla est.

Τὸ νεκρὸν καθ' ἑαυτὸν est destitui actu primo & for- ma inesse debitæ;ista benificetiæ miseration. & liber- tatis forma aberat ab hypocrita Jacobæo dicente egenis: Ite in pace, calefiite. Nam καθ’ ἑαυ- τὴν est in semetipsa, intrinsece, ut Ebr. VI. 13. (Gen. XXII. 16.) Matth. XXII. 25. 26. Quod exemplum temere Grotius pro suo pleonasmo allegat, & con- tra fidem omnium Codicum pro καθ’ ἑαυτῆς legi vult ἐφ’ ἑαυτῆν: quemadmodum & reliqua pleonasmi exempla temere adducta sunt, quum potius ex inspectione locorum constet, non citra emphasin peculiarem vocem illam additam esse. Et cum vers. ult. corpus mortuum esse ex Spiritus absentia, fides mortua ex operum absentia docetur, mortuum non tantum de suspensione actuum ani- malium aut naturalium, salva facultate vitali; sed de carentia vitæ quoad actum primum intelligi, ne ipse Grotius sua interpretatione diffiteri potuit. Didymus Alexandr. in h. l. Notandum, inquit, quia cum fides mortua sit præter opera, jam neque fides. Nam neque homo mortuus est homo. Ephrem Syrus de vita spirit. §. 91. explicat hoc dictum, fides sine operibus mortua est, de iis, qui dicunt se nosse Deum, factis autem negant, quos negat esse fideles, affirmat esse vere mortuos: & §. 88. (quem locum adducunt Biblia magna Duacensium) cum de fide disputas, inquit, considera, utrum habeas opera fidei congruentia: Nam si discendi tantum & audiendi studiosus es, illud in te jacietur: Fides sine operibus mortua est. Profecto enim mortui sunt omnes, qui Deum nosse se profitentur, factis autem negant, cum sint, ut Apostolus ait, increduli, & ad omne opus bonum reprobi. Mortuum ergo esse est incredulum esse. Non ergo fides mor- tua essentiam vel naturam fidei habere potest. Chrysostomus homil. II. in Gen. Fides, inquit, sine operibus mortua est, & opera sine fide mortua. Ut ergo opera extra fidem facta non sunt vere bona: ita, ex mente Chrysostomi, nec fides operibus ca- rens vere bona est. Cyrillus Alexandrinus in c. IV. Mal. Si quis post justificationem revertatur ad ea, quæ carnis sunt, & mundi, occidit quasi in se- ipso fidem. Damasc. libr. IV. de orthod. fide cap. 10. Oportet enim virtute servare nos ipsos puros ab iniquitatis operibus. Fides enim sine operibus mor- tua est, similiter & opera sine fide. Nam vera fi- des per opera comprobatur. Isidorus Pelusiota l. III. ep. 73. Videris ea ignorare, quæ etiam PUE- RULIS nota & perspicua sunt. Neque enim hoc existimes, quod fides (si tamen licet fidem appella- re, quæ operibus suis refutatur) salutem tibi affer- re possit. Etenim fides ea, quæ primum justifica- vit, actiones consentaneas sibi exigit. Et ep. 403. Cum sanis dogmatibus pietatem conjungere oportet: Siquidem illud verum est, ut certum est, fidem sine operibus mortuam esse. Simeon Junior T. XII. Bibl. Patr. part. I. f. 749. Christum confiteri, ait, & Chri- sto obedire, quanquam duo videntur: tamen non duo, sed unum quiddam sunt. Nec enim unum si- ne altero constat: Tametsi IGNORANTES quidam aliter sentiant. Audi Apostolum: Fi- des sine operibus mortua est, cum malis operibus ne fides quidem est. Mortuum enim, si recens est, vel- ut modo exanimatum dicitur mortuum. Quod si multorum jam dierum est, non mortuum, sed putri- dum, corruptum, & fœtidum vocatur. Quoniam ergo duo sunt genera operum, Deo placentia & exo- sa: si fides sine operibus mortua est, ut scriptum legi- mus, fides illa, quæ non solum operibus Deo acceptis cared, sed & opera Deo invisa habet, quo nomine af- ficietur? Mortua? Imo magis putrida & corrupta nominari debet, aut ut verius loquar, incredulitas & impietas. E quibus abunde constat, non mor- tuam dici fidem propter solam absentiam operum externorum, sed propter extinctionem, vel absenti- am principii vitalis, non per syncopen tantum seu deliquium motus extrinsecus impediens, sed per carentiam vitæ, adeoque vere mortuam in seipsa: nec actu tantum secundo servandi destitutam fi- dem, sed quæ nullam facultatem intrinsecam ser- vandi habeat, designari, uti ab exemplis adductis à Groctio etiam patet Rom. IV. 19. Ebr. XI. 12. Cor- pus Abrahami νενεκρωμένον & νέκρωσις τῆς μήτρας Saræ, non tantum quoad suspensionem actus secun- di in facultate generatrice, sed quoad extinctio- nem hujus facultatis ob corpus jam effœtum, & ste- rilitatem ob cessationem muliebrium (Gen. XVIII. 11.) intelligi, quum de novo δύναμιν εἰς καταβο- λὴν σπέρματος acceperint, Ebr. XI. 11. 12. Loca au- tem proprie parallela, quo pacto vere mortua dica- tur fides sine operibus explicantia, dissimulata hic à Groctio, videantur Mat. VIII. 22. Luc. XV. 24. 32. Eph. II. 15. Col. II. 13. Eph. V. 14. Apoc. III. 1. Jud. v. 13.

Nonnullis placet determinationem illam καθ' ἑαυτὴν ad fidem referre, non ad vocem νεκρὰν, ut eam Syrus reddidit, sola, vel quæ solitaria est, sine spe, sine charitate, ut Augustinus loquitur, l. I. sent. 8. Sed fidei solitariæ περίφρασις jam erat expressa verbis, ἐὰν μὴ ἔργα ἔχῃ, præstat ergo ad prædica- tum referre, quod talis fides in seipsa mortua sit.

Quæ vero de actu fidei nõ quidem naturali, nec ei debito; sed à DEO liberaliter concesso SER- VANDI nos, suspicatus hic est B. Hülsemannus, nimis vera esse posteriora, imprimis scripta Grotiana docuere: nimirum patrocinari ipsum no- luisse Papistis, Socinianis & Arminii discipulis, fidei actum à merito & morali valore suo, quem Dei li- beralitas & ἐπιείκεια, ipsaq; moralis congruitas ei tribuit, æstimantibus, quum tamen juxta scriptu- ram fides non nisi instrumentaliter salvet, quatenus accipit bonum oblatum, non ob dignitatem ali- quam sui, nec in fide actus naturalis supernaturali contradistingui possit, sed fides tota sua essentia donum supernaturale sit, nec nisi à supernaturali principio facultatem salvandi habeat, quam natu- ram quia fidei indidit Deus, inde actus ille natu- ralis fidei non immerito dicitur, postquam DEO placuit per fidem nos servare, fidemque justifi- cam & salvificam efficere. Competit enim id na- turæ fidei ex œconomia Divina, ut possit salvare, Gal. III. 11. 1. Petr. I. 9. quemadmodum Verbo Evan- gelii naturale est, esse vivum & efficax Ebr. IV. 12.

## 2:18
Ver. 18. Ἀλλ' ἐρεῖ τις] But someone, well accustomed to doing good, will deservedly say to him who proclaims his faith to be void of works.

Σὺ πίστιν ἔχεις] You have faith, and you boast of it greatly. Κἀγὼ ἔργα] But I, saying nothing of my faith, devote my effort to pious deeds.

Δεῖξόν μοι τὴν πίστιν σου ἐκ τῶν ἔργων] Since very many manuscripts, and that best one which we use, and the Latin, and the Syriac, and the Arabic have read τὴν πίστιν σου χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων, it is altogether better that we follow that reading, in this sense: Show that faith of yours by words as much as you like, for the deeds are not present: And see how much godly men will value it, and from that infer what God will do.

Κἀγὼ δείξω σοι ἐκ τῶν ἔργων μου τὴν πίστιν μου] This second person is used for any man whatsoever: I, not boasting of my faith, but devoting constant effort to modesty, patience, and love, will easily convince anyone, even while silent, that there is true faith in me. For that perpetual holiness and constancy in adversity, such as appeared in that age, could have no other cause than true faith. Therefore he says this: All the pious will greatly prefer my faith, demonstrated by deeds, to yours, boasted of in words. How much more will God?

Grotius had handed down the very same things in his earlier commentary. It is pleasing, however, to add those things, so that nothing may be lacking.

Vers. 18. Ἀλλ' ἐρεῖ τις, σὺ πίστιν ἔχεις, κἀγὼ ἔργα ἔχω] But someone will say, you have faith, and I have works- I have. A pious person might deservedly say to a man who boasts of his faith in many words: you boast of your faith, but I, in silence, apply myself to pious deeds.

Show me your faith by your works. He adds: Since faith is situated in the mind, it is easily boasted of even by those who do not possess it, so that not even men can be certain of another's faith in a human way, unless pious deeds testify to it, the best indicators of faith. For such excellent and frequent deeds, such as were observed among Christians in that age, could not but proceed from faith.

And I will show you my faith by my works. I, not seeking glory for my faith, am wholly concerned with this, that by the piety of my life I may show not only to God and my conscience, but also to others, that I am a Christian: Finally, what need is there for words, let us be judged by our actions?

A non-saving, but historical and dogmatic faith is conceded to the boaster, namely that which consists solely in the assent to things to be believed: But because he boasts of a true and integral faith, he is challenged to demonstrate it by works, without which there is no true and integral faith. Three speakers are not introduced, of whom one, relying on faith, neglects works; another, indeed, valuing works, trusts in them, having neglected faith; the third, St. James, asserting that neither suffices for salvation, and that both must be joined, as Erasmus perverts it. For there are only two speakers, nor is there any dispute here about works without faith: nor is it false; but it is true that faith alone suffices for salvation: but it is false that both faith and works together contribute to obtaining salvation. The particle ἀλλὰ is not adversative in this place, but is equivalent either to 'therefore', or 'furthermore', or 'nay rather', 'indeed', so that it is either inferential, or continuative, or exaggerative. Nor is it said merely by Mimesis, 'you have faith', as Piscator, Pareus, and the Belgian Interpreters wish, as if to say, 'if you have faith as you say'. For St. James concedes that a certain man has that faith, just as he adds: 'You believe that God is one, you do well': But he denies that he has that which is saving. Pareus thinks that a Synecdoche or Metonymy must be established in the words, 'and I have works': so that it is understood as working faith, or works which are the effects of justifying faith. But there is no need for that. For even if only works are named, 'I have works', it is nevertheless manifest from the consequences that truly good works are understood, which demonstrate faith, and have no place without faith, Rom. XIV. 29. For from them, as from the fruits of faith, faith itself can be known.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Ἀλλ' ἐρεῖ τις] At merito fidem suam ab ope- ribus vacuam prædicanti dicet pius aliquis bene suetus a- gere.

Σὺ πίστιν ἔχεις] Habes fidem, eamque multum jactas. Κἀγὼ ἔργα] Ego vero de fide mea tacens do operam piis factis.

Δεῖξόν μοι τὴν πίστιν σου ἐκ τῶν ἔργων] Cum & Manu- scripti plurimi, & ille optimus, quo utimur, & Latinus, & Syrus & Arabs legerint τὴν πίστιν σου χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων, omnino præstat, eam lectionem nos sequi, hoc sensu: Illam tuam fidem ostende verbis quantumlibet, nam fa- cta non adsunt: Et vide, quanti eam facturi sint homines pii, & inde collige, quid facturus sit Deus.

Κἀγὼ δείξω σοι ἐκ τῶν ἔργων μου τὴν πίστιν μου] Ista se- cunda persona ponitur pro homine quolibet: Ego fidem meam non jactitans, sed perpetuam dans operam mode- stiæ, patientiæ, dilectioni, facile cuivis persuadebo, eti- am tacens, esse in me veram fidem. Nam perpetua illa sanctitas & in malis constantia, qualis illo seculo appare- bat, causam aliam, quam veram fidem habere non pote- rat. Hoc ergo dicit: Pii omnes fidem meam factis demon- stratam præ tua verbis jactata multum præferent. Quanto magis Deus?

Eadem prorsus tradiderat Grotius in priori commentatione. Adjicere tamen illa, ne quid defit, placet.

Vers. 18. Ἀλλ' ἐρεῖ τις, σὺ πίστιν ἔχεις, κἀγὼ ἔργα ἔχω] Sed dicet quis, tu fidem habes, & ego opera- habeo. Merito dicat aliquis pius, homini, fidem suam multis verbis prædicanti: tu de fide te jactitas, ego vero ta- citus do operam piis factis.

Δεῖξόν μοι τὴν πίσιν σου ἐκ τῶν ἔργων σου] Ostende mihi fi- dem tuam ex operibus tuis. Addit ille: Fides cum in a- nimo sita sit, facile etiam ab eam non habentibus jacta- tur, ita ne homines quidem de alterius fide humano mo- do certi esse possunt, nisi pia facta eam testentur, optima fidei indicia. Nam tam egregia ac frequentia facta, qualia in Christianis ista ætate spectabantur, non poterant non ex fide procedere.

Κἀγὼ δείξω σοι ἐκ τῶν ἔργων μου τὴν πίσιν μου] Et ego ostendam tibi ex operibus meis fidem meam. Ego de fi- de mea glorias non sectans in hoc totus sum, ut vitæ pie- tate non Deo tantum ac conscientiæ meæ, sed & aliis o- stendam, me esse Christianum: Denique quid verbis opus est, spectemur agendo?

Conceditur jactatori fides non salvifica, sed hi- storica & dogmatica, ea nempe, quæ in solo assensu credendorum consistit: Sed quia jactat veram & in- tegram fidem, eam ut demonstret operibus, sine quibus fides vera atque integra nulla est, provoca- tur. Non tres inducuntur colloquentes, quorum al- ter fretus fide opera negligat; alter nimirum æsti- mans opera his fidat, neglecta fide; tertius S. Jaco- bus, neutrum ad salutem sufficere, jungi utrumque debere asserat, ut Erasmus pervertit. Duo enim tan- tum sunt colloquentes, nec disputatio ulla hic est de operibus sine fide: neque falsum est; sed verum, fidem solam sufficere ad salutem: falsum autem, & fidem & opera conjunctim ad salutem consequendam fa- cere. Particula ἀλλὰ non est adversantis h. l. sed vel idem valet, quod ergo, vel quod præterea, vel quin imo, imò verò, ut sit vel inferentis, vel continuantis, vel exaggerantis. Neque per Mimesin dicitur tan- tum, tu fidem habes, ut Piscator, Pareus, Interpre- tes Belgici, volunt, si ita, ut dicis, te habere fidem. Nam concedit S. Jacobus, aliquem hominem illam habere fidem, quemadmodum addit: Tu credis, quod Deus sit unus, bene facis: Negat autem illam habere, quæ salvifica est. In verbis, & ego opera ha- beo, Synecdochen vel Metonymiam statuendam esse, censet Pareus: ut intelligatur fides operans, vel opera, quæ sunt fidei justificantis effectus. Sed ea opus non est. Etsi enim opera tantum nominentur, ego opera habeo, è consequentibus tamen manifestum, opera verè bona intelligi, quæ fidem demonstrant, nec locum habent sine fide, Rom. XIV. 29. Ex illis enim tanquam ex fructibus fidei cognosci potest ipsa fides.

## 2:19
Vers. 19. You believe that God is one. In the Manuscript: 'that God is one', he takes that which is first among things to be believed, and by which the Jews were separated not only from the atheists, but also from the Greeks: that God exists and is one, Deut. IV. 35, 39; VI. 4, upon which also the whole faith in Christ depends. For Christ's authority is from that one and true God, John XIV. 1; XVII. 3.

You do well? He says this: Thus far your affairs are in a good state. But he implies that this does not suffice for salvation.

And the demons believe. The demons, as the Rabbis call them שׁעירים, as the LXX also interpret in Isaiah XIII. 21.

And they shudder. They fear Him as the avenger of their malice, 2 Pet. II. 4; Jude 6. Thus you also ought to fear the same God, if you imitate the deeds of the Devil. For φρίσσουσι the Syrian has רצלין, they tremble. The Arab has יריוד in the same sense. By Metonymy that word signifies great fear, and is translated in the glossary as 'I shudder', 'I tremble'. Hence φρικῶς, Wisd. VI. 5, and φρικτὸν שׂערוריה, Jer. V. 30; XVIII. 13; XXIII. 14; φρικῶδες, Hos. VI. 10.

We add things not dissimilar to what had been handed down in the previous commentary.

You believe that God is one. You have bid farewell to those gods which human audacity invented, and you acknowledge God to be one, shown in the Law, more openly revealed in the Gospel. See Deut. VI. 4; Mark XII. 29, 32; John XVII. 3. Concerning the many things that are to be believed, he placed this as an example, which is the first, and upon which the mission and authority of Christ depend.

You do well. This is well, but it does not suffice.

Καὶ τὰ δαιμόνια πιςεύεσι] And the demons believe. This knowledge is so far from being sufficient that it is common to you with the wicked spirits.

Καὶ φρίσσουσι] And they shudder. Not only do they have no salvation to hope for, but also, because of their wickedness, they expect more severe torments with fear. See Matt. VIII. 28. 2 Pet. II. 4. Jude 6. Rev. XX. 10.

Therefore, it is taught here to believe that it is good: that faith is not vain and falsely called. Καλῶς ποιεῖς: And yet that faith is not saving. And therefore that James is dealing here with a different faith than that to which the Apostle attributes justification, Rom. III. For James's faith is the faith of demons. No one would say that Paul's faith is a faith common to men with demons. James's faith carries trembling with it: They believe, he says, and shudder, Φρίσσουσι, by which word a huge and horrible trembling is denoted, which is Φρὶξ, the roaring and horror of the sea and waves: Cf. Matt. VIII. 29. 2 Pet. II. 4. Jude v. 6. Rev. XX. 10. Paul's faith frees from all fear and brings peace, Rom. V. 1. ch. VIII. 1. James's faith is completed by bare knowledge and the ratification of things to be believed: Paul's faith is θάρσος, or confidence or trust, 2 Cor. V. 6, 8. Heb. XIII. 6. Cf. Matt. IX. 2, 22. Luke VIII. 48. John XVI. 33. Acts XXIII. 11. & ὑπόστασις τῶν ἐλπιζο- μένων, Heb. X. 1. which does not apply to demons. James's faith is unfruitful, destitute of works, indeed dead in itself. But to call Paul's faith, by which he teaches us to be saved, unfruitful, void of works, and dead, is to contradict the Holy Spirit openly. See Eph. II. 8, 9. Gal. V. 6. ch. II. 20. 2 Pet. I. 8.

From these things, therefore, it is manifest that there is one kind of faith which the truly faithful person seeks to be demonstrated to him, and another which he concedes the boaster and hypocrite has, which he also says is found in demons. For the former is living and justifying, such as even the Jesuits themselves would not say the latter is. Lorinus certainly, on v. 19, at the word, 'They believe'; 'Wherefore,' says Augustine, in sermon XLI on the word of the Lord, 'Christ did not wish to turn stones into bread, Matt. IV. 2, because the Devil (even having seen this miracle) was not going to believe in Him,' he understands it of living faith, to which charity is joined, which faith the Devil cannot have. Bellarmine, in order to extricate himself from the objection that faith without works is compared with the faith of demons, who it is agreed do not have true and justifying faith, replies in book I de justif. c. XV. that the faith of wicked men differs from the faith of demons in that the faith of men is free, with the pious will indeed capturing the intellect into the obedience of Christ, whereas the faith of demons is forced and extorted by the very evidence of things, because they believe while shuddering, that is, unwillingly and under compulsion. But that wicked men capture the intellect with a pious will, that they are wicked, and that they capture the intellect under the obedience of Christ, is a σιδηρόξυλον (iron-wood/absurdity). But that demons shudder when they believe is a consequence of their knowledge and assent, namely, the trembling and horror arising from the fact that they believe those things which have been revealed concerning God and eternal judgment to be true; because, as Grotius holds, they shudder because they not only have no salvation to hope for, but also, because of their wickedness, expect more severe torments with fear. But it is not the antecedent, or the same thing, that they are compelled to believe, nor does it accord with the common opinion of the Papists that revealed things are evident, or that the articles of faith have evidence, who make both the faith which is believed and that by which it is believed non-evident. But what Estius urges, that the faith such as that of demons is true because they are said to do well who believe in this way, Bellarmine himself limits in the aforementioned place, teaching that The faith of wicked men [is] with the faith of demons in this, namely that both are true and right faith on the part of the object. Therefore, it cannot be concluded from this that it is simply true, certainly not that it is so true that it has the form of justifying faith, and that it is active through love, since Bellarmine acknowledges it to be fruitless. It is true when it is taken for assenting or, as they call it, dogmatic faith, not when it is taken for justifying and saving faith. For even if faith is said to justify at least dispositively, are demons justified dispositively through faith, is there in them a disposition toward justification? Moreover, the Apostle's present argument from the insufficiency of historical and assenting faith is as follows: If historical faith is insufficient for salvation, the mere boasting of faith will be less sufficient. But the former is true: because even the demons believe, but (καὶ as an adversative, like the Syrian) they shudder.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Σὺ πιστεύεις, ὁ Θεὸς εἷς ἐστι] In Manuscripto: ὅτι εἷς ἐστιν ὁ Θεὸς, sumit id quod inter credenda primum est, & quo Judæi non tantum παρὰ τῶν ἀθέων, sed & πα- ρὰ τῶν Ἑλλήνων, separabantur: Deum esse & esse unum, Deut. IV. 35. 39. VI. 4. unde etiam pendet tota in Chri- stum fides. Nam Christo autoritas est ab illo uno ac vero Deo, Joh. XIV. 1. XVII. 3.

Καλῶς ποιεῖς;] Hoc dicit: Hactenus res tuæ bene se ha- bent. Sed sufficit hoc ad salutem non sufficere.

Καὶ τὰ δαιμόνια πιστεύει] Mali Spiritus idem credunt. Τὰ δαιμόνια Rabbinis שׁעירים quomodo & LXX. interpre- tantur Esa. XIII. 21.

Καὶ φρίσσουσι] Timent eum malitiæ suæ vindicem, 2. Petr. II. 4. Judæ 6. Sic & tu timere debes eundem De- um, si Diaboli facta imitaris. Pro φρίσσουσι Syrus רצלין tremunt. Arabs יריוד eodem sensu. Per Meto- nymiam id verbum ingentem metum significat, vertitur- que in glossario horreo, horresco. Inde φρικῶς Sap. VI. 5. & φρικτὸν שׂערוריה, Jer. V. 30. XVIII. 13. XXIII. 14. φρικῶδες Os. VI. 10.

Addimus quæ in priori commentatione tradi- derat non absimilia.

Σὺ πιστεύεις, ὅτι ὁ Θεὸς εἷς ἐστι] Tu credis quoniam unus est Deus. Valedixisti illis Diis, quos humana audacia invenit, agnoscisque Deum esse unum in le- ge monstratum, in Evangelio apertius revelatum. Vi- de Deut. VI. 4. Marc. XII. 29. 32. Joh. XVII. 3. de plu- ribus, quæ credenda sunt, id posuit exempli causa, quod primum est, atque unde pendet Christi missio & au- toritas.

Καλῶς ποιεῖς] Bene facis. Bene hoc se habet, sed non sufficit.

Καὶ τὰ δαιμόνια πιςεύεσι] Et Dæmones credunt. Ista cognitio adeo non sufficit, ut cum pravis Spiriti- bus tibi sit communis.

Καὶ φρίσσουσι] Et contremiscunt. Non modo salu- tem nullam sperandam habent, sed & pro sua pravitate graviora tormenta cum metu expectant. Vide Matth. VIII. 28. 2. Petr. II. 4. Judæ 6. Apoc. XX. 10.

Docetur ergo hic credere illud bonum esse: Non esse vanam & falso dictam fidem. Καλῶς ποιεῖς: Et fidem tamen non esse salvificam. Ideoque de alia fi- de hic agere Jacobum, quam de illa, cui justifica- tionem tribuit Apostolus, Rom. III. Jacobi enim fi- des est Dæmonum fides. Pauli fidem esse fidem ho- minibus communem cum Dæmonib9 nemo dixe- rit. Jacobi fides tremorem secum fert: Credunt, inquit, & contremiscunt, Φρίσσουσι, qua voce in- gens & horribilis tremor notatur, qui Φρὶξ est, fre- mitus & horror maris ac fluctuum: Conf. Matth. VIII. 29. 2. Petr. II. 4. Jud. v. 6. Apoc. XX. 10. Pauli fi- des liberat ab omni metu, ac pacem affert, Rom. V. 1. cap. VIII. 1. Jacobi fides nuda notitia & ratihabiti- one credendorum absolvitur: Pauli fides θάρσος est, vel confidentia vel fiducia, 2. Cor. V. 6. 8. Ebr. XIII. 6. Conf. Matth. IX. 2. 22. Luc. VIII. 48. Johan. XVI. 33. Act. XXIII. 11. & ὑπόστασις τῶν ἐλπιζο- μένων, Ebr. X. 1. quæ in Dæmones non cadit. Jacobi fides infructuosa est, operibus destituta, imò in se mortua. At Pauli fidem, qua servari nos docet, in- fructuosam, operibus cassam, mortuam dicere, est Spiritui sancto palam contradicere. Vid. Eph. II. 8. 9. Gal. V. 6. cap. II. 20. 2. Petr. I. 8.

Ex his ergo manifestum est, aliam fidei speciem esse, quam vere fidelis sibi demonstrari petit, aliam quam concedit jactatorem & hypocritam habere, quam etiam in Dæmonib9 inveniri ait. Illam enim esse vivam & justificantem, qualem hanc esse nec ipsi Jesuitæ dixerint. Lorinus certe ad v. 19. ad ver- bum, Credunt; Quocirca, inquit Augustinus, cum affirmat serm. XLI. de verbo Dom. Christum noluisse lapides in panem convertere, Matth. IV. 2. quia Diabo- lus, (etiam viso hoc miraculo) non erat crediturus in eum, intelligit de fideviva, cui charitas conjun- cta est, quam fidem Diabolus habere non potest. Bellarminus ut se expediat objectione, quod fides sine operibus comparata sit cum fide Dæmonum, quos constat fidem veram & justificantem non ha- bere, respondet l. I. de justif. c. XV. fidem hominum improborum à fide Dæmonum eo differre, quod ho- minum fides libera est, captivante nimirum pia vo- luntate intellectum in obsequium Christi, fides verò Dæmonum sit coacta & extorta, ab ipsa rerum evi- dentia, quia credant contremiscentes, id est, inviti & coacti. Sed homines impios pia voluntate intelle- ctum captivare, impios esse, & captivare intelle- ctum sub obsequium Christi, σιδηρόξυλον est. Quod verò Dæmones contremiscunt, cum credunt, conse- quens est notitiæ, & assensus ipsorum, tremor nem- pe, & horror inde oriundus, quod vera esse cre- dant, quæ de Deo & æterno judicio revelata sunt; quia, ut Grotius habet, contremiscunt, quod non mo- do salutem nullam sperandam habeant, sed & pro sua pravitate graviora tormenta cum metu expe- ctent. Non autem antecedens est, aut idem, quod cogantur, ut credant, neque revelata evidentia esse, vel articulos fidei evidentiam habere, Papistarum communi sententiæ congruit, qui & fidem, quæ cre- ditur, & qua creditur, inevidentem faciunt. Quod verò Estius urget, fidem, quaiis Dæmonum, veram esse, quia καλῶς facere dicuntur, qui ita credunt, id limitat ipse Bellarm. l. c. docens, quod conveniat fides hominum improborum cum fide Dæmonum in eo, nempe quod utraque est vera & recta fides ex parte objecti. Non ergo simpliciter veram esse inde concludi potest, non certè, quod ita vera sit, ut for- mam fidei justificantis habeat, & ut per dilectionem operosa sit, quum infructuosa esse agnoscat Bellarmi- nus. Vera est, qua pro fide assensitiva accipitur vel dogmatica, quam vocant, non qua pro fide justifica & salvifica. Nam etiamsi fides saltim dispositive ju- stificare dicatur, num Dæmones per fidem justifi- cantur dispositive, num in illis dispositio est ad ju- stificationem? Cæterum argumentum Apostoli præsens ab insufficientia fidei historicæ & assensitivæ tale est: Si historica fides insufficiens est ad salutem, minus sufficiens erit nuda fidei jactantia. At verum prius: quia & dæmonia credunt, at (καὶ adversati- vum, ut Syrus) exhorrescunt.

## 2:20
Vers. 20. Θέλεις δὲ γνῶναι] That is, do you wish to be taught this also by proofs from the Old Testament?

Ὦ ἄνθρωπε κενὲ] רֵיקָא, concerning which word it was spoken in Matt. V. 22. The Syrian here [uses] חַלָּשׁ, weak in judgment, that is to say: the Arab [uses] אלבטאל, vainly. Christ prohibits anger bursting forth into such words: not the words themselves, where they are used by masters to correct disciples, and much less where certain men are not marked in this way, but certain kinds of men. This appears in Matt. XXIII. 17, 18; Luke XXIV. 25; Gal. I. 13. They are deservedly called vain, who feed themselves on vain hope.

Ὅτι ἡ πίστις χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων νεκρά ἐστι] That faith without works cannot produce that which you hope for. χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων, the same as often ἐὰν μὴ ἔργα ἔχῃ.

In the prior commentary on that clause, Grotius has it thus.
