Θέλεις δὲ γνῶναι, ὦ ἄνθρωπε κενὲ, ὅτι ἡ πίστις χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων νεκρά ἐστι] Do you wish to know, O vain man, that faith without works is dead? Ἄνθρωπε κενὲ, that is, vain. In Syriac, Rica or Raca. Thus Jud. XI. 3. The Greeks translate, ἄνδρες κενοί. And thence Hesychius, ῥακὰ κενός. Therefore, it is not to be taken altogether universally that Christ forbids anyone to be called by such a word, but where it is out of hatred and uncontrolled anger: not where it is with a brotherly spirit of correction, especially if he who speaks thus has some authority or oversight over the other. Thus Christ called them μωροὺς, fools, in Matt. XXIII. 17, 18, and ἀνοήτους, senseless, both Christ in Luke XXIV. 25, and by his example Paul in Gal. III. 1, 3. But at the same time it must be noted both here and in those Apostolic words of Christ that it is not some certain man, but a kind of man, and indeed one tinged with some depraved quality or persuasion, that is addressed in this way, when he says Θέλεις γνῶναι, do you wish to know? he means this: Do you wish to be shown by examples taken from the sacred code, which you say you believe, that what I have said is true?

Κενὸς denotes not only one weak in judgment and feeding himself on vain hope, i.e., one whose persuasion is vain, but also a hypocrite, who namely boasts that he has faith, which, however, he does not demonstrate by works: for this vanity is the greatest, and it is designated not as true saving faith, but as vain and mere hypocrisy, since true and saving faith cannot exist without works. For the description of this ἀνθρώπου κενοῦ from his hypocritical kindness toward a needy brother in v. 15, 16, teaches that such a one does not labor so much from ignorance of the true and the decent, or from weakness of judgment, as from a lack of sincerity. Thus κενὰ in Acts IV. 25 not only denotes inept plans lacking the hoped-for effect, but also connotes deceitful pursuits. Κενὴ ἀπάτη, Eph. V. 6, not only denotes fruitless seduction, but also that which is malicious against the dictates of reason: And κενόδοξοι and κενοδοξία do not only designate an opinion born of ignorance, but also involve deceit and malice, Phil. II. 3; Gal. V. 26. And therefore James, with these words ὦ ἄνθρωπε κενὲ, not only corrects a false opinion in a refutatory manner, but also at the same time intends to confound the hypocrisy of such people in a corrective manner, by the contrary example of Abraham. B. Brochmand wishes to designate here who they are against whom the Apostle disputes, namely against the empty, void, and vain boasters of faith: who, because they gloriously boasted of a faith that was not true, being sterile of works, as if it were a true and living faith, for that reason the Apostle calls them empty and void men, alluding without doubt to empty vessels. For just as empty vessels, if they are struck, give forth a more sonorous sound and a clearer ringing than those which are filled to the very brim with any best liquid: So hypocrites boast and proclaim the faith, which they do not have, more verbosely than the truly faithful and pious. But that which the Apostle wishes to show is not that trust in the merit of Christ without works is dead or ineffective for justification, or as Grotius [says], that it cannot effect that which a vain man hopes for. For St. James had not argued by a single word against trust in Christ, but against the false boasting of it, and the vain profession of faith, or faith that is merely historical or dogmatic, void of works: which he had called dead καθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν, because it is destitute of the principle generating true trust in Christ—namely good works, both internal and external—nor can it demonstrate itself through works. Nor does the Apostle treat here of the justification of man before God, or the causes of the same, much less does he intend to demonstrate that faith and good works are συνάιτια & concausas (co-causes) of it, but he teaches this: that faith which is boasted of without the demonstration of good works is as null as words given to the poor without the contribution of alms, as from v. 15, 16, 17; that faith which does not have good works is not true, but false; nor is it the same faith in species as that which demonstrates itself through works, v. 18, 19. Which he proved, both from the faith of demons, whose faith is not that true salvific faith, but is beyond all doubt different in species from it, and from the faith of Abraham, to whose example, as the Father of believers, faith that is truly imputable to righteousness and truly proper to believers is recalled by Paul, Rom. IV. Dead, says the Apostle, that is, faith without works is dead. But it is one thing to be dead, another not to be able to produce salvation. That which is dead is nothing: therefore dead faith is nothing. A dead man is called a man equivocally. Therefore the faith of hypocrites, because it is not trust in the merit of Christ, is called faith only equivocally. It is dead, not only because of the lack of a second act, or the non-sensible production of good works: but especially because of the lack of a first act, or the principle that would generate good works. Whence it follows that such a principle generating good works is of the essence and definition of salvific faith, but the effect itself of this principle, or the internal and external good works themselves, are not of the definition and essence of justifying faith, but only an inseparable consequence, as the blessed Hülsemann rightly says here.

Latin:

Vers. 20. Θέλεις δὲ γνῶναι] Id est, vin' tibi hoc doceri e- tiam documentis è Veteri Testamento?

Ὦ ἄνθρωπε κενὲ] רֵיקָא, de qua voce dictum Mat. V. 22. Syrus hic חַלָּשׁ debilis judicio scilicet: Arabs אלבטאל vane. Christus prohibet iracundiam in ta- les voces prorumpentem: non ipsas voces, ubi à magistris ad corrigendos discipulos usurpantur, multoque minus, ubi non certi homines sic notantur, sed certa hominum genera. Apparet hoc Matth. XXIII. 17. 18. Luc. XXIV. 25. Gal. I. 13. Merito autem vani vocantur, qui vana spe se lactant.

Ὅτι ἡ πίστις χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων νεκρά ἐστι] Fidem sine operi- bus producere non posse id, quod speras. χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων, idem quod sæpe ἐὰν μὴ ἔργα ἔχῃ.

In priori commentatione de isto commate sic habet Grotius.

Θέλεις δὲ γνῶναι, ὦ ἄνθρωπε κενὲ, ὅτι ἡ πίστις χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων νεκρά ἐστι] Vis autem scire, ô homo inanis, quod fides sine operibus mortua est? Ἄνθρωπε κενὲ id est, vane. Syriace Rica vel Raca. Sic Jud. XI. 3. Græci vertunt, ἄνδρες κενοί. Et inde Hesychius ῥακὰ κενός. Non igitur omnino universim sumendum, quod Christus vetat tali vocabulo quempiam appellari, sed ubi id ex odio & impotenti ira sit: non ubi frater- no corrigendi animo, præsertim si, qui ita loquitur, imperium aliquod in alterum aut inspectionem ha- beat. Sic μωροὺς stultos dixit Christus Matth. XXIII. 17. 18. & ἀνοήτους tum Christus, Luc. XXIV. 25. tum ejus exemplo Paulus, Gal. III. 1. 3. Sed simul notandum & hic & illis Christi Apostolicis verbis non certum ali- quem hominem, sed hominum genus, & quidem prava aliqua qualitate aut persuasione tinctum ita compellari, cum dicit Θέλεις γνῶναι, vis scire? hoc vult: Vin' tibi exemplis è sacro codice, cui credere te ais, depromptis ostendi, verum esse, quod dixi?

Κενὸς non debilem tantum judicio & vana spe se lactantem, f. cujus vana est persuasio, sed hypocritam etiam notat, qui scilicet jactitat, se fidem habere, quam verò operibus non demonstrat: Hæc enim vanitas summa est, nec veram salvificam fidem, sed vanam esse ac mera hypocrisin, designatur, quum vera & salvifica fides sine operibus esse non possit. Descriptio enim hujus ἀνθρώπου κενοῦ ab hypocritica benignitate erga fratrem egenum v. 15. 16. docet, non tam laborare talem ignorantia veri, & decentis vel debilitate judicii, quam sinceritate. Sic κενὰ Act. IV. 25. non tantum inepta consilia notant carentia spe- rato effectu, sed dolosa quoque studia connotant. Κενὴ ἀπάτη, Eph. V. 6. non solum notat infructuo- sam seductionem, sed etiam malitiosam contra di- ctamen rationis: Et κενόδοξοι, ac κενοδοξία non solam opinionem ex ignorantia natam designant, sed dolum quoque & malitiam involvunt, Phil. II. 3. Gal. V. 26. Ideoque Jacobus verbis istis ὦ ἄνθρωπε κενὲ, non solum in genere Elenctico corrigit falsam opinionem, sed etiam in Epanorthotico simul talium hypocrisin, exemplo contrario Abrahami confun- dere intendit. B. Brochmand. hic designari vult, quinam sint, contra quos Apostolus disputet, videlicet contra inanes, vacuos, & vanos fidei jactatores: qui quoniam fidem non veram, quippe operum sterilem, gloriose jactabant, tanquam veram & vivam fidem, idcirco eos vocat Apostolus homines vacuos & ina- nes, aliudens procul dubio ad vasa vacua. Nam veluti inania vasa, si pulsentur, magis sonorum so- num, & clariorem tinnitum edunt, quam quæ optimo quovis liquore ad summum usque repleta sunt: Ita hypocritæ fidem, quam non habent, verbosius jactant & deprædicant quam vere fideles & pii. Id autem, quod ostendere vult Apostolus, non est, fiduciam in Christi meritum sine operibus mortuam aut ineffi- cacem esse ad justificationem, vel ut Grotius, efficere non posse id, quod homo vanus sperat. Nam adversus fiduciam in Christum nullo verbo egerat S. Jaco- bus, sed adversus falsam ejus jactantiam, ac vanam fidei professionem, vel fidem merè historicam, seu dogmaticam, operibus cassam: quam καθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν mortuam dixerat, quia principio bona opera, tum interna, tum externa, generante vera in Christum fiducia destituitur, nec se per opera demonstrare potest. Nec de justificatione hominis coram Deo hic tractat Apostolus, aut causis ejusdem, multo mi- nus intendit demonstrare συνάιτια & concausas il- lius esse fidem & bona opera, sed id docet, fidem, quæ jactatur sine demonstratione bonorum operum tam esse nullam, quam verba data pauperibus sine collatione eleemosynæ, ut è v. 15. 16. 17. fidem, quæ non habet bona opera non esse veram, sed falsam; nec ullam eandemq; esse specie fidem cum illa, quæ se demonstrat per opera v. 18. 19. Quod probavit, cum è Dæmonum fide, quorum fides non est illa vera sal- vifica fides, sed ab ea citra omnem dubietatē, spe- cie diversa est, tum è fide Abrahami, ad cujus ceu Patris credentium exemplum fides vera imputabi- lis ad justitiam, & verè fidelibus propria, à Paulo revocatur, Rom. IV. Νεκρὰν, inquit, Apostol9, id est, mortuam esse fidem sine operibus. Aliud autem est, mortuum esse, aliud producere non posse salutem. Quod mortuum est, nullum est: fides ergo mortua nulla. Homo mortuus æquivoce homo dicitur. Fi- des ergo hypocritarum, quia non est fiducia in Christi meritum, æquivoce tantum fides dicitur. Mortua est, non tantum ob carentiam actus secundi, seu non sensibilem productionem bonorum o- perum: Sed præcipuè ob carentiam actus primi, seu principii generaturi bona opera. Unde conse- quens est, tale principium generans bona opera esse de essentia & definitione salvificæ fidei, ipsum autem effectum hujus principii, seu ipsa bona opera interna & externa non esse de definitione & essentia justifi- cantis fidei, sed tantum inseparabile consequens, ut rectè hic B. Hülsemannus.

## 2:21
Vers. 21. Abraham our father] Even according to the flesh. For he is writing to Hebrews.

Was he not justified by works] δικαιοῦσθαι sometimes signifies to be made just, sometimes to be loved and treated as just. For most Hebrew words of that form have a double meaning. Although it is certain that a man is made just through faith, and then also more just through continuous works, nevertheless the whole context of this discourse, and especially those things which will now follow, demand that we take δικαιοῦσθαι here in the latter sense, and indeed in such a way that it is understood that both Abraham and Rahab were treated by God in the way that those who are just are accustomed to be treated, not only regarding their faith, but also the works that proceeded from faith. But if that faith of Abraham, so highly praised in Gen. XV. 6, was indeed profitable, but not alone, why is it that others should promise themselves more from their own non-working faith? If Abraham had believed that faith was sufficient for himself to conciliate and retain the favor of God, he would have abstained from the sorrowful work of which this writer is now speaking.

Much more prolix is Grotius in his often-mentioned peculiar treatise on this clause, not so much an interpretation as a dissertation, composed to pervert the Apostle's meaning, which we bring here in its entirety.

Abraham our father, was he not justified by works? Which many of the ancients, and among them Augustine in his book On Faith and Works, judge; and it is probable that this epistle, and the first of John, and that of Jude, and that which is called the second of Peter, were written against those who, interpreting the Pauline epistles perversely, said that faith without good morals was sufficient for salvation, both from the final words of that epistle which is ascribed to Peter, and because this James uses the example of the same Abraham to prove that works are required for salvation in the sense we explained above, from whose example Paul had inferred that men are justified by faith without works, Rom. III. 27 and IV. throughout. Moreover, that Paul himself does not at all conflict with these Apostles, Augustine teaches most clearly by the saying of the same Paul in Gal. V. 6: In Christ neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but that faith which works through love; to which Augustine also added another passage from 1 Cor. XIII. 2, where he who has faith but does not have love is said to be nothing. But where, the same Augustine adds, this faithful love works, without doubt one lives well. The same Augustine, On Free Choice, ch. VII: But men, not understanding what the Apostle himself says, think that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law; they thought he meant that faith is sufficient for a man, even if he lives badly and does not have good works. Far be it that the vessel of election should think so, who, when he had said in a certain place: For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, he immediately added: But faith, which works through love. This is the faith that separates the faithful of God from the unclean demons. For they too, as the Apostle James says, believe and tremble, but they do not work well. Reconciling both, the same Augustine in Volume IV, book of 83 Questions, question LXXVI, speaks thus: Therefore the opinions of the two Apostles, Paul and James, are not contrary to each other, when one says that a man is justified by faith without works, because the former speaks of works that precede faith, the latter of those that follow faith, as Paul himself also shows in many places: Excellent. For Paul does not oppose to faith works that proceed from faith, and are often even included under the very name of faith in a certain broader sense, as appears from the passages of Paul cited at the beginning of this treatise, Rom. X. 10, Tit. I. 1. But those which can be performed without faith, or from the native powers of men and human instruction alone, such as all rituals, then also the abstinence from evil actions for the sake of avoiding punishment, and furthermore certain other things which are wont to be done out of a desire for convenience or honor. The Jews attributed very much to rites: Of the forbidding precepts, they urged only those to which a penalty is attached; they denied that even a deliberate thought was liable to punishment before God: but they said that the omission of commanding precepts was easily expiated. This was the Jewish piety, by which, puffed up, they despised foreigners, however much they had turned from false gods to the true God, and from a wicked life to a holy one. Disputing against these, Paul shows that no works please God for the giving of salvation which are not produced from a soul purified by faith in eternal life, and kindled above the care of temporal things to the love of God and neighbor, and on the contrary, that evil works do not hinder salvation in those who have turned themselves from them through such faith, and have dedicated themselves and a holy life to God. Augustine, in the aforementioned book of questions, quest. LXXVI: This passage of this epistle (namely, James) explains how the same sense of the Apostle Paul is to be understood, and therefore he uses the example of Abraham more, that faith is empty if it does not work well, because the Apostle Paul also used the example of Abraham to prove that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law. For when he commemorates the good works of Abraham, which accompanied his faith, he sufficiently shows that the Apostle Paul does not teach through Abraham that a man is justified by faith without works in such a way that, if anyone has believed, it does not pertain to him to work well, but rather to this end, that no one should think that he has arrived at the gift of justification, which is in faith, by the merits of prior good works. In the same place, having adduced the passages of Paul, Gal. V and 1 Cor. VI, by which sentences, he says, he teaches most manifestly that they did not arrive at the justification of faith through past good work, nor was that grace given to them by their merits, when he says: And such were you: But when he says, those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God, he sufficiently shows that, from the time they believed, they ought to work well:

which James also says, and in many places altogether the same Apostle Paul proclaims quite openly, that all who have believed in Christ must live rightly, lest they arrive at punishments. The Greek word δικαιοῦν, to justify, corresponds to the Hebrew הצדיק, as appears both to the writers of the New Testament and to the interpreters of the Old. But the voices of that form which is called Hiphil by the Hebrews sometimes signify a double act, that is, of making another do something, sometimes something similar, for instance to declare, just as the word הצדיק, and its opposite הרשיע, to unjustify, are taken in the sense of absolving and condemning respectively, both elsewhere and in Deut. XXV. 2 and Prov. XVII. 15; likewise to treat as such: for instance to praise, as that word is placed in Matt. XI. 19, Luke VII. 29, X. 29, XVI. 15, 1 Tim. III. 16, and Ecclesiasticus I. 28, XXXI. 5; likewise to do good to someone, as 1. Reg. VIII. 32. Just as סכך, which is to make innocent, the Chaldean translates in Exod. XXXIV. as to spare, so he who is loved by God as if he were plainly guiltless, is gifted with the Spirit of God, and becomes certain of eternal salvation in that state, is sometimes said to be δικαιοῦσθαι, although the word itself is otherwise found elsewhere in that primitive and more proper meaning in Dan. XII. 3. Ap. XXXII. 11. That one may please God in that way is obtained not through the native works of men, but through faith. That it is held by divine oracles, where it has reached the purpose of obedience, and is indeed preserved through pious deeds, all Christians, Greek, Latin, and African, have believed and taught with unanimous, manifest, and perpetual consent, and have demonstrated that they so believe, both by the individual deeds of each and by the rules established in common by all concerning baptism and repentance. Concerning the Eucharist, Justin says thus: Ἧς οὐδενὶ ἄλλῳ μετασχεῖν ἐξόν ἐστιν, ἢ τῷ πιστεύοντι ἀληθῆ εἶναι τὰ διδασκόμενα ὑφ' ἡμῶν, καὶ λουσαμένῳ τὸ ὑπὲρ ἀφέσεως ἁμαρτιῶν, καὶ εἰς ἀγένεσιν λουτρὸν, καὶ οὕτω βιοῦντι, ὡς ὁ Χριστὸς παρέδωκε, of which it is lawful for no one else to partake, except him who believes that the things taught by us are true, and has been washed in the laver which is instituted for the remission of sins and for regeneration, and so lives as Christ commanded. But Paul opposes the Pharisaic opinions in many ways; for he shows that ritual matters were partly tolerated by God, and partly instituted for the sake of the times and the nature of the people to avoid idolatrous worship, but were not held in esteem for their own sake; and then, that to abstain from crimes—which even human laws, in this respect in agreement with the law of Moses, restrain with severe punishments—has nothing in itself worthy of praise, much less of divine reward: or anything in which anyone ought to boast; where he also incidentally sprinkles this, that many who boasted of the law had not even performed that innocence, after, of course, the capital judgments, by the fear of which they were restrained, had ceased among them and the Roman laws or governors connived at many crimes. But indeed, that method of leading men to salvation, which God had roughly outlined in Abraham and the affairs of his descendants, but had shown most fully perfected in the Gospel, is most worthy of God and most useful to men. For modesty and submission of mind, when one must deal with God, are most greatly impressed upon us by the fact that we know we are led to the hope of eternal life not ἐκ συναλλάγματος, or by an equal covenant, but through the mercy of God and the forgiveness of even grave sins, since the law of Moses was (to use the words of Livy speaking of human law) a deaf and inexorable thing regarding such matters: 'Αδυνάτῳ ἡ τῆς κολάσεως παραίτησις νόμου παραβαίνοις, there was no room for the deprecation of punishment for him who had sinned against the law, says Josephus against Apion, because we obtain the knowledge of that very life—I mean a firm one, and for the sake of which any inconveniences and dangers are despised—not by our own reasoning or the authority of any human wisdom, but because God has deigned to reveal His counsels to us by His goodness, and to seal the same in our hearts through the Holy Spirit: because God judges us, now insisting upon that way, not by the highest law but by paternal clemency. But the submission of mind born from these things both drives us to prayers and to acknowledging the huge benefits of God: it removes pride and the contempt of others. But that firm persuasion concerning eternal life causes us to consider nothing great in comparison with the love of God who is so beneficent, and the salvation of our neighbor who is commended to us by Him and is in His place: especially since Christ Himself, the author of our salvation, not only taught that way but also demonstrated it by example. To these, however, are compared the Jewish ceremonies, and that thin innocence according to the prescription of the law, whether human or divine, insofar as it is understood after the manner of human beings, and μέχρι τῶν πράξεων ἐγκράτεια, continence standing within deeds, as Chrysostom speaks on Rom. VIII, deservedly seem base: indeed, even that opinion concerning the easy expiation of faults that consist in omission throws up a great hindrance to progress; for all these things are such that they not only fail to cleanse the mind, but, unless other aids are added by divine grace, they rather turn the mind away from the sense of its own diseases. But since this most wise plan of divine economy was difficult to persuade to the Hebrews, who prided themselves on the title of both ancestral virtues and the law given to them alone, and who envied salvation to uncircumcised foreigners, even though it had testimonies among men not entirely stubborn—the precepts of Christ above the law, his death and return to life, the life of foreigners converted to Christ much holier than the Jewish one, and much stronger patience in adverse circumstances, and furthermore the conspicuous gifts of the Holy Spirit taken from the synagogue and transferred to the Church—Paul, to crush that ferocity, denies that God owes an account of his plan to anyone, since both as Creator he has a master's right over us, and eternal life and heavenly happiness are not owed to man by his own nature. Nevertheless, at the end of these prescriptions, he liberally shows that no plan more glorious to God or more useful to men could have been devised. And this indeed is the chief purpose of the Pauline epistle to the Romans, piously observed by all the ancients, although they do not all interpret the individual members and words in the same way, which will seem least surprising to one who, with Irenaeus, Origen, and Jerome, has learned through much reading and intensity of mind while reading that there are in that writer many hyperbata, parentheses, confusions, anacolutha, superjections, interpositions, confusions, transitions, unfinished comparisons, and things said concisely, others abruptly. But these ought not to cast a cloud over the saving doctrines proposed both by the same Apostle and by other holy writers, often and openly. We must beware lest we fall into that which Tertullian says against Marcion IV. Heretics always snatch either naked or simple words with conjectures, wherever they wish, or again they dissolve conditional and rational ones by the condition of simplicity: Which Aristotle would say: They take what is said simply as if it were in a certain respect, and what is said in a certain respect, as if it were simply: They accept what is said simply as in a certain respect, against what is said in a certain respect, simply. And against Praxeas: This is the property of all heretics: For because there are few things that can be found in the forest, they defend the few against the many. Thus also in the book on modesty: It is, he says, a custom for heretics to be armed against an army of sentences of the whole instrument by the occasion of some ambiguous chapter. And on the resurrection: It is certainly fair that uncertain things be judged by certain ones, and obscure things by manifest ones, so that faith may not be dissipated, truth endangered, and Divinity itself branded as inconstant amidst the discord of certain and uncertain, manifest and obscure things. Which agrees well with those things of Origen VI against Celsus: I know well that they will take some things from the Scripture; which even these (namely the evils) wishing to dare to say have happened from God, not being able to demonstrate in the height of the Scripture, which blames those who sin, but accepts those who do well, and nevertheless says nothing less than evils, which it seems to distract, being few, those who read the divine scriptures ignorantly. I know that some will seize upon sayings of scripture, who also say that these things are from God, since they cannot bring forward for themselves a perpetual tenor of scripture, which everywhere accuses those who do evil and approves those who do well, and yet says those things which, being few, seem to detain those who read the scriptures unskillfully. Whence the prudent saying of Clement of Alexandria in Strom. VI does not depart: All things are right before those who understand, says the scripture, that is, those who, receiving the explanation of the scriptures made clear by him according to the Ecclesiastical canon, preserve it; and the Ecclesiastical canon is the harmony and agreement of the law and the prophets, with the covenant which is handed down by the coming of the Lord. All things are right to those who understand, says the scripture, that is, to those who accept and keep the sense of scripture made clear by him according to the Ecclesiastical canon; and the Ecclesiastical canon is the harmony and agreement of the law and the Prophets, with that covenant which was given through the coming of the Lord. And no less useful is that of Vincent: Then he will take pains to consult and question the opinions of the elders brought together among themselves, of those only who, although in different times and places, remaining in the communion and faith of one Catholic Church, have proven to be reliable teachers. And whatever he discovers that not one or two only, but all together with one and the same consent have openly, frequently, and perseveringly held, written, and taught, let him understand that this also is to be believed by him without any doubt: Which the same writer briefly expresses thus: That the line of Prophetic and Apostolic interpretation be directed according to the norm of the Ecclesiastical and Catholic sense. And again: This is finally done if we follow universality, antiquity, and consent. Forewarned by these things, the reader will easily understand what James means for himself, namely that Abraham himself, who was called the Father of believers, labored in every way to ensure that, having obtained the favor of God through faith, he would preserve it by good works, in that way making his calling and election sure, as Peter speaks of Christians in II Epistle 1.10. Just as we obtain this life by the act of our parents, but preserve it through nourishment. Thus that state in which God accepts us as innocent is sought by faith, but is preserved by good works. But a saving birth, not accepted but guarded, gives life, as Cyprian says in Epistle VII.

Grotius brings forward three interpretations as analogous to the faith: The first is that of the Papists, that a man is made just through faith, and more just through continuous works, who call the former justification, and the latter a second one, and they wish for this to be what is designated here by James. Concerning which Bellarmine, in Book I on Justification, chapter I, says: just as it is commonly said that not only he who becomes hot from being cold is heated, but also he who becomes hotter from being hot: so also he is said to be justified not only who from being impious becomes just, but also he who from being just becomes more just, where he cites that passage of James, chapter II: You see that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only. But that distinction of justification into first and second is neither found anywhere in Scripture, nor does it agree with Scripture or this Apostolic passage, nor could it prove itself to the ancient Papists. For first, the justification of a sinful man before God is only one, and is accomplished by faith alone, without works, Rom. III. 28. Next, Paul brought forward the example of Abraham, Rom. IV. 3, not at the beginning of his conversion, but when he had already obeyed God for some years, whom he nevertheless confirms from Gen. XV was justified not by works, but by faith alone. Thirdly, he proves by the testimony of David that not only justification, but also eternal blessedness is attained through faith, Rom. IV. 6. Fourthly, the Apostle expressly describes the beginning of faith, and the middle, and the end, Rom. V. 1, seq. There is held there, as the blessed Chemnitz observes in the Examination of the Council of Trent, an illustrious distribution: The first concerning the beginning: Through Christ we have had access by faith into this grace, so that justified by faith we have peace with God. The second concerning the middle: In that same grace by faith we stand. The third concerning the end: In that same grace by faith we boast of the glory of God: that is, just as by faith we had access into grace: so also we hope, by the same faith and grace, that we shall arrive at glorification. In addition to these, fifthly, in Phil. III, Paul, as the blessed Chemnitz further says, delivers the doctrine of justification in the same way through a distribution, which was his righteousness before God unto eternal life, namely first, when he was converted from Pharisaism, secondly then when he was writing to the Philippians, thirdly when he is to meet the resurrection of the dead. But he does not say that his justification was one thing at the beginning of his conversion, and another afterwards, when he was writing from his chains, or when he is to meet the resurrection. This he certainly does not say, but he describes one and the same righteousness, namely of faith, in the beginning, middle, and end. But this fictitious distinction of the Papists has been dealt with elsewhere. Which sixthly proceeds solely from a false hypothesis, as if justification behaves as a physical act, such as heating, and the infusion of the habit of justice, whereas forensic justification is to be understood by the phrase and sense of Scripture, by which a man is pronounced just before the divine tribunal and is absolved from sins. Seventh, that that sense does not agree with this passage, that a man is said to be made more just by works: it is evident from this, that the question here is not how justice is nourished and increased, but that it must be taught that faith is dead, not living, true, and justifying, which is destitute of good works. But it is one thing for justice to be made greater by works, and another for one who has no works not to have faith. Add eighth, that according to this exposition it must be said that the boasters, with whom James is dealing, were indeed just by the infused habit of justice, or as regards primary justification, but were to be reproved because they did not, by the example of Abraham, increase their infused justice by the exercise of good works. But who will admit that hypocrites were truly just? Or justified by a demonic faith, as Augustine calls it? Finally, we here commit Estius with other Papists: That which some say for the sake of reconciliation, that Paul speaks of primary justification and James of secondary, seems to be said with little solidity. For the works of faith are required for primary justification, of which James speaks: and the works of the law, of which Paul speaks, are useless for secondary justification. Thus, therefore, Estius reconciles it: The Apostle Paul denies that anyone can be justified by the works of the law, that is, by those works which precede faith in the Mediator and proceed from the mere knowledge of the law. James, however, deals with works that follow faith, and sprout from faith, and are directed by faith. Similarly, Cornelius à Lapide, as also Vasquez, Tom. II. in I. 1. D. 210. c. 8., admit that both Apostles speak of both justifications. That Paul excludes works which are done by the sole powers of free will without faith in Christ. But that James includes works done from faith, and attributes to them the power of justifying.

And to this point goes the other Grotian explanation, which he delivered in his former commentary. 1. He says that faith without works produces salvation: but does not lead to salvation those who live longer: in which way the Pontificians distinguish between justification and salvation, that we are indeed justified by faith alone, but are not saved unless, given time and opportunity, good works follow. Bellarmine, book IV. de justif. cap. VII. We, on the contrary, understand that good works are necessary for men who have the use of reason, and who survive for so long after obtaining the grace of remission until the occasion of fulfilling the law occurs. 2. When Grotius says that Paul opposes to faith, not works which proceed from faith, but those which can be performed without faith or from the native powers of men and human instruction alone: he explains it thus, that they are all rituals, then also abstinences from evil actions for the sake of avoiding punishment, furthermore certain other things which are wont to be done out of a desire for convenience or honor. To which returns the opinion of Dominicus à Soto, Toletus, Pererius, Salmeron, Justinianus, Estius, as also Cornelius à Lapide in Rom. III.; from whom Cornelius: When the Apostle, he says, thus everywhere separates and distinguishes faith from works, he understands the works of the law not only ceremonial and judicial, but also moral or of the Decalogue. But as for that distinction between justification and salvation, it agrees neither with Paul nor with James. For Paul attributes not only justification, but also blessedness to faith alone without works, and constitutes the same causes of salvation and justification, as was said before. James also teaches not only that faith which is without works does not save, but that faith which does not have attendant works does not justify; nay, he demonstrates that such faith is demonic, dead in itself, and nothing. As for the distinction between works done before faith and those proceeding from faith: works, when they are done from the powers of nature alone and before faith, are nothing, because whatever is not of faith is sin, Rom. XIV. last; nor do good works precede the one to be justified, but follow the one justified. Nor are the works of the law understood as those which are done before faith, but those which are conformable to the law, and thus all good works are excluded from justification, even if they flow from faith. Because all works have a relation to the law as a norm, and it is necessary that they be conformable to it. Furthermore, since works both proceed from faith and follow the one to be justified, how can they be the cause of justification? For a cause does not follow an effect, but must be prior to it: Whence the Sophists cannot extricate themselves here, how James, speaking of justification, if the discourse is about that justification which is before the tribunal of God, can say that Abraham was justified by faith, if indeed it is certain that works follow not only faith but also justification. For that by which Abraham was justified before God, as the cause of justification itself, could not but be prior to justification itself, in the order of nature.

Which perhaps was the reason why Grotius, having dismissed that interpretation of his former commentary, in the annotations to this passage adopted another, which is the third, that to be justified here is not to be made just, but to be loved and treated as just, as it is understood that both Abraham and Rahab were so treated by God as those who are just are wont to be treated, not only regarding their faith, but also works proceeding from faith. Which, although they can be admitted without prejudice to orthodoxy; for there is no doubt that God regards both faith and works, and that the works of those justified by faith are pleasing to God, and that they themselves are loved and treated by God as just. Grotius, however, fosters in this explanation a ὕπóυλόν τι [something festering underneath], which comes out later: that the faith of Abraham, proclaimed in Gen. 15:6, was beneficial, but not alone, for justification: for it is treated in Genesis concerning him: that faith did not suffice for Abraham to procure and retain the favor of God, the effect destined for him, as he is later to say, (salvation) that faith cannot obtain [it] ἅνευ συναιτίων [without contributing causes] of good works, which are, of course, purely Papist errors. On the contrary, Paul vindicates justification to faith alone in Rom. 4 from that passage of Genesis ch. 15:6; he teaches that we both obtain and retain the grace of justification by faith alone, which we previously taught from Rom. ch. 4 and 5 and Phil. 3, and it is evident from 1 Pet. 1 that we are guarded through faith unto salvation. Scripture has constituted faith alone, on our part, as the cause of salvation, with works excluded: Rom. 4:8. Blessedness is his, to whom God imputes righteousness without works. How, therefore, could good works make συναίτια [contributing causes] of blessedness? This would certainly be an open ἅντιλογία [contradiction].

But let us see what that prolix Grotian commentary has in reserve? First, he brings forward the occasion of this epistle, and of the former of John, and of Jude, and of the latter of Peter, that they were directed against those who, interpreting the Pauline epistles perversely, said that faith without good morals sufficed for salvation. But that is evident from neither this nor other epistles by any indication. And although they teach that faith which is without good works does not save, they do not therefore constitute both faith and good works as causes of salvation, nor do they assert that good works contribute with faith to obtaining salvation. Nor is it probable from the final words of Peter that the doctrine concerning justification is designated by the τὰ δύσνόητα [things hard to be understood], which the oi̓ a̓́μαθεις κ̓ ἄστήρικτοι [the unlearned and unstable] have depraved, which are more correctly referred by others and by most of the ancients to the Epistle to the Hebrews, to which this Petrine letter was also inscribed. Nor can it be admitted that James here proves that works are required for salvation: since his scope is to teach only this, that the faith by which we are justified is not without works: just as neither was the faith of Abraham, which alone was imputed to him for righteousness, without works, but manifested itself through works, so that he was justified, that is, acknowledged as righteous, and openly declared, from his works, especially when he offered his son Isaac. But that this was reckoned by the ancients among the false interpretations of the Pauline epistles, that faith without morals suffices for salvation, can be proved by no testimony; nor does Gal. V. 6 or 1 Cor. XIII. 2 contribute anything to it, nor did Augustine hand down any such thing, whose words from chapter VII of De Libero Arbitrio we embrace with both hands, as those by which it is only refuted that faith suffices for a man, even if he lives wickedly and does not have good works, which we have already refuted at length. The reconciliation of Paul and James also holds up very well in the Augustinian manner, and agrees entirely with the Augsburg Confession: that Paul teaches that a man is justified by faith without works; James, that faith without works is empty: the former speaks of works that precede faith, which Paul teaches are as nothing; so it is also clear that no one can be justified by them, since all have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God, and the whole world is subject to God, Rom. III. 19, 23. And therefore we must be justified freely, by grace, through faith in the blood of Christ alone, v. 24, 25. The latter, however (James), speaks of those works which follow faith, which Augustine does not understand in the sense as if we were justified by them before God, but that by them we demonstrate ourselves to be righteous and are acknowledged as righteous. Nor indeed from the fact that it is said that it is Paul's doctrine that Abraham did not attain to grace and glory through works preceding faith, does the other disparate point follow: That Abraham at least attained to salvation through works following faith. The author does not infer this, but only that after faith Abraham worked well, and thus also showed us the debt by working well after we have believed. We also readily grant what he has in book LXXXIII. Qq. q. 76 (even if it is disputed whether that book is by Augustine) that Paul does not teach through Abraham that a man is justified by faith without works in such a way that if anyone has believed, it does not pertain to him to work well, but rather to this end, that no one should think that he has attained to the gift of justification, which is in faith, by the merits of pious good works. We admit that Paul teaches that men, from the time they have believed, ought to work well, and that all who have believed in Christ must live rightly, lest they come to punishment.

Furthermore, secondly, he appeals here to the proper meaning of the word הצדיק, that in its primitive and more proper meaning according to the Hiphil form it denotes a double act, that is, of one making another do, bring about, Dan. XII. 3, Apoc. XXII. 11. But that rule, that verbs of the third conjugation of the Hebrews denote either a double act, that is, to make another do, or something similar, such as to declare, etc., is not universal, but proceeds only in those verbs, and not even everywhere, which in the first conjugation, Kal, denoted a simple act. But those which are intransitive and neuter in Kal denote a simple act in Hiphil, and since according to R. D. Kimchi, Pagninus, and Bertram, verbs whose meaning is intensified are increased in the third conjugation, either by an accumulation of acts, if the Hiphil verbs denoted a simple act in Kal, or by an alteration of meaning, so that they become active in Hiphil from being neuter in Kal, therefore because צדק in Kal is by the consensus of most intransitive, 'he was righteous,' not 'he did righteously'; therefore in Piel and Hiphil it alters its meaning, and denotes to pronounce righteous, to declare, to make, through information about the way of acquiring righteousness, absolution from guilt, declaration, etc. never when it is used of God justifying and man being justified, to infuse a new habit of righteous and holy men, by the power of which habit the subject having suffered it may henceforth produce righteous and holy actions, or to make someone righteous so that he himself also acts righteously, which double act Grotius assigns. Furthermore, if one must proceed from an induction of many places, the word הֵצְרִיק is most frequently to declare, to pronounce righteous, just as Grotius himself acknowledges, that that word is taken for the act of absolving, the opposite of הִרְשִׁיעַ, to unjustify, for a condemnatory sentence, Deut. XXV. 2, Prov. XVII. 15, who produced no more than a single place from the Old Testament for the meaning which he calls primitive, Dan. XII. 3, which however does not denote that double act, but information about the way of acquiring righteousness, as Jerome rendered it, 'those who instruct many unto righteousness.' Nor did Grotius have any other place to bring forward from the New Testament than that one, Apoc. XXII. 12, from which, however, how it denotes either its primitive meaning or that acceptance of the word which occurs when the mode and reason by which God justifies man is treated, since there the discourse is not about that mode, but about the actions of the justified man, nor does 'to justify' in the words 'let him be justified still' denote the infusion of a habit of righteousness, but to act righteously from a habit or a passing impulse of piety, which no Papal interpreter denies, just as it is explained by the Council of Trent itself, sess. VI, c. 10, concerning the increase of received justification, and that not as infused by God by way of a habit, but elicited by the man himself.

Furthermore, if we admit that the word δικαιόω here means to treat as just, to praise, and to do good, what does this prove either against our orthodoxy or for the Papist-leaning and Socinian-leaning Grotius? That Abraham was praised for his works, and that benefits were shown to him by God on account of his obedience—does it follow immediately from that that he obtained eternal salvation through works? Thus, the process goes from the undistributed to the distributed, from the genus to a specific species.

But that Paul teaches that one may please God in such a way that he is loved by God as if entirely innocent, is gifted with the Spirit of God, and is made certain of eternal salvation in that state—and that this is obtained not through the native works of men, but through faith applied to Divine oracles, when it has reached the purpose of obeying—this can neither be shown from the Pauline Epistle to the Romans, which Grotius here considers, and it contradicts the Apostolic treatment, both because he understands faith applied to divine oracles as mere assent, and, as it appears, restricts it with the Socinians to oracles concerning existing eternal life: and also because he judges that only the native works of men are excluded from justification, whereas the Apostle excludes all works of which the law is the norm: and also because he says that faith reaches the purpose of obeying, as if this contributes to the perfection of faith, when it is only an effect of faith according to the Apostle, and does not truly pertain to its integrity and definition; and also because he wishes justifying grace, which consists in the non-imputation of our injustice and the imputation of the justice of Christ, to be preserved through pious works, which, as it is uniquely received and obtained through faith, is thus also uniquely preserved through faith, Rom. V. 1. seqq. cap. X. 20. 2. Cor. I. 24. Joh. XV. 1. 1. Petr. I. 5. 9. Meanwhile, the benevolence of God and the benefit of justification are preserved and increased through pious deeds objectively, and by the occasion of wishing well to those who do well, just as the misery of the sufferer provokes and increases the compassion of the one who pities, Ezech. XVI. 5. 6. Luc. X. 33. as also impetratory (in distinction to that impetration which is called meritorious) for this reason, because God promised that He would give greater grace to one who has and works well, and that He would preserve one who works well in a state of grace, Matt. XIII. 11. John XV. 2. we do not deny. For just as God degrees of grace to them.

But that pious deeds contribute anything to the grace of justification, whether to be obtained with faith in eternal life proposed for obedience, or to be preserved, that ALL Christians, Greeks, Latins, Africans, are asserted to have believed, taught, and demonstrated that they so believe by UNANIMOUS and MANIFEST and PERPETUAL CONSENT, both by the individual deeds of each and by the rules established in common concerning baptism and penance, that is indeed a most bold and most mendacious statement, altogether unworthy of so great a man and polymath. To prove which he brought forward a too weak and trivial argument, the single opinion of Justin concerning the Eucharist, that it is not lawful for anyone to become a participant of it, unless he has believed that those things which are taught among us are true, and has been washed with the washing which was instituted for the remission of sins and for regeneration, and so lives as Christ commanded to live. For Justin did not testify as a Doctor of the universal Greek, Latin, and African Church, nor concerning the faith and rites of all Churches, but of his own nation and diocese: Nor did he include in that testimony anything concerning those controversial points, namely, that the benefit of justification and salvation is obtained through assent held to divine oracles concerning eternal life, insofar as or because that assent has the purpose of obeying the decalogue or divine laws: Likewise: that the benefit of justification and salvation is preserved through pious deeds; much less that all and individual Christians demonstrated that they so believe, both with individual deeds and with common statutes. And how could the universal Church believe so, without the whole Church having erred in the truly fundamental article of justification, since those opinions are diametrically contrary to the doctrine of Paul, who even opposed the works of Abraham, long since reborn and justified, to the faith of the same, and taught that he obtained justification and the continuation of that grace through it alone. Rom. IV. 2. seqq. And he likewise opposes the works of all the reborn, or whatever works there are, to faith regarding the act and office of justifying. And to him who does not work, but believes, faith is imputed for righteousness. Blessedness is of the man to whom faith is imputed without works, etc. But concerning these things, which pertain to the discussion of the present Grotian commentary, as far as the argument of the epistle to the Romans is concerned, we have already spoken in the Prolegomena to the same epistle.

Ἀνενέγκας Ἰσαὰκ τὸν ὑἱὸν ἁυτῦ ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιασήριον) He placed his only son by Sarah, bound, as is the custom for victims, upon the altar, prepared even to slaughter him, if God had persisted in the command. Concerning this matter, see what we have said on Heb. XI. 17.

Concerning which the former commentary has this: Ἀνενέγκας Ἰσαὰκ τὸν ὑἱὸν ἁυτῦ ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιασήριον) Offering Isaac his son upon the altar. Many works of Abraham could be brought forward after the faith held in the words of God: But none more exalted than that he prepared his only son, born to him in the old age of both by his most beloved wife, as a victim for God, so that it did not stand by him that he did not also give him to death. This preparation, in which nothing was lacking except the lethal blow, causes him to have obtained from God the praise of the deed as if it were accomplished, Gen. XXII. 12. and in this sense Abraham is said here, and Heb. XI. 17, to have offered his son. Salvianus says it best: As far as the purpose of the heart pertains, he sacrificed. However, it is not credible that a father loving his son would have done that, if he had thought that he could retain the benevolence of God toward him without works of obedience. But he significantly adds, ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιασήριον upon the altar, from Gen. XXII. 9. as if he were saying to a certain death, as he himself judges, which was accustomed to follow victims thus placed upon the altar and bound for it. That custom of binding victims also appears in Virgil, where Sinon, destined for the altar, says: I broke the bonds. And in Ovid, Book III of the Pontic Elegies, Elegy II, where there is talk of Pylades and Orestes in Tauris: Straightway they are led to the cruel altar of Trivia, their hands bound behind their backs.

We acknowledge that this preparation caused Abraham to obtain from God the praise of the deed as if it were accomplished, Gen. XXII. 12.; but we deny that through the same Abraham was justified before the tribunal of God, because he was justified long before, namely 30 years, concerning which Moses Gen. XV. and from him Paul Rom. IV. and that through faith χωρὶς ἔργων without works. That it is also not credible that a father loving his son would have done those things, if he had thought that he could retain the benevolence of God toward him without works of obedience, is stated ambiguously, either that it could have been retained even if that obedience had not been added, but the Patriarch had been disobedient to the divine command, which persuasion would have been altogether most false, or that he believed that he could not retain the grace of justification without works of obedience, but that those works were altogether necessary for retaining that grace of justification, which sense Grotius intends, but rashly attributes to the Patriarch, as one to whom, not working but believing, and without works, Paul clearly testified that God imputed righteousness.

But what of James? Was not Abraham our father justified by works? Piscator here wishes the word 'works' to be taken metonymically: Ἐξ ἔργων, that is, by such faith as was joined with good works, namely by bringing them forth from itself as native fruits. A metonymy of the effect, since the procreating cause is signified by the effect: so that the sense may be: Abraham was justified by faith, which brought forth good works from itself. Indeed, this explanation of Piscator was so pleasing to Pareus that, in a commentary on this epistle dedicated to him, he testified that he had been not slightly helped by his analysis and observations, especially in the discussion of chapter II concerning justifying faith. He called it alternatively a synecdoche or a metonymy of the effect, warning that James, although in verses 20, 24, and 25 he seems to attribute justification to works, in reality does not attribute it, since there (just as before in verse 18) he calls by WORKS, synecdochically or by metonymy of the effect, faith itself made conspicuous by works, and understands Abraham and Rahab to have been justified by such faith. Jacobus Laurentius also explained it thus in his commentary on this passage. To which explanation, although analogous to the faith, we judge that one should not add one's vote for these reasons: 1. Because one should not depart to a trope where the matter can be resolved without a trope. 2. Because that trope, by which works signify faith pregnant with works, is unusual and unaccustomed in Scripture. 3. Because faith and works are here opposed to each other, and therefore works cannot be taken for faith. 4. Because works are always taken properly in the preceding parts of this whole discussion: verse 14, 17, 18, three times in verse 19. and in the following parts themselves, verse 22 twice, as also verse 26 once; and thus they undoubtedly obtain their proper sense nine times, and are distinguished from faith. Why, therefore, would the Apostle, in a similar thread of discourse and in the same argument of treatment, leave the proper signification and betake himself to a tropical one twice? Could it not be believed that he had thus studiously involved the matter? Far be it from us to presume that. 5. Because that opposition of faith and works is also found in that place where Piscator and Pareus understand 'active faith' by 'works' synecdochically or metonymically, namely in verse 24. 6. What James understands by works, he declares by adding an example, and in verse 21: 'Abraham our father, was he not justified by works, offering Isaac his son upon the altar?' For that offering was not active faith, but a work proceeding from faith. And verse 26. Similarly, was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, receiving the messengers? Although this work also may have arisen from the faith of Rahab, Hebrews XI, yet not as an example of faith producing works from itself is brought forward here, but as an example of the good work by which Rahab was acknowledged and declared righteous. 7. The scope of the Apostle is not to treat of justification before God, insofar as it is brought about and continued, but insofar as it is shown. 8. Because those Reformed, by a facility of interpretation, understand 'faith working' by metonymy or synecdoche through works, the Papists will say with the same facility that in Rom. III and IV, works themselves together with faith, or flowing from faith, can be understood by faith synecdochically. Add that 9. Piscator himself, at v. 23, explains these words, 'and the Scripture was fulfilled,' in such a way that it was then known in the Church that Abraham was endowed with true faith, and therefore justified by faith, just as Moses had testified in that statement in Gen. XV even before the narration of that offering. And in the Scholia: Καὶ ἐπληρώθη ἡ γραφὴ, that is, it was thus made manifest that Abraham was endowed with true faith, and therefore justified by God, as the Scripture testifies in Gen. XV. Whence the blessed Menzer, in disp. XI, Tom. V, Giessen, p. 225, argues thus: If Abraham was justified before God by true faith in the promised Messiah, that is, thirty years, to be sure, before Isaac was offered: it cannot be said that Abraham was justified (in one and the same signification of the word) before God by the offering of Isaac. The former Moses affirms, and Paul and all the pious confess. Wherefore the latter must be denied. And consequently, the word 'to justify' is taken in one way in the Pauline disputation, and in another way in James. Pareus, at v. 22, says that it seems to be said according to the mind of James, that faith cooperated with his works or work in justification. How? Because Abraham was justified by faith conspicuous in this work, or because faith, declaring itself not idle but working through that tremendous work, wrought justification, and therefore considers justification against its own intention, not as it is before God, but as it is acknowledged by men to have been done before God. John Camero, however, acknowledges in Myroth. p. 340 that this metonymy of Piscator might seem harsh and little used in Scripture. The blessed Hopfner argued against that explanation and the reasons of Pareus proposed for it in disp. XII, de justif. p. 1115, seqq.

Wherefore it is altogether better to say that justification is not taken in these examples in the present for absolution from sins, or the justification which takes place in judgment and before the tribunal of God, but for the declaration or acknowledgment of a just person, by which someone is held to be just before the world: Whether the word δικαιοῦσθαι is believed to be taken in that sense, which is acknowledged by Grotius as not infrequent in the Scriptures, when someone is praised, as Matt. XI. 10, Luke VII. 29, ch. X. 29, ch. XVI. 15, 1 Tim. III. 16. Eccles. I. 24, ch. XXXI. 5, or by a most well-known Hebraism, by which a thing is said to be done when it is manifested or acknowledged as justified by works, that is, praised or justified, acknowledged and manifested by works, especially those which shone forth openly when he offered his son Isaac upon the altar, or was doing everything, as far as it lay with him, to execute the divine command and offer his son, intending to offer him entirely, had he not been restrained by God. For this was an illustrious and public specimen of justifying faith and Abrahamic justification: Which sense is demanded by the antecedents, the consequents, and the scope of the whole treatment: The antecedents, because the Apostle had treated in v. 18 of faith being demonstrated by works, and that which is not demonstrated by them, or is not demonstrable, is vain, but true and saving faith is such that it exerts and demonstrates itself through works. and according to the immediately preceding verse, he institutes more fully and clearly to convince the empty man, both because of his vain persuasion and because of his emptiness of good works, that faith which is without works is dead, that is, is not acknowledged as living, but is understood as dead, so that it can be known and acknowledged that it is altogether dead. For it is to be noted that the same so-called Hebraism obtains here: and faith is said to be dead which is acknowledged and manifested to be dead. For the absence of works declares it to be dead, not living, and therefore not justifying: just as by the illustrious example of the Father of believers, faith is shown on the contrary not to be dead, but living and justifying, through those signal works, most known to the whole world, that he was willing to offer his son upon the altar. 'But do you want to know, O empty man, that faith without works is dead,' that is, is acknowledged to be so, so far is it from being able to justify or save faith that has no works. Was not Abraham our father justified by works, that is, was it not acknowledged and manifested that he was truly justified and just, and therefore endowed with true justifying faith, without which he could by no means have performed those works.

The consequents are 1. The Apostolic inference: 'You see that faith cooperated with his works' in that offering of his son, because although they proceeded from the zeal of obeying God, yet without faith neither that zeal had a place, nor the works that followed from it: Faith therefore cooperated, by strengthening Abraham in the zeal of obedience, which operation of faith can be seen and acknowledged from those illustrious works, just as the zeal of most holy and truly admirable obedience shone forth from it: just as in Heb. XI that offering is said to have been made from faith. 'You see that faith was acknowledged to cooperate' with Abrahamic obedience in executing those works which looked toward the rendering of obedience. For faith no less than obedience and reverence, although both lay hidden intrinsically in the heart, openly betrayed and manifested itself in these works, namely that huge confidence which the Patriarch had in God, that He would entirely fulfill His promise concerning the blessed seed, which was to be fulfilled only in the seed about to come from Isaac by the power of the divine oracle, even if, obeying the divine command, he were to slaughter Isaac, for he believed that the same son in number could be restored and resurrected from the ashes alive in turn.

2. A further conclusion, which is this: and by works faith was perfected. How perfected by works? Is it by reason of itself and its essential perfection? That cannot be said. For since Abraham was already justified by faith 30 years before, it was necessary that his faith was not imperfect, but perfect, as regards essential perfection. For how would the Patriarch have been justified by an imperfect faith? But if not by reason of itself, then by what other reason was it perfected, if not by reason of others, and insofar as it was manifested to others, and acknowledged by others?

3. The fulfillment of Scripture v. 23. And the Scripture was fulfilled, saying: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness. How then was the Scripture finally fulfilled, unless this is understood likewise by reason of becoming known, that it was openly declared by that illustrious deed that Abraham had been truly justified by faith in Christ? For such works are the fruits of justification, and they testify no less to justification than to justifying faith, since good works do not precede the one to be justified, but follow the one who has been justified. For a Scripture, or some prophecy, or any divine oracle whatsoever, is said to be fulfilled most of all when its completion becomes openly known or can become known through some remarkable effect. Namely, that it is most true, which was handed down by that oracle of Scripture.

4. The appellation Friend of God. He was already a friend of God for many good years. He was therefore called a friend of God then, not because he first obtained the grace of God, and was admitted to friendship with God, but because from this so remarkable and public specimen he was acknowledged and openly manifested as a friend of God. Indeed, to be called To be called a friend of God indeed presupposes the truth of an intervening friendship between God and Abraham, and it also adds a notoriety among men. See Wis. 3:13, 15; Gen. 41:1; Prov. 21:24, ch. 24:8; Isa. 1:27; Job 15:15. The Mosaic history is added in Gen. 22:13, 17, 18, and in that place the manifestation and recognition of both true faith and the friendship of God regarding Abraham shines forth: the former from the words of the Lord: 'Now I know that you truly fear God, because you did not spare your only son for my sake,' where from the evidence of Abraham's external obedience shown in the offering of his son, God, in an anthropopathic manner, testifies that He has known the truth and sincerity of the internal affection, which indeed could not exist without faith in him. If one explains it effectively regarding the knowledge made known to men, as Ambrose does in 'On Faith' ch. 8, 9; Augustine in book 4 of 'On Genesis to the Letter'; Hilary in book 9 of 'On the Trinity'; Gregory the Great in book 28, of 'Morals' ch. 7, it is likewise a manifestation and making known that is inferred: just as the Gloss, Lyra, Abulensis, Sa, Estius, and other Papist interpreters acknowledge. Thus, therefore, God Himself used this mode of inferring, so that He might show the truth of the Abrahamic faith to men through the offering of Isaac. Was not the friendship of God toward Abraham also most clearly declared when God confirmed with an oath the blessing of his family and the promise concerning the Messiah, which confirmation indeed testified no less to the faith of Abraham in God and the divine promises, from which the offering was made (Heb. 11:17), than to his justification and the love of God toward him? For this is to be observed, that in the words of God, Gen. 22:15, 16, 'because you have done this thing, and have not spared your only son, in blessing I will bless you, because you have obeyed my voice,' the obedience of Abraham is brought forward, not as the cause of the blessing or justification, but as a testimony and sign of the same, by which he is made more certain of the blessed seed to be born from his loins, and of the spiritual blessing obtained through it, as well as of the outcome of the remaining divinely promised blessings, which is still to come. Wherefore the particle כי, 'because,' signifies not the cause of the blessing itself, but only the cause of knowing the blessing and its continuation, and consequently it hints that the discourse there is about blessing or justification, not insofar as it is before God, because it is described as such when considered through the imputation of faith unto righteousness, but insofar as it is notified to men that it has been done before God, and insofar as faith through this work, as its secondary exercise, is effective and industrious, and is made more certain, just as it is said in Heb. 11:17: 'By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested, and he was offering his only begotten, in whom he had received the promise,' as the blessed Hopfner has it in his 12th disputation on justification, page 1079.

Finally, the scope of James's treatment of justification by works, and not by faith only, is this: to show that the mere profession of faith without works, by which it is demonstrated, is nothing but a vain and empty boast of true faith, for which he used the example of Abraham: whose faith is entirely different from such a naked profession, as one whose faith and justification through faith and the fruits of grace through works were openly made known, and were recognized and manifested primarily by that notable deed of the offering of Isaac. This sense even the Papists themselves cannot deny, even if they willingly insert here their own fabrication about Abraham being rendered more just through works. Thus the Ordinary Gloss on this passage: 'Here it is a matter of works which follow faith, on account of which he (Abraham) is further justified, when he was already just through faith.' Whence Paul: 'By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested.' This offering is a work and testimony of faith and justice. Thomas in ch. 3 of Galatians and in ch. 2 of James explains this also regarding the showing and manifestation of justice: and

in the former place indeed it is thus: 'And in this way a man is justified, that is, is shown to be just from works performed.' Lyranus on this passage: 'And similarly the greatness of Abraham's faith appeared from his obedience in offering his son, for which it was said to him by the Lord: "Now I know that you fear the Lord," that is, I have made others know.' Folengius explains the word 'justification' in James 2: 'Shown to be just, and, such as he already was in heaven, declared.' Guil. Estius on this passage: 'James,' he says, 'deals with works that follow faith, and sprout from faith, and are directed by faith; without which faith is vain, sterile, and unfruitful, and consequently useless. From works of this kind, therefore, a man is justified, because through them, as through an actual justice, he is and is declared truly just, and on that account is pleasing to God.' Grotius himself will profess that he performed works to prove the benevolence of God: which He promised only to the just.

Latin:

Vers. 21. ᾽Αβραὰμ ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν] Etiam secundum carnem. Nam Ebræis scribit.

Οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη] δικαιοῦσθαι modo significat ju- stum reddi, modo ut justum amari atque tractari. Ha- bent enim pleræque voces Ebraicæ ejus formæ significa- tum duplicem. Quanquam verò certum est, hominem justum fieri per fidem, deinde etiam justiorem per opera continua, tamen totus hujus sermonis contextus, & ma- ximè ea, quæ jam sequentur, exigunt, ut δικαιοῦσθαι hic sumamus in sensu posteriore, & quidem ita, ut intelli- gantur tum Abraham tum Rahab à Deo tractati, ita ut ii, qui justi sunt, tractari solent, non tantum respiciente ipso- rum fidem, sed & ex fide profecta opera. Quod si A- brahami fides illa adeò prædicata, Gen. XV. 6. profuit quidem, sed non sola, quid est cur alii de sua fide non o- perante plus promittere sibi debeant? Abraham si fidem ad favorem Dei conciliandum ac retinendum sibi credidisset suf- ficere, abstinuisset opere tam luctuoso, de quo jam loque- tur hic Scriptor.

Multò prolixior est Grotii in peculiari sæpius dicto tractatu super hoc comma nõ tam interpre- tatio, quam dissertatio, ad pervertendam Apostoli sententiam composita, quam integram hic addu- cimus.

'Aβραὰμ ὁ Πατὴρ ἡμῶν ἐκ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη] A- braham Pater noster nonne ex operibus justificatus est? Quod veterum multi, atque inter eos Augusti- nus libro de fide & operibus censent, & hanc epi- stolam & Johannis primam, & Judæ, & eam, quæ Petri secunda dicitur, scriptas adversus eos, qui Pau- linas epistolas prave interpretantes fidem dicebant sine bonis moribus ad salutem sufficere, probabile sit, tum ex ultimis epistolæ illius, quæPetro adscribitur, verbis, tum quod hic Jacobus ejusdem Abrahami exemplo uti- tur, ut probet opera ad salutem requiri eo quem supra explicavimus sensu, ex cujus exemplo intu- lerat Paulus justificari homines per fidem sine operibus, Rom. III. 27. & IV. toto. Cæterum ipsum Paulum mi- nimè pugnare cum his Apostolis, clarissime docet Au- gustinus Pauli ejusdem dicto ad Gal. V. 6. in Christo ne- que circumcisionem valere quicquam, neque præputi- um, sed eam fidem, quæ per charitatem operatur, cui & alterum locum adjecit Augustinus ex 1. Cor. XIII. 2. ubi is qui fidem habeat, charitatem non habeat, nihil esse dicitur. Ubi autem, subjicit idem Augustinus, hæc si fidelis charitas operatur, sine dubio bene vivitur. I- dem Augustinus de libero Arb. cap. VII. Homines au- tem non intelligentes, quod ait ipse Apostolus, arbi- trantur justificari hominem per fidem sine operibus legis putaverunt eum dicere, sufficere homini fidem, etiamsi male vivat, & bona opera non habeat. Quod absit, ut sentiret vas electionis, qui cum dixisset quodam in lo- co : In Christo Jesu enim neque circumcisio quic- quam valet, neque præputium, mox addidit : Sed fi- des, quæ per dilectionem operatur. Ista est fides, quæ fideles Dei separat ab immundis Dæmonibus. Nam & ipsi, sicut dicit Apostolus Jacobus, credunt & con- tremiscunt, sed non bene operantur. Utrumque con- cilians idem Augustinus Tomo IV. libr. LXXXIII. Qq. quæstione LXXVI. sic loquitur : Quapropter non sunt sibi contrariæ duorum Apostolorum sen- tentiæ, Pauli & Jacobi, cum dicit unus, justificari hominem per fidem sine operibus, quia ille dicit de ope- ribus, quæ fidem præcedunt, iste de iis, quæ fidem se- quuntur, sicut etiam ipse Paulus multis locis often- dit : Optimè. Opponit enim Paulus fidei non opera, quæ ex fide procedunt, ac sæpe etiam sub ipso fidei no- mine sensu quodam extensiore comprehenduntur, ut apparet ex citatis ad initium hujus tractationis Pauli locis, Rom. X. 10. Tit. I. 1. Sed ea quæ sine fide, sive ex nativis hominum viribus, & humana tantum insti- tutione præstari possunt, qualia sunt ritualia omnia, de- inde etiam malarum actionum abstinentia pœnæ vi- tandæ causa, præterea alia quædam, quæ commodi honorisve studio fieri solent. Judæi plurimum tribue- bant ritibus : Præceptorum vetantium ea sola urge- bant quibus apposita est pœna cogitationem quam- vis deliberatam negabant pœna etiam apud Deum esse obnoxiam : omissionem vero præceptorum ju- bentium facilè dicebant expiari. Hæc erat pietas Ju- daica, qua inflati contemnebant alienigenas, quan- tumvis à Diis falsis ad verum Deum, à flagitiosa vi- ta ad sanctam conversos. Adversus hos disputans Pau- lus, ostendit neque Deo placere ad dandam salutem ulla opera, quæ non ex animo per fidem vitæ æternæ pur- gato, & supra rerum temporalium curam ad mortem Dei proximique accenso eduntur, & contra nihil im- pedire salutem mala opera in iis, qui se per talem fi- dem ab iis averterint, Deoque se & sanctæ vitæ dica- verint. Augustinus dicto quæstionum libro quæst. LXXVI. Locus iste hujus epistolæ ( nempe Jacobi ) eundem sensum Pauli Apostoli quomodo sit intelli- gendus exponit, ideoque magis Abrahæ utitur exem- plo, vacuam esse fidem, si non bene operetur, quo- niam Abrahæ exemplo etiam Paulus Apostolus usus est, ut probaret, justificari hominem per fidem sine operi- bus legis. Cum enim bona opera commemorat Abrahæ, quæ ejus fidem comitata sunt, satis ostendit Paulum Apostolum non ita per Abrahamum docere, justifi- cari hominem per fidem sine operibus, ut, si quis cre- diderit, non ad eum pertineat bene operari, sed ad hoc potius, ut nemo meritis priorum bonorum operum arbitretur, se pervenisse ad donum justificationis, quæ est in fide. Ibidem adductis locis Pauli Gal. V. & 1. Cor. VI. quibus sententiis, ait, manifestissime do- cet, non eos præterito bono opere ad fidei justificatio- nem pervenisse, nec meritis eorum istam gratiam datam, quando dicit : Et hæc quidem fuistis : Sed cum dicit, qui talia agunt, regnum Dei non possidebunt, satis ostendit, jam ex quo crediderunt, bene operari debere:

quod & Jacobus dicit, & multis omnino locis idem Apostolus Paulus satis aperteque prædicat, recte vi- vendum omnibus, qui in Christo crediderunt, ne ad pœnas perveniant. Vox Græca δικαιοῦν justificare respondet Ebræo הצדיק, ut & vox novi fœderis scriptoribus, & ex veteris Interpretibus apparet. E- jus autem formæ, quæ Hiphil Ebræis dicitur, voces modo actum duplicem, id est, facientis, ut alter fa- ciat, significant, modo aliquid simileputa declarare, quomodo & vox הצדיק, & ei opposita הרשיע, injustificare, illud in absolvendi, hoc in condemnan- di sensu sumuntur tum alibi, tum Deut. XXV. 2. & Prov. XVII. 15. item tractare tanquam talem: puta laudare, quomodo vox ea ponitur Matth. XI. 19. Luc. VII. 29. X. 29. XVI. 15. 1. Tim. III. 16. & Ecclesi- astici I. 28. XXXI. 5. item alicui benefacere, ut 1. Reg. VIII. 32. quomodo & סכך, quod est innocentifica- re, Chaldæus Exod. XXXIV. vertit parcere, ita qui tan- quam planè infons à Deo amatur, Spiritu Dei donatur, certus fit in eo statu æternæ salutis, interdum dicitur δι- καιῶσθαι, cum alioqui vox ipsa alibi in significatu illo primitivo & magis proprio reperiatur Dan. XII. 3. Ap. XXXII. 11. Ut quis eo modo Deo placeat, obtineri non per nativa hominum opera, sed per fidem. Divi- nis oraculis habitam, ubi ea ad propositum obediendi pervenerit, conservari verò per pia facta, omnes Chri- stiani Græci, Latini, Africi unanimi ea manifesto per- petuoque consensu crediderunt, docuerunt, & ita se credere tum singularibus quisque factis, tum constitu- tis in commune circa baptismum & pœnitentiam regulis universi demonstrarunt. De Eucharistia sic ait Justi- nus: Ἧς οὐδενὶ ἄλλῳ μετασχεῖν ἐξόν ἐστιν, ἢ τῷ πιστεύ- οντι ἀληθῆ εἶναι τὰ διδασκόμενα ὑφ' ἡμῶν, καὶ λουσαμέ- νῳ τὸ ὑπὲρ ἀφέσεως ἁμαρτιῶν, καὶ εἰς ἀγένεσιν λο- τρὸν, καὶ οὕτω βιοῦντι, ὡς ὁ Χριστὸς παρέδωκε, cujus neminem fas est participem fieri, nisi qui crediderit, quæ apud nos docentur, & ablutus sit lavacro, quod insti- tutum est pro remissione peccatorum & ad regeneratio- nem, & sic vivat, quomodo Christus vivi jussit. Mul- tis autem modis Pharisæicas sententias oppugnatPaulus, ostendit enim ritualia partim à Deo tolerata, partim & pro temporum ingeniorumque ratione ad vitandos cultus idololatricos, instituta, non autem per se in pre- cio habita, tum verò a facinoribus, quæ & humanæ leges cum Mosis lege hac in parte congruentes, gravi- bus suppliciis coërcent abstinere, nihil in se habere lau- de, nedum præmio divino dignum: aut tale, in quo jactare se quisquam debeat; ubi obiter & hoc aspergit, multos, qui se de lege jactabant, ne istam quidem præ- stitisse innocentiam, postquam scilicet judicia capita- lia, quorum metu coërcebantur, apud ipsos cessave- rant & Romanæ leges aut præsides ad multa facinora connivebant. At verò eam rationem homines ad salu- tem ducendi, quam Deus in Abrahamo, ejusque po- sterorum rebus ruditer delinea verit, plenissime autē con- summatam in Evangelio ostenderit, Deo esse dignissi- mam, hominibus verò utilissimam.
