Nam modestiam ac submissionem animi, ubi cum Deo agendum est, co nobis maximè imprimi, quod sciamus, non ἐκ συναλλάγ- ματος, sive æquo fœdere, sed per Dei misericordiam, & peccatorum etiam gravium condonationem nos ad spem vitæ æternæ perduci, cum lex Mosis esset (ut Livii de lege humana loquentis utar verbis) res surda & inexo- rabilis circa talia: 'Αδυνάτῳ ἡ τῆς κολάσεως παραί- τησις νόμου παραβαίνοις, nullia patebat pœnæ depre- catio ei, qui in legem peccasset, ait contra Appionem Josephus, quod ejus ipsius vitæ cognitionem, fir- mam dico, & cujus causa quævis in commoda ac peri- cula despectentur, non nostrapter ratiocinatione, aut ullius humanæ sapientiæ autoritate, sed Dei bonitate sua consilia nobis patefacere, eandemque per Spiritum sanctum in cordibus obsignare dignati, apiscamur: quod eam jam viam insistentes non summo jure sed paterna clementia Deus judicet. Ex his autem nascens animi submissio & ad preces nos adigit, & agnoscenda ingen- tia Dei beneficia: demit autem superbiam aliorum- que contemptum. Firma autem illa de vita æterna persuasio efficit, ut præ Dei tam benefici amore & commendati nobis ab ipso, & ipsius vice proximi sa- lute nihil magni ducamus: præsertim cum ipse Chri- stus salutis nostræ autor eam viam non docuerit tan- tum, sed & exemplo monstravit. Ad hæc autem com- paratæ cæremoniæ Judaicæ, & tenuis illa ad præscriptum legis, sive humanæ sive divinæ, quatenus ea ad humanæ modum intelligitur innocentia & μέχρι τῶν πράξεων ἐγκράτεια intra facta stans continentia, ut Chrysosto- mus loquitur in Rom. VIII. merito sordent : Imò & illa de facili culparum, quæ in omittendo consistunt, expiatione opinio magnum profectui impedimen- tum objicit : cuncta autem ista talia sunt, ut non modo animum non purgent, sed nisi alia divinitus accedant, animum magis à sensu morborum suo- rum avertant. Cum autem ista ratio divinæ ὀἰκονο- μίας sapientissima, Ebræis, qui & avitarum virtutum, & legis sibi solis datæ titulo semet efferebant, alie- nigenis autem non circumcisis invidebant salutem, difficulter persuaderetur, etiamsi maxima apud ho- mines non planè contumaces habebat testimonia, Christi præcepta supra legem, ejus mortem & redi- tum in vitam, alienigenarum ad Christum converso- rum vitam Judaica multo sanctiorem, fortiorem- que multo in rebus adversis patientiam, Spiritus præterea sancti dona conspicua à synagoga sublata, translata ad Ecclesiam, ut eam ferociam contunde- ret Paulus, negat Deum consilii sui debere cuiquam rationem cum & opifex herile jus in nos habeat, & vita æterna cœlestisque felicitas homini ex suapte natura non debeatur. Attamen fine harum præ- scriptionum fraude liberaliter ostendit, neque Deo gloriosam magis, neque utiliorem hominibus ratio- nem iniri potuisse. Et hoc quidem est Paulinæ ad Romanos epistolæ præcipuum propositum, à vete- ribus cunctis piè observatum, cum tamen membra singula & voces non eundem in modum omnes in- terpretentur, quod minime mirum videbitur ei, qui cum Irenæo, Origene, Hieronymo multa lectione, & inter legendum animi intentione didicerit, mul- tas esse in eo Scriptore ὑπερβολάς, παρενθέσεις, συγχύσεις, ὑπέρβατα ἀνακόλουθα, superjectiones, in- terpositiones, confusiones, transilitiones, compa- rationes inconsummatas & concise alia, alia ex abru- pto dicta. Sed hæc salutiferis dogmatibus & ab eo- dem Apostolo, & ab aliis sanctis Scriptoribus & sæ- pe & aperte propositis nubem objicere non debent. Cavendum ne incidamus in illud, quod dicit Ter- tullianus adversus Marcionem IV. Semper hæretici aut nudas aut simplices voces conjecturis, quo vo- lunt, rapiunt, aut rursus conditionales & rationales simplicitatis conditione dissolvunt : Quod Aristote- les diceret : Τὸ ἁπλῶς λεγόμενον ὡς κατά τι λαμβά- νεσι, τὸ δὲ κατά τι, ὡς ἁπλῶς : Simpliciter dictum accipiunt secundum quid, contra quod secundum quid dicitur, simpliciter. Et adversus Praxeam : Pro- prium hoc est omnium hæreticorum : Nam quia pauca sunt, quæ in sylva inveniri possunt, pauca adversus plura defendunt. Sic & libro de pudicitia : Solenne esse, ait, hæreticis, alicujus capituli ancipitis occasione adver- sus exercitum sententiarum totius instrumenti armari. Et de resurrectione : Utique æquum est, incerta de cer- tis, & obscura de manifestis præjudicari, ut ne in- ter discordiam certorum & incertorum, manifesto- rum & obscurorum fides dissipetur, veritas pericli- tetur, ipsa Divinitas ut inconstans denotetur. Qui cum bene conveniunt illa Origenis VI. adversus Cel- sum : Εὖ οἶδα, ὅτι ἱπτάτινα παραλήψονται τῆς γραφῆς· Οἳ κὰι ταῦτα (nempe τὰ κακὰ) βυλόμενοι τολμᾶν φάσ- κειν ἀπὸ Θεοῦ γεγονέναι, μὴ δυνάμενοι ἐν ὕψει ἀποδεί- ξαι τῆς γραφῆς, αἰτιωμένης μὲν τὰς ἁμαρτάνοντας, ἀπο- δεχομένης δὲ τὰς εὖ πράττοντας, κὰι οὐδὲν ἧττον κάκοια λεγόσης ἅτινα περισπᾷν δοκεῖ ὀλίγα ὄντα τὰς ἀμαθῶς τὰ θεῖα γράμματα ἀναγινώσκοντας. Scio aliqua scriptu- ræ dicta arrepturos, qui & ista dicunt à Deo esse, cum non possint afferre pro se tenorem scripturæ perpe- tuum, quæ ubique accusat malè agentes bene agentes ap- probat, & tamen illa dicit, quæ pauca, detinere videntur eos, qui scripturas imperitè legunt. Unde non abit prudens Clementis Alex. dictum Strom. VI. Ἄπαντα ὀρθὰ ἐνώπιον τῶν συνιέντων, φησὶν ἡ γραφὴ, τῆτ’ ἔστι, τῶν ὅσοι ὑπ’ αὐτῶ σαφηνισθεῖσαν τῶν γραφῶν ἐξήγησιν κατὰ τὸν Ἐκκλησιαστικὸν κανόνα ἐκδεχόμενοι διασώζουσι· Κανὼν δὲ Ἐκκλησιαστικός ἡ συνῳδία κὰι συμφωνία νόμου τε κὰι προφητῶν, τῇ τὴν παρουσίαν Κυρίου παραδιδομέ- νῃ διαθήκῃ. Omnia recta intelligentibus, ait scriptura, id est, iis qui ab ipso patefactum scripturæ sensum se- cundum Ecclesiasticum canonem accipiunt & servant Canon autem Ecclesiasticus est convenientia & consen- sus legis & Prophetarum, cum eo fœdere, quod per Do- mini adventum datum est. Nec minus utile illud Vincentii : Tunc operam dabit, ut collatas inter se majorum consulat interogetque sententias, eorum duntaxat, qui diversis licet temporibus & locis, in unius tamen Ecclesiæ Catholicæ communione & fi- de permanentes magistri probabiles extiterunt. Et quicquid non unus aut duo tantum, sed omnes pari- ter uno eodemque consensu apertè, frequenter, per- severanter tenuisse, scripsisse, docuisse cognoverit, id sibi quoque intelligat absque ulla dubitatione cre- dendum: Quod breviter idem scriptor sic exprimit: Ut Propheticæ & Apostolicæ interpretationis linea se- cundum Ecclesiastici & catholici sensus normam di- rigatur. Et rursum: Hoc ita demum fit, si sequa- mur universitatem, antiquitatem, consensionem. His præmunitus lector facile intelliget, quod sibi Jaco- bus velit, nimirum ipsum Abrahamum, qui cre- dentium Pater dicebatur, in id omni modo laboras- se, ut favorem Dei per fidem adeptus eum bonis o- peribus conservaret, eo modo βεβαίαν τὴν ἀυτῶ κλῆ- σιν καὶ ἐκλογὴν ποιήμενος certam faciens suam vocati- onem & electionem, ut Petrus de Christianis loquitur II. epist 1. 10. Sicut vitam hanc parentum facto adipi- scimur, per alimenta autem conservamus. Sic status ille, in quo Deus nos tanquam innocentes acceptat, fi- de quæritur, conservatur autem bonis operibus. Na- tivitas autem salutaris non accepta, sed custodita vivifi- cat, ut ait Cyprianus epist. VII.

Tres adfert Grotius interpretationes ceu fidei analogas: Prior est Pontificiorum, hominem justum fieri per fidem, justiorem per opera continua, qui primam illud justificationem, hoc secundam di- cunt, eamque hic à Jacobo designari volunt. Quo de Bellarminus libr. I. de justif. cap. I. quemadmo- dum usitate dicitur calefieri non solum, qui fit cali- dus ex frigido, sed etiam ex alido qui fit calidior: Sic etiam justificari dicitur non solum is, qui ex impio fit justus, sed ille quoque, qui ex justo fit justi- or, ubi adfert illud Jacobi cap. II. Videtis quod ex operibus justificetur homo, & non ex fide tantum. Sed ea distinctio justificationis in primam & secun- dam neque in scriptura uspiam invenitur, neque scripturæ vel huic loco Apostolico congruit, nec veteribus Pontificiis sese probare potuit. Primò enim justificatio hominis peccatoris coram Deo non nisi unica est, & sola fit fide, sine operibus, Rom. III. 28. Deinde Paulus exemplum Abrahami adduxit, Rom. IV. 3. non sub initium conversionis, sed quan- do jam per aliquot annos conversus Deo obedie- rat, quem tamen non operibus, sed fide solum ju- stificatum esse è Gen. XV. confirmat, Tertio non so- lum justificationem, sed etiam beatitudinem æternam per fidem cõtingere testimonio Davidis compro- bat, Rom. IV. 6. Quarto disertè & principium fidei describit Apostolus, & medium & finem, Rom. V. 1. seq. Illustris ibi, ut B. Chemnitius observat in Exam. conc. Trid. habetur distributio: Prima de principio: Per Christum habuimus accessum fide in hanc gra- tiam, ut fide justificati habeamus pacem in Deum. Secunda de medio: In illa ipsa gratia fide stamus. Tertium de fine: Illa ipsa gratia fide gloriamur de gloria Dei: hoc est, sicut fide habuimus accessum in gratiam: Ita & speramus, eadem fide & gratia nos perventuros ad glorietionem. Ad hæc quinto Phil. III. Paulus, dicente porrò B. Chemnitio, eodem mo- do per distributionem tradit doctrinam justifica- tionis, quæ fuerit sua justitia coram Deo ad vitam æternam, scilicet primo, cum ex Pharisaismo con- verteretur, secundo tunc cum ad Philippenses scriberet: tertio quando occursurus est in resur- rectionem mortuorum. Non verò dicit aliam fuisse suam justificationem in principio conver- sionis, & aliam postea, cum ex vinculis scriberet, vel quando occursurus est ad resurrectionem. Hoc certè non dicit, sed unam & eandem ju- stitiam, fidei scilicet, in principio, medio & fi- ne describit. Sed adversus hanc Papicolarum com- mentitiam distinctionem alias actum est. Quæ sexto unicè ex falsa hypothesi procedit, quasi justifica- tio sese habeat ceu actus physicus, qualis est calefa- ctio, & infusio habitus justitiæ, cum phrasi, & sensu scripturæ justificatio forensis sit intelligenda, qua homo justꝫ pronunciatur coram tribunali divino, & à peccatis absolvitur. Septimo non cõvenire huic loco illum sensum, quod homo justus justior fieri dicatur per opera: vel inde liquet, quod hic non quæratur, quomodo justitia alatur & augescat, sed docendum sit, fidem mortuã esse, non vivam, ve- ram, & justificam, quæ destituta est operibus bonis. Aliud autem est, justitiam auctiorem fieri per opera, aliud fidem non habere, qui opera non habet. Adde octavò, quod juxta hanc expositionem dicendum, jactatores, cum quibus res est Jacobo, justos quidem fuisse infuso justitiæ habitu, vel quoad justificatio- nem primam, sed reprehendendos, quod non ex- emplo Abrahami justitiam infusam exercitio bono- rum operum augeant. Quis verò admittet, hypocri- tas verè justos fuisse? Aut per fidem Dæmoniacam, ut vocat Augustinus, justificatos? Denique com- mittimus hic Estium cum aliis Papistis: Quod au- tem aliqui pro conciliatione dicunt, Paulum agere de prima justificatione, & Jacobum de secunda, parùm solidè videtur dici. Nam & ad primam justificatio- nem opera fidei requiruntur, de quibus loquitur Ja- cobus: Et ad secundam justificationem inutilia sunt opera legis, de quibus Paulus. Ita ergo conciliat Estius: Negat Apostolus Paulus justificari quen- quam posse ex operibus legis, id est, ex iis operibꝫ, quæ fidem Mediatoris antecedunt, & ex sola legis cognitione proficiscuntur. Jacobus autem de ope- ribus agit fidem consequentibus, & ex fide pullu- lantibus atque à fide directis. Similiter Cornelius à Lapide, ut & Vasquez Tom. II. in I. 1. D. 210. c. 8. utrumque Apostolum de utraque justificatione loqui admittunt. Paulum excludere opera, quæ fiunt solis liberi arbitrii viribꝫ absque fide in Chri- stum. Jacobum verò includere opera facta ex fide, & iisdemque tribuere vim justificandi.

Atque huc abit altera explicatio Grotiana, quam in priori commentatione tradidit. 1. Fidem sine operibus salutem parere dicit: non autem perdu- cere ad salutem diutius viventes: quo pacto Ponti- ficii distinguunt inter justificationem & salutem, quod per fidem solam quidem justificemur, at non salvemur, nisi dato tempore & occasione pia opera sequantur. Bellarminus libr. IV. de justif. cap. VII. Nos contra intelligimus, bona opera esse necessaria hominibus rationis usum habentibus, & qui tamdiu post adeptam remissionis gratiam supervivunt, do- nec occasio implendæ legis occurrat. 2. Cum ait Gro- tius, Paulum fidei, non opera quæ ex fide proce- cunt, sed ea, quæ sine fide sive ex nativis hominum viribus & humana tantum institutione præstari possunt, opponere: id ita explicat, quod sint ritua- lia omnia, deinde etiam malarum actionum absti- nẽtiæ pœnæ vitandæ causa, præterea alia quædam, quæ commodi, honorisve studio fieri solent. Quo redit Dominici à Soto, Toleti, Pererii, Salmeronis, Justiniani, Estii, ut & Cornelii à Lapide in Rom. III. sententia; è quibus Cornelius: Cum Apostolus, ait, sic passim fidem ab operibus separat & distinguit, ope- ra intelligit legis non solum ceremonialia, & judicia- lia, sed etiam moralia sive Decalogi. Cæterum quod ad distinctionẽ illam inter justificationem & salu- tem attinet, ea nec Paulo convenit, nec Jacobo. Paulus enim non tantum justificationem, sed & beatitudinem fidei soli tribuit sine operibus, & eas- dem salutis ac justificationis causas constituit, ut antea dictum. Jacobus etiam non modo fidem, quæ sine operibus est, non servare docet, sed nec justifi- care fidem, quæ non habet pedisequa opera, imò fa fidem talem Demoniacam, mortuam in semetipsa, nullam esse, demonstrat. Quod ad distinctionem in- ter opera ante fidem facta, & ex fide profecta: opera, quum ex solis naturæ viribus & ante fidem fiant, nulla sunt, quia quicquid non est ex fide peccatum est, Rom. XIV. ult. nec opera bona præcedunt justi- ficandum, sed sequuntur justificatũ. Nec per opera legis intelliguntur, quæ ante fidẽ fiunt, sed quæ le- gi conformia sunt, adeoque omnia opera bona à justificatione excluduntur, etiamsi ex fide fluant. Quia opera omnia ad legem ceu normam relatio- nem habent, eique conformia sint, oportet. Porrò quum opera & ex fide proficiscantur, & justifican- dum sequantur, quomodo causa esse possunt justi- ficationis? Causa enim non sequitur effectum, sed prior eodem sit, oportet: Unde hic se expedire ne- queunt Sophistæ, quomodo Jacobus de justificatio- ne loquens, si de ea justificatione sermo est, quæ co- ram tribunali Dei sit, Abrahamum ex fide justifica- tum dicat, siquidem opera non fidem tantum, sed & justificationem consequi certum sit. Id enim per quod Abraham coram Deo justificatus est, tan- quam per causam justificationis ipsius, non potuit non prius esse ipsa justificatione, ordine naturæ.

Quæ fortassis causa fuit, cur Grotius missa illa in- terpretatione prioris suæ commentationis in anno- tatis ad h. l. aliam, quæ tertia est, assumpserit, quod δικαιῶσθαι hic sit non justum reddi, sed ut justum a- mari atque tractari, ut intelligitur tum Abraham, tum Rahab ita à Deo tractati, ut ii, qui justi sunt tra- ctari solent, nõ tantum respiciente ipsorum fidem, sed & opera ex fide profecta. Quæ quanquã ortho- doxia salva admitti possint; nam & fidem & opera Deum respicere, & justificatorum per fidem opera Deo grata esse, ipsosque ceu justos à Deo amari, atque tractari, dubium nullum est. Fovet tamen hac explicatione Grotius ὕπóυλόν τι, quod postea prodit: Abrahami fidem Gen. XV. 6. prædicatam profuisse, sed non solam, scilicet ad justificationem: nam de eo in Genesi agitur: non suffecisse Abraha- mo fidem ad favorem Dei conciliandum & reti- nendum effectum sibi destinatum, ut postea dictu- rus est, (salutem) fidem non consequi non posse a̔́νευ συναιτίων bonorum operum, scilicet, qui merè Papistici sunt errores. Ex adverso soli fidei justifica- tionem vindicat Paulus Rom. IV. ex illo Geneseos loco cap. XV. 6. sola fide gratiam justificationis nos & consequi & retinere docet, quod è cap. IV. & V. ad Rom. & Phil. III. antea docuimus, & è 1. Petr. I. quod per fidem custodiamur ad salutem, constat. Solam fidem ex parte nostri causam salutis consti- tuit scriptura, exclusis operibus: Rom. IV. 8. Beati- tudo est ejus, cui Deus imputat justitiam absque ope- ribus Quomodo ergo bona opera faceret συναίτια beatitudinis? Aperta sanè hæc esset a̔́ντιλογία.

Videamus autem, quid prolixa illa commenta- tio Grotiana in recessu habeat? Primum occasionem affert scriptæ hujus, & prioris Johannis, & Judæ, & posterioris Petri epistolæ, quod directæ illæ adver- sus eos, qui epistolas Paulinas pravè interpretantes fidem sine bonis moribus dixere ad salutem sufficere. Sed illud neque ex hac, neque ex aliis epistolis ullo indicio constat. Et quamvis fidem, quæ sine bonis operib9 est, non servare doceant, non tamen & fi- dem & bona opera causas salutis constituunt, aut bona opera cum fide ad salutẽ consequendam cõ- ferre asserunt. Nec ex ultimis Petri verbis proba- bile sit, doctrinã de justificatione per tà δύσνόητα de- signari, quam à Paulo in epistola ad Romanos tra- ctatam oi̓ a̓́μαθεις κ̓ ἄστήρικτοι depravarint: quę re- ctius ab aliis & plerisque veteribus referuntur ad Epistolam ad Ebræos, quibus hæc Petrina etiã in- scripta. Neque admitti potest, Jacobum hic pro- bare, opera ad salutem requiri: quum ejus scopus fit, id tantum docere, quod fides, qua justificamur, non sit sine operibus: quemadmodum nec Abra- hami fides, quæ sola ipsi imputata est in justitiam, fu- it sine operibus, sed per opera sese manifestavit, ut justificatus, id est, justus agnitus, & palam declaratus fuerit, ex operibus suis, imprimis cum Filium suum Isaacum offerret. A veteribus autem id inter ψευ- δεγμηνείαν Paulinarum epistolarum recensitum esse, quod fides sine moribus ad salutem sufficiat, nullo testimonio probari potest; nec eo quicquam facit, Gal. V. 6. 1. Cor. XIII. 2. aut tale quid tradi- dit Augustinus, cujus verba è cap. VII. de lib. Arb. ambabus manibus amplectimur, utpote quibus solum reprobatur, sufficere homini fidem, etiamsi male vivat, & bona opera non habeat, quod antea prolixe reprobavimus. Conciliatio etiam Pauli & Jacobi Augustinianæ optime se habet, & cum Augustana confessione ex asse convenit: Paulum docere, hominem justificari fide sine operibus; Jacobum, inanem esse fidem sine operibus: illum loqui de operibus, quæ fidem præcedunt, quæ ut nulla esse docetPaulus; ita nec iis quenquam justi- ficari posse in aprico est, siquidem omnes peccave- rint, & gloria Dei caruerint, totusq; mundus Deo obnoxius sit, Rom. III. 19. 23. Ideoque gratis, per gratiam, per fidem in sanguinem Christi unicè nos justificari oporteat v. 24. 25. Istum autem (Jaco- bum) loqui de iis operibus, quæ fidem sequuntur, quod non intelligit Augustinus eo sensu, quasi co- ram Deo iisdem justificemur, sed quod per ea ju- stos nos demonstremus, & justi agnoscamur. Nec verò ex eo, quod dicitur, Pauli doctrinam esse, quod Abraham non pervenerit ad gratiam & gloriam per opera fidem præcedentia, sequitur alterum dispara- tum: Quod Abraham saltem per opera fidem con- sequentia ad salutem pervenerit. Non hoc infert Autor, sed id solum, quod post fidem Abraham bene operatus fuerit, adeoque & nobis, postquam credi- derimus, bene operando debitum ostenderit. Largi- mur etiam ultro, quæ libro LXXXIII. Qq. q. 76. ha- bet (etsi librum illum Augustini esse, κρινόμενον sit) Paulum non ita per Abraham docere, justificari homi- nem per fidem sine operibus, ut si quis crediderit, non ad eum pertinere bene operari, sed ad hoc potius, ut nemo meritis piorum bonorum operum arbitre- tur, se pervenisse ad donum justificationis, quæ est in fide. Admittimus, quod doceat Paulus, homines, ex quo crediderunt, bene operari debere, omnibus- que recte vivendum, qui in Christo crediderunt, ne ad pœnas perveniant.

Porrò secundo ad verbi הצדיק significatum pro- prium hic provocat, quod id significatu primitivo & magis proprio juxta formam Hiphil actum dupli- cem, id est, facientis, ut alter faciat, inferat, Dan. XII. 3. Apoc. XXII. 11. Sed regula illa, quod verba tertiæ Conjugationis Ebræorum modo actum du- plicem, id est, facere, ut alter faciat, notent, modo aliquid simile, puta declarare &c. non est universa- lis, sed procedit tantum in iis verbis, nec ubiq; ta- men, quæ in prima Conjugatione Kal actum simpli- cem notarunt. Quæ verò in Kal sunt intransitiva, & neutra, ea in Hiphil simplicem actum notant, & quum secundum R. D. Kimchi, Pagninum & Ber- tram, verba, quorum significatio intenditur, in ter- tia conjugatione augeantur, vel accumulatione actuum, si verba Hiphil in Kal actum simplicem no- tarunt, vel alteratione significati, ut ex Neutris in Kal fiant in Hiphil activa, proinde quia צדק in Kal plerorumque consensu est intransitivum, justus fuit, non justè fecit; ideò in Piel & Hiphil alterat si- gnificationem, & notat justum pronunciare, decla- rare, facere, per informationem de modo acquiren- dae justitiae, absolutione de culpa, declarationem &c. nunquam quando de Deo justificante, & homine justificato usurpatur, justorum sanctorumque no- vum habitum infundere, cujus habitus vi subje- ctum passum justas deinceps sanctasque actiones edat, vel facere aliquem justum, ut ipse quoque ju- ste faciat, quem actum duplicem assignat Grotius. Porrò si ex plurium locorum inductione proce- dendum, vox הֵצְרִיק frequentissimè est justum de- clarare, pronunciare, quemadmodum Grotius ipse agnoscit, vocem illam pro actu absolvendi, oppo- situm הִרְשִׁיעַ injustificare pro sententia condemna- toria sumi Deut. XXV. 2. Prov. XVII. 15. qui non nisi unicum locum è Veteri Testamento pro- duxit pro significatu, quem vocat, primitivo, Deut. XII. 3. qui tamen non notat actum illum duplicem, sed informationem de modo acquirendae justitiae, ut Hieronymus reddidit, qui erudiunt multos ad justi- tiam. Neque è Novo Testamento nisi unicum illu locum afferre habuit Grotius Apoc. XXII. 12. ex quo vero quomodo vel primitivum significatum suum vel acceptionem vocis eam, quae occurrit quando de modo ratione, qua Deus hominem justifi- cat, agitur, quũ ibi non de modo illo sermo sit, sed de hominis justificati actionibus, nec justificare in ver- bis justificetur adhuc, habitus justitiae infusionem notat, sed ex habitu vel impulsu transeunte pietatis justè operari, quod nemo Interpretum Papalium diffitetur, quemadmodum ab ipso Conc. Trid. sess. VI. c. 10. de acceptae justificationis incremento, eoque non à Deo per modum habitus subinde infuso, sed elicito ab ipso homine explicatur.

Porrò si admittamus, vocem δικαιόω hic esse tractare tanquã justum, laudare, ac benefacere, quid hoc vel adversus nostram orthodoxiam, vel pro Papizante & Socinianizante Grotio, Abrahamum ex operibus laudatum, eique ob obedientiam be- neficia à Deo exhibita esse, num idcò statim per opera salutem aeternam consequutus est? Ita à non distributo processus sit ad distributum, à genere ad certam speciem.

Quod verò Paulus id doceat, ut quis eo modo Deo placeat, ut tanquam planè infons à Deo ame- tur, Spiritu Dei donetur, ac certus fiat in eo statu aeternae salutis, id obtineri nõ per nativa hominum opera, sed per fidem Divinis oraculis adhibitam, ubi ea ad propositum obediendi pervenerit, nec è Paulina ad Romanos Epistola, quam hic respicit Grotius, ostendi potest, & contrariatur tractationi Apostolicae tum quodfidèm divinis oraculis habi- tam de nudo assensu intelligat, & ut apparet, ad ora- cula de vita aeterna exiftentia cum Socinianis re- stringat: tum quod nativa tantum opera hominum à justificatione excludi censeat, quum omnia ope- ra, quorum lex est norma, excludat Apostolus: tum quod fidem ad propositum obediendi pervenire dicat, quasi hoc ad fidei perfectionẽ faciat, quum effectus tantum fidei sit, secundum Apostolum, non vero ad integritatem & definitionem ejus spe- ctet, tum quod gratiam justificantem, quae in non imputatione injustitiae nostrae, & imputatione ju- stitiae Christi consistit, conservari per pia opera ve- lit, quae uti per fidem unicè recipitur, & obtinetur Ita unice per fidem etiam conservatur, Rom. V. 1. seqq. cap. X. 20. 2. Cor. I. 24. Joh. XV. 1. 1. Petr. I. 5. 9. Interim conservari, & augeri benevolentiam Dei & justificationi beneficium per pia facta objectivi, & per occasionem bene cupiendi bene agentibus, quo- modo miseria patientis provocat, & auget misera- tionem miserantis, Ezech. XVI. 5. 6. Luc. X. 33. ut & impetratorie (contradistincta impetratione illi mo- do, qui dicitur meritorius) ea de causa, quia Deus promisit, se daturum esse habenti & bene operanti majorem gratiam, se conservaturum bene operan- tem in statu gratiæ, Matt. XIII. 11. Joh. XV. 2. non in- ficiamur. Quemadmodum enim Deus majores gra- dus gloriæ promisit piis sanctisq; operibus: Ita non negamus, quin majores gradʉ gratiæ iis promiserit.

Quod autem ad justificationis gratiam, vel obti- nendam cum fide vitæ æternæ propositum obediendi, vel conservandam pia facta quicquam faciant, id OMNES Christianos, Græcos, Latinos, Afros UNA- NIMI ac MANIFESTO, PERPETUOQUE CONSENSU CREDIDISSE, docuisse, & ita se credere, tum singularibus quisque factis, tum consti- tutis in commune circa baptismum & pœnitentiam regulis universi demonstrasse adseritur, id verò & audacissimum & mendacissimum est effatum, tanto viro, & polyhistore prorsus indignum. Cujus pro- bandi causa nimis infirmum ac leviculum protulit argumentum, unicam Justini de Eucharistia senten- tiam, cujus neminem fas est participem fieri, nisi qui crediderit, quæ apud nos docentur, & ablutus sit la- vacro, quod institutum est pro remissione peccatorum, & regeneratione, & sic vivat, quomodo Christus vivere jussit. Justinus enim non universalis Ecclesiæ Græcæ, Latinæ, & Africanæ Doctor, nec de fide, ac ritibus omnium Ecclesiarum, sed suæ gentis ac diœ- ceseos testatus est: Nec quicquam de istis punctis controversis illa testificatione complexus est, quod nempe justificationis, & salutis beneficium obtinea- tur per assensum divinis oraculis de vita æterna ha- bitum, quatenus vel quia assensus ille propositum ha- bet obediendi decalogo vel legibus divinis: Item: Ju- stificationis & salutis beneficium conservari per pia facta; nedum universos & singulos Christianos cum factis singularibus tum statutis communibus ita se cre- dere demonstrasse. Et quomodo ita credere potuit universalis Ecclesia, quin tota Ecclesia errasset in articulo justificationis vere fundamentali, quum il- læ sententiæ Pauli doctrinæ καθδιάμετρον contra- riæ sint, qui etiam opera Abrahami, dudum renati & justificati, opposuit fidei ejusdem, & per eam so- lam justificationem, & continuationem illius gra- tiæ obtinuisse docuit. Rom. IV. 2. seqq. Et omnium renatorum opera, vel quicquid operum est, pariter opponit fidei quoad actum & officium justificandi. Et qui non operatur, sed credit, imputatur fides ad ju- stitiam. Beatitudo est hominis, cui imputatur fides sine operibus &c. Sed de hisce, quæ ad præsentis commentationis Grotianæ discussionem, quantum argumentum epistolæ ad Romanos attinet, faciunt, in Prolegomenis ad eandem epistolam jam diximus.

Ἀνενέγκας Ἰσαὰκ τὸν ὑἱὸν ἁυτῦ ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιασήριον) Filium de Sara unicum vinctum, ut fieri mos victimis, imposuit aræ, paratus etiam eum mactare, si Deus in jusso persti- tisset. De hac re vide quæ diximus Ebr. XI. 17.

Quo de prior commentatio hæc habet: Ἀνενέγκας Ἰσαὰκ τὸν ὑἱὸν ἁυτῦ ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιασήριον) Of- ferens Isaac filium super altare. Multa afferri o- pera poterant Abrahami post fidem Dei verbis habi- tam: Sed nullum excelsius, quam quod filium uni- cum ex matrefamilias sibi charissima in senectute utriusque genitum paravit Deo victimam, ita ut per eum non steterit, quo minus etiam eum morti daret. Hæc præparatio, in qua præter lethalem ictum nihil aberat, facit, ut rei, tanquam peractæ, laudem sit à Deo consecuutus, Gen. XXII. 12. & hoc sensu obtulisse fi- lium suum Abrahamus & hic dicitur, & Ebr. XI. 17. Optime Salvianus: Quantum ad defunctionem cor- dis pertinet, immolavit. Credibile autem non est, amantem filii patrem id facturum fuisse, si putasset, se Dei in se benevolentiam absque obedientiæ operibus posse retinere. Significanter autem addit, ἐπὶ τὸ θυσια- σήριον super altare, ex Gen. XXII. 9. quasi diceret ad cer- tam, ut ipse arbitratur, mortem, quæ victimas ita altari impositas, & in id ligatas solebat sequi. Mos ille victi- mas ligandi etiam in Virgilio apparet, ubi Sinon aræ de- stinatus ait: Ego vincula rupi. Et apud Ovidium III. li- bri de Ponto Elegia II. ubi de Pylade & Oreste in Tauris sermo : Protinus immitem Triviæ ducuntur ad aram Evincti geminas ad sua terga manus.

Hanc præparationem fecisse, ut rei, tanquam per- actæ laudem à Deo consequutus sit Abraham Gen. XXII. 12. agnoscimus; sed per eandem Abrahamum coram tribunali Dei justificatum fuisse negamus, quia jam pridem justificatus fuit, ante 30. nempe annos, quo de Moses Gen. XV. & ex eo Paulus Rom. IV. id- que per fidem χωρὶς ἔργων sine operibus. Credibile etiam non esse, amantem filii Patrem illa facturum fuisse, si putasset, se benevolentiam Dei in se absque obedientiæ operibus posse retinere, ambiguè dicitur, vel quod retineri ea potuisset, etiamsi obedientia illa non accessisset, sed inobediens divino mandato fuisset Patriarcha, quæ persuasio omnino fuisset falsissima, vel quod crediderit, se justificationis gra- tiam retinere posse non absque operibus obedien- tiæ, sed opera illa factura omnino ad retinendum il- lam gratiam justificationis, quem sensum intendit Grotius, sed temere affingit Patriarchæ, utpote cui non operanti, sed credenti, & sine operibus Deum imputasse justitiam, Paulus luculenter testatus est.

Sed quid Jacobus? Abraham Pater noster nonne ex operibus justificatus est? Piscator hic operum vocem accipi vult Metonymice: Ἐξ ἔργων, id est, ex tali fide, quæ conjuncta fuit cum bonis operibus, pariendo scil. illa ex se, tanquam nativos fructus. Metonymia effe- cti, quippe quæ ex effectu significatur causa procreans: ut sensus sit: Abraham justificatus est ex fide, quæ bona opera ex se peperit. Pareo verò hæc Piscatoris expli- catio tam grata fuit, ut commentario in hanc epi- stolam ipsi dedicato testatus fuerit, se analysi & ob- servationibus ejus non leviter adjutum fuisse, cumpri- mis in disputatione cap. II. de fide justificante. Voca- vit autem alternativè Synecdochen vel Metonymiam effecti, monens quod Jacobus, quamvis v. 20. 24. 25. justificationem tribuere operibus videatur: revera tamen non tribuat, quoniam ibi (sicut prius v. 18.) OPERA Synecdochice seu per Metonymiam effecti vo- cat ipsam fidem operibus conspicuam, & tali fide Abra- hamum & Rahab justificatam intelligat. Sic etiam exposuit Jacobus Laurentius in comment. super h. l. Cui explicationi, etsi fidei analogæ, ob hasce cau- sas calculum haud adjiciendum censemus 1. quod ad tropum non discedendum, ubi sine tropo res ex- pediri potest. 2. Quod tropus ille, quo opera signi- ficent fidem operibus fætam, insolens & inusitatus Scripturæ sit. 3. Quod fides & opera hic sibi oppo- nantur, ideoq; opera pro fide accipi non possint. 4. Quod opera semper in antecedentibus accipian- tur proprie in hac disputatione tota v. 14. 17. 18. ter v. 19. & in ipsis etiam consequentibus v. 22. bis, ut & v. 26. semel; adeoque indubitato novies proprium sensum obtineant, & à fide distinguantur. Qui ergo binis vicibus in simili orationis filo, eodemque tra- ctationis argumento Apostolus relicta propria si- gnificatione ad tropicam se reciperet? Nonne ita studiose rem involvisse credi posset? Quod absit, ut præsumamus. 5. Quod etiam illa oppositio fidei & operum eo loco reperiatur, ubi Synecdochice vel Metonymice Piscator & Pareus per opera fidem operosam intelligunt, utpote v. 24. 6. Quid per ope- ra intelligat Jacobus, addito exemplo declarat, & v. 21. Abraham pater noster, annon ex operibus justi- ficatus est, offerens Isaac filium suum super altare: Oblatio enim illa non erat fides operosa, sed opus ex fide profectum. Et v. 26. Similiter Ra- hab meretrix nonne operibus justificata est susci- piens nuncios: Etsi hoc opus etiam ex fide Rahab oriundum sit, Ebr. XI. non tamen ut exemplum fidei parientis ex se opera hic adducitur, sed ut exem- plum boni operis quo justa agnita & declarata est Rahab. 7. Scopus Apostoli non est de justificatione coram Deo, quatenus fiat & continuetur, agere, sed quatenus ostendatur. 8. Quia facilitate Reformati illi per opera fidem operantem intelligunt Meto- nymice, aut Synecdochice, eadem facilitate dicent Pontificii intelligi Rom. III. & IV. posse per fidem Synecdochice ipsa opera simul cum fide, vel è fide profluentia. Adde quod 9. Piscator ipse ad v. 23. ver- ba ista, & impleta est Scriptura, ita explicet, quod tum cognitum sit in Ecclesia, Abrahamum vera fide esse præditum, ac proinde fide esse justificatum, sicut Moses illo dicto Gen. XV. jam ante illius oblationis narrationem fuerat testatus. Et in Scholiis: Καὶ ἐπλη- ρώθη ἡ γραφὴ, id est, ita patefactum fuit, Abraha- mum vera fide esse præditum, ac proinde à Deo justifi- catum, sicut testatur scriptura Gen. XV. Unde B. Menzerus disp. XI. Tom. V. Giessenf. p. 225. ita ar- gumentatur: Si Abraham justificatus est coram Deo vera fide in promissum Messiam, hoc est, triginta ni- mirum annis, antequam offerretur Isaac: dici non potest, Abrahamum esse justificatum (in una & ea- dem vocis significatione) coram Deo per oblationem Isaaci. Prius affirmat Moses, Paulus & omnes pii fa- tentur. Quare posterius negandum est. Et per conse- quens aliter verbum justificandi in disputatione Pau- lina, aliter apud Jacobum accipitur. Pareus ad v. 22. Ad mentem Jacobi, ait, dicendum videtur, fidem cooperatam esse operibus seu operi ejus in justificatio- ne. Quomodo? Quia fide in hoc opere conspicua Abraham fuit justificatus, seu quia fides per tremen- dum illud opus se non otiosam sed operantem esse de- clarans justificationem operata est, ideoque justifi- cationem contra intentionem suam considerat, non ut sit coram Deo, sed ut coram Deo facta esse agnoscitur ab hominibus. Johannes Camero verò agnoscit Me- tonymiam istam Piscatoris duram ac parum usita- tam in Scriptura videri posse in Myroth. p. 340. Plu- ribus contra illam explicationem, & rationes Parei pro illa propositas disputavit B. Hopfnerus disp. XII. de justif. p. 1115. seqq.

Quapropter omnino præstat dicere, non accipi justificationem in his exemplis in præsenti pro ab- solutione à peccatis, vel justificatione, quæ fit in judi- cio, & coram tribunali Dei, sed pro justi declaratio- ne vel agnitione, qua habetur quis justus coram mundo: Sive vox δικαιοῦσθαι credatur accipi eo sensu, qui in scripturis non infrequens agnoscitur à Grotio, cum quis laudatur, ut Matth. XI. 10. Luc. VII. 29. c. X. 29. c. XVI. 15. 1. Tim. III. 16. Eccles. I. 24. c. XXXI. 5. sive per Ebraismum notissimum, quo res tum fieri dicitur, cum manifestatur vel agnoscitur ju- stificatus ex operibus, id est, laudatus vel justificatus, agnitus & manifestatus fuit ex operibus, imprimis illis, quæ palam effulgebant, cum offerret Isaacum filium suum super altare, vel omnia, quantum ad ipsum erat, efficiebat, ut mandatum divinum exe- queretur, & filium suum offerret, oblaturus omni- no, nisi à Deo inhibitus fuisset. Hoc enim illustre, ac publicum specimen erat fidei justificantis & ju- stificationis Abrahamiticæ: Quem sensum postu- lant tum antecedentia, tum consequentia, tum sco- pus totius tractationis: Antecedentia, quia de fide demonstranda per opera, &, quæ per ea non demon- stratur, vel demonstrabilis est, vana, vera autem, & salvifica, tum talis, quæ per opera sese exerat, & de- monstret, egerat Apostolus v. 18. & juxta immedia- te antecedens comma hominem inanem, & ob va- nam persuasionem & ob vacuitatem bonorum ope- rum convincere instituit uberius & luculentius, quod fides, quæ est sine operibus, mortua sit, id est, non viva agnoscatur, sed mortua intelligatur, ut sciri possit & agnosci, eam omnino mortuam esse. Notandum enim, quod hic itidem Ebraismus di- ctus obtineat:& mortua esse dicatur fides, quæ mor- tua esse agnoscitur & manifestatur. Nam mortuam esse, non vivam, adeoque justificantem, declarat absentia operum: quemadmodum illustri exemplo Patris credentium ex adverso ostensa fides non mortua, sed viva & justificans, per opera illa insi- gnia,orbiq; toti notissima,quod filium suum offer- re voluerit super altare. Vis autem scire,o homo ina- nis, quoniam fides sine operibus mortua est, id est, agnoscitur, tantum abest, ut justificare possit, vel servare fides, quæ opera non habet. Abraham Pa- ter noster nonne ex operibus justificatus est, id est, agnitus est, & manifestatus, quod vere justificatus & justus esset,adeoque fide vera justificante prædi- tus, sine qua ea opera patrare minime potuisset.

Consequentia sunt 1. Illatio Apostolica: Vides quo- niam fides cooperata est operibus ejus in illa filii ob- latione, quia etsi ex studio obediendi Deo ea pro- fecta sint, sine fide tamen nec studium illud locum habuit,nec opera inde sequuta: Fides itaque coope- rata est,Abrahamum confortando in obsequii stu- dio, quæ fidei operatio videri & agnosci potest ex operibus istis illustribus, æque ut obsequii sanctissi- mi & vere admirandi studium inde effulsit: quem- admodum Ebr. XI. ex fide oblatio illa facta dicitur. Vides quoniam fides cooperari agnita est obsequio Abrahamitico in exequendis illis operibus, quæ ad obedientiam præstandam spectabant. Non minus enim fides quam obedientia, & reverentia, etsi utra- que intrinsecus in corde latebat, palam in operibus istis sese prodebat, & manifestabat, ingens scilicet illa fiducia,quam inDeum habebat Patriarcha,im- pleturum omnino suam promissionem de semine be- nedicto, quæ non nisi in semine ex Isaaco prodituro implenda erat vi oraculi divini, etiamsi obsequens jussui divino Isaacum mactaret,posse enim eundem numero filium ex cineribus vicissim vivum restitui ac resuscitari.

2. Ulterior conclusio, quæ hæc est: & ex operibus fides consummata est. Quomodo consummata ex operibus? Num ratione sui & perfectionis essentia- lis? Id dici non potest. Quia enimAbraham per fi- dem justificatus jam ante 30. annos fuit, oportuit fidem non imperfectam fuisse,sed perfectam,quoad essentialem perfectionem.Quomodo enim per fidem imperfectam justificatus fuisset Patriarcha? Si au- tem non ratione sui, qua ergo alia ratione consum- mata, nisi ratione aliorum, & quatenus aliis manife- stata, & ab aliis agnita?

3. Scripturæ impletio v.23. Et suppleta est Scriptu- ra dicens: Credidit Abraham Deo, & reputatum est illi ad justitiam. Quomodo tum impleta demum scriptura, nisi intelligatur hoc itidem ratione inno- tescentiæ, quod palam id declaratum illustri illo fa- cinore fuerit, Abrahamum vere justificatum fuisse per fidem in Christum. Nam opera talia fructus sunt justificationis, & non minus de justificatione te- stantur, quam de fide justificante,quum bona opera non præcedant justificandum, sed sequantur justi- ficatum. Dicitur enim Scriptura seu vaticinium aliquod, seu quodcunque oraculum divinum, vel maxime tunc impleri, quando complementum ejus per insignem quendam effectum palam inno- tescit aut innoscere potest. Verissimum nempe esse, quod illo Scripturæ oraculo traditum.

4.Amici Dei appellatio.AmicusDei jam fuit per an- nos bene multos. Appellatus ergo amicusDei tum est, non quod primum gratiamDei consequutus sit, & ad amicitiam cum Deo admissus, sed quod ex hocce tam insigni publicoq; specimine agnitus, & palam manifestatus fuerit amicusDei.Imò κληθῆναι vocari amicum Dei supponit quidem veritatem in- tercedentis amicitiæ inter Deum & Abrahamum, & superaddit etiam notorietatem apud homines. Vid. Sap. III. 13. 15. Gen. XLI. 1. Prov. XXI. 24. cap. XXIV. 8. Es. I. 27. Job. XV. 15. Accedit historia Mo- saica Gen. XXII. 13. 17. 18. & quo loco utriusq; mani- festatio & agnitio tum veræ fidei, tum amicitiæ Dei quoad Abrahamum, elucescit: illius quidem è ver- bis Domini: Nunc cognovi, quod Deum vere timeas, quia filio tuo unico propter me non pepercisti, ubi ab e- videntia extrinsecæ obedientiæ Abrahami in obla- tione filii ostensæ Deus ἀνθρωποπαθῶς testatur, se veritatem & sinceritatem affectû intrinseci cogno- visse, qui verò sine fide in ipso existere non potuit. Si exponat id effectivè de facta hominibq notitia, uti ab Ambrosio de fide cap. VIII. IX. Augustino libr. IV. de Gen. ad lit. i. Hilario libr. IX. de Trin. Greg. M. l. XXIIX. Moral. cap. 7. sit, itidem manifestatio & in- notescentia infertur: quemadmodum glossa, Lyra Abulensis, Saa, Estius, aliiqve Pontificii Interpp. agnoscunt. Ita ergo Deus ipse hoc inferendi modo usus est, ut veritatem fidei Abrahamiticæ homini- bus ostenderet per oblationem Isaaci. Amicitia etiam Dei erga Abrahamum annon luculentissimè declarata est, quando Deus juramento confirmavit benedictionem familiæ ipsius, & promissionem de Messia, quæ profectò confirmatio non minus testa- batur de fide Abrahami in Deum & promissiones divinas, ex qua facta est oblatio Ebr. XI. 17. quàm de justificatione ejusdem, & amore Dei erga ipsum. Id enim observandum, quod in verbis Dei, Gen. XXII. 15. 16. quia fecisti hanc rem, & non pepercisti filio tuo unico, benedicendo benedicam tibi, eo quod obediisti voci meæ, obedientia Abraha adducatur, non ut causa benedictionis sive justificationis, sed ut testimo- nium ejusdem & signum, quo magis certioratur de semine benedicto ex lumbis suis nascituro, & per illud obtenta benedictione spirituali, nec non de reliquarum benedictionum divinitus promissarum eventu adhuc futuro. Quapropter particula כי quia significat non causam benedictionis ipsius, sed tantum causam co- gnoscendi benedictionem, ejusque continuationem, ac proinde ibi sermonem esse innuit de benedictione seu justificatione, non quatenus sit coram Deo, quia ea sic considerata describitur per imputationem fidei in ju- stitiam, sed quatenus notificatur hominibus, quod co- ram Deo sit facta, & quatenus fides per hoc opus ceu exercitium suum secundarium efficax sit, & operosa est, accertioratur magis, sicut Ebr. XII. 18. dicitur: Fide obtulit Abraham Isaac cum tentaretur, & uni- genitum offerebat, in quo susceperat repromissionem, ut habet B. Hopfnerus disp. XII. de justif. pag. 1079.

Denique scopus Jacobæ tractationis de justifi- catione ex operibus, & non per fidem tantum hic est, ut ostendat fidei solam professionem sine ope- ribus, quibus ea demonstretur, non esse nisi vanam & inanem fidei veræ jactantiam, ad quod usus est exemplo Abrahami: cujus fidei prorsus difformis est talis nuda professio, utpote cujus fides & justifi- catio per fidem ac fructus gratiæ per opera palam innotuit, atq; agnoscebatur & manifestabatur im- primis illo insigni facinore oblationis Isaaci. Quem sensum nec ipsimet Papistæ diffiteri possunt, etsi suum etiam commentum de Abrahamo justiore reddito per opera hic libenter inferant. Ita Glossa ordinaria in h. l. Hic de operibus agitur, quæ sequun- tur fidem, propter quæ amplius justificatur (Abra- ham) cum jam per fidem esset justus. Unde Paulus: Fide Abraham obtulit Isaacum, cum tentaretur. Hæc oblatio est opus & testimonium fidei & justi- tiæ. Thomas in c. III. Gal. & in c. II. Jac. explicat hoc etiam de ostensione & manifestatione justitiæ: &

priori quidem loco ita habet: Et hoc modo homo ju- stificatur, id est, justus ostenditur ex operibus opera- tis. Lyranus in h. l. Et similiter magnitudo fidei Abra- hæ apparuit, ex ejus obedientia offerendo filium, pro- pter quod dictum fuit sibi à Domino: Nunc cognovi, quod timeas Dominum, id est, cognoscere feci alios. Folengius verbum justificationis Jac. II. exponit: Ju- stus ostensus, &amp;, qualis jam esset in cœlo, declaratus. Guil. Estius in h. l. Jacobus, inquit, de operibus agit, fi- dem consequentibus, &amp; ex fide pullulantibus, atque à fide directis; sine quibus vana, sterilis, &amp; infructuo- sa, ac proinde inutilis est fides. Ex hujusmodi igitur operibus homo justificatur, quia per ea tanquam per actualem justitiam est, &amp; declaratur vere justus, eóq; nomine Deo gratus. Grotius ipse ad arguendam Dei benevolentiam opera fecisse jam profitebitur: quam non nisi justis promiserit.

## 2:22
Verse 22. Βλέπεις) Do you see?

Ὅτι ἡ πίστις συνήργει τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ) Likewise both faith and works concurred to retain and prove the benevolence of God, which He promised only to the just.

The frequently mentioned Grotian commentary has this to say on these words:

Βλέπεις ὅτι ἡ πίστις συνήργει τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ) You see that faith was working together with his works. Lest anyone should think that works are required here apart from faith, he well notes that for the sake of protecting that state of grace before God, both faith and works concurred in Abraham: faith, which runs from the beginning of that state until its consummation; works, as following faith and necessary at a given time and occasion for preserving that state. When he says συνήργει, 'was working together,' we are taught that it is not wrong to say that both faith and the works of faith can be called a cause of justification; thus also of salvation (for justification, when retained, brings salvation), provided we do not understand the primary cause, which is God's εὐδοκία, good pleasure, or free decree in φιλανθρωπία, out of His love toward men (Eph. 2:4, Tit. 3:4), but conditions which are often called causes without which not, or causes of their own kind.

That faith and works concurred equally to the retaining of God’s benevolence, neither does James intend here to prove, nor do those words bear that meaning: that faith was a co-worker with works in the offering of Isaac, which means not only that works or the zeal of obedience, but also faith along with them acted here, which was to be done: that faith was a co-worker with works is not said in regard to justification: Faith συνήργει τοῖς ἔργοις, was a co-worker with works, namely to this end, that they might be good. It worked, I say, with them, and through them, so that both the works might be good, and faith itself might be conspicuous through the works, as Pareus explains, l. IV. de justif. contr. Bellarm. c. 18. p. 1156. Concerning which see Pererius, disp. I. in cap. IV. ad Rom. n. 4. To whomever is working, faith cooperates, both teaching what is to be done, and inciting to action, and moderating in the acting, and directing the action to that end to which the matter ought to be referred, and propping up and sustaining the agent, lest he fail and desist from acting. Nor did Estius acknowledge an equal cooperation (συνέργειαν) of faith and works here, and therefore he disapproved of Erasmus's translation concerning 'aid': 'Cooperated', in Greek συνήργει, which Erasmus interprets as 'was an aid'. But our Interpreter well and properly translates it 'cooperated'. For the Apostle wishes to intimate a certain inseparable partnership between faith and works: so that just as faith ought not to be without works, so neither should works be without faith: although the parts of faith are superior, as being that which directs, as I have said, and commands. Then if the concurrence is understood in relation to justification, it must be explained according to the subject matter, not concerning justification being retained or increased, but concerning the same being manifested or demonstrated: Whence Thomas in this place interprets that it cooperated not in the act of justification, but in the exercise and declaration of the justice received, because faith led him to works. And who does not know that συνεργεῖν means to cooperate, and that συνεργὸς can be called fellow-workers or colleagues, who concerning diverse objects work together at the same, or a different time or place, at least for the same supreme end, which is the glory of God. See Rom. VIII. 29. 1 Cor. XVI. 16. B. Hopfner, however, admits a συνέργειαν [cooperation] of the same kind, but for the purpose of showing justification, not effecting it, namely that the profession of faith cooperates with works in the office of notifying saving faith and justification. Concerning which, see the cited dissertation, p. 1082 et seqq.

And by works faith was perfected) Faith is perfected by love, says Tertullian in the fifth book against Marcion. Every thing is perfected when it produces its destined effect. Faith cannot attain that ἄνευ συναυτῶν [without them].

He had said the same things, but not so crudely, in his previous commentary: Καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἔργων αὐτῶ ἡ πίστις ἐτελειώθη) And by works faith was consummated. Namely, through works it was brought about that faith did not fall short of its hoped-for effect. Faith is perfected by love, as Tertullian speaks in Against Marcion V. For not, as Cyprian rightly says in the already mentioned epistle, the attainment, but the consummation saves a man for God. It had preceded: It is a small thing to have been able to attain something: it is more, that you have attained, to be able to keep it.

We do not deny that faith is perfected by love in a certain sense. For a thing is understood to be perfected according to the usage of Scripture, which either acquires a just perfection of parts or degrees, or also becomes known more evidently to others by its excellence. And thus we do not deny that faith was intrinsically strengthened by reason of degrees through these notable works of obedience; that it became more known extrinsically to all those who were to hear of them now and in the past, no one can doubt. But in this latter sense, perfection must be understood with regard to the Apostle's purpose, from which it could be known that Abraham's faith was true faith, and most different from hypocritical faith devoid of works.

In which sense charity is also said to be perfected, 1 John IV. 17, or to strive toward this perfection, so that we may have confidence in the day of judgment, certainly of divine love toward us, concerning which Salmero explains: The supreme degree shines forth from the fact that nothing can deter us on the day of judgment from the certainty of salvation; but also that is the highest perfection of our love for God in this life, that we are not tormented by the fear of damnation, v. 18. For the most illustrious evidence of love is if it casts out fear, and does not tremble on the day of judgment. Thus also the power of God is said to be perfected in weakness, that is, to be seen more evidently in a subject that is in itself weaker, 1 Cor. XIII. 9. Where certainly it cannot be said that our weakness adds anything to the power of God, and thus nothing else is noted than that the power of God exerts itself in our weakness, and shows how powerful it is: Thus here faith is not strengthened by works, because it receives any virtue from them, but because it shows how great it is in works. Nor did Dionysius the Carthusian explain it otherwise, saying that Abraham's faith was consummated by works, because the magnitude of the faith with which Abraham then believed God was afterwards approved by God, and declared to others by the fact that he was prepared to offer his son to God: thus then it became publicly and consummately known, what was previously known almost only to God and Abraham, namely that Abraham could trust God so greatly. Tertullian: He does not speak of the form of faith, but of a perpetual accident, that faith is exercised, perfected, exerted, and shown through love, comparing the passage Gal. V. 6. Cyprian also does not teach Rogatian and the other confessors about the essential parts of saving faith, or about the confluence of good works into the acquisition of salvation, but about the duty of persevering both in trust toward God and in the confession of truth and faith before tyrants. What? That faith is even said to be guarded by perseverance negatively, namely by not admitting apostasy, and that through Abraham's obedience it was brought about that faith did not fall short of its hoped-for event, which pertains to the privative effect of works, insofar as it was hindered, lest through disobedience the grace of God and salvation, as the hoped-for event of faith, should be lost: yet it should not be concluded from this that works preserved Abraham in a state of grace, much less that they were co-causes [συναίτια] of salvation with faith. For even if Abraham had died before these works concerning the offering of Isaac were completed: he would undoubtedly have attained eternal salvation, as the hoped-for event, and his faith would have been altogether perfect, as regards formal perfection and the power of saving Abraham. But after the command concerning the offering of Isaac was received, if he had been disobedient, he would certainly have fallen short of the hoped-for event. However, there is no analogy [ἀναλογία] in this proposition: Whose absence of obedience privatively intercepts the hoped-for event of salvation, its presence positively effects that one obtains that hoped-for event. D. Hopfner, in the cited place, p. 1089, explains faith consummated as the profession of faith: Justification, he says, of a sinful man before God does not receive more and less, nor is it doubled, so that one is first, another second, one by habit, another by act of faith. Wherefore the external profession of faith is said to be consummated when, joined with works as that collateral sign, it becomes an absolutely perfect sign of saving faith and justification. The sense, therefore, of the words of James is: faith, that is, the external profession of faith in cooperating with works for the demonstration of saving faith and justification, was consummated by works, that is, it was made a perfect sign of Abraham's saving faith and justification.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Βλέπεις) Viden'?

Ὅτι ἡ πίστις συνήργει τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ) Pariter &amp; fides & opera concurrêrunt ad retinendam arguendamque Dei be- nevolentiam, quam non nisi justis promisit.

Commentatio Grotiana sæpius dicta ita ad hæc verba habet:

Βλέπεις ὅτι ἡ πίστις συνήργει τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ) Vides quo- niam fides cooperabatur operibus illius. Ne quis puta- ret, hic opera seposita fide exigi, bene notat ad statum illum gratiæ apud Deum tutandum, concurrisse in Abrahamo &amp; fidem &amp; opera, fidem quæ ab initio ejus status ad consummationem usque decurrit, opera ut fidem subsequentia &amp; dato tempore ac occasione ad conservandum eum statum necessaria. Cùm συνήργει cooperabatur dicit, docemur non male &amp; fidem &amp; ope- ra fidei posse dici causam ut δικαιώσεως justificatio- nis; ita salutis (nam δικαίωσις retenta salutem affert) modo non intelligamus causam primariam, quæ est Dei εὐδοκία, beneplacitum, sive liberum decretum in φιλανθρωπίας, ex sua in homines dilectione, Eph. II. 4. Tit. III. 4. sed conditiones, quæ sæpe causæ sine quibus non, aut sui generis causæ, dicuntur.

Quod fides &amp; opera pariter concurrerint ad reti- nendam Dei benevolentiam, nec Jacobus intendit hic probare, nec verba illa præ se ferunt: coopera- tam esse fidem operibus in oblatione Isaaci, quod non solum opera vel obedientiæ studium, sed cum illis etiam fides hic egerint, quod agendum erat: Cooperatam esse fidem operibus, ad justificationem non dicitur: Fides συνήργει τοῖς ἔργοις, cooperabatur operibus, nempe ad hoc, ut bona essent. Operata est, inquam, cum illis, &amp; per illa, ut &amp; opera essent bona, &amp; ipsa per opera foret conspicua, ut explicat Pareus l. IV. de justif. contr. Bellarm. c. 18. p. 1156. Quo de Pererius disp. I. in cap. IV. ad Rom. n. 4. Cuicunque operanti fides cooperatur, &amp; docens, quid agendum sit, &amp; incitans ad agendum, &amp; moderans in agendo, &amp; dirigens actionem in eum finem, in quem referri res oportet, &amp; fulciens, &amp; sustentans agentem, ne defi- ciat, &amp; ab agendo desistat, Neque parilem hic συνέρ- γειαν fidei &amp; operum agnovit Estius, ideoque Eras- mi translationem de adjumento improbavit: Coo- perabatur, Græce συνήργει, quod Erasmus interpreta- tur, adjumento fuit. Sed bene noster Interpres ac pro- prie vertit cooperabatur. Vult enim Apostolus innue- re societatem quandam individuam inter fidem & opera: ut sicut fides sine operibus esse non debet: Ita nec opera sine fide: tametsi partes fidei po- tiores sunt, utpote dirigentis, ut dixi, &amp; impe- rantis. Tum si concursus ad justificationem intelli- gatur, pro subjecta materia explicandus erit, non de justificatione retinenda vel augenda, sed de ea- dem manifestanda vel arguenda: Unde Thomas in h. l. interpretatur, quod cooperata fuerit non in actu justificationis, sed in exercitio &amp; declaratione justi- tiæ acceptæ, quia fides eum duxit ad opera. Et quis nescit, συνεργεῖν cooperari, ac συνεργὸς colla- boratores collegas dici posse, qui circa diversa obje- cta eodem, aut diverso tempore aut loco, eodem saltim fine supremo, qui est gloria Dei, simul ope- rantur. Vide Roman. VIII. 29. 1. Cor, XVI. 16. B. Hopfnerus tamen admittit συνέργειαν ejusdem ra- tionis, sed ad justificationem ostendendam, non efficiendam, quod nempe fidei professio coopere- tur operibus in officio notificandi fidem salvificam & justificationem. Quo de videatur disp. laudata p. 1082. seqq.

Καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἔργων ἡ πίστις ἐτελειώθη) Perficitur per dile- ctionem fides, ait Tertullianus adversus Marcionem quinto. Perficitur res quæque cum effectum sibi destina- tum parit. Eum fides consequi non potest ἄνευ συναυτῶν.

Eadem, sed non tam crasse, dixerat in commen- tatione priori: Καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἔργων αὐτῶ ἡ πίστις ἐτελειώθη) Et ex operibus fides consummata est. Nempe per opera factum est, ne fides sperato effectu excideret. Perficitur per dilectio- nem fides, ut Tertullianus loquitur adversus Marcio- nem V. Nec enim, ut recte Cyprianus, dicta jam epi- stola, consecution, sed consummatio hominem Deo ser- vat. Præcesserat: Parum est, adipisci aliquid potuisse: plus est, quod adeptus es, posse servare.

Perfici per dilectionem fidem certa ratione non negamus. Perfici enim res intelligitur ex usu Scri- pturæ, quæ vel justam partium vel graduum perfe- ctionem acquirit, vel etiam à præstantia sua aliis evidentius innotescit. Atq; ita etiam intrinsecè ra- tione graduum roboratam fuisse fidem per hæc in- signia obedientiæ opera non diffitemur: extrinsecè magis innotuisse omnibus iis, qui nunc & olim de iis audituri erant, dubitari à nemine potest. Hac au- tem posteriori ratione perfectio intelligenda est ratione scopi Apostoli, ex qua scilicet inotescere po- tuerit, Abrahami fidem fuisse veram fidem, maxi- meq; diversam à fide hypocritica operibus vacua.

Quo sensu etiam charitas dicitur perfici, 1. Joh. IV. 17. vel ad hanc perfectionem contendere, ut fidu- ciam habeamus in die judicii, amoris certe divini erga nos, de quo explicat Salmero: Supremus gra- dus elucescit ex eo, quod nihil nos deterrere possit in die judicii à certitudine salutis; sed & amoris nostri in Deum illa summa in hac vita est perfectio, quod damnationis metu non cruciamur, v. 18. Illustrissi- mum enim dilectionis indicium est, si foras mittat timorem, nec contremiscat in die judicii. Sic etiam virtus Dei in infirmitate dicitur perfici, id est, evi- dentius conspici in subjecto per se infirmiori, 1. Cor. XIII. 9. Ubi certe dici nequit addere infirmitatem nostram aliquid potentiæ Dei, adeoque nihil aliud notatur, quam quod Dei virtus se in infirmitate no- stra exerat, & ostendat quam potens sit: Ita hic non confortatur fides per opera, quod ab iis aliquid virtutis accipiat, sed quod ostendat, quanta sit in ope- ribus. Nec aliter exposuit Dionysius Carthusianus, consummatam ex operibus fidem Abrahæ dicens, quia magnitudo fidei, qua tum Abraham credidit Deo, postmodum est approbata Deo, ac aliis decla- rata per hoc, quod filium suum paratus fuerit Deo offerre: tum itaque publice & consummate inno- tuit, quod antea Deo & Abrahamo fere soli notum erat, Abrahamum nimirum tantopere Deo fidere posse. Tertullianus: Non de forma loquitur fidei, sed de perpetuo accidente, quod fides exerceatur, perficia- tur, exeratur, ostendatur per dilectionem, conferens locum Gal. V. 6. Cyprianus etiam Rogatianum & cæ- teros confessores non docet de partibus essentiali- bus fidei salvificæ, aut de confluentia bonorum operum in acquisitionem salutis, sed de debito perseveran- di tam in fiducia erga Deum, quam in confessione veritatis & fidei coram tyrannis. Quid? quod etiam dicatur fides custodiri per perseverantiam negativè, non admittendo scilicet apostasiam, & per obedientiam Abrahami factum esse, ne fides sperato eventu excideret, quod ad privativum ope- rum effectum, quatenus impeditum est, ne per ino- bedientiam gratia Dei & salute, ceu sperato fidei e- ventu excideret: nec tamen inde concludendum sit, quod opera Abrahamum in statu gratia conserva- rint, nedum cum fide salutis συναίτια fuerint. Nam etiamsi Abraham ante hæc opera circa oblationem Isaaci expedita decessisset: salutem æternam sine dubio consequutus fuisset, ceu speratum eventum, & perfecta omnino fuisset fides ejusdem, quod ad formalem perfectionem, & ad vim servandi Abraha- mum. Post acceptum autem de oblatione Isaaci mandatum, si inobediens fuisset, sperato eventu utique excidisset. Nulla autem est ἀναλογία in hac propositione: Cujus obedientiæ absentia privati- ve intervertit speratæ salutis eventum, ejus præsen- tia positive efficit, ut sperato illo eventu quis po- tiatur. D. Hopfnerus l. c. p. 1089. fidem consummatam explicat de professione fidei: Justificatio, inquiens, hominis peccatoris coram Deo non recipit magis & mi- nus, nec duplicatur, ut alia sit prima, alia secunda, alia per habitum, alia per actum fidei. Quare fidei professio externa dicitur consummari, quando conjun- cta cum operibus ceu signo illo collaterali fit absolute perfectum signum fidei salvifica & justificationis. Sen- sus itaque verborum Jacobi est, fides, id est, professio fidei externa in cooperando cum operibus ostensionem fidei salvifica & justificationis fuit consummata per opera, id est, facta est perfectum signum fidei salvifica & justificationis Abrahami.

## 2:23
Vers. 23. And the scripture was fulfilled which saith) Before indeed that had been said concerning Abraham when he offered Isaac, as is to be seen in the cited place Gen. XV. 6. But it is the custom of the Hebrews to say, this נתקיים, that is, was fulfilled, when another thing similar to a matter narrated somewhere else happens. For then out of faith Abraham offered victims to God, and now a much more precious victim. In a similar way that saying, it was reckoned to him for righteousness, the writer of the first book of Maccabees II. 52 refers to the time of Isaac being offered: Abraham was not found faithful in temptation, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness.

Concerning these things he had annotated thus in the former treatise: And the scripture was fulfilled which saith, and Abraham believed God) And the scripture was fulfilled saying: Abraham believed God. He uses the same saying of Moses which Paul had used for commending faith. But someone might say, this was placed by Moses long before he had arrived at the history of the offered Isaac, where namely he had narrated that an innumerable offspring was promised to Abraham, and that faith was held by him in that promise. But it must be known that it is frequent among the Hebrews to say נתקיים, that is, was fulfilled, or this or that place of Holy Scripture was verified, as often as something similar to the matter commemorated in that place happens, especially where a like event follows a like cause. That faith of Abraham, which was so pleasing to God that on account of it He received Abraham as if he were entirely innocent from the beginning, appeared often: at that time, of which that place of Genesis XV. 6 treats, and again in Gen. XVII. when a son was promised to him from Sarah, which Paul executes in Rom. IV. 17. & seq. But it never shone forth more evidently than when he girded himself to obey the command of God concerning killing his son. For that faith was immense and like unto Evangelical faith, thinking so of the power of God, and of constancy in performing His own sayings, that he believed his son, upon whom the other magnificent promises depended, could be restored to him even from death, Heb. XI. 18.

Grotius rightly says that the faith of Abraham shone forth most evidently when he girded himself to obey God in killing his son: But that this saying is used by Paul in the same way is not to be admitted. For Paul applies it to that effect of faith which is the justification of Abraham before God. James, however, says that that Scripture was fulfilled, not when Abraham was justified before God, but when his faith and righteousness were publicly declared, and could be acknowledged by all. Nor did a like event follow a like cause there. For faith is one cause, works another; justification is one event, the showing of justification another. For Scripture is said to be fulfilled also when that which was handed down by divine oracle is openly manifested or becomes known: which sense even the Papists themselves admit here, such as Salmero, Cornelius à Lapide, Paëz, Tirinus, Estius, and especially Lorinus, who explains that phrase at length, because the magnitude of Abrahamic faith—which was not idle, not dead, but active, efficacious, and accompanied by good works—showed itself most greatly in the immolation of his son, and became known to others. which is accustomed to be expressed by מתקיים, whatever may be the case with more recent Hebrews, does not agree with the style of Scripture, in which that is never observed; but קיים denotes either the first institution, as Esth. IX. 21, 27, 29, 31, 32, or the confirmation of a new contract, Ruth IV. 7, or the assertion of a present statement, Ezech. XIII. 6, or the moral confirmation of the mind in a good purpose, Psal. CXIX. 28, 106. But especially it deserves censure, because he says that Abrahamic faith had only a certain likeness of Evangelical faith. For the Apostle sets it before us as an example and an idea of true Evangelical and justifying faith, Rom. IV, and makes the object of that faith the multiplication of the seed of Abraham, the principal object of which was the promise that the Son of God would be Abraham's shield and great reward, and that promise of the seed to be multiplied was made only on account of that μοναδικὸν seed, in which blessing reaches all the nations of the earth, Gen. XII. 3, ch. XV, 1, seqq., Gal. III. 16, Rom. IV. 3, seqq. Finally, God did not receive Abraham as if he were entirely innocent from the beginning on account of faith, but through faith: so that faith is to be regarded as the instrument by which the grace of God is received, not as a moral virtue on account of which we are received into grace.

Καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην) That is, that faith was held by God as an excellent thing, such as things are accustomed to be called by the name of justice. You have the same kind of speech in Psal. CVI. 31, where the zeal of Phinehas is said to have been reckoned to him for justice, that is, made great by God and rewarded with the great reward of the high priesthood.

v. Grotius had executed these things more prolixly in his former commentary;

Καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην) And it was reckoned to him for justice. The Hebrew word, for which the Greeks put λογίζεσθαι, is frequently used when a thing or some man is held as if he were in another way than he is, whether that is done by right or by wrong, and the word נחשב, which is equivalent, is used in the same way, as Es. LIII. 12, which the Interpreters rendered by λογίζεσθαι, Matth. XV. 28, Luc. XXII. 37. Thus when one excellent work is held for many, it is said to be λογίζεσθαι or reckoned for justice, as concerning Phinehas, Psal. CVI. 30. Thus ἡ ἀκροβυςία, the state of an uncircumcised man, is said εἰς περιτομὴν λογίζεσθαι, Rom. II. 27, that is, to be worth as much as the state of a circumcised man. Justin to Zenas: Ἀνοήτῳ γὰρ ἐπερωτήσαντι σοφίαν, σοφία λογισθήσεται. For to the ignorant man asking for wisdom, wisdom is reckoned, that is, ἡ ἐπερώτησις εἰς σοφίαν λογισθήσεται, the asking will be held for wisdom. Theophilus Antiochenus, ἡ πίσις σου εἰς ἀπισίαν λογίζεται, thy faith is reckoned for infidelity. Tertullian in the Apologeticus concerning the games of the gentiles: The occasion of luxury will be reckoned as religion. The same author in the book on patience, speaking of Abraham: But God, whom he had reckoned for justice, knew. Chrysostom, 1 Cor. ch. II: Λογισθήσεται τῷ ἕλληνι εἰς πίσιν ἡ προσκύνησις ἐκείνη: That adoration will be reckoned to the Greek for faith. Therefore, for something to be λογίζεσθαι εἰς δικαιοσύνην to someone, to be reckoned for justice, is worth the same as that he who has it is held ὡς δίκαιον καὶ ἀναμάρτητον, as if he were entirely just and had never sinned. Justin in the dialogue with Trypho: Εἰ γὰρ Χρηστότης καὶ ἡ φιλανθρωπία τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ τὸ ἀμέτρον τοῦ πλούτου αὐτοῦ τὸν μετανοοῦντα ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων ὡς δίκαιον καὶ ἀναμάρτητον ἔχοι, καὶ τὸν ἀπὸ εὐσεβείας ἢ δικαιοπραξίας μετατιθέμενον ἐπὶ ἀδικίαν ἀκραταλὸν καὶ ἄδικον καὶ ἀσεβῆ ἐπίςαται. For God's goodness and love toward men and the immensity of his riches holds him who is led to repentance for sins as just and free from sin; but on the contrary, he holds him who falls away from piety or justice to iniquity as a sinner, and unjust, and impious. The Greeks also speak of this by ἀποδέχεσθαι, to accept, as ὁ Θεὸς τὴν μετάνοιαν εἰς ἀρετὴν

ἀποδέχεσθαι: God accepts repentance for virtue. Philo expresses this very thing, which is said here, by circumlocution in the book, Who is the heir of divine things: Ἀναγκαίως ἔτι ἐπιλέγεται· Ἐπίστευσεν δὲ Ἀβραὰμ τῷ Θεῷ πρὸς ἔπαινον τοῦ πιστεύσαντος, καίτοι τάχ' ἄν τις εἴποι, τοῦτ' ἄξιον ἐπαίνου κρίνεται; Τίς δὲ οὐκ ἂν λόγοντι καὶ ὑπισχνουμένῳ Θεῷ προσέχοι τὸν νοῦν, κἂν ἁπάντων ἀδικώτατος καὶ ἀσεβέστατος ὢν τυγχάνων; πρὸς ὃν ἐροῦμεν· μὴ, μὴ, ὦ γενναῖε, ἀνεξετάστως ᾗ τὸν σοφὸν ἀφίλη τὰ πρέποντα ὀγκώματα, ᾗ τοῖς ἀναξίοις τὴν τελειοτάτην τῶν ἀρετῶν πίστιν μαρτυρήσῃς, ἢ τὴν ἡμετέραν περὶ τούτων γνῶσιν αἰτιάσῃ. For if you should wish to make a deeper, and not a very superficial, investigation, you will clearly know that to believe in God alone, without the additional taking up of another, is a task for a great and Olympian mind, because of the kinship we have with the mortal to which we are yoked, which persuades us to believe in wealth, and glory, and authority, and friends, and the health and strength of the body, and many other things. But to wash away each of these, and to disbelieve in a creation that is in all things untrustworthy of itself, and to believe only in God, who is also the only one truly trustworthy, is the work of a great and Olympian mind, no longer enticed by any of the things among us. Well, therefore, is it said, "his faith was reckoned to him as righteousness." For nothing is so righteous as to use a faith toward God alone that is pure and unmixed. Necessario igitur additur, credidit Abraham Deo ad laudem ipsius, qui credidit. At forte dicat aliquis: Hoc ne dignum laude existimatis? Who would not give credence to God speaking and promising, even if he were the most unjust or most impious of men? To whom we reply: Ah, good man, do not either take away from a wise man the praises that are owed to him, or attribute the most perfect of virtues to the unworthy, or condemn our opinion on this matter. For if you wish to make a deeper inquiry into this matter, and not one that merely floats on the surface, you will recognize that it is not so easy to give, to God alone, without assuming any other thing, one's belief, because of the kinship that exists within us with our mortal frame, which is indeed the reason why we trust in money, and glory, and honors, and friends, and good health, and bodily strength, and other goods of this kind. To be purged of all these, and to distrust created things which are in themselves untrustworthy, but to trust in God alone, who is truly the only one who is always faithful, is the work of a great and heavenly mind, and of one who is no longer captured by any of the allurements of those things which we see. But it is very well said that faith was reckoned to him for righteousness. For nothing is so just as to rely with pure and sincere faith upon God. And what follows there is truly worthy of reading. The same Philo in his book On the Confusion of Tongues: Ὁ δὲ σοφὸς πρῶτον μὲν κτῆται γέρας παρὰ τοῦ ἑστῶτος ἀεί. Θεοῦ συγγενὲς αὐτῷ τὴν ἀκλινῆ καὶ ἄῤῥεπη πρὸς πάντα δυνάμει λαβών, εἴρηται γάρ· Σὺ δὲ αὐτοῦ στῆθι μετ' ἐμοῦ, ἵνα εὐδοιασμοὺ κᾐ ἐπαμφοτερισμὸν ἀβεβαίου ψυχῆς διαθέσεως, ἀποδυσάμε- νος τὴν ὀχυρωτάτην κᾐ βεβαιοτάτην διάθεσιν καὶ πίστιν ἐν- δύσηται. The wise man first has received from God, who always stands, a reward consistent with the immutable and invariable power of God. For it has been said: But you stand here with me, namely, that by casting off the hesitation and alternation of an unstable soul's disposition, he may put on the most fortified and most certain disposition, namely, faith. If anyone should rightly consider these things, he will find that they agree very well with what the writer to the Hebrews, breathing something of Philo, as it seems to Jerome, wrote: Ἔστι δὲ πίστις ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων: Faith is the substance of things to be hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. The same Philo in the aforementioned book On the Heir of Divine Goods explains the nature of faith thus, saying: Τὸ μὲν ἀπορεῖν ἐνδοιάζοντος, τὸ δὲ μηκέτι ζητεῖν, πεπιστευκότος ἔργον εἶναι: To doubt is the work of one who is wavering, but to inquire no further is the work of one who has believed. Where ἐνδοιάζειν to waver is the same as δισάζειν, Matt. 14:31, and διακρίνεσθαι, Matt. 21:21, and in this epistle of James 1:6. But James wisely, when he was commending works, also mixed in the illustrious titles of faith, lest he seem to cast it down more than is right, showing that works themselves are to be credited to faith, and all the more so, the more illustrious they are. Chrysostom on the fourth chapter to the Romans: Τὸ γὰρ μὴ κλέψαι, μηδὲ φο- νεῦσαι καὶ τῶν τυχόντων ἐσίν. Τὸ δὲ πιστεῦσαι ὅτι τὰ ἀδύνατα δύναται Θεὸς μεγαλοφυοῦς τινὸς δεῖται ψυχῆς, κᾐ σφό- δρα δι' αὐτοῦ περιεστηκότης: For not to steal, nor to murder, is even for ordinary people. But to believe that God can make the impossible happen requires a sublime soul, and one very well disposed toward God. The same man, immediately comparing the believer to him who only exhibits works: Δείκνυσι πιστεύοντα ἐργαζομένου μᾶλλον ᾗ ἐκείνου, κᾐ πλείονος δεό- μενον δυνάμεως, κᾐ πολλῆς τῆς ἰσχύος. He shows that the believer does more than that man, and requires more power and much strength for that work.

We have stated what it means for faith to have been reckoned to Abraham for righteousness, both in our Illustrious Bible of the Old Testament on Gen. XV, as well as in our commentary on Genesis, likewise in our commentary on Rom. IV, and also in our preface to the Epistle to the Romans. The Grotius paraphrase does not exhaust the sense of the phrase, whether as presented by Moses or as explained more fully by Paul, as if to say that that faith was held by God as an extraordinary thing, because it is said to be reckoned for righteousness for the reason that by that faith the Patriarch was justified before God. Nor is this a parallel passage to be held

Ps. CVI. 31. For there the discourse is not about justification before the divine tribunal, or about the righteousness of a person, but about the righteousness of a singular deed, which was considered just extraordinarily and extrajudicially, not when Phinehas was being brought before the tribunal and judgment of God, about to render an account for all things done throughout his whole life, and whether he was to be condemned for sins or absolved in view of faith, by the example of Abraham, from sins. Furthermore, since the passages of Philo consider faith as an act and a moral virtue, they must be judged irrelevant here. For Moses teaches that faith, viewed instrumentally, or rather objectively as the thing believed, or faith, not by which one believes, but which is believed, was reckoned for righteousness: that the righteousness or obedience of Christ, apprehended by true faith, was reckoned to Abraham as his own righteousness, just as that sentence in Rom. IV. 3. brought by Paul from Moses is explained, v. 6, that righteousness is reckoned to a man without works, which is or can be no other than the righteousness or obedience of Christ, by which we are constituted righteous, Rom. V. 19, Phil. III. 9. For the quality of faith is not regarded here, as if it were worthy to be reputed for righteousness, as Pererius, Bonfrerius, Marius, Tirinus on Gen. XV. 6, Justinianus, Estius on Rom. IV, Lorinus, Paëz in this place, and Vasquez I. 2. disp. 222. c. 1. interpret τὸ λογίζεσθαι as a divine estimation which results from the nature and quality of faith: which is opposed by those in the Papacy, who accept it for such an estimation and reputation of God as faith does not merit of itself, but which proceeds from the purpose of grace, just as in the Sixtine and Clementine Vulgate editions it is added at the end of the verse: According to the purpose of grace of God: As Cardinal Toletus in Rom. IV. ann. 7. Cornelius à Lapide, Salmero, Menochius, etc. Which sense the scope of the Apostle entirely demands, as do those words κατὰ χάριν, according to grace. For to this imputation is opposed another, which is made κατὰ τὸ ὀφείλημα, according to debt.

Καὶ φίλος Θεῦ ἐκλήθη) Namely because he had offered his son, as is said in Gen. XXII. 16, where God, which He had not done before, entered into a sworn covenant with Abraham, just as Kings are accustomed to do with friends: and the cause is added; because you have done this thing, and have not spared your only son for my sake. How much such a sworn covenant ought to be valued, the writer to the Hebrews VI. 13 seqq. explains excellently. He was called the friend of God, that is, and was, in Hebrew idiom, examples of which we have in Is. I. 16, XLVIII. 8, LXII. 4, Jer. XXXIII. 16, Ezech. XLVIII. 35. Thus to become children of God in John I. 12 is the same as to be called children of God in 1 Epist. III. 1. But the name adhered to Abraham from the fact, as we see in Is. XLI. 8 and 2 Chron. XX. 7. Clement in his epistle to the Corinthians: Ἐμαρτυρήθη μεγάλος Ἀβραὰμ, καὶ φίλος προσηγορεύθη τῦ Θεῦ.

In the other commentary these things are read, not very different, but containing many erroneous things:

Καὶ φίλος Θεῦ ἐκλήθη) And he was called the friend of God. After he rendered his own to faith, he returns to preaching the power of works. Ἐκλήθη, he was called, is not to be referred to the estimation of men (for no witness had been present at this deed of Abraham offering his son, so highly praised, as sacred history teaches us) but to the thing itself in Hebrew idiom, by which someone is said to be called by a name by which he was never called, but which beautifully expresses his state. Thus John said in 1 Epist. III. 1, ἴδετε, ποταπὴν ἀγάπην δέδωκεν ἡμῖν ὁ Πατὴρ, ἵνα τέκνα Θεῦ κληθῶμεν. See what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be named children of God. Which he had said in the Gospel ch. I. 12, ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ἐξουσίαν τέκνα Θεῦ γενέσθαι, he gave them power to become children of God. See Is. I. 16, XLVIII. 8, LXII. 4, Jer. XXXIII. 16, Ezech. XLVIII. 35. But what is said here φίλος Θεῦ ἐκλήθη, he was called the friend of God, pertains to those things which we have in Gen. XXII. 16 & seqq., where God, because he had not spared his son for the love of God, enters into a new covenant with Abraham, and confirms that very thing by an oath, the value of which see in Heb. VI, and thus receives him into a closer degree of friendship: to which also that pertains which is in Is. XLI. 8 and 2 Chron. XX. 7. Thus James excellently shows how much both faith and works proceeding from faith avail before God.

But first, we find a lack of connection here.
