For he does not return in these words to preaching the power of works, after he rendered his own to faith, because he both preached true faith in the example of Abraham, and did not cease to preach his works: and the Apostle adheres strictly to his scope, that the Patriarch was justified by faith, but faith which demonstrated itself through works. And that that faith and justification were clearly acknowledged and manifested primarily by those works which he performed in the offering of Isaac through faith. And thus also that he was truly called the friend of God, that is, that he was not only so in reality, but was also named and held as such. For we said before that that appellation implies notoriety of the fact in addition to the truth. The second thing, therefore, that we find lacking in Grotius here, is that he explains τὸ κληθῆναι only by 'to become,' that he then became the friend of God. He was already a friend of God, yet he can be said to have been made so, because a closer friendship had approached: But that word does not refer to being made [something] bare: It also brings in, by the force of its own meaning, the naming and notoriety of the thing, that it became known that he was such, and therefore was deservedly so called. The divine conversation with Abraham, as of a friend with a friend, testifies to the truth of this, as does the friendly, nay, sworn confirmation of the covenant entered into with him, and the assurance of the promises, and the reason for the same rendered by God himself, which He set forth in most friendly words: Because you have done this, and have not spared your only son: and therefore because you have obeyed my voice. Which, as they have become known and celebrated throughout the Church along with the deed of Abraham: So the Holy Spirit here testifies that Abraham was named and held to be the friend of God; and this also appears from those passages Isa. XLI. 8, 2 Chron. XX. 7, and Judith VIII. 22. Nor do those things which Grotius compares teach only that he was made a friend. For 1. 1 John III. 1, we are said both to be called and to be children of God; Isa. I. 26, chap. XLVIII. 8, chap. LXII. 4, besides the truth of attribution, the public notoriety of such a denomination is also insinuated. In the passage of Isa. XLVIII. 35, the word for calling does not indeed occur, but it is manifest that the notoriety of the Church throughout the world is designated. But the passage Jerem. XXXIII. 16 is foreign to the matter, concerning which [we shall speak] in its own place. Thirdly, we do not deny that the friendship of God toward Abraham was increased by the obedience of the Patriarch; but that justification, which consists in the remission of sins, was therefore increased, is by no means a consequence, nor do we admit that a second justification is denoted by the infusion of more abundant habits of faith: nay, not even Toletus among the Papists admits it, appealing to the ancients in ann. V. on Rom. IV. The second righteousness made him not a friend, but a more pleasing friend. Therefore it is necessary to understand this testimony concerning the first righteousness; just as Paul also understood it, and the ancient Fathers also understood it. Justinianus does not admit it. And yet I do not know whether those words, by which he affirms that Abraham was made the friend of God, can be adapted to a second justification. For by what reasoning is he said to have been made a friend of God, who was already long since a friend and righteous. And subsequently: Therefore I have always thought that both Paul and James spoke of the first justification. For Paul indeed, who commended the faith of Christ and his grace against the arrogance of the Jews, attributes the justification of Abraham to faith, as to a root and source: but James, who acted against those who boasted of faith alone and naked, shows that Abraham was indeed justified by faith, Nor does Gabriel Vasquez admit this, disp. 210. in l. 2. c. 8. Nor does Seraphinus Cameranus in Concil. LL. CC. F. III. contra pos. 9. Nor Estius in h. l. What then? That not even Bellarmine himself agrees with himself here. For although he maintains that James is speaking here of secondary justification: yet regarding Rahab, who is said here to have been justified, he interprets it as meaning that she was made a believer from an unbeliever, l. IV. de justif. c. 18. §. Quarto ex eo. Fourthly, God does not make a new covenant, Gen. XXII. 16. but confirms by an oath that which he had already entered into with Abraham, and had repeated and renewed several times, Gen. XI. 34. 35. cap. XIII. 13. seqq. cap. XV. 5. 6. 18. cap. XVII. 2. seqq. cap. XVIII. 18. cap. XXI. 12.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Καὶ ἐπληρώθη ἡ γραφὴ ἡ λέγουσα ) Ante quidem id dictum fuerat de Abrahamo quum Isaacum offerret, ut vi- dere est dicto loco Gen. XV. 6. Sed mos est Ebræis dicere, hoc נתקיים, id est ἐπληρώθη, cum rei alicubi narratæ similis alia contingit. Nam tunc ex fide Abraham Deo victimas ob- tulit, & nunc victimam multo pretiosiorem. Pari modo di- ctum illud, reputatum est ei ad justitiam ad tempus Isaaci oblati refert Scriptor primi Maccabaici II. 52. ᾿Αβραὰμ οὐχ ἐν πειρασμῷ εὑρέθη πιστὸς, καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην.

De hisce ita annotarat in priori tractatu: Καὶ ἐπληρώθη ἡ γραφὴ ἡ λέγουσα, ἐπίσευσε δὲ ᾿Αβραὰμ τῷ Θεῷ) Et suppleta est scriptura dicens: Credidit Abraham Deo. Eodem Mosis dicto utitur, quo ad commendan- dam fidem Paulus usus fuerat. Atqui dicat aliquis, multo hoc ante positum à Mose est, quam ad historiam oblati Isaaci pervenerat, ubi scilicet Abrahamo promissam so- bolem innumeram, eique promisso fidem ab ipso habi- tam narraverat. Sed sciendum est, apud Ebræos frequens esse, ut dicant נתקיים id est, ἐπληρώθη, sive compre- batus est hic vel ille Scripturæ sacræ locus, quoties rei lo- co illo commemoratæ simile quid accidit, maxime ubi parem causam par eventus sequitur. Fides illa Abrahami, quæ Deo ita grata fuit, ut propter eam Abrahamum, velut plane ab initio innocentem susciperet, sæpe appa- ruit: eo tempore, de quo agit ille locus Geneseos XV. 6. iterum Gen. XVII. cum promissus ei esset ex Sara filius, quod exequitur Paulus Rom. IV. 17. & seq. Nunquam au- tem evidentius emicuit, quam cum se ad parendum præ- cepto Dei de filio occidendo accinxit. Erat enim ea fides ingens & Evangelicæ instar, ita & de potentia Dei, & in dictis suis faciendis constantia existimans, ut filium, un- de cætera magnifica promissa pendebant, vel à morte si- bi restitui posse crederent, Ebr. XI. 18.

Recte dicit Grotius, fidem Abrahami eviden- tissime emicuisse, cum se ad parendum Deo in filio occidendo accinxit: Sed eodem modo hoc dictum adhiberi à Paulo non admittendum. Pau- lus enim ad illum fidei effectum, qui est justifi- catio Abrahami coram Deo, adhibet. Jaco- bus vero impletam dicit illam Scripturam, non cum justificatus coram Deo est Abraham, sed ubi fides & justitia ejus publice declarata est, & ab omnibus agnosci potuit. Neque ibi parem cau- sam par eventus sequutus est. Nam alia causa est. fides, alia opera, alius eventus est justificatio, alius justificationis ostensio. Impleri enim dicitur Scri- ptura etiam, cum id, quod oraculo divino tra- ditum est, palam manifestatur vel innotescit: quem sensum hic ipsimet etiam Papistæ admittunt, utpote Salmero, Cornelius à Lapide, Paëz, Tirinus, Estius, & imprimis Lorinus, qui multis eam phrasin explicat, quod magnitudo fidei Abrahamiticae, quod non otiosa, non mortua, sed actuosa, efficax, & comitata bonis operibus esset, in filii immolatio- ne se maxime ostenderit, & innotuerit aliis. Quod de forma loquendi πληρωθῆναι τὴν γραφὴν exprimi solita per מתקיים tradit Grotius, quicquid de Ebraeis sit recentioribus, stylo scripturae non con- gruit, in qua id nunquam observatur, sed קיים vel primam institutionem notat, ut Esth. IX. 21. 27. 29. 31. 32. vel confirmationem novi contractus Ruth. IV. 7. vel assertionem dicti praesentis, Ezech. XIII. 6. vel mo- ralem confirmationem animi in bono proposito, Psal. CXIX. 28. 106. Sed imprimis censuram me- retur, quod fidem Abrahamiticam tantum instar quoddam fidei Evangelicae habuisse ait. Nam eam in exemplum sistit nobis, & ideam verae Evangelicae & justificae fidei Apostolus Rom. IV. quodque ob- jectum ejus fidei facit multiplicationem seminis Abrahami, cujus praecipuum objectum fuit pro- missio, quod Filius Dei Abrahae scutum & merces magna esse velit, ac promissio illa seminis multipli- candi non nisi ob μοναδικὸν illud semen facta, in quo benedictio obtingit omnibus nationibus ter- rae, Gen. XII. 3. cap. XV, 1. seqq. Gal. III. 16. Rom. IV. 3. seqq. Denique non propter fidem Deus suscepit Abrahamum velut ab initio plane innocentem, sed per fidem: Ita ut fides spectanda sit ceu instru- mentum, quo accipitur gratia Dei, non ceu mora- lis virtus, propter quam in gratiam recipimur.

Καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην) Id est, fides illa à Deo habita est pro re egregia, quales res justitiae nomine ap- pellari solent. Habes idem loquendi genus Psal. CVI. 31. ubi zelus Phineae dicitur ei reputatus in justitiam, id est, magno à Deo factus, magnaque mercede sacerdotii summi remuneratus.

v. Prolixius haec exequutus erat Grotius in priori commentatione;

Καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην) Et reputatum est illi ad justitiam. Vox Ebraea, pro qua λογίζεσαι ponunt Graeci, frequenter sumitur, cum res aut homo aliquis ita habetur, quasi alio modo haberet, quam se habet, sive id jure, sive injuria fiat, eodemque modo sumitur verbum ἰσοδυναμῶν נחשב, ut Es. LIII. 12. quod per λογίζεσαι reddidere Interpretes Matth. XV. 28. Luc. XXII. 37. Sic cum opus unum egregium pro multis habetur, dicitur id in justitiam λογίζεσθαι sive reputari, ut de Phi- nea Psal. CVI. 30. Sic ἡ ἀκροβυςία praeputiati hominis status dicitur εἰς περιτομὴν λογίζεσθαι Rom. II. 27. id est, tantundem valere, quantum status hominis circum- cisi. Justinus ad Zenam Ἀνοήτῳ γὰρ ἐπερωτήσαντι σοφίαν, σοφία λογισθήσεται. Imperito enim & interroganti sa- pientiam, sapientia reputatur, id est, ἡ ἐπερώτησις εἰς σο- φίαν λογισθήσεται, interrogatio pro sapientia habebi- tur. Theophilus Antiochenus, ἡ πίσις σου εἰς ἀπισίαν λογίζεται, fides tua in infidelitatem reputatur. Tertul- lianus Apologetico de ludis gentium: Occasio luxu- riae religio deputabitur. Idem libro, de patientia de Abrahamo loquens: Caeterum Deus, quem justitiae de- putasset, sciebat. Chrysostomus 1. Cor. cap. II. Λο- γισθήσεται τῷ ἕλληνι εἰς πίσιν ἡ προσκύνησις ἐκείνη: Repu tabitur Graeco ad fidem adoratio illa. Idem ergo valet aliquid alicui λογίζεσθαι εἰς δικαιοσύνην, reputari ad justi- tiam, quod eum, qui id habeat, haberi ὡς δίκαιον καὶ ἀνα- μάρτητον, quasi justus plane esset, neque unquam pec- casset. Justinus colloquio cum Tryphone: Εἰ γὰρ Χρη- σότης καὶ ἡ φιλανθρωπία τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ τὸ ἀμέτρον τοῦ πλούτου αὐτοῦ τὸν μετανοοῦντα ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων ὡς δίκαιον καὶ ἀναμάρ- τητον ἔχοι, καὶ τὸν ἀπὸ εὐσεβείας ἢ δικαιοπραξίας μετατιθέ- μενον ἐπὶ ἀδικίαν ἀκραταλὸν καὶ ἄδικον καὶ ἀσεβῆ ἐπίςαται. Dei enim bonitas & erga homines dilectio & immen- sum divitiarum ejus poenitentia ob peccata ductum pro justo & peccati exorte habet; at contra eum, qui à pietate aut justitia deficit ad iniqua, pro peccatore, & injusto, & impio habet. Idem & per ἀποδέχεσθαι acce- ptare Graeci loquuntur, ut ὁ Θεὸς τὴν μετάνοιαν εἰς ἀρετὴν

ἀποδέχεσθαι: Deus pœnitentiam pro virtute acceptat. Id vero ipsum, quod hic dicitur, sic circum loquendo exprimit Philo in libro, quis rerum divinarum hæres: Ἀναγκαίως ἔτι ἐπιλέγεται· Ἐπίστευσεν δὲ Ἀβραὰμ τῷ Θεῷ πρὸς ἔπαινον τοῦ πιστεύσαντος, καίτοι τάχ' ἄν τις εἴποι, τοῦτ' ἄξιον ἐπαίνου κρίνεται; Τίς δὲ οὐκ ἂν λόγοντι καὶ ὑπισχνου- μένῳ Θεῷ προσέχοι τὸν νοῦν, κἂν ἁπάντων ἀδικώτατος καὶ ἀσε- βέστατος ὢν τυγχάνων; πρὸς ὃν ἐροῦμεν· μὴ, μὴ, ὦ γενναῖε, ἀνεξε- τάστως ᾗ τὸν σοφὸν ἀφίλη τὰ πρέποντα ὀγκώματα, ᾗ τοῖς ἀνα- ξίοις τὴν τελειοτάτην τῶν ἀρετῶν πίστιν μαρτυρήσῃς, ἢ τὴν ἡμετέραν περὶ τούτων γνῶσιν αἰτιάσῃ. Βαθύτεραν γὰρ εἰ βουλη- θείης ἔρευναν, κᾐ μὴ σφόδρα ἐπιπόλαιον ποιήσασθαι, σαφῶς γνώσῃ, ὅτι μόνῳ Θεῷ χωρὶς ἑτέρου προσπαραλήψεως ἐφ' ἕ- δους πιστεῦσαι, διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸ θνητὸν, ᾧ συνεζεύγμεθα συγ- γένειαν, ὅπερ ἡμᾶς κᾐ χρήμασι, κᾐ δόξῃ, κᾐ ἀρχῇ, κᾐ φίλοις, ὑγείᾳ τε κᾐ ῥώμῃ σώματος, κᾐ ἄλλοις πολλοῖς ἀναπείθει πεπι- στευκέναι. Τὸ δὲ ἐκνίψασθαι τούτων ἕκαστον, κᾐ ἀπιστῆσαι γενέσει τῇ πάντα ἐξ ἑαυτῆς ἀπίστῳ, μόνῳ δὲ πιστεῦσαι Θεῷ, τῷ κᾐ πρὸς ἀλήθειαν μόνῳ πιστῷ, μεγάλης καὶ ὀλυμπίου διανοίας ἔργον ἐστι, πρὸς οὐδενὸς ὑκέτι δελεαζομένης τῶν παρ' ἡμῖν. Εὖ δὲ τὸ Φάναι, λογισθῆναι τὴν πίστιν εἰς δικαιοσύνην αὐτῷ. Δίκαιον γὰρ οὕτως οὐδὲν ὡς ἀκράτῳ κᾐ ἀμιγεῖ τῇ πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν μόνου κε- χρῆσθαι. Necessario igitur additur, credidit Abraham Deo ad laudem ipsius, qui credidit. At forte dicat ali- quis: Hoc ne dignum laude existimatis? Quis non Deo loquenti & pollicenti fidem adhibeat, etiamsi sit hominum injustissimus vel maxime impius? Cui re- spondemus: Ah ne, vir bone, aut viro sapienti aufer, quæ ei debentur præconia, aut indignis perfectissi- mam virtutum attribue fidem, aut nostram hac de re damna sententiam. Nam si profundiorem velis, non autem in summo natantem hac de re inquisitionem facere cognosces, dare non adeo esse facile, Deo soli, re alia non assumpta, credere, propter eam quæ in nobis est, cum mortali compage cognationem, quæ quidem causa est, cur fidamus pecuniis, & gloriæ, & honori- bus, & amicis, & bonæ valetudini, & corporis robori, & aliis ejusmodi bonis. Ab his purgari omnibus, & diffidere genitis rebus per se infidis, uni autem Deo confidere, qui revera solus semper fidus est, magni & cœlestis animi est opus, & ejus, qui nullis amplius ca- piatur earum, quas videmus, rerum illecebris. Optime autem dictum, fidem ipsi esse ad justitiam reputatam. Nihil enim tam justum, quam pura & sincera in Deum fide niti. Et quæ ibi sequuntur, digna sane le- ctu. Idem Philo libro de confusis linguis: Ὁ δὲ σοφὸς πρῶτον μὲν κτῆται γέρας παρὰ τοῦ ἑστῶτος ἀεί. Θεοῦ συγγενὲς αὐτῷ τὴν ἀκλινῆ καὶ ἄῤῥεπη πρὸς πάντα δυνάμει λαβών, εἴρηται γάρ· Σὺ δὲ αὐτοῦ στῆθι μετ' ἐμοῦ, ἵνα εὐδοιασμοὺ κᾐ ἐπαμφοτερισμὸν ἀβεβαίου ψυχῆς διαθέσεως, ἀποδυσάμε- νος τὴν ὀχυρωτάτην κᾐ βεβαιοτάτην διάθεσιν καὶ πίστιν ἐν- δύσηται. Sapiens ille primum habet acceptum à Deo semper stante præmium consentaneum potentiæ Dei indemutabili atque invariabili. Dictum enim est: Tu autem sta mecum, nempe ut hæsitationem & alterna- tionem instabilis animi affectiones exuens induat constitutionem omnium firmissimam atque constan- tissimam, fidem scilicet. Quæ si quis recte conside- ret, inveniet optime convenire cum eo, quod scriptor ad Ebræos, Philoneum aliquid spirans, ut Hierony- mo videtur, scripsit: Ἔστι δὲ πίστις ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων: Est fides speranda- rum substantia rerum, argumentum non apparen- tium. Naturam fidei idem Philo dicto libro de hæ- rede bonorum divinorum sic explicat, dicens: Τὸ μὲν ἀπορεῖν ἐνδοιάζοντος, τὸ δὲ μηκέτι ζητεῖν, πεπιστευκότος ἔργον εἶναι: Dubitare alternantis est, nihil autem sci- scitari credentis opus. Ubi ἐνδοιάζειν alternare idem est, quod δισάζειν, Matth. XIV. 31. & διακρίνεσθαι, Matth. XXI. 21. & in hac Jacobi epistola I. 6. Sapienter au- tem Jacobus, cum opera commendaret, immiscuit & fidei præclaros titulos, ne eam plus æquo dejicere videretur, ostendens ipsa opera fidei accepta ferenda, eoque magis, quo præclariora. Chrysostomus in IV. caput ad Romanos: Τὸ γὰρ μὴ κλέψαι, μηδὲ φο- νεῦσαι καὶ τῶν τυχόντων ἐσίν. Τὸ δὲ πιστεῦσαι ὅτι τὰ ἀδύνατα δύναται Θεὸς μεγαλοφυοῦς τινὸς δεῖται ψυχῆς, κᾐ σφό- δρα δι' αὐτοῦ περιεστηκότης: non furari, non occidere ho- minum est vulgarium. At credere Deo, quod possit impossibilia effecta dare, animum requirit sublimem, & optime in Deum affectum. Idem mox creden- tem ei qui tantum opera exhibet conferens: Δείκνυσι πιστεύοντα ἐργαζομένου μᾶλλον ᾗ ἐκείνου, κᾐ πλείονος δεό- μενον δυνάμεως, κᾐ πολλῆς τῆς ἰσχύος. Ostendit cre- dentem plus illo agere, & majore ad id opus vi & efficacia.

Quid sit fidem imputatam esse Abrahamo ad ju- stitiam, & in Bibliis Illustr. V. T. ad Gen. XV. ut & in comment. ad Genesin, item in comment. ad Rom. IV. nec non in præfat. ad epist. Rom. diximus. Non exhaurit sensum phraseos, sive prout à Mose exhi- bita, sive prout à Paulo uberius explicata Grotiana paraphrasis, q. d. fidem illam pro re egregia à Deo habitam, quia imputata dicitur ad justitiam ea ra- tione, quod per fidem illam justificatus coram Deo sit Patriarcha. Neque parallelus habendus locus

Psal. CVI. 31. Ibi enim non de justificatione coram tribunali divino sermo est, aut de justitia personæ, sed de justitia singularis facti, quod extraordinariè, & extrajudicialiter justum habitum est, non quan- do Pinehas coram tribunali & judicio Dei sisteba- tur, de omnibus per totam vitam gestis rationem redditurus, ac sive ob peccata condemnandus, seu absolvendus intuitu fidei, exemplo Abrahami, à peccatis. De cætero quum Philonis loca fidem ut actum & virtutem moralem considerent, aliena censenda hic sunt. Siquidem Moses de fide instru- mentaliter spectata, vel potius objective de re credi- ta, vel fide, non quâ creditur, sed quæ creditur, do- ceat, eam in justitiam imputatam : quod justitia vel obedientia Christi vera fide apprehensa Abraha- mo imputata fuerit ceu propria justitia, quemad- modum illa sententia Rom. IV. 3. à Paulo è Mose ad- ducta explicatur, v. 6. quod justitia homini impute- tur sine operibus quæ nulla alia est aut esse potest, quam justitia vel obedientia Christi, qua justi nos constituimur, Rom. V. 19. Phil. III. 9. Non enim re- spicitur hic qualitas fidei, quasi illa digna sit reputari pro justitia, uti Pererius, Bonfrerius, Marius, Tirinus ad Gen. XV. 6. Justinianus, Estius ad Rom. IV. Lorinus, Paëz in h. l. Vasquez I. 2. disp. 222. c. 1. τὸ λογίζεσθαι interpretantur pro æstimatione divina, quæ re- sultet ex indole & qualitate fidei : quibus repu- gnant in Papatu, qui illud pro tali æstimio ac repu- tatione Dei accipiunt, qualem fides pro se non me- reatur, sed quæ proficiscatur ex proposito gratiæ, quemadmodum in Vulg. Sixtinis & Clementinis editionibus additur sub finem versus : Secundum propositum gratiæ Dei: Utpote Cardinalis Toletus in Rom. IV. ann. 7. Cornelius à Lapide, Salmero, Me- nochius &c. Quem sensum scopus Apostoli omni- no poscit, ut & voces illæ κατὰ χάριν secundum gra- tiam. Huic enim imputationi opponitur altera, quæ fit κατὰ τὸ ὀφείλημα secundum debitum.

Καὶ φίλος Θεῦ ἐκλήθη) Nempe quia filium obtulerat, ut dicitur Gen. XXII. 16. ubi Deus quod ante non fece- rat, juratum fœdus cum Abrahamo iniit, sicut Reges cum amicis solent : additurque causa; quia fecisti hanc rem, & non pepercisti filio tuo unico propter me. Quanti autem tale fœdus juratum fieri debeat, egregiè explicat scriptor ad Ebr. VI. 13. seqq. Amicus Dei vocatus est, id est, & fuit, loquutione Ebræa, cujus exempla habemus Es. I. 16. XLVIII. 8. LXII. 4. Jerem. XXXIII. 16. Ezech. XLVIII. 35. Sic fieri filios Dei Joh. I. 12. idem est quod 1. epist. III. 1. vocari filios Dei. Ex re autem nomen illud Abrahamo adhæsit, ut videmus Es XLI. 8. & 2. Par. XX. 7. Clemens in epistola ad Corinthios: Ἐμαρτυρήθη μεγάλος Ἀβραὰμ, καὶ φίλος προσηγορεύθη τῦ Θεῦ.

In altero commentario hæc leguntur non ad- modum diversa, plura autem erronea continen- tia:

Καὶ φίλος Θεῦ ἐκλήθη) Et amicus Dei appellatus est. Postquam fidei suum reddidit, ad operum vim prædicandam redit. Ἐκλήθη appellatus est, non ad ho- minum existimationem referendum (nemo enim te- stis adfuerat isti facto Abrahami filium offerentis tan- topere prædicato, ut sacra nos docet historia) sed ad rem ipsam loquutione Ebræa, qua vocari aliquis di- citur nomine, quo nunquam appellatus est, sed quod ipsius statum pulchre exprimit. Sic Johannes dixit 1. Epist. III. 1. ἴδετε, ποταπὴν ἀγάπην δέδωκεν ἡμῖν ὁ Πατὴρ, ἵνα τέκνα Θεῦ κληθῶμεν. Videte qualem charitatem pater dedit nobis Pater, ut filii Dei nominemur. Quod in Evangelio dixerat cap. I. 12. ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ἐξουσίαν τέκνα Θεῦ γενέσθαι, dedit eis potestatem, filios Dei fieri. Vide Es. I. 16. XLVIII. 8. LXII. 4. Jer. XXXIII. 16. Ezech. XLVIII. 35. Quod autem hic dicitur φίλος Θεῦ ἐκλή- θη, amicus Dei appellatus est, pertinet ad ea, quæ ha- bemus Gen. XXII. 16. & seqq. ubi Deus cum Abra- hamo, ideo quod filio suo præ Dei amore non peper- cisset, fœdus novum paciscitur, idque ipsum sancit ju- rejurando, quod quanti sit faciendum, vide Ebr. VI. & sic eum in propiorem amicitiæ recipit gradum: quo & illud spectat, quod est Esa. XLI. 8. & 2. Paral. XX. 7. Ita egregie ostendit Jacobus, quantum apud Deum valeant & fides, & ex fide profecta opera.

Primum autem hic nexum desideramus. Non enim redit his verbis ad operum vim prædican- dam, postquam fidei suum reddidit, quia & fidem veram in exemplo Abrahami prædicavit, nec ope- ra ejus prædicare intermisit: ac scopo suo inhæret presse Apostolus, fide, sed quæ per opera se demonstra- vit, Patriarcham justificatum. Illam autem fidem, & justificationem luculenter agnitam, & manifestatam fuisse imprimis operibus illis, quæ in oblatione Isaaci per fidem facta exequutus est. Atque ita etiam ami- cum Dei ex vero appellatum esse, id est, non fuisse tantum reapse, sed etiam nuncupatum ac habitum esse. Nam istam appellationem præter veritatem etiam notorietatem rei inferre antea diximus. Al- terum ergo, quod hic desideramus in Grotio, est, quod τὸ κληθῆναι solum per fieri explicat, quod tum amicus Dei factus sit. Erat jam amicus Dei, fa- ctus tamen dici potest, quod amicitia arctior acces- serit: Sed non nudum fieri vox illa respicit: Infert etiam vi propriæ significationis nuncupationem & notorietatem rei, quod talem esse innotuerit, adeo- que merito ita vocatus sit. De sei veritate testatur divina cum Abrahamo, ceu amici cum amico, col- loquutio, fœderisque cum eodem initi amica imò juratoria confirmatio, & promissionum certio- ratio, ejusdemque reddita à Deo ipso ratio, quam amicissimis verbis exposuit: Quia fecisti hoc, & filio tuo unico non pepercisti: & ideo quod voci meæ pa- ruisti. Quæ uti passim in Ecclesia cum facto Abra- hami innotuere & celebrata sunt: Ita Abraham nominatum & habitum esse amicum Dei, Spiritus Sanctus hic testatur; idque etiam ex locis illis Esa. XLI. 8. 2. Paral. XX. 7. & Judith. IIX. 22. apparet. Nec ea, quæ confert Grotius, solum amicum fa- ctum docent. Nam 1. Joh. III. 1. & appellari & esse filii Dei dicimur Esa. I. 26. cap. XLIIX. 8. cap. LXII. 4. præter veritatem attributionis etiam publica no- torietas talis denominationis insinuatur. In loco vero Esa. XLVIII. 35. non occurrit quidem ver- bum vocandi, manifestum autem est, notorie- tatem Ecclesiæ per orbem designari. At alienus est locus Jerem. XXXIII. 16. de quo suo loco. Tertio amicitiam Dei erga Abrahamum auctam fuisse ex obsequio Patriarchæ non abnuimus; sed justificationem, quæ in remissione peccatorum sita est, ideo auctam esse, minimè consequens est, neque justificationem secundam per copiosioris fidei habitus infusionem notari admittimus: imò ne admittit quidem è Pontificiis Toletus ad anti- quos provocans ann. V. ad Rom. IV. Secunda ju- stitia non amicum, sed gratiorem amicum fecit. Er- go de prima justitia necesse est intelligere hoc te- stimonium; sicut & Paulus intellexit, & antiqui Patres etiam intellexerunt. Non admittit Justi- nianus. Atqui haud scio, an ea verba, quibus affirmat Abrahamum Dei amicum factum esse, secundæ justificationi aptari queant. Quæ enim ratione dicitur factus amicus Dei, qui jam pridem erat ami- cus & justus. Et deinceps: Itaque semper existimavi, tam Paulum, quam Jacobum de prima justificatione disputare. Nam Paulus quidem, qui fidem Chri- sti ejusque gratiam adversus Judæorum arroganti- am commendabat, justificationem Abrahæ tribuit fi- dei, tanquam radici ac fonti: Jacobus autem, qui contra eos agebat, qui solam nudamque fidem ja- ctabant, ostendit justificatum quidem Abrahamum ex fide, non tamen elumbi, otiosa & languida, sed conjuncta cum pœnitentia, spe, & charitate. Nec admittit Gabriel Vasquez disp. 210. in l. 2. c. 8. Neq; etiam Seraphinus Cameranus in Concil. LL. CC. F. III. contra pos. 9. Neque Estius in h. l. Quid? quod nec Bellarmino ipsi secum hîc conveniat. Nam licet statuat de justificatione secunda hic lo- qui Jacobum: De Rahaba tamen, quod hic dici- tur, eandem justificatam esse, ita interpretatur, quod ex infideli facta fuerit fidelis, l. IV. de justif. c. 18. §. Quarto ex eo. Quarto non paciscitur Deus fœ- dus novum, Gen. XXII. 16. sed juramento confir- mat, quod cum Abrahamo jam inierat, & repe- tierat aliquoties ac renovarat, Gen. XI. 34. 35. cap. XIII. 13. seqq. cap. XV. 5. 6. 18. cap. XVII. 2. seqq. cap. XVIII. 18. cap. XXI. 12.

## 2:24
Vers. 24. See then) Learn from this example of a very great man.

That a man is justified by works, and not by faith only) Unless works are added to faith, God will never hold anyone as righteous. For all these things are accustomed to be included under the name הַצְדִּיק in a secondary meaning. It is the same thing to say ἐκ πίστεως μόνον as it is ἐκ πίστεως μόνης. Thus μόνον, an adverb, is placed in the stead of an adjective, Matth. V. 47. XXI. 19. Joh. XIII. 9. Act. XI. 19. Rom. III. 20. and elsewhere.

What is read in the previous treatise concerning these matters is as follows:

Vers. 24. See then, that a man is justified by works and not by faith only) You see that a man is justified by works, not by faith alone. Clement in his epistle to the Corinthians, Ἔργοις καὶ δικαιούμενος, καὶ μὴ λόγοις, justified by works and not by words, δικαιοῦται is justified. In these places, it must be understood entirely as being before God, as the preceding words and the passage brought from Genesis prove. To which arguments let this also be added, that faith, being something internal to a man, does not appear to other men, and thus one cannot be said to be justified before men. He says this, therefore, that he who has already believed may be treated by God as entirely innocent and good, or that he may have God as a friend and patron (for these things come to the same thing), that faith is not sufficient, but if time and opportunity are given, good works are also required, such as those Abraham performed. For the same thing he placed δικαιωθῆναι to be justified, and Φίλος Θεοῦ κληθῆναι, to be called a friend of God. Thus δικαιωθῆναι, to be justified, is explained by εἰρήνην ἔχειν πρὸς Θεὸν, to have peace with God, Rom. V. 1. These two, faith and works joined together, or faith which is effective through love, Paul calls a new creature, and also the keeping of the commandments of God, as appears by comparing the passages Gal. V. 6. VI. 15. and 1. Cor. VII. 19. Salvianus, in his book on the government of God, book IV, teaches from this passage of James that it is said by the Holy Spirit that faith cannot profit Christian men without good works, nay, that without them the fruit of faith is fruitless.

Many things occur in these that are to be marked with a black coal. 1. It is Ἄγραφον (unwritten) that a man is justified by works BEFORE GOD. For even if he can be said to be declared or manifested as righteous by God through works: yet this does not fit the phrase of Scripture, that anyone is declared righteous BEFORE GOD ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ by works: because Scripture is accustomed to designate the same God as established on the tribunal, when a man is accused by the voice of the law, but is absolved by grace on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by true faith, Psal. CXLIII. 2. Rom. III. 20. c. IV. 2. 2. Although the passage of Genesis deals with justification before God, it is not said to be fulfilled in this place, because Abraham attained that justification when he offered Isaac, nor is the question at present about that justification and its causes, but about the necessary consequence of justifying faith, through which it exerts and manifests itself. 3. But although faith lies hidden within, and for that reason neither it, nor justification, which is the effect of faith, appears to other men, yet the faith of Abraham was openly made known by that external and remarkable specimen of heroic obedience, and from the very revelation of God, from the Mosaic account, that he was treated as a friend, just as the same was abundantly established from the visitation of Abraham, made by the Son of God, and the familiar conversation with Abraham, and the very friendly admission of his intercession, Gen. XIIX. seqq. Then if faith could in no way be demonstrated by works, why did James challenge that boaster: Show me your faith by your works? Why did he testify: And I will show you my faith by my works? 4. To that end, that he who has already believed may be treated by God as entirely innocent, it is entirely sufficient before God that one persevere in faith, to which the beginning and middle and consummation of salvation is attributed: but works are not required, as if they flowed together with faith to this effect, namely eternal salvation, for this is repugnant to Paul, Rom. VI. v. ult. Eph. II. 8. 9. Even if they are otherwise necessary by reason of the Divine command: nay, even by reason of faith itself as inseparable consequences of faith, and they are profitable for the increase of holiness and glory. 5. Not only if time and opportunity are given, but simply good works are required for faith, so that at no time is it, or can it be, without good works, internal or external. 6. It is not equivalent to be treated by God as entirely innocent and good, and to have God as a friend and patron. For did not Job, did not Paul, did not other saints, nay, did not Christ himself, have God as a friend, who nevertheless were not treated by God as entirely innocent? 2. While the necessity of good works is restricted to the presence of opportunity, is it not thereby taught that good works are not always required to retain the grace of God, but only then, when the fear of committing an opposite or contrary act is present, and the Divine command urges one to do good here and now; and that good works are not necessary by the necessity of a means, otherwise they would always be necessary, and thus one could obtain salvation by another means even in the absence of works. That even the Papists do not deny this is evident from Vasquez, book 1; where he shows that faith alone, without any other works, justifies a man even in secondary justification, when no commandment to do good occurs: whence it follows that faith is necessary for justification always and for all time: but works only then, when the memory occurs of doing good here and now: and thus the necessity and influence of each upon justification and salvation are not equal. 8. To be justified and to have peace with God are not the same, but the latter is a consequence of the former, as the Apostle testifies, Rom. 5:1. 9. That faith and works together are called a new creature, or likewise the keeping of the commandments of God, is not evident from a comparison of the passages cited: but rather the whole worship of Christians is designated, and to avail in Christ, according to the blessed Hopfner, is to make a true Christian. Meanwhile, that is attributed to faith alone in Gal. 5:6, whereas justification is expressly denied to works there, v. 4. Rightly does the blessed Luther say of this passage in his Commentary: Paul depicts the whole Christian life in this place, so that a Christian may be absolutely such inwardly before God through faith, and outwardly before men through charity.

10. The Apostolic conclusion in this place tends to this, as is evident from the premises, that a just man is recognized and manifested by works, not by the profession of faith alone. For many profess faith who are not recognized as just, Matt. 7:21. For it was concerning that justification that the discussion in the premises had been, namely, that by which one is recognized and manifested as just, to which mere profession, or naked faith, does not suffice, but there is need of works, as undoubted consequences and signs of saving faith. B. Menzerus, disp. XI, Tom. V, Giess., interprets it in a combined sense; namely, that the profession of faith is joined with works to demonstrate justification, th. 51. For here James says, concluding v. 24: You see that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only. This is: it is demonstrated and certainly concluded that that man is judged and commended as righteous before men, who not only professes true faith with his voice, but also expresses and confirms the same with deeds, just as Abraham did. St. Paul, however, affirms that a man is justified before God, that is, absolved from sins and received into grace, not by works or by working, but by faith or by believing, by the example of Abraham. And thus, according to Paul, faith alone justifies without works, that is, faith alone (not also works) is the instrument apprehending Christ, and in him the remission of sins and eternal righteousness. According to James, however, faith and works justify together, that is, not the mere profession of faith, but also those works conformable to it argue and declare a man truly justified. Which is also the interpretation of B. Hopfner, disp. XII, de justif., p. 1122. Justification is not viewed by James as being before God, but is shown as having been done before GOD, and its presence is acknowledged by men; and therefore the mind of the Apostle is this: A man is justified, that is, is declared and acknowledged to be righteous from works following faith, and not from faith only, that is, from the mere external profession of faith. And thus this verse agrees with the first chapter of James, verse 22. Be doers and not hearers only, likewise v. 25, he who is not a forgetful hearer, this one is blessed in his operation, that is, he is acknowledged to be blessed. And the following page: The sense, therefore, of the words of James in chapter II, v. 24, is none other than that an infallible certainty concerning justification cannot be had from faith or external profession only; but that works are also required for the complete infallibility of this knowledge, as σύνεργα, for the efficiency of this certainty.

Moreover, these can be taken in our judgment in the opposite sense: that a man is justified by works, that is, is acknowledged and declared righteous: and not by faith alone, that is, by the naked profession of faith, even if it is not said that the profession of faith cooperates to demonstrate faith. Concerning which Ephrem Syrus, book IV, de vita spir.: Consider whether you have works congruent with faith. For if you are studious only of speaking and hearing, that will be cast at you: Faith without works is dead. And Salvianus, book IV, de provid.: The Apostle James indicates that the good acts of Christian faith are as it were witnesses, because unless a Christian has done good works, he cannot approve his faith, and because he is not able to prove that it is so, it must be held entirely that it is not. The words of James can also be explained concerning internal faith, that a man is justified, that is, is pronounced righteous by God himself also, not in the primary sense, which brings about the remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, but in the secondary sense, by which he who is so justified that he is treated as righteous, as Grotius speaks, is pronounced, held, and acknowledged as righteous by God and men, not from faith alone, which, if it is destitute of works, is dead in itself, but from works, as being the undoubted witnesses of faith. You see, therefore, that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only: because, namely, you have seen that Abraham, clear through faith clothed with works, is pronounced by God to be righteous and the friend of God: so that it is not the cause of justification, why a man is pronounced righteous even by God himself, but the subject is designated, that, namely, he is finally held and declared righteous even by God himself, who shows the truth of his faith by works, who does not have faith without works, but faith which is active through love. Which explanation is approved by B. Hülsemann, and is confirmed in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession, Art. IV, in response to the arguments of the adversaries. James rightly denies that we are justified by such faith as is without works. But that he says we are justified by faith and works, he certainly does not say that we are reborn (or justified) through works, nor does he say this, that Christ is partly the propitiator and our works are partly the propitiation: Nor does he describe here the MODE of Justification: but he describes WHAT KIND of people the righteous are, after they are JUSTIFIED AND REBORN. And to be justified here does not signify to be made righteous from being ungodly, but in forensic usage to be pronounced righteous: Just as here: The doers of the law shall be justified: Just as, therefore, these words (the doers of the law shall be justified) have nothing inconvenient in them: so we feel about the words of James. A man is justified not only by faith, but also by works: Because certainly men having faith and good works are pronounced righteous. For good works in the saints, as we have said, are of righteousness, and they please because of faith (because of Christ apprehended by faith). For James proclaims only those works which faith produces, as he testifies when he says of Abraham: Faith helps his works, etc. To which also goes the opinion of Augustine, book de fid. et operibus, chapter 14: It must be shaken out from religious hearts, lest they lose their salvation through evil security, if they think that faith alone is sufficient to obtain it, but neglect to live well and to keep the way of God by good works.

It pleases some that assentive faith be understood, which is shown only by external profession, and is not also acknowledged through works: Which seems to be the explanation of Fulgentius, book II, de remiss. Pecc., chapter 1: A good life is not truly called such, which is depraved by the perverse vice of belief, nor does the faith of one who believes rightly suffice for salvation, if the conversation is disturbed by obscene morals and works: And from the Greeks, Chrysostom, hom. XIV, in 1 Tim. V. 8: Let life harmonize with the dogmas of faith, and let dogmas preach life. For faith without works is dead, and works are dead without faith. For even if we hold sound doctrine, but neglect life, doctrines will profit us nothing. Again, if we have taken diligent care of life, but have limped in the tenets of faith, not even so will there be any gain for us.

There remains the interpretation of those who wish for hypocritical faith to be considered, in this way: You see therefore that a man is justified, that is, acknowledged as just, by works and not by faith only, that is, absolutely not by faith alone or solitary, idle, and hypocritical: since it is evident from the premises that μόνον is an exclusive of the subject, and it is entirely denied to this faith, which is solitary justification before men, and the same is ascribed to works flowing from true faith. This is confirmed both by the Apostle's theme in v. 14, that such faith can save no one: and by the comparison concerning charity, which gives nothing but words, v. 15, 16, to which is compared faith void of works, dead in itself: and by the lack of demonstration, v. 18: and by the insufficiency and uselessness for salvation of mere assentual faith, from which it is gathered that the mere boasting of faith is of little benefit: and by the example of Abraham, that just as he conducted himself, and his faith behaved, so all the justified ought to conduct themselves, and so their faith ought to behave, which certainly was not hypocritical, but ἀνυπόκριτος, not ineffectual and idle, but effectual and industrious with unusual obedience. To which the example of Rahab, which now follows, also tends.

Latin:

Vers. 24. Ὁρᾶτε τοίνυν) Discite hoc viri maximi exemplo.

Ὅτι ἐξ ἔργων δικαιοῦται ἄνθρωπος, καὶ οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως μό- νον) Nisi ad fidem opera accedant, nunquam Deus ali- quem pro justo habebit. Hæc enim omnia sub nomine הַצְדִּיק in significatu secundario comprehendi solent. Idem est ἐκ πίστεως μόνον, quod ἐκ πίστεως μόνης. Sic μόνον Adverbium vice Adjectivi ponitur, Matth. V. 47. XXI. 19. Joh. XIII. 9. Act. XI. 19. Rom. III. 20. & alibi.

Quæ in priori tractatu de hisce leguntur, hæc sunt:

Vers. 24. Ὁρᾶτε τοίνυν, ὅτι ἐξ ἔργων δικαιοῦται ἄνθρω- πος καὶ οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως μόνον) Videtis quoniam ex operibus justificatur homo, non ex fide solum. Cle- mens in epist. ad Corinth. Ἔργοις καὶ δικαιούμενος, καὶ μὴ λόγοις, operibus justificatus non verbis, δικαιοῦται justificatur. Omnino his in locis intelligi debet apud Deum, ut verba præcedentia & adductus ex Genesi locus evincunt. Ad quæ argumenta & hoc acce- dat, quod fides, utpote internum aliquid homini, ho- minibus aliis non apparet, ac sic apud homines ali- quem justificari dici non potest. Hoc ergo dicit, ut qui jam credidit, à Deo tanquam plane intons, bo- nusque tractetur, sive ut Deum habeat amicum & fautorem (hæc enim eo recidunt) non sufficere fi- dem, sed si tempus detur & occasio, requiri & bona opera, qualia præstitit Abrahamus. Pro eodem po- suit δικαιωθῆναι justificari, & Φίλος Θεοῦ κληθῆναι, ami- cum Dei vocari. Sic δικαιωθῆναι justificari, per εἰρή- νην ἔχειν πρὸς Θεὸν, pacem habere apud Deum, expo- nitur Rom. V. 1. Hæc duo fidem & opera conjuncta, sive fidem, quæ per dilectionem efficax est, Paulus ap- pellat novam creaturam, item observationem præce- ptorum Dei, ut collatis locis Gal. V. 6. VI. 15. & 1. Cor. VII. 19. apparet. Salvianus de gubernatione Dei libr. IV. ex hoc Jacobi loco docet à Spiritu san- cto dici, nec fidem Christianis hominibus, sine bo- nis operibus posse prodesse, imo sine iis fidei fructum esse infructuosum.

Multa in his occurrunt atro carbone notanda. 1. Ἄγραφον est, quod homo operibus justificetur CO- RAM DEO. Nam etiamsi à DEO possit dici justus declarari vel manifestari operibus: non tamen Scripturæ phrasi hoc convenit, quenquam CO- RAM DEO ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ justum declarari ex operibus: quia solet Scriptura eadem Deum in tri- bunali constitutum, cum accusatur homo voce legis, absolvitur vero ex gratia propter meritum Christi, vera fide apprehensum, designare, Psal. CXLIII. 2. Rom. III. 20. c. IV. 2. 2. Quamvis lo- cus Geneseos agat de justificatione coram Deo, non tamen impletus dicitur hoc loco, quod tum justifi- cationem illam consequutus sit Abraham, cum obtulit Isaacum, nec de illa justificatione, ejusque causis in præsenti quæstio est, sed de fidei justifican- tis necessario consequente, per quod illa se exerit ac manifestatur. 3. Etsi autem fides interius lateat, eaque ratione nec ipsa, nec justificatio, quæ effectus fidei, aliis hominibus appareat, manifestata tamen fides Abrahami externo illo insigni specimine obe- dientiæ heroicæ, & ex ipsa Dei revelatione, ex Mo- saica relatione palam innotuit ipsum tanquam amicum tractari, quemadmodum ex visitatione Abrahæ, à Filio Dei facta, & colloquio cum Abraha- mo familiari, ac intercessionis admissione peramica idem affatim constitit, Gen. XIIX. seqq. Tum si nul- lo modo fides per opera demonstrari possit, cur provocavit Jacobus jactatorem illum: Demonstra mihi fidem tuam ex operibus tuis? cur testatus est: Et ego demonstrabo tibi fidem meam ex operibus meis? 4. Ad id, ut qui jam credidit, à Deo tanquam plane infons tractetur, sufficit omnino penes De- um, ut quis perseveret in fide, cui initium & medi- um & consummatio salutis tribuitur: non vero re- quiruntur opera, quasi confluerent cum fide ad hunc effectum, æternam nempe salutem, hoc enim repu- gnat Paulo, Rom. VI. v. ult. Eph. II. 8. 9. Etiamsi alias necessaria sint ratione mandati Divini: imo etiam ratione ipsius fidei ceu consequentia insepara- bilia fidei, & ad augmentum sanctitatis & gloriæ prosint. 5. Non tantum si tempus & occasio detur, sed simpliciter requiruntur bona opera ad fidem, adeo, ut nullo tempore sine bonis operibus inter- nis, aut externis sit aut esse possit. 6. Non sunt æquipollentia, tractari à Deo tanquam plane inson- tem bonumque, & Deum habere amicum & fauto- rem. Annon enim Job, annon Paulus, annon alii sancti, imo annon Christus ipse, amicum habuere Deum, qui tamen non tractati à Deo sunt tanquam plane in fontes? 2. Dum restringitur necessitas bo- norum operum ad occasionis præsentiam, annon eo ipso docetur, bona opera non semper requiri ad gra- tiam Dei retinendam, sed tum demum, quando metus oppositi aut contrarii committendi adest, & præceptum Divinum urget, hic & nunc bene operan- di; neque necessaria esse bona opera necessitate medii, aliàs semper forent necessaria, adeoque alio medio obtinere posse salutem etiam absentibus operibus. Quod neque Pontificios diffiteri, è Vas- quez l. 1. constat; ubi ostendit, fidem solam sine ullis aliis operibus justificare hominem etiam justificatione secunda, quando nullum præceptum bene operandi occurrit: unde consequitur, fidem esse ad justifica- tionem necessariam semper & pro semper: Opera ve- ro tunc solum, quando memoria occurrit de hic & nunc bene operando: adeoque non esse parem utri- usque necessitatem & influentiam in justificatio- nem & salutem. 8. Non sunt idem justificari, & pacem habere cum Deo, sed hoc consequens illius est, teste Apostolo, Rom. V. 1. 9. Fidem & opera conjunctim appellari novam creaturam, item ob- servationem præceptorum Dei è collatione loco- rum adductorum non patet: Sed totus Christiano- rum cultus potius designatur, & valere in Christo, juxta B. Hopfnerum est efficere verum Christianum. Interim id Gal. V. 6. soli fidei tribuitur, operibus autem justificatio expresse ibi denegatur, v. 4. Re- cte de isto loco B. Lutherus in Comment. Totam Christianam vitam hoc loco Paulus pingit, ut sic ab- solute sit Christianus intus coram Deo per fidem foris coram hominibus per charitatem.

10. Conclusio Apostolica hoc loco eo tendit, quemadmodum ex præmissis constat, quod homo justus agnoscatur & manifestetur ex operibus, non ex sola fidei professione. Multi enim fidem profi- tentur, qui justi non agnoscuntur, Matth. VII. 21. De ea enim justificatione in præmissis actum erat, nimirum, qua justus quis agnoscitur & manifesta- tur, ad quod professio sola, vel nuda fidei non fa- cit, sed opus est operibus, ceu indubitatis conse- quentibus & signis fidei salvificæ. B. Menzerus disp. XI. Tom. V. Giess. in sensu copulato interpretatur; professionem nempe fidei cum operibus conjungi ad demonstrandam justifi- cationem th. 51. Hic enim Jacobus: Videtis, inquit, concludendo v. 24. quoniam ex operibus justificatur homo, & non ex fide tantum. Hoc est demonstra- tur & certo concluditur hominem illum coram ho- minibus pro justo censeri & commendari, qui non so- lum voce veram fidem profitetur, verum etiam ean- dem factis exprimit & confirmat, quemadmodum fecit Abrahamus. D. Paulus autem affirmat, ju- stificari hominem coram Deo, hoc est, à peccatis ab- solvi, & in gratiam recipi, non operibus sive operan- do, sed fide sive credendo, exemplo Abrahami. Et sic sola fides justificat apud Paulum sine operibus, hoc est, sola fides, (non etiam opera) & instrumentum apprehendens Christum, & in ipso remissionem pec- catorum & æternam justitiam. Apud Jacobum au- tem fides & opera simul justificant, hoc est non sola professio fidei, verum etiam opera illa conformia ar- guunt & declarant hominem vere justificatum. Quæ etiam est interpretatio B. Hopfneri disp. XII. de ju- stif. p. 1122. Justificatio à Jacobo non spectatur, ut sit coram Deo, sed ostenditur ut facta coram DEO, ejusq́; præsentia agnoscitur ab hominibus, ideoque mens Apostoli hæc est: Homo justificatur, id est, justus esse declaratur & agnoscitur ex operibus fidem con- sequentibus, & non ex fide tantum, id est, sola exter- na professione fidei. Atque ita concordat hic ver- sus cum cap. I. Jacobi. vers. 22. Estote factores & non auditores tantum, item v. 25. qui non est obliviosus Auditor, hic beatus est in operatione sua, id est, bea- tus esse agnoscitur. Et pag. seq. Sensus itaque ver- borum Jacobi in cap. II. v. 24. nullus alius est, quam de justificatione certitudinem infallibilem haberi non posse ex fide seu externa professione tantum; sed re- quiri ad completam hujus notitiæ infallibilitatem etiam opera, tanquam σύνεργα, ad hujus certitudi- nis efficientiam.

Cæterum accipi hæc possunt nostro judicio in sensu opposito: quod ex operibus justificetur homo, id est, justus agnoscatur & declaretur: & non ex fi- de sola, id est, professione nuda fidei, etiamsi non di- catur professio fidei ad demonstrandam fidem cooperari. Quo de Ephrem. Syrus libr. IV. de vi- ta spir. Considera, utrum habeas opera fidei congru- entia. Nam si dicendi tantum & audiendi studio- sus es, illud in te jacietur: Fides sine operibus mor- tua est. Et Salvianus libr. IV. de provid. Jacobus Apostolus indicat, actus bonos Christianæ fidei quasi testes esse, quia Christianus nisi bona opera fecerit, fi- dem suam approbare non possit, ac quia probare non valeat, quod sit sic, omnino habendum, quod non sit. Explicari etiam possunt verba Jacobi de fide inter- na, quod homo justificetur, id est, justus pronun- cietur ab ipsomet quoque Deo non sensu prima- rio, qui infert remissionem peccatorum & imputa- tionem justitiæ Christi, sed secundario, quo qui ju- stificatus ita est, ut justus tractatur, ut Grotius lo- quitur, justus pronunciatur, habetur, agnoscitur à Deo & hominibus, non ex fide sola, quæ, si destituta est operibus, mortua in seipsa est, sed ex operibus, utpote fidei testibus indubitatis. Videtis itaque ju- stificari hominem ex operibus, non fide tantum: quia nempe vidistis, Abrahamum fide operibus vestita clarum, à Deo pronunciari justum & amicum Dei: Ut non causa justificationis, cur justus homo pro- nuncietur etiam à Deo ipso, sed subjectum desi- gnetur, quod nempe is demum etiam ab ipso Deo habeatur ac declaretur justus, qui fidei suæ verita- tem operibus ostendit, qui non fidem habet sine operibus, sed fidem, quæ per charitatem operosa est. Quæ explicatio B. Hülsemanno probatur, & in Confess. August. Apolog. confirmatur Art. IV. resp. ad argum. adversar. Jacobus recte negat, nos tali fide justificari, quæ est sine operibus. Quod autem dicit, nos justificari fide & operibus, certe non dicit, nos per opera renasci (seu justificari) neque hoc di- cit, quod partim Christus sit propitiator, partim ope- ra nostra sint propitiatio: Nec describit hic MO- DUM Justificationis: sed describit, QUA- LES sint justi, postquam sunt JUSTIFICATI ET RENATI. Et justificari hic non significat ex impio justum effici, sed usu forensi justum pronun- ciari: Sicut hic: Factores legis justificabuntur: Sic- ut igitur hæc verba (factores legis justificabuntur) nihil habent incommodi: ita de Jacobi verbis senti- mus. Justificatur homo non solum ex fide, sed etiam ex operibus: Quia certe justi pronunciantur homines habentes fidem & bona opera. Nam bona opera in sanctis, ut diximus, sunt justitiæ, & placent propter fidem (propter Christum fide apprehen- sum) Nam hæc tantum opera prædicat Jacobus, quæ fides efficit, sicut testatur, cum de Abraham dicit: Fides adjuvat opera ejus, &c. Quo etiam abit Au- gustini sententia l. de fid. & operibus cap. 14. Ex- cutiendum est à cordibus religiosis, ne mala securita- te salutem suam perdant, si ad eam obtinendam suffi- cere solam fidem putaverint, bene autem vivere, & bonis operibus viam Dei tenere neglexerint.

Nonnullis placet fidem assensitivam intelligi, quæ solum ostenditur per externam professionem, & non etiam per opera agnoscitur: Quæ videtur Fulgentii explicatio l. II. de remiss. Pecc. cap. 1. Vi- ta bona non veraciter dicitur, quæ perverso creduli- tatis vitio depravatur, neque sufficit ad salutem fides recte credentis, si conversatio moribus atque operi- bus turbatur obscænis: Et è Græcis Chrysostomi hom. XIV. in 1. Tim. V. 8. Vita consonet fidei do- gmatis, & dogmata prædicent vitam. Fides enim si- ne operibus mortua est, & mortua sunt sine fide opera. Nam temetsi sanam teneamus doctrinam, vitam autem negligamus, nihil nobis proderunt do- ctrinæ. Rursus si vitæ curam diligentem gesserimus, in fidei autem placitis claudicaverimus, neque sic nobis aliquid lucri fuerit.

Restat eorum interpretatio, qui fidem hypocri- ticam respici volunt, hoc modo: Videtis igitur ju- stificari, id est, justum agnosci hominem ex operibus & non ex fide tantum, id est, prorsus non ex fide sola vel solitaria, otiosa, & hypocritica: siquidem è præ- missis constet, μόνον esse exclusivam subjecti, & omnino denegetur huic fidei, quæ solitaria justifica- tio coram hominibus eademque adscribatur operi- bus è vera fide profluentibus. Quam confirmat tum thema Apostoli v. 14. quod fides ejusmodi ne- minem servare possit: tum simile de charitate, quæ non nisi verba dat, v. 15. 16. cui confertur fides ope- ribus cassa, in se mortua: tum demonstrationis defe- ctus, v. 18. tum insufficientia, & inutilitas ad salu- tem solius fidei assensualis, unde minus prodesse solam fidei jactantiam colligitur: tum exemplum Abrahami, quod uti sese ille gessit, & fides ejus ha- buit: Ita se gerere debeant omnes justificati, & ita se fides eorum habere debeat, quæ certe non fuit hypocritica, sed ἀνυπόκριτος, non inefficax & otio- sa, sed efficax & operosa obsequio inusitato. Quo etiam Rahabæ exemplum, quod jam sequitur, tendit.

## 2:25
Vers. 25. Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ Ῥαὰϐ ἡ πόρνη) Because many foreigners also, in the same way as the believing Jews

had joined the Church, James adds another example, very much to their point, of a woman and a stranger to the blood of Abraham, and of a previously sinful life, such as most of the Gentiles had been. Concerning this Rahab and the word πόρνης we spoke at Heb. XI. 30, where the faith of this woman is proclaimed just as her works are here.

- - - - - - - Thus one thing asks for the help of another and conspires in a friendly manner.

Was she not justified by works?) Interrogative. Did she not achieve this by works, that she might receive the reward of righteousness from God, saved by the sole command of God, when all her countrymen were being killed, and then deemed worthy of marriage to a man eminent among his own people, Boaz.

Having received the messengers) Having received the spies, Heb. XI. 31. This is a great deal in a woman. Although she knew that they were scouts sent by the enemies of the people of Jericho, she nevertheless received them with hospitality and hid them, out of reverence for the one God, whom she had learned was worshipped by the Hebrews, and whom she had understood to be the author of this war for the Hebrews. The scouts are also rightly called messengers, because they are sent for this purpose, that they may report what they have seen. But some codices have κατασκόπους here as well. And the Syriac and Arabic translate it thus.

And having sent them out by another way) By another way than that by which they were thought to be going. For she both let them down through the wall and showed them devious paths, so that they would not be caught by the people of Jericho. She would have done none of these things if she had hoped for salvation from naked faith.

Concerning these, the previous commentary has this: Ver. 25. Likewise also Rahab) The example of Abraham ought to have sufficed for the Hebrews converted to Christ: But because James is also writing to Gentiles who have embraced Christ, he added the example of a foreign woman.

The harlot) a prostitute. The Greeks translate the word זונה in the book of Joshua ch. II, where this history is related, as πόρνην, whom James follows here, and the writer of Heb. XI. 30. The word indeed seems properly to signify a hostess, πανδοκεύτριαν, as Chrysostom speaks of this very woman in his second sermon on repentance. But usually, hostesses also engaged in such trade: See the law: Concerning adultery. C. de adulteriis. Among the descendants of Abraham, even before the law, it was a grave crime for a woman to be a prostitute, as Philo notes. Not so among the more corrupt Gentiles, from whom those who came were considered by the Apostles to need special instruction, lest they consider prostitution a light matter, as can be seen in Acts XV. 29. But what is said here, ἡ πόρνη, the harlot, is to be understood as one who had been such before she converted to the true God, having been taught by her Hebrew guests. Thus in Matt. XXI. 31, the harlots are said to enter the kingdom of heaven. Chrysostom in the said sermon: If she lives, why is she called a harlot? If she is a harlot, why is it said that she lives? I say, he says, her former state, so that you may marvel at the second transformation: Thus, if she lives, why is she called a harlot? If she is a harlot, why is it said, let her live? He means this: Recall her former state to yourself, so that you may marvel at the subsequent restoration. Rahab most excellently bears the figure of those who from foreign nations have believed in Christ: For even for their salvation, a previous shameful life was no obstacle. Thus Chrysostom in the said place: Rahab bears the figure of the Church which was once polluted by the prostitution of demons.

Was she not justified by works?) Was she not justified by works? Faith had preceded, by which she had acknowledged GOD as the one Lord of heaven and earth, Jos. II. 31, Heb. XII. 31, which, how great a thing it was in those most corrupt times, and with the frequent lapses of the Hebrews concerning this very thing, is sufficiently understood. But he judged that works were to be added to this faith.

Having received the messengers) receiving the messengers. She also, after she had believed, judged that works were to be added so that she might be saved, when she not only received into her house the Hebrews sent to her, who were considered by the city as enemies, but also hid them in secret places, so that they could not be found.

And having sent them out by another way) and sending them out by another way. Then she also let them down unharmed by a rope through a window joined to the wall of the city, and showed them the way by which they might deceive the inquisitors sent from the city; she would have done none of these things, unless she had believed that works were necessary after faith to preserve the benevolence of God toward her.

Grotius therefore explained justification here as the attainment of salvation or the reward of righteousness, which he says Rahab hoped for and obtained, not from naked faith, but also from works. But justification is taken in this place in no other sense than in the preceding example of Abraham, that is, that she was demonstrated and acknowledged to be righteous by her works. There is no mention of faith here. Only works, and specifically the receiving of the messengers and their cautious dismissal, are commemorated. That these were necessary for the benevolence of God, if it is understood concerning the grace of justification, and for attaining salvation, is taught by no indication: nor does it appear from the testimony of James that Rahab believed this. Indeed, since she is said to be justified and saved ὁμοίως, similarly, as Abraham, it is not permitted to presume that she is understood to be justified before God by works. For this is denied directly concerning Abraham, Rom. IV. 1. seqq. And Paul testifies concerning Rahab, Heb. XI. 30, that she escaped death and condemnation not by her own works, but by faith: that she did not perish by that kind of death by which her fellow citizens perished, who perished not by a temporal, but by an eternal death. She believed immediately, and therefore the end followed: For when all had perished, she alone was saved, says Chrysostom, homil. XXVII. on Hebrews. For the end of faith is salvation, 1 Pet. I. 9. How then could he say she was justified from sins, and from their punishment, condemnation, and absolved by works? She is therefore said to be justified by works, that is, she was declared and acknowledged to be righteous through works.

Latin:

Vers. 25. Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ Ῥαὰϐ ἡ πόρνη) Quia multi etiam alienigenæ in eandem cum Judæis credentibus

Ecclesiam coaluerant, alterum Jacobus exemplum ad- dit, valde ad eorum rem appositum, fœminæ & extraneæ à sanguine Abrahami, & vitæ antea mendosæ, quales & plerique ex gentibus fuerant. De hac Rahabe & de vo- ce πόρνης diximus Ebr. XI. 30. ubi tam fides hujus mulie- ris prædicatur, quam hic ejus opera.

- - - - - - - alterius sic Altera poscit opem res & conjurat amice.

Οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη) Interrogative. Nonne ope- ribus id consequuta est, ut justitiæ præmium à Deo refer- ret, solo Dei jussu servata, cum omnes ejus populares in- terficerentur, deinde dignata conjugio viri eminentis inter suos Boozi.

Ὑποδεξαμένη τοὺς ἀγγέλους) Δεξαμένη τοὺς κατασκόπους, Ebr. XI. 31. Multum hoc in fœmina. Cum sciret il- los esse exploratores ab hostibus Hierichuntinorum mis- sos, tamen eos hospitio excepit texitque, reverentia unius Dei, quem ab Ebræis coli, quemque hujus belli autorem esse Ebræis intellexerat. Exploratores recte etiam nun- tii dicuntur, quia in id mittuntur, ut spectata renuntient. Sed quidam Codices etiam hic habent κατασκόπους. Et sic vertunt Syrus & Arabs.

Καὶ ἑτέρᾳ ὁδῷ ἐκβαλοῦσα) Alia via, quam qua ituri putabantur. Nam & per murum eos demisit, & devia itinera monstravit, ne ab Hierichuntinis deprehenderen- tur. Hæc omnia non factura, si salutem ex nuda fide sperasset.

De his prior commentatio hæc habet: Vers. 25. Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ Ῥαάϐ) Similiter & Ra- ab) Abrahami exemplum Ebræis ad Christum con- versis sufficere debebat: Sed quia etiam alienigenis Christum amplexis scribit Jacobus, adjunxit exem- plum fœminæ extraneæ.

Ἡ πόρνη) meretrix. Vocem זונה & Josuæ libro c. II. ubi hæc refertur historia, vertunt Græci πόρνην, quos & Jacobus hic sequitur, & Scriptor Ebr. XI. 30. Videtur quidem vox proprie cauponam significare, πανδοκεύτριαν, ut loquitur Chrysostomus de hac ipsa fœmina sermone de pœnitentia secundo. Sed ple- rumque cauponæ talem quæstum etiam faciebant: Vide legem: Quæ adulterium. C. de adulteriis. In- ter Abrahami posteros etiam ante legem grave cri- men fuit fœminæ scortari, ut Philo notat. Non item apud gentes corruptiores, à quibus qui venirent eos Apostoli specialiter instituendos duxere, ne scortari pro levi haberent, ut videre est Act. XV. 29. Quod au- tem hic dicitur ἡ πόρνη, meretrix, intelligendum, quæ talis fuerat, antequam ad verum Deum ab Ebræis ho- spitibus edocta se converteret. Sic Matth. XXI. 31. αἱ πόρναι meretrices dicuntur intrare in regnum cœ- leste. Chrysostomus dicto sermone: Εἰ ζῇ, ὀφείλει διὰ τί πόρνη; εἰ πόρνη, διὰ τί ζῆται; λέγω, φησὶ τὴν προτέραν κατάστασιν, ἵνα θαυμάσῃς τὴν δευτέραν μετάστα- σιν: Sic vivere debet cur meretrix dicitur? Si meretrix est, cur dicitur, vivat? Hoc vult: Priorem tibi statum ejus memora, ut secutam mireris restitutionem. Opti- me autem Rahab figuram gerit eorum, qui ex genti- bus extraneis in Christum credidere: Nam & horum saluti vita prior flagitiosa nihil obstitit. Sic Chry- sostomus dicto loco: Εἰκὼν τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἡ Ῥαὰϐ τῆς πότε πεφυρμένης τῇ πορνείᾳ τῶν δαιμόνων. Rahab figu- ram gerit Ecclesiæ, quæ olim polluta erat scortatione cum Dæmonibus.

Οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη;) Nonne ex operibus ju- stificata est? Fides præcesserat, qua DEUM agnorat unum cœli terræque Dominum, Jos. II. 31. Ebr. XII. 31. quod quantum fuerit istis corruptissimis tempo- ribus, & frequentibus Ebræorum circa idipsum lapsi- bus satis intelligitur. Sed fidei huic addenda censuit opera.

Ὑποδεξαμένη τοὺς Ἀγγέλους) suscipiens nuntios. Il- la quoque postquam crediderat, ut servari posset, ad- jungenda censuit opera, cum missos ad se Ebræos, qui pro hostibus à civitate habebantur, non tantum in domum recepit, sed & latebris, ne reperiri possent, abdidit.

Καὶ ἑτέρᾳ ὁδῷ ἐκβαλοῦσα) & alia via dimittens. De- inde etiam fune per fenestram muro urbis injunctam dimisit incolumes, viamque monstravit, per quam in- quisitores ex urbe missos fallerent; hæc omnia non factura, nisi ad conservandam Dei in se benevolentiam opera post fidem necessaria credidisset.

Justificationem ergo hic exposuit Grotius per consequutionem salutis vel præmii justitiæ, quam Rahabam non ex nuda fide, sed etiam ex operibus sperasse, & obtinuisse ait. Sed non alia ratione ju- stificatio hoc accipitur loco, quam in praecedenti Abrahæ exemplo, hoc est, quod justa demonstrata & agnita fuerit ex operibus. De fide hic nulla men- tio. Solum opera, & in specie susceptio nunciorum & cauta dimissio commemorantur. Ad benevo- lentiam Dei, si de gratia justificationis intelligatur, & ad salutem consequendam ea necessaria fuisse, nullo docetur indicio: nec id credidisse Rahabam, Jacobi testimonio constat. Imo quum ὁμοίως, si- militer, ut Abraham, justitificata dicatur & servata, non licet præsumere, ipsam coram Deo intelligi per opera justificatam. Hoc enim directe de Abra- hamo negatur, Rom. IV. 1. seqq. Et testatur Paulus de Rahaba, Ebr. XI. 30. eam non operibus suis, sed fide mortem & damnationem effugisse: non periisse eo genere mortis, quo perierunt concives, qui non temporali, sed æterna morte periere. Statim cre- didit, ideo & finis sequutus est: Cum enim omnes pe- riissent, ipsa sola salvata est, ait Chrysostomus homil. XXVII. ad Ebr. Finis enim fidei salus est, 1. Petr. I. 9. Quomodo ergo justificatam a peccatis, eo- rumque pœna, damnatione, absolutam diceret ex operibus? Justificata itaque dicitur ex operibus, id est, justa declarata & agnita est per opera.

## 2:26
Vers. 26. For as the body without the spirit is dead) that is, it does not produce the functions appropriate to a man. For we noted above that the word νεκρῷ is taken in this way. But he calls that substance here πνεῦμα, which provides life to the body, Luke XXIII. 46, Acts VII. 59. So also faith without works is dead) i.e., it does not cause a man to be reckoned righteous by God, and thus to attain the Spirit of God and eternal life, which we have confirmed and illustrated in many places of the ancients in that more extensive commentary.

To the last verse these things are annotated in the previous commentary: Vers. 26. For as the body without the spirit is dead) Just as the body is dead without the Spirit. The conclusion of this whole most useful treatment follows. When the Hebrews speak of the soul, they understand life itself, but they call that substance which vivifies πνεῦμα, spirit, as can be seen in Luke XXIII. 46, Acts VII. 59, and elsewhere. Where that substance has departed, the body is left νεκρὸν, that is, it does not produce from itself those acts which are appropriate to a human body. So also faith without works is dead) Thus also faith without works is dead. Faith, unless works follow it at a given time and opportunity, does not produce that which it ought to produce, namely, the continuation of Divine favor, and consequently eternal salvation. Chrysostom on the Epistle to the Romans, chap. III. But since after this grace, by which we have been justified, there is need of a good life, let us show a zeal worthy of virtue; And soon in chapter VI. Thus also a Christian will perhaps have no profit if he has faith and the gift from baptism, but is subject to all passions, thus also a Christian will gain nothing if he has faith and the gift of baptism, but is subject to base affections. And chap. VIII. For it is not possible that one who becomes sluggish after faith should be saved. For the struggles are easy, so that you may win by contending, not so that you may sleep, nor so that you may use the greatness of grace as a pretext for sluggishness, wallowing again in the former mire. For it cannot be that he who becomes sluggish after faith is saved. The struggles have been made easy for you, so that you may win by contending, not so that you may abuse the greatness of grace as an occasion for laziness, wallowing again in the former mire. Then, so that if you lose the grace of the spirit while you are here, and do not depart with it safe, you have perished entirely, even if you had risen. And chap. XI. He did not say by faith, but by goodness, that is, if you do things worthy of God's love for men, for faith alone is not required. The same in chapter I of the second epistle to the Corinthians, v. 1. For the release from sins, and having become a friend, to wallow in the former things, to return again to enmity, is not to have received the grace in vain. For there is no profit from the gift.

we are benefited unto salvation, living impurely, but we are also harmed more greatly by being burdened by this and in our sins, because after this knowledge, and the gift, we returned to former evils, for if anyone liberated from sins and made a friend of God should wallow again in former things, that truly is to return to enmity, and to have received grace in vain. For we obtain nothing great from grace unto salvation if we live impurely; rather, on the contrary, we are harmed, since a heavier weight is added to our sins because after that knowledge and those gifts we revert to former evils. To the Galatians ch. V. v. 4. So that you may not, having heard that he chose, think that faith alone suffices, he also adds life, so therefore, when you hear, he chose, do not think faith alone suffices, therefore he also adds life. In the fourth book on the priesthood: No profit from sound faith if the way of life is corrupted.

We could admit, without prejudice to the analogy of faith, that by πνεῦμα the soul is understood in terms of substance, just as Flacius and Brochmand admitted, and from the Reformed, Piscator, Drusius, along with Paëzius, Justinianus, Estius: yet it is better to understand it as respiration or vital breath, with the blessed Menzer, the blessed Gerhard, the blessed Hopfner, the blessed Hülsemann, Pareus, the Belgian Interpreters, and from the Papists, Lyranus, Cajetan, Faber Stapulensis, and also Cornelius a Lapide. It stands against Paëzius and his followers that if πνεῦμα is taken essentially as the soul, the form of the animated body, it would follow that faith, which is without works, is called faith at least equivocally, just as an animated thing, when the soul expires, is no longer what it was, except equivocally. Concerning which Guillandus says: As a corpse or a statue has indeed the appearance of a man, but not the power and works of a man: So also is faith without charity and works. But that faith without works is called faith only equivocally is repugnant to the opinion of the Papists, who hold it as faith properly so-called, and make a species of faith distinct from formed faith: Just as Grotius also says that true faith can exist in men without works. Add that to Bellarmine himself it is absurd that the intrinsic form of salvific faith, which they call formed, should be good works. And therefore others take it effectively concerning the motion of the soul, and especially respiration, as the proper, immediate, and necessary effect of the indwelling soul, and a certain argument of life. For as a body that no longer breathes is dead: So also faith, which does not exert itself through good works, is dead, since faith can be just as true and alive without works as an animated and living body can be without respiration. For St. James in this treatise is not dealing with the form and constitution of faith, but with its effects and declaration.

Nor is it true what Grotius says, that among the Hebrews רוּחַ is used only for the soul, and נֶפֶשׁ for life, since נֶפֶשׁ is also used for a habit, Job XLI. verses 10, 11, and also for desire, Exod. XV. 9, for will, Psalm CV. 21, etc., and the word πνεῦμα among the LXX likewise occurs for respiration, Job VII. 15, ch. XXVII. 2, ch. XXX. 16, and in the New Testament denotes the affections of the concupiscible and irascible faculty, not always a vivifying substance, Acts XVII. 16, ch. XVIII. 5. But what will accrue from this to the Papists, or to Grotius, even if works are said to be the life and soul of faith? For it is a question here of the bare absence of works (in the words 'faith, which is without works, is dead'), not of the impotence of justifying without the co-influence of works in justification. Whence Lorinus has it thus: The force of the comparison consists in this, that just as when the soul, or breath, spirit, respiration is absent from the body, the body lies dead and destitute of all life: So with the absence of charity, which is the worker of good works, or of works which have a vital similarity to functions, faith indeed remains, but as if lifeless, bloodless, dead, emitting no true sign of life. Among the ancients, they explain Spirit as respiration and breath, Gaudentius of Brescia, ep. to Germ.

T. III. Bibl. Patr. p. 830. Chrysost. hom. II. in Gen. Bernard, sermon II: on the resurrection: works attest to the life of faith, just as it is written: The works which the Father gave me, these testify of me. Nor do those seem to differ from this opinion who assert that faith without works is dead in itself. For just as we discern the life of this body from its motion: So also the life of faith from good works. Which explanation the ordinary gloss, Lyranus, and the Douay theologians repeat and make their own. Cajetan likewise understands breath by Spirit. Because as an animal body, if it does not breathe, is dead, so a good operation is the effect of living faith. Nor does Salmero disapprove of this explanation of Cajetan, but calls it not inept. What Grotius gathered toward the end from Chrysostom is nothing to the point: they teach the necessity of works, or of the conjunction of faith and works; but they do not hint by a single iota that works are necessary for justification and salvation, either to be obtained or to be preserved. Or they testify that they are required, lest through voluntary sloth, or abstinence from doing good, or through the commission of the opposite evil, we lose the benefits received and promised: but not so that we may acquire or obtain the benefit of justification and salvation through good works, or preserve it by way of a preserving cause, in the way that food preserves the human body. The penultimate passage in Eph. I. 4. (which was falsely cited as Gal. V. 4.) is read thus in Chrysostom: So that you may not, because he chose, think that faith alone suffices, he also adds life. Gentianus Hervetus Aurelius, Canon of Reims, translated it: Do not therefore think that it suffices alone that He chose our faith, He adds life also: Therefore, he says, He chose us also for this, that we might be holy and immaculate. Which have been changed by Grotius. But even if they are read according to the same, they do nothing for the τὸ κρινόμενον [the point at issue], that faith alone does not suffice for salvation, that is to say, for obtaining it. For they have nothing concerning this end: On the contrary, however, Chrysostom everywhere ascribed salvation to faith alone. Clearer than the sun are those words on Rom. III. v. 27. But what is the law of faith? To be saved by grace. By these he shows the power, that He not only saved, but also justified, and led into boasting, asking for no works, requiring faith only. And hom. XIV. on chap. VIII. 21. This one gift of GOD we have brought, that we believe Him promising future things. And only by this way have we been saved. If we have lost this way, we have lost the whole sum of our comparison. And a little later: What therefore made you safe? Only that you hoped in God, and believed His promises: And you could not bring more to this matter. Likewise in Eph. II. verse 8. How did faith make one safe from works? This very thing is the gift of God, lest anyone should boast, so that He might make those who think well of His grace (grateful). What then? Did He prohibit being justified from works? By no means. But no one, he says, has been justified from works, so that the grace and Φιλανθρωπία [philanthropy/love for mankind] of God might be shown. He does not reject those having works, but He saved those who are conspicuous by works, freely, so that no one might have a cause for boasting. More have been adduced elsewhere from Chrysostom. These can easily suffice at present to vindicate his mind.

It is helpful, however, in place of a conclusion to the present Jacobean treatment, to add Beza's not inelegant paraphrase, which is as follows: Those people were relying on that false appearance of faith, that is, the knowledge of God: it was necessary to show them that this was not true faith, but a dead image. But James nevertheless calls that faith by concession (lest he seem to litigate about words). Verse 14. Suppose, he says, you have that faith which you say you have, what else is it than a useless thing? V. 15. 16. he illustrates this by applying a comparison: If anyone If one should say to a hungry man: Be filled, and yet in the meantime provide him with nothing, who would call this true liberality? V. 17. So if you boast that you have knowledge of GOD, (which you call faith) and yet in the meantime do not apply it to use, this will not properly be faith, but a phantom of faith: just as if you were to call a lifeless body a man. V. 18. What then? Surely that is faith at last, which you can demonstrate by works. V. 19. Then he proceeds to arguments: If that which you call faith were faith, what would prevent the Devil from being a believer himself? For the Devil believes what you call faith: yet he does not trust, but trembles. Therefore the faith which you boast of is not true faith, nor that upon which you can securely rely. V. 20. Do you wish to know this further? V. 21. Compare that faith which you boast of with the example of Abraham. For there is no doubt that he had true faith. What then did he do? Did he not offer up Isaac? V. 22. Therefore he did not have a faith which works did not follow, but the thing itself shows that he was truly justified through faith, since he produced a work of righteousness. From the fact, therefore, that he showed his faith by his deeds, it clearly appeared that his faith was not dead, but living and complete in all its parts. V. 23. And then it was fully revealed how deservedly it was written concerning him that he had believed God, and that it had been reckoned to him for righteousness. V. 24. From this it is concluded that he is not truly justified who has that faith which you boast of, but rather that which can be shown by its effects. V. 25. Do you seek another example? For perhaps that one deters you. Let us take that harlot Rahab, to whom you will be ashamed to be found unequal. Did she not show by the deed itself that she had a faith far different from that dead one, which is common even to the devils themselves? For she preferred the glory of GOD and charity toward her neighbor to her own life, when she saved and sent away the spies of God. V. 26. Let us conclude, therefore, that that faith of yours is like a corpse: and so there is no reason for you to be proud of its title, as if you were justified by it. For that faith which shines forth in the deeds of the justified is living, not dead.

Latin:

Vers. 26. Ὥσπερ γὰρ τὸ σῶμα χωρὶς τοῦ πνεύματος νεκρόν ἐστι) id est, functiones hominis convenientes non edit. Sic enim vocem νεκρῷ sumi supra annotavimus. Πνεῦμα autem hic vocat eam substantiam, quæ corpori vitam sub- ministrat, Luc. XXIII. 46. Act. VII. 59. Οὕτω καὶ ἡ πίστις χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων νεκρά ἐστι) i. e. non effi- cit, ut homo justus a Deo censeatur, & sic Spiritum Dei, vi- tamque æternam consequatur, quod multis veterum locis in illa uberiori commentatione confirmavimus atque illu- stravimus.

Ad versum ultimum hæc annotata sunt in prio- ri commentatione: Vers. 26. Ὥσπερ γὰρ τὸ σῶμα χωρὶς τοῦ πνεύματος νεκρόν ἐστι) Sicut enim corpus sine Spiritu mortuum est.
