Sequitur conclusio totius hujus utilissimæ tra- ctationis. Ebræi animam cum dicunt, vitam ipsam intelligunt, substantiam autem eam, quæ vivificat, vocant πνεῦμα, spiritum, ut videre est Luc. XXIII. 46. Act. VII. 59. & alibi. Ea substantia, ubi abiit, re- linquitur corpus νεκρὸν, id est, non edit ex se eos actus, qui humano corpori conveniunt. Οὕτω καὶ ἡ πίστις χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων νεκρά ἐστι) Sic & fi- des sine operibus mortua est. Fides, nisi eam dato tempore & occasione opera sequantur, non producit id, quod producere debeat, continuationem scilicet Divini favoris, & consequenter salutem æternam. Chrysostomus in epistolam ad Romanos cap. III. Ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ μετὰ τὴν χάριν ταύτην, δι' ἧς ἐδικαιώθημεν, πρὸς πολιτείας χρεία, ἀξίαν ἐπιδείξασθαι τῆς ἀρετῆς τὴν σπουδὴν; sed quia post eam, qua justificati sumus gratiam vita opus est bona, ostendamus studium virtute dignum; Et mox capite VI. Οὕτω καὶ χριστιανῷ οὐδὲν ἴσως κέρδος ἐκ πίστεως μὲν ἔχοντι, καὶ τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ βαπτίσματος δωρεὰν, πᾶσι δὲ τοῖς πάθεσι προκειμένῳ, sic & Christianus nihil lucrifaciet, si fidem quidem habeat & baptismi do- num, pravis autem subjaceat affectibus. Et cap. VIII. Οὐδὲ γὰρ δυνατὸν, ἵνα μετὰ τὴν πίστιν ῥαθυμεῖται σωθῆναι. Εὔκολα γὰρ τὰ παλαίσματα, ἵνα νικήσῃς ἀγωνιζόμενος, ὄχι ἵνα καθεύδῃς, οὐδ' ἵνα τῷ μεγέθει τῆς χάριτος πρὸς ῥαθυ- μίας ὑπόθεσιν ἀποχρήσῃ, τῷ βορβόρῳ πάλιν ἐγκαλινδού- μενος τὴν προτέρῳ. Fieri enim non potest, ut salvetur, qui post fidem torpescit. Faciles tibi factæ sunt lu- ctæ, ut vincas certans, non ut magnitudine gratiæ ad occasionem pigritiæ abutaris, rursum volutatus in lu- to priore. Deinde ὥστε ἂν ἀπολάσῃς ἐνταῦθα ὢν τοῦ πνεύματος τὴν χάριν, καὶ μὴ ὁσίαν αὐτῷ ἔχων ἀπέλθῃς, ἀπολῇ πάντως, κἂν ἀνέστης quod si dum hic es, expellas spiritus gratiam, neque ea tibi sospite decedas, periisti quanquam surrexeras. Et cap. XI. Οὐκ εἶπε τῇ πίστει, ἀλλὰ τῇ χρηστότητι, τουτέστιν ἂν ἀξία τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ φιλανθρω- πίας πράττῃ, ἢ γὰρ πίστις δεῖ μόνον, non dixit fide, sed bonitate, id est, si digna agas Dei erga homines dile- ctione, non enim fides sola requiritur. Idem in ca- put I. epistolæ secundæ ad Corinthios v. 1. Τὴν γὰρ ἀπαλλαγὴν ἐπὶ ἁμαρτημάτων, κὶ φίλον γενόμενον τοῖς προτέ- ροις ἐγκαλινδεῖσθαι, πάλιν ἐπ' ἔχθραν ἐπανελθεῖν, οὐχὶ εἰς κενὸν τὴν χάριν δέξασθαί. Οὐδὲν γὰρ ἀπὸ τοῦ χαρίσματος ὠφέλη-

ὠφελώμεθα εἰς σωτηρίαν, ἀκαθάρτως ζῶντες, ἀλλὰ καὶ βλα- πτόμεθα μειζόνως ταύτῃ βαρύμενοι καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἁμαρτήμα- σιν, ὅτι μετὰ ἐπίγνωσιν ταύτην, καὶ δωρεὰν ἐπὶ τὰ πρότερα ἐπανήλθομεν κακὰ, nam si quis liberatus a peccatis & amicus factus Dei iterum in prioribus volutetur, -id vero est ad inimicitiam redire, & frustra accepisse gra- tiam. Nihil enim magni ex gratia consequimur ad salutem, si impure vivamus, imo contra lædimur, cum ad peccata gravius inde pondus accedat, quod post cognitionem illam & illa dona ad mala priora revertimur. Ad Galatas cap. V. v. 4. Ἵνα τοίνυν μὴ ἀκούσας ὅτι ἐξελέξατο τὴν πίστιν ἀρκεῖν νομίσῃς μόνον, καὶ τὸν βίον προστίθησι, ne igitur, ubi audis, elegit solam putes sufficere fidem, ideo & vitam addit. Libro quarto de sacerdotio: Οὐδὲν κέρδος ὑγιοῦς πίστεως τῆς πολιτείας διεφθαρμένης nihil lucri ex sana fide, si vita sit cor- rupta.

Per πνεῦμα animam substantiæ ratione intelligi, salva quidem fidei analogia admittere possemus, quemadmodum admisit Flacius & Brochmand, & e Reformatis, Piscator, Drusius, cum Paëzio, Justinia- no, Estio: præstat tamen respirationem seu halitum vitalem intelligere, cum B. Menzero, B. Gerhardo, B. Hopfnero, B. Hülsemanno, Pareo, Interpp. Belgi- cis, & e Pontificiis Lyrano, Cajetano, Fabro Stapulen- si, nec non Cornelio a Lapide. Paëzio & asseclis id obstat, quod si essentialiter accipiatur πνεῦμα de anima, corporis animati forma, sequatur fidem, quæ est sine operibus, æquivoce saltem fidem dici, ficuti animatum, ubi expirat anima, non est amplius, quod erat, nisi ὁμωνύμως. Quo de Guillandus: Ut cada- ver aut simulachrum speciem quidem hominis, non autem vim & opera hominis habet: Ita & fides sine charitate & operibus. At fidem sine operibus æqui- voce tantum fidem dici repugnat Pontificiorum sententiæ, qui eam pro fide proprie dicta habent, & speciem fidei distinctam a fide formata faciunt: Quemadmodum & Grotius veram fidem existere in hominibus posse ait absque operibus. Adde quod Bellarmino ipsi absurdum sit, fidei salvificæ, quam formatam vocant, intrinsecam formam esse bona opera. Ideoque alii effective de motu animæ, & potissimum respiratione, ceu proprio, immediato & necessario effectu animæ ἐνσωμάτου, certaque vi- tæ argumento accipiunt. Ut enim corpus, quod amplius non respirat, mortuum est: Sic & fides, quæ se non exerit per bona opera, mortua est, quum æq; fides possit esse vera & viva absque operibus, atque corpus animatum & vivum sine respiratione. Agit enim in hoc tractatu S. Jacobus non de fidei forma & constitutione, sed effectis & declaratione.

Nec verum est, quod Grotius ait Ebræis רוּחַ de anima tantum adhiberi, נֶפֶשׁ vero de vita, cum & נֶפֶשׁ de habitu adhibeatur, Job. XLI. verf. 10. 11. nec non de desiderio, Exod. XV. 9. de voluntate, Psal. CV, 21. &c. & vox πνεῦμα apud LXX. pro re- spiratione itidem occurrat, Job. VII. 15. cap. XXVII. 2. cap. XXX. 16. & in Novo Testamento affectio- nes notet facultatis concupiscibilis & irascibilis non semper substantiam vivificam, Act. XVII. 16. cap. XVIII. 5. Quid vero accedet inde Pontificiis, vel Grotio, si maxime opera dicantur vita & anima fi- dei? Nam de nuda hic absentia operum (verbis fi- des, quæ sine operibus est, mortua est) non de impoten- tia justificandi citra coinfluentiam operum in justi- ficationem agitur. Unde Lorinus ita habet: Vis comparationis in eo consistit, quod quemadmodum cum abest a corpore anima, vel flatus, halitus, respira- tio, jacet corpus mortuum, omnique vita destitutum: Sic absente operatrice bonorum operum charitate, aut operibus, quæ habeant similitudinem vitalem functionum, remanet quidem fides, sed veluti exani- mis, exsanguis, mortua, nullum vere vitæ signum edens. E. veteribus Spiritum de respiratione & ha- litu exponunt Gaudentius Brixiensis ep. ad Germ.

T. III. Bibl. Patr. p. 830. Chrysost. hom. II. in Gen. Bernhardus serm: II: de resurrēct. fidei vitam opera attestantur, sicut scriptum est: Opera qua mihi dedit Pater, ista testificantur de me. Nec discre- pare videntur ab hac sententia, qui fidem sine operi- bus mortuam asserunt in semetipsa. Sicut enim cor- poris hujus vitam ex motu suo dignoscimus: Ita & fidei vitam ex operibus bonis. Quam explicatio- nem repetunt, suamque faciunt glossa ordin. Lyra- nus & Duacenses. Cajetanus itidem per Spiritum intelligit flatum. Quia ut corpus animale, si non spirat, est mortuum, ita operatio bona est effectus fidei viva. Neque improbat hanc Cajetani explicatio- nem Salmero, sed non ineptam dicit. Quae sub finem è Chrysostomo conglomeravit Grotius ὐδὲν πρὸς ἔπῶ : Necessitatem operum, vel conjunctionis fidei & operum docent: necessaria au- tem esse opera ad justificationem, & salutem vel obtinendam vel conservandam, nullo apice innu- unt. Aut requiri testantur, ne per voluntariam segnitiem, vel abstinentiam à bene operando, vel per commissionem mali oppositi perdamus beneficia ac- cepta, & promissa: non autem ut per bona opera ju- stificationis & salutis beneficium acquiramus, impe- tremus, vel per modum causae conservantis, quomo- do alimenta conservant corpus humanum, confer- vemus. Locus penultimus in Eph. I. 4. (qui falso adductus Gal. V. 4.) ita in Chrysostomo legitur: Ἵνα μὴ τοίνυν, ὅτι ἐξελέξατο, τὴν πίσιν ἀρκεῖν νομί- σῃς μόνον,ὴ τὸν βίον προστίθησι. Gentianus Hervetus Aurelius, Rhemensis Canonicus interpretatus est: Ne ergo existimes, solum sufficere, quod fidem no- stram elegit, vitam etiam addit: Propterea, inquit, nos elegit etiam ad hoc, ut essemus sancti & immacu- lati. Quae immutata sunt à Grotio. Sed etiamsi juxta eundem legantur, nihil faciunt ad τὸ κρινόμενον, fi- dem solam non sufficere ad salutem, scilicet conse- quendam. De hoc enim fine nihil habent: Ex ad- verso autem Chrysostomus passim soli fidei adscri- psit salutem. Sole clariora sunt illa ad Rom. III. v. 27. Qua autem est lex fidei? Salvari per gratiam. His potentiam ostendit, quod non solum salvavit, sed & justificavit, & in gloriationem induxit, nulla pe- tens opera, fidem tantum requirens. Et hom. XIV. in cap. VIII. 21. Hoc unum attulimus DEI do- num, quod credimus promittenti futura. Et tan- tum hac via salvati sumus. Hanc viam si amiseri- mus, totam summam collationis nostrae amisimus. Et paulo post: Quod itaque te salvum fecit? Tantum quod in Deum sperasti, ejusque promissionibus credi- disti: Et plura in hanc rem afferre non potuisti. Item in Eph. II. vers. 8. Quomodo fides salvum fecit ab operibus? Hoc ipsum est Dei donum, ne quis glorie- tur, ut de gratia ipsius bene sentientes (gratos) faci- at. Quid ergo? Prohibuitne ex operibus justifica- ri? Nequaquam. Sed nullus, inquit, justificatus est ex operibus, ut ostendatur Dei gratia & Φιλανθρω- πία. Non abjicit habentes opera, sed eos, qui conspi- cui sunt operibus, gratis salvavit, ut nemo gloriandi causam haberet. Plura alias adducta sunt è Chry- sostomo. Haec in praesenti facile ad mentem ejus vin- dicandam sufficere possunt.

Juvat autem coronidis loco ad praesentem tra- ctationem Jacobaeam paraphrasin Beza non in- concinnam addere, quae ita habet: Nitebantur isti falsa illa fidei specie, id est, notitia Dei: hanc illis oportuit ostendi veram fidem non esse, sed mortuum simulacbrum. Sed illam tamen Jacobus per concessio- nem, (ne de verbis litigare videatur) fidem vocat. Versus 14. Esto, inquit, fidem illam habeatis, quam vos habere dicitis, quid aliud est, quam res inutilis? V. 15. 16. hoc illustrat adhibita comparatione: Si quis famelico dixerit: Satur esto, nec interim quicquam illi suppeditaverit, quis veram hanc esse liberalita- tem dixerit? V. 17. Ita si DEI notitiam vos habere gloriemini, (quam fidem vocatis) nec interim eam ad usum accommodetis, non erit haec fides proprie, sed fidei simulacrum: ut si corpus inanime hominem di- cas. V. 18. Quid ergo? Nempe fides ea demum est, quam ex operibus possis ostendere. V. 19. Deinde ad argumenta accedit: Si illud, quod fidem vocas, fides esset, quid impediret Diabolum, quo minus & ipse fi- delis esset? Nam credit Diabolus, quod tu fidem vo- cas: nec tamen confidit, sed contremiscit. Ergo fides, quam jactas, vera fides non est, nec qua secure niti possis. V. 20. Vis autem hoc amplius cognoscere? V. 21. Confer fidem illam, quam jactas, cum Abrahami exemplari. Neque enim dubium est, quin hic veram fidem habuerit. Quid igitur ille? Nonne Isaacum obtulit? V. 22. Itaque non habuit fidem, quam opera non consequerentur, sed illum vere per fidem justifi- catum fuisse res ipsa ostendit, quum opus ederet justi- tiae. Ex eo igitur, quod factis ostendit fidem, liqui- do apparuit, non mortuam, sed vivam, & suis nume- ris absolutam fuisse ipsius fidem. V. 23. Tumque ple- ne patefactum est, quam merito scriptum esset de eo, quod credidisset Deo, idque ei imputatum esset ad ju- stitiam. V. 24. Inde efficitur, vere justificatum esse non eum, qui fidem illam habeat, quam jactatis, sed eam, quae ex effectis ostendi possit. V. 25. Aliud exem- plum quaeritis? Nam istud fortasse vos deterret. Su- mamus meretricem illam Rahab, cui vos pudebit im- pares fieri. Illa nonne re ipsa ostendit, se longe aliam fidem habere, quam mortuam illam, cum Diabolis ipsis communem? Nam DEI gloriam & proximi charitatem vitae suae anteposuit, servatis & emissis Dei speculatoribus. V. 26. Concludamus igitur, fi- dem illam vestram quasi cadaveris instar esse: itaq; non esse, quod vos illius titulo superbietis, quasi per eam justificati. Viva enim est, non mortua illa fides, quae in justificatorum factis elucet.

## 3:1 Argument
PART III. OF THE PARENETIC EPISTLE. SECTION I. GENERAL. CHAPTER III. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He warns about bridling the tongue in rash judgment of one's neighbor, and avoiding other slips of the tongue, since horses can be bridled and ships steered by a small rudder, and that small member accomplishes great things by inflaming our whole body; and he teaches that the tongue is more difficult for man to bridle than untamed animals, with which we both praise and curse, whereas sweet and bitter waters do not bubble forth from the same source, and he exhorts to the demonstration of true wisdom, and meekness, and mercy without lying, and hypocrisy, and contention.

There are two parts. I. On bridling the tongue, to v. 12. II. On true wisdom to be demonstrated particularly in the moderation of the tongue, to v. 18.

PART I. On bridling the tongue.

Vers. 1. Μὴ πολλοὶ διδάσκαλοι γίνεσθε, ἀδελφοί μου)

Let not just anyone covet the office of Teacher, that is, of a Bishop so eminently called: Τῶν προεστώτων, τῶν κοπιώντων ἐν λόγῳ etc. Not that it is not an excellent thing: but that few are equal to it. Διδάσκαλοι רבים מורים or. A similar admonition in Ecclesiastes VII. 17.

Εἰδότες ὅτι μεῖζον κρῖμα ληψόμεθα) That is, God will require more from us, who are Teachers of others, than from others. But if this is true in those who have complied with the judgment of others, how much more so in those who thrust themselves forward? Chrysost. in XIII. ad Ebræos Βαβαὶ πόσος ὁ κίνδυνος. Τί ἄν τις εἴποι πρὸς τὰς ἀθλίας, τὰς ἐπιῤῥιπτούσας ἑαυτὰς τοσαύτῃ τιμωριῶν ἀβύσσῳ; πάλιν ὧν ἄρχεις γυναικῶν, καὶ ἀνδρῶν, καὶ παιδίων, σὺ λόγον δίδως. Τοσούτῳ πυρὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν ὑποτίθης; θαυμάζω εἴ τινά ἐστι τῶν ἀρχόντων σωθῆναι πρὸς τῇ τοιαύτῃ ἀπειλῇ καὶ τῇ παρούσῃ ῥᾳθυμίᾳ, ὁρῶν ὅτι καὶ ἐπιτρέχουσί τινες, καὶ ἐπιῤῥίπτουσιν ἑαυτοὺς τῷ τοσούτῳ ὄγκῳ τῆς ἀρχῆς. Εἰ γὰρ οἱ ἀνάγκῃ ἑλόμενοι οὐδεμίαν ἔχουσι καταφυγὴν καὶ ἀπολογίαν, κακῶς τὸ πρᾶγμα οἰκονομοῦντες κἀμελοῦντες. Ἐπεὶ καὶ Ἀαρὼν ἠπειλήθη κἀκινδύνευσε. Καὶ Μωσῆς πάλιν ἐκινδύνευσε πολλάκις παραιτησάμενος. Καὶ Σαὺλ ἑτέραν ἐμπιστευθεὶς ἀρχὴν μετὰ τὸ παρακληθῆναι ἐκινδύνευσεν, ἐπειδὴ κακῶς αὐτὴν ᾠκονόμησε. Πόσῳ μᾶλλον οἱ σπουδῇ ταύτην τίθεμενοι καὶ ἐπιῤῥίπτοντες ἑαυτούς. Ὁ δὲ τοιοῦτος πολλῷ πλέον ἑαυτὸν ἀποστερήσει πάσης συγγνώμης. Δεδοικότας γὰρ χρὴ καὶ τρέμειν, καὶ διὰ τὸ συνειδὸς καὶ διὰ τὸν ὄγκον τῆς ἀρχῆς, and what follows there, which will contribute primarily to understanding this passage.

The general admonition is about being cautious of the mastery of the tongue over others, because the whole chapter deals with restraining the tongue without restriction to a specific order. Therefore, it should not be drawn to the Ecclesiastical office: he who desires this, desires a good work, as Paul testifies, 1 Tim. III. 1. Some divide the chapter into three exhortations: on avoiding arrogance in correcting brothers v. 1, 2; on restraining the tongue from v. 3 to v. 13; and on showing gentleness, avoiding envy and strife to the last verse. But all things can be recalled to the same exhortation which B. Brochmand makes concerning avoiding unjust and untimely censure, and a licentious mastery of observing others: We generally establish the sum concerning restraining the tongue: 1. In the correction of others v. 1, 2. 2. In the direction of the whole body and conversation: where the prior cause of restraining the tongue is simultaneously involved by its convenience, if it is restrained v. 2, 3, 4, 5, and if it is not restrained, by the damage and inconvenience, v. 5, 6. The latter, however, is from the difficulty of the matter, even though it is most necessary, v. 7, 8. 3. In the execration of one's neighbor, which cannot consist with the blessing of God, for which the tongue was granted, v. 9 to 12. 4. In contention, which is not a document of heavenly wisdom, but earthly, animal, and Demoniacal, v. 13 seqq., nor does it produce fruit, except bad ones, v. 16, whereas on the contrary, the fruit of the wisdom which is from above is not only purity, but also peace and mercy, as well as justice, v. 17, 18. Therefore, all things generally look to the right use of the tongue. There is nothing that teaches that it specifically regards the office of Teachers: and therefore neither that Grotian gloss, even though not only Justinianus and Estius the Papists, but also Drusius from the Reformed, and Luc. Osiander from our own favor it, that the duty of teaching should not be ambitiously affected; nor the one akin to it by Thomas Anglicus and Cornelius à Lapide, that there should not be many Bishops of one place and city, deserves approval; indeed, not even the explanation of certain Ancients, such as Augustine in the prologue to book 1 of the Retractations and Bede, which Salmero cites and approves, that since Christ is the only Rabbi, Matt. XXIII. 8, one must be cautious that there are not many Masters, that is, such Doctors who bring doctrine dissenting from the doctrine of the only Master. The interpretation of others is truer, who by the name of διδασκάλων understand those who take upon themselves a censorial right over others. For that fits 1. συνέχεια of the treatment, which there is no need to fetch from chapter I. 19 with Estius, since a closer and more elegant reason for the coherence can be rendered either with the preceding chapter concerning the vain boasting of faith, so with B. Brochmand you may say this admonition coheres, because those who vainly boast of faith are accustomed to inquire severely into the faith and life of others, but to indulge themselves a little more, or because the doctrine concerning true religion, to which, as in the case of the visitation of the needy and the avoidance of προσωποληψίας [partiality], so generally the demonstration of faith through charity and the pursuit of good works look, conveniently follows an exhortation to bridle the tongue, through which, when not governed, both one's neighbor is rashly judged, and the whole body is defiled, and the wheel of our birth is set on fire, and the execration redounds upon God himself, nor can heavenly wisdom, purity, peace, or any fruit of justice have a place. 2. Contextus συνάφεια [connection]. For here the discourse is not so much about a διδασκαλία [teaching] that is dangerous, such as that of an ecclesiastical office, as it is about one that is vicious and necessarily brings a heavier judgment, verse 1. 3. The cause of the prohibited mastership, which is that in many things we all stumble. This is not a reason for not seeking the Episcopate. For thus no one ought to seek or assume the Episcopate, because there is no one who does not stumble in many things, as the Apostle testifies: No one is so perfect that he does not stumble in speech alone. 4. The advantage of a bridled tongue, that it contributes to perfection and the moderation of the whole body, verse 2 seqq. Does the intermission of seeking the Episcopate bring this advantage? 5. The harm of an unbridled tongue: Which likewise looks not to the doctoral office, but in general to the abuse of the tongue, since it is a world of iniquity, etc. Whence Flacius, Beza, Hemmingius, Piscator, Pareus, and other Belgian interpreters join in this general explanation. B. Brochmandus: Since all the reasons, he says, which are subjoined, contain the inconveniences of a petulant tongue, everyone easily sees that those are to be understood here under the name of διδασκάλων [teachers], who are accustomed to call the words and deeds of others to account, and meanwhile do not see that which is in the wallet on their back, Matt. VII. 11. Luke VI. 37. What Heinsius brings forth here on page 590 is too subtle, thinking that πολὺς διδάσκαλος [many a teacher] in this place is ὁ μέγας διδάσκαλος [the great teacher], so that this name, brought forward with expressed magnitude, goes off into a reproach of the supreme Teacher, Matt. XXIII. verse 8. The context certainly shows that the Apostle is sharpening his pen against the importunate chastisers of the life and faith of others: of which kind of censors and masters he teaches there are many, when he says: Μὴ πολλοὶ διδάσκαλοι γίνεσθε [Be not many teachers]. Therefore the sense of the words of St. James is: Let us not importunately arrogate to ourselves a mastership over the faith, life, and morals of others.

However, the name πολλοὶ [many] can be referred to the multitude of affected mastership by reason of the same subject, lest any one person be πολὺς [many] or μέγας [great] or a Master of many. For such Aristarchuses and Censors are accustomed to take mastership to themselves over many, indeed all, and perhaps recall everyone under their Censorian rod, since in their own judgment they alone are wise, while others flit about like shadows. They do not take upon themselves the role of one master only, but of many, as those who are like several Doctors for passing judgment on others, and easily suffice alone to judge countless people. Such, however, will bring a heavier judgment, both because the kind of people they show themselves to be in judging others without mercy, such a God they will find in turn in judging them, James II. verse 13. Matt. XVIII. verse 25. Luke VI. verse 37. both because he who professes himself a leader of others, and himself stumbles in those things for which he reproves others, deserves a heavier punishment, Rom. II. v. 17. 18. Matt. XV. v. 14. Luke VII. verse 41. 42.

Latin:

PARS III. EPISTOLAE PARENETICA. SECTIO I. GENERALIS. CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Monet de frenanda lingua in judicio temerario de proximo, & cavendis aliis lapsibus linguae, cum equi frenari, naves a modico guberna- culo dirigi possint, & parvum illud mem- brum magna efficiat inflammando totum corpus nostrum; docetque linguam aegrius quam indomita animantia ab homine fre- nari, qua tum laudamus, tum maledici- mus, quum contra non ebulliant e fonte eo- dem & dulces & amarae aquae, ac hortatur ad ostendendam veram sapientiam, & mansuetudinem, ac misericordiam citra mendacium, & hypocrisin ac contentionem.

Partes duae sunt. I. De lingua frenanda, ad v. 12. II. De vera sapientia in linguae moderamine pecu- liariter demonstranda, ad v. 18.

PARS I. De lingua frenanda.

Vers. 1. Μὴ πολλοὶ διδάσκαλοι γίνεσθε, ἀδελφοί μου)

Ne quivis ambiat munus Doctoris, id est, Episcopi sic eminenter dicti: Τῶν προεστώτων, τῶν κοπιώντων ἐν λόγῳ etc. Non quod non præclara ea res sit: sed quod pauci sint pares. Διδάσκαλοι רבים מורים aut. Similis admonitio Ecclesiastæ VII. 17.

Εἰδότες ὅτι μεῖζον κρῖμα ληψόμεθα) Id est, plura à nobis, qui Doctores aliorum sumus, requiret Deus, quam ab aliis. Quod si hoc verum in iis, qui aliorum judicio morem gessere, quanto magis in iis, qui se ingerunt? Chrysost. in XIII. ad Ebræos Βαβαὶ πόσος ὁ κίνδυνος. Τί ἄν τις εἴποι πρὸς τὰς ἀθλίας, τὰς ἐπιῤῥιπτούσας ἑαυτὰς τοσαύτῃ τιμωριῶν ἀβύσσῳ; πάλιν ὧν ἄρχεις γυναικῶν, καὶ ἀνδρῶν, καὶ παιδίων, σὺ λόγον δίδως. Τοσούτῳ πυρὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν ὑποτίθης; θαυμάζω εἴ τινά ἐστι τῶν ἀρχόντων σωθῆναι πρὸς τῇ τοιαύτῃ ἀπειλῇ καὶ τῇ παρούσῃ ῥᾳθυμίᾳ, ὁρῶν ὅτι καὶ ἐπιτρέχουσί τινες, καὶ ἐπιῤῥίπτουσιν ἑαυτοὺς τῷ τοσούτῳ ὄγκῳ τῆς ἀρχῆς. Εἰ γὰρ οἱ ἀνάγκῃ ἑλόμενοι οὐδεμίαν ἔχουσι καταφυγὴν καὶ ἀπολογίαν, κακῶς τὸ πρᾶγμα οἰκονομοῦντες κἀμελοῦντες. Ἐπεὶ καὶ Ἀαρὼν ἠπειλήθη κἀκινδύνευσε. Καὶ Μωσῆς πάλιν ἐκινδύνευσε πολλάκις παραιτησάμενος. Καὶ Σαὺλ ἑτέραν ἐμπιστευθεὶς ἀρχὴν μετὰ τὸ παρακληθῆναι ἐκινδύνευσεν, ἐπειδὴ κακῶς αὐτὴν ᾠκονόμησε. Πόσῳ μᾶλλον οἱ σπουδῇ ταύτην τίθεμενοι καὶ ἐπιῤῥίπτοντες ἑαυτούς. Ὁ δὲ τοιοῦτος πολλῷ πλέον ἑαυτὸν ἀποστερήσει πάσης συγγνώμης. Δεδοικότας γὰρ χρὴ καὶ τρέμειν, καὶ διὰ τὸ συνειδὸς καὶ διὰ τὸν ὄγκον τῆς ἀρχῆς, & quæ ibi sequuntur ad hunc locum intelligendum apprime conducentia.

Admonitio generalis est de magisterio linguæ in alios cavendo, quia de lingua refrenanda sine restri- ctione ad certum ordinem totum caput agit. Non ergo ad officium Ecclesiasticum trahenda est: quod qui desiderat, bonum opus desiderat, teste Paulo, 1. Tim. III. 1. Dispescunt nonnulli caput in tres pa- raneses: de cavenda arrogantia in corripiendis fratribus v. 1. 2. de frenanda lingua à v. 3. ad v. 13. & de mansuetudine præstanda, cavenda invidia & rixis ad vers. ult. Sed omnia ad eandem exhortationem revocari possunt, quam B. Brochmand. facit de ca- venda iniqua & intempestiva censura, & licentioso in alios animadvertendi magisterio: Nos γενικῶς summam constituimus de frenanda lingua: 1. In aliorum correptione v. 1. 2. 2. In totius corporis & conversationis directione: ubi causa frenandæ lin- guæ prior simul involvitur ab ejusdem tum com- modo, si frenetur vers. 2. 3. 4. 5. tum si non frene- tur, damno & incommodo, v. 5. 6. Posterior verò est à difficultate rei, etsi maxime necessariæ, v. 7. 8. 3. In proximi execratione, quæ consistere nequit cum benedictione Dei, ob quam concessa est lingua, v. 9. ad 12. 4. In contentione, quæ non sapientiæ cœlestis documentum est, sed terrenæ, animalis & Dæmoniacæ, v. 13. seqq. nec fructus pa- rit, nisi malos, v. 16. quum contra sapientiæ, quæ non superius est fructus non solum puritas, sed pax etiam atque misericordia sit, nec non justitia, v. 17. 18. Omnia itaque generatim ad rectum linguæ usum spectant. Nihil est, quod doceat peculiati ter respi- ci officium Doctorum: ideoque nec illa Grotiana glossa, etsi non tantum Justinianus & Estius Pontifi- cii, sed etiam Drusius è Reformatis, & Luc. Osiander è nostris ei faveant, ne docendi munus ambitiose affe- ectetur; nec affinis eidem Thomæ Anglici ac Cornelii à Lapide, ne plures sint unius loci & urbis Episcopi calculum meretur, imo nec Veterum quorundam utpote Augustini prolog. in libr. 1. Retract. ac Be- dæ, quam Salmero adducit, ac probat, explicatio, quum Christus unicus Rabbi sit Matth. XXIII. 8. cavendum esse, ne plures sint Magistri, id est, tales Doctores, qui afferunt doctrinam, ab unici Magi- stri doctrina dissentientem. Verior est interpreta- tio aliorum, qui nomine διδασκάλων intelligunt eos, qui in alios jus censorium sibi sumunt. Nam illi congruit 1. συνέχεια tractationis, quam non opus est, cum Estio à cap. I. 19. arcessere, quum propin- quior & concinnior reddi possit cohærentiæ ratio sive cum præcedenti capite de vana fidei jactantia, ita cum B. Brochmand. dicas hanc admonitionem cohaerere, quod qui fidem vane jactant, in alienam fidem & vitam severe inquirere, sibimet vero pluscu- lum indulgere soleant, seu quod commode doctri- nam de vera religione, ad quam ut in specie visita- tio indigentium, ac fuga προσωποληψίας; ita ge- neratim fidei per charitatem ac studium bonorum operum demonstratio, spectant, sequatur adhorta- tio ad linguam frenandam, per quam non guberna- tam & proximus temere judicatur, & totum corpus maculatur, ac rota nativitatis nostrae inflammatur, & in Deum ipsum redundat execratio, nec locum habere potest coelestis sapientia, puritas, pax, aut ullus justitiae fructus. 2. Contextus συνάφεια. Nam hic de διδασκαλία non tam periculosa, qualis est Ecclesiastici muneris, quam vitiosa, & necessa- rio gravius judicium afferente, vers. 1. sermo est. 3. Prohibiti magisterii causa, quae est, quod in multis labamur omnes. Haec non est ratio non expetendi Episcopatus. Sic enim nemo Episco- patum petere, aut assumere deberet, quia nemo est, qui non labatur in multis, teste Apostolo: Ne- mo tam perfectus est, ut in sermone tantum non labatur. 4. Franata lingua commodum, quod faci- at ad perfectionem, totiusque corporis modera- tionem vers. 2. seqq. Num intermissio expetendi Episcopatum hoc commodum affert? 5. Linguae non franatae damnum: Quod itidem non ad docto- rale munus, sed in genere ad abusum linguae, quum mundus iniquitatis sit, &c: spectat. Unde huic ge- nerali explicationi accedunt Flacius, Beza, Hem- mingius, Piscator, Pareus, Interpp. Belgici alii. B. Brochmandus: Cum rationes omnes, inquit, quae subjunguntur, petulantis linguae incommoda conti- neant, nemo non facile videt, quod hi nomine διδα- σκάλων hic veniant intelligendi, qui aliena dicta & facta sub censum vocare solent, ac interim id man- ticae, quod a tergo est, non vident, Matth. VII. 11. Luc. VI. 37. Justo subtiliora sunt, quae hic promit Heinsius pag. 590. ratus, quod πολὺς διδάσκαλος hoc in loco sit ὁ μέγας διδάσκαλος, ita ut hoc no- men, cum expressa magnitudine adductum, ad su- premi Doctoris contumeliam abeat Matth. XXIII. vers. 8. Contextus certe monstrat, quod Apostolus in importunos alienae vitae ac fidei castigatores ca- lamum stringat: cujus generis censores & magistros multos esse docet, quando dicit: Μὴ πολλοὶ διδάσκα- λοι γίνεσθε. Verborum itaque D. Jacobi sensus est: Ne in alienam fidem, in alienam vitam & mores ma- gisterium importune nobis arrogemus.

Nomen tamen πολλοὶ referri potest ad affectati magisterii multitudinem ratione ejusdem subjecti, ne unus aliquis πολὺς multus vel μέγας magnus seu multorum Magister sit. Solent enim tales Ari- starchi, & Censores in multos imo omnes magi- sterium sibi sumere, omnesque forte sub virgulam Censoriam revocare, quum suo judicio ipsi soli sa- piant, caeteri volitent sicut umbrae. Non uni- us tantum Magistri vicem sibi sumunt, sed mul- torum, ut qui sint instar plurium Doctorum ad censuram de aliis ferendam, sufficiantque facile soli ad innumeros judicandos. Tales autem gra- vius judicium afferent, tum quia quales se in alios sine misericordia judicandis praebent, talem in se judicandis vicissim Deum invenient Jac. II. vers. 13. Matth. XIIX. vers. 25. Luc. VI. vers. 37. tum quia qui Ducem aliorum se profitetur, & in iis ipse labitur, ob quae alios reprehendit, graviorem poe- nam meretur, Rom. II. v. 17. 18. Matth. XV. v. 14. Luc. VII. vers. 41. 42.

## 3:2
Verse 2.

Πολλὰ γὰρ πταίομεν ἅπαντες [For in many things we all stumble]) All, that is, most, as the following teaches. It is the custom of great men through a certain modesty to add themselves to the weaker ones. Πταίειν [to stumble], in Syriac שרע [to slip], is said here of some error which can happen to those who teach: for which reason Paul, though conscious of no evil in himself, yet does not say he is entirely free from this, namely from errors, 1 Cor. IV., where see the remarks. The mortal condition does not allow a man to be pure from every stain, says Lactantius VI. 13. Philo on Agriculture: For it is difficult, just as for runners who have started on the road to piety, to direct their course without stumbling and without falling, since ten thousand things fall in the way of one who is born, and with some things inserted, which it would be long to transcribe: But rare are those to whom God will grant to walk through life from beginning to end without having stumbled or slipped, but by the force and speed of their nature to fly over both kinds of offenses, voluntary and involuntary. See also Ecclesiastes VII. verse 20. But yet so that you remember these things are to be understood differently in that imperfect time, and differently under the Gospel.

Three things are to be noted here in Grotius: 1. The depravation of the word ἅπαντες [all]. And it denotes all, as is evident. Perversely, therefore, Grotius makes most out of all: nor does he have any argument for this thing from what follows. The universal pronouncement of James also agrees with Scripture everywhere, admitting no restriction or exception, 1 Kings VIII. verse 46. Eccles. VII. verse 21. Rom. III. verse 23. 1 John I. verse 8. And the catholic admonition requires the same universality. For the Apostle exhorts not some, but all. Therefore he brings forward the infirmity and proclivity to stumbling of all in the place of reason. Nor does the Apostle except himself, or at least through a certain modesty joins himself to the weaker ones. This infirmity, however, is common to all, which Grotius himself afterwards professed by the testimony of Lactantius and Philo, and indeed of Solomon himself. 2. The narrower explanation of stumbling. He restricts Τὸ πταίειν here to error, which can happen to those who teach. By what argument? For that word is general. Furthermore, if it is understood concerning errors in doctrine, how could James include himself out of modesty, when he could thus render his own doctrine suspect, and modesty ought not to detract from the truth. How could Grotius pronounce that Paul was not free from errors of such a kind? For that detracts from his Apostleship. And why does he think Paul truly (although through a misinterpretation of the passage 1 Cor. IV. verse 4) professed himself not to be immune from every error in doctrine? But that James only through modesty counted himself among those who slip in doctrine? Does he establish Paul as not as much inspired by God as James? Not only do all teachers slip in many things, nor only in doctrine (we except the Apostles, who were moved by the Holy Spirit, who as teachers of the universal Church had to be led into all truth by the force of Christ's promise, John XVI. verse 13), but also in life. Others slip equally as well. And this is the opinion of James. The Papists restrict the word πταίειν to venial sin, which is to slip, to stumble, and is less than to fall, as for instance Justin, Paëz, Estius. But the thing itself teaches that James does not excuse πταίσματα: indeed, he testifies rather, chap. II. verse 10, whoever has kept the whole law, but has slipped in one point, is held guilty of all. What, I ask, says the blessed Brochmand, would be the force of the Apostolic speech? Do not exercise censure too importunately upon others: for you will incur a more severe judgment. Since indeed we all commit lighter aberrations. Add to these the complaints of the saints, Job IX. 1, 2, 3, Psalm XXXIII. 6, Psalm CXLIII. verse 2, Dan. IX. verse 5, 10, Rom. VII. verse 14, following. 3. The third thing worthy of note in Grotius is that he again brings in his distinction of the time before the Gospel, which he calls imperfect, by reason of the precepts and observance of the same, and under the Gospel, which is more perfect, which savors not of Scripture, but of the Socinian lamp.

If any man offend not in word.] Who neither says what he does not have certain knowledge of, and observes the times in which each thing is either to be said or kept silent. This admonition is directed especially at quarrelsome disputants, as the following shows.

But that does not appear from what follows. Not only are quarrelsome disputations noted, but all slips of the tongue. Therefore, it is not enough not to say what you do not have certain knowledge of, and to observe the times in which each thing is to be said, which fits others more than quarrelsome disputants, and is common to absolutely everyone. The tongue can also slip in other ways, namely by any idle word, Matt. 12:36.

This is a perfect man.] This man is excellent; 1 Cor. 2:6, 14:20, Phil. 3:15. He can say: אשמרה דרכי מחטוא בלשוני as it is in Psalm 39:2.

Not only an excellent man, but such a one is truly perfect. There is no reason why we should depart from the literal meaning of the word. For never to slip with the tongue is a sign of perfection, which does not fall to this life. Which the Psalmist had indeed proposed to himself, but did not attain, nor does anyone attain. For every man is a liar, Psalm 116:11. All have become useless, there is none who does good, not even one, Psalm 14:3. And we slip with the tongue not only regarding sins of commission, but also of omission. But who is so perfect that he does not slip in this way? Therefore, this is only an assertion, not an application. A major proposition, which presents the idea of a perfect man; under which, however, no one can subsume himself; for he who says that he is perfect who does not slip with his tongue does not by that very fact assert that anyone is found to be so perfect. The consequence from a precept to a possibility is not valid: much less to existence. Nay, by this conditional, perfection is denied to all from the greater to the less. For if that which seems more likely to be present is not present; much less will that be present which is less credible to be present: If even the smallest member cannot be restrained from a slip, how much less other members, the whole body, the mind itself? Indeed, his ἀδυναμία (inability) is expressly held in verse 8. No man can tame the tongue. It is an evil that you cannot restrain. Cf. Sir. 19:17. And Estius confesses that no one is found here who can avoid the smallest offenses of words. Therefore, the Apostle wants us to acknowledge our imperfection, lest like many Masters we presume to judge others; because not even we ourselves are of that perfection that we do not slip in speech: But as all slip in many things, so also all slip often in speech. Whence we have no cause to judge the slips of others in speech more rigidly, if we observe our own. There is no trace here of the body of the Church. He who does not slip in speech teaches what kind of body is understood as the subject; the less he slips with his tongue, the more apt he is to rule his whole body: the predicate teaches: that he is a perfect man (ἀνὴρ τέλειος). Therefore, the body of any man is noted, not the Church. The relation of the tongue in each one, who is warned to bridle it, teaches [it refers] to the whole body of the man. The comparison of a horse governed by a bridle to the whole body being ruled teaches it. Finally, the comparison in verse 6 of the defilement of the whole body, which the tongue often brings, teaches it. Therefore, a man is also said to be justified and condemned by his speech, Matt. 12:37. The sense, therefore, is, as the blessed Brochmand rightly says, that he who can moderate his tongue, to him it is also easy to rule the other members of the body, the eyes, ears, hands, and their actions. For since no member of the body is more prone to transgression than the tongue, and no aberrations are less cared for than those which are committed by the tongue, certainly he who can rule the tongue will also easily be going to govern the remaining members. For he who can do that which is most difficult, why will he not perform what is easier?

Able to bridle also the whole body.] He is finally apt to rule the whole body of the Church. For it usually happens that the people follow the tongue of the Doctor. We had χαλιναγωγεῖν (to bridle) also above at 1:26. The Syrian here has שעבד (to make to serve). Σῶμα (body) for the Church, 1 Cor. 12:20, 25, 27, Eph. 4:12, 16, Col. 1:18. This name, just as it belongs to the universal Church by a certain right: so also to individual churches in their own way. For every college is also called a body in law.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Πολλὰ γὰρ πταίομεν ἅπαντες) Omnes, id est, plerique, ut docet sequentia. Mos est magnorum virorum per modestiam quandam se addere infirmioribus. Πταίειν Syro שרע lapsare hic dicitur de errore aliquo, qui docen- tibus potest obvenire : qua de causa Paulus nullius sibi mali conscius, non tamen ab hoc se plane liberum ait, ab erroribus scilicet , 1. Cor. IV. ubi dicta vide. Mor- talis conditio non patitur esse hominem ab omni macu- la purum, ait Lactantius VI. 13. Philo de Agricultura: Χαλεπὸν γάρ, ὥσπερ τοὺς δρομεῖς ἀρξαμένους ὁδοῦ τῆς πρὸς εὐσέ- βειαν ἀπταίστως καὶ ἀπτῶσι διευθῦναι τὸν δρόμον, ἐπεὶ μυρία ἐμποδὼν πίπτι τῷ γενομένῳ, & quibusdam interjectis, quæ longum sit transscribere : Σπάνιοι δὲ, οἷ ταῖ δωρήσεται ὁ Θε- ὸς ἀπ' ἀρχῆς ἄχρι τέλους βαδιεῦσαι τὸν βίον μητ' ὀκλάσαντι, μητ' ὀλισθήσαντι, ἀλλ' ἑκατέρας φύσει ἀδικημάτων ἐκουσίων τε καὶ ἀκουσίων, ῥύμῃ καὶ φορᾷ τάχους ὑπερπτῆναι. Vide & Ec- clesiasten VII. vers. 20. Sed ita tamen ut memineris aliter hæc in illo tempore imperfecto, aliter sub Evangelio in- telligenda.

Tria hic notanda in Grotio : 1. vocis ἅπαντες depravatio. Et omnes, uti constat, denotat. Per- verse ergo ex omnibus plerosque facit Grotius : nec ex sequentibus ullum habet ejus rei argumen- tum. Consonat etiam universali Jacobi pronun- ciato passim scriptura, nullam admittens restrictio- nem, vel exceptionem, 1. Reg. VIII. vers. 46. Ec- cles. VII. vers. 21. Rom. III. vers. 23. 1. Joh. I. vers. 8. Et requirit eandem universalitatem ca- tholica admonitio. Nam hortatur non quos- dam, sed omnes Apostolus. Omnium ergo infir- mitatem ac proclivitatem ad lapsum rationis lo- co adducit. Nec sese excipit, vel saltem per mo- destiam quandam infirmioribus adjungit Aposto- lus. Hæc vero infirmitas omnibus communis est, quod testimonio Lactantii & Philonis imo ipsius Salomonis Grotius ipse deinde professus est. 2. La- psus angustior explicatio. Τὸ πταίειν hic restringit ad errorem, qui docentibus evenire potest. Quo ar- gumento ? Vox enim illa generalis est. Porrò si de erroribus in doctrina intelligatur, quomodo per modestiam se includeret Jacobus, quum ita suspe- ctam reddere posset doctrinam suam, nec modestia veritati derogare debeat. Quomodo Paulum ab erroribus ejusmodi non fuisse liberum pronuncia- re potuit Grotius ? Id enim Apostolatui ejusdem derogat. Et cur Paulum ex vero putat (quam- vis per ψευδερμηνείαν loci 1. Cor. IV. vers. 4.) se non immunem ab errore omni in doctrina esse professum. Jacobum autem tantum per modestiam iis, qui in doctrina labuntur, se accensuisse ? An Paulum non tam θεόπνευστον statuit, quàm Jaco- bum ? Non Doctores tantum in multis labuntur omnes, nec in doctrina solum (Apostolus ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγία Φερομένους excipimus, qui ceu uni- versalisEcclesiæDoctores in omnem veritatem de- duci debuerunt vi promissionis Christi Joh. XVI. vers. 13.) sed etiam in vita. Labuntur pariter & alii. Atq; hæc est Jacobi sententia. Pontificii re- stringunt verbum πταίειν ad peccatum veniale, quod sit labi, impingere, ac minus sit, quam cade- re, utpote Justin. Paëz, Estius. Sed Jacobum πταί- σματα non excusare, res ipsa docet : imo testatur potius, cap. II. vers. 10. qui universam legem serva- rit, πταίσει δὲ ἐν ἑνὶ, lapsus vero fuerit in uno, omni- um reus tenetur. Quæ, quæso, inquit B. Brochman- dus, foret Apostolice orationis valentia. Nolite in alios exercere importunius censuram : nam eò gra- vius auferetis judicium. Siquidem omnes leviores aberrationes committimus. Adde hisce sanctorum querelas Job. IX. 1. 2. 3. Psal. XXXIII. 6. Psal. CXLIII. vers. 2. Dan. IX. vers. 5. 10. Rom. VII. vers. 14. seqq. 3. Tertium quod in Grotio animad- versione dignum, est, quod iterum ingerit suam distinctionem temporis ante Evangelium, quod imperfectum vocat, ratione præceptorum & ob- servationis eorundem, & sub Evangelio, quod per- fectius, quæ non Scripturam, sed Socinianam lu- cernam olet.

Εἴ τις λόγῳ ὐ πταίσει.] Qui neq; dicit quod non comper- tum habeat, & tempora observet, quibus quidque aut dicen- dum aut silendum sit. Hæc admonitio maxime directa est in rixosos disputatores, ut sequentia ostendunt.

Id vero è sequentibus non apparet. Non tan- tum rixosæ notantur disputationes, sed omnes linguæ lapsus. Nec ergo sufficit, non dicere, quod non habeas compertum, & tempora observare, quibus quidque dicendum, quod magis in alios quadrat, quam rixosos disputatores, & omnibus omnino commune est. Labi etiam aliis modis lingua pot- est, nimirum quovis otioso verbo, Matth. XII, 36.

Οὗτος τέλειος ἀνήρ.] Hic vir est egregius; 1. Cor. II, 6. XIV, 20. Phil. III, 15. Is potest dicere : אשמרה דרכי מחטוא בלשוני ut est in Psalm. 39. v. 2.

Non tantum vir egregius, sed vere perfectus talis est. Nulla causa est, cur à vocis proprietate disce- damus. Nam nunquam labi lingua perfectionis signum est, quæ non cadit in hanc vitam. Quod proposuerat quidem sibi Hieoropsaltes, sed non as- sequutus est, neque quisquam assequitur. Omnis enim homo mendax est, Psal. CXVI, 11. Omnes facti sunt inutiles, non est, qui facit bonum, ne unus qui- dem, Psalm. XIV, 3. Et labimur lingua non tan- tum quoad peccata commissionis, sed etiam omissio- nis. Ecquis vero ita perfectus, ut sic non labatur. Hic ergo assertio tantum est, non applicatio. Ma- jor propositio, quæ ideam sistit viri perfecti; sub qua vero subsumere nequit quisquam; Non enim qui dicit, illum perfectum esse, qui lingua non labi- tur, eo ipso aliquem inveniri ita perfectum asserit. A præcepto ad posse non valet consequentia: nedum ad esse. Imo hac conditionali à majori ad minus omnibus perfectio negatur. Si enim id non inest, quod magis inesse videtur; multo minus inerit, quod minus credibile est inesse: Si vel minimum membrum à lapsu cohiberi non potest, quanto mi- nus membra alia, totum corpus, animus ipse? Illi- us vero ἀδυναμία vers. 8. habetur diserte. Lin- guam nullus hominum domare potest. Malum est, quod coërcere non possis. Conf. Sir. XIX. vers. 17. Et fatetur Estius, hic non inveniri quenquam, qui minimas verborum offensas vitare possit. Vult ergo Apostolus, agnoscamus nostram imperfectio- nem, ne multorum Magistrorum instar alios judi- care præsumamus; quia ne ipsi quidem ejus sumus perfectionis, ut sermone non labamur: Sed ut omnes in multis, ita etiam in sermone sæpe labun- tur omnes. Unde nec aliorum lapsus in sermoni- bus rigidius censendi causam habemus, si nostros ipsi observamus. De corpore Ecclesiæ hic nullum vestigium. Quale corpus intelligatur subjectum, docet is, qui in sermone non labitur, quo minus labitur lingua, eo magis aptus ad regendum totum corpus suum: docet prædicatum: quod sit ἀνὴρ τέ- λειος. Viri ergo cujusvis corpus notatur, non Ec- clesiæ. Docet relatio linguæ in unoquoque, qui commonetur ad eam frenandam, ad totum homi- nis corpus. Docet comparatio equi freno guber- nati ad totum corpus regendum. Docet denique collatio vers. 6. totius corporis commaculatio, quam sæpe lingua affert. Ideo etiam ex sermone homo justificandus & condemnandus dicitur, Matth. XII, 37. Sensus ergo est, ut recte B. Broch- mandus, quod qui linguæ moderari potest, huic etiam facile sit, cætera corporis membra, oculos, aures, ma- nus, & eorum actiones regere. Etenim cum nullum corporis membrum ad transgressionem proclivius sit lingua, nec ullæ aberrationes minus curentur, quam quæ lingua committuntur, certe qui linguam regere potest, hic etiam reliqua membra facile gubernaturus est. Nam qui potest id, quod est difficillimum, quidni quod est facilius præstabit?

Δυνατὸς χαλιναγωγῆσαι καὶ τὸ ὅλον σῶμα.] Is demum aptus est ad regendum totum corpus Ecclesiæ. Plerumque enim evenit, ut Doctoris linguam sequatur plebs. Χαλιναγωγεῖν ha- buimus & supra I, 26. Syrus hic שעבד facere ut serviat. Σῶ- μα pro Ecclesia, 1. Cor. XII, 20. 25. 27. Eph. IV, 12. 16. Coloss. I, 18. Nomen hoc sicut universæ Ecclesiæ jure quodam com- petit: Ita & Ecclesiis singulis suo modo. Nam & omne col- legium in jure corpus dicitur.

## 3:3
Verse 3.

And if we put bits into the mouths of horses, that they may obey us, and we turn about their whole body.] By an apt similitude he shows that things are often small which move great things. See Psalm 32:9. Hence to bridle for to rule, not only among poets, but also among orators. And the skin adhering to the tongue is called a persuasive bridle (χαλινὸς πειθόϊος). Thus we say, the chariot does not heed the reins.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Εἰδὲ τῶν ἵππων τοὺς χαλινοὺς εἰς τὰ στόματα βάλλομεν, πρὸς τὸ πείθεσθαι αὐτοὺς ἡμῖν, καὶ ὅλον τὸ σῶμα αὐτῶν μετάγομεν.] Apposita similitudine ostendit, sæpe exigua esse quæ res ma- gnas moveant. Vide Psalm. XXXII, 9. Hinc frænare pro re- gere, non apud Poëtas tantum, sed & apud oratores. Et pel- licula linguæ adhærens dicitur χαλινὸς πειθόϊος שמש. Sic dicimus, nec audit currus habenas.

## 3:4
V. 4. Behold also the ships, being so great.] Those great ships (ציים אדירים) Isa. 33:21, of which Virgil says: - - - You would believe the Cyclades were floating, torn up. The Egyptian kings had house-boats, the length of which was half a stadium. Καὶ (and) here is for as, just as Job 5:7.

And driven by fierce winds.] He adds this to the difficulty of steering, that they are also tossed hither and thither by the waves. Σκληρῶν ἀνέμων (fierce winds) is רוחות גדולות in Jonah 1:4.

It is turned about by a very small rudder.] Aristotle proposes this question: Why does the rudder, being small and at the very end of the ship, have such power that by a small tiller, and by the strength of a man, and that a quiet one, the great masses of ships are moved? And he gives the reason in his Mechanical Problems, chapter 5.

Wherever the impulse of the pilot wills.] Ὁρμὴ here signifies the will, not the primary motion, as the philosophers take it: but as historians often do. Ὁ εὐθύνων here is for εὐθυντὴς, a participle for a verbal noun, in the Hebrew manner. The Greeks also call the pilot of a ship εὐθυντῆρα and a ruler, as do the Latin poets.

Latin:

V. 4. Ἰδὲ καὶ τὰ πλοῖα τηλικαῦτα ὄντα.] Magna illa navigia ציים אדירים Esa. 34. v. 21. de quibus Virgilius: - - - Credas innare revulsas Cycladas. Reges Ægyptii thalamegos habere, quarum longitudo se- mistadii. Καὶ hîc est pro sicut, quemadmodum Job. V, 7.

Καὶ ὑπὸ σκληρῶν ἀνέμων ἐλαυνόμενα.] Difficultatem regi- mini & hoc addit, quod & fluctibus huc illuc agitantur. Σκλη- ρῶν ἀνέμων רוחות גדולות Jon. I, 4.

Μετάγεται ὑπὸ ἐλαχίστου πηδαλίου.] Proponit hanc quæstio- nem Aristoteles: Διὰ τί τὸ πηδάλιον μικρὸν ὂν, κᾀ ἐπ᾿ ἐσχάτῳ τῷ πλοίῳ τοσαύτην δύναμιν ἔχει, ὥστε ὑπὸ μικρᾶ οἴακος, καὶ ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπου δυνάμεως καὶ ταύτης ἠρεμαίας μεγάλα κινεῖσθαι με- γέθη πλοίων. Et rationem reddit 2. μηχανικῶν capite 5.

Ὅπου ἂν ἡ ὁρμὴ τοῦ εὐθύνοντος βούληται.] Ὁρμὴ hic volun- tatem significat, non τὴν πρώτην κίνησιν, ut sumunt Philo- sophi: Sed quomodo historici sæpe. Ὁ εὐθύνων hic est pro εὐθυντὴς participium pro verbali, more Ebræo. Etiam Græ- ci gubernatorem navis εὐθυντῆρα vocant & rectorem, Latini Poëtæ.

## 3:5
Even so the tongue is a little member.] It is a small member, with regard to the human body, and much more so with regard to the social body.

And boasts great things.] Magna erat (it was great) is translated as μεγαλαυχεῖν in Ezekiel 16:49, Zephaniah 3:11, and עזץ in Psalm 10:18. Isocrates and other good Greek writers use this verb. In the Glossary, μεγαλαυχῶ means I magnify, I boast. In Psalm 12:4, מדברת גדלות is translated into Greek as γλῶσσαν μεγαλοῤῥήμονα (a tongue speaking great things). In Psalm 18:71, דברו בגאות is ἐλάλησεν ὑπερηφανίαν (it spoke pride); but in Daniel 7:20, וממלל רברבן is λαλοῦν μεγάλα (speaking great things).

See how great a forest a little fire kindles.] Thus Ben Sira: A burning fire kindles many heaps. Ὕλη does not necessarily mean a forest, but everything that can be burned. This is apparent in Sirach 28:10.

We have already warned that these are wrongly restricted to the social body or the Church. However, Heinsius notes that the word μεγαλαυχεῖν, although it properly pertains to words, is nevertheless rightly referred to deeds as well. See the LXX Interpreters on Ezekiel 16:50, Zephaniah 3:11. For it is in general to lift up one's neck boastfully, which is done by words, gestures, and deeds. Here, however, the tongue's 'boasting great things' is not said so much of empty vanity, as the Vulgate seems to have understood, rendering it 'magnifies great things,' and Beza 'magnificently carries itself.' For the similar examples brought from the bridle and the rudder teach how great the power of the tongue is in directing the rest of the body, which does not so well suit the vanity of the tongue; rather, it is said of the effect of things: so that it is implied that the tongue can both boast great things and effect them. And indeed these are not to be taken only in a good sense, as Piscator and Estius wish, that it 'effects great things,' or at least in a bad one, as Heinsius, that it 'commits great sins,' but in a middle sense, which is the opinion of Pareus. For as bridles cause horses to obey, and the rudder and the ship's tiller cause the ship to be carried wherever the director wills: so also the tongue has the whole body in its power, to speak good or evil, and furthermore to effect things by its speech, and on that account it as it were lifts up its neck, and its head it removes, even if it is a small member. Afterwards, the subject is treated specifically regarding the depravity of the tongue, through the comparisons of a small fire, setting a huge amount of material ablaze. Ὀλί- γον πῦρ is a small fire: A spark of fire, which can accomplish that: Then also of wild animals v. 7. finally of lethal poison v. 8. These things, therefore, are not undeservedly explained even more generally, just as B. Luther elegantly rendered it: R grosse Dinge an.

Latin:

Οὕτω καὶ ἡ γλῶσσα μικρὸν μέλος ἐστὶ.] Parvum est mem- brum, ratione habita corporis humani, multoque magis ra- tione habita corporis socialis.

Καὶ μεγαλαυχεῖ.] Magna erat גבר vertitur μεγαλαυχεῖν Ezech. XVI, 49. Soph. III, 11. & עזץ Psalm. X. v. 18. Utitur hoc verbo Isocrates & alii bene Græci. In Glossario μεγα- λαυχῶ magnifico, glorior. In Psalm. XII, 4. מדברת גדלות Græce vertitur γλῶσσαν μεγαλοῤῥήμονα. Psalm. XVIII, 71. דברו בגאות ἐλάλησεν ὑπερηφανίαν; Danielis vero VII, 20. וממלל רברבן λαλοῦν μεγάλα.

Ἰδὲ ὀλίγον πῦρ ἡλίκην ὕλην ἀνάπτει.] Sic Bensyra ignis ar- dens accendit multos acervos. Ὕλη non utique nemus si- gnificat, sed omne quod incendi potest. Apparet id Sirach. XXVIII, 10.

Hæc ad corpus sociale vel Ecclesiæ restringi perpe- ram, jam monuimus. Verbum autem μεγαλαυ- χεῖν etsi proprie ad verba spectet, tamen ad facta quoque referri recte, notat Heinsius. Vid. LXX. Interpp. Ezech. XVI, 50. Soph. III, 11. Est enim in genere cervices gloriose erigere, quod fit verbis, ge- stibus & factis. Hic autem linguam μεγαλαυχεῖν non tam de inani jactantia dicitur, ut Vulgatus vi- detur intellexisse, reddens, magna exaltat, & Beza magnifice se effert. Similia enim à freno & guber- naculo adducta, quanta sit linguæ potestas in reli- quum corpus dirigendum, docent, jactantiæ lin- guæ non adeo conveniunt; quam de rerum effe- ctione: ut lingua magna & jactare & efficere in- nuatur. Et quidem non vel in bonam tantum par- tem hæc accipienda sunt, ut Piscator & Estius volunt, res magnas efficit, vel saltim in malam, ut Heinsius, magna committit peccata, sed in mediam, quæ Pa- rei est sententia. Nam ut frena faciunt, ut equi pa- reant, gubernaculum & navis procignaculum ut navis vehatur, quamdiu director voluerit: Ita et- iam lingua totum corpus in sua potestate habet, bonum vel malum loqui, ac porro sermone suo ef- ficere, eoque nomine cervices quasi erigit, caputq; tollit, etsi exiguum membrum sit. Postmodum in specie de pravitate linguae agitur, per similitudines ignis exigui, ingentem materiam incendentis. Ὀλί- γον πῦρ ignis exiguus est: Scintilla ignis, quae id ef- ficere potest: Tum etiam ferorum animalium v. 7. denique veneni lethalis v. 8. Haec ergo genera- lius adhuc non immerito explicantur, quemad- modum eleganter reddidit B. Lutherus: R grosse Dinge an.

## 3:6
Ver. 6.

So also the tongue is a fire, the world of iniquity, thus the tongue is established among our members.] These things do not cohere. The manuscript has: And the tongue is a fire, the world of iniquity, the tongue is established among our members, to which reading the Latin Interpreter comes close. But the Syrian seems to have read it best: The tongue is a fire to the world of iniquity is established &c. The tongue is accustomed to be compared to fire: Therefore the interpreter of Ben Sira, explaining the parable already mentioned, says: Just as a small fire consumes many heaps of grain, so there is nothing that devastates the world more than an evil tongue. You see here also that the world is placed in the stead of the material which the fire ignites, exactly as the Syrian perceived. Moreover, the evil tongue is said to be the fire of iniquity, because it stirs up the fires of hatreds, dissensions, seditions, and wars, all of which are rightly called by the name of iniquity. Thus Prov. XVI, an evil man is described in this way: In his lips is a burning fire. And Psalm CXX, 3. 4. a deceitful tongue is compared to coals. Is established among our members. In Syrian איתוהי בהדמין, it is one of the number of so many members & indeed a small one, and yet it accomplishes such great things, just as a bridle, a rudder, a flame. Euripides: From a small beginning the tongue provides great strife for men. And a Latin Proverb useful for this matter: From a spark, a conflagration.

That which defiles the whole body.] The mouth defiles the flesh, Ecclesiastes V, 5. Namely, when one comes from flatteries to adulteries. But here more correctly, as we have already said, body is taken for the body of the Church, which is often driven into the most serious dissensions through the tongue of one or another. To defile is to stain, Wisd. XV, 4. Jude 23. מכתם in Syrian. A stain is also said of any foul thing XXIIX, 6. Where it is transferred to the mind, it signifies to infect with vices, exactly as to defile in Heb. XII, 15.

And setting on fire the wheel of nature.] I think it should be written wheel. The books of those times did not have accents, which everyone later added according to their own judgment. Nature is the course of life, as we said above I, 23. The course of nature is a periphrasis of life. Varro: Fortune allows no one to slide from the starting gate of the course, unhurt, to the white finish line. Thus also old age is the turning point of life in Herod's mimiambs. Such also is that: I have lived and finished the course which fortune had given. Setting on fire, Dan. III, 28. Pf. 67, 3. Hesychius: to set on fire, to burn. And being set on fire by hell.] Present for Future, unless it should be written being set on fire, how the Syrian seems to have read it. Just as it itself sets on fire; so also it itself, namely with the body, will bring the fire of Gehenna. The sense is the same as Matt. V, 22. See also Matt. 18, 9. Mark 9, 47. For by hell, the Syrian has in the fire, the Arab in the fire, that is, by the fire. See Dan. VII, 9.

Some say that the elliptical expression should be supplied thus: The tongue is a fire, the world of iniquity is the material, so that this apodosis may be: The tongue is a fire, the world of iniquity, which is full of iniquity, 1 John V, 19. it is the material, which an unbridled tongue inflames in the manner and way of dry wood, so that the evil lurking before within the breast reveals itself, and spreads itself into the destruction of many, which B. Brochmand has. But I do not see why one should depart from the common reading and B. Luther's version. For the apodosis is to be supplied from the preceding. Also the tongue is such a fire, viz. setting a huge amount of material ablaze, the world of iniquity, and the tongue is also a fire, a world full of unrighteousness. Oecumenius & Isid. Pelusiota book IV, chap. 10, explain it as an ornament or covering of iniquity, because every iniquity is accustomed to be adorned and covered by the tongue, whence the phrase of scripture, to contrive deceits with the tongue, Job VI, 26. Psalm L, 19. Prov. XII, 19. As if he were to say: that the torch of eloquence, when it adorns those who are planning great things, seems to be an ornament of

truth, as Isidore has it, an ornament of diction, a torch when it adorns those who have fallen gravely, seems to paint over the truth. Yet Isidore also brings forward other interpretations, because world in Scripture signifies the multitude, the world did not ask him, that is, the multitude or the common people. The tongue, therefore, he says, is either a fire, burning the multitude iniquitously, or a receptacle of the multitude of unjust fire. To Heinsius, the world of iniquity is an instrument of iniquity. Others take it as a proverbial expression, as if it were a thing most full of iniquity, an Iliad of evils, and a sea of evils. Thus Calvin, Beza, Piscator, Drusius, Pareus, the Belgian Interpreters, Cornelius à Lapide, Estius, Brochmand. To which the Vulgate version also tends: A universe of iniquity. Which explanation seems most convenient. To this point belong the eight species of the evil tongue according to Thomas Anglicus: the slanderous of detractors, etc. XVIII. 6. the false of flatterers chap. XII, 18. the boastful of the proud, Ps. XI, 4. the viperous of heretics, Job XX, 16. the blasphemous of those who curse, chap. XV, 5. the deceitful of hypocrites, Ps. CXIX, 2. the defiled of the lustful, Sir. LI, 3. the iniquitous of advocates Prov. XVII. v. 2. The particle of comparison thus was added by Grotius without the authority of the Greek Codices. But the thus which follows is correct. Moreover, they cohere very well: Even the tongue is a world of iniquity. Now the apodosis of the comparison of fire is explained more expressly, as also the other epithet concerning the world of iniquity. Thus, I say, the tongue is established among our members (equally small, by comparison with other members) and defiling the whole body and setting on fire the wheel of our birth, and set on fire by hell. The body cleansed by the blood of Christ is entirely defiled through the tongue. It is an Iliad, and a sea of iniquity, and it is set on fire by the same, as a fire suddenly igniting, the vows of iniquity. The word body

Grotius perverts it again, explaining the Church as the mystical body of Christ: When the discourse is about his body, whose tongue is noted. The wheel of birth is explained as the course of nature or life. For thus πρόσωπον γενέσεως is the native countenance, James 1:23. Τροχὸς indeed [means] a wheel and everything circular, τρέχο [means] a runner, it rotates. The matter therefore comes to the same thing, whichever way you read it. For the course of our nature or life is also noted by the wheel through a metaphor. For the evil tongue inflames the whole curriculum of life, it sets all the ages of life on fire with anger, lust, pride, and other crimes. That Augustine explains trochon or wheel as a kind of punishment for men seems indeed ingenious and apt to Cornelius; so that the wheel of birth is the punishment of our nature, and Serarius says that such a native wheel is any perturbation whatsoever, [this] is foreign, because it is not about perturbation, but about the tongue that is treated here, not about the evil of punishment, but of fault. Kaj For (for it is also accustomed to be taken causally) it is inflamed by hell, because the devil kindles this fire, John 8:44, Rev. 12:10, Luke 11:24. The punishment of a wicked tongue is not expressed in hell, because the Apostle is properly occupied in designating the fault and its cause. He teaches how great an evil of fault the wickedness of the tongue is, a world of iniquity, defiling the whole body, and a fire, setting on fire the whole life; since it is kindled by hell, that is, by Metonymy, by the devil in hell: Or Catachrestically and by similitude, because it is evidently so slanderous, and so pestilent, and burning, that it does not seem to be kindled by earthly, but by infernal fire. For in hell the damned, out of desperation, with an ignited, furious tongue, curse God, etc. Nor will the tongue only be inflamed in hell, but the whole body, nay the whole man, who is entirely defiled and set on fire by the tongue throughout all age. He who is headlong into unjust censures, who is a liar, who uses impure speech, this man belches forth hellish flame, and he who hears, approves, and admits such words, admits hellish flame into his inmost breast, says Blessed Brochmand. How the tongue harms like an arrow, wounds like a sword, burns like fire, see Psalm 57:5, Proverbs 16:27, Jeremiah 9:8.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Οὕτω καὶ ἡ γλῶσσα πῦρ, ὁ κόσμος τῆς ἀδικίας, οὕτως ἡ γλῶσ- σα καθίσταται ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ἡμῶν.] Haec non cohaerent. Ma- nuscriptus habet: Καὶ ἡ γλῶσσα πῦρ, ὁ κόσμος τῆς ἀδικίας, ἡ γλῶσσα καθίσταται ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ἡμῶν, ad quam lectionem prope accedit Interpres Latinus. Sed Syrus optime legisse vi- detur: Ἡ γλῶσσα πῦρ τῷ κόσμῳ τῆς ἀδικίας καθίσταται &c. Solet lingua igni comparari: Itaque interpres Bensyrae dictam jam παραβολὴν explicans, ait: Sicut exiguus ignis multos fru- gum acervos consumit, ita nihil est, quod magis devaftat mundum quam mala lingua. Vides hic quoque mundum poni vice materiae, quam ignis accendit, plane ut sensit Syrus. Dicitur autem mala lingua esse πῦρ τῆς ἀδικίας, quia incen- dia suscitat odiorum, dissidiorum, seditionum, bellorum, quae omnia ἀδικίας nomine recte appellantur. Sic Prov. XVI. vir malus describitur hoc modo: In labiis ejus ignis ardens. Et Psalm. CXX, 3. 4. lingua dolosa carbonibus comparatur. Κα- θίσταται ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ἡμῶν. Syro איתוהי בהדמין, unum est de numero tot membrorum & quidem exiguum, & ta- men res tantas efficit, quomodo frenum, gubernaculum, flamma. Euripides: Σμικρᾶς ἀπ' ἀρχῆς νεῖκος ἀνθρώποις μέγα γλῶσσ' ἐκπορίζει. Et Latinum Proverbium in hanc rem utile: Ex scintilla in- cendium.

Ἡ σπιλῦσα ὅλον τὸ σῶμα.] Os inquinat carnem, Ecclesia- stae V, 5. Nempe cum ex blanditiis ad adulteria venitur. Sed hic rectius, ut jam diximus, σῶμα sumitur pro corpore Eccle- siae, quae saepe per unius atque alterius linguam in gravissimas diffensiones impellitur. Σπιλῦν est maculare Sap. XV, 4. Ju- dae 23. מכתם Syro. Σπίλωμα etiam de re quavis foeda dici- tur XXIIX, 6. Ad animum ubi transfertur, significat vitiis inficere, plane ut μιαίνειν Ebr. XII, 15.

Καὶ φλογίζυσα τὸν τροχὸν τῆς γενέσεως.] Puto scriben- dum τρόχον. Libri illorum temporum accentus non ha- buere, quos postea quisque addidit pro suo arbitrio. Γένεσις est natura, ut diximus supra I, 23. Cursus naturae est περί- φασις vitae. Varro: Nemini fortuna cursum carcere emissum intimo Labi inoffensum per aequas candidum ad calcem sinit. Sic & senectus βίε καμπτὴρ Herodi in mimiambis. Tale & illud: Vixi & quem dederat cursum fortuna peregi φλογίζω הרך Dan. III, 28. לחט Pf. 67, 3. Hesychius φλογίζω, καίω. Καὶ φλογιζομένη ὑπὸ τῆς γεέννης.] Praesens pro Futuro, nisi scribendum φλογισομένη, quomodo legisse videtur Syrus. Sicut ipsa incendit; ita & ipsa nempe cum corpore incendium feret Gehennae. Sensus idem, qui Matth. V, 22. Vide & Matth. 18, 9. Marci 9, 47. Pro ὑπὸ τῆς γεέννης. Syrus habet בנורא, Arabs באלדאל id est, ab igne. Vid. Dan. VII, 9.

Nonnulli Ellipticam loquutionem dicunt ita supplendam: Ἡ γλῶσσα πῦρ ἐστιν, ὁ κόσμος τῆς ἀδικίας ὕλη, ut apodosis haec sit: Lingua ignis est, mundus iniquitatis, qui plenus iniquitate est, 1. Joh. V, 19. materia est, quam lingua effrenis more ac modo lignorum aridorum inflammat, adeo ut la- tens antea intra pectus malum se prodat, & in per- niciem multorum se diffundat, quod habet B. Brochmandus. Sed non video, cur à communi le- ctione, ac B. Lutheri versione discedendum sit. Apodosis enim supplenda è superioribus. Etiam lingua est ignis talis, scil. ingentem materiam in- cendens, mundus iniquitatis, und die Zunge ist auch ein Feuer, eine Welt voll Ungerechtigkeit. Oecumenius & Isid. Pelusiota libr. IV. cap. 10. ex- ponunt ornamentum vel velamentum iniquitatis, quia lingua omnis iniquitas ornari & velari solet, unde phrasis scripturae, linguam concinnare dolos, Job. VI, 26. Psalm. L, 19. Prov. XII, 19. Quasi di- cat: ὅτι ὁ τῆς εὐγλωττίας πυρσὸς, ὅταν τὰς με- γάλα πλάοντας κοσμῇ, ἐγκαλλώπισμα δοκεῖ τῆς

ἀληθείας, ut habet Isidorus, ornatus dictionis, fax ubi eos, qui graviter lapsi sunt, exornat, fucum facere videtur veritati. Affert tamen & alias interpretatio- nes Isidorus, quod mundus in Scriptura significet multitudinem, mundus eum non rogavit, hoc est, multitudo seu plebs. Lingua igitur, inquit, aut ignis est, multitudinem inique comburens, aut receptacu- lum multitudinis ignis injusti. Heinsio κόσμος ἀδι- κίας est σκεῦος instrumentum iniquitatis. Alii pro loquutione habent proverbiali, quasi plenissimam iniquitatis rem, ἰλιάδη κακῶν, & mare malorum. Ita Calvinus, Beza, Piscator, Drusius, Pareus, Interpre- tes Belgici, Cornelius à Lapide, Estius, Brochman- dus. Quo etiam abit Vulgata versio: Universitas ini- quitatis. Quæ explicatio convenientissima vide- tur. Huc faciunt octo species malæ linguæ apud Thomam Anglicum maledica detractorumper, & c. XIIX. 6. falsa adulatorum cap. XII, 18. magniloqua superborum, Psal. XI, 4. viperea hæreticorum, Job. XX, 16. blasphema maledicentium, cap. XV, 5. do- losa hypocritarum, Ps. CXIX, 2. coinquinata luxu- riosorum, Sir. LI, 3. iniqua advocatorum Prov. XVII. v. 2. Particula similitudinis ὕτω à Grotio addita est sine autoritate Græcorum Codicum. Quæ autem sequitur ὕτως, recte se habet. Cohærent autem optime: Etiam lingua est mundus iniquitatis. Jam expreffius Apodosis similitudinis ignis explicatur, ut & alterum epitheton de mundo iniquitatis. Sic, inquam, lingua constituta est inter membra nostra (pariter exigua, comparatione aliorum membro- rum) & maculans totum corpus & inflammans ro- tam nativitatis nostræ, & inflammata à gehenna. Corpus mundatum sanguine Christi totum com- maculatur per linguam. Ilias est, & mare iniquita- tis, & inflammatur per eandem, ceu ignem subito incendentem, vota iniquitatis. Vocem σώματος

iterum pervertit Grotius, de corpore mystico Christi Ecclesia explicans: Quum sermo fit de ejus corpo- re, cujus lingua notatur. Rota nativitatis explica- tur naturæ seu vitæ curriculum. Nam ita πρόσωπον γενέσεως vultus nativus est, Jac. I, 23. Τροχὸς vero rotam & omne orbiculare, τρέχο cursor rotat. Res ergo eodem redit, utrovis modo legas. Nota- tur enim etiam per rotam naturæ vel vitæ nostræ cur- sus ejusdem per metaphoram. Totum enim curri- culum vitæ inflammat lingua mala, omnes vitæ æ- tates accendit ira, libidine, superbia, aliisq; sceleri- bus. Quod trochon vel rotam de supplicii genere Augustinus viros explicat, ingeniosum quidem & appositum Cornelio videtur; ut rota nativitatis sit supplicium naturæ nostræ, & Serarius rotam ejus- modi nativam esse quamlibet perturbationem ait, alienum est, quia non de perturbatione, sed de lin- gua hic agitur, non de malo pœnæ, sed culpæ. Kaj Nam (solet enim etiam causaliter accipi) inflammatus est à gehenna, quia ignem hunc accendit diabolus, Jo- han. IIX, 44. Apoc. XII, 10. Luc. XI, 24. Non pœna linguæ improbæ in gehenna exprimitur, quia Apo- stolus in culpa, ejusque causa designanda proprie occupatur. Docet quantum in semalum culpæ sit improbitas linguæ, mundus iniquitatis, commacu- lans totum corpus, & ignis, incendens totam vitam; siquidem accendatur à gehenna, id est, per Metony- miam, à diabolo in gehenna: Vel Catachrestice & per similitudinem, quia scilicet tam maledica, & tam pestilens, urensque, ut non videatur non terreno, sed infernali igne succensa. In inferno enim damna- ti ex desperatione lingua ignita, furibunda, maledi- cent Deo, &c. Neque lingua tantum inflammabi- tur in gehenna, sed totum corpus, imo totus homo, qui totus per linguam commaculatur & incendi- tur per omnem ætatem. Qui in iniquas censuras præceps est, qui mendax est, qui sermone utitur im- puro, hic flammam infernalem eructat, & qui ta- lia verba audit, approbat, admittit, flammam infer- nalem intra penitum pectus admittit, ait B. Broch- mandus. Quomodo lingua lædat instar sagittæ, vulneret instar gladii, urat instar ignis, vide Psalm. LVII, 5. Prov. XVI, 27. Jerem. IX, 8.

## 3:7
Verse 7. For every nature of beasts and of birds, of creeping things and of things in the sea is tamed and has been tamed by the human nature.] Euripides: 'Small is the strength of man. But by the varied devices of the mind he tames the tribes of the sea, and the creatures of the earth and of the air.' James added serpents here. For human industry captures them too, and draws the poison from them. He says δαμάζεται καὶ δεδάμασται, to show that this is perpetual: and as it is now, so it has always been done. Δαμάζειν is חשׂל in Daniel 2:40. Φύσις here is the Arabic טבע, which is the טבע of the Rabbis.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Πᾶσα γὰρ φύσις θηρίων τε καὶ πετεινῶν, ἑρπετῶν τε κᾀ ἐναλίων δαμάζεται καὶ δεδάμασται τῇ φύσει τῇ ἀνθρωπί- νῃ.] Euripides: Βραχύ τοι σθένος ἀνέρος. Ἀλλὰ ποικιλίαις πραπίδων Δαμᾷ φῦλα πόντου Χθονίων τ’ αἰθερίων τε παιδεύματα. Adjecit hic Jacobus serpentes. Nam & illos capit humana industria, & venenum eis detrahit. Dicit autem δαμάζεται καὶ δεδάμασται, ut ostendat perpetuum hoc esse : & ut nunc sit, ita factum semper. Δαμάζειν חשׂל Dan. II, 40. Φύσις hic Arabi טבע, quod est Rabbinorum טבע.

## 3:8
Verse 8. But no man is able to tame the tongue.] The tongue, namely another's, no one can tame, just as we tame wild animals.

An unruly evil.] Supply 'is'. Which the following member shows. It is an evil that cannot be restrained.

Full of deadly poison.] Again, understand 'is'. Cicero called a false accusation a poisoned weapon. You have the word θανατηφόρῳ not only among Greek poets, but also in the Greek of Job 33:23 and Numbers 18:22. The same is θανάσιμον in Mark 16:18. To the Rabbis, ἰὸς θανατηφόρος is סם המות; we have it in the same sense in Deuteronomy 32:33, 'the cruel venom of asps.' Cleanthes: 'There is nothing more wicked than slander.'

It is not about another's tongue, as Grotius thinks with Estius, but one's own, which everyone is commanded to tame as much as he can, Psalm 39:1. The reason, however, why wild beasts can be tamed, but the human tongue cannot be fully tamed, and is that uncontrollable evil, is that their fervor and fury are from nature, but this one's is from Gehenna, which never ceases, while a man survives in life, to inflame the tongue, and finds in us 'the sin which doth so easily beset us,' which is never not working, Hebrews 12:1, Romans 7:14 ff. Therefore, the difficulty here is not just that which Lorinus, Cornelius à Lapide, Piscator, as well as Pareus and the Belgian Interpreters hold, but the impossibility of total restraint is indicated, Sirach 19:17. It is difficult to restrain the tongue. But to tame it completely is impossible in this infirmity of life. How necessary it is, however, that we strive to tame it, the comparison with lethal poison teaches. For the wickedness of the tongue is like such poison. As poison extinguishes the native heat, upon the extinction of which death follows: so it extinguishes the heat of charity, which is proper to the faithful not by generation, but by regeneration, without which spiritual life cannot consist, 1 John 4:16. A similar, not dissimilar, passage is found in Psalm 140:4. Cf. Proverbs 18:21. That lethal poison is both native and is breathed in through the inflammation of the tongue. A slanderer, however, is a triple homicide. For he kills him whom he slanders by defamation, and him before whom he slanders by scandal, and himself by guilt. Is not the tongue of the detractor a most ferocious viper? Clearly indeed, which so lethally infects three with one breath. Truly also most sharp, which pierces three with one blow, says Bernard in his sermons.

Regarding the reading of verse 7, where in the Greek it is ἐναλίων 'of the sea,' while the Vulgate has 'of the rest' [cæterorum]; some suspect the Interpreter read ἄλλων 'of others': to Estius it is more likely that he wrote cætorum, which he testifies is the text in some copies, along with Erasmus. Whatever the case, the error lies in the Vulgate, not the Greek text, in which there is a wonderful agreement of all codices here, as also of the Syriac and other interpreters.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Τὴν δὲ γλῶσσαν ὀυδεὶς δύναται τῶν ἀνθρώπων δαμά- σαι.] Linguam, nempe alienam, nemo domare potest, sicut animalia fera mansuefacimus.

Ἀκατάσχετον κακόν.] Supple ἐστί. Quod ostendit mem- brum sequens. Malum est quod inhiberi nequit.

Μεστὴ ἰοῦ θανατηφόρου.] Iterum subaudi ἐστί. Falsum cri- men quasi venenatum telum dixit Cicero. Vocem θανατη- φόρῳ habes non tantum apud Poëtas Græcos, sed & in Græ- co Job. 33, 23. & Num. 18, 22. Idem θανάσιμον Marc. 16, 18. Rabinis ἰὸς θανατηφόρος est סם המות eodem sensu ha- bemus Deuter. 32, 33. ראשׁ פתנים אכזר venenum aspi- dum crudele. Cleanthes. Κακουργότερον ὀυδὲν διαβολῆς ἐστί που.

Non de lingua aliena, ut cum Estio Grotius, sed propria agitur, quam quisque domare, quantum potest, jubetur, Psal. XXXIX, 1. Causam vero, cur feræ domari possint, lingua vero humana domari plene non possit, & incoërcibile illud malum sit, est, quod illarum fervor & furia à natura sint, hujus à gehenna, quæ nunquam cessat, dum homo in vita superat, linguam inflammare, & τὴν ἐυπερίστατον ἁμαρτίαν in nobis nunquam non cooperantem in- venit, Ebr. XII, 1. Rom. VII, 14. seqq. Non ergo hic tantum difficultas, quod Lorinus, Cornelius à Lapide, Piscator item & Pareus ac Interpretes Bel- gici volunt, sed impossibilitas coercitionis totalis indicatur, Sir. XIX, 17. Difficile est, linguam frena- re. Penitus autem domare, est impossibile in hac vi- tæ infirmitate. Quam vero necessarium sit, ut stu- deamus eam domare, comparatio cum veneno le- thifero docet. Siquidem improbitas linguæ talis veneni instar est. Ut venenum calorem nativum extinguit, quo extincto mors sequitur: Ita calorem charitatis, qui non per generationem, sed regenera- tionem fidelibus proprius est, extinguit, sine qua spiritualis vita consistere nequit, 1. Joh. IV, 16. Si- mile non dissimile habetur, Psal. CXL, 4. Conf. Prov. XIIX, 21. Venenum illud lethiferum tum nativum est, tum adspiratur per inflammationem linguæ. Maledicus vero ter homicida est. Occi- dit enim eum, cui detrahit per diffamationem, & eum, apud quem detrahit per scandalum, & seipsum, per culpam. Numquid non vipera est lingua de- tractoris ferocissima? Plane nimirum, quæ tam le- thaliter tres inficiat flatu uno. Profecto & acutis- sima, quæ tres penetret uno ictu, ait Bernhardus in sermonibus.

Circa lectionem vers. 7. ubi in Græco est ἐναλίων marinorum, quum Vulgata habeat cæterorum; qui- dam suspicantur Interpretem legisse ἄλλων alio- rum: Estio verisimilius est, eum scripsisse cætorum, quod in nonnullis exemplaribus textum testatur cum Erasmo. Quicquid sit, in mendo cubat Vulga- ta, non Græcus textus, in quo Codicum omnium mira hic consonantia, ut & Syri, aliorumque Inter- pretum.

## 3:9
Verse 9. With it we bless God and the Father.] Εὐλογεῖν with the accusative is frequent both in the Interpreters of the Old Testament and in the writers of the New. You have εὐλογεῖν τὸν Θεὸν in Psalm 67:8, Luke 2:25, and often elsewhere. That καὶ here is explanatory, as above in 1:27. Ἐν here is 'by'. In the manuscript it is εὐλογοῦμεν τὸν Κύριον, that is, Christ.

And with it we curse men.] Καταρᾶσθαι ארר properly means to devote to curses: but it is taken for any manner of speaking evil, as we have said at Matt. V, 44. These things agree beautifully with the saying of Aesop: That the tongue is both the best and the worst thing. There is an excellent dissertation on both sides in Plutarch, περὶ ἀκοῦς. And the Hebrews say life and death are in the power of the tongue.

Those who have been made according to the likeness of God.] In the Manuscript γεγεννημένους, that is, πεποιημένους, Gen. I, 26, 27. See the notes made by us on that passage, if you have time.

Latin:

Vers. 9. Ἐν αὐτῇ εὐλογοῦμεν τὸν Θεὸν καὶ Πατέρα.] Εὐλογ γεῖν accusativo frequens & Interpretibus Veteris Testamenti & Scriptoribus Novi. Εὐλογεῖν τὸν Θεὸν habes Ps. 67, 8. Luc. 2, 25. & alibi sæpe. Illud καὶ hic est ἐξηγητικὸν, ut supra I, 27. Ἐν hic est per. In Manuscripto εὐλογοῦμεν τὸν Κύριον, id est, Christum.

Καὶ ἐν αὐτῇ καταρώμεθα τοὺς ἀνθρώπους.] Καταρᾶσθαι ארר proprie est diris devovere: sed sumitur pro quolibet modo maledicere, ut diximus ad Matth. V, 44. Pulchre hæc conveniunt cum Æsopi dicto: Linguam & optimam esse & pessimam. Est in utramque partem egregia dissertatio apud Plutarchum περὶ ἀκοῦς. Et Ebræi dicunt vita & mors in ma- nu linguæ.

Τοὺς κατ᾽ ὁμοίωσιν Θεοῦ γεγονότας.] In Manuscripto γε- γεννημένους. id est, πεποιημένους, Gen. I, 26. 27. Ad quem lo- cum a nobis notata vide, si vacat.

## 3:10
Vers. 10. Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing.] Just as that man in Aesop was warming and cooling with the same breath. For ἐξέρχεται the Arabs have תבע, it emanates, just as he translates it βρύει.

My brethren, these things ought not so to be.] It becomes a good man to be constant in what is good.

He implies, therefore, that a curse cast upon a neighbor redounds to God Himself, just as an insult offered to the image of a King is considered to redound to the King himself.
