What kind of monster the tongue is, is understood even from this, that with it we both bless God and at the same time curse men: since nature has so ordered things that contrary things do not proceed from the same source: How absurd it is, therefore, for one and the same fountain to pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same stream, and for a fig tree to produce grapes, and a vine to produce figs, since they are fruits of a different species: it is just as monstrous for the tongue to bring forth both the blessing of God and the execration of a neighbor, Ps. L, 16. Ps. XV, 13. 2. Moreover, man is said to be made to the image of God, not such as he is now, but such as he was before the fall, to which, however, he is here repaired again through Christ, Eph. IV, 24. Col. III, 9. 2 Cor. V, 17.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ στόματος ἐξέρχεται εὐλογία καὶ κα- τάρα.] Sicut ille apud Æsopum eodem flatu calefaciebat & refrigerabat. Pro ἐξέρχεται Arabs habet תבע emanat, quomodo & βρύει vertit.

Οὐ χρὴ ἀδελφοί με ἀγαπητοὶ ταῦτα οὕτω γείνεσθαι.] Virum bonum decet in bono esse constantem.

Maledictionem ergo in proximum jactatam in Deum ipsum redundare innuit, non secus atque contumelia Regis imagini illata in Regem ipsum redundare censetur. Quale itaque monstrum lin- gua sit, vel ex eo intelligitur, quod eadem & bene- dicamus Deo, & simul maledicamus: siquidem na- tura res ita comparavit, ut ab eodem principio non prodeant contraria: Quam itaque absonum est unum & eundem fontem ex eodem rivo funde- re dulcem & amaram aquam, & ficum uvas, & vi- tem ficus proferre, quum sint diversæ speciei fru- ctus: tam monstrosum est, linguam & benedictionem Dei promere, & execrationem proximi, Ps. L, 16. Ps. XV, 13. 2. Ad imaginem autem Dei homo factus dicitur, non qualis nunc est, sed qualis ante lapsum erat, ad quam tamen hic iterum reparatur per Christum Eph. IV, 24. Col. III, 9. 2. Cor. V, 17.

## 3:11
Vers. 11. Doth a fountain send forth at the same place sweet water and bitter?] From the same hollow. For it happens sometimes from neighboring hollows that sweet water flows from one, and bitter or salt from another, as the natural philosophers note. Βρύει means it emanates. In the Glossary, βρύει means I gush forth. This is what the Hebrews say יקיר מתוך בער.

Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olive berries? either a vine, figs?] A similar sentiment is in Matt. VII, 16. Thus Marcus Antoninus the Emperor: He who does not wish the wicked man to sin is like one who does not wish the fig tree to produce juice in its figs.

Neither can any fountain yield salt water and fresh.] He had already said this: For under the name πικρῷ (bitter), salt is also included: as 'Doris may not mingle her bitter waves': Thus also the Greek Poet concerning Alpheus: --- And the bitter salt of the sea.

Wherefore the Manuscript is correct here: Οὔτε ἁλυκὸν γλυκὺ ποιῆσαι ὕδωρ, that is, how I think the Latin Interpreter wrote: Neither can salt water make sweet. The sea does not produce sweet waters from itself.

Estius also suspects that the Greek codices sometimes rendered this meaning, because the Syriac supports the Latin reading: rendering it thus: Neither can salt waters be made sweet: But because no Greek Codex has been found that has it so, and all here agree entirely, the authentic text is not to be changed for the sake of the Latin and Syriac version: because it is not new or unusual for the same sentiment to be repeated in almost similar words, as is evident even from verses 9 and 10: With it (the tongue) we bless God, and with it we curse man. Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing, where Cornelius says: He exaggerates the indignity of the evil, and insists upon and repeats it to press the point. Therefore, blessing and cursing proceed from the same mouth, which is clearly so wicked and unworthy in itself that it does not need, nay, cannot be exaggerated by other words. Add that in this place the conclusion can be taken morally: Whence Cornelius warns from the former similitude, that sweet and bitter water does not flow from the same fountain, and that it cannot be proved and concluded morally, that is, it ought not to be that blessing and cursing proceed from the same mouth: And this similitude is the same as the first. But why could it not have been repeated in the conclusion after the proofs were added, that which the Apostle wished to prove, he had said, that a fountain cannot pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening, v. 11. He proves it v. 12. and illustrates it: Can, my brethren, the fig tree [produce] grapes (or rather, as it is in the Greek and Syriac, ἐλαίας olives, with which there is a greater antithesis, as Cornelius admits, for figs are sweet, but olives are bitter: Estius acknowledges that Bede and some ancient Greek copies agree with this) or the vine figs: As the fig tree cannot produce both figs and olives, or the vine both grapes and figs: So the salt fountain cannot produce both salt and sweet water. Such inferences and repetitions are frequent in James, as is evident even from c. II.

PART II. Concerning true wisdom, to be demonstrated by the moderation of the tongue.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Μή τι ἡ πηγὴ ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς ὀπῆς βρύει τὸ γλυκὺ καὶ τὸ πικρόν.] Ex eodem cavo. Nam ex vicinis cavis sit inter- dum, ut hinc dulcis fluat aqua, inde amara aut salsa, ut Phy- sici notant. Βρύει emanat. In Glossario βρύει scaturio. Hoc est, quod Ebræi dicunt יקיר מתוך בער.

Μὴ δύναται, ἀδελφοί με, συκῆ ἐλαίας ποιῆσαι, ἢ ἄμπελος σῦκα.] Similis sententia Matth. VII, 16. Sic M. Antonius Imperator: Ὁ μὴ θέλων τὸν φαῦλον ἁμαρτάνειν, ὅμοιός τῷ μὴ θέλοντι συκῆν ὀπὸν ἐν τοῖς συκοῖς φέρειν.

Οὐδὲ μία πηγὴ ἁλυκὸν καὶ γλυκὺ ποιῆσαι ὕδωρ.] Hoc jam dixerat: Nam sub πικρῷ nomine comprehenditur & salsum: ut Doris amara suas non intermisceat undas: Sic & Græcus Poëta de Alphæo: - - - Καὶ ἅλθια πικρὰ θαλάσσης.

Quare recte hic Manuscriptus: Οὔτε ἁλυκὸν γλυκὺ ποιῆ- σαι ὕδωρ, id est, quomodo Latinum Interpretem puto scripsis- se: Neque salsa dulcem potest facere aquam. Mare non edit de se aquas dulces.

Ita etiam suspicatur Estius, Græcos codices ali- quando hunc sensum reddidisse, quia Latinæ le- ctioni Syriaca patrocinatur: Sic reddens: Nec aquæ salsæ possunt effici dulces: Sed quia nullus repertus Codex Græcus, qui ita habeat, & omnes hic ex asse consentiunt, in gratiam Latinæ & Syriacæ versionis textus authenticus immutandus non est: quia non novum est aut insolens, sententiam eandem verbis fere similibus repeti, ut vel è v. 9. & 10. constat: Illa (lingua) benedicimus Deum, & in illa maledicimus homini. Ex ipso ore egreditur benedictio & male- dictio, ubi Cornelius: Exaggerat mali indignitatem, illudque insistendo & repetendo perurget. Ex eodem ergo ore procedit benedictio & maledictio, quod in se tam iniquum & indignum esse liquet, ut aliis verbis magis exaggerari non egeat, imo nequeat. Adde quod hoc in loco conclusio moraliter accipi possit: Unde Cornelius monet ex priori similitudine, quod ex eodem fonte non manet aqua dulcis & amara, probari, & concludi moraliter, non posse, id est, non debere ex eodem ore prodire benedictionem & male- dictionem: Eandemque esse hanc similitudinem cum prima. Quidni vero in conclusione repeti po- tuerit post adjectas probationes, id, quod probare volebat Apostolus, dixerat, non posse fontem de eodem foramine dulcem & amaram aquam funde- re, v. 11. Probat id v. 12. & illustrat: Numquid potest, fratres mei, ficus uvas (vel potius, ut in Graeco & Syro est, ἐλαίας olivas, quibus cum major est antithesis, fatente Cornelio, ficus enim sunt dulces, olivæ vero amaræ: Bedam, ac nonnulla antiqua exemplaria Gra- cis adstipulari agnoscit Estius) facere aut vitis ficus: Quam non potest ficus & ficus, & olivas, vel vitis & uvas & ficus proferre: Tam non potest fons salsus & salsam & dulcem aquam edere. Tales illationes & re- petitiones frequentes Jacobo, ut vel è c. II. patet.

PARS II. De vera sapientia, linguæ moderamine demon- stranda.

## 3:13
Ver. 13. If any one is wise and understanding among you.] Thus we have wisdom and understanding in Col. I, 9. In Hebrew you would say מִי חָכָם וְיָבֵן, as in Hos. XIV, 10. However, he seems to be called wise who knows many things, and understanding, who also possesses the manner of instruction, who can instruct others. Let him show out of good conduct his works in meekness of wisdom.] That is, in meek wisdom, as the Syriac rightly explains here. Thus - - - - Mitis sapientia læti. The meaning is: In his social life let him produce works which testify to a meek wisdom. You have the word conduct in the same sense in Gal. I, 13. Eph. IV, 22. 1 Tim. IV, 12. Heb. XIII, 7. and several times in Peter. The preposition out of here signifies the occasion, and to show means to produce, as in John X, 31. A sentiment not far from this is in Prov. X, 2. וְאֶת־צְנוּעִים חָכְמָה, where the Greeks say: The mouth of the humble meditates wisdom.

Grotius, along with Estius and Cornelius à Lapide, again understands these things as referring to Teachers. But it is a general admonition, just as he had previously exhorted everyone, not just teachers, to bridle the tongue, as they themselves admit. Nor is there any need to say that a digression was made to the vices of the tongue: since the whole chapter tends toward that. For the pursuit of meekness and peace, and the flight from envy and contentiousness, can also be said to be prescribed as a medicine for the abuse of the tongue, as Pareus and the Belgian Interpreters judged. Disciplined is rendered by the Vulgate for understanding; so that, as Cornelius interprets, it may be signified that a wise man ought to be not only speculative, but also practical, because discipline is the ordered correction of morals. According to Estius, wisdom denotes the knowledge of divine things, and understanding the knowledge of human things. It is more correctly said that both are joined for the sake of emphasis, because he is to be considered neither wise nor knowing anything who cannot demonstrate it by the moderation of his tongue. He therefore proposes both things to be done and things to be avoided by the truly wise and intelligent man: As for the former, that he should show good conduct and meekness. Good conduct is to be taught not so much by speech and censure as by life and example, Matt. V, 16. Rom. II, 17. seqq. 1 Pet. III, 1. 2. The meekness of wisdom, which he requires to be shown by the works of our conduct, demands that harsh words should never be used where we can succeed with kinder ones. For that is of charity, which is the index of true wisdom, 1 Cor. XIII, 4. 7. Gal. VI, 1. 2. The meekness of wisdom is by Hebraism a wise meekness, or one joined with wisdom and proceeding from it, so that by meekness we may overcome offenses, bear injuries, not be easily irritated, but prudently discern by what we ought, or ought NOT, to be offended. And by such meekness we demonstrate our good works in our conduct with our brethren and neighbors, so that from the same may shine forth meekness, tempered by prudence.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Εἴ τις σοφὸς καὶ ἐπιστήμων ἐν ὑμῖν.] Sic σοφίαν & σύνεσιν habemus Coloss. I, 9. Ebraice diceres מִי חָכָם וְיָבֵן, ut Os. XIV, 10. Videtur autem dici σοφὸς qui multa novit, ἐπιστήμων, qui etiam habet τὸν τρόπον τῆς παιδείας, qui alios instituere potest. Δειξάτω ἐκ τῆς καλῆς ἀναστροφῆς τὰ ἔργα ἀυτοῦ ἐν πραΰτητι σοφίας.] Id est, in σοφίᾳ πραείᾳ, ut hic recte explicat Syrus. Sic - - - - Mitis sapientia læti. Sensus est: In convictu producat opera, quæ mitem sapien- tiam testentur. Vocem ἀναστροφῆς eodem sensu habes Gal. I, 13. Eph. IV, 22. 1. Tim. IV, 12. Ebr. XIII, 7. & apud Petrum aliquoties. Præpositio ἐκ hic significat occasionem, Δειγνύειν autem producere, ut Joh. X, 31. Sententia non longe hinc alie- na, Proverb. X, 2. וְאֶת־צְנוּעִים חָכְמָה, ubi Græci: Στόμα ταπεινῶν μελετᾷ σοφίαν.

De Doctoribus hæc iterum intelligit Grotius cum Estio & Cornelio à Lapide. Sed generalis est admoni- tio, uti antea ad linguam frenandam hortatus erat omnes, non doctores tantum, iisdem fatentibus. Nec opus est, ut digressionem factam ad linguæ vitia dicamus: quum eo caput totum tendat. Nam & mansuetudinis ac pacis studium, fugamque inviden- tiæ & rixositatis pro medicina abusus linguæ præ- scribere dici potest, ut Pareus & Interpretes Belgici judicarunt. Ἐπιστήμων disciplinatus à Vulgata reddi- tur; ut, interprete Cornelio, significetur, sapientem non speculativum tantum, sed & Practicum esse de- bere, quia disciplina est morum ordinata correctio. Secundum Estium sapientia Divinarum, scientia, humanarum notitiam notat. Rectius emphaséos causa utrumque conjungi dicitur, quod neque sa- piens, neque quicquam sciens habendus sit, qui non demonstrare id possit linguæ moderamine. Propo- nit ergo tum facienda, tum fugienda vere sapienti & intelligenti: Quoad illa, ut ostendat bonam con- versationem & mansuetudinem. Bona conversa- tio non tam sermone & censura, quam vita & exem- plo docenda est, Matth. V, 16. Rom. II, 17. seqq. 1. Petr. III, 1. 2. Πραότης σοφίας, qua opera conver- sationis nostræ ostendenda requirit, ut nunquam verba asperioda adhibeantur, ubi benignioribus proficere possumus. Id enim charitatis est, quæ veræ sapientiæ index, 1. Cor. XIII, 4. 7. Gal. VI, 1. 2. Mansuetudo sapientiæ per Ebraismum est mansue- tudo sapiens, seu cum sapientia conjuncta, & ex ea procedens, ut mansuetudine vincamus offensas, feramus injurias, ne facile irritemur, prudenter ve- ro discernamus, quibus offendi oporteat, vel non OPORTEAT. Ejusmodi vero mansuetudine opera no- stra demonstramus bona cum fratribus & proxi- mis conversatione, ut ex eadem effulgeat mansue- tudo, prudentia temperata.

## 3:14
But if you have bitter zeal, and contentiousness in your heart.] In the Manuscript: But if indeed zeal. You have zeal and contentiousness as related terms in 2 Cor. XII, 20. and Gal. V, 20. where consult the passages cited. And he well adds that bitter to contentiousness, so that he might make it clearer toward what those similitudes above in III, 11. 12. were tending.

Do not boast and lie against the truth.] In the Manuscript, do not boast, do not please yourselves by arrogating to yourselves the title of wise against the truth. There is, however, a pleonasm in that do not lie against the truth. Thus I speak the truth, I do not lie, Rom. IX, 1. we lie and do not the truth 1 John I, 6.

Bitter zeal, or envy and contentiousness, are to be avoided, which are the fountains of more wicked censures and of the petulance of the tongue: because out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, Matt. XII, 34. Fountains which pour forth nothing but bitter things from themselves, however much envious and contentious men may boast of wisdom, they boast rashly and lie against the truth. It is not angelic wisdom, but diabolical, proceeding from the author of envy, contentions, calumnies, and malice. Therefore, he tacitly exhorts to block those fountains with a conditional: If YOU HAVE, tempering the reproof. He said bitter zeal, so that he might distinguish it from the praiseworthy, Gal. IV, 7. For it is bitter when we are indignant and seethe without cause out of mere envy, or not according to knowledge, Rom. X, 2. which is called bitter because it arises from the effusion of black bile or gall. Envy is bitter, from which that zeal arises: this fervor and heat of the mind is bitter, because bitter bile seethes, both yellow and black, that is, both cholera and melancholy, so much so that the envious person bears a dark, bilious, and livid color on his face; and it produces bitter fruits both for others and for him who labors under envy, as one who is wonderfully tormented by the torture of envy when he sees another preferred to himself, or equaled in wisdom, virtue, or glory. Whence Aristotle is said to have called envy the antagonist of the fortunate. Chrysologus, sermon 172, says that envy has always been the executioner of its own people. Nazianzen, oration XXVII, says: Envy, he says, is alone of all the affections the most unjust and at the same time the most just. The most unjust, because it is against all good things. The most just, because it consumes and destroys its own masters.

The Apostle likewise wishes to block self-seeking, the lust for contention, which bursts forth from the heart and betrays itself through a contentious tongue, Matt. 15:15, just as Paul also joined 'strifes' and 'zeal' in the catalog of the works of the flesh, Gal. 5:19. He who carries the gall of envy in the stomach of his heart is eager to exhale it through his mouth, and to contradict everyone, and to contend with everyone. Conversely, meek men always despise quarrels; as Bernard says in his book on the manner of living, ch. 17. Whence he warns: strive to contend in no cause, unless it be to please God alone. In the words, 'do not boast and lie,' the reason for the dissuasion against levity is contained, because those who indulge in envy and brawls boast indeed that they are Christians, and wish to appear wise and knowledgeable above others, but they lie against the truth, because they are not truly what they boast and brag that they are. Cornelius à Lapide thinks it is signified that zeal, or envy, is the mother and fountain of contention, boasting, and lies: as if to say, if you feel in your mind an ardor for contending, do not follow it, and do not cast it out and exert it through your mouth and words, so that you may gloriously and mendaciously attack the truth, but rather repress this ardor with silence, and restrain it with reason. For to contend, according to Augustine, book 4 of On Christian Doctrine, ch. 28, is not to care how error may be overcome by truth, but how your own speech may be preferred to the speech of another.

Latin:

Εἰ δὲ ζῆλον πικρὸν ἔχετε, καὶ ἐρίθειαν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν.] In Manuscripto: Εἰ δὲ ἄρα ζῆλον. Ζῆλον & ἐρίθειαν, ut affinia habes 2. Cor. XII, 20. & Gal. V, 20. ubi dicta consule. Et be- ne addit ἐκίθειαν illud πικρὸν, ut apertius faceret, quo tende- rent istæ similitudines supra III, 11. 12.

Μὴ κατακαυχᾶσθε καὶ ψεύδεσθε κατὰ τῆς ἀληθείας.] In Manuscripto, μὴ καυχᾶσθε, ne vobis ipsis placete, contra ve- ritatem vobis arrogando sapientis titulum. Est autem Pleo- nasmus in illo μὴ ψεύδεσθε κατὰ τῆς ἀληθείας. Sic ἀλήθειαν λέγω, ὀ ψεύδομαι, Rom. IX, 1. ψευδόμεθα καὶ ὀ ποιῦμεν τὴν ἀλήθειαν 1. Joh. I, 6.

Fugienda sunt zelus amarus, vel invidia & con- tentiositas, qui fontes sunt iniquiorum censurarum, & petulantiæ linguæ: quia ex abundantia cordis os loquitur, Matth. XII, 34. Fontes, qui non nisi ama- ra quæq; de se fundunt, utcunq; de sapientia glo- rientur homines invidi, & contentiosi, temere glo- riantur, & adversus veritatem mentiuntur. Non est Angelica sapientia, sed diabolica ab autore in- vidiæ, contentionum, calumniarum & maledicen- tiæ profecta. Ad fontes ergo illos obstruendos tacite hortatur conditionali: Si HABETIS, ex- probationem temperans. Ζῆλον πικρὸν dixit, ut distinguat à laudabili, Gal. IV, 7. Amarus enim est, cum indignamur, & æstuamus sine causa ex mera invidia, vel non, secundum scientiam, Rom. X, 2. qui amarus dicitur, quia ab atra bilis vel fellis effu- sione oritur. Invidia amara est, unde oritur zelus ille: amarus est iste fervor, & æstus animi, quia bilis exæstuat amara, tam flava, quam atra, hoc est, tam cholera quam melancholia, adeo, ut invidus in vul- tu atrum, felleum, lividumque colorem præ se fe- rat; & fructus gignit amaros tum aliis, tum illi, qui invidia laborat, utpote qui mire cruciatur invidiæ cruciatu, cum alium sibi videt præferri, vel æquari sapientia, virtute, vel gloria. Unde invidiam Ari- stoteles dicitur dixisse antagonistam fortunatorum. Chrysologus serm. 172. ait, invidiam suorum semper extitisse carnificem. Nazianzenus orat. XXVII. So- lus, inquit, ex omnibus affectibus iniquissimus simul & æquissimus est invidia. Iniquissimus, quia bonis omni- bus adversus est. Æquissimus, quia Dominos suos exest & conficit.

Ἐρίθειαν libidinem contendendi pariter obstrui vult Apostolus, quæ è corde prorumpit, & lingua contentiosa se prodit, Matth. XV, 15. quomodo & Paulus ἔρεις & ζῆλος in catalogo operum carnis conjunxit, Gal. V, 19. Qui fel invidiæ gerit in cordis stomacho, ille gestit illud ore exhalare, omnibusque contradicere, & cum omnibus contendere. Contra viri mites semper despiciunt lites; dicente Bernhar- do libr. de modo viv. c. 17. Unde monet: in nulla causa decertare studeas, nisi ut soli Deo placeas. Ver- bis, ne gloriamini & mentimini, contra levitatem dehortationis ratio continetur, quia qui invidiæ & rixis indulgent, gloriantur quidem, se esse Christia- nos, videri volunt præ aliis sapientes, & scientes, sed mentiuntur contra veritatem, quia vere non sunt, quos se esse gloriantur, & jactitant. Cornelius à La- pide censet significari zelum, sive invidiam esse ma- trem & fontem contentionis, jactantiæ, & mendacio- rum: q. d. Si sentitis in mente ardorem contenden- di, nolite illum sequi, eumque per os verbaque egerere & exerere, ut gloriose & mendaciter oppugnetis ve- ritatem, sed potius ardorem hunc silentio reprimite, & ratione compescite. Contendere enim, secundum Augustinum libr. IV. de doctrina Christiana cap. 28. est non curare, quomodo error veritate vinca- tur, sed quomodo tua dictio dictioni præferatur al- terius.

## 3:15
Verse 15. 'This is not the wisdom that comes down from above.' This is not that true wisdom, such as the Holy Spirit works

Etus. Thus ἄνωθεν καταβαῖνον [coming down from above] supra I, 17. See John XV, 26. Ἀπ᾽ ἐπίγειον.] Fitting for minds concerned with earthly things. Thus τὰ ἐπίγεια φρονεῖντες [minding earthly things], Phil. III, 19. Ψυχική.] They are called ψυχικοὶ [natural/soulish] who do not have the Spirit of God, Jude 19. That wisdom is from nature, not from God. The Syrian here says from the thoughts of the soul. Through it men are σοφοὶ ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ [wise in this age] 1 Cor. III, 18. Δαιμονιώδης.] For the Demon is accustomed to mix himself in earthly cares 2 Cor. IV, 4. Eph. II, 2. The Syrian here [uses] מן שׁאדא [from the] destroyer. For that is how they call the Demon. Satanic in the Arabic.

That wisdom is not descending from above from the Father of lights, from whom is every good thing, James I, 17. Therefore it is not good, true, or pleasing to God. But it is ἐπίγειος [earthly], worldly, accustomed to the world, and therefore evil, 1 John II, 16. chap. V, 19. ψυχικὴ [natural/soulish], animal or carnal, 1 Cor. II, 14. Jude 19. δαιμονιώδης [demonic], brought in by the devil, the author of lies and contentions John VIII, 44. Rev. XII, 10. Cornelius a Lapide distributes those epithets according to the reason of the different vices, because earthly wisdom exists on account of avarice, which seeks earthly riches; animal [wisdom] on account of gluttony and luxury, by which it desires the sensible pleasures of the belly and of Venus. Diabolical [wisdom], on account of pride, by which it aspires to excel and be honored above others, and thus finds subtle modes of pain and heat, of which the devil is the author. But the epithets are general to envy and contention, since they feign zeal for the glory of God and the study of truth, assigned without distribution.

Latin:

Vers. 15. Οὐκ ἔστιν αὕτη ἡ σοφία ἄνωθεν κατερχομένη.] Non hæc est illa vera sapientia, qualem operatur Spiritus San-

Etus. Sic ἄνωθεν καταβαῖνον supra I, 17. Vide Joh. XV, 26. Ἀπ᾽ ἐπίγειον.] Conveniens curis in terras animis. Sic τὰ ἐπίγεια φρονεῖντες, Phil. III, 19. Ψυχική.] Ψυχικοὶ dicuntur, qui Spiritum Dei non habent, Judæ 19. Ista sapientia a natura est, non a Deo. A cogitatio- nibus animæ dicit hic Syrus. Per eam sunt homines σοφοὶ ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ 1. Cor. III, 18. Δαιμονιώδης.] Nam terrestribus curis Dæmon solet se admiscere 2. Cor. IV, 4. Eph. II, 2. Syrus hic מן שׁאדא vastatore. Ita enim illi Dæmon appellant. Satanica apud Arabem.

Non est ista sapientia desursum descendens a Pa- tre luminum, a quo omne bonum, Jac. I, 17. Non ergo est bona, vera, Deo placens. Est autem ἐπί- γειος terrena, mundana, mundo consueta, eoque mala, 1. Joh. II, 16. cap. V. 19. ψυχικὴ animalis vel carnalis, 1. Cor. II, 14. Job. III, 5. δαιμονιώδης a dia- bolo ingesta, autore mendacii & contentionum Joh. IIX, 44. Apoc. XII, 10. Cornelius a Lapide distri- buit illa epitheta pro ratione vitiorum diverso- rum, quod sapientia terrena sit ob avaritiam, quæ quærit opes terrenas; animalis ob gulam & luxu- riam, qua concupiscit voluptates sensibles ven- tris, & Veneris. Diabolicas, ob superbiam, qua am- bit præ cæteris excellere & honorari, atque adeo subtiles modos dolor & æstus adinvenit, quorum Autor diabolus est. Sed epitheta generalia sunt invidia & contentioni, cum illa zelum & gloriæ Dei & veritatis studium mentiuntur, sine distri- butione assignata.

## 3:16
Verse 16. Ὅπου γὰρ ζῆλος καὶ ἐρίθεια [For where there is zeal and strife.] He names those vices which were most apparent, as above [in verse] 14. Ἐκεῖ ἀκαταστασία [There is disorder.] Tumult or seditions, as Luke XXI, 9. 2 Cor. VI, 5. XII, 20. In the Manuscript, not badly: ἐκεῖ καὶ ἀκαταστασία [there is also disorder]. Καὶ πᾶν φαῦλον πρᾶγμα [And every evil thing.] Hyperbole. For he wishes to say: From rivalry, and the bitter contention that follows it, many evils are born.

Ἀκαταστασία [disorder] is rendered as inconstancy by the Vulgate, as tumult by others. But properly it is the disturbance of an unordered thing, just as Plutarch, in 'On the Cessation of Oracles', joins ἀκατάστατον [unsettled] and ἐμπαθῆ [passionate], meaning disturbed and subject to passions. Paul denies that God is a God of ἀκαταστασίας [disorder], and opposes εἰρήνη [peace] to it. For the envious and contentious disturb the peace of the Church and the Republic. Thence πᾶν φαῦλον πρᾶγμα [every evil thing] follows, every wicked work for the overthrow of private and public affairs; indeed, evils of every kind. For where things are disturbed by quarrels and contentions, and moved from their place, it cannot be but that every kind of vice prevails, and rushes in as if in swarms. St. Cyprian, Sermon on Zeal and Envy, page 192: 'There is no reason for anyone to think that this evil is contained in one form, or concluded in brief terms and a narrow end. The manifold and fruitful ruin of zeal extends widely: it is the root of all evils and the fountain of disasters, the seedbed of offenses, the material of faults.' Thence hatred arises, thence animosity proceeds; zeal inflames avarice, while one cannot be content with his own, seeing another wealthier. Zeal excites ambition, while one perceives another higher in honors, with zeal blinding our senses, and bringing the secrets of the mind into its own dominion. The fear of God is spurned, the teaching of Christ is neglected, the day of judgment is not provided for. Pride inflates, cruelty exacerbates, perfidy prevaricates, impatience shakes, discord rages, anger boils. Nor can he now restrain or rule himself, who has been made [a subject] of another's power. Hence the bond of the Lord's peace is broken, hence brotherly charity is violated, hence truth is adulterated, unity is split, [and one] rushes headlong into heresies and schisms.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Ὅπου γὰρ ζῆλος καὶ ἐρίθεια.] Ea vitia nominat, quæ maxime apparebant, ut supra 14. Ἐκεῖ ἀκαταστασία.] Tumultus sive seditiones, ut Luc. XXI, 9. 2. Cor. VI, 5. XII, 20. In Manuscripto non male: ἐκεῖ καὶ ἀκαταστασία. Καὶ πᾶν φαῦλον πρᾶγμα.] Ὑπερβολή. Vult enim dicere: Ex æmulatu, & quæ eum sequitur acerba contentione, pluri- ma nasci mala.

Ἀκαταστασία inconstantia a Vulgato, tumultuatio ab aliis redditur. Sed proprie est rei inordinatæ perturbatio, uti Plutarchus de defect. orari jungit ἀκατάστατον, καὶ ἐμπαθῆ perturbatum & passioni- bus obnoxium. Paulus Deum negat ἀκαταστασίας Deum, eique εἰρήνην opponit. Invidi enim, & con- tentiosi Ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ pacem perturbant. Inde πᾶν φαῦλον πρᾶγμα sequitur omne opus pra- vum ad eversionem rei privatæ & publicæ; imo omnis generis mala. Nam ubi rixis & contentio- nibus res perturbantur, locoque moventur, fieri non potest, quin omne genus vitii obtineat, & vel- uti catervatim irruat. S. Cyprianus serm, de zel. & liv. pag. 192. Non est quod aliquis existimet, ma- lum istud una specie contineri, aut brevibus terminis & angusto fine concludi. Late patet zeli multiplex & fe- cunda pernicies: radix est omnium malorum & fons cladium, seminarium delictorum, materia culparum. Inde odium surgit, animositas inde procedit, avari- tiam zelus inflammat, dum quis non potest suo esse con- tentus, videns alterum ditiorem. Ambitionem zelus excitat, dum cernit quis alium in honoribus altiorem, zelo excæcante sensus nostros, ac in ditionem suam mentis arcana redigente. Dei timor spernitur, magi- sterium Christi negligitur, judicii dies non provide- tur. Inflat superbia, exacerbat sævitia, perfidia pre- varicatur, impatientia concutit, furit discordia, ira fervescit. Nec se jam potest cohibere, nec regere, qui factus est potestatis alienæ. Hinc Dominicæ vinculum pacis rumpitur, hinc charitas fraterna violatur, hinc adulteratur veritas, unitas scinditur, ad hæreses at- que schismata prosilitur.

## 3:17
Verse 17. Ἡ δὲ ἄνωθεν σοφία [But the wisdom from above] Given by God above nature. Πρῶτον μὲν ἁγνή ἐστι [First indeed it is pure] Pure from those earthly studies. The Syrian [uses] מכיא שכיסא.

Wisdom, which is from above, is first called ἁγνὴ [pure] chaste, because it is alien to impure love, and keeps us undefiled, continually recalling to our mind and memory that we should keep the faith, given to Christ the bridegroom, inviolate, 2 Cor. XI, 2.

Ἔπειτα εἰρηνικὴ, ἐπιεικής [Then peaceable, gentle.] Interpreting everything as much as possible in the better light. See 1 Cor. XIII, 4. See Phil. IV, 5. 1 Tim. III, 3. Tit. III, 2. The Syrian translates מכיכא, that is, modest.

There follows the pursuit of peace, the chastity of faith, by which it is brought about that we are able εἰς τὸ ἓν εἰρεῖν [to join into one], to join minds, whence εἰρήνη [peace] is named, Matt. 5, 9. Heb. 12, 4. True wisdom has peace as its companion. 'Have salt in yourselves,' says Christ, Mark IX, v. last (salt is a symbol of wisdom), 'and have peace among yourselves.' Bernard, Sermon 36 on the Song of Songs: 'Much knowledge ingested into the stomach of the soul, if it has not been adorned with charity, is converted into wicked and harmful humors, and causes swellings and torments of the mind.' But in order for there to be a place for peace, there is need of ἐπιεικεία [gentleness/equity], so that no one may urge or pursue his own right, but for the sake of friendship and peace may rather concede something of his right, mindful of how much God remits of His own right, Matt. V, 7. chap. XVIII, 28. [and that one] may also interpret everything in the better light, and show to another that equity which he himself would wish for himself.

Εὐπειθὴς.] Compliant, the Syrian [version] משתמעניא. Philo and Galen use this word in this way.

The Vulgate renders it 'persuadable,' others 'courteous,' 'tractable,' 'affable in speech,' without moroseness and adulation. The word is active and passive, meaning 'persuadable,' says Pareus, which in ambiguous matters persuades better things, and willingly obeys those who persuade good things. Courtesy is not inappropriately opposed to zeal and envy. It is included in the following epithet, 'full of good fruits.' The Vulgate adds here another: 'consenting to good things.' But that is neither in the Greek, nor in the Syrian, nor is it read in Prosper on Free Will, nor in Cajetan, nor in Gagney, nor Catharinus, etc. It is likely, as Estius says, that it was transcribed here from another translation, in which 'consenting to good things' was read instead of the word 'persuadable.' For the Greek word ἐυπειθὴς does not reject this interpretation either, so that to consent to good things is to acquiesce to the admonitions and counsels of good men. Estius therefore acknowledges that the text authentic to the Papists lies here once again in error.

Μεστὴ ἐλέους.] Full of beneficence. For we have said elsewhere and above at II, 13, that ἐλέου is taken by our people in this way.

Καρπῶν ἀγαθῶν.] 'Full' must be repeated here. He calls works 'fruit' here, Matt. III, 8, 16. Gal. V, 22. Eph. V, 9. Phil. I, 11.

By the name ἐλέους, mercy, whose nature is to sympathize with the misfortunes of others, the duties of charity of every kind are designated, according to others, just as by the fullness of good fruits. We do not, however, reject the interpretation of Grotius, provided that heavenly wisdom is described more fully in this way, to which the fruits of the Spirit and good works pertain no less according to the first than the second table, so that now everything is reduced as it were into a sum, and the totality of good things is comprehended, unless it is better to understand it as referring to other good fruits which had not yet been specifically expressed.

Ἀδιάκριτος.] Which does not distinguish men according to the flesh. See above II, 4. ודלא פלגותא without partition, namely, unjust.

The Vulgate, 'not judging.' Beza, 'without disputation': To which the blessed Brochmand agrees, explaining it as wisdom ignorant of contentious disputation. I would prefer to side with Grotius, in this sense, that it is ἄνευ προσωποληψίας (without respect of persons). To which Piscator also leans: Which does not distinguish between neighbors out of partiality, as does Estius, comparing chapter II, 4. Thus the blessed Luther: 'Unpartheyisch' (impartial).

Ἀνυπόκριτος.] Not, as is the custom of ambition, having one thing locked in the breast and another ready on the tongue, as is found in Sallust. Such is that man in Homer: 'Who hides one thing in his heart, but speaks another.' See Rom. XII, 9. 2 Cor. VI, 6. 1 Tim. I, 5. 2 Tim. I, 5. 1 Pet. I, 22. Wisd. V, 19. ch. XVIII, 16.

This wisdom, void of hypocrisy, requires not only that we speak the truth from the heart, Eph. IV, 24. but that we cherish faith unfeigned, 2. Cor. VI, 6. and charity, and brotherly love likewise unfeigned, Rom. XII, 9. 1. Petr. I, 22. These eight eulogies of true wisdom contribute particularly to the moderation of the tongue, especially also in judging one's neighbor. For because suffer us to be defiled by the slander of the tongue, and our tongue, consecrated to Christ the bridegroom, dedicated to the glory of God and the uses of our neighbor, to be set on fire by hell, v. 6. Because it is peaceable, it does not permit envy and contention to rule; because it is equitable, it does not exaggerate the flaws of one's neighbor, it does not rigidly discuss the words and deeds of others, Matth. VII, 1, 2. because it is easy to be entreated, it believes all things, hopes all things, 1. Cor. XIII, 7. nor does it easily take upon itself the censor's rod, Matth. VII, 3. because, full of mercy, it does not judge, it does not condemn others, Luc. VI, 36. 37. because, full of good fruits, it does not burn with hatred, malice, envy, nor does it leave room for contentions, calumnies, or similar evil fruits or wicked works; because it is without partiality, it does not judge according to the outward appearance; because it is without hypocrisy, it proves sincerity in conversation, and utters nothing with the mouth other than what it cherishes in the heart, which is the worst abuse of the tongue, a Machiavellian fraud, and wisdom truly devilish. Even though Pseudo-Politicians today are not afraid to call it Politics.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ἡ δὲ ἄνωθεν σοφία ] A Deo data supra naturam. Πρῶτον μὲν ἁγνή ἐστι ] Pura a terrestribus illis studiis. Sy- rus מכיא שכיסא.

Sapientia, quæ desuper est, primum ἁγνὴ casta di- citur, quia aliena est ab impuro amore, nosque im- pollutos custodit, jugiter nobis in mentem ac me- moriam revocans, ut fidem, Christo sponso datam, inviolatam servemus, 2. Cor. XI, 2.

Ἔπειτα εἰρηνικὴ, ἐπιεικής.] Omnia quantum fieri potest in meliorem partem interpretans. Vide 1. Cor. XIII, 4. vide Phil. IV, 5. 1. Tim. III, 3. Tit. III, 2. Syrus vertit מכיכא, id est, modesta.

Sequitur pacis stadium, fidei castitatem, quo id agitur, ut possimus εἰς τὸ ἓν εἰρεῖν, in unum nectere, jungere animos, unde εἰρήνη dicta, Matth. 5,9.Ebr.12, 4. Sapientia vera pacem habet comitem. Habete in vobis sal, inquit Christus Marc. IX. v. ult. (sal est symbolum sapientiæ) & pacem habete inter vos. Bernhard. serm. 36. in Cant. Multa scientia ingesta stomacho animæ, si charitate decorata non fuerit, convertitur in pravos noxiosque humores, atque in- flationes, mentisque tormina facit. Ut autem paci lo- cus sit, opus est ἐπιεικεία æquitate, ne quis suum jus urgeat aut persequatur, sed amicitiæ, & pacis causa de jure suo potius aliquid concedat, memor, quan- tum Deus de jure suo remittat, Matth. V, 7. cap. XVIII, 28. omnia etiam in meliorem partem in- terpretetur, & eam æquitatem alii exhibeat, quam ipse sibi optet.

Εὐπειθὴς.] Obsequiosa Syrus משתמעניא. Utuntur sic hac voce Philo & Galenus.

Vulgata reddit suadibilis, alii comis, tractabilis, affabilis in sermone, sine morositate & adulatione. Vox active & passive est suasibilis, inquit Pareus, quæ in ambiguis suadet meliora, & suadentibus bo- na libenter obtemperat. Comitas non incommo- de zelo, & invidiæ opponitur. Obsequiosas se- quenti epitheto plena fructuum bonorum com- prehenditur. Addit hic Vulgata aliud: Bonis con- sertens: Sed id nec in Græco est, nec in Syro, nec a Prospero de libero Arb. nec a Cajetano, nec a Ga- gnejo, nec Catharino &c. legitur. Estio verisimile est, huc transcriptam esse ex alia translatione, in qua pro vocabulo suasibilis legebatur bonis consentiens. Nam Græca vox ἐυπειθὴς etiam hanc interpretatio- nem non respuit, ut bonis consentire sit acquiescere bo- norum monitis & consiliis. Agnoscit ergo Estius, authenticum Papistis textum hic iterum in mendo cubare.

Μεστὴ ἐλέους.] Plena beneficentia. Nam sic sumi a nostris ἐλέου diximus & alibi & supra II, 13.

Καρπῶν ἀγαθῶν.] Repetendum hic μεστή. Καρπὸς hic vo- cat opera, Matth. III, 8. 16. Gal. V, 22. Eph. V, 9. Phil. I, 11.

Nomine ἐλέους misericordia, cujus est alienis ma- lis condolere, uti plenitudine fructuum bonorum omnis generis officia charitatis designantur juxta alios. Non abnuimus tamen Grotianæ interpre- tationi, fiquidem ita plenius sapientia cœlestis de- scribatur, ad quam fructus Spiritus, & bona opera non minus juxta primam, quam secundam tabulam pertinent, ut quasi in summam nunc omnia redi- gantur, & universitas bonorum comprehendatur, nisi præstet de cæteris fructibus bonis, qui non dum speciatim expressi erant, intelligere.

Ἀδιάκριτος.] Quæ non discernit homines secundum carnem. Vide supra II, 4. ודלא פלגותא fine partitione, nempe iniqua.

Vulgata, non judicans. Beza, absque discepta- tione: Cui annuit B. Brochmandus, exponens de sa- pientia rixotæ disceptationis nescia. Malim Grotio accedere, hoc sensu,quod sit ἄνευ προσωποληψίας. Quo etiam abit Piscator: Quæ non discernit inter proximos ex prosopolepsia, ut & Estius conferens cap. II, 4. Sic B. Lutherus: Unpartheyisch.

Ἀνυπόκριτος.] Non, ut mos est ambitionis, aliud clausum in pectore, aliud promptum in lingua habens, ut est apud Sallustium. Talis ille apud Homerum: Ὅς χ᾽ ἕτερον μὲν κέυθει ἐνὶ φρεσὶν, ἄλλο δὲ βάζει. Vide Rom. XII, 9. 2. Cor. VI, 6. 1. Tim. I, 5. 2. Tim. I, 5. 1. Petr. I, 22. Sap. V, 19. c. XVIII, 16.

Requirit hæc sapientia,hypocriseos expers,non tantum ut veritatem ex animo loquamur, Eph. IV, 24. sed ut fidem foveamus ἀνυπόκριτον, 2. Cor. VI,6. & charitatem, ac Φιλαδελφίαν pariter ἀνυπόκριτον, Rom. XII, 9. 1. Petr. I, 22. Hæc octo elogia veræ sapientiæ peculiariter faciunt ad moderamen lin- guæ, imprimis etiam in judicando proximo. Nam quia sapientia, quæ ἄνωθεν est, pura ac casta est, non patitur, nos linguæ maledicentia commaculari, lin- guamque nostram Christo sponso consecratam, gloriæ DEI & proximi usibus dicatam à gehenna inflammari v. 6. Quia pacifica est, non permittit invidiam, & contentionem regere; quia æqua, non exaggerat nævos proximi, non rigide discutit alio- rum dicta, & facta, Matth. VII, 1,2. quia ἐυπειθὴς, omnia credit, omnia sperat, 1. Cor. XIII, 7. nec faci- le censoriam virgulam sibi sumit, Matth. VII, 3. quia plena misericordia non judicat, non condemnat alios, Luc. VI, 36. 37. quia plena fructuum bonorum, non ardet odio, livore, invidia, nec contentionibus, calumniis aut similibus malis fructibus, vel pravis operibus locum relinquit; quia ἀδιάκριτος est, non judicat secundum externam faciem; quia ἀνυπόκρι- τος, candorem in conversatione probat, nec aliud ore promit, quam quod in corde fovet, qui pessi- mus est linguæ abusus, fraus Machiavellica, & σο- φία vere δαιμονιώδης. Etsi Pseudo-Politici hodie eam Politicam vocitare non vereantur.

## 3:18
Vers. 18. And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace.] A double Antanaclasis. For he uses the word fruit, which he just used regarding works, now regarding the reward of works, and he takes the word peace first for prosperous things (for it is said in peace for into peace) and then for concord. And righteousness is taken here generally, so that it comprehends all things which are our duty, as Matth. V, 20. Act. X, 35. Rom. III, 21. 22. Phil. I, 11. and elsewhere. The comparison of sowing is frequent in this matter, as 2. Cor. IX, 6. Gal. VI, 7. 8. Thus the Latins say: As you sow, so shall you reap. Then to make peace is to devote effort to peace, just as to do righteousness, 1. Joh. II, 29. c. III, 7. which in Act. X, 35. is to work righteousness and to perform righteousness above I, 20. to devote effort to justice. Just as the Hebrew word for 'to do' is frequent among the Hebrews.

It does not appear why we should take peace in a different way, and leave the proper sense of the preposition in. For these words do not sound of a term to which and a consequence, but of the manner of sowing, in peace it is sown, and the Apostle is engaged in the commendation of the pursuit of peace, so that he may extirpate contentions and sow concord, from which he described heavenly wisdom as peaceable. It is sown, he says, the fruit of righteousness, that is, it is acquired, the antecedent for the consequent, because fruit follows sowing, not that it is acquired by our labor, as the mercenary Papists boast, but that the fruit emerges by the free and gracious blessing of God. For farmers, from whom the metaphor is taken, do not earn a harvest from their seed from God: Must not the Divine blessing be acknowledged, that God hears the heaven, and the heaven hears the earth, and the earth hears the corn, and the wine and the oil, and these hear Israel, Hos. II, 21. 22. To whom indeed is that fruit sown? To those who make peace. For Christ declares these blessed, Matth. V, 9. By whom? By the peacemakers themselves. For these sow for themselves, not for others, Gal. VI, 8. Just as a farmer confers fields upon himself and his own, and reaps, and thus acquires fruits, not for others. How? In peace, or by a most common Hebraism, through peace. For peace, or the pursuit of peace, is that seed which sprouts into the fruit of righteousness. What is that fruit? Paul names eternal life, using this same similitude: Gal. VI, 20. which is the reward of righteousness and the pursuit of peace, but a free one. For eternal life is the gift of God, Rom. VI, 23. Therefore, the merit of our righteousness cannot be carved out from this. What? That Estius judges it to be more in the mind of the Apostle that the fruit of righteousness be understood as the fruit which is righteousness itself, for those cultivating peace, rather than the fruit which is gathered from righteousness: But that we should take righteousness according to its increments and perfection, as Phil. I, 11. Ebr. XII, 11. Because peace cherishes charity, which contentions diminish or extinguish. But Grotius rashly draws here to initial righteousness that more abundant righteousness, by which we enter the kingdom of heaven, Matth. V, 20. the righteousness of God, which is manifested without the law, which is by the faith of Jesus Christ, that is, the imputed righteousness and obedience of the God-man Christ, by which we are justified before God, and are constituted righteous, Rom. III, 21. 22. cf. c. V, 9.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Καρπὸς δὲ τῆς δικαιοσύνης ἐν εἰρήνῃ σπείρεται τοῖς ποιοῦσιν εἰρήνην.] Duplex Ἀντανάκλασις. Nam & vocem καρ- ποῦ, quam modo usurpavit de operibus, nunc usurpat de præ- mio operum, & εἰρήνης vocem sumit primum pro rebus pro- speris (est enim ἐν εἰρήνῃ dictum pro εἰς εἰρήνην) deinde pro concordia. Et δικαιοσύνη hic generaliter sumitur, ita, ut omnia comprehendat, quæ nostri sunt officii, ut Matth. V, 20. Act. X, 35. Rom. III, 21. 22. Phil. I, 11. & alibi. Comparatio satio- nis in hac re frequens, ut 2. Cor. IX, 6. Gal. VI, 7. 8. Sic Latini dicunt: Uti seres, ita metes. Deinde ποιεῖν εἰρήνην est dare operam paci, quomodo ποιεῖν δικαιοσύνην, 1. Joh. II, 29. c. III, 7. quod Act. X, 35. Ἐργάζεσθαι δικαιοσύνην & κατεργά- ζεσθαι δικαιοσύνην supra I, 20. justitiæ operam dare. Quo- modo עשׂה frequens apud Ebræos.

Non apparet, cur pacem diversimode accipere debeamus, & Præpositionis ἐν sensum proprium re- linquere. Non enim de termino ad quem & con- sequenti, sed de modo sationis hæc sonant ἐν εἰρήνῃ σπείρεται, & versatur Apostolus in commendatio- ne studii pacis, ut contentiones extirpet, ac con- cordiam serat, à qua sapientiam cœlestem ceu εἰρη- νικὴν descripsit. Seminatur, inquit, fructus justitiæ, id est, comparatur, antecedens pro consequenti, quia sationem sequitur fructus, non quod labore nostro acquiratur, ut Papistæ mercenarii jactitant, sed quod gratuita & gratiosa Dei benedictione fru- ctus emergat. Non enim agricolæ, à quibus meta- phora petita est, semine suo à Deo messem meren- tur: Nonne agnoscenda benedictio Divina, quod Deus exaudiat cælum, & cælum exaudiat terram, & terra exaudiat triticum, & vinum & oleum, & hæc ex- audiant Israël, Hos. II, 21. 22. Quibus vero seritur ille fructus? Pacem facientibus. Hos enim beatos prædicat Christus Matth. V, 9. A quo? Ab ipsismet pacificis. Hi enim sibi, non aliis serunt, Gal. VI, 8. Sicut agricola sibi, & suis conferit agros, & metit, adeoque acquirit fructus, non aliis. Quomodo? In pace, vel per Ebraismum usitatissimum, per pa- cem. Pax enim seu pacis studium est semen illud, quod in fructum justitiæ pullulat. Quis ille fructus? Vitam æternam nominat hac eadem similitudine utens Paulus: Gal. VI, 20. quæ præmium est justi- tiæ, studiique pacis, sed gratuitum. Donum enim Dei est vita æterna, Rom. VI, 23. Non ergo hinc ju- stitiæ nostræ meritum exsculpi potest. Quid? quod Estius magis ex mente Apostoli esse censeat, ut fructus justitiæ intelligatur fructus, qui est ipsa justitia, colentibus pacem, quam fructus, qui ex justitia colligitur: Sed ut justitiam accipiamus se- cundum incrementa sua, & perfectionem, ut Phil. I, 11. Ebr. XII, 11. Quia pax charitatem fovet, quam contentiones minuunt aut extinguunt. Temere autem hic ad justitiam inchoatam trahit Grotius justitiam illam abundantiorem, qua regnum cælorum adimus, Matth. V, 20. justitiam Dei, quæ sine lege manifestatur, quæ est per fidem Jesu Christi, hoc est, imputatam Christi θεανθρώπυ justitiam & obe- dientiam, qua coram Deo justificamur, & justi constituimur, Rom. III, 21. 22. conf. c. V, 9.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

The admonition begun concerning the fleeing of contention is continued; of which he delivers the origin from wicked pleasure, the fruit, which is none but harmful, the non-hearing of prayers, the hatred of God: as also the means, that we should submit ourselves to God, resist the devil, and mourn our sins with true repentance, and neither condemn our neighbor, nor rashly presume about the morrow, mindful of the fleeting nature of life, which is like a vapor, nor ambitiously exalt ourselves. There are two parts. I. A dehortation from the pursuit of contending to v. 12. II. An admonition to flee presumption about the morrow to v. 17. and the last.

PART I.

A dehortation from the pursuit of contending.

Vers. 1. Whence come wars and fightings among you.] Whence among you, namely Israelites, are quarrels and wars? He understands those movements of the Philadelphian Jews against those who were in Perea, the faction of the sons of Judas of Galilee, the fights with the Samaritans, and the arms of the Svarii, concerning which see Josephus, book XX. It is credible that some who were Christians more in name than in reality were also carried away by these movements. He admonishes both: the latter that they should correct themselves to the norm of the Gospel, the former that they should come to the Gospel.

Οὐκ ἐντεῦθεν ἐκ τῶν ἡδονῶν ὑμῶν τῶν ςρατευομένων ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ὑμῶν.] By metonymy he calls pleasures the desires for voluptuous or non-necessary things for life. And the Syrian translated it as desires, both in this verse and below in chapter 3. Porphyry, in the fourth book on abstinence from animal food, when he had described that life under Saturn, content with few and necessary things, adds: 'But indeed there were no wars for them, nor sedition against one another. For there was no prize of any note set in the middle, for which anyone would have stirred up such a dispute, so that the sum of life happened to be leisure and ease from necessary things, and friendship.' Tibullus: 'This vice belongs to the riches of gold: nor were there wars when the beech cup stood before the feasts.' Cicero, On Ends, book one: 'From desires arise hatreds, dissensions, discords, seditions, and wars.' Jamblichus: 'For indeed wars and seditions and battles are provided by nothing else than the body, and the desires of that time.' Thus also Diogenes used to say that wars are not stirred up for the sake of vegetables and fruits, but for the delights of meats and banquets; and Pliny says that the outcomes of wealth tend toward crimes, slaughters, and wars. We have brought forward many other excellent things on this matter in book I of On the Law of War and Peace, chapter 5, both in the context and in the annotations, to which I refer the reader. James excellently says ςρατευομένων, because those external wars would not exist unless there had first been an internal one, namely, of those desires against right and sound reason. In a similar sense we have ἀντιςρατεύεσθαι in Romans 7:23.

Why we should understand this concerning public disturbances, we see no reason in the text. The exhortation is too general to be restricted to the disturbances of the Philadelphian Jews: nor is it certain that the Christians were involved in them, who, as if disarmed by the Romans, could not wage wars. The Apostle had begun to treat, on the occasion of unjust judgments, of the contentions which arise from them; he therefore pursues that subject: as is clear from verse 12, where it is concluded finally, a thorough treatment concerning the slanders, censures, and condemnations of the brethren. Since, therefore, those are the causes of contentions, from which tumults and the shaking of the republic and of private life arise, v. 16, chap. III, he traces the origin of these evils more deeply, namely, that the zeal for accusing, contending, and fighting redounds from a depraved concupiscence or the law of sin in the members, warring against the law of the mind, of which Rom. VII. 23 speaks, where the Apostle also said νόμον ἀντισρατευόμενον, which parallel passage Grotius makes for ours. Therefore, the cause of contentions is not to be sought in Tibullus or Cicero and other Gentiles ignorant of this true origin, which not even Paul himself had acknowledged under Pharisaism, Rom. VII, 7, which does not reside in the desire for voluntary things, but in the depraved concupiscence innate in all, Joh. III, 5. Therefore, some make the theme of this chapter that carnal concupiscences must be opposed and restrained, whose pernicious effects the blessed Brochmand wishes to be recounted here: wars, fights, contentions, v. 1; the vain labor of efforts, v. 2; and the preposterous manner of attaining those things which are lacking, v. 2; vain prayers, v. 3; enmity with God, v. 4; envy, v. 5; pride, v. 6; and the remedies, which are: to submit to God, to cleanse hands, to purify hearts, v. 8; to weep over sins, v. 9; to humble oneself seriously, v. 10; to avoid backbiting, v. 11, 12; to avoid empty confidence in undertaking business, v. 13, 14; to commit oneself solely to Divine providence, v. 15 seqq. Which opinion can be supported from chap. I, 14, where he taught that the cause of sin is depraved concupiscence, and opposed to it regeneration and religion, both toward God and toward one's neighbor, for which faith and good works are required, chap. I and II, for which cause he exhorted against unjust censures toward one's neighbor and the abuse of the tongue, which is naturally untamed and is a world of iniquity, and he exhibited the distinction between true and false wisdom and religion, chap. III, and now further exhorts to restrain carnal concupiscences. Pareus agrees without difficulty: In the fourth chapter, James pursues the argument of the third more fully. For he continues to tear out more sharply the intimate roots of the disease of the tongue, which he had previously gravely censured and begun to cure with certain special remedies—namely, carnal concupiscences, avarice, envy, luxury, love of the world, and pride—as well as its pestilent fruits, strifes and fights, and he prescribes a certain catholic antidote for curing those evils: serious conversion to God and repentance, joined with true humiliation before God and love of the brethren. In the last part, however, he disagrees and assigns a new theme with us: The reproof of the vain confidence of some, who were ignorant of themselves and of divine providence. Now, therefore, he refutes the zeal for contending, understanding by wars and fights not those in which opposing armies clash with weapons, but rather quarrels, contentions, and more bitter brawls, as Terence says in the Eunuch: In love, all these vices are present: injuries, suspicions, enmities, truces, war, and peace again.

He calls pleasures, ἡδονὰς, carnal concupiscences and depraved desires, which are so called because they are sweet to the flesh, and men given over to their own affections take pleasure from them, such as pride, avarice, lust of the flesh, etc.

He calls wars the conflicts and struggles over those things which they were wickedly desiring, such as over prizes, honors, or even over those things which would serve only for pleasure, as Estius says: who notes also that forensic litigations can be understood, which he had already reproached them for in chap. II, 6: whence he here opens up their source.

Thomas Anglicus refers litigations too restrictively to those litigating before judges, and wars to violent men who attempt to claim things for themselves through violence and injury; others also reduce duels to this. They are said to war in our members both because the enemies are intimately in our vitals, and because they wage war against the law of the mind, and are as it were armed soldiers for our destruction. By the name of members, however, he understands not only external organs prepared for fulfilling depraved desires, but primarily the internal faculties of the soul, in which concupiscence especially dominates. Therefore, they are said to war against the soul, 1 Pet. II, 11; Matt. XV, 19; Rom. VI, 13; 1 John II, 16. Concupiscence in the members, as Cornelius à Lapide says, wars in such a way that they dominate regarding sudden and indeliberate acts, which forestall reason and liberty; but regarding human, free, and deliberate acts, they do not dominate, but both they themselves and the members are subject to the will and free choice, by which they are governed not despotically, as a brute is governed by a man, but politically, as a citizen is governed by a magistrate, whom he can contradict and resist. Wars arise, however, primarily from the concupiscences of riches and honors. All litigations and wars arise because of mine and thine. Take away these two pronouns from the world, or at least from the minds of men, there will be no litigations, no wars, says Chrysostom. Anabaptists, however, rashly conclude from this passage that wars are entirely illicit for Christians. Something else is had from the instruction of John, Luke III, 14, as well as from approved examples, Matt. VIII, 10; Acts X, 2 seqq.

Latin:

CAPUT IV.

ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Continuatur admonitio cœpta de fugienda con- tentione; cujus tradit ortum è prava volu- ptate, fructum, qui nullus nisi noxius, pre- cum non exauditio, Dei odium: ut & me- dium, ut Deo nos subdamus, diabolo resista- mus, ac vera pœnitudine peccata lugeamus, nec proximum nostrum condemnemus, ne- que temere de crastino præsumamus, memo- res fugacitatis vitæ, quæ vaporis instar est, nedum ambitiose nos extollamus. Partes duæ sunt. I. Dehortatio à contendendi stu- dio ad v. 12. II. Commonitio ad fugiendam præsum- ptionem de crastino ad v. 17. & ultimum.

PARS I.

Dehortatio à studio contendendi.

Vers. 1. Πόθεν πόλεμοι καὶ μάχαι ἐν ὑμῖν.] Unde inter vos, nempe Israëlitast, rixæ & bella? Intelligit motus illos Judæorum Philadelphensium contra eos, qui in Peræa erant, factionem filiorum Judæ Galilæi, pugnas cum Samaritanis, & Svariorum arma, de quibus vide Josephum libr. XX. Cre- dibile est istis motibus abreptos fuisse etiam quosdam nomi- ne magis quem re Christianos. Admonet utrosque, hos ut se corrigant ad Evangelii normam, illos ut ad Evangelium ve- niant.

Οὐκ ἐντεῦθεν ἐκ τῶν ἡδονῶν ὑμῶν τῶν ςρατευομένων ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ὑμῶν.] Μετωνυμικῶς voluptates appellat cupiditates rerum voluptariarum sive non necessariarum ad vitam. Et cupiditates posuit Syrus, tum hoc commate, tum infra 3. Por- phyrius quarto de non esu animalium, cum vitam illam sub Saturno descripsisset, paucis iisque necessariis contentam, addit: Ἀλλὰ μὴν ὐδὲ πόλεμοι ἀντοῖς ἦσαν, ὐδὲ ςάσις πρὸς ἀλ- λήλες. Ἄθλον γὰρ ὐδὲν ἀξιόλογον ἐν τῷ μέσῳ προκείμενον ὑπῆρ- χεν, ὑπὲρ ὅτε τις ἂν διαφορὰν τοσαυτην ἐνςήσατο, ὥςε τὸ κε- φάλαιον εἶναι τῶ βίυ συνέβαινε σχολὴν ῥᾳθυμίαν ἀπὸ τῶν ἀναγ- καίων ὀγίασαν, φιλίαν. Tibullus: Divitiis hoc vitium est auri: nec bella fuere Faginus adstabat cum scyphus ante dapes. Cicero de finibus primo: Ex cupiditatibus odia, dissidia, discordiæ, seditiones, bella nascuntur. Jamblichus: καὶ γὰρ πολέμες καὶ ςάσεις, καὶ μάχας ὐδὲν ἄλλο παρέχει ἢ τὸ σῶμα, καὶ αἱ τότε ἐπιθυμίαι. Sic & Diogenes dicebat bella non pro victu olerum & pomorum, sed pro carnium & epularum de- liciis excitari & Plinius opulentiz exitus ait ad scelera, cædes & bella tendere. Multa alia præclara ad hanc rem attulimus libr. I. de jure belli & pacis II, 5. tum in contextu, tum in an- notatis, ad quæ lectorem remitto. Egregie autem dicit Jacobus ςρατευομένων quia bella illa externa non essent nisi prius fuis- set internum, cupiditatum scil. istarum cum recta sanaque ra- tione. Pari sensu ἀντιςρατεύεσθαι habemus Rom. VII, 23.

De publicis motibus cur hoc intelligamus, nullam videmus in textu rationem. Generalior est paræne- sis, quam ut restringenda sit ad motus Judæorum Philadelphensium: nec constat iis involutos fuisse Christianos, qui ceu exarmati à Romanis bella ge- rere non poterant. Cœperat Apostolus occafione iniquiorum judiciorum de contentionibus, quæ in- de oriuntur, agere; illam igitur materiam perfequi- tur: quemadmodum è vers. 12. liquet, concludi ibi demum penitus tractationem de calumniis, censu- ris, & condemnationibus fratrum. Quum ergo illæ causæ sint contentionum, è quibus tumultus, & concussiones reipublicæ & privatæ oriuntur, v. 16. cap. III. altius ducit originem istorum malorum, quod nempe studium criminandi, contendendi, & præliandi è prava concupiscentia vel lege peccati in membris repugnante legi mentis, de qua Rom. VII. 23. redundet, ubi etiam νόμον ἀντισρατευόμενον di- xit Apostolus, quem locum parallelum nostro facit Grotius. Non ergo in Tibullo aut Cicerone aliisq; gentilibus hujus veræ originis ignaris, quam nec Paulus ipse sub Pharisaismo agnoverat, Rom. VII, 7. quærenda causa contentionum, quæ non in re- rum voluntariarum cupiditate, sed in concupiscen- tia prava omnibus congenita hæret Joh. III, 5. Ideo nonnulli thema hujus capitis faciunt, oppugnan- das & coërcendas esse concupiscentias carnales, qua- rum & effecta perniciosa hic recensita vult B. Broch- mand. bella, pugnas, contentiones v. 1. irritum cona- tuum laborem v. 2. & præposterum ea, quæ desunt, assequendi modum, v. 2. irritas preces, v. 3. inimici- tiam cum Deo, v. 4. invidiam v. 5. superbiam v. 6. & remedia, quæ sunt, subjici Deo, emundare manus, purificare corda, v. 8. peccata deflere, v. 9. serio se humiliare, v. 10. obtrectationes vitare, v. 11. 12. in ne- gotiis suscipiendis inanem confidentiam vitare, vers. 13. 14. Divinæ providentiæ sese unice committere, v. 15. seqq. Quæ sententia juvari potest è cap. I, 14. ubi causam peccati docuit esse pravam concupi- scentiam, eique opposuit regenerationem, & reli- gionem, cum erga Deum, tum erga proximum, ad quam fides & bona opera requiruntur cap. I. & II. cujus causa dehortatus est ab iniquis adversus pro- ximum censuris, & abusu linguæ natura indomitæ, quæ mundus iniquitatis est, veraque ac falsa sapien- tiæ & religionis discrimen exhibuit, cap. III. & nunc porro adhortatur ad compescendas concupiscentias carnales. Consentit haud ægre Pareus: Capite quarto Jacobus argumentum tertii fusius persequi- tur. Morbi enim linguæ, quem prius graviter per- strinxit, & specialibus quibusdam remediis curare cœpit, intimas radices, carnales concupiscentias, avaritiam, invidiam, luxuriam, mundi amorem & superbiam, nec non pestilentes ejus fructus, lites & pugnas, acrius revellere pergit, atque malis istis cu- randis catholicum quoddam ἀντίδοτον præscribit, se- riam ad Deum conversionem & resipiscentiam, cum vera coram Deo humiliatione & fratrum dilectione conjunctam. In postremo tamen discrepat, ac no- vum thema nobiscum assignat: Reprehensionem vanæ quorundam confidentiæ, qui seipsos & provi- dentiam divinam ignorabant. Jam ergo contenden- di studium redarguit, bella & pugnas intelligens, non quibus copiæ adversæ armis invicem confli- gunt, sed jurgia, contentiones, & rixas acerbiores, quomodo Terentius in Eunucho: In amore hæc omnia insunt vitia, injuriæ, suspiciones, inimicitiæ, in- duciæ, bellum, pax rursus.

Voluptates vero dicit ἡδονὰς carnales concupi- scentias, & prava desideria, quæ ita vocantur, quia suavia sunt carni, & voluptatem ex illis capiunt ho- mines affectibus suis dediti, quales sunt superbia, avaritia, libido carnis &c.

Bella vocat conflictus, & concertationes de iis rebus, quas male concupi- scebant, ut de præmiis, honoribus, aut etiam de iis, quæ ad solam voluptatem facerent, ut ait Estius: qui notat etiam lites forenses intelligi posse, quas cap. II, 6. jam exprobrarat iisdem: unde hic earum fontem aperit.

Thomas Anglicus lites nimis restrictè refert ad litigantes coram judicibus, bella ad violentos, qui rem per violentiam & injuriam sibi vendicare co- nantur; alii huc duella etiam reducunt. Militare dicuntur in membris nostris tum quod hostes inti- me sint in visceribus nostris, tum quod bellum ge- rant contra legem mentis, & veluti armati milites sint in nostram perniciem. Membrorum autem no- mine non externa tantum organa, ad explendas pravas cupiditates parata, sed imprimis internas animæ facultates intelligit, in quibus concupiscen- tia maxime dominatur. Ideo dicuntur militare ad- versus animam, 1. Petr. II, 11. Matth. XV, 19. Rom. VI, 13. 1. Job. II, 16. Concupiscentia in membris, di- cente Cornelio à Lapide, ita militant, ut dominentur quoad actus subitos & indeliberatos, qui rationem & libertatem præveniunt, quoad actus vero humanos, liberos, & deliberatos non dominantur, sed tam ipsa, quam membra subsunt voluntati & libero arbitrio, à quo reguntur non despotice, uti brutum regitur ab homine, sed politice, uti civis regitur à magistratu, cui contradicere & reluctari potest. Oriuntur au- tem bella imprimis ex concupiscentiis opum & ho- norum. Omnes lites & bella oriuntur propter meum & tuum. Tolle hæc duo pronomina à mundo, aut sal- tim è mentibus hominum, nullæ erunt lites, nulla bella, inquit Chrysostomus. Temere autem ex hoc loco bella Christianis prorsus illicita esse colligunt Anabaptistæ. Aliud ex informatione Johannis ha- betur Luc. III, 14. nec non à probatis exemplis, Matth. VIII, 10. Act. X, 2. seqq.

## 4:2
Ver. 2. You desire and do not have.] The more you covet, the less you have, as God punishes you. This pertains first to the scarcity of grain, then to the famine, which occurred in the times of Claudius: concerning which see Acts 11:28, the words being taken from Proverbs 13:4.

You murder and covet, and are not able to obtain, you fight and wage war, and you do not have.] These are indeed absent in the manuscript. But the omission seems to have occurred because of the 'you do not have' being repeated twice, the scribe overlooking what is in the middle. Instead of 'you murder' (Φονεύετε), there are those who read 'you envy' (Φθονεῖτε), not badly, unless one prefers 'you rage' (Φονεῖτε) against one another: and you envy the fortunate and yet you cannot reach their good fortune. A Greek poet indeed says: O the greatest wickedness of envy. One hates the fortunate man, whom God loves.

Another: When one happens to find a man whom God loves, he brings upon himself the greatest folly. For he openly contends with God himself, having received the greatest anger from envy. For one ought to love him, whom God loves.

Apuleius: For he who envies the blessed torments himself.

Cyprian: It is a calamity without remedy to hate the fortunate. Furthermore he says, You even fight and wage war: and yet you do not attain, namely, a tranquil life, for the sake of which wars are undertaken.

Because you do not ask.] God has promised to those who pray, not to those who fight, Matthew 7:7. 'To ask' (αἰτεῖσθαι) instead of 'to ask' (αἰτεῖν) is Attic, as in Matthew 18:19, 20:22, Luke 11:9, and elsewhere.

Nothing is held here concerning the scarcity of grain, nothing concerning the famine, nor did famine or scarcity of grain prevail everywhere where the twelve tribes were dispersed. He notes the litigants, because they take no fruit from their litigations: and not only contentions, but also the desires from which those arise: by which they weary themselves in vain; nay, they render God angry toward themselves, so that they do not obtain anything from him even by prayers. He expresses first avarice, 'you covet,' then illicit zeal, 'you kill and you emulate,' then contentions, 'you fight and you wage war,' that is, you indulge in fights and wars. But with what effect? 'And you do not have,' you cannot attain what you want, you have nothing, that is, you perceive no advantage. He teaches, therefore, that the avaricious, the envious, and the quarrelsome attain nothing by their desires, and he gives the reason, that they do not ask from God: for those pleasures hinder prayers, and those devoted to them, having neglected prayers, which are the means of obtaining something from God divinely prescribed, James 1:10, strive to obtain by illicit means what they desire, Haggai 1:6.

As for the covetous, they are said to lust (which lust is called the lust of the eyes, 1 John 2:16; the desire for riches, 1 Timothy 6:9), but not to have, which is fulfilled in them not only when they obtain nothing and their desire is vain, but also because avarice never has enough, its desire is never fully satisfied, Proverbs 29:15; and the covetous man does not so much possess the thing lusted after as he is held and possessed by it, as if by a master, nay, a tyrant, Proverbs 13:7. Furthermore, the Apostle testifies that those who seek with envy are also unable to attain what they pursue: which seems to be said of the proud and ambitious, because honor follows the one who flees it, and flees the one who follows it. Concerning those who contend and wage war, it is likewise pronounced, 'you have not.' For often, neither by contentions, whether private or forensic, nor by violence, can what is sought be obtained. From avarice and ambition, contentions and quarrels are wont to follow. Moreover, in the Greek Codices, φθονεῖτε nowhere occurs, but φονεύετε, which the Vulgate also reads, as does the Syriac, and in his time, Oecumenius. Erasmus, however, amended it from mere suspicion: 'Perhaps it was written φθονεῖτε,' and Beza followed him. But as Estius rightly says, the customary reading ought not to have been changed from mere conjecture without the aid of Codices, which he thinks can be explained thus: 'You kill,' that is, you hate one another, from 1 John 3:15. Cornelius à Lapide interprets it thus: 'You kill in an act not perfected, but begun,' that is, you think to kill, you plot murder. For envy and anger always grow, and at length erupt into murders. Whence they are neighbors as in name, so also in fact and operation, φόνος and φθόνος, that is, envy and killing. Orators, when they inveigh against a vice, are wont to recount and exaggerate its extreme and most grievous harms, though they be rare, so as to impel the hearers more toward hatred of the vice. The sense can also be 'You kill and are jealous,' almost to the same effect as 'you are jealous.' Heinsius in this place interprets it thus: He deals with the perverse desires of men, which rarely, or for the most part do not, attain their end: among whom are οἱ φονεύοντες, not those who kill, but those who for the most part either wish for another's death, or who threaten another's life, as in Psalm 62:3, 'How long will you set upon a man? You all kill.' For so the Hellenists followed their own judgment, not those who took it otherwise. It is therefore φονεύειν, which the Greeks commonly call φονᾷν. But no one for the most part attains his end less than he who wishes for another's death and does not expect it.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Ἐπιθυμεῖτε καὶ οὐκ ἔχετε.] Quo plura concupisci- tis, eo minus habetis, Deo vos puniente. Pertinet hoc ad ca- ritatem primum annonæ, deinde famem, quæ fuit Claudia- nis temporibus: De qua Act. XI, 28. sumpta verba ex Prov. XIII, 4.

Φονεύετε καὶ ζηλοῦτε, καὶ οὐ δύνασθε ἐπιτυχεῖν, μάχεσθε καὶ πολε- μεῖτε, καὶ οὐκ ἔχετε.] Hæc absunt quidem in Manuscripto. Sed videtur omissio evenisse ob id οὐκ ἔχετε bis repetitum, ea quæ in medio sunt prætervidente librario. Pro Φονεύετε sunt qui legunt Φθονεῖτε non male, nisi quis malit Φονεῖτε sævitis alii in alios: & felicibus invidetis & tamen ad eorum felicitatem pertingere non potestis. Poëta Græcus quidem: Ὦ τῆς μεγίστης τοῦ φθόνου πονηρίας. Τὸν εὐτυχῆ μισεῖ τις, ὃν Θεὸς φιλεῖ.

Alius: Ὅταν τυχῇ τις ἄνδρα τὸν Θεὸς φιλεῖ, Οὗτος μεγίστην μωρίαν κατεσνάγει Φανερῶς γὰρ αὐτῷ τῷ Θεῷ κορύσσεται, Χόλον μέγιστον ἐκ φθόνου δεδεγμένος. Δεῖ γὰρ φιλεῖν ἐκεῖνον, ὃν Θεὸς φιλεῖ.

Apulejus: Nam sese excruciat, qui beatis invidet.

Cyprianus: Calamitas sine remedio est odisse felicem. Præterea ait, Pugnatis etiam & bellatis: nec tamen consequi- mini, nempe vitam tranquillam, cujus causa bella suscipiun- tur.

Διὰ τὸ μὴ αἰτεῖσθαι ὑμᾶς.] Deus promisit precantibus, non pugnantibus Matth. VII, 7. Αἰτεῖσθαι pro αἰτεῖν Attice, ut Matth. XVIII, 19. XX, 22. Luc. XI, 9. & alibi.

Nihil de caritate annonæ, nihil de fame hic habe- tur, nec ubique, quo dispersæ erant XII. tribus, fa- mes, aut annonæ caritas vigebat. Litigantes notat, quod nullum è litigiis fructum capiant: nec conten- tiones tantum, sed & cupiditates, unde illæ oriuntur: quo frustra se iisdem fatigent; imo Deum iratum sibi reddant, ut nec precibus quicquam ab ipso ob- tineant. Exprimit autem primum avaritiam, con- cupiscitis, deinde zelum illicitum, occiditis, & æmu- lamini, tum contentiones, pugnatis & belligeramini, hoc est, indulgetis pugnis & bellis. Sed quo effectu? Et non habetis, non potestis assequi, quod vultis, nihil habetis, id est, nihil commodi percipitis. Avaros itaque invidos, rixosos, nihil suis cupidita- tibus consequi docet, ac rationem reddit, quod non petant à Deo: Voluptates enim illæ impedi- unt preces, & dediti iisdem, posthabitis precibus, quæ medium sunt aliquid à Deo obtinendi divini- tus praescriptum Jac. I, 10. mediis illicitis, quae de- siderant, consequi contendunt Hagg. I, 6.

Quod ad avaros, dicuntur illi concupiscere, (quae concupiscentia vocatur oculorum, 1. Joh. II, 16. desiderium divitiarum, 1. Tim. VI, 9.) sed non ha- bere, quod in illis impletur, non tantum cum nihil impetrant, & vanum est illorum desiderium, sed etiam quia nunquam satis habet avaritia, nunquam impletur plene ejus desiderium, Prov. XXIX, 15. & avarus non tam habet rem concupitam, quam ab ea habetur & possidetur, quasi ab hero, imo ty- ranno, Prov. XIII, 7. Porro qui cum invidia am- biunt, eos etiam non posse assequi, quod sectantur Apostolus testatur: quod in superbos & ambitio- sos dictum videtur, quia honor fugientem sequi- tur, & sequentem fugit. De contendentibus item, & belligerantibus pronunciatur, οὐκ ἔχετε. Saepe enim nec contentionibus, sive privatis, sive foren- sibus, nec violentia obtineri potest, quod expeti- tur. Ex avaritia & ambitione sequi solent con- tentiones & jurgia. Caeterum in Graecis Codici- bus nuspiam occurrit φθονεῖτε, sed φονεύετε, quod etiam Vulgatus legit & Syrus, ut & suo tempore Oecumenius. Ex nuda vero suspicione emenda- vit Erasmus: Forte scriptum fuit φθονεῖτε, eum- que sequutus est Beza. Sed ut recte Estius, non debuit ex nuda conjectura sine Codicum ope le- ctio consueta mutari, quam ita explicari posse censet: Occiditis, id est, odio habetis alius alium è 1. Joh. III, 15. Cornelius à Lapide ita interpretatur: Occiditis in actu non perfecto, sed inchoato, id est, occidere cogitatis, caedem machinamini. Invidia enim & ira semper crescunt, ac tandem in caedes erumpunt. Unde vicina sunt uti nomine, ita & re ac operatione, φόνος καὶ φθόνος, id est, invidia & occisio. Solent oratores cum vitium insectan- tur, extrema & gravissima ejus damna, licet rara, recensere & exaggerare, ut Auditores magis ad vitii odium impellant. Potest etiam sensus esse Occiditis & zelatis, fere ad eadem zelatis. Hein- sius in h. l. ita interpretatur: Agit de perversis ho- minum cupiditatibus, quae finem suum raro, aut plerumque non assequuntur: Inter quos sunt oi φο- νεύοντες, non qui occidunt, sed qui mortem ut plu- rimum aut alienam optant, aut qui vitae alienae im- minent, ut cum Psal. LXII, 3. ἕως πότε ἐπιτίθεσθε ἐπʼ ἄνθρωπον; φονεύετε πάντες ὑμεῖς. Ita enim Hellenistae suum sequuti judicium, non eos, qui ali- ter id acceperunt. Est igitur φονεύειν, quod φονᾷν vulgo dicunt Graeci. Nemo autem minus finem as- sequitur plerumque, quam qui alienam optat, nec expectat mortem.

## 4:3
Verse 3.

You ask and do not receive, because you ask amiss, that you may spend it on your pleasures.] Some could say: but others do not pray to God, we do pray. He answers even these, that it is no wonder if they are not heard, because they pray amiss, not that they may serve God having the necessities, but that they may have what they may spend on pleasures. But God has not promised such things, Matthew 6:32. We said above in 1:5 and Matthew 18:19 that it is given to those who ask, but if they ask rightly, that is, if they ask for necessities humbly and with the intention of using them rightly.

He asks amiss, not only he who does not ask from the one God, or who asks on account of his own merits or those of the saints, not in the name of the one Mediator Christ, or who does not ask for a good thing, or what God wills to be asked, but also he who does not ask with a good end: not for the glory of God, for his own salvation, or that of his neighbor; but for pleasures and luxury, by which he may satisfy carnal desires, as the covetous man satisfies avarice, the envious zealot envy, the contentious man his own evil will. They are not heard because they do not pray according to the will of God, John 5:14.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Αἰτεῖτε καὶ ὀ λαμβάνετε, διότι κακῶς αἰτεῖτε, ἵνα ἐν ταῖς ἡδο- ναῖς ὑμῶν δαπανήσητε.] Poterant quidam dicere: at vero alii non precantur Deum, nos precamur. Etiam his respon- det, non mirum esse si non exaudiantur, quia male precantur, non ut habentes necessaria Deo serviant, sed ut habeant quae in voluptates impendant. Talia autem non promisit Deus, Matth. VI, 32. Diximus supra I, 5. & Matth. XVIII, 19. dari petentibus, sed si recte petant, id est, si petant necessaria hu- militer, & animo recte utendi.

Male petit, non tantum, qui non à Deo uno pe- tit, aut qui ob merita propria vel sanctorum, non in nomine unius Mediatoris Christi petit, vel qui non petit bonum, vel quod Deus vult peti, sed etiam qui non bono fine petit: non ob gloriam Dei, ob salutem propriam, vel proximi; sed ob volupta- tes & luxum, quo carnales cupiditates, ut avarus avaritiam, invidus zelotes invidiam, contentio- sus malam suam voluntatem expleat. Illi non ex- audiuntur, quia non orant juxta voluntatem Dei, Johan. V, 14.

## 4:4
Adulterers and adulteresses. For μοιχαλὶς is an adulteress, Romans 7:3. Here, however, these words are to be taken in a figurative sense. For those who do not adhere to the one God, nor desire to obey Him in all things, but accommodate themselves partly to God and partly to the world, are like those spouses who, not content with their own sweet spouse, admit external loves.

Do you not know that the friendship of the world is enmity with God.] That is, friendship with the world, or with the vicious actions of the world, is held by God as hostility against Himself: who demands the whole man for Himself. The same sense is in Matthew 12:30, where see the remarks. Ἔχθρα Θεοῦ, with the genitive taken objectively, is the same as ἔχθρα εἰς Θεὸν, Romans 8:7.

Whoever wishes to be a friend of the world, becomes an enemy of God.] May he be hateful to God. Thus φίλῷ Θεõ above II, 23. beloved of God.

By pleasures and depraved desires, having abandoned God, to whom we have been betrothed through faith 2 Cor. XI, 2, we commit fornication with the world, since love is enmity toward God, as the Apostle says concerning the Φρονήματι τῆς σαρκὸς, Rom. VIII, 7, that it is ἔχθρα εἰς θεὸν, so they love the world, with the love of God spurned, who conform themselves to the world or to this age, Rom. XII, 2, and who follow those things which are in the world, 1 John II, 15. The world, therefore, is to be understood as the malice of the world, such as avarice, lusts, pride, frauds, contentions, etc., in a word, any lawlessnesses, by which, as we are turned away from the law of God, so we are turned away from God himself. For he who is a transgressor of the law is an enemy of God. Just as it is impossible to serve God and mammon: So it is to be a friend of GOD and of the world at the same time, says Didymus in this place. However, that enmity of GOD can be understood reciprocally, for the lover of the world is not only an enemy of God, but also has God as a foe and enemy; just as is clear from verse 6, as also from verse 5, that the Spirit of God is borne hostilely against envy. In a similar way, fornication occurs throughout in a metaphorical sense: See Jerem. XIII, 27, Ezech. XXIII, 44, 45, Hosea II, 2. Which sense pleased most interpreters. But B. Brochmand preferred to understand it as πορνείᾳ, which is committed in mind, gesture, words, and deed, Matth. V, 28.

Latin:

Μοιχοὶ καὶ μοιχαλίδες.] Adulteri & adulteræ. Nam μοι- χαλὶς est mœcha Rom. VII, 3. Hic tamen hæ voces sumen- dæ in sensu figurato.
