Nam qui Deo uni non adhærent, nec ei per omnia parere cupiunt, sed partim Deo, partim mundo se accommodant, similes sunt iis conjugibus, qui suo suavè conjuge non contenti externos amores admiscent.

Οὐκ ὄιδατε, ὅτι ἡ φιλία τõ κόσμυ ἔχθρα τõ Θεõ ἐσι.] Id est, amicitia cum mundo, sive cum mundi vitiosis actionibus, à Deo habetur pro hostilitate in se: qui totum hominem sibi poscit. Idem sensus Matth. XII, 30. ubi dicta vide. Ἔχθρα Θεõ genitivo objective sumpto, idem quod ἔχθρα εἰς Θεὸν, Rom. VIII, 7.

Ὃς ἂν ἦν βυληθῆ φίλῷ εἶναι τõ κόσμυ, ἐχθρὸς τõ Θεõ κα- θίςαται.] Deo sit exosus. Sic φίλῷ Θεõ supra II, 23. amâ- tus Deo.

Voluptatibus & concupiscentiis pravis, relicto Deo, cui per fidem desponsati sumus 2. Cor. XI, 2. fornicamur cum mundo, cum amor est inimici- tia Dei, uti de Φρονήματι τῆς σαρκὸς, Rom. VIII, 7. Apostolus ait, quod sit ἔχθρα εἰς θεὸν, ita mundum amant, amore Dei spreto, qui mundo vel huic se- culo confìgurantur, Rom. XII, 2. quique ea se- ctantur, quæ in mundo sunt, 1. Joh. II, 15. Mundus ergo de malitia mundi intelligendus, ut sunt ava- ritia, libidines, fastus, fraudes, contentiones &c. uno verbo, quævis ἀνομίαι, quibus ut à lege Dei, sic à Deo ipso divaricamur. Qui enim legis transgressor est, inimicus est Dei. Sicut impossibile est, servire Deo & mammone: Ita amicum DEI esse simul & mundi, ait Didymus in h. l. Potest tamen illa DEI inimicitia reciproce intelligi, non enim tantum Dei hostis est, amator mundi, sed Deum etiam ho- stem & inimicum habet; quemadmodum è versu 6. liquet, ut & è v. 5. quod Spiritus Dei hostiliter fe- ratur adversus invidiam. Simili modo fornica- tio passim occurrit sensu Metaphorico: Vid. Jerem. XIII, 27. Ezech. XXIII, 44. 45. Ose. II, 2. Qui sen- sus plerisque Interpretibus placuit. B. Brochman- dus vero maluit de πορνείᾳ intelligere, quæ animo, gestu, verbis & opere fit Matth. V, 28.

## 4:5
Verse 5.

Do you think that the Scripture speaks in vain? The spirit that dwells in us yearns for envy.] These are not the very words, but the sense taken from two places in Gen. VI, namely 3 and 5. For what is there מַחְשׁבֹת [thoughts] of the mind, here is ἐπιποθεῖ [yearns]. That 'the spirit that dwells in us' is from verse 3, and it is worth the same as 'heart' in verse 5, which in the same verse 5 is עַץ [evil]. In the Greek, 'for evil things' is here 'envy,' because among the kinds of evils, envy is not the least, and those to whom this epistle is written were most akin to it. That Spirit given to men by God, and dwelling in men by his command, that is, the mind, was daily made worse through evil examples, and desiring those things which not love, but envy suggests. For φθόνῳ [envy] is taken here metonymically, as I have just shown.

By the Spirit, Gen. VI, 3, not the mind of man, but the Holy Spirit is understood, because Moses said the Spirit of God, not the spirit of man, which we are taught to distinguish in 2 Cor. II, 11. Nor in this place is the mind of man denoted by the Spirit, but the Holy Spirit, or according to others, that which is in man from regeneration, John III, 6. Therefore, it does not refer to Gen. VI, 5, where it deals with the depravity of the concupiscence of the human heart: But, if you listen to Osiander, it refers to Gal. V, 7, where the Spirit is said to lust against the flesh. For there, among the works of the flesh, envyings are listed. Although it is not displeasing to take 'envy' here synecdochically for the works of depraved concupiscence and the depraved concupiscence itself, which Paul expressed by the name of flesh. Osiander concludes from this, however, that this epistle is not canonical; because it alleges the Scripture of Paul by the name of 'Scripture.' But it is certain that Peter himself also appeals to the writings of Paul, 2nd epistle, III, 15, 16, nor would the Holy Spirit have done this without cause, but so that by that reason the Apostles might bear witness to one another of Canonical authority, James, and Peter to Paul, just as also to Peter, Judas, in most places repeating the sayings and sentences from 2 Epist. II. Citations alone indeed do not make a Canonical book, but when they are made in the name of Scripture or the Holy Spirit, or with a similar eulogy, that testimony to the cited author is of Canonical authority. Bede, however, refers these words, that Scripture does not speak in vain, to the preceding. Oecumenius, however, to that which is brought forward in v. 6 from Prov. III, 34. Cornelius a Lapide despairs of finding that alleged place in Scripture. He seeks, however, the sense of Exod. XX, 5, Nah. I, 2, that God is a jealous God, explaining it thus: To covet unto envy is the same as to be jealous. Therefore, that God is jealous of the soul, not suffering a rival, namely, that the world is hinted at. Gagnejus, Cajetanus, Catharinus, Salmero, Mariana, and Lorinus do not depart much from that interpretation, whose sense Cornelius reports and approves thus: That God envies the world, because it entices and destroys souls from GOD: But the exposition of those who wish the Holy Spirit to be said to covet to or against envy is simpler. Their interpretation comes to almost the same thing, who understand the words interrogatively, but in a negative sense: Does the Spirit of God, who dwells in you, tend toward envy, that is, does he inflame us to envy? For by the Spirit, who dwells in us, in the phrase of Scripture, nothing but the Holy Spirit is understood, 1 Cor. III, 16, Rom. IIX, 11, nor does the following verse permit anything else, μείζονα δὲ χάριν δίδωσι, which is a truly divine predicate, and therefore does not befit the human spirit. And that the particle πρὸς sometimes signifies against, is evident from Luke XX, 19, Heb. II, 4. And this, besides those already mentioned, Justinianus, Junius, Piscator, Pareus, and the Belgian Interpreters urge. Hugo also explained it thus: i.e., The Spirit covets to envy, that is, against envy. Estius notes that some also handed down this sense in Bede: The Spirit of God, dwelling in you through baptism, desires that the disease of envy be overcome and extirpated from your minds. For Scripture says that in those places where it condemns envy. And B. Brochmand: He who dwells in us, the Spirit of regeneration, ἐπιποθεῖν πρὸς φθόνον, that is, to covet against envy, or seriously to exhort us that we beware of all envy. Pareus says: You ought to hate the world, because, as Scripture testifies, the Spirit of God, who is in us, and has already long ago dwelt in our people, ἐπιποθεῖ, desires, covets, that is, by his instinct makes us covet and instigates πρὸς φθόνον namely τοῦ κόσμου, to envy, that is, the hatred and flight of the world, for he commands and persuades us to hate the world. Thus φθόνος would be for μῖσος. But even with the propriety of the word retained, the sentence will not be absurd, but very congruent, if we understand πρὸς φθόνον as κατὰ φθόνε, against envy: Just as μάχεσθαι πρός τινα is to fight against someone, and ἐπιποθεῖ desires, is carried hostilely, in this sense: You ought not to love the world: because the Spirit of God dwelling in us is carried hostilely, or is angry against the envy rampant in the world, namely with the remaining vices: A synecdoche of the species for the genus.

Therefore, the discourse is not about the propensity of the human mind to envy, which Hugo, Saa, Thomas Anglicus, and Estius wish, or to desires against God, as Heinsius wishes, bringing in the voice of the Lord, πρὸς φθόνον κυρίου, and that φθόνος is παροργισμὸς, anger, indignation, and that ἐπιποθεῖν πρὸς φθόνον is to provoke to anger, which is asserted without a suitable example.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Ἡ δοκᾶτε, ὅτι κενῶς ἡ γραφὴ λέγει; πρὸς φθόνον ἐπιποθεῖ τὸ πνεῦμα ὃ κατῴκησεν ἐν ἡμῖν.] Non sunt ipsa verba, sed sensus sumptus ex duobus locis Gen. VI. nempe 3. & 5. Nam quod ibi est מַחְשׁבֹת διανοῖται, hic est ἐπιποθεῖ. Illud τὸ πνεῦ- μα ὃ κατῴκησεν, ἐν ἡμῖν est ex commate 3. & idem valet quod commate 5. לִבּוֹ, quod eodem commate 5. est עַץ. In Græ- co ἐπὶ τὰ πονηρὰ hic est φθόνον, quia in malorum genere in- vidìa non minimum est, & maxime ei affines erant illi, ad quos hæc epistola scribitur. Spiritus ille à Deo hominibus datus, & ejus jussu in hominibus habitans, id est, animus, indies per mala exempla pejor erat factus, & ea desiderans, quæ non dilectio, sed invidia suggerit. Nam φθόνῳ hic με- τωνυμικῶς sumitur, ut modò ἐδειξα.

Per Spiritum, Gen. VI, 3. non animus hominis, sed Spiritus sanctus intelligitur, quia Spiritum Dei dixit Moses, non hominis Spiritum, quæ distinqui docemur 2. Cor. II, 11. Nec hoc in loco per Spiritum hominis animus, sed Spiritus Sanctus, vel juxta alios id, quod in homine ex regeneratione est, Joh. III, 6. denotatur. Ideo non Gen. VI, 5. ubi de pravitate concupiscentiæ humani cordis agitur: Sed, si O- siandrum audias, Gal. V, 7. respicit, ubi Spiritus ad- versus carnem concupiscere dicitur. Illic enim inter opera carnis Φθόνοι recensentur. Quanquam non displiceat, Synecdocbice Φθόνον hic accipere de ope- ribus pravæ concupiscentiæ & ipsa concupiscentia prava, quam carnis nomine expressit Paulus. Colli- git autem inde Osiander, hanc epistolam non esse Canonicam; eo quod illa Pauli Scripturam alleget nomine γραφῆς. At constat, quod & Petrus ipse ad scripta Pauli provocet, 2. epist. III, 15. 16. nec citra causam Spiritus sanctus hoc fecisset, sed ut ea ra- tione Apostoli sibi invicem testimonium perhibe- rent autoritatis Canonicae, Jacobus, & Petrus Pau- lo, quemadmodum etiam Petro, Judas, in plerisque repetens e 2. Epist. II. dicta, & sententias. Solae qui- dem citationes non faciunt librum Canonicum, sed cum Scripturae vel Spiritus sancti nomine fiunt, aut cum simili elogio, testimonium illud autori citato est autoritatis Canonicae. Beda autem haec, quod non inaniter Scriptura dicat, ad praecedentia re- fert. Oecumenius vero ad id, quod v. 6. e Prov. III, 34. adducitur. Cornelius a Lapide desperat de loco illo allegato in scriptura inveniendo. Sensum au- tem quaerit Exod. XX, 5. Nah. I, 2. quod Deus zelo- tes sit, ita exponens: Ad invidiam concupiscere idem est, quod esse zelotypum. Deum ergo zelotypum animae non pati rivalem, mundum scilicet innui. Non multum ab ea interpretatione abeunt Ga- gnejus, Cajetanus, Catharinus, Salmero, Mariana, Lorinus, quorum sensum ita refert & approbat Cor- nelius: Deum invidere mundo, quod animas a DEO se pelliceat ac perdat: Simplicior autem est eorum expositio, qui Spiritum sanctum ad vel adversus invidiam concupiscere dici volunt. Quo fere redit eorum interpretatio, qui interrogative, sed sensu ne- gativo verba intelligunt: An Dei Spiritus, qui in vo- bis habitat, ad invidiam fertur, hoc est, nos ad invi- diam inflammat? Per Spiritum enim, qui in nobis habitat, phrasi scripturae non nisi Spiritus sanctus intelligitur, 1. Cor. III, 16. Rom. IIX, 11. neque aliud permittit versus sequens, μείζονα δὲ χάριν δίδωσι, quod praedicatum vere divinum est, ideoque non convenit humano spiritui. Et particulam πρὸς quan- doq; contra significare, e Luc. XX, 19. Ebr. II, 4. con- stat. Idque urgent praeter jam dictos Justinianus, Junius, Piscator, Pareus, Interpp. Belgici. Sic expo- suit etiam Hugo: q. d. Spiritus concupiscit ad invi- diam, id est, contra invidiam. Quem sensum etiam nonnullos apud Bedam tradidisse monet Estius: Invidiae morbum debellari, atque a vestris mentibus extirpari desiderat Spiritus Dei per baptismum, ha- bitans in vobis. Id enim Scriptura dicit iis locis, qui- bus invidiam damnat. Et B. Brochmand. Eum qui in nobis habitat, regenerationis Spiritum, ἐπιποθεῖν πρὸς φθόνον, id est, concupiscere contra invidiam, seu serio hortari nos, ut ab omni invidia caveamus. Pa- reus dicit: Debetis odisse mundum, quia, Scriptura teste, Spiritus Dei, qui in nobis est, & in populo nostro jam olim habitavit, ἐπιποθεῖ, desiderat, concupiscit, hoc est, instinctu suo nos concupiscere facit & insti- gat πρὸς φθόνον nempe τοῦ κόσμου, ad invidiam, hoc est odium & fugam mundi, pro jubet & suadet odisse mundum. Sic φθόνος esset pro μῖσος. Sed etiam re- tenta proprietate vocis non absurda, sed valde con- grua erit sententia, si πρὸς φθόνον intelligamus κατὰ φθόνε, contra invidiam: Sicut μάχεσθαι πρός τινα contra aliquem pugnare, & ἐπιποθεῖ desiderat, fer- tur hostiliter, hoc sensu: Non debetis amare mun- dum: quia Spiritus Dei in nobis habitans fertur ho- stiliter, seu irascitur adversus invidiam grassantem in mundo, nempe cum reliquis vitiis: Synecdoche speciei pro genere.

Non ergo de propensione animi humani ad invi- diam sermo est, quod Hugo, Saa, Thomas Angli- cus & Estius volunt, aut ad cupiditates adversus Deum, ut Heinsius vult, Domini vocem ingerens, πρὸς φθόνον κυρίου, & φθόνος sit παροργισμὸς ira, indignatio, & ἐπιποθεῖν πρὸς φθόνον, sit ad iram provocare, quod sine exemplo idoneo adseritur.

## 4:6
Vers. 6.

Μείζονα δὲ δίδωσι χάριν.] God, namely, at this time. For it was an old saying concerning the Messiah, that he would correct the יצר הרע, namely both by the precepts which we have in Matt. V, 28 and elsewhere, and by eternal and heavenly promises, and furthermore by that Spirit of his, that is, an excellent one. The same sense is in 1 Peter III, 19 and following, where the time of Christ is similarly compared with the time of the flood. These words taken μυσικῶς can be seen from Prov. IV, 19. Διὸ λέγει. Κύριος ὑπερηφάνοις ἀντιτάσσεται, ταπεινοῖς δὲ δίδωσι χάριν.] These are the very words of the LXX, Prov. III, 34. But since they are absent from the best manuscripts, and from some Latin codices, it is credible that this passage, as being alien to what is treated here, had been annotated in the margin from 1 Pet. V, 6, and then, as is wont to happen, crept into the text. And with these omitted, the sense coheres better.

The subject is to be repeated from the preceding v. 5, which is τὸ πνεῦμα. It is not, however, to be brought in at will. To which the following verb διὸ λέγει also agrees. Therefore, divine and personal predicates are attributed here to the Holy Spirit, as to a truly divine person. For to give greater saving grace and to speak through the Prophets: and in the Scriptures, is the person of a divine one. But that greater grace, which the Holy Spirit gives to those in whom he dwells, who covets against envy and sins, not only makes our spirit covet against any wicked desires of the heart, but also effects that we be perfected in sanctification from day to day, from glory to glory, and be reformed to the image of God, not only that the outer man be corrupted, but also that the inner man be renewed from day to day, 2 Cor. IV, 16. The suspicion which Grotius has about the words διὸ λέγει is rash. For most Codices, and those ancient ones, have this pericope. All the Latins both read and interpret it. The Syrian Interpreter also gives it, whence Estius does not doubt that it was written by James. Nor could it have crept in from Peter. For the words διὸ λέγει, therefore he says, are prefixed, which are not prefixed in the Petrine passage. Nor does the scruple about coherence move us. For he had spoken before of the grace which the Holy Spirit gives greater to his own, and he now teaches that it happens to men, and not having read the proud,

And because pride is the beginning of all sin, and impels one to all kinds of sins, Sir. X, 15. whence also a great part of contentions, and quarrels, and wars arise, therefore the Apostle particularly dissuades from this vice, and at the same time thus builds for himself an approach to the remedy of repentance, which pride hinders most of all: because God resists the proud (ὑπερηφάνοις are those who, out of ambition, exalt themselves above others, from ὑπερφάινομαι, I appear above, I overtop), or as Cyprian in his epistle to Novatus says, he stands against, the Syrian says he depresses, he crushes (the proud.) In the Greek there is the emphatic verb ἀντιτάσσεται, which among Plutarch and others means to stand in battle array against. Whence also Chrysostom hom. III. on the words of Isaiah. The Apostle did not simply say: God dismisses the proud, and abandons them in their sins, and strips them of his help, but he resists and opposes them as if in battle array; not that God has need of a battle array or a fight, since there is nothing weaker than a proud man, inasmuch as he is blinded in the eyes with which he might see God, and is exposed to the injury of all: whereas for God, however strong and powerful a proud man might be, his will suffices to overturn everything. He resists, therefore, to declare his vehement hatred toward the proud. Jerome epist. XLV. What kind of evil must it be, which has God as its adversary.

But he GIVES GRACE TO THE HUMBLE. The streams of grace flow downward, not upward. Waters seek sloping places: Thus grace does not flow, except into humble hearts. Bernard serm. IV. on Missus est: Just as humility is the seat of waters in the valleys: So humility is the seat of grace in men. The valleys are irrigated by heavenly rivers, and become more fertile than the highest summits of the mountains. Whence St. Aug. warns in ser. xvi. on the martyrs. Do you seek height? Through the valley one arrives at the mountain. You seek the seat of brightness: first drink the cup of humility. And Fulgentius, epistle 6, chapter 9: Let the humility of mind grow in you, which is the true and integral sublimity of a Christian: and you will know that the grace of God grows in you all the more, the more you see the humility of heart abound in you.

In the Hebrew text it is, he (the Lord) will mock the mockers, and will give grace to the meek. James, however, having followed this, as also in the parallel passage St. Peter, 1 epistle 5, 6, the LXX interpreters κατὰ πόδα do not differ from the authentic text. For the proud are truly mockers, who with a high brow despise and laugh at those who advise better things: whom God resists, and by resisting mocks them, so that they may be confounded. The humble, however, are the meek, as opposed to the irascible, proud, and boastful. Estius wrongly gathers from this a doctrine which he calls Catholic, but is truly non-Catholic, that a justified man merits an increase of grace by good works and especially by humility. On the contrary, the Holy Spirit calls this not merit, but grace and a gratuitous gift, which are opposites, Romans 11, 6.

Moreover, that the Holy Spirit gives greater grace is not to be restricted to the times of the New Testament, nor does the comparison tend that way. For in the Old Testament the grace of the Holy Spirit was not denied. But the benefits obtained by Christ look backward and forward, Hebrews 13, 8. Nor are those to be learned from the blind Rabbinical doctors, that the Messiah had to come to correct the evil figment (how old that saying was, Grotius did not teach), there is no doubt among Christians. But that this was done through precepts, through promises, and the Holy Spirit, whence will it be taught? Precepts manifest, they do not remove or correct that evil, for the removal of which it was necessary that Christ should take upon himself the sin of the world, Isaiah 53, 9; John 1, 29; Hebrews 5, 21. For the sake of the precepts there was also no need for the advent of Christ, which in the Old Testament had already been fully and perfectly handed down, nor could they receive greater perfection from Christ, John 1, 17. Scripture nowhere teaches that the promises of eternal life correct evil: nor does it teach that they were brought by Christ as new promises. We do not deny that the Holy Spirit corrects it, but if it is understood legally, or regarding the precepts, there is no true correction from this unless the Gospel is added, which hands down the mode and reason for the cleansing of sins through the blood of Christ, 1 John 1, 7, which the Holy Spirit applies in justification, and daily thereafter corrects and cleanses us in renewal. Grotius therefore omitted the proper benefit of Christ, that He acquired for us by His blood and death the cleansing of sins, and that equally for all men, whether they live under the Old Testament or under the New Testament.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Μείζονα δὲ δίδωσι χάριν.] Deus nempe hoc tempore. Nam de Messia vetus erat dictum, futurum ut corrigeret יצר הרע nempe & praeceptis, quae habemus Matth. V, 28. & alibi, & promissis aeternis ac coelestibus, ac praeterea Spi- ritu illo suo, id est, eximio. Idem sensus 1. Petri III, 19. & sequentibus, ubi similiter tempus Christi comparatur cum tempore diluvii. Videri possunt hæc verba μυσικῶς sumpta de Prov. IV, 19. Διὸ λέγει. Κύριος ὑπερηφάνοις ἀντιτάσσεται, ταπεινοῖς δὲ δίδωσι χάριν.] Sunt hæc ipsa verba LXX. Prov. III, 34. Sed cum absint ab optimis manuscriptis, & à Latinis codicibus nonnullis, credibile est hunc locum, ut ab eo, quod hic tra- ctatur alienum, annotatum fuisse in margine, ex 1. Petr. V, 6. deinde, ut fieri solet, irrepsisse in textum. Et his omissis sen- sus melius cohæret.

Subjectum è v. 5. præcedenti repetendum, quod est τὸ πνεῦμα. Non vero pro arbitrio ingerendum. Cui etiam convenit sequens verbum διὸ λέγει. Spi- ritui S. ergo tribuuntur hic prædicata divina, & personalia, ceu personæ vere divinæ. Nam dare gratiam majorem salutiferam & loqui per Prophe- tas : & in Scripturis, persona est divinæ. Gratia au- tem illa major, quam Spiritus sanctus dat illis, in quibus habitat, qui concupiscit adversus invidiam, & peccata, non solum nostrum Spiritum concupi- scere faciat adversus quaslibet pravas cordis cupi- ditates, sed etiam efficiat, ut in sanctificatione de die in diem, de claritate in claritatem perficiamur, & ad imaginem Dei reformemur, non solum ut exte- rior homo corrumpatur, sed etiam, ut interior homo renovetur de die in diem, 2. Cor. IV, 16. Quam Gro- tius de verbis διὸ λέγει habet suspicionem, teme- raria est. Plerique enim Codices, iique vetusti, habent hanc pericopen. Latini omnes & legunt & interpretantur. Dat eam etiam Syrus Interpres, unde non dubitat Estius, quod à Jacobo scripta fuerit. Nec è Petro potuit irrepsisse. Nam præ- mittuntur verba διὸ λέγει, propterea dicit, quæ non præmittuntur in loco Petrino. Neque scrupulus nos movet de cohærentia. Nam & de gratia, quam dat Spiritus sanctus majorem suis, dixerat antea, & eam contingere hominibus jam docet, neque lectis superbis,

Et quia superbia initium omnis peccati est, & ad omnis generis peccata impellit, Sir. X, 15. unde et- iam magnam partem contentiones, & jurgia atque bella oriuntur, ideo peculiariter dehortatur Apo- stolus ab hoc vitio, & simul ita ad pœnitentiæ re- medium, cui maxime officit superbia, aditum sibi struit: quia Deus superbis (ὑπερηφάνοις sunt, qui ex ambitione super alios sese efferunt ab ὑπερφάινομαι super appareo, superemineo) resistit, vel ut Cyprianus epist. ad Novat. contrastitit, Syrus deprimit, conte- rit (superbos.) In Græco est verbum emphaticum ἀντιτάσσεται, quod apud Plutarchum & alios est ex adverso stare instructa acie. Unde & Chrysostomus hom. III. de verb. Esa. Non simpliciter dixit Aposto- lus: Deus superbos dimittit, & in peccatis deserit, suo quoque nudat auxilio, sed resistit & adversatur quasi in oppositum bene disposita acie; non quod in- structa acie aut pugna Deo sit opus, tum superbo ni- hil sit infirmius, utpote quia oculis orbatus est, qui- bus videat Deum, & omnium expositus injuriæ: Deo autem, quamlibet superbus, validus ac potens esset, voluntas sufficiat ad invertenda omnia. Resistit ergo, ut vehemens odium declaret erga superbos. Hiero- nymus epist. XLV. Quale malum sit oportet, quod adversarium habet Deum.

HUMILIBUS autem DAT GRATIAM. Fluenta gratiæ deorsum, non sursum fluunt. Aquæ loca quærunt declivia : Sic gratia non fluit, nisi in corda humilia. Bernhardus serm. IV. super Missus est: Quemadmodum aquarum sedes humilitas est val- lium : Ita gratiæ sedes humilitas est hominum. Valles fluviis cœlestibus irrigantur, & fiunt fœcundiores quam summa montium cacumina. Unde monet S. Aug. ser. xvi. de mart. Altitudinem quæritis? Per valte pervenitur ad montem. Sedem quæritis claritatis: Prius bibite calicem humilitatis. Et Fulgentius epist. VI. cap. 9, Crescat in te humilitas animi, quæ vera est & integra sublimitas Christiani: Et tanto ma- gis cognosces in te gratiam Dei crescere, quanto ma- gis tibi humilitatem cordis videris abundare.

In Ebræo textu est, ipse (Dominus) deludet illu- sores, & mansuetis dabit gratiam. Sequutus autem Jacobus, ut & in loco parallelo S. Petrus 1. epist. V, 6. LXX. Interp. κατὰ πόδα non dissentiunt à textu authentico. Superbi enim vere sunt illusores, qui alto supercilio contemnunt, ridentque rectiora monentes: quibus resistit Deus, & resistendo elu- dit eosdem, ut confundantur. Humiles vero man- sueti sunt, ut contra iracundi superbi & jactabun- di. Perperam vero exinde Estius colligit doctri- nam, quam vocat Catholicam, vere acatholicam, hominem justificatum bonis operibus ac imprimis humilitate mereri gratiæ augmentum. Ex adverso Spiritus sanctus id vocat non meritum, sed gratiam & donum gratuitum, quæ opposita sint, Roman. XI, 6.

Cæterum quod Spiritus Sanctus majorem gra- tiam dat, non restringendum ad tempora Novi Te- stamenti, nec comparatio eo tendit. Nam in Veteri Testamento non denegata fuit gratia Spiritus san- cti. Beneficia autem à Christo parta retrorsum & antrorsum spectant, Ebr. XIII, 8. neque illa discen- da Rabbinis cæcis Doctoribus, Messiam venire de- buisse, ut corrigeret figmentum malum (quod quam vetus fuerit dictum, non docuit Grotius) du- bium nullum est inter Christianos. Sed id factum esse per præcepta, per promissa, & Spiritum sanctum, unde docebitur? Præcepta manifestant, non tol- lunt aut corrigunt illud malum, ad quod tollen- dum opus fuit, ut Christus peccatum mundi in se susciperet, Esa. LIII, 9. Joh. I, 29. Ebr. V, 21. Præce- ptorum causa etiam opus non erat adventu Chri- sti, quæ in Vet. Test. plene ac perfecte jam tradita erant nec potuere majorem perfectionem à Chri- sto accipere, Jop. I, 17. Promissa vitæ æternæ corri- gere malum nuspiam Scriptura tradit: nec à Christo allata esse ceu nova promissa docet. Spiritum San- ctum vero corrigere id non negamus, sed si intelli- gatur legaliter, vel quoad præcepta, non vera hinc correctio est, nisi accedat Evangelium, quod mo- dum & rationem mundationis peccatorum tradit, per sanguinem Christi, 1. Joh. I, 7. quam Spiritus sanctus applicat in justificatione, ac quotidie dein- ceps nos corrigit & emundat in renovatione. Omi- sit ergo proprium Christi beneficium Grotius, quod nobis acquisiverit sanguine & morte sua mundationem peccatorum, idque ex æquo omni- bus, seu qui sub Veteri Testamento, seu qui sub No- vo Testamento vivunt, hominibus.

## 4:7
Verse 7. Submit yourselves therefore to God. Since God now gives much greater gifts than in the time of the flood, it is right that you allow yourselves to be ruled by Him, not by that human spirit long since corrupted. Ὑποτάγητε is a passive used as a reciprocal, that is, submit yourselves, just as the same word is taken in Romans 10, 3; 13, 1, 5; 1 Corinthians 16, 10; Ephesians 5, 21, 22, 24; Colossians 3, 18; Titus 2, 5, 9; 3, 1; 1 Peter 2, 13, 18; 3, 1, 3; 5, 5.

Resist the devil. The same sense as 1 Peter 5, 9. One must resist through the wisdom of God that demonic wisdom, of which above 3, 15. In the manuscript, 'but resist'.

And he will flee from you. Repulsed often, just as by Christ our head, he will flee away. See Matthew 4, 11 and what is said there. That spirit is proud, and does not easily return to where he has often been triumphed over.

He commands submission towards God, to whom He said He gives grace to the humble. Men, depraved by sin, draw up a battle line as it were against God, whom God in turn opposes: and the humble indeed submit themselves to God. Therefore He receives them into His faith and protection. The Apostle had handed down the dangerous effects of carnal pleasures. Now therefore he adds fruitful remedies: which are to be subject to God, and to resist the devil, so that the devil, who inflames desires, may flee, and God, who resists through His Spirit, may be rendered closer to us. But in order that we may be subject to God, resist the devil, and God may approach us through grace, it is necessary that we approach God through repentance, and amend the lust for slandering, which is a fruit of repentance, and this was to be urged again here particularly, where the Apostle had dealt against contentions. The word ὑποτάσσω is to place under or to subject, just as in Romans 13, 1, the subjection owed to the magistrate is designated by that word, the subjection of women, Ephesians 5, 22. It therefore properly signifies an inferior being subjected to an order established by a superior, and in this place it introduces the obedience owed to the divine order or ordinance, or the subjection to be performed according to the prescription of the divine word. He who obeys God cannot obey the temptations of the devil, but resists, which is done through the word, prayers, and faith in Christ, who destroyed the works of the devil, 1 Peter 5, 8; 1 John 3, 8. The fruit and outcome of the struggle against the devil is his flight. Since he insults us again from time to time, even if he is put to flight, we must never cease to be vigilant, so that he may be resisted: until, the struggle and course being fully completed, we carry off the crown of life, 2 Timothy 4, 7; Revelation 2, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ὑποτάγητε ὧν τῷ Θεῷ.] Cum Deus multo majo- ra nunc det dona, quam diluvii tempore, æqvum est, ut ab ipso vos regi sinatis, non ab humano illo Spiritu pridem cor- rupto. Ὑποτάγητε passivum pro reciproco, id est, subjicite vos ipsos, quomodo eadem vox sumitur Rom. X, 3. XIII, 1. 5. 1. Cor. XVI, 10. Eph. V, 21. 22. 24. Col. III, 18. Tit. II, 5. 9. III, 1. 1. Petr. II, 13. 18. III, 1. 3. V, 5.

Ἀντίστητε τῷ διαβόλῳ.] Idem sensus 1. Petr. V, 9. Resisten- dum est per Dei sapientiam illi sapientiæ δαιμονιώδει, de qua supra III, 15. In Manuscripto ἀντίστητε δέ.

Καὶ φεύξεται ἀφ' ὑμῶν.] Repulsus sæpe, sicut à Christo capite nostro, aufugiet. Vide Matth. IV, 11. & ibi dicta. Superbus est ille Spiritus, nec facile eo redit, ubi sæpe est tri- umphatus.

Submissionem erga Deum præcipit, quem humi- libus gratiam dare dixit. Homines per peccatum depravati aciem quasi contra Deum instruunt, quos Deus ex adverso oppugnat: ac humilesqui- dem Deo sese subdunt. Eos ergo in fidem ac tute- lam suam recipit. Effecta voluptatum carnalium pe- riculosa tradiderat Apostolus. Jam itaque remedia fructuosa subjungit: Quæ sunt subjici Deo, & resi- stere diabolo, ut diabolus, qui inflammat cupidita- tes, fugiat, Deus, qui per Spiritum suum resistit, iis- dem nobis propior reddatur. Ut autem Deo subji- ciamur, diabolo resistamus, nobisq; Deus appro- pinquet per gratiam, opus est, ut nos Deo appro- pinquemus per pœnitentiam, & emendemus obtre- ctandi libidinem, qui est fructus pœnitentiæ, & hic peculiariter iterum urgendus erat, ubi adversus contentiones Apostolus egerat. Verbum ὑποτάσ- σω est subcolloco vel subjicio, quomodo Rom. XIII, 1. subjectio magistratui debita illo verbo designata, subjectio fœminarum, Eph. V, 22. Significat ergo proprie inferiorem subjici ordini à superiori con- stituto, & hoc in loco obsequium τάξει vel ordina- tioni divinæ debitum infert vel ὑποταγὴν juxta præscriptum verbi divini præstandam. Qui autem Deo paret, diaboli tentationibus parere non pot- est, sed resistit, quod fit per verbum, preces, & fidem in Christum, qui opera diaboli destruxit, 1. Petr. V, 8. 1. Joh. III, 8. Fructus & eventus luctæ adversus dia- bolum est fuga ejusdem. Qui quum subinde nobis iterum insultet, etiamsi fugetur, nunquam non no- bis vigilandum est, ut eidem resistatur: donec cer- tamine & cursu plene consummato coronam vitæ reportemus, 2. Tim. IV, 7. Apoc. II, 2.

## 4:8
Verse 8.

“Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you.” קָרַב to draw near to God, is to pray to God and to be willing to obey Him. Conversely, God is said to come to us when He helps us both against the desires of the flesh and against the assaults of the devil, of which he has already treated. This is the mystical sense of the words of Jer. IV, 1.

As through sins we are turned away from God and separated, Is. LIX, 2. So through conversion from sins we return again to God, and draw near to God, not with the steps of the body, but of the heart, of which it is treated not in a mystical sense but a literal one, Jer. IV, 1. God, however, draws near to us by grace and benefits. Let us therefore draw near to God not only through prayers and the purpose of obedience, but also through contrition and faith, which the purpose of new obedience necessarily presupposes, nor without it can it be pleasing, Heb. XI, 6. God, moreover, draws near to us not only by helping us against enemies, but also by affecting and crowning us with manifold grace. But when we are commanded to draw near to God, so that He may draw near to us, neither is the beginning of conversion established in the faculty of man, nor is the beginning of meriting an increase implied. Not the former, because a divine commandment teaches our duty, but it does not demonstrate the faculty of our powers: nor does the Apostle here address those yet to be converted, but those already converted. Finally, God does not only command, but by the grace of His Spirit He works both to will and to perform, Phil. II, 13. Not the latter, because by the testimony of Christ, no one can come to Him, unless the Father has drawn him, John VI, 44. from whose grace is both the beginning, and the middle, and the completion, and although it is given to him who has, Mark IV, 25, it is not, however, because he has it, or as if he merits it: But because God has defined that order, that the grace following, working upon the preceding, should receive it, if the first is not rejected.

“Cleanse your hands, you sinners.” טַהֲרוּ restore ill-gotten goods, Jon. III, 8.

“And purify your hearts, you double-minded.” We also had the word δίψυχοι above at I, 8. Ἁγνίσατε καρδίας קַדְּשׁוּ purify your hearts, namely, using both the present favor and help of God, by prayers and every effort, expel that inconstancy which now draws you to God, now repels you to the world. See 1 Pet. I, 22. 1 John III, 3. where the same word ἁγνίζειν is used.

Repentance is described a posteriori through the cleansing of the hands and the purification of the hearts; the former of which looks to external actions, the latter to internal movements of the soul: because the hands are the instrument of external actions, the pollution of which through sins, Isa. 1:15, ch. 59:3, Matt. 5:13. Thus, cleansing or purity from the stain of sins is designated Gen. 20:5, 1 Sam. 26:18, Job 9:30, Ps. 7:4, 18:21. But that purification is effected through the blood of Christ, 1 John 1:7, Heb. 9:14, and through faith, Acts 15:9. By ἁμαρτωλὸς, notable sinners, who practice the art of sinning as it were, are denoted, Matt. 9:10 seqq., ch. 11:19, Luke 15:2, who are here called δίψυχοι, because they divide their heart between Belial and God, 1 Kings 18:21, or between the world and God, since they wish to serve both, Matt. 6:24, which James, with Christ above, has testified cannot be done. This is to approach the Lord truthfully, namely to have purity of work and simplicity of heart, says Bede in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Ἐγγίσατε Θεῷ, καὶ ἐγγιεῖ ὑμῖν.] קָרַב ἐγγίζειν Θεῷ, est Deum orare & eidem obedire velle. Deus contra dicitur ad nos venire, cum nos adjuvat tum contra cupiditates carnis, tum contra diaboli insultus, de quibus jam egit. Hic est sen- sus mysticus verborum Jerem. IV, 1.

Ut per peccata à Deo avertimur & sequestramur Es. LIX, 2. Ita per conversionem à peccatis ad Deum iterum revertimur, & Deo appropinquamus, non corporis, sed cordis passibus, de qua non sensu my- stico sed literali agitur, Jer. IV, 1. Deus vero appro- pinquat nobis gratia & beneficiis. Appropinqua- mus ergo Deo non tantum per preces & obedientiæ propositum, sed etiam per contritionem & fidem, quam novæ obedientiæ propositum necessario præsupponit, nec sine illa gratum esse potest, Ebr. XI, 6. Deus autem appropinquat nobis non tantum contra hostes nos adjuvando, sed etiam multiplici gratia nos afficiendo & coronando. Cum autem jubemur Deo appropinquare, ut appropinquet nobis, non vel initium conversionis in facultate ho- minis constituitur, vel initium mereri augmentum innuitur. Non illud, quia præceptum divinum de- bitum nostrum docet, non vero virium nostrarum facultatem demonstrat: neque hic alloquitur A- postolus adhuc convertendos, sed jam conversos. Denique non præcipit solum Deus, sed Spiritus sui gratia etiam tum velle tum perficere operatur, Phil. II, 13. Non hoc, quia Christo teste, nemo venire ad ipsum potest, nisi Pater traxerit eum, Joh. VI, 44. à cujus gratia & initium, & medium, & complemen- tum est, & quanquam habenti detur Marc. II, 25. non tamen, quia habet, vel quasi id mereatur: Sed quia Deus ordinem illum definivit, ut primam gratiam sequens, prævenientem operans excipiat, si prima non respuatur.

Καθαρίσατε χεῖρας ἁμαρτωλοὶ.] טַהֲרוּ reddite male ra- pta Jon. III, 8.

Καὶ ἁγνίσατε καρδίας δίψυχοι.] Vocem δίψυχοι etiam supra habuimus I, 8. Ἁγνίσατε καρδίας קַדְּשׁוּ purgate corda, nem- pe utentes tam præsenti Dei favore & auxilio, precibus & omni conatu expellite istam inconstantiam, quæ vos modo ad Deum trahit, modo ad mundum repellit. Vide 1. Petr. I, 22. 1. Joh. III, 3. ubi idem verbum ἁγνίζειν.

Pœnitentia à posteriori describitur per emunda- tionem manuum & purificationem cordium; qua- rum illa spectat externas actiones, hæc internos animi motus:quia manus instrumentum sunt actio- num externarum,quarum ut pollutio per peccata, Esa.I,15. cap.LIX,3.Matth.V,13. Ita emundatio vel mundities à peccatorum labe designatur Gen. XX, 5. 1.Sam.XXVI,18. Job.IX, 30. Ps. VII, 4. XIIX, 21. Fit autem illa purificatio per sanguinem Christi, 1. Job.I,7. Ebr.IX,14. & per fidem, Actor. XV, 9. Per ἁμαρτωλὸς insignes peccatores,qui veluti peccandi artem exercent, Matth.IX,10. seqq. cap. XI, 19. Luc. XV, 2. notantur, qui hic δίψυχοι dicuntur, quod cor inter Belialem & Deum dividant, 1. Reg. XVIII, 2. vel inter mundum & Deum, cum utrique servire volunt, Matth. VI, 24. quod fieri non posse Jaco- bus cum Christo supra testatus est. Hoc est vera- citer appropinquare Domino, operis videlicet mun- ditiam & cordis simplicitatem habere, ait Beda in h. l.

## 4:9
Verse 9.

Ταλαπωρήσατε, καὶ πενθήσατε καὶ κλαύσατε.] For Christians who have fallen into grave sins, there is no return to a good life except through mournful repentance: to express the force of which, James placed these words. Ταλαπωρήσατε, שׁדד to afflict, namely yourselves with fasts and other bodily σκληραγωγίαις (harsh treatments). Πενθήσατε, אבל put on mourning attire, sackcloth and haircloth, as penitent Christians were accustomed to do. For this is the force of that word, as can be seen in Gen. 37:23, 2 Sam. 13:37, ch. 16:2, and elsewhere. κλαίειν, בכה to weep, is usually joined with fasting, as 1 Sam. 1:7, 2 Sam. 1:12, ch. 12:22, and with the verb πενθεῖν, as Nehem. 1:4, ch. 8:11.

Ὁ γέλως ὑμῶν εἰς πένθος μεταστραφήτω, καὶ ἡ χαρὰ εἰς κατήφειαν.] As much as you have previously laughed and rejoiced, when it was permitted to take vengeance on your enemies and plunder their goods, so much now take up sorrow and sadness. Κατήφεια among the poets, Plutarch, and others is that sorrow which betrays itself even in the countenance, which the Hebrews call נפלו פנים. He tacitly hints that the destruction of Jerusalem and the dispersion of the Jewish nation is imminent.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Ταλαπωρήσατε, καὶ πενθήσατε καὶ κλαύσατε.] Christianis in gravia lapsis non datur reditus ad bonam frugem,nisi per pœ- nitentiam luctuosam : cujus vim ut exprimeret Jacobus, hæc verba posuit. Ταλαπωρήσατε שׁדד affligere, nempe vos- metipsos jejuniis & aliis corporis σκληραγωγίαις. Πενθήσατε אבל lugubrem habitum induite, saccum & cilicia, ut pœ- nitentes Christiani solebant. Hæc enim vis est istius vocis, ut videre est Gen. 37, 23. 2. Sam. 13, 37. c. 16, 2. & alibi κλαίειν בכה flere, solet plerumque jungi cum jejunio, ut 1. Sam. I, 7. 2. Sam. I, 12. c. XII, 22. & cum verbo πενθεῖν, ut Nehem. I, 4. c. IIX, 11.

Ὁ γέλως ὑμῶν εἰς πένθος μεταστραφήτω, καὶ ἡ χαρὰ εἰς κα- τήφειαν.] Quantum antea risistis & gavisi estis,ubi ultionem vobis de inimicis sumere, & res eorum rapere licuit, tantum nunc suscipite dolorem ac mœstitiam. Κατήφεια apud Poëtas, Plutarchum & alios est is mœror, qui ipso etiam vultu se pro- dit,quod Ebræi dicunt נפלו פנים. Tacite innuit,imminere excidium Hierosolymorum & disjectionem Judaicæ gentis.

## 4:10
Verse 10. Ταπεινώθητε ἐνώπιον τοῦ Κυρίου ] With humble prayers, ענו Lev. 16:29 and elsewhere. Before the Lord, that is, Christ.

Καὶ ὑψώσει ὑμᾶς.] ירוממכם he will lift you up, or will make you exalted with his gifts, concerning which see above 1:17.

A priori, repentance is described both through the internal affliction of the heart and through external mourning and weeping: whence even outward laughter is to be converted into mourning, just as inward joy is to be converted into sadness; then through humiliation in the sight of the Lord, not only that which is in external signs, but that which is viewed in the innermost recesses of the heart, which God, the καρδιογνώστης (knower of hearts), searches. Examples may be seen in David in the penitential Psalms, Mary in Luke 7:38, the prodigal son in Luke 15:18, the publican in ch. 18:13, etc. The word ταλαιπωρήσατε is from ταλαίπωρος, Rom. 7:24, which descends ἀπὸ τοῦ τλῆναι τὸν πῶρον, it is to sustain misery and brings about anxiety of heart, Rom. 3:15. Πένθος and κλαυθμὸς are joined also elsewhere, Mark 16:10, Luke 6:25, Rev. 15:9, ch. 18:11. Regarding the observation of order, κατήφεια and κατηφὴς is derived from καταβάλλων τὰ φάη, casting down the eyes, as if one has relaxed the forehead and eyebrows out of sorrow. The joy which sinners receive from pleasures must be converted into sorrow, if repentance is to be truly performed, Ps. 6:7, Joel 2:16, Matt. 5:4. We ought to be humbled before the Lord, so that, having acknowledged our unworthiness, we do not exalt ourselves, but prostrate ourselves before the divine majesty, and, struck by the fear of deserved wrath, we, submissive and humble, may supplicate the divine mercy, Lam. 3:19, 41, 42, Dan. 9:28. He who weeps does not act proudly; he who mourns is humbled, says Ambrose, book 5 on Luke. James adds the fruit of the humiliation of penitents, and the Lord will exalt you, from the epiphonema of Christ concerning the repentance of the humble publican, Luke 18:14, 'He who humbles himself shall be exalted.' Cf. Prov. 29:23, Job 22:29, 1 Pet. 5:6. Grotius rashly says that anything is hinted here about the Jerusalemite destruction and the dispersion of the Jewish nation: because there is no trace of it in the text.

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ταπεινώθητε ἐνώπιον τοῦ Κυρίου ] Demissis pre- cibus ענו Levit. XVI, 29. & alibi. Coram Domino, id est, Christo.

Καὶ ὑψώσει ὑμᾶς.] ירוממכם attollet vos,sive sublimes faciet donis suis, de quibus supra I, 17.

A priori pœnitentia describitur tum per internam afflictionem cordis, tum per externum luctum & plo- ratum: Unde risus etiam exterior in luctum con- vertendus,uti gaudium interius in mœrorem; tum per humiliationem in conspectu Domini, non tan- tum quæ sit signis exterioribus, sed quæ in intimis cordis recessibus spectetur, quos Deus καρδιογνώ- στης scrutatur. Exempla videantur Davidis in Psal- mis pœnitentialibus,Mariæ Luc.VII,38. filii prodi- gi Luc. XV, 18. publicani, cap. XIIX, 13. & c. Verbum ταλαιπωρήσατε à ταλαίπωρος est, Rom. VII, 24. quod descendit ἀπὸ τοῦ τλῆναι τὸν πῶρον,est sustine- re miseriam & cordis anxietatem infert, Rom. III, 15. Πένθος & κλαυθμὸς conjunguntur etiam alias, Marc.XVI,10. Luc.VI, 25. Apoc.XV, 9. cap.XIIX, 11. circa observationem ordinis,κατήφεια & κατηφὴς à καταβάλλων τὰ φάη deducitur, dimittens lumi- na,quasi frontem &supercilia remisit præ mœrore. Gaudium, quod è voluptatibus accipiunt pecca- tores, in mœrorem convertendum, si vere agenda pœnitentia, Ps. VI, 7. Joël. II, 16. Matth.V, 4. Hu- miliari coram Domino debemus, ita ut agnita indi- gnitate nostra non efferamus, sed prosternamus nos coram divina majestate,& iræ promeritæ metu perculsi submissi atque humiles divinæ misericor- diæ supplicemus, Thren.III, 19. 41. 42. Dan. IX, 28. Qui flet, non superbit, qui luget, humiliatur, ait Am- brosius libr.V. in Luc. Addit Jacobus humiliatio- nis pœnitentium fructum, & exaltabit vos Domi- nus, ex Epiphonemate Christi circa pœnitentiam humilis publicani, Luc. XIIX, 14. Qui se humilia- verit, exaltabitur. Conf. Prov. XXIX, 23. Job. XXII, 29. 1. Petr. V, 6. De excidio Hierosolymitano, & disje- ctione Judaicæ gentis hic quicquam innui temere di- cit Grotius: quia nullum de eo in textu vestigium.

## 4:11
Verse 11. Μὴ καταλαλεῖτε ἀλλήλων ἀδελφοὶ.] He returns to that which he had touched upon above, 3:9, 10. We also say καταλαλεῖν κατά τινὸς, Num. 21:7, Ps. 50:19, and more briefly καταλαλεῖν τινός, Ps. 77:19, Job 19:3. Thus also 1 Pet. 2:12, ch. 3:16. In the glossary, καταλαλῶ means I speak against. Hence the noun καταλαλος, Rom. 1:30, where see the remarks made.

Ὁ καταλαλῶν ἀδελφοῦ, καὶ κρίνων τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἀυτοῦ.] Namely, concerning those things which Christ does not condemn in the Gospel, such as the observation of days, foods, and the like. The sense is the same as Rom. 14:3, 4. In the Manuscript, ἢ κρίνων is used disjunctively.

He speaks against the law and judges the law.] Such a man scorns and condemns the Evangelical doctrine (which he also calls by the name of law several times above, as Paul also does in Gal. VI, 2) as imperfect. For Christ does not condemn such people, as stated in the Roman passage.

But if you judge the law.] If you condemn the Evangelical doctrine as imperfect.

You are not a doer of the law, but a judge.] You who ought to have obeyed the law, take upon yourself judgment over the law. Those who do the things which the law commands are also called doers of the law in Rom. II, 13, by metonymy, οἱ ποιῦντες τὰ τοῦ νόμου, as Paul says in the same place. In Hebrew עשים כל־המצות Deut. VI, 25. The same elsewhere is τηρεῖν νόμον &c. φυλάσσειν.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Μὴ καταλαλεῖτε ἀλλήλων ἀδελφοὶ.] Redit ad id, quod supra attigerat III, 9. 10. Dicimus & καταλαλεῖν κατά τινὸς Num. 21, 7. Psal. 50, 19. & brevius καταλαλεῖν τινός. Ps. 77, 19. Job. 19, 3. Sic & 1. Petr. 2, 12. c. 3, 16. In glossario κα- ταλαλῶ obloquor. Hinc nomen καταλαλος Rom. I, 30. ubi dicta vide.

Ὁ καταλαλῶν ἀδελφοῦ, καὶ κρίνων τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἀυτοῦ.] Nempe ob eas res, quas Christus in Evangelio non damnat, qualia sunt observationes dierum, ciborum, & similia. Idem sensus, qui Rom. XIV, 3. 4. In Manuscripto ἢ κρίνων disjunctive.

Καταλαλεῖ νόμου καὶ κρίνει νόμον.] Doctrinam Evangelicam (quam & supra aliquoties legis nomine appellavit, ut & Pau- lus Gal. VI, 2.) homo talis spernit & damnat ut imperfectam. Christus enim tales non damnat Rom. dicto loco.

Εἰ δὲ νόμον κρίνεις.] Si Evangelicam doctrinam damnas ut imperfectam.

Οὐκ εἶ ποιητὴς νόμου, ἀλλὰ κριτής.] Qui obsequi legi de- bueras, judicium tibi in legem sumis. Ποιηταὶ νόμου dicuntur & Rom. II, 13. per μετωνυμίαν ii, qui faciunt ea, quæ lex præ- cipit, οἱ ποιῦντες τὰ τοῦ νόμου, ut eodem loco dicit Paulus. E- braice עשים כל־המצות Deut. VI, 25. Idem alibi τη- ρεῖν νόμον &c. φυλάσσειν.

## 4:12
There is one lawgiver.] For us, not Moses, but Christ, Heb. VIII, 6. A manuscript here adds καὶ κριτής, and the Latin, Syriac, and Arabic versions read it thus.

He who is able to save and to destroy.] That word δυνάμενος here signifies right and power, as in Acts IV, 20; 2 Cor. XIII, 9. Christ, the Judge of all given by God, has the right and power both to save us and to destroy us. Therefore, the judgment concerning doubtful matters must be left entirely to Him.

But who are you, who judge another.] Who do you make yourself out to be? Are you not a man? Neither the Author of the law, nor a Judge of souls appointed by God? For τὸν ἕτερον the manuscript has τὸν πλησίον with the same meaning, and the Syriac and Latin versions read it so.

That nothing is more opposed to humility than the zeal for contending and detracting: for the humble man esteems himself inferior to all, whence he disparages no one: Thus the Apostle returns here again to exclude it. For this vice is common, so that it easily mixes itself with all, even the pious: Concerning which Jerome says in his epistle to Celantia: So great a lust for this evil has invaded the minds of men, that even those who have retreated far from other vices fall into this one, as if into the final snare of the devil. For there is no true repentance where a neighbor is detracted: by which he teaches that not only the brother is judged, but the law itself is judged, and the office of the divine Judge is prejudiced. Which things, therefore, are wrongly explained by Grotius as concerning not judging a brother on account of the distinction of foods and other indifferent matters, since they are general, and not to be restricted to those times. Nor is it a matter here of Evangelical doctrine, but of the law, which James says the detractor speaks against, who furthermore introduces God as the lawgiver, who alone can save and destroy, so that it cannot be doubted that the discourse is not about the Gospel, but about the law. For the Gospel is a proclamation of grace in Christ, who came not to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him, John III, 17. Καταλαλεῖν is to speak against someone, Num. XX, 44; Ps. VII, 13; 1 Pet. II, 12; ch. III, 16. We speak against or detract from a brother by: 1. Imputing a false crime to him. 2. By exaggerating a vice too much, 3. by revealing a secret, 4. by interpreting a good deed badly, or by extending it, or by praising it coldly, or by concealing virtues and praises when we ought to spread and recount them. This is a grave vice, because it harms not only charity, but also justice, which requires that we give to each his own, that we harm no one; furthermore, because as no one is without sin, so he who censures the sin of another condemns his own by this very act, which he ought to have amended first, Luke VI, 42. Therefore Jerome, epistle to Ruffinus: Detract from no one, nor think yourself holy in this, if you lacerate others. We often accuse what we do, and eloquent against ourselves, we inveigh against our own vices, etc. But that vice is truly much more serious, and deservedly so, which James refutes here: namely, that by it we speak against the law itself, not in word, but in deed, not by a formal and explicit judgment, but by a virtual and tacit one: as Cornelius à Lapide, from Dionysius, Catharinus a brother and disparages him not only transgresses the law, Lev. XIX, 16, but is also considered to speak against the law, as if it were rashly enacted regarding not disparaging. Therefore, by judging his brother, he judges the law that forbids this judgment of the brother, and he tacitly argues against and condemns it, as if it had wrongly forbidden this, which is done most of all by those who disparage others for works of virtue, as when they call a patient man weak, or one who gives his own to the poor a spendthrift, etc. For thus they condemn what the law commands. In this way, Oecumenius, Lyranus, Hugo, and Gagneius explain it. But he who speaks against the law is not a ποιητὴς νόμου ἀλλὰ κριτὴς, not an observer of the law, but a judge: nay, he flies into the judicial office of God, since this belongs to God alone, as the sole legislator, just as it is to destroy, so also to judge and to condemn, who alone has both in his power, both to save and to destroy, and to absolve and to condemn, Prov. XXXII, 39, Isa. XXXIII, 22. Now, while God is called the one legislator, it is implied that He is the supreme legislator, who has supreme power, not only of saving and destroying the body, but also the soul, Matt. X, 25. By which very fact it is plain that the νομοθετικὴν power and the right of the political magistrate, or even the power of the keys of the Ecclesiastical ministry, are not taken away, Matt. XIII, 1, seqq., John XX, 22, 23, Matt. XVIII, 12, 2 Chron. XIX, 6, 1 Cor. IV, 1. Those who judge by an office committed to them by God do not judge another's servant: but those who take upon themselves judgment against a brother, judge another as one not committed to them. Cf. Rom. XIV, 4. Let us not judge anyone, warns Ephrem, Paraen. IV, because we do not know his repentance; gold is sometimes hidden in earthen vessels.

PART II. Admonition to avoid presumption.

Latin:

Εἷς ἐστιν ὁ νομοθέτης.] Nobis non Moses, sed Christus, Ebr. VIII, 6. Manuscriptus hic adjicit καὶ κριτής, & sic legere Latinus, Syrus, Arabs.

Ὁ δυνάμενος σῶσαι καὶ ἀπολέσαι.] Illud δυνάμενος hic jus potestatemque significat, ut Act. IV, 20. 2. Cor. XIII, 9. Chri- stus Judex omnium à Deo datus jus potestatemque habet & servandi nos & perdendi. Illi igitur integrum relinquendum est judicium de rebus dubiis.

Σὺ δὲ τίς εἶ, ὃς κρίνεις τὸν ἕτερον.] Quem te facis? Nonne homo es? Neque legis Autor, neque Judex animorum à Deo constitutus? Pro τὸν ἕτερον Manuscriptus habet τὸν πλησίον sensu eodem, & ita legerunt Syrus & Latinus.

Ut nihil magis humilitati adversatur, quam con- tendendi & obtrectandi studium: Humilis enim se omnibus inferiorem æstimat, unde nulli detrahit: Ita ad eam excludendam hic iterum redit Aposto- lus. Nam hoc vitium commune est, ut omnibus, et- iam piis se facile immisceat: Quo de Hieronymus in epist. ad Celantiam: Tanta hujus mali libido mentes hominum invasit, ut etiam, qui procul ab aliis vitiis re- cesserunt, in istud tamen, quasi in extremum diaboli laqueum incidant. Neque enim vera est pœnitentia, ubi obtrectatur proximus: quo non fratrem tan- tum, sed & legem ipsam judicari, Deique Judicis officio præjudicari docet. Quæ proinde de fratre non judicando ob ciborum discrimen & alia ἀδιάφορα à Grotio perperam explicantur, quum generalia sint, nec ad tempora ista restringenda. Neq; de Ev- angelica doctrina hic agitur, sed de lege, cui obloqui obtrectatorem ait Jacobus, qui præterea & νομοθέτην introducit Deum, qui solus potest servare & per- dere, ut dubium esse nequeat, non de Evangelio, sed de lege sermonem esse. Evangelium enim con- cio gratiæ est in Christo, qui venit, non ut judicaret mundum, sed ut servaretur mundus per ipsum, Joh. III, 17. Καταλαλεῖν est obloqui alicui Num. XX, 44. Of. VII, 13. 1. Petr. II, 12. c. III, 16. Obloquimur autem vel detrahimus fratri 1. Falsum crimen eidem impin- gendo. 2. Vitium nimis exaggerando, 3. occultum pro- dendo, 4. benefactum male interpretando, vel exten- dendo, vel frigide laudando, seu reticendo virtutes & laudes, cum eas debeamus pandere ac recitare, Grave hoc vitium, quia lædit non tantum charita- tem, sed & justitiam, quæ requirit, ut unicui- que suum tribuamus, neminem lædamus, deinde quia ut nemo sine peccato est, ita qui alterius pecca- tum censet, hoc ipso suum condemnat, quod prius emendare debebat, Luc. VI, 42. Ideo Hieron. epist. ad Ruffin. Nulli detrahas, nec in eo te sanctum putes, si cæteros laceres. Accusamus sæpe, quod facimus, & contra nos ipsos diserti in nostra vitia invehimur &c. Sed multo profecto adhuc gravius vitium illud, & merito, redarguit hic Jacobus : quod nempe per id ipsi legi obloquamur, non verbo, sed facto, non judi- cio formali & explicito, sed virtuali & tacito: ut Cornelius à Lapide, è Dionysio, Catharino, Cajetano, Salmerone. Qui enim fratri obloquitur, eumque obtrectat, non modo legem transgreditur, Levit. XIX, 16. sed etiam legem obtrectare censetur, quasi temere latam de non obtrectando. Judicando ergo fratrem judicat legem hoc fratris judicium vetan- tem, illamque tacite arguit & condemnat, quasi ipsa perperam hoc vetarit, quod maxime illi faci- unt, qui aliis ob opera virtutum detrahunt, ut dum patientem vocant vecordem, sua pauperibus dan- tem prodigum &c. Ita enim, quæ lex præcipit, con- demnat. Quo pacto explicant Oecumenius, Ly- ranus, Hugo, Gagneius. Qui autem legem obtrectat, non ποιητὴς νόμου ἀλλὰ κριτὴς, non observator legis, sed judex est : imo involat in judiciarium Dei offi- cium, quum hoc solius Dei sit, ceu unici legislato- ris, ut perdere, ita & judicare & damnare, qui solus utrumque in potestate sua habet & servare & per- dere, & absolvere, & damnare, Prov. XXXII, 39. Esa. XXXIII, 22. Dum autem unus legislator Deus dicitur, supremum ipsum esse legislatorem, qui su- premam potestatem habet, non tantum servandi & perdendi corpus, sed etiam animam innuitur, Matth. X, 25. Quo ipso planum est, non tolli pote- statem νομοθετικὴν, & jus magistratus politia, vel etiam potestatem clavium ministerii Ecclesiastici, Matth. XIII, 1. seqq. Joh. XX, 22. 23. Matth. XVIII, 12. 2. Chron. XIX, 6. 1. Cor. IV, 1. Qui ex officio à Deo commisso judicant, non judicant alienum : Sed qui sibi sumunt judicium adversus fratrem, alium ut- pote sibi non commissum judicant. Conf. Roman. XIV, 4. Non judicemus quemquam, monet Ephræm Paræn. IV. quia non novimus ejus pœnitentiam, in te- staceis vasis aurum quandoque reconditur.

PARS II. Commonitio ad fugiendam præsumptio- nem.

## 4:13
Vers. 13. Ἄγε νῦν οἱ λέγοντες.] That ἄγε here, and below V, 1, is worth as much as it is among the Prophets. Now I turn my speech to you, namely. Xenophon and Plutarch also use it this way. It is also accustomed to be said with more words, as in Homer. Ἀλλ᾿ ἄγε μίμνετε πάντες. Xenophon: Ἄγε δὴ ἀκούσατε.

Some give this connection: Who are you who judge your brother? You are, of course, a rash, free, inconsiderate man, who promises yourself a long life, and does not think that death is imminent, in which an account of rash judgment will have to be rendered. B. Brochm. establishes a new remedy for resisting the pleasures of the flesh, since nothing feeds carnal concupiscences more than such empty presumption. But the sentence is general, taxing the stupidity of those who, intent entirely on profits and the business of the world, arrange the future at their own discretion, as if they were free and masters of life and time, as Bede noted, cf. Luke XII, 17.

Οἱ λέγοντες σήμερον καὶ αὔριον πορευσόμεθα εἰς τὴν δὲ τὴν πόλιν.] Other codices have σήμερον ἢ αὔριον: as the Syriac and Latin read. Πορευσόμεθα and the words that follow, both here and below in 15, the Syriac, Latin, and Arabic read in the future: And thus the best Greek codices have it, not in the potential. Εἰς τὴν δὲ τὴν πόλιν, in Syriac כמדינתא אידא, that is, into this city or that, say Damascus, Alexandria, Antioch. Thus we say regarding persons πρὸς τὸν δεῖνα.

Καὶ ποιήσομεν ἐκεῖ ἐνιαυτὸν ἕνα.) We will stay there for a year. You have this way of speaking in Acts XV, 33, XVIII, 23, XX, 3, 2 Cor. XI, 25. And among the Hebrews in Ecclesiastes VII, 1.

But the Latins also say 'to do' (facere) with someone a few days, many years, as the learned have noted. Καὶ ἐμπορευσόμεθα καὶ κερδήσομεν.) Thus they arrange their plans regarding uncertain things, as if they had them in their hand.

By way of example, trade is brought forward, because of the desire for gain, so that avarice may be noted at the same time, primarily because those who are devoted to it scarcely think of the end of life, and thus seek gain and riches in such a way that they neglect the gain of the soul and heavenly treasures, Matt. XVI, 26, ch. VI, 20, cf. Wis. XV, 12. Regarding the avaricious, Ambrose, book on Naboth, ch. 12, says: You serve, O rich, and a miserable servitude indeed, you who serve error, cupidity, and avarice, which cannot be satisfied. Wealth is captive, poverty is free.

Moreover, not every solicitude regarding future things is forbidden here. For he who would say this would be opposed by Solomon, Prov. VI, 6 and XXX, 25, and refuted by the examples of Joseph, Gen. XLI, 39, seq., Christ, John XII, 6 and XIII, 29, and the Apostles, Acts XI, 29. Therefore, only that solicitude is forbidden which either hinders us from seeking the kingdom of God, Matt. VI, 33, or which arises from diffidence toward God, Matt. VI, 30, or which precedes and does not follow the solicitude for the kingdom of God, Matt. VI, 33, or finally which excludes divine providence and blessing, James IV, 13.

Latin:

Vers. 13. Ἄγε νῦν οἱ λέγοντες.] Illud ἄγε hic, & infra V, 1. tantum valet, quantum apud Prophetas. Jam ego ad vos nempe sermonem meum converto. Utuntur sic & Xeno- phon & Plutarchus. Solet etiam pluribus id dici, ut apud Homerum. Ἀλλ᾿ ἄγε μίμνετε πάντες. Xenophon: Ἄγε δὴ ἀκούσατε.

Connexionem nonnulli hanc dant: Tu quis es, qui judicas fratrem tuum ? Nimirum es homo præ- ceps, liber, inconsideratus, qui longam tibi vitam polliceris, nec cogitas, mortem imminere, in qua judicii temerarii reddenda erit ratio. B. Brochm. remedium novum ad resistendum voluptatibus carnis constituit, quum nihil magis alat concupi- scentias carnales, quam inanis præsumptio ejusmo- di. Generalis autem est sententia, eorum taxans stoliditatem, qui toti lucris, mundique negotiis in- tenti, pro arbitratu futura disponunt, quasi liberi, vitæque & temporis Domini, ut Beda notavit, conf. Luc. XII, 17.

Οἱ λέγοντες σήμερον καὶ αὔριον πορευσόμεθα εἰς τὴν δὲ τὴν πόλιν.] Alii Codices σήμερον ἢ αὔριον: Quomodo legerunt Syrus & Latinus. Πορευσόμεθα & quæ sequuntur verba tum hic tum infra 15. in futuro legerunt Syrus, Latinus, Arabs : Et sic optimi habent Græci codices, non in potentiali. Εἰς τὴν δὲ τὴν πόλιν, Syro כמדינתא אידא, id est, in urbem hanc vel illam, puta Damascum, Alexandriam, Antiochiam. Sic de personis dicimus πρὸς τὸν δεῖνα.

Καὶ ποιήσομεν ἐκεῖ ἐνιαυτὸν ἕνα.) Manebimus ibi per an- num. Habes hoc loquendi genus Act. XV, 33. XVIII, 23. XX, 3. 2. Cor. XI, 25. Et apud Ebræos Ecclesiastæ VII, 1.

Sed & Latini dicunt facere cum aliquo paucos dies, annos multos, ut notaverunt eruditi. Καὶ ἐμπορευσόμεθα καὶ κερδήσομεν.) Ita super rebus incertis consilia sua disponunt, tanquam ea haberent in manu.

Exempli loco affertur mercatura, ob lucrandi studium, ut simul notetur avaritia, imprimis ideo, quod qui illi dediti sunt, vix finem vitæ cogitent, & ita lucrum ac divitias quærunt, ut animæ lucrum, & cælestes thesauros negligant, Matth. XVI, 26. cap. VI, 20. conf. Sap. XV, 12. De avaris Ambrosius l. de Naboth, cap. 12. Servitis, inquit, divites, ac mi- seram quidem servitutem, qui servitis errori, cupidi- tati, avaritiæ, quæ expleri non potest. Captiva est opu- lentia, paupertas libera.

Cæterum non quævis hic de rebus futuris solici- tudo interdicitur. Hoc enim, qui dixerit, ei adver- sabitur Salomon Prov. VI, 6. & XXX, 25. ac confuta- bunt exempla Josephi Gen. XLI, 39. seq. Christi Job. XII, 6. & XIII, 29. Apostolorum, Actor. XI, 29. Ea ergo tantum interdicitur solicitudo, quæ aut impe- dit, quo minus regnum Dei quæramus, Matth. VI, 33. aut quæ à diffidentia adversus Deum oritur, Matth. VI, 30. aut quæ præcedit, & non sequitur so- licitudinem regni Dei, Matth. VI, 33. aut denique quæ divinam providentiam & benedictionem exclu- dit, Jac. IV, 13.

## 4:14
Ver. 14.

Οἵτινες οὐκ ἐπίστασθε τὸ τῆς αὔριον.) The manuscript has τὰ τῆς αὔριον. They do not know what is going to happen tomorrow, what the morrow is going to bring forth, as Solomon speaks in Prov. 27, v. 1. Favorinus: Being a man, never say what will happen tomorrow. No one has had the gods so favorable that he can promise himself tomorrow. Horace: God in his wisdom hides the outcome of future time in dark night. Τὰ τῆς αὔριον, that is, the things that will happen on the morrow. Seneca’s warning on the shortness of life, 3 & 4, is not foreign to this argument. Recall to your memory, when you have been certain of a plan, how many days have turned out as you had intended. And then: You will hear most people saying: At fifty I will retire to leisure, my sixtieth year will release me from my duties. And who, pray, do you accept as a surety for a longer life? Who will allow those things to go as you arrange them? Ποία γὰρ ἡ ζωὴ ὑμῶν.) How fleeting a thing is this life of ours. Life is given to be used, given to us as a loan without interest, and not to be repaid on a fixed day. Ἀτμὶς γάρ ἐστιν ἡ πρὸς ὀλίγον φαινομένη, ἔπειτα δὲ καὶ ἀφανι- ζομένη.) ἐστι is more correct than ἔσται, as it is in certain codices. And the Syriac, Latin, and Arabic read it thus. Ἀτμὶς for ὥσ- περ ἀτμὶς. A vapor or smoke is seen for a little time, then it disappears. Ἀτμὶς for smoke, Lev. 16:13, Ezek. 8:11, Sir. 20:27, ch. 24:18, ch. 37:34. Thus Aeschylus on human life: And an image of a shadow, or a shadow of smoke. Thus also the Hebrews compare human life to shadows, 1 Chron. 29:15, Job 8:9, Psalm 102:12, 144:4, and among the Greeks, Sophocles in more than one place. These things from οἵτινες to ἀφανι- ζομένη should be taken as parenthetical.

He alludes, as Cornelius notes, to that axiom and epiphonema of Eccles. 1:1, Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity; for which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, and all the others, except the LXX, as Jerome says in the same place, translate: Vapor of vapors, and all is vapor. For what is more vain than vapor, which immediately vanishes into thin air. Estius rightly notes that uncertainty is comprehended under brevity. For that also is considered brief which is exposed to accidents on all sides, so that one can promise oneself nothing regarding its duration. Since, therefore, life itself, which is the basis of human actions, is most uncertain to us, is it not a foolish presumption to extend an absolute definition regarding the actions themselves, and their success, even into a long period of time?

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Οἵτινες οὐκ ἐπίστασθε τὸ τῆς αὔριον.) Manuscriptus τὰ τῆς αὔριον. Nesciunt quid cras sit eventurum, quid pariturus sit dies crastinus, ut loquitur Salomon Prov. 27. v. 1. Favorinus: Ἄνθρωπος ὢν μηδέποτε φῇς ὅτι γίνεται αὔριον. Nemo tam divos habuit faventes Crastinum ut possit sibi polliceri. Horatius: Prudens futuri temporis exitum Caliginosa nocte premit Deus. Tὰ τῆς αὔριον, id est, τὰ συμβησόμενα τῆς αὔριον ἡμέρας. Est non aliena ab hoc argumento monitio Senecæ de brevitate vitæ 3. & 4. Repete memoria tecum, quando certus consilii fueris, quotusquisque dies, ut destinaveras, recefferit. Et deinde : Audies plerosque dicentes: A quinquagesimo in otium secedam sexagesimus annus ab officiis me dimittet. Et quem tandem longioris vitæ prædem accipis? Quis ista, sicuti disponis, ire patiatur? Ποία γὰρ ἡ ζωὴ ὑμῶν.) Quam caduca res est vita hæc nostra. Vita data est utenda, data est sine fœnore nobis Mutua, nec certa persolvenda die. Ἀτμὶς γάρ ἐστιν ἡ πρὸς ὀλίγον φαινομένη, ἔπειτα δὲ καὶ ἀφανι- ζομένη.) Rectius ἐστι, quam ut in codicibus quibusdam ἔσται. Et sic legere Syrus, Latinus, Arabs. Ἀτμὶς pro ὥσ- περ ἀτμὶς. Vapor aut fumus pauxillum ad tempus vide- tur, deinde dispares. Ἀτμὶς pro fumo Levit. XVI, 13. E- zech. 8, 11. Sir. 20, 27. c. 24, 18. c. 37, 34. Sic Æschylus de vita humana: Καὶ σκιᾶς εἴδωλον, ἢ καπνῶ σκιὰ. Sic & umbræ vitam humanam conferunt Ebræi 1. Paral. 29, 15. Job. 8, 9. Psalm. 102, 12. 144, 4. & inter Græcos Sopho- cles non uno loco. Debent autem ista ab οἵτινες ad ἀφανιζο- μένη sumi ut παρενθετικά.

Alludit, notante Cornelio, ad illud axioma & epi- phonema Ecclef. I, 1. Vanitas vanitatum, & omnia vanitas; pro quo Aquila, Symmachus & Theodo- tion, cæterique omnes, exceptis LXX. ut ait ibidem Hieronymus, vertunt: Vapor vaporum, & omnia vapor. Quid enim vanius vapore, qui illico tenues vanescit in auras. Recte notat Estius sub brevi- tate comprehendi incertitudinem. Nam & illud breve censetur, quod undique casibus expositum est, ut de ejus diuturnitate nihil polliceri quis sibi possit. Cum ergo vita ipsa, quæ basis est humana- rum actionum, sit nobis incertissima, annon stulta præsumptio est, de ipsis actionibus, earumque succes- su definitionem absolutam in longum etiam tempus extendere.

## 4:15
Vers. 15. Instead of your saying, if the Lord wills and we live, and we do this or that] The Latin and the Syriac read more correctly, we shall do, without the preceding and: although that little word is often accustomed among the Hebrews writing in Greek to be redundant or taken for then. The sense is: If God grants that we live, we shall do this and that. For and is often explanatory. Of what is prescribed here, we have examples in Acts 18:21, God willing, 1 Cor. 4:19, if the Lord (that is, Christ) wills. Moreover, there is an old saying of the Hebrews in Ben Sira: לעולם אל יאמר אדם שום דבר אלה בגמר השם Let a man never say he will do anything, unless he first says: If God wills. Nor was this unknown to Plato, in whose work, when Alcibiades says: But how must one speak, Socrates replies: That if God wills. Proclus, regarding that passage in the Timaeus: I shall certainly not fail in anything according to my power, says: He has sufficiently represented what is secure in promises, and what is moderate in words about oneself.

However, this admonition of the Apostle is not to be taken in such a way that we always say such things with our tongue: But primarily that we always carry in our mind the knowledge of divine providence and of our own mortality: sometimes also that we express such a condition with our voice. Those who determine their future actions without God act just as if someone, after receiving a sentence of death, wished to arrange certain matters of impostors without the will of the Judge. Cf. Jer. 10:23.

Latin:

Vers. 15. ἀντὶ τοῦ λέγειν ὑμᾶς, ἐὰν ὁ κύριος θελήσῃ καὶ ζήσω- μεν, καὶ ποιήσωμεν τοῦτο ἢ ἐκεῖνο] Rectius Latin. & Syrus legere, ποιήσομεν, absque καὶ præcedente: quanquam solet sæpe ea vo- cula apud Ebræos Græce scribentes πλεονάζειν aut sumi pro tunc. Sensus est: SiDeus dederit ut vivamus, faciemus hoc & hoc. Nam καὶ sæpe est ἐξηγητικόν. Quod hic præscribi- tur, ejus exempla habemus Actorum 18, 21. τοῦ Θεοῦ θέλον- τος, 1. Cor. 4, 19. ἐὰν ὁ κύριος (id est Christus) θέλῃ. Est autem vetus sententia Ebræorum apud Bensiram: לעולם אל יאמר אדם שום דבר אלה בגמר השם Nunquam dicat homo facturum se quicquam, nisi prius di- cat: Si Deus voluerit. Neque ignoratum id Platoni, apud quem dicenti Alcibiadi? Ἀλλὰ πῶς χρὴ λέγειν, respondet So- crates: ὅτι ἐὰν Θεὸς ἐθέλῃ. Proclus ad illud in Timæo: Κατὰ δύναμιν γοῦν οὐδὲν ἐλλείψομαι, ait: Τὸ ἀσφαλὲς ἐν ταῖς ὑποσχέσεσι, καὶ τὸ μέτριον ἐν τοῖς περὶ αὑτοῦ λόγοις ἱκανῶς παρέστησεν.

Non autem ita accipiendum est hoc Apostoli monitum, ut semper lingua talia dicamus: Sed im- primis ut divina providentia, nostræque mortalita- tis cognitionem semper animo geramus: interdum etiam voce conditionem ejusmodi exprimamus. Qui de suis actionibus in futurum sine Deo sta- tuunt, perinde faciunt, atque si quis post acce- ptam mortis sententiam vellet absque voluntate Judicis de quibusdam adhuc impostorum agendis disponere. Conf. Jer. X. 23.

## 4:16
Vers. 16. But now you boast in your arrogances] You please yourselves in those boastings about the future. In the Glossary, arrogancy is boasting.

Therefore, the Apostle means this, as interpreted by our blessed Brochmand: you speak with such audacity and confidence about success in your business without any mention of divine providence, as if you were certain both of God's will and of the duration of your life. Plutarch notes in book II of his Paedia that those are called arrogant who pretend to be richer and more energetic than they are, and promise things they cannot perform. Thus, therefore, they are truly arrogant who initiate long-term hope and proudly promise themselves success in lucrative business, without even a mention of divine providence. Cf. Prov. 16:33, Ps. 127:1.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Νῦν δὲ καυχᾶσθε ἐν ταῖς ἀλαζονείαις ὑμῶν] Pla- cetis vobis in istis jactantiis de futuro. In Glossario ἀλα- ζονεία jactantia.

Id ergo vult Apostolus, interprete B. Brochman- do nostro, tanta audacia & confidentia loquimini de successu in negotiis vestris sine ulla divina provi- dentiæ mentione, ac si & de Dei voluntate, & de vita vestra duratione certi essetis. Notat Plu- tarchus lib. II. Pædiæ, ἀλάζονας vocatos, qui se ditiores & magis strenuos simulant esse, quam sint, & ea pollicentur, quæ præstare non possunt. Ita ergo vere ἀλάζονες sunt, qui spem longam in- choant, & successum in negotiis lucrofsis sibi super- be promittunt, ne facta quidem providentiæ divi- næ mentione. Conf. Prov. XVI. v. 33. Ps. 127. v. 1.

## 4:17
Vers. 17.

to him therefore who knows to do good, and does not do it, to him it is sin] Compare the saying, as in John 9:41. The sense is the same in Luke 12:47. See what we have said in both places, and those things are opposed to those who think that a man always and necessarily wills according to the measure of what is in the intellect: which I think is sufficiently refuted by everyone's own experience within themselves. The Syriac reads: to him therefore who knows the good, without to do: not badly. Thus the Lacedaemonians about the Athenians: That they knew what was right, but did not want to do it. This is what James means: You have been warned by me: You cannot plead ignorance, if you say anything of the sort hereafter, the guilt will be heavier. He who sins after being warned, his sin is rebellion, Num. 15:30, pride.

This is either referred to the nearest admonition, so that it is an addition: We know that we can do nothing without the nod and will of God, the response: It is not enough to know this, unless you also perform it in deed, but you, having dismissed those arrogances and rash presumptions, commit yourselves solely to divine providence: Or it is a conclusion of the admonitions of this and the preceding chapter, as if he were saying: I have now warned you enough about all these things, and you will not be able to pretend ignorance hereafter. Therefore, if you do not obey, you will sin. For to him who knows, and does not do it, it is sin. Which is to be preferred; but the sin is to be understood as more serious, John 15:22. Cf. Luke 12:47. Therefore, he does not mean that he is not held by sin who does not do what he does not know must be done: but he teaches that he is made guilty of a much heavier sin who, knowing what must be done, nevertheless does not do it. For ignorance lightens the guilt of the former, while knowledge weighs down that of the latter. Moreover, Ephrem rightly gathers from this in his sermon on repentance: If it is sin to him who knows the good and does not do it, it will be sin to him who knows the evil and does it, much more so.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

εἰδότι οὖν καλὸν ποι εῖν, καὶ μὴ ποιοῦντι, ἁμαρτία αὐτῷ ἐστι] Comparate dictum, ut Joh. IX. 41. Sensus idem Luc. XII. 47. Vide quæ utroque loco à nobis dicta, & ea op- pene iis, qui putant hominem semper ac necessario velle pro modo ejus, quod est in intellectu: quod ego satis puto cujusque intra se experientia refelli. Syrus legit: εἰδότι οὖν τὸ καλὸν sine ποιεῖν: non male. Sic Lacones de Athe- nienfibus: Scire eos, quid rectum esset, sed facere nolle. Hoc vult Jacobus: Moniti estis à me: Ignorantiam non potestis obtendere, si quid posthac tale dixeritis, gravior erit cul- pa. Qui monitus peccat, ejus peccatum est רמה, Num. XV. 30. ὑπερηφανία.

Id vel refertur ad proximum monitu, ut sit ad πρόσληψιν, Scimus nos sine Dei nutu ac voluntate nihil posse, responsio: Non sufficit hoc scire, nisi & facto præstetis, at vos unice divinæ providentiæ missis illis ἀλαζονείαις & temerariis præsumptio- nibus, committatis: Vel conclusio est monitorum hujus & præcedentis capitis, quasi dicat: Jam de his omnibus satis vos monui, nec deinceps poteritis ignorantiam prætexere. Proinde, si non pareatis, peccabitis. Nam scienti, & non facienti pecca- tum est. Quod præferendum; peccatum autem intelligendum gravius, Johan. 15, 22. Conf. Luc. 12, 47. Non ergo id vult, eum non teneri pecca- to, qui non facit, quod faciendum nescit: sed eum multo gravioris reum fieri peccati docet, qui sciens, quid faciendum sit, non tamen facit. Nam illius culpam ignorantia elevat, hujus scien- tia gravat. Recte autem Ephrem. serm. de pœ- nit. hinc colligit: Si scienti bonum & non facienti peccatum est, illi multo magis malum scienti & illud facienti peccatum erit.

## 5:1 Argument
SECTION II. Presenting special exhortations. CHAPTER V. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

He denounces punishments to the greedy and unjust rich who withhold the wages of laborers, who feed themselves on pleasures, and who oppress the just. He stirs up the oppressed, however, to patience, by the comfort of the approaching Lord, by patience similar to the farmer's, by the example of the Prophets and of Job, and by divine mercy: He dissuades from oaths, and teaches the faithful how they ought to conduct themselves in adversity and prosperity: finally, he instructs on the power of intercessions and prayers, and on the calling back of brothers into the way. There are three parts: I. Comminatory regarding the greedy and unjust rich, up to verse 16. II. Consolatory regarding the oppressed and afflicted, up to verse 11. III. Informative regarding oaths, prayers, and the restoring of brothers, up to the final verse 20.

PART I. THREATENING, Regarding covetous and unjust rich men.

Vers. 1. Ἄγε νῦν] See above c. 4. 13. οἱ πλoύσιοι] He addresses the rich Jews, among whom Christians were mingled. For he will soon turn his speech properly to Christians. For he had spoken of other rich men above in c. 2, 6. But he did not address them, as not being of his flock. The Apostles and their hearers do not expel those who are rich and wish to remain such: But they show them that their state is dangerous, and that they have need of very many cautions, in order to be saved. See 1 Tim. 6, 17. However, these things could be useful even to good Christians, for converting to the Gospel the Jews, to whom Judaism had profited so little.

That this epistle was directed to Jews not converted to the faith of Christ is not at all likely. For even if James afterwards specifically calls the oppressed whom he consoles 'brethren,' it is not to be gathered that these rich men were still strangers to the profession of Christianity. For it is customary for the Apostle, when he begins a new exhortation, to use the name of brethren, just as from v. 10, 11, 19 and the preceding chapter v. 11, c. 3, 1, c. 2, v. 1, c. 1, v. 2, 16, 19. But when he institutes a correction, he omits the name of brethren, c. 4, 1, c. 3, 14. Nor yet are only the faithful addressed even there, but all who professed Christ, or this speech is directed to Jews not yet converted to Christ. Nor were there lacking among Christians rich men whom James might deservedly rebuke for avarice and illiberal tenacity and injustice. But concerning others still established outside the assembly of Christians, Paul says: What have I to do with those who are outside? 1 Cor. 5, 12. And the correction coheres with the preceding chapter 4, 9. Ταλαπωρήσατε, καὶ πειθήσατε, καὶ κλαύσατε. by which the Hebrews were invited to repentance, who professed the name of Christ but were given to depraved desires, whom he had reproved for relying in lucrative businesses not so much on divine providence and blessing as on their own labors. Whose insolent ἀλαζονείαν he had taxed, to them he now denounces punishment, the ταλαιπωρίας or miseries that are to come.

κλαύσατε ὀλολύζοντες] He seems to refer to the passage in Zechariah 11, 2 and Joel 1, 5, where what is in Hebrew הילילו is translated in Greek as ὀλολύξατε.

ἐπὶ ταῖς ταλαιπωρίαις ὑμῶν ταῖς ἐπερχομέναις] ἐπὶ here is 'on account of,' as in Matthew 26, 50 and often elsewhere. He pre-signifies the calamities about to happen to the Jews, concerning which we have said something above ch. 4, 9. For the time predicted by Christ was drawing near. After Jerusalem was destroyed, the dispersed nation, the Jews, began to be treated very badly also in other places, among whom Christians were then hiding under that name.
