See book VII of Josephus on the Jewish War. Even the didrachma, which they were accustomed to give for the uses of the temple, was spent for the uses of the Capitol. See what is said at Matt. 7, 24.

The coming calamities do not so much concern those which were impending over the Jews in the destruction of Jerusalem or the dispersion of the nation, as Oecumenius and Cornelius à Lapide have explained: because those happened without distinction to the poor and the rich, the oppressors and the oppressed, with some even who had been converted to the faith of Christ being involved in that universal cataclysm, as they concern those miseries which await those rich, greedy, unjust, and voluptuous men, both in this life and in the future, unless they repent. The word ὀλολύζειν for Homer and Demosthenes is to cry out horribly, or to vociferate with a certain wailing, by which he indicates immense grief, Jer. 4, 8. Joel 2, 10. 13. Matt. 1, 8. and a horrible wailing, such as was that of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, when they went down alive into hell, Num. 16, 31. seqq. For those miseries are truly horrible, which await such rich men not so much in this life, where they often flourish well enough, as is evident from Ps. 37. and 73, and daily experience confirms, as in the other, Luke 16, 15. not that all rich men are to be condemned, but such as are noted here, namely those who either greedily hoard riches, ver. 2, 3, 4, or spend them on luxuries, ver. 5, or abuse them to oppress others, ver. 6, of whom Christ says in Matt. 19, 24: It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God, and Luke 11, v. 34: Woe to you rich, for you have your consolation. Cf. Isa. 5, 8. Amos 6, 1. It is difficult, says Jerome in Epistle XXXIV, nay impossible, for one to enjoy both present and future goods, and to fill the belly here and the mind there, so as to pass from luxuries to luxuries.

Latin:

SECTIO II. Paræneses speciales exhibens. CAPUT V. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Pœnas denunciat divitibus avaris, & iniquis mercedem operariis detinentibus, volupta- tibus se pascentibus, justos opprimentibus. Excitat verò oppressos ad patientiam, sola- tio appropinquantis Domini, patientia si- mili agricolæ, exemplo Prophetarum, & Iobi, ac divina misericordia: Dehortatur à juramentis, ac quales se in adversis, & prosperis gerere debeant fideles docet: po- stremò de intercessionum & precum vi, de- que fratrum in viam revocatione instruit. Partes sunt tres: I. Comminatoria quoad divi- tes avaros & iniquos, ad vers. 16. II. Consolatoria quoad oppressos & afflictos, ad v. 11. III. Informa- toria de juramentis, de precibus, & reducendis fra- tribus, ad v. 20. finalem.

PARS I. COMMINATORIA, Quoad divites avaros & iniquos.

Vers. 1. Ἄγε νῦν] Vide supra c. 4. 13. οἱ πλoύσιοι] Divites Judæos alloquitur, quibus Christi- ani erant permixti. Nam proprie adChristianos mox vertet sermonem. Nam de aliis divitibus loquutus erat supra c. 2, 6. At non eos alloquutus, ut non sui gregis. Apostoli & eorum auditores non expellunt eos, qui divites sunt & ta- les manere volunt: Sed ostendunt eis, periculosum esse eo- rum statum, & plurimis eos opus habere cautionibus, ut ser- ventur. Vide 1. Tim. 6, 17. Poterant autem hæc utilia esse etiam bonis Christianis, ad convertendos ad Evangelium Ju- dæos, quibus Judaismus parum adeo profuisset.

Ad Judæos non conversos ad Christi fidem hane directam fuisse epistolam, haud verisimile est. Etiamsi enim postea fratres speciatim vocet op- pressos, quos consolatur Jacobus, non tamẽ hosce divites alienos adhuc fuisse à professione Christia- nismi colligendum. Solenne enim est Apostolo, cum novam incipit parænesin, fratrum nomine uti, quemadmodum è v. 10.11.19. & cap. præceden- ti v. 11. c. 3, 1. c. 2, v. 1. c. 1, v. 2. 16. 19. Cum vero E- panorthosin instituit, fratrum nomen omittere c. 4, 1. c. 3, 14. Nec tamen vel illic soli fideles compellan- tur, sed omnes Christum professi, vel hic sermo directus est ad Judæos, ad Christum nondum con- versos. Neque deerant inter Christianos divites, quos ob avaritiam & illiberalem tenacitatem ac iniquitatem merito reprehenderet Jacobus. De aliis autem extra cœtum Christianorum adhuc constitutis Paulus: Quid ad me, qui foris sunt? 1. Cor. 5, 12. Et cohæret epanorthosis cum præce- denti cap. 4, 9. Ταλαπωρήσατε, καὶ πειθήσατε, καὶ κλαύσατε. qua ad pœnitentiã invitabantur Ebræi, nomen Christi professi, sed pravis concupiscen- tiis dediti, quos redarguerat in lucrosis negotiis, non tam divina providentia & benedictione, quam laboribus suis nitentes. Quorum insolentem ἀλα- ζονείαν taxarat, illis jam pœnam denunciat, ταλαι- πωρίας vel miserias venturas.

κλαύσατε ὀλολύζοντες] Videtur respicere locum Zachar. 11, 2. & Joel. 1, 5. ubi quod in Ebræo est הילילו in Græco vertitur ὀλολύξατε.

ἐπὶ ταῖς ταλαιπωρίαις ὑμῶν ταῖς ἐπερχομέναις] ἐπὶ hic est propter, ut Matth. 26, 50. & alibi sæpe. Præsignificat eventuras Judæis calamitates, de quibus aliquid diximus supra cap. 4, 9. Prope enim adventabat tempus à Christo prædictum. Post excisa Hierosolyma, gentem dispersam, pessime etiam aliis in locis tractari cœpere Judæi, quorum tunc sub nomine latebant & Christiani. Vide librum VII. Josephi de bello Judaico. Etiam didrachmum, quod soliti erant dare in usus templi, impensum fuit in usus Capitolii. Vi- de quæ dicta ad Matth. 7, 24.

Eventuræ calamitates non tam respiciunt eas, quæ imminebant Judæis in excidio Hierosolymitano aut gentis dispersione, ut Oecumenius exposuit & Cornelius à Lapide : quia illæ sine discrimine pauperibus & divitibus oppressoribus & oppres- sis evenere, nonnullis etiam ad Christi fidem conversis in isto universali cataclysmo iisdem in- volutis, quam miserias illas, quæ tum in hoc, tum in futuro seculo manent illos divites, avaros, iniquos, & voluptarios, nisi pœnitentiam agant. Verbum ὀλολύζειν Homero & Demostheni est hor- rendum clamare, seu cum quodam ululatu voci- ferari, quo ingentem dolorem indicat, Jerem. 4, 8. Joel. 2, 10. 13. Matth. 1, 8. & ejulatum hor- rendum, qualis erat Coræ, Dathan & Abiram, cum vivi in infernum descenderent, Num. 16, 31. seqq. Miseriæ enim illæ vere horribiles sunt, quæ non tam in hac vita divites ejusmodi manent, ubi sæpe felices satis vigent, ut è Psal. 37. & 73. & expe- rientia quotidiana constat, quam in altera, Luc. 16, 15. non quod divites omnes damnandi, sed quales hic notantur, utpote qui vel divitias ava- rè recondunt, vers. 2. 3. 4. aut delitiis insumunt, vers. 5. aut ad opprimendos alios iisdem abutun- tur, vers. 6. de qualibus Matth. 19, 24. Christus: Facilius est, camelum per foramen acus transire, quam divites in regnum Dei introire, & Luc. 11. v. 34. Væ vobis divitibus, quia habetis consolatio- nem vestram. Conf. Esa. 5, 8. Amos. 6, 1. Difficile, inquit Hieronymus Epist. XXXIV. imo impossibile est, ut præsentibus quis & futuris fruatur bonis, & hic ventrem & ibi mentem expleat, ut de delitiis transeat ad delitias.

## 5:2
Ver. 2.

ὁ πλῦτος ὑμῶν σέσηπε] This is the active for the passive, as in the Glossary σήπω I rot, I stink: for so it must be read there. Then it is a species placed for the genus. For he wishes to say that things so sought, so kept, often perish uselessly not for others, but for themselves, which is the mystical sense of that which was signified in the Manna, Exod. 16, 20, where in Hebrew it is יבאש and in Greek ἐπώζεσε.

καὶ τὰ ἱμάτια ὑμῶν σητόβρωτα γέγονε] The moth is said to eat garments, Isa. 51, 9. You have the word σητόβρωτα in Job 13, 28, where in Hebrew it is אכלו עש. A similar composition is in σκωληκόβρωτος, Acts 12, 23. The garments, with which you could have relieved the misery of the poor, often kept too long beyond human use perish for you, whether eaten by moths or otherwise. See Matt. 6, 19. 20. Luke 12, 33.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

ὁ πλῦτος ὑμῶν σέσηπε] Est hic activum pro passivo, ut in Glossario σήπω tabeo, puteo: ita enim ibi legen- dum. Deinde est species posita pro genere. Vult enim dicere res ita quæsitas, ita asservatas, sæpe non aliis, sed & ipsis inutiliter perire, qui est sensus mysticus ejus, quod in Manna significatum Exod. 16, 20. ubi in Ebræo יבאש in Græco ἐπώζεσε.

καὶ τὰ ἱμάτια ὑμῶν σητόβρωτα γέγονε] Tinea dicitur co- medere vestimenta, Esa. 51, 9. Vocem σητόβρωτα habes Job. 13, 28. ubi in Ebræo אכלו עש. Similis compositio in σκωληκόβρωτος, Actor. 12, 23. Syntheses, quibus sub- levare potuistis miseriam pauperum, sæpe nimis diu extra usum humanum asservatæ vobis pereunt, sive à tineis corrosæ, sive aliter. Vide Matth. 6, 19. 20. Luc. 12, 33.

## 5:3
Ver. 3.

ὁ χρυσὸς ὑμῶν καὶ ὁ ἄργυρος κατίωται] He persists in similar figures: For just as clothes are accustomed to be corrupted by moths, so iron by rust. Menander:

And all things that corrupt are within, As, for instance, rust for iron, if you look, And moths for the garment.

But what was proper to iron, he also transferred to gold and silver, not that this is accustomed to happen, but that the result is often the same. Cf. the passage of Job 41, 27. Ezek. 24, 11. χαλκὸς ἰῶται Sirach 12, 9. and it is said of a mirror κατίωσις.

καὶ ὁ ἰὸς αὐτῶν εἰς μαρτυρίαν ὑμῶν ἔσται] Concerning this expression see at Matt. 8, 4. ch. 10, 18. ch. 24, 14. Mark 1, 44. ch. 7, 11. ch. 12, 9. Luke 5, 14. ch. 21, 13. It is not that one should be ashamed to have detained those things so uselessly, so that they perished both for you and for others, sought moreover often through injustice and lack of mercy, as he will now say. See Matt. 6, 24 and what is said there.

and will eat your flesh, as fire you have stored up in the last days] The Arabs seem to have read ὡς πῦρ ὁ ἐθησαυρίσατε. Not badly, the manuscript repeats the word ὁ ἰὸς after σάρκας ὑμῶν. Φάγεται is good Greek. For the Greeks say φάγομαι, ἔδομαι, πίομαι & thus φάγεσαι, ἔδεσαι, πίεσαι,

& φάγεται, ἔδεται, πίεται, instead of φαγοῦμαι ἔδομαι & so on. This came into common use from the Aeolic dialect. The sense, however, is: Those goods of yours, kept in such abundance, beyond the uses of men, so that they often perish uselessly, will be the cause of most grievous punishments for you after the time of judgment, just as if you had stored up fire in your evil. Fire is said to eat flesh, Ps. 21:10, Isa. 30:27, ch. 33:11, and under the name of fire, divine wrath or its instruments is usually denoted. Take θησαυρίζειν here as in Rom. 2:5, ἐν ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις for εἰς ἐσχάτας ἡμέρας. That expression, however, when the discourse is to the Jews, is usually referred to the time of the destruction of Jerusalem, and of the temple and the republic, at which time immense thousands of Jews perished most miserably, especially by fire, which is an omen of the universal judgment.

He used putrefaction for corruption, the species for the genus: he understands riches in that part where they are subject to putrefaction, as are stored wood, and the fruits of fields and trees, as Estius says here. The word σήπειν, used of the stench exhaling from a corpse, as in Jer. 22:19, hints that riches will one day be more troublesome by their stench, Isa. 66:24. Cf. Job 20:6 seqq. The rich exalt themselves with precious garments, gold and silver; therefore he threatens that garments are to be devoured by moths, and gold and silver to be corrupted by rust, because they despise, in comparison with earthly riches, the treasure which moths cannot consume and rust cannot corrupt, Matt. 6:19, which, however, will not be able to deliver them in the day of wrath, Ezek. 7:19, Zeph. 1:18. Those things, however, still speak properly of the guilt rather than of the punishment of the avaricious; which follows thereafter. He is evidently rebuking the rich because they would rather have their riches putrefy, their garments eaten by moths, and their gold and silver corrupted, than bestow anything of them upon the poor. Moreover, the rust of gold and silver will testify against them for a twofold reason: both because they have placed their trust in a thing subject to corruption, and because they preferred that their gold and silver be destroyed by rust than be spent on the necessary uses of the poor. The rich prefer that their grain, meat, and wine putrefy than be given to the poor. A similar phrase concerning the judgment of God is found in Hos. 5:12: And I will be as a moth to Ephraim, and as rottenness to the house of Judah. Just as almsgiving makes the rich, so unmercifulness and avarice impoverish, to such an extent that the wealth of such people consumes itself like a moth, and by the sending of locusts, moths, rust, and enemies, the crops and fruits of the avaricious are destroyed, Prov. 11:26. Caesarius of Arles, homily II. Because perhaps, he says, it happens sometimes that through negligence my garments, which the poor ought to have received, were devoured by moths, I fear lest they be brought forth as a testimony against me myself on the day of judgment, according to that which the Apostle James terribly rebukes. The avaricious rich bury their heart in the earth with their gold and silver: therefore they will be turned entirely into hell, into a pool burning with fire and brimstone with idolaters, to whom they are akin, Eph. 5:5, Apoc. 21:8. Many, says Ambrose, lib. II de Jacob. et vita beata ch. 7, brood over buried gold: their gold is under the earth, and their heart is under the earth. Beware, therefore, lest you also bury your heart in the earth while you are alive.

The rust will eat your flesh like fire, which Cornelius explains thus: Because you, out of avarice, allowed rust to eat your gold: hence likewise rust will eat your flesh, not physically, but morally, because by its demerit and on account of it you will burn in the fire of Gehenna; Luke 16:24. Oecumenius interprets it thus: Your wealth, which you have stored up like fire, will eat your flesh, and in the last days, namely of the coming of the Lord, you will find your wealth like fire laid up and treasured unto your destruction. The Vulgate adds the word 'wrath,' which Beza also reads and the Syriac renders: YOU HAVE STORED UP WRATH FOR YOURSELVES IN THE LAST DAYS; as if he were saying, you wished to zealously hoard true gold, but you did not hoard gold, but a treasure of wrath, a treasure of hellfire, Rom. 2:5. Cf. Job 27:19-20. Luke 12:30. That [phrase]: And it shall eat your flesh like fire, the blessed Brochmand notes can be understood in two ways. Either because the anxious solicitude of keeping money consumes the avaricious like fire, Matt. 6: from verse 25 to the end: or because the hoarding of gold and silver without use is the material for kindling divine wrath, which like fire consumes the avaricious, Matt. 19:21. Luke 16:9. 1 Tim. 6:9. But the latter explanation is more suitable on account of the words ἐν ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις: which the punctuation of others absolutely demands, approved by Heinsius along with the Syriac, so that the sense is ἐθησαυρίζατε ὡς πῦρ, or simply πῦρ, as others read, εἰς ἐσχάτας ἡμέρας, or ἐσχάτην ἡμέραν, & Wis. 16:27, θησαυρίζῃ πῦρ. What wonder, he says, if he who is impious, and provokes divine wrath, for the last day, which is said to be the one that determines human life and actions (or the last days of life), is said to gather and store up fire for himself! Even if the Vulgate punctuation is retained, the sense remains the same, which Estius rendered thus: The speech is figurative, by which rust is fashioned as both a witness and an executioner. The sense, however, is that it will happen at some time, namely in the judgment of God, that their own conscience will bear witness against them, namely by presenting to them their gold and silver avariciously kept, and corrupted by rust, so that just as rust once ate their money: so then that same thing, haunting their memory and biting their conscience, will consume their flesh not with light torture, but like fire. For by these words is signified not so much consumption as the magnitude of the punishment, which will not only affect the souls, but will also torture the bodies, even though they are never to be consumed.

And further: You rejoice and congratulate yourselves on the treasures of money which you have avariciously stored up for many years. But by doing that you have heaped up for yourselves wrath and a curse for the last day, that is, for the day of the final judgment. Osiander paraphrases thus: Your riches are corruptible, a thing which you can also see daily: while grain is consumed and flies away, garments are corrupted by moths, money and precious furniture perish either by rust or by fire. Daily experience can teach you this: Therefore those corruptible riches will bear witness against you on the last day, because you have acted impiously and foolishly, because you have placed your hope in uncertain riches rather than in the living God. And indeed your corruptible riches, unjustly acquired, will torture you in hell: you will pay heavy penalties on that account. Your ill-gotten goods, and those which you have shamefully misused, will burn upon you in hell. Osiander, however, does not refer the final part about storing up and the last days to the treasures of wrath, but to earthly treasures in this way: In this last part of the world, when you ought to be preparing yourselves for the coming of the Savior, that being neglected, you have given yourselves entirely to accumulating riches. So also the Weimar paraphrase: But we easily agree here with Grotius, Heinsius, and others who take ἐν for εἰς, yet acquiescing to the punctuation of the Vulgate, so that the distinction is established after the word πῦρ and the particle of comparison ὡς is retained. For one should not rashly depart from the customary reading and punctuation. You have stored up, therefore, he says, for the last days,

(just as in verse 5, ἐν ἡμέρᾳ σφαγῆς for εἰς ἡμέραν σφαγῆς, which sense Grotius admits) or having admitted the very common enallage, for the last day. Who, however, have stored up for themselves is not expressed: but from the preceding words it is easily gathered, namely that which he had said, or certainly to that, ἐκβατικῶς, so that then they may eat their flesh eternally, devouring them like fire, but never consuming them, to which also that commentary of Oecumenius tends: In the last days, namely the coming of the Lord, you will find your riches, like fire, hidden and stored up for your own destruction. That this expression is said to be accustomed to be referred to the Jerusalem destruction rather than to the last day of the world is not proven, nor did that judgment of God follow because of avarice primarily, but because of the innocent blood of the righteous, and especially because of the slaughter of the Son of God himself. Nor was this present passage easily understood by ancient and recent interpreters as referring to the last days of the Jewish polity.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

ὁ χρυσὸς ὑμῶν καὶ ὁ ἄργυρος κατίωται] Perstat in figuris similibus: Nam sicut vestes per tineas corrumpi solent, ita ferrum rubigine. Menander:

Καὶ πάντα τὰ λυμαινόμεν’ ἔνεστιν ἔνδοθεν Οἷον, ὁ μὲν ἰὸς τὸν σίδηρον, ἂν σκοπῇς Τὸ δ’ ἱμάτιον οἱ σῆτες.

Quod vero proprium erat ferri, id etiam ad aurum & ar- gentum transtulit, non quod id fieri soleat, sed quod sæpe par sit eventus. Conf. locum Jobi 41, 27. Ezech. 24, 11. χαλκὸς ἰῶται Sirach. 12, 9. & de speculo dicitur κα- τίωσις.

καὶ ὁ ἰὸς αὐτῶν εἰς μαρτυρίαν ὑμῶν ἔσται] De hac loquu- tione vide ad Matth. 8, 4. cap. 10, 18. cap. 24, 14. Marc. 1, 44. cap. 7, 11. cap. 12, 9. Luc. 5, 14. cap. 21, 13. Non est quod pudeat ista ita detinuisse inutilia, ut & vobis & aliis perirent, quæsita præterea sæpe per injustitiam & im- misericordiam, ut jam dicet. Vide Matth. 6, 24. & ibi dicta.

καὶ φάγεται τὰς σάρκας ὑμῶν, ὡς πῦρ ἐθησαυρίσατε ἐν ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις] Arabs videtur legisse ὡς πῦρ ὁ ἐθησαυ- ρίσατε. Non male, manuscriptus repetit vocem ὁ ἰὸς post σάρκας ὑμῶν. Φάγεται bene Græcum. Dicunt enim Græ- ci φάγομαι, ἔδομαι, πίομαι & sic φάγεσαι, ἔδεσαι, πίεσαι,

& φάγεται, ἔδεται, πίεται, pro φαγοῦμαι ἔδομαι & sic cætera. Ex Æolica dialecto venit hoc in usum commu- nem. Sensus autem est: Bona ista vestra in tantam copi- am asservata, extra hominum usus, ut sæpe inutiliter pa- reant, causa vobis erunt gravissimarum pœnarum post tempus judicii, plane quasi ignem in vestro malo asservas- setis. Ignis dicitur carnes comedere, Psal. 21, 10. Esa. 30, 27. cap. 33, 11, Et sub ignis nomine solet notari ira divina aut ejus instrumenta. Θησαυρίζειν hic sume, ut Rom. 2, 5. ἐν ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις pro εἰς ἐσχάτας ἡμέρας. Ista au- tem loquutio, quum ad Judæos sermo est, solet referri ad tempus excidii Hierosolymorum, & templi & reipublicæ, quo tempore immensa Judæorum millia pessime peri- ere, maxime incendio, quod omen est judicii univer- salis.

Putrefactionem posuit pro corruptione, speciem pro genere: divitias intelligit ea parte, qua pu- trefactioni sunt obnoxia, ut sunt congesta ligna, & agrorum atque arborum fructus, ut hic Estius. Verbum σήπειν de fœtore è cadavere exhalante, sicut Jerem. 22, 19. adhibitum divitias fœtore suo ma- gis molestas olim futuras innuit, Esa. 66, 24. Conf. Job. 20, 6. seqq. Divites se efferunt vesti- bus pretiosis, auro & argento, vestes ergo ti- neis vorandas, aurum & argentum ærugine cor- rumpendum minatur, quia thesaurum, quem tineæ depascere, ægruo corrumpere nequeunt, præ divitiis terrenis contemnunt, Matth. 6, 19, quæ vero ipsos in die iræ liberare non poterunt, Ezech. 7, 19. Zephan. 1, 18. Loquuntur autem illa proprie adhuc de culpa potius, quam de pœ- na avarorum; quæ deinde sequitur. Nimirum arguit divites, quod divitias suas potius putre- fieri, vestes à tineis exedi, aurum & argentum corrumpi malint, quam pauperibus de iisdem quicquam largiri. Gemina autem ratione te- stabiur rubigo auri & argenti contra ipsos, tum quod fiduciam in rè corruptioni obnoxia collo- caverint, tum quod maluerint ærugine perdi aurum & argentum, quam necessariis pauperum usibus insumi. Divites malunt sua frumenta, carnes & vina putrescere, quam pauperibus da- ri. Phrasis similis de judicio Dei habetur Hos. 5, 12. Et ego quasi tinea Ephraim, & quasi putre- do ero domui Judæ. Sicut Eleemosyna facit di- vites, ita immisericordia & avaritia depauperat, adeo ut opes talium seipsas instar tineæ consu- mant, ac immissis locustis, tineis, ærugine, hostibus segetes & fruges avarorum perduntur, Prov. 11, 26. Cæsarius Arelat. homil. II. Quia for- te, inquit, aliquoties evenit, ut per negligentiam vestimenta mea, quæ debuerunt accipere paupe- res, devorarentur à tineis, timeo ne mihi ipsi pœ- ni ad testimonium proferantur in die judicii se- cundum illud, quod Jacobus Apostolus terribiliter increpat. Divites avari defodiunt cor suum in terram cum auro & argento: ideo in infernum toti convertentur, in stagnum igne & sulphu- re ardens cum idololatris, quibus gemini sunt, Ephes. 5, 5. Apoc. 21, 8. Multi, inquit Ambro- sius lib. II. de Jacob. & vita beata cap. 7. defosso au- ro incubant: aurum eorum sub terra, & cor eo- rum sub terra. Cave ergo ne & tu cor tuum terra vivus infodias.

Ærugo manducabit carnes vestras sicut ignis, quod ita exponit Cornelius: Quia vos ex avaritia permisistis æruginem manducare aurum: hinc pariter ærugo manducabit carnes vestras, non physice, sed moraliter, quia ejus demerito ac propter illam ardebitis in igne gehennæ; Luc. 16, 24. Oecumenius sic interpretatur: Opes ve- stræ, quas sicut ignem thesaurizastis, comedent car- nes vestras, & in novissimis diebus adventus scilicet Domini reperietis opes vestras sicut ignem in perni- ciem vestram reconditas & thesaurizatas. Vul- gata addita voce iræ, quam etiam Beza legit & Syrus reddidit: THESAURIZATIS VOBIS IRAM IN NOVISSIMIS DIE- BUS; quasi dicat, voluistis studiose coacerva- re aurum verum, at non coacervastis aurum, sed thesaurum iræ, thesaurum ignis inferni, Rom. 2, 5. Conf. Job. 27, 19. 20. Luc. 12, 30. Illa: Et exedit carnes vestras sicut ignis, duobus mo- dis accipi posse notat B. Brochmand. Sive quia anxia solicitudo asservandi pecuniam avaros velut ignis conficit, Matth. 6: à vers. 25. usque ad finem: sive quia auri & argenti sine usu asservatio mate- ria est inflammandæ iræ divinæ, quæ instar ignis avaros absumit, Matth. 19, 21. Luc. 16, 9. 1. Tim. 6, 9. Sed posterior explicatio ob verba ἐν ἐσχά- ταις ἡμέραις convenientior est: quam omninò postulat aliorum distinctio, Heinsio cum Syro probata, ut mens sit ἐθησαυρίζατε ὡς πῦρ, vel simpliciter πῦρ, ut alii legunt, εἰς ἐσχάτας ἡμέ- ρας, vel ἐσχάτην ἡμέραν, & Sap. 16, 27. θησαυρίζῃ πῦρ. Quid mirum, inquit, si, qui impius est, ac iram provocat divinam, in postremum diem, qui de vita actionibusque statuis humanit (vel po- stremos vitæ dies) colligere ignem sibi ac reponere dicatur! Etiamsi autem retineatur vulgata di- stinctio, sensus idem recte habet, quem sic tra- didit Estius: Figuratus est sermo, quo ærugo fin- gitur & testis & carnifex. Sensus autem est, ali- quando futurum, nempe in Dei judicio, ut testimo- nium adversus eos dicat ipsorum conscientia, vi- delicet eis repræsentans aurum suum & argentum avarè servatum, & ærugine corruptum, adeo ut quemadmodum ærugo quondam pecunias eorum ex- edit: Ita tunc eadem ipsa memoriam obsidens, & conscientiam mordens exesura sit eorum carnes non levi cruciatu, sed tanquam ignis. Nam his ver- bis non tam consumptio, quam pænæ magnitudo si- gnificatur, quæ non solum animas afficiet, sed etiam corpora cruciatura sit, etsi nunquam consumenda.

Et porro: Gaudetis & gratulamini vobis de the- sauris pecuniarum, quas avarè recondidistis in multos annos. Atqui id faciendo vobis coacerva- stis iram & maledictionem in diem novissimum, id est, in diem extremi judicii. Osiander sic παρα- φράζει: Opes vestræ sunt corruptibiles, id quod etiam quotidie videre potestis: dum frumenta con- sumuntur & avolant, vestimenta à tineis corrum- puntur, pecunia & supellex pretiosa vel ærugine vel incendio perit. Hæc vos quotidiana experien- tia docere potest: Itaque opes illæ corruptibiles te- stimonium contra vos dicent in die novissimo, quod impie & stulte egeritis, quod spem vestram potius in divitiis incertis, quam in Deum vivum collocave- ritis. Et quidem opes vestræ corruptibiles inju- ste partæ vos cruciabunt in inferno: dabitis eo nomine graves pænas. Euer übel gewonnen Gut, und dessen ihr schändlich mißbraucht, wird auf euch in der Hölle verbrennen. Ultima vero de the- saurizatione ac novissimis diebus non ad thesauros iræ refert Osiander, sed ad thesauros terrenos hoc modo: In postrema hac mundi parte, cum ad Salvato- ris adventum vos præparare debeatis, illo neglecto, divitiis cumulandis vos totos tradidistis. Sic etiam paraphrasis Vinariensis: Sed facile hic annuimus Grotio, Heinsio, aliisque ἐν pro εἰς accipientibus, acquiescentes tamen distinctioni Vulgatæ, ut ita distinctio statuatur post vocem πῦρ & particula si- militudinis ὡς retineatur. Non enim temere ab usitata lectione, ac distinctione discendendum Thesaurizastis ergo, inquit, in novissimos dies,

(quemadmodum vers. 5. ἐν ἡμέρᾳ σφαγῆς εἰς ἡμέ- ραν σφαγῆς, quem sensum admittit Grotius) vel admissa enallage usitatissima in diem novissimum. Qui autem sibi thesaurizaverint, non exprimi- tur: at è verbis præcedentibus id facile colligi- tur, nimirum id quod dixerat, vel certe ad id, ἐκ- βατικῶς, ut tum comedant in æternum carnes suas, instar ignis easdem vorantes, nunquam au- tem absumentes, quo etiam abit ille Oecumenii commentarius: In extremis diebus adventus scili- cet Domini divitias vestras, sicut ignem, in perni- ciem vestram reconditas & thesaurizatas reperie- tis. Ad Hierosolymitanum autem excidium lo- quutionem istam referri potius quam ad novissi- mum mundi diem consuevisse dicitur, non proba- tur, neque propter avaritiam præcipue!, sed pro- pter innocuum justorum sanguinem, atque impri- mis propter cædem ipsiusmet Filii Dei sequutum est illud Dei judicium. Nec facile de novissimis diebus politiæ Judaicæ ab Interpretibus priscis & recentioribus præsens locus intellectus fuit.

## 5:4
Verse 4.

Behold the wages of the laborers who have reaped your fields, which have been kept back by you, cry out]. He reproaches those rich men not only for ungenerous stinginess, but also for injustice against the precepts not only of Christ, but also of the law given through Moses, as can be seen in Lev. 19:13, Deut. 24:15. Namely, they delayed paying the wages of rustic labor, so that they might brood over the money longer, and use it for the market. Sins that so openly disturb human society are said to cry out to God, as we see in Gen. 4:10, Exod. 22:23, 27, and elsewhere. He rightly says μισθὸν ἀπεστερημένον, just as לא תעשק in Deut. 24:14 is translated as 'you shall not defraud' (ἀποστερήσεις) the wages, because he also pays less, as the jurisconsults say, who pays less in time.

And the cries of those who have reaped have entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth]. The sense is from Deut. 24:15. יהוה צבאות is frequent in the sacred scriptures, it signifies the God of the stars and of the Angels, and therefore the most powerful. The LXX are accustomed to leave the Hebrew name Sabaoth, and so Paul in Rom. 9:29. Among those names which the Gnostics used was Iao-Sabaoth, as can be seen in Irenaeus, book 1, 34, and Epiphanius on heresies 37. That, however, is יה אל צבאות.

Στερεῖν is to deprive, ἀποστερεῖν to defraud and to cheat, according to Plutarch, Demosthenes, and Aristophanes. The passage Deut. 24:14 is correctly applied.

It is therefore a grave sin to withhold wages, as it is reckoned among the other sins crying out to heaven, such as murder, Gen. 4:10, shameful lust, Gen. 18:20, and the oppression of the poor, Exod. 3:7; the unjust withholding of wages is also added, according to the common verse:

The voice of blood cries out to heaven, and that of the Sodomites, The voice of the oppressed, and the withheld wages of laborers.

Therefore, he who sheds blood and he who defrauds a hireling are called brothers, Eccl. 34:27. This cry is nothing other than the enormity and atrocity of the crime, so that it cannot be excused or hidden, which strikes the ears and eyes of God and impels Him to wrath and vengeance, and thus from Salvian, lib. 1, de gubern. Dei, p. m. 29: 'But why does He testify that the sins of men, as it were, cry out? Namely, because God says that the cries of sinners reach His ears, so that the punishment of sinners is not delayed. And truly it is a cry, and a great cry, when the piety of God is overcome by the cries of sinners, so that He is compelled to punish the sinners.' Therefore, the Lord shows how reluctantly He punishes even the gravest sinners, saying that the cry of the Sodomites has ascended to Him; that is to say, my mercy indeed persuades me to spare, but yet the cry of the sinners compels me to punish. Cf. Wis. 10:17. Prayer is said to enter into the ears of the Lord from Ps. 18:7. The entering of a prayer is its acceptance, says Augustine in Ps. 87. Conversely, the prayer of him who stops his ear to the cry of the poor is excommunicated from the church of heaven, says Hugo Cardinalis. the Lord however is called Zebaoth not only by reason of the stars and the angels, but of all creatures, because heaven and earth, and all that are in them, dispose themselves at the nod of God, and like a most orderly and most powerful army, they invade, infest, and overturn the enemies of God at the command of this supreme and most general Commander. Ps. 148, 2. seqq.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

ἰδὺ ὁ μισθὸς τῶν ἐργατῶν τῶν ἀμησάντων τὰς χώρας ὑ- μῶν ὁ ἀπεστερημένος ὑφ’ ὑμῶν κράζει]. Non tantum ilibera- lem tenacitatem divitibus illis exprobrat, sed & injustiti- am contra præcepta non Christi modo, sed & legis per Mo- sen datæ, ut videre est Levit. 19, 13. Deut. 26, 15. Nimirum differebant mercedes operis rustici solvere, quo diutius pe- cuniæ incubarent, & ea ad mercatum uterentur. Peccata tam aperte humanam societatem perturbantia dicuntur ad Deum clamare, ut videmus Gen. 4, 10. Exod. 22, 23.27. & alibi. Recte autem dicit μισθὸν ἀπεστερημένον, quomodo לא תעשק Deut. 24, 14. vertitur ἐκ ἀποστερήσεις μισθὸν quia & minus solvit, ut ajunt Jurisconsulti, qui tépore min9 solvit.

καὶ αἱ βοαὶ τῶν θερισάντων εἰς τὰ ὦτα τοῦ κυρίε Σαβα- ὼθ εἰσεληλύθασιν] Sensus ex Deut. 24, 15. יהוה צבאות frequens in sacris literis, significat Deum siderum & Ange- lorum, ac proinde potentissimum. Nomen Ebræum LXX. relinquere solent Σαβαὼθ, & sic Paulus Rom. 9, 29. In illis nominibus, quæ Gnostici usurpabant, erat ἰγαλοσαβαὼθ, ut vi- dere est apud Irenæum libr. 1. 34. & Epiphanium de hæresibus 37. Id vero est יה אל צבאות.

Στερεῖν est privare, ἀποστερεῖν fraudare & de- fraudare apud Plutarchum, Demosthenem, Ari- stophanem. Recte adhibetur locus Deut. 24, 14.

Grave itaque peccatum est, mercedem detinere, ut de peccatis ad cœlum clamantibus reliquis, ceu sunt cædes, Gen. 4, 10. pudenda libido, Gen. 18, 20. pauperum oppressio Exod. 3, 7. accensetur etiam iniqua mercedis detentio juxta tritum versicu- lum:

Clamitat in cœlum vox sanguinis, & Sodomorum, Vox oppressorum, merces detenta laborum.

Ideo fratres dicuntur, qui effundit sanguinem & qui fraudem facit mercenario, Eccl. 34, 27. Clamor hic non est aliud, quam enormitas & atrocitas sceleris, ut excusari vel occultari nequeat, quæ Dei aures & oculos verberat, eumque ad iram & vindictam impellit, adeoque de Salvian. lib. 1. de gubern. Dei p. m. 29. Quare autem peccata homi- num quasi clamare testatur? Scilicet quia cædi au- tes suas Deus dicit clamoribus peccatorum, ne diffe- ratur pœna peccantium. Et vere clamor & gran- dis clamor est, quando pietas Dei peccatorum cla- moribus vincitur, ut peccantes punire cogatur. Ostendit ergo Dominus, quam invitus puniat etiam gravissimos peccatores, dicens, quod clamor Sodo- morum ad se ascenderit, hoc est dicere, misericordia quidem mea mihi suadet, ut parcam, sed tamen pec- catorum clamor cogit, ut puniam. Conf. Sap. 10, 17. Introire in aures Domini dicitur oratio è Ps. 18, 7. Ingressio orationis acceptatio ejus est, inquit Au- gustinus in Psal. 87. Ex adverso excommunicatur ab Ecclesiæ cæli oratio ejus, qui ad pauperis clamo- rem obturat aurem, ait Hugo Cardin. Dominus autem Zebaoth Deus dicitur non tantum ratione siderum & Angelorum, sed omnium creaturarum, quod coelum & terra, & omnia, quae in, iis sunt, ad nutum Deo se componant, & instar ordinatis- simi & potentissimi exercitus hostes Dei ad Impe- toris hujus summi & generalissimi mandatum in- vadant, infestent, & evertant Psal. 148, 2. seqq.

## 5:5
Ver. 5.

ἐτρυφήσατε ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς κὺ ἐσπαταλήσατε] התענגו ותעלסו. See Isa. 57, 3. and Ezek. 16, 49. Luke 7, 25. 1 Tim. 5, 6. You have placed your joys and used them beyond measure in this earthly life.

Τρυφᾷν means to live delicately and luxuriously, 2 Pet. 2, 13. σπαταλᾶν denotes the same, 1 Tim. 5, 6. Interpreters judge that the luxury of feasts, of clothes, and of all delights, by which hearts and bodies are snatched toward lust, is designated. The Syrian translates, you have acted with mockery, by metalepsis, because gluttons are accustomed to be wanton and to break out into taunts and mockery. Some of the rich are so tenacious that they do not dare to use their amassed wealth, lest the heap of money be diminished: of whom it has already been spoken. Others squander it on luxury and feasts, so unconcerned with helping the poor that they even strive to destroy them with calumnious arts. Against these the Apostle now inveighs. Gluttons are elegant and liberal to themselves, but stingy and cruel to others, and they deny them not only alms but also the wages due for their labor, so that they may scrape together wealth with which to prepare feasts, whence James aptly places feasts after the wages denied to the laborers, as if it were the cause and the end. Therefore, feasting and unmercifulness, gluttony and cruelty are inseparable companions, as Cornelius a Lapide rightly says here. Cf. Ezek. 16, 40. Jer. 22, 13. Amos 6, 6. Concerning gluttons, Clement of Alexandria, book II, Strom. chap. 1, says thus: 'A demon presides over those who are inclined to the luxury of tables and who nourish their own diseases for themselves, a greatest beast, whom I will not fear to call the demon of the belly, and the worst and most pernicious of demons.' Cf. Phil. 3, 19. Basil the Great, homily on Paradise. The body, he says, abundantly fattened, and the soul immersed in it and made prone to sin, is a certain shortcut to wantonness and impudence, and at the same time to all things that are forbidden.

ἐθρέψατε τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν ὡς ἐν ἡμέρᾳ σφαγῆς] τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν, that is, yourselves. Thus בלבו is translated ἐν αὑτῷ Exod. 4, 14. Esther 6, 6. and בלבך ἐνσεαυτῷ, Job 10, 13. and לבבי ἐμαυτῷ Job 27, 6. For ἐν ἡμέρᾳ in the manuscript it is ἐν ἡμέραις, it is taken as כיום, which the Syrian has here, corresponding to the Hebrew ומי, as can be seen, Gen. 32, 54. Prov. 7, 14. and ch. 17, 1. Amos 5, 25. זבחים is translated σφάγια.

- A twofold exposition is found among interpreters: The former is 'as in the day of slaughter or of a victim,' so that the comparison is from sacrificial feasts, which are accustomed to be more elegant than common ones, i.e., you have thought of daily banquets, as if all days were festive for you, in which victims are accustomed to be slaughtered. This sense is also favored by Luther's marginal gloss, 'As one slaughters for a wedding or for a feast.' Luke 15, 23. 'Slaughter a fattened calf.' Matt. 22, 4. 'My oxen and fattened cattle are slaughtered.' Which the Weimar editors also embraced. Some understand the victim to be the just man killed, over whom the rich oppressors, as if having obtained their wish, rejoice and exult: who, as Cornelius observed, referring 'in the day of slaughter' to what follows, explain it concerning Christ and Christians, i.e., in the day of slaughter, that is, of the Passover, on which you are accustomed to kill the paschal lamb, you have condemned and killed the just one, namely Christ, the true lamb who takes away the sins of the world, thus Oecumenius, Bede, Hugo, Dionysius, Gagnejus,

Catharinus, Salmeron, and others. Cornelius adds: 'Again, more simply, you have killed the just one, that is, the just Christians, in a public and solemn day, which you destined for their slaughter,' says Lyranus, 'and finally you will soon kill me, James, surnamed the Just, on a similar day.' But these are forced. The other explanation is 'as for the day of slaughter,' as the Syrian rendered it, because gluttons feed and fatten themselves as if for that time in which they are to be slaughtered, just as cattle are accustomed to be fattened with diligent care for the victim, so that the day of slaughter is the day of judgment, when a feast will be prepared for the demons from the flesh of the impious, Ezek. 39, 4. Rev. 19, 21. Estius, in which manner it is said of the impious in Jer. 12, 3: 'Gather them for the victim like a flock, and sanctify them for the day of slaughter.' LXX: εἰς ἡμέραν σφαγῆς. For it is not unusual for εἰς to be put for ἐν, as from Rom. 2, 4. Jas. 5, 4. which explanation Heinsius prefers, as do Osiander and Brochmand, to which Oecumenius's interpretation also tends, although he wishes it to refer to the day of the conquest of the Jews by the Romans, when it is more correctly understood as the day of the last judgment, or of any mortal, like that glutton in Luke 16, 19, or of all at the end of the age. For who, says Heinsius, when either ἡμέρα σφαγῆς or πρόβατα σφαγῆς occurs in this sense, would call them sheep of a feast or a day of a feast? And who would dare to translate it thus in Jeremiah when he said of the impious, 'Gather them like a flock for a sacrifice, and sanctify them for the day of slaughter,' which is also used of men who are taken from the midst: who, however, have nothing to do with a feast: That saying of Job is known, 'But if their sons become many, they shall be for the slaughter.' And it is familiar, what he says: 'As cattle destined for slaughter greedily devour what is set before them, and the more greedily the more they are fattened, secure about their destruction, and about that day for which they are being fattened: so the impious fill their heart with every pleasure, nor do they think of the day that is imminent, in which they are to be slaughtered,' indeed, just as I do not even agree with those who interpret it in the Syrian as the day of a feast, not of slaughter or killing. Cf. Ps. 44, 22. Ezek. 32, 14. To which contributes that of Clement of Alexandria, book II, Paedagogus, chap. 1: 'But it is alien to reason and useless, and by no means human, to be nourished for death, fattened like cattle.' And Chrysostom, homily LIV to the people of Antioch: 'Are we to be slaughtered because we fatten ourselves?' Also Theodore the Studite, Sermon XXXVII: 'You are therefore like pigs that are fattened for slaughter.' Which sense we prefer.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ἐτρυφήσατε ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς κὺ ἐσπαταλήσατε] התענגו ותעלסו. Vide Esa. 57, 3. & Ezech. 16, 49. Luc. 7, 25. 1. Timoth. 5, 6. Gaudia vestra posuistis & supra modum usurpastiis in hac vita terrestri.

Τρυφᾷν est delicate ac luxuriose vivere, 2. Petr. 2,13. σπαταλᾶν idem notat 1. Tim. 5,6. luxum epula- rum, vestium, omniumque deliciarum, quibus rapiuntur corda & corpora ad libidinem, designa- ri censent Interpretes. Syrus vertit, sannas egistis, per Metalepsin, quia epulones solent lascivire, at- que in scommata & sannas erumpere. Divitum alii ita tenaces sunt, ut opibus congestis uti non audeant, ne pecuniarum acervus minuatur: de quibus jam dictum est: Alii eas profundunt in luxum & epulas, adeo non soliciti pauperum ju- vandorum, ut eos etiam calumniosis artibus per- dere nitantur. In hos nunc invehitur Aposto- lus. Epulones sibi lauti & liberales, aliis parci & crudeles sunt, iisque non tantum eleemosynas, sed & mercedem labori debitam negant, ut corrogent opes, quibus epulas instruant, unde apposite mercedi ope- rariis negatae Jacobus subjicit epulas, quasi causam & finem: Comites ergo individuae sunt epulatio & immisericordia, crapula & crudelitas, ut recte hic Cornelius a Lapide. Conf. Ezech. 16, 40. Jerem. 22, 13. Amos 6, 6. De epulonibus Clem. Alexan- drin. libr. II. Strom. cap. 1. ita: Illis, qui ad luxum mensarum propensi sunt, & suos sibi morbos enu- triunt praeest Daemon, belluo maximus, quem ego non verebor appellare ventris Daemonem, Daemonum autem pessimum & perniciosissimum. Conf. Phil. 3, 19. Basilius M. homil. de Parad. Corpus, inquit, abunde saginatum, & anima illi immersa & ad pec- candum proclivis facta compendium quoddam est ad lasciviam ac procacitatem, & simul omnia, quae vetita sunt.

ἐθρέψατε τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν ὡς ἐν ἡμέρᾳ σφαγῆς] τὰς καρ- δίας ὑμῶν, id est, vosmetipsos. Sic בלבו vertitur ἐν αὑτῷ Exod. 4, 14. Esther 6, 6. & בלבך ἐνσεαυτῷ, Job. 10, 13. & לבבי ἐμαυτῷ Job. 27, 6. Pro ἐν ἡμέρᾳ in Manu- scripto est ἐν ἡμέραις, sumitur כיום, quod hic habet Syrus, respondens Ebraeo ומי, ut videre est, Gen. 32, 54. Prov. 7, 14. & c. 17. 1. Amos 5, 25. זבחים vertitur σφάγια.

- Gemina reperitur apud Interpretes expositio: Prior sicut in die mactationis vel victimae, ut com- paratio sit ab epulis sacrificialibus, quae lautiores esse solent vulgaribus, q. d. quotidiana cogitastis convivia, tanquam dies omnes vobis essent festi, in quibus solent caedi victimae. Cui sensui etiam favet Glossa marginalis Lutheri, Wie man zur hochzeit oder auf ein Fest schlachtet. Luc. 15, 23. Schlachtet ein gemästet Kalb. Matth. 22, 4. Meine Ochsen und Mastvieh ist geschlachtet. Quem etiam Vinarienses amplexi sunt. Non- nulli victimam intelligunt justum occisum, super quo divites oppressores tanquam voto potiti lae- tantur & exultant: qui τὸ in die occisionis, ut ob- servavit Cornelius, referentes ad sequentia, expli- cant de Christo & Christianis, q. d. in die occisionis, id est Paschatis, quo occidere soletis agnum pascha- lem, addixistis & occidistis justum, puta Christum verum agnum, qui tollit peccata mundi, ita Occu- menius, Beda, Hugo, Dionysius, Gagnejus,

Catharinus, Salmeron & alii. Addit Cornelius: Rursum simplicius justum, id est, justos Chri- stianos occidistis in die publico & solenni, quem occasioni eorum destinastis, inquit Lyranus, ac denique me Jacobum cognomento justum simili die mox occidetis. Sed haec coacta sunt. Altera explicatio est, sicut ad diem mactationis, ut Sy- rus reddidit, quod epulones sese pascant, ac sa- ginent, tanquam in illud tempus, quo mactan- di sint, quomodo pecora diligenti cura solent saginari ad victimam, ut dies mactationis sit dies judicii, quando de carnibus impiorum pa- rabitur epulum Daemonibus, Ezech. 39, 4. Apoc. 19, 21 Estius, quo pacto Jerem. 12, 3. de impiis dici- tur: Congrega eos ad victimam quasi gregem, & sanctifica eos in diem occisionis. LXX. εις ημέραν σφαγής. Etenim pro είς poni non insolens est, ut è Rom. 2, 4. Jac. 5, 4. quam explicationem Hein- sius praefert, ut & Osiander ac Brochmand. quo abit etiam Oecumenii interpretatio, quanquam is respici velit diem expugnationis Judaeorum à Romanis, quum rectius dies judicii novissimi, sive cujusvis mortalium, ut epulonis istius Luc. 16, 19. sive omnium in fine seculi intelligatur. Quis enim, inquit Heinsius, cum vel ημέρα σφαγής vel πρόβατα σφαγής hoc sensu occurrit, oves epuli aut diem epuli dicat? Et quis ita apud Jeremiam ver- tere ausit cü de impiis dixit συνάγαγε αυτὲς ὡς ποί- μνιον εις θυσίαν, κ' ἄγνισον ἀυτὲς εἰς ἡμέραν σφα- γῆς, quod & de hominibus, qui è medio tolluntur, usurpatur: qui tamen nihil ad epulum: No- tum illud Jobi, ἐὰν δὲ πολλοὶ γένωνται οἱ ὑοὶ ἀυ- τῶν, εἰς σφαγὴν ἔσονται. Et familiare est, quod dicit: Sicut pecudes mactationi destinatae vorant cupide, quae apponuntur, eoque avidius, quo ma- gis saginantur, de exitio securi, ac de illo, in quem saginantur, die: Ita impii cor omni voluptate re- plent, nec de die cogitant, qui instat, quo ma- ctandi sunt, nimirum quemadmodum ne illis as- sentior quidem, qui in Syro diem epuli, non occi- sionis aut mactationis interpretantur. Conf. Psal. 44, 22. Ezech. 32, 14. Quo facit illud Clemen- tis Alexandr. lib. II. Paedagog. cap. 1. Est autem ratione alienum & inutile, & nequaquam huma- num, pecudum more pinguefactum morti nutriri. Et Chrysostomi homil. LIV. ad popul. Antioch. Numquid mactandi sumus quoniam nos ipsos sagi- namus? Necnon Theodori Studitae Sermon. XXXVII. Similes ergo estis porcis, qui saginan- tur ad mactationem. Quem sensum praeferi- mus.

## 5:6
Ver. 6.

κατεδικάσατε, ἐφονεύσατε τὸν δίκαιον] I agree with those who refer these words to the killing of Christ procured by the Jews. For He is also called ὁ δίκαιος by way of excellence, Acts 3:14, ch. 22:14, and ὁ ἅγιος 1 John 2:20. And the Jews are rightly said to have done that, of which they were not only the authors, but also the instigators, Acts 2:23, 37, ch. 3:15, 1 Cor. 2:8.

Oecumenius, Bede, Faber Stapulensis, Cornelius à Lapide interpret it of Christ; others of Stephen, with Lorinus; most, however, more correctly understand any righteous person whatsoever. For the subject is Jews converted to the Christian religion. Nor does Scripture impute the death of Christ to the rich, but to the Princes and Priests of the Jews. And the consolation of the oppressed subjoined, 'be patient therefore,' sufficiently teaches that Christ is not meant, but the poor, upon whom the wicked rich were inflicting violence. Estius, also Piscator, Pareus, the Dutch Interpreters, Osiander, the Weimar Paraphrasts, B. Brochmand, and others, [interpret it] of any righteous persons whatsoever. Estius observes: That the discourse is emphatic in the singular number, by which it is signified that every single righteous poor person, although he may seem solitary and deserted, and therefore exposed to the prey of the rich, yet on the other hand, as if he were alone and unique, he is singularly cared for by God. For thus also elsewhere Scripture opposes the just to the rich and powerful, as in Isa. 57: The just man has perished, and there is no one who considers in his heart. And Ps. 93: They will lie in wait for the soul of the just, and will condemn innocent blood. And elsewhere in the Psalms. Such oppressors are noted as rich, Jerem. 22, 3. who, even if not always with their hands, yet by frauds kill the just, Isa. 1, 15. just as the word κατεδικάσατε also previously, which the Vulgate explained as 'you have condemned' (some wrongly read 'you have brought'—it is understood not only of condemnation, but of accusation, you have acted as the prosecutor, which Estius prefers for the Vulgate). Since here the Apostle does not address judges, but private rich men, just as in general other vices of the rich were noted above, avarice, luxury, and the withholding of wages, so now violence and the calumnious oppression of just poor men, which even proceeds to the plotting of death.

ὀυκ ἀντιτάσσεται ὑμῖν] In the Hebrew manner, a verb for a participle. He who was not opposing you: it is a litotes. For on the contrary, he was profiting you greatly, by expelling demons, healing diseases, and correcting life both by words and example. Ἀντιτάσσεται is a passive used for a reciprocal, which happens with many verbs, especially those derived from τάσσω: Then a metonymy. For those who oppose themselves to others are accustomed to seek that, in order to harm them.

The Vulgate rendered it: And he did not resist you. But in the Greek the tense is present, and he does not resist you, which does not quite suit Christ suffering: Whence it is twisted by some thus: Christ is still silent, and does not resist you, O Jews. Therefore, the daily violences of the rich are noted, which the oppressed cannot resist. Wherefore the oppressors ought to fear the avenging hand of the Lord all the more, Ps. 9, v. 9, 13, 19.

PART II. CONSOLATORY Regarding the oppressed.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

κατεδικάσατε, ἐφονεύσατε τὸν δίκαιον] Assentior iis, qui haec referunt ad interfectionem Christi ab Judaeis procura- tam. Nam & is ὁ δίκαιος per excellentiam dicitur, Act. 3, 14. c. 22, 14. & ὁ ἅγιος 1. Joh. 2, 20. Et recte dicuntur Ju- daei id fecisse, cujus non autores tantum, sed & impulsores fu- ere, Act. 2, 23.37. c. 3, 15. 1. Cor. 2, 8.

De Christo interpretantur Oecumenius, Beda, Faber Stapulensis, Cornelius à Lapide, alii de Ste- phano cum Lorino, plerique tamen rectius ju- stum quemlibet intelligunt. Agitur enim de Ju- daeis ad Christianam religionem conversis. Neque mortem Christi divitibus imputat Scriptura, sed Principibus ac Sacerdotibus Judaeorum. Et con- solatio oppressorum subjuncta, patientes igitur estote, satis docet, non intelligi Christum, sed pau- peres, quibus vim inferebant iniqui divites. De justis quibusvis Estius, etiam Piscator, Pareus, In- terpretes Belgici, Osiander, Paraphraste Vinarien- ses, B. Brochmandus alii. Estius observat: In nu- mero singulari emphaticum esse sermonem, quo si- gnificetur, unumquemque pauperem justum, quamvis solitarius ac desertus videatur, ideoque divitum prædæ expositus, è diverso tamen, atque si solus & unicus esset, singulariter à Deo curari. Sic enim & alibi justum divitibus ac potentibus op- ponit Scriptura, ut Esa. 57. Justus periit, & non est, qui recogitet in corde suo. Et Psal. 93. captabunt in animam justi, & innocentem sanguinem conde- mnabunt. Et alibi in Psalmis. Tales oppressores divites notati, Jerem. 22, 3. qui etsi non manibus semper, fraudibus tamen justos occidunt Es. 1, 15. quemadmodum prius etiam verbum κατεδικάσα- τε, quod Vulgatus exposuit addixistis (aliqui per- peram legunt adduxistis (non de condemnatione solum, sed accusatione intelligitur, reum egistis, quod præfert Vulgatæ Estius. Siquidem hic non Judices compellet Apostolus, sed divites privatos, ut in genere alia divitum vitia in superioribus no- tata sunt, avaritia, luxus, & mercedis detentio, ita jam violentia, & calumniosa justorum pauperum oppressio, quæ etiam usque ad mortis machinatio- nem procedit.

ὀυκ ἀντιτάσσεται ὑμῖν] Ebræo more, verbum pro parti- cipio. Eum qui vobis nihil obstabat: Est λιτότης. Nam contra plurimum proderat, expellendo dæmonas, sanando morbos, corrigendo vitam & verbis & exemplo. Ἀντι- τάσσεται passivum pro reciproco, quod plurimis verbis e- venit, maxime vero iis, quæ à τάσσω derivantur: Deinde μετωνυμία. Nam qui se aliis opponunt, id quærere solent, ut eis noceant.

Vulgata reddidit: Et non restitit vobis. In Græ- co autem tempus præsens est, & non resistit vobis, quod non adeo convenit Christo patienti: Unde ita torquetur à nonnullis: Christus adhuc tacet, & non resistit vobis Judæi. Notantur ergo divitum violentiæ quotidianæ, quibus resistere non pos- sunt oppressi. Quo magis metuere manum ul- tricem Domini debent oppressores, Psal. 9, v. 9. 13. 19.

PARS II. CONSOLATORIA Quoad oppressos.

## 5:7
Vers. 7. Μακροθυμήσατε ἓν ἀδελφοὶ ἕως τῆς παρουσίας τοῦ κυρίου] The word ἀδελφοὶ notes that here the discourse is turned to those Israelites who had embraced the doctrine of Christ, and for that very reason were suffering many things from others, as has already been touched upon in II. 6, 7. He wishes these to bear these evils patiently in the hope of better things. For that is what μακροθυμεῖν means, as in Heb. 6, 5 and elsewhere. Παρουσία κυρίου seems here to signify both the judgment of Christ upon the Jewish nation, which is also signified by the word ἐπανελθεῖν, Luke 19, 15, and at the same time his judgment upon the whole human race, which the ancient Christians suspected would be joined together in close intervals of time, for the reason that they had learned nothing certain about that matter, and had always been ordered to be intent upon that last day, which was to free the good from every vexation of evils. See 2 Thess. 2, 1. Conf. Rom. 8, 23.

How weak the argument from the word ἀδελφοὶ is, we have already said. It is not likely that both the particular day of judgment upon the Jews and the universal one upon the whole human race are designated: nor is the day of destruction usually expressed by the 'coming of the Lord' in the books of the New Testament, and Grotius presumes ἅτερ γραφῆς (without Scripture) that the faithful at that time believed the same day of universal judgment was near. Certainly, from those places 2 Thess. 2, 1 and Rom. 8, 23, that cannot be gathered. Therefore Estius is more correct: Now he applies consolation to the afflicted and oppressed poor, exhorting them to bear injuries patiently until that time when they themselves shall receive the reward of their patience, and the rich shall pay the punishments worthy of their crimes. For this is the time he signifies by the coming of the Lord, namely, Christ to judgment. For although particular judgments may precede, they are meanwhile hidden from us, nor do they happen at one time, and they are not of men, but of souls only. Therefore, the universal judgment is proposed everywhere in the Scriptures, to which all should look, as that in which the whole human race is to be judged manifestly at the same time. Wherefore Oecumenius less correctly judges the coming of the Lord to be that by which Christ came to the destruction of Jerusalem through Titus and Vespasian. In Greek ἕως τῆς παρουσίας, that is, until the presence of the Lord, as if he were to say, the Lord will come, and will present himself present to you, and by his presence will plainly console you, as Cornelius does here. For although the Lord is present to us in this life, Matt. 28, 20, yet his coming is expected, by which he will present himself present to all, and will be seen by all, Matt. 25, 31, Acts 1, 11. Presence in this life does not exclude afflictions, Acts 14, 22, Rom. 8, 17. But that in the other life, with the wicked separated from the good, will admit no calamity, Matt. 13, 9, Apoc. 21, 4.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Μακροθυμήσατε ἓν ἀδελφοὶ ἕως τῆς παρουσίας τοῦ κυρίου] Verbum ἀδελφοὶ notat, hic sermonem verti ad illos Israeli- tas, qui Christi doctrinam erant amplexi, & ob id ipsum ab aliis multa patiebantur, ut jam attigit II. 6. 7. Hos vult pa- tienter hæc mala ferre in spem meliorum rerum. Id enim μακροθυμεῖν, ut Ebr. 6, 5. & alibi. Παρουσία κυρίου videtur hic significare & judicium Christi in gentem Judaicam, quod & voce ἐπανελθεῖν significatur, Luc. 19, 15. & simul judici- um ejusdem in humanum genus universum, quæ propin- quis inter se temporum spatiis fore juncta Christiani veteres suspicabantur, ideo quod nihil certi ea de re didicissent, & se- per jussi essent intenti esse in ultimum illum diem, qui bonos ab omni malorum vexatione erat liberaturus. Vide 2. Thess. 2, 1. Conf. Rom. 8, 23.

Quam infirmum sit argumentum à voce ἀδελ- φοὶ, jam diximus. Diem & judicii in Judæos par- ticularis & in totum humanum genus universalis defignari non verisimile est: neque per adventum Domini exprimi solet dies excidii in libris Novi Testamenti, & eundem vicinum diem pantocri- ticum isto tempore fideles credidisse, ἅτερ γραφῆς præsumit Grotius. E locis certe illis 2. Thess. 2, 1. Rom. 8, 23. id colligi non potest. Rectius ergo Estius: Nunc pauperibus afflictis & oppressis conso- lationem adhibet, exhortans eos, ut patienter ferant injurias usque in illud tempus, quo & ipsi suæ patien- tiæ præmium accepturi sint, & divites condignas suis sceleribus pœnas daturi. Hoc enim tempus si- gnificat per adventum Domini, videlicet Christi ad judicium. Quamvis enim judicia particularia præcedant: ea nobis interim occulta sunt, nec uno tempore fiunt, eademque non hominum sunt, sed ani- marum tantum. Idcirco passim judicium univer- sale proponitur in Scripturis, ad quod omnes spe- ctent, ut in quo manifeste simul universum homi- num genus judicandum sit. Quare minus recte Oecumenius adventum Domini dici censet, quo Christus venit ad excidium Hierosolymæ per Titum & Vespasianum. Græce ἕως τῆς παρουσίας, id est, usque ad præsentiam Domini, quasi dicat, adve- niet Dominus, seque præsentem vobis sistet, ac sua præsentia vos plane consolabitur, ut hic Cornelius. Quanquam enim Dominus præsens nobis in hac vita sit, Matth. 28, 20. Adventus tamen ejus ex- pectatur, quo omnibus se præsentem sistet, & ab omnibus videbitur, Matth. 25, 31. Actorum 1, 11. Præsentia in hac vita non excludit afflictiones, Actor. 14, 22. Rom. 8, 17. At illa in altera vita, separatis improbis à probis, nullam admittet ca- lamitatem, Matth. 13, 9. Apoc. 21, 4.

## 5:7
ἰδὲ ὁ γεωργὸς ἐκδέχεται τὸν τίμιον καρπὸν τῆς γῆς, μακροθυ- μῶν ἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ, ἕως ἂν λάβῃ ὑετὸν πρώϊμον καὶ ὄψιμον] Hope nourishes farmers. Ὁ γεωργὸς, that is, any farmer. He spoke excellently of the 'precious fruit of the earth,' the produce by which we are most nourished. For there is always great honor for that produce both among the Jews and among the Christians. Tertullian on the crown: We suffer anxiously if even something of our cup or bread is dropped onto the ground. Ὑετὸν πρώϊμον καὶ ὄψιμον, that is, the autumnal and the pre-harvest rain, of which the former is for the Hebrews יורה or מורה, but the latter מלקוש, Deut. 11, 14, Prov. 16, 16, Jerem. 5, 24, Hos. 6, 3, Joel 2, 23, Zach. 10, 1. ἕως ἂν here does not signify the end of hope, but the intervening time, in which way the Hebrew עד is also often taken. See Gen. 28, 15, and what we have said on Matt. 1, 25.

Latin:

ἰδὲ ὁ γεωργὸς ἐκδέχεται τὸν τίμιον καρπὸν τῆς γῆς, μακροθυ- μῶν ἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ, ἕως ἂν λάβῃ ὑετὸν πρώϊμον καὶ ὄψιμον] Spes alit agricolas. Ὁ γεωργὸς, id est, quivis agricola. Egregie dixit τὸν τίμιον καρπὸν ἀρέσης, frugem qua maxime alimur. Ejus enim frugis magnus semper honos & apud Judæos & apud Christianos. Tertullianus de corona: Calicis aut panis etiam nostri aliquid decuti in terram anxie patimur. Ὑετὸν πρώϊμον καὶ ὄψιμον, id est, sementalem & antemessi- vum, quorum ille Ebræis יורה vel מורה hic vero מלקוש Deut. 11, 14. Prov. 16, 16. Jerem. 5, 24. Ose. 6, 3. Joel. 2, 23. Zach. 10, 1. ἕως ἂν hic non finem spei significat, sed tempus intercedens, quomodo & Ebræum עד sæpe sumitur. Vide Gen. 28, 15. & quæ diximus ad Matth. 1, 25.

## 5:8
Vers. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

## 5:8
μακροθυμήσατε καὶ ὑμεῖς] Under the hope of much greater fruit, irrigated meanwhile by the rain of the Holy Spirit.

στηρίξατε τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν] Strengthen yourselves, חזקו ויאמץ לבבכם Ps. 32, 25. Endure, and save yourselves for favorable things.

ὅτι ἡ παρουσία τοῦ κυρίου ἤγγικε] See what we said above at v. 6, and Phil. 4, 5, Heb. 10, 25. ἤγγικε is a past tense in form, but present in sense, as in Matt. 3, 2, ch. 4, 17, ch. 26, 45, Rom. 13, 12, 1 Pet. 4, 7.

Lyra explains it concerning the early and latter fruit, which the land of promise yielded annually, which Paul of Burgos denies from the silence of Scripture, which celebrates the praises of that land. But the Greek text is clear, concerning the early and latter rain, as is also the Syriac: with which the passages of the Old Testament remarkably agree. For the Apostle consoles the delay in two ways in the protasis: first, from the fruit, which he calls τίμιον, which is rightly held in price and honor: because it is a singular gift of God, granted for the nourishing of our bodies: then from the divine blessing, from which meanwhile there is the early and latter rain, which serves the crops both for drawing them from the earth, and for maturing and completing them, to sustain the patience of the farmer, Deut. 28, 12. Just as, he says, according to Estius' interpretation, the patience of the farmer is commended, not only in that he expects the fruit, but also in that he expects the opportune rains for obtaining the fruit: So you must, amidst the afflictions of this life, with patience expect from God not only the fruit of eternal life, but also spiritual consolations for the time being, by which, as if by rains given from heaven, you may be irrigated and bear present evils more lightly, and become more fit for attaining the fruit of eternity. Which last point, however, we admit only regarding subjective fitness, such as that of the earth, not active, much less meritorious. The early rain, he says, is preventing grace, the latter rain is subsequent grace. The coming of the Lord is said to draw near, because his day gradually becomes closer, and when it has come, it will be understood how truly near it was: although the coming of the Lord can also be understood in relation to every believer, who prays daily, 'thy kingdom come.'

Latin:

μακροθυμήσατε καὶ ὑμεῖς] Sub spe frugis multo majoris, irrigati interim imbre Spiritus Sancti.

στηρίξατε τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν] Vosmetipsos obfirmate חזקו ויאמץ לבבכם Psal. 32, 25. Durate, & rebus vosmet servate secundis.

ὅτι ἡ παρουσία τοῦ κυρίου ἤγγικε] Vide quod diximus supra v. 6. & Phil. 4, 5. Ebr. 10, 25. ἤγγικε sono præteritum, sensu præsens, ut Matth. 3, 2. cap. 4, 17. cap. 26, 45. Rom. 13, 12. 1. Petr. 4, 7.

Lyra de temporaneo & serotino fructu explicat, quem terra promissionis quotannis reddiderit, quod verò negat Paul. Burgensis è silentio Scriptu- ræ, laudes terræ istius decantantis. Sed textus Græcus luculentus est, de pluvia tempestiva & se- rotina, ut & Syrus: cui loca Veteris Testamenti eximie congruunt. Solatur nempe Apostolus moram duobus modis in προτάσει, primum à fru- ctu, quem τίμιον dicit, qui in pretio & honore ju- re habeatur: quia singulare Dei donum est, alen- dis corporibus nostris concessum: tum à benedi- ctione divina, à qua interea pluvia est matutina & serotina, quæ serviat frugibus & eliciendis è ter- ra, & maturandis atque consummandis, ad susten- tandam agricolæ patientiam, Deut. 28, 12. Quem- admodum, inquit, Estio interprete, agricolæ pa- tientia commendatur, non in eo solum, quod expe- ctat fructum, verum etiam quod pluvias opportunas ad fructum consequendum: Ita vos oportet inter afflictiones hujus vitæ cum patientia à Deo exspecta- re non solum fructum vitæ æternæ, sed & spiritua- les pro tempore consolationes, quibus velut pluviis è cœlo datis irrigati & mala præsentia levius feratis, & ad fructum æternitatis assequendum fiatis aptio- res. Quod postremum tamen de aptitudine solum subjectiva, qualis terræ est, non activa nedum meritoria admittimus. Imber temporaneus, in- quit, est gratia præveniens, serotinus est gratia sub- sequens. Dicitur autem adventus Domini appro- pinquare, quia dies ejus paulatim fit propior, & quum venerit, intelligetur, quam revera propin- quus fuerit: quanquam & adventus Domini in- telligi possit ratione cujus vis fidelis, qui precatur quotidie, adveniat regnum tuum.

## 5:9
Verse 9.

μὴ στενάζετε κατ' ἀλλήλων ἀδελφοί] It is the same as above, ch. 4, 2. Do not envy one another. For it is a metonymy. For envy is accustomed to groan at the good things of others. Moreover, the history of Cain is not obscurely referred to: who, when he envied his brother, heard from God, why are you angry? Gen. 4, 6.

ἵνα μὴ κριθῆτε] That is, κατακριθῆτε, lest God punish you, as he did Cain. See Rom. 2, 29. Gal. 5, 21. Tit. 3, 3.

There is no necessity that we should descend from the proper sense of the word to a metonymical one. It is not about envy, but about complaint and sighing when we groan to the Lord because of the impotence of our mind and impatience, and demand vengeance: from which the Apostle dissuades, since we ought to bless our neighbor and pray for him, not curse and groan against him, Matth. 5, 44. THAT YOU MAY NOT BE JUDGED, because such persons, as if unmindful of the Lord's command, nay, of the law of nature, Matth. 7, 12, and unmerciful toward their neighbor, will receive judgment without mercy, Jas. 2, 13. Matth. 18, 23. We do not deny, however, that envy is not rarely joined to such groanings. For the poor and afflicted are accustomed to groan and complain, now about their own injury and affliction, now about the fortune and tyranny of the wicked, and by groaning to murmur against the rich, to be impatient for themselves, to envy their neighbor, and even to complain against God himself. Heinsius is singular here, and thinks that στενάζειν is the same as to raise a clamor, so that the quarreling and contention of those who come through these steps to judgments and the forum may be noted, as if to say, do not contend among yourselves with clamor and quarrels, or get into a fight. But it is better to persist in the proper and more famous signification of the word, which is to groan, Mark 7, 34. Rom. 8, 23. 2 Cor. 5, 2, 4. Heb. 13, 17, just as also στεναγμὸς is not a quarrelsome clamor, but a sigh or groan, Acts 7, 34. Rom. 8, 26.

ἰδὺ κριτὴς πρὸ τῶν θυρῶν ἕστηκεν] The same sense as the words of God to Cain: Sin, [that is, the punishment of sin] lies at the doors. This also refers to the punishments now imminent upon the Jewish nation.

The words spoken to Cain sound of sin, not of the punishment of sin. But here it is not a matter of sin, nor of the punishment of sin, but of Christ the Judge, as far as the immediate sense is concerned. The punishment is already designated by the preceding words, THAT YOU MAY NOT BE CONDEMNED. Now it is indicated that the Judge is near. Estius thinks these things can seem to be added for a twofold reason, either because the brother is not to be judged by us, because he has a Judge who will soon come: or because we are not to groan against a brother: because the Judge is before the doors. But it is manifest that the former does not fit here: and therefore he himself prefers the latter. Cornelius à Lapide, however, brings forward a double sense: First, that Christ the Judge from heaven looks down upon all our things close at hand, Ps. 102, 10. Second, that He will soon come to judgment, both universal and particular, by which He will crown our patience: but will condemn the tyranny of those who persecute us. For from the particular judgment, which will soon arrive, depends the sentence of each one in the universal judgment. By which pact it is most true that the day of judgment is near with respect to individuals and is imminent for each one. The sense, therefore, is that the Judge is not far away, in the manner and mode of those who, when they have approached the door, prepare to enter. To this contributes the sentiment of St. Augustine, Epist. XX to Hesychius: In whatever state his own last day finds each one, in that state the last day of the world will overtake him: since such as each one dies on that day, such will he be judged on that day. Cornelius indeed explains it also of Christ the Judge assisting before our door, and looking upon all things before Him: because the Vulgate renders it: Behold the Judge stands before the door: But he acknowledges that sense as moral, not literal, from Augustine in Solil. cap. 14. A great necessity is imposed upon us of living justly and rightly, who do all things before the eyes of a Judge who sees all things.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

μὴ στενάζετε κατ' ἀλλήλων ἀδελφοί] Idem est quod supra c. 4, 2. Ne invidete alii aliis. Est enim μετωνυμία. Nam in- vidıa solet aliis bonis ingemere. Respicitur autem non ob- scure Caini historia: qui cum fratri invideret, à Deo audiit, quare iratus es? Gen. 4, 6.

ἵνα μὴ κριθῆτε] Id est, κατακριθῆτε, ne Deus vos puniat, ut Cainum. Vide Rom. 2, 29. Gal. 5, 21. Tit. 3, 3.

Nulla necessitas est, ut à proprio verbi sensu ad Metonymicum descendamus. Non de invidia, sed querela & suspiratione cum ad Dominum ge- mimus præ impotentia animi & impatientia vin- dictam exposcimus: à quo dehortatur Aposto- lus, quum benedicere proximo debeamus, & pro eo precari, non maledicere, & adversus eum in- gemiscere, Matth. 5, 44. UT NON JUDI- CEMINI, quia tales ceu præcepti Dominici, imo juris naturæ immemores, Matth. 7, 12. & im- misericordes erga proximum judicium sine mise- ricordia ferent, Jac. 2, 13. Matth. 18, 23. Conjun- ctam tamen esse invidiam talibus gemitibus non raro, haud negamus. Solent enim pauperes & afflicti gemere & queri nunc de sua injuria & affli- ctione, nunc de impiorum fortuna & tyrannide, & ingemiscendo divitibus obmurmurare sibi im- patientes esse, proximo invidere, adeoque etiam de Deo ipso queri. Heinsius hic singularis est, ac στενάζειν idem esse censet, ac clamorem edere, ut rixa & contentio eorum notetur, qui per istos gradus ad judicia ac forum veniunt, q. d. ne clamo- re & rixis inter vos contendite, aut committamini. Sed præstat in vocis propria & famosiori signifi- catione persistere, quæ est ingemiscere, Marc. 7. 34. Rom. 8, 23. 2. Cor. 5, 2. 4. Ebr. 13, 17. quemadmo- dum & στεναγμὸς non rixosus clamor est, sed suspi- rium gemitus Act. 7, 34. Rom. 8, 26.

ἰδὺ κριτὴς πρὸ τῶν θυρῶν ἕστηκεν] Idem sensus, qui verbo- rum Dei ad Cainum: Peccatum, [id est, peccati pœna] in fo- ribus cubat. Etiam hoc respicit pœnas Judaicæ genti jamjam imminentes.

Verba ad Cainum dicta de peccato sonant, non de peccati pœna. Hic vero neque de pecca- to, neque de pœna peccati, sed de Christo Judice, quod ad immediatum sensum attinet, agitur. Pœ- na verbis præcedentibus, UT NON CON- DEMNEMINI, jam designata. Nunc in pro- pinquo esse Judicem indicatur. Estius geminam ob causam hæc addi videri posse putat, sive quod fra- ter à nobis judicandus non sit, quia Judicem habet brevi venturum: sive quod non ingemiscendum sit contra fratrem: quod Judex præ foribus sit. Sed manifestum est, priorem hic non convenire: Ideoque posteriorem etiam ipse præfert. Sensum autem duplicem affert Cornelius à Lapide: Pri- mum; quod Christus Judex è cœlo cominus o- mnia nostra intueatur Psal. 102, 10. Alterum, quod brevi venturus sit ad judicium tum univer- sale, tum particulare, quo patientiam nostram co- ronabit: persequentium vero tyrannidem da- mnabit. Nam ex judicio particulari, quod cito adveniet, pendet sententia cujusque in judicio universali. Quo pacto verissimum est, judicii diem prope esse respectu singulorum & cuique immi- nere. Sensus ergo est, non longe abesse Judicem, more & modo eorum, qui, cum ad januam acces- serint, ingressum parant. Quo facit sententia S. Augustini Epist. XX. ad Hesych. In quo quem- que invenerit suus novissimus dies, in hoc eum com- prehendet mundi novissimus dies: quoniam qualis in die isto quisque morietur, talis in die illo judicabi- tur. Explicat quidem Cornelius etiam de Christo Judice assistente ante januam nostram, & omnia co- ram intuente: quia Vulgata reddit: Ecce Judex ante januam assistit: Sed eum sensum moralem, non li- teralem agnoscit ex Augustin. in Solil. cap. 14. No- bis magna est indita necessitas juste recteque viven- di, qui cuncta facimus ante oculos judicis cuncta cernentis.

## 5:10
Verse 10. ὑπόδειγμα λάβετε ἀδελφοί με τῆς κακοπαθείας καὶ μακροθυμίας τῆς προφήτας τῷ ὀνόματι Κυρίυ] ὑπόδειγμα is an example, to which we ought to fashion ourselves, as John 13, v. 15. κακοπαθεῖν is to be vexed with evils, as 2 Tim. 2, 9, below v. 13. Hence κακοπάθεια Malach. 1, 13. 2 Macc. 2, 27, 28. In the Glossary κακοπάθεια is vexation; labor. Cebes and others use it. Concerning these evils, which the Prophets endured, see Heb. 11, 35, 36, 37, 38, and what is said there. Μακροθυμία here is constant patience in adversities, as Heb. 6, 12. In the Manuscript here it is: ὑπόδειγμα ἀδελφοί τῆς κακοπαθείας τῆς μακροθυμίας ἔχετε τῆς προφήτας. That ὀνόματι Κυρίυ, or as other codices have it, ἐν ὀνόματι Κυρίυ, signifies by the command of God: For although Κύριος in the New Testament is accustomed to be said of Christ; yet where it is a matter of Old Testament affairs, it is accustomed, after the manner of the LXX Interpreters, to be put for יהוה, which is read אדני, as Matth. 1, 22, ch. 2, 15, ch. 3, 3. Acts 2, 21, ch. 3, 22, ch. 15, 17, and elsewhere.

The Vulgate wrongly rendered it as an evil outcome, when the Greek word κακοπαθείας denotes the suffering of evils, or the enduring of evils; it also added of its own the name of labor, which is not in the Greek, as Cornelius à Lapide and Estius admit. The Grotian observation about the word κυρίᾳ is not universal: which even those examples Matth. 3, 3, Acts 2, 21 testify, concerning which let those things be seen which we said in the parallel places of the Old Testament. Add Matth. 22, 43, Luke 1, 76, Acts 7, 31, Rom. 10, 13, ch. 14, 11, 1 Cor. 1, 31, Heb. 1, 10. In which places by the word κυρίυ Christ is understood, even if the sayings of the Old Testament are brought forward. That the name יהוה is to be read אדני we have elsewhere refuted, especially in Theol. nat. & rev.

Latin:

Vers. 10. ὑπόδειγμα λάβετε ἀδελφοί με τῆς κακοπαθείας καὶ μακροθυμίας τῆς προφήτας τῷ ὀνόματι Κυρίυ] ὑπόδειγμα est exemplum, ad quod nos ipsos fingere debemus, ut Joh. 13, v. 15. κακοπαθεῖν est malis vexari, ut 2. Tim. 2, 9. in- fra v. 13. Hinc κακοπάθεια Malach. 1, 13. 2. Macc. 2, 27. 28. In Glossario κακοπάθεια vexatio; labor. UtiturCebes & alii. De his malis, quæ Prophetæ pertulerunt vide Ebr. 11, 35. 36. 37. 38. & ibi dicta. Μακροθυμία hic est constans in adversis patientia, ut Ebr. 6, 12. In Manuscripto hic est: ὑπόδειγ- μα ἀδελφοί τῆς κακοπαθείας τῆς μακροθυμίας ἔχετε τῆς προ- φήτας. Illud ὀνόματι Κυρίυ, vel ut alii codices habent, ἐν ὀνό- ματι Κυρίυ, significat Dei mandato: Nam quanquam Κύριος in novo fœdere de Christo solet dici; tamen ubi agitur de re- bus Veteris Testamenti, solet more LXX. Interpretum poni pro יהוה, quod legitur אדני, ut Matth. 1, 22. cap. 2, 15. c. 3, 3. Act. 2, 21. c. 3, 22. c. 15, 17. & alibi.

Vulgata perperam exitum malum reddidit, quum vox Græca κακοπαθείας malorum passionem, vel malorum perpessionem notet, de suo etiam addidit nomen laboris, quod in Græco non habe- tur, fatente Cornelio à Lapide & Estio. Grotiana observatio de voce κυρίᾳ non est universalis: quod vel exempla illa Matth. 3, 3. Act. 2, 21. testan- tur, de quibus videantur, quæ in locis parallelis Veteris Testamenti diximus. Adde Matth. 22, 43. Luc. 1, 76. Actor. 7, 31. Rom. 10, 13. cap. 14, 11. 1. Cor. 1, 31. Ebr. 1, 10. In quibus locis voce κυρίυ Christus intelligitur, etsi Veteris Testamenti dicta addu- cantur. Nomen יהוה legendum esse אדני alias profligavimus, imprimis in Theol. nat. & rev.

## 5:11
Verse 11.

ἰδὲ μακαρίζομεν τῆς ὑπομένοντας] In the manuscript it is better as τῆς ὑπομείναντας, as both the Syriac and Latin versions read. We still praise the constancy of those who endured such evils, and we proclaim them blessed on this account. Μακάρι- ό ὑπομένων is found in Dan. 12, 12. Μακαρίζειν is אשׁר Gen. 30, 13. Num. 24, 17. Job 29, 11. Ps. 41, 2, and elsewhere, Luke 1, 48. Hence μακαρισμὸς in Rom. 4, 6, 9.

Why should all other codices be corrected here from a single manuscript? Beza certainly preferred the common reading of the Greeks, which was also done by Pagninus, the Tigurines, and others, rendering it: who (adversities) endure: Nor does it stand in the way that Cornelius à Lapide, according to the saying of Solon to Croesus, says: No one should be called blessed in life, but only after death: because by the phrase of Scripture, those who are still on the way are also called blessed. These do not speak of the blessed departed, but of those who still act on earth, like the disciples of Christ in Matt. 5, 11.

τὴν ὑπομονὴν τῶ Ἰὼβ ἀκύσατε] Having lost his children and goods, his body twisted by the most severe pains, his friends slandering him. For it is, as we said regarding the book of Job, a true history, but treated poetically.

Job is brought forward above others, whom St. Cyprian, in 'On the Good of Patience,' raised to the highest pinnacle of praise by the virtue of his patience; Tertullian, in 'On Patience,' ch. 14, says that in him God built a bier for the Devil and raised a banner over the enemy of His glory. Hilary, in Psalm 68, called him the glorious and blessed painter of all human sufferings. For this reason also the writing of Job is commended, in which we have an example of patience, which is joined to the Prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord, as a writer equally θεόπνευστος. Prosper, part 1, 'Predictions,' ch. 22, p. 28: From the seed of Esau came the Idumean nation, in which, among other leaders, that Job, the most valiant athlete of God, shone forth, brought forward as an example of all patience, so that in an agonistic contest he might overcome the Prince of the whole militia, the Devil, supported by the help of God.

Καὶ τὸ τέλος τοῦ Κυρίου εἴδετε] This is a genitive of cause. You have seen, he says, that is, you have known by reading, what end God gave to him: good and firm health: many and flourishing children: fame and honors, and riches.

Ὅτι πολύσπλαγχνος ἐστι καὶ οἰκτίρμων] The former of these seems to be referred to affection, as also σπλάγχνα, Luke 1:78; the latter to acts corresponding to the affection. The sense is the same in Ex. 34:6; 2 Sam. 24:14.

The interpretation of those who understand Christ by 'the Lord' and his death by 'the end' is foreign here, along with Abbot Guerric, Serm. 3 on Palm Sunday: 'The patience of Job was until the return of his substance, the patience of the Lord until the end of his life.' This is also the opinion of Augustine, Book 1, De symbolo ad Catechumenos, ch. 3, and Epistle 120, ch. 10; Bede, the Gloss, and Hugo; which they prove from the word 'you have seen': because many in that age had seen the death of Christ, but no one had seen the end of Job. This argument is too weak, because 'to see' in Scripture is often the same as 'to know,' whether it happens by sight, by hearing, or by another sense, and it is understood as mental vision. It is more correctly understood as the end which Job obtained from the Lord: because an explanation of the end is added, namely, that the Lord was known to be merciful and compassionate toward Job, while He granted him a happy end to his miseries.

PART III. INFORMATORY.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

ἰδὲ μακαρίζομεν τῆς ὑπομένοντας] In Manuscripto melius τῆς ὑπομείναντας, quomodo legerunt & Syrus & Latinus. Laudamus adhuc constantiam eorum, qui talia mala pertu- lere, beatosque eos hoc nomine prædicamus. Μακάρι- ό ὑπομένων est apud Dan. 11, 12. Μακαρίζειν אשׁר Gen. 30. v. 12. Num. 24, 17. Job. 29, 11. Psal. 41, 2. & alibi, Luc. 1, 48. Hinc μακαρισμὸς Rom. 4, 6. 9.

Cur è Manuscripto unico hic emendandi cæte- ri codices omnes?
