Beza utique prætulit commu- nem Græcorum lectionem, quod etiam à Pagnino, Tigurinis, aliisque factum, reddens: qui (ad- versa) tolerant: Neque obstat, quod Cornelius à Lapide juxta Solonis dictum ad Crœsum ait: Non in vita beatum quenquam dicendum, sed duntaxat post mortem: quia phrasi Scripturæ beati etiam dicuntur, qui adhuc in via sunt. Non de defun- ctis beatis hæc loquuntur, sed de iis, qui ad- huc in terris agunt, ut discipuli Christi Matth. 5, 11.

τὴν ὑπομονὴν τῶ Ἰὼβ ἀκύσατε] Amissis liberis & bonis, torto per gravissimos dolores corpore, amicis eum calumni- antibus. Est enim, ut ad Jobi librum diximus, vera hæc hi- storia, sed tractata Poëtice.

Job præ aliis adducitur, quem S. Cyprianus de bono patient. ad summum fastigium laudis pa- tientiæ virtute provectum, Tertullianus de pa- tient. cap. 14. in quo Deus feretrum de Diabolo extruxerit, vexillum de inimico gloriæ suæ ex- tulerit. Hilarius in Psalm. LXVIII. universa- rum passionum humanarum gloriosum & beatum pictorem dixit. Hac etiam ratione Jobi scri- ptum commendatur, in quo exemplar patientiæ habeamus, quod jungitur Prophetis, qui loquuti sunt in nomine Domini, ceu scriptor æque θεό- πνευςος. Prosper part. I. Prædict. cap. 22. p. m. 28. Ex semine Esau Idumæa gens, in qua inter cæteros Duces, Job ille fortissimus athleta Dei enituit, in exemplum omnis patientiæ productus, ut agonistico certamine Principem to- tius militiæ Diabolum superaret, fultus auxilio Dei.

Καὶ τὸ τέλος τοῦ Κυρίου εἴδετε] Est hic Genitivus causæ. Vi- distis, inquit, id est, legendo cognovistis, quem exitum ei De- us dederit: bonam ac firmam valetudinem : plurimos ac flo- rentes liberos : famam & honores, & divitias.

Ὅτι πολύσπλαγχνος ἐστι καὶ οἰκτίρμων] Horum prius ad affectum referri videtur, ut & σπλάγχνα, Luc. I. 78. alte- rum ad actus affectui congruentes. Sensus idem Ex. XXXIV. 6. 2. Sam. XXIV. 14.

Aliena hic est eorum interpretatio, qui per τὸν Κύριον intelligunt Christum, & per τὸ τέλος mor- tem ejus cum Guerrico Abbate Serm. III. de Dom. Palm. Sufferentia Jobi fuit usque ad reditum sub- stantiæ, sufferentia Domini usque ad exitum vitæ. Quæ etiam Augustini sententia l. I. de symbol. ad Catech. c. 3. & epist. CXX. cap. X. Beda, Glossa, Hugonis; quam è verbo vidistis probant : quia multi ævo isto mortem Christi viderant, Jobi fi- nem nemo. Nimis infirmum hoc argumentum, quia videre in Scriptura sæpe idem est, quod co- gnoscere, sive visu, sive auditu, sive alio sensu fi- at, & de visione mentali accipitur. Rectius de fine, qui à Domino Jobo obtigit, intelligitur: quia addi- tur explicatio finis, quod nempe cognitus fuerit Dominus misericors & miserator in Jobum, dum illi felicem exitum miseriarum concessit.

PARS III. INFORMATORIA.

## 5:12
Verse 12. Πρὸ πάντων δὲ ἀδελφοὶ] Because the Jews were very prone to oaths, and that custom could not easily be rooted out, James therefore seriously warns Christians to remember the precept which Christ gave, about which we have said much on Matt. 5:33, 34, 35, 36, 37, and in [De Jure Belli ac Pacis] Book 2, 13.21. Moreover, we are accustomed to say that those things which we wish to be strictly avoided must be avoided above all else.

The information pertains especially to those things which concern the use and abuse of the tongue, about which he had also treated in chapter 3. For it deals with oaths, prayer, psalms, prayers for the sick, confession of sins, mutual intercession, and the calling back of those who are wandering into the way, all of which pertain to the second commandment of the Decalogue. As for oaths, the gloss of Lyranus, 'above all,' that is, 'do not, as you are accustomed, prefix an oath to all your words,' is deservedly rejected by those skilled in language as unworthy of refutation. However, we easily agree with Grotius here.

Μὴ ὀμνύετε] Namely, by promising something about an uncertain matter. Not that one should not also abstain from an assertory oath, as much as the honor of God and the commands of superiors allow, but because the context of the passage shows that this is not what is being discussed here. The Essenes also abstained from such oaths, and following their example, the Pythagoreans, namely περὶ τῶν ἐνδεχομένων καὶ ἀορίστων τῆς ἐκβάσεως ἐχόντων τὸ πέρας, as we have made clear from Hierocles.

Why should we restrict this to promissory oaths, which in general sound like they refer to oaths? If, as Grotius acknowledges, one must also abstain from assertory ones, why does James not rebuke the same here, pronouncing absolutely: 'Do not swear!' Although these concern both assertory and promissory oaths, not all oaths are simply prohibited, which Josephus is the authority for stating that the Essenes held (Book 2, De Bell. Jud. ch. 7). The Pelagians also held, as Jerome testifies, that oaths were entirely abolished, at least in the New Testament. The Anabaptists in the Emden colloquy also made this their dogma in the previous age, though they testified to a sounder mind in the Frankenthal colloquy. About the Socinians, it has been said elsewhere. But how could one be forbidden from either judicial oaths, which the Magistrate imposes, or others which the glory of God, public and private safety, or even our reputation, or any other unavoidable necessity demands? Nor indeed is it forbidden to them, since the precepts and laws concerning oaths, Deut. 6,

Latin:

Vers. 12. Πρὸ πάντων δὲ ἀδελφοὶ] Quia Judæi valde proni erant ad juramenta; nec facile evelli ea consuetudo potuit, ideo Christianos monet serio Jacobus, ut memine- rint ejus præcepti, quod Christus dedit, de quo multa diximus ad Matth. V. 33. 34. 35. 36. 37. & II. de Jure Belli & Pacis XIII. 21. Quæ autem valde caveri volumus, ea dicere solemus caven- da ante omnia.

Informatio ad ea potissimum spectat, quæ usum & abusum linguæ concernunt, de quo cap. III. etiam egerat. Versatur enim circa ju- ramenta, orationem, psalmos, preces pro ægrotis, confessionem peccatorum, mutuam intercessionem, & errantium in viam revocationem, quæ omnia ad secundum Decalogi præceptum pertinent. Quod ad juramenta, Lyrani glossa, ante omnia, id est, o- mnibus dictis vestris nolite, ut soletis, juramen- tum præmittere, merito reprobatur à linguæ me- ritis, refutatione indigna. Grotio autem facile hic accedimus.

Μὴ ὀμνύετε] Nempe promittendo aliquid de re incerta. Non quod non & assertorio juramento abstinendũ sit, quan- tum Dei honos & superiorum jussa id sinunt, sed quia de eo hic non agi sententiæ nexus ostendit. Etiam Esseni à talibus juramentis abstinebant, & eorum exemplo Pythagorici, nem- pe περὶ τῶν ἐνδεχομένων καὶ ἀορίστων τῆς ἐκβάσεως ἐχόντων τὸ πέ- ρας, ut ex Hierocle apertum fecimus.

Cur restringamus ad juramenta promissoria, quæ in genere sonant de juramentis? Si, quod agnoscit Grotius, etiam ab assertoriis abstinendum, quidni eadem hic reprehendat Jacobus, abso- lute pronuncians: Ne juretis! Quanquam vero hæc tam assertoria, quam promissoria concernant, non tamen omnia simpliciter juramenta prohi- bita sunt, quod Essenos statuisse, autor est Jose- phus libr. II. de Bell. Jud. c. 7. Statuerunt & Pela- giani, Hieronymo teste, juramenta saltim in Novo Testamento prorsus sublata esse. Quod dogma suum quoque fecerunt superiori ævo Anabaptistæ in Embdano colloquio, qui tamen in Franskenth. col- loq. saniorem mentem testati sunt. De Socini- anis alibi dictum. At quomodo vel judicialibus, quæ Magistratus imponit, vel aliis, quæ postulat Dei gloria, salus publica & privata, vel etiam fama nostra, aut alia inevitabilis necessitas quæcunque, interdici potuit? Neque vero interdictum iis esse, cum præcepta & leges de juramentis, Deut. VI.

## 5:12
Μήτε τὸν ὀρανὸν, μήτε τὴν γῆν.] The more superstitious Jews (as we have observed from Philo) did not explicitly use the name of God for common oaths, but other things, such as heaven and earth. But Christ wishes for these also to be abstained from. For just as Ulpian said that he who swears by his own safety is seen to swear by God, because he swears with respect to the divine Power, so he who swears by heaven prays, if he deceives, that heaven be unwholesome to him, and he who swears by the earth, that the earth be unfruitful, all of which depend on God.

Μήτε ἄλλον τινὰ ὅρκον] For example, by Jerusalem, by the temple, by the altar, by κεφαλὴν, by his own head, Matt. V. 35, XXIII. 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22.

This particle is understood either as a limitation of the previous prohibition, which pleases some, or as a more specific commandment, which seems more appropriate. He had already warned that one should not swear rashly: now, that one should not swear by created things, which still clung to the converted Jews from the custom of the Pharisees; because they did not even consider those to be oaths. But just as Christ had refuted the Pharisees, Matt. V and XXIII, so now Christians are warned not to utter those oaths, or not to consider them as oaths. There are those who say those are indirect oaths, but according to the mind of the swearer and custom, they are entirely direct: because the confirmation of those things which are said is intended by them, not merely naked, nor only vehemently assertive, but greater than any exception, which might put an end to controversies, such as a truly promissory oath is, Heb. VI. v. 16. But it is easily evident that those oaths are illicit, indeed sacrilegious, because that worship is owed to God alone, the inspector and judge of hearts, and it implies both an invocation of the Divine Being from our soul, which we would not wish to deceive, and a solemn imprecation that He be the avenger if we do deceive, Deut. VI. 13, c. X. 20. Therefore, they are condemned as profane, Exod. XXIII. 13, Jer. VII. 5, and it is decreed by Innocent III in C. Etsi Christus concerning the oath, from Jerome, that Christ in Matthew prohibited swearing by creatures for the sake of the honor of the Creator. In the Fourth Council of Carthage, it is established that a cleric swearing by creatures is to be most severely rebuked, and if he persists in the vice, he is to be excommunicated. Let the Papists see, therefore, with what piety they either swear by Saints or Angels, or assert that it is possible to swear by them!

Let your yes be yes, and your no, no] That is, what you promise with a word, fulfill with a deed, whether it consists in doing or in not doing. 'Yes' signifies both the promise and the fulfillment of the promise, as can be seen in 2 Cor. I. v. 18, 19, 21. There is, therefore, a ploke here, as also in a similar saying of the Jews. The just man's 'yes' is 'yes', and there is no 'no'. That 'yes' is of the one promising, like 'yes' or 'certainly' to the Greeks.

Oecumenius more correctly: i.e., let your speech be a simple affirmation or negation without an oath, so that you say simply that what is, is, and what is not, is not. Others, most correctly of all: Instead of an oath, use rather a constant and doubled affirmation or negation. Nor do we think these should be restricted, with Heinsius and the Dutch interpreters, to familiar conversation. For they are spoken generally to exclude any rash oaths. A Christian, says St. Augustine, Book I de Serm. Dom. in monte, should speak the truth, and commend the truth not by frequent swearing, but by the integrity of his morals. Compare what is said on that passage regarding this and the similar warning proposed by Christ in Matt. V. 35.

Lest you fall into hypocrisy] Lest you be found liars. Thus, lest I lie. Prov. ch. XXX. v. 9. For 'hypocrisy' is taken for a lie, 1 Tim. ch. IV. v. 2, and 'to play the hypocrite' for to lie, Prov. XVI. 28, in the version of Symmachus. And 'hypocrite' for a liar, Job XXXIV. 30, XXXVI. 13. This locution not being well understood seems to have been the reason why the Syriac, Latin, and Arabic versions read, 'lest you fall under judgment'.

Rightly he deserts the Vulgate here, which Estius defends in vain with Beza, with no more than the single codex of Robert Stephanus, which had 'under judgment'. Heinsius also observes the same as Grotius: There was no reason why the learned, who expressed 'under judgment' instead of 'into hypocrisy', should judge that this passage ought to be changed. For a hypocrite is one who says what is false, a hypocrite is one who swears what is false. Of which kind were those caviling oaths with which he dealt. But we [deal with this] more fully on Matthew. Add that he who easily and often swears anything, easily lies, and easily perjures himself: which is 'to fall into hypocrisy'. Whence Prov. XXX. 8, 9, which passage clearly makes for this. 'Appoint for me what is necessary, and what is sufficient, lest being filled I become a liar and say, who sees me? or being impoverished I steal, and swear by the name of the Lord.' It is known what 'chaneph' is, and how widely it extends, especially indeed to perjurers and liars, nor is that saying of the Apostle unknown, 'in the hypocrisy of liars', 1 Tim. IV. 2. Others, however, with Pagninus, the Tigurine, Cajetan, and Clarius, prefer to render it 'into simulation', i.e., lest you swear fictitiously and feignedly, swearing with the mouth, not with the heart, and saying, I have sworn with my tongue, I keep my mind unsworn.

Latin:

Μήτε τὸν ὀρανὸν, μήτε τὴν γῆν.] Judæi superstitiosiores, (quemadmodum ex Philone observavimus) ad vulgaria juramenta non diferte Dei nomen usurpabant, sed res alias, ut cœlum & terram. Sed his quoque abstineri vult Christus. Nam sicut Ulpianus dixit, eum, qui per salu- tem suam jurat, videri Deum jurare, quia respectu divini Numinis jurat, ita qui cœlum jurat, precatur, si fallat, cœlum sibi insalubre, & qui terram, terram infrugiferam, quæ omnia a Deo pendent.

Μήτε ἄλλον τινὰ ὅρκον] Puta per Hierosolyma, per templum, per altare, per κεφαλὴν, per caput suum, Matth. V. 35. XXIII. 16. 17. 18. 19. 20. 21. 22.

Hæc particula vel ut limitatio intelligitur, quod nonnullis placet, prioris interdicti, vel ut specialiùs præceptum, quod convenientius vide- tur. Prius non esse temere jurandum monu- erat: jam non jurandum in creaturis, quod ex Pharisæorum consuetudine Judæis conversis ad- huc hærebat; quia illa ne quidem pro juramen- tis habebant. Sed ut Pharisæos Christus redargu- erat, Matth. V. & XXIII. Ita jam Christiani mo- nentur, ne illa juramenta emittant, aut non ha- beant pro juramentis. Sunt qui dicant ea ju- ramenta indirecta, sed ex mente jurantis & con- suetudine directa omnino sunt: quia confir- matio eorum, quæ dicuntur, intenditur iisdem non nuda, nec vehementer tantum as- severatoria, sed omni exceptione major, quæ finem faciat controversiarum, qualis revera ju- ratoria est, Ebr. VI. v. 16. Illicita autem illa jura- menta, imò sacrilega esse facile constat, quia cultus ille soli Deo cordium inspectori ac Ju- dici debetur, ac tum invocationem Numinis im- portat de animo nostro, quod non velimus fallere, tum imprecationem solennem, ut vindex sit, si fal- lamus, Deut. VI. 13. c. X. 20. Ideo ceu profana da- mnantur, Exod. XXIII. 13. Jer. VII. 5. & ab Inno- centio III. in C. Etsi Christus de jurejurando ex Hi- eronym. decernitur, Christum apud Matthæum pro- hibuisse juramentum per creaturas ob honorificen- tiam Creatoris. In Concilio Carthaginensi IV. statuitur, Clericum per creaturas jurantem acer- rime esse objurgandum, quod si perstiterit in vitio, excommunicandum. Viderint ergo Pontificii, qua pietate per Sanctos aut Angelos vel jurent, vel jurari posse asserant!

Ἤτω καὶ ὑμῶν τὸ ναὶ, ναὶ, καὶ τὸ ὂ, ὂ] Id est, quod verbo promittitis, id facto implete, sive id in agendo sive in non- agendo consistat. Ναὶ & promissum significat & promissi implementum, ut videre est 2. Cor. I. v. 18. 19. 21. Est igi- tur hic πλοκὴ, ut & in simili dicto Judæorum. Justi יאך est יאך, & non est non. Illud יאך est promittentis, ut ναὶ vel μάλιςα Græcis.

Rectius Oecumenius: q. d. Sermo vester sit simplex affirmatio aut negatio sine juramento, ut, quod est, dicatis simpliciter esse, quod non est, non esse. Rectissimi omnium alii: Pro juramento utamini potius constanti ac geminata seu affirma- tione seu negatione. Neque hæc tantum cum Heinsio ac Belg. Interpretibus restringenda cense- mus ad conversationem familiarem. Generaliter enim dicta ad excludenda juramenta quævis te- meraria. Christianus, inquit S. Augustinus l. I. de Serm. Dom. in monte, verum loquatur, ne- que jurationibus crebris, sed morum probitate commendet veritatem. Conf. quæ de hoc & simili Matth. V. 35. à Christo proposito monito ad illum locum dicta.

Ἵνα μὴ εἰς ὑπόκρισιν πέσητε] Ne inveniamini men- daces. Sic ne mentiar. Prov. cap. XXX. vers. 9. Nam ὑπόκρισις pro mendacio sumitur, 1. Tim. cap. IV. v. 2. & ὑποκρίνεσθαι pro mentiri, Prov. XVI. 28. in versione Sym- machi. Et ὑποκριτὴς pro mendace, Job. XXXIV. 30. XXXVI. 13. Videtur hæc loquutio non bene percepta causa fuisse, cur Syrus, Latinus, Arabs legerint, ἵνα μὴ ὑπὸ κρίσιν πέσητε.

Merito hic Vulgatam deserit, quam nequic- quam cum Beza tuetur Estius, non nisi unico Ro- berti Stephani codice, qui habuerit ὑπὸ κρίσιν. Idem quod Grotius, observat quoque Heinsius: Nihil erat causa, quare eum locum mutandum ju- dicarent eruditi, qui ὑπὸ κρίσιν pro εἰς ὑπόκρισιν expresserunt. Nam ὑποκριτὴς qui falsum dicit, ὑποκριτὴς qui falsum jurat. Cujus generis cavil- latoria ea juramenta erant, de quibus egit. Nos autem ad Matthæum fusius. Adde quod qui fa- cile ac sæpe quidvis jurat, facile mentitur, facile & pejerat: quod est εἰς ὑπόκρισιν πίπτειν. Unde Prov. XXX. 8. 9. qui locus plane huc facit. Σύντα- ξον δέ μοι τὰ δέοντα, καὶ τὰ ἀυτάρκη, ἵνα μὴ πλη- σθεὶς ψευδὴ γένωμαι καὶ εἴπω, τίς με ὁρᾷ; ἢ πε- νωθεὶς κλέψω, καὶ ὀμόσω τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Κυρίου. Notum quid sit חנף, & quam late se extendat, imprimis verò ad perjuros καὶ ψευδολόγος, nec ignotum illud Apo- stoli, ἐν ὑποκρίσει ψευδολόγων, 1. Tim. IV. 2. Alii ta- men cum Pagnino, Tigur. Cajet. Clario reddere malunt in simulationem, q. d. ne ficte & simulate juretis, ore jurantes, non corde, ac dicentes, juravi lingua, mentem injuratam gero.

## 5:13
v. 13, ch. 10, v. 20, Ps. 66:12, Jer. 4:2, as well as the examples of the Saints teach, Gen. 14:22, ch. 26:31, Josh. 14:9, to which are added the oaths of the most holy God Himself, to whom we ought to be conformed. See Ps. 110:4, Is. 45:23, Jer. 22:5, ch. 44:26, Ezek. 18:32, ch. 33:11, Am. 4:2. It is also predicted that they would have a place in the New Testament, Is. 65:16, Jer. 12:16, such as holy men of God also performed, as is the example of Paul, Rom. 9:1, 2 Cor. 11:23, ch. 13:21, Phil. 1:8, which finally they wished to be the end of all controversy, Heb. 6:13.

What Grotius objects concerning the connection of the sentence relies on τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐπιλύσει, as if those words ναὶ, ναὶ, ὀ, ὀ, had this meaning: that which you promise with a word, fulfill with a deed. But these are more correctly accepted in a general sense, that it is indeed fitting for the faithful to assert something strongly, if the situation demands it, by doubling the ναὶ, or even to deny it by repeating the particle of denial ὀ, but it is not fitting to promise or assert something rashly by interposing an oath, by which we easily abuse the name of God. This is what reverence for the divine name demands, and the truth and faith of the pious, which ought to be so great that one should be believed entirely without oaths, as Clement of Alexandria warns in book VII of the Stromata. Augustine rightly says of the parallel passage, Matt. V. 35: The Lord commanded not to swear, so that no one might seek an oath as a good thing, and so that no one might slip into perjury through the habit of swearing. He, therefore, who understands that an oath is to be held not among good things, but among necessary ones, restrains himself as much as he can, so as not to use it unless by necessity, when he sees that men are lazy to believe what is useful to them unless it is confirmed by an oath. Whence Thomas, not inappropriately in Opusculum IV, warned that an oath should be used no differently than a medicine, only when necessity compels. And in II. 2. q. 89. art. 3, he says: An incautious oath lacks judgment, a lying oath lacks truth, an unjust oath lacks justice. A false oath, according to Augustine in Sermon XXVIII on the Words of the Lord, is destructive; a true oath is dangerous; no oath is secure.

Latin:

v. 13. c. X. v. 20. Psal. LXVI. 12. Jerem. IV. 2. tum exempla Sanctorum docent, Genes. XIV. vers. 22. cap. XXVI. 31. Jos. XIV. 9. quibus ipsius Dei san- ctissimi, cui nos conformes esse debemus, juramen- ta accedunt. Vid. Psal. CX. 4. Es. XLV. 23. Jerem. XXII. 5. cap. XLIV. 26. Ezech. XIIX. 32. c. XXXIII. 11. Am. IV. 2. In Novo etiam Testamento locum ea habitura prædictum, Es. LXV. 16. Jer. XII. v. 16. qualia etiam sancti Dei homines præstitere, ut ex- emplo est Paulus, Rom. IX. 1. 2. Cor. XI. 23. c. XIII. v. 21. Phil. I. 8. quæ denique finem omnis contro- versiæ esse voluere Ebr. VI. 13.

Quod de nexu sententiæ obvertit Grotius, τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐπιλύσει nititur, quasi verba illa ναὶ, ναὶ, ὀ, ὀ, hunc habeant sensum, quod verbo promittitis, id facto implete. Quæ vero generatim rectius ac- cipiuntur, quod fideles quidem deceat fortiter a- liquid asseverari, si res poscat, geminato nēpe ναὶ, vel etiam negare repetita negandi particula ὀ, nō autem deceat temere juramento interposito, quo facile nomine Dei abutimur, aliquid vel promit- tere, vel asserere. Quod divini nominis reveren- tia postulat, & veritas ac fides piorum, quæ tanta esse debet, ut injuratis omnino credendum sit, mo- nente Clem. Alexandr. libr. VII. Strom. Recte Au- gustinus de loco parallelo, Matth. V. 35. Dominus præcepit, ne juretur, ne quis tanquam bonum appe- tat jujurandum, & ne quis assiduitate jurandi in perjurium dilabatur. Qui igitur intelligit, non in bonis, sed in necessariis jurationem habendam, refre- nat se, quantum potest, ut ea non utatur, nisi neces- sitate, cum videt, homines pigros esse ad credendum, quod eis utile est, nisi juratione firmetur. Unde Thomas non inconcinne opusc. I V. juramentum monuit non aliter ac medicamentum non nisi co- gente necessitate usurpandum. Et in II. 2. q. 89. art. 3. Judicio, inquit; caret juramentum incau- tum, veritate juramentum mendax, justitia jura- mentum iniquum. Falsa juratio, Augustino Serm. XXIIX. de Verb. Dom. exitiosa, vera juratio pericu- losa est, nulla juratio secura.

## 5:13
Vers. 13.

Is anyone among you suffering adversity] If anyone is pressed by adversities. See above 10.

Let him pray] You have examples in Matt. XXVI. 39, Acts ch. XXI. 5.

Concerning sorrow, Chrysostom, Sermon II on Providence: The spirit of sorrow is more powerful for doing harm than any diabolical action. For the demon overcomes almost everyone he overcomes through sorrow. If you take that away, no one will be able to be harmed by the demon. Concerning prayers and Psalms, he has this to say in Psalm XIV: A Psalm is a most sharp weapon against demons: nor do stags flee as demons flee the Psalms of David. David took his lyre and played, and the evil spirit departed from Saul, and the believing demon fell, like a stag struck by an arrow and wounded in the breast.

Is anyone cheerful] If anyone rejoices because of goods received from God. Thus 'becoming cheerful', Acts XXVII. 36. Let him sing] Let him give thanks to God, even with singing. See 2 Cor. XIV. 15, Eph. V. 19. 'To sing' properly is to play on strings, but it is taken more broadly among our people.

We must sing, both so that we may give thanks to God, and so that we may foster and increase our joy in the Lord. The Psalm, as Chrysostom says on Psalm CXXXIV, holds pleasure with utility; its principal profit is to speak hymns to God, to purge the soul, to lift the thought on high, etc. What? That in the Psalms we emulate the angels, eternally singing with a joyful voice, Holy, Holy, Holy Lord God of Sabaoth, Is. VI. 3, compare Eph. V. 19.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Κακοπαθεῖ τις ἐν ὑμῖν] Si quis premitur adversis. Vide supra 10.

Προσευχέσθω] Exempla habes Matth. XXVI. 39. Act. c. XXI. 5.

De mœrore Chrysostomus Serm. II. de pro- vid. omni Diabolica actione potentior ad nocen- dum est mœroris Spiritus. Dæmon enim quos- cunque fere superat, per mœrorem superat. Eum si auferas, nemo a Dæmone lædi poterit. De precibus vero & Psalmis in Psal. XIV. ita habet: Psalmus est acutissimum telum contra Dæmones: nec cervi ita fugiunt, ut Psalmos David Dæmones. Sumsit Da- vid citharam & pulsavit, & a Saule recessit malus Spiritus, & credens Dæmon cecidit, ut cervus sagitta percussus, & in pectore sauciatus.

Εὐθυμεῖ τις] Si quis lætatur ob accepta à Deo bona. Sic εὔθυμοι γενόμενοι, Act. XXVII. 36. Ψαλλέτω] Deo gratias agat, etiam cum cantu. Vide 2. Cor. XIV. 15. Eph. V. 19. Ψάλλειν proprie est fidibus canere, sed latius sumitur apud nostros.

Psallendum est, & ut Deo gratias agamus, & ut gaudium in Domino foveamus & augeamus. Ha- bet Psalmus, Chrysostomo in Psal. CXXXIV. dicen- te, voluptatem cum utilitate; principale ejus lucrum est ad Deum hymnos dicere, animam expurgare, co- gitationem in altum extollere &c. Quid? quod Psalmis Angelos æmulemur, æternum læta voce cantantes Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus Dominus Deus Zebaoth, Es. VI. 3. conf. Eph. V. 19.

## 5:14
Vers. 14. Is any sick among you?] That is, if anyone is ill. This word is taken thus in Matt. 10:8, 25:36, Mark 6:56, Luke 4:40, Phil. 2:26, 27, and often elsewhere. The Syriac כריה is in the same color. That word corresponds to the Hebrew חלה, as can be seen in Prov. ch. 22:35. What is ἀσθενεῖν here, is soon κάμνειν.

Let him call for the elders of the Church.] The Syriac is לקשישא דעדתא. It is customary for seven elders to be employed for this matter in the East.

And let them pray over him] ἐπ' αὐτὸν is עלוהו, that is, for him.

Anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord] According to the institution of Christ, Mark 6:13. Namely, because oil among the Hebrews signified divine grace: as also the laying on of hands, which itself was also accustomed to be used around the sick, Mark 16:18, Acts ch. 28:8. Moreover, all these things were done in the name of Christ, Mark 16:17, Acts 3:6, 16, 19:13. Proculus the Christian once cured the Emperor Severus through oil. Tertullian is the witness in his letter to Scapula.

Grotius seems to wish to gratify the Papists, who strive to extract the sacrament of extreme unction from this passage: whom, however, he deserts again when he brings here the passages concerning the miraculous anointing for healing the sick from Mark 6 and 16: which the Papists, in Cajetan who interprets the present passage concerning it, disapprove, relying on their councils, the Florentine in the decree of union, and especially the Tridentine, Sess. 14, Can. 1 seqq., and ch. 1 on extreme unction. We oppose these arguments to the Papists and their supporters: First, from the Efficient cause. For the Sacraments of the New Testament were instituted by Christ himself, as Thomas admits, p. 3, q. 64, art. 2, q. 72, art. 1. But most Papists, along with Lombard, acknowledge that this anointing, of which we are speaking at present, was not instituted by Christ. Next, the form pertains to a Sacrament, which Cornelius à Lapide calls the prayer of faith here. But neither St. James, nor any other of the Apostles, much less Christ himself, ever defined the formula in extreme unction sanctioned by the Synod of Trent, 'by this anointing,' etc. Thirdly, they make the matter oil blessed by a Bishop: here mention is made of oil, but no mention of a blessing, much less one performed by a Bishop. Fourthly, the subject to be anointed in this place is not one who is in the death throes or lying mortally ill. The word ἀσθενεῖ denotes any infirmity, not only the extreme and deadly one: nor is one who is lying mortally ill or about to die designated only by κάμνοντα, but any sick person, as the Vulgate itself rendered it, or one who is sick, as the Syriac has explained. Fifth, the effect of the Jacobean anointing is not the remission of sins: which Cajetan, among others, urges: It can be gathered neither from the words nor from the effect that these words speak of sacramental extreme unction, but rather of the anointing which the Lord Jesus instituted in the Gospel to be exercised by the disciples upon the sick. For the text does not say, if anyone is sick unto death, but absolutely, if anyone is sick, and it calls the effect the relief of the sick person, and it speaks of the remission of sins only conditionally, since extreme unction is not given except near the point of death, and directly, as its form sounds, tends toward the remission of sins. Add that James speaks of such an anointing whose end is health. The Papists, however, wish their anointing to be applied only to those who are in danger of life. Sixth, the cause, those administering regarding James's anointing are designated as many. Seven are said to be employed by Grotius. That, indeed, is not observed in the extreme unction of the Papists. Whence Cajetan says: James, he says, commands many presbyters to be called to one sick person, both praying and anointing, which is foreign to the rite of extreme unction. What? That Bellarmine, in On Extreme Unction, ch. 11, acknowledges that the anointing designated in Mark ch. 6 is not sacramental, because it was related only or chiefly to the healing of a bodily disease. Whence it follows, since Dionysius the Carthusian, Lyranus, and others admit that Mark and James are dealing with the same anointing, that this passage is not to be taken as referring to the sacrament of anointing. Finally, how greatly the Jacobean anointing differs from the Papistic is easily evident from these things: that the Pontificians do not anoint simply with oil, but the eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth, hands, feet, etc. that in the anointing of each member they use certain particular formulas, that they wish that anointing to be beneficial ex opere operato, whereas James ascribes it to the prayer of faith against health, that they invoke not only God, but also the saints. What? That the Apostolic anointing looks to those who possessed the gift of miracles, and certainly the special gift of healings, which gifts were proper to the primitive Church: and they did not always use oil, much less consecrated oil, but sometimes cured diseases by word alone, or by the touch of a hand, or by a shadow. That this gift granted to the Apostles and others in the primitive Church, as from Matt. 10:17, Mark 6:13, ch. 16:18, flourished still at this time when this epistle was written: And the Council of Trent itself, Sess. 14, ch. 1, acknowledges that James is dealing here with the same anointing which was insinuated by Christ in Mark 6:13. But Bellarmine proves (although Maldonato in ch. 6 of Mark grumbles) that that anointing, of which Mark 6 speaks, was not sacramental, first because it was referred only or chiefly to the healing of a bodily disease; second because the Apostles were not yet priests at that time; third because they anointed any sick persons indiscriminately; fourth because they did not ask whether those who were to be anointed were baptized or not. Bellarmine says that this opinion of his is that of Ruard, Jansenius, Dominicus à Soto, and others; and Aegidius Coningk agrees. Add that Bede has handed down that it was lawful for not only presbyters, but all Christians, in urgent necessity, to anoint the sick. Furthermore, to the Apostles and others, along with the gift of the power of healing, the gift of the discernment of spirits was also granted, so that it might be certain to which sick persons specifically the symbol of miraculous healing should be applied, lest by applying it rashly they might either profane the symbol of anointing or expose it to the mockery of infidels. And healing was obtained primarily by prayers, just as the Apostle here commends the power of prayer at length. Augustine (or whoever that author is) on the rectitude of Catholic conversation: Whenever any infirmity occurs to anyone, let not enchanters, diviners, or sorcerers be sought, etc., but let him who is sick trust in the mercy of God alone, and receive the Eucharist with faith and devotion, and faithfully seek blessed oil from the Church, with which his body may be anointed, and according to the Apostle, the prayer of faith will save the sick. Simeon Metaphrastes in his commentary on the deeds of the saints. milk, oil, with the prayer of the priest, he says, is held as a medicine for disease.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ἀσθενεῖ τις ἐν ὑμῖν;] Id est, si quis ægrotat. Ita verbum hoc sumitur Matth. X. 8. XXV. 36. Marci VI. 56. Luc. IV. 40. Phil. II. 26. 27. & alibi sæpe. Syrus כריה in co- lore est. Respondet ea vox Ebrææ חלה, ut videre est Prov. c. XXII. 35. Quod hic est ἀσθενεῖν, mox est κάμνειν.

Προσκαλεσάσθω τῆς πρεσβυτέρους τῆς Ἐκκλησίας.] Syrus לקשישא דעדתא. Solent ac hanc rem in Oriente adhi- beri presbyteri septem.

Καὶ προσευξάσθωσαν ἐπ' αὐτὸν] ἐπ' αὐτὸν עלוהו, id est, pro ipso.

Ἀλείψαντες αὐτὸν ἐλαίῳ ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Κυρίυ] Ex institu- to Christi Marci VI. 13. Nempe quia oleum apud Ebræos divinam gratiam significabat: ut & manuum impositio, quæ & ipsa circa ægrotos adhiberi solebat, Marci XVI. 18. Actor. c. XXVIII. 8. Omnia autem ista fiebant in nomine Christi, Marci XVI. 17. Act. III. 6. 16. XIX. 13. Proculus Christianus Seve- rum Imperatorem per oleum aliquando curavit. Testis Ter- tullianus ad Scapulam.

Pontificiis videtur gratificari velle Grotius, qui hinc sacramentum extremæ unctionis exsculpere satagunt: Quos vero rursus deserit, cum loca de miraculosa ad sanandum ægrotos unctione è Marc. VI. & XVI. huc affert: quod Papistæ in Ca- jetano locum præsentem de ea interpretante im- probant conciliis suis Florentino in decreto unio- nis & imprimis Tridentino Sess. XIV. Can. I. seqq. & cap. I. de extr. unct. innitentes. Pontificiis & eorum parastatis hæc opponimus argumenta: Pri- mum à causa Efficiente. Nam Sacramenta Novi Testamenti ab ipso Christo instituta sunt, fatente Thoma p. III. q. 64. art. 2. q. 72. art. 1. Unctionem autem hanc, de qua in præsenti, à Christo institu- tam non esse agnoscunt plerique Pontificii cum Lombardo. Deinde ad Sacramentum pertinet forma, quam hic orationem fidei dicit Cornelius à Lapide. Sed formulam in unctione extrema à Synodo Trid. sancitam, per istam unctionem &c. nuspiam vel S. Jacobus, vel quisquam alius ex Apo- stolis, nedum Christus ipse definivit. Tertio materiam faciunt oleum ab Episcopo benedictum: hic olei mentio fit, benedictionis mentio nulla, nedum ab Episcopo factæ. Quarto subjectum ungendum hoc in loco non est, qui in agone constitutus est vel lethaliter decumbens. Verbum ἀσθενεῖ infirmitatem quamvis notat, non extre- mam tantum & mortiferam: neque per κά- μνοντα solum lethaliter decumbens, aut jam- jam moriturus designatur, sed quivis infir- mus, ut Vulgata ipsa reddidit, vel qui ægrotat, ut Syrus exposuit. Quinto effectus un- ctionis Jacobeæ non est remissio peccatorum: quod urget inter alia Cajetanus: Nec ex verbis, nec ex effectu colligi potest, quod hæc verba loquantur de sacramentali extrema unctione, sed magis de un- ctione, quam instituit Dominus Jesus in Evangelio à discipulis exercendam in ægrotis. Textus enim non dicit, infirmatur quis ad mortem, sed absolute, infirmatur quis, & effectum dicit infirmi allevatio- nem, & de remissione peccatorum non nisi condi- tionaliter loquitur, cum extrema unctio non nisi prope articulum mortis detur, & directe, ut ejus forma sonat, tendat ad remissionem peccatorum. Adde quod Jacobus de tali unctione loquatur; cu- jus finis sit sanitas. Pontificii autem suam un- ctionem non nisi illis adhiberi velint, qui de vita periclitantur. Sexto causa administrantes circa Jacobi unctionem plures designantur. Septem à Grotio adhibiti dicuntur. Id vero in extrema unctione Papistarum non observatur. Unde Cajetanus: Jacobus, inquit, ad unum ægrotum multos presbyteros tum orantes, tum ungentes, vo- cari mandat, quod ab extremæ unctionis ritu alie- num est. Quid? quod unctionem etiam; Marci c. VI. designatam sacramentalem non esse agnoscit Bellarminus de extr. unctione cap. 11. quia relata fuerit solum aut præcipue ad curationem morbi corporalis. Unde consequens est, quum de ea- dem unctione Marcum & Jacobum agere, Dio- nysius Carthus. Lyranus & alii fateantur, neque hunc locum de sacramento unctionis accipien- dum esse. Quantopere denique distet Jacobea unctio à Papistica, ex hisce facile patet: quod Pon- tificii non simpliciter oleo ungant, sed oculos, au- res, nares, os, manus, pedes &c. quod in cujusque membri inunctione certas precularem formulas adhibeant, quod illam unctionem ex opere operato prodesse velint, quum Jacobus contra sanitatem orationi fidei adscribat, quod non Deum solum, sed etiam sanctos invocent. Quid? quod Apo- stolica unctio ad eos, qui pollebant miraculorum, & certe speciali sanationum dono, spectat, quæ dona primitivæ Ecclesiæ propria fuere: nec sem- per oleo adhibito, nedum consecrato oleo, sed so- lo interdum verbo, vel manus contactu, vel umbra morbos curarunt. Quod donum Apostolis, a- liisque in primitiva Ecclesia concessum, ut è Matth. X. 17. Marc. VI. 13. cap. XVI. 18. viguit ad- huc isto tempore, quo hæc exarata est epistola: Et de eadem unctione, quæ à Christo Marci VI. vers. 13. insinuata est, agere hic Jacobum agnoscit ipsummet Concilium Trident. Sess. XIV. cap. 1. Illam vero unctionem, de qua Marc. VI. non fuisse sacramentalem, probat Bellarminus l. c. (etsi frendente Maldonato in cap. VI. Marci) primum quia illa referebatur solum vel præcipue ad curatio- nem morbi corporalis; secundo quia Apostoli tum nondum erant Sacerdotes; tertio quia promiscue un- gebant quosvis ægrotos; quarto quia non quærebant, an essent baptizati, qui ungendi erant, necne? Quam suam sententiam Bellarminus dicit esse Ruardi, Jansenii, Dominici, à Soto & aliorum; annuitq; Æ- gid. Coningk. Adde quod Beda non solum Presbyte- ris, sed omnibus Christianis, urgente necessitate, lici- tum fuisse ægrotos ungere, tradiderit. Porro Apo- stolis aliisq; una cum dono δυνάμεως θεραπευτι- κῆς etiam donum discretionis Spirituum concessum, ut quibus præcise ægrotis miraculosæ sanationis symbolum applicandum esset, constaret, ne te- mere id adhibendo vel prophanarent unctionis symbolum, vel infidelium exponerent ludibrio. Et precibus imprimis obtinebatur sanatio, quem- admodum ideo Apostolus precum vim hic pro- lixe commendat. Augustinus (vel quisquis ille Autor) de rectitudine conversationis Catholicæ: Quoties aliqua infirmitas occurrerit alicui, non quæ- rantur præcantatores, non divini, non sortilegi &c. sed qui ægrotat, in sola Dei misericordia confidat, & Eucharistiam cum fide & devotione accipiat, ole- umque benedictum fideliter ab Ecclesia petat, unde corpus suum ungatur, & secundum Apostolum ora- tio fidei salvabit infirmum. Simeon Metaphr. in comment. rero gestar. lac, oleum, cum oratione Sa- cerdotis habitum dicit pro morbi medicina.

## 5:15
Verse 15.

And the prayer of faith shall save the sick person] The prayer of the presbyters as well as of the sick person himself, proceeding from faith in Christ. (For here too the genitive denotes the cause) obtains for the sick person the health of the body: namely, unless it is otherwise expedient for him for eternal salvation. See 2 Cor. 12:9, 1 Tim. 5:23, 2 Tim. ch. 4:20. To save is taken here as how to be saved, Matt. 9:21, 22, 14:30, Mark 6:56, and often elsewhere. And the Lord shall raise him up.] It will be Christ, not the presbyter, who will raise him up from his sickness. Thus Mark 1:31, coming to her, he raised her up. He will raise up. The expression is from there because those who are seriously ill are accustomed to lie down. Hence also the Latins say that those who recover their health rise. And if he has committed sins] Because sins are often the causes of diseases, Matt. 11:6, John 5:14, 1 Cor. 11:30. They shall be forgiven him] Namely, to a certain effect, so that he may not be absorbed by the disease. Moreover, he who was thus healed ought to take penance from the Church according to the manner of his sins, and fulfill it once taken, and thus be received to the full right of communion.

Therefore, restoration is not attributed to the oil, much less the remission of sins, but to the prayer of faith. Let the defenders of the Council of Trent see, therefore, how they can defend that, when they assert that there are two effects of anointing: one, that it heals the body, if it is so expedient for the soul; the other, that it wipes away the remnants of sins. This great champion certainly could not defend that. What Grotius hands down concerning penance to be taken by the Church from the sick person who has been restored, because they are said without any authority, they are refuted by the same authority by which they are affirmed. That all sick persons had fallen away from the communion of the Church in the primitive Church, so that they had need of some reception to the full right of communion, is in no way made plausible. Often, says Grotius, sins are the causes of diseases. Therefore, not all who are sick are to be accused of grave sins, so that they must be received into the full right of ecclesiastical communion by public penance.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Καὶ ἡ εὐχὴ τῆς πίςεως σώσει τὸν κάμνοντα] Oratio tam Presbyterorum quam ipsius ægrotantis, profecta ex fide in Christum. (Nam & hic genitivus causam notat) impe- trat ægroto salutem corporis: nempe nisi aliter ei expediat ad salutem æternam. Vide 2. Cor. XII. 9. 1. Tim. V. 23. 2. Tim. c. IV. 20. Σώζειν hic sumitur quomodo σώζεσθαι, Mat. IX. 21. 22. XIV. 30. Marc. VI 56. & alibi sæpe. Καὶ ἐγερεῖ αὐτὸν ὁ Κύριος.] Christus erit, non Presbyter, qui eum ex morbo eriget. Sic Marci I. 31. προσελθὼν ἤγει- ρεν αὐτήν. הקים Loquutio inde quia qui graviter ægro- tant, solent cubare. Hinc & Latini surgere dicunt eos, qui sanitatem recuperant. Κἂν ἁμαρτίας ἦ πεποιηκὼς] Quia sæpe peccata morborum causæ, Matth. XI. 6. Job. V. 14. 1. Cor. XI. 30. Ἀφεθήσεται αὐτῷ] Nempe ad certum effectum, ne à morbo absorbeatur. Cæterum debebat is, qui sic erat sa- natus, pro peccatorum modo pœnitentiam sumere ab Ec- clesia, & sumptam implere, & sic ad plenum jus communi- onis recipi.

Non ergo oleo tribuitur restitutio, nedum pec- catorum remissio, sed orationi fidei. Viderint er- go concilii Tridentini propugnatores, quomodo id tueri queant, cum asserunt, effectus unctionis duos esse: unum quod sanet corpus, si ita expediat animæ, alterum, quod abstergat reliquias peccatorum. Non potuit certe hic magnus Hyperaspites id tueri. Quæ de pœnitentia pro peccatorum modo ab ægroto restituto sumenda ab Ecclesia Grotius tradit, quia sine omni autoritate dicuntur, parili autoritate re- probantur, qua affirmantur. Ægrotos omnes ab Ecclesiæ communione excidisse in primitiva Ec- clesia, ut receptione quadam ad plenum jus com- munionis opus habuerint, nullo modo fit verisi- mile. Sæpe, inquit Grotius, peccata morborum causæ. Non ergo semper, qui ægrotant, gravium peccatorum sunt arguendi, ut pœnitentia publica recipi in communionis Ecclesiasticæ plenum jus debeant.

## 5:16
Verse 16.

Ἐξομολογεῖσθε ἀλλήλοις τὰ παραπτώματα] In the manuscript this is connected not badly with the preceding in this way: Ἐξομολογεῖσθε οὖν ἀλλήλοις τὰς ἁμαρτίας. Nor does the Latin read otherwise: Confess, he says, your sins: namely because the Church prays more effectively for sins known to it, applying at the same time suitable remedies to the evil, so that one does not fall back into it. See what we have said at Matt. III. 6. Acts XIX. 18. Add if you please Maimonides on Repentance.

This is a new precept, not pertaining to the sick: nor is the reading of one MS. to be preferred to other Codices: nor is the custom of the Christian Church to be learned from Maimonides. The subject here is mutual confession. But that is not mutual which is instituted by a sick person to Presbyters. The Papists strive to prove their special confession of sins from this passage. But the subject here is not confession to be instituted before Priests, nor did Grotius dare to affirm that expressly. Vasquez, however, in his treatise on penance, art. 1, quest. 60, openly denies that the precept of confession is proved from that passage, because many interpret it as concerning the confession which ought to be made mutually between brothers, so that they may be corrected. That is evident from Erasmus and Cajetan, indeed also from the interlinear gloss, and also from Scotus, 4 Sent. dist. 74. By saying, he says, confess one to another, he does not say more, confes- that confession must be made to a Priest, rather than to others. For he adds, pray for one another, that you may be saved. The Gloss on Penance, dist. V. de pœnit., denies that confession was instituted by James in the New Testament, and derives it from the tradition of the universal Church rather than from the authority of the New or Old Testament, and from there it determines that it is not used among the Greeks, because such a tradition did not emanate among them. How then that tradition of the universal Church, which emanated only among the Latins? Estius himself acknowledges that there is no lack of probability in the expositions of others, who interpret it either as that confession of sins by which the faithful acknowledge their guilt and seek pardon from those whom they have injured in some way, Matt. V. 24, or as that by which sins are uncovered to brothers for the sake of seeking counsel or the aid of prayers, and that Catholics hand down this latter one. Thence he leaves it free to choose which interpretation one wishes from these two, and that third one, which we have already noted among the Papists.

And pray for one another) In the Manuscript, pray (proseuchesthe). Standing, pray for the fallen. That you may be healed (Hopos iathete) That God may cleanse you who have fallen from your sins. For that does not happen to everyone.

It is not urged here that only those standing, nor are they commanded to pray only for the fallen, but it is enjoined that any faithful should pour out prayers for any Christians whatsoever, so that one may pray for another in every necessity, whether bodily or spiritual. The words 'for one another' openly imply mutual intercession. Whence many, as Estius admits, prefer that it be a general precept, by which the faithful are commanded to pray for one another; Nor does James say, 'that God may cleanse you who have fallen from your sins,' but 'that you may be healed' (hopos iathete): Which concern bodily health, just as the example of Elijah praying concerned the bodily good of the granting of rain.

The prayer of a righteous man avails much, being worked (energoumenē)] See John IX. 31, where we also cited the Greek verse: God is not a hearer of a righteous prayer. And he well added 'being worked,' that is, intent, efficacious, not languid. For in the Hebrew manner, the participle is used for the verbal 'energetic,' 1 Cor. XVI. 9, Philem. v. 26, Heb. IV. 12.

He understands the prayer not of just anyone, but of a righteous man, who has been justified through faith, and has a heart purified by faith, and pours out prayers in faith, James I. 6, ch. IV. 8, Acts XV. 9, Rom. V. 1, Eph. III. 12. A righteous man is a friend of God, and therefore has the right before Him to obtain, if he asks for something for another, that which pertains to salvation. But the prayer of a sinner, unless he has already departed from sin, as if proceeding from an enemy, is ungrateful to God, says Estius. Of great weight, says Basil, hom. 2 on prayer, is the aid of those who can bend God with prayers, and mutual supplications are not only salutary in this life, but when we depart from this life, they will provide us with abundant provisions for the future life.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Ἐξομολογεῖσθε ἀλλήλοις τὰ παραπτώματα] In manu- scripto connectitur hoc cum superioribus non male hoc mo- do: Ἐξομολογεῖσθε οὖν ἀλλήλοις τὰς ἁμαρτίας. Nec aliter Latinus legit: Fatemini, inquit, peccata: nempe quia effi- cacius orat Ecclesia pro peccatis sibi cognitis, adhibens si- mul idonea remedia malo, ne in id recidatur. Vide quæ di- ximus ad Matth. III. 6. Act. XIX. 18. Adde si placet Maimoni- dem de Pœnitentia.

Novum hoc est præceptum, non ad ægrotos pertinens: neque unius MS. lectio aliis Codicibus præferenda: aut Ecclesiæ Christianæ usus è Mai- monide discendus. Agitur hic de mutua exomo- logesi. At ea mutua non est, quæ ab ægroto Presby- teris instituitur. Pontificii ex hoc loco specialem suam peccatorum confessionem probare nitun- tur. Sed hic de confessione penes Sacerdotes instituenda non agitur, nec id diserte affirmare au- sus est Grotius. Vasquez vero tr. de pœnit. art. 1. quæst. 60. aperte negat probari ex illo loco præ- ceptum confessionis, quia multi interpretentur de confessione, quæ invicem fieri debet inter fratres, ut corrigantur. Patet id ex Erasmo & Cajetano, imo & è glossa interlineari, nec non è Scoto 4. Sent. dist. 74. Dicendo, inquit, confite- mini alterutrum, non magis dicit, confes- confessionem faciendam esse Sacerdoti, quam alii. Subdit enim, orate pro invicem, ut salvemini. Glossa in pœnitentia dist. V. de pœnit. negat confessionem institutam esse à Jacobo in Novo Testamento, & deri- vat eam ex universalis Ecclesiæ traditione potius, quam ex Novi vel Veteris Testamenti autoritate, & inde apud Græcos non adhiberi statuit, quia non emanavit apud illos traditio talis. Quomodo ergo illa universalis Ecclesiæ traditio, quæ tantum apud Latinos emanavit? Estius ipse agnoscit alio- rum expositionibus, qui vel interpretantur de ea peccatorum confessione, qua culpam agnoscunt, & veniam petunt fideles ab iis, quos aliqua injuria affecerunt, Matth. V. 24. vel de ea, qua peccata re- teguntur fratribus petendi consilii, vel precum au- xilii causa, non deesse probabilitatem, & hanc po- steriorem catholicos tradere. Inde liberum relin- quit, eligendi quam velit interpretationem ex hisce duabus, & illâ tertiâ, quam in Pontificiis jam notavimus.

Καὶ εὔχεσθε ὑπὲρ ἀλλήλων) In Manuscripto προσεύχεσθε. Stantes pro lapsis orate. Ὅπως ἰαθῆτε) Ut vos lapsos Deus à peccatis repurget. Non enim omnibus id contingit.

Non hic stantes solum compellantur, nec pro lapsis solum orare jubentur, sed ut quilibet fideles pro quibusvis Christianis preces fundant, præci- pitur, ut altero pro altero in omni necessitate sive corporali sive spirituali oret. Mutuam intercessi- onem verba ὑπὲρ ἀλλήλων aperte inferunt. Unde plerique, fatente Estio, malunt generale esse præce- ptum, quo jubeantur fideles orare pro sese mutuo; Nec dicit Jacobus, ut vos lapsos Deus à peccatis repurget, sed ὅπως ἰαθῆτε, ut sanemini: Quæ sa- nitatem corporalem respiciunt, quemadmodum & Eliæ precantis exemplum concernebat bonum corporale pluviæ concessionem.

Πολὺ ἰσχύει δέησις δικαίου ἐνεργουμένη] Vide Joh. IX. 31. ubi & Græcum versum attulimus: Εὐχῆς δικαίας ἐκ ἀνήκοος Θεός. Et bene addidit ἐνεργουμένη, id est, intenta, efficax, non lan- guida. Est enim more Ebræo participium pro verbali ἐνερ- γὴς 1. Cor. XVI. 9. Philem. v. 26. Ebr. IV. 12.

Orationem non cujusvis, sed justi, qui per fidem justificatus est, & cor habet purgatum fide, ac in fi- de preces fundit, Jac. I. 6. cap. IV. 8. Act. XV 9. Rom. V. 1. Eph. III. 12. intelligit. Justus amicus est Dei, & proinde jus apud eum habet impetrandi, si quid pro alio petat, quod ad salutem pertineat. Pecca- toris autem oratio, nisi jam à peccato recesserit, tan- quam ab hoste profecta, ingrata est Deo, inquit E- stius. Magni ponderis, inquit Basilius orat. 2. de precat. eorum auxilium est, qui possunt precibus fle- ctere Deum, & supplicationes mutuæ cum in hac vita salutares sunt, tum cum ex hac vita decedemus, co- piosum nobis viaticum ad futuram vitam suppedi- tabunt.

## 5:17
Ver. 17. Elijah was a man of like passions with us] And subject to the evils of death and life no less than we. We have the same noun 'homoiopathes' in Acts XIV. 15 and Wisd. VII. 3. Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus use it.

Adducing the example of Elijah, lest anyone say it was singular, he premises, he was a man like us, passible, 'homoiopathes.' The Gloss explains it as similar in the frailty of mind and flesh. Concerning the efficacy of his prayers, Chrysostom, hom. XVI, from various places in Matthew: The tongue of Elijah, he says, was as it were the key of heaven: for he was made as an arbiter, by whose nod rains were both restrained and flowed: Cf. Ambrose, book on Elijah, ch. 2. Augustine on faithful prayer, Sermon CCXXVI de tempore: The prayer of the righteous is the key of heaven: prayer ascends, and the mercy of God descends.

And he prayed with prayer] That is, he prayed intently: 'Energetically.' For verbal nouns added to verbs among the Hebrews signify vehemence. That it might not rain] 'tou' that is, 'heneka tou' (for the sake of). In Scripture we only have the drought predicted by Elijah and then the rain. But tradition adds that this was done at his prayers, and it is credible in itself. For the worship of Baal, accepted everywhere, extorted from a man full of zeal for God (for the whole history shows him to have been such) a demand for punishment, and conversely, the people having changed for the better, he himself easily turned to milder things. James did not derive this from tradition, but had it from divine inspiration. Prayer can also be understood in the words of Elijah, 1 Kings XVII. v. 1: The Lord lives, if there shall be dew or rain these years, except by the Word of my mouth. Tertullian, book against Psych., ch. 6, says that his (Elijah's) prayer was strengthened by fasting and abstinence: Chrysostom, Sermon II on Elijah, Vol. I of his works, p. 647. When the most holy Prophet Elijah saw the people had apostatized, and perceived that Baal and the groves were being worshipped by the sacrilegious, the Lord being despised, and that the whole people, having despised the Creator, had addicted themselves to figments and groves; moved by zeal for God, he condemned the land of Judea with a sentence of drought and sterility of rains. Then suddenly the earth gasps, the heaven is dried up, the rivers thirst, the fountains dry up. All moisture seeks the depths, deserts the heights, the air burns, serenity torments, tranquility is a punishment. The nights swelter, the days dry up, the crops are scorched, the shrubs sicken, the meadows fail, the groves languish, the fields fast, the earth is squalid, it destroys the herbs which it produced, all creation testifies to the wrath of God. Hunger is troublesome, where necessity finds that what it hungers for is lacking. Finally, punishment, because it torments: and guilt deserved a fitting punishment at some time. Late vengeance deserved a usurious punishment: and that which would eventually intervene worthily and deservedly was long delayed.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ἠλίας ἄνθρωπος ἦν ὁμοιοπαθὴς ἡμῖν] Et morti & vitæ malis obnoxius non minus, quam nos. Idem nomen ὁμοιοπαθὴς habemus Act. XIV. 15. & Sap. VII. 3. Utitur Pla- to, Aristoteles, Theophrastus.

Adducens Eliæ exemplum, ne quis singulare id dicat, præmittit, homo similis erat nobis passibilis, ὁμοιοπαθής. Glossa exponit, similis mentis & car- nis fragilitate. De efficacia precum ejus Chrysosto- mus hom. XVI. ex variis Matth. locis: Eliæ, in- quit, lingua fuit quasi cæli clavis: factus enim est vel- ut arbiter, cujus nutu & cohiberentur, & defluerent imbres: Cons. Ambros. l. de Elia c. 2. Augustinus de fideli oratione Serm. CCXXVI. de tempore: Ora- tio justi clavis est cæli: ascendit precatio, & descen dit Dei miseratio.

Καὶ προσευχῇ προσηύξατο] Id est, intente oravit: Ἐνεργῶς. Nam verbis addita verbalia apud Ebræos vehementiam significant. Τῦ μὴ βρέξαι] τῦ id est, ἕνεκα τῦ. In Scriptura tantum habemus prædictam ab Elia ἀνομβρίαν & deinde imbrem. Sed traditio addit factum hoc ad ipsius preces, & est id per se credibile. Nam & cultus Baalis passim receptus viro pleno ardoris pro Deo (talem enim eum fuisse tota ostendit historia) extorsit pœnæ postulationem, & contra populo ad meliora mutato facile & ipse ad mitiora se vertit. Non ex traditione hoc Jacobus deprompsit, sed ex inspiratione divina habuit. Potest etiam precatio in verbis Eliæ intelligi, 1. Reg. XVII. v. 1. Vivit Dominus, si erit his annis ros, aut pluvia, nisi per Verbum oris mei. Ejus (Eliæ) orationem jejunio atque abstinentia fuisse roboratam Tertull. l. advers. Psych. c. 6. ait: Chrysostomus, Serm. II. de Elia Tom. I. oper. p. 647. Cum Elias Propheta sanctissimus populum prævaricatum aspiceret, cumque Baal & lucos, despecto Domino, coli à sacrilegis pervideret, cumque creatore despecto, figmentis sese, nemoribusque omnis populus addixisset; zelo Dei commotus, Judæam terram siccitatis sententia & pluviarum sterilitate addixit. Tunc subito anhelat terra, siccatur cælum, sitiunt amnes, fontes arescunt. Omnis humor petit ima, supera deserit, aër fervet, serenitas torquet, tranquillitas pœna est. Æstuant noctes, dies arescunt, sata torrentur, arbusta ægrotant, prata deficiunt, nemora languent, campi jejunant, squallet terra, herbas, quas produxit, interimit, iram Dei universa creatura testatur. Molesta est fames, ubi quod esurit, necessitas deesse invenit. Tandem pœna, quod torqueat: & culpa meruit competens aliquando supplicium. Sera ultio fæneratam meruit pœnam: & diu dilatum est, quod quandoque digne ac merito interveniret.

## 5:17
And it did not rain upon the earth] In the lands of the ten tribes. Menander mentions this drought in the history of the Phoenicians, as Josephus teaches us in VII. 7. Three years and six months] So also in Luke IV. 25, where there is no need for what was said by us to be repeated here. And he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain] 1 Kings ch. XVIII. 45. And the earth brought forth its fruit] For the drought had been the cause of the failure of the crops, as we see in 1 Kings XVIII. 2. Add Deut. XXVIII. 12, 23, 24. Conversely, timely rain is the cause of fertility, Is. XXX. 23, and above 7. That he prayed again is gathered from 1 Kings XVIII: Elijah went up to the top of Carmel, and bowed himself down to the earth and put his face between his knees, namely for the sake of praying. For this prostration of the body and composition of the limbs was that of one praying humbly. And that he prayed seven times to obtain rain is apparent from the fact that he sent his servant as many times to go toward the sea, to see if any cloud might rise there. He meanwhile repeating the turns of prayer, until he was heard: concerning which furthermore Chrysostom in the same place says: After the Lord saw the shattered people, having had pity, He commands Elijah to descend from the mountain, He commands him to gather the whole people, so that with the sacrifice completed he might cause the rains to come, which he had previously denied to the wicked people: and that Elijah might be the author of the rains being brought, so that he who had shown the anger of a moved God might also demonstrate the benevolence of a placated one. Finally, Elijah stood in the middle between God and the people. He stood, I say, a holy man among the sacrilegious, a just man among sinners, a devout man among the profane, about to provide advocacy for all the peoples; he rebukes the people, he beseeches GOD, he averts the anger of the LORD, and he recalled the erring people from the worship of gods to the worship of GOD. He joins the Lord to the people, and the people to God. Through Elijah a single concord is made between God and man, between the people and the parent. And that all might say, truly the Lord God himself is God, the word of the most holy Elijah is the key of heaven. For he commands, and it is closed; he prays afterwards, and it is opened. He closes, he says, heaven and opens it, binds and looses, unlocks what he has shut.

Latin:

Καὶ ἐκ ἔβρεξεν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς] In terris decem tribuum. Hujus ἀνομβρίας in Phœnicum historia meminit Menander, ut Josephus nos docet VII. 7. Ἐνιαυτὸς τρεῖς κὴ μῆνας ἓξ] Sic & Luc. IV. 25. ubi quæ à nobis dicta nihil opus hic repeti. Καὶ πάλιν προσηύξατο, καὶ ὁ ὐρανὸς ὑετὸν ἔδωκε] 1. Reg. c. XVIII. 45. Καὶ ἡ γῆ ἐβλάστησε τὸν καρπὸν ἀυτῆς] ἀνομβρία enim causa fuerat deliquii frugum, ut videmus 1. Reg. XVIII. 2. Adde Deut. XXVIII. 12. 23. 24. Contra pluvia tempestiva causa fœcunditatis, Es. XXX. 23. & supra 7. Quod iterum orarit è 1. Reg. XIIX. colligitur: Elias ascendit in Carmeli verticem, & pronus in terram posuit faciem suam inter genua sua, scilicet orandi causa. Nam hæc corporis abjectio, membrorumque compositio erat humiliter orantis. Et septies eum orasse pro impetranda pluvia inde apparet, quod toties miserit puerum suum ad proficiscendum contra mare, num ibi nubes aliqua adscendat? Ipse interim orandi vices repetens, donec exaudiretur: de quo porro Chrysostomus l. c. Postquam Dominus populum quassatum vidit, miseratus jubet Eliam de monte descendere, jubet eum universum populum congregare, ut sacrificio perfecto pluvias venire faceret, quas scelerato populo antea denegasset: afferendisque pluviis Elias autor existeret, ut qui commoti Dei iram ostenderat, iedem & placati benevolentiam demonstraret. Denique stabas Elias medius inter Deum & populum. Stabat, inquam, inter sacrilegos sanctus, inter peccatores justus, inter profanos devotus, advocationem populis cunctis præstiturus objurgat populum, exorat DEUM, iram DOMINI avertit, & errantem populum à Dei cultura ad Dei latriam revocavit. Conjungit Dominum populo, & Deo populum. Fit per Eliam una concordia inter Deum & hominem, inter populum & genitorem. Et ut u- niversi dicerent, vere Dominus Deus ipse est Deus, clavis cæli sit sermo Eliæ sanctissimi. Jubet enim, & clauditur, orat postmodum & aperitur. Clau- dit, inquit, cælum & aperit, ligat & solvit, rese- rat quod conclufit.

## 5:18
Verse 18.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

## 5:19
Vers. 19. Brethren, if any of you do err from the truth.] He calls that way of life the way of truth, which the Gospel prescribes, which is eminently called truth Rom. XV. v. 8. 2. Cor. IV. 2. chap. VI. v. 7. Gal. II. v. 5. 14. chap. III. v. 1. chap. V. v. 7. Eph. I. v. 13. chap. IV. v. 24. Coloss. I. v. 5. 2. Thessal. II. v. 10. 12. 13. 1. Tim. II. v. 4. chap. III. v. 15. here above I. 18. 1. Petr. I. 22.

And if any one turn him) If any one leads him away by good admonitions from injustice, from envy, from hatred, from the facility of swearing, and similar things. The mystical sense of the precept, which is Deut. XXII. 1.

These things concern not only those seduced by sins, but also those who fall away from the Evangelical doctrine, and thus are to be led back into the way of truth. If any one shall have erred from the truth, which brings in not life primarily, but the doctrine of truth, from which we fall away both through apostasy from the faith and through sins that shake off faith. Truth, says Estius, he calls the right rule of living, which comprises these two things: sound faith and holy conversation. Heretics err from sound faith; bad Christians from holy conversation. Therefore, to err from the truth is a periphrasis for a sinner. But he is said to convert this person who applies those external aids, with the subsequent effect, which God has established to be applied to sinners being recalled from error, such as prayers to God, doctrine, exhortation, correction, chastisement, although otherwise it is God alone who can properly turn the hearts of men to himself. The Apostle had admonished about helping brothers, that they might be healed; now he admonishes about helping them, that they might be led back into the way. That concerned the health of the body; this, the health of the soul. He wanted that to be done by prayers or intercessions; this, by information, though prayers are not neglected. He had admonished: Confess your sins one to another, and pray for one another. Now, therefore, he indicates of what importance it is to procure the conversion of one's neighbor, both by information and by prayer; Compare Matt. XVIII. 15. seqq. Gal. VI. 1. seqq. No good man, says Leo in his Sermon on St. Lawrence, is good to himself alone, nor is the wisdom of any wise man friendly to himself only, and this is the nature of true virtues, that they lead many away from dark error.

Latin:

Vers. 19. Ἀδελφοὶ, ἐάν τις ὑμῶν πλανηθῇ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀληθείας.] Viam veritatis vocat illam vitæ rationem, quam præscri- bit Evangelium, quod eminenter veritas dicitur Rom. XV. v. 8. 2. Cor. IV. 2. cap. VI. v. 7. Gal. II. v. 5. 14. c. III. v. 1. cap. V. v. 7. Eph. I. v. 13. c. IV. v. 24. Coloss. I. v 5. 2. Thessal. II. v. 10. 12. 13. 1. Tim. II. v. 4. cap. III. v. 15. hic supra I. 18. 1. Petr. I. 22.

Καὶ ἐπιστρέψῃ τις αὐτόν) Si quis eum bonis abducat mo- nitis ab injustitia, ab invidia, ab odio, à facilitate jurandi & similibus. Sensus mysticus præcepti, quod est Deut. XXII. 1.

Non tantum per peccata seductos hæc concer- nunt, sed etiam eos, qui à doctrina Evangelica de- ficiunt, adeoque in viam veritatis reducendi sunt. Si quis erraverit ἀπὸ τῆς ἀληθείας, quæ non vitam primo, sed doctrinam veritatis inferunt, à qua deficimus tum per apostasiam à fide, tum per peccata excutientia fidem. Veritatem, inquit Estius, vocat rectam vivendi regulam, quæ comple- ctitur hæc duo, sanam fidem, & sanctam conversa- tionem. A sana fide aberrant hæretici, à conver- satione sancta mali Christiani. Errare igitur à ve- ritate est periphrasis peccatoris. Hunc autem con- vertere dicitur, qui ea foris adhibet adminicula sub- sequente effectu, quæ revocandis ab errore peccatori bus adhibenda Deus constituit, ut preces ad Deum, doctrinam, exhortationem, correptionem, castigatio- nem, cum alioqui solus Deus sit, qui hominum corda proprie possit ad se convertere. Monuerat Aposto- lus de juvandis fratribus, ut sanentur, jam de iis ju- vandis, ut in viam reducantur, monet. Illud con- cernebat sanitatem corporis, hoc sanitatem ani- mæ. Illud precibus vel intercessionibus fieri vo- lebat, hoc informatione, non neglectis tamen pre- cibus. Monuerat: Confitemini invicem peccata vestra, & orate pro invicem. Jam ergò indicat, quanti momenti sit, procurare proximi conversio- nem tum informatione, tum oratione; Confer. Matth. XIIX. 15. seqq. Gal. VI. 1. seqq. Nullus bonus inquit Leo Serm. de S. Laurent. sibi soli bonus est, nec cujusquam sapientis sibi tantum amica est sapien tia, & hæc verarum natura virtutum est, ut mul- tos a tenebroso abducant errore.

## 5:20
Vers. 20. He shall save a soul from death) In the Manuscript, his soul. He will be the cause of salvation to him who had sinned. A similar expression Rom. XI. 14. 1. Tim. IV. 16. Jude v. 23. But he is rightly said to be snatched from death not only he who is first led to Christianity, but also he who is led back from a vicious life to a life convenient to Christianity. See the example 1. Cor. III. 15.

That a soul may be saved from death, it is necessary that the ignorance of the mind be driven away, the hardness of the heart be removed, and finally that the whole man give himself to justice and holiness, Acts chap. XXVI. 18. Eph. I. 14. chap. IV. 18. seqq. Ezech. XI. v. 19. A great thing is the soul, which, redeemed by the blood of Christ, exclaims Bernard, epistle LIV.

And shall cover a multitude of sins) He will cause God to dissimulate those former sins of the now converted person, and as it were place them out of his sight. To cover is to forgive, as can be seen in Ps. XXXII. 1. where in the Greek, whose sins have been covered. In this sense, a wise man is said to cover the sins of others in the Talmud, title Balthra, section VIII.

Grotius more rightly understands these things concerning the sins of those who had been snatched away from the way of truth and justice, than either Pope Zacharias in Epistle I to Boniface and Bede concerning the sins of him who converts the seduced, or even Salmero, Lorinus, Corn. à Lapide, who drag these to the sins of both the converter and the converted. For his sins are covered, that is, are remitted, whose soul is said to be saved. Therefore, those are not to be heard who think this refers to the passage of Prov. X. 12, charity covers all sins, which is the persuasion not only of the Papists, Cornelius à Lapide, and Estius, but also of Pareus and the Belgian Interpreters. For those erring are not led back into the way of truth by charity, but by information. Charity does not cover sins otherwise than by patiently bearing, excusing, and interpreting everything in the better part, as far as is permitted, 1. Cor. XIII. 5. seq. But he who converts a soul by the divine word covers sins by urging repentance and by setting forth the redemption and merit of Christ, so that those who are converted may obtain remission of sins through repentance and faith, Acts II. 38. chap. III. 19. 1. Tim. IV. 16. The blessing of him who is about to perish comes upon him, says Gregory the Great concerning such a one, book XIX of Morals, chap. 12, when he prevents the destruction of the sinner, and when he leads him back from the pit of guilt with holy exhortations. If any one has recalled an erring person into the way, he has done a greater work than if he had recalled a dead person to life, because he snatched a miserable man from the jaws of hell, says Osiander. CONVERT US, AND WE SHALL BE CONVERTED; FOR THOU ART THE LORD OUR GOD! Jerem. XXXI. 18.

TO THEE, O LORD, BE GLORY FOR EVER AND EVER! AMEN!

Latin:

Vers. 20. Σώσεὶ ψυχὴν ἐκ θανάτε) In Manuscripto τὴν ψυχὴν ἀυτοῦ. Causa erit salutis ei, qui peccaverat. Par lo- quutio Rom. XI. 14. 1. Tim. IV. 16. Judæ v. 23. Recte autem à morte eripi dicitur non tantum qui primum ad Christianismum perducitur, sed & qui à vita vitiosa ad vi- tam Christianismo convenientem reducitur. Vide exem- plum 1. Cor. III. 15.

Ut animæ à morte servetur, opus est, ut mentis ignorantia pellatur, cordis durities tollatur, totus denique homo se justitiæ & sanctitati dedat, Act. c. XXVI. 18. Eph. I. 14. cap. IV. 18. seqq. Ezech. XI. v. 19. Magna res anima, quæ Christi sanguine redem- pta, exclamat Bernhardus epist. LIV.

Καὶ καλύψει πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶν) Efficiet ut illa jam con- versi peccata priora Deus dissimulet, & quasi extra con- spectum suum ponat. Καλύπτειν כסה est condonare, ut videre est Pf. XXXII. 1. ubi in Græco ὧν ἐπεκαλύφθησαν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι. Hoc sensu vir sapiens dicitur tegere aliorum pec- cata in Thalmude titulo Balthra, sectione VIII.

Rectius ita Grotius hæc de peccatis eorum, qui à via veritatis & justitiæ abrepti fuerant, intelligit, quam vel Zacharias Papa Epist. I. ad Bonif. & Beda de peccatis ejus, qui seductum convertit, vel etiam Salmero, Lorinus, Corn. à Lapide, qui ad peccata tam convertentis, quam conversi hæc abripiunt. Ejus enim peccata teguntur, hoc est, remittuntur, cujus anima servari dicitur. Non ergo audiendi, qui respici hic putant locum Prov. X. 12. charitas omnia peccata operit, quæ non modo Pontificiorum, Cornelii à Lapide, & Estii, sed etiam Paræi & Inter- pretum Belg. persuasio est. Nam non charitate, sed informatione reducuntur errantes in viam verita- tis. Charitas non aliter operit peccata, quam pa- tienter ferendo, excusando, & in meliorem partem, qua licet, omnia interpretando, 1. Cor. XIII. 5. seq. At qui verbo divino animam convertit, peccata operit, pænitentiam urgendo, ac redemptionem & meritum Christi sistendo, ut, qui convertuntur, per resipiscentiam & fidem remissionem peccatorum consequantur, Act. II. 38. c. III. 19. 1. Tim. IV. 16. Be- nedictio perituri super eum venit, inquit de tali Gre- gorius M. l. XIX moral. cap. 12. cum peccatoris inte- ritum prævenit, & cum sanctis exhortationibus à culpa fovea reducit. Si quis errantem in viam re- vocaverit, majus opus fecit, quam si mortuum in vi- tam revocasset, quia ex inferni faucibus miserum hominem eripuit, ait Osiander. CONVERTE TU NOS, ET CONVERTEMUR; QUIA TU DOMINE DEUS NO- STER ES! Jerem. XXXI. 18.

TIBI, DOMINE, SIT GLORIA IN ÆTERNA SECULA! AMEN!

# 1 Peter

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
IN THE NAME OF JESUS. ANNOTATIONS ON THE FIRST EPISTLE OF PETER.

Latin:

IN. J. ANNOTATA AD PRIOREM PETRI EPISTOLAM.

## 1:1 Introduction: Prolegomena
PROLEGOMENA.

The inscription of the Epistle reads thus: Πέτρε τῶ Ἀπο- sόλε ἐπισολὴ καθολικὴ πρώτη: Which indeed did not proceed from Peter, as the word πρώτη sufficiently teaches, nor from any of the Apostles, none of whom would easily have added the word καθολικὴ, which was also omitted by the Syrian; yet it is without doubt ancient, and as to the matter itself, not to be rashly called into doubt: except that

Erasmus gathers from chapter V. 12 that Peter had written some other epistle before this one, which can move no one: since if reference is made there to this very epistle, just as Paul, Heb. ch. XIII. 23, says, 'I have written to you in few words,' pointing to no other than the same epistle in which these things are read. That this is the first is sufficiently indicated by the second epistle, ch. III. 1. 'This, behold, beloved, I write to you as the second epistle,' he writes. But if you listen to Grotius, this is to be believed not the first, but the only one

Peter's epistle, and therefore that one: 'This now, beloved, I write to you as the second epistle,' will not be able to have a relation to that which is at hand. Whence not only a different Simon had to be invented by him, but also the name of Peter and of the Apostle had to be expunged in the latter, and the former [epistle] of the fictitious Simon must be established first, consisting of two chapters, so that chapter III may be heard as the second epistle of the same. Concerning which portent of opinion or of the new Critic at the beginning of the second epistle. There were also found at one time some who received this first [epistle] of Peter alone, which we shall likewise examine there. But concerning this one, no doubt at all was raised in the Church. Eusebius is a witness, book III of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 3: 'Of Peter, one epistle, the one called his former, is acknowledged; and the ancient elders have used this in their own writings as an undisputed one.' And afterwards: 'But the things named of Peter, of which I have known only one genuine epistle, and [it is] acknowledged among the ancient elders [so much].' See also St. Athanasius in the Synopsis, Jerome in the catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers and in the epistle to Paulinus, Innocent I in the fourth epistle to Exuperius, the Council of Laodicea, last chapter. Carthaginian [Council] III, chapter 47. Augustine, book II on Christian doctrine, chapter 8. Gelasius, the holy Roman [Council], distinction XV.

Concerning the Author of the Epistle, there is no reason for us to say more here, since the inscription will still suggest an occasion for speaking. To which we also reserve those to whom the epistle is written.

They bring forward a triple occasion. The first is the corruption of the Apostolic doctrine concerning faith, as if that could be true which is destitute of true piety: which Augustine handed down in 'On Faith and Works', chapter 14. The second was the doubt of some concerning the agreement of Peter's doctrine with Paul's, for the sake of refuting which Paul even betook himself to Jerusalem to Peter and James, Galatians 1:18, 19; 2:12, and approved the Pauline epistles with a notable eulogy, 2 Epistle 3:16. The third was the persecution of those to whom the Apostle wrote, concerning which one may read in chapter 2:12, 4:14 ff., 5:9, 10. The argument is clear from the recapitulation of chapter 5:12 itself: 'I have written to you in few words, exhorting and testifying that this is the true grace of God in which you stand.' The state of the epistle, therefore, is first of all exhortatory, that they may persist in faith and piety just as they had been informed and established, and not allow themselves to be led away by the false persuasions of others or even by grave persecutions; that this is the ultimate scope, the exhortations and conclusions always tending toward that in this epistle testify. Then, indeed, it is informative, because they are further instructed in the doctrine of the Christian religion, which is a super-attestation, if I may so call it, that is, a further testimony beyond that which they had received, whether from Paul or from other Apostles, or from Peter himself, a testimony concerning Christ and his benefits, and concerning the duties of those called to Christ and reborn. Concerning which Athanasius in the Synopsis: 'He wrote this epistle rather for the sake of teaching to the Jews converted to Christianity, who were established in the dispersion. For after many from among the Jews believed, he confirms them.' Therefore Flacius [says] of this epistle: 'Its form, he says, seems indeed to be parenetic, but yet it is also didactic.' What? That if one considers the order of the treatment, it is first didactic: but in the second part it is finally parenetic: since from that information exhortations are deduced, and furthermore the exhortations are so instituted that doctrines are mixed in from time to time, and those [exhortations] are fortified by them.

Therefore, having premised the inscription in chapter 1:1, 2, which is so adorned that they may be informed summarily at the same time concerning the benefits of election, sanctification, and redemption exhibited by the Father in the power of the Holy Spirit through Christ, he begins from the blessing of God; on account of regeneration, faith, and joy, even in temptations: accordingly, he teaches concerning regeneration and its causes: concerning faith, from which [he teaches] its origin, and its preservation, and its probation, and its end: concerning the hope of salvation: and salvation itself: concerning spiritual joy; concerning the cross and affliction, and its use: concerning the acquisition of salvation, and its prediction both by the Prophets in the Old Testament, as regards the afflictions of Christ and the glories that would follow them, and the announcement made in the New Testament through the Apostles and other heralds of the Gospel, up to verse 12. Whence is built up an exhortation to faith, and new obedience, and holiness, verses 13, 14, 15, 16, 17. But in such a way that the argument of the exhortation is deduced from the redemption of Christ previously insinuated, and for that reason the Apostle returns to this principal doctrine concerning the ransom of the blood of Christ, so that we may have faith and hope, verses 18, 19, 20, 21, and likewise a tacit reminder is inferred both concerning fostering the obedience of faith and concerning keeping mutual charity: because they are therefore reborn through the Word of the living God, remaining forever, that is, the Gospel brought to them, verses 22, 23, 24, 25.
