From which benefit of regeneration, the duty of owed piety is further deduced parenetically in chapter 2, both in general, when the Apostle exhorts to the growth of the reborn, verse 1. and 2, but in such a way that he seems to pursue the teaching more, celebrating the kindness of the Lord which the reborn have tasted, verse 3, and describing him as a living and chief stone, upon whom the faithful are built, to the end that they may offer spiritual sacrifices to God through faith, and not stumble through unbelief, verse 4 ff., and exhibiting the benefit of conversion, through which they were made a chosen race to preach the grace of God, verses 9, 10, then in particular, partly regarding the parts of the duty of the faithful, which are to abstain from carnal lusts, verse 11, and honest conversation among the Gentiles, verse 12, partly regarding diverse states, especially of subjects, whom the Apostle exhorts to obedience, verse 13 ff., and of servants, whom he wishes to be subject even to wicked masters with fear, verse 18 ff. Whence it is clear that the former part of chapter II is more didactic: And although a most sweet exhortation was interjected for the growth of the newly begotten: yet the doctrinal part of the epistle is rightly extended to v. 10 of the second chapter: since not only those things which are handed down concerning the kindness of the Lord, and concerning that precious stone, pertain to doctrine, but also those things which were said concerning the ἀδόλῳ milk of the Word, through which we grow; just as also in the first chapter the constancy of faith was primarily inculcated, with which indeed the Apostle taught that holiness and Φιλαδελφίαν, v. 13 seqq., and also 21 seq., cohere in an inseparable bond, so that the exhortations to the pursuit of piety might flow in more sweetly, offered with the milky sweetness of divine benefits.

There follows, therefore, the other part of the epistle, to be denominated thus from the more important [part] as Parenetic, from v. 13 of ch. II to the votive epilogue at ch. V. 9, in which, however, doctrines are continuously inserted, not only concerning our duties, but also concerning the benefits of Christ our Redeemer, so that they may be consolidated primarily in faith. For as regards those [duties], in ch. II information is handed down concerning the Efficient cause and the end of the Magistrate, v. 13, 14, concerning the will of God, v. 15, 16, concerning the good pleasure of God, v. 19; but as regards these [benefits], it pleased the Holy Spirit to set forth the passion of Christ a little more prolixly, not only as an example, but also as to its merit, so that from this faith might be confirmed, and from that patience might be sharpened, and for the sake of the calling and conversion of the faithful it might be recalled to mind, v. 21 to the very end of the chapter.

The Apostle proceeds, however, to special exhortations, ch. III, regarding the duties of wives v. 1 & seqq. and of husbands v. 7. & in general of all, v. 8. 9. the doctrine concerning the end of the calling is inserted again, with the inheritance of the blessing, which he fortifies with Davidic authority, v. 10. et seqq. exhorting primarily to the enduring of persecutions by a constant profession of faith, v. 13. et seqq. having proposed the example of the obedience of Christ in his passion, v. 18. and the disobedience of the first age, v. 19. 20. as well as the end of baptism prefigured by the flood, v. 21. 22. On which occasion he again performed the office of instruction, and concerning the end of the passion of Christ, concerning the descent of the quickened Christ to the underworld, concerning the incredulity of the antediluvian world, the cause of the condemnation of the same: concerning the efficacy of baptism, and the cause of the same, of Christ delivered to death for us, his resurrection, and his exaltation to the right hand of God.

Similarly he continues in chap. IV. the exhortation to newness of life, having proposed both the state of conversion, v. 2. 3. 4. and the final judgment, which is imminent, v. 5. 6. 7. admonishing primarily concerning the duty of sobriety and charity, to verse 11. as well as concerning the patiently bearing of the cross, verse 12. et seqq. with a caution, that no one be afflicted for misdeeds, verse 15. setting forth both Christ, who suffered for us in the flesh; and the blessedness of those who are afflicted in the name of Christ, and the divine ordination and will, concerning which v. 17. 18. 19.

In the last chapter he exhorts the Presbyters to the true care of rightly feeding the flock of Christ, v. 1. et seqq. and stirs up the younger to perform their duty especially toward the elders, v. 4. 5. Finally, he commends to all humility toward God, v. 5. 6. trust in divine providence, v. 7. vigilance against the Devil, whom one must resist through faith, v. 8. 9. With an epilogue added, which consists of a prayer for the strengthening of the faithful, v. 10. as for whose sake the Apostle had exhorted his own to it, and a δοξολογίᾳ v. 11. as well as a brief ἀνακεφαλαιώσει, v. 12. and salutations announced, v. 13. and commanded, with a final wish, v. 14.

There are therefore three parts of the epistle: I. Εἴσοδος, c. I. v. 1. 2. II. Διέξοδος, from v. 3. to chap. V. v. 9. III. Ἔξοδος or ἐπίλογος, v. 10. et seqq. The middle part or the treatment itself is two-fold: First, dogmatic concerning the benefits of Christ, c. I. 3. to c. II. 10. second, Parenetic concerning the duties of Christians: the titles of which, if anyone desires them specifically, in the former is contained both the application of salvation in regeneration, chap. I. 3. et seqq. and the acquisition of salvation, v. 10. et seqq. and the commendation of both doctrines, as sincere milk, so that the regenerate may grow, and being built up through faith upon the stone rejected by men, but chosen by God, they may be built as living stones, c. II. 1. et seqq. In the latter, however, occur the rules of living, first special ones concerning subjects and servants, though with general ones premised, verse 11. et seqq. chap. II. & concerning wives and husbands with exhortations subjoined; both concerning the performing of good, and the tolerating of evil: chap. III. Which are further declared in c. IV. how, as far as the former is concerned, one must live not according to the lusts of men, but according to the will of God, so that as far as we are concerned in sobriety, as far as our neighbor in charity, as far as God in the holy distribution of his gifts and graces, we may pass our whole life: but as far as the latter is concerned, that we may patiently bear the cross and persecution. Then c. V. rules are prescribed for Presbyters and the younger in particular, with peculiar rules also added concerning humility and trust toward God, and vigilance against the Devil.

Among the Interpreters, eminent from the ancients are Didymus, Bede, Oecumenius; from ours B. Huss, B. Selneccer, B. Gerhard. From the Reformed Bullinger, and Fr. Gomarus: From the Papists Cajet. Estius, Corn. à Lap. and Lorin.

Latin:

PROLEGOMENA.

INscriptio Epistolæ ita habet: Πέτρε τῶ Ἀπο- sόλε ἐπισολὴ καθολικὴ πρώτη: Quæ nõ qui- dē profecta est à Petro, quod satis docet vox πρώτη, nec ab Apostolorũ quopiam, quorũ null9 facile adjecisset vocem καθολικὴ, à Syro etiam prætermissâ; vetusta tamẽ sine dubio est, nec quo- ad rẽ ipsam temere in dubium vocanda: nisi quod

Erasmus Petrum ante hanc epistolam adhuc aliã quandam scripsisse è cap. V. 12. colligit, quod ne- minem movere potest: Siquidem ibi respiciatur hæc ipsa epistola, quemadmodum & Paulus, Ebr. c. XIII. 23. Perpaucis, inquit, scripsi vobis, non aliam, quam eandem, in qua hæc leguntur, indigitans epi- stolam. Hanc autem primam esse satis indicatur epistola posteriori, c. III. 1. Hanc ecce vobis, charis- simi, secundam scribo epistolam, scribens. Grotium v. si audias, hæc non prima, sed unica credenda est

Petri epist. ideoq; illa: Ταύτην ἤδη, ἀγαπητοὶ, δευτέ- ραν ὑμῖν γράφω ἐπισολὴν, relationem ad eam, quæ præ manib9 est, habere nõ poterunt. Unde fingen- dus ipsi non solum alius Simon fuit, sed etiam Petri & Apostoli nomen expungendum in posteriori, & illa fictitii Simonis prior constituenda, duo- bus nempe capitibus constans, ut cap. III. au- dire possit epistola secunda ejusdem. De quo por- tento opinionis vel novelli Critici sub initium al- terius epistolæ. Reperti etiam quondam nonnulli, qui hanc primam Petri solam recepere, quod pari- ter illic expendemus. De hac autem nullum plane dubium in Ecclesia motum fuit. Testis est Euse- bius libr. III. Hist. Eccles. cap. 3. Πέτρε μὲν ἓν ἐπι- ςολὴ μία, ἡ λεγομένη ἀυτὲ προτέρα ἀνωμολόγηται· Ταύτῃ δὲ κὴ οἱ πάλαι πρεσβύτεροι ὡς ἀναμφιλέκτῳ ἐν τοῖς σφῶν ἀυτῶν κατακέχρηνται συγγράμμασιν. Et postea: Ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν ὀνομαζόμενα Πέτρε, ὧν μίαν μόνην γνησίαν ἔγνων ἐπισολὴν, καὶ παρὰ τοῖς πάλαι πρεσβυτέροις ὁμολογημένον [τοσαῦτα]. Vid. & S. Athanasius in Synopsi, Hieronymus in catal. Scri- ptor. Eccles. & in epist. ad Paulin. Innocentius I. in epist. IV. ad Exuperium, Concilium Laodic. c. ult. Carthaginens. III. c. 47. August. libr. II. de doctr. Christian. cap. 8. Gelasius C. sancta Romana dist. XV.

De Autore Epistolæ non est, quod plura hic di- camus, quo de ἐπιγραφῇ occasionem dicendi ad- huc suggeret. Quo etiam reservamus eos, ad quos scripta est epistola.

Occasionem triplicem afferunt. Prima est corru- ptela doctrinæ Apostolicæ de fide, quasi ea vera esse possit, quamvis destituatur vera pietate: Quam Au- gustinus tradidit de fide & oper. c. 14. Altera fuit dubitatio quorundam de consensu doctrinæ Petri cum Paulina, cujus profligandæ gratia etiam Pau- lus Hierosolymam ad Petrum & Jacobum se con- tulit, Gal. I. 18. 19. II. 12. & Paulinas epistolas insigni elogio comprobavit, 2. Ep. III. 16. Tertia fuit perse- quutio eorum, ad quos scripsit Apostolus, de qua le- gere est c. II. 12. IV. 14. seqq. V. 9. 10. Argumentum è recapitulatione ipsius cap. V. 12. liquet, scripsi vobis paucis παρακαλῶν κὴ ἐπιμαρτυρῶν ταύτην εἶναι ἀ- ληθῆ χάριν τῆ θεῶ, εἰς ἣν ἑςήκατε, exhortans & su- perattestans, illam esse veram Dei gratiam, in qua sta- biliti estis. Status ergo epistolæ est primo quidem exhortatorius, ut in fide ac pietate, quemadmodum informati & stabiliti erant, persistant, non vero ab ea se per aliorum falsas persuasiones, aut graves etiam persecutiones abduci patiantur, quem sco- pum ultimum esse, paræneses & conclusiones eò semper tendentes in hac epistola testantur. Dein- de vero informatorius, quia in doctrina religionis Christianæ ulterius instruuntur, quæ est superatte- statio, ut ita vocem, hoc est, ulterior testificatio su- pra eam, quam acceperant, sive à Paulo, sive ab aliis Apostolis, ipso etiam Petro, testificationem de Christo, ejusque beneficiis, & de vocatorum ad Christum atque renatorum officiis. Quo de Atha- nasius in Synopsi: Potius docendi gratia epistolam hanc Judæis ad Christianismum conversis, in disper- sione constitutis, scripsit. Postquam enim ex Judæis multi crediderunt, confirmat eos. Ideo Flacius de hac epistola: Videtur quidem, inquit, ejus forma esse Pa- rænetica, sed tamen est etiam Didactica. Quid? quod ordine tractationis pensi habito primum Didactica sit: In altera vero parte demum Parænetica: quum ex illa informatione deducantur adhortationes, ac præterea adhortationes ita instituantur, ut subinde doctrinæ immisceantur, iisque illæ munian- tur.

Præmissa itaque ἐπιγραφῇ cap. I. 1. 2. quæ sic ad- ornata est, ut de beneficiis electionis, sanctificatio- nis & redemptionis à Patre in virtute Spiritus Sancti per Christum exhibitis, summatim si- mul informentur, ab εὐλογία Dei incipit; ob regenerationem, fidem, & lætitiam, etiam in tentationibus: Proinde docet de regeneratione, ejusque causis: de fide, qua originem, & con- servationem ac probationem, & finem ejus- dem: de spe salutis: ac salute ipsa: de lætitia spirituali; de cruce & afflictione, ejusque usu: de salutis acquisitione, ejusque tum à Prophetis in Veteri Testamento prædictione, quod ad Christi & afflictiones, & eas consequuturas glorias, tum in Novo Testamento facta per Apostolos, aliosq; Evangelii præcones annunciatione ad v. 12. Unde extruitur exhortatio ad fidem, & novam obedien- tiam, ac sanctitatem v. 13. 14. 15. 16. 17. Sed ita, ut argumentum παρακλήσεως deducatur è redempti- one Christi antea insinuata, eaque ratione red- eat Apostolus ad præcipuam hanc doctrinam de λυτρώσει sanguinis Christi, ut fidem & spem habea- mus, v. 18. 19. 20. 21, ac inferatur itidem commone- factio tacita tum de obsequio fidei fovendo, tum de charitate mutua custodienda: quod ideo rena- ti sint per Verbum viventis Dei, manens in æter- num, hoc est, Evangelium ad eos delatum, v. 22. 23. 24. 25. Ex quo regenerationis beneficio porro de- ducitur παραινετικῶς cap. II. pietatis debitæ offici- um, cum in genere, cum exhortatur Apostolus ad incrementa renatorum v. 1. & 2. sed ita ut dida- σκαλίαν magis persequi videatur, celebrans be- nignitatem Domini, quam gustarint renati, v. 3. eundemq; describens, ceu lapidem vivum ac præ- cipuum, super quem extructi sunt fideles, ea fini, ut offerant Deo hostias spirituales per fidem, non vero impingant per incredulitatem, v. 4. seqq. ex- hibensque beneficium conversionis, per quam fa- cti sunt genus electum ad prædicandam Dei grati- am v. 9. 10. tum in specie, partim quoad partes offi- cii fidelium, quæ sunt abstinere à carnalibus concu- piscentiis, v. 11. & conversatio honesta inter gen- tes, v. 12. partim quoad status diversos, imprimis subditorum, quos ad obsequium hortatur Aposto- lus, vers. 13. seqq. & servorum, quos cum timore etiam pravis dominis subjici vult, v. 18. seq. Unde luculentum est, partem priorem cap. II. magis esse Didacticam: Et quamvis suavissima interjecta fue- rit ad incrementum recens genitorum exhorta- tio: Doctrinalem tamen partem epistolæ recte extendi ad v. 10. capitis secundi: quum ad doctri- nam pertineant non tantum illa, quæ de benigni- tate Domini, deque lapide isto pretioso traduntur, sed etiam quæ de lacte Verbi ἀδόλῳ, per quod ado- lescimus, dicta sunt; quemadmodum & priori capi- te constantia fidei imprimis inculcata est, cum qua vero indivulso nexu cohærere sanctitate & Φιλα- δελφίαν, v. 13. seqq. nec non 21. seq. docuit Aposto- lus, ut eo suavius influerent paræneses ad pietatis studium cum lactea beneficiorum divinorum dul- cedine propinatæ.

Sequitur ergo pars epistolæ altera, à potiori sic denominanda Parænetica, à v. 13. c. II. ad epilogum usque votivum c. V. 9. in qua tamen doctrinæ jugiter inseruntur, non tantum de nostris officiis, sed etiam de Christi Redemptoris nostri beneficiis, ut imprimis in fide consolidentur. Nam quoad illa c. II. infor- matio traditur de causa Efficiente, ac de fine Magi- stratus, v. 13. 14. de voluntate Dei, v. 15. 16. de com- placentia Dei, v. 19. quoad hæc verò placuit Spiritui Sancto, paulo prolixius passionem Christi non in exemplum solum sistere, sed etiam quoad meri- tum, ut hinc fides confirmaretur, illinc vero pa- tientia acueretur, vocationis, & conversionis gratia fidelibus in mentem revocaretur, v. 21. ad finem usque capitis.

Pergit autem Apostolus adhortationes speciales, c. III. quoad officia uxorū v. 1. & seqq. & virorum v. 7. & in universum omnium, v. 8. 9. inserta iterum do- ctrina de fine vocationis, hæreditate benedictionis, quæ autoritate munit Davidica, v. 10. seqq. exhor- tans imprimis ad tolerandas persecutiones con- stanti fidei professione, v. 13. seqq. proposito exem- plo obedientiæ Christi in passione, v. 18. & inobe- dientiæ primi seculi, v. 19. 20. nec non fine baptismi per diluvium præfigurati, v. 21. 22. Qua occasione iterum informationis munere functus est, deque passionis Christi fine, de vivificati Christi descensu ad inferos, de incredulitate mundi antediluviani, causa condemnationis ejusdem: de efficacia ba- ptismi, & causa, ejusdem Christi in mortem pro no- bis traditi resurrectione, & evectione ad dextram Dei.

Similiter pertexit cap. IV. parænesin ad novita- tem vitæ, proposito tum conversionis statu, v. 2. 3. 4. tum judicio novissimo, quod imminet v. 5. 6. 7. commonefaciens imprimis de sobrietatis, & charitatis debito, ad vers. 11. nec non de patien- ter ferenda cruce vers. 12. seqq. cum cautione, ne quis ob maleficia affligatur, vers. 15. sistens tum Christum, qui pro nobis passus est in carne; tum beatitudinem eorum, qui nomine Christi affligun- tur, tum ordinationem & voluntatem divinam, de qua v. 17. 18. 19.

Postremo capite Presbyteros hortatur ad veram curam recte pascendi gregis Christi, v. 1. seqq. exci- tatque juniores ad faciendum officium præsertim erga seniores, v. 4. 5. Denique omnibus commen- dat humilitatem erga Deum, v. 5. 6. fiduciam in providentiam divinam v. 7. vigilantiam adversus Diabolum, cui resistendum per fidem, v. 8. 9. Ad- dito epilogo, qui constat comprecatione corrobora- tionis fidelium, v. 10. utpote cujus causa ad eam hortatus fuerat suos Apostolus, & δοξολογίᾳ v. 11. nec non brevi ἀνακεφαλαιώσει, v. 12. ac salutationi- bus annuntiatis, v. 13. & demandatis, cum voto finali, v. 14.

Sunt ergo tres epistolæ partes: I. Εἴσοδος, c. I. v. 1. 2. II. Διέξοδος, à v. 3. ad cap. V. v. 9. III. Ἔξοδος vel ἐπίλογος, v. 10. seqq. Media pars vel tractatio ipsa bimembris est: Primùm dogmatica de Christi beneficiis, c. I. 3. ad c. II. 10. secundo Parænetica de Christianorum officiis: quarum titulos specialîs si quis desiderat, in priori habetur tum salutis appli- catio in regeneratione, cap. I. 3. seqq. tum salutis ac- quisitio, v. 10. seqq. tum doctrinæ utriusque, ceu la- ctis sinceri commendatio, ut regeniti adolescant, & extructi per fidem super lapidem ab hominibus reprobratum, apud Deum vero electum, tanquam lapides vivi ædificentur, c. II. 1. seqq. In posteriori vero occurrunt regulæ vivendi, primum de sub- ditis ac servis speciales, præmissis tamen gene- ralibus, vers. 11. seqq. cap. II. & de uxoribus ac viris subjunctis adhortationibus; tum de præ- stando bono, tum de tolerando malo: cap. III. Quæ ulterius declarantur c. IV. quomodo, quan- tum ad prius, non concupiscentiis hominum, sed voluntati Dei vivendum, ut quoad nos in sobrieta- te, quoad proximum in charitate, quoad Deum in ejus munerum ac donorum sancta distributione vi- tam omnem transigamus: quantum vero ad poste- rius, patienter crucem & persequutionem fera- mus. Deinde c. V. Presbyteris & junioribus in specie regulæ præscribuntur, additis peculiaribus etiam regulis de humilitate & fiducia erga Deum, ac vi- gilantia adversus Diabolum.

Ex Interpretibus eminent è veteribus Didymus, Beda, Oecumenius; è nostris B. Hussus, B. Selneccer. B. Gerhard. E Reformatis Bullinger, & Fr. Goma- rus: E Pontificiis Cajet. Estius. Corn. à Lap. & Lorin.

## 1:1 Argument
PART I. OF THE EPISTLE DIDACTIC, Concerning the Benefits of Christ. CHAPTER I. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

After the inscription and the wish, Peter celebrates God, who regenerated the faithful unto salvation through the resurrection of Christ, he describes the salvation acquired through Christ, and exhorts to constant faith, and holiness, on account of the redemption made through the blood of Christ, and regeneration through the Word of the Gospel. There are three parts: I. The inscription, v. 1. 2. II. The description of the grace of God in Christ, v. 3. et seqq. regarding the application of salvation in regeneration to v. 10. and the acquisition of the same made through Christ, both predicted, v. 10. 11. and announced, v. 12. III. The commendation of the doctrine concerning the grace of God exhibited in Christ, so that we may hope in it, passing our life in filial fear, v. 13. et seqq. and that we may consider both our precious redemption, v. 18. et seqq. and the gracious regeneration of God, v. 21. et seqq.

PART I. OF CHAPTER I. The inscription of the epistle.

Vers. 1. Peter) The same name as Cephas, just as Thomas and Didymus are the same name. : This epistle has a vehemence, fitting the character of the Prince of the Apostles.

The inscription contains first the author of the Epistle; then the object, or those to whom it was written; thirdly, the wish. The author is described by his name and office. As to the name, he was called Peter and Cephas at his calling to the hope of the Apostleship, John 1:43, who was called Simon at his circumcision, son of Jonah, whence he was called now Peter, Gal. 2:14, now Cephas, 1 Cor. 3:22, 9:5, 15:5, Gal. 2:9, of which the former is a Greek name, the latter a Syriac one, and not, as Bellarmine foolishly prattles in his Analectus, in the supposititious Epistle 3, Tom. 1 of the councils, and in his book 1 on the Roman Pontiff, ch. 18, as if Cephas meant head in Greek, which Gomarus refutes at length here, and Cornelius à Lapide says it is clear that this is not the genuine etymology from the Greek language, but that it is a Syrian name. But he trifles perhaps, that Christ in this naming looked to a very high, rocky hill, which was called Kepha, near Jerusalem, from which the whole city could be seen: because, what this hill is to Jerusalem, that Peter is to the Church: which things are more worthless than fig-leaf trifles. We admit that Peter was the Prince of the Apostles, because he was first in order, by reason of his calling, Matt. 4:18, and I add, by a certain reason of dignity: but he ought not therefore to be considered the head of the Apostles: whom Cyprian testifies to have been of equal power in his work on the simplicity of prelates. Of which elsewhere. Peter calls himself not Prince of the Apostles, but a fellow-elder of the elders, ch. 5:1. Although this epistle is most excellent, yet the Pauline ones do not yield to it: That one certainly which was written to the Ephesians can easily compete with this in elegance, and in the weight of doctrine and words. And concerning all the Catholic ones, Jerome in his epistle to Paul. James, Peter, John and Jude published epistles as mystical as they are succinct and short, and equally long, short in words, long in meanings, so that there is rarely anyone who does not go blind in reading them. For the rest, Estius is correct: Whoever wishes to know how much Peter and Paul agree in doctrine, let him run through the sentences and every principal precept of this epistle: and he will find them wonderfully to agree with those things which Paul delivers in various epistles, and he will not doubt that the doctrine of both has proceeded from one Spirit.

Apostle of Jesus Christ) The Apostles are not accustomed to omit this dignity of theirs, which is indeed very great, at the beginnings of their epistles, so that their authority, and that the greatest, may be established in their writings. The name Apostle exhibits the office taken in a special sense, by which those are called Apostles who were called immediately by Christ to preach the Gospel throughout the world. However, we have already noted before that the name Apostle is not always prefixed to their Epistles.

Elect) To Christians, as Rom. VIII. 33. XV. 13. Col. III. v. 12. 2. Timoth. II. 10. Tit. I. 1. below II. 6. 9. To the Jews, clearly, for Peter was destined especially for them. It is a title taken from the Old Testament, in which the Israelites are בחירים elect, Is. LXV. v. 8. and elsewhere. Therefore the Apostles adapted the same name, and certainly with much better right, to those who believe in Christ. Whom GOD set apart for Himself for much greater holiness, as will follow now. See John ch. XV. v. 19.

He calls those to whom the epistle is written elect first: which Grotius, as it appears, understands generally of called Christians, just as in 1 Cor. I. 26, 27, the called are said to be elect, as also in Psalm CV the Israelites, and the Hebrews called to Christ, 1 Pet. ch. II. v. 9, and also the Colossians, ch. III. 12. But the elect here are rather to be understood in a special sense as those predestined to eternal life, as 2 Tim. II. 10, Tit. I. 1, which the added description teaches: because they are said to be elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father in sanctification of the Spirit unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ, v. 2, which is a description of the election made from eternity unto eternal life, Rom. VIII. 33, 2 Thess. II. v. 13, Eph. I. 4, not that he considered all to whom he writes to be elect, which certainly would not have been consistent with the truth, but because denomination is accustomed to be made from the more worthy part. For as Augustine says on the unity of the Church, ch. 12. Prophets and Apostles are accustomed to argue against those who are reprehensible in some people, as if all in that people were being argued against: and thus to address those who are praiseworthy, as if all were being praised. But that Christians are said to be Elect with a much better right than the Israelites cannot be admitted: for Christians, who were converted from the Gentiles to Christ, have approached the communion of the Israelites, Eph. II. 13, seqq. But the Israelites of the Old Testament were Messianic just as much as those who, after the coming of Christ, were called Christians converted from among the Israelites to faith in Jesus, because they were not saved by any other reason than these, and both obtained salvation through the grace of Christ, Acts XV. 11. Peter nowhere says that these were set apart for much greater holiness; indeed, he requires the same holiness that Moses did in the Old Testament, v. 16, from Levit. XIX. v. 2, than which also there can be none greater.

Moreover, Grotius understands here the elect from the Jews to whom the epistle was written, which also seemed right to most others, such as Eusebius, l. III. Hist. Eccl. cap. IV., Jerome in the catalogue, Didymus, Oecumenius, Cajetan, Erasmus, and also Cano, l. II. de loc. Theolog., Baronius, T. I. Annal., Ribera in the preface to the Hebrews, and others, nor does it displease us, provided it was written to those παρ᾽ ἐπιδήμοις διασπορᾶς, who were among the Gentiles, among whom the Jews were dispersed and were sojourners, and therefore they are commanded to have good conduct among the Gentiles, c. II. v. 12, and that the later one was also written to the Jews, which was written to the same people to whom the former was. Compare 2 epist. III. v. 15, cap. II. 1, just as also the ministry of the circumcision was committed particularly to Peter, Gal. II. 7. It must be noted, however, that although this epistle was written to the dispersed Jews, there were nevertheless among the Gentiles some converts also, with whom the Jewish Christians lived, to whom it is clear this epistle also pertains from ch. II. v. 10, where a prophecy from Hos. II. 23 is cited, which is explained by the Apostle as concerning the conversion of the Gentiles, Rom. IX. 25, and mention is made of the former state of paganism, ch. V. 14, ch. VI. 3, whence August. book XXII. against Faust. c. 89, Joh. Hesselius in this place, B. Luther, Osiander, Winckelmann, maintain that it was written to the Gentiles, which opinion, if it be accepted in the stated way, that it pertained primarily to the Jews and secondarily to the Gentiles, seems to be admissible. Although those Gentiles were not in the dispersion, which Gomarus urges for understanding it as Jews only, they nevertheless belonged to those sojourners, and together with them constituted one communion, which takes its name from the more worthy part. For the Gentiles were only proselytes with respect to the Jewish Church converted to Christ. Compare Acts II. and X. chapters. In which way B. Gerhard, with Estius, judged that both opinions could be reconciled.

Παρεπιδήμοις) תושבים. For that word is so translated in Gen. XXIII. 9 and Psalm XXXIX. 13; it signifies those dwelling abroad. See Heb. XI. 13, as below II. 11.

There are those who, as Estius notes, take sojourners metaphorically for those who, as pilgrims in this world, are tending toward the heavenly fatherland, as all Christians are called from 1 Epist. II. 11. But in this way one departs from the proper meaning, and the naming of particular places teaches that it was not directed to all Christians, although it is certain that by reason of use not only this epistle, but the whole Scripture is common to all Christians. Others understand proselytes who had been converted from paganism to Judaism, and thence to Christianity, in which way Lyranus interprets sojourners: But proselytes are one thing, sojourners another. Maldonatus in John VII. 35 understands Gentiles by sojourners: for these, dispersed throughout the whole world, were called the dispersion. Some interpret sojourners as Jews, COMING TO Christ and converted, which Cornelius attributes to Jerome, Athanasius, Didymus, Oecumenius, Ambrose, Catharinus, and Cajetan. He acknowledges, however, more correctly that the Christian Jews are indicated as the strangers of the dispersion of Pontus, Galatia, etc., who, both at other times and recently on account of the persecution stirred up by the Jews after the death of Stephen, Acts VIII. 1, had fled dispersed from Judea into Pontus, Galatia, etc., and were guests and strangers there.

Διασπορᾶς) Thus are called all the places in which the Israelites lived outside their homeland, at whatever time, and for whatever occasion those migrations had occurred, whether in wars, as through Tiglath-Pileser, Shalmaneser, and Nebuchadnezzar, or to avoid internal evils, for which reasons many withdrew both into Syria and into Egypt, and into other places of the Roman Empire. Nor should that dispersion be omitted here which had occurred after the death of Stephen, concerning whom Luke uses the word διασπαρέντες in Acts VIII. 4 and XI. 19. These are the נפצים of Isaiah LVI. v. 8. See also what we have said at James I. 1.

Πόντου) From this first-named region this epistle is said to be to the Pontians, as Tertullian calls them, and Cyprian, who follows him in many things. Moreover, all the regions named here are of the Roman Empire, not the Parthian, in which Babylon was. I think those are mistaken who either think only two dispersions are mentioned, or think Babylon was the head of those Jews who were throughout Asia, subject to the Romans. Media, Hyrcania, and those situated further away were under the Babylonian Patriarch: but Egypt, Libya, and those nearest to them were under the head of the Sanhedrin of Alexandria. All others were under the prince, that is, the נשי of the Jerusalemites, who later settled in Tiberias. In Colchis there were already long ago some of the Israelite nation from the deportation of Shalmaneser and Nebuchadnezzar, as we said in the Annotations to the first book on the truth of the Christian religion. But here it is a question of the Jews, of whom also in Acts II. 10, where mention is also made of Cappadocia and Asia, namely that in which Ephesus is. All these did not use the Chaldean version, but the Greek, and in that language Paul addressed them. In Philo, Agrippa says of Jerusalem: Μητρόπολις δὲ οὐ μιᾶς χώρας ἰουδαίας, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν πλείστων, διὰ τὰς ἀποικίας, ἃς ἔπεμ-

Latin:

PARS I. EPISTOLÆ DIDACTICA, De Christi Beneficiis. CAPUT I. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Post inscriptionem & votum celebrat Petrus Deum, qui regenuit fideles ad salutem per resurrectionem Christi, describit salutem per Christum acquisitam, & hortatur ad fi- dem constantem, ac sanctitatem, ob redem- ptionem per sanguinem Christi factam, & regenerationem per Verbum Evangelii. Partes tres sunt: I. Inscriptio, v. 1. 2. II. Gratia Dei in Christo descriptio, v. 3. seqq. quoad salutis ap- plicationem in regeneratione ad v. 10. ejusdemq; acquisitionem per Christum factam, tum prædi- ctam, v. 10. 11. tum annunciatam, v. 12. III. Do- ctrina de gratia Dei in Christo exhibita commen- datio, ut in eam speremus, in filiali timore vitam transigentes, v. 13. seqq. atque cogitemus tum pre- tiosam nostri redemptionem, v. 18. seqq. tum gra- tiosam Dei regenerationem, v. 21. seqq.

PARS I. CAPITIS I. Epistolæ inscriptio.

Vers. 1. Πέτρὸς) Idem nomen, quod Κηφᾶς, sicut idem nomen Θωμᾶς & Δίδυμος. : Habet hæc epistola τὸ σφοδρὸν, conveniens ingenio Principis Apostolorum.

Inscriptio primo Autorem Epistolæ; tum ob- jectum, seu eos, ad quos scripta; tertio votum con- tinet. Autor à nomine & officio describitur. Quod ad nomen, Petrus & Cephas dictus fuit in vocatione ad spem Apostolatus, Joh. I. 43. qui Si- mon in circumcisione vocatus est, filius Jonæ, unde promiscue modo Petrus, Gal. II. 14. modo Cephas appellatus est, 1. Cor. III. 22. IX. 5. XV. 5. Gal. II. 9. quorum illud Græcum, hoc Syriacum nomen est, non vero ut ineptit cum Analecto suo supposititio Epist. III. Tom. I. concil. Bellarminus l. I. de Rom. Pont. c. 18. quasi Κηφᾶς Græce significet caput, quod prolixè hic refellit Gomarus, Corn. à Lap. patere sit dicit, quod id non sit genuinum Etymon è Græca lingua, sed quod nomen Syrum sit. Nugatur autem forte, Christum respexisse hac nuncupatione ad præaltum scopulosum collem, qui Kepha vocatus sit, Hierosolymæ vicinus, ex quo tota urbs videri po- tuerit: quia, quod hic collis est Hierosolymæ, hoc Petrus sit Ecclesiæ: Quæ gerris ficulis vaniora sunt. Petrum Apostolorum Principem fuisse, quod pri- mus in ordine, ratione vocationis, Matth. IV. 18. addo & dignitatis certa ratione admittimus: non autem ideo Apostolorum caput haberi debet: quos paris potestatis fuisse Cyprianus testatur de simplici- tate prælator. De quo alias. Petrus non Principem Apostolorum, sed συμπρεσβύτερον se vocat Presbyte- rorum c. V. 1. Quanquam autem præstantissima hæc sit epistola, non tamen Paulinæ cedunt eidem: Ea certe quæ ad Ephesios exarata est, certare cum hac facile potest elegantia, ac doctrinæ & verborum pondere. Ac de omnibus Catholicis Hieronymus epist. ad Paul. Jacobus, Petrus, Johannes & Judas epistolas ediderunt tam mysticas, quam succinctas & breves pariter & longas, breves in verbis, longas in sententiis, ut rarus sit, qui in earum lectione non ca- cutiat. De cætero recte Estius: Qui volet co- gnoscere, quam consentiant in doctrina Petrus & Paulus, percurrat hujus epistolæ sententias & præcepta quæque præcipua: & inveniet, ea mirifice convenire cum iis, quæ Paulus tradit in variis epi- stolis, nec dubitabit ab uno Spiritu profectam esse utri- usque doctrinam.

᾿Απόστολος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) Non solent in epistolarum ini- tiis hanc suam dignitatem, sane maximam, omittere Apo- stoli, ut inde etiam scriptis ipsorum sua constet, eaque ma- xima, autoritas. Officium Apostoli nomen exhibet sensu præci- puo acceptum, quo Apostoli dicti, qui à Christo immediate vocati sunt ad prædicandum Evange- lium per orbem terrarum. Non autem semper Apostoli nomen præmissum esse Epistolis ipso- rum jam ante monuimus.

Ἐκλεκτοῖς) Christianis, ut Rom. VIII. 33. XV. 13. Col. III. v. 12. 2. Timoth. II. 10. Tit. I. 1. infra II. 6. 9. Judæis scilicet, nam illis præcipue destinatus erat Petrus. Est titulus sum- ptus ex Veteri Testamento, in quo Israëlitæ בחירים ἐκλεκτοὶ Es. LXV. v. 8. & alibi. Ideo Apostoli idem no- men, & certe multo meliori jure in Christum credentibus aptarunt. Quos DEUS sibi seposuit ad multo majo- rem sanctimoniam, ut jam sequetur. Vide Joh. cap. XV. v. 19.

Eos, ad quos scripta epistola est, primum electos dicit: quod generaliter, ut apparet, Grotius intelli- git de vocatis Christianis, quomodo 1. Cor. I. 26. 27. vocati dicuntur electi, ut & Psal. CV. Israëlitæ & Ebræi ad Christum vocati, 1. Petr. cap. II. v. 9. necnon Colossenses, c. III. 12. Sed electi hic potius speciali sensu intelligendi prædestinati ad æter- nam vitam, ut 2. Tim. II. 10. Tit. I. 1. quod descriptio addita docet: quia electi dicuntur secundum præ- scientiam Dei Patris in sanctificatione Spiritus ad obedientiam & aspersionem sanguinis Jesu Christi, v. 2. quæ est electionis ab æterno ad vitam æternam factæ descriptio, Rom. VIII. 33. 2. Thess. II. v. 13. Eph. I. 4. non quod omnes, ad quos scribit, electos censuerit, quod certe non fuisset veritati conso- num, sed quia à potiori parte solet fieri denomina- tio. Nam ut Augustinus de unitate Ecclesiæ cap. 12. Prophetæ & Apostoli sic arguere solent repre- hensibiles in aliquo populo, quasi omnes in aliquo po- pulo arguantur: Et sic alloqui laudabiles, quasi omnes laudentur. Christianos autem multo po- tiori jure Electos dici, quam Israëlitas, admitti ne- quit: Accessere enim Christiani ad IsraëExpression commu-nionem, qui è gentibus conversi sunt ad Christum, Eph. II. 13. seqq. Israëlitæ vero Veteris Testamenti Messiani æque fuere, ac qui post ad- ventum Christi dicti sunt Christiani ex Israëlitis ad fidem in Jesum conversi, quia non alia ratione illi, quam hi salvati, & utrique per gratiam Christi salutem adepti sunt, Act. XV. 11. Ad multo majorem sanctimoniam hos sepositos esse nuspiam dicit Petrus, imo eandem sanctimoniam, quam Moses in Veteri Testamento, requirit v. 16. è Levit. XIX. v. 2. qua etiam major nulla esse potest.

Cæterum Grotius electos è Judæis hic intelli- git, ad quos scripta sit epistola, quod etiam aliis plerisque, utpote Eusebio l. III. Hist. Eccl. cap. IV. Hieronymo in catal. Didymo, Oecumenio, Cajetano, Erasmo, nec non Cano l. II. de loc. Theolog. Baro- nio T. I. Annal. Riberæ in proœm. ad Ebr. aliisque visum, neque nobis displicet, siquidem παρ᾽ ἐπιδή- μοις διασπορᾶς, quæ inter gentes erat, scripta sit, a- pud quos Judæi dispersi, & advenæ fuere, ideoque inter gentes bonam jubentur habere conversationem, c. II. v. 12. & ad Judæos posterior quoque exarata sit, quæ ad eosdem scripta, ad quos prior. Confer. 2. epist. III. v. 15. cap. II. 1. quemadmodum etiam Petro peculiariter ministerium circumcisionis com- missum fuit, Gal. II. 7. Monendum autem, etsi ad Judæos dispersos scripta hæc epistola, fuisse tamen inter gentes nonnullos etiam con- versòs, quibus cum vixere Judæi Christiani, ad quos pertinere quoque hanc epistolam è cap. II. v. 10. patet, ubi adducitur prophetia ex Os. II. 23. quæ de gentium conversione explicatur ab Aposto- lo, Rom. IX. 25. & pristini gentilismi status mentio fit, cap. V. 14. cap. VI. 3. unde August. libr. XXII. contr. Faust. c. 89. Joh. Hesselius in h. l. B. Lutherus, Osiander, Winckelmannus, ad gentiles eam scri- ptam statuunt, quæ sententia, si dicto modo ac- cipiatur, quod πρώτως ad Judæos, δευτέρως ad gen- tes ea pertinuerit, admittenda videtur. Genti- les illi etsi non fuerint in dispersione, quod pro solis Judæis intelligendis urget Gomarus, pertinebant tamen ad advenas illos, & cum iisdem unam con- stituebant communionem, quæ à potiori parte nomen sortitur. Nam gentiles tantum proselyti erant respectu Ecclesiæ Judaicæ ad Christum con- versæ. Conf. Act. II. & X. capp. Quo pacto utramque sententiam conciliari posse cum Estio censuit B. Gerhardus.

Παρεπιδήμοις) תושבים. Ea enim vox sic vertitur Gen. XXIII. 9. & Psal. XXXIX. 13. significat peregre habi- tantibus. Vide Ebr. XI. 13. sicut infra II. 11.

Sunt, qui, notante Estio, metaphoricè advenas ac- cipiunt de iis, qui in hoc mundo peregrini ad cœ- lestem patriam tendunt, ut è 1. Epist. II. 11. vocan- tur omnes Christiani. Sed ita disceditur à pro- pria significatione, nec ad omnes Christianos di- rectam eam fuisse, docet locorum particularium denominatio, quamvis ratione usus omnibus Christianis non hanc tantum epistolam, sed totam Scripturam communem esse, certum sit. Alii in- telligunt proselytos, qui è gentilismo conversi e- rant ad Judaismum, & inde ad Christianismum, quomodo Lyranus advenas interpretatur: Sed alii sunt proselyti, alii παρεπίδημοι. Maldonatus in Joh. VII. 35. per advenas intelligit gentiles: Hi enim toto orbe dispersi vocabantur dispersio. Nonnulli advenas Judæos, ad Christum ADVEN- TANTES & conversos interpretantur, quod Cornelius tribuit Hieronymo, Athanasio, Didymo, Oecumenio, Ambrosio, Catharino & Cajetano. Agnoscit autem rectius Judæos Christianos indigi- tari advenas dispersionis Ponti, Galatiæ &c. qui tum alias, tum recenter ob persecutionem à morte Ste- phani à Judæis excitatam, Actor. VIII. 1. è Judæa dispersi fugerant in Pontum, Galatiam &c. ibique hospites, & advenæ erant.

Διασπορᾶς) Sic vocantur loci omnes, in quibus Israëlitæ extra patriam vivebant, quocunque tempore, quacunque occasione illæ migrationes evenissent, sive in bellis, ut per Tiglathphalasaram, Salmanasarem, & Nabuchodonosor rum, sive ad vitanda mala interna, quibus de causis multi & in Syriam & in Ægyptum, & in alia loca Romani imperii concessere. Nec omittenda hic illa dispersio, quæ post Stephani mortem evenerat, de quibus verbum διασπαρέντες usurpat Lucas Act. VIII. 4. & XI. 19. Hi sunt נפצים Es. LVI. v. 8. Vide & quæ diximus ad Jac. I. 1.

Πόντου) Ex hac primum nominata regione epistola hæc dicitur ad Ponticos, quomodo eam appellant Tertullianus, & eum in multis sequens Cyprianus. Sunt autem omnes, quæ hic nominantur regiones Romani imperii, non Par- thici, in quo erat Babylon. Falli puto eos, qui aut duas tantum dici putant διασπορὰς, aut Babylonem putant fuisse caput eorum Judæorum, qui erant per Asiam, parentem Ro- manis. Media, Hyrcania & longius sita erant sub Patriar- cha Babylonensi: At Ægyptus, Lybia, & eis proxima sub capite Synedrii Alexandriæ. Alii erant omnes sub principe, id est נשי Hierosolymitarum, qui postea Tiberiade consedit. In Colchis jam olim quidam fuere gentis Israëliticæ ex deportatione Salmanasaris & Nabuchodonosori, ut dixi- mus in Annot. ad libr. primum pro veritate religionis Chri- stianæ. Sed hic de Judæis agitur, de quibus & Act. II. 10. ubi & Cappadociæ & Asiæ, ejus scilicet, in qua Ephesus, mentio. Omnes isti non Chaldaica versione utebantur, sed Græca, & ea lingua eos alloquutus est Paulus. Apud Philonem Agrippa de Hierosolymis: Μητρόπολις δὲ ὖ μιᾶς χώρας ἰουδαίας, ἀλλὰ κὶ ̇τ πλείστων, διὰ τὰς ἀποικίας, ἃς ἔπεμ-

## 1:1
Galatia) In which there were many Jews, as appears from Paul's epistle to the Galatians.

Cappadocia) See the cited passage of Acts,

Asia) Ionia, in which is Ephesus, in which region there were very many Jews, Josephus XII. 3. XIV. 17. In the edict of Dolabella & XVI, 3. where he says there was a huge multitude of Jews in the cities of Ionia. See the passage which we mentioned in Acts, & VI. 9 & in the same book XIV. 2. 8. 10. 13. 33.

And Bithynia) Bithynia is near the Pontus. Galatia & Asia are so called specifically. See the Geographers.

What was said about these things in the preliminaries to James; that this epistle seems to Scaliger to have been written to the sojourners of the Asian dispersion, and the same to have been sent from the metropolis itself, Babylon. It does not appear why that opinion should be rejected, since there were many Christians in Babylon of Chaldea, to whom St. Peter betook himself by virtue of the agreement entered into with St. Paul, Gal. II. 7. However, this does not seem to be referable to the dispersion in Egypt, because these provinces, which are enumerated here, looked toward Asia, and indeed toward Asia Minor, which is enclosed by the Euphrates on the East, the Mediterranean Sea on the South and West, and the Euxine Pontus on the North, today entirely subject to the Turkish empire. The more recent distribution of the Patriarchate is too late to be brought in here. Meanwhile, we readily admit that the Greek of the LXX Interpreters was generally common to the Jews dispersed everywhere. But just as there were Jews from Pontus, Cappadocia, & Asia in Jerusalem at the feast of Pentecost, Acts II, so it is likely that some of them were converted by Peter's sermon. It is established that Asia is spoken of in three ways. For that word sometimes denotes the third or rather the fourth part of the globe, which is separated from Europe by the Danube river, and from Africa by the Nile: At other times that region which is between the Cyprian sea and the Pontus; finally, at other times only that region which is around Ephesus, and has that as its metropolis. In which there were not a few Jews. It is established from the epistle of Paul given to the Galatians that Galatia, being nearest to the Pontus, also fostered Jews. This Bithynia in Asia is different from the other in Europe, and is called the greater. Phrygia, in which are two primary cities, Nicaea and Chalcedon, famous for Ecumenical Synods. Peter had already filled Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia with the laws of evangelical preaching, as Leo says in Sermon I on the Apostles. Of Peter & Paul: therefore by this epistle he institutes a reminder of those things which he had handed down, as 2 Pet. I. 12. 13. chap. III. 1. indicates: Since, even by the testimony of Jerome in book I against Jovinian, Peter himself traveled through those provinces, and joined them to the Church of Christ by his preaching. Although indeed the peoples of Asia and Galatia were converted by the preaching of Paul, it is not therefore to be denied that Peter preached there, who, as Epiphanius testifies in his work on heresies, visited Pontus and Bithynia often, so he is to be believed to have gone to the other aforementioned regions as well, and to have preached to them by word of mouth, to whom he now directs the present epistle for the sake of a reminder.

Latin:

Γαλατίας) In qua multi Judæi, ut ex epistola Pauli ad Galatas apparet.

Καππαδοκίας) Vide dictum Actorum locum,

Ἀσίας) Ioniæ, in qua Ephesus, in qua regione plurimi Judæi, Josephus XII. 3. XIV. 17. In Dolabellæ edicto & XVI, 3. ubi in Ioniæ urbibus ingentem ait fuisse Judæorum multitudinem. Vide locum, quem diximus, in Actis, & VI. 9 & eodem libro XIV. 2. 8. 10. 13. 33.

Καὶ Βιθυνίας) Bithynia vicina Ponto. Galatiæ & Asiæ sic peculiariter dictæ. Vide Geographos.

Dictum de his ad Jacob. in præliminaribus; ad advenas dispersionis Asianæ scriptam Scaligero videri hanc epistolam, eandemque ex ipsa metropoli Babylone missam. Non apparet, cur reprobanda sit ea sententia, quum in Babylone Chaldææ multi Christiani fuerint, ad quos se vi conventionis cum S. Paulo, Gal. II. 7. initæ, contulit S. Petrus. Non autem videtur ad dispersionem in Ægypto hæc referenda, quia hæ provinciæ ad Asiam spectabant, quæ hic recensentur, & quidem ad Asiam minorem, quæ ab Ortu Euphrate, à Meridie & Occasu mari Mediterraneo, à Septentrione Ponto Euxino clauditur, Turcico imperio hodie tota subjecta. Patriarcham distributio recentior est, quam ut huc afferri debeat. Interim Græcam LXX. Interpp. fere communem fuisse Judæis passim dispersis, facile admittimus. Ut autem è Ponto, Cappadocia, & Asia Hierosolymis fuere Judæi festo Pentecostes, Act. II, ita ex illis nonnullos Petrina concione fuisse conversos verisimile est. Asiam autem tribus modis dici constat. Nam ea vox alias tertiam vel potius quartam orbis partem notat, quæ ab Europa Danai fluvio, & ab Africa Nilo disterminatur: Alias regionem illam, quæ est intra Cyprium mare & Pontum; denique alias tantum istam regionem, quæ est circa Ephesum, eamque metropolin habet. In qua Judæi erant non pauci. Galatiam Ponto proximam etiam Judæos fovisse ex epistola Pauli ad Galatas data constat. Bithynia hæc in Asia ab alia in Europa diversa est, & vocatur major. Phrygia, in qua duæ urbes primariæ Nicæa, & Chalcedon Synodis Oecumenicis celebres. Impleverat Petrus jam Pontum, Galatiam, Cappadociam, Asiam atque Bithyniam legibus Evangelicæ prædicationis, ut Leo ait Serm. I. in Apost. Petri & Pauli: proinde hac epistola ὑπόμνησιν eorum, quæ tradiderat, instituit, ut 2. Petr. I. 12. 13. cap. III. 1. indigitat: Siquidem Hieronymo etiam teste libr. I. contr. Jovin. Petrus provincias illas ipse peragravit, & sua prædicatione Ecclesiæ Christi conjunxerit. Quanquam vero Pauli præconio Asiæ & Galatiæ populi conversi, non tamen ideo negandum, Petrum ibi prædicasse, qui ut Pontum sæpe, ac Bithyniam visitavit, Epiphanio in hær. Corp. testante, ita & alias regiones prædictas adiisse, iisque viva voce prædicasse credendus est, ad quas nunc præsentem epistolam ὑπομνήσεως causa dirigit.

## 1:2
ANNOTATIONS ON 1 PETER CHAP. I. v. 2.

Psysis [says] the neighboring ones, Egypt, Phoenicia, Syria, both the other and that called Coele, and as for those far distant, Pamphylia, Cilicia, and most of Asia as far as Bithynia and the recesses of the Pontus. Then, after many things interposed, he comes to the places beyond the Euphrates: he says, however, that in his own time there were no Jews in Babylon.

Latin:

ANNOTATA AD 1. PETRI CAP. I. v. 2.

Ψησὶς τὰς μὲν ὁμόρους, Αἰγυπτίων, Φοινίκην, Συρίαν τήν τε ἄλλην κὰι τὴν Κοίλην προσαγορευομένην, ὡς δὲ τὰς πόῤῥω διηνπισμένας Παμφυλίαν, Κιλικίαν, τὰ πολλὰ τ᾽ Ἀσίας ἄχρι Βιθυνίας καὶ τ’ τῦ Πόντε μυχῶν. Deinde multis interjectis venit ad loca trans Euphratem: Babylone autem suo tempore nullos ait fuisse Judæos.

## 1:2
Verse 2. According to the foreknowledge of God the Father) This, by hyperbaton, is to be referred to that 'elect' which preceded. Foreknowledge here, however, signifies not prescience, but an antecedent decree, as also in Acts II. 23. the same sense which is in Eph. I. 4.

Foreknowledge properly signifies prescience, nor is there any reason why it should be taken otherwise here: nor does it occur with a different meaning in Acts II. 23. or even Rom. XI. 2: the election was therefore made according to the prevision of faith, by which God from eternity foresaw those who were about to believe, 1 Tim. I. 16. rich in faith, Jas. II. 15. whom he foreknew he also predestined, Rom. VIII. 29. Oecumenius with Cyril on the true faith refers foreknowledge to the words 'Apostle of Jesus Christ'; but what follows teaches that it pertains to the elect, which Bede and other Interpreters acknowledge.

Ἐν ἁγιασμῷ Πνεύματος) That is, εἰς ἁγιασμὸν Πνεύματος, as the Latin also accepts. He chose and loved us in such a way that He might also sanctify us through His Spirit. Πνεύματος is a genitive denoting the cause.

Εἰς ὑπακοὴν) Which Spirit causes us to obey God much more excellently than before.

Καὶ ῥαντισμὸν αἵματος Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ) This does not treat of the remission of sins, which precedes the gift of the Holy Spirit: but here again it is a genitive of cause. See Rom. III. 25. V. 9. Ephes. I. 7. II. 13. Coloss. I. 19. Heb. IX. 19. X. 19. 29. XII. 24. XIII. 12. But the word ῥαντισμῦ is taken from the law of Moses, where both the people and the priests, before they entered into the earthly sanctuary, were sprinkled with a certain liquid, Exod. ch. XXIV. 8. Num. XXXI. 23. So also we, that we may enter into the heavenly sanctuary, must be sprinkled with the blood of Christ, that is, follow His example in sufferings, Heb. XII. 29. Αἷμα ῥαντισμῦ is called the blood of Christ by a genitive of effect, but here ῥαντισμὸς τῦ αἵματος Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ is by a genitive of efficient cause: because that sanctification, that is, the right of entering into the heavenly sanctuary, does not befall us except through the blood of Christ, which is proposed to us as an example of both passion and glory. he was made sin, the just one died for the unjust, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him, 2 Cor. V. v. 21. 1 Pet. III. 18. For our sake he was made obedient even unto the death of the cross, and for our sake he was exalted, and received a name above every name, Phil. II. 8. 9. delivered for our sins, raised for our righteousness, Rom. IV. v. last. Therefore we are not justified or saved by our own righteousness, but by the obedience of that one man many are made righteous; Rom. V. 19. and through his blood we have παῤῥησίαν access into the holy of holies, that is, into heaven, Heb. X. 19.

The sanctification of the Spirit is not the very right of entering into the heavenly sanctuary, nor does our holiness, which Grotius wishes to be regarded, give us any right, being too imperfect and polluted, but the holiness and righteousness of Christ, who has been made for us by God righteousness and holiness and redemption, so that he who boasts, may boast in the Lord, 1 Cor. I. 30. 31. By grace we are saved through faith and this is not of ourselves, it is the gift of God, lest anyone should boast, Eph. II. 8. On the contrary, our righteousness is to be held as σκυβάλοις [refuse] in respect to the righteousness of Christ, Phil. ch. III. 7. 8. 9. since all our righteousness is as a menstruous cloth: Is. LXIV. 6. Nor is the sanctification of the Spirit here to be understood passively, either as that by which our spirit is sanctified, as Salmero wishes, or as that by which the holiness produced in us is regarded, which appears to be the mind of Grotius; but the active sanctification of the Holy Spirit, by which he regenerates us and works faith in us, which benefit Peter has already celebrated in v. 3. Whether the preposition ἐν be rendered IN the sanctification of the Spirit: or whether, as some prefer, according to the common Hebraism, it is said to be put for διὰ [through], as Erasmus explained, because through the sanctification of the Spirit, which is done by the ministry of the Word, John XVII. 19. salvation comes to us: Which sense the blessed Gerhard prefers: The ministry of the Spirit as a medium on the part of God, and the obedience of faith, that is, faith itself, which is the obedience of the Gospel, Acts VI. 7. Rom. X. 16. the obedience of Christ, Heb. V. 9. the obedience of faith, Rom. I. 5. ch. XVI. 26. is said to be understood: in that 2. Thess. II. 13. the sanctification of the Spirit and the faith of the truth are joined, or that which is held to the truth of the Gospel, Mark I. 14. But since in that place we are said to be elect ἐν ἁγιασμῷ Πνεύματος κὶ πίςει ἀληθείας [in sanctification of the Spirit and faith of the truth]: Here, however, indeed ἐν ἁγιασμῷ [in sanctification] of the Spirit, but not ἐν πίςει [in faith] or ὑπακοῇ πίσεως [obedience of faith], but εἰς ὑπακοὴν [unto obedience], we consider the explanation given before to be simpler, that it is unto obedience not of faith, but which follows faith, as it is effective δι᾽ ἀγάπης [through love], Gal. V. 6. nor does it allow us to be ἀκάρπες [unfruitful], 2. Petr. I. 8. we are elect, namely, that we may be holy, Eph. ch. I. 4. since by that reasoning the full force is left to the preposition εἰς [unto], and the words εἰς ὑπακοὴν καὶ ῥαντισμὸν [unto obedience and sprinkling] are most conveniently accepted through a hendiadys, which the blessed Gerhard admits here, into the obedience of the sprinkling of the blood of Christ made through the sprinkler of the ministry of the Word, or the proclamation of the Gospel, and received by true faith, which is ἐν τῷ ἀυτῶ αἵματι [in the same blood], Rom. III. 25.: which faith we said is included in the word προγνώσεως [foreknowledge]. For it is not to be doubted that the application of the benefits by the death and blood of Christ, which is done through faith, is hinted at, by which hearts are purified, Acts XV. 9. Since Christ cleanses our conscience from dead works by his blood, Heb. IX. 14. and from all sin, 1 John I. 7. Cf. Ps. LI. 7. where the Greeks explain the word חטא [sin] as purified through ῥαντίζειν [to sprinkle], and Is. LII. 15. as well as the typical sprinkling, Exod. XXIV. v. 8. ch. XXIX. 21. Lev. VIII. 30. Heb. IX. 20. The blessed Luther, Vol. II. Jena, German, on this epistle, fol. 321. 'To sprinkle means to preach that Christ has shed his blood, and he steps before his Father for us, and says: Dear Father, there you see my blood, which I have shed for this sinner. If you believe that, then you are sprinkled.' Whence it is clear that our election does not depend on the obedience of works or merits, which Estius is forced to confess here: He says they are elect according to the foreknowledge of God, that is, elect by the eternal foreordination and predilection of God, so that every thought of merits of any kind preceding this election, which could be imagined on our part, is excluded, so that, with thanksgiving, the faithful may understand that they were predestined to salvation by the grace of God alone. Which same thing Paul teaches at greater length in Rom. IX. and Eph. I. There is also here a notable testimony of the Holy Trinity: God the Father gives us salvation through gratuitous election: the Son merits it through the shedding of blood: the Holy Spirit applies the benefits and merits of the Son through the preaching of the Gospel.

Grace to you and peace be multiplied) Both the favor of God, and the prosperity proceeding from it, may grow for us daily. The same prayer in the same words 2 Pet. I. 2. and in nearly the same words in Jude v. 2. Also in Paul 1 Cor. I. 3. and in very many other places. A similar prayer Num. VI. 24. 25. 26.

The inscription is followed by a prayer. Now, grace is wished for first, by which some understand the benefits of grace through metonymy: but it is more correctly understood as grace itself, which in Jude v. 2 is rendered ἔλεος. Compare below v. 13. Then peace, which is accustomed to embrace every happiness in the Hebrew phrase, Gen. XLIII. 27, Ps. CXIX. 65, Jer. ch. XXIX. 7, and thus it can also be accepted here, provided that primarily that spiritual happiness is regarded, by which those justified by faith have peace with God, Rom. V. 1, which he wishes to be multiplied, that is, to receive increase and be dilated with grace in the hearts of the elect. Now the grace of God is increased both as to the sense and taste of the same, just as the love of God is said to be poured out in our hearts, Rom. V. 5, and as to effects and gifts, even if grace in itself, the favor of God, is not multiplied. The sum of the whole Gospel is contained here in the Apostolic wish. For in the Gospel the grace of God is offered to us in Christ and on account of Christ, which he who receives by faith has peace toward God, in God, and with God: spiritual and heavenly peace, internal and eternal, peace guarding our hearts in Christ Jesus, Phil. IV. 7. Blessed Luther on this passage: Grace is God's favor, which now begins in us, but must work on and on, and increase until death. Whoever now recognizes and believes this, that he has a gracious God, he has Him, thus his heart also gains peace, and fears neither the world nor the devil, for he knows that God, who is powerful over all things, is his friend, and wants to help him out of death, hell, and all misfortune. Therefore his conscience has peace and joy.

PART II. Description of grace in Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Κατὰ πρόγνωσιν Θεὓ Πατρὸς) Hoc per trajectionem referendum ad illud ἐκλεκτοῖς, quod præcessit. Πρόγνωσις autem hic non præscientiam, sed antecedens decretum significat, ut & Act. II. 23. idem sensus, qui Ephes. I. 4.

Πρόγνωσις significat proprie præscientiam, nec ratio est, cur aliter hic accipiatur: neque alia significatione Act. II. 23. aut etiam Rom. XI. 2. occurrit: facta ergo electio secundum prævisionem fidei, quâ τὰς μέλλοντας πιστεύειν Deus ab æterno prævidit 1. Tim. I. 16. divites in fide, Jac. II. 15. ὃς προέγνω ἃ προώρισε, Rom. VIII. 29. Oecumenius cum Cyrillo de recta fide πρόγνωσιν refert ad verba Apostolus Jesu Christi; sed quæ sequuntur, docent, ad electos pertinere, quod Beda aliique Interpretes agnoscunt.

Ἐν ἁγιασμῷ Πνεύματος) Id est, εἰς ἁγιασμὸν Πνεύματος, quomodo accept & Latinus. Ita nos felegit & amavit, ut etiam per Spiritum suum nos sanctificaret. Πνεύματος Genitivus causam denotans.

Εἰς ὑπακοὴν) Qui Spiritus facit, ut multo quam ante excellentius Deo obediamus.

Καὶ ῥαντισμὸν αἵματος Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ) Non agitur hic de remissione peccatorum, quæ donum Spiritus Sancti præcedit: Sed est hic rursus Genitivus causæ. Vide Rom. III. 25. V. 9. Ephes. I. 7. II. 13. Coloss. I. 19. Ebr. IX. 19. X. 19. 29. XII. 24. XIII. 12. Sed vox ῥαντισμῦ sumpta est ex lege Mosis, ubi & populus & Sacerdotes, antequam in sanctuarium terrestre intrarent, humore quodam aspersi sunt, Exod. c. XXIV. 8. Num. XXXI. 23. Sic & nos, ut in sanctuarium cœleste intremus, aspergi debemus Christi sanguine, id est, ejus exemplum in perpessionibus sequi, Ebr. XII. 29. Αἷμα ῥαντισμῦ dicitur sanguis Christi per Genitivum Effecti, hic vero ipse ῥαντισμὸς τῦ αἵματος Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ per Genitivum Efficientis: quia illa sanctificatio, id est, jus intrandi in sanctuarium cœleste non contingit nobis, nisi per sanguinem Christi, qui nobis pro exemplari & passionis & gloriæ proponitur. factus est peccatum, mortuus justus pro injustis, ut nos in ipso redderemur justitia Dei, 2. Cor. V. v. 21. 1. Petr. III. 18. Pro nobis obediens factus est usque ad mortem crucis, atque nostri causa exaltatus est, & nomen accepit supra omne nomen, Phil. II. 8. 9. traditus propter peccata nostra, resuscitatus pro- pter justitiam nostram, Rom. IV. v. ult. Non ergo propria nostra justitia vel justificamur vel salva- mur, sed per unius illius obedientiam justi con- stituuntur multi; Rom. V. 19. & per sanguinem ejus habemus παῤῥησίαν aditus in sanctum sanctorum, hoc est, in cœlum, Ebr. X. 19.

Sanctificatio Spiritus non est ipsum jus intran- di in sanctuarium cæleste, nec nobis sanctitas no- stra, quam Grotius respici vult, jus aliquod dat, utpote nimis imperfecta & polluta, sed sanctitas & justitia Christi, qui factus nobis à Deo est justi- tia & sanctitas & redemptio, ut qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur, 1. Cor. I. 30. 31. Gratia salvi sumus per fidem & hoc non ex nobis, Dei donum est, ne quis glorietur, Eph. II. 8. Contrà justitia nostra pro σκυβάλοις habenda respectu justitiæ Christi, Phil. c. III. 7. 8. 9. cum omnis nostra justitia sit ceu pan- nus menstruatæ: Es. LXIV. 6. Neque hic sanctifi- catio Spiritus passiva intelligenda, sive quâ Spiritus noster sanctificatur, ut Salmero vult, sive qua sancti- tas in nobis producta respicitur, quam mentem Grotiiesse apparet; Sed sanctificatio Spiritus San- cti activa, quâ nos regenerat, & fidem in nobis operatur, quod beneficium jam celebravit Petrus v. 3. Sive reddatur præpositio ἐν IN sanctificatione Spiritus: sive quod nonnulli malunt, juxta usitatum Ebraismum dicatur poni pro διὰ, ut Erasmus ex- posuit, quia per sanctificationem Spiritus, quæ fit Verbi ministerio, Joh. XVII. 19. salus nobis obtin- git: Quem sensum præfert B. Gerhardus: Ministe- rium Spiritus ceu medium ex parte Dei, & obe- dientiam fidei, hoc est, fidem ipsam, quæ obedientia Evangelii, Act. VI. 7. Rom. X. 16. obedientia Chri- sti, Ebr. V. 9. obedientia fidei, Rom. I. 5. cap. XVI. 26. dicatur, intelligens: eo quod 2. Thess. II. 13. conjun- gatur sanctificatio Spiritus & fides veritatis, vel quæ habetur veritati Evangelii, Marc. I. 14. Sed quum in isto loco ἐν ἁγιασμῷ Πνεύματος κὶ πίςει ἀ- ληθείας electi dicamur: Hic verò ἐν ἁγιασμῷ qui- dem Spiritus, non autem ἐν πίςει vel ὑπακοῇ πίσεως, sed εἰς ὑπακοὴν, simpliciorem censemus explicatio- nem antea traditam, quod ad obedientiam non fi- dei, sed quæ fidem sequitur, utpote quæ efficax est δι᾽ ἀγάπης, Gal. V. 6. nec sinit nos esse ἀκάρπες, 2. Petr. I. 8. electi simus, ut nempe sancti simus, Eph. c. I. 4. quum ea ratione præpositioni εἰς vis integra relinquatur, & verba εἰς ὑπακοὴν καὶ ῥαντισμὸν per hendyaden, quam hic admittit B. Gerhardus, com- modissime accipiantur, in obedientiam aspersionis sanguinis Christi per Verbi ministerii aspergillum, vel præconium Evangelii, factæ, & vera fide, quæ est ἐν τῷ ἀυτῶ αἵματι, Rom. III. 25. receptæ: quam fidem in voce προγνώσεως includi diximus. Ap- plicationem enim beneficiorum morte & san- guine Christi, quæ fit per fidem, innui, non ambi- gendum, qua corda purificantur, Act. XV. 9. Siqui- dem sanguine suo Christus emundet conscientiam nostram ab operibus mortuis, Ebr. IX. 14. & ab omni peccato, 1. Joh. I. 7. Conf. Ps. LI. 7. ubi verbum חטא purificavit per ῥαντίζειν exponunt Græci, & Es. LII. 15. nec non typicam aspersionem, Exod. XXIV. v. 8. c. XXIX. 21. Lev. IIX. 30. Ebr. IX. 20. B. Lutherus T. II. Jen. Germ. in hanc epist. f. 321. Besprengen heisset predigen, dass Christus sein Blut habe ver- gossen, und tritt für uns zu seinem Vater, und spricht: Lieber Vater, da siehest du mein Blut, das ich für diesen Sünder vergossen habe. Gláubest du das, so bist du besprenget. Unde luculentum est, electionem nostram non pendere ab operum obe- dientia vel meritis, quod hic fateri coactus est E- stius: Electos dicit secundum præscientiam Dei, id est, electos æterna Dei præordinatione & prædilectio- ne, ut omnis cogitatio meritorum qualiumcunque hanc electionem prævenientium, quæ ex parte nostra fingi possent, excludatur, utŕ, cum gratiarum actione fideles intelligant, se sola Dei gratia ad salutem esse prædestinatos. Quod idem pluribus docet Paulus Rom.IX. & Eph.I. Habetur etiam hic insigne testi- monium SS.Trinitatis: Deus Pater salutem nobis donat per gratuitam electionem: Filius eam pro- meretur per sanguinis effusionem: Spiritus S. be- neficia & merita Filii applicat per Evangelii præ- dicationem.

Χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη πληθυνθείη) Et favor Dei, & inde pro- cedens prosperitas nobis crescat indies. Eadem precatio iis- dem verbis 2. Petr. I. 2. & prope iisdem verbis Judæ v. 2. Apud Paulum quoque 1.Cor I. 3. & aliis locis plurimis. Si- milis precatio Num. VI 24. 25. 26.

Ἐπιγραφὴν sequitur εὐχή. Vovetur autem primo χάρις, per quam nonnulli intelligunt beneficia gra- tiæ per Metonymiam: Sed rectius ipsa gratia intel- ligitur, quæ Jud. v.2. ἔλεος redditur. Conf. infra v. 13. tum εἰρήνη, quæ omnem felicitatem phrasi Ebræa complecti solet, Gen. XLIII. 27. Ps. CXIX. 65. Jer. c. XXIX. 7. atque ita etiam hic accipi potest, modo imprimis respiciatur spiritualis illa felicitas, qua ju- stificati fide pacem habent cum Deo, Rom. V. 1. quam πληθυνθῆναι multiplicari, & incrementum capere, ac dilatari cum gratia optat in cordibus electorum. Gratia autem Dei augetur tum quoad sensum & gustum ejusdem, uti charitas Dei effusa dicitur in cordibus nostris, Rom. V. 5. tum quoad effecta & dona, etsi in se gratia, favor Dei non multiplice- tur. Summa hic continetur totius Evangelii in vo- to Apostolico. In Evangelio enim offertur nobis Dei gratia in Christo & propter Christum, quam qui fide recipit, pacem habet ad Deum, in Deo, & cum Deo: Pacem spiritualem, & cælestem internam, & æternam, pacem custodientem corda nostra in Christo Jesu, Phil. IV. 7. B. Lutherus in h. l. Gnad ist GOttes Hulde, die fáhet jest in uns an, muß aber für und für wircken, und sich mehren biß in den Tod. Wer nun das erkennet und glaubet, daß er ei- nen gnádigen GOTT habe, der hat ihn, so gewin- net sein Hertz auch Friede, und fürchtet sich weder für der Welt, noch für dem Teuffel, denn er weiß, daß GOtt, der aller Ding gewaltig ist, sein Freund ist, und will ihm aus Tod, Hölle und allem Unglück helffen. Drum hat sein Gewissen Fried und Freude.

PARS II. Gratia in Christo descriptio.

## 1:3
Verse 3. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ) A frequent formula for giving thanks, 2 Cor. I. 3, Eph. I. 3. Similar to Dan. II. 20.

Who according to His abundant mercy) You have similar things in Eph. ch. II. v. 4. כרוב חסדר.

Having begotten us again) He uses this word also below in 23. He said Γεννηθῆναι ἄνωθεν in John III. 3, concerning the sense of which words and the word παλιγγενεσίας we spoke there. He made us other men, far more truly than that which was once said of Saul, 1 Sam. X. 6. God is also said to have begotten the people of Israel, when He made them a free people, Deut. XXXII. 18. But this generation is much more exalted toward eternal things, as follows.

Unto a living hope) That new life here excites in us a living hope, that is, a vivifying one, namely unto eternity. We observed the same kind of speaking in John VI. 50, Heb. X. 20. The Syriac here says: into the hope of life.

Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead) For that resurrection of Christ both shows the thing to be possible, and at the same time shows Him to be truthful, who promised us the resurrection. For why else would God have raised Him up? Or to deceive all men? That is by no means consistent with the truth of God.

For the same reason, mention of the resurrection of Christ is made below in v. 21 and III 21.

The inscription had handed down the election made from eternity in Christ. Therefore, the grace of God exhibited in Christ, which we enjoy in time, and which concerns the execution of the election, now follows; the former was referred to the will, the latter is exhibited under the formula of blessing: by which he celebrates God, first on account of the regeneration to faith at v. 4, which they had attained. For the word blessed (εὐλογητός) denotes not just thanksgiving, which we call eucharistia rather than eulogia, but celebration, and the verb 'let be' is understood: blessed be God! Moreover, he sets forth the causes of regeneration: both the supreme efficient cause, God, Jas. 1:18 and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, where the particle 'and' is taken exegetically, as Matt. 13:41, Col. 2:8; and the internal impulsive cause, His great mercy, Eph. 2:4, Tit. 3:7. Sir. 2:23; then the formal cause, by the word 'having regenerated' (ἀναγεννήσας), which we have discussed regarding the parallel passage in John 3, namely that by which we are born of God so that we may live by faith in the Son of God, and through it be rendered children of God and be constituted heirs, through which the powers of believing are granted to us in God, we who were alienated in mind from God and from the life which is in God: which, however, Grotius confuses with renewal, by which we turn out to be other men, and a new creature in Christ, 2 Cor. 5:17, when we are renewed in the spirit of our mind, and put on the new man created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth, Eph. 4:23-24, which benefits of the Holy Spirit are distinct, Tit. 3:5; then the final cause, which is partly intermediate, namely hope, 'unto a living hope' (εἰς ἐλπίδα ζῶσαν); which there is no need to take metaleptically for vivifying hope, since it can properly be understood as living hope, just as faith is called living; indeed, by hope, faith itself is rightly designated, with the approval of the blessed Gerhard and the interlinear gloss, which holds thus: through faith Christ rises in us, just as through infidelity He dies in us; since these are not rarely interchanged in sacred writings, to trust in God and to hope in the Lord, or in the Lord. Moreover, the new life in the sense of Grotius, i.e., the pursuit of holiness, is so far from exciting a vivifying hope unto eternity in us that, if it were to be derived from our life, we would never have solid hope, let alone vivification, from it: because however much one may be conscious of nothing in himself with Paul, he is not justified by that, 1 Cor. 4:4, cf. Job 9:2-3; partly ultimate, which is the heavenly inheritance: then the meritorious cause, which is the resurrection of Christ from the dead, not excluding but including the death of Christ, which the phrase itself imports, because by His death and resurrection Christ merited for us regeneration and the heavenly inheritance, being delivered for our sins and raised for our justification, Rom. 4:last v., cf. 1 Cor. 15:3-4, 22. We are said to be regenerated 'by the resurrection' (δι' ἀναστάσεως), that is, through the resurrection of Christ, which to explain with Grotius as meaning that Christ's resurrection teaches that our regeneration is possible and the promise of our resurrection is true, is too diluted. For it is not what is taught by the resurrection, or what is syllogistically gathered from it, but what the resurrection of Christ contributes energetically to our regeneration, and how it concurs with it, namely when it is taken complexly with the passion and death of Christ, of which it is the terminus, and death is the triumph over death and the Devil, who is understood to have the empire of death, in the resurrection, it concurs expiatorily and meritoriously. For thus Christ merited for us regeneration, faith, and living hope, as also the heavenly inheritance itself: just as baptism, which is the washing of regeneration, is said to save us through the resurrection of Christ, 1 Pet. 3:21. Blessed Gerhard in this place, p. 58. Christ, he says, regenerates us through His resurrection, because by the resurrection of Christ all His merits were sealed, and because Christ was therefore raised from the dead and ascended into heaven, and sat at the right hand of God, so that He might apply to us through faith the benefits procured by His passion and death. Grotius, however, with the Socinians, seems to make the death of Christ not a ransom and expiation, but only a testimony, which had been proven by the resurrection, which heresy has been refuted elsewhere. Beautifully, blessed Luther here: 'Therefore one should teach thus: Do you see, Christ has died for you, has taken upon Himself sin, and death, and hell, and laid Himself under them, but nothing could suppress Him, for He was too strong, but He has risen from under them, and has overcome all that, and brought it under Himself, and that so that you might be free from it, and become a lord over it.' If you believe that, then you have it.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Εὐλογητὸς Θεὸς καὶ Πατὴρ τῦ Κυρίε ἡμῶν Ἰησῦ Χρι- στῦ) Frequens gratias agendi formula 2. Cor. I. 3. Eph. I. 3. Simile Dan. II. 20.

Ὁ κατὰ τὸ πολὺ αὑτῦ ἔλεος) Similia habes Eph. c.II. v. 4. כרוב חסדר.

Ἀναγεννήσας ὑμᾶς) Utitur hac voce & infra 23. Γεννη- θῆναι ἄνωθεν dixit Joh. III. 3. de quarum vocum sensu & voce πα- λιγγενεσίας ibi diximus. Fecit nos homines alios longe veri- us, quam id olim de Saule dictum, 1. Sam. X. 6. Dicitur Deus & populum Israëlis genuisse, cum eum fecit populum liberum, Deut. XXXII. 18. At hæc generatio multo excelsior ad res æternas, ut sequitur.

Εἰς ἐλπίδα ζῶσαν) Illa vita hic nova spem in nobis excitat viventem, id est, vivificantem, nempe in æternum. Idem lo- quendi genus observavimus, Joh. VI. 50. Ebr. X. 20. Syrus hic in spem vitæ.

Δι᾿ ἀναστάσεως Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ ἐκ νεκρῶν) Nam illa Christi re- surrectio & rem ostendit possibilem esse, & simul ostendit ipsum esse veracem, qui nobis resurrectionem promisit. Nam quorsum alioqui Deus ipsum resuscitasset? An ad o- mnes homines fallendos? Minime id convenit Dei veritati.

Eadem de causa resurrectionis Christi fit mentio infra v. 21. & III 21.

Electionem ab æterno factam in Christo, in- scriptio tradiderat. Gratia ergo Dei in Christo ex- hibita, qua in tempore fruimur, quæque executio- nem concernit electionis, jam sequitur; illa ad vo- tum referebatur, hæc sub formula ευλογιας exhi- betur: qua Deum celebrat primo ob regeneratio- nem ad fidem ad v. 4. quam consequuti erant. Voce enim ευλογητος benedictus non gratiarum actio- nem tantum, quam ευχαρισιαν potiùs, quam ευλο- γιαν dicimus, notat, sed celebrationem, & subintel- ligitur verbum εςω, benedictus sit Deus! Regene- rationis autem causas sistit tum Efficientem supre- mam Deum, Jac. I. 18. & Patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi, ubi particula και εξηγητικως accipitur, ut Matth. XIII. 41. Col. 2, 8. tum impulsivam internam, magnam ejus misericordiam, Eph. II. 4. Tit. III. 7. Sir. II. 23. tum formalem, voce ἀναγεννήσας, quæ quid inferat, circa locum parallelum Joh. III. dixi- mus, nimirum qua nos ex Deo nascimur, ut viva- mus fide Filii Dei, & per eam filii Dei reddamur, & hæredes constituamur, per quam vires credendi nobis conceduntur in Deum, qui mente alienati sumus à Deo, & à vita, quæ est in Deo: quam vero confundit Grotius cum renovatione, qua alii homi- nes evadimus, & nova creatura in Christo, 2. Cor. V. 17. cum renovamur spiritu mentis nostræ, & induimus novum hominem creatum secundum Deum in justitia & sanctitate veritatis, Eph. IV. 23. 24. quæ beneficia Spiritus Sancti distincta sunt, Tit. III, 5. tum fina- lem, quæ est partim intermedia, spes nempe, εις ἐλ- πίδα ζωϲαν; quam metaleptice accipere opus non est pro spe vivificante, quum proprie intelligi pos- sit spes viva, uti fides viva dicitur, imo per spem re- cte designata ipsa fides dicitur, annuente B. Gerhar- do, & glossa interlineari, quæ ita habet, per fidem Christus resurgit in nobis, sicut per infidelitatem mo- ritur in nobis; quum ea permutentur in sacris non rara, confidere in Deo & sperare in Domino, vel in Dominum: Vita autem nova sensu Grotii, h. e. stu- dium sanctitatis spem vivificantem in æternum adeo non excitat in nobis, ut si ex vita nostra de- rivanda illa sit, nunquam spem solidam, nedum vi- vificationem inde habituri simus: quia quantumvis quis nihil sibi conscius sit cum Paulo; non tamen per id justificatur, 1. Cor. IV, 4. conf. Job. IX. 2. 3. partim ultima, quæ est hæreditas cælestis: tum me- ritoria causa, quæ est resurrectio Christi à mortuis, non exclusa, sed inclusa morte Christi, quam phra- sis ipsa importat, quia morte ac resurrectione sua Christus nobis meruit regenerationem & hæredi- tatem cælestem, utpote traditus propter peccata nostra, & resuscitatus propter justitiam nostram, Rom. IV. v. ult. conf. 1. Cor. XV. 3. 4. 22. Regeniti di- cimur δι' ἀναστάσεως, id est, per resurrectionem Chri- sti, quod cum Grotio ita explicare, quod Christire- surrectio regenerationem nostram possibilem, & pro- missionem resurrectionis nostræ veracem esse doceat, nimis dilutum est. Non enim quid doceatur per re- surrectionem, vel ex ea colligatur συλλογισικῶς, sed quid conferat ad nostri regenerationem Christi resurrectio ἐνεργητικῶς, & quomodo ad eam con- currat, nimirum cum complexe accipitur cum pas- sione & morte Christi, cujus est terminus & mors triumphatio de morte & Diabolo, qui imperium mortis, in resurrectione, intelligitur, ἱλασικῶς & meritorie concurrit. Sic enim promeruit nobis Christus regenerationem, fidem & spem vivam, ut & ipsam hæreditatem cælestem: quomodo etiam baptismus, qui lavacrum est regenerationis, nos dicitur salvare per resurrectionem Christi 1. Petr. c. III. 21. B. Gerh. in h. l. p. 58. Christus, inquit, per re- surrectionem suam nos regenerat, quia resurrectione Christi omnia ipsius merita obsignata, & quia Chri- stus ideo ex mortuis suscitatus in cælos ascendit, & ad dextram Dei consedit, ut beneficia passione & morte sua parta per fidem nobis applicaret. Grotius autem cum Socinianis mortem Christi non ἀντί- λυτρον & ἱλασμὸν, sed tantum μαρτύριον, quod per resurrectionem comprobatum fuerit, facere vide- tur, quæ hæresis alias profligata est. Pulchre B. Lu- therus hic: Darum soll man also lehren: Sihest du, Christus ist für dich gestorben, hat auff sich ge- nommen Sünd, und Tod, und die Hölle, und sich darunter geleget, aber es hat ihn nichts können un- terdrucken, denn er war zu starck, sondern er ist dar- unter auffgestanden, und hat das alles überwun- den, und unter sich bracht, und das darum, daß du davon ledig, und ein Herr darüber würdest. Gláu- best du das, so hast du es.

## 1:4
Ver. 4. 'To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away' (Εἰς κληρονομίαν ἄφθαρτον, καὶ ἀμίαντον, καὶ ἀμάραντον) The object and effect of that hope is the inheritance, that is, a firm possession (נחלה) (concerning this word see Acts 20:32, Gal. 3:18, Eph. 1:14, 18, Col. 1:12, 24, Heb. 9:15) which can neither perish, nor be defiled from without, nor rot within. We have the word 'incorruptible' (ἄφθαρτον) also in 1 Cor. 9:25, 15:52, and 'incorruption' (ἀφθαρσίαν), 1 Cor. 15:42, 50, 53, 54, 2 Tim. 1:10; it is worth the same as (לא תתחבל) Dan. 2:44. 'Undefiled' (ἀμίαντον), Heb. 7:26, Jas. 1:27, and 'to defile' (μιαίνειν) is accustomed to be said of diseases, as we noted at Heb. 12:17. 'That fadeth not away' (ἀμάραντον) we have in Wis. 6:12, and in the same sense 'unfading' (ἀμαράντινος), below v. 4, and the verb 'to fade' (μαραίνεσθαι), Jas. 1:10, (מכך) Job 24:24.

Not the object, but rather the end of hope, or of living faith, is designated here as the heavenly inheritance, which as ἄφθαρτος is opposed to the earthly inheritance, as being fleeting and corruptible, just as below gold and silver are called φθαρτὰ v. 18.
