It is ἀμίαντος in contrast to the pleasures of this age that defile us, and ἀμάραντος like a flower that does not wither, called heliochrysum by Galen, because it displays the brilliance of gold in its leaves that curl into a circle at the reflection of the Sun, in contrast to the goods of earthly life, which like flowers wither with life itself; Job ch. XIV. 2. Ps. XC. 6. Ps. CIII. 5. 6. 1. Petr. I. 24. Conf. 1. Petr. V. 4. Sap. VI. 12. That inheritance is incorruptible in itself, it is undefiled by another, it is unfading in time. It is incorruptible, because it never fails, so that it is touched neither by old age, nor by disease, nor by any other sadness. It is undefiled, because it receives nothing unclean. It is unfading, because not even in the very minds of the blessed is that heavenly conversation able to become cheapened through long use, Job. Hussus on this passage & from him B. G. Gerhardus p. 59.

Τετηρημένην ἐν ὐρανοῖς εἰς ὑμᾶς) That is, ὑμῖν, as the Syriac and Arabic translate this. Τηρεῖσθαι here is the same as ἀποκεῖσθαι, 2. Tim. IV. 8. & Coloss. I. 9. In the same way τηρεῖν is said of punishment, 2. Petr. II. 17.

It denotes the inheritance 1. as eternal by the word τετηρημένη in the perfect tense, having been preserved long ago, just as an inheritance is accustomed to be preserved by parents for their children. Conf. Matth. XXV. 34. 2. Thess. II, 13. 2. As certain, being placed in the hand of God, Joh. X. 28. Matth. VI. v. 20. 3. As still hidden, Col. III. 3. 4. 1. Joh. III. v. 2.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Εἰς κληρονομίαν ἄφθαρτον, καὶ ἀμίαντον, καὶ ἀμά- ραντον) Objectum, & effectum illius spei est hæreditas, id est, possessio firma נחלה (de hac voce vid. Act. XX. 32. Gal. III. 18. Eph. I. 14, 18. Col. I. 12. 24. Ebr. IX. 15.) quæ neque peri- re potest, neque extrinsecus fœdari, neque intus marcescere. Vocem ἄφθαρτον habemus & 1. Cor. IX. 25. XV. 52. & ἀφθαρ- σίαν, 1. Cor. XV. 42. 50. 53. 54. 2. Tim. I. 10. idem valet לא תתחבל Dan. II. 44. Ἀμίαντον, Ebr. VII. 26. Jac. I. 27. & μιαίνειν de morbis dici solet, ut notavimus Ebr. XII. 17. ἀμάραντον habemus Sap. VI. 12. & eodem sensu ἀμαράντινος, infra V. 4. & verbum μαραίνεσθαι, Jac. I. 10. מכך Joc. XXIV. v. 24.

Non objectum, sed potius finis spei, vel vivæ fi- dei hic designatur hæreditas cœlestis, quæ ceu ἄ- φθαρτος opponitur hæreditati terrenæ, utpote ca- ducæ & corruptibili, ut infra aurum & argentum φθαρτὰ dicuntur v. 18. quâ ἀμίαντος voluptatibus hujus seculi nos inquinantibus, ceu ἀμάραντος à flore non marcescente, heliochryso Galeno dicto, quod ad Solis repercussum comantibus in orbem foliis fulgorem auri præ se ferat, vitæ terrenæ bonis, quæ instar florum cum ipsa vita marcescunt; Job. c. XIV. 2. Ps. XC. 6. Ps. CIII. 5. 6. 1. Petr. I. 24. Conf. 1. Petr. V. 4. Sap. VI. 12. Hæreditas illa est incorrupti- bilis à se, est incontaminata ab alio, est immarcesci- bilis tempore. Est incorruptibilis, quia nunquam de- ficit, ut nec senio, nec morbo, nec alia mœstitia tanga- tur. Est incontaminata, quia nihil immundum reci- pit. Est immarcescibilis, quia nec in ipsis beatorum mentibus ex longo usu cælestis illa conversatio valet aliquando vilescere, Job. Hussus in h. l. & ex eo B. G. Gerhardus p. 59.

Τετηρημένην ἐν ὐρανοῖς εἰς ὑμᾶς) Id est, ὑμῖν לכן, quomo- do hoc vertunt Syrus & Arabs. Τηρεῖσθαι hic quod ἀποκεῖ- σθαι, 2. Tim. IV. 8. & Coloss. I. 9. Pari modo τηρεῖν de pœna dicitur, 2. Petr. II. 17.

Notat hæreditatem 1. æternam verbum τετηρη- μένη in forma perfecta, jam olim asservatam, sicut à parentibus liberis solet asservari hæreditas. Conf. Matth. XXV. 34. 2. Thess. II, 13. 2. Certam, utpote in manu Dei positam, Joh. X. 28. Matth. VI. v. 20. 3. Adhuc absconditam, Col. III. 3. 4. 1. Joh. III. v. 2.

## 1:5
Vers. 5. Τὺς ἐν δυνάμει Θεῦ φρυρυμένυς διὰ πίστεως) Through faith you have obtained the Holy Spirit, who guards you in the grace of God. The Holy Spirit is called δύναμις Θεῦ in Luc. XXIV. v. 49.

Indeed, we are said to be guarded by the infinite power of God to obtain that inheritance through faith: by which manner it is hinted that this is a work not of human strength, but of divine power, and that we are guarded for salvation not through our works, but solely through faith. For whether δύναμις Θεῦ is taken essentially, or personally concerning the Holy Spirit, the matter comes to the same thing, that it is not by our power, but by divine power and grace in us, and through faith, that we are guarded and the inheritance is obtained. No one by the power of his own free will is able to be guarded in good things, but the help of Him from whom we have received the beginning of a good action must be sought through all things, as Bede says in this place. And this is the second benefit of God, which is celebrated here, for which God is to be glorified, that He preserves us by His gracious power through faith unto the heavenly inheritance, εἰς σωτηρίαν unto salvation, which we have obtained as children of God by the title of inheritance, having been regenerated by God, so that that inheritance, eternal salvation, may not be snatched away or subverted from us by the force or fraud of enemies. Φρουρεῖσθαι is a military word, and denotes being fortified with garrisons, 2 Cor. 11:32, Judith 3:7. Cf. Gal. 3:23, Phil. 4:7. For the power of God is our safest garrison. Regeneration is attributed to divine mercy, preservation to divine power: because in the former mercy, in the latter power, exerts itself. But that power of God is not to be concluded as irresistible with the Calvinists, or the grace of remission as unloseable, which is guarded by the power of God: Because God does not use His power absolutely, nor does He act in the faithful even from absolute grace, but He binds them to the use of means, which if they neglect, they fall from grace by their own fault, and are deprived of the protection of divine power. And therefore we are warned that we should remain in the word of Christ, John 8:31, that no one may fail of the grace of God, Heb. 12:15, that we may not receive the grace of God in vain, 2 Cor. 6:1.

unto salvation ready to be revealed in the last time). The benevolence of God toward you tends to this, that you may obtain salvation, which will be made manifest on the last day, ἑτοίμην ἀποκαλυφθῆναι .עתיד להגלות By the last day he understands the day of judgment: John ch. 6:39, ch. 11:24, ch. 12:48. Salvation, therefore, is said to be prepared to be revealed on the day of judgment, which is kept for us still hidden in God, Col. 3:3, 4. But it will then be revealed openly to all: from which, however, it is not to be denied that salvation does not reach or is not revealed to the souls of the just before the last day. For blessed are they ἀπάρτι, from now on, who die in the Lord, Rev. 14:13.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Τὺς ἐν δυνάμει Θεῦ φρυρυμένυς διὰ πίστεως) Per fidem obtinuistis Spiritum Sanctum, qui vos custodit in Dei gratia. Spiritus Sanctus δύναμις Θεῦ dicitur Luc. XXIV. v. 49.

Imo virtute Dei infinita custodiri dicimur ad hæreditatem illam consequendam per fidem: quo pacto non humanarum virium, sed virtutis di- vinæ hoc opus esse, neque per opera nostra, sed unice per fidem nos custodiri ad salutem innui- mur. Sive enim δύναμις Θεῦ essentialiter acci- piatur, sive de Spiritu Sancto personaliter, res eo- dem redit, non nostra, sed divina virtute & gratia in nobis, & per fidem custodiri & hæreditatem obtineri. Nullus sua libertatis potentia custodiri valet in bonis, sed illius quærendum per omnia auxi- lium, à quo initium bonæ actionis accepimus, ut Beda in h. l. Atque hoc est alterum beneficium Dei, quod hic celebratur, ob quod Deus glorifi- candus est, quod nos conservet gratiosa sua virtu- te per fidem ad hæreditatem cœlestem, εἰς σω- τηρίαν ad salutem, quam ceu filii Dei hæreditatis titulo consequuti sumus, regeniti à Deo, ut ne illa hæreditas, salus æterna, per vim aut fraudem ho- stium nobis eripiatur aut intervertatur. Φρουρεῖ- σθαι est verbum militare, ac notat præsidiis muni- ri, 2. Cor. XI. 32. Judith III. 7. Conf. Gal. III. 23. Phil. IV. 7. Virtus enim Dei præsidium nobis est tutissimum. Regeneratio divinæ misericordiæ, con- servatio divinæ potentiæ tribuitur: quia in illa magis misericordia, in hac potentia sese exerit. Non autem virtus illa Dei cum Calvinianis irresi- stibilis, aut gratia remissionis inamissibilis conclu- denda, quæ virtute Dei custoditur: Quia Deus non absolutè utitur potentia, vel ex absoluta etiam gratia agit in fidelibus, sed eos adstringit ad mediorum usum, quæ si negligant, culpa sua gratia excidunt, & præsidio divinæ virtutis de- stituuntur. Ideoque monemur, ut maneamus in sermone Christi, Joh. VIII. 31. ne desit quis gratiæ Dei, Ebr. XII. 15. ne gratiam Dei in va- num accipiamus 2. Cor. VI. 1.

Εἰς σωτηρίαν ἑτοίμην ἀποκαλυφθῆναι ἐν καιρῷ ἐσχάτῳ). Dei in vos benevolentia huc tendit, ut adipiscamini sa- lutem, quæ patebit in ultimo die, ἑτοίμην ἀποκαλυφθῆναι .עתיד להגלות Per ἐσχάτην ἡμέραν diem judicii intelligit: Joh. c. VI. 39. cap. XI. 24. cap. XII. 48. Salus ergo parata revelari dicitur in die judicii, quæ asservatur no- bis adhuc abscondita in Deo, Col. III. 3. 4. Revelabi- tur autem tum omnibus palam: ex quo vero ne- gandum non est, justorum animabus salutem non contingere aut revelari ante novissimum diem. Beati enim sunt ἀπάρτι, à modo, qui moriuntur in Domino, Apoc. XIV. 13.

## 1:6
Verse 6. In which you rejoice) That 'in which' refers not to one noun, but to the whole matter. Those great expected goods fill you with joy, Matt. 5:12. So also below 8, ἀγαλλιᾶσθε in the indicative. A little while now (if it is necessary) having been grieved in various temptations) With joy, he says, these things fill you, although even now for some time (namely, while this short life lasts), if the situation so requires, you may feel sadness from various temptations, which both unbelieving Gentiles and Jews bring upon us. Ἄρτι is rightly translated 'now', Matt. 26:29, John 13:7, 33, 16:12, 1 Cor. 4:11, and elsewhere ὀλίγον 'for a little while', as Mark 6:31, ברגע קטן Is. 54:7, εἰ δέον ἐστὶ.

This third benefit is spiritual joy and exultation, which is not subverted by any temptations among the faithful. The prayer rises: God not only preserves the reborn through faith in dangers: But also raises them up in adversities, and fills them with joy as well, so that they can glory in tribulations, Matt. 5:12, Rom. 5:2, 3, 2 Cor. 6:10, 1 Pet. 4:13. He therefore hints not only at an external manifestation of joy, but at an inward exultation in the Spirit, Luke 1:47, ch. 10:21. The Vulgate is to be corrected here, rendering 'if it is necessary to be grieved'. But by temptations all afflictions are understood universally, as those by which God sustains, 1 Pet. 4:12, James 1:12, cf. Luke 22:28, Acts 20:19, 2 Pet. 2:9.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Ἐν ᾧ ἀγαλλιᾶσθε) Illud ᾧ non ad unum no- men, sed ad totam rem refertur. Illa magna bona expectata perfundunt vos gaudio, Matth. V. 12. Sic & infra 8. ἀγαλ- λιᾶσθε in Indicativo. Ὀλίγον ἄρτι (εἰ δέον ἐστὶ) λυπηθέντες ἐν ποικίλοις πειρα- σμοῖς) Gaudio, inquit, vos ista perfundunt, quanquam etiam nunc ad tempus aliquod (nempe dum brevis hæc vita durat) si res ita ferat, tristitiam sentiatis ex variis tentationibus, quas nobis inferunt & gentes incredulæ, & Judæi. Ἄρτι nunc rectè vertitur, Matth. XXVI. 29. Job. XIII. 7. 33. XVI. 12. 1. Cor. IV. 11. & alibi ὀλίγον aliquantïsper, ut Marc. VI. 31. ברגע קטן Es. LIV. 7. εἰ δέον ἐστὶ.

Tertium hoc beneficium est lætitia & exultatio spiritualis, quæ nullis tentationibus intervertitur penes fideles. Assurgit oratio: Deus non tan- tum conservat renatos per fidem in periculis: Sed etiam erigit eos in adversis, ac lætitia quoque per- fundit, ut in tribulationibus gloriari possint, Matth. V. 12. Rom. V. 2. 3. 2. Cor. VI. 10. 1. Petr. IV. 13. Non ergo tantum externam lætitiæ significatio- nem, sed interiorem in Spiritu exultationem innu- it, Luc. I. 47. c. 10. X. 21. Castiganda hic Vulgata, red- dens, si oportet contristari. Per πειρασμοὺς au- tem universim omnes afflictiones intelliguntur, ut- pote quibus Deus sustentat, 1. Petr. IV. 12. Jac. I. 12. conf. Luc. XXII. 28. Act. XX. 19. 2. Petr. II. 9.

## 1:7
Verse 7. That the trial of your faith) That is, your faith, clearly as in James 1:3. The testing of your faith, namely through those temptations. Much more precious than gold) That is, than the trial of gold, such as that, having obtained a laurel greater than all triumphs, that is, the laurel of all triumphs, because that testing is useful for a small time, this one for eternity.

Perishing) That is, which is at some time going to perish; for gold is worn away as filings secretly depart. A ring is consumed by use.

But being tested by fire) Even that thing, though not always going to last, is nevertheless tested by fires, so that it may shine more brightly, Job ch. 23:10, Prov. 17:3, Mal. 3:5. Δοκιμαζόμενος מְזֻקָק, 1 Chron. 28:18, 29:4. Where the Greeks [use] δοκίμῳ.

May be found unto praise and honor and glory at the revelation of Jesus Christ) Then that testing will result in the highest honor, praise, and glory for you, when Christ shall appear. We have ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι in the same sense in Luke 17:30. Peter has gathered many words, so that he might declare the magnificence of the matter. So also Eph. 1:6, 12, 13, Phil. 1:10, and Rom. 2:27.

B. Gerhard here assigns the fourth benefit, which is the testing of faith through the cross. The end of afflictions and the cause why they rejoice, though as it were sorrowful, 2 Cor. 6:10, and are rejoicing in hope, Rom. 12:12, the reborn, is explained, because they know that they are not being punished through afflictions, but that their faith is being tested so that it may be rendered more brilliant, and thus it is declared why he called them πειρασμοὺς (trials). Gold is tested by fire when it is purged of dross, and when inquiry is made into its integrity: so faith is tested by the heat of the cross, when the dross of distrust and the desire to sin, of negligence in praying and in searching the Word of God is smelted out, 2 Cor. 1:8 ff., Isa. 26:16, and when faith is explored as to whether it is sincere and firm, Psalm 118:21, Rom. 5:3. Τὸ δοκίμιον πίστεως (the testing of faith) by Hebraism for tested faith. In the Vulgate, the word τοῦ ἀπολλυμένου (of that which perishes) is rashly omitted, in which lies the emphasis of the opposition: for gold is worn away when it is tested: but nothing is lost from faith, nay, it is rendered more perfect. If that is valued so highly by men, that they wish it to be tested by fire, so that it may obtain its just price among them; why should not God test our faith, so that its light and preciousness may appear more before Him? Which may become publicly known to men at the revelation of Jesus Christ, so that from it the elect may obtain praise, glory, and honor, when Christ shall be revealed from heaven, 2 Thess. ch. 1:7, Jas. 1:12. Some distinguish those words, that ἔπαινος (praise) is usually done by words, τιμὴ (honor) by things and gestures, δόξα (glory) is a sound judgment concerning someone's virtue. More simply, the elect are said to be about to have praise, because then there will be praise for each from God, 1 Cor. 4:5; honor, because the Father will honor them, John 12:26; glory, because they will bring back the crown of glory, 1 Pet. 5:4. Moreover, the coming of Christ is called ἀποκάλυψις (revelation) here and in v. 13, as also 1 Cor. 1:7, Φανέρωσις (manifestation) of Christ, 1 Pet. 5:4, Col. 3:4, 1 John 2:28, so that we may understand that Christ is not now absent from us, even if He does not appear: but then His presence will be revealed: whence it is called by Paul ἐπιφάνεια τῆς παρουσίας (the appearing of His coming), 2 Thess. 2:8. Ambrose, book VII in Luke, ch. X: Concerning Christ, he says, although He is everywhere and, standing in the midst of us, is not seen by us, there will nevertheless be a time when all flesh will see Him returning.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Ἵνα τὸ δοκίμιον ὑμῶν τῆς πίστεως) Id est ἡ πίστις ὑ- μῶν, plane ut Jac. I. 3. Exploratio fidei vestræ, nempe per il- las tentationes. Πολὺ τιμιώτερον χρυσίου) Id est τοῦ δοκιμίου τοῦ χρυσίου, quale illud, omnium triumphorum lauream adepte majorem, id est laurea omnium triumphorum, quia illa exploratio ad exiguum tempus est utilis, hæc in æternum.

Ἀπολλυμένῳ) Id est, quod aliquando periturum est; atteritur enim aurum abscedentibus latenter ramentis. Consumitur annulus usu.

Διὰ πυρὸς δὲ δοκιμαζομένῳ) Etiam illa res non semper duratura tamen ignibus exploratur, ut magis eniteat Job. cap. XXIII. 10. Prov. XVII. 3 Malach. III. 5. Δοκιμαζό- μενος מְזֻקָק, 1. Paral. XXVIII. 18. XXIX. 4. Ubi Græci δο- κίμῳ.

Εὑρεθῇ εἰς ἔπαινον καὶ τιμὴν καὶ δόξαν ἐν ἀποκαλύψει Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ) Tunc illa exploratio summo vobis honori, lau- di, gloriæque cedet, cum Christus apparebit. Ἀποκα- λύπτεσθαι eodem sensu habemus Luc. XVII. 30. Multas voces congessit Petrus, ut rei magnificentiam declararet. Sic & Eph. I. 6. 12. 13. Phil. I. 10. & Rom. II. 27.

B. Gerhardus hic assignat quartum beneficium, quod sit fidei per crucem probatio. Finis afflictio- num & causa, cur quasi tristes tamen gaudeant, 2. Cor. VI. 10. & spe gaudentes sint, Rom. XII. 12. renati, exponitur, quia per afflictiones non se- se puniri, sed fidem suam probari, ut fulgidior reddatur, sciunt, adeoque declaratur, cur πει- ρασμοὺς eas dixerit. Aurum probatur per ignem, cum à scoriis repurgatur, & cum de pro- bitate ejus inquiritur: Ita fides per æstum cru- cis probatur, cum scoriæ diffidentiæ & studii pec- candi, negligentiæ precandi, & Verbum Dei scru- tandi excoquitur, 2. Cor. I. 8. seqq. Es. XXVI. 16. & cum fides, sitne sincera & firma exploratur, Psalm. CXIIX. 21. Rom. V. 3. Τὸ δοκίμιον πίστεως per Ebraismum pro fide probata. In Vulgata te- mere omittitur vox τοῦ ἀπολλυμένου, in qua oppo- sitionis emphasis: Aurum enim atteritur, cum probatur: fidei autem nihil decedit, imo perfe- ctior redditur. Si illud tanti æstimatur ab ho- minibus, ut illud velint igne probari, quo justum apud ipsos obtinere possit pretium; quidni Deus fidem nostram, ut ejus lux & pretiositas coram ipso magis appareat? Quæ publice innotescat hominibus in revelatione Jesu Christi, ut inde laudem, gloriam, & honorem consequuturi sint electi, cum Christus de cœlo revelabitur, 2: Thess. c. I. 7. Jac. I. 12. Distinguunt nonnulli voces illas, quod ἔπαινος fieri soleat verbis, τιμὴ rebus & ge- stibus, δόξα sanum sit judicium de alicujus virtute. Simplicius dicuntur electi habituri laudem, quia tunc cuique erit laus à Deo, 1. Cor. IV. 5. honorem, quia Pater eos honorabit, Joh. XII. 26. gloriam, quia gloriæ coronam reportabunt, 1. Petr. V. 4. Adventus autem Christi ἀποκάλυψις dicitur hic & v. 13. ut & 1. Cor. I. 7. Φανέρωσις Christi, 1. Petr. V. 4. Col. III. 4. 1. Joh. II. 28. quo intelligamus, Christum non absentem nobis jam esse, etsi non appareat: tum autem revelatum iri ejus præsentiam: unde ἐπιφάνεια τῆς παρουσίας Paulo dicta, 2. Thess. II. 8. Ambrof. l. VII. in Luc. cap. X. De Christo, licet, in- quit, ubique sit & stans in medio nostrum non cerna- tur à nobis, erit tamen tempus, quo universa caro se aspiciet revertentem.

## 1:8
Vers. 8.

Whom not knowing you love) It is a great thing to love Him whom you have not known by sight.

In whom now not seeing, but believing you rejoice) You neither saw Him acting on earth, nor do you now behold His glory, but you believe, and by believing you rejoice. Εἰς ὃν (in whom) pertains to πιστεύοντες (believing), μὴ ὁρῶντες (not seeing) is inserted in passing.

With joy unspeakable) With joy, which cannot be expressed in words, ineffable: Thus you have ἀλαλήτοις (unutterable) in Rom. 8:26, ἀνεκδιηγήτῳ (inexpressible), 2 Cor. 9:15.

And glorified) That is, with joy worthy of the highest praise. The Syrian in this sense משבחא. In Hebrew you would say נאדרי, as in Exod. 15:6.

This is the fifth benefit for B. Gerhard, the love of Christ not yet seen. He wishes the converted to be praised by a double name, both because in their first conversion to Christ they received Him by faith, even though not seen, and because in the progress of Christianity, not even now seen, by a faith so firm they adhere, so that from that faith a spiritual joy of the heart may arise in them. That word therefore μὴ ὁρῶντες is not inserted incidentally. The Vulgate and the Syriac, as also B. Luther, understand it concerning future joy, looking to ἀποκάλυψιν and the epithets of joy; but the time is present, as the Syriac also rendered it, and the joy of the pious is ἀνεκλάλητον, surpassing all speech, just as spiritual peace surpasses all understanding, Phil. 4, 7, and δεδοξασμένον, worthy of glory, and solid in respect to worldly joy, which is joined with disgrace, unstable, and evanescent; nay, that joy of the pious is a certain πρόγευσμα, and an earnest of that ineffable and glorious joy of the world to come, Heb. 6, verse 5, Eph. 1, verse 14.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Ὃν οὐκ εἰδότες ἀγαπᾶτε) Multum est, amare eum, quem de facie non noveris.

Εἰς ὃν ἄρτι μὴ ὁρῶντες, πιστεύοντες δὲ ἀγαλλιᾶσθε) Neque illum in terris agentem vidistis, neque nunc ejus gloriam conspicitis sed creditis, & credendo gaudetis. Εἰς ὃν ad πι- στεύοντες pertinet, μὴ ὁρῶντες obiter insertum.

Χαρᾷ ἀνεκλαλήτῳ) Gaudio, quod verbis exprimi nequit, ineffabili: Sic ἀλαλήτοις habes Rom. VIII. 26. ἀνεκδιηγήτῳ, 2. Cor. IX. 15.

Καὶ δεδοξασμένῃ) Id est, gaudio summa laude digno. Syrus hoc sensu משבחא. Ebraice dicas נאדרי, ut Exod. V. 6.

Quintum beneficium hoc est B. Gerhard o, Christi nondum visi dilectio. Vult autem duplici laudari nomine conversos, tum quod in prima sua ad Christum conversione fide eum, etsi non visum, receperint, tum quod in Christianismi progressu, ne nunc quidem viso fide tam firma adhæreant, ut ex fide illa spirituale cordis gau- dium exoriatur in illis. Illud ergo μὴ ὁρῶντες non insertum est obiter. Vulgata & Syrus, ut & B. Lutherus de gaudio futuro intelligunt, respi- cientes ἀποκάλυψιν & gaudii epitheta; sed tem- pus præsens est, sicut Syrus etiam reddidit, & ἀνεκλάλητον est piorum gaudium, superans omnem loquelam, uti pax spiritualis omnem intellectum, Phil. 4, 7. & δεδοξασμένον gloria dignum, & so- lidum respectu mundani gaudii, quod cum de- decore conjunctum, instabile, ac evanidum, imo illud piorum gaudium est πρόγευσμα quod- dam, & arrha gaudii illius ineffabilis & glo- riosi venturi seculi, Ebr. 6. vers. 5. Ephes. 1. vers. 14.

## 1:9
Vers. 9.

κομιζόμενοι) Instead of κομισάμενοι. But he preferred to use the present tense because of the certainty of the matter. We have κομίζεσθαι in the sense of a reward also in 2 Cor. 5, 10, Eph. 6, 8, Col. 3, 25, Heb. 10, v. 36, c. 11, 39.

τὸ τέλος τῆς πίσεως ὑμῶν) That is, the reward. The reward, because it is given at the end of the work. The Hebrews call it אַחֲרִית, as in Jeremiah 29, 11, likewise עֵקֶב, which signifies the heel, Ps. 19, 12, where in the Greek it is ἀνταπόδοσις. The word פּוּרעָנָא signifies exactly the same thing, which the Syriac here uses entirely.

σωτηρίαν ψυχῶν) Our salvation, which is περιποίησις ψυχῆς, Heb. 10, 39. You have σῶσαι ψυχὴν in James 1, v. 20.

This sixth benefit is called the eternal possession of salvation: but the beginning of salvation is not understood, as in Rom. 4, verse 6, chap. 8, verse 24, Eph. 2, v. 8, Tit. 3, verse 5, or salvation begun, even if it is called the salvation of souls: But consummated salvation, because τέλος is called the end of faith: Which word Grotius and Piscator wrongly interpret as reward along with the Papists, since it properly signifies the end, and only metaphorically a reward: Concerning which Bellarmine himself in book V de justif. cap. 3 says: The end and the reward are not the same. For the end has a relation to the means, whether they be merits or not; the reward has a relation to merits alone: Which is true concerning a reward of debt properly so called, but not concerning a reward of grace, or one improperly so called, Matt. 5, 46, Ps. 127, 4. We are said to obtain the end of faith, however, when we no longer walk by faith, but by sight, 2 Cor. 5, 7. We rejoice therefore in the present, as being about to obtain one day the end of faith.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

κομιζόμενοι) Pro κομισάμενοι. Sed præsenti tempore uti maluit ob rei certitudinem. Κομίζεσθαι in sensu præ- mii habemus & 2. Cor. 5, 10, Eph. 6, 8. Col. 3, 25. Ebr. 10. v. 36. c. 11, 39.

τὸ τέλος τῆς πίσεως ὑμῶν) Id est mercedem. Merce- dem, quia in fine operis datur. Ebræi vocant אַחֲרִית, ut Jeremiæ 29, 11. item עֵקֶב, quod calcem significat, Pf. 19, 12. ubi in Græco ἀνταπόδοσις. Idem- plane significat פּוּרעָנָא, quod hic prorsus Syrus.

σωτηρίαν ψυχῶν) Salutem nostram, quæ περιποίη- σις ψυχῆς, Ebr. 10, 39. σῶσαι ψυχὴν habes Jac. 1. v. 20.

Sextum hoc beneficium dicitur æterna salutis possessio: non autem initium salutis intelligitur, ut Rom. 4. vers. 6. cap. 8. vers. 24. Ephes. 2. v. 8. Tit. 3. vers. 5. vel salus inchoata, etsi salus ani- marum dicatur: Sed consummata salus, quia τέλος finis fidei dicitur: Quam vocem perpe- ram cum Papistis mercedem interpretatur Gro- tius & Piscator, quum proprie finem significet, nec nisi Metaphorice mercedem: De quo Bellar- minus ipse libr. V. de justif. cap. 3. Non est idem finis & merces. Nam finis relationem habet ad media sive sint merita, sive non sint; Merces re- lationem habet ad sola merita: Quod de merce- de debita proprie sic nuncupata verum, non ta- men de mercede gratiæ, vel improprie ita dicta Matth. 5, 46. Psal. 127, 4. Reportare autem fi- nem fidei dicimur, quando non amplius ambula- mus per fidem, sed per speciem, 2. Corinth. 5, 7. Gau- demus ergò in præsenti, utpote reportaturi olim finem fidei.

## 1:10
Vers. 10.

περὶ ἧς σωτηρίας ἐξεζήτησαν καὶ ἐξηρεύνησαν οἱ προφῆται) They saw that something great was reserved for our late times. But what that might be, they could not foresee. The same sense is in Luke 10, 24. Moses saw that it was far from his own times, Deut. 32.

οἱ περὶ τῆς εἰς ὑμᾶς χάριτος προφητεύσαντες) They predicted those good things which have happened to us, but under the shadows of victories over the nations, of liberation from Babylon, and from Antiochus: few directly, and few things.

B. Gerhard now wishes to add to the proof from the enumeration of benefits a proof from the consensus of Prophetic and Apostolic doctrine, so that it may be taught that the doctrine concerning Christ, which the converted Jews had received, is true. According to our analysis, after the application of salvation, the discussion now concerns the acquisition of that salvation, both predicted and investigated by the Prophets, and announced by those who evangelized to the Jews. Therefore, it is said of that salvation, which was to be acquired through Christ, that the Prophets sought and searched. In the compound word ἐκζητεῖν there is a singular emphasis, because they inquired with the greatest zeal, as if they wished to search it out thoroughly. Similarly in the verb ἐξερευνᾶν, in which Chrysostom (Hom. XXI on Genesis and XL on John) notes a metaphor taken from miners of metals, who search the innermost caverns of the earth. Cf. Prov. 1, v. 4. Moreover, the Prophets are described who prophesied concerning the grace that was to come to us, which, namely, was to be fulfilled in the time of the New Testament, which is to be understood concerning the redemption to be performed by the blood of Christ. But how did they seek and search concerning it? I answer: partly by solicitously investigating and searching out divine revelations concerning these things, if any were had either by themselves or by others before them, and partly by seeking and desiring the fulfillment through pious prayers, John 8, 16; Luke 10, 24. Nor indeed did the Prophets see these things almost only under shadows: nor were so few of them direct. The contrary was shown from our vindications of the Old Testament, where many oracles were indeed asserted, prophesying directly concerning the grace of Christ: which Grotius, and for the most part Calvin before him, and his defenders, Paraeus, Rivetus, and others among the Christians, but especially the more recent Jews, whom Grotius loves to follow, have corrupted. The most diligent and most learned English author of the Synopsis of Critics and Interpreters, Matthew Poole, frankly acknowledged the force of these vindications in the Church and school of the Reformed, who preferred to erect a trophy to the truth than to follow the unhappy camp of Calvin in impugning the Prophetic oracles, and he openly professed this in the preface to the second volume of his work. I cite the man's words as an example of candor to others: For virtue is to be praised even in an enemy. Calovius, he says, who learnedly and solidly vindicates many passages of the Psalms (and of other books that follow), which were rightly and deservedly understood of Christ by almost the whole Christian world, both ancient and new, but which some have rashly twisted into a foreign sense; these, because I neither wished nor dared to be wanting to the common Christian cause, I have been pleased to represent faithfully here.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

περὶ ἧς σωτηρίας ἐξεζήτησαν καὶ ἐξηρεύνησαν οἱ προφῆται) Viderunt aliquid magni in nostra sera tempora reservari. Sed quale id esset, non potuerunt pervidere. Idem sensus Luc. 10, 4. 24. Longe illud à suis temporibus abesse vidit Moses Deut. 32.

οἱ περὶ τῆς εἰς ὑμᾶς χάριτος προφητεύσαντες) Prædixe- runt bona illa, quæ nobis evenere, sed sub umbris victoria- rum de gentibus, liberationis è Babylone, & ab Antiocho: pauci directe, & pauca.

B. Gerhardus probationi à beneficiorum enu- meratione addi jam vult probationem à consen- su Prophetica & Apostolicæ doctrinæ, ut docea- tur, doctrinam de Christo, quam conversi Ju- dæi acceperant, veram esse. Secundum nostram ἀνάλυσιν post applicationem salutis jam de acqui- sitione tum prædicta, & indagata à Prophetis, tum annunciata ab iis, qui Judæis evangelizabant, agitur. Dicuntur ergo de ea salute, quæ acqui- renda erat per Christum, exquisivisse ac scrutati esse Prophetæ. In voce composita ἐκζητεῖν sin- gularis emphatis est, quod summo studio inqui- siverint, quasi penitus exquirere voluerint. Si- militer in verbo ἐξερευνᾶν, in quo Metaphoram à fossoribus metallorum petitam notat Chrysostomus hom. XXI. in Gen. & XL. in Joh. qui intimas ter- ræ cavernas perscrutantur. Conf. Prov. 1. v. 4. Describuntur autem Prophetæ, qui de futura in se nobis gratia prophetarunt, quæ scilicet tempo- re Novi Testamenti implenda erat, quod de re- demptione sanguine Christi præstanda intelli- gendum. Quomodo autem de ea exquifiverunt & scrutati sunt? Resp. partim solicite divinas de hisce revelationes, si quas vel ipsi, vel ante ipsos alii habuere, indagando & perscrutando, par- tim precibus piis impletionem expetendo & de- siderando, Johan. 8, 16. Luc. 10, 24. Nec vero adeò sub umbris fere tantum ea viderunt Prophe- tæ: nec ita pauci directè. Contrarium patuit è vindiciis nostris ad Vetus Testamentum, ubi be- ne multa asserta sunt oracula, directè de Christi gratia vaticinantia: quæ Grotius & magnam par- tem ante ipsum Calvinus, & hyperaspistæ ejus, Paræus, Rivetus, & alii è Christianis, maxime au- tem Judæi recentiores, quos sequi amat Grotius, depravarunt. Quarum vindiciarum vim inge- nue in Ecclesia & schola Reformatorum agnovit Diligentissimus, & Eruditissimus Synopseos Cri- ticorum & Interpretum Autor Anglicanus, Mat- thæus Polus, qui maluit veritati trophæum erige- re, quam castra infelicia Calvini in impugnandis oraculis Propheticis sectari, & palam id professus est in Secundi Tomi Operis præfatione. Sisto viri verba, in exemplum candoris aliis: Nam & in hoste laudanda virtus. Calovius, inquit, qui mul- ta Psalmorum (& aliorum, qui insequuntur, li- brorum) loca, à toto fere orbe Christiano, tum ve- teri tum novo, de Christo jure merito intellecta, nonnullis temere in alienum sensum detorta, erudite solideque vindicat, quæ, quia communi causa Chri- stiana deesse nec volui, nec ausus sum, fideliter hîč repræsentare placuit.

## 1:11
Verse 11.

Searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify) He indicates Daniel most of all, who inquired of the Angel concerning the time, as can be seen in Dan. 9, 22. 23. Which time, that is, in what week of years: what manner of time, that is, under a free people, or a serving one, or a semi-free one. He calls it the Spirit of Christ from the object, the Spirit pre-signifying the things of Christ, and who was given to them for the sake of Christ. Barnabas at the end of his epistle: The Prophets, having the gift from Him, prophesied concerning Him. ἐδήλου, signifying, he was designating by predicting.

The sufferings for Christ) εἰς χριστὸν, more correctly for χριστῷ, as just now, εἰς ὑμᾶς. And ἀποβησόμενα is understood. The Prophets pre-signify that Christ would suffer many things, Luke 24, 25. 26; Acts 26, 23. But some more obscurely, others more clearly. The Hebrews call these חבלי משיח.

And the glories after these) The resurrection of Christ, the ascension into heaven, the mission of the Holy Spirit, the calling of the Gentiles.

Not only Daniel, although he calculated the count more specifically, but others also inquired about the time, the Patriarch Jacob himself also, Gen. 49, 10; Haggai likewise, ch. 2; and Malachi ch. 3 and 4, when they gave certain characters of the coming of the Messiah, looking to the time of the same, to say nothing of others now. But the Spirit of Christ is said not from the object, because it pre-signified the things of Christ, since these are already designated by the words 'predicting the sufferings and glories which are in Christ': But because the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Son of God, proceeding from Him from eternity, just as He is said to be the Spirit of the Father for the same reason on account of the eternal procession from the Father, John 15, 16. Concerning which in System. Theol. Vol. III. Concerning that pre-testification, Christ, Luke 24, 26. 27. 44; and Peter, Acts 10, 43.

Latin:

Vers 11.

ἐρευνῶντες εἰς τίνα ἡ ποῖον καιρὸν ἐδήλου τὸ ἐν αὐτοῖς πνεῦμα χριστοῦ προμαρτυρόμενον) Danielem maximè indicat, qui tempus ab Angelo inquisivit, ut videre est Dan. 9, 22. 23. quod tempus, id est, qua annorum hebdomade: quale tempus, id est, libero populo, an serviente, an semilibero. Spiritum Christi vocat ex objecto, Spiritum res Christi præsignificantem, & qui Christi causa ipsis datus erat Bar- nabas fine epistolæ: Prophetæ ab ipso habentes donum in il- lum prophetarunt, ἐδήλα προμαρτυρόμενον, prædicendo de- signabat.

τὰ εἰς χριστὸν παθήματα) εἰς χριστὸν, rectius pro χριστῷ, ut modo, εἰς ὑμᾶς. Et subauditur ἀποβησόμενα. Præsignifi- cant Prophetæ, Christum passurum multa, Luc. 24, 25. 26. Actor. 26, 23. Sed alii obscurius, alii clarius. Ebræi hæc vo- cant חבלי משיח.

καὶ τὰς μετὰ ταῦτα δόξας) Resurrectionem Christi, ascen- sum in cœlos, missionem Spiritus Sancti, gentium voca- tionem.

Non Daniel tantum, etsi hic calculum inierit specialius, sed alii etiam tempus inquisivere, ipse quoque Patriarcha Jacobus, Gen. 49, 10. Hag- gæus item, cap. 2. & Malachias cap. 3. & 4. cum characteres certos adventus Messiæ, tempus ejus- dem respicientes, dedere, ut alios jam taceamus. Spiritus autem Christi dicitur non ex objecto, quod res Christi præsignificarit, quia hæc jam designantur per verba prænuncians, eas, quæ in Christo sunt, passiones & glorias: Sed quod Filii Dei Spiritus sit Spiritus Sanctus ab æterno ex ipso procedens, uti Spiritus Patris eadem ratione dici- tur ob æternam à Patre processionem, Joh. 15, 16. Quo de in System. Theol. Tom. III. De illa præte- stificatione Christus, Luc. 24, 26. 27. 44. & Petrus Act. 10, 43.

## 1:12
Verse 12.

Οἷς ἀπεκαλύφθη, ὅτι ὀὐχ’ ἑαυτοῖς, ὑμῖν δὲ διηκόνουν αὐτὰ) The whole matter was not laid open to them, but they understood this, that they had administered these things, that is, had foretold them (for every announcement of the divine word is διακονία, Acts 6:4, Rom. 11:13, 1 Cor. 4:1, ch. 5:18, 1 Tim. 1:12, 2 Tim. 4:5), which were to come to pass not in their own time, but in yours. Magnus It is truly an honor that the Prophets served not themselves, but us. They saw through a lattice what we clearly behold. In the Manuscript: Οἷς ἀπεκαλύφθη ἀυτὰ ὀυχ ἑαυτοῖς, ὑμῖν δὲ διε- κόνων. But I prefer that which this Latin follows. ἅ νῦν ἀνηγγέλη ὑμῖν διὰ τῶν ἐυαγγελισαμένων ὑμᾶς ἐν Πνεύ- ματι ἁγίῳ ἀποσταλέντι ἀπ᾿ ὀυρανῦ) Those great things have been fully explained to us by the Apostles and their helpers, gifted from heaven with the Holy Spirit, that is, with greater gifts than the Prophets themselves had, and of which the Prophets themselves spoke, as Joel 2:28. ἀναγγέλειν is a word very well suited to this matter, Acts 14:27, c. 15:4, c. 20:20, 37, Rom. 15:21, 1 John 1:5. חזה. ἐυαγγελίζειν or ἐυαγγελίζεσθαι in an active sense not rarely governs the accusative of the person instead of the dative among our writers, Luke 3:18, Acts 8:25, 40, c. 13:32, c. 14:15, 21, Gal. 1:9. The Spirit is said to be sent, as in Luke 24:49. John 14:26, c. 15:26, c. 16:6.

It was not only revealed to the Prophets that the Messiah was not to come in their own time, Dan. 9:24, ch. 12:9, 13, Heb. 11:13, which some here wish to be implied, but the Apostle says that a revelation was made to them concerning those things which concern the person, office, and benefits of the Messiah, that all those things are to be fulfilled in the New Testament which are now announced as fulfilled through the Gospel. Which things, however, are by no means to be drawn to the conclusion as if they did not pertain to the believers of the Old Testament: because they also were saved through the grace of Jesus Christ, Isa. 45:24, Acts 4:12, ch. 15:11, Rom. 3:21, Heb. 11:10, ch. 13:13. Indeed, because the Prophets searched concerning that grace, it is to be gathered that neither were they excluded from its communion, nor others to whom they preached it, so that they might receive it by faith, Ps. 2, last verse, Isa. 45:23. To say nothing of the fact that particles negative in sound are often comparative in sense: they ministered not so much to themselves as to us, Gen. 32:28, Exod. 16:8, 1 Sam. 8:7, Mark 9:37, Luke 14:12, John 5:39, 1 Cor. 1:17. The Spirit of Christ in the Prophets, the Spirit of Christ in the Apostles. Thus it appears that the Prophets and Apostles announce the same salvation, says the Glossa ordinaria on this passage. But the Apostles and their coadjutors evangelized ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ, in the Holy Spirit, sent from heaven, Acts 2:14, ch. 3:12, ch. 4, v. 8, 31, 33, ch. 6:10. Nor does Peter, as some suspect, indicate that he was not an evangelist to those to whom he writes, but that he was not the only one.

εἰς ἅ ἐπιθυμῦσιν ἄγγελοι παρακύψαι) ἅ here signifies all those things of which he had treated, which the Angels themselves, not previously known, now behold with supreme joy; Irenaeus also accepted it, book V, 67. Those good things were predicted, into which the Angels desired to look. For παρακύψαι is taken here as in James 1:25. ἐπιθυμῦσιν אבו, that is, they love, as in Ps. 119:20, 40, and often elsewhere. That Angels progress through men is an old opinion of the Hebrews in Rabbi Israel on the Soul, ch. 1. There is, however, again in these words an allusion to the Cherubim, whose eyes looked toward the ἱλαστήριον.

Bede refers the relative to the glories of Christ, but more correctly to all things which have been fulfilled and announced through the Gospel; indeed, even to those mysteries, such as those which are ὁμολογουμένως without controversy great, which are handed down in the Gospel concerning Christ manifested in the flesh, or concerning the incarnation of the Son of God, the personal union of the two natures, the passion and satisfaction of the Son of God, and his exaltation and kingdom, the mysteries of godliness, 1 Tim. 3:16. For it is not said εἰς ὃν, as some codices read, but according to the consensus of the approved Greek and Latin codices εἰς ἅ, into which, whence Irenaeus, book IV, ch. 77, accepted these things concerning the promises of the Prophets which Christ fulfilled upon coming. Παρακύπτειν is properly said of those who incline themselves with the zeal of looking and peering more deeply, and look at all things more accurately, Luke 24:12, John 20:5, and thus it is used for accurate inspection, James 1:25, ch. 2:5. Wherefore, not only is the sublimity and depth of the mysteries concerning Christ, Rom. 11:35, Eph. 3:18, and their dignity thus denoted, but also the fervor and diligence of desire and zeal from religion toward God, and love toward the human race, of which Luke 15:10, Eph. 3:8, 1 Tim. 3:16, and the consonance and conformity of Prophetic Theology in the Old Testament, Evangelical in the New Testament, and Angelic in heaven are expressed.

PART III. A commendation of the grace of God exhibited in Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Οἷς ἀπεκαλύφθη, ὅτι ὀὐχ’ ἑαυτοῖς, ὑμῖν δὲ διηκόνουν αὐτὰ) Non patefacta illis est res tota, sed hoc intellexere, se eas administrasse, id est, prædixisse, (nam omnis ver- bi divini annunciatio est διακονία, Actorum 6, 4. Rom. 11, 13. 1. Cor. 4, 1. c. 5, 18. 1. Tim. 1, 12. 2. Tim. 4, 5.) quæ eventuræ erant non ipsorum, sed vestro tempore. Magnus sane honor, quod Prophetæ non sibi, sed nobis inserviere. Viderunt per transennam, quæ nos clare conspicimus. In Manuscripto: Οἷς ἀπεκαλύφθη ἀυτὰ ὀυχ ἑαυτοῖς, ὑμῖν δὲ διε- κόνων. Sed præfero id, quod Latinus hic sequitur. ἅ νῦν ἀνηγγέλη ὑμῖν διὰ τῶν ἐυαγγελισαμένων ὑμᾶς ἐν Πνεύ- ματι ἁγίῳ ἀποσταλέντι ἀπ᾿ ὀυρανῦ) Res illæ magnæ nobis ple- ne explicatæ sunt per Apostolos, & eorum adjutores, cœ- litus donatos Spiritu Sancto, id est, donis majoribus, quam ipsi Prophetæ habuere, & de quibus ipsi Prophetæ sunt lo- quuti, ut Joel. 2, 28. ἀναγγέλειν vox valde accommodata huic rei, Actor. 14, 27. c. 15, 4. c. 20, 20. 37. Rom. 15, 21. 1. Joh. 1, 5. חזה ἐυαγγελίζειν aut ἐυαγγελίζεσθαι sensu activo non raro apud nostros scriptores accusativum personæ regit vici Dative Luc. 3, 18. Actor. 8, 25. 40. c. 13, 32. c. 14, 15. 21. Gal. 1, 9. Spiritus mitti dicitur, ut Luc. 24, 49. Johan. 14, 26. c. 15, 26. c. 16, 6.

Non tantum id revelatum est Prophetis, quod non ipsorum tempore adventurus sit Messias, Dan. 9, 24. cap. 12, 9. 13. Ebr. 11, 13. quod non- nulli hic innui volunt, sed etiam de iis revela- tionem ipsis factam dicit Apostolus, quæ Mes- siæ personam, officium, & beneficia concernunt, quod omnia illa complenda sint in Novo Testa- mento, quæ nunc per Evangelium annuncian- tur completa. Quæ vero neutiquam eo trahen- da, quasi illa non spectarint ad fideles Veteris Testamenti: quia illi etiam per gratiam Jesu Christi salvati sunt, Esa. 45, 24. Actorum 4, 12. cap. 15, 11. Rom. 3, 21. Ebr. 11, 10. cap. 13, 13. Imo quia de illa gratia scrutati sunt Prophetæ, ideo nec ipsos ab ejus communione exclusos fuisse, colligere est, nec alios, quibus eam prædica- runt, ut fide susciperent, Psal. 2. v. ult. Esa. 45, 23. Ut taceam, quod particulæ quoad sonum negativæ sæpe comparativæ sint quoad sensum: non tam sibi quàm nobis ministrarunt, Gen. 32, 28. Exod. 16, 8. 1. Sam. 8, 7. Marc. 9, 37. Luc. 14, 12. Johan. 5, 39. 1. Corinth. 1, 17. Spiritus Christi in Prophetis, Spiritus Christi in Apostolis. Ita apparet, quod Prophetæ & Apostoli eandem salu- tem nuncient, inquit Glossa ordin. in h. l. Evan- gelizarunt autem Apostoli & coadjutores eorum ἐν Πνεύματι ἁγίῳ, in Spiritu Sancto, misso de cœ- lo, Actorum 2, 14. cap. 3, 12. cap. 4. v. 8. 31. 33. cap. 6, 10. Neque vero Petrus, quod quidam su- spicantur, indicat, se non fuisse eorum, ad quos scribit, Evangelistam, sed non fuisse solum.

εἰς ἅ ἐπιθυμῦσιν ἄγγελοι παρακύψαι) ἅ hic significat omnes res istas, de quibus egerat, quas Angeli ipsi, an- tea non percognitas, cum summo gaudio nunc perspi- ciunt; ita accepit & Irenæus l V. 67. Ea prædicta sunt bona, in quæ concupiscebant Angeli intendere. Παρακύψαι enim hic sumitur, ut Jacob. 1, 25. ἐπιθυμῦσιν אבו, id est, amant, quomodo Psal. 119, 20. 40. & alibi sæpe. Angelos proficere per homines vetus est Ebræorum sen- tentia apud Rabbinum Israelem de Anima cap. 1. Est au- tem iterum in his verbis allusio ad Cherubinos, quorum oculi versus ἱλαστήριον spectabant.

Relativum ad Christi glorias refert Beda, sed rectius ad omnia, quæ impleta sunt, & per Evangelium annunciata; imo etiam ad myste- ria illa, qualia sunt ὁμολογουμένως citra contro- versiam magna, quæ de Christo manifestato in carne, vel de Filii Dei incarnatione, personali duarum naturarum unione, Filii Dei passione & satisfactione, ejusdemque exaltatione & regno in Evangelio tradita sunt pietatis mysteria, 1. Ti- moth. 3, 16. Non enim dicitur εἰς ὃν, ut qui- dam Codices legere, sed juxta consensum pro- batiorum Codicum Græcorum & Latinorum εἰς ἅ, in quæ, unde Irenæus libr. IV. cap. 77. de promissis Prophetarum, quæ Christus adve- niens implevit, hæc accepit. Παρακύπτειν pro- prie de iis dicitur, qui studio intuendi ac peni- tius introspiciendi se inclinant, & omnia accu- ratius intuentur, Luc. 24, 12. Johan. 20, 5. adeoque de accurata inspectione adhibetur, Jac. 1, 25. cap. 2, 5. Quapropter non tantum my- steriorum de Christo sublimitas & profunditas, Rom. 11. 35. Ephes. 3, 18. ac dignitas ita denotatur, sed etiam desiderii studiique è religione erga Deum, & amore erga genus humanum, quo de Luc. 15, 10. fervor & sedulitas, Ephes. 3, 8. 1. Tim. 3, 16. ac Theologiæ Propheticæ in Veteri Testamento, Evangelicæ in Novo Testamento, & Angelicæ in cœlo consonantia & conformitas exprimitur.

PARS III. Gratia Dei in Christo exhibita commenda- tio.

## 1:13
Verse 13.

Διὸ) Since such great honor is destined for you, that you know what the Prophets did not foresee, and the Angels themselves become more learned from your successes. ἀναζωσάμενοι τὰς ὀσφύας τῆς διανοίας ὑμῶν) The members and acts of the body are accustomed to be transferred to the mind. Those who prepare themselves for some bodily ministry are accustomed to gird their loins, concerning which matter see what is said in Luke 12:35, Eph. 6:14. But specifically here the Paschal rite is looked to, Exod. 12:11. The sense is: Be attentive. νήφοντες) That is, having a mind not at all disturbed. See 1 Thess. 5:6, 8, 2 Tim. 4:5. τελείως ἐλπίσοντες) That is, even to the end, as Judith 11:5. למנצח. See Matt. 10:22. ἐπὶ την φερομένην ὑμῖν χάριν ἐν ἀποκαλύψει Ἰησοῦ Χριςῦ) There is here first a transposition for εἰς τὴν χάριν τὴν φερομένην ὑμῖν ἐν ἀποκαλύψει Ἰησοῦ Χριςῦ. Then χάρις is put for the supreme effect of divine benevolence, that is, eternal life. The same is χάρισμα in Rom. 6:23. φέρein and κομίζειν are reciprocal to each other. What God brings to us, we bring back. Take ἐν ἀποκαλύψει Ἰησοῦ Χριςῦ here as above in v. 7.

That grace of God, which He has exhibited to us in Christ, is now commended to the converted, so that they may likewise diligently examine it, attentively weigh it, and receive it with the holy obedience of faith, and persevere in that faith even to the end, and demonstrate that faith in the innocence of life and character. Rightly, therefore, Blessed Luther above others: That is an exhortation to faith, and this is the meaning: Because such things have been given and proclaimed to you through the Gospel, in which even the angels rejoice and have a desire to look; so hang on to it now, and place your confidence upon it, with full consideration, so that it may be a genuine faith, and not a feigned or fabricated delusion and dream. The metaphor of the loins of the mind is taken from the Orientals, who used loose garments, and therefore had need, when about to undertake a journey or some work, to gird up their loins. Thus, with the loins of the mind girded, we ought to be intent upon the grace of the Gospel, just as it was predicted by the Prophets and announced by the Evangelists and Apostles, lest νοήματα and ὑψώματα, exalting themselves against the knowledge of God, be a hindrance to us, 2 Corinthians 10:5. To which end let us also be νήφοντες, that is, vigilant, as Jerome translates against Vigilantius. Be awakened, the Syriac renders it, not so much by the vigilance and excitement of the body as of the spirit and prudence, but as children of light, whose directress is the Prophetic and Apostolic scripture. The Vulgate interpreted it as sober; but it is the sobriety of the mind that is to be understood. Whence Blessed Luther explained these things thus: But the spiritual girding (of which the Apostle speaks here) proceeds thus. As a virgin is bodily pure and uncorrupted: Thus the soul is spiritually unmoved through faith, through which it becomes the bride of Christ. But if it falls from faith into false doctrine, it must come to shame. Hence Scripture everywhere calls idolatry and unbelief adultery and whoredom, that is, when the soul clings to human doctrines and thus lets go of faith and Christ. St. Peter now forbids this here, when he bids us gird the loins of the mind, as if he would say: You have now heard the Gospel, and have entered into faith, therefore see to it that you remain therein, and do not let yourselves be moved by false doctrine, so that you do not waver, and run here and there with works. And furthermore: Mind is what we call being minded, as when I say: That seems right to me, and as Paul speaks: Thus we hold it, thus we are minded. With this he hits upon the faith properly, and wishes to say: You have formed a righteous mind, that one must be justified through faith alone, in that mind remain now, gird it well, hold fast to it, and do not let yourselves be torn away from it, then you stand well. For many false teachers will arise, and set up human doctrine, so that they move your mind, and loosen the belt of faith, therefore be warned, and grasp it well in your minds.

Others explain the word τελείως as perfectly. But Grotius's explanation is not inconvenient: Inasmuch as it is not so much the perfection of faith that is required, as final perseverance. For ἐλπίζειν in the phraseology of Scripture is to trust, 2 Samuel 22:13, 1 Chronicles 10:14, Job 13:13, Psalm 2, last verse. Faith can be firm and sincere, but in whom will it be found perfect? Through χάριν, however, is understood not only eternal life, which is the gift of God in Christ, Rom. 6:23, but the grace brought by Christ and offered to us in the Gospel: for φερομένη is not put for the future, but can and ought to be taken properly for the grace which is offered in the present, as Erasmus [says] in that grace which is brought to you. By ἀποκάλυψιν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ [is meant] not that which is expected on the last day, as verse 7 is designated in the present, but that which happens through the Word of the Gospel, as Luke 2:23, Rom. 16:25, Gal. 1:12, 16. Ephes. 1:17, as Erasmus: while Christ is manifested to you. Thus there is no need to take the preposition ἐν for εἰς.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Διὸ) Cum tantus vobis honor destinatus sit, ut noritis, quæ Prophetæ non perviderunt, & ex vestris successibus ipsi Angeli fiant doctiores. ἀναζωσάμενοι τὰς ὀσφύας τῆς διανοίας ὑμῶν) Solent mem- bra & actus corporis transferri ad animum. Accingi lumbos solent, qui se ad corporale aliquod ministerium parant, de qua re vide dicta Luc. 12, 35. Eph. 6, 14. Specialiter autem hic respicitur ritus Paschalis, Exod. 12, 11. Sensus est: Esto- te attenti. νήφοντες) Id est, animum habentes minime perturba- tum. Vide 1. Thess. 5, 6. 8. 2. Tim. 4, 5. τελείως ἐλπίσοντες) Id est, ad finem usque, ut Judith. 11, 5. למנצח . Vide Matth. 10, 22. ἐπὶ την φερομένην ὑμῖν χάριν ἐν ἀποκαλύψει Ἰησοῦ Χριςῦ) Est hic primum trajectio pro εἰς τὴν χάριν τὴν φερομένην ὑμῖν ἐν ἀποκαλύψει Ἰησοῦ Χριςῦ. Deinde χάρις ponitur pro summo effectu divinæ benevolentiæ, id est, vita æter- na. Idem χάρισμα Rom. 6, 23. Sunt inter se ἀντίςροφα φέρειν & κομίζειν. Quæ Deus nobis apportat, nos re- portamus. ἐν ἀποκαλύψει ἰησοῦ Χριςῦ hic sume, ut supra v. 7.

Commendatur jam conversis gratia illa Dei, quam exhibuit nobis in Christo, ut eam pari- ter diligenter scrutentur, attente expendant, & sancta obedientia fidei excipiant, atque in ea fide ad finem usque perseverent, eamque fidem in vitæ & morum innocentia demon- strent. Recte itaque B. Lutherus præ aliis: Das ist eine Vermahnung zum Glauben, und ist das die Meynung: Weil euch solches gegeben und verkündiget ist, durch das Evangelium, deß sich auch die Engel freuen, und Lust haben zu schauen; So hanget nun dran, und setzet eure Zuversicht drauff, mit ganzem Erwegen, also, daß es ein rechtschaffener Glaube, und nicht ein ge- färbter oder erdichteter Wahn und Traum sey. Metaphora de lumbis mentis ab Orientalibus pe- tita est, qui laxis vestibus utebantur, adeoque opus habebant, ut iter vel opus aliquod aggres- suri lumbos præcingerent. Ita succincti lumbis mentis intenti esse debemus in gratiam Evange- lii, prout à Prophetis ea prædicta, ab Evange- listis & Apostolis annunciata est, ne nobis impe- dimento sint νοήματα & ὑψώματα, se efferentia adversus cognitionem Dei, 2. Corinth. 10. v. 5. Qua fini etiam νήφοντες simus, id est, vigilantes, ut Hieronymus adversus Vigilant. vertit. Exci- tamini, reddit Syrus, non tam vigilantia & exci- tatione corporis, quam spiritus, ac prudentia, sed filiorum lucis, cujus directrix est scriptura Prophetica & Apostolica. Vulgata exposuit so- brii; sed intelligenda sobrietas mentis. Unde B. Lutherus hæc ita exposuit: Aber das geistliche Gürten (davon hie der Apostel sagt) gehet also zu. Wie eine Jungfrau leiblich rein und unverruckt ist: Also ist die Seele geistlich durch den Glauben un- verruckt, durch welchen sie Christus Braut wird Wenn sie aber von dem Glauben fället auf falsch Lehre, so muß sie zu schanden werden. Dahe die Schrifft allenthalben die Abgötterey und Un glauben einen Ehebruch und Hurerey nennet, das ist, wenn die Seele an Menschen-lehren hänget und also den Glauben und Christum fallen lässet. Das verbeut nun hier S. Petrus, wenn er uns heisset die lenden des Gemüths gürten, als woll er sagen: Ihr habt nun das Evangelium gehö- ret, und seyd in Glauben getreten, darum sehet darauff, daß ihr darinnen bleibet, und euch nicht verrucken lasset durch falsche lehre, daß ihr nicht wancket, und hin und her laufft mit Wercken. Et porro: Gemüth heisset, das wir sprechen, gesinnet seyn, als wenn ich sage: Das düncket mich recht, und wie Paulus redet: Also halten wirs, also sind wir gesinnet. Damit triffet er eigentlich den Glau- ben, und will also sagen: Ihr habt einen recht- schaffenen Sinn geschöpfft, daß man allein müsse durch Glauben gerecht werden, in dem Sinn blei- bet nun, gürtet den wohl, haltet vest daran, und lasset euch davon nicht reissen, so stehet ihr wohl. Denn es werden viel falsche Lehrer aufftreten, und Menschen-lehre auffrichten, daß sie euren Sinn verrucken, und den Gürtel des Glaubens auff- lösen, darum seyd gewarnet, und fasset es wohl zu Sinnen.

Vocem τελείως alii exponunt perfe- cte. Sed non inconveniens est Grotii explica- tio: Siquidem requiratur fidei non tam perfe- ctio, quam finalis perseverantia. Ἐλπίζειν enim phrasi Scripturæ est confidere, 2. Samuel. 22, 13. 1. Paral. 10, 14. Job. 13, 13. Psal. 2. v. ult. Fides firma & sincera esse potest, perfecta autem in quonam reperietur? Per χάριν vero non solum vita æterna, quæ donum est Dei in Christo, Rom. 6, 23. sed gratia à Christo parta, & in Evangelio nobis oblata intelligitur: non enim φερομένη pro futuro ponitur, sed proprie accipi potest ac de- bet pro gratia, quæ in præsenti offertur, ut Erasmus in eam, quæ ad vos defertur, gra- tiam. Per ἀποκάλυψιν Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ non illa, quæ in extremo die expectatur, ut verf. 7. designa- tur in præsenti, sed quæ fit per Verbum Evan- gelii, ut Luc. 2, 23. Rom. 16, 25. Galat. 1, 12. 16. Ephes. 1, 17. quomodo Erasmus: dum vobis ma- nifestatur Christus. Sic opus non est, præpositio- nem ἐν pro εἰς accipere.

## 1:14
Verse 14.

ὡς τέκνα ὑπακοῆς) בּנֵי מִשׁמַע. Thus τέκνα φωτὸς, Eph. 5:8, thus we said that τέκνα is to be understood for that πίσεως, Heb. 10:39, on the other hand we have τέκνα ὀργῆς, Ephes. 2:3, and κατάρας below chapter 6:3. μὴ συσχηματιζόμενοι ταῖς πρότερον ἐν τῇ ἀγνοίᾳ ὑμῶν ἐπιθυμίαις) Thus μὴ συσχηματίζεσθε τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, Rom. 12:12. But he rightly distinguishes the times of ignorance from the times of knowledge. This other age demands other customs. The same sense [is in] verse 8 seq. See also John 9:39 and Acts 17:30, Eph. 4:18. Then they had lived as desire dictated, Eph. 2:3, now as Christ has taught.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

ὡς τέκνα ὑπακοῆς) בּנֵי מִשׁמַע. Sic τέκνα φωτὸς, Eph. 5, 8. sic ad illud πίσεως subaudiri τέκνα diximus Ebr. 10, 39. contra τέκνα ὀργῆς habemus Ephes. 2, 3. & κατάρας infra cap. 6, 3.. μὴ συσχηματιζόμενοι ταῖς πρότερον ἐν τῇ ἀγνοίᾳ ὑμῶν ἐπι- θυμίαις) Sic μὴ συσχηματίζεσθε τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, Rom. 12, v. 12. Bene autem distinguit tempora ignorantiæ à tem- poribus notitiæ. Alia hæc ætas alios mores exigit. Idem sensus v. 8. seq. Vide & Joh. 9, 39. & Act. 17, 30. Eph. 4, 18. Tunc vixerant ut cupido dictabat, Eph. 2, 3. nunc ut Chri- stus docuit.

## 1:15
Verse 15.

ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸν καλέσαντα ὑμᾶς ἅγιον, καὶ αὐτοὶ ἅγιοι ἐν πάσῃ ἀναστροφῇ γενήθητε) The following words show that God is indicated here by the name of holy. And Isaiah often uses the word holy in this way. But our calling is often ascribed to God the Father of Christ, as the principal cause, Rom. 9:12, 24, 1 Cor. 7:15, Gal. 1:6, and elsewhere. Concerning the word ἀναστροφῆς see Heb. 13:7, James 3:13.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸν καλέσαντα ὑμᾶς ἅγιον, καὶ αὐτοὶ ἅγιοι ἐν πά- σῃ ἀναστροφῇ γενήθητε) Deum hic indicari sancti nomine ostendunt sequentia. Et sæpe vocem sancti sic usurpat Esaias. Vocatio autem nostra sæpe Deo Patri Christi ad- scribitur, ut causæ principi, Rom. 9, 12. 24. 1. Corinth. 7. v. 15. Gal. 1, 6. & alibi de voce ἀνασροφῆς Vide Ebr. 13, 7. Jac. 3, 13.

## 1:16
Verse 16.

διότι γέγραπται, ἅγιοι γίνεσθε, ὅτι ἐγὼ ἅγιός εἰμι) Levit. 11:44 and 19:2. If this was said to the Israelites at that time, how much more at this time, which requires more holiness. In the manuscript, instead of γίνεσθε there is ἔσεσθε, as in the LXX in the two places in Leviticus.

By ὑπακοὴν (obedience) can be understood either Evangelical obedience or legal. Most assume the latter. But either the former seems to be noted, as blessed Luther explains, or certainly both. For children of obedience is a Hebrew phrase for those who are obedient, both by believing the Gospel and by rendering obedience to the law. Just as the Apostle had spoken of the girding of the loins of the mind as a requirement of faith, of faith to be kept until the end, and of the grace of God offered through the revelation of the Gospel to be embraced trustingly as the object of faith, so he now warns that we should show ourselves as those who are reborn of God and children of God through faith, not children τῆς ἀπειθείας (of disobedience), Eph. 2, 2. ch. 5, 6. Coloss. 3, 6. or unbelieving men, but children ὑπακοῆς τῆς πίστεως (of the obedience of faith), Rom. 1. v. 5. that is, believers, observing the commandment of God the Father, which is that we should believe in the name of His Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, 1 John 3, 13. For we are not (τέκνα) (children) of withdrawal, but of faith, Heb. 10, 39. reborn to this by the Word of truth, that we might be the firstfruits of His creatures, James 1, 18. Before, without faith, without Christ, without God, the Gentiles had lived in the world, in ignorance and various wicked desires, Eph. 2, 12. 1 Pet. 4, 3. For ignorance of Christ is the cause of all impurity and impiety, Eph. 4, 18. Now, therefore, having been converted to Christ and reborn, they are warned not to be conformed to the former desires of Gentile ignorance. Those who have been received as children render obedience to the Father, Mal. 1, 6. by adhering to Him with sincere faith, by restraining carnal desires, and by exhibiting true holiness in all conduct. He therefore involves the arguments of his exhortation from the duty of the children of God, from the modern state of conversion, and from the example of the heavenly Father, by whom they have been called. Where one must marvel at Grotius, that he believed a greater holiness could be required than that which is demanded by the example of God in the law. For what more can be prescribed than that we should be holy as God is? That, however, was required no less of the Israelites than in our time. Nor does Peter require more of us than Moses, whose precept, and according to it the highest degree of holiness, he exhibits and had required. Add also Levit. 20, v. 7, 26. ch. 21, v. 8, where the same thing that occurs here regarding the calling is added, Levit. 20, v. 26: Because I have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine. The Papal abuse of this sentence, with Innocent's Epist. II, ch. 9, distinct. 31, by which he rashly wished to carve out the celibacy of priests because it is written, 'be holy,' etc., we deem unworthy of refutation. To which, however, Siricius preceded in Epist. I, ch. 7, in the same distinction, ch. 'plurimis': Who does not see that the holy order of God, which is a sacrament to the Pontificals, is thus affected with the highest insult, and that it would have to be prohibited for that reason not only to priests, but to all pious people?

Latin:

Vers. 16.

διότι γέγραπται, ἅγιοι γίνεσθε, ὅτι ἐγὼ ἅγιός εἰμι) Levit. 11, 44. & 19, 2, Si hoc dictum Israelitis illo tempore, quan- to magis hoc tempore plus sanctitatis requirente. In Ma- nuscripto pro γίνεσθε est ἔσεσθε, quomodo apud LXX. duo- bus Levitici locis,

Per ὑπακοὴν intelligi potest vel obedientia Evangelica, vel legalis. Plerique hanc assumunt. Sed vel illa notari videtur, ut B. Lutherus explicat, vel certe utraque. Filii enim obedientia phrasi Ebræa sunt obedientes, tum Evangelio credendo, tum legi obedientiam præstando. Ut de lumborum mentis cinctura, ceu requisito fidei, de fide ad finem usque servanda, de gratia Dei per revelationem Evangelii oblata fiducialiter amplectanda ceu objecto fidei dixerat Apostolus, ita nos exhibeamus, jam monet, tanquam eos, qui renati sunt à Deo, & filii Dei per fidem, non filii τῆς ἀπειθείας incredulitatis, Eph. 2, 2. cap. 5, 6. Coloss. 3, 6. vel homines increduli, sed filii ὑπακοῆς τῆς πίστεως obedientiæ fidei, Rom. 1. v. 5. id est, fideles, observantes mandatum Dei Patris, quod est, ut credamus in nomen Filii ejus Jesu Christi, & diligamus nos invicem, 1. Johan. 3, 13. Non enim sumus (τέκνα) ὑποστολῆς, ἀλλὰ πίστεως Ebr. 10, 39. ad id regeniti Verbo veritatis, ut simus primitiæ creaturarum ejus, Jacob. 1, 18. Ante sine fide, sine Christo, sine Deo vixerant gentiles in mundo, in ignorantia variisque desideriis pravis, Eph. 2, 12. 1. Petr. 4, 3. Christi enim ignorantia est omnis impuritatis & impietatis causa, Ephes. 4, 18. Jam ergo ad Christum conversi & renati monentur, ne prioribus ignorantiæ gentilis desideriis configurentur. Qui recepti in filios sunt, Patri præstant obedientiam, Malach. 1, 6. sincera fide ipsi adhærendo, desideria carnalia compescendo, veram sanctitatem in omni conversatione exhibendo. Involvit ergo argumenta suæ adhortationis à debito filiorum Dei officio, à moderno conversionis statu, ab exemplo Patris cælestis, à quo vocati sunt. Ubi mirari oportet Grotium, quod majorem sanctitatem postulari posse crediderit, quam quæ exemplo Dei requisita est in lege. Quid enim amplius præscribi potest, quam ut ita sancti simus, ut Deus est? Illud autem requirebatur non minus Israëelitarum, quam nostro tempore. Nec amplius requirit Petrus à nobis, quam Moses, cujus præceptum, & juxta id supremum sanctitatis gradum exhibet, requisiverat. Adde & Levit. 20. vers. 7. 26. cap. 21. vers. 8. ubi eadem, quæ hic à vocatione occurrit, addita est, Levit. 20. vers. 26. Quia separavi vos à populis, ut essetis mei. Sententiæ hujus abusum Papalem, cum Innocentiis Epist. II. cap. 9. distinct. 31. temere cælibatum Sacerdotum inde exsculpere voluit, quia scriptum est, sancti estote &c. indignum censemus refutatione. Cui tamen præivit Siricius Epist. I. cap. 7. distinctio- ne eadem c. plurimis: Quis non videt, ita sanctum Dei ordinem, qui Pontificiis sacramentum est, summa contumelia affici, nec Sacerdotibus tantum, sed omnibus piis eundem ea ratione prohibendum fore?

## 1:17
Vers. 17. καὶ εἰ πατέρα ἐπικαλεῖσθε (and if you call upon the Father) Namely, through Christ. τὸν ἀπροσωπολήπτως κρίνοντα κατὰ τὸ ἑκάστου ἔργον (who judges impartially according to each one's work) Namely, that He may give or take away His Spirit. Ἀπροσωπολήπτως (impartially) He judges, Job 34, 18. He will not hold you excused any more than those born from the Gentiles, Acts 9, 34. Rom. 2, 11. Eph. 6, 9. Col. 3, 25. ἔργον (work) singular for plural, as James 1, 4, 25. Thus in Job 34, 12, כי פעל אדם ישלם לו, where the Greeks [say], ἀποδιδῷ ἀνθρώπῳ κατὰ ποιεῖ (He renders to man according to what he does). ἐν φόβῳ (in fear) With the highest reverence for God, Eph. 6, 5. Phil. 2, 12. τὸν τῆς παροικίας ὑμῶν χρόνον ἀναστράφητε (pass the time of your sojourning) He comforts them because they live abroad, signifying that all men are pilgrims here. On this matter, see what we have brought forward on Hebrews ch. 11, v. 13, and following. τὸν χρόνον (the time) is the accusative of duration. Παροικία (sojourning) is מגור, Psalm 119, 54. In Latin, incolatus (residence/sojourning).

The particle εἰ is not conditional, but assertive, not of one doubting, but presupposing a known fact: because you call upon him as Father. It seems to refer to the Lord's Prayer, Matt. 6:9. Because you name him, and by naming him you call upon him; because you profess yourselves his children, and in your prayers and desires you turn to him as Father: where an argument is introduced from the judgment of God, by which he is about to judge without respect of persons according to the work of each one, not by giving or taking away the Spirit, for the Spirit is not given according to our works, but out of grace: But in such a way that he bestows rewards upon those who do good, and renders punishments to those who do evil. Κατὰ denotes not cause, but quality, as in Matt. 23:3, and is rendered in Rev. 22:12 as their work shall be. For Peter means that before the tribunal of God there is no place for respect of persons, but that the sincerity of the heart is estimated, and works are judged by Him not according to external appearance, but according to the good or evil quality of the heart.

Furthermore, he insinuates another argument from our sojourn, because we are only strangers in this world, and are not truly of the world, John 15:19, and therefore we ought not to conform ourselves to the world, but to pass our life in the fear of the Lord, by whom we have been called; because we are only sojourners here, not having a stable dwelling in this world, but aspiring to that one, Heb. 13:14, and therefore let us live here in such a way, as those about to depart shortly, lest we be excluded from that abiding city. It is not so much a comfort for those living abroad, as an allusion to the state of those dispersed into foreign shores: and from there is drawn an exhortation concerning strangers in this world with respect to the heavenly fatherland.

Latin:

Vers. 17. καὶ εἰ πατέρα ἐπικαλεῖσθε) Nempe per Christum. τὸν ἀπροσωπολήπτως κρίνοντα κατὰ τὸ ἑκάστου ἔργον) Nempe ut det aut auferat Spiritum suum. Ἀπροσωπολήπτως judicat Job. 34, 18. Non magis vos excusatos habebit, quam è gentibus natos, Actor. 9, 34. Rom. 2, 11. Ephes. 6, 9. Col. 3, 25. ἔργον singulare pro plurali, ut Jac. 1, 4. 25. Sic Jobi 34, 12. כי פעל אדם ישלם לו, ubi Græci, ἀποδιδῷ ἀνθρώπῳ κατὰ ποιεῖ. ἐν φόβῳ) Cum Dei reverentia summa, Eph. 6, 5. Phil. 2, 12. τὸν τῆς παροικίας ὑμῶν χρόνον ἀναστράφητε) Solatur eos, quod peregre habitent, significans omnes homines hic esse peregrinos. Hac de re vide, quæ attulimus ad Ebræos cap. 11. v. 13, & sequentia, τὸν χρόνον accusativus durationis, Παροικία מגור Psal. 119, 54. Latine incolatus.

Particula εἰ non est conditionalis, sed assertiva, non dubitantis, sed rem notam præsupponentis: quia Patrem eum invocatis. Respicere videtur orationem Dominicam Matth. 6, 9. quia nomi- natis & nominando invocatis; quia profitemini vos filios ejus, & in precibus ac desideriis vestris ad eum tanquam Patrem vos convertitis: ubi argumentum ingeritur à judicio Dei, quo sine personarum acceptione judicaturus est secundum unius cujusvis opus non Spiritum vel dando vel auferendo, non enim secundum opera nostra datur Spiritus, sed ex gratia: Sed ita, ut tribuat bene operantibus præmia, male agentibus autem pœnas retribuat. Κατὰ non causam, sed qualita- tem notat, ut Matth. 23, 3. & redditur Apoc. 22. ὡς τὸ ἔργον αὐτῶν ἔσται. Id enim vult Petrus apud Dei tribunal non esse personæ respectui locum, sed cordis sinceritatem æstimari, ac opera non ex specie externa, sed ex cordis qualitate bona vel mala ab ipso judicari.

Porro aliud etiam insinuat argumentum ab incolatu, quia peregrini sumus tantum in hoc mun- do, non vero de mundo sumus, Johan. 15, 19. ideo- que non debemus nos mundo configurare, sed vi- tam in timore Domini, à quo evocati sumus, tra- ducere; quia advenæ hic tantum sumus, stabile habitaculum in mundo hoc non habentes, sed ad id adspirantes, Ebr. 13, 14. ideoque ita hic vivamus, ut brevi migraturi, ne à civitate illa manente ex- cludamur. Non tam solatium est peregre habi- tantium, quam allusio ad dispersorum in oras peregrinas statum: & inde petita exhortatio de peregrinis in hoc mundo respectu patriæ cœle- stis.

## 1:18
Verse 18. εἰδότες) Considering, as in Acts 23:5. So that he may return to further information concerning the salvation acquired through Christ in this admonition to innocence of life, he recalls to their memory the benefit of Christ's redemption, as that from which the duty of our piety flows.

ὅτι ὀ φθαρτοῖς ἀργυρίῳ ἢ χρυσίῳ) See above v. 7. ἐλυτρώθητε) וגאלתם. The same word in the same sense in Tit. 2:14, and the noun λυτρώσεως in Heb. 9:12, 26.

ἐκ τῆς ματαίας ὑμῶν ἀναστροφῆς πατροπαραδότου) From the observance of rites, with the mind not cleansed, which your fathers, that is, your teachers, had taught you was sufficient for salvation. Thus the name of Fathers is taken in 1 Cor. 4:15. Hence Pirkei Avot.

Latin:

Vers. 18. εἰδότες) Considerantes, ut Actor. 23, 5. Ut redeat ad informationem ulteriorem de sa- lute per Christum acquisita in hac νουθεσίᾳ ad in- nocentiam vitæ, in memoriam ipsis revocat redem- ptionis Christi beneficium, utpote è quo fluit debi- tum pietatis nostræ officium.

ὅτι ὀ φθαρτοῖς ἀργυρίῳ ἢ χρυσίῳ) Vide supra v. 7. ἐλυτρώθητε) וגאלתם. Idem verbum in eodem sensu Tit. 2, 14. & nomen λυτρώσεως Ebr. 9, 12. 26.

ἐκ τῆς ματαίας ὑμῶν ἀναστροφῆς πατροπαραδότου) Ex ob- servatione rituum, animo non emundato, quam sufficere ad salutem Patres vestri, id est magistri vos docuerant. Sic Patris nomen sumitur 1. Cor. 4, 15. Hinc פרקיו אבות.

## 1:19
Verse 19. ἀλλὰ τιμίῳ αἵματι, ὡς ἀμνῶ ἀμώμυ κὴ ἀσπίλυ χριστ̃) It must be a great thing, for which God gave his Son to death. Therefore our liberation is often attributed to the blood of Christ, Eph. 1:7, c. 2:13, Col. 1:14, 20, Heb. 9:14, c. 10:19, or even to his life itself, namely lost for our sake, Matt. 20:28, 1 Tim. 2:6, or even to his death endured for our sake, Rom. 5:10, Col. 3:22, Heb. 2:14. The paschal lamb had to be תמים perfect, Exod. 12:5, πρόβατον λευκὸν in the Greek. For that it was required that no necessary part should be missing from it, nor indeed should there be any other notable deformity in it. To the former refers ἄμωμος; to the latter ἄσπιλος. Christ is truly the Paschal lamb, that is, that which was signified by that Lamb. Through him we have been liberated from servitude, and from the destroying Angel, John 1:29, 1 Cor. 5:7, and he was without sin, John 8:46, below C. 2:22.

Latin:

Vers. 19. ἀλλὰ τιμίῳ αἵματι, ὡς ἀμνῶ ἀμώμυ κὴ ἀσπίλυ χριστ̃) Ma- gna res sit oportet, ob quam Deus Filium suum morti de- derit. Ideo liberatio nostra sæpe tribuitur sanguini Chri- sti, Eph. 1, 7. c 2, 13. Coloff. 1, 14. 20. Ebr. 9, 14. c. 10, 19. aut etiam vitæ ipsius nempe ob nos amissæ, Matth. 20, 28. 1. Tim. 2, 6. aut etiam morti ob nos toleratæ Rom. 5, 10. Coloff. 3, 22. Ebr. 2, 14. Agnus paschalis debebat esse תמים perfectus, Exod. 12, 5. πρόβατον λευκὸν in Græco. Ad id requirebatur ut nulla pars neceffaria ei deesset, neque vero alia notabilis in èo aliqua esset deformitas. Ad illud refer- tur ἄμωμος; ad hoc ἄσπιλος. Christus vere agnus Pascha- lis, id est, id, quod per illum Agnum significabatur. Per illum liberati sumus à servitute, & ab Angelo vastante, Joh. 1, 29. 1. Cor. 5, 7. & fuit is sine peccato, Johan. 8, 46. infra C. 2, 22.

## 1:20
Verse 20. προεγνωσμένου μὲν πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου) Already from the beginning of the world God had destined to send Christ. See what we said on John 17:5. Take προγνώσκειν here as πρόγνωσιν above v. 2.

Φανερωθέντος δὲ) Shown to the world: Thus also it is called ἐπιφάνειᾳ in Luke 1:79. See John 1:19 and 1 Tim. 3:16.

ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάτων τῶν χρόνων) That is, finally after a long expectation, as in the Hebrew, thus Heb. 1:1. See 2 Tim. 3:1, Jude v. 18. In the Manuscript, ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάτου τῶν χρόνων, just as ἐπ᾿ ἐσχάτου τῶν καιρῶν, Num. 24:14.

δι ὑμᾶς) For your good.

He sets forth, moreover, both the price of redemption, which is not corruptible silver or gold, but the precious (incorruptible, by way of opposition) blood of Christ; and the subject of the redeemer, which is Christ, the immaculate and undefiled Lamb, by which description is regarded the Paschal lamb, by whose blood the destroying Angel was warded off, Exod. 12; and the sacrificial one, by whose blood the expiation of sins was made, Levit. 12, 6. chap. 14, 10. Exod. 29, 30. Num. 28, 11; and the highest principle of redemption, which is the divine foreknowledge, made before the foundation of the world, not simple, but joined with the divine purpose: Whence the sufficiency and dignity of redemption, partly because the price is of the highest value, the proper blood of the Son of God himself, Acts 20, 28. Rom. 9, 32. partly because all that depends upon the divine ordination, that Christ is destined as our Redeemer: Which was done πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, that is, from eternity, which is expressed by another phrase in Apoc. 13, 8. ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου in the same sense. Conf. Matth. 25, 34. Apoc. 17, 8. & Psal. 12, 3. Prov. 8, 24. For this is a description of eternity: and then the completion of redemption, which was done in the last times, on account of this, says the Apostle, concerning which conf. Heb. 12, 40. which nevertheless pertains here not only to the completion of redemption, but also of its manifestation; which, on account of those believers to whom St. Peter writes, was done through those who preached the gospel to them. For the Lamb was manifested in the last times partly through the manifestation of God (the Word) in the flesh, 1 Tim. 3, 16, partly through the demonstration of the same by John, John 1, 29. to the Apostles and other disciples, by God the Father from heaven, Matth. 3, 17, by Christ himself through miracles, John 1, 14, chap. 20, last, and by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, John 14, 26, chap. 15, 16, chap. 16, 14, 1 Pet. 1, 11, having been done, to which pertains the manifestation of the ministry, Rom. 16, 26, Eph. 3, 10, Col. 1, 26, 2 Tim. 1, v. 9, 10. Tit. 1, 2. and then the form and merit of redemption: that it is not a simple liberation, but satisfactory, by which he redeemed us with the price of his blood paid for us, satisfying divine justice, and meritorious, by which he so redeemed from the wrath of God, from the power of Satan, from death and condemnation, from sin, that he acquired for us the grace of God, dominion over Satan, life, salvation, and eternal righteousness: and then the term of redemption, from which, a vain conversation, formerly propagated to us through the fathers, that is, sin both original and actual: and then the term of redemption to which, since they have been brought back again to God through the same, so that they might adhere to him through faith, and purify their souls through the Holy Spirit, and consecrate them to him.

In the Grotian solution, that is especially to be desired, that he interprets that conversation as the observation of rites handed down by the teachers of the Jews as sufficient for salvation. For Peter addresses not only the Jews, but also the Gentiles converted to Christ, and ignorance in the former conversation, which was especially that of the Gentiles, by Grotius himself from Acts 17, 30, Eph. 4, 18. & c. 5, 14. the interpreter of this passage had noted in those places that the redemption of Christ did not pertain either to the Jews alone or particularly, who observed the rites or ceremonial laws, and to whom those traditions had descended only from the Fathers; nor does the benefit of redemption from vain conversation, which Christ provided by the λύτρῳ of his blood, consist in the liberation of the Jews from the observation of rites, but in the propitiation of the whole human race, or the expiation of the sins of the world, and liberation from guilt and punishment, which even those passages confirm which Grotius collected Tit. 2, 14. Heb. 2, 14. ch. 9, 12. 14. 26. ch. 10, 19.

Ephes. 1, 7. chap. 2, 13. Coloss. 1, 14. 20. chap. 3, 22. Matth. 20, 28. 1. Tim. 2, 6. Rom. 5, 10. abundantly testify. Finally, the Jewish masters did not teach that the observation of rites alone was sufficient for salvation, requiring also the external performance of the moral law, and striving to erect their own righteousness. Add that this Petrine description does not fit this Gloss. For since the Fathers can be understood properly, one should not turn aside to an improper meaning without necessity, so as to understand them as masters: rather, the opposition to the heavenly Father God should be noted, whom they ought to imitate in the conversation of life, having been redeemed from the former conversation handed down by the Fathers and ancestors. That vain conversation is also not the observation of ceremonial laws; because that was not vain in itself, but holy, divinely instituted. Furthermore, ἀναστροφὴ nowhere denotes the observation of rites. But we learn that that vain [conversation], which is the ἀναστροφὴ ἐν ματαιότητι of the Gentiles Acts 14, 15. Rom. 1, 21. Ephes. 4, 17. and of other reprobates 2. Pet. 2, 18. 1. Cor. 3, 20. and the vanity to which the creature is subjected through the abuse of men Rom. 8, 20.: from the vanity of the mind, in which the unregenerate walk, whose understanding is darkened, and who are alienated from the life of God Ephes. 4, 17. 18. according to which former conversation (προτέραν ἀναστροφὴν) the old man corrupts himself according to the desires of error Ephes. 4, 22. concerning which former conversation of the elect (ἀναστροφῇ) among the Gentiles (ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσι) S. Peter chap. 2, 12. [we learn] how God delivered (ἐῤῥύσατο) the just Lot, oppressed by the luxurious conversation of the wicked (ἀσελγείᾳ ἀναστροφῆς), 2. Pet. 2, 7.

But that ἀναστροφὴ πατροπαράδοτος is so called, because it is a vain conversation or custom of conversing and living propagated from the Fathers, from which Christ redeemed us, just as He delivered us from the present evil age (ἐκ τοῦ ἐνεστῶτος αἰῶνος πονηροῦ), Galat. 1, 4. Which vain and depraved manner of living we receive from our fathers with carnal propagation, because that which is born of the flesh is flesh, John 3, 5. Who can give the clean from an unclean seed, Job 14, 3. no less than by the imitation of paternal examples.
