The Vulgate rendered πατροπαράδοτος as 'paternal tradition': Erasmus, 'which you had received from the tradition of the Fathers': Augustine in Ps. 146, 'conversation handed down from the Fathers,' because they had received it from their ancestors through evil examples, and had expressed it in themselves through imitation. Concerning this exhortation, see Beza in loc. The greater the price is by which you have been redeemed from the corruption of carnal life, the more you ought to fear, lest by returning to the corruption of vices you offend the mind of your Redeemer. Concerning the price of redemption, B. Luther: 'What is now the treasure with which we are redeemed? Not corruptible gold or silver, but the precious blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. The treasure is so precious and noble that no human mind and reason can grasp it: so that only a little drop of this innocent blood would have been enough for the sin of the whole world. Yet the Father wished to pour out his grace upon us so abundantly, and to show himself so much, that he let his Son Christ shed all his blood, and gave us the treasure entirely.'

Latin:

Vers. 20. προεγνωσμένου μὲν πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου) Jam à mundi initio Deus Christum mittere destinaverat. Vide quæ dixi- mus ad Joh. 17, 5. Προγνώσκειν hic sume ut πρόγνωσιν supra v. 2.

Φανερωθέντος δὲ) Ostensi mundo: Sic & ἐπιφάνειᾳ dicitur Luc. 1, 79. Vide Joh. 1, 19. & 1. Tim. 3, 16.

ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάτων τῶν χρόνων) Id est, tandem post longam ex- pectationem כאשר יתהיטום, sic Ebr. 1, 1. Vid. 2. Tim. 3, 1. Judæ v. 18. In Manuscripto, ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάτου τῶν χρόνων, quomodo ἐπ᾿ ἐσχάτου τῶν καιρῶν, Num. 24.

δι ὑμᾶς) Vestro bono.

Proponit autem tum redemptionis pretium, quod non est argentum vel aurum corruptibile, sed pretiosus (incorruptibilis, vi oppositionis) san- guis Christi; tum redemptoris suppositum, quod est Christus, Agnus immaculatus & incontami- natus, quâ descriptione respicitur agnus cum Pa- schalis, cujus sanguine arcebatur Angelus vasta- tor, Exod. 12. tum sacrificialis, cujus sanguine fie- bat peccatorum expiatio, Levit. 12, 6. cap. 14, 10. Exod. 29, 30. Num. 28, 11. tum redemptionis princi- pium summum, quod est πρόγνωσις divina, ante mundi constitutionem facta, non simplex, sed cum προθέσει divina conjuncta: Unde redemptio- nis sufficientia & dignitas, partim quia pretium est summi valoris ipsius Filii Dei proprius sanguis, Actor. 20, 28. Rom. 9, 32. partim quia totum id à divina ordinatione dependet, quod Christus de- stinatus est Redemptor noster: Quod πρὸ κατα- βολῆς κόσμου factum, id est, ab æterno, quod alia phrasi effertur Apoc. 13. 8. ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου eo- dem sensu. Conf. Matth. 25, 34. Apoc. 17, 8. & Psal. 12, 3. Prov. 8, 24. Est enim hæc descriptio æternitatis: tum redemptionis complementum, quod novissimis temporibus factum, propter hoc, inquit Apostolus, quo de conf. Ebr. 12, 40. quod tamen hic non ad complementum tantum redem- ptionis, sed etiam manifestationis pertinet; quæ propter illos fideles, ad quos scribit S. Petrus, fa- cta est per eos, qui ipsis evangelizarunt. Agnus enim manifestatus temporibus novissimis partim per Φανέρωσιν Θεῦ (λόγου) in carne, 1. Tim. 3, 16. partim per demonstrationem ejusdem à Johan- ne, Johan. 1, 29. Apostolis & discipulis aliis, Deo Patre de cœlis Matth. 3, 17. ipso Christo per mi- racula Johan. 1, 14. cap. 20. ult. & à Spiritu Sancto de cœlis misso Johan. 14, 26. cap. 15, 16. cap. 16, 14. 1. Petr. 1, 11. factam, quo pertinet manifestatio mi- nisterii, Rom. 16, 26. Eph. 3, 10. Col. 1, 26. 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. 10. Tit. 1, 2. tum redemptionis formam & meri- tum: quod non sit simplex liberatio, sed satisfa- ctoria, qua nos redemit pretio sanguinis sui so- luto pro nobis satisfaciens justitiæ divinæ, & me- ritoria, qua ita redemit ab ira Dei, à potestate Sa- tanæ, à morte & condemnatione, à peccato, ut nobis gratiam Dei, dominium in Satanam, vi- tam, salutem, & æternam justitiam acquisiverit: tum redemptionis terminum, à quo, conversatio- nem vanam, pristinam per patres ad nos propaga- tam, hoc est, peccatum tam originale quàm actua- le: tum redemptionis terminum ad quem, siqui- dem ad Deum per eandem iterum adducti sint, ut eidem per fidem adhæreant, & animas suas per Spiritum Sanctum purificent, eique conse- crent.

In Grotiana ἐπίλυσεί id imprimis desideran- dum, quod illam ἀναστροφὴν, de observatione ri- tuum à Magistris Judæorum ceu sufficienti ad sa- lutem tradita interpretetur. Nam nec solos Ju- dæos, sed gentes etiam ad Christum conversas alloquitur Petrus, & ἄγνοιαν in priori ἀναστρο- φῇ, quæ gentilium imprimis erat, ipso Gro- tio ex Actor. 17, 30. Eph. 4, 18. & c. 5, 14. hujus lo- ci interprete, in illis notarat, neque redemptio Christi vel ad Judæos sive tantum sive peculiari- ter pertinebat, qui ritus observabant, vel leges ceremoniales, & ad quos traditiones illæ à Pa- tribus solum dimanarant; neque beneficium re- demptionis à vana conversatione, quam Chri- stus sanguinis sui λύτρῳ præstitit, situm est in liberatione Judæorum à rituum observatione, sed totius generis humani propitiatione, vel peccatorum mundi expiatione, & à culpa & pœna libera- tione, quod vel loca illa, quæ contulit Grotius Tit. 2, 14. Ebr. 2, 14. cap. 9, 12. 14. 26. cap. 10, 19.

Ephes. 1, 7. cap. 2, 13. Coloff. 1, 14. 20. cap. 3, 22. Matth. 20, 28. 1. Tim. 2, 6. Rom. 5, 10. affatim testantur. Nec denique rituum observationem tantum Ma- gistri Judæorum ad salutem sufficere docebant, requirentes etiam externam legis moralis præsta- tionem, propriamque justitiam erigere sata- gentes. Adde quod descriptio illa Petrina non conveniat huic Glossæ. Nam cum Patres intel- ligi propriè possint, præter necessitatem non est divertendum ad impropriam significationem, ut magistros intelligamus: imo oppositio potius Dei cœlestis Patris attendenda, quem imitari debent in vitæ conversatione, redempti à conversatione pristina à Patribus & majoribus traducta. Vana etiam illa conversatio non est observatio legum ce- remonialium; quia illa non vana erat in se, sed sancta, divinitus instituta. Adhæc ἀναστροφὴ nuspiam notat rituum observationem. Vana au- tem illa, quæ sit ἀναστροφὴ ἐν ματαιότητι gentilium Actorum 14, 15. Rom. 1, 21. Ephes. 4, 17. & repro- borum aliorum 2. Petr. 2, 18. 1. Corinth. 3, 20. ac vanitate, cui subjicitur creatura per abusum hominum Rom. 8, 20. discimus: è vanitate men- tis, in qua ambulent non renati, quorum intel- lectus obtenebratus est, & qui alieni sunt à vi- ta Dei Ephes. 4, 17. 18. juxta quam προτέραν ἀνα- στροφὴν vetus homo se corrumpit secundum deside- ria erroris Ephes. 4, 22. de qua ἀναστροφῇ electo- rum pristina ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσι S. Petrus cap. 2, 12. quo- modo ἐῤῥύσατο eripuit Deus justum Lothum, op- pressum à nefandorum luxuriosa conversatione ἀσελγείᾳ ἀναστροφῆς, 2. Petr. 2, 7.

Dicitur autem illa ἀναστροφὴ πατροπαράδοτος, quia è Patribus propagata vana conversatio vel conversandi & vivendi consuetudo, à qua nos Christus redemit, quemadmodum liberavit nos ἐκ τοῦ ἐνεστῶτος αἰῶνος πονηροῦ à præsenti seculo ma- lo, Galat. 1, 4. Quam vanam & pravam viven- di rationem à patribus accipimus cum propaga- tione carnali, quia quod ex carne natum est, ca- ro est, Johan. 3, 5. Quis potest dare mundum de immundo natum semine, Job. 14, 3. non minus quam imitatione exemplorum paternorum. Vul- gata πατροπαράδοτος reddidit paterna traditio- nis: Erasmus, quam ex Patrum traditione acce- peratis: Augustinus in Psal. CXLVI. à Patribus tradita conversatione, quia per mala exempla à majoribus suis eam acceperant, ac per imita- tionem in semetipsis expresserant. De hac pa- rænesi Beza in h. l. Quanto majus est pretium, quo redempti estis à corruptione vitæ carnalis; tan- to amplius timere debetis, ne forte ad corru- ptelam vitiorum revertendo animum vestri Re- demptoris offendatis. De pretio redemptionis B. Lu- therus: Welches ist nun der Schatz, damit wir erlöset seyn? Nicht vergänglich Gold oder Silber, sondern das theure Blut JEsu Christi, des Sohnes GOttes. Der Schatz ist so köstlich und edel, daß es keines Menschen Sinn und Vernunfft begreiffen kan: Also, daß nur ein Tröpfflein von diesem un- schuldigen Blute übrig gnug gewesen wäre für al- ler Welt Sünde. Noch hat der Vater seine Gna- de über uns so reichlich wollen ausschütten, und sich so viel sehen lassen, daß er seinen Sohn Christum hat sein Blut alles vergiessen lassen, und uns den Schatz gantz geschenckt.

## 1:21
Verse 21.

those who through him believe in God who raised him from the dead, and gave him glory) It appears that this was done for your good: For through him you firmly believed in God the Father: not as one who delivered you from Egypt or Babylon, but as one who delivered Christ from death, and exalted him with supreme glory, so that through him as the author you might also receive the same blessings. Concerning that exaltation of Christ, see Phil. 2, 9, 10. Heb. 2, 9, 10.

so that your faith and hope might be in God) Your countrymen object to you in vain that, because you place your faith and the hope connected with faith in Christ, you are failing God. For that very faith and hope of yours tends through Christ to that God whose worshippers they profess themselves to be.

They are said to be faithful in God, who raised Christ from the dead, not exclusively, but inclusively, as is clear from Rom. 4, 24. 25. For there this description is explained, which concerns the object of faith, which embraces both: that Christ was delivered for our sins, and that he was raised for our justification. Therefore, one should not think of an example here; since the proper object of our faith is Christ by reason of merit, without whom there is no faith, no hope in God. For how could anyone who is not reconciled to God through the blood of Christ trust or hope in him? For God, when not appeased, is a consuming fire, Deut. 4. Heb. 12, last verse. And therefore we are said to believe in God through Christ. Cf. John 14, 1. 6. Through the resurrection of Christ and the bestowing of glory, we are certainly confirmed that full satisfaction has been made for our sins, and that we are perfectly reconciled to God: whence our faith and hope in God can be firm. Add that that glory was given to Christ the Mediator so that, sitting at the right hand of God, and flowing into the Church, his mystical body, with the gifts and grace of the Spirit, he might be able to regenerate us, to work faith and hope in us, and to lead us through faith to salvation, Acts 2, 33. ch. 10, 40.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

τοὺς δι’ αὐτοῦ πιστεύοντας εἰς Θεὸν τὸν ἐγείροντα αὐτὸν ἐκ νε- κρῶν, καὶ δόξαν αὐτῷ δόντα) Apparet id factum vestro bo- no: Nam per eum firmiter credidistis in Deum Patrem: non ut qui vos liberaverit ex Ægypto aut Babylone, sed ut quo Christum à morte liberaverit, summaque gloria auxerit, ut illo autore eadem bona & vos acci- peretis. De illa evectione Christi vide Phil. 2, 9, 10. Ebr. 2, 9, 10.

ὥστε τὴν πίστιν ὑμῶν καὶ ἐλπίδα εἶναι εἰς Θεὸν) Frustra popu- lares vestri vobis objiciunt, vos quia in Christum fidem & connexam fidei spem collocatis, Deo deficere. Nam illa ipsa fides vestra & spes per Christum in eum Deum tendit, cujus illi se cultores profitentur.

Fideles esse dicuntur in Deum, qui suscitavit Christum à mortuis, non exclusive, sed inclusive, ut è Rom. 4, 24. 25. liquet. Nam ibi explicatur hæc descriptio, quæ concernit objectum fidei, quod complectatur utrumque, & quod traditus Christus sit propter peccata nostra, & quod resuscitatus sit propter justitiam nostram. Non ergo hic de exemplo cogitandum; siquidem objectum proprium fidei nostræ Christus est ratione meriti, sine quo nulla est fides, nulla spes in Deum. Quomodo enim Deo non-reconciliatus per sanguinem Christi confidere, vel in eum sperare quis posset? Deus enim non-placatus ignis consumens est, Deut. 4. Ebr. 12, vers. ult. Ideoque per Christum in Deum credere dicimur. Conf. Johan. 14, 1. 6. Per resurrectionem Christi & collationem gloriæ certo confirmati sumus, plene satisfactum esse pro peccatis nostris, nosque Deo perfecte reconciliatos esse: unde fides ac spes nostra in Deum firma esse potest. Adde quod gloria illa data Christo Mediatori sit, ut ad dextram Dei sedens, & in Ecclesiam, caput mysticum, donis & gratia Spiritus influens, nos regenerare, fidem ac spem in nobis operari possit, nosque per fidem ad salutem perducere, Act. 2, 33. c. 10, 40.

## 1:22
Verse 22.

having purified your souls) This does not concern that first purification, but the exaction, as the following mention of the Spirit shows, see John 13, 10. ch. 15, 2.

in the obedience of the truth) That is, into the obedience of the truth, so that the Gospel may be obeyed more and more. For the Gospel is preeminently called the truth. See James 5:19.

through the Spirit) Through the Spirit of God, who most exactly purges even the affections. This is missing in the Manuscript, no less than in the Latin and Syriac.

into unfeigned brotherly love) In human friendships there is much simulation: that is sincere and without pretense which coalesces through Christ and for the sake of Christ. The word brotherly love appears also in Rom. 12:10, 1 Thess. 4:9, Heb. 13:1, 2 Pet. 1:7; and unfeigned in Rom. 12:9, 2 Cor. 6:6, in which places love is the same as brotherly love here. The Latin does not translate into unfeigned brotherly love badly as with simple love.

love one another fervently from a pure heart) Do therefore what the Spirit urges. Thus love from a pure heart is required in 1 Tim. 1:5; add Matt. 5:8, 2 Tim. 2:22. In the Manuscript there is only from the heart, as in Rom. 6:17, and so the Latin reads. Fervently, vehemently, not perfunctorily. Thus we have fervent love also below in 1 Pet. 4:8, and fervent prayer in Acts 12:5.

He connects the purification of souls with faith, which is done through faith, Acts 15:9, and thus in the obedience of the truth: and because faith is effective through love, Gal. 5:6. He demands unfeigned brotherly love. He had warned that grace must be constantly cherished by faith, and that the time of our sojourning must be spent in fear, verse 17. Which he had deduced from salvation acquired through the passion and glory of Christ, to the enjoyment of which they were called by God. Now, having more copiously expounded the redemption of Christ, he concludes from it again that our souls must not only be purified through faith; but also that brotherly love must be demonstrated: since we were born again for that reason through the Word of God. Thus, therefore, he teaches both the application and the end of redemption, and explains the nature and fruit of regeneration. The word having purified is of the past tense, although the participle could be resolved into a gerund, by purifying your souls, so that it may agree with the exhortation, which is clear from the subjunctive imperative, love one another. Unless indeed the soul is justified through faith, love from a pure heart has no place, which is the consequence and fruit of true faith. The Vulgate lies here in a threefold error: For instead of ἡγνικότες it has 'cleansing', instead of ὑπακοῇ τῆς ἀληθείας, it has 'obedience not of truth', as the Syriac, but 'of charity', finally it omits the word διὰ πνεύματος, whereas the Apostle means this, that through faith, by which you have obeyed the truth, you have purified your souls, or by purifying your souls through the obedience of the truth. Cf. Rom. 1, 5. ch. 16, 26. ch. 6, 17. where the obedience of faith occurs. Which obedience is not brought about except through the Holy Spirit 1 Cor. 12, 3. Therefore he describes faith metaphorically as the chastity or purity of the soul from all false doctrine, which is a spiritual adultery, just as idolatry is often described as abhorrent and alien. He describes charity, however, both in terms of its form or mode, that we ought to love one another through brotherly love, as Oecumenius explains the particle εἰς by διὰ, because as they are children of God by believing, so they are brothers among themselves, whence mutual Φιλαδελφία is required, Rom. 12, 10, 2 Pet. 1, 17. Although it can also be rendered 'into brotherly charity', that is, so that your love towards all may overflow or pass into brotherly love by the very deed; where he furthermore wishes Φιλαδελφίαν to be ἀνυπόκριτον, void of simulation, 1 John 3, 8. and then in terms of its principle, that it ought to proceed ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας, from a pure heart: Cf. 1 Tim. 1, 14. Augustine lib. IV. de virgin. cap. 18. The virginity of the mind, he says, consists in the sincerity of faith, and the purity of the heart from wicked burnings: then also in terms of its increase by the word ἐκτενῶς, by which, according to the Blessed Gerhard, is demanded not only an extensive increase of charity, so that it may never cease, but also an intensive one, so that we may love intensely, ardently and with all our strength, because ἐκτενῶς means continually, Joel 1, 14. Judith 4. v. 10. and intensely, Luke 22, 44.

Latin:

Vers. 22.

τὰς ψυχὰς ὑμῶν ἡγνικότες) Agitur hic non de prima illa purgatione, sed de exactione, ut sequens mentio Spiritus monstrat, vide Joh. 13, 10. c. 15, 2.

ἐν τῇ ὑπακοῇ τῆς ἀληθείας) Id est, εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τῆς ἀληθείας, ut magis magisque Evangelio obediatur. Evangelium enim eximie vocatur ἀλήθεια. Vide Jac. 5, 19.

διὰ πνεύματος) Per Spiritum Dei exactissime purgantem etiam affectus. Deest hoc in Manuscripto non minus quam in Latino & Syriaco.

εἰς φιλαδελφίαν ἀνυπόκριτον) In humanis amicitiis multum est simulationis: sincera & sine fuco illa est, quæ per Christum & propter Christum coalescit. φιλαδελφίας vox apparet etiam Rom. 12, 10. 1. Thess. 4, 9. Ebr. 13, 1. 2. Petr. 1, 7. ἀνυποκρίτου vero Rom. 12, 9. 2. Cor. 6, 6. quibus in locis ἀγάπη, idem quod hic φιλαδελφία. Latinus εἰς φιλαδελφίαν ἀνυπόκριτον non male vertit amore simplici.

ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας ἀλλήλους ἀγαπήσατε ἐκτενῶς) Facite ergo quodSpiritus suadet. Sic ἀγάπη ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας exigitur 1. Tim. 1, 5. adde Matth. 5, 8. 2. Tim. 2, 22. In Manuscripto tantum est ἐκ καρδίας, quomodo Rom. 6, 17. & ita legit Latinus. Ἐκτενῶς, vehementer non perfunctorie. Sic ἀγάπην ἐκτενῆ habemus & infra 1.Petr.4,8. προσευχὴν ἐκτενῆ Act. 12, 5.

Cum fide connectit animarum purgationem, quæ fit per fidem, Actorum 15, 9. adeoque in obedientia veritatis: & quia fides per charitatem efficax est, Gal. 5, 6. Φιλαδελφίαν postulat ἀνυπόκριτον. Monuerat fide gratiam constanter fovendam, & in timore tempus nostri incolatus transigendum esse verf. 17. Quod ex salute per Christi passionem & gloriam acquisita, ad cujus fruitionem vocati sint à Deo, deduxerat. Jam redemtione Christi copiosius exposita iterum inde concludit, animas nostras non tantum per fidem purgandas esse; sed etiam charitatem fraternam demonstrandam: siquidem renati ideo sumus per Verbum Dei. Sic ergo & redemptionis applicationem, ac finem docet, & regenerationis naturam ac fructum explicat. Verbum ἡγνικότες præteriti temporis est, quanquam resolvi possit Participium in Gerundium, purificando animas vestras, ut exhortationi conveniat, quæ ex subjuncto Imperativo, diligite invicem, luculenta est. Nisi enim enim per fidem anima justificata sit, ex corde puro dilectio locum non habet, quæ veræ fidei conse- quens & fructus est. Vulgata in triplici menda hic cubat: Nam pro ἡγνικότες habet castigantes, pro ὑπακοῇ τῆς ἀληθείας, obedientiam non veritatis, ut Syrus, sed charitatis habet, denique verbum διὰ πνεύματος omittit, quum id velit Apostolus, quum per fidem, qua obedistis veritati, animas ve- stras purificaveritis, vel purificando obedientia ve- ritatis animas. Conf. Rom. 1, 5. cap. 16, 26. c. 6, 17. ubi obedientia fidei occurrit. Quæ obedientia non nisi per Spiritum Sanctum fit 1. Cor. 12, 3. Fi- dem itaque metaphorice ceu castitatem vel puri- tatem animæ describit ab omni falsa doctrina, quæ adulteratio spiritualis est, quemadmodum sæpius idololatria describitur abhorrentem & alienam. Charitatem autem describit tam ratio- ne formæ vel modi, quod per fraternum amorem nos invicem diligere debeamus, ut Oecumenius particulam εἰς per διὰ explicat, quia ut credentes Dei filii, ita inter se fratres sunt, unde Φιλαδελ- φία requiritur mutua, Rom. 12, 10, 2. Petr. 1, 17. Quanquam etiam reddi possit in fraternam cha- ritatem, id est, ita ut amor vester erga omnes redundet vel transeat in amorem fraternum ope- re ipso; ubi ἀνυπόκριτον insuper vult esse Φιλαδελ- φίαν, simulationis expertem, 1. Johan. 3, 8. tum ra- tione principii, quod ἐκ καθαρᾶς καρδίας, è puro corde proficisci debeat: Conf. 1. Tim. 1, 14. Au- gustinus lib. IV. de virgin. cap. 18. Virginitas men- tis, inquit, consistit in fidei sinceritate, & cordis à pravis ustionibus puritate: tum etiam ratione augmenti voce ἐκτενῶς, qua juxta B. Gerhardum postulatur non solum augmentum charitatis ex- tensivum, ut nunquam desinat, sed etiam inten- sivum, ut impense diligamus, ardenter ac totis vi- ribus, quia ἐκτενῶς est jugiter, Joel. 1, 14. Judith. 4. v. 10. & impense, Luc. 22, 44.

## 1:23
Vers. 23. Ἀναγεγεννημένοι) See above v. 3. ἐκ ἐκ σπορᾶς φθαρτῆς) The seed of mortal man does not beget except to mortal life. ἀλλὰ ἀφθάρτυ) Namely σπορᾶς: and understand ἀφθάρτυ effectively: from a seed leading to immortal life, just as we had ἐλπίδα ζῶσαν above v. 3. Διὰ λόγε ζῶντος Θεῦ, καὶ μένοντος εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) In the Manuscript: ζῶντος Θεῦ, so that it is clear that ζῶντος is joined here with the word Θεῦ and not with the word λόγυ. For the words are taken from Dan. 6, 26. where in the Greek it is αὐτός ἐστι Θεὸς ζῶν καὶ μένων. It is no wonder if the seed leads to immortality, which proceeds from God, who has always lived and is about to live. To call God a sower is frequent among the Hebrews, as we said at Matt. 13, 4. where we showed that the word of doctrine is also compared to seed by the Greeks.

He had made mention of brotherhood. Now therefore he teaches whence that is, namely not from the first, but from the second generation. As he had celebrated the benefit of regeneration in the doxology: So now, having set forth the meritorious cause of the same, he explains the medium by which we are regenerated: Which is the Word of God, which he therefore calls seed. But it is called incorruptible seed not only effectively, but also formally: because the Word of God is in itself void of all corruption, and remains forever, which the Apostle proves from Isaiah. And therefore the Word is the seed of regeneration to an incorruptible inheritance, because it is itself incorruptible. Those who are born from corruptible seed are corruptible. That which is born of the flesh is flesh. Wherefore it is necessary for us to be reborn from incorruptible seed, so that we may be able to enter into the heavenly inheritance. For flesh and blood (corruptible) cannot inherit the kingdom of God, both of which are taught by the testimony of Isaiah: both that all men by nature are flesh, and corruptible grass, and that the Word of the Lord is incorruptible, and remains forever. Other seeds, in order for something to be generated from them, must first be corrupted: Just as the earth changes and corrupts the seeds conceived. But the seed of the divine Word, remaining incorruptible and immutable, changes and regenerates men who conceive it by faith. Nor does Luke 8, 11. seqq. regarding the corruption of seed stand in the way. For it is not corrupted in itself, but only with respect to unbelieving men, and the utility which the Word could have brought forth in them; therefore it perishes in a way to them, which otherwise persists by itself, as Gomarus acknowledges. But the Apostle does not say ἐκ λόγʊ, but διὰ λόγʊ, because the Word of God is not the spiritual matter of birth, but its medium. Those epithets ζῶντῶ, καὶ μένοντῶ are more correctly referred to the Word, both because the Apostle is occupied in explaining it as the medium of regeneration, not in declaring the nature of God: and because he teaches how the Word of God is incorruptible seed: Seed, because it is living, since seed has life in itself; but incorruptible, because it remains forever: and because the proof brought from Isaiah clearly demonstrates that it is not said here that God remains forever, but the Word of God: and because the words themselves are so ordered that it appears the epithets are adapted to the Word of God. For if they were joined to God, they would rather have been placed thus: διὰ λόγʊ Θεῦ ζῶντῶ κὶ μένοντʊ, and because God living and remaining forever does not pertain so much to the present matter. For the efficacy of the Word of God had to be proven, that it makes for regeneration, for eternal life, to which the life and eternity of God does not directly look, and because those epithets of the Word are consistent from parallel passages. For the Word is called living, Heb. 4, 12. Spirit and life, John 6, 68. and to remain forever, Luke 21, 33. and because the Syriac version rendered it by the living word of God. Whence rightly from this passage the efficacy of the divine Word against the Photinians and Calvinists, as well as the fanatics, who prefer to refer these epithets in this place to God, as is evident from Cajetan, Aretius, Schwenckfeld, Rathmann: Or certainly to the hypostatic Word, of which there is no trace here, and which cannot be said to be indicated by Isaiah, to whom finally the explanation of the Apostle himself does not at all agree: This is the Word, which has been preached to you. Cf. Rom. 10, 17. it is confirmed by this apostolic saying: because for the same reason it is called λόγʊ ζῶν κὶ ἐνεργὴς Heb. 4, 12. Word of life, John 6, 68. Acts 5, 20. Phil. 2, 16. indeed δύναμις Θεῦ εἰς σωτηρίαν Rom. 1, 16. ζωὴ αἰώνιω, John 12, 5. It is, however, by accident that the law kills and is the ministry of death on account of the corruption of our nature, 2 Cor. 3:6, Rom. 7:10, whereas in itself it is the Word of life, Acts 7:38. That the Word is established as the medium of regeneration is not to be taken exclusively, since baptism is also a medium of regeneration, John 3:6, Tit. 3:5, which is accustomed to be called the ῥητόν word; for Paul it is the washing of water by the Word, Eph. 5:27, concerning which Bede says in this place: Just as the price of the Lord's passion, by which we have been redeemed, is incorruptible: so also is the sacrament of the sacred font, by which we are reborn, incorruptible; these are so connected to one another that one cannot confer salvation upon us without the other. Here, however, the discourse is properly about the Word of God. Cf. Luke 7:11, 1 Cor. 4:15, James 1:18. The opinion of Estius is to be noted here, which the force of truth wrung from him: Peter therefore teaches that a man is reborn as if from the seed of the word of Evangelical preaching, which is the same as the Word of faith, insofar as it is received by faith. Wherefore nothing else is signified by words of this kind than that a man is reborn, cleansed, justified, and saved through faith, by which he believes the Gospel announced to him.

Latin:

Vers. 23. Ἀναγεγεννημένοι) Vide supra v. 3. ἐκ ἐκ σπορᾶς φθαρτῆς) Semen hominis mortalis non gignit nisi ad vitam mortalem. ἀλλὰ ἀφθάρτυ) Nempe σπορᾶς: & ἀφθάρτυ intellige effective: ex semine ducente ad vitam immortalem, quomo- do ἐλπίδα ζῶσαν habuimus supra v. 3. Διὰ λόγε ζῶντος Θεῦ, καὶ μένοντος εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα) In Ma- nuscripto: ζῶντος Θεῦ, ut apertum sit ζῶντος cum voce Θεῦ non cum voce λόγυ hic conjungi. Sumpta enim ver- ba ex Dan. 6, 26. ubi in Græco αὐτός ἐστι Θεὸς ζῶν καὶ μένων. Non mirum est si immortalitatem ducit semen, quod profi- ciscitur à Deo, qui semper vixit, victurusque est. Deum satorem vocare frequens apud Ebræos, ut diximus ad Matth. 13, 4. ubi ostendimus etiam à Græcis verbum do- ctrinæ comparari semini.

Fraternitatis mentionem fecerat. Jam ergo unde illa sit, nimirum non ex prima, sed secunda generatione docet. Ut in δοξολογίᾳ regenera- tionis beneficium celebrarât: Ita nunc exposita causa meritoria ejusdem medium, quo regenera- mur, explicat: Quod est Dei Verbum, quod ideo semen vocat. Dicitur autem semen incorrupti- bile non tantum effective, sed etiam formaliter: quia Verbum Dei in se omnis corruptionis ex- pers est, & in æternum manet, quod ex Esaia probat Apostolus. Atque ideo Verbum semen est regenerationis ad hæreditatem incorruptibi- lem, quia ipsum est incorruptibile. Qui ex semi- ne corruptibili nascuntur, corruptibiles sunt. Quod ex carne natum est, caro est. Quapropter ex semine incorruptibili nos renasci oportet, ut hæreditatem cœlestem adire possimus. Caro enim & sanguis (corruptibilis) regnum Dei hæredita- re non potest, utrumq; Esaiæ testimonio docetur: & quod omnes homines natura caro sint, & fœ- num corruptibile, & quòd Verbum Domini incor- ruptibile sit, & in æternum maneat. Semina reli- qua, ut ex iis aliquid generetur, prius corrumpan- tur necesse est: Sicut terra concepta semina mutat ac corrumpit. Sed semen Verbi divini incorrupti- bile permanens & immutabile, homines, qui id concipiunt, fide mutat, ac regenerat. Nec obstat Luc. 8, 11. seqq. de corruptione seminis. Nam non in se corrumpitur, sed tantum respectu hominum infidelium, & utilitatis, quam in iis Verbum pro- ferre potuisset; ipsis igitur quodammodo perit, quod alioquin per se perstat, ut agnoscit Gomarus. Non autem dicit Apostolus ἐκ λόγʊ, sed διὰ λόγʊ, quod Verbum Dei non sit materia spiritualis nati- vitatis, sed ejus medium. Epitheta illa ζῶντῶ, καὶ μένοντῶ rectius ad Verbum referuntur, tum quia in eo ceu medio regenerationis explicando versa- tur Apostolus, non in declaranda Dei natura: tum quia quomodo incorruptibile semen sit Dei Ver- bum docet: Semen, quia vivum est, quum semen vitam in se habeat; incorruptibile autem, quia ma- net in æternum: tum quia probatio ex Esaia addu- cta, non Deum hic dici manere in æternum, sed Verbum Dei, luculenter demonstrat: tum quia ver- ba ipsa ita ordinata sunt, ut Dei Verbo aptata esse epitheta appareat. Nam si Deo jungerentur, sic potius illa posita essent διὰ λόγʊ Θεῦ ζῶντῶ κὶ μέ- νοντʊ, tum quia Deum vivere & in æternum ma- nere non adeo ad rem præsentem facit. Nam probanda erat efficacia Verbi Dei, quod ad rege- nerationem, ad vitam æternam faciat, quò dire- cte non spectat Dei vita & æternitas, tum quia è locis parallelis ea Verbi epitheta constant. Dicitur enim Verbum vivum, Ebr. 4. 12. Spi- ritus & vita, Johan. 6. 68. ac manere in æternum, Luc. 21, 33. tum quod Syriaca versio reddiderit per sermonem vivum Dei. Unde recte ex hoc loco efficacia Verbi divini contra Photinianos & Calvinianos, nec non fanaticos, qui malunt ista epitheta hoc loco ad Deum referre, út de Ca- jetano, Aretio, Schwenckfeld, Rathmanno con- stat: Vel certe ad Verbum hypostaticum, de quo hic nullus apex, quodque ab Esaia indigitari dici nequit, cui denique haud convenit explicatio ipsius Apostoli: Hoc est Verbum, quod prædi- catum est ad vos. Conf. Rom. 10, 17. hoc dicto Apostolico confirmatur: quod ob eandem di- citur λόγʊ ζῶν κὶ ἐνεργὴς Ebr. 4, 12. Verbum vi- tæ, Job. 6, 68. Actor. 5, 20. Phil. 2, 16. imo δύναμις Θεῦ εἰς σωτηρίαν Rom. 1, 16. ζωὴ αἰώνιω, Joh. 12, 5. Ex accidenti autem est, quod lex occidat, & mini- sterium mortis sit propter corruptionem naturæ nostræ, 2. Cor. 3, 6. Rom. 7, 10. quum per se Verbum vitæ sit, Actor. 7, 38. Quod autem Verbum medium regenerationis constituitur, non exclusive acci- piendum, quum etiam baptismus regenerationis medium sit, Johan. 3, 6. Tit. 3, 5. qui verbum ὄγατὸν solet dici, Paulo est lavacrum aquæ in Verbo, Eph. 5, 27. de quo Beda in h. l. Sicut incorruptibile est pretium Dominicæ passionis, quo redempti su- mus: Ita enim incorruptibile est sacramentum fontis sacri, quo renascimur, quæ ita sibi invicem connectuntur, ut unum nobis sine altero salutem conferre nequeat. Hic tamen propriè de Verbo Dei sermo est. Conf. Luc. 7, 11. 1. Cor. 4, 15. Jac. 1. v. 18. Notanda hic Estii sententia, quam vis veri- tatis ei expressit: Docet igitur Petrus, hominem re- nasci velut ex semine verbo prædicationis Evange- licæ, quod idem est Verbum fidei, quatenus fide susci- pitur. Quare non aliud hujusmodi verbis signi- ficatur, quam renasci, mundari, justificari, salva- ri hominem per fidem, qua credit Evangelio sibi an- nunciato.

## 1:24
Verse 24.

For all flesh is as grass.] The sense is the same as in Sirach ch. 14, 17. Nor is that Homeric line to be distrusted: 'As is the generation of leaves, so is that of men,' praised by Simonides. For flesh in this place signifies man, grass signifies herb.

And all the glory of man as the flower of grass.] Everything that is considered magnificent in human affairs, beauty, bodily strength, human learning, riches, honors, are as the greenness of herbs. For we said that this is the flower of grass at James 1, 11.

The grass withered, and the flower thereof fell away.] James has nearly the same words in the aforementioned place, so that it appears these were used as a proverb. See what was said on James.

The passage in Sirach ch. 14, 17 is different: 'All flesh is as a garment that grows old.' Whence Sixtus Senensis, book VIII, Bibl. hær. 9, and Jodocus Coccejus, Vol. I, thes. book VI, art. 7, page 680, appeal to the same Petrine allegation to assert its canonical authority. Claud. Guillandus, Lorinus, Salmero, Dominicus à Soto, Justinianus, Estius, and others acknowledge that this testimony is not brought from that passage, but from Isaiah 40. For there, in the LXX Interpreters, the same words are read: 'All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass, the grass withered, and the flower fell away,' where also the other sentence concerning the Word of God brought here is held in almost the same words: 'But the word of our God abides forever.' However, from the similar passage of James, as regards the former sentence, it is not gathered that those things were used as a proverb, but that he looked to the same passage of the Prophet and cited it in part. Moreover, by the name of flesh it is manifest that man born of flesh, subject to corruption, is noted, John 3, 6, which is also called flesh, Gal. 5, 17, who is like grass, which flourishes in the morning, is cut down about evening, and withers, Psalm 90, 6, cut down by the scythe of death, it withers. But through the Word of the Lord, which abides forever, he is reborn to eternal life. But this Word, says Estius, abides forever, because the Gospel, that is, the preaching of Christ crucified for our salvation and raised from the dead, perceived by faith, is effective from the certain, firm, and immutable promise of God to bestow eternity upon believers, that is, eternal life. This, therefore, is what St. Peter leaves to be gathered from the things said, that those who are reborn from incorruptible seed, that is, from the Word of God, will be incorruptible and immortal. Thus John, 1st epistle 2: 'He who does the will of God abides forever.'

Latin:

Vers. 24.

Διότι πᾶσα σὰρξ ὡς χόρτος.] Sensus idem Siracidæ c. 14, 17. Nec diffidet Homericum illud: Οἵη περ φύλλων γενεὴ, τοίηδε κὴ ἀνδρῶν laudatum Simonidi. Caro enim hoc loco hominem significat, χόρτος herbam.

Καὶ πᾶσα δόξα ἀνθρώπε ὡς ἄνθος χόρτου.] Omne id, quod in rebus humanis magnificum ducitur, forma, vires corporis, eruditio humana, divitiæ, honores, ita sunt ut her- bæ viror. Nam id esse ἄνθος χόρτου diximus ad Jac. I, 11.

Ἐξηράνθη ὁ χόρτος, καὶ τὸ ἄνθος αὐτοῦ ἐξέπεσε.] Prope eadem verba habet Jacobus dicto loco, ut appareat fuisse hæc proverbio usurpata. Vide ad Jacobum dicta.

Locus Sir. cap. 14, 17. diversus est: Πᾶσα σὰρξ ὡς ἱμάτιον παλαιοῦται. Unde Sixtus Senensis l. VIII. Bibl. hær. 9. Jodocus Coccejus T. I. thes. l. VI. art. 7. pag. 680. ad ejusdem allegationem Petrinam provocant pro asserenda ejus autoritate Canonica. Non ex illo loco, sed Esa. 40. testimonium istud adduci agnoscunt Claud. Guillandus, Lorinus, Salmero, Dominicus à Soto, Justinianus, Estius, alii. Ibi enim in LXX. Interpp. eadem verba leguntur: Πᾶσα σὰρξ χόρτος, καὶ πᾶσα δόξα ἀνθρώπω ὡς ἄνθος χόρτου, ἐξηράνθη ὁ χόρτος, καὶ τὸ ἄνθος ἐξέπεσεν, ubi etiam altera de Verbo Dei sententia hic adducta iisdem pene verbis habetur: Τὸ δὲ ῥῆμα τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα. E Jacobi autem loco consimili, quod ad priorem sententiam, non id colligitur, quod proverbio illa adhibita sint, sed quod eundem Prophetæ locum respexerit, & μερικῶς allegarit. Cæterum carnis nomine manifestum est, hominem ex carne natum, corruptioni obnoxium notari, Joh. III, 6. quæ caro etiam dicitur, Gal. 5, 17. qui instar graminis est, quod mane floret, circa vesperam decerpitur, & exarescit, Psal. 90, 6. falce mortis resectus exarescit. Per Verbum autem Domini, quod in æternum manet, ad æternam vitam renascitur. Manet autem, inquit Estius, hoc Verbum in æternum, quia Evangelium, id est prædicatio Christi pro nostra salute crucifixi, & à morte resuscitati fide percepta; ex certa, firma, & immutabili Dei promissione efficax est, ut credentibus tribuat æternitatem, id est, vitam æternam. Hoc igitur est, quod ex dictis colligendum S. Petrus relinquit, eos qui renati sunt ex semine incorruptibili, id est, ex Verbo Dei incorruptibiles & immortales futuros. Ita Johannes 1. epist. 2. Qui facit voluntatem Dei, manet in æternum.

## 1:25
Verse 25.

But the word of the Lord abides forever.] From Isaiah 40, 8, where this sentence follows that very one which preceded. The same in Psalm 119, 89.

And this is the word which was preached as good news unto you.] Again 'unto you' for 'for you', לכם, as above v. 4. He wishes to say that those words of Isaiah have a most excellent sense if they are understood concerning the Gospel. For other words of God also abide, that is, they are not retracted by God, but only the Gospel produces fruit that is truly eternal. In the Manuscript more briefly: 'And this is that which was preached as good news unto you.'

He introduces a clearly different sense from his own interpretation. Peter explains simply of what word the Prophet said these things, namely that which had been preached as good news to them, or concerning the Word of the Gospel. Grotius wishes that Peter indicates by these words that the words of the Prophet have a most excellent sense if they are understood concerning the Gospel. Where these hypotheticals, and what need for the same, when Peter teaches that they are to be understood in no other way than absolutely concerning the Gospel? Where concerning a most excellent sense, as if a less excellent sense were also given, and consequently there were a double sense of that saying? Nor indeed is the Gospel called eternal only by reason of fruit, but also in itself, because the Gospel never ceases, even if the ministry of the Gospel should cease. Therefore an 'eternal gospel' is introduced, Rev. 14, verse 6. But impiously and ineptly, as Fr. Gomarus notes, in this place.

Theodoricus Philippi, a leader of the Anabaptists, in his handbook in the treatise on the incarnation, distorts this passage to prove that Christ was not incarnated from human seed, but from the incorruptible seed of the Father. The matter here is about the regeneration of man born in sin: But what is this to Christ and his temporal birth? And how is incorruptible seed, which concurs not to spiritual but to bodily generation, attributed to God the Father?

Latin:

Vers. 25.

Τὸ δὲ ῥῆμα τοῦ Κυρίου μένει εἰς αἰῶνα.] Ex Esa. 40, 8. ubi hæc sententia illam ipsam, quæ præcessit, sequitur. Idem Psalm. 119, 89.

Τοῦτο δέ ἐστι τὸ ῥῆμα τὸ εὐαγγελισθὲν εἰς ὑμᾶς.] Rursus εἰς ὑμᾶς pro vobis, לכם, ut supra v. 4. vult dicere, illa verba Esaiæ sensum habere excellentissimum, si intelligantur de Evangelio. Nam & alia Dei verba manent quidem, id est, à Deo non retractantur, sed solum Evangelium fructum producit vere æternum. In Manuscripto brevius: Τοῦτο δέ ἐστι εὐαγγελισθὲν εἰς ὑμᾶς.

Plane alium sensum infert è propria ἐπιλύσει. Petrus explicat simpliciter, quo de verbo hæc dixerit Propheta, nimirum quod evangelizatum erat ipsis vel de Verbo Evangelii. Grotius vult, Petrum istis indicare, verba Prophetæ habere sensum excellentissimum, si intelligantur de Evangelio. Ubi hæc hypothetica, & quid eadem opus, quum non aliter intelligenda esse, quam de Evangelio absolute doceat Petrus? Ubi de sensu excellentissimo, ac si minus excellens sensus etiam detur, ac proinde dicti istius geminus sensus sit? Nec vero tantum Evangelium æternum dicit ratione fructus. sed etiam in se, quod nunquam desinat Evangelium, etsi ministerium Evangelii cesset. Ideo εὐαγγέλιον αἰώνιον introducitur, Apoc. 14. vers. 6. Impie autem & inepte, notante Fr. Gomaro, in h. l.

Theodoricus Philippi Anabaptistarum coryphæus in enchiridio suo tractatione de incarnatione hunc locum detorquet, ut probet Christum non ex semine humano, sed ex incorruptibili Patris semine in- carnatum. Agitur hic de regeneratione hominis in peccato nati: Quid vero hoc ad Christum, ejusque nativitatem temporalem? Et quomodo Deo Patri semen incorruptibile, quod concurrat non ad spi- ritualem, sed corporalem generationem, tribuitur?

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

The Apostle admonishes that, having laid aside malice, they should desire the sincere milk of the Gospel, and grow in Christ, to whom they have been converted, whom he proposes as a living stone (from Isa. 28, 16; ch. 8, 14) upon whom we are to be built, in whom those who believe are not confounded, just as those elect have been made the people of God (according to the prophecy of Hos. 2, 23). Whom he therefore exhorts to lead a good life among the Gentiles not yet converted, that they be subject to the Magistrate, and that servants be subject to their masters, even the harsh ones, with patience, to whom he sets forth Christ as an example (from Isa. 53, 9) and presents the final cause of that same expiatory sacrifice, that they might live to righteousness, healed by his wounds, who had been like wandering sheep (Isa. 53, 5, 6) but have therefore been converted to the shepherd of their souls.

There are two parts: The former is more Didactic concerning the growth of the newly born, and Christ the living stone, to whom they have been brought, up to verse 10, which still pertains to the completion of the first part. The other is more Parenetic, by which the second part of the epistle begins, concerning the duty of good conduct and of subjects and servants, up to verse 25.

PART I. OF CHAPTER II. Didactic concerning the growth of the reborn.

Ver. 1.

Ἀποθέμενοι ὖν πᾶσαν κακίαν.] We have the verb ἀποτίθεσθαι in a similar sense in Eph. 4, 22, 25; Coloss. 3, 8; Jac. 1, 21. Κακία is elsewhere a noun of genus, here of species, like the Latin malitia. Thus Rom. 1, 29; 1 Cor. V, 8; Eph. IV, 31; Col. III, 8; Tit. III, 3. Arabic עול. That denotes especially those vices which had reigned most widely among the Jews. Compare James.

Καὶ πάντα δόλον.] Rom. V, 29.

Καὶ ὑποκρίσεις.] Feigned goodness. When a bad man feigns good, then he is at his worst. See Matth. 6, 2; ch. 23, 8; Marc. 12, 15; Luc. 12, 1; 1 Tim. 2, 2.

Καὶ φθόνες.] Rom. 2, 29; Gal. 5, 21; Phil. 1, 15; 1 Tim. 6, 4; Tit. 3, 3; Jac. 4, 5.

Καὶ πάσας καταλαλιάς.] 2 Cor. 12, 20; Rom. 1, 30.

We are taught here, both how we can grow in Christ, by laying aside the malice that hinders growth, v. 1, by desiring the sincere milk of the Gospel, in which we taste the sweetness of the Lord, v. 2, 3, and by building ourselves upon the living stone, to whom we have been brought, v. 4 sqq.; and why we ought to grow in Christ, where the cause is brought forward and confirmed by the prophecies of the Old Testament. The cause is twofold, why we ought to grow in the Lord from time to time, partly because Christ is that living stone, upon whom we have been built as living stones through faith in him, whence we ought to be built up more and more upon him as a spiritual house; partly because we are his holy priesthood for offering spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Christ, v. 4, 5. The confirmation, besides the fact that it is already insinuated by words accumulated from the Old Testament, is still delivered particularly regarding the former cause from Isa. 28:16, concerning the cornerstone and its proper end, why it was placed in Zion or the Church, that we might believe in it, and also the accidental [cause], that it was made a stone of stumbling to the unbelieving, v. 6, 7, from Isa. 8:14; regarding the latter, that the Royal priesthood and His holy people are believers converted to Christ, even the Gentiles according to the oracles, Hos. 1:10, ch. 2:23, compared with Exod. 19:5, 6. By various comparisons, therefore, this Apostolic information is illustrated: from the growth of infants who are nourished with milk when they are newly born in Christ; and the structure of a building when the foundation has been laid and the superstructure must be built; from the old priesthood and the people of God, who were once a Royal priesthood, that, having been thus assumed by the Lord, they ought to progress more and more in true holiness and announce His mighty works no less by life than by doctrine, as Priests and the chosen people of the Lord. The Apostle commemorates the regeneration of the elect; therefore, he now teaches how the regenerate ought to grow in faith and holiness. But there is need both of ἀφαιρέσει (removal) of those things by which spiritual growth is hindered, such as are malice, guile, hypocrisy, envy, backbiting; and of θέσει (position) or admission of those things by which it is promoted, such as is the sincere milk of the Gospel, which must be eagerly drunk; and also the spiritual union and communion with Christ, by which we ourselves, as living stones joined by faith to the true living stone, are built up in Him into the mystical temple of the Lord, which he teaches is likewise done through faith, since the faithful are made by Christ not only living stones and temples of the Lord, but also mystical Priests, Apoc. 1:6, ch. 5:6, to offer sacrifices pleasing to God through faith, and to consecrate themselves wholly to Him, as a people of acquisition, called to the marvelous light of the Lord by the tenor of both their calling and their redemption: Which is the sum of the first part of the present chapter, delivered a little more fully.

Blessed Gerhard wishes the proposition to be held here first, which contains both an ἀποτροπήν (turning away) from the vices of Christian charity, to which he had exhorted in v. 22, and an ἐπιτροπήν (turning toward) to the study of progressing from the word of the Gospel in true faith and holy life. Then he wishes the confirmation to be subjoined, and finally the conclusion, or the repetition of the proposition in v. 11. But there begins the second part of both the chapter and the epistle, with a new address, ἀγαπητοὶ (beloved), which is more νουθετικὴ (admonitory). Although a paranesis is instituted here so that our duty of laying aside malice may be connected with the benefit of regeneration, the Apostle nevertheless returns immediately to the doctrine concerning the regenerate regarding the growth of the newly born, and concerning Christ and faith in Christ, and the state of Christians or the faithful, which have the form of information, even if the information directed toward paranesis is not properly theoretical, but practical. And ἀποθέμενοι ὖν (laying aside, therefore), says the Apostle, not in the present, as the Vulgate renders it, 'laying aside,' but since it is an aorist, 'after you have laid aside,' or as Augustine has it, 'having therefore laid aside all malice.' For it signifies, according to the interpretation of Blessed Gerhard, that in the regeneration and renewal made through baptism, that laying aside of malice has indeed begun, but must still be continued daily: in which sense he also says that the verb of the present tense rightly agrees with this passage. For it is not to be believed that everything which has the nature of sin is extinguished through baptism. See Rom. 7:14, Heb. 12:1. Contained here, however, is the required desire of the regenerate for the sincere milk, just as James ch. 1:21 also warns the regenerate that, ἀποθέμενοι πᾶσαν ῥυπαρίαν καὶ περισσείαν κακίας ἐν πραότητι (laying aside all filthiness and overflow of wickedness, in meekness), we should receive the engrafted Word. For malice hinders the Word from being received, nor can the milk of purer doctrine be eagerly sought or drunk, as if to say: after you have therefore laid aside malice, seek with desire and drink that sincere milk, that being regenerate through the Gospel you may grow through it. For through the Word of truth we are not only reborn, but we also grow in faith and the holiness that follows it. The name κακίας (wickedness), although it is understood specifically by some, is more rightly explained generally, as below in v. 16 and Acts 8:22, because all malice in general must be laid aside as far as it can be done in this imperfection, and especially all guile and simulation, as well as envy and all backbitings regarding one's neighbor, which cannot consist with Φιλαδελφίᾳ ἀνυποκρίτῳ (unfeigned brotherly love). Δόλος (guile) is a machination of fraud to circumvent someone by words or deeds. It is defined by Servius as a machination for the sake of deceiving another; by Blessed Gerhard it is said to be a lie in words, 1 Pet. 2:22; in works, simulation, Acts 13:10; in the heart, a machination of fraud, Matt. 26:4. Ὑπόκρισις (hypocrisy) here is also said with respect to one's neighbor regarding the feigned simulation of love, Matt. 22:18. Guile is opposed to simplicity and truth; hypocrisy to candor, when someone promises something with the mouth, and silently hides another thing under the breast. Hypocrisy, says Origen in Homily XV on Matthew, is not a good thing, but a simulation of good, nor is it justice, but a figment of justice, but in reality it is mostly iniquity and the worst evil. Φθόνος (envy) or ill-will is inwardly in the heart, when someone receives the good things of his neighbor with a sick mind and grieves over them. Καταλαλιαὶ (backbitings) are done with the mouth, when someone detracts from the reputation of another; both are most adverse to brotherly charity. Because the Apostle said πάσας καταλαλιὰς (all evil speakings), B. Huss noted that detraction is committed in many ways: either by denying the good, or by obscuring it, or by diminishing it, or by ascribing evil, or by perverting the intention in a good work. If anyone objects that Paul himself used guile, 2 Cor. 12:16, 'Being crafty, I caught you with guile,' I reply that this is said κατ' ἄνθρωπον (after the manner of men) or κατ' ἀνθυποφοράν (by way of objection). For he is reciting the objection of the Apostles, he does not concede it to them. St. Augustine presents these vices in Book 50 of his homilies, homily 20: What is malice, but a love of harming? What is guile, but to do one thing and simulate another? What is flattery, but seduction by fallacious praise? What is envy, but hatred of another's happiness? What is detraction, but a reproach more biting than it is truthful? Malice delights in another's evil; Envy is tormented by another's good. Guile doubles the heart, flattery the tongue, detraction wounds the reputation.

Latin:

CAPUT II. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Monet Apostolus, ut deposita malitia lac since- rum Evangelii concupiscant, & in Christo crescant, ad quem conversi sunt, quem pro- ponit ceu lapidem vivum (ex Esa. 28, 16. cap. 8, 14.) super quo extruendi sumus, in quem qui credunt, non confunduntur, quem- admodum electi illi populus Dei, (secundum prophetiam Ose. 2, 12) facti. Quos proin- de hortatur, ut bonam conversationem du- cant inter gentes nondum conversas, subditi subjecti sint Magistratui, servi Do- minis etiam duris cum patientia, quibus Christum in exemplum sistit (ex Esa. 53, 9.) ac sacrificii ejusdem expiatorii causam fina- lem exhibet, ut justitiæ vivant, vulneribus ejus sanati, qui ovium errantium instar fuerint (Esa. 53, 5. 6.) ad pastorem vero animarum ideo conversi sint.

Partes duæ sunt: Prior magis Didactica de in- cremento recens genitorum, & Christo lapide vi- vo, ad quem adducti sunt, ad v. 10. quæ ad comple- mentum partis primæ adhuc pertinet. Altera est Parænetica magis, qua inchoatur secunda epistolæ pars, de bonæ conversationis & subditorum ac ser- vorum debito, ad vers. 25.

PARS I. CAPITIS II. Didactica de renatorum incremento.

Vers. 1.

Ἀποθέμενοι ὖν πᾶσαν κακίαν.] Verbum ἀποτίθεσθαι in pari sensu habemus Eph. 4, 22. 25. Coloss. 3, 8. Jac. 1, 21. Κα- κία alibi nomen generis, hic speciei, ut Latinum malitia. Sic Rom. 1, 29. 1. Cor. V, 8. Eph. IV, 31. Col. III, 8. Tit. III, 3. Arabs עול. Illa maxime notat vitia, quæ inter Judæos latis- sime regnaverant. Confer Jacobum.

Καὶ πάντα δόλον.] Rom. V, 29.

Καὶ ὑποκρίσεις.] Simulatam bonitatem. Malus bonum cum simulat, tunc est pessimus. Vide Matth. 6, 2. c. 23, 8. Marc. 12, 15. Luc. 12, 1. 1. Tim. 2, 2.

Καὶ φθόνες.] Rom. 2, 29. Gal. 5, 21. Phil. 1, 15. 1. Tim. 6, 4. Tit. 3, 3. Jac. 4, 5.

Καὶ πάσας καταλαλιάς.] 2. Cor. 12, 20. Rom. 1, 30.

Docemur hic, tum quomodo crescere in Christo possimus, deponendo malitiam incrementum impe- dientem, v. 1. concupiscendo lac sincerum Evangelii, in quo gustamus suavitatem Domini, v. 2. 3. & ex- struendo nos super lapidem vivum, ad quem adducti sumus v. 4. sqq. tum cur in Christo debeamus cresce- re, ubi causa affertur, & è Veteris Testamenti va- ticiniis confirmatur. Causa gemina est, cur subin- de in Domino crescere debeamus, partim quia Christus est lapis ille vivus, super quem exstructi sumus per fidem in ipsum lapides vivi, unde magis magisque ædificari debeamus super ipso ceu domus spiritualis; partim quia nos sumus sanctum ejus sa- cerdotium ad offerendas hostias spirituales, acce- ptas Deo per Christum, v. 4. 5. Confirmatio præ- terquam quod verbis è Veteri Testamento accu- mulatis jam insinuata sit, peculiariter adhuc tradi- tur quoad priorem causam ex Esa. 28, 16. de lapide angulari & fine ejus proprio, cur in Sion vel Ecclesia positus sit, ut credamus in ipsum, nec non acciden- tario, quod factus sit incredulis lapis offensionis, v. 6. 7. ex Esa. 8, 14. quoad posteriorem, quod Re- gale sacerdotium & sanctus ejus populus sint cre- dentes ad Christum conversi etiam gentiles secun- dum oracula, Ose. 1, 10. cap. 2, 23. collata cum Exod. 19, 5. 6. Diversis ergo comparationibus iis insi- gnibus illustratur hæc informatio Apostolica, ab incremento infantum, qui lacte aluntur, quum re- cens geniti sint in Christo: Et structura ædificii, cum jactum est fundamentum, & superædificatio fieri debet: à sacerdotio veteri, & populo Dei, qui quondam Regale sacerdotium erat, quod sic as- sumpti à Domino magis magisque in vera sancti- tate proficere debeant, ejusque virtutes annuncia- re non minus vita, quam doctrina, ceu Sacerdotes, populusque electus Domini. Commemorat A- postolus regenerationem electorum, jam ergo quomodo regeniti crescere debeant in fide & san- ctitate docet. Opus autem est tum ἀφαιρέσει & remotione eorum, quibus impeditur spirituale in- crementum, ceu sunt malitia, dolus, hypocrisis, invi- dia, detrectatio: tum θέσει seu admissione eorum, quibus promovetur, ceu sunt sincerum lac Evange- lii, quod avide hauriendum; nec non spiritualis cum Christo junctura & communio, qua ipsi ceu vi- vi lapides vero lapidi vivo per fidem juncti in ipso subinde ædificamur in templum Domini mysti- cum, quod itidem per fidem fieri docet, quum fi- deles non tantum lapides vivi ac templa Domini, sed etiam Sacerdotes mystici à Christo sint effecti, Apoc. 1, 6. cap. V, 6. sacrificia per fidem Deo grata offerre, eique totos se consecrare debent, ceu po- pulus acquisitionis, vocatus ad lumen Domini mi- rabile tenore tum vocationis tum redemptionis ipsorum: Quæ summa est partis prioris capitis præsentis, paulo plenius tradita.

B. Gerhardus propositionem hic primum habe- ri vult, quæ tum ἀποτροπήν à vitiis charitati Chri- stianæ, ad quam v. 22. hortatus fuerat, contineat, tum ἐπιτροπήν ad studium proficiendi è verbo Ev- angelii in fide vera & vita sancta. Deinde sub- jungi confirmationem, ac demum conclusionem, seu propositionis repetitionem v. 11. Sed ibi incipit alte- ra pars & capitis & epistolæ, nova compellatione ἀγαπητοὶ, quæ magis νουθετικὴ est. Quanquam vero hic instituatur parænesis, ut connectatur cum regenerationis beneficio nostrum officium depo- nendi malitiam, redit tamen statim Apostolus ad doctrinam de renatis quoad recens genitorum in- crementum, & de Christo ac fide in Christum, sta- tuque Christianorum seu fidelium, quæ formam habent informationis, utut ad parænesin directa informatio Theologica proprie non theoretica est, sed practica. Et ἀποθέμενοι ὖν, inquit Apo- stolus, non in præsenti, ut Vulgata reddit, deponen- tes, sed quum aoristus sit, postquam deposuistis, vel ut Augustinus habet, deposita igitur omni malitia. Significat enim, interprete B. Gerharde, in regene- ratione ac renovatione per baptismum facta depo- sitionem illam malitiæ fieri quidem cœpisse, sed adhuc quotidie continuandam esse: quo sensu et- iam verbum præsentis temporis huic loco recte con- gruere ait. Non enim credendum per baptismum omne, quod peccati rationem habet, extingui. Vid. Rom. 7, 14. Ebr. 12, 1. Continetur autem hic requisitum desiderii renatorum lactis sinceri, quemadmodum & Jacobus c. 1, 21. renatos monet, ut ἀποθέμενοι πᾶσαν ῥυπαρίαν καὶ περισσείαν κα- κίας ἐν πραότητι Verbum insitum suscipiamus. Im- pedit enim malitia, ut suscipi nequeat Verbum, nec avide expeti vel hauriri lac doctrinæ purioris, q. d. postquam igitur deposuistis malitiam, expe- tite cum desiderio & imbibite lac illud sincerum, ut renati per Evangelium crescatis per illud. Nam per Verbum veritatis non renascimur tantum, sed crescimus etiam in fide, eamque insequenti sancti- tate. Κακίας nomen, quanquam à nonnullis specia- liter intelligatur, generaliter rectius exponitur, ut infra v. 16. & Actor. 8, 22. quia & omnis malitia in genere deponenda est quoad ejus fieri potest in hac imperfectione & imprimis omnis dolus, & si- mulatio, nec non invidia, & detrectationes omnes quantum ad proximum, quæ cum Φιλαδελφίᾳ ἀνυποκρίτῳ consistere nequeunt. Δόλος est ma- chinatio fraudis ad aliquem circumveniendum verbis vel factis. A Servio definitur machinatio al- terius decipiendi causa, à B. Gerhardo in verbis dici- tur esse mendacium, 1. Petr. 2, 22. in operibus simula- tio, Actor. 13, 10. in corde fraudis machinatio, Matth. 26, 4. Ὑπόκρισις hic etiam respectu proximi dicitur de fucata amoris simulatione, Matth. 22, 18. Dolus opponitur simplicitati ac veritati: Hypocrisis can- dori, cum quis ore aliquid promit, taciteque aliud sub pectore condit. Hypocrisis, inquit Origenes homil. XV. in Matth. non est bonum, sed simulatio boni, nec justitia, sed figmentum justitiæ, re ipsa au- tem maxime iniquitas & pessimum malum. Φθόνος vel invidentia in corde interius, cum quis animo ægro bona proximi suscipit, & de iis dolet. Κατα- λαλιαὶ detrectationes ore fiunt, cum quis famæ al- terius detrahit, utrumque charitati fraternæ maxi- me adversum est. Quia Apostolus πάσας κατα- λαλιὰς dixit, B. Hussius notavit, multis modis de- trectationem committi, aut bonum negando, aut ob- fuscando, aut diminuendo, aut malum adscribendo, aut intentionem in bono opere pervertendo. Si quis objiciat, Paulum ipsum dolum adhibuisse, 2. Cor. 12, 16. Cum essem astutus, dolo vos cepi; resp. id dici κατ' ἄνθρωπον vel κατ' ἀνθυποφοράν. Recitat enim Apostolorum objectionem, non concedit id iis- dem. Vitia hæc ita exhibet S. Augustinus libr. L. homiliar. hom. 20. Quid est malitia, nisi nocendi amor? Quid dolus, nisi aliud agere, aliud simulare? Quid adulatio, nisi fallaci laude seductio? Quid in- vidia, nisi odium felicitatis alienæ? Quid detrecta- tio, nisi mordacior quam veracior reprehensio? Ma- litia malo delectatur alieno; Invidia bono cruciatur alieno. Dolus duplicat cor, adulatio linguam, detre- ctatio vulnerat famam.

## 2:2
Verse 2.

Ὡς ἀρτιγέννητα βρέφη.] כעוללים: as newborn infants, namely, from the time you received the Word of the Gospel. See above chapter 1:3. We must live according to Christianity, not according to Judaism.

Τὸ λογικὸν ἄδολον γάλα.] Τὸ λογικὸν, that is, μυσικὸν (mystical), τὸ νοητὸν (intellectual); see Rom. 12:1 and what was said at Matt. 26:29, Luke 22:16. The Syrian rightly translates it as 'spiritual.' Milk has various translations. Elsewhere it is opposed to solid food, but here it is opposed to mixed and therefore insincere things.

Ἐπιποθήσατε.] Love ardently, unless perhaps it should be ἐπιποτίζετε.

Ἵνα ἐν ἀυτῷ ἀυξηθῆτε.] That is, that you may progress more and more in piety. A similar comparison is in Eph. 4:13. This manuscript, along with the Syrian and Latin, correctly adds εἰς σωτηρίαν (unto salvation). For that growth looks to nothing else but eternal salvation.

The Word of the Gospel is compared to mother's milk, the reborn to newborn infants, the zeal for progressing in the knowledge of heavenly doctrine and faith to the desire for mother's milk in infants, and the spiritual progress of the same. He had compared it to a woman, from whom the pious are reborn; now he compares it to milk, from which they are spiritually nourished. By the word ἐπιποθεῖν a huge desire is noted, Ps. 131, 2. Rom. 1, 11. Phil. 1, 8.

By γάλα λογικὸν, the milk of the Word is designated, as the Syriac correctly [translates] as to the sense: Desire the word itself as pure and spiritual milk. The added epithet does not denote a quality added to the thing, but the subject or the thing itself, about which the discourse is. Conf. 1 Pet. 2, 13. ch. 3, ver. 8. For the adjunct follows with the word ἄδολον, so that the milk of the word may be understood as sincere, and not corrupted by any human addition, just as infants seek pure milk, not adulterated with water, 2 Cor. 2, ver. 17. ch. 4, ver. 2. But it is to be desired for this end, that in it or through it, by a common Hebraism, we may grow, and receive spiritual strength and increase, Isa. 38, ver. 16. Matt. 4, v. 4. Eph. 4, 13. But the addition, which Grotius approves, is rejected by approved authentic codices. Nor does the explanation of Clement of Alexandria, book 1, deserve assent. Pæd. ch. 6, which understands the incarnate Word through verbal milk. Nor is the gloss of the Socinians to be admitted, as if λογικὸν were rational, whence Smalcius concludes against Frantz, page 421, that nothing is to be believed which is contrary to reason. Nor is the explanation of Estius and Salmeron regarding the Eucharist sufficiently fitting. The Word is also otherwise compared to milk, Cant. 4, 11. ch. 5, 1. Isa. 51, 1. 1 Cor. 3, 2. Heb. 5, 12. on account of its purity, Ps. 19, 8. sweetness, Ps. 19, 13. Ps. 119, 29. and power to nourish, as also to cleanse, Lam. 4, ver. 7. Cant. 5, ver. 11. John 15, 3.

Moreover, 1 Cor. 3, ver. 2, Heb. 5, ver. 12, by the name of milk the elementary doctrine of the weak is specifically noted, but here in general the Evangelical doctrine, through which both the weak and the perfect are nourished unto eternal life. Christ crucified is both milk to those who are fleeing and food to those who are progressing, says Augustine, tract. 98 in John. For as long as we live here, we are little children, with respect to the manly and perfect age, which we shall attain only in the other century, Eph. 5, 13. Ps. 131, 1. 1 Cor. 13, ver. 11. Concerning the Word of God, Tertullian, book on the resurrection of the flesh: The Word of God is to be sought for the sake of life, to be devoured by hearing, to be ruminated by the intellect, to be digested by faith. Between those breasts, from which the milk of heavenly doctrine is drawn, the beloved bridegroom of the Church ought to dwell like a bundle of myrrh, that is, Christ suffered and crucified ought always to be preached in the Church and the memory of his passion continually recalled, Cant. 1, 13. as the blessed Luther beautifully [says] in this place. Concerning heretics, Irenaeus says in book 3, ch. 19, that they mix gypsum with milk, that is, they infect heavenly doctrine with the poison of their error.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Ὡς ἀρτιγέννητα βρέφη.] כעוללים: tanquam recens na- ti, nempe ex quo Verbum Evangelii recepistis. Vide supra cap. I, 3. secundum Christianismum nobis vivendum est, non secundum Judaismum.

Τὸ λογικὸν ἄδολον γάλα.] Τὸ λογικὸν, id est, μυσικὸν τὸ νοητὸν, vide Rom. 12, 1. & quæ dicta ad Matth. 26, 29. Luc. 22, 16. Spirituale bene vertit Syrus. Lac varias habet translatio- nes. Alibi opponitur cibo solido, at hic rebus mixtis ac pro- inde non sinceris.

Ἐπιποθήσατε.] Adamate, nisi forte fuerit ἐπιποτίζετε.

Ἵνα ἐν ἀυτῷ ἀυξηθῆτε.] Id est, magis magisque proficiatis in pietate. Par similitudo Eph. 4, 13. Adjicit hic Manuscri- ptus cum Syro & Latino εἰς σωτηρίαν recte. Non enim incre- mentum illud alio spectat, quam ad salutem æternam.

Verbum Evangelii lacti materno confertur, re- nati infantibus recens natis, studium proficiendi in cognitione doctrinæ cœlestis & fide desiderio la- ctis materni in infantibus spiritualem profectum eorundem. Comparaverat id feminæ, ex quo pii renascantur, jam comparat lacti, ex quo spi- ritualiter nutriuntur. Verbo ἐπιποθεῖν ingens desiderium notatur, Psal. 131, 2. Rom. I, 11. Phil. I, 8.

Per γάλα λογικὸν γάλα τῶ λόγꙋ lac Verbi desi- gnatur, uti Syrus recte quoad sensum : Concupisci- te ipsum sermonem tanquam lac mundum, & spiri- tuale. Epitheton adjectum non adjunctam rei qualitatem notat, sed subjectum seu rem ipsam, de qua sermo est. Conf. 1. Petr. II, 13. cap. III. vers. 8. Adjunctum enim sequitur voce ἄδολον, quod sin- cerum, nec additamento aliquo humano corru- ptum lac verbi intelligatur, sicut infantes lac pu- rum, non aqua adulteratum expetunt, 2. Corinth. 2. vers. 17. cap. 4. vers. 2. Eo autem fine id deside- randum, ut in illo vel per illud, per usitatum Ebræ- ismum, crescamus, & spirituale robur, ac incre- mentum capiamus, Esa. 38. vers. 16. Matth. 4. v. 4. Eph. 4, 13. Additamentum autem, quod probat Grotius, reprobant codices probati authentici. Neque assensum meretur Clementis Alex. libr. 1. Pæd. cap. 6. explicatio, qui per lac verbale Verbum incarnatum intelligit. Neque Socinianorum glossa admittenda, quasi λογικὸν sit rationale, unde colligit Smalcius contra Franztum pagin. 421. nihil credendum esse, quod rationi adversetur. Nec satis convenit Estii & Salmeronis explicatio lactis de Eucharistia. Verbum etiam alias lacti con- fertur, Cant. 4, 11. cap. 5, 1. Esa. 51, 1. 1. Corinth. 3, 2. Ebr. 5, 12. ob puritatem, Psalm. 19, 8. suavitatem, Psalm. 19, 13. Psalm. 119, 29. & nutriendi virtutem, ut & mundandi, Thren. 4. vers. 7. Cantic. 5. vers. 11. Joh. 15, 3.

Cæterum 1. Corinth. 3. vers. 2. Ebr. 5. vers. 12. lactis nomine doctrina elementaris infirmorum speciatim notatur, hic vero in genere doctrina Ev- angelica, per quam & infirmi, & perfecti ad vitam æternam nutriuntur. Christus crucifixus & lac fugentibus & cibus est proficientibus, inquit Augu- stinus tract. XCVIII. in Joh. Quamdiu enim hic vivimus, parvuli sumus, respectu virilis ac perfectæ ætatis, quam in altero demum seculo conseque- mur, Ephes. 5, 13. Psalm. 131, 1. 1. Corinth. 13, vers. 11. De Verbo Dei Tertullianus l. de resurrect. carn. Sermo DEI in causam vitæ appetendus, auditu devo- randus, intellectu ruminandus, fide digerendus. Inter ubera illa, ex quibus lac doctrinæ cœlestis hauri- tur, dilectus Ecclesiæ sponsus instar fasciculi myr- rhæ debet commorari, hoc est, Christus passus & crucifixus semper in Ecclesia debet prædicari & passionis memoria jugiter recoli, Cant. I, 13. ut pulchre B. Lutherus in h. l. De hæreticis ait Irenæus l. III. c. 19. quod gypsum lacti immisceant, id est, erroris sui veneno doctrinam cœlestem inficiant.

## 2:3
Ver. 3.

Εἴπερ.] As if he were to say: I know you will do that, if only you are those whom I hope. Ἐγεύσασθε, ὅτι Χρηστὸς ὁ Κύριος.] טעמו כי טוב יהוה, Ps. 34, 9. where the Greeks [have] γεύσασθε, ὅτι Χρηστὸς ὁ Κύριος: but there the Lord is God the Father in the manner of the Old Testament, but here it is Christ. Γεύεσθαι here is not to taste lightly, but to experience, as Matt. 16, 28. Mark 9, 1. Luke 9, 27. John 8, 52. Heb. 2, 9. ch. 6, 4. For the Hebrews are accustomed to borrow words from any external sense to signify internal senses. Therefore the LXX in the Psalm placed γεύσασθε καὶ ἴδετε, and the Syriac [is] no different. Ὅτι here is 'that'. And Χρηστὸς is 'sweet', so that the translation taken from tasting may proceed better. See Luke 5, 39 and what is said there. And thus the ancient versions have it in the Psalms.

The Apostle had commended the Evangelical doctrine for its sincerity and power to nourish; now he also proclaims the same for the sweetness and pleasantness with which it commends itself to the new man. Which he confirms from the object, because it exhibits the sweetness of the Lord, by Davidic authority.

Davidic authority. But here the transition is not from the Lord to the Lord, as Grotius wishes, but it is taught that through the Lord, whose sweetness David proclaims, our Lord Jesus Christ is to be understood. For the argument is firm: He, whose sweetness David proclaims there, is the Lord Jehovah, God blessed forever. Christ is he, whose sweetness David proclaims there, as witnessed by St. Peter. Therefore Christ is Jehovah, God blessed forever. But Grotius less correctly introduces a doubt, which the Vulgate also hints at by the particle 'if' added on its own, which is found neither in the Greek, nor in the Syriac, nor in other Latin codices: Since on the contrary the particle εἴπερ is to be taken not in the sense of one doubting but of one supposing and as a causal, for ἐπειδήπερ 'since', as Rom. 8, ver. 9. 2 Thess. 1, 16. As the Lord טוב is good, and kind and beneficent: So we taste and perceive his goodness in the Word of the Gospel: Which is proper to the faithful, who lay aside malice and strive to put it off. By how much more the bitter root of malice is laid aside, by so much more the goodness of the Lord is tasted, how sweet the Lord is. The Lord is sweet in contemplation for meditating (Cant. 2, 3), in the spiritual ear for hearing (Cant. 5, 13), in prospect for seeing (Sir. 23, 37), says John Huss in this place. Conf. Matt. 11, 28. Isa. 55, 1 seqq. But he who tastes nothing of the supernal sweetness in his mind, it is no wonder if he does not avoid defiling it with earthly allurements, says Bede in this place.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Εἴπερ.] Quasi dicat : Scio vos id facturos, si modo ii estis, quos spero. Ἐγεύσασθε, ὅτι Χρηστὸς ὁ Κύριος.] טעמו כי טוב יהוה, Ps. 34, 9. ubi Græci γεύσασθε, ὅτι Χρηστὸς ὁ Κύριος : sed ibi Κύριος more Veteris Testamenti est Deus Pater, hic vero Chri- stus. Γεύεσθαι hic non est leviter degustare, sed experiri, ut Matth. 16, 28. Marc. 9, 1. Luc. 9, 27. Joh. 8, 52. Ebr. 2, 9. c. 6, 4. Solent enim Ebræi ad significandos sensus internos vocabula de quovis sensu externo mutuari. Ideo LXX. in Psalmo po- suerunt γεύσασθε καὶ ἴδετε, nec aliter Syrus. Ὅτι hic est quam. Et Χρηστὸς est suavis, ut à gustu sumpta translatio melius pro- cedat. Vide Luc. V, 39. & ibi dicta. Et sic habent vetustæ versiones in Psalmis.

Commendaverat Apostolus doctrinam Evan- gelicam à sinceritate, & nutriendi virtute, jam etiam à dulcedine & suavitate, qua sese novo homini commendat, deprædicat eandem. Quam ab ob- jecto, quia Domini suavitatem exhibet, autoritate

Davidica confirmat. Non autem hic transitus sit à Domino ad Dominum, ut Grotius vult, sed per Dominum, cujus suavitatem deprædicat David, intelligendum esse Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum docetur. Argumentum enim firmum: Is, cujus suavitatem deprædicat ibi David, est Do- minus Jehovah, Deus benedictus in secula. Chri- stus est is, cujus suavitatem deprædicat ibi David, teste S. Petro. Ergo Christus est Jehovah, Deus benedictus in secula. Minus recte autem Grotius dubitationem ingerit, quam etiam Vulgatus parti- cula si tamen de suo addita innuit, quæ nec in Græ- cis, nec in Syriacis, nec in aliis Codicibus Latinis reperitur: Quum ex adverso particula εἴπερ non sensu dubitantis sed supponentis & causali accipi- enda sit pro ἐπειδήπερ siquidem, ut Roman. 8. vers. 9. 2. Theffal. 1, 16. Ut Dominus טוב bonus est, & be- nignus ac beneficus: Ita bonitatem ejus in Ver- bo Evangelii gustamus, ac percipimus: Quod fi- delibus proprium est, qui malitiam deponunt, & exuere conantur. Quanto magis deponitur ma- litia amara radix, tanto magis gustatur bonitas Domini, quam dulcis sit. Dulcis est Dominus in con- templatione ad meditandum (Cantic. II, 3.) in aure spirituali ad audiendum (Cant. V, 13.) in prospectu ad videndum (Sir. 23, 37.) ait Johan. Hussus in h. l. Conf. Matth. 11, 28. Es. 55, 1. seqq. Qui vero nihil de superna suavitate animo gustat, non est mirum, si hunc terrestribus illecebris sordidare non evitat, ait Beda in h. l.

## 2:4
Ver. 4.

Πρὸς ὃν προσερχόμενοι.] This word signifies worship and obedience, see Heb. 4:16, ch. 7:25, ch. 10:1, 22, ch. 11:6. קָרַב.

Λίθον ζῶντα, ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων μὲν ἀποδεδοκιμασμένον, παρὰ δὲ Θεῷ ἐκλεκτὸν, ἔντιμον.] That word ζῶντα signifies an allegory, just as the word λογικὸν does now, elsewhere πηρὸν, elsewhere πληθυόμενον or πλουματικὸν and the like. Reference is made to the passages Ps. 118:22, and Isa. 8:14, and ch. 28:16, concerning which we have spoken at Matt. 21:42 and Acts 4:11. By men here understand the Jews, but especially those who were in the Sanhedrin. Ἀποδεδοκιμασμένον סוּסַר, thus also Matt. 21:42, Mark 12:10, Luke 20:17, for the same is ἐξουθενηθεὶς in Acts 4:11, which in the Psalm is, made into the cornerstone, that is, by which the whole building might be sustained. He said this here in other words with the same sense from Isa. 28:16, ἐκλεκτὸν is בְּחִיר to the Hebrews, as the LXX read, in the already mentioned passage of Isaiah, where commonly it is מָסָד. The Syrian is גבא, as it is translated here, then יקר made of the greatest value by GOD.

An argument from the sweetness of the Gospel according to the blessed Gerhard succeeds now from the dignity of the pious, that they are the spiritual house of God, and Priests of God, and therefore ought to lay aside all uncleanness. After he required for the growth of the reborn a desire and zeal for drawing in, embracing by faith, and as it were imbibing the Evangelical doctrine, and also for converting it into juice and blood; now he teaches that there is also a need, using another metaphor, for us to be built up into a temple of the Lord, and to offer spiritual sacrifices daily, so that we may progress in the Lord. We have been consecrated in baptism, and through the Word of the Lord into mystical temples, because whoever hears the Word of God, God comes to him, and makes his dwelling with him, John 14:23, and Christ dwells in us through faith, Eph. 2:17, as many as have been baptized into Christ, have put on Christ, Gal. 3, v. 27. But it is necessary that we do not destroy the temple of the Lord through unbelief, but remain the spiritual house of the Lord through faith, 1 Cor. 3:16, 17. We have been built by faith upon that living stone, built up upon the same, Mark 16:17, into a habitation of God in the Spirit, Eph. 2, verses 20, 22, 1 Cor. 3, verse 11. But it is necessary that through the same Spirit we, who have life from Him through faith in Christ, should build ourselves up upon that Rock more and more continually.

We have been made spiritual priests, washed by the blood of Christ, Apoc. 1:5, anointed with the oil of the Spirit in baptism and the Word, 1 John 2:30; wherefore it is necessary that through the Holy Spirit we should continually offer spiritual sacrifices, which are accepted to God in Christ Jesus. The temple of the Lord needed to be kept clean, not polluted, Levit. 15:31, ch. 21:12, Num. 19:13. Priests were required to study purity and holiness, Levit. 21:8. But through faith our hearts are purified, Acts 15:9, and consciences are cleansed by the blood of Christ sprinkled by faith, Heb. 9:14, without which it is impossible to please God, Heb. 12:6. When you received the doctrine of the Gospel, says the Apostle, interpreted by the blessed Gerhard, p. 165, you already began to approach CHRIST, and to be built up like living stones upon Him as the cornerstone. It is therefore right that you should persevere constantly in this your calling, and by daily progress in faith, approaching Christ, you yourselves as living stones should be more and more built up upon Him, and thus take on ever greater increments in the spiritual life. As therefore he declares the progress in true faith by the similitude of building upon a living stone, namely that by it the faithful are as it were glued and coalesce more with Him: so he illustrates the progress of the faithful in holiness by the comparison of priests, comparing the faithful to priests and good works to sacrifices, which spiritual priests ought to offer through faith.

He informs us thus both about Christ, who is the living stone rejected by men in the passion by which He redeemed us, but chosen and honored before God in the constitution of the foundation of the Church, by which He built the whole Church upon this chosen stone, Matt. 16:17; and about Christians, who as living stones built upon Christ are constructed into a spiritual house, and who also are a holy priesthood anointed for that purpose through Christ, and through Christ offering sacrifices acceptable to God.

The word προσερχόμενοι is rendered by the Vulgate as 'approaching'; the Syriac renders it 'you have approached'; it implies a continuous act of approaching, which happens through faith, Heb. 11:6, to CHRIST, whose sweetness they are said to taste: who is that living stone, sustaining the whole house of the Church, and providing it with firmness against the very gates of hell, Matt. 16:18; who not only has life in Himself, John 5:25, 1 John 5:20, nay, is life itself, but also gives life to the stones built upon Him, that is, those adhering to Him by faith, John 6:88, ch. 5:28-29, ch. 10:28, not only by reason of merit and acquisition, but also by reason of efficacy and application. Moreover, it is said ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων ἀποδεδοκιμασμένῳ, which, although some extend it to all the reprobate, it is clear from Psalm 118:22, compared with Acts 4:11, that the rejection is understood as having been done in the passion of CHRIST by those foolish architects, the priests, Scribes, and Pharisees; cf. here verse 7 concerning the reprobate in general, who are opposed to those building themselves upon the living stone, and who stumble through unbelief, which will be dealt with subsequently, verse 78. Furthermore, παρὰ δὲ τῷ θεῷ ἐκλεκτὸν calls this living stone 'excellent' (ἐξοχικῶς), because it is properly 'before God,' not as the Vulgate has it 'chosen BY GOD,' that is, not merely beloved, but excellent, because, in Hebrew phrase, 'chosen' is 'outstanding' and 'excellent,' 1 Tim. 5:21, because such things are accustomed to be preferred in free election, Isa. 42:1, Matt. 22:48. Ἔντιμον, precious, because before God Himself it is a most precious gem: upon which single gem the whole heavenly Jerusalem, truly also gem-like, but built by the power and virtue of this gem, is constructed, Apoc. 21:19; upon which as one foundation rest the twelve foundations, that is, the Apostles, Eph. 2:20. Cf. Matt. 13:46 and Isa. 54:11-12. Who, although He was rejected by men, was nevertheless held in esteem before GOD. He is honored, says Lyranus in this place, in the working of miracles, in the resurrection, in the ascension, in the mission of the Holy Spirit. But here He should be understood as honored especially in the constitution of the foundation of the Church. Blessed Luther: 'Before God's eyes the stone is chosen, and a chosen precious stone, which means so much that He takes away death, pays for sin, and rescues from hell, and in addition gives the kingdom of heaven.' Concerning the saying of the Psalm which is looked at here, see the Bibl.
