But βασίλειον is added here, so that Christians may be understood to have been made Priests through Christ in such a way that they are at the same time Kings, after the example of Christ: not like the Israelites, of whom that was said, Exod. 19:6, on account of the sacred Passover, and on account of the liberty common to all, and magnificent victories, but because they offer those things to God of which we have already spoken before; and because they are free from vices, and conquer the flesh, the world, and the devil. For that can truly be applied to a Christian man: He is a king who fears nothing. He is a king who desires nothing. And what Cicero says in defense of Sulla, that it is kingly to serve no desire. The same sense is in Apocal. 1:6, ch. 5:10.

Just as the faithful in the New Testament are called a Royal Priesthood, so the same were also called such in the Old Testament. For they too offered spiritual sacrifices, as Priests, Psalm 51:19, 21, and conquered spiritual enemies as Kings, which the catalog of the ancient faithful, Heb. 11, who are set before us as an example both by Paul in that cloud of witnesses, and elsewhere, as well as by Peter, 1 epist. 3:6, 2 epist. 2:5, 8, etc. For the rest, we readily agree that this appellation alludes to the Priests and Kings of the Israelites, provided that those titles are not denied to the ancient faithful even before Kings and Priests were solemnly instituted and anointed: Just as CHRIST is said to have made those whom He washed with His blood Priests and Kings to GOD the Father: But He did not wash with His blood only the men who live in the time of the New Testament: But the redemption made by His blood pertains to all men of all ages and centuries.

Ἔθνος ἅγιον.] Above ch. 1:15. The words are taken from Deut. 7:6 and ch. 14:2, where in Hebrew it is עם קדוש. The assembly of the Church is called a holy people not regarding external holiness, in the way the Israelite people were separated from other peoples and unclean nations by a ceremonial holiness situated in portions, the distinction of clean and unclean foods, and other rites of that kind, but regarding internal holiness, which that designated and prefigured, Exod. 22:31, Levit. 20:44, 45, ch. 20:26, Num. 15:40, John 17:17, Ephes. 1:4, ch. 5:27, Heb. 13:12. Nor is it called ἔθνος ἅγιον without cause, when he could have said λαὸν ἅγιον, because the name of 'nations' was hateful to unbelieving Jews, but pleasing to the faithful, and it was rendered more pleasing in that the nations were consecrated to God and were holy no less than the believing Jews, Acts 10:34, Gal. 3:28, Col. 3:11.

Λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν.] That is, for salvation, as Heb. 11, 39. Exod. 19, 6. והייתם לי סגלה in Greek ἔσεσθέ μοι λαὸς περιούσιος, and Malachi 3, v. 17. אשר אני עשה סגלה, or, ἵνα ποιῶ εἰς περιποίησιν. The Vulgate translated it 'a people of acquisition.' In the Old Testament it is called a people of peculiar possession, Deut. 7, 6. ch. 14, 2. ch. 26, 18. Mal. 3, 17. The word סגלה signifies a precious thing, which is held in the place of a treasure, whence Pagninus in Exod. 19, 5 rendered it: 'You shall be to me as a beloved treasure.' The LXX Interpreters: λαὸς περιούσιος, a peculiar people, as Paul has it in Tit. 2, 14. But here it is called λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν, which word-for-word is not a people for salvation, but into acquisition, or redemption, which is a redeemed people; the Syriac translated it, 'whom He acquired for Himself,' πε- ριεποιήσατο God with His own blood, Acts 20, 28. But 1. Thess. 4, 9. we are said to be placed εἰς περιποίησιν σωτη- ρίας for the acquisition of salvation: whence not undeservedly in this place it is explained as a people placed for the acquisition of salvation, that is, placed by Divine ordination to obtain salvation, compare 2 Thessal. II, ch. 14. Heb. X, 39.

That you may proclaim the mighty works of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.] The word ἀρετὴ sometimes signifies upright habits, as in Phil. 4:8. But when it is said of God, as here, it corresponds to the word הוד, as in Hab. 3:3, Zech. 6:13, or to the word תהלה, as in Isa. 42:8, 12, ch. 43:21, ch. 63:7, in which places it is, as here, in the plural, ἀρετὰς in the sense of power. The Syriac translates it as praise. It is God who called us, Rom. 9:12, 24, 1 Cor. 7:15, Gal. 1:6, 15, ch. 5:8, 1 Thess. 1:12, ch. 5:24, 2 Thess. 2:14, 2 Tim. 1:9. Darkness is called the time before the Gospel, Matt. 4:16, Luke 1:79, John 3:19, Acts 26:18, Rom. 13:11, Eph. 5:8, Col. 1:13, 1 Thess. 5:4, 5. Light is the Gospel itself and the life consistent with it, as can be seen in the same places, and Rom. 13:12, Col. 1:12. But that word marvelous is added here, just as true in John 1:9, 1. John 2:8, to denote the excellence of this light, thus great and marvelous, Rev. 15:1. This is the mystical sense of the passage in Isa. 42:6, 7 and Job 37:21.

Darkness does not designate the pre-Evangelical time, except regarding the Gentiles who sat in darkness, but the state before the communion of the true light, which enlightens every man, John 1:9. For even before the coming of the Son of God in the flesh, the faithful were walking in the light of the knowledge of the true God and of the Messiah, not in the darkness of ignorance, as the Gentiles, Acts 17:30. But in that state of darkness all the unregenerate are established, at whatever time they may live, therefore they are to be turned from darkness to light, Acts 26:8, Eph. 5:8, Col. 1:13. By light, the Gospel itself and the life consistent with it, proper to the time of the New Testament, as Grotius wishes, is noted; whence will this be taught? The light of knowledge is of all times, and no one would rashly say that the Patriarchs, and Abraham himself, the father of believers, who is set forth by Paul as an example of faith to all, were destitute of it. But Christ is called the light of the Gentiles, Isa. 42:6, as also ch. 49:6, not in a mystical sense, but literal, as noted regarding those passages. But the passage in Job 37:21 is clearly irrelevant here. By ἀρετὰς, mighty works, are understood not those which Christ works in us, or of the called, as Cornelius wishes, but the mighty works of God himself, who called us, being Divine power, wisdom, grace, and justice, which shine forth most in the business of vocation and conversion, cf. 2 Pet. 1:3. By darkness, from which God called us, the Apostle understands not only the darkness of ignorance, and of errors or superstitions, and idolatries and sins, and impieties, but also of miseries, and of temporal and eternal death, and thus the whole power of darkness is designated, Col. 1:13. Therefore, by light he designates not only the light of the Gospel or of knowledge and faith, dispelling both ignorances and errors, but also the light of grace, blessing, and salvation, both in this life and in the other in the kingdom of light, which is opposed to the kingdom of darkness. Which light is truly marvelous, both because faith is occupied with the marvelous things of God, Psalm 119:18, and because that grace of the faithful, which they enjoy in the kingdom of grace and glory, is to be marveled at.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Ὑμεῖς δὲ γένος ἐκλεκτὸν.] Vide supra c. I, 1. ipsa verba γένος ἐκλεκτὸν habes Esa. 43, 20.

Electum genus dicitur non sensu generali, ut vocati quivis ad regnum gratiae electi dicuntur, Deut. 3. 37. cap. 7, 6. cap. 10, 15. cap. 14, 2. qui etiam videtur locum habere Esa. 43. vers. 20. sed specia- liori de electis ad regnum gloriae, quod tituli re- liqui confirmant, vel si de toto Ecclesiae coetu accipiantur, certum tamen est, quod ratione partis potioris illi tributi sint, quemadmodum in Scripturis illa sponsa Christi, Cantic. 4. vers. 10. Esa. 61. vers. 10. Johan. 3. vers. 29. intus ornata & gloriosa, Psalm. 45. vers. 14. tota pulchra & abs- que macula, Cant. 4. vers. 7. sancta & inculpata, Eph. 5, 27. corpus Christi, 1. Cor. 12, 24. Eph. 1, 29. cap. 4, 16. domus Dei spiritualis, 1. Timoth. 3. v. 15. Ebr. 3, 6. 1. Petr. 3, 6. &c. vocatur.

Βασίλειον ἱεράτευμα.] Ἱεράτευμα sunt, ut supra vers. 5. Sed additur hic βασίλειον, ut intelligantur Christiani per Chri- stum ita facti Sacerdotes, ut simul & Reges sint ad Christi exemplum: non ut Israelitæ, de quibus id dictum, Exod. 19, 6. ob sacrum Paschale, & ob libertatem omnibus commu- nem, & magnificas victorias, sed quia ea offerunt Deo, de quibus jam ante diximus; & quia liberi sunt a vitiis, & vin- cunt carnem, mundum, diabolum. Christiano enim homini vere illud aptari potest: Rex est, qui metuit nihil. Rex est, qui cupiit nihil. Et quod Cicero dicit pro Sylla, Regium esse, nulli servire cu- piditati. Idem sensus Apocal. I, 6. c. V, 10.

Quemadmodum fideles in Novo Testamen- to Regale Sacerdotium dicuntur, ita iidem in Ve- teri Testamento quoque dicti sunt. Nam & illi offerebant sacrificia spiritualia, ceu Sacerdotes, Psalm. 51. vers. 19. 21. & vincebant hostes spiritua- les ceu Reges, quod catalogus fidelium prisco- rum, Ebr. 11. qui nobis in exemplum sistun- tur tam a Paulo in ista testium nube, & alibi, tum a Petro 1. epist. 3. vers. 6. 2. epist. 2, 5. 8. &c. De cætero ad Sacerdotes & Reges Israelitarum alludi hac appellatione facile annuimus, dum- modo priscis fidelibus etiam ante institutos Re- ges & Sacerdotes solenniter unctos illa elogia non denegentur: Sicuti CHRISTUS, quos suo abluit sanguine, fecisse DEO Patri dicitur Sa- cerdotes & Reges: Non autem abluit sanguine suo tantum homines, qui tempore Novi Testa- menti vivunt: Sed pertinet redemptio sanguine ejus facta ad omnes omnium ætatum & seculorum homines.

Ἔθνος ἅγιον.] Supra cap. I, 15. Sumpta verba ex Deut. 7, 6. & c. 14, 2. ubi in Ebræo עם קדוש. Sanctus populus dicitur Ecclesiæ cœtus non quoad externam sanctitatem, quemadmodum populus Israeliticus separabatur ab aliis populis & immundis gentibus ceremoniali sanctitate in portionibus, discrimine ciborum mundorum & im- mundorum, aliisque ejusmodi ritibus sita, sed quoad sanctitatem internam, quam illa designabat, & præfigurabat Exod. 22. vers. 31. Levit. 20. vers. 44. 45. cap. 20, 26. Num. 15, 40. Johan. 17. vers. 17. Ephes. 1, 4. cap. 5, 27. Ebr. 13, 12. Nec præter cau- sam ἔθνος ἅγιον dicitur, quum λαὸν ἅγιον dicere potuisset, quia gentium nomen incredulis Judæis invisum, fidelibus gratum erat, ac gratius ita red- debatur, quod gentes Deo consecratæ sanctæque fuerint non minus, quam Judæi fideles, Act. 10, 34. Gal. 3, 28. Col. 3, 11.

Λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν.] Id est ad salutem, ut Ebr. 11, 39. Ex- od. 19, 6. והייתם לי סגלה Græce ἔσεσθέ μοι λαὸς περιού- σιος, & Malachiæ 3. v. 17. אשר אני עשה סגלה, ἢ, ἵνα ποιῶ εἰς περιποίησιν. Vulgata exposuit populum acquisitionis. In Ve- teri Testamento dicitur populus peculii Deut. 7, 6. cap. 14, 2. cap. 26, 18. Mal. 3, 17. Vox סגלה rem ta- men pretiosam, quæ thesauri loco habetur, significat, unde Pagninus Exod. 19, 5. reddidit: Eritis mihi tanquam thesaurus dilectus. LXX. Interpretes: λαὸς περιούσιος, populus peculiaris, ut habet Paulus Tit. 2, 14. Hic vero λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν dicitur, quod κατὰ πόδα non est populus ad salutem, sed in acquisitionem, vel redemptionem, quod populus re- demptus Syrus exposuit, quem sibi acquisivit, πε- ριεποιήσατο Deus proprio sanguine, Act. 20, 28. At 1. Thess. 4, 9. positi dicimur εἰς περιποίησιν σωτη- ρίας in acquisitionem salutis: unde non immerito hoc loco exponitur populus ad acquisitionem sa- lutis, hoc est, consequendam salutem Divina or- dinatione positus, cons. 2. Thessal. II, cap. 14. Ebr. X, 39.

Ὅπως τὰς ἀρετὰς ἐξαγγείλατε τῦ ἐκ σκότος ὑμᾶς καλέσαν- τος, εἰς τὸ θαυμαςὸν ἀυτῦ φῶς.] Vox ἀρετὴ, interdum signi- ficat rectos habitus, ut Phil. 4, 8. At ubi de Deo dicitur, ut hic, respondet voci הוד, ut Abac. 3, 3. Zach. 6, 13. aut voci תהלה, ut Esa. 42, 8. 12. cap, 43, 21. cap. 63, 7. in quibus locis est, ut hic, pluraliter, ἀρετὰς in significatu potentiæ. Syrus laudem vertit. Deus est, qui nos vocavit, Rom. 9, 12. 24. 1. Corinth. 7, 15. Gal. I, 6. 15. cap. 5, 8. 1. Thess. I, 12. cap. 5, 24. 2. Thess. 2, 14. 2. Timoth. I, 9. Σκότος vocatur tempus ante Evangelium, Matth. 4, 16. Luc. 1, 79. Joh. 3, 19. Actor. 26, 18. Rom. 13, 11. Ephes. 5, 8. Coloss. I, 13. 1. Thess. 5, 4. 5. Φῶς ipsum Evangelium & vita ei congruens, ut iis- dem locis videre est, & Roman. 13, 12. Coloss. I, 12. Additur autem hic illud θαυμαστὸν, sicut ἀληθινὸν Joh. I, 9. 1. Joh. 2, 8. ad denotandam hujus lucis excellentiam, sic μέγα καὶ θαυμαστὸν Apoc. 15, 1. Hic est sensus mysticus loci Esa. 42, 6. 7. & Job. 37, 21.

Σκότος non tempus ante-Evangelicum, nisi quo- ad gentiles, qui sederunt in tenebris, sed statum ante communionem veræ lucis, quæ illuminat omnem ho- minem, Job. I, 9. designat. Nam & ante adven- tum Filii Dei in carnem fideles in luce versabantur cognitionis veri DEI, & Messiæ, non in tenebris ignorantiæ, ut gentiles, Actor. 17, 30. In illo vero statu tenebrarum omnes non renati constituti sunt, quocunque vivant tempore, ideo conver- tendi à tenebris ad lucem, Act. 26, 8. Eph. 5. 8. Col. I, 13. Per Φῶς ipsum Evangelium, & vitam ei con- gruentem, tempore Novi Testamenti propriam, ut vult Grotius, notari, unde docebitur? Lux cogni- tionis omnium est temporum, qua destitutos fuisse Patriarchas, ipsumque Abrahamum, Patrem cre- dentium, qui omnibus in exemplum fidei sistitur à Paulo, nemo temere dixerit. Christus vero lux gentium dicitur, Esa. 42, 6. ut & cap. 49, 6. non sen- su mystico, sed literali, ut circa loca illa monitum. Locus autem Job. 37, 21. hic plane ἀλλότριος est. Per ἀρετὰς virtutes non quas Christus in nobis opera- tur, vel vocatorum, ut Cornelius vult, sed virtutes ipsius Dei, qui nos vocavit, intelliguntur, utpote Di- vina potentia, sapientia, gratia, & justitia, quæ elu- cent maxime in negotio vocationis & conversionis, conf. 2. Petr. I, 3. Per tenebras, à quibus vocavit nos Deus, non ignorantia tantum, & errorum vel superstitionum, ac idololatriarum atque peccatorum, & impietatum tenebras intelligit Apostolus, sed & miseriarum, & mortis temporalis, & æternæ, adeoq; tota tenebrarum potestas designatur, Coloff. I, 13. Per lucem ergo non tantum Evangelii vel cognitio- nis, & fidei lux dispellens & ignorantias & errores, sed etiam lucem gratiæ, benedictionis & salutis, tum in hac tum in altera vita in regno lucis, tene- brarum regno opposito, designat. Quod lumen vere admirabile est, tum quod fides circa admiran- da Dei occupetur, Psalm. 119, 18. tum quod admi- randa sit illa gratia fidelium, qua fruuntur in regno gratiæ & gloriæ.

## 2:10
Verse 10.

Who once were not a people, now are also the people of God.] That word God from the latter member ought to be understood in the former as well, as the passage which is referred to here shows, Hos. 2:23. Paul adapts that passage to those who arose from the Gentiles, Rom. 9:25. But it is not badly applied also to the Jews, who were so poorly instructed that they became children of hell, Matt. 23:15. Who had not obtained mercy, now have also obtained mercy.] I will have mercy on her who had not obtained mercy, in the cited passage of Hosea, formerly not loved because of vices, now loved because of purification. For also in the passage of Hosea some versions have, I will love her who was not loved.

He confirms this vocation from the prediction of the Holy Spirit, and teaches that it is purely gratuitous. The Syriac explained it in this way: You who formerly were reckoned not a people, but now are the people of God, also there was no mercy toward you, but now mercy has been poured out upon you. But Paul does not only adapt the passage of Hosea to the Gentiles, but from it he proves the vocation of the Gentiles. Therefore, it is rightly understood here of the Gentiles as well. For although the epistle may have been directed to the Jews dispersed here and there, yet they were those dispersed among the Gentiles, from whom not a few, also brought to the faith of Christ, belonged to the same Church. And therefore Estius gathers from this passage: This epistle is not written to the Jews alone, but also to the Gentiles, with whom the Jews, placed in dispersion, were intermingled and communicated through faith and the Sacraments, so that for that reason the Apostle directs his speech partly to the Jews, partly to the Gentiles, but at other times to both together. Although he also thinks it can be said that the prediction of the Prophet pertains only to the Israelites dispersed among the Gentiles, to whom the Prophet, after the repudiation was introduced, promises the grace of reconciliation, which promise Peter teaches is now fulfilled. What is to be thought of the prediction of Hosea, we have said at the Prophetic passage, with which compare what was said at Rom. IX, v. 25.

PART II OF CHAPTER II. Concerning the duty of the conversation of the faithful, especially of subjects and servants. In which the SECOND PART OF THE EPISTLE, WHICH IS PARENETIC, begins. Concerning the Duty of Christians.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Οἱ ποτὲ ὀυ λαὸς, νῦν καὶ λαὸς Θεῦ.] Illud Θεῦ ex membro posteriore etiam in priore subaudiri debet, ut ostendit locus qui hic respicitur, Ose. 2, 23. Aptat eum locum Paulus iis, qui ex gentibus orti, Rom. 9, 25. Verum non male etiam Judæis applicatur, qui ita male instituebantur, ut filii fierent gehennæ, Matth. 23, 15. Οἱ ὀυκ ἠλεημένοι, νῦν καὶ ἐλεηθέντες.] רחמתי את לא רחמה dicto Oseæ loco, olim non amati ob vitia, nunc amati ob purgationem. Nam & in lo- co Oseæ quædam versiones habent, ἀγαπήσω τὸν ὀυκ ἠγα- πημένον.

Confirmat hanc vocationem è prædictione Spiritus sancti, docetque eam esse mere gratuitam. Syrus exposuit hoc modo: Qui antea reputa- bamini non populus, nunc autem populus Dei, etiam non erat erga vos misericordia, nunc autem effusa est super vos misericordia. Non aptat autem tantum Paulus locum Oseæ gentibus, sed ex eo gentium vocationem probat. Ideo de gentibus etiam me- rito hic intelligitur. Etsi enim epistola ad Judæos directa fuerit hinc inde dispersos, erant tamen illi dispersi inter gentes, è quibus non pauci etiam ad Christi fidem perducti ad eandem Ecclesiam per- tinebant. Ideoque ex hoc loco colligit Estius: Non ad solos Judæos scribi hanc epistolam, sed etiam ad gentiles, quibus permixti Judæi in dispersione po- siti, fide & Sacramentis communicabant, ut propterea partim ad Judæos, partim ad gentiles, alias vero ad utrosque simul sermonem dirigat Apostolus. Quan- quam & dici posse idem arbitretur, prædictionem Prophetæ ad solos pertinere Israëlitas in gentibus di- sporsas, quibus Propheta post inductum repudium gratiam reconciliationis promittat, quam promif- sionem nunc impletam esse Petrus docet. Quid de prædictione Oseæ habendum sit, diximus ad locum Propheticum, quo cum confer; quæ ad Rom. IX. v. 25. dicta.

PARS II. CAPITIS II. De conversationis fidelium, imprimis subdi- torum & servorum debito. Qua inchoatur PARS ALTERA EPISTOLÆ PARÆNETICA. De Officio Christianorum.

## 2:11
Verse 11.

Ἀγαπητοὶ.] Thus also James 1:16, 19; ch. 2:5.

Παρακαλῶ ὡς παροίκες καὶ παρεπιδήμους.] Πάροικοι are those who have a residence outside their fatherland: παρεπίδημοι are those who are traveling outside their fatherland. From their present state he warns them of the condition common to all men, who live on earth for a short time, and not as if in their own [home], clearly as above in ch. 1:17, where see the notes.

Having shown the foundation of salvation, upon which we are built up through faith; by the method used by the Apostles, he exhorts to the flight from evils and the pursuit of good works: And after he warns concerning the dignity and happiness of Christians, which they obtain from the benefit of redemption, calling, and promised glorification, that they might respond to such great dignity with a worthy manner of life. Cornelius therefore, from the fact that we are called strangers, wrongly concludes that our soul comes down from heaven and from God into the earth and this mortal body: Because we are entirely πάροικοι, that is, as interpreted by Grotius, established outside our fatherland both in soul and body: Which is called fatherland, not by reason of the origin of the soul, which we draw from our parents by the vigor of the blessing made to the Protoplast: But partly by reason of primeval creation, because both the body was formed and the soul was inspired by the heavenly Father by the common fate of mortals; partly by reason of regeneration, because we are reborn by the heavenly Father not to this, but to another life: partly by reason of temporary sojourn, because in these lands we are strangers and only traveling, nor do we have a remaining city here, but we seek one to come, Heb. 13:14, cf. Psalm 39:12, Psalm 119:19, Heb. 11:13 ff. Every man, says Augustine, q. 91 in Leviticus, is a stranger by being born, since he is compelled to migrate by dying. Hence we are deservedly called παρεπίδημοι, because we not only live outside our fatherland, but we also wander and travel here with an uncertain residence: for nothing is stable in these lands and therefore we must always think that we are pilgrims here, and we should not cling to this age, 1 Chron. 29:15, and that we should value all things in it as if they were foreign and strange, in the manner of pilgrims, and not fix our heart on worldly things. True happiness, says Eucherius in his epistle to Valerian, is to despise the happiness of the age, and having neglected earthly things, to burn for Divine things. Therefore, let us pant for our homeland, and with that hope let us bravely overcome the difficulties of this pilgrimage. He who does not groan as a pilgrim will not rejoice as a citizen, because the desire is not in him, says Augustine in Psalm 145 and in Psalm 137. This life is a small tribulation; if there is no tribulation, there is no pilgrimage. But if it is a pilgrimage, you either love your homeland too little, or you are undoubtedly in tribulation. For who would not be in tribulation, not being with that which he desires?

Abstain from fleshly lusts.] That one may abstain from fulfilling those desires which not reason, but the flesh suggests. Fleshly lusts, which are the lusts of the flesh, Gal. 5:16, Eph. 2:3, 1 John 2:6.

The argument of the Apostle is this: You are guests and pilgrims in this world. Therefore, do not love the world. He who is a pilgrim on earth considers all earthly things as foreign to himself, much more so carnal concupiscence, since he uniquely desires spiritual delights and is delighted by them, and desires heavenly and eternal things in abundance. A soul burning with heavenly greed, says Basil in his admonition to his spiritual son, is coupled to the love of Christ when, while living on earth, it meditates continually on heavenly things, tramples upon the pleasures of the age, and no care of the age separates it from the love of Christ, but it seems to move among men as if in a figure, and its whole conversation is in heaven. Nor does Estius speak inconveniently: Carnal desires are called so from the flesh, that is, concupiscence, or the tinder of sin, exciting them in us. But we are commanded to abstain from them, not so that we may be entirely without them, which in this corruption of life cannot happen, but so that we may not follow them either by deed or by consent.

Which war against the soul.] They fight directly against the good of your soul, that is, they hinder you from being able to attain eternal life, which ought to be your homeland. A similar metaphor is in the word to war, Rom. 7:23, James 4:1. Concerning the word soul, see Heb. 10:39.

They not only fight against the good of the soul, but also against the very nature of the regenerated soul, which is spiritual. For the flesh and the Spirit are opposed. And not only the soul, but the whole inner man, which has been renewed by the Holy Spirit, is understood; compare Rom. 7:23, James 4:1. Carnal concupiscence is not only an impediment to the way, Wisd. 4:1, but also a poison to life. For it kills the soul of the pilgrim to heaven, and thrusts him into hell, Gal. 5:17 ff., Rom. 8:13, Rev. 21:8. Carnal concupiscences war against the soul, and are in the soul itself as in a seat. The fight is the more dangerous for that reason: They war not by force, but by sweet enticements: For that reason they are the more to be avoided, James 2:14.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Ἀγαπητοὶ.] Sic & Jac. I, 16. 19. c. II, 5.

Παρακαλῶ ὡς παροίκες καὶ παρεπιδήμους.] Πάροικοι sunt qui sedem habent extra patriam : παρεπίδημοι qui extra pa- triam peregrinantur. Ex præsente ipsorum statu eos admo- net fortis communis omnium hominum, qui in terris agunt ad tempus breve, nec tanquam in suo, plane ut supra c. I, 17. ubi annotata vide.

Ostenso fundamento salutis, cui per fidem su- perædificamur; methodo Apostolis usitata hor- tatur ad fugam malorum & studium bonorum ope- rum: Et postquam de Christianorum dignitate & felicitate, quam ex beneficio redemptionis, vo- cationis, & promissæ glorificationis obtinent, mo- net, ut tantæ dignitati conversatione digna re- spondeant. Cornelius ergo ex eo, quod adve- ne dicamur, perperam concludit, animam no- stram cælestem & à DEO creatam venire in ter- ram, & corpus hoc mortale: Quia nos toti πά- ροικοι sumus, hoc est, interprete Grotio, extra patriam & anima & corpore constituti: Quæ patria dicitur, non ratione originis animæ, quam à parentibus, vigore benedictionis Protoplastis factæ, trahimus: Sed partim ratione primævæ creationis, quia à Patre cœlesti & corpus forma- tum, & anima inspirata est communi morta- lium fatori; partim ratione regenerationis, quia à cœlesti Patre non ad hanc, sed ad alteram vi- tam regignimur: partim ratione temporariæ com- morationis, quia in hisce terris advenæ sumus & peregrinamur tantum, nec civitatem manen- tem hic habemus, sed futuram quærimus, Ebr. 13. vers. 14. conf. Psalm. 30. vers. 13. Psalm. 119. v. 119. Ebr. 11. vers. 13. seqq. Omnis homo, inquit Augu- stinus q. XCI. in Levit. advena est nascendo, quo- niam compellitur migrare moriendo. Hinc merito παρεπίδημοι dicimur, quia non solum extra pa- triam degimus, sed incerta etiam sede hic oberra- mus & peregrinamur: nihil n. stabile his in terris est. Ideoque id nobis semper cogitandum, nos hic peregrinos esse, nec huic seculo adhærescamus, 1. Paral. 29, 15. & ut omnia in eodem velut aliena & peregrina more peregrinantium æstimemus, nec cor nostrum mundanis affigamus. Vera beatitudo est, inquit Eucherius epist. ad Valerian. seculi beati- tudinem spernere, neglectisque terrenis ad Divina flagrare. Quapropter anhelemus ad patriam, eaq́; spe difficultates hujus peregrinationis fortiter supere- mus. Qui non gemit peregrinus, non gaudebit ci- vis, quia desiderium non est in illo, ait Augustinus in Psalm. CXLV. & in Psalm. CXXXVII. Vita ista parva tribulatio est, si non est tribulatio, non est pere- grinatio. Si autem peregrinatio est, aut parum pa- triam diligis, aut sine dubio tribularis. Quis enim non tribuletur, se non esse cum eo, quod desiderat?

Ἀπέχεσθε τῶν σαρκικῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν.] Ut abstineatur ab implendis cupiditatibus illis, quas non ratio, sed caro sug- gerit. Ἐπιθυμίαι σαρκικαὶ, quæ ἐπιθυμίαι σαρκὸς, Gal. 5, 16. Eph. 2, 3. 1. Joh. 2, 6.

Argumentum Apostoli hoc est: Hospites estis, & peregrini in hoc mundo. Ergo non amate mun- dum. Qui peregrinatur in terra, peregrina sibi æstimat omnia terrena, multo magis concupiscentiam carnalem, cum unice delicias spirituales concupiscat, iisq́ue oblectetur, cœlestesque & æternas affatim deside- ret. Aviditate cœlesti anima flagrans, inquit Basi- lius admonit. ad filium spiritual. Christi amori copu- latur, cum in terris agens de cœlestibus jugiter medi- tatur, calcat seculi voluptates, nec ulla seculi cura eam segregat ab amore Christi, sed ut figura quadam inter homines versari videtur, & tota ejus conversatio in cœlis est. Nec incommode Estius: Carnalia desi- deria dicuntur à carne, id est concupiscentia, seu fo- mite peccati, ea in nobis excitante. Ab iis autem ab- stinere jubemur, non ut prorsus iis careamus, quod in hac vitæ corruptione fieri non potest, sed ut nec opere, nec consensu ea sequamur.

Αἵτινες στρατεύονται κατὰ τῆς ψυχῆς.] Directe pugnant cum animæ vestræ bono, id est, impediunt, ne vitam æter- nam, quæ patria vobis esse debet, possitis consequi. Par me- ταφορα in voce στρατεύεσθαι Rom. 7, 23. Jac. 4, 1. De voce ψυχῆς vide Ebr. 10, 39.

Non tantum pugnant cum animæ bono, sed et- iam cum ipsa animæ regenitæ natura, quæ spiritua- lis est. Caro enim & Spiritus opposita sint. Nec tantum anima, sed totus homo interior, quæ per Spiritum sanctum renovatus est, intelligitur, conf. Rom. 7, 23. Jac. 4, 1. Concupiscentia carnalis non tantum impedimento est ad viam, Sap. 4, 1. sed etiam veneno ad vitam. Occidit enim ani- mam peregrinantis in cœlum, truditque eum in infernum, Galat. 5, 17. seqq. Rom. 8, 13. Apoc. 21, 8. Militant concupiscentiæ carnales adversus ani- mam, & sunt in ipsa anima ceu sede. Eo pe- riculosior est pugna: Militant non vi, sed sua- vibus irritamentis: Eo magis cavendæ sunt, Ja- cobi II, 14.

## 2:12
Verse 12.

Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles.] See James 3:13. Among the Gentiles, in the sight of the nations among whom you live, by whom you are observed because of the diversity of your religion.

The information of the inner man is followed by the form of external conversation. For first, the account of conscience before GOD, then also the account of reputation and honest conversation among men must be held. The Syriac rendered it, let your conversations be elegantly pleasant and grateful. What he says among the Gentiles argues that this epistle was written to the Jews. For writing to the Gentiles, he would not say among the Gentiles, but among the unbelievers, or those who are outside, or with an addition, as elsewhere, among the Gentiles who do not know God, as Estius has it here.

That in that wherein they speak against you as evildoers.] For the very reason for which they traduce you as guilty, that is, because of the Christian religion. In a similar sense we have the little word in, Eph. 3:13.

Vulgate: In that, wherein they speak against you, as of evildoers. Syriac, who speak evil words against you. Peter brings forward a twofold cause, namely, that false crimes may be declined, and that others may be excited to glorify GOD. For the Gentiles were accusing (compare Phil. 2:15) Christians of being despisers of Princes, of the Divinity, and of the gods, of being voluptuous, of practicing promiscuous intercourse, which the Gnostics did, of eating human flesh, not understanding the mystery of the Eucharist, of being less obedient to Princes and Magistrates and Ethnic Lords under the pretext of religion and liberty, etc., and all calamities were imputed to them, and from that they persecuted them most atrociously. If the Tiber, says Tertullian in his Apology, rises to the walls, if the Nile does not rise to the fields, if the earth quakes, if there is famine, if there is plague, immediately the Christians to the lions. See the Apology of Justin, Athenagoras, Cyprian, Clement of Alexandria, Arnobius, etc.

Ἐκ τῶν καλῶν ἔργων ἐποπτεύσαντες.] That is, ἀ ἐπώπτευ- σαν, having observed your good works.

Δοξάσωσι τὸν Θεὸν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἐπισκοπῆς.] Let them praise God in the time of probation, as the Syriac here, that is, in hard times, for thus the word ἐπισκοπῆς is used in Isaiah 10:3 and elsewhere: The sense is: when those nations see that the Christians alone are immune from those evils which, because of their turbulent and seditious natures, threaten the Jews everywhere. The things that follow immediately require this sense.

Conf. 2 Peter 3:16. Matthew 5:16. The day of visitation is to be understood as a gracious visitation of the slanderers rather than a visitation of wrath, because through the good works of the faithful they learn to think more rightly, and through examples, when they harmonize with doctrine, they are led to recognize the truth of the Christian religion, so that that unmerited detraction may be turned into the praise and glorification of GOD. Compare Luke 19:44. Bede interprets it as the day of final judgment, others as the day of visitation which occurs through the cross leading to recognition, Oecumenius as the day of human inquiry, others interpret it otherwise. See Cornelius à Lapide. The explanation which we have given is the simplest, which Cornelius also followed, to the effect that the Gentiles shall glorify GOD at the time when GOD shall visit them with the light of His grace, so that they may see the truth and holiness of CHRIST and of Christians, and embrace it, as if he were saying, your good conversation will be a sharp stimulus to them for conversion and faith. In support of this opinion he cites the Gloss, Dionysius, Gagnejus, Catharinus, Vatablus, and Salmeron. Thus was Justin converted, who in Apol. II professes concerning himself that, while he was still a Gentile, he thought it impossible that Christians could pursue those prodigious pleasures of which they were accused, seeing that they met death so steadfastly for CHRIST. Eusebius, Book X, chapter 10, and Ruffinus, Book I, chapter 10, record that the Iberians, a people of Spain, were converted to Christ by the obedience, patience, devotion, and mighty works of a certain captive Christian woman.

But the holy life of Christians would never profit for the conversion of infidels and malevolent people, unless God, by special grace, looked upon them as if by the benign illumination of His countenance, just as Christ looked upon Peter, Luke 22, as Estius rightly warned in this place. God was also glorified when the Gentiles, having recognized the innocence of Christians, bore public testimony to them, which was done, as Eusebius relates in book III of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 12, by the Emperor Antoninus, so that he decreed that if anyone should proceed to bring any trouble or charge against any Christian because he is a Christian, the one against whom the charge was brought, even if he were found to be a Christian in fact, should be acquitted: but he who accused him should undergo the just and due punishment.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Τὴν ἀναστροφὴν ὑμῶν ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἔχοντες καλήν.] Vid. Jac. III, 13. Ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, in conspectu gentium inter quas vivitis, à quibus ob religionis diversitatem obser- vamini.

Informationem interioris hominis sequitur for- ma externæ conversationis. Primum enim con- scientiæ ratio coram DEO, deinde etiam famæ, & honestæ apud homines conversationis ratio ha- benda. Syrus reddidit, sint conversationes ve- stræ eleganter jucundæ & gratæ. Quod ait in- ter gentes, arguit epistolam hanc ad Judæos scri- ptam esse. Nam ad gentiles scribens, non diceret inter gentes, sed inter incredulos, aut eos, qui foris sunt, aut cum addito, ut alibi, inter gentes, quæ Deum ignorant, ut hic habet Estius.

Ἵνα ἐν ὧ καταλαλῶσιν ὑμῶν ὡς κακοποιῶν.] Ob idipsum ob quod vos tanquam sontes traducunt, id est, ob reli- gionem Christianam. Pari sensu voculam ἐν habemus Eph. III, 13.

Vulgata: In eo, quod detrectant de vobis, tanquam de malefactoribus. Syrus, qui loquun- tur contra vos sermones malos. Causam gemi- nam affert Petrus, nempe ut falsa crimina de- clinentur, & ut alii ad DEUM glorificandum excitentur. Criminabantur quippe gentiles (con- fer. Philipp. II. vers. 15.) Christianos esse con- temptores Principum, Numinis, ac Deorum, voluptuarios, usurpare promiscuos concubitus, quod faciebant Gnostici, vesci carnibus huma- nis, non intelligentes mysterium Eucharistiæ, prætextu religionis & libertatis Principibus ac Magistratibus & Dominis Ethnicis minus obsequi, &c. iisque omnes calamitates imputabantur, at- que inde persequebantur eos atrocissime. Si Ti- beris, ait Tertullianus in Apol. ascendit in mœnia, si Nilus non ascendit in arva, si terra movet, si fames, si lues, statim Christianos ad Leones. Vide Apologiam Justini, Athenagoræ, Cypriani, Cle- mentis Alexandr. Arnobii &c.

Ἐκ τῶν καλῶν ἔργων ἐποπτεύσαντες.] Id est, ἀ ἐπώπτευ- σαν, spectatis bonis operibus vestris.

Δοξάσωσι τὸν Θεὸν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἐπισκοπῆς.] Laudent Deum tempore probationis, ut hic Syrus, id est,in temporibus duris, ita enim ἐπισκοπῆς vox ponitur Esa. X, 3. & alibi: Sensus est: cum conspicient gentes illæ solos Christianos immunes ab illis malis, quæ Judæis ob turbulenta ac seditiosa ipsorum ingenia ubique locorum impendent. Hunc sensum postulant ea, quæ ἀμέσως sequuntur.

Conf. 2. Petr. III. vers. 16. Matth. V. vers. 16. Dies visitationis de gratiosa potius maledicorum visitatione intelligenda, quam de visitatione iræ, quia per fidelium opera bona rectius sentire il- li discunt, & per exempla, cum doctrinæ con- sonant, ad veritatem religionis Christianæ co- gnoscendam deducuntur, ut ita immerita illa detractio in laudem & glorificationem DEI con- vertatur. Confer. Luc. XIX. vers. 44. Beda de die extremi judicii, alii de die visitationis, quæ fit per crucem ad agnitionem perducentem, Oecumenius de die inquisitionis humanæ, alii aliter interpretantur. Vid. Cornelius à Lapide. Simplicissima autem est illa, quam dedimus, explicatio, quam etiam sequutus est Cornelius, q. d. ut gentiles glorificent DEUM tunc, quando DEUS eos visitabit lumine gratiæ suæ, ut videant veritatem & sanctitatem CHRISTI & Chri- stianorum, eamque amplectantur, quasi dicat, vestra bona conversatio acer erit eis stimulus ad conversionem & fidem. In quam senten- tiam affert Glossam, Dionysium, Gagnejum, Ca- tharinum, Vatablum, Salmeronem. Ita con- versus est Justinus, qui Apol. II. de se profite- tur, quod, cum adhuc gentilis esset, cogitarit, impossibile esse, Christianos prodigiosas illas, qua- rum rei agebantur, sectari voluptates, qui tam constanter pro CHRISTO mortem obirent. Eu- sebius Libr. X. cap. 10. Ruffinus Libr. I. cap. 10. commemorant: Iberos, Hispaniæ populos obe- dientia, patientia, devotione & virtute captivæ cujusdam Christianæ ad Christum conversos esse.

Nunquam autem sancta Christianorum vita ad in- fidelium & malevolorum conversionem proficeret: nisi Deus speciali gratia, tanquam benigna vultus sui illuminatione eos respiceret, quomodo Christus Pe- trum respexit, Luc. 22. ut recte monuit h. l. Estius. Glorificatus etiam Deus est, cum gentiles agnita Christianorum innocentia publica ipsis tulere te- stimonia, quod ita ab Antonino Imperatore, Eusebio l. III. hist. Eccles. cap. 12. referente factum, ut de- creto fanciuerit, quod si quispiam cuiquam Chri- stiano, quia Christianus sit, pergat quicquam mo- lestiae aut criminis inferre, ille cui crimen illatum fuerit, etiamsi re ipsa Christianus deprehensus sit, absolvatur: qui autem illum accusaverit, justum debitumque supplicium subeat.

## 2:13
Vers. 13.

ὑποτάγητε ὗν.] A passive for the Hithpael, which is frequent in other verbs as well, but especially in those which come from τάσσω. Conduct yourselves as subject, thus Luke 2:51, Rom. 8:7, 1 Cor. 16:16, Eph. 5:22, 24, Col. 3:18, Tit. 2:5, 9, ch. 3:1, Jas. 4:7.

Πάσῃ ἀνθρωπίνῃ κτίσει.] That is, to that ordinance which has and ought to have a place among men living on earth. For כון ארכא among other things also signifies to ordain, as we have said in the Prolegomena to the New Testament. Add Sirach 7:6, ch. 39:30, 34, 36, ch. 40:1, 9. Someone might perhaps think it was written κρίσει. For to the Hellenists κρίνειν is to rule after the manner of the Hebrew שפט.

Διὰ τὸν Κύριον.] On account of Christ's precept, Matt. 22:21.

He descends from a general exhortation to special precepts of a holy and honest conversation, and because all Christians were then subjects, and furthermore Jews were commonly ill-spoken of among the Gentiles as refractory to the laws, on the occasion of Judas the Galilean, who had taught that the Jews, as the people of God, were free from taxes and ought not to be subject to the Roman Emperor as a Gentile, he prescribes subjection in the first place. Cf. Acts 5:37. Jerome in his epistle to Titus, ch. II. Augustine, epistle V. Chrysostom on ch. XIII to the Romans. Lest, forsooth, the Gentiles should say that Christianity brings about the subversion of the state, as Oecumenius holds in this place. ὑποτάσσεσθαι properly is to be subordinated, and thus it implies that the order between magistrate and subjects was established by God, by virtue of which subjects ought to be subject to the Magistrate, Rom. 13:1. Some understand creation abstractly by the name of κτίσεως, and they take it either concerning the ordinance of laws, which however agrees neither with the signification of the word, since it nowhere denotes a law; nor with the following distribution, whether to the King or to Governors; or concerning τάξει and πολιτείᾳ, the ordinance and disposition of civil government, which explanation Cornelius à Lapide approves: but it is repugnant to this that the Magistrate in the abstract is not a human ordinance, but a Divine creature, otherwise than the Papists think: See Prov. 8:15, 16, Rom. 13:1, 2, Psalm 81:6, and B. Hülfemann, Manual of the Augsburg Confession, disp. XIV.

§. IV. seqq. but concretely concerning the persons holding the Magistracy, which is called an human creation, because Magistrates are created or ordained by men as regards the application of this Divine power to certain subjects, as Didymus explains. Moreover, all ought to be subject to the Magistrate, whoever he may be, whether he be a Christian or a Gentile, etc. The Apostle says 'every', as Cajetan notes, not distinguishing between Ethnics and believers. And Estius: At the time when this epistle was written, the Prince of the Roman empire was Domitius Nero, the most severe persecutor of Christians, under whom Peter himself, who writes this, and Paul suffered martyrdom. It is clear, therefore, from the Apostolic doctrine that even infidel and very evil Princes must be obeyed. Which is to be observed against the hypothesis of the Pontificians concerning not tolerating a heretical or infidel King and against Brutus, Rossaeus, Boucher, and others denying obedience to a Tyrant. He who gave the empire to Marius, the same gave it to Gaius Caesar, he who to Augustus, the same to Nero, he who to Vespasian either to the Father or to the Son, most sweet Emperors, the same to the apostate Julian, says Augustine in book V of the City of God, chapter 21.

Διὰ τὸν Κύριον, by which is denoted not so much a command, because the imperative was already introducing that, as the supreme cause of such creatures, which, even if they exist as to their moral being through men, are nevertheless ordained by God, who institutes whatever power there is. Therefore, it is called a human creature on account of the instrumental cause, because the Divine ordinance is instituted through men on account of the principal cause, which is God. The power of the King or the president is not called a human creature, but the King or the President, says B. Hülsemann, S. XXIII, p. 592, and he adds further: that a human creature is not said in this place efficiently and constitutively, as if men were the active principle of the creature: But it is said, he says, a human creature materially and subjectively, because it consists of men and among men, not that it was constituted by men, and therefore men are the passive, not active, principle of this κτίσεως, which he proves from the common meaning of this word (ἀνθρώπινη), which does not denote anything that has drawn its origin from human industry or law, but that which is done and seen among men and in men, Rom. 6, 19. Galat. 3, 15. 1 Cor. 10, 13. Jac. 3, v. 7. Therefore, on account of God, subjection is to be rendered to them for conscience' sake, Rom. 13, 1, 2, 5, whose place they also hold, Ps. 81, 6, not against the Lord, but according to the Lord. Conf. Eph. VI, 1.

Εἴτε βασιλεῖ.] That is, to Caesar. The Romans called them Emperors, not Kings, due to the ancient religion of the oath, as Cyprian says. But the Greeks did not hesitate to call them βασιλέας, and the Jews similarly מלכים, doubtless because they used a plainly Royal, that is, a most free power, as Dion teaches us. When this epistle was written, suppose that Claudius was reigning.

Ὡς ὑπερέχοντι.] As placed above all, this ἐξουσία ὑπερέχουσα, Rom. XIII, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

ὑποτάγητε ὗν.] Passivum pro Hithpaël, quod frequens in aliis quoque verbis, sed maxime in iis, quæ à τάσσω veniunt. Subjectos vos gerite, sic Luc. 2, 51. Rom. 8, 7. 1. Cor. 16, 16. Eph. 5, 22. 24. Col. 3, 18. Tit. 2, 5. 9. c. 3, 1. Jac. 4, 7.

Πάσῃ ἀνθρωπίνῃ κτίσει.] Id est, ordinationi isti, quæ inter homines in terris agentes locum habet & habere debet. Nam כון ארכא inter alia & ordinare significat, ut diximus in Prolegomenis ad Novum Testamentum. Adde Sirac. 7, 6. c. 39, 30. 34. 36. c. 40, 1. 9. Aliquis forte putaret scriptum κρίσει. Nam κρίνειν Hellenistis est regere ad modum Ebræi שפט.

Διὰ τὸν Κύριον.] Propter Christi præceptum, Matth. XXII, 21.

A generali exhortatione ad specialia præcepta sanctæ & honestæ conversationis descendit, & quia Christiani omnes tum erant subditi, adhæc Judæi vulgo male audiebant inter gentiles, tan- quam legum refractarii, occasione Judæ Galilæi, qui docuerat, Judæos, utpote populum Dei, libe- ros esse à vectigalibus, nec subjici debere Impera- tori Romano ceu gentili, primo loco subjectio- nem præcipit. Conf. Actor. V, 37. Hieronymus in epist. ad Tit. cap. II. Augustin. epist. V. Chrysost. in cap. XIII. ad Rom. Ne scilicet dicerent genti- les, quod politiæ subversionem afferat Christianis- mus, ut habet hoc loco Oecumenius. ὑποτάσσεσθαι proprie est subordinari, adeoque innuit ordinem inter magistratum & subditos Divinitus esse con- stitutum, vi cujus subditi Magistratui subjici debe- ant, Rom. 13, 1. Κτίσεως nomine abstractive crea- tionem nonnulli intelligunt, & eam vel de legum ordinatione accipiunt, quod vero nec vocis signifi- cationi convenit, quum nuspiam legem denotet; nec distributioni sequenti, sive Regi, sive Ducibus; vel de τάξει & πολιτείᾳ ordinatione & civilis guber- nationis dispositione, quam explicationem Cornelius à Lapide approbat: Cui vero repugnat, quod Ma- gistratus in abstracto non humana sit ordinatio, sed creatura Divina, secus atque Papistæ arbitran- tur: Vid. Prov. 8, 15. 16. Rom. 13, 12. Psalm. 81, 6. & B. Hülfemannus Manual. Aug. Conf. disp. XIV.

§. IV. seqq. sed concretive de personis Magistratum gerentibus, quæ ἀνθρωπίνη κτίσις dicitur, quod per homines quoad applicationem hujus Divinæ po- testatis ad certa subjecta creentur vel ordinentur Magistratus, ut Didymus explicat. Subjici autem debent omnes Magistratui, cuicunque, sive Chri- stianus sit, sive gentilis &c. Dicit Apostolus omni, notante Cajetano, non distinguendo inter Ethnicos & fideles. Et Estius: Quo tempore scri- pta fuit hac epistola, Princeps imperii Romani erat Domitius Nero, Christianorum gravissimus persecu- tor, sub quo Petrus ipse, qui hac scribit, & Paulus martyrium subierunt. Liquet ergo ex doctrina A- postolica, Principibus etiam infidelibus & valde ma- lis obediendum esse. Quod contra Pontificiorum hypothesin de non tolerando Rege hæretico aut infi- deli & contra Brutum, Rossæum, Boucherium, & alios Tyranno obedientiam denegantes, observan- dum. Qui Mario imperium dedit, ipse Cajo Cæ- sari, qui Augusto, ipse & Neroni, qui Vespasiano vel Patri, vel Filio, suavissimis Imperatoribus, ipse Apostatæ Juliano, ait Augustinus libr. V. de Civit. Dei cap. 21.

Διὰ τὸν Κύριον, quo non tam præceptum notatur, quia id jam Imperativus inferebat, quam suprema causa creaturarum talium, quæ etsi per homines quoad esse morale existant, à Deo tamen instituente potestatem quamvis, ordinati sunt. Humana er- go creatura dicitur propter causam instrumenta- lem, quia per homines instituitur Divina ordina- tio ob causam principalem, quæ est Deus. Non Regis, non præsidis potestas dicitur humana crea- tura, sed Rex, sed Præses, inquit B. Hülsemannus S. XXIII. pag. 592. additque porro: Humanam creaturam non dici hoc loco efficienter & constitutive, quod homines sint principium activum creaturæ: Sed dicitur, inquit, humana creatura materialiter & subjective, quod ex hominibus & inter homines constet, non ab hominibus constituta sit, adeoǵ, homi- nes sint principium hujus κτίσεως passivum, non acti- vum, quod probat ex communi hujus vocis (ἀνθρώ- πινη) significatione, quæ non notat quippiam, quod ex humana industria aut lege originem traxerit, sed id, quod inter homines & in hominibus fit & conspici- tur, Rom. 6, 19. Galat. 3, 15. 1. Cor. 10, 13. Jac. 3. v. 7. Idcirco propter Deum subjectio illis præstanda propter conscientiam Rom. 13, 1. 2. 5. cujus etiam vices gerunt Psal. 81, 6. non contra Dominum, sed juxta Dominum. Conf. Eph. VI, 1.

Εἴτε βασιλεῖ.] Id est Cæsari. Romani eos vocabant Im- peratores, non Reges, religione jurisjurandi veteri, ut ait Cy- prianus. At Græci non dubitabant, eos appellare βασιλέας, & Judæi similiter מלכים nimirum quia plane Regia, id est, liberrima utebantur potestate, ut Dion nos docet. Cum hæc epistola scriberetur, puta imperasse Claudium.

Ὡς ὑπερέχοντι.] Tanquam super omnes posita hæc ἐξουσία ὑπερέχουσα, Rom. XIII, 1.

## 2:14
Vers. 14.

Εἴτε ἡγεμόσι.] To the proconsuls of both Asia and Bithynia. For ἡγεμόνων is a general name for all those governing provinces, as we said at Matth. XXVII, 2.

Ὡς δι᾽ αὐτοῦ πεμπομένοις.] As sent by Caesar, that is, deriving their power from him. For this is also signified by πέμπειν, as in John XX, 21 and elsewhere. Therefore, if a Proconsul orders one thing and an Emperor another, we ought to choose to serve the greater, as Augustine says, who also says elsewhere that such power was given to Pilate that he himself was also under Caesar's power. Wherefore, as Christians, they were not to adhere to Furius Camillus Scribonianus against Claudius. Those who instruct peoples otherwise both resist the doctrine of the Apostles and disturb empires. The supreme power is in every empire, to which pagans and soldiers swear allegiance, whose laws all obey, from whose judgments there is no appeal, whose image the coin bears.

Therefore it is not true and perfect obedience to obey only the supreme Magistrate, but to deny obedience to inferior Magistrates. For the Apostle joins Kings and Presidents. In inferior Magistrates we ought to see and revere the King as superior, and in the King, God Himself. For the pronoun δι᾽ αὐτοῦ, according to Estius, whom B. Gerhard follows, is referred not to the King, but to God: For the Apostle, he says, wishes this to be considered in these presidents, that God sent them, which is what ought to move them to obey. And to pass over the fact that presidents were set over provinces not so much by the authority of Caesar as by the Senate, that which follows, 'for the punishment of evildoers, etc.,' does not fit that other relation, which goal evil Kings did not always have proposed. More correctly therefore it is referred to God, who prescribes this end for all magistrates. Whence also Paul Rom. XIII. For he is God's minister to you for good; and again: He is God's minister, a revenger to wrath upon him who does evil. From which it also appears that those sent by God must be understood here to be not only leaders or governors, but also the King himself, to whom, by syllepsis, that part, as being sent by him, also pertains. Add that the Apostle thus explains that 'for the Lord's sake,' that the magistrate is sent by the Lord.

For the punishment of evildoers, but for the praise of those who do well) He says clearly the same thing that Paul says in Rom. XIII. 3, 4, 5. Namely, from the ancient opinions of the Hebrews. We have this custom from those who hold public authority for the most part: for both crimes are punished by them: and rest is provided as a reward for those who love rest. If at any time they sin through ignorance or passions, God will compensate for the injuries thus inflicted. Indeed, He will also punish wicked Princes, undoubtedly in the other life, and not rarely in this very one.

This is not taken from the opinions of the Hebrews, nor does it look only to what usually happens: But to what ought always to happen by divine institution. Not that all Kings, as Bede says here, or leaders, know how to punish evildoers or praise the good, but it simply narrates what the action of a good Judge ought to be, that is, that he should restrain those doing evil and reward those doing good. Which also consists with the light of nature. Whence Plato said that the Republic is held together by rewards and punishments. Solon, in Cicero in the Brutus, asserts that the Republic is best governed if the good are invited by rewards and the bad are restrained by punishments. Cf. Rom. XIII. 3.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Εἴτε ἡγεμόσι.] Proconsulibus tum Asiæ, tum Bithyniæ. Est enim ἡγεμόνων, nomen generale omnibus provincias re- gentibus, ut diximus ad Matth. XXVII, 2.

Ὡς δι᾽ αὐτοῦ πεμπομένοις.] Tanquam à Cæsare missis, id est, potestatem suam ducentibus. Nam & hoc significatur per πέμπειν, ut Joh. XX, 21. & alibi. Itaque si Proconsul aliquid jubeat, & aliquid Imperator, eligere debemus servire majori, ut ait Augustinus, qui & alibi Pilato talem datam ait potestatem, ut esset etiam ipse sub Cæsaris potestate. Quare Christiano, Furio Camillo Scriboniano contra Claudium non erant adhæsuri. Qui populos aliter instituunt, & Apo- stolorum doctrinæ repugnant, & imperia turbant. Summa potestas in quoque imperio est, cui fidem pagani & milites jurant, cujus legibus omnes parent, à cujus judiciis non pro- vocatur, cujus imaginem nummus præfert.

Non ergo est vera & perfecta obedientia. Su- premo tantum Magistratui parere, inferioribus au- tem Magistratibus obedientiam denegare. Con- jungit enim Apostolus Reges & Præsides. In Ma- gistratibus inferioribus Regem tanquam superio- rem, in Rege Deum ipsum intueri ac revereri de- bemus. Pronomen enim δι᾽ αὐτοῦ secundum Estium, quem sequitur B. Gerhardus, non ad Re- gem, sed ad Deum refertur: Nam Apostolus, in- quit, vult hoc in præsidibus istis considerari, quod Deus eos miserit, id quod ad obediendum eos movere debet. Ac ut taceam, quod Præsides provinciis præ- ficiebantur, non tam autoritate Cæsaris, quam Sena- tus, illi alteri relationi non quadrat quod sequitur, ad vindictam malefactorum &c. quem scopum mali Reges non usque quaq́; habebant propositum. Rectius igitur ad Deum refertur, qui hunc finem omnibus magistratibus præscribit. Unde & Paulus Rom. XIII. Dei enim Minister est tibi in bonum; ac rursum: Dei minister est, vindex in iram ei, qui male agit. Ex quo etiam apparet, missos à Deo intelligi hic debere non solum Duces seu præsides, sed etiam Regem ipsum, ad quem per syllepsin illa pars, tanquam ab eo missis, etiam pertineat. Adde quod Apostolus ita expli- cet illud propter Dominum, quod Magistratus à Domino missus sit.

Εἰς ἐκδίκησιν μὲν κακοποιῶν, ἔπαινον δὲ ἀγαθοποιῶν) Idem plane dicit, quod Paulus Rom. XIII. 3. 4. 5. Nimirum ex veteribus Ebræorum sententiis. Habemus hunc usum ab iis, qui publica imperia obtinent ἐπιτοπολὺ: nam & scelera per eos puniuntur: & quietem amantibus quies præstatur pro præmio. Si quando ignorantia aut affectibus peccant illatas sic injurias Deus repensabit. Imo & Principes iniquos puniet, haud dubie in altero seculo, non raro & in hoc ipso.

Non hoc vel ex Ebræorum sententiis deprom- ptum est, vel respicit id tantum, quod plerumque fit: Sed quod ex instituto divino fieri semper de- bet. Non quod omnes quidem Reges, ut hic Beda, aut Duces, vel malefactores punire vellaudare bonos noverint, sed quæ esse debeat actio boni Judicis, sim- pliciter narrat, hoc est, ut malefacientes coërceat, bene agentes remuneret. Quod etiam è naturæ lu- mine constitit. Unde Plato dixit præmiis & pœnis Rempublicam contineri. Solon apud Ciceronem apud Brutun. Rempublic. optime gubernari asse- ruit, si boni præmiis invitentur, mali pœnis coercean- tur. Conf. Rom. XIII. 3.

## 2:15
v. 15. For so is the will of God) namely in the Gospel, Matt. X. 16.

Here Grotius harbors something suspicious, as if this will of God were handed down not in the Old Testament, but only in the New. But did not God will in the Old Testament that the pious should do good? Did He not arrange that their innocence should be brought to light through good deeds? Ps. XXVI. v. 1. Ps. XXXIV. 14. sqq. Ps. XXXVII. v. 6. 7. &c.

By doing good to muzzle the ignorance of foolish men) By doing good to obstruct the mouth of the ignorance (that is, of things arising from ignorance) of men who are not wise, namely concerning divine things. To do good is sometimes to confer benefits, for which it is also called to do good works. But here it simply signifies to act rightly, as also below II. 20. III. 6. 17. 3 John v. 11. in which sense we have already had the adjective 'well-doing,' and Sirach XL. 20. and 'well-doing' below IV. 15. I muzzle in the Glossary I restrain. I am muzzled I am silenced, I become mute, I become silent. Hesychius: Muzzling, silencing. See Matt. XXII. v. 12. 34. Mark I. 25. 39. Luke IV. 35. I know some who would like 'tonguelessness' to be read here instead of 'ignorance,' because to be tongueless is to blaspheme according to Hesychius. By suffering evils and not resisting, we best muzzle the mouths of our enemies.

The sense is, as interpreted by B. Gerhard: If you cannot even by your innocence obtain that others, by the sight of it, may be converted to God and glorify Him, which outcome is often intercepted by the malice of the Devil and the stubbornness of men; you will nevertheless be able to obtain this, that the mouths of calumniators may be obstructed. There is attributed to those detractors of the pious both ignorance of God and the divine Word, like the persecutors of Christ, John XVI. 3. or even of the state and conversation of the pious: and also foolishness, because, destitute of the true knowledge of God, they are stupid, and those who weigh all things less prudently dare to pour out stupid and irrational speeches against the innocent with blind judgment. Four causes are therefore noted for rendering obedience to Magistrates: 1. that we may honor God, who commanded them, 2. that we may avoid the punishment of violated civil justice, 3. that we may obtain from the magistrate the praise and defense of justice, 4. that we may obstruct the mouths of slanderers.

Latin:

v. 15. Ὅτι ὅτως ἐστὶ τὸ θέλημα τῦ Θεῦ) nempe in Evan- gelio, Matth. X. 16.

Hic ὕπυλόν τι fovet Grotius, quasi non in Vete- ri Testamento, sed Novo demum hæc voluntas Dei tradita sit. At annon in Veteri Testamento Deus voluit, ut benefacerent pii? Annon ut in- nocentia eorum in lucem produceretur per bene- facta disposuit? Psal. XXVI. v. 1. Psal. XXXIV. 14. sqq. Pf. XXXVII. v. 6. 7. &c.

Ἀγαθοποιοῦντας φιμοῦν τὴν τῶν ἀφρόνων ἀνθρώπων ἀγνωσίαν) Bene agendo os obstruere ignorantiæ (id est, dictis ex igno- rantia orientibus) hominum nihil sapientium, nempe circa divina. Ἀγαθοποιεῖν interdum est beneficia conferre, pro quo & ἀγαθοεργεῖν dicitur. Sed hic simpliciter significat recte agere, ut & infra II. 20. III. 6. 17. 3. Joh. v. 11. quo sensu & adjectivum ἀγαθοποιὸς jamjam habuimus, & Si- rach. XL. 20. & ἀγαθοποιΐα infra IV. 15. φιμῶ in Glossario compesco. Φιμῶμαι commuteo, obmuteo, commutesco. Hesychius Φιμῶν, ἐπιστομίζων. Vide Matth. XXII. v. 12. 34. Marc. I. 25. 39. Luc. IV. 35. Novi qui pro ἀγνωσίαν vellet hic legi ἀγλωσσίαν, quia ἀγλωσσεῖν est βλασφημεῖν Hesychio. Patiendo mala, nec resistendo optime inimicis os frenamus.

Sensus est, interprete B. Gerharde: Si vel maxi- me non potestis vestra innocentia hoc obtinere, ut alii ejus intuitu ad Deum convertantur, ipsumque glorificent, qui eventus Diaboli malitia & hominum pertinacia sæpius intervertitur; hoc tamen obtinere poteritis, ut calumniatoribus ora obstruantur. Tri- buitur autem obtrectatoribus illis piorum tùm ἀγνωσία ignorantia Dei & Verbi divini, uti perse- cutoribus Christi, Joh. XVI. 3. vel etiam status & conversationis piorum: tum ἀφροσύνη stultitia, quia vera Dei agnitione destituti stolidi sunt, & qui minus prudenter omnia expendunt, cæco ju- dicio sermones stolidos & irrationabiles contra innocentes effundere audent. Quatuor itaque causæ notantur præstandæ Magistratibus obedien- tiæ, 1. ut honoremus Deum, qui ea præcepit, 2. ut evitemus pœnam violatæ civilis justitiæ, 3. ut à magistratu justitiæ laudem, ac defensionem obti- neamus, 4. ut maledicorum ora obstruamus.

## 2:16
Vers. 16.

As free) Free, namely from vices, John VIII. 32. 36. Rom. VI. 18. 22.

And not as having liberty as a cloak for wickedness) Not taking Christian liberty as a pretext for evil things, as those did who said that Christians were free from all public laws. Setting aside authority, as Judas says. 'Cloak' is well translated as pretext. Thus Gellius: Who under the pretext of the name of Philosophy pursue useless leisure and the darkness of language and life. But as servants of God) Servants of God, and therefore also servants of those whom God commands us to serve. This part is to be construed with the previous verb 'be subject,' as was done by Chrysostom and Oecumenius, not with the participle 'doing good,' as Bede wishes. For this is of a different case. The word 'as' is not of one comparing; but of one asserting, i.e., obey Princes freely and liberally, as if the free men of Christ, and sons of obedience. That the Gnostics once abused Christian liberty for every disgrace and wickedness, Cornelius observes here, and therefore that Peter means this: You have been made free by Christ, but from sin, not from the law of God, nor from obedience to Princes: do not therefore use the liberty of Christ as a pretext for your disobedience, malice, and turpitude. For this is not liberty, but the slavery of sin, Gal. V. v. 13. Estius notes: That some who had given their name to Christ abused the pretext of a double liberty for sinning. For the Jews indeed, because they were the peculiar people of God, wanted to be free from the laws of foreign Princes, and from paying tributes. But some, interpreting perversely the liberty with which we have been gifted through Christ, thought that they were so free from the law that they could do whatever they pleased. Against whom Paul, Rom. VI. Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. And at Galatians 5: 'You have been called to liberty, only do not give liberty as an occasion to the flesh.' From this were born the Gnostics, of whom blessed Peter speaks in his 2nd epistle, chapter 2: 'Promising them liberty, while they themselves are slaves of corruption,' and blessed Jude in his epistle: 'Turning the grace of our God into luxury.' However, it is likely, as Estius thinks, that Peter in this passage is looking primarily at the former pretext of liberty. For he is writing to the Jews, and is occupied with inculcating the precept of obedience to be shown to magistrates. Compare Deuteronomy 12:15, John 5:33. Both respects can, however, be joined, as blessed Gerhard judges, who rendered this meaning: You are indeed free, but that liberty, being spiritual, ought not to be changed into carnal license, nor ought you to abuse that liberty as a cloak of malice. You have been freed by Christ from the servitude of sin, so that henceforth you may be servants of God. Because, therefore, God requires obedience toward the Magistrate, the liberty obtained through Christ does not in the least abolish that obedience. Just as servants, who are free, both liberally serve and obey not only God, but also all Magistrates, whom God has ordained as His vicars and our superiors. For to serve God is to reign. He (God), says Augustine in 'On the Quality of the Soul', chapter 34, frees from all things, to serve whom is most useful to all, and in whose service to please perfectly is the only liberty. The word 'cloak' according to Cornelius alludes to the veil or white garment, which the baptized received in baptism, both so that they might be mindful of preserving the purity of soul received in baptism, and so that they might show spiritual joy and the hope of eternal life by their attire, and also to indicate the liberty obtained through Christ, so that the soul, clothed in the liberty of a new life, might be able to fight bravely against the Devil with divine help, as Augustine says, book 4 'On the Creed to the Catechumens', chapter 9; see Tertullian, book 5 'Against Marcion'. But from where will it be taught that this rite was already accepted in Peter's time?

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Ὡς ἐλεύθεροι) Liberi, nempe à vitiis, Joh. VIII. 32. 36. Rom. VI. 18. 22.

Καὶ μὴ ὡς ἐπικάλυμμα ἔχοντες τῆς κακίας τὴν ἐλευθερίαν) Non libertatem Christianam sumentes obtentui ad res ma- las, ut illi faciebant, qui Christianos ab omnibus publicis legibus dicebant esse liberos. Κυριότητα ἀθετοῦντες, ut ait Judas. Ἐπικάλυμμα מסך bene vertitur obtentus. Sic Gel- lius: Qui obtentu Philosophici nominis inutile otium, & linguæ vitæque tenebras sequuntur. Ἀλλ' ὡς δοῦλοι Θεοῦ) Servi Dei, ac proinde etiam eorum servi, quibus Deus servire nos jubet. Construenda est hæc pars cum superiori verbo ὑποτάγητε, ut à Chrysostomo & Oecumenio factum, non cum Participio ἀγαθοποιοῦντες, ut Beda vult. Hoc enim casus diversi est. Vox quasi non est affi- milantis; sed asseverantis, q.d. obedite Principibus libere liberaliter, qs. liberi Christi, & obedien- tiæ filii. Abusos esse olim Gnosticos libertate Chri- stiana ad omne dedecus & nefas, observat hic Cor- nelius, ideoque Petrum id velle: Facti estis liberi à Christo, sed à peccato, non à lege Dei, nec ab obedi- entia Principum: nolite ergo inobedientiæ, malitiæ & turpitudini vestræ prætexere libertatem Christi. Hæc enim non est libertas, sed peccati servitus, Gal. V. v. 13. Estius notat: Duplicis libertatis prætextu quosdam, qui Christo nomen dederant, abusos fuisse ad peccandum. Nam Judæi quidem, quod essent Dei populus peculiaris, liberos se esse volebant à legi- bus Principum alienorum, & à tributis pendendis. Nonnulli vero libertatem, qua per Christum donati sumus, perverse interpretantes, existimabant ita se esse à lege liberos, ut quicquid liberet, agere possent. Contra quos Paulus, Rom. VI. Permanebimus in pec- cato, ut gratia abundet? Absit. Et ad Gal. V. Vos in libertatem vocati estis, tantum ne libertatem in occa- sionem detis carnis. Inde nati Gnostici, de quibus B. Petrus in 2. epist. c. II. Libertatem illis promittentes, cum ipsi servi sint corruptionis, & S. Judas in sua epistola: Dei nostri gratiam transferentes in luxu- riam. Verisimile autem Estio est: Petrum præcipue hoc loco respicere ad prætextum libertatis priorem. Scribit enim ad Judæos, & versatur in inculcando præcepto obedientiæ magistratibus exhibendæ. Conf. Deut. XII. 15. Job. V. 33. Conjungi tamen uterque respectus potest, ut B. Gerhardus censet, qui hunc reddidit sensum: Estis quidem liberi, sed libertas illa, utpote spiritualis non debet mutari in licentiam car- nalem, nec debetis libertate illa abuti pro velamine malitiæ. Per Christum à peccati servitute liberati estis, ut imposterum sitis Dei servi. Quia ergo Deus obedientiam erga Magistratum requirit, ideo liber- tas per Christum parta obedientiam illam minime tollit. Sicut servi, qui liberi, & liberaliter serviunt & obediunt non tantum DEO, sed & omni- bus Magistratibus, quos Deus sibi vicarios no- strosque superiores ordinavit. Servire enim Deo regnare est. Ille (Deus) ab omnibus, inquit Augu- stinus de Qualit. animæ cap. 34. liberat, cui ser- vire omnibus utilissimum est, & in cujus servitio placere perfecte, sola libertas est. Vox velamen juxta Cornelium alludit ad velum sive vestem can- didam, quam baptizati accipiebant in baptismo, tum ut memores essent servandi candoris animæ baptismo accepti, tum ut lætitiam spiritualem ac spem vitæ æternæ habitu ostenderent, tum ad in- dicandam libertatem per Christum obtentam, ut anima libertate novæ vitæ induta adversus Diabo- lum cum adjutorio divino valeat fortiter dimicare, dicente Augustino, l. IV. de symbol. ad Catech. cap. 9. vid. Tertull. l. V. adversus Marc. Sed ritum istum Petri tempore jam receptum fuisse, unde docebitur?

## 2:17
Verse 17.

Honor all men) Namely those to whom some honor is owed, as in Romans 13:7; he will now explain this general statement through its species. More correctly, blessed Gerhard: This is a brief conclusion of the immediately preceding points, and because the Apostle joins the honor due to all, the love to be bestowed upon the brethren, and the fear to be rendered to GOD with the special honor of obedience due to the King, signifying that neither can God be truly feared, nor His own right be rendered to each, nor civil society be preserved, unless the political order binding the Magistrate and subjects to one another is inviolably kept, and the obedience due to the Magistrate is rendered. The Apostle also signifies that that honor of obedience, which is due and deferred to Kings, ought to arise from the true fear of God and the love of men, and therefore is perpetually joined with them. He who truly and from the heart fears God, the Author of the Magistrate, he also will not deny the honor of obedience to the King or Magistrate, because God has commanded this honor to be deferred to the King. Conversely, he who loves his brethren, and embraces the whole human race with the affection of humanity, benevolence, and love that is fitting, he likewise will not deny the honor of obedience to the Magistrate, because the Magistrate is instituted for the salvation of the human race, and the advantage of the brethren, that is, the Church, 1 Tim. II. v. 1 & 2. He warns, however, that all should be honored, because the Jews and Gentiles, Rom. XIV. v. 3, despised one another, Jas. II. v. 3. Therefore he wishes that they reverently acknowledge the gifts of God in others, and despise no one, Rom. XII. 10, Phil. II. 3. Understand, however, in this precept: Honor all, namely, those whom God has willed to be honored, Rom. XIII. v. 7. It is to be noted, moreover, that under honor all kinds of duties are comprehended. Therefore Ambrose explained that passage in Rom. XII, 'preventing one another with honor,' thus: 'Preventing one another with mutual obediences.'

Τὴν ἀδελφότητα ἀγαπᾶτε) You have Τὴν ἀδελφότητα in 1 Macc. II. 10, 17, אחוה, Zech. XI. 14. But here this word, as also below in v. 9, does not signify the relationship itself, but the flock of the brethren, just as ἱεράτευμα signifies the order of priests. He wishes, therefore, that the assemblies of the faithful, in which we live, be honored by loving them.

Hence the Syrian rightly translates: Love your brethren. But the Apostle understands brethren not by reason of carnal generation, but of spiritual regeneration, chap. I. 23. We ought indeed to honor and love all; yet we should embrace the Church and its citizens with a special love, Gal. VI. v. 10, Rom. XII. 10, 2 Pet. I. 7.

Τὸν Θεὸν φοβεῖσθε) that is, obey Him without exception. See Eph. VI. 5, Phil. II. 12.

In general, some understand the entire worship of GOD; but it is more correctly explained specifically as the filial fear of God, and that filial fear in relation to the honor to be exhibited to the Magistrate, Acts V. 29. The King is to be honored, says Tertullian in Scorpiac. c. 14, when he insists upon his own affairs; when he is far from divine honors.

Τὸν βασιλέα τιμᾶτε) Exhibit to the Emperor the highest honors that human nature can receive.

A special honor is now inculcated, due to the King by reason of his eminence, and by that reason the Apostolic precept, which he has hitherto chiefly treated, is concluded. The King or Emperor at that time was not only a Gentile, but also covered with all crimes, and a persecutor of the true Church. The Apostle therefore repeats this precept about honoring the King with obediences, lest on account of the diversity of religion, the wickedness of his life, and his cruelty, he might seem to some less worthy of honor, as here B. Gerhard.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Πάντας τιμήσατε) Nempe quibus honos aliquis debetur, ut Rom. XIII, 7. hoc dictum generale jam per species suas explicabit. Rectius B. Gerhardus: Est hæc brevis conclusio proxime præcedentium, ac quia honorem omnibus debitum, amorem fratribus impendendum, & ti- morem DEO prestandum cum speciali obsequii ho- nore Regi debito Apostolus conjungit, significat, nec Deum vere timeri; nec jus suum cuique reddi, nec civilem societatem conservari posse, nisi politicus or- do Magistratum & subditos invicem devinciens in- violate servetur, & Magistratui debita obedientia præstetur. Significat etiam Apostolus, honorem illum obsequii, qui Regibus debetur ac defertur, ex vero Dei timore atque hominum charitate oriri debere, ac proinde cum illis perpetuo conjunctum esse. Qui Deum Magistratus Autorem vere & ex animo timet, is etiam Regi sive Magistratui honorem obse- quii non denegabit, quia Deus hunc honorem Regi deferri præcepit. Vicissim qui fratres suos amat, & totum genus humanum, quo decet humanitatis, be- nevolentiæ, & amoris affectu amplectitur, is itidem Magistratui honorem obsequii non denegabit, quia Magistratus in salutem humani generis, & fratrum, id est, Ecclesiæ commodum est institutus, 1. Timoth. II. v. 1. & 2. Monet autem, ut omnes honorent, quia Judæi & gentes, Rom. XIV. vers. 3. se mutuo despiciebant, Jac. II. v. 3. Ideo vult, ut dona Dei in aliis reverenter agnoscant, neminemque con- temnant, Rom. XII. 10. Phil. II. 3. Subintellige tamen in hoc præcepto: Omnes honorate, scili- cet, quos Deus honorari voluit, Rom. XIII. v. 7. Notandum insuper, quod sub honore omnis ge- neris officia comprehendantur. Ideo Ambrosius illud Rom. XII. honore invicem prævenientes ita exposuit: Mutuis obsequiis invicem prævenientes.

Τὴν ἀδελφότητα ἀγαπᾶτε) Τὴν ἀδελφότητα habes 1. Macc. II. 10. 17. אחוה, Zach. XI. 14. Verum hic ea vox, ut & infra V. 9. non ipsam σχέσιν, sed gregem fratrum significat, quomodo ἱεράτευμα Sacerdotum ordinem. Vult ergo cœ- tus fidelium, in quibus vivimus, honorari diligendo.

Inde Syrus recte vertit: Fratres vestros diligi- te. Fratres autem intelligit Apostolus non ratione carnalis generationis, sed spiritualis regeneratio- nis, cap. I. 23. Debemus quidem omnes honorare & amare; speciali tamen amore Ecclesiam & ejus- dem cives amplecti, Gal. VI. vers. 10. Rom. XII. 10. 2. Petr. I. 7.

Τὸν Θεὸν φοβεῖσθε) id est, ei sine exceptione parete. Vide Eph. VI. 5. Phil. II. 12.

In genere nonnulli universum DEI cultum in- telligunt;sed rectius speciatim de filiali Dei timore explicatur, eoque filiali, in ordine ad honorem Magistratui exhibendum Act. V. 29. Honorandus est Rex ait Tertull. in Scorpiac. c. 14. cum suis re- bus insistit; cum à divinis honoribus longe est.

Τὸν βασιλέα τιμᾶτε) Imperatori summos exhibete hono- res, quos capit humana natura.

Honor specialis jam inculcatur Regi eminentiæ causa debitus, eaque ratione præceptum Aposto- licum, quod hactenus præcipue tractavit, conclu- ditur. Rex sive Imperator tum temporis non solum erat Ethnicus, sed etiam omnibus sceleribus cooper- tus, & veræ Ecclesiæ persecutor. Apostolus igitur hoc præceptum de Rege obsequiis honorando repetit, ne propter religionis diversitatem, vitæ improbitatem ac crudelitatem minus honorandus alicui videri pos- set, ut hic B. Gerhardus.

## 2:18
Vers. 18.

Οἱ οἰκέται) who are δοῦλοι to Paul, Eph. VI. v. 5, Col. III. v. 22, Tit. II. 9. Thus he said δεσπότας whom Paul called κυρίους.

From the genus of political subjection he descends to certain other forms of subjection, such as servants obeying masters, and wives their husbands. Estius observes that they are called domestics, not slaves, and likewise masters, not Lords, because he is writing to the Jews, to whom, as the people of GOD, it was burdensome to be called slaves and to have Lords, so that he might mitigate an odious thing by the gentleness of the words. But who would admit that the Apostle wished to pander to that vain persuasion about liberty, simply promised to the people of God? It is more likely, therefore, that the name οἰκετῶν is taken generally, so that freedmen with slaves, and servants of both a harsher and a more tolerable condition, are comprehended.

Ὑποτασσόμενοι ἐν παντὶ φόβῳ τοῖς δεσπόταις) Supply ἐστὲ. Ὑποτασσόμενοι is an active for a Hithpael, as we just said, ἐν παντὶ φόβῳ, explain as that of Paul in the same matter, μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου, Eph. VI. 5.

In all fear, that is, with much reverence. For he understands fear not as servile, but joined with love, which is called reverence. See Acts IX. 31. 2 Cor. V. 1. Phil. II. 11. IN ALL, that is, according to Lyranus and Hugo, perfect fear, which includes love; according to Cornelius à Lapide, ALL, because fear is manifold: 1. of punishment, lest they be punished by their masters if they are disobedient; 2. of sin, lest they offend God through disobedience, concerning which Oecumenius speaks; 3. of scandal, lest by their disobedience they provoke their masters to hatred of the faith, but showing good faith in all things, that they may adorn the doctrine of our Savior God in all things, Tit. II. v. 9. Eph. VI. 5. Col. III. 22.

Not only to the good and gentle, ἠπίοις as Homer speaks. See Phil. IV. 5. 1 Tim. III. 3. Tit. III. 2. Jas. III. 17.

But also to the froward) Ἀλλὰ καὶ δυσκόλοις the Latin reads, and as I think, the Arab. Δύσκολος is harsh, as Jer. XLIX. 7. In the glossary: δύσκολος is morose, difficult, truculent. Menander had written a comedy, the name of which is δύσκολος. Agathias mentions it in an epigram, Anth. VIII. And Julian in the Misopogon. But the Syrian has two adjectives קשיא ולעיסקא. Wherefore it seems he read δυσκόλοις καὶ σκολιοῖς. It could easily happen, however, that one of two neighboring words was omitted by the scribes. Σκολιοὶ are crooked. See Acts II. v. 40. Phil. II. 15. נלוזים Prov. II. 15. III. 32. from לוז σκολιάζειν, Prov. XIV. 2.

The Vulgate has: But also to the dyscolis. But it is not to be presumed from that, that it was so read in the Greek. Our Interpreter, says Estius, rendered a Greek word with another Greek word, which perhaps was in use among the Latins. A certain old version, as Bede reports, reads 'more difficult'. Blessed Peter wishes that Christian servants, even if they are treated harshly and unjustly, and heavier burdens are imposed than are just, should not refuse authority, nor take to flight. For it is not permitted for a servant to flee on account of any injury whatsoever; indeed, it is unjust, since a servant is the possession of his master. But Hugo and the Gloss speak ignorantly, saying that 'dyscolos' is called rustic, rude, unlearned, as if alien to school and studies, which make men civil, polite, and benign. Which Cornelius himself refutes. For δύσκολος is said in Greek, not δύσχολος, and it signifies a morose and difficult person, who creates weariness and disgust for himself and others.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Οἱ οἰκέται) qui δοῦλοι Paulo Eph. VI. v. 5. Col. III. v. 22. Tit. II. 9. Sic δεσπότας dixit quos Paulus κυρίυς.

A genere subjectionis Politicæ ad quasdam alias subjectionis formas descendit, ut sunt servos pa- rere dominis, & uxores maritis. Illos autem fa- mulos vocari, non servos, item heros, non Domi- nos observat Estius, quia ad Judæos scribit, quibus ceu populo DEI molestum erat vocari servos & habere Dominos, ut ita rem odiosam mitiget le- nitate vocum. Sed Apostolum vanæ illi persuasio- ni de libertate, simpliciter populo Dei promissa, velificari voluisse, ecquis admittet? Verisimilius ergo οἰκετῶν nomen generaliter accipi, ut liberti cum mancipiis, servique cum durioris, tum tole- rabilioris conditionis comprehendantur.

Ὑποτασσόμενοι ἐν παντὶ φόβῳ τοῖς δεσπόταις) Supple ἐστὲ. Ὑποτασσόμενοι activum pro Hithpael, ut modo diximus, ἐν παντὶ φόβῳ, explica ut illud Pauli in re eadem μετὰ φόβου καὶ τρόμου, Eph. VI. 5.

In omni timore, id est, cum multa reverentia. Nam timorem intelligit non servilem, sed cum amore conjunctum, qui reverentia vocatur. Vid. Act. IX. 31. 2. Cor. V. 1. Phil. II. 11.
