IN OMNI, id est, secundum Lyranum & Hugonem, perfecto timore, qui amorem includit, secundum Cornelium à Lapide OMNI, quia multiplex est timor, 1. pænæ, ne ab heris, si inobedientes sint, puniantur, 2. cul- pæ, ne Deum per inobedientiam offendant, de quo Oecumenius. 3. scandali, ne sua inobedientia provocent heros ad odium fidei, sed in omnibus bonam fidem ostendentes, ut doctrinam Salva- toris nostri Dei ornent in omnibus, Tit. II. v. 9. Eph. VI. 5. Col. III. 22.

Οὐ μόνον τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς καὶ ἐπιεικέσιν) Bonis ac lenibus, ἠπίοις ut Homerus loquitur. Vide Phil. IV. 5. 1. Timoth. III. 3. Tit. III. 2. Jac. III. 17.

Ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς σκολιοῖς) Ἀλλὰ καὶ δυσκόλοις legit Latinus & ut puto Arabs. Δύσκολος est durus, ut Jerem. XLIX. 7. In glossario: δύσκολος morosus, difficilis, truculentus. Menan- der comœdiam scripserat, cui nomen δύσκολος. Ejus me- minere Agathias in epigrammate Anth. VIII. Et Julianus Mysopogone. At Syrus duo habet Adjectiva קשיא ולעיסקא. quare videtur legisse δυσκόλοις καὶ σκολιοῖς. Fa- cile autem fieri potuit, ut à librariis de duabus vicinis vo- cibus altera omitteretur. Σκολιοὶ sunt pravi. Vide Act. II. v. 40. Phil. II. 15. נלוזים Prov. II. 15. III. 32. à לוז σκολιάζειν, Prov. XIV. 2.

Vulgata habet: Sed etiam dyscolis. Non autem inde præsumere licet, in Græco sic lectum fuisse. Noster Interpres, inquit Estius, Græcam vocem alia Græca reddidit, quæ forte Latinis erat in usu. Quæ- dam vetus versio, referente Beda, legit difficilioribus. Vult B. Petrus, servos Christianos, etiamsi dure & inique tractentur à dominis, ac justo graviora im- ponantur onera, non tamen imperium recusare, sed nec fugam arripere. Nam servo fugere propter quam- libet injuriam non licet, imo injustum id est, cum servus sit possessio domini sui. Imperite autem Hu- go & Glossa dyscolos, inquiunt, vocatur agrestis, rudis, indoctus, quasi alienus à schola & studiis, quæ homines reddunt civiles, politos, benignos. Quod refellit ipse Cornelius. Δύσκολος enim Græce di- citur, non δύσχολος, ac significat morosum ac diffi- cilem, qui sibi & aliis tædium & fastidium creat.

## 2:19
v. 19. For this is grace) The Manuscript adds παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ, just as the Syrian also reads. It is indeed a metonymy. For he wishes to say, this procures for us the highest favor of God.

Others understand praise or glory by the name of grace, as follows later. For what glory is it? Or the work of grace, an effect proceeding from the grace of God, and the same worthy of exceptional praise. But these explanations almost amount to the same thing, as if to say: it is a work very pleasing to GOD, and worthy of singular praise, if anyone for God's sake, that is, so that he may please God, whom he keeps in his mind, patiently bears sad and troublesome things, while he is afflicted unjustly and without merit. The abstract is put for the concrete. Moreover, we cannot procure the grace of God for ourselves either by the tolerance of injuries or by any work of ours: for it is merely gratuitous, Rom. 11, 6.

If for conscience of God one bears sorrows) Συνείδησις Θεῦ is said here by metonymy of the object, the conscience of that which one owes to God. Ὑποφέρειν is placed here, as in 2 Tim. III. v. 11. And λύπας is another metonymy, for τὰ λυπηρὰ, sad things.

Gagnejus explains it concerning the conscience of God himself: On account of God, who is conscious both of his patience and of their wickedness. But more correctly, the conscience of God is a conscience about God, because he is conscious that God wills this, and that it is pleasing to God. This is certain, says the blessed Gerhard, that it is not the conscience which God has that is understood, but that which a man has before God, by which he takes care not to offend God. Therefore, by the conscience of God is understood in this place a good conscience before God, by which servants solicitously take care not to offend God by their disobedience, sedition, or rebellion against their masters. Some, even Cornel. à Lapide, explain it thus: On account of the conscience of God, that is, because you are worshippers of the true God, namely, for that reason hateful to your masters. But as Estius warns, Peter does not yet seem to be dealing with the affliction of Christians on account of righteousness, and because they are Christians, which he finally deals with after the middle of the following chapter, and again in chapter IV.

Suffering unjustly) Here that 'unjustly' refers to the active [verb] corresponding to the suffering: And it is a construction according to the sense.

The Apostle says these things on the occasion of servants afflicted by harsh masters; but his discourse is general, and therefore it pertains to all who suffer innocently in any way, and he encourages and consoles them to endure bravely.

Latin:

v. 19. Τοῦτο γὰρ χάρις) Addit Manuscriptus παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ, quomodo legit & Syrus. Est vero μετωνυμία. Vult enim dicere, hoc summum nobis Dei favorem conciliat.

Alii gratiæ nomine laudem vel gloriam intel- ligunt, ut postea sequitur. Quæ enim est gloria? Aut effectum gratiæ opus à gratia Dei profectum, idemque eximia laude dignum. Sed hæ explica- tiones fere eodem recidunt, q. d. opus esse DEO valde gratum, & singulari laude dignum, si quis Dei respectu, id est, ut Deo placeat, quem animo ge- rit, tristia, & molesta patienter ferat, dum injuste ac præter meritum affligitur. Abstractum positum est pro concreto. Gratiam autem Dei nobis neque injuriarum tolerantia, neque ullo opere nostro con- ciliare possumus: Est n. mere gratuita, Rom. 11, 6.

Εἰ διὰ συνείδησιν Θεῦ ὑποφέρει τις λύπας) Συνείδησις Θεῦ hic per μετωνυμίαν objecti dicitur conscientia ejus, quod quis Deo debet. Ὑποφέρειν hic ponitur, ut 2. Timoth. III. v. 11. Et λύπας alia μετωνυμία, pro τὰ λυπηρὰ, tristia.

Gagnejus de conscientia ipsius Dei explicat: Pro- pter Deum, qui & suæ patientiæ & illorum nequitiæ conscius est. Sed rectius conscientia Dei est con- scientia de Deo, quia conscius est, id Deum velle, & Deo gratum esse. Certum hoc est, inquit B. Ger- hardus, non intelligi conscientiam, quam Deus habet, sed quam homo coram Deo habet, qua cavet, ne Deum offendat. Ergo per conscientiam Dei intelligitur hoc loco bona coram Deo conscientia, qua solicite cavent servi, ne sua adversus heros inobedientia, seditione, rebellione Deum offendant. Nonnulli, etiam Cornel. à Lapide, ita exponunt: Propter Dei conscientiam, id est, quia veri Dei cultores estis, videlicet eo no- mine dominis vestris exosi. Sed Estio monente nondum videtur Petrus de Christianorum affli- ctione propter justitiam, & quia Christiani sunt, agere, de qua demum agit post medium cap. sequ. & rursum c. IV.

Πάσχων ἀδίκως) Hic illud ἀδίκως refertur ad activum respondens passioni: Et est constructio κατὰ τὸ σημαινόμενον.

Occasione servorum à duris heris afflictorum hæc dicit Apostolus; sed sermo ejus generalis est, ideoque ad omnes, qui quomodo libet innocentes patiuntur, pertinet, eosque ad fortiter tolerandum animat & consolatur.

## 2:20
v. 20. For what glory) Namely, before God.

If you sin and are buffeted and endure) Both the Syriac and the Arabic seem to have read 'being punished' [kolazomenoi], which is a word proper to the penalties which public laws impose upon violators of human society. Although 'being buffeted' [kolaphizomenoi] can also be borne, so that it is a species for a genus, as in 1 Cor. 4:11 and 2 Cor. 12:7. 'Endure' here signifies not patience, but only suffering, as in Heb. 2:7.

The sense is: What is great or singular, so that one might expect praise or glory for it, if one is beaten on account of a fault? Therefore, it is not to be restricted to God.

But if doing good and suffering you endure) that is, you endure sufferings, you bear tortures. A similar kind of speaking to that which is above [at] 12.

This is thanks before God) Explain as above [at] 19.

Here Estius corrects the Vulgate: In Greek, he says, 'but if doing good and suffering you endure,' just as it is read in certain Latin manuscripts and in Bede. The Syriac also agrees with this reading, and thus it corresponds to the preceding part, 'sinning and being buffeted.' It also agrees with those things which are in ch. III. 17. But an unskilled scribe changed what he did not understand into that which seemed more ready. The sense is: But if you suffer, if you endure with an even mind, when you do good and yet suffer, that is, are affected by evils, it is glory for you; that endurance will procure for you praise and glory. However, the same man wrongly observes that, according to Peter, he who patiently endures deserved punishments for his faults in the Republic will not lack the reward of his patience before God. Since Peter expressly says that there is no praise for him, and that one merits nothing before God by patiently suffering deserved punishments.

Latin:

v. 20. Ποῖον γὰρ κλέος) Nempe apud Deum.

Εἰ ἁμαρτάνοντες καὶ κολαφιζόμενοι ὑπομενεῖτε) Videntur & Syrus & Arabs legisse κολαζόμενοι, quæ vox propria pœnis, quas indicunt leges publicæ in societatis humanæ violato- res. Quanquam potest & κολαφιζόμενοι ferri, ut sit species pro genere, quomodo 1.Cor.4,11.& 2.Cor.12,7. Ὑπομένετε hic non patientiam, sed solam passionem significat, ut Ebr.2,7.

Sensus est: Quid magnum aut singulare, ut de eo laudem quis expectet aut gloriam, si propter deli- ctum cæditur? Non ergo restringendum ad Deum.

Ἀλλ' εἰ ἀγαθοποιοῦντες καὶ πάσχοντες ὑπομενεῖτε) id est παθή- ματα ὑπομενεῖτε, cruciatus fertis. Simile loquendi genus ei, quod supra 12.

Τοῦτο χάρις παρὰ Θεῷ) Explica ut supra 19.

Castigat hic Vulgatam Estius: Græce, inquit, sed si benefacientes & patientes sustinetis, quemadmo- dum & in Latinis quibusdam MSS. legitur & apud Bedam. Cui lectioni etiam Syrus annuit, & ita re- spondet parti præcedenti, peccantes & colaphizati. Congruit etiam his, quæ sunt c. III. 17. Verum impe- ritus scriba, quod non intellexit, mutavit in id, quod promptius videbatur. Sensus est: Sed si suffertis, si sustinetis æquo animo, quum benefacitis, & tamen patimini, id est, malis afficimini, gloria vobis est, ea sustinentia laudem & gloriam vobis pariet. Perpe- ram autem idem observat, secundum Petrum eum, qui pro delictis suis in Republica meritas pœnas sustinet patienter, mercede patientiæ suæ non ca- riturum apud Deum. Siquidem diserte Petrus laudem nullam ei esse dicat, & nihil, sufferendo patienter pœnas promeritas, aliquem apud Deum mereri.

## 2:21
v. 21. For to this you were called) We were called by this law, that we should endure all hard things for the sake of conscience, 1 Cor. 1:19. Thus also we are said to be called to peace, to holiness, Col. 3:15, 2 Thess. 2:14.

Because Christ also suffered for us) 'For you' [is in the] manuscript, which rightly coheres with what follows. In the manuscript 'for you,' just as it often has elsewhere, where in the Vulgate editions it is 'for us'.

Leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps) Let us not wonder that what happened to Christ happens to us. In the Glossary, 'hypogrammos' is 'a copy': which word Cicero also uses. The word seems to have come first from craftsmen, who mark out lines with red lead, which they follow in their work. It is taken metaphorically for everything that is to be imitated. Another metaphor is in 'following the steps,' which is 'to walk in the steps' in Rom. 4:12, 'to walk in the steps' in 2 Cor. 12:18. In Hebrew, 'halakh be-aqba': The Syriac [says] 'halakh ahar'. The Latins also say 'to insist upon the footsteps of someone' for 'to imitate someone'.

The Apostle employs a twofold argument: the first from the calling of Christians, as those who have been called to tolerance, i.e., you have been called to Christ and to the fellowship of Christ's kingdom under this law: that you may do good, and while suffering evils, endure them with the same patience; the second from the example of Christ, who patiently endured injuries. Whence we, who are his members, ought also to endure them patiently; where, so that the example of Christ may move us more, he presents Christ as our Mediator and Redeemer, who suffered for us, and therefore it becomes us all the more to follow in the footsteps of the same as our Redeemer. He proposes, therefore, both his merit, that his passion is vicarious and satisfactory, by which he suffered for us, Matt. 20:28, Mark 10:45, 1 Tim. 2:6, and his example, that he has left us an ὑπογραμμον, that is, a form delineated and prescribed, as Budaeus interprets it. Which word is taken from painters and teachers who propose to their disciples a model, to which they look back while painting images and writing letters. The Syrian expresses such a word, which arose from the Greek τύπος, which he also interpreted as ὑπόδειγμα, John 8:15, 1 Cor. 10:6, 2 Thess. 3:9. The other metaphor is taken from a guide on a road, whose footsteps he presses who, ignorant of the road, follows him. Bede on this passage says: You hear that Christ suffered for you, and you rejoice that he died for you; attend to what follows, leaving us an example, that you should follow his footsteps, an example of tribulations, etc. Cf. Rom. 8:29, Gal. 6:17, 2 Tim. 2:11, 12. Augustine says in Ps. 36: A Christian is one who does not spurn the way of Christ, but wishes to follow the way of Christ through his passions. Do not wish to go by any other way than that by which he himself went. It seems hard, but it is the safe way. Another perhaps has delights, but it is full of robbers. We are called Christians in vain, says Leo the Great, sermon 5 on the nativity of Christ, if we are not imitators of Christ, who for this reason said he was the way, so that the conversation of the Master might be the form of the disciple, and the servant might choose that humility which the Lord followed. Blessed John Huss observes: Peter does not express what Christ suffered, but simply says, Χριστὸς ἔπαθεν, to imply that Christ endured every kind of passion for us. In that, therefore, let us imitate God, so that whatever is imposed upon us, we may patiently endure, and that in such a way that we demonstrate trust, Ps. 16:2, Ps. 22:1, obedience, Phil. 2:8, patience, Is. 53:7, and hope of liberation, Ps. 16:10, according to the example of Christ, and reverently implore the help of God, and commit all things to him, Heb. 5:7, Matt. 26:42. The footsteps of Christ are marked by his blood, and therefore easy to find, obvious, and certain.

Latin:

v. 21. Εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ ἐκλήθητε) Ea lege vocati sumus, ut du- ra omnia conscientiæ causa sustineremus, 1. Cor. I. 19. Sic & ad pacem, ad sanctitatem vocati dicimur, Col. III, 15. 2. Thess. II. 14.

Ὅτι καὶ χριστὸς ἔπαθεν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν) περὶ ὑμῶν Manuscriptus, quod recte cohæret cum sequentibus. In Manuscripto περὶ ὑμῶν, quomodo & alibi sæpe habet, ubi in Vulgatis est ὑπὲρ.

Ὑμῖν ὑπολιμπάνων ὑπογραμμὸν, ἵνα ἐπακολουθήσητε τοῖς ἴχνεσιν αὐτοῦ) Non miremur nobis evenire, quod Christo evenit. In Glossario ὑπογραμμὸς præscriptum: qua voce etiam Cicero utitur. Videtur à fabris primum venisse vox, qui minio lineas designant, quas opere persequuntur. Μετα- φορικῶς sumitur pro omni eo, quod imitandum est. Alia Metaphora in ἐπακολουθεῖν τοῖς ἴχνεσι, quod στοιχεῖν τοῖς ἴχνεσι Rom. IV. 12. περιπατεῖν τοῖς ἴχνεσι 2. Cor. XII. 18. Ebræis, הלך בּעקבֿא : Syrus fic. הלך אחר. Latini quoque dicunt vestigiis alicujus insistere, pro aliquem imitari.

Geminum adhibet argumentum Apostolus, alterum à vocatione Christianorum, utpote qui ad tolerantiam vocati sunt, q. d. ea lege ad Christum, & regni Christi consortium vocati estis: ut bene agatis, & mala patientes eadem cum patientia suf- tineatis: alterum à Christi exemplo, qui patienter injurias sustinuit. Unde nos, qui membra ejus su- mus,etiam debeamus eas patienter sustinere,ubi,ut Christi exemplum magis moveat, Christum, ceu Mediatorem & Redemptorem nostrum sistit, qui pro nobis passus est, ideoque eò magis nos decet, vestigiis ejusdem ceu Redemptoris nostri insistere. Proponit ergo ipsius tum meritum, quod passio ejus sit vicaria & satisfactoria, qua pro nobis passus est, Matth. 20, 28. Marc. 10, 45. 1. Tim. 2, 6. tum exemplum, quod nobis ὑπογραμμον, hoc est, for- mam delineatam ac præscriptam, ut interpretatur Budæus, reliquerit. Quæ vox pictoribus & præ- ceptoribus discipulis suis exemplar proponenti- bus, ad quod pingentes imagines & literas respi- ciunt,petita est. Syrus ejusmodi voce,quæ à Græco τύπος orta,exprimit,quam etiam ὑπόδειγμα, Joh. 8, 15. 1. Cor. 10, 6. 2. Thess. 3, 9. interpretatus est. Al- tera metaphora à via Duce desumpta est, cujus ve- stigia premit,qui viæ ignarus ipsum sequitur. Beda in h. l. Audis, inquit, quia Christus passus est pro no- bis,& gaudes, quia pro te mortuus est; attende quod sequitur, relinquens nobis exemplum, ut sequamini vestigia ejus, exemplum tribulationum &c. Conf. Rom. 8, 29. Gal. 6, 17. 2. Tim. 2, 11, 12. Christianus, inquit Augustinus in Ps. 36. est, qui non aspernatur viam Christi, sed vult viam Christi sequi per passio- nes ipsius. Noli per aliam viam velle ire, quam per illam, qua ipse ivit. Dura videtur, sed ipsa est tuta via. Alia forte delicias habet, sed latronibus plena est. Frustra appellamur Christiani, inquit Leo M. serm. 5. de nativ. Christi, si imitatores non simus Christi, qui ideo se viam dixit esse, ut conversatio Magistri forma esset discipuli, & illam humilitatem eligeret servus, quam sequutus est Dominus. B. Joh. Hussus observat; Petrum non exprimere, quid Christus passus sit, sed simpliciter dicere, Χριστὸς ἔπαθεν, ut innuat omne passionis genus Christum pro nobis tole- rasse. In eo ergo imitemur Deum, ut, quæcunque nobis imponuntur, patienter sustineamus, idque ea ratione, ut ad exemplum Christi fiduciam, Ps. 16, v. 2. Ps. 22, 1. obedientiam, Phil. 2. v. 8. patientiam, Es. 53, 7. spem liberationis, Ps. 16, 10. demonstre- mus, & auxilium Dei reverenter imploremus, eiq; omnia committamus, Ebr. 5. v. 7. Matth. 26, 42. Vestigia Christi sanguine ejus signata sunt, ideo- que inventu facilia, obvia & certa.

## 2:22
v. 22. Ὃς ἁμαρτίαν ἐκ ἐποίησεν, ἐδὲ εὑρέθη δόλος ἐν τῷ ςόματι αὐτῶ from Is. 53:9. Where in the Greek: ὅτι ἀνομίαν ἐκ ἐποίησεν, ἐδὲ δόλον ἐν τῷ ςόματι αὐτῶ: but in some codices: ἐδὲ δόλος εὑρέθη ἐν τῷ ςόματι αὐτῶ, which is more correct. For in the Hebrew ולא מרמה is implied, there was, which is correctly expressed by εὑρέθη, as in Rom. 7:10 and others, just as the Hebrews also take נמצא, which is translated by ἦν in Is. 39:2. Christ was led to death by no crime of his own, Luke 23:41, John 8:46.

He illustrates the example of patience by a comparison of unlikes: Christ patiently endured injuries of any kind, even though he deserved nothing; therefore, Christians, who are not free from sin, ought much more to endure injuries patiently. They note here a Hebraism. Among the Hebrews, that which is, is also said to be found; that which is not, not to be found, Gen. 2:20, ch. 16:26, Exod. 16:24, 2 Chron. 21:1, Is. 22:63. Which the Apostles also imitated in the New Testament, Phil. 2:8, Rev. 14:5, ch. 20:15. By the name ἁμαρτίας the Apostle seems to understand all sins committed by deed, by the name δόλος, those committed by mouth, so that he might thus designate sinlessness in every way. See Heb. 7:26, 27, 2 Cor. 5:21, Dan. 9:24.

Ὃς λοιδορέμενος ἐκ ἀντελοιδόρει) When he was attacked with revilings, he did not return revilings. See Matt. 26:63, 68, 27:12, 29, 39, and following. Thus Polycarp to the Philippians, rendering evil for evil, and reviling for reviling.

Because he treats of the patience of Christ, he teaches through the distribution that Christ sustained not only curses, but also evil deeds, not only verbal, but also real injuries. λοιδορεῖν is to assail someone with insults and curses, and to harass with reproaches. Αντιλοιδορεῖν is to return curses for curses. Cyprian renders it, to curse back. Cornelius observes that he was not striking back when he was being struck, to put the Greek before; but he produces no Greek codex as testimony. That he says canon XXVIII of the Apostles reads thus: it is of as much importance as those canons, that is, of none. What he said to the Jews in John VIII. 44, you are from your Father the Devil, was not a recrimination, because nothing similar had been objected to him before then: but a true and just excuse.

Latin:

v. 22. Ὃς ἁμαρτίαν ἐκ ἐποίησεν, ἐδὲ εὑρέθη δόλος ἐν τῷ ςόματι αὐτῶ ex Es. LIII. 9. Ubi in Græco: ὅτι ἀνομίαν ἐκ ἐποίησεν, ἐδὲ δόλον ἐν τῷ ςόματι αὐτῶ: at in nonnullis codi- cibus: ἐδὲ δόλος εὑρέθη ἐν τῷ ςόματι αὐτῶ, quod rectius. Nam in Ebræo ולא מרמה subauditur יהוה fuit, quod recte exprimitur per εὑρέθη, ut Rom. VII. 10. & aliis, quo- modo & Ebræi sumunt נמצא, quod per ἦν vertitur Es. XXXIX. 2. Christus nullo suo crimine in mortem actus est, Luc. 23. v. 41. Joh. VIII. 46.

Exemplum patientiæ illustrat collatione dissimi- lium: Christus sustinuit patienter injurias quas- cunque,etsi nihil meritus: ideò multo magis Chri- stiani peccati non expertes sustinere patienter de- bent injurias. Notant hic Ebraïsmum. Ebræis etiam inveniri dicitur, quod est; non inveniri,quod non est, Gen. 2, 20. c. 16, 26. Exod. 16, 24. 2. Paral. 21, 1. Es. 22, 63. Quod etiam in Novo Testamento Apostoli sunt imitati, Phil. 2, 8. Apoc. 14, 5. c.20, 15. Nomine ἁμαρτίας videtur Apostolus intelligere omnia peccata opere, nomine δόλος, ore commis- sa,ut omni modo ἀναμαρτησίαν ita designaret. Vid. Ebr.7,26.27. 2. Cor.5,21. Dan.9,24.

Ὃς λοιδορέμενος ἐκ ἀντελοιδόρει) Cum convitiis impe- teretur, convitia non reddidit. Vide Matth. 26. vers. 63. 68. XXVII. 12. 29. 39. & fequentibus. Sic Polycarpus ad Phi- lippenses, ἀποδιδόντες κακὸν ἀντὶ κακῶ, καὶ λοιδορίαν ἀντὶ λοιδορίας.

Quia de patientia Christi agit, per distributionem Christum non maledicta tantum, sed etiam malefacta, non verbales tantum, sed etiam reales injurias sustinuisse docet. λοιδορεῖν est convitiis & maledictis aliquem incessere, ac probris insectari. Αντιλοιδορεῖν maledicta maledictis regerere. Cyprianus reddit, remaledicere. Graeca praemittere, cum percuteretur, non repercutiebat, observat Cornelius; sed nullum Graecum codicem in testimonium producit. Quod canonem XXVIII. Apostol. ita legere ait: tanti est momenti, quanti canones illi, hoc est nullius. Quod Judaeis dixit Johan. VIII. 44. vos ex Patre Diabolo estis, non recriminatio fuit, quia nihil simile prius tunc ei fuerat objectum: sed vera, & justa excusatio.

## 2:23
Πάσχων οὐκ ἠπείλει) He who had prostrated his adversaries with one word, when he was led away captured, bound, beaten with scourges, and nailed to the cross, did not utter even a threatening word, so that he might give us a more perfect example of patience.

Christ in his passion not only did not return evil for evil, but he never even threatened that he would return evils. Prosper to Demetrius has: He did not threaten the one striking him. See Matthew XII. 23, chapter XXVI. 68, chapter XXVII. 42, John VIII. 49, chapter XVIII. 30, etc. It is indeed read that Christ sometimes threatened and denounced woe to cities that would not receive his doctrine, as in Matthew X and XI, likewise to the Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, and those corrupting the doctrine delivered by GOD. But he did not threaten then, when he was suffering, lest he might seem to have done so not out of zeal for justice, but moved by the affections of anger and hatred. Nor did he do it for his own sake, that is, to avenge himself upon them, but for their own sake, and out of love for their salvation, so that by denouncing divine wrath and eternal fire to the wicked, he might recall them from wickedness and hell. St. Cyprian, tract on the passion. Christ, he says, with fear set aside, as if using a more powerful authority among the spectacles and blows and other mockeries, disturbs the insane minds of his persecutors with patience and gentleness, and in that, because Jewish malice feels itself despised among the injuries and insults, it is more vehemently exacerbated, and the sweetness and piety of CHRIST triumphs over impiety and malice.

Παρεδίδυ δὲ τῷ κρίνοντι δικαίως) Some noun is understood after παρεδίδυ. The Syrian not badly supplies a verbal from the following verb, as if it were written, παρεδίδυ δὲ κρίσιν, he committed his cause to him who judges justly, always, that is. For men often judge unjustly, as the sanhedrin and Pilate. God is called a just Judge, Psalm VII. 12. The same sense is in Psalm XCVI. 10, XCVIII. 10, Jeremiah XI. 20, and elsewhere. This whole passage looks back to those things which we have in Isaiah L. 6, 7, 8, 9.

The Vulgate has: He was delivering himself to him who judges unjustly, so that the sense is, he was delivering himself, contradicting nothing, nor murmuring to Pilate, to be judged by an unjust Judge. But Estius warns: That in the Greek there is an entirely different reading: He was delivering himself to him who judges justly: Which the Syrian interpreter also paraphrastically renders thus: But he was delivering his judgment to the Judge of justice. The sense therefore of the Greek reading is: Christ was not avenging himself, but was delivering, or committing his cause to God, who judges justly, to be judged and avenged. According to that of Deuteronomy XXXII, repeated by Paul, Romans XII and Hebrews X: Vengeance is mine, I will repay. Blessed Peter can be seen to have alluded to that said in the person of Christ by Jeremiah chapter XI: But you, O Lord of Hosts, who judge justly and test the reins and hearts, let me see your vengeance upon them. For to you I have revealed my cause. Judge, O Lord, those who do me harm. That indeed is to give place to wrath, namely divine, just as Paul commands, Romans XII. It is likely that our interpreter translated nothing other than what is read in all the Greek [codices]: But since it was not understood, it had long ago been changed by the ignorance of scribes into a more obvious sense. Otherwise, certainly Augustine, tract XXI on John, agrees with the Greeks, reading thus: But he was commending [it] to him who judges justly. Similarly Fulgentius to Trasimundus chapter 11: But he was commending [it] to him who judges justly. These things Estius [states] most correctly. The Vulgate, however, has been left in error by the Reverend Fathers. This, of course, is their infallibility. Compare Jeremiah XI. verse 28, chapter XX. verse 12, Psalm VII. verse 2, Psalm XXVI. verse 16, XXXV. 24, John XV. verse 25. Some explain the word παρεδίδου as committed, that is, commended, Jeremiah XI. verse 21. Didymus and the ordinary gloss. alien, and beside the Apostolic scope: He commended his torturers and persecutors to God the Father by praying for them, Luke XXIII. verse 34. Cornelius a Lapide wishes this to be the genuine sense: He delivered himself to God the Father to death, by obeying him. But in the Greek that pronoun HIMSELF is not held, and therefore the interpretation already brought forward by Estius is to be preferred, by whom also the judgment of Cornelius, that the Latin reading is truer and more appropriate, has already been refuted. The authority of Clement of Alexandria, who in his commentary read as the Vulgate has, can move no one, because those commentaries are of no authority: Concerning which Bellarmine on Ecclesiastical writers page 79. Cassiodorus mentions in book I of the Divine Institutions the explanation of Clement of Alexandria on the Canonical epistles, which explanation, whether it is that which is found in the Library of the Holy Fathers, I cannot easily judge. Others appeal to Didymus. But the explanation of Didymus on the epistle Canonical, which is held in Tom. IX of the Library of the Fathers, is likewise of doubtful authority. Paulinus is also brought forward, epistle II. The ordinary and interlinear gloss, but they followed the Latin reading, they did not inspect the Greek text. And yet it is not read that Christ commended vengeance to God. Resp. Although it is not read elsewhere, here however we are taught about it by the Holy Spirit. Although in the Psalms such things are read entirely, by which he commended vengeance to GOD, Ps. LXIX. verse 23 seqq., Ps. CIX. v. 6 seqq. But he commended it thus, unless they repent; he prayed indeed at the same time for them, that pardon might be granted to those repenting: Luke XXIII. verse 34, Hebrews XII. 24.

v. 23. Who himself bore our sins in his body to the tree) ἀνήνεγκεν, here it is 'took away', as the following words show, just as we noted the same word in Heb. 9:28. In the same sense is αἴρειν ἁμαρτίαν in John 1:29, and נשא and סבל in Isa. LIII. 4, where the Greeks have φέρει. He killed our vices just as those who are affixed to a cross are accustomed to be killed. A similar manner of speaking is in Col. II. 14. See also Rom. VI. 6. Gal. II. 20. V. 24. But this is a μετάληψις (transumption). For Christ did not properly take away our vices when he was crucified, but he gave the causes through which they might be taken away. For the cross of Christ is the foundation of preaching, but preaching is of repentance, and repentance indeed takes away vices ἐν τῷ σώματι αὐτοῦ, with his body. A locution such as is in Matt. VI. 29, Rom. XV. v. 29, Eph. VI. 2, and elsewhere. Just as his body was driven onto the cross: so also our vices were as it were driven onto the cross. Particles signifying a likeness are often left unsaid, and thus the discourse is more effective.

That sense of the word ἀνήνεγκε, that it means 'took away', serves the Socinians. Perhaps it is said that Christ did not take away, did not kill our sins: Nay, he himself was killed on account of our sins, Rom. IV. last verse. Our sins were cast upon him, and he was wounded, and thus he himself was slain on account of our sins, Isa. LIII. v. 8. He therefore bore them both by reason of the guilt which he took upon himself, and by reason of the punishment which he paid for us and in our place, 2 Cor. V. 19, 20, 21. But he bore them in his body, because he paid for our sins in his own person. He bore them to the wood of the cross, because on the wood of the cross he especially paid for our sins. Ἀναφέρομαι is 'I lift up', 'I carry up'. Which word the LXX Interpreters also used in Isa. LIII. 12, from which the Prophet also took that emphatic pronoun αὐτὸς, of which the first usage is in Gen. 3:15. The Syriac: He bore all our sins, and took them up in his body to the cross. Athanasius, Oration IV against the Arians: Bearing our sins to the cross together with his body. The cross of Christ was that sublime altar, onto which Christ ascended, about to offer himself, burdened with our sins to have carried them in his body, however, not because his soul was devoid of sufferings. For his soul labored, Isa. 53:11, and he himself laid down his soul for a sin offering, v. 20. But because he hung visibly in his body on the cross. Meanwhile, the animated body and the whole human nature of Christ is understood by synecdoche; just as he is said to have suffered and been put to death in the flesh, that is, in his human nature, 1 Pet. 3:18. Compare Flacius in Clavis Scripturae, p. 1, col. 882. Estius rendered this sense: He who himself by himself took up and carried not his own sins, but ours, as a heavy weight in his body upon the wood of the cross, to which he was affixed, that is, hanging on the cross he himself received and paid the penalties owed for our sins. Cornelius à Lapide thought that reference is made to the scapegoat, concerning which Lev. 16:21. Therefore, not only the penalty, which he himself wishes, but also the guilt was taken away by Christ. That sense of Peter's words: He himself carried our sins in his body upon the wood of the cross, that is, just as his body was driven onto the cross: so also your vices as if driven onto the cross; is hitherto unheard of in the Church, and is forced. There is no particle of comparison here, nor can one be understood. For the body of Christ is not compared with our sins by reason of crucifixion or killing: But that our sins were carried by Christ crucified on the wood of the cross and punished in Christ is taught from the collation of Isaiah: concerning which passage we have dealt more fully with these matters. There is no reason why one should depart to such an unusual μετάληψιν (transference). It can indeed be admitted in a Catholic sense: that the cross of Christ is the foundation of preaching, because if Christ had not been crucified and died for us, there would be no preaching of the remission of sins in the name and through the name of Christ, Luke 24:47. Nor do we deny that the preaching of the Gospel concerning Christ crucified is the foundation of repentance, insofar as this includes faith in Christ crucified for our sins: We also concede that repentance takes away vices, but not in such a way that they are killed or extirpated, but that they are pardoned and remitted, not that they are not present, but that they are not imputed, as Augustine speaks. But we deny that these things are affirmed in these words of Peter. The carrying and expiation of our sins is noted, because he carried them in order to expiate them; and therefore in that respect the ἀθέτησις (annulment) of sins has a place here, Heb. 9:26, insofar as satisfaction has been made for them, sins have been expiated, and their guilt has been removed. In which manner Paul says the handwriting which was against us, on account of our sins or debts, was deleted and affixed to the cross, Col. 2:14, and the Principalities were despoiled, who have no right, no power over sins, the handwriting having been deleted. Whence Origen, homily 8. on John. Visibly, he says, the Son of God was crucified in the flesh, but invisibly on that cross the Devil with his Principalities and powers was affixed to the cross. The Apostle had called Christ an example of having suffered for us. He therefore both explains and confirms this by using prophetic words, how he suffered for us, namely because he bore our sins in his body when he was lifted up onto the cross: which pertains to his merit; and how he became an example to us, because he bore our sins and underwent death for them on the cross, so that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness. He had warned servants to insist on the footsteps of Christ, who endured sufferings with the utmost patience.

But lest this should seem to concern only servants, he now changes the person, and speaks in the first person, that Christ bore OUR sins, so that WE might live to righteousness. The Syriac explained that indefinite proposition by a universal: that Christ bore all our sins. Compare 1 John 2:2, v. 24. Ἵνα ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἀπογενόμενοι) having become far from sins. For ἀπογίνεσθαι also signifies this among the Greeks, and Ambrose took it so here. The manuscript: ἵνα ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἡμῶν. It is considered more correct that Peter wished to express the Pauline ἀποθανόντες (having died), Rom. 6:10, so that ἀπογίνεσθαι is to be taken from the midst, to depart, just as the Vulgate rendered it, dead, which the opposition of life teaches. We are said to die to sins, however, in that we are exempted from their dominion and yoke, so that it may no longer rule and live in us, nor we live to it.

Latin:

Πάσχων οὐκ ἠπείλει) Ille qui uno verbo adversantes prostraverat, cum captus duceretur, vinciretur, flagris caederetur, affigeretur cruci, ne verbum quidem minax edidit, quo perfectius nobis daret exemplar patientiae.

Christus in passione sua non modo malum malo non retulit, sed nec aliquando mala se relaturum esse, comminatus est. Prosper ad Demetr. habet: Percutienti se non comminatus est. Vid. Matth. XII. 23. cap. XXVI. 68. cap. XXVII. 42. Joh. VIII. 49. cap. XIIX. 30. &c. Legitur quidem Christus aliquando minatus fuisse, & vae denunciasse civitatibus, quae doctrinam ipsius non reciperent, ut Matth. X. & XI. item Scribis & Pharisaeis, hypocritis, & Doctrinam a DEO traditam corrumpentibus. Sed non minatus fuit tunc, quando patiebatur, ne non ex zelo justitiae, sed affectibus irae & odii commotus id fecisse videretur. Nec id fecit propter se, ut scilicet se de iis vindicaret, sed propter ipsos, & ex amore salutis ipsorum, ut scilicet denunciando sceleratis iras divinas & ignem aeternum eos revocaret a scelere & gehenna. S. Cyprianus tract. de pass. Christus, ait, postposito timore, quasi utens potentiori autoritate inter spectamenta & colaphos & reliqua ludibria patientia & mansuetudine vesanas persecutorum mentes conturbat, & in eo, quod inter injurias & convitia malitia Judaica se sentit contemptam, vehementius exacerbatur, & de impietate & malitia suavitas pietasque CHRISTI triumphat.

Παρεδίδυ δὲ τῷ κρίνοντι δικαίως) Subauditur nomen aliquod post παρεδίδυ. Syrus non male supplet verbale a verbo sequenti, quasi scriptum esset, παρεδίδυ δὲ κρίσιν, causam suam commisit ei, qui juste judicat, semper scilicet. Nam homines saepe injuste judicant, ut synedrium & Pilatus. Deus justus Judex vocatur, Psal. VII. 12. Idem sensus Psal. XCVI. 10. XCVIII. 10. Jerem. XI. 20. & alibi. Totus hic locus respicit illa, quae habemus, Es. L. 6. 7. 8. 9.

Vulgata habet: Tradebat autem se judicanti injuste, ut sensus sit, tradebat se nihil contradicens, nec obmurmurans Pilato, judicandum injusto Judici. At monet Estius: In Graecis omnino diversa lectio nem esse: Tradebat autem judicanti juste: Quam & Syrus Interpres paraphrastice sic reddit: Sed tradebat judicium suum Judici justitiae. Sensus igitur Graecae lectionis est: Christus non seipsum vindicabat, sed tradebat, seu committebat causam suam Deo, qui juste judicat, judicandam & vindicandam. Juxta illud Deut. XXXII. a Paulo repetitum, Rom. XII. & Ebr. X. Mihi vindicta, ego retribuam. Videri potest allusisse B. Petrus ad illud in persona Christi dictum a Jeremia cap. XI. Tu autem Domine Zebaoth, qui judicas juste & probas renes & corda, videam ultionem tuam ex eis. Tibi enim revelavi causam meam. Judica Domine nocentes mihi. Id vero est dare locum irae, scilicet divinae, quemadmodum praecipit Paulus, Rom. XII. Verisimile est, Interpretem nostrum non aliud vertisse, quam quod in omnibus Graecis legitur: Sed cum non intelligeretur, librariorum inscitia jam olim fuisse mutatum in sensum obvium magis. A- lioqui certe August. tract. XXI. in Joh. cum Graecis convenit, ita legens: Sed commendabat illi, qui juste judicat. Similiter Fulgentius ad Trasimundum ca- pit. 11. Commendabat autem judicanti juste. Haec Estius rectissime. Vulgata tamen in mendo reli- cta est a RR. PP. Haec scilicet eorum est infallibi- litas. Conf. Jer. XI. vers. 28. cap. XX. vers. 12. Psal. VII. vers. 2. Psal. XXVI. vers. 16. XXXV. 24. Johan. XV. vers. 25. Verbum παρεδίδου nonnulli explicant commisit, id est, commendavit, Jer. XI. vers. 21. Didymus & glossa ordin. aliene, & praeter scopum Apostolicum: Commendavit suos torto- res, & persecutores Deo Patri pro eis orando, Luc. XXIII. vers. 34. Cornelius a Lapide hunc genuinum esse vult sensum: Tradidit se Deo Patri ad mortem, eidem obediendo. Sed in Graeco non habetur pronomen illud SE, ideoque praeferenda Estii adducta jam interpretatio, a quo etiam Cornelii judicium, quod lectio Latina verior sit, magis- que apposita, jam profligatum est. Autoritas Clementis Alexandr. qui in commentario legerit, ut Vulgata habet, neminem movere potest, quia commentarii illi nullius sunt autoritatis: De qui- bus Bellarm. de scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis pag. 79. Meminit Cassiodorus in l. I. Div. Inst. explanationis Clementis Alexandr. in epistolas Canonicas, quae explanatio an ea sit, quae in Bibliotheca S. Patrum invenitur, non facile judicare possum. Alii ad Di- dymum provocant. Sed explicatio Didymi in epist. Canon. quae habetur Tom. IX. Bibl. Patr. pariter dubia est autoritatis. Adducitur & Paulinus epist. II. Glossa ordin. & interlin. sed illi sequuti sunt le- ctionem Latinam, textum Graecum non inspexe- re. Atqui non legitur, Christum vindictam Deo commendasse. Resp. Licet id alibi non legatur, hic tamen de eo a Spiritu sancto edocemur. Quam- vis in Psalmis omnino talia legantur, quibus vin- dictam DEO commendarit, Ps. LXIX. vers. 23. seqq. Ps. CIX. v. 6. seqq. Sic autem commenda- vit, nisi resipiscant; oravit vero simul pro ipsis, ut venia resipiscentibus concederetur: Luc. XXIII. vers. 34. Ebr. XII. 24.

v. 23. Ὅς τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν αὐτὸς ἀνήνεγκεν ἐν τῷ σώματι αὑτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον) ἀνήνεγκεν, hic est abstulit, quod sequen- tia ostendunt, quomodo idem verbum semi notavimus Ebr. 9, 28. eodem sensu αἴρειν ἁμαρτίαν Joh. 1, 29. & נשא & סבל Es. LIII. 4. ubi Graeci φέρει. Vitia nostra ita interfecit, sicut qui cruci affiguntur, interfici solent. Simile loquendi- genus, Col. II. 14. Vide & Rom. VI. 6. Gal. II. 20. V. 24. Est autem hic μετάληψις. Non enim proprie Christus cum crucifigeretur, vitia nostra abstulit, sed causas dedit, per quas auferrentur. Nam crux Christi fundamentum est prae- dicationis, praedicatio vero poenitentiae, poenitentia vero aufert vitia ἐν τῷ σώματι αὐτοῦ cum corpore suo. Loquutio- ne qualis est Matth. VI. 29. Rom. XV. v. 29. Eph. VI. 2. & alibi. Sicut corpus ejus in crucem actum est: Ita & vitia nostra quasi in crucem acta. Particulae similitudinem signi- ficantes saepe subticentur, sitque sic oratio efficacior.

Sensus ille vocis ἀνήνεγκε, quod sit abstulit, So- cinianis velificatur. Fortasse dicitur peccata no- stra Christus, non abstulisse, non interfecisse: Imo ipse interfectus est ob peccata nostra, Rom. IV. ult. Peccata nostra in ipsum injecta sunt, & vulnera- tus, adeoque occisus est ipse ob peccata nostra, Es. LIII. v. 8. Portavit ergo illa tum ratione cul- pae, quam in se suscepit, tum ratione poenae, quam pro nobis, & nostri loco luit, 2. Cor. V. 19. 20. 21. Portavit autem in corpore suo, quia in propria per- sona sua luit pro peccatis nostris. Portavit ea in lignum crucis, quia in ligno crucis imprimis luit pro peccatis. Ἀναφέρομαι est sustollo, sursum tollo. Quod verbum LXX. Interpp. Es. LII. 12. etiam usurparunt, e quo Propheta etiam illud Pronomen emphaticum αὐτὸς desumptum est, cujus primus usus Gen. III. 15. est. Syrus: Bajulavit omnia pec- cata nostra, eaque sustulit in corpore suo ad crucem. Athanasius orat. IV. contr. Arian. Efferens pecca- ta nostra in crucem una cum corpore suo. Crux Christi fuit sublime illud altare, in quod Christus seipsum oblaturus ascendit onustus peccatis no- stris: quod onus sequutus ascendere fecit vel sustu- lit in crucem. In corpore autem portasse dici- tur: non quod anima expers fuerit passionum. Laboravit enim anima ejus Es. 53, 11. posuitque ipse animam suam pro delicto v. 20. Sed quia corpore fuo pependit visibiliter in cruce. Interim corpus animatum, & tota natura humana Christi intelli- gitur per synecdochen; quemadmodum in carne passus & mortificatus dicitur, id est, in natura hu- mana, 1. Petr. 3, 18. Confer. Flacius in Clav. Script. p. 1. col. 882. Sensum hunc reddidit Estius: Qui ipse per se peccata non sua, sed nostra, tanquam grave pondus sustulit ac portavit in suo corpore super lignum crucis, cui erat affixus, id est, pendens in cruce ipse pœnas recepit ac persolvit peccatis nostris debitas. Respectum haberi ad hircum emissarium existima- vit Cornelius à Lapide, de quo Levit. XVI. 21. Non ergo pœna tantum, quod ipse vult, sed etiam culpa à Christo ablata. Sensus ille verborum Petri: Peccata nostra portavit ipse in corpore suo super lignum cru- cis, id est, sicut corpus ejus in crucem actum est: Ita & vitia tua quasi in crucem acta; inauditus hactenus in Ecclesia, & contortus est. Nulla hic comparatio- nis particula est, nec subaudiri potest. Non enim comparatur corpus Christi cum peccatis nostris ratione crucifixionis vel interfectionis: Sed pecca- ta nostra à Christo crucifixo in ligno crucis porta- ta & in Christo punita esse è collatione Esaiæ doce- tur: ad quem locum de his uberius egimus. Cur ad ejusmodi inusitatam μετάληψιν discedendum sit, causa nulla est. Admitti quidem potest sensu Ca- tholico: Crucem Christi fundamentum esse pre- cationis, quia nisi Christus pro nobis crucifixus & mortuus esset, nulla esset prædicatio remissionis peccatorum in nomine & per nomen Christi, Luc. 24. v. 47. Neq; id negamus, prædicationem Evange- lii de Christo crucifixo esse fundamentum pœni- tentiæ, quatenus hæc fidem includit in Christum pro peccatis nostris crucifixum: Pœnitentiam etiam auferre vitia, sed non ita, ut ea interficiantur vel extirpentur, sed ut condonentur & remittan- tur, non ut non insint, sed ut non imputentur, ut Augustinus loquitur, concedimus. Sed ista in hisce Petri verbis affirmari, negamus. Peccatorum no- strorum portatio & expiatio notatur, quia portavit ea, ut expiaret; ideoq; ea ratione peccatorum ἀθέ- τησις hic locum habet, Ebr. 9, 26. quatenus pro iis satisfactum, peccata expiata, eorumque reatus ab- latus est. Quo pacto Paulus chirographum, quod ad- versus nos erat, ob peccata vel debita nostra dele- tum, & cruci affixum dicit Col. 2, 14. & expoliati Prin- cipatus, qui nullum jus, nullam potestatem habent peccatorum, chirographo deleto. Unde Origenes homil. IIX. in Joh. Visibiliter quidem, ait, Filius Dei in carne crucifixus est, invisibiliter vero in ea cruce Diabolus cum Principatibus suis & potestatibus af- fixus est cruci. Dixerat Apostolus Christum pro nobis passum exemplum. Id ergo & explicat, & con- firmat verbis Propheticis adhibitis, quomodo pro nobis sit passus, quia scilicet peccata nostra bajulavit in corpore suo, cum in crucem sublatus est: quod ad meritum ejus pertinet; & quomodo exemplum fa- ctus nobis est, quia peccata nostra pertulit, & mor- tem pro iis in cruce subiit, ut peccatis mortui justi- tiæ viveremus. Monuerat servos, ut vestigiis Christi insistant, qui passiones summa patientia sustinuit.

Ne autem solos id servos concernere videretur, personam jam mutat, & in prima persona loquitur, peccata NOSTRA Christum pertulisse, ut Nos justitiæ viveremus. Indefinitam illam propositio- nem Syrus per universalem exposuit: quod Christus omnia peccata nostra portaverit. Conf. 1. Joh. 2, 2. v. 24. Ἵνα ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἀπογενόμενοι) longe facti à peccatis. Nam ἀπογίνεσθαι etiam hoc significat apud Græcos, & ita hic sumpsit Ambrosius. Manuscriptus: ἵνα ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἡμῶν. Rectius censetur Petrus exprimere ea voce vo- luisse Paulinum ἀποθανόντες, Rom. 6, 10. ut ἀπογί- νεσθαι sit è medio tolli, defungi, quemadmodum Vulgata reddidit, mortui, quod oppositio vitæ do- cet. Peccatis autem mori dicimur, qua dominio & jugo eorum eximimur, ne amplius in nobis do- minetur & vivat, nec nos illi vivamus.

## 2:24
Τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ ζήσωμεν) For it is not enough to abstain from evils, but effort must also be devoted to Christian virtues. To live to righteousness is said here just as to live to God, Rom. 6:10, Gal. 2:19. John said Ποιεῖν δικαιοσύνην (to do righteousness) for the same thing several times.

We live to righteousness when we are devoted to righteousness and holiness, so that it may live and rule in us, and sin may be mortified in us through the Spirit. Peter joins both benefits of the death of Christ, that through it our sins have been expiated for their pardon in justification, and that through its power sin has been mortified in us, and we have been reformed to a life of righteousness and holiness, which pertains to sanctification and renewal.

Οὗ τῷ μώλωπι αὐτοῦ ἰάθητε, ) A Hebraism. For the Hebrews are accustomed to say אשר בו and לא אשר and similar things. The words are taken from Isa. 53:5. Τῷ μώλωπι αὐτοῦ ἡμεῖς ἰάθημεν (by his stripe we are healed), חבורתו, which is translated as μώλωψ (stripe), properly signifies a bruise from a contusion, as it is taken figuratively for any pain, as Gen. 5:27, Exod. 21:25, Ps. 38:6, Isa. 50:1, Prov. 20:19, Sirach 23:11, 28:21, Judith 9:13. Indeed, in many ways the pains of Christ healed us from vices. But here it looks most of all to the example which he gave us of obedience, patience, gentleness, and love in the midst of pains, as the preceding things show.

It does not at all appear from the preceding that an example is primarily being referred to here: for Peter has spoken in the preceding no less about merit than about example. Isaiah, however, from whom these things are taken, dealt properly with the merit of the death of Christ. He does indeed allude to the stripes and wounds of servants inflicted by harsh masters, but in order that they may patiently endure all things, he sets forth not only the example of the suffering Christ, who bore stripes, but also the merit of the same, because for our sake he willed to be beaten with stripes in the manner of servants, so that he might heal the wounds of our souls, so that on account of his holy wounds, servants might also endure their own wounds from unjust masters with a calm mind. The healing of the wounds of the soul, therefore, does not so much concern sanctification as justification, namely, that through his stripes and wounds he has merited for us liberation from the stripes of sin, which is the removal of the guilt of our sins, by which our soul is wounded, and the application of the obedience of Christ through faith, so that we may be affected by no sickness on account of sins, and may rejoice in blameless health in Christ through the most perfect righteousness of the same. The Syriac rendered 'wounds' as 'stains,' by which it understands the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, by which his whole body was stained: being sprinkled with which, we are freed from spiritual leprosy, and are quickened to eternal life by Christ, who is our life. Tauler, in his meditations on the life of Christ, says: 'That we might live, it was necessary for him to die; that we might be gladdened, he himself was saddened; that we might be healed, he himself was wounded; that we might be cleansed, he himself shed his blood.' The blood of the Physician was shed, and it was made the medicine of the sick man. Christ heals us by his wounds, both so that we may be saved from the wounds of the soul, and so that we may obtain new strength to abstain from evil and to perform good, lest we suffer a relapse.

Latin:

Τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ ζήσωμεν) Non enim sufficit à malis absti- nere, sed danda & virtutibus Christianis opera. Zῆν δικαιο- σύνῃ hic dicitur quomodo ζῆν Θεῷ, Rom. VI. 10. Gal. II. 19. Ποιεῖν δικαιοσύνην pro eodem dixit aliquoties Johannes.

Justitiæ vivimus, cum dediti sumus justitiæ & san- ctitati, ut illa in nobis vivat, & dominetur, & per Spiritum peccatum in nobis mortificetur. Conjun- git Petrus utrumq; mortis Christi beneficium, quod per eandem peccata nostra expiata sint ad eorum condonationem in justificatione, & quod per illius virtutem peccatum in nobis mortificatum sit, nos- que ad vitam justitiæ & sanctitatis reformati, quod ad sanctificationem & renovationem pertinet.

Οὗ τῷ μώλωπι αὐτοῦ ἰάθητε, ) Ebraismus. Solent enim Ebræi dicere אשר בו & לא אשר & similia. Sumpta verba ex Es. LIII. 5. Τῷ μώλωπι αὐτοῦ ἡμεῖς ἰάθημεν חבורתו, quod μώλωψ vertitur, proprie livorem ex contusione signifi- cat, ut figurate pro quovis dolore sumitur, ut Gen. V. 27. Exod. 21, 25. Ps. 38, 6. Es. 50, 1. Prov. 20, 19. Sirach. 23, 11. 28, 21. Judith. 9, 13. Multis quidem modis Christi dolores nos à vitiis sanarunt. Sed hic maxime respicitur exemplum, quod nobis dedit obedientiæ, patientiæ, mansuetudinis, dilectio- nis in mediis doloribus, ut antecedentia ostendunt.

Ex antecedentibus minime apparet, imprimis exemplum hic respici: nam non minus de merito quam de exemplo loquutus in antecedentibus est Petrus. Esaias vero, ex quo hæc deprompta, egit proprie de merito mortis Christi. Alludit quidem ad plagas & vibices servorum, à duris dominis in- flictas, sed ut patienter sustineant omnia, non tan- tum exemplum Christi patientis sistit, qui plagas pertulit, sed etiam meritum ejusdem, quod pro- pter nos more servorum plagis cædi voluerit, ut animarum nostrarum vulnera sanaret, ut propter sanctas illius vibices, servi etiam suas vibices à dominis iniquis æquo animo sustineant. Sanatio itaque vulnerum animæ non tam respicit sanctifi- cationem, quam justificationem, quod nempe per plagas & vibices suas promeruerit nobis à plagis peccati liberationem, quæ sit reatus peccatorum nostrorum, quibus anima nostra sauciata est, remo- tione, & obedientiæ Christi per fidem applicatio- ne, ut nullâ ægritudine ob peccata afficiamur, & sanitate inculpata in Christo per ejusdem justitiam perfectissimam gaudeamus. Syrus vibices reddidit maculas, per quas intelligit aspersionem sanguinis Christi, quo totum ejus corpus maculatum fuit: quo conspersi nos à spirituali lepra liberamur, & à Christo, qui vita nostra est, ad æternam vitam vivi- ficamur. Taulerus meditat. vitæ Christi ait: Ut nos viveremus, ipsum mori oportuit; ut nos exhilaremur, ipse tristatus est; ut nos sanaremur, ipse vulneratus est, ut nos mundaremur, ipse fudit sanguinem. Fusus est sanguis Medici, & factus est medicamentum ægroti. Sanat nos Christus vulneribus suis, & ut salvemur à vulneribus animæ, & ut vires novas consequamur à malo abstinendi bonumque ope- randi, ne recidivam patiamur.

## 2:25
v. 25. Ἦτε γὰρ ὡς πρόβατα πλανώμενα) And this is from Is. 53, 6. with which the passage in Jer. 50, 6 agrees, but also Ps. 119, 176, the explanation of which you have in Matt. 9, 36, where see what is said.

But you have now returned) שׁוּבְתֶם. To the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls) It is customary for ἐπιστρέψαι to have ἐπὶ or πρὸς after it; then that ὡς here is explanatory, returning those who have wandered. For when he had mentioned the Shepherd to pursue the simile, he now explains how Christ is the Shepherd, namely because He cares for souls, just as a Shepherd cares for sheep. See above I, 9. Ἐπίσκοπος is פָּקִיד or בָּקוּר, or מִפְקַר, he who takes care of something; as Num. 4, 16; c. 31, 14; Jud. 9, 28; 2 Reg. 11, 16, 19; 2 Paral. 34, 12, 17; Nehem. 11, 9, 14. The comparison of the Shepherd fits Christ very well, John 10, 11, 14, 16; Heb. 13, 20; below c. 5, 4.

Because he had said from Isaiah that we were healed by Christ's stripe; he indicates from the same source the disease from which we have been healed, namely that we were all like wandering sheep, who languish and fail for want of good pasture, or perish having been cast into dangers through pathless places, or are exposed to the prey of wolves and are torn apart: He also explains the effect of Christ's passion, the salvation of souls, by a comparison with our former miserable state, in which we were like wandering sheep, outside the way of salvation on the road leading to hell: A sheep is a stupid animal: thus before conversion we were destitute of true wisdom, which consists in the saving knowledge of God. Sheep are subject to various diseases, and as Aristotle relates in book IV de part. animal. c. 2, to as many diseases as men: Thus before conversion we are spiritually sick, and are in need of the healing of the soul. Wandering sheep are destitute of a Shepherd and are separated from the flock: Thus before conversion we were separated from Christ and from the assembly of the saints. When therefore we have been converted to Christ, let us serve Christ as obedient sheep, and piously and patiently; and let us follow in the footsteps of Him as our Shepherd. In the same, says Blessed Luther, we once stuck in the mud of misery, in which those who afflict us also stick. It is better, therefore, to make vows for their conversion to God than to rule them with curses. He who converts us can also convert our masters. One must not despair, says Augustine, sent. 184, concerning the wicked, but one must pray more zealously for them, that they may become good, because the number of the saints is always increased from the number of the impious. Those who are goats today can be sheep tomorrow; those who are tares today can be wheat tomorrow. You were like wandering sheep, destitute of a shepherd, torn by the thorns of vices, and wandering through the precipices of vices, as the interlinear gloss has it.

The name of Shepherd is taken from the Old Testament, where it is attributed to Christ by David, Ps. 23, 1; Ps. 95, 7; to Asaph, Ps. 80, 1; to Isaiah, c. 40, 14; to Ezekiel, c. 34, 11; to Zechariah, c. 10, 2; c. 13, 7. Which name fits here very well not only because of the correlate of sheep, and the common office of shepherds, which is to seek wandering sheep, to bring back those that are found, Luke 15, 1, and to heal the sick, Ezek. 34, 16. But also to lay down His life for the redeeming of the sheep, John 10, 11, just as the Apostle had hinted that Christ as the Lamb of God had borne our sins: so now he calls Him the Shepherd, who laid down His soul for His sheep. He is also called Bishop, that is, Inspector, from Ezek.

34, 11. I will visit my sheep, where the LXX have ἐπισκέψομαι: because He bears constant care for our salvation, considering our necessities and infirmities with a watchful eye. Beautifully Epiphanius, haer. 55: He who offered Himself for the whole world, He Himself is the victim, He Himself the sacrifice, He Himself the priest, He Himself the altar, He Himself God, He Himself man, He Himself King, He Himself Pontiff, He Himself the sheep, He Himself the lamb, having become all things in all for us, so that He might become life for us in all ways, and might make the immutable foundation of His priesthood for the ages. He is called Shepherd and Bishop of souls, not because He does not care for our bodies, but because He is distinguished as a spiritual Shepherd from a bodily Shepherd. Nor is the positing of one the exclusion of the other: and it is most well known that a denomination is made from the more important. Add that He is the Bishop of bodies, insofar as the salvation of bodies is directed to the salvation of souls. Otherwise, the salvation of bodies pertains to a Physician, not to a Bishop. From the fact that before conversion we were like wandering sheep, it is gathered against the Pelagians, Semi-Pelagians, and Synergists that we could not return and be converted to God by our own powers: Which Cornelius a Lapide acknowledges here: You have been converted now not by yourselves, but by Christ, calling through His grace, and drawing to Himself, according to that John 6, 44: No one can come to me, unless the Father, who sent me, draws him, and that of Paul: It is God who works in you both to will and to perform, Phil. 2, 13: and that of the Psalmist, Ps. 58, 11: His mercy prevents me. And that: Convert us, O Lord, to Thee, and we shall be converted, Lam. 5, 21. And that Jer. 31, v. 18: Thou hast chastised me and I was instructed, as an untamed calf: Convert me, and I shall be converted, because Thou art the Lord my God. For after Thou didst convert me, I did penance.

Latin:

v. 25. Ἦτε γὰρ ὡς πρόβατα πλανώμενα) Et hoc ex Es. 53, 6. quo cum convenit locus Jerem. L. 6. sed & Psal. 119, 176. quo- rum explicationem habes Matth. 9, 36. ubi quæ dicta vide.

Ἀλλ' ἐπεστράφητε νῦν) שׁוּבְתֶם. Ἐπὶ τὸν ποιμένα καὶ ἐπίσκοπον τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν) Solet ἐπι- στρέψαι post se habere ἐπὶ vel πρὸς, deinde illud ὡς hic est ἐξη- γητικὸν, ἐπιστρέφοντες τὰ ἀποπεπλανημένα. Nam cum dixisset Pastorem ad persequendam similitudinem, nunc explicat, quomodo Christus sit Pastor, nimirum quia animas curat, sicut Pastor oves. Vide supra I. 9. Ἐπίσκοπος est פָּקִיד vel בָּקוּר, vel מִפְקַר, is qui alicujus rei curam gerit; ut Num. 4, 16. c. 31, 14. Jud. 9, 28. 2. Reg. 11, 16. 19. 2. Paral. 34, 12. 17. Nehem. 11, 9. 14. Comparatio Pastoris optimè Christo convenit, Joh. 10, 11. 14. 16. Ebr. 13, 20. infra c. 5, 4.

Quia Christi livore nos sanatos ex Esaia dixe- rat; morbum, à quo sanati sumus, ex eodem indi- cat, quod nempe similes fuerimus omnes ovibus errantibus, qui inopia boni pabuli languescunt ac deficiunt, vel per avia in pericula præcipitati pere- unt, aut luporum prædæ exponuntur, & dilaceran- tur: Explicat etiam effectum passionis Christi salutem animarum, collatione pristini status miseri, in quo eramus instar ovium errantium, extra salutis viam in via ad infernum ducente: Ovis est animal stoli- dum: sic ante conversionem destituti sumus vera sapientia, quæ in salvifica Dei cognitione consistit. Oves variis morbis sunt obnoxiæ, & ut Aristoteles l. IV. de part. animal. c. 2. tradit; tot morbis, quot ho- mines: Sic ante conversionem spiritualiter ægro- tamus, ac sanatione animæ indigemus. Oves er- rantes destituuntur Pastore & à grege separatæ sunt: Ita ante conversionem à Christo & à cœtu sanctorum separati sumus. Quum ergo ad Christum conversi sumus, ut oves obedientes, ac pie & pati- enter Christo serviamus: ejusq; ceu Pastoris nostri vestigiis insistamus. In eodem, inquit B. Lutherus, olim miseriæ luto hæsimus, in quo illi, qui nos affligunt. Satius igitur est, pro conversione eorum ad Deum vota facere, quam maledictis regere. Qui nos con- vertit, etiam dominos nostros convertere potest. Non est desperandum, inquit Augustinus sent. 184. de malis, sed pro ipsis, ut boni fiant, studiosius suppli- candum est, quia numerus sanctorum semper est de numero auctus impiorum. Qui hodie sunt hædi, cras oves esse possunt: qui hodie zizania, cras triticum esse possunt. Eratis sicut oves errantes, destituti pa- store, dilacerati spinis vitiorum, ac per abrupta vi- tiorum vagantes, ut habet glossa interlin.

Pastoris nomen è Veteri Testamento desum- ptum, ubi Christo tribuitur à Davide, Psal. 23, 1. Psal. 95, 7. Assapho Psal. 80, 1. Esaia c. 40, 14. Eze- chiele c. 34, 11. Zacharia c. 10, 2. c. 13, 7. Quod no- men hic optime convenit non tantum ob correla- tum ovium, & Pastorum commune officium, quod est oves errantes quærere, inventas reducere, Luc. 15, 1. morbidasque curare, Ezech. 34, 16. Sed etiam pro ovibus redimendis vitam profundere, Joh. 10, 11. quemadmodum innueraτ Apostolus, Christum ut Agnum Dei peccata nostra portasse: ita nunc Pa- storem vocat, qui animam suam posuit pro ovibus suis. Vocatur & Episcopus, id est Inspector ex Ezech.

34, 11. visitabo oves meas, ubi LXX. habent ἐπισκέψο- μαι: quia assiduam salutis nostræ curam gerit, ocu- lo vigilante necessitates & infirmitates nostras considerans. Pulchre Epiphanius hær. 55. Qui pro toto mundo obtulit se, ipse victima, ipse sacrificium, ipse sacerdos, ipse altare, ipse Deus, ipse homo, ipse Rex, ipse Pontifex, ipse ovis, ipse agnus, omnia in omnibus pro nobis factus, ut nobis vita omnibus mo- dis fieret, & sacerdotii sui immutabile firmamentum efficeret in sœcula. Pastor a. dicitur & Episcopus ani- marum, non quod corpora nostra non curet, sed quod à corporali Pastore ceu spiritualis Pastor di- stinguatur. Neque vero unius positio est alterius exclusio: & à potiori fieri denominationem no- to- tissimum est. Adde quod Episcopus corporum sit, quatenus salus corporum dirigitur ad salutem animarum. Alioqui enim salus corporum ad Me- dicum spectat, non ad Episcopum. Ex eo quod ante conversionem sicut oves errantes fuerimus, colli- gitur adversus Pelagianos, Semi-Pelagianos, & Sy- nergistas viribus nos propriis ad Deum redire & converti non potuisse: Quod agnoscit hic Corne- lius a Lapide: Conversi estis nunc non a vobis, sed a Christo, per gratiam suam vocante, & trahente ad se, juxta illud Joh. 6, 44. Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum, & illud Pauli: Deus est, qui operatur in vobis & velle & perficere, Phil. II. 13: & illud Psaltis Psal. 58, 11. Misericordia ejus prævenit me. Et illud: Converte nos Domine ad te, & convertemur, Thren. V. 21. Et illud Jer. 31. v. 18. Castigasti me & eruditus sum, quasi juvenculus indomitus: Converte me, & convertar, quia tu Do- minus Deus meus. Postquam enim convertisti me, egi pænitentiam.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Wives are admonished concerning subjection toward their husbands, and chaste conversation, and interior adornment after the example of holy women: Husbands concerning due cohabitation, and the honor to be shown to the female sex, as to a weaker vessel: All in common are exhorted to concord and charity, with Davidic warnings and promises brought forward, and to rendering an apology for the faith, and Christian patience in enduring persecutions, with the example and merit of Christ again proposed: as also the punishments of the unbelievers in the time of Noah, who were convicted by the descent of Christ into hell of the guilt of their own condemnation, and of the means of salvation, baptism, figured in the flood, as also of the dominion of Christ over all things, and the angelic powers themselves.

There are three parts: I. It contains special exhortations to wives and husbands, up to verse 7. II. Universal exhortations to charity and holiness, up to verse 13. III. It presents peculiar exhortations to tolerance, when we suffer for righteousness, and to perseverance in the faith. By dichotomy: The former part is proper to the economic state as yet: The latter is common, concerning both the pursuit of piety and the state of confession and constancy in the faith. The former is merely parenetic, the latter is both exhortatory and informative concerning the passion of Christ, concerning the descent into hell, concerning the resurrection and its power exerting itself in baptism, concerning the ascension into heaven, and the session at the right hand of God.

PART I. Special exhortation to wives and husbands.

v. 1. Ὁμοίως αἱ γυναῖκες ὑποτασσόμεναι τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν) 'is' must be supplied here again, as above l. 18. and 'being subject' is to be taken as Hithpael, as we said there. The sense is the same as Eph. V. 22, 24. Col. III. 18. These agree with Gen. III. 16. Πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα σου ἡ ἀποστροφή σου. Ἵνα καὶ εἴ τινες ἀπειθοῦσι τῷ λόγῳ διὰ τῆς τῶν γυναικῶν ἀναστροφῆς, ἄνευ λόγου κερδηθήσωνται) There were already examples of this thing, as we see 1 Cor. VII. 16. For while they themselves were silent, modesty, chastity, obedience, care of domestic affairs, and other virtues commended to the husbands not only their wives, but also the truly divine philosophy in which they were instructed. They said what Libanius said: Alas, what women the Christians have! Ἀπειθοῦσι τῷ λόγῳ) To those still resisting the Gospel, just as we have 'disobeying the truth', Rom. VII. 8. Concerning the word ἀναστροφῆς, see above l. 15. II. 12. and what was said there, and concerning the word

they shall be gained, Matt. 18:15; 1 Cor. 9:19, 20, 21, 22. Without a word: because silence brings ornament to women.

He proceeds from servants to wives. Estius gives this reason why he does not remind masters of their duty: that these writings were for Jews in the dispersion, many of whom were indeed servants, but very few were masters who had servants. The cause of this exhortation, however, is believed to have been the calumny and rumor of the Gentiles, who wished the wives of Christians to be free from subjection to their husbands because of the liberty obtained by Christ. Augustine deduces that subjection from the very law of nature in Quaest. sup. Gen. c. 133: 'There is a natural order among men, that women should serve their husbands; because this is justice for them, that the weaker reason should serve the stronger: and in this there is clear justice in dominions and servitudes, that those who excel in reason should excel in dominion.' Therefore, a wife ruling over her husband, and a husband suffering the rule of his wife, is called a monster. The Apostle adds the emphatic word 'own' (idios), to admonish wives of chastity and to call them away from the suspicious attentions of other men. He advises, however, that wives be subject to their own husbands indefinitely, whether they be faithful or unfaithful, which the reason subjoined teaches, that through holy conversation the unfaithful may be converted, 1 Cor. 7:16. By 'the word' (ton logon) in both places is understood the word of the Evangelical proclamation. Grotius, in the latter place, seems to take the word 'Word' differently, concerning the word of the wives' admonition. Oecumenius interprets it as 'without the word of contradiction' of the husbands. But John Huss more correctly as 'without the word of public preaching.' Wives are said to 'gain' their husbands—understand: for Christ or the Church—and by the name of gain is insinuated both the price of souls and the holy delight from the conversion of the unfaithful, 2 Cor. 1:14, Phil. 4:1, as also Matt. 18:15, 1 Cor. 9:19, Phil. 3:18. Cf. Matt. 25:14. Luke 19:12. When a woman is gracious and is loved by her husband, and is constantly with him, she glides into his mind like water into a sponge, gradually and imperceptibly, and occupies him and bends him where she wishes, as Chrysostom says, Hom. 60 in John.

Latin:

CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Monentur uxores de subjectione erga maritos, & casta conversatione, ornatuque interiore ad exemplum sanctarum mulierum: Viri de cohabitatione debita, & honore muliebri se- xui, tanquam infirmiori vasi exhibendo: Omnes in communi hortatur ad concor- diam, & charitatem, monitis & promissis Davidicis adductis, & ad apologiam fidei reddendam, ac patientiam Christianam in tolerandis persecutionibus, proposito iterum Christi exemplo, & merito: nec non sup- pliciis incredulorum tempore Noachi, qui convicti per descensum Christi ad inferos de culpa propria condemnationis, ac medio salutis baptismo, in diluvio figurato, ut & Dominio Christi super omnia, ipsasque pote- states Angelicas.

Partes tres sunt I. Adhortationes ad uxores & viros speciales continet ad v. 7. II. Adhortationes ad charitatem & sanctitatem universales, ad v. 13. III. Adhortationes ad tolerantiam, cum patimur ob justitiam & perseverantiam in fide peculiares exhibet. Per διχοτομίαν: Prior pars est propria ad- huc statui Oeconomico: Posterior est communis tum studium pietatis, tum statum confessionis & con- stantiam in fide concernens. Illa mere Parænetica, hæc tum adhortatoria, tum informatoria de passio- ne Christi, de descensu ad inferos, de resurrectione, ejusque vi in baptismo se exerente, de ascensione in cœlum, & sessione ad dextram Dei.

PARS I. Adhortatio specialis ad uxores, & viros.

v. 1. Ὁμοίως αἱ γυναῖκες ὑποτασσόμεναι τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν) iterum supplendum hic ἐστὶ, ut supra l. 18. & ὑποτασσόμεναι sumendum ut Hithpael, ut ibi diximus. Sensus idem Eph. V. 22. 24. Col. III. 18. Conveniunt hæc cum Gen. III. 16. Πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα σου ἡ ἀποστροφή σου. Ἵνα καὶ εἴ τινες ἀπειθοῦσι τῷ λόγῳ διὰ τῆς τῶν γυναικῶν ἀναστρο- φῆς, ἄνευ λόγου κερδηθήσωνται) Erant jam exempla ejus rei, ut videmus 1. Cor. VII. 16. Nam ipsis tacentibus modestia, casti- tas, obedientia, cura rei familiaris aliæque virtutes com- mendabant maritis non ipsorum uxores tantum, sed & philo- sophiam vere divinam, in qua erant institutæ Dicebant quod dicebat Libanius: Proh quales fœminas habent Christiani! Ἀπειθοῦσι τῷ λόγῳ) Reluctantibus adhuc Evangelio, quomodo ἀπειθοῦσι τῇ ἀληθείᾳ habemus, Rom. VII. 8. De voce ἀναστροφῆς, vide supra l. 15. II. 12. & ibi dicta, & de voce

κερδανθήσονται, Matth. XVIII. 5. 1. Cor. IX. 19. 20. 21. 22. ἄνευ λόγου : quia γυναιξὶ κόσμον ἡ σιγὴ φέρει.

A servis progreditur ad uxores. Cur autem Do- minos non commonefaciat officii, reddit Estius hanc rationem, quod scripta haec sint Judaeis in di- spersione, quorum multi quidem servi fuerint, per- pauci vero Domini, qui servos habebant. Causa au- tem hujus adhortationis fuisse creditur calumnia, & rumor gentium, quae uxores Christianorum ob libertatem a Christo partam liberas esse voluerint a subjectione erga maritum. Subjectionem illam Augustinus ex ipsa lege naturae deducit in quaest. sup. Gen. c. 133. Est ordo naturalis in hominibus, ut serviant foeminae viris; quia & illis justitia est haec, ut infirmior ratio serviat firmiori: & hac in dominatio- nibus & servitutibus clara justitia est, ut qui excellunt ratione, excellant dominatione. Ideo monstrum dici- tur uxor viro imperans, & vir uxoris imperium pati- ens. Addit Apostolus emphaticam vocem ἰδίοις, ut castitatis uxores admoneat, avocetque a suspectis obsequiis virorum alienorum. Monet autem, ut subjectae sint uxores viris propriis indefinite, sive fideles illi sint, sive infideles, quod ratio subjuncta docet, quod per conversationem sanctam infideles converti possint, 1. Cor. 7, 6. Per τὸν λόγον utrobique intelligitur verbum praeconii Evangelici. Grotius. posteriori loco ἄνευ λόγου aliter vocem Verbi acci- pere videtur, de Verbo commonitionis uxorum. Oe- cumenius interpretatur sine verbo contradictionis maritorum. Sed rectius Joh. Hussus sine verbo prae- dicationis publicae. Lucrari autem uxores dicuntur maritos subintellige Christo vel Ecclesiae, & infi- nuatur nomine lucri tum pretium animarum, tum sancta delectatio e conversione infidelium, 2. Cor. I. 14. Phil. 4, 1. ut & Matth. 18, 15. 1. Cor. 9, 19. Phil. 3, 18. Conf. Matth. 25, 14. Luc. 19, 12. Mulier cum sit gratiosa & ametur a viro, eique jugiter adsit, in ejus animum sicut aqua in spongiam sensim sine sensu illabitur, illumque occupat & flectit, quo vult, di- cente Chrysostomo hom. LX. in Joh.

## 3:2
Verse 2.

Having beheld your chaste conversation in fear) 'In fear,' namely of God, as Acts 2:43, 5:5, 2 Cor. 7:15, and elsewhere, and 'o' for 'sun' as often elsewhere. 'Chaste conversation,' a chaste life. See Phil. 4:8. Tertullian, Ad Uxorem, book 2: 'That among the saints the duties of the sex may be transacted with honor to the necessity itself, as if under the eyes of God, modestly and moderately.'

He wishes fear with respect to God to be joined with subjection with respect to the husband, of which the interlinear gloss also understands 'fear,' and chaste conversation with respect to others: if by his consideration or inspection the husbands are to be led to the faith. 'Epopteuein' denotes accurate inspection and consideration. Cf. ch. 2:12. By 'chaste conversation' is required not only conjugal fidelity, 1 Cor. 7:4, and bodily chastity; but especially also purity of mind, Matt. 5:28. By the word 'your' (humon), as Lyranus notes, the mode of speaking is changed from the third person to the second, the cause of which Blessed Huss gives: he turns his speech to the women, so that by a mode of speaking which is more familiar, he may entice them to good.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Ἐποπτεύσαντες τὴν ἐν φόβῳ ἁγνὴν ἀναστροφὴν ὑμῶν) Ἐν φόβῳ nempe Θεοῦ, ut Act. II. 43. V. 5. 2. Cor. VII. 15. & alibi, & ὀ. pro σὺν ut alibi saepe. Ἁγνὴν ἀναστροφὴν vitam ca- stilimam. Vide Phil. IV. 18. Tertullianus ad uxorem secun- do: Ut penes sanctos officia sexus, cum honore ipsius neces- sitatis tanquam sub oculis Dei modeste & moderate tran- sigantur.

Cum subjectione respectu mariti conjunctam esse vult timorem respectu Dei, de quo etiam φόβον glossa interlin. intelligit, castam conversationem re- spectu aliorum: si ejus consideratione vel inspe- ctione mariti ad fidem perducendi. Ἐποπτεύειν ac- curatam inspectionem & considerationem notat. Conf. cap. II. 12. Ad τὴν ἁγνὴν ἀναστροφὴν non tan- tum fides conjugalis illibata, 1. Cor. VII. 4. & ca- stitas corporis; sed imprimis etiam animi puritas requiritur, Matth. V. 28. Voce ὑμῶν mutatur, no- tante Lyrano, modus loquendi de persona tertia ad secundam, cujus causam reddit B. Hussius: con- vertit sermonem ad mulieres, ut ex modo loquendi, qui magis familiaris est, alliciat eas ad bonum.

## 3:3
Verse 3.

Whose adorning let it not be the outward plaiting of hair) This passage is to be compared with the Pauline one, 1 Tim. 2:9. 'Plaits' (emplokai) here is what 'braids' (plegmata) is there, [Hebrew: ma'aseh miqsheh]. See Isa. 3:24. See what is said there.

And the wearing of gold) namely, of necklaces made of gold.

Or the adorning of putting on of apparel) namely, of 'costly' apparel, which is added in Paul. In the Glossary: 'Kosmos gunaikeios,' ornament. The Latins distinguish a woman's 'mundus' (attire) from her 'ornatus' (ornament). But the Greeks comprehend both in one word.

Peter instructs women as to how they ought to conduct themselves toward others, and now as to how they should conduct themselves regarding their own selves: by avoiding excessive outward bodily adornment, and by pursuing the inward adornment and decoration of the Spirit. He therefore dissuades them from luxury in attire, which is the plaiting of hair, the wearing of gold, and the putting on of garments: which he brings forward by way of example only: for more things are recounted elsewhere, and especially in Isaiah 3:16 sqq. Ἐμπλέκεσθαι means to entangle, to be knotted, 2 Tim. 2:4, 2 Pet. 2:10. Paul, 1 Tim. 2:9, μὴ ἐν πλέγμασιν, not with braided hair. Female pride has devised various entanglements of hair, some of which Jerome recounts in his letter to Demetrias: for some women curl their hair with art, some twist it back, knot it, and arrange it in curls, some divide it into ringlets and horns with curling irons, some even attach foreign and artificial hair to themselves, and some let hair hang down from the forehead. By τὰ χρύσια any gold ornaments are understood, such as necklaces, chains, rings, earrings, headbands, etc. Paul, 1 Tim. 2:9, μὴ ἐν μαργαρίταις. For women are accustomed to adorn themselves now with pearls, now with gold. St. Jerome to Laeta on the education of a daughter: Do not, he says, burden your head with gems, nor redden your hair, and thereby invite upon yourself some of the fires of Gehenna. For they were accustomed to color their hair and face with white lead, antimony, and other pigments, and those who prepared these were called cinerarii and cinislones from the ash of cosmetics, as Teraquell has it, leg. 2. concub. n. 27. St. Cyprian gravely rebukes such women in his book on the discipline and attire of virgins. Women, he says, lay hands upon God when they strive to reform and transfigure that which He formed, not knowing that everything which is born is the work of God, and whatever is reformed is the work of the Devil. Your Lord says: You cannot make one hair white or black, and you, to overcome the voice of your Lord, wish to be more powerful. With bold attempt and sacrilegious contempt you dye your hair. Do you not fear, I pray, you who are such a person, that when the day of resurrection comes, your Maker will not recognize you, and will remove and exclude you as you come to His rewards and promises, rebuking you with the vigor of a censor and judge, saying: This is not my work, nor is it our image. You have polluted your skin with false medicine, you have changed your hair with an adulterous color, your face has been conquered by a lie, your figure is corrupted, your countenance is foreign. You will not be able to see God, when the eyes are not yours, which God made, but which the Devil has infected. By τὰ ἱμάτια not only outer garments, such as cloaks, are understood, Matt. 9:20, ch. 21:7, but in general any garments, as Matt. 11:8, ch. 27:35. Paul has in its place, 1 Tim. 2:9, μὴ ἐν ἱματισμῷ πολυτελεῖ. These things are not to be taken as if all adornment whatsoever were forbidden by Peter, as Jerome refutes in his first book against Pelagius, because according to the customary Hebraism, negative words are put for comparative ones, 1 Tim. 2:8, or because those things pertain only to the faithful in Peter's age: But because excess and adornment are always, and in every age, to be shunned. A modest and honest bodily adornment and decoration is to be used according to the reason of the condition and status of each person: How much more are garments and ornaments devised for lasciviousness to be avoided?
