Concerning which St. Jerome in his epistle on the life of the coenobites: The caliga (shoe) of the walker, black and shining, calls young men to itself with its creaking; the breasts are compressed with bands, and the chest is tightened more narrowly with a curling angle, the hair flows down either onto the forehead or the ears, the little cloak sometimes falls, so as to bare the shining shoulders, etc. A double adornment, says Tertullian on the attire of women, belongs to a woman, namely, the womanly world in gold, gems, and clothes, and the adornment, which it is fitting to call the womanly uncleanliness, in the care of the hair, the skin, and of those parts of the body which draw the eyes. We charge the former with the crime of ambition, the latter with that of prostitution.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Ὧν ἔστω οὐχ ὁ ἔξωθεν ἐμπλοκῆς τριχῶν) Conferendus hic locus cum Paulino, 1. Tim. II. 9. Ἐμπλοκαὶ hic quod ibi. dem πλέγματα מעשה מקשה. Ef III. 24. Vide ibi dicta.

Καὶ περιθέσεως χρυσίων) monilium scilicet ex auro.

Ἢ ἐνδύσεως ἱματίων κόσμος) ἱματίων nempe πολυτελῶν, quod apud Paulum additur. In Glossario: Κόσμος γυναι- κεῖος, ornamentum. Latini distinguunt mundum mulieris ab ornatu. At Graeci utrumque una voce comprehendunt.

Informatat Petrus mulieres, quales se gerere debeant erga alios, jam quales quoad semet ipsas: vitando nimium corporis cultum exteriorem, se- ctando cultum & ornatum Spiritus interiorem. De- hortatur itaque à luxu in habitu, quæ plicaturam capillorum; circumpofitionem auri, & amictum vestimentorum: Quæ exempli causa tantum af- fert: Plura enim recensentur alias, & imprimis Ef. LIII. 16. sqq. Ἐμπλέκεσθαι est implicare, innoda- ri, 2. Tim. II. vers. 4. 2. Petr. II. vers. 10. Paulus 1. Tim. II. vers. 9. μὴ ἐν πλέγμασιν, non intortis crinibus. Implicationes capillorum varias excogita- vit fastus muliebris, quarum nonnullas recenset Hieronymus ad Demetriad: Quædam enim fœmi- næ capillos arte crispant, quædam eos retorquent, innodant, & in cincinnos componunt, quædam in cir- ros & cornua calamistris eos discriminant, quædam etiam alienos & factitios crines sibi apponunt, quæ- dam à fronte crines demittunt. Per τὰ χρύσια quæ- libet aurea ornamenta comprehenduntur, ut sunt monilia, catenæ, annuli, inaures, frontalia, &c. Paulus 1. Tim. II. vers. 9. μὴ ἐν μαργαρίταις. So- lent enim modo margaritis modo auro se ornare fœminæ. Sanct. Hieronymus ad Lætam de instit. filiæ: Nec caput, ait, gemmis oneres, nec capillum irrufes, & ei aliquid de gehennæ ignibus auspiceris. Consueverant enim crines & vultum cerussa, sti- bio, aliisque pigmentis colorare, & qui hæc pa- rabant, à cinere fucorum vocabantur cinerarii & cinislones, ut habet Teraquell. leg. 2. concub. n. 27. Fœminas ejusmodi graviter redarguit S. Cypria- nus l. de discipl. & habit. virgin. Fæminæ, inquit, manus Deo inferunt, quando id, quod ille formavit, reformare, & transfigurare contendunt, nescien- tes, quia opus Dei est omne, quod nascitur, Dia- boli, quodcunque reformatur. Dominus tuus dicit: Non potes facere capillum unum album aut nigrum, & tu ad vincendam Domini tui vocem vis te esse potiorem. Audaci conatu, & sacrilego contemptu crines tuos inficis. Non metuis oro, quæ talis es, ne cum resurrectionis dies venerit, artifex tuus te non recognoscat, & ad sua præmia & promis- sa venientem removeat, & excludat, increpans vigore censoris & judicis dicat: Opus hoc meum non est, nec imago nostra est. Cutem falso medi- camine polluisti, crinem adultero colore mutasti, expugnata est mendacio facies, figura corrupta est, vultus alienus est. Deum videre non poteris, quando oculi non tui sunt, quos Deus fecit, sed quos Diabolus infecit. Per τὰ ἱμάτια non tantum ex- teriora, ut pallia sunt, Matth. IX. vers. 20. cap. XXI. vers. 7. sed in genere quævis vestimenta, ut Matth. XI. vers. 8. cap. XXVII. vers. 35. intelligun- tur. Paulus ejus vice habet, 1. Tim. II. vers. 9. μὴ ἐν ἱματισμῷ πολυτελεῖ. Hæc non eo accipienda, quasi vel omnis omnino cultus à Petro prohibea- tur, ut in Pelagio refellit Hieronymus lib. 1. contr. Pelag. quia secundum usitatum Ebraïsmum verba negantia pro comparatis ponuntur, 1. Tim. II. v. 8. vel quod tantum illa ad fideles Petri ævo perti- neant: Sed quod excessus & cultus semper, & omni ævo fugiendus sit. Modestus vero & hone- stus corporis cultus & ornatus adhibendus pro conditionis & status cujusvis ratione: Quanto ma- gis vitanda ad lasciviam excogitata vestimenta & ornamenta? Quo de S. Hieronymus epist. de vita contubern. Caliga (calceus) ambulantis nigella ac nitens stridore ad se juvenes vocat: papillæ fasciolis comprimuntur, & crispanti angulo angustius pectus arctatur, capilli vel in frontem vel in aures diffluunt, palliolum interdum cadit, ut nitidos nudet humeros, &c. Duplex, inquit Tertull. de habit. mulier. est cultus fæminæ, sc. mundus muliebris in auro, gem- mis & vestibus, & ornatus, quem immundum mulicbrem convenit dici, in cura capilli, cutis & earum partium corporis, quæ oculos trahunt. Illi crimen ambitionis intendimus, huic prostitutionis.

## 3:4
v. 4. But the hidden man of the heart) He uses the masculine, although he is speaking of women, because this precept is such that it can apply to either sex: The hidden man of the heart is the same as the inward man, Rom. 7:22, where see the notes: In like manner the Jew in secret, Rom. 2:29, and the secrets of the heart, 1 Cor. 14:25. For the heart, לֵב, is taken by the Hebrews for the internal parts of the soul, Ecclesiastes 11:9, 10, and elsewhere. Mystical sense, Psalm 45:13 and Exodus 28:13.

In the incorruptible of the meek and quiet spirit) that is, with a gentle and modest disposition, which does not allow itself to be corrupted by evil examples. I take spirit here for a disposition of the soul, as in 1 Cor. 4:21, Gal. 6:1. For the Hebrews often take רוּחַ in this way. Incorruptible here means that which does not allow itself to be spoiled. Thus in incorruptibility, Eph. 6:4. Paul requires incorruptibility in a similar way, Tit. 2:7. What quietness is, see 1 Tim. 2:11, 12.

Cornelius à Lapide interprets the hidden man of the heart as the immortal soul hidden by man; but from the opposition of the interior and exterior man, it is clear that the man, insofar as he is reborn, comes under the name of the interior man, and that this name cannot be restricted to the mind alone, just as regeneration does not pertain to the mind alone. However, there is no doubt that the soul is especially regarded, which he requires to be quiet and modest, especially in women. Ambrose, epistle 27, says: The exterior man has very many members in himself: but the interior man of the heart is entirely wisdom, full of grace, full of beauty. By incorruptibility, Cornelius understands chastity and purity of spirit, which is opposed to the corruption of the body, as well as the integrity of a meek soul, which is not corrupted by any sicknesses of the passions, no anger, pride, envy, etc. But the former explanation is less suitable: for incorruptibility is said in relation to a quiet and modest spirit, not absolutely. It indeed pleases Jerome (l. c.), Bede, and the Ordinary Gloss, saying: because your exterior man is corrupted, and you cease to have the blessedness of integrity which is proper to virgins, imitate the incorruption of the spirit through abstinence. But the sanctification of body and soul cannot be denied to pious spouses, 1 Tim. 2:15, Rev. 14:4. Therefore the latter is more correct, with which the Grotius interpretation agrees: The external adornment of the body is perishable and corruptible: the internal adornment of the soul is constant and incorruptible. Nazianzen, against women adorning themselves ambitiously, says: To noble women, not gold, not purple, not pigments bring ornament, but their ornament is the probity of their morals and elegance. Tertullian, On the Apparel of Women: Come forth, he says, now you women, instructed with the ornaments of the Apostles, taking candor from simplicity, a blush from modesty, painting your eyes with bashfulness and your spirit with silence, inserting the word of God into your ears, binding the yoke of Christ to your necks, submit your heads to your husbands, and you will be sufficiently adorned. Keep your hands occupied with wool, fix your feet at home, and you will please more than in gold: Clothe yourselves in the silk of probity, the fine linen of holiness, the purple of modesty: Thus painted, you will have God as your lover. By spirit here, Athanasius (to Serapion) understands the Holy Spirit, whose fruit is modesty, Gal. 5:22. But the human spirit is more correctly understood, with Ambrose, Book 1, On Duties, chapter 18.

Which is in the sight of God of great price.) That 'which' refers to the whole preceding clause. Other things are of value among men: hair, gold, splendid garments: but before God, a gentle and modest soul, and one uncorrupted against evil morals. Of great price is used of ointment in Mark 14:3, and of women's clothing in 1 Tim. 2:9. It corresponds to the Hebrew יָקָר in Proverbs 1:13.

The Vulgate refers that 'which' to the spirit: Which spirit is rich in the sight of God. And Ambrose, Book 4, ep. 27: Truly rich, who can seem rich in the sight of God, in whose sight the earth is small, the world itself is narrow. But God knows only him to be rich who is rich for eternity, who stores up not the fruits of wealth but of virtues. But who is rich before God except a quiet and

modest spirit, which is never corrupted. Does he not seem rich to you who has peace of soul, the tranquility of quietness, so that he desires nothing, is agitated by no storms of desires, nor loathes the old and seeks the new, and by always desiring becomes needy in the midst of great riches. That is the peace that is truly rich, which surpasses all understanding, rich peace, rich modesty, rich faith (for to the faithful the whole world is a possession), rich simplicity. For there are also riches of simplicity, which discusses nothing, thinks nothing contracted, suspicious, or fraudulent, but pours itself out with a pure affection, etc. Estius renders the sense thus: Which spirit or soul, adorned with such virtues, is a thing precious in the sight of God, that is, very pleasing to God.

Latin:

v. 4. Ἀλλ᾽ ὁ κρυπτὸς τῆς καρδίας ἄνθρωπος) Masculino uti- tur, cum de fœminis loquatur, quia præceptum hoc tale est, ut possit utrique sexui convenire: Ὁ κρυπτὸς τῆς καρδίας ἄν- θρωπος idem, quod ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος, Rom. 7, 22. ubi dicta vide: Pari modo ὁ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ Ἰουδαῖος, Rom. II. 29. & τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς καρδίας, 1. Cor. 14, 25. Καρδία enim לֵב Ebræis su- mitur pro internis animi, Ecclesiastæ 11, 9. 10. & alibi. My- sticus sensus Psal. 45, 13. & Exod. XXVIII, 13.

Ἐν τῷ ἀφθάρτῳ τοῦ πραέος καὶ ἡσυχίου πνεύματος) id est cum affectu leni & modesto, qui se à malis exemplis corrum- pi non sinit. Spiritum hic sumo pro affectu animi, ut 1. Cor. 4. v. 21. Gal. 6, 1. Nam Ebræi רוּחַ sæpe sic sumunt. Ἄφθαρτον hic quod vitiari se non patitur. Sic ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ Eph. 6, 4. Ἀφθαρσίαν pari modo exigit Paulus, Tit. II. 7. Quid sit ἡσυχία. Vide 1. Tim. II. 11. 12.

Absconditum cordis hominem de anima immor- tali ab homine abscondita interpretatur Cornelius à Lapide; sed ex oppositione interioris, & exterioris hominis patet, hominem qua renatus est, interioris nomine venire, nec ad hominis mentem solam id nominis restringi posse, quemadmodum nec ad mentem solam pertinet regeneratio. Maxime ta- men animum respici, dubium non est, quem im- primis in fœminis requirit quietum & modestum. Ambrosius epistola 27. Exterior homo, ait, plurima in se membra habet: interior autem cordis homo totus sapientia est, plenus gratiæ, plenus decoris. Per ἀφθαρ- σίαν Cornelius castitatem, & puritatem Spiritus in- telligit, quæ opponatur corruptioni corporis, nec non integritatem animi mansueti, qui nullis passio- num ægritudinibus, nulla ira, superbia, invidia &c. corrumpatur. Sed prior explicatio minus conve- nit: dicitur enim ἀφθαρσία relate ad quietum & mo- destum Spiritum, non absolute. Placet quidem Hie- ronymo l. c. Beda & Gloss. Ordin. q. d. quia exterior vester homo corruptus est, & beatitudinem integrita- tis, quæ propria est virginum, habere desistis, imita- mini incorruptionem Spiritus per abstinentiam. Sed ἁγιασμὸς corporis & animi denegari non potest piis conjugibus, 1. Tim. 2, 15. Apoc. 14, 4. Rectius ergo se habet posterior, cui Grotiana convenit: Ex- ternus corporis cultus est caducus, & corruptibilis: Internus animi cultus est constans & incorruptibi- lis. Nazianzenus adversus mulieres ambitiose se ornantes: Nobilibus, ait, fœminis non aurum, non purpura, non pigmenta ornamentum afferunt, sed earum ornatus est morum probitas, & elegantia. Tertullianus de habitu mulierum: Prodite, inquit, jam vos mulieres ornamentis instructæ Apostolorum, sumentes de simplicitate candorem, de pudicitia ru- borem, depictæ oculos verecundia & Spiritus taci- turnitate, inserentes in aures sermonem Dei, anne- ctentes cervicibus jugum Christi, caput maritis subji- cite, & satis ornatæ eritis. Manus lanis occupatæ, pe- des domi figite, & plus quam in auro placebitis: Vestite vos serico probitatis, byssino sanctitatis, purpura pu- dicitiæ: Taliter pigmentatæ Deum habebitis ama- torem. Per Spiritum hic Athanasius ad Serap. Spi- ritum S. intelligit, cujus fructus est modestia, Gal. 6, 22. Sed rectius Spiritus humanus intelligitur cum Ambrosio l. I. Officior. cap. 18.

Ὁ ἐστιν ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ πολυτελές.) Illud ὅ ad totum præce- dens membrum refertur. Alia apud homines sunt in pretio, coma, aurum, splendidæ vestes: at apud Deum animus lenis ac modestus, & contra malos mores incorruptus. Πολυτε- λὲς de unguento habes Marc. 14. v. 3. de veste muliebri, 1. Tim. 2, 9. Respondet Ebræo יָקָר Prov. I. 13.

Illud ὃ refert ad Spiritum Vulgata: Qui Spiritus in conspectu Dei est locuples. Et Ambrosius l. 4. ep. 27. Vere dives, qui in conspectu Dei potest dives videri, in cujus conspectu terra exigua, mundus ipse angustus est. Sed solum illum Deus divitem novit, qui sit dives æternitati, qui non opum sed virtutum fructus recon- dat. Quis autem ante Deum dives nisi quietus &

modestus Spiritus, qui nunquam corrumpitur. Nonne tibi videtur dives, qui habet pacem animi, tranquillitatem quietis, ut nihil concupiscat, nullis exagitetur cupiditatum procellis, nec vetera fasti- diat & nova quaerat, & semper desiderando fiat in summis divitiis inops. Ea est pax vere dives, quae su- perat omnem mentem, dives pax, dives modestia, dives fides (fideli enim totus mundus possessio est) di- ves simplicitas. Sunt enim & divitiae simplicitatis, quae nihil discutit, nihil contractum, nihil suspectum aut fraudulentum putat, sed puro se effundit affectu, &c. Sensum Estius ita reddit: Qui Spiritus sive animus ejusmodi virtutibus ornatus res est in con- spectu Dei pretiosa, id est, Deo valde grata.

## 3:5
v. 5. For after this manner in the old time the holy women also, who trusted in God, adorned themselves) Namely, with the virtues of the soul. He says holy women, who trusted in God, in which sense to trust is accustomed to have after it 'in' or 'upon', just as the Hebrew בטח draws after it ב. In the manuscript here there is 'in' instead of 'upon'.

Being in subjection to their own husbands) as above v. 1. If the matrons of the old covenant did this, how much more those who belong to Christ?

As if, indeed, the matrons of the old covenant had not belonged to Christ? Paul taught the contrary by the example of Sarah and Rahab, Heb. 11. If they were without Christ, how could they have obtained salvation, which is nothing outside of Christ, Acts 4:12. The Synod of Jerusalem also defined the contrary, Acts 15:11. And did not Grotius himself profess afterwards concerning Christian women: You were daughters (of Sarah) by flesh; but through the Gospel you have been made daughters also by her character. Which must be said even more of faith, which is the mother of all virtues pleasing to God. The Apostle wishes to say this: With these virtues the holy women of old, your progenitors, whose hope was in God, adorned themselves, being subject to their own husbands, namely with a meek and quiet Spirit, as if to say, they considered themselves beautifully adorned and decorated only if they showed themselves subject and obedient to their husbands. Strength and beauty are her clothing, says Solomon concerning the holy woman, Prov. 31:25. Crates from the Philosophers says: That which makes a woman more honorable adorns her: but it is not gold, not emerald, not scarlet that makes her such, but whatever things have the mark of gravity, moderation, and modesty. Saint Peter here designated the virtues of a woman: 1. obedience toward husbands, 2. chastity, 3. fear of God, 4. pure conversation, 5. moderate bodily adornment and clothing, 6. meekness, 7. a tranquil Spirit. All those shine forth in the example of Sarah, concerning whom it follows now.

Latin:

v. 5. Οὕτω γάρ ποτε καὶ αἱ ἅγιαι γυναῖκες, αἱ ἐλπίζουσαι ἐπὶ τὸν Θεὸν, ἐκόσμουν ἑαυτὰς) Nempe animi virtutibus. Foeminae inquit sanctae, quae Deo confidebant, quo sensu ἐλπίζειν solet post se habere εἰς vel ἐπὶ sicut Ebraeum בטח post se tra- hit ב. In Manuscripto hic est εἰς pro ἐπὶ.

Ὑποτασσόμεναι τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν) ut supra v. 1. Si veteris foederis matronae hoc fecere, quanto magis eae, quae ad Christum pertineant?

Quasi vero matronae foederis veteris ad Chri- stum non pertinuissent? Contrarium exemplo Sarae & Rahabis docuit Paulus Ebr. 11. Si sine Chri- sto fuere, quomodo salutem adipisci potuerunt, quae nulla est extra Christum, Act. 4, 12. Contra- rium etiam definivit Synodus Hierosolymitana, Act. 15, 11. Et annon postea de Christianis foeminis professus est ipse Grotius: Eratis carne (Sarae) filiae; sed per Evangelium factae estis & moribus ejus filiae. Quod magis de fide dicendum, quae mater omnium virtutum Deo gratarum. Id vult dicere Apostolus: His virtutibus olim sanctae mulieres progenitrices vestrae, quarum spes erat in Deo, sese ornabant, subjectae propriis viris, scilicet cum mansueto & quieto Spiritu, q. d. ita demum se reputabant pul- chre comptas & ornatas, si viris suis subditas & obedientes semetipsas exhiberent. Fortitudo & decor indumentum ejus, inquit Salomo de sancta muliere, Prov. 31, 25. E Philosophis Crates: Ornat, inquit, mulierem, quod honestiorem facit: Talem vero praestat non aurum, non Smaragdus, non coccus, sed quaecunque gravitatis, moderationis & pudoris spe- cimen habent. Sanctus Petrus hic virtutes mulieris designavit, primo obedientiam erga maritos. 2. ca- stitatem, 3. timorem Dei, 4. puram conversationem, 5. moderatum corporis cultum & vestitum, 6. man- suetudinem, 7. tranquillum Spiritum. Omnes illae in exemplo Sarae pellucent, de qua jam sequitur.

## 3:6
v. 6. As Sarah obeyed Abraham) Often an article must be added to proper Hebrew names to recognize the case in indeclinable words. You see the obedience of Sarah in Gen. 12:5, ch. 18:6, ch. 20:1, and elsewhere: and note that Sarah is called by this name, as if you were to say 'queen,' for the reason that many kings were to proceed from her.

Calling him Lord) אדני, as it is in Gen. 18:12; they were accustomed to say בעלי in the same sense, as in Gen. 20:3, Exod. 21:3, Joel 1:8, and sometimes this is in the book of morals. The Attics imitated this in the Knights of Aristophanes: 'You will lead Smicythus and the Lord.' To which place the Scholiast says: 'It is customary in the introductions of accusations to hide [the name], whenever an accusation is brought against a woman: For thus they are accustomed to challenge in the court. Such-and-such a woman and the Lord, that is, the husband.' At Rome also, it was the custom to speak thus in the past. With corrupted morals, the contrary custom grew, so that wives were called 'mistresses' by their husbands.

She herself was called Sarah by God, that is, mistress: Nevertheless, she does not conduct herself as a mistress, but acknowledges Abraham as lord.

Whose children you have become) You were her daughters by flesh, but through the Gospel you have been made her daughters also by character. A similar expression, Matt. 3:9, John 8:39, Rom. 9:7-8, Gal. 4:28.

Doing good) Just as Sarah received guests.

And not fearing any terror) That is, toward no terror, fearful of no terrors, namely, of betraying their modesty, which the provincial magistrates often attempted even with threats. Just as Sarah did not yield to the desire of Abimelech, Gen. 20. You have 'terror' in Luke 21:9, 24:37.

By the word 'doing good' not only beneficence, but the pursuit of good works is designated in general, as in ch. II. 14, 15, 20, ch. III. 17, ch. IV. 19, and here in the Syriac, which renders it 'in good works': just as 'confidence' is added to them, meaning that they ought to be μεγαλόψυχοι (great-souled), not fearing any disturbance, as the Vulgate has it, but resting in the protection of God with great confidence of mind and strength. Πτόησις properly signifies not disturbance, nor can it be explained as lust, as Salmero wishes, because Aristotle calls the excessive ardor of lust in women by that name, which sense Cornelius à Lapide criticizes as less chaste, but it signifies dread and consternation from πτοεῖσθαι, which is to be made afraid, Luke 21:9, ch. 24:37, in which sense it occurs frequently among the LXX Interpreters, Exod. 19:16, Jos. 7:5, 1 Par. 22:13, Job 23:15, Hab. 3:6. By 'dread,' however, the evil which is the cause of dread is understood, Prov. 1:26, ch. 3:25, as if to say: pious and faithful wives are not held by any dread, but so trust in the gracious protection of GOD that they do not fear any evil for themselves in a preposterous way. For just as they are called children of Abraham who follow the footsteps of the faith of Abraham, Rom. IV. v. 12, so also they are daughters of Sarah who imitate the faith of Sarah. Compare Isa. LI. 1, seqq.

Latin:

v. 6. Ὡς Σάῤῥα ὑπήκουσε τῷ Ἀβραάμ) Saepe nominibus propriis Ebraicis debet addi Articulus ad noscendum casum ἐν τοῖς ἀκλίτοις. Obedientiam Sarae vides Gen. 12, 5. c. 18, 6. c. 20, 1. & alibi: & nota Saram dictam hoc nomine, quasi ἄνασ- σαν dicas, ideo quod multi ab ea Reges erant prodituri.

Κύριον αὐτὸν καλέσα) אדני, ut est Gen. 18, 12. solebant & בעלי sensu eodem dicere, ut Gen. 20, 3. Exod. 21, 3 Joel. 1, 8. & aliquoties est hoc in libro מוסר. Imitati Attici sic in equi- tibus Aristophanis: Διάξεις Σμικύθην καὶ Κύριον. Ad quem locum Scholiastes: ἔστιν ἐν ταῖς εἰσαγωγαῖς τῶν ἐγκλημάτων κρύπτειν εἰώθασιν, ἐπειδὰν γυναικὶ ἐπιφέρεται ἔγκλημα· Οὕτω γὰρ προκαλεῖσθαι εἰώθασιν ἐν τῷ δικαστηρίῳ. Ἡ δεῖνα κᾀ ὁ Κύριος τουτέστιν ὁ ἀνὴρ, Romae & olim sic loqui mos erat. Corruptis moribus mos inolevit contrarius, ut uxores a maritis do- minae vocarentur.

Vocata est ipsa a Deo Sara, id est, domina: Ni- hilominus non ceu dominam se gerit, sed Abra- hamum dominum agnoscit.

Ἧς ἐγενήθητε τέκνα) Eratis carne ejus filiae, sed per Evan- gelium factae estis & moribus ejus filiae. Par loquutio, Matth 3, 9. Joh. VIII. 39. Rom. IX. 7. 8. Gal. IV. 28.

Ἀγαθοποιοῦσαι) Sicut Sara excepit hospites.

Καὶ μὴ φοβούμεναι μηδεμίαν πτόησιν) Id est πρὸς μηδεμίαν πτόησιν, ad nulla terriculamenta pavidae, nempe ad proden- dam pudicitiam, quam magistratus provinciarum saepe etiam minis attentabant. Sicut Sara Abimelechi cupiditati non cessit, Gen. XX. Πτοήσεως habes Luc. XXI. 9. XXIV 37.

Voce ἀγαθοποιοῦσαι non tantum beneficentia, sed studium bonorum operum in genere designatur, ut cap. II. 14. 15. 20. cap. III. 17. cap. IV. 19. & hic apud Syrum reddentem in operibus bonis: quem- admodum illi additur fiducia, quod nempe de- beant esse μεγαλόψυχοι, non pertimentes ullam perturbationem, ut habet Vulgata, sed in Dei prote- ctione magna animi fiducia & robore acquiescen- tes. Πτόησις proprie non perturbationem signifi- cat, nec de libidine explicari potest, ut Salmero vult, quod Aristoteles nimium ardorem libidinis in fœminis ita vocet, quem sensum ceu minus castum perstringit Cornelius à Lapide, sed pavorem & con- sternationem significat à πτοεῖσθαι, quod est pave- fieri, Luc. 21, 9. cap. 24, 37. quo sensu apud LXX. Interpretes frequenter occurrit, Exod. 19. v. 16. Jos. 7, 5. 1. Par. 22, 13. Job. 23, 15. Hab. 3, 6. Per pa- vorem autem malum, quod est pavoris causa, in- telligitur, Prov. 1, 26. c. 3, 25. q. d. uxores piæ & fideles non tenentur ullo pavore, sed ita in gratio- so DEI præsidio confidunt, ut à nullo malo præ- postere sibi timeant. Ut enim filii Abrahæ dicun- tur, qui fidei Abrahæ vestigia sectantur, Rom. IV. v. 12. ita etiam filiæ Saræ sunt, quæ fidem Saræ imi- tantur. Conf. Es. LI. 1. seqq.

## 3:7
v. 7. Οἱ ἄνδρες ὁμοίως (Likewise, ye husbands) that is, in turn. Συνοικοῦντες κατὰ γνῶσιν (dwelling with them according to knowledge) Here also 'be' is understood. Συνοικεῖν is properly said of spouses, as can be seen in the Greek Gen. XX, 3, Deut. XX, 7, XXII, 13, XXIV, 1, Prov. XXX, 23, Isa. LXII, 5, Sirach XXV, 11, XLII, 13, 15. It comprehends, however, by a certain synecdoche, all the duties of spouses toward one another. Κατὰ γνῶσιν, that is, according to that knowledge of the divine will which you have obtained through the Gospel. See Rom. XV, 14, 1 Cor. VI, 6. Ὡς ἀσθενεστέρῳ σκεύει τῷ γυναικείῳ ἀπονέμοντες τὴν τιμὴν (giving honor unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel) σκεῦος signifies everything that we use, and is also said of men, as Acts IX, 15, Rom. IX, 21, 22. The wife is the instrument of the husband. Aristotle, Polit. l. 3, 'weaker' than the man, as the same Aristotle speaks, l. 3, of the Economics. Quintilian rightly explains this in Declamation CCCVIII: 'Woman is a weak thing, and it adds no small weight to her natural infirmity that she is a widow.' Therefore the wife is to be treated gently, which here says 'to have honor,' which expression is also in the book Musar: 'Just as a certain honor is held for crystal vessels, because they are handled with care.'

He subjoins the duties of men to the duties of women, just as was also done by Paul, Eph. 5:33, Col. 3:18, 19, 1 Tim. 2:8, 9. Knowledge is required in men. For a man in the house is as an eye, a lamp, and a Sun teaching and illuminating the whole house, as Bede says here. By 'honor,' however, is not meant abstinence from the use of marriage, as Jerome l. 1 against Jovinian and Hessel, with Estius not denying it, or the conjugal debt, as Lorinus from Turrianus, but what 'honor' properly denotes is signified, as Oecumenius explains, and under it gentleness is comprehended. Which sense Cornelius à Lapide approves. We do not, however, deny that prudent moderation is also to be applied in the act of marriage, and that it is simultaneously comprehended here, just as the word συνοικεῖν occurs specifically regarding that in Deut. 22:13, compare 1 Cor. 7:5, but that pertains to τὸ συνοικεῖν κατὰ γνῶσιν, and not indeed to τιμὴν, as Lorinus wishes. By which word the honor appropriate to women is noted. Nor indeed by τὸ σκεῦος 1. Thess. 4:4, is the wife understood, but the body of each man as the dwelling place of the soul. Here, however, wives are compared to vessels because they are instruments divinely ordained for the generation and education of children and the administration of family affairs. For a woman by her own nature is timid, modest, and faint-hearted: the medicine for this fear, modesty, and faint-heartedness is honor, if she sees, namely, that she is honored by her husband. For women are weak, both in sex and constitution, and in mind and judgment, and in art, industry, and wisdom for managing affairs. Compare 1 Cor. 13:22. Whence Chrysostom, hom. 26 on 1 Corinthians: 'Consider that a woman is a weak vessel. You, however, husband, having been made a Prince and given in the place of a head, so that you may bear the weakness of the subject. You wish therefore to illustrate your leadership; you will do that if you do not insult the subject, etc.' Where he praises the example of Isocrates, who, when asked how he tolerated the ways of a wicked and drunken wife, replied: 'So that I may have a gymnasium and a wrestling school of philosophy (patience) at home.' For I shall be, he said, gentle with others, since I am trained in tolerating her daily.

Ὡς καὶ συγκληρονόμοι χάριτος ζωῆς (As being heirs together of the grace of life) that is, life-giving, as we said above I. 3. Both men and women are participants of the Evangelical grace, which leads to eternal life. In the Manuscript it is ποικίλης χάριτος ζωῆς (of the manifold grace of life) because of the various gifts of the Spirit.

Although unequal in sex, women are nevertheless equal to their husbands in grace. The Greek συγκληρονόμοι seems to refer to the husbands; but if husbands are co-heirs with their wives, wives in turn are co-heirs with their husbands: although the Greek can also be taken in that way, as Estius notes, as if the women themselves were co-heirs of the grace of life, as the Syriac has it here. The 'grace of life' is not the Evangelical grace leading to life, but it is the grace bestowing life, Rom. VI, last, because they are called co-heirs not by reason of the Gospel, but by reason of salvation, which is our inheritance, 1 Pet. I:4. It is called the grace of life by a certain species of metonymy for life to be given from grace, as the Syriac rendered it. Jerome also reads: 'And as co-heirs of manifold grace.' But because that does not agree with either the Greeks or the Latins, it seems credible to Estius that the blessed Jerome, citing from memory, took that word from ch. IV:10.

That your prayers be not hindered) The Latin correctly reads ἐγκόπλεσθαι. For that is to be hindered, as in Acts 24:4, Rom. 15:22, Gal. 5:7, 1 Thess. 2:18. Whence ἐγκοπὴ, 1 Cor. 9:12. From harsh treatment follow quarrels and strife, which hinder prayers, that is, the power and efficacy of prayers. For prayers do not please GOD unless they proceed from a tranquil mind.

It is not right to emend Greek Codices from Latin ones. Ἐκκόπλεσθαι, as Cornelius admits, means they are broken off, intercepted. For if a woman is treated harshly by her husband, through that strife and quarreling, prayers are intercepted, to which nothing is so contrary as anger, strife, and perturbation of mind. Cf. Matt. 10:23, Sir. 25:1. Thus ἐκκόπτειν is to cut out or cut off, Matt. 3:10, ch. 5:30, to cut through or intercept in Herodian, book 7. This is what the Greek ἐκκόπλεσθαι signifies, says Cornelius, as if to say, lest the power of your prayer be cut into or cut off and enervated. For it is cut into and dashed to pieces by dissension and discord, but it grows together and is strengthened by concord, Matt. 18:19. The interpretation of Jerome, Bede, and the gloss, as also of Estius, is inappropriate: 'impart honor, that is, the conjugal debt to the wife: yet so that your prayers be not hindered.' For that restriction is not found in the Greek, and therefore the former explanation, which is that of Hugo, Dionysius, Lyranus, and others, is deservedly preferred. However, honor is not to be shown to a spouse with the fear prescribed for wives, Eph. 5:33: Nor does a despotic lordship befit a husband, but a marital one over a spouse; and love and honor are reciprocal between spouses, yet neither weakens the husband's lordship or the wife's subjection. A wife is deservedly honored through harmonious cohabitation and gentle governance, yet the wife ought not on that account to exempt herself from subjection. And although the husband is the head of the woman, 1 Cor. 11:3, both spouses are nevertheless equally obligated to the fruit of concord and mutual love, 1 Cor. 7:4, Eph. 5:29, Col. 3:19.

PART II. General exhortations to charity and holiness.

Latin:

v. 7. Οἱ ἄνδρες ὁμοίως) id est vicissim. Συνοικοῦντες κατὰ γνῶσιν) Hic quoque subauditur ἔστε. Συνοι- κεῖν proprie de conjugibus dicitur, ut videre est in Græco Gen. XX, 3. Deut. XX. 7. XXII. 13. XXIV. 1. Prov. XXX. 23. Es. LXII, 5. Sirach. XXV. 11. XLII. 13. 15. Comprehendit autem per συνεκδοχὴν quandam omnia inter se conju- gum officia. Κατὰ γνῶσιν id est secundum eam notitiam divinæ voluntatis, quam per Evangelium estis adepti. Vide Rom. XV. 14. 1. Cor. VI. 6. Ὡς ἀσθενεστέρῳ σκεύει τῷ γυναικείῳ ἀπονέμοντες τὴν τιμὴν) σκεῦος omne id, quo utimur, significat, diciturque etiam de hominibus, ut Act. IX. 15. Rom. IX. 21. 22. Uxor ὄργανον viri. Aristoteles Polit. l. 3. ἀσθενέστερον viro, ut loquitur idem Aristot. l. 3. Oeconomicorum. Quintilianus id recte ex- plicat declamatione CCCVIII. Imbecilla res est fœmina, & affert infirmitati naturali non leve pondus, quod vidua est. Propterea leniter tractanda uxor, quod hic dicit τιμὴν ἔχειν, quæ loquutio & in libro Musar: Sicut honor quidam habetur crystallinis, quia solicite tractantur.

Officiis mulierum subjungit Officia virorum, sicut etiam à Paulo factum Eph. 5, 33. Col. 3, 18. 19. 1. Tim. 2, 8. 9. Scientia in viris requiritur. Est n. vir in domo quasi oculus, lucerna, & Sol totam domum do- cens, & illuminans, ut hic Beda. Per honorem autem non vel abstinentia ab usu matrimonii, ut Hieronym. l. 1. contra Jovin. & Hessel. non abnuente Estio, vel debitum conjugale, ut ex Turriano Lorinus, sed quod proprie notat honor, significatur, ut Oecu- menius explicat, & sub eo lenitas comprehenditur. Quem sensum probat Cornelius à Lapide. Non tamen negamus, etiam in συνουσίᾳ adhibendam prudentem moderationem, eamq; simul hic com- prehendi, uti vox συνοικεῖν de eo peculiariter oc- currit Deut. 22, 13. conf. 1. Cor. 7. 5. sed id ad τὸ συνοι- κεῖν κατὰ γνῶσιν, non vero ad τιμὴν, ut Lorinus vult, pertinet. Qua voce honor mulieribus conveniens notatur. Neque vero per τὸ σκεῦος 1. Thess. 4, 4. uxor intelligitur, sed corpus hominis cujusque ceu animæ habitaculum. Hic vero vasis comparantur uxores, quia sunt instrumenta ad generationem & educationem liberorum ac rei familiaris admini- strationem divinitus ordinata. Mulier enim sua na- tura est timida, verecunda & pusillanimis: timoris hujus, pudoris & pusillanimitatis pharma- cum est honor, si videat scilicet, se à marito ho- norari. Infirmæ enim sunt mulieres tum sexu & complexione, tum animo & judicio, tum arte, industria & sapientia ad res gerendas. Conf. 1. Cor. 13. v. 22. Unde Chrysostomus hom. 26. in 1. ad Co- rinth. Considera, mulierem debile vas esse. Tu autem vir propterea Princeps factus & capitis loco datus, ut subdita feras imbecillitatem. Velis igitur tuum illustrare principatum, id facies, si subdita non insul- taveris &c. Ubi laudat exemplum Isocratis, qui rogatus, quomodo mores uxoris pravæ & temulentæ toleraret, respondit, ut gymnasium & palæstram philosophiæ (patientiæ) domi habeam. Ero enim, inquit, cum aliis mansuetus, quum in ea quotidie toleranda erudiar.

Ὡς καὶ συγκληρονόμοι χάριτος ζωῆς) id est ζωοποιούσης, quo- modo diximus supra I. 3. Gratiæ Evangelicæ, quæ ad vi- tam æternam ducit, participes sunt & viri & fœminæ. In Manuscripto est ποικίλης χάριτος ζωῆς propter varia Spi- ritus dona.

Etsi sexu impares, gratia tamen pares maritis sunt mulieres. Græcum συγκληρονόμοι videtur referri ad maritos; sed si cohæredes mariti sunt uxoribus, uxores vicissim cohæredes sunt maritis: quan- quam & Græca ita accipi possint, notante Estio, Tan- quam & coheredes sint gratiæ vitæ ipsæ scilicet mu- lieres, ut hic habet Syrus. Gratia vitæ non est gratia Evangelica ad vitam ducens, sed est gratia vitam largiens Rom. VI. ult. quia cohæredes dicuntur non ratione Evangelii, sed ratione salutis, quæ est hæreditas nostra, 1. Petr. I. 4. Dicitur gratia vitæ per speciem quandam Metonymiæ pro vita ex gra- tia danda, ut Syrus reddidit. Legit & Hieronym. Et sicut cohæredibus multiplicis gratiæ. Sed quia id nec cum Græcis nec cum Latinis consonat, cre- dibile Estio videtur, B. Hieronymum de memoria citantem accepisse verbum istud ex cap. IV. 10.

Εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐγκόπλεσθαι τὰς προσευχὰς ὑμῶν) Latinus recte legit ἐγκόπλεσθαι. Id enim est impediri, ut Act. XXIV. v. 4. Rom. 15, 22. Gal. V. 7. 1. Thess. II. 18. Unde ἐγκοπὴ, 1. Cor. IX. 12. Ex dura tractatione sequuntur jurgia & rixæ, quæ impediunt preces, id est precum vim & efficaciam. Non enim placent DEO preces, nisi quæ ex tranquillo profici- scuntur animo.

Non emendare fas est Græcos Codices è Lati- nis. Ἐκκόπλεσθαι fatente Cornelio est refringantur, intercipiantur. Nam si duriter tractetur mulier à viro, per illam rixam & jurgia preces intercipiun- tur, quibus nihil tam contrarium, quam ira, rixa, animique perturbatio. Conf. Matth. X. 23. Sir. XXV. 1. Ita ἐκκόπτειν est excidere vel exscindere, Matth. III. vers. 10. cap. V. v. 30. intercidere vel intervertere apud Herodianum l. 7. Hoc significat Græcum ἐκκόπλεσθαι, inquit Cornelius, q. d. ne inci- datur vel excidatur & enervetur vis orationis vestræ. Inciditur enim & eliditur per dissidium & discor- diam, coalescit vero & corroboratur per concordiam, Matth. 28, 19. Inconveniens est Hieronymi, Bedæ, & glossæ, ut & Estii interpretatio, impertite honorem, id est, debitum conjugale uxori: Sic tamen, ut non impediantur orationes vestræ. Illa enim re- strictio non habetur in Græco, ideoque prior ex- plicatio, quæ Hugonis, Dionysii, Lyrani & aliorum est, merito præfertur. Non autem honor conjugi exhibendus cum timore uxoribus, Eph. V. v. 33. præ- scripto: Neque convenit marito dominium δεσπο- τικὸν, sed γαμικὸν in conjugem; & amor & ho- nor reciprocus est inter conjuges, neuter tamen vel dominium mariti, vel subjectionem uxoris la- befactat. Merito honoratur uxor per concordem cohabitationem, & mansuetam gubernationem, non tamen uxor propterea à subjectione se exi- mere debet. Et quamvis vir sit mulieris caput, 1. Cor. XI. 3. uterque tamen conjugum ad fructum concordiæ & amorem mutuum æqualiter obliga- tur, 1. Cor. VIII. 4. Eph. V. 29. Col. III. 19.

PARS II. Adhortationes generales ad charitatem, & sanctitatem.

## 3:8
v. 8. Finally) סוֹף דָּבָר, Eccles. 12:13. The sum of my admonitions returns to those things which I shall now say.

From conjugal charity, the Apostle proceeds to the charity to be shown to the neighbor in common. He had spoken of the interior adornment of women; now he subjoins the spiritual adornment of all the pious. The Apostle, says Lyranus, here returns to instructing everyone in common, ordering them first toward the neighbor, v. 9; second toward God, v. 15; third toward oneself, in the following chapter. The first part is subdivided into two, because first he orders them in the conferring of good, v. 9; second in the enduring of evil, v. 10. Moreover, not only Lyranus reads here IN FIDE, instead of in fine, but also Bede, Hugo, and others, since in the Greek Codices it is consistently held as τὸ δὲ τέλος, whom the Syrian follows, as do the more correct Latin Codices.

Πάντες ὁμόφρονες) again, ἐστέ is understood. These admonitions pertain not to men of a certain lot, as some of the preceding ones do, but to all Christians. Moreover, the sense of this admonition is the same as in Rom. XII. 16, XV. 5.

This concord of minds embraces agreement both in the truth of faith and in the holiness of life, which is the foundation of true charity. The Syrian rendered it: Be all in unanimity. Compare especially Rom. XV. 5, 6; 1 Cor. I. 10; 2 Cor. XIII. 11; Eph. IV. 3; Phil. II. 2; c. III. 16.

Συμπαθεῖς) feeling pain for the evils of others. For an example, see Heb. X. 34.

Where there is ὁμόνοια, there is also συμπάθεια, Rom. 12, 15, 16; Phil. II. 1, by which one esteems the misery of others as one's own, and by compassion makes it, as it were, one's own. The Syrian renders it: As those grieving with those who grieve. Compare 1 Cor. XII. 26.

Φιλάδελφοι) The same sense as above II. Hence φιλαδελφία in Rom. XII. 10; 1 Thess. IV. 4; Heb. XIII. 1; 2 Pet. I. 7.

This is [the state] in which we embrace the neighbor, especially the companion in faith, with brotherly love, 1 Pet. I. 22.

Εὔσπλαγχνοι) you have the same word in Eph. IV. 32. It signifies that we ought to be prone to helping others. See Phil. II. 1; Col. III. 12; 1 John III. 7, where there is the noun σπλάγχνα, corresponding to the Hebrew רחמים.

Σπλάγχνα are the bowels, from which the heart is most excellent. By the name of the heart, metonymically, the movements of the heart toward commiseration and beneficence are noted, such as are found especially in parents because of the 5οργή implanted by nature, 1 Kings 3, 29; compare Jer. 31, 10; Prov. 12, 10. Mercy, according to Augustine, book 9 of The City of God, ch. 5, is a certain compassion in our heart for the misery of another, by which, indeed, if we are able, we are compelled to assist.

Φιλόφρονες) Courteous; thus φιλοφρόνως, courteously, Acts XXVIII. v. 7 and 2 Macc. III. 9. In the Manuscript, instead of φιλόφρονες, there is ταπεινόφρονες, which word you have in Prov. XVIII. 23. And it is from this that certain Latin Codices have 'humble'.

Cornelius a Lapide argues here that the Greek text is corrupt, because the Vulgate has two words, 'modest, humble'. But most Greek Codices read Φιλόφρονες; few have ταπεινόφρονες. Those in Acts 28, 7 are called courteous and affable, such as both the modest and the humble are; whence also the Syrian used that word which denotes the meek and humble. B. Luther rendered it 'freundlich'. Therefore, it designates the sweetness of manners in common life, courtesy, affability, and humanity: which is altogether required by those who desire to pursue charity and lead a tranquil life; in Col. III. 12 and Eph. IV. 23 it is called χρησότης. Meekness and humility are like foster-sisters, says St. Bernard in Apoc. XII.

Latin:

v. 8. Τὸ δὲ τέλος) סוֹף דָּבָר, Eccles. XII. 13. Summa monitorum meorum ad ea redit, quæ jam dicam.

A charitate conjugali ad charitatem in com- muni proximo praestandam progreditur Aposto- lus. Dixerat de interiori ornatu mulierum, jam subjungit spiritualem ornatum omnium piorum. Apostolus, inquit Lyranus, hic revertitur ad infor- mandum omnes communiter ordinando primo eos ad proximum v. 9. secundo ad Deum, v. 15. tertio ad seipsum cap. seq. Prima pars subdividitur in duas, quia primo ordinat eos in collatione boni v. 9. secun- do in perpessione mali v. 10. Caeterum legit hic non Lyranus tantum IN FIDE, pro in fine, sed etiam Beda, Hugo aliique, quum in Graecis Codicibus constanter habeatur τὸ δὲ τέλος, quos sequitur Syrus, sequuti & correctiores Codd. Latini.

Πάντες ὁμόφρονες) iterum subauditur ἐστέ. Pertinent haec monita non ad certae sortis homines, ut quaedam praece- dentium, sed ad omnes Christianos. Est autem hujus moniti sensus idem, qui Rom. XII. 16. XV. 5.

Haec concordia animorum consensionem tum in fidei veritate, tum in vita sanctitate, quae funda- mentum est verae charitatis, complectitur. Syrus reddidit: Sitis omnes in unanimitate. Conf. impri- mis Rom. XV. 5. 6. 1. Cor. I. 10. 2. Cor. XIII. 11. Eph. IV. 3. Phil. II. 2. c. III. 16.

Συμπαθεῖς) indolentes alii aliorum malis. Exemplum vid. Ebr. X. 34.

Ubi ὁμόνοια, ibi etiam συμπάθεια, Rom. 12, 15. 16. Phil. II. 1. qua aliorum miseriam quis pro sua aestimat, eamque compassione quasi suam facit. Syrus reddit: Sicut dolentes cum iis, qui dolent. Conf. 1. Cor. XII. 26.

Φιλάδελφοι) Idem sensus qui supra II. Hinc φιλαδελ- φία Rom. XII. 10. 1. Thess. IV. 4. Ebr. XIII. 1. 2. Petr. I. 7.

Haec est cum amore fraterno proximum, im- primis fidei socium complectimur, 1. Petr. I. 22.

Εὔσπλαγχνοι) habes eandem vocem Eph. IV. 32. Signi- ficat pronos nos esse debere ad juvandos alios. Vide Phil. II. 1. Col. III. 12. 1. Joh. III. 7. ubi est nomen σπλάγχνα respondens Ebraeo רחמים.

Σπλάγχνα viscera sunt, e quibus cor praestan- tissimum. Cordis autem nomine Metonymice mo- tus cordis ad commiserationem & beneficentiam notatur, quales maxime in parentibus ob 5οργὴν natura implantatam reperire est, 1. Reg. 3, 29. conf. Jerem. 31, 10. Prov. 12, 10. Misericordia, secundum Augustinum libr. 9. de civit. Dei, c. 5. est alienae mi- seriae quaedam in corde nostro compassio, qua utique, si possumus subvenire, compellimur.

Φιλόφρονες) Comes, sic φιλοφρόνως comiter Act. XXVIII. v. 7. & 2. Macc. III. 9. In Manuscripto pro φιλόφρονες est τα- πεινόφρονες, quam vocem habes Prov. XIIX. 23. Et inde est, quod Latini quidam Codices habent humiles.

Cornelius a Lapide textum Graecum hic corru- ptionis arguit, quia Vulgata duas voces habet, modesti, humiles. Sed plerique Codices Graeci le- gunt Φιλόφρονες, pauci habent ταπεινόφρονες. Illi Act. 28, 7. comes & affabiles dicuntur, quales & modesti & humiles sunt; unde & Syrus ea voce usus, quae notat mansuetos & humiles. B. Lutherus reddidit freundlich. Designatur ergo suavitas mo- rum in vita communi, comitas, affabilitas, & hu- manitas: quae omnino requiritur ab iis, qui chari- tatem sectari, & vitam tranquillam ducere cupiunt, Col. III. 12. & Eph. IV. 23. dicitur χρησότης. Mansue- tudo & humilitas sunt velut sorores collactaneae, ait S. Bernhardus in Apoc. XII.

## 3:9
v. 9. Not rendering evil for evil) You have the same in Rom. XII. 17. where there is also more on this matter.

Or railing for railing) See above II. 22.

But contrariwise, blessing) Rather, on the contrary, praying well for them, Matth. V. 44.

Knowing that hereunto you were called) By this law you were called. So also above II. 10. That word 'knowing' is missing in the Manuscript, and in the Syriac.

That you should inherit a blessing) for the partaking of eternal goods. There is an antanaklasis in the word 'blessing,' which signifies now good words, now good deeds. Is God so liberal to you in things: and would you be sparing in words?

To the commandment of Christian charity is subjoined the interdict of private revenge, which is most opposed to it, by which is prohibited the vengeance of both real and verbal injuries, such as Christians suffered most from the infidels in whose midst they lived. Compare Prov. XX, 22. chap. XXIV, 29. 1. Thess. V, 5. Luc. VI, 37. Under 'blessing,' however, he also includes 'beneficence,' as is evident from Matth. V. 14. He adds an argument from the will of God, who called us to this, that not only the curse under which we were might be taken away, but also that a blessing might be conferred upon us in Christ, Eph. I, 3. Gal. III, 8. sqq. The emphasis is on the word 'knowing,' therefore it is not to be omitted. That 'that' (ἵνα), however, is not to be referred to the more remote 'rendering,' but to 'you were called,' that is, a blessing is not promised to those blessing their enemies, but the end of the vocation is designated, the inheritance of blessing, so that the sense may be: Those who are one day to obtain the heavenly kingdom by inheritance, since they receive a spiritual and eternal blessing from God through faith, and have been called to that, in turn bless others, even if undeserving, out of charity. By 'blessing' are understood benefits of every kind, temporal and eternal, but especially these, Eph. I, 3. compare Matth. VI. 15. The pious, therefore, when injured by a neighbor, ought to call to mind that God did not pour out His curse upon them, even though they were as deserving of it as other men, but rather blessed them with every heavenly blessing, Eph. I. 4. from which very fact they should acknowledge themselves warned not to return curses to those who are worthy of a curse, but rather to wish them eternal happiness from the heart, as the blessed Gerhard piously advises here. Hemmingius in Glassius on the 5th Sunday after Trinity, page 1146. The Apostle wishes that we pray well for those who curse us, and from the heart forgive the offense to those who have injured us, which he confirms from the condition of our vocation. As if he were to say: We so often offended God, and were worthy that God should curse us eternally; but since He Himself, having forgiven every offense, calls us to the possession of a perpetual blessing, it is right that we imitate His example, provided we wish to be His genuine children. Because this is a common duty of Christians, it by no means removes or overturns the duty of those whose office it is to chastise and restrain others in the fear of God, lest the scab of a few infect the whole flock. The blessed Glassius adds another explanation of the blessed Hieron. Weller. He adds concerning the reason why they should not grow weary of doing good to both friends and enemies; nor render evil for evil. Because, he says, your condition and fortune is far better than that of the impious. God has called you to the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven, that you may be children of God, and joint-heirs of Christ, and partakers of the divine nature, as he says elsewhere. On the contrary, the impious are rejected from the face of God, excluded from that heavenly inheritance. It behooves you to consider these things, and always to refer the eyes of your heart to that treasure of yours laid up in heaven. Thus at last it will come to pass that you may easily extinguish all the flames of hatred, anger, and envy, and conceive a kind mind toward friends and enemies alike. By the word 'to inherit,' however, is noted both the manner by which we obtain those things, namely through adoption, Joh. I. v. 12. Rom. VIII. 17. and the perpetuity: for what we obtain by inheritance, we possess perpetually, 1. Petr. I. 4. To this pertain the admonitions of Chrysostom, homily 18 on Matthew. Nothing so restrains those who injure as the patience and modesty of the injured. Fire is not extinguished by fire, but by water. Thus injury and anger are not extinguished by the retaliation of anger, but by meekness, humility, and benefits. And of Isidore of Pelusium, book III, Epistle. Enmity is to be written in water, so that it may slip from mind and memory: but friendship must be carved into them, so that it may cling to the mind continually: As also Gregory of Nazianzus says: Let us concede something small, that we may obtain something greater: namely, concord: let us suffer ourselves to be conquered, that we may conquer. Observe the custom of athletes and the contests of wrestlers, who often by this very fact, that they have been thrown, conquer their adversaries who are pressing upon them. It is a good thing to conquer audacity with gentleness, and to make those who do injury better, which we tolerate by suffering. Each one of us owes much to Christ; let us grant pardon, that we may obtain it; let us remit, that it may be remitted to us. Chrysostom thunders against anger and the desire for vengeance in Homily XXIX and the following, to the people of Antioch. Anger is a kind of drunkenness, nay rather, it is more difficult than drunkenness, and more miserable than a demon. And further: Anger does not permit one to see, but just as in a night battle, binding everything, both eyes and ears, so it operates. Let us therefore be delivered from this demon when we restrain it at its beginning, let us place a seal upon our breast as a kind of bridle. Likewise: It is better for a nail or a viper to lie hidden in your heart than anger and rancor. For those things leave us suddenly: but this one always remains, fixing its teeth, pouring in poison, learning heavy thoughts.

Latin:

v. 9. Μὴ ἀποδιδόντες κακὸν ἀντὶ κακῦ) Idem habes Rom. XII. 17. ubi & plura ad hanc rem.

Ἤ λοιδορίαν ἀντὶ λοιδορίας) Vide supra II. 22.

Τὸὐναντίον δὲ, ἐυλογῦντες) Imo contra illis bene precantes, Matth. V. 44.

Εἰδότες ὅτι εἰς τῦτο ἐκλήθητε) Hac lege vocati estis. Sic & supra II 10. Illud εἰδότες deest in Manuscripto, & in Syro.

Ἵνα ἐυλογίαν κληρονομήσατε) ad aeterna bona participan- da. Est ἀντανάκλασις in voce ἐυλογίας, quae modo bo- na verba, modo benefacta significat. Deus adeo rebus in vos liberalis est: & vos effetis parci in verbis?

Christianae charitatis mandato subjungitur pri- vatae vindictae, quae illi maxime adversatur, interdi- ctum, quo prohibetur tum realium tum verbalium injuriarum, quales Christiani maxime ab infideli- bus, in quorum medio vivebant, patiebantur, ultio. Conf. prov. XX, 22. cap. XXIV, 29. 1. Thess. V, 5. Luc. VI, 37. Sub εὐλογία autem complectitur etiam εὐεργεσίαν, ut e Matth, V. 14. constat. Addit argumentum a Dei voluntate, qui ad hoc nos vo- cavit, ut non solum maledictio, sub qua eramus, auferretur, sed etiam benedictio nobis in Christo conferretur, Eph. I, 3. Gal. III, 8. sqq. Emphasis est in voce εἰδότες, ideo non omittenda. Illud ἵνα au- tem non ad remotius ἀποδίδοντες, sed ad ἐκλήθητε referendum, hoc est, non promittitur benedictio benedicentibus inimicis suis, sed finis vocationis designatur, benedictionis haereditas, ut sensus sit: Qui regnum coeleste aliquando haereditate conse- quuturi sunt, illi, quum spiritualem & aeternam benedictionem a Deo per fidem recipiant, & ad id vocati sint, vicissim aliis, etsi immeritis ex chari- tate benedicunt. Per εὐλογίαν omnis generis bene- ficia temporalia & aeterna, maxime vero haec in- telliguntur, Eph. I, 3. conf. Matth. VI. 15. Pii ergo a proximo laesi in memoriam sibi revocare debent, quod Deus non effuderit super ipsos maledictionem suam, etiamsi eam aeque ac caeteri homines essent promeriti, sed potius omni benedictione coelesti benedixerit ipsis, Eph. I. 4. a quo ipso se moneri agnoscant, ne maledicta regerant illis, qui maledictione digni sunt, sed ater- nam potius felicitatem illis ex animo apprecantur, ut pie hic monet B. Gerhardus. Hemmingius apud Glassium apud Dom. V. Trin. pag. 1146. Vult Apo- stolus, ut bene precemur iis, qui nobis maledicunt, & ex animo condonemus offensam iis, qui nos laeserunt, id quod ex vocationis nostrae conditione confirmat. Ac si diceret: Nos toties Deum offendimus, & fui- mus digni, quibus aeternum malediceret Deus; ve- rum cum ipse condonata omni offensa, vocat nos ad possessionem perpetuae benedictionis, par est, ut ejus exemplum imitemur, modo ipsius filii germani esse velimus. Hoc quia commune est officium Christiano- rum, nequaquam tollit aut evertit ipsorum officium, quorum est alios in timore Dei castigare & coërcere, ne scabies paucorum totam inficiat gregem. Addit Beat. Glassius aliam Beat. Hieron. Welleri explica- tionem. Addit de causa, cur non defatigentur bene- facere tum amicis tum inimicis; nec malum pro ma- lo reddant. Quia, inquit, vestra longe potior est conditio & fortuna, quam impiorum. Deus vos ad regni coelorum haereditatem vocavit, ut sitis filii Dei, cohaeredes autem Christi, ac θείας κοινωνοὶ φύσεως, sicut alibi inquit. E contra impii sunt rejecti a facie DEI, exclusi ab illa coelesti haereditate. Haec vos considerare oportet, semperque oculos cordis ad illum thesaurum vestrum in coelo repositum referre. Ita demum futurum est, ut facile omnes flammas odii, irae, & invidiae extinguatis, & benignam mentem erga amicos pariter & inimicos concipiatis. Verbo autem κληρονομεῖν tum modus notatur, quo illa consequimur, nimirum per υἱοθεσίαν, Joh. I. v. 12. Rom. VIII. 17. tum perpetuitas: quae enim per hae- reditatem consequimur, ea perpetuo possidemus, 1. Petr. I. 4. Huc pertinent monita Chrysost. homil. XIIX. in Matth. Nihil ita laedentes coërcet, ut pa- tientia modestiaque laesorum. Non extinguitur ignis igne, sed aqua. Sic injuria & ira non extingui- tur ire talione, sed mansuetudine, humilitate, beneficiis. Et Isidori Pelus. libr. III. Epist. Inimicitia scribenda est in aqua, ut statim è mente & memoria effluat: amicitia vero incidenda in es, ut jugiter menti inhæreat: Ut & Gregorii Na- zianzeni: Concedamus aliquid exiguum, ut majus impetremus: nempe concordiam: patiamur nos vin- ci, ut vincamus. Videte athletarum consuetudinem, & luctatorum certamina, qui sæpe hoc ipso, quod sup- positi sunt, adversarios sibi incumbentes vincunt. Bonum est, mansuetudine audaciam vincere, & me- liores efficere eos, qui injuriam faciunt, quæ tolera- mus patiendo. Unusquisq́, nostrum multum Christo debet, veniam demus, ut impetremus, remittamus, ut nobis remittatur. Detonat in iram & vindictæ cupiditatem Chrysostom. Hom. XXIX. & seqq. ad popul. Antioch. Ebrietas quædam est ira, imò verò difficilior ebrietate, & dæmone miserabilior. Et por- rò: Ira videre non permittit, sed velut in pugna no- cturna colligans omnia, & oculos & aures sic opera- tur. Ab hoc igitur Dæmone liberemur cum corripia- mus incipientem, sigillum pectori quasi quoddam fre- num imponamus. Item: Satius est unguem vel vipe- ram in corde tuo latere quàm iram & rancòrem. Illa namque nos repente relinquunt: Hæc autem semper remanet, dentes infigens, infundens venenum, gra- ves addiscens cogitationes.

## 3:10
v. 10. (For he that will love life, and see good days) The Syriac reads more correctly, 'For he that will of life, and loving to see good days'; for it is from Psalm 34:13, where in the Greek it is: 'What man is there that desireth life, and loveth to see good days.' But there, life and days pertain to this age: here, however, as all Evangelical promises, it is referred to eternity.

Let him refrain his tongue from evil, and his lips that they speak no guile: This is from the same place in the Psalms, except that there it is in the second person 'refrain' (παῦσον), and in like manner 'your tongue' (γλῶσσάν σε) and 'your lips' (χέιλη σε). Let him beware both of evil-speaking and of lying. 'To refrain' (παύειν) here is to abstain, as in Acts 6:13, 13:10. In the Hebrew it is נצר, for which the Syriac is נטר, with the same meaning, changing the צ into ט, which is frequent for the Syrians. That 'his' (αὑτῦ) in both places is absent in the Manuscript. See for the explanation of this sentence the place from the book of Musar, which Drusius cited.

He not only confirms the admonition about not speaking evil with a Davidic passage, but also at the same time exhorts to the pursuit of holiness, which is the second part of the Apostolic exhortation. To this, however, both this and what are further brought forward from the Psalm pertain. But there is no necessity that we should prefer the Syriac phrasing. For the Apostles are not accustomed to follow the text, whether Greek or Hebrew, word for word; and the sense is the same: he who wishes to love life, that is, he who wishes and loves life, or who by loving loves, or vehemently loves life, etc. Nor is the Psalmist to be considered to be speaking of the life of this age: for thus the blessing of eternal life could not have been confirmed from it: But the Holy Spirit looks to both the present and the future life, to good days in this and in the other age, in both the Psalm and this text. For those who guard themselves from evil with their tongue, and from guile with their lips, who turn away from the wicked and strive for good and holiness, have the promise of this and the future age, 1 Tim. 4:8. The Apostle therefore teaches what vices of the tongue must be avoided by those who desire to lead a blessed life in this and the future age, both that they ought not to be abusive, indulging in the petulance of the tongue and returning insults for insults; and that they ought not to be fraudulent and deceitful, bringing forth one thing with the tongue, but carrying another thing hidden in the heart. There is the manifest injury of the tongue against a neighbor, evil-speaking: here is the hidden and secret injury, fraudulence: Compare Ps. 39:2, Sir. 22:33, ch. 28:28, 30, James 3:5. Under these species, however, all other sins of the tongue are insinuated or comprehended, and the contrary virtues are commanded, according to the customary Hebraism: which Estius acknowledges here.

Latin:

v. 10. Ὁ γὰρ θέλων ζωὴν ἀγαπᾷν, καὶ ἰδεῖν ἡμέρας ἀγαθὰς) Syrus rectius legit, ὁ γὰρ θέλων ζωῆς, καὶ ἀγαπῶν ἰδεῖν ἡμέρας ἀγαθὰς; est enim ex Psal. XXXIV. 13. ubi in Græco: Τίς ἐστιν ἄνθρωπος, ὁ θέλων ζωὴν, ἀγαπῶν ἡμέρας ἰδεῖν ἀγαθάς. Sed ibi vita & dies ad hoc seculum pertinent: hic vero, ut omnia promissa Evangelica, ad æternitatem refertur.

Παυσάτω τὴν γλῶσσαν αὑτῶ ἀπὸ κακῦ, καὶ χείλη αὑτῶ τῦ μὴ λαλῆσαι δόλον: Est hoc ex eodem loco Psalmorum, nisi quod ibi in secunda persona παῦσον, & pari modo γλῶσσάν σε & χείλη σε. Caveat tum à maledicentia, tum à menda- cio. Πάυειν hic est abstinere, ut Act. VI. 13. XIII. 10. In Ebræo נצר, pro quo Syrus נטר significatu eodem mutato צ in ט, quod Syris frequens. Illud ἀυτῦ utroque loco abest in Manuscripto. Vide ad explicationem hujus sententiæ locum ex libro מוסר, quem adduxit Drusius.

Non tantum confirmat loco Davidico monitum de non maledicendo, sed etiam simul ad sanctitatis studium hortatur, quæ altera pars paræneseos A- postolicæ est. Eo autem & hæc, & quæ porro è Psalmo adducuntur, pertinent. Non est autem ul- la necessitas, ut Syri locutionem præferamus. Non enim solent κατὰ πόδα textum sive Græcum, sive Ebræum sequi Apostoli; & sensus idem est: qui vult diligere vitam, id est, qui vult, & diligit vitam, vel qui diligendo diligit, vel vehementer diligit vitam &c. neque Hierophaltes censendus est de vita hu- jus seculi loqui: Sic enim non potuisset inde confir- mari benedictio æternæ vitæ: Sed vitam tum præ- sentem, tum futuram, dies bonos in hoc & in alte- ro seculo, utrobique & in Psalmo, & in hoc textu respicit Spiritus Sanctus. Nam qui lingua sibi ca- vent à malo, & labiis à dolo, qui declinant à pravo, & student bono ac sanctitati, promissionem habent hujus & futuri seculi, 1. Tim. IV. 8. Docet ergo Apostolus quæ linguæ vitia cavenda sint illis, qui beatam in hoc & futuro seculo vitam traducere cupiunt, tum quod non debeant esse contumeliosi petulantiæ linguæ indulgentes, & convitia convi- tiis regerentes; tum quod non debeant esse frau- dulenti & dolosi, aliud quidem lingua proferen- tes, aliud vero in corde absconditum gerentes. Ibi est manifesta linguæ adversus proximum injuria, maledicentia: hic injuria latens & occulta, frau- dulentia: Conf. Pf. XXXIX. 2. Sir. XXII. 33. cap. XXVIII. 28. 30. Jac. III. 5. Sub his autem speciebus insinuantur vel comprehenduntur cætera omnia linguæ peccata, & præcipiuntur contrariæ virtu- tes, juxta usitatum Ebraismum: quod agnoscit hic Estius.

## 3:11
v. 11. (Let him turn away from evil, and do good) And this is from the same place in the Psalm, with the person changed. The former is to abstain from wicked things: It is a virtue to flee vice, and the first wisdom, to have lacked folly. The latter is to apply oneself to good acts. See above 1:19, 2:1, 2.

He confirms from the Davidic passage that one should not return insult for insult: now he confirms that one should not return evil for evil: There he regulates the tongue, here he regulates deeds. By the word 'let him turn away' (ἐκκλινάτω) he warns that we should turn away from the way of impiety and malice, and convert ourselves to the way of the Lord's commandments, Job 31:7, Ps. 119:32, because 'to turn away' (ἐκκλίνειν) is properly to deflect from the way, Num. 22:23, Judg. 14:5. 'To turn away from evil' (ἐκκλίνειν ἀπὸ κακῦ) also occurs in Ps. 36:25, Prov. 3:7, ch. 14:6. But we must not only turn away from evil, but also do good, Ps. 37:27, Eph. 1:16, Rom. 12:9. First it is necessary to extirpate vices, then to implant virtues, just as a farmer clears a garden of briars and thorns before he commits fruit-bearing seeds to it.

Let him seek peace, and pursue it. From the same place in the Psalm with a like change. From the same place are those things which follow up to 'and who'. The sense of this member, which is in Matt. 5:9.

Some think these are added as the goal of the precepts delivered, which look to this, that we may be able to live peaceably with our neighbor. But the Apostle does not intend only that: rather he exhorts to holiness in general, to which the pursuit of peace is particularly required: confirming what he had commanded concerning concord by this Davidic precept. 'To seek' (ζητεῖν) is to look for something with great zeal and solicitude, Matt. 2:13, ch. 6:33, ch. 21:46, Luke 2:45. 'Seek peace' is a Hebraism, that is, strive exceedingly for peace, Jer. 29:7, ch. 38:4. Similarly 'to pursue' (τὸ διώκειν) is to follow after with great zeal and fervor, Rom. 9:30, 31, ch. 12:14, 1 Tim. 6:11, 1 Thess. 5:15. Interlinear Gloss: Let him inquire for peace, as a hidden thing, and pursue it, as a fugitive thing. Compare Rom. 12:18, ch. 14:19, Heb. 12:14.

Latin:

v. 11. Ἐκκλινάτω ἀπὸ κακῦ, καὶ ποιησάτω ἀγαθὸν) & hoc ex eodem Psalmi loco, mutata persona. Prius est à pravis ab- stinere: Virtus est vitium fugere, & sapientia prima, Stultitia caruisse. Alterum actibus bonis incumbere. Vide supra I. 19. II. 1. 2.

Confirmat è loco Davidico, non reddendum convitium pro convitio : jam confirmat non redden- dum malum pro malo: Ibi linguam, hic opera mo- deratur. Voce ἐκκλινάτω monet, ut à via impietatis ac malitiæ declinemus, & ad viam mandatorum Domini nos convertamus, Job. XXXI. 7. Pf. CXIX. vers. 32. quia ἐκκλίνειν proprie est à via deflectere, Num. XXII. 23. Jud. XIV. 5. Ἐκκλίνειν ἀπὸ κακῦ oc- currit & Pf. 36, 25. Prov. 3, 7. c. 14, 6. Non autem tantum à malo declinare debemus, sed etiam bo- num facere, Psal. 37, 27. Ef. 1, 16. Rom. 12, 9. Primo oportet extirpare vitia, deinde virtutes inferere, sicut agricola sentibus & spinis prius hortum libe- rat, antequam frugifera semina ipsi committat.

Ζητησάτω εἰρήνην, καὶ διωξάτω αὐτὴν) Ex eodem Psalmi loco pari mutatione. Indidem sunt quæ sequuntur usque ad καὶ τίς. Sensus hujus membri, qui Matth. V. 9.

Hæc addi censent nonnulli, ceu scopum præce- ptorum traditorum, quæ eo spectent, ut pacificè cum proximo vivere possimus. Sed non id solum intendit Apostolus: imò ad sanctitatem in genere hortatur, ad quam peculiariter requirit pacis stu- dium : id quod de concordia præceperat, hoc pa- cto Davidico præcepto confirmans. Ζητεῖν est ma- gno studio & solicite aliquid quærere, Matth. 2, 13. c. 6, 33. c. 21, 46. Luc. 2, 45. Quærite pacem, Ebraïsmus est, id est, fummopere studete paci, Jerem. 29, 7. c. 38, 4. Similiter τὸ διώκειν est magno studio & zelo per- sequi, Rom. 9, 30. 31. c. 12, 14. 1. Tim. 6, 11. 1. Thess. 5, v. 15. Glossa Interlin. Inquirat pacem, ut rem abscondi- tam, & persequatur eam, ut rem fugitivam. Conf. Rom. 12, 18. c. 14, 19. Ebr. 12, 14.

## 3:12
Ver. 12.

For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears unto their supplication) God looks upon the pious with favor and hears them, John IX, 31. James V. 16.

But the face of the Lord is against them that do evil) ἐπὶ and what is in Hebrew אל is here placed for against, as Luke X. 17. There follows in the Psalm, which is here omitted for the sake of brevity, to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth.

He confirms the promise of a pleasant and blessed life from divine kindness, because God looks upon all who are justified through faith with gracious eyes, and hears them with a benevolent ear; but because he had commanded those who do not obey to turn away from evil, he threatens the angry face of God. By the eyes of God is noted his fatherly favor, by the ears the readiness to hear. This is an anthropopathy. For those whom we love and whom we favor, we cast our eyes upon them, we look upon them gently and kindly, and we receive their speech with ready ears. But those at whom we are angry, we are accustomed to look upon with a stern countenance. Compare concerning the former Num. 6. v. 25. 26. Ps. 31, 17. Ps. 80, 4. concerning the latter Lev. 17, 10. c. 20, 5. Ps. 68. v. 3. The sense therefore is, as Estius notes: that the Lord indeed looks even upon those who do evil, but not with a benign countenance, but with the stern aspect of his indignation, not that he may save and hear, but that he may at some time destroy and abolish them from the earth, that is, from among men their memory, so that there is no one among the living who speaks of them honorably. Which, as it mostly happens to the wicked in this age, so it will happen perfectly and without exception in the future.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Ὅτι ὀφθαλμοὶ Κυρίου ἐπὶ δικαίους, καὶ ὦτα αὐτῦ εἰς δέησιν αὐτῶν) Deus pios propitius respicit & exaudit, Joh. IX, 31. Jac. V. 16.

Πρόσωπον δὲ Κυρίου ἐπὶ ποιῦντας κακά) ἐπὶ & quod in E- bræo est אל hic ponitur pro contra, ut Luc. X. 17. Sequitur in Psalmo, quod hic brevitatis causa subticetur τῦ ἐξολο- θρεῦσαι ἐκ τῆ τὸ μνημόσυνον αὐτῶν.

Confirmat promissionem vitæ jucundæ & bea- tæ à divina benignitate, quia Deus cunctos. per fi- dem justifactos & gratiosis oculis respicit, & aure benevola exaudit; at quia declinare à malo jusserat illis, qui non parent, vultum Dei iratum minatur. Per oculos Dei paternus ejus favor, per aures prom- ptitudo exaudiendi notatur. Est hic ἀνθρωποπά- θεια. Quos enim diligimus & quibus favemus, in illos oculos conjicimus, eos blande & amice in- tuemur, eorumque sermonem promptis auribus excipimus. In quos vero irascimur, eos torvo vul- tu intueri solemus. Conf. de illo Num. 6. v. 25. 26. Pf. 31, 17. Pf. 80, 4. de hoc Lev. 17, 10. c. 20, 5. Pf. 68. v. 3. Sensus ergo est, notante Estio : Dominum respi- cere quidem etiam eos, qui mala faciunt, verum non vultu benigno, sed torvo suæ indignationis aspectu, non ut servet & exaudiat, sed ut aliquando perdat & aboleat de terra, id est, ex hominibus memoriam eo- rum, adeo ut viventium nemo sit, qui de eis honorifice loquatur. Quod ut plerumque contingit malis in hoc seculo, ita perfecte & sine exceptione continget in fu- turo.

## 3:13
v. 13. And who is he that will harm you, if ye be followers of that which is good?) This means: There will be few who wish to harm you, if you always imitate those things which are clearly good. We have the word κακῶσ for to treat badly, Acts VII. 6. 19. XII. 1. XVIII. 10. Τῦ ἀγαθῦ for τῶν ἀγαθῶν, of good things, as the Syriac and Latin have it here. A manuscript has ζηλωταὶ instead of μιμηταὶ, not badly. See Acts XXI. 20.

Another argument is for the pursuit of peace and holiness, that to those devoted to these, trouble cannot easily be caused, and because experience itself teaches that peaceful men win over the minds of others to themselves, so that by God's blessing they can lead a peaceful and quiet life. Thus this can be referred at the same time to the preceding, as if to say: No one will be able to harm you if you pursue the good of patience and virtue, both because virtue overcomes all evils is the tutor and protector of virtue and of those who cultivate it. No adversity will harm you, if no iniquity dominates. Cf. Chrysostom’s oration that no one is harmed except by himself: In which way Estius also not inappropriately refers this to good days, i.e., that promise written by David: Who is the man who desires life, etc., although it should be referred primarily to the life of the future age, it nevertheless pertains in its own way also to the present age. For it happens for the most part that those who govern their tongue well, and love peace, and strive to do good to all, and to harm no one, live tranquilly and happily, and are certainly less exposed to the injuries of wicked men: which is to see good days according to the manner of the present life. There is no one who can harm you by inflicting true harm, Rom. VIII. v. 28. concerning which B. Huss in this place. To those who have holiness of life, no one can do harm, or would wish to do harm: because the minds of even enemies are accustomed to be soothed by patience and the pursuit of peace. But this is to be understood of that which is accustomed to happen for the most part, Prov. XV. v. 1. Some with Augustine, sermon 107 de divers. c. 6. 7., refer the word τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ to God or Christ: But it is better to understand it substantively with most others as the good which he previously commanded to do.

PART III. Particular exhortations to tolerance, when we suffer for the sake of justice and perseverance in the faith.

Latin:

v. 13. Καὶ τίς ὁ κακώσων ὑμᾶς, ἐὰν τῦ ἀγαθῦ μιμηταὶ γένη- σθε;) Hoc vult: Pauci erunt, qui vobis nocere velint, si sem- per ea, quæ plane bona sunt, imitemini. Verbum κακῶσ pro male tractare habemus, Act. VII. 6. 19. XII. 1. XVIII. 10. Τῦ ἀγαθῦ pro τῶν ἀγαθῶν, rerum bonarum, quomodo hic Syrus & Latinus. Manuscriptus pro μιμηταὶ habet ζηλωταὶ, non male. Vide Act. XXI. 20.

Aliud argumentum est pro studio pacis, & san- ctitatis, quod illi deditis non facile molestia creari- possit, quodque ipsa experientia doceat, homines pacificos aliorum animas sibi conciliare, ut Dei beneficio vitam pacatam & tranquillam ducere possint. Sic referri hoc simul ad superiora poterit, q. d. Nemo vobis nocere poterit, si bonum patientia, & virtutis sectemini, tum quia virtus omnia mala superat, tum quia virtutis, eamque colentium est tutor & protector. Nulla vobis nocebit adversi- tas, si nulla dominabitur iniquitas. Conf. Chryso- stomi orat. quod nemo læditur, nisi à seipso: Quo pacto etiam ad dies bonos id non incommode re- fert Estius, q. d. promissionem illam à Davide scri- ptam: Quis est homo, qui vult vitam, &c. etsi prin- cipaliter referenda sit ad vitam futuri seculi, perti- nere tamen suo modo etiam ad præsens seculum. Fit enim ut plurimum, ut qui linguam suam bene mo- derantur, & pacem amant, omnibusque student benefacere, lædere neminem, tranquille & feliciter agant, certe minus obnoxii sint hominum improbo- rum injuriis: quod est dies videre bonos juxta mo- dum vitæ præsentis. Nemo est, qui vobis nocere possit, verum nocumentum inferendo, Rom. VIII. v. 28. quo de B. Hussus in h. l. Habentibus sanctita- tem vitæ nemo nocere potest, vel nocere velit: quia patientia & studio pacis etiam inimicorum animi demulceri solent. Sic autem id intelligendum de eo, quod plerumque fieri consuevit, Prov. XV. v. 1. Nonnulli cum Augustino serm. 107. de divers. c. 6. 7. vocem τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ad Deum vel Christum referunt: Sed præstat id substantive cum aliis ple- risque de bono, quod ante facere jussit, intelligere.

PARS III. Adhortationes peculiares ad tolerantiam, cum patimur ob justitiam & perseveran- tiam in fide.

## 3:14
v. 14. But if even you should suffer for the sake of justice) because he saw that the cruelty of magistrates could be objected on account of religion, therefore he responds to that. Δικαιοσύνη is the profession of the Gospel, in which God is obeyed, than which nothing is more just. Thus also Matt. V. 10. In the Manuscript: but if you should suffer.

Blessed) by that very fact you are happy, as is also said in the cited place of Matthew. For great is the reward.

Therefore he wishes to say this. If even the wicked should try to harm you, and so it happens that you are afflicted on account of justice: nothing nevertheless is lost to your blessedness on that account, indeed you will be blessed in it. Your persecutors will not only not be able to harm you, but will even promote your salvation beyond their intention. Thus the Apostle digresses at the same time to these exhortations. And when he has exhorted in general to patience, now he reminds them in particular of patience for the sake of justice and the profession of the name of the Lord, and he commands it in such a way that without fear we may sanctify the Lord, even by apology and profession of faith. As he had previously removed boldness in returning evil: so he now removes inordinate fear in sustaining evil. But by justice he understands both in general the pursuit of piety, of which he had warned, and especially the confession of heavenly truth, which is a certain part of Christian justice, concerning which Christ properly speaks, Matt. V. 10. Which is also evident from the apology which he requires. Add also c. IV. 16.

But do not fear their fear, nor be troubled) that is, on account of the fear, as above 6. and the Genitive αὐτῶν here designates the object. Do not be afraid or perturbed for fear of them, namely the magistrates. And this, and what follows, is from Is. VIII. 12. 13. where in the Greek: You shall not fear his fear, nor be troubled.

Some here apply Peter’s words, with a slight inflection of the Prophet’s words concerning the fear with which the wicked and persecutors are preposterously feared, to the fear which the wicked haughtily strike into others. But in the Prophet it concerns the fear of the Jewish people, with which they feared the evils hanging over them, when they ought rather to have trusted in the Lord; the Apostle also requires the same, that the converted Jews should not fear the persecutors, or the fear and the formidable things which they threaten, so that there is a Metonymy in the word fear: For he does not note the act of fear here but the object, as the Syrian has rendered it here. Cf. Job III. verse 20. Ps. XCI. v. 5. Prov. I. 25. To be troubled signifies to be vehemently disturbed, Matt. II. v. 3. ch. XIV. v. 25. Luke I. v. 12. Job XIV. 1. 22. He warns therefore not to be perturbed too much on account of the threats or injuries of the persecutors, but to demonstrate constancy of mind even in the dangers themselves. He who fears God, and trusts in Him, does not fear the threats of men, Ps. XXVII. verse 1. Ps. LVI. verse 5. For death is the punishment of the one being born, if it is paid for justice and piety, it becomes the glory of the one being reborn, as St. Augustine says, lib. VI. de C. D. c. 13. Therefore, as Ambrose warns in Ps. CXVIII. octon. 21., the just man is restrained by no injuries, is bitten by no dangers, is tempted by no storms, whether death may impend, or life, or the Angels of the heavens, nor may he be cast down by adversities, nor exalted by successes, may his affection never be infirm.

Latin:

v. 14. Ἀλλ' εἰ καὶ πάσχοιτε διὰ δικαιοσύνην) quia videbat objici posse sævitiam magistratuum religionis causa, ideo ad id respondet. Δικαιοσύνη est Evangelii professio, in qua Deo obeditur, quo nihil justius. Sic & Matth. V. 10. In Manuscripto: εἰ δὲ πάσχοιτε.

Μακάριοι) eo ipso felices estis, ut & dicto Matthæi loco dicitur. Magna enim merces.

Hoc ergo vult dicere. Si vel maxime mali co- nentur vobis nocere, adeoque contingat, vos pro- pter justitiam affligi: nihil tamen propterea bea- titudini vestræ decedit, imo in eo beati eritis. Per- secutores vestri non solum non poterunt vobis nocere, sed etiam salutem vestram præter inten- tionem promovebunt. Ita digreditur simul Apo- stolus ad has Paræneses. Et quum adhortatus fuerit in genere ad patientiam, jam in specie commonefa- cit de patientia ob justitiam, & professionem nominis Domini, eamque ita præcipit, ut sine timore, san- ctificemus Dominum, etiam apologia & professione fidei. Ut antea removerat audaciam in malo re- pendendo: Sic removet jam timorem inordina- tum in malo sustinendo. Per justitiam autem tum in genere pietatis studium, de quo monuerat, tum imprimis confessionem veritatis cælestis, quæ est justitiæ Christianæ quædam pars, intelligit, de qua proprie Christus, Matth. V. 10. Quod etiam ex apologia, quam requirit, patet. Adde & c. IV. 16.

Τὸν δὲ φόβον αὐτῶν μὴ φοβηθῆτε, μηδὲ ταραχθῆτε) id est διὰ τὸν φόβον, ut supra 6. & Genitivus αὐτῶν hic objectum designat. Ne pavescite aut perturbamini præ metu illorum, nempe magistratuum. Et hoc, & quod sequitur, est ex Es. VIII. 12. 13. ubi in Græco: Τὸν φόβον αὐτοῦ οὐ μὴ φοβηθῆ- τε, μηδὲ ταραχθῆτε.

Nonnulli hic Petrum levi quadam inflexione verba Prophetæ de timore, quo præpostere mali & persecutores timent applicare ad timorem, quem mali aliis fastuosi incutiunt. Sed in Propheta de populi Judaici timore, quo mala metuebant sibi impendentia, agitur, quum in Domino confidere potius deberent, idem etiam requirit Apostolus, ut ne metuant conversi Judæi persecutores, vel timorem & formidabilia, quæ illi minantur, ut Metonymia sit in voce timoris: Non enim timoris actum sed objectum hic notat, ut Syrus hic reddidit. Conf. Job. III. vers. 20. Psal. XCI. v. 5. Prov. I. 25. Ταράττεσθαι significat vehementer turbari, Matth. II. v. 3. cap. XIV. v. 25. Luc. I. v. 12. Job, XIV. 1. 22. Monet ergo ne perturbentur nimium ob minas vel injurias persecutorum, sed animi constantiam in ipsis periculis etiam demonstrent. Qui Deum timet, ipsique confidit, non timet hominum mi- nas, Psal. XXVII. vers. 1. Psal. LVI. vers. 5. Mors enim pœna nascentis, si pro justitia pietateque penda- tur, fit gloria renascentis, dicente S. Augustino lib. VI. de C. D. c. 13. Nullis ergo, monente Ambrosio in Psal.
