CXVIII. octon. 21. justus frenatur injuriis, nullis mordetur periculis, nullis tentatur procellis, sive mors ingruat, sive vita, sive Angeli cælorum, neque dejiciatur adversis, nec extollatur secundis, numquam sit ejus infirmus affectus.

## 3:15
v. 15. But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts) In the Greek of Isaiah in the cited place, Sanctify the Lord himself. But ἁγιάζειν signifies in this place indeed to give thanks, to glorify, in which way קדש is sometimes translated. Thus Cyprian, having heard his condemnation, gave thanks to God, and other martyrs.

To terror and consternation is opposed the sanctification of the Lord in the heart, and the holy and intrepid confession of the same which is made by the mouth, as well as the brave endurance of all persecutions for the sake of his name. Lyranus expresses these three things thus: The first is that faith be strengthened in the heart; regarding this he says: Sanctify the Lord Christ. The second is that this faith be derived to others; regarding this he adds: always prepared for a defense. The third is that for the sake of any adversities whatsoever a man be not torn away from the faith; and regarding this it is added: For it is better, if the will of God should will it, that you suffer for doing good. Therefore ἁγιάζειν is not to glorify, but what the word properly signifies, to sanctify, which is done by the true acknowledgment of the Lord and by a confident apprehension, or by the placing of a constant trust in the same, when we acknowledge not only the truth, justice, wisdom, power, and truth of God, and whatever has been handed down concerning him as a support for our faith; but we also place the trust of our heart in the goodness and power of the Lord, and we rely upon and acquiesce in his promises with true faith. Nor is such sanctification required only regarding the Word of the Lord, but also regarding the actions and deeds of the Lord: Whence Blessed Luther on this passage: When I consider as good and holy whatever is sent by God, then I sanctify him. That sanctification is done in our hearts, because with the heart one believes unto righteousness, Rom. X. 10. and it has as its object the Lord, in whom one must believe, and particularly in Isaiah it treats of Christ, whom he calls the Lord of hosts: because he names him Immanuel, which is the proper name of Christ. Cf. Is. VII. 14, c. VIII. 13. 14, and he affirms concerning him that he is a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, which it is established pertains to Christ from 1 Pet. II. 6, Luke II. 34, Rom. IX. 33, and he is said to be sanctification to the faithful, because he has been made for us by God sanctification, 1 Cor. I. 30, whence a firm argument is had for the Deity of Christ, since Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς and Jehovah of hosts is none other than the true and eternal God, nor ought we to sanctify any but the true God in our hearts through faith.

Ἕτοιμοι δὲ ἀεὶ πρὸς ἀπολογίαν) Be prepared to render an account why you are Christians. Thus we have ἀπολογίαν in Philipp. I. 7, 17, 2 Tim. IV. 16, Acts XXII. 1.

To everyone who asks you for a word concerning the hope that is in you.] In the manuscript, ἀπαιτῶντι is not bad, if someone should demand from you the cause of the religion, which is here called by the name of hope joined to it, as also in Acts XXVI. 7. Περὶ is redundant here, as it often is.

External sanctification must be joined with internal sanctification: the profession of the mouth with the faith of the heart. Nor can the profession of the mouth be true and pleasing to God unless it overflows from the interior sanctification of the heart, Psalm CXVI. 10; 2 Cor. IV. 13. The cause also and the reason why we ought to confess the name of God is faith and sanctification, which cannot lie hidden or be concealed in the heart, but comes forth and breaks out in external profession, in the praise and celebration of the Lord. Therefore, true Christians are always prepared to give a reason for their faith, which is called ἀπολογία, because faith is accustomed to be torn apart by slanders, against which it must be defended. For ἀπολογία is properly called that which is done with words, Acts XXII. 1; 1 Cor. IX. 3; 2 Cor. VII. 11; concerning such an apology of faith, see Phil. I. 7, 17; 2 Tim. IV. 16. The Syrian here rendered it as the production of the Spirit, because the confidence of the mind opens the mouth, which fear closes. It is called the reason of hope. Fulgentius II. to Thrasimund reads 'of faith and hope'; the Syrian, 'of the hope of faith.' Salmero therefore thinks the word 'faith' is missing in the Greek, but that it should be supplied. Truly, that was found in no codex. Hope, however, is put for faith by the customary phrase of Scripture, through Metonymy, because faith is the foundation of the hope of the heavenly inheritance. We must always be prepared, but we are not bound to give a reason at all times. St. Peter indeed says, 'to everyone who asks,' but that is to be understood of him who asks seriously, who asks by right, or for the sake of information, and when the Divine glory demands it, not when it is joined with damage to the glory of the divine name or the salvation of the Church: for a profession not opposed to the sanctification of the divine name, but consistent with it, is required. Cornelius à Lapide: It is not necessary, he says, to always actually give a reason for our faith and hope, e.g., when mockers ask for a reason in order to mock, when they are incapable, when through this harm is created for those asking or for others, Matt. VI. 7. Therefore, not only when the Magistrate demands it, as the Jesuits answered in the colloquy of Ratisbon, which is also the restriction of Perkins, l. II. de cas. Consc. c. 13. q. 1, but to anyone who asks, provided he acts seriously, and in a competent place and time, the reason must be given. But all ought to be prepared to give a reason for their faith, not only Priests and Teachers, to whom alone Cornelius wishes this to pertain, but also the Laity, because it is a universal precept, and as not only Priests, but also the Laity are reminded to suffer for righteousness, and to sanctify the Lord in their hearts; so also, when a reason is required of them, all are admonished for the apology of faith, and the Apostle speaks of all, Rom. X. 10: 'With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation,' etc. For all who have the same spirit of faith, that passage of Ps. CXVI. 10 has a place: 'I believed, therefore I spoke,' 2 Cor. IV. 13. And this is to confess, or to give an ἀπολογίαν τῆς ἐλπίδος, which is afterwards explained by λόγον, a reason, not that a disputation or a proof of the articles of faith by arguments is required from the Laity, but that they may know what they believe, as Cornelius confesses; St. Peter demands a response, not a disputation: nor yet is it to be given only to infidels in the origin of the Church, not to heretics once the faith is confirmed, which Cornelius contends. For this precept pertains to all believers of all times, and teaches that a reason must be given to everyone who demands it; nor a response or confession of implicit faith, as Cornelius wishes: The Laity, he says, when asked by heretics why they believe Christ is present in the Eucharist, should answer because the Church believes and has believed it in every age: But that they should explicitly profess those things which are to be believed, and not rely in these on the authority of the Church, but on that of Scripture, which is the ultimate reason for believing. For not even Priests and Teachers, let alone the Laity, can easily and certainly affirm or say that the Church has believed so in every age: so that even the simplest Laity can have it ascertained that it is held in Scripture in the words of the institution, looking at the naked words: 'Take, this is my body; drink, this is my blood.' Furthermore, St. Augustine, l. XIV. de Trin. c. 1, rightly says: 'It is one thing to know only what a man ought to believe for the sake of obtaining the blessed life; but it is another thing to know how this very thing may both help the pious and be defended against the impious.' Estius renders this sense: Since infidels boast that your hope, which you have in Christ concerning life and future glory, is empty: therefore I advise that you always have in readiness, as if from meditation, a response by which you may show your hope, or faith in the hoped-for glory, to be reasonable, whether it be an adversary or anyone desirous of learning and knowing, who demands from you a reason why you suffer such hard things in the present life, despising the goods of this life. But what Christ says, 'Do not premeditate,' Matt. X. 19, either pertains to those who were immediately moved by the Holy Spirit, or it was said against excessive anxiety joined with diffidence: to which due preparation with confidence in divine assistance is not repugnant.

Μετὰ πραΰτητος καὶ φόβου] In the manuscript, not badly, but with gentleness and fear, and he has joined these well. One must abstain from harsh words: yet nothing should be withheld that is relevant to the matter, and that for the sake of reverence for God, who is called fear here.

The Vulgate has 'with modesty,' the Syriac 'with humility.' Modesty is the companion and certain indicator of gentleness and humility. Therefore, he means that an account of the hope of faith must be rendered to those who ask, not arrogantly or immodestly, but gently and reverently. That reverence is referred either to God, so that we do not dissemble anything to please men; or to the person questioning, to whom the honor that is owed to him must not be denied: especially indeed if an account must be rendered before a judge or anyone superior in dignity, there is need of reverence, Rom. 13:7. Immodesty and untimely zeal often bring more harm than fruit. A soft answer breaks wrath, a harsh word stirs up fury, Prov. 15:1. By the exhortation of kindness and by enticing blandishment, [one should] openly clear away the cloud of error from the ways of truth that have been shown, so that each one may not begin to be dragged, but to follow the one going before: harder things must always be bent, lest the curvature, inclined by force, should break and pour out a fragment before it comes into a circle, says Athanasius, or whoever is the author of the Exhortation to Monks.

Latin:

v. 15. Κύριον δὲ τὸν Θεὸν ἁγιάσατε ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν) In Græco Esaiæ dicto loco Κύριον αὐτὸν ἁγιάσατε. Signifi- cat autem ἁγιάζειν hoc quidem in loco gratias agere, δοξά- ζειν quomodo קדש interdum vertitur. Sic Cyprianus audita damnatione sua gratias Deo egit, & martyres alii.

Terrori, & consternationi opponitur Domini in corde sanctificatio, ejusdemque sancta & intrepi- da, quæ ore fit, confessio, nec non pro ejusdem no- mine fortis omnium persecutionum toleratio. Quæ tria sic effert Lyranus: Primum est, quod fi- des corde firmetur, quantum ad hoc, dicit: Dominum Christum sanctificate: Secundum, ut hæc fides ad alios derivetur. Quantum ad hoc, subdit: parati semper ad satisfactionem. Tertium est, quod pro- pter quæcunque adversa homo à fide non evellatur: Et quantum ad hoc, subditur: Melius est enim be- nefacientes pati. Est ergo ἁγιάζειν non glorificare, sed quod proprie vox sonat, sanctificare, quod fit vera Domini agnitione ac fiduciali apprehensio- ne, vel constanti fiduciæ in eundem collocatione, cum non tantum veritatem, justitiam, sapientiam, potentiam ac veritatem Dei agnoscimus, & quic- quid de ipso ad fidei nostræ fulcrum traditum est; Sed etiam in Domini bonitate ac potentia cordis fiduciam ponimus, ac promissionibus ejusdem ve- ra fide nitimur & acquiescimus. Neque talis san- ctificatio requiritur tantum quoad Domini Ver- bum, sed etiam quoad actiones & facta Domini: Unde B. Lutherus in h. l. Quando bonum & sanctum duco, quicquid â Deo immittitur, tunc sanctifico ipsum. Illa sanctificatio in cordibus nostris fit, quia corde creditur ad justitiam, Rom. X. 10. & pro objecto habet Dominum, in quem credendum est, ac pe- culiariter apud Esaiam de Christo, quem Domi- num exercituum vocat, agitur: quia nominat eum Immanuel, quod proprium est Christi nomen. Conf. Es. VII. 14. c. X. 10. 11. & de eo affirmat, quod sit lapis offensionis & petra scandali, quod ad Christum pertinere è 1. Petr. II. 6. Luc. II. 34. Rom. IX. 34. constat, diciturque eundem fore fide- libus sanctificationem, quia factus nobis à Deo est sanctificatio, 1. Cor. I. 30. unde firmum argu- mentum habetur Deitatis Christi, quum Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς & Jehovah exercituum non sit, nisi verus & æternus Deus, nec nisi verum Deum in cordibus nostris sanctificare per fidem debeamus.

Ἕτοιμοι δὲ ἀεὶ πρὸς ἀπολογίαν) Parati estote causam reddere, cur sitis Christiani. Sic ἀπολογίαν habemus Phi- lipp. I. 7. 17. 2. Tim. IV. 16. Act. XXII. 1.

Παντὶ τῷ αἰτῶντι ὑμᾶς λόγον περὶ τῆς ἐν ὑμῖν ἐλπίδος.] In Manuscripto non male ἀπαιτῶντι, fi quis causam à vobis po- poscerit religionis, quæ hic ex adjuncto spei nomine vocatur, ut & Act. XXVI. 7. Περὶ hic πλεονάζει, ut sæpe.

Cum sanctificatione interna conjuncta esse de- bet sanctificatio externa: cum fide cordis professio oris. Nec potest vera Deoque grata esse oris pro- fessio, nisi redundet ex interiori cordis sanctifi- catione, Psal. CXVI. 10. 2. Cor. IV. 13. Causa etiam ac ratio, cur nomen Dei confiteri debeamus, est fi- des, & sanctificatio, quæ latere nequit vel abscondi in corde, sed prodit ac prorumpit externa professi- one, laude ac celebratione Domini. Parati ergo se- per sunt veri Christiani ad reddendam fidei ratio- nem, quæ ἀπολογία dicitur, quia fides calumni- is proscindi solet, adversus quas defendenda est. Ná ἀπολογία proprie dicitur, quæ verbis fit, Act. XXII 1. 1. Cor. IX. 3. 2. Cor. VII. 11. de tali fidei apologia v. Phil. I. 7. 17. 2. Tim. IV. 16. Syrus hic reddidit ad pro- ductionem Spiritus, quia fiducia animi os aperit, quod timor occludit. Ratio spei dicitur. Fulgentius II. ad Thrasm. legit de fide & spe, Syrus, de spe fidei. Salmero ergo putat in Græco deesse verbum fides, sed supplendum id esse. Verum id in nullo codice repertum fuit. Spes autem ponitur pro fide usitata scripturæ phrasi, per Metonymiam, quia fides est fundamentum spei cœlestis hæreditatis. Parati esse semper debemus, non autem semper rationem red- dere tenemur. Dicit quidem S. Petrus, omni petenti, sed id intelligendum de eo, qui serio petit, qui petit jure, vel informationis causa, & cum id postulat gloria Divina, non cum id cum damno gloriæ divi- ni nominis, aut salutis Ecclesiæ conjunctum est: nam professio non opposita sanctificationi nomi- nis divini, sed eidem conveniens requiritur. Corne- lius à Lapide: Non oportet, inquit, semper actu dare rationem fidei & spei nostræ, v. g. cum irrisores po- scunt rationem ut irrideant, cum incapaces sunt, cum per hoc rogantibus vel aliis damnum creatur, Matth. VI. 7. Non ergo tantum cùm Magistratus exigit, ut Jesuitæ in colloquio Ratisbon. responderunt, quæ etiam restrictio Perkinsi est l. II. de cas. Consc. c. 13. q. 1. sed cuivis petenti, modo rem serio agat, & in lo- co ac tempore competente, ratio reddenda. Omnes autem parati esse debent ad reddendam rationem fidei, non tantum Sacerdotes & Doctores, ad quos solos hæc pertinere Cornel. à Lapide vult, sed etiam Laici, quia præceptum universale est, & ut ad pati- endum propter justitiam non Sacerdotes tantum, sed etiam Laici, & ad sanctificandum Dominum in cordibus suis commonefiunt; sic & ad apologiam fidei cum ratio ab iis requiritur, omnes admonen- tur, ac de omnibus Apostolus, Rom. X. 10. Corde cre- ditur ad justitiam, ore fit confessio ad salutem &c. De omnibus τὸ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα τῆς πίστεως habentibus locum habet illud Ps. CXVI. 10. ἐπίστευσα διὸ ἐλά- λησα, 2. Cor. IV. 13. Atque hoc est confiteri, vel ἀπο- λογίαν τῆς ἐλπίδος reddere, quod postea exponi- tur per λόγον rationem, non quod à Laicis requira- tur disputatio, vel articulorum fidei per argumenta comprobatio, sed ut norint, quid credant, ut Corne- lius fatetur; responsionem exigit S. Petrus, non dispu- tationem: neque tamen dandam solum infidelibus in origine Ecclesiæ, non hæreticis confirmata jam fide, quod Cornelius contendit. Nam præceptum hoc ad omnes fideles omnium temporum pertinet, & omni exigenti rationem dandam docet; neque re- sponsionem, vel confessionem fidei implicitæ, prout Cornelius vult: Laici, inquit, rogati ab hæreticis, cur credant Christum esse præsentem in Eucharistia, respondeant, quia id credit & credidit Ecclesia omni seculo: Sed ut explicite profiteantur, ea quæ credenda sunt, nec in iis Ecclesiæ, sed Scripturæ au- toritate, quæ ultima est ratio credendi, nitantur. Nam omni seculo ita credidisse Ecclesiam, ne Sa- cerdotes quidem ac Doctores, nedum Laici facile, ac certò affirmare, vel dicere possunt: ut ita in scri- ptura in verbis institutionis haberi etiam simplicis- simi Laici possunt exploratum habere, verba nuda intuentes. Edite hoc est corpus meum, bibite, hoc est sanguis meus. De cætero recte S. Augustinus l. XIV. de Trin c. 1. Aliud est scire tantummodo, quid homo credere debeat propter adipiscendam vitam beatam; aliud autem scire, quemadmodum hoc ipsum & piis opituletur, & contra impios defendatur. Estius hunc reddit sensum: Quoniam infideles spem ve- stram, quam in Christo habetis de vita & gloria fu- tura jactitant inanem esse: propterea moneo, ut sem- per habeatis in promptu, velut ex meditato responsi- onem, qua spem vestram seu fidem gloriæ speratæ rati- onabilem ostendatis, sive sit adversarius, sive quispi- am discendi & sciendi cupidus, qui rationem à vobis e- xigat, cur in præsenti vita tam dura patiamini, conte- mnentes bona vitæ hujus. Quod vero Christus ait, nolite præmeditari, Matth. X. 19. vel ad eos perti- net, qui immediate agebantur à Spiritu sancto, vel versus nimiam solicitationem cum diffidentia con- junctam, dictum est: cui debita præparatio cum confidentia divinæ assistentiæ non repugnat.

Μετὰ πραΰτητος καὶ φόβου] In Manuscripto non male ἀλλὰ μετὰ πραΰτητος καὶ φόβου, & bene hæc conjunxit. Ab- stinendum à verbis asperis: attamen nihil reticendum, quod ad rem faciat, idque ob Dei reverentiam, qui hic φό- βος dicitur.

Vulgatus habet cum modestia, Syrus cum humi- litate. Mansuetudinis & humilitatis comes & index certus est modestia. Id ergo vult rationem spei fi- dei poscentibus reddendam esse non arroganter, vel immodeste, sed mansuete, & reverenter. Illa reve- rentia vel ad Deum refertur, ne in gratiam hominũ quicquam dissimulemus; vel ad personam interro- gantem, cui honor, qui ipsi debetur, non denegan- dus est: Imprimis vero si apud Judicem aut digni- tate superiorem quemvis ratio sit reddenda, reve- rentia opus est, Rom. XIII. 7. Immodestia & zelo intempestivo plus sæpe damni quã fructus affertur. Responsio mollis frangit iram, sermo durus suscitat furorem, Prov. XV. 12. Magis benignitatis adhorta- tione & illicitente blandimento viæ veritatis ostensæ nu- bem erroris aperte, ut non trahi incipiat unusquis- que, sed sequi præcedentem: semper duriora flectenda sunt, ne viribus inclinata curvatio priusquam in cir- culum veniat, fatiscens, fragmen effundat, ait Atha- nasius, vel quisquis est Autor exhort. ad Monach.

## 3:16
Συνείδησιν ἔχοντες ἀγαθὴν] Keeping a good conscience in every act, Acts 23:1, 1 Tim. 1:5, 19, 3:9, 2 Tim. 1:3, and so also below 3:25.

A good conscience must be kept even in the act of confession, so that we do not profess anything against our conscience, or mock God and men by a crafty evasion of distinction between an elicited and an commanded act of the will, and wound our own conscience, or even by a mental reservation; or deceive those to whom the confession is to be made by some cunning condition: and it must be proven in a life consistent with faith, lest the purity of faith be contaminated by the impurity of life, as Oecumenius says: St. Peter, he says, advises that our responses be confirmed also by our life, which is what he calls conscience. It seems to me, says St. Augustine, Epist. 211 to Proba, that the manner of living is worth more in this inquiry than the manner of speaking. But if the life does not correspond to the profession, not only will there be no progress, but loss also follows among those who judge of the speech by the morals. He blushes, although excellent doctrine, which one's own conscience rebukes, says Jerome in his epistle to Principia. Add that a good conversation provides confidence in speaking, Acts XXIII. 1. Verse 16. Ἵνα ἐν ᾧ καταλαλῶσι ὑμῶν ὡς κακοποιῶν] the same speech, which is above II. 12. Καταισχυνθῶσιν οἱ ἐπηρεάζοντες ὑμῶν τὴν ἀγαθὴν ἐν Χριστῷ ἀνατροφὴν] Here again understand διὰ τὸν Χριστὸν, according to the precepts of Christ. They will speak evil of you, because you are Christians. But this very thing will be a shame to them, when it shall appear from your deeds how upright and pure the Christian religion is. Concerning the word ἐπηρεάζειν see Matthew V. 44, Luke VI. 28. Estius says the reading of the Syriac text is probable, which is this: as men who slander your good conversation, which is in Christ, in this sense: It will come to pass that those who speak evil of you, as if you were evildoers and wicked men, they themselves in turn, as slanderers of your holy conversation, will be ill-spoken of and will blush. It is possible, he says, that the particle ὡς in the Greek text was omitted long ago, either by the injury or the ignorance of the scribes, who thought it superfluous. Furthermore, as to the words, 'that they detract from you,' in the Greek is added, 'as evildoers,' which in the Syriac text is also added in this way, 'as evil men,' [but] it is omitted in the Latin. This seems to Estius to have been added from chapter II. 12. But the cause for suspicion is not sufficient in either case. For the Greek words yield an excellent sense, which Estius himself exhibits thus: It will come to pass that your detractors, who slander your conversation—that is, the life which you lead according to the doctrine of Christ—as wicked and hypocritical, will at length be convicted of their own sycophancy and wickedness, and will be ashamed and forced to be silent. So also Cornelius à Lapide: By your holy conversation you powerfully refute their detractions, and they will blush for their falsehood and slander. The mouths of slanderers are not only stopped by the good conversation of the pious, so that they are forced to be silent, 1 Peter II. 15, but the slanderers themselves are also confounded and blush, Psalm XXV. 3, XXXV. 4, 26. Verse 17. Κρεῖττον γὰρ ἀγαθοποιοῦντας εἰ θέλοι τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ πάσχειν, ἢ κακοποιοῦντας] This is the very thing which Socrates used to say to his wife: but he was not so instructed regarding the straight path, nor the end to which it tends, as Christians are. He who suffers for crimes has no hope of recompense: he who suffers for God has the greatest. Whence above II. 20. The expression is Hebrew, noted by the learned, אם רו ירצה רצוך האל, equal to that which is in 1 Corinthians IV. 19, James IV. 15. But here it is used concerning adversities, as in the prayer, 'Thy will be done.' See also Matthew 26, Luke XXII. 42. Θέλημα elsewhere signifies the thing which God wills, but here the act of willing. In the manuscript, instead of εἰ θέλοι is εἰ θέλει. Some Latins translate, 'if the Spirit of God wills,' because the words written by abbreviation θμα̃ and πμα̃ are similar. It does not mean what seemed so to Cornelius: 'It is good to suffer as a guilty person, but it is better to suffer as an innocent one.' But the comparison is improper. He is criticizing, says Bede, some who, if they suffer for a fault, bear it patiently, but if they suffer while innocent, they murmur, and thus they lose the good of innocence through the fault of impatience, when they ought rather to increase and adorn it by the merit of patience. The patience of Christians, says Origen in Homily VII on Judges, overcomes the impudence of persecutors. To do good and suffer evil is far better than to do evil and suffer evil on that account, which in truth is not good, except insofar as the deserved punishment is sustained with patience, Luke XXIII. 41. Compare 1 Peter II. 15, 16. The Syrian conveniently expressed this improper comparison: 'It helps you when you suffer evils while doing good works, and not when you yourselves do evils.' 'If the will of God wills,' the Syrian: 'If only it be so, or if the will or good pleasure of God bears it.' Which St. Augustine explained in Book XXII against Faustus, ch. 20: 'If it pleases God to permit persecutions and calamities.'

by the will, he says, of the Spirit of God they suffer while doing good; the just are not spared, but when they are doing evil, sinners are not spared. Yet according to His will both come to pass, He who says, 'I will not spare the just nor the sinner,' the former by scourging him as a son, the latter by punishing him as an impious man. But Lorinus is wrong at this place: 'It is indeed good to bear the punishments due to sins, and if one tolerates them patiently, he satisfies and merits, and it is better not to have deserved them.' For although patience in punishments pleases God, it does not appease God. He is pleased through faith in Christ, who alone appeased God by His satisfactory passion.

Latin:

Συνείδησιν ἔχοντες ἀγαθὴν] In omni actu bonam servan- tes conscientiam, Actor. XXIII. 1. 1. Tim. I. 5. 19. III. 9. 2. Tim. I. 3. sic & infra III. 25.

Bona conscientia & in actu confessionis servanda, ne quicquam invita conscientia profiteamur, vel subdolo distinctionis maleferiatorum effugio inter actum voluntatis elicitum, & imperatum Deo & hominibus illudamus, conscientiamque nostram sauciemus, aut reservato etiam mentali; vel conditi- one aliqua veteratoria eos, quib9 confessio edenda, decipiamus: & in vita fidei consentanea probanda, ne fidei puritas vitæ impuritate contaminetur, quo- modo Oecumenius: S. Petrus, inquit, consulit, ut re- sponsiones à vita etiam nostra comprobentur, id quod conscientiam vocat. Mihi videtur, inquit S. August. epist. 211. ad Probam. plus valere in hac inquisitione vivendi, quam loquendi modum. Quod si vita profes- sioni non respondeat, non modò nullus erit profe- ctus, sed sequitur etiam dispendium apud eos, qui de sermone ex moribus judicant. Erubescit, quamvis præclara doctrina, quam propria reprehendit consci- entia, ait Hieronymus in epist. adPrincip. Adde quod conversatio bona loquendi præbeat fiduciam Act. XXIII. 1. Vers. 16. Ἵνα ἐν ᾧ καταλαλῶσι ὑμῶν ὡς κακοποιῶν] ea- dem loquutio, quæ supra II. 12. Καταισχυνθῶσιν οἱ ἐπηρεάζοντες ὑμῶν τὴν ἀγαθὴν ἐν Χριστῷ ἀνατροφὴν] Hic iterum subaudi διὰ τὸν Χριστὸν, secundum Christi præcepta. Male de vobis loquentur, quod Christi- ani sitis. At hoc ipsum eis pudori erit, ubi apparuerit ex fa- ctis vestris, quam recta & pura sit Christiana religio. De ver- bo ἐπηρεάζειν vide Matth. V. 44. Luc. VI. 28. Estius Syriaci textus lectionem probabilem di- cit, quæ hæc est, tanquam viri,qui calumniantur con- versationes vestras bonas, quæ sunt in Christo, hoc sensu: Ita fiet, ut qui male de vobis loquuntur, tan- quam de maleficis & sceleratis hominibus, ipsi vi- cissim tanquam calumniatores sanctæ vestræ con- versationis male audiat & erubescant. Fieri potest, inquit, ut particula ὡς inGræco textu jam olim vel injuria vel imperitia scribentium, qui superfluam putarent, omissa fuerit. Porrò quod ad verba, quod detrahunt vobis, in Græco additur, tanquam malefactoribus, quod inSyriaco textu etiam addi- tur hoc modo, tanquam hominibus malis, inLatino omissum est. Id additum videtur Estio è cap. II.12. Sed causa suspicionis in neutro idonea est. Sensum enim Græca optimum reddunt, quem ita exhibet Estius ipse: Ita futurum est, ut obtrectatores vestri, qui conversationem vestram, id est, vitam, quam agitis juxta Christi doctrinam, calumniantur ut ma- leficam ac fucatam, sua sycophantia & improbitatis tandem convicti, pudeant, & obmutescere cogan- tur. Ita etiam Cornelius à Lapide: Cum sancta conversatione valide confutatis eorum detrectationes, & calumnias erubescent de falsitate & calumnia sua. Calumniatorum ora non solum per bo- nam piorum conversationem obstruuntur, ut ob- mutescere cogantur, 1. Petr. II, 15. sed ipsi etiam calumniatores confunduntur & erubescunt, Psal. XXV.3. XXXV.4.26. Vers. 17. Κρεῖττον γὰρ ἀγαθοποιοῦντας εἰ θέλοι τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ πάσχειν, ἢ κακοποιοῦντας] Hoc est ipsum, quod uxo- ri suæ dicebat Socrates: sed neque de via recta, neque de fi- ne, quo ea tendit, ita edoctus, ut Christiani. Qui ob facino- ra patitur, spem non habet repensationis: qui ob Deum pa- titur, habet maximam. Unde supra II. 20. Loquutio est Ebræa ab eruditis annotata אם רו ירצה רצוך האל par ei quæ est 1.Cor. IV. 19. Jac. IV. 15. Sed hic ea de adversis usurpatur, ut in precatione, fiat voluntas tua. Vid. & Matth. 26. Luc. XXII. 42. Θέλημα alibi significat rem, quam Deus vult, hic vero volendi actionem. InManuscripto pro εἰ θέλοι est εἰ θέλει. Quidam Latini vertunt, si velit Spiritus Dei, quia voces per compendium scripta θμα̃ & πμα̃ vicina sunt. Non id vult, quod Cornelio visum: Bonum est pati nocentem, at melius est pati innocentem. Est au- tem comparatio impropria. Perstringit, ait Beda, quosdam, qui si pro culpa patiuntur, patienter fe- runt, sin inculpati patiuntur, murmurant, itaque bo- num innocentiæ perdunt per culpam impatientiæ, cum potius illud augere & ornare deberent merito patien- tiæ. Patientia Christianorum, inquit Origenes hom. VII. in Jud. vincat impudentiam persecutorum. Be- ne agere & mala pati longe satius est, quam male a- gere & propterea mala pati, quod revera bonũ nõ est, nisi quatenus cum patientia sustinetur prome- rita pœna, Luc. XXIII. 41. Confer. 1. Petr. II. 15.16. Quam impropriam comparationem Syrus com- mode expressit: Juvat vos cum facientes opera bona sustinetis mala, & non cum facitis ipsi mala. Si velit Dei voluntas, Syrus: Si modo ita sit vel ferat volun- tas sive beneplacitum Dei. Quod S. Augustinus ex- posuit l. XXII. contr. Faust. c. 20. Si Deo placeat permittere persecutiones ac calamitates.

voluntate, inquit, Spiritus Dei patiuntur benefaci- entes, non parcitur justis, cum autem malefacientes, non parcitur peccatoribus. Secundum illius tamen voluntatem fit utrumque, qui ait, non parcam justo nec peccatori, illum flagellando ut filium, hunc puni- endo ut impium. Perperam autem Lorinus ad h. l. Bonum quidem supplicia ferre peccatis debita, & si patienter quis toleret, satisfacit ac meretur, ac me- lius, non commeruisse. Etsi enim patientia in pœnis Deo placeat, non tamen Deum placat. Placet per fi- dem in Christum, qui solus placavit Deum passio- ne sua satisfactoria.

## 3:18
Verse 18. Ὅτι καὶ Χριστὸς ἅπαξ περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἔπαθε δίκαι- ος ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων] ἅπαξ here signifies nothing other than 'once' or 'at some time,' as Hebrews IX. 7, Psalm LXXXIX. 36. If Christ died on the occasion of our sins, and that for our good, we who were then evil, how much more ought we to be prepared to die or to suffer evils for His glory and the edification of Christians? Περὶ and ὑπὲρ sometimes signify the occasion, sometimes the benefit of another, as can be seen here. The Syrian in both places used חלף. Compare what is in Romans V. 6. In the manuscript more fully: Περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἔπαθε δίκαι- ος ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων.

By the example of Christ he now exhorts to patience in sufferings for the sake of justice. The little word ἅπαξ is properly 'once,' nor is it taken otherwise in Hebrews IX. 7, and the same sense is convenient in Psalm LXXXIX. 36. Cornelius à Lapide observes that by the word 'once' is noted: 1. That Christ at once and once for all underwent all kinds of torments, and drank up the whole sea, while we only drink up brief, small, and scattered sufferings. 2. That Christ by a single heroic act of patience exhausted the whole force of sufferings, and became the victor and triumpher over all: and therefore we also ought to decide with a single heroic resolution to suffer patiently any adversities whatsoever by the example of Christ. 3. That the single passion and patience of Christ was so great that by that thing He redeemed the whole world, Hebrews X. 14. This last reason especially prevails here, which Estius alone holds: He says 'once', in order to declare the efficacy of the death of Christ, which alone, and never to be repeated, is sufficient to blot out all the sins of all ages. The Syriac rendered it 'at one time' through a Hebraism. The Vulgate has: 'Christ died once for our sins.' But in the Greek and Syriac the pronoun 'our' is not held, nor 'died', but 'suffered' in the Greek. There is no doubt, however, as Estius says, but that Peter speaks of the passion of death, especially because he adds 'once'. For so also Paul, Rom. VI: 'He died to sin once', and Heb. IX: 'By his own blood he entered once into the holy places.' And again: 'Christ was offered once to exhaust the sins of many.' But the Syriac also in this place expressed the passion of death. Christ, however, died not only by occasion, but also by the merit of our sins, because he was delivered up for our sins, Rom. IV, last verse; nor do περὶ and ὑπὲρ ever denote only occasion in this matter, nor only, when Christ is said to have died for us, do they note the end, that he died for our good, which Grotius now teaches in favor of the Socinians, whereas he previously taught more correctly, namely that a substitution is signified, which the Syriac חלף also implies. Namely, he underwent death in our stead, having suffered and died for our sins, that is, because of our sins, the just for the unjust, that is, in the stead of the unjust. For if one died ὑπὲρ πάντων for all, then all have died, 2 Cor. V. 15. As regards the preposition ὑπὲρ, Grotius used to say in his Defense of the Catholic Faith concerning the Satisfaction of Christ, chap. IX, page 117, it is first to be noted that it also, not indeed always, but often, is worth the same as ἀντί. Paul desires to be ἀνάθεμα for his brethren, that is, in the stead of the Jews, whom he knew would otherwise, by persisting in unbelief, be ἀνάθεμα. Rom. IX. 3.

The Apostles ὑπὲρ τῆ Χρισῦ πρεσβεύυσι, that is, they are ambassadors in the place of Christ himself, 2 Cor. 5:20. Wherefore, since ἀντὶ necessarily signifies a commutation, and ὑπὲρ is sometimes accustomed to be put for the same, what prevents one from interpreting a word of doubtful notation from a certain one, especially when the argument concerns the same subject? But especially that passage 2 Cor. 5:14 seems to require this interpretation: If one died for all, then all died. Furthermore, even if the word were ambiguous in those places where ὑπὲρ was used, but it had been openly said that Christ died for our benefit, yet by this very fact that commutation would not be excluded; indeed, by comparing other passages, it would rather be included. For he who dies in this way, so that by that very act he frees another from death, dies for his benefit. Nor can this sense be rejected because in some places Christ's deed is proposed to us as an example. For an example, it is sufficient that there be a certain general similarity, even if there is a difference in the special mode, the mention of which is sometimes made for the sake of denoting the thing more certainly. This is manifestly clear from Peter's exhortation, 1 Pet. 2:19 ff. He wants us to be patient in enduring the afflictions which we suffer innocently. He brings forward the example of Christ: who, he says, also himself suffered: This was enough for the comparison. But he added ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, which does not pertain to the comparison, but clearly designates the thing itself, that is, the passion of Christ. The patience, therefore, is common; the mode differs. Otherwise, Paul would ask in vain whether Paul was crucified for the believers, 1 Cor. 1:13. For he himself could also be crucified for the Church, that is, for the use of the Church, just as he said he suffered for the Church, Col. 1:24, and afterwards he himself was struck by the sword for the great good of the Church, and Peter and the other Apostles were crucified. But in the way in which Christ was crucified, by bearing punishments in our stead, neither Paul could, nor anyone else. That word 'for' therefore denotes something peculiar here, which cannot be communicated to the Apostles. It could, however, if the utility of Christ's death were separated from the death of the Apostles only by degree, and not also by its own end. Christ does not only excite us to patience by the example of his death, so that we may similarly sustain death and other passions with a patient mind when we suffer for righteousness, just as he himself suffered—which example he also inculcated above in 1 Epist. 2:19—but he also obtained by the merit of his death that we have no need to suffer for our sins, which he himself expiated, and that we are able to sustain patiently the passions which are unjustly inflicted upon us by men: therefore, as above in the special exhortation to servants to patience, the Holy Apostle had brought forward both the example and the merit of Christ: So he does the same here in the general exhortation to all Christians to patience.

Ἴνα ἡμᾶς προσαγάγη τῷ Θεῷ] προσάγειν, here, is what καταλλάσσειν is, Rom. 5:10. Just as προσερίχεσθαι Θεῷ is to worship God, as we have seen several times, so προσάγειν is to make [us] fit to worship God, which Christ performed, both by providing us an example of obedience and by sealing the truth of his doctrine with his blood. The Syrian [translates] ונקברככן as 'that he might offer us to God,' as victims, namely, similar to himself. For also קרב, when it concerns victims, is accustomed to be translated by προσάγειν in very many places of Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers.

It is one thing to καταλλάσσειν, to reconcile to God, which is done through the expiation of sins; it is another to προσάγειν, to bring to God, which is done through conversion. Reconciliation was made through satisfaction for our sins; when Christ suffered for our sins, the just for the unjust. But the bringing to God is the source of that reconciliation; therefore it is said, ἵνα ἡμᾶς προσάγαγη τῷ θεῷ, if you explain it as 'to make fit to worship God,' the same is also done through our regeneration and conversion, but not only by providing an example and sealing the truth of the doctrine with blood. For the Apostles also did both of these, yet they neither reconciled men by their own blood, which belongs to Christ alone, Rom. 5:10, nor did they suffer for others and for the sins of others, so that they might make them fit to

worship God, or bring them to God. The Vulgate and B. Luther take the word προσάγειν in a sacrificial sense: But it properly signifies to bring, as Augustine rendered it in Ep. 99 and Book 1 de merit. et remiss. pecc. See Luke 9:41, Acts 12:6, ch. 16:20, in which sense the Syriac word can also be taken, as 'to make you approach God.' This προσ- αγωγή of conversion to God is the cause of the fiducial approaching of the converted to God through prayers, of which [we read] Rom. 5:2, Eph. 2:17, 18, ch. 3:12. It can, however, be said that Christ offers us to God as a sacrifice, in that he made us spiritual priests to God the Father, so that we may offer ourselves to the same as living hosts, and pleasing to God, Apoc. 1:6, Rom. 12:1, 1 Pet. 2:5.

Θανατωθεὶς μὲν σαρκὶ] He died indeed, as far as pertains to this fragile and perishable life, which is accustomed to be signified by the name of flesh, as 2 Cor. 5:16, Heb. 5:7, 1 Tim. 3:16. It is clearly the same as what is said in 2 Cor. 13:4, ἐσταυρώθη ἐξ ἀσθενείας.

Ζωοποιηθεὶς δὲ τῷ πνεύματι] Vivified to life through that Divine power which appeared in him even while he was acting on earth. This is what is said in the aforementioned place 2 Cor. 13:4, ἐκ δυνάμεως Θεῦ. Thus also the Spirit of God, which is in us, will be the cause of our resuscitation, as we said at Rom. 1:1 and Heb. 9:14. That τῷ is absent in the Manuscript. Σάρξ and Πνεῦμα are opposed, as John 6:63.

Flesh and Spirit in Christ denote not natural, perishable life and the Holy Spirit, but the human and divine nature of Christ. For thus σὰρξ and Πνεῦμα are opposed in Christ, John 1:14, Rom. 1:3, 4, ch. 9:5, 1 Tim. 3:16, Heb. 2:14. The passage John 6:63 is foreign here: for that cannot be taken concerning the flesh or Spirit of Christ, unless it be impiously said that the flesh of Christ profits nothing. Therefore he is said to be put to death in the flesh, that is, as regards his human nature. But he was made alive in the Spirit, or by the power of the divine nature, according to which he had power from himself to lay down his life and to take it up again, John 10:17, 18. But this one is God and eternal life, 1 John 5:20. By the name of flesh, says Blessed Gerhard, according to the common phrase of Scripture, is understood the whole human nature of Christ, in which Christ sustained passion and death, John 1:14. For although the soul of Christ, being an immortal Spirit, was not dead, nor could it die, yet it sustained the most grievous agonies in his passion, whence he is said to have labored, Isa. 53:11, and to have been sorrowful even unto death, Matt. 26:38, and in death it was separated from the body. Τῷ Πνεύματι is put for διὰ Πνεύματος, by the Spirit, namely, of the Deity. Whence Oecumenius explains it: By the force and power of the Divinity, which is the most pure Spirit. So also Athanasius in Bede. Augustine, sermon 95 on the Words of the Apostle, and from the Papists, Isidorus Clarius. For although he was affected by death, on account of the nature of the flesh assumed; yet by the Spirit and Divinity (since God is Spirit, John 4:24) he always lives. Whence also he can save by himself those who approach God through him, Heb. 7:25. That Cornelius à Lapide understands the soul by Spirit and the body of Christ by flesh is foreign to the manner of speaking of Scripture, which, in the opposition of flesh and Spirit when the discourse is about the person of Christ, is not accustomed to speak thus, nor does it suit the present subject, because Christ did not profit by the soul alone, as one who profited after ζωοποίησιν or having been made alive. Nor does Estius altogether disapprove of our sense; Christ, while he was suffering, was indeed killed and died in the flesh, which he bore as mortal and weak: but by the power of the Divinity, which was not separated from him through death, or (which is the same thing) by the power of the Holy Spirit, he was made alive, that is, resurrected to life. Thus Oecumenius and Augustine in the places already cited. Likewise Athanasius and the aforementioned V. Bede. This sense agrees with that which Paul writes about Christ, 2 Cor. last. For although he was crucified out of weakness, yet he lives by the power of God. Add that the soul of Christ did not raise his body by itself by its own power, but by the power communicated by the Word brought it back into life. Put to death in the flesh, says Augustine in Epistle 99, he is said to be, because he died according to the flesh alone: But brought to life in the Spirit: because by that Spirit working, in whom he came to those to whom he was preaching, even that very flesh was brought to life and rose again, in which manner he comes to men. And although the offering of Christ was made even in death through the eternal Spirit or the Deity of Christ, because that action is theandrikē, yet Christ died according to the flesh, because death is a property of human nature. The reading of certain Latin codices, put to death indeed in the flesh, but brought to life in the Spirit, although Bede, the author of the Gloss, Lyranus, Gagnejus, Catharinus, Arias, and Schvoarez have followed it, is deservedly rejected by Cornelius and Estius, and the Greek and Latin-Roman reading is preferred, as is the Syriac reading, put to death indeed in the flesh, but brought to life in the Spirit, which is that of Clement of Alexandria, Book VI of the Stromata, and of Epiphanius, Heresy 51 and 77. Augustine, Epistle 99; Rufinus in his Exposition of the Creed; Cyril, On the Faith to Regina; Peter of Alexandria in the Council of Ephesus, Vol. II, 7; Jerome on Isaiah 54; Oecumenius, and others.

Latin:

Vers. 18. Ὅτι καὶ Χριστὸς ἅπαξ περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἔπαθε δίκαι- ος ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων] ἅπαξ hic nihil aliud significat, quam ali- quando, ut Ebr. IX. 7. Psal. LXXXIX. 36. si Christus mor- tuus est occasione peccatorum nostrorum, idque nostro bo- no, qui tunc eramus mali, quanto magis nos parati esse de- bemus mori, aut mala perpeti ad ipsius gloriam & Christia- norum ædificationem? Περὶ & ὑπὲρ modo occasionem signi- ficant, modo alterius utilitatem, ut hic videre est. Syrus utroque loco posuit חלף. Confer quæ sunt Rom. V. 6. In Manuscripto plenius: Περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἔπαθε δίκαι- ος ὑπὲρ ἀδίκων.

Exemplo Christi jam ad patientiam in passionibus propter justitia exhortatur. Vocula ἅπαξ proprie est semel, nec aliter accipitur Ebr. IX. 7. idemque sensus commodus Psal. LXXXIX. 36. Cornelius à Lapide observat, voce semel notari 1. Christum si- mul & semel omnia cruciatuum genera subiisse, to- tumque mare absorpsisse, nos tantum breves, exi- guas, & dispersitas passiones ebibere. 2. Christum unico heroico patientiæ actu omnem passionum vim expunxisse, omniumque factum esse victorem & triumphatorem: ideoque & nos unica heroica resolutione decernere debere, quælibet adver- sa Christi exemplo patienter pati. 3. Unicam Chri- sti passionem & patientiam tantam fuisse, ut ea re- demerit totum mundum, Ebr. X. 14. Quæ ratio po- strema hic præcipue obtinet, quam unam Estius ha- bet: Dicit autem semel, ut efficaciam mortis Christi declaret, quæ una, nec unquam iteranda, valet ad o- mnia omnium seculorum peccata delenda. Syrus red- didit uno tempore per Ebraismum. Vulgatus habet: Christus semel pro peccatis nostris mortuus est. Sed in Græco & Syriaco Pronomen nostris non habetur, nec mortuus, sed passus est in Græco. Non dubium tamen, Estio dicente, quin de passione mortis loqua- tur Petrus, maxime quia addit semel. Sic enim & Paulus, Rom. VI. Peccato mortuus est semel, & Ebr. IX. Per proprium sanguinem introivit semel in san- cta. Et iterum: Christus semel oblatus est ad multo- rum peccata exhaurienda. Sed & Syrus hoc loco pas- sionem mortis expressit. Christus vero mortuus est non tantum occasione, sed & merito peccatorum no- strorum, quia traditus est propter peccata nostra, Rom. IV. v. ult. neque περὶ & ὑπὲρ occasionem tan- tum uspiam in hac materia, nec solum cum pro no- bis mortuus dicitur Christus, finem notant, quod nostro bono mortuus sit, quæ in gratiam Socinia- norum nunc tradit Grotius, quum prius rectius do- cuerit, nimirum commutationem significari, quam etiam infert Syriacum חלף. Na vice nostri mortem subiit passus & mortuus pro peccatis, id est, pro- pter peccata nostra, justus pro injustis, id est, vice injustorum. Si enim unus ὑπὲρ πάντων pro omnibo mortuus est, utiq; omnes mortui sunt, 2. Cor. V. 15. Præpositionem ὑπὲρ quod attinet, inquiebat Grotius defens. fidei Cath. de satisf. Christi cap. IX. pag. 117. primum notandum est, illam quoque non qui- dem semper, at sæpe idem valere, quod ἀντί. Optat Paulus ἀνάθεμα esse ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀδελφῶν, hoc est, vice Judæorum, quos alioqui perseverantes in incredulitate sciebat futuros ἀνάθεμα. Rom. IX. 3.

Apostoli ὑπὲρ τῆ Χρισῦ πρεσβεύυσι h. e. legati sunt ipfius Christi vice, 2. Cor. V. 20. Quare cum ἀντὶ necessa- rio commutationem significet, ὑπὲρ autem pro eodem poni nonnunquam foleat, quid vetat vocem notatio- nis dubiæ ex certa interpretari, præsertim cum eodem de argumento agitur? Imprimis vero eam interpre- tationem videtur requirere locus ille 2. Cor. V. 14. Si unus pro omnibus mortuus, omnes ergo mortui. Dein- de vero etiamfi vox on per se ambigua ὑπὲρ iis in lo- cis esset usurpata, sed aperte esset dictum, Christum bono nostro mortuum, hoc ipso tamen commutatio illa non excluderetur, imo collatis aliis locis includere- tur potius. Nam & qui in hoc moritur, ut eo ipso al- terum à morte liberet, ejus bono moritur. Neq; potest hic sensus rejici, quia alicubi Christi factum nobis in exemplum proponitur. Nam ad exemplum fufficit, generalem quandam esse similitudinem, etsi differen- tia sit in modo speciali, cujus tamen mentio fit inter- dum rei certius denotandæ gratia. Quod manifesto liquet ex Petri adhortatione 1. Petr. II. 19. feqq. Vult nos patientes esse in tolerandis afflictionibus, quas in- fontes patimur. Affert Christi exemplum: qui inquit & ipfe passus est: Satis hoc erat ad comparationem. Sed addidit ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, quod ad comparationem non per- tinet, sed rem, ipfam, hoc est, Christi passionem clare designat. Commune ergo est patientia, modus differt. Alioqui frustra Paulus quæreret, an Paulus pro fide- libus esset crucifixus, 1. Cor. I 13. Poterat enim & ipse pro Ecclesia, hoc est, in usum Ecclefiæ crucifigi, sicut pati se dixit pro Ecclesia, Col. I. 24. & postea magno Ecclefiæ bono ipse gladio percussus est, Petrus, aliique Apostoli crucifixi. Sed eo modo, quo Christus crucifi- gi, pœnas vice nostra ferendo, nec Paulus poterat, nec alius quisquam. Vox ergo illa pro peculiare hic ali- quid notat, quod Apostolis communicari non potest. Posset autem, si mortis Christi utilitas gradu tantum à morte Apostolorum, non etiam fine proprio segre- garetur. Christus non mortis tantum suæ exemplo nos ad patientiam excitat, ut similiter animo pa- tienti mortem sustineamus, aliasque passiones, cum ob justitiam patimur, quemadmodum ipse passus est, quod exemplum etiā supra 1. epist. II. 19. incul- carat, sed etiam mortis suæ merito id impetravit, ut pro peccatis nostris pati opus non habeamus, quæ ipfe expiavit, utque passiones, quæ ab hominibus injuste nobis inferuntur, patienter sustinere vale- amus: ideo ut supra in fervorum exhortatione spe- ciali ad patientiā S. Apostol9 & exempl. & meritũ Christi adduxerat: Ita idem hic facit in Christiano- rum omnium generali ad patientiā exhortatione.

Ἴνα ἡμᾶς προσαγάγη τῷ Θεῷ] προσάγειν, hic est, quod καταλλάσσειν, Rom. V. 10. Sicut προσερίχεσθαι Θεῷ est De- um colere, ut vidimus aliquoties, ita προσάγειν idoneos ad Deum colendum facere, quod Christus præstitit, & exem- plum nobis præbendo obedientiæ, & suo sanguine obfignan- do doctrinæ suæ veritatem. Syrus ונקברככן ut offerret nos Deo, ut victimas, nimirum ipsi similes. Nam & קרב ubi de victimis agitur, verti solet per προσάγειν plurimis lo- cis Exodi, Levitici & Numerorum.

Aliud est καταλλάσσειν reconciliare Deo, quod fit per expiationem peccatorum, aliud προσάγειν adducere ad Deum, quod fit per conversionem. Recō- ciliatio per satisfactionẽ pro peccatis nostris facta est; quando Christus passus est pro peccatis nostris, justus pro injustis. Adductio autem ad Deum fons est illi9 recōciliationis, ideo dicitur, ἵνα ἡμᾶς προσ- αγάγη τῷ θεῷ, si exponas, idoneos facere ad colẽ- dum Deum, idem etiam fit per regenerationem & cōversionem nostram, non autẽ tantum exemplum præbendo & sanguine obsignando doctrinæ veri- tatem. Nam hoc utrumque fecere etiam Apostoli, nec tamẽ illi vel reconciliarunt homines sanguine suo, quod uni Christo convenit, Rom. V. 10. vel passi sunt pro aliis, & aliorum peccatis, ut eos idoneos ad

Deum colendum facerent, vel ad Deum adduce- rent Vulgata & B. Lutherus verbum προσάξειν sen- su sacrificiali accipiunt: Sed id proprie significat ad- ducere, ut Augustinus reddidit ep. XCIX. & l. 1. de merit. & remiss. pecc. Vid. Luc. IX. 41. Act. XII. 6. c. XVI. 20. quo sensu etiam verbum Syriacum accipi potest, ut appropinquare vos faceret Deo. Quæ προσ- αγωγή conversionis ad Deum causa est fiducialis conversorum per preces ad Deum appropinquati- onis, de qua Rom. V. 2. Eph. II. 17. 18. c. III. 12. Dici tamen potest, Deo nos in sacrificium offerre Chri- stum, qua nos fecit spirituales Sacerdotes Deo Pa- tri, ut nos eidem offeramus in hostias vivas, Deoq; placentes, Apoc. I. 6. Rom. XII. 1. 1. Petr. II. 5.

Θανατωθεὶς μὲν σαρκὶ] Mortuus quidem est, quod atti- net ad vitam hanc fragilem & caducam, quæ carnis nomine significari solet, ut 2. Cor. V. 16. Ebr. V. 7. 1. Tim. III. 16. Plane idem est, quod 2. Cor. XIII. 4. dicitur ἐσταυρώθη ἐξ ἀσθενείας.

Ζωοποιηθεὶς δὲ τῷ πνεύματι] Vivificatus ad vitam per vim illam Divinam, quæ in ipso etiam in terris agente apparuit. Hoc est quod dicitur dicto loco 2. Cor. XIII. 4. ἐκ δυνάμεως Θεῦ. Sic & Spiritus Dei, qui in nobis est, causa erit nostræ resuscitationis, ut diximus ad Rom. I. 1. & Ebr. IX. 14. Il- lud τῷ abest in Manuscripto. Σάρξ & Πνεῦμα opponuntur, ut Joh. VI. 63.

Caro & Spiritus in Christo non vitam naturalem caducam, & Spiritum S. sed Humanam & Divinam Christi naturam notant. Nam ita opponitur σὰρξ & Πνεῦμα in Christo Joh. I. 14. Rom. I. 3. 4. c. IX. 5. 1. Tim. III. 16. Ebr. II. 14. Locus Joh. VI. 63. hic ἀλλότριος est: Ille enim de carne vel Spiritu Christi accipi non potest, nisi impie dicatur carnem Christi nihil prod- esse. Mortificatus ergo carne dicitur, seu quod ad humanam naturam. Vivificatus autem Spiritu, vel virtute divinæ naturæ, secundum quam à semetipso potestatẽ habuit vitam ponendi & vicissim sumen- di, Joh. X. 17. 18. Hic autem Deus est & vita æterna, 1. Joh. V. 20. Carnis nomine, inquit B. Gerhardus, juxta Vulgatam scripturæ phrasin intelligitur tota natura Humana Christi, in qua passionem & mortem Chri- stus sustinuit, Joh. I. 14. Quamvis enim anima Christi, utpote immortalis Spiritus, non fuerit mortua, nec po- tuerit mori, illa tamen gravissimos angores in passione sustinuit, unde dicitur laborasse, Es. LIII. 11. ac περί- λυπος fuisse usque ad mortem, Matth. XXVI. 38. & in morte fuit à corpore separata. Τῷ Πνεύματι ponitur pro διὰ Πνεύματος, per Spiritum, videlicet Deitatis. Unde Oecumenius exponit: Vi & potentia Divi- nitatis, quæ est Spiritus purissimus. Sic etiam A- thanasius apud Bedam. Augustinus serm. XCV. de Verb. Apost. & è Pontificiis Isidorus Clarius. Nam etsi morte affectus est, ob carnis naturam acceptam; Spiritu tamen ac Divinitate, (siquidem Deus) Spiri- tus est Joh. IV. 24.) semper vivit. Unde & salvare potest per seipsum accedentes per ipsum ad Deum, Ebr. VII. 25. Quod Cornelius à Lapide per Spiritum animam, per carnem corpus Christi intelligit, alie- num est à modo loquendi scripturæ, quæ in opposi- tione carnis & Spiritus, cum de Christi persona ser- mo est, ita non solet loqui, nec convenit materiæ præsenti, quia non sola anima profectus est Chri- stus, utpote qui post ζωοποίησιν vel ζωοποιηθεὶς profectus est. Nec omnino improbat sensum nostru Estius; Christus dum pateretur, carne quidem, quam mortalem & infirmam gerebat occisus est & mortuus: sed virtute Divinitatis, quæ per mortem ab eo non fuit separata, vel (quod idem est) virtute Spiritus S. vivi- ficatus est, id est, ad vitam resuscitatus. Sic Oecumeni- us & locis jam citatis August. Item Athanasius & V. Beda allegatus. Convenit hic sensus cum eo, quod Paulus scribit de Christo 2. Cor. ult. Nam etsi crucifi- xus est ex infirmitate, sed vivit ex virtute Dei. Adde quod anima Christi corpus suum non per se sua vir- tute, sed communicata τῦ λόγε potentia in vitam reduxit. Mortificatus carne, inquit Augustinus ep. XCIX. dictus est, quia secundum solam carnem mor- tuus est : Vivificatus autem Spiritu: quia Spiritu illo operante, in quo ad quos veniebat & prædicabat ipsa etiam caro vivificata surrexit, in quo modo ad homi- nes venit. Etsi autem oblatio Christi in morte etiam facta sit per Spiritum æternum vel Deitatem Chri- sti, quia actio illa est θεανδρικὴ, mortuus tamen Christus est secundum carnem, quiamori proprie- tas est humanæ naturæ. Lectio Latinorum quorun- dam Codicum, mortificatos quidem carne, vivifica- tos autem Spiritu, etsi eam sequutus sit Beda, Autor Glossæ, Lyranus, Gagnejus, Catharinus, Arias & Schvoarez, merito rejicitur à Cornelio & Estio, præferturque Græca, & Latina-Romana, ut & Syra lectio, mortificatus quidem carne, vivificatus autem Spiritu, quæ est Clem. Alexandr. l. VI. Strom. Epi- phanii hæresi LI. & LXXVII. Augustini ep. XCIX. Ruffini in expos. symboli, Cyrilli de fide ad Regin. Petri Alex. in concil. Ephes. T. II. 7. Hieronymi in Es. LIV. Oecumenii & aliorum.

## 3:19
v. 19. In whom] Through which Spirit of God sent into the Apostles. And to the spirits in prison he went and preached] he went after he ascended into heaven, as shortly in v. 22. John 14:2, 3, 12, 28; 15:17, 28. Christ is said to have preached to the Gentiles, because the Apostles did this in his name and by his power, 2 Cor. 5:20; Acts 13:47; Rom. 15:16; Gal. 2:8; Eph. 2:17. But because Peter wished to add a comparison from the times of Noah, to show how much better things have proceeded now through Christ than then through Noah, he therefore takes the words from that history. For God says in Gen. 6:3, לא ידון רוחי באדם, where the Greeks say, 'My Spirit shall not remain,' or 'My Spirit shall not abide in these men,' but if we follow the propriety of the words, it says this: 'It shall not be that my Spirit is held as if in a sheath in man': that is, the mind which I gave him (Wisdom 12:1) shall not be useless, like a sword in a sheath, which accomplishes nothing of that for which it was made. A prison is accustomed to be called phylakē, as in Gen. 40:3, 4, 7; 41:10; 42:17, 19; Lev. 24:17; Judg. 16:22, 26; 2 Sam. 22:27; 1 Kings 22:27; 2 Kings 4:17; 24:47, 48; 2 Chron. 13:26; Isa. 42:7; Jer. 32:2, 8, 12; 33:1; 37:4, 14, 17, 21; 52:27; Ezek. 19:9. Moreover, a sheath is as it were a prison for a sword. The Chaldeans call the human body a sheath, nadan, in the same way, as in Dan. 7:15 and often in the Talmudic writings. Thus also Tertullian calls the flesh the sheath of the breath of God, in his book On the Resurrection of the Flesh. This interpretation is not new, but is Jerome's on Isaiah.

Latin:

v. 19. Ἐν ᾧ] Per quem Dei Spiritum missum in Apostolos. Καὶ τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασι πορευθεὶς ἐκήρυξεν] πορευ- θεὶς postquam in cœlum ascendit, ut mox v. 22. Joh. XIV. 2. 3, 12. 28. XV. 17. 28. Dicitur Christus prædicasse gentibus, quia Apostoli id ejus nomine ac virtute fecerunt, 2. Cor. V. 20. Act. XIII. 47. Rom. XV. 16. Gal. II. 8. Eph. II. 17. Quia verò Petrus adjungere voluit similitudinem à tempori- bus Noë, ut ostendat quanto res nunc melius per Christum quam tunc per Noën processerit, ideo verba desumit ex illa hi- storia. Nam dicit Deus Gen. VI. 3. לא ידון רוחי באדם, ubi Græci ὐ μὴ καταμείνῃ, aut ὐ καταμενεῖ τὸ πνεῦμά με ἐν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις τύτοις, at si proprietatem vocum sequimur, id dicit: non erit ut in vagina detentus sit Spiritus meus in homine: id est, non erit inutilis animus, quem ei dedi, (Sap. XII. 1.) sicut ensis in vagina, qui nihil efficit ejus, ad quod factus est. Carcer solet dici φυλακὴ, ut Gen. 40, 3. 4. 7. 41, 10. 42, 17. 19. Levit. 24, 17. Jud. 16, 22.26. 2. Sam. 22, 27. 1. Reg. 22. 27. 2. Reg. 4, 17. 24, 47. 48. 2. Pa- ral. 13, 26. Es. 42, 7. Jer. 32, 2. 8. 12. 33, 1. 37, 4. 14. 17. 21. 52, 27. Ezech. 19, 9. Est autem vagina velut carcer gla- dio. Chaldæis נדן vagina eodem modo corpus homi- nis Chaldæi vocant, ut Dan. VII. 15. & in Thalmudicis sæpe. Sic & Tertullianus caro vagina afflatus Dei, libro de resurrectione carnis. Hæc interpretatio non nova est, sed Hi- eronymi ad Esaiam.

## 3:20
Verse 20. To those who were disobedient at one time, when the patience of God was waiting once for all in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared] What kind of minds did not obey long ago in the times of Noah. He speaks as if they had been the same, and they had been the same spirits or minds, not in number, as Aristotle speaks, but in kind, that is, minds equally useless to God, namely those who did not believe Noah's preaching. Men completely alienated from God did not believe Noah; they believed Christ. See regarding a not dissimilar way of speaking what we said in Book II of The Law of War and Peace, 9.3, in the text and in the annotations. The patience of God waited for them, as long as the ark was being built for 120 years. See Heb. 11:7. The word apekdechomai is not infrequent in our writers. See Rom. 7:9; 8:23; 1 Cor. 1:7; Gal. 5:5; Phil. 3:20; Heb. 9:28.

This commentary is truly new and unheard-of. For as to his appealing now to Jerome on Isaiah, he ought to have designated the place or chapter. But we are entirely certain that such a marvelous explanation is not found in Jerome. Yet Socinus's gloss seems related, from which perhaps this was taken, for Grotius loves to 'Socinianize' in his later works; in his explanation of certain passages of Scripture, Socinus has it thus on this passage, p. 113 (which explanations were added to the explanation of the first part of chapter 1 of John): 'For it came to pass that, although he was killed on account of the weakness of the flesh and tasted death, yet by divine force and power he was afterwards restored to immortal life.' Through the same divine force and power, however, when he had departed from here to the Father, having sent his disciples and ministers throughout the whole world, who would preach and openly testify to such a great victory of his over death, he clearly preached and revealed the truth to the minds and souls of those men also, who were held captive by malice and ignorance as if by a kind of force, as if they were prisoners of God, and had been stubborn at one time. Which happened no differently than when, in the age of Noah, the gentleness and clemency of God awaited the repentance of stubborn men, whom the ark, which was being built by Noah himself according to divine prescription, sufficiently warned of their duty and of the divine punishment that was impending.' Which gloss of Socinus, Schlichtingius interpolated in almost the same way as Grotius, in his commentary on this passage: 'Christ went through the Holy Spirit, insofar as he, remaining in heaven, sent that Spirit, received from the Father, in his own place.' He preached, however, through the same Spirit, insofar as he instructed his Apostles with it, who, inspired and instructed by it, preached the Gospel. And further: 'He preaches to the spirits through the Spirit,' that is, to the souls of men, whose spiritual prison is a prison. For spirits cannot be in any other prison than a spiritual one: which prison is what else but sin, and the damnation that follows sin? He adds: 'Those to whom Christ preached had been disobedient at one time, namely in the days of Noah, because they were the same in kind, likewise spirits in prison, likewise damned sinners, but not the same in number.' Related also might seem the comment of John Hessels of Louvain, who thinks that the calling of the Gentiles through Apostolic preaching is described here a priori, because infidel Gentiles are described by the Prophets as bound, darkened, and shut up with iron bars and bronze gates, Isa. 42:7; 49:7. In this Grotius interpretation, however, I desire these things especially: 1. That by 'Spirit' he understands the Holy Spirit, whereas the opposition of flesh and the supposition or person of Christ sufficiently teaches that the name 'Spirit' should rather be understood as the Divinity of Christ. 2. That which the Apostle says was done concerning the Spirit of Christ after His ζωοποίησιν (vivification), Grotius rejects to the times of the Apostles after the ascension of Christ. 3. In order, according to St. Peter, follow the passion and death of Christ, His vivification, and the journey or descent of the Spirit into the prison of hell, the resurrection, the journey or ascension into heaven, the sitting at the right hand of God, and the subjection of the angels by His power, just as it is most well known that these things follow one another in the second article of the Apostolic Creed. 4. The calling of the Gentiles does not immediately follow the vivification of Christ, but followed after His resurrection and ascension into heaven. 5. That which is attributed to Christ or the Spirit of Christ by St. Peter, Grotius attributes to the Apostles. 6. St. Peter speaks of spirits in prison, Grotius of the souls of men in the body. Because this seemed less appropriate to Schlichting, he interpreted the prison not as the body, but as sin, and as a new damnation by a strange interpretation. For he says, 'Sin is the prison of the soul, not of the body, and the spirit is held by the prison of damnation even when bodies are extinct.' But where in the Holy Scriptures is sin called the prison of the soul? Rom. 11:32, God is indeed said to have shut up all under unbelief. But the Apostle does not call sin φυλακὴν or a prison. And were those who were held in the prison of damnation after their bodies were extinct called to repentance and the remission of sins by the preaching of the Apostles? 7. Peter speaks of the unbelievers in the time of Noah, Grotius of the unbelievers in the time of the New Testament, similar to those who lived in the time of Noah. 8. Peter of those spirits to whom Noah once preached, Grotius of different ones, imagining that Peter speaks of different ones, as if they had been the same. Which is to attribute to Peter a speech that is less appropriate, to use the most moderate term. 9. Peter of the spirits of those who remained in unbelief: Grotius of those who were indeed once useless to God and unbelievers (namely, under paganism) but afterwards believed in Christ. 10. Peter of the preaching made to those who, because they did not believe it, were condemned and shut up in the infernal prison, Grotius of the proclamation received through faith, made to those who were saved by believing in Christ.

Enjedinus sometimes invents a τελείαν ςιγμὴν [perfect stop], relying on some copy, after a word: And he separates the other words by the inserted particle AS, i.e., that the nations were once disobedient, under the Old Testament & in the time of Christ: As in the days of Noah. But that word of SIMILARITY appears nowhere in any codex; nor can it be admitted through the relation of the little words ὅτε, πότε, which suffer no perfect punctuation; but they teach that the spirits were once incredulous, namely when the long-suffering of God was waiting for them in the time of Noah. When once, says Schlichtingius, we are accustomed to speak thus, when we narrate that something happened at some time. In the days of Noah: He expresses when this expectation of God took place, namely then when Noah was living. It is manifest, therefore, that the Petrine discourse is distorted by Enjedinus & by Grotius into a sense that is entirely alien. Not to mention the comparison of the Mosaic passage, which is instituted here by Grotius, most alien and a most perverse distortion; concerning which it has been dealt with in the commentary on Genesis and in the Bibl. Illustr.

As for the genuine mind of the Holy Apostle, some explain it concerning the journey and preaching made in the time of Noah by the Spirit of Christ, in which manner Beda: He who in our times coming in the flesh preached the way of the journey to the world, he himself also before the flood preached to those who were then incredulous and living carnally, coming as a Spirit. He himself, however, through the Holy Spirit was in Noah and the other saints who were then, and through their good conversation preached to the depraved men of that age, so that they might be converted to better things. Which sense Augustin had handed down in epistle XCIX to Evodius, that Christ preached to the incredulous in the time of Noah not in the flesh, because at that time he had not yet come into the flesh, but in the Spirit: because the spirits are not in prison in an infernal prison, but souls are as if shut up in the prison of the flesh and the darkness of ignorance. Thomas followed the same exposition in part III, q. 53, articles 2 & 3. Hugo, the Author of the ordinary gloss, Lyranus, Carthufianus, Titelmannus, Joh. Benedictus; to whom B. Gerhardus also accedes thus far, along with B. Winckelmannus, as also Andradius in book II of the defense of Trent, by whom this preaching made in the time of Noah is established. The sense, he says, on this passage p. 466, is this: Christ in the Spirit, that is, by his Divinity, or according to his divine nature, having journeyed, preached, namely through Noah, the herald of righteousness, to the antediluvian men, whose souls are in the prison of hell, namely those who were unwilling to have faith in this preaching.

Many others, however, interpret it not concerning the journey and preaching of Christ made in the time of Noah, but after Christ was put to death in the flesh and made alive again in the Spirit, not to antediluvian men, but to their spirits, who were in the infernal prison, and thus they explain it concerning the descent of Christ into hell. Which interpretation seems to be preferred 1. because the subject is Christ the God-man, and not indeed the Son of God without flesh. 2. It concerns Christ put to death according to the flesh or human nature, of whom also in chapter IV. 1, Christ having suffered for us in the flesh, but made alive through the Spirit. Therefore not concerning those things which were done under that in the time of Noah. 3. Christ having been made alive is said to have journeyed and preached, but these things cannot be said of the Word before the incarnation. 4. Nor does a journey properly befit him before the incarnation, and there is no reason why one should depart from the propriety of the word. 5. Just as he is said to have journeyed into heaven, v. 22. So also he journeyed and preached v. 19. But there a properly spoken journey is understood. 6. The series of the acts and passions of Christ demands that we accept these not concerning a journey in the time of Noah, but after the passion of Christ, because they follow in order: mortification, vivification, the journey to the spirits established in prison. How therefore can this return be made regarding the acts of Christ to the times of Noah? 7. He is said to have journeyed to the spirits, and to have preached to them themselves. Therefore antediluvian men who are still surviving cannot be understood here. For nowhere are living men understood by the name of spirits, when viewed as to substance. Joh. IV. 1, seqq. The word Spirits, as is evident from the opposition to the Spirit of God, designates not seducing men, but the spirit by which they are agitated, or at least they are viewed not by reason of substance, but of doctrine. B. Gerhardus himself observes p. 484. That the name 'Spirit' is used unusually of men living in the flesh.

8. The holy Apostle indicates not only to whom he went, but also when and where, namely τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ; some codices add κατακεκλεισμένοις, which indeed we do not admit because of better codices, yet the thing itself teaches that it is to be understood. Those spirits, therefore, when Christ preached to them, were already shut up in the infernal prison. If you say, how could repentance be preached to them? I answer: He did not preach so that they might repent, but because they had not repented; not so that they might be converted, but so that they might be convinced of their infidelity and the merit of their condemnation, whether that was done by words or by the factual presentation of his victory over Satan and sin, which they had despised when it was set before them by Noah, the herald of righteousness, through their infidelity. We have here again the like-minded blessed Gerhard, who replies to those objecting that preaching is not conveniently said to have been done in hell: The preaching is understood not so much as verbal, but real (just as in Heb. 12:24, the speech is not verbal, but real), by which Christ preached to the souls of the impious not for conversion and liberation, as he had done in his ministry on these earths, but for their refutation and confusion, so that they might understand to their great harm that they had despised this herald of righteousness who had once preached to them through Noah. For just as in the final judgment the impious in their bodies are to see the Judge himself and feel the punishments from the face of the Lord, 1 Thess. 1:9, Apoc. 1:7, so also their souls, constituted outside their bodies, saw him as a glorious conqueror in hell, and by this vision the torment in them was increased. The sense, therefore, is this: Christ descended to the lower regions by divine power and appeared there to the spirits damned for their unbelief, not to liberate them from there, nor to grant them a time for repentance, Heb. 9:27, but to show them that he had now come in the flesh and had provided the price of redemption, which they had once, in the times of Noah, stubbornly despised when it was preached to them.

9. He who is said to have presented himself ἐν φυλακῇ, for the purpose of πορευθεὶς, that he might preach to those who were once unbelieving, when the long-suffering of God waited for their repentance, is understood not to have preached πορευθεὶς some centuries before, when they were not ἐν φυλακῇ, but were living on earth and could still repent.

10. Blessed Gerhard himself brings forward, among other things, this proof: Just as in his ascension Christ showed his glory and majesty to the spirits of the just: So in his descent to the lower regions he showed his glorious victory to the majesty of the spirits of the damned, to the former indeed for glorification and exultation, but to the latter for ignominy and confusion. 11. The parallel passage, Eph. 4:9-10, makes for this: 'He who descended is the same who ascended above all heavens, that he might fill all things.' For here too, πορευθεὶς is said to have gone into the prison by descending into hell, just as he went into heaven by ascending, v. 19, 22.

12. Those to whom Christ preached WERE in prison when he preached, as the Vulgate and the ancients render ERANT, not SUNT. And the Syriac: He preached to those souls which were detained in hell. If anyone denies that the name Φυλακῆς is taken from hell, let him be convinced from chapter XX. 7. compare v. 3. & Matt. V. 25. c. XVIII. 30. Luke XII. 58. Whence the Syrian rendered this as in hell. If anyone should urge: Why is it said that he preached only to those who had been incredulous in the time of Noah, and not also to others in hell? Resp. It is not to be taken exclusively, but rather the whole is to be understood from a part; but they are named particularly, so that it might be taught that the antediluvians also ought to have believed in Christ, and were damned on account of incredulity, and that the reason of the type of the flood might be explained regarding the antitype of baptism. 13. Most of the Fathers agree with this opinion, which the blessed Gerhard likewise acknowledges: Most of the Ancients, he says, accept this passage concerning the descent of Christ into hell in this sense: Christ was put to death in the flesh, because the union of body and soul was dissolved in death, but he was made alive in the Spirit, because through his divine virtue and power the soul was in turn united to the body, and life was restored to it 2 Cor. XIII. 4. in which divine virtue according to the soul and according to the mode of a glorified and spiritual body, as a glorious conqueror he set out and descended to the spirits in prison established in the prison of hell, who had once been incredulous, and on account of their incredulity had come to this place, and he preached to them, that is, he refuted their incredulity, and manifested his divine Majesty and victory. He brought forward Athanasius in the epistle to Epictetus, Cyril on the true faith to Theodosius. Ambrose on Eph. IV. Bellarmine l. IV. de Christo c. 13. Clement of Alexandria l. VI. Strom. Athanasius in the book on the incarnation. Cyril on the true faith to Theodosius & l. XII. in John c. 36. Hilary on Ps. CXVIII. Ambrose on c. X. Rom. Rufinus in the exposition of the Creed. Although they do not agree on the mode and end of the descent into hell: yet most accept the words of Peter concerning the descent into hell. Justin Martyr in the dialogue with Trypho p. m. 132. brings forward some things which existed in certain copies, but were cut out by the Jews, which seem to pertain to this. Similarly, they cut these things out from the sayings of Jeremiah: The Lord God remembered his dead of Israel, who slept in the land of the mound (that is, in tombs and sepulchers) and descended to them, to preach his salvation to them. Irenaeus l. III. against heresies c. 23. commemorates Isaiah saying such things. Isaiah says, and the holy Lord of Israel remembered his dead, because they slept in the land of burial, and he descended to them to preach the salvation which is from him, that he might save them. But those things are found neither in Isaiah, nor in Jeremiah, whether in the Hebrew, or among the LXX Interpreters. They teach, however, not indeed that St. Peter received these from there, which seems likely to Cornelius à Lapide, but that Justin and Irenaeus wished to prove the descent of Christ into hell, which they drew from the words of Peter, from the O.T., from wherever they may have received those things.

The Papists also support the view that the descent of Christ into hell is exhibited by these words of St. Peter, although they err in this, that they wish the limbo of the Fathers to be understood by the prison, which is the opinion of Bellarmine and Cornelius à Lapide, who here acts very foolishly, that the Paradise promised and delivered to the thief was into eternal glory, and that Christ descended into hell to fully undergo and pay the penalties of our sins, and others' opinion, or purgatory, which Fr. Turrianus l. IV. for the epistles of the Popes cap. 12. or both, which Estius wished for this passage. For into neither can the ἀπειθεῖς, that is, the ἄπιστοι incredulous (see John II. 26. Acts XIV. 2. Rom. VII. 8. Heb. III. 8. 1 Pet. III. 1. 4.) be sent, whose punishment is eternal condemnation in hell, just as on the contrary the retribution of the faithful is free eternal life in heaven Rom. VII. v. last. John III. 15. 16. 18. Mark XVI. 16. Therefore Augustine epist. XCIX. warns that the Apostle does not make mention of the Holy Fathers, but of those who were incredulous in the times of Noah. And why would he name the time of Noah particularly, when the Papists place all the Saints up to the time of the descent of Christ in limbo? What? That not only Andradius rejects that explanation, but also Lorinus refutes Salmeron, Fevardentius, Catharinus, Saa, Bellarmine, Suarez and Valentius, because they established that Peter means that their souls, which repented at the time of the flood, received the news of their redemption from Christ, and he teaches that Peter speaks of the damned who perished in the flood, and says it is uncertain whether Christ then led any souls out of purgatory, and that it is improbable that those souls were in purgatory for so long, which also seems less credible to Cornelius à Lapide, concerning which matter Bellarmine also fluctuates vehemently with his Thomas l. IV. de Christo, cap. 16. §. Fourth. He acknowledges that Christ preached to the damned, by arguing their infidelity. Haegerus, Paez l. VII. de symb. cap. 20. Nor can the figment of Calvin l. II. Instit. cap. 16. §. 9. & in Psychopannychia (to which, however, the Osiandrian paraphrase seems to favor) be proven in any way in this place, concerning souls not being admitted immediately after death to the beatific vision of God, which appears analogous to the limbo of the Fathers.
