Which exaltation of Christ is celebrated by Leo the Great, sermon 1 on the Ascension: thus: Truly great and ineffable was the cause for rejoicing when, in the sight of the holy multitude, the nature of the human race ascended above the dignity of all heavenly creatures, about to surpass the Angelic orders and to be raised beyond the height of the Archangels, nor would it have had a limit to its advancement in any heights, unless, having been received into the session of the eternal Father, it were associated in the glory of Him to whose nature it was joined in the Son. From which, however, Cornelius and Lorinus, here, Gregory of Valencia 3. p. disp. I. q. 8. point 3, Suarez 3. part. tom. I. disp. 43. sect. 1 and 2, conclude not without rashness that the Angels also obtained grace and glory from the merits of Christ, for this would have pertained to the dignity of Christ, and to a greater association of the Church, which consists of Angels just as much as of men. For as Christ nowhere took hold of Angels, but the seed of Abraham, Heb. II. 16, so He merited grace and glory not for Angels, but for us, who came only for the sake of sinners, and to seek that which had perished, with the Angels confirmed and destined to persist in glory, even if men had not been created, much less fallen, or Christ had not come into the world. Therefore, no greater glory could accrue to Christ from that, nor do the Angels make for a greater association of the Church on earth, but in heaven, which Christ merited not for the Angels, who are in no way in need of it, but for men, albeit for the joy of the Angels.

Latin:

Vers. 22. Ὅς ἐστιν ἐν δεξιᾷ τοῦ Θεοῦ]. Eadem loquutio Rom. VIII. 34. Similis Ebr. I. 3. Hic in quibusdam Græcis codici- bus aliquanto plus fuisse docet Latina versio.

Additur hoc non tantum, ut viam in cælum no- bis patere per baptisma significetur, quæ Bedæ ratio est, sed etiam ut alteri9 stabiliatur fides de perfecta satisfactione Christi, qui non ad dextram Dei eve- ctus fuisset, nisi peccatorum omnium expiationem fecisset, ac salutem generis humani consummasset, Ebr. I. 3. deque sufficientissima Christi Mediatoris nostri virtute ad nos ad salutem æternam conser- vandos: nec solum ut soletur pios, quod tueri pos- sit suos, sed etiam ut terreat impœnitentes, quod eos potenter prosternere valeat. Postremo, inquit Flacius, celebrat bic Christum, ejusque istam victori- am de peccato, Satana, & morte: quo tum fœderis istius firmitatem efficaciamque ex victoria ac resur- rectione Christi dependentem stabiliat, tum pios con- soletur in cruce & lucta cum Satana & propriis in- firmitatibus, vetereque bomine, dum audiunt se ha- bere tam præpotentem Patronum servatoremque: tum etiam impios ejus contemptores perterrefaciat damnetque, dum audiunt, sibi inimicitias esse cum tam potente gloriosoque & jam redivivo adven- sario.

Verba quæ in Vulgata hic adjiciantur, degluti- ens mortem, ut vitæ æternæ hæredes efficeremur, in- terpretationis gratia à quopiam adjecta in textum irrepsisse videntur. Unde non mirum ea Bedam, & glossam ordinariam aliosque exposuisse, ac Ful- gentium l. de fid. ad Petrum c. 8. repetiisse. Estius hanc pericopen in Græcis & Syriacis codicibus non haberi, nec videri eam agnovisse Ruffinum in exposit. symb.& parum commode post illud, qui est in dextera Dei, subjungi, nisi præsens accipiatur loco Præteri- ti, apte autem connecti, quod sequitur, profectus in cælum, cum illa parte, qui est in dextera Dei, agnoscit. Πορευθεὶς εἰς ὐρανὸν] Vide supra 20. Recte Estius: Observa, Petrum nunc dicere pro- fectum in cælum, quem paulo ante dixerat profe- ctum ad inferos. Utitur enim utrobique eodem vo- cabulo Græco πορευθεὶς, ex quo collige contra Cal- vinum, etiam priorem locum secundum naturam as- sumptam exponendum esse.

Ὑποταγέντων αὐτῷ Ἀγγέλων καὶ ἐξουσιῶν καὶ δυνάμεων] An- geli hic nomen est speciei non generis, ut & Rom. VIII. 38. Crescit enim oratio Ἐξουσίας & habes Eph. I. 21. & Col. I. 16. II. 10. Δυνάμεων vero Rom. VIII. 38. Eph. I. 21. ad quæ loca, quæ diximus, vide.

Vulgatus exposuit subjectis sibi Angelis, sed Græ- cum proprie est, cum ei subjecti essent Angeli scilicet à Patre: Quod etiam observatum Estio. Conf. 1. Cor.XV. 27. Ebr. II.8. Eph. I. 20. seqq. ex quo loco id etiam liquet, hosce tres ordines Angelorum non exclusive intelligendos esse, sed inclusive. Sessio enim ad dextram Dei non tantum subjectionem a- liquorum, sed omnium Angelorum, imo omnium creaturarum infert. Quæ proinde nō restringenda cum Estio & Lorino tantum ad bonos Angelos, eti- amsi soli hoc in loco nominentur, quia constitutus super omne nomen non solum quod nominatur in hoc, sed & in futuro seculo, nec quicquam exceptum est, quod non subjectum ei sit, Ebr. II. 18. etsi non- dum appareat, subjecta esse omnia: neque definien- da ex prædicamento situs cum Calvinisequis, sed ex prædicamento actionis, quod sit omnium in cælo & in terra præsentissima atque potentissima guber- natio, & πλήρωσις τῶν ἑπάντων, Eph. IV. 10. Quæ Christi exaltatio à Leone M. serm. 1. de ascens. ita celebratur: Revera magna & ineffabilis erat causa gaudendi cum in aspectu sanctæ multitudinis super omnium cælestium creaturarum dignitatem huma- ni generis natura conscenderet, supergressura Ange- licos ordines & ultra Archangelorum altitudinem elevanda nec ullis sublimitatibus modum provectionis suæ habitura, nisi æterni Patris recepta consessu il- lius gloria sociaretur in throno, cujus naturæ copula- batur in Filio. Ex quo vero non nisi temere Cor- nelius & Lorinus, hic, Gregorius de Valentia 3. p. disp.I. q.8. puncto 3. Suarez. 3. part. tom. I. disp. 43. sect. 1. & 2. concludunt, Angelos quoque ex meritis Christi gratiam & gloriam consequutos esse, hoc enim pertinuisse ad dignitatem Christi, & ad majorem consociationem Ecclesiæ, quæ constet Angelis perinde & hominibus. Nam ut Christus nusquam Angelos assumpsit, sed semen Abrahæ, Ebr. II. 16. ita non Angelis, sed nobis meritus est gratiam, & gloriam, qui non venit nisi propter peccatores, & ad id quæ- rendum quod perierat, Angelis in gloria confir- matis ac perstituris, etiamsi homines non conditi, nedum lapsi essent, aut Christus in mundum nō ve- nisset. Non ergo inde major gloria Christo acce- dere potuit, neque ad consociationem Ecclesiæ majo- rem faciunt Angeli in terris, sed in cælis, quam me- ruit Christus non Angelis ea minime indigis, sed hominibus, etsi in Angelorum lætitiam.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV. ARGUMENT, AND PARTITION.

He draws again from the passion of Christ, by merit and example, an exhortation that we should tolerate sufferings, desist from sin, and live not according to our desires, but to the will of God, renouncing our former impiety, since for this reason the Gospel was preached even to the dead, and the end of all things is imminent: Therefore, having exhorted to prayers, charity, and the administration of mutual duties, he teaches how we ought to sustain temptations and suffer insults, provided that no one suffers for evil deeds. There are three parts: I. An exhortation to patience and innocence of life, to v. 7. II. An exhortation to prayers and the duties of charity, to v. 11. III. An instruction concerning the act of sufferings, to v. 19.

PART I. Exhortation to patience and innocence of life.

Vers. 1. Χριστῦ ὖν παθόντῶ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν σαρκὶ] He repeats what he had said above III, 18.

Καὶ ὑμεῖς τὴν αὐτὴν ἔννοιαν ὁπλίσασθε] It is again a passive used for a reciprocal verb. Arm yourselves with a firm purpose to bear anything for Christ. Thus ἐνδύσασθαι τὰ ὅπλα τῦ φωτὸς Rom. XIII. 12. ἐνδύσασθαι πανοπλίαν τῦ Θεῦ, τὸν θώρακα τῆς πίστεως, Eph. VI. 11. 1. Thess. V. 8. ἐνδύσασθαι καινὸν ἄνθρω- πον Eph. IV. 24. Col. III. 10. לבש.

He rightly understands τὴν αὐτὴν ἔννοιαν as a firm purpose to sustain anything for the name of Christ, which, however, is not understood alone, but with armor against concupiscences. For that refers partly to the preceding warning, chap. III. 17, that it is better to suffer ἀγαθοποιῦντας ἢ κακοποιῦντας: In explaining which the Apostle is now occupied, both as to the sufferings τῶν ἀγαθοποιούντων, and as to the sufferings τῶν κακοποιούντων v. 15, and for that reason he dissuades from impiety and exhorts to vigilance and the pursuit of charity and piety: and partly to the benefit of the passion of Christ endured for us: which, as to merit and example, he had exhibited before, so that we might put on that very mind of which he had warned, and which he had set before the faithful by the proposed passion of Christ, just as Paul commanded in Phil. II. 5: τῦτο γὰρ φρονεί- σθω ἐν ὑμῖν, ὃ κὶ ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησῦ. For Christ promptly sustained the most dire sufferings, complying not with his own, but with the Father's will, Matth. XXVI. 42. John X. 18. Psalm XL. 8. and by suffering σαρκὶ, in the flesh or human nature, deriving upon himself for our sake both our guilt and our punishment, since he himself could not sin, 2 Cor. 5, 21, he rendered obedience to the Father even unto death, even the death of the cross, Phil. II. 8, and left us an ὑπογραμμὸν, that we might follow in his footsteps, 1 Petr. II. 21. And therefore let us also with patience sustain our sufferings, we who are not devoid of sin, and let us live not to our own will, which is only evil, but to the will of God, since Christ suffered for us for this reason, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness, 1 Petr. II. 24. Bede in this place. After he had constructed the example of the Lord's resurrection and our washing, which takes place in baptism, from the sacrament of the ark and the flood, he returns to what he had begun to say, that, imitating the work of our redemption, we should patiently tolerate the wickedness of the evil within the good things that we do. Schlichtingius in this place. The Apostle rightly infers this warning and command from Christ's death for us. For this is what Christ merited for us by his death and sufferings, this is what he demands from us by his right, this is the profession of us all who believe in him and have been baptized. By the word σαρκὶ, which is the proper subject of suffering, is noted, according to Fulgentius, book III to Thrasimund, ch. 9, that he confesses Christ suffered in the flesh, whose Divinity he knew to remain entirely impassible. The Vulgate interpretation wrongly omitted that ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, in which great force of argument is situated, which Jerome reads in book I against Jovinian, the Syrian did not neglect, and it fits perfectly with the preceding chapter III, 18, and the thing itself. For us, says Schlichtingius, namely, having suffered the punishment of the cross and death. For us, namely, as a victim for sinners, so that by his blood he might wash away our crimes, and bless us with many other and greatest goods through his sufferings and death. Καὶ ὑμεῖς τὴν αὐτὴν ἔννοιαν ὁπλίσασθε. The Vulgate explained it, and be ye armed with the same thought. The Syrian, according to the same thought, just as Oecumenius supplies the particle κατὰ which is understood. It is not badly explained, put on the same thought, as a kind of spiritual armor. Since Christ in his passion demonstrated both singular patience and all-manner of innocence, it behooves you also, for whom Christ suffered, and who have been washed through baptism, to whom baptism is συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα εἰς Θε- ὸν, a stipulation of a good conscience toward God, to be armed and instructed with the same mind and thought, with the same intention and purpose, to sustain any sufferings whatsoever and to keep innocence of life.

Ὅ παθὼν ἐν σαρκὶ] In the Manuscript ὁ παθὼν σαρκι τετέ- λεσται, he who has crucified and killed the carnal affections in himself, Rom. VI. 2. 7. Gal. V. 24. Col. III. 5.

Πέπαυται ἁμαρτίας] He abstains henceforth from sins, δεδικαίωται ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας, Rom. VI. 2. חדל הרע Is. I. 17.

Latin:

CAPUT IV. ARGUMENTUM, ET PARTITIO.

E passione Christi merito, & exemplo parane- sin iterum deducit, ut passiones toleremus, à peccato desistamq, nec cupiditatibus nostris, sed voluntati Dei vivamus, pristina impie- tatem abnegantes, quu etiam ideo mortuis Evangelium prædicatum sit, & finis rerum omnium immineat:Ideo ad preces & chari- tatem ac officiorum mutuoru administrati- onem hortatus, quomodo tentationes susti- nere, contumelias pati debeamus, dummo- do non patiatur, quis ob malefacta, edocet. Partes tres sunt I. Ad patientiam & vitæ innocen- tiam adhortatio ad v. 7. II. Ad preces & charitatis officia exhortatio, ad v. 11. III. De actu passionum in- formatio, ad v. 19.

PARS I. Adhortatio ad patientiam & vitæ inno- centiam.

Vers. 1. Χριστῦ ὖν παθόντῶ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν σαρκὶ] Repetit quod dixerat supra III, 18.

Καὶ ὑμεῖς τὴν αὐτὴν ἔννοιαν ὁπλίσασθε] Est rursus passivum pro verbo reciproco. Firmo proposito quidvis pro Christo ferendi vosmet armate. Sic ἐνδύσασθαι τὰ ὅπλα τῦ φωτὸς Rom. XIII. 12. ἐνδύσασθαι πανοπλίαν τῦ Θεῦ, τὸν θώρακα τῆς πίστεως, Eph. VI. 11. 1. Thess. V. 8. ἐνδύσασθαι καινὸν ἄνθρω- πον Eph. IV. 24. Col. III. 10. לבש.

Recte de firmo proposito quidvis pro Christi nomine sustinendi τὴν αὐτὴν ἔννοιαν accipit, quod tamen solum non intelligitur, sed cum armatura adversus concupiscentias. Illa enim respicit partim præcedaneum monitum, cap. III. 17. quod melius sit pati ἀγαθοποιῦντας ἢ κακοποιῦντας: In quo ex- plicando jam occupatur Apostolus, tum qua passi- ones τῶν ἀγαθοποιούντων, tũ qua passiones τῶν κα- κοποιούντων v. 15. eoque nomine dehortatur ab im- pietate, & hortatur ad vigilātiā & charitatis ac pie- tatis studium: partim passionis Christi pro nobis exanclatæ beneficium: quam quoad meritum, & exemplum ante exhibuerat, ut induamus illam ipsam mentem, de qua monuerat, & quam propo- sita Christi passione fidelibus stiterat, quemadmo- dum Paulus Phil. II. 5. præcepit: τῦτο γὰρ φρονεί- σθω ἐν ὑμῖν, ὃ κὶ ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησῦ. Christo enim prom- pte passiones dirissimas sustinuit, nō suæ, sed Patris voluntati obsecundans, Matth. XXVI. 42. Job. X. 18. Psal. XL. 8. ac patiendo σαρκὶ carnem vel natu- ram Humanam pro nobis nostram & culpam & pænam in se derivans, quum peccatum ipse non posset, 2. Cor. 5, 21. obedientiam Patri præstitit usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, Phil. II. 8. no- bisque ὑπογραμμὸν reliquit, ut vestigiis ejus insi- stamus, 1. Petr. II. 21. Ideoque & nos cum patientia sustineamus passiones nostras, qui peccati expertes non sumus & voluntati non nostræ, quæ tantum mala, sed Dei vivamus, quum ideo pro nobis pas- sus sit Christus, ut peccatis mortui justitiæ vivamus 1. Petr. II. 24. Beda in h. l. Postquam exemplum resurrectionis Dominicæ & ablutionis nostræ, quæ fit in baptismo de arcæ ac diluvii sacramento adstru- xerat, revertitur ad hoc, quod dicere cœperat, ut imi- tantes opus redemptionis nostræ intra bona qua faci- mus, patienter malorum nequitiam toleremus. Schlichtingius in h. l. Merito monitum ac præce- ptum istud ex Christi pro nobis morte infert Aposto- lus. Hoc enim Christus sua pro nobis morte & pas- sionibus est meritus, hoc suo à nobis exigit jure, hac nostra omnium, qui in ipsum credimus, & baptizati sumus, professio est. Voce σαρκὶ quæ passionis pro- prium est subjectum notatur Fulgentio l. III. ad Thrasim. c. 9. Propterea Christum fatetur passum in carne, cujus Divinitatem noverat prorsus impas- sibilem permanere. Vulgata interpretatio perperam omisit illud ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, in quo magna vis argumẽ- ti sita est, quod Hieronymus libr. I. contra Jov. legit, Syrus non neglexit, & antecedentibus cap. III, 18. reique ipsi apprime congruit. Pro nobis, inquit Schlichtingius, passo scilicet crucis supplicium & mortem. Pronobis, tanquam victima scilicet pro pec- catoribus, ut sanguine suo crimina nostra elueret, & multis aliis maximisque bonis per suas perpessiones & mortem nos bearet. Καὶ ὑμεῖς τὴν αὐτὴν ἔννοιαν ὁπλίσασθε. Vulgatus exposuit, & vos eadem cogita- tione armamini. Syrus juxta eandem cogitationem, quomodo & Oecumenius supplet particulam κατὰ subintellectam. Non male exponitur, induite eandem cogitationem, velut spiritualem quandam armaturam. Quum Christus in sua passione & sin- gularem patientiam, & omnimodam innocentiam demonstravit, vos etiam, pro quibus Christus pas- sus est, quique per baptismum abluti estis, quibus baptismus συνειδήσεως ἀγαθῆς ἐπερώτημα εἰς Θε- ὸν, stipulatio bonæ conscientiæ in Deum est, eadem me- te & cogitatione, eadem intentione & proposito armatos & instructos esse decet, ad passiones quas- vis sustinendas & vitæ innocentiam custodiendam.

Ὅ παθὼν ἐν σαρκὶ] In Manuscripto ὁ παθὼν σαρκι τετέ- λεσται, qui affectus carnales in se crucifixit atque interfecit, Rom. VI. 2. 7. Gal. V. 24. Col. III. 5.

Πέπαυται ἁμαρτίας] Abstinet imposterum à peccatis, δεδικαίωται ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας, Rom. VI. 2. חדל הרע Es. I. 17.

## 4:2
Vers. 2. Εἰς τὸ μηκέτι ἀνθρώπων ἐπιθυμίαις ἀλλὰ θελήμα- τι Θεῦ τὸν ἐπίλοιπον ἐν σαρκὶ βιῶσαι χρόνον] Here εἰς τὸ means 'so that'. And ἀνθρώπων ἐπιθυμίαι are called those desires which are accustomed to be present in the greatest part of men. To live to the Divine will is to live according to God's precepts, which is called living to God in Rom. VI. 10, 11, Gal. II. 19, and living to the Lord in Rom. XIV, 8. And in the word σαρκὶ there is an ἀντανάκλασις. For flesh had been taken before for the affections which serve the flesh alone: here, however, it is for the fleeting and fragile life, just as in Gal. II. 20.

On account of the authority of one manuscript, it is not fitting to disregard all other codices, and they are read more correctly altogether with the preposition ἐν. For here the discourse is about the sufferings which are sustained in our fragile flesh, which is subject to passions and mortality; nor is there any need that we should take these metaphorically concerning the mortification of the flesh, as is done by some; indeed, the argument here is exhibited from the end of sufferings, which are imposed for this reason, that those who suffer in the flesh may cease from sins, as an armor for our patience and the innocence of life, or so that we may suffer while doing good. Through Divine providence, by adverse things and afflictions, as if by a certain medicine, a man is freed from his intended malice and rendered healthier, says Justin, q. 137. What the file is to iron, what the furnace is to gold, what the flail is to grain, this is tribulation to a righteous man. The spiritual progress of the pious consists in large part in the cross, says Tauler. Afflictions of the body are called tribulation of the flesh, 1 Cor. VII. 28. Those who are rendered conformable to Christ through sufferings and afflictions are restrained by tribulations as if by a certain bridle, lest they satisfy the desires of corrupt nature, because the cross is a prophylactic against sin, to which our flesh is prone. It is not so fitting to say that through the mortification of the flesh we are rendered conformable to the passion of Christ: And how does that inference stand: As Christ suffered in the flesh: So you also ought to crucify the flesh with all its concupiscences, Gal. V. 24. For he himself did not have flesh which was to be crucified with its lusts. Therefore, this passage does not seem to be an antanaclasis. That is certainly not necessary. And concerning the end of the sufferings, it follows further that he who suffers tribulations should desist from sins, and ought to desist by the intention of God who sends the sufferings; because the words of the acts sometimes denote a duty, so that he may devote his effort not to the lusts of men, but to the Divine will, which surpasses life in the flesh. It is nowhere stated that to mortify the flesh is to suffer in the flesh. If you render it thus, 'he who suffers in the flesh, that is, mortifies the flesh, rests from sin,' how will this fit the example of Christ? And is not the same thing said thus in v. 2, that we may no longer live for our lusts, which is what remains in the flesh? Where, besides, there will be need of another meaning for the expression ἐν σαρκὶ. The former explanation is therefore simpler; which is also favored by the use of the particle ὅτι, which is argumentative rather than exegetical.

But the Socinian gloss is not free from impiety, since the subject ὁ παθὼν ἐν σαρκὶ is explained as referring to Christ. For if Christ ceased from sins, it must be that he sinned at some time, especially if the following is added, 'that he might no longer live for the lusts of men.' But did he ever live for them, he who was separated from sinners, Heb. VII, and knew no sin, 2 Cor. V. 21? These words, which are immediately placed as the subject and sound as if they concern the same subject, do not allow that gloss; namely, that to desist from sin is to be exempt from afflictions, which Crellius brought forward against Grotius, p. 10, along with Socinus in Part II, De Servatore Christo, c. 22. But Schlichtingius, his disciple, in his commentary on this passage, did not think it should be approved at all, explaining the present passage thus: He brings forward the cause why they ought to think of and consider themselves dead to the flesh, because he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin: he has suffered, that is, he has died: in the flesh, according to the flesh, or through the flesh: He has ceased from sin: He had no further business with sin. The dead do not sin, therefore you also will cease from sin when you consider yourselves dead in the flesh. Although this gloss is cold enough; for how will anyone imagine himself to be dead when he feels that he is alive? Or what will that false imagination do toward desisting from sin? Yet it shows that Schlichtingius did not wish to understand 'to desist from sin' improperly, as 'to be exempt from afflictions,' nor to take those words concerning Christ with Socinus and Crellius; nor did Socinus himself rest in his explanation, as is evident from his wavering in his letter III. to Smalcius, p. 518: Insofar as those words, he says, 'he has suffered in the flesh,' refer to Christ, they signify his death and the passion of the cross, so that the sense is that he was freed by the passion of the cross from those things which are usually the punishments of sins. Insofar as it refers to us, it signifies that by the killing or rejection of carnal desires we cease from sinning. Yet Titelmannus and Salmero in the Papacy also approved an interpretation akin to Socinus's comment, although they greatly twist the words of Peter, teaching us that Christ ceased not from his own, but from our sins, and was raised living a spiritual life in the flesh. Everyone sees how ineptly Τὸ ἐπιλοι- πὸν ἐν σαρκὶ is explained as referring to Christ acting in our flesh after the resurrection. It is too clear that it concerns our life, which we still have to pass in this fragile flesh. See 2 Cor. X, verse 3; Gal. II, verse 10. Phil. I, verse 12. Which sense is also demanded by the antithesis in verse 3 to the life previously passed before conversion.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Εἰς τὸ μηκέτι ἀνθρώπων ἐπιθυμίαις ἀλλὰ θελήμα- τι Θεῦ τὸν ἐπίλοιπον ἐν σαρκὶ βιῶσαι χρόνον] Hic εἰς τὸ valet, ita ut. Et ἀνθρώπων ἐπιθυμίαι dicuntur cupiditates illæ, quæ adesse solent maximæ hominum parti. Vivere volun- tati Divinæ est vivere secundum Dei præcepta, quod vivere Deo dicitur Rom. VI. 10.11. Gal. II. 19. vivere Domino Rom. XIV, 8. Et in voce σαρκὶ est ἀντανάκλασις. Caro enim prius sumpta fuerat pro affectibus, qui carni soli ser- viunt: hic vero pro vita caduca & fragili, quomodo Gal. II. 20.

Ob unius Manuscripti autoritatem non conve- nit omnes alios codices posthabere, & rectius omnino, cum præpositione ἐν hæc leguntur. Nam hic de passionibus, quæ in carne nostra fragili, pas- sionibus & mortalitati obnoxia, sustinentur, sermo est; neque opus est, ut metaphoricè de mortificatio- ne carnis, quod ab aliquibus fit, hæc accipiamus; imò armaturæ nostræ ad patientiam, & vitæ inno- centiam, vel ut ἀγαθοποιῦντες patiamur, argu- mentũ hic exhibetur à fine passionum, quæ ideo im- ponuntur, ut, qui patiuntur in carne, desinăt à pecca- tis. Per Divinam providentiam rebus adversis & afflictionibus tanquam medicina quadam à desti- nata malitia sua liberatus homo sanior redditur, ait Justinus q. 137. Quod lima ferro, quod fornax auro, quod flagellum grano, hoc tribulatio viro justo. Spi- ritualis piorum profectus magna ex parte in cruce consistit, ait Taulerus. Afflictiones corporis vo- cantur tribulatio carnis, 1. Cor. VII. 28. Qui per pas- siones & afflictiones Christo conformes reddun- tur, illi tribulationibus tanquam freno quodam coërcentur, ne desideriis corruptæ naturæ satisfa- ciant, quia crux est προφυλακτικὸν peccati, ad quod caro nostra proclivis est. Per mortificationem carnis passioni Christi nos reddi conformes non a- deo convenit: Et quomodo sese habet illa illatio: Sicut Christus passus est carne: Ita & vos crucifigere carnem debetis cũ omnibg concupiscentiīs, Gal. V. 24. Nam ipse carnem, quæ crucifigenda esset cum con- cupiscentiis, non habuit. Antanaclasi itaque non videtur hic locus esse. Necessaria certe illa non est. Et de fine passionum sequitur porro, quod, qui tri- bulationes patitur, à peccatis desistat, ac desistere ex intentione Dei passiones immittentis debeat; quia verba actuum quandoque debitum notant, ut non concupiscentiis hominum, sed voluntati Di- vinæ, quod vitæ in carne superat, impendat. Carnem mortificare nuspiam effertur pati in carne. Si red- das ita, qui patitur in carne, id est, carnem mortifi- cat, quiescit à peccato, quomodo ad exemplum Christi hoc congruet? Et annon idem dicitur ita v. 2. ut non amplius concupiscentiis nostris, quod residu- um est in carne, vivamus. Ubi præterea alia ite- rum vocis ἐν σαρκὶ opus erit significatione. Sim- plicior ergo est superior explicatio; cui etiam fa- vet particulæ ὅτι usus, qui potius ratiocinativus est, quam exegeticus.

Sociniana vero glossa impietate non vacat, quum subjectum ὁ παθὼν ἐν σαρκὶ de Christo ex- plicatur. Si enim à peccatis desiit Christus, ali- quando ipsum peccasse oportet, imprimis si adda- tur sequentia, ut non amplius concupiscentiis homi- num viveret. Num autem usquam illis vixit, qui segregatus fuit à peccatoribus, Ebr. VII. & pecca- tum non novit, 2. Cor. V. 21. Quæ verba immedia- te subjecta, & de eodem subjecto sonantia non per- mittunt glossam illam; quod à peccato desistere sit afflictionibus exemptum esse, quam cum Socino part. II. de Serv. Christo c. 22. Crellius contra Grotium p. 10. attulit. Schlichtingius vero ejus discipulus in comment. ad h. l. minime probandam duxit, sic explicans præsentem locum: Causam affert, cur se carne mortuos cogitare ac ducere debeant, quia qui passus est carne, cessavit à peccato: passus est, scilicet mortuus est: in carne, secundum carnem, seu per carnem: Cessavit à peccato: Nullum amplius ipsi cum peccato negotium fuit. Mortui non peccant, proinde & vos à peccato cessabitis, cum vos in carne mortuos ducetis. Quæ glossa etsi frigida satis; quomodo enim quis si- bi imaginabitur, se mortuum esse, quum se vivere sentiat? Aut quid illa falsa imaginatio ad desisten- dum à peccato faciet? Docet tamen Schlichtingium noluisse τὸ desistere à peccato improprie intellige- re, pro exemptum esse ab afflictionibus, nec verba ill de Christo cum Socino, & Crellio accipere; neq; in explicatione sua acquievisse ipsumet Socinum è fluctuatione ejus epist. III. ad Smalc. pag. 518. pa- tet: Quatenus illa verba, inquit, passus est in carne, ad Christum referuntur, significant ejus mortem & crucis passionem, ut sit sensus, illum per crucis passio- nem liberatum fuisse ab iis, quæ pœnæ peccatorum esse solent. Quatenus vero refertur ad nos, signi- ficat per interemptionem seu abjectionem carnalium desideriorum à peccando cessare. Affinem tamen Socini commento interpretationem probarunt eti- am in Papatu Titelmannus, & Salmero, etsi valde torqueant Petrina verba, Christum desiisse non à suis, sed à nostris peccatis & suscitatum in carne vi- ventem spiritualem vitam nos docuisse. Τὸ ἐπιλοι- πὸν ἐν σαρκὶ quam inepte de Christo post resurre- ctionem in carne nostra agente explicetur, nemo non videt. De nostra vita, quam in carne hac fra- gili traducere adhuc habemus, agi nimis luculen- tum est. Vid. 2. Cor. X. vers. 3. Gal. II. vers. 10. Phil. I. vers. 12. Quem sensum etiam postulat an- tithesis vers. 3. sequenti vitæ prioris ante conversi- onem transactæ.

## 4:3
Verse 3.

᾿Αρκετὸς γὰρ ὑμῖν παρεληλυθὼς ὁ χρόνος τοῦ θεοῦ τὸ θέλη- μα τῶν ἐθνῶν κατεργάσασθαι] The manuscript has better κατείρ- γασθαι, as the Syriac also seems to have read.

twice owes the past time, in which you, although Jews, lived in the manner of the Gentiles, corrupted by wicked teachers. Thus Martial: 'You have played: it is enough.' Compare the passage on the life of the Jews, Rom. II. 21, 22. And here κατείργασθαι is placed for εἰς τὸ κα- τείργασθαι, to do those things which please other Gentiles, as the Latin correctly takes it: He will now explain specifically what those things are. Ἀρκετὸς רב.

I do not see why the received reading should be postponed to the Grotian manuscript. For the sense is correct: 'For it is enough for us that the past time of life we have worked the will of the Gentiles': or if the ἀνα- κοίνωσις, by which Peter numbers himself with them, is harsh, let us read ὑμῖν with other codices, 'it is enough for you,' which Grotius also chose, and the Syriac. For it is enough for that time which has passed, in which you worked the will of the Gentiles, since the Apostle also speaks in the second person in the 1st and 4th verses. In the word 'it is enough' there is a litotes, by which the Apostle mitigates the severity of the reproach, Ezek. XLIV, 6; ch. LIV, 9; Mark XIV, 41. They explain Τὸ θέλημα τῶν ἐθνῶν as τὰς ἐπιθυμίας ἀν- θρώπων, the lusts of men, who are nothing other than men, in whom there is nothing of the Spirit of God. Man without God, says Estius, is entirely carnal, and executes not the will of God, but of the flesh: such as the Gentiles were, alienated from God. Whence the Syriac explained the word ἐθνῶν as 'of the profane.' For they were held as profane and impure, Matt. VI. 5; ch. X. 15; ch. XVIII, 7. That the Apostle indicates that the Jews also lived in the manner of the Gentiles, which Schlichtingius also wanted here, although it can be admitted, because it is credible concerning some, yet there is no doubt that the Gentiles are meant, inasmuch as the epistle was directed to them as well, and among whom the converted Jews lived, 1 Pet. II. 12. Which the parallel passage especially confirms, Eph. IV. 17, seqq. The connection of the argument is: before your conversion, when you were still wandering in the darkness of Gentile ignorance, you conformed yourselves to the will of the Gentiles, who are devoid of God: but this life demands other morals: Cf. Rom. VI. 19; ch. XVI, 11; 1 Cor. VI, 11; 1 Thess. V. 6; 2 Pet. II. 10.

Πεπορευμένους ἐν ἀσελγείαις] Πορεύεσθαι הלך means to follow a certain way of life. See what ἀσελγείαις are in Mark VII. 2. Rom. XIII. 13. 2 Cor. XII. 21. Gal. V. 19. Eph. IV. 19. 2 Pet. II. 7, 18. Jude 4.

The emphasis is on the word πορεύεσθαι, not only because of the customary description of human life, which is compared to a journey, but also because of the zeal for tending and proceeding in vices after the manner of those who are striving toward some destination, implying that they are advanced from vice to vice, which the interlinear gloss notes. See similar expressions in 2 Pet. II. 10, ch. III. 3, Jude v. 16, 18, as also Luke I. 6; therefore this word was rashly omitted by the Syriac. Ἐν ἀσελγείαις, the Vulgate [renders as] 'luxuries'. Ἀσελγὴς is petulant, as is 'lascivious'. Lucian [says] ἀσελγέστεροι τῶν ὄνων, 'more lascivious than donkeys'. Therefore Blessed Luther rendered it as 'Unzucht' (unchastity).

Ἐπιθυμίαις] With the mind always burning for new lusts. See Rom. I. 28, VI. 12, XIII. 14, Gal. V. 16, 24, Eph. II. 3, IV. 22, Col. III. 5, 1 Thess. IV. 5, 1 Tim. VI. 9, 2 Tim. III. 6, IV. 3, Tit. II. 12, III. 3, above I. verse 14, 2 Pet. I. v. 4, II. v. 10, 18, III. v. 3, Jude 16, 18.

Therefore Lyranus on this passage: Just as he denotes external acts of intemperance regarding sexual matters through 'luxuries', so he denotes internal acts, when the opportunity for external ones is lacking, through 'concupiscences'.

Οἰνοφλυγίαις] This word is found in Plutarch's Otho. Οἰνόφλυξ in Xenophon, from φλύειν, 'to have an impulse toward something', says the writer of the Etymologicum. Οἰνοφλυγεῖν in the LXX, Deut. XXI. 20, Isa. LVI. 12, for סבא, whence σαβάζειν.

The Vulgate rendered it as 'vinolentiis' (drunkenness). Oecumenius explained it as 'unrestrained impulses toward wine'. One is called οἰνόφλυξ who belches wine, greedy for wine. The Syriac rendered it more generally: 'In drunkenness'. So also Blessed Luther.

Κώμοις (Revelries).] See Rom. XIII, 13. Gal. V, 21. The Vulgate says 'in comessationibus' (in carousings): because κῶμος is a convivial gathering, from which someone eventually falls into a deep sleep, as Eustathius says. Here, because πότοι (drinking bouts) are added, an inordinate greed for gluttony is denoted.

Πότοις (Drinking bouts).] Constant banquets, even if drunkenness is absent, are not without fault. Thus מִשְׁתֶּה (drinking/feast) is used in Gen. 19, 3; c. 40, 20; Jud. 14, 10, 12, 17; 1 Sam. 25, 36; 2 Sam. 3, 15; Esth. 1, 5, 8, 9, 11, 18; c. 5, 6; c. 6, 14; c. 7, 1; Job 1, 4, 5; Prov. 23, 30; Eccles. 7, 3; Isa. 25, 6; Jer. 16, 6; Dan. 1, 5, 8; indeed, just as the Greeks say συμπόσια (symposia). The Vulgate says 'in potationibus' (in drinking bouts), regarding the gluttony of drinking; see Eph. 5, 11, 12; Prov. 23, 30. Blessed Gerhard takes οἰνοφλυγίας (drunkenness) regarding the vicious habit and effect, and πότος regarding the act of drinking.

Καὶ ἀθεμίτοις εἰδωλολατρείαις (And unlawful idolatries).] עבודות זרות (strange worships), the cults of false deities, which were called εἰδωλολατρείαι (idolatries) by the Hellenistic Jews, because they were not accustomed to be practiced without images. But such cults are in themselves illicit, because they transfer to others what belongs to the one God, against His will. Therefore, they are called here ἀθέμιτοι (unlawful), which word you also have in Acts X, 28. In the glossary, ἀθέμιτον is an unspeakable crime, illicit. Ἀθέμιτα ἔργα (unlawful works) is found in Herodotus. Such things are גְלוּלִים (idols) to the Hebrews. Moreover, idolatry is a certain species of being present at the συσσιτίοις (common meals) of sodalities, which are given to false gods. And it is highly credible that in this matter especially, those Jews, before they were Christians, had accommodated themselves to the customs of the Gentiles.

The Vulgate says 'illicitis idolorum cultibus' (in unlawful cults of idols): the Syriac says 'servitio dæmoniorum' (service of demons). Augustine, Homily 26, among others, says 'nefandis idolorum servitutibus' (in unspeakable services of idols), which expresses the Greek word more accurately. Blessed Luther says 'greulichen Abgötteren' (abominable idolatries). And therefore this Grotian restriction of idolatry does not fit well enough. Cornelius à Lapide gathers more correctly from this that this epistle, although written primarily to the Jews, was also directed to the Gentiles who were given to idolatry. Since the Jews, after the return from Babylon, did not worship idols anymore. But Gregory of Valencia, Book II, on Idolatry, ch. 7, p. 718, ineptly gathers from 'illicitis idolorum cultibus' (in unlawful cults of idols) that there is some lawful cult of idols; no differently than Marcion and the Manichaeans would gather a bad God from a good God: because that word is not διακριτικὴ (distinguishing), but ὁριστικὴ (descriptive), through which all idolatry is rather established as illicit, although Estius acknowledges that it is translated more correctly as 'in nefariis idolorum cultibus' (in nefarious cults of idols).

Latin:

Vers. 3.

᾿Αρκετὸς γὰρ ὑμῖν παρεληλυθὼς ὁ χρόνος τοῦ θεοῦ τὸ θέλη- μα τῶν ἐθνῶν κατεργάσασθαι] Melius Manuscriptus κατείρ- γασθαι, quomodo videtur legisse & Syrus.

bis debet præteritum tempus, quo vos quanquam Judæi vixi- ftis gentium more, corrupti à pravis Doctoribus. Sic Mar- tialis: Lufistis: Satis est. Confer de Judæorum vita locum Rom. II. 21. 22. Et hic κατείργασθαι positum pro εἰς τὸ κα- τείργασθαι, ad ea facienda, quæ gentibus aliis allubescunt, quomodo recte accipit Latinus: Ea quæ sint, jam speciatim explicabit. Ἀρκετὸς רב.

Non video cur lectio recepta Manuscripto Grotiano postponenda sit. Sensus enim recte ha- bet: Sufficit enim nobis præteritum tempus vitæ vo- luntatem gentium operatos fuisse: aut si dura sit ἀνα- κοίνωσις, qua se Petrus illis annumeret, cum aliis Co- dicibus ὑμῖν legamus, sufficit vobis, quod etiam Grotius elegit, & Syrus. Sufficit enim tempus istud, quod præteriit, in quo operati estis voluntatem gentium, quum & in 1. & 4. versu in secunda perso- na loquatur Apostolus. In voce sufficit litotes est, qua mitigat Apostolus exprobrationis severitatem Ezech. XLIV, 6. cap. LIV, 9. Marc. XIV, 41. Τὸ θέλημα τῶν ἐθνῶν explicant τὰς ἐπιθυμίας ἀν- θρώπων concupiscentias hominum, qui nihil aliud sunt quam homines, in quibus nihil est Spiritûs Dei. Homo sine Deo, inquit Estius, totus carnalis est, nec Dei, sed carnis voluntatem exequitur: quales gen- tes erant à Deo alienæ. Unde vocem ἐθνῶν Syrus exposuit profanorum. Habebantur enim pro pro- fanis & impuris, Matth. VI. 5. cap. X. 15. c. XIIX, 7. Judæos autem gentium more vixisse, quod & Schlichtingius hic voluit, indicare Apostolum, etsi admitti possit, quia de nonnullis id credibile est, non tamen dubium, πάντως gentiles respici, utpote ad quos simul directa epistola, & inter quos Judæi conversi vivebant, 1. Petr. II. 12. Quod imprimis locus parallelus confirmat, Eph. IV. 17. seqq. Ne- xus argumenti est: ante conversionem vestram, cum adhuc in tenebris ignorantiæ gentilis versare- mini, voluntati gentium vos conformastis, quæ ex- pertes sunt Dei: hæc vero vita alios mores postu- lat: Conf. Rom. VI. 19. cap. XVI, 11. 1. Cor. VI, 11. 1. Thess. V. 6. 2. Petr. II. 10.

Πεπορευμένους ἐν ἀσελγείαις] Πορεύεσθαι הלך est certum vitæ institutum sequi. Ἀσελγείαις quæ sint vide Marc. VII. 2. Rom. XIII. 13. 2. Cor. XII. 21. Gal. V. 19. Eph. IV. 19. 2. Petr. II. 7. 18. Judæ 4.

Emphasis est in voce πορεύεσθαι non tantum ob vitæ humanæ usitatam descriptionem, quæ profe- ctioni comparatur, sed etiam ob tendendi & per- gendi in vitiis eorum more, qui aliquo contendunt, studium, quod de vitio in vitium provehantur, quod notat glossa interlinearis. Vide similes lo- quutiones 2. Petr. II. 10. cap. III. 3. Jud. v. 16. 18. ut & Luc. I. 6. ideo temere hæc vox à Syro præter- missa est. Ἐν ἀσελγείαις Vulgata luxuriis. Ἀσελγὴς est petulans, ut & lascivus. Lucianus ἀσελγέστεροι τῶν ὄνων asinis lasciviores. Ideo B. Lutherus reddi- dit in Unzucht.

Ἐπιθυμίαις] Ad novas semper libidines inardescente animo. Vide Rom. I. 28. VI. 12. XIII. 14. Gal. V, 16. 24. Eph. II. 3. IV. 22. Col. III. 5. 1. Thess. IV. 5. 1. Timoth. VI. 9. 2. Timoth. III. 6. IV. 3. Tit. II. 12. III. 3. supra I. vers. 14. 2. Petri I. v. 4. II, v. 10. 18. III. v. 3. Judæ 16. 18.

Ideo Lyranus in h. l. Sicut externos actus intem- perantiæ circa veneres denotat per luxurias: Ita in- ternos actus, quando facultas externorum deest, denotat per concupiscentias.

Οἰνοφλυγίαις] Est hæc vox apud Plutarchum Othone. Οἰνόφλυξ apud Xenophontem, παρὰ τὸ φλύειν, ὁρμὴν πρός τι ἔχειν, ait Scriptor Etymologici. Οἰνοφλυγεῖν apud LXX. Deut. XXI. 20. Es. LVI, 12. pro סבא, unde σα- βάζειν.

Vulgata reddidit vinolentiis. Oecumenius expo- suit τὰ ἐπὶ τὸν οἶνον ἀκρατεῖς ὁρμὰς. Οἰνόφλυξ dici- tur, qui vinum eructat, vini avidus. Syrus reddidit generalius: In ebrietate. Sic & B. Lutherus.

Κώμοις.] Vide Rom. XIII, 13. Gal. V, 21. Vulgatus in comessationibus: quia κῶμος est comportatio convivialis, ex qua tandem aliquis in- cidit in somnium profundum, ut ait Eusthatius. Hic quia πότοι adduntur, inordinata vorandi avi- ditas denotatur.

Πότοις.] Assidua convivia,etiamsi absit ebrietas,culpa non carent. Sic מִשְׁתֶּה. sumitur Gen.19,3. c.40,20. Jud.14,10.12.17. 1.Sam.25,36. 2.Sam.3,15. Esth.1,5.8.9.11.18. cap.5,6. c.6,14. c.7,1. Job.1,4.5. Prov.23,30. Eccles.7,3. Esa.25,6. Jer.16,6. Dan.1,5. 8. nimirum quomodo Græci dicunt συμπόσια. Vulgata in potationibus, de ingluvie potandi, vid. Ef.5,11.12. Prov.23.30. B. Gerh. οἰνοφλυγίας de vitio- so habitu & effectu, πότος de potandi actu accipit.

Καὶ ἀθεμίτοις εἰδωλολατρείαις.] עבודות זרות cultus falsorum numinum, qui à Judæis Hellenistis dicti εἰδωλολα- τρείαι, quia non sine simulacris exerceri solebant. Tales au- tem cultus per se sunt illiciti, quia, quod unius Dei est, ipso nolente in alios transferunt.Ideo hic dicuntur ἀθέμιτοι quam vocem habes & Act.X,28. In glossario ἀθέμιτον infandum nefas,illicitum. Ἀθέμιτα ἔργα apud Herodotum. Talia Ebræis גְלוּלִים. Est autem idololatria quædam species, adesse soda- litiorum συσσιτίοις, de quibus profecta falsis Diis dantur. Et in hac maxime re credibile est Judæos illos, antequam Chri- stiani essent, accommodasse se gentium moribus.

Vulgata illicitis idolorum cultibus: Syrus servi- tio dæmoniorum. Augustinus hom. 26. inter L. ne- fandis idolorum servitutib9,quod magis exprimit Græcam vocem. B. Lutherus greulichen Abgötteren- en. Ideoque non satis convenit hæc Grotiana ido- lolatriæ restrictio. Rectius colligit inde Cornelius à Lapide, hanc epistolam licet primario ad Judæos scriptam,ad gentes quoq; directam esse,quæ idolo- latriæ vacarunt.Siquidem Judæi post reditum è Ba- bylonia idola non coluerint amplius.Inepte autem Gregorius de Valentia libr. II. de idol. c. 7. p. 718. ex illicitis idolorum cultibus colligit, aliquem esse lici- tum idolorum cultum; non secus atq; Marcion, & Manichæi ex Deo bono colligerent Deum malum: quia vox illa διακριτικὴ est, distinctiva, sed ὁριστικὴ, descriptiva, per quam omnis idololatria potius sta- tuitur illicita, quanquam Estius agnoscat, rectius verti, in nefariis idolorum cultibus.

## 4:4
Verse 4. Ἐν ᾧ ξενίζονται μὴ συντρεχόντων ὑμῶν εἰς τὴν αὐτὴν τῆς ἀσωτίας ἀνάχυσιν (In which they think it strange that you do not run with them into the same flood of dissipation).] They marvel at this, those not yet converted, that you do not run with them to such luxurious banquets. We have ξενίζεσθαι (to think it strange) also below in verse 12. Thus Polybius: Ξενιζόμενοι τοῖς τῶν ὀργάνων κατασκευαῖς (being surprised at the construction of the instruments), and ἐξενίσθη διὰ τὸ παράδοξον (he was surprised because of the paradox). Ἀνάχυσις (flood/overflow) is taken here for the Chaldean פרה (to overflow) or אתפשטותא (extension): by which is signified that which far exceeds the limit, just as the Latins call a prodigal person 'profusum' (profuse). Ἀσωτία (dissipation) is זֹלֵל (glutton/prodigal) in Prov. 28, 7.

He rendered the Greek 'in quo peregrinantur' (in which they are strangers) as to the sense; the Vulgate says 'in quo admirantur' (in which they marvel); Augustine, Ep. 99, 'in quo stupescunt' (in which they are astonished), as also the scholia say θαυμάζωσιν (they marvel); and the Syriac says 'obstupescunt' (they are astonished), or even 'indignantur' (they are indignant). The verb ξε- νίζεσθαι is properly to be a guest, Acts 10, 6, 18, 32; c. 12, 16. Metaleptically, therefore, they marvel, as those who are traveling are wont to do when they see new cities, houses, and monuments, Acts 17, 20. Ἐν ᾧ (in which) looks not only to the immediately preceding vice, but to all the preceding ones, which are comprehended under the name τῆς ἀσωτίας (of dissipation), not running together, as the Vulgate has it, with you into the same confusion of luxury, because ἀσωτία has an influx into all kinds of vices. From luxury and intemperance of food and drink, lusts arise, and idolatry is usually joined to it, as spiritual whoredom with bodily whoredom, Exod. 32, 6; 1 Cor. 10, 7; and the Gentiles worshipped the goddess Victua, who would provide food, and Potua, who would provide drink. Arnobius, Book 3, against the Gentiles. Drunkenness is the fuel of lust, the incentive of insanity, the poison of foolishness, says Ambrose in 'On Elijah and Fasting', ch. 16. Ἀνά- χυσις in the Greek scholia is explained by σύγχυσιν (confusion), though others prefer 'refusionem' (refusion) or even 'profusionem' (profusion). According to Hesychius, it denotes a certain βλακείαν (sluggishness) and ἔκλυσιν (languor) of the mind, a dissolution of strength, softness, which

dissipation eventually dissolves the powers of mind and body. According to Blessed Gerhard, it can not absurdly be thought that, in particular, regard is had to the festival of Bacchus, to which the Gentiles were wont to run with a certain insane impulse, and in it to practice those unspeakable outrages which Peter enumerates in the preceding verse.

Βλασφημῦντες (Blaspheming).] That is, cursing us besides, for thus that word is taken in Matt. 27, 39; Mark 15, 29; Luke 23, 39; Acts 13, 45; c. 18, 6; Rom. 3, 8; and elsewhere. They were cursing them, however, as deserters of civil society. They were blaspheming not only the Christians, but the Christian religion itself, and not so much because of the deserted civil society as because of the other way of life assumed.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Ἐν ᾧ ξενίζονται μὴ συντρεχόντων ὑμῶν εἰς τὴν αὐτὴν τῆς ἀσωτίας ἀνάχυσιν.] De eo mirantur illi nondum conversi, quod non cum ipsis cursitent ad talia luxuriosa convivia. Ξε- νίζεσθαι mirari habemus & infra 12. Sic Polybius: Ξενιζόμενοι τοῖς τῶν ὀργάνων κατασκευαῖς, & ἐξενίσθη διὰ τὸ παράδοξον. Ἀ- νάχυσις hic sumitur pro Chaldæo פרה vel אתפשטותא: Per quæ significatur id, quod modum longe excedit,sicut La- tini prodigum vocant profusum. Ἀσωτία זֹלֵל Prov. 28, 7.

Græcum in quo peregrinantur reddidit quoad sensum, Vulgata, in quo admirantur, August. ep.99. in quo stupescunt,ut & scholia θαυμάζωσιν : ac Syrus obstupescunt, vel etiam indignantur. Verbum ξε- νίζεσθαιproprie est diversari, Act.10,6.18.32. c.12,16. Metaleptice ergo mirantur, quod peregrinantes so- lent, novis civitatibus, domibus, monumentis vi- sis, Act.17, 20. Ἐν ᾧ non tantum immediate antece- dens vitium,sed omnia antegressa respicit,quæ no- mine τῆς ἀσωτίας comprehenduntur,non concur- rentibus, ut Vulgata habet, vobis in eandem luxu- riæ confusionem, quia ἀσωτία influxum habet ad omnis generis vitia. Ex luxuria & intemperantia ci- bi & potus libidines oriuntur,& conjuncta esse solet idololatria, ceu scortatio spiritualis cum scortatione corporali, Exod.32,6. 1. Cor.10,7. colebantq; gentiles Deam victuam, quæ victum, potuam, quæ potum præberet. Arnobius libr. 3. contra gent. Ebrietas est fomentum libidinis, incentivum insaniæ, venenum in- sipientiæ ait Ambrosius de Elia & jejunio cap.16.Ἀνά- χυσις in Græcis scholiis per σύγχυσιν exponitur, alii tamen malunt refusionem, vel etiam profusionem. Hesychio autore notat quandam animi βλακείαν κὴ ἔκλυσιν, virium exolutionem, mollitiem, quod

ἀσωτία animi & corporis vires tandem dissolvat. B. Gerh. autore non absurde cogitari potest, in specie haberi respectum ad Bacchi festum, ad quod insano quodam impetu gentiles concurrere sole- bant, inque eo nefanda illa flagitia exercere, quæ Petrus versu præcedenti enumerat.

Βλασφημῦντες.] Id est, maledicentes insuper nobis, nam sic id verbum sumitur Matth. 27, 39. Marc. 15, 29. Luc. 23, 39. Act. 13, 45. cap. 18, 6. Rom. 3, 8. & alibi. Maledicebant autem illis tanquam desertoribus civilis societatis. Non Christianos tantum, sed ipsam etiam religio- nem Christianam blasphemabant, nec illos tam ob desertam civilem societatem, quam ob aliud vi- vendi genus assumptum.

## 4:5
Ver. 5. Who shall give an account.] That is, their wicked deeds shall come to the examination of Christ. See Heb. 13, 7.

To him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.] A circumlocution for Christ, who is prepared to judge both those who will be alive when he comes, and those who have died before. Thus you have ἑτοίμως ἔχειν in Acts 21, 13; 2 Cor. 12, 14; and Dan. 13, 15, where in the Chaldee it is אותיין עתידין.

These things are said not only for consolation on account of accusation, but also for dissuasion from former crimes. A great necessity, says Augustine in Soliloquies ch. 14, is laid upon us to live justly and rightly, since we do all things before the eyes of a judge who sees all things. For ἑτοίμως ἔχοντι the Syrian uses the word עתיד here, which is also rendered thus by the LXX interpreters, and which denotes not only being ready, but also being imminent, being near, Deut. 32, 35; Esth. 3, 14; Dan. 3, 5. To which meaning verse 7 of this place corresponds. Compare James 5, 9. But when he is called the Judge of the living and the dead, by the living are understood those whom he will find alive and surviving at his coming to judgment, Acts 10, 42; 2 Tim. 4, 1, so that a universal future judgment is implied. Maximus of Turin, homily on the exposition of the creed: The living and the dead are said to be judged, so that it may be believed that there is care for all men before God.

Latin:

Vers. 5. ὁι ἀποδώσυσι λόγον.] Id est, maledicta illorum ad examen venient Christi. Vide Ebr. 13, 7.

Τῷ ἑτοίμως ἔχοντι κρῖναι ζῶντας κὶ νεκρές.] Circumscriptio Christi, qui paratus est judicare & tunc victuros, cùm veniet, & præmortuos. Sic ἑτοίμως ἔχειν habes Act. 21, 13. 2. Cor. 12, 14. & Dan. 13, 15. ubi in Chaldæo אותיין עתידין.

Hæc non tantum ob consolationem propter cri- minationem, sed etiam ob dehortationem à pristinis criminibus dicuntur. Magna, inquit Augustinus in solil. c. 14. nobis indita est necessitas juste recteque vi- vendi, qui cuncta facimus ante oculos judicis cuncta cernentis. Pro ἑτοίμως ἔχοντι Syrus voce עתיד hic utitur, quæ sic etiam redditur à LXX. Interpretibus, quæque notat non solum promptum esse, sed etiam imminere, in proximo esse, Deuter. 32, 35. Esth. 3, 14. Dan. 3, 5. Cui significatui congruit v. 7. h. l. Conf. Jac. 5, 9. Cum autem Judex vivorum & mortuorum dicitur, per vivos intelliguntur, quos vivos, & su- perstites inveniet in adventu ad judicium, Act. 10, 42. 2. Tim. 4, 1. ut universale futurum innuatur ju- dicium. Maximus Taurinensis hom. in expos. symb. Vivi judicandi referuntur & mortui, ut omnium ho- minum esse apud Deum cura credatur.

## 4:6
Ver. 6. For to this end was the gospel preached also to the dead.] Namely by Christ, by the same locution which is in Gal. 1, 16. The little word κί shows that here νεκροῖς is to be taken in the same way as νεκρὺς, which had preceded. However, the νεκροὶ are not to be understood as those who were dead when Peter wrote these things, in the same way as it is said in Ruth 1, 18, καθὼς ἐποιήσατε μετὰ τῶν τεθνηκότων עם המתים. For even there they are called dead who were dead at the time when Naomi said these things, not when the kindness was done to them. Christ wished to be announced even to those who are already dead. Therefore he will judge not only the living, but also the dead. Otherwise, it would have been announced to them in vain: they would have believed and endured hardships in vain.

Peter teaches that the dead also are to be judged by Christ, because the Gospel concerning Christ was preached to them also while they were among the living, which sounded perpetually not only in the New Testament but also in the Old, since all are to render an account to Christ. Blessed Gerhard thinks that this exposition can be entirely tolerated, and we, since one should not depart from the literal meaning without necessity, judge it to be preferred to others: since the text also holds together very well in this way.

Those who explain the preaching of the Gospel as having been done to the dead in prison, from 1 Pet. 3, 19, do not attend to the end subjoined here, that they might live according to God in the spirit. Certainly, it does not befit those established in hell, just as the announcement of the Gospel does not. It is repugnant to others, who explained it as the preaching done to the blessed in heaven, that it is said of them that they are to be judged according to men in the flesh. Augustine, Ep. 99, explains it concerning the spiritually dead. It is possible that he called the infidels dead, that is, dead in soul. For therefore in this life it was evangelized even to the dead, that is, to the infidels and the unrighteous, so that when they have believed, they may indeed be judged according to men in the flesh, that is, in various tribulations and in the very death of the flesh, whence the same Apostle says in another place that it is time for the judgment of God to begin at the house of God, but that they may live according to God in the Spirit, because they also had been mortified in it when they were held by the death of infidelity and impiety. But because the proper meaning is not rashly to be abandoned, furthermore, that the discourse is about the dead, of whom Christ is said to be Judge just as He is of the living, the context indicates, and moreover the particle καὶ leads us to this, as does the continuation of the discourse concerning the end of all things, which is joined with the final judgment; we prefer to understand the dead as those who have departed, to whom in preceding times, even before Christ, the Gospel concerning Christ was announced, so that it may be established that the proclamation of the Gospel of Christ is no less universal than the final judgment of Christ. Because he said that God would judge, says Flacius, not only those whom He will find alive, but also those who were dead before the last day and will then be resurrected: therefore, so that he might, as it were, take away every excuse from everyone on the last day, he says that for this very purpose the Gospel was preached even to the ancients who had already died at this time of Christ and the Apostles, to this very end, that their flesh or old man might be judged, or punished and mortified, but the new and spiritual man might be generated, vivified, and grow. To this point contribute the observations of B. Gerhard on page 591. Those who take the name of the dead indefinitely concerning any dead persons whatsoever, they establish the sense to be that the Gospel is not only preached to men still living in the flesh, but was also preached to those who are already dead, so that they too might be converted to God in their sins and escape the sentence of condemnatory judgment. They therefore report such a connection. 1. The Apostle meets a tacit objection. For someone could think, how will not only the living, but also the dead be judged, since they have already perished? The Apostle answers that the dead are to be judged no less than those who now live, since the Gospel was also announced to the dead, namely to those who are indeed already dead, but formerly lived. For just as the dead will be judged, who have indeed already perished, but will then be restored to life: so the Gospel was preached to the dead, who have indeed already perished, but formerly lived. 2. Such a reason for the connection can also be given: An objection could be raised that those who died before the advent of Christ into these lands would have an excuse in the judgment, because they did not hear the preaching of the Gospel. Peter denies this and teaches that the Gospel was preached even to the dead, since the doctrine concerning the Messiah has sounded perpetually in the Church not only in the New, but also in the Old Testament. 3. But this connection can also be given, that it may be said that the Apostle wished to teach by these words that death is no obstacle to Christ being nonetheless our vindicator and liberator. For however much liberation may not happen in this life, but we are forced to struggle for the truth of the Gospel even unto blood and death (Heb. 12:4), the hope of our redemption will not therefore be vain or void, because the power of this our liberator extends even to the dead.

Ἵνα κριθῶσι μὲν κατὰ ἀνθρώπους σαρκὶ, ζῶσι δὲ κατὰ Θεὸν πνεύματι.] That is, so that although condemned to death by men, they may nevertheless live again by the power of God. Ἵνα signifies what the outcome of the preaching made to them would be. Κατ' ἀνθρώπους, as much as it was in the power of men, who can kill the body, but not the soul (Matt. 10:28). Thus in the opposite member, κατὰ Θεὸν, which is in God. Κριθῶσι σαρκὶ is briefly stated, so condemned that the loss of the flesh occurs: which, when these things were written, had happened to Stephen, James, and others. Add Rev. 14:13. ζῆν πνεύματι is to live that eternal life, which is also spiritual (1 Cor. 15:46).

Schlichtingius also provided this sense: That they may indeed be judged, i.e., condemned, torn apart by blasphemies and insults on account of Christ's name and His righteousness. He puts the cause for the effect. According to men, namely the infidels, according to their opinion, judgment, pleasure, and will. Thus also below in verse 14, in the flesh, i.e., through the flesh, or as regards the flesh. For the adversaries can do nothing except against the flesh of the pious, God permitting. He opposes life to judgments, because the judgment of men brings condemnations and deaths to Christians. According to God, i.e., the Divine will revealed through Christ. In the Spirit, i.e., through the Spirit, or as regards the Spirit, both the natural one, or the rational soul, and the Spirit drawn and received from Christ. But here the end of the Gospel preached to the dead is expressed, which regards not only the pious, but all to whom it is preached, nor is it an obstacle that those to whom it is preached are torn apart by insults and killed, for this happens accidentally, not from the Divine intention, according to which the Gospel was preached to all. Nor is the end of the proclamation only that they may live after natural death in the other life, as Grotius accepted, but that they may live here in the kingdom of grace according to God in the Spirit. To which the opposition of flesh and Spirit also leads us, with Schlichtingius not denying it: Christians, he says, ought not to live by the flesh, but to be judged, condemned, afflicted, and suffer by the flesh: they ought to live by the Spirit, and mortify the actions of the flesh (Rom. 8:12, 13, 14), where, however, Schlichtingius confuses the diverse use of the word flesh, when it is taken for the body in a physical sense opposed to the soul, or naturally, and when it is taken for the old exterior man, or as he is not reborn, and is opposed to the Spirit, or the new and interior man, as he is a reborn man, just as the flesh lusts against the Spirit (Gal. 5:17), just as that confusion also occurs in the explanation of the Spirit, to which he attributes such disparate meanings in these words of Peter against hermeneutical laws, so that he denotes both the natural Spirit or rational soul, and the Spirit drawn and received from Christ. Although Flacius thinks these things can be understood concerning the death of the body and the vivification of the soul, as if to say the preached Gospel accomplished this, that although it did not rescue believers from this temporary destruction before the last day, since it is necessary for all to die in the human manner, yet at least their souls might live in the bosom of Abraham, awaiting with joyful spirit the final judgment and eternal glory, so that believers have not entirely perished, however much they may appear to our fleshly eyes to perish just like other impious people. Nevertheless, he seems to establish the former opinion as truer, that that expression signifies this, that they are judged according to men in the flesh, so that their flesh or old Adam may be mortified, so that it can no longer live in the manner and custom of corrupt men, but the Spirit or new man, regenerated by the Holy Spirit, may be so much the more vivified and progress, living according to the will and Word of God. For he adds: The same opinion clearly seems to be in Rom. Chapter eight, verse ten: The body is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of righteousness. Similarly, the blessed Gerhard judges that this exposition, that the Gospel has been preached to men from the beginning of the world, so that even if they are punished in the flesh in the human manner because of sins, yet they live and are saved in the Spirit before God, does not conflict with the analogy of faith. However, he most simply establishes that by the phrase 'to be judged according to men in the flesh' is understood the condemnation and abolition of the old man, that is, of carnal conversation walking according to men in carnal lusts. But by the phrase 'to live according to God in the Spirit' is understood spiritual life according to the new man, conformed to the Divine will. For since sin clings to the nature of men, and is intimately fixed to it, Heb. 12, 1, therefore he says 'according to man,' which you can also take as 'according to men,' that is, who are merely men, as before in verse 2. ἐπιθυμίας ἀνθρώπων the Apostle had said. In which sense the word 'to judge' is taken in 1 Cor. 11:31, if we were to judge ourselves in true repentance through the mortification of the flesh. For the end of the preached Gospel is the mortification of the flesh and the renewal of the Spirit, just as the blessed Bede also explained, as you judge, that is, that having spurned carnal desires they may live spiritually. And B. Huss: That they may be judged, viz. in the present, by themselves, viz. through the mortification of the flesh concerning their human deeds, which they committed while living carnally in the flesh. But let them live a spiritual life, which is according to God. Similarly also B. Luther: You must understand 'flesh' thus, as I have said above, that the whole man is called flesh, as he lives, just as he is also called whole spirit, when he strives after that which is spiritual. This is now so mingled together, as I speak of a man who is wounded, that he is whole and yet wounded, thus so that the healthy part is greater than the wounded one, yet he is called wounded only according to the part that is struck: Thus here also the spirit should take precedence. Therefore he says that they are condemned according to the outward being, but according to the inner, that is, according to the spirit, they would be preserved, and live. Cornelius à Lapide collects many other senses; concerning most of them one may consult B. Gerhard.

he said in the plural, both because there are diverse kinds of prayer, 1 Tim. II, 1, and because it is always necessary to pray and not to faint, which reason B. Huss gives, cf. Luke XVIII, 1. It behooves us to watch always, so that while we do not know the certain moments of the future judgment, always established as if on watch, and placed on a certain watchtower of virtue, we may decline the habit of sinning, lest the day of the Lord overtake us among vices, says Ambrose, book V de fide, ch. 8.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Εἰς τῦτο γὰρ κί νεκροῖς ἐυηγγελίσθη.] Nempe Chri- stus, eadem loquutione, quæ est Gal. 1, 16. Vocula κί ostendit hic νεκροῖς sumendos, quæmodo νεκρὺς, quod præcesserat. In- telligendi autem νεκροὶ non qui mortui erant, cum Petrus hæc scriberet, plane quomodo dicitur Ruth. 1, 18. καθὼς ἐποίησα- τε μετὰ τῶν τεθνηκότων עם המתים. Nam & ibi mortui dicuntur, qui tunc erant mortui, cum ista diceret Naëmi, non cum eis benefieret. Christus voluit annuntiati etiam iis, qui jam sunt mortui. Ergo non vivos tantum, sed & mortu- os judicabit. Alioqui frustra illis annuntiatus esset: Frustra illi credidissent, & dura pertulissent.

Docet Petrus etiam mortuos à Christo judicandos, quia & illis, dum in vivis erant, prædicatũ est Evan- gelium de Christo, quod non tantum in N. T. sed & in V. perpetuo sonuit, siquidem omnes Christo ra- tionẽ reddituri sint. Quam expositionem omnino tolerari posse B. Gerh. existimat, nosque cum citra necessitatem à proprietate literæ non sit discedendũ, aliis præferendā censemus: siquidem optime etiam textus ita se habeat συνέχεια.

Qui de prædicatione Evangelii mortuis in carcere facta, è 1. Petr. 3, 19. ex- plicant, finem hic subjunctum non attendunt, ut vi- vant secundum Deum spiritu. Certe in inferno con- stitutis non convenit, quemadmodũ nec Evangelii annunciatio. Aliis, qui de prædicatione beatis in cæ- lis facta exposuere, repugnat, quod dicitur de illis secundum homines in carne judicandis. De Spiri- tualiter mortuis explicat Aug. ep. 99. Fieri potest, ut mortuos dixerit infideles, hoc est in anima mor- tuos. Propterea enim in hac vita & mortuis evan- gelizatum est, id est, infidelibus & iniquis, ut cum crediderint, judicentur quidem secundum homines in carne, hoc est, in diversis tribulationibus, & in ipsa morte carnis, unde idem Apostolus alio in loco dicit tempus esse, ut incipiat judicium Dei à domo Domini, vivant autem secundum Deũ Spiritu, quia & in ipso fuerant mortificati cum morte infidelita- tis & impietatis detinerentur. Sed quia non teme- re significatio propria relinquenda, adhæc de mor- tuis, quorum æque ut viventium Christus Judex dicitur, sermonem esse, contextus indicat, & præ- terea eo particula καὶ nos deducit ut & continuatio sermonis de fine rerum omnium, qui conjunctus est cum judicio novissimo, malumus mortuos intelli- gere eos, qui decesserunt, quibus præcedentibus temporibus, etiam ante Christum, Evangelium de Christo annuntiatum fuit, ut constet, non minus universale esse Evangelii Christi præconium, quam novissimum Christi judicium. Quia dixit Deum judicaturum, inquit Flacius, non tantum eos, quos vivos reperiet, sed etiam qui mortui ante extremum diem fuerint & tunc resuscitabuntur: ideo, ut veluti omnibus omnem excusationem in extrema die adi- meret, dicit ad hoc ipsum etiam veteribus, qui hac tempore Christi & Apostolorum jam mortui fuerant, in hunc ipsum finem esse prædicatum Evangelium, ut caro aut vetus eorum homo judicaretur, seu punire- tur & mortificaretur, novus vero & spiritualis gene- raretur, vivificaretur & cresceret. Quo faciunt quæ observat B. Gerhardus pag. 591. Qui nomen mor- tuorũ indefinite accipiunt de quibusvis mortuis, illi statuunt sensum esse eum, quod Evangeliũ non- solum prædicetur hominibus in carne adhuc vi- ventibus, sed etiam prædicatum fuerit illis, qui jam mortui sunt, ut ipsi quoq; in peccatis ad Deum con- verterentur, & judicii damnatorii sententiam effu- gerent. Tradunt igitur ejusmodi connexionem. 1. Occurrit Apostolus tacitæ objectioni. Poterat enim quispiam cogitare, quomodo non solum vivi, sed etiam mortui judicabuntur, cum illi jam interie- rint? Respondet Apostolus, non minus judicandos mortuos, quam eos, qui nunc vivunt, siquidem & mortuis Evangelium sit annunciatum, nempe illis, qui jam quidem mortui sunt, olim autem vivebant. Sicut enim judicabuntur mortui, qui jam quidem interierunt, tum autem vitæ restituentur: ita prædi- catum Evangelium esse mortuis, qui jam quidem interierunt, olim autem vivebant. 2. Potest etiam talis dari connexionis ratio: Objici poterat, illos, qui ante Christi in has terras adventũ mortui sunt, excusationem in judicio habituros, quod prædica- tionem Evangelii non audierint, Negat hoc Petrus & docet etiam mortuis prædicatum fuisse Evange- lium, cum doctrina de Messia non solum in N. sed etiam in V. T. perpetuo in Ecclésia sonuerit. 3. Sed & hæc potest dari connexio, ut dicatur, Apostolum hisce verbis docere voluisse, mortem nihil obstare, quin Christus nihilominus sit vindex & liberator noster. Utcunque enim in hac vita non contingat liberatio, sed cogamur usq; ad sanguinem & mor- tem pro veritate Evangelii decertare Ebr. XII, 4. non tamen inanis aut irrita propterea erit spes no- stræ redemptionis, quia virtus hujus nostri libera- toris etiam ad mortuos extenditur.

Ἵνα κριθῶσι μὲν κατὰ ἀνθρώπους σαρκὶ, ζῶσι δὲ κατὰ Θεὸν πνεύματι.] Id est, ut quamvis ab hominibus damnati ad mor- tem, Dei tamen virtute rursus vivant. Ἵνα significat quis futu- rus sit eventus prædicationis ipsis factæ. Κατ' ἀνθρώπους quan- tum in hominibus fuit, qui corpus interficere possunt, non & animum, Matth. X, 28. Sic in opposito membro κατὰ Θεὸν, quod in Deo est. Κριθῶσι σαρκὶ est breviter dictum, ita da- mnati, ut carnis jactura fiat: quod, cum hæc scriberentur, eve- nerat Stephano, Jacobo & aliis. Adde Apoc. 14, 13. ζῆν πνεύματι est vivere vitam illam æternam, quæ & spiritualis 1. Cor. 15, 46.

Hunc sensum tradidit & Schlichtingius: Ut judi- centur quidem, i. e. damnentur, blasphemiis, convitiis proscindantur propter Christi nomen & ejus justitiam. Causam ponit pro effectu. Secundum homines, nempe infideles, secundum eorum opinionem, sententiam, pla- citum, voluntatem. Sic & infra 14. carne, i. e. per car- nem, seu quod ad carnem. Nihil enim adversarii pos- sunt, nisi in carnem piorum, Deo permittente. Vitam opponit judicia, quod judicium hominum afferat Chri- stianis damnationes & mortes. Secundum Deum, i. e. Divinam voluntatem per Christum revelatam. Spiri- tu, i. e. per Spiritum, seu quod ad Spiritum tam natu- ralem, seu animam rationalem, quam Spiritum ex Christo haustum & acceptum. Sed hic finis exprimi- tur Evangelii mortuis prædicati, qui non pios tan- tum, sed omnes, quibus id prædicatur, respicit, ne- que obest, quod illi, quibus prædicatur, convitiis proscindantur & occidantur, hoc enim accidenta- liter evenit, non ex intentione Divina, secundum quam prædicatum Evangelium omnibus. Nec finis præconii tantum est ut vivant post mortem natu- ralem in altera vita, ut Grotius accepit, sed ut hic in regno gratiæ secundum Deum Spiritu vivant. Quo et- iam oppositio carnis & Spiritus nos deducit, non diffitente Schlichtingio: Christiani, inquit, vivere non debent carne, sed carne judicari, damnari, affligi, pati: Spiritu debent vivere, & actiones carnis mortificare, Rom. 8, 12. 13. 14. ubi tamen confundit Schlichtingius usum vocis carnis diversimodum, cum pro corpore accipitur animæ sensu physico opposito, vel natura- liter, &cũ pro homine veteri exteriore, vel qua non re- natus est, & opponitur Spiritui, vel homini novo & interiori, qua homo renatus est, prout caro con- cupiscit adversus Spiritum, Gal. V, 17. quemadmo- dum ea confusio etiam occurrit in explicatione Spiritus, cui tam disparatos in hisce Petri verbis contra leges hermeneuticas tribuit significatus, ut tum Spiritum naturalem seu animam rationalem, tum Spiritum à Christo haustum, & acceptum no- tet. Flacius etsi posse hæc de morte corporis & vivi- ficatione animæ accipi censeat, q. d. Evangelium prædicatum id perfecit, ut licet non vindicarit ab hoc interitu temporario credentes ante extremam diem, quandoquidem omnes more humano mori necesse est, at saltem eorum animæ in sinu Abrahæ viverent, læto animo expectantes ultimum judicium & gloriam æter- nam, ut credentes non plane perierint, quantumvis nostris carneis oculis perinde interire videantur, sicut & alii impii. Priorem tamen sententiam veriorem videtur statuere, ut id significet illa loquutio, ut judi- centur secundum homines carne, ut caro aut vetus eo- rum Adam mortificetur, ne amplius possit modo more- que corruptorum hominum vivere, sed Spiritus aut no- vus homo, per Spir. S. regeneratus, tanto magis vivifi- cetur & proficiat, vivendo secundum voluntatem Verbumq́; Dei. Nam addit: Eadem plane sententia videtur esse Rom. Cap. octavo vers. decimo: Corpus mortuum est propter peccatum, spiritus autem vivit propter justitiam. Similiter B. Gerhardus exposi- tionem istam, quod Evangelium inde à mundi initio fuerit hominibus prædicatum, ut etiam si more huma- no propter peccata in carne castigentur, tamen Spiri- tu coram Deo vivant & salventur, non pugnare censeat cum fidei analogia. Simplicissime tamen per τὸ judicari secundum homines carne intelligi statuit damnationem & abolitionem veteris hominis, h. e. carnalis conversationis secundum homines in car- nalibus concupiscentiis ambulantes. Per τὸ vivere autem secundum DEUM Spiritu vitam spiritua- lem secundum novum hominem Divinæ volunta- ti conformem. Quum enim peccatum in natura hominum hæreat, eiq; intime sit infixum, Ebr. 12, 1. ideo dicit secundum hominem, quod etiam accipere possis secundum homines, id est, qui mere homines sunt, ut antea vers. 2. ἐπιθυμίας ἀνθρώπων dixerat Apostolus. Quo sensu verbum judicandi accipi- tur 1. Cor. XI, 31. si nos ipsos judicaremus in vera pœnitentia per carnis mortificationem. Finis enim prædicati Evangelii est carnis mortificatio, & Spiri- tus renovatio, quemadm. odum & Beda exposuit, ut judicatis, id est, spretis carnalibus desideriis spiri- tualiter vivant. Et B. Huffus: Ut judicentur, scil. in praesentia, semetipsis scil. per mortificationem carnis de factis suis humanis, quae commiserunt in carne carnaliter viventes. Vivant autem vita spirituali, quae est secundum Deum. Similiter & B. Lutherus: Fleisch must du also verstehen, wie ich oben gesagt habe, daß der gantze Mensch Fleisch heisse, wie er le- bet, wie er auch gantz Geist heisset, wenn er nach dem trachtet, das geistlich ist. Das ist nun so in einan- der gemenget, wie ich spreche von einem Menschen, der verwundet ist, daß er heil und doch verwundet sen, also doch, daß das gesunde Theil grösser sey, denn das verwundete, doch heisset er allein nach dem Theil, das getroffen ist, verwundet: Also soll hier auch der Geist vorgehen. Darum sagt er, daß sie nach dem eusserlichen Wesen verdammet werden, aber nach dem inneren, das ist, nach dem Geist, be- halten würden, und leben. Alios sensus plures col- legit Cornelius à Lapide, de plerisque conferri po- terit B. Gerhardus.

tem in plurali dixit, tum quia diversae sunt oratio- nis species, 1. Tim. II, 1. tum quia semper oportet orare & non deficere, quam rationem reddit B. Hussius, conf. Luc. XVIII, 1. Vigilare semper nos opor- tet, ut dum certa futuri judicii momenta nescimus, semper tanquam in excubiis constituti, & in quadam virtutis specula collocati peccandi consuetudinem de- clinemus, ne nos inter vitia dies Domini deprehendat, ait Ambrosius l. V. de fide cap. 8.

## 4:7
Vers. 7. Πάντων δὲ τὸ τέλος ἤγγικε.] קץ הכל That judgment is not far off. For so Peter thought, as we also said concerning Paul, 1 Cor. XV, 33. 1 Thess. IV, 17. Πάντων of all things of this age, as the Syrian also understood.

A new reason, or an elucidation of that which he had said, that the judge is imminent, or the cause of the study of innocence and holiness is rendered; because no one knows about the day of judgment, on account of which it must be thought of as always near, and such a thought represses carnal vices, says Lyranus. The consideration of the approaching end of all things contributes much both to patience in adversities and to the innocence of life in the perverse pursuits of the world. By τὰ πάντα are understood not the prophecies of the Prophets, but all visible created things except man, for this one is reserved for judgment. Cf. James V, 8, 9. 1 Cor. X, 11. 1 John II, 18. The time intermediate between the first and second coming of Christ is called the last, because no further illustrious and universal manifestation of God is to be expected in this age, Heb. I, 1. B. Luther: Not so much time, he says, remains until the day of judgment as has flowed away. That Peter alone thought humanly that the end of all things was imminent is said less piously. For Peter did not write these things ἀνθρωπίνως, but θεοπνεύστως.

PART II. Excitation to sobriety, charity, and the holy dispensation of charisms.

Be of sound mind, therefore, and be sober unto prayers.] Σωφρονῶν is to conduct oneself modestly, as in Tit. II, 6. Νήφων is to be of a mind undisturbed by any evil affections, as we said in 1 Thess. V. Both are profitable for praying rightly. See above III, 7.

An exhortation is now drawn from the approaching end of all things, that we may live soberly as regards ourselves, dutifully as regards our neighbor, and holily as regards the use of divine gifts: and to the general exhortation to live according to the will of God, special precepts are subjoined. The Vulgate rendered Σωφρονήσατε: Be prudent. Others: Be sober, such as the Syriac, Oecumenius, Erasmus, Pagninus, Vatablus: Since σωφρονεῖν means to act prudently, to be temperate, and moderate, and thus it refers to the sobriety of both mind and body. The former meaning is found in Mark V, 15, Luke VIII, 35, Rom. XII, 3. The latter in Tit. II, 6. D. Glassius, Dom. Exaud. p. 358, says that that word σωφρονήσατε comprises two things: attention and temperance. The Vulgate rendered Νήψατε: Watch. The Syriac: Be watchful, aroused, cf. 2 Tim. IV, 5, 1 Pet. I, 13, Luke XXI, 31, which is joined with the former, because they are not fit for vigils unless they are sober. B. Glassius wishes the word νήψατε primarily to denote sobriety, but also to imply repentance. Προσευχὰς au- Vers. 9. ὅτι ἡ ἀγάπη καλύψει τὸ πλῆθος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν.] The same sentiment as in James V, 20, where we say that καλύπτειν does not mean to forgive. Love is regarded especially in this, that we draw others away from sins, the consequence of which is that God overlooks the former sins of a man who has now been amended. In the Manuscript: Ἀγάπη καλύπτει.

Grotius seems to take it concerning Divine forgiveness. But the discourse is about the charity of men, not, as Clement of Alexandria lib. VI. Strom. and Bernard Serm. XXIII. in Cant. [say], about God's [forgiveness], and about the forgiveness which is done to a neighbor, since that κάλυψις [covering] signifies not only the covering of a neighbor's faults, but also the dissimulation and remission of injuries brought upon us by him, which are proper to charity. The word for covering seems to look back to the history of Noah, whose nakedness was covered by his sons Shem and Japheth, Gen. IX, 23, and it hints at the ease of the thing. For nothing is easier than to cover oneself or one's neighbor with a garment, says Caesarius of Arles, hom. IX. de Eleem. Furthermore, if we cover the sins of our neighbor, GOD will also cover our sins, Matth. VI, 14. Abbot Pastor in the Lives of the Fathers, book V, ch. 9, n. 6. At whatever hour we cover the sin of our brother, God also covers ours, and at whatever hour we have betrayed the faults of our brothers, GOD will likewise betray ours, 1. Cor. XIII, 7. Jas. V, 20. However, this κάλυψις (covering) does not remove either the rebuke of public persons, which is done for the sake of duty, or that which is owed to a neighbor for necessary correction, Matt. XVIII, 25. The sins of a neighbor, says Anselm in his book on beatitude, are never to be uncovered, unless for the benefit of the sinners or others. One must also distinguish between public and private, notorious and occult, or secret offenses. For as Augustine advises in his explanation of the passage in Matt. XVIII, 5, charity itself demands that those things which are sinned more secretly should be corrected secretly. Where the evil happens, there let it also die. For if you alone know it, and you wish to correct it before everyone, you are not a corrector, but a betrayer.

Nor does that κάλυψις (covering) serve for the covering of one's own sins, as Cornelius à Lapide contends, saying: Charity covers all sins, one's own and another's: one's own, because it arises from the charity of God, which abolishes all sins and sanctifies man: But the charity with which God loves us does indeed cover our sins, because sins are remitted to us out of mere grace, but not that with which we love God: That the discourse here is about charity toward a neighbor, covering his sins, the Solomonic passage Prov. X, 12 teaches, with Lyranus as interpreter, meaning this: Just as hatred through anger manifests the defects of others: So charity conceals them, unless fraternal correction requires otherwise. That fraternal charity is signified, says Estius, that is, that with which a neighbor is loved, is evident from the preceding part, and no less from the antithesis which the Wise Man makes between hatred and charity.
