For he does not refer hatred to men and charity to God, but both to men. The same sentence of the Wise Man shows that the discourse is about the offenses of neighbors, and not of the one whose charity is being commended. For what the Wise Man says is like this: Just as hatred stirs up quarrels and dissensions with others whom one hates: So charity, on the contrary, not only does not sow or stir up quarrels and dissensions, but even composes and settles those that have been stirred up, and covers offenses and injuries, which are wont to be the cause of quarrels, by tolerating, dissimulating, and excusing them; finally, it forgives whatever is a sin in itself, and intercedes and obtains that God may forgive. Lorinus also interprets it as charity, how it refreshes others and easily forgives the sins of others, because Peter had just before dealt with mutual charity, and suddenly gives the reason, because charity covers a multitude of sins, bringing forward in that sentiment Chrysostom in his homily. IV. on the Acts of the Apostles. Council of Ilerda c. 7. Augustine book 1 on baptism c. 17. Ambrose on Psalm CXVIII. Beautifully B. Luther on this passage: The merit of Christ apprehended by faith covers sins before God, but charity covers the sins of a neighbor. Just as God covers our sins with His charity: So we ought to cover the sins of our neighbor with our charity.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Πάντων δὲ τὸ τέλος ἤγγικε.] קץ הכל Non longe abeft illud judicium. Ita enim Petrus existimabat, ut & de Paulo diximus 1. Cor. XV, 33. 1. Thess. IV, 17. Πάντων rerum omnium hujus seculi, quomodo & Syrus accepit.

Nova ratio, vel ejus, quod dixerat imminere ju- dicem, dilucidatio, aut causa studii innocentiae & sanctitatis redditur; quia de die judicii nemo scit, propter quod cogitanda est tanquam semper pro- pinqua, & talis cogitatio reprimit carnalia vitia, inquit Lyranus. Consideratio appropinquantis fi- nis rerum omnium tum ad patientiam in adversis, tum ad vitae innocentiam in perversis mundi studi- is plurimum facit. Per τὰ πάντα non vaticinia Pro- phetarum, sed omnia creata visibilia praeter homi- nem intelliguntur, hic enim judicio reservatur. Conf. Jac. V, 8. 9. 1. Cor. X, 11. 1. Job.II, 18. Tempus inter primum & secundum Christi adventum inter- medium vocatur novissimum, quia nulla amplius il- lustris & universalis Dei patefactio in hoc seculo expectanda, Ebr. I, 1. B. Lutherus: Non tantum, in- quit, temporis ad diem judicii restat, quantum ef- fluxit. Petrum solum humanitus existimasse finem omnium imminere, minus pie dicitur. Petrus enim non ἀνθρωπίνως haec scripsit, sed θεοπνεύςως.

PARS II. Excitatio ad sobrietatem, charitatem, & chari- smatum sanctam dispensationem.

Σωφρονήσατε ἦν καὶ νήψατε εις τὰς προσευχάς.] Σωφρονῶν est modeste se gerere, ut Tit. II, 6. Νήφων animo esse nullis malis affectibus turbato, ut diximus 1. Thess. V. Utrumque prodest ad recte faciendas preces. Vide supra III, 7.

Deducitur jam à fine rerum omnium appropin- quante exhortatio, ut sobrie quod ad nos, officiose quoad proximum, & sancte quoad usum divino- rum charismatum vivamus: ac generali ad viven- dum secundum voluntatem Dei paraenesi, subjun- guntur praecepta specialia. Σωφρονήσατε Vulgata reddidit: Estote prudentes: Alii sobrii sitis, utpote Syrus, Oecumenius, Erasmus, Pagninus, Vatablus: Si- quidem σωφρονεῖν fit prudenter agere, temperan- tem esse, ac moderatum, adeoque & ad animi & ad corporis sobrietatem refertur. Illa significatio ha- betur Marc. V, 15. Luc. IIX, 35. Rom. XII, 3. Haec Tit. II, 6. Voceni illam σωφρονήσατε duo complecti ait D. Glassius Dom. Exaud. p. 358. attentionem & tem- perantiam. Νήψατε Vulgata reddidit: Vigilate. Sy- rus vigilantes sitis, excitati, conf. 2. Tim. IV, 5. 1. Petr. I, 13. Luc. XXI, 31. quod cum illo conjungitur, quia ad vigilias apti non sunt, nisi sobrii. B. Glassius vocem νήψατε primario sobrietatem notare vult, inferre autem etiam poenitentiam. Προσευχὰς au- Vers. 9. ὅτι ἡ ἀγάπη καλύψει τὸ πλῆθος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν.] Eadem sententia, quae Jacobi V, 20. ubi dicimus καλύπτειν non esse condonare. Dilectio maxime in eo spectatur, ut alios à peccatis abstrahamus, cui consequens est, ut Deus ho- minis jam emendati priora peccata dissimulet. In Manuscri- pto: Ἀγάπη καλύπτει.

De condonatione Divina videtur accipere Grotig. Sed de charitate hominum sermo est, non, ut Clem. Alexandr. lib. VI. Strom. & Bernh. Serm. XXIII. in Cant. de Dei, & de condonatione, quae fit proximo, quum κάλυψις illa non modo naevorum proximi ob- tectionem, sed etiam injuriarum nobis ab illo illatarum dissimulationem, & remissionem. quae charitati pro- pria sunt. Verbum tegendi respicere videtur histo- riam de Noacho, cujus pudenda tecta sunt à filiis Se- mo & Japheto, Gen. IX, 23. innuitq; facilitatem rei. Nihil enim facilius, quam seipsum vel proximum ve- ste tegere, ait Cæsarius Arelatensis hom. IX. de Eleem. Porro si peccata proximi tegimus, DEUS etiam peccata nostra teget, Matth. VI, 14. Abbas Pa- stor in vitis Patrum l. V. c. 9. n. 6. Quacunque ho- ne tegimus peccatum fratris nostri, tegit etiam Deus nostrum, & quacunque hora prodiderimus culpas fratrum, etiam DEUS nostras similiter prodet, 1. Cor. XIII, 7. Jac. V, 20. Non autem haec κάλυ- ψις tollit vel correptionem, quae officii causa fit, per- sonarum publicarum, vel etiam quae proximo debe- tur ob necessariam emendationem, Matth. XIIX, 25. Peccata proximi, inquit Anselmus l. de beatit. nunquam detegenda sunt, nisi ob utilitatem peccan- tium, vel aliorum. Distinguendum etiam inter de- licta publica & privata, notoria & occulta, vel secre- ta. Nam ut Augustinus in explic. loci Matth. XIIX, 5. monet, ipsa charitas postulat, ut secreto corrigan- tur, quae peccantur secretius. Ubi contingit malum, ibi moriatur etiam. Nam si solus nosti, & vis coram omnibus corrigere, non es corrector, sed proditor.

Neque etiam illa κάλυψις facit ad tectionem pecca- torum propriorum, uti contendit Cornelius à La- pide, Charitas, inquiens, operit universa delicta, propria & aliena: propria ideo, quia oritur ex cha- ritate Dei, quae omnia peccata abolet, hominemque sanctificat: Sed charitas, qua Deus nos diligit, no- stra quidem peccata tegit, quia ex mera gratia re- mittuntur nobis peccata, non autem illa, qua nos Deum diligimus: De charitate erga proximum, peccata ejus operiente hic sermonem esse, locus Sa- lomoneus Prov. X, 12. docet, interprete Lyrano, id volens: Sicut odium per iram manifestat defe- ctus aliorum: Sic charitas celat, nisi quantum cor- rectio fraterna requirit. Charitatem significari fra- ternam, inquit Estius, id est, eam, qua proximus di- ligitur, ex parte praecedenti constat, nec minus ex an- tithesi, quam facit Sapiens inter odium & charita- tem. Non enim odium ad homines, charitatem ad Deum refert, sed ad homines utrumque. Ostendit eadem Sapientis sententia, sermonem esse de delictis proximorum, non autem ejus, cujus charitas com- mendatur. Nam quod Sapiens dicit, tale est: Sicut odium suscitat rixas & dissidia cum aliis, quos odio quis habet: Ita charitas è diverso non solum rixas & dissidia non serit aut suscitat, sed etiam suscitata componit ac sedat, & delicta atque offensiones, quae rixarum causa esse solent, tolerando ac dissimulan- do atque excusando operit, denique, quicquid in se peccatum est, condonat, & ut Deus condonet, inter- cedit & impetrat. De charitate etiam, ut reficit alios & aliorum facile peccata condonat, interpreta- tur Lorinus, quia proxime ante Petrus de charitate mutua egerat, ac subito rationem reddit, quia cha- ritas operit multitudinem peccatorum, adducens in eam sententiam Chrysostomum homil. IV. in Act. Apost. Concilium Ilerdense c. 7. Augustinum l. 1. de bapt. c. 17. Ambrosium in Psal. CXIIX. Pulchre B. Lutherus in h. l. Peccata coram Deo tegit meritum Christi fide apprehensum, sed peccata proximi tegit charitas. Sicut Deus sua charitate tegit nostra pec- cata: Sic nostra charitate tegere debemus proximi peccata.

## 4:8
Vers. 8. Πρὸ πάντων δὲ.] The same locution as in James V, 12. Τὴν εἰς ἑαυτοὺς ἀγάπην ἐκτενῆ ἔχοντες.] Supply ἐσὲ, and εἰς ἑαυτοὺς for εἰς ἀλλήλους, as Col. III, 16. 1 Thess. V, 13. Ἐκτενῆ.] As above ἐκτενῶς 1, 22.

As for prayer and piety toward God, both the vigilance of the mind and the sobriety of the body are required; so the foundation of the duties which we owe to our neighbor is charity, which covers the errors of brothers, and is the producer and nurse of mutual duties. Πρὸ πάντων, he says, because charity is the most excellent virtue, 1 Cor. XII, 21, ch. XIII, 2, seqq. But the Apostle did not here intend a comparison of charity toward one's neighbor with piety toward God, as if the former were to be preferred to the latter, but he turns himself to those things from which charity stands out entirely, q. d. furthermore, or what remains. For that is to be understood, above all have charity one toward another. For that is the bond of perfection among us mutually for guarding the unity of the mystical body, Col. III, 14. And charity is the greatest virtue, not absolutely, but in συγκρίσει to the ministering gifts, 1 Cor. XII, v. ult. Augustine, enchir. ch. 121. The study of charity, he says, ought to be commended above all, for to it all Divine precepts are referred. Furthermore, that εἰς ἑαυτοὺς is poorly rendered in the Vulgate as 'in vobismetipsis' (in yourselves): and therefore the exposition of some is vain, 'in the heart, not in outward signs,' since mutual charity is denoted, as the Syrian, Augustine, book de grat. & lib. arb. c. 7, Erasmus, and others have it. Others render the word ἐκτενῆ extensively with Oecumenius as 'long,' 'prolonged,' 'persevering': others intensively, 'vehement' with Erasmus, 'Brünstig' with B. Luther, which is more suitable. See Luke XXII, 44. 1 Pet. I, 22. Charity is compared to fire, Cant. VIII, 6. Our charity, says B. Luther in Exod. XXVI, ought to be twice-dyed scarlet, which can tolerate hatreds and detractions. We are kinsmen, says S. Bernard, by the blood of Christ. See therefore how greatly we ought to love one another, viz. as blood and kinsmen both of ours and of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 8. Πρὸ πάντων δὲ.] Eadem loquutio, quae Jacobi V, 12. Τὴν εἰς ἑαυτοὺς ἀγάπην ἐκτενῆ ἔχοντες.] Supple ἐσὲ, & εἰς ἑ- αυτὸς pro εἰς ἀλλήλες, ut Col. III, 16. 1. Thess. V, 13. Ἐκτενῆ.] Ut supra ἐκτενῶς 1, 22.

Ut ad orationem & pietatem erga Deum requiri- tur tum mentis vigilantia, tum corporis sobrietas; ita officiorum, quae proximo debemus, fundamen- tum est charitas, quae errata fratrum tegit, & est ef- fectrix, atque nutrix mutuorum officiorum. Πρὸ pávtων, inquit, quia charitas est virtus excellentis- sima, 1. Cor. XII, 21. cap. XIII, 2. seqq. Non autem hic respexit Apostolus comparationem charitatis proximi cum pietate erga Deum, quasi huic illa praferenda sit, sed convertit sese ad ea, è quibus eminet omnino charitas, q. d. de cœtero, vel quod su- pereft. Id enim subintelligendum, ante omnia cha- ritatem habete alii ad alios. Illa enim vinculum per- fectionis inter nos mutuo ad unitatem corporis my- stici custodiendam Col. III, 14. Et maxima virtus est charitas, non absolute, sed in συγκρίσει ad dona mi- nistrantia, 1. Cor. XII. v. ult. Augustinus enchir. cap. 121. Charitatis, inquit, studium ante omnia debet esse commendatum, ad eam enim omnia praecepta Divina referuntur. Caeterum illud εἰς ἑαυτὸς male in Vul- gata redditur in vobismetipsis: Ideoq; vana est non- nullorum expositio in corde, non in signis exterio- ribus, quum mutua charitas denotetur, ut Syrus, Augustinus l. de grat. & lib. arb. c. 7. Erasmus, & alii habent. Vocem ἐκτενῆ extensive alii reddunt cum Oecumenio in longum, prorsusum, perseverantem: alii intensive, vehementem cum Erasmo, Brünstig cum B. Luthero, quod convenientius. Vid. Luc. XXII, 44. 1. Petr. I, 22. Charitas confertur igni Cant: IIX, 6. Charitas nostra, inquit B. Lutherus in Exod. XXVI. debet esse coccus bis tincta, quae possit tolerare odia & detrectationes. Consanguinei, inquit S. Bernh. sumus sanguine Christi. Vide ergo, quan- topere diligere nos invicem debeamus, scil. ut sangui- nem & consanguineos tam nostros, quam Christi.

## 4:9
Φιλόξενοι εἰς ἀλλήλους.] Ready to receive pilgrim brothers with hospitality. See 2. Tim. III, 2. Tit. I, 8. Rom. XII, 13. Heb. XIII, 2.

Because among the works of charity hospitality is most to be celebrated at the final judgment, Matt. XXV, 35, therefore the Apostle commemorates it here particularly, after he had designated the day of judgment, especially because the Pontics are believed to have been inhospitable, as witnessed by Arnobius book VIII against the Gentiles. The discourse, however, is about hospitality toward needy pilgrims, exiles for the sake of religion. For there were many exiles then because of the persecutions of Christians. And hospitality contains within itself all mutual offices of mercy and charity. Compare Rom. XII, 13 and 3. John v. 5. Ambrose says: Let us beware, lest if we are hard and negligent in receiving guests, the hospitality of the saints be denied to us also after the course of this life.

XXIII. in the Gospel. Receive Christ at your tables, so that you may be able to be received by Him to eternal banquets: provide hospitality to the pilgrim Christ now, so that He may not desert you in judgment as if you were pilgrims, but may receive you as His own into the kingdom.

Ἄνευ γογγυσμῶν.] Content with your lot. See Phil. II, 14. This should not be referred, with Hugo, to those who are received with hospitality, so that they may be content with what is set before them, but it pertains to those who provide hospitality, that they may do it without murmuring, whether silent or expressed, with idle reproach of benefits, and therefore with a joyful and cheerful mind, Phil. II, 14. 2. Cor. IX, 7. Rom. XII, 8. Charity is not dispensed from a purse, says Augustine in his first discourse on Psalm CV, but chiefly from the heart and will, in which it has its seat; if the purse does not have what to give, the heart and will have it.

Latin:

Φιλόξενοι εἰς ἀλλήλους.] Prompti ad hospitio excipiendos fratres peregrinos. Vide 2. Tim. III, 2. Tit. I, 8. Rom. XII, 13. Ebr. XIII, 2.

Quia inter opera charitatis maxime hospitalitas in extremo judicio celebranda, Matth. XXV, 35. ideo eam hic peculiariter commemorat, postquam judicii diem designarat Apostolus, imprimis quia Pontici creduntur inhospitales fuisse, teste Arno- bio l. IIX. c. gent. Sermo autem est de hospitalitate erga peregrinos egenos, religionis causa exules. Erant enim tum ob persecutiones Christianorum multi exules. Et continet hospitalitas in se omnia mutua misericordiae & charitatis officia. Conf. Rom. XII, 13. & 3. Joh. v. 5. Ambrosius: Caveamus, inquit, ne si nos duri & negligentes fuerimus in recipiendis hospitibus, etiam nobis post hujus vitae cursum sancto- rum hospitia denegetur.

XXIII. in Evang. Ad mensas vestras Christum susci- pite, ut vos ab eo suscipi ad eterna convivia valeatis: præbete modo peregrino Christo hospitium, ut vos in judicio non quasi peregrinos deserat, sed ut proprios recipiat ad regnum.

Ἄνευ γογγυσμῶν.] Contenti vestra sorte. Vide Phil. II, 14. Non cum Hugone id ad eos referri debet, qui hospitio excipiuntur, ut sint appositis contenti, sed ad eos pertinet, qui hospitio excipiunt, ut faciant id sine murmure, sive tacito, sive expresso, cum otiosa beneficiorum exprobratione, adeoq; læto & hila- ri animo, Phil. II, 14. 2. Cor. IX, 7. Rom. XII, 8. Cha- ritas non de sacculo erogatur ait Augustinus conc. I. in Psal. CV. sed ex corde præcipue & voluntate, in qua sedem habet; si non saccus habet, quod donet, habet cor & voluntas.

## 4:10
Vers. 10. Ἕκαστος καθὼς ἔλαβε χάρισμα.] Under the name of grace accepted generally, he understands here not only the gifts of the Spirit, but also those of the body and of faculties, as the following words declare. This passage is to be compared with that which is in Rom. XII, 6, 7.

Εἰς ἑαυτὺς αὐτὸ διακονῦντες.] Again εἰς ἑαυτὺς for εἰς ἀλλήλους: And διακονεῖν here is general, soon it is taken specially. See above I, 12.

As good stewards of the manifold grace of God. What a steward is, see 1 Cor. IV, 1, 2; Tit. I, 7. Manifold grace, just as manifold powers, Heb. II, 4.

Most interpreters understand this concerning the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Some, however, include under 'charismata' also the various functions, from 1 Cor. XII, 4 ff., just as mention is subsequently made of manifold grace, and of the Teachers of the Word and Deacons, v. 10 and 11, and 'stewards' also especially look to this, 'of the mysteries of God' 1 Cor. IV, 1. To the duties of charity belong both the ministering gifts and the ministries entrusted to us, that we may expend them for the use of our neighbor, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. The Apostle warns that those things are received from God, and are not properly ours except as stewards, by right of ownership they belong to God, and for that purpose they were committed to us by God, so that each one may serve the other with them, and therefore not all things were given to one, but some to others, so that individuals may assist others, and that that variety of gifts and offices may be a bond for maintaining concord among men, and that all may direct and turn their charismata to the glory of God with a unanimous mind. Humbly, says Gregory the Great, hom. VI in Ezech., expend the good to your neighbors, because you know that what you have is not from yourselves, and l. XXIX moral. c. 6: Then the manifold grace of God is well dispensed, when the received gift is believed to be also his who does not have it, when it is thought to be given to oneself for the sake of him to whom it is expended. The word ποικίλης has greater emphasis than the Latin 'multiformis' in the Vulgate. Jerome, epist. L. to Pammach., rendered it: 'multiplicis'; l. I. contr. Jovin. c. 4. 'variæ' (various).

Latin:

Vers. 10. Ἕκαστος καθὼς ἔλαβε χάρισμα.] Sub nomine gratiæ generaliter acceptæ hic intelligit non tantum dona Spiritus, sed & corporis & facultatum, ut sequentia declarant. Conferendus hic locus cum eo, qui est Rom. XII, 6. 7.

Εἰς ἑαυτὺς αὐτὸ διακονῦντες.] Rursus εἰς ἑαυτὺς pro εἰς ἀλλήλυς: Et διακονεῖν hic generale est, mox specialiter sumi- tur. Vide supra I, 12.

Ὡς καλοὶ ὀικονόμοι ποικίλης χάριτος Θεῦ.] Quid sit ὀικονό- μος, vide 1. Cor. IV, 1. 2. Tit. I, 7. Ποικίλης χάριτος sicut ποι- κίλαις δυνάμεσιν, Ebr. II, 4.

De donis Spiritus sancti plerique interpretes ac- cipiunt. Sub charismati tamen comprehendunt nonnulli etiam diversas functiones, è 1. Cor. XII, 4. seqq. quemadmodum multiformis gratiæ, ac Docto- rum Verbi & Diaconorum deinceps peculiaris et- iam facta mentio v. 10. & 11. & ὀικονόμοι huc etiam imprimis spectant τῶν μυστηρίων τῦ Θεῦ 1. Cor. IV, 1. Ad charitatis officia faciunt tum dona ministrantia, tum ministeria nobis credita in usum proximi im- pendamus, sicut boni dispensatores multiformis gratiæ Dei. A Deo illa accepta, non nostra esse proprie nisi ut dispensatorum jure dominii ad De- um pertinere, eoque fine nobis à Deo commissa esse monet Apostolus, ut unusquisque alteri iisdem inserviat, atque ideo non uni omnia, sed alia aliis data, ut singuli aliis subveniant, utque varietas illa donorum & munerum vinculum sit retinendæ in- ter homines concordiæ, omnesque sua charismata ad Dei gloriam unanimi mente dirigant ac con- vertant. Humiliter, inquit Gregorius M. hom. VI. in Ezech. impendite bonum proximis, quia scitis vo- bis non à vobis esse quod habetis & l. XXIX. moral. c. 6. Tunc bene multiformis Dei gratia dispensatur, quando acceptum donum & ejus, qui hoc non habet, creditur, quando propter eum, cui impenditur, sibi datum putatur. Vox ποικίλης majorem emphasin habet, quam Latina in Vulgata multiformis. Hiero- nymus epist. L. ad Pammach. reddidit: multiplicis l. I. contr. Jovin. c. 4. variæ.

## 4:11
Vers. 11. If any man speak, as the oracles of God. Supply 'let him speak', he who teaches the people, 'he who labors in the word', as it is said 1 Tim. V, 17, let him teach the Gospel not as a human word, but as the word of God. You have 'oracles of God' in Acts VII, 38; Rom. III, 2; Heb. V, 12; Num. XXIV, 4; in the Psalms often enough.

The particle 'as' in the Hebrew is not of similarity here, but of truth, as in John I, 14. If anyone has received, says Estius, from God the grace of elocution or speech, (to which must be referred those things which Paul enumerates in Rom. 12 and 1 Cor. 12: the word of wisdom and knowledge, the gift of prophecy, of teaching, of exhortation, of interpretation, etc.) and someone is called to such an office in the Church, let him speak, (for that must be supplied, just as the Syriac paraphrase supplies it) as the oracles of God, of whom he is a minister and vicar in that function; let him bring forth nothing that is not consistent with the Word of God, whether written or handed down. Let him not teach the inventions of men, let him not report false miracles, let him not treat of useless questions, but let him announce the will of God from the Divine oracles.

therefore it is not about the form and manner, but about the matter of the preaching. Only the Word of God can instruct us concerning the will of God regarding those things which make for our salvation, 1 Tim. III, 15, 16. Only the Word of God is living and effective, Heb. IV, 12, and the power unto salvation, Rom. I, 16. Concerning the sayings of the Gentiles and profane histories, we have no such promise, as the blessed Gerhard gravely warned here; in the house of God, which is the Church, 1 Tim. III, 15, let nothing else sound forth but the Word of God: The prophet who has a dream, let him tell the dream, and he who has my word, let him speak my word truly: What is the chaff to the wheat, says the Lord, Jer. XXIII, 28.

If any man ministers.] Here that word is taken specifically to designate the care for the poor, as in Acts VI, 2. Not only those things which pertain to the care of the poor, but all other offices in the Church distinct from the Doctor's office are designated: Which the parallel passages Rom. XII, 6, 7, 1 Cor. XII, 28 teach.

As of the strength which God supplies.] According to the strength of the body. For young men used to be chosen for ministries, who could easily run here and there. Not only the strength of the body, but primarily of the mind is regarded, so that one may not act remissly and languidly, but according to the strength which God supplies, faithfully and sincerely, 1 Cor. IV, 2, and thus may not trust in his own prudence, but in Divine grace and assistance, and humbly seek strength from God. The more humbly, says Bede, let each one expend for his neighbor every good that he can, the more certainly he knows that he cannot have from himself what he expends.

That in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.] i.e., that all who see your acts may praise God, because through Jesus Christ He has produced such mighty works in men. The Syrian adds: That in all things which you are doing, from 1 Cor. X, 31. Cf. Matt. V, 16. It is added 'through Jesus Christ,' because not only are those gifts distributed through Him as the head of the Church, Eph. I, 22, ch. IV, 8, but because they are also acquired by His merit and are expended for the glory of God and the public salvation, Apoc. I, 6, nor are our actions or doxologies otherwise pleasing to GOD than in the name of Jesus Christ and through Christ, Col. III, 17. Just as all benefits descend to us from God through Christ, so in turn, by humble thanksgiving through Christ, all things ought to be referred to the glory of God. The blessed Bernard, sermon against ingratitude: Happy is he who, for every gift of grace, returns to Him in whom is the fullness of all graces.

To whom is the glory and the power for ever and ever. Amen.] A similar acclamation pertaining to Christ is 2 Tim. IV, 18. Glory and power are wont to be joined, as below V, 11, Apoc. I, 6, V, 13, and jointly 'the power of the glory,' Col. I, 11. Thus 'honor and power,' 1 Tim. VI, 16. 'Power and authority,' Jude v. 25. 'To whom is the glory,' that is, to whom alone all glory is owed, and to whom strength and power is or belongs. It is not a wish but rather an assertion, therefore it is said not 'let it be' but rather 'it is,' nor is the particle 'amen' in this place so much of one wishing as of one confirming, as Matt. V, 26, 2 Cor. I, 20. And it is the same as 'truly,' cf. Luke XXI, 3, Mark XII, 43, Jer. XXIX, 6. But the pronoun is rightly referred to Christ, as the immediate antecedent, and by the force of the parallels, Apoc. I, verse 6, ch. V, 12.

PART III. Information concerning the craftiness of persecutions.

Latin:

Vers. 11. Εἴ τις λαλεῖ, ὡς λόγια Θεῦ.] Supple λαλείτω, qui populum docet, ὁ κοπιῶν ἐν τῷ λόγῳ, ut dicitur 1. Tim. V, 17. do- ceat Evangelium non ut verbum humanum, sed ut verbum Dei. Λόγια Θεῦ habes Actor. VII, 38. Rom. III, 2. Ebr. V, 12. Num. XXIV, 4. in Psalmis satis sæpe.

Particula ὡς ut Ebr. non similitudinis hic est, sed veritatis, ut Joh. I, 14. Si quis accepit, inquit Estius, à Deo gratiam elocutionis sive sermonis, (quo referen- da sunt, quæ Paulus numerat Rom. 12. & 1. Cor. 12. sermo sapientiæ & scientiæ, donum prophetiæ, doctrinæ, exhortationis, interpretationis &c.) & ad hujusmodi munus aliquis in Ecclesia vocatur, is loquatur, (id enim supplendum, quemadmodum supplet Syra para- phrasis) tanquam Dei sermones, cujus in ea functio- ne minister est & vicarius, nihil proferat, quod Verbo Dei vel scripto vel tradito non sit consentaneum. Non hominum commenta doceat, non falsa miracula re- ferat, non inutiles tractet quæstiones, sed Dei vo- luntatem ex eloquiis Divinis annunciet.

ergo de forma & modo, sed de materia prædicatio- nis agitur. Solum Dei Verbum de voluntate Dei nos instruere potest de iis, quæ ad salutem nostram fa- ciunt, 1. Tim. III, 15. 16. Solum Dei Verbum vi- vum est & efficax, Ebr. IV, 12. & potentia ad salu- tem, Rom. I, 16. De gentilium dictis & profanis historiis non habemus ejusmodi promissionem, quod hic graviter monuit B. Gerhardus; in domo Dei, quæ est Ecclesia, 1. Tim. III, 15. nihil aliud sonet quam Verbum Dei: Propheta qui habet somnium,narret somnium, & qui habet sermonem meum, loquatur sermonem meum vere: Quid paleis ad triticum, di- cit Dominus Jerem. XXIII, 28.

Εἴ τις διακονεῖ.] Hic vox illa specialiter sumitur ad desi- gnandam curam circa pauperes, ut Act. VI, 2. Non tantum ea, quæ ad curam pauperum spe- ctant, sed alia omnia officia in Ecclesia à Doctorali munere distincta designantur: Quod loca parallela Rom. XII, 6. 7. 1. Cor. XII, 28. docent.

῾Ως ἐξ ἰσχύος, ἧς χορηγεῖ ὁ Θεός.] Pro corporis viribus. Nam juvenes ad διακονίας eligi solebant, qui huc illuc facile discursarent. Non vires tantum corporis, sed imprimis animi respiciuntur, ne remisse ac languide quis agat, sed pro viribus, quas Deus suppeditat fideliter ac sin- cere, 1. Cor. IV, 2. adeoque nec suæ prudentiæ, sed Divinæ gratiæ & assistentiæ confidat, & vires à Deo humiliter expetat. Tanto humilius, inquit Beda, impendat quisque proximo omne bonum, quod pot- est, quanto certissime novit, quod à semetipso non potest habere, quod impendat.

Ἵνα ἐν πᾶσι δοξάζηται ὁ Θεὸς διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.] i.e.ut omnes, qui vestros actus vident, Deum laudent, quod per JesumChri- stum virtutes tales in hominibus produxerit. Syrus addit: Ut in omnibus quæ facientes estis vos, è 1. Cor. X, 31. Conf. Matth. V, 16. Additur per Je- sum Christum, quod non tantum illa χαρίσματα per ipsum ceu caput Ecclesiæ distribuantur Eph. I, 22. c. IV, 8. Sed quod etiam ejus merito acquisita sint & impendantur gloriæ Dei & saluti publicæ, Apocal. I, 6. neque aliter gratæ sint DEO nostræ actiones vel δοξολογίαι,quam in nomine JesuChri- sti & per Christum, Col. III, 17. Sicut à Deo per Christum omnia beneficia ad nos descendunt, ita vicissim humili gratiarum actione per Christum omnia ad Dei gloriam referri debent. B. Bernhar- dus serm. contra ingratitud. Felix est, qui ad singu- la gratiæ dona redit ad eum, in quo est plenitudo omnium gratiarum.

Ὧι ἐστιν ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.] Simi- lis acclamatio ad Christum pertinens est 2.Tim. IV, 18. Δόξα & κράτος conjungi solent, ut infra V, 11. Apoc. I, 6. V, 13. & junctim κράτος τῆς δόξης Coloss. I, 11 Sic τιμὴ καὶ κράτος, 1. Tim. VI, 16. Κράτος καὶ ἐξουσία Judæ v. 25. Cui est gloria, id est, cui soli debetur omnis glo- ria, & cui est vel competit robur & potestas. Non votum sed asseveratio potius est, ideo non ἔστω sed ἐστὶ potius dicitur, nec particula ἀμὴν tam optantis hoc loco est, quam confirmantis, ut Matth. V, 26. 2. Cor. I, 20. Estque idem, quod ἀληθῶς, conf. Luc. XXI, 3. Marc. XII, 43. Jer. XXIX, 6. Recte au- tem Pronomen ad Christum refertur, ceu imme- diate antecedens, & vi parallelorum, Apocal. I. vers. 6. cap. V, 12.

PARS III. De astu persecutionum informatio.

## 4:12
Vers. 12. Beloved, do not be surprised.] Do not wonder, do not be stupefied, as above 4. Cyprian translates: Do not wonder. He prefaces the most sweet address 'beloved,' concerning which Oecumenius says: By that very name, he says, he signifies that afflictions happen to them, not because they are held in hatred, but because they are very dear (to GOD) and are vehemently loved. He does not indeed say 'beloved' with respect to God, but to himself, and because the Holy Spirit spoke through the Apostle, Oecumenius judged that He deemed them worthy of this name. Cf. Prov. III, 12, Heb. XII, 6, Apoc. III, 19. The sweetness of Divine love tempers the bitterness of the cross. An exhortation to patience was most necessary at that time on account of grave persecutions, therefore he is occupied with it again and again, so that he may strengthen Christians in patience and console them in afflictions. 'Do not be surprised' is do not wonder and do not esteem it a strange thing. Vain therefore are the expositions of Bede and Hugo: Do not esteem yourselves strangers from God and Christ, as if cast off by Him, as also Lyranus: Do not, on account of afflictions, become pilgrims, that is, alienate yourselves from the faith and love of God, or flee to foreign shores. For the Greeks, says Estius, are said to be 'surprised' who are disturbed with wonder on account of some new, insolent, or strange thing. But what wonder is it, says Salvianus, lib. III de providentia: If we endure all evils, we who serve as soldiers to tolerate all things?

By the burning among you which is happening to you for a trial.] 'By' for 'upon.' He calls adverse things a 'burning' because of the similar effect. For just as metals are tested by flame, so men are tested by adversities: which testing is called here and elsewhere 'trial.' Thus 'He burned them for a testing,' Judith VIII, 21. Concerning metals you have Prov. XXVII, 21, 'the fining pot for silver and the furnace for gold.' And hence, as I said, the similarity Ps. LXVI, 9, 'You have burned us, as silver is burned,' and the same is Zach. XIII, 9, and Jer. IX, 7, 'behold I will burn them and try them.' Similar sense. Dan. XI, 35, take here 'trial,' as James I, 2.

Burning, to some, is proof and exploration by fire. The Syrian rendered it 'temptations,' Oecumenius 'proofs by fire.' But the Greek word properly denotes a burning, that is, a grave affliction. The Vulgate interprets it as 'fervor,' Cyprian, lib. IV, epist. 6, as 'ardor.' Cf. Eccles. XXVII, 6, Wisd. III, 3. Ephrem Syrus, in a sermon on patience, observes that just as a potter or goldsmith adjusts the furnace to the earthen vessel or the gold which he is cooking, so that he does not burn it too much or too little: So also God adapts the temptation to the strength of the man and the grace which He gives him, nor does He suffer a man to be tempted above his strength, 1 Cor. X, 13. He adds therefore that a 'burning' happens for a 'trial,' so that He may mitigate the pain of the burning, because it happens not for destruction, but only for temptation. Which temptation, however, does not regard God as tempting, who knows intimately what is in man, but the men who are tempted, so that they may learn to know themselves.

Ὡς ξένου ὑμῖν συμβαίνοντος.] As if a strange thing were happening to you. It ought not to seem new, strange, and unusual to the faithful of Christ, that which was decreed from eternity, Rom. VIII, verse 29; that which was so often predicted in the Scriptures, Matth. X, verse 17, Luc. XXI, verse 12, Johann. XV, verse 20, chap. XVI, verse 32, Actor. XIV, verse 22, 2. Tim. III, verse 11; that which was prefigured in Christ the head, Matth. XVI, verse 2, Luc. IX, verse 23, Joh. XV, verse 20; that which has been customary for all the pious ever since the beginning of the world, 2. Tim. III, 11, 2. Corinth. I, verse 8, Matth. XXIII, verse 34, etc.; that which is necessary for the mortification of the old man for all who are to be saved, 2. Cor. IV, 10, as Blessed Gerhard p. 693.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Ἀγαπητοὶ μὴ ξενίζεσθε.] Ne admiremini, ne ob- stupefcite, ut supra 4. Cyprianus vertit: Nolite mirari. Præmittit compellationem suavissimam ἀγα- πητοὶ, de qua Oecumenius: Eo ipso nomine, inquit, significat, non quia odio habeantur, sed quia val- de chari sint (DEO) vehementerque amentur, afflictiones ipsis contingere. Non quidem dicit ἀγαπητοὺς respectu Dei, sed sui, & quia Spiritus sanctus per Apostolum loquutus est, eosdem ipsum hoc nomine dignari Oecumenius censuit. Conf. Prov. III, 12. Ebr. XII, 6. Apocal. III, 19. Amaritiam crucis temperat suavitas Divinæ dile- ctionis. Maxime necessaria erat isto tempore ob graves persecutiones ad patientiam exhortatio, ideo iterum iterumq; in eo occupatur, ut confor- tet Christianos in patientia & consoletur in affli- ctionibus. Μὴ ξενίζεσθε est nolite admirari & rem peregrinam æstimare. Vanæ ergo sunt expositio- nes Bedæ & Hugonis: Nolite vos peregrinos æstima- re à Deo & Christo, quasi ab eo projectos, ut & Ly- rani: Nolite ob afflictiones peregrinari, id est, alienare vos à fide & amore Dei, aut fugere in alie- nas oras. Græci enim, inquit Estius, ξενίζεσθαι di- cuntur, qui ob rem aliquam novam, insolentem aut pe- regrinam cum admiratione turbantur. Quid au- tem mirum est, inquit Salvianus lib. III. de provi- dentia: Si mala cuncta perferimus, qui ad toleranda universa militamus?

Τῇ ἐν ὑμῖν πυρώσει πρὸς πειρασμὸν ὑμῖν γινομένῃ.] Τῇ pro ἐπὶ τῇ. Vocat πύρωσιν res adversas ob similem effectum. Nam sicut metalla per flammam, ita homines per adversa ex- plorantur: quæ exploratio hic & alibi dicitur πειρασμός. Sic ἐκείνους ἐπύρωσεν εἰς ἐτασμόν. Judith VIII, 21. De metallis ha- bes Prov. XXVII, 21. δοκίμιον ἀργυρίῳ καὶ χρυσῷ πύρωσις. Et hinc, ut dixi, similitudo Psal. LXVI, 9. Ἐπύρωσας ἡμᾶς, ὡς πυροῦται τὸ ἀργύριον, idemque est Zach. XIII, 9. & Jerem. IX, 7. ἰδὲ ἐγὼ πυρώσω ἀυτούς καὶ δοκιμῶ ἀυτούς. Par sensus. Dan. XI, 35. sume hic πειρασμόν, ut Jac. I, 2.

Πύρωσις quibusdam est probatio & exploratio per ignem. Syrus tentationes, Oecumenius pro- bationes per ignem reddidit. Sed vox Græca proprie ustionem, id est, gravem afflictionem notat. Vulgata fervorem, Cyprianus l. IV. epist. 6. ardo- rem interpretatur. Conf. Eccles. XXVII, 6. Sap. III, 3. Ephrem Syrus serm. de patient. observat, quod sicut figulus vel aurifaber fornacem attempe- rat fictili vasi, vel auro, quod coquit ne illud nimis urat, vel nimis parum: Ita & Deus tentationem ac- commodat viribus hominis & gratiæ, quam ei dat, nec patitur hominem supra vires tentari, 1. Cor. X, 13. Addit ergo ad πειρασμὸν fieri πύρωσιν, ut ustionis dolorem mitiget, quod non ad exitium, sed solum ad tentationem contingat. Quæ vero tentatio non Deum tentantem respicit, qui intime novit, quod in homine sit, sed homines tentatos, ut se- ipsos nosse discant.

Ὡς ξένου ὑμῖν συμβαίνοντος.] Tanquam res inopinata vobis eveniret. Christi fidelibus non debet videri novum peregri- num ac insolitum, quod ab æterno decretum Rom. VIII. vers. 29. quod in Scripturis toties prædictum, Matth. X. vers. 17. Luc. XXI. vers. 12. Johann. XV. vers. 20. cap. XVI, vers. 32. Actor. XIV; vers. 22. 2. Tim. III. vers. 11. quod in Christo capite præfigu- ratum, Matth. XVI. vers. 2. Luc. IX. vers. 23. Joh. XV. vers. 20. quod jam inde à mundi origine omni- bus piis usitatum 2. Tim. III, 11. 2. Corinth. I. vers. 8. Matth. XXIII. vers. 34. &c. quod ad mortificatio- nem veteris hominis omnibus salvandis necessarium, 2. Cor. IV, 10. ut B. Gerhardus p. 693.

## 4:13
Vers. 13.

Ἀλλὰ καθὸ κοινωνεῖτε τοῖς τοῦ χριστοῦ παθήμασι χαίρετε.] Καθὸ here is the same as καθ' ὅτι, Luc. I, 7, XIX, 9. To share in the sufferings of Christ, as it is here, is to be a partaker of the sufferings of Christ, as 2. Cor. I, 7, to suffer with Christ, Rom. 8, 17, is to suffer to bear witness to the doctrine of Christ, for which cause Christ also suffered. For this reason he wishes them to rejoice. Thus James, dealing with afflictions: Count it all joy, and Heb. X, 34, you accepted the plundering of your goods with joy. Add Act. V, 41. This is a great comfort: that the affliction of the pious is a communion with Christ: whence he is also said to bear the cross of Christ, Matt. XI, 28. To carry about the mortification of Jesus, 2 Cor. IV, 10, to bear the marks of Jesus, Gal. VI, 17, and his reproach, Heb. 13, 13. By martyrdom, says Cyprian on the praise of martyrdom, you are adorned as if with the blood of your companion Christ. And reciprocally, Christ is also said to suffer in his members because of this κοινωνίαν [communion], Acts IX, 4. Do not, says Oecumenius in his paraphrase of this passage, consider this strange for the friends of God, since it is proper and glorious for them that, like gold, they are tested, purified, and brightened by the fire of tribulation, and that they are conformed to the suffering Christ, so that they may be conformed to the same as he rises again. We commune, however, in the passions of Christ not because of a practical satisfaction, as the Council of Trent intended in Sess. XIV, c. 14, but only regarding the affliction, even though the end of the passions of Christ and our own is very different, and those are of infinite value because of the infinity of his person.

That you may rejoice and be glad also in the revelation of his glory] They also rejoice who anticipate great joys with a certain hope. Christ indeed already has glory, but it does not appear to all, as it will appear on the supreme day; which is here the revelation of the glory of Christ, and the revelation of the Lord above I, 7, 13, 2 Thess. I, 7. See also Luke XVII, 30.

From the argument of the example of Christ and communion with Christ, he adds another from the salutary outcome of afflictions, whence they ought not only not to be saddened or stunned, but even to rejoice because of the afflictions. Rejoice in mind, exulting in body: because the saints will have joy internally and externally, corporal and spiritual, says Blessed Huss. The passion is corporal, the joy is spiritual, which begins on the cross and lasts for eternity, says Blessed Luther. Ἀγαλλιώμενοι [rejoicing] are those leaping for joy: which will happen in the revelation of his glory, on the day of the final judgment, 1 Pet. I, 7, where before all the Elect, indeed before all men, he will publicly manifest his glory, Matt. XVI, 27, ch. XXIV, 30, ch. XXV, 31. For then those who were here partners in the passions will also be partners in the glory, Rom. VIII, 17, 2 Tim. II, 11, Luke XXII, 28.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Ἀλλὰ καθὸ κοινωνεῖτε τοῖς τοῦ χριστοῦ παθήμασι χαίρετε.] Καθὸ hic idem quod καθ' ὅτι, Luc. I, 7. XIX, 9. Κοινωνεῖν πα- θήμασι χριστοῦ, ut hic est κοινωνὸν εἶναι τῶν τοῦ χριστοῦ παθημάτων, ut 2. Cor. I, 7. συμπάσχειν Χριστῷ Rom. 8, 17. est pati ad testimo- nium reddendum doctrinæ Christi, qua de causa & Christus passus est. Ob id gauderi vult. Sic Jacobus de afflictionibus agens: Πᾶσαν χαρὰν ἡγήσασθε, & Ebr. X, 34. τὴν ἁρπαγὴν ὑπαρχόντων μετὰ χαρᾶς προσεδέξασθε. Adde Act. V, 41. Magnum hoc solatium: Piorum afflictionem esse cum Christo communicationem: unde etiam Christi crucem dicitur ferre, Matth. XI, 28. Mortificatio- nem Jesu circumferre, 2. Cor. IV, 10, stigmata Jesu portare, Gal. VI, 17. & improperium ejus, Ebr. 13, 13. Martyrio, inquit Cyprianus de laude martyrii velut socio Christi cruore decoraris. Et reciproce Christus etiam in membris suis pati dicitur propter hanc κοινωνίαν, Act. IX, 4. Nolite, inquit Oecume- nius in paraphrasi hujus loci, hoc ab amicis DEI extraneum ducere, cum hoc eis proprium & glo- riosum sit, quod ut aurum igne tribulationis pro- bentur, purgentur & illustrentur, quodque Chri- sto patienti conformentur, ut eidem resurgenti configurentur. Communicamus autem passioni- bus Christi non quod satisfactionem practicam, ut Conc. Trid. voluit Sess. XIV. c. 14. sed quoad afflictionem tantum, etsi finis passionum Christi & nostrarum diversissimus sit, illae etiam ob personae infinitatem valoris sint infiniti.

Ἵνα καὶ ἐν τῇ ἀποκαλύψει τῆς δόξης αὐτῶ χαρῆτε ἀγαλλιώ μενοι] Gaudent & qui magna gaudia spe certa praesumunt. Christus jam quidem gloriam habet, sed ea non omnibus ap- paret, sicut apparebit supremo die; Quae hic ἀποκάλυψις δό- ξης Christi, & ἀποκάλυψις Κυρίε supra I, 7. 13. 2.Thessal. I, 7. Vide & Luc. XVII, 30.

Argumento ab exemplo Christi & communica- tione cum Christo addit aliud à salutari afflictionum eventu, unde non solum non contristari aut obstu- pescere, sed etiam gaudere debeant propter affli- ctiones. Gaudeatis mente, exultantes corpore: quia sancti habebunt gaudium interius & exterius, corporale & spirituale ait B. Hussius. Passio est cor- poralis,gaudium spirituale, quod in cruce incipit, durat in aeternum, ait B. Lutherus. Ἀγαλλιώμενοι sunt exilientes prae gaudio: quod fiet ἐν ἀποκαλύ- ψει τῆς δόξης αὐτῶ, in die extremi judicii, 1.Petr.I, 7. ubi coram omnibus Electis,imo omnibus homi- nibus gloriam suam publice manifestabit, Matth. XVI, 27. cap. XXIV, 30. cap. XXV, 31. Tum enim qui hic fuere consortes passionum, consortes etiam erunt gloriae, Rom. VIII, 17. 2. Tim. II, 11. Luc. XXII, 28.

## 4:14
Verse 14. If you are reproached in the name of Christ, blessed are you.] Here 'in the name of Christ', which is 'for the sake of Christ' in the saying of the same sense, Matt. V, 11. See also above III, 14.

He proceeds from passions to insults: because the faithful are tempted in two ways primarily, then by afflictions, then by reproaches; the former affect the body, the latter the mind, Wis. II, 19, 1 Tim. IV, 10. And in the primitive Church, because of the name of Christians alone, the faithful were subject to both punishments and reproaches out of hatred for the name of Christ, just as Christ had predicted, Matt. XXIV, 9, Luke XXI, 37. That they would be blessed, however, only in the kingdom of glory: which the Vulgate implies through the future verb: You shall be: But that they are already in the kingdom of grace even in the passions themselves, those who suffer for the name of Christ and are affected by reproaches, St. Peter had from the mouth of Christ VIII, 15, 1 Pet. III, 14. Which sense the added reason confirms.

For the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.] In the Manuscript: For the Spirit of glory, and of power, and of God rests upon you. But the true reading is the Spirit of glory and of power, the Spirit of God, etc. Why, he says, would you not rejoice even in the midst of evils? You have a great cause. The Spirit of God, who does not desert you in evils, but remains with you, rests, that is, שכן [dwelt], whence שכינה [Shekhinah]. And he says 'upon you' just as the same Spirit is said to 'come upon', Luke I, 33, Acts I, 8. Thus שכן עליו [he dwelt upon him] Exod. XL, 35. But he calls this Spirit also of glory, that is, glorious, as the Syrian rightly takes it here, and of power, that is, very powerful and effective. Truly a great power, to speak in tongues, to heal the sick, to cast out demons, and to predict the future. And from this, the greatest honor for them among upright men. But if such is the earnest, how great and what kind will the price itself be.

There is no need for a new reading to be invented. The same sense emerges if the particle x̀ is taken exegetically. Of glory, that is, or which is the same, the Spirit of God. For that Spirit of glory, which brings glory to us, and seals it in us even in the passions themselves, and is himself the God of glory, is the Spirit of God. He confirms the blessedness in afflictions, because the Spirit of God rests upon the faithful as the Spirit of glory, which is the pledge and earnest of glory: whence we already have here the kingdom of God, and in it joy in the Holy Spirit, Rom. XIV, 17, ch. V, 2, 3. The Vulgate interpreter rendered it thus: Because the glory and the Spirit of God rests in us. But the Syrian more correctly: The Spirit of the glory of God, or the glorious Spirit: Which Spirit of God is opposed to the spirit of the world. Our persecutors are agitated by the spirit of the world: but upon us, who suffer from them, the Spirit of God rests, because to suffer reproaches patiently for the name of Christ is a most certain sign of the Holy Spirit dwelling in us, Gal. V, 22, who is also the Spirit of gentleness, Gal. VI, 1. Upon Christ the Spirit rested not by measure, Isa. XI, 1, John III, 34. Because we have communion with Christ, it also rests upon us according to the measure of the gift of Christ, Eph. IV, 7. Dionysius the Carthusian says that this rest of the Holy Spirit brings an inherent quality, which formally justifies and strengthens. But the indwelling of the Holy Spirit is a consequence of justification, which does not consist in an inherent quality, but in the remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, Gal. IV, 6.

On their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified.] This is absent from the Manuscript, no less than from the Latin, the Syrian, and the Arabic.

Yet it should not therefore be called into doubt, or considered an addition with Lorinus. For the Greek Codices agree, and the commentaries of the Greeks read it, as does Cyprian, book IV, ep. 6, who introduces it in this way: Which indeed according to them is blasphemed, but according to us is honored, referring those predicates to the name of Christ, not to the Spirit. But since τὸ Πνεῦμα immediately precedes, it is more correctly referred to it by Oecumenius: The Spirit of GOD is indeed blasphemed among them, but among us is glorified, because the reproaches which are brought on account of the name of Christ redound to the Spirit of glory himself, both because those who suffer them, professing the name of Christ, are ruled by the Holy Spirit, and because those reproaches are so arranged that they do not concern persons, but dogmas, when the Word of God is torn by calumnies, and the profession of the faith delivered by the Holy Spirit is traduced under the name of apostasy, heresy, sedition, and contumacy against the Magistrate, etc. Among the faithful, however, the Holy Spirit is glorified, while they constantly profess His Word and glorify the name of the Lord.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Εἰ ὀνειδίζεσθε ἐν ὀνόματι Χριστῶ μακάριοι.] Hic ἐν ὀνόματι χριστῶ, quod ἕνεκα χριστῶ in ejusdem sensus dicto, Matth. V, 11. Vide & supra III, 14.

A passionibus ad contumelias progreditur: quia fideles duobus imprimis modis tentantur, tum afflictionibus, tum opprobriis, illa corpus, hac animum afficiunt, Sap. II, 19. 1. Tim. IV, 10. Et in primitiva Ecclesia ob solum Christianorum no- men ex odio nominis Christi cum suppliciis tum opprobriis obnoxii erant fideles, quemadmodum praedixerat Christus, Matth. XXIV, 9. Luc. XXI, 37. Beatos autem fore tantum in regno gloriae: Quod Vulgata innuit per Verbum futurum: Eri- tis: Sed jam esse in regno gratiae in ipsis etiam pas- sionibus, qui ob nomen Christi patiuntur, & op- probriis afficiuntur ex ore Christi habuit S. Petrus VIII, 15. 1. Petr. III, 14. Quem sensum ratio ad- juncta comprobat.

Ὅτι τὸ τῆς δόξης καὶ τὸ τῶ Θεῶ Πνεῦμα ἐφ' ὑμᾶς ἀναπαύε- ται.] In Manuscripto: Ὅτι τὸ τῆς δόξης, καὶ δυνάμεως, καὶ τὸ τῶ Θεῶ πνεῦμα ἐφ' ὑμᾶς ἀναπαύεται. Sed vera lectio est τὸ τῆς δόξης καὶ δυνάμεως, τὸ τῶ Θεῶ Πνεῦμα &c. Cur non gau- deretis, inquit, etiam in mediis malis? Causam habetis ma- gnam. Spiritum Dei, qui in malis vos non deserit, sed vo- biscum manet, ἀναπαύεται, id est שכן unde שכינה. Et dicit ἐφ' ὑμᾶς quomodo ἐπέρχεσθαι dicitur idem Spiritus, Luc. I, 33. Actor. I, 8. Sic שכן עליו Exod. XL, 35. Hunc Spiritum autem appellat & gloriae, id est, gloriosum, ut hic recte accipit Syrus, & potentiae, id est, potentem valde atque efficacem. Magna sane potentia, loqui linguas,sanare aegro- tos, ejicere daemonas, & praedicere futura. Et maximus inde illis honor apud homines æquos. Quod si talis est arrhabo, quantum & quale erit ipsum pretium.

Non opus est, nova fingatur lectio. Sensus idem emergit, si particula x̀ ἐξηγητικῶς accipiatur. Glo- riæ, hoc est, vel qui idem est Dei Spiritus. Nam Spiritus ille gloriæ, qui nobis gloriam affert, atque eam etiam in ipsis passionibus in nobis obsignat, estque ipse Deus gloriæ, est Spiritus Dei. Beati- tudinem confirmat in afflictionibus, qui super fide- libus requiescit Spiritus Dei, ceu Spiritus gloriæ, qui pignus & arrhabo est gloriæ: unde hic jam ha- bemus regnum Dei, & in eo gaudium in Spiritu sancto, Rom. XIV, 17. cap. V, 2.3. Vulgatus Inter- pres sic reddidit: Quoniam gloria & Spiritus Dei in nobis requiescit. Sed rectius Syrus: Spiritus glo- riæ Dei, vel Spiritus gloriosus: Qui Spiritus Dei op- ponitur Spiritui mundi. Persecutores nostri Spi- ritu mundi agitantur: super nos vero, qui ab ipsis patimur, Spiritus Dei quiescit, quia patienter op- probria sustinere propter nomen Christi & signum certissimum inhabitantis in nobis Spiritus sancti, Gal. V, 22. qui & Spiritus lenitatis est, Gal. VI, 1. Super Christum requiescebat Spiritus non ad men- suram, Esa. XI, 1. Joh. III, 34. Quia communio- nem habemus cum Christo, etiam super nos quie- scit κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δωρεᾶς τῶ χρισᾶ, Eph. IV, 7. Hanc Spiritus sancti requiem Dionysius Carthusia- nus inferre qualitatem inhærentem ait, quæ formali- ter justificet atque corroboret. Sed Spiritus san- cti inhabitatio consequens est justificationis, quæ non in qualitate inhærente consistit, sed in remis- sione peccatorum & imputatione justitiæ Christi, Gal. IV, 6.

Κατὰ μὲν ἀυτὸς βλασφημᾶται, κατὰ δὲ ὑμᾶς δοξάζεται.] Abest hoc à Manuscripto, non minus quam à Latino & Sy- ro & Arabe.

Nec tamen in dubium ideo vocandum, vel cum Lorino pro additamento habendum. Consenti- unt enim Græci Codices, leguntque id Græcorum commentarii, ut & Cyprianus l. IV. ep. 6. qui hoc modo id adducit: Quod quidem secundum illos blasphematur, secundum nos autem honoratur, re- ferens ea prædicata ad nomen Christi, non ad Spi- ritum. Sed quum proxime τὸ Πνεῦμα præcedat, rectius eo refertur ab Oecumenio: Spiritus DEI apud ipsos quidem blasphematur, apud nos autem glorificatur, quod opprobria, quæ ob nomen Christi inferuntur, in ipsum Spiritum gloriæ redundent, tum quia à Spiritu sancto illi reguntur, qui ea pa- tiuntur, nomen Christi profitentes, tum quia ita comparata sunt opprobria illa, ut non personas concernant, sed dogmata, cum Verbum Dei calu- mniis proscinditur, fidei à Spiritu sancto traditæ professio apostasias, hærefeos, seditionis, contuma- ciæ adversus Magistratum nomine traducitur &c. Apud fideles autem Spiritus sanctus glorificatur, dum Verbum ejus constanter profitentur, & no- men Domini glorificant.

## 4:15
Vers. 15.

Μὴ γάρ τις ὑμῶν πασχέτω ὡς φονευς.] It is a happy thing to suffer for a good cause. The same sense as above II, 20. You have the word φονεὺς in Wisd. 12, 5. Acts 3, 14. ch. 7, v. 52. ch. 28, v. 4. Rev. 21, v. 8. ch. 22, v. 15. It signifies him who unjustly takes away a man's life. Here γάρ stands for ὅτι, as in Exod. 25, 40.

Ἤ κλέπτης.] See 1 Cor. 6, v. 10. A thief is one who unjustly seizes what belongs to another.

Ἤ κακοποιός.] By this general name he designates those who in any way offend against public laws, such as perjurers, forgers, adulterers. See John 18, 30. above ch. 2, v. 12, 14. ch. 3, v. 16.

Since some persecutors wished to appear to be harassing Christians not on account of that name, but on account of the crimes with which they were burdened, the Apostle warns them to take care that they do not suffer for misdeeds, which is not it brings no glory to them, but brings ignominy both to them and to the Christian name. Thus, infanticide and Thyestean banquets were charged against them by the Gentiles, as Minucius testifies in his Octavius, Tertullian in Apologeticus c. 9, and Augustine in his oration to Antoninus Pius: Therefore they are warned to abstain from true homicide: and when Christians were subjected to the same infamous punishment as thieves, and seemed to be partners in the guilt of those whose punishment they were forced to undergo, they are warned to beware of the crime of theft, &c. Justice is not certain from suffering, but suffering is glorious from justice, says Augustine, l. IX, epist. Parm. c. 7. It is not the punishment that makes a martyr of Christ, but the cause, says the same, lib. III, c. Crescon. cap. 7.

Η᷍ ὡς ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοπος.] As a meddler in others' affairs: Thus Tertullian in Scorpiace. By this name is denoted a busybody, and one who is garrulous.

The Vulgate rendered it: A coveter of others' things, which Estius defends thus: namely, as one who is such in effect, that is, greedily gaping after the things of others, and taking them where he can. But that pertains to theft. Others more correctly take it regarding πολυ- πραγμοσύνῃ (meddlesomeness), by which someone invades the boundaries of another's office, and as an inspector of others' affairs claims for himself a censorship over the affairs of others, because he is called ἀλλοτρίων ἐπίσκοπος according to Budaeus, who takes upon himself the administration of another. Cyprian, l. c., rendered it as one who manages the cares of others, as did also Augustine in his unfinished commentary on Romans: It is likely that Christians, living among Jews and Gentiles, sometimes took upon themselves a censorship of others out of rashness, or intruded themselves too curiously into the affairs of others; he forbids that, since they could easily incur the crime of meddlesomeness from it.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Μὴ γάρ τις ὑμῶν πασχέτω ὡς φονευς.] Lætum est pati pro bona causa. Idem sensus, qui supra II, 20. Vocem φονεὺς ha- bes Sap. 12, 5. Act. 3, 14. c. 7. v. 52. c. 28. v. 4. Apoc. 21. v. 8. c. 22. v. 15. Significat eum, qui injuste homini vitam eripit. Est hic γάρ pro ὅτι, ut Exod. 25, 40.

Ἤ κλέπτης.] Vide 1. Cor. 6. v. 10. Fur est, qui alienum in- juste arripit.

Ἤ κακοποιός.] Nomine hoc generali eos designat, qui quo- vis modo in leges publicas delinquunt, ut perjuri, falsarii, a- dulteri. Vide Joh. 18, 30. supra c. 2. v. 12. 14. c. 3. v. 16.

Quum persecutores nonnulli videri voluerint Christianos sese non ob nomen illud, sed ob cri- mina, quib9 onerabantur, infestare, monet Aposto- lus, caveant, ne ob maleficia patiantur, quod non modo nullam ipsis gloriam, sed & ipsis & nomini Christiano ignominiam affert. Ita infantici- dii ac cœnæ Thyesteæ à gentilibus arguebantur, teste Minutio in Octavio, Tertulliano in Apolo- get. c. 9. Augustino in orat. ad Anton. Pium : Ideo ut à vero homicidio abstineant, monentur : & quum infami cum furibus supplicio afficerentur Christiani, eorumque in culpa socii viderentur, quorum pœnam subire cogebantur, à furti crimi- ne sibi caveant monentur, &c. non ex passione certa est justitia, sed ex justitia passio gloriosa, ait Augusti- nus l. IX. epist. Parm. c. 7. Martyrem Christi non pœna facit, sed causa ait idem lib. III. c. Crescon. cap. 7.

Η᷍ ὡς ἀλλοτριοεπίσκοπος.] Ut alieni speculator : Ita Ter- tullianus scorpiaco. Denotatur hoc nomine percunctator, idemque garriens.

Vulgatus reddidit: Alienorum appetitor, quod ita tuetur Estius : scilicet cum effectu talis, hoc est, cupide rebus alienis inhians, & tollens, ubi potest. Sed id ad furtum pertinet. Rectius de πολυ- πραγμοσύνῃ alii accipiunt, qua quis fines alieni offici invadit, & ceu alienorum inspector censu- ram in aliena sibi vendicat, quia ἀλλοτρίων ἐπίσκο- πος dicitur secundum Budæum, qui alienam pro- curationem sibi sumit. Cyprianus l. c. alienas cu- ras agens reddidit, ut & Augustinus in comment. ad Rom. inchoato : Verisimile est, Christianos inter Judæos & gentes agentes alienorum è teme- ritate censuram sibi quandoque sumsisfe, aut cu- riosius rebus alienis sese ingessisse, id prohibet quum inde πολυπραγμοσύνης crimen facile in- currere potuerint.

## 4:16
Vers. 16.

Εἰ δὲ ὡς Χριστιανός.] Concerning the origin of this name, you have it in Acts 11:26.

Estius says that name was imposed by outsiders, not assumed by the faithful. But the contrary appears from this passage, which Estius himself seems to have acknowledged at 1 Cor. 1:12. Outsiders or infidels called Christians Galileans, as Theodoret testifies, l. III, A. C. c. 8, and they turned the name of Christians into Chrestians.

Μὴ αἰσχυνέσθω.] If it was not a thing to be ashamed of to die with Phocion, how much less for Christ?

For the passions which we suffer as Christians, and therefore as innocent, do not bring us ignominy, but glory. Passions endured for the name of Christ are precious pearls before God. Therefore, a Christian ought to be no more ashamed of them than a virgin of her pearls and gems. Theodore the Studite to Naucratius: Is it not, he says, more glorious than the diadem of those who wear it, to bear the stigmata of Christ, his life-giving passions, as crowns? See especially St. Cyprian, l. V, epist. 12, on how great a thing it is to suffer as a Christian.

Δοξαζέτω δὲ τὸν Θεὸν ἐν τῷ μέρει τούτῳ.] Let him give thanks to God on this account, see above 3:14. Ἐν τούτῳ τῷ μέρει means what pertains to this matter, as 2 Cor. 3:10, 9:3, Col. 2:16. In the Manuscript it is in Latin phrasing: Ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τούτῳ. Nor does the Syriac read it otherwise.

He could have read it otherwise, even if he rendered it thus. For he did not always render word for word. For the sense is the same, whether the name is taken for the cause, or whether the name of Christ is understood. Which must also be held regarding the Vulgate, 'but let him glorify God in this name.' Not only let him not be ashamed, but let him even rejoice, and not only rejoice, but also count it as his glory, and give thanks to God that he is held worthy to suffer for Christ, Acts 5:41, Phil. 1:29. Chrysostom, hom. 5 on Job: He who is inflamed with the love of Christ will choose rather to be bound for Christ than to inhabit the heavens, and will hold this more clearly than to sit upon twelve thrones, as long as it is the will of God that he should suffer.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Εἰ δὲ ὡς Χριστιανός.] De origine hujus nominis habes Act. XI, 26.

Nomen illud ab externis impositum dicit Estius, non à fidelibus assumptum. Sed contra- rium ex hoc loco apparet, quod etiam agnovisse videtur Estius ad 1. Cor. I, 12. Externi sive infideles Christianos vocabant Galilæos teste Theodor. l. III. A. C. c. 8. & Christianorum nomen in Chre- stianorum convertebant.

Μὴ αἰσχυνέσθω.] Si non pudendum fuit cum Phocione mori, quanto minus ob Christum ?

Passiones enim, quas ut Christiani, adeoque ut innocentes patimur, non ignominiam nobis, sed gloriam afferunt. Passiones ob Christi nomen tole- ratæ pretiosæ sunt coram Deo margaritæ. Tam igi- tur de illis non erubescere debet Christianus, quam virgo de margaritis & gemmis. Theodorus Studita ad Naucratium : Annon, ait, diadema ge- stantium gloria mirabilior stigmata ferre Christi vi- vificas ejus passiones ceu coronas. Videatur impri- mis S. Cyprianus l. V. epist. 12. quantum sit pati ut Christianum.

Δοξαζέτω δὲ τὸν Θεὸν ἐν τῷ μέρει τούτῳ.] Gratias Deo agat hoc nomine, supra III, 14. Ἐν τούτῳ τῷ μέρει valet quod ad hanc rem attinet, ut 2. Cor. 3, 10. c. 9, 3. Col. 2, 16. In Manu- scripto est loquutione Latina : Ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τούτῳ. Nec aliter legit Syrus.

Potuit aliter legisse, etiamsi ita reddiderit. Non enim semper verbum verbo reddidit. Sensus enim idem est, sive nomen pro causa accipiatur, sive et- iam Christi nomen intelligatur. Quod de Vulgata quoque habendum, glorificet autem Deum in isto nomine. Non modo non erubescat, sed etiam gau- deat, nec gaudeat solum, sed etiam gloriæ sibi du- cat, ac Deo gratias agat, quod pro Christo pati di- gnus habeatur, Act. V, 41. Phil. I, 29. Chrysostomus hom. V. de Jobo : Qui amore Christi aduritur, eliget potius vinctum esse pro Christo, quam cælos inhabitare, clariusque hoc habebit, quam super duodecim sedes se- dere, quamdiu voluntas Dei est, quod patiatur.

## 4:17
Verf. 17. Ὅτι ὁ καιρὸς τῦ ἄρξασθαι τὸ κρῖμα ἀπὸ τῦ οἴκυ τῦ Θεῦ.] In the Manuscript: ὅτι καιρὸς as in Mark 11:13. The time is imminent when Christians will suffer most grievous evils, predicted by Christ in Matt. 24:19. Moreover, κρῖμα in this place is clearly as in Rom. 5:16, מִשְׁפָּט, the decree of God, namely, concerning the sending of adversities, as the preceding shows, namely, to purge some, to test others, and to set them forth as an example. Εἰ δὲ πρῶτον ἀφ᾿ ἡμῶν ] If we are the first to bear evils. Τί τὸ τέλος τῶν ἀπειθούντων τῷ τοῦ Θεῦ εὐαγγελίῳ.] He deals with the Jews, and predicts the destruction of that nation. You have Τὸ τέλος in a similar sense in Matt. 24:14; it refers to the passage in Daniel 9:27, where there is כלה συντέλεια.

It is not the case that this should be restricted to the times at the beginning of the primitive Church of the New Testament, because this decree of God is for all times, that in the first order the house of GOD should experience the judgment of the Lord; just as the pious are forced to suffer afflictions first, 2 Tim. 3, 2. And the Apostle seems to look to similar places of the Old Testament, Jer. 10, 13. 14, 18. 19. 29. 30. 31. ch. 49, 12. Ezek. 9, 6. ch. 21, 4. Amos 3, 24. Oecumenius here praised the saying of Basil the Great: It is provided by nature that we are indignant against those who are most familiar to us when they sin against us. It is taught here also in general, why the faithful ought to glorify God if they suffer as Christians, because it is a sign that they belong to the house of God, Heb. 12, 6. By τὸ κρῖμα however here is understood not punishment, but paternal chastisement, as regards the faithful, as 1 Cor. 11, 31. 32. because no one is entirely innocent before God, Exod. 34, 7. Judgment begins from the house of God or the Church and the faithful, 1 Tim. 3, 15. Heb. 3, 6. But it is defined and completed in the unfaithful, and especially in impenitent persecutors. If God, says the Apostle, afflicts his own household, and even his beloved sons in this life above others, what will become of the unbelievers who are alien to the family of God. The Vulgate rendered it of those who do not believe. But there is greater emphasis in the word ἀπειθούντων, by which is signified positive unbelief and a stubborn contempt of the Gospel: Cf. Acts 13, 46. Augustine in Psalm 93. If the sons are scourged, what ought the most wicked servants to hope for? How then will the ungodly be with you, when you do not even spare your own faithful, so that you may exercise and instruct them? Otherwise, says Bede in Psalm 36, God scourges a servant so that he may expel him, otherwise a son, whom he may receive into his inheritance.

Latin:

Verf. 17. Ὅτι ὁ καιρὸς τῦ ἄρξασθαι τὸ κρῖμα ἀπὸ τῦ οἴκυ τῦ Θεῦ.] In Manuscripro: ὅτι καιρὸς ut Marc. XI, 13. Tempus imminet, quo Christiani gravissima mala patiantur, prædictum Christo Matth. XXIV, 19. Est autem κρῖμα hoc loco plane, ut Rom. V, 16. מִשְׁפָּט Dei constitutio, de immittendis scilicet ad- versis, ut ostendunt præcedentia, nempe ad alios purgandos, alios explorandos, & proponendos in exemplum. Εἰ δὲ πρῶτον ἀφ᾿ ἡμῶν ] Si nos primi ad mala ferenda. Τί τὸ τέλος τῶν ἀπειθούντων τῷ τοῦ Θεῦ εὐαγγελίῳ.] De Ju- dæis agit, & ejus gentis excidium prædicit. Τὸ τέλος pari sensu habes Matth. XXIV, 14. respicitur Danielis locus IX, 27. ubi est כלה συντέλεια.

Non est,ut hoc restringatur ad tempora sub ini- tium primitivæ Ecclesiæ Novi Testamenti, quia decretum hoc Dei est omnium temporum, primo ordine domum DEI judicium Domini experiri; quemadmodum pii primum afflictiones pati co- guntur, 2. Tim. 3, 2. Et videtur Apostolus respicere similia Veteris Testamenti loca, Jer. X, 13. XIV, 18. 19. 29. 30. 31. cap. XLIX, 12. Ezech. IX, 6. cap. XXI, 4. Amos III, 24. Oecumenius hic laudavit Basilii M. di- ctum: Natura comparatum est, ut contra eos, qui familiarissimi nobis sunt, cum in nos peccant, indi- gnemur. Docetur hic etiam in communi, cur Deum glorificare fideles debeant, si patiantur, ut Christiani, quia signum id est,quod pertineant ad domum Dei, Ebr. XII, 6. Per τὸ κρῖμα autem hic non pœna, sed castigatio paterna, quod ad fideles, intelligitur, ut 1. Cor. XI, 31. 32. quia nemo coram Deo prorsus in- nocens est, Exod. XXXIV, 7. Incipit judicium à domo Dei seu Ecclesia & fidelibus, 1. Tim. III, 15. Ebr. III, 6. Sed definit & completur in infidelibus, & imprimis persecutoribus impœnitentibus. Si Deus, inquit Apostolus, domesticos suos, adeoque filios dilectos in hac vita præ aliis affligit, quid fu- turum incredulis à Dei familia alienis. Vulgatus reddidit eorum, qui non credunt. Sed major em- phasis est in voce ἀπειθούντων, qua significatur in- credulitas positiva & pertinax Evangelii contem- ptus: Conf. Act. XIII, 46. Augustinus in Psalm. XCIII. Si flagellantur filii, quid debent sperare servi nequissimi? Quomodo ergo erunt tecum iniqui, quando nec tuis fidelibus parcis, ut exerceas & eru- dias eos? Aliter, inquit Beda in Psal. XXXVI. fla- gellat Deus servum, ut expellat, aliter filium, quem in hæreditatem recipiat.

## 4:18
Verf. 18. Καὶ εἰ ὁ δίκαιος μόλις σώζεται.] It is from the Greek version of Prov. 11, 31. where in the Hebrew: הֵן צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ יְשֻׁלָּם אַפַּכִּי רָשָׁע וְחוֹטֵא. Μόλις here signifies not without adversities. Thus μόλις πῶς in Xenophon with difficulty. Μόλις ἐπαίρουσι τὰ βλέφαρα in Galen. The Syrian here למחסן with force. Thus μόλις and μετὰ ποῖs, as they are placed as equals. Sir. 9, 16. And μόλις is in a similar sense in Isocrates in his oration to Demonicus.

Thus the little word μόλις occurs in Acts 14, 18. ch. 27, 7. it is also the same as μόγις, whence μογέω I endure labors, I suffer hardships, and therefore the adversities of the just are implied, Acts 14, 22. But when it is said that the just is scarcely saved, regard is had not to divine power, but to human infirmity, whence St. Augustine from these words proves the necessity of divine grace everywhere against the Pelagians, book II de peccat. merit. & remiss. ch. 19. book 4 contr. Julian. ch. 2. etc. Also to be noted here against the Papistic perfection of works is that of Estius in this place: Why is the just man scarcely saved, unless because he is scarcely just? that is, because he has an imperfect justice, since he fails in many things, and the very works of justice which he does, for the most part have something of filth mixed in, either from an impure intention, or from some other circumstance.

Ὁ ἀσεβὴς καὶ ἁμαρτωλὸς πῦ φανεῖται;] The ungodly toward God, the wicked toward men, where will he be found? Will it not be in the greatest evils? Take ἁμαρτωλὸς here, as Rom. 5, 8. Gal. 2, 15. You have ἀσεβεῖς καὶ ἁμαρτωλοὺς joined together also in 1 Tim. 1, 9.

A sentiment very similar to this is found in Rabbi Solomon on Num. 10. When the holy, blessed God executes judgment upon the righteous, the Holy One is exalted and praised: For if He does this to them, how much more to the impious? See also Jer. 45:29 and Luke 23:3 and the statements there. The writer on the life and death of Moses: But if God recompenses the righteous for the least things they do, how much more does He recompense sinners for the great things they commit?

This is not referred to the house of God, as it has seemed to some, but the judgment of God is regarded, in which the impious cannot stand, Psalm 1:5. Lyranus: Where will he appear? i.e., nowhere, because they will be hidden in the depths of hell. Bede cites the text of Solomon in this place: Such is the fragility of mortal life that not even the righteous, who are to be crowned in heaven, pass through it without tribulation on account of the countless stain of corrupted nature: how much more do those who are exiles from heavenly grace await the certain outcome of their perpetual damnation? Draconites in this place. If one repenting from sins and an heir of eternal life is afflicted because of sin inherent in the flesh, how much more will the impious, sinning contumaciously and dying in their sins, if not here, like the pious, yet in the other life be tormented more harshly and perpetually: Didymus of Alexandria in this place seems to distinguish the impious and the sinner equally, calling the former one who is entirely outside the Lord; but the latter one whom God contains, but he himself despises Him while he transgresses His laws: But they seem to be synonyms in this place; for both are opposed to the righteous. Cf. Gen. 13:14. Estius has it thus here: Those to whom the Gospel has been preached are indeed impious and sinners, yet not guilty of unbelief. But all those are guilty of unbelief who are not saved. The distinction between believers and non-believers, those to be saved and those to be damned, is adequate. And not only positive, but also privative unbelief condemns.

Latin:

Verf. 18. Καὶ εἰ ὁ δίκαιος μόλις σώζεται.] Est ex Græca versione Prov. XI, 31. ubi in Ebræo: הֵן צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ יְשֻׁלָּם אַפַּכִּי רָשָׁע וְחוֹטֵא. Μόλις hic significat non sine adversis. Ita μόλις πῶς apud Xenophontem cum dif- ficultate. Μόλις ἐπαίρουσι τὰ βλέφαρα apud Galenum. Sy- rus hic למחסן cum vi. Sic μόλις & μετὰ ποῖs, ut paria po- nuntur. Sir. IX, 16. Et μόλις pari sensu est apud Isocratem si- ne ad Demonicum.

Sic vocula μόλις occurrit Actor. XIV, 18. cap. XXVII, 7. est & idem quod μόγις, unde μογέω la- bores tolero, ærumnas patior, ideoque adversitates justorum subinnuuntur, Act. XIV, 22. Quando au- tem dicitur, justum vix salvari, respectus habetur non ad divinam virtutem, sed ad humanam infirmi- tatem,unde S. Augustinus ex his verbis gratiæ divinæ necessitatem passim probat contra Pelagianos l. II. de peccat. merit. & remiss. cap. XIX. l. 4. contr. Julian. c. 2. &c. Observanda etiam hic contra operum per- fectionem Papisticam illa Estii in h. l. Quare justus vix salvetur, nisi quia vix est justus? id est, quia im- perfectam habet justitiam, cum delinquat in multis, & ipsa justitiæ opera, quæ facit, plerumque sordium aliquid habeant admixtum, vel ex intentione non pura, vel ex alia circumstantia.

Ὁ ἀσεβὴς καὶ ἁμαρτωλὸς πῦ φανεῖται;] Impius in Deum, in homines improbus ubi invenietur? Nonne in sum- mis malis? Ἁμαρτωλὸς hic sume, ut Rom. V, 8. Galat. II, 15. Conjunctim ἀσεβεῖς καὶ ἁμαρτωλοὺς habes & 1. Timoth. 1, 9.

Sententia huic valde par est apud Rabbinum Salomonem ad X. Num. Cum Deus sanctus, benedictus judicium facit in justos, sanctus extollitur & laudatur: Nam si in illis hoc fa- cit, quanto magis in impiis? Vide & Jerem.XLV, 29. & Luc. XXIII. vers. 3. & ibi dicta. Scriptor de vita & morte Mo- sis: Quod si justis retribuit Deus, minimum quod faciunt, quanto magis peccatoribus multum, quod committunt, re- tribuit?

Non ad domum Dei hoc refertur, ut nonnullis visum, sed judicium Dei respicitur, in quo impii stare non possunt, Psalm. I. 5. Lyranus: Ubi compa- rebit? q. d. nuspiam, quia in profundo inferni erunt absconditi. Beda textum Salomonis ita citat in h. l. Tanta est vita mortalis fragilitas, ut ne justi quidem, qui in cœlo coronandi sunt, hanc sine tribulatione propter innumeram vitiatæ naturæ labem transeant: quanto magis hi, qui cælestis sunt gratiæ extorres certum suæ perpetuæ damnationis exitum expectant? Draconites in h. l. Si à peccatis resipiscens & hæres vitæ æternæ propter inhærens carni peccatum affligi- tur, quanto magis impii contumaciter peccantes, & in peccatis morientes, si non hic, ut pii, tamen in alte- ra vita durius & perpetuo cruciabuntur: Didymus Alexandrinus in h. l. impium & peccatorem pariter distinguere videtur illum dicens, qui omnino extra Dominum est: hunc autem, quem Deus continet, sed ipse contemnit eum, dum transgreditur leges ejus: Sed videntur hoc loco esse Synonyma; Uter- que enim opponitur justo. Conf. Gen. XIII, 14. Estius hic ita habet: Quibus Evangelium est præ- dicatum impii quidem sunt, & peccatores, non ta- men incredulitatis rei. Sed omnes illi rei incredufi- tatis sunt, qui non servantur. Adæquata est creden- tium & non credentium, salvandorum & damnan- dorum distinctio. Nec tantum positiva, sed etiam privativa incredulitas damnat.

## 4:19
Verse 19.

Ὥστε καὶ οἱ πάσχοντες κατὰ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ.] To suffer here is to be agitated by adversities, as above 2:19, 20, 23; 3:14, 17; above 15. According to the will of God, God thus dispensing, as above 3:17. It is not a question here of some common permission, but of a special decree of God, by which He calls the pious to the cross by the example of Christ.

The Apostle instructs, as Blessed Gerhard warns, those who suffer persecution, how they ought to conduct themselves in it; 1. let them acknowledge that afflictions are sent to them only by the will of God, 2. let them commend the outcome to God in true patience and humility, 3. let them not depart from the zeal of doing good because of their troubles, 4. in all these things let them imitate the example of Christ.

Ὡς πιστῷ κτίστῃ] To God, of course, who is the Creator, and therefore has a right over us: furthermore He is faithful, and therefore will stand by His promises, and will compensate for the evils endured with the greatest goods.

Παρατιθέσθωσαν τὰς ψυχὰς ἑαυτῶν ἐν ἀγαθοποιΐᾳ.] Let them commit themselves entirely, as much as they are, to the will of GOD, and let them not grow weary in doing good. We have already had the word ἀγαθοποιΐα in this sense several times, above 2:24, 15, 20; 3:6, 17. Παρατίθεσθαι, to commit, in the Hebrew idiom means to give oneself over, as we said on Matt. 10:39.

Some render κτίστῃ as possessor from κτάω, I possess, but it is more correctly explained as Creator from κτίζω, I create, which seems to agree more with the following verb, because God the creator of our souls is the most faithful guardian, into whose hands the care of this deposit is resigned most safely, who will not neglect His work in the least, but will deign to preserve it, as the most faithful, and will be able to, as the most powerful. By the verb παρατιθέσθωσαν it seems that Ps. 31:6 is regarded; therefore we also properly understand the soul here, since there is no necessity for a synecdochical meaning, cf. Matt. 10:28, ch. 11:29. The passage Eccl. 12:7 also seems to be regarded. However, the words of the Apostle are not to be understood exclusively, but preeminently, because the soul is to be given the primary consideration. For our bodies also are in the hand of God, who is at some time going to raise them from the dust of the earth. But that God is called the Creator of souls, it is wrongly inferred from that, that God still creates souls today. Bellarmino himself notes in his book on the state of sin, ch. 1, that it is indeed proven from this that God is the founder of souls, but not the manner in which they were founded by GOD, whether by creation out of nothing, or by propagation from the soul of the first man.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Ὥστε καὶ οἱ πάσχοντες κατὰ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ.] Πάσχειν hic est adversis agitari, ut supra II, 19. 20. 23. III, 14. 17. supra 15. Κατὰ τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ, Deo sic dispensante, ut supra III, 17. Non agitur hic de communi quadam permissione, sed de speciali Dei decreto, quo pios Christi exemplo ad crucem vocat.

Instruit Apostolus, monente B. Gerhardo, eos, qui persecutionem patiuntur, quomodo in ea se gerere debeant; 1. agnoscant afflictiones non nisi voluntate Dei sibi immitti, 2. eventum in vera patientia & hu- militate Deo commendent, 3. à studio benefaciendi propter ærumnas minime discedant, 4. in hisce omni- bus exemplum Christi imitentur.

Ὡς πιστῷ κτίστῃ] Deo scilicet, qui Creator est, ideoque jus in nos habet: deinde fidus, ideoque stabit promissis, & mala tolerata maximis bonis repensabit.

Παρατιθέσθωσαν τὰς ψυχὰς ἑαυτῶν ἐν ἀγαθοποιΐᾳ.] Se to- tos, quanti quanti sunt, DEI arbitrio permittant, neque in bene agendo defatigentur. Verbum ἀγαθοποιΐα jam aliquo- ties in hoc sensu habuimus, supra II, 24. 15. 20. III, 6.17. Πα- ρατίθεσθαι הפק יד, ψυχὰς ἑαυτῶν loquutione Ebræa va- let, seipsos, ut diximus ad Matth. X, 39.

Nonnulli κτίστῃ reddunt possessori à κτάω possi- deo, sed rectius exponitur Creatori à κτίζω creo, quod verbo sequenti magis videtur congruere, quia Deus creator animarum nostrarum custos fi- delissimus est, in cujus manus cura depositi hujus resignatur tutissime, qui opus suum minime negli- get, sed conservare dignabitur, ut fidelissimus, & poterit, ut potentissimus. Verbo παρατιθέσθωσαν respici videtur Psal. XXXI, 6. ideo etiam animam hic proprie intelligimus, quum nec ulla sit Synec- dochicæ significationis necessitas, conf. Matth. X, 28. cap. XI, 29. Videtur quoque respici locus Eccl. XII, 7. Non tamen Apostoli verba exclusive in- telligenda, sed ἐξοχικῶς, quia animæ præcipuæ est habenda ratio. Nam & corpora nostra in manu Dei sunt, qui ea aliquando excitaturus est è terræ e pulvere. Quod autem Deus animarum Creator dicitur, ex eo perperam relinquitur, Deum adhuc hodie animas creare. Bellarminus ipse notat l. de stat. pecc. cap. 1. probari quidem hinc, animarum conditorem Deum esse, sed non modum, quo à DEO conditæ sint, utrum per creationem ex nihilo, an per propagationem ex anima primi hominis.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

Presbyters are warned particularly how they ought to feed the flock of Christ, and to all in common humility toward one's neighbor, trust toward God and His providence, and resistance against the devil are commended, with a promise of divine strengthening, and with the recapitulation of the epistle subjoined, with greetings added, and finally the epistle is concluded with a brief prayer.

There are three parts: The first is a special exhortation to the Presbyters, up to verse 4. The second is a general exhortation concerning humility, confidence, and vigilance against Satan, up to verse 11. The third is the conclusion of the epistle, up to verse 14.

PART I. A special exhortation directed to the Presbyters.

Ver. 1.

Πρεσβυτέρους τοὺς ἐν ὑμῖν παρακαλῶ.] He understands both the leaders of the assembly, those who labor in the word, and the others associated with them for governance.

He is not addressing the leaders of the assembly, but those who feed the flock of the Lord with the word. Others say that those superior in both age and dignity and priesthood are being addressed, such as Cornelius à Lapide, who nevertheless acknowledges later that these things concern the Pastors of the Church, just as Grotius could not deny that these things concern those who labor in the word. But if he understands by the others associated with them for governance the Lay presbyters, as they are called, who preside over discipline and external governance, this appendix is by no means appropriate: for the discourse is about the pasturing of the word, and Grotius later explains those Presbyters in verse 2 as Bishops, comparing the passage Acts 20:28, which looks solely to the Pastors of the word. Therefore, Cornelius is correct: He addresses, he says, Priests and Bishops, as Pastors of the Church, and commands them to feed the flock of the faithful committed to them by God strenuously, for whom he therefore prescribes the ideal of pastoral life in a few, but vigorous, words. Whence among the Syrians this part of the epistle is accustomed to be read at the election and ordination of Bishops, as the Syrian notes here.
