Hence also, presently, for 'providing' in Greek it is ἐπισκοποῦντες; so St. Jerome, Oecumenius, and others throughout. That primarily only Bishops are addressed, as Estius holds, is by no means to be conceded: For as to the pasturing of the word, it is equally committed to all pastors, Acts 20:28. Therefore Estius says: He turns the exhortation to Ecclesiastical Pastors, that is, Bishops or Presbyters. But what he adds: With the same authority with which he admonishes the Bishops of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, which regions he named at the front of the epistle, he could also admonish all other Bishops established anywhere; we concede this regarding Apostolic authority, which he has in common with other Apostles: But that he wishes to infer this primacy over the universal Church is a non sequitur. Furthermore, that Estius, even though he acknowledges that the name of Presbyter is general, even by the usage of the Apostles, so that all who are of the Priestly order, may include, Phil. I. 1. Tim. III. & V. Tit. I., he says that Bishops alone are properly and in the full sense pastors of the Lord's flock; that is foreign to the phraseology of Scripture, whatever may be the case regarding the Canons and certain of the Ancients. Paul, when naming Pastors and Teachers in Eph. IV, [did not mean] only Bishops it pertains to Bishops not only to preach the word of God and administer the Sacraments, but also to lay down laws, and punish transgressors, and cast the contumacious out of the Church by excommunication. But how will it be taught that these things are suitable and proper to Bishops, such as they are defined in Scripture? Not divine constitutions, but human sanctions claim these for Bishops—not genuine ones, but Papistical ones. Therefore, Cornelius à Lapide wishes the priesthood in general to be noted here, whether it be lesser and common, or greater, such as the Episcopate. And Salmero notes: that Peter does not mention the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, which has so many ranks of Bishops, Archbishops, Patriarchs, etc., because it consists of Ecclesiastical and Canonical institution, and they are not of divine law. Presbyters are called Pastors, however, because they ought to be πρεσβύτεροι, if not in age, then at least in senile prudence. Ambrose on A&olio: Truly that old age is venerable which grows white not with gray hairs, but with merits. For that is a reverend grayness which is the grayness of the soul, shining forth in gray thoughts and works, whence it cannot be proven—as Erasmus reports—that in the Papacy men are more often chosen for Ecclesiastical benefices, even those they call 'cured' (that is, those which have the care of souls joined to them), who are still of immature age. The Vulgate inserts the illative particle 'therefore' (ergo), which Cornelius wishes to be referred both to all the preceding things, which, although they pertain to all the faithful, yet pertain especially to Pastors, who ought to inculcate them to the faithful, and also properly to verses 11 and 17. But in most Greek Codices the particle οὖν is not found, and if it were to be referred to all the preceding things for that reason, because all things that are handed down in the scriptures ought to be inculcated by Presbyters, then all things would have to be referred to Presbyters, to whom the whole of Holy Scripture is indeed entrusted, 2 Tim. III, 15 seqq. But all the faithful pertain to the house of the Lord, whether they be Teachers or hearers. Therefore, that illative particle is more correctly absent.

The word παρακαλῶ here signifies 'I beseech' more than 'I exhort,' Cornelius advises, because for the sake of modesty Peter does not so much command as pray and beseech: But he says that in favor of the Vulgate. But why should Peter, an Apostle of God, writing by divine authority and furthermore by the impulse of the Holy Spirit, not exhort? These are indeed precepts which are handed down here, and are proposed imperatively: Feed the flock of God. παρακαλεῖν more commonly signifies to exhort than to beseech, says Estius.

ὁ συμπρεσβύτερος.] Thus also Roman Emperors call their soldiers fellow-soldiers: and the senate say that they are a part of themselves.

This comparison without doubt tends toward ensuring that this name is not believed to prejudice the primacy and Oecumenical papacy of the Roman Pontiff. But that had to be demonstrated above all things from the scriptures, not only concerning Peter, who never accepted it, never claimed it, but also concerning the Roman Pontiffs, who falsely boast themselves to be the Successors of Peter in that axiom. Although we detect this pride only in the Bishops of Rome of later times. Concerning Gregory the Great, this very Cornelius à Lapide certainly admits: St. Gregory, Roman Pontiff, did not wish to be called universal Bishop, lest he should seem to derogate from or diminish the right of the Episcopate for other Bishops, as if he alone were truly a Bishop, and the others only in name, and merely his vicars or suffragans. He did this to blunt the insolence of John, Archbishop of Constantinople, who was arrogating to himself the name of universal Patriarch, against whom St. Gregory, lib. 7, epist. 69, to Eusebius, says: If one is universal, it remains that you are not Bishops. And l. 4, epist. 36, to Eulogius: If one is called universal Patriarch, the name of Patriarch is derogated from the others. He should have added also this sentiment of Gregory the Great, lib. VI, epist. 30, to Maurice Augustus: I say confidently that whoever calls himself universal Priest, or desires to be called so in his election, is a precursor of the Anti-Christ, because by pride he sets himself before others: and the decree C. primæ sedis distinct. XCIX, from the African Council: Let the Bishop of the first see not be called Prince of Priests, or supreme Priest, or anything of this kind, but only Bishop of the first see. Moreover, let not even the Roman Pontiff be called universal. Out of modesty, indeed, he calls himself a fellow-elder with Peter, because as an Apostle he far excelled other Presbyters or Pastors, but that he excelled even other Apostles as Pope or Oecumenical Bishop will never be demonstrated. Therefore, Oecumenius, looking at him here not as a Pontiff but as an Apostle, gives this paraphrase: If I, who was a spectator of such miracles, and am a teacher of them to you, do not disdain to call myself your fellow-elder and companion, neither ought you to exalt yourselves above those who are subject to you. He calls himself a fellow-elder in this exhortation, however, to hint that he has a certain right to admonish other Presbyters, since he is one of their number. To these things he does not compel by commanding as a Pope, but exhorts by observing as a fellow-elder, and therefore the Roman Pontiff departs greatly from the manner of Peter, whose successor he nevertheless claims to be, when he publishes his mandates, diplomas, bulls, and briefs under the gravest threats, punishments, and I know not what indignation of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul.

Καὶ μάρτυς τῶν τοῦ Χριστοῦ παθημάτων.] Peter saw him bound. Then, which history does not teach, but is credible, hearing that he was crucified, he wished to be a spectator of that event also, but from a distance and in the crowd. The Apostles are eminently distinguished by the name of witnesses, Luke XXIV, 48, Acts I, 8, 22, II, 32, III, 15, V, 32, X, 39, 41.

St. Peter could be an unaccountable witness of the sufferings of Christ, even if he did not behold all his acts before his eyes: because he also testified of those things which do not fall into the senses of mortals, much less were seen by him, from infallible θεοπνευσίᾳ [divine inspiration]. He calls himself, however, a witness of the sufferings, which for a great part he usurped with his own eyes, so that they might the more obey his admonition concerning feeding the flock, which the Lord purchased for himself with his own blood, Acts XX, 28, since he himself could testify from the truth how much the Lord endured for that reason. These things do nothing for enduring sufferings on account of Christ, unless in so much as this witness, along with the other Apostles, found it necessary to endure much for the sake of his testimony, which John said he was made a partaker of in tribulation, Apoc. I, 9, which, however, is by no means hinted at by these words. Therefore, the explanations of Cornelius are foreign, not only that one, that he calls himself a witness of the sufferings of Christ, namely those which Christ suffers in his own, but also that one, that he voluntarily exposed himself to sufferings for Christ, neither of which is indicated in this place. But Cornelius says that Peter rightly remembered the sufferings of Christ, both because he carried them in the inmost marrow of his soul, and by them was excited to an ardent love of Christ, and to tolerating any labors and sorrows whatsoever for him: and also that by the same he might excite the pastors of the Church to the imitation of them, so that by the love of Christ they might endure whatever they might suffer and do to feed his sheep, and for them exhaust their blood, spirit, and life, just as Christ exhausted his. Ὁ καὶ τῆς μελλούσης ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι δόξης κοινωνός.] Supply 'future'. Thus 'partakers of the consolation', 2 Cor. 1:7. You have 'the glory that shall be revealed' also in Rom. 8:18. Now we have the right, the thing itself lies hidden. It is not called 'partaker' (κοινωνὸς) actively, because he hands down faith and the hope of glory to be revealed in heaven by preaching to others, as Lyranus and Carthusianus [think], but passively; nor does it refer to the glory of Christ seen on Mount Tabor, as Cajetanus [thinks], or in the resurrection, ascension, and mission of the Holy Spirit, as the Gloss, Hugo, and others wish; but to the glory which he was certain he would participate in after this life, which Oecumenius hands down and Cajetanus acknowledges, cf. Rom. 8:17, 1 Pet. 1:5, 2 Cor. 4:7. Blessed Gerhard says the nerve of the argument is such: 'My heavenly glory will be a reward common to me with you in the office of faithfulness, if you yourselves also apply due diligence in the office. Therefore it is fair that a place for my admonition be left by you.' He mentions heavenly glory, says Cornelius, both because his mind was occupied with the heavens and he was panting for heavenly glory, and to snatch the souls of pastors and the faithful to heavenly things, and to animate them by their hope to undergo all labors and struggles for Christ, v. 4. Therefore the Vulgate does not correctly render it 'Communicator' [partaker], because it is active: which fault Estius not undeservedly noted: 'Communicator,' he says, 'is not properly called one who becomes a partner, but one who makes others partners,' which Peter did not wish to ascribe to himself. That Peter was certain of his own salvation, these things teach; whether he had this from a special revelation, or whether these words are only those of a good and Christian hope, is not clear to Estius. Lorinus, however, says that he had it not only from a foretaste of felicity, but that he also wishes others to argue from thence that it will come to pass that when the Prince of Pastors shall appear, they shall receive the crown of glory: Cf. Rom. 8:29, 2 Cor. 4:13, 14.

Latin:

CAPUT V. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Monentur peculiariter Presbyteri, quomodo gregem Christi pascere debeant, omnibusque in communi humilitas erga proximum, fiducia erga Deum ejusque providentiam, resistentia adversus diabolum commendatur, cum pollicitatione divinæ confortationis, & subjuncta ἀνακεφαλαιώσει epistolæ, additis salutationibus, ac voto brevi tandem concluditur epistola.

Partes tres sunt: Prima adhortatio ad Presbyteros specialis, ad v. 4. Secunda adhortatio communis de humilitate, confidentia & contra Satanam vigilantia ad v. 11. Tertia conclusio epistolæ ad v. 14.

PARS I. Adhortatio specialis ad Presbyteros directa.

Vers. 1.

Πρεσβυτέρους τοὺς ἐν ὑμῖν παρακαλῶ.] Intelligit & Principes cœtus, κοπιῶντας ἐν λόγῳ, & cæteros ad regimen eis sociatos.

Non Principes cœtus, sed qui pascunt verbo gregem Domini, alloquitur. Alii superiores tum ætate tum dignitate & sacerdotio compellari dicunt, ut Cornelius à Lapide, qui tamen agnoscit postea, hæc concernere Pastores Ecclesiæ, quemadmodum nec Grotius diffiteri potuit, τοὺς κοπιῶντας ἐν λόγῳ hæc concernere. Si autem per cæteros ad regimen eis sociatos presbyteros Laicos, quos vocant, intelligat, qui disciplinæ & externo regimini præsunt, minimé convenit hæc appendix: nã de pastura verbi sermo est, & Presbyteros illos ad v. 2. de Episcopis explicat postea Grotius locum conferens, Act. XX, 28. qui ad Pastores verbi unice spectat. Recte ergo Cornelius: Compellat, inquit, Sacerdotes & Episcopos, quasi Ecclesiæ Pastores, eosque jubet, ut strenue pascant gregem fidelium, à Deo sibi commissum, quibus proinde ideam vitæ pastoralis paucis, sed nervose præscribit. Unde apud Syros hæc epistolæ pars legi solet in electione & ordinatione Episcoporum, ut notat hic Syrus. Hinc & mox pro providentes Græce est ἐπισκοποῦντες; ita S. Hieronymus, OEcumenius, & alii passim. Principaliter solos Episcopos compellari, ut Estius habet, minime concedendum est: Nam quod ad pasturam verbi, æque ea omnibus commissa est pastoribus, Act. XX, 28. Ideo Estius: Ad Ecclesiasticos, inquit, Pastores, id est, Episcopos sive Presbyteros exhortationem convertit. Quod autem addit: Eadem autoritate, qua admonet Episcopos Ponti, Galatiæ, Cappadociæ, Asiæ & Bithyniæ, quas regiones in fronte epistolæ nominavit, potuit & reliquos Episcopos omnes ubivis constitutos admonere; concedimus, quod ad autoritatem Apostolicam, quam cum aliis Apostolis communem habet: Quod autem hunc primatum colligere vult super universam Ecclesiam, ἀνακόλουθον est. Porro quod Estius, etsi agnoscat, nomen Presbyteri generale esse etiam usu Apostolorum, ut omnes, qui sunt ordinis Sacerdotalis, complectatur, Phil. I. 1. Tim. III. & V. Tit. I. Episcopos solos proprie & plena ratio- ne Dominici gregis pastores esse ait, id à phrasi scri- pturæ alienum est, quicquid sit de Canonibus, & quibusdam è Veteribus. Paulum Eph. IV. Pastores & Doctores nominantem solos Episcopos intelle- xisse negamus, nec id probari potest. Ad Episcopos pertinere non solum prædicare Dei verbum, & Sa- cramenta administrare, sed etiam leges ponere, & transgressores punire, & contumaces ab Ecclesia per excommunicationem ejicere. Hæc vero Epi- scopis, quales in Scriptura definiuntur, convenire ac propria esse, quomodo docebitur? Non divinæ illud constitutiones, sed humanæ sanctiones Epi- scopis non germanis, sed Papisticis vendicant. Ideo Cornelius à Lapide sacerdotium in genere hic no- tari vult, sive id minus sit & vulgare, sive majus, puta Episcopatus. Et Salmero notat: Petrum ideo non meminisse Hierarchiæ Ecclesiasticæ, quæ tot habet gradus Episcoporum, Archi-Episcoporum, Patri- archarum &c. quia institutione Ecclesiastica & Ca- nonica constat, non juris divini sunt. Vocantur au- tem Pastores Presbyteri, quia debent esse πρεσβύ- τεροι, si non ætate, senili tamen prudentia. Ambro- sius de A&olio: Vere senectus illa venerabilis est, quæ non canis, sed meritis albescit. Ea est enim reve- renda canities, quæ est canities animæ in canis co- gitationibus & operibus effulgens, unde probari non potest, quod Erasmo referente in Papatu sæ- pius eligantur ad beneficia Ecclesiastica etiam cu- rata, quæ vocant, hoc est, quæ curam animarum conjunctam habent, qui ætate adhuc sunt immatu- ra. Vulgata inserit particulam illativam ergo, quam referri Cornelius vult tum ad omnia præcedentia, quæ licet ad omnes fideles spectent, maxime tamen ad Pastores, qui ea fidelibus inculcare debeant tum proprie ad v. 11. & 17. Sed in plerisque Codicibus Græcis non habetur particula ὖν, ac si ideo ad omnia præcedentia hæc referenda, qui à Presbyte- ris inculcari omnia debent, omnia quæ in scriptu- ris traduntur, ea ratione ad Presbyteros referenda erunt, quibus tota utique Scriptura sacra commen- data est, 2. Tim. III, 15. seqq. Ad domum autem Domini pertinent omnes fideles, seu Doctores seu auditores sint. Rectius itaque abest illa illativa particula.

Verbum παρακαλῶ hic magis significare obse- cro, quam hortor, monet Cornelius, quod modestiæ causa Petrus non tam jubeat, quam precetur & ob- secret: Sed id in gratiam Vulgatæ dicit: Quidni vero Petrus deu Apostolus autoritate divina, ac præterea impulsu Spiritus sancti scribens horte- tur? Præcepta hæc utique sunt, quæ hic tradun- tur, & imperative proponuntur: Pascite gregem Dei. παρακαλεῖν usitatius adhortari significat, quam obsecrare, ait Estius.

ὁ συμπρεσβύτερος.] Sic & Imperatores Romani milites suos commilitones vocant: & senatus partem se esse dicunt.

Comparatio hæc sine dubio eo tendit, ut prima- tui & papatui Oecumenico Pontificis Romani hoc nomen præjudicare ne credatur. Sed ille de- monstrandus ante omnia erat è scripturis non mo- do de Petro, qui nunquam illum accepit, nunquam vendicavit, sed etiam de Pontificibus Romanis, qui falso se Petri eo in axiomate Successores jactitant. Quanquam in sequiorum solum temporum Epi- scopis Romanis hunc fastum deprehendamus. De Gregorio M. certe fatetur hic ipse Cornelius à Lapi- de: S. Gregorius Romanus Pontifex noluit appellari universalis Episcopus, ne cæteris Episcopis videre- tur jus Episcopatus derogare aut minuere, quasi ipse solus revera esset Episcopus, cæteri tantum nomine- nus, ejusque duntaxat vicarii aut suffraganei. Id fecit ad retundendam insolentiam Johannis Archiepiscopi Constantinopolitani, qui nomen universalis Patriar- chæ sibi arrogabat, contra quem S. Gregorius lib. 7. epist. 69. ad Euseb. Si unus, ait, universalis est, restat ut vos Episcopi non sitis. Et l. 4. epist. 36. ad Eulog. Si unus Patriarcha universaliter dicitur, Patriarcha- rum nomen cæteris derogatur. Addere debuisset & hanc Gregorii M. sententiam libr. VI. epist. 30. ad Mauritium Augustum: Ego fidenter dico, quia quis- quis se universalem Sacerdotem vocat, vel vocari de- siderat in electione sua, Anti-Christum præcurrit, quia superbiendo se cæteris præponit: & decretum C. primæ sedes distinct. XCIX. è Concilio Africa- no: Primæ sedis Episcopus non appelletur Princeps Sacerdotum, vel summus Sacerdos, aut aliquid hu- jusmodi, sed tantum primæ sedis Episcopus. Uni- versalis autem nec etiam Romanus Pontifex appelle- tur. Ex modestia quidem Petrum se consenio- rem vocat, quia ut Apostolus longe aliis Presby- teris vel Pastoribus præeminebat, sed ut Papam vel Episcopum Oecumenicum præeminuisse et- iam super alios Apostolos, nunquam demonstra- bitur. Ideo Oecumenius non ut Pontificem, sed Apostolum eum hic spectans hanc dat paraphra- sin: Si ego, qui talium miraculorum spectator fui, at- que eorum vobis præceptor sum, non dedignor, com- presbyterum & socium vestrum me ipsum vocare, ne- que vos supra illos efferre, qui vobis subsunt, debetis. Compresbyterum autem se in hac exhortatione vocat, ut innuat se jure quodam alios Presbyteros monere, quum sit unus ex eorum numero. Ad hæc non imperando cogit ut Papa, sed observan- do exhortatur, ut consenior, ideoque maxime abit Pontifex Romanus à Petri more, cujus tamen se successorem venditat, cum sub gravissimis com- minationibus, pœnis, & indignatione, nescio qua, S. Apostolorum Petri & Pauli sua mandata, diplo- mata, bullas & brevia publicat.

Καὶ μάρτυς τῶν τοῦ Χριστοῦ παθημάτων.] Vidit eum Petrus vinctum. Deinde quod historia non docet, sed credibile est, audiens crucifixum, ejus quoque rei spectator esse vo- luit, sed eminus & in turba. Apostoli testium nomine emi- nenter insigniuntur Luc. XXIV, 48. Actor. I, 8. 22. II, 32. III, 15. V, 32. X, 39. 41.

Testis passionum Christi S. Petrus esse potuit ἀνυπεύθυνος, etsi non omnes actus coram intuitus sit: quia de illis etiam testatus est ex infallibili θεο- πνευσίᾳ, quæ in sensus mortalium non cadunt, ne- dum ab ipso visa sunt. Nominat autem se testem passionum, quas magnam partem oculis suis usur- pavit, ut admonitioni suæ de pascendo grege, que Dominus suo sanguine sibi mercatus est, eo ma- gis pareant, Act. XX, 28. quum ipse, quantum ideo sustinuerit Dominus, testari possit ex vero. Ad pas- siones propter Christum sustinendas hæc nihil fa- ciunt, nisi quantum testis hic cum aliis Apostolis multum testimonii sui causa sustinere necesseum ha- buit, quod Johannes se participem factum in tri- bulatione dixit, Apoc. I, 9. quod vero his verbis mi- nime innuitur. Alienæ ergo sunt explicationes Cor- nelii, non illa tantum, quod testem passionum Chri- sti se dicat, earum scilicet, quas Christus in suis pa- titur, sed etiam illa, quod passionibus se pro Christo ultro exposuerit, quorum neutrum hoc loco indi- catur. Recte autem meminisse Petrum passionum Christi, ait Cornelius, tum quia eas in intimis animæ medullis gerebat, iisque excitabatur ad ardentem Christi amorem, ac labores & dolores quoslibet pro eo tolerandos: tum ut iisdem excitaret pastores Ec- clesiæ ad eorum imitationem, ut Christi amore dura qualibet paterentur & agerent ad oves ejus pascendas, pro eisque sanguinem, spiritus, & vitam exhaurirent, uti exhausit Christus. Ὁ καὶ τῆς μελλούσης ἀποκαλύπτεσθαι δόξης κοινωνός.] Supple futurus. Sic κοινωνοὶ τῆς παρακλήσεως, 2. Cor. I, 7. δόξαν μέλλουσαν ἀποκαλυφθῆναι habes & Rom. IIX, 18. Nunc jus habemus, res ipsa latet. Non κοινωνὸς dicitur active, quod aliis prædicando fidem & spem gloriæ in cælo revelandæ tradat, ut Lyranus & Carthusianus, sed passive; nec id gloriæ Christi in monte Thabor, ut Cajetanus, aut in resurrectione, ascensione ac missione Spiritus sancti conspectæ, ut Glossa, Hugo, & alii volunt; sed gloriæ, quam post hanc vitam se participaturum certus erat, quod Oecumenius tradit & Cajetanus agnoscit, conf. Rom. IIX, 17. 1. Petr. I, 5. 2. Cor. IV, 7. Nervum argumenti talem esse, dicit B. Gerhardus: Gloria cælestis mea in officio fidelitatis merces mihi vobiscum communis erit, si ipsimet quoque debitam in officio diligentiam adhibueritis. Ergo æquum est, admonitioni meæ locum à vobis relinqui. Gloriæ cælestis meminit, inquit Cornelius, tum quia mente versabatur in cælis, & ad gloriam cælestem anhelabat, tum ut Pastorum & fidelium animos ad cælestia raperet, eorumque spe animaret ad omnes labores & agones, pro Christo fortiter subeundos v. 4. Non ergo recte reddit Vulgatus Communicator, quod activum est: quod vitium notavit non immerito Estius: Communicator inquit proprie non dicitur, qui fit consors, sed qui consortes alios facit, quod Petrus adscribere sibi non voluit. Certum autem fuisse Petrum de salute sua hæc docent, quod utrum ex speciali revelatione habuerit, an vero bonæ ac Christianæ spei hæc tantum verba sint, Estio non liquet. Lorinus autem ex prægustu felicitatis non tantum ipsum habuisse ait, sed quod etiam inde argumentari alios id velit, fore ut cum apparuerit Princeps Pastorum, gloriæ coronam percipiant: Conf. Rom. IIX, 29. 2. Cor. IV, 13. 14.

## 5:2
Ver. 2.

Feed the flock of God which is among you.] What Christ had commanded Peter, John 21:15, 16, 17, Peter commands others. To feed (ποιμαίνειν) is to rule, as appears both from the cited place of John and Matt. 2:6, thus also Acts 20:28; thus the Hebrew רָעָה is also attributed to Kings, as 2 Sam. 5:2, ch. 7:7, Psalm 78:71. But the things which follow here sufficiently show that royal government is not understood here, but that which is exercised by persuading, not by compelling. 'Among you' (ἐν ὑμῖν), that is, the flock which is in your localities.

The word 'to feed' (ποιμαίνειν) is translated by the Vulgate not as 'to rule' but 'to feed', thus also John 21:17, and rule is forbidden to Pastors by Peter, 'not as being lords over the clergy', and John Hesselius explains that 'to rule' in Estius in this way: 'The sheep of Christ are ruled pastorally while the food of Christian doctrine is provided to them, not only by public preachings and exhortations, but also by secret and private instructions, consolations, and corrections. Likewise: While the sacraments of Christ are diligently administered to them, while the best examples of life are proposed to them, then their temporal necessities are cheerfully relieved, while useful laws and precepts are prescribed, while one prays, groans, weeps, and sacrifices for them most solicitously and frequently before God.' Such rule, provided that which is added about laws and sacrifice is easily admitted to befit Bishops: namely, that which is done by the staff of the word. Bernard, sermon on the resurrection. Feed, he says, with the mind, feed with the mouth, feed with the work: Feed with the prayer of the soul, the exhortation of the word, the exhibition of example. Christ provides the example, Ezek. 34:15, 16, Ps. 23:1 ff., John 10:11. Concerning such an office of feeding, also Jer. 3:15, Ezek. 34:1 ff. That 'among you' (ἐν ὑμῖν) Erasmus and Calvin wrongly [translate as] 'as much as is in you', for that is τὸ καθ'

you. Arias also absurdly [translates] 'in you', 'within yourselves', as if the flock of God were in individual men, that is, that individuals belong to this flock. A peculiar argument of the admonition lies in the word 'flock of God', because they ought to care for the same as God's property, Acts 20:28, and because it is not their own flock, but God's, to whom an account must be rendered concerning it. But how Papal Bishops and Prelates perform their duty to Peter, let them see to it themselves. Claudius Espensaeus certainly, in 1 Tim. 1:11, digress. ch. 1, 2, complains about it at length: 'How many of the greater or lesser Prelates seem to teach their own people.' Therefore, if it is said that it is enough to labor through a vicar, the answer is not badly returned to them: 'Then let it be enough also to eat through a vicar.' For it is written, he who does not labor, let him not eat. The name of Pastor, as Maldonatus has in summ. quaest. 10, art. 3, signifies a personal action, just like the name 'physician'. Therefore, just as no one can cure through another: So no one can feed his sheep through another.

Taking the oversight (Ἐπισκοποῦντες).] פקדים. Thus also Presbyters are called 'overseers' (ἐπίσκοποι), Acts 20:28, which name adhered to the Prince of the assembly by excellence.

Not from the usage of Scripture, but of the later Church. The Vulgate rendered it 'providing', Hieronymus in epistle 85 to Evagrius 'superintending'. Augustine in book 19 of The City of God, ch. 19: 'If we wish to say Ἐπισκοπεῖν in Latin, we can say 'to superintend', so that he understands that he is not a Bishop who has loved to preside, not to be useful.' For Ἐπισκοπεῖν is to take diligent care of someone, Heb. 12:15, Deut. 11:12. Ambrosius on the dignity of the priesthood, ch. 6, interprets a Bishop as a 'super-inspector'. The Syrian rendered it by the name of visitor or curator. To which it contributes that in the Old Testament the Prophets were called 'watchmen', Isa. 52:8, ch. 56:10, Jer. 6:17, Ezek. 3:17, ch. 33:2, Hos. 9:8. Just as Isidorus, book 7, Etymologies, ch. 12, in C. Cleros dist. 21: 'Bishops are interpreted in Greek, in Latin as watchmen.' Pastors ought not only to feed (ποιμαίνειν), but also to oversee (ἐπισκοπεῖν). It is the duty of pastors to watch, says Bernard, over the flock for three necessary reasons, namely for discipline, for protection, for prayers: For discipline, for the correction of morals, lest the flock committed to them fail through its own trouble: For protection, because of diabolical suggestion, lest it be seduced by hostile cunning; for prayers, because of the urgency of temptations, lest it be overcome by faint-heartedness.

Μὴ ἀναγκαστῶς, ἀλλ᾽ ἑκουσίως.] That is, do not grieve as if a burden were imposed; but do with a joyful mind what is your duty. Thus Thucydides: Ἀναγκαστοὶ ἐκβάντες, when they went out unwillingly. The Chaldeans would say מֵאֹנוּס, for that which is here ἀναγκαστῶς; the Apostle Paul said in a similar matter ἄκων, 1 Cor. IX, 17. ἑκουσίως with a ready mind בִּבְרָכָה, Psalm LIV, 7. In the manuscript it is ἑκουσίως κατὰ τὸν Θεὸν, that is, for God's sake. And thus the Latin reads. Thus Philo also opposes doing things by necessity and willingly: Μὴ φόβῳ τὸ δίκαιον δρῶντες, ἀλλ᾽ ἑκουσίῳ γνώμῃ. For things done not by necessity, the unaccountable achievement is more honorable everywhere.

That ἀναγκαστῶς does not refer to the flock, in that commands ought not to be given to them by force, which Nazianzen seems to have wished in his Apology and Cornelius contends, but to the Pastors, that they ought not to perform their duty by compulsion or unwillingly, which is done by hirelings, but with a prompt and liberal mind, whence the office of shepherding should not be thrust upon one who is unwilling or reluctant, just as Gregory the Great, book IV, epistle 35, professes of himself, that he never wished to force anyone into the Episcopate. And Blessed Luther on this passage says: those who perform their duty by compulsion do not provide useful service to the Church.

Μηδὲ αἰσχροκερδῶς.] Not that you should turn this function into an occasion for gain. You have the same in 1 Tim. III, 3, 8; Tit. I, 7. Add 1 Tim. VI, 8, 9. The Hebrews would say: לֹא לְבֶצַע. Do not be like that shepherd of whom Zechariah XI, 16 speaks.

The Vulgate [says] not for the sake of filthy lucre, but voluntarily, which Erasmus explained as with willing minds, others as with a ready mind. See Rom. I, 15. Acts XVII, 11. 2 Cor. VIII, 11. ch. IX, 2. 1 Chron. XXIX, 17. Johannes Huss from Gilbert in this place: He is not spontaneous whom poverty urges, nor voluntary whom greed draws. Primasius on 1 Tim. III: Filthy lucre, he says, is to seek earthly wealth from heavenly sacraments. Where the greed for gain reigns, says B. Luther in this place, pastors easily become mercenaries, nay, wolves: Cf. Ezek. XIII, 18. There is nothing that more hinders the Episcopal function and dishonors the name of Bishop than the corruption of gifts, says Guillandres in this place. And therefore Bede here commends the example of the Israelites in the construction of the tabernacle, where both the whole multitude of the children of Israel offered the firstfruits to the Lord with a most ready and devoted mind, and the craftsmen themselves offered themselves willingly to do the work.

But willingly.] ישׁרהוּ לבב with a right mind, that is, most excellently, affected toward the people. The Syrian here [has] מן כלה לבבך from all your heart.

The Apostle removes three vices: 1. ἀκηγίαν, weariness, sloth, and drowsiness, to which he opposes alacrity; 2. ἀισχροκερδίαν, or avarice, to which he opposed readiness; 3. Φιλοπρωΐαν, the lust for dominating, to which he opposes being a pattern of the flock and humility. For those who arrogate lordship to themselves do not shine forth to their hearers by the example of a holy life and especially of humility, but compel them by command. Concerning which Bede in this place: Being made a pattern of the flock, so that, namely, the humility which he desires that you have both toward those subject to you and toward one another, you yourselves may first demonstrate, and keep in your mind, entirely.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Ποιμάνατε τὸ ἐν ὑμῖν ποίμνιον τοῦ Θεοῦ.] Quod Christus Petro præceperat, Joh. XXI, 15. 16. 17. idem Petrus aliis. Ποιμαίνειν est regere, ut apparet tum dicto Johannis loco, tum Matth. II, 6. sic & Act. XX, 28. sic Ebræum רָעָה etiam Regibus tribuitur, ut 2. Sam. V, 2. c. VII, 7. Psalm. LXXVIII, 71. Sed quæ hic sequuntur, satis ostendunt non Regiam hic gubernationem intelligi, sed eam, quæ suadendo, non quæ cogendo exerceatur. Ἐν ὑμῖν, id est, gregem, qui in vestris est locis.

Vox ποιμαίνειν à Vulgata non regere sed pascere vertitur, sic & Joh. XXI, 17. & prohibetur regimen Pastoribus à Petro, non dominantes clero, explicatque Joh. Hesselius illud regere apud Estium hoc modo: Reguntur autem oves Christi pastoraliter, dum eis præbetur pabulum doctrinæ Christianæ, non tantum publicis prædicationibus & exhortationibus, sed etiam secretis atque privatis institutionibus, consolationibus, correptionibus. Item: Dum eis sedulo administrantur sacramenta Christi, dum eis optima vitæ exempla proponuntur, tum temporalibus eorum necessitatibus hilariter succurritur, dum utiles leges & præcepta præscribuntur, dum admodum sollicite frequenterque pro eis apud Deum oratur, ingemiscitur, ploratur, sacrificatur. Quale regimen modo id, quod de legibus & sacrificio additur, facile admittimus Episcopis convenire: quod scilicet pedo verbi fit. Bernardus serm. de resurr. Pasce, inquit, mente, pasce ore, pasce opere: Pasce animi oratione, verbi exhortatione, exempli exhibitione. Exemplum præbet Christus Ezech. XXXIV, 15. 16. Psal. XXIII, 1. seqq. Joh. X, 11. De tali pascendi officio etiam Jerem. III, 15. Ezech. XXIII, 1. seqq. Illud ἐν ὑμῖν perperam Erasmus & Calvinus, quantum in vobis est, id enim est τὸ καθ'

ὑμᾶς. Absurde etiam Arias in vobis, intra vos ipsos, quasi in singulis hominibus sit grex Dei, hoc est, singuli pertineant ad hunc gregem. Latet ad- monitionis peculiare argumentum in voce gregis Dei, quod eundem ceu Dei peculium curare de- beant, Asct. XX, 28. quodque non proprius ipso- rum, sed Dei grex sit, cui reddenda de illo ratio. Quomodo autem Episcopi & Prælati Papales Pe- tro morem gerant, viderint ipsi. Claudius certe Espensæus in 1. Tim. I, 11. digress. c. 1, 2. queritur de eo prolixe: Quotusquisque Prælatorum majorum minorumve populum suum docere videtur. Itaque si dicatur satis esse per vicarium laborare; respon- sum non male redditur ipsis: Satis ergo esto etiam per vicarium manducare. Nam scriptum est, qui non laborat, non manducet. Nomen Pastoris, ut Mal- donatus habet summ. quæst.10. art.3. significat actio- nem personalem, sicut nomen medicus. Itaque sicut nemo per alium potest curare: Ita nemo potest suas oves per alium pascere.

Ἐπισκοποῦντες.] פקדים. Sic & Presbyteri vocantur ἐπί- σκοποι, Actor. XX, 28. quod nomen per excellentiam Principi cœtus adhæsit.

Non ex usu scripturæ, sed sequioris Ecclesiæ. Vulgatus reddidit providentes, Hieronymus epist. XXCV. ad Evagrium superintendentes. Augustinus libr. XIX. de civ. Dei c. 19. Ἐπισκοπεῖν si velimus La- tine superintendere possumus dicere, ut intelligat, non se esse Episcopum, qui præesse dilexerit, non prodesse. Ἐπισκοπεῖν enim est curam alicujus diligenter ge- rere, Ebr. XII, 15. Deut. XI, 12. Ambrosius de dignit. sacerd. c. 6. Episcopum interpretatur superinspecto- rem. Syrus visitatoris vel curatoris nomine red- didit. Quo facit, quod in Veteri Testamento Pro- phetæ speculatores dicti, Esa. LII, 8. cap. LVI, 10. Jerem. VI, 17. Ezech. III, 17. cap. XXXIII, 2. Ose. IX, 8. Quomodo Isidorus l. VII. Etym. c. 12. in C. Cle- ros dist. XXI. Episcopi Græce, Latine speculatores in- terpretantur. Pastores non solum debent ποιμαίνειν, sed etiam ἐπισκοπεῖν. Pastorum est vigilare, inquit Bernhardus, super gregem propter tria necessaria, videlicet ad disciplinam, ad custodiam, ad preces: Ad disciplinam propter morum correctionem, ne grex commissus propria molestia deficiat: Ad custo- diam propter diabolicam suggestionem, ne hostili seducatur calliditate; ad preces, propter tenta- tionum instantiam, ne vincatur à pusillanimi- tate.

Μὴ ἀναγκαστῶς, ἀλλ᾽ ἑκουσίως.] Id est, ne dolete quasi one- re imposito; sed læto animo facite quod vestri officii est. Sic Thucydides: Ἀναγκαστοὶ ἐκβάντες, cum inviti exirent. Chal- dæi dicerent מֵאֹנוּס, pro eo, quod hic est ἀναγκαστῶς dixit in re pari ἄκων Apostolus Paulus 1. Cor. IX, 17. ἑκουσίως alacri animo בִּבְרָכָה, Psal. LIV, 7. In Manuscripto est ἑκουσίως κα- τὰ τὸν Θεὸν, id est, Dei causa. Et sic legit Latinus. Sic necessi- tate & sponte facere opponit & Philo: Μὴ φόβῳ τὸ δίκαιον δρῶντες, ἀλλ᾽ ἑκουσίῳ γνώμῃ. Τὰ γὰρ μὴ’ ἀνάγκης τὸ ἀνυπεύ- θυνον κατόρθωμα τιμιώτερον πανταχοῦ.

Non ad gregem illud ἀναγκαστῶς spectat, quod illi non debeant coacta dari imperia, quod videtur voluisse Nazianz. in Apol. & contendit Cornelius, sed ad Pastores, quod non coacti vel inviti officium facere debeant, quod à mercenariis fit, sed prom- pto & liberali animo, unde nec invito vel reluctan- ti pascendi munus obtrudendum, quemadmo- dum Gregorius M. l. IV. epist. 35. de se profitetur, quod neminem unquam ad Episcopatum cogere voluerit. Et B. Lutherus in h. l. qui coacti, inquit officium faciunt, non præstant utilem Ecclesiæ operam.

Μηδὲ αἰσχροκερδῶς.] Non ut functionem hanc in occa- sionem lucri vertatis. Idem habes 1. Tim. III, 3. 8. Tit. I, 7. Adde 1. Tim. VI, 8. 9. Ebræi dicerent: לֹא לְבֶצַע. Ne sitis similes isti pastori, de quo Zach. XI, 16.

Vulgatus neque turpis lucri gratia, sed voluntarie, quod Erasmus animis propensis, alii prompto animo exposuere. Vid. Rom. I, 15. Actor. XVII, 11. 2. Cor. IIX, 11. cap. IX, 2. 1. Par. XXIX, 17. Johannes Huss ex Gilberto in h. l. Non est spontaneus, quem paupertas urget, aut voluntarius, quem cupiditas trahit. Primasius in 1. Tim. III. Turpe lucrum, inquit, est, de cœlestibus sacramentis terrenas opes conquirere. Ubi lucri cupiditas regnat, ait B. Lutherus in h. l. Pastores facile fiunt mercenarii, imo lupi: Conf. Ezech. XIII, 18. nihil est, quod magis Episcopalem functionem impediat, & Episcopi nomen dehonestet, quam munerum corruptela, inquit Guillandres in h. l. Ideoque Beda hic commendat exemplum Israëlitarum in constructione tabernaculi, ubi & omnis multitudo filiorum Israël obtulit mente promptissima atque devota primitias Domino, & ipsi artifices sponte obtulerunt se ad faciendum opus.

Α᾿λλὰ προθύμως.] ישׁרהוּ לבב animo recto, id est, optime, erga plebem affecto. Syrus hic מן כלה לבבך ex toto corde.

Tria removet Apostolus vitia, 1. ἀκηγίαν tædium, ignaviam ac somnolentiam, cui opponit alacritatem, 2. ἀισχροκερδίαν sive avaritiam, cui opposuit προθυμίαν, 3. Φιλοπρωΐαν, dominandi libidinem, cui typum esse gregis & humilitatem opponit. Qui enim dominium sibi arrogant, non prælucent Auditoribus sanctæ vitæ & imprimis humilitatis exemplo, sed cogunt eos imperio. Quo de Beda in h. l. Forma gregis facti, ut videl. humilitatem, quam subditos & ad vos & ad invicem habere desiderat is, ipsi prius ad demonstretis, & in animo servetis, ex integro.

## 5:3
Verse 3. Neither as lording it over the heritages.] Formerly the Israelite people [were] the heritage, or patrimony of God, Deut. VI, 20. IX, 29. Now the Christian people, whose individual parts, as is wont to happen, in things of the same kind, participate in the same name. And so the Syrian here placed המסרעתא for the flock; to lord it is רדה, to rule in a kingly manner, at one's pleasure, as we said at Matt. XX, 25. and in book II of the Law of War and Peace XXII, 14. in the text and annotations. The Syrian [says] not as Lords of the flock: The Vulgate: Neither as lording it over the clergy. It is not tyrannical domination that is forbidden, as Cornelius explains with Bellarmine, book V de R. P. ch. 10, but domination simply, which Grotius acknowledged here: Therefore not only the word 'lording it' (κατακυριεύειν), which could be taken in a bad sense because of the particle 'kata', but 'to rule' (κυριεύειν) is also forbidden, or domination itself, just as that word 'lording it' is taken in Acts XIX, 15, and it is evident from a comparison of Matt. XX, 25, Luke XXII, 29, 2 Cor. I, 24. Ecclesiastical persons are ministers of the Church, therefore they ought not to preside as Lords and Princes by example, as a pattern of the flock, not by command, by the force of the Apostolic opposition. Augustine in his Rule, praised by Cornelius à Lapide, says of himself: Let him who presides over you consider himself happy not by dominating greed, but by fervent charity. Erasmus in this place: Do not dominate in the manner of Kings, but feed by example, overcome by good deeds. Now the crowd of Bishops hears nothing from learned flatterers but lordships, dominions, swords, keys, powers, and hence the pride of some is more than royal, their cruelty more than tyrannical. Estius: Not only are they said to dominate over others who turn and refer the power which they have over them to their own utility, such as the power of Masters over servants: But also those who rule in the manner of the Princes of this age with an ostentation of power, and do not go out in public except with a retinue and a pomp of followers, namely to strike terror into their subjects. Yet Christ wished that in the Pastors and Rulers of the Church humility and gentleness should appear more than the ostentation and severity of power, and love more than terror: So that there may be absent not only the mind, but even the appearance of dominating over the subject people, and that they may rather conduct themselves through humility as their Ministers, procuring their spiritual utility with all zeal, according to what the Lord consequently commands in the same place: But whoever wishes to become greater among you, let him be your Minister. Which ministry indeed consists not only in teaching and commanding, but also in exhibiting examples of holy conversation.

By the name of the heritages is not understood the clergy, whom the Papists call [so], or the sacred assembly assigned to the ministry of the altar, as Salmero wished, and indeed even Jerome in his epistle to Nepotianus, which sense Cornelius said was very fitting. [It is] the flock of God, as the Apostle called it in the preceding verse, just as not only in the cited places, but also Deut. XXXII, 9, 2 Sam. XXI, 3, Ps. XXXIII, 12, Ps. LXXIV, 2, Ps. LXXVIII, 71, Isa. XIX, 25, and elsewhere Israel is called the inheritance of the Lord. Moreover, by the plural name are designated the portions which, as if by lot, fall to the Bishops by divine lot, as is wont to happen in an inheritance, cf. Ps. LXXVIII, Judg. I, 3, ch. XX, 4. Which sense of the heritages Cyril [gives in] book I on Isaiah, oration 3. Bede and Oecumenius in this place, as well as Jansenius in Psalm 77, approve, and Estius confirms it in this way: It is far more probable that by 'cleros' are understood the portions of the Lord's flock which have fallen to individual Bishops to be fed and governed as if by lot, according to that which Cyprian says, that the Church is one, of which individual bishops hold individual portions in their entirety. The phrase is taken from lot (for κλῆρος signifies a lot) which the ancients also used by God's command in distributing the land to individuals for possession. For hence the parts which had fallen to individuals were called κλῆροι, that is, lots. Whence Psalm 77: 'If you sleep among the middle of the lots,' that is, in the middle of your lots. Certainly, the adversative which Peter makes sufficiently argues that the whole flock is understood here by the name of 'clerus': 'Not lording it over the clergy, but being made patterns of the flock,' as if 'clerus' and 'flock' were the same. Wherefore the Syriac Interpreter also wrote 'flock' instead of 'clergy,' not 'the Lord's flock.' Finally, it is not customary to call Clerics 'cleros' in the plural, but 'clerus' as a collective noun. Therefore, Cornelius wrongly notes here the ancient appellation of 'clerus' attributed to Clerics, as they are called, comparing Acts 1:17. For even if the occasion for this name could have arisen from there, because Matthias was chosen by lot, yet neither there nor anywhere in the scriptures is that name attributed to an Ecclesiastical person.

Ἀλλὰ τύποι γινόμενοι τοῦ ποιμνίου.] Teach those things which you yourselves also do, otherwise than the Scribes and Pharisees, Matt. 23:4. Τύπος in this place signifies a pattern, as also Exod. 25:40, Philip. 3:17, 1 Thess. 1:7, 2 Thess. 3:9, 1 Tim. 4:12, Tit. 2:7. Latinus Pacatus: 'He is most gently commanded by example.' Cicero on the Senate: 'Let that order be free from vice: let it be a specimen to the rest.'

Cornelius rightly says: he opposes this form to domination, as if to say, do not lord it over them by command, but by example, so that they may prescribe a form of holy life to the faithful by living holily. Chrysostom, Tit. 2:7: 'Let your teaching be a pattern to all, and your life a mirror of your virtue, which is proposed to all for imitation, like some primary image, having in itself all things which are good and honest.' Let life command, let the tongue persuade, says Athanasius to the Monks. Gregory the Great, part 1, Pastoral Care, ch. 3: 'Let the Pastor,' he says, 'be preeminent in action, so that he may proclaim the way of life to his subjects by living it, and the flock, which follows the voice and manners of the Pastor, may walk better by examples than by words. That voice penetrates the hearts of the hearers more willingly which the life of the speaker commends: And the best pastures of all are the examples of the Pastor.' And in ch. 28 of Job: 'The law is laid upon preachers, that they fulfill what they hasten to urge by speaking. For the authority of speaking is lost when the voice is not aided by action. That voice penetrates the heart of the listener which confirms by action what it has sounded. Here Estius again corrects the Vulgate: The Greek and Syriac do not have the addition, 'from the heart'; Bernard also does not add it, citing this passage in epistle 237. Furthermore, there is not the form in the Greek, but τύποι, forms, in the plural number, which many approved Latin Codices, both ancient and more recent, also read. Nor is the word added in the Seventh Synod, canon 4, or in Ephrem the Syrian.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Μηδ᾽ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων.] Olim populus Israëlïticus κλῆρος, sive patrimonium Dei, Deut. VI, 20. IX, 29. Nunc populus Christianus, cujus singulæ partes, ut fieri solet, ἐν ὁμογένοις, idem nomen participat. Itaque Syrus hic posuit המסרעתא gregi, κατακυριεύειν רדה est Regio more imperare, pro lubitu, ut diximus ad Matth. XX, 25. & libro II. de jure belli & pacis XXII, 14. in textu & annotatis. Syrus non tanquam Domini gregis: Vulgata: Neque ut dominantes in cleris. Prohibetur non tyrannicus dominatus, ut Cornelius exponit cum Bellarm. l. V. de R. P. c. 10. sed dominatus simpliciter, quod hic agnovit Grotius: Ideo non solum τὸ κατακυριεύειν, quod in malam partem accipi posset ob particulam κατὰ, sed κυριεύειν etiam prohibetur, vel ipse dominatus, uti vox illa κατακυριεύειν, Act. XIX, 15. accipitur, & è collatione Matth. XX, 25. Luc. XXII, 29. 2. Cor. I, 24. constat. Personæ Ecclesiasticæ ministri sunt Ecclesiæ, non ergo Domini ac Principes exemplo præesse debent, ceu typus gregis, non imperio, vi oppositionis Apostolicæ. Augustinus in Regula laudante Cornelio à Lapide de se ait: Qui vobis præest, æstimet se non dominante cupiditate, sed charitate fervente felicem. Erasmus in h. l. Non dominantes more Regum, sed exemplo pascite, benefactis vincite. Nunc Episcoporum vulgus nihil audit àb assentatoribus doctis nisi dominia, ditiones, gladios, claves, potestates, atque hinc fastas quorundam plus quam Regius, sævitia plusquam Tyrannica. Estius: Non solum dominari dicuntur in alios, qui potestatem, quam super illos habent, ad suam ipsorum convertunt ac referunt utilitatem, cujusmodi potestas est Dominorum in servos: Verum etiam qui more Principum hujus seculi imperant cum ostentatione potestatis, nec nisi cum satellitio & pompa asseclarum prodeunt in publicum, scilicet ut terrorem subditis incutiant. Atqui Christus voluit in Pastoribus & Rectoribus Ecclesiæ magis apparere humilitatem & mansuetudinem, quam potestatis ostentationem atque severitatem, & amorem magis, quam terrorem: Ut absit non solum animus, sed species etiam dominandi in plebem subjectam, patiusque sese per humilitatem gerant, ut Ministros eorum, quibus præsunt, utilitatem ipsorum spiritua- lem omni studio procurantes, juxta quod Dominus ibidem consequenter præcipit: Sed quicunque vo- luerit inter vos major fieri, sit vester Minister. Quod quidem ministerium consistit non solum in docendo ac præcipiendo, verum etiam in exhibendis sanctæ conversationis exemplis.

Nomine τῶν κλήρων non intelligitur clerus, quem Papistæ vocant, vel sacer cœtus ministerio altaris adscriptus, ut Salmero voluit, imo & Hieronymus in epist. ad Nepot. quem sensum valde congruum dixit Cornelius. Tò ποίμνιον τοῦ Θεοῦ, uti Apostolus vocavit v. præcedente, quemadmodum non tan- tum locis citatis, sed & Deut. XXXII, 9. 2. Sam. XXI, 3. Psal. XXXIII, 12. Psal. LXXIV, 2. Psal. LXXIIX, 71. Esa. XIX, 25. & alibi Israel hæreditas Domini dicitur. Plurali autem nomine portio- nes designantur, quæ veluti sortito Episcopis obti- gere divina sorte, ut in hæreditate fieri solet, conf. Psal. LXXIIX, Jud. I, 3. cap. XX, 4. Quem sen- sum τῶν κλήρων Cyrillus l. I. in Es. orat. 3. Beda & Oecumenius in h. l. necnon Jansenius in Psalm. LXXVII. approbant, confirmatque Estius hoc modo: Longe probabilius est, per cleros intelligi gre- gis Dominici portiones, quæ singulis Episcopis pa- scendæ ac regendæ velut sortito obtigerunt, juxta id, quod Cyprianus dicit, Ecclesiam esse unam, cujus singulas portiones singuli Episcopi in solidum tenent. Phrasis desumpta à sorte (nam slerus sortem signifi- cat) qua veteres etiam ex Dei præcepto utebantur in distribuenda terra singulis in possessionem. Hinc enim partes, qua singulis obvenerant, κλῆροι, id est, sortes vocabantur. Unde Psal. LXXVH. Si dormia- tis inter medios cleros, id est, in medio sortium ve- strarum. Sane totum gregem nomine cleri hic intelli- gi satis arguit adversativa, quam Petrus facit: Non dominantes in cleris, sed formæ facti gregis, tanquam idem sit clerus & grex. Quapropter & Syrus Inter- pres pro cleris gregem scripsit, non tanquam Domini gregis. Denique nec consuetum est Clericos appellare cleros pluraliter, sed clerum nomine collectivo. Perpe- ram ergo Cornelius hic antiquam appellationem cleri Clericis, quos vocant, tributam notat, confe- rens Act. I, 17. Nam etsi inde occasio hujus nomi- nis oriri potuerit, quod Matthias sorte electus, nec ibi tamen, nec uspiam in scripturis id nominis tri- butum est personæ Ecclesiasticæ.

Ἀλλὰ τύποι γινόμενοι τοῦ ποιμνίου.] Ea præcipite, quæ & ipsi faciatis, aliter quam Scribæ & Pharisæi, Matth. 23, 4. Τύπος hoc loco exemplar significat, ut & Exod. 25, 40. Philip. 3, 17. 1.Thess. I, 7. 2. Thess. 3, 9. 1.Tim. 4, 12. Tit. 2, 7. Latinus Paca- tus: Blandissime jubetur exemplo. Cicero de Senatu: Is or- do vitio vacato: Cæteris specimen esto.

Recte Cornelius: formam hanc opponit domi- nationi, q. d. non dominentur imperio, sed exemplo, ut formam vitæ sanctæ sancte vivendo fidelibus præscribant. Chrysostomus Tit. II, 7. Sit omnibus do- ctrina exemplar que tuæ virtutis speculum vita, quod omnibus ad imitandum proponitur, veluti primaria quædam imago, omnia in se habens, qua bona & ho- nesta sunt. Vita jubeat, lingua persuadeat, ait Atha- nasius ad Monach. Gregor. M. part. I. pastor. c. 3. Sit Pastor, inquit, operatione præcipuus, ut vitæ viam subditis vivendo denunciet, & grex, qui Pasto- ris vocem, moresque sequitur per exempla melius, quam per verba gradiatur. Illa vox libentius audi- torum corda penetrat, quam dicentis vita comen- dat: Et optima omnium pascua sunt exempla Pa- storis. Et in cap. XXVIII. Jobi: Lex est prædicato- ribus posita, ut impleant, quod loquendo suadere festinant. Nam loquendi autoritas perditur, quando vox opere non adjuvatur. Illa vox cor audientis penetrat, quæ hoc, quod sonuerit, opere confirmat. Emendat hic iterum Vulgatam Estius: Græca & Syra non habent additum, ex animo, Bernhardus quoque non addit, citans hunc locum epistola 237. Deinde nec est in Græco forma, sed τύποι formæ, plurali numero, quod & legunt multi probatique Codices Latini tam vetusti, quam recentiores. Nec additum verbum ex animo Synodo VII. can. 4. aut apud Ephrem Syrum.

## 5:4
Verse 4.

And when the chief shepherd shall appear.] We have the word ἀρχιποίμην in 2 Kings 3:4; such is that one in Seneca's Oedipus: 'The crowd of shepherds under him was smaller.' For the same, the writer to the Hebrews said τὸν μέγαν ποιμένα in chapter 13:20. Φανερωθέντος is said as in Colossians 3:4, 'when Christ shall appear' (ὅταν ὁ Χριστὸς φανερωθῇ).

You shall receive the unfading crown of glory.] Κομίζεσθαι is elegantly used regarding a reward, as above 1:9, Hebrews 10:36, 11:39, 2 Corinthians 5:10, Ephesians 6:8. στέφανος δόξης is עטרת תפארת, Jeremiah 13:8, Proverbs 16:31, Ezekiel 16:12, chapter 23:42. Thus those crowns were called which were taken during festive times or in the height of joy. Peter, however, elegantly added ἀμαράντινον here. For among the crowns that were given to those who deserved well among the Greeks and other nations, there were στέφανοι ἀμαράντινοι, as Philostratus teaches us in his Heroicus. Pliny, however, on the Amaranth, book 20: 'The sum of its nature is in its name, so called because it does not wither.' Hence this allegory is drawn, simultaneously looking back to that of Psalm 1:3, 'His leaf shall not fall.' Thus also above 1:4 he said κληρονομίαν ἀμάραντον; you have the opposite in Isaiah 40:7, נבל ציץ, James 1:10, 11, above 1:24.

By the example of the Master, he proposes to the Pastors the hope of a reward in heaven, Matthew 24:45, chapter 25:4. Compare Daniel 12:3, 2 Timothy 4:8. The coming of Christ is Φανέρωσις, 1 John 2:28; ἐπιφάνεια τοῦ Χριστοῦ, 1 Timothy 6:14, 2 Timothy 4:1; τῆς δόξης, Titus 2:13; τῆς παρουσίας, 2 Thessalonians 2:8; ἀποκάλυψις, 1 Corinthians 1:7, 2 Thessalonians 3:7; therefore he affirms the presence of Christ, he does not remove it, as the Calvinists wish, even if it is now invisible, Matthew 18:20, chapter 28:19, which will be conspicuous on that day. By the crown of glory, however, is not designated an aureola or laureola of faithful Pastors, or a higher degree of eternal life above others, as Hugo, Thomas Anglicus, and Salmero wish, but eternal life itself: Concerning which Estius says: Hesselius wants a very glorious crown. For he says it does not simply signify eternal life, but a higher degree above others. Whence in Daniel 12, when it had been said that the good would go into eternal life, concerning the eminent reward of Pastors it follows: 'But they that are learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and they that instruct many to justice, as stars for all eternity.' There are those who interpret this crown as an aureola, which is attributed to Doctors, such as Hugo Cardinalis and Thomas Anglicus. But it is more probable that the principal reward is understood, which is also accustomed to be signified elsewhere by the name of a crown, as in James 1. Στέφανος δόξης is said, either so that it is a genitive of species, 'you will receive glory, which will be as a crown,' or it is placed in the position of an adjective through a Hebraism, that is, a very glorious crown. It is called a crown, both because we will be heirs of the heavenly kingdom and Kings, and because the glory will be eternal, as Lyranus says in this place. Eternal life is a crown, because it has neither beginning nor end. He calls it unfading, as Estius advises, in contrast to the crowns which are given among us to victors. For they are woven from flowers and leaves, which wither a little later. But that heavenly crown will neither wither nor grow old ever, but will always retain the grace of freshness and bloom. But what he infers concerning merit is an anacoluthon: For every comparison is dissimilar: for the Apostle does not imply that we, by fighting and conquering, merit the glory of the heavenly kingdom, but that we attain heaven, as it is a gratuitous reward, Romans 6:last. Heavenly glory, says Lyranus in chapter 10 of John, is rendered to the faithful, just as an inheritance to children, for which reason it does not have the nature of a wage.

PART II. A common exhortation concerning humility, confidence, and vigilance.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Καὶ φανερωθέντος τοῦ ἀρχιποιμένος.] Vocem ἀρχιποίμην habemus 2. Reg. III, 4. talis ille in Oedipode Senecæ: Minor sub illo turba pastorum fuit. Pro eadem τὸν μέγαν ποιμένα dixit scriptor ad Hebræos c. XIII, 20. Φανερωθέντος dictum ut Coloss. III, 4. ὅταν ὁ Χριστὸς φανερωθῇ.

Κομιεῖσθε τὸν ἀμαράντινον τῆς δόξης στέφανον.] Κομίζεσθαι eleganter de præmio dicitur ut supra I, 9. Ebr. X, 36. XI. 39. 2. Cor. V, 10. Eph. VI, 8. στέφανος δόξης עטרת תפארת Jer. 13, 8. Prov. 16, 31. Ezech. 16, 12. c. 23, 42. Ita dicebantur coronæ illæ, quæ sumebantur temporibus festis aut in summo gaudio. Eleganter autem Petrus hic addidit ἀμαράντινον. Nam inter coronas, quæ dabantur bene meritis apud Græcos & gentes alias erant στέφανοι ἀμαράντινοι, ut nos docet Philostratus heroicis. Plinius autem de Amaranto libr. XX. Summa natura ejus in nomine est, appellato, quoniam non marcescat. Hinc ducta hæc allegoria, simul respiciens ad illud Psalmi I, 3. Τὸ φύλλον αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἀποῤῥυήσεται. Sic & supra I, 4. dixit κληρονομίαν ἀμάραντον, contrarium habes Es. XL, 7. נבל ציץ Jac. I, 10. 11. supra I, 24.

Exemplo Magistri proponit Pastoribus spem mercedis in cælo, Matth. XXIV, 45. cap. XXV, 4. Conf. Dan. XII, 3. 2. Tim. IV, 8. Adventus Christi Φανέρωσις 1. Joh. II, 28. ἐπιφάνεια τοῦ Χριστοῦ 1. Tim. VI, 14. 2. Tim. IV, 1. τῆς δόξης Tit. II, 13. τῆς παρουσίας 2. Thess. II, 8. ἀποκάλυψις 1. Cor. I, 7. 2. Thess. III, 7. ideo præsentiam Christi firmat, non tollit, ut Calviani volunt, etsi invisibilis jam ea sit, Matth. XVIII, 20. c. XXVIII, 19. quæ conspicua in illo die erit. Per coronam autem gloriæ non designatur aureola vel laureola Pastorum fidelium, vel celsior gradus æternæ vitæ præ cæteris, ut Hugo, Thomas Anglicus & Salmero volunt, sed ipsa æterna vita: Quo de Estius: Hesselius vult coronam valde gloriosam. Non enim simpliciter, inquit vitam æternam significat, sed altiorem præ cæteris gradum. Unde Dan. XII. cum dictum esset bonos ituros in vitam æternam, de eminenti Pastorum præmio sequitur: Qui autem docti fuerint fulgebunt sicut splendor firmamenti, & qui ad justitiam erudiunt multos, quasi stellæ, in perpetuas æternitates. Hanc coronam, sunt, qui aureolam interpretentur, quæ Doctoribus attribuitur, ut Hugo Cardin. & Thomas Anglicus. Sed probabilius est, principale præmium intelligi, quod & alibi coronæ nomine significari solet, ut Jacobi I. Στέφανος autem δόξης dicitur, vel ut Genitivus speciei sit, percipietis gloriam, quæ erit veluti corona, vel positus loco adjectivi per Ebraismum, id est, corona valde gloriosa. Dicitur corona, tum quia hæredes regni cœlestis & Reges erimus, tum quia æterna erit gloria, uti Lyranus in h. l. Vita æterna corona est, quia nec principium, nec finem habet. Immarcescibilem vocat, ut monet Estius, ad discrimen coronarum, quæ apud nos dantur victoribus. Nectuntur enim ex floribus & foliis, quæ paulo post marcescunt. At illa corona cœlestis nec marcescet, nec veterascet unquam, sed viroris ac floris gratiam semper retinebit. Quod vero de merito infert, ἀνακόλουθον est: Nam simile omne dissimile: neque enim nos pugnando ac vincendo meriti gloriam regni cœlestis, sed consequi cœlum innuit Apostolus, utpote quæ præmium est gratuitum, Rom. VI. ult. Gloria cœle- stis, inquit Lyranus in cap. X. Joh. redditur fideli- bus, sicut hæreditas liberis, propter quod non habet rationem mercedis.

PARS II. Adhortatio communis de humilitate, confi- dentia & vigilantia.

## 5:5
Verse 5.

Likewise, you younger, be subject to the elders.] The sense is the same as in Hebrews 13:17. But Paul commands this especially to the young, because that age suffers itself to be ruled with more difficulty.

He proceeds from the elders to the younger. Afterwards he exhorts all in general, and having given precepts to the Pastors, he turns himself to common rules. And as he forbade them lordship, so he here reminds all of subjection. Nor indeed is there any reference here to Pastors, but the name of presbyters is now of age, not of dignity. These things therefore pertain to common life, in which the younger are taught to be subject to the elders, and all to one another. But they do not have the same sense as that which is in Heb. 13:17. Certainly there are not wanting those who wish subjection to the Pastors to be enjoined upon the people here, such as Bede, Dionysius, Cajetan, Hesselius, to which sense Estius agrees, because of the word ὁμοίως, and because obedience is not properly owed to elders by age, but reverence; or even those who wish subjection toward a Bishop to be demanded of a simple Presbyter, with Salmeron. But others more correctly understand elders here generally, whether they be such by the dignity of their office or by age, and by subjection and the kind of subjection and duty which the younger owe to the elders, viz. that they ought to rise before the elders, to honor them with words, gestures, and the very work itself, to obey their admonitions, to yield to them, and so to hold their venerable gray hair in value, Lev. 19:32. ὑποτάσσεσθαι is properly to be subordinated. Elders are strong in authority, counsel, and prudence. It requires, therefore, that the younger allow themselves to be ruled by the counsels of the elders, and follow them with due reverence. Add that humility is the mother of all other virtues. He who judges himself inferior to another, reveres him, complies with his counsels, and accommodates himself to his manners. The Apostle, however, understands not old men in years without prudence and piety, of whom Isa. 65:20, but those in whom true wisdom dwells, Job 12:12. Sir. 25:6.

Πάντες δὲ ἀλλήλοις ὑποτασσόμενοι.] He wishes individuals to yield to the consent of the whole Church. For ἀλλήλοις is to be taken here as in Jas. 5:16. Concerning the word ὑποτάσσεσθαι, that it is of reciprocal sense, we have already said often. But in the Manuscript ὑποτασσόμενοι is missing, and those words πάντες δὲ ἀλλήλοις cohere with what follows, as also in the Latin and Syriac.

If by ἀλλήλυς individuals are understood, the sentence must be inverted. For not all, that is, the whole assembly of the Church, ought to yield to individuals, according to Grotius. More correctly, therefore, these are judged to commend a mutual subordination toward one another, which is of humility, according to the parallel admonition, Phil. II, 3, and Eph. V, 21. The sense is not, says Estius, that all ought to be subject to all, but some to others, inferiors to superiors, wives to husbands, children to parents, servants to masters, just as Paul declares consequently in the same place. But in a certain sense, as is evident from the passage Phil. II, 11, all ought to be subordinate to all, and one ought to anticipate another in humility. For we are members one of another. Some wish the word μᾶλλον to be understood, that altogether the younger ought to be subject to the older, but rather all ought to be subject to one another, Rom. 12, 10, Sir. III, 20. Thus, therefore, he girds himself for the exhortation to humility. For it is certain that he does this both for mutual subjection and for the flight of pride. For through humility it happens that no one, however much he may shine with sublimity despise the other, but rather anticipate the other in honor, treat him humanely, acknowledge his own infirmity and the gifts in others, 1 Tim. IV. 12. and thus by this correction the Apostle wishes to bring all to equality and concord. It is no great thing, says Bernard in sermon IV on 'missus est', to be humble in abjection; humble humility is a truly great and rare virtue.

Clothe yourselves with humility) The manuscript has ἐγκομβώσατε, that is indeed 'put on', but it is not used except regarding a servile habit. Pollux in book IV: 'To the exomis and small garment of slaves a white thing is added, which is called an egkomboma.' The allegory is therefore well drawn here to express the force of humility. For Christ also 'emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,' Phil. II. 7.

The Vulgate and Bede have 'insinuate': whence Cornelius thinks that ἐγκολπώσασθαι was read, 'hide or have in the bosom,' as the interlinear gloss explains: or from the bosom not of the chest but of the garments, as Cornelius wishes, whose very winding commentary does not deserve to be cited here; and since this sense of the word is not suitable, and the explanation of Salmeron is also forced, 'insinuare' properly is to join and as it were secretly and cautiously to insert oneself into the bosom; others with Lyranus prefer to explain it as 'demonstrate by words and works,' so that you may mutually excite one another to works of humility. But neither does that fit well, and everyone sees that all these things depart from the Greek text, which must be looked upon here as God-breathed. Agreeing with this, the Syriac rendered it: 'Clothe yourselves,' (adding 'inwardly' to express the preposition ἐν, just as the word ἐγκομβώσασθαι is also used in Hesychius, whence Oecumenius rendered it: 'Surround yourselves') 'Embrace humility on every side, so that you may seem to be clothed and wrapped in it on all sides.' Conf. Col. III. 12. Some say that a garment tied in a knot is referred to, and that slaves used such a thing: to which the explanation of others also returns, 'knot, bind, tightly fasten humility to yourselves,' and that of Erasmus, 'have it fixed,' and of Vatablus, 'have humility fixed to you, or tightly, or held bound with knots.' Heinsius: 'Nothing could be said more charmingly; the egkomboma was a humble garment of slaves, who, when they wore short tunics, which they call epomides, were accustomed to put on over these an egkomboma, a most vile but white small cloak, which the ancients, as they observe, also called an epiblema.' Camerarius: 'Bind, fasten together.' Others explain it as 'adorn yourselves': because in Suidas 'kombomata' are 'kallopismata' or ornaments, and Hesychius interprets 'kombosasthai' as 'gylisasthai' or to be adorned. This, therefore, is what he wants, that we should put on humility as a garment and an ornament, and be tightly knotted to it.

For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble) From the Greek of Proverbs III. 34. A similar sentiment is in Luke I. 51, 52, Matthew XXIII. 12, Luke XIV. 11, XVIII. 14. 'Tapeinois' here and often elsewhere is equivalent to 'tapeinophrosi' (humble-minded). 'Tapeinois kardia' (humble in heart), Matthew XI. 29.

Eustathius notes that 'hyperephanon' is said with a pleonasm of the letter 'eta' from 'hyperphainomai', 'I am eminent above others,' and he explains that word as 'hyperphronountes' (those who think highly of themselves), because contempt for others arises from pride. The Syriac rendered it: 'Those who elevate and exalt themselves.' The verb 'antitassesthai' is to be at war, as it were to draw up a battle line against, as Budaeus observes, to resist by word and deed, Acts XVIII. 6, Romans XIII. 2. The Syriac explained it as 'meets, opposes.' Chrysostom notes in homily III on the words of Isaiah, that it is not said, 'God dismisses the proud,' withdrawing His help and grace from them, but 'antitassetai,' He opposes and positively resists, not that God has need of a drawn-up battle line or fight, since nothing is weaker than a proud man before God, but because He resists him by His mere nod, blasts him, destroys him, annihilates him, if He wills. Ambrose in Psalm CXVIII, oct. 7: 'What therefore does he think to be worse than this sin, which began from an injury to God?' Therefore Scripture says, 'The Lord resists the proud,' as if a repeller of His own insult, He has undertaken a kind of special contest against pride. The LXX use the word 'tapeinos' for one who is of a cast-down and humiliated spirit, compressed in spirit, Psalm XXXIII. 18, Proverbs XI. 2. The Syriac explained it by 'humble.' It is noted not as the humiliation of affliction, or a humble status, but a cast-down and humble act, Luke I. 52. The same sentiment is held in James IV. 6.

Vers. 5.

Ὁμοίως νεώτεροι ὑποτάγητε πρεσβυτέροις.] Sensus idem, qui Ebr. XIII, 17. Sed præcipue juvenibus id præcepit Paulus, quod illa ætas difficilius regi se patiatur.

A senioribus ad juniores progreditur. Postmo- dum omnes in universum adhortatur, & præceptis Pastoribus datis ad regulas communes se convertit. Et ut illis dominatu interdixit, ita omnes hîc ad subjectionem commonefacit. Neque vero hîc re- latio ad Pastores habetur, sed nomen presbytero- rum jam ætatis est, non dignitatis. Ad communem ergo vitam hæc pertinent, in qua juniores seniori- bus, omnesque sibi invicem subjecti esse docentur. Non autem eundem sensum habent, qui est Ebr. XIII, 17. Sane non desunt, qui hic plebi erga Pasto- res subjectionem præcipi velint, utpote Beda, Dio- nysius, Cajetanus, Hesselius, cui sensui annuit Estius, ob vocem ὁμοίως, & quod proprie Senioribus æta- te obedientia non debeatur, sed reverentia; vel et- iam ssimplici Presbytero subjectionem erga Episco- pum demandari velint cum Salmerone. Sed rectius alii seniores intelligunt hic generali9, sive tales sint officii dignitate, sive ætate, ac per subjectionem ac subjectionis & officii genus, quod juniores debent senioribus, videl. quod debeant senioribus assur- gere, eos verbis, gestibus & opere ipso honorare, eorum monitis parere, ipsis cedere, adeoq; vene- randam ipsorum canitiem in pretio habere, Lev.19, 32. ὑποsάτsesdaı proprie est subordinari. Seniores valent autoritate, consilio & prudentia. Requirit ergo, ut juniores seniorum consiliis se regi patian- tur, eosque debita reverentia prosequantur. Ad- de quod humilitas sit mater omnium virtutum re- liquarum. Qui altero se inferiorem judicat, ipsum reveretur, consiliis ejus obsequitur, & moribus ipsius se accommodat. Intelligit autem Apostolus non senes annis sine prudentia ac pietate, de qua- libus Esa. LXV, 20. sed in quibus vera habitat sa- pientia, Job. XII, 12. Sir. XXV, 6.

Πάντες δὲ ἀλλήλοις ὑποτασσόμενοι.] Vult singulos cedere consensui totius Ecclesiæ. Nam ἀλλήλοις hic sumendum, ut Jac. V, 16. De voce ὑποτάσsesdaı esse eam sensus reciproci, jam diximus sæpe. At in Manuscripto deest ὑποτασσόμενοι, & illa πάντες δὲ ἀλλήλοις cohærent cum jam sequentibus, ut & in Latino & Syro.

Si per ἀλλήλυς singuli intelliguntur, invertenda erit oratio. Non enim omnes, id est, totus cœtus Ec- clesiæ cedere debent singulis, juxta Grotium. Re- ctius ergo mutuam erga nos invicem subordina- tionem, quæ humilitatis est, hæc commendare cen- sentur juxta monitum parallelum, Phil. II, 3. & Eph. V, 21. Non sensus est, inquit Estius, omnes omnibus subditos esse debere, sed alios aliis, inferiores superiori- bus, uxores viris, filios parentibus, sirvos Dominis, quemadmodum Paulus ibidem consequenter decla- rat. Sed certa ratione, ut è loco Phil. II, 11. constat, omnes omnibus subordinari debent, & humilitate al- ter alterum prævenire. Sumus enim invicem membra. Nonnulli volunt subaudiendam esse vocem μᾶλ- λον, omnino juniores subjici debent senioribus, sed omnes potius debent sibi invicem subjici, Rom. 12, 10. Sir. III, 20. Sic ergo accingitur ad exhortationem ad humilitatem. Nam & subjectionem mutuam & superbiæ fugā eo facere certum est. Per humilita- tẽ enim sit, ut nemo quantavis sublimitate fulgeat alterum despiciat, sed honore potius alterum præ- veniat, humaniter ipsum tractet, infirmitatem suam & dona in aliis agnoscat, 1. Tim. IV. 12. adeo- que per hanc correctionem ad æquabilitatem & concordiam omnes redigere vult Apostolus. Non magnum est, ait Bernardus serm. IV. super missus est, esse humilem in abjectione, magna prorsus & rara virtus honorata humilitas.

Τὴν ταπεινοφροσύνην ἐγκομβώσασθε) Manuscriptus ἐγκομ- βώσατε, id est quidem induimini, sed non usurpatur, nisi de servili habitu. Pollux libro IV. Τῇ τ̄ τ̄ δούλων ἐξωμίδι καὶ ἱμα- τίδιόν τι πρόσκειται λευκόν, ὃ ἐγκόμβωμα λέγεται. Bene ergo hic ducta ἀλληγορία ad vim ταπεινοφροσύνης exprimendam. Nam & Christus ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε, μορφὴν δούλου λαβών, Phil. II. 7.

Vulgata & Beda habent insinuate: unde Corne- lius putat lectum esse ἐγκολπώσασθαι in sinu re- condite vel habete, ut glossa interlin. explicat: vel a sinu non pectoris sed vestium, ut vult Cornelius, cujus valde sinuosus commentarius hic referri non me- retur; & quum hic sensus vocis non sit conveni- ens, coacta etiam sit explicatio Salmeronis, insi- nuare proprie est conjungere & quasi latenter & caute in sinum se immittere; alii cum Lyrano ex- plicare malunt, verbis & operibus demonstrate, ut excitetis vos mutuo ad opera humilitatis. Ve- rum nec id satis congruit, & a Græco textu, qui hic spectandus est ut θεόπνευστος, ista omnia abire nemo non videt. Cui consentiens Syrus reddidit: Amicite vos, (addens intrinsecus ad exprimendam præpositionem ἐν, quemadmodum vox ἐγκομ- βώσασθαι etiam apud Hesychium adhibetur, un- de Oecumenius reddidit: Vobis circumdate) Hu- militatem omni ex parte complectimini, ut ea un- diq; amiciri & involvi videamini. Conf. Col. III. 12. Vestem ea respici in nodum constrictam ajunt nonnulli, talique servos usos esse: quo redit alio- rum etiam explicatio, innodate, illigate, arcte vo- bis constringite humilitatem, & Erasmi, infixam habete, & Vatabli, humilitatem vobis infixam ha- bete, vel arcte, seu nodis obligatam tenete. Hein- sius: Nihil dici potuit venustius, ἐγκόμβωμα vestis humilis & servorum erat, qui cum breves tunicas, quas ἐπωμίδας vocant, gestarent, super has ἐγκόμβω- μα induere solebant, palliolum vilissimum, sed can- didum, quod & ἐπίβλημα, ut observant antiqui, di- cebant. Camerarius: Devincite, compingite. Alii exponunt, ornate vos: quia Suidæ κομβώματα sunt τὰ καλλωπίσματα ornamenta, & κομβώσασθαι He- sychius interpretatur γυλίσασθαι ornari. Hoc ergo vult, ut induamus humilitatem ceu vestimentum, & ornamentum, eidemque arcte innodemur.

Ὅτι ὁ Θεὸς ὑπερηφάνοις ἀντιτάσσεται, ταπεινοῖς δὲ δίδωσι χάριν) Ex Græco Proverb. III. 34. Similis sententia Luc. I. 51. 52. Matth. XXIII. 12. Luc. XIV. 11. XVIII. 14. Τα- πεινοῖς hic alibi sæpe valet ταπεινόφροσι. ταπεινοῖς καρδίᾳ, Matth. X, 9.

Ὑπερήφανον cum pleonasmo literæ η dici ab ὑπερ- φαίνομαι, super alios emineo, notat Eustathius, & vocem illam exponit per ὑπερφρονῶντες, quia ex su- perbia oritur contempus aliorum. Syrus reddidit: Illis qui sese elevant atque exaltant. Verbum ἀντι- τάσσεσθαι est militare, ex adverso quasi aciem in- struere, ut Budæus observat, verbo & factis resiste- re, Act. XIIX. 6. Rom. XIII, 2. Syrus exposuit oc- currit, adversatus est. Notat Chrysostomus hom. III. de verb. Esaiæ, non dici, Deus superbos dimittit, suam eis opem gratiamque subducens, sed ἀντιτάσσε- ται adversatur, & positive resistit, non quod instructa acie aut pugna Deo sit opus, cum superbo nihil Deo sit infirmius, sed quod solo nutu ei resistat, eum afflet, perdat, annihilet, si velit. Ambrosius in Ps. CXIIX. oct. 7. Quid igitur hoc peccato putet esse deterius, quod a Dei cepit injuria? Ideo Scriptura dicit, Do- minus superbis resistit, tanquam sua contumelia pro- pulsator, veluti quoddam suscepit adversus super- biam speciale certamen. Voce ταπεινὸς LXX. utun- tur pro eo, qui animo demisso & humiliato est, compressus spiritu, Ps. XXXIII. 18. Prov. XI. 2. Sy- rus per humilem exposuit. Notatur non humilia- tio afflictionis, vel humilis status, sed demissus & humilis actus, Luc. I. 52. Sententia eadem habetur Jac. IV. 6.

## 5:6
v. 6. Be humbled therefore under the mighty hand of God) That is, permit yourselves to be ruled by God, which admonition we had in other words above at IV. 19. You have 'cheira krataian' (mighty hand) regarding God in Exodus III. 19, 'yad chazaqah'. The Apostle persists, as B. Gerhard notes, in a military metaphor. Men corrupted and depraved by sin draw up a battle line as it were against God, whom God opposes from the other side, and the humble indeed submit themselves under His powerful hand, whom He also receives into His faith and protection, but the proud, continuing to move arms against Him, are prostrated by the powerful hand of God. It is also explained in this way as the mode and manner of humbling ourselves, that we subject ourselves to God, and for God's sake to men, which commands that we humble ourselves not only to Him, but also to our neighbor. So that if you humble yourself to others, you humble yourself to God: If on the contrary you exalt yourself above others, you exalt yourself against God. The subject here is that humiliation by which one acknowledges his own infirmity, humbles himself in true fear before God, and reverently subjects himself to others, honoring the gifts of God in them. Through that powerful hand of God, however, He strikes fear into the swollen, but raises up the humble and oppressed by the power of God. There are, as it were, two hands of God, under which we ought to humble ourselves; one depresses the proud, the other extols the humble. If God casts you down, says Augustine in sermon LIII on the Words of the Lord, God raises you up; if God extols you, He casts you down. A similar passage is James IV. 6, 7.

that He may exalt you in time) If not before, certainly at the time of judgment. Thus 'en kairois idiois' (in due times), 1 Tim. VI. 15, 'en kairo eschato' (in the last time) above at I. 5. A sentiment similar to this is in James IV. 10. In the manuscript: 'En kairo tes episkopes' (In the time of visitation). The word 'episkopes' is accustomed to be taken now in a good, now in a bad sense. Hence 'episkope' is to be understood as the time of liberation, as Genesis L. 23, 24, Exodus III. 16, XIII. 19.

That manuscript added that determination either from the Vulgate, in which an addition is held regarding the time of visitation, or from chapter II. 12. It is not found in the more approved Greek codices, nor in the Syriac, which set forth only καιρὸν concerning a convenient or just time: just as Erasmus also rendered it, that he may exalt you when it shall be opportune, when he shall judge it expedient for you either in this age or on the day of judgment. Therefore, there is no reason that we, with Estius, should restrict the exaltation to the final time of retribution, which Cornelius a Lapide acknowledges, explaining: that he may exalt you either in this or in the future age. Two arguments for humility are therefore insinuated here; the one from the power of God designated by the mighty hand of God, the other from divine grace, by which he exalts those who humble themselves, Luke XIV. 11, ch. XVIII. 14. The end of humility is glory: the end of pride is ignominy, Job V. 11, ch. XXII. 9, Ps. XVIII. 28, Prov. XI. 2, ch. XXIX. 23. But Lorinus rightly says: We ought not to propose exaltation to ourselves as the primary end in humility: yet this has a connection with that, and one can be stirred by the hope of reward to propose God alone as the end for oneself first. Nor should Estius's observation be passed over: He says, it manifestly signifies that the exaltation of the future age is included under the name of grace, concerning which he had said: he gives grace to the humble.

What can be opposed to Estius himself regarding the parallel passage James IV. 6, noting these things: This sentence, God gives grace to the humble, confirms the Catholic doctrine, which teaches that a justified man merits the increase of grace by good works and especially by humility ment. For if that which God gives to the humble is grace, and a free gift, it is certainly not given out of merit. For grace is not grace in any way if it is not free in every way, Rom. XI. 6. For even the increase of grace is merely free, just as the end itself, eternal life, is a χάρισμα, Rom. XVI. 23. concerning which Estius on v. 5 says: To the humble, he says, by this very fact that they are already humble, having been anticipated by the grace of God, he gives more abundant grace, increasing what he gave, and heaping upon former gifts new gifts of his grace in succession, finally exalting them through glory in the world to come, which is itself also grace, as Paul testifies: The grace of God is eternal life, Rom. VI. Which Peter also signifies in the following verse.

Latin:
