v. 6. Ταπεινώθητε ὖν ὑπὸ τὴν κραταιὰν χεῖρα τῦ Θεῦ) Id est, Deo regendos vos permittite, quod monitum aliis verbis supra IV. 19. habuimus χεῖρα κραταιὰν de Deo habes Exod. III. 19. יד חזקה Persistit Apostolus, notante B. Gerhardo, in me- taphora militari. Homines per peccatum corrupti ac depravati aciem quasi contra Deum instruunt, quos Deus ex adverso oppugnat, ac humiles quidem se sub potenti ipsius manu submittunt, quos etiam in suam fidem ac tutelam recipit, superbi vero adversus ipsum arma movere pergentes potenti manu Dei pro- sternuntur. Exponitur etiam ita modus ac ratio humiliandi nos, ut Deo nos subjiciamus, ac pro- pter Deum hominibus, qui non tantum sibi, sed etiam proximo nos humiliemus, præcipit. ut si alii te humilies, Deo te humilies: Si contra efferas te supra alios, contra Deum te efferas. Agitur hic de illa humiliatione, qua quis infirmitatem suam agnoscit, in vero timore se coram Deo humiliat, & aliis reverenter se subjicit, dona Dei in illis hono- rans. Per illam autem potentem Dei manum tur- gidis timorem incutit, humiles vero & oppressos virtute Dei erigit. Duæ quasi sunt manus Dei, sub quibus nos humiliare debemus, una deprimit super- bos, altera extollit humiles. Si Deus dejicit te, ait Au- gustinus serm. LIII. de Verb. Dom. Deus elevat te, si extollit te Deus, dejicit te. Similis locus est Jac. IV. 6. 7,

ἵνα ὑμᾶς ὑψώσῃ ἐν καιρῷ) Si non ante, certe judicii tem- pore. Sic ἐν καιροῖς ἰδίοις, 1. Tim. VI. 15. ἐν καιρῷ ἐσχάτῳ su- pra I. 5. Sententia huic similis Jac. IV. 10. In Manuscripto: Ἐν καιρῷ τ᾽ ἐπισκοπῆς. Solet vox ἐπισκοπῆς nunc in bonam nunc in malam partem sumi. Hinc ἐπισκοπὴ intellige tem- pus liberationis, ut Gen. L. 23. 24. Exod. III. 16. XIII. 19.

Manuscriptum illud vel e Vulgata, in qua addi- tum habetur in tempore visitationis, vel e cap. II. 12. illum προσδιορισμὸν adjecit. In Græcis proba- tioribus Codd. non reperitur, nec in Syro, qui και- ρὸν solum exposuit de tempore conveniente sive justo: quemadmodum & Erasmus reddidit, ut vos extollat cum erit opportunum, cum judicabit id vobis expedire vel in hoc seculo, vel in die judicii. Proinde non est, ut cum Estio exaltationem re- stringamus ad extremum tempus retributionis, quod agnoscit Cornelius a Lapide, explicans: ut vos exaltet sive in hoc sive in futuro seculo. Duo ergo argumenta humiliationis hic insinuantur; al- terum a Dei potentia per manum Dei potentem designata, alterum a divina gratia, qua exaltat sese humiliantes, Luc. XIV. 11. c. XVIII. 14. Finis hu- militatis gloria: Finis superbiæ ignominia, Job. V. 11. c. XXII. 9. Ps. XVIII. 28. Prov. XI. 2. c. XXIX. 23. Recte autem Lorinus: Non debemus in hu- militate nobis proponere pro fine primario ex- altationem: Hæc tamen cum illa nexum habet, potestque quis præmii spe excitari primum sibi proponendi finem Deum solum. Nec prætereun- da Estii observatio: Manifeste, inquit, significat exaltationem illam futuri seculi gratiæ nomine com- prehendi, de qua dixerat: humilibus dat gratiam.

Quæ opponi potest ipsimet Estio ad locum paral- lelum Jac. IV. 6. hæc annotanti: Confirmat hæc sententia, Deus humilibus dat gratiam, Catholicam doctrinam, quæ tradit, hominem justificatum bonis operibus ac imprimis humilitate mereri gratiæ aug- mentum. Si enim id, quod Deus humilibus dat, gratia est, & donum gratuitum, utiq; non datur ex merito. Gratia enim non est gratia ullo modo, si non sit gratuita omni modo, Rom. XI. 6. Nam & augmentum gratiæ est mere gratuitum, ut & finis ipse vita æterna χάρισμα est, Rom. XVI. 23. quo de Estius ad v. 5. Humilibus, inquit, hoc ipso, quo jam humiles sunt, a Dei gratia præventis gratiam dat ampliorem, augens quod dedit, & novis subinde gra- tiæ suæ donis priora cumulans, denique eos exaltans per gloriam in seculo futuro, quæ & ipsa gratia est, Paulo testante: Gratia Dei vita æterna, Rom. VI. Quod & Petrus significat versu sequente.

## 5:7
v. 7. Casting all your care upon him) ἐπιῤῥίπτειν here is what גל is in Prov. XVI. 3, Psal. XXII. 8, or השׁלך as in Psal. LV. 23, a sense which is in Matth. VI. 25 and the following verses, where see the stated passages.

The exaltation of those who humble themselves belongs to divine providence. To him, therefore, let us commit ourselves, the Apostle commands; especially because the humble are not rarely supplanted by the more powerful, so that by casting our care upon the Lord, humility may be peaceful. Therefore, the aorist is used in the participle ἐπιῤῥίψαντες [ταπεινώθητε, so that it may indicate that this humiliation requires the casting of all our cares upon God, whence with humility filial trust is deservedly required. It should therefore be rendered not as the Vulgate, casting all your anxiety upon him, but since it is an aorist, all your anxiety having been cast upon him, as Erasmus, all care having been thrown upon him. The same ἐπιῤῥίψας is found in Ps. LV. 23, where in the Hebrew it is הַשְׁלֵךְ, cause to be cast, or cast upon the Lord thy burden or load, Luke XIX. 35. That word concerning a hurried casting occurs, from which these things can be taken in such a way that we ought not to struggle for a long time with the weight of our cares, but immediately relieve ourselves of it and cast it upon the Lord. He brings in, however, especially that casting which is done with a serious affection of the heart and inward sighs, concerning which Blessed Luther, Tom. VIII. Jen. fol. 315: 'Oh, if one could learn this throwing well, he would experience that it is certainly so. But whoever does not learn such throwing must remain a cast-off, broken, subjected, thrown-out, thrown-away, and overturned person.' They wish μέριμναν to be said from μερίζειν τὸν νοῦν, because care divides the mind into different parts, as it were. He wishes us, therefore, to cast care upon the Lord, lest it distract us: which is to be understood concerning the care of this age, which drags us away into various parts in this world, anxiety about food and clothing, and about dangers and evils that occur, Psal. XXXVII. 5. Matth. VI. 27. Luke XII. 22. chap. XXI. 34. Phil. IV. 6. Care, therefore, is not prohibited as an office or when ordered, but when inordinate or joined with distrust; Cf. Rom. XII. 2.

for he cares for you) He takes care of you, Matth. II. 26, 30.

In the praised Psalm it is held, and he will nourish you, he will not give a shaking to the righteous forever. Peter gathers the genus from the species. He has care for you, regarding all things necessary for this and the future life, Matth. VI. 32. Phil. IV. 5. Theodoret on Psal. LV: Cast your thought upon the Lord, against the fluctuating manner of the mind, the anchor of hope must be cast into God amidst the waves of anxieties, for he himself is the pilot. Bernard, sermon LXVIII. on the Canticles, warns: Peter did not say 'cast all your anxiety upon him so that he may have care for you,' but 'because he has care for you,' openly showing that the Church of the saints was not only loved, but that it had been loved first, i.e., attend to him, because he attends to you. He has care for us. Therefore, we ought to cast our care upon him. Do not be anxious, says Chrysostom, hom. LVI.

to the people of Antioch. your own, but permit those things to God. For if you are busy, you are busy as a man, but if you let go, God will provide.

Latin:

v. 7. Πᾶσαν τὴν μέριμναν ὑμῶν ἐπιῤῥίψαντες ἐπ’ αὐτὸν) ἐπιῤῥίπτειν hic est, quod גל Prov. XVI. 3. Psal. XXII. 8. aut השׁלך ut Psal. LV. 23. sensus qui Matth. VI. 25. & sequen- tibus, ubi dicta vide.

Exaltatio humiliantium sese est divinæ provi- dentiæ. Ei ergo nos committamus, jubet Aposto- lus; imprimis quia humiles non raro a potentiori- bus supplantantur, ut projecta cura in Dominum pacata sit humilitas. Ideo adhibetur aoristus in participio ἐπιῤῥίψαντες [ταπεινώθητε, ut nempe indi- cetur, humiliationem illam postulare omnium cu- rarum nostrarum in Deum projectionem, unde cum humilitate merito requiritur filialis fiducia. Reddendum ergo non cum Vulgata, omnem soli- citudinem vestram projicientes in eum, sed quum aoristus sit, omni solicitudine vestra projecta in eum, ut Erasmus, omni cura conjecta in eum. Idem ἐπιῤῥίψας habetur Pf. LV. 23. ubi in Ebræo est הַשְׁלֵךְ fac mitti, vel projice super Dominum pon- dus vel onus tuum, Luc. XIX. 35. Verbum illud de festinata projectione occurrit, unde hæc ita accipi possunt, quod cum pondere curarum nostrarum non diu luctari debeamus, sed statim nos eo levare, & in Dominum illud conjicere. Infert autem im- primis eam injectionem, quæ serio cordis affectu, & intimis suspiriis fit, quo de B. Lutherus Tom. VIII. Jen. fol. 315. Ach, wer das Werffen wohl lernen könnte, der würde erfahren, daß es gewiß also sey. Wer aber nicht lernet solch Werffen, der muß blei- ben ein verworffen, zerworffen, unterworffen, aus- geworffen, abgeworffen und umgeworffen Mensch. Μέριμναν a μερίζειν τὸν νοῦν dici volunt, quod cu- ra mentem in partes diversas velut dividat. Cu- ram ergo, ne nos distrahat, in Dominum rejici vult: quod de cura hujus seculi, quæ nos in hoc mundo in varias partes abripit, solicitudine de vi- ctu & amictu, deque periculis & malis obvenien- tibus intelligendum Psal. XXXVII. 5. Matth. VI. 27. Luc. XII. 22. cap. XXI. 34. Phil. IV. 6. Cura ita- que non officii aut ordinata, sed inordinata aut cum diffidentia conjuncta prohibetur; Conf. Rom. XII. 2.

ὅτι αὐτῷ μέλει περὶ ὑμῶν) Curam ille vestri agit, Matth. II. 26. 30.

In Psalmo laudato habetur, & ipse nutriet te, non dabit nutationem justo in seculum. Petrus ex specie colligit genus. Ipsi cura est de te, quoad omnia necessaria ad hanc & futuram vitam, Matth. VI. 32. Phil. IV. 5. Theodor. in Psal. LV. Jacta cogi- tatum tuum super Dominum, adversus fluctuantem animi morem solicitudinum fluctibus ancora spei in Deum jactanda, ipse enim gubernator est. Bern- hardus sermon. LXVIII. in Cantic. monet; Petrus non dixit omnem solicitudinem projicite in eum, ut sit ipsi cura de vobis: sed quia ipsi cura est de vobis, aperte monstrans, Ecclesiæ sanctorum, non modo quoniam dilecta, sed quod prius dilecta fue- rit, q. d. intendite illi, quia ipse intendit vobis. Ipsi est cura de nobis. Ergo in ipsum curam conjicere debemus. Ne cures, inquit Chrysostomus hom. LVI.

ad popul. Antioch. tua, sed ea Deo permitte. Nam si satagis, tanquam homo satages, si vero dimittis, Deus providebit.

## 5:8
Be sober) See above I. 13. IV. 7. Be watchful) The same admonition in Matth. XXIV. 42. XXV. 13. Mark XIII. 35, 37. Acts XX. 31. 1 Cor. XVI. 13. 1 Thess. V. 6. Rev. III. 2, 3. XVI. 15. He now commends sobriety and vigilance against the snares of the Devil. The former is sobriety, then follows vigilance. Calvin wishes sobriety of mind to be understood, but because Peter seems to have looked to the warning of Christ in Luke XXI. 34, we refer it to the sobriety of the body: for the sobriety of the mind is comprehended under vigilance, which is altogether necessary against the Devil. For this vigilance implies both prudence in avoiding the snares of Satan, and the flight from security and sins, and the spiritual watches of the children of light, so that, having been clothed in the armor of the Holy Spirit, they may keep watch with the sword of the word and diligently pray, Eph. VI. 11 seqq. Augustine, sermon XXIII. on the Words of the Lord, c. 10. Watch with the heart, watch with faith, watch with hope, watch with charity, watch with works. One must watch especially in prayer, Eph. VI. 18, which is a sacrifice pleasing to God, the safest protection for man, and a scourge to the Devil. Concerning the watch, Estius not inappropriately: The watch, he says, signifies attentive care for salvation against hostility. The metaphor is taken from military sentinels. Which is required not only from Clerics, but from any of the faithful, which Lorinus noted against some associates: We must all watch, lest we be intercepted by the snares of Satan, who sagaciously seeks all ways of doing harm and is most greedily panting for our prey. Wherefore this passage does not pertain to Bishops alone and Priests who are Ministers of the Eucharist, although Valentia also thinks so with Turrianus. See Turrianus, book II. on dogmatic characteristics, Valentia, Tom. IV. disp. 9. point 5. §. 1.

v. 8. Your adversary the Devil, as a roaring lion walketh about, seeking whom he may devour. The Devil is here called the adversary of the godly, just as he is called enemy, Matt. XIII. 39. As a roaring lion אריה שאג, Jud. XIV. 5. Ps. XXII. 13. Jer. II. 15. Ezech. XXII. 25. Hos. XI. 11. Zeph. III. 4. Zech. XI. 3. The lion roars when he is angry. He walketh about refers to the passage in Job I. 7. שוט where in the Greek it is ἐμπεριπατήσας. Thus he passeth through is used of the same in Matt. XII. 43. He seeks whom he may harm, Luke XXII. 31. To devour בלע. By these are contained the reasons for the exhortation, and almost every single word presents individual arguments: 1. because we are not without an adversary, but have an implacable enemy: whom he calls adversary, because he not only observes us to accuse us before God, Rev. XII. 10, since an adversary is one litigating in court, Matt. V. 25, a man of strife, Is. XLI. 11, but also opposes us on every side with perpetual hostility. The Syriac here rendered it lord or possessor of hatred. In Hebrew adversary should be translated שטן, Num. XXII. 12, 1 Sam. XXIX. 4, which name is attributed by antonomasia to the Devil, Job I. 6, 2 Cor. XII. 7, Rev. XII. 9, XX. 2. Therefore, 2. he is called our enemy in this place, devil, from slandering, because he slanders God and men, as Chrysostom teaches, Homily II on 2 Corinthians. Gregory the Great, book 2, Morals, ch. 5, says: The ancient adversary, when he finds no evils to accuse, seeks to bend the very good deeds themselves toward evil: and when he is overcome in works, he scrutinizes our words for the sake of accusing: when he finds no accusation even in words, he strives to darken the intention of the heart, as if good deeds were not done with a good spirit, and therefore should not be weighed by a good judge. 3. He is compared to a lion, and that primarily on account of cruelty, just as cruel men are also accustomed to be designated by that name, Ps. XXII. 22, XXXV. 17, 1. Tim. IV. 17. The Syriac explained it as a great lion, which now seizes and tears its prey; for that is what the word אריה denotes. Augustine, Sermon XLVI on various subjects, ch. 2.

Christ, he says, is the Lion (Rev. 5:5) on account of his strength, the Devil on account of his ferocity: The former is a Lion for conquering, the latter a lion for harming. Yet Satan can also be compared to a lion for his audacity and desire to harm, for his power and validity, for his craftiness and cunning, Ps. 10:10. 4. He is called a roaring lion, such as are hungry lions roaring from the impatience of hunger, concerning which Ambrose, book VI, Hexaëm. ch. 3, says that a hungry lion strikes terror into living creatures with its voice, so that they fail as if drawn by force. When he is hungry, says Pliny, book VIII, ch. 10, the lion roars more savagely. Cf. Ps. 104:21. For the Devil ineffably desires our destruction, and no prey suffices for him.

5. He is described as a Peripatetic: for he is called περιπατῶν (walking about), roaming like a hungry lion, solicitously seeking prey, which the continuation of the metaphor implies. He is also compared for this reason to a hunter, Ps. 91:3, who spares no cares and labors to track down his prey. Cyprian sets forth here a metaphor from an enemy of a besieged city surveying the walls by circuit, in his sermon on jealousy and envy: He goes around us one by one, and like an enemy besieging closed walls, he explores and tests whether there is any part of the members less stable and less faithful, by whose entrance he might penetrate to the interior, etc. Cf. Luke 11:24.

6. The word ζητεῖν (to seek) itself is added, which is to seek with the highest zeal.

7. And for this purpose, that he may swallow up, not merely harm in any way, but utterly devour. He goes about seeking, says Chrysostom, homily 22 to the people of Antioch, not whom he may bite or break, but whom he may devour. Lyranus: Seeking whom he may devour, by incorporating them into himself through mortal sin.

Although Christ has overcome Satan by his passion and resurrection, and has acquired for us life and security from the infernal enemy, and makes us participants in his own victory; yet that most impudent Spirit does not cease to lay snares even for the faithful, therefore there is need for perpetual vigilance against him, because we are still in the Church militant, not yet in the triumphant. The Devil, says Cyprian, book I, ep. 1, does not seek those whom he has already subdued, or desire to overthrow those whom he has already made his own. The enemy and foe of the Church, those whom he has alienated from the Church and led outside, he despises as captives and the defeated and passes them by; he proceeds to harass those in whom he knows Christ dwells.

However, these things are to be understood not ἐξοχικῶς (pre-eminently) concerning the Prince of evil Spirits, who is called the Devil, Matt. 25:41, Rev. 12:9, nor συναγωγικῶς (collectively) concerning the whole phalanx, which does not always lie in wait for everyone, but κοινῶς (commonly), because it is proper to all evil spirits to lie in wait for men: and if they are from among men, others pant after others as desired prey. Therefore, let these things move us to sobriety and vigilance because of that most grave danger which perpetually threatens us from these enemies. Such is our life, says Blessed Luther in this place, as if a stranger were coming into an inn where all the inhabitants were thieves; there he would certainly be vigilant, arm himself, and fortify himself. Against all the snares of the Devil, says Cyprian, loc. cit., whether deceitful or open threats, the mind ought to stand instructed and armed, as prepared always to resist as the enemy is always prepared to attack.

Latin:

Νήψατε) Vide supra I. 13. IV. 7. Γρηγορήσατε) Eadem admonitio Matth. XXIV. 42. XXV. 13. Marc. XIII. 35. 37. Act. XX. 31. 1. Cor. XVI. 13. 1. Thess. V. 6. Apoc. III. 2. 3. XVI. 15. Sobrietatem jam & vigilantiam commendat ad- versus Diaboli insidias. Prior est sobrietas, deinde sequitur vigilantia. Calvinus sobrietatem mentis intelligi vult, sed quia videtur Petrus respexisse monitum Christi Luc. XXI. 34. ad sobrietatem cor- poris referimus: mentis enim sobrietas sub vigilan- tia comprehenditur, qua omnino adversus Diabo- lum opus est. Vigilantia enim hæc tum pruden- tiam in cavendis Satanæ insidiis, tum fugam secu- ritatis & peccatorum, tum excubias filiorum lucis spirituales, ut nempe armatura Spiritus Sancti in- duti gladio verbi excubent ac sedulo precibus vi- gilent, Eph. VI. 11. seqq. Augustinus serm. XXIII. de Verb. Dom. c. 10. Corde vigila, fide vigila, spe vigila, charitate vigila, operibus vigila. Vigilandum im- primis oratione, Eph. VI. 18. quæ gratum Deo est sacrificium, tutissimum homini præsidium, Diabo- lo vero flagellum. De vigilia Estius non inconve- nienter: Vigilia, inquit, significat attentam curam salutis adversus hostilitatem. Sumpta Metaphora a castrensibus excubitoribus. Quod requiritur non tantum a Clericis, sed a quibusvis fidelibus, quod contra nonnullos socios notavit Lorinus: Vigilan- dum nobis omnibus, ne intercipiamur Satanæ in- sidiis, omnes nocendi vias sagaciter quærentis, & avidissime ad prædam nostram inhiantis. Quocir- ca non pertinet hic locus ad Episcopos solos & Sa- cerdotes Eucharistiæ Ministros, licet cum Tur- riano ita quoque sentiat Valentia. Vid. Turrianus l. II. de dogm. charact. Valentia Tom. IV. disp. 9. punct. 5. §. 1.

v. 8. Ὁ ἀντίδικος ὑμῶν Διάβολος, ὡς λέων ὠρυόμενος περι- πατεῖ, ζητῶν τίνα καταπίῃ) Diabolus hic vocatur piorum ἀν- τίδικος, quomodo ἐχθρός, Matth. XIII. 39. ὡς λέων ὠρυόμενος אריה שאג, Jud. XIV. 5. Ps. XXII. 13. Jer. II. 15. Ezech. XXII. 25. Os. XI. 11. Soph. III. 4. Zach. XI. 3. Rugit leo cum irasci- tur. Περιπατεῖ respicit locum Jobi I. 7. שוט ubi in Græco ἐμπεριπατήσας. Sic διέρχεται de eodem Matth. XII. 43. quærit is, cui noceat Luc. XXII. 31. Καταπίειν בלע devorare. His continentur rationes adhortationis, ac singu- la pene verba singula exhibent argumenta, 1. quia non destituimur adversario, sed hostem habemus ἄσπονδον: Quem ἀντίδικον vocat, quod non tantum nos observet ut accuset nos coram Deo, Ap. XII. 10. quum ἀντίδικος adversarius sit in judicio litigans, Matth. V. 25. vir litis, Es. XLI. 11. sed & perpetua ho- stilitate nobis undiq; adversetur. Syrus hic reddi- dit Dominum vel possessorem odii. In Ebræo ἀντί- δικος vertatur שטן adversarius Num. XXII. 12. 1. Sam. XXIX. 4. quod nomen per ἀντονομασίαν tri- buitur Diabolo Job. I. 6. 2. Cor. XII. 7. Apoc. XII. 9. XX. 2. Ideo 2. vocatur hostis noster hoc loco διάβο- λος a calumniando, quia Deum & homines calu- mniatur, ut docet Chrysostomus homil. II. in 2. ad Corinth. Gregorius M. l. 2. Moral. c. 5. Antiquus ad- versarius, inquit, cum quæ accuset mala non invenit, ipsa ad malum inflectere bona quærit: cumq́; de operi- bus vincitur ad accusandum verba nostra perscruta- tur: cum nec in verbis accusationem reperit, intentio- nem cordis fuscare contendit, tanquam bona facta bo- no animo non fiant, & idcirco perpendi a judice bono non debeant. 3. Leoni comparatur, idq; imprimis ob crudelitatem, quemadmodum & homines crude- les eo nomine designari solent, Ps. XXII. 22. XXXV. 17. 1. Tim. IV. 17. Syrus leonem grandprofilem exposuit, qui jam prædam rapit & discerpit; id enim vox אריה notat. Augustinus serm. XLVI. de divers. c. 2.

Christus, inquit, Leo, Apoc. V. 5.) propter fortitudi- nem, Diabolus propter feritatem: Ille Leo ad vincen- dum, hic leo ad nocendum. Leoni tamen etiam con- ferri potest Satanas ob audaciam & nocendi cupi- ditatem, ob robur & validitatem, ob astutiam & calliditatem, Ps. X. 10. 4. Leo rugiens dicitur, qua- les sunt famelici leones præ impatientia famis ru- gientes, quo de Ambrosius l. VI. Hexaëm. c. 3. leo- nem famelicum voce sua terrorem animantibus in- cutere, ut quasi vi attracta atq;, ista deficiant. Cum esurit, inquit Plinius l. VIII. c. 10. sævius rugit leo. Conf. Ps. CIV. 21. Diabolus enim perniciem no- stram ineffabiliter appetit, nec ulla præda ei suffi- cit.

5. Describitur ut Peripateticus: dicitur enim περιπατῶν obambulare instar leonis famelici, soli- cite prædam inquirentis, quod continuatio Meta- phoræ infert. Comparatur etiam ejus causa vena- tori, Ps. XCI. 3. qui nullis parcit curis & laboribus, ut prædam investiget. Cyprianus ponit hic Meta- phoram ab hoste civitatis obsessæ muros per circui- tum lustrante, serm. de zelo & livore: Circumit il- le nos singulos, & tanquam hostis clausos obsi- dens muros explorat & tentat, an sit pars aliqua membrorum minus stabilis, & minus fida, cujus aditu ad interiora penetretur, &c. Conf. Luc. XI. 24.

6. Additur ipsum ζητεῖν, quod est summo studio quærere.

7. Idq; eo fine, ut deglutiat, non lædat qualitercunq; sed prorsus devoret. Circuit quærens ait Chrysostomus hom. XXII. ad pop. Antioch. non quem mordeat vel frangat, sed devoret. Lyranus: Quærens quem devoret, incorporando sibi per mor- talem culpam.

Quamvis autem Christus passione ac resurre- ctione sua Satanam superarit, nobisq; vitam ac se- curitatem ab hoste infernali acquisiverit, suæ etiam victoriæ nos participes reddat; non cessat tamen Spiritus impudentissimus etiam fidelibus insidias struere, ideo opus est perpetua adversus ipsum vi- gilantia, quia adhuc sumus in Ecclesia militante, nondum in triumphante. Non quærit, inquit Cypri- anus l. I. ep. I. Diabolus eos, quos jam subegit, aut ge- stit subvertere, quos jam suos fecit. Inimicus & hostis Ecclesiæ, quos alienavit ab Ecclesia & foras duxit, ut captivos & victos contemnit & præterit eos, pergit lacessere, in quibus Christum novit habitare.

Intelligenda autem hæc non ἐξοχικῶς de Princi- pe malorum Spirituum, qui Diabolus dicitur Matt. XXV. 41. Apoc. XII. 9. neq; συναγωγικῶς de tota phalange, quæ non semper cuivis insidiatur, sed κοι- νῶς, quod omnibus malis spiritibus hoc sit pro- prium, hominibus insidiari: atq; si illi ex homini- bus, alii aliis ceu prædæ desideratæ inhient. Hæc itaq; nos ad sobrietatem & vigilantiam moveant ob periculum illud gravissimum, quod ab istis ho- stibus nobis perpetuo imminet. Talis vita nostra, inquit B. Lutherus in h. l. ac si peregrinus veniret in hospitium, in quo omnes incolæ essent latrones, ibi cer- te vigilaret, sese armaret, ac muniret. Contra omnes Diaboli, inquit Cypr. l. c. vel fallaces insidias, vel a- pertas minas stare debet instructus animus & arma- tus tam paratus semper ad repugnandum, quam est ad impugnandum paratus semper inimicus.

## 5:9
ᾧ ἀντίστητε (whom resist) is an imperative. Thus ἀντιστῆναι τῷ πονηρῷ (to resist the evil one), Eph. 6:13.

Στερεοὶ τῇ πίστει) Firm in faith חֲזָקִים. Thus the foundation of the faith, Col. II. 5.

Sobriety and vigilance were required so as not to admit the enemy who prowls about, and resistance was required to repel him when he attacks us. And since he has depicted the power and ferocity of this enemy under the figure of a lion, he now teaches with what strength such a great enemy is to be resisted, namely not with our own, but with that of the Lion of the tribe of Judah, who is far more powerful than the infernal lion, whose victory and power may be ours through faith, Apoc. V. 5. Concerning which Bernard, sermon XIII. on Psalm XCI. Your adversary as a roaring lion, says Peter. Thanks be to that great Lion of the tribe of Judah. That one can roar, he cannot wound. Let him roar as much as he wants, provided the sheep of Christ does not flee. How much he threatens, how much he exaggerates, how much he attempts, let us not be beasts, so that he may prostrate us; that roaring is empty. True faith embraces Christ with all his benefits, and unites us with Christ, so that he may dwell in our hearts, Eph. III. 15, so that he may remain in us and we in him, John XV. 4, so that we may be one Spirit with the Lord, 1 Cor. VI. 17. Therefore, as one possesses Christ the victor over Satan: so one uses his power in the battle against Satan, Phil. IV. 13. However, fortitude or rather solidity in faith is required. The Vulgate rendered it: Resist him, strong in faith. The Syriac: Stand or rise up against him, strengthened, established, or confirmed in faith. Cf. Eph. VI. 13. seqq. James IV. 7. 1 John V. 4. B. Luther on this passage: If you have the Word of God, he says, in your heart, and keep it by faith, the Devil cannot triumph over you, but is forced to yield. Salmero on this passage. The Apostle wishes them to be strong in faith, namely in the confidence of divine mercy, and by which one embraces Christ himself, fighting for us: Estius: The blessed Peter teaches, he says, that the temptations of the Devil, whether open or hidden, are to be resisted by the firmness of faith, by which, clearly, we not only believe the promises of God without doubt, but also stir up in ourselves the confidence of obtaining them, with the power and truth and mercy of God through Christ set before our eyes. For grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, John I, and this is the victory that overcomes the world, our faith, 1 John V. If the world, then also the Prince of the world, the Devil. By the unbelieving, says Isidore, book III. de sum. bon. c. 5, the Devil is feared as a lion; by those strong in faith, he is despised as a worm. The sign of the cross, says Anthony in Athanasius, and faith in the Lord is an impregnable wall for us. For the Lord, says Dionysius, or whoever is the author of Eccl. Hierar. c. 2, as he is supremely clement and good, conquers in his warriors, while dwelling in them he fights for their salvation and victory against the empire of death and corruption.

V. 9. εἰδότες τὰ αὐτὰ ὧ̃ παθημάτων τῇ ἐν κόσμῳ ὑμῶν ἀδελ- φότητι ἐπιτελεῖσθαι) Concerning the word ἀδελφότητι see above II. 17. I take ἐπιτελεῖσθαι here as it is used in Lucian, ἄθλον ἐπι- τελεῖν, and ἐπιτελεῖν ἀποφορὰν in Herodotus: You know how many Christian flocks there are throughout the whole world, that they undergo equal labors and adversities. We had the word παθήματα above l. 11. IV. 13. and here 1. it is frequent in Paul.

By brotherhood in the world, spiritual brothers dispersed here and there in the world are understood. Some wish the temptations of the world to be understood in this way: But the words themselves teach that the discourse is about the temptations of Satan, to which brothers in the world are also subject. The Vulgate rendered the word ἐπιτελεῖσθαι as 'to be done', but it is more emphatic: For it denotes to be perfected, completed, consummated, Luke XIII. 32. Rom. XV. 28. 2 Cor. VII. v. 1. For they are completed just as they were decreed by God, Rom. VIII. 29. Τὰ αὐτὰ τῶν παθημάτων are τὰ αὐτὰ πα- θήματα. Therefore the Apostle means this: No one ought to seek or imagine a better lot for himself. A common fatherhood and a common inheritance require a common lot of brotherhood. A common battle also against the enemy makes for hope of victory, because united strength is stronger: They are not only partakers of our sufferings, but also our allies in prayers and in the battle against the common enemy. The weight, says Oecumenius, is lightened by the society of companions, so that it may provide greatness of soul against the adversary the Devil, because we are not alone in fighting with him, but all the good and the Elect of Christ. Above c. IV. 12. that temptations are not something strange, now he teaches equally about the temptations of the Devil, that they are common to them with all brothers or believers, as many as are in the world.

Latin:

ᾧ ἀντίστητε) Est imperativus. Sic ἀντιστῆναι τῷ πονηρῷ, Eph. VI. 13.

Στερεοὶ τῇ πίστει) Firma fide חֲזָקִים. Sic στερέωμα τῆς πίστεως, Col. II. 5.

Sobrietas, & vigilantia requisita fuit ad hostem, qui obambulat, non admittendum, resistentia ad eum, cum aggreditur nos, repellendum. Et quum potentiam & feritatem hostis hujus sub figura leo- nis depinxerit, jam quibus viribus tanto hosti re- sistendum sit, docet, nimirum non nostris, sed leo- nis de tribu Juda, qui infernali leone longe poten- tior est, cujus victoria & virtus nostra sit per fi- dem, Apoc.V.5. Quo de Bernhardus serm. XIII. in Psal. XCI. Adversarius vester tanquam leo rugiens, inquit Petrus. Gratia magno illi Leoni de tribu Ju- da. Rugire iste potest, ferire non potest. Rugiat quan- tum vult, tantum non fugiat ovis Christi. Quanta minatur, quanta exaggerat, quanta intentat, non simus bestiæ, ut nos prosternat, vacuus ille rugitus. Vera fides Christum cum omnibus suis beneficiis complectitur, & cum Christo nos unit, ut habitet in cordibus nostris, Eph. III. 15. ut maneat in nobis & nos in ipso Joh. XV. 4. ut unus Spiritus simus cum Domino, 1. Cor. VI. 17. Ut ergo Christum vi- ctorem Satanæ possidet: Ita potentia ejus in pugna contra Satanam utitur, Phil. IV. 13. Requiritur au- tem fortitudo vel potius soliditas in fide. Vulgata reddidit: Cui resistite fortes in fide. Syrus: State vel insurgite contra cum corroborati, stabiliti, vel confir- mati in fide. Conf. Eph. VI. 13. seqq. Jac. IV. 7. 1. Joh. V. 4. B. Lutherus in h. l. Si Verbum Dei, inquit, habes in corde, illudq; fide servas, Diabolus non potest de te triumphare, sed cogitur cedere. Salmero in h. l. Apo- stolus fortes vult esse in fide scilicet fiducia divina misericordiæ, & qua Christum ipsum complectitur, pro nobis pugnantem: Estius: Docet, inquit, B. Pe- trus, Diaboli tentationibus sive apertis sive occultis resistendum esse firmitate fidei, qua videlicet non so- lum indubitanter credamus promissionibus Dei, ve- rum etiam fiduciam in nobis excitemus eas conse- quendi, proposita nobis ante oculos, Dei potentia & veritate & misericordia per Christum. Nam gratia & veritas per Jesum Christum facta est, Joh. I. & hæc est victoria, quæ vincit mundum, fides nostra, 1. Joh. V. Si mundum, igitur & mundi Principem Diabo- lum. Ab incredulis, inquit Isidorus l. III. de sum. bon. c. 5. Diabolus timetur ut leo, a fortibus in fide ut vermis contemnitur. Signum crucis, ait Antonius apud Athan. & fides ad Dominum inexpugnabilis nobis murus est. Dominus enim, inquit Dionysius, vel quisquis autor Eccl. Hierar. c. 2. ut est summe, clemens & bonus, in suis bellatoribus vincit, dum in illis habitans pro illorum salute & victoria ad- versus mortis & corruptionis imperium pugnat.

V. 9. εἰδότες τὰ αὐτὰ ὧ̃ παθημάτων τῇ ἐν κόσμῳ ὑμῶν ἀδελ- φότητι ἐπιτελεῖσθαι) De voce ἀδελφότητι vide supra II. 17. ἐπιτελεῖσθαι hic sumo, quomodo apud Lucianum, ἄθλον ἐπι- τελεῖν, & ἐπιτελεῖν ἀποφορὰν apud Herodotum: Scitis quot sunt per orbem omnem Christiani greges, eos paribus la- boribus & adversis fungi. Vocem παθήματα habuimus supra l. 11. IV. 13. & hic 1. frequens est apud Paulum.

Per fraternitatem in mundo fratres spirituales in mundo hinc inde dispersi intelliguntur. Nonnulli mundi tentationes ita respici volunt: Sed de Sata- næ tentationibus, quibus fratres in mundo etiam obnoxii sunt, sermonem esse, verba ipsa docent. Verbum ἐπιτελεῖσθαι Vulgatus reddidit fieri, sed ἐμ- φατικώτερον est: Denotat enim perfici, compleri, consummari, Luc. XIII. 32. Rom. XV. 28. 2. Cor. VII. v. 1. Complentur enim sicut a Deo decretum, Rom. VIII. 29. Τὰ αὐτὰ τῶν παθημάτων sunt τὰ αὐτὰ πα- θήματα. Id ergo vult Apostolus: Nemo debet me- liorem sibi sortem expetere aut imaginari. Com- munis paternitas & communis hæreditas com- munem fraternitatis sortem requirit. Communis etiam adversus hostem pugna spem victoriæ facit, quia virtus unita fortior est: Non solum sunt pas- sionum nostrarum συμμέτοχοι, sed etiam in preci- bus & pugna contra communem hostem nostri σύμμαχοι. Gravitatem, inquit, Oecumenius, alle- vat societas consortum, ut animi magnitudinem contra adversarium Diabolum præstet, quia non soli sumus, qui cum eo pugnamus, sed omnes boni & Christi Electi. Supra c. IV. 12. tentationes non esse aliquid peregrini monuerat, jam de tentationibus Diaboli pariter docet, eas ipsis communes esse cum omnibus fratribus vel fidelibus, quotquot in mundo sunt.

## 5:10
v. 10. ὁ Θεὸς πάσης χάριτος) The most merciful God אל חנון Exod. XXXIV. 6. 2. Paral. XXX. 9. Neh. IX. 17. 31. Jonæ IV. 3. & often in the Psalms. Some begin the conclusion of the epistle here, but it is more correctly established here as the conclusion of the exhortation regarding not considering the heat of the cross as something strange. For just as the Apostle had concluded the previous exhortations with a doxology in chapter IV. 11, so he now finishes with a vow and a doxology that which he had begun there in v. 12, and to which he had returned after inserting certain common matters by way of digression to the Pastors and others in chapter V. 8, 9. He appends the final vow, pertaining to the conclusion of the whole epistle, in the last verse. In this conclusion, however, he provides arguments for both the new exhortation to resist the Devil through faith and for consolation regarding certain victory, from the abundance of divine grace, from the kindness of the divine calling, from the brevity of sufferings, from the variety of divine benefits, and from the certainty of our preservation and consummation. These are therefore added not by way of a vow or prayer, as it seemed to some, but by way of a promise, so that the faith of those fighting against the Devil may be strengthened. Emphatically, therefore, he calls God the God of all (πάσης) grace, which word 'all' was not to be omitted by the Syrian, and he connects it with the following 'will perfect' (καταρτίσει), showing thus, as the blessed Gerhard warns, that from the same fountain of grace both the first calling to heavenly glory and the final consummation of this benefit, namely preservation in good and introduction into heavenly glory, proceed. St. Augustine, sermon XVI. on the words of the Apostles: He predestined us before we were, called us when we were converted, justified us when we were sinners, glorified us when we were mortal. ὁ καλέσας ἡμᾶς εἰς τὴν αἰώνιον ἀυτῶ δόξαν ἐν χριστῷ ἰησοῦ) Who called us through Jesus Christ to the fellowship of His glory. See 1 Cor. I. 9, 1 Tim. VI. 12. The determination (προσδιορισμὸς) 'through Jesus Christ' is rightly referred to the word 'called' (καλέσας), because the calling to eternal life comes to us on account of Christ's merit, to whom all spiritual benefits are to be ascribed: election, Eph. I. 3, 4; calling, 1 Cor. I. 2, Gal. I. 6, 2 Tim. I. 9; eternal glorification, Rom. VI. 23. As for the following 'having suffered a little' (ὀλίγον παθόντας), it is to be referred to 'on account of Christ', as some have wished. ὀλίγον παθόντας) ὀλίγον here is 'for a short time', as above I. 6. Truly all this life is short compared to eternity. Some take that 'little' not as opposed to long duration, but to magnitude. But it is better to take it regarding time, as in James IV. 24 and Rev. XVII. 11. Αὐτὸς καταρτίσαι ὑμᾶς, στηρίξαι, σθενώσαι, θεμελιῶσαι) In the Manuscript it is καταρτίσει, στηρίξει, σθενώσει; 'you' (ὑμᾶς) is absent, but it is understood, nor is 'found' (θεμελιώσει) present, nor does the Latin read otherwise. Καταρτίζει is כונן in Deut. XXXII. 6. See 1 Cor. I. 10, 2 Cor. XIII. 11, Heb. XIII. 21. Στηρίξει is יסמך in Ps. LI. 13, Is. LIX. 16, Rom. XVI. 25, 2 Thess. II. 17, III. 3. Σθενώσει is ויאמץ, He will make you perfect, will sustain, will strengthen. The pronoun 'He' (ὁ ἀυτὸς) is not redundant, but has emphasis, as we said at v. 10. The blessed Gerhard has diligently dealt with the diverse reading here. Estius prefers the verbs to be read in the optative, having the authority of the Vulgate approved by the Council of Trent in every way. However, a doxology fits a promise better than a vow, and not only the Royal and other Stephanus Codices have the reading in the future, but also some Latin ones, and among them the author of the book on the calling of the nations, book I, chapter 24, and others following the Vulgate version. The word καταρτίζειν not only means to adapt and restore, 2 Cor. XIII. 11, Gal. VI. 1, but also signifies to perfect, Luke VI. 40, 2 Cor. I. 30, 1 Thess. III. 10, Heb. XIII. 20, 21, and is used by the LXX Interpreters for כון 'prepared, adorned', Ps. LXXIII. 17; for כּוֹנֵן 'arranged', Ps. X. 13; for יָסַד 'founded', Ps. VIII. 3; for תָּמַךְ 'sustained', Ps. XVI. 6, Is. IV. 12, and brings in firmness and perfection. By the Syrian it is explained as חַיִל in Hithpaël, 'he was strengthened, he was corroborated'; by the Vulgate, 'he will perfect'. Lyranus: 'he will perfect', namely, for that which your virtue does not suffice. Dionysius: 'God will perfect that which He began.' Blessed John Huss: 'He will perfect the victory of glory.' Blessed Luther elegantly: 'will prepare'. Blessed Gerhard accumulates various meanings: that God prepares us, because there is no ability (ἱκανότης) in us; perfects us, when He supplies our defects; restores us, when we are preoccupied by a fall. But it is better to understand it with Blessed Luther and others as a full adaptation or apt consummation, by which He renders us perfect in faith and fills us with His gifts, supplies our defects, and completes and consummates our blessedness.

Στηρίζειν is to stabilize, to prop up, Luke XXII. 32, Rom. I. 11, 1 Thess. III. 1, 2 Thess. II. 16, III. 3, 2 Peter I. 12; and it is hinted that God props up our infirmity in faith by the strength of the Spirit, so that we do not fail in temptations. Σθένειν is to be strong, to prevail, whence ἀσθένεια is the weakness of strength. Therefore the Vulgate rendered the preceding and this with one word: which was also done by the Syrian. Θεμελιῶν is to found, Matt. VII. 25, Luke VI. 48, Eph. III. 18. Heb. I. 10, that God founds and solidifies us in faith, just as the Vulgate rendered it: 'will solidify'. From which word Blessed Gerhard gathers that this whole passage is metaphorical: For just as for the construction of a fortress it is required that it be founded on a firm rock, that it be stabilized with columns, that it be propped up with beams so that it does not collapse, that it be fortified and surrounded with ramparts, that it be covered so that it is not damaged by rains: so in the spiritual building God provides all these things for us out of grace; He founds and stabilizes us in faith, restores us in virtues, instructs us with the strength of the Spirit so that our renewal may take increments daily; He arms us to sustain the temptations of Satan, He preserves and confirms us in true piety, so that we may be able to stand against all the insults of the Devil, the world, and the flesh, and not allow ourselves to be moved from true faith and piety by any threats or terrors. In summary, whatever pertains to the beginning, middle, and end of our salvation, Peter encompasses all of that in these four words. Lorinus has things not unlike these on this passage. It is probable, as Gagnejus hints, that the same matter is exaggerated by many words signifying almost the same thing, namely how great is the power of faith and patience or perseverance against the Devil, etc. The Syriac Interpreter seems to have intended this also in the present passage. So that when we have endured these slight oppressions, we may be strengthened and confirmed and persist in Him (Christ Jesus) forever; nevertheless, the Greek words have great force, besides the word καταρτίσαι (which means to restore, compose, fit, complete, instruct, perfect), namely στηρίξαι, to establish firmly and prop up, and by metaphor to confirm what is doubtful; σθενῶσαι, from σθένος, to strengthen; θεμελιῶσαι, from θεμέλιον, to found; all of which aptly suit faith, which is the first foundation in the spiritual edifice and the ὑπόστασις, Heb. 11:1, and therefore Christ said it pertains to that to strengthen (στηρίζειν) the brethren, for whose faith He had prayed that it might not fail, Luke 22:32, and upon whom He had founded His Church, Matt. 16:18. Whence it is entirely to be gathered that we ought not to doubt concerning salvation, but that we can be certain that He who began a good work in us will bring it to completion until the day of Jesus Christ, Phil. 1:6, and that perseverance and salvation depend not on our works, but solely on the grace of God.

Latin:

v. 10. ὁ Θεὸς πάσης χάριτος) Deus clementissimus אל חנון Exod. XXXIV. 6. 2. Paral. XXX. 9. Neh. IX. 17. 31. Jonæ IV. 3. & in Psalmis sæpe. Hic conclusionem epistolæ nonnulli inchoant, sed rectius hic constituitur conclusio adhortationis de non peregrino habendo æstu crucis. Quemadmodum enim priores paræneses δοξολογίᾳ concluserat A- postolus cap. IV. 11. sic eam, quam ibi v. 12. cœpe- rat, & ad quam post insertas quasdam per digres- sionem communes ad Pastores aliosque redierat cap. V. 8. 9. jam voto & δοξολογίᾳ finit. Votum ve- ro finale ad conclusionem totius epistolæ perti- nens versu ultimo subjungit. In hac vero conclu- sione nova cum adhortationis ad resistendum Dia- bolo per fidem, tum consolationis de certa victo- ria subministrat argumenta a divina gratia uber- tate, a vocationis divina benignitate, a passionum brevitate, a beneficiorum divinorum varietate, & conservationis ac consummationis nostræ certitudi- ne. Quæ proinde non per modum voti vel preca- tionis, quod quibusdam visum, sed per modum promissionis adjiciuntur, ut fides pugnantium ad- versus Diabolum corroboretur. Emphatice itaq; Deum πάσης, omnis gratiæ vocat, quæ vox omnis a Syro prætermittenda non erat, & connectit illud cum sequentibus καταρτίσει, ostendens ita, monen- te B. Gerhardo, ex eodem gratiæ fonte, & primam ad gloriam cœlestem vocationem, & ultimam hu- jus beneficii consummationem, videlicet conser- vationem in bono, & introductionem in gloriam cœlestem provenire. S. Augustinus serm. XVI. de Verb. Apostoli: Prædestinavit nos, antequam esse- mus, vocavit, cum conversi essemus, justificavit cum peccatores essemus, glorificavit, cum mortales essemus. ὁ καλέσας ἡμᾶς εἰς τὴν αἰώνιον ἀυτῶ δόξαν ἐν χριστῷ ἰησοῦ) Qui nos vocavit per Jesum Christum ad gloriæ suæ con- sortium. Vide 1. Cor. I. 9. 1. Tim. VI. 12. Recte refertur προσδιορισμὸς per Jesum Chri- stum ad verbum καλέσας, quia vocatio ad vitam æternam propter Christi meritum nobis obtingit, cui omnia beneficia spiritualia accepta ferenda, e- lectio, Eph. I. 3. 4. vocatio, 1. Cor. I. 2. Gal. I. 6. 2. Tim. I. 9. æterna glorificatio, Rom. VI. 23. Ad sequentia ὀλίγον παθόντας, q. d. propter Christum ὀλίγον παθόντας referri, quod nonnulli voluere. ὀλίγον παθόντας) ὀλίγον hic est ad breve tempus, ut supra I. 6. Brevis sane omnis hæc vita æternitati comparata. Nonnulli non ut oppositum diuturnitati, sed magnitudini modicum illud accipiunt. Sed præstat de tempore accipere, ut Jac. IV. 24. & Apoc. XVII. 11. Αὐτὸς καταρτίσαι ὑμᾶς, στηρίξαι, σθενώσαι, θεμελιῶσαι) In Manuscripto καταρτίσει, στηρίξει, σθενώσει, abest ὑμᾶς, sed sub- auditur, nec adest θεμελιώσει, nec aliter legit Latinus. Κα- ταρτίζει כונן Deut. XXXII. 6. Vide 1. Cor. I. 10. 2. Cor. XIII. 11. Ebr. XIII. 21. Στηρίξει יסמך Psal. LI. 13. Es. LIX. 16. Rom. XVI. 25. 2. Thess. II. 17. III. 3. Σθενώσει ויאמץ, Perfectos vos faciet, sustentabit, roborabit. Pronomen ὁ ἀυτὸς non redundat, sed emphasin habet, ut diximus ad v. 10. De diversa lectione se- dulo hic egit B. Gerhardus. Estius verba in optativo mavult legi, fusq; deque Vulgati autoritatem Con- cilio Tridentino probatam habens. Promissioni autem magis, quam voto congruit δοξολογία, & le- ctionem in futuro non solum Regii aliiq; Stepha- ni Codices habent, sed etiam Latini nonnulli, & inter eos autor libr. de vocat. gent. l. I. c. 24. aliique Vulgatam versionem sequentes. Vox καταρτίζειν non modo adaptare & instaurare, 2. Cor. XIII. 11. Gal. VI. 1. sed etiam perficere significat Luc. VI. 40. 2. Cor. I. 30. 1. Thess. III. 10. Ebr. XIII. 20. 21. & a LXX. Interpretibus adhibetur pro כון præparavit, ador- navit, Pf. LXXIII, 17. pro כּוֹנֵן concinnavit, Pf. X. 13. pro יָסַד fundavit Pf. VIII. 3. pro תָּמַךְ sustentavit Pf. XVI. 6. Es. IV. 12. ac firmitatem & perfectionem infert. A Syro חַיִל in Hithpaël exponitur, confor- tatus, corroboratus est, a Vulgato perficiet. Lyranus perficiet, scilicet ad quod vestra virtus non sufficit. Dionysius: Perficiet Deus id, quod incepit. B. Joh. Hussus: Perficiet victoriam gloriæ. B. Lutherus eleganter vollbereiten. B. Gerhardus cumulat va- ria significata, quod Deus nos præparet, quia in nobis nulla est ἱκανότης, perficiat, cum defectus nostros suppleat, restauret, cum lapsu præoccupe- mur: Sed præstat cum B. Luthero & aliis de plena adaptatione vel apta consummatione, qua nos perfectos in fide reddat, & donis suis impleat, de- fectus nostros suppleat, & beatitudinem com- pleat ac consummet, intelligere.

Στηρίζειν est stabilire, fulcire, Luc. XXII. 32. Rom. I. 11. 1. Thess. III. 1. 2. Thess. II. 16. III. 3. 2. Petr. I. 12. ad- euq; innuitur, Deum in fide robore Spiritus fulci- re ac infirmitatem nostram sublevare, ne in tenta- tionibus deficiamus. Σθένειν est valere, pollere, un- de ἀσθένεια virium imbecillitas. Ideo Vulgatus præ- cedens & hoc uno verbo reddidit: Quod & a Syro factum. Θεμελιῶν est fundare, Matt. VII. 25. Luc. VI. 48. Eph. III. 18. Ebr. I. 10. quod Deus nos in fide fun- det ac solidet, quemadmodum Vulgata reddidit: solidabit: Ex quo verbo B. Gerhardus colligit, to- tum hunc locum esse Metaphoricum: Quemadmo- dum enim ad arcis extructionem requiritur, ut ea fundetur in firma petra, ut stabiliatur columnis, ut fulciatur tignis, ne corruat, ut muniatur & circum- valletur aggeribus, ut tegatur, ne a pluviis lædatur: sic in spirituali ædificio Deus hæc omnia ex gratia nobis præstat, in fide nos fundat ac stabilit, in vir- tutibus instaurat, Spiritus robore nos instruit, ut re- novatio nostra indies incrementa sumat: ad tenta- tiones Satanæ sustinendas nos armat, in vera pietate nos conservat & confirmat, ut adversus omnes Dia- boli, mundi & carnis insultus consistere possimus, nec ullis minis vel terriculamentis a vera fide & pietate nos dimoveri patiamur. Summatim quicquid ad sa- lutis nostræ principium, medium, & finem pertinet, illud omne Petrus quatuor hisce verbis comprehen- dit. Quibus non absimilia habet Lorinus in h. l. Pro- babile est, quod innuit Gagnejus, rem eandem verbis multis idem fere significantibus exaggerari, nimi- rum quanta sit fidei vis ac patientiæ seu perseveran- tiæ contra Diabolum &c. Hoc videtur etiam in præ- senti loco voluisse Syrus Interpres. Ut cum sustinue- rimus has oppressiones exiguas, roboremur & confir- memur atq; perstemus in eo (Christo Jesu) in æter- num, nihilominus habent vim magnam Græca verba præter verbum καταρτίσαι (quod significat reficere, componere, aptare, complere, instruere, perficere) nempe στηρίξαι statuere firmiter ac fulcire & per translationem confirmare quod dubium est, σθενῶσαι a σθένος roborare, θεμελιῶσαι a θεμέλιον fundare, quæ omnia apte conveniunt fidei, quæ primum in æ- dificio spirituali fundamentum est & ὑπόστασις, Ebr. I. 1. ac proinde ad illam spectare Christus dixit, fratres στηρίζειν pro cujus fide rogaverat, ne deficeret, Luc. XXII. 32. ac super quem fundaverat Ecclesiam suam, Matth. XVI. 18. Unde colligere omnino est, dubi- tandum nobis non esse de salute, sed certos nos es- se posse, quod qui cepit opus bonum, in nobis illud consummaturus sit, usq; in diem Jesu Christi, Phil. I. 6. nec ab operibus nostris, sed unice a gratia Dei pendere perseverantiam & salutem.

## 5:11
v. 11. To Him be the glory and the power forever and ever) In the Manuscript there is only 'to Him be the power' etc. see above IV. 15.

I would prefer the glory of God to be accepted here in a holy manner concerning the properties of God, power, majesty, perfection of God, etc.: who is therefore called the God of glory and glorious, Acts 7:2. Which is taken relatively, as we are said to give glory to God: Because from thence He fulfills the promise of the confirmation of our faith, because to Him belongs glory, power, wisdom, majesty, and this is celebrated by this Apostolic doxology. Therefore the sense is not, to Him is glory as a preaching, but to Him is glory: which confirms the other, to Him is κράτος power. He does not wish, or command, that the glory and power of God be celebrated, but he professes concerning God, that He is the God of glory, having immense power and infinite strength. conf. 1 Pet. 4:11.

PART III. Conclusion of the whole epistle.

Latin:

v. 11. Αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα, καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τ. αἰώνων) In Manascripto tantum est αὐτῷ τὸ κράτος &c. vide sup. IV. 15.

Gloriam Dei hic malim accipi ὀσιωδῶς de pro- prietatibus Dei, virtute, majestate, perfectione Dei &c: qui ideo Deus gloriae & gloriosus dicitur, Act. VII. 2. quam σχετικως prout accipitur, cum di- cimur Deo gloriam dare: Quia inde promissionem confirmationis fidei nostrae implet, quia ei est glo- ria, virtus, sapientia, majestas, & haec celebratur hac δοξολογία Apostolica. Non ergo sensus est, ipsi est gloria deprædicatio, sed ipsi est gloria: quod confir- mat alterum, ipsi est κράτος potestas. Non optat, aut præcipit, ut celebretur Dei gloria & potestas, sed profitetur de Deo, quod sit Deus gloria, im- mensam potestatem & robur infinitum habens. conf. 1. Petr. IV. 11.

PARS III. Conclusio totius epistolae.

## 5:12
v. 12. By Silvanus to you the faithful brother (as I reckon) I have written in few words) as I reckon, I interpret, if I remember correctly. He testifies to his affection when he says that he is not writing to them now for the first time, but that he had also written before, although briefly, and that, as far as he remembers, through Silvanus or Silas. For the same Silas is in the Acts, and 2 Corinthians, and both epistles to the Thessalonians, and here Silvanus, as we have said at those places. This exposition seems most convenient, so that Peter may appear neither to doubt the faith of Silas, nor to be uncertain whether these few things are many, which he now writes. The praise which is given here to Silas is similar to that which Paul gives to Timothy, 1 Cor. 4:17, and to Tychicus, Col. 4:7. That gloss, if I remember correctly, is new, and does not sufficiently agree with the Word of the Apostle, let alone the inspiration of the Holy Spirit; and on that account also it is to be rejected, because Grotius draws these things to some other epistle of Peter, I know not which, which are to be understood of the present one. For that there was another epistle written by Peter before this one to the dispersed converted Hebrews, is not inferred by any point in this place, nor is it handed down anywhere in the Scriptures, nor does it have even obscure traces in all of antiquity. That the present epistle is the first of St. Peter, however, is received by common suffrage, if by chance you except one, Erasmus, therefore 2 Pet. 3:1 his second epistle is called posterior: Behold, beloved, I write this second epistle to you. And the Syrian here notably: I have written these few things to you, indicating this very epistle. Nor indeed does that parenthesis ὡς λογίζομαι make Peter uncertain about whether they are few or many things which he now writes, as the Syrian and the Vulgate seem to imply, by rendering, through Silvanus a faithful brother to you, as I think, I have written briefly, which sense Estius handed down with Cajetan, referring it to the brevity of the epistle, concerning which, however, how could the Apostle have doubted? Or even concerning the faithfulness of Silvanus, as Schlichtingius thinks, for the reason that Silvanus was not so well known to Peter as to Paul. For the word λογίζομαι, which is altogether to be referred to the epithet πιστῦ, as the order in the authentic text has τῦ πιστῦ ἀδελφῦ (ὡς λογίζομαι), does not signify to think or to suppose, but to determine certainly. For so it is taken Rom. 3:28, 6:11, 8:18, Heb. 11:19. Wisdom 8:18, so that it may note that, having weighed the reasons, he firmly determines with himself, and thus it implies that he is certain, not doubtful, of the Apostle: and this parenthesis is added, as Calvin notes, so that they may certainly know that Peter speaks from the sense of his own mind. For it was absurd not to subscribe to the judgment of such an Apostle, I add that it would have been impious, not merely absurd: because the Apostle was writing this ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίε Φερόμενος. The Syrian rendered the word, as I judge, which if that λογίζομαι is taken concerning the persuasion which Peter had as a man, there are not lacking similar places concerning Paul, Rom. 15:14, Gal. 5:10, 2 Thess. 3:4, 2 Tim. 1:5. Some refer the Greek pronoun ὑμῖν to πιστὸν in this way: Through Silvanus the brother, who performs a faithful ministry to you, but it is more correctly referred to the word ἔγραψα. That by Silvanus is understood Silas, who with Paul and Timothy wrote both epistles to the Thessalonians, and was Paul's colleague in preaching the Gospel, Acts 15:10, 16:19, 25, 29, 17:14, which Jerome also thinks in epistle 14 to Damasus, Oecumenius, as also Lorinus and Cornelius in this place. Whom Peter might seem to have employed for this reason, lest it be spread about that Peter preached something other than Paul, Gal. 2:2. Others urge that because in Silas in Greek, if it be written with an Iota or an Upsilon, they seem to be distinct persons, just as Dorotheus also in his synopsis, and the Menologium of the Greeks on the first of August distinguishes the same. But whatever may be the case regarding Dorotheus, they are mistaken in the writing, since both names are found written with an Iota, and therefore we easily agree that the same Silas and Silvanus are one, which Chytræus in his Onomasticon and others of ours admit. That Peter used Silvanus here as an amanuensis, however, seemed so to Lyranus; and to the author of the interlinear gloss. it pleased that the same was employed as a legate or messenger, which sense from a similar place Rom. 16:22 seems to be preferred.

Exhorting and testifying that this is the true grace of God, in which you stand) He repeats with what intent that short epistle was, so that if they received it, they might know it was written by him, not supposed by someone else. It had been useful, however, that the Galatians, whom Paul had converted to Christ, be confirmed also by the authority of Peter. He calls doctrine here grace, which has proceeded from the supreme goodness of God. And εἰς ἣν for ἐν ᾗ by a commutation frequent in our times. Paul Rom. 5:2, The grace in which we stand, where see what is said. For it is the past for the present, and it signifies that it is faith which preserves you from falls. In the Manuscript it is ἐν ᾗ στῆτε, so that it may be of one exhorting.

This is not a sign of some other epistle which may have been lost, but a recapitulation of the present one, which is partly didactic, which is signified by the word ἐπιμαρτυρῶν, Acts 10:43, and partly hortatory, which the word παρακαλῶν implies, and since exhortation makes up both pages, as it is said, therefore the Apostle places τὸ παρακαλεῖν first in this summary conclusion; B. Gerhard interprets χάριν as doctrine, along with Lyranus, who says that grace here signifies the Catholic faith. The sense therefore is: I have written to you for this reason, that I might not only exhort you to the pursuit of piety and holiness, but also that I might confirm by testimony that doctrine and religion which you have embraced, and which you profess in persecutions, to be that one true doctrine and religion by which God wills to be worshipped. The Apostle confirms, says Flacius, those to whom he writes in the doctrine already rightly received perhaps from Paul and his hearers, who had reached those places. Perhaps there were those who tried to disturb them, saying repeatedly that Paul, by abolishing circumcision and diminishing the righteousness of works and the law, was a less than sincere Evangelist, as also appears from Acts 15 and from the Galatians. This is the true grace in which you stand, that is, the doctrine concerning the grace of God.

Latin:

v. 12. Διὰ Σιλυανῦ ὑμῖν τῦ πιστῦ ἀδελφῦ (ὡς λογίζομαι) δι' ὀλίγων ἔγραψα) ὡς λογίζομαι, interpretor, si recte memini. Affectum suum testatur, cum dicit, se non nunc primum eis scribere, sed & scripsisse antehac, quanquam breviter, & id, quantum meminit, per Silvanum sive Silam. Idem enim Silas in actis, & 2. ad Corinthios & utraque ad Thessalo- nicenses, & hic Silvanus, ut ad illa loca diximus. Hæc ex- positio videtur commodissima, ut neque de fide Silæ vi- deatur dubitare Petrus, neque incertus esse an hæc pauca an multa sint, quæ nunc scribit. Laus quæ hic Silæ datur, similis est ei, quam dat Timotheo Paulus 1. Cor. IV. 17. & Tychico Coloss. IV. 7. Glossa illa, si recte memini, nova est, nec Verbo Apostoli satis convenit, nedum inspirationi Spiri- tus Sancti; atque eo nomine quoque reprobanda est, quod ad aliam quandam Petri epistolam, ne- scio quam, hæc trahat Grotius, quæ de præsenti in- telligenda sunt. Nam aliam ante hanc scriptam à Petro fuisse epistolam ad dispersos Ebræos con- versos, nec ulla hoc in loco apice inferitur, aut us- piam in Scripturis traditum est, neque in universa antiquitate vel obscura saltim habet vestigia. Præ- sentem autem epistolam primam esse S. Petri, com- muni suffragio receptum est, si forte unum exci- pias Erasmum, ideo 2. Petr. III. 1. posterior secunda ejus epistola dicitur: Hanc ecce vobis, charissimi, secundam scribo epistolam. Et Syrus hic notanter: Hæc pauca scripsi vobis, hanc ipsam innuens episto- lam. Nec verò illa parenthesis ὡς λογίζομαι Petrum incertum facit de eo, an pauca sint, an multa, quæ nunc scribit, ut Syrus & Vulgata videtur innuere, reddendo, per Silvanum fidelem fratrem vobis, ut arbitror, breviter scripsi, quem sensum Estius cum Cajetano tradidit, referens eam ad brevitatem epi- stolæ, de qua vero quomodo dubitare potuit Apo- stolus? vel etiam de fidelitate Silvani, ut Schlichtin- gius putat, eo quod non adeò cognitus fuerit Petro Silvanus ac Paulo. Nam verbum λογίζομαι, quod o- mnino ad epitheton πιστῦ referendum, ut ordo in textu authentico habet τῦ πιστῦ ἀδελφῦ (ὡς λογί- ζομαι) non significat putare vel arbitrari, sed certo statuere. Ita enim accipitur Rom. III. 28. VI. 11. VIII. 18. Ebr. XI. 19. Sap. VIII. 18. ut notet subductis ratio- nibus firmiter apud se statuere, adeoque certum esse, non dubium innuit Apostolum: additurq; hæc pa- renthesis, notante Calvino, ut certe sciant, Petrum ex animi sui sensu loqui. Erat enim absurdum, eos tanti Apostoli judicio non subscribere, addo impium id fu- turum fuisse, non absurdum modo: quia scribebat Apostolus hoc ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίε Φερόμενος. Syrus reddidit verbum, ut judico, quod si de per- suasione, quam Petrus habuit, ut homo, accipia- tur illud λογίζομαι, non desunt similia de Paulo lo- ca, Rom. XV. 14. Gal. V. 10. 2. Thess. III. 4. 2. Tim. I. 5. Græcum Pronomen ὑμῖν nonnulli ad πιστὸν re- ferunt hoc modo: Per Silvanum fratrem, qui fide- le vobis ministerium præstat, sed rectius refertur ad verbum ἔγραψα. Per Silvanum Silam intelligi, qui cum Paulo & Timotheo utramque epistolam ad Thessalonicenses scripsit, & Pauli in prædican- do Evangelio collega fuit, Act. XV. 10. XVI.19.25. 29. XVII. 14. quod & Hieronymus putat epist. XIV. ad Damasum, Oecumenius, ut & Lorinus & Cor- nelius in h. l. Quem ideo adhibuisse Petrum videri possit, ne spargerétur, Petrum aliud quid prædica- re, quam Paulum, Gal. II,2. Alii urgent, quod in Si- la Græco per Jota, si Ypsilon scribatur, distinctæ personæ videantur, quemadmodum etiam Doro- theus in synopsi, & Menelogium Græcorum l. Au- gusti eundem distinguit. Quicquid autem sit de Dorotheo, in scriptione falluntur, quum utrumq; nomen per Jota scriptum reperiatur, ideoque faci- le annuimus, eundem Silam & Silvanum esse, quod Chytræus in Onomast. aliique è nostris admittunt. Silvano autem hic usum esse Petrum, ut amanuensi Lyrano visum est; autori glossæ interlin. placuit eundem adhibitum fuisse ceu legatum sive nunci- um, qui sensus è simili loco Rom. XVI. 22. præfe- rendus videtur.

Παρακαλῶν καὶ ἐπιμαρτυρῶν ταύτην εἶναι ἀληθῆ χάριν τοῦ Θεοῦ, εἰς ἣν ἑστήκατε) Repetit quo tenore fuerit brevis illa epistola, ut si eam receperint, sciant eam à se scriptam, non ab aliquo suppositam. Fuerat autem utile, Galatas, quos Paulus ad Christum converterat, etiam Petri autoritate fir- mari. Χάριν vocat hic doctrinam ex summa profectam Dei bonitate. Et εἰς ἣν pro ἐν ᾗ frequenti nostris temporibus commutatione. Paulus Rom. V. 2. Τὴν χάριν ταύτην ἐν ᾗ ἑστήκαμεν, ubi dicta vide. Est enim præteritum pro præsen- ti, & significat fidem esse, quæ vos à lapsibus servat. In Ma- nuscripto est ἐν ᾗ στῆτε, ut sit hortantis.

Non hoc est signum alterius cujusdam epistolæ, quæ deperdita sit, sed ἀνακεφαλαίωσις præsentis, quæ partim didactica est, quod voce ἐπιμαρτυρῶν signi- ficatur, Act. X. 43. partim parænetica, quod vox πα- ρακαλῶν innuit, & quum adhortatio utramq; quod dicitur, paginam in ea faciat, ideo præmittit Apo- stolus τὸ παρακαλεῖν in hac summaria complexio- ne, χάριν de doctrina pariter interpretatur B. Ger- hardus, cum Lyrano, qui gratia, inquit, significat hic fidem Catholicam. Sensus igitur est: Ideo vobis scripsi, ut non solum vos exhortarer ad studium pie- tatis & sanctitatis: Sed etiam ut testimonio confirma- rem doctrinam & religionem illam, quam amplexi estis, & quam in persecutionibus profitemini, solam esse veram illam doctrinam & religionem, qua Deus coli velit. Confirmat, inquit Flacius, Apostolus eos, ad quos scribit in doctrina jam recte accepta forte à Paulo, ejusq́; auditoribus, qui in ea usq́; loca pervene- rat. Forsitan fuerunt, qui eos perturbare sint conati, dictitantes, quod Paulus abolens circumcisionem & extenuans justitiam operum legiq́;, sit parum since- rus Evangelista, ut etiam ex Act. XV. è Galatis appa- ret, Hanc esse veram gratiam, in qua statis, id est do- ctrinam de gratia Dei.

## 5:13
v. 13. She who is in Babylon, elect together with you, greets you. To the word συνεκλεκτὴ both the Syriac and the Arab and the Latin add the name of the Church: rightly. For he writes to the Church. And both this one and that one are equally chosen by God, that is, separated from the world. Thus Paul often calls Christians fellow-heirs and fellow-partakers. Concerning Babylon, the ancient and modern interpreters disagree. The ancients interpret it as Rome, where no true Christian will deny that Peter was; the moderns, as Babylon in Chaldea. I agree with the ancients: for the fact that he called Rome Babylon did not only serve the purpose that, if the epistle were intercepted, it could not be known from it in what places he was living, but also that the people of Pontus might consider that, just as they themselves were now being vexed by the Roman empire, so their ancestors had once been vexed in those very places by the Babylonian empire, yet had been pious in the city of Babylon, and were now in Rome: and that just as God exacted punishment from Babylon, so He would also exact it from Rome: and just as the Jews were once freed from the yoke of Babylon, so the Christians would be freed from Roman cruelty. See Orosius 2.2 for very many congruences between Babylon and Rome. Hence Babylon is a figure of the Roman city for Tertullian in Against the Jews and Against Marcion 4. Here is mystically fulfilled what is in Ps. 87:3.

He brings forward two expositions concerning Babylon: the one is im- proper, concerning Rome, the other proper, concerning the chief city in Chaldea; but a third is given, which is likewise proper. For by this name comes not only the metropolis of Chaldea, but also a certain city of Egypt. Grotius prefers the first opinion, but if you depart from the authority of the ancients, he builds it upon nothing but conjectures and congruities. But one must not depart from the proper signification of names, especially proper names, for mere conjectures, and both those conjectures are ludicrous; the former, which he perhaps received from Baronius, T. I. Annal. ann. 85, n. 16, that he called Rome Babylon so that it could not be known in what places Peter was living: for why would Peter have concealed this? It was rather in the interest of the dispersed faithful that they should not be ignorant of where he was acting, while to others, or from elsewhere, it could have been sufficiently established that Peter was staying at Rome, if he had held the Episcopate or Pontificate there, as the Papists wish. The other [opinion], concerning similar pressures of the Roman faithful, such as those of the Babylonians were of old, and concerning the punishment of persecutors and the similar liberation of the afflicted, which the Papists ought to have conjectured from this appellation, vanishes by its own futility. For what Oedipus would have attained such things by divining, and why would the Apostle have indicated it so obscurely, who could easily have alleged the example of the faithful Jews and the Old Testament, and he had already tacitly embraced that at the same time in chapter IV. 12. Furthermore, the congruities which intervene between Rome and Babylon will only then be relevant here, when it has been established that Rome is understood by Babylon. There remain, therefore, only the authorities of the ancients, whose testimonies are wont to be brought forward in great number; but in them this distinction must be observed, that while most of them teach that Rome is indeed understood by Babylon, they do not assert this precisely of this Petrine passage, but look to the apocalyptic passages, even if some do treat of this passage as well. However, the nature of those places is different: for in the Apocalypse, where many mystical things occur wrapped in figures and images, it is not inconvenient to the nature of that prophetic writing for Rome to be designated by the name of Babylon. But here, in an epistle given to the Pontics, it is not at all probable that Rome is designated by a mystical and figurative name: nor will a similar example be easily found in the Apostolic letters. And that opinion concerning Rome being signified by Babylon in this place took its origin from a writer of not much judgment, Papias, according to Eusebius, Hist. Eccl. book II, ch. 15, whom Jerome seems to have followed in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers under the entry for Mark, as well as Bede and Oecumenius. Add that it has not yet been sufficiently proven that St. Peter ever stayed at Rome, which Grotius ought not to have merely asserted and assumed as indubitable, but to have solidly proven. For we have warned elsewhere that there were not lacking among Christians those who doubted this, and indeed denied it. Meanwhile, if anyone, with the blessed Chemnitz in Harm. Evang. ch. L, asserts that Peter came to Rome around the end of his life in the last years of Nero, we will not greatly object. But that will be able to help Grotius not at all; but certainly, from the fact that Peter only came to Rome toward the end of Nero's reign, it appears even from this that this epistle was not written at Rome, because mention is made of Mark in it. For Mark died at Alexandria in the eighth year of Nero. They report that he established the Alexandrian Church and held the Episcopate there for a long time: whence likewise he could not have been present with Peter at Rome. Nor are there lacking those among the Papists themselves, most of whom abuse this passage to maintain that St. Peter was at Rome—of which, however, no trace, or at least no obscure one, is detected here—who have acknowledged that Babylon is not understood as Rome here. Erasmus in this place: Greetings, he says, the congregation of Christians bids you; which, together with us, God has chosen for Himself in Babylon, and in the midst of more wicked idolaters follows piety, in the midst of those living most corruptly embraces purity of life. And in the argument: He says that he called this [epistle] written from Babylon: For he bids them greetings in the words of this Church, if the fabrication about Rome is not approved by anyone. Francis Coster the Jesuit in Enchir. ch. 3: From the Babylon of Egypt, he says, it is not inappropriately said that his former epistle was written.

Furthermore, the reasons by which the Papists contend that one must depart from the propriety of the word Babylon here can be solved without any difficulty; for what Baronius, loc. cit., warns concerning the Babylon of Chaldea, that in the time of Gaius Augustus, according to Josephus, Antiq. book XVIII, ch. 12, the Jews who were at Babylon were expelled, can easily be refuted concerning the Babylon of Egypt, because it is a place clearly obscure and not worthy of the name of a town, and no Church was gathered there; since it cannot be denied that there were Christians in the Babylon of Assyria in the time of Peter, whence it is to be gathered that Peter betook himself there for the sake of preaching the Gospel, and that by virtue of the pact entered into with Paul, Gal. II. 7, since he spent some years in Syria, as Luke testifies in the Acts, how easily could he have approached Babylonia? But that Babylon in Egypt was an obscure town does not prevent a Church from having been gathered there, and since Mark, the disciple of Peter, held the Episcopate at Alexandria in Egypt, why could Peter not have stayed in Egypt as well? See Bunting in Itin. book II, p. 61, and Funccius in Chronol. Salmero says Babylon in Egypt is called Memphis, which is called Cairo today, according to Cornelius. Considered the largest city in the world, whose Bishop Baronius designated in the 5th century: in which, however, in the time of the Apostles, who preached throughout the whole world, there is no cause for doubting that the Gospel was announced and a Church gathered. Ps. 137, 4, does not indeed treat only mystically, but in the literal sense, of the Gospel being preached by the Babylonians also in the time of the New Testament, nor is it necessary to understand Rome precisely by Babel there, although we do not doubt that, with a few nations named, others are simultaneously indicated in the manner of Scripture.

and Mark my son) Why we think that not John Mark, mentioned in the Acts, but the companion of Peter, whose Gospel we have, is signified, we have said at the inscription of his Gospel. The Apostles were accustomed to call those whom they themselves had instructed sons, as you see 1 Cor. IV. 17, 1 Tim. I. 2, 18, 2 Tim. I. 2, ch. II. 1. And Mark had the Jewish name Mordecai, as Silvanus had Silas.

Concerning these, because we have likewise spoken at the prolegomena of Mark, we do not wish to do what has already been done.

Latin:

v. 13. Ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς ἡ ἐν Βαβυλῶνι συνεκλεκτὴ) Ad vo- cem συνεκλεκτὴ & Syrus & Arabs & Latinus addunt nomen Ecclesiæ:recte. Nam & ad Ecclesiam scribit. Et hæc & illa pa- riter à Deo electa, id est, à mundo segregata. Sic Christianos συγκληρονόμους, συγκοινωνοὺς sæpe vocat Paulus. De Babylone dissident veteres & novi Interpretes. Veteres Romam inter- pretantur, ubi Petrum fuisse, nemo verus Christianus nega- bit: novi, Babylonem in Chaldæa. Ego veteribus assentior: Nam quod Romam Babylonem vocavit, non in hoc tan- tum serviit, ut si deprehenderetur epistola, non posset inde sciri, quibus in locis viveret, verum etiam ut cogitarent Pon- tici, sicut nunc ipsi vexarentur ab imperio Romano, ita olim majores suos, & quidem illis ipsis in locis vexatos fuisse ab imperio Babylonico, fuisse tamen pios in urbe Babylone, & nunc esse Romæ: at sicut Deus pœnas exegit de Babylone: ita & exacturum de Roma: Et sicut olim Judæi a Babylonis jugo liberati fuere: Ita & Christianos à Romana sævitia li- beratum iri. Congruentias plurimas inter Babylonem & Romam vide Orosii II.2. Hinc Babylon Romanæ urbis figu- ra Tertulliano adversus Judæos, & adversus Marcionem IV. Hic mystice impletum, quod est in Ps. LXXXVII. 3.

Duas de Babylone affert expositiones, altera im- propria est de Roma, altera propria de civitate in Chaldæa præcipua; sed datur tertia, quæ itidem pro- pria est. Nam hoc nomine non tantum venit me- tropolis Chaldææ, sed etiam civitas quædam Ægy- pti. Præfert Grotius primam sententiam, sed eam si ab autoritate veterum discesseris, non nisi conje- cturis & congruentiis superstruit. At primum à propria significatione nominum imprimis pro- priorum ob meras conjecturas discedendum non est, & ludicra utraq; illa conjectura est, prior, quam à Baronio T.I. Annal. ann. 85. n. 16. forte accepit, quod Romam Babylonem vocarit, ut non possit sciri, quibus in locis viveret Petrus: nam cur hoc dissimu- lasset Petrus? intererat potius dispersis fidelibus, ne ignorarent, ubi ageret, aliis vero vel aliunde id satis constare poterat, Romæ Petrum degere, si Episcopatu vel Pontificatu, quod Papistæ volunt, ibidem functus fuit. Altera de similibus Romanen- sium fidelium pressuris, quales olim erant Babylo- niorum, deq; persecutorum pœna & afflictorum liberatione simili, quam ex hac appellatione con- jectare Pontici debebant, futilitate sua evanescit. Ecquis enim Oedipus talia divinando assequutus fuiffet, & cur id tam obscure indicasset Apostolus, qui facile poterat exemplum fidelium Judæorum & Vetus Testamentum allegare, taciteque id simul complexus jam erat cap.IV. 12. Congruentiæ porro, quæ Romæ & Babyloni intercedunt, tum demum huc facturæ sunt, ubi constiterit per Babylonem Romam intelligi. Restant ergo solum autoritates veterum, quorum testimonia magno numero ad- duci solent; sed in iis id discriminis observandum, quod pleraque per Babylonem Romam quidem intelligi doceant, non autem præcise de hoc loco Petrino id asserant, sed apocalyptica loca respiciant, etsi nonnulla de hoc etiam loco agant. Est autem dispar locorum istorum ratio: nam in apocalypsi, ubi multa mystica figuris & imaginibus involuta occurrunt, Romam nomine Babylonis designari scripti istius Prophetici indoli non inconveniens est. At hic mystice & figurato nomine in epistola ad Ponticos data Romam designari haud probabile est: nec simile facile exemplum in literis Apostolicis invenietur. Et originem illam de Roma per Ba- bylonem hoc loco significata opinio cepit à scri- ptore non multi judicii Papia apud Eusebium l. II. Hist. Eccl. c. 15. quem sequutus videtur Hierony- mus in catal. script. Eccles. sub voce Marci, Beda, & Oecumenius. Adde quod nondum satis proba- tum sit, S. Petrum unquam Romæ egisse, quod non nude tantum asserere debuit Grotius, & pro indu- bitato assumere, sed solide probare. Non defuisse enim inter Christianos, qui de eo dubitarint, imo id negarint, alias monuimus. Interim si quis cum B. Chemnitio in Harm.Evang. c.L. asserat, Petrum circa finem vitæ suæ ultimis annis Neronis Romam venisse, non adeo refragabimur. Id vero Grotium nihil juvare poterit; sed eo certe, quod Petrus Ro- mam demum sub finem Neronis venerit, hanc e- pistolam Romæ scriptam non esse vel inde appa- ret, quod Marci in ea mentio fiat. Marcus enim jam anno octavo Neronis Alexandriæ mortuus est: Quem Alexandrinam Ecclesiam constituisse, ibiq; diu Episcopatu functum fuisse tradunt: unde iti- dem Romæ Petro non potuit adfuisse. Neque de- sunt è Pontificiis ipsis, quorum pleriq; hoc loco abutuntur, ut obtineant, Romæ S. Petrum fuisse, de quo vero nullum hic vel obscurius saltem ve- stigium deprehenditur, qui agnoverint per Baby- lonem hic non intelligi Romam. Erasmus in h. l. Sal- vere, inquit, vos jubet congregatio Christianorum; quam una nobiscum Deus sibi delegit Babylone, & in medio iniquiorum idololatrarum sequitur pietatem, in medio corruptissime viventium amplectitur vitæ puritatem. Et in argumento: Hanc scriptam, in- quit, appellaret ex Babylone: Nam hujus Ecclesiæ verbis jubet eos salvere, si cui de Roma commentum non probatur. Franciscus Costerus Jesuita in Enchir. cap. 3. Ex Babylone Ægypti, inquit, non incommode dicitur ipsius prior epistola scripta.

Porro nullo negotio solvi possunt rationes, qui- bus hic à proprietate vocis Babylonis discedendum esse contendunt Papisequæ, quod de Babylone Chaldææ Baronius l.c. monet, Caji Augusti tempore Josepho l. XVIII. antiq. c. 12. Judæos, qui Babylone agebant, expulsos fuisse, de Babylone vero Ægypti, quod obscurus plane locus, nec oppidi dignus no- mine fuerit, & nulla ibi collecta Ecclesia sit, dilui fa- cile potest; Siquidem in Babylone Assyriæ Christianos fuisse tempore Petri negari non possit, unde collige- re est, Petrum eo se contulisse Evangelii prædican- di ergo, idque vį pacti cum Paulo initi, Gal. II. 7. quum in Syria aliquot annis egerit, teste Luca in A- ctis, quam facile potuit adire Babyloniam? Quod autem Babylon in Ægypto fuerit obscurum oppi- dum, haud obstat, quo minus illic Ecclesia collecta fuerit, & quum Marcus Petri discipulus Alexan- driæ in Ægypto Episcopatu functus sit, quidni po- tuerit Petrus in Ægypto etiam egisse? Vid. Bün- ting. in itin. l. II. p. 61. & Funccius in Chronol. Sal- mero Babylon in Ægypto Memphis dicitur, quæ Cai- rus hodie vocatur, teste Cornelio. Urbs maxima ha- bita in orbe, cujus Episcopum seculo 5. designavit Baronius: in qua verò Apostolorum tempore, qui per totum orbem prædicarunt, Evangelium an- nunciatum, & Ecclesiam collectam esse, dubitandi causa nulla suppetit Pf. 137, 4. non mysticè quidem tantum, sed sensu literali agit de Evangelio à Ba- byloniis etiam prædicando tempore N. Test. nec per Babel ibi Romam præcise intelligere necessum est, quanquam paucis nominatis gentibus alias si- mul subindicari more Script. non dubitemus.

καὶ Μάρκος ὁ ὑός με) Cur non Johannem Marcum in actis memoratum, sed Petri comitem, cujus habemus Evangelium, significari putemus, diximus ad ejus Evangelii inscriptionem. Solebant Apostoli eos, quos ipsi instituerant, filios vocare, ut vides 1. Cor. IV. 17. 1. Tim. I. 2. 18. 2. Tim. I. 2. c. II. 1. Et Marco nomen Judaicum fuit Mardochæus, ut Silvano Silas.
