De his quia itidem diximus ad Marci prolego- mena, nolumus actum agere.

## 5:14
v. 14. Greet one another with a kiss of love) after the manner of the East, concerning which we have spoken at Luke VII. 45, ch. XXII. 48, Rom. XVI. 16, 1 Cor. XVI. 20, 2 Cor. XIII. 12, 1 Thess. V. v. 26, of love, namely, Christian love. The Syriac reads ἐν φιλήματι ἁγίῳ, as is very often the case in Paul.

Concerning that custom of the East, see Justin, Apology to Antoninus; Tertullian, book on prayer; Cyril of Jerusalem, Mystagogic Catechesis V; Augustine, Question LXXXVII on Genesis. From that custom of the East, therefore, and not, as Baronius wishes (Vol. I, annals for the year 45, no. 13), did the holy kiss take its origin from the Romans, concerning which Augustine says in sermon LXXXIII on various topics: After the prayer, which you have received and returned, it is said 'peace be with you,' and Christians kiss one another with a holy kiss, a true kiss, a kiss of peace, a dove-like kiss, not deceitful, not polluted, such as Joab used to kill Amasa, such as Judas used to betray the Savior, such as those who speak peace with their neighbor, but evils are in their hearts. Therefore, those who do not love in word or in tongue, but in deed and in charity, greet one another with that holy kiss.

Peace be to you all) שלום לכם, the Hebrew custom of greeting. The Syriac here has: שלמא עם כלכון.

Some think the word πληθυνθείη should be supplied from ch. I. 2 and from the epistle of Jude v. 2, but the substantive verb can be understood, which is a more common ellipsis.

Interlinear gloss. To all throughout the world the churches; whence Bede gathers that this epistle is catholic, pertaining to all Christians; But the pronoun ὑμῖν refers to those to whom the epistle is directed, whom he says are in Christ Jesus, namely through faith. If this were an acclamation of the Church, it would not be a part of the Θεοπνεύςꙋ canon, which must not be conceded, concerning which we have warned before. # 2 Peter

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
In the Name of Jesus. Annotations on the second epistle of St. Peter.

Latin:

I. N. J. ANNOTATA AD EPISTOLAM POSTERIOREM S. PETRI.

## 1:1 Introduction: Prolegomena
Prolegomena.

Grotius did not preface things peculiarly only concerning the inscription of the epistle, but also some things about the name of the Author, who is called Simon, about the Author, whether he is Peter the Apostle, or indeed some other one called Simon, about the unity of the epistle, about the sincerity of the inscription, and also some things on occasion about the Canonical authority, about the style of diction, about the time of writing, about the Syriac translation, and about those to whom this epistle was delivered, which, as they were handed down by him, we will first exhibit. Then, with the order slightly changed, we will examine them, and finally, we will add some things that pertain to the prolegomena. The inscription then presents the persons, namely the author by whom the epistle was written, and those to whom it was written, and then it contains a vow. The things that deal with the persons properly pertain here to the Prolegomena, and they are as follows: Σίμων Πέτρꙋ δῦλος καὶ Ἀπόςολος Ἰησῦ Χριςῦ) Other books say Συμεὼν. But that is the same thing. For this is the Hebrew name שמעון, that one is bent from the Hebrew into a more Greek form, as Jason from Jesus. Thus 1 Macc. 2:65 in Greek is Συμεὼν, in Latin Simon. And Josephus writes it by this name. Now long ago many of the ancients believed this epistle not to be of the Apostle Peter, by the argument both of the diction being much different from the former epistle, which Eusebius and Jerome acknowledge, and because many churches long ago did not receive it. I will add another argument, why this seems not to be Peter's? Peter died under Nero. But this epistle, or the epistle, as we think, annexed to it, which makes the third chapter, was written after the destruction of Jerusalem. For no Christian believed that the last day of the world would come, unless after the overthrow of the Jewish state had happened. But after that, the ruin of the world would follow very shortly, was in the minds of many, as we said at 2 Thess. 2 and elsewhere. But here the writer wants Christians to be patient still in the expectation of that day, if perhaps it arrives later than hoped: That this is a sign of the great patience of God, who still wishes many from the Jews and Gentiles to be converted to Himself. I think, however, the writer of this epistle is Simeon, or Simon the Bishop after the death of James at Jerusalem, and the successor and imitator of the same James, whose epistle we have had. For the name of that Bishop is written in both ways, both Simeon and Simon, in Eusebius and others, whence it is also evident that he lived after the destruction of Jerusalem until the times of Trajan, and was then crucified for the name of Christ. I think, however, the title of the epistle was: Συμεὼν δῦλος Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ, as both James and Jude write: but that those who wanted to make this epistle more respectable and marketable added Πέτρꙋ and Ἀπόςολος, and below 3:15, to the name of Paul, ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελφός. I believe it will be found so, if anyone finds copies of this epistle older than those we have. In the old books of the Syrians, this epistle is absent. Tertullian never uses a testimony taken from here.

without doubt. Here, before the word Σωτῆρος, the article is omitted, clearly as in Tit. 2:13.

As for what first concerns the name of Simon, little depends on it, whether it is written Σίμων, or indeed Συμεών. Nor do we add anything about the origin. However, there occur in the N.T. in this latter form Συμεὼν, besides the name of the tribe so called, Rev. 7:7, and Simeon, who was among the ancestors of Christ, the son of Judah, Luke 3:30, that pious man who took the infant Jesus in his arms, Luke 2:25, a certain Simeon surnamed Niger, Acts 13:1, numbered among the Prophets and Teachers of Antioch. But in the former form, besides Simon Magus, Acts 8:9, 13, 18, 24, Simon the father of Judas Iscariot, John 6:71, Simon the leper, Matt. 26:6, Simon the Cyrenian, ch. 27:32, Simon the tanner, Acts 9:43, in the college of the Apostles Simon the Canaanite, Matt. 10:4, and Simon surnamed Peter, v. 2, son of Jonah, John 1:42, therefore called in the Syriac idiom Bὰρ Ἰωνᾶ, Matt. 16:17. Whom the inscription teaches to be the author of this epistle.

Grotius, however, denies that he is the author of it: and appeals to the authority of the ancients, because many of them believed that this epistle is not of the Apostle Peter. Grotius did not name those ancients, whom if he had investigated, perhaps he would not have found so many. Eusebius indeed, l. 3 Hist. Eccl. c. 3, says that among the presbyters of old he had discovered only one epistle of Peter that was acknowledged: yet he named only Origen, who himself did not speak from his own opinion: His words are these, l. 6 c. 25. Peter has left one epistle acknowledged, let there be also a second, for it is doubted. He left one epistle approved by common confession. Let there be also a second. For it is doubted. Origen did not say by whom, nor did he absolutely give his assent, but he indicated not obscurely that he himself was in doubt. Nor was Eusebius more certain. Jerome followed these in his catalogue of Illustrious men. On Peter: The second epistle, he says, is denied by many to be his on account of the dissonance of the style. Gregory the Great, Homily XVIII on Ezekiel, reports some who indeed conceded that this is an epistle of Peter, but denied that it is of Peter the Apostle, and attributed it to some other Cephas or Peter, whom Paul withstood to his face, Gal. II. 11. But no one else is understood there than the Apostle. And Gregory the Great refutes that opinion sufficiently in book 5. If they had wished to weigh the words of the same epistle, they could have thought far otherwise. For in it is written concerning the voice that descended to him of this kind from the magnificent glory: This is my beloved Son, and it is subjoined: And we heard this voice, when we were with him in the holy mount. Let them read, therefore, the Gospel, and they will immediately recognize that when that voice came from heaven, Peter the Apostle stood with the Lord. He therefore wrote this epistle, who heard this voice on the mount concerning the Lord.

Furthermore, the reasons by which it is called into doubt that it is of the Holy Apostle are of no strength. The first from

To them that have obtained like precious faith with us) ἰσότιμον, ἰσόμοιρον, ἰσόπεδον, are words accepted by the more elegant Greeks, such as are not few in the Maccabean books. Such also is λαγχάνειν for to receive in the book of Wisdom. The faith of all Christians tends to the same honor, namely, eternal life. This epistle, however, was sent to the Jews by nation, Christians by religion, who were in various places of the earth.

In the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ) Among other things, a part of justice is to stand by promises. Christ promised, and through Christ God, eternal life to those believing in him, namely, by that faith which has obedience as its companion. He will perform that in diction, much different from the former, is brought forward not indeed by Eusebius, but by Jerome, and that primarily from the opinion of others. For he himself did not conclude from that that Peter was not the author of it, but only that Peter had a different interpreter, writing thus in Epist. ad Hedib. quaest. II: The two epistles which are attributed to Peter differ from each other in style and character, and in the structure of the words. From which we understand that, because of the necessity of the circumstances, he used different interpreters. Although this opinion concerning the different interpreters whom the holy Apostle used does not have a foundation, nor does it agree in any way. For did Peter write in any other than the Greek language, and did he employ another interpreter for the translation into the Greek language? Or did he dictate only his own thoughts and permit the character of the writing to an amanuensis? Is this epistle not thus rendered of doubtful authority regarding the Greek text, or regarding the character of the diction and words, as to whether the interpreter was inspired by God? Estius explains Jerome regarding the diversity of interpreters in such a way that by interpreter he understands only a scribe or amanuensis: but a different character of diction cannot proceed from a scribe, who only receives and records what is dictated, just as it is dictated. Therefore, that opinion of Jerome, resting on no authority of the ancients, is more safely set aside; to which that of Clement of Alexandria, lib. VII. Strom., might indeed seem similar, that Mark performed the duty of an interpreter for Peter, and a certain Glaucias, whom Basilides falsely boasted was his master: But Baronius, ad ann. 45. num. 37, understands the office of interpretation not as the translation of writings, but of sermons, or even the explanation of those things which the Apostles had spoken with difficulty. Nor indeed is that dissimilarity of style so great that it proves a different author, since it is not only established, as Cajetan rightly observes here, that one and the same man sometimes writes in a different style, which is sufficiently apparent even from the epistles of Paul himself, provided that a diversity of subject matter sometimes demands a different character or style: but also learned men here not undeservedly doubt that discrepancy of style. Erasmus indeed quite boldly in his annotations to this epistle: The difference of style, he says, both in the thoughts and in the words, is too clear to be concealed. Others, however, as Estius holds, do not acknowledge this dissimilarity of character, of which among the ancients only Jerome makes mention, so much so that even the Magdeburg Centuriators affirm that the style of this epistle seems to them very similar to the former: In which matter, says Estius, we Catholics easily agree with them. For the opinion of the dissimilarity of style seems to have been born from the diversity of the subject matter. Otherwise, even in the judgment of Calvin, this epistle has nothing unworthy of Peter, so much so that it expresses the power and grace of the Apostolic Spirit everywhere. Thus Estius. The Magdeburg Cent. I. lib. II. cap. 4. col. 54. have it thus: The style and composition do not differ much from the former epistle of Peter. In both occurs an artificial brevity joined with the highest majesty.

The second reason of Grotius is that many churches did not receive this epistle. But by this reasoning, not so much Peter as a ministerial author, but the supreme author of this epistle, and its canonical authority, could be called into doubt, if there were any weight in it. But in truth, the doubt of certain churches, unless it rests on solid arguments, cannot prejudice the truth. Although Eusebius reports not of the doubt of entire churches, but only of certain ancients, and on the contrary, both the divine authority and the author, the holy Apostle Peter, are established by firmer arguments than that this doubt could move anyone, of which hereafter.

Grotius adds a third reason why it does not seem to be Peter's, taken from the time: That this epistle was written after Nero, under whom Peter met his death, indeed after the destruction of Jerusalem. But that glutton of antiquity could prove this first point by no document from antiquity. Then the conjecture which he draws from it, that in this epistle the last day of the world is hinted at as being briefly imminent, is utterly futile: No Christian, he says, believed that the last day of the world would come (he wished to add 'briefly', otherwise he would have made all those Christians scoffers), until after the overthrow of the Jewish state had happened. But after that, the ruin of the world following very briefly was present to the minds of many. But neither this nor that rests on any suitable witnesses, but both are merely asserted nakedly. But what he adds: This writer indeed wishes Christians to be patient still in the expectation of that day, if perhaps it arrives later than hoped, proves nothing. For he acts against the scoffers, who were utterly denying the final advent, and he takes care that they are not seduced by the same. But to have believed that the writer believed Christ would come briefly to judgment detracts entirely from the direction of this author by the Holy Spirit immediately, and thus from the canonical authority of the epistle. For thus he would have believed a falsehood, which cannot be said of an author inspired by God. Add that those things concerning the extreme advent of Christ occur only in the third chapter, which Grotius considers a peculiar epistle. What then do those things do to the author of the first and second chapters, which according to the same constitute a proper and different epistle?

Finally, Grotius offers some conjecture or divination, that the writer of this epistle is Simeon, Bishop of Jerusalem after the death of James. But who among the ancients has handed this down? Who among the moderns has ever even dreamed of such a thing? Then indeed, if two are to be established from this later, as it is called, epistle, whose author is that Simeon to be considered? That of the former, or of the other, or of both? If of the other, that is, of the third chapter only, why does he claim both, or more correctly this whole epistle, for the same person? If of the first two chapters only, that argument from time falls, as I have said. If of all three chapters, not only the author but also the truth of the epistle is called into doubt, although the truth is also endangered by the reasoning of the third chapter, if someone other than the Apostle is believed to be the author, as we are about to say. Finally, the canonical authority of the epistle cannot but be endangered in this way. For that Simeon was not an Apostle or θεόπνευστος (divinely inspired).

Therefore, having dismissed that profane desire of Grotius to call into doubt divinely inspired (θεόπνευσα) writings, we prove that St. Peter the Apostle is the author of the present epistle, first from the inscription itself. For the author is indicated not only by the name Simeon, or, as some other codices have it, Simon, which alone would be sufficient, because no one in the evangelical history or in the Acts of the Apostles is called by that name among the divinely inspired (θεοπνεύστοις) men, without a determining addition (προσθήκῃ) except Simon Peter the Apostle. See Matt. XIII. v. 53, ch. XVII, 25, Mark I. 16, ch. VI. v. 3, ch. XIV. v. 37, Luke IV. v. 38, ch. V. v. 3, 4, 5, 10, ch. XXII. v. 31, ch. XXIV. 34, John I. v. 41, but also by the surname Πέτρα (Rock); when both names are joined, it perpetually denotes Peter the Apostle in the scriptures, and it is not rarely accustomed to be joined, Matt. XVI. v. 16, Luke V. v. 18. John I. v. 40, ch. VI. v. 8, 68, ch. XIII. v. 6, 24, 36, ch. XVIII. v. 10, 15, 25, ch. XX. v. 2, 6, ch. XXI. v. 2, 3, 7, 11, 15. Indeed, there is added besides the name of the office, δοῦλος καὶ Ἀπόστολος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, so that no doubt remains that Peter is the author of the epistle. Grotius affirms that this title is corrupted no less impiously than rashly, since other parts of Scripture could be called into doubt with equal ease, so that finally nothing certain would be left in the Holy Scriptures. For he could not deny that all Greek codices exhibit this inscription with the highest consensus: Indeed, it grieved the man that he found no exemplar consistent with his own invention. And yet he dared to believe and persuade others that older exemplars of this epistle, if they were found, would support his opinion. Although he could not produce the slightest shred of evidence from antiquity for his most vain suspicion. Of how great audacity, therefore, that untimely Aristarchus of the Holy Scriptures was, can be established even from this example, that he judges those two names, Πέτρος καὶ Ἀπόστολος, to be so confidently expunged.

Then from the testimony concerning the vision of the glory of Christ and the hearing of the voice from heaven made to Christ by God the Father, when this Simon was with Christ on the holy mount, chap. I, v. 16, 17, 18. For this provides an argument above all exception, that no other Simon than Peter the Apostle is the author of this epistle, who was with Christ at His transfiguration with John and James on the mount, Matt. XVII, v. 1. And with what appearance of truth could that Simon, Bishop of Jerusalem, have professed this of himself? Hugo indeed wished to twist these words concerning the heavenly voice heard on the mount by Peter and the other two Apostles to another manifestation, but those writings are under the rays of the sun and such circumstances that a significant violence must be inflicted upon the words, whence the man, who seems to have been born for the purpose of rendering Scripture doubtful in every way, again retreated to a most miserable hiding-place, indeed an impious invention of corruption admitted even in that passage: Concerning which, when we have arrived at that place.

Thirdly, from the mention of the later epistle. This, he says, chap. III, v. 1, is the second epistle which I write to you, in which I stir up your sincere mind by way of reminder: Which have a relation to the former epistle of Peter, whether we look to those to whom both epistles were written, or attend to the scope of both; whence it is gathered not obscurely that both proceeded from no other Simon than Peter the Apostle.

Fourthly, from the inclusion of the Author under the name of the Apostles, 2 Peter III, v. 2, καὶ τῆς τῶν Ἀποστόλων ἡμῶν ἐντολῆς. For these sound as if one of the Apostles were speaking: which is a trifle to Grotius, because he thinks that pronoun is an interpolation, by which reasoning all trifles could be held to be in the Scriptures. For what, in the end, could not be struck out in such a way, since that is infinite in the Holy Scriptures? For all codices add the pronoun, and in most it is read ἡμῶν, not ὑμῶν, whence also Blessed Luther rendered it: And of our commandment, who are Apostles of the Lord and Savior. Concerning which Schlichtingius in his commentary adds his own and the other Apostles' commandment concerning faith in Christ Jesus and perfect righteousness and holiness. And afterwards: He calls himself an Apostle, but he also adds other Apostles, as if to say, not of me as the only Apostle, but also of all the other Apostles.

Fifthly, from Paul's συναδελφίᾳ. For the author of the epistle calls Paul his brother, chap. III, v. 15. Which fits Peter, but not Simon, the Bishop of Jerusalem. Whence Grotius also suspects the text here to be corrupted, and that ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελφός was added to the name of Paul by those who wished to make this epistle more respectable and more marketable. But what would the hands of Harpies not dare in the Holy Scriptures, if it were permitted to scrape away or eliminate whatever one pleases without any authority of codices or antiquity?

Sixth, from the collation of the Epistle of Jude. For this is as it were a compendium of the Petrine epistle, and especially of the second chapter. But who would believe that Jude would have wished to reduce a writer who is not θεόπνευστον [divinely inspired] into a compendium, or that the Holy Spirit had brought it about that those things which are not Apostolic should be repeated through the Apostle, or, as Grotius loves to speak at 2 Peter II, v. 3, that Jude should have transferred most things from Simeon of Jerusalem.

To these arguments from the bowels of the text are added the testimonies of sound antiquity; since most Fathers attributed this epistle to Simon Peter the Apostle, indeed all who acknowledged that it pertains to the Testamentary books and the canon of Scripture: but if Grotius believed it did not pertain to it, why did he rank it with other ἐνδιαθήκοις [canonical] writings without any indication of disparate authority, or that it pertains least to the canon? This epistle is cited by the name of Peter by ancient Doctors: by Athanasius in the Synopsis, Epiphanius haer. LXXVI, Jerome to Paulinus, Augustine lib. III de doctr. Christian. c. 8, Gregory the Great hom. XVIII in Ezech., Damascene lib. IV orthod. fid. c. 18. And Amphilochius in his Iambics to Seleucus, Nazianzen in his poem on the Scriptures, Rufinus of Aquileia in his exposition of the creed, Innocent I in his third epistle to Exuperius, and Isidore lib. VI Etymol. c. 1, testify that it is Peter's. The present epistle is also placed in the canon by Councils under the name of Peter, such as the Laodicean can. 59, as also the third Council of Carthage, cap. 47. Likewise the Council of 70 Bishops under Gelasius I. Bede, indeed, in the preface to his commentary on this epistle, wonders that anyone should doubt that the author of this epistle is St. Peter, since he expresses his own name and testifies that he was on the mount with the Lord. We have mentioned above that Gregory the Great also used this argument. But no one has been found who ever established that Simeon, Bishop of Jerusalem, was the author.

From which also the canonical authority of this epistle, which is the third chapter of the things prefaced, is easily gathered: because if Peter the Apostle, a man of God, ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίε φερόμενος [borne along by the Holy Spirit], is the author of the Epistle, it cannot be doubted that the Epistle, inspired by the Holy Spirit, is of divine and canonical authority: which is therefore confirmed by intrinsic criteria, by the majesty and sublimity of the epistle, both as regards the most divine subject matter, and as regards the style of speaking and the Apostolic Spirit, by the all-encompassing truth and harmonic consensus with other θεοπνεύστοις [divinely inspired] writings, by the efficacy and divine power which exerts itself in the souls of men through this epistle also; from the testimony, as regards the express letter, superior to any exception, by which the author names himself Peter the Apostle, a spectator of the glory of Christ on the holy mount, and a hearer of the proclamation of the heavenly voice, a colleague of the Apostles, and a sharer in the same authority as the Prophets, a fellow-brother of Paul, and takes upon himself the role of approving the Pauline epistles and commending so great an Apostle, and finally from the divine preservation of this epistle, which has been propagated uncorrupted along with the other canonical books of the New Testament. To these must be added the extrinsic arguments from the testimonies of the Doctors and Councils already praised, as those by which this epistle is referred to among the canonical scriptures, from the consensus of the Church, both express and interpretative. For if there has been any doubt, it has been doubted by a few, of whom we have spoken before. Estius warns that it is not found in the Syriac: but he observes to the contrary, that the excellent Syrian Doctors Ephrem and John Damascene sometimes cite testimonies from this epistle as sacred, and that Damascene weaves the same into his catalogue of the Scriptures. But Edward Pococke also published the same Syriac version together with the second and third epistles of John and the epistle of Jude from a Manuscript of the Bodleian Library of Oxford in the year 1630; it was also published in the Polyglot Bibles. Finally, there are no reasons why the canonical authority of the epistle can be called into doubt: nor do we see why, on account of the hesitation of some, we ought to call it deuterocanonical: since that hesitation was based on no reasons, and canonical authority, if we wish to speak more accurately, admits of no degrees, nor does it properly depend on the testimonies of men.

Fourthly, the uncorrupted sincerity of the epistle is acknowledged by all, except that Grotius, with a profane mind, has attempted to render it suspect, but he is instructed by no evidence: regarding what Estius brings forward from the commentary of Didymus of Alexandria, the teacher of Jerome, on this epistle, which concludes it thus: It is not therefore to be ignored that the present epistle is falsified, which although it is published (that is, read publicly for the laws of the Church), it is not however in the Canon; the same Estius warned about this, that Didymus is mistaken in this, and that he gathers it poorly from those things which are held at the end of the epistle concerning the renovation of the world, where he thinks Platonic revolutions are taught. But the blessed Gerhard adds, not without merit, that it is not without reason that some suspect those words were inserted into the book of Didymus by another, since he neither shows in what way this epistle was falsified, nor is it likely that such a great man would have wished to publish commentaries on an Apocryphal Epistle.

Fifthly, the unity of this epistle must be weighed. Grotius imagines that not one, but two epistles are exhibited in these three chapters; the one indeed in the two former, the other in the third. This is a new and unheard-of opinion, nor does it rest on any foundation, according to which it is doubtful whether these three chapters proceeded from the same or from different authors? And now there will not be only two, but three epistles, which were taken for two: nay, not three, but four epistles of Simon are to be believed to have been written, even if according to Grotius they are different: for Grotius maintains that two epistles were also written by Simon Peter, 1 Peter 5:12. All of which are new discoveries, entirely worthy of such an Aristarchus and Dictator of the sacred letters. On the contrary, all consistently attribute these three to the same acknowledged Author, and say that they constitute one and the same epistle. It has been believed until now that two, and no more, epistles were written by Simon, and he the Apostle, surnamed Peter, of which the first is canonical, completed in five chapters, and this second one in three chapters.

Sixthly, the personal object, or those to whom the epistle was sent, are described by the faith which they have received. However, by faith is understood either the doctrine, which is the faith that is believed, or properly the faith by which one believes that ἰσότιμος, not only by reason of the end, because it tends to the same honor, namely eternal life; but also by reason of intrinsic dignity, because it is most worthy of honor, as much as to the matter, or those things about which it is concerned, which are truly divine, such as both precepts and mysteries, as also as much as to the form, because the doctrine of faith is not of any human thing, but because of the Spirit, which is united to the Word or heavenly doctrine, from whence the efficacy of the Word and divine virtue flows, it is truly divine. Moreover, there is no need for us to take faith improperly or metonymically for doctrine when the proper acceptance has a place, approved by most

interpreters, because the faith of all believers is ἰσότιμος; both by reason of the object, from which it has all its honor, which is the most precious righteousness or obedience of Christ, both active and passive, and by reason of divine estimation or imputation, because God imputes faith to us for righteousness, which is the highest price and the highest honor of faith. The Vulgate rendered ἰσότιμον ἡμῖν as equal to us. But it is properly faith equally precious with us. He compares the faithful Jews with the Apostles, just as the pronoun ἡμῶν is taken in chapter 3, verse 2, or as the blessed Gerhard prefers, the converted Gentiles with other faithful Jews. For the faith of all is the same, by reason of the object, and equally precious before God on account of the object, which is the merit of Christ, which it itself embraces, even if by reason of degrees there is a diversity in the subjects, concerning which the blessed Luther beautifully says: A giant embraces a gem enclosed in a golden ring, and a little boy also embraces it. Although the giant embraces it more strongly than the little boy; yet the ring remains equally precious, and the gem equally precious, whether the giant or the little boy embraces it. The gift is equally precious which is received by a weak hand, and which is apprehended by a robust hand: because the price is not from the receiver, or of the receiving or apprehension itself, but in the excellence of the gift itself. And therefore it is added ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ in the RIGHTEOUSNESS of God and our Savior, because faith is borne toward the righteousness of Christ, relies upon it, rests solely in it, and is properly the apprehension of the righteousness of Christ itself, which believers are said to have received, because it is given to them freely, so that they may believe, Phil. 1:29, and faith is a gift of God, John 6:29. For λαμβάνειν is to receive something by lot, but those things which happen by lot, happen freely without merit, Acts 1:17, Eph. 1:11, Col. 2:12.

That doctrine of faith also consists properly in the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ. Which is to be read in one spirit, and accepted in a combined sense, namely that Jesus Christ is our God and Savior, which the omission of the article and the comparison of the passage v. 11 below, as well as c. III. 18, and also Tit. II. 13, made here by Grotius himself confirms, whose righteousness is especially the object of the obedience of faith, because Moses and the Prophets testify of it, Rom. III. v. 21, cap. X. v. 4, Act. X. 43. But God did not only promise eternal life through Christ, but Christ, God blessed forever over all, merited the same for us, Rom. IX. v. 5, since he himself was given for the life of the world, John VI. v. 51. For it could not have been promised to us, unless Christ had satisfied for our sins, and had merited eternal salvation for us, because we were under wrath and eternal condemnation, Rom. III. 19, cap. XI. v. 32. He promised, however, that it is to be obtained by faith, which has obedience as its companion, even though it is not obtained through obedience, but by faith alone.

Grotius acknowledges those to whom the epistle was sent as Jews by race, Christians by religion, and as for their location, dispersed in various places of the earth. And therefore this latter epistle was written entirely to the same people as the former, just as is expressly taught in cap. III, 1. Peter Aureolus is therefore mistaken when he says in his Compendium of Scripture that the latter epistle of Peter was written to the Romans: for since the former was directed to the Jews dispersed through Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, the same cannot be denied of the latter, which they also gather from 1 Pet. I. 19, because the Prophetic word was made to the Jews, not to the Gentiles, and theirs were the τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ, Rom. III. v. 20. Add that 2 Peter III. v. 15 refers not to the epistle of Paul to the Romans, as that Aureolus wished, but to the epistle to the Hebrews let it be considered, as we shall show regarding that passage. Yet we do not deny that this epistle was directed also to the Gentiles, among whom those faithful Jews were dispersed, just as we observed above regarding the former.

As for the seventh point, regarding the place of writing, it is not indeed as clearly defined as in the former, yet it seems likely to many that this epistle was also sent from Babylon. Schlichtingius supports this opinion on chapter III, verse 1, concluding that Rome cannot be understood by Babylon: Hence it appears, he says, that this second epistle was directed to the same people to whom the former was specifically inscribed, namely to the Jews dispersed through Pontus, Galatia, Bithynia, Cappadocia, and Asia, who professed the name of Christ. Whence it may be conjectured that this epistle, like the former, was sent from Babylon, to which those regions are nearer than to Rome, being situated in the same part of the world; which I say against those who, without any probable reason, claim that Rome was signified by the name of Babylon in the former epistle.

Eighth, the occasion for the epistle was provided both by those who were more remiss in the pursuit of piety and faith, who therefore needed to be stirred up, and by those who were busy seducing the faithful, or were foreseen to be about to seduce them, against whom they needed to be fortified and forewarned; such as, in part, the false prophets who denied the Master who had bought them, and in part the scoffers who rendered the final coming of the Lord ambiguous. Therefore, just as tyrants and persecutors provided the handle for the former epistle, so did heretics and seducers for this latter one, as Hugo and Dionysius warn. Whence Blessed John Huss says: In the former epistle, Peter led those to whom he writes to remain in the goodness of grace, lest they succumb through the adversities of tribulations. In this latter one, he leads them to persevere in the truth of Christian grace, lest they be perverted by the false doctrine of heretics and false apostles.

Ninth, therefore, the scope of the epistle is now not obscure, and it is twofold: first, διέγερσις (stirring up) to piety, and especially to constancy in faith, which is the root of all virtues; and second, ὑπόμνησις (reminding), by which he wished to recall to the memory of the faithful the commands of the Prophets and Apostles, so that they might be instructed against any seducers whatsoever: both of which ends and scopes he joins in chapter III, verses 1 and 2, as also in chapter II, verses 12 and 13.

Whence tenth, Athanasius in his Synopsis establishes the argument of the epistle as follows: This epistle, he says, is a ὑπόμνησις (a refreshing of memory) of the former. For when Peter had learned that the ἀνάλυσιν (departure) of his body would soon take place, he diligently acted so that all might be admonished of those things about which they had been instructed before through the doctrine of the Gospel. And first, indeed, he discourses about faith, and shows that it was announced by the Prophets, and that the prophecies concerning the Savior are not human, but were foretold by God. Then he warns them not to pay attention to seducers, predicting their future destruction, just as punishment was taken upon the transgressing Angels. Moreover, this epistle signifies the future days in which scoffers will be going about everywhere, and will attempt to seduce some, saying that the future coming of the Savior is preached by us in vain, for the reason that, although it is always being preached, it has not yet come. Therefore he commands them to abstain from these, teaching us not to lose heart for the sake of the delay, because the whole of time produces no slowness before the Lord, with one day being like a thousand years and a thousand years like one day. At the same time, he affirms and declares that the day of the Lord will be soon, and commands all to be prepared for His coming in good works, and to embrace what has been written by the Apostle, and not to lend their ears to those who slander these things, since the same people also slander all the divine scriptures. After, therefore, he has admonished and taught everyone so that they may know these future things, he exhorts that no one should stray from the faithful scope, and thus he ends the epistle.

According to St. Athanasius, therefore, the epistle will not be incorrectly distributed into a θέσιν (thesis) concerning the Evangelical doctrine once foretold by the Prophets, which is to be retained, and an ἀντίθεσιν (antithesis) concerning the heterodoxy of false prophets and seducers, which is to be avoided. The former is exhibited in chapter I, the latter in II and III. It pleased Blessed Gerhard to designate the two parts of the epistle thus: that the former is νυθεσία (exhortation) to constancy and progress in faith and the pursuit of piety, and the latter is προφητεία (prediction) both concerning false prophets and seducers, and concerning the scoffers and mockers who deny the final coming of Christ. Both partitions can be conveniently joined, and therefore let it be

PART I. EPISTLES. A hortatory thesis on guarding the faith and adorning it with virtues.

Latin:

ΠΡΟΛΕΓΌΜΕΝΑ.

Non præfatus est peculiariter Grotius solum circa ἐπιγραφὴν epistolæ nonnulla de nomine Autoris, qui Simon vocatur, de Autore, an Petrus sit Apostolus, an verò alius quidam Simon vocatus, de epistolæ unitate, de inscriptionis sinceritate, quædam etiam ex occa- sione de autoritate Canonica, de dictionis genere, de scriptionis tempore, de translatione Syriaca, de iis, ad quos scripta hæc epistola tradidit, quæ uti ab ipso tradita sunt, primum exhibebimus. Deinde ordine paululum immutato expendemus, deniq; aliqua, quæ ad τὰ προλεγόμενα faciunt, subjicie- mus. Ἐπιγραφὴ tum personas sistit, autorem nempe à quo scripta epistola, & hos, ad quos ea perscripta, tum votum continet. Quæ de personis agunt propriè huc ad Prolegomena pertinent, atque ita habent: Σίμων Πέτρꙋ δῦλος καὶ Ἀπόςολος Ἰησῦ Χριςῦ) Alii libri Συμεὼν. Sed id perinde est. Hoc enim est nomen Ebræum שמעון, illud ex Ebræo in Græciorem formam deflexum, ut ex Jesu Jason. Sic 1. Macc. II. 65. in Græco Συμεὼν, in Latino Simon. Et hoc nomine ita scribit Josephus. Jam olim vete- rum multi credidere hanc epistolam non esse Apostoli Petri, argumento tum dictionis ab epistola priore multum diver- sæ, quod agnoscunt Eusebius & Hieronymus, tum quod multæ olim Ecclesiæ hanc non receperint. Ego aliud addam argumentum, cur hæc non Petri esse videtur? Petrus sub Ne- rone obiit. At hæc epistola, aut epistola, ut nos arbitramur, huic subnexa, quæ facit caput tertium, scripta est post exci- dium Hierosolymorum. Nemo enim Christianus ultimum mundi diem venturum credidit, nisi postquam evenisset eversio Judaici status. Post eam vero brevi admodum secu- turam mundi ruinam, multorum animo obversabatur, ut di- ximus ad 2. Thessal. II. & alibi. Hic vero scriptor Christianos vult patientes adhuc esse in illius diei expectatione, si forte sperato tardius adveniat: Esse hoc signum magnæ Dei patien- tiæ, qui adhuc multos ex Judæis & gentibus ad se velit con- verti. Scriptorem autem hujus epistolæ arbitror esse Simeo- nem, sive Simonem Episcopum post Jacobi mortem Hie- rosolymis, ejusdemq; Jacobi, cujus epistolam habuimus, suc- cessorem & imitatorem. Nomen enim ejus Episcopi utroque modo & Simeon & Simon scribitur apud Eusebium & alios, unde etiam constat, vixisse hunc post excidium Hierosoly- morum ad Trajani tempora, & tunc pro Christi nomine crucifixum. Puto autem titulum epistolæ fuisse: Συμεὼν δῦ- λος Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ, quomodo & Jacobus & Judas scribunt: sed eos qui spectabiliorem & vendibiliorem voluerunt fa- cere hanc epistolam, adjecisse Πέτρꙋ & Ἀπόςολος, & infra III. 15. ad nomen Pauli ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελφός. Credo ita comperturum, si quis antiquiora quam nos habemus, episto- læ hujus exemplaria invenerit. In Syrorum libris veteribus abest hæc epistola. Tertullianus nunquam deprompto hinc testimonio utitur.

procul dubio. Est hic ante vocem Σωτῆρος omissus articu- lus, plane ut Tit. II. 13.

Quod primum ad nomen Simonis, in eo parum situm est, an Σίμων scribatur, an verò Συμεών. Neq; de origine quicquam addimus. Occurrunt autem in N. T. hac posteriori forma Συμεὼν præter no- men tribus ita nuncupatæ, Apoc. VII. 7. & Simeonem, qui inter majores Christi fuit, Judæ filius Luc. III. 30. pius ille, qui ulnis excepit Jesulum, Luc. II. 25. quidam Simeon cognomine Niger, Act. XIII. 1. Pro- phetis & Doctoribus Antiochenis annumeratus. Priori verò forma præter Simonem Magum Act. VIII. 9. 13. 18. 24. Simonem Judæ Iscariotidos paren- tem, Joh. VI. 71. Simonem leprosum, Matth. XXVI. v. 6. Simonem Cyreneum, c. XXVII. 32. Simonem co- riarium Act. IX. 43. in collegio Apostolorum Si- mon Cananæus, Matth. X. 4. & Simon cognomina- tus Petrus, v. 2. filius Jonæ, Joh. I. 42, ideo Syriaco idiomate Bὰρ Ἰωνᾶ dictus, Matth. XVI. 17. Quem autorem hujus epistolæ esse inscriptio docet.

Grotius tamen eum autorem ejusdem esse ne- gat: & ad veterum autoritatem provocat, quod multi eorum crediderint, hanc epistolam non esse Apostoli Petri. Non nominavit veteres illos Gro- tius, quos si indagasset, forte non adeò multos in- venisset. Eusebius quidem l. III. Hist. Eccl. c. 3. apud Presbyteros olim unam tantum Petri ὁμολογεμέ- νην se deprehendisse ait: Origenem tamen solum nominavit, qui nec ipse è propria sententia loquu- tus est: Ejus verba sunt hæc l. VI. c. 25. Petrus μίαν ἐπιςολὴν ὁμολογεμένην καταλέλοιπεν, ἔςω δὲ καὶ δευτέραν, ἀμφιβάλλεται γὰρ, unam epistolam com- muni confessione probatam reliquit. Esto autem & alteram. De ea enim ambigitur. Non dixit à qui- bus, nec absolutè assensum præbuit, sed dubium seipsum esse haud obscure innuit Origenes. Neque certior fuit Eusebius. Sequutus holce Hieron. in catal. Illustr. viror. in Petro: Secunda, inquit, Petrâ epistola à plerisque ejus esse negatur propter styli disso- nantiam. Gregor. M. Homil. XVIII. in Ezech. re- fert quosdam, qui concesserint quidem Petri hanc esse epistolam, at negarint, eam esse Petri Apostoli, & tribuerint alii cuidam Cephæ seu Petro, cui Pau- lus in faciem restiterit, Gal. II. 11. Sed ibi nullus alius, quam Apostolus intelligitur. Et refellit eam opinionem satis Gregor. M. l. 5. Si ejusdem epistolæ verba pensare voluissent, longe aliter pensare pote- rant. In ea quippe scriptum est de voce delapsa ad eum hujusmodi à magnifica gloria: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, atq; subjungitur: Et hanc vocem nos au- divimus, cum essemus cum ipso in monte sancto. Le- gant itaq; Evangelium, & protinus cognoscent, quia cum vox ista de cælo venit, Petrus Apostolus cum Do- mino stetit. Ipse ergo hanc epistolam scripsit, qui hanc vocem in monte de Domino audivit.

Porro rationes, quibus S. Apostoli eam esse in dubium vocatur, nullius roboris sunt. Prima à

Τοῖς ἰσότιμον ἡμῖν λαχῦσι πίςιν) ἰσότιμον, ἰσόμοιρον, ἰσό- πεδον, voces sunt ab elegantioribus Græcis acceptæ, quales non paucæ in Maccabaicis. Tale est & λαγχάνειν pro accipere in libro Sapientiæ. Fides omnium Christianorum ad eun- dem honorem tendit, nempe vitæ æternæ. Missa autem hæc epistola ad gente Judæos, religione Christianos, qui erant in variis terrarum locis.

Ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ τῶ Θεῶ ἡμῶν καὶ Σωτῆρος Ἰησῦ Χριςῦ) Ju- stitiæ inter alia pars est, stare promissis. Promisit Christus, & per Christum Deus, vitam æternam credentibus sibi, nem- pe ea fide, quæ obedientiam habeat comitem. Id præstabit dictione, a priori multum diversa non ab Eusebio quidem, sed ab Hieronymo, idq; imprimis ex mente aliorum affertur. Ipse enim inde non concIusit, Petrum ejusdem autorem non esse, sed tantum di- versum Petrum habuisse Interpretem, in epist. ad Hedib. quaest. II. ita scribens: Duae epistolae, quae feruntur Petri, stylo inter se & charactere discre- pant, structuraq; verborum. Ex quo intelligimus, pro necessitate rerum diversis eum usum Interpreti- bus. Quanquam nec haec de diversis Interpreti- bus, quibus usus fuerit S. Apostolus, sententia fun- damentum habeat, aut ullo modo conveniat. Num enim Petrus alia, quam Graeca lingua scri- psit, & ad translationem in Graecam linguam alium Interpretem adhibuit? Aut num sensus dictavit tantum suos & characterem scriptionis permisit amanuensi? Annon ita haec epistola dubiae reddi- tur autoritatis quoad Graecum textum, sive quoad characterem dictionis & verborum, an Interpres θεόπνευστος fuerit? Estius exponit Hieronymum de diversitate Interpretum ita, ut per Interpretem scribam solum vel amanuensem intelligat: sed a scriba non potest proficisci alius character dictio- nis, qui tantum excipit & consignat, quae dictan- tur, prout dictantur. Tutius ergo illa Hieronymi sententia nulla veterum autoritate nixa reponitur; cui similis quidem videri possit illa Clementis Ale- xandr. libr. VII. Strom. quod Interpretis munere apud Petrum functus fuerit Marcus, & Glaucias quidam, quem Basilides falso suum jactitarit Ma- gistrum: Sed interpretationis officium non de trans- latione scriptorum, sed concionum, vel etiam ex- planatione eorum, quae difficilia loquuti fuissent Apostoli, intelligit Baronius ad ann. 45. num. 37. Nec vero illa styli dissimilitudo tanta est, ut diver- sum autorem probet, quum non modo constet, ut recte Cajetanus hic observat, unum atq; eundem ho- minem stylo quandoq; diverso scribere, quod vel ex ipsis Pauli epistolis satis apparet, fiquidem etiam materia diversitas diversum quandoq; characterem aut stylum postulet: sed & de illa styli discrepantia eruditi hic non immerito ambigant. Erasmus quidem audacter satis in annot. ad hanc epistolam: Styli, inquit, discrimen tum in sensibus, tum in ver- bis clarius est, quam ut possit dissimulari. Alii ta- men, ut Estius habet, hanc characteris dissimilitu- dinem, cujus inter veteres solus Hieronymus memi- nit, non agnoscunt, adeo ut etiam Magdeburgenses (Centuriatores) affirment, stylum hujus epistolae cum priori valde similem sibi videri: Qua in re, inquit Estius, nos Catholici facile iis assentimur. Nam opinio dissimilitudinis styli ex materia diversitate nata videtur. Alioqui etiam, Calvino judice, nihil habet haec epistola Petro indignum, ita sane, ut vim Spiritus Apostolici & gratiam ubique exprimat. Haec Estius. Magdeburg. Cent. I. lib. II. cap. 4. col. 54. ita habent: Stylus & compositio a priori epistola Petri non admodum discrepat. In utraque occurrit artificiosa brevitas cum summa majestate conjuncta.

Altera ratio Grotii est, quod multa Ecclesia hanc epistolam non receperint. Sed hac ratione non tam Petrus autor ministerialis, quam autor su- premus hujus epistolae, ejusdemque autoritas Ca- nonica in dubium vocari posset, si quod illi mo- mentum inesset. Verum enim vero quarundam Ecclesiarum dubitatio, nisi solidis ea innitatur ar- gumentis, veritati non potest praejudicare. Quan- quam nec de integrarum Ecclesiarum, sed de quo- rundam tantum veterum dubitatione Eusebius re- ferat, & ex adverso firmioribus argumentis & au- toritas divina, & autor S. Petrus Apostolus con- stet, quam ut ista dubitatio quemquam movere possit, de quibus deinde.

Tertiam addit Grotius rationem, cur Petri esse non videatur, à tempore desumptam: Quod post Neronem, sub quo mortem obiit Petrus, exarata sit epistola hæc, imò post excidium Hierosolymorum. Sed id primum nullo ex antiquitate documento probare potuit heluo antiquitatis. Deinde conje- ctura, quam inde petit, quod in hac epistola mun- di dies extremus ceu brevi imminens innuatur, prorsus futilis est: Nemo, inquit, Christianus ulti- mum mundi diem (brevi addere voluit, alioquin empæctas fecisset omnes illos Christianos) ven- turum credidit, nisi postquam evenisset eversio Ju- daici status. Post eam verò brevi admodum sequu- turam mundi ruinam multorum animis obversaba- tur. At neque hoc, neque istud ullis testibus ido- neis nititur, sed nudè tantùm asseritur utrumque. Quod verò addit: Hic scriptor verò Christianos pa- tientes adhuc esse vult in illius diei expectatione, si forte sperato tardius adveniat, nihil probat. Agit enim contra empæctas, qui prorsus negabant ad- ventum novissimum, & ne ab iisdem seducantur cavet. Credidisse autem Scriptorem, brevi ven- turum Christum ad judicium, derogat omnino autoris hujus directioni à Spiritu S. immediatæ, adeoque epistolæ autoritati Canonicæ. Ita enim falsum credidisset, quod de θεοπνεύστῳ autore dici non potest. Adde, quod illa de extremo Christi adventu in tertio demum capite occurrant, quod pro peculiari epistola habet Grotius. Quid ergò ista faciunt ad capitis primi & secundi, quæ pro- priam & diversam juxta eundem constituunt epi- stolam, autorem?

Tandem conjecturam vel divinationem ali- quam affert Grotius, quod Scriptor hujus epistolæ sit Simeon Episcopus post mortem Jacobi Hieroso- lymis. Ecquis verò veterum id tradidit? Ecquis re- centiorum vel somniavit tale quid unquam? Tum verò, si duæ constituendæ ex hac posteriori, quæ vocatur, epistolæ, cujusnam Autor Simeon ille ha- bendus? An prioris, an alterius, an utriusque? Si alterius, hoc est capitis tertii tantùm, cur utram- que vel rectiùs totam hanc epistolam eidem vindi- cat? Si priorum duorum capitum solum, cadit, ut dixi, illa à tempore ratio. Si omnium trium capi- tum, non jam Autor tantum, sed veritas etiam epistolæ in dubium vocatur, quanquam & tertii capitis ratione periclitetur veritas, si alius quàm Apostolus Autor credatur, uti jam dicturi sumus. Deinique non potest non ita periclitari autoritas Canonica epistola. Simeon enim ille non fuit Apo- stolus vel θεόπνευστος.

Missa ergo prophana illa in dubium vocandi scripta θεόπνευσα libidine Grotiana S. Petrum A- postolum Autorem præsentis epistolæ esse proba- mus primum ex ipsa inscriptione. Indicatur enim Autor non solùm nomine Simeonis, vel, ut alii quidam codices habent, Simonis, quod solum suf- ficiens foret, quia nemo in historia Evangelica, vel in Actis Apostolicis eo nomine appellatus est è viris θεοπνεύστοις, sine προσθήκῃ determinante præ- ter Simonem Petrum Apostolum. Vid. Matth. XIII. v. 53. cap. XVII, 25. Marc. I. 16. cap. VI. v. 3. cap. XIV. v. 37. Luc. IV. v. 38. cap. V. v. 3. 4. 5. 10. cap. XXII. v. 31. cap. XXIV. 34. Joh. I. vers. 41. sed etiam cognomine Πέτρα, utrumque nomen cum conjungitur, Petrum Apostolum perpetuo in scri- pturis notat, nec raro conjungi solet, Matth. XVI. v. 16. Luc. V. v. 18. Joh. I. v. 40. cap. VI. v. 8. 68. cap. XIII. v. 6. 24. 36. cap. XVIII. v. 10. 15. 25. cap. XX. v. 2. 6. cap. XXI. v. 2. 3. 7. 11. 15. Imò ad- ditur præterea nomen officii δοῦλος καὶ Ἀπόστολος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ne dubium ullum superfit, Petrum Autorem esse epistolæ. Quem titulum non minus impie, quam temerarie corruptum esse, affirmat Grotius, quum parili facilitate cæteræ Scripturæ in dubium vocari queant, ut nihil deni- que certi in sacris literis relinquatur. Omnes enim codices Græcos summo consensu hanc in- scriptionem exhibere diffiteri non potuit: Imo id homini doluit, quod nullum exemplar invenerit commento suo congruum. Et credere tamen aliisque persuadere ausus est, antiquiora exem- plaria epistolæ hujus, si inveniantur, suæ opinioni suffragatura. Quum ne minimum ex antiquitate suspicionis vanissimæ proferre potuerit docu- mentum. Quantæ ergo audaciæ intempestivus ille sacrarum literarum Aristarchus fuerit, vel ab hoc exemplo constare potest, quod tam confiden- ter expungenda duo illa nomina Πέτρος καὶ Ἀπό- στολος judicet.

Deinde e testificatione de gloriæ Christi visio- ne & auditu vocis de cælo ad Christum a Deo Pa- tre factæ, quum in monte sancto fuit hic Si- mon cum Christo, cap. I. v. 16. 17. 18. Hæc enim argumentum præbet omni exceptione superius, non alium Simonem, quam Petrum Apostolum hujus epistolæ Autorem esse, qui cum Christo in transfiguratione ipsius cum Johanne & Jacobo in monte fuit, Matth. XVII. v. 1. Et qua veritatis specie Simon ille Hierosolymitanus Episcopus id de se profiteri potuisset. Detorquere quidem voluit Hugo hæc verba de voce cœlesti in monte a Petro, aliisque duobus Apostolis audita ad aliam mani- festationem, sed scripta illa Solis radiis & talibus circumstantiis, ut vis insignis verbis inferenda sit, unde denuo se ad miserrimum κρησφύγετον, imo impium commentum corruptelæ in illo etiam lo- co admissæ recepit homo, qui ad id natus videtur, ut undiquaque Scripturam dubiam redderet: Quo de, quum ad locum istum devenerimus.

Tertio e posterioris epistolæ mentione. Hæc, in- quit cap. III. v. 1. est secunda epistola, quam ad vos scribo, in quibus excito vestram in commonitione sinceram mentem: Quæ ad priorem epistolam Pe- tri relationem habent, sive eos respiciamus, ad quos scripta utraque epistola est, sive scopum utriusque attendamus; unde non ab alio Simone, quam a Petro Apostolo utramque profectam esse haud obscure colligitur.

Quarto ex Autoris sub Apostolorum nomine complexione 2. Petri III. v. 2. καὶ τῆς τῶν Ἀποστόλων ἡμῶν ἐντολῆς. Hæc enim ita sonant, quasi unus ex Apostolis loqueretur: quod leviculum Grotio est, quia infarstum pronomen illud putat, qua ratio- ne omnia levicula in scripturis haberi possent. Ec- quid enim tandem non elidi ita posset, quod infi- nitum id sacris literis sit. Codices enim omnes pronomen addunt, & in plerisque legitur ἡμῶν non ὑμῶν, unde etiam B. Lutherus reddidit: Und an unser Gebot, die wir sind Apostel des HErrn und Heylandes. De quo Schlichtingius in comment. Prophetis adjungit suum & aliorum Apostolorum mandatum de fide in Christum Jesum & perfecta justitia & sanctitate. Et postea: Apostolum se di- cit, sed & alios Apostolos adjungit, q. d. non mei unius Apostoli, sed & omnium aliorum Apostolorum.

Quinto a Pauli συναδελφίᾳ. Vocat enim Pau- lum fratrem suum Autor epistolæ cap. III. v. 15. Quod in Petrum congruit, non vero in Simonem Hierosolymitanum Episcopum. Unde & hic tex- tum corruptum suspicatur Grotius, & ad nomen Pauli ab iis, qui spectabiliorem & vendibiliorem voluerunt facere hanc epistolam, adjectum esse ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελφός. Quid vero non aude- rent tandem Harpyiæ manus in sacris literis, si citra ullam codicum vel antiquitatis autoritatem radere vel eliminare liceret, quicquid lubet?

Sexto ex epistolæ Judæ collatione. Hæc enim veluti compendium est epistolæ Petrinæ, & præ- cipue capitis secundi. Quis autem credat? Judam voluisse scriptorem non θεόπνευστον in compen- dium redigere, aut Spiritum S. id egisse, ut per A- postolum ea, quæ non sunt Apostolica, repeteren- tur, vel ut Grotius ad 2. Petri II. v. 3. loqui amat, ut Judas pleraq́; e Simeone Hierosolymitano transferri beret.

Quibus argumentis e visceribus textus acce- dunt testimonia sanæ antiquitatis; siquidem Patres plerique hanc epistolam Simoni Petro Apostolo tribuerint, imo omnes, qui ad libros Testamen- tarios & canonem Scripturæ eandem pertinere agnoverunt: ad quem autem si non pertinere cre- didit Grotius, cur cæteris scriptis ἐνδιαθήκοις sine ullo indicio disparis autoritatis, vel quod ad ca- nonem minime pertineat, accensuit? Adducitur hæc epistola nomine Petri a Doctoribus antiquis. ab Athanasio in synopsi, Epiphanio hær. LXXVI. Hieronymo ad Paulin. Augustino lib. III. de doctr. Christian. c. 8. Gregorio M. hom. XVIII. in Ezech. Damasceno lib. IV. orthod. fid. c. 18. Et testantur eandem Petri esse Amphilochius in Jambis ad Se- leucum, Nazianzenus in carm. de script. Ruffinus Aquilejens. in exposit. symb. Innocentius I. ad Exu- per. epist. III. Isidorus lib. VI. Etymol. c. 1. A Con- ciliis etiam epistola præsens in canone collocatur sub nomine Petri, utpote Laodiceno can. 59. ut & Carthagin. III. cap. 47. Concilio item LXX. Epi- scoporum Gelas. I. Beda vero in proœm. com- mentar. in hanc epist. miratur, quenquam dubitare de Autore epistolæ hujus S. Petro, quum nomen suum exprimat, seq́; in monte cum Domino fuisse testetur. Quo argumento etiam usum fuisse Gregorium M. supra commemoravimus. Nemo autem repertus est, qui Simeonem Hierosolymitanum Episco- pum Autorem esse, unquam statuerit.

E quibus etiam jam autoritas Canonica hujus epistolæ, quod tertium sit τῶν προλεγομένων caput, facile colligitur: quia si Petrus Apostolus, Vir Dei, ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίε φερόμενος, Autor Epistolæ est, dubium esse nequit, Epistolam a Spiritu S. inspi- ratam, divinæ & canonicæ autoritatis esse: Quod proinde argumentis ab intrinsecis κριτηρίοις confir- matus a majestate & sublimitate epistolæ, tum quo- ad materias divinissimas, tum quoad dicendi genus & Spiritum Apostolicum, ab omnimoda veritate & harmonico consensu cum aliis scriptis θεοπνεύστοις, ab efficacia & vi divina, quæ se exerit in animis ho- minum per hanc etiam epistolam; a testificatione, quoad expressam literam, omni exceptione su- periori, qua se Autor Petrum Apostolum specta- torem gloriæ Christi in monte sacro, & auditorem proclamationis vocis cælestis, collegam Apostolorum, & ejusdem cum Prophetis autoritatis consortem, confratrem Pauli nominat, & partes approbandi epistolas Paulinas, & commendandi tantum Apo- stolum sibi sumit, a conservatione denique divina hujus epistolæ, quæ cum cæteris libris Novi Testa- menti canonicis in corrupta propagata est. Quibus addenda extrinseca argumenta a testimoniis Docto- rum & Conciliorum jam laudatis, utpote a quibus inter Canonicas scripturas hæc epistola refertur, a consensu tum expresso, tum interpretativo Eccle- siæ. Si qua enim forte dubitatum est, a paucis du- bitatum est, quo de antea dictum. Estius monet, quod in Syriaco non habeatur: sed observat con- tra, quod Syri Doctores egregii Ephrem, & Joh. Damascenus ex hac epistola interdum testimonia pro sacris citent, quodque Damascenus eandem ex黙reffe catalogo Scripturarum intexat. Sed & edidit eandem Syriacam Eduardus Pococke una cum secunda & tertia Johannis & Judæ epistola ex Bibliothecæ Bodlejanæ Oxoniensis Manuscripto Anno 1630. edita etiam est in Bibliis Polyglottis. Denique causæ nullæ sunt, cur in dubium vocari possit autoritas epistolæ Canonica: neque etiam videmus, cur ob dubitationem quorundam δευτε- ροκανονικὴν eandem dicere debeamus: Siquidem nullis rationibus innixa fuerit illa dubitatio, & Canonica autoritas, si accuratius loqui velimus, gradus nullos admittat, neq; ab hominum testimo- niis propriè dependeat.

Quarto sinceritas epistolæ incorrupta ab omni- bus agnoscitur, nisi quod profana mente Grotius eandem suspectam reddere conatus sit, sed docu- mento instructus nullo: quod è Didymi Alex. Hieronymi Præceptoris commentario in hanc epi- stolam affert Estius: quod eandem ita concludat: Non est igitur ignorandum, præsentem epistolam esse falsatam, quæ licet publicetur (id est, publice pro Ecclesiæ legatur) non tamen in Canone est, de eo monuit idem Estius, Didymum in hoc falli, idque male colligere ex iis, quæ in fine epistolæ habentur de mundi renovatione, ubi tradi putat revolutiones Platonicas. Addit autem non immerito B. Ger- hardus, haud sine ratione quosdam suspicari, verba illa in librum Didymi esse ab alio inserta, cum nec ostendat, in quo falsata fuerit hæc epistola, nec veri- simile sit, tantum virum in Epistolam Apocrypham commentarios edere voluisse.

Quinto epistolæ hujus unitas expendenda. Fingit Grotius non unam, sed duas epistolas tribus hisce capitibus exhiberi; alteram quidem duobus prioribus, alteram tertio. Nova hæc & inaudita est sententia, nec ullo nititur fundamento, secun- dum quem dubium, an ab eodem, an a diversis autoribus hæc tria capita profecta? Nec jam duæ tantum, sed tres erunt epistolæ, quæ pro duabus habitæ: imo non tres, sed quatuor Simonis, etsi juxta Grotiurn diversi, epistolæ exaratæ credendæ: nam a Simone Petro etiam duas scriptas esse epi- stolas 1. Petri V. v. 12. statuit Grotius. Quæ omnia nova εὑρήματα sunt, tanto sacrarum literarum Aristarcho ac Dictatore prorsus digna. Contra omnes consentienter eidem Autori tribuunt ista tria agnita, & unam eandemque epistolam con- stituere ajunt. Duas non plures epistolas à Simo- ne, eoque Apostolo, Petro cognominato exara- tas esse hactenus creditum est, quarum prima ca- nonica capitibus quinque, hæc secunda altera tri- bus capitibus absoluta.

Sexto objectum personale, vel illi, ad quos missa epistola, describuntur a fide, quam accepere. In- telligitur autem per fidem vel doctrina, quæ fides est, quæ creditur, vel proprie fides, qua creditur illa ἰσότιμος, non ratione finis tantum, quod ad eundem honorem tendat, vitæ nempe æternæ; sed etiam ratione intrinsecæ dignitatis, quod honore dignissima sit, quantum ad materiam, vel ea, circa quæ versatur, quæ vere divina sunt, puta tum præ- cepta tum mysteria, ut & quantum ad formam, quia doctrina fidei non est humani quid, sed ob Spiritum, qui unitus est Verbo vel doctrinæ cæle- sti, unde Verbi efficacia, & virtus divina fluit, vere divina est. Cæterum non opus est, ut fidem improprie, vel metonymice accipiamus pro doctrina quum propria acceptio locum habeat, plerisque

Interpretibus probata, quia fides omnium cre- dentium ἰσότιμος est; tum ratione objecti, à quo omnem habet honorem, quod est pretiosissima Christi justitia vel obedientia cum activa tum pas- siva, tum ratione dignationis vel imputationis di- vinæ, quia Deus fidem nobis imputat ad justitiam, quod est summum pretium & summus honor fi- dei. ἰσότιμον ἡμῖν coæqualem nobiscum reddidit Vulgatus. Sed propriè est æquè pretiosam fidem nobiscum. Confert fideles Judæos cum Apostolis, quemadmodum pronomen ἡμῶν accipitur cap. III. v. 2. vel quod B. Gerhardus mavult, gentiles conversos cum aliis Judæis fidelibus. Fides enim omnium eadem est, ratione objecti, & æque pre- tiosa coram Deo propter objectum, quod est meri- tum Christi, quod ipsum amplectitur, etsi ratione graduum in subjectis diversitas detur, quo de pul- chrè B. Lutherus: Gemmam annulo aureo inclu- sam amplectitur Gigas, amplectitur & puerulus. Licet Gigas fortius cum amplectatur, quam pueru- lus; tamen manet annulus æque pretiosus, & gemma æque pretiosa, sive Gigas, sive puerulus eum ample- ctatur. Munus æque pretiosum est, quod manu infirma accipitur, & quod apprehenditur manu robusta: quia pretium non est ab accipiente, vel ipsius acceptionis seu apprehensionis, sed in ipsa muneris præstantia. Atque ideo adjicitur ἐν δι- καιοσύνῃ in JUSTITIA Dei & Servatoris nostri, quia fides in justitiam Christi fertur, ea nititur, in ea unice recumbit, estque proprie ipsius justitiæ Christi apprehensio, quam fidem accepisse dicun- tur credentes, quod ipsis gratis detur, ut credant, Phil. I. v. 29. ac fides donum Dei sit, Joh. VI. v. 29. Nam λαμβάνειν est forte aliquid accipere, quæ au- tem forte obtingunt, sine merito gratis obtin- gunt, Actor. I. v. 17. Eph. I. v. 11. Col. II. v. 12.

Doctrina etiam illa fidei proprie consistit in ju- stitia Dei nostri, & Servatoris Jesu Christi. Quæ uno spiritu legenda, accipienda sensu conjuncto, quod nempe Jesus Christus sit Deus noster & Servator, quod omissio articuli & collatio loci v. 11. infra, nec non c. III. 18. ut & Tit. II. 13. ab ipso Grotio hic facta confirmat, cujus justitia est potissimum obe- dientia fidei objectum, quia de ea testantur Moses & Prophetæ, Rom. III. v. 21. cap. X. v. 4. Act. X. 43. Non autem promisit tantum Deus per Christum vitam æternam, sed promeruit eandem nobis Christus Deus benedictus in secula super omnia, Rom. IX. v. 5. quum datus ipse est pro mundi vita, Job. VI. v. 51. Nec enim promitti nobis potuisset, nisi satisfecisset Christus pro peccatis nostris, & promeruisset nobis æternam salutem, quia eramus sub ira & condemnatione æterna, Rom. III. 19. cap. XI. v. 32. Promisit autem obtinendam fide, quæ obedientiam habet comitem, etsi non obtineatur per obedientiam, sed sola fide.

Illos autem, ad quos epistola missa est, gentis ratione Judæos, religione Christianos, quoad sedem vero variis terrarum locis dispersos, agnoscit Gro- tius. Ideoque ad eosdem scripta omnino hæc po- sterior epistola, ad quos prior, quemadmodum & cap. III, 1. diserte docetur. Fallit ergo Petrus Aureolus, dum in compend. script. posteriorern Petri ad Romanos scriptam, dicit: Quum enim prior ad Judæos per Pontum, Galatiam, Cappado- ciam, Asiam & Bithyniam dispersos directa sit, idem etiam de posteriori negari nequit, quod etiam è 1. Petr. I. 19. colligunt, quia sermo Propheticus ad Judæos factus fuit, non ad gentiles, illorumque erant τὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ, Rom. III. v. 20. Adde quod 2. Petri III. v. 15. non epistola Pauli ad Romanos, quod Aureolus ille voluit, sed epistola ad Ebræos respiciatur, quemadmodum circa istum locum ostendemus. Nec tamen negamus ad gentiles, inter quos dispersi erant Judæi illi fideles, simul directam fuisse hanc epistolam, quemadmodum de priori id supra observavimus.

Quod ergo septimo ad scriptionis locum, non est ille quidem adeo definitus, ut in priori, verisimile tamen plerisque videtur, Babylone etiam hanc missam esse epistolam. Cui sententiæ suffragatur Schlichtingius ad cap. III. v. 1. concludens Romam per Babylonem intelligi non posse: Hinc apparet, inquit, istam secundam epistolam ad eosdem dire- ctam, quibus prior speciatim fuit inscripta, id vero per Pontum, Galatiam, Bithyniam, Cappadociam, Asiam, dispersis Judæis nomen Christi profitentibus. Unde conjectari licet, epistolam hanc, ut & priorem Babylone missam esse, cui regiones istæ viciniores sunt, quam Romæ, quippe in eadem orbis parte posi- tæ, quod adversus illos dico, qui Babylonis appella- tione Romam significatam fuisse dicunt in epistola priori, nulla probabili ratione.

Octavo occasionem epistolæ dedere, tum qui in studio pietatis & fide remissiores erant, qui pro- inde excitandi, tum qui fideles seducere fatage- bant, aut deinceps seducturi prævidebantur, ad- versus quos muniendi ac præmonendi erant, qua- les partim Pseudo-Prophetæ, abnegantes herum, qui ipsos mercatus erat, partim Empactæ adventum Domini novissimum ambiguum reddentes. Ut ergo epistolæ priori ansam præbuere tyranni & per- secutores: ita huic posteriori hæretici & seductores, monente Hugone & Dionysio. Unde B. Johannes Huss. in priore epistola, inquit, Petrus induxit eos, quibus scribit, ad permanendum in gratiæ bonitate, ne succumberent per adversitates tribulationum. In hac posteriori inducit eos ad perseverandum in gratiæ Christianæ veritate, ne pervertantur per fal- sam doctrinam hæreticorum & Pseudo-Apostolo- rum.

Nono itaque scopus epistolæ haud obscurus jam est, qui geminus est: tum διέγερσις excitatio ad pietatem, & imprimis ad constantiam in fide, quæ omnium virtutum radix est, tum ὑπόμνησις, qua in memoriam revocare voluit fidelibus mandata Prophetarum & Apostolorum, ut adversus sedu- ctores quosvis instruantur: quem utrumque fi- nem & scopum conjungit cap. III. vers. 1. 2. ut & cap. II. v. 12. 13.

Unde decimo argumentum epistolæ Athana- sius in synopsi tale constituit: Est autem hæc epi- stola, inquit, ὑπόμνησις refricatio priorum. Cùm enim cognovisset Petrus, cito futuram corporis sui ἀνάλυσιν, diligenter hoc egit, ut omnes admoneren- tur eorum, de quibus antea per Evangelii doctrinam erant instructi. Et primum quidem de fide disserit, atque ostendit, quod a Prophetis illa sit annunciata, & quod prophetiæ de Salvatore non sint humanæ, sed a Deo prænunciatæ. Deinde denunciat illis, ne seductores attendant, illorum perditionem futuram prædicens, quemadmodum & de Angelis transgres- soribus pœna sumpta est. Significat autem hæc epi- stola futuros dies, quibus illusores passim circuituri sint, conaturiq́; ut aliquos seducant, dicentes, quod inaniter a nobis prædicatur adventus Salvatoris fu- turus, eo, quod is, cum semper prædicatur, nondum tum venerit. Ab his igitur abstinere præcipit, do- cens ne moræ gratia animum despondeamus, propter- ea quod nihil tarditatis universum tempus gignat apud Dominum, uno die instar mille annorum exi- stente & mille annis instar unius diei. Affirmat si- mul & declarat cito futurum Domini diem, præci- pitq́; omnibus, ut ad illius adventum parati sint in bonis operibus, & amplectantur, quæ ab Apostolo scripta sunt, nec aures accommodent his, qui ea ca- lumniantur, quandoquidem iidem & universas scri- pturas divinas calumnientur. Postquam igitur quosvis admonuit ac docuit, ut ista futura sciant, hortatur, ne quisquam a fideli scopo aberret, atque ita finit epistolam.

Juxta S. Athanasium itaque epistola non inre- cte distribuetur in θέσιν de doctrina Evangelica a Prophetis olim prænunciata retinenda, & ἀντίθε- σιν, de falsorum Prophetarum & seductorum hete- rodoxia cavenda. Illa cap. I. hæc II. & III. exhibetur. B. Gerhardo placuit duas partes epistolæ ita desi- gnare, quod prior sit νυθεσία, exhortatio ad con- stantiam & profectum in fide ac studio pietatis, altera sit προφητεία, prædictio tum de falsis Prophe- tis ac seductoribus, tum de empactis & illusoribus ultimum Christi adventum negantibus. Conjungi commode utraque partitio potest, ideoque esto

PARS I. EPISTOLÆ Θέσις νυθετικὴ de fide custodienda, & virtutibus ornanda.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

With a preliminary inscription and Apostolic vow, the divine grace through the knowledge of Him who called us, and the greatest promises of partaking in the divine nature, are recalled to memory; and the faithful are thence admonished that, fleeing the corruption of depraved concupiscence, they should supply virtues in their faith, and not allow the knowledge of Christ to be unfruitful, and should make their calling and election firm, so that an entrance may be provided to the heavenly kingdom: for which purpose he reminds them of these things before he lays aside the tabernacle of the body, and brings forward both the vision of the glory of Christ and the hearing of the heavenly voice on the holy mount, and especially the Prophetic word, to which attention must be paid, as having proceeded from the Holy Spirit.

There are two parts: I. The entrance and preparation of the epistle, by which the subscription, as they call it, the inscription, and the Apostolic prayer, v. 3. II. The elaboration or treatment, by which the exhortation to retain the faith, and its motives, v. 3, 4, and its elements, v. 5, 6, 7, 8, illustrated by the contrary, v. 9, and by its fruit, v. 10, 11: and by the commemoration of the causes, both of the duty undertaken of stirring them up, namely the imminent departure, v. 12, 13, 14, 15, and of the obedience due from those to whom he writes, because St. Peter was an eyewitness of the glory, and an ear-witness of the proclamation of Christ made by the heavenly voice, v. 16, 17, 18, and because the Prophets agree, v. 19, 20, 21.

PART I. OF CHAPTER I. The entrance of the epistle, and preparation.

v. 1. Simeon Peter, etc.) Here the words of Grotius already alleged above from the prolegomena may be repeated.

We have already weighed the glosses of Grotius regarding the subscription of the author's name, 'Simon Peter, a servant and an Apostle of Jesus Christ,' and the inscription or designation of those to whom the epistle is written, 'to them that have obtained a like precious faith with us in the righteousness of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ': Now we only observe that this periphrasis fits perfectly with the purpose of the Apostle, who exhorts to guard the faith and to beware of defection from the faith, which from its preciousness and cause, from which, namely, the righteousness of God and of our Savior Jesus Christ has value, he commends, and makes common with the Apostles: and thereby he equates them to the Apostles regarding the equality of faith, so that they may apply due solicitude to retaining it, not losing it.

Latin:

CAPUT I. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Prævia inscriptione, ac voto Apostolico in me- moriam revocantur gratia divina per cogni- tionem ejus, qui vocavit nos, & promissa maxima participandæ divinæ naturæ, mo- nenturq; inde fideles, ut corruptionem pra- væ concupiscentiæ fugientes in fide admini- strent virtutes, nec infrugiferam esse sinant cognitionem Christi, firmamque reddant vocationem & electionem suam, ut aditus præbeatur ad regnum cœleste: quo fine de illis ipsos commonefacit, antequam deponat tabernaculum corporis, adducitq; cum visio- nem gloriæ Christi & auditum vocis cœlestis in monte sancto, tum imprimis sermonem Propheticum, cui attendendum, utpote a Spiritu S. profectum.

Partes duæ sunt: I. εἴσοδος & præparatio epi- stolæ, qua subscriptionem, ut vocant, inscriptionem & Apostolicam precationem, v. 3. II. Ἐξεργασία vel tractatio, qua adhortationem ad retinendam fidem, ejusq; motiva, v. 3. 4. & momenta, v. 5. 6. 7. 8. a contrario, v. 9. & fructu, v. 10. 11. illustrata: & causarum commemoratione tum suscepti muneris excitandi imminentis nempe ἀναλύσεως, v. 12. 13. 14. 15. & debiti eorum, ad quos scribit, obsequii, quod S. Petrus ἐπόπτης fuerit gloriæ, & αὐτήκοος præconii Christi voce cœlesti facti, v. 16. 17. 18. quodque Prophetæ consonent, v. 19. 20. 21.

PARS I. CAPITIS I. Εἴσοδος epistolæ, & præparatio.

v. 1. Συμεὼν Πέτρος &c.) Huc Grotii verba supra jam allegata repeti poterunt ἐκ τῶν προλεγομένων.

Glossas Grotii qua subscriptionem nominis au- toris, Simon Petrus servus & Apostolus Jesu Christi, & inscriptionem vel designationem eo- rum, ad quos scripta est epistola, iis, qui coæqua- lem nobiscum fortiti sunt fidem in justitia Dei nostri & Salvatoris Jesu Christi antea jam expen- dimus: Jam tantum observamus, optime conve- nire hanc περίφρασιν instituto Apostoli, qui ad fi- dem custodiendam, & defectionem a fide caven- dam hortatur, quam a pretiositate sua & causa, a qua sc. pretium habet justitia Dei & Salvatoris nostri Jesu Christi, commendat, & cum Apostolis communem facit: eoq; Apostolis quoad fidei ἰσο- τιμίαν ipsos æquat, ut de ea retinenda, non amit- tenda debitam solicitudinem adhibeant.

## 1:2
Verse 2.

Grace to you and peace be multiplied) He imitates Peter I. v. 2. as also Jude 2: be multiplied ירב

in the knowledge of God, and of Jesus our Lord) In the manuscript, 'our' is absent. ἐπίγνωσις is knowledge and experience, and it is called now 'the knowledge of the Son of God', Eph. IV. 13, now 'the knowledge of God', as Col. I. 10.

The Apostle prays for the grace of God, which is the fruitful mother of all spiritual and bodily goods, especially however of those together with peace, which is most internal, which is the tranquility of the conscience, and indeed for the multiplication of grace and peace, which the faithful, though not destitute of grace or peace, nevertheless have need of the preservation and multiplication of both. But as grace and peace are obtained and fostered through faith: so his prayer involves at the same time a silent warning, lest they themselves cast away grace and peace through sins against the conscience, or apostasy from the faith. And therefore he wishes for multiplication in the knowledge of God, and of Jesus our Lord, in the knowledge both of GOD, whose grace he prays for, and of JESUS, who is our Lord by the peculiar right of redemption, whose redemption we embracing by faith, and acknowledging him with Thomas as our Lord and our God, John XX. v. 28. and we enjoy the grace of God, and we have peace with God Rom. V. 1. ἐπίγνωσις is taken for simple γνῶσις, Rom. III, 20. chap. X. 2. But ἐπίγνωσις is acknowledgment here, not bare or theoretical, but practical or fiduciary, and thus faith is denoted, as John XVII. 3. Luke I. 77. Isa. LIII. 11. because grace and peace are obtained through faith, and once obtained are multiplied. Faith, through which we acknowledge and embrace God, and Jesus Christ whom He sent, is the medium through which we are made partakers of the grace of God, are preserved in the state of grace, and perceive and feel its power more and more in our heart, and are enriched with the gifts of grace: through which also we attain peace with God, and are strengthened in that peace. And therefore the preposition ἐν is the same here as BY, as it is rightly rendered by the blessed Luther.

PART II. Elaboration, or treatment.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη πληθυνθείη) Imitatur Petrum I. v. 2. ut & Judas 2: πληθυνθείη ירב

ἐν ἐπιγνώσει τοῦ Θεῦ, καὶ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν) In Ma- nuscripto abest ἡμῶν. Est ἐπίγνωσις cognitio & experientia, diciturque modo ἐπίγνωσις τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ, Eph. IV. 13. modo ἐπίγνωσις τοῦ Θεοῦ, ut Coloff. I. 10.

Gratiam Dei, quæ fœcunda est mater omnium bonorum spiritualium & corporalium, imprimis tamen istorum cum pace maxime interna, quæ conscientiæ est tranquillitas, precatur Apostolus, & quidem multiplicationem gratiæ & pacis, quam fideles nec gratia nec pace destituti, utriusque ta- men conservatione ac multiplicatione indigue- rint. Ut autem gratia & pax per fidem obtinetur & fovetur: ita ejus precatio tacitam commonitio- nem simul involvit, ne ipsimet gratiam & pacem excutiant per peccata contra conscientiam, vel apostasiam a fide. Ideoque multiplicationem vo- vet ἐν ἐπιγνώσει τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν, in cognitione tum DEI, cujus gratiam precatur, tum JESU, qui Dominus noster est peculiari redem- ptionis jure, cujus redemptionem fide ample- ctentes, ipsumque cum Thoma agnoscentes Do- minum nostrum & Deum nostrum, Joh. XX. v. 28. & gratia Dei fruimur, & pacem habemus cum Deo Rom. V. 1. Ἐπίγνωσις sumitur pro simplici γνώσει, Rom. III, 20. cap. X. 2. Est autem ἐπίγνωσις agnitio hic non nuda vel theoretica, sed practica vel fidu- cialis, adeoque fides notatur, ut Joh. XVII. 3. Luc. I. 77. Efa. LIII. 11. quia gratia & pax per fidem ob- tinetur, & obtenta multiplicatur. Fides, per quam Deum, &, quem ille misit, Jesum Christum agno- scimus, & amplectimur, est medium, per quod gratiæ Dei participes reddimur, in statu gratiæ conservamur, ac vim ejus magis magisq; in corde nostro percipimus ac sentimus, gratiæque donis locupletemur: per quod etiam pacem cum Deo consequimur, & in pace illa corroboramur. Ideo- que præpositio ἐν idem hic est, quod PER, uti recte a B. Luthero redditur.

PARS II. Ἐξεργασία, vel tractatio.

## 1:3
Verse 3.

As all things to you of his divine power have been given for life and godliness through the knowledge of him who called you through glory and virtue) He means this: that he does not magnify that knowledge in vain, since divine power through it bestows upon us all things which make for the life of the other world and for piety in this world; it would have been enough to say 'through the knowledge of him', but the Hebrews love to place nouns in place of pronouns. Nor is this circumlocution of God empty. For he is known from the very manner of calling as full of glory, which shone forth in Christ, John I. 14, and full of power.
