In the manuscript it is 'by his own glory and virtue': but virtue here is power. Διὰ here is causal, and 'having given' is a middle verb in an active sense.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Ὡς πάντα ὑμῖν τῆς θείας δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ τὰ πρὸς ζωὴν καὶ εὐσέβειαν δεδωρημένης διὰ τῆς ἐπιγνώσεως τοῦ καλέσαντος ὑμᾶς διὰ δόξης καὶ ἀρετῆς) Hoc vult: non frustra se magnificare il- lam notitiam, quandoquidem divina potentia per eam no- bis largiatur omnia, quæ faciunt ad vitam alterius seculi & ad pietatem in hoc seculo, satis fuerat dicere διὰ τῆς ἐπιγνώ- σεως αὐτοῦ, sed Ebræi amant nomina ponere vice pronomi- num. Nec inanis est hæc Dei circumscriptio. Noscitur enim ex ipso vocandi modo plenus gloriæ, quæ in Christo refulsit, Joh. I. 14. & plenus potentiæ. In Manuscripto est ἰδίᾳ δόξῃ καὶ ἀρετῇ: Est autem ἀρετὴ hic potentia. Διὰ hic est αἰτιολογικὸν & δωρησαμένης, verbum medium sensu activo.

## 1:4
Verse 4.

Through which) Through which the glory and power of God shining forth in Christ.

The precious and greatest promises have been given to us) Given to us are the promises of eternal life, than which promises nothing is greater or more honorable. But they were given with great testimonies, both of the divine voice and the transfiguration of Christ on the mount, which are referred to glory, and through very many miracles, which are referred to power.

ἵνα διὰ τούτων γένησθε θείας κοινωνοὶ φύσεως) That through these promises you might become participants, that is, imitators of divine goodness. For the word φύσεως here pertains to the properties of God, as ὑποστάσεως in Heb. 1:3; in the Glossary φύσις is nature, φύσεως ζώων, Wisdom 7:20. Hierocles: God promises the following, to make from the weak, as far as it is possible for a man, to become God.

Grotius refers these things to what precedes, to which the Vulgate also seems to incline when it rendered: How all things of his divine power, which have been given to us for life and godliness through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and virtue; in what way the Jesuit Gretser attempted to defend the Vulgate version, Tom. 1, defens. Bellarm. lib. 1, de V. D. c. 14, that those things are to be referred to the preceding wish in this way: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in such a way as all things of his divine power have been given to you. But in this way the wish is extended further than is just and customary, since it is more correct that the ἐξεργασία of the epistle begins here, as is sufficiently evident from a comparison of other epistles of Paul and other Apostles, and of Saint Peter himself, whose wishes are presented more succinctly, and also from the series of the Apostolic πραγματείας. Therefore, others say more conveniently that the divine benefits which the faithful had already received are commemorated here; so that by that commemoration they might be excited to those things which he intends to inculcate. We have said that arguments and motives are placed before the keeping of the faith, because through the knowledge of him who called us, that is, through faith, all the gifts of divine power have been given to us, which are necessary for life and godliness. The particle ὡς here is therefore not one of similarity or explanation, or of admiration or exclamation, but rather of reasoning and inferring, so that it is the same as ἐπεὶ, after or since, as B. Luther and the Syriac rendered it. B. Gerhard compares this sentiment to Luke 1:23, 24; 2:15; 4:25; 5:4. The pronoun αὐτοῦ is referred by some to the immediately preceding name of Christ, by others to the more remote God: but the matter comes to the same thing, since the Father and the Son are one, John 10:30. However, we do not deny that the participle δεδωρημένης is to be taken actively, as Grotius wishes, and not passively with the Vulgate, just as the verb δεδώρηται is also taken in verse 4, and rendered by the Vulgate, so that the sense may be: After his divine power has graciously given us all things that make for eternal life and godliness: Let us flee the corruption that is in the world through lust. For life, he says, both of grace and of glory, both spiritual and heavenly, and thus to obtain eternal life, and for the pursuit of godliness, lest having fallen into sins we lose life and salvation. By fiducial knowledge, however, or by faith, he understands that God gives us τὰ τῆς θείας δυνάμεως, the charisms of his divine power, not by bare knowledge, just as before he had wished grace and peace to be multiplied through fiducial knowledge, or that which is joined with assent and trust.

Some indeed refer what is subjoined, διὰ δόξης κὶ ἀρετῆς, to those who are called, and understand it terminatively as to glory and virtue. But that explanation is simpler which is referred to God who calls, and is taken causally, because God called us through the glory of grace or glorious grace and his power. For in our calling that glory of God shines forth most greatly with his virtue and power, Eph. 1:7, 19; 2:7; 2 Tim. 1:9; 1 Pet. 5:10; 2:9. Grotius, with certain others, wishes the glory of the glorification of Christ, which shone on the mountain, and the power which shone in the miracles, to be indicated. But the discourse here is not about those things which concern Peter or other Apostles, but which concern all who are called. B. Gerhard wishes ἀρετὴν to designate the kindness and philanthropy of God, and explains it by a hendiadys as the glorious kindness of God, which interpretation will easily agree with ours. By that glorious virtue of God let us understand the virtue of grace and divine power. For these ἀρεταὶ or divine properties exert themselves primarily in our calling and conversion: because calling is understood comprehensively, not without but with conversion, or as others speak, not only by reason of the term from which, of God calling, but at the same time by reason of the term to which, of men receiving the calling and benefits offered in the word. Through that glorious power, therefore, have been given to us those precious and greatest promises; but what those promises are, the following explains, namely that through them (which make for life and godliness) we may be partakers of the divine nature. Blessed Gerhard prefers to refer this to the promises, and explains the same metonymically concerning the goods which are promised, as Heb. X. 36, spiritual and heavenly, such as are the redemption of the human race, reconciliation with God, the remission of sins, adoption as sons of God, the donation of righteousness and eternal life, 1 Cor. I. 20, Hos. II. 25.

The Grotian gloss, that by those promises we are excited to become imitators of the divine goodness, born from the opinions of the Socinian and Arminian heresy, is not indeed consistent with the analogy of faith. For neither do bare promises cause us to imitate the goodness of God, but it is necessary that He work that in us by His power through the Holy Spirit; nor is the κοινωνία τῆς θείας φύσεως (communion of the divine nature) completed by the imitation of divine goodness, since communication implies union, which altogether intervenes between the faithful soul and God, and some participation of divine attributes by the force of that gracious union, if indeed we are filled with all the divine fullness through the indwelling of Christ in our hearts by faith, Eph. III. 19, according to the nature of the mystical and spiritual union. No essential μεταμόρφωσις (transformation) is to be imagined here, which does not even have a place in the hypostatic union, which is far closer, nor yet does a mere change of qualities and a certain restoration of the divine image exhaust this κοινωνίαν (communion). For we possess the divine nature itself, according to the gracious ἐνοίκησιν (indwelling) John XIV. 23, Eph. III. 17, and we are made partakers of divine attributes. Concerning which the blessed Luther in this place: What is the nature of GOD? Eternal truth, righteousness, wisdom, eternal life, peace, joy, and pleasure, and whatever good can be named. Whoever, therefore, is a partaker of the divine nature, he obtains all these things, so that he may live forever, and obtain eternal peace, joy, and pleasure, so that he may be clean, righteous, and omnipotent against the Devil, sin, and death. Blessed John Huss on 1 John III: Then we shall be, he says, Gods by participation, not by a fellowship of equality, but of participation through grace in this, through glory in the future age. Blessed Gerhard refers here to the adoption as sons of God, from which this phrase in verse 4. κοινωνία τῆς θείας φύσεως (communion of the divine nature) can be illustrated to a certain extent, but only so that it may be taught that we truly become partakers of the divine nature, but not in what that κοινωνία (communion) consists: Just as God, when He produced Adam, whom Luke calls the son of God in chapter III, last verse, breathed into his face, and gave him human and animal life: Gen. II. 7. So when He receives someone as a son, He makes him a partaker of spiritual life, which is from God, Ephes. IV. 18, and communicates to him certain divine properties, and a right to all the inheritance of God. It can also be illustrated from the mystery of the personal union, which is the foundation of our spiritual union and communion with Christ. For as the Son of God was made a partaker of human nature through the personal union, the human nature of Christ was made a partaker of the divine, as that whose whole fullness dwells in it, Col. II. 9. Thus the faithful are made partakers of the divine nature through spiritual union. God was made man, says Athanasius in his 5th oration against the Arians, that He might deify us in Himself. And Ambrose, book V de fide, ch. 5: Christ, he says, offered Himself as a partner of our fragility in the flesh, that He might make us partners of the divine nature in His divine power.

The Apostle changes the person, however, not without cause, now using the second for the first: lest anyone presume that only the Apostles were made partakers of this honor, whence he applies it here to those to whom he writes, so that they may know that they belong to the fellowship of the same honor.

ἀποφυγόντες τῆς ἐν κόσμῳ ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ φθορᾶς (having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust)] The writer calls φθορὰν (corruption) here not only here, but also below in chapter II, verses 12 and 19, corrupt morals, to which is opposed ἀδιαφθορία (incorruptibility), Tit. II. 17, which is also ἀφθαρσία (incorruption) Ephes. VI. 4. For κόσμῳ in the Manuscript ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, which is more frequent. This corruption of morals is said to be in the world, because the greatest part of the world labors under it, 1 John V. 19, and it is said to be ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ (in lust), that is, διὰ ἐπιθυμίας (through lust), because it is born from concupiscence, James I. 15. Ἀποφυγὼν (having escaped) can govern the accusative because of the verb φεύγειν (to flee), and it is so constructed below in chapter II. 20. But it can also govern the genitive because of the force of the preposition ἀπὸ (from), as if it were written, φυγόντες ἀπὸ τῆς φθορᾶς (having fled from the corruption).

Thus far he has brought forward divine benefits and motives, the collation of all things which are necessary for life and godliness, to which he refers faith or saving knowledge, the gracious calling, the greatest donation of divine promises, and the communication of the divine nature itself. Now he proceeds to the admonitions, if indeed all those things have been given to them, so that fleeing that corruption which is in the world in concupiscence, and applying all diligence to that end, they may supply in their faith virtue, etc., where the Apostle prescribes both things to be fled and things to be done. For these things are not said conditionally, if you have escaped, because in that consisted neither the cause nor the medium of that κοινωνίας (communion), nor conditionally, if we have escaped evil concupiscences, and have supplied virtue in faith, are we made partakers of the divine nature, since these things follow that κοινωνίαν (communion). Nor are these things said merely assertively, that through that κοινωνίαν [communion] that which we escape the lusts of the world is obtained for us: but prescriptively, because the Apostle, from the fact that we have been made partakers of the divine nature, deduces these admonitions, that we ought to escape the desires of the world, and supply virtue in faith, lest we render ourselves unworthy of such great benefits and fall away. Therefore he embraces the things to be fled under the name τῆς ἐν κόσμῳ ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ φθορᾶς [of the corruption that is in the world through lust]. By which φθορὰν [corruption] is not understood destruction, but the corruption of vices, not only through foul lusts, by which human nature is disgraced, approved by Simon Magus and his followers, to whom the epistle is opposed, but in general whatsoever corruption of depraved desires, through which our will is corrupted: therefore it is generally named ἐπιθυμία [lust] and is hinted at by the phrase τῆς ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ φθορᾶς [of the corruption that is in lust]. For depraved concupiscence, which is of all vices, Gal. V. v. 17, 19, 24, brings about the corruption of the mind and will; therefore φθορὰ [corruption] is taken in an active sense, because depraved concupiscences corrupt the mind, heart, and all the faculties of man, and therefore those who have been made partakers of the divine nature, and have been renewed to the image of God, ought to take the greatest care that they may be ἀποφυγόντες (ἀπὸ) τῆς ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ φθορᾶς [having escaped (from) the corruption that is in lust], from that corruption which is in and from depraved concupiscence, which is ἐν κόσμῳ [in the world], because the whole world lies in wickedness, 1 John V. 19, and all that is in the world is the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes and the pride of life, 1 John II. 16. This world is taken not substantially, or concerning the system of heaven and earth, or concerning the earth alone or men on the earth, but by reason of a vicious quality, because in worldly and earthly men depraved concupiscences hold sway, to which world are opposed the faithful, who are not of the world, John XV. 19.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Δι' ὧν) Per quam Dei gloriam & potentiam in Christo refulgentem.

Τὰ τίμια ἡμῖν καὶ μέγιστα ἐπαγγέλματα δεδώρηται) Data no- bis sunt promissa vitæ æternæ, quibus promissis nihil ma- jus aut honoratius. Data autem sunt cum testimoniis ma- gnis tum vocis divinæ, & clarificationis Christi in monte, quæ ad gloriam referuntur, tum per plurima miracula, quæ ad potentiam.

ἵνα διὰ τούτων γένησθε θείας κοινωνοὶ φύσεως) Ut per ista promissa excitati participes fieretis, id est, imitatores divi- næ bonitatis. Nam φύσεως vox hic ad proprietates Dei per- tinet, ut ὑποστάσεως Ebr. I. 3. in Glossario φύσις ingenium, φύσεως ζώων, Sap. VII. 20. Hierocles : τὰ ἑξῆς ἐπαγγέλλε- ται Θεὸς ἐξ ἀσθενῶν ποιήσειν ἐφ᾽ ὅσον οἷόν τε ἀνθρώπῳ Θεὸν γενέσθαι.

Ad præcedentia hæc refert Grotius, quo etiam Vulgatus abire videtur, cum reddidit: Quomodo omnia nobis divinæ virtutis suæ, quæ ad vitam & pietatem donata sunt per cognitionem ejus, qui vo- cavit nos propria gloria & virtute, quo pacto Vul- gatam versionem tueri conatus est Jesuita Gretse- rus Tom. I. defens. Bellarm. lib. I. de V. D. c. 14. quod referenda sint illa ad præcedens votum hoc modo: Gratia & pax vobis ita multiplicetur, quo- modo omnia virtutis divinæ sua vobis donata sunt. Sed ita votum justo & solito amplius extenditur, quum rectius hic ἐξεργασία inchoëtur epistolæ, ut e collatione aliarum epistolarum Pauli, & alio- rum Apostolorum, ipsiusque Sancti Petri, qua- rum vota succinctius exhibentur, nec non e serie πραγματείας Apostolicæ satis constat. Conve- nientius proinde alii hic commemorari ajunt be- neficia divina, quæ jam acceperant fideles; ut ea commemoratione excitentur ad ea, quæ inculcare instituit. Argumenta, & motiva diximus præmitti custodiendæ fidei, quia per cognitionem ejus, qui vocavit nos, hoc est, per fidem, donata sunt nobis omnia divinæ virtutis dona, quæ ad vitam & pie- tatem necessaria sunt. Particula ergo ὡς hic non est vel similitudinis aut explicantis, vel admirantis aut exclamantis, sed potius ratiocinantis & infe- rentis, ut idem sit, quod ἐπεὶ postquam vel siqui- dem, ut B. Lutherus & Syrus reddidere. In quam sententiam confert B. Gerhardus Luc. I. v. 23. 24. c. II. 15. c. IV. 25. c. V. 4. Pronomen αὐτῦ a nonnul- lis ad immediate præcedens nomen Christi, ab aliis ad remotius Dei refertur: sed res eodem recidit, cum Pater & Filius unum sint, Joh. X. 30. Non au- tem abnuimus, active, ut Grotius vult, non vero passive cum Vulgata participium δεδωρημένης acci- piendum esse, quemadmodum etiam v. 4. verbum δεδώρηται accipitur, & a Vulgata redditur, ut sen- sus sit: Postquam divina ejus virtus nobis omnia, quæ ad vitam æternam & pietatem faciunt, gratiose donavit: Fugiamus eam, quæ in mundo est, concupi- scentia corruptionem. Ad vitam, inquit, & gratiæ & gloriæ, & spiritualem & cœlestem, adeoque æternam consequendam, & ad pietatis studium, ne prolapsi in peccata vita & salute excidamus. Per cognitio- nem autem fiducialem, vel per fidem Deum nobis donare τὰ τῆς θείας δυνάμεως, divinæ suæ potentiæ charismata intelligit non per nudam cognitio- nem, quemadmodum ante gratiam & pacem per cognitionem fiducialem, vel quæ cum assensu & fiducia conjuncta est, multiplicari optarat.

Quæ subjunguntur διὰ δόξης κὶ ἀρετῆς nonnulli quidem referunt ad vocatos, & terminative intelli- gunt ad gloriam & virtutem. Sed simplicior est illa explicatio, quæ ad Deum vocantem refertur, & accipitur causaliter, quia per gloriam gratiæ seu gratiam gloriosam & potentiam suam vocavit nos Deus. Nam in vocatione nostra maxime elucet illa Dei gloria cum virtute ac potentia ejusdem, Eph. I. 7. 19. c. II. 7.2, Tim. I. 9. 1. Petr. V. 10. c. II. 9. Grotius cum aliis quibusdam gloriam glorificatio- nis Christi, quæ in monte, ac potentiam, quæ in miraculis refulsit, indigitari vult. Sed hic non de iis, quæ Petrum aliosve Apostolos, sed quæ omnes vocatos concernunt, sermo est. B. Gerhardus ἀρε- τὴν benignitatem & Φιλανθρωπίαν Dei designare vult, & per hendyaden de gloriosa Dei benignitate explicat, quæ interpretatio facile cum nostra con- veniet. Per illam gloriosam Dei virtutem intelli- gamus virtutem gratiæ & potentiæ divinæ. Hæ enim ἀρεταὶ vel proprietates divinæ exerunt sese imprimis in vocatione & conversione nostra: quia vocatio intelligitur complexim, non abs- que, sed cum conversione, vel ut alii loquuntur, non solum ratione termini à quo, Dei vocantis, sed simul ratione termini ad quem, hominum vocationem & beneficia in verbo oblata suspicientium. Per eam ergo virtutem gloriosam data sunt nobis pretiosa, & maxima illa promissa; quænam autem illa promissa sint, sequentia explicant, ut nempe per illa (quæ ad vitam & pietatem faciunt) participes simus divinæ naturæ. B. Gerhardus ad promissa mavult, eademque metonymicè explicat de bonis, quæ promissa sunt, ut Ebr. X. 36. spiritualibus & cælestibus ceu sunt generis humani redemptio, reconciliatio cum Deo, peccatorũ remissio, in filios Dei adoptio, justitiæ & vitæ æternæ donatio, 1. Cor. I, 20. Ose. II. 25.

Glossa Grotiana, ut per illa promissa excitati imitatores fiamus divinæ bonitatis, è Socinianæ & Arminianæ hæreseos opinionibus enata, non verò analogiæ fidei congrua est. Nam nec promissa nuda faciunt, ut imitemur bonitatem Dei, sed necesse est, ut operetur id in nobis virtute sua Spiritu S. neque κοινωνία τῆς θείας φύσεως absolvitur divinæ bonitatis imitatione, quum communicatio inferat unionem, quæ omnino intercedit animæ fideli cum Deo, & participationem aliquam divinorum ἀυχημάτων vi gratiosæ istius unionis, siquidem omni plenitudine divina repleamur per inhabitationem Christi in cordibus nostris per fidem, Eph. III. 19. pro natura mysticæ & spiritualis unionis. Nulla quidem hîc fingenda essentialis μεταμόρφωσις, quæ ne quidem in hypostatica unione longè arctiori locum habet, nec tamen sola qualitatum mutatio & imaginis divinæ quædam restauratio exhaurit hanc κοινωνίαν. Possidemus enim ipsammet divinam naturam, secundum gratiosam ἐνοίκησιν Joh. XIV. 23. Eph. III. 17. & participes reddimur divinorum ἀυχημάτων. Quo de B. Lutherus in h. l. Quid est natura DEI? Æterna veritas, justitia, sapientia, æterna vita, pax, gaudium, & voluptas, & quicquid boni nominari potest. Qui ergo naturæ divinæ particeps sit, ille hæc omnia consequitur, ut vivat in æternum, & æternam pacem, gaudium & voluptatem obtineat, ut sit mundus, justus & omnipotens contra Diabolum, peccatum & mortem. B. Joh. Hussus in 1. Joh. III. Tunc erimus, inquit, Dii participatione non consortio æqualitatis, sed participationis per gratiam in hoc, per gloriam in futuro sæculo. Refert huc B. Gerhardus adoptionem in filios Dei, è qua phrasis hæc v. 4. κοινωνὶ τῆς θείας φύσεως quadantenus illustrari potest, sed tantum ut doceatur, quod vere participes fiamus divinæ naturæ, non autem in quonam κοινωνία illa sita sit: Sicut Deus cum produxit Adamum, quem Lucas vocat Dei filium cap. III. v. ult. inspiravit in faciem ejus, & dedit ei vitam humanam ac animalem: Gen. II 7. Sic cum aliquem in filium recipit, participem eum facit vitæ spiritualis, quæ est ex Deo, Ephes. IV. 18. ac communicat ei divinas quasdam proprietates, & jus ad omnem Dei hæreditatem. Illustrari etiam potest è mysterio unionis personalis, quod fundamentum est spiritualis nostræ cum Christo unionis & communionis. Nam ut Filius Dei & humanæ naturæ particeps factus est per unionem personalem, humana Christi natura divinæ particeps est facta, utpote cujus tota plenitudo in ipsa habitat, Col. II. 9. Sic fideles participes redduntur divinæ naturæ per unionem spiritualem. Deus factus est homo, inquit Athanasius orat. V. contra Arian. ut nos in seipso Deificaret. Et Ambrosius l. V. de fid. c. 5. Christus, inquit, nostræ fragilitatis in carne se præbuit consortem, ut nos in virtute sua divina faceret naturæ consortes.

Mutat autem Apostolus personam non citra cau- sam pro prima secundam jam adhibens: ne quis praesumat, solos Apostolos honoris hujus participes factos, unde hic applicat ad eos, ad quos scribit, ut ad ejusdem honoris consortium se pertinere sciant.

ἀποφυγόντες τῆς ἐν κόσμῳ ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ φθορᾶς] Φθορὰν hic scriptor non hic tantum, sed & infra cap. II. v. 12. 19. vocat mores corruptos, quibus opponitur ἀδιαφθορία, Tit. II. 17. quæ & ἀφθαρσία Ephes. VI. 4. Pro κόσμῳ in Ma- nuscripto ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, quod frequentius. Hæc morum corruptio in mundo esse dicitur, quia maxima pars mundi ea laborat, 1. Joh. V. 19. & dicitur esse ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ, id est, διὰ ἐπιθυμίας, quia ex concupiscentia nascitur, Jac. I. 15. Ἀπο- φυγὼν potest regere accusativum propter verbu φεύγειν, & sic construitur infra c. II. 20. Sed potest & genitivum regere propter vim præpositionis ἀπὸ, quasi scriptum esset, φυγόν- τες ἀπὸ τῆς φθορᾶς.

Hactenus beneficia divina & motiva adduxit, omnium quæ ad vitam & pietatem necessaria sunt, collationem, quò refert fidem vel cognitionem salvificam, vocationem gratiosam, promissorum divinorum maximam donationem, ipsiusque na- turæ divinæ communicationem. Jam ad monita accedit, siquidem ista omnia ipsis donata sint, ut fugientes illam, quæ in mundo est in concupiscentia corruptionem, & in id contra omne studium adhiben- tes administrent in fide virtutem &c. ubi tum fu- gienda tum facienda præscribit Apostolus. Nec enim hæc dicuntur conditionaliter, si effugeritis, quia in eo nec causa, nec medium constitit κοινω- νίας istius, neque conditionaliter, si effugerimus pravas concupiscentias, & in fide virtutem ministra- verimus, divinæ naturæ participes reddimur, quum hæc consequantur illam κοινωνίαν. Neque assertivè tantum hæc dicuntur, quod per illam κοι- νωνίαν id obtingat nobis, quod effugiamus mundi concupiscentias: sed præceptivè, quia Apostolus ex eo, quod divinæ naturæ participes facti simus, monita hæc deducit, quod effugere debeamus mundi cupiditates, & ministrare in fide virtutem, ne tantis beneficiis nos indignos reddamus & ex- cidamus. Fugienda itaque complectitur nomine τῆς ἐν κόσμῳ ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ φθορᾶς. Per quam φθορὰν non intelligitur exitium, sed corruptio vitiorum, non solum per fœdas libidines, quibus humana natura dehonestatur, Simoni Mago, & sectatoribus ejus probatas, quibus epistola opposita, sed in ge- nere quæcunq; corruptio pravarum cupiditatum, per quas corrumpitur nostra voluntas: ideo ge- neraliter ἐπιθυμία nominatur atq; innuitur phrasi τῆς ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ φθορᾶς. Concupiscentia enim prava, quæ est vitiorum omnium, Gal. V. v. 17. 19. 24. in- fert mentis, & voluntatis corruptionem; proinde φθορὰ sensu activo accipitur, quia concupiscentiæ pravæ corrumpunt mentem, cor, & facultates o- mnes hominis, ideoque qui divinæ naturæ con- sortes facti, & ad imaginem Dei renovati sunt, summo studio debent id curare, ut sint ἀποφυγόν- τες (ἀπὸ) τῆς ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ φθορᾶς, ab illa corruptione, quæ est in & à concupiscentia prava, quæ est ἐν κόσμῳ, in mundo, quia mundus totus in maligno positus est, 1. Joh. V. 19. & omne quod est in mundo, est concupi- scentia carnis & concupiscentia oculorum, & super- bia vitæ, 1. Joh. II. 16. Mundus hic accipitur non substantialiter, sive de systemate cœli & terræ, aut de terra solum aut hominibus in terra, sed ra- tione vitiosæ qualitatis, quia in hominibus munda- nis ac terrenis concupiscentiæ pravæ dominen- tur, cui mundo opponuntur fideles, qui non sunt de mundo, Joh. XV. 19.

## 1:5
Vers. 5.

κὶ αὐτὸ τῦτο δὲ σπυδὴν πᾶσαν παρεισενέγκαντες] In the Manuscript: κί αὐτοὶ δὲ σπυδὴν πᾶσαν παρεισενέγκαντες: that is, since you have received such great benefits from God, devote all your effort to cultivating them. Nor does it seem that Latinus read it otherwise. God has done what is His; do you also what is yours.

Now follow the things to be done, and these are placed in the middle, by which zeal is excited, καὶ αὐτὸ τοῦτο δὲ σπουδὴν πᾶσαν παρεισενέγκαντες, which respects both the preceding, with which the 'escaping the corruptions of the world' is connected, and what follows, the 'supplying virtue in faith,' for which effort must be expended on both. Moreover, the particle κατὰ or πρὸς is understood with the words αὐτὸ τοῦτο, and 'applying all effort to this very thing': the preposition παρὰ can also be brought back here from the word παρεισενέγκαντες, that besides that escaping, indeed also all diligence must be brought to bear, or one must apply oneself to this, that you supply virtue in faith, in which way the things to be done are more openly joined to those things to be fled. However, it is foreign that Estius draws these to the preceding things concerning divine donation, so that besides that donation of God we also bring all effort, so that the synergy of free will with the grace of the Holy Spirit may be confirmed. Which Grotius also seems to intend, praising the Vulgate version for that reason, because it renders it SUBINFERENTES. For although we admit a synergy in the reborn, not through the powers of nature, but of grace, not from generation, but regeneration, yet that παρὰ cannot be snatched here, since there is something closer to which it may be referred, and indeed among those things which are commanded by the Apostle. Nay, it is also certain that compound words are often used for simple ones, so that in that word παρεισφέρειν the emphasis is not to be sought in the particle παρὰ; nor does the Apostle mean that we ought to contribute something of our own to God's grace and faith, but that faith ought to exert itself through virtues, and not be unfruitful, and Estius himself acknowledges that the cooperation of free will is to be attributed to the help of God, working in us both to will and to perform, Phil. II. v. 13.

Ἐπιχορηγήσατε ἐν τῇ πίστει ὑμῶν τὴν ἀρετὴν] There is an excellent discussion in this period. And ἐπιχορηγεῖν in this place is to add, and ἐν is redundant. Thus ἐπιχορήγημα in Athenaeus is an addition to a feast. The word ἀρετῆς cannot be taken here as generally as in Phil. IV. 8 and among the philosophers. For many names of virtues follow, ἐγκράτεια, ὑπομονὴ, etc. Wherefore I think that ἀρετὴν can here rightly be taken as fortitude in faith, just as we noted above II. v. 11, 19 that ἀρετὰς is said for power.

The Vulgate rendered it 'minister,' the Syrian explained it as 'add.' Nor is this explanation inconvenient, because virtue is altogether to be added to faith or for faith, not so that faith may be perfected, but so that it may exert and exercise itself through the works of virtue. However, there is no need for us to expunge the preposition ἐν, or consider it to be πλεονάζειν, since it can be taken for εἰς, so that virtue is added to faith. By ἀρετὴν, however, fortitude is not understood, which it is not our place to add to faith, but what ἀρετὴ usually sounds, virtue. For δυνάμις is one thing, which introduces power, fortitude, and strength, and ἀρετὴ is another, which in a more famous meaning denotes virtue, and indeed virtue in general, whence Bede says he put virtue for good conversation, which is rightly to be joined to faith, lest it be idle and dead without works.

Yet it is not therefore to be concluded with Estius that faith is unformed without virtue, even if virtues necessarily follow faith as fruits of faith. Therefore they cannot be the form of faith; just as the fruits of a tree are not its form: nor do good works add a soul or strength to faith, but they receive all dignity and vigor from faith, Rom. XIV. v. ult., Heb. XI. v. 6. Faith is the mother and root of good works, says Augustine, Epist. LXIII. Faith is the mother of good will and just action, says Lombard, lib. III. dist. XL. from Ambrose. Although indeed the special names of virtues follow thereafter, nothing prevents the genus from being placed first, and some species being subjected to it afterwards: nor is there need for us to posit a gradation here, since only the connection or conjunction of those things is hinted at, which the Apostle requires together with faith or wishes to be added to faith, even if there is a certain order among them, since order does not immediately imply the dependence of one upon another: or even if we explain the preposition ἐν concerning causality through the subsequent members: since by itself it does not imply the same.

Moreover, the gradation which Socinus invents here in his explanation of the Loca Scripturae, page 115, is heretical. This is the true connection of this chain: that from the assent applied to the preaching of the Gospel, it proceeds that a Christian man afterwards conducts himself manfully and gathers strength. Hence he seeks true and solid knowledge and understanding of divine things. From that it is born that he restrains himself from every desire of the flesh. And in this he does violence to himself, endures, and perseveres, which the word ὑπομονή contains. Now he is not only continent, which is a virtue toward oneself, or (and it can be explained thus) he does not harm others, but he also becomes pious, that is, having spurned the pleasures of the flesh and cast aside the care of worldly things, he turns himself wholly to God and religion. Thus affected, he loves the brethren, and finally exercises the charity which is described in 1 Corinthians 13, and does not refuse to lay down his life for a brother. For ἀγάπη embraces more than Φιλαδελφία. For it is imagined in such a way that assent alone causes a Christian man to conduct himself manfully, whereas for fortitude in the Lord, not only assent but primarily trust is needed, without which there is no spiritual fortitude, and countless people offer assent to the Gospel who nevertheless do not conduct themselves manfully. Nor does γνῶσις or knowledge of divine things arise from that fortitude, which rather must necessarily precede assent. For how can I offer assent to a thing not known? Indeed, the Apostle had already warned before about abstinence from every concupiscence of the flesh and the world, and that it overflows from the mere knowledge of divine things is likewise false. For many are most expert in them who by no means restrain themselves from the desires of the flesh, nor do they become pious: nor is εὐσέβεια in this exhortation a conversion to God. For those whom the Apostle commands to add virtue to faith are already converted, and thus also to pursue piety, which is denoted by εὐσέβεια. Nor, finally, does ἀγάπη embrace more than Φιλαδελφία, but vice versa, common love yields to brotherly love, inasmuch as we ought especially to love the brethren and the household of faith, Galatians 6:10.

Ἐν δὲ τῇ ἀρετῇ τὴν γνῶσιν)

The particle ἐν can be retained here in its customary meaning: because γνῶσις must be applied in virtue, inasmuch as it is to be performed and restrained with prudence, which directs and moderates all virtues, so that in their exercise we may not sin in excess or in defect, nor wander from the due end, in which sense of the word γνῶσις the blessed Gerhard brings forward these passages: 1 Corinthians 8:6, 2 Corinthians 6:6, 1 Peter 3:7, and of the related ἐπίγνωσις, Romans 10:12. Bernard, sermon 49 on the Song of Songs, says: Practical knowledge, or spiritual prudence, is the charioteer of all virtues. Whence Dionysius on this passage: By knowledge is understood discretion, which is the directress and charioteer of the virtues, teaching us to observe moderation, the fitting place, the apt time, so that all things may be done in order, and we may travel the Royal road, so that our service may be reasonable. Blessed Luther: Because prudence, he says, is the eye of all virtues, without which virtues easily degenerate into vices; therefore, the Apostle teaches that prudence must be joined to virtue. Grotius does not explain how γνῶσις follows from virtue, but in his gradation he omitted this member. Those who explain it thus, that fortitude produces knowledge of faith, that is, experience, so that one who was able to perform something then certainly knows (which he did not know before when he believed) that it could be performed, are philosophizing too subtly, if I am not mistaken, and are making the effects of faith out of its adjuncts.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

κὶ αὐτὸ τῦτο δὲ σπυδὴν πᾶσαν παρεισενέγκαντες] In Manu- scripto: κί αὐτοὶ δὲ σπυδὴν πᾶσαν παρεισενέγκαντες: id est, cum tanta acceperitis Dei beneficia, vos in iis excolen- dis omne studium conferte. Nec videtur aliter legisse La- tinus. Deus fecit quod suum est, vos quoque quod vestrum est, facite.

Sequuntur jam facienda, & hæc in medio po- sita, quibus studium excitatur, καὶ αὐτὸ τοῦτο δὲ σπου- δὴν πᾶσαν παρεισενέγκαντες tam præcedens, cum quo connectitur τὸ effugere concupiscentias mun- di, quam quod sequitur, τὸ administrare in fide vir- tutem respicit, quod utrique studium impenden- dum sit. Subintelligitur autem ad verba αὐτὸ τοῦτο particula κατὰ vel πρὸς & circa vel ad hoc ipsum ve- ro adhibentes omne studium: potest etiam è verbo παρεισενέγκαντες præpositio illa παρὰ huc redu- ci, præter illud effugere vero etiam omnis diligentia conferenda, vel in id incumbendum est, ut in fide administretis virtutem, quo pacto conjunguntur apertius facienda illis fugiendis. Alienum autem est, quod Estius hæc ad superiora de donatione di- vina trahit, ut præter illam Dei donationem nos quoque omne studium conferamus, ut συνέργεια liberi arbitrii cum gratia Spiritus S. confirmetur. Quam etiam intendere videtur Grotius, laudans ideo Vulgatam versionem, quod reddat SUBIN- FERENTES. Licet enim in renatis συνέργειαν admittamus nonper vires naturæ, sed gratiæ, non ex generatione, sed regeneratione, huc tamen ab- ripi illud παρὰ nequit, cum propinquius adsit, ad quod referatur, & quidem inter ea, quæ ab Apo- stolo præcipiuntur. Imo constat etiam, composita sæpe pro simplicibus usurpari, ut in illa voce πα- ρεισφέρειν in particula παρὰ non sit quærenda em- phasis; nec Apostolus id velit, quod de nostro ad Dei gratiam & fidem aliquid subinferre debea- mus, sed quod fides sese exerere debeat per vir- tutes, nec infrugifera esse, & agnoscit Estius ipse liberi arbitrii cooperationem attribuendam esse Dei auxilio, operantis in nobis & velle & perficere, Phil. II. v. 13.

Ἐπιχορηγήσατε ἐν τῇ πίστει ὑμῶν τὴν ἀρετὴν] Est in hac periodo egregia tractatio. Et est ἐπιχορηγεῖν hoc loco adji- cere & in abundat. Sic ἐπιχορήγημα apud Athenæum cœ- næ accessio. Vox ἀρετῆς non potest hic ita generaliter su- mi, ut Phil IV. 8. & apud Philosophos. Sequuntur enim mul- ta virtutum nomina ἐγκράτεια, ὑπομονὴ &c. Quare ἀρετὴν hic recte puto accipi posse fortitudinem in fide, sicuti ἀρετὰς pro potentia dici, notavimus supra II. v. 11. 19.

Vulgatus reddidit ministrate, Syrus exposuit addite. Nec incommoda hæc explicatio, quia fi- dei vel ad fidem addenda omnino est virtus, non ut fides perficiatur, sed ut exerat & exerceat sese per virtutis opera. Non autem opus est, ut Præ- positionem ἐν expungamus, vel πλεονάζειν censea- mus, quum accipi queat pro εἰς, ut ad fidem adji- -ciatur virtus. Per ἀρετὴν autem non fortitudo in- telligitur, quam nostrum non est adjicere fidei, sed quod usitate sonat ἀρετὴ virtus. Nam aliud est δυνάμις, quæ potentiam, fortitudinem & vires infert, aliud ἀρετὴ, quæ famosiori significatu vir- tutem notat, & quidem in genere quamvis virtu- tem, unde Beda virtutem inquit, pro conversatione bona posuit, quæ fidei recte jungenda est, ne sine operi- bus otiosa sit & mortua.

Nec tamen ideò cum Estio concludendum, fi- dem informem esse sine virtute, etsi necessario con- sequantur virtutes fidem ceu fructus fidei. Non ergo fidei forma esse possunt; uti fructus arboris non sunt forma ejusdem: neque bona opera ad- dunt animam, vel vires fidei, sed accipiunt à fide omnem dignitatem, ac robur, Rom. XIV. v. ult. Ebr. XI. v. 6. Fides mater est & radix bonorum ope- rum, ait Augustinus epist. LXIII. Fides est geni- trix bonæ voluntatis, & justæ actionis, ait Lombar- dus lib. III. dist. XL. ex Ambrosio. Quanquam ve- ro sequantur deinde nomina virtutum specialia, nihil tamen obstat, quo minus genus præmitta- tur, & subjiciantur postmodum eidem species non- nullæ: neque opus est, ut vel gradationem hic sta- tuamus, quum simpliciter tantum connexio vel conjunctio eorum innuatur, quæ Apostolus, unà cum fide requirit vel fidei adjici vult, etsi inter ea quidam sit ordo, quum ordo non statim inferat dependentiam unius ex alio: vel etiam præpo- sitionem ἐν de causalitate explicemus per membra subsequentia: quum per se non inferat eandem.

Hæretica autem est gradatio, quam Socinus hic fingit in explic. Loc. Scr. pag. 115. Hic est verus nexus hujus catenæ, ut ex assensu prædicationi Ev- angelii adhibito proficiscatur, ut homo Christia- nus postea viriliter sese gerat & vires sumat. Hinc veram ac solidam cognitionem ac scientiam rerum divinarum petat. Inde nascitur, ut sese contineat ab omni carnis cupiditate. Et in hoc sibi vim faciat, toleret, & perseveret, quæ continet verbum ὑπομο- νή. Nunc non tantum continens est, quæ est virtus erga seipsum, vel (& ita potest explicari) alii non no- cet, sed pius etiam evadit, hoc est, spretis carnis vo- luptatibus & abjecta rerum mundanarum cura to- tus ad Deum & religionem se convertit. Ita affectus amat fratres, & denique charitatem, quæ describi- tur 1. Corinth. XIII. exercet, neque vitam suam pro fratre ponere recusat. Nam ἀγάπη plus com- plectitur, quam Φιλαδελφία. Nam ita fingitur, so- lum assensum efficere, ut homo Christianus virili- ter se gerat, quum ad fortitudinem in Domino non assensu tantum, sed imprimis fiducia opus sit, sine qua nulla est fortitudo spiritualis, & innumeri assensum præbeant Evangelio, qui tamen virili- ter sese non gerunt. Neque ex ista fortitudine ori- tur γνῶσις vel cognitio rerum divinarum, quæ an- tecedat potius assensum necesse est. Quomodo enim rei non cognitæ assensum præbere possum? De abstinentia vero ab omni carnis & mundi con- cupiscentia jam ante monuerat Apostolus, quam ex sola rerum divinarum notitia redundate itidem falsum est. Multi enim earum peritissimi sunt, qui nequaquam à cupiditatibus carnis se conti- nent, neque pii evadunt: neque εὐσέβεια in hac parænesi est conversio ad Deum. Nam conversi jam sunt, quos jubet Apostolus ad fidem adjicere virtutem, adeoque & pietati studere, quæ per εὐ- σέβειαν denotatur. Nec denique ἀγάπη plus com- plectitur quam Φιλαδελφία, sed vice versa amor communis cedit amori fraterno, siquidem præci- puè fratres diligere debeamus, ac fidei domesticos Gal. VI. 10.

Ἐν δὲ τῇ ἀρετῇ τὴν γνῶσιν)

Particula ἐν usitata significatione hic retineri potest: quia in virtute adhibenda est γνῶσις, ut- pote quæ cum prudentia est præstanda & coër- cenda, quæ omnes virtutes dirigit & moderatur, ut in earum exercitio nec in excessu, nec in defe- ctu peccemus, nec à debito fine aberremus, in quem sensum vocis γνώσεως affert B. Gerhardus hæc loca 1. Corinth. VIII. v. 6. 2. Corinth. VI. 6. 1. Petr. III. v. 7. & cognatæ ἐπιγνώσεως, Rom. X. 12. Bernhardus serm. XLIX. in Cant. Scientia practi- ca, inquit, sive spiritualis prudentia est omnium virtutum auriga. Unde Dionysius in h. l. Per scien- tiam intelligitur discretio, quæ est directrix & auriga virtutum, docens observare moderamen, congruum locum, tempus aptum, ut omnia ordinate agantur, & Regia via tendamus, ut sit rationabile nostrum obsequium. B. Lutherus: Quia pruden- tia, inquit, est oculus omnium virtutum absque qua virtutes facile in vitia degenerant, ideò virtuti pru- dentiam conjungendam esse, Apostolus docet. Gro- tius non explicat, quomodo ex virtute γνῶσις se- quatur, sed in sua gradatione membrum hoc omi- sit. Qui ita exponunt, quod fortitudo fidei scien- tiam, id est, experientiam pariat, ut qui aliquid præstare potuit, tum certo sciat (quod antea cùm crederet, nesciebat) id præstari potuisse, nimis ar- gutè, ni fallor, philosophantur, & ex adjunctis fidei faciunt ejusdem effecta.

## 1:6
Vers. 6.

ἐν δὲ τῇ γνώσει τὴν ἐγκράτειαν] A severe abstinence from all pleasures. See Acts XXIV. 26. Gal. V. 23. Joined with prudence, Christian temperance (ἐγκράτεια) ought to be the moderator of virtues, and in prudence, continence or moderation of mind and sobriety must be administered. For since knowledge puffs up, 1 Cor. VIII. v. 1, therefore he requires that moderation of mind be joined with it, so that we may be wise εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν, Rom. XII. v. 1, says the blessed Gerhard here. He does not deny, however, that moderation in food and drink is simultaneously included; indeed, he calls this the simplest explanation: that the Apostle joins temperance with prudence because prudence cannot have a place without temperance. A prudent soul is said to dwell in a dry place, and σωφροσύνη is said to be, as it were, σώζεσα τὴν φρόνησιν. He does not, however, embrace Bede's interpretation, abstinence in knowledge, so that when they have learned to do good, they may immediately abstain from evil, lest the knowledge of heavenly things be in vain if one has neglected to restrain oneself from earthly allurements. That abstinence was already forbidden in v. 4. Here, therefore, moderation of mind and body is insinuated, not severe abstinence from pleasures.

ἐν δὲ τῇ ἐγκρατείᾳ τὴν ὑπομονὴν] The constant endurance of evils, Luke XXI. 19. Rom. V. 3. VIII. 25. XV. 4. 2 Cor. I. 6. 1 Tim. VI. 11. 2 Tim. III. 10. Tit. II. 1. Heb. X. 36. XII. 1. Jas. I. 3. 4. V. 11. The blessed Gerhard rightly says: It is required of the pious not only that they moderate the desires of food and drink, which is proper to continence, but also that they bear injuries and afflictions with an even mind, which is proper to patience.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

ἐν δὲ τῇ γνώσει τὴν ἐγκράτειαν] Severam ab omnibus vo- luptatibus abstinentiam. Vide Act. XXIV. 26. Gal. V. 23. Conjuncta cum prudentia Christiana virtutum moderatrix debet esse ἐγκράτεια temperantia, & in prudentia administranda est continentia vel ani- mi moderatio & sobrietas. Quum enim scientia inflet, 1. Cor. VIII. v. 1. ideò cum ea moderatio- nem animi conjungi requirit, ut sapiamus εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν, Rom. XII. v. 1. ait hic B. Gerhardus. Mo- derationem tamen in cibo & potu simul compre- hendi non negat, imò simplicissimam hanc expli- cationem dicit: Apostolum ideò cum prudentia conjungere temperantiam, quia prudentia non po- test habere locum sine temperantia. Anima pru- dens in sicco dicitur habitare, ac σωφροσύνη dicitur quasi σώζεσα τὴν φρόνησιν. Non autem amplecti- tur Bedæ interpretationem, in scientia abstinen- tiam, ut cum bona facere didicerint, mox à malis abstineant, ne in vacuum cœlestium scientia ce- dat, si se ab illecebris terrestribus quis continere neglexerit. Illa abstinentia v. 4. jam prohibita. Hic ergo moderatio animi & corporis insinuatur, non severa à voluptatibus abstinentia.

ἐν δὲ τῇ ἐγκρατείᾳ τὴν ὑπομονὴν] Malorum sufferentiam constantem, Luc. XXI. 19. Rom. V. 3. VIII. 25. XV. 4. 2. Cor. I. 6. 1. Tim. VI. 11. 2. Tim. III. 10. Tit. II. 1. Ebr. X. 36. XII. 1. Jac. I. 3. 4. V. 11. הקנו Recte B. Gerhardus: Non solum à piis requiritur, ut cupiditates cibi & potus moderentur, quod est proprium continentiæ, sed etiam injurias & affli- ctiones æquo animo ferant, quod est proprium pa- tientiæ.

## 1:6
ἐν δὲ τῇ ὑπομονῇ τὴν εὐσέβειαν] that is, a huge increase of godliness, how this and what follows are to be understood. See 1 Tim. II. 2. III. 16. IV. 7. 8. VI. 3. 6. 11. Tit. I. 1. above 3. The Apostle adds nothing about a huge increase of godliness. But godliness is to be administered or performed in patience, because not only is the true patience of Christians, as the blessed Gerhard holds, distinguished from the semblance of patience shining in the Gentiles in that the truly pious in the cross look to the providence of God and to the promises concerning liberation from the cross and the most bountiful reward to follow in eternal life: But also in the very endurance of evils, one must not desert godliness, but must adhere to the pursuit of it, and true Christians devote effort to godliness with patience in adversities, because they know that it cannot be otherwise for those who wish to live godly in Christ, 2 Tim. III. v. 12. Finally, in patience the worship of God is most especially performed, when we patiently tolerate adversities for the honor of God, and hoping in God, and religiously worshipping Him, we await liberation from all adversities in filial confidence.

Latin:

ἐν δὲ τῇ ὑπομονῇ τὴν εὐσέβειαν] id est, incrementum in- gens pietatis, quomodo intelligenda & quæ sequuntur. Vide 1. Tim. II. 2. III. 16. IV. 7. 8. VI. 3. 6. 11. Tit. I. 1. supra 3. Nihil addit Apostolus de incremento ingenti pietatis. In patientia autem ministranda vel præ- standa pietas, quia non modo vera Christianorum patientia, ut B. Gerhardus habet, in eo à simulacro patientiæ in Ethnicis relucente distinguitur, quod vere pii in cruce respiciunt ad Dei providentiam & ad promissiones de liberatione ex cruce & largissima remuneratione in vita æterna secutura: Sed etiam in ipsa malorum sufferentia pietatem non deserere, sed ejusdem studio inhærere oportet, & veri Chri- stiani cum patientia in adversis pietati operam na- vant, quod sine adversitate norint esse haud posse, qui pie in Christo vivere volunt, 2. Timoth. III. v. 12. Denique in patientia maxime cultus Dei præstatur, cum patienter in honorem Dei adversa toleramus, & in Deum sperantes, eumque reli- giose colentes liberationem ex omnibus adversis in filiali fiducia expectamus.

## 1:7
Vers. 7.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

## 1:7
And in piety, brotherly love] The love of those who are likewise Christians, 1 Peter 1:22, 3:8, Romans 12:10, 1 Thessalonians 4:9, Hebrews 13:1. God cannot be rightly worshipped and loved unless we love our brothers, as John testifies in his 1st epistle, chapter 4, verse 20. Just as we love God, as the most benevolent Father, for His own sake, so let us love His children, our brothers—that is, all who confess Christ—for His sake. 'No one,' says Bernard in his book On Loving God, 'can love his neighbor purely who does not love God.' It is necessary, therefore, that God be loved first, so that the neighbor may also be loved in God. However, it is not understood as a common or inferior degree of love, as Socinus wishes, but as the intimate love with which a brother pursues a brother, just as the Syriac rendered it 'the intimate love of brotherhood'; since by the word רחם, derived from the womb, the bowels of maternal love are denoted, so that such love is designated as that which a mother has toward the children whom she has carried in her womb.

And in brotherly love, love] Love toward all men, even those who are not Christians. It does not, therefore, point to the love of God, as Bede wanted, or a superior degree of love, as Socinus, but to the common love with which we embrace all men, which is manifested in brotherly love, because we ought to love brothers primarily in such a way that we do not neglect others. Blessed Gerhard, concerning this exhortation, warns that the little word ἐν signifies the same as 'with,' as in Matthew 25:16, Acts 7:38, and the prefix ב in Genesis 32:1, 1 Samuel 1:24. Hosea 4:3, chapter 5:6, so that not so much the origin of one virtue from another is described, as a certain collection of the most beautiful and principal virtues, and thus one should not labor greatly over the reason for the order, just as Flacius also observes, that in this gradation one should look not so much at the natural sequence of things as at the necessary conjunction of all these virtues with faith: yet Blessed Gerhard does not deny that there is a certain connection in these degrees of virtues, which may be usefully investigated, even if the former is not always the cause of the latter.

Latin:

ἐν δὲ τῇ εὐσεβείᾳ τὴν φιλαδελφίαν] Dilectionem eorum, qui pariter Christiani sunt, 1. Petri I. 22. III. 8. Rom. II. 10. 1. Thess. IV. 9. Ebr. XIII. 1. Deus recte coli atque diligi non potest, nisi di- ligamus fratres nostros, teste Johanne 1. epist. IV. v. 20. sicut Deum amamus, velut benignissimum Patrem propter seipsum: Ita filios ipsius nostros fratres, hoc est, omnes, qui Christum confiten- tur, diligamus propter ipsum. Proximum, inquit Bernhardus lib. de dilig. Deum; pure diligere non potest, qui Deum non diligit. Oportet ergoDeum di- ligi prius, ut in Deo diligatur & proximus. Intelli- gitur autem dilectio non vulgaris aut inferior di- lectionis gradus, ut Socinus vult, sed intimus amor quo frater fratrem prosequitur, uti Syrus reddidit intimum amorem fraternitatis; siquidem voce רחם ab utero deducta viscera materni amoris de- notentur, ut designetur talis amor, qualis matris erga liberos est, quos in utero suo gestavit.

ἐν δὲ φιλαδελφίᾳ τὴν ἀγάπην] Dilectionem erga homines omnes, etiam non Christianos. Non ergo vel Dei amorem, quod Beda voluit, vel superiorem dilectionis gradum, ut Socinus, sed communem amorem, quo omnes homines complectimur, indigitat: qvii in φιλαδελφίᾳ præ- statur, quod ita fratres imprimis diligere debea- mus, ut tamen alios non negligamus. B. Gerhar- dus circa hanc adhortationem monet, voculam ἐν idem significare, quod cum, ut Matth. XXV. 16. Act. VII. 38. & præfixum ב Gen. XXXII. 1. 1. Sam. I. 24. Ose. IV. 3. cap, V. 6. ut non tam origo unius virtutis ex altera, quam congeries quædam pul- cherrimarum ac præcipuarum virtutum descri- batur, sicque de ratione ordinis non sit magnopere laborandum, quemadmodum & Flacius observat, in gradatione hac non tam rerum naturalem con- secutionem, quam harum omnium virtutum neces- sariam cum fide conjunctionem spectandam esse: neque tamen negat B. Gerhardus, esse quandam in hisce virtutum gradibus connexionem, quæ utiliter investigetur, etiamsi prior non semper sit causa posterioris.

## 1:8
Verse 8.

For if these things are present in you] Not only will they be present, but they will also increase daily. Πλεονάζων, 'abounding.' In the manuscript, instead of ὑπάρχοντα, it is παρόντα. 'He does not make you idle or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ'] Here εἰς τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν is put for ἐν τῇ ἐπιγνώσει, which the Latin interpreter rightly saw. These things will cause the knowledge of Christ, that is, of the Gospel, which you have attained, to be neither useless to others nor unfruitful to you. Ἀργὸς, 'idle'; ἀκάρπως, 'unfruitful'.

The Apostle had promised to the faithful that grace would be multiplied in the knowledge or faith of God and Christ, verse 2. He had said that things were given divinely through knowledge and faith, through which we are made partakers of the divine nature, verses 3 and 4; therefore he had warned that they should flee the lusts of the world and supply virtue in faith; now, therefore, he confirms that for that reason knowledge or faith will not be empty and unfruitful. For these are the excellent fruits of faith. He had warned to exercise virtue, but so that we might apply all diligence, he therefore says not only: 'For if these things are present in you' (if these things are with you), but also 'and abounding' (the Vulgate renders it 'superent,' more correctly 'exuberent'). From which, however, it is by no means permitted to infer works of supererogation or the perfection of works, nor being full of good works, Acts 9:36, and what is prescribed to the rich of this world, 1 Timothy 6:18, that they should be rich in good works, 1. Timothy 6:18, implies this: nor is the absolute perfection of good works asserted anywhere; indeed, in this imperfection, because of the remnants of sin, it has no place in any of the reborn. Nor, indeed, with Lorinus, can the future judicial knowledge of Christ be understood by 'knowledge,' as if good works constitute us perfect for it, since this phrase nowhere occurs regarding the judicial knowledge of Christ, and it is too manifest that this is the sense of the Apostle's words, which Lorinus himself also preferred, that those works do not render us unfruitful in the faith and knowledge of Christ. Perhaps those things are not inappropriately referred to the preceding matters, concerning which v. 3, or to all things which precede, because the rest flow from these, as if to say: If through those things which God has given you by faith, having become partakers of the divine nature you have applied all care to such virtues, certainly your faith will not be empty and unfruitful, since on the contrary (as follows next) that man is blind, and does not fall away from true faith, to whom such things are not present. Thus the Greek word καθίςησι, which is of the present tense, must be rendered in the present, not in the future as the Vulgate does, 'constituent'.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Ταῦτα γὰρ ὑμῖν ὑπάρχοντα] Ubi hæc omnia vobis non aderunt non tantum, sed & accrescent in dies. Πλεονάζων ערף. In Manuscripto pro ὑπάρχοντα est παρόντα. Οὐκ ἀργὸς ἐδὲ ἀκάρπες καθίστησιν εἰς τὴν τῆ Κυρία ἡμῶν Ἰη- σᾶ Χριστᾶ ἐπίγνωσιν] Hic εἰς τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν positum est pro ἐν τῇ ἐπιγνώσει, quod recte vidit Latinus Interpres. Ista effi- cient ut cognitio Christi, id est, Evangelii, quam adepti e- stis, neque inutilis sit aliis, neque vobis infructuosa. Ἀργὸς בטלים, עקרים ἀκάρπως.

Voverat Apostolus fidelibus gratiam multipli- cari in cognitione vel fide Dei & Christi, v. 2. Dixe- rat donata esse divinitus per cognitionem & fi- dem, per quæ divinæ naturæ consortes reddimur, vers. 3. & 4. ideo monuerat, ut concupiscentias mundi fugiant, & in fide virtutem ministrent, jam ergò confirmat, ea ratione non fore cognitio- nem vel fidem inanem & infrugiferam. Hi enim egregii fructus sunt fidei. Monuerat ad virtutum exercitium, sed ut omne studium adhibeamus, ideo non tantum ait: Ταῦτα γὰρ ὑμῖν ὑπάρχοντα, hæc si vobiscum adsint, sed etiam καὶ πλεονάζοντα, VVulgatus reddit superent, rectius exuberent. E quo tamen minimè opera supererogationis aut ope- rum perfectionem colligere licet, neque plenum esse bonis operibus, Actor. IX. v. 36. & quod di- vitibus hujus seculi præscribitur, 1. Timoth. VI. 18. ut divites sint in bonis operibus, 1. Timoth. VI. v. 18. id infert: neque uspiam perfectio bonorum ope- rum omnimoda asseritur, imò in hac imperfe- ctione ob reliquias virtutis locum non habet in ullo renatorum. Nec verò cum Lorino per ἐπί- γνωσιν futura Christi judiciaria cognitio intelligi potest, quasi perfectos constituant nos bona ope- ra ad eandem, quum de cognitione judiciaria Christi hæc phrasis nuspiam occurrat, & manife- stum nimis sit, hunc esse verborum Apostoli sen- sum, quem Lorinus ipse etiam prætulit, quod ope- ra ista non reddant nos in fide & cognitione Christi infrugiferos. Referri forte non incommode illa poffint ad fuperiora, de quibus v. 3. vel ad omnia, quæ præcedunt, quia ex iftis reliqua fluunt, q. d. Si per illa, quæ Deus per fidem vobis donavit, divi- næ naturæ participes facti talibus virtutibus omnem curam impenderitis, certe fides vestra non erit inanis & infrugifera, quum ex adverso (ut porro fequi- tur) cæcus ille sit, veraque fide non excidat, cui ta- lia non adfunt. Sic verbum Græcum καθίςησι, quod præsentis temporis est, in præsenti redden- dum, non ut Vulgata in futuro constituent.

## 1:9
Ver. 9.

For he to whom these things are not present] These things just mentioned, 5, 6, 7. Τυφλός ἐστι μυωπάζων] The one is an explanation of the other, or an ἐπανόρθωσις (correction). Something similar is in Apoc. XVII. v. 18. The writer means this: I call him blind, namely because he does not see with his mind things placed far away, that is, in heaven. Μυωπάζειν are called (says Aristotle) those who see things near, but do not see things from a distance.

He confirms the matter by the contrary: For he to whom these things are not present is blind, and groping with his hand, as the Vulgate, groping for the way with his hand, as Erasmus. Robertus Stephanus in his Thesaurus of the Greek language rendered it: seeing nothing at all, from the same passage of Aristotle: which Grotius followed. But there is no need for an ἐπανόρθωσις, rather τυφλὸς should be retained in its proper sense; he is not merely dim-sighted, or sees with blinking eyes, as if from μύων ὦπα, or is unable to see things placed far off, but is plainly blind, who is destitute of these. Therefore Erasmus more correctly derives the word μυωπάζων from μυῶν, mice, as from a Greek scholium, from subterranean mice, which they call moles, because they grope for the way in the manner of the blind, cf. Deuter. XXVIII. v. 28, 29. Joh. V. v. 14. cap. XII. v. 25. Esa. LIX. 10. Therefore B. Gerhard opposes those who, in the manner of Grotius, wish to have these things added by way of a certain correction, as if to say: he is blind, or if not entirely blind, he is dim-sighted, he is dim-sighted like a dim-sighted person, as one who does not rightly look at and value the benefit of purification from sins, which in this reasoning would have required the insertion of the disjunctive particle ἢ, τυφλός ἐστιν, ἢ μυωπάζων.

Having forgotten the purification of his old sins] He does not remember, he says, the baptism in which he professed that he wished to abandon all vices. See Actor. V. v. 5. 1. Cor. VII. 1. Tit. II. v. 4. Ebr. IX. v. 23. Jac. IV. 8. 1. Joh. I. v. 17. But especially Eph. V. 26.

Even if mention were made here specifically of the purification performed through baptism, which Oecumenius understands, yet not only the profession made in baptism, but primarily the benefit of the purification of sins, which happens through baptism, would be regarded, which even those places incorrectly alleged by Grotius, Actor. II. v. 38. 1. Cor. VI. v. 11. Tit. III. v. 5. Ebr. X. vers. 23, as also Ephes. V. v. 26, testify. The Vulgate rendered the word: receiving oblivion: The Syriac: He has forgotten the purification of former sins, because to the word πάλαι one must understand the word πεποιημένων, so that the sense is: he who does not flee those lusts which are in the world corrupting it, nor applies effort to virtues, is blind, and gropes like a blind man, showing by the very fact that he has forgotten that he was purified from old sins: or neglecting and holding in low esteem the very benefit of purification, which he obtained in baptism or after baptism in repentance through faith: Which is the greatest blindness, to despise both the benefit by which we have been purified from sins and snatched from eternal damnation, and also to neglect the end of that purification, which is that we may serve God with a pure heart, Ebr. X. v. 22. ff. Conf. 1. Joh. II. v. 9. 19. He who neglects the pursuit of good works shows by the very fact that he has forgotten the benefit received and the remission of sins, since he does not show himself grateful for it, as was fitting, says B. Gerhard.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Ὧ γὰρ μὴ πάρεστι ταῦτα] Ista modo dicta, 5. 6. 7. Τυφλός ἐστι μυωπάζων] Alterum est alterius explicatio, fi- ve ἐπανόρθωσις. Simile quid Apoc. XVII. v. 18. Hoc vult hic scriptor: Græcum eum dico, nimirum quia longe po- sita, in cœlo scilicet, animo non videt. Μυωπάζειν λέ- γονται (ait Aristoteles) οἱ τὰ μὲν ἐγγὺς βλέποντες, τὰ δὲ ἐξ ἀ- ποστάσεως οὐχ ὁρῶντες.

A contrario rem confirmat: Cui enim non præ- sto sunt hæc, cæcus est, & manu tentans, ut Vul- gatus, manu viam tentans, ut Erasmus. Robertus Stephanus in thesauro lingv. Græc. reddidit: ni- hil prorsus cernens ex eodem Aristotelis loco: Quem sequutus Grotius est. Sed non opus est ἐπα- νορθώσεως, quin τυφλὸς proprio sensu retineri debet non tantum cæcutit, vel conniventibus oculis vi- det, quasi μύων ὦπα, aut procul posita videre ne- quit, sed plane cæcus est, qui illis destitutus est. Ideo rectius Erasmus vocem μυωπάζων ἀπὸ μυῶν muribus deducit, ut è Græco scholio à muribus subterraneis, quos talpas vocant, quod more cæ- corum viam prætentent, conf. Deuter. XXVIII. v. 28.29. Joh. V. v. 14. cap. XII. v. 25. Esa. LIX. 10. Ideo B. Gerhardus illis, qui more Grotii hæc per cor- rectionem quandam subjici volunt, q. d. cæcus est, aut si non prorsus cæcus, lusciosus, instar lusciosi cæcutit, ut qui non recte aspiciat atque æstimet beneficium purgationis a peccatis, opponit, quod hac ratione inseri debuisset particula disjunctiva ἢ, τυφλός ἐστιν, ἢ μυωπάζων.

Λήθην λαβὼν τῦ καθαρισμῦ τῶν πάλαι αὐτῦ ἁμαρτιῶν] Non meminit, inquit, baptismi, in quo profeffus fuit, se vitia omnia velle deserere. Vide Actor. V. v. 5. 1. Cor. VII. 1. Tit. II. v. 4. Ebr. IX. v. 23. Jac. IV. 8. 1. Joh. I. v. 17. Sed maxi- me Eph. V. 26.

Etiamsi peculiariter purgationis per baptismum factæ hic mentio fieret, de qua Oecumenius intelli- git, non tamen professio tantum in baptismo fa- cta, sed imprimis beneficium purgationis peccato- rum, quæ per baptismum contingit, respiceretur, quod etiam loca illa corrupte allegata à Grotio A- ctor. II. v. 38. 1. Cor. VI. v. 11. Tit. III. v. 5. Ebr. X. vers. 23. ut & Ephes. V. v. 26. testantur. Vulgatus verbum reddidit: oblivionem accipiens: Syrus: Oblitus est priorum delictorum purgationis, quia ad voce͂ πάλαι subintelligendum verbum πεποιη- μένων, ut sensus sit: qui non fugit eas, quæ in mundo sunt concupiscentias corrumpentes, nec studium adhibet in virtutibus, cæcus est, & pal- pat instar cæci, oblitum sese ostendens reipsa, quod à veteribus peccatis purgatus sit: vel negligens & insuper habens tantum purgationis beneficium, quam in baptismo sive post baptismum in pœni- tentia per fidem consequutus est: Quæ maxima est cæcitas contemnere tum beneficium, quo à peccatis purgati & à damnatione æterna erepti sumus, tum etiam finem istius purgationis negli- gere, qui est, ut puro corde Deo serviamus, Ebr. X. v. 22. feqq. Conf. 1. Joh. II. v. 9. 19. Qui stu- dium bonorum operum negligit, reipsa ostendit, se accepti beneficii & remissionis peccatorum effe oblitum, cum pro eo sefe gratum, uti decebat, mi- nimè præstat, ait B. Gerhardus.

## 1:10
Ver. 10.

Therefore rather. Make your calling and election sure] Devote effort, so that both the calling which came to you through the Gospel, and the election following it, by which you have become the people of God, may be ratified, that is, may obtain the hoped-for outcome. For that is what it means to become βέβαιον or to be confirmed. See Rom. IV. v. 6. cap. XV. v. 8. Ebr. II. v. 2. cap. IX. v. 17. In that manuscript which we use, and many others, we read more fully: Σπουδάσατε ἵνα διὰ τῶν καλῶν ὑμῶν ἔργων βεβαίαν ὑμῖν τὴν παράκλησιν καὶ ἐκλογὴν ποιῆσθε. The Latin in his Greek had: Διὰ τῶν καλῶν ἔργων: but κλῆσιν, not παράκλησιν.

An exhortation flowing from the preceding. For because all things have been given to us which are necessary for life and godliness, through calling, pains must be taken diligently, so that we may make firm and certain the calling made in time, to the kingdom of grace, and our election, by which we have been predestined to the kingdom of glory. Vulgate: Wherefore, brethren, be the more diligent, that by good works you may make your calling and election certain. That addition 'by good works' is foreign, because it is not held in the authentic text, except in a few codices, and those more recent, into which it crept from the Vulgate version. Whence Lorinus rashly accuses B. Luther, because he exposed it, when he ought rather to have argued against the Vulgate, because it added the same, just as Cajetan, Erasmus, Vatablus, Isidorus, Clarius, Adam Sasbouth, and Gagnejus acknowledge that those words 'by good works' are superfluous. Estius doubts: Perhaps, he says, Peter did not add it: nor do the antecedents demand them: For the pronoun ταῦτα does not look to καλὰ ἔργα, but to those things concerning which the Apostle had previously commanded: the flight from desires, and the zeal to provide virtue in faith, of which he had spoken in verse 8: Ταῦτα ὑπάρχοντα ὐκ ἀργὲς, ὐδὲ ἀκάρπες καθίστησιν; and verse 9: ᾧ μὴ πάρεσι ταῦτα, τυφλός ἐσιν. Or, if anyone prefers, let the pronoun ταῦτα in this place be referred to the immediately preceding admonition, 'be diligent, that you may make your calling and election firm': if you do these things: The matter comes to the same thing. The Vulgate translated it as 'making certain', Estius prefers 'firm', because that is what the word βεβαία properly signifies, Romans IV, verse 16, 2 Corinthians I, verse 7, Hebrews II, verse 2, 2 Peter I, verse 15, and the following verse 21. and the following is opposed to firmness, this firmness is not to be opposed to certainty, but is joined with certainty; nor is it right for Papists to desert the Vulgate translation, for which there is also no cause here. For the calling and election is made firm not on the part of God, whose gifts are ἀμεταμέλητα, Romans XI, verse 29, but on our part, so that we may be certain that we are so called that we are also elected, since many otherwise are called, few are chosen, Matthew XX, verse 15, and XXII, verse 14. But the calling is understood as that which is joined with the effect divinely intended, with acceptance on our part and justification through faith, Romans VIII, verse 30, 2 Timothy I, verse 9. What is firm, it is necessary that it also be certain. Therefore Estius himself interpreted it as 'certain and firm', which he explains truly concerning certainty in the class of individual probable things. But although from good works a certain moral and conjectural certainty, as they call it, of our election might be had, yet from the internal testimony of the Spirit we have the certainty of divine faith, Romans VIII, verse 16, not to mention that conjectural certainty is a σιδηρόξυλον. Thomas himself certainly acknowledges this, paraphrasing the true certainty here thus: That by good works, namely external ones, you may make it certain, that is, show

your calling to faith in time, and election through predestination from eternity, so that you may indeed be certain that you are called and elected by God. What? That each person can be entirely certain of his own faith through the exploration of himself, and through a reflexive act, 2 Cor. XIII. 5, and through the proof of interior renewal, and the argument of the struggle between flesh and spirit, Gal. V. v. 17, the flight from vices, and the pursuit of virtues, which are certain signs of faith, Gal. V. 22, 1 John II. v. 3, 4, ch. III. v. 14, whence he is also rendered certain of justification, which happens through faith, and consequently of salvation, which is the end of faith, provided he does not fall away from faith and grace through apostasy and sins against conscience, nor neglect or despise the means of preserving faith: the hearing of the Word of God, the use of the Sacraments, and the pursuit of prayers and supplications. For the certainty of salvation is not absolute, but hypothetical, nor does it rely so much on our piety, which often languishes, as on the divine promise, which is infallible, Phil. II. v. 12, 1 Cor. I. v. 9, ch. X. v. 3, and on the power, which is most sufficient, 2 Tim. I. v. 12, and on the merit of Christ, and his intercession for us, Rom. VIII. v. 34, 38. Meanwhile, the reborn, with the grace of the Holy Spirit assisting, can avoid mortal sins, and seriously propose this to themselves, but they should not trust in their own strength, and thus they should perpetually seek divine grace through pious prayers. Concerning which Augustine says in 'On the Gift of Perseverance', ch. 22: 'You ought to hope for the very perseverance of obeying from the Father of lights, and to ask for it in daily prayers, and by doing this, to trust that you are not aliens from the predestination of his people, because he himself grants that you may do even this.' Ταῦτα γὰρ ποιοῦντες οὐ μὴ πταίσητε] that is, you shall not fall from the things hoped for לא תמוט. See Rom. XLI. Ps. XV. 5. לא ימוט Ps. CXIX. v. 164. ואין למו מכשול.

The Vulgate explains this concerning the fall of sin, not concerning falling away from the goods hoped for, rendering it: 'You shall not sin at any time.' Similarly, Ambrose, book III 'On Faith', ch. 6, and Idacius against Varimundus: 'You shall not err at any time.' And thus this word occurs in Jas. II. v. 3, 10, Rom. XI. v. 11, and it is a metaphorical expression taken from those who stumble while running; cf. Phil. I. v. 10, Jude, penultimate verse. Therefore, it is not understood as simple sin, but that such persons are not to offend, not to fall into mortal sins, as the ordinary gloss has it: 'You shall avoid crimes, from which he who has devoted himself to the aforementioned virtues may remain immune with God's help.'

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Διὸ μᾶλλον ] Potius ergo. Σπουδάσατε βεβαίαν ὑμῶν τὴν κλῆσιν καὶ ἐκλογὴν ποιεῖσθαι] Date operam, ut & vocatio, quæ vobis contigit per Evan- gelium, & electio eam sequuta, qua facti estis Dei po- pulus, rata sint, id est, speratum eventum consequantur. Id enim est βέβαιον γίνεσθαι sive βεβαιοῦσθαι. Vide Rom. IV. v. 6. cap. XV. v. 8. Ebr.II. v.2. cap.IX. v. 17. In Manuscripto illo, quo utimur, & aliis multis plenius legimus : Σπουδά- σατε ἵνα διὰ τῶν καλῶν ὑμῶν ἔργων βεβαίαν ὑμῖν τὴν παράκλησιν καὶ ἐκλογὴν ποιῆσθε. Latinus in suo Græco habuit: Διὰ τῶν καλῶν ἔργων: sed κλῆσιν, non παράκλησιν.

Adhortatio è superioribus fluens. Nam quia omnia donata nobis, quæ ad vitam & pietatem necessaria sunt, per vocationem, opera danda sedulo, ut vocationem in tempore factam, ad regnum gratiæ, & electionem nostram, qua ad regnum gloriæ prædestinati sumus, firmam & certam faciamus. Vulgata: Quapropter, fra- tres, magis satagite, ut per bona opera certam ve- stram vocationem & electionem faciatis. Ille προσ- διορισμὸς per bona opera alienus est, quia non ha- betur in textu avthentico, exceptis paucis codici- bus, iisque recentioribus, in quos ex Vulgata ver- sione irrepsit. Unde Lorinus temere B. Luthe- rum accusat, quod illum expunerit, cum potius Vulgatum arguere debuerit, quod eundem addi- derit, quemadmodum Cajetanus, Erasmus, Va- tablus, Isidorus, Clarius, Adamus Sasbouth, Ga- gnejus agnoscunt, voces illas per bona opera su- perfluere. Estius dubitat: Forte, inquit, Petrus non addidit: nec ea poscunt antecedentia: Nam pronomen ταῦτα non respicit καλὰ ἔργα, sed ea, de quibus antea præceperat Apostolus: fugam cu- piditatum, & studium præstandi in fide virtutem, de quibus vers. 8. dixerat : Ταῦτα ὑπάρχοντα ὐκ ἀργὲς, ὐδὲ ἀκάρπες καθίστησιν; & vers.9. ᾧ μὴ πά- ρεσι ταῦτα, τυφλός ἐσιν. Aut, si quis malit, refe- ratur pronomen ταῦτα hoc loco ad immediate præcedens monitum, satagite, ut vocationem & electionem vestram firmam faciatis: hæc si feceritis: Res eodem recidit. Certam reddi vocationem Vulgatus exposuit, Estius mavult firmam, quia id vox βεβαία proprie significat, Roman. IV. vers. 16. 2. Corinth. I. vers. 7. Hebræor. II. vers. 2. 2. Petr. I. vers. 15. & lapsus vers. 21. & sequente opponitur firmitati, est hæc firmitas non opponenda certi- tudini, sed conjuncta est cum certitudine; neque integrum est Papistis Vulgatam translationem de- serere, cujus etiam causa hic nulla est. Nam firma redditur vocatio & electio non ex parte Dei, cu- jus dona sunt ἀμεταμέλητα, Roman. XI. vers. 29. ex parte nostri, ut nos certi simus, nos esse ita vo- catos, ut etiam electi simus, quum multi alioquin sint vocati, pauci electi, Matth. XX. v. 15. & XXII. v. 14. Vocatio autem intelligitur ea, quæ cum ef- fectu divinitus intento conjuncta est, cum acce- ptione ex parte nostra & justificatione per fidem, Rom. VIII. vers. 30. 2. Timoth. I. vers. 9. Quod firmum est, id etiam certum sit oportet. Ideo Estius ipse interpretatus est, certam firmamque, quod vero de certitudine in genere singulorum bene probabilium explicat. Sed licet ex bonis operibus tantum moralis quædam & conjecturalis certitudo, ut vocant, electionis nostræ habere- tur, ex interno tamen Spiritus testimonio habe- mus certitudinem fidei divinæ, Roman. VIII. v. 16. ne dicam, quod certitudo conjecturalis sit σιδηρό- ξυλον. Agnoscit utique Thomas ipse, hic veram certitudinem sic παραφάζων: Ut per bona opera, scilicet exteriora, certam faciatis, hoc est, osten-

catis vestram vocationem ad fidem in tempore, & electionem per prædestinationem ab æterno, ut scili- cet certi sitis, vos vocatos & à Deo electos. Quid? quod de fide sua quisque omnino certus esse pos- sit per suiipsius explorationem, & per actum re- flexum, 2. Corinth. XIII. 5. & per renovationis in- terioris documentum, ac luctæ carnis & spiritus argumentum, Gal. V. v. 17. vitiorum fugam, ac virtutum studium, quæ singa certa sunt fidei, Galat. V. 22. 1. Johan. II. v. 3. 4. cap. III. v. 14. unde etiam de justificatione, quæ contingit per fidem, certus redditur, & per consequens de sa- lute, quæ est finis fidei, modo per apostasiam, & peccata contra conscientiam fide ac gratia non excidat, nec media conservandæ fidei negligat, aut contemnat, Verbi Dei auditum, Sacramento- rum usum, precum & orationum studium. Est enim certitudo salutis non absoluta, sed hypothe- tica, nec tam nititur nostra pietate, utpote quæ sæpe languet, quam divina promissione, quæ infallibilis, Phil. II. v. 12. 1. Corinth. I. v. 9. cap. X. v. 3. ac virtute, quæ sufficientissima est, 2. Tim. I. v. 12. & Christi merito, ac pro nobis intercessione, Roman. VIII. v. 34. 38. Interim possunt renati as- sistente Spiritus Sancti gratia cavere peccata mor- talia, sibique hoc serio proponunt, sed suis ne fi- dant viribus, adeoque precibus piis per petuo di- vinam ambiant gratiam. Quo de Augustinus de dono persever. cap. 22. ipsam obediendi perseve- rantiam à Patre luminum sperare debetis, & quoti- dianis orationibus poscere, atque hoc faciendo confi- dere, non vos esse à prædestinatione populi ejus alie- nos, quia etiam hoc ut faciatis, ipse largitur. Ταῦτα γὰρ ποιοῦντες οὐ μὴ πταίσητε] id est, non excidetis speratis לא תמוט. Vide Rom. XLI. Psal. XV. 5. לא ימוט Psal. CXIX. v. 164. ואין למו מכשול.

De lapsu peccati Vulgatus exponit, non de ex- cidentia à bonis speratis, reddens: Non peccabitis aliquando. Similiter Ambrosius lib. III. de fide cap. 6. & Idacius contra Varimundum non errabitis aliquando. Atque ita vox hæc occurrit Jac. II. v. 3. 10. Roman. XI. v. 11. & metaphorica est loquu- tio ab illis petita, qui inter currendum impingunt, conf. Philipp. I. v. 10. Juda vers. penult. Non er- go simplex peccatum intelligitur, sed quod tales non sint offensuri, non ruituri in peccata morta- lia, ut glossa ordinaria habet: Crimina vitabitis, à quibus immunis juvante Deo permaneat, qui supra dictis virtutibus sese mancipaverit.

## 1:11
Verse 11.

For so shall the entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ be richly provided for you] πλουσίως is abundantly, as in Col. III. v. 16, 1 Tim. VI. v. 17, Tit. III. v. 6, but here by metonymy it signifies with God's most ready affection. And ἐπιχορηγηθήσεται, here, is, shall be granted, as in 2 Cor. IX. 10, Gal. III. 5.

Therefore, the Vulgate did not translate it quite conveniently as 'abundantly'. For it denotes a free and open entrance into the eternal kingdom, which God will provide or grant out of grace to those who supply virtue in faith, not out of the merit of virtues, Rom. VI. last verse. To those who are rich in good works, the entrance into the kingdom of Christ our Savior is granted πλουσίως, not because of good works, but because of Christ the Savior and his merits, who makes us πλουσίως by his own poverty, 2 Cor. IX. v. 19, and by the gratuitous mercy of God, who is rich in mercy, Eph. II. 4, rich unto all who call upon him in true faith, Rom. X. 12, who chose πλουσίως ἐν πίςει, Jas. II. 5.

PART III. A commemoration of the causes both for being reminded of the received duty and for obeying the admonitions.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Οὕτω γὰρ πλουσίως ἐπιχορηγηθήσεται ὑμῖν ἡ εἴσοδος εἰς τὴν αἰώνιον βασιλείαν τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ] πλουσίως est co- piose, ut Coloss. III. v. 16. 1. Timoth. VI. v. 17. Tit. III. v. 6. sed hic per μετωνυμίαν significat promptissimo Dei affectu. Et ἐπιχορηγηθήσεται, hic est, concedetur, ut 2. Cor. IX. 10. Gal. III. 5.

Non ergo satis commode reddidit Vulgata abundanter. Notatur enim liber & apertus in- gressus in æternum regnum, quem Deus ex gra- tia illis suppeditabit vel præstabit, qui submini- strant in fide virtutem non ex merito virtutum, Roman. VI. vers. ult. Qui divites sunt in operibus bonis, illis πλουσίως introitus in regnum Christi Servatoris nostri conceditur non propter bona opera, sed propter Christum Servatorem ejusque merita, qui sua inopia nos facit πλουσίως, 2. Cor. IX. v. 19. & gratuita Dei misericordia, qui dives est in misericordia Ephes. II. 4. dives in omnes, qui invocant eum vera fide, Rom. X. 12. qui elegit πλουσίως ἐν πίςει, Jac. II. 5.

PARS III. Causarum cum suscepti muneris commonendi, tum parendi monitis, commemo- ratio.

## 1:12
Verse 12.

Wherefore] since this matter is of such great moment. I will not be negligent to remind you always of these things] to remind תזכיר, 2 Tim. 2, 14, Tit. 3, 1. It is also useful to remind those who are mindful, Phil. 3, 1. In the Manuscript: Wherefore I will delay, unusually. And yet the Latin seems to have read it thus. The reason why Peter now reminds his converts of this is that the laying aside of the tabernacle is imminent, so that after his death they may have a memorial. Others assign a triple cause here: 1. From the utility of the reminder, which is insinuated by the illative word 'wherefore', because it contributes to the promotion of their salvation. 2. From the Apostolic office, by virtue of which this is incumbent upon him. 3. From the nearness of his death. The Vulgate interprets οὐκ ἀμελήσω less correctly as 'I will begin', which Grotius tacitly but rashly excuses, and Estius more openly. For the Greek codices agree on the word ἀμελήσω, and all have the negative 'not'. But what makes for the Vulgate, which rendered it 'I will begin'?
