On the contrary, however, according to the Greek reading, the sense is clear: 'I will not neglect', that is, according to the custom of Scripture, I will take care of it with zeal. The negation is placed with emphasis for the contrary affirmation: See Exod. XX. v. 7, Lev. X. v. 1, 1 Sam. XII. v. 21, Job XIV. v. 18. What is the sense of the Vulgate, I pray? 'I will always begin to remind you.' Whence Estius finally acknowledges: 'Because the future μελλήσω is hardly in use among the Greeks, although it may be read somewhere in Plato, certainly nowhere in the sacred writings, therefore I consider that reading to be truer which all or almost all Greek codices have. For all have the negation, and almost all have ἀμελήσω: which word fits this place very well.' As he says, 'So that you may receive ample rewards from God, I will not neglect to exhort you to exercise good works,' that is, I will assiduously and solicitously remind and exhort you. Although you know] Thus Hesiod: 'Now I will speak to those who are wise themselves.' And established in the present truth] This does not pertain to all, but to the greater, certainly the better part of those to whom he writes. Established נסמכים. See 1 Pet. V. 11. In the present truth, in that truth which you profess up to this point, namely, the Evangelical. Thus 'in the word of the truth of the Gospel which is present unto you', Col. I: 5. The Vulgate 'and indeed knowing', more correctly, 'although knowing', as B. Luther and the Syriac. Similar places are to be compared here, Rom. XV. v. 14, 15, 1 John II. 21, Jude v. 5, 2 Pet. III. 1, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Διὸ] cum haec res tanti sit momenti. Οὐκ ἀμελήσω ἀεὶ ὑμᾶς ὑπομιμνήσκειν περὶ τούτων] ὑπομί- μνησκειν תזכיר, 2. Tim. 2, 14. Tit. 3, 1. Utile est etiam me- mores monere, Phil. 3, 1. In Manuscripto: Διὸ μελλήσω, in- usitate. Et tamen videtur Latinus sic legisse. Causa cur nunc commonefaciat conversos Pe- trus suos haec est, quod immineat tabernaculi de- positio, ut post obitum habeant μνημόσυνον. Tri- plicem causam alii hic assignant 1. A commonefa- ctionis utilitate, quae insinuetur voce illativa διὸ, quod ad promovendam salutem ipsorum ea faciat. 2. Ab Apostolico munere, vi cujus id ipsi incum- bat. 3. A mortis sua propinquitate. Οὐκ ἀμελήσω Vulgatus minus recte' interpretatur incipiam, quem tacite sed temere excusat Grotius, apertius Estius. Consonant enim Graeci codices in verbo ἀμε- λήσω, & negativam ἐκ habent omnes. Quid autem pro Vulgata, quae reddidit incipiam, hoc facit? Ex adverso vero juxta Graecam lectionem sensus est luculentus non negligam, id est, ex more Scri- pturae studio id curabo. Negatio ponitur cum em- phasi pro contraria affirmatione: Vid. Exod. XX. v. 7. Levit. X. v. 1. 1. Sam. XII. v. 21. Job. XIV. v. 18. Vulgatae quis sensus obsecro? Semper incipiam vos commonere. Unde agnoscit tandem Estius: Quia Futurum μελλήσω vix est in usu apud Graecos, licet alicubi apud Platonem legatur, certe nusquam in sacris literis, idcirco veriorem arbitror eam le- ctionem, quam habent omnes aut pene omnes Graeci codices. Nam omnes habent negationem, pene omnes ἀμελήσω: Quod verbum optime convenit huic loco. Ut, inquit, ampla praemia recipiatis à Deo, non negligam vos ad exercenda bona opera ex- hortari, id est, assidue atque solicite vos commonefa- ciam & adhortabor. Καίπερ εἰδότας] Sic Hesiodus: Νῦν δι αἰνὸν βασιλεῦσ᾽ ἐρέω φρονέουσι καὶ αὐτοῖς. καὶ ἐστηριγμένους ἐν τῇ παρούσῃ ἀληθείᾳ] Hoc non ad omnes, sed ad majorem, certe meliorem eorum, quibus scribit par- tem pertinet. Εστηριγμένους נסמכים. Vide 1. Petr. V. 11. ἐν τῇ παρούσῃ ἀληθεία in ea veritate, quam huc usque pro- fitemini, Evangelica scilicet. Sic ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τ ἀληθείας τοῦ Ευαγγελείου τοῦ παρόντος εἰς ὑμᾶς, Col. I: 5. Vulgata & quidem scientes, rectius, etsi scien- tes, ut B. Lutherus & Syrus. Conferenda hic simi- lia loca, Rom. XV. v. 14. 15. 1. Joh. II. 21. Judae v. 5. 2. Petr. III. 1. 2.

## 1:13
Verse 13.

Δίκαιον δὲ ἡγοῦμαι εφ᾽ ὅσον εἰμὶ ἐν τούτῳ τῷ σκηνώματι] In this body. The Hebrews call the body משכן. That is called in Greek σκῆνος, as in Wisdom 9:15 and among the Pythagoreans, or σκήνωμα, as here, and a little later. Διεγείρειν ὑμᾶς ἐν ὑπομνήσει] To stir you up to duty by frequent reminding.

Dicitur hic δίκαιον, quod ratione officii incumbit. See also Ephesians 6:1, Philippians 1:7. Εφ' ὅσον that is to say, time. The word for tabernacle occurs in the same sense in 2 Corinthians 5:1, 4. Some also compare here Isaiah 38:12. Whence they wish to see a reference to military and pastoral tabernacles, in which soldiers only dwell in time of war, and shepherds in time of guarding, which are constructed of cheap and weak material, and are easily taken down. Compare Job 4:19, in which also the Patriarchs dwelt as pilgrims, having no fixed dwelling. Hebrews 11:9, 13, chapter 13:14, 2 Corinthians 5:6. The designation of the Pythagoreans and Platonists here does nothing. For they dreamed that the human body is as it were a prison and sepulcher of the soul; whereas on the contrary the body pertains equally to the constitution of man, as does the soul. Concerning which elsewhere against the Socinians and Remonstrants. Furthermore, our soul dwells in our body in this life as in a tabernacle: it will dwell in eternal life in the same glorious body as in a temple. In the word διεγείρειν a metaphor occurs from those who awaken from sleep, Matt. 8, 25. Luke 8, 24. John VI. v. 18. and therefore they are awakened, if any are sluggish.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Δίκαιον δὲ ἡγοῦμαι εφ᾽ ὅσον εἰμὶ ἐν τούτῳ τῷ σκηνώματι] In hoc corpore. Ebraei corpus משכן vocant. Id Graece dicitur σκῆνος, ut Sap. IX. 15. & apud Pythagoricos, aut σκήνωμα, ut hic, & paulo post. Διεγείρειν ὑμᾶς ἐν ὑπομνήσει] Excitare vos ad officium sae- pe commonefaciendo.

Dicitur hic δίκαιον, quod ratione officii incumbit. Vid. & Ephes. VI. v. 1. Philipp. I. v. 7. Εφ' ὅσον scili- cet χρόνον. Tabernaculi vox eodem sensu 2. Cor. V. v. 1. 4. occurrit. Nonnulli etiam conferunt hic Isa. XXXVIII. v. 12. Unde respici volunt taber- nacula militaria & pastoralia, in quibus tantum belli milites, & custodiae tempore pastores habi- tant, quae ex vili & imbecilli materia constructa sunt, ac facile deponuntur. Conf. Job. IV. 19. in qualibus etiam Patriarchae habitabant ceu pe- regrinantes, nullamque certam mansionem ha- bentes. Ebr. XI. v. 9. 13. cap. XIII. v. 14. 2. Cor. V. v. 6. Pythagore & Platonicorum nuncupatio huc nihil facit. Somniarunt enim corpus humanum esse veluti custodiam & sepulchrum animæ; quum contra corpus æque ad constitutionem hominis pertineat, uti anima. Quo de alias contra So- cinianos & Remonstrantes. De cætero anima no- stra habitat in corpore nostro in hac vita tan- quam in tabernaculo: habitabit in vita æterna in corpore eodem glorioso tanquam in templo. In voce διεγείρειν metaphora occurrit ab illis, qui à somno excitant, Matth. 8, 25. Luc. 8, 24. Joh. VI. v. 18. ideoque excitantur, si qui torpescunt.

## 1:14
Ver. 14.

Knowing that the putting off of my tabernacle is speedy, even as our Lord Jesus Christ showed me] A similar prediction of Paul concerning himself 2 Timothy IV. v. 6. Something not dissimilar happened also to Cyprian and Chrysostom. And that the gift of prophecy was then frequent in the churches in Jerusalem, we shall see in the Apocalypse: I believe, however, that this epistle was written by Simeon the Bishop while Trajan was already reigning. To put off ἀποτίθεσθαι is properly said of garments, as Acts VII. 58. By a certain similarity concerning the tabernacle, or concerning the body as a tabernacle, just as also those who are outside the body are called γυμνοὶ, see 2 Cor. V. 2.

That the fictitious author Simeon of Jerusalem had the gift of prophecy while Trajan was reigning, and that the time of his death was divinely indicated to him, is a Grotian fable. Concerning Peter, who is the genuine author of the epistle, some wish this prediction made by Christ in John XXI. v. 18. to be designated: But the time of his departure (ἀναλύσεως) was not expressed in it, and therefore there is no doubt that a special revelation was given by Christ to Simon Peter concerning the time of his death: concerning which, although some authors report something, they are of uncertain authority, such as those which Surius reports from Simeon Metaphrastes, which Estius himself acknowledges in this place, or at any rate they do not pertain to this. Tirinus judged it likely that the revelation happened to Peter in the Mamertine prison.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Εἰδὼς ὅτι ταχηή ἐστιν ἡ ἀπόθεσις τῦ σκηνώματός με, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν Ἰησῦς Χριστὸς ἐδήλωσέ μοι] Similis præ- dictio Pauli de se 2 Timoth. IV. v. 6. Cypriano quoque & Chrysostomo aliquid evenit non dissimile. Et in Hie- rosolymis tunc Ecclefiæ frequens fuisse donum Prophetiæ, videbimus in Apocalypsi: Credo autem scriptam à Simeone Episcopo hanc epistolam imperante jam Trajano. Depone- re ἀποτίθεσθαι proprie de vestibus dicitur, ut Actor. VII. 58. Per similitudinem quandã de tabernaculo, aut de corpore ve- lut tabernaculo, quomodo & γυμνοὶ dicuntur, qui extra cor- pus sunt, vide 2.Cor. V.2.

Fictitium autorem Simeonem Hierosolymita- num donum prophetiæ habuisse imperante Tra- jano, eique obitus sui tempus divinitus indicatum esse, fabula Grotiana est. De Petro, qui genui- nus autor epistolæ, nonnulli hanc prædictionem factam à Christo Joh. XXI. v. 18. designari volunt: Sed ea non expressum fuit tempus, ἀναλύσεως, id- eoque peculiarem revelationem à Christo datam Simoni Petro de tempore mortis, dubium nullum est: de qua etsi autores nonnulli aliquid referant, incertæ tamen fidei ea sunt, qualia quæ ex Sime- one Metaphr. Surius refert, agnoscit Estius ipse in h. l. aut certe huc non faciunt. Tirinus in carce- re Mamertino Petro contigisse revelationem verisi- mile censuit.

## 1:15
Ver. 15.

But I will endeavor at all times to have you, after my departure, make a remembrance of these things] Since I feel that I am about to die shortly, I wish this to be so deeply fixed in your minds: that you cannot, even after my death, fail to remember them often. We noted that death is called an exodus (ἔξοδος) at Luke IX. v. 31. Here is an exit figured by that one from Egypt.

This interpretation prostrates the Popish figment, to wit, that Peter, because he wishes to remember those to whom he writes in his prayers or his intercession in the heavens, which Salmero, Gagnejus, Lorinus, Cornelius, Tirinus, and other interpreters here, and elsewhere Bellarmine, Costerus, Joseph à Costa, and many others teach, in order to obtain that the Saints after death take care of the living, and so are to be religiously invoked. That it is not a matter of prayers after death, but of memory before death, which he wishes to inculcate in these very letters, so that they may retain the same even after his death, is acknowledged even by the Papists themselves, the author of the Ordinary Gloss, Thomas, Lyranus, Hugo Cardinalis, Dionysius Carthusianus, Cajetanus, Erasmus, Guillaudus, Emanuel Saa, Lorinus, Estius. The word ἔχειν is not referred to Peter: but to those to whom he was writing: I will take pains that you may have that which you may remember after my death. The gloss of Bellarmine, lib. I. de Beat. Sanct. cap. 8, is very inept: I will take pains that I may have you, namely commended, so that you may make a remembrance of these things. Certainly, if we listen to Estius, it was not fitting that he should say, I will take pains, I will take care, σπυδάσω, since the saints do that without care and solicitude. Still more inept is the Cornelian: I will act, I will direct and impel you, so that you may remember these things. For Peter, he says, is the charioteer of the Church, driving and urging the faithful to good, even when he enjoys God in the heavens; For where is ἔχειν the same as to drive or impel? Where is anything held concerning that which Peter wishes to do after death? Concerning the true sense, Lorinus says thus: The more common opinion of the expositors is that it signifies that Peter, because he must shortly depart from this life, wishes to take care that he leaves behind such a monument of his epistles and the warnings in them, so salutary, lest they ever fall out of their memory. Rightly, therefore, Flacius observes in this place that it is the custom of the Apostolic writings that all posterity until the end of the world may be instructed and confirmed thereby.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Σπυδάσω δὲ ἑκάστοτε ἔχειν ὑμᾶς μετὰ τὴν ἔξοδον τὴν τύτων μνήμην ποιεῖσθαι] Cum sentiam brevi me moriturum, ita alte hoc volo infigi vestris animis: ut non possitis nec post meam mortem sæpe eorum recordari. Ἔξοδος dici mortem notavimus ad Luc. IX. v. 31. Hic exitus figuratus per illum ex Ægypto.

Hæc interpretatio prosternit figmentum Pa- pisticum, q. d. Petrus, quod eorum, ad quos scri- bit, meminisse velit} in precibus vel intercessione sua in cælis, quod hic Salmero, Gagnejus, Lori- nus, Cornelius, Tirinus, alii Interpretes, & alibi Bellarminus, Costerus, Josephus à Costa, aliique plurimi tradunt, ut obtineant, Sanctos post ob- itum curam gerere viventium, adeoque religiose invocandos esse. Non de precibus post mortem, sed memoria ante mortem, quam ipsis hisce literis inculcare vult, ut post mortem etiam suam ean- dem retineant, agi, agnoscunt etiam è Papistis ipsis, Autor Glossæ ordinariæ, Thomas, Lyranus, Hugo Cardinalis, Dionysius Carthusianus, Cajeta- nus, Erasmus, Guillaudus, Emanuel Saa, Lori- nus, Estius. Verbum ἔχειν non refertur ad Pe- trum: sed ad eos, ad quos scribebat: Dabo operam, ut habeatis, cujus post obitum meum recordemini. Perquam inepta est glossa Bellarmini lib. I. de Be- at. Sanct. cap. 8. operam dabo, ut habeam vos, sci- licet commendatos, ut horum memoriam faciatis. Certe si Estium audiamus, non congruebat, ut diceret, dabo operam, curabo, σπυδάσω, cum il- lud sancti faciant absque cura & solicitudine. Adhuc ineptior est Corneliana: Agam, dirigam & im- pellam vos, ut horum reminiscamini. Petrus enim, inquit, est auriga Ecclesiæ, fideles agens & agi- tans ad bonum, etiam cum in cælis Deo fruitur; Ubi enim ἔχειν idem est, quod agere vel impel- lere? Ubi de eo, quod post obitum agere velit Petrus, quicquam habetur? De vero sensu ita Lorinus: Magis communis expositorum sententia est, significare Petrum, se, quia brevi ex hac vita sibi discedendum sit, curare velle, ut hoc epistola- rum & monitorum in iis tam salutarium relinquat monumentum, ne illis unquam excidat de memo- ria. Recte ergo observat Flacius h. l. Usum A- postolicorum scriptorum esse, ut omnis posteritas usque ad finem mundi inde erudiatur & confirme- tur.

## 1:16
Ver. 16.

For we have not followed cunningly devised fables when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ] Μύθοις σεσοφισμένοις, fables made by art. Σοφίζομαι, to cavil, to invent, in the Glossary. Thus πλαστοῖς λόγοις below c. 2, 3. Δύναμιν καὶ παρουσίαν, one by two, for a powerful coming. Moreover, παρουσία is said of every operation. See 2 Thess. 2, 9. Ἀλλ' ἐπόπται γενηθέντες] such as the witnesses are called αὐτόπται in Luke in the preface, who testify not from another's, but from their own sight, עיניך הראת, Deut. 3, 21. τῆς ἐκείνου μεγαλειότητος] that is, of his miracles. For it is a Metonymy, such as Luke 9, 23. The same miracles are called μεγαλεῖα τοῦ Θεοῦ, Acts 2, 11.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Οὐ γὰρ σεσοφισμένοις μύθοις ἐξακολουθήσαντες ἐγνωρίσαμεν ὑμῖν τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ δύναμιν καὶ παρουσίαν] Μύ- θοις σεσοφισμένοις, fabulis arte factis. Σοφίζομαι cavil- lor, comminiscor in Glossario. Sic πλαστοῖς λόγοις infra c. 2, 3. Δύναμιν καὶ παρουσίαν ἓν διὰ δυοῖν pro δυνατὴν παρουσί- αν. Dicitur autem παρουσία omnis operatio. Vide 2. Thess. 2, 9. Ἀλλ' ἐπόπται γενηθέντες] quales testes αὐτόπται dicuntur Lucae in praefatione, qui non de alieno, sed de suo visu te- stantur עיניך הראת, Deut. 3, 21. τῆς ἐκείνου μεγαλειότητος] id est, miraculorum ejus. Est enim Metonymia, qualis Luc. 9, 23. Eadem miracula di- cuntur μεγαλεῖα τοῦ Θεοῦ, Act. 2, 11.

## 1:17
Vers. 17.

For having received from God the Father honor and glory] Supply ἦν, such as the eyewitnesses we have already often had. τιμὴν καὶ δόξαν, honor most glorious.

Peter sets forth the reasons for the duty of obedience in receiving his admonition and the doctrine of Christ delivered by him, both because he received the doctrine of Christ confirmed by a heavenly voice, heard on the holy mount: and because it is strengthened by the same prophetic word, to which those who attend, in their hearts arises that heavenly Day-star through faith. He proves, therefore, his doctrine and commends it to them by authority, because he delivers not human inventions, but divine oracles. By μύθους σεσοφισμένους he understands not speeches composed by art, as Oecumenius and Gagnejus wish, but fables shrewdly and sophistically, or fraudulently devised, looking to the matter, not the manner of proposing, because μύθοι are fables, 1 Tim. I. v. 4. cap. IV. v. 7. 2 Tim. IV. v. 4. Tit. I. vers. 14. Σοφίζεσθαι σοφίζεσθαι Aristoph. in the Clouds is to invent shrewdly; in Demosthenes it is to devise something deceitfully and cunningly, such as vafrous and deceitful fables, which it is evident from chapter II. verse 3 are primarily intended. Oecumenius thinks the Valentinians are indicated, who invented βυθὸς & σιγὴν, depths and silence. It is likely, however, that they had already begun to arise at that time. Concerning the Gnostics, Augustine, book on heresies, chapter VI, says: They hand down, he says, dogmas full of most fabulous figments, and those who believe them they make not to excel in much knowledge, as they think, but to vanish away in much, if I may so say, fabulosity. But because those heretics, as being later than the Apostles, could not be followed by them, it seems there was no need for that heresy, and so it is more likely that Peter had regard to Jewish fables, such as are noted in 1 Tim. I. v. 4, cap. IV. v. 7, 2 Tim. IV. v. 4, Tit. I. v. 14. are noted, and those of the Gentiles, of the kind which occur in Hesiod's Theogony and Ovid's Metamorphoses, or similar things.

By the power and coming of Christ our Lord is understood the power of the advent, either in the advent, or his conspicuous presence. Which παρουσία we understand not of the second advent, as Estius wishes, nor does it displease Lorinus, to whom also our B. Gerhard and the Weimar Gloss agree, but of the first advent, with Vatablus, Cajetan, Clarius, Salmeron, Erasmus, Gagnejus, Fevardentius, Saa, Flacius, and Osiander, whose paraphrase is this: That what concerning Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, Redeemer and Savior of the world (who defeated Satan), we have taught, namely that he has already come into this world, this we learned neither from the fables and trifles of the Jews nor of the Greeks (which they invent without the Word of God). For it concerns that advent through which all things that pertain to life and godliness have been given to us, verse 3; through whom and on account of whom the greatest and most precious promises have come to us, and we have been made partakers of the divine nature, verse 4; and we have an entrance into the eternal kingdom of Christ, verse 11, in which the divine power had already been demonstrated, which the Apostles had known in Christ the Lord, not from fables, but from their own inspection of the majesty of Christ, verse 16. For the discourse is not about a power of Christ that is yet to be demonstrated on the last day, but one already demonstrated and known in the days of his flesh, of which Peter and other Apostles were eyewitnesses (ἐπόπται), just as it is said in John 1:14, 'The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the Only Begotten of the Father.' It concerns the power that shone forth in his doctrine and miracles, which the Apostles, as eyewitnesses who had heard the Word of life and life itself manifested in the flesh, and had seen it with their own eyes, were bound to announce to others. John 1:2, so that they might be led to the faith and knowledge (ἐπίγνωσιν) of Christ, about which those to whom Peter was writing could be informed and confirmed even from the Prophetic Scriptures themselves, so that the day of saving knowledge might shine upon them more and more, and the Daystar might arise in their hearts more clearly; which power and presence (παρουσίαν) both the Prophets in the Old Testament foretold and the Apostles in the New Testament were bound to announce. Concerning which the Father also testified from heaven on the Holy Mount, whence the Apostles, being present, hearing the heavenly voice and beholding the majesty of the glorified Christ, were able to notify others of it and render others more certain about Christ the Son of God, in whom God is well pleased, and about his doctrine which is to be heard by all. Concerning which knowledge (ἐπιγνώσει) of Christ the Apostle had also said in verse 12 that the same was to be called to their memory, although they knew and were established in the present truth. This present truth, knowledge (ἐπίγνωσις), and reminder (ὑπόμνησις) certainly do not concern that particle of the heavenly doctrine of Christ regarding the last advent, which the mockers had called into doubt, but the entire saving doctrine of Christ, concerning which the Apostle therefore says, 'We have made known to you the power and presence (παρουσίαν) of our Lord Jesus Christ.' What Estius says, that the first advent of Christ was in infirmity and humility, we admit, but it also consisted well with the glory and majesty which subsequently shone forth in him in the days of his flesh. For he was in the form of God, and he frequently manifested his glory as of the Only Begotten of the Father even in the time of his humiliation (ταπεινώσεως), because all things had been given into his hands, John 3:35, chapter 13:2, concerning which even the Pharisees themselves testified, John 3:2. It is concerning this power and glory of Christ that the matter here treats, of which the Apostles were indeed eyewitnesses (ἐπόπται), and not that which will only be revealed on the last day. To this point are those things of Gerhard: By majesty (μεγαλειότητα) is understood the glory and majesty of Christ, which shone forth in him during all that time in which he lived with the Apostles in these lands, John 1:14, 'We beheld (Ἐθεασάμεθα) his glory, the glory as of the Only Begotten of the Father.' The author of the book on the miracles of Scripture, Vol. III, Augustine, book 3, chapter 10: 'The Divinity, hidden in the body, granted a small portion of its light to be seen outwardly by those who could see.' He uses the related word greatness (μεγαλωσύνης) concerning CHRIST in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 1:3 and chapter 8:1. Moreover, the word majesty (μεγαλειότητος) itself is used concerning the miracles of CHRIST in Luke 9:43, since from these his divine majesty and power shone forth. As for what Estius further says, that the transfiguration of CHRIST on the mount was a certain type of the second advent: I reply. That it is brought forward not as a type of the glory of CHRIST to be manifested one day or of the second advent of CHRIST, just as the transfiguration of CHRIST was not done for that purpose, in which no conversation was instituted about the last advent of CHRIST, but about the departure which he had to fulfill in his first advent in Jerusalem, Luke 9:31. It was therefore done for this end, that the disciples of CHRIST and others might be confirmed concerning the advent of the Son of GOD into the flesh, that this Jesus of Nazareth is the beloved Son of GOD, in whom is all the good pleasure (εὐδοκία) of the Father, of whom Moses and the Prophets (among whom Elijah is commemorated here) prophesied, and whom the heavenly voice revealed so that he might be heard by all, which does not pertain to the last day, but to the time of grace, in which he is to be heard. Which end of the gospel-writing (εὐαγγελιογραφίας) the Holy Spirit assigns, John 20:31. What is finally brought forward by Estius from chapter 3:4, as if it concerned the advent which some wished to render doubtful, saying, 'Where is the promise of his presence (παρουσίας)?'—this is the very thing in question. The epistle was directed not only against those who called the second advent of CHRIST into doubt, but also against those who denied the power and first advent of CHRIST, which he teaches was confirmed by a heavenly voice, and who denied the Master who bought them, which redemption was indeed accomplished through his first advent, chapter 2:1. For the heresies of destruction and feigned words of these false prophets are opposed by the prophetic word and the Apostolic doctrine, which we have not received in cunningly devised fables, but from the mouth of him concerning whom the Father proclaims from heaven: 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased (εἰς ὃν ἐγὼ εὐδόκησα), hear him,' which the continuity of the first and second, the conclusion of the former, and the beginning and scope of this chapter teach.

Nor is it an objection that elsewhere the word παρουσία almost always denotes the second advent of CHRIST, since the determination must be sought not from other passages, but primarily from the context, and the advent of grace is also called the παρουσία of the Son of man only once, Matt. XXIV. verse 27, and thus nothing prevents the advent of the incarnation from being designated in this way also only once, since that advent is designated by the name τῆς ἐπιφανείας only once: nor is it permissible to conclude, because that word elsewhere always denotes the second advent of CHRIST, 2 Thess. 2, v. 8, 1 Tim. 6, v. 14, 2 Tim. 4, v. 1, 8, Tit. 2, v. 13, that also in 2 Tim. 1, v. 10, the second, and not the first advent, is denoted by the same.

By μεγαλειότητα, or majesty and magnificence, which was seen in the miracles, is designated, so that its confirmation by the voice made from heaven may be considered as being added, or that magnificence is declared from the act of the transfiguration of CHRIST, in which he received τιμὴν καὶ δόξαν, honor and glory, or honor most glorious. Neither explanation is repugnant, and the blessed Gerhard joins both. The latter, however, seems simpler, according to which St. Peter speaks of himself and the two other Apostles taken with him onto the mountain, that they were then ἐπόπται

of the majesty, when he received honor and glory through the heavenly voice, and through the same is to be understood the magnificence of the glorification of Christ, which shone forth in that illustrious transfiguration of the body of Christ; which, however, is not to be confused with honor and glory, inasmuch as what it was, and how great it was, is to be learned from the heavenly voice. Honor and glory not only of the glorified body, but of the person of Christ, not temporal, but perpetual, such as indeed is brought about by being the Son of God, not by grace, but by nature, and thus consubstantial and coequal with God the Father; and the Messiah, the Redeemer of the world, in whom and for whom is all good pleasure. Honor, I say; both of the person of the Son of God, and of his same Mediatorial office, which is not finite, but truly infinite, immense, and divine, since all ought to honor the Son, even as they honor the Father, John 5:23. and to Christ the Mediator and Savior of all, knees ought to bow themselves, and divine and religious honor ought to be exhibited to him, Is. 45:23 seqq., Rom. 14:11, Phil. 2:10. Therefore, he confirms the certainty of Christian doctrine from the authority and majesty of Christ, from whom he received it: he confirms the authority and majesty of Christ from the glory and honor conferred upon him in the transfiguration, in which he was constituted the public Teacher of the whole world by the voice of the heavenly Father, as here Blessed Gerhard. But it pleased him to distinguish glory and honor, so that he understood the former as the glory of the body, of which Matt. 17:2, Mark 9:3, Luke 9:29, because its splendor was so great that it exerted itself through the very garments, otherwise dark and not at all diaphanous: but the latter as that excellent honor with which Christ was affected by his heavenly Father, by a voice fallen from heaven.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Λαβὼν γὰρ παρὰ Θεοῦ Πατρὸς τιμὴν καὶ δόξαν] Supple ἦν, quales ἐπόπται saepe jam habuimus. τιμὴν καὶ δόξαν hono- rem maxime gloriosum.

Causas debiti obsequii in suscipienda sua com- monitione, ac doctrina Christi abs se tradita proponit Petrus, tum quod doctrinam Christi confirmatam acceperit voce coelesti, in monte sacro audita: tum quod eodem sermone pro- phetico roboretur, cui qui attendunt, in illorum cordibus oritur Phophorus iste coelestis per fi- dem. Probat ergo doctrinam suam & commen- dat ipsis ab autoritate, quod non humana com- menta, sed divina oracula tradat. Per μύθους σε- σοφισμένους non sermones arte compositos, ut Oe- cumenius & Gagnejus volunt, sed fabulas argute & sophistice, vel fraudulenter excogitatas intelligit, materiam respiciens, non modum proponendi, quia μύθοι fabulae sunt, 1. Timoth. I. v. 4. cap. IV. v. 7. 2. Timoth. IV. v. 4. Tit. I. vers. 14. Σοφίζεσθαι σοφίζεσθαι Aristoph. in Nub. est argute comminisci, Demo- stheni est dolose & callide aliquid excogitare, qua- les μύθους vafros & dolosos imprimis intelligi e cap. II. vers. 3. constat. Oecumenius putat Valen- tinianos indicari, qui βυθὸς & σιγὴν comminisce- bantur profunda & silentium. Verisimile autem esse, eos illo tempore jam suboriri coepisse. De Gno- sticis Augustinus lib. de haeres. cap. VI. Tradunt, inquit, dogmata fabulosissimis plena figmentis & illos, qui eis credunt, faciunt non multa, ut putant, scientia pollere, sed multa, ut ita dicam, fabulosi- tate vanescere. Sed quia illos haereticos ceu po- steriores Apostolis hi sequi non poterant, illa ἅρεσει opus non fuisse videtur, adeoque verisi- milius est, Petrum fabulas Judaicas, quales 1. Ti- moth. I. vers. 4. cap. IV. v. 7. 2. Tim. IV. v. 4. Tit. I. v. 14. notantur, & gentilium, cujusmodi in Hesi- odi Theogonia & Ovidii Metamorphosi ocurrunt, aut similes respexisse.

Per Christi Domini nostri δύναμιν καὶ παρου- σίαν intelligitur potentia adventus vel in adventu, vel praesentia ejus conspicua. Quam παρουσίαν non de adventu secundo, ut Estius vult, nec displi- cet Lorino, quibus accedit etiam B. Gerhardus no- ster & Glossa Vinar. sed de adventu primo intel- ligimus cum Vatablo, Cajetano, Clario, Salme- rone, Erasmo, Gagnejo, Fevardentio, Saa, Flacio, & Osiandro, cujus paraphrasis haec est: Quod de Je- su Christo æterno Dei Filio mundi Redemptore & Salvatore (qui Satanam devicit) docuimus, eum jam in hunc mundum venisse, id neque ex Judæo- rum neque ex Græcorum fabulis & nugis, (quas si- ne Dei Verbo comminiscuntur,) didicimus. Nam de eo adventu agitur, per quem omnia nobis, quæ ad vitam & pietatem spectant, donata sunt vers. 3. per quem & propter quem obtigerunt nobis ma- xima & pretiosissima promissa, factique sumus con- sortes divinæ naturæ, vers. 4. nosque ingressum habemus in æternum Christi regnum, vers. 11. in quo demonstrata jam erat divina potentia, quam cognaverant in Christo Domino Apostoli non ex fa- bulis, sed è propria inspectione magnificentiæ Chri- sti vers. 16. Non enim de adhuc in novissimo die demonstranda, sed jam in diebus carnis demonstrata, cognitaque Christi potentia ser- mo est, cujus ἐπόπται fuere Petrus, & alii A- postoli, quemadmodum Johann. I. 14. dicitur, Verbum caro factum est, & habitavit in nobis, & vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam velut Unigeni- ti à Patre. De potentia, quæ in doctrina & miraculis ejus effulsit, quam ceu testes oculati, qui Verbum vitæ & vitam ipsam manifestatam in carne audierant, oculisque suis viderant, aliis annunciare debebant Apostoli 1. Johan. 1. vers. 2. ut ad fidem & ἐπίγνωσιν Christi perducantur, de qua ex ipsis etiam Propheticis Scriptis infor- mari poterant, & confirmari illi, ad quos scri- bebat Petrus, ut illucescat illis magis magisque dies cognitionis salutiferæ, & Phosphorus oriatur in cordibus ipsorum dilucidius, quam potentiam & παρουσίαν & Prophetæ in Veteri Testamento prænunciarunt, & Apostoli in Novo Testamento annunciare debuere. De qua etiam testatus est Pater de cœlo in monte Sancto, unde & Apo- stoli præsentes, vocem cœlestem audientes, & magnificentiam Christi glorificati intuentes aliis eam notificare, aliosque de Christo Filio Dei, in quo Deo complacuit, deque ejusdem doctrina ab omnibus audienda certiores redde- re potuere. De qua Christi ἐπιγνώσει etiam v. 12. Apostolus dixerat, eandem ipsis in me- moriam revocandam esse καίπερ εἰδότας καὶ ἐ- στηριγμένυς ἐν τῇ παρούσῃ ἀληθείᾳ. Quæ præ- sens veritas ἐπίγνωσις & ὑπόμνησις certe non concernunt particulam illam cœlestis Christi do- ctrinæ de novissimo adventu, quam Empæctæ in dubium vocarant, sed universam doctrinam sa- lutiferam Christi, de qua proinde Apostolus ἐγνωρίσαμεν, inquit, ὑμῖν τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ δύναμιν καὶ παρουσίαν: Quod Estius ait, primum Christi adventum fuisse infirmitate & humilitate admittimus, sed & probe consistebat cum gloria & majestate, quæ subinde in eodem effulsit in diebus carnis. Nam in forma Dei erat, & gloriam suam ceu Unigeniti à Patre etiam tempore ταπεινώσεως sua frequenter manife- stabat, quod omnia essent data in manus ejus, Johann. 3, vers. 35. cap. 13, vers. 2. de qua ipsiet- iam Pharisæi testabantur, Johann. 3, vers. 2. De qua potentia & gloria Christi hic agitur, cujus nempe ἐπόπται fuere Apostoli, non vero qua ad- huc demum patefiet in die novissimo. Quo fa- ciunt illa Gerhardi: Per μεγαλειότητα intelligitur Christi gloria & majestas, quæ in ipso eluxit toto illo, quo cum Apostolis in his terris versatus est, tem- pore, Johann. I. vers. 14. Ἐθεασάμεθα vidimus glo- riam ejus, gloriam quasi unigeniti à Patre. Au- tor libr. de mirabilibus Scripturæ Tom III. Au- gustinus libr. 3. cap. 10. Divinitas latens in corpore luminis sui portiunculam conspiciendam foris vi- dentibus quantam poterant concessit. Cognata voce μεγαλωσύνης de CHRISTO utitur epist. Ebr. capite I. vers. 3. & cap. VIII. vers. 1. Ipsa autem μεγαλειότητος vox de miraculis CHRI- STI usurpatur Luc. IX. v. 43. quippe ex quibus divina ipsius majestas & potentia reluxit. Quod porro Estius ait, quod secundi adventus typus qui- dam fuerit transfiguratio CHRISTI in monte: Resp. Eandem adduci, non ut typum gloria CHRI- STI olim manifestanda vel adventus CHRISTI secundi, quemadmodum nec eo fine facta est transfiguratio CHRISTI, in qua non de ad- ventu CHRISTI novissimo colloquium insti- tutum est, sed de exitu, quem in adventu primo complere debuit in Jerusalem, Lucæ 9, vers. 31. Facta itaque in hunc finem est, ut confirmaren- tur discipuli CHRISTI, aliique de adventu Filii DEI in carnem, quod hic JESUS Naza- renus sit Filius DEI dilectus, in quo omnis εὐ- δοκία est Patris, de quo Moses & Prophetæ, è qui- bus Elias hic commemoratur, vaticinati sunt, quemque vox cœlestis patefecit, ut ab omnibus audiatur, quod ad novissimum diem non facit, sed ad tempus gratiæ, quo audiendus est. Quem finem εὐαγγελιογραφίας assignat Spiritus Sanctus, Johann. XX. vers. 31. Quod denique affertur ab Estio è cap. III. v. 4. quasi de adventu, quem du- bium reddere volebant nonnulli, dicentes, ubi est promissio τῆς παρουσίας adventus ejus, ageretur, hic agatur, id est ipsum τὸ κρινόμενον. Non tantum contra eos directa fuit epistola, qui secundum adventum CHRISTI in dubium vocarunt, sed etiam contra illos qui CHRISTI potentiam & adventum primum, quem cœlesti voce confir- matum docet, inficiabantur, quique abnegabant τὸν ἀγοράσαντα αὐτοὺς δεσπότην, quæ utique re- demptio facta est per primum ejus adventum, cap. II. v. 1. Horum enim Pseudoprophetarum αἱρέσεις ἀπωλείας & πλαστοὶ λόγοι opponuntur λό- γῳ τῷ προφητικῷ & doctrinæ Apostolicæ, quam non ἐν σεσοφισμένοις λόγοις, sed ex ore ejus, de quo Pa- ter de cœlo proclamat: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, εἰς ὃν ἐγὼ εὐδόκησα, hunc audite, quod συνέχεια pri- mi & secundi, conclusio illius, & initium ac scopus hujus capitis docet.

Nec obstat, quod alias ferè semper vox πα- ρουσίας adventum CHRISTI secundum notet, quum non ex aliis locis, sed è contextu imprimis determinatio petenda sit, & adventus gratiæ et- iam semel tantum παρουσία Filii hominis nomi- netur, Matth. XXIV. vers. 27. adeoque nihil ob- stet, adventum incarnationis semel etiam tan- tum ita designari, quum adventus ille τῆς ἐπιφανείας nomine semel tantum designatus est: neque con- cludere licet, quia vox illa alias semper notat se- cundum CHRISTI adventum, 2. Thess. 2, v. 8. 1. Tim. 6, v. 14. 2. Tim. 4, v. 1. 8. Tit. 2, v. 13. etiam 2. Tim. 1. v. 10. secundum, non vero primum ad- ventum eadem notari.

Per μεγαλειότητα vel majestas & magnificentia, quæ in miraculis conspecta fuit, designatur, ut ejus confirmatio per vocem de cælo factam sub- jecta censeatur, vel magnificentia illa ex actu transfigurationis CHRISTI, in quo τιμὴν καὶ δόξαν honorem & gloriam vel honorem maxime gloriosum accepit, declaratur. Neutra explica to repugnat, & conjungit utramque B. Gerb. Posterior tamen simplicior videtur, juxta quam de se & duo- bus aliis Apostolis secum assumptis in mon- tem S. Petrus loquitur, quod tum ἐπόπται fuerint

τῆς μεγαλειότητος, quum honorem & gloriam per vocem cælestem accepit, & per eandem intelli- genda erit magnificentia glorificationis Christi, quæ in illustri illa transfiguratione corporis Chri- sti effulsit; quæ tamen non confundenda cum ho- nore & gloria, utpote quæ, qualis & quanta fue- rit, è voce cælesti discendum. Honor & gloria non corporis tantum glorificati, sed personæ Chri- sti, non temporalis, sed perpetua, qualem nem- pè infert τὸ esse Filium Dei, non τῇ χάριτι ta- lem, sed τῇ φύσει, adeoque ὁμοούσιον καὶ ὁμότι- μον Deo Patri; & Messiam Redemptorem mun- di, in quo & propter quem est omnis εὐδοκία Ho- nor, inquam; tum personæ Filii Dei, tum officii ejusdem Mediatorii, qui non finitus est, sed vere infinitus, immensus & divinus, quum omnes Fi- lium honorare debeant, ut Patrem Joh. V. 23. & Christo Mediatori ac Salvatori omnium genua sese flectere, ac divinum & religiosum honorem ipsi exhibere debeant, Es. XLV. 23. seqq. Rom. XIV. 11. Phil. II. 10. Certitudinem itaque doctrinæ Christianæ confirmat ab autoritate & majestate Christi, à quo illam acceperit: Autoritatem & ma- jestatem Christi confirmat à gloria & honore in transfiguratione ipsi collato, in qua publicus totius Orbis Doctor voce Patris cælestis fuerit constitu- tus, ut hic B. Gerhardus. Cui vero placuit di- stinguere δόξαν & τιμὴν, ut illam de gloria cor- poris, de qua Matth. XVII. 2. Marc. IX. 3. Luc. IX. 29. quod tantus fuerit ejus splendor, ut per i- psas vestes, alioquin obscuras, ac minime diaphanas sese exeruerit: hanc vero de eximio il- lo honore, quo Christus à Patre suo cælesti, vo- ce cælitus delapsa fuit affectus, intellexerit.

## 1:18
Vers. 18.

A voice being borne to him such as this from the magnificent glory, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, and this voice we heard, borne from heaven, being with him in the holy mountain] These words are commonly wont to be referred to that voice heard on a certain mountain of Galilee, of which Peter was a witness with John and James, whose opinion we also followed when we were writing our notes on that history, narrated by Matthew 17. Now, what makes me think otherwise is not only our opinion just proposed regarding the writer of this epistle, but also that 'holy mountain' among the Hebrews signifies no other mountain than Mount Moriah, on which the temple was, and therefore I refer these words to that which John 28 narrates. For many were present at that event: among whom we need not wonder that there was this Simeon, who is called by Eusebius an eyewitness and hearer of the Lord, who died, according to Hegesippus, when he was 120 years old. Nor is that incredible, since the most eloquent writer, who is usually appended to Tacitus when dealing with the causes of the changed eloquence, teaches us that those who had seen Caesar the dictator lived until the age of Vespasian. However, that voice mentioned by John happened, as far as can be gathered from the text, while Jesus was passing through the court of the Gentiles, which is a part of Mount Moriah. One thing stands in the way, that John reports that voice in other words, namely, I have glorified and will glorify again. Whence the suspicion occurred to me that these words: 'Such as this, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,' as certain others, were added by those who altogether wished this to be believed as an epistle of the Apostle Peter. Let the older copies also be consulted here, if any can be found. In the Manuscript: From heaven. 'Magnificent glory' for God himself, as 'kabod' often is for the Hebrews. 'Power' for Matt. 26:64.

Grotius brings forward arguments that are too futile for this novel and unheard-of gloss: First, namely, that false persuasion about an author of the epistle other than Peter, which we refuted before, and showed that the Fathers solidly demonstrated from this very revelation that no other than Simon Peter was the author of the epistle, and then the denomination of the holy mountain. For nowhere in the New Testament, except in this one place, does 'holy mountain' occur, nor is there a need that by the holy mountain we precisely understand the mountain

of Moriah or the temple; it was truly a holy mountain because of that most holy presence and the solemn divine manifestation of the most holy Trinity, which took place on that mountain. Why then could St. Peter not name that mountain so? These things cannot be drawn to the manifestation in John 12:29, because it did not happen on a mountain, nor even in the temple, as far as is known (Grotius certainly could not prove that), nor does it pertain to the present place, regarding that voice 'This is my Son,' etc., which Grotius suspects, according to his own ingenuity, to have crept in here, but which cannot be taught by any, not even a single, codex, whether Greek, or Latin, or Syriac, or of any language whatsoever. Finally, it is expressly asserted here that that voice, of which Peter speaks, was heard not by all indiscriminately, but by Peter and those who were with him on the holy mountain. Therefore, that public voice of John 12, which could reach even those at a distance, does not look to this. However, this voice was heard only by those present on the mountain; which he calls high, as do the Evangelists, whence Jacobus Faber and Franc. Lucas conclude it was Lebanon; yet most understand Mount Tabor, the height of which, according to Josephus, Book IV of the Jewish War, ch. 2, rose up to thirty stadia. Which opinion was held by the Greeks Cyril of Jerusalem, Catech. XII, Euthymius on Ps. 89, Damascenus in his sermon on the transfiguration of the Lord, and from the Latins by Jerome, Epistle 27 in the epitaph of Marcella, Bede on the holy places, ch. 17, Philo of Carpathia in his commentary on Canticles, and others. Moreover, the heavenly voice is repeated in the present passage in that manner as it is read in Matt. 17:5, except that for 'in whom I am well pleased' there is in this place 'in whom I am well pleased,' which construction does not vary the sense, and is found in Matt. 12:18, 'in whom my soul is well pleased.' However, 'hear him' is added in Matthew, which the Apostle omitted here as being sufficiently known. For although this precept also occurs in the Vulgate, the Greek codices nevertheless consistently omit it. Furthermore, the double article in the words of the heavenly voice, which is also read in Matt. 3:17, is not without emphasis. Οὗτός ἐσιν ὁ ὕός μυ ὁ ἀγαπητὸς, this is that Son of mine, of whom the Father had spoken in Ps. 2:7: Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee, that beloved one, in whom I am well pleased, of whom in Isa. 42:1. Therefore the person of Christ is expressed, that Jesus is the Son of God, not adoptive, but natural, proper, and Only-begotten, John 1:14, ch. 3:16. Rom. 8:32, since the office, which is that he is the Mediator, in whom the Father has good pleasure, so that all the fullness of the Godhead may dwell in Christ, Col. 1:19, ch. 2:9, and that through him all things may be reconciled unto him, Col. 1:20, in whom the Father has good pleasure and rests, which the word רצה implies, on account of the obedience, both active and passive, of this just and elect Servant, Isa. 42:1, ch. 53:11, whom Isaiah had predicted would act prudently, and by whose hand the purpose of the Lord would succeed, whose soul would labor, and who was to deliver his life as a sacrifice for sins, v. 10, 11, who in John 8:29 says, I always do those things that are pleasing to the Father, in whom ἐπὶ γῆς εἰρήνη ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἐυδοκία, Luke 2:14, in whom ἠγαπημένῳ ἐχαρίζωσεν, the Father has embraced us with his grace in the beloved, Eph. 1:6, who in John 17:26 entreated this for us with most efficacious prayers: I pray, Father, that the love with which you love me may also be in them or toward them. The Syriac uses a word in this place concerning that beloved Son, which by etymological reasoning implies he cherished in his bosom, loved most tenderly, because that beloved Son is in the bosom of the Father, John 1:18. That good pleasure Augustine, book II.

In his work on the harmony of the Gospels, chapter 14, he explains it thus: I have established my pleasure in you; through you I have decreed to fulfill what pleases me, so that henceforth I shall not say, 'I repent that I have made man.' For in this Son alone the εὐδοκία (good pleasure) of the heavenly Father rests and acquiesces, outside of whom no one can become a participant in His εὐδοκία; on account of whom it is God's εὐδοκία that He wills to give the kingdom of God to those who believe in Him, Luke 12:32. It is His εὐδοκία that He predestined us to adoption, Ephesians 1:5; that He makes known to us the mystery of His will concerning our salvation in the Gospel, Ephesians 1:9; that He works in us both to will and to perform, Philippians 2:13; in whom God has deposited all His good pleasure, so that in Him alone we may find grace.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Φωνῆς ἐνεχθείσης αὐτῷ τοιᾶσδε ἀπὸ τῆς μεγαλοπρεποῦς δόξης, οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ὑός μου ὁ ἀγαπητὸς, εἰς ὃν ἐγὼ εὐδόκησα καὶ ταύ- την φωνὴν ἡμεῖς ἠκούσαμεν, ἐξ ὐρανοῦ ἐνεχθεῖσαν σὺν ἀυτῷ ὄντες ἐν τῷ ὄρει τῷ ἁγίῳ] Solent hæc verba vulgo referri ad vo- cem illam auditam in monte quodam Galilææ, cujus testis fuit Petrus cum Johanne & Jacobo, quorum sententiam & nos sequebamur, cum ad illam historiam, narratam à Matthæo XVII. nostra scriberemus. Nunc ut aliter sentiam facit, non modo nostra de scriptore hujus epi- stolæ proposita modo sententia, sed & quod ὄρος ἅγιον apud Ebræos non alium montem significat, quam mon- tem Moriæ, in quo erat templum, ideoque hæc verba refero ad illud quod narrat Johan. XII. 28. Ei enim rei plurimi adfuere: quos inter non est quod miremur fuisse hunc Simeonen, qui Eusebio dicitur αὐτόπτης καὶ ἀυτήκοος τοῦ Κυρίου, mortuus Hegesippo teste, cum annotum esset CXX. Nec id incredibile, cum ad Vespasiani ævum vixisse, qui Cæsarem dictatorem vidissent, doceat nos disertissi- mus Scriptor, qui de causis mutatæ eloquentiæ agens Ta- cito subjungi solet. Contigit autem illa vox Johanni me- morata, quantum ex textu colligi potest, Jesu transe- unte per subdiale gentium, quæ pars est montis Moriæ. Obstat unum quod vocem illam aliis verbis Johannes re- fert, nempe ἐδόξασα καὶ πάλιν δοξάσω. Unde suspicio mihi incidit, hæc verba: Τοιᾶσδε οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ὑός μου ἀγαπητὸς, εἰς ὃν ἐγὼ ἐυδόκησα, ut alia quædam, addita ab illis qui o- mnino hanc epistolam Petri Apostoli credi voluerunt. Con- sulantur & hic vetustiora exemplaria, fi qua reperiri pos- sunt. In Manuscripto: Ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ. Μεγαλοπρεποῦς δό- ξης pro ipso Deo, ut כבוד sæpe Ebræis. Δύναμις pro Matth. XXVI. 64.

Novellæ hujus, & inauditæ glossæ argumenta nimis futilia affert Grotius: Primo nempe falsam illam persuasionem de alio, quam Petro, autore epi- stolæ, quam antea confutavimus, Patresque ex hac ipsa revelatione non alium quam Simonem Petrum Autorem epistolæ esse solide demonstras- se ostendimus, & deinde montis sacri denomina- tionem. Nuspiam enim in Novo Testamento nisi hoc unico in loco ὄρος ἅγιον occurrit, nec o- pus est, ut per montem sacrum præcise montem

Moria vel templum intelligamus, vere erat mons sacer ob illam sanctissimam praesentiam, & solen- nem divinam manifestationem sacrosanctae Tri- nitatis, quae in isto monte facta. Quidni ergo montem illum ita nominare potuerit S. Petrus? Ad manifestationem Johann. XII. vers. 29. haec trahi non possunt, quia nec in monte illa facta ac ne in templo quidem, quod constet (probare certe id non potuit Grotius) nec ad locum prae- sentem facit, de voce ista ὗτός ἐσιν ὁ ὕός μυ &c. quam huc irrepsisse pro ingenio suo suspicatur Grotius, nullo autem nec unico, sive Graeco, sive Latino, sive Syro, sive cujuscunque idioma- tis codice doceri potest. Denique non ab o- mnibus promiscue, sed a Petro, & qui cum ipso in monte sacro fuerunt, auditam esse vocem illam, de qua Petrus, expresse hic asseritur. Non ergo huc spectat illa publica vox Johann. XII. quae ad distantes etiam pervenire potuit. Haec autem vox solum a praesentibus in monte audita est; quem excelsum dicit, ut Evangeli- stae, unde Libanum fuisse colligunt Jacobus Faber & Franc. Lucas; montem tamen Thabor pleri- que intelligunt, cujus altitudo secundum Jose- phum l. IV. de Bell. Jud. c. 2. ad trigesimum usque stadium assurtexit. Quae sententia e Graecis Cyril- li Hierosol. Catech. XII. Euthymii in Ps. LXXXIX. Damasceni in serm. de transfigur. Dom. e Latinis Hieronymi epist. XXVII. in epitaph. Marcellae, Bedae de locis sanctis cap. 17. Philonis Carpathii in comm. Cant. & aliorum fuit. Repetitur autem in praesenti vox coelestis ea ratione, uti Matth. XVII. 5. legitur, nisi quod pro ἐν ὧ εὐδόκησα hoc loco habeatur εἰς ὃν ἐυδόκησα, quae constructio sen- sum non variat, & habetur Matth. XII. 18. εἰς ὃν ἐυδόκησεν ἡ ψυχή μυ. Additur autem apud Mat- thaeum, ἀυτῦ ἀκύετε, quod hic ceu satis notum praetermisit Apostolus. Etsi enim apud Vulga- tam etiam hoc praeceptum occurrat, Codices ta- men Graeci constanter illud praetereunt. Caeterum emphasi non caret articulus geminus in verbis coelestis vocis, qui etiam Matth. III. 17. legitur. Οὗτός ἐσιν ὁ ὕός μυ ὁ ἀγαπητὸς, hic est ille Filius meus, de quo scilicet Psal. II. 7. dixerat Pater: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te, ille dilectus, in quo mihi complacitum, de quo Es. XLII. 1. Exprimitur ergo persona Christi, quod Jesus sit Filius Dei non adoptivus, sed naturalis, pro- prius & Unigenitus, Johan. I. v. 14. cap. III. v. 16. Roman. VIII. 32. cum officium, quod Mediator sit, in quo beneplacitum habet Pater, ut habi- tet in Christo omnis plenitudo Deitatis, Coloss. I. 19. cap. II. 19. utque per ipsum concilientur o- mnia in ipsum, Coloss. I. 20. in quo Pater bene- placitum habet & requiescit, quod verbum רצה infert, ob obedientiam tum activam tum pas- sivam Servi hujus justi & electi, Es. XLII. 1. cap. LIII. 11. quem prudenter acturum, & per cu- jus manum propositum Domini successurum praedixerat Esaias, cujus anima laboratura, & Vitam suam in victimam pro peccatis traditurus erat vers. 1. 10. 11. qui Johan. VIII. 29. quae placita sunt Patri, inquit, facio semper, in quo ἐπὶ γῆς εἰ- ρήνη ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἐυδοκία, Luc. II. 14. in quo ἠγα- πημένῳ ἐχαρίζωσεν dilecto nos gratia sua complexus est Pater, Ephes. I. 6. qui Joh. XVII. 26. id effica- cissimis precibus nobis exoravit: Oro Pater, ut di- lectio, qua me diligis, sit etiam in iis vel erga eos. Sy- rus de dilecto illo Filio vocem hoc loco adhibet, quae infert Etymi ratione in sinu fovit, tenerrime dilexit, quia Filius ille dilectus est in sinu Patris Johan. I. 18. Beneplacitum illud Augustinus l. II.

de consens. Evangel. cap. 14. sic explicat : Placitum meum in te constitui, per te decrevi implere, quod mihi placet, ut deinceps non dicam pœnitet me fecisse hominem. In hoc enim Filio unice recumbit & acquiescit cœlestis Patris εὐδοκία, extra quem nemo εὐδοκίας ejus particeps fieri potest, ob quem Dei εὐδοκία est, quod velit credentibus in ipsum regnum Dei dare, Luc. XII. 32. εὐδοκία est, quod nos prædestinavit in adoptionem, Ephes. I. 5. quod notum nobis facit mysterium voluntatis suæ de salute nostra in Evangelio, Ephes. I. 9. quod operatur in nobis velle & perficere, Phil. II. 13. in quem Deus omne suum beneplacitum deposuit, ut in eo solo gratiam inveniamus.

## 1:19
Verse 19.

And we have the prophetic word more sure] that is, the speech of the Prophets indeed always had authority among us. But now it has much greater, since we see the events so beautifully agreeing with the sayings about the Messiah. We have βεβαιῶ (to confirm) used in this way also in Mark 16:20, 1 Corinthians 1:6, Hebrews 6:16, and it corresponds to the Hebrew הֵקִים.

It is more correct to establish here a new confirmation of Christian doctrine than a confirmation of Prophetic authority, which interpretation is entirely new. The particle καὶ is the same as 'furthermore.' The prophetic word is called 'more sure' not intrinsically: for in that way all revelations are equally firm, but extrinsically, not by reason of itself, but by reason of us, or with regard to those converted Hebrews, to whom that word of the Prophets was more certain than that revelation, even though confirmed by Petrine authority. St. Peter uses that 'we have' by a figure of communication, even though he does not refer to himself, but to the faithful Jews themselves, whom he is now addressing, among whom the Prophetic word was firmer and more certain or of greater authority through Petrine attestation, just as the Apostles themselves appealed to the Prophets and gave assurance to their own sayings by their authority. Therefore, it was necessary for that to be more certain, lest they be said to have proven an uncertain thing by an equally uncertain thing, or a doubtful thing by an equally doubtful thing. In this sense, Augustine, Sermon 27 on the Words of the Apostle: 'Who of us would not wonder that the prophetic word is called by the Apostle more certain than the voice brought from heaven?' He certainly said 'more certain,' not 'better.' For that word from heaven is as true as the prophetic word, as good, as useful. What then is 'more certain,' if not that in which the Hearer is more confirmed? In which sense it is also explained by Bede, Thomas, Hugo, Lyranus, the Carthusian, Cajetan in Opuscula, Vol. II, tract 1, chapter 1, and commentary on this passage; Salmeron on this passage; Barradius, Vol. I, Concordance of the Gospels, book 1, chapter 17; Gretser, Vol. I, defense of Bellarmine, treatise on recognizing the Canonical Scripture, chapter 7, page 1908; B. Gerhard in his observations; Lorinus in his commentary on Acts 26:22. Peter, he says, calls the prophetic word firmer than the transfiguration of Christ himself, which he had seen, that is, more apt for convincing the Jews, who accept the Prophets. Estius notes on this passage that the first comparative 'firmer' is not referred to the voice of the Father brought from heaven (for the voice of the Father had supreme authority among the Jews as the voice of God) but to the Apostolic testimony, which immediately preceded it. 'And we heard this voice,' etc. Next, a distinction of the word 'firmer' is needed. For either something is called firm in itself, because it has immovable truth, in which way every Word of God is equally firm, whether it comes to us through a voice formed in the air, or through the mouth of the Prophets, or through the preaching of the Apostles: or it is called firm in the mind of man, that is, certain, known for certain. Thus, what is firm and certain to one can be doubtful and uncertain, or less certain, to another. In this way, therefore, the prophetic word was firmer to the Jews converted to Christ than that Apostolic attestation from which they had learned that that revelation had occurred on the holy mount. For the authority of the Prophets in that people was already established and strengthened by the passage of time and the consensus of the elders; not so the authority of the Apostles, which was still recent, and therefore was not yet received with such veneration. For the Apostles themselves also confirmed their doctrine with the sayings of the Prophets, especially as often as they dealt with the Jews. From which it is evident that the testimony of the Scriptures is far firmer than the testimony of the Church. Contrary to what the Papists contend, since even the testimony of Peter himself, whom they hold as Pope, was firmer.

Where you do well in paying attention] You do rightly because you turn the volumes of the Prophets by hand night and day.

To pay attention denotes not only reading, but especially the attentiveness of those reading, for which the faithful are praised: See Matthew 7:15, chapter 10:17, chapter 16:6, Luke 12:1, chapter 17:3, 1 Timothy 4:13. It is explained by 'to search' (ἐρευνᾶν) in John 5:39.

As to a lamp shining in a dark place until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts] that is, until you yourselves obtain the prophetic gift from God. Prophecy is called a 'dropping' in Micah 2:11, Ezekiel 21:2. Therefore, a dry place is a man not having the gift of prophecy, Micah 4:8. עפל is translated as 'dark/squalid' (αὐχμώδης). Prophecy is also called 'illumination' (φωτισμός), as in Jude 13:8, Daniel 5:14, and 'Lucifer' (morning star) in Isaiah 9:2. For הילל is properly 'Lucifer' to the Hebrews. He who does not yet have the light in himself needs to borrow it for the time being from another. There is no need to carry wood into the forest. Philo on the constitution of a Prince: 'To a prophet nothing is unknown, having the intelligible sun within himself.'

Nothing here about the Prophetic gift. Ἀυχμηρὸς τόπος is not a dry place, nor is it so called in Mich. IV. 8. αὐχμώδης. Grotius himself rendered it there as a misty and squalid (family) long neglected. Properly αὐχμηρὸς is squalid, because squalor adheres to dark places, a dark or gloomy place, and the darkness of our hearts is looked to, in which light arises through the Word of God, which is lucid, and light, illuminating our hearts, a lamp to our feet and a light to our paths, Psal. CXIX. 105. Proverb. VI. 23. since outside the Word we sit in darkness Es. IX. 2. and in the Word of God alone is the morning light for us, Es. VIII. 20. the Prophetic gift is not for everyone. But everyone ought to attend to the Prophetic word, until the day of divine illumination shines in their hearts and the Morning Star arises. By λόγον Προφητικὸν Erasmus wrongly understands the voice of the heavenly Father, when the context clearly speaks of Prophetic Scripture. By λύχνον is understood a lit lamp, a torch, and a lantern, by which our darkness is dispelled, Matth. V. 5. Marc. IV. 21. Luc. VIII. 16. cap. XI. 33. By τόπον αὐχμηρὸν the human heart without the Word of God is to be understood as dark, which the opposite light, by which it shines in our hearts, having dispelled those darknesses of ignorance and errors, shows, which is attributed to the Prophetic word.

The day therefore dawning is not the day of the final judgment, because the light arises in the hearts of those attending to Prophetic Scripture still in this life, nor is the Morning Star in the other life only the forerunner of the Sun, but the Sun of righteousness itself will shine forth with full radiance, nor that through the reading or attention to Scripture, but through the communication of the light of glory and the vision of the Lord face to face, 1. Cor. XIII. 12. 2. Cor. V. Nor by the dawning day is the day of clearer knowledge proper to the New Testament understood, as if attention to Scripture this knowledge of the Prophetic [Scripture] may follow, and be as it were its limit. For even in the time of the Old Testament, not only under the New, did Prophetic Scripture shine in a dark place, and day dawned through the same saving knowledge and faith, which is evident from the examples of the Patriarchs and other believers of the Old Testament, who were converted from darkness even to light. What then? The day is said to dawn in the heart of any attentive reader of the Prophetic word, at any time, through the power of that light shining in a dark place, because the darkness of night, of ignorance, and of errors is dispelled by it, and light arises just as when the day dawns and when the Morning Star arises. If this Morning Star is applied spiritually, it is Christ himself, that morning star, Apoc. XXII. 16, but by reason of the manifestation, or the light viewed, by which he scatters [light] in our hearts, or, which is the same thing, the knowledge of Christ, by which our hearts are illuminated. For one must attend to the Prophetic word until the illumination of faith follows, and that Morning Star arises in our hearts, where, however, that Hermeneutical Rule is to be observed, that the particle 'until' sometimes signifies continuity and perpetuity, as in Ps. CXXIII. 2: 'Our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us'; Matt. XXVIII. 20: 'Behold, I am with you until the end of the age.' Cf. Acts III. 20; Rom. V. 13; 1 Tim. IV. 13: 'attend to reading' ἕως ἔρχομαι 'until I come'. There is, therefore, no reason why that dawning day and the Morning Star should be referred to the clearer light of the New Testament, and the Prophetic lamp to the dimmer light of the Old Testament, with Estius: since even in the Old Testament, through Prophetic preaching, such a day shone, and can even now shine for Jews and others, so that the Morning Star of saving knowledge can arise, and on that account, attention to Prophetic Scripture is commended even to the believers themselves, because through it, as a sufficiently clear light, the darkness in the dark place of the human heart is dispelled, and the day dawns, and the Morning Star of knowledge.

Therefore, the interpretation of Estius, which he chose along with Hasselanus, Adam, and Arias, is not pleasing: that Prophetic Scripture, like a lamp lit in the darkness, exhibits a faint and restricted light, which, however, is to be used in the meantime until the day arrives, which will provide a clear and widely diffused light. Likewise, by the words 'until the day dawns,' is signified the progress and increase of faith, while a more certain, purer, more sincere, and more explicit knowledge of the mysteries of Christ is received little by little, just as when the day dawns. And further concerning the Morning Star: 'Until, with the darkness of night dispelled, a clearer light, as of the rising Morning Star, shines into your minds,' that is, until you are so illuminated by the light of faith that your minds are no longer troubled by any scruples of doubt. For many of the Jews who had believed had not yet arrived at this perfection of faith. Because all these things compare Prophetic Scripture with the light of the Gospel, as far as the light of faith is concerned, which is certain and without the waves of doubt, they detract from Prophetic Scripture not only in comparison to the Apostolic regarding a clearer degree of perspicuity and light, but also regarding that perfection of knowledge which is required in believers so that they may be able to overcome temptations; if this is detracted from it, how could the believers of the Old Testament have been certain, and have retained a firm faith against the temptations to which they were subject just as we are?

In short, a comparison between Prophetic and Apostolic Scripture is not being instituted, but the certainty and power of the Prophetic word for the illumination of our heart is being declared, and thus the Prophetic word is not compared to a lamp shining in the time of night, and the word of the Gospel to the morning star bringing the full light of day; indeed (as the blessed Gerhard himself also observes), what the Apostle asserts here specifically about Prophetic Scripture can also be accommodated to Apostolic Scripture, and thus to the whole of Scripture: The blessed Gerhard also observes this, ad h. l., that the whole time of life is compared to the light of eternal life as a certain dark night, but that eternal life will be brighter than the midday light, Apoc. XXI. 23, in which way, with Augustine tr. XXXV in John, Bede, the Glossa Ordinaria, and Cajetan ad h. l., Peter likens the entire state of this life to a dark place needing the light of a lamp, which is Holy Scripture. The future life is likened to a clear day, because the Morning Star, that is, Christ, arises not corporally, but spiritually in the hearts of men. Which explanation, however, is by no means proper to this passage. The state of the present and future [life] is not compared here in this way, but the natural state, which brings mere darkness, and the state of grace, in which the Morning Star and the day dawns. The state of glory is not commemorated here, in which, however, the Sun of righteousness will shine in full radiance, and Christ is going to illuminate us far more perfectly. Nevertheless, the end of the dawning of the Morning Star in our hearts in the time of grace is the illumination which is hoped for in the kingdom of glory, 1 Pet. I. 9; Apoc. XXII. 5, 23, where there is no night, no cloud, no darkness, but immense and eternal brightness and perpetual day.

The Papists are refuted by this passage, that the reading of Scripture is not to be prohibited to the laity, since Peter pronounces that those who read it do rightly, and that Prophetic Scripture is clear and contributes to the illumination of our heart, because it is compared to a lamp shining in a dark place until the day dawns. Therefore, Clement of Alexandria in Protrept. says: 'The Word is hidden from no one; it is a light common to all, it shines for all.' Cf. Is. VIII. 20. Nor is there any reason for Gretser to object (T. I. defens. Bellarm. p. 1794) that the Prophetic word had a wider scope than Prophetic Scripture. For Peter is speaking of that Prophetic word which the converted Hebrews had and to which they attended. But that was none other than what was contained in Prophetic Scripture.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Καὶ ἔχομεν βεβαιότερον τὸν προφητικὸν λόγον] id est, sermo Prophetarum habuit quidem semper apud nos autoritatem. At nunc multo majorem habet, ex quo videmus eventus tam pulchre congruere dictis de Messia. Sic βεβαιῶ habemus & Marci XVI. 20. 1. Cor. I. 6. Ebr. VI. 16. respondetque Ebræo הֵקִים.

Rectius hic nova confirmatio doctrinæ Christianæ, quam confirmatio autoritatis Propheticæ, quæ interpretatio omnino nova, constituitur. Particula καὶ idem est quod præterea. Βεβαιότερος dicitur sermo Propheticus non intrinsece : Sic enim omnes revelationes æque firmæ sunt, sed extrinsece, non ratione sui, sed ratione nostri, vel quoad illos conversos Ebræos, quibus certior erat sermo ille Prophetarum, quam illa revelatio, etsi autoritate Petrina confirmata. Illud ἔχομεν per communicationis figuram adhibet S. Petrus, etsi non se, sed ipsos Judæos fideles respiciat, quos jam alloquitur, apud quos erat firmior certiorque aut majoris autoritatis sermo Propheticus attestatione Petrina, quemadmodum Apostoli ipsi provocarunt ad Prophetas, ipsorumque autoritate suis dictis fidem fecerunt. Illam ergo oportuit certiorem esse, ne incertum per æque incertum, aut dubium per æque dubium probasse dicantur. Quo sensu Augustinus serm. XXVII. de Verb. Apost. Quis nostrum non miretur delata voce de cælo certiorem sermonem Propheticum ab Apostolo dictum esse? Certiorem sane dixit, non meliorem. Tam enim verus ille sermo de cælo, quam verus sermo Propheticus, tam bonus, tam utilis. Quid est ergo certiorem, nisi in quo magis confirmetur Auditor? Quo sensu explicari etiam à Beda, Thoma, Hugone, Lyrano, Carthusiano, Cajetano in opuscul. Tom. II. tract. 1. cap. 1. & comment. in h. l. Salmer. in h. l. Barradio Tom. I. Concord. Evang. l. I. cap. 17. Gretser. Tom. I. defens. Bellarm. tr. de agnosc. Script. Canon. cap. 7. pag. 1908. B. Gerhardus observat. Lorinus in comm. Act. XXVI. 22. Petrus, inquit, Propheticum sermonem, quam ipsius Christi transfigurationem, quam viderat, firmiorem dicit, hoc est, aptiorem ad convincendos Judæos, qui Prophetas recipiunt. Estius in h. l. notat, primum comparativum firmiorem non referri ad vocem Patris de cælo allatam (nam vox Patris apud Judæos supremam habebat autoritatem utpote vox Dei) sed ad testimonium Apostolicum, quod proxime præcessit. Et hanc vocem nos audivimus &c. Deinde distinctione opus est vocabuli firmiorem. Aut enim firmum aliquid dicitur in se, quia immobilem habet veritatem, quomodo omne Dei Verbum æque firmum est, sive per vocem in aëre formatam, sive per os Prophetarum, sive per Apostolorum prædicationem ad nos perveniat: Aut firmum dicitur in mente hominis, id est certum, certo cognitum. Ita quod uni firmum ac certum est, al- teri dubium ac incertum, aut minus certum esse potest. Hoc igitur modo sermo Propheticus Ju- dæis ad Christum conversis erat firmior Apostoli- ca illa attestatione, ex qua didicerant, revelatio- nem illam factam in monte sancto. Erat enim Prophetarum autoritas in illo populo diuturnitatis tempore & consensu majorum firmata jam & robo- rata: non item autoritas Apostolorum, qua recens adhuc erat, ac proinde nondum tanta cum veneratio- ne suscipiebatur. Nam & ipsi Apostoli suam do- ctrinam confirmabant dictis Prophetarum maxi- me quoties cum Judæis agerent. E quibus constat, Scripturarum testimonium longe firmius esse testi- monio Ecclesiæ. Secus atque Papistæ contendunt, siquidem etiam ipsius Petri, quem pro Pontifice habent, testimonium firmius erat.

Ὧ καλῶς ποιεῖτε προσ-έχοντες] Recte facitis quod Prophe- tarum volumina nocturna & diurna manu versatis.

Προσ-έχειν non tantum lectionem, sed maxime attentionem legentium denotat, ob quam cele- brantur fideles: Vid. Matth. VII. 15. cap. X. 17. c. XVI. 6. Luc. XII. 1. c. XVII. 3. 1. Tim. IV. 13. Expo- nitur per ἐρευνᾷν scrutari Joh. V. 39.

Ὡς λύχνῳ φαίνοντι ἐν αὐχμηρῷ τόπῳ ἕως οὗ ἡ ἡμέρα διαυ- γάσῃ καὶ φωσφόρος ἀνατείλῃ ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν] id est, donec vos ipsi donum Propheticum a Deo consequamini. Prophetia vocatur stillatio Micheæ II. r. Ezech. XXI. 2. Er- go locus siccus, est homo non habens donum prophetiæ, Michææ IV. 8. עפל vertitur αὐχμώδης. Dicitur Prophe- tia & φωτισμὸς, ut Jud. XIII. 8. Daniel. V. 14. & Lucifer Es. IX. 2. Nam הילל proprie Lucifer Ebræis. Qui non- dum in se lucem habet, opus est eam tantisper ab alio fœ- neretur. In sylvam ligna ferre nihil opus. Philo de Principis constitutione: Προφήτῃ δὲ οὐδὲν ἄγνωστον, ἔχοντι νοητὸν ἥλιον ἐν ἑαυτῷ.

Nihil hic de dono Prophetico. Ἀυχμηρὸς τό- πος non est locus siccus, nec ita Mich. IV. 8. αὐχμώδης dicitur. Reddidit ibi Grotius ipse ne- bulosam & squalidam (familiam) diu neglectam. Proprie αὐχμηρὸς est squalidus, quia locis caligi- nosis squalor adhæret, caliginosus vel tenebrico- sus locus, & respiciuntur tenebræ cordis nostri, in quibus lux oritur per Verbum Dei, quod est lucidum, & lux, illuminans corda nostra, lucer- na pedibus nostris & lumen semitis nostris, Psal. CXIX. 105. Proverb. VI. 23. quum extra Verbum in tenebris sedeamus Es. IX. 2. & in solo Dei Ver- bo matutina lux nobis sit, Es. VIII. 20. donum Propheticum non est omnium. At omnes at- tendere debent sermoni Prophetico, donec in eorum cordibus dies illucescat divinæ illumina- tionis & Phosphorus oriatur. Per λόγον Προ- φητικὸν perperam Erasmus vocem Patris cœlestis intelligit, quum contextus luculenter de Scriptu- ra Prophetica loquatur. Per λύχνον lucerna ac- censa, fax, & lampas intelligitur, qua nostræ te- nebræ discutiuntur, Matth. V. 5. Marc. IV. 21. Luc. VIII. 16. cap. XI. 33. Per τόπον αὐχμηρὸν cor humanum absque Verbo Dei tenebricosum intel- ligendum, quod opposita lux, qua effulget in cordibus nostris, discussis illis tenebris ignoran- tiæ & errorum, ostendit, quæ tribuitur sermoni Prophetico.

Dies itaque illucescens non est dies extremi judicii, quia lux exoritur cordibus attendentium Scriptu- ræ Propheticæ adhuc in hac vita, neque in altera tantum Phosphorus anteambulo Solis, sed ipse Sol justitiæ pleno jubare affulgebit, nec id per lectionẽ vel attentionem Scripturæ, sed per luminis gloriæ communicationem & Domini visionem a facie ad faciem, 1. Cor. XIII. 12. 2. Cor. V. Neque per diem il- lucescentem dies clarioris notitiæ Novo Testamen- to propriæ intelligitur, quasi attentionem Scriptu- ræ Propheticæ hæc notitia sequatur, ejusque vel- uti terminus sit. Nam etiam Vet. Testamenti tem- pore, non demum sub Novo Scriptura Prophetica lucebat in loco caliginoso, & dies illucescebat per eandem cognitionis & fidei salvifica, quod Patriar- charum aliorumque fidelium Veteris Testamenti exemplis constat, qui à tenebris etiam ad lucem conversi sunt. Quid ergo? Dies illucescere dicitur in corde cujusvis attenti lectoris sermonis Propheti- ci, quovis tempore, per lucis istius vim, lucen- tis in loco tenebricoso, quia tenebræ noctis, igno- rantiæ & errorum per eandem dispelluntur ac lux oritur non secus, ac cum dies illucescit, & cum Phosphorus oritur. Qui Phosphorus si spirituali- ter applicetur, ipse Christus est, stella illa matutina, Apoc. XXII. 16. sed ratione manifestationis, seu lucis spectatæ, quâ spargit in cordibus nostris, vel, quod idem est, cognitio Christi, qua corda nostra illumi- nantur. Eo usque enim attendendum est sermoni Prophetico, donec sequatur illuminatio fidei, & Phosphorus ille oriatur in cordibus nostris, ubi ta- men observanda Regula illa Hermineutica, parti- culam donec quandoque continuitatem & perpe- tuitatem significare, uti Psal. CXXIII. 2. Oculi no- stri ad Dominum Deum nostrum, donec misereatur nostri, Matth. XXVIII. 20. Ecce ego vobiscum sum ad consummationem seculi. Conf. Act. III. 20. Rom. V. 13. 1. Tim. IV. 13. attende lectioni ἕως ἔρχομαι do- nec venio. Non ergo est, quod dies ille illucescens, & Phosphorus ad clariorem Novi Testamenti lu- cem: Prophetica vero lucerna ad tenuiorem lucem Veteris Testamenti referatur cum Estio: Siqui- dem & in Veteri Testamento concione Prophe- tica tanta dies illuxerit, atque etiamnum Judæis aliisque illucescere possit, ut Phosphorus salutaris cognitionis oriri possit, & eo nomine commen detur ipsis etiam fidelibus attentio Scripturæ Pro- pheticæ, quod per eam ceu lucem satis dilucidam tenebræ in loco caliginoso cordis humani dispel- lantur, & dies illucescat, ac Phosphorus cogniti- onis.

Non itaque placet Estiana interpretatio, quam cum Hasselano, Adamo & Aria elegit: Scriptura Prophetica more lucernæ in tenebris accensæ tenuem & restrictam lucem exhibet, qua tamen interim utendum sit, donec dies adveniat, clarum lateque diffusum lumen præbitura. Item per illa, ut dies illucescat, significatur profectus & incrementum fidei, dum paulatim certior, purior ac sincerior ma- gisque explicita de Christi mysteriis accipitur cogni- tio, velut die illucescente. Et porro de Lucifero: Donec depulsis noctis tenebris clarius lumen velut exorientis Luciferi mentibus vestris infulgeat, id est, donec ita sitis illustrati lumine fidei, ut nullis du- bitationum scrupulis animi vestri amplius inquie- tentur. Ad hanc enim fidei perfectionem, multi Ju- dæorum, qui crediderant, nondum pervenerant. Quæ omnia quia comparant Scripturam Propheti- cam cum luce Evangelii, quantum ad lumen fidei, quæ certa sit, & absque dubitationum flucti- bus, derogant Scripturæ Propheticæ non tantum in συνκρίσει ad Apostolicam quoad clariorem gra- dum perspicuitatis & lucis, sed etiam, quoad eam perfectionem cognitionis, quæ in credentibus re- quiritur, ut tentationes superare possint, quæ si ipsi derogetur, quomodo fideles Veteris Testa- menti certi esse potuere, fidemque adversus tenta- tionem, quibus æque ac nos subjecti fuerunt, fir- mam retinere?

Paucis, non instituitur comparatio Scripturæ Propheticæ & Apostolicæ, sed declaratur certitudo & vis sermonis Prophetici ad illuminationem cordis nostri, adeoque non comparatur sermo Propheti- cus lucernæ tempore noctis lucenti, sermo Evan- gelii lucifero plenam diei lucem afferenti, imo (quod observat etiam ipse B. Gerhardus,) quod de Scriptura Prophetica in specie hoc loco adserit Apostolus, ad Scripturam etiam Apostolicam, adeoque ad totam Scripturam accommodari po- test: B. Gerhardus & hoc observat. ad h. l. totum vita tempus comparatum ad vitæ æternæ lucem esse obscuram quandam noctem, vitam vero æternam fore luce meridiana clariorem Apoc. XXI. 23. quo- modo cum August. tr. XXXV. in Joh. Beda, Glos- sa ordin. Cajetanus ad h. l. Petrus universum sta- tum hujus vitæ assimilat loco caliginoso egenti lucer- næ lumine, quod est Scriptura Sacra. Futura vita assimilatur diei claro, quod Lucifer, hoc est, Chri- stus oritur non corporaliter, sed spiritualiter in cor- dibus hominum. Quæ tamen explicatio huic loco minime propria est. Non ita confertur hic status diei præsentis & futuræ, sed status naturalis, qui meram caliginem infert, & gratiæ, in quo Phos- phorus & dies illucescit. Status gloriæ hic non commemoratur, in quo vero pleno jubare fulge- bit Sol justitiæ, nosque longe perfectius Christus illuminaturus est. Finis tamen illucescentiæ Phos- phori in cordibus nostris in tempore gratiæ est, il- luminatio, quæ speratur in regno gloriæ 1. Petr. I. 9. Apoc. XXII. 5. 23. ubi nulla nox, nulla nubes, nulla caligo, sed immensa & æterna claritas & dies perpetuus.

Convincuntur ex hoc loco Pontificii, laicis pro- hibendam non esse Scripturæ lectionem, quum Pe- trus recte eos facere, qui legunt eandem, pronun- ciet & Scripturam Propheticam dilucidam esse, & ad illuminationem cordis nostri facere, quia comparatur lucernæ in loco caliginoso lucenti, donec dies illucescat. Ideo Clemens Alex. in Pro- trept. Nullis, inquit, celatum est Verbum, lux est communis omnibus, illucescit omnibus. Conf. Es. VIII. 20. Nec est, quod excipiat Gretserus T. I. defens. Bellarm. p. 1794. Sermonem Propheticum latius patuisse, quam Scripturam Propheticam. Loquitur enim Petrus de sermone illo Prophetico, quem habebant & cui attendebant Ebræi conversi. At ille alius nullus erat, quam qui Scriptura Pro- phetica comprehensus.

## 1:20
v. 20. Knowing this first] πρῶτον, that is, above all בּרִאשׂוֹנָה. ὅτι πᾶσα προφητεία γραφῆς ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως ὐ γίνεται] I entirely agree with those who think that ἐπηλύσεως should be read here. Prophecy is not a matter of our own impulse. He who wishes does not possess it. The Spirit blows where He wishes. I am not unaware that חָתַר in Gen. XII. 12 is translated by some interpreters as ἐπιλύειν, for which the Chaldeans say פשׁר, whence פִּשׁרָן in Dan. V. 12, and that in the Chaldean of Cant. 1 it is said that what Isaiah predicted was explained, and that for Philo in 'On the Contemplative Life' the explanation of Scripture is called ἐπίλυσιν. But what I have just said is simpler, and coheres better with what follows.

This rule concerns not the origin, but the interpretation of Scripture, whether προφητεία γραφῆς is explained as scriptural prophecy, or by Hypallage as Prophetic Scripture with Cornelius, or as the interpretation of Scripture with Bede, which is called προφητεία, Rom. XII. 26, 1 Cor. XIII. 2, XIV. 16, 1 Thess. V. 20, because materially Scripture and its sense and interpretation are the same. The origin of Scripture is treated in the following [verse], and the same is brought forward as an argument. Who will admit that the same thing is proved by the same thing?
