And therefore the reading is not to be changed, as Calvin wished without the authority of any codex, nor is a new explanation of the word ἐπίλυσις to be devised with Beza and Hemmingius for 'impulse' or 'impetus,' which is destitute of any proven example in that place. Ἐπίλυσις is explanation, Mark IV. 24, Gen. III. 21. Every Prophecy is not, that is, by a Hebrew idiom, no Prophecy is of ἰδίας, its own or private explanation. V. 21. For prophecy was never brought by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit] They spoke of future things, not when they themselves wished, but when the Spirit of God moved them. Φερόμενοι is proper to this matter. For among the Greeks also such are Θεοφόρητοι. Concerning the force of this word, see Heb. I. 3. That very thing is what is expressed by נשא. Jud. XIII. 25. The sense is the same as here in Dan. II. 27. 28. Ἠνέχθη is בא. For Θεῦ there is τῶ Θεῶ in the Manuscript, it is a man of God, ἅγιοι τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωποι : אנשי אלהים הקדשים. To the Hebrews thus איש אלהים, that is, a Prophet, 2 Kings IV. 40. and elsewhere.

An argument is brought forward concerning Scripture not being explained by private ἐπιλύσει: because it was not published by private authority, but proceeded by divine authority. Prophecy was never brought by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit. By which Spirit, says Bernard in his epistle to the brothers of the mount, the scripture of God was made, by that same Spirit it is desired to be read, and by Him it must be understood. But that Φορὰ embraces both the internal illumination of the mind, and the suggestion of those things which were to be said or written, as well as the external motion, so that not less the tongue or the pen, than the mind and spirit, acted by that impulse, whatever it did, and not only the matter or things were suggested; but also the words were placed in the mouth, or dictated to the pen by the Holy Spirit, as if to His own amanuenses, the Men of God. And therefore it is also called Prophecy, namely, on account of divine inspiration. Whatever cannot be written except by the instinct of God, Origen teaches in Homily II on Exodus is Prophecy. Although indeed they can be said to have spoken not only future things, but whatever they spoke, contained in the sacred letters, not when, nor as they themselves wished, but when and as the Holy Spirit moved them, yet that is not to be understood as if the Holy Spirit so moved and impelled the holy men of God that they did not understand what they were saying, nor had it in their power not to speak: which Bede here refutes as a most impudent error. How, he says, would they give such sound counsels of living to those who hear, if they themselves, like madmen, did not know what they were saying? Why then are they called Prophets who see? For what reason is the word written, which Isaiah or some Prophet sees, unless because in the secret of celestial visions they knew with the most lucid intuition of the mind the mysteries which they would openly bring forth to their hearers in whatever words? But when Peter thus proves that Scripture is not of private ἐπιλύσεως, by private ἐπίλυσις he understands every interpretation which is brought forth outside of Scripture, whether it is brought forth by some private person or by a public person, or the Church: since no ἐπίλυσις is to be admitted except that which is drawn from Scripture itself. According to Hilary, book I de Trin., the best reader is one who expects the understanding of what is said from the things said rather than imports it, and reports it rather than brings it, nor forces it to seem contained in the words, which he had despised understanding before reading. The Glossa ordinaria from Bede on this passage has it thus: Just as the Prophets wrote not their own words, but the words of God: So the reader ought not to use his own interpretation, lest he deviate from the faith, but should labor to attend to how He who wrote wished His words to be understood: This is the gloss. For just as the Prophets spoke and wrote what they spoke and wrote only by the impulse of the Holy Spirit: So the Holy Spirit is the only Interpreter of His own words, who also has exposed His own mind in Scripture and through Scripture sufficiently clearly: because He wished it to be a lamp shining in a dark place, so that the Morning Star might arise in our hearts. If Scripture itself were obscure, how would it shine in a dark place, how would it cause the dawning of the day and the rising of the Morning Star, and for that reason would its attention be commended to us? As He is the best Interpreter of Himself: so Scripture interprets itself best, if the propriety of the words, and the context and scope of any place, as well as the parallelism of other places, and the analogy of faith are diligently attended to. That the Spirit for infallibly interpreting the Holy Scriptures has been promised to any one person, or even to a communion, or a Council, just as most Papists boast concerning their Pope and Councils, while others claim the same rather for a general Council, will be proven at the Greek Calends. That the opinion of one private person is to be preferred to the definition of the Pope, if that opinion rests on better reasons than the decision of the latter, Gerson, Panormitanus, Picus Mirandula, and others admit.

PART II. OF THE EPISTLE. Prophetic Antithesis.

SECTION I. The opposite doctrine of false Teachers predicted by the Apostle, with their description.

Latin:

v. 20. Τῦτο πρῶτον γινώσκοντες] πρῶτον, id est imprimis בּרִאשׂוֹנָה. ὅτι πᾶσα προφητεία γραφῆς ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως ὐ γίνεται] O- mnino assentior iis, qui hic legendum censent ἐπηλύσεως. Non est prophetia res nostri impetus. Non habet eam qui vult. Spiritus ubi vult spirat. Non ignoro חָתַר Gen. XII. 12. à nonnullis Interpretibus verti ἐπιλύειν, pro quo Chaldæi dicunt פשׁר, unde פִּשׁרָן Dan. V. 12. & Chal- dæo Cant. l. dici explicatum ab Esaia, id quod Esaias præ- dixit, & Philoni de vita contemplativa explicationem Scri- pturæ dici ἐπίλυσιν. Sed quod jam dixi simplicius est, & cum sequentibus melius cohæret.

Non hæc regula originem, sed interpretationem Scripturæ concernit, sive προφητεία γραφῆς expli- cetur prophetia scripturalis, aut per Hypallagen Pro- phetica Scriptura cum Cornelio, sive interpretatio Scripturæ cum Beda, quæ προφητεία dicitur, Rom. XII. 26. 1. Corinth. XIII. 2. XIV. 16. 1. Thess. V. 20. quia materialiter idem sunt Scriptura ejusque sen- sus, & interpretatio. De origine Scripturæ v. sequ. agitur, eademque argumenti loco affertur. Idem per idem probari ecquis admittet? Ideoque non immutanda sive lectio, ut Calvinus voluit citra ulli- us codicis autoritatem, sive vocis ἐπίλυσις expli- catio nova excogitanda cum Beza & Hemmin- gio pro impetu vel impulsu, quæ exemplo probato ibidem destituitur. Ἐπίλυσις explicatio est, Marc. IV. 24. Gen. III. 21. Omnis Prophetia non est, id est idiotismo Ebraico, nulla Prophetica est ἰδίας propria vel privatæ explicationis. V. 21. Οὐ γὰρ θελήματι ἀνθρώπε ἠνέχθη ποτὲ προφητεία, ἀλλ᾽ ὑπὸ Πνεύματος ἁγίε φερόμενοι ἐλάλησαν ἅγιοι Θεῦ ἄν- θρωποι] Loquuti sunt futura, non cum ipsi vellent, sed cum eos ageret Dei Spiritus. Φερόμενοι proprium hujus rei. Nam & Græcis tales Θεοφόρητοι. De hujus vocis vi vide Ebr. I. 3. Illud ipsum est, quod per נשא exprimitur. Jud. XIII. 25. Sensus idem qui hic Dan. II. 27. 28. Ἠνέχθη est בא. Pro Θεῦ est τῶ Θεῶ in Manuscripto est viri Dei, ἅγιοι τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωποι : אנשי אלהים הקדשים Ebræis sic איש אלהים, id est Propheta, 2.Reg.IV. 40. & alibi.

Argumentum adducitur de non explicandâ, privata ἐπιλύσει, Scriptura: quia non privata auto- ritate edita est, sed divina autoritate prodiit. Non voluntate humana allata est unquam Prophetia, sed à Spiritu Sancto agitati loquuti sunt sancti Dei homines. Quo Spiritu, inquit Bernhardus in epist ad fratr. de monte, Dei scriptura facta sunt, eo Spi- ritu legi desiderant, ipso etiam intelligendæ sunt Φορὰ autem illa complectitur tum illuminationem mentis internam, & suggestionem eorum, quæ dicenda, vel scribenda fuere, tum externam mo- tionem, ut non minus lingua, vel calamus, quam mens & animus impulsu isto egerit, quicquid e- git, neque materia tantum, vel res suggestæ sint; sed etiam verba in os posita, vel dictata in cala- mum à Spiritu Sancto, ceu amanuensibus propriis, Viris Dei. Atque ideo dicitur etiam Prophetia ob inspirationem scilicet divinam. Quicquid nisi Dei instinctu scribi potest, Prophetiam esse docet homil. II. in Exod. Origenes. Quanquam vero loquuti di- ci possint non futura tantum, sed quicquid loquu- ti sunt, in sacris literis comprehensum, non cum, nec prout ipsi vellent, sed cum, & prout eos egit Spiritus Sanctus, id tamen non est ita intelligen- dum, quasi Spiritus Sanctus ita egerit, & impule- rit sanctos Dei homines, ut non intellexerint quæ loquerentur, nec in potestate sua habuerint non loqui: quod refellit hic Beda ceu impudentissimum errorem. Quomodo, inquit, audientibus tam sana vivendi consilia darent, si insanis similes ipsi, quæ lo- querentur, nescirent? Quare videntes appellantur Prophetæ? Qua ratione scriptum est verbum, quod videt Esaias aut aliquis Propheta, nisi quia in occul- to visionum cælestium lucidissimo mentis intuitu cognoscebant arcana, quæ foras suis auditoribus pa- lam verbis qualibuscunque efferrent? Cum autem ita probat Petrus non esse privatæ ἐπιλύσεως Scri- pturam, per privatam ἐπίλυσιν omnem, quæ ex- tra Scripturam affertur, interpretationem sive à privato quopiam sive à persona publica, vel Ec- clesia afferatur, intelligit: siquidem non nisi ea admittenda ἐπίλυσις, quæ ex ipsa Scriptura depro- mitur. Optimus secundum Hilarium l. I. de Trin. lector est, ut dictorum intelligentiam expectet ex dictis potius, quam importet, & retulerit magis, quam attulerit, nec cogat id videri dictis contineri, quod ante lectionem contempserit intelligendum. Glossa ordin. ex Beda in h. l. ita habet: Sicut Pro- phetæ non sua, sed Dei verba scribebant: Ita lector non sua interpretatione uti debet, ne à fide exorbi- tet, sed laboret attendere, quomodo verba sua volue- rit intelligi, quis scripsit: Hæc glossa. Ut enim non nisi Spiritus Sancti impulsu ea loquuti sunt & scripserunt Prophetæ, quæ loquuti sunt & scri- psere: Ita non nisi Spiritus Sanctus verborum suo- rum Interpres est, qui etiam suam mentem in Scri- ptura & per Scripturam satis luculenter exposuit: quia eam voluit lucernam esse lucentem in loco ca- liginoso, ut Phosphorus oriatur in cordibus no- stris. Si obscura esset ipsa Scriptura, quomodo luceret in loco tenebricoso, quomodo ad illu- cescentiam diei, & exortum Phosphori faceret, ejusque causa nobis commendaretur illius atten- tio. Ut idem sui Interpres optimus est: ita Scri- ptura semetipsam optime interpretatur, si verbo- rum proprietas, & contextus ac scopus loci cu- jusvis proprius, nec non parallelismus aliorum locorum, & analogia fidei sedulo attendatur. Spiritum ad infallibiliter interpretandum S. lite- ras uni alicui personæ, vel etiam communioni, aut Concilio promissum esse, quemadmodum Pontificii plerique de Papa suo & Conciliis jacti- tant, aliis tamen Concilio potius generali eun- dem vindicantibus, ad Calendas Græcas probabi- tur. Unius privati sententiam Papæ definitioni præferendam esse, si illa sententia nitatur meliori- bus rationibus, quam hujus decisio, admittunt Gerson, Panormitanus, Picus Mirandula, alii.

PARS II. EPISTOLÆ ᾿Αντίθεσις Προφητική.

SECTIO I. Opposita doctrina falsorum Doctorum ab Apo- stolo prædicta, cum eorum descriptione.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II. ARGUMENT, AND PARTITION.

Opposed to the Evangelical Doctrine is the Doctrine of the Pseudo-Prophets, whom he predicts will introduce sects of perdition, denying Him who bought them, with their own destruction and that of those who will follow them: which he confirms by the example of the Angels who sinned, and the former world punished by the flood, as well as the overthrow of the Sodomites, from whom only Lot was snatched, as also by the judgment of God, which awaits the impure, the despisers of dominion, and the blasphemers, the voluptuous, and the covetous imitators of Balaam, such as the false Teachers are noted to be, fountains without water driven by storms, proud, shameless, and seducing others to sins, and involving them with themselves in the pollutions of the world, whose last state is worse than the first.

There are two parts: I. Prophetic, in which the doctrine and destruction of false Prophets, up to verse 9. II. Prosopography, in which the vices and life of false Teachers with the addition of their punishment, up to v. 22.

PART I. The prophecy, by which the doctrine of false Prophets.

V. 1. ᾿Εγένοντο δὲ καὶ ψευδοπροφῆται ἐν τῷ λαῷ] It coheres well with the preceding. For not all who call themselves such are Prophets of God. Many falsely assume that name for themselves. Many are agitated by a Diabolical Spirit. ᾿Εν τῷ λαῷ, in the Israelite people, See 1 Kings XXII. 6. Jer. XXVIII. Ezek. XIII. 2. XXII. 25. 28. Zeph. III. 4.

After he spoke about the true Prophets in the Old Testament and was about to predict the false ones, teaching that there were also false Prophets in the past, he takes the occasion of his prophecy from that to speak of the false Teachers who would arise under the New Testament, and he proceeds from the doctrine, which he had commended to be kept holy, to the ἀντίθεσιν of contrary doctrine to be diligently guarded against and avoided. In the Old Testament, besides the Baalites, 1 Kings XIX, there were also those who they opposed themselves to the prophecies of others, and championed idolatry, and seduced the people with false prophecies and various promises, and strengthened them in impiety, security, and impenitence.

ὧς καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν ἔσονται ψευδοδιδάσκαλοι] He understands especially Carpocrates and his associates, who were in the times of Hadrian.

οἵτινες παρεισάξουσιν αἱρέσεις ἀπωλείας] Pernicious sects. The word αἱρέσεως is by its own nature neutral, but it is distinguished by the addition. Παρεισάξουσι, they will introduce secretly. See Gal. II. 4.

καὶ τὸν ἀγοράσαντα αὐτὸς δεσπότην, ἀρνούμενοι] That is Jesus, who is for the most part called Κύριος in the New Testament, but also sometimes δεσπότης, as is very often to be seen in the books of responses to the orthodox and other books of Christians. Christ redeemed them too, inasmuch as he died for all. Such words do not always signify the effect, especially the final one, but often the efficacy. Thus σώζειν is taken in 2 Tim. I. 9. But they denied Jesus, because they detracted from his highest honor, saying he was born of the father Joseph, and that many of the flock of Carpocrates were his equals, and some even his superiors, Iren. I. 24.

That Carpocrates and his associates are understood specifically does not appear. Generally, all are understood who in future times, not only in that age but also in other ages to follow, are about to introduce heresies of perdition, and primarily those who are about to deny the Lord who bought them. By which periphrasis are designated those who were about to deny both the Deity of Christ, which the word δεσπότης denotes, and the meritorious satisfaction of the same, that he bought us with a price, as were Ebion and Cerinthus in the time of the Apostles, the Donatists and Pelagians in the third and fourth centuries, Abailard in the eleventh century, Servetus and the Socinians in the previous and modern century, which we show in a special Historical-Theological dissertation. Παρεισάξωσιν is 'they will subintroduce,' because they are about to bring into the Church ἑτεροδοξίαν, besides that true doctrine concerning Christ, by whatever means, Gal. II. 4. Therefore in the parallel place of Jude v. 4. it is said of them παρεισέδυσάν τινες ἄνθρωποι, certain men crept in, because they slip in stealthily, as self-called. Conf. Acts XX. 29, 30. We do not find the word αἱρέσεως used except in a bad sense in the New Testament, Acts IV. 17, ch. XV. 5, 1 Cor. XI. 19, Gal. V. 20, nor is it taken otherwise in Acts XXIV by Tertullian, or by the Jews in ch. XXVIII. v. 22, who held their religion as a pestilent heresy, or by Paul in Acts XXVI. 5, by whose judgment Pharisaism was indeed a pernicious heresy, even if it carried the appearance of holiness with singular hypocrisy. But in Acts ch. XXIV. 14, Paul does not call the Christian religion a heresy from his own judgment, but from that of the Jews. Therefore the word ἀπωλείας is not restrictive here, but descriptive, since every heresy brings about perdition. But what is added, 'by the denial of the Master who bought them,' is not to be referred to the sects of perdition, as if by the very fact that they introduce sects of perdition they deny the Lord who bought them; but to the false teachers, whose specification is had here, because it is prophesied here specifically concerning those who are about to attack the Deity and redemption of Christ. For it is not without cause that that periphrasis of the 'Master' is added: nor does that denial of the Lord as Redeemer occur in every heresy, and the parallel passage of Jude v. 4 is clear, by which those heretics are openly described thus by the very head of their heresy, 'denying the only Master God and our Lord Jesus Christ,' just as in the thesis of true Evangelical doctrine, to which this antithesis is opposed, both the Deity of Christ and the truth of his Redemptive office are exhibited, as confirmed by the very voice of the heavenly Father.

We have therefore against the Christ-fighters an invincible argument for the Deity of Christ, and a most grave judgment of the Apostle, that the denial of the Deity of Christ and his redemption is αἵρεσις ἀπωλείας, a destructive heresy. The argument for the Deity of Christ stands thus: Whoever is called μοναδικῶς in the singular Δεσπότης in the New Testament, he is the Lord called ἐξοχικῶς, or the most absolute Lord of all things, and therefore is God. But Christ is called μοναδικῶς Δεσπότης in the New Testament, Therefore. The major is proved: Because that name is vindicated uniquely to that one Master and Lord of all things by the usage of the sacred Scriptures of the New Testament, which is also evident from the induction of places, Luke II. 29, Acts IV. 24, Rev. VI. 10, etc. nor can the adversaries deny it: They follow in this part the Holy Writers of the New Testament, as in many others, the Hellenists, the authors of the Apocryphal books of the Old Testament, who likewise use the word δεσπότης uniquely of God, both absolutely, Wisd. XIII. 39, Sirach XXXIV. 26, 2 Macc. V. 17, IX. 13, Susanna v. 5, and also when the word 'of all' is added, ὁ πάντων Δεσπότης, Wisd. VI. 7, VIII. 3, Sir. XXXVI. 1, or something else describing God, as Sir. XXIII. 1, Δεσπότα ζωῆς μꙋ, 2 Macc. V. 20, τꙋ μεγάλꙋ Δεσπότꙋ. Nor do the LXX, the Elder Interpreters of the Old Testament, use the word Δεσπότην otherwise than of the dominion of the one God, by which they were accustomed to render the word משל, he has dominion (whence Christ is called משל, ruler, Mic. V. 2), see Ps. XXII. 29, LIX. 14, LXVI. 7, LXXXIX. 10, CIII. 19. But they also employ δεσπότης concerning the supreme Lord of things, explaining either the essential name of God יהוה, Prov. XXIX. 26, or אדני, which likewise is proper only to God, Is. I. 24, or even the word אדון, Gen. XV. 2, Josh. V. 14, Is. III. 1, X. 33, or finally the word אל, which likewise befits none but the one God, Job V. 8.

The minor premise is confirmed from this passage: τὸν ἀγοράσαν- τα ἀυτὸς Δεσπότην ἀρνόμενοι, denying that Master who redeemed them. That Christ is noted here is evident both from the added description, because ἀγορασμὸς is attributed to no one but Christ in the Scriptures, and never to God the Father, Gal. III. 13. IV. 5. V. 19; and from the mention of the Pseudo-Prophets, because false teachers who arose in the Church are not read to have denied the Father so much as Christ our Redeemer; impiously denying partly his divine lordship, that he is not that Δεσπότης, and partly his ἀγορασμὸν, the redemption made by the price of his blood. Concerning these heresies we have treated in a previously mentioned Historical-Theological Diatribe.

We add a parallel passage from Jude v. 4. Where Christ is designated not only as Δεσπότης, but as ὁ μόνος Δεσπότης, God and our Lord, so that it is established that he is the same supreme and absolute Lord, as of all things, so also of the Church and the faithful, who is none other than that one God. We shall teach that that passage is to be understood concerning Christ when we arrive at it. Now we compare the passage 2 Tim. II. 21. It will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful τῷ Δεσπότῃ, to the Master. It is certain that the Master of the Church, which is described as the house of God, is to be understood. But who does not know that in the New Testament Christ is particularly called the Lord of the Church, which the adversaries do not deny to be the house of Christ? Add that the mention of Christ had been made immediately before, as the one whose name all members of the Church profess: for which reason they are commanded to depart from injustice. Finally, how can it be doubted that Christ is the spiritual Lord, the absolute and supreme master of the Church, since he is ὁ κατασκευάσας ἀυτὴν, who built and prepared it, whose house therefore all the faithful are called, Heb. III. 3, 6. We finally subjoin the passage Rev. VI. 10. Oc- the souls of the slain martyrs cry out: How long, O Master, the holy and the true, do you not judge? From which words it is gathered that Christ is being addressed, because all judgment has been given to Christ, and he executes all judgment, John 5:22. To whom also the name of the true and the holy is peculiarly vindicated in this book of the Apocalypse, Chapter 3:7, These things says the holy, the true, and verse 14, the faithful and the true. What? That it is said to be his proper name in Apoc. 19:11, called faithful and true, which is translated as Faithful and True.

Now, as far as concerns ἀγορασμὸς, a redemption made by a price, and thus that a satisfaction is designated, against the Socinians who deny the same, it is evident both from the proper meaning of the word, from which one must not depart unless necessity compels; because ἀγοράζειν and ἀγορασμὸς properly denote a redemption which is made by the payment of a price, and not a simple liberation: and also from the explicit mention of the price, that we were redeemed not with corruptible gold or silver, but with the precious blood of the immaculate Lamb, 1 Pet. 1:18-19, Apocal. 5:9, and 1 Cor. 6:20, for you were bought with a price, and also from the proper confession of the adversaries. Socinus in Synops. de justif. p. 7 says: The word to redeem signifies to liberate by a given price; indeed, if you look at the force of the word itself, it declares an act of buying, which cannot happen without a price. Smalzius in Ex. 157. Error. n. 51. We confess, he says, that the blood of Christ is the true price of our redemption, and that it had the force of a price in redeeming us, because the blood of Christ truly performed for us that which a price performs in redeeming any captive.

But as to what he says, that the requirements of redemption are not present, since there is no one to whom the blood of Christ was given for us, he is mistaken in that. For just as other requirements are present, verse 9, the object of redemption, which are captive men, Zech. 9:11, Gal. 3:22-23, the Redeemer Christ, Rom. 3:24, and the λύτρον, which is his blood, Matt. 20:28, Mark 10:45, Eph. 1:7, Col. 1:14, 1 Pet. 1:18, so also is not lacking that one to whom the λύτρον is paid. For it had to be paid to God, who principally detained us as captives, since the devil is only the jailer, from whose hand Christ redeemed us, Hos. 13:14. But God, as a just Judge, consigned us to prison and submitted us to the hand of the devil because of sin, by the force of His justice, Gal. 3:22, Rom. 11:32. Therefore, the payment and satisfaction were rendered to God. For Christ offered himself to God, Eph. 5:2, Heb. 9:14. But to whom Christ offered himself as a sacrifice for our sins, to the same he rendered the payment for us. As God by the force of His justice demanded a λύτρον for our liberation, so by the force of His mercy He accepted an ἀντίλυτρον in our stead, which was paid for us by Christ. Which is a true satisfaction, as we have shown elsewhere from the nature of satisfaction.

But since Christ is said to have redeemed even those who deny him and bring swift destruction upon themselves, the Calvinists, who insist that only the elect were redeemed by Christ, are powerfully refuted. But Polanus, Tossanus, and Piscator rashly contend that this is not said κατ᾽ ἀλήθειαν (in truth), but only κατὰ δόξαν (in appearance). For the words themselves teach that St. Peter speaks from his own mind. He does not say, as they think, but that they were redeemed. And how would that harmonize with their heresy, which is, he denies the Master who redeemed them? He who believes he has been redeemed by the Lord does not deny the Lord the Redeemer, but by that very fact acknowledges Him. Add that they are said to have escaped the pollutions of the world before through the knowledge of Christ, verses 18, 20, not apparently, but truly. Therefore, they were previously believers, truly liberated from the pollutions of the world, and thus redeemed by the blood of Christ from their vain conversation, 1 Pet. 1:18. If you say with Estius: That it is indeed well gathered from these words that Christ redeemed certain reprobates, namely those who became participants in his redemption according to some effects, such as were these of whom Peter speaks, being regenerated through faith in baptism and having obtained the forgiveness of sins, although they later relapsed into the old slavery of sin. Which is the same doctrine of the Council of Valence held nearly 800 years ago in Gaul, Chapter 5, affirming that the redemption of Christ pertains to those who, even if they are not saved because they do not persevere, were nevertheless regenerated by baptism and washed from their sins in the blood of Christ. But do not gather from this that the effect of redemption extends to all men whatsoever. Resp. If those effects of the redemption of Christ belong to the reprobate through faith, to be regenerated in baptism and to obtain the forgiveness of sins, it must be that Christ also acquired regeneration and the remission of sins for the reprobate. What then can be lacking here in the redemption of Christ? For where there is regeneration, there is the inheritance to which we are regenerated; where there is the remission of sins, there is salvation. But that they fall away from the grace of regeneration and the remission of sins (which Estius acknowledges; but Calvinists contend it is impossible for true believers) does not argue a defect of the Redemption, but the fault of the redeemed: but it confirms that they were truly redeemed; and that this redemption extends to all is evident from this, that for all captives, as regards redemption, the reason is the same, and an ἀντίλυτρον was paid for all, 2 Tim. 4:6. Whence Cornelius à Lapide on 2. Petr. III. was compelled to admit that they err who think that Christ did not suffer for all, but only for the predestined. See Heb. II. ver. 9. 2 Cor. V. ver. 19. 1 John II. ver. 1. Isa. LIII. ver. 4. et seqq. Moreover, it is evident from this passage that Calvinists are also among those who deny the Lord who bought them, who bring upon themselves swift destruction, and that therefore their dogma is a heresy τῆς ἀπωλείας. And how can they believe in Christ, that He redeemed them, who deny that Christ redeemed all? How can they apply to themselves the redemption and the price of redemption, who deny that all were redeemed, and that the price of redemption was paid for all? See Gründlicher Beweiß Facultat. Theol. Witteb. daß die Calvinischen Irrthümer den Grund des Glaubens betreffen, und der Seligkeit nachtheilig seyen, part. II. cap. II. 248. et seqq. Furthermore, the Papists, because they join Mary and the Saints to Christ the Redeemer and Mediator, and say that they can obtain salvation by their own works, merits, and satisfactions, deny that Christ is the one Lord who redeemed them, etc.

Ἐπάγοντες ἑαυτοῖς ταχινὴν ἀπώλειαν.) In the war of Bar Kokhba, to which they adhered, as worldly men.

It is not a question of temporal destruction, but eternal; not of the war of Bar Kokhba, of which there is no trace here, but of heresy as the cause of destruction: not of those who adhered to Bar Kokhba, but of all who deny the Lord who bought them, Christ Jesus. What is clearer than that it is a question of the same ἀπωλεία from which heresies are named, and that by the same, not some war of seditious men is accelerated, that ἀπώ-

tion. Finally, that by ταχινὴν ἀπώλειαν [swift destruction] eternal condemnation is denoted, verse 3, is most clearly evident, where τὸ κρῖμα καὶ ἡ ἀπώλεια [the judgment and the destruction] are joined for the sake of explanation, and τὸ κρῖμα [the judgment] is declared by the example of the Angels, who, having been dragged down by the ropes of hell, were delivered to be tormented in Tartarus? Whence Jude says they were long ago προγεγραμμένους [written beforehand] to that judgment, verse 4, whether in the prophecies or in the judicial decree of GOD.

Latin:

CAPUT II. ARGUMENTUM, ET PARTITIO.

Doctrinæ Evangelicæ opposita est Doctrina Pseu- do-Prophetarum, quos prædicit, sectas hæ- rum, qui mercatus ipsos est, abnegantes in- troducturos cum propria & eorum, qui ipsos sequentur, pernitie: quam confirmat exem- plo Angelorum, qui peccarunt, & mundi prioris per diluvium puniti, nec non eversio- nis Sodomitarum, è quibus ereptus tantum Loth, ut & judicio Dei, quod impuros, domi- nationis contemptores, & blasphemos, volu- ptuarios, & avaros Balaami imitatores ma- net, quales falsi Doctores notātur esse fontes sine aqua à turbinib9 agitatos, superbos, im- pudicos, aliosque ad peccata seducentes, & mundi inquinamentis secum involventes, quorum novissima sunt deteriora prioribus.

Partes duæ sunt: I. Prophetica, qua falsorum Prophetarum doctrinam & exitium, ad vers. 9. II. Προσωπογραφία, qua falsorum Doctorum vitia & vitam addito eorundem supplicio, ad v. 22.

PARS I. Prophetia, qua falsorum Prophetarum doctrinam.

V. 1. ᾿Εγένοντο δὲ καὶ ψευδοπροφῆται ἐν τῷ λαῷ] Bene co- hæret cum superioribus Non enim omnes Dei Prophetæ sunt, qui tales se dicunt. Multi falso sibi sumunt id nomen. Multi Diabolico Spiritu agitantur. ᾿Εν τῷ λαῷ, in populo Israëlitico, Vid. 1. Reg. XXII. 6. Jer. XXVIII. Ezech. XIII. 2. XXII. 25. 28. Soph. III. 4.

Postquam de veris Prophetis in Veteri Testa- mento dixit ac falsos prædicturus, etiam olim fal- sos fuisse Prophetas docens, occasionem prophe- tiæ suæ inde sumit de falsis Doctoribus sub Novo Testamento exorituris, & à doctrina, quam com- mendarat sancte custodiendam, ad ἀντίθεσιν do- ctrinæ contrariæ sedulo cavendam & fugiendam progreditur. In Veteri Testamento præter Baa- litas, 1. Reg. XIX. etiam fuere, qui Esaiæ, Jeremiæ, aliorum prophetiis sese opposuerunt, & idolo- latriam propugnarunt, & populum falsis prophe- tiis, variisque promissis seduxerunt, & in impie- tate, securitate ac impoenitentia corrobora- runt.

ὧς καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν ἔσονται ψευδοδιδάσκαλοι] Carpocratem & ejus socios praecipue intelligit, qui fuere Adriani tem- poribus.

οἵτινες παρεισάξουσιν αἱρέσεις ἀπωλείας] Sectas pernicio- sas. Est vox αἱρέσεως suapte natura media, sed addita- mento distinguitur. Παρεισάξουσι, latenter introducent. Vide Gal. II. 4.

καὶ τὸν ἀγοράσαντα αὐτὸς δεσπότην, ἀρνούμενοι] Id est Jesum, qui plerumque Κύριος in Novo Testamento voca- tur, sed & δεσπότης interdum, ut saepissime videre est in li- bris responsionum ad orthodoxos, & aliis libris Christiano- rum. Christus & illos redemit, quippe pro omnibus mortu- us. Verba talia non semper effectum, praesertim ultimum, sed saepe efficaciam significant. Sic σώζειν sumitur 2. Tim. I. 9. Abnegabant autem illi Jesum, quia honorem ei sum- mum detrahebant, dicentes eum natum patre Josepho, & multos de Carpocratis grege ipsi pares, quosdam & superiores esse, Iren. I. 24.

Carpocratem, & ejus socios peculiariter intelli- gi, non apparet. Generaliter omnes intelliguntur, qui futuris temporibus, non seculo isto tantum, sed aliis etiam aetatibus secuturis sub introducturi sunt haereses perditionis, & imprimis negaturi Dominum, qui eos mercatus est. Qua περιφάσει de- signantur, qui cum Deitatem Christi, quam voce δεσπότης denotat,tum satisfactionem ejusdem me- ritoriam, quod pretio nos emerit, abnegaturi e- rant, ceu fuerunt Ebion, & Cerinthus Apostolo- rum tempore, Donatistae, & Pelagiani seculo ter- tio, & quarto Abailardus seculo undecimo, Ser- vetus, & Sociniani superiori & moderno seculo, quod ostendimus peculiari diatriba Historico-Theologi- ca. Παρεισάξωσιν est subintroducent, quod praeter illam veram de Christo doctrinam in Ecclesiam ἑτεροδοξίαν invecturi sint quacunque ratione, Gal. II.4.Ideo in loco parallelo Judae v.4. ipsis dicuntur παρεισέδυσάν τινες ἄνθρωποι, subintroierunt quida homines, quod furtim, ut αὐτόκλητοι irrepant. Conf. Act. XX. 29. 30. Vocem vero αἱρέσεως non in- venimus nisi in malam partem usurpatam in Novo Testamento, Act. IV. 17. cap. XV. 5. 1. Corinth. XI. 19. Gal. V. 20. nec aliter Act. XXIV. à Tertulliano ac- cipitur, aut a Judaeis c. XXVIII. v. 22. qui uti reli- gionem pro pestilenti haeresi habebant, aut à Pau- lo Act. XXVI. 5. ex cujus sententia Pharisaismus vero erat pernitiosa haeresis, etsi singulari hypo- crisi sanctitatem prae se ferret. Actorum vero cap. XXIV. 14. Paulus non ex sua, sed Judaeorum sententia Christianam religionem haeresin vocat. Proinde vox ἀπωλείας non est hic restrictiva, sed descriptiva, cum omnis haeresis perditionem in- ferat. Quod autem additur denegatione heri,qui ipsos redemit, non referendum ad sectas perdi- tionis, quasi eo ipso, quod sectas perditionis in- troducunt, Dominum abnegent, qui ipsos merca- tus est; Sed ad falsos Doctores, quorum specificatio hic habetur, quod peculiariter de illis hic vatici- netur, qui Christi Deitatem, & redemptionem im- pugnaturi sunt. Non enim absque causa περίφρα- σις illa heri adjecta est: nec in omni haeresi ea ne- gatio Domini, ceu Redemptoris occurrit, & luculentus est locus parallelus Jud. v. 4. quo hae- retici illi aperte ita describuntur à proprio hae- reseos suae capite τὸν μόνον δεσπότην Θεὸν καὶ Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησῦν Χριστὸν ἀρνύμενοι, quemadmodum & in θέσει verae doctrinae Evangelicae, cui haec ἀν- τίθεσις opposita est, cum Christi Deitas, tum of- ficii ejus Redemptorii veritas exhibita est, ceu ipsa voce Patris coelesti confirmata.

Habemus itaque contra χριστομάχες argumen- tum Deitatis Christi invictum, & judicium Apostoli gravissimum, quod negatio Deitatis Christi & redemptionis ejus sit αἵρεσις ἀπωλείας exitiosa hæ- resis. Argumentum Deitatis Christi sic habet: Qui- cunque μοναδικῶς in singulari vocatur Δεσπότης in Novo Testamento, is est Dominus ἐξοχικῶς ita di- ctus, vel Dominus rerum omnium absolutissimus, adeoque sumus Deus. At Christus μοναδικῶς vo- catur Δεσπότης in Novo Testamento, Ergo. Major probatur: Quia nomen illud vindicatur unice uni illi hero, & Domino rerum omnium ex usu Scri- pturarum sacrarum Novi Testamenti, quod & ex inductione locorum constat, Luc. II. 29. Act. IV. 24. Apoc. VI. 10. &c. nec diffiteri possunt adversa- rii: Sequuntur hac in parte Scriptores Sanctos Novi Testamenti, ut in aliis multis, Hellenistas A- pocryphorum librorum Veteris Testamenti Au- tores, qui itidem unice de Deo utuntur voce δε- σπότης, tum absolute Sap. XIII. 39. Syrach. XXXIV. 26. 2. Macc. V. 17. IX. 13. Susan. v. 5. tum etiam cum ad- ditur vox omnium ὁ πάντων Δεσπότης, Sap. VI. 7. VIII. 3. Sir. XXXVI. 1. aut aliud quid Deum descri- bens, ut Sir. XXIII. 1. Δεσπότα ζωῆς μꙋ, 2. Macc. V. 20. τꙋ μεγάλꙋ Δεσπότꙋ. Nec aliter verbum Δεσπό- την usurpant LXX. Seniores Interpretes Veteris Te- stamenti, quam de dominio unius Dei, quo reddere consueverunt vocem משל dominatus est, (unde Christus משל dominator dictus est Mich. V. 12.) vid. Psal. XXII. 29. LIX. 14. LXVI. 7. LXXXIX. 10. CIII. 19. Sed & δεσπότης adhibent de summo rerum Do- minos explicantet, eodem vel nomẽ Dei essentiale יהוה Prov. XXIX. 26. vel אדני, quod itidem so- li Deo proprium Es. I. 24. vel etiam vocem אדון Gen. XV. 2. Jos. V. 14. Es. III. 1. X. 33. vel denique vocem אל, quæ pariter non nisi uni Deo conve- nit Job. V. 8.

Minor confirmatur ex hoc loco τὸν ἀγοράσαν- τα ἀυτὸς Δεσπότην ἀρνόμενοι, negantes herum il- lum, qui redemit illos. Christum notari tum è de- scriptione addita patescit, quia ἀγορασμὸς nõ nisi Christo tribuitur in Scripturis, nuspiam autem Deo Patri, Gal. III. 13. IV. 5. V. 19. tum è Pseudo- Prophetarum mentione, quia falsi Doctores in Ecclesia exorti non tam Patrem leguntur negasse, quam Christum Redemptorem nostrum; partim ejus divinum dominium, quod non sit Δεσπότης il- le, partim ejꙋ ἀγορασμὸν, redemptionem pretio san- guinis factam, impie abnegantes. De quibus hære- sibus peculiari Diatribe antea nominat a Historico- Theologica egimus.

Addimus parallelum lolum è Jud. v. 4. Ubi Christus nõ modo Δεσπότης, sed ὁ μόνος Δεσπότης, Θεὸς κὶ Κύριος ἡμῶν indigitatur, ut constet eundẽ esse summum & absolutum, ut rerum omnium, ita etiam Ecclesiæ & fidelium Dominum, qui non est nisi unus ille Deus. De Christo autem intelligen- dum esse locum illum docebimus, cum eo devene- rimus. Jam conferimus locum 2. Tim. II. 21. Vas erit in honorem sanctificatum & utile τῷ Δεσπότῃ, Hero. Intelligi Herum Ecclesiæ, quæ ceu domus Dei de- scribitur, certum est. At quis nescit, particulariter in Novo Testamento Christum vocari Dominum Ecclesiæ, quam domum Christi esse, non diffiten- tur Adversarii. Adde quod proxime Christi men- tio facta fuerit, utpote cujus nomen omnia Eccle- siæ membra profitentur: Qua de causa recedere ju- bentur ab injustitia. Denique qui dubitari potest, quod Christus sit Dominus spiritualis Ecclesiæ herus absolutus & summus, quum is sit ὁ κατασκευάσας ἀυτὴν, qui fabricavit & præparavit eam, cujus proinde domus dicuntur omnes fideles, Ebr. III. 3. 6. Subjicimus denique locum Apoc. VI. 10. Oc- cisorum martyrum animæ clamant: Quousq́; non judicas ὁ Δεσπότης, ὁ ἅγιος, κ̓ ὁ ἀληθινὸς, quibus verbis compellari Christum inde colligitur, quod Christo omne judicium datum sit, isque omne judicium exequatur Joh. V, 22. Cui etiam τοῦ ἀληθινοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἁγίoυ nomen peculiariter vindicatur in hoc apocalypseos libro Cap. III, 7. τὰ δὲ λέγει ὁ ἅγιος, ὁ ἀληθινὸς, & vers. 14. ὁ πιστὸς κ̓ ἀληθινὸς. Quid? quod proprium ejus nomen esse dicatur Apoc. XIX. v. 11. καλόυμενος πιστὸς καὶ ἀληθινός, quod vocatur Fidelis & Verus.

Jam quod ad ἀγορασμὸν attinet, redemptionem pretio factam, adeoque satisfactionem designari contra Socinianos eandem negantes constat tum è propria vocis significatione, à qua discedendum non est, nisi cogat necessitas; quia ἀγοράζειν, & ἀγορασμὸς proprie notat redemptionem, quæ fit solutione pretii, non vero simplicem liberationem: tum è diserta pretii mentione, quod non corruptibili auro vel argento, sed pretioso sanguine Agni immaculati redempti simus, 1. Petr. I. vers. 18. 19. Apocal. V. vers. 9. & 1. Corinth. VI, 20. ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς, pretio enim redempti estis, tum ex adversariorum propria confessione. Socinus in synops. de justif. pag. 7. Redimendi verbum, inquit, pretio dato liberare significat, imo si ipsius verbi vim spectes, emtionem id omnino declarat, quæ sine pretio fieri nequit. Smalzius in Ex. 157. Error. n. 51. Fatemur, inquit, sanguinem Christi verum pretium esse redemptionis nostræ, & vim pretii in redimendis nobis habuisse, quia vere id nobis præstitit sanguis Christi, quod pretium in redimendo aliquo captivo præstat.

Quod autem ait, non adesse redemptionis proprie requisita, cum nemo sit, cui sanguis Christi datus sit pro nobis, in eo fallitur. Nam uti alia requisita adsunt, vers. 9. objectum redemptionis, quod sunt homines captivi, Zach. IX. vers. 11. Galat. III. vers. 10. 22. 23. Redemptor Christus, Rom. III, 24. & λύτρον, quod sanguis ejus est, Matth. XX, 28. Marc. X. vers. 45. Eph. I. vers. 7. Coloss. I. vers. 14. 1. Petr. I. v. 18. Ita nec deeft ille, cui λύτρον solvitur. Deo enim id persolvendum fuit, qui principaliter nos captivos detinuit, quum diabolus carcerarius tantum sit, è cujus manu nos redemit Christus, Ose. XIII. vers. 14. Deus vero, ceu justus Judex, nos carcere manciparit, & manui diaboli submiserit ob peccatum, vi justitiæ suæ, Gal. III. vers. 22. Rom. XI. vers. 32. Deo itaque præstita est solutio & satisfactio. Deo enim sese obtulit Christus, Eph. V, 2. Ebr. IX, 4. Cui autem se obtulit Christus in sacrificium pro peccatis nostris, eidem solutionem præstitit pro nobis. Deus ut vi justitiæ suæ λύτρον exegit pro nostri liberatione: Ita vi misericordiæ suæ ἀντίλυτρον suscepit vice nostri, quod pro nobis à Christo solutum est. Quæ vera est satisfactio, ut alias è natura satisfactionis ostendimus.

Cum autem Christus etiam eos redemisse dicatur, qui eum abnegant, & celerem perditionem sibi accersunt, potenter refelluntur Calviniani, qui solos electos à Christo redemptos esse dictitant. Temere autem Polanus, Tossanus, & Piscator hoc non κατ᾽ ἀλήθειαν, sed κατὰ δόξαν tantum dici contendunt. Nam ex mente propria loqui S. Petrum ipsa verba docent. Non dicit, qui putant, sed redemptos esse. Et quomodo id consonaret hæresi ipsorum, quæ est, negat Herum, qui ipsos redemit? Qui credit se redemptum esse à Domino, non negat Dominum Redemptorem, sed eo ipso agnoscit eundem. Adde quod effu- si gisse illi dicantur prius per cognitionem Christi in- quinamenta mundi vers. 18. 20. non apparenter, sed vere. Fuerunt ergo antea fideles, ab inqui- namentis mundi vere liberati, adeoque sangui- ne Christi a vana conversatione redempti, 1. Petr. I. vers. 18. Si dicas cum Estio: Bene quidem ex his verbis colligi, Christum redemisse quosdam repro- bos, nimirum illos, qui redemptionis ejus secun- dum aliquos effectus facti sunt participes, cujus- modi erant hi, de quibus Petrus loquitur, utpote per fidem in baptismo regenerati, & peccatorum veniam consecuti, licet postea in veterem peccati servitutem relapsi. Quae eadem est doctrina Con- cilii Valentini ante annos pene 800. in Gallia ha- biti Cap. V. affirmantis Christi redemptionem ad eos pertinere, qui etsi non salventur, quia non per- severant, baptismo tamen regenerati fuerunt, & in sanguine Christi a peccatis suis abluti. Sed ne hinc colligas, ad omnes omnino homines effectum redem- tionis extendi. Resp. Si illi effectus redemptio- nis Christi conveniunt reprobis per fidem, in ba- ptismo regenerari & peccatorum veniam conse- qui, oportet Christum reprobis etiam acquisi- visse regenerationem, & remissionem peccato- rum. Quid ergo desiderari hic potest in redem- ptione Christi? Ubi enim regeneratio, ibi hære- ditas, ad quam regeneramur, ubi remissio pec- catorum, ibi salus. Quod autem regenerationis, & remissionis peccatorum gratia excidunt (quod agnoscit Estius; Calviniani vero ἀδύνατον esse de veris fidelibus contendunt) id non arguit defe- ctum Redemptionis, sed culpam redemptorum: confirmat autem, vere ipsos redemptos esse; hanc vero redemptionem ad omnes extendi hinc con- stat, quod omnium captivorum, quod ad redem- ptionem, eadem sit ratio, & pro omnibus ἀντί- λυτρον solutum sit, 2. Tim. IV. vers. 6. Unde Cor- nelius à Lapide ad 2. Petr. III. fateri coactus est, errare, qui censent Christum non pro omnibus esse passum, sed tantum pro prædestinatis. Vid. Ebr. II. vers. 9. 2. Corinth. V. vers. 19. 1. Joh. II. vers. 1. Esa. LIII. vers. 4. seqq. Patet autem ex hoc loco, Calvinianos etiam esse inter eos, qui negant Do- minum, qui mercatus est illos, qui celerem sibi perditionem attrahunt, adeoque dogma eorum hæresin esse τῆς ἀπωλείας. Et quomodo in Chri- stum possunt credere, quod se redemerit, qui ne- gant, Christum omnes redemisse? Quomodo ap- plicare sibi possunt redemptionem & redemptio- nis pretium, qui omnes redemptos, pro omnibus pretium redemptionis solutum esse inficiantur? Vid. Gründlicher Beweiß Facultat. Theol. Wit- teb. daß die Calvinischen Irrthümer den Grund des Glaubens betreffen, und der Seligkeit nach- theilig seyen, part. II. cap. II. 248. seqq. Porro Pontificii, quia adjungunt Christo Redemptori & Mediatori Mariam, & Sanctos, cum operibus, me- ritis, & satisfactionibus propriis sese obtinere salu- tem posse ajunt, Christum unum esse herum, qui eos redemit, negant, &c.

Ἐπάγοντες ἑαυτοῖς ταχινὴν ἀπώλειαν.) Bello Barchochebæ, cui adhæserunt, ut homines mundani.

Non de perditione temporali, sed æterna, non de bello Barchochebæ, de quo nullum hic vesti- gium, sed de hæresi, ceu causa perditionis, hic agitur: Non eorum, qui Barchochebæ adhæsere, sed omnium, qui Herum abnegant, qui ipsos mer- catus est, Christum Jesum. Quid luculentius est, quam quod de eadem ἀπωλείᾳ agatur, à qua de- nominantur αἱρέσεις, quodque per eandem non bellum aliquod seditiosorum acceleretur illa ἀπώ-

λειαν. Denique quod per ταχινὴν ἀπώλειαν con- demnatio æterna denotetur vers. 3. luculentissi- me constat, ubi τὸ κρῖμα καὶ ἡ ἀπώλεια explica- tionis causa conjunguntur, & τὸ κρῖμα exemplo Angelorum, qui rudentibus inferni detracti in tartarum traditi sunt cruciandi, declaratur? Un- de Judas eos dicit olim ad illud judicium προγε- γραμμένους vers. 4. sive in vaticiniis, sive in decreto DEI judiciario.

## 2:2
Verse 2. And many shall follow their lasciviousness.

For they both gave love potions and held works of impurity ἐν ἀδιαφόροις [among things indifferent]. Irenaeus in the cited place and Epiphanius. Theodoret of them: Making licentiousness a law. The same author in another place calls Carpocrates and his associates teachers of lasciviousness and lawlessness. Augustine says of Carpocrates: He taught every shameful operation and every invention of sin.

Those love potions of shameless love have nothing to do with this. In some Codices ἀπωλείαις [destructions] is found, as Jerome also reads in the Greek Concordance of Stephanus, and Isidorus Clarius, Vatablus, Cajetan, and B. Luther have rendered it. But although the more approved Codices have ἀσελγείαις [lasciviousnesses], with which the parallel passage in Jude verse 4 and below verse 18 also agrees, as does the Syriac Interpreter. Therefore, the false teachers are described here by the lasciviousnesses which those who adhere to them imitate: not inebriated by love potions, but following the same vices by their own lust. However, it seems that not only a luxurious life is noted here, but primarily the doctrine by which many were to be seduced into luxuries. For those false teachers are said to be τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν χάριν μετατιθέντες εἰς ἀσέλγειαν [turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness], and he adds that they are τὸν μόνον Δεσπότην ἀρνόμενοι [denying the only Master], Jude verse 4. As this pertains to their doctrine, by which they deny that one Master: so also does that, that they transfer the grace of GOD into lasciviousness or petulance and forwardness. For ἀσελγὴς [lascivious] is also petulant and forward. B. Luther: They draw the grace of GOD into wantonness. That this has been done by many heretics, their catalogs teach, who fostered sins and luxuries or lasciviousnesses with their false and impious dogmas. The Simonians, Carpocratians, and Manichaeans said that the decalogue was not a precept of the law of GOD, but of some unfortunate nature. The same Simonians and Carpocratians, as also the Nicolaitans, wished for the use of wives to be common. The Cataphrygians approved of incest; the Adamites and Feri, in the manner of the Cynics, removed all shame. The Messalians established the Christian life in idleness and inertia, and said that it was permitted to lie. The Cerinthians placed eternal life in bodily pleasure; the Audaeans and others admitted anyone, even the most wicked, without repentance. How likewise the foundations of piety are undermined by the doctrines of the Photinians, Calvinists, and Papists, B. Gerhard has learnedly taught in special disputations.

By reason of whom the way of truth shall be blasphemed.] The evangelical doctrine, which is called ὁδὸς [way] (דֶּרֶךְ) Acts 20:9, below 15. Conversely, evil institutions also come under the name below 15, Jude v. 11. He says, however, that the Gospel will be ill-spoken of because of both their doctrine and their morals, because they also wished to be called Christians. Similar to Rom. 2:24, 1 Tim. 6:1, Tit. 2:5. Irenaeus concerning the Carpocratians: Nay, they themselves are sent by Satan for the detraction of the divine name and the Church, just as the Gentiles are, so that, according to one way or another, men hearing what is theirs, and thinking that we are all such, turn away their ears from the preaching of the truth, or seeing what is theirs, blaspheme us all. Epiphanius says the same in heresy 27. In the Manuscript it is ἡ δόξα τῆς ἀληθείας [the glory of the truth].

The pronoun ἧς [whose] ordinarily pertains to the nearer [antecedent], nor does it appear why it should be taken otherwise here. But the nearer was αὐτῶν [their] own, of the false teachers. Through them primarily the way of truth of the Christian religion was blasphemed, even by their own impious dogmas and most wicked life. For they wished to be considered Christians, which is evident not only of the Carpocratians but also of other heretics. The way of truth is a Hebrew phrase for doctrine divinely revealed and specifically the Christian religion, Acts 9:2, ch. 19:9, 23, ch. 22:4, ch. 24:14, which is called the way of salvation, as also the way of God, the way of the Lord. Compare Acts 16:17, ch. 18:25, 26.

Latin:

Vers. 2. Καὶ πολλοὶ ἐξακολουθήσουσιν αὐτῶν ταῖς ἀσελγείαις.

Nam & philtra dabant, & impudicitiæ opera habebant ἐν ἀδιαφόροις. Irenæus dicto loco & Epiphanius. Theodorews de illis : Νόμον τὴν ἀκολασίαν ποιούμενοι. Idem alio loco Carpocratem, ejusque socios vocat τῆς ἀσελγείας καὶ τῆς παρανομίας διδασκάλους. Docebat, ait de Carpocrate Au- gustinus, omnem turpem operationem, omnemque adinven- tionem peccati.

Nihil huc illa impudici amoris philtra. In non- nullis Codicibus habetur ἀπωλείαις, uti etiam Hieron. Stephani in Concord. Græc. legit, ac Isidorus Clarius, Vatablus, Cajetanus, & B. Luthe- rus reddidere. Sed quamvis probatiores Codi- ces ἀσελγείαις habeant, quibus consonat etiam locus parallelus Jud. vers. 4. & infra vers. 18. ut & Interpres Syrus. Describuntur ergo hic falsi Doctores ab ἀσελγείαις, quas imitantur illi, qui ipsis adhærent: non philtris inebriati, sed pro- pria libidine vitia eadem sectantes. Non autem tantum vita luxuriosa hic notari videtur, sed im- primis doctrina, qua ad luxurias seducendi erant plurimi. Nam falsi illi Doctores dicuntur τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν χάριν μετατιθέντες εἰς ἀσέλγειαν, addit- que quod sint τὸν μόνον Δεσπότην ἀρνόμενοι, Judæ vers. 4. Ut hoc ad doctrinam ipsorum pertinet, qua abnegant unum illum Herum : Ita etiam il- lud, quod gratiam DEI transferant in lasciviam vel petulantiam & proterviam. Ἀσελγὴς enim et- iam est petulans & protervus. B. Lutherus: Zie- hen die Gnade GOttes auff Muthwillen. Quod à multis hæreticis factum esse, docent eorum ca- talogi, qui peccata & luxurias vel lascivias fove- bant suis falsis & impiis dogmatibus. Simonia- ni, Carpocratiani, Manichæi decalogum legis non DEI, sed infaustæ cujusdam naturæ præceptio- nem dicebant esse. Iidem etiam Simoniani & Car- pocratiani, ut & Nicolaitæ uxorum usum communem esse volebant. Cataphryges incestus probabant, Adamitæ & Feri more Cynicorum omnem pudo- rem tollebant. Messaliani in otio & inertia vitam Christianam constituebant, & mentiri licere aje- bant. Vitam æternam in corporis voluptate Ce- rinthiani ponebant, sine pœnitentia quoslibet et- iam sceleratiffimos admittebant Audæani &c. Quo- modo item per doctrinas Photinianorum, Calvi- nianorum, & Pontificiorum fundamenta pietatis la- befactentur, peculiaribus disputationibus erudite docuit B. Gerhardus.

Δι' ὃς ἡ ὁδὸς τῆς ἀληθείας βλασφημηθήσεται.] Evangelica doctrina, quæ ὁδὸς דֶּרֶךְ dicitur Actor. XX, 9. infra 15. Con- tra & mala instituta nominę veniunt infra 15. Judæ v. 11. Dicit autem propter ipsorum & doctrinam & mores male au- diturum Evangelium, quia & ipsi dici volebant Christiani. Simile Rom. II. vers. 24. 1. Tim. VI. vers. 1. Tit. II, 5. Irenæ- us de Carpocratianis. Quin & ipsi ad detrectationem divini nominis & Ecclesiæ, quemadmodum & gentes à satana præ- missi sunt, uti secundum alium & alium modum, quæ sunt il- lorum audientes homines,& putantes nos omnes tales esse, aver- tant aures suas à præconio veritatis, aut ut videntes, quæ sunt illorum, omnes nos blasphement. Paria dicit Epiphanius hære- si XXVII. In Manuscripto est ἡ δόξα τῆς ἀληθείας.

Pronomen ἧς ad propinquius pertinet ordi- narie, neque hic aliter cur accipiendum sit ap- paret. Propinquius autem erat αὐτῶν ipsorum, Doctorum falsorum. Per illos πρώτως via veri- tatis religionis Christianæ blasphemabatur, ipsis etiam dogmatibus eorum impiis & vita pessima. Volebant enim haberi Christiani, quod non tantum de Carpocratianis, sed etiam aliis hæreti- cis constat. Via veritatis phrasi Ebræa est do- ctrina divinitus patefacta & speciatim religio Christiana, Actor. IX. vers. 2. cap. XIX. vers. 9. 23. cap. XXII, 4. cap. XXIV, 14. quæ via salutis dici- tur, ut & via Dei, via Domini. Conf. Act. XVI. v. 17. cap. XVIII. vers. 25. 26.

## 2:3
Verse 3.

And through covetousness shall they with feigned words make merchandise. With feigned names (for they used to pretend the names of faith and love, as Irenaeus and others teach us) they made merchandise through avarice. For ἐν [in] here, in the Hebrew manner, is equivalent to διὰ [through]. Those who promise salvation to those not correcting their life, they draw many disciples to themselves, and scrape together much from them, whence they live pleasantly. We have the verb ἐμπορεύεσθαι [to make merchandise] also in James 4:3. It corresponds to the Hebrew סחר, as can be seen in Gen. 34:21, ch. 42:34, 2 Chron. 9:14, Prov. 4:14, ch. 31:19, Ezek. 27:21. Cicero and others often use 'to make merchandise' in that sense.

Feigned words are proper to heretics, words skillfully and deceitfully constructed, not only putting forward a zeal for charity, but also flowing pleasantly under the guise of truth. Paul calls them in Rom. 16:18 χρηςολογία καὶ ἐυλογία [fair speech and flattery], by which they deceive the hearts of the simple. Covetousness is almost the pathognomonic vice of heretics, who are said to make merchandise for this reason, that they exercise a kind of market and negotiation with their heresy, which this word implies, Matt. 22:5, James 4:3.

Whose judgment now of a long time lingereth not, and their destruction slumbereth not. Long ago God determined to send impostors, by whom such men, being deceived, might perish most miserably, Matt. 24:24, John 5:43. But the words of Moses are not obscurely referred to, Deut. 32:35. Thus Jude, who transcribed most of this epistle, to show that what was predicted here had already happened. They who were of old written beforehand to this judgment, to whom it does not linger, that is, to whom it hangs over.

This divine destination is to be understood concerning the permission in 1 Kings XXII. verse 22, or concerning the judicial destination of the consequence of the will, lest God be established as the Author of imposture. However, the matter here is not about that which God destined concerning impostors, but about the judgment which threatens the impostors from God. Concerning the words of Jude in their proper place. Moreover, it cannot be asserted that the things which are predicted here happened at that time, unless it is certain that Jude was later than Simeon, Bishop of Jerusalem, whom Grotius believed to be the Author of this epistle. Which will be more correctly believed concerning Simon Peter. By the word ἔκπαλαι, reference is made to ἔκπαλαι; either divine reprobation made from eternity on account of foreseen final incredulity, Isa. XXX. verse 30, Matt. XXV. verse 34, or the Prophetic prediction of the Old Testament, as Dionysius holds: The judgment of reprobation long ago pronounced concerning them by the holy writers is not revoked, nor finished. Hugo & Glossa Interlin. The present verb οὐκ ἀργεῖ & μὴ νυστάζει refers to the present remorse of conscience, which is some part of Gehenna, but this is too narrow. It is not that the judgment is already beginning, but it is hinted that it will certainly come, or that it threatens sooner than expected. He who is idle and drowsy puts off what is incumbent upon him to perform. Therefore, he denies that the judgment and condemnation of these false Teachers is idle and drowsy, because at the time divinely appointed, it will oppress them both certainly and sooner than expected.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Καὶ ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ πλατοῖς λόγοις ἐμπορεύσονται. Fictis nominibus (prætexebant enim nomina fidei & dile- ctionis, ut Irenæus nos docet & alii) nundinabantur per ava- ritiam. Nam ἐν hic Ebræo more valet διὰ. Qui promit- tunt salutem, vitam non corrigentibus, ii multos discipulos sibi attrahunt, & ab illis multa corradunt, unde suaviter vi- vant. Verbum ἐμπορεύεσθαι habemus & Jac. IV, 3. Re- spondet Ebræo סחר, ut videre est Genes. XXXIV. vers. 21. cap. XLII. vers. 34. 2. Paral. IX. vers. 14. Proverb. IV. v. 14. c. XXXI, 19. Ezech. XXVII, 21. Nundinari eo sensu sæpe usurpat Cicero & alii.

Proprii sunt hæreticis πλαςοὶ λόγοι voces affa- bre, & dolose confictæ, non tantum charitatis studium præ se ferentes, sed etiam suaviter sub specie veritatis influentes. Paulo vocantur Rom. XVI. vers. 18. χρηςολογία καὶ ἐυλογία, quibus ἐξα- πατῶσι τὰς καρδίας τῶν ἀκάκων, πλεονεξία fere παθογνωμονικὸν hæreticorum vitium est, qui ideo ἐμπορεύεσθαι dicuntur, quod hæresi sua mercatu- ram quasi exerceant & negotiationem, quod vox hæc infert, Matth. XXII, 5. Jac. IV, 3.

Οἷς τὸ κρῖμα πάλαι ἐκ ἀργεῖ, καὶ ἀπώλεια ἀυτῶν ὐ νυσάζει. Pridem Deus destinavit mittere impostores, quibus tales homines decepti pessime pereant, Matth. XXIV, 24. Joh. V, 43. Respiciuntur autem non obscure verba Mosis, Deuter. XXXII. vers. 35. Sic Judas, qui pleraque hujus epistolæ transscripsit, ut ostenderet, quæ hic prædicta sunt, jam eve- nisse. Οἱ πάλαι προγεγραμμένοι εἰς τῦτο τὸ κρῖμα, οἷς ἐκ ἀργᾶ, id est, quibus impendet.

Destinatio hæc divina de permissione intelli- genda 1. Reg. XXII. vers. 22. vel de judiciaria vo- luntatis consequentiæ destinatione, ne Deus impo- sturæ Autor statuatur. Agitur autem hic non de eo, quod destinavit Deus circa impostores, sed de judicio, quod imminet à Deo impostoribus. De Judæ verbis suo loco. Eo autem tempore evenisse, quæ hic prædicta sunt, asseri nequit, ni- si constet Judam posteriorem fuisse Simeone Hierosolymitano Episcopo, quem Autorem hu- jus epistolæ credidit Grotius. Quod de Simone Petro rectius credetur. Voce ἔκπαλαι respicitur ἔκπαλαι; vel divina reprobatio ob prævisam finalem incre- dulitatem ab æterno factam, Esa. XXX. vers. 30. Matth. XXV. vers. 34. vel prædictio Veteris Testa- menti Prophetica, ut Dionysius habet: Reproba- tionis judicium dudum de iis pronunciatum à san- ctis scriptoribus non est revocatum, neque fini- tum. Hugo & Glossa Interlin. verbum præsens ἐκ ἀργεῖ & μὴ νυσάζει ad præsentem conscientiæ remor- sum, qui pars gehennæ nonnulla est, refert, sed hoc angustius est. Non quod jam incipiat, sed quod certo venturum sit judicium, vel opinione citius immineat, innuitur. Qui otiatur & dormitat, il- le quid peragendum sibi incumbit, differt. Negat ergo judicium, & damnationem horum falsorum Doctorum otiari, & dormitare, quia tempore di- vinitus constituto, & certo & opinione citius eos opprimet.

## 2:4
Verse 4.

For if God did not spare the angels who sinned.)

He treats of those angels whom Jude calls 'those who did not keep their own beginning, but left their own habitation': whose head 'did not stand in the truth,' John 8, verse 42, and drew many others with him, of whom that one in Genesis 3, verse 1, was denoted.

But having cast them into chains of gloom, he delivered them to be kept for judgment.)

Jude: 'He has kept them in eternal chains under gloom for the judgment of the great day.' The book which is attributed to Enoch said for the same: 'subjected to chains in the earth.' But to understand these things, Philo on Abraham brings us light: 'And the light in the wilderness is pure and unmixed with darkness, but in the air beneath the moon it appears mixed with gloomy air.' Thus also Plutarch in his book on Homeric poetry says that Hades is 'air,' adding: 'For he calls this gloomy air, such as it is, not having it from itself, but it is illuminated by the sun and the moon and the other stars.' But those apostate angels, when they had had their seat in the highest heaven, the dwelling place of the purest light, were thrust down from there below the entire starry region into the places of the air near the earth, whence their Prince is called 'ruler of the authority of the air,' Ephesians 2, verse 2. But they are called chains or bonds, just as Pindar also, speaking of the souls of the impious, calls it an 'inescapable yoke,' that law of God which forbids demons to wander beyond assigned places, nay, not even to act except by permission, Revelation 20, verse 2. But 'to cast into Tartarus' is nothing other than to cast down. For 'Tartarus' is so called because it is the lowest thing in any matter, whether in the earth, or in the water, or as here, in the air. Truly from the Syriac 'tahtha'. Homer called it 'gloomy Tartarus' in the Iliad 9, and in the same book: 'And deep Tartarus all around.' The same called it 'gloomy air' in the Iliad 15 and 21. But both this writer and Jude say that those deserting angels are kept in that air, as in a prison, until the day of judgment, when they are to bear punishments worthy of their crimes, which is indicated also in Matthew 8, verse 29.

Some think that 'kai' should be read instead of 'ei'. But since all the codices have 'ei', it must be established here as an 'anantapodoton' (a sentence with a missing apodosis), which seems to be the case to some: or, which I would prefer, it is to be connected to verse 9. If God did this, it is manifest from these examples, both that the Lord knows how to rescue his own from temptations, and indeed to reserve the unjust to be punished on the day of judgment. Which explanation I see is not disapproved of by the Greek scholia, but especially pleases Bede, who says regarding verse 9: 'Many verses are closed without one: the Lord knows how to rescue the pious from temptation.' Some place a 'meiosis' in the words 'did not spare,' as if the negation is used for the contrary affirmation: he did not spare, that is, he punished most severely. But there is no need for that: because it is 'emphatikoteron' (more emphatic), that he did not spare even them, just as it is said also of the only-begotten Son of God, that God did not spare him, Romans 8, verse 32. For 'alla' follows, but not explaining the punishment, as if already generically designated, nor exegetically, but it is to be understood in its proper sense or adversatively, namely that he so far from spared them, that he even, casting them into Tartarus with ropes of gloom, delivered them kept for judgment and condemnation. Where 'chains of gloom' are not referred to the projection into Tartarus, as if by those means he sent them down into hell, but to the word 'delivered,' that he delivered them kept by ropes or chains of gloom, as a means of custody. For 'chains,' Augustine in 'City of God' book 11, chapter 33, and book 21, chapter 23, as also in 'On the Nature of the Good' chapter 33, and also Fulgentius in book 1 'To Thrasimundus,' have 'prisons,' whether because they read it so, or because they used the name 'prisons' for 'enclosures,' as Ludovicus Vives notes regarding Augustine, or through a metonymy of the container for the contained they placed 'prison' for 'chains in prison'. The Vulgate rendered it 'rudentibus,' that is, nautical ropes; whence from ignorance of the Greek language some wrote 'rugientibus inferni' (roaring of hell), which

Bede refers the word either to heavenly pride or to wailing in punishments. Through 'chains' Bede understands pride. But because those chains of gloom look to punishment, not guilt, B. Gerhard makes this metaphorical sense, that God bound the devils with gloom as if with certain chains. And afterwards: 'Chains,' he says, 'by which evil angels are held bound after the fall signify (1) that they are restrained by divine power, so that they cannot harm men without God's permission. (2) That they have fallen from a state of happiness into extreme misery, from concreated liberty into servitude.' Thus far, therefore, Grotius's opinion can be admitted, that 'seirai' or 'desmoi' are that law of God, or divine power and sentence, by which they are bound as if by certain bonds, so that they cannot wander outside of hell at will, nay, not even do anything except by permission. The force of the Apostolic argument from a similar inference, Augustine, tractate 95 on John, we seek: 'Lest hard pride of mortals think that it is spared, it must be terrified by the punishment of the angels.' If God so turns away from the uncleanness of sin, that those golden vessels of angelic nature, adorned with the most precious gems of most shining gifts, for the very reason that he saw they had contracted the uncleanness and rust of pride, he crushed with the eternal sentence of condemnation as if with an iron rod, and cast into the dunghill of hell forever, what do you believe will happen to man, who is a vessel of clay and earth, when he has been defiled with the uncleanness and filth of sins? Although we have not precisely stated that the first sin of the devil was pride, which the Scholastics boldly affirm, since it is not for us to define anything certain when the Scriptures are silent, nevertheless it is not doubtful to us that in the fall of sin, elation against GOD had a place, just as he also seduced men to pride: In which sense Ambrose rightly in Book X, Epistle XXIV: Pride took its beginning from the devil, who, because he was pleased with his own power and dignity which he had received from the Creator, and compared himself to the glory of his Author, was cast down from heavenly sublimity along with those angels whom he had drawn into the consent of his impiety. See System. Theol. Vol. IV, chap. III, page 315.

As for the seat of the devil, which Grotius assigns to the places of the air near the earth, there are indeed not lacking those among the Fathers who maintain that demons are detained in the dark and foul air as if in a prison. But whether that opinion was transferred into the Church by philosophers, or arose from the words of the Apostle in Ephesians VI, verse 12, and Chapter II, verse 2, being less correctly understood, it deserves no approval. For as to the fact that the Apostle calls them τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις, Jerome indeed, whom Haymo follows, explained it as being in those things which are under the sky, that is, in the air. But in the Greek it is not ὑπεράνιος, but ἐπουράνιος; nor does it designate a place, but the object about which the malignant spirits are chiefly occupied, as we have taught regarding that passage. The ruler of the power of the air is called so in the other passage, not because he has his seat in the air, but because he not rarely exercises power there. Thus, therefore, nothing can be brought forward from the Scriptures for an aerial seat. To the book

Grotius betook himself to Enoch, and to Philo, Plutarch, and Homer; likewise to excellent interpreters of divine things, about whom we are to be informed only from the sacred writings. That the angels had their seat placed in the highest heaven above the starry firmament and the region of the highest planets is a human invention. Which heaven the Scholastico-Calvinian System. Theol. Vol. III.

Art. V. Quest. II. page 996. et seqq. we have destroyed. How then shall we believe that they were thrust down from that fictitious heavenly region into the air nearest to the earth? Nor indeed is the air designated by τάρταρον according to the sacred scriptures, which must be consulted here, not Homer or Plutarch, but the lowest and most profound seat of the underworld, which is called the abyss, Luke VIII. verse 31. Romans X. verse 7. Apocalypse IX. verse 1. chap. XI. verse 7. chap. XVII. verse 8. chap. XX. verses 1, 3. to which the name ζόφυς of darkness and ἅδης is more appropriate, on account of the extreme darkness, which is not assigned to the air, seeing that it has something of light mixed in, and is sometimes even serene, but to the abyss or hell. Who, I ask, will admit that Capernaum ἕως ἅδε, cast down even to the air, Matt. XI. verse 23, Luke X. verse 15, that πύλας ἅδε, the gates of the air, are spoken of, Matt. XVI. verse 18, that the soul of Christ was not to be left in the air, Acts II. verse 27, is asserted? Or will he explain the triumph of the elect thus: Where is your air, O victory? 1 Cor. XV. verse 15. Or will he believe that the air, along with death, is to be cast into the lake of fire according to Apoc. XX. verse 14. Away with such absurdities, where the sacred scriptures are to be handled!

It seems that this opinion also stuck with Grotius, that the devil does not yet feel punishment before the day of judgment, but will only feel it on the day of judgment. Although indeed demons are kept for the day of judgment bound in chains of darkness, they are not, however, currently devoid of punishment. Heavier punishments will certainly await the demons when they are judged on that all-judging day, and the devil will be cast into the lake of fire and brimstone with his angels, Matt. XXV. verses 41, 46. Apocalypse XX. verse 10. Therefore they complain, Matt. VIII. verse 29: Have you come here to torment us before the time? Which will also happen to the unfaithful: yet neither the former nor the latter experience no punishments in hell before the day of judgment, as was believed concerning the Sethian devils, and also concerning the impious Socinians and some of the Fathers. For as the impious suffer the torments of hell immediately after their departure, Luke XVI. verse 24 et seqq., so also the demons were cast into Tartarus immediately after they left their own οἰκητήριον, and are bound by eternal chains of darkness, verse 6 of the epistle of Jude. This is also hinted at here by the phrase: He did not spare those who sinned: Namely, that the judgment of GOD followed sin without delay, just as the Scholastics conclude from this that the demons sinned in such a way at the beginning that GOD granted them no delay of time for repentance. On which see Lorinus on this passage. Furthermore, that the punishment of evil angels will have no end, contrary to Origen and the Anabaptists, is evident from these very δεσμοῖς ἀϊδίοις. Compare Augustine, book XXI. de civ. Dei, ch. 23. But concerning the guilt and punishment of evil angels, see System. Theol. Vol. IV. Art. I. ch. III.

Latin:

Verf. 4.

Εἰ γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς Ἀγγέλων ἁμαρτησάντων οὐκ ἐφείσατο.)

Agit de illis Angelis, quos Judas vocat μὴ τηρήσαντας τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἀρχὴν, ἀλλὰ ἀπολιπόντας τὸ ἴδιον οἰκητήριον: Quorum caput ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ οὐχ ἕστηκεν, Johann. VIII. vers. 42. & mul- tos secum traxit alios, quorum fuit ille Gen. 3. vers. 1. deno- tatus.

Ἀλλὰ σειραῖς ζόφου ταρταρώσας παρέδωκεν εἰς κρίσιν τηρουμένους.)

Judas: Εἰς κρίσιν μεγάλης ἡμέρας δεσμοῖς ἀϊδίοις ὑπὸ ζόφον τετήρηκεν. Liber, qui Enocho tribuitur, pro eodem dixit: δεσμοῖς ὑποβληθέντας ἐν γῇ. Ad intelligenda autem hæc lu- cem nobis affert Philo de Abrahamo: Καὶ τὸ φῶς ἐν ἐρημίᾳ μὲν ἄκρατον καὶ ἀμιγὲς σκότους ἐστὶν, ἐν δὲ τοῖς ὑπὸ σελήνην ἀέρι ζοφερῷ κεκραμένον φαίνεται. Sic & Plutarchus libro de Ho- merica poësi, ᾅδην dicit esse ἀέρα addens: Τοῦτον γὰρ λέγει ζό- φον ἠερόεντα, ὁποῖός ἐστιν οὐκ οἴκοθεν ἐκ ἔχων, ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ ἡλίου καὶ σε- λήνης καὶ τῶν ἄστρων ἄλλων καταλάμπεται. Defectores autem isti Angeli, cum sedem habuissent in summo cœlo, domicilio purissimæ lucis, inde infra omnem astriferam regionem de- trusi sunt in aëris loca terræ propinqua, unde eorum Princeps ἄρχων τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ ἀέρος dicitur Ephes. 2. vers. 2. Dicun- tur autem σειραὶ sive δεσμοὶ, sicut & Pindaro de impiorum animabus loquenti ζεύγλαν ἄφυκτον, DEI lex illa, quæ dæ- monas ultra loca assignata vagari vetat, imo nec agere nisi ex permissu Apocal. XX. vers. 2. Ταρταρῶν autem nihil aliud est, quam dejicere. Nam τάρταρος dicitur, quod in quaque re infimum est, sive in terra, sive in aqua, sive ut hic in aëre. Nimirum ex Syriaco תחתא. Τάρταρον ἠερό- εντα dixit Homerus Iliados 9, & eodem libro: Βαθὺς δέ τε Τάρταρος ἀμφίς. Idem ζόφον ἠερόεντα Iliados Μ. & φ. Di- cit autem & hic Scriptor, & Judas, Angelos illos desertores servari in isto aëre, velut in carcere, in diem judicii, cum con- dignas laturi sunt suis criminibus pœnas, quod indicatur & Matth. 8. vers. 29.

Nonnulli καὶ pro εἰ legendum putant. Sed quum omnes Codices εἰ habeant, statuendum hic ἀνανταπόδοτον, quod quibusdam videtur: vel, quod malim, connectendus vers. 9. Si hoc Deus fecit, manifestum est ab his exemplis, tum quod suos ex tentationibus norit Dominus eripere, tum vero injustos ad diem judicii puniendos reserva- re. Quam etiam explicationem Græcorum scho- liis non improbari, sed imprimis Bedæ placere video, qui ad vers. 9. multi, inquit, versiculi sine uno clauduntur: novit Dominus pios de tentatio- ne eripere. In verbis μὴ ἐφείσατο μείωσιν quidam ponunt, quasi negatio pro contraria affirmatione adhibeatur: non pepercit, id est, gravissime pu- nivit. Sed ea opus non est: quia ἐμφατικώτε- ρον est, quod ne illis quidem pepercerit, quem- admodum dicitur & de Filio DEI unigenito, quod ei non pepercerit DEUS, Roman. VIII. vers. 32. Sequitur enim ἀλλὰ, sed non explicans pœnam, ceu jam generice designatam, nec exe- getice, sed proprio sensu vel adversative intelli- gendum, quod nempe adeo non pepercerit iis, ut etiam funibus caliginis eos in tartarum pro- jiciens tradiderit ad judicium & damnationem servatos. Ubi σειραὶ ζόφου catenæ vel funes ca- liginis non referuntur ad projectionem in tarta- rum, quod illis quasi mediis eos in infernum demiserit, sed ad verbum παρέδωκε, quod tra- diderit eos funibus vel catenis caliginis reserva- tos, ceu medio custodiæ. Pro catenis Augusti- nus XI. de civit. DEI cap. 33. & l. XXI. cap. 23. ut & de natura boni cap. 33. nec non Fulgentius l. I. ad Thrasim. habent carceribus, sive quod ita legerint, sive quod nomine carceribus pro claustris usi sint, ut Ludovicus Vives de Augusti- no monet, aut per Metonymiam continentis pro contento carcerem pro catenis in carcere posue- rint. Vulgatus reddidit rudentibus, hoc est, fu- nibus nauticis; unde ex ignorantia linguæ Græ- cæ nonnulli scripserunt rugientibus inferni, quod

Beda ad vocem vel supernæ elationis, vel ejulatus in pœnis refert. Per catenas Beda superbiam in- telligit. Sed quia ad pœnam, non culpam illæ caliginis catenæ spectant, Methaphoricum hunc sensum facit B. Gerhardus, quod caligine velut catenis quibusdam diabolos constrinxerit DEUS. Et postea: Catenæ, inquit, quibus mali Angeli post lapsum tenentur constricti significant (1.) quod divina potentia coërceantur, ne possint absque per- missione DEI hominibus nocere. (2.) quod ex statu felicitatis in extremam miseriam, ex liber- tate concreata in servitutem sint prolapsi. Hacte- nus ergo admitti potest Grotii sententia, quod σειραὶ vel δεσμοὶ sint lex illa DEI, vel potestas & sententia divina, qua veluti vinculis quibusdam constringuntur, ut vagari extra infernum pro lu- bitu non possint, imo nec agere quicquam nisi ex permissu. Vim argumenti Apostolici ex illatio- ne simili August. tract. XCV. in Johan. peti- mus: Ne sibi parci existimet superbia dura mor- talium, de supplicio superborum terrenda est An- gelorum. Si DEUS immunditiem peccati ita aversatur, ut vasa illa aurea Angelicæ naturæ, pretiosissimis donorum fulgentissimorum gem- mis ornata eo ipso, quod vidit immunditiem & æruginem superbiæ contraxisse, æterna damna- tionis sententia tanquam virga ferrea contrivit, & in sterquilinium inferni in æternum proje- cit, quid futurum credis de homine, qui vas est fictile & terreum, cum peccatorum immunditia ac fordibus fuerit inquinatum? Etsi autem præ- cise non dixerimus primum diaboli peccatum superbiam fuisse, quod Scholastici audacter affir- mant, cum Scripturis tacentibus nostrum non sit aliquid certi definire, non tamen dubium nobis est, in lapsu peccati elationem adversus DEUM locum habuisse, quemadmodum homines etiam ad superbiam seduxit: Quo sensu Ambrosius recte l. X. Epist. XXIV. Superbia à diabolo sumpsit ex- ordium, qui, quoniam sua, quam à Creatore ac- ceperat, potentia & dignitate sibi placuit, ses, Auto- ris sui gloriæ comparavit, cum iis Angelis, quos in consensum impietatis suæ traxerat, à cælesti subli- mitate dejectus est. Vid. System. Theol. T. IV. cap. III. pag. 315.

Quod ad sedem diaboli, quam assignat Gro- tius loca aëris terræ propinqua, non desunt qui- dem è Patribus, qui dæmonas aëre caliginoso, & tetro velut carcere detineri, statuant. Sed sive à Philosophis ea opinio in Ecclesiam traducta sit, sive enata ex verbis Apostoli Ephes. VI. vers. 12. & Cap. II. vers. 2. minus recte intellectis, calcu- lum minime meretur. Nam quod Apostolus eos vocat τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανί- οις Hieronymus quidem, quem Haymo sequitur, exposuit, in illis, quæ sub cælo sunt, hoc est, in aëre. Verum in Græco non est ὑπεράνιος, sed ἐπου- ράνιος; neque locum designat, sed objectum, cir- ca quod potissimum occupantur Spiritus ma- ligni, ut ad illum locum docuimus. Ἄρχων au- tem τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ ἀέρος dicitur altero loco, non quod sedem habeat in aëre, sed quod ibi pote- statem non raro exerceat. Sic ergo è Scripturis nihil afferri potest pro aërea sede. Ad librum

Enochi se contulit Grotius, & ad Philonem, Plu- tarchum & Homerum; item egregios rerum di- vinarum Interpretes, de quibus non nisi è sacris literis informandi sumus. In summo cœlo supra stelliferum firmamentum & regionem summa- rum Planetarum posito sedem habuisse Angelos, commentum est humanum. Quod cœlum Scho- lastico - Calvinianum System. Theol. Tom. III.

art. V. Quæst. II. pag. 996. seqq. destruximus. Quomodo ergo ex ista fictitia regione superna in aërem terræ proximum detrusos credemus? Neque vero per τάρταρον juxta sacras literas, quæ hic consulendæ sunt, non Homerus aut Plutarchus, aër designatur, sed ima & profundissima inferorum sedes, quæ abyssus vocatur, Luc. VIII. vers. 31. Roman. X. vers. 7. Apocal. IX. vers. 1. cap. XI. vers. 7. cap. XVII. vers. 8. cap. XX. vers. 1. 3. cui potius convenit ζόφυς caliginis nomen, & ἅδης, ob summam caliginem, quæ non in aëre, utpote qui admixtum aliquid lucis habet, quandoque etiam serenus est, sed in abysso vel inferno assignatur. Quis quæso Capernaum ἕως ἅδε usque ad aërem præcipitatam Matth. XI. vers. 23. Luc. X. vers. 15. πύλας ἅδε portas aëris dici, Matth. XVI. vers. 18. animam Christi non in aëre relinquendam Actor. II. vers. 27. asseri admittet? Aut triumphum electorum ita explicabit: Ubi aër tua victoria? 1. Cor. XV. vers. 15. Aut aërem cum morte in stagnum ignis præcipitandum credet juxta Apoc. XX. vers. 14. Apage tales ineptias, ubi sacræ tractandæ literæ!

Videtur & hoc opinionis hæsisse Grotio, quod diabolus nunc ante diem judicii nondum pœnam sentiat, sed demum in die judicii sensurus sit. Quanquam vero serventur dæmones in diem judicii catenis caliginis vincti, non tamen nunc expertes pœnæ sunt.
