Graviores sane manebunt dæmonas pœnæ, quando judicabuntur in die illo Pantocritico, inque stagnum ignis & sulphuris præcipitabitur diabolus cum angelis suis, Matth. XXV. vers. 41. 46. Apocalyps. XX. vers. 10. ideo queruntur Matth. VIII. vers. 29. Venisti huc nos torquere ante tempus: quod etiam infidelibus eveniet: nec tamen vel illi vel isti pœnas nullas experiuntur in inferno ante diem judicii, quemadmodum de diabolis Sethianis, de impiis etiam Socinianis ac nonnullis Patribus persuasum fuit. Nam ut impii statim post excessum inferni tormenta patiuntur, Luc. XVI. vers. 24. seqq. ita & dæmones in tartarum præcipitati statim sunt, postquam proprium οἰκητήριον reliquerunt, & vinculis caliginis æternis constringuntur, vers. 6. epist. Judæ. Id etiam hic innuit phrasis: Peccantibus non pepercit: Quod nempe sine mora judicium DEI sequutum sit peccatum, quemadmodum Scholastici inde colligunt, dæmones ita primo peccasse, ut nullam temporis moram ad resipiscentiam illis DEUS contulerit. Quo de conferendus Lorinus in h. l. Porro Angelorum malorum pœnam nullum finem habituram contra Origenem & Anabaptistas ex his ipsis δεσμοῖς ἀϊδίοις constat. Conf. Augustinus l. XXI. de civ. Dei c. 23. Sed de culpa & pœna malorum Angelorum vid. System. Theol. Tom. IV. Art. I. cap. III.

## 2:5
Verse 5.

Καὶ ἀρχαίε κόσμε ἐκ ἐφείσατο.] He calls the ancient world the race of men before the flood. Ἀλλ’ ὄγδοον Νῶε δικαιοσύνης κήρυκα ἐφύλαξεν.] It is a form of speech such as is found in Martial: Tell me how many and for how much you wish to dine. For he is said to be the eighth who was saved, who was one of the eight saved, 1 Pet. III, 20. But Noah is called a herald of righteousness, because he devoted all his effort to converting the men of his age to righteousness, that is, to a more upright life, as can be seen in the already mentioned passage of Peter, and Matt. XXIV, 37. Whence he is also said to have condemned that world, Heb. XI, 7. Κατακλυσμὸν κόσμῳ ἀσεβῶν ἐπάξας.] He rightly calls the world of the ungodly men who from their earliest age think of nothing good, such as are described in Gen. VI. Κατακλυσμὸς, a deluge, flood, inundation in the Glossary. We have this word

Matt. XXIV. verses 38, 39. Luke XVII. verse 27. Plato uses it often, but also Varro in Censorinus. ἐπάξας, said for exacto: hence the ἐπαγωγαὶ of Sirach, all evils sent by God.

The first example of divine judgment which the Apostle proposed to heretics and their followers were the evil angels. The second are the unfaithful men from Cain down to the antediluvians: such as are not those who in their first age think of nothing good, Gen. VI. verse 5. For this description is common to all mortals, the cause of which is original sin, as is evident from a comparison of the passage in Genesis VIII. verse 21 and the explanation of both provided in the commentary on Genesis; but those who, through unbelief, spurned Noah, the herald of the righteousness which is through faith in Christ, Heb. XI, 7. For the adequate cause of condemnation is ἀπιστία, John III. v. 18, Mark XVI. verse 16. For of whatever righteousness Noah was constituted an heir, that he also preached to the ancient world, so that it too might become an heir of the same righteousness, and because the antediluvian world neglected it, it was condemned. Noah was constituted heir of that righteousness which is by faith. Cf. our disputation on antediluvian faith. The Vulgate interprets the original world, whence Gagnejus thinks it read ἀρχικὸν, not ἀρχαῖον, which it wishes to signify not so much ancient, as rude and unskilled, as if to say: If God did not spare that world, still rude and unskilled and ignorant of divine things: What is He going to do to false teachers, who have turned aside from the way of truth once understood. But Lorinus refutes Gagnejus, and teaches that ἀρχαῖον denotes ancient: See Matt. V, verses 21, 27, 33. Luke IX, 8. Acts XV, verses 20, 21, chap. XXI, 16. Rev. XII, verse 9, chap. XX, verse 2. He says that men of the first age are designated, which he reckons from the transgression of the parents up to the time of the flood.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Καὶ ἀρχαίε κόσμε ἐκ ἐφείσατο.] Antiquum mundum vocat hominum genus ante diluvium. Ἀλλ’ ὄγδοον Νῶε δικαιοσύνης κήρυκα ἐφύλαξεν.] Est loquutio, qualis apud Martialem: Dic quotus & quanti cupias cœnare. Nam octavus dicitur servatus, qui unus fuit ex octo servatis, 1. Petr. III, 20. Dicitur autem Noe præco justitiæ, quia operam omnem dedit, ut homines suæ ætatis ad justitiam, id est, ad vitam rectiorem converteret, ut videre est dicto jam Petri loco, & Matth. XXIV, 37. unde & mundum illum damnasse dicitur, Ebr. XI, 7. Κατακλυσμὸν κόσμῳ ἀσεβῶν ἐπάξας.] Merito κόσμον ἀσεβῶν vocat homines à prima ætate nihil boni cogitantes, quales describuntur Gen. VI. Κατακλυσμὸς diluvies, diluvium, inundatio in Glossario. Habemus hanc vocem

Matth. XXIV. vers. 38. 39. Luc. XVII. vers. 27. Utitur Pla- to sæpe, sed & Varro apud Censorinum. ἐπάξας, exacto dictum : inde ἐπαγωγαὶ Siracidæ, omnia mala divinitus immissa.

Primum judicii divini exemplum, quod hæ- reticis eorumque sectatoribus proposuit Apo- stolus, mali angeli fuere. Alterum sunt homines infideles inde à Caino antediluviani : quales non sunt in prima ætate nihil boni cogitantes, Gen. VI. vers. 5. Hæc enim descriptio est communis omnibus mortalibus, cujus causa est peccatum originale, ut è collatione loci Genes. VIII. vers. 21. & utriusque explicatione in commentario ad Ge- nesin tradita patescit; sed qui Noam præconem ju- stitiæ, quæ est per fidem in Christum, Ebr. XI, 7. per incredulitatem spreverunt. Causa enim con- demnationis adæquata est ἀπιστία, Joh. III. v. 18. Marc. XVI. vers. 16. Cujus enim justitiæ hæres constitutus est Noah, eam etiam prædicavit mun- do antiquo, ut & ille ejusdem justitiæ hæres eva- deret, eamque quia mundus antediluvianus ne- glexit, condemnatus est. At justitiæ illius hæres constitutus fuit Noah, quæ est per fidem. Conf. disputatio nostra de fide antediluv. Vulgata mun- dum originalem interpretatur, unde Gagnejus pu- tat legisse ἀρχικὸν, non ἀρχαῖον, quod non tam antiquum significare vult, quam rudem & impe- ritum, q. d. Si Deus seculo illi rudi adhuc & im- perito, rerumque divinarum ignaro non peper- cit: Quid facturus est falsis Doctoribus, qui à via veritatis intellecta deflexerunt. Sed refellit Gagnejum Lorinus, & ἀρχαῖον priscum notare do- cet: Vid. Matth. V. vers. 21. 27. 33. Luc. IX, 8. Act. XV. vers. 20. 21. cap. XXI, 16. Apoc. XII. vers. 9. cap. XX. vers. 2. designari ait homines ætatis primæ, quam à parentum censeat transgressione usque ad tempus diluvii.

## 2:6
Vers. 6. And turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah into ashes, condemned them with an overthrow.

It is the custom of the LXX interpreters to speak of Sodom in the plural, as Jerusalem, whom Matthew follows X, 15, 23, 24, Mark VI, v. 11, Luke X, 12, chap. XVII, verse 29. Nor does Strabo do otherwise. Τεφρώσας, turned to ashes. Strabo says that all that land is ash-colored. Solinus says it crumbles into loose dust. He compares those places to a brand snatched from the fire, Amos IV, verse 11. καταστροφὴ, subversion, destruction. In the Glossary. It corresponds to the word הפכו in this very history, Gen. XIX, 29.

Making them an example to those who should live ungodly.

Take Ὑπόδειγμα here for an example, as in James V, 10. The ungodly can see in it what punishment awaits them. For that was a specimen of eternal fire, as Jude says, v. 7.

The third example of divine judgment is that of the Sodomites. For the Apostle wished to use examples of judgment that were both most ancient and universal, so that all might beware of the cause of judgment, sin; and as for examples of judgment exercised against men from the ancient world, he brought forward the hearers of Noah, whom he wished to lead to repentance and faith in the Messiah, as a herald of the righteousness of faith: But from the recent world, the illustrious example of the Sodomites, whom Lot the righteous, and the same herald of righteousness, likewise strove to convert, not only spurned by them, but most grievously afflicted; from which examples it is also evident, which is taught in 2 Peter III, verse 9, that God does not wish anyone to perish, but all to be converted to repentance; Jude also used the same example, verse 7. Moreover, he demonstrates this primarily by this example, that since God has most severely punished the ungodly, He will much more punish those who seduce to impiety: such as he notes here, the false teachers, denying the Lord who bought them, whose judgment does not idle, and whose damnation does not slumber. For such seduce to infidelity, and thus to impenitence. B. Gerhard observes that this example is brought forward, both because heresy is spiritual whoredom, and because those false Teachers were addicted to whoredoms. Concerning the cities of Σοδόμων (by which name two others destroyed by sulphur and heavenly fire, namely Adama and Seboim, seem to be included: perhaps because those were subject to the Sodomites) and Γομόῤῥας, see Gen. XIX. and what we have said concerning that history in our commentary and Bibl. Illustr. Τεφρώσας the Vulgate rendered reducing to ashes, the Syriac burned, consumed: another Syriac, made them ashes, as Dionysius interpreted it. Καταστροφῇ κατέκρινε, he condemned by utterly overturning, with which word καταστρέφειν the LXX Interpreters use in Gen. XIX. verse 25. 29. and it is to subvert in Matth. XXI. verse 22. Mark XI. verse 15. The word ὑποδείγματι involves not only the nature of an example but also of a type, Heb. VIII. verse 5. chap. IX. verse 23. which Jude explains in verse 7.

Latin:

Vers. 6. Καὶ πόλεις Σοδόμων καὶ Γομόῤῥας τεφρώσας καταστροφῇ κατέκρινεν.]

Σόδομα pluraliter dicere, ut Ἱεροσόλυμα mos est Interpre- tibus LXX. quos sequitur Matth. X, 15. 23. 24. Marc. VI. v. 11. Luc. X; 12. c. XVII. vers. 29. Nec aliter Strabo. Τεφρώσας cinefactas. Strabo terram illam omnem dicit esse τεφρώδη. Solinus fatiscere in vagum pulverem. Comparat ea loca tor- ri rapto ex incendio Amos IV. vers. 11. καταστροφὴ subversio, excidium. In Glossario. Respondet voci הפכו in hac ipsa historia Gen. XIX, 29.

Ὑπόδειγμα μελλόντων ἀσεβεῖν τεθεικώς.]

Ὑπόδειγμα hic sume pro exemplari, ut Jac. V, 10. Videre in eo possunt impii, quæ pœna ipsos maneat. Fuit enim illud δεῖγμα πυρὸς αἰωνίου, ut ait Judas v. 7.

Tertium exemplum judicii divini est Sodomo- rum. Voluit enim Apostolus uti exemplis judi- cii, & antiquissimis, & universalibus, ut omnes causam judicii, peccatum, caveant, & quoad exempla judicii adversus homines exerciti è mun- do antiquo adduxit auditores Noæ, quos ille ad pœnitentiam & fidem in Messiam perducere vo- luit, ceu præco justitiæ fidei: E mundo vero re- centi exemplum illustre Sodomorum, quos Loth justus, idemque justitiæ præco, pariter convertere sategit, non spretus tantum ab iis, sed gravissime afflictus, è quibus exemplis id etiam constat, quod 2. Petr. III. vers. 9. docetur, Deum non velle quenquam perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam con- verti, usus eodem exemplo est & Judas vers. 7. Demonstrat autem id imprimis hoc exemplo, quod cum gravissime DEUS impios puniverit, multo magis seductores ad impietatem punitu- rus sit: quales hic notat falsos Doctores, Domi- num, qui ipsos mercatus est, abnegantes, quo- rum judicium non otiatur, & quorum damnatio non dormitat. Tales enim seducunt ad infideli- tatem, adeoque ad impoenitentiam. B. Gerhar- dus observat hoc exemplum adduci, tum quia hae- resis est scortatio spiritualis, tum quia falsi illi Do- ctores dediti fuerint scortationibus. De civita- tibus Σοδόμων (quo nomine duae aliae sulphure & igni coelesti deletae, Adama nempe & Seboim com- prehendi videntur: forte quod illae Sodomitis sub- jectae fuerint) & Γομόῤῥας, vid. Gen. XIX. & quae ad istam historiam diximus in comment. & Bibl. Il- lustr. Τεφρώσας Vulgatus reddidit in cinerem re- digens, Syrus succendit, combussit : Syrus alter, fe- cit eos cineres, uti Dionysius interpretatus est. Κα- ταστροφῇ κατέκρινε, funditus evertendo damna- vit, qua voce καταστρέφειν utuntur LXX. Interpre- tes Gen. XIX. vers. 25. 29. estque subvertere Matth. XXI. vers. 22. Marc. XI. vers. 15. Vox ὑποδείγμα- τι non tantum exempli sed etiam typi rationem involvit, Ebr. VIII. vers. 5. cap. IX. vers. 23. quam explicat Judas vers. 7.

## 2:7
Vers. 7.

Καὶ δίκαιον Λώτ.] Thus he calls him, compared with those among whom he dwelt, although he had not reached the height of wisdom, as Philo says speaking of him in his book on the life of Moses.

Καταπονούμενον ὑπὸ τῆς τῶν ἀθέσμων ἐν ἀσελγείᾳ ἀναστροφῆς ἐῤῥύσατο.] It wearied him to live among such inhospitable and flagitious people. Whom he calls ἀθέσμους, because they did not live according to that primitive law, partly of nature, partly of tradition. Thus also ἄνομα ἔργα in the following member.

As an example of divine goodness and grace was inserted before in Noah: so now in the preservation of Lot. The word Καταπονέμενον implies not weariness but the oppression of Lot. See Acts VII. v. 24. 2 Maccab. VIII. verse 2. and Genesis XIX. verse 8. The Syriac explained it: Who was being crushed. That the Sodomites had only the law of nature and tradition, and that they are to be argued against because of its neglect, is by no means to be conceded. For they had Lot as a preacher of righteousness throughout. In Suidas ἄθεσμον is ἄδικον. They are therefore opposed to Lot the righteous, who was righteous through faith, and strove for true righteousness and holiness. But they, spurning both the righteousness of faith and the holiness which the teaching and example of Lot commended to them, remained ἀθεσμοι, and persevered in the conversation or perversity, as the Syriac rendered ἀναστροφὴν. Ἐν ἀσελγείᾳ, lasciviousness, or rather petulance and forwardness: because it was not only one kind of wickedness to which they were addicted, although they were particularly famous for impudicity and obscene lusts, Gen. XIX, 5. which it is clear are also especially looked to here from Jude verse 7. They were evil, says the Holy Spirit, Gen. XIX. verse 13. He adds for the sake of emphasis, and sinners, namely pre-eminently, and furthermore sinners before the Lord, who openly in the sight of GOD, without any fear of God, were prevaricating and transgressing the laws of the Lord. Finally, he adds an intensive particle: They were very great sinners, so that their sins cried out to heaven. It is expressed in detail in the said place, that they went after the flesh in concupiscence, that they were ἀῤῥενοκοῖτοι. Compare Genesis XIX. verse 5.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Καὶ δίκαιον Λώτ.] Sic eum vocat, comparatum cum illis, inter quos habitabat καί τοι γ' οὐκ ἐπ' ἄκρον ἧκε σοφίας, ut ait Philo de eo loquens libro, de vita Mofis.

Καταπονούμενον ὑπὸ τῆς τῶν ἀθέσμων ἐν ἀσελγείᾳ ἀναστροφῆς ἐῤῥύσατο.] Tædebat eum vivere inter tam inhospitales atque flagitio- sos. Quos ἀθέσμους vocat, quod secundum illam primævam partim naturæ, partim traditionis legem non viverent. Sic & ἄνομα ἔργα membro sequente.

Ut exemplum divinæ bonitatis & gratiæ in Noæ antea inserebatur: ita jam in Lothi conser- vatione. Verbum Καταπονέμενον non tædium sed oppressionem Lothi infert. Vid. Actor. VII. v. 24. 2. Maccab. VIII. vers. 2. & Genes. XIX. vers. 8. Syrus exposuit: Qui contundebatur. Habuisse So- domitas tantum naturæ & traditionis legem, ob eamque neglectam argui minime concedendum est. Nam habuere omnino Lothum Præconem justitiæ. Suidæ ἄθεσμον est ἄδικον. Opponuntur ergo Lotho δικαίῳ, qui per fidem justus erat, ac veræ justitiæ, & sanctitati studebat. Illi vero ut justitiam fidei ita & sanctitatem, quam doctrina & exemplo Loth illis commendabat, spernentes ἄθεσμοι permanebant, & in conversatione vel perversitate, uti Syrus ἀναστροφὴν reddidit, perse- verabant. Ἐν ἀσελγείᾳ, lascivia, vel potius pe- tulantia & protervia: quia non unum tantum ge- nus flagitii erat, cui ipsi dediti, etsi peculiariter ce- lebres fuerint ob impudicitiam & obscœnas libidi- nes, Gen. XIX, 5. quas etiam maxime hic respici ex Jud. vers. 7. liquet. Erant mali, inquit Spiritus sanctus Gen. XIX. vers. 13. Addit emphaseos cau- sa, & peccatores, scilicet ἐξοχικῶς, ac porro pecca- tores coram Domino, qui palam in DEI conspectu, sine ullo Dei timore, prævaricabantur, & leges Domini transgrediebantur. Denique αὐξητικὴν addit particulam: Erant peccatores valde, ut pecca- ta ipsorum in cælum clamarint. In specie exprimi- tur dicto loco, quod abierint post carnem in concupi- scentia, quod fuerint ἀῤῥενοκοῖτοι. Conf. Genes. XIX. vers. 5.

## 2:8
Verse 8.

For by sight and hearing the righteous man dwelling among them day after day was tormenting his righteous soul with lawless deeds.] They advise correctly, those who refer those words 'by sight and hearing' to 'was tormenting' and take this active verb as a reciprocal one. He was torturing himself not only because he heard, but also because he was forced to see their flagrant crimes; they sinned so openly, as is said in Gen. 13:13 and Isa. 3:9. 'Day after day' יום יום for sixteen years, that is, from the time he had departed from Abraham.

Grotius departs from the Vulgate, which rendered it:

For by sight and hearing the righteous man was, dwelling among them, who day after day were tormenting his righteous soul with unjust works. Although the verb 'was tormenting' is of the singular number, it can nevertheless be taken distributively: each one of the Sodomites was tormenting, namely with his 'lawless deeds,' with words and actions, which the righteous man, that righteous one who lived among them, was forced to hear and see; who was no less righteous in sight than in hearing, so that he could neither see such unjust deeds nor hear profane words without his soul being most grievously tormented by them and condemning them. Regarding the eulogy of Lot, Bede has this to say in this place: 'He conducted himself so circumspectly that neither by the sight of their flagrant crimes nor by the hearing of them did he stain the intuition of his chaste mind in any way, but with tireless intention he insisted upon the acts of his justice.' Or certainly he was righteous in sight and hearing, because those present saw nothing in him but works of justice and heard nothing but discourses, and fame spread nothing about him among those absent except what pertained to justice. However, the blessed Glassius prefers the other grammatical sense, S. page 274. 'By sight and hearing' (that is, wherever he had applied either his eyes or his ears, whatever he might perceive or hear) 'the righteous Lot, dwelling among them' (the Sodomites), 'day after day was tormenting' (ἐβασάνιζεν) 'his righteous soul' (his own) 'with the unjust works' (of the Sodomites), that is, he had continuous torments, and his soul felt them on account of those unjust works of the Sodomites. Beza: 'He dragged out a life anxious and consumed with sorrows, laboring no less than if he had been placed upon the rack.' The article 'the righteous one' seems to favor this opinion, and the blessed Luther does not deny it.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Βλέμματι γὰρ καὶ ἀκοῇ ὁ δίκαιος ἐγκατοικῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς ἡμέραν ἐξ ἡμέρας ψυχὴν δικαίαν ἀνόμοις ἔργοις ἐβασάνιζεν.] Recte monent, qui illa βλέμματι καὶ ἀκοῇ referunt ad ἐβα- σάνιζεν & verbum hoc activum sumunt pro reciproco. Cru- ciabat se non modo quod audiret, sed & quod videre cogere- tur eorum flagitia, adeo aperte peccabant, ut dicitur Gen. 13. v. 13. & Esa. 3. v. 9. ἡμέραν ἐξ ἡμέρας יום יום per annos nem- pe sexdecim, ex quo ab Abrahamo abierat.

Discedit à Vulgata Grotius, quæ reddidit:

Aspectu enim & auditu justus erat, habitans apud eos, qui de die in diem animam justam injustis ope- ribus cruciabant. Quanquam vero verbum ἐβα- σάνιζε numeri singularis sit, potest tamen distribu- tive accipi: Sodomitarum unusquisque cruciabat, scilicet ἔργοις ἀνόμοις iniquis operibus suis, verbis & factis, quæ cogebatur audire, & videre ὁ δίκαιος, justus ille, qui inter ipsos habitabat, qui non mi- nus aspectu, quam auditu justus erat, ut nec vi- dere talia iniqua facta, nec audire verba profana potuerit, quin gravissime illis torqueretur anima eademque reprehenderet. De elogio Lothi ita habet Beda in h. l. Tam circumspecte se gerebat, ut nec visis illorum flagitiis nec auditis in aliquo castæ suæ mentis fucaret intuitum, sed indefessa intentione cœptis suæ justitiæ insistebat actibus. Vel certe aspectu, & auditu justus erat, quia nihil in eo præsentes nisi justitiæ & opera cernebant, & audiebant eloquia, nihil fama de illo per absentes, nisi quod ad justitiam pertineret, vulgabat. B. Glas- sio tamen placet alter sensus Gramm. S. pag. 274. Aspectu & auditu, (hoc est, quocunque vel oculos vel aures applicuisset, quicquid cerneret vel audiret) justus Loth habitans apud eos (Sodomitas) de die in diem animam justam (suam) iniquis operibus (Sodomitarum) ἐβασάνιζεν excruciabat, hoc est, cruciatus continuos habebat, & anima sua sentiebat ob iniqua illa Sodomitarum opera. Beza: Anxiam ac doloribus confectam vitam trahebat non minus la- borans, quam si equuleo fuisset impositus. Cui sen- tentiæ favere videtur articulus ὁ δίκαιος, neque abnuit B. Lutherus.

## 2:9
Verse 9.

The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment.] It is the present for the future: 'being punished' for 'those who will be punished.' And from one noble example he infers a general judgment.

The inference from the preceding examples, both regarding the rescue of the faithful by the example of Noah and Lot, and regarding the reservation of the ungodly for the day of judgment by the example of the ancient world and the Sodomites, and indeed also of the evil angels. The verb 'knows' implies not only knowledge and power, but also thanks, according to the idiom of the Hebrews, by which words of knowledge include affection. 'The godly' are those who, by the example of Noah and Lot, apprehend the justice of Christ through faith and are devoted to true piety. Regarding the rescue of the pious, see Psalm 34:20, Psalm 91:7, Jer. 38:2, ch. 41:5, Ezek. 9:6, Amos 3:12. To these are opposed here the 'unjust,' who insist upon the footsteps of the Cainites and Sodomites in infidelity, various crimes, and impenitence. Who are reserved for the day of judgment 'being punished.' The 'day of judgment' is that day of the universal judge, Jude v. 5, ch. 3:7, Acts 17:31. For which they are reserved, not to be tormented only at long last, as the Vulgate rendered the Greek verb in the future, but 'having been tormented,' as the Syriac has it, or 'already giving satisfaction,' namely according to the soul, unless one prefers to understand them as 'tormented' or 'punished,' since they were taken from the midst by that horrible punishment, which nevertheless was the beginning of eternal torments for the impenitent. Whence Dionysius the Carthusian, from Bede, explains that 'to be tormented' thus: 'He says the unrighteous are reserved to be tormented for the day of judgment, not because they do not pay the penalties for their merits even before the day of judgment, having been released from the body, but because more severe torments await them in the judgment when the body is received, who are now tormented in the soul alone.'

PART II. PROSOPOGRAPHIA, concerning the vices and life of false Teachers.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Οἶδε κύριος εὐσεβεῖς ἐκ πειρασμϿν ῥύεσθαι, ἀδίκυς δὲ εἰς ἡμέραν κρίσεως κολαζομένυς τηρεῖν.] Est Præsens pro Futuro: κολαζομένυς pro κολασθησομέ- νυς. Et ex uno exemplo nobili sententiam infert generalem.

Illatio è superioribus exemplis tum quoad fi- delium ereptionem exemplo Noæ, & Lothi; tum quoad impiorum in diem judicii reservationem exemplo mundi prisci & Sodomorum, imo & Angelorum malorum. Verbum οἶδε non solum scientiam, & potentiam, sed etiam gratiam infert ex idiotismo Ebræorum, quo verba notitiæ af- fectum includunt. Εὐσεβεῖς sunt, qui exemplo Noachi, & Lothi per fidem justitiam Christi apprehendunt, ac pietati veræ dediti sunt. De piorum ereptione vid. Psalm. XXXIV. vers. 20. Psalm. XCI. vers. 7. Jerem. XXXVIII. vers. 2. cap. XLI. vers. 5. Ezech. IX. vers. 6. Amos III. vers. 12. Quibus ἄδικοι injusti hic opponuntur, qui Cai- nitarum & Sodomitarum vestigiis insistunt in in- fidelitate, variis sceleribus & impœnitentia. Qui reservantur in diem judicii κολαζόμενοι. Ἡμέρα κρίσεως est dies illa παντοκριτικὴ Jud. vers. 5. cap. III. vers. 7. Actor. XVII. vers. 31. In quam re- servantur, non olim demum cruciandi, ut ver- bum Græcum in futuro reddidit Vulgatus, sed cruciati, ut Syrus habet, vel pœnas jam dantes, scilicet secundum animam, nisi quis malit crucia- tos vel punitos intelligi, cum per horribile il- lud supplicium de medio sublati sunt, quod ta- men initium fuit quoad impœnitentes æternorum cruciatuum. Unde Dionysius Carthus. ex Beda illud cruciandos ita exponit: Iniquos dicit in diem judicii cruciandos reservari, non quia etiam an- te diem judicii soluti corpore non luant pœnas pro meritis, sed quia graviora eos in judicio tormenta exspectent corpore recepto, qui nunc in anima sola cruciantur.

PARS II. ΠΡΟΣΩΠΟΓΡΑΦΙΑ, Qua falsorum Doctorum vitia & vitam.

## 2:10
V. 10. But chiefly those who walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness.] To walk after is to follow, Luke 21:8. Jude said for the same thing, to go after other flesh. Moreover, by the word flesh we rightly understand here all flesh, whether of our own or of the other sex, which is not our own, that is, outside of marriage. All such things are pollutions שקצים. For only in marriage is the bed undefiled, Heb. 13:4. Irenaeus concerning the Carpocratians: They are so unbridled in madness that they say they have the power to practice all those things which are irreligious and impious. For they consider business to be good or evil only by human opinion. Epiphanius explains: An unspeakable and unlawful practice, which it is not lawful to bring upon the body. And every kind of sodomy, and more lustful intercourse with women in every member of the body.

From the doctrine of false Teachers bringing destruction, which he had confirmed by the judgment of the Angels who fell from God, and of the ancient world and the Sodomites, who not only perished temporally but are reserved for the final judgment to be afflicted with the eternal punishments of hell along with the evil Angels, he proceeds to the life of the false Teachers, and graphically describes their morals, of whom, although he has already noted some, avarice and licentiousness, which were implicated in their doctrine; here, however, he is properly occupied with the life itself and the vices to which he predicted the false Teachers would be addicted, not neglecting those things which resulted from the doctrine itself. Whom, therefore, he judges should be punished most especially, as being immersed not simply unjustly, but in the most grave and altogether most detestable crimes, and because they join a wicked life with a damnable doctrine. Of which vices he names first perverse lust not containing itself within the mind, but breaking forth with full force, noting those who walk after the flesh, who follow nefarious lusts, walking without discrimination after any flesh whatsoever (Compare Jude v. 6). In the lust of uncleanness (so the Vulgate) or rather of pollution; where the preposition in denotes not so much the way by which they walk, as the preceding cause which impels them to walk. Bede in this place, by those who walk after the flesh in lust, understands fornicators: the Apostle, who for the guilt of their corruption will suffer greater torments in judgment than general wicked men. Examples of such false Teachers, especially also of those who defile themselves with Sodomy, are most prevalent in Rome. Jerome, book III against Jovinian, testifies that the heresy of Jovinian being rampant, Rome had already been defiled in his own time by the filth of the Sodomitic crime. Udalricus, Bishop of Augsburg, in the ninth century wrote in an epistle to Nicholas I: That Papal Pontiffs, Bishops, and Clerics are driven so headlong into lust that they do not know how to shrink from the most shameful embrace of either males or beasts. Sixtus IV was a Sodomite, and granted that crime to be practiced by his familiar Cardinals for three summer months, June, July, and August. Julius III approved an apology for that crime. Johannes de la Casa, Archbishop of Benevento, composed an entire book on the praises of Sodomy, which Grappa and Anastasius also commended in public writings, as witnessed by Wolff, Vol. II, Memorabilia, page 421, etc.

And despising dominions.] Dominions is the abstract for the concrete, as in Eph. 1:21, Col. 1:16. But there it concerns Angels, here it concerns men: nor are dominions here anything other than authorities, Rom. 13:1. All those placed in commands. Thus also the Latins say powers.

Presumptuous, self-willed.] Presumptuous, full of heart, daring everything. Self-willed, contumacious, Tit. 1:7. Thus someone attacks the arrogance of the Stoics in Tacitus, adding that men become turbulent from that sect.

Glories, that is, those in glory, holding honor, namely, the higher authorities, Rom. 13:1. So far from reverencing those placed in the highest honors, that they even atrociously speak evil of them, against the precept of Exod. 22:28. To tremble here by metonymy is to revere, as in Dan. 5:19, ch. 6:26.

The other crime is the contempt of the Savior, or the only Redeemer, and the blasphemy of Christ the Lord, and that Master, of whom the Apostle had spoken in v. 1: which was likewise common to many heretics, and also dominates excellently in the Papacy. But it should be read dominion, not as the Complutensian and Royal Bibles have despising dominions: for this word is constructed not with the accusative, but with the genitive, which we judge should be understood of Christ, with Lyra, and the interlinear Gloss, and Cornelius à Lapide, not of Angels with Estius, nor of Magistrates with most recent writers, here comparing Luke 22:25, 1 Tim. 3:15, Acts 25:26. Some take it of Ecclesiastical Principalities: But the Apostles and Doctors of the Church are nowhere called dignities or powers; indeed, to rule is denied to them, Luke 22:25, 2 Cor. 1:24, 1 Pet. 5:3. For which name such persons are also called τολμηταὶ, bold, or as Grotius rightly says, daring everything, and thus holding the dominion of the Lord of lords in contempt, and despising it, and αὐθάδεις, proud, the Vulgate says 'pleasing themselves,' as if it were derived from αὐτὸς and ἅδειν, to please, or for others as if it were αὐτὸς ἐφ’ ἑαυτῦ, the same from himself, ἰδιογνώμονες. Whence the Vulgate rendered it 'proud' in Tit. 1:7. The Syriac in this place explained it as 'elated.' And to Hesychius, the synonyms are αὐθάδης, ὑπερήφαντος, θυμιώδης, παράνομος, αὐτάρεσκος, ἐξυσιαστικὸς, proud, unpleasant, lawless, self-pleasing, of one's own right. Blessed Luther: 'eigensinnig' (headstrong). All of which usually coincide, and are the cause of contempt for others. Therefore, also to the Greeks, αὐθάδες are refractory, stubborn. Augustine, in his book 'On Pastors,' ch. 8, says: 'In different places, he says, there are different heresies, but one mother, pride, has begotten them all.' To the same crime pertain those things which are added, δόξας οὐ τρέμουσι βλασφημοῦντες, Jude verse 8. δόξας δὲ βλασφημοῦσι, that is, according to some, the highest dignities, Emperors, Kings, Princes by metonymy, for glory belongs to these; (which is also Grotius's explanation) they do not revere, nay, they blaspheme. Others, however, prefer to explain it as 'they do not fear to blaspheme,' so that the participle, by a common Grecism, is put for the infinitive, as the Syriac and Blessed Luther rendered it. According to whom, blasphemy here denotes not reviling against God, but evil-speaking. To the exaggeration of this vice also contributes verse 11 and 12, concerning which Estius says thus: 'If, however, he says, one should prefer to understand by glories men excelling in glory (rather than angels), the exaggeration of their crime, who speak evil of these, taken from the angels, will nonetheless be valid.' But that blasphemy is taken properly, by which heretics were tearing apart the glories of Jesus our Lord, will be taught in the apostolic age concerning the parallel passage. But the Vulgate ineptly explained that δόξας οὐ τρέμουσι βλασφημοῦντες as: 'They do not fear to introduce sects, blaspheming.' For although δόξα may also signify an opinion, it is nowhere taken for a sect. Nor is there anything here about introduction. Jude simply says: Δόξας δὲ βλασφημοῦσι, who would render this 'but they blaspheme sects'? The Vulgate explained it: 'But they blaspheme majesty': which crime Cornelius a Lapide imputes to Blessed Luther. But he reproved the vices of the magistrate, he did not truly despise majesties, much less affect them with curses. But concerning the Popes, it is notorious how greatly they despise the supreme powers themselves, the Monarchs, casting them down from their throne if they do not wish to adore their decrees, and trampling them underfoot: who are ordered to kiss the feet of the Pontiffs, to provide water for their hands, to carry the chair in which they are carried, to hold the stirrup, to lead the horse by the hand. See Book III of the Roman Ceremonial, Title 2. They blaspheme the State of the Magistracy, as one in which a person can with difficulty be saved, and therefore they persuade them to abdicate the throne and enter a monastery: they excommunicate the same to the fourth and ninth generation. See B. Luther, book against the falsely called spiritual state. We pass over in silence that they exempt all Clerics from the power of the Magistrate, even if they commit the crime of high treason, and that they derogate from his authority in the matter of religion, which was once done by the Donatists, etc.

Latin:

V. 10. Μάλισα δὲ τὸς ὀπίσω σαρκὸς ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ μιασμῦ πο- ρευομένως.] Πορεύεσθαι ὀπίσω est sectari, Luc. 21, 8. Judas pro eodem dixit, ἀπελθῦσαι ὀπίσω σαρκὸς ἑτέρας. Ceterum voce σαρκὸς recte hic intelligimus omnem carnem, sive nostri, sive alterius sexus, quæ non est nostra, id est, extra conjugium. Omnia talia μιασμοὶ שקצים. Nam sola in matrimonio κοί- τη ἀμίαντος Ebr. XIII, 4. Irenæus de Carpocratianis: In tan- tum insania effrænati sunt, uti ea omnia, quæcunque sunt ir- religiosa & impia potestatem habere se operandi dicant. Sola enim humana opinione negotia bona & mala ducunt. Expli- cat Epiphanius: Ἀῤῥητυργίαν καὶ ἀθέμιτον πρᾶξιν, ἣν ὐ θεμιτὸν ἐπὶ σόμα[τος] φέρειν ἐπιπράττεσι. Καὶ πᾶν εἶδος ἀνδροβασίας, καὶ λαγνεστέραν ὁμιλίαν πρὸς γυναῖκας ἐν ἑκάσῳ μέλει σώματος.

A doctrina falsorum Doctorum exitium infe- rente, quod confirmaverat judicio Angelorum, qui defecerunt à Deo, & prisci mundi ac Sodomi- tarum, qui non tantum temporaliter interierunt, sed reservantur ad extremum judicium pœnis in- ferni æternis cum malis Angelis afficiendi, ad vitam progreditur falsorum Doctorum, moresque eorum graphice describit, quorum etsi aliquos jam nota- rit, avaritiam, & ἀσέλγειαν, qui doctrinæ ipsorum implicabantur; hic tamen in ipsa vita & vitiis, qui- bus deditos fore falsos Doctores prædixit, proprie occupatur, non neglectis iis, quæ ex doctrina ipsa redundabant. Quos proinde μάλιςα maxime, præ- cipue puniendos censet, ceu non ἀδίκως simpliciter, sed gravissimis omnino & maxime detestandis fla- gitiis immersos, & quia cum damnahili doctrina sceleratam vitam conjungunt. E quibus vitiis no- minat primo pravam libidinem non intra animum sese continentem, sed pleno impetu prorumpen- tem notans τὰς ὀπίσω σαρκὸς πορευομένως, quine- farias libidines sectantur, sine discrimine post carnem quamcunque ambulantes (Conf. Jud. v. 6.) Ἐν ἐπι- θυμίᾳ μιασμῦ in concupiscentia immunditiæ (ita Vulgata) vel potius pollutionis; ubi præpositio ἐν non tam viam, qua ambulant, quam causam προη- γεμένην, quæ ad ambulandum impellit, notat. Be- da in h. l. per eos, qui post carnem in concupiscentia ambulant, fornicatores intelligit: Apostolus, qui pro reatu suæ corruptionis majora in judicio, quam gene- rales iniqui tormenta patientur. Talium falsorum Doctorum, imprimis etiam eorum, qui Sodomia se coinquinant, exempla Romæ maxime prostant. Hieronymus lib. III. contr. Jovin. Vigente hæresi Joviniani jam dum suo tempore fœdata Romam fuis- se spurcitia sceleris Sodomitici, testatur. Udalricus Episc. August. seculo nono in epist. ad Nicol. I. scripsit: Pontifices, Episcopos & Clericos Papales in libidinem ita agi præcipites, ut nec masculorum nec pecudum turpissimo amplexu sciant abhorrere. Six tus IV. Sodomita fuit, & concessit illud flagitium familiaribus Cardinalibus tribus mensibus æsti- vis Junio, Julio & Augusto exercendum. Julius III. approbavit apologiam pro isto scelere. Jo- hannes de la Casa Archi-Episcopus Benevent. li- brum composuit integrum de laudibus Sodomiæ, quam etiam Grappa & Anastasius publicis scriptis commendarunt teste Wolffio Tom. II. Memorab. pag. 421. &c.

Καὶ κυριότητας καταφρονῦντας.] Κυριότητας est abstractum pro concreto, ut Eph. I, 21. Col.I, 16. Sed ibi de Angelis agi- tur, hic de hominibus: nec aliud sunt κυριότητες hic quam ἐξυσίαι Rom. XIII, 1. Omnes in imperiis positi. Sic & Lati- ni dicunt potestates.

Τολμηταὶ, αὐθάδεις.] Τολμηταὶ מלאים לב, nihil non audentes. Αὐθάδεις contumaces, Tit. I, 7. Sic Stoicorum ar- rogantiam apud Tacitum insectatur quidam, addito, ex ea secta homines turbidos fieri.

Δόξας, id est, τὺς ἐν δόξῃ, honore fungentes, summo scil. ἐξυσίας ὑπερεχόσας, Rom. XIII, 1. Adeo non reverentes in summis honoribus positos, ut etiam eis atrociter maledicant, contra præceptum Exod. XXII, 28. Τρέμειν hic per μετωνυ- μίαν est revereri, ut Dan. V, 19. c. VI, 26.

Alterum scelus est comtemtus Servatoris, vel Re- demtoris unici, & blasphemia Christi Domini, ac Dominatoris illius, de quo v. 1. dixerat Aposto- lus: quod pariter multis hæreticis commune fuit, & in Papatu quoque excellenter dominatur. Le- gendum autem κυριότητα, non uti Biblia Com- plutensia, & Regia habent κυριότητας καταφρονῦν- τας: nam Verbum hoc non cum accusativo, sed Genitivo construitur, quod de Christo intelligen- dum censemus, cum Lyra, & Glossa interlin. ac Cornelio à Lapide, non de Angelis cum Estio, ne- que de Magistratibus cum plerisque recentiori- bus, hic conferentibus Luc. XXII, 25. 1. Tim. III. vers. 15. Actor. XXV. vers. 26. De Ecclesiasticis Principatibus accipiunt nonnulli: Sed Apostoli, & Doctores Ecclesiæ nuspiam dignitates, vel po- testates nuncupantur, imo derogatur ipsis τὸ κυ- ριέυειν, Luc. XXII. vers. 25. 2. Corinth. I. vers. 24. 1. Petr. V. vers. 3. Quo nomine tales etiam di- cuntur τολμηταὶ audaces, vel ut recte Grotius, ni- hil non audentes, adeoque dominationem Do- mini dominantium despicuati habentes, ac sper- nentes, & αὐθάδεις superbi, Vulgatus sibi placen- tes, quasi dicatur ab αὐτὸς & ἅδειν placere, aliis quasi αὐτὸς ἐφ’ ἑαυτῦ idem ex seipso, ἰδιογνώμονες. Unde superbos Tit. I, 7. reddidit Vulgata. Syrus hoc loco elatos exposuit. Et Hesychio Synonyma sunt αὐθάδης, ὑπερήφαντος, θυμιώδης, παράνο- μος, αὐτάρεσκος, ἐξυσιαστικὸς, superbus, imcun- dus, exlex, sibi placens, proprii juris. B. Luthe- rus eigensinnig. Quæ omnia coincidere solent, & causa esse contemptus aliorum. Ideo etiam Græcis αὐθάδες refracti, pervicaces. Augusti- nus lib. de Pastoribus c. 8. Diversis locis, inquit, diversæ sunt hæreses, sed una mater superbia omnes genuit. Ad idem crimen spectant, quæ addun- tur, δόξας ἐ τρέμυσι βλασφημῦντες, Jud. vers. 8. δόξας δὲ βλασφημῦσι, hoc est, secundum non- nullos, summas dignitates, Imperatores, Reges, Principes per Metonymiam, his enim convenit gloria; (Quæ etiam est Grotii explicatio) non re- verentur, imo blasphemant. Alii tamen malunt ex- ponere, non metuunt blasphemare, ut Participium, usitato Græcismo, ponatur pro Infinitivo, ut Syrus & B. Lutherus reddidit. Juxta quos blasphemia hic non convitium in Deum, sed maledicentiam deno- tat. Ad exaggerationem hujus vitii facit etiam v. 11. & 12. de quo ita Estius: Si tamen, inquit, per glorias quis intelligere maluerit homines gloria præ- cellentes, (quam Angelos) nihilominus valebit cri- minis eorum, qui his maledicunt, exaggeratio ab An- gelis sumpta. Sed blasphemiam proprie accipi, qua δόξας Jesu Domini nostri proscindebant hæretici, Apostolorum ætate circa locum parallelum doce- bitur. Inepte autem Vulgata illa δόξας ὐ τρέμεσι βλασφημῦντες exposuit: Sectas non metuunt intro- ducere blasphemantes. Etsi enim δόξα opinionem quoque significet: nuspiam tamen pro secta acci- pitur. Nec de introductione hic quicquam habetur. Judas simpliciter: Δόξας δὲ βλασφημῦσι, quis hic reddat, sectas autem blasphemant. Vulgata exposuit: Majestatem autem blasphemant: quod crimen B. Luthero imputat Cornelius Lapideus. Sed hic vitia magistratus reprehendit, non vero majestates con- tempsit, nedum maledictis affecit. De Pontifici- bus autem notorium est, quantopere despiciant ipsas supremas potestates, Monarchas solio suo deturbantes, si placita eorum adorare nolint, pedi- busque concultantes: qui jubentur pedes Pontifi- cum osculari, aquam manibus præbere, sellam, qua vehuntur, portare, stapedem tenere, equum manu deducere. Vid. l. III. Cerem. Rom. Tit. 2. Blasphe- mant Statum Magistratus, utpote in quo difficulter quis salvari possit, ideo abdicato solio monaste- rium ingredi suadent: excommunicant eosdem in quartam & nonam generationem. Vid. B. Lutherus lib. contra falso dictum statum spiritual. Tacemus, quod Clericos omnes Magistratus potestati exi- mant, etiamsi crimen læsæ Majestatis committant, illique autoritatem in religionis negotio dero- gent, quod olim à Donatistis factum &c.

## 2:11
Verse 11.

Where Angels, being greater in strength and power.] Angels are more capable and powerful than Kings, as appeared in Egypt and in Sennacherib. Angels are called גברי כח, strong ones, powers, Psalm 103, verse 20.

They do not bring against them a blasphemous judgment before the Lord.] That 'before the Lord' is absent in the Manuscript, and rightly so. When Angels speak of Kings and Princes, whether impious or wicked, they never speak except modestly; not with curses, as can be seen both elsewhere and in 1 Kings 22:20, Daniel 4 and 12, and Zechariah 3. Naturally, even Angels show reverence to the power which God has granted them by special providence. A blasphemous judgment, or, as in Jude, a judgment of blasphemy, is vengeance, which is exercised by cursing. For 'judgment' is put for 'vengeance' (Prov. 6:34, Isa. 34:4, 35:4). They reserve that vengeance for God alone, just as Michael did against the devil, as one to whom even they themselves have been given a certain power by God, which is an argument from the greater that Jude adds.

Very many interpretations of this passage occur in Lorinus, Estius, and others, of which the blessed Gerhard has brought forward thirteen: among them the twelfth is that which Grotius made his own. But from the parallel passage of Jude, and also from the very words of Peter, it is clear that the discourse in this place is indeed about good Angels (not, as most expositions wish, about evil ones), such as Michael is, but not about Angels, since they have business with Magistrates, but where they are with the adversaries of their own nature, 'against them' instead of 'against themselves,' just as some Codices have, and sometimes those pronouns are accustomed to be interchanged, they do not bring against themselves, that is, against one another, a blasphemous judgment; which some explain as 'cursing'. For since they themselves are most holy Spirits, says Tirinus, and at the same time most pure, they shudder to bring against themselves an execrable judgment, that is, they shudder even to use a cursing or execratory word with their voice alone, lest they seem to contaminate their Angelic mouth even by a shadow; so Oecumenius, Sasboldus, Gagnejus, Clarius, Salmeron, à Lapide, and others: But by St. Jude v. 9 it is explained as a judgment of blasphemy, or concerning blasphemy. 'Before the Lord,' or in the sight of the Lord, whose sight they fear, and to whom they leave the judgment: which words the Complutensian and Royal Codices, and, as Luke of Bruges testifies, some Latin ones also have, even though the Vulgate and the Syriac omit them. Even if they (the Angels) are greater in strength and virtue than any false Doctors, even the most eminent ones (and thus the Pope himself!): or rather than devils, with whom the confirmation of strength is instituted: for they did not retain or keep their 'arche,' their Principality. In what manner Jude v. 9 speaks of Michael: And Michael the Archangel, when contending he disputed with the devil about the body of Moses, did not dare to bring a judgment of blasphemy, but said: The Lord rebuke you. Jerome handed down the sense in chapter 3 to Titus: The devil deserved a curse: But blasphemy ought not to have come out through the mouth of the Archangel. But more on the sense of the words of St. Jude in its proper place.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Ὅπου Ἄγγελοι ἰσχύϊ καὶ δυνάμει μείζονες ὄντες.] Angeli plus possunt pollentque, quam Reges, ut apparuit in Ægypto & in Sennacheribo. Vocantur Angeli גברי כח fortes, robora, Psalm. CIII. vers. 20.

Οὐ φέρουσι κατ' αὐτῶν παρὰ Κυρίῳ βλάσφημον κρίσιν.] Illud παρὰ Κυρίῳ abest in Manuscripto, & recte. Angeli cum de Regibus ac Principibus aut impiis aut vitiosis loquuntur, nus- quam loquuntur, nisi modeste; non eum maledictis, ut vide- re est tum alibi, tum 1. Reg. XXII, 20. Dan. IV. & XII. & Zach. III. Nimirum etiam Angeli reverentiam exhibent potestati, quam eis speciali providentia Deus concessit. Βλάσφημος κρί- σις, aut, ut apud Judam, est κρίσις βλασφημίας, est vindicta, quæ maledicendo exercetur. Nam κρίσις ponitur pro נקם Prov. VI, 34. Esa. XXXIV, 4. XXXV, 4. Deo soli vindictam illam reservant, sicut & contra diabolum, utpote cui & ipsi potestas quædam à Deo data sit, fecit Michaël, quod argumen- tum à majori addit Judas.

Plurimæ occurrunt hujus loci interpretatio- nes apud Lorinum, Estium, alios, quarum tre- decim adduxit B. Gerhardus: Inter eas duodeci- ma est, quam suam fecit Grotius. Sed è loco Ju- dæ parallelo, necnon ex ipsis Petri verbis patet, de Angelis quidem bonis, (non, ut pleræque ex- positiones volunt, de malis hoc loco sermonem esse) qualis est Michaël, sed non de Angelis, cum eis res est cum Magistratibus, sed ubi cum ἀντιπάλοις suæ naturæ, κατ' αὐτῶν pro καθ' ἑαυ- τῶν, quemadmodum quidam Codices habent, & quandoque illa pronomina permutari solent, non ferunt adversus seipsos, hoc est, adversus se mutuo judicium blasphemum; quod nonnulli exponunt maledicum. Cum enim ipsi sint Spiritus sanctis- simi, inquit Tirinus, simul & purissimi, horrent portare adversum se execrabile judicium, id est, horrent vel sola voce usurpare verbum maledicum vel execratorium, ne videantur vel per umbram os suum Angelicum contaminare; ita Oecumenius, Sasboldus, Gagnejus, Clarius, Salmeron, à Lapide & alii: Sed à S. Juda v. 9. exponitur κρίσις βλα- σφημίας judicium blasphemiæ, vel de blasphemia. Παρὰ Κυρίῳ coram Domino, vel in conspectu Domi- ni, cujus conspectum verentur, & huic relinquunt judicium: Quas voces Complut. & Regii Codd. ac teste Luca Burgensi, nonnulli etiam Latini habent, etsi Vulgata & Syrus omittant. Etsi robore & virtu- te majores sint (Angeli) quibuscunque Doctori- bus falsis etiam eminentissimis, (adeoque ipso- met Papa :) vel potius diabolis, quibus cum insti- tuitur fortitudinis confirmatio: illi enim neque retinuerunt vel servarunt ἀρχὴν, Principatum su- um. Quo pacto de Michaële Judas v. 9. Atque Mi- chaël Arch-Angelus, cum adversus diabolum certans disputaret de corpore Mosis, non est ausus judicium blasphemiæ ferre, sed dixit: Increpet te Dominus. Sen- sum ita tradidit Hieronymus in cap. III. ad Tit. Me- rebatur diabolus maledictum: Sed per Arch-Angeli os blasphemia exire non debuit. Sed de verborum S. Judæ sensu suo loco.

## 2:12
Verse 12. But these as irrational animals, naturally born for capture and destruction, in those things which they do not understand, blaspheming, in their own destruction shall be destroyed.

In the Manuscript: 'Naturally born.' But the Latin has 'by nature,' which I think is correct; thus they will perish, just as mute animals perish, which are destined by nature for this, that they may be caught and killed by men. He predicts the outcome of the war of Bar Kokhba. You have similar comparisons in Jer. 10:18, Ps. 141:10, Hab. 1:15. 'Irrational animals' are 'beasts.' He rightly says that this will happen to them, because they attack with curses those things which they do not understand. For they do not understand how great is the utility of empires 'in their destruction,' that is, when the time of their ruin has arrived. A metonymy. And 'in those things' is for 'into which.' See 2 Kings 19:6.

To these vices is added, by the antithesis of the understanding and blessed Angels to the false teachers, first the antecedent ignorance in blaspheming, from which that proud cursing arises, whether it be ignorance by negation, or of simple denial, of knowledge and lack of knowledge, or by disposition of a depraved state, or one affected and overflowing from arrogance: then the consequent destruction in corruption. C. à Lapide says that St. Peter compared the heresiarchs of his age, for instance the Simonians and Gnostics, because of pride, avarice, and lust, first to demons, second to impious men drowned in the flood and the Sodomites, and now thirdly he compares them to wild beasts, which are driven not by reason, but by the heat or fury of their bestial nature, and therefore they fall, or rather rush, and drag others with them into the snares of hunters, so that they may be caught and killed. However, there is no reason why we should purge the clear Greek fountain from the muddy Latin stream: not to mention that, with Erasmus, they can be called 'natural' for capture, just as one is born for learning, so that it is not necessary to say that one has read another Vulgate: just as B. Luther, reading nothing else in the Greek, rendered it: 'Those who are born for this by nature.' The sense from the Greek 'as irrational animals, natural' can be conveniently rendered as: like brute animals, natural, which are led only by nature or natural desires and impulses, not by reason, just as in 1 Cor. 9:14 the 'natural man' is spoken of, who uses only the natural light of reason, is led by animal affections, and is not ruled by the Spirit of God: which sense the mention of ignorance also confirms, as well as the parallel passage in Jude.

[They] are said to be born for capture and destruction, not actively, as if only rapacious animals were being noted; but passively, so that they may be captured and perish, just as in the apodosis to false teachers corruption is also attributed. Cf. James 5:5. In the words ἐν οἷς ἀγνοοῦσι βλασφημοῦντες, an ellipsis seems to be established in this way: Ἐν ἐκείνοις, ἃ ἀγνοοῦσι, and the preposition ἐν, after the manner of the Hebrews or against Gen. 26:12, Num. 12:1, Isa. 10:13, as if it circumscribes the accusative, is to be taken, as in Ps. 20:3, to call upon in the name, i.e., to blaspheme the name in these things, i.e., those things, who ἐν τῇ φθορᾷ ἀυτῶν καταφθαρήσονται, shall be corrupted in their corruption. Luther emphatically: They shall perish in their corrupt nature; whether you understand corruption as the pernicious cause, or as the punishment, or as the destruction itself, contracted by a just judgment. The former, however, is more agreeable. For the punishment is designated in the word 'shall be corrupted,' the guilt in the phrase 'in their corruption,' in their vices, by which they corrupt themselves. Brute beasts are led only by natural desires: but these men are not only prone by nature to depraved lusts, but also by a depraved habit of sinning. Those are born for capture and destruction; these, even if they are by nature children of wrath, could nevertheless escape through conversion, but they indulge in corruption, and in it they are lost on the day of judgment, as if by some snare of those about to be captured and to perish. Thus also in Jude verse 10, it is held concerning the corruption of both punishment and guilt, which verse corresponds to the twelfth verse in this Petrine passage. For what is said here 'blaspheming in those things which they do not know,' Jude expresses thus:

But these men, whatever they know, they blaspheme: what Peter says here ἐν τῇ φθορᾷ αὐτῶν καταφθαρήσονται, is rendered by Jude together with the preceding words ὡς ζῶα ἄλογα φυσικὰ thus: ὅσα δὲ φυσικῶς ὡς ἄλογα ζῶα ἐπίσανται ἐν τέτοις φθείρονται, which they know naturally like brute animals without reason by the sole aid of nature, so that they are carried away in that sensitive appetite, because the words of knowledge imply affection or appetite, as irrational animals are carried away into such things, e.g., food, drink, Venus, in these they are corrupted: of which the former is of guilt, the latter of punishment. For that punishment is being treated here, the following words in our text confirm.

Latin:

Vers. 12. Οὗτοι δὲ ὡς ἄλογα ζῶα φυσικὰ γεγενημένα εἰς ἅλωσιν καὶ φθοράν, ἐν οἷς ἀγνοοῦσι βλασφημοῦντες ἐν τῇ φθορᾷ αὐτῶν καταφθαρήσονται.]

In Manuscripto: Γεγενημένα φυσικά. At Latinus φύσει, quod rectum puto, ita peribunt illi, sicut pereunt muta animalia, quæ per naturam in id destinata sunt, ut ab hominibus capiantur & interficiantur. Prædicit exitum belli Barchochebæ. Similes comparationes habes Jer. 10, 18. Ps. 141, 10. Abac. I, 15. ἄλογα ζῶα sunt בעירים. Merito autem hoc eis eventurum ait, quia maledictis insectantur ea, quæ non intelligunt. Neq; enim intelligunt, quanta sit imperiorum utilitas ἐν τῇ φθορᾷ ἀυτῶν, id est, cum advenerit tempus exitii eorum. Metonymia. Et ἐν οἷς est pro εἰς ἅ. Vide 2. Reg. 19, 6.

Additur hisce vitiis per ἀντίθεσιν Angelorum intelligentium & beatorum ψευδοδιδασκάλων, tum antecedens ignorantia in blasphemando, è qua illa superba maledicentia, sive sit ignorantia κατ' ἀπόφασιν, vel simplicis negationis, scientiæ & inscitiæ, sive κατὰ διάθεσιν pravæ dispositionis, vel affectata ex ἀυθαδείᾳ redundans: tum consequens interitus in corruptione. Comparavit, inquit C. à Lapide, S. Petrus hæresiarchas sui ævi, puta Simonianos & Gnosticos, ob superbiam, avaritiam, & libidinem primo dæmonibus, secundo hominibus impiis mersis diluvio ac Sodomitis, nunc tertio comparat eos feris & bestiis, quæ non ratione, sed natura ferinæ ardore vel furore aguntur, ideoque incidunt, imo ruunt, aliosq́; secum trahunt in laqueos venatorum, ut capiantur & occidantur. Non est autem, quod ex Latino turbido rivo limpidum fontem Græcum repurgemus: ne dicam, quod cum Erasmo naturalia ad captionem dici possint, quemadmodum quis natus ad discendum, ut ita aliud legisse Vulgatum dicere opus non sit: quemadmodum nec B. Luth. aliud in Græco legens reddidit: Die von Natur darzu geboren sind. Sensus ex Græco ὡς ἄλογα ζῶα φυσικὰ commode reddi potest, velut bruta animalia, naturalia, quæ à natura sive naturalibus concupiscentiis & motibus tantum, non ratione ducuntur, uti 1. Cor. IX, 14. ψυχικὸς ἄνθρωπος dictus, qui naturali tantum rationis lumine utitur, animalibus affectibus ducitur, non vero Spiritu Dei regitur: Quem sensum etiam mentio ignorantiæ confirmat, nec non locus parallelus Jud.

Genita dicuntur ad capturam & perniciem non active, quasi animalia rapacia tantum notentur; sed passive, ut capiantur & pereant, quemadmodum in ἀποδόσει falsis Doctoribus φθορὰ etiam tribuitur. Conf. Jac. V, 5. In verbis ἐν οἷς ἀγνοοῦσι βλασφημοῦντες ellipsis videtur statuenda hoc modo: Ἐν ἐκείνοις, ἃ ἀγνοοῦσι, & Præpositio ἐν more Ebræorum vel contra Gen. XXVI, 12. Num. XII, 1. Es. X, 13. velut circumscribat Accusativum, accipienda, ut Ps. 20, 3. invocare in nomine, i. e. nomen blasphemare in iis, i. e. ea, qui ἐν τῇ φθορᾷ ἀυτῶν καταφθαρήσονται, in corruptione sua corrumpentur. Lutherus emphatice: Sie werden von ihrem verderblichen Wesen umkomen; sive φθορὰν intelligas de causa pernitiosa, sive de pœna, vel exitio ipso, justo judicio contracto. Prius tamen magis consentaneum est. Nam pœna in verbo corrumpentur, culpa in nomine in corruptione sua, in vitiis suis, quibus se corrumpunt, designatur. Bruta pecora naturalibus ducuntur tantum concupiscentiis: Hi vero non natura tantum proni sunt in pravas cupiditates, sed etiam prava peccandi consuetudine. Illa generantur in captionem & pernitiem, hi etsi natura filii iræ sint: evadere tamen possent per conversionem, sed indulgent corruptioni, inque ea perduntur in die judicii, ceu laqueo quodam capiendi & perituri. Sic etiam Judæ vers. 10. de corruptione & pœnæ & culpæ habetur, qui versus respondet duodecimo commati in hoc loco Petrino. Nam quod hic dicitur ἀγνοοῦσι βλασφημοῦντες, id Judas sic effert:

Οὗτοι δὲ ὅσα μὲν οἶδασι, βλασφημοῦσιν: quod hic Petrus ait ἐν τῇ φθορᾷ αὐτῶν καταφθαρήσονται, id à Juda una cum antecedentibus ὡς ζῶα ἄλογα φυσικὰ sic redditur: ὅσα δὲ φυσικῶς ὡς ἄλογα ζῶα ἐπίσανται ἐν τέτοις φθείρονται, quæ naturali- ter sicut bruta animalia citra rationem solo naturæ adminiculo cognoscunt, ita ut in eo appetitufen- sitivo ferantur, quia verba notitiæ affectum vel appetitum inferunt, uti animalia irrationalia fe- rantur in talia v. g. cibum, potum, Venerem, in iis corrumpuntur: quorum illud culpæ hoc pœnæ est. Nam de pœna hic agi verba sequentia in no- stro textu confirmant.

## 2:13
Ver. 13.

- Receiving the reward of unrighteousness.] Concerning this meaning of the word κομίζων we spoke at 1 Pet. V, ver. 4. Ἀδικίας here signifies a life outside the laws.

The Vulgate rendered it 'receiving'. But the Greek word is of the future tense, 'about to receive'. Although some explain ἀδικίαν as unrighteousness against the seventh Commandment, here, however, it is more correctly taken more generally, since it treats of the punishment of nefari- ous lusts, of contempt for the Lord, and also of banquetings and other vices. See 1 John V, 17; Rom. I, 15.

Ἡδονὴν ἡγόμενοι τὴν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τρυφὴν] it will perhaps have been τροφήν. They count it a pleasure to be pampered for the day, nor do they see that this is happening to them, as to cattle, which are soon to be slaughtered. Ἐν ἡμέρᾳ, that is, for a short time.

But why should the word τρυφήν not be retained? Which is read in all the codices, and agrees with the following word τρυφῶντες, and fits the present matter entirely, and corresponds to the Syriac text, which has 'delights': as this word is taken in Luke VII, ver. 25; Wisd. XIX, ver. 11. This is the third vice of the false teachers: thinking the pleasure of banquetings and delights to be τρυφήν, luxury and delights: Τὴν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ, which last for a short time, or as others explain, the day of this life. Oecumenius explains it as daily luxury. But thus it would be καθ' ἡμέραν, as in Luke XVI, ver. 19, or ἡμέραν from ἡμέρας as above ver. 8.

Σπίλοι καὶ μῶμοι.] Σπιλάδες of Jude, that is, disgraces of Christianity. Μῶμο- מום is a bodily defect, as can be seen in Lev. 21 and 25; Num. 19, 2; Deut. 15, 21; ch. 17, 1; but it is also transferred to the soul, as can be seen in Deut. 32, 5; as also ἄμωμο Eph. I, 4; ch. 5, 27; Col. I, 22; Heb. 9, 14; 1 Pet. I, 19; Jude ver. 24; Apoc. 14, 5. Σπίλο- filth, as we said at Eph. V, 27; whence σπιλῶν Jas. 3, 6; Jude v. 23.

Σπίλ properly signifies a spot, Eph. V, 26; ἀσπιλέω I spot, I contaminate, Jas. III, ver. 6; Jude v. 23. Μῶμο reproach from μωμάομαι to reproach, 2 Cor. VI, 3; ch. III, 20. The abstract, spot and defilements, or of disgrace, is put for the concrete, on account of emphasis, just as a notably wicked person is called 'wickedness' by the Latins.

Ἐντρυφῶντες ἐν ταῖς ἀπάταις ἀυτῶν συνευωχόμενοι ὑμῖν.] The Latin rightly reads ἀγάπαις, just as Jude also speaks, likewise subjoining συνευωχόμενοι ὑμῖν. But that ἀυτῶν, which the Arab does not read, must be removed. Ἀγάπαι were called those banquets in which rich and poor Christians used the same food. For by the expense of the rich, the poor were helped by that sort of refreshment, and therefore it was called what 'love' is among the Greeks, as Tertullian says in his Apologeticus. Those banquets were accustomed to be closed with the sacrament of the Lord's passion, as can be seen in Acts II, 42, 46; which custom remained in Africa on the very day on which the supper was instituted by the Lord, as we learn from the Councils and Augustine. And therefore formerly as much was eaten as the hungry could take: as much was drunk as was useful for the modest, as Tertullian says in the aforementioned book. But the historian Socrates teaches us that intemperance was first introduced into those agapae in Egypt, which was the reason why it was later instituted that the Sacrament should not be taken except by those who were fasting. That very intemperance is noted here, and it is shown that its origin was from the Carpocratians.

Nay, the Latin does not read correctly. For the Greeks constantly have ἀπάταις. Jude, however, adds the word ἀγάπαις for the sake of explanation, and that to the word σπιλάδες v. 12. Οὗτοι πίςιν ἐν ταῖς ἀγάπαις ὑμῶν σπιλάδες: Which are different. For here nothing else is said than that they are turning aside in their deceits, that is, those things which they have scraped together through deceits and frauds, as being those of which he foretold in ver. 3, ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ πλαστοῖς λόγοις ὑμᾶς ἐμπορεύσονται. To the word ἀπάταις also the pronoun ἀυτῶν fits better, which Grotius would therefore gladly strike out. But all the Greek Codices stand in the way; it also fits better what is added συνευωχόμενοι ὑμῶν, which the Vulgate renders 'luxuriating with you'. Augustine, in his book De Fide et Operibus ch. 25, more correctly [renders it] 'feasting together'. For ἐνωχία signifies a feast, and among Pollux a public banquet, and ἐνωχόμεν in Judith 1, 16 is 'holding luxurious banquets'. But luxury was already expressed here in the participle ἐντρυφῶντες: Here, therefore, public banquets are noted in general, which the false teachers, luxuriating in those things which they had amassed through deceptions, used to institute with their listeners, which Judas hints was also done by false teachers at the Agapae. Although in these [passages] it is predicted that this would happen regarding collections for the Agapae, but in those [passages] regarding what was scraped together through the fraud of seducers. Συνευωχόμενοι ὑμῖν is ἐνωχώμενοι σὺν ὑμῖν. How truly that was predicted, both by the examples of the ancient heretics in the very age of the Apostles, as the Pseudo-Apostles are a proof, and by the clergy of the Papists, of whom Blessed Luther [writes in] Vol. II, Jena German edition, fol. 112. Who, I ask, are they who live luxuriously as if on the goods of others? Who think it sufficient for themselves that delicacies of every kind are available? Does the text need a gloss? For it is known to the public that luxury reigns in the courts of Popes, Cardinals, Bishops, and Prelates. Platina in the life of Gregory IV: The ecclesiastical order has poured itself into every luxury. It is not necessary to speak of silver vessels and their royal furnishings, and of their food, since if you look at these, the feasts of Sicily, the Attalic ornaments, and the Corinthian vessels could be called of no value. Concerning which Bernard also complained in Sermon XXXIII on the Song of Songs: They are ministers of Christ, and they serve the Anti-Christ; they walk about honored with the goods of the Lord, to which Lord they do not render honor: hence the splendid table with both foods and cups, hence the carousings and drunkenness, hence the citharas and lyres and flutes, hence the overflowing winepresses and storehouses full, belching from this into that. For such things as these, the provosts of churches, deans, archdeacons, bishops, archbishops, etc., wish to be and are. What? That the same complaint is echoed even regarding monks bound by a vow of poverty by Erasmus in Method. Theolog. p. 139: they call themselves monks mixed into the bowels of the world, and while affecting royal luxury, they use mendicancy as a pretext. Ludovicus Vives in the book of Augustine De Civitate Dei, ch. 26: But if Augustine were to see now the wealthiest and most ample brotherhoods demanding alms from those to whom they should rather distribute their own, with which they overflow and abound, while meanwhile he who gave gnaws on dry and coarse bread, setting up a table of vegetables, and with earthenware vessels filled only with water, looked upon by his children, for whom he is anxious night and day and works intently, while he who received, an opulent beggar, buries himself in white and fine bread, partridges, capons, and generous wine. Cornelius Agrippa de vanit. scient. chapter on beggars: Hence those sects of friars, monks, and other mendicants were born, from whose number are those who, promising indulgences and dispensations, hunt for riches under the pretext of alms, etc., and think that by such arts of mendicancy and remarkable cunning of frauds (we have here the ἀπάτας noted by the Apostle) they offer themselves as most holy sacrifices to GOD and the saints, as often as they are laden with booty in that manner with great

At the expense of the people and the detriment of the Republic, the satellites of their household staff fatten the idle, etc. More may be seen concerning monastic luxury in Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, around the year 1180, book VI, epistle 87, and in countless others. Concerning the ἀπάταις (deceptions) also, by which they scrape together riches for such luxury, long-winded complaints are met with everywhere, e.g., concerning indulgences, taxes for penitentiaries, votive offerings, and others for the building of temples, for the feeding of the poor, and a thousand others. Nicholas of Clemanges, in his book describing the state of the Church, chapter XXII, p. 20, concerning monks: Are they not, he says, ravenous wolves, wearing the coverings of sheep, who assert with their own word that they have abandoned all things that are of this kind, but in the very act they seek out temporal things from every side with incredible ardor, desire, snares, frauds, and lies. Cf. Platina, book II, on the true good; Polydore Vergil, book VII, on the inventors of things. Grievances of the German Nation. In the year 1523; offered in the Diet of Nuremberg, etc.

Latin:

Verf. 13.

- Κομιόμενοι μισθὸν ἀδικίας.] De hoc significatu vocis κο- μίζων diximus 1. Petr. V. vers. 4. Ἀδικίας hic vitam extra leges significat.

Vulgatus reddidit percipientes. Sed Græcum verbum est futuri temporis reportaturi. Quan- quam vero aliqui ἀδικίαν de injustitia contra septi- mum Præceptum explicent, hic tamen rectius ge- neralius accipitur, siquidem de pœna tum libidinum nefariarum, tum contemptus Domini, tum etiam comeffationum & aliorum vitiorum agatur. Vid. 1. Joh. V, 17. Rom. I, 15.

Ἡδονὴν ἡγόμενοι τὴν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τρυφὴν] fuerit forte τροφήν. Voluptati ducunt saginari in diem, nec vident id sibi fieri, sicut pecoribus, quæ mox mactanda sunt. Ἐν ἡμέρᾳ, id est, ad breve tempus.

Cur vero non retinenda vox τρυφήν? Quæ & in codicibus omnibus legitur, & verbo sequenti τρυφῶντες convenit, & ad rem præsentem omni- no quadrat, textuique Syro, qui delicias habet, congruit: uti hæc vox accipitur Luc. VII. vers. 25. Sap. XIX. vers. 11. Tertium hoc vitium est Docto- rum falsorum: Comeffationum, & delitiarum vo- luptatem existimantes τρυφὴν luxum & delicias: Τὴν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ, quæ brevi durant tempore, vel quod alii explicant, die hujus vitæ. Oecumenius expo- nit de quotidiano luxu. Sed ita esset καθ' ἡμέραν, ut Luc. XVI. vers. 19. vel ἡμέραν ex ἡμέρας ut su- pra vers. 8.

Σπίλοι καὶ μῶμοι.] Σπιλάδες Judæ, id est dedecora Christia- nismi. Μῶμο- מום est vitium corporis, ut videre est Levit. 21. & 25. Num. 19, 2. Deut. 15, 21. c. 17, 1. sed & ad animum transfertur, ut videre est Deut. 32, 5. ut & ἄμωμο Eph. I, 4. c. 5, 27. Col. I, 22. Ebr. 9, 14. 1. Petr. I, 19. Judæ vers. 24. A- pocal. 14, 5. Σπίλο- sordes, ut diximus ad Ephes. V, 27. unde σπιλῶν Jac. 3, 6. Judæ v. 23.

Σπίλ maculam proprie significat Eph.V, 26. ἀσπιλέω maculo, contamino Jac. III. vers. 6. Judæ v. 23. Μῶμο vituperium à μωμάομαι vituperare 2. Cor. VI, 3. cap. III, 20. Abstractum macula, & inquinamenta, vel dedecoris, ponitur pro concreto, propter emphasin, quemadmodum insigniter sce- leratus scelus Latinis dicitur.

Ἐντρυφῶντες ἐν ταῖς ἀπάταις ἀυτῶν συνευωχόμενοι ὑμῖν.] Recte Latinus legit ἀγάπαις, quomodo & Judas loquitur, itidem subjungens συνευωχόμενοι ὑμῖν. Sed auferendum il- lud ἀυτῶν, quod Arabs non legit. Ἀγάπαι dicebantur convi- via illa, in quibus Christiani divites & pauperes pari victu utebantur. Divitum enim sumptu pauperes isto quasi refri- gerio juvabantur, ideoque id vocabatur, quod dilectio apud Græcos, ut in Apologetico ait Tertullianus. Ea convivia clau- di folebant sacramento Dominicæ passionis, ut videre est Act. II, 42. 46. qui mos ipso die, quo instituta est à Domino cœna, mansit in Africa, ut ex Conciliis & Augustino discimus. Ideo- que olim edebatur, quantum esurientes caperent: bibebatur, quantum pudicis erat utile, ut ait dicto libro Tertullianus. At docet nos historicus Socrates in Ægypto primum introdu- ctam in illas agapas ἀκρασίαν, quæ causa fuerit cur postea institutum sit, ut ne Sacramentum, nisi à jejunis sumeretur. Ea ipsa ἀκρασία hic notatur, oftenditurque ejus origo fuisse à Carpocratianis.

Imo non recte legit Latinus. Nam Græci con- stanter habent ἀπάταις. Judas vero explicationis causa addit vocem ἀγάπαις, idque ad vocem σπι- λάδες v. 12. Οὗτοι πίςιν ἐν ταῖς ἀγάπαις ὑμῶν σπι- λάδες: Quæ diversa sunt. Hic enim nihil aliud dicitur, quam quod sint declinantes in deceptioni- bus suis, hoc est, iis, quæ per deceptiones & fraudes corraserunt, utpote de quibus vers. 3. prædixit ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ πλαστοῖς λόγοις ὑμᾶς ἐμπορεύσονται. Voci etiam ἀπάταις rectius convenit pronomen ἀυτῶν, quod proinde libenter excuteret Grotius. Sed obstant omnes Græci Codices; convenit etiam melius, quod additur συνευωχόμενοι ὑμῶν, quod Vulgatus reddit luxuriantes vobiscum. Rectius Au- gustinus libr. de fid. & operibus c. 25. coëpulantes. Nam ἐνωχία significat epulum, & apud Pollucem convivium publicum, & ἐνωχόμεν Judith. 1, 16. est luxuriosa convivia agitans. Sed luxuria hic jam in participio expressa erat ἐντρυφῶντες: Hic ergo notantur in genere convivia publica, quæ Docto- res falsi luxuriantes in iis, quæ per deceptiones coacervarant, cum auditoribus suis instituebant, quod in Agapis quoque fieri à falsis Doctoribus Judas innuit. Quamvis in his de collectis ad aga- pas, in istis autem de corrasis per fraudem sedu- ctorum id futurum prædictum sit. Συνευωχόμενοι ὑμῖν est ἐνωχώμενοι σὺν ὑμῖν. Quam vere id prædi- ctum, tum veterum hæreticorum exemplis con- stitit ipsorum etiam Apostolorum ætate, ut do- cumento sunt Pseudo-Apostoli, tum Cleri Ponti- ficiorum, de quibus B. Lutherus Tom. II. Jenens. Germ. fol. 112. Quinam sunt, quæso, qui quasi alio- rum bonis luxuriose vivunt? Qui sufficere putant sibi omnis generis delitias suppetere? Num textus in- diget Glossa. Nam in aulis Pontificum, Cardina- lium, Episcoporum ac Prælatorum luxum regnare in vulgus notum est. Platina in vita Greg. IV. In omnem luxum se effudit ordo Ecclesiasticus. De ar- genteis vasis, & Regia eorum fupellectile, deque ciba- riis non attinet dicere, cum & Siciliæ dapes, & Atta- lica ornamenta & vasa Corinthia, si hæc inspicias, nullius pretii dici possint. Quo de etiam Bernhardus serm. XXXIII. in Cant. questus est: Ministri Chri- sti sunt, & Anti-Christo serviunt, honorati incedunt de bonis Domini, cui Domino honorem non defe- runt: Inde splendida mensa & cibis & scyphis, inde comeffationes & ebrietates, inde citharæ & lyræ & tibiæ, inde redundantia torcularia & promptuaria plena ex hoc in aliud eructantia. Pro hujusmodi vo- lunt esse & sunt Ecclesiarum Præpositi, Decani, Ar- chi-Diaconi, Episcopi, Archi-Episcopi &c. Quid? quod etiam de Monachis paupertatis voto adstri- ctis eadem querela ingeminetur ab Erasmo in Method. Theolog. p. 139. ipsos mundi visceribus im- mixti monachos se vocant, & Regium luxum affectan- tes mendicitatem prætexunt. Ludov. Vives in libr. Aug. de Civ. Dei c. 26. Quod si nunc videret Au- gustinus ditissima & amplissima sodalitia ab iis po- scere stipem, quibus deseret potius sua impertiri, qui- bus redundant & affluunt, cum interea, qui dedit, arrodat siccum & cibarium panem, olerum mensam instruens, & fictilibus vasis aqua duntaxat plenis, liberis circumspectus, pro quibus noctes & dies solici- tus operi intentus agit, qui accepit opulens mendicus candido & siligineo pane, perdicibus, capisque gene- roso vino, ac lenti se obruat. Cornelius Agripp. de vanit. scient. cap. de mendicis: Hinc illa fratrum, Monachorum, cæterorumque quæstuariorum scete nate sunt, è quorum numero sunt, qui indulgentias & dispensationes pollicentes eleemosynarum prætextu venantur divitias &c. putantq; per hujusmodi men- dicitatis artes, insignesque fraudum versutias (ha- bemus hic ἀπάτας ab Apostolo notatas) sese DEO atque sanctis sanctissima offerre sacrificia, quoties ad istum modum onusti prada magno

Populi dispendio ac Reipublicæ detrimento sui famu- litii satellites saginent otiosos &c. Plura videan- tur de luxu Monastico apud Petr. Cluniacensem Abbatem circa ann. 1180. l. VI. epist. 87. & in- numeros alios. De ἀπάταις etiam quibus di- vitias ad ejusmodi luxum corradunt, prolixæ querelæ passim obviæ sunt, v. g. de indulgentiis, taxic Pænitentiariis, donariis votivis, aliisque pro templorum ædificatione, pro alendis pauperibus & mille aliis. Nicolaus de Clemangis libr. descript. Eccles. stat. cap. XXII. p. 20. de Monachis: An- non, inquit, lupi rapaces sunt, velamina ovium gestantes, qui omnia, qua hujusmodi sunt, verbo suo se deseruisse asserunt, facto autem ipso tempora- lia incredibili ardore concupiscentia, insidiis, frau- dibus atque mendaciis undique exquirunt. Conf. Platina l. II. de vero bono, Polydorus Virgilius l. VII. de rerum inventoribus. Gravamina Na- tion. German. Anno 1523; in Comitiis Norimb. ob- lata &c.

## 2:14
Verse 14. Having eyes full of an adulteress. In the manuscript: μοιχαλίας (of adultery): which I think is correct, so that it is from μοιχαλὶς (adulteress), μοιχαλία (adultery), just as from μοιχὸς (adulterer), μοιχεία (adultery). And the Latin reads thus, which translates it as 'of adultery,' saying 'eyes full of adultery,' doing nothing else but enticing women to adultery. For great is the power of the eyes in love, as we said on Matthew V, v. 28. Add Proverbs VI, 26; Sirach XXVI, 1.

And unceasing sin. The Latin reads better as ἀκαταπαύσε (unceasing). Their eyes do not only pursue adulteries, but also other foul things, and that assiduously. In the Glossary: Ἀκατάπαυσος, inaccessible, unceasing. It is the same as השקט לא יוכל (cannot be quiet) Isaiah LVII, 20.

Enticing unstable souls. They easily bait souls. But whose? The inconstant. The word δελεάζειν (to bait/entice) is very proper for this matter, which is also found in James I, 14 and below 18. Thus also you have ἀστηρίκτες (unstable) below III, 16.

Having a heart exercised in covetousness. He repeats the colors often, so that they may be better known. The manuscript also has πλεονεξίας (of covetousness), not πλεονεξίαις (with covetousnesses), as other codices. And it is a participle for a verbal, in the Hebrew manner, as if you were to say, a heart skilled in avarice. It is no wonder if doctors who grant leave to sin attract many disciples and make profit from it, as we have already said before.

Children of a curse. בני ארורים (cursed children). But the locution is such as Matthew XI, 19; 1 Peter I, 14; John XVII, 12; Ephesians II, 2. Thus בן הכות (son of smiting) is translated as worthy of stripes, Deuteronomy XXV, 1.

From a gluttonous throat it proceeds to eyes full of adultery, and restless from sin (namely, the lustful looks of women, or from lust) to the tongue, by which they bait (they persuade and entice with flattering words, as the Syriac rendered it, and bait into sins, James I, 14) unstable souls (men not sufficiently grounded in the study of faith and piety: Jerome: They deceive souls not yet robust in the charity of Christ), and finally to a heart exercised in avarice. The former of these still pertain to the voluptuous life of those false doctors: the latter specifically explains their notable avarice: whence he said πλεονεξίας (of covetousness) in the plural (according to the more approved codices), in which they are especially exercised from long study: which are also directed to this end, that they may have that from which they can live luxuriously. Their punishment is added again, while they are called κατάρας τέκνα (children of a curse), that is, cursed men, by a common Hebraism. But this fourth kind of vice, namely avarice, he now pursues more fully and illustrates with the example of Balaam the false prophet.

We do not concern ourselves with the petulant Grotius-like emendations of the original text, since they are of no necessity, nor is it permitted to depart from the consenting Greek codices on account of a single manuscript which suffers from various faults, or a Latin version teeming with countless errors. For why can it not be said 'having eyes full of adultery'? Either because the concrete is put for the abstract in the Hebrew manner, as Deuteronomy XXIX, 19; Daniel IX, 24; Ephesians VI, 12; or because it is implied that those lustful men carry the adulteress as it were in their very eyes, and look at nothing else but adulteresses for the sake of fulfilling their lust. As Oecumenius says: Furthermore, while they feast with you, they do not do it out of charity, but so that they may find an opportunity to deceive women. For these, while they have eyes, look at nothing else but adulteresses. B. Luther explains the eyes of an adulteress thus, loc. cit. What are the eyes of an adulteress? Without doubt a wanton, bold, and impudent life: Just as an impudent adulteress casts her eyes on anyone and prostitutes herself to anyone. Furthermore, why can it not be said that false doctors have unceasing eyes of sin, as some Latin codices also have: that is, they have eyes that do not know how to cease from sinning, they do not desist from sin, as soon as they look at a woman with their eyes, they burn with the flames of lust toward her. From seeing comes loving. Cf. Job XXXI, 1; Ambrose, book on Joseph, ch. 3. The first weapons of an adulteress are her eyes, the second are her words, but he who is not captured by the eyes can resist the words. Cyprian, book on the simple, serves for the explanation of the place. Prel. They are utterly insane, he says, they burn with desire for women, as many as do not yield to this prohibition, and gaping at obscenities they prefer to die than to be content to be torn away by any separation from the sides of women, so that to satisfy the gluttony of their greed they are not without the pleasure of a woman even for a point of time, and they have this fruit in women, that with their intention always fixed upon them they may satiate the desires of their eyes, so that not even any moment may pass when they are in need of what they crave. Thus integrity dies among them, where every dwelling together, whether by winking at or by living together, is defiled by corrupt affections, which S. Peter designated, saying: Having eyes full of adultery. We see here, however, both that spiritual and bodily whoredom are for the most part joined together: and that false teachers are accustomed to be given to avarice, just as Jerome pronounces in book III on Zechariah, chapter XIV, concerning heretics, that they do everything for the sake of gain and glory.
