The Papacy provides examples of both in abundance: which were previously touched upon in part.

Latin:

Vers. 14. Ὀφθαλμὸς ἔχοντες μετὲς μοιχαλίδος.] In Manuscripto μοιχαλίας: quod rectum puto, ut sit à μοιχαλὶς μοιχαλία, sicut à μοιχὸς μοιχεία. Et ita legit La- tinus, qui vertit adulterii, oculos plenos adulterii dicit, nihil agentes aliud, nisi ut mulieres ad adulteria alliciant. Magna enim in amoribus vis oculorum, ut diximus Matth. V. v. 28. Adde Prov. VI, 26. Sir. XXVI, 1.

Καὶ ἀκαταπαύσες ἁμαρτίας.] Melius legit Latinus ἀκαταπαύσε. Oculi eorum non adul- teria tantum sectantur, sed & alia fœda, idque assidue. In Glossario: Ἀκατάπαυσος, inaccessibilis, indesinens. Idipsum est השקט לא יוכל Esa. LVII, 20.

Δελεάζοντες ψυχὰς ἀστηρίκτες.] Inescant facile animos. At quos? inconstantium. Vox δελεάζειν valde est huic rei propria, quæ invenitur & Jac. I, 4. & infra 18. Sic & ἀστηρίκτες habes infra III, 16.

Καρδίαν γεγυμνασμένην πλεονεξίας ἔχοντες.] Sæpe repetit colores, ut melius noscantur. Πλεονεξίας ha- bet & Manuscriptus, non πλεονεξίαις, ut Codices alii. Et est participium pro verbali, more Ebræo, quasi dicas, cor peritum avaritiæ. Doctores, qui commeatum dant peccandi, non mi- rum est, si multos discipulos attrahant, & inde lucrum faci- ant, ut jam ante diximus.

Κατάρας τέκνα.] בני ארורים. Sed loquutio est, qualis Matth. XI, 19. 1. Petr. I, 14. Joh. XVII, 12. Eph. II, 2. Sic בן הכות vertitur ἄξιος πληγῶν, Deut. XXV, 1.

A gula luxuriante progreditur ad oculos plenos adulterio, & irrequietos à peccato (videlicet aspe- ctus libitinosi mulierum, vel à libidine) ad lin- guam, qua inescant (verbis adulatoriis persuadent & alliciunt, ut Syrus reddidit, & ad peccata in- escant, Jacob. I, 14.) animas ἀςηρίκτες, (homines in fidei & pietatis studio non satis fundatos: Hie- ronymus: Decipiunt animas necdum Christi chari- tate robustas) ad cor denique avaritia exercitatum. Quorum priora ad vitam voluptuariam illorum fal- sorum Doctorum adhuc pertinent: posterius ava- ritiam eorum insignem peculiariter explicat: un- de πλεονεξίας in plurali (juxta probatiores Codi- ces) dixit, in quibus ex diuturno studio imprimis exercitati sint: quæ etiam eo directæ sunt, ut ha- beant, ex quo luxuriari possint. Additum ite- rum supplicium eorum, dum κατάρας τέκνα filii maledictionis, id est, homines maledicti per usita- tum Ebraismum dicuntur. Quartum autem hoc vitiorum genus, avaritiam nempe uberius jam persequitur & exemplo Bileami Pseudo-Prophetæ illustrat.

Petulantes textus originalis emendationes Gro- tianas nihil moramur, quum nullius sint necessita- tis, nec ob unicum Manuscriptum, quod variis la- borat vitiis, aut Latinam versionem erratis innu- meris scatentem, à Græcis Codicibus consentien- tibus discedere liceat. Quidni enim dici possit ocu- los habentes plenos adulterii? Sive quod concretum pro abstracto more Ebræo ponatur, ut Deuter. XXIX, 19. Dan. IX, 24. Eph. VI, 12. sive quod in- nuatur libidinosos istos adulterum quasi in ipsis ocu- lis gestare, & nihil aliud quam adulteras libidinis implendæ causa spectare. Quomodo Oecumenius: Quin etiam dum vobiscum epulantur, non ob charitatem id faciunt, sed ut occasionem ad deci- piendas mulieres nanciscantur. Hi enim cum ocu- los habeant, non aliud, quam adulteras aspiciunt. B. Lutherus oculos adulteræ ita explicat l. c. Quid sunt oculi adulteræ? Procul dubio proterva, procax & impudens vita: Sicut impudens adultera oculos in quosvis conjicit, & cuivis se prostituit. Porro quid- ni dici possit habere falsos Doctores oculos inceffa- biles delicti, ut Latini etiam Codices nonnulli ha- bent: id est, habent oculos à peccando cessare ne- scios, non desistunt à peccato, quamprimum fœ- minam oculis intuentur, flammis libidinis erga eam exardescunt. Ἐκ τῦ ὁρᾷν γίνεται τὸ ἐρᾷν. Conf. Job. XXXI, 1. Ambrof. l. de Joseph. c. 3. Prima adulteræ oculorum tela sunt, secunda verborum, sed qui non capitur oculis, verbis potest resistere. Expli- cationi loci inservit Cyprianus l. de simpliciter. Præl. Insaniunt, inquiens, prorsus, ardent desiderio fœmi- narum, quotquot huic interdictioni non cedunt, & obscœnitatibus inhiantes malunt mori, quam con- tenti sint à lateribus mulierum aliqua disjunctione divelli, ut ad explendam suæ aviditatis ingluviem etiam puncto temporis non sint sine fœminæ volupta- te, & hunc habent in mulieribus fructum, ut in illis semper defixa intentione desideria satient ocu- lorum, ne vel momentum aliquod transeat, quando indigeant, quod affectant. Sic inter eos integritas emoritur, ubi omnis commoratio sive connivendo sive commanendo corruptis affectionibus inquinatur, duos S. Petrus designavit, dicens: Oculos habentes plenos mæchationibus. Videmus autem hic tum quod spiritualis & corporalis scortatio plerumque conjuncta sint: tum quod falsi Doctores avaritiæ dediti esse soleant, quemadmodum Hieronymus l. III. in Zach. cap. XIV. de hæreticis pronuntiat, quod omnia lucri & gloriæ causa faciant. Utrius- que exempla Papatus affatim præbet: Quæ antea ex parte tacta.

## 2:15
Καταλιπόντες εὐθεῖαν ὁδὸν.]

That way which the Apostles had shown. Thus it was said to Elymas: Οὐ παύσῃ διαςρέφων τὰς ὁδὺς τῶ Κυρία τὰς εὐθείας, Acts XIII, 10. It is an introduction to the comparison which follows. For it was said to Balaam in Num. 22, 32: כי ירט הדרך לנגדי.

Vers. 15. Ἐπλανήθησαν.] תעו.

To which Judas refers in verse 12, who calls them ἀςέρας πλανήτας, wandering stars.

Ἐξακολυθήσαντες τῇ ὁδῷ τῶ Βαλαὰμ τῶ Βοσὸρ;

Instead of Prophets and Apostles, they followed a false prophet. Moreover, the comparison is very apt, as the following will show. Τῦ Βοσὸρ, namely, a place. We indeed have the name Bosoc in Greek for בשור 1 Sam. 30, 9, likewise בצר Deuteronomy 4, 43 and 1 Macc. v. 20. But those places do not pertain here, but that place is designated which was once called פתורה Num. 22, 5. The name of that place, however, was changed by later Syrians into בשר, because it is frequent for them to change into ב, just as Joel I, v. 1, פתואל in Greek is Βαθυὴλ, and the change of ת into ש is no less frequent, just as the same is פתור & פשור, and many others. But the Arab reads here Βεὼρ, and has prefixed a word which signifies son. Which I do not disapprove of, if the ancient copies favor it. For בעור is the father of Balaam, as appears in the already mentioned place of Numbers.

The name of a region is not indicated by the word Βοσὸρ, as Grotius wishes with the Vulgate, but it is the name of the Father according to the Hebrew custom of speaking, which the Syrian and Arab have rightly followed, even if he read here Βεὼρ. Although indeed the parent of Bileam is not called Bofor, but Beor, Num. XXII, 5, Micah VI, 5, it could nevertheless be the same synonym, or בעור was changed by the Interpreters into Βοσὸρ, such as Changes in proper names and in the Hebrew text are not frequent. Estius also acknowledges that the Father is noted: The former interpretation, which recent writers Erasmus, Cajetan, Gagnejus, Adamus, and others hand down, is favored by the article τοῦ, which is more accustomed to designate a parent than a place of birth.

Latin:

Καταλιπόντες εὐθεῖαν ὁδὸν.]

Eam viam, quam Apostoli monstraverant. Sic Elyma di- ctum: Οὐ παύσῃ διαςρέφων τὰς ὁδὺς τῶ Κυρία τὰς εὐθείας, Act. XIII, 10. Est introductio ad comparationem, quæ sequitur. Nam Balaamo dictum est Num. 22, 32. כי ירט הדרך לנגדי.

Vers. 15. Ἐπλανήθησαν.] תעו.

Quo facit Judas vers. 12. qui eos vocat ἀςέρας πλανήτας, sidera errantia.

Ἐξακολυθήσαντες τῇ ὁδῷ τῶ Βαλαὰμ τῶ Βοσὸρ;

Pro Prophetis & Apostolis sequuti sunt Pseudoprophetam. Est autem comparatio valde apposita, ut sequentia ostendent. Τῦ Βοσὸρ nempe χωρίον. Habemus quidem nomen Bosoc in Græco pro בשור 1. Sam. 30, 9. item בצר Deuter, 4, 43. & 1. Mace. v. 20. Sed ea loca huc non pertinent, sed is locus designatur, qui olim dictus פתורה Num. 22, 5. Ejus vero loci nomen a Syris posterioribus mutatum est in בשר quia frequens illis mutare in ב quomodo Joel I. v. 1. פתואל in Græco est Βαθυὴλ, nec minus frequens mutatio ת in ש, quomodo idem est פתור & פשור, multaque alia. At Arabs legit hic Βεὼρ, & præposuit vocem, quæ filium fignificat. Quod non improbein, si exemplaria vetera faveant. Nam בעור pater Balaami, ut apparet dicto jam Numerorum loco.

Non regionis nomen indicatur voce Βοσὸρ, ut cum Vulgata Grotius vult, sed id Patris nomen est ex Ebræo consuetudine loquendi, quam Syrus & Arabs recte sequutus est, etsi hic Βεὼρ legerit. Quanquam vero parens Bileami non Bofor, sed Beor vocatur, Num. XXII, 5. Mich. VI, 5. potuit tamen idem esse συνώνυμον, vel בעור ab Interpretibus mutatum in Βοσὸρ fuit, quales mutationes in nominibus propriis & in Ebræo textu non frequentes sunt. Patrem notari agnoscit & Estius: Priori intellectui, quem tra- dunt recentiores Erasmus, Cajetanus, Gagnejus, Adamus & alii, favet Articulus τοῦ, qui magis solet parentem designare, quam locum nativita- tis.

## 2:16
Ver. 16. Who loved the wages of unrighteousness.

See how good a comparison corresponds. Balaam persuaded [them to] debauchery, and that for the sake of gain. So also [do] they. Tradition in this place has supplied what is passed over in Scripture. See what we have said in Num. XXIV. v. 25. chap. XXXI. v. 8. Take ἀδικίας here, as above 13. Μισθὸν ἀδικίας [is] שכר שקר in Hebrew with an excellent paronomasia. Balaam, having accepted the reward, perished a little later. So also they will perish.

It is called the reward of unrighteousness, because he hoped for it for an unjust and impious work, Num. XXII, 5, namely for the cursing of the people. Therefore, he did not receive the reward because he persuaded [them to] debauchery, which Grotius rashly fetches here from I know not what tradition, even though he did give the counsel that the daughters of the Moabite people should entice the Israelites both into love for themselves and into idolatry.

But he had a rebuke for his own lawlessness, a speechless beast of burden.

Note the history from Num. XXII, 28; however, the comparison proceeds very well. The donkey rebuked him: [it rebukes] these [men] by almost all mute animals, because they observe the laws of sex: some even [observe] conjugal chastity. The same sense is in Jude ver. 10. Ὑποζύγιον is a noun general in itself, like the Latin jumentum. But among the Greek interpreters of Holy Scripture, it is always said of a donkey or a mule, as in Gen. 36, 24. Exod. 4, 20. chap. 9, 3. chap. XX, 17. chap. 22, 9. 10. chap. 23, 4. 5. 12. chap. 34, 20. Deut. 5, 14. 20. Josh. 6, 21. chap. 7, 14. Judg. 1, 14. chap. 5, 10. chap. 19, 3. 10. 21. 28. 2 Sam. 16, 2. 2 Chron. 18, 15. Job 24, 3. Zech. 9, 6. and no otherwise in Matt. 21, 5. This happens because Judea did not bear horses. And it is called ἄφωνον here, because it lacks speech, with the more excellent species signified by the name of the genus. The Latin here reads παρανοίας instead of παρανομίας, which word is found in Aristophanes, Plato, and others.

St. Peter implies no such third point of comparison: he compares [them] only with Balaam, whose way the false teachers are said to follow, by reason of avarice joined with false doctrine, because Balaam was not obedient to the mouth of the Lord for the sake of gain, which is especially looked to here. Moreover, Balaam is said to have been rebuked by the donkey concerning his transgression and foolishness: because from that stupendous miracle of the speaking donkey, especially because it refused to proceed, he could have understood that his way was contrary to God.

Speaking with a human voice, it restrained the madness of the prophet.

The γὰρ is missing here as above 9, just as כִּי is often missing among the Hebrews. If men were silent, the stones would speak, Luke 19, 40. Thus, when men become brutish, brute animals speak for God. And note that he is called a prophet not because he was such, but because he called himself such. For often the name נָבִיא is used in the sacred writings according to what is thought, not what is. And in that sense, interpreters sometimes translate it as prophet, often as false prophet, as in Jer. 6, 13. chap. 26, 7. 8. 11. 16. chap. 27, 7. c. 28, 1. c. 29, 1. 8. Zech. 13, 2. Παραφρονία is an unusual word. In Greek it is called either παραφροσύνη, as in Plato in his Epistle, or παραφρόνησις, as in Zech. 12, 4.

Grotius rashly denies that Balaam was a prophet. For it is evident from Moses that he sought and obtained oracles from God, Num. XXII, 8. 13. 18. 19. and that Jehovah met Balaam and put a word in his mouth, Num. XXIII. ver. 5. 16. just as he also brought forth an oracle concerning the Messiah from divine revelation, chap. XXIV, 16. 17.

And although in the Vulgate Num. XXII. verse 5, he is called a soothsayer; yet in the Hebrew no such thing exists, but the word פְּתוֹרָה is a proper name of a place in Syria, as it is accepted in the Targum and among the LXX Interpreters, and is rendered by the Vulgate itself in the parallel passage Deut. XXIII. verse 4. Then if it be granted at all that Balaam also sometimes used magical arts, which some deduce from the appellation קוסם Jos. XIII. v. 22 (which, however, also simply denotes one who is prescient of the future, and one who prophesies, Isa. III. verse 2. Mich. III. verse 11, even if he is not a Magus), yet it does not seem to be denied for that reason that he truly received oracles and responses from GOD at times, since this very thing is most clear from the passages previously cited, nor is it judged inconsistent that Balaam, however much a Prophet of God, sometimes used illicit divinations and, as in Num. XXIII. verse 5, first wished to elicit an oracle concerning cursing the Israelites by magical arts, and thus erected altars on different occasions. See Ambrose l. VI. epist. 37, Nyssenus lib. de vita Mos., Cyril l. VI. de orat., Augustine q. 48 in Num., Theodoret q. 40, Jerome qq. Ebr. from Num. XXII. 'First,' he says, 'a holy man and Prophet of GOD, afterwards through disobedience and the desire for gifts, when he wishes to curse Israel, he is called by the name of a diviner.' Estius's suspicion does not seem improbable: that Balaam, a man of avarice, for the sake of gain among the infidel peoples, among whom he was dwelling, also exposed his services for sale for illicit divinations.

Latin:

Vers. 16. Ὃς μισθὸν ἀδικίας ἠγάπησεν.]

Vide quam bona similitudo respondeat. Balaam suasit stupra, idque lucri causa. Sic & illi. Traditio in hoc lo- co supplevit, quod reticetur in Scriptura. Vide quæ diximus Num. XXIV. v. 25. cap. XXXI. v. 8. Ἀδικίας hic sume, ut supra 13. Μισθὸν ἀδικίας שכר שקר in Ebræo cum egre- gia παρονομασίᾳ. Balaam accepta mercede paulo post periit. Sic & illi peribunt.

Merces injustitiæ dicitur, quia pro opere in- justo & impio eam sperabat, Num. XXII, 5. nimi- rum pro maledictione populi. Non ergo quod stupra suaserit, mercedem accepit, quod hic te- mere è traditione nescio qua accersit Grotius, etsi consilium dederit, ut filiæ populi Moabitici & in sui amorem & ad idololatriam Israelitas pel- licerent.

Ἔλεγξιν δὲ ἔσχεν ἰδίας παρανομίας ὑποζύγιον ἄφωνον.]

Nota historia ex Numer. XXII, 28. optime autem procedit comparatio. Illum asina arguit: hos animalia muta prope omnia, quod sexus leges servant: quædam etiam pudicitiam conjugalem. Idem sensus apud Judam vers. 10. Ὑποζύγιον est nomen per se generale, ut Latinum jumentum. Sed apud Græcos sacræ Scripturæ Interpretes semper de asino aut mulo dicitur, ut Genes. 36, 24. Exod. 4, 20. cap. 9, 3. cap. XX, 17. cap. 22, 9. 10. cap. 23, 4. 5. 12. cap. 34, 20. Deuteronom. 5, 14. 20. Jos. 6, 21. cap. 7, 14. Jud. 1, 14. cap. 5, 10. cap. 19, 3. 10. 21. 28. 2. Sam. 16, 2. 2. Paral. 18, 15. Job. 24, 3. Zachar. 9, 6. nec aliter Matth. 21, 5. Id eo evenit, quod Judæa equos non fer- ret. Et ἄφωνον hic dicitur, quod sermone caret, specie excel- lentiore significata per nomen generis. Latinus hic pro παρανομίας, legit παρανοίας, quæ vox est apud Aristopha- nem, Platonem & alios.

Nullum tale comparationis tertium innuit S. Petrus: Solum cum Balaamo, cujus viam sequi ψευδοδιδάσκαλοι dicuntur, comparat ratione ava- ritiæ cum falsa doctrina conjunctæ, quia Balaam non obediens fuit ori Domini lucri causa, quod hic præcipue respicitur. Dicitur autem ab asina cor- reptus de transgressione & insipientia sua Bileam: quia ex stupendo illo asinæ loquentis miraculo, cumprimis quia illa progredi renuit, intelligere potuit, viam suam Deo adversam esse.

Ἐν ἀνθρώπου φωνῇ φθεγξάμενον ἐκώλυσε τὴν τοῦ προ- φήτου παραφρονίαν.]

Deest hic γὰρ ut supra 9. quomodo כִּי sæpe deest apud E- bræos. Si homines tacerent, lapides loquerentur, Luc. 19, 40. Sic cum homines brutescant, bruta animantia pro DEO lo- quuntur. Et nota προφήτην vocari non qui talis erat, sed qui talem se dicebat. Sæpe enim nomen נָבִיא in sacris lite- ris usurpatur secundum id, quod putatur, non quod est. Et in eo sensu Interpretes vertunt interdum προφήτην, sæpe ψευδο- προφήτην. ut Jer. 6, 13. cap. 26, 7. 8. 11. 16. cap. 27, 7. c. 28, 1. c. 29, 1. 8. Zach. 13, 2. Παραφρονία vox est inusitata. Græcis dici- tur aut παραφροσύνη, ut Platoni in Epistola, aut παραφρόνη- σις, ut Zach. 12, 4.

Temere negat Grotius, Bileamum Prophe- tam fuisse. Nam è Mose constat, quod oracu- la à DEO petierit & impetrarit, Numer. XXII, 8. 13. 18. 19. quodque Jehovah occurrerit Bileamo, & verbum in ejus ore posuerit Num. XXIII. vers. 5. 16. quemadmodum & oraculum de Messia ex revelatione divina protulit, cap. XXIV, 16. 17.

Et quanquam in Vulgata Num. XXII. vers. 5. ario- lans vocetur; in Ebræo tamen tale quid non ex- tat, sed vox פְּתוֹרָה est nomen proprium loci in Syria, ut in Thargum, & apud LXX. Interpretes accipitur, & à Vulgato ipso in loco parallelo Deut. XXIII. vers. 4. redditur. Tum si omnino concedatur, quod Bileam etiam magicis arti- bus quandoque usus sit, quod nonnulli ex ap- pellatione קוסם Jos. XIII. v. 22. deducunt (quæ vero etiam simpliciter præscium futurorum, & qui vaticinatur, notat, Esa. III. vers. 2. Mich. III. vers. 11. etsi Magus non sit) non tamen ideo ne- gandum videtur eum vere oracula & responsa à DEO quandoque accepisse, quum hoc ipsum è locis antea adductis clarissimum sit, nec in- conveniens judicetur, Bileamum utut Prophe- tam Dei quandoque illicitis divinationibus et- iam usum fuisse ac Num. XXIII. vers. 5. prius Ma- gicis artibus oraculum de maledicendis Israelitis elicere voluisse, adeoque diversis vicibus altaria, erexisse. Vid. Ambrosius l. VI. epist. 37. Nyssenus lib. de vita Mos. Cyrillus l. VI. de orat. Augusti- nus q. 48. in Num. Theodoretius q. 40. Hierony- mus qq. Ebr. ex Num. XXII. Primum, inquit, vir sanctus & Propheta DEI, postea per inobedien- tiam & desiderium munerum, cum Israel maledice- re cupit, divini vocabulo nuncupatur. Estio non im- probabilis videtur suspicio: Bileam hominem avaritiæ quæstus causa apud populos infideles, inter quos mo- rabatur, etiam ad illicitas divinationes operam suam venalem exposuisse.

## 2:17
Verse 17. These are wells without water.

He depicts the character of those men with many comparisons. Wells without water are called wells, but they are not. Just as an eye that does not see is not an eye to Aristotle. So they are Christians in name only.

Clouds carried about by a tempest.

Clouds are called both nubes and nebulæ, which themselves are a kind of abortion in the genus of clouds, dark and not rain-bearing. Hence Juvenal also spoke of a cloud of errors. And this manuscript has ὁμίχλαι more distinctly instead of νεφέλαι. Now, a mist (ὁμίχλη) is defined by Aristotle as a certain vaporous exhalation devoid of water, thicker than air but thinner than a cloud. See Wisd. II verse 4, Sirach 24 verse 3, chap. 43 verse 47. The Hebrew ערפל is usually translated this way, as in Job 38 verse 9, Joel 2 verse 2, Zeph. I verse 6. And Jude, mixing this comparison with the preceding one, says clouds without water carried about by winds. That which is light is more easily agitated; a mist by winds, nebulones (worthless fellows) by their own desires. Thus Cicero often compares the movements of the mind to winds and storms.

These two other, but related, vices, and the former indeed shadows forth the empty talk, the latter the levity and inconstancy of false Teachers: Nor are they mixed by Jude, but the latter, which he alone brings forward, is explained when he says they are nebulas ἀνύδρους, destitute of water, and thus dark clouds, not rain-bearing, agitated by winds, which Peter here designates as clouds carried about by whirlwinds. Cf. Prov. XIV. verse 14. By the former comparison it is signified that false Teachers promise many things in words, but perform nothing in reality, boast of holiness but do not exhibit it, or, as Augustine explains in Book 2 of On Faith and Works: He calls them wells because they have received the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. But dry, because they do not live accordingly. It can also be said, Wells without water refer to the boastfulness of true doctrine, by which false Teachers assert themselves, but rashly and falsely; inasmuch as they abandon the fountain of living water of the Word of God, and hand down broken cisterns, which are not able to contain waters, of traditions or human inventions, Jerem. II. verse 13. They boast that they wish to provide a salutary drink to the thirsty, but they do not have water springing up into life or of saving wisdom and life-giving consolation, Zachar. IX. verse 11, John IV. verse 14. Jerome lib. II. contra Jovin. and from him Bede on this passage. They open fountains of knowledge which do not have the water of doctrine narum: They promise rain like the clouds of the Prophets, to which the truth (virtue) of God arrives, and they are agitated by the whirlwinds of demons and vices. Blessed Huss with the interlinear Gloss on this passage has it thus: Where there is a fountain without water, there is mud and mire. So in these there is no water of overflowing grace, but the mud of unexpected malice. Nor is it a wonder, because they have abandoned the fountain of living water. They are therefore fountains not overflowing, but rather polluting, not calming the heat of pleasure, but more truly stirring it up, not refreshing, but infecting, not sanctifying, but defiling. On the contrary, however, pious Doctors are compared to clouds fruitful with saving rain. See Isa. 60:8, Deut. 32:2, Joel 2:23.

By the latter simile, the inconstancy of false Doctors is noted, because they are carried about by various winds of doctrine, Eph. 4:14; as well as their fraudulence, because they entice men with false promises, like clouds making a hope of rain and not pouring out rain; as well as their harmful effects, concerning which Blessed Huss says: Clouds agitated by winds stir up a storm and obscure the splendor of the Sun: Thus heretics disturb the quiet of minds, and with the darkness of errors obscure the Sun of righteousness.

Οἷς ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους εἰς αἰῶνα τετήρηται.] The punishments of the other life are described sometimes under the figure of fire, sometimes under the figure of darkness, as Matt. 8:12, ch. 22:13, ch. 25:30. The significance is increased, however, when not only ζόφος is said, but ζόφος σκότους, as also in Jude v. 13. Thus it is said χθονὸς πέδον, συμφορὰ πάθους, mire of mud, and the like: And the punishment corresponds to the guilt. Let a dark life be punished by darkness. Τετήρηται is said here of punishment, as of a reward in 1 Pet. 1:4.

Such dark gloom is expressed through outer or outermost darkness, most remote from the region of light, and therefore most dense, Matt. 8:12, ch. 22:13, ch. 25:30. Understood, however, are not natural darknesses, but spiritual ones of ignorance and errors, Isa. 42:9, Luke 1:27, and of a perverse will, Eph. 5:11. The Vulgate wrongly omitted here, εἰς αἰῶνα, considered by Estius to be more sincere than the Greek text, though preposterously. Since the Greek Codices consistently read these things.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Οὗτοί εἰσι πηγαὶ ἄνυδροι.

Multis similitudinibus depingit illorum hominum inge- nium. Fontes sine aqua dicuntur fontes, sed non sunt. Sicut oculus, qui non videt, Aristoteli non est oculus. Ita illi, no- mine tantum Christiani.

Νεφέλαι ἀπὸ λαίλαπος ἐλαυνόμεναι.

Νεφέλαι & nubes dicuntur & nebulæ, quæ ipsæ abortus quidam sunt in nubium genere, tenebricosæ & non imbri- feræ. Inde errorum nebulam dixit & Juvenalis. Et Manu- scriptus hic pro νεφέλαι distinctius habet ὁμίχλαι. Defini- tur autem ὁμίχλη Aristoteli ἀτμώδης ἀναθυμίασις τις ἄγονος ὕδατος, ἄερος μὲν παχυτέρα νέφους δὲ ἀραιοτέρα. Vide Sap. II vers. 4. Sirach. 24. vers. 3. cap. 43. vers. 47. Solet ita verti Ebræum ערפל, ut Job. 38. vers. 9. Joël. 2. vers. 2. Soph. I. vers. 6. Et Judas hanc comparationem cum præcedente per- miscens ait νεφέλαι ἄνυδροι ὑπὸ ἀνέμων παραφερόμεναι. Fa- cilius agitatur id, quod leve est; nebula à ventis, nebulones à cupiditatibus suis. Sic motus animi ventis & procellis sæ- pe comparat Cicero.

Similitudines hæ alia duo, sed cognata vitia, & prior quidem vaniloquentiam, posterior vero levitatem & inconstantiam falsorum Doctorum adumbrant: Nec à Juda commiscentur, sed po- sterior, quam solam affert, explicatur, cum di- cit, eos nebulas ἀνύδρους, aquis destitutas, adeo- que nubes tenebricosas, non imbriferas, ventis agi- tatas, quas Petrus hic nebulas turbinibus exagi- tatas indigitat. Conf. Prov. XIV. vers. 14. Prio- ri similitudine significatur, quod falsi Doctores verbis multa promittant, reipsa nihil præstent, sanctitatem jactitent, non autem exhibeant, vel, ut Augustinus Libr. de fid. & operibus cap. 2. explicat: Fontes vocat, quod acceperint cognitio- nem Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Siccos autem, quia non congruenter vivunt. Dici etiam potest, Fontes sine respici doctrinæ veræ jactantiam, qua sese esse- aqua. runt falsi Doctores, sed temere & falso; utpote qui fontem aquæ vivæ Verbi Dei relinquunt, ac cisternas dissipatas, quæ aquas continere non va- lent, traditionum vel inventionum humanarum tradunt, Jerem. II. vers. 13. Jactitant se potum sa- lutarem præbere velle sitientibus, sed non ha- bent aquam in vitam scaturientem vel sapientiæ salvificæ & consolationis vivificæ, Zachar. IX. vers. 11. Johann. IV. vers. 14. Hieronymus lib. II. contra Jovin. & ex eo Beda in hunc locum. Ape- riunt fontes scientiæ, qui aquam non habent doctri- narum: Promittunt imbrem velut nubes Propheti- cæ, ad quas pervenit veritas (virtus) Dei, & turbi- nibus exagitantur dæmonum atque vitiorum. B. Huf- fus cum Glossa interlin. in h. l. ita habet: Ubi fons est sine aqua, ibi est lutum & limus. Sic in istis non est aqua inundantis gratiæ, sed lutum inopinantis ma- litiæ. Nec mirum, quia dereliquerunt fontem aquæ vivæ. Sunt ergo fontes non inundantes, sed potius coinquinantes, non calorem voluptatis se- dantes, sed verius suscitantes, non reficientes, sed inficientes, non sanctificantes, sed polluentes. Ex adverso vero Doctores pii nubibus salutari pluvia fœcundis comparantur. Vid. Esa. LX, 8. Deuter. XXXII, 2. Joel. II, 23.

Posteriori similitudine notatur Doctorum falsorum tum inconstantia, quod variis ventis do- ctrinæ circumferantur, Ephes. IV. v. 14. tum frau- dulentia, quod falsis promissis homines lactent, ut nubes spem pluviæ facientes, & pluviam non effundentes: tum effecta noxia, de quibus B. Huf- sus: Nubes ventis agitata tempestatem excitant, & Solis splendorem obsuscant: Sic hæretici mentium quietem turbant, tenebris errorum Solem justitiæ obsuscant.

Οἷς ὁ ζόφος τοῦ σκότους εἰς αἰῶνα τετήρηται.] Pœnæ alterius seculi modo sub incendii, modo sub tenebrarum figura de- scribuntur, ut Matth. 8, 12. c. 22, 13. c. 25, 30. Augetur au- tem significatio, cum non ζόφος tantum dicitur, sed ζόφος σκότους, ut & Judæ v. 13. Sic dicitur χθονὸς πέδον, συμφορὰ πάθους, cœnum luti & similia: Et respondet pœna culpæ. Tenebricosa vita tenebris puniatur. Τετήρηται dictum hic de pœna, ut de præmio 1. Petr. I, 4.

Talis caligo tenebricosa per tenebras exte- riores seu extimas à regione lucis remotissimas, adeoque densissimas exprimitur Matth. VIII, 12. cap. XXII, 13. cap. XXV, 3. Intelliguntur autem non tenebræ naturales, sed spirituales ignorantiæ, & errorum, Esa. XLII, 9. Luc. I, 27. voluntatis per- versæ, Eph. V, 11. Perperam hic Vulgata omisit, εἰς αἰῶνα, præpostere ab Estio sincerior textu Græco habita. Siquidem Codices Græci con- stanter ista legant.

## 2:18
Vers. 18.

Ὑπέρογκα γὰρ ματαιότητος φθεγγόμενοι.] They speak inflated and vain things. In the Glossary, ὑπέρογκος is inflated. Jude says of the same: Their mouth speaks great swelling words, namely, about the virtue sent into them, by which they could escape the makers of the world: they used to say, as Tertullian says in his book On the Soul, that their souls were conceived from a sublime virtue, a despiser of the world and of the powerful Principalities. The passage Dan. 11:36 is referred to, ודבר נפלאת, where the Greeks say λαλήσει ὑπέρογκα. The same word is in Deut. 32:11, 2 Sam. 13:2. In the same sense is ממלל רברב, a mouth speaking great things, Dan. 7:18.

These things are not to be restricted to a few; they are common, like the rest, to most heretics: They certainly fit those whom the Apostle foretold in this place. Therefore, every such over-swollen false-speaking is noted generally, by which, in the manner of waterless clouds, they sound only pompously, but are dissipated into air and smoke. Yet with proud and pompous words they ensnare others, and entice them to look upon the lusts of the flesh, promising them liberty, but precipitating them into destruction. By the proud phrase of vanity are meant proud vanities: Bede on this passage: They speak great things, and their whole discourse is pride, Jude verse 16. Their mouth speaks great swelling words.

Δελεάζουσι.] above 14

Thus false Doctors are compared with fishermen, who catch fish with a hook, and bird-catchers, who entice birds so that they may enclose them in a net. The lusts of the flesh are that bait by which they entice men.

Ἐν ἐπιθυμίαις τῆς σαρκὸς, ἀσελγείαις.] The Manuscript also has it without the conjunction: nor is that unusual, where one is an exposition of the other, as Luke 2:14. Concerning the matter, see above 7 and 10; is here is per.

The Vulgate is not to be admitted, rendering it, in the desires of the flesh, of luxury: Which Estius excuses in vain, as if it were read not ἀσελγείας, but ἀσελγείαις. For the preposition ἐν is repeated in most Codices as ἐν ἀσελγείαις.

Τοὺς ὀλίγον ἀποφυγόντας.] In the Manuscript it is ὀλίγως, which is infrequent. The sense is, those who have escaped for a time, namely such desires. Thus we also had ὀλίγον in 1 Pet. 1:6. In the thing itself they had escaped, not in appearance. They had been corrected, but have relapsed into old ways, as the following clearly indicate.

The more approved codices do not read ὀλίγον, nor as Erasmus & Vatablus ὄντως, but ὄντως; which B. Luther also followed. Therefore, the judgment of Piscator's Gloss does not fit, that it refers only to charity, since according to the truth it is implied that those who are seduced, and in turn relapse to their former ways, have escaped desires. Cf. Heb. VI, 4. 5.

Τοὺς ἐν πλάνῃ ἀναστρεφομένους.] Those who now, having been received, return, namely to those things which they had escaped. Ἀναστρέφεσθαι is to return, Matt. 17, 22. Acts 5, 22. ch. 15, 16. And in very many places of the Old Testament שוב is translated thus. For the same word below, ἐπιστρέψας.

Vulgatus: Those who walk in error: Which some refer to the more remote Φθεγγόμενοι, to whom, however, the accusative case in Greek is repugnant. B. Luther rendered the sense here, he did not render word for word. Others explain it thus: They entice those who had truly escaped those who walk in error. Grotius's explanation would not be inconvenient, if ἐν πλάνῃ were taken for εἰς πλά νην. The preceding explanation therefore seems simpler, which also pleased Estius; it is governed, he says, in the judgment of some by the verb 'entice', by which τοὺς ἀποφυγόντας was governed, as if the Apostle were saying: They entice those who have escaped a little: Those, I say, who walk in error. But that sense does not fit. For they do not entice those who are erring. Furthermore, how do they walk in error, who have already escaped? Therefore it must rather and altogether be said that it is governed by the nearest participle ἀποφυγόντας, so that this is the structure: They entice those who had escaped a little from those (or by those) who walk in error. Thus he speaks a little later, 'For if having escaped the pollutions of the world &c.' with the same participle.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Ὑπέρογκα γὰρ ματαιότητος φθεγγόμενοι.] Inflata lo- quuntur & vana. In Glossario ὑπέρογκος inflatus. Judas de iisdem: Τὸ στόμα αὐτῶν λαλεῖ ὑπέρογκα, nempe de virtute in se missa, qua mundi fabricatores effugere possent: dicebant, ut ait Tertullianus, libro de Anima, suas animas de sublimi virtute conceptas, despectrice mundi potentium Principa- tuum. Respicitur locus Daniel. XI, 36. ודבר נפלאת, ubi Græci λαλήσει ὑπέρογκα. Est eadem vox Deuteron. 32. 11. 2. Sam. 13, 2. Eodem sensu ממלל רברב στόμα λαλοῦν με- γάλα, Dan. 7. v. 18.

Non restringenda hæc ad paucos, communia sunt, uti cætera, plerisque hæreticis: Illis certe, quos prædixit hoc loco Apostolus, conveniunt. Notatur itaque generaliter omnis ejusmodi præ- tumida falsiloquentia, qua more nubium ἀνύδρων fastuose tantum sonant, sed in aërem & fumum dissipantur. Superbis tamen & fastuosis verbis alios inescant, & ad spectandas carnis concupi- scentias alliciunt, libertatem iis pollicitando, sed in exitium eos præcipitando. Superba vanita- tis phrasi Ebræa sunt superbæ vanitates: Beda in h. l. Loquuntur grandia, & totus eorum sermo su- perbia est, Judæ vers. 16. Τὸ στόμα αὐτῶν λαλεῖ ὑπέρογκα.

Δελεάζουσι.] supra 14

Comparantur ita falsi Doctores cum pisca- toribus, qui hamo pisces capiunt, & aucupibus, qui volucres inescant, ut reti eas concludant. Concupiscentiæ carnis sunt esca illa, qua homines illiciunt.

Ἐν ἐπιθυμίαις τῆς σαρκὸς, ἀσελγείαις.] Sic habet & Ma- nuscriptus sine copula: nec id inusitatum, ubi alterum alte- rius est expositio, ut Luc. II, 14. De re vide supra 7. & 10. is hic est per.

Non admittenda Vulgata reddens, in desideriis carnis, luxuriæ: Quam nequicquam excusat Estius, quasi lectum sit non ἀσελγείας, sed ἀσελγείαις. Repetitur enim in plerisque Codicibus præposi- tio ἐν ἀσελγείαις.

Τοὺς ὀλίγον ἀποφυγόντας.] In Manuscripto est ὀλίγως, quod infrequens. Sensus est, qui ad tempus effugerunt, nempe tales cupiditates. Sic ὀλίγον etiam habuimus in 1. Petr. I. vers. 6. Re ipsa effugerent, non in speciem. Cor- recti fuerant, sed in vetera sunt relapsi, ut sequentia clare indicant.

Probatiores Codices legunt non ὀλίγον, nec ut Erasmus & Vatablus ὄντως, sed ὄντως; Quod etiam B. Lutherus sequutus est. Non ergo congruit Glossa Piscatoris judicium charitatis tantum respi- ci, quum secundum veritatem cupiditates effugisse innuantur, qui seducuntur, & vicissim ad priora relabuntur. Conf. Ebr. VI, 4. 5.

Τοὺς ἐν πλάνῃ ἀναστρεφομένους.] Qui nunc recepti rede- unt, nempe ad ea, quæ effugerant. Ἀναστρέφεσθαι est re- dire Matth. 17, 22. Actor. 5, 22. cap. 15, 16. Et plurimis lo- cis Veteris Testamenti שוב sic vertitur. Pro eodem infra ἐπιστρέψας.

Vulgatus: Qui in errore conversantur: Quod referunt nonnulli ad remotius Φθεγγόμενοι, qui- bus vero casus Accusativus in Græco repugnat. B. Lutherus sensum hic tradidit, non verbum verbo reddidit. Alii ita exponunt: Pelliciunt eos, qui revera effugerant illos, qui in errore con- versantur. Non incommoda foret Grotiana explicatio, si ἐν πλάνῃ acciperetur pro εἰς πλά- νην. Simplicior itaque videtur præcedens ex- plicatio, quæ etiam Estio placuit, Regitur, inquit, quorundam judicio à verbo pelliciunt, à quo regebatur τοὺς ἀποφυγόντας, tanquam di- cat Apostolus: Pelliciunt eos, qui paululum effu- gerunt: Eos, inquam, qui in errore conversantur. Verum sensus iste non congruit. Non enim pelli- ciunt eos, qui errant. Deinde quomodo in errore conversantur, qui jam effugerunt? Ergo potius & omnino dicendum, quod regatur à participio proxi- mo ἀποφυγόντας, ut hæc sit structura: Pelliciunt eos, qui paululum effugerant eos (vel ab illis) qui in errore conversantur. Ita paulo post loquitur, Si enim refugientes coinquinationes mundi &c. parti- cipio eodem.

## 2:19
Vers. 19.

Ἐλευθερίαν αὐτοῖς ἐπαγγελλόμενοι.] Doubtless they thus called the liberty of doing all things: And thus they said their soul was freed from all things, as Irenaeus testifies.

Αὐτοὶ δοῦλοι ὑπάρχοντες τῆς φθορᾶς.] How could they free others, who themselves are slaves of the most corrupt morals? For φθορὰ is taken here, as above I, 8. In the manuscript it is δοῦλοι ὄντες, it makes no difference.

This also pertains to the vain talk of false teachers, inasmuch as they not only bait with the desires of the flesh and lasciviousness, but also permit liberty, as if by the liberty which Christ acquired for us, a license for sinning were obtained for us, against which seduction the holy Apostle warned in 1 Epist. II, 16. and Paul in Gal. V, 13. But those are said to promise liberty who themselves are not free, but are slaves of corruption, that is, of every depraved concupiscence, through which they corrupt themselves. Cf. above II, 12.

ᾯ γάρ ἄν τις ἡττήθῃ τούτῳ καὶ δεδούλωται.] The same sense as Rom. VI, 16. and John VIII, 34. where we have brought forward some things from the philosophers of equal sense. Estius notes here an argument from the right of war: By whom anyone is overcome in war, by him he is reduced to slavery. Since, therefore, false teachers themselves have been overcome by the devil through the depraved lusts of the flesh, they have certainly been made slaves or reduced to slavery by him: Cf. John VIII, 34. Romans VI, 16. And therefore they are slaves of the devil as regards guilt, and consequently also as regards punishment, Rom. VI, 23. Heb. II, 14, 15. Which argument Catholics also rightly use against the Pelagians, Papists, and Synergists, demonstrating the slavery of free will brought in by the fall, with St. Augustine leading the way in Enchir. cap. 30. Man, using free will badly, destroyed both himself and it. For just as he who kills himself certainly kills himself by living, but by killing himself he does not live, nor will he be able to resuscitate himself when he has killed himself: So when one sinned by free will, free will was lost by the victory of sin: for by whom anyone is overcome, to him he is also addicted as a slave. For that is the sentiment of the Apostle Peter, which, since it is true, what liberty, I ask, can a slave addicted to sin have, except when it pleases him to sin? For he serves liberally who willingly does the will of his master: And by this he is free to sin, who is a slave of sin. And these are the chief attributes of heretics, namely that they are given to wicked lusts, despisers of the Lord, and blasphemers, stubborn, voluptuous, greedy, vain-talkers, unstable, loosening the reins of the lust of the flesh; how these things agree with the Papists, B. Luther shows clearly in his commentary on this place and on the state of false teachers, Vol. II, Jena. German [edition] shows clearly.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Ἐλευθερίαν αὐτοῖς ἐπαγγελλόμενοι.] Nimirum sic voca- bant libertatem omnia operandi: Et sic animam suam dice- bant ab omnibus liberatam, teste Irenæo.

Αὐτοὶ δοῦλοι ὑπάρχοντες τῆς φθορᾶς.] Quomodo alios libe- rarent, qui ipsi servi sunt morum corruptissimorum? φθορὰ enim hic sumitur, ut supra I, 8. In Manuscripto est δοῦλοι ὄντες, nihil refert.

Pertinet & hoc ad vaniloquentiam falsorum Doctorum, utpote qui non tantum inescant desi- deriis carnis & lasciviis, sed libertatem etiam per- mittunt, quasi per eam, quam nobis acquisivit li- bertatem Christus, parta nobis sit peccandi licentia, adversus quam seductionem præmonuit S. Aposto- lus 1. Epist. II, 16. & Paulus Gal. V, 13. Promittere autem libertatem dicuntur illi, qui ipsi non liberi, sed servi sunt corruptionis, hoc est, pravæ cujus- que concupiscentiæ, per quam seipsos corrum- punt. Conf. supra II, 12.

ᾯ γάρ ἄν τις ἡττήθῃ τούτῳ καὶ δεδούλωται.] Sensus idem, qui Rom. VI, 16. & Joh. IIX, 34. ubi nonnulla ex Philosophis at- tulimus paris sensus. Notat hic Estius argumentum à jure belli: A quo quis in bello superatur, ab eo in servitutem redigitur. Quum ergo falsi Doctores ipsimet superati sint à diabolo per pravas concupiscen- tias carnis, servi utique facti vel in servitutem ab eo redacti sunt: Conf. Joh. VIII, 34. Roman. VI, 16. Ideoque servi diaboli sunt quoad cul- pam, & consequenter etiam quoad pœnam, Rom. VI, 23. Ebr. II, 14. 15. Quo argumento etiam contra Pelagianos, Pontificios, & Synergistas, recte utuntur Catholici demonstrantes servi- tutem liberi arbitrii per lapsum invectam, præ- eunte S. Augustino in Enchir. cap. 30. Libero arbitrio male utens homo & se perdidit & ipsum. Sicut enim qui se occidit, utique vivendo se occi- dit, sed se occidendo non vivit, nec seipsum poterit resuscitare, cum occiderit: Ita cum libero peccare- tur arbitrio, victore peccato amissum est liberum arbitrium: à quo enim quis devictus est, huic & servus addictus est. Petri enim Apostoli est ista sententia, quæ cum vera sit, qualis quæso potest ser- vi addicti esse libertas, nisi quando eum peccare de- lectat. Liberaliter enim servit, qui Domini sui voluntatem libenter facit: Ac per hoc ad pecca- tum liber est, qui peccati servus est. Atque hæc sunt præcipua attributa hæreticorum, quod nempe sint nefandis libidinibus dediti, contemto- res Domini, ac blasphemi, pervicaces, voluptarii, avari, vaniloqui, instabiles, concupiscentia carnis frena laxantes; quæ quomodo conveniant in Pontificios, B. Lutherus comment. in h. l. & de statu falso dictor. spirit. T. II. Jen. Germ. luculen- ter ostendit.

## 2:20
Verse 20.

Οἱ γὰρ ἀποφυγόντες τὰ μιάσματα τοῦ κόσμου.] See above 10. Other books have εἰ γὰρ. But the true reading is οἱ γὰρ, as the series of what follows indicates.

Ἐν ἐπιγνώσει τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ Σωτῆρος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.] For the knowledge of the Gospel has the power of freeing us from sins, John VIII, 36.

Τούτοις δὲ πάλιν ἐμπλακέντες ἡττῶνται.] The δὲ is redundant, as elsewhere. ἐμπλέκεσθαι is also found in Prov. 28, 18; Plato and Polybius also use it. They are held entangled.

Γέγονεν αὐτοῖς τὰ ἔσχατα χείρονα τῶν πρώτων.] You have the same words in Matt. 12, 45 and Luke 11, 6. Similar in Matt. 27, 64, John 5, 14, Hermas 3, 9. Some, however, of them have stained themselves, and have been cast out from the race of the just, and have returned again to their former state, and even worse than they had escaped before, says Socrates in Xenophon, Book II, that some think that those who have been just do not become unjust: but he himself thinks quite otherwise, and that this change happens through bad examples and the neglect of practicing virtue.

Some understand these things of the seducers, others of the seduced, but it is a general sentiment, concerning all, by which it is taught that we ought not, after conversion from the pollutions of the world, to be entangled again in the same. Μιάσματα to physicians are the seeds of pestilential contagion in corrupt air, such as are here both doctrines and life. He commands to beware, lest we be reduced again into the slavery of sin and the devil, from which we have been freed, lest the latter things become worse than the former. Cf. Luke XII, 47. Concerning which Chrysostom, homily on the first fall of man: Do not sin after forgiveness, do not be wounded after the cure, do not be defiled after grace. Consider, O man, that guilt is more serious after forgiveness, a renewed wound is worse than the pain after the cure, it is more troublesome for a man to be defiled after grace. Wherefore he is ungrateful for indulgence, who sins after receiving pardon: he is unworthy of health, who wounds himself after he has been cured, nor does he deserve to be cleansed, who defiles himself after grace.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Οἱ γὰρ ἀποφυγόντες τὰ μιάσματα τοῦ κόσμου.] Vide supra 10. Alii libri habent εἰ γὰρ. Sed vera lectio est οἱ γὰρ, ut se- ries sequentium indicat.

Ἐν ἐπιγνώσει τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ Σωτῆρος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.] Cognitio enim Evangelii vim habet, nos à peccatis liberandi, Johan. VIII, 36.

Τούτοις δὲ πάλιν ἐμπλακέντες ἡττῶνται.] Abundat δὲ. ut & alibi. ἐμπλέκεσθαι habet & Prov. 28, 18. utuntur & Plato & Polybius. Tenentur irretiti.

Γέγονεν αὐτοῖς τὰ ἔσχατα χείρονα τῶν πρώτων.] Habes eadem verba Matth. 12, 45. & Luc. 11, 6. Similia Matth. 27, 64. Joh. 5, 14. Hermas 3, 9. Quidam tamen ex eis macula- verunt se, & projecti sunt de genere justorum, & iterum redierunt ad statum pristinum, atque etiam deteriores, quam prius evaserant, ait Socrates apud Xenophontem lib. II. quos- dam existimare,qui justi fuere, injustos non fieri: se vero pla- ne aliter existimare, atque eam immutationem fieri per mala exempla & neglectum exercendæ virtutis.

Nonnulli hæc de seductoribus, alii de seductis intelligunt, sed est generalis sententia, omnes concernens, qua docetur, non debere nos post conversionem ab inquinamentis mundi liberos rursus implicari iisdem. Μιάσματα Medicis sunt seminaria luis pestilentialis in aëre corrupto, qualia hic sunt tum doctrinæ tum vitæ. Caveri jubet, ne in servitutem iterum redigamur pecca- ti, & diaboli, è qua liberati sumus, ne posterio- ra deteriora evadant prioribus. Conf. Luc. XII, 47. Quo de Chrysostomus homil. de laps. prim. hom. Noli peccare post veniam, noli vulnerari post curam, noli sordidari post gratiam. Cogita, ô homo, graviorem esse culpam post veniam, renova- tum vulnus pejus dolore post curam, molestius homi- nem sordidari post gratiam. Quare indulgentia in- gratus est, qui post veniam peccat: Sanitate indi- gnus est, qui semetipsum, postquam curatus est, vul- nerat, nec mundari meretur, qui semetipsum post gra- tiam sordidat.

## 2:21
Verse 21.

For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered unto them.] Here κρεῖττον, that is, better, is said of that which is less evil. Thus καλὸν ἦν is used in Matthew 26:24, which elsewhere is called ἀνεχτότερον, Matthew 10:15, ch. 11:22, 24, Mark 9:11, Luke 10:12, 14. The way of righteousness here is the Gospel, which is called above the way of truth and the straight way. For righteousness here comprehends all things which are pleasing to God, as 1 Peter 2:24. The same holy commandment by excellence, 1 Timothy 6:4. Moreover, the Gospel is said to have been delivered to them by the Apostles, namely, as will be said below III, 2, where the same word commandment occurs. Thus Jude 3 calls it the faith delivered. And Paul says of himself, I delivered unto you, 1 Corinthians 11:2, 23, ch. 15:3. There are, however, similar sentiments in Philo, as in his work On Agriculture: These things having been added to me, and the beginning often harmed many. But against Flaccus: To him who sins through ignorance of the better, pardon is given; but he who sins from knowledge has no defense, having already been condemned in the court of his conscience. Sirach 34:30: He that washeth himself after the touching of a dead body, if he touch it again, what availeth his washing? So is a man that fasteth for his sins, and goeth again, and doeth the same; who will hear his prayer? See also Luke 22:48 and what is said there. In the Manuscript in this place it reads thus: If they turn back to the things behind from the holy commandment delivered to him, etc. Thus you have to turn back for שׁוּב in Exodus 32:26, Judges 11:39, 2 Samuel 1:22, ch. 8:14, 1 Kings 12:20, 1 Chronicles 19:5, Job 39:1, Jeremiah 31:5, Ezekiel 1:14, ch. 7:13, ch. 9:8. To the things behind means backward, as Mark 13:16, Luke 9:62, ch. 17:31, John 18:6, ch. 20:14, אחור.

The doctrine of the Gospel is called the way of righteousness, because in it is delivered the way of obtaining righteousness that is valid before God, and consequently eternal life, which he had therefore designated before by the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ: and afterwards by the name of the holy commandment delivered: Compare 1 John 3:23.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Κρεῖττον γὰρ ἦν αὐτοῖς μὴ ἐπεγνωκέναι τὴν ὁδὸν τῆς δικαιο- σύνης, ἢ ἐπιγνοῦσιν ἐπιστρέψαι, ἐκ τῆς παραδοθείσης αὐτοῖς ἁγί- ας ἐντολῆς.] Hic κρεῖττον, id est, melius, dicitur id, quod mi- nus malum est. Sic καλὸν ἦν sumitur Matth. 26, 24. quod alibi dicitur ἀνεχτότερον, Matth. 10, 15. c. 11, 22. 24. Marc. 9, 11. Luc. 10, 12. 14. ὁδὸς τῆς δικαιοσύνης hic est Evangelium, quod supra ὁδὸς ἀληθείας & ὁδὸς εὐθεῖα. Nam δικαιοσύνη hic omnia comprehendit, quæ Deo grata sunt, ut 1. Petr. 2. v. 24. Eadem ἁγία ἐντολὴ per excellentiam, 1. Tim. 6, 4. Dicitur autem Evangelium ipsis traditum per Apostolos nempe, ut dicetur infra III, 2. ubi eadem vox ἐντολῆς. Sic παραδοθεῖσαν πίστιν dicit Judas 3. Et Paulus de se παρέδωκα ὑμῖν, 1. Cor. 11, 2. 23. c. 15, 3. Sunt autem huic sententiæ similes apud Philonem, ut de Agricultura: Τύτους μοὶ προσγενομένους, καὶ τὸ ἄρξασθαι πολλάκις μεγάλα πολλοὺς ἔβλαψεν. Adversus Flaccum ve- ro: Τῷ μὲν ἀγνοίᾳ τοῦ κρείττονος ἁμαρτάνοντι συγγνώμη δίδο- ται· ὁδ᾽ ἐξ ἐπιστήμης ἀδικῶν ἀπολογίαν οὐκ ἔχει, προεαλωκὼς ἐν τῷ τοῦ συνειδότος δικαστηρίῳ. Siracides 34, 30. Βαπτιζόμενος ἀπὸ νεκροῦ καὶ πάλιν ἁπτόμενος αὐτοῦ, τί ὤφελησεν ἐν τῷ λουτρῷ αὐτοῦ; ἕτως ἄνθρωπος νηστεύων ἐπὶ ταῖς ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτοῦ, κὴ πά- λιν πορευόμενος, καὶ ταῦτα ποιῶν τὴν προσευχὴν αὐτοῦ τίς ἐξα- κούσεται. Vide & Luc. 22, 48. & ibi dicta. In Manuscripto hoc loco sic legitur: Εἰ ὑπογύρισι εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω ἀνακάμψαι ἀπὸ τῆς παραδοθείσης ἀυτῷ &c. Sic ἀνακάμψαι pro שׁוּב habes Exod. 32, 26. Jud. 11, 39. 2. Sam. I, 22. c 8, 14. 1. Reg. 12, 20. 1. Pa- ral. 19, 5. Job. 39, 1. Jerem. 31, 5. Ezech. 1, 14. c. 7, 13. c. 9, 8. Εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω valet retro, ut Marc. 13, 16. Luc. 9, 62. c. 17, 31. Joh. 18, 6. c. 20, 14. אחור.

Doctrina Evangelii via justitiæ dicitur, quod in ea tradatur via consequendi justitiam coram Deo valentem, adeoque vitam æternam, quam proin- de per ἐπίγνωσιν τοῦ Κυρίου κὴ Σωτῆρος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ antea designarat: & postea nomine τῆς παραδο- θείσης ἁγίας ἐντολῆς: Conf. 1. Joh. III, 23.

## 2:22
Verse 22.

For it has happened to them according to the true proverb, The dog that has turned back to its own vomit.) This is a true proverb, or mashal, Proverbs 26:11, where the Greek has it thus: As a dog when it returns to its own vomit, and becomes hateful, so a fool in his own wickedness returns to his own sin.

And the sow that was washed to the wallowing in the mire.) Aratus: The sow wallowing in the mire. Philo: in the manner of a sow wallowing in the mire. Into the wallowing place: as Ambrose cites it: For the same he said wallowing place. Proverbs 2:18. Terence, Hecyra: For I see you have been turned back again into the same life.

When a dog has greedily gorged itself with food, having eaten a certain herb, it induces vomiting, but as it is an animal by nature unclean and voracious, it soon re-absorbs the ejected food: But the sow is a friend of mud: Therefore, even if it has been washed, it immediately wallows in it again. Gregory the Great applies these things to those who return to the filth of sin after repentance, part III, Pastoral Care, admonition 31. Those who lament their admitted sins, yet do not abandon them, must be admonished to know how to consider solicitously that they cleanse themselves in vain by weeping, who defile themselves wickedly by living, since they wash themselves with tears for this reason, that they may return clean to filth. For hence it is written: The dog returned to his own vomit, and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire. For when a dog vomits, it surely casts out the food that was weighing down its chest, but when it returns to the vomit from which it had been relieved, it is burdened again. And those who lament their admitted sins surely cast out the wickedness with which they had been evilly sated, and which the habit of the mind's inner parts was weighing down, which, when they repeat it after confession, they resume. But the sow in the wallowing place of mud, when it is washed, is rendered filthier, and he who laments an admitted sin, yet does not abandon it, subjects himself to a nearly graver fault, because he despises the very pardon he could have obtained by weeping, and wallows in himself as if in muddy water, because while he withdraws the cleanliness of life from his weeping, he makes even the tears themselves filthy before the eyes of God. St. Augustine on the former similitude, homily 2 on Psalm 30. See, he says, to what a horrible thing he has compared them. It is certainly a horrible thing to re-absorb one's own vomit, not practiced by anyone even in the greatest famine. And in Psalm 93.

A dog returned to its own vomit. For your conscience was pressing upon your breast because of your sins: having received indulgence, as if you had vomited, your breast was relieved. A good conscience was made out of a bad conscience: why do you turn back again to your vomit? If a dog doing this is loathsome to your eyes, what will you be to the eyes of God?

The application of the latter similitude was made by Origen, homily I on Psalm XXXVII. His admonition looks to this: He says that those who delight in the stenches of sins are called similar to swine, just as swine, who seek out every stench as if it were a most sweet odor. Consider, therefore, the sinner who delights in his sins, and is joyful in his evils, since he himself wallows in the foul dung, and perceives no sense of his stench, which arises from the dung of sin, and he delights as if in the highest pleasures and most grateful delicacies.

Cornelius a Lapide applies all these things throughout the whole chapter to the false Doctors in his recapitulation of the same, which it is pleasing to repeat, even though the accommodation of them to the Lutherans, made from a diabolical lust for slandering, could with the most just title be made to the Papists through all their members, which the very notoriety of the matter proves. This, therefore, he says, is the idea of a heretic (such as, for instance, the Papists are, addicted to the profession of the Tridentine Conventicle), which St. Peter graphically painted to the life in this whole chapter as if with these colors of character. First, v. 1: Heretics, he says, are false prophets and lying teachers. Second, they introduce sects of perdition. Third, they deny the Lord who bought them. Fourth, v. 2: many follow their luxuries. Fifth, by them the way of truth is blasphemed. Sixth, v. 3: in avarice they trade with the Devil concerning the body and soul of the faithful. Seventh, they are hypocrites and flatterers: for they use feigned and smooth-talking words, and those composed for seducing. Eighth, their perdition hastens. Ninth, v. 8: they are similar to demons and Lucifer. Tenth, v. 5: they are similar to the carnal ones drowned by the flood and the Sodomites. Eleventh, v. 10: they walk after the flesh in the concupiscence of uncleanness. Twelfth, they despise dominion. Thirteenth, they are bold. Fourteenth, they are self-pleasing. Fifteenth, they are blasphemous. Sixteenth, v. 12: they are as irrational beasts born for capture and perdition. Seventeenth, they blaspheme things they do not understand. Eighteenth, v. 13: they are voluptuaries, stains and blemishes, flowing with delicacies. Nineteenth, reveling in their feasts, having eyes full of adultery and incessant sin. Twentieth, v. 14: they entice unstable souls. Twenty-first, they have a heart exercised in avarice. Twenty-second, they are children of the curse. Twenty-third, v. 15: forsaking the right way, they wander. Twenty-fourth, they follow the way of Balaam, who loved the wages of iniquity, and therefore perished. Twenty-fifth, v. 17: they are fountains without water. Twenty-sixth, they are clouds driven by whirlwinds, for whom the mist of darkness is reserved. Twenty-seventh, v. 18: they speak proud things of vanity. Twenty-eighth, they entice those who have newly turned away from error through the bait of pleasures and luxury. Twenty-ninth, v. 19: they promise liberty, when they themselves are slaves of corruption. Thirtieth, v. 20: their latter end becomes worse than the former. Thirty-first, v. 22: they are as dogs returned to their vomit, and as washed sows returned to the wallowing in the mire.

And these things concerning the second chapter.

SECTION II. ANTITHESIS OF TRUE DOCTRINE, of those mocking who call the latest coming of Christ into doubt, with their refutation.

The doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles, recalled to memory, predicts that mockers will come in the last days, who will call the coming of the Lord to judgment into doubt: and it teaches that, just as the heaven and earth were constituted by the Word of God, so the world also will perish by fire, by the word of God: that the last day is deferred as far as we are concerned, since with God one day is as a thousand years, because of divine long-suffering, but that it will come unexpectedly, with the destruction of the heavens, the elements, and the creatures of the earth, whence it warns that we should strive that we may be found immaculate, and that we should count the long-suffering of the Lord as our salvation: appealing to the support of the Pauline epistles, which it commends as being from divine wisdom, even though they are perverted by the unlearned alongside other Scriptures, and it exhorts finally that they should not allow themselves to be seduced, but should grow in the knowledge of Christ, and it concludes with a doxology.

There are two parts: I. The refutation of the mockers denying the coming of the Lord, up to v. 10. II. The exhortation to preparation for the coming of the Lord, up to v. 18.

PART I. The refutation of the mockers denying the coming of the Lord.
