Vers. 22.

Συμβέβηκε γὰρ ἀυτοῖς τὸ τῆς ἀληθοῦς παροιμίας κύων ἐπι- στρέψας εἰς τὸ ἴδιον ἐξέραμα.) Est hæc ἀληθὴς παροιμία, sive משל Prov. XXVI, 11. ubi Græca sic habent: Ὥσπερ κύων ὅ- ταν ἐπὶ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ ὀματὸν, καὶ μισητὸς γένηται, ὕτως ἄφρων τῇ ἑαυτοῦ κακίᾳ ἀναστρέψας ἐπὶ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἁμαρτίαν.

Καὶ ὗς λυσαμένη εἰς κύλισμα βορβόρου.) Aratus: Σύες φορυντὰ ὕει μαργαίνουσαῃ. Philo συὸς τρόπον ἐν βορβόρῳ διαλυομένης. Εἰς κύλισμα in volutabrum: quomodo citat Ambrosius: Pro eodem κυλισ- μὸν dixit Theodotion. Prov. II, 18. Terentius Hecyra: Nam in eandem vitam te revolutum dehuo Video esse.

Canis cum se avidus cibo ingurgitavit, herba quadam comesa, vomitum ciet, sed ut animal na- tura immundum & vorax est, mox resorbet cibos ejectos: Sui autem lutum amicum est: Ideo etsi lota sit; statim sese rursus in eo volutat. Hæc applicat post pœnitentiam ad peccati sordes redeuntibus Gregorius M. part. III. cur. pastor. admon. 31. Admonendi sunt, qui admissa plan- gunt, nec tamen deserunt, ut considerare solicite sciant, quia flendo inaniter se mundant, qui viven- do se nequiter inquinant, cum idcirco se lacrymis lavant, ut mundi ad sordes redeant. Hinc enim scriptum est: Canis reversus ad suum vomitum, & sus lota in volutabro luti. Canis quippe cum vomit, profecto cibum, qui pectus deprimebat, pro- jicit, sed cum ad vomitum revertitur, unde levigatus fuerat, rursus oneratur. Et qui admissa plangunt, profecto nequitiam, de qua male satiati fuerant, & quæ mentis intima deprimebat consuetudo, proji- ciunt, quam post confessionem dum repetunt, resu- munt. Sus vero in volutabro luti, cum lavatur, sordidior redditur, & qui admissum plangit, nec tamen deserit, pene graviori culpa se subjicit, quia ipsam quam potuit flendo impetrare veniam, con- temnit, & quasi in lutosa aqua semetipsum volvit, quia dum fletibus suis vitæ munditiam subtrahit, ante Dei oculos sordidas etiam ipsas lacrymas fa- cit. S. Augustinus de priori similitudine hom. II. in Psalm. XXX. Vide, inquit, quam horribili res eos comparaverit. Horribilis certe res est, propri- um resorbere vomitum, nec in summa quidem fa- me a quoquam usurpatum. Et in Psalm. XCIII.

Canis reversus ad suum vomitum. Premebat enim pectus conscientia peccatorum: Accepta indulgentia, quasi vomuisses, relevatum est pectus tuum. Facta est bona conscientia ex mala conscientia: quid rursus converteris ad vomitum? Sicanis hac faciens hor- ret oculis tuis, tu quid eris oculis Dei?

Posterioris similitudinis applicatio facta est ab Origene homil. I. in Psal. XXXVII. Cujus com- monitio huc spectat: Porcis, inquit, similes di- cuntur ii, qui peccatorum fætoribus delectantur, sicut porci, qui omnem fætorem tanquam odorem suavissimum expetunt. Considera ergo peccatorem, qui peccatis suis delectatur, & lætus est in malis suis, quoniam & ipse in stercore fætido volutatur, & nullum fætoris ejus, qui ex peccati stercore oritur, percipit sensum, ac velut in summis voluptatibus & gratissimis deliciis delectatur.

Omnia hæc per totum caput ad falsos Docto- res applicat Cornelius a Lapide in ἀνακεφαλαιώσει ejusdem, quam repetere placet, etsi accommoda- tio eorum ad Lutheranos ex Diabolica calumni- andi libidine facta, titulo justissimo ad Papistas per omnia membra fieri possit, quam ipsa rei no- torietas comprobat. Hæc est ergo, inquit, idea hæretici, (quales ex grat. Pontificii sunt, professio- ni Conciliabuli Tridentini addicti) quam toto hoc capite graphice hisce moribus quasi coloribus ad vivum pinxit S. Petrus. Primo v. 1. Hæretici, inquit, sunt Pseudo-Prophetæ & Magistri menda- ces. Secundo introducunt sectas perditionis. Ter- tio eum, qui emit eos, Dominum negant. Quarto v. 2. multi sequuntur eorum luxurias, Quinto per eos via veritatis blasphematur. Sexto v. 3. in avaritia de fidelium corpore & anima cum Dæmo- ne negotiantur. Septimo sunt hypocritæ & adula- tores: utuntur enim verbis fictis & blandiloquis, & ad seducendum compositis. Octavo perditio eorum accelerat. Nono v. 8. similes sunt Dæmonibus & Lucifero. Decimo v. 5. similes sunt carnalibus mersis diluvio ac Sodomitis. Undecimo v. 10. post carnem in concupiscentia immunditiæ ambulant. Duodecimo, dominationem contemnunt. Decimo tertio sunt audaces. Decimo quarto sibi placentes. Decimo quinto blasphemi. Decimo sexto v. 12. sunt velut irrationabilia pecora nata in captionem & perditionem. Decimo septimo, quæ non intelligunt blasphemant. Decimo octavo v. 13. sunt voluptua- rii coinquinationes & maculæ, deliciis affluentes. Decimo nono in convivio luxuriantes, oculos haben- tes plenos adulterii & incessabilis delicti. Vigesimo vers. 14. pelliciunt animas instabiles. Vigesimo primo cor habent avaritia exercitatum. Vigesimo secundo sunt maledictionis filii. Vigesimo tertio v. 15. derelinquentes viam rectam errant. Vigesimo quar- to sequuntur viam Balaam, qui mercedem iniquita- tis amavit, ideoque periit. Vigesimo quinto v. 17. sunt fontes sine aqua. Vigesimo sexto sunt nebulæ turbinibus exagitatæ, quibus caligo tenebrarum re- servatur. Vigesimo septimo v. 18. superba vanita- tis loquuntur. Vigesimo octavo pelliciunt per escam voluptatum & luxuriæ noviter ab ea conversos. Vigesimo nono v. 19. promittunt libertatem, cum ipsi sint servi corruptionis. Trigesimo v. 20. fiunt ejus posteriora deteriora prioribus. Trigesimo pri- mo v. 22. sunt velut canes reversi ad vomitum, & velut sues lotæ reversæ ad volutabrum luti.

Atque hæc de secundo capite.

SECTIO II. ANTITHESIS VERÆ DOCTRINÆ, Empactarum novissimum Christi adventum in dubium vocantium, cum eorum con- futatione.

In memoriam revocata doctrina Prophetarum & apostolorum prædicit Empæctas in no- vissimis diebus venturos, qui adventum Domini ad judicium in dubium vocaturi sint: docetque, ut Verbo Dei cælum & ter- ra constitit, sic interiturum orbem quoque igne, Dei verbo: differi autem quoad nos diem vovissimum, quum apud Deum unus dies mille annorum instar sit, ob longani- mitatem divinam, sed venturum inopina- to, cum interitu cælorum, elementorum & creaturarum terræ, unde monet, studea- mus, ut immaculati reperiamur, & lon- ganimitatem Domini salutem nostram du- camus: provocans ad epistolarum Pauli- narum suffragia, quas a divina sapientia commendat, etsi ab indoctis juxta cum aliis Scripturis pervertantur, hortaturque postremo, ne patiantur sese seduci, sed cre- scant in cognitione Christi, & concludit δοξολογίᾳ.

Partes duæ sunt: I. Empæctarum adventum Domini negantium confutatio, ad v. 10. II. Ad præparationem ad adventum Domini exhortatio, ad v. 18.

PARS I. Empæctarum adventum Domini negan- tium confutatio.

## 3:1 Argument
Ver. 1. This is now, beloved, the second epistle I write unto you

This is the beginning of a new epistle of the same Simeon to those Jews in Egypt who had professed the discipline of Christ.

This novel opinion concerning a new epistle of Simeon rests on no reason at first, is furthermore destitute of all probability, and is easily refuted both from the very beginning and from the continuity and end of the preceding chapter. For at the beginning no introduction of a new epistle appears, just as in the conclusion of the second chapter no indication of a finished epistle is detected: nay, both the prophecy and the exhortation, by which Pseudo-Teachers and Mockers are to be shunned, and the conclusion of the whole epistle, by which they are finally warned to avoid those who deprave the sacred Scriptures, clearly teach that the present chapter coheres and pertains to the same epistle. What? That the holy author immediately indicates here that this is the second epistle, not the third. Concerning which it was treated in the Prolegomena. Moreover, this latter epistle was not written to the Jews in Egypt, but to the same ones to whom the prior Petrine epistle was inscribed, and thence from the Babylon of Egypt, concerning which likewise before.

In which I stir up your sincere mind by way of remembrance.

In which, that is, both in this and in that epistle which was written heretofore, which is comprised in the two chapters which we have already had. In remembrance, that is, by putting in mind. It is the same expression as above I. 13. To stir you up by putting you in remembrance. Thus we have to put in remembrance for הִזְכִּיר in John XIV. ver. 26. 2 Tim. II. ver. 14. and above chapter I. ver. 12. But what he says, your sincere mind, is that of one flattering and hoping well. Paul commends sincerity to us, 1 Cor. V. ver. 8. and indeed by his own example, 2 Cor. I. ver. 12. chap. II. ver. 17. Mind, Matthew XXII. ver. 37. Mark XII. ver. 30. Luke X. ver. 27. Eph. I. ver. 8. Heb. VIII. ver. 10. chap. X. ver. 16. 1 Pet. I. ver. 13. We have the scope of both epistles designated here, both the first of Peter and the second, not indeed only of the two preceding chapters, but also of the present third. For a stirring up and a reminding of this kind was also made in the first Petrine epistle, where all states were aroused and warned, and the doctrine was recalled to their memory, both of the Prophets 1 Pet. 1. vers. 10. 11. and of the Apostles, vers. 12. because the former was delivered through the Spirit of Christ, and the latter likewise sent from heaven through the Holy Spirit, exhibiting grace through the manifestation of Jesus Christ, of which Apostolic word they are also reminded in vers. 25. and thence are aroused to lay aside hypocrisy, and to expect the sincere milk of the Evangelical doctrine, chap. II. vers. 1. 2. in which epistle the Apostle likewise warned of the end of the world and of the final judgment chap. IV. 5. 7. and exhorted to constancy of faith and vigilance vers. 12. seqq. chap V. vers. 8. 9. And the recapitulation in chap. V. vers. 12. teaches that this was the same end of the former epistle: 'I have written, exhorting and testifying that this is the true grace of God, in which you stand.' The construction therefore 'in which' refers to the sense, not to the words. 'In which' namely 'epistles'. 'In reminding' is put for 'through reminding', as in chap. I. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 1. Ταύτην ἤδη, ἀγαπητοὶ, δευτέραν ὑμῖν γράφω ἐπιστολὴν)

Hoc est initium novæ epistolæ ejusdem Simeonis ad illos in Ægypto Judæos, Christi disciplinam professos.

Novella hæc de nova epistola Simeonis opinio nulla primum ratione nititur, ad hæc omni proba- bilitate destituitur, & tum ex ipso initio, tum e συνεχείᾳ & fine capitis præcedentis facile refelli- tur. Nam in initio nullum apparet novæ episto- læ εἰσόδιον, uti in conclusione capitis secundi nul- lum deprehenditur finitæ epistolæ indicium: imo cohærere, & ad eandem epistolam pertinere præ- sens caput luculenter utraque tum prophetia, tum parænesis, qua fugiendos Pseudo-Doctores & Empæctas, nec non conclusio totius epistolæ, qua ultimo monentur de vitandis iis, qui sacras Scri- pturas depravant, edocet. Quid? quod hic al- teram hanc esse epistolam, non tertiam, statim in- dicet sanctus autor. De quo in Prolegomenis actum. Non autem Judæis in Ægypto, sed ad eosdem, quibus prior Petrina epistola inscripta fuit, hæc posterior exarata est, indeque e Babylo- ne Ægypti, quo de itidem antea.

Ἐν αἷς διεγείρω ὑμῶν ἐν ὑπομνήσει τὴν εἰλικρινῆ διάνοιαν.

In quibus, id est, & in hac, & in ea, quæ antehac scripta est epistola, quæ comprehensa est capitibus duobus, quæ jam habuimus. Ἐν ὑπομνήσει, id est commonefaci- endo. Est eadem loquutio quæ sura I. 13. Διεγείρειν ὑμᾶς ἐν ὑπομνήσει. Sic ὑπομιμνήσκειν pro הִזְכִּיר habemus Joh. XIV. vers. 26. 2. Tim. II. vers. 14. & supra cap. I. vers. 12. Quod vero ait τὴν εἰλικρινῆ διάνοιαν, est blan- dientis & bene sperantis. Εἰλικρίνειαν commendat no- bis Paulus, 1. Cor. V. vers. 8. & quidem suo exemplo, 2. Corinth. I. vers. 12. cap. II. vers. 17. Διάνοια mens Matth. XXII. vers. 37. Marc. XII. vers. 30. Luc. X. vers. 27. Ephes. I. vers. 8. Ebr. VIII. vers. 10. cap. X. vers. 16. 1. Petr. 1. vers. 13. Utriusque epistolae scopum tum prima Petri- na, tum secunda hic designatum habemus, non vero tantum duorum praecedentium capitum, sed & praesentis tertii. Nam ejusmodi διέγερσις καὶ ὑπόμνησις etiam facta est in prima Petrina, ubi omnes status excitati & commoniti sunt, & in memoriam ipsis revocata doctrina tum Prophe tarum 1. Petr. 1. vers. 10. 11. tum Apostolorum, vers. 12. quod illa per Christi Spiritum tradita, haec itidem per Spiritum Sanctum de coelo mis- sa sit exhibens gratiam per manifestationem Je su Christi, de quo Apostolico verbo etiam con monefiunt vers. 25. atque inde excitantur ad deponendam hypocrisin, & expectandum lac sincerum doctrinae Evangelicae, cap. II. vers. 1. 2. in qua epistola pariter de fine mundi monuit Apostolus & de judicio novissimo cap. IV. 5. 7. & hortatus est ad constantiam fidei & vigilanti- am vers. 12. seqq. cap V. vers. 8. 9. Atque hunc eundem finem prioris epistolae fuisse ἀνακεφα- λαίωσις cap. V. vers. 12. facta docet : Ἔγραψα παρα- καλῶν καὶ ἔτι μαρτυρῶν ταύτην εἶναι ἀληθῆ χάριν τῦ Θεῦ, εἰς ἣν ἑστήκατε. Constructio ergo ἐν αἷς ad sensum, non ad verba refertur. Ἐν αἷς scilicet ἐπιστολαῖς. Ἐν ὑπομνήσει ponitur pro δι' ὑπο- μνήσεως per commonitionem, ut cap. I. 13.

## 3:2
Vers. 2.

Μνησθῆναι τῶν εἰρημένων ῥημάτων ὑπὸ τῶν ἁγίων Προφη- τῶν καὶ τῆς τῶν Ἀποστόλων ἡμῶν ἐντολῆς τῦ Κυρίε καὶ Σωτῆρος.)

For 'your' others have 'our', namely as if one of the Apostles were speaking. I think both are inserted, and that it is a transposition for 'the commandment of the Apostles of the Lord and Savior'. Thus Jude, who follows this writer much, 'by the Apostles of the Lord Jesus Christ'.

He wishes that 'our', which approved Codices have, to be expunged, lest the Author be believed to be Simon Peter the Apostle; but he cuts his own vines, when he affirms that Jude follows this author much. For who would believe that Jude the Apostle wished to follow a non-Apostolic writer much or in most things, nor one inspired by God? We have, however, here a Petrine confirmation of the sacred canon comprised in Prophetic and Apostolic writings. For by the name of 'words spoken by the holy Prophets and the Apostles' are designated the Scriptures, as of the Prophets, who do not speak to us otherwise than through the Scriptures; so also of the Apostles. And since Apocrypha are not in the number of the Prophetic writings of the Old Testament, therefore the same, even if canonized by the council of Trent, cannot be received with an equal affect of piety alongside the Prophetic ones.

The Vulgate must be corrected here; 'that you may be mindful of those words which I foretold by the holy Prophets', by which the most lucid Greek text is obscured, provided the transposition most customary to Peter is observed, 1. Epist. I. vers. 11. chap. III. vers. 21. 2. Pet. I. 19. How Erasmus rendered it correctly, 'that you may be mindful of our commandment, who are Apostles of the Lord and Savior', that is, 'that you may be mindful of the commandment which you received from us, the Apostles of the Lord and Savior', as B. Luther also rendered it: 'and of the commandment of us the Apostles of the Lord and Savior'. In which way the parallel passage Jude vers. 17. agrees. To which sense Estius also acceded, having disregarded the Vulgate version. By that precept, however, is understood the whole doctrine delivered by the Apostles, conf. chap. II. vers. 21. under which is also comprehended the warning made peculiarly by Jude vers. 18. concerning avoiding the doctrines of demons 1. Timoth. IV. vers. 1. and the associations of the impious, 2. Tim. III. v. 1.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Μνησθῆναι τῶν εἰρημένων ῥημάτων ὑπὸ τῶν ἁγίων Προφη- τῶν καὶ τῆς τῶν Ἀποστόλων ἡμῶν ἐντολῆς τῦ Κυρίε καὶ Σωτῆρος.)

Pro ὑμῶν alii habent ἡμῶν, nempe quasi unus ex Apo- stolis loqueretur. Ego utrumque insertum puto, & esse trajectionem pro τῆς ἐντολῆς τῶν Ἀποστόλων τῦ Κυρίε καὶ Σωτῆρος. Sic Judas, qui hunc scriptorem multum se- quitur, ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀποστόλων τυ Κυρίε Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ.

Illud ἡμῶν, quod habent probati Codices, ex- punctum vult, ne Autor Simon Petrus Aposto lus credatur; sed propria vineta caedit, cum Ju- dam hunc Autorem multum sequi affirmat. Ec- quis enim credat, Judam Apostolum multum vel in plerisque sequi Scriptorem non Apostolum voluisse, nec θεόπνευστον? Habemus autem hic confirmationem Petrinam canonis sacri Scri- ptis Propheticis & Apostolicis comprehensi. Nomine enim εἰρημένων ῥημάτων ὑπὸ τῶν ἁγίων Προφητῶν καὶ τῶν Ἀποστόλων designantur Scriptu rae ut Prophetarum, qui non aliter loquuntur no- bis, quam per Scripturas; ita & Apostolorum. Et quum in numero Propheticorum scriptorum Veteris Testamenti Apocrypha non sint, ideo eadem, etsi a concilio Trident. canonizata non posse juxta cum Propheticis pari pietatis affectu suscipi.

Corrigenda autem hic Vulgata; ut memores sitis eorum, quae praedixi verborum a Sanctis Pro- phetis, quibus obscuratur textus Graecus lucu- lentissimus, modo observetur trajectio Petro usitatissima, 1. Epist. I. vers. 11. cap. III. vers. 21. 2. Pet. I. 19. Quomodo reddidit recte Erasmus, ut memores sitis mandati nostri, qui sumus Apo- stoli Domini & Salvatoris, hoc est, ut memores sitis mandati, quod accepistis a nobis Domini & Salvatoris Apostolis, ut B. Lutherus etiam red- didit: καὶ τῆς ἐντολῆς ἡμῶν τῶν Ἀποσόλων τῦ Κυ- ρίε καὶ Σωτῆρος. Quo pacto consonat locus Parallelus Jud. vers. 17. Cui sensui etiam acces- sit Estius, susque deque habita versione Vulga- ta. Per praeceptum autem illud intelligitur tota doctrina ab Apostolis tradita, conf. cap. II. vers. 21. sub qua etiam comprehenduntur com- monitio peculiariter a Juda vers. 18. facta de ca- vendis doctrinis Dæmoniorum 1. Timoth. IV. vers. 1. & commerciis impiorum, 2. Tim. III. v. 1.

## 3:3
Vers. 3.

Τῦτο πρῶτον γινώσκοντες, ὅτι ἐλεύσονται ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάτω τῶν ἡμερῶν ἐμπαῖκται) 'first' here is again 'above all', as above 1. 2. 'In the last of the days' does not designate a certain time, but signifies 'at length' or 'hereafter'. Thus Num. XXIV, v. 14. אחרית הימים: In Sirach: 'in the last of the days'. Jude in the same matter said 'in the last time'. V. x 'mockers' is in the Greek, Isa. III. 3. where in the Hebrew העלולים. The meaning is similar in the Hebrew לצים. Men are called thus, who mock piety. In the Manuscript it is 'in mockery mockers', for 'in mockery', for it is said both 'mockery' and 'mockery', 'a mockery'. It is, however, a custom for the Hebrews to add substantives to adjectives for the sake of emphasis. And thus the Latin reads, translating: 'In deception mocking'. Augustine cites it more expressly to the Greek: 'mocking with illusion'. I interpret those Ἐμπαίκτας, who were to come, as before, the Carpocratians, who denied that the resurrection of the body was to come, as Augustine expressly teaches us, and all the more boldly because, with Jerusalem already destroyed, they still saw this machinery of the world standing, contrary to what most Christians, even the Apostles, had thought would happen, because they had received nothing certain about that matter from the Lord, except that Jerusalem would be destroyed before the world. When I said Apostles here, I understand [it] before the time of the Revelation made to John.

St. Peter speaks expressly of the last days, as also St. Jude of the last time, from which clear text one should not depart without cause. Nor does the passage Num. XXIV. 14 fit here. For there, κατά τι, the extreme times are understood concerning the conversation of that Moabite with the Israelites: here, the extreme days of the age. Therefore, these things are perversely snatched away to the Carpocratians, concerning whose heresy it is not even certain that they denied the last coming of the Lord. Carpocrates is said to have denied the resurrection of the flesh, and that around the year of Christ 140, but in such a way that he asserted μετεμψύχωσιν, namely, that souls are sent into other bodies because they had not sufficiently satisfied themselves with pleasures. The fable about the belief in the coming of Christ being connected with the destruction of Jerusalem is repeated, not proven, by Grotius; which, however, cannot consist with the promise of the Holy Spirit, who was to lead the Apostles into all truth, if the Apostles themselves are believed to have been subject to this error. Estius explains Empæctas as impostors; but others interpret it more correctly as mockers, because ἐμπαίζειν is to mock, Matt. XX. 19, ch. XXVII. 29, 31, etc. They mocked, however, as Bede has it, the faith and hope of Christians, not because of a delayed coming, like that wicked servant, Matt. XXIV. 47, but because none is to be expected. For are not such questions formed by the particles 'is it not', 'what', 'where', 'how' accustomed to deny simply? Gen. XVIII. 14, 17, Ps. CXIII. 5, Matt. XII. 26, 34, Luke XIV. 5, Job III. 4, Rom. III. 3, see especially Ps. XLII. 4, Ps. LXXIX. 10. Which the other words of the Empæctas also teach. But that the words IN DECEPTION were rashly inserted by the Vulgate is confirmed both by the consensus of the Greek Codices and by a comparison with Jude v. 18.

Walking according to their own desires) The same words in Jude v. 6. See also above II. 10. But it is no wonder if those who do not believe in the resurrection indulge the flesh in all things, as Paul teaches us 1 Cor. XV. 32.

It is signified that those Empæctas, having shaken off the fear of God and having put the word of God behind them, are serving depraved pleasures, especially gluttony and lust, according to their own desires. Cf. Jude v. 18, 2 Tim. III. 1 seqq.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Τῦτο πρῶτον γινώσκοντες, ὅτι ἐλεύσονται ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάτω τῶν ἡμερῶν ἐμπαῖκται) πρῶτον hic rursus est imprimis, ut supra 1. 2. Ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάτω τῶν ἡμερῶν non designat certum tempus, sed significat tandem aut posthac. Sic Num. XXIV, v. 14. אחרית הימים: In Siraco: ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάτῳ τῶν ἡμερῶν. Judas in re eadem dixit ἐν ἐσχάτῳ χρόνῳ. V. x ἐμπαῖκται est in Græco, Esa. III. 3. ubi in Ebræo העלולים. Par ser- me significatio in Ebræo לצים. Dicuntur sic homines, qui pietatem irrident. In Manuscripto est ἐν ἐμπαιγμονῇ ἐμ- παῖκται, pro ἐν ἐμπαιγμῇ, dicitur enim & ἐμπαιγμὸς & ἐμ- παιγμὸς, ἐμπαίγμα. Est autem mos Ebræis augendi causa addere substantiva Adjectivis. Et sic Latinus legit ver- tens: In de eptione illuso es. Augustinus citat expressius ad Græcum: illusione illudentes. Ἐμπαίκτας illos, qui futuri erant, interpretor, ut ante, Carpocratianos, qui resurrectionem corporis negabant venturam, ut expresse nos docet Augu- stinus, eoque audacius, quod excisis jam Hierosolymis adhuc viderent stare hanc mundi machinam, contra quam plerique Christianorum, etiam Apostoli, existimaverant futurum, quia nihil certi ea dere acceperant a Domino, nisi ante fore ut exscinderentur Hierosolyma, quam mun- dus. Apostolos hic cum dixi, intelligo ante tempus Re- velationis Johanni factæ.

Loquitur S. Petrus expresse de diebus novissi- mis, ut & S. Judas de novissimo tempore, a qua lite- ra diserta sine causa non est discedendum. Ne- que locus Num. XXIV. 14. huc quadrat. Ibi enim κατά τι extrema tempora de conversatio- ne istius Moabitarum cum Israelitis intelliguntur: hic extremi dies seculi. Perverse ergo hæc ab- ripiuntur ad Carpocratianos, de quorum hæresi etiam haud constat, quod negarint adventum Do- mini novissimum. Carnis resurrectionem negasse dicitur Carpocrates, idque circa annum Christi 140. sed ita ut μετεμψύχωσιν asseruerit, in alia nem- pe corpora animas immitti, quod non satis se vo- luptatibus expleverint. Fabula de connexo cre- dito adventu Christi cum interitu Hierosolymo- rum repetitur, non probatur a Grotio; Quæ vero cum promissione Spiritus Sancti, Apostolos in omnem veritatem ducturi, consistere nequit, si Apostoli ipsi etiam huic errori obnoxii fuisse credantur. Empæctas Estius explicat imposto- res; sed rectius alii interpretantur, illusores, quia ἐμπαίζειν est illudere, Matth. XX. 19. cap. XXVII. 29. 31. &c. Illuserunt autem, ut Beda habet, fidei & spei Christianorum, non ob dilatum adventum, ut servus ille malus, Matth. XXIV. 47. sed quod nullus expectandus sit. Tales enim interrogatio- nes per particulas nunquid, quid, ubi, quomodo formatæ solent simpliciter negare? Gen. XVIII. 14. 17. Ps. CXIII. 5. Matth. XII. 26. 34. Luc. XIV. 5. Job. III 4. Rom. III. 3. vid. imprimis Ps. XLII. 4. Ps. LXXIX. 10. Quod etiam verba Empæctarum cætera docent, Illa vero verba IN DECEPTIO- NEM temere a Vulgata inserta esse tum consen- sus Græcorum Codicum, tum collatio Jud. v. 18. confirmat.

Κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἁυτῶν πορευόμενοι) Eadem verba Jud. v. 6 Vide & supra II. 10. Non mirum autem esse, si carni per omnia indulgent, qui resurrectionem non credant, docet nos Paulus 1. Cor. XV. 32.

Significatur Empæctas illos excusso Dei ti- more, & verbo Dei posthabito, pravis voluptati- bus, gulæ imprimis ac libidini secundum propria desideria servientes. Conf. Jud. v. 18. 2. Tim. III. 1. seqq.

## 3:4
Ver. 4.

And saying: where is the promise of his coming) His, that is, Christ's, whose name preceded a little before, and, if that were not the case, it could still be sufficiently understood from the matter itself, as Heb. XIII. 5. In a similar way, the impious mocked the prophecies of Ezekiel, ch. XII. 27. And it was said to Malachi: Where is that God of judgment, that is, who is to judge? ch. II. 17.

For from the time the fathers fell asleep) from the time, understand the word 'day'. And take 'day' for 'time'. All things so remain from the beginning of the creation) Manilius: Even then when the ships of Danaus were ravaging Pergamum, the Bear and Orion were going with opposing fronts. Conf. Eccles. I. 9.

The promise of the presence, that is, the coming, chap. I. 16. chap. III. 12. Matt. XXIV. 27. 37. 39. 1 Cor. XV. 23. or the promised coming, namely the second, as it is called from Heb. IX. 28. The name of Christ seems to have been omitted by the mockers through a weakening of the expression. For he recites their words. Cornelius teaches that such were the Dositheans after the Sadducees, Hymenæus and Philetus, the Gnostics, the Florians, etc. But Peter here designates the mockers of the last days. More correctly, therefore, he would have named certain Pontiffs.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Καὶ λέγοντες· πῦ ἐστιν ἡ ἐπαγγελία τῆς παρυσίας ἀυτῦ) Αὐτῦ, id est, Christi, cujus nomen paulo ante præcessit, &, si id non esset, tamen ex re ipsa satis poterat intelligi, ut Ebr. XIII. 5. Simili modo impii illudebant Ezechielis va- ticinia cap. XII. 27. Et Malachiæ dicebatur: Ubi Deus ille judicii, id est, judicaturus? cap. II. 17.

Ἀφ' ἧς γὰρ οἱ πατέρες ἐκοιμήθησαν) ἀφ' ἧς subintellige ἡμέρας. Et ἡμέραν fume pro tempore. Πάντα ὕτως διαμένει ἀπ' ἀρχῆς τῆς κτίσεως) Manilius: Jam tum cum Danaæ vastarent Pergama puppes, Arctos & Orion adversis frontibus ibant. Conf. Eccles. I. 9.

Promissio παρουσίας, id est adventus cap. I. 16. cap. III. 12. Matth. XXIV. 27. 37. 39. 1. Cor. XV. 23. vel promissus adventus, secundus scilicet, ut ex Ebr. IX. 28. vocatur. Nomen Christi videtur per ἐξαθενισμὸν ab Empæctis prætermissum. Eorum enim verba recitat. Tales fuisse post Sadducæos Dositheanos, Hymenæum & Philetum, Gnosticos, Florianos, &c. Cornelius docet. Sed Petrus no- vissimorum dierum Empæctas hic designat. Re- ctius ergo Pontifices quosdam nominasset.

## 3:5
Ver. 5. For this escapes them, who wish it)

There is a certain ignorance that partakes much of the voluntary. Therefore it is said of some, they did not want to understand. If they read Moses, they can know that this world consists of corruptible things, and therefore it is no wonder if it is to be that it also itself be corrupted. That the heavens were of old and the earth consisting out of water and through water) It is a zeugma. For 'consisting' refers as much to the heaven as to the earth. The earth emerged from water, that is, from that moist mass which the Greeks, from the books of the Phoenicians, called 'matter', as we noted in the Annotations to the first book on the truth of the Christian religion and in the annotations to Genesis. The same earth stands 'through water', that is, in the midst of waters. For 'through' is also put for 'in the midst of', that is, between. See 1 Pet. III. 20. 'Consisting', that is, having its constitution, as the physicists also speak, as we said at Col. I. 17. Thus also you have 'constitution of the world' in Wisd. VII. 17. For both the earth together with the water makes one globe, and under the earth are huge receptacles of waters, into which all the seas insinuate themselves, and from where rivers arise, and in them they often hide themselves again. See Psalm XXIV. 2. Eccl. I. 7. and what is said there. The heaven also consists of water. For all heaven, as much as we call air as what we call ether, is called by one name by the Hebrews, and is considered to be a vapor from the waters, as we showed at Genesis. The same heaven also stands 'through water' because of the clouds which are in the heaven, and partly above the heaven, as can be seen in Gen. I. 7. chap. VII. 12. Ps. CXLVIII. 4. 'Of old' [Greek] [Hebrew] from days of old, Isa. XXXVII. 26.

To others it seems more convenient that we understand the word 'created' (heavens), since no necessity compels us to a zeugma or syllepsis, as Cornelius notes: Even if that verb 'consisting' is read in the singular, not in the plural 'consisting' [plural], as Oecumenius preferred. Nor therefore is it to be granted, as with Lessius on the Divine attributes, book XIII, chap. 10, and with Cornelius a Lapide, that 'out of water' should be referred to the heavens, and 'through water' to the earth, since both ought to be referred to the earth, if indeed the earth emerged 'out of water', since water had previously enveloped the whole earth, Gen. I. 9, 10. And the earth consists 'through water', which is not indeed said to float on the waters, as Grotius wishes, for it is not in the midst of the waters, but Peter says the earth consists through water; but it can be said to be 'consisting' [compacted] and solidified through water, both so that it would not crumble into dust, and so that it would be fit for the production and conservation of mixed bodies, the product of plants and animals, which causes Philo brings forward in his book on the creation of the world. Whence Oecumenius applies it thus: the earth from water indeed as from a material principle, but through water as through a perfecting principle. For water contains the earth like a certain glue, which is present to it, which if it did not happen to it, it would be necessary for it to be dissolved and turned into air. To which Beda also has similar things here: But if the verb 'consisting' is referred even to the heavens by a zeugma, so that there is no need to understand the word 'created' (even if that is easily deduced from the previous verse from the beginning of the creation) it would not, however, be necessary for those words 'out of water, and through water' to be referred also to the heavens, since those can be taken as if they look only to the earth, in this way: That the heavens were of old (from the beginning of the creation) and

the earth consisting out of water and through water by the word of God, so that those words 'out of water and through water', just as they are not added to the heavens but to the earth, may be understood of the earth and not of the heaven. But the words 'consisting by the word of God' alone are referred to the heavens and to the earth, both because the nerve of the Apostolic argument consists in them, regarding the destruction of the whole system of heaven and earth, that He who constituted heaven and earth by the Word alone, so that they might consist, can in turn destroy heaven and earth by the power of the Word alone, so that they are no longer: that He who from the beginning of the creation, which the mockers conceded, created them from nothing, and gave them a beginning, can annihilate them again, and bring an end to them: and because those adhering to the earth, and relying at least on earthly goods, pretended that all things remain in it as they were created from the beginning of the creation, so as to persuade that there would be no end of the world at all, they could be confounded regarding the earth, by an instance taken from the flood, if indeed this had not escaped them, nor could it be denied, that the earth had not remained as it was created in the beginning, but just as it emerged from water, and was constituted through water, so also it had been overwhelmed by water and destroyed and corrupted through water. There is no need here to inquire about the heavens, how they were constituted out of water, or through waters, which it is agreed were created out of nothing, and are of a substance entirely different from the elements and especially from water; unless we say that the stars, created from primordial light, which approach a nature more fiery than watery, were produced from waters: or how the heavens perished through the flood, and to restrict that to the aerial heavens, and indeed only to the lowest regions of the air, when on the contrary the Apostle names οὐρανοὺς in the plural: That certainly will never be proven, that the air is also comprehended under the name of the heavens, and that all those heavens, which Grot. calls both air and ether, are vapor from waters: concerning which it has been spoken of at Genesis. Piscator wrongly explains that ἔκπαλαι as concerning the time of Noah: because it is clear that it deals with the first creation, by which the heaven and earth consist: Nor did the heaven and earth, which were created from the beginning, perish at the time of Noah, but men and other living creatures in the world: which suffices for the refutation of the assertion of the scoffers, that all things thus persevere from the beginning of the creation, and for asserting the possibility of the destruction of the world. For there is no doubt that He who destroyed the world, which had stood for 1656 years, contrary to the expectation of the scoffers of that time, by the flood of water, is also able to destroy the same totally by fire, inasmuch as He once created it out of nothing. Not to mention that the air is falsely understood as heaven by Piscator, and that it is not consistent that he says the air perished in the flood, and thus that heaven and earth perished then. The world that was then denotes primarily men and living creatures, yet with the external form of the ancient world, which it is certain was greatly changed by the flood. Finally, what Grotius says, that the heaven δι' ὕδατοs stands in the midst of waters because of the clouds which are in the heaven, and partly above the heaven, that is foreign both to the present passage and to the phraseology of Scripture. It is not said here that the heavens consist δι' ὕδατοs, but the earth alone is said to be δι' ὕδατοs συνεστῶσα, nor are clouds ever said in the Scriptures to be either in the heavens or above the heavens. But in Gen. I. 7 and Ps. CXLVIII. 4 there is discourse concerning the supercelestial waters; in Gen. VII. 11 the windows of the heavens are said to be opened, concerning which in its own place. It is unheard of in all Theology as well as Philosophy that clouds are above the heaven, and thus that the heavens are constituted between waters, that is, between the clouds which are in the heavens and those which are above the heavens.

By the Word of God) See what we have said at the beginning of the Gospel of John. Add the passage of Philo on the life of Moses: 'For by the Word the changes and the annual seasons are established in a fixed and stable manner.' He means that those things which are in heaven and on earth are, by God's command and power, as much contained as they are released; just as fire is also.

Grotius confuses the imperative and the hypostatic word, as the passage in John 1:1-2 deals with the latter. What Grotius says about fire, that it is contained and released in heaven by divine command, is unwritten. Philosophers have dreamed something about fire under the concave of the Moon, but that fire has long since been extinguished, or to speak more correctly, that dream has been solidly refuted and exploded in sounder philosophy.

Vers. 5. Λανθάνει γὰρ ἀυτὰς τῦτο θέλοντας)

Est quædam ignorantia multum trahens de voluntario. Ideo de quibusdam dicitur, noluerunt intelligere. Si Mo- sen legerunt, scire possunt, mundum hunc constare ex cor- ruptibilibus, ideoq; non mirum si futurum est, ut & ipse corrumpatur. Ὅτι ἐρανοὶ ἦσαν ἔκπαλαι κỳ γῆ ἐξ ὕδατος κỳ δι' ὕδατος συνε- τῶσα) Est ζεῦγμα. Nam συνεστῶσα tam ad cœlum, quam ad terram refertur. Terra ex aqua emersit, id est, ex massa illa humida, quam ὕλην vocabant ex Phœnicum libris Græci, ut in Annot. ad librum primum pro veritate religionis Christ. & ad Genesin annotavimus. Eadem terra stat δι' ὕδατος, id est, in mediis aquis. Nam διὰ ponitur etiam pro בתוך, id est, inter. Vide 1. Petr. III. 20. Συνεστῶσα, id est, σύστασιν suam habens, quomodo & Physici loquuntur, ut diximus ad Col. I. 17. Sic & σύστασιν κόσμε habes Sap. VII. 17. Nam & terra simul cum aqua unum efficit globum, & sub terra ingentia sunt aquarum conceptacula, in quæ tota se maria insinuant, & unde amnes oriuntur, & in iis se sæpe rursus occultant. Vide Psalm. XXIV. 2. Eccl. I. 7. & ibi dicta. Cœlum quoque ex aqua constat. Nam cœlum omne, tam quod aërem, quam quod ætherem dicimus, Ebræis uno appellatur nomine, censeturque esse vapor ex aquis, ut ad Genesin ostendimus. Idem cœlum stat etiam δι' ὕδατος ob nubes, quæ in cœlo sunt, ac partim supra cœ- lum, ut videre est Gen. I. 7. cap. VII. 12. Psal. CXLVIII. 4. ἔκπαλαι מֵימֵי קֶדֶם ἐξ ἡμερῶν ἀρχαίων Es. XXXVII. 26.

Aliis convenientius videtur, ut subintelliga- mus vocem καταθέντες (ὐρανοὶ) quum ad Zeugma vel Syllepsin, ut notat Cornelius, nulla cogat ne- cessitas: Etsi in singulari legatur verbum illud συνεστῶσα, non in plurali συνεστῶτα, ut placuit Oe- cumenio. Neque ergo concedendum est, ut cum Lessio de attrib. Div. l. XIII. cap. 10. & cum Corne- lio a Lapide τὸ ἐξ ὕδατος ad cælos, τὸ δι' ὕδατος ad terram referatur, quum ad terram utrumque referri debeat, siquidem ἐξ ὕδατος emerserit ter- ra, quum aqua totam terram prius involverit, Gen. I. 9, 10. & δι' ὕδατος consistat terra, quæ non aquis quidem innatare dicitur, ut Grotius vult, nec enim in medio aquarum, sed per aquas consistere ter- ram, ait Petrus, per aquam autem συνεστῶσα com- pacta, & solidata dici potest, tum ut ne in pulve- rem fatisceret, tum ut apta esset productioni & conservationi corporum mixtorum productum plantarum atque animalium, quas causas affert Phil. l. de mundi opific. Unde ita applicat Oecumenius; terra ex aqua quidem tanquam ex materiali principio, per aquam vero tanquam per principium perfectivum. Aqua enim continet terram velut glutten quoddam, quod ipsi adest, quod nisi ipsi contingeret, necesse esset, illam dis- solvi, & verti in aërem. Quibus gemina etiam hic habet Beda: Quod si maxime per Zeugma verbum συνεστῶτα etiam ad cælos referatur, ut opus non sit subintelligere verbum κτισθέντες (etsi id e v. præc. ἀπ' ἀρχῆς κτίσεως facile deducatur) non ta- men necessum fuerit ad cælos etiam referri illa ἐξ ὕδατος, καὶ δι' ὕδατος, quum illa possint accipi, tanquam ad solam terram ea spectent, hoc modo: Ὅτι οἱ ὐρανοὶ ἦσαν ἔκπαλαι (ἀπ' ἀρχῆς κτίσεως) καὶ

γῆ ἐξ ὕδατοs, καὶ δι' ὕδατοs συνεστῶσα τῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ λό- γῳ, ut illa ἐξ ὕδατοs καὶ δι' ὕδατοs, quemadmo- dum non coelis addita sunt, sed terrae, de terra non de coelo intelligantur. Verba autem συνεστῶσα τῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ λόγῳ sola ad coelos & ad terram referan- tur, tum quia in illis nervus argumenti Apostolici consistit, quoad interitum totius systematis coeli & terrae, quod, qui solo Verbo coelum & terram constituit, ut constent, solius Verbi virtute coe- lum & terram vicissim destruere possit, ut non sint amplius: qui a̓πὸ ἀρχῆs κτίσεως, quod concede- bant Empaectae, ea ex nihilo condidit, iisque ini- tium dedit, eadem annihilare iterum, iisque finem afferre queat: tum quia terrae adhaerentes, bonis- que terrenis saltem nitentes omnia in eo mane- re, quemadmodum ab initio creationis fuerunt condita, praetendebant, ut finem mundi prorsus nullum fore persuaderent, confundi poterant de terra, per instantiam a diluvio petitam, siquidem hoc non latuerit illos, nec negari poterat, terram non mansisse, qualis initio condita erat, sed quem- admodum ex aqua emersit, & per aquam consti- tuta fuit, ita etiam aqua obrutam & per aquam perditam, & corruptam fuisse. Hic opus non est disquirere de caelis, quomodo illi ex aquis, vel per aquas constituti sint, quos ex nihilo conditos es- se constat, & substantiae esse prorsus diversae ab elementis & imprimis ab aqua; nisi sidera ex luce primigenia condita, quae ad igneam potius natu- ram, quam aqueam accedunt, ex aquis producta dicamus: vel quomodo coeli per diluvium interie- runt, & ad coelos aëreos id restringere, & qui- dem tantum ad infimas aëris regiones, quum con- tra Apostolus οὐρανοὺς in plurali nominet: Id cer- te nunquam probabitur, quod caelorum nomine etiam aër comprehendatur, & omnes isti coeli, quos Grot. vocat, tam aër quam aether, vapor sint ex aquis: de quibus ad Genesin dictum. Piscator il- lud ἔκπαλαι perperam de Noae tempore explicat: quia de prima creatione agi luculentum est, qua coelum & terra consistere: Nec Noae tempore coelum & terra, quae ab initio condita, perire, sed homines & animantia alia in mundo: quod sufficit ad confutationem assertionis Empaectarum, quod omnia sic perseverent ab initio creaturae, & adse- rendam possibilitatem destructionis mundi. Qui enim mundum, qui per annos 1656. constitit, praeter Empaectarum istius temporis expectatio- nem per aquae diluvium destruxit, idem etiam eundem quin destruere per ignem possit totali- ter, utpote quem ex nihilo olim condidit, dubi- tandum non est. Ut taceam, falso aërem intelligi per coelum a Piscatore, neque consentaneum esse, quod ait aërem in diluvio interiisse, adeoque caelum & terram tum periisse. Mundus qui tunc erat, homi- nes imprimis, & animantia notat, cum forma ta- men externa antiqui mundi, quam per diluvium valde immutatum certum est. Quod denique ait Grotius coelum δι' ὕδατοs, stare in medio aquarum ob nubes, quae in coelo sunt, ac partim supra coelum, id & a praesenti loco, & a phrasi Scri- pturae alienum est. Non hic coeli dicuntur δι' ὕδα- τοs consistere, sed terra sola dicitur δι' ὕδατοs συνεστῶσα, nec uspiam in Scripturis nubes vel in coelis, vel supra coelos esse dicuntur. Sed Gen. I. 7. & Psal. CXLVIII, 4. de aquis supracoelestibus sermo est Gen. VII. 11. coeli cataractae apertae di- cuntur, quo de suo loco. Inauditum est in omni tum Theologia, tum Philosophia nubes supra coelum esse, & ita coelos inter aquas con- stitui, hoc est inter nubes, quae in coelis & quae supra coelos sunt.

Τῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ λόγῳ) Vide quæ diximus ad initium Evangelii Johannis. Adde locum Philonis de vita Mosis: λόγῳ γὰρ οἱ τροπαὶ καὶ ἐτήσιοι ὥραι τεταγμένῃ καὶ παγίῳ συνίστανται Hoc vult a- quas illas, quæ in cœlo terraque sunt, Dei imperio ac po- tentia ut contineri, ita & laxari; sicut & ignem.

Confundit Grotius verbum προστακτικὸν & ὑποστατικὸν, utpote de quo locus Joh. I. 1. 2. agit. Quod de igne ait Grotius, eundem in cœlo divino imperio contineri & laxari, ἄγραφον est. Somnia- runt aliquid Philosophi de igne sub concavo Lunæ, sed ignis ille jam pridem extinctus est, vel ut re- ctius dicam, somnium illud in saniori Philoso- phia solide discussum & explosum.

## 3:6
Ver. 6.

By which) that is, for which reason. For thus the Greeks say 'for which things,' 'from which things,' denoting not something specific, but the whole matter which has been discussed. For which reason, that is, because the constitution of both the earth and the heaven was such as we have said.

Concerning the various explanation of the words 'by which,' see among others B. Gerhard. It is not displeasing to explain it as 'for which reason,' and to refer it to the whole matter which has been discussed, namely that the heavens and the earth stood by the Word of God alone, and that the earth emerged from the waters and was solidified by the power of the Word of God; whence it follows that it is not because the constitution of heaven and earth was such as Grotius said, but because heaven and earth were produced and solidified by the power of the divine Word alone, as we have shown from Moses, and by that same power the earth, inundated by water, perished. That depravation of the words 'by which' as 'by the word and the water' is not suitable, if only because a pleonasm would arise: 'the world which then was, perished, inundated by water, by the Word and the water.' Therefore, the explanation of Beza, Piscator, and Tossanus is more suitable: because the earth consists from water and in water, it happened that it was overwhelmed by the waters in the flood, with the waters reclaiming their ancient seats, by the command of Him by whose authority they had once receded from the earth. Therefore, those words 'by which' must be rendered as an illative 'wherefore' or 'for which reason,' with the genitive placed for the accusative, just as in 2 Peter 1:4 the words 'by which' are also intended to be taken as illative; since 'dia' with the accusative signifies 'on account of' (John 6:57, Rom. 3:25). For the cause is brought forward here as to why the earth perished by water: and therefore the explanation of Bede does not fit, who refers these 'by which' to heaven and earth, that the earth was submerged, and the heavens according to the quantity and spaces of the air: nor does the interlinear Gloss 'by which things,' that is, in which parts, the air and the earth, the world perished by the waters. For the object that perished by the waters is not expressed by the words 'by which,' but the cause is indicated as to why the world perished by water. Finally, the opinion of Salmeron is refuted from this, that by 'water,' from which the earth is said to have been made, the prime matter is understood, from which he also wishes to imply that the heaven was made. For Peter understands the same thing there by the name of water that he says here was overwhelmed with water. But who would say that the world was inundated by prime matter? By the name of water, says Estius in this place, some wish prime matter to be signified, but in a sense alien to the Scriptures.

The world that then was) That which was in the times of Noah. 'The ancient world' above in 2:15, the men who were then.

It is not understood as the men who were then only, nor of other living creatures alone, as Heinsius does from the Greeks, but primarily of the earth, which he had said consisted from water and by water, and which the scoffers had pretended persisted along with the heavens in the same manner as it had been established from the beginning of creation. Therefore, there is no reason for that 'then' to be restricted to the times of Noah, since it ought rather to be explained from the preceding words 'from the beginning of creation,' so that it may answer the objection of the scoffers. It is not true that the whole world remained as it was from the beginning: this earthly world perished, overwhelmed and inundated with those things which it contained, the waters, from which and by which it consisted, and it lost much of its ancient form. And therefore both the soul of the earth and the earth itself had need of a new divine blessing (Gen. 8:17, 22; 9:2, 3). Concerning which, see Bede in this place. The earth perished, because, being submerged and covered by waters, it not only lost the state of fruitfulness implanted in it for so long a time, but also received in most places a face unlike that which it had first received.

Scholastic and Papist interpreters dispute whether and how the waters of the heavens perished in the flood: whom Bede had preceded with an inconvenient interpretation of the passage, as Augustine did for him in book XX of The City of God, chapter 18. Estius, on verse 5, says: 'Not only almost all later theologians, both those who write on the Sentences and the commentators on this epistle, but also Augustine and Bede, understand the aerial heaven here.' He asserts, therefore, that the Apostle is speaking of the aerial heaven, and not even the whole of it, but that part which contains the lowest and middle region of the air, from which the birds of the heaven and the clouds and the rain are called the heaven. For the waters of the flood reached to these regions of the heaven, and no higher. They will scarcely be able to explain that the lowest and middle regions of the air were changed into another state; but as for the highest region of the air, they themselves see that this cannot be said, nor did the waters of the flood penetrate that far. Piscator, agreeing with them, says that the air perished for a time during the flood. St. Peter speaks of those heavens which were established of old by the Word, which indeed did not perish in the flood when the earth perished, or was destroyed by waters, but which, with the earth, are kept for fire on the day of judgment and the destruction of ungodly men, v. 7. But these are the ethereal heavens, not the aerial. For they are contrasted with the elements, v. 10 and 12, under which the air is included. Salmero, among the Papists, acknowledges this: 'For first,' he says, 'we show that the aerial and elemental heavens are never understood by the name of heavens in the plural number, and Peter, after naming the heavens, adds: The elements shall be dissolved with heat.' Cornelius a Lapide on Ez. XXXIV. 4: 'That exposition by which some, in the Apostolic passage 2 Pet. III, understand the air by the heavens, does not sufficiently agree with v. 10 and 12, where the Apostle opposes the heavens to the elements. Therefore, he understands not the aerial, but the sidereal heavens.' Blasius de Viegas in his commentary on Apoc. XXI, p. 812, confesses that in the words of Peter, v. 10, 'the heavens shall pass away with a great noise,' the celestial bodies themselves are understood. Cornelius a Lapide observes that most of the Fathers also establish this on v. 10 of this Petrine passage.

ὕδατι κατακλυσθεὶς ἀπώλετο) It perished, submerged by waters bursting forth both from the earth and from the heaven, as the history of Moses shows; see what we have brought forward from Seneca on that passage.

Nothing is read in Moses about waters bursting forth from the earth at the time of the flood, but about the opening of the fountains of the great deep: nor about waters from those heavens of which Peter had made mention here, but about waters sent down by the opening of the windows of heaven, which is a periphrasis for rains. Grotius wished to serve his hypothesis.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Δι' ὧν) id est, qua de causa. Sic enim Græci dicunt ἀνθ' ὧν, ἐξ ὧν, non certi aliquid, sed rem totam, de qua actum est, denotantes. Qua de causa, id est, quia talis erat, qualem di- ximus, constitutio & terræ & cœli.

De vocum δι' ὧν varia explicatione vid. inter alios B. Gerhardus. Non displicet explicari qua de causa, & ad rem totam, de qua actum est, refer- ri, nempe quod cœli & terra solo Dei verbo con- stiterint, & quod terra ex aquis emerserit, & per aquam solidata fit Verbi Dei virtute, unde non quia talis constitutio cœli & terræ, qualem Gro- tius dixit, sed quia ita producta & solidata cœlum & terra virtute solius Verbi divini, quemadmo- dum e Mose ostendimus, eadem etiam virtute per aquam terra inundata perierit. Illa verborum δι' ὧν depravatio per illa, id est, per verbum & a- quam, vel ideo non convenit, quod Pleonasmus oriturus sit, per Verbum & aquam mundus, qui tum erat, aqua inundatus interiit. Quapropter convenientior est Bezæ, Piscatoris & Tossani ex- plicatio: quia terra ex aqua & in aqua consistit, inde factum, ut aquis in diluvio fuerit obrata, anti- quas nimirum sedes aquis repetentibus, mandato illius, cujus imperio olim a terra recesserant. Red- denda ergo illa δι' ὧν illative quapropter, quamob- rem, genitivo posito pro accusativo, quemadmo- dum etiam 2. Pet. I. 4. verba δι' ὧν illative accipi volunt; siquidem διὰ cum Accusativo propter significat, Joh. VI. 57. Rom. III. 25. Affertur enim hic causa, cur aqua perierit terra: ideoque expli- catio Bedæ haud quadrat, referentis hæc δι' ὧν ad cœlum & ad terram, quod terra submersa sit, & cœli secundum quantitatem & spatia aëris: nec Glossa interlin. per quæ, hoc est, in quibus partibus, aëre & terra mundus interiit aquis. Non enim objectum vocibus δι' ὧν exprimitur, quod interiit aquis, sed causa, cur aqua interierit mundus, indi- gitatur. Refellitur denique hinc Salmeronis opi- nio, per aquam, ex qua terra facta dicitur, mate- riam primam intelligi, e qua etiam cœlum fa- ctum innui vult. Nam idem aquæ nomine Petrus ibi intelligit, quod hic cum aqua obrutum mun- dum dicit. At quis dicturus est, materia prima mundum inundatum? Aquæ nomine, inquit Estius in h. l. materiam primam nonnulli significatam vo- lunt, sed sensu a Scripturis alieno.

Ὁ τότε κόσμος) Is qui erat Noæ temporibus. ὁ κό- σμος ἀρχαῖος supra II. 15. homines, qui tum erant.

Non de hominibus, qui tunc erant tantum, nec de animantibus aliis solum, ut e Græcis Heinsius, sed imprimis de terra, quam ex aqua & per aquam constitisse dixerat, & quam juxta cum cœlis ea- dem ratione perseverare, uti ab initio creationis condita erat, Empæctæ obtenderant, ὁ κόσμος in- telligitur. Ideo nec est, ut illud τότε ad tempora Noæ restringatur, quum potius e verbis præceden- tibus ἀπ' ἀρχῆς κτίσεως explicari debeat, ut ob- jectioni Empæctarum respondeat. Non verum, mansisse mundum universum, qualis ab initio erat: interiit mundus hic terrenus cum iis, quæ continuit, aquis, ex quibus & per quas constitit, obrutus & inundatus, multumque de antiqua sua forma perdidit. Ideoque nova etiam benedictio- ne divina & anima terræ, & terra ipsa opus habu- re, Gen. VIII. 17. 22. cap. IX. 2. 3. Quo de Be- da in h. l. Periit terra, quia submersa & cooperta aquis, non solum tanto tempore insitum sibi fructi- ficandi statum perdidit, sed & dissimilem plerisque in locis ab ea, quam primo acceperat, faciem recepit.

Disputant Scholastici & Pontificii Interpretes, num & quomodo cœli aquæ diluvio perierint: quibus ex incommoda loci interpretatione præ- iverat Beda, uti huic Augustinus l. XX. de Civ. Dei, cap. 18. Cælum aëreum, inquit Estius ad v. 5. intelli- gunt hic non solum posteriores Theologi omnes fere, tam sententionarii, quam hujus epistolæ commenta- tores, verum etiam Augustinus & Beda. Asserit ergo Apostolum loqui de cælo aëreo, nec eo toto, sed qua parte continet infimam & mediam aëris regionem, a qua volucres cœli & nubes ac pluvia cœli vocantur. Ad has enim cœli regiones, & non altius aquæ diluvii pervenerunt. Vix illi explicare poterunt regiones aëris infimam & me- diam in alium statum commutatas esse; de supre- ma autem aëris regione vident ipsimet, id dici non posse, nec eo usque aquas diluvii penetrasse. Piscator illis consonans aërem per diluvium ad tempus dicit interiisse. S. Petrus de illis cœlis lo- quitur, quod constituti olim sint Verbo, qui non quidem diluvio interierint, cum terra periit, vel perdita est aquis, sed qui cum terra igni servantur in die judicii & interitus impiorum hominum v. 7. At hi sunt cœli ætherei, non aërei. Contradistin- guuntur enim elementis. v. 10. & 12. sub quibus aër comprehenditur. Quod agnoscit e Pontifi- ciis Salmero: Nam imprimis, inquit, ostendimus, nunquam cælorum nomine in plurium numero aë- reos & elementares cælos accipi, ac Petrus post cæ- los nominatos subdit: Elementa calore solventur. Cornelius a Lapide ad Ez. XXXIV. 4. Expositio illa, qua quidam in loco Apostolico, 2. Pet. III. per cælos intelligunt aërem, non satis convenit v. 10. & 12. ubi cælos Apostolus opponit elementis. Ergo per cælos non aëreos, sed sidereos intelligit. Blasius de Vie- gas in comment. Apoc. XXI. p. 812. fatetur in ver- bis Petri v. 10. cœli magno impetu transibunt, ipsa cælestia corpora intelligi. Quod etiam Pa- tres plerosque statuere observat Cornelius a La- pide ad v. 10. hujus Petrini loci.

ὕδατι κατακλυσθεὶς ἀπώλετο) Periit mersus aquis tum e terra, tum e cœlo erumpentibus, ut Mosis historia osten- dit, ad quem locum quæ attulimus ex Seneca vide.

De aquis e terra erumpentibus tempore diluvii nil in Mose legitur, sed de apertis fontibus abyssi magna: nec de aquis e cœlis illis, quorum hic mentionem fecerat Petrus, sed de aquis apertis ca- taractis cæli, quæ pluviarum est περίφρασις, de- missis. Voluit Grotius τῇ ὑποθέσει δυλεύειν.

## 3:7
Vers. 7. Οἱ δὲ νῦν ὐρανοὶ) The air and the ether. Καὶ ἡ γῆ) This earth restored to us after the flood.

Nowhere in the Scripture of the New Testament is the air and ether understood by the name of τῶν ὐρανῶν, especially where ἡ γῆ is joined to them. For then the whole world is always understood collectively. Add that the air here is referred to the elements rather than opposed to the heavens in v. 10 and 12, and is not included under the name of heavens. Salmero on this passage says: 'Although heaven is sometimes taken for the air, according to that saying, the birds of the heaven, he who covers the heaven with clouds, etc., yet the heavens in the plural number are never taken for the air: but here we read of the heavens and the earth in the plural number. Furthermore, even if 'heaven' in the singular may have a place, yet where 'heaven and earth' is said absolutely, the name of heaven is always accustomed to be taken for the true heaven, where earth is opposed to it, as the Apostle does here. For heaven and earth is a sphere with a center, and therefore signifies by synecdoche the whole universe. But what is said οἱ δὲ νῦν ὀυρανοὶ (but the heavens that now are), has respect not to τὸ ἔκπαλαι (that of old) v. 5, but to τὸ τότε (that then) v. 6, where the world, that is, the earth indeed, is said to have perished by water at that time, but the heavens which now are did not perish then, but still exist, as they were constituted ἔκπαλαι ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς κτίσεως (of old from the beginning of the creation), they remain, even if they were not corrupted by waters, but with the earth, which emerged again from the waters, they are stored up as if in a treasury by the word of God, reserved for fire. Heinsius renders it thus: But what is it that escapes them? The heaven and the earth, which were created out of water and by the Word of God upon it: Whence the same earth, that world perishing, was again overwhelmed by water: But the heavens, which we see now (or literally, which now are) [are] such as will not be in the future, but, as he says presently, new.

Τῷ αὐτῷ λόγῳ (By the same word) that is, by the word of God, as above [v.] 8. The Latin reads τῷ ἀυτοῦ λόγῳ (by his word), not badly.

The Latin is wrongly praised to the prejudice of the Greek and the authentic text in the more approved codices, the sense of which B. Gerhardus teaches is ἐμφατικώτερον (more emphatic), otherwise than it seemed to Beza: For the pronoun ἀυτῶ, he says, has this sense: It is God who by his word once created the world; the same who by his word once destroyed the world; the same is he who by his word preserves the world as if in a treasury, so that it may be destroyed by fire at some time. Since he himself is omnipotent, he could therefore accomplish all things by his word, indeed by his nod, and by his word, indeed by his nod, he will at some time destroy the world.

Τεθησαυρισμένοι εἰσὶ (They are stored up) that is, they are left untouched for a time, like those things which are locked in a chest. For we have said that the name θησαυρῶν (of treasures) extends so widely at Matt. II. 11, and thence θησαυρίζειν (to treasure up), Matt. VI. 19, 20, Luke XII. 21, Rom. II. 5, 1 Cor. XVI. 2, 2 Cor. XIV. 14, James V. 3.

Others express this sense thus: those heavens and that earth are preserved by the word and divine truth as if in a certain treasury, not so that they may remain forever, but so that they may be destroyed at the appointed time. The explanation of others is more subtle: that the word of God is a kind of treasury, as it were, from which he himself draws forth all things: and that those passages are referred to here in which God is said to open his treasury, where he exercises particular judgments, Deut. 32:24, Jer. 50:25. The comparison itself teaches the disparity, and therefore we acquiesce in the Grotian explanation, as being simpler.

Πυρὶ τηρέμενοι (Reserved for fire) τηρεῖσθαι (to be reserved) here signifies distinction (perhaps detention), as above II. vers. 4, 9, 17, 1 Pet. II. 4. This is a most ancient tradition confirmed by Christ. We have shown in the annotations to book I of De Veritate Religionis Christianae, near the end, that the testimonies of that tradition existed among Hystaspes, the Sibyls, and Sophocles, and exist even now among Ovid, Seneca, and Lucan. The same Seneca, Natural. III. 13: fire is the end of the world: naturally from the Stoics, who called that end of the world ἐκπύρωσιν (conflagration). Zeno, being a Cittiean, had received that from the Phoenicians. For Cittium is a Phoenician colony in Cyprus. Heraclitus had the same from the Pythagoreans, Pythagoras from the Jews. Mention of this tradition is in the book which is called The Cedar of Lebanon. Just as God once loosened the reins for the waters: so he will loosen them for the fire: Ὅταν πυρὸς γέμοντα θησαυρὸν σχάσῃ χρύσωπος αἰθήρ (When the golden-faced ether shall open the treasury full of fire).

says Sophocles. Fire was not in that first moist mass, but God created it afterwards. Moses calls it light, because the same thing that is bright is also hot. From this light the stars are compacted, whence fires flow down into the earth, and fires are generated under the earth. With these fires coming together among themselves, just as the waters came together, that conflagration fatal to the world will be born. With all matter burning in one fire, whatever now shines by arrangement will burn, says Seneca to Marcia. Among Minucius, Caecilius says of the Christians: They threaten the whole globe and the world itself with its stars with a conflagration.

Those things about the fire of the stars, and fires flowing down into the earth from the stars, as if they were to come together from subterranean fires into the world, have no foundation in the Scriptures. How those fires also behave according to philosophy, and how they can come together, let others see. Philosophers say the stars are hot not formally, but virtually. They will not easily admit that fires fall from the stars to the earth. Nor, therefore, will that coming together of fires be easily proven by them. Finally, what kind of fire it is by which the world will burn is not sufficiently certain. Of what kind that fire is, says Augustine, book XX of The City of God, and in what part of the world or of things it will be, we think no man knows.

Εἰς ἡμέραν κρίσεως καὶ ἀπωλείας τῶν ἀσεβῶν ἀνθρώπων (For the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men) Matt. XXV. 41, Jude v. 7, Matt. XIII. 40.

The ἀπώλεια (perdition) of the impious does not bring about total destruction or annihilation; but eternal perdition and death: to which, although they are subject as to the soul after departure: yet they will be subjected in soul and body finally on the day of judgment.

Latin:

Vers. 7. Οἱ δὲ νῦν ὐρανοὶ) Aer & æther. Καὶ ἡ γῆ) Terra hæc ex diluvio nobis reddita.

Nuspiam in Scriptura Novi Testamenti nomi- ne τῶν ὐρανῶν aër & æther intelligitur, imprimis ubi ἡ γῆ iisdem adjungitur. Tum enim semper totus mundus intelligitur complexim. Adde quod aër hic ad elementa potius cælis opposita v. 10. & 12. referatur, quam sub nomine cælorum compre- hendatur. Salmero in h. l. Etsi cælum, inquit, in- terdum pro aëre sumatur, juxta illud volucres cæli, qui operit cælum nubibus &c. nunquam tamen cæli plurali numero pro aëre accipiuntur: hic autem plurium numero legimus cælos & terram. De- inde etiamsi maxime cælum in singulari locum ha- beat, ubi tamen absolute dicitur cælum & terra, semper nomen cæli pro vero cælo accipi solet, ubi illi opponitur terra, ut hic facit Apostolus. Est enim cælum & terra sphæra cum centro, ac proinde signi- ficat per Synecdochen totum universum. Quod autem dicitur οἱ δὲ νῦν ὀυρανοὶ, respectum habet non ad τὸ ἔκπαλαι v. 5. sed ad τὸ τότε v. 6. ubi mundus, hoc est terra quidem aqua tum periisse dicitur, qui vero nunc sunt cœli, tum non periere, sed ad- huc dum sunt, uti constituti ἔκπαλαι ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς κτίσεως sunt, permanent, etsi aquis non fuerint corrupti, sed cum terra, quæ ex aquis iterum emersit, verbo Dei velut in thesauro reconditi sunt, igni reservantur. Heinsius ita reddit: Quid autem latet eos? Cælum terramque, quæ ex aqua & super ea DEI Verbo creata: Unde eadem terra, pereunte illo mundo, aqua rursus obruta: Cælos au- tem, quos videmus nunc (aut ad verbum qui nunc) tales olim non futuros, sed, ut loquitur mox, novos.

Τῷ αὐτῷ λόγῳ) id est τῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ λόγῳ, ut supra 8. Latinus legit τῷ ἀυτοῦ λόγῳ, non male.

Latinus perperam laudatur in præjudicium Græci & authentici textus in probatioribus Co- dicibus, cujus sensum ἐμφατικώτερον esse, secus at- que Bezæ visum docet B. Gerhardus: Pronomen enim ἀυτῶ, inquit, hunc habet sensum: Deus est, qui verbo suo olim creavit mundum; idem qui ver- bo suo olim mundum destruxit; idem est, qui ver- bo suo mundum velut in thesauro conservat, ut per ignem aliquando destruatur. Ipse cum sit omnipo- tens, ideo verbo suo imo nutu omnia præstare potuit, ac verbo suo, imo nutu, mundum aliquando de- struet.

Τεθησαυρισμένοι εἰσὶ) id est, intacta relinquuntur ad tempus, ut ea, quæ arca clauduntur. Tam late enim pate- re θησαυρῶν nomen diximus ad Matth. II. 11. & inde θησαυρίζειν, Matth. VI. 19. 20. Luc. XII. 21. Rom. II 5. 1. Corinth. XVI. 2. 2. Corinth. XIV. 14. Jac. V. 3.

Quem sensum ita alii efferunt: isti cæli & ista terra verbo & veritate divina velut in thesauro quodam conservantur, non ut in æternum permane- ant, sed ut constituto tempore destruantur. Argutior est aliorum explicatio: Verbum Dei quendam qua- si thesaurum esse, ex quo ipse cuncta depromat: & quod huc illa loca referuntur, in quibus Deus di- citur thesaurum suum aperire, ubi particularia ju- dicia exercet, Deut. 32, 24. Jer. L. 25. Collatio ipsa docet disparitatem, ideoque explicationi Grotianæ, ceu simpliciori, acquiescimus.

Πυρὶ τηρέμενοι) τηρεῖσθαι hic distinctionem (forte deten- tionem) significat, ut supra II. vers. 4. 9. 17. 1. Petr. II. 4. Est hæc antiquissima traditio a Christo confirmata. Ejus tra- ditionis testimonia fuisse apud Histaspen, Sibyllas & So- phoclem, extare etiam nunc apud Ovidium, Senecam, Lu- canum oftendimus annotatis ad librum I. de verit. Relig. Christ. circa finem. Idem Seneca Natural. III. 13. ignis exitus mundi est: nimirum ex Stoicis, qui illum mundi exi- tum ἐκπύρωσιν vocabant. Id Zeno, quippe Cittienfis a Phœnicibus acceperat. Nam Cittium Phœnicum in Cy- pro colonia. Idem habuit a Pythagoricis Heraclitus, Py- thagoras ab Judæis. Mentio ejus traditionis in libro, qui dicitur Cedrus Libani. Sicut Deus olim aquis frena laxa- vit: ita laxabit igni: Ὅταν πυρὸς γέμοντα θησαυρὸν σχάσῃ χρύσωπος αἰθήρ.

ait Sophocles. Ignis non erat in prima illa humenti mo- le, sed eum Deus postea condidit. Lucem vocat Moses, quia lucida eadem, quæ calida. Ex hac luce compacta sunt astra, unde ignes in terram defluunt, & sub terra ignes ge- nerantur. His ignibus inter se coeuntibus, quomodo aquæ coiere, nascetur incendium illud mundo fatale. Omni flagrante materia uno igne, quicquid nunc ex disposito lucet, ardebit, ait ad Marciam Seneca. Apud Minutium Cæcilius de Christianis. Toti orbi & ipsi mundo cum sideribus suis minantur incendium.

Illa de igne astrorum, & ignibus in terram deflu- entibus ex astris, ut ex ignibus subterraneis in sive mundi coituris, in Scripturis fundamentum non habent. Quomodo etiam ignes illi se habeant juxta Philosophiam, & quomodo coire possint, alii viderint. Astra calida dicunt Philosophi non formaliter, sed virtualiter. Ex astris ignes in terram cadere non facile admittent. Nec ergo facile illa coitio ignium ipsis probabitur. Qualis deniq; ignis sit, quo mundus conflagrabit, non satis constat. Cujusmodi ille ignis, inquit Au- gustinus l. XX. de Civ. Dei, & in qua mundi vel rerum parte futurum sit, nullum hominem scire arbitramur.

Εἰς ἡμέραν κρίσεως καὶ ἀπωλείας τῶν ἀσεβῶν ἀνθρώπων) Matth. XXV. 41. Judæ v. 7. Matth. XIII. 40.

Impiorum ἀπώλεια non totalem interitum vel annihilationem infert; sed perditionem ac mor- tem æternam: cui etsi quoad animam post exces- sum subjecti sint: anima tamen & corpore de- mum die judicii subjicientur.

## 3:8
V. 8. Ἓν δὲ τοῦτο μὴ λανθανέτω ὑμᾶς, ἀγαπητοὶ (But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing) that is, know this above all.

That one day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day) It is as easy for Him to execute His judgments suddenly as it is slowly, and that a day with God is a thousand years is a frequent saying among the Hebrews, as may be seen in Ps. XC. 4. and the Midrash there. Sirach XVIII. and in the Zohar, Parashah Bereshit. Seneca praises the saying of Heraclitus in epistle XII. One day is equal to all. Pythagoras in Iamblichus says: To the gods nothing is long. Plutarch in his Consolation: For a thousand and ten thousand years, according to Simonides, is an indefinite moment when looking toward the infinite age. And in his On the Delays of Divine Vengeance: To the gods the whole interval of human life is nothing, and 'now,' rather than 'thirty years ago,' is the same thing, just as it is for a slave to be tortured or hanged now rather than in the morning, for the wicked man. Zosimus in book II. For all time is short to the Divine, which is always existing and of equal measure. The author of this epistle applies these things, which are accustomed to be said of God, to Christ, as many things said of God in the Old Testament are accustomed to be adapted to Christ in the New.

He wishes no one, unless perhaps he to whom the Divine Spirit has shown it, to believe that with certainty. He says less with Huss as author, and signifies more, that you may be certain of it. Moreover, the number one thousand is put for any revolution of times whatsoever. For with God there is no change or succession of times. Since, therefore, Christ is understood here by the name Lord (Κυρίῳ), 1 Cor. VIII. 6, 2 Pet. I. 2, 8, ch. II. 14, 16, ch. II. 20, ch. III. 2, 9, 10, 15, 18, the eternal and immutable Deity of Christ is rightly gathered from this. For the application of those things which are proper to God to another who is not God is not to be admitted: since God would not wish to give His glory to another, Is. 42, 8. Therefore that inference is firm: He with whom a thousand years are as one day, He is the eternal and immutable God, Ps. XC. 4. But with Christ, etc. Therefore. But those who from this sentiment, that a thousand years are as one day before God, gather that the world, which was created in the space of six days, will be preserved for six thousand years, even if they rely on very many authorities of the Fathers, especially as regards the thesis itself, in the judgment of Estius himself, who with the remaining Papists makes an apodictic argument from the consensus of the Fathers, they are vain; who says that those conjectures are of superstitiously curious men, entirely uncertain and foreign to the sense of this passage. For who will be taught that Peter wished to compare the six days of creation with the duration of the world? Who teaches only this, that it is not according to the clock of our time, or human estimation, but according to divine eternity and providence, to which all times are present, and do not bring anything but a certain moment. Lyranus on this passage: By a thousand years is understood any revolution of times whatsoever, which is small, and of no moment, compared to divine eternity. Ephrem. Tom. I. Serm. exhort. ad piet. A thousand years of this age in that eternal and incorruptible world have as much comparison as the smallest grain of sand of the sea with all the sand of the same. Conf. Sir. XVIII. 8. But there is not even such a comparison and succession in eternity. "Nothing is temporal with God," says Justin in his Questions and Answers.

Latin:

V. 8. Ἓν δὲ τοῦτο μὴ λανθανέτω ὑμᾶς, ἀγαπητοὶ) id est, hoc imprimis scitote.

Ὅτι μία ἡμέρα παρὰ Κυρίῳ ὡς χίλια ἔτη, καὶ χίλια ἔτη, ὡς μία ἡμέρα) Tam facile ei est, judicia sua subito, quam tarde exequi, & contra diem apud Deum esse mille annos, di- ctum est frequens Ebræis, ut videre est Psal. XC. 4. & ibi Midrasch. Sirach. XVIII. & in Zoar, Parasche Bereschith. Heracliti dictum laudat Seneca epistola XII. Unus dies par omni est. Pythagoras apud Jamblichum dicit: Θεοῖς οὐδὲν μακρὸν εἶναι. Plutarchus Consolatione: Τὰ γὰρ χίλια, καὶ τὰ μύρια κατὰ Σιμωνίδην ἔτη στιγμή τίς ἐστιν ἀόριστος πρὸς τὸν ἄπειρον ἀφορῶσιν αἰῶνα. Et de sera Numinis vindicta: Τοῖς Θεοῖς πᾶν ἀνθρωπίνου βίου διάστημα τὸ μηδέν ἐστι, καὶ τὸ νῦν, ἀλλὰ μὴ πρὸ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα, ταὐτόν ἐστιν, οἷον δὲ δούλης, ἀλλὰ μὴ πρωῒ στρεβλοῦν ἢ κεκρεμασμένου, τὸν πονηρόν. Zosimus libro II. Πᾶς γὰρ χρόνος τῷ θείῳ βραχὺς ἀεί τε ὄντι καὶ ἰσο- μέτρῳ. Hæc de Deo dici solita Scriptor hujus epistolæ Chri- sto applicat, ut solent multa de Deo dicta in Veteri Testa- mento aptari Christo in Novo.

Neminem, nisi forte cui Spiritus Divinus ostendit, vult, ut certo id credant. Minus dicit Husso autore, & plus significat, id certi sitis. Nu- merus autem millenarius ponitur pro quacunque temporum revolutione. Apud Deum enim nulla est temporum mutatio, vel successio. Quum ergo hic nomine Κυρίῳ Christus intelligatur, 1. Cor. VIII. 6. 2. Petr. I. 2. 8. cap. II. 14. 16. cap. II. 20. cap. III. 2. 9. 10. 15. 18. recte hinc colligitur æterna & immutabilis Christi Deitas. Non enim appli- catio eorum, quæ Dei propria sunt, ad alium, qui non sit Deus, admittenda: Siquidem Deus glori- am alteri dare non velit, Es. 42, 8. Firma est ergo illa illatio: Apud quem sunt mille anni sicut unus dies, ille est æternus & immutabilis Deus, Ps. XC. 4. At apud Christum &c. Ergo. Qui vero ex hac sententia, quod mille anni sint velut dies una co- ram Deo, colligunt, mundum, qui sex dierum spa- tio conditus est, sex millibus annorum conservatum iri, etsi Patrum autoritatibus plurimis imprimis, quantum ad thesin ipsam, nitantur, judicio ipsius Estii, qui cum Papistis reliquis argumentum a Patrum consensu apodicticum facit, vani sunt; qui conjecturas illas esse, ait, hominum superstitiose curiosorum, prorsus incertas & alienas ab hujus loci sensu. Qui enim docebitur, Petrum hexaëmeron creationis voluisse cum duratione mundi con- ferre? Qui id solum docet, non esse ex horologio nostri temporis, seu humana æstimatione, sed ex divina æternitate & providentia, cui omnia tem- pora præsentia sunt, nec nisi aliquale momentum inferunt. Lyranus in h. l. Per millenarium in- telligitur quantacunque revolutio temporum, quæ modica est, & nullius momenti, comparata divinæ æternitati. Ephrem. Tom. I. Serm. exhort. ad piet. Mille anni hujus seculi in æterno & incor- ruptibili illo mundo tantam habent comparationem, quantum minima arena maris cum tota arena ejusdem. Conf. Sir. XVIII. 8. Sed nè tanta qui- dem est comparatio, imo nulla, nulla plane pro- portio. Simplex hic est negatio temporis, & successionis in æternitate. Οὐδὲν ἔγχρονόν ἐστι πα- ρὰ τῷ Θεῷ, ait Justinus qq. & resp.

## 3:9
Verse 9.

"The Lord does not delay the promise" (I might think it was written "the promises," just as "I do not delay salvation," Isa. XLVI. 13. God never prefixed a certain time. Therefore it is not a delay. In the Manuscript it is "Lord," not "the Lord." Hab. II. 3. "Coming he will come and will not delay." "As some count slackness") And because of this they also call the promised thing itself into doubt. "But is longsuffering toward us") Patient toward us, that is, toward the human race, Apoc. VI. 10, 11. In the Manuscript it is "for our sake."

That emendation of the Greek text is frivolous. For it can also be rendered intransitively: The Lord does not delay the promise, by a Hebrew phrase, just as the Lord of the covenant is spoken of, Gen. XIV. 13. The Lord of the oath, Nehem. VI. 18. And transitively, so that there is a change of cases, or the word "for the sake of" is understood, the Lord does not delay for the sake of the promise. But to delay and to defer or to make a wait differ. For he who makes a wait does not immediately delay, but only he who defers beyond what is due, Hab. II. 3. And although he may seem to delay regarding the punishment of the wicked, Apoc. VI. 10, he does not however delay, as men are wont to do out of some forgetfulness or negligence; but he defers out of mere longsuffering, Rom. II. 4. conf. Es. XXX. 14. The heavenly Father prefers repentance to punishment, says Justin in his Apology to Antoninus.

"Not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance." Just as before the destruction of the Jews he long awaited the repentance of the Jews; so also now he awaits it in the scattered remnants of the Jews. He wills this, however, not plainly and absolutely, but as much as suffices for his justice and goodness, Conf. Ezech. XVIII. 23, XXXIII. 11, 1 Tim. II. 4.

These things do not only concern the Jews, or the scattered remnants of the Jews, or a certain time: But it is a Catholic axiom concerning all men of all times. For the cause of the delayed coming of the Lord is brought forward, longsuffering, and divine grace, which is not restricted to a certain age or nation, but is truly universal, by the force of this Apostolic utterance, whence he concludes, because God does not will that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance or be converted, therefore he still defers the day of judgment. Grotius rightly understands this will of God not of the absolute, but of the ordained will of God. For he does not absolutely will that all be converted. For all things which God absolutely wills, he does, Ps. CXV. 3, Ps. CXXXIV. 6, "all my will shall be done." Isa. XLVI. 10. God therefore wills seriously, and by an internal good pleasure, that all should come to repentance, and that no one should perish, not by an irresistible will, Rom. IX. 19, absolute and mere, but under a certain order of means: by an antecedent will, not a consequent one, as Chrysostom in Homily I on Ephesians and Damascene in Book II on the Orthodox Faith, chapter 29, explain. Conf. 1 Tim. II. 4. God, says Dionysius the Carthusian in this place, does not will that anyone should perish, but that all should be saved, speaking of the antecedent will, that is, by considering men as they are men, as being of a rational nature and capable of happiness: but not speaking of the consequent will, as by considering them as such and such: just as an earthly King wills all his subjects to prosper and live, in so far as they are his subjects, but not in so far as some of them are evildoers, and rebels, thieves, murderers, robbers. We have here, therefore, an invincible argument against the absolute Calvinist decree. For he who does not will that anyone should perish, but that all should be converted to repentance, he certainly is not to be said to have predestined the greatest part of men to eternal destruction out of an absolute good pleasure. He who wills all to come to repentance, that all may be saved, and that no one should perish; he surely did not choose only a very few men for eternal salvation out of an absolute and simple good pleasure. Therefore, against the Calvinists and the Pontifical Scotists and Dominicans, the disciples of Bannes and Medina, who follow the heresy of the Predestinarians, we rightly oppose this Petrine sentence.
