Let Hemmingius whisper this to the Calvinists in this place: Learn, he says, the Apostle pronounces without any ambiguity, both of words and of sense, that God does not will any to perish, but that all should be gathered to repentance. Wherefore let us keep this saying in memory, that we may fortify ourselves against those who today deny that the grace of God is universal. Let Cornelius a Lapide remind the Dominicans and their twins: Hence it is clear, he says in this place, that God wills the salvation of all, and does not will the damnation of anyone, and consequently reprobates no one before his demerits and death in sin, which will is not only in God of sign, as some have judged, but also of good pleasure, as Gabriel Vasquez solidly shows, Book I, q. 19, disp. 83, c. 2.

Nor is there any reason why Beza and Piscator, and Maccovius in his Collection on Predestination, disp. I, from the Reformed, and Estius from the Papists, should accept that these things are said only of the elect, that God wills none of them to perish. For that St. Peter speaks of all is too clear. Doubtless God wills none of those to perish whom he wills to come to repentance. But God wills all men to come to repentance, not only the elect, as Peter pronounces with a clear voice. Therefore God wills no man to perish. He calls not only the elect to repentance, but also the reprobate, Luke XXIV. 46, Acts XVII. 30, Matt. XXIII. 37, he wills not only the elect to come to repentance, but also the reprobate, who treasure up for themselves wrath against the day of wrath, Rom. II. 5. He wills all to come to the knowledge of the truth and to be saved, 1 Tim. II. 4. What Hemmingius himself observed against Beza, and which Tossanus here acknowledged: God, he says, exhorts all to repentance, even the impious, and grants them time for repentance. For those to whom God grants time for repentance, and whom he exhorts to repentance, them he certainly wishes to come to repentance. Daniel Chamier T. III. Panstrat. de Prædest. l. VII. c. 6. What is weaker, he says, than if you say, God does not wish any of those who are saved to perish. Likewise: That is harsh, not wishing any to perish, to bend it to kinds of individuals. Of the Papists, Lorinus on this passage: It is a general proposition, not to be restricted to kinds of individuals, or to the predestined. Tirinus on this passage: Therefore the Lord does not delay the promised coming of Christ absolutely or with respect to an infallible judgment, but only with respect to fallacious judgment and human opinion. And that not to our detriment, but to our good, so that we may have a more extended space for repenting, and for changing our life for the better. For he does not wish (by an antecedent will, as Calvin raves) to destroy any, but as far as it depends on him, he desires all, even the most impious and blinded and obstinate, to be converted to repentance, and thus to be saved, as even St. Paul, and indeed Christ himself teaches. See Molina, Vasquez, Valencia.

But what Chamier objects, by distinguishing between εὐδοκίαν and εὐαρεστίαν, that God is patient to wait for repentance by the will of εὐαρεστίας, because conversion is more pleasing to Him, and therefore the salvation of the sinner, than damnation, but not by the will of εὐδοκίας: And others distinguish between the approving and the decreeing will: Vain are the evasions regarding the gracious will of God. For God would not only delight in the repentance and salvation of those whom He calls (and He calls also the reprobate) if they were to repent and be saved, but He also wills by His divine good pleasure that they should repent, that they should not perish, but be saved, 1 Tim. II. 4, which is His true εὐδοκία, from which He calls and exhorts even the reprobate to repentance; for He wills to have mercy on all, Rom. XI. 32, that no one should perish, not only by the will of the sign and externally, but internally and by His good pleasure, of which the exhortations, the even sworn protestations, the threats, and the divine complaints bear witness: where the exception of Sam. Rhætorf. Exercit. V. apol. pro divin. is impious. grat. p. 331, the exception, that the exhortation of God sets forth that God wills the salvation of the reprobate, and yet He does not will their salvation, but intends their inexcusability. For Τὸ χρηστὸν, the goodness of God ἄγει εἰς μετάνοιαν, leads to repentance those who despise the μακροθυμίαν (long-suffering) of GOD, and the riches of divine goodness, Rom. II. 4. Why then would He not intend their repentance? Nor would God only approve if they were converted, but He also decreed for them the means by which they might be converted. He destined and sent to them Christ the Savior of the world, He decreed to call them, and in act He calls them to repentance. D. Joh. Bergius professes this concerning himself and his own in his treatise on the difference and agreement of the Evangelicals, q. 53. Our Doctors, he says, do not deny that God wills the salvation of all men insofar as He has testified in the Word, as in a sign of His will, to which the secret will of His good pleasure is in no way contrary; which some, with Damascenus, also call the antecedent will, when here it is considered what God of Himself, before all our works, according to the will of His goodness and grace, has willed, namely (1) by an approving will, that He of Himself delights not in the perdition, but rather in the salvation of them, Ezek. XVIII. v. 32, ch. XXXIII. 11, 1 Tim. II. 4, 2 Pet. III. v. 9. (2) By a commanding and promising will, that He has ordained and prepared for all the necessary means which by duty devolve upon them for salvation, such as the knowledge of God, repentance, faith, love, and obedience; and has seriously commanded, and thus has faithfully promised salvation to all, Mich. VI. 8, Eccl. XII. 13, Rom. I. 21, Act. XVII. 30. Es. XLV. v. 22, Tit. II. 11. (3) By an operating will, that He even leads to repentance by His efficacious goodness, and wills to provide all things for their salvation, as He shall judge congruent and sufficient for His wisdom, goodness, justice, and truth, so that they ought to be converted, whereby every excuse is taken away from them, as if the defect were not in their own will, but in the grace of God, that they cannot be converted, Rom. II. 4, etc. (4) Not, however, by necessity, as if He willed that all should inevitably and necessarily, or certainly and infallibly be saved, but that in very many who reject His goodness and grace, He wills to exercise and demonstrate His most just wrath against sins in their condemnation, which they call the consequent will. Not as if the antecedent will is changed by it, or is contrary to this consequent one, but that according to the works of men and their ways, He has so ordained by the will of His just judgment, Rom. II. 5. & IX. 22, 23, & XI. 20, 22, Act. XIII. 46. Thus Bergius. But we have said more about the Calvinists in the 'gründlichen Beweiß' (thorough proof), which was published in the name of the Theological Faculty, part II, ch. III, q. III, seqq. From the Papists, Bellarminus, l. II, de Grat. & libr. arb. c. V, compares the present passage with 1 Tim. II. 4 and Joh. I. 9, explaining the same from Augustine, l. de Spir. & lit. c. XXXIII, whose opinion he teaches was this: That God wills all to be saved, because He gives to all that whereby they can will to believe and be saved, yet so that if they themselves do not will it, they are not saved, but are destined for eternal punishments. Bellarminus adds: This was also the exposition of S. Prosper, l. II, de vocat. gent. cap. 23, 25, & 28. Likewise of the commentaries which are attributed to Ambrose, likewise of Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius. He praises among others the opinion of Chrysostom, homil. VII. in Joh. If He illuminates, he says, every man coming into this world, in what way do so many men remain without light? For not all know Christ, how therefore does He illuminate every man? He illuminates indeed, as far as it is in Him, but if any, of their own accord, with the eyes of their mind closed, do not wish to direct their gaze to the rays of this light, they have remained in darkness not from the nature of the light, but from their own malice, and have of their own accord rendered themselves unworthy of the holy gift.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Οὐ βραδύνει ὁ Κύριος τῆς ἐπαγγελίας) Putem scriptum fuisse τὰς ἐπαγγελίας, quomodo σωτηρίαν οὐ βραδύνω, Esa. XLVI. 13. Certum tempus nunquam præfixit Deus. Ita- que non est trico. In Manuscripto est Κύριος, non ὁ Κύ- ριος. Abbac. II. 3. Ἐρχόμενος ἥξει καὶ οὐ μὴ χρονίσῃ. Ὡς τινες βραδυτῆτα \u1fηγοῦνται) Et propterea ipsam quo- que rem promissam in dubium trahunt. Ἀλλὰ μακροθυμεῖ εἰς ἡμᾶς) Patiens erga nos, id est, erga humanum genus, Apoc. VI. 10. 11. In Manuscripto δι’ ἡμᾶς, nostri causa.

Frivola est illa textus Græci emendatio. Nam & intransitive reddi potest: Non tardat Dominus promissionis, phrasi Ebræa, ut Dominus fœderis di- citur, Gen. XIV. 13. Dominus juramenti, Nehem. VI. 18. & transitive, ut ἑτέρωσις sit casuum, vel subau- diatur vox ἕνεκα, non tardat Dominus τῆς ἐπαγ- γελίας ἕνεκα. Tardare autem & differre sive moram facere differunt. Non enim qui moram facit, sta- tim tardat, sed is demum, qui ultra debitum differt Hab. II. 3. Et quamvis videatur tardare quoad supplicium impiorum Apoc. VI, 10. non tamen tardat, ut homines solent ex quædam oblivione aut negligentia; sed differt ex mera μακροθυμίᾳ, Rom. II. 4. conf. Es. XXX. 14. Pœnitentiam ma- vult Pater cælestis quam pœnam, ait Justinus in Apol. ad Antonin.

Μὴ βυλόμενός τινας ἀπολέσθαι, ἀλλὰ πάντας εἰς μετά- νοιαν χωρῆσαι) Sicut ante excidium Judæorum diu expe- ctavit Judæorum pœnitentiam; ita & nunc eam expectat in sparsis Judæorum reliquiis. Vult autem hoc non plane & absolute, sed quantum justitiæ bonitatique ejus sufficit, Conf, Ezech. XVIII, 23. XXXIII, 11. 1. Tim. II, 4.

Non hæc tantum Judæos, aut sparsas Judæo- rum reliquias, vel certum tempus spectant: Sed axioma est Catholicum omnes homines omnium temporum concernens. Nam causa affertur dila- ti adventus Dominici, μακροθυμία, & gratia divi- na, quæ non restringitur ad certam ætatem, aut gentem, sed vere universalis est, vi effati hujus A- postolici, unde concludit, quia non vult Deus, ut quisquam pereat, sed ut omnes ad pœnitentiam veni- ant vel convertantur, ideo adhuc differt diem judi- cii. Recte autem Grotius hoc velle Dei intelligit non de absoluta, sed ordinata Dei voluntate. Non enim absolute vult, ut omnes convertantur. Nam omnia quæ absolute vult Deus facit, Ps. CXV. 3. Ps. CXXXIV. 6. omnis voluntas mea fiet. Esa. XLVI. 10. Vult ergo Deus serio quidem, & inter- no beneplacito, ut omnes ad pœnitentiam veni- ant, nec ullus pereat, non voluntate irresistibili Rom. IX, 19. absoluta & mera, sed sub certa τάξει mediorum: voluntate antecedente, non consequen- te, ut Chrysostomus hom. I. in Eph. & Damascenus l. II. de orth. fid. cap. 29. explicant. Conf. 1. Tim. II. 4. Deus, inquit Dionysius Carthusianus in h. l. non vult, quenquam perire, sed omnes salvari, lo- quendo de voluntate antecedente, hoc est consideran- do homines secundum quod homines sunt, utpote ra- tionalis naturæ, ac felicitatis capaces: non autem lo- quendo de voluntate consequente, utpote conside- rando eos ut tales & tales: quemadmodum Rex terrenus vult omnes subditos suos prosperari ac vivere, in quantum sunt subditi sui, non autem in quantum quidam eorum malefici sunt, & rebel- les, fures, homicidæ, latrones. Invictum itaque hic argumentum habemus adversus absolutum de- cretum Calvinianum. Qui enim non vult quen- quam perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam conver- ti, is certe dicendus non est maximam partem ho- minum ex absoluto beneplacito ad æternum exi- tium prædestinasse. Qui omnes vult venire ad pœnitentiam, ut omnes salventur, nec quisquam pereat; is utique non paucissimos tantum homi- nes ex absoluto & simplici beneplacito ad æter- nam salutem elegit. Calvinianis itaque & e Pon- tificiis Scotistis ac Dominicanis, Bannis & Medi- næ Discipulis, Prædestinatianorum hæresin se- quentibus, merito hanc Petrinam sententiam op- ponimus. Calvinianis hoc insusurret Hemmin- gius in h. l. Discite, inquit, absque omni ambiguita- te tum verborum, tum sensus pronunciat Apostolus, Deum non velle ullos perire, sed omnes ad pœniten- tiam colligi. Quare hoc dictum memoria tenea- mus, ut nos muniamus adversus eos, qui hodie negant gratiam Dei universalem esse. Dominicanos eisque gemellos commonefaciat Cornelius a Lapide: Hinc patet, inquiens in h. l. Deum velle omnium salutem, & nolle alicujus damnationem ac conse- quenter neminem reprobare ante ejus demerita & mortem in peccato, quæ voluntas non tantum in Deo est signi, ut quidam censuerunt, sed etiam bene- placiti, ut solide ostendit Gabriel Vasquezius l. I. q. 19. disp. 83. c. 2.

Nec est, quod de solis electis hæc Beza & Pi- scator, ac Maccovius Coll. de prædestin. disp. I. e Reformatis, Estius e Papistis accipiant, quod eo- rum neminem Deus perire velit. Nam de omni- bus S. Petrum loqui, nimis luculentum. Nimirum eorum nullum perire vult Deus, quos ad pœni- tentiam venire vult. At Deus omnes homines vult ad pœnitentiam venire, non solos electos, ut λευκάδι φωνῇ Petrus pronunciat. Ergo nullum ho- minum vult Deus perire. Non solos electos ad pœnitentiam vocat, sed etiam reprobos, Luc. XXIV. 46. Act. XVII. 30. Matth. XXIII. 37. non electos solos venire ad pœnitentiam vult, sed et- iam reprobos, qui sibi iram ad diem iræ thesauri- zant, Rom. II. 5. Omnes vult ad agnitionem veri- tatis venire & salvari, 1. Tim. II, 4. Quod contra Bezam Hemmingius ipse observavit, agnovitque hic Tossanus: Deus, inquit, omnes ad pœnitentiam hortatur, etiam impios, ac concedit ipsis tempus pœ- nitentiæ. Quibus enim Deus concedit tempus pœnitentiæ, quosq; hortatur ad pœnitentiam, eos utique venire vult ad pœnitentiam. Daniel Cha- mier T. III. Panstrat. de Prædest. l. VII. c. 6. Quid infirmius, inquit, quam si dicas, Deus non vult ul- lum perire eorum, qui servantur. Item: Durum est illud, nolens ullos perire, flectere ad genera singulo- rum. E Pontificiis Lorinus in h. l. Est generalis propositio, non restringenda ad genera singulorum, vel ad prædestinatos. Tirinus in h. l. Non ergo absolute aut respectu infallibilis judicii tardat Dominus pro- missum Christi adventum, sed solum respectu falla- cis judicii & opinionis humanæ. Idq; non in da- mnum, sed in bonum nostrum, ut prolixius habeamus spatium pœnitendi, & vitam in melius commutan- di. Neq; enim vult (voluntate antecedente, ut Calvi- nus delirat) aliquos perdere, sed quantum ex se est, optat omnes etiam maxime impios & excæcatos at- que obstinatos ad pœnitentiam converti, atq; ita salvos fieri, ut etiam S. Paulus, adeoque & ipse Christus docet. Vide Molinam, Vasquez, Valentiam.

Quod vero Chamier excipit, distinguendo inter εὐδοκίαν, & εὐαρεστίαν, Deus patiens sit exspectare ad pœnitentiam voluntate εὐαρεστίας, quia gratior ei conversio, ideoque & salus peccato- ris, quam damnatio, non autem voluntate εὐδοκίας: Aliique distinguunt inter voluntatem approban- tem & decernentem: Vanæ sunt elusiones gratio- sæ Dei voluntatis. Deus enim non delectaretur solum pœnitentia & salute eorum, quos vocat, (vocat autem non solum electos, sed etiam re- probos) si pœnitentiam agerent ac salvarentur, sed etiam vult divino beneplacito, ut agant pœ- nitentiam, ut non pereant, sed salventur, 1. Tim. II. 4. quæ vera ejus εὐδοκία est, ex qua vocat & hortatur etiam reprobos ad pœnitentiam, vult enim omnium misereri, Rom. XI. 32. neminem pe- rire non voluntate signi tantum & externa, sed in- terna & beneplaciti, de qua testantur adhortatio- nes, protestationes etiam juratoriæ, comminationes & querelæ divinæ: ubi impia est Sam. Rhætorf. Exercit. V. apol. pro divin. grat. p. 331. exceptio, hortatio Dei præ se fert Deum velle salutem repro- borum, & tamen non vult eorum salutem, sed in- tendit eorum inexcusabilitatem. Τὸ χρηστὸν enim, bonitas Dei ἄγει εἰς μετάνοιαν ducit ad pœniten- tiam eos, qui μακροθυμίαν DEI, & divitias boni- tatis divinæ contemnunt, Rom. II. 4. Quidni ergo intenderet pœnitentiam eorum? Nec approba- ret tantum Deus, si converterentur, sed decrevit etiam ipsis media, quibus converti queant. De- stinavit misitque ipsis Christum Salvatorem mun- di, decrevit eos vocare, actuque vocat ad pœni- tentiam. Id de se & suis profitetur D. Joh. Ber- gius tr. de differ. & conven. Evangel. q. 53. No- stri, inquit, Doctores non diffitentur, Deum omni- um hominum salutem eatenus velle, quatenus in verbo, tanquam in voluntatis signo, cui nec arcana voluntas beneplaciti ullo modo contraria est, testa- tus est; quam etiam quidam cum Damasceno vo- luntatem antecedentem nominant, quum hic consi- deretur, quid Deus per se ante omnia nostra opera secundum bonitatis & gratiæ suæ voluntatem vo- luerit, nempe (1) voluntate approbante, quod per se non perditione, sed potius salute ipsorum delectetur, Ezech. XVIII. v. 32. cap. XXXIII. 11. 1. Tim. II. 4. 2. Petr. III. v. 9. (2) Præcipiente & promittente, quod etiam necessaria media, quæ ad salutem ex officio ipsis incumbunt, utpote agnitionem Dei, pœ- nitentiam, fidem, amorem & obedientiam omnibus ordinarit & præpararit; serioq; mandarrit, atq; ita salutem omnibus fideliter promiserit, Mich. VI. 8. Eccl. XII. 13. Rom. I. 21. Act. XVII. 30. Es. XLV. v. 22. Tit. II. 11. (3) operante, quod etiam efficaci bonitate sua ad pœnitentiam ducat, omniaq; ad sa- lutem ipsorum præstare velit, prout sapientiæ, boni- tati, justitiæ & veritati congruum & sufficiens ju- dicabit, ut converti debeant, quo omnis excusatio ipsis adimatur, quasi defectus non in ipsorum vo- luntate, sed in Dei gratia sit, quod converti neque- ant, Rom. II. 4. &c. (4) Non tamen necessitate, quasi omnes inevitabiliter & necessario, vel certo & infallibiliter salvare velit, sed quod in quampluri- mis bonitatem & gratiam suam repudiantibus ju- stissimam suam iram adversus peccata in ipsorum condemnatione exercere & demonstrare velit, quam quidem consequentem voluntatem nuncupant. Non quasi antecedens voluntas per eam immutetur, vel huic consequenti contraria sit, sed quod juxta ho- minum opera & vias ipsorum justi judicii sui vo- luntate ita ordinarit, Rom. II. 5. & IX. 22. 23. & XI. 20. 22. Act. XIII. 46. Hæc Bergius. Sed de Calvinianis plura diximus im gründlichen Be- weiß, quod scriptum nomine Facultatis Theol. prodiit, part. II. cap. III. q. III. seqq. E Pontificiis Bellarminus l. II. de Grat. & libr. arb. c. V. con- con- fert locum præsentem cum 1. Tim. II. 4. & Joh. I. 9. exponens eundem ex Augustino l. de Spir. & lit. c. XXXIII. cujus hanc docet fuisse sententiam: Deum velle omnes salvos fieri, quia dat omnibus, unde possint velle credere & salvari, sic tamen ut si ipsi noluerint, non salventur, sed ad supplicia de- stinentur æterna. Addit Bellarminus: Hanc etiam fuisse expositionem S. Prosperi l. II. de vocat. gent. cap. 23. 25. & 28. Item commentariorum, qui tri- buuntur Ambrosio, item Chrysostomi, Theophylacti, Oecumenii. Laudat inter alia Chrysostomi senten- tiam homil. VII. in Joh. Si illuminat, inquit, omnem hominem, venientem in hunc mundum, quo- nam pacto tot homines sine lumine permanent? Ne- que enim omnes Christum cognoscunt, quomodo er- go illuminat omnem hominem. Illuminat profecto, quantum in ipso est, si qui autem sponte sua mentis oculis conniventibus ad hujus lucis radios aciem dirigere noluerint, non ex luminis natura in tene- bris perstiterunt, sed ex malitia sua sponte sancto se dono indignos reddiderunt.

## 3:10
Vers. 10.

The day of the Lord will come) That last day, on which Christ will judge men, of which those judgments upon the Jews are a pledge, Luc. XVII. vers. 24, 1 Cor. I. 8, V. 5, 2 Cor. I. vers. 4, Phil. I. vers. 10.

As a thief in the night) Suddenly. Matth. XXIV. vers. 43, Luc. XII. vers. 39, 1 Thess. V. vers. 2. A thief in the night, שדר לילה, Abdia I. 5.

There is no trace here of the judgments of God upon the Jews. But by the similitude of a thief, those predictions of Christ are recalled to memory, so that they may be confirmed regarding the certainty of the final advent of Christ, which the designation of the manner made by Christ, that He Himself is to come unexpectedly like a thief, also establishes. He adds the same also for this reason, that they should not abuse the long-suffering of the Lord for security, but should always be prepared for the advent of the Lord: in which way He prepares the path for Himself for the admonition which He is about to subjoin, conf. Matth. XXIV. 43, Luc. XII. v. 39, Apoc. III. 3, cap. XVI. 15. But the Vulgate wrongly omitted that 'in the night', in which there is emphasis, yet the time of the advent of Christ is not to be determined from it, as some Fathers have done, quite confidently, but without Scripture, which was done by Tirinus in this place: In the Greek, he says, it is added, 'in the night', and Chrysostom, Theophylact, Euthymius report it, on that Matth. XXV. 6. At midnight a cry was made, etc. That Christ will come at night for judgment, and indeed at Passover, specifically at the same hour in which He once struck the firstborn of the Egyptians; indeed, St. Jerome says that this is an Apostolic tradition. And I could easily believe that the advent of Christ will be begun at night, namely that the fire of the conflagration will then be excited by an unusual agitation of the air. But I would prefer, with Thomas, 3rd part, in the supplement, q. 77, art. 3, Abulensis on Matthew XXV, Suarez, part 3, Vol. II, disp. 57, and others, to reserve the actual descent of Christ for judgment for the morning twilight, so that the judgment may be carried out most clearly in bright light. But if the world has already burned at night, what day or light can be expected from the Sun, when it has ceased to exist?

Ἐν ᾗ οὐρανοὶ ῥοιζηδὸν παρελεύσονται)

Ἐν ᾗ, namely ἡμέρᾳ, at which time. Ῥοιζηδὸν παρελεύσονται, they will perish with a great rushing sound. In the Glossary, ῥοῖζος is a rushing sound. The Scholiasts of Homer also interpret it as ὁρμὴν. The air and the ether will perish, because the appearance and form will be changed. Things seem to be absent, say the Jurisconsults, even those whose body remains, if the form has been changed, where body is said for matter, as we noted at L. Mulieris, and §. res abesse. D. de verb. signif. Concerning the word παρέρχεσθαι, see Matthew V. 18. The Hebrews use עבר in the same sense, as in Psalm XXXVII. 36 and elsewhere. It is placed for it and אבד, Psalm CII. 27.

The heavens (oi oὐρανοὶ) do not refer to the air and the ether, but only to the heavens: because it follows next concerning the elements. Much less, therefore, is it fitting to understand only the air here, as Blasius de Viegas does in his commentary on Apocalypse XXI, p. 812. That by the name of heavens are understood not the sidereal, but the aerial heavens, is also contended by Estius and Gregorius de Valentia, Vol. IV, commentary on Thomas, p. 2277; Barradius, Book IX, in Conc. Ev., ch. XI, p. 592; Ambrosius Catharinus in this place, in Sixtus Senensis, Bibliotheca, Book VI, annotation 340. That he speaks truly of the heavens, and not of the air, is evident: for after he said, in which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, he added, but the elements shall be dissolved with heat: which seems to pertain to the air and to the water, which are to be dissolved by fire. Concerning the earth, however, he says specifically: But the earth, etc. Tirinus, however, thinks that both the sidereal and the aerial heavens can be accepted, along with Cajetan and Suarez, disputation LVIII, section 3. and a Lapide, citing for the same opinion (but falsely) Blasius de Viegas in Apocalypse XXI. As to the word

παρελεύσονται (they shall pass away) implies not only a change of appearance and form, but a total destruction, which is to be learned not from a comparison of legal texts, but from Scripture, and indeed those passages which Grotius brought forward, Matthew V, v. 18, Psalm CII, 27, confirm it. Add Matthew XXV, 35, Mark XIII, 31, Luke XXI, v. 33, chapter XVI, 17, Apocalypse XXI, 1. Nor is there any other sense of the word in Psalm XXXVII, v. 36, than that the wicked has ceased to be, of whom there is speech there. We showed at Psalm CII, 27, the substantial destruction of the material heavens, that they are to pass away completely, to perish, and to be no more. Here the heavens are said to be reserved for fire, and to pass away with a great noise, to be dissolved, kindled by fire, which implies not an accidental change, but a substantial destruction. For that which passes away in such a way that it is consumed by fire is substantially abolished: therefore, in Apocalypse XXI, 1, the heaven is said to be about to pass away in such a way that it will no longer exist, nor will its place be found any more.

The gloss of Salmeron is jejune, because he wished God to declare through Peter and the other Prophets that all things were to perish and be reduced almost to nothing, so that we might acknowledge His omnipotence: And Barradius, Book X, Conc. Ev., ch. 1: The heavens shall perish, that is, they can perish; for it is not taught what divine omnipotence can do, but what divine omnipotence is going to do; nor is the possibility of the destruction of the world, but the actual destruction, handed down here. Lorinus retreats to hyperbole, but in vain: because one must not depart from the literal sense in those things which consist solely of the revelation of Scripture. Still more inept are those who understand this passing away only as local motion, or as a cessation from motion. To Tirinus it is probable that the sidereal heavens are then to be agitated more swiftly, so that they may carry with them the aerial heavens, full of thick vapor and habit, to excite a swifter kindling of the fire by which the world will burn; and thus it can be aptly understood how the heavens are to pass away and be moved. For that passing away implies not local motion, but destruction. Blasius de Viegas, in the place cited, refutes those who understand the passing away as from motion to rest, along with the Scholastics, as Ambrosius Catharinus does in his commentary on Hebrews I: How shall the heavens perish? Most say, as regards local motion. But this is not to perish nor to grow old, which tends toward destruction, as the Apostle says below, and that which grows old is near to destruction. Furthermore, St. Peter left this testimony concerning the heaven: The heavens shall pass away with a great noise, the heavens shall be dissolved burning, but we look for new heavens. Moreover, the beloved in the Apocalypse I saw a new heaven and a new earth: For the first heaven and the first earth passed away: And our Lord himself: Heaven and earth shall pass away. From these testimonies of the Scriptures, therefore, unless we wish to do violence to the words, we are compelled to confess that there will be some truly great alteration of the heavens through fire, and not merely the cessation of motion alone, through which alteration new heavens will be in a way delivered, and will become far more beautiful than they are now. Salmeron in this place: That some interpret this passing away through the cessation of the heavens from motion seems to me clearly violent and forced. For the heavens to be dissolved by fire through cessation from all motion is in my judgment far less than to be dissolved, kindled by fire, and it signifies rather through alteration and corruption that the heavens perish. But even Tirinus himself, however much he may explain the passing away as a commotion, acknowledges that the heavens are said to be changed, dissolved, burned, and to perish in another sense, namely, that they are to be transferred into greater light and glory, which Cornelius explained in the same manner as Blasius had previously set forth that it would happen, and taught that it was explained by others, at verse 10. Distinguished Theologians and Philosophers assert that the sidereal heavens will burn and be liquefied by the fire of the conflagration, as being compacted, constricted, and as it were glued together from water, so that they may be purged from all filth and dross, and become purer and more subtle. For St. Peter says this clearly here, and Isaiah chapter XXXIV, 4, chapter L, 6, and among the more recent ones, our Tannerus at length in his dissertation on the heavens, question XI.

Although indeed some of the ancients went so far as to say—Jerome, book 18 on Isaiah, that we shall not see other heavens and another earth, but the old and ancient ones changed for the better; Gennadius in the book on Church Dogmas, chapter 70, and Oecumenius in this passage, that the world will not tend entirely toward corruption, but toward renewal, just as we are accustomed to melt certain corporeal things with fire, not to assign them absolute destruction, but to provide them with purity and sincerity: of whom you may see more in B. Gerhard, On the Consummation of the Age, § 32—yet that explanation does not agree with the emphatic words of Scripture concerning the destruction of the world, the passing away and dissolution of the heavens, nor is anything handed down in the sacred writings about the innovation of the present heavens, but rather about the existence of new heavens. Nor does that hypothesis about the starry heavens being compacted from water rest on the foundation of Scripture, nor is it certain concerning the filth and dregs of the heavens, whence Estius here denies that the celestial bodies are to be purged by fire, although he thinks they will receive a transmutation for the better: And Sixtus Senensis observes in book 6 of the Bibliotheca, Annotation 340, that Clement of Rome in Recognitions II and Hilary in Canon 4 on Matthew assert the destruction of the heavens according to substance, and that Jerome in book 14 on Isaiah infers that opinion, disapproved by some, from the present testimony of Peter. Salmero also contradicts himself in the explanation of this passage, which he teaches is indicated, that the heavens are about to perish, in such a way that they will not be. For whatever fire seizes, it is accustomed by its force and efficacy to convert, like wood and stones, into ashes. When the Apostle says they will pass away with a great rush, it seems to be similar to that which the Lord says, heaven and earth will pass away, to which He opposes: But my words will not pass away. Therefore they will not pass away in such a way that they remain only without motion, but THEY WILL PASS AWAY ENTIRELY, SO THAT THEY CEASE TO BE. Those things which cease to be are reduced to nothing. Similarly, Cornelius cuts his own vines in his Commentary on Isaiah 34, verse 4. For although he establishes both opinions—concerning destruction according to substance and according to qualities—as probable, and confesses that they have weighty authors, and says that the latter is even more conformable to Aristotelian philosophy; the former he acknowledges to be more conformable to Scripture, from which this matter must be judged entirely; and therefore Cornelius adds, not without rashness and perversity: which may be the truer, we shall discuss elsewhere. For whatever opinion concerning matters of faith is more conformable to Scripture, that is also, without any doubt, the truer one. We subjoin, however, what he has besides on these matters there: Adamus, says Pererius in Apoc. VI. and the Scholastics passim with Augustine, book XX de Civit. Dei, ch. 14, St. Jerome on Isaiah LI, Gregory, Moral. XVII, ch. 5, and others, believe that the heaven and the stars are to be changed and renewed only according to light and other qualities, but not according to form and substance, for in Psalm CXLVI it is said that God founded them for ever and ever: and because according to Aristotle and the philosophers the form of the heavens is incorruptible, and Aristotle deduces that from the fact that it is eternal. For he himself believes the world to have been from eternity, indeed uncreated, as some opine, in which it is clear he has erred. Many Fathers, however, and recent authors, who wish philosophy to be subjected to the sacred letters, and not the contrary, hold that heaven and earth will perish even as to substance, and are to be changed into another new heaven and another new earth. For that seems to be said most clearly here and elsewhere, as ch. LI. 6, ch. LXV. v. 17, Apoc. VI. 14, and ch. XXI. 1, Ecclesiasticus XVII. v. 30, Ps. CI. 27, Matthew XXIV. 35, 2 Peter III. 7, 12. Where note that the Holy Scripture speaks far more effectively of the mutation of the heavens and the elements than of the blessed bodies in the resurrection, and clearly signifies that the mutation of the former will be far greater than that of the latter; because the former will be substantial, the latter only accidental. Again, since light naturally flows as it were from the essence of the heavens, and will then be far greater and more noble, it seems likewise that it will flow from another more noble substantial form. For light as great as it will then be is not connatural to the form of the Sun as it now is. Thus think Chrysostom, hom. XIV in Epist. ad Rom., and after him Theodoret and Oecumenius, Justin q. 93, Ambrose book I Hexaëm. c. 6, Basil hom. III Hexaëm., Nyssenus book de creat. hom. ch. 24, Clement books 2 and 3 Recognit., Sibylla in St. Augustine de Civit. Dei book XVIII, ch. 3. The same is taught at length by Hieronymus Magius book II de exustione mundi ch. 6 and 7, and Valesius sacr. Philos. ch. 89, and our Molina tr. de opere sex dier. diff. 3. Which things are indeed so limited by Cornelius, that he wishes the same to be understood only of the form of heaven, not of the matter. For he adds then: Furthermore, that Scripture says elsewhere that the heavens and the earth will stand for ever does not conflict with this opinion. For the same earth, the same Sun, and the same heavens will remain generically: for the earth will retain the form of earth, and the heavens the generic form of heavens, even if they receive another and more excellent one specifically. For there will then be an innovation, reformation, and recreation of the whole world. But if the created heavens are reduced to nothing along with other creatures, except man and Angel, they will certainly perish not only according to form, but also according to matter; indeed, since the end and consummation of the world is predicted in the sacred letters, how will the heavens or other things remain according to matter? Therefore, heaven and earth are said to stand for ever, not as to absolute eternity, but defined, namely until the consummation of all things, until the αἰῶνας ἐπερχομένους Eph. II. 7, while this ὁ αἰὼν οὗτος lasts, Matthew XII, and to the ends of the ages, 1. Cor. X. 21, to the συντέλειαν τῶν αἰώνων, Heb. IX. 25, to which those phrases contribute: until there is no Moon, Psalm LXXII. 7, until the consummation of the world, v. 8, until the Sun remains v. 17, the end of the world or age, Matthew XIII. 39, ch. XXIV. 3, ch. XXVIII.

p. 20, the end of all things 1 Peter IV. 7. Hilary certainly, whom Sixtus Senensis praised, believed that the heavens would perish not only according to form, but also as to matter, in Enarr. ad Psal. CXXII: This heaven, which in our times is subject to change through its matter, which like smoke was solidified and received both the nature and name of a firmament, will pass away and will not be, but the seat of the Lord remains for ever. Similar things the same Senensis notes from Clement of Rome, that Peter teaches two heavens, one higher and indestructible, perpetual and eternal, which the blessed Spirits inhabit, the other lower, visible, distinguished by various stars, corruptible, and to be dissolved and utterly abolished at the consummation of the age. Nor will the fire, by which the world will burn, tend toward the mutation of form, but toward the destruction of matter, as in other bodies, with man alone excepted: so also in heaven. Concerning which Augustine book XX de civit. DEI ch. 18, in this place indeed understanding only the aerial heavens, but judging in Psalm CII. 27 that no heaven is left which he did not say would perish. For where, he says, it is said the heavens are the works of his hands, they themselves will perish, as none of them is separated from the work of GOD, so none of them is separated from destruction: See more in B. Gerhard de consumm. seculi §. 39 seqq., to which opinion is also brought from the Reformed §. 47 Beza, Tilenus, Chassanio, Polanus, Socinus c. Puccium p. 143, Schlichtingius in h. l. the heavens will be changed from being to non-being.

Στοιχεῖα δὲ καυσούμενα λυθήσεται) here he calls the stars and water στοιχεῖα. For a special mention of the earth will follow. Compare Wisd. XIX. 17. Λύεσθαι here, which Euripides in the tragedy Chrysippos called διακρίνεσθαι, is to depart from the former form. Καυσούμενα, burning. This word is found in Dioscorides.

Καὶ γῆ καὶ τὰ ἐν ἀυτῇ ἔργα κατακαήσεται) Ἔργα here is worth מלאכות, under which name are comprehended both living creatures, as Gen. XXXIII. 13, and other things which are possessed by men, as trees and crops. Thus the labors of oxen among the Poets, κατακαήσονται, will not be scorched, but will be burned up. For that is κατακαίεσθαι Exod. III. 2, Isaiah XLIII. 2, LXIV. 2, Jerem. XLIX. v. 2, 2 Kings XXIII. v. 11, Deut. VII. 5, 1 Macc. IV. 38, and elsewhere.

By what argument, indeed, will it be taught that στοιχεῖα denotes stars and water? Stars pertain to the heavens, not to the elements. However, most think that air is referred here to τὰ στοιχεῖα or elements along with water, because it follows distinctly from the earth in the next words, and they judge that fire is applied for destruction by way of an agent: because the elements are said to be burned up by the heat of fire, and to be dissolved, or rather destroyed, by that heat, as λύειν is used in Job II. 19, Acts XXVII. 42, 1 John III. 8. B. Luther rendered it: Die Elementen werden für Hitze zerschmelzen: concerning the earth it is added particularly because of the works that are in it, which must be burned up with them. Since Grotius concedes that these are to be entirely burned up, why should the same not be said of the elements, if indeed all these things are afterwards called λυόμενα in verse 11, and particularly concerning the heavens in verse 12, ὀυρανοὶ πυρούμενοι λυθήσονται; and concerning the elements, τὰ στοιχεῖα καυσούμενα καήσεται. Therefore, the Papists rashly except the upper region of the air: concerning which they trifle thus, with Barradius as interpreter, lib. IX. comm. in Evang. Conc. cap. XI. p. 592. It is asked how far the fire is to ascend? The interlinear gloss on 2 Peter III. answers with these words: the fire of judgment ascends only as far as the water of the flood ascended. But the water of the flood ascended fifteen cubits above the mountains, Genesis VII. The fire will ascend just as much. The ordinary gloss on 2 Thess. I. The fire will be in the world, which will precede Christ, occupying as much space as the water occupied in the flood. The same is The opinion of the Master and the Scholastics: Who indeed dictated these things to the Glossators and to the Master? If all the elements will perish by fire, how will the highest region of the air be excepted? Tirinus philosophizes thus in the same place concerning the upper region of the air, without any Word of GOD: The aerial heavens will be disturbed by such thick clouds, such horrible thunders, lightnings, comets, falling stars, and other meteors, storms, and tempests, that even the highest heavens themselves will seem to burn, and to be torn from their hinges, undermined, and to vanish. But what of that disturbance, which they dream of regarding the conflagration or dissolution and destruction of the aerial heavens? But the elements, for instance fire, the lower region of the air near the earth, and water or the seas will be dissolved by heat, that is, by burning and ardor, that is, they will be attenuated by the force of fire, and will be liquefied as if gold in a crucible, so that vapors, exhalations, and all dregs already mixed with them may be separated from them: thus St. Thomas and other Doctors. Let that which is in the air, flammable matter, be consumed, therefore; in the sea, whatever is earthy, congealed or mixed. Against this, Ribera on Apoc. XXI says that water after the end of the world will not be fluid, but consolidated and conglobated like a sphere. But the Apostle treats not of the attenuation or consumption of flammable matter in the air, not of the separation of earthy matter in water, or of the concretion of the sea, but of the destruction of air and water. And in Apocal. XXI. verse 1, it is said of the sea, ἡ θάλασσα ὐκ ἔτι. Barradius l. X. conc. cap. 1. pag. 611. Water, he says, in the new world will be like crystal, air like heaven, fire like the luminaries of the world. But where are such things written? Is it not clearly said that the sea will no longer exist? A new heaven and a new earth, say Primasius and Beda on Apoc. XXI. verse 1, but we do not read that there will also be a new sea.

Concerning fire, Gregorius de Valentia, Tom. IV. Comm. in Thom. pag. 2276, divines: It is probable that the fire by which the earth will burn will ascend to its natural sphere. The fire that will be in its natural sphere, since it does not have foreign qualities mixed in there, will not be altered by that fire of conflagration, but only the remaining elements, and any fires that will then be found impure in lower places. But those things concerning the natural sphere of fire under the concave of the Moon have no foundation in nature. Nor is it known to any mortal whether the natural or elemental fire, or what finally that world-devouring or πανολέθριος fire will be: For the Apostle implies that not just some elements, but indefinitely the elements will be consumed by that fire: then when the fire has no fuel, it itself also is extinguished and perishes, if it pleases one to philosophize thus. But it is safer to assert with Scripture the destruction of the whole universe than to except some parts at will. Certainly, not only Beda, but also Andreas Caesariensis, Aretes, Anselmus, Haymo, and Rupertus on Apoc. XXI agree with Lorinus, who admits the destruction of fire and water. Philippus Solitarius, Dioptr. c. 6. 7, removes all elements from the midst after the resurrection and judgment. But Estius is injurious to divine omnipotence when he says that the elements will be dissolved, the dissolution of which into primary matter is impossible; since not even their total destruction should be believed impossible, nay, it should even be asserted. The inanities of the Papists about the cross of Christ and other instruments of his passion being preserved forever are unworthy of refutation: If anyone desires to know them, let him approach B. Gerhard on this passage and on the Consummation of the Age, as also Harim. Evang. c. 161.

PART II. Exhortation to preparation for the coming of the Lord.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Ἥξει δὲ ἡ ἡμέρα τοῦ Κυρίου) Illa ultima, qua Christus homines judicabit, cujus arrhabo sunt judicia illa in Ju- dæos, Luc. XVII. vers. 24. 1. Cor. I. 8. V. 5. 2. Cor. I. vers. 4. Phil. I. vers. 10.

Ὡς κλέπτης ἐν νυκτὶ) Subito. Matth. XXIV. vers. 43. Luc. XII. vers. 39. 1. Thess. V. vers. 2. Κλέπτης ἐν νυκτὶ שדר לילה, Abdia I. 5.

De judiciis Dei in Judæos nullum hic vestigi- um. Furis autem similitudine in memoriam re- vocantur illæ Christi prædictiones, ut confirmen- tur de certitudine adventus Christi novissimi, quam etiam designatio modi a Christo facta, quod instar furis inopinato adventuris ipse sit, statuminat. Addit autem eandem etiam ideo, ut ne μακροθυμίᾳ Domini abutantur ad securitatem, sed semper ad adventum Domini parati sint: quo pacto sibi ad admonitionem, quam subjuncturus est, viam parat, conf. Matth. XXIV. 43. Luc. XII. v. 39. Apoc. III. 3. cap. XVI. 15. Perperam autem illud ἐν νυκτὶ omisit Vulgatus, in quo emphasis est, non tamen inde tempus adventus Christi de- terminandum, cum Patribus quibusdam, quem- admodum satis confidenter, sed ἄτερ γραφῆς, id a Tirino hoc in loco factum: In Græco, inquit, additur, in nocte, traditq; Chrysostomus, Theophy- lactus, Euthymius, in illud Matth. XXV. 6. Media nocte clamor factus est &c. Christum noctu ven- turum ad judicium, & quidem in Paschate, puta eadem hora, qua olim percussit primogenita Ægy- ptiorum, imo S. Hieronymus ait, hanc esse Apostoli- cam traditionem. Et quidem facile crediderim, no- ctu inchoatum iri adventum Christi, nempe ignem conflagrationis ex insolita aëris agitatione tunc ex- citandum. Sed ipsum Christi descensum ad judici- um malim cum Thoma 3. p. in suppl. q. 77. art. 3. Abulensi in Matth. XXV. Suarez. p. 3. T. II. disp. 57. & aliis matutino crepusculo reservare, ut judi- cium in clara luce clarissime peragatur. Sed si mun- dus jam conflagravit noctu, quænam a Sole dies vel lux expectari poterit, ubi ille esse desiit?

Ἐν ᾗ οὐρανοὶ ῥοιζηδὸν παρελεύσονται)

Ἐν ᾗ nempe ἡμέρᾳ quo tempore. Ῥοιζηδὸν παρελεύ- σονται peribunt magno impetu. In Glossario ῥοῖζος im- petus. Etiam Scholiastæ Homeri interpretantur ὁρμὴν Aër & æther peribunt, quia species & forma mutabitur. Res abesse videntur, ajunt Jurisconsulti, etiam hæ quarum corpus manet, forma mutata est, ubi corpus dicitur pro materia, uti notavimus ad L. Mulieris, & §. res abesse. D. de verb. signif. De voce παρέρχεσθαι vide Matth. V. 18. Ebræi עבר eodem sensu usurpant, ut Ps. XXXVII. 36. & alibi. Ponitur pro ea & אבד, Psal. CII. 27.

Non de aëre & æthere oi oὐρανοὶ, sed de cælis solum sonant: quia de elementis deinde sequitur. Multo ergo minus solum aërem hic intelligere convenit, uti Blasius de Vigeas in comment. Apoc. XXI. p. 812. Cælorum nomine non sidereos, sed aëreos cælos intelligi, quod etiam contendit Estius & Gregorius de Valentia Tom. IV. comm. in Thom. p. 2277. Barradius l. IX. in Conc. Ev. c. XI. p. 592. Ambrosius Catharinus in h. l. apud Sixt. Sen. Bibl. l. VI. annot. 340. Quod vero de cælis loquatur proprie, & non de aëre patet: Postquam enim dixit, in quo cæli magno impetu solventur, adjecit, elementa vero calore solventur: quod ad aërem & ad aquam pertinere videtur, quæ per ignem solvenda sunt. De terra autem particulariter ait: Terra autem &c. Tirinus tamen putat, accipi posse tam sidereos, quam aëreos cælos, cum Cajetano Suarez disp. LVIII. sect. 3. & a Lapide, adducens in eandem sententiam, (sed falso) Blasium de Viegas in Apoc. XXI. Quod ad verbum

παρελεύσονται, non tantum speciei & formæ mutationem, sed totalem interitum infert, quod non e collatione textuum juris, sed Scripturæ discendum, & sane vel illa loca, quæ adduxit Grotius, Matth. V. v. 18. Psal. CII. 27. confirmant. Adde Matth. XXV. 35. Marci XIII. 31. Luc. XXI. v. 33. cap. XVI. 17. Apoc. XXI. 1. Nec alius sensus vocis est Psal. XXXVII. v. 36. quam quod esse desierit impius, de quo ibi sermo. Substantialem interitum cælorum materialium, quod penitus transituri, interituri, nec amplius futuri sint, ad Psalm. CII. 27. ostendimus. Hic igni reservari dicuntur cæli, & magno impetu transituri, igne succensi solvendi, quæ non Accidentalem mutationem, sed substantialem destructionem inferunt. Quod enim ita transit, ut igne exuratur, id substantialiter aboletur: ideo Apoc. XXI. 1. ita transiturum cælum dicitur, ut futurum amplius non sit, nec locus ejus amplius inveniatur.

Jejuna est glossa Salmeronis, quod voluerit Deus per Petrum, & alios Prophetas declarare, omnia peritura & in nihilum fere redigenda, ut agnoscamus omnipotentiam ejus: Et Barradii l. X. conc. Ev. c. 1. Cæli peribunt, hoc est perire possunt; nam non quid divina omnipotentia possit, sed quid divina omnipotentia factura sit, docetur; nec possibilitas destructionis mundi, sed actualis destructio hic traditur. Ad hyperbolen se recipit Lorinus, sed frustra: quia a litera discedendum non est in his, quæ sola Scripturæ revelatione constant. Ineptiores adhuc sunt, qui transitum hunc de motu locali solum intelligunt, vel de cessatione a motu. Tirino probabile est, cælos sidereos velocius tunc agitandos, ut secum rapiant cælos aëreos pingui vapore, & habitu plenos ad celeriorem accensionem ignis, quo mundus conflagrabit, excitandam; atq; ita apte intelligi posse, quomodo cæli transituri & commovendi sint. Ille enim transitus non motum localem, sed interi- tum infert. Blasius de Viegas l. c. transitum a motu ad quietem intelligentem cum Scholasticis ita refellit Ambrosius Catharinus in comment. ad Ebr. I. Quomodo peribunt cæli? Dicunt plerique, quantum ad motum localem. At hoc non est perire neque veterascere, quod ad interitum tendit, ut ait Apostolus inferius, & quod veterascit, prope interitum est. Præterea S. Petrus de cælo hoc testimonium reliquit: Cæli magno impetu transibunt, cæli ardentes solventur, novos vero cælos expectamus. Adhæc dilectus in Apocal. Vidi cælum novum & terram novam: Primum enim cælum & prima terra abiit: Et ipsemet Dominus no- ster: Cœlum & terra transibunt. Ex his ergo Scri- pturarum testimoniis, nisi prorsus velimus verbis vim inferre, cogimur fateri futuram vere ali- quam magnam cælorum alterationem per ignem, & non solius tantum motus cessationem, per quam alterationem novi quodammodo tradentur cæli, & longe fient pulchriores, quam nunc sunt. Salmero in h. l. Quod quidam hunc transitum per cessa- tionem cælorum a motu interpretantur, plane mi- hi violentum & extortum videtur. Solvi enim cæ- los igne per cessationem a motu omni est meo ju- dicio longe minus, quam succensos igne solvi, & potius per alterationem & corruptionem significat cælos perire. Sed & Tirinus ipse, utut transitum de commotione explicet, agnoscit, immutandos, dissolvendos, arsurros ac perituros cælos alio sensu dici, nempe quod in majorem lucem & gloriam transferendi sint, quod ad eundem modum, uti antea Blasius futurum exposuit, & ab aliis ex- poni docuit Cornelius ad vers. 10. Insignes Theo- logi & Philosophi afferunt cælos sidereos per ignem conflagrationis arsuras & liquandos, utpote ex aqua compactos, constrictos, & quasi conglutinatos, ut ab omni sorde & fæce purgentur, fiantque purio- res & subtiliores. Id enim diserte ait hic S. Petrus, & Esa. cap. XXXIV. 4. cap. L. 6. ac inter recentio- res fuse noster Tannerus dissert. de cælis q. XI.

Quanquam vero nonnulli veterum eo etiam abierint, Hieronymus l. XIIX. in Esaiam, non alios cœlos & aliam terram videbimus, sed veteres & antiquos in melius commutatos; Gennadius in libr. de Eccles. dogmat. cap. 70. & Oecume- nius in h. l. non penitus ad corruptionem tendet mundus, sed ad renovationem, sicut igne fundere solemus res quasdam corporeas, non ut absolu- tum interitum eis tribuamus, sed ut puritatem ac sinceritatem iisdem præstemus: quorum plures vide sis B. Gerhard. de Consummat. Seculi §. 32. non tamen convenit illa explicatio verbis Scri- pturæ emphaticis, de destructione mundi, transi- tu & dissolutione cœlorum, nec uspiam in sa- cris de cœlorum præsentium innovatione ali- quid traditum, sed de novorum cœlorum exi- stentia. Neque illa hypothesis de cælis sidereis ex aqua compactis fundamento Scripturæ nititur, nec de sorde & fæce cœlorum constat, unde E- stius hic negat, corpora cœlestia igne purganda esse, tametsi transmutationem in melius acce- ptura putet: Et observat Sixtus Senensis l. VI. Bibl. Annot. 340. Clementem Romanum in re- cognit. II. Hilarium Can. IV. in Matth. interitum cælorum secundum substantiam asserere, ac Hie- ronymum l. XIV. in Esa. inferre sententiam illam, a quibusdam improbatam, præsenti Petri testimo- nio. Salmero etiam ipse contradicit sibi in hu- jus loci explicatione, quem docet indicari, quod cæli perituri sint, ita ut non sint. Quicquid enim arripit ignis, solet vi sua & efficacia, ut ligna & saxa in cineres convertere. Cum ait Apostolus ma- gno impetu transibunt, videtur simile esse ei, quod Dominus ait, cælum & terra transibunt, quibus opponit: Verba autem mea non transibunt. Er- go non ita transibunt, ut maneant tantum sine mo- tu, sed OMNINO TRANSIBUNT, UT DESINANT ESSE. Quæ esse desinunt, ea in nihilum rediguntur. Similiter propria vineta cædit Cornelius Commentar. in Esa. XXXIV. vers. 4. Etsi enim utramque sententiam de in- teritu secundum substantiam & secundum qua- litates probabilem statuat, gravesque habere au- tores fateatur, posteriorem etiam Philosophiæ Aristotelicæ esse conformiorem dicat; priorem tamen magis Scripturæ conformem esse agnoscit, e qua omnino hæc res dijudicanda; ideoque non nisi temere ac perverse subjungit Cornelius: utra sit verior alibi pertractabimus. Quæ enim senten- tia de rebus fidei Scripturæ conformior, ea citra omnem dubietatem etiam verior est. Subjicimus tamen, quæ de his illic præterea habet: Adamus, inquit Pererius in Apoc. VI. & passim Scholastici cum Augustino l. XX. de Civit. Dei cap. 14. S. Hie- ronymo in LI. Esaiæ, Gregor. XVII. Moral. cap. 5. & aliis censent, cælum & astra mutanda & inno- vanda esse tantum secundum lucem, aliasq; quali- tates, non autem secundum formam & substantiam, nam Psal. CXLVI. dicitur Deus ea fundasse in secu- lum seculi: & quia secundum Aristotelem & Phi- losophos forma cælorum est incorruptibilis, idque Aristoteles deducit ex eo, quod sit æterna. Censet enim ipse mundum fuisse ab æterno, imo increatum, ut nonnulli opinantur, in quo errasse eum clarum est. Multi tamen Patres & recentiores, qui Philo- sophiam exigendam volunt ad sacras literas, non contra, volunt cælum & terram peritura etiam quoad substantiam, ac mutanda in aliud cælum novum, & aliam terram novam. Id enim hic & alibi clarissime dici videtur, ut cap. LI. 6. cap. LXV. v. 17. Apoc. VI. 14. & cap. XXI. 1. Ecclesiastici XVII. v. 30. Ps. CI. 27. Matth. XXIV. 35. 2. Petr. III. 7. 12. Ubi nota, sacram Scripturam longe efficacius loqui de mutatione cælorum & elementorum, quam cor- porum beatorum in resurrectione, planeq; significa- re, longe majorem fore mutationem illorum, quam horum; quia illa substantialis, hæc tantum acci- dentalis erit. Rursum cum lux naturaliter quasi profluat ex essentia cælorum, tumq; futura sit longe major & nobilior, videtur pariter, quod ex alia forma substantiali nobiliori manabit. Nam lux tan- ta, quanta tunc erit, non est connaturalis formæ Solis, qua jam est. Ita sentiunt Chrysostomus hom. XIV. in Epist. ad Rom. & post eum Theodoretus & Oecumenius, Justinus q. 93. Ambrosius l. I. Hexaëm. c. 6. Basilius hom. III. Hexaëm. Nyssenus l. de creat. hom. cap. 24. Clemens l. 2. & 3. Recognit: Sibylla apud S. Augustinum de Civit. Dei l. XVIII. cap. 3. Idem fuse docet Hieronymus Magius l. II. de exu- stione mundi cap. 6. & 7. & Valesius sacr. Philos. c. 89. & noster Molina tr. de operc sex dier. diff. 3. Quæ vero ita a Cornelio limitantur, ut de forma tantum cæli eadem intellecta velit, non de mate- ria. Nam addit deinde: Porro quod alibi ait Scri- ptura, quod cæli & terra in æternum stabunt, non repugnat huic sententiæ. Manebit enim eadem ter- ra, idem Sol, & iidem cæli generice: Terra enim formam terræ, cæli formam cælorum genericam re- tinebunt, esto specifice aliam eamq; præstantiorem accipiant. Erit enim tunc totius mundi innovatio, reformatio & recreatio. Sed si in nihilum redi- gentur cæli creati cum aliis creaturis, excepto ho- mine, & Angelo, certe non tantum secundum formam, sed etiam secundum materiam peribunt, imo quum omnium finis & consummatio mundi in sacris literis prædicetur, quomodo secundum materiam cæli aut aliæ res supererunt. In æter- num ergo stare cælum & terra dicitur, non quoad æternitatem absolutam, sed definitam, nimirum usq; ad rerum omnium consummationem, usque ad αἰῶνας ἐπερχομένους Eph. II. 7. dum durat ὁ αἰὼν οὗτος, Matth. XII. & ad fines τῶν αἰώνων, 1. Cor. X. 21. ad συντέλειαν τῶν αἰώνων, Ebr. IX. 25. quo faciunt illæ phrases: donec non erit Luna, Psalm. LXXII. 7. usque ad consummationem mundi, v. 8. quousque Sol manebit v. 17. finis mundi vel se- culi, Matth. XIII. 39. cap. XXIV. 3. cap. XXVIII.

p. 20. finis omnium 1. Petr. IV. 7. Hilarius certe, quem laudavit Sixtus Senensis, non tantum secun- dum formam, sed etiam quoad materiam cœlos perituros censuit in Enarr. ad Psal. CXXII. Cœ- lum hoc, quod vicibus nostris per materiam sui subjacet, quod tanquam fumus solidatum firma- menti & naturam & nomen accepit, præteribit & non erit, sedes autem Domini manet in æternum. Qualia idem Senensis notat e Clemente Romano, Petrum duos cœlos docere, unum superius & in- ruibile, perpetuum & æternum, quod beati Spiri- tus incolunt, alterum inferius, visibile, variis di- stinctum sideribus, corruptibile, & in consun- matione seculi dissolvendum, prorsusque abo- lendum. Nec ignis, quo conflagrabit mundus, ad formæ immutationem, sed ad materiæ destructio- nem tendet, ut in aliis corporibus solo homine excepto: ita etiam in cœlo. Quo de Augustinus l. XX. de civit. DEI cap. 18. in hoc quidem loco cœlos aëreos tantum intelligens, in Psalmo autem CII. 27. judicans, nullum cœlorum relinqui, quod periturum esse non dixerit. Ubi enim, inquit, di- citur opera manuum suarum sunt cœli, ipsi peri- bunt, quam nullum eorum ab opere DEI, tam nullum eorum a perditione secernitur: Vid. plu- ra apud B. Gerhardum de consumm. seculi §. 39. seqq. in quam sententiam etiam adducitur e Reformatis §. 47. Beza, Tilenus, Chassanio, Pola- nus, Socinus c. Puccium p. 143. Schlichtingius in h. l. cœli mutabuntur ab esse ad non esse.

Στοιχεῖα δὲ καυσούμενα λυθήσεται) στοιχεῖα hic vocat astra & aquam. Nam terræ specialis mentio sequetur. Conf. Sap. XIX. 17. Λύεσθαι hic quod διακρίνεσθαι dixit Euripides tragœdia Chrysippos, est de forma priore exire. Καυσού- μενα æstuantia. Est ea vox apud Dioscoridem.

Καὶ γῆ καὶ τὰ ἐν ἀυτῇ ἔργα κατακαήσεται) Ἔργα hic valet מלאכות, sub quo nomine comprehenduntur & animantia, ut Gen. XXXIII. 13. & alia, quæ ab hominibus possidentur, ut arbores & sata. Sic boumque labores apud Poëtas, κατακαήσονται, non adurentur, sed exurentur. Id enim κατακαίεσθαι Exod. III. 2. Esaiz XLIII. 2. LXIV. 2. Jerem. XLIX. vers. 2. 2. Reg. XXIII. vers. 11. Deuter. VII. 5. 1. Macc. IV. 38. & & alibi.

Quo vero argumento docebitur, στοιχεῖα astra & aquam notare? Astra ad cœlos non ad elemen- ta pertinent. Ad τὰ στοιχεῖα autem vel elementa cum aqua aërem huc referri, quia de terra distin- ctim sequitur in verbis proximis, plerique pu- tant, ignem vero ad destructionem per modum agentis adhiberi censent: quia elementa ignis ar- dore comburenda dicuntur, & per istum ardorem dissolvenda, vel potius destruenda, uti λύειν adhi- betur Job. II. 19. Actor. XXVII. 42. 1. Joh. III. 8. B. Lutherus reddidit: Die Elementen werden für Hitze zerschmelzen: de terra peculiariter additur ob opera, quæ in ipsa sunt, quod cum illis exu- renda sit. Quæ quum omnino exurenda conce- dat Grotius, cur de elementis idem non dicen- dum, siquidem communi verbo postmodum ista omnia dicantur λυόμενα v, 11. ac peculiariter de cœlis v. 12. ὀυρανοὶ πυρούμενοι λυθήσονται; de elemen- tis τὰ στοιχεῖα καυσούμενα καήσεται. Temere ergo Pontificii superiorem aëris regionem excipiunt: de qua ita nugantur, interprete Barradio l. IX. comm. in Evang. Conc. cap. XI. p. 592. Quæritur quousque ignis sit ascensurus? Respondet glossa interlinearis 2. Petr. III. his verbis, tantum ascen- dit ignis judicii, quantum ascendit aqua diluvii. Ascendit autem aqua diluvii quindecim cubitis super montes, Genes. VII. Totidem ascendet ignis. Glossa ordinaria 2. Thess. I. Ignis erit in mundo, qui præcedet Christum, tantum spatium occupans, quantum occupavit aqua in diluvio. Eadem est Magistri & Scholasticorum sententia : Quis vero dictavit Glossatoribus ista & Magistro ? Si ele- menta omnia igne peribunt, quomodo excipie- tur aëris suprema regio ? Tirinus de superiori re- gione aëris ita philosophatur ibidem, sine ullo DEI Verbo : Cæli aërei tam spissis nubibus, tam horrendis tonitribus, fulgetris, cometis, stellis ca- dentibus, aliisque meteoris, procellis, tempestatibus perturbabuntur, ut ipsi etiam supremi cæli ardere, & e suis cardinibus convelli, subrui & evanescere videantur. Quid vero illa perturbatio, quam so- mniant ad aëreorum cælorum conflagrationem vel dissolutionem & destructionem ? Elementa vero, ignis puta, inferior aëris regio terræ vicina, & aqua seu maria calore, id est, æstu & ardore sol- ventur, id est, vi ignis extenuabuntur, & quasi au- rum in conflatorio liquabuntur, ut ab iis separen- tur vapores, exhalationes & fæces omnes eis jam permixtæ : ita S. Thomas & alii Doctores. Abfu- metur ergo, quicquid in aëre est, materia inflam- mabilis, in mari, quicquid terrenum est, concre- tum vel mixtum. Contra Ribera ad Apoc. XXI. aquam post finem mundi non fluidam fore dicit, sed consolidatam & instar sphæræ conglobatam. Ast Apostolus non de extenuatione vel absum- ptione materiæ inflammabilis in aëre, non de terrenæ materiæ in aqua separatione, vel de ma- ris concretione, sed de aëris & aquæ destructio- ne agit. Et in Apocal. XXI. vers. 1. dicitur de mari, ἡ θάλασσα ὐκ ἔτι. Barradius l. X. conc. cap. 1. pag. 611. Aqua, inquit, in novo mundo erit sicut crystallus, aër ut cælum, ignis ut lumi- naria mundi. Ast ubi talia scripta sunt? Annon clare dicitur, mare non futurum amplius ? Cæ- lum novum & terram novam, inquit, Primasius & Beda ad Apoc. XXI. vers. 1. non autem & mare novum futurum legimus.

De igne Gregor. de Valentia Tom. IV. Comm. in Thom. pag. 2276. hariolatur : Verisimile est, ignem, quo terra conflagrabit, ascensurum ad sphæ- ram suam naturalem. Ignis, qui erit in sphæra sua naturali, cum ibi non habeat admixtas qua- litates alienas, non alterabitur, ab igne illo confla- grationis, sed tantum reliqua elementa, & ignes ali- qui, qui in inferioribus locis tunc reperientur im- puri. Sed illa de sphæra ignis naturali sub con- cavo Lunæ in natura fundamentum nullum ha- bent. Neque an ignis naturalis aut elementaris vel qualis denique sit futurus ille mundi devora- torius, vel πανολέθριος ignis, ulli mortalium con- stat: Non enim aliqua tantum elementa, sed in- definite elementa consumptum iri igne isto Apo- stolus innuit: tum ubi ignis pabulum nullum ha- bet, ipse etiam extinguitur & perit, si ita philo- sophari lubeat. Tutius autem est cum Scriptura totius universi interitum asserere, quam partes aliquas pro lu- bitu excipere. Interitum certe ignis & aquæ non Beda tantum, sed Lorino fatenti Andreas Cæsa- riensis, Aretes, Anshelmus, Haymo, & Rupertus in Apoc. XXI. accedunt. Elementa omnia post re- surrectionem & judicium de medio tollit Philip- pus Solitarius Dioptr. c. 6. 7. Injurius autem in divinam omnipotentiam est Estius, cum ait, disso- lutum iri elementa, quorum dissolutionem in ma- teriam primam esse impossibilem; quum ne qui- dem omnimoda eorum destructio impossibilis credenda, imo asserenda sit etiam. Ineptiæ Papi- starum de cruce Christi aliisque instrumentis pas- sionis ejus in æternum servandis indigna confu- tatione sunt : Si quis ea nosse cupiat, B. Gerhar- dum in h. l. & de Consummatione Seculi, ut & Harim. Evang. c. 161. adeat.

PARS II. Adhortatio ad præparationem ad adven- tum Domini.

## 3:11
Vers. 11.

Τούτων ὧν πάντων λυομένων) If God does not spare these such beautiful works, how much less the impious?

Ποταποὺς δεῖ ὑπάρχειν ὑμᾶς ἐν ἁγίαις ἀναστροφαῖς καὶ εὐσε- βείαις) Ποταπὸς is something more than ποῖος. For it is said of excellent things, Matt. VIII. 27. Mark XIII. 1. Luke I. 29. VII. 39. 1 John III. 1. ἀναστροφὴ and εὐσέβεια are accustomed to be said in the singular. But it is the custom of the Hebrews to give plurals to all such nouns. And so they say צדקות חמים and the like.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Τούτων ὧν πάντων λυομένων) Si istis tam pulchris operi- bus Deus non parcit, quanto minus impiis?

Ποταποὺς δεῖ ὑπάρχειν ὑμᾶς ἐν ἁγίαις ἀναστροφαῖς καὶ εὐσε- βείαις) Ποταπὸς est aliquid plus quam ποῖος. Dicitur enim de rebus eximiis, Matth. VIII. 27. Marc. XIII. 1. Luc. I. 29. VII. 39. 1. Joh. III. 1. ἀναστροφὴ & εὐσέβεια solent singulariter dici. Sed Ebræorum mos est omnibus talibus nominibus dare plurales. Itaque dicunt צדקות חמים & similia.

## 3:12
Vers. 12.

Looking for and hastening the coming of the day of God) Expecting & desiring. Thus σπεύδω τὸ σὸν ἀγαθὸν in Thucydides, see also 2 Macc. IX. 14. The day of God is the same as that of Christ. For in Christ God will show himself.

This present tense is used for the future, λυομένων for λυσομένων, on account of the certainty, and because it is imminent, and the dissolution of τούτων πάντων, of all those things which he had named, of the heavens, of the elements specifically of the earth, and of all its works, is as it were already beginning. However, as regards others, a zeal for holiness or justice is required; as regards God, piety; as regards ourselves, vigilance, and therefore sobriety and chastity, so that we may expect, nay, hasten as if to meet it with prayers, desires, and fitting preparation, Luke XII. 35, Tit. II. 13. That σπεύδοντας is not 'accelerating,' as Erasmus rendered it, but 'hastening,' so that by the ellipsis of the preposition εἰς, it is 'unto the coming,' just as the wise virgins went out with lamps to meet the bridegroom, Matt. XXV. 1. For a transitive meaning does not occur in the New Testament: see Luke II. 16, ch. XIX. 5, 6, Acts XX. 16, ch. XXII. 18. But the day is called of God, not because God will show himself in Christ, but because Christ is God blessed for ever over all, Rom. IX. 5. And since mention is always made in the Scriptures of one day, which is the last day, the day of the Lord, and in which the judgment is to be held, the opinion of the Mahometans concerning the space of fifty thousand years in which the judgment is to be celebrated, is deservedly to be exploded.

Estius seeks the force of the Apostolic argument from the burning up of the works on the earth, by which he understands sins, but wrongly: as if he were exhorting the faithful that, since all these things are to be dissolved, they should apply themselves to holy conversations and pieties as if to heavenly works, expecting and hastening unto the coming of that day, and as if, should they act otherwise, their works as if earthly would be burned up together with the earth, and they themselves would perish, or at least suffer loss. But sins are not called works on the earth, much less can they be burned, nor do they pertain to the system of the world, which is what is treated here, because he descends from heaven to the elements and finally to the works on the earth. The passage 1 Cor. III is indeed irrelevant, because there the discourse is about the fire of temptation: nor does that connection deserve the approval of Estius. The world, which was created for our sake, will be dissolved by fire, will be purged, will be renewed, so that it may become a receptacle for us, that is, for the elect and the just; how much therefore does it behoove us to be pure and holy, so that we may be received into that dwelling-place. For neither is the renewal of the world to be admitted, since a new world is rather to be expected, much less is it to be believed that the world is to be renewed for the end that the elect may dwell in the same: but least of all does our spiritual renewal contribute to this. For what commerce or analogy has that spiritual renewal of man, which is a new creature in Christ, with the renewal of the material world?

The reason for the connection, however, is this: since the whole world is to perish, and God alone with the holy angels, besides men, is to remain eternally, that we ought not to cling to worldly things, much less to be devoted to the vices that are in the world, as they draw us away from God, but rather to devote ourselves solely to the true and eternal God in true faith and piety, so that we may enjoy his eternal communion when heaven and earth shall pass away, and may be able to rejoice eternally in the company of the holy Angels after the destruction of all other creatures, 1 Cor. 7:29, 1 John 2:15, 17. Therefore it is established, says Gregory of Nazianzus in his tract on the life of travelers, that all things of this life are uncertain and unstable, so that we may burn with love and desire for firm and stable things. And since, as Augustine says in Epistle 21, on the same day that the world is to be destroyed, Christ is to come for judgment, and we are all to be stationed before his tribunal, let us therefore live in the true fear of God, and serve him in holiness and justice. Thus Lorinus on this passage. The Apostle urges from these words an exhortation that we prepare ourselves for the judgment which we await, quickly and zealously, certain that God will not spare sinners, who has determined to purge (or more correctly, to destroy) even the senseless creatures that are devoid of reason, because of some stain contracted in a way from the sins of men, by a general conflagration. We must hasten, however, to meet the Lord, as if we look to this one thing, and do this one thing. This is that one thing truly necessary: this is the best thing, which we should choose, Luke 10, last chapter, 21, verse 36.

By reason of which,) namely, the parousia. Through that supreme power of God, which will show itself on that day, that is, at that time.

The heavens being on fire shall be dissolved) the heavens, the air and the ether, the two heavens. Being on fire, melted by fire, as metals are accustomed to be melted. צרופים, 1 Sam. 20:31, Ps. 12:7, Isa. 1:25, Dan. 12:9, Zech. 13:9, and elsewhere.

And the elements being on fire shall melt) Here, under the name of elements, the earth can also be included. They shall melt, they will flow away like wax, Mic. 1:4. In Isaiah 64:1, הרים נזלו is translated 'the mountains shall melt'.

St. Peter again inculcates the destruction of both the heavens and all the elements, so that he might the more establish the consummation of the universe, which philosophy persuaded us would endure forever, and, with the material parts of the heaven and earth destroyed, might assign a new heaven and a new earth to the elect, different in their entire nature. He says that the heavens, to which the air cannot be referred, as it is included under the elements, are not to be melted, but consumed or destroyed by fire. For this is what 'being on fire they shall be dissolved' means. If they were to be melted like metals, they would not be destroyed. For we said at verse 10 that the word 'to dissolve' implies destruction. 'Being on fire' means kindled and inflamed by fire, just as the elements are said to be 'burning' or about to blaze with the heat of fire. 'They shall melt' certainly means to liquefy, like wax brought near a fire. The Vulgate rendered it 'wasting away'. Augustine, book 20, On the City of God, chapter 18, they shall be boiled down; it is also rendered by כלה, 'it has ceased entirely, it has failed', Job 11:20, chapter 17:5; for תכלינה, 'it was consumed', Ezek. 24:10, which meanings are most appropriate here: because in verse 10 it is said of the heavens that 'they shall pass away', here the manner is expressed, they shall perish and be consumed by the burning of fire, which is added so that no one might think that while the earth and all the elements are to perish by fire, the heaven will be immune from the conflagration of fire: which total consummation is also confirmed by the introduction of a new heaven and a new earth. For it is not a renovated heaven, but a new one, not an improvement of the earth, but a completely new earth, and one most different from the former, that is promised to the elect. But St. Peter, or the entire Scripture, does not hint by any word that the just are to be purged by a destructive fire, as the Papists, Salmero, and others on this passage wish: for such spiritual purging, material fire does nothing; but there is need of the fire of the Holy Spirit and faith, Matt. 3:11, Acts 15:9, and the clean water of baptism, Zech. 13:1, Heb. 10:22, 1 Cor. 6:11, and the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, 1 Pet. 1:2. Which purging, indeed, happens perpetually in the Church, and is not to happen finally at the end of the world, much less after the resurrection: which opinion Lorinus refutes in some of the Fathers: 'It is against all reason,' he says, 'that the just, already raised, should in any way feel fire, since they are already blessed, or have deserved no punishment, or have satisfied for it before the resurrection.' Therefore, the opinion of Joseph Acosta, book 4, On the Last Things, page 639, cannot be proven. I think that the wicked will burn in that fire which will precede the face of the judge already descending, as it rages everywhere; and that the upright and just will indeed be purged, if any stain has settled upon them, as the Apostle insinuates in 1 Cor. 3, but not that they will be killed. Salmero certainly maintains that this purging will happen before the resurrection, and will contribute to the glorious resurrection and a greater merit of the eternal crown. Estius refers that fire to the purging of the world, along with most others, not to the elect. What of the fact that some, according to Estius, teach that the fire of the world's conflagration will arise only after the universal judgment is finished, by which the world is then renewed, and the impious, caught up, are dragged into the depths to be tormented?

Although Estius says that the common opinion, and the one more conformable to Scripture, is that that fire will precede the judgment, by which the human race, which will remain from the preceding plagues, will be consumed and perish, and at the same time the purging and renovation of the world will take place, so that the elect, with their bodies raised to immortality, may be introduced into the new world, which fire, however, is to remain during the judgment until it drags the impious with it into the depths: yet how that opinion is more conformable to Scripture does not appear. as much on account of the hypotheses which he introduces, which are purely precarious, about which there is nothing in Scripture, such as the all-consuming fire (πανολεθρίῳ), that this same fire is the one by which the impious will be tormented in hell, about the world being renewed and purged, about men who will perish by fire, who will survive alive on the last day, about the elect being resurrected and introduced into a renewed and purged world, about the fire remaining during the judgment, about the fire consuming the impious first, and after they are resurrected dragging them with it into the underworld (but how indeed will that fire not consume when it drags away, since it is about to consume all things, or how will the dragging away of the impious be consistent with fire?), as well as on account of the order of these last things, which Scripture has not defined, which is rather designated by Augustine in book XX of The City of God in such a way God, chapter 14, that the judgment precedes, and the consummation of the universe follows: After the judgment is finished, he says, then this heaven and this earth will cease to be, when the new heaven and the new earth will begin to be: compare also chapters 16, 18, and 30, where however he seems to prefer to withhold judgment. For although it might perhaps be said not inappropriately that the judgment is to be administered before the universe is yet consumed, so that the creatures may first be as it were witnesses of how they had to serve the abuse of the sons of men; just as St. Peter also says that the heaven and earth are reserved for the day of judgment and the destruction (ἀπώλειαν) of impious men; verse 7. On the other hand, however, the heaven is said to be about to pass away when the day of the Lord is to come as a thief, and the heavens and elements are to be destroyed by the presence of the Lord: unless it be said that the beginning of the shaking of the heavens and elements will indeed precede, and the resurrection of the dead and the snatching away of the elect to meet the Lord, but the conflagration and the total consummation of the universe will follow finally, not only after the resurrection, but also after the final judgment. And in that sense we admit that statement of Augustine, ch. 18: After the judgment is finished, the world will burn, which he himself explains in ch. 38 concerning the total conflagration. After Christ's judgment, I believe the resurrection of the dead (which will precede it) and the separation of the good and the bad will be followed by the conflagration of the world. To B. Gerhard it seems more probable that the extreme judgment will precede the total conflagration of the world itself: yet that this will happen before the impious are thrust into hell and the pious are raised into heaven: Vol. VIII. de Noviss. in gen. §. 11. & 13.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Προσδοκῶντας καὶ σπεύδοντας τὴν παρουσίαν τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμέρας) Expectantes & optantes. Sic σπεύδω τὸ σὸν ἀγα- θὸν apud Thucydidem, vide & 2. Macc. IX. 14. Dei dies eadem, quæ Christi. Nam in Christo ostendet se Deus.

Præsens hoc pro futuro λυομένων pro λυσομέ- νων ponitur ob certitudinem, & quod immineat, & quasi jam incipiat dissolutio τούτων πάντων il- lorum omnium, quæ nominarat, cælorum, ele- mentorum in specie terræ, & operum ejus omni- um. Requiritur autem quoad alios studium san- ctitatis vel justitiæ, quoad Deum pietas, quoad nos vigilantia, adeoque sobrietas & castitas, ut ex- pectemus, imo properemus velut in occursum precibus, desideriis, ac decenti præparatione, Luc. XII. 35. Tit. II. 13. Illud σπεύδοντας non acce- lerantes est, ut Erasmus reddidit, sed properantes, ut ellipsi sit Præpositionis εἰς, in adventum, uti virgines sapientes cum lampadibus obviam ive- runt sponso, Matth. XXV. 1. Transitiva enim signi- ficatio in Novo Testamento non occurrit: Vid. Luc. II. 16. cap. XIX. 5. 6. Act. XX. 16. cap. XXII. 18. Dicitur autem dies τοῦ Θεοῦ, non quod in Christo se ostendet Deus, sed quod Christus sit Deus be- nedictus in secula super omnia, Rom. IX. 5. Et quum unius diei mentio semper fiat in Scripturis, qui dies novissimus, dies Domini, & in quo judicium habendum, sententia Mahumetanorum de spatio quinquaginta millium annorum, quo celebran- dum judicium, merito explodenda est.

Argumenti Apostolici vim Estius petit ab ope- rum in terra exustione, per quæ intelligit pecca- ta, sed perperam: quasi hortetur fideles, ut quo- niam hæc omnia dissolvenda sunt, sanctis conver- sationibus & pietatibus tanquam operibus cœle- stibus incumbant, expectantes & properantes in adventum illius diei, ac si secus egerint, opera eorum velut terrena simul cum terra exurantur, & ipsi pereant, vel certe detrimentum patiantur. Sed peccata non dicuntur opera in terra, multo minus comburi possunt, aut ad Systema mundi pertinent, de quo hic agitur, quia cœlo ad elementa & de- nique ad opera in terra descendit. Locus vero 1. Cor. III. ἀλλότριος est, quia illic de igne tenta- tionis sermo est: Neq; illa συνέχεια Estii calculum meretur. Mundus, qui nostri causa conditus est, incendio solvetur, purgabitur, innovabitur, ut no- strum, hoc est electorum & justorum fiat recepta- culum, quantum igitur nos ipsos, ut in habitacu- lum illud recipiamur, puros & sanctos esse conve- nit. Nam nec innovatio mundi admittenda, quum novus mundus expectandus potius sit, nedum eo fine innovandus mundus credendus, ut electi in eodem habitent: minime vero omnium huc facit spiritualis nostra innovatio. Quid enim ille spi- ritualis hominis ἀνακαίνωσις, quæ est nova crea- tura in Christo, cum mundi materialis innovatio- ne commercii aut analogiæ habet?

Ratio autem connexionis hæc est: quum mundus universus interiturus sit, solus Deus cum S.
