Angelis præter homines æternum maneat, non debere nos adhærere rebus mundanis, nedum vitiis, quæ in mundo sunt, deditos esse, utpote quæ a Deo abs- trahunt, sed unice vero & æterno Deo nos dede- re in vera fide ac pietate, ut æterna ejus commu- nione, cum cœlum & terra transibunt, frui san- ctorum Angelorum societate post omnium alia- rum creaturarum interitum æternum gaudere possimus, 1. Cor. VII. 29. 1. Joh. II. 15. 17. Ideo con- stitutum est, inquit Gregorius Nazianzenus tract. de vit. itiner. ut res omnes hujus vitæ incertæ sint, ac instabiles, ut rerum firmarum stabiliumǫ; amo- re ac desiderio inardescamus. Et cum, dicente Augustino epist. XXI. eodem die, quo mundus destruendus, Christus ad judicium sit venturus, & omnes ad tribunal ejus sistendi simus, ideo in vero DEI timore vivamus, in sanctitate & justitia ipsi serviamus. Ita Lorinus in h. l. Urget Apo- stolus ex dictis hortationem, ut nos ad judicium, quod expectamus, propere ac studiose compa- remus, certi, non parciturum peccatoribus Deum, qui sensus etiam creaturas expertes ob nescio quam quodammodo ex hominum peccatis labem contractam purgare (rectius destruere) constitue- rit exustione generali. Properandum autem in oc- cursum Domini, quasi hunc unum spectemus, hoc unum agamus. Hoc est unum illud vere neces- sarium: hoc optimum, quod eligamus Luc. X. ult. cap. XXI. vers. 36.

Δι' ἧν,) nempe παρουσίαν. Per illam summam Dei vim, quæ illo die, id est, illo tempore se ostendet.

Οὐρανοὶ πυρούμενοι λυθήσονται) οὐρανοὶ aër & æther, duo cœli. Πυρούμενοι fusi igne, ut metalla fundi solent. צרופים, 1. Sam. XX. vers. 31. Psal. XII. 7. Es. I. 25. Dan. XII. vers. 9. Zach. XIII. vers. 9. & alibi.

Καὶ στοιχεῖα καυσόμενα τακήσεται) Hic sub nomine ele- mentorum etiam terra comprehendi potest. Τακήσονται diffluent ut cera, Mich. I. 4. Apud Esaiam LXIV. vers. 1. הרים נזלו vertitur ὄρη τακήσεται.

Iterum inculcat S. Petrus cum cœlorum, tum elementorum omnium destructionem, ut eo ma- gis consummationem universi, quod in æternum duraturum Philosophia persuadebat, adstrueret, & destructis universi partibus materialibus cœli & terræ, novum cœlum & novam terram electis assignaret, toto genere diversam. Cœlos, ad quos aër referri nequit, utpote sub elementis compre- hensus, non fundendos dicit, sed incendio con- summandos vel destruendos. Nam hoc est πυρό- μενοι λυθήσονται. Si ut metalla funderentur, non destruerentur. Nam verbum λύειν destructionem inferre ad v. 10. diximus, Πυρούμενοι est igne accensi & inflammati, quemadmodum & elementa καυ- σόμενα exarsura vel ardore ignis exæstuatura di- cuntur. Τακήσεται sane est liquefcient, instar ceræ igni admotæ. Vulgatus reddidit tabescens. Augu- stinus l. XX. de Civ. DEI cap. 18. decoquentur, redditur autem etiam per כלה omnino cessavit, defecit, Job. XI. 20. cap. XVII. 5. pro תכלינה con- sumptus fuit Ezech. XXIV. 10. quæ significatio- nes hic maximè conveniunt: quia vers. 10. de cœlis dicitur παρελεύσονται, hic modus exprimi- tur, ignis exustione peribunt & consumenttur, quod additur, ne quis censeat, terram quidem & ele- menta omnia igne peritura, cœlum vero a con- flagratione ignis immune futurum: quam tota- lem consummationem etiam firmat novi cœli & novæ terræ introductio. Non enim cœlum reno- vatum, sed novum, non melioratio terræ, sed prorsus nova terra, & a priori cum maxime di- versa electis promittitur. Igne autem πανολεθρίῳ justos purgandos, quod Papistæ volunt, Salmero, & alii in h. l. nullo verbo innuit S. Petrus, vel Scriptura universa: ad quam spiritualem purga- tionem ignis materialis nihil facit; sed igne Spi- ritus Sancti & fide opus est, Matth. III. 11. Act. XV. 9. & aqua munda baptismi Zach. XIII. v. 1. Ebr. X. 22. 1. Cor. VI. 11. ac ῥαντισμῷ sanguinis Christi, 1. Petr. I. 2. Quæ vero purgatio in Eccle- sia fit perpetuo, non sub finem mundi demum futura est, nedum post resurrectionem: quam sententiam in Patribus nonnullis refellit Lorinus: Jam suscitatos justos, inquit, contra omnem ratio- nem est ignem ullo modo sentire, cum jam sint bea- ti, vel nullam pœnam meruerint; vel ei satisfece- rint ante resurrectionem. Probari ergo non potest Josephi Acostæ sententia l. IV. de noviss. temp. pag. 639. Illo igne, qui faciem judicis jam descen- dentis præcedet, ubique grassante, sceleratos arsuras puto; probos & justos purgandos quidem, si quid la- bis insederit, ut insinuat Apostolus 1. Cor. III. sed non necandos. Salmero certe ante resurrectionem eam purgationem futuram statuit, & facturam ad gloriosam resurrectionem, ac majus meritum coronæ æternæ. Estius ad mundum purgandum ignem illum refert cum plerisque aliis, non ad electos. Quid? quod doceant nonnulli apud Estium, ignem conflagrationis mundi peracto de- mum universali judicio oriturum esse, quo & mundus tunc innovetur, & impii involuti in tar- tara rapiantur cruciandi.

Quanquam vero Estius communem sententiam & Scripturæ conformiorem dicat, ignem illum an- tecessurum esse judicium, quo genus humanum, quod à plagis præcedentibus reliquum erit, consumptum intereat, simul & mundi purgatio ac renovatio fiat, ut in novum mundum electi resuscitatis ad im- mortalitatem suis corporibus introducantur, qui tamen ignis durante judicio sit permansurus, donec impios in tartara secum abripiat: ea tamen sen- tentia quomodo Scripturæ conformior sit, non apparet: tam propter hypotheses, quas admiscet, mere precarias, de quibus nihil in Scriptura, ut- pote de igne πανολεθρίῳ, quod idem ille sit ignis, quo cruciabuntur impii in inferno, de mundo innovando & purgando, de hominibus igne interi- turis, qui vivi supererunt in die novissimo, de electis resuscitandis in mundum renovatum & pur- gatum introducendis, de igne durante judicio per- mansuro, de igne absumpturo primum impios, & post resuscitatos in tartara secum abrepturo (quo- modo vero ignis ille non consumet, quando ab- ripiet, qui omnia consumpturus est, aut quomo- do igni conveniet abreptio impiorum?) tum pro- pter istorum novissimorum ordinem, quem Scri- ptura non definivit, qui potius ita ab Augusti- no l. XX. de Civ. Dei cap. 14. designatur, ut an- tecedat judicium, & sequatur consummatio uni- versi: Peracto, inquit, judicio tunc esse desinet hoc cœlum & hæc terra, quando incipiet esse cœlum no- vum & terra nova: conf. & cap. XVI. XVIII. & XXX. ubi tamen τὸ ἐπέχειν præstare videtur. Nam etsi non inconcinne forte dici possit, universo nondum consummato judicium administrandum, ut creaturæ quasi testaturæ primum sint, quomo- do ad abusum servire debuerint filiis hominum; quemadmodum etiam AD DIEM judicii, & ἀπώλειαν impiorum hominum cœlum & terram τηρημένυς dicit S. Petrus; vers. 7. ab altera tamen parte cœlum transiturum dicitur, cum venturus est dies Domini, ut fur, & per præsentiam Do- mini destruendi cœli & elementa: nisi dicatur, ini- tium quidem concussionis cœlorum & elementorum, præcessurum, & resurrectionem mortuorum & ob- reptionem electorum in occursum Domini, con- flagrationem autem & consummationem universi omnimodam sequuturam demum, non modo post refuscitationem, sed & post judicium novissimum. Atque eo sensu admittimus illud Augustini c. 18. Post factum judicium mundus ardebit, quod ipse cap. 38. de totali conflagratione explicat. Post Christi judicium, mortuorum resurrectionem (quæ præcedet) bonorum malorumque direm- ptionem existimo seqvuturam mundi conflagra- tionem. B. Gerhardo probabilius videtur, quod judicium extremum antecessurum sit ipsam mundi conflagrationem totalem : hanc tamen prius futu- ram, quam impii in infernum detrudantur, & pii in cælum evehantur: Tom. VIII. de Noviss. in gen. §. 11. & 13.

## 3:13
Verse 13.

And we look for a new heaven and a new earth according to his promise) that is, a new universe. For the Hebrews are accustomed to express this with the names of heaven and earth, as we said at Gen. I. 1. See also Gen. II. 1. Ps. XXXIII. 6. CXXIV. 8. CXLVI. verse 6. Acts XIV. 15. XVII. 14. Rev. XXI. 1. There will be a pure earth in a pure heaven, as Plato says in the Phaedo, whom Origen follows in VII against Celsus. From the remains of the ancient mass a better one will rise. Irenaeus in the fragments: The substance, nor the essence of the creation is destroyed, that is, the matter, the forest has not perished. Thus also Eusebius explains Plato in XI of the Preparation. See the responses to the orthodox XCIV. XCV. Tertullian in the Apologeticus: He says that philosophers differ on whether this world is to pass away or to remain. In the Manuscript it is not according to his promise, but according to his promises. We look for not only a new world, but also those great promises of Christ, the resurrection of bodies and eternal life. Thus you have promises in Eph. II, verse 12. Heb. VI. 17. and elsewhere. Nor does the Latin read otherwise here.

What he understands by a new universe, whether he wishes the system of heaven and earth to be renewed including in heaven the stars and planets, both fixed and wandering, and on earth brute animals, or at least vegetative things, trees, plants, herbs, he does not explain. There were those who said that the earthly Paradise was to be reserved for the other age, not only Moses Bar-Cepha in his book on Paradise, ch. 18, excepting it from the fire of the conflagration; but also certain more recent Papists, who asserted that it was destined for little children for all eternity; whom Lorinus and Cornelius contradict. Tirinus in this place says: B. Anselm (in Elucidar.), William of Paris in Dionysius (in IV. dist. 49.), Pico della Mirandola. (in Heptapl.) Abulensis (in Matt. XXV. q. 542. 548.), Cajetan, Salmero, a Lapide, and Serarius (in Judith XVI. q. 2.) judge that infants who died without baptism will have their dwelling on the earth, which they say will be perpetually adorned again with new and never-fading fragrant flowers, gems, trees, fountains, and other ornaments. For from what place will those little children be able to contemplate the Sun, the heavens, the stars, the sea, and other created things better and more conveniently, so that from them they may rise to loving and praising God, and pass their life without sorrow, weariness, or idleness eternally? See also Vasquez in 2. disp. 34. c. 3. and Lessius de attrib. Div. l. XIII. 23. cap. Cornelius produced similar earthly and childish thoughts here at greater length, that not only is the earth to be adorned with new beauty, purity, and brightness, so that it is as it were glorified along with the saints whom it served, and delights their eyes and minds; but that also those infants, when they resume their bodies on the day of judgment, because the limbo of children will not hold their bodies, will have a convenient place on earth: to receive the punishment of loss (the lack of the beatific vision), not of sense, to be perfected in intellect, will, and other faculties of nature; which and other trifles, more vain than Sicilian nonsense, can be read there. Add that at Rev. XXII. 2, the same Cornelius, following the Scholastics and other Doctors of his, places such things in heaven itself and assigns to the blessed what he himself with Tirinus attributes to infants who died without baptism on the new earth. For the blessed, he says, will be in the Empyrean heaven, as if in a most sweet and happy ether, which therefore, like our air, can be cut and divided (lest the Blessed be as if compacted in it like a wall), teaches St. Thomas in 2. d. 2. q. 4. a. 2; Richard in 4. d. 49. q. 4. a. 3. indeed St. Basil, Ambrose, Damascenus, whom I cited at Gen. I. v. 6. and Sebastian Barradius Vol. III. l. 10. and others. Finally, all teach that the senses of the Blessed will have their own proper and wonderful pleasures and delights, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, in heaven, St. Thomas, Scotus, D. Soto, Henricus, Major, and others, whom Suarez cites and follows in 3. p. tom. 2. diss. 47. in the last section, and Johannes Salas 1. 2. q. 5. art. 5. tract. 2. diss. 14. sect. 14. This is what the Psalmist sighed for: I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. Wherefore these trees and fruits can be taken literally, as they sound. For what stands in the way? For if Adam enjoyed them twice in the earthly Paradise, much more will the Blessed enjoy them in the heavenly Paradise: for the earthly one was a specimen and image of this. But why does Cornelius not also add brute animals, which Lucas Trelcatius also referred to the other age, and which are more worthy? But let us leave those inventions and earthly delights, which Papists dream of in the other age in the manner of Jews and Mahometans, to them: which things, however, conflict diametrically with the total consummation of the universe. And therefore Bellarmine, lib. VI. de amiss. grat. & stat. pecc. c. 6, denies that there will be plants on the new earth. For, as the Theologian Doctors, he says, teach by common consent, after the day of judgment there will be no plants, no animals, no mixed bodies, with the exception of humans only: and Thomas in Addit. quest. 91. art. 5. Plants and animals belong to the perfection of the universe according to this state of mutability, not according to the state of newness. Nor could that opinion of Catharinus and Salmeron concerning the earthly Paradise of unbaptized infants, which has been listed among errors by Cocceius, be proven by Bellarmine in the place cited, or by Cocceius in part 2, Thesis, book 10, question 2, page 1047.

Although Scripture, when it speaks of the present age, expresses the whole universe by the name of heaven and earth, it is not therefore to be concluded that when it deals with the future age, a new universe is designated by the name of a new heaven and a new earth. For it speaks of heavenly things using phrases taken from worldly things, which, however, are not to be understood in a worldly manner. Furthermore, neither Plato, nor Origen or anyone else where he follows Plato, deserves to be heard here. For Plato and his followers did indeed receive something from the Church concerning the mysteries of the faith, but they wrapped them in the figments of their own philosophy, so that Scripture is not to be explained from Plato, but Platonic dogmas are to be corrected from Scripture: just as Theophilus of Alexandria observes in book 1 against the Gentiles: that the Gentiles perceived some things from the school of the Patriarchs in Egypt; and Theophilus of Antioch in book 2 to Autolycus. Regarding the conflagration of the world, they say, the philosophers, whether they like it or not, agree with the Prophets: although with respect to time they are much younger here; yet they have stolen these things from the Law and the Prophets. Whence Plato, says Justin Martyr in his first exhortation to the Greeks, having conceived an opinion about the dissolution of the heaven, wrote thus: Did he not think that this very thing which he perceived from the sacred prophets was derived from them? Scripture, however, knows nothing of that fiction that a better world is to rise again from the remains of the old mass, and Grotius rightly observes that the philosophers themselves, as Tertullian notes, differ as to whether this world is to pass away or to remain. And the Fathers are no less divided in their opinions on that matter. disagree, and they do not subscribe to the assertion of Irenaeus, lib. V. adv. haeret. c. 36, that neither the subsistence nor the nature of the condition is destroyed, concerning which see B. Gerhardus de consummat. sec. §. 46.

But here we urge primarily the literal statement of Holy Scripture, which alone is to be heard in these matters, not only regarding the total destruction of heaven and earth, but also regarding the creation of a new heaven and a new earth, Is. 65:17, ch. 66:22. For as that creation differs greatly from a renovation, and heaven and earth are not said to be renovated or glorified with new beauty, but a new heaven and a new earth are to be created, and indeed in such a way that no memory of the old ones will remain. St. Peter also simply names new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness is to dwell. St. John saw a new heaven and a new earth, and that the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and that the sea was no more, Rev. 21:1. All of which, along with other things touched upon before and to be treated more fully elsewhere, substantially imply a new heaven and a new earth. By the introduction of a better heaven, says Justin, it is necessary that the firmament recently made be taken away, etc., in qq. & resp. ad Orthod. q. 44. Minutius Felix in Octavius: Who of the wise doubts, who is ignorant that the heaven with all things that are contained in heaven, so as they had begun, shall cease? Hilary, Can. XXVI. in Matth.: And so that there might be certain faith in future things, by saying Amen (Christ) adds the profession of truth, that our generation cannot pass away unless all these things have passed by, and those things which are considered firm, heaven and earth, shall not be, but his words cannot not be, because those things, from the condition of their creation, that is, having proceeded from nothing, have this of necessity in themselves, that they should not be: but these things, derived from eternity, contain this of power in themselves, that they should remain. Moreover, although a new heaven and a new earth are distinctly named, yet it is not one dwelling designated by the name of heaven and another by the name of earth, but Scripture speaks of the future in the manner of the present age: but it often names heaven without naming earth, yet in the same sense.

The words κατὰ τὸ αὐτοῦ ἐπάγγελμα are not to be questioned on account of the Grotius MS. But he who agrees with the Greek codices appeals in vain to the Latin, in the more approved copies, which Estius himself acknowledges. That in certain Latin codices it is read for 'according to his promises', and 'promises' is not read in the manuscripts which are with us, which are more approved, just as it is not read at all in the Greek texts existing today. Although we do not read that promise made to Christ in the days of Christ's flesh according to the letter, it was nevertheless made according to the διάνοια (thought) when, with heaven and earth destroyed, he promised the kingdom prepared for the elect ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου (from the foundation of the world) or from eternity, Matt. 25:34, which certainly is not rising again from the remains of the ancient mass as something better, it is not this whole universe renovated. And here are regarded the promises made by Christ's Spirit, who was in Isaiah, 1 Pet. 1:11, made in ch. 65:17, ch. 66:22.

Ἐν οἷς δικαιοσύνη κατοικεῖ (In which righteousness dwells). In that state there will be pure righteousness without vice: not as in this age, where the good are mixed with the bad. The parable in Matt. 13:39 and the passage in Matt. 25:31 look to this. In the manuscript it is ἐνοικεῖ, that is, ἐνοικήσει (it will dwell), it will be perpetually, as Rom. ch. 8:11, 2 Cor. ch. 6:16, 2 Tim. 1:14.

If righteousness is said to be placed in the abstract for the righteous, the excellence or perfection of righteousness will be designated, that the righteousness of the inhabitants of heaven is consummated: for abstract terms are wont to be put for concrete ones for the sake of excellence: but it can be understood as righteousness itself: namely, that nothing but righteousness dwells in the heavens. But the perpetuity is sufficiently implied by the present verb ἐνοικεῖ, namely, an eternal and continuous act; and therefore there is no need to establish that the present is put for the future on account of the certainty of the thing.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Καινὸς δὲ ὀρανὸς καὶ γῆν καινὴν κατὰ τὸ ἀυτᾶ ἐπάγγελμα προσδοκῶμεν) id est novum universum. Nam id Ebræi no- minibus cæli & terræ solent exprimere, ut diximus ad Gen. I. 1. Vid. & Gen. II. 1. Psal. XXXIII. 6. CXXIV. 8. CXLVI. vers. 6. Actor. XIV. 15. XVII. 14. Apoc. XXI. 1. Erit γῆ καθαρὰ ἐν καθαρῷ ὀρανῷ, ut ait Plato Phædone, quem sequitur Origenes VII. contra Celsum. Ex reliquiis molis antiquæ resurget melior. Irenæus in fragmentis : Οὐχ ἡ ὑπόστασις, ἐδὲ ἡ ὐσία τῆς κτίσεως ἀφανίζεται, id est materia, sylva non periit. Sic & Eusebius Platonem expli- cat XI. προπαρασκευῆς. Vide responsa ad orthodoxos XCIV. XCV. Tertullianus in Apologetico : Deceffurusne an man- surus sit hic mundus variare ait Philosophos. In Manu- scripto non est κατὰ τὸ ἀυτᾶ ἐπάγγελμα, sed κατὰ ἐπαγγέλ- ματα ἀυτᾶ. Expectamus non tantum orbem novum, sed & illa Christi promissa magna, resurrectionem corporum & vitam æternam. Sic ἐπαγγελίας habes Eph. II, vers. 12. Ebr. VI. 17. & alibi. Nec aliter hic legit Latinus.

Quid per novum universum intelligat, num in cœlo etiam sidera & stellas tum fixas, tum er- rantes, in terra animantia bruta, vel saltim vege- tativas res, arbores, plantas, herbas, cum systema- te cœli & terræ renovatum iri velit, non explicat. Fuerunt qui Paradisum terrenum alteri seculo reservandum dixere, non Moses Barcephe tantum in libr. de Parad. cap. 18. ab igne conflagratio- nis eundem excipiens; sed etiam Pontificii qui- dam recentiores, qui eundem parvulis destinatum in omnem æternitatem asseruere; quibus contra- dicunt Lorinus, & Cornelius. Tirinus in h. l. B. Anshelmus, inquit, (in Elucidar.) Wilhelmus Pa- riensis apud Dionys. (in IV. dist. 49.) Picus Mi- randulan. (in Heptapl.) Abulensis (in Matth. XXV. q. 542. 548.) Cajetanus, Salmero, a Lapi- de, & Serarius (in Judith. XVI. q. 2.) censent par- vulos sine baptismo defunctos habitationem suam habituros in terra, quam dicunt novis rursum & qui nunquam marcescent floribus odoriferis, gem- mis, arboribus, fontibus, aliisque ornamentis perpe- tuo decorandam. Ex quo enim loco poterunt par- vuli illi melius commodiusque contemplari Solem, cælos, astra, mare, cæteraque creata, ut ex iis ad Deum amandum laudandumque assurgant, & vitam sine mœrore, tædio, vel otio æternum transigant? Vide etiam Vasquez in 2. disp. 34. c. 3. & Lessium de attrib. Div. l. XIII. 23. cap. Similes terrenas & pueriles cogitationes prodidit hic Cornelius pro- lixius, quod non tantum terra novo decore, puri- tate, & fulgore ornanda sit, ut cum sanctis, quibus servivit, quasi glorificetur, eorumque oculos & mentes oblectet; sed quod etiam infantes isti, cum novis corpora in die judicii resumentes, quia cor- pora eorum limbus puerorum non capiet, in terra locum commodum habituri sint: excepturi pœnam damni (visionis beatificæ carentiam,) non sensus, perficiendi in intellectu, voluntate, aliisque natu- ræ facultatibus; quæ & aliæ nugæ gerris Siculis vaniores legi ibi possunt. Adde quod ad Apoc. XXII. 2. idem Cornelius e Scholasticis, aliisque suis Doctoribus in ipso cœlo talia collocet, ac bea- tis assignet, quæ in terra nova ipse cum Tirino infantibus sine baptismo defunctis tribuit. Erunt enim, inquit, beati in cœlo Empyreo, quasi in æthe- re suavissimo & felicissimo, quem proinde instar aëris nostri scindi & findi posse (ne Beatis in eo quasi in muro compacti sint) docet D. Thomas in 2. d. 2. q. 4. a. 2; Richard. in 4. d. 49. q. 4. a. 3. imo S. Basilius, Ambrosius, Damascenus, quos citavi Gen. I. v. 6. & Sebastian Barradius Tom. III. l. 10. & alii. Denique omnes sensus Beatorum proprias & mirificas voluptates & sua oblectamen- ta, quæ nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, in cœlo habituros docent D. Thomas, Scotus, D. Soto, Hein- ricus, Major, & alii, quos citant & sequuntur Suarez 3. p. tom. 2. diss. 47. sectione ultima, & Johannes Salas 1. 2. q. 5. art. 5. tract. 2. diss. 14. sect. 14. Hoc est, quod Psaltes suspirabat: Credo videre bona Domini in terra viventium. Quo- circa flavius hic arbores & poma ad literam, uti sonant, accipi possunt, Quid enim obstat? Nam si bis in Paradiso terrestri fruitus est Adam, mul- to magis iisdem fruentur Beati in Paradiso cœle- sti: Hujus enim specimen & imago fuit terrestris. Cur vero non etiam bruta animantia addit Cor- nelius, quæ Lucas Trelcatius etiam ad alterum se- culum retulit, quæque digniora sunt. Sed com- menta ista & delicias terrenas, quas Judæorum & Mahumetanorum more in altero seculo somni- ant Papistæ, ipsis relinquamus: Quæ vero cum totali consummatione universi pugnant e diame- tro. Ideoque Bellarminus lib. VI. de amiss. grat. & stat. pecc. c. 6. negat plantas futuras in nova terra. Nam, ut Theologi Doctores, inquit, commu- ni consensu docent, post diem judicii nulla erunt plantæ, nulla animalia, nulla corpora mixta, homi- nibus duntaxat exceptis: & Thomas in Addit. quæst. 91. art. 5. Plantæ & animalia sunt de perfectio- ne universi secundum statum istum mutabilitatis, non secundum statum novitatis. Neque probari potuit Bellarmino l. c. vel Coccejo part. 2. Thes. lib. 10. q. 2. p. 1047. illa Catharini opinio & Sal- meronis de Paradiso terrestri infantum non-bapti- zatorum, quæ inter errores a Coccejo relata est.

Etsi autem cum de præsenti seculo loquitur Scriptura, nomine cæli & terræ totum universum exprimat, non tamen ideo cum de seculo futuro agit, novi cæli & novæ terræ nomine novum uni- versum designari concludendum. Nam loquitur phrasibus a rebus mundanis desumptis de rebus cœlestibus, quæ vero non sunt more mundano accipiendæ. Porro nec Plato, nec ubi Platonem sequitur Origenes aut alius quisquam hic audiri meretur. Nam Plato cum suis ab Ecclesia aliquid de mysteriis fidei accepit quidem, sed figmentis propriæ suæ Philosophiæ ea involvit, ut non e Platone explicanda sit Scriptura; sed e Scriptura emendanda Platonica dogmata: quemadmodum Theophil. Alexandr. l. I. contra gentes observat: Gentiles ex schola Patriarcharum in Ægypto non- nulla percepisse; & Theophil. Antioch. l. II. ad Au- tolyc. Quoad conflagrationem mundi, inquiunt, nolentes volentes consentiunt Prophetis Philosophi: quamvis temporis respectu hic multo sint juniores; at- tamen ea ex lege & Prophetis suffurati sunt. Unde Plato, inquit Justinus Martyr in paræn. 1. ad Græc. de cœli dissolutione opinione concepta ita scripsit: Annon idipsum quod, ex sacris percepit vatibus atq́; ab ipsis sit hoc ductum esse arbitratus est? Scriptura vero de illo commento, quod ex reliquiis molis antiquæ melior resurrectura sit, nihil novit, & Philosophos ipsos, notante Tertulliano, decessurusne an man- surus sit hic mundus variare recte observat Gro- tius. Nec minus vero Patres ea de re in sententiis discrepant, neque Irenæi assertioni lib. V. adv. hæret. c. 36. nec subsistentia nec natura conditionis exterminatur, subscribunt omnes, de quo vid. B. Gerhardus de consummat. sec. §. 46.

Urgemus autem hic imprimis τὸ ῥητὸν Scripturæ Sacræ, quæ sola in his audienda, non solum qua omnimodam cœli & terræ destructionem, sed etiam qua novi cœli & novæ terræ creationem, Es. LV. 17. cap. LXVI. 22. Nam uti creatio illa ma- xime differt à renovatione, nec renovanda dicun- tur, aut novo decore glorificanda cœlum & ter- ra, sed novum cœlum & nova terra creanda, & quidem ita, ut veterum nulla superatura sit me- moria. S. Petrus etiam simpliciter novos cœ- los & novam terram nominat, in quibus habi- tatura sit justitia. S. Johannes vidit novum cœ- lum & terram novam, & cœlum primum ac terram primam transiisse, ac mare non fuisse amplius, Apoc. XXI. 1. Quæ omnia cum aliis antea tactis alibique plenius tractandis, substantialiter no- vum cœlum & novam terram innuunt. Inductione melioris cæli, inquit Justinus, recens facti firma- mentum tolli necesse est &c. in qq. & resp. ad Or- thod. q. 44. Minutius Felix in octav. Quis sapien- tum dubitat, quis ignorat cælum cum omnibus, quæ in cælo continentur, ita, ut cepissent desinere? Hi- larius Can. XXVI. in Matth. Atque ut fides certa esset futurorum, Amen dicendo professionem verita- tis adjicit (Christus) generationem nostram præ- terire non posse, nisi universa ista transcurrerint, ea- que, quæ firma existimantur, cælum & terra non fu- tura, verba autem sua non posse non esse, quia illa ex conditione creationis suæ, id est, profecta de nihi- lo, habeant id in se necessitatis, ut non sint: hæc autem ex æternitate deducta id in se contineant vir- tutis, ut maneant. Cæterum etsi distincte no- minetur novum cœlum & nova terra, non tamen aliud cœli, aliud terræ nomine designatur habi- taculum, sed more seculi præsentis de futuro lo- quitur Scriptura: sæpius autem cœlum nominat terra non nominata, eodem tamen sensu.

Verba κατὰ τὸ αὐτοῦ ἐπάγγελμα solicitanda ob Grotti MS. haud sunt. Ad Latinum autem frustra provocat, qui Græcis codicibus consen- tit, in probatioribus exemplaribus, quod agnoscit ipse Estius. Quod in Latinis quibusdam codi- cibus pro secundum promissa, legatur, & promissa, in Manuscriptis, quæ apud nos sunt, probatioribus non legitur, ut nec omnino in Græ- cis hodie extantibus. Promissum illud Christo etsi in diebus carnis Christi factum non legamus quoad literam, factum tamen quoad διάνοιαν cum cœlo & terra destructis regnum electis ἀπὸ κατα- βολῆς κόσμου vel ab æterno paratum pollicitus est, Matth. XXV. 34. quod certe non est ex reliquiis molis antiquæ resurgens melior, non est univer- sum hoc renovatum. Et respiciuntur hic promissa à Christi Spiritu', qui in Esaia erat, 1. Petr. I. 11. facta cap. XXV. 17. c. XXVI. 22.

Ἐν οἷς δικαιοσύνη κατοικεῖ In illo statu erit justitia pura si- ne vitio: non ut in hoc seculo, boni malis permixti. Huc spectat parabola, Matth. XIII. 39. & locus Matth. XXV. 3. In Manuscripto ἐνοικεῖ, id est, ἐνοικήσει, erit perpetuo, ut Rom. cap. VIII. vers. 11. 2. Corinth. cap. VI. vers. 16. 2. Tim. I. 14.

Si justitia in abstracto dicatur posita pro justis, excellentia vel perfectio justitiæ designabitur, quod consummata sit cœlicolarum justitia: Solent enim abstracta pro concretis poni excel- lentiæ causa: Sed intelligi potest ipsa justitia: quod nempe in cœlis nihil nisi justitia habitet. Satis autem præsenti verbo ἐνοικεῖ perpetuitas f innuitur, æternus nempe & continuus actus; id- eoque nec opus est statuere, præsens positum esse pro futuro ob rei certitudinem.

## 3:14
Vers. 14.

Διὸ ἀγαπητοὶ, ταῦτα προσδοκῶντες (Therefore, beloved, looking for these things)] Expecting such great rewards.

Σπουδάσατε ἄσπιλοι καὶ ἀμώμητοι αὐτῷ εὑρεθῆναι ἐν εἰρήνῃ (Be diligent to be found by him without spot and blameless in peace). In the manuscript it is ἄμωμοι, as in Eph. 1:4, 5:27, Col. 1:22, Jude v. 24, Rev. 14:5. Devote every effort that he himself (God, whose mention preceded) may find you without stains and vice, and that for your own good. Ἄσπιλοι καὶ ἄμωμοι is the opposite of what he said above, σπίλοι καὶ μῶμοι 2:13. And it is a mystical explanation of the laws concerning victims. See Jas. 1:27, Phil. 2:15, and the places already mentioned. Εὑρεθῆναι αὐτῷ, that is, παρ᾽ αὐτῷ, a manner of speaking familiar to Greeks and Latins. Thus Demosthenes: Τῶν ἐμοὶ πεπραγμένων (Of the things done by me). Ἐν εἰρήνῃ, that is, εἰς εἰρήνην (for peace), for your good, for your prosperity: לשלמכם.

From the destruction of heaven and earth the Apostle had drawn an exhortation to the pursuit of holiness and piety: now he draws a similar one from the promise of a new heaven and a new earth, as being those in which nothing but righteousness dwells. But it is not for us to depart from the proper meaning of the preposition ἐν (in). For the Apostle requires this primarily, that at the coming of Christ we may be found in peace, since the peacemakers are blessed, because they shall be called, that is, shall be, the children of God, Matt. 5:9, which external peace with one's neighbor, however, is presupposed by our peace or reconciliation with God, 2 Cor. 5:20, and the internal peace of conscience, Rom. 5:1. And therefore we must strive that we may be found in peace with God and neighbor.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Διὸ ἀγαπητοὶ, ταῦτα προσδοκῶντες] Tanta præmia exspe- ctantes.

Σπουδάσατε ἄσπιλοι καὶ ἀμώμητοι αὐτῷ εὑρεθῆναι ἐν εἰρήνῃ] In Manuscripto ἄμωμοι, quomodo Eph. I. 4. V. 27. Co- loss. I. 22. Judæ v. 24. Apoc. XIV. 5. Omnem date ope- ram, ut ipse (Deus, cujus præcessit mentio) vos reperiat sine sordibus vitioque, & id bono vestro. Ἄσπιλοι καὶ ἄμωμοι contrarium ei, quod supra dixit σπίλοι καὶ μῶμοι II. 13. Et est mystica explicatio legum de victimis. Vide Jac. I. 27. Phil. II. 15. & loca jam dicta. Εὑρεθῆναι αὐτῷ, id est, παρ᾽ αὐτῷ, loquendi genus Græcis ac Latinis familiare. Sic Demosthenes: Τῶν ἐμοὶ πεπραγμένων. Ἐν εἰρήνῃ, id est, εἰς εἰρήνην ad bonum vestrum, ad prosperitatem vestram: לשלמכם.

E cæli & terræ destructione adhortationem ad studium sanctitatis & pietatis deduxerat Apo- stolus: jam similem deducit è cæli novi & ter- ræ novæ promissione, utpote in quibus non nisi justitia habitat. Non est autem, ut discedamus à Præpositionis ἐν propria significatione. Id enim imprimis requirit Apostolus, ut sub adven- tum Christi in pace inveniamur, quum beati sint pacifici, quia filii Dei vocabuntur, hoc est, erunt. Matth. V. 9. quæ tamen pax externa cum proxi- mo præsupponitur è pace vel reconciliatione nostra cum Deo, 2. Cor. V. 20. & pace conscientiæ interna, Rom. V. 1. Ideoque studere debemus, ut inveniamur in pace cum Deo & proximo.

## 3:15
Vers. 15.

Καὶ τὴν Κυρίου ἡμῶν μακροθυμίαν σωτηρίαν ἡγεῖσθε] There is a similar expression to this in James 1:2, πᾶσαν χαρὰν ἡγήσασθε, and here above in 11, ἡδονὴν ἡγούμενοι τὴν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τρυφὴν; the sense is, believe that this patience of Christ is salutary for you and others, if you use it rightly.

He has therefore taken the substantive for the adjective; determine firmly that that long-suffering of the Lord, because He does not immediately present Himself for judgment, but defers His coming, is your salvation, that is, is salutary for you. But the substantive can also be retained, that it is salvation, that is, that it conduces to salvation. The verb ἡγεῖσθαι implies a certain persuasion of the mind, Acts 26:2, 2 Cor. 9:5, Phil. 2:25, ch. 3:8, 1 Tim. 1:12.

Καθὼς καὶ ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελφὸς Παῦλος] We have said above why we believe those words ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελφὸς were added by scribes wishing to give Apostolic authority to this epistle.

This excessive license of Grotius, to delete from the sacred Scriptures those things which do not agree with his preconceived opinion. Woe to those who add, woe to those who take away! says Tertullian. Nor does he only delete what he wishes, but he does not even fear to strip the divine Scriptures of their authority. For does this not openly derogate from the divine authority of the Petrine epistle? Moreover, Peter confirms here what he said with Pauline testimony, and refers them to it, so that they may be more fully instructed about those things from there, at the same time thus asserting the Canonical authority of the Pauline epistles. He had confirmed his own words with the words of Christ, which he used concerning the coming of the Lord and the last day, that He will come like a thief in the night, and concerning the passing away of heaven and earth, as well as the exhortations of Christ to preparation for the last coming: as also the promises of a new heaven and a new earth made by the Lord. Now he confirms the same things with the Pauline writings, which are of the same vote, to strengthen the faith of his own, and to confound the impiety of the scoffers. Peter calls the Apostle Paul brother, because they had given each other the right hand of fellowship, Gal. ch. 2:9, and they were Co-Apostles.

According to the wisdom given to him he wrote to you] Namely in the epistle to the Romans, in which there are many things pertaining properly to the Jews. Nor is it in vain that he attributes wisdom to Paul, namely heavenly: See 2 Cor. II. 6, 7; XII. 8; Eph. I. v. 8, 17; Col. II. 9, 28; III. 16; Jas. I. 5; III. 13, 15, 17.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Καὶ τὴν Κυρίου ἡμῶν μακροθυμίαν σωτηρίαν ἡγεῖσθε] Est lo- quutio similis cum ista Jac. I. v. 2. πᾶσαν χαρὰν ἡγήσασθε, & hic supra 11. ἡδονὴν ἡγούμενοι τὴν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ τρυφὴν, sensus est, credite istam Christi patientiam vobis & aliis esse saluta- rem, si ea recte utamini.

Substantivum ergo pro adjectivo accepit, sta- tuite firmiter longanimitatem illam Domini, quod non statim ad judicium se sistit, sed adven- tum differt, salutem vestram, id est, salutarem vobis esse. Sed retineri etiam substantivum potest, salutem esse, hoc est, ad salutem condu- cere. Verbum ἡγεῖσθαι certam animi persuasio- nem infert, Act. XXVI. 2. 2. Cor. IX. 5. Phil. II. v. 25. cap. III. 8. 1. Tim. I. 12.

Καθὼς καὶ ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελφὸς Παῦλος] Cur illa ἀγαπητὸς ἡμῶν ἀδελφὸς adjecta credamus à librariis huic epistolæ Apostolicam autoritatem dare volentibus diximus supra.

Nimia hæc Grotii licentia, delere è Scriptu- ris sacris, quæ præceptæ opinioni non conveni- unt. Væ addentibus, væ detrahentibus! ait Tertullianus. Nec delet tantum quæ vult, sed exautorare etiam non veretur divinas scripturas. Annon enim hoc autoritatem divinam epistolæ Petrinæ palam derogat? Cæterum confirmat hic, quæ dixit Petrus Paulino testimonio, eoque remittit, ut uberius de illis inde instruantur, simul ita asserens Paulinis epistolis Canonicam autoritatem. Firmarat sua verbis Christi, quæ de adventu Domini & die novissimo adhibuit, quod venturus sit instar furis nocturni, & de cœli ac terræ transitu, necnon exhortationibus Christi ad præparationem ad adventum novis- simum: ut & promissis cæli novi & terræ novæ à Domino factis. Jam confirmat eadem Scri- ptis Paulinis ὁμοψήφοις ad roborandam suorum fidem, & confundendam Empæctarum impie- tatem. Fratrem vocat Petrus Apostolum Pau- lum, quia dederant sibi invicem dextram fra- ternitatis, Gal. cap. II. vers. 9. & Co-Apostoli erant.

Κατὰ τὴν αὐτῷ δοθεῖσαν σοφίαν ἔγραψεν ὑμῖν] Nempe in epistola ad Romanos, in qua multa sunt ad Judæos proprie pertinentia. Non frustra autem sapientiam Paulo tribuit, nempe cœlestem: Vide 2. Cor. II. 6. 7. XII. 8. Eph. I. v. 8. 17. Col. II. 9. 28. III. 16. Jac. I. 5. III. 13. 15. 17.

## 3:16
Verse 16.

As also in all the epistles] In those others, eight of which remain to us.

Speaking in them about these things] About judgment, about eternal life, and about the conditions prescribed for those wishing to obtain it, namely living without filth and vices, and about patiently awaiting the resurrection of the bodies, Rom. ch. VIII. v. 23; Eph. ch. IV. 31.

But why in the epistle to the Romans? Schlichtingius brings forward the reason, because in Rom. II. 3, 4, 5, it also deals with the longsuffering of God: But that 'as' is to be referred to all the preceding things which the Apostle wrote against the scoffers and to fortify and stir up the faithful, not only to that which precedes immediately concerning longsuffering: Because all those things had to be confirmed, and the Apostle of the Gentiles also wrote about all those things according to the wisdom given to him, just as Grotius admits it is said here that the Apostle wrote in all other epistles about those things, about judgment and eternal life, and the method of obtaining it. And although there are many things in the epistle to the Romans pertaining properly to the Jews, it is not to be concluded that the Apostle looked properly to that here, since the epistle directed to the Hebrews themselves is rather looked to: 'He wrote to you'. Peter clearly distinguishes that epistle which was written to the converted Hebrews from the rest which Paul wrote, which are not only eight, but thirteen: so that one ought to wonder how Grotius counted only eight. But he teaches that Paul wrote about the same matters in all of them. He wrote especially in the epistle to the Hebrews about the same subjects through all the chapters: about the eternal throne of Christ, about the destruction of the world, about the inheritance of salvation, ch. I; how we shall see all things subjected at the end of the world, and about salvation and glory obtained through Christ, ch. II; about the time of grace and faith to be kept until the end, ch. III; about the eternal sabbath and the diligence to be applied so that we may enter into rest, ch. IV; about Christ the eternal High Priest, his expiation and the merit of eternal salvation, ch. V; about the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment, and the powers of the world to come, and the entry into the interior of the veil, ch. VI. about the introduction of a better hope and the salvation of those who approach God through Christ, ch. VII; about the High Priest sitting for our sake in heaven at the right hand of Majesty, and a more excellent ministry and a new Testament, ch. VIII; about eternal redemption and the promise of eternal inheritance, and also the return of Christ for the sake of those who await him for salvation, ch. IX; about our boldness regarding the entry into the holy place through the blood of Christ and life to be obtained through faith, ch. X; about the heavenly country and the city having foundations, whose Builder is God, ch. XI; about the eternal vision of God and the heavenly Jerusalem, ch. XII; about the city that is to come and remains, ch. XIII; all of which, with the exhortations to perseverance in faith, the expectation of divine promises, and the pursuit of piety found here and there in this epistle, especially ch. X, likewise about the patience of God, inviting us and promising grace while it is still TODAY, ch. III. what else do they testify than that St. Peter here looked to this very Epistle to the Hebrews? Although therefore Oecumenius asserts here that the epistle to the Romans is also indicated, to which Lorinus agrees, while Salmero refers these things to the epistle to the Galatians: yet other ancients more correctly judge that the epistle to the Hebrews is designated here, with most Papists agreeing, Baronius

Vol. I. ad Ann. 60. Pererius in Prolegomena to the epistle to the Romans, no. 64. Ribera on Hebrews, p. 37, and Estius in this place. Nor does it stand in the way that Paul wrote not to the Hebrews in the dispersion, but to those who were in Judea, because that 'to you' is to your nation, nor is any other epistle to the Hebrews found written by Paul, and about the same argument and the same materials. Whence it is invincibly concluded from this passage that Paul is the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, as we have noted elsewhere.

Concerning the wisdom of Paul given by GOD, the passage 2 Cor. ch. XII is also brought forward, but although Paul there [mentions] those things which are of the highest wisdom revealed in the third heaven; yet they were unspeakable words to him, and therefore he could not comprehend those things in writing. Gal. ch. I, verse 12, is more correctly applied here. But how Paul wrote in all the epistles about those things which are noted here, there is no need for us to inquire much, since those things are obvious concerning the final judgment, and the perfect liberty of the elect, and the redemption of bodies which is expected, as well as the glorious inheritance, Rom. ch. II and VIII; concerning the resuscitation of the dead, and glorious bodies, 1 Cor. ch. XV; concerning the heavenly tabernacle, and the beatitude of vision, 2 Cor. V; concerning the inheritance of the children of God and the harvest of eternal life, Gal. III, IV, VI; concerning the blessing in heavenly places, the pledge of inheritance, salvation and the kingdom of God, Gal. I and V. concerning the gain of death, the expectation of the Savior Christ from heaven, and the glorification of our bodies, Phil. I and II; concerning the hope laid up in heaven and the inheritance of the saints in light, Col. ch. I, verse 11; concerning the coming of the LORD JESUS CHRIST, and the elect being caught up to meet Christ in the air and other things looking to that, as also concerning the day of the Lord coming like a thief, 1 Thess. ch. III, IV, and V; concerning the glorious appearance and flames of fire, and the destruction of the wicked, and the manifestation of the coming of the Lord, 2 Thess. ch. I and II; concerning the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ, concerning future treasures, and eternal life, 1 Tim. ch. VI; concerning that day and the salvation of the elect and the crown of righteousness and the appearance of the just Judge, 2 Tim. I, II, IV; concerning the blessed hope to be expected, and the appearance of the glory of the great God and our Savior JESUS CHRIST, and heirs of true life, Tit. ch. II and III. On the knowledge of every good which we have in Christ and faith in Christ, Philem. vers. 5, 6. No less in all of Paul's epistles are exhortations to faith and piety read, and in most of them [are read] concerning preparation for the coming of the LORD, not to mention the warnings about avoiding pacts and the impiety of the last times delivered in the same, and the testimonies of μακροθυμίας and divine grace inviting us to repentance, and demonstrating the same gracious invitations and admonitions.

In which are some things hard to understand ] The manuscript has ἐν αἷς. The things which he indicates as hard to understand are concerning the spiritual body in 1 Cor. ch. XV, vers. 44, which the Carpocratians wished to be understood in this way, as if salvation were promised to souls alone: likewise concerning faith opposed to the works of the law, which they took as if faith were sufficient, without any good works which might be exercised through the body, and as if faith and love could stand and progress with any works of the body whatsoever.

That MS. reading is not to be admitted, which Estius does not dare to affirm is true. Salmero, however, confesses that ἐν οἷς refers to the word περὶ τέτων: And Lorinus says, that 'in which' is not referred to the epistles, but to those things concerning which it is treated in the epistles. For the Greek pronoun οἷς is not of the feminine gender, of which the noun ἐπιστολῶν is. Therefore, the obscurity of the Pauline epistles is not noted here, but the difficulty of the subject matters, concerning which Peter has treated in this place, is noted in them; not concerning the phrase or the less perspicuous speech, but concerning the thing or object δυσνοήτῳ, difficult to understand, such as certainly are those things which were delivered by St. Paul concerning the last things, 1 Corinthians ch. XV, 2 Corinthians ch. VI, 1 Thessalonians ch. IV, 2 Thessalonians ch. I & II, and elsewhere. Therefore, those things contribute nothing to the obscurity of scripture, which the Papists argue. For things that are not evident to faith can also be delivered in clear and not at all obscure words, which are difficult to understand, not because of the obscurity of the mode of proposing, but because of the sublimity of the mysteries of faith exceeding our grasp, so that the cause of that difficulty is not to be sought in the λέξει of scripture, but in the dullness of our intellect and the height of heavenly things, 1 Cor. ch. II, v. 14, 2 Corinthians X, 4. And δυσνόητα occur not only in those things which concern the last things, but also in the way and manner of obtaining eternal salvation, concerning which Paul has treated especially clearly. Furthermore, because that mystery, as Justin says, is ὑπὲρ νοῦν, ὑπὲρ λόγον, ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν τῆς κτιστῆς φύσεως, therefore to human reason it is foolishness, nor can it understand it. It does not appear that the Carpocratians alone or especially are noted here, who, when they feigned that faith without works [was taught] by the Apostle against the Pseudo-Apostles along with other false teachers, were indeed defeated; but one must nevertheless beware here of the other extreme, by which the merit of Christ is not a little shaken, nor is that Lord who bought us with the price of his blood any longer left as the only one, 2 Peter ch. II, v. 2, inasmuch as a place is entrusted to the merits of the saints and our own in the manner of obtaining eternal salvation. Which way of salvation is also subverted by those who, under the pretext of the words of the Apostle, Heb. ch. VI, v. 4, ch. X, v. 16, denying repentance after a fall to the reborn, which places some think are specifically looked to here: Nor do we deny that the dogma delivered there is δυσνόητον: for it concerns that difficult argument concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit: But without doubt more things, and especially those which we have mentioned, are comprehended under the title of those δυσνόητων. From these things, therefore, it is clear that Cornelius rashly urges the present passage against us, because the scriptures are not easy and perspicuous to every unlearned person, which is not absolutely asserted by us, much less, as Estius has it here, that sacred scripture is everywhere easy and accessible to all in understanding: for we do not exclude hermeneutical means, which are not found in every subject, nor do we deny that many things in the scriptures are obscure, but with Augustine, l. II. de vit. Christ. ch. 9, we profess that in those things which are openly placed in the scriptures are found all things which contain faith and the morals of living. For the rest, we repeat the observation of the Blessed Luther in his diatribe on the enslaved will against Erasmus: Dogmas in themselves are obscure, but insofar as they are proposed in scripture, they are manifest, if we wish to be content with that knowledge which GOD has proposed to the Church in the scriptures.

Ἃ οἱ ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστήρικτοι στρεβλοῦσιν] An adulterated sense obstructs the truth as much as a corrupting style. Tertullian on the prescription of heretics. Therefore, where the sense of the τῷ ῥητῷ comes into controversy, tradition comes to the aid, within which the lines of interpretation are to be governed. He calls them ἀμαθεῖς because they do not consider the series and purpose of the Apostle. ἀστηρίκτους because they do not hold themselves to that doctrine which sounded from the beginning through the Churches. ἀμαθεῖς סכלים. ἀστήρικτους we had also above ch. II, v. 14. στρεβλοῦσι פתל, 1 Sam. ch. XXII, verse 7. In the Glossary στρεβλῷ is perverse. The Rabbis say חמס תורה στρεβλοῖ τὸν νόμον.

Nothing here concerning tradition, which ought to aid sacred scripture; nor is the interpretation of the same to be drawn from tradition, but from scripture itself, as was said at 1 Peter ch. I, verse 20. If tradition ought to aid scripture, scripture will be imperfect, or not sufficient to render us ἀρτίους for every good work and wisely instructed for salvation, which is against Paul, 2 Timothy III, v. 15, 16; nay, tradition will be of greater dignity, perfection, and perspicuity than scripture, which it ought to aid, when yet those axioms of perfection and perspicuity are nowhere attributed to tradition, but sacred scripture is celebrated for perfection and perspicuity. Nor are we taught anywhere that the lines of interpretation are to be governed within tradition, but we are commanded only to attend to scripture and to search it, 1 Peter ch. I, verse 19, John ch. V, v. 39. But concerning these Papist errors approved by Grotius, see System. Theol. Tom. I, ch. III, q. I, II, ch. IV, q. XII. By ἀμαθεῖς are understood those who do not allow themselves to be taught by the scriptures, which alone are the infallible rule of doctrine: by ἀστηρίκτους, those who have not acquired for themselves any solidity of faith from the sacred letters, but are tossed to and fro by every wind of doctrine, inasmuch as they are destitute of the unique foundation of faith, which are the writings of the Prophets and Apostles, Ephesians ch. II, verse 20. Thus, as Heinsius rightly warns, he does not ascribe τὸ δυσνόητον to the author as a fault. But he condemns the readers as ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστήρικτους: but he manifestly extols the author himself. For firstly, he attributes σοφίαν to him. But what kind? Infused and heavenly. Secondly, he places the epistles of the Apostle in the canon, when he adds: ὡς καὶ τὰς λοιπὰς γραφάς. Thirdly, he accuses or commends those whom he says στρεβλοῦσι or distort, but with eternal destruction, which are very well said by him.

Στρεβλῶσι they deprave into a foreign sense, they snatch away by the neck, as the saying goes, they twist, contort, and retort. The metaphor is derived from torturers, because they twist Scripture as if on racks and pulleys to suit their own purposes. Clement of Alexandria, book VII of the Stromata: They use the Scriptures, he says, not all of them, then not the perfect ones, nor as the body and context of the prophecy dictates, but choosing those things which are said ambiguously, they translate them to their own opinions, plucking a few words here and there, not considering what is signified by them, but using the bare diction itself.

Ὡς καὶ λοιπὰς γραφὰς] He seems to understand the books of the Gospels and the Acts, which were already in hand when this epistle was written. Chrysostom on the 7th chapter to the Romans: You see that if we do not select the words with the proper reverence, and look to the Apostolic purpose, we shall see countless absurdities. And in the 8th to the Romans: You see how many absurdities are born if we interpret what is said simply. The same, 2 Corinthians, chapter X: He (Paul) was not a man of many colors, but simple and clear; but these men twisted the words to their own thoughts. Origen, third against Celsus, concerning Paul: For if he gives himself to reading with attention, I know well that he will admire the mind of the man who, in common speech, thinks of great things, or if he does not admire him, he himself will appear ridiculous, either explaining as if he had understood the intention of the man, or even attempting to contradict and overturn what he imagined him to have understood. The same, in that place which we have in chapter IX of the Philocalia, when he had said that the expression is often ambiguous, and there is no perpetual order in the words of the Apostle, he adds: And this is in many places the cause of it seeming to have no syntax, nor sequence.

the whole of the other scripture, and especially as the Prophetic and the Apostolic [scripture] pre-exist, and especially the Apostolic epistle to the Romans, in which the things concerning the law are named differently, and are set down concerning different matters.

In grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ] It is a hendiadys. For that grace is understood, through which Christ is known, by experimental knowledge. See above I. 5. Compare 2 Cor. IV. 6.

He understands the remaining divinely inspired scriptures, namely the Apostolic ones of Matthew and John, (the reason is the same for James and Jude) and those of the non-Apostolic Evangelists, such as Mark and Luke, and indeed the Prophetic ones too. Bede in this place: Heretics pervert all scriptures. For there is no book of either the Old or New Testament in which they have not perversely understood many things. But they have also often perverted the scriptures themselves in their own state by removing, adding, or changing whatever their perfidy had dictated.

In this closing of the epistle, first there is a dissuasion concerning avoiding impostors and apostasy from the faith. Then an exhortation to growth in grace and the knowledge of Christ, which corresponds to the initial prayer, 2 Pet. I. 2. There is no need, however, for these to be explained by a hendiadys: because an increase in both grace and the knowledge of Christ, that is, of faith, was necessary for them. That foreknowledge, however, as is clear from the context, concerns false teachers and their destructive doctrine, not precisely the coming of Christ, except insofar as it is called into doubt by them. Lawless men are wicked, or those who wish to be without law: such are those who treat and twist the law, that is, divine scripture, wickedly.

To their own destruction] Deservedly: because they bring an evil mind to the reading, and prejudices taken from the flesh. Furthermore, even in matters not so evil, it is not reckoned as a fault that they are ignorant, as Augustine speaks, but that they neglect to seek what they are ignorant of. But let us seek, says Tertullian, in our own [scriptures], and from our own [people], and concerning our own [matters]: and that only which can come into question without prejudice to the rule of faith. Which rule having been recited, he adds: Otherwise, while its form remains in its order, you may seek and discuss as much as you like, and pour out all the lust of curiosity; if anything seems to you to hang in ambiguity or to be overshadowed by obscurity, there is certainly some brother, a Doctor gifted with knowledge: there is someone experienced among the learned, someone curious, yet seeking with you. Then: Let curiosity yield to faith, let glory yield to salvation. Certainly, let them either not object, or let them be quiet. The passage is from the Prescription against Heretics.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Ὡς καὶ ἐν πάσαις ταῖς ἐπισολαῖς] In illis aliis, quarum o- cto nobis restant.

Λαλῶν ἐν αὐταῖς περὶ τέτων] De judicio, de vita æterna, deque conditione eam adipifci volentibus præscripta, viven- di nempe sine sordibus ac vitiis, deque patienter expectanda corporum resurrectione, Rom. cap. VIII. v. 23. Eph. cap. IV. 31.

Cur vero in epistola ad Romanos? Schlichtingius causam affert, quia Rom. II. 3. 4. 5. etiam de lon- ganimitate Dei agitur: Sed illud καθὼς ad omnia præcedentia, quæ contra Empæctas, & ad munien- dos excitandosque fideles scripsit Apostolus, re- ferenda non solum ad id, quod immediate de μα- κροθυμίᾳ præcedit: Quia illa omnia confirmanda erant, & de omnibus illis scripsit quoque gentium Apostolus secundum datam ipsi sapientiam, quem- admodum & in aliis epistolis omnibus de illis de judicio & vita æterna, & ratione eam adipiscendi scripsisse Apostolum hic dici fatetur Grotius. Etsi vero in epistola ad Romanos multa sint, proprie ad Judæos pertinentia, non tamen hic eo proprie Apostolum respexisse colligendum, quum respi- ciatur potius epistola ad ipsos Ebræos directa: Ἔγραψεν ὑμῖν. Distinguit aperte Petrus eam, quæ ad Ebræos conversos exarata est, epistolam à reli- quis, quas Paulus scripsit, quæ non octo tantum sunt, sed tredecim: ut quomodo octo tantum nu- merarit Grotius, mirari oporteat. In omnibus au- tem illis de iisdem rebus scripsisse Paulum docet. Scripsit cumprimis in epistola ad Ebræos de iisdem materiis per omnia capita de throno æterno Christi, de mundi destructione, de hæreditate salutis, c. I. quomodo omnia subjecta esse in fine mundi vi- suri simus, & de salute ac gloria per Christum parta cap. II. de tempore gratiæ & fide ad finem usque ser- vanda, cap. III. de sabbatismo æterno & diligentia adhibenda, ut requiem ingrediamur, cap. IV. de Christo æterno Pontifice, ejus expiatione & merito æternæ salutis, cap. V. de resurrectione mortuorum ac æterno judicio, & virtutibus venturi seculi, & ingressu in interiora veli, cap. VI. de introductione melioris spei & salute eorum, qui per Christum ac- cedunt ad Deum, cap. VII. de Pontifice nostri causa in cælis ad dextram Majestatis sedente, ac præstan- tiori λειτουργίᾳ & novo Testamento, cap. VIII. de redemptione æterna & promissione hæreditatis æ- ternæ, nec non reditu Christi ob eos, qui expe- ctant ipsum ad salutem, cap. IX. de παῤῥησίᾳ no- stra quoad ingressum in sanctum per sanguinem Christi & vita per fidem obtinenda, cap. X. de pa- tria cœlesti & civitate fundamentum habente, cujus Conditor est Deus, cap. XI. de æterna Dei vi- sione & Hierusalem cœlesti, cap. XII. de civitate futura manente, cap. XIII. quæ omnia cum ex- hortationibus ad perseverantiam in fide, expe- ctationem divinarum promissionum, studiumq; pietatis passim in hac epistola obviis, imprimis cap. X. de patientia itidem Dei, nos, dum ad- huc HODIE est, invitantis & gratiam pro- mittentis, cap. III. quid aliud testantur, quam hanc ipsam ad Ebræos Epistolam S. Petrum hic respexisse? Quamvis ergo hic Oecumenius Epi- stolam ad Romanos indigitari etiam asserat, cui Lorinus annuit, Salmero vero ad epistolam ad Galatas hæc referat: rectius tamen alii veteres epistolam ad Ebræos hic designatam censent, ad- stipulantibus plerisque Pontificiis, Baronio

Tom. I. ad Ann. 60. Pererio in Prolegom. epist. ad Rom. num. 64. Ribera ad Ebr. pag. 37. & Estio in h. l. Nec vero obstat, quod Paulus E- bræis non in dispersione, sed qui in Judæa e- rant, scripserit, quia illud ὑμῖν vobis, est genti vestræ, nec alia reperitur epistola ad Ebræos à Paulo exarata, deque argumento eodem ac materiis iisdem. Unde ex hoc loco invicte col- ligitur, Paulum esse autorem Epistolæ ad Ebræos, ut alias monuimus.

De sapientia Pauli à DEO data affertur etiam locus, 2. Corinth. cap. XII. sed quanquam ibi Paulus ea, quæ summæ sapientiæ sunt in ter- tio cœlo revelata; fuerunt tamen ipsi ἄῤῥητα ῥήματα, ideoque ista literis comprehendere ne- quivit. Rectius huc facit, Gal. cap. I. vers. 12. Quomodo autem in omnibus epistolis Paulus de illis, quæ hic notantur, scripserit, non o- pus est, multum disquiramus, quum obvia illa sint de judicio novissimo, ac libertate electo- rum perfecta, & ἀπολυτρώσει corporum, quæ expectatur, necnon hæreditate gloriosa, Rom. cap. II. & VIII. de resuscitatione mortuorum, & gloriosis corporibus, 1. Corinth. cap. XV. de tabernaculo cœlesti, & beatitudine visio- nis 2. Corinth. V. de hæreditate filiorum Dei & messe vitæ æternæ, Gal. III. IV. VI. de benedi- ctione in cœlestibus, pignore hæreditatis, sa- lute & regno Dei, Gal. I. & V. de lucro mor- tis, expectatione Servatoris Christi de cœlo, & glorificatione corporum nostrorum, Phil. I. & II. de spe in cœlo reposita & hæreditate san- ctorum in luce, Coloss. cap. I. vers. II. de adventu DOMINI JESU CHRISTI, & in occur- sum Christi in aëre rapiendis electis aliisque eo spectantibus, ut & de die Domini instar furis venturo, 1. Thess. cap. III. IV. & V. de glo- riosa apparitione & flammis ignis, atque exitio impiorum, & de manifestatione adventus Do- mini, 2. Thess. cap. I. & II. de apparitione Do- mini nostri Jesu Christi, de thesauris futuris, & vita æterna, 1. Timoth. cap. VI. de die illo ac sa- lute electorum & corona justitiæ & justi Judicis apparitione, 2. Timoth. I. II. IV. de expectanda beata spe, & apparitione gloriæ magni Dei & Salvatoris nostri JESU CHRISTI, ac hæ- redibus veræ vitæ, Tit. cap. II. & III. de co- gnitione omnis boni, quod habemus in Chri- sto & fide in Christum, Philem. vers. 5. 6. Nec minus in omnibus Pauli epistolis exhortationes ad fidem & pietatem leguntur, & in plerisque de præparatione ad adventum DOMINI, ut tace- am præmonitiones de fugiendis empactis, & novis- simorum temporum impietate in iisdem traditas, ac μακροθυμίας & gratiæ divinæ nos ad pœni- tentiam invitantis testimonia, eandemque de- monstrantes gratiosas invitationes ac commo- nitiones.

Ἐν οἷς ἐστι δυσνόητά τινα ] Manuscriptus ἐν αἷς. Δυσνόητα quæ indicat, sunt de corpore spirituali 1. Corinth. cap. XV. vers. 44. quæ Carpocratiani volebant accipi hoc mo- do, quasi solis animabus salus promitteretur: item de fide opposita operibus legis, quæ illi sumebant, quasi fides sufficeret, sine ullis bonis operibus, quæ per corpus exercerentur, & quasi fides & dilectio stare possent, & proficere cum quibuslibet corporis ope- ribus.

Non est admittenda illa MS. lectio, quam veram esse Estius affirmare non audet. Sal- mero autem fatetur ἐν οἷς referriad verbum περὶ τέτων: Et Lorinus, non refertur illud, inquit, in quibus, ad epistolas, sed ad ea, de quibus tra- statur in epistolis. Nam Graecum pronomen οἷς non est foeminini generis, cujus est nomen ἐπιστο- λῶν. Non ergo hic obscuritas epistolarum Paulinarum, sed difficultas materiarum, de quibus hoc loco egit Petrus, in iisdem notatur, non de phrasi vel sermone minus perspicuo, sed de re vel objecto δυσνοήτῳ intellectu difficili, qua- lia certe sunt, quae de novissimis à S. Paulo tra- dita, 1. Corinth. cap. XV. 2. Corinth. cap. VI. 1. Thess. cap. IV. 2. Thess. cap. I. & II. & alibi. Nihil ergo illa ad obscuritatem scripturae, quam arguunt Papistae, faciunt. Nam possunt etiam res in- evidentes fidei verbis perspicuis, minimeque ob- scuris tradi, quae intellectu difficiles sunt, non ob modi proponenti obscuritatem, sed ob myste- riorum fidei captum nostrum excedentium sub- limitatem, ut causa istius difficultatis non in scri- pturae λέξει quaerenda sit, sed in intellectus nostri hebetudine, & rerum caelestium altitudine, 1. Cor. cap. II. v. 14. 2. Corinth. X. 4. Nec tantum in iis, quae novissima concernunt, δυσνόητα occurrunt, sed etiam in via ac ratione consequendi salutem aeternam, de qua imprimis luculenter egit Pau- lus. Caeterum quia mysterium illud, Justino dicente, est ὑπὲρ νοῦν, ὑπὲρ λόγον, ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν κατάληψιν τῆς κτιστῆς φύσεως, ideo rationi huma- nae id stultitia est, nec potest id intelligere. Car- pocratianos vel solos vel praecipue hic notari haud apparet, qui cum fingebant, fidem sine o- peribus ab Apostolo in Pseudo-Apostolos cum aliis falsis Doctoribus, profligata quidem sunt; sed cavendum tamen hic alterum extre- mum, quo meritum Christi non parum labe- factatur, nec ipse solus amplius relinquitur herus ille, qui sanguinis suo pretio nos mercatus est, 2. Petr. cap. II. v. 2. utpote cum meritis san- ctorum & propriis nostris locus concreditur in ratione consequendi aeternam salutem. Quae salutis via etiam intervertitur ab iis, qui prae- textu verborum Apostoli, Ebr. cap. VI. v. 4. cap. X. v. 16. poenitentiam post lapsum renatis denegantes, quae loca specialiter hic respici nonnulli censent: Neque diffitemur, dogma ibi traditum δυσνόητον esse: agitur enim de diffi- cili illo argumento de peccato in Spiritum San- ctum: Sed plura sine dubio & imprimis ea, quae diximus, sub istorum δυσνοήτων titulo comprehenduntur. Ex his ergo liquet temere contra nos locum praesentem urgere Cornelium, quod scripturae non sint faciles, & cuique idiotae perspicuae, quod non absolute à nobis asseritur, nedum, ut Estius hic habet, scri- pturam sacram ubique facilem esse, & omnibus intellectu perviam: nam non excludimus media hermeneutica, quae in quovis subjecto non re- periuntur, neque diffitemur, multa in scri- pturis obscura esse, sed cum Augustino l. II. de vit. Christ. cap. 9. profitemur, in illis, quae aperte in scripturis posita sunt, inveniri omnia, quae continent fidem moresque vivendi. De caetero repetimus B. Lutheri observationem diatr. de serv. arbitr. c. Erasm: Dogmata in se sunt obscura, sed quatenus in scriptura proponun- tur, sunt manifesta, si velimus illa cognitione esse contenti, quam DEUS Ecclesiae in scripturis proposuit.

Ἃ οἱ ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστήρικτοι στρεβλοῦσιν] Tantum veritati obstrepit adulter sensus, quantum & corruptor stylus. Ter- tullianus de praescriptione haereticorum. Ideo ubi τῷ ῥητῷ sensus in controversiam venit, subvenit traditio, intra quam interpretationis lineae regendae sunt. Ἀμαθεῖς vo- cat illos, quia seriem propositumque Apostoli non con- siderant. Ἀστηρίκτους quia non tenent se in ea doctrina, quæ ab initio per Ecclesias sonuit. Ἀμαθεῖς סכלים. Ἀ- στηρίκτους habuimus & supra cap. II. v. 14. Στρεβλῦσι פתל, 1. Sam. cap. XXII. vers. 7. In Glossario στρεβλῷ pravo. Rabbini dicunt חמס תורה στρεβλοῖ τὸν νόμον.

Nihil hic de traditione, quæ scripturæ sacræ subvenire debeat; neque ex traditione, sed ex ipsa scriptura ejusdem depromenda est interpre- tatio, ut ad 1. Petr. cap. I. vers. 20. dictum. Si subvenire scripturæ traditio debet, scriptura erit imperfecta, vel non sufficiens ad nos ἀρτί- ος reddendos ad omne opus bonum, & sapi- enter instruendos ad salutem, quod est contra Paulum, 2. Timoth. III. v. 15. 16. imo traditio ma- joris dignitatis, perfectionis, & perspicuitatis erit, quam scriptura, cui subvenire debet, quum tamen nuspiam illa axiomata perfectio- nis & perspicuitatis traditioni tribuantur, scri- ptura vero sacra a perfectione & perspicuitate celebretur. Nec uspiam docemur, intra tra- ditionem interpretationis lineas regendas esse, sed solum attendere jubemur scripturæ, eamque scrutari, 1. Petr. cap. I. vers. 19. Joh. cap. V. v. 39. Sed de Pontificiis hisce erroribus Grotio pro- batis vid. System. Theol. Tom. I. cap. III. q. I. II. cap. IV. q. XII. Per ἀμαθεῖς intelliguntur, qui se scripturis doceri non patiuntur, quæ solæ doctrinæ regula infallibilis sunt: per ἀστηρίκτους, qui nullam fidei soliditatem sibi compararunt e sacris literis, sed quovis vento doctrinæ hinc inde agitantur, utpote unico fidei fundamento, quod Prophetarum & Apostolorum scripta sunt, Ephes. cap. II. vers. 20. destituti. Sic non autori, ut recte monet Heinsius, τὸ δυσνόητον ut vitium adscribit. Sed lectores ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστηρίκτους damnat: ipsum autem manifeste extollit. Primo etenim σοφίαν ei tribuit. Qualem vero? Infusam ac cælestem Secundo epistolas Apostoli in canone reponit, cum addit: ὡς καὶ τὰς λοιπὰς γραφὰς. Tertio accusat seu commendat eos, quos στρεβλῦν seu detorquere sed cum exitio æterno ait, quæ ab eo optime dicuntur.

Στρεβλῶσι depravant in alienum sensum, ob- torto, quod dicitur, collo abripiunt, torquent, contorquent & retorquent. Metaphora est a tortoribus deducta, quod scripturam quasi fidi- culis & equuleis ad suos torqueant. Clemens Ale- xandr. libr. VII. Strom. Scripturis, inquit, utuntur non omnibus, deinde non perfectis, ne- que ut dictat corpus & contextus Prophetiæ, sed eligentes ea, quæ dicta sunt ambigue, traducunt, ad proprias opiniones, paucas voces sparsim car- pentes, non id considerantes, quod ex ipsis significa- tur, sed ipsa nuda dictione utentes.

Ὡς καὶ λοιπὰς γραφὰς] Videtur intelligere libros Evangeliorum, & Acta, quæ jam in manibus erant, cum hæc epistola scriberetur. Chrysostomus in VII. ad Romanos: Ὁρᾷς ὅτι ἂν μὴ μετὰ τῆς προσηκούσης εὐλαβεί- ας τὰς λέξεις ἐκλεξώμεθα, καὶ πρὸς τὸν Ἀποστολικὸν ἴδω- μεν σκοπὸν, μυρία ὄψεται ἄτοπα. Et in VIII. ad Ro- manos: Ὁρᾷς πόσα ἄτοπα τίκτεται, ἐὰν ἁπλῶς τὰ λε- γόμενα ἐκδεξώμεθα. Idem 2. Corinth. cap. X. Οὐ ποί- κιλόν τις ἦν (ὁ Παῦλος) ἀλλ' ἁπλῶς καὶ σαφής· οὗτοι δὲ πρὸς τὰς οἰκείας διέστρεψαν τὰ ῥήματα ἐννοίας. Origenes tertio contra Celsum de Paulo: ἐὰν γὰρ ἐπιδῷ ἑαυτὸν τῇ μετὰ τοῦ προσέχειν ἀναγνώσει, εὖ οἶδ' ὅτι θαυμάσεται τὸν νοῦν τοῦ ἀνδρὸς ἐν ἰδιωτικῇ λέξει μεγάλα περινοοῦντος, ἢ μὴ θαυ- μάσας αὐτὸς καταγέλαστος φανεῖται εἴτε διεγούμενος ὥσπερ νενοηκὼς τὸ βούλημα τοῦ ἀνδρὸς, ἢ καὶ ἀντιλέγειν καὶ ἀνα- τρέπειν πειρώμενος ἃ ἐφαντάσθη αὐτὸν νενοηκέναι. Idem in eo loco quem habemus cap. IX. Φιλοκαλίας, cum dixis- set sæpe loquutionem esse ambiguam, neque ordinem perpetuum in verbis Apostoli, addit: Καὶ τῦτο πολ- λαχῦ αἴτιόν ἐστι τοῦ δοκεῖν μὴ ἔχειν σύνταξιν, μηδὲ ἀκολου-

ὅλαν τὴν ἄλλην γραφὴν, καὶ μάλιςα ὡς προϋπάρχειν τὴν Προφητικὴν, κἀι τὴν Ἀποςολικὴν, κἀι μάλιςα τὰς Ἀποςολικὰς τὴς πρὸς Ῥωμαίους ἐπιςολὴ, ὅι ἧ τὰ περὶ νόμο διαφόρως ὀνομάζετα, κἀι ἐπὶ διαφόρων πραγμάτων κείμενα.

Ἐν χάριτι κἀι γνώσει τῦ Κυρίυ ἡμῶν καὶ Σωτῆρος Ἰησῦ Χριςῦ] Est ἓν διὰ δυοῖν. Intelligitur enim illa gratia, perquam Christus cognoscitur, cognitione experimentali. Vide supra I. 5. Conf. 2. Cor. IV. 6.

Intelligit scripturas divinitus inspiratas reliquas, Apostolicas nempe Matthæi, & Johannis, (de Jacobo & Juda par est ratio) & Evangelistarum non-Apostolorum, quales Marcus & Lucas, imo & Propheticas. Beda in h. l. Omnes scripturas hæretici depravant. Nullus enim est vel Veteris vel Novi Testamenti liber, in quo non multa perverse intellexerint. Sed & ipsas sæpe scripturas in suo statu perverterunt vel demendo, vel addendo, vel immutando, quæcunque illorum perfidia dictasset.

In clausula hac epistolæ primum ἀποτροπὴ de cavendis impostoribus & apostasia à fide habetur. Deinde προτροπὴ ad incrementum in gratia & cognitione Christi, quæ voto initiali convenit, 2. Petr. I. 2. Non opus autem, ut hæc per hendyaden exponantur: quia & gratiæ & notitiæ Christi fiducialis, seu fidei incrementum ipsis necessarium erat. Præscientia autem illa, ut è συνεχείᾳ liquet falsos Doctores respicit, eorumque doctrinam exitiosam, non Christi adventum præcise, nisi qua is in dubium vocatus ab illis est. Ἄθεσμοι homines sunt nefarii, vel qui sine lege esse volunt: quales sunt, qui legem, hoc est, scripturam divinam nefariè tractant & torquent.

Πρὸς τὴν ἰδίαν ἀυτῶν ἀπώλειαν] Merito: quia afferunt ad lectionem malum animum, & præjudicia à carne sumpta. Præterea etiam in non adeo malis non deputatur ad culpam, quod ignorant, ut Augustinus loquitur, sed quod negligunt quærere, quod ignorant. Quæramus autem, inquit Tertullianus, & in nostro & à nostris & de nostro: idque duntaxat, quod salva regula fidei potest in quæstionem devenire. Qua regula recitata addit: Cæterum manente forma ejus in suo ordine, quantumlibet quæras & tractes, & omnem libidinem curiositatis effundas, si quid tibi videtur vel ambiguitate pendere, vel obscuritate obumbrari, est utique frater aliquis, Doctor gravis scientia donatus: est aliquis inter xercitatos conversatus, aliquis curiosus, tecum tamen quærens. Deinde: Cedat curiositas fidei, cedat gloria saluti. Certe aut non obstrepant, aut quiescant. Locus est de præscriptione contra Hæreticos.

## 3:17
Verse 17.

ὑμεῖς ἓν, ἀγαπητοὶ, προγινώσκοντες] Forewarned of the dangers. See Matt. XXIV. 25.

Φυλάσσεσθε, ἵνα μὴ τῇ ᾗ ἀθέσμων πλάνῃ συναπαχθέντες ἐκπέσητε τῦ ἰδίυ ςηριγμῦ] πλάνη here signifies deception, מרמה, as in Prov. XIV. 8. See also Eph. IV. 14. Those are called Ἄθεσμοι for the same reason as the inhabitants of Sodom above, II, 7. Συναπάγεσθαι, to be carried away, as in Gal. II. 13. Στηριγμὸς, משען, 2 Pet. III. 17, in this place is that constancy by which faith is retained. ᾿Εκπεσεῖν ςηριγμῦ is said just as Χάριτος ἐκπιπτειν, Gal. V. verse 4, to lose firmness, to lose grace.

᾿Αυτῷ ἡ δόξα καὶ νῦν καὶ εἰς ἡμέραν ἀιῶνος. Ἀμήν. To Him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

ὑμεῖς ἓν, ἀγαπητοὶ, προγινώσκοντες] Præmoniti de periculis. Vide Matth. XXIV. 25.

Φυλάσσεσθε, ἵνα μὴ τῇ ᾗ ἀθέσμων πλάνῃ συναπαχθέντες ἐκπέσητε τῦ ἰδίυ ςηριγμῦ] πλάνη hic deceptionem significat מרמה ut Prov. XIV. 8. Vide & Eph. IV. 14. Ἄθεσμοι dicuntur isti pari de causa, qui supra Sodomorum habitatores II, 7. Συναπάγεσθαι abripi, ut Gal. II. 13. Στηριγμὸς משען, Ef. III. 1. hoc loco est constantia illa, per quam retinetur fides. ᾿Εκπεσεῖν ςηριγμῦ sic dicitur sicut Χάριτος ἐκπιπτειν, Gal. V. vers. 4. amittere firmitatem, amittere gratiam.

᾿Αυτῷ ἡ δόξα καὶ νῦν καὶ εἰς ἡμέραν ἀιῶνος. Ἀμήν.

## 3:18
To Him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.] The word 'day' here, as in 1 Pet. II. 12, signifies time in the Hebrew manner. But the 'day of eternity' is the 'eternal day', everlasting time. The sense is similar to 1 Tim. VI. 16.

Oecumenius is more serious here: The perdition of those who killed the Prophets and Apostles is equal to that of those who corrupted their writings and sermons, and they are both liable to the same judgment of God and to damnation and vengeance. For the former killed the Prophets and Apostles so that others would not follow their salutary doctrine. But the latter pervert their sermons and writings so that others, desiring a right and sincere understanding, might not be saved.

The whole epistle is concluded with a doxology attributed to CHRIST, now and to the day of eternity, eternity being estimated as one day, which is perpetual and has no vicissitude or night, no succession, Apoc. ch. XXII. v. 5. Before GOD, the whole of eternity is a single day lacking evening, says Caesarius Dial. 3. There is one day there, but everlasting, which is neither preceded by a yesterday nor excluded by a tomorrow, says Augustine Tract. XXXI. on John, which the natural Sun does not produce, since it has been destroyed, but Christ the Sun of righteousness, Apoc. ch. XXII. verse 5. And since eternal glory belongs to GOD alone, and such a doxology or glorification, which is a species of the worship of latria, Rom. ch. XVI. verse 27. Phil. ch. IV. verse 20. 1 Tim. ch. VI. verse 16. 2 Tim. ch. IV. verse 18. Heb. ch. XIII. v. 20 & 21. 1 Pet. ch. I. verse 10. Jude v. 25. The Divinity of CHRIST is confirmed from this, as Estius admits, and Papists are convicted of idolatry from the opposite, as often as they join Mary and other Saints to GOD in such doxologies. Finally, the sealing is done with the word Amen. With which doxology and celebration of CHRIST we also conclude:

Latin:

᾿Αυτῷ ἡ δόξα καὶ νῦν καὶ εἰς ἡμέραν ἀιῶνος. Ἀμήν.] Ἡ μέρα hic ut 1. Petr. II. 12. Tempus more Ebræo significat. Ἡμέρα autem ἀιῶνός est ἡμέρα ἀιώνιος, tempus æternum. Sensus similis 1. Tim. VI. 16.

Gravius hic Oecumenius: Par eorum perditio est, qui Prophetas & Apostolos occiderunt, atque eorum, qui scripta & sermones eorum corruperunt, eidemque judicio Dei & damnationi ac vindictæ utrinque sunt obnoxii. Illi enim occiderunt Prophetas & Apostolos, ne alii doctrinam eorum salutarem sequerentur. Hi vero sermones eorum & scripta depravant, ne alii rectam & sinceram intelligentiam cupientes salvi fiant.

Concluditur tota epistola δοξολογίᾳ CHRISTO tributa, nunc & in diem æternitatis, æstimata æternitate pro una die, quæ perpetua est, nullamque vicissitudinem aut noctem, nullam successionem habet, Apoc. cap. XXII. v. 5. Apud DEUM vespere carens & unicus dies est tota æternitas, ait Cæsarius Dial. 3. Dies est ibi unus, sed sempiternus, qui nec præceditur hesterno, nec excluditur crastino, ait Augustinus Tract. XXXI. in Johan. quem non Sol naturalis efficit, utpote qui destructus est, sed Christus Sol justitiæ, Apoc. cap. XXII. vers. 5. Et quum soli DEO gloria æterna conveniat, & δοξολογία vel glorificatio ejusmodi, quæ est species cultus λατρείας, Rom. cap. XVI. vers. 27. Phil. cap. IV. vers. 20. 1. Timoth. cap. VI. vers. 16. 2. Timoth. cap. IV. vers. 18. Ebr. cap. XIII. v. 20. & 21. 1. Petr. cap. I. vers. 10. Jud. v. 25. Divinitas CHRISTI hinc confirmatur fatente Eftio, & ex adverso idololatrias convincuntur Papistæ, quoties in δοξολογίαις talibus Mariam, aliosque Sanctos DEO conjungunt. Tandem obsignatio fit voce Ἀμήν. Qua δοξολογίᾳ & celebratione CHRISTI etiam nos finimus:

# 1 John

## 1:1 Introduction
[Abraham Calov, Biblia Novi Testamenti Illustrata (Vol. 2, Part 2). English: machine translation, The Faith Received (Mere Orthodoxy); the original follows each comment.]
I. N. J. ANNOTATIONS ON THE FIRST EPISTLE OF JOHN. PROLEGOMENA. GROTIUS'S PREFACE.

That this epistle is the Apostle John’s has never been doubted in the Church, as Eusebius, Jerome, and others teach us. It was once called the epistle to the Parthians, as Augustine testifies: that is, to the Jews who professed CHRIST, who lived not under the Roman, but the Parthian empire, in places across the Euphrates, where there was a huge multitude of Jews, such as in Nearda, Nisibis, and other places. See Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews XVIII. 9. And this I think is the reason why this epistle neither in the front bears the name and title of the Apostle, nor does it contain at the end the greetings of Apostolic custom. For, as it happens, this epistle was being sent through Ephesian merchants into lands hostile to the Romans, and it could have done much harm to the Christians if this correspondence, however innocent, had been discovered. I think, however, that this epistle was written, as I have said elsewhere, from Patmos, not long before the destruction of Jerusalem, for two main reasons: first, that the Christians of those parts might cultivate peace and friendship among themselves, and not allow themselves to be implicated in those factions which were miserably tearing apart the Jews beyond the Euphrates, but should devote effort to being distinguished from the rest of their countrymen by a zeal for concord. Then, lest a report be brought there that there were some in Judea who claimed to be sent by God to liberate the people, and they themselves might run to them along with other Jews, but rather that they should firmly hold that no one had been sent by God who brought things contrary to those which Jesus, truly the Messiah and truly the liberator of the people, had brought: and at the same time, in those impostors, they might recognize the truth of the prediction of Jesus.
