Concerning such impostors, who are also called ἀντίχριστοι, because they claimed for themselves either the title or the office of Christ, we spoke at Matthew XXIV. v. 5. To those add Simon Barjona, whom certain Jews, by confusing similar names, call the former Barchochebas, and those of whom Josephus speaks in Jewish War VI. 30.

OBSERVATIONS.

The author of the epistle is, beyond controversy, St. John the Apostle and Evangelist: But for the sake of proving this matter, not so much the testimonies of certain Doctors, which occupy the last place in the class of proofs, as other documents, primarily taken from internal κριτηρίοις (criteria), must be brought forward. From which those very Doctors themselves have been confirmed in their opinion. Eusebius certainly, in book VII of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 25, by the words of Dionysius of Alexandria, based on the character of the style and similar internal τεκμηρίοις (proofs), establishes that the author of the present epistle is the same one who consigned the Gospel ascribed to John, urging the singular harmony of both: For the Gospel and the epistle mutually agree with each other, and they begin in the same way. For thus the Gospel begins: In the beginning was the Word: But the epistle: That which was from the beginning. In the former it is said: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us: And we saw his glory, the glory as of the Only-begotten of the Father. But this one has the same things, only slightly changed: That which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life: and the life was manifested. For these things he puts forward as if they were preludes of a melody, against those who denied that Christ had come in the flesh, as he shows in what follows. Wherefore he deliberately added: And that which we have seen we testify, and announce to you the eternal life, which was with the Father, and appeared to us. That which we have seen and heard, we announce to you. Thus he hangs entirely upon himself and does not depart even a hair's breadth from his own propositions, but pursues everything with almost the same headings and words. From which we shall indeed suggest a few things briefly. But whoever reads it attentively will find in both, quite often, life, light, the flight of darkness, frequently truth, thanks, joy, the flesh and blood of the Lord, judgment, the remission of sins, the love of God toward us, the commandment of mutual love among us, and that all commandments must be kept. Furthermore, the pronouncement of condemnation against the world, the Devil, and the Anti-Christ, the promise of the Holy Spirit, the adoption of the sons of God, the faith to be performed by us in all things: Father and Son are named everywhere and occur throughout in both. Finally, in all things, if you examine it rightly, one and the same genius of both writings, namely of the Gospel and the Epistle, evidently appears: And a little later: The Gospel indeed and the epistle are written not only correctly, as far as the Greek language is concerned, but also with the highest elegance both in words and in arguments, and in the whole composition of the discourse. It is so far from the case that any barbarism or solecism, or finally any idiom, is discovered in them. For the Evangelist was endowed with both, namely language and knowledge, since the Lord himself had granted him these two, knowledge and eloquence at the same time. Nor do the Papists themselves, Cornelius à Lapide, Estius, Tirinus, and others, neglect these documents; Cornelius in his Proemium: The Orthodox likewise agree that the author of the Epistle is Saint John the Apostle, as its inscription holds. The style of the epistle sufficiently indicates the same thing, agreeing in all respects with the Gospel of John, being as it is candid and honeyed with charity, clearly indicating its source, namely the candid and charity-honeyed breast of St. John. Furthermore, he inculcates the same things in this epistle as in the Gospel; as Eusebius skillfully notes. That argument from the same manner of speaking was most thoroughly examined by Flacius in his gloss on the proemium to St. John, that in the Gospel and in this epistle John has his own properties: 1. he uses many explanations everywhere; 2. frequent antitheses; 3. very frequently he confirms by placing one of the contraries affirmatively and negatively, or positively and privatively, by extolling the other; 4. there are many repetitions in them; 5. frequent epanalepses, no asyndeta, not a few appendices of sentences, or appositions placed at the end of a sentence: Also that he has certain words and phrases as if they were his own, or which he uses much more than others. Which is demonstrative, and in this he uses a certain great evidence and efficacy, etc. Which can be read there. For the rest, not to touch upon other marks now, the testimony of the Church has great weight here: since not only does Eusebius in book III, chapter 25, admit the first epistle among the writings of John besides the Gospel, both by recent authors and by the Ancients concerning the controversy. And Jerome in his catalogue: Which is approved by all Ecclesiastical and learned men: But also Augustine, in his tractate or on the 1st Epistle of John: It is a canonical epistle, he says, it is recited by ALL NATIONS; it is retained by the authors of the WHOLE WORLD, it has built up the whole world. However, we do not acknowledge this common sense of the whole Church as a suitable argument, with Cornelius and other Papists, because it was expressed in the Council of Trent, Sess. IV, which is notoriously false to have represented the universal Church; nor do we think that room should be left for the Cornelian distinction handed down here, that there are two kinds of Canonical books of Scripture: the first kind, Proto-Canonical, as if of the first canon, in that they have been held as Canonical by all in every age; and the second kind, Deutero-Canonical, in that the Church or the Fathers have sometimes doubted their authority; yet in a later age they have been received into the canon by all. To which kind, with Sixtus Senensis in his Bibliotheca, book I, page 42, he adds not only the book of Tobit, Judith, and other Apocrypha of the Old Testament; but also certain parts of the Gospel of St. Mark, Luke, and John, the Epistle to the Hebrews, James, Second Peter, Second and Third John, Jude, and the Apocalypse. He calls this first Epistle of John Proto-Canonical, except for one particle of it, which Cornelius does not actually specify. In which distinction many things can be found wanting, both because it attributes to the Church the power to receive some books into the canon; and because it posits one first canon, another second canon; since there is only one canon of Scripture; both because it ascribes canonical authority to the Apocryphal books of the Old Testament, which we have otherwise refuted; and because it makes equal to them the second epistle of Peter, as well as the second and third of John, and also the Apocalypse, nay even the epistle of James, concerning which in the preface he had professed that it was canonical by the faith of God, as well as certain parts of the three Evangelists, all of which are to be received with equal affection of piety, as was defined in the Council of Trent. But of these elsewhere.

We approach those to whom the epistle was written, whom Grotius calls Parthians, because it is called the epistle to the Parthians by Augustine in Lib. II. Quæst. Evang. c. 39. Indeed, doubt was moved concerning this not only by Fr. Junius in animadvers. contr. Bellarm. l. II. de Verbo Dei, cap. 15. n. 22., understanding by Parthians not the inhabitants of Parthia, but pious exiles dispersed outside their native soil, who were once so called in the Scythian language, according to Justin l. 41.; but also Serarius, warning that for 'Parthians' one should read 'Pathmians', because John, having been relegated to the island of Patmos by Domitian, converted the inhabitants to Christ. Sixtus Senensis l. II. Biblioth. pag. 87. says he does not have a sufficiently clear view as to whether that which is called 'to the Parthians' by Augustine is the first of John, or some other of his. But since the words which St. Augustine cited in the same place are read in the first of John, there is no doubt that he pointed to it itself; just as Possidius also in Indic. Tom. of Augustine, and Higynius in epist. I., as also John II. in the epistle to Valerius, allege this epistle under that name: and it can easily be admitted that by Parthians are understood the inhabitants of Parthia, whom Baronius thinks John had visited before, and Cornelius conjectures that they migrated there from Asia after their conversion by John; Sophronius in 'De viris illustribus' handed down that the Parthians were converted by Simon the Canaanite, Bartholomew, and Thomas, and the Persians neighboring them. But Luke in Acts II. commemorates that Parthians were present at the first Pentecost; from whom it is likely that some were converted: to whom, however, we do not deny that others were added, brought to the faith of Christ either by John or by others. For those opinions are not opposed, but subordinated. John the Apostle wrote to the Parthians, says Estius (which nation was situated between the rivers Tigris and Indus near the Medes), because in that region and the surrounding places there were very many Jews from the ancient captivity and dispersion of the ten tribes. Whence also in Acts II., where it treats of the Jews who had come to Jerusalem from various parts of the world, the Parthians, Medes, and Elamites are mentioned in the first place. Therefore, just as Peter gave an epistle to the Jews of the dispersion of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, whom Luke enumerated there in a later place, so also John wrote to the Jews established in the East, that is, in Parthia with the adjacent places: not so, however, that each Apostle did not also wish his epistle to be communicated to the Gentiles of the same regions who had believed in Christ, as being members of the same Church and partakers of the same Sacraments, and called to the same hope of the heavenly kingdom, which Peter signifies in more than one place of his epistle. Indeed, Antonius Quadrius the Jesuit in the East Indies, and Michaël Barulus in the epistles given at Goa in the year of Christ 1555, write that even now some of the Persians profess the Christian faith, and attribute it to St. John, as this Cornelius and from him Tirinus. In these things, however, that this epistle was written to the Parthians, and also that it was written to the Jews, I would not wish to fix that certainty which Grotius established with his customary boldness, even though he is instructed by no sufficient authority: of which he will perhaps be warned below at chapter II.

That the epistle lacks an inscription and final greetings, because it was sent into hostile lands, which is the conjecture of Grotius, is hardly probable: for such fear does not seem to be attributable to St. John. That it was sent from Patmos does not please most, since they wish it to have been written after his return from exile: to others, however, it seems to have been written before the exile. Which opinion is to be preferred in our judgment. That it was written in old age seems to be gathered by Cornelius from his own words, by which he calls himself an elder, and the faithful his little children. But I do not see St. John using the name of Elder for himself in this epistle. Cornelius adds that it also appears from the fact that, as if an old man, he inculcates almost nothing but charity; and from Thomas Anglicus it has it thus: St. John seems now an old man, and as if forgetful of all earthly things and panting for Christ, here just as in the Gospel, absorbed by the magnitude of the mystery and charity of Christ, having omitted the name just as the greeting, he begins from the very mystery so sublime, so that he may carry the reader with him, and thus insinuate that he is the author of this epistle and the Gospel. The words of the first epistle, with which he is wonderfully delighted and ravished with Christ incarnate, sufficiently indicate the same thing (with Cornelius as author). But those are not sufficiently firm. Perhaps those things which others observe are more certain, primarily that this epistle was not written until after Jerusalem was destroyed. Baronius in the year of Christ 99. He rejects the writing to the twenty-fifth year of Nerva from the destruction of Jerusalem. That he lived after all the Apostles is undoubted in Ecclesiastical Antiquity: some also gather from John XXI. 22 that he was an eyewitness of the destruction. But most affirm that John wrote this epistle in his extreme old age, just as Ambrose also in Ps. XXXVI. says: that John, now an old man, began to write the Gospel and the Epistles. And the Glossa ordinaria observes that John wrote both the Gospel and the Epistles after he returned from Patmos. But Domitian, the successor of Titus, had forced him into exile, whence according to this opinion it is necessary that these writings of St. John are later than the destruction of Jerusalem. Just as most say that the Apocalypse was written shortly before the death of St. John, which as it is written today is the last in the Biblical canon: So also it is believed to be the last written among the Johannine monuments, with which the holy Apostle and Evangelist sealed the canon of the New Testament, placing a colophon upon it, as the last among the Apostles in age, with the addition of a most grave attestation concerning adding nothing, taking away nothing, by which was concluded by him as his prophetic Apocalypse, so the entire revelation of the divinely inspired New Testament scripture. Although indeed Epiphanius in Section XXIV teaches against the Basilidians, especially the offspring of the Simonians, that this epistle was directed: yet most others think that it was written primarily against Cerinthus and Ebion. It is certainly opposed to their heresy no less than to that of the Basilidians. But Cerinthus and Ebion were later than the destruction of Jerusalem. Therefore Bartholomew Petri does not deserve approval in his annotations on 1 John 5:8, because this epistle was written long before the destruction of the city. For whence will that be taught? Which nevertheless Grotius did not hesitate to assert, that the present epistle was written before that destruction at 1 John 2:17. But for what purpose he contends this, we shall see in that place.

The cause Grotius assigns a twofold cause for the writing of this epistle: the one, that the Apostle might urge a zeal for concord; the other, that he might command that Pseudo-Prophets and Anti-Christs be guarded against. But in this way the chief reason and proper scope of the epistle is neglected; which, if it be weighed more accurately, is not so much an exhortation concerning a zeal for peace and concord, or mutual love, as it is an instruction concerning the λόγῳ, the incarnation of the Son of God, and communion with the same, from which afterwards υἱοθεσία is derived, not only toward one's neighbor, but primarily toward God; inasmuch as He, by His supreme and inestimable love, out of which He gave us His Son, and by which we are rendered partakers of communion with God the Father Himself and of the sonship of God, and have eternal life in Him, does not so much excite us to the love of Himself as inflame us. In which sense Gregory rightly says (hom. XV. in Ezech.): Do we seek to be kindled in our heart by the fire of charity? Let us weigh the words of John, all of whose speech is vaporized by the fire of charity. And Augustine in the preface to the Epistle: Charity is most highly commended; for he is about to speak much, and almost everything, about charity. He who has within himself that from which he may hear, it is necessary that he rejoice at what he hears. For thus will that reading be to him like oil on a flame. Furthermore, St. Jerome also says of him in Ezech. c. II: John, he says, reclined on His breast, that he might draw the streams of wisdom, that he might be able to say: In the beginning was the Word. And Epiphanius (hæres. LXXIII): John, truly the son of thunder, through his own grandiloquence, as if from certain clouds, persuaded us of a pious understanding concerning the Son from the enigmas of wisdom. The doctrine concerning Christ and His benefits certainly holds the primacy in this epistle, so that those who believe in Christ may be rendered certain of eternal life, which St. John also made the scope of his εὐαγγελογραφίας, chapter 20, 31. Therefore, charity is brought forward as the consequence and evidence and τεκμήριον of faith in Christ, so that it may render us certain a posteriori of the grace of God in Christ, of communion with God, of regeneration, of υἱοθεσία, and of eternal life, just as he wished to render us more certain of salvation a priori from the testimony of the three witnesses in heaven, that is, of the Most Holy Trinity, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit: as well as from the testimony of the three witnesses on earth, through whom the Most Holy Trinity perpetually testifies in the Church and seals the faithful concerning salvation and eternal life. Wherefore he does not so much command as commend charity, and with arguments that are most effective and that greatly inflame the hearts of the faithful: nor does he, in the Pauline manner, treat distinctly first of faith and then of charity, and perform the parts of teaching and admonishing separately, but he immediately intermixes the duties of charity with doctrine, and thus deduces from it, as it were, πορισματικῶς with remarkable δεινότητι, and informs rather than commands concerning the debt of charity, and demonstrates its necessary connection with faith, and shows the use of faith and love and divine grace toward us rather than demands it; yet he adheres to his chief scope and intention, namely, the doctrine concerning Christ and faith in Christ, with an exhortation to perseverance in the same, and the flight of heretics who overturn the same. Flacius therefore rightly weighed the matter when he wrote thus concerning the scope and argument of this: Authors have discussed the argument of this epistle in entirely different ways: to me, however, it seems that here too the Evangelist is likewise showing only that Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, and exhorting all to embrace Him with a sincere heart, and in turn to flee from all contrary things that pull us away from Him, whether they be errors and seducers, or even the allurements of the world and an unpious life. And afterwards: Thus this whole epistle shows and celebrates Christ and His most gracious Father, together with His benefits, and most ardently stimulates us to embrace and retain Him by faith: so that it is entirely, according to the very name of the author, a certain Evangelical grace-discourse, but yet, from time to time, as occasion offers, it endeavors to excite and increase love toward one's neighbor also, as a stream flowing from the most abundant fountain of the love of God toward us. Which may also become clear from the economy of the parts of the epistle, and the reason and method of its treatment, which Flacius has not inconveniently set forth. He presents it thus: But so that we may nevertheless agree with other expositors that there are more scopes or principal parts for the sake of teaching, let them indeed be four in number: of which the first, in the first two chapters, treats mostly of embracing Christ and His benefit of justification and the flight of those things which draw us away from Him. The second part, chapter III, discusses adoption and regeneration and its fruits, whether externally and toward others, or even toward ourselves, and then also our own toward our neighbor. The final part, in the last chapter, treats of faith and its object, namely, of the testimonies upon which it depends, and of the benefits or goods which follow it. Concerning the mode and method of treatment, he has this: The reason and method of the treatment of this epistle may seem to be such as is usually that of solicitous fathers when they instruct and correct their most beloved children, and such as the necessity of the tender children and little ones of Christ demands, so that they may more often instill the same things, which they indeed also deem to be most necessary for them, and propose the primary documents of piety as if comprehended in brief summaries or aphorisms. He nevertheless produces the principal propositions of this epistle from their sources, which, being repeatedly iterated and inculcated, he fortifies and establishes with other and different arguments and reasons: but the whole epistle mostly shows and celebrates and offers that Passover of ours, sacrificed for us, and applies it most aptly to that method indicated before. Not discordant with these are those things which [are found] in the preface to the Gospel of John. are observed by B. Luther: Luther, of pious memory, in his Domestic Postil also notes that property of the speech and doctrine of this Evangelist, that for the most part he first leads men to Christ, then through Him to the Father: so that he may teach the sinner first, after contrition, to acknowledge this only Lamb of God taking away his sins: when he has acknowledged His immense kindness toward him through His passion and benefits, he may embrace Him with his whole heart: and thus further begin, through this Legate and Mediator, to acknowledge and embrace the Father Himself also, and His more than paternal or maternal spirit toward us, who bestowed this most beloved Son upon us for a most sorrowful death, and who, as the interpreter of His will, and the witness and most certain pledge of His love toward us, as if drawn from His own bosom, sent Him away into this sad valley of miseries for the sake of our salvation, when we were still entirely His enemies.

The Athanasian Synopsis agrees no less: it says this epistle was written in order to remind (ὑπομιμνήσκειν) those who had already believed in the Lord. And first indeed, it says, he discourses in this epistle also concerning the Divinity of the Word, showing that It is always in GOD, and teaching that the Father is light, so that we may thus know the Word to be from the Father, as brightness from Light. But while discoursing concerning the Divinity of the Word, he sets forth our faith's mystery as not a new thing, but as eternal from the beginning, now however manifested in the Lord, because He is eternal life and the true God. He also sets forth the cause for which the Word came to us and appeared, namely, that He might dissolve the works of the Devil, and deliver us from death, and cause us to acknowledge the Father, and the Son our Lord Jesus Christ. He writes therefore to every age, to children, to adolescents, to the old, that God has made Himself known, and that the diabolical operation has henceforth been deleted and conquered by death. And these things are concerning the principal argument. As for the rest, Athanasius continues, throughout the whole epistle he teaches love, wishing that we should love one another, for the reason that Christ also loved us. And afterwards: He exhorts throughout the whole epistle those who believe in the Lord, that they should not be of a dejected spirit if they are held in hatred in this world, but rather that they should rejoice: for the reason that the hatred of this world declares that believers have migrated from this world, and henceforth converse in the heavens. And at the foot of the epistle he warns again that the Son of God is eternal life and the true God, and that we should serve Him, and keep ourselves from idols. The comparison of the Pauline and Johannine treatment observed by Flacius in the cited place also contributes to this: In the Epistles this Evangelist seems to distinguish the parts of doctrine less openly than Paul, who for the most part urges first contrition, afterwards justification, and lastly new obedience: first showing the evil tree, accusing and as it were cutting it down: then planting and generating a good one: lastly describing its good fruits, and as it were producing them: here he passes from time to time by occasion from the doctrine of faith and Christ to the documents of charity, and conversely returns from there to here. Nor indeed has the Apostle spoken so much about avoiding factions as about the kind of mutual love to be exhibited, and he commends it most effectively.

Furthermore, as to the other cause of the writing of St. John touched upon by Grotius concerning the rumor of certain ones behaving as liberators of the Jewish people sent by God; nothing can be brought forward concerning that which pertains to this, nor does St. John hint at it with any word. Nor are those AntiChrists designated by St. John who sold themselves as the Messiah, the liberator of the Jews; but those who denied that Jesus is the Son of God, the Christ, the Savior of men, such as were primarily Ebion and Cerinthus with Carpocrates; as Tertullian notes in his book on prescription, chapter 48. After him (Carpocrates) the heretic Cerinthus broke out, teaching similar things. For he himself also proposes Christ as a man born from the seed of David, contending that he was made that man without Divinity. That Cerinthus scattered this heresy in Asia, Epiphanius, heresy 28, is the author; with John preaching in the same place, concerning which also Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 3. Similar things concerning the heresy of Ebion have been handed down by Tertullian on the flesh of Christ, Epiphanius, heresy 30, Eusebius, book 3, chapter 23. And Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 11, testifies that John wished to remove that error concerning the Word which had been sown by Cerinthus. Jerome in the prologue to Matthew: When John, he says, was in Asia, and already then the seeds of the heretics Cerinthus, Ebion, and others were sprouting, who deny that Christ has come in the flesh, he was compelled by almost all the Bishops of Asia at that time and by the embassies of many Churches to write more deeply concerning the Divinity of the Savior and to break forth to the Word of God himself, if I may so say, with a boldness not so much audacious as happy. Epiphanius, heresy 51: After, he says, Ebion and Cerinthus and their accomplices preached in Asia that Christ was a mere man from the womb, the Holy Spirit there produced for the world this holy herb or shrub, putting the serpent to flight and destroying the tyranny of the Devil. For there St. John, after his old age, is commanded by the Holy Spirit to preach, and to turn back the erring into the way, not by force, but by will, revealing to believers the light of God, which is in the holy doctrine of God. Blessed Luther observes in his preface to John: As in the Gospel he urges faith, so in this Epistle, which ought deservedly to follow it, he must encounter those who boast of faith without works, and teach that works do not fail where faith is: If they fail, that faith is not true faith, but a lie and darkness. Which, however, he professes is also opposed to the Cerinthians, who denied that Christ came in the flesh; and he observes that the spirit of AntiChrist also tends toward this: Because he who wishes to be justified and saved by his own works does the same as if he denied Christ. For indeed Christ came into the flesh for this reason, that He might justify and save us without works, solely through His blood. And therefore Blessed Luther warns that this epistle fights against both parties, both against those who boast of faith without works; and those who wish to be justified by works, and to hold a middle way, that through faith we are freed from sins, justified, and once justified we exercise good works and charity promptly without any impulse. That error concerning the necessity of good works for salvation flows from the doctrine of Cerinthus, that Christ was a man naked as to matter, and was himself subject to the law, whence no place is left for either satisfaction or his merit, nor can his obedience, whether passive or active, be imputed to us for salvation, but it behooves us to obtain salvation by our own works. In which manner says Cyril, exegesis to Valerius on the incarnation of the Word: Could one who died for all pay the price for all, the just for the unjust, if we say that that suffering was of a mere man! Unless God had granted salvation, says Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 20, we would not firmly possess it, and unless man had been joined to our God, he (man) could not have become a participant in incorruptibility. Which therefore Irenaeus urges against the Ebionites, book 3, chapter 59. How can the Ebionites be saved, unless it is God who has worked their salvation upon the earth, and how shall man pass to God, if God does not (pass) into man, namely through the incarnation or ἐνανθρώπησιν? And therefore Eusebius joins both errors in the heresy of the Ebionites, book 3, chapter 27, that the Ebionites defended both. For him, he says, they considered simple and common, and nothing other than a man, who had been made righteous by the progress of virtue: but begotten from the intercourse of a man with Mary. Furthermore, they considered the observance of the law to be entirely necessary for themselves, as if they were not able to obtain salvation through faith in Christ alone and the life led from it. Therefore Jacobus Nauclerus, vol. II, Chronogr. gener. p. 464, says: Ebion judged that the observance of the law must be kept, and that faith in Christ was not sufficient for salvation. Regarding Cerinthus, Epiphanius also observes, heresy 98, that he was one of the pseudo-apostles who caused disturbances when James and those who were with him wrote letters to Antioch (Acts 15), and that he, along with his followers, was noted by Paul, Galatians 2:3, to whom the Apostle opposes, Galatians 2:21, this sentiment: I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me. For the life which I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me. I do not frustrate the grace of God. For if you wish to be justified by the law, you have fallen from grace. But we through the Spirit wait for the hope of righteousness by faith, etc. Tertullian teaches that these heretics were noted as Antichrists by St. John, in his book concerning Prescription against Heretics, chapter 33. But in his epistle (John) calls those especially Anti-Christs, who deny that Christ has come in the flesh, and who do not think that Jesus is the Son of God. Marcion championed the former, Hebion the latter. Likewise: Writing to the Galatians (Paul) inveighs against the observers and defenders of circumcision and in what way the Apostle inveighs against the observers of the law in that epistle, we have taught in its proper place: namely, in that they establish that they obtain salvation through the observation of the law, and that it is necessary for salvation.

Since, therefore, it is evident from these things that the present epistle is more didactic than hortatory, its distribution according to the chapters of doctrine is to be established: the first of which is concerning the person and office of Christ, where first concerning the incarnation of the eternal Word, or the manifestation of eternal life, which he confirms as an αὐτόπτης καὶ ἀυτήκοος witness, and concerning the chief end of that, communion with the Father and the Son, and the joy arising thence, as well as concerning that which is necessarily προσκειμένῳ to those who have communion with God, that since God is light, in whom there is no darkness, they themselves must walk in the light, not in darkness, inasmuch as they have both been purged from all sin by the blood of Christ, and on account of the same, provided they perform repentance, they obtain the remission of sins, chapter 1. Which

Chapter II illustrates partly by the duty of our office, that we may not sin, partly by the propitiatory office of Christ: there showing the necessity of the observation of the commandments, etc., but here explaining the benefits of Christ, the incarnation of the Word, asserting that the doctrine concerning Christ is not new, but ancient, and diligently commending it to the faithful, both universally and to individuals, elders, juniors, and little children, with an exhortation concerning the fleeing from and the love of the world, both as to life and as to doctrine, the Anti-Christ, inasmuch as they are contrary to our duties, and to the benefits of Christ, and repugnant to the doctrine of Christ, concerning which the Holy Spirit confirms the faithful. Whence they are warned that they should remain in the doctrine of Christ, who promised us eternal life, and having left the seducers, they should acquiesce in those things which the anointing, that is, the Holy Spirit, teaches, and that they should have confidence in the coming of Christ, and that they should do justice; since he himself is just. Concerning this chapter, therefore, Flacius judges thus, that it is shown in the same the medium through which the Savior is apprehended with the Father, namely, by embracing his true doctrine from the heart; yet there is interspersed there in four verses a precept concerning love, and immediately one returns in verse 12 to the doctrine concerning embracing this Savior together with his benefits; thence in verse 15 he begins to warn concerning avoiding those contrary things which abstract us from Christ and his salvation, and first indeed concerning the flight from the desires, allurements, and frauds of the world: but soon in verse 18 he teaches that seducers are to be avoided, and that one must persist most constantly in the received Gospel and Christ, to which they themselves are also warned and impelled by the indwelling Holy Spirit and the new man.

There follows now in the third chapter concerning the other end of the coming of the Son of God, our adoption or ὑοθεσίᾳ, how great this good is, and joined to it both our purification and the confidence of our heart. He confirms the former partly from this, that he came into the world to take away our sins and to dissolve the works of the Devil; partly that the regenerate do not sin, but exercise justice, and love the brethren; partly that the doctrine of Christ tends to this, and whence our translation from death into life is recognized: partly that in this also Christ has gone before us by his own example, who laid down his soul for us. But this (our confidence), he establishes from divine virtue and his gracious care and hearing, and repeats the sum of the doctrine of Christ, which embraces faith in Christ and mutual love.

To this information he subjects again in Chapter IV a brief warning concerning testing the Spirits and concerning loving one's neighbor, which duty of love he deduces from regeneration and the highest benefit of divine love toward us by the mission of the Only-Begotten Son, and he teaches that love toward one's neighbor cannot be separated from the love of God, and that the union of the faithful with God has the love of God and neighbor as its companion.

In the final chapter, he treats explicitly of faith in Christ Jesus, both its fruit, love and victory over the world, and its confirmation by the signs and proofs of Christ's advent; by the baptism of water and blood poured out on the cross, as also by the Spirit testifying to the truth of the Word, and also by the testimony partly of the three witnesses in heaven concerning Jesus the Son of God, Christ and Savior of the world, and partly of the three witnesses on earth in the Church, by the ministry of the Word, as also by the Sacrament of Baptism and the Holy Eucharist; then the end, eternal life, which we have in the Son of God through faith; then the adjunct, the confidence of being heard in prayers even for a sinning brother, provided he does not commit the sin against the Holy Spirit, and abstinence from voluntary sins. Finally, he repeats the sum of saving faith through a certain ἀνακεφαλαίωσις, which is completed both by the advent of the Son of God and by the gift of the knowledge of the true God and communion with the same in his Son Christ Jesus, inasmuch as he is the true God and eternal life, with a final warning to flee idols, which cannot coexist with the True God.

Therefore, two parts of the epistle can be established: The first concerning the incarnate Word and his benefits, in the first four chapters: the first of which is communion with God, to which is subjoined a warning concerning the love of the brethren, and fleeing the world and the spirit of the Anti-Christ, ch. I and II. The second is ὑοθεσία and adoption, ch. III, to which is again attached a warning concerning testing the spirits and concerning the love of one's neighbor, ch. IV. The latter is concerning faith in Christ, ch. V.

Interpreters of the first Johannine [epistle], besides the common ones, are found to be St. Augustine, Bede, Nicetas, Oecumenius, Augustinus de Ancona, Petrus Aureolus, Adam Sasbouth, Claudius Guillaudus, Johan. Gagnejus, Joh. Antoninus Dalphinus, Johan. Heffelius, Joh. Lorinus, Nicol. Serarius, Libertus Fromondus, Joh. Mariana, Thomas Naogeorgius, Erasmus, Valla, Joh. à Loranio. From our own: B. Luther, Johan. Huss, Johan. Baptista, Henricus Eckardi, Eilhardus Lubinus, Johan. Camirus, Ægidius Hunnius, Nicol. Selneccerus, Erasmus Sarcerius, Victor. Strigelius. From the Reformed: Zwingli, Johan. Calvin, Henricus Bullinger, Rudolphus Gualtherus, Franc. Gomarus, Johannes Buxtorf, Guilh. Perkins, as also Nicol. Hemmingius. From the Anti-Trinitarians: F. Socinus and Jonas Schlichtingius.

PART I. OF THE EPISTLE, Concerning the incarnation of the Word and its fruits.

Latin:

I. N. J. ANNOTATA AD PRIOREM JOHANNIS EPISTOLAM PROLEGOMENA. GROTIANUM PRÆLOQUIUM.

HÆc epistola quin sit Apostoli Johannis, nunquam in Ecclesia dubitatum est, ut nos docent Eusebius, Hieronymus, alii. Vocata olim fuit epistola ad Parthos, ut Augustinus testatur: id est, ad Judæos CHRISTUM professos, qui non sub Romanorum, sed Parthorum vivebant imperio, in locis trans Euphratem, ubi ingens Judæorum erat multitudo, ut Neardæ, Nisibi & aliis in locis. Vide Josephum antiquæ historiæ XVII. 12. Et hanc causam puto, cur hæc epistola neque in fronte nomen titulumque Apostoli, neque in fine salutationes Apostolici moris contineat. Quia nimirum in terras ho- stiles Romanis hæc epistola per mercatores Ephesios mit- tebatur, multumque nocere poterat Christianis, si depre- hensum fuisset hoc, quanquam innocens, literarum com- mercium. Puto autem scriptam, ut & alibi dixi ex Patmo hanc epistolam, non multo ante excidium Hie- rosolymorum, duabus maxime de causis: primum ut Christiani illarum partium pacem amicitiamque inter se colerent, neque factionibus illis, quæ Judæos Trans- Euphratenses misere lacerabant, paterentur se implica- ri, sed operam darent, ut concordiæ studio à cæteris po- pularibus suis dignoscerentur. Deinde ne fama illuc per- lata esse aliquos in Judæa, qui se à Deo missos dicerent ad populum liberandum, ad eos & ipsi cum Judæis aliis concurrerent, sed firme tenerent, neminem esse à Deo missum, qui contraria afferret iis, quæ Jesus vere Mes- sias & vere populi liberator attulerat: simulque in im- postoribus illis prædictionem Jesu veritatem agnoscerent. De talibus impostoribus, qui & ἀντίχριστοι dicuntur, quia Christi aut titulum aut munus sibi vindicabant, di- ximus ad Matth. XXIV. v. 5. Illis adde Simonem Barjo- nam, quem Judæi quidam confusis nominibus vicinis pri- orem Barchochebam vocant, & illos, de quibus Josephus Belli Judaici VI. 30.

OBSERVATIONES.

Autor epistolæ citra controversiam est S. Johannes Apostolus & Evangelista: Sed ejus rei probandæ causa non tani Docto- rum quorundam testimonia, quæ postremum in classe probationum locum occupant, quam a- lia documenta imprimis ab internis κριτηρίοις de- sumpta, afferenda. E quibus ipsimet Doctores illi de sua sententia confirmati sunt. Eusebius certe l. VII. hist. Eccles. cap. 25. verbis Dionysii Alexan- drini è styli charactere ac similibus internis τεκμη- ρίοις, eundem esse præsentis epistolæ Autorem, qui Evangelium Johanni adscriptum consignavit, statuminat, utriusque singularem consonantiam urgens: Nam Evangelium & epistola sibi mutuo consonant, & eodem ordiuntur modo. Sic enim incipit Evangelium: In principio erat Verbum: Epistola vero: Quod fuit ab initio. In illo dicitur: Et Verbum caro factum est, & habitavit in nobis: Et vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam quasi Unigeniti à Patre. Hæc vero eadem habet, paulisper tantum immutata: Quod audivimus, quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod perspeximus, & manus nostræ contre- ctaverunt, de Verbo vitæ: & vita manifestata est. Hæc enim ille veluti modulationis præludia præmit- tit, adversus eos, qui Christum in carne advenisse ne- gabant, ut in sequentibus ostendit. Quamobrem de industria subjunxit: Et quod vidimus testamur, & annuntiamus vobis vitam æternam, quæ erat apud Patrem, & apparuit nobis. Quod vidi- mus & audivimus, nuntiamus vobis. Adeo totus ex se ipse pendet & à propositionibus suis ne latum quidem unguem discedit, sed iisdem pene capitibus ac verbis cuncta prosequitur. Ex quibus nos qui- dem nonnulla breviter suggeremus. Qui vero attente perlegerit, in utroque sæpius vitam, lucem, fugam te- nebrarum, frequenter veritatem, gratiam, gaudium, carnem & sanguinem Domini, judicium, peccato- rum remissionem, Dei erga nos dilectionem, mutua inter nos dilectionis præceptum, & universa præcepta servanda esse reperiet. Adhæc condemnationis elo- gium adversus mundum, Diabolum, & Anti-Chri- stum, promissio Sancti Spiritus, adoptio filiorum Dei, fides in omnibus à nobis præstanda: Pater & Filius ubique nominati in utroque passim occurrunt. De- nique in omnibus, si recte examinaveris, unus idemq; utriusq; scriptionis genius Evangelii nimirum & Epistolæ evidenter apparet: Et paulo post: Evan- gelium quidem & epistola non modo emendate, quod ad Græcum sermonem attinet, verum etiam cum summa elegantia tum in verbis tum in argumenta- tionibus, & in tota orationis compositione perscri- ptæ sunt. Tantum abest, ut barbarismus aliquis aut solæcismus, aut denique idiotismus quispiam in illis deprehendatur. Utroque enim præditus erat Evangelistes, sermone nimirum ac scientia, cum hæc duo ipsi Dominus concessisset, scientiam simul & elo- quentiam. Nec negligunt ea documenta ipsimet Pontificii Cornelius à Lapide, Estius, Tirinus alii, Cornelius in Procœmio: Consentiunt pariter Or- thodoxi, autorem Epistolæ esse sanctum Johannem Apostolum, uti habet ejus inscriptio. Idipsum sa- tis indicat stylus epistolæ, per omnia consentiens Ev- angelio Johannis, utpote candidus & charitate mel- leus, plane indicans suum fontem, puta pectus S. Jo- hannis candidum & charitate melleum. Adhæc eadem in hac epistola, quæ in Evangelio inculcat; ut solerter advertit Eusebius. Argumentum illud ab eodem dicendi genere cum maxime exæquu- tus est Flacius in glossa in procœmio in S. Johannem, quod in Evangelio & in hac epistola Johannes suas habeat proprietates 1. multas ubique adhi- beat explicationes; 2. crebras antitheses; 3. valde crebro affirmative & negative seu positive & privative ponendo alterum contrariorum ex- tollendo alterum confirmet; 4. multæ in iis re- petitiones; 5. crebræ epanalepses, asyntheta nulla, appendices sententiarum non paucas, vel ap- positiones fini sententiæ subjectas: Item quod habeat quædam vocabula & phrases quasi pro- prias, aut quibus ipse præ aliis multum utitur. Quod demonstrativum hoc est, & in hoc ma- gna quadam evidentia & efficacitate adhibeat &c. Quæ illic legi poterunt. De cætero ut alia jam non attingamus γνωρίσματα, magnum omnino mo- mentum hic habet Ecclesiæ testimonium: quum non tantum Eusebius l. III. c. 25. inter Johannis scri- pta præter Evangelium prior quoque epistola, tum à recentioribus, tum ab Antiquis circa controver- siam admittitur. Et Hieronymus in catal. Quæ ab universis Ecclesiasticis & eruditis viris probatur: Sed etiam Augustinus tr. vel in epist. 1. Johann. Canonica, inquiat, est ipsa epistola, per OMNES GENTES recitatur; ORBIS TERRÆ autoribus retinetur, orbem terrarum ipsa ædificavit. Hu- jus tamen communis Ecclesiæ totius sensus argu- mentum idoneum non agnoscimus cum Cornelio aliisque Papisequis, quod expressum sit in Concilio Tridentino, Sess. IV. quod Ecclesiam universam re- præsentasse notorie falsum est; neque distinctioni Cornelianæ hic traditæ locum relinquendum cen- semus, quod duplicis generis libri Canonici Scri- pturæ sint, primi generis, Proto-Canonici, quasi primi canonis, eo quod omni ævo apud omnes ha- biti sint Canonici; & secundi generis Deutero-Ca- nonici, eo quod aliquando Ecclesia aut Patres de eorum autoritate dubitarint; posteriori tamen æ- vo ab omnibus in canonem sint recepti. Cui generi cum Sixto Senensi Biblioth. l. I. pag. 42. ac- censet non tantum librum Tobiæ, Judith, aliosq; Veteris Testamenti Apocryphos; sed & partes quasdam Evangelii S. Marci, Lucæ, & Johannis, Epistolam ad Ebræos, Jacobi, Secundam Petri, Se- cundam & tertiam Johannis, Judæ & Apocaly- psin. Proto-Canonicam autem hanc primam Jo- hannis dicit, excepta una ejus particula, quam vero non exprimit Cornelius. In qua distinctione multa desiderari possunt, tum quod Ecclesiæ po- testatem tribuat libros aliquos in canonem reci- pere; tum quod alium primum canonem, alium secundum canonem constitnat; quum non nisi unus tantum canon sit Scripturæ; tum quod libris Vet. Test. Apocryphis Canonicam autoritatem adscribat, quam alias profligavimus; tum quod iisdem pares faciat epistolam posteriorem Petri, necnon secundam ac tertiam Johannis, ut & Apo- calypsin, imo epistolam Jacobi quoque, de qua in procœmio professus erat de fide Dei eam esse Ca- nonicam, necnon partes quasdam trium Evange- listarum, quæ vero omnia pari pietatis affectu suscipienda, ut in Concilio Tridentino definitum. Sed de his alibi.

Accedimus ad eos, ad quos perscripta epistola, quos Parthos dicit Grotius, quia ab Augustino epi- stola ad Parthos vocata l. II. Quæst. Evang. c. 39. Dubium vero movit de eo non tantum Fr. Junius in animadvers. contr. Bellarm. l. II. de Verbo Dei, cap. 15. n. 22. per Parthos non incolas Parthia intelli- gens, sed pios exules dispersos extra natale solum, qui sermone Scythico teste Justino l. 41. olim ita dicti; Sed & Serarius pro Parthos monens legendum esse Pathmios, quia in Pathmos insulam à Domitiano relegatus Johannes incolas ad Christum convertit. Sixtus Senensis l. II. Biblioth. pag. 87. non satis per- spectum se habere ait, an illa ab Augustino ad Par- thos dicta prior Johannis sit, an alia quædam ejus- dem. Sed quum verba, quæ ibidem adduxit S. Augustinus, in prima Johannis legantur, quin ipsam indigitarit, dubium nullum est; quemadmodum & Possidius in Indic. Tom. Augustini & Higynius in epist. I. ut & Johannes II. in epist. ad Valerium hanc epistolam sub isto nomine allegant: facileque ad- mitti potest, Parthos intelligi Parthiæ incolas, quos antea Johannem adiisse Baronius putat, ex Asia post conversionem à Johanne factam eo migrasse con- jectat Cornelius; à Simone Cananæo, Bartholomæo & Thoma conversos Parthos, eisque vicinos Per- sas tradidit Sophronius de viris illustribus. Sed jam in prima Pentecoste Parthos præsto fuisse Lucas Act. II. commemorat; è quibus nonnullos conversos esse verisimile est: quibus tamen alios accessisse sive à Johane, sive ab aliis etiam ad fidem Christi perductos, non repugnamus. Non enim oppositæ sunt illæ sententiæ, sed subordinatæ. Scripsit ad Parthos, inquit Estius, Johannes Aposto- lus (quæ gens sita erat inter flumina Tygrim & In- dum juxta Medos) quod in ea regione locisque circum- vicinis plurimi essent Judæi ex antiqua captivitate & dispersione decem tribuum. Unde & Act. II. ubi de Judæis, qui ex variis mundi partibus Hierosolymam venerant, agitur, primo loco referuntur Parthi, Me- di, Elamitæ. Igitur quemadmodum Petrus epistolam dedit ad Judæos dispersionis Ponti, Galatiæ, Cappado- ciæ, Asiæ, Bithyniæ, quos Lucas illic enumeravit loco posteriore, sic & Johannes scripsit ad Judæos in Oriente constitutos, id est, in Parthia cum locis adjacentibus: non ita tamen, quin uterque Apostolus suam episto- lam etiam communicatam voluerit gentilibus ea- rundem regionum, qui in Christo crediderant, ut- pote membris ejusdem Ecclesiæ & eorundem Sacra- mentorum consortibus, & ad eandem spem regni cœ- lestis vocatis, id quod Petrus non uno loco suæ epistolæ significat. Sane Antonius Quadrius Jesuita in In- dia orientali, & Michaël Barulus in Epistolis Goa datis Anno Christi 1555. scribunt, etiamnum non- nullos è Persis fidem Christianam profiteri, eam- que S. Johanni acceptam ferre, ut hic Cornelius & ex eo Tirinus. In istis tamen, quod hæc epi- stola ad Parthos, etiam quod ad Judæos perscri- pta sit, nolim eam certitudinem figere, quam pro solita audacia Grotius constituit, etsi nulla suffi- ciente instructus autoritate: Quo de infra ad cap. II. forte monebitur.

Inscriptione autem ac salutationibus finalibus quod careat epistola, quod in terras hostiles mis- sa, quæ Grotii est conjectura, vix probabile est: Talis enim metus non videtur S. Johanni tribu- endus. Ex Pathmo eandem missam, plerisque haud placet, quum eam post reditum ab exilio scriptam velint: aliis tamen videtur ante exi- lium eandem exaratam esse. Quæ sententia no- stro judicio præferenda est. In senio scriptam ex verbis ipsius, quibus se seniorem vocat, fideles vero filiolos, colligi videtur Cornelio. Sed non video nomen Senioris de se usurpare in hac qui- dem epistola S. Johannem: Addit Cornelius, id etiam ex eo apparere, quod quasi senex non a- liud pene quam charitatem inculcet; & ex Tho- ma Anglico ita habet: Videtur S. Johannes jam Senex, & omnium quasi terrenorum oblitus ac an- helans ad Christum, hic æque ac in Evangelio, ma- gnitudine mysterii & charitatis Christi absorptus omisso nomine æque ac salutatione ab ipso mysterio tam sublimi ordiri, ut eo secum rapiat lectorem, itaque insinuet, se epistolæ hujus ac Evangelii esse Autorem. Idipsum (Cornelio Autore) satis indi- cant primæ epistolæ verba, quibus cum Christo in- carnato mire deliciatur & diffuaviatur. Non autem sunt illa satis firma. Certiora forte sunt, quæ alii observant, imprimis quod epistola hæc non sit scripta, nisi post Hierosolymam ever- sam. Baronius in ann. Christi 99. Nervæ I. vi- gesimum quintum ab excidio Hierosolymitano scriptionem rejicit. Vixisse eum post omnes Apostolos, in Antiquitate Ecclesiastica indubi- um: nonnulli etiam è Joh. XXI. 22. colligunt, eundem testem excidii oculatum fuisse. Plerique vero in ultima senecta Johannem hanc epistolam scripsisse affirmant, quomodo & Ambrosius in Ps. XXXVI. ait: Johannem jam Senem scribere cœpisse Evangelium & Epistolas. Et Glossa ordi- naria observat, tum Evangelium tum Epistolas Johannem scripsisse, postquam è Pathmo rediit. In exilium autem eundem coëgerat Domitianus Titi successor, unde juxta hanc sententiam ne- cessum est excidio Hierosolymitano posteriora esse ista scripta S. Johannis. Quemadmodum Apo- calypsin plerique paulo ante mortem S. Johannis scriptam dicunt, quæ uti hodie scriptum est ul- timum in canone Biblico: Ita etiam inter Johan- nea monumenta scriptum esse ultimum creditur, quo obsignarit canonem Novi Testamenti S. Apostolus & Evangelista, eidem imponens colo- phonem, ceu ætate postremus inter Apostolos, addita gravissima attestatione de nihil addendo, nihil demendo, qua conclusa ab ipso est ut Pro- phetica ejus ἀποκάλυψις, ita universa revelatio scripturæ Novi Testamenti divinitus inspiratæ. Quanquam vero Epiphanius Sect. XXIV. doceat contra Basilidianos, potissimum, Simonianorum sobolem, hanc epistolam directam esse: plerique tamen alii censent, scriptam imprimis esse adver- sus Cerinthum & Ebionem. Eorum certe hæresi non minus, quam Basilidianorum opposita est. Ce- rinthus autem & Ebion posteriores fuerunt excidio Hierosolymitano. Non ergo Bartholomæus Petri in annot. ad 1. Joh. V. 8. calculum meretur, quod diu hæc epistola ante excidium urbis scripta sit. Unde enim id docebitur? Quod tamen non dubitavit etiam asserere Grotius, ante excidium illud exara- tam esse præsentem epistolam ad 1. Joh. II. 17. Sed id quo fine contendat, istic loci visuri sumus.

Causam Causam scriptionis hujus epistolæ geminam assignat Grotius, alteram ut concordiæ studium suaderet, alteram ut Pseudo-Prophetas & Anti- Christos caveri juberet Apostolus: Sed ita præ- cipua ratio & scopus proprius epistolæ negligitur: quæ si accuratius expendatur, non tam est exhorta- tio de pacis & concordiæ studio, aut mutua dilectio- ne, quam informatio de τῷ λόγῳ, Filii DEI in- carnatione, ejusdem communione, è qua post- modum υἱοθεσία ad charitatem non proximi tan- tum, sed imprimis Dei deducitur, utpote qui summa sua & inæstimabili dilectione, ex qua nobis Filium suum donavit, nosque in ipso com- munionis cum ipso Deo Patre & filiationis Dei participes reddamur ac vitam æternam in ipso ha- beamus, nos ad sui dilectionem non tam excitat, quam inflammat. Quo sensu recte Gregorius hom. XV. in Ezech. Succendi cor nostrum igne charita- tis quærimus? Johannis verba pensemus, cujus omne, quod loquitur, charitatis igne vaporatur. Et Augustinus in præfat. Epist. Maxime commenda- tur charitas: Loquuturus enim est multa & prope omnia de charitate. Qui habet in se unde audiat, necesse est gaudeat ad quod audit. Sic enim erit illi lectio ista tanquam oleum in flamma. De cætero etiam de ipso S. Hieronymus in Ezech. c. II. Jo- hannes, ait, recubuit in pectore ejus, ut hauriret fluenta sapientiæ, ut posset dicere: In principio erat Verbum. Et Epiphanius hæres. LXXIII. Johan- nes revera tonitrua filius per propriam suam grandi- loquentiam velut ex quibusdam nubibus à sapien- tiæ ænigmatibus piam nobis de Filio intelligentiam persuasit. Τὸ πρωτεῖον certe in hac epistola obti- net doctrina de Christo ejusque beneficiis, ut qui in Christum credunt, de salute æterna certi reddantur, quem fere etiam εὐαγγελογραφίας suæ scopum fecit S. Johannes cap. 20, 31. ideo adducitur cha- ritas ceu fidei in Christum consequens & indicium ac τεκμήριον, ut à posteriori nos certos reddat de gratia Dei in Christo, communione cum Deo, regeneratione, υἱοθεσίᾳ & vita æterna, quemad- modum de salute nos certiores reddere voluit à priori è testimonio trium testium in cælo, hoc est SS. Trinitatis, Patris, Verbi & Spiritus Sancti: necnon à testimonio trium testium in terra, per quos SS. Trinitas perpetuo testatur in Ecclesia ac obsignat fideles de salute & vita æterna. Qua- propter non tam præcipit quam commendat charitatem & argumentis maxime efficacibus & corda fidelium valde accendentibus: neque mo- re Paulino distincte, de fide tum de charitate agit, ac partes docendi & commonendi seor- sim exequitur, sed immiscet doctrinæ statim officia charitatis, adeoque ex ista πορισματικῶς quasi deducit cum insigni δεινότητι, & magis in- format, quam præcipit de charitatis debito, ejusque necessariam cum fide connexionem, & ad fidem ac dilectionem & gratiam divinam erga nos demonstrandam usum demonstrat po- tius, quam demandat, ac præcipuo tamen scopo & intentioni suæ inhæret, doctrinæ nem- pe de Christo & fide in Christum, cum exhorta- tione ad perseverantiam in eadem, & fugam hæ- reticorum eandem evertentium. Recte itaque rem expendit Flacius, cum ita de scopo & ar- gumento hujus scripsit: Varie omnino autores de hujus epistolæ argumento disseruerunt: mihi ta- men videtur, hic quoque Evangelista perinde o- stentare solum illum Dei agnum, peccata mun- di tollentem, omnesque ad eum corde sincero am- plectendum hortari, & vicissim ad fugam omnium contrariarum hinc nos avellentium, sive errorum ac seductorum, sive etiam illecebrarum mundi & parum pia vita excitare. Et postmodum: Sic tota hac epistola omnino Christum ipsiusque simul ac no- strum gratiosissimum Patrem cum suis beneficiis monstrat, ac celebrat, ac ad eum fide complecten- dum retinendumque ardentissime extimulat: ut sit omnino juxta ipsum autoris nomen Evangelica qua- dam gratia concio, sed tamen subinde per occasio- nem, dilectionem quoque erga proximum, tan- quam rivulum ex uberrimo fonte dilectionis Dei erga nos profluentem excitare augereque conetur. Quod ex oeconomia quoque partium epistolæ, ac ratio- ne & methodo tractationis ejusdem, quam Fla- cius non incommode tradidit, elucescat. Illam sic exhibet: Quo vero nihilominus cum aliis ex- positoribus faciamus plures ejus scopos aut principa- les partes docendi gratia, sint sane illæ quatuor nume- ro: quarum prima primis duobus capitibus agit potissimum de complectendo Christo, ejusque benefi- cio justificationis fugaque eorum, quæ nos ab illo abs- trahunt. Secunda pars cap. III. differit de adoptione & regeneratione ejusque fructibus, sive ad extra & erga alios, sive etiam erga nos, tum & nostra erga proximum. Postrema pars ultimo capite agit de fide & ejus objecto, nempe de testimoniis, unde ea dependet, & de beneficiis bonisve, quæ illa consequi- tur. De modo & methodo tractationis ita habet: Ratio autem methodusque tractationis hujus epistolæ videri possit talis esse, qualis solicitorum Patrum esse solet, cum dilectissimos filios informant & corri- gunt, qualemque etiam necessitas tenerorum libero- rum ac pusillorum Christi postulat, ut eadem, quæ quidem etiam maxime illis necessaria esse opinantur, sæpius instillent, & primaria documenta pietatis ve- luti brevibus summis aut aphorismis comprehensa, proponant. Producit autem nihilominus principa- les hujus epistolæ propositiones ex suis fontibus, quas subinde iteratas atque inculcatas aliis atque aliis argumentis rationibusque munit & constabilit: to- ta vero epistola potissimum illud Pascha nostrum ac pro nobis immolatum ostentat ac celebrat offertq́, ac ad illam prius indicatam methodum aptissime appli- cat. Quibus non absona sunt, quæ in præfat. in Evang. Joh. è B. Luthero observant: Lutherus p. m. in Domestica Postilla etiam illam proprietatem ser- monis doctrinæque hujus Evangelistæ annotat, quod plerumque primum homines ad Christum deducat, de- inde per eum ad Patrem: ut nempe doceat primum peccatorem post contritionem agnoscere hunc uni- cum agnum Dei sua peccata tollentem: cujus cum immensam erga se benignitatem ex passione benefi- ciisque agnoverit, toto eum pectore complectatur: & sic porro incipiat, per hunc Legatum ac Mediato- rem agnoscere & complecti ipsum quoque Patrem, ejusque plus quam paternum aut maternum erga nos animum, qui hunc dilectissimum filium nobis in tri- stissimam mortem largitus sit, eumque ut suæ volun- tatis interpretem, testemque ac certissimum & pignus sui erga nos amoris ex suo sinu quasi depromptum in hanc tristem vallem miseriarum ad nos salutis nostræ causa, cum adhuc omnino inimici essemus, ablegaverit.

Nec minus convenit Synopsis Athanasiana: Scri- ptam hanc epistolam dicit, ut commonefaceret, (ὑπομιμνήσκειν) eos, qui jam in Dominum credi- derant. Et primum quidem, inquit, ita & in hac epistola de Verbi Divinitate differit, ostendens illud in DEO semper esse, ac docens, Patrem esse lucem, ut ita Verbum cognoscamus ex Pare esse, tanquam fulgorem è Luce. Differens au- tem de Divinitate Verbi, exponit fidei nostræ mysterium non esse rem novitiam, sed esse sempiter- num ab initio, nunc vero manifestatum in Do- mino, quia vita est sempiterna & verus Deus. Causam etiam, ob quam verbum ad nos venerit & apparuerit, ponit hanc videlicet, ut opera Diaboli dissolveret, ac nos a morte liberaret, effice- retque, ut Patrem agnosceremus, & Filium Domi- num nostrum Jesum Christum. Scribit ergo ad quamvis ætatem, ad pueros, ad adolescentes, ad senes, quod Deus innotuerit, diabolica vero operatio dein- ceps deleta morte devicta sit. Atque hæc de prin- cipali argumento. Quod reliquum est, pergit Athanasius, per totam epistolam dilectionem docet, volens, ut nos invicem alius alium diligamus, pro- pterea quod & Christus dilexit nos. Et postmo- dum : Hortatur autem per totam epistolam Domi- no credentes, ne animo sint abjecto, si odio habean- tur in hoc mundo, sed magis gaudeant : ob id quod odium mundi hujus declaret credentes migraf- se ex hoc mundo, & posthac conversari in cælis. Et in calce epistolæ iterum admonet, Filium Dei esse vitam æternam ac verum Deum, & ut illi servia- mus, nosque ipsos a simulacris custodiamus. Facit huc etiam collatio tractationis Paulinæ & Joanneæ à Flacio l. c. observata : In Episto- lis hic Evangelista minus videtur aperte distingue- re partes doctrinæ, quam Paulus, qui plerum- que primum contritionem, postea justificationem, postremo novam obedientiam urget : primum ma- lam arborem monstrans, accusans ac veluti succi- dens : deinde bonam plantans & generans : po- stremo ejus bonos fructus describens, & quasi pro- ducens : hic per occasionem subinde à doctrina de fide Christoque ad charitatis documenta transit, & contra hinc illuc regreditur. Neque vero tam de factionibus fugiendis, quam de genere, de mutua exhibenda dilectione loquutus est Aposto- lus, eamque efficacissime commendat.

Porro quod ad alteram causam scriptionis S. Johannis à Grotio tactam de fama de quibusdam sese pro liberatoribus populi Judaici à Deo missis gerentibus; nihil de illa, quod huc faciat, afferri po- test, nec ullo verbo eam innuit S. Johann. neque AntiChristi illi à S. Johanne designantur, qui se pro Messia Judæorum liberatore venditarunt; sed qui Jesum esse Dei Filium, Christum, Salva- torem hominum inficiati sunt, quales imprimis fuere Ebion & Cerinthus cum Carpocrate; no- tante Tertulliano l. de præscript. cap. 48. Post hunc (Carpocratem) Cerinthus Hæreticus erupit, similia docens. Nam & ipse Christum ex semine David natum proponit hominem illum factum sine Divinitate contendens. Quam hæresin Cerin- thum in Asia sparsisse, Epiphanius hær. 28. Au- tor est; prædicante ibidem Johanne, quo de etiam Irenæus l. 3. c. 3. Similia de hæresi Ebionis tradidere Tertullianus de carne Christi, Epipha- nius hæres. 30. Eusebius l. 3. cap. 23. Testaturque Irenæus l. 3. c. 11. Johannem voluisse auferre eum, qui à Cerintho seminatus erat, errorem de λόγῳ. Hi- eronymus in prologo Matth. Quum Johannes, inquit, esset in Asia, & jam tum hæreticorum semina pullularent Cerinthi, Ebionis & cæterorum, qui ne- gant Christum venisse in carne, coactus est ab omni- bus pene tunc Asiæ Episcopis & multarum Ecclesia- rum legationibus de Divinitate Salvatoris altius scribere & ad ipsum, ut ita dicam, Dei Verbum non tam audaci quam felici temeritate prorumpere. E- piphanius hær. 51. Postquam, inquit, Christum ex afflictu nudum hominem prædicavit Ebion & Ce- rinthus & ipsorum complices in Asia, illic Spiritus Sanctus produxit mundo hanc sanctam herbam sive fruticem fugantem serpentem & Diaboli tyranni- dem destruentem. Illic enim S. Johannes post ætatem senectam jubetur à Spiritu Sancto prædicare, & re- flectere errantes in viam non coacte, sed ex voluntate, credentibus lumen Dei revelans, quæ est in sancta Dei doctrina. B. Lutherus observat in præfat. Johann. Ut in Evangelio fidem urget, ita in hac Epistola, quæ illud merito sequi debeat occurrere illis, qui fi- dem jactant sine operibus, ac docere, opera non deficere, ubi fides est: Si deficiant, fidem non esse veram fidem, sed mendacium & tenebras. Quam tamen Cerinthianis etiam oppositam esse, qui Christum negarunt in carne venisse, profite- tur; eoque etiam Spiritum AntiChristi tendere observat: Quia qui operibus suis justificari ac sal- vari vult, perinde facit, ac si Christum negaret. Si- quidem Christus ideo in carnem venerit, ut nos si- ne operibus solum per sanguinem suum justifica- ret & salvaret. Ideoque monet B. Lutherus, milita- re hanc epistolam adversus utramque partem, tum contra eos, qui fidem jactant sine operibus; tum qui per opera justificari volunt, viamque mediam tenere, quod per fidem à peccatis liberemur, ju- stificemur, justificati opera bona & charitatem exerceamus prompte sine omni impulsu. Fluit er- ror ille de bonorum operum necessitate ad salutem è Cerinthi doctrina, quod Christus nudus quoad materiam homo fuerit, legique ipse subditus, un- de neque satisfactioni neque merito ejus locus relinquitur, nec imputari nobis obedientia ejus seu passiva seu activa ad salutem potest, sed propri- is operibus salutem nos consequi oportet. Quo pacto ait Cyrill. exeg. ad Valer. de Verbi incarn. Unus pro omnibus mortuus justum pro omnibus pre- tium exsolvere potuit, si perpessionem illam puri homi- nis fuisse dicamus! Nisi Deus donasset salutem, ait I- rænæus l. 3. c. 20. non firmiter haberemus eam, & nisi homo conjunctus fuisset Deo nostro, non potuisset particeps (homo) fieri incorruptibilitatis. Quod proinde contra Ebioneos urget Irenæus l. 3. c. 59. Quomodo possunt salvari Ebionitæ, nisi Deus est, qui salutem ipsorum super terram operatus est, & quomodo transeat homo ad Deum, si non Deus in hominem (transit) scil. per incarnationem vel ἐνανθρώπησιν? Ideoque conjungit Eusebius utram- que errorem in hæresi Ebioneorum l. 3. cap. 27. quod utrumque propugnarint Ebionitæ. Eum enim, inquit, simplicem ac vulgarem, nec aliud, quam hominem esse censebant, qui profectu virtutis justus factus fuisset: Cæterum ex viri cum Maria concubitu procreatum. Porro legis observatio- nem sibi omnino necessariam ducebant quasi per so- lam fidem in Christum vitamque ex ea traductam salutem consequi non valerent. Ideo Jacobus Nau- clerus vol. II. Chronogr. gener. p. 464. Ebion, in- quit, censuit custodiendam legis observationem, nec Christi fidem ad salutem sufficere. De Cerintho etiam Epiphanius hær. XCVIII. observat, quod unus fuerit è Pseudo-Apostolis, qui turbas dederit, cum Jacobus & qui cum eo erant, literas Antiochi- am scripserunt (Act. XV.) hunc etiam cum asseclis suis notatum à Paulo, Gal. 2, 3. quibus opponit Apostolus, Galat. 2, 21. hanc senten- tiam: Vivo ego, sed non ego, sed Christus vivit in me. Nam quod vivo in carne, vivo in fide Filii Dei, qui me dilexit, & tradidit semetipsum pro me. Non abjicio Dei Gratiam. Nam si per legem justificari vultis, & gratia excidistis. Nos autem in Spiritu per fidem expectamus justitiam &c. Hos autem hæreticos ceu Anti-Christos no- tatos esse à S. Johanne docet Tertullianus l. de præscript. adv. hæret. cap. 33. At in epistola (Jo- hannes) eos maxime Anti-Christos vocat, qui Christum negant in carnem venisse, & qui non putant, Jesum esse Filium Dei. Illud Marcion, hoc Hebion vindicavit. Item: Ad Galatas scribens (Paulus) invehitur in observatores & defensores circumcisionis & legis. Ebionis hæresis est. Quo- modo autem in legis observatores invehatur Apostolus in ista epistola, suo loco docuimus: scilicet qua per observationem legis salutem se consequi, eámque ad salutem necessariam sta- tuunt.

Quum ergo ex his constet, præsentem episto- lam magis esse Didacticam quam Paræneticam, ejusdem destributio secundum capita doctrinæ instituenda: quorum primum est de Christi per- sona & officio, ubi primum æterni Verbi incar- natione, vel vitæ æternæ manifestatione, quam ceu testis αὐτόπτης καὶ ἀυτήκοος confirmat, ac istius fine præcipuo, communione cum Patre ac Filio, & inde oriundo gaudio, necnon de eo- rum, qui communionem habent cum Deo, neces- sario προσκειμένῳ, quod cum Deus lux sit, in quo tenebræ non sunt, ipsis in luce, non in te- nebris ambulandum sit, utpote qui & sanguine Christi purgati sunt ab omni peccato, & pro- pter eundem, modo pœnitentiam agant, pec- catorum remissionem consequuntur cap. 1. Quod

Cap. II. illustrat partim qua muneris nostri debi- tum, ne peccemus, partim qua officium Christi propitiatorium: Illic ostendens necessitatem ob- servationis mandatorum &c. hic vero beneficia Christi, incarnationis Verbi explicans, doctri- nam de Christo non novam, sed antiquam esse asserens, eamque sedulo commendans fidelibus tum universis, tum singulis senioribus, junio- ribus & parvulis, cum adhortatione de fugien- do & amore mundi qua vitam, & qua doctrinam, Anti-Christo, utpote contrariis officiis nostris, Christique beneficiis, ac repugnantibus doctri- næ Christi, de qua Spiritus Sanctus fideles con- firmat. Unde monentur, ut in doctrina Chri- sti percepta, qui promisit nobis æternam vi- tam, maneant, & relictis seductoribus, iis, quæ unctio, hoc est, Spiritus Sanctus docet, ac- quiescant, tum ut fiduciam habeant in adventu Christi, tum ut justitiam faciant; siquidem ipse justus est. De hoc ergo capite Flacius ita censet, quod monstretur in eodem medium, per quod Salvator apprehendatur cum Patre, nempe veram ejus doctrinam ex animo ample- ctendo; interferatur tamen ibi quatuor versibus præceptum de dilectione, ac protinus redeatur vers. 12. ad doctrinam de amplectendo hoc Sal- vatore una cum suis beneficiis; inde v. 15. inci- piat monere de cavendis iis contrariis, quæ nos à Christo & ejus salute abstrahunt, ac primum quidem de fuga cupiditatum, illecebrarum & fraudum mundi: mox autem v. 18. doceat, ca- vendos esse seductores, & persistendum constan- tissime in recepto Evangelio & Christo, ad quos ipsos etiam ab inhabitante Spiritu Sancto & novo homine moneri ac impelli.

Sequitur jam tertio capite de altero fine adven- tus Filii Dei adoptione vel ὑότητι nostra, quan- tum hoc bonum sit, eique conjuncta tum puri- ficatione nostra, tum fiducia cordis nostri. Illam confirmat partim inde, quod ad tollenda pec- cata nostra & dissolvenda opera Diaboli in mun- dum venerit; partim quod regeniti non peccent, sed justitiam exerceant, & fratres diligant; par- par- tim quòd tendat doctrina Christi, & unde agnosca- tur translatio nostra de morte in vitam: partim quod in eo etiam exemplo suo nobis præiverit Christus, qui animam suam posuit pro nobis. Hanc vero (fiduciam nostram), è divina virtute ac gratiosa nostri cura & exauditione statuminat, repetitque summam doctrinæ Christi, quæ fi- dem in Christum & dilectionem mutuam com- plectitur.

Huic informationi subjicit iterum Cap. IV. paucis monitum de probandis Spiritibus & de diligendo proximo, quod dilectionis officium è regeneratione ac summo dilectionis divinæ er- ga nos beneficio missione Filii Unigeniti deducit, & dilectionem erga proximum à dilectione Dei sejungi non posse, fideliumque unionem cum Deo amorem Dei & proximi comitem habere docet.

Postremo capite de fide in Christum Jesum tra- ctat explicite ejus tum fructum, dilectionem ac victoriam mundi, tum confirmationem ab ad- ventus Christi signis ac documentis; baptismo aquæ & sanguine in cruce effuso, ut & Spiritu testificante de Verbi veritate, nec non à testi- monio partim trium in cœlo testium de Jesu Filio Dei Christo & Salvatore mundi, partim trium in terris in Ecclesiâ testium Verbi ministerio, ut & Baptismi & S. Eucharistiæ Sacramento, tum finem vitam æternam, quam in Filio Dei nos habere per fidem, tum adjunctum fiduciam exauditionis precum etiam pro fratre peccante, modo non committat peccatum in Spiritum S. & abstinentiam à peccatis voluntariis. Tandem summam repetit Fidei salvificæ per ἀνακεφαλαίω- siv quandam, quæ absolvitur tum Filii Dei ad- ventu, tum donatione cognitionis veri Dei, & communionis cum eodem in Filio ejus Christo Jesu, utpote qui verus Deus est & æterna vita, cum commonitione finali fugiendorum idolorum, quæ cum Vero Deo consistere ne- queunt.

Partes itaque epistolæ duæ constitui possunt: Prima de Verbo incarnato ejusque beneficiis: prioribus quatuor capitibus: quorum primum est communio cum Deo, cui subjungitur com- monitio de fratrum dilectione, fugiendo mun- do & Spiritu Anti-Christi cap. I. & II. Alterum est ὑοθεσία & adoptio, cap. III. cui iterum attexi- tur monitum de probandis Spiritibus, & de dilectio- ne proximi cap. IV. Posterior est de fide in Chri- stum, cap. V.

Interpretes prioris Johánneæ præter com- munes inveniuntur S. Augustinus, Beda, Nicetas, Oecumenius, Augustinus de Ancona, Petrus Au- reolus, Adam Sasbouth, Claudius Guillaudus, Jo- han. Gagnejus, Joh. Antoninus Dalphinus, Johan. Heffelius, Joh. Lorinus, Nicol. Serarius, Libertus Fromondus, Joh. Mariana, Thomas Naogeorgius, Erasmus, Valla, Joh. à Loranio. E nostris B. Lu- therus, Johan. Hussus, Johan. Baptista, Henricus Eckardi, Eilhardus Lubinus, Johan. Camirus, Ægidius Hunnius, Nicol. Selneccerus, Erasmus Sarcerius, Victor. Strigelius. E Reformatis Zuvinglius, Johan. Calvinus, Henricus Bullinger, Rudolphus Gualtherus, Franc. Gomarus, Johan- nes Buxtorfius, Guilh. Perkinsus, ut & Nicol. Hem- mingius. Ex Anti-Trinitariis F. Socinus, & Jonas Schlichtingius.

PARS I. EPISTOLÆ, De Verbi incarnatione ejusque fructibus.

## 1:1 Argument
CHAPTER I. ARGUMENT, AND PARTITION.

He describes the incarnate Word, which was from eternity with the Father, and was manifested in the flesh, seen, heard, and handled by the Apostles. And its chief benefit, communion with the Father, and the perfect joy of believers: and he deduces from thence an admonition, that we should walk in the light, just as God is light: and he celebrates the benefit of the cleansing of the blood of Christ, of which we are made partakers, when we acknowledge and confess our sins.

There are two parts: The former is the announcement and testimony concerning the incarnation of the Word and its end, our communion with God, up to verse 4. The latter is the announcement concerning the requirements of those who have communion with God; that they should walk in the light, and seeking expiation of sins through the blood of Christ, should not deny their sins.

PART I. Announcement concerning the incarnate Word, and its chief benefit.

Ver. 1.

Ὁ ἦν ἀπ' ἀρχῆς] Some think that the beginning of the preaching is looked at, as in Mark 1:1, Luke 1:2, Acts 11:25. But I judge it more correct that the same time is noted as in the first words of the Gospel of John and in Genesis: so that the sense is, that those things which the Apostles perceived with their senses had been destined by God already from the very beginning of the world, and from that time prefigured by many shadows, and predicted by many prophecies, against those who accused the doctrine of the Gospel of novelty. ἀπ' ἀρχῆς and ἐν ἀρχῇ ought not to be distinguished. For they signify the same thing. See Matthew 19:4, 8.

Ὁ ἀκηκόαμεν] That which had long been hidden with God, that was certainly made manifest to us, as will follow presently. We heard not only God speaking the words of life, but also God the Father rendering to Him from heaven a testimony greater than the Prophets or even Moses.

Ὁ ἑωράκαμεν τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς ἡμῶν, ὁ ἐθεασάμεθα] An effective expression. For it was not enough to say we saw, but he adds with our eyes: just as the Latins also say: I have seen with these eyes. Then he adds we beheld, that is, we contemplated for a long time and much to satiety so many and such great miracles of Jesus, so many men healed, loaves multiplied, sight returned to the blind, life to the dead.

καὶ αἱ χεῖρες ἡμῶν ἐψηλάφησαν] He adds a third sense, touch. For that also intervened both elsewhere and in the multiplied loaves and in Lazarus.

περὶ τοῦ λόγου τῆς ζωῆς] In so many ways we have known that the doctrine of the Gospel is true, which is called λόγος ζωῆς, or ῥήματα ζωῆς, Phil. 2:16, John 6:68, Acts 2:28, ch. 5:20.

This Epistle is ἄτιτλος, as that which is inscribed to the Hebrews, ἄνευ ἐπιγραφῆς κͅ προσφωνήσεως. Socinus attributes an exordium or proem to it up to verse 5. But others, to whom Schlichtingius has also joined himself, determine more correctly that the proposition itself is exhibited immediately without a proem. For the verb, which follows in verse 3, looks to completing the sense of the proposition: We announce to you that which was from the beginning, which we heard, which we saw, etc., therefore those things are repeated in verse 3. That, I say, which we saw and heard, we announce to you, so that the sense may be clearer, which on account of the παρένθεσιν in verse 2, which almost everyone acknowledges, could have seemed in some way doubtful. It seems, however, that he proposes the matter immediately ἄνευ προοιμίꙋ, because he wished to conform the beginning of the epistle to the beginning of his Gospel, and to indicate that the sentiment is the same in both places. It does not seem wrong to Estius that these very words have a certain appearance of a greeting and good news, so that there is no need for another greeting. For he soon testifies that he is announcing to those to whom he writes those good things than which nothing more joyful could be wished for. Ὃ ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς some take concerning the person, others concerning the doctrine. Grotius, with Socinus, understands it concerning the doctrine: interpolating the opinion of Socinus, who interprets it concerning the Gospel of Christ, in such a way that he includes with the doctrine the very things which the Apostles apprehended with their senses. But it must be understood entirely as the person: because this is demanded by 1. The words, that which was from the beginning, compared with the beginning of the Gospel: In the beginning was the Word; where it is most clear that the discourse is about the hypostatic Word. 2. The predicates, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon or contemplated, which our hands have handled. Which signify not doctrine or things of any kind, but a person. Doctrine can indeed be heard, but not looked upon, or handled with the hands. Things, however, which are done, even if some have been perceived by the eyes, are not here implied to have been heard, or announced from hearsay. 3. Nor did it seem that this should be announced as something singular and with such a great apparatus of words, that the Apostles, who it was established had been with Christ, heard his doctrine and saw the things done, but that they recognized that Word which is from eternity, and saw and heard it manifested in the flesh, which is the happiness proper to the Apostles, Luke 10, 23. 24. concerning which St. John also testifies in chapter 1, 14. The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, the glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father. This is ὁμολο- γꙋμένως μέγα μυστήριον, concerning which the Apostle 1. Timoth. 3, 16. that God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, and seen even by the Angels themselves not without the highest delight, who desire παρακύψαι this, which the Apostles announce to them as seen and looked upon 1. Petr. 1, vers. 12. 4. One must not depart from the propriety of words without necessity. But Socinus and Grotius depart, when they understand what is said about vision and handling metaphorically, not properly. Socinus says: Nothing prevents John from having used these metaphors of seeing and handling with the very eyes and hands to declare certain knowledge of the matter: But what cause compels us to betake ourselves to metaphors, especially where they are said not only to have seen, but to have seen with their own eyes, to have looked upon and contemplated the Word, nay even to have felt and handled with their own hands, which was most true of the hypostatic Word, but could not be said of the spoken word? That which they saw and handled with their hands is explained as being ἡ ζωὴ life, and ἡ ζωὴ αἰώνιꚙ eternal life, which is expounded concerning Christ by John, chapter 1, verse 4, and in this epistle, chapter 5, v. 20. This is the true God, and eternal life, and also by Christ himself, John 11, 25. chapter 14, 6. I am the life. 6. The same is called λόγꙙ τῆς ζωῆς the Word of life, just as 1. Joh. 5, 7. 20. the same is called ὁ λόγꙙ ζωὴ αἰώνιꚙ; and those names are peculiarly proper to the Son of God. 7.
