By Life and λόγꙙ is understood he to whom the predicate ἡ ζωὴ ἐφανερώ- θη applies, which is Φανέρωσις ἐν σαρκὶ, 1. Tim. 3, 16. λόγꙋ ἐνσάρκωσις Joh. 1, 14. Φανέρωσις τꙋ ὑιꙋ τꙋ Θεꙋ 1. Joh. 3, 8. doubtful. Concerning the doctrine of Christ, it is not said that ἐφανερώθη (he was manifested). Apparition properly belongs to a suppositum or a person. The life is treated here, ἥτις ἦν πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα, which was with the Father, verse 2. Which St. John testifies to have been ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς (from the beginning): just as in the Gospel ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν (in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God), chap. 1, 1. ότι ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν (that he was in the beginning with God), verse 2. whom he calls λόγον ζωῆς (the Word of life) verse 4, 9. That φανέρωσις (manifestation) of eternal life is explained concerning the advent of the Son of God, John 3, verses 5, 8. concerning his mission into the world, that we might live through him, 1 John 4, v. 9. just as St. John likewise spoke of this apparition, chap. 4, v. 14. & nos vidimus & testamur quod Pater miserit Filium Servatorem mundi (and we have seen and testify that the Father sent the Son, the Savior of the world), & chap. 5, 11. Et hoc est testimonium, quod vitam æternam dedit nobis Deus, & vita illa est in Filio ejus (And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and that life is in his Son), as also verse 20. Scimus quod Filius Dei venit, hic est verus Deus & vita æterna (We know that the Son of God has come, this is the true God and eternal life). 10. Opposed to this announcement concerning the incarnation of the Word and the advent of the Son of God is the contrary doctrine of the Anti-Christs, who deny that Jesus is the Christ, 1 John 2, v. 22. who do not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, chap. 4, v. 3. which ἀντίθεσις (antithesis) is shown in verse 14. 11. Not only do most other interpreters, even by Socinus's own admission, explain this concerning Christ, but Schlichtingius himself does so concerning the Word of life, that is, concerning Jesus, whom he calls the Word in his own fashion. Rightly, therefore, says the blessed Hunnius: First, he calls Christ λόγον (the Word), understanding not a certain dissoluble, vanishing word, but the ὑπόστασιν (hypostasis) of the Son subsisting in the Trinity. For it is familiar to John to call the Son of God λόγον (the Word); which is no less clear from the beginning of his Gospel. Which appellation he borrowed from the history of the creation of the world, where God is read to have founded all things by speaking or by the Word, just as the same thing is repeated in Psalm 33. The reason for the name is that the Son within the Trinity is, as it were, the speech and character of the Father's glory and Majesty, and then also because he is that Orator who, having been brought forth from the bosom of the Father, declared to us the everlasting Gospel concerning the reconciliation of the world: as it is written: In these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, through whom he also created the ages, Heb. 1.

Therefore, concerning the person of Christ, this ὃ ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς (THAT which was from the beginning) must be accepted, he says, using the neuter pronoun for the masculine, through the customary commutation of genders, primarily because in λόγῳ (the Word) he wished to note ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο (one thing and another), a different nature and a different nature, as the pious Ancients say, that in Christ there is not indeed ἄλλος καὶ ἄλλος (one person and another), or a double person, yet there is in Christ ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο (one thing and another), a double nature: he designates the Divine when he says, ὃ ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς (that which was from the beginning), the Human when he says, ὃ ἀκηκόαμεν, ὃ ἑωράκαμεν (that which we have heard, that which we have seen), which (manifested in the flesh) we have heard, which we have seen. Therefore, the argument of Socinus is null, that the Gospel must be understood [as referring to a thing], because the Apostle uses not the masculine, but the neuter gender. For what he says, that the neuter is never placed for the masculine when the discourse is about a person, is false. See Matt. 1, 20. Luke 1, 35. John 3, 6. Heb. 7, 7. And the parallel passage John 1, 1 clearly shows that here the neuter is placed for the masculine. For what John says here: ὃ ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς (that which was from the beginning), he expresses there thus: ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος (in the beginning was the Word): which passages Grotius himself compares here. The Vulgate rendered the verb ἦν (was): fuit (was/has been), others more correctly, ERAT (was). Cornelius à Lapide acknowledges this: Note, it is better to say, the Word was, than the Word has been, because 'has been' signifies that the thing has passed away, 'was' [signifies] that it still is, or is perennial: Thus St. Chrysostom, Cyril, Theophylact, and others on chapter 1 of the Gospel of St. John. However much, says Basil in book II against Eunomius, you may wish to run backward with the inquiry of your mind, you will not be able to pass through THAT WHICH WAS and be carried beyond it with your thoughts. Enjedinus, however, says it appears that the Apostle proposes principally that he is not going to speak about the Word of life, but about a certain thing adhering to the Word itself, namely, that which existed from the beginning. Concerning the nature belonging to the hypostatic Word, we shall more correctly say that which existed from eternity, which is his divine nature.

Therefore, by the words ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς (from the beginning) is not understood the ἄναρχον (beginningless) beginning, God the Father, as Cyril and Origen [do] in the Gospel of St. John, nor the beginning of the Gospel, as Socinus and Schlichtingius explain, but the same beginning that is designated in John 1, 1, the beginning of the world or of time, as Augustine, Bede, Chrysostom, and Theophylact explain, which sense Grotius also acknowledges: nor indeed is it indicated by that phrase that the subject of whom the Apostle speaks only began with the beginning of the world; but ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἦν, he WAS from the beginning, just as ἐν ἀρχῇ (in the beginning) ἦν (he WAS), says John, that is, he did not begin to be, but already existed, and the Word WAS with the Father: so likewise in this place ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς (he WAS from the beginning), he says, he did not begin to be from the beginning of the world. St. Ambrose, book I de fide, chap. 5, says: John, in his Epistle, says that he was in the beginning; 'was' is extended indefinitely, whatever you may have thought, the Son was: that which was in the beginning is not included in time, is not anticipated by a beginning. Augustine, sermon VI de tempore: He who was in the beginning, he says, concludes every beginning within himself. And Nazianzen, oration de fid.: Whatever beginning you may wish to assign, you will have it prejudiced, because he was in the beginning. But St. Cyril, book I in John 1, more expressly: In the beginning, he says, if indeed it retains the definition of a beginning, nothing is more ancient, for the beginning of a beginning can never be conceived: for if something else is understood before the beginning, it will surely fall away, nor will it be truly a beginning. Furthermore, if something else can be found before the true beginning, we will have to proceed to infinity, always seeking one thing before another, and not resting in one simple beginning: Which things Cornelius brought forward. For he is ζωὴ ἀιώνιος (eternal life), and thus from eternity, he is the first and the last, the beginning and the end, Apoc. 1, 8. cap. 21, 6. cap. 23, 13. which is the description of the eternal God, Isa. 41, 4. cap. 44, 6. He is that Lord, who is, who was, who is to come, Rev. 1, 8. by which periphrasis John had designated the eternity of God the Father, Rev. 1, 4. Therefore, one should not seek a difference in the bare words ἐν ἀρχῇ and ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς as some do, but the whole phrase must be considered, ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ and ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς, and the ἰσοδυναμία (equivalence) will appear, because by both the existence of the Word is expressed, which must be well observed here especially against the Socinians. Add that the preposition ἀπὸ by a customary Hebraism, as Flacius notes, signifies BEFORE, and that ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς also denotes eternity, 2 Thess. 2, 13. 1 John 2, 13. Cf. Eph. 1, 4. 2 Tim. 1, 9. Ps. 78, 2. Isa. 55, 20. For the induction from the usage of Scripture is firm: Wherever the word from the beginning or in the beginning occurs absolutely, and no restriction is added in the context, the beginning of all things is always to be understood. Nor should it be passed over that for the same reason the eternity of the Father is described by John in this epistle, cap. 2, 13, since you have known τὸν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς him who is from the beginning, that is, from eternity. Beza here also gives the reason why St. John in this place preferred to use the phrase ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς rather than ἐν ἀρχῇ, namely, because he is speaking here indeed of Christ as God, yet not simply, but as clothed in flesh: just as if he were saying that that visible and palpable Christ did not begin to exist then, when he was seen and touched, but had always existed besides, namely according to his Deity, in respect of which he already existed even then, when all created things received the beginning of their existence: and therefore that a dual nature is thus also more conveniently signified than if he had said, ὃς ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ, ὃν ἑωράκαμεν, &c. Estius's simple equivalence pleases me: That, he says, is certain, that by this expression, what was from the beginning, eternity is signified, by which because it always was, just as also there, in the beginning was the Word. For it is said to have been in the beginning and from the beginning, because it was in such a way that nothing was prior to it: which is the most certain notion of eternity, as if he had said: What was from eternity. Wherefore it is immediately declared to us here that Christ the Son of God is coeternal with the Father. However, Enjedinus achieves nothing here by comparing the passage in Luke 1, for that is clearly different: for there the context convinces that ἀπ' ἀρχῆς is to be understood concerning the beginning of the Gospel; nor is it less clear that the words cannot be explained otherwise, because the Apostles are eyewitnesses ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, who it is certain did not exist from the beginning of the world or from eternity. But here that eternal λόγος is regarded, ὁ ἀληθινὸς, ἡ ζωὴ αἰώνιος.

The word ἦν, therefore, is not to be understood concerning destination, or prediction, or prefiguration, but, as it sounds, and as its proper sense holds, concerning true and real existence: just as also in the prologue of the Gospel, which Grotius makes parallel to this, it denotes not destination, but ὕπαρξιν and existence, and the words ἥτις ἦν πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα, compared with John 1:1, ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν, openly teach that the existence of the λόγος with God the Father is denoted, that at the beginning of the creation of all things, before anything existed outside of God, he already existed with God, and so, since before creation there was mere eternity, he was from eternity with the Father. The antiquity of the Evangelical doctrine is not asserted here, which Grotius wishes, but not without ἑαυτομαχίᾳ, because he himself argues the doctrine of the Gospel, which he says is being defended here against those who accused it of novelty, as being novel in many places: But the eternity of the Word, the Son of God, Jesus our Savior, is built up, which Ebion and Cerinthus denied, blasphemously contending that he only began to exist when he was born of Mary.

Against these, therefore, the Apostle builds up the eternal existence of the Word, and the Deity or divine nature of Jesus with these words, that which was from the beginning, and with the explanation subjoined, we announce to you the eternal life, which was with the Father. Then, indeed, he affirms that the same Word was manifested in the flesh, heard by him, seen, looked upon, and touched, lest with those heretics he should distinguish and tear the Word away from Jesus, whom the Apostles were announcing, in which manner Eusebius observes in Book III of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 27, that the Ebionites said Jesus was λιτὸν καὶ κοινὸν κατὰ προκοπὴν ἀυτὸ μόνον ἄνθρωπον δεδικαιωμένον, and that they denied προϋπάρχειν ἀυτὸν Θεὸν, λόγον ὄντα καὶ σοφίαν: And Ignatius in his Epistle to the Philadelphians. If anyone says that there is indeed one God, but confesses also Christ Jesus, yet thinks the Lord is a mere or naked man, not the Only-begotten God, and the Wisdom and Word of God, but judges him to consist only of soul and body, that man is a false serpent and a seducer, preaching for the perdition of men, and he is that poor-minded one, as he is called by the surname Ebion. Indeed, Ebion, as others also did, divided Jesus and Christ, although according to Epiphanius, there was much vertigo in him. Some of them feigned that Christ was created from the supernal spirits before all creatures, and came into Jesus, as Ebion's teacher Cerinthus, with Epiphanius himself as author in heresy XXVIII, blasphemed that Christ, when Jesus was an adult, came from the supernal realms into Jesus in the form of a dove, and when he himself suffered, he in turn flew up from him; but that Jesus suffered, while Christ remained unharmed. But Saint John teaches that Jesus is the Christ the Son of God, the eternal Word, the eternal life, the true God, whom they heard in the flesh, saw with their eyes, and contemplated, and touched with their hands. Tertullian arranges these things differently, and constructs them differently, but without the authority of the authentic Codices, namely in this way: That which we have seen, that which we have heard, we have seen with our eyes, and our hands have touched concerning the word of life. He adds: testimony is false everywhere, if the sense of the eyes and ears and hands lies by nature.

Now therefore, as Beza also notes, he approaches the humanity, so that afterwards he may establish one person of Christ from two natures, not confused but distinct. Moreover, the word ἀκήκοεν does not signify in this place receiving something from the narration of others, but hearing something with one's own ears. I heard, he says, him speaking, I saw with my own eyes, I touched with my own hands the true God made true man: and not I alone, but others besides, who were with me. But to what end this, John? Namely, there had already arisen those who denied the divine nature, and those who denied the human nature of Christ. Concerning which we heard Tertullian before: that John thus refutes Ebion and Marcion, of whom the former with Cerinthus denied that Jesus was the Son of God, as Basilides did before him, and the latter denied that Christ came into the flesh. Rightly Cornelius a Lapide: John inculcates and exaggerates the incarnation and appearance of the Word in the flesh in so many words for three reasons. The first, that against Basilides, who in that age taught that Christ had assumed an apparent and phantastical flesh, not a true one, and therefore was not truly crucified, but only in image, he might teach that Christ assumed a true and real flesh, and in it really suffered, and really redeemed and sanctified us, thus Epiphanius, heresy 24. The second, that he might fully confirm the faithful in the faith of the incarnation, and persuade the unfaithful of its truth, having sought an argument from the three senses, which are held to be the most faithful and most perspicacious: for such are sight, hearing, and touch. He asserts, therefore, that he with the Apostles saw, heard, attentively looked upon, and touched the incarnate Word. Thus Peter proves that Christ rose again by his own eyewitness testimony and that of the Apostles, Acts 10:40. The third, that he might show the condescension of the Word and the dignity of the Apostles. For the Word deigned to descend from heaven to earth, and to associate and bind itself to clay, I mean to our flesh formed from clay, and to bind God to man by the closest bond of the same hypostasis and person, so that all the attributes of God are the attributes of man and vice versa, and consequently through the attributes of man He showed the Deity and its attributes to the Apostles. For this reason the Word was made flesh, that the intangible might become tangible, says Nazianzen, oration 38, and thence knowable.

He speaks, however, in the plural, because He speaks of Himself and the other Apostles, or in the person of the rest of the Apostles at the same time, who were likewise witnesses, ἀυτήκοοι καὶ ἀυτόπται; as was also done in the Gospel, John 1:14, 'We beheld His glory.' Furthermore, that hearing is referred to Jesus, the Word of life, not to the Father speaking from heaven, of whose testimony it is treated in chapter 5, 7; but here by no means. For whom they heard, Him they also saw with their own eyes, and with their hands con- handled, which cannot be said of the Father. Nor does the vision pertain immediately to miracles, but to the author of the miracles, the Word of life, whose glory the Apostles saw manifested in the miracles; and the Apostle proceeds to a firmer sense of sight, and appeals to their own eyes, lest they be thought to have seen only with the eyes of others, nor does he look only at the miracles being performed, but also at the man conversing in human flesh. Because these things pertain to the human nature, and to the asserting of the unity of the person, which, both that which was from eternity, and also that which the Apostles heard and saw, was consistent. We have seen, says Estius as interpreter, the man conversing in human flesh, eating with men, drinking, and doing and suffering the other things which are human. We have seen him transfigured and shining on the mountain: We have seen him affixed to the cross and dying. Finally, we have seen him alive again from death, and ascending into heaven. These things are said against those who denied that Jesus had come in the flesh: I add: Indeed, even against those who divided Christ from JESUS.

The Apostle adds in the gradation the word ἐθεασάμεθα, which implies that they did not simply see, but accurately contemplated and observed, lest it be considered some phantom, which Marcion later dared to accuse it of being. Θεᾶσθαι according to Oecumenius is to look upon with admiration and astonishment. It is also to contemplate publicly as if in a theater a wonderful and new spectacle. Nay, he subjoins: Which our hands have handled, by which he further precludes every doubt about a phantom and specter, just as by that reason Christ himself after the resurrection deigned to remove all doubt from the Apostles and the infirm Thomas, Luke 24:37 ff., John 20:20, 27. Therefore there is no need here to invent a hyperbole with some, as if nothing else is implied than that he dwelt among them, John 1:14. For why should they not have truly handled him with their hands before the resurrection, when being found in the likeness of men, and in fashion as a man, Phil. 2:7-8, he conversed among them, when, having entered into glory through his passion, he offered himself not only to be seen, but also to be handled by their hands? Who is it, says Augustine in this place, who handles the Word with his hands, if not because the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us? And further: What is this? They themselves saw, they handled with their hands the Word of life. He was from the beginning, for a time the only Son of God was made visible and palpable.

Enjedinus clamors here that that particle, 'which was from the beginning,' cannot be separated from the rest, so that the former is taken concerning the eternity, and the latter concerning the humanity of Christ; first because the Apostle has without doubt executed what he proposed: but he says nothing anywhere in this whole epistle about the eternity of Christ. Secondly, because a copula should have been interposed, by which it would be signified that there was to be a discussion about several things. Thirdly, because in the individual clauses the article is repeated, by which the clauses are connected, so that it is certain that the discourse is held about the same and not about another. But these things are futile. For as to the first, he does not propose things to be treated here in such a way that it is a bare proposition, distinct from the confirmation, but he immediately begins the matter, and proposes and confirms at the same time with arguments what he asserts; he confirms, namely, that the same subject is that which was from eternity, and that which they themselves in time saw, heard, and handled with their hands: that this Word of life is not one person, and Jesus, whom they heard, etc., another; lest that Word be a bare man, but true and eternal God. For to that end he uses both his Apostolic authority, and the testimony of the other Apostles, and the undoubted evidence of the sense of hearing, sight, and touch: by which that same Word, which was from eternity as true God, with whom they conversed as true man, demonstrated himself to them. Nor does he only confirm this here, but subsequently also, especially indeed in chapter 5, where he gave the coming of the Son of God proven by documents and testimonies of witnesses both divine and earthly. Moreover, St. John immediately in the very next verse established the eternity of Christ himself, when he designated him the eternal life, which was with the Father from the beginning, and also in chapter 5:20, where he taught that he is the true God and eternal life: to say nothing of other things. As to the second, the lack of a copula does not argue for the same nature, but for the same person; since it had to be asserted that Jesus and Christ, and the Son of God or the Word of God are not different persons; but that Jesus is Christ the Son of God and the eternal Word. Finally, as to the third article, it is certain that it is repeated with emphasis; nor do we refer those clauses to one and another, but we urge that the discourse is about the same and not about another. But that identity of person does not prevent some clause from being able to be referred to his divine nature, and the rest to his human nature. And therefore those words 'concerning the Word of life' do not look, as Grotius wishes, following Socinus, to the 'spoken word' (the doctrine of the Gospel), but to Christ the 'hypostatic Word,' which, as we showed before, also serves this distinction of natures in Christ. For the anomaly of apposition is not to be posited for 'the Word' with Piscator, but that particle is used with emphasis, as if he were saying, I am speaking about that Word of life. For as the little word περὶ joined to the genitive is a commemorative particle, as skilled lexicographers note, and in this place sends us away to consider the Word of life itself in the assumed true humanity, by which he was seen, heard, and handled by the Apostles, as if to say, I am speaking about the Word of life and the eternal Son of God, who was made God-man by assuming human nature, and not about some 'mere man,' as the blessed Glassius has in Grammat. S. p. 74. Nor does Beza advise unsuitably here: Again, considering distinctly one thing and another in Christ, he preferred to write 'concerning the Word of life' rather than 'the Word of life,' lest he should seem to think that that which he had seen and handled was the same as that which was from the beginning (by which reasoning he would have confounded the natures) or to posit him who was from the beginning as another from him whom he had seen and handled, that is, to divide the person by separated natures. But soon in the following verse he will most clearly declare the hypostatic union. The article is also emphatic, hinting at that very Word, through which all things were made, and in which alone is life, as the Syrian also explains. There are those who refer the little word περὶ to the fact that we know here only something περὶ λόγε, and that even that knowledge which the Apostles had was only a partial knowledge. But it is not a question of intellectual knowledge, but here the discourse is properly about sensual experience. Lorinus says it is a Hebraism, such as in Acts 2: 'I will pour out of my Spirit' for that which is in Joel, when it is read: 'I will pour out my Spirit.' Estius: It must be said, he says, in that which he says, 'of the Word of life,' that it is a transitive locution, to be expressed in this direct way: The Word of life itself, which was from the beginning, and which clothed in flesh we heard and saw and handled. Thus, he says, the beginning of this epistle corresponds perfectly with the beginning of the Gospel: In the beginning was the Word. This syntax is found in Augustine in his exposition of this epistle and in others. The Syriac interpreter clearly expressed the same. The method of explanation is different. But the sense comes to the same thing. Concerning the Word of life, says Cornelius à Lapide, that is, the Word of life itself, which was from the beginning, we announce to you: and thus Lyranus, Hugo, Catharinus, and Gagnejus hold. Our B. Hunnius: He does not rashly, he says, nor without reason call Christ the Word of life. Since he alone truly is and lives, whose essence is nothing other than life, which he possesses in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit, as Christ himself says: Just as the Father has life in himself: so he has given to the Son also to have life in himself, John V. Wherefore in the following words he does not hesitate to call him eternal life itself by an abstract term. Then indeed, and for this reason, he is so called, because by the merit of his obedience he acquired eternal life for us. Therefore, with this most august title and eulogy, John commends his Deity.

Moreover, he is called the Word of life, not only because he is life itself essentially as God, John V, 69 [sic], and hypostatically as man, John VI, verses 48, 50, but also because he is the Author of life self-actively, from whom is both natural life, because all things exist through him, and all things consist in him, Colossians I, 16, 17, and spiritual and heavenly life. John XIV, 6. Chapter XI, 25. He makes alive whom he wills, John V, 21. He is called the Word of life, therefore, for a double reason: both because he is the living Word, nay, life itself, and because he is the life-giving Word, that is, bringing life and salvation to men. Estius seems to have signified the former mode here, as the following things declare, though with respect to the latter mode, who also judges that the place of the Gospel is to be understood in the same way: In him was life, and the life was the light of men.

Latin:

CAPUT I. ARGUMENTUM, ET PARTITIO.

Describit Verbum incarnatum, quod ab æterno fuit apud Patrem, & in carne manifesta- tum, visum, auditum & contrectatum est ab Apostolis. Ejusque beneficium præci puum communionem cum Patre, & gau- dium credentium perfectum: & deducit inde monitum, ut in luce ambulemus, quemadmodum Deus lux est: celebratque beneficium mundationis sanguinis Christi, cujus participes reddimur, cum agnoscimus & confitemur peccata.

Partes duæ sunt: Prior est annunciatio & testi- ficatio de Verbi incarnatione ejusque fine, nostra cum Deo communione, ad v. 4. Posterior est annunciatio de requisitis eorum, qui communionem habent cum Deo; ut in luce ambulent, & expiatio- nem peccatorum per Christi sanguinem expeten- tes peccata sua non diffiteantur.

PARS I. Annunciatio de Verbo incarnato, ejusque præ- cipuo beneficio.

Vers. 1.

Ὁ ἦν ἀπ' ἀρχῆς] Putant quidam spectari initium prædi- cationis, ut Marc. 1, 1. Luc. 1, 2. Actor. 11, 25. Sed re- ctius arbitror, idem tempus notari, quod in primis verbis Evangelii Johannis & in Geneseos: ut sensus sit, eas res, quas Apostoli sensibus suis percepere, fuisse a Deo destinatas jam ab ipso mundi primordio, & ab eo tempore multis um- bris præfiguratas, multis vaticiniis prædictas, contra eos, qui Evangelii doctrinam novitatis accusabant. Non de- bent distingui ἀπ' ἀρχῆς & ἐν ἀρχῇ. Idem enim significant. Vide Matthæum 19, 4. 8.

Ὁ ἀκηκόαμεν] Quod apud Deum diu reconditum fuerat, id nobis certo fuit patefactum, ut mox sequetur. Audivi- mus non Deum tantum loquentem verba vitæ, sed & De- um Patrem ipsi e cœlo reddentem testimonium majus Pro- phetis aut etiam Mosi.

Ὁ ἑωράκαμεν τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς ἡμῶν, ὁ ἐθεασάμεθα] Efficax loquutio. Non enim satis fuit dicere vidimus, sed addit oculis nostris: Sicut & Latini dicunt: Hisce oculis vidi. De- inde addit spectavimus, id est, diu multumque ad satie- tatem contemplati sumus tot & tanta Jesu miracula, tot ho- mines sanatos, panes multiplicatos, redditum visum cæcis, vitam mortuis.

καὶ αἱ χεῖρες ἡμῶν ἐψηλάφησαν] Tertium sensum adjicit, tactum. Nam is quoque intervenit tum alibi, tum in pa- nibus multiplicatis & in Lazaro.

περὶ τοῦ λόγου τῆς ζωῆς] Tot modis cognovimus, verum esse Evangelii doctrinam, quæ λόγος ζωῆς dicitur, aut ῥήματα ζωῆς, Phil. 2, 16. Johann. 6, 68. Actorum 2, 28. c. 5, 20.

Est hæc Epistola ἄτιτλος, ut illa, quæ ad E- bræos inscribitur, ἄνευ ἐπιγραφῆς κͅ προσφωνήσε- ως. Socinus exordium ei tribuit vel procœmium us- que ad v. 5. Sed rectius sine procœmio ipsam statim propositionem exhiberi alii statuunt, qui- bus accessit etiam Schlichtingius. Nam verbum, quod v. 3. sequitur, ad complendum sensum pro- positionis spectat: Annunciamus vobis illud, quod erat a principio, quod audivimus, quod vidimus &c. ideo repetuntur illa v. 3. Quod, inquam, vidimus & audivimus, annunciamus vobis, ut lu- culentior sensus sit, qui ob παρένθεσιν vers. 2. quam plerique omnes agnoscunt, dubius quo- dammodo videri potuisset. Videtur autem ἄνευ προοιμίꙋ statim rem proponere, quod initium epistolæ voluerit conformare initio Evangelii sui, atque indicare, eandem utrobique esse sententiam. Non male Estio videtur, hæc ipsa verba speciem habere quandam salutationis ac boni nuncii, ut alia salutatione non sit opus. Mox enim testatur, se illis, ad quos scribit, annunciare bona illa, quibus lætiora voveri non possint. Ὃ ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς alii de persona, alii de doctrina accipiunt. Grotius cum Socino de do- ctrina intelligit: Socini sententiam, qui de Ev- angelio Christi interpretatur, ita interpolando, ut cum doctrina res ipsas, quas Apostoli sensi- bus suis apprehendere, complectatur. Sed in- telligenda omnino est persona: quia id poscunt 1. Verba, quod erat a principio, collata cum initio Evangelii: In principio erat Verbum; ubi de Verbo ὑποστατικῷ sermonem esse liquidissi- mum est. 2. Prædicata, quod audivimus, quod vidimus oculis nostris, quod spectavimus vel con- templati sumus, quod manus nostræ contrecta- runt. Quæ non doctrinam aut res quas cunque, sed personam significant. Doctrina audiri qui- dem potest, non autem spectari, vel manibus contrectari. Res vero, quæ geruntur, etsi ocu- lis nonnullæ usurpatæ sint, non tamen hic audi- tæ, vel ex auditu annunciatæ innuuntur. 3. Ne- que id ut singulare tantoque verborum appara- tu annunciandum videbatur, quod Apostoli, quos Christo affuisse constabat, ipsius doctri- nam audierint, & res gestas viderint, sed quod agnoverint Verbum illud, quod ab æterno est, idque in carne manifestatum viderint & audive- rint, quæ est beatitudo Apostolorum propria, Luc. 10, 23. 24. qua de testatur etiam S. Johan- nes cap. 1, 14. Verbum caro factum est, & ha- bitavit in nobis, & vidimus gloriam ejus, glo- riam velut Unigeniti à Patre. Hoc est ὁμολο- γꙋμένως μέγα μυστήριον, de quo Apostolus 1. Ti- moth. 3, 16. quod Deus manifestatus in carne, ju- stificatus est in Spiritu, ipsisque etiam Angelis non sine summa oblectatione visus, qui deside- rant παρακύψαι hoc, quod annunciant sibi vi- sum ac spectatum Apostoli 1. Petr. 1, vers. 12. 4. A proprietate vocum citra necessitatem ab- eundum non est. Abit autem Socinus & Gro- tius, cum quæ de visione, & contrectatione dicun- tur, Metaphorice intelligunt, non proprie. Dicit Socinus: Nihil prohibere, quo minus Jo- hannes, ut rei scientiam certam declararet hisce Metaphoris videndi & contrectandi oculis ipsis & manibus usus fuerit: Sed quæ causa nos cogit, ut ad Metaphoras nos recipiamus, imprimis ubi non tantum vidisse, sed etiam oculis suis vidis- se, spectasse ac contemplati esse dicuntur Ver- bum, imo manibus suis etiam palpasse & con- trectasse, quod de Verbo hypostatico verissi- mum, de verbo προφορικῷ vero dici non pote- rat. Explicatur id, quod viderunt & mani- bus contrectarunt, quod sit ἡ ζωὴ vita, & ἡ ζωὴ αἰώνιꚙ vita æterna, quod de Christo exponi- tur à Johanne, cap. 1, vers. 4. & in hac epistola, cap. 5. v. 20. Hic est verus Deus, & vita æterna, necnon ab ipso Christo, Joh. 11, 25. cap. 14, 6. Ego sum vita. 6. Idem dicitur λόγꚙ τῆς ζωῆς Verbum vitæ, quemadmodum 1. Joh. 5, 7. 20. idem ὁ λόγꚙ ζωὴ αἰώνιꚙ dicitur; suntque illa nomina peculiariter propria Filio Dei. 7. Vita & λόγꚙ in- telligitur, cui convenit prædicatum ἡ ζωὴ ἐφανερώ- θη, quæ est Φανέρωσις ἐν σαρκὶ, 1. Tim. 3, 16. λόγꙋ ἐνσάρκωσις Joh. 1, 14. Φανέρωσις τꙋ ὑιꙋ τꙋ Θεꙋ 1. Joh. 3, 8. De doctrina Christi non dicitur, quod ἐφανε- ρώθη. Apparitio proprie est suppositi vel personæ. De vita hic agitur, ἥτις ἦν πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα, quæ fuit apud Patrem, vers. 2. quam ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς fuisse S. Johannes testatur: quemadmodum in Evangelio ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν. cap. 1, 1. ότι ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν θε- ὸν, vers. 2. quem λόγον ζωῆς vocat vers. 4. 9. Φα- νέρωσις illa æternæ vitæ explicatur de adventu Fi- lii Dei, Johann. 3, vers. 5. 8. de missione ejus in mundum, ut vivamus per ipsum, 1. Johan. 4, v. 9. quemadmodum S. Johanes pariter de ista appa- ritione loquutus est, cap. 4, v. 14. & nos vidimus & testamur quod Pater miserit Filium Servato- rem mundi, & cap. 5, 11. Et hoc est testimonium, quod vitam æternam dedit nobis Deus, & vita illa est in Filio ejus, ut & vers. 20. Scimus quod Filius Dei venit, hic est verus Deus & vita æterna. 10. Huic annunciationi de Verbi incarnatione & adventu Filii Dei opponitur contraria doctri- na Anti-Christorum, qui negant Jesum esse Chri- stum, 1. Johan. 2, v. 22. qui non confitentur Je- sum Christum in carne venisse, cap. 4, v. 3. quæ ἀντίθεσις monstratur vers. 14. 11. Non plerique omnes alii Interpretes tantum fatente Socino ex- plicant de Christo, sed etiam Schlichtingius ipse de Sermone vitæ, id est, de Jesu, quem suo more Sermonem appellat. Recte itaque inquit B. Hunnius: Primo Christum λόγον nominat, in- telligens non verbum quoddam dissolubile evani- dum, sed in Trinitate subsistentem ὑπόστασιν Filii. Familiare enim est Johanni Filium Dei λόγον ap- pellare; quod non minus ex principio Evangelii ejus liquet. Quam appellationem ex historia creatio- nis mundi est mutuatus, ubi Deus dicendo seu Ver- bo omnia condidisse legitur, sicut id ipsum Psal. 33. repetitum extat. Ratio nominis est, quod Filius intra Trinitatem, quasi sermo & character sit Pa- ternæ gloriæ & Majestatis, tum vero etiam, quod hic est Orator ille, qui sempiternum Evangelium de reconciliatione mundi è sinu Patris prolatum no- bis enarravit: sicut scriptum est: Novissime loquu- tus est nobis per Filium, per quem & secula condi- dit, Ebr. 1.

De persona ergo Christi hæc accipienda ὃ ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς, inquit, QUOD erat à principio, pro- nomine neutro utens pro Masculino, per usitatam generum commutationem, imprimis quia in λόγῳ annotare voluit ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο aliam atque aliam na- turam, ut loquuntur pii Veteres, quod in Chri- sto sit non quidem ἄλλος καὶ ἄλλος alius atque alius, vel gemina persona, sit tamen in Christo ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο, natura gemina: Divinam designat, cum ait, ὃ ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς, Humanam, cum ait, ὃ ἀκηκόαμεν, ὃ ἑωράκαμεν, quod (in carne mani- festatum) audivimus, quod vidimus. Ideo argu- mentum Socini nullum est, Evangelium intelligen- dum esse, quia non Masculino, sed Neutro gene- re utitur Apostolus. Quod enim ait, Neutrum pro Masculino nuspiam poni, cum de persona sermo est, falsum est. Vid. Matth. 1, 20. Luc. 1, 35. Joh. 3, 6. Ebr. 7, 7. & ostendit luculenter locus parallelus Joh. 1, 1. hic Neutrum pro Masculino poni. Nam quod hic Johannes: ὃ ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς, id ibi sic effert, ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος : quæ loca hic confert ipse Grotius. Verbum ἦν Vulgatus reddidit: fuit, alii rectius, ERAT. Agnofcit id Cornelius à Lapide: Nota, potius dici, erat Verbum, quam fuit Verbum, quia fuit significat rem præteriisse, erat, etiamnum esse, sive esse perennem: Ita S. Chrysostomus, Cyrillus, Theophylactus & alii in caput I. Evang. S. Johan- nis. Quantumcunque, inquit Basilius l. II. con- tra Eunom. volueris mentis inquisitione retro- currere, pertransire tamen QUOD ERAT & ultra illud ferri cogitationibus non poteris. Enje- dinus tamen apparere ait, Apostolum proponere principaliter, se non de Verbo vitæ, sed de re quadam ipsi Verbo adhærente dicturum esse, nempe quæ ab initio extiterit. De natura Verbo hypostatico conveniente rectius dice- mur, quæ ab æterno extitit, quæ est natura e- jus divina.

Per verba itaque ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς non intelligitur i- nitium ἄναρχον Deus Pater, ut Cyrillus & Orige- nes in Evang. I. Johan. nec principium Evangelii, ut Socinus & Schlichtingius explicant, sed idem ini- tim, quod Joh. 1, 1. designatur, principium mun- di vel temporicum, ut Augustinus, Beda, Chrysosto- mus, & Theophylactus explicant, quem sensum etiam agnoscit Grotius: nec vero ea phrasi indica- tu tantum cum mundi principio cœpisse subje- ctum istud, de quc Apostolus; sed ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἦν, ERAT à principio, uti ἐν ἀρχῇ in principio ἦν ERAT, inquit Johannes, id est, non incipiebat esse, sed exiftebat jam, & apud Patrem ERAT ὁ λόγος: ita pariter hoc loco ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ERAT, inquit, non esse incipiebat à principio mundi. S. Ambrosius lib. I. de fide cap. 5. Johannes, ait, in Epistola dicit, quod erat in principio, indefinite tenditur erat, quicquid cogitaveris, erat Filius: quod erat in principio, non includitur tempore, non principio prævenitur. Augustinus serm. VI. de tem- pore: Qui in principio erat, inquit, intra se conclu- dit omne principium. Et Nazianz. orat. de fid. Quodcunque principium assignare volueris, præju- dicatum habebis, quia in principio erat. Expressius vero S. Cyrillus l. I. in Joh. 1. In principio, inquit, si- quidem definitionem principii retinet, nihil anti- quius est, nunquam enim principii principium po- terit excogitari: nam si aliud quiddam ante princi- pium intelligitur, excidet profecto, nec erit vere principium Præterea, si ante vere principium aliud inveniri poterit, in infinitum nobis erit proceden- dum, aliud semper ante aliud quærentibus, nec in uno simpliciter principio consistentibus: Quæ addu- xit Cornelius. Est enim ζωὴ αἰώνιος æterna vita, adeoque ab æterno, est primus & novissimus, principium & finis, Apoc. 1, 8. cap. 21, 6. cap. 23, 13. quæ est descriptio æterni Dei, Esa. 41, 4. cap. 44, 6. Est Dominus ille, qui est, qui erat, qui venturus est, Apoc. 1, 8. qua περιφράσει æternitatem Dei Pa- tris designarat Johannes, Apoc. 1, 4. Non ergo in verbis nudis ἐν ἀρχῇ & ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς cum nonnul- lis diversitas quærenda, sed spectanda tota phrasis, ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ & ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς, & apparebit ἰσοδυνα- μία, quod utraque λόγυ existentia sit expressa, quod adversus Socinianos imprimis hic probe observandum. Adde quod præpositio ἀπὸ usi- tato Ebraïsmo, Flacio notante, significet ANTE, quodque ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς etiam æternitatem notet, 2. Thess. 2, 13. 1. Johan. 2, 23. Conf. Ephes. 1, 4. 2. Tim. 1, 9. Psal. 78, 2. Esa. 55, 20. Nam firma est inductio ex usu Scripturæ: Ubicunque vox à principiop vel in principio absolute occurrit, nec in contextu aliqua additur restrictio, semper principium rerum omnium intelligendum. Ne- que id prætereundum, quod eadem ratione æter- nitas Patris à Johanne describatur in hac episto- la cap. 2, 13. quoniam cognovistis τὸν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς eum, qui est ab initio, id est, ab æterno. Beza hic etiam rationem reddit, cur S. Jo- hannes h. l. maluerit phrasi ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς uti, quam ἐν ἀρχῇ, quod scilicet hic de Christo quidem ut Deo loquatur, non tamen simpliciter, sed ut carne induto: perinde ac si diceret, Christum illum visibilem & palpabilem non tunc cœpisse existere, quum videretur & palpareur, sed semper præterea extitisse, nempe secundum Deitatem, cujus respe- ctu jam tum erat, quum res omnes creatæ princi- pium existentiæ reciperent: ideoque naturam du- plicem sic commodius quoque significari, quam si dixisset, ὃς ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ, ὃν ἑωράκαμεν, &c. Estio simplex æquipollentia placet: Illud, inquit, constat, hac locutione, quod fuit ab initio æterni- tatem significari, qua quia semper fuit, quemadmo- dum & illic, in principio erat Verbum. Nam in principio & à principio fuisse dicitur, quòd ita fuit, ut nihil eo fuerit prius: qua certissima notio est æter- nitatis, ac si dixisset: Quod fuit ab æterno. Quo- circa nobis statim hic declaratur, Christum Dei Fi- lium esse Patri coæternum. Nihil autem hic pro- ficit Enjedinus, conferens locum Luc. I. nam ille plane diversus est: Ibi enim ἀπ' ἀρχῆς de prin- cipio Evangelii intelligendum esse contextus convincit; nec aliter verba explicari posse lucu- lentum est, quia ἀπ' ἀρχῆς ἀυτόπται sunt Aposto- li, quos à principio mundi vel ab æterno non fuis- se constat. Sed hic λόγος ille æternus respicitur, ὁ ἀληθινὸς, ἡ ζωὴ αἰώνιος.

Verbum itaque ἦν non de destinatione acci- piendum, aut de prædictione, aut præfiguratio- ne, sed, uti sonat, & ut proprius ejus sensus ha- bet, de existentia vera & reali: quemadmodum etiam in proœmio Evangelii, quod huic paral- lelum facit Grotius, non destinationem, sed ὕπαρ- ξιν & existentiam notat, & verba ἥτις ἦν πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα, collata cum Joh. 1, 1. ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν aperte docent, existentiam λόγου apud Deum Patrem denotari, quod in principio creationis rerum omnium, antequam quicquam fuit extra Deum, jam extiterit apud Deum, adeoque, quum ante creationem mera fuerit æternitas, ab æterno apud Patrem fuerit. Non asseritur hic antiquitas doctrinæ Evangelicæ, quod vult Gro- tius, sed non sine ἑαυτομαχίᾳ, quia doctrinam Evangelii, quam hic vindicari adversus eos, qui illam novitatis accusabant, ait, ipse passim no- vitatis arguat: Sed adstruitur æternitas Verbi, Filii Dei, Jesu Servatoris nostri, quam nega- bant Ebion & Cerinthus, eundem cœpisse de- mum cum è Maria natus est, blaspheme conten- dentes.

Contra hos ergo æternam Verbi existentiam, & Deitatem vel divinam naturam Jesu verbis hisce, quod erat à principio, & ἐξηγήσει subjun- cta annunciamus vobis vitam æternam, quæ erat apud Patrem, adstruit Apostolus. Dehinc vero idem Verbum in carne manifestatum, à se audi- tum, visum, spectatum & contrectatum affir- mat, ne cum hæreticis illis Verbum, à Jesu, quem Apostoli annunciabant, distingat ac di- vellat, quo pacto observat Eusebius lib. III. Hist. Eccles. cap. 27. Ebioneos Jesum dixisse λιτὸν καὶ κοινὸν κατὰ προκοπὴν ἀυτὸ μόνον ἄνθρωπον δεδικαι- ωμένον, inficiatos esse, προϋπάρχειν ἀυτὸν Θεὸν, λό- γον ὄντα καὶ σοφίαν: Et Ignatius Epist. ad Phila- delph. Si quis dicat unum quidem Deum, confiteatur vero etiam Christum Jesum, merum autem vel nu- dum hominem esse existimet Dominum, non Deum Unigenitum, & Sapientiam & Verbum Dei, sed ex anima & corpore ipsum solum constare arbitretur, ille serpens est falsus & seductor, prædicans ad per- ditionem hominum, & est iste pauper mente, ut di- ctus cognomento Ebion. Nimirum dividebat Ebion, ut & alii etiam, Jesum & Christum, quanquam Epiphanio dicente, multa apud ipsum fuerit vertigo. Nonnulli eorum Christum ex su- pernis esse spiritibus prae omnibus creatum, & venisse in Jesum fingebant, uti Praeceptor Ebio- nis Cerinthus, eodem Epiphanio autore haer. XXVIII. Christum, cum adultus fuit Jesus, de su- pernis in Jesum venisse in specie columbae, & ubi ipse passus est, vicissim ab ipso sursum volasse, blasphemabat; passum autem Jesum esse, Chri- stum vero illaesum mansisse. Verum S. Johannes docet Jesum esse Christum Filium Dei, Verbum aeternum, vitam aeternam, verum Deum, quem in carne audierint, oculis suis viderint ac contempla- ti sint, manibusque suis contrectarint. Quae ali- ter ordinat, aliterque construit, sed citra autori- tatem Codicum authenticorum Tertullianus, ni- mirum hoc modo: Quod vidimus, quod audivi- mus, oculis nostris vidimus, & manus nostrae contre- ctarunt de sermone vitae. Addit: falsa ubique te- statio, si oculorum & aurium & manuum sensus natura mentitur.

Jam ergo, notante etiam Beza, ad humanita- tem accedit, ut postea ex duabus non confusis sed di- stinctis naturis unam Christi personam statuat. Verbum autem ἀκήκοεν non significat hoc in loco ex aliorum narratione aliquid accipere, sed suis auri- bus aliquid audire. Audivi inquit loquentem, vi- di ipse meis oculis, contrectavi meis manibus verum Deum verum hominem factum: nec ego solus, sed alii praeterea, qui mecum fuerunt. Quorsum haec autem Johannes? Nempe jam insurrexerant, & qui naturam divinam, & qui naturam humanam Christi negarent. Quo de Tertullianum antea au- divimus: Johannem ita Ebionem & Marcionem refellere, quorum ille cum Cerintho Jesum nega- vit esse Filium Dei, ut ante eum Basilides, hic Christum in carnem venisse. Recte Cornelius a Lapide: Johannes tot verbis inculcat & exaggerat Verbi incarnationem & apparitionem in carne tri- bus de causis. Prima ut contra Basilidem illo aevo docentem Christum assumpsisse carnem apparentem & phantasticam, non veram, ac proinde non vere esse crucifixum, sed in imagine duntaxat, doceret Christum veram & realem carnem assumpsisse, in eaque realiter passum, realiter nos redemisse & san- ctificasse, ita Epiphan. haeres. 24. Secunda ut fideles in fide incarnationis plene confirmet, infidelibus ve- ro ejus fidem persuadeat, petito argumento a tribus sensibus, qui fidelissimi & perspicacissimi habentur: tales enim sunt visus, auditus & tactus. Asseverat ergo se cum Apostolis Verbum incarnatum vidisse, audivisse, attente perspexisse & contrectasse. Sic Petrus Christum resurrexisse probat testimonio ocu- lari suo & Apostolorum Actor. 10, 40. Tertia ut ostendat Verbi dignationem & Apostolorum digni- tatem. Verbum enim dignatum est e caelo in terram descendere, ac se limo, carni inquam nostrae ex limo formatae, ac Deum homini arctissimo ejusdem hypo- staseos, & personae vinculo sociare & nectere, ita ut omnia attributa Dei sint attributa hominis & vice versa, ac proinde per attributa hominis Deitatem ejusque attributa Apostolis ostendit. Hac de causa Verbum caro factum est, ut intactile fieret tactile, ait Nazianz. orat. 38. indeque cognoscibile.

Loquitur autem in plurali, quia de se & aliis A- postolis, vel in persona simul caeterorum Aposto- lorum, qui pariter testes fuere ἀυτήκοοι καὶ ἀυτόπται loquitur; uti etiam in Evangelio factum, Johan. I. v. 14. Vidimus gloriam ejus. Caeterum auditus ille ad Jesum refertur Verbum vitae, non ad Patrem de caelo loquentem, de cujus testimonio cap. 5, 7. agitur: hic vero minime. Nam quem audiverunt, eum etiam oculis suis viderunt, manibusque con- trectarunt, quod de Patre dici nequit. Neque visio immediate ad miracula, sed ad autorem mi- raculorum Verbum vitæ, cujus gloriam in mira- culis manifestatam viderunt Apostoli, pertinet, progrediturque Apostolus ad sensum firmiorem visum, & ad oculos proprios provocat, ne alienis tantum oculis vidisse censeantur, nec miracula tantum patraniem, sed etiam hominem in huma- na carne conversantem respicit. Quia pertinent hæc ad humanam naturam, & ad adserendam uni- tatem personæ, quæ, & quod ab æterno fuit, et- iam eo quod Apostoli audiverunt & viderunt, constabat. Vidimus, inquit, Estio interprete, ho- minem in humana carne conversantem, cum homini- bus edentem, bibentem, ac cætera, quæ humana sunt, agentem ac patientem. Vidimus in monte transfi- guratum & splendentem: Vidimus cruci affixum & morientem. Denique vidimus à morte redivivum, & in cælos ascendentem. Hæc contra illos dicuntur, qui Jesum negabant in carne venisse: Addo: Imo etiam contra eos, qui Christum à JESU divi- debant.

Addit in gradatione Apostolus verbum ἐθεα- σάμεθα, quod non simpliciter viderint, sed accu- rate contemplati sint, & observavint, ne qua phan- tasma, quod Marcion deinde ausus est criminari, censeretur. Θεᾶσθαι secundum Oecumenium est cum admiratione & stupore inspicere. Est etiam publice quasi in theatro mirum novumque specta- culum contemplari. Quin subjungit: Quod ma- nus nostræ contrectarunt, quo adhuc magis omne dubium de phantasmate ac spectro præcludat, quemadmodum ea ratione Christus ipse post re- surrectionem Apostolis & infirmo Thomæ Luc. 24, 37. seqq. Joh. 20, 20. 27. dubitationem omnem adimere dignatus est. Non ergo hic opus est, hy- perbolen cum nonnullis fingere, quasi nihil aliud innuatur, quam quod inter ipsos habitavit, Job. 1. v. 14. Quidni enim vere ipsum manibus ante re- surrectionem contrectarint, cum ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀν- θρώπων γενόμενος, καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρω- πος, Phil. II, 7. 8. inter ipsos conversatus est, quum in gloriam per passionem ingressus seipsis non vi- dendum tantum, sed etiam manibus contrectan- dum præbuit? Quis est, inquit Augustinus in h. l. qui manibus tractet Verbum, nisi quia Verbum caro factum est & habitavit in nobis? Et porro: Quid est hoc? Ipsi viderunt, contrectarunt manibus Verbum vitæ. Ab initio erat, ad tempus visibilis & palpabilis factus est unicus Filius Dei.

Obstrepit hic Enjedinus, non posse illam par- ticulam, quod fuit ab initio, à cæteris separari, ut illa de æternitate, hæc de humanitate Christi acci- piantur; primo quia Apostolus id procul dubio execu- tus est, quod proposuit: at nihil usquam in tota hac epistola dicit de Christi æternitate. Secundo quia co- pula interjici debuisset, quo significaretur de rebus pluribus fore disputationem. Tertio quia in singulis clausulis articulus repetitus est, quo clausulæ conne- ctuntur, ut constet de eodem & non de alio ser- monem haberi. Sed hæc futilia sunt. Nam quod ad primum, non ita hic proponit tractanda, ut nuda sit propositio, à confirmatione distincta, sed statim materiam orditur, ac proponit & confir- mat simul argumentis, quod asserit; firmat nimi- rum idem esse suppositum, quod ab æterno fuit, & quod ipsimet in tempore viderunt, audiverunt, manibus contrectarunt: non esse aliam personam Verbum istud vitæ, alium Jesum, quem audive- runt &c. ne Verbum illud nudum esse homi- nem, sed verum & æternum Deum. In eam enim rem & autoritate sua Apostolica, & Apostolorum cæterorum testimonio, & sensum auditus, visus, tactusque indubitato documento utitur: quibus idem illud Verbum, quod ab æterno ceu Verus Deus fuit, cum quo conversati sunt ceu vero ho- mine, sese ipsis demonstravit. Neque hic tantum id firmat, sed deinceps etiam, imprimis vero c. 5. ubi adventum Filii Dei documentis & testimoniis divinorum pariter & terrenorum testium com- probatum dedit. Æternitatem autem ipsam Chri- sti versu statim proximo adstruxit S. Johannes, quum æternam eum vitam, quæ ἀπ' ἀρχῆς apud Patrem fuit, indigitarit, nec non C. V, 20. ubi eum verum Deum & vitam æternam esse docuit: ut alia jam taceamus. Quod ad alterum, defectus copulæ non arguit eandem naturam, sed eandem perso- nam; quum id asserendum fuerit, Jesum & Chri- stum, ac Filium Dei vel Verbum Dei non diver- sas esse personas; sed Jesum esse Christum Dei Fi- lium & Verbum æternum. Quod denique ad tertium articulum, repeti cum emphasi certum est; neque clausulas illas ad alium atque alium re- ferimus, sed de eodem & non de alio sermonem esse urgemus. Illa vero personæ identitas non ob- stat, quo minus aliqua clausula ad divinam, cæte- ræ ad humanam ejus naturam referri possint. Ideoq; verba illa περὶ τῦ λόγε τῆς ζωῆς non respi- ciunt, ut Socino præeunte Grotius vult, λόγον προ- φορικὸν doctrinam Evangelii, sed Christum λόγον ὑποστατικὸν, quod ut antea ostendimus, ita etiam huic naturarum distinctioni in Christo inservit. Non enim cum Piscatore anomalia appositionis pro τὸν λόγον statuenda, sed cum emphasi adhibi- ta est illa particula, quasi dicat, de λόγῳ illo vitæ lo- quor. Ut enim vocula περὶ Genitivo juncta par- ticula memorativa, ut periti Lexicographi no- tant, & h. l. ad ipsum λόγον τῆς ζωῆς in assumpta humanitate vera, qua conspectus, auditus, con- trectatus fuit ab Apostolis, considerandum nos ablegat, q. d. de Verbo vitæ & æterno Dei Filio loquor, qui factus est θεάνθρωπος assumpta Hu- mana natura non vero de quodam ψιλανθρώπῳ, seu nudo homine, ut habet B. Glassius Gram- mat. S. p. 74. Nec incommode hic monet Beza: Rursum distincte considerans in Christo aliud atque aliud, maluit scribere περὶ λόγε τῆς ζωῆς quam τὸν λόγον τῆς ζωῆς, ne scilicet sentire videretur idem esse id, quod viderat & palpaverat, at- que id, quod erat à principio (qua ratione confudis- set naturas) vel alium statuere eum, qui erat à principio, ab eo, quem viderat & palpaverat, id est, personam separatis naturis dividere. Mox vero versu sequenti apertissime hypostaticam unio- nem declarabit. Articulus etiam emphaticus est, innuens ipsum illud Verbum, per quod omnia facta sunt, & in quo uno vita est, uti Syrus quo- que explicat. Sunt qui voculam περὶ eo re- ferant, quod aliquid tantum περὶ λόγε hic cogno- scamus, & partialis solum notitia etiam illa fue- rit notitia, quam Apostoli habuere. Verum non agitur de notitia intellectuali, sed de experientia sensuali hic proprie sermo est. Lorinus Ebrai- smum esse dicit, qualis Actor. II. effundam de Spi- ritu meo pro eo, quod apud Joëlem, cum legitur: Effundam Spiritum meum. Estius: Dicendum, inquit, in eo, quod ait, de Verbo vitæ, loquutio- nem esse transitivam, hoc recto modo exprimen- dam: Ipsum Verbum vitæ, quod fuit à principio, quodque carne indutum audivimus & vidimus & contrectavimus. Ita, inquit, respondet opti- me exordium hujus epistolæ cum exordio Evangelii: In principio erat Verbum. Hæc Syntaxis est apud Augustinum in exposit. hujus epist. & apud alios. Eandem Syrus Interpres clare expressit. Modus explicandi est diversus. Sed sensus eodem redit. De Verbo vitæ, inquit Cornelius à Lapide, id est, ipsum Verbum vitæ, quod fuit ab initio, annun- tiamus vobis: atque ita Lyranus, Hugo, Catha- rinus, Gagnejus habent. B. Hunnius noster: Non temere, inquit, nec abs re Christum λόγον vitæ no- minat. Siquidem ipse solus vere est & vivit, cu- jus essentia nihil aliud est quam vita, quam cum Patre & Spiritu sancto communem obtinet, dicen- te ipsomet Christo. Sicut Pater habet vitam in se- metipso: Sic dedit & Filio habere vitam in semet- ipso Johan. V. Quamobrem verbis sequentibus non dubitat, illum abstracta voce vitam æternam ipsam nuncupare. Deinde vero & hanc ob causam sic dici- tur, quod obedientia suæ merito vitam æternam no- bis acquisivit. Ergo hoc augustissimo titulo & elogio Deitatem ipsius commendat Johannes.

Dicitur autem λόγος τῆς ζωῆς, non modo quod vita ipsa sit ὀσιωδῶς ut Deus, Joh. V, 69. & ὑποστα- τικῶς ut homo Joh. VI. vers. 48. 50. sed etiam quod Autor vitæ sit αὐτοενεργητικῶς, à quo est tum vita naturalis, quia omnia per ipsum existunt, & consistunt omnia in ipso, Coloss. I, 16. 17. tum vita spiritualis & cœlestis. Joh. XIV, 6. Cap. XI, 25. vi- vificat quos vult, Joh. V, 21. Vocatur ergo Ver- bum vitæ duplici ratione, & quia Verbum vivens est, imo ipsa vita, & quia Verbum vivificum, id est, vitam ac salutem afferens hominibus. Vi- detur autem Estio prior modus hic significatus, uti sequentia declarant, cum respectu tamen ad modum posteriorem, qui eodem modo etiam lo- cum Evangelii intelligendum censet: In ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux hominum.

## 1:2
Verse 2.

And the life was manifested, and we have seen.] For the eternal life of Christ has also been made conspicuous to us by his example. See 2 Timothy I, 10.

And we bear witness.] Here 'and' signifies 'this very thing,' he says, we testify, having discovered it by our own senses, Acts I, 8; c. 2, 32; c. 3, 15; c. 4, 20; c. 5, 32; c. 10, 40. See what has been said by us on the preface to Luke, and 2 Peter I, 16.

And we announce to you the eternal life.] Relying on such great pledges, we make you also certain concerning eternal life. The word 'we announce' fits this business. See Acts XXVI, 20. In the Manuscript: 'We announce also to you.' We announce these things even to you who are so far away.

Which was with the Father.] It had long lain hidden in the decree of God. See what is said at the cited place, John I, 2. Add Ephesians III, 5.

And was manifested to us.] Here 'and' signifies 'but.' But to us, he says, it has been revealed, not to the Patriarchs, not to the Prophets, Romans XVI, 25; Colossians I, 26; Hebrews VIII, 6.

It is now explained in what way he predicates concerning the Word both 'that which was from the beginning' by reason of existence, which is the divine nature, and 'to be heard, seen, looked upon, handled' by reason of temporary conversation, as regards the human [nature], and 'to be the Word of life' by reason of both natures. As regards the divine nature, it is called 'eternal life, which was with the Father': As regards the human, 'manifestation' is attributed to them, because he is not God without flesh, but in the flesh, manifested in the flesh, 1 Timothy 3, 16, and because he was seen in the flesh by the Apostles, who testify of him and announce him, preaching the coming of the Son of God into the world, or the eternal life, which was with the Father from eternity, and appeared to them, having assumed human nature in the fullness of time: Which to testify was the proper office of the Apostles. This, therefore, is what the Apostle says, in the interpretation of Flacius, that life-giving Word, from the bosom of the Father, where he was and will be in all eternity, came to us through the incarnation and most familiar conversation and instruction: so that it has been made entirely most known to us, and we preach to you things most fully ascertained. Most manifestly in these things both the two natures of Christ, divine and human, and the unity of his person or hypostasis are asserted, while he says that that very Word was that Jesus whom they heard, saw, and touched. He was manifested, says Augustine in his exposition on the epistle of John, life itself in the flesh, because it was placed in manifestation, so that the thing which can be seen only by the heart might be seen also by the eyes, so that it might heal hearts. For the Word is seen only by the heart, but flesh is seen also by bodily eyes. There was a way for us to see the flesh, but there was not a way for us to see the Word. The Word was made flesh, which we could see, so that that by which we might see the Word might be healed in us. Therefore, 'the life' and 'the eternal life' are said with the emphasis of the article concerning hypostatic life, just as John I, 4, 'and the life was the light of men,' and John XIV, 6; Chapter XI, 25, 'I am the life,' Colossians III, 4, 'when Christ your life shall appear': just as also 'the Word of life' is said concerning the hypostatic Word: and the Apostle himself explains it thus, 1 John V, 20, concerning the Word, whom he had called in verse 7, affirming, 'this is the true God, and the eternal life'; and Revelation XIX, 13, concerning 'the true one, and his name is called the Word of God.' Eternal life was not finally to be manifested by the Apostle, as the faithful of the Old Testament also had knowledge of it; unless one wishes to invent with the Socinians that Christ was the first herald of eternal life, and to make the Patriarchs and Prophets and other saints devoid of it. But that Jesus is he who had been promised, not as a herald of eternal life, but as the procurer of the same, who by his obedience and death had to acquire eternal life for us, that is, that he is the Messiah whom the ancients were expecting, and whom they believed would come, through whom we believe just as they did, that we are to obtain salvation through his grace, Acts 15:11. This, indeed, is what the Apostles announced.

But Grotius's gloss is futile: Eternal life was made conspicuous to us by the example of Christ. Thus, it could already be said to have been made conspicuous by the example of Enoch and Elijah. Therefore, it could also have been said in those times: καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἐφανερώθη, καὶ ἑωράκαμεν. Nor indeed did any of the Apostles behold eternal life or eternal blessedness with their own eyes, except Paul, who, however, having been caught up out of the flesh into the third heaven, it is doubtful whether he saw eternal life with his own eyes. And lest anyone object with John's ἀποκάλυψιν, John is speaking here of that which other Apostles saw at the same time; it is likely that the ἀποκάλυψιν happened only after this epistle. Finally, eternal life cannot be seen in the example of Christ so that we might likewise aspire to it; because Christ is not ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος, but θεάνθρωπος, and he knew no sin, and by his own power, triumphing over the devil and death, he entered into glory. Which example is without example.

Furthermore, ἀπαγγέλλειν does not mean to make certain by giving a pledge, but to announce: nor can we be made certain of obtaining eternal life by the example of Christ: but by his merit, apprehended by faith, we are made certain that we have eternal life in Christ. Moreover, it is a question here of hypostatic life, just as it is of the λόγῳ ὑποστατικῷ: of that life which was with God the Father; which does not sound of a long-lasting concealment in the decree of the Father, but of eternal existence with the Father; from which propriety of sense we are loath to deflect to an improper and figurative one: nay, as we have said, it is false that salvation and eternal life were not manifested to the Patriarchs and Prophets, but only finally to the Apostles. For did not Abraham with others expect eternal [life] by faith

and the heavenly fatherland? Did not David describe the joy of eternal life in Psalm 16, last verse, and Psalm 17, last verse, and elsewhere? Did not Isaiah describe the joy of eternal blessedness quite often in Ch. 25:7, Ch. 31:10, Ch. 60:19 ff., Ch. 65:17-18, Ch. 66:22-23, Daniel Ch. 12:1, etc., and others? But this error of Grotius is too shameful, and born from the dung-heap of Pelagius and Socinus. Most interpreters agree that these things are to be understood concerning the hypostatic manifestation in the flesh. Cornelius is correct: The Word, which is immortal and blessed life, both formal and causal, as I have already said, but hidden with GOD in the bosom of the Father, has now manifested itself through the incarnation, and has presented itself to men as visible and tangible: Therefore we Apostles, who have seen that, testify and announce to you the eternal life, which was with the Father, and now at the end of the ages has appeared to us through the assumed flesh. This is what Isaiah predicted in Ch. 40:5. The glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see together what the mouth of the Lord has spoken, namely, as St. Luke explains in Ch. 3:5. And all flesh shall see the salvation of God, that is, every man shall see the Christ of GOD, as St. Ambrose says in the same place. Cassian, book 5, on the incarnation, Ch. 6. Then, he says, he adds the Word life and the manifested life: that he saw this, that he announces this, that he protests this, at the same time, of course, fulfilling the duty of faith and instilling terror into unbelief: so that when he certainly protests that he is preaching, he might impute his danger to himself, who would not want to hear him.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἐφανερώθη, καὶ ἑωράκαμεν.] Nam & vita æterna Christi exemplo facta nobis est conspicua. Vid. 2. Tim. I, 10.

Καὶ μαρτυρῶμεν.] Καὶ hic valet hoc ipsum, ait, testamur, sensibus compertum propriis, Actor. I, 8. c. 2, 32. c. 3, 15. c. 4, 20. c. 5, 32. c. 10, 40. Vide quæ dicta à nobis ad Lucæ præfationem, & 2. Petr. I, 16.

Καὶ ἀπαγγέλλομεν ὑμῖν τὴν ζωὴν τὴν αἰώνιον.] Tantus freti pignoribus certos & vos reddimus de vita æterna. Vox ἀπαγ- γέλλομεν aptat huic negotio. Vid. Actor. XXVI, 20. In Manu- scripto: Ἀπαγγέλλομεν καὶ ὑμῖν. Etiam vobis hæc nuntiamus tam longe dissitis.

Ἥτις ἦν πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα.] In decreto Dei diu latuerat. Vi- de quæ dicto loco Joh. I, 2. Adde Eph. III, 5.

Καὶ ἐφανερώθη ἡμῖν.] καὶ hic valet sed. Sed nobis, inquit, patefacta est, non Patriarchis, non Prophetis, Rom. XVI, 25. Col. I, 26. Ebr. VIII, 6.

Explicatur jam, qua ratione de λόγῳ prædica- cit & τὸ ἦν ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς ratione existentiæ, quod di- vinam naturam, & τὸ audiri, videri, spectari, contre- ctari ratione conversationis temporariæ, quoad Humanam, & τὸ esse λόγον τῆς ζωῆς ratione utrius- que naturæ. Quoad naturam divinam dicitur ζωὴ αἰώνιος, ἥτις ἦν πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα: Quoad Hu- manam Φανέρωσις ipsis tribuitur, quod nempe non sit Deus ἄσαρκος, sed ἔνσαρκος, manifestatus in carne 1. Tim. 3, 16. quodque in carne visus Aposto- lis sit, qui de eo testantur, eumque annuntiant, prædicantes adventum Filii Dei in mundum, vel vitam æternam, quæ apud Patrem erat ab æterno, ipsisque apparuit, assumpta humana natura in ple- nitudine temporis: Quod testari proprium erat Apostolorum officium. Hoc itaque est, quod dicit Apostolus, interprete Flacio, vivificum illud Ver- bum, ex sinu Patris, ubi in omni æternitate fuit & erit, venit ad nos per incarnationem, familiarissi- mamque conversationem & institutionem: ut no- bis sit factum prorsus notissimum, vobisque tantum compertissima prædicemus. Manifestissime hisce tum duæ naturæ Christi, divina & humana, tum & unitas ejus personæ aut hypostaseos asserta est, dum illud ipsum Verbum dicit fuisse eum Jesum, quem illi audiverint, viderint ac palpaverint. Manife- stata est, inquit Augustinus exposit. in epist. Joh. ipsa vita in carne, quia in manifestatione posita est, ut res, quæ solo corde videri potest, videretur & ocu- lis, ut corda sanaret. Solo enim corde videtur Verbum, caro autem & oculis corporalibus videtur. Erat unde videremus carnem, sed non erat, unde videremus Verbum. Factum est Verbum caro, quam videre possemus, ut sanaretur in nobis, un- de Verbum videremus. Dicitur ergo ἡ ζωή, & ἡ ζωὴ ἡ αἰώνιος cum emphası articuli de vita ὑποστατικῇ, quemadmodum Joh. I, 4. καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἦν τὸ φῶς τῶν ἀνθρώπων, & Joh. XIV, 6. Cap. XI, 25. ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ζωὴ, Coloss. III, 4. cum apparebit Christus vita ve- stra: prout etiam ὁ λόγος τῆς ζωῆς de λόγῳ ὑπο- στατικῷ dicitur: idque ita explicat Apostolus ipse, 1. Joh. V, 20. de τῷ λόγῳ, quem vocarat vers. 7. affirmans, ὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς, καὶ ἡ ζωὴ αἰώ- νιος; & Apoc. XIX, 13. de τῷ ἀληθινῷ, καὶ καλεῖται τὸ ὄνομα ἀυτῦ ὁ λόγος τῦ Θεῦ. Vita æterna non demum manifestanda erat ab Apostolo, utpote cujus notitiam etiam fideles Veteris Testamenti habuere; nisi cum Socinianis fingere libeat, pri- mum vitæ æternæ præconem fuisse Christum, & Patriarchas & Prophetas, aliosque sanctos ex- pertes facere. At Jesum esse illum, qui promis- sus erat non ut præco vitæ æternæ, sed ut pararius ejusdem, qui nobis obedientia ac morte sua vi- tam æternam acquirere debuerit, hoc est, Mes- siam illum esse, quem expectabant veteres, & quem venturum credebant, per quem æque nos ut illi credimus, quod per gratiam ejus salutem consequuturi simus, Actor. XV, 10. Hoc vero est, quod annunciarunt Apostoli.

Futilis autem est Grotii Glossa: Vita æterna Christi exemplo nobis facta est conspicua. Sic jam Enochi & Eliæ exemplo conspicua facta dici posset. Ergo & istis temporibus potuisset dici: καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἐφανερώθη, καὶ ἑωράκαμεν. Nec vero vitam seu beatitudinem æternam quisquam Apo- stolorum oculis suis usurpavit, nisi Paulus, qui tamen extra carnem raptus in tertium cœlum an oculis suis vitam æternam viderit, dubium est. Ac ne quis obvertat Johannis ἀποκάλυψιν, loqui- tur hic Johannes de eo, quod viderunt simul alii Apostoli, verisimile est, post hanc epistolam de- mum contigisse ἀποκάλυψιν. Denique in exem- plo Christi vita æterna videri nequit, ut nos pari- ter ad eam adspiremus; quia Christus non ψιλὸς ἄνθρωπος, sed θεάνθρωπος est, nec peccatum ullum novit, & propria virtute de diabolo & mor- te triumphans in gloriam ingressus est. Quod ex- emplum est sine exemplo.

Porro ἀπαγγέλλειν non est pignore dato certum reddere, sed annunciare: nec de vita æterna con- sequenda exemplo Christi certi reddi possumus: Sed merito ejus fide apprehenso certi reddimur, nos habere in Christo vitam æternam. Adhæc de vita hypostatica, perinde ut de λόγῳ ὑποστατι- κῷ agitur hic: De ea vita, quæ erat apud Deum Patrem; quod non de delitescentia in decreto Pa- tris diuturno, sed de æterna existentia apud Pa- trem sonat; à qua sensus proprietate ad impro- prium & figuratum deflectere religio nobis est: imo, ut diximus, falsum est, manifestatam salu- tem & vitam æternam non fuisse Patriarchis & Prophetis, sed demum Apostolis. Annon enim fide Abraham cum aliis expectavit æternam

& coelestem patriam? Annon David lætitiam vitæ æternæ Psalm. XVI. v. ult. & Pf. XVII. v. ult. & alibi descripsit? Annon Esaias descripsit gau- dium æternæ beatitudinis sæpius C. 25, 7. C. 31, 10. C. 60, 19. seqq. C. 65, 17. 18. C. 66, 22. 23. Daniel Cap. 12, 1. &c. aliique? Sed hic error Grotii ni- mis pudendus, eque Pelagii, & Socini sterquili- nio enatus. Consonant plerique Interpretes, hæc de vita hypostatica in carne manifestatione in- telligenda esse. Recte Cornelius: Verbum, quod est vita immortalis & beata, tum formalis, tum cau- salis, uti jam dixi, sed abscondita apud DEUM in sinu Patris, jam per incarnationem sese manifesta- vit, ac hominibus aspectabilem & tractabilem se- se præbuit: Itaque nos Apostoli, qui vidimus illud, testamur & annunciamus vobis vitam æternam, quæ erat apud Patrem, & nunc in fine seculorum per carnem assumptam apparuit nobis. Hoc est, quod prædixit Esaias Cap. 40, 5. Revelabitur gloria Do- mini, & videbit omnis caro pariter, quod os Domi- ni loquutum est, nimirum ut explicat S. Lucas Cap. III, 5. Et videbit omnis caro salutare Dei, id est, videbit omnis homo Christum DEI, ut ibidem S. Ambrosius. Cassianus lib. V. de incarnat. Cap. 6. Deinde, ait, addit Verbum vita & vitam manife- statam: hoc se vidisse, hoc annunciare, hoc protesta- ri, simul scilicet, exequens officium fidei, & ingerens terrorem incredulitati: ut cum ille utique protesta- tur se prædicare, sibi imputaret periculum suum, qui eum noluisset audire.

## 1:3
Verse 3.

That which we have seen and heard, we announce to you, that you also may have fellowship with us.] We render this testimony to you so certain, not only so that you may know these things to be true, when many histories are narrated, but so that you yourselves, no less than we, may perceive the fruit from it, fellowship with God and with Christ, here in holiness, hereafter in blessedness. Κοινωνίαν ἔχειν is the same as κοινωνεῖν 1 Pet. 4:13, κοινωνὸν εἶναι 2 Cor. 1:7, or γενέσθαι 2 Pet. 1:4, μέτοχον γενέσθαι Heb. 6:4, ch. 12:8.

And our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.] Namely, it happens, which the Latin supplies. He explains what that fellowship is, about which he began to speak below in ch. 3:2 and 2 Tim. 2:12. It is a pleonasm. For καὶ remains with the following δέ. Similar abundance in John 6:51.

We admit that the second comma, which we said was exegetical, should be read in the parenthesis. Now therefore he returns to that which the Apostle had said: That, I say, which we have seen and heard. (We announce to you that Word manifested in the flesh, that it has indeed come.) Estius thinks the text becomes clearer if it is supplied in this way: Which we also saw, of which therefore we also testify, and which we announce to you, the life, I say, eternal. Again, however, what is said here agrees with those things which are held in the Gospel. For what he says there, and the Word was with God, this he now says of the life, which was with the Father: And what there: The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, here he says of the life, and appeared to us. Flacius: Again, he says, resuming in the manner customary to the Hebrews through Epanalepsis from the first member of the sentence that which we heard, and from the second, we announce: He further adds what benefit they themselves are to perceive from this, or what at last is the end and fruit or effect of that Savior and his doctrine: namely, that most excellent one, that all his true followers may have communion with the Apostles and Prophets, and indeed with the sacred Triad itself.

The Apostle therefore adds the end and fruit of this advent or manifestation, and of this proclamation or announcement, that you may have communion with us, which is our communion with the Father and with his Son JESUS Christ. The particle καὶ

(that you also) is an argument that the discourse is not about the benefit and fruit of the Incarnation absolutely, which pertains to all, since the Son of GOD came for the sake of the salvation of all and acquired salvation for all, but by reason of the modern announcement, by which indeed that communion with GOD acquired for all was also announced to them, so that they might enjoy the same together with the Apostles. According to the Vulgate version, the sense is: And that our society, that is, yours joined with us, may be with GOD the Father and the Son. But if vero is to be supplied, as the particle δὲ (but) seems to demand (for Erasmus also approves this more in his annotation), it will be an assumption to that which precedes, so that the sense is: Our society, however, that is, that which we Apostles have among ourselves (lest I seem to promise you a thing not very much to be desired) is common to us with the Father and his Son JESUS Christ. Which society is certainly to be desired with all prayers. Wherefore if you enter into society with us, consequently you will be together with us partners of the Father and the Son, as Estius says here. This is the highest and chief effect and fruit of both the advent of the Son of God and the Evangelical proclamation, communion with the Father, by which we are partakers of the divine nature, 1 Pet. 1:4, we turn out to be one with GOD, 1 Cor. 6:17, because communion presupposes union; we live in God, or of the life which is from God, Eph. 4:18, Gal. 2:20, and we turn out to be partners of GOD, and how great and how lovable a society this is, so that all may understand, it is expressed by the name of friendship, which St. James alleges as a great thing, that Abraham was called the friend of GOD, Ch. 2:23, which communion, society, and friendship also brings about the participation of divine goods, just as the goods of friends are common; which we enjoy here through faith, and one day we shall enjoy according to sight, 2 Cor. 5:7. Since, on the contrary, we were separated from GOD by sin, Isa. 59. v. 2, destitute of the life which is from GOD, Eph. 4. v. 18, dead in transgression, Eph. 2. v. 1, deprived of the friendship of God, subject to the hatred and abomination of God, and shut up under the wrath of GOD, Rom. 3. v. 19, Chap. 11. v. 32, despoiled of all divine goods, Rom. 3. v. 23, and subject to all evils, and finally to eternal death and condemnation, which brings the heap of all evils, Gen. 2. v. 17, Deut. 27. v. 26, Rom. 6. v. ult. Since indeed in this miserable state we would have had to perish eternally, unless we had been delivered through Christ the Mediator and brought to the communion of God: Therefore it is added: Καὶ μετὰ τῦ ὑιῦ ἀυτῦ Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ, because we do not arrive at communion with the Father except in Christ Jesus, John 14. v. 6, Acts 4. v. 12. Wherefore it was necessary that the Son of God should become a partaker of our flesh and blood, so that we might be rendered partakers of the divine nature in Him, Heb. 2. v. 14. Jesus of Nazareth, therefore, was made Christ, Messiah, or the Anointed of the Lord, when the eternal Word was made flesh, John 1. v. 14, and the Son of God was born man, Gal. 4. v. 4, so that He might be our Mediator, Redeemer and Savior, our High Priest, who would reconcile us to GOD by His merit and intercession, our Prophet, who would bring to us the knowledge of GOD from the bosom of the Father, and our King, who would rule and protect us in the kingdom of grace, and lead us to the kingdom of glory. The Son of GOD, says Irenaeus lib. V. cap. 1, because of His immense love became what we are, that He might perfect us to be what He Himself is; He was made a partaker of our nature, that we might be rendered partakers of the divine nature, and cap. XIV. The Word of God was made man, assimilating Himself to man, and man to Himself, so that through that likeness which is toward the Son, man may become precious to the Father. Augustine, book 9, On the City of God, ch. 15: Blessed and beatifying God, having been made a participant of our humanity, provided a compendium of participating in his divinity. See also concerning the communion of the Son of God, 1 Cor. 1:9. Nor indeed do we have communion with the Father only through Jesus the Son of God; but we have communion also with Christ Jesus himself, the Son of God: because we are also one as regards the mystical union with the Father and the Son, as also with the Holy Spirit, and thus we enjoy communion with the undivided, sacrosanct Trinity, to which also the human nature of Christ, received into the hypostasis of the Son of God, pertains. Which John does not deny. Hesselius, Lorinus, Cornelius: of whom the latter, in this place, has it thus: This society or communion of ours with Christ, as much God as man, is as of Lord and Servant, Father and adopted son, illuminator and illuminated, justifier and justified, ruler and subject, giver and receiver, hearer and invoker, donor and one giving thanks for gifts, beatifier and blessed. Finally, that he who adheres to God may be one spirit with him, and walking in the light, just as he himself is in the light, may have society with him. Therefore also Christ calls us his friends by virtue of this society, John 15:15, Song of Songs 5:10. Compare Hosea 2:19, 2 Cor. 11:2. Furthermore, our blessed Hunnius fixes an exhortation here, which we do not deny is done tacitly; even though the Apostle is properly occupied in teaching, and designates the end of the Evangelical proclamation concerning the hypostatic communion, which he had hinted at before. For since to be seen and to be touched are not proper to the Deity, but to the Humanity alone; yet they are truly and really attributed to the Word, the Son of God, which is done for this reason, because in true communion, as the blessed Hunnius advises, he personally united himself to this flesh. Indeed, just as each of us has his own proper body and soul: so also the Word has been made a participant of flesh and blood, and thus of the entire humanity in a similar way, Heb. 2. And he so personally united this flesh to himself, that whatever is said of it, that is said and believed of the Son of God himself, from which it is possible to estimate how sublime and ineffable a communion intervenes between the Word and the assumed nature, so that the flesh cannot be touched or seen, without the Son of God being immediately touched and seen by that very fact.

From that personal communion, therefore, of the Word and our human nature, the Apostle proceeds to the spiritual communion which intervenes between us and the Word, or the economy of the incarnation, as the end and fruit of the same. Which the blessed Hunnius presents thus: He descends to the exhortation proposed to himself, by which he strives to persuade men that they should embrace this doctrine concerning the incarnate Word, the Lord Jesus Christ, with true faith.
