He uses an argument taken from dignity, not indeed that which the doctrine of the Gospel shines with of itself by reason of the sublimity and majesty of its subject matter, of which he had spoken before, but that which it confers and conciliates to us men, while by the benefit and power of this doctrine we arrive into the communion or society not of some Prince, not of a King, not of an Emperor or earthly Monarch, but of God himself, who is the King of Kings and Lord of Lords. We announce, he says, to you, that having received this doctrine you may have society with us, and not with us only, but that our society may be with God the Father and his Son Jesus Christ. Which society and familiarity is not human, but divine, not earthly, but heavenly, containing an ineffable dignity joined with the highest and perpetual beatitude. Indeed, the hinge of our eternal felicity turns on this familiarity with God and the beneficial fruition of him, by which he deigns to communicate himself and his treasures to us in eternal life, by reason of which communication he himself is to be our sufficiency, and thus all in all, 1 Cor. 15. And further: And these things we write to you, etc. That is, this doctrine at last and no other can excite true and solid joy in us, so that in the midst of afflictions it may be permitted to you to exult under the hope of that everlasting communion and society with the highest good, God the Best and Greatest. Flacius distinguishes communion with the Father and communion with the Son. The former he calls the association with him by which we are reconciled to him, and are his household, and thus sons and heirs: The latter, by which, perceiving by faith all the merits of Christ, we are brothers and members and co-heirs of him, and through him are justified and saved, and use him as our perpetual King, Priest, and advocate. He adds: Communion with the Holy Spirit is that by which we are illuminated, ruled, and sanctified by him unto eternal life. Communion with the Church is to be so inserted into it through baptism that you are a participant of its ministry, of the Word and Sacraments, of prayers, and altogether of all its goods, by which also you are a fellow-member of all other pious people in this body of the Church, and under one head, Christ, and finally by which you are also a participant of both his confession and his cross.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Ὁ ἑωράκαμεν καὶ ἀκηκόαμεν, ἀπαγγέλλομεν ὑμῖν, ἵνα καὶ ὑμεῖς κοινωνίαν ἔχητε μεθ' ἡμῶν.] Testimonium hoc tam certum vobis reddimus, non tantum ut noritis hæc esse vera, quando historiæ multæ narrantur, sed ut & vos ipsi non minus quam nos fructum inde percipiatis, societatem cum Deo & cum Christo, hic in sanctitate, imposterum in beatitudine. Κοινω- νίαν ἔχειν idem quod κοινωνεῖν 1. Petr. 4, 13. κοινωνὸν εἶναι 2. Cor. I, 7. aut γενέσθαι 2. Petr. I, 4. μέτοχον γενέσθαι Ebr. 6, 4. c. 12, 8.

Καὶ ἡ κοινωνία δὲ ἡ ἡμετέρα μετὰ τῦ Πατρὸς καὶ τῦ ὑῖῦ ἀυτῦ Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ.] Nempe, fit, quod supplet Latinus. Explicat, quæ sit illa societas, de qua loqui cœpit infra c. 3, 2. & 2. Tim. 2, 12. Est pleonasmus. Nam καὶ superest sequente δὲ. Par abundantia Joh. 6, 51.

Admittimus in parenthesi legendum comma secundum, quod primi diximus exegeticum. Jam ergo redit ad id, quod dixerat Apostolus: Quod, inquam, vidimus & audivimus. (Verbum illud in carne manifestatum annunciamus vobis, quod nempe id venerit) Planiorem putat Estius textum fieri, si suppleatur hoc modo: Quam & vidimus, de qua proinde & testificamur, quamque vobis an- nunciamus, vitam, inquam, æternam. Rursus autem, quæ hic dicuntur, conveniunt cum iis, quæ habentur in Evangelio. Quod enim illic ait, & Verbum erat apud Deum, hoc de vita nunc dicit, quæ erat apud Patrem: Et quod illic: Ver- bum caro factum est, & habitavit in nobis, hic de vita dicit, & apparuit nobis. Flacius: Iterum, inquit, more Ebræis usitato per Epanalepsin resu- mens ex primo orationis membro illud, quod audi- vimus, & ex secundo, annuntiamus: Attexit por- ro, quid ipsi hinc commodi sint percepturi, seu quis tandem finis & fructus effectusve sit istius Servato- ris ejusque doctrinæ: nempe ille longe præclarissimus, ut omnes ejus veri sectatores habeant communionem cum Apostolis & Prophetis, atque adeo cum ipsamet sacra Triade.

Addit ergo Apostolus hujus tum adventus vel manifestationis, tum præconii vel annunciatio- nis finem & fructum, ut communionem habeatis nobiscum, quæ communio nostra est cum Patre & cum Filio ejus JESU Christo. Particula καὶ

(ἵνα καὶ ὑμεῖς) argumento est, de beneficio & fru- ctu Incarnationis non absolute, quæ ad omnes pertinet, quum omnium salutis causa advenerit Filius DEI, omnibusque salutem acquisiverit, sed ratione modernæ annunciationis sermonem esse, qua nempe illa communio cum DEO omnibus acquæsita ipsis etiam annunciabatur, ut eadem fruerentur juxta cum Apostolis. Juxta vulga- tam versionem sensus est: Utque societas nostra, id est, vestra nobiscum adunata sit cum DEO Pa- tre & Filio. Quod si vero est suppleatur, ut postu- lare videtur particula δὲ autem (nam & Erasmus id magis probat in annotatione) erit assumptio ad id, quod præcedit, ut sensus sit: Nostra autem societas, id est, ea, quam nos Apostoli inter nos habemus (ne rem non admodum expetendam pro- mittere vobis videar) nobis communis est cum Pa- tre, & Filio ejus JESU Christo. Quæ profecto so- cietas omnibus votis est expetenda. Quare si no- biscum inieritis societatem, consequenter una eritis nobiscum socii Patris & Filii, ut hic Estius. Sum- mus & præcipuus hic effectus & fructus est tum adventus Filii Dei, tum præconii Evangelici κοι- νωνία μετὰ τῦ Πατρὸς, qua κοινωνοὶ sumus θείας φύσεως, 1. Petr. I, 4. unum evadimus cum DEO, 1. Cor. 6. vers. 17. quia κοινωνία præsupponit unio- nem; vivimus in Deo, vel vitæ, quæ est ex Deo, Ephes. 4. vers. 18. Galat. 2. vers. 20. & socii evadi- mus DEI, quæ quanta sit & quam amabilis so- cietas, ut omnes intelligant, exprimitur nomi- ne amicitiæ, quod ceu magnum allegat S. Ja- cobus, quod nempe Abraham amicus DEI ap- pellatus, Cap. 2. vers. 23. quæ communio, societas, & amicitia infert etiam bonorum divinorum par- ticipationem, quemadmodum amicorum bona sunt communia; quibus hic fruimur per fidem, olim fruemur secundum speciem, 2. Corinth. V, 7. Quum ex adverso per peccatum essemus divulsi à DEO, Esa. 59. vers. 2. expertes vitæ, quæ est ex DEO, Ephes. 4. v. 18. mortui in prævaricatio- ne, Ephes. 2. vers. 1. privati amicitia Dei, odio & abominationi Dei obnoxii, & sub ira DEI con- clusi, Rom. 3. v. 19. Cap. 11. v. 32. omnibus bonis divinis spoliati, Rom. 3. vers. 32. omnibus malis, æternæ denique morti & condemnationi, quæ cumulum omnium malorum infert, subjecti, Gen. 2. v. 17. Deut. 27. v. 28. Rom. 6. vers. ult. Quum vero in hoc miserabili statu æternum nobis pereundum fuiffet, nisi per Christum Mediatorem liberati & ad communionem Dei adducti fuissemus: Ideo additur: Καὶ μετὰ τῦ ὑιῦ ἀυτῦ Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ, quia non nisi in Christo Jesu nos ad communionem cum Patre pervenimus, Joh. 14. vers. 6. Actor. 4. v. 12. Quapropter opus fuit, ut Filius Dei carnis & sanguinis nostri particeps fieret, ut nos in ipso divinæ naturæ consortes redderemur, Ebr. 2. vers. 14. Jesum Nazarenum ergo ita Christum, Mes- siam, vel unctum Domini factum, cum æternum Verbum caro factum, Johan. I. vers. 14. Filius Dei homo natus est, Gal. 4. vers. 4. ut esset noster Mediator, Redemptor & Salvator, Pontifex no- ster, qui nos DEO reconciliaret merito & in- tercessione sua, Prophetæ, qui DEI cognitio- nem nobis è sinu Patris afferret, & Rex noster, qui nos in regno gratiæ regeret ac tueretur, & ad regnum gloriæ perduceret. Filius DEI, in- quit Irenæus lib. V. cap. 1. propter immensam suam dilectionem factus est, quod nos sumus, ut nos per- ficeret esse, quod est ipse, factus est particeps na- turæ nostræ, ut nos redderemur consortes naturæ divinæ, & cap. XIV. Verbum Dei factum est ho- mo, seipsum homini, & hominem sibi ipsi assimilans, ut per eam, quæ est ad Filium, similitudinem pretio- sus homo fiat Patri. Augustinus l. 9. de C. D. c. 15. Beatus & beatificus Deus factus particeps humanita- tis nostræ compendium præbuit participandæ divini- tatis suæ. Videatur etiam de communione Filii Dei 1. Cor. I, 9. Nec vero tantum per Jesum Filium DEI communionem habemus cum Patre; sed communionem etiam habemus cum ipso Christo Jesu Filii Dei: quia unum etiam sumus quoad unionem mysticam cum Patre & Filio, ut & Spiritu Sancto, adeoque communione cum indivisa sacro- sancta Trinitate fruimur, ad quam etiam Huma- na Christi natura recepta in hypostasin Filii DEI pertinet. Quod non diffitentur Joh. Hesselius, Lorinus, Cornelius: è quibus hic in h. l. ita habet: Societas sive communio hæc nostra cum Christo tam Deo, quam homine, est tanquam Domini & Servi, Patris & filii adoptivi, illuminantis & illuminati, justificantis & justificati, regentis & subditi, dan- tis & accipientis, exaudientis & invocantis, donan- tis, & pro muneribus gratias agentis, beatificantis & beati. Denique ut adhærens Deo unus cum illo sit Spiritus, & in luce ambulans, sicut ipse est in luce, societatem habeat cum ipso. Ideo & Christus nos amicos suos dicit vi hujus societatis, Joh. 15, 15. Cant. 5, 10. Conf. Ose. 2, 19. 2. Cor. 11. 2. Cæte- rum B. Hunnius noster exhortationem hic figit, quam tacite fieri non abnuimus; etsi Apostolus proprie in διδασκαλίᾳ versetur, & finem præconii Evangelici de κοινωνίᾳ hypostatica designet, quam antea innuerat. Quum enim videri, tangi non sint Deitatis propria, sed solius Humanitatis; ea tamen vere ac realiter tribuantur λόγῳ Filio DEI, quod ideo fit, quia vera κοινωνίᾳ, ut monet B. Hunnius, se huic carni personaliter univit. Siquidem ut no- strum quisque suum habet proprium corpus & ani- mam: Sic & λόγος carnis & sanguinis, adeoque integre humanitatis consimiliter particeps est factus, Ebr. II. Et hanc carnem ita personaliter sibi uni- vit, ut quicquid de ea dicitur, id de ipsomet Filio Dei dicatur & credatur, ex quo æstimare licet, quam sublimis & inenarrabilis κοινωνία inter λόγον & na- turam assumptam interveniat, ut nec tangi, nec vide- ri possit caro, quin protinus eo ipso tangatur & videa- tur Filius Dei.

Ab illa ergo κοινωνίᾳ personali λόγε & Humanæ nostræ naturæ ad κοινωνίαν spiritualem, quæ nobis cum λόγῳ intercedit, vel οἰκονομίαν incarnatio- nis progreditur Apostolus, ceu finem & fru- ctum ejusdem. Quod ita exhibet B. Hunnius: Descendit ad propositam sibi exhortationem, qua persuadere nititur hominibus, ut hanc de incar- nato Verbo Domino JESU Christo doctrinam vera fide amplectantur. Argumento utitur sumpto à dignitate, non ea quidem, quæ ipsamet per se doctrina Evangelii ob materiæ sublimitatem ac majestatem fulget, de qua prius dixerat, sed ea, quam nobis hominibus confert & conciliat, dum beneficio ac virtute hujus doctrinæ pervenimus in κοινωνίαν seu societatem non alicujus Principis, non Regis, non Imperatoris aut Monarchæ terreni, sed ipsiusmet DEI, qui Rex Regum est, & Do- minus dominantium. Annuntiamus, inquit, vo- bis, ut suscepta hac doctrina societatem habeatis no- biscum, nec nobiscum duntaxat, sed ut societas no- stra sit cum DEO Patre & Filio ejus Jesu Christo. Quæ societas & familiaritas non humana, sed divi- na est, non terrena, sed cælestis, continens inenarra- bilem dignitatem cum summa perpetuaque beatitu- dine conjunctam. Siquidem æterna nostra felicitati- cardo vertitur in hac cum Deo familiaritate & bene- fica ipsius fruitione, qua dignatur se suosque the- sauros in vita æterna nobis communicare, ratione cu- jus communicationis ipse nostra sufficientia, adeoque omnia in omnibus futurus est, 1. Cor. XV. Et porro: Et hæc scribimus vobis &c. Id est, hæc doctrina de- mum & nulla alia verum solidumque gaudium in nobis excitare potest, ut in mediis afflictionibus liceat vobis exultare sub spe illius sempiternæ κοινωνίας ac societatis cum summo bono, DEO Optimo Maximo. Flacius communionem cum Patre, & communio- nem cum Filio distinguit. Illam dicit consociatio- nem cum eo, qua reconciliamur illi, & simus ejus domestici, atque adeo filii & hæredes: Hanc qua percipientes fide omnia Christi merita simus fra- tres & membra atque cohæredes ipsius, perque ipsum justificamur & servamur, eoque perpetuo Rege, Sacerdote & advocato utimur. Addit: Com- munio cum Spiritu Sancto est, qua illuminamur, re- gimur & sanctificamur ab eo ad vitam æternam. Communio cum Ecclesia est, per baptismum ita in eam inseri, ut sis particeps ejus ministerii, verbi & Sacra- mentorum, precum, & omnino omnium ejus bonorum, qua etiam sis aliorum piorum omnium commembrum in hoc corpore Ecclesiæ, subque uno capite Christo, & denique qua etiam sis particeps tum confessionis, tum & crucis ejus.

## 1:4
Verse 4. And these things we write to you. The plural nominative of the first person does not always have the significance of magnitude, but often of modesty, where we share our honors with others. Servius notes this on that line of Virgil: And we too have borne some name and honor. When he says, 'These things we write,' he designates the principal argument of this epistle.

That your joy may be full. The manuscripts and very many of the best have 'your', rightly. We take up this labor to the end that you also may enjoy full joy here. All joys undertaken concerning the goods of this life become turbid by the fear of both loss and death. But pure joy is to have a certain hope of immortality. See Heb. 11:15, John 16:24, Rom. 5:13, ch. 14:17, Col. 1:11, 1 Pet. 1:8.

That joy can be understood either as the joy of the faithful in the present life in the kingdom of grace, or as the joy in the future life and the kingdom of glory; both arise both from the announcement of the coming of Christ, who merited that joy for us, and from communion with GOD in Christ, by which we are admitted into the participation of this joy in the kingdom of God; and also from the preaching of the Gospel, by which, not only as a good message, we are suffused with solid joy, but it also works in us by the virtue and efficacy of the Holy Spirit a true and perfect joy: which, however, will be most consummated in the other life. Conf. Luke 2:10, John 13:22, 23, Rom. 5:2, Ch. 14:17, Phil. 4:4, 1 Pet. 1:8, Rev. 12:12, Ch. 19:17, etc. Nothing, however, prevents us from understanding all these things. For all the joy of mortal men, whether received in this or in the future age, must be attributed to Christ, in whom every blessing comes to us, Gen. 12:3, Eph. 1:3. The intermediate end is spiritual joy, or joy in the Holy Spirit, and begun in the present age, Rom. 14:17. The ultimate end is heavenly joy, and consummated in the blessed vision and fruition of the most holy Trinity, 1 John 3:2. These things I have spoken to you, says Christ, John 17:3, that my joy may be in you, and your joy may be fulfilled. St. Augustine, Book 10 of Confessions, ch. 22: Far be it, he says, O Lord, far be it from the heart of thy servant, who confesses to thee, far be it that I should think myself blessed by any joy whatsoever. For there is a joy which is not given to the ungodly, but to those who worship thee freely, whose joy thou thyself art, and this is the blessed life, to rejoice in thee and of thee. You, and for Your sake; It is Itself, and there is no other: but those who think there is another, pursue a different joy, and not the true one: For the blessed life is joy in the truth, for this is joy in You, who are the truth, GOD my illumination, the salvation of my countenance. And in Soliloquies, ch. 35. Enter into the joy without sadness, which contains eternal gladness. The vision of the blessed Deity is the joy of the LORD your GOD. O joy above joy, overcoming every joy, outside of which there is no joy! When shall I enter into You, that I may see my GOD, who dwells in You! St. Anselm in the same, ch. 26. They will rejoice as much as they will love, they will love as much as they will know. Cyprian, sermon on the Ascension, ch. 9. The saints will exult in glory, they will see God and will rejoice, they will be glad and will be delighted, and they will enjoy glory, and will be joyful in eternal happiness. Flacius has these things concerning the joy of the faithful in this place: This spiritual joy of the faithful is called full and perfect for many reasons, and that especially by comparison and in respect to the joy of the ungodly and of this world: First, it is perfect by reason of the object apprehended, from which this joy arises, namely by reason of God, and His true goods, which, since they are solid, also provide a solid and sincere joy. This perfect joy Christ describes through that parable of the one acquiescing in the found treasure or pearl: And the Psalm in which the pious man says that he seeks nothing else, provided he has God. Conversely, earthly joy, arising from imperfect and indeed fallacious goods, also exists as imperfect. But that perfection of joy is twofold, one in the state of grace in this life, the other in the state of glory in the other life. Here is the perfection of joy only as regards its essence, which could more be called sincerity than true perfection: But in the other life there will be the perfection of this joy according to all its parts, and the highest degrees of those parts. Secondly, the joy of the pious is called perfect because it is stable and enduring, so that no one can take it from us, and no sickness can disturb it, just as worldly joys easily perish, are taken away, and their laughter is quickly turned into mourning, just as Christ Himself explains this perfection of joy, that no one will take it from us, and that our mourning, however much it may intervene, is quickly turned into laughter. Thirdly, this joy is called perfect because it is sincere and true, whereas on the contrary Virgil rightly says of earthly joys, expressing the gladness of the Trojans thinking they were now freed from the danger of war: We spent the last night in empty joys. For the ungodly world laughs even when it laughs a Sardonic laugh, and like those who are deranged, it thinks it is doing well and is healthy. Therefore, spiritual joy is sincere and solid, but that earthly one is painted over, whence Augustine rightly calls the former that of truth, the latter that of vanity. Fourthly, spiritual joy is sincere, and has nothing of evil mixed in, just as most earthly joys have more gall than honey mixed in, and indeed, if they had no other evil, yet they have that greatest one, namely the wrath of God and sin. Whence Solomon rightly testifies: It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting. Finally, this spiritual joy is perfect by reason of its manifold and immense use, because it can be opposed to all evils and adversities. This one thing, so to speak, is a medicine that can be opposed to all diseases, both spiritual and also bodily, and it is valid for all things, and truly heals and removes all things, however much we may not feel this health due to the stupidity of our old Adam. Therefore, let us oppose this joy of a good conscience, justified and pacified through Christ, and feeling the spiritual consolation of God, as a wall against all adversities, always approaching God with confidence, and obtaining all help from Him, according to that of Christ in John XVI: Ask and you shall receive, that your joy may be full, and Psalm XCIV says: According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, Thy consolations have gladdened my soul.

PART III. The announcement concerning the requirements of those who have communion with GOD.

Latin:

Vers. 4. Καὶ ταῦτα γράφομεν ὑμῖν.] Pluralis Nominativus primæ personæ non semper per magnitudinis, sed sæpe mo- destiæ habet significationem, ubi nostra decora cum aliis par- timur. Notat hoc Servius ad illud Virgilii: - - - Et nos aliquod nomenque decusque Gessimus. Hæc scribimus, cum dicit, toties epistolæ hujus præcipuum argumentum designat.

Ἵνα ἡ χαρὰ ὑμῶν ἦ πεπληρωμένη.] ὑμῶν habent Codices & plurimi optimi, recte. Sumimus hunc laborem in id, ut & hic pleno fruamini gaudio. Omnia de bonis hujus vitæ su- scepta gaudia tum jacturæ, tum mortis metu fiunt turbida. Purum vero gaudium est, certam habere spem immortalita- tis. Vide Ebr. 11, 15. Joh. 16, 24. Rom. 5, 13. c. 14, 17. Col. I, 11. 1. Petr. 1, 8.

Illud gaudium intelligi potest vel de gaudio fi- delium in vita præsenti in regno gratiæ, vel de gau- dio in vita futura & regno gloriæ; utrumque ori- tur tum ex adventus Christi annuntiatione, qui promeruit nobis id gaudium, tum communione cum DEO in Christo, qua admittimur in par- ticipationem hujus gaudii in regno Dei; tum è prædicatione Evangelii, quo non tantum ceu bono nuncio, gaudio solido perfundimur, sed id operatur etiam in nobis virtute & efficacia Spiritus S. gaudium verum & perfectum: Quod tamen maxime consummatum erit in altera vita. Conf. Luc. 2, 10. Joh. 13, 22. 23. Rom. 5, 2. C. 14, 17. Phil. 4, 4. 1. Petr. 1, 8. Apocal. 12, 12. C. 19, 17. &c. Nihil autem obstat, quin hæc omnia intelliga- mus. Omne enim gaudium mortalium homi- num sive in hoc sive in futuro seculo acceptum ferendum est Christo, in quo omnis benedi- ctio nobis obtingit Gen. 12, 3. Ephes. 1, 3. Finis in- termedius est gaudium spirituale vel in Spiritu San- cto, & inchoatum in præsenti seculo, Rom. XIV. v. 17. Finis ultimus est gaudium cæleste, & con- summatum in beata visione, ac fruitione sacro- sanctæ Trinitatis 1. Johann. III, 2. Hæc loquutus sum vobis, inquit Christus, Joh. XVII, 3. ut gau- dium meum in vobis sit, & gaudium vestrum im- pleatur. S. Augustinus l. X. conf. cap. 22. Absit, ait, Domine, absit à corde servi tui, qui confitetur tibi, absit, ut quocunque gaudio gaudeam, beatum me putem. Est enim gaudium, quod non datur im- piis, sed iis, qui te gratis colunt, quorum gaudium Tu ipse es, & ipsa est beata vita, gaudere ad Te, & de Te, & propter Te; Ipsa est, & non est altera: qui autem aliam putant esse, aliud sectantur gau- dium, neque ipsum verum: Beata quippe vita est gaudium de veritate, hoc est enim gaudium de Te, qui veritas es DEUS illuminatio mea, salus faciei mea. Et in soliloqu. c. 35. Intra in gaudium sine tristitia, quod continet æternam lætitiam. Beatæ Deitatis visio est gaudium Domini DEI tui. O gaudium super gaudium, vincens omne gaudium, extra quod non est gaudium! Quando intrabo in Te, ut videam DEUM meum, qui habitat in Te! B. Anshelmus in pro cap. 26. Tantum gaude- bunt, quantum amabunt, tantum amabunt, quan- tum cognoscent. Cyprianus serm. de Ascens. c. 9. Exultabunt sancti in gloria, videbunt Deum & gaudebunt, lætabuntur & delectabuntur, & fruentur gloria, & in felicitate jucundabuntur æterna. Flacius de gaudio fidelium hæc habet hoc loco: Gaudium istud spirituale fidelium mul- tis de causis dicitur plenum ac perfectum, idque potissimum collatione & respectu gaudii impiorum & mundi hujus: Primum est perfectum ratione objecti apprehensi, unde hoc gaudium oritur, nempe ratione Dei, ejusque verorum bonorum, quæ cum sint solida, solidum etiam sincerumque gaudium præ- stant. Hoc gaudium perfectum Christus describit per illam parabolam de acquiescente in reperto the- sauro aut margarita: Et Psalmus in quo pius di- cit, se nihil aliud expetere, modo Deum habeat. Contra gaudium terrenum, oriens ex imperfectis imo & fallacibus bonis imperfectum etiam existit. Illa autem gaudii perfectio duplex est, alia in statu gratiæ in hac vita, alia in statu gloriæ in altera vita. Hic est perfectio gaudii tantum quoad essentiam, quæ magis dici posset sinceritas, quam vera perfectio: In altera autem vita erit gaudii istius perfectio se- cundum omnes partes, partiumque summos gra- dus. Secundo piorum gaudium dicitur perfectum, quia est stabile & perdurans, ita, ut id nemo no- bis auferre possit, nullaque ægritudo id interturba- re, sicut mundana gaudia facile pereunt, au- feruntur, & cito risus eorum in luctum conver- tuntur, sicut Christus ipse istam gaudii perfectio- nem exponit, quod nemo id à nobis auferet, quod- que luctus noster, ut maxime quis interveniat, cito vertatur in risum. Tertio istud gaudium dicitur perfectum, quia est sincerum & verum, cum contra de terrenis gaudiis recte dicat Virgilius, exprimens lætitiam Trojanorum putantium, se jam periculo belli esse liberatos: Egimus extremam per inania gaudia noctem. Ridet enim impius mundus etiam cum ridet Sardo- nium risum, & phreneticorum instar putat se be- ne habere ac valere. Gaudium igitur spirituale est sincerum & solidum, istud vero terrenum est fucatum, unde merito Augustinus vocat verita- tis, hoc vanitatis. Quarto gaudium spirituale est sincerum, & nihil habet admixtum mali, sicut plerumque omnia terrena gaudia habent plus ad- mixtum fellis quam mellis, & sane, si nihil aliud haberent mali, at habent illa summa, videlicet iram Dei & peccatum. Unde recte Salomon te- statur: Melius esse ire in domum luctûs, quam in domum convivii. Postremo hoc gaudium spiritua- le est perfectum ratione multiplicis ingentisque usus, quia omnibus malis & adversis opponi potest. Hoc unum, ut ita dicam, medicamen omnibus morbis tum spiritualibus, tum etiam corporalibus opponi pot- est, & ad omnia valet, omniaque vere sanat ac tol- lit, utcunque nos istam sanitatem nostri veteris Ada- mi stupiditate non sentiamus. Hoc igitur bona con- scientiæ gaudium per Christum justificatæ & pacifi- catæ, Deique spiritualem consolationem sentientis omnibus adversis tanquam murum opponamus, sem- per cum fiducia Deum accedentes, & omnem opem ab eo impetrantes, juxta illud Christi Joh. XVI. Pe- tite & accipietis, ut gaudium vestrum sit plenum, & Psalm. XCIV. inquit: Secundum multitudinem dolorum in corde meo consolationes tuæ lætificaue- runt animam meam.

PARS III. Annunciatio de requisitis eorum, qui commu- nionem habent cum DEO.

## 1:5
Verse 5.

And this is the message.] The manuscript has ἀγγελία. Nor does the Syriac or the Latin read otherwise. The word ἀγγελία is found in 2 Sam. 4:4, Proverbs 12:26, ch. 25:26, ch. 26:16, Isaiah 28:9, Jeremiah 48:34, Ezekiel 7:20, ch. 21:7. In the Glossary, ἀγγελία is announcement. This is what it means to say: Christ did not bring us only promises, but also explained the conditions and the causes of those conditions.

Which we have heard from Him.] We have known this much more openly through Christ than before in the law.

Estius here, having finished the preface, wishes an entry to be made to the exhortation: But the things that precede have exhibited the primary part of the things to be treated, from which now this tacit admonition, an open denunciation, is deduced only by way of corollary. He had previously dealt with the benefit of Christ, which we obtain through His incarnation and His preaching. Now he deals with our duty. Previously about our communion with GOD and with the Son: Now about the things attached to those who enjoy that communion. But these are not proposed as conditions, as Grotius wishes, but as adjuncts cohering in an inseparable bond. For we do not have communion with God under this condition or for this cause, because we walk in the light, even though those who have communion with GOD walk in the light. This communion rather, which is obtained through faith in Christ, is the cause of walking in the light, because through this, the zeal for holiness is understood, which Grotius wishes to be understood. Moreover, two προσκείμενα are handed down concerning those with whom there is κοινωνία with God: first, walking in the light; second, the enjoyment of the expiation of sins made through the blood of Christ. For because those who have not been purified from sins cannot rejoice in the communion of God, and when they do rejoice in the same, they easily fall into sins, James 3:2, it is necessary that they enjoy the purification made by Christ, both to obtain and to continue or to restore that blessed communion.

No necessity compels us to another reading. For ἐπαγγελία denotes an announcement, and it has a good place here as a promise: because we are not only commanded to walk in the light and to be cleansed by the blood of Christ, but the grace of both is also promised to us—the former through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, the latter through the application of Christ's expiation; because we enjoy both through blessed communion with God and Christ. Therefore, there is no need for a metonymy, so that we might understand the announcement for the thing announced. Moreover, St. John shows that the fellowship of the faithful with GOD does not indeed consist in this, that they walk in the light of knowledge, obedience, and love of God, in that GOD is light itself, in which if we remain, we are made invincible to sin, as Cornelius wishes. These things, however, are joined with that spiritual κοινωνία with God. But as for the fact that the Apostle professes that he heard this ἐπαγγελίαν from Christ, in the person also of the other Apostles, it is not for that to be accepted, as if those things were not handed down in the Old Testament: For Christ himself also referred to Moses and the Prophets, Luke 16:29. And the same was done by Paul, Acts 16:22. And by Peter, 2 Epist. 1:19. Nor are the testimonies in the Old Testament doubtful or obscure concerning GOD, that He is light, or that He is pure and holy, and concerning the faithful, that they must walk in the light of knowledge and holiness, 1 Pet. 1:15, 16. and Levit. 18. Deut. 32:4. God is faithful, and without any iniquity, just and upright.

That God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all.] That GOD is so pure that nothing of impurity can please Him. See below chapter 2, 3. Light is a most pure thing. Therefore it is taken for purity. See Luke 16:8. Acts 26:18. Rom. 13:12. Eph. 5:8. 1 Thess. 5:5. The power of Satan is called the power of darkness, Luke 22:53. By purity we approach most closely to God, Matt. 5:8. John 4:24. Add 1 Pet. 1:15, where we are warned that we should be holy, just as GOD is holy.

God is said to be light not in a literal sense, as the Manichaeans have trifled, but metaphorically: Just as darkness is also understood metaphorically: and this both essentially and causally. Essentially, by reason of the purity of His nature, and by reason of the light of the omniscient divine mind, because He is full of intelligence, knowing most clearly Himself (who is the primary truth) and in Himself all other things: And by reason of the holiness of the divine will, because He is supreme goodness, supreme justice and uprightness: Causally, because from this light is all the light that is in creatures, all purity, all true knowledge, all true holiness: From the Father of lights are all good gifts, and every perfect gift, James 1:17. And therefore He is called light because of the effect of light in us, because indeed GOD is so much light in Himself, most pure and mixed with no darkness, that He is also the fountain of all light, that is, of truth, goodness, and justice, which is in us, and He not only illuminates us by teaching what we ought to do through the illustration of the mind: but also effectively works in us so that we may act through the sanctification of the will, so that our mind, bathed in the rays of that light, may be freed from the darkness of ignorance, and the will may be purged of depravity. Therefore he adds: And darkness is not in Him. By light is also designated divine grace and efficacy, because as light is not only most pure, but also most efficacious, bringing splendor, heat, life, and vigor and joy: So all these things belong to divine grace: which finally leads to eternal light, glory, and joy, just as sins lead to the lowest darkness, and supreme ignominy and sadness. As in the Gospel, mention of light is added to the naming of life. John 1:4. In Him was life, and the life was the light of men, because there is no life except for those who have the light, John 17:3. So here the light of life is added. For GOD, who is light, as Saint John says, is not only the Father, but also the Son, with whom we have communion equally, as with the Father: whom as he had called life: so now he also honors with the name of light. For the Son is that true light enlightening every man, John 1:9, the light of the world, whom whoever follows does not walk in darkness, John 8:12. The Son of God is light from light, true GOD from true GOD. Concerning Christ the Mediator, Saint Augustine beautifully says in homily 43 among the 50. Therefore Christ came as an illuminator, because the devil had been a blinder. The supreme Physician made an eye-salve of infinite value, so that He might heal blinded eyes. See what kind of, and how salutary, the eye-salve was from the Word and flesh. The Word, he says, was made flesh. But the eyes of the restored man are so, and thus illuminated, that they can equal the eyes of the Angels, and behold the celestial glory of God Himself. For the Apostle refers to these words: And this is the promise or announcement which we have heard from Him, the sermons of Christ, in which He delivered such things about Himself. Concerning which the Blessed Hunnius says: But because the Apostle refers us with these words to the very sermon and proclamation of Christ, it must be considered where CHRIST taught this. He seems to have referred especially to those sermons which are read to have been delivered by Christ in John 3:8 and 12. Where Christ, under the same metaphor of light and darkness, in the same way clearly exhorts to a pure and holy conversation. For in John 3 he indeed says: The light came into the world, and men loved darkness more than light, for their works were evil. Everyone who does evil hates the light, and does not come to the light, lest his works should be reproved. But he who works truth comes to the light, so that his deeds may be made conspicuous, that they are done through GOD. And John 8: I am the light of the world, he who follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life. Similarly John 12: Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. He who walks in darkness does not know where he is going. While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may be sons of light. And a little later: I have come as a light into the world, that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness. Looking back, therefore, to these most serious exhortations, John affirms that this is that announcement which they heard from Christ Himself. Where he first explains the nature of God, so that having shown it, he may subsequently stimulate us to purity and sincerity of life. But how GOD is said to be light, the late lamented one explains thus: GOD is called light, that is, a most sincere and most pure essence, to which nothing of vice, nothing of ignorance and malice is mixed, light namely without darkness, that is, wisdom without ignorance, truth without falsehood, innocence without the stain of crime, justice and holiness without any iniquity. The antithesis, which the Apostle adds according to his custom for the sake of greater emphasis, and darkness is not in Him at all, is referred by some to the Light, that God is such a light, in which there is no darkness, or which is mere light, as Jerome has in book 2 of the Dialogue against the Pelagians, chapter 3. When John says that no darkness is found in the light of GOD, he shows that all the lights of others are stained with some filth. Most others, and more correctly according to the custom of those ἀντιθέσεων (antitheses), refer it to God, even though the sense is the same. For God is mere light without darkness; and therefore in God, in that most pure light, there are no shadows, whether of ignorance, or of errors, or of vices, nor can they arise from that light; both are repugnant to the immutability, simplicity, perfection, truth, goodness, and holiness of God, and utterly overturn the nature of God. For God cannot deny himself, 2 Tim. II, 13. It is impossible for God to lie, Heb. VI, 17. With the Father of lights there is no variation of light and darkness, James I, v. 17, which words also seem to be spoken here against the blasphemy of those who, already in the Apostolic age, as we observed on the passage in James, were spreading impious dogmas about God being the author of sin, when the antithesis is added, & in him there is no darkness. Although the Apostle also goes further, looking at the same time at the contrary operation of God in us, which explanation Estius has handed this down, and we do not disagree with him. The sense, he says, is: All the darkness of error and ignorance and sin is so alien to that eternal light, which is God, that it also expels the darkness of errors and sins from us. And this sense is sufficiently gathered from what follows, and is consistent with what the same Apostle writes in chapter 1 of his Gospel concerning the Word of God: The life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it: where he calls men darkened by errors and sins 'darkness'. And chapter 12: I have come as a light into the world, that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness. Where he certainly understands by darkness the sins and errors for the dissipating of which Christ the true light came into the world. For he aims at this, that walking in the light of faith and new obedience, we may flee from the darkness of sins. He warns, therefore, that we should dwell and live in the light, having taken the argument from the nature of God, who, since He is light, admits no one into His fellowship unless he himself also walks in the light. Flacius vigorously comprehends all these things: This light embraces first the omniscience and truthfulness of God, who both knows all things, and is supremely delighted by truth, and proposes it to men, and demands it from them: Secondly, it indicates justice, because God loves all things right and holy, and utterly abhors the contrary, and for that reason also both enjoins justice upon men and restores it when lost: thirdly, it notes life and blessedness, which, just as He has in Himself, so He also communicates to men: but joined with these is also mercy, and the highest zeal for doing good to men. Therefore, by this very brief expression, the Apostle, embracing huge goods, testifies that God has offered Himself to the world most sincerely and most mercifully, as an immense treasure of every good and happiness. But that he excludes contrary evils by antithesis in the Hebrew manner, he does so in order to indicate all the more clearly that the human race is overwhelmed and buried by these very same huge evils: But that that heavenly Father wishes, by sending and giving them that very Word in whom is the life and light of men, to liberate them most mercifully from them, namely from ignorance and error, and injustice and death, and to communicate His contrary goods to them most liberally through Him.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Καὶ ἔστιν αὕτη ἡ ἐπαγγελία.] Manuscriptus ἀγγελία. Nec aliter legere aut Syrus aut Latinus. Reperitur vox ἀγγε- λίας 2. Sam. 4, 4. Proverb. 12, 26. cap. 25, 26. c. 26, 16. Esa. 28, 9. Jerem. 48, 34. Ezech. 7, 20. c. 21, 7. In Glossario ἀγγελία nunciatio. Hoc vult dicere: non promissa sola attulit no- bis Christus, sed & conditiones & earum conditionum causas explicavit.

Ἣν ἀκηκόαμεν ἀπ' ἀυτῦ.] Multo apertius per Christum hoc cognovimus quam ante in lege.

Estius hic finito procœmio ingressum vult fieri ad exhortationem: Sed quæ antecedunt, prima- riam partem tractandorum exhibuere, è qua jam tantum πορισματικῶς hæc tacita parænesis, aperta denunciatio deducitur. Prius de Christi beneficio, quod per incarnationem ejusque prædicationem, consequimur, egerat. Jam de nostro officio agit. Prius de communione nostra cum DEO & cum Filio: Jam de προσκειμένοις eorum, qui com- munione illa gaudent. Non autem hæc tanquam conditiones, ut vult Grotius, proponuntur, sed ceu adjuncta indivulso nexu cohærentia. Non enim sub hac conditione vel ex hac causa cum Deo communionem habemus, quia in luce ambula- mus, etsi, qui cum DEO communionem habent, ambulent in luce. Hæc potius communio, quæ per fidem in Christum obtinetur, causa est am- bulationis in luce, quia per hanc studium sanctita- tis intelligitur, quod intelligi vult Grotius. Duo autem προσκείμενα traduntur eorum, quibus in- tercedit κοινωνία cum Deo, primo ambulatio in lu- ce, deinde expiationis peccatorum per Christi san- guinem factæ fruitio. Nam quia nec in commu- nione Dei gaudere possunt, qui purificati à pecca- tis non sunt, & cum eadem gaudent, facile in pec- cata labuntur, Jacobi III, 2, opus est, ut purifica- tione à Christo facta & ad obtinendam & ad con- tinuandam aut ad redintegrandam communio- nem illam beatam fruantur.

Ad aliam lectionem nulla nos impellit neces- sitas. Nam & ἐπαγγελία notat annunciationem, & promissioni hic bene locus est: quia non ju- bemur tantum in luce ambulare ac mundari san- guine Christi, sed utriusque etiam gratia no- bis promittitur illius per Spiritus Sancti illu- minationem, hujus per expiationis Christi ap- plicationem; quia utraque fruimur per bea- tam cum Deo & Christo communionem. Ideo opus non est Metonymia, ut annunciationem pro re annunciata intelligamus. Ostendit autem S. Johannes, societatem fidelium cum DEO non quidem consistere in eo, ut ambulent in luce co- gnitionis, obedientiæ & amoris Dei, eo quod DEUS sit ipsa lux, in qua si permaneamus, in- victi peccato efficiamur, ut vult Cornelius. Hæc tamen conjuncta esse cum κοινωνίᾳ illa spirituali cum Deo. Quod vero hanc ἐπαγγελίαν audi- visse se à Christo Apostolus in persona etiam cæterorum Apostolorum profiteatur, non eo accipiendum, quasi in Veteri Testamento ea tradita non sint: Nam & Christus ipse remisit ad Mosen & Prophetas, Luc. XVI, 29. idemque a Paulo factum, Actor. XVI, 22. & a Petro 2. epist. I, 19. neque dubia aut obscura sunt in Veteri Testa- mento testimonia de DEO, quod lux sit, vel quod purus sit & sanctus, ac de fidelibus, quod in luce ipsis ambulandum sit cognitionis & sanctita- tis, 1. Petr. I. v. 15. 16. & Levit. XVIII. Deut. XXXII. v. 4. Deus fidelis est, & absque ulla iniquitate, ju- stus & rectus.

Ὅτι ὁ Θεὸς φῶς ἐστι, καὶ σκοτία ἐν ἀυτῷ οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδε- μία.] DEUM ita esse purum, ut nihil impuritatis ei pla- cere possit. Vide infra cap. 2, 3. Lux res purissima. Ideo pro puritate sumitur. Vid. Luc. 16. vers. 8. Actor. 26. v. 18. Rom. 13. vers. 12. Ephes. 5. v. 8. 1. Thess. 5. v. 5. Contra sa- tanæ ἐξουσία dicitur τοῦ σκότους, Luc. 22. v. 53. Puritate pro- xime ad Deum accedimus, Matth. 5. v. 8. Joh. 4. v. 24. Adde 1. Petr. I. v. 15. ubi monemur, ut sancti simus, sicut & DEUS sanctus est.

Lux Deus esse dicitur non sensu proprio, ut Manichæi nugati sunt, sed Metaphorice: Quem- admodum & tenebræ Metaphorice intelligun- tur: idque tum essentialiter, tum causaliter. Es- sentialiter, ratione puritatis naturæ, & ratione lucis omnisciae mentis divinæ, quia plenus est intelligentia clarissime seipsum (qui est prima veritas) & in seipso omnia alia agnoscens: Et ratione sanctitatis divinæ voluntatis, quia summa bonitas est, summa justitia & rectitudo: Cau- saliter, quia ab hac luce omnis, quæ in creatu- ris est, lux, omnis puritas, omnis cognitio ve- ra, omnis vera sanctitas est: A Patre luminum omnia dona bona, & omne donum perfectum est, Jacobi I. vers. 17. Ideoque lux dicitur ob effe- ctum lucis in nobis, quia nimirum ita DEUS in seipso lux est purissima, nullisque permixta te- nebris, ut etiam fons sit omnis lucis, id est ve- ritatis, bonitatis ac justitiæ, quæ in nobis est, nec solum nos illuminet, docendo quid agere debeamus per illustrationem mentis: sed etiam efficaciter in nobis operetur, ut agamus per vo- luntatis sanctificationem, ut radiis illius lucis mens nostra perfusa ab ignorantiæ tenebris libe- retur, & voluntas a pravitate purgetur. Pro- pterea addit: Et tenebræ non sunt in eo. Luce etiam designatur gratia divina & efficacia, quia ut lux non purissima modo est, sed & efficacis- sima afferens splendorem, calorem, vitam, ac vigorem & lætitiam: Ita hæc omnia gratiæ di- vinæ conveniunt: quæ denique ad æternam du- cit lucem, gloriam & lætitiam, ut peccata ad imas ducunt tenebras, summamque ignomini- am, & tristitiam. Ut in Evangelio vitæ nomi- nationi lucis addita mentio est. Joh. I. vers. 4. In ipso vita erat, & vita erat lux hominum, quia vita non est nisi iis, quibus lux est, Joh. XVII. vers. 3. ita hic vitæ lux additur. DEUS enim, qui lux est, dicente Sancto Johanne, non Pa- ter solum est, sed etiam Filius, cum quo pari- ter, ut cum Patre, communionem habemus: quem uti vitam dixerat: ita etiam nunc lucis appellatione honorat. Est enim Filius lux illa vera omnem hominem illuminans, Joh. I. vers. 9. lux mundi, quem qui sequitur, non ambulat in tenebris, Joh. VIII. vers. 12. Filius Dei est lumen de lumine, DEUS verus de DEO vero. De Chri- sto etiam Mediatore pulchre Sanctus Augustinus homil. 43. inter 50. Ideo venit Christus illumi- nator, quia diabolus fuerat excæcator. Fecit sum- mus Medicus infiniti collyrium pretii, ut excæcatos sanaret oculos. Vide quale, quamque salutare fuerit collyrium ex Verbo & carne. Verbum, in- quit, caro factum est. Refecti autem hominis ocu- li ita sunt, itaque illuminati, ut Angelorum exæ- quare possint oculos, Deique ipsius cælestem glori- am tueri. Respicit enim Apostolus hisce ver- bis: Et hæc est promissio vel annunciatio, quam ex ipso audivimus, conciones Christi, quibus talia de semetipso tradidit. Quo de Beat. Hun- nius: Quia vero Apostolus hisce verbis ad ipsius Christi concionem ac denunciationem nos remittit, considerandum fuerit, ubi hoc CHRISTUS docue- rit. Respexisse potissimum videtur ad eas concio- nes, quæ Joh. III. vers. 8 & 12. à Christo habitæ le- guntur. Ubi Christus sub eadem Metaphora lucis ac tenebrarum eodem plane modo ad puram san- ctamque conversationem hortatur. Nam Joh. III. quidem ait: Venit lux in mundum, & dilexerunt homines tenebras magis, quam lucem, erant enim eorum opera mala. Omnis, qui agit mala, odit lucem, nec venit in lucem, ne arguantur opera ejus. Qui autem operatur veritatem, venit in lucem, ut conspicua fiant facta ipsius, quod per DEUM sint facta. Et Johann. VIII. Ego sum lux mun- di, qui sequitur me, non ambulat in tenebris, sed habebit lumen vitæ. Similiter Joh. XII. Ambula- te, donec lucem habetis, ne vos tenebræ occupent. Qui ambulat in tenebris, nescit quo vadat. Dum lucem habetis, credite in lucem, ut filii lucis sitis. Et paulo post: Ego lux in mundum veni, ut omnis, qui credit in me, in tenebris non maneat. Ad has igi- tur gravissimas exhortationes respiciens Johannes af- firmat, hanc esse annunciationem illam, quam ex ipso Christo audiverint. Ubi primo Dei naturam explicat, ut ostensa ea deinceps & nos ad puritatem sinceritatemque vitæ extimulet. Quomodo vero lux dicatur DEUS, ita explicat ὁ Μακαρίτης: Lux dicitur DEUS, hoc est, sincerissima plane, purissima- que essentia, cui nihil vitii, nihil ignorantiæ malitiæ- que sit admixtum, lux scilicet absque tenebris, hoc est, sapientia absque ignorantia, veritas sine mendacio, in- nocentia sine labe criminis, justitia & sanctitas abs- que ulla iniquitate. Antithesis, quam pro con- suetudine sua majoris emphaseos gratia addit A- postolus, καὶ σκοτία ἐν ἀυτῷ ἐκ ἔστιν ὀυδεμία, à qui- busdam ad τὸ Φῶς refertur, quod talis lux sit Deus, in qua nullæ sint tenebræ, seu quæ mera lux sit, ut habet Hieronymus l. II. Dial. contr. Pelag. cap. 3. quando dicit Johannes, nullas tenebras in DEI lu- mine reperiri, ostendit omnia aliorum lumina ali- qua sorde maculari. Alii plerique omnes & re- ctius ex more istarum ἀντιθέσεων ad Deum refe- runt, etsi sensus idem sit. Deus enim mera lux est sine tenebris; ideoque in Deo, in luce illa puris- sima nullæ tenebræ sunt, sive ignorantiæ, sive er- rorum, sive vitiorum, nec ab ista luce oriri pos- sunt; utrumque repugnat inmutabilitati, sim- plicitati, perfectioni, veritati, bonitati ac san- ctitati divinæ, Deique naturam penitus evertit. Deus enim seipsum abnegare non potest, 2. Tim. II, 13. Impossibile est, Deum mentiri, Ebr. VI, 17. Apud Patrem luminum nulla est vicissitudo lu- cis & tenebrarum, Jac. I. v. 17. quæ contra bla- sphemiam eorum, qui jam Apostolico sæcu- lo, ut ad locum Jacobeum observavimus, im- pia dogmata de Deo autore peccati spargebant, hic etiam dicta videntur, cum additur antithe- sis, & tenebræ non sunt in eo. Quamvis & ulterius abeat Apostolus, respiciens simul operationem Dei contrariam in nobis, quam explicationem tradidit Estius, neque eidem abnuimus. Sensus est, inquit: Ita tenebras omnis erroris & ignoran- tiæ & peccati ab illa luce æterna, quæ Deus est, alie- nas esse, ut etiam à nobis errorum & peccatorum te- nebras expellat. Et hic sensus satis colligitur ex sequentibus, estque consentaneus iis, quæ scribit idem Apostolus cap. I. sui Evangelii de Verbo DEI: Vita erat lux hominum, & lux in tenebris lucet, & tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt : ubi te- nebras vocat homines erroribus & peccatis obteue- bratos. Et cap. XII. Ego lux in mundum veni: ut omnis, qui credit in me, in tenebris non maneat. Ubi tenebras utique peccata & errores intelligit, qui- bus dissipandis Christus lux vera venit in mundum. Id enim agit, ut in luce fidei & novæ obedientiæ ambulantes à peccatorum tenebris refugiamus. Monet ergo, ut in luce versemur ac vivamus, sum- pto argumento à natura Dei, qui cum lux sit, ne- minem in suam societatem admittit, nisi ipse quoq; in luce ambulet. Nervose hæc omnia compre- hendit Flacius: Complectitur autem hic lux primum omnisapientiam veracitatemque DEI, qui & sciat omnia, & veritate summe delectetur eamque ho- minibus proponat, & ab illis exigat: Secundo indi- cat justitiam, quod Deus amet omnia recta & sancta, & à contrariis prorsus abhorreat, eoque etiam justi- tiam hominibus tum injungat, tum & amissam resti- tuat : tertio notat vitam ac beatitudinem, quam sic- ut ille in sese habeat: ita hominibus quoque commu- nicet: cum hisce vero conjuncta est etiam misericor- dia, & summum benefaciendi hominibus studium. Hac igitur brevissima loquutione Apostolus ingentia bona complectens testatur Deum sese mundo sinceris- fime & clementissime obtulisse, tanquam immensum thesaurum omnis boni ac felicitatis. Quod autem more Ebræo per antithesin contraria mala excludit, facit ideò, ut tanto clarius indicet humanum genus istis ipsis ingentibus malis obrutum, sepultumq; esse: Verum Patrem illum cælestem velle, misso donatoque eis isto ipso Verbo, in quo sit vita & lux hominum,ipsos ab illis clementissime liberare, nempe inscitia ac errore, injustitiaque ac morte, & contraria sua bona illis per illud liberalissime communicare.

## 1:6
Ver. 6.

Ἐὰν εἶπωμεν, ὅτι κοινωνίαν ἔχομεν μετ' ἀυτῶ.] That is, that we are friends to God. For friendship is the greatest fellowship.

Καὶ ἐν τῷ σκότει περιπατῶμεν.] Let us do impure works, John 3. v. 19. Rom. 13. v. 12.

Ψευδόμεθα καὶ ἐ ποιῦμεν τὴν ἀλήθειαν.] We do not act according to the truth, thus Cyprian, that is, we do not act sincerely. Thus John ch. 5. verse 21. ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν, he who acts sincerely. Thus also Ezech. 18. v. 9. The Hebrews love, when they wish to affirm something strongly, to add the negation of the contrary to a word once placed, Roman. 4. v. 1. and just now above 5.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Ἐὰν εἶπωμεν, ὅτι κοινωνίαν ἔχομεν μετ' ἀυτῶ.] Id est, nos DEO amicos esse. Nam amicitia maxima est so- cietas.

Καὶ ἐν τῷ σκότει περιπατῶμεν.] Faciamus opera impura, Joh. 3. v. 19. Rom. 13. v. 12.

Ψευδόμεθα καὶ ἐ ποιῦμεν τὴν ἀλήθειαν.] Non agimus ex veritate, sic Cyprianus, id est, non sincere agimus. Sic Joh. c. 5. vers. 21. ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν, qui sincere agit. Sic & Ezech. 18. v. 9. Amant Ebræi, cum quid valde affirmare vo- lunt, verbo aliquo posito addere negationem contrarii, Ro- man. 4. v. 1. & jam jam supra 5.

## 1:7
Ver. 7.

Ἐὰν δὲ ἐν τῷ φωτὶ περιπατῶμεν.] If we live purely, that is, according to the precepts of Christ.

Ὡς αὐτός ἐστιν ἐν τῷ φωτὶ.] He is always engaged in the purest actions.

Κοινωνίαν ἔχομεν μετ' ἀλλήλων.] That matter makes us friends among ourselves. It is the way of friends to want and not want the same things. This is friendship among the good, among the bad it is faction. Those who are bound with God are necessarily also bound among themselves. See Ephes. II. verse 6. In the Manuscript, instead of μετ' ἀλλήλων, there seems to have been μετ' ἀυτῶ. The erasure indicates this, not holding more letters.

To walk in darkness is not only to do impure works; but they also and especially walk in darkness who do not rejoice in the true light, which is Christ, and without Christ, and thus without GOD, are in this world, who is the self-originated light & Father of lights, Eph. II, 12, established in ignorance of the true light & in errors concerning the true GOD: For he who does not have the Son does not have the Father, 1 John II, v. 23, who are said to sit in darkness & the shadow of death, Is. IX, 1, Ch. XLII, 7, Luke I, 79, nay even to be darkness, Eph. V, v. 8, & in the parallel passage, John I, 5, the light, THAT LIGHT, concerning the Word, was shining in darkness, & the darkness did not comprehend it. He declares why he has brought in here the mention of light and darkness, as if he were saying, if God is light, admitting no darkness, and the man himself walking in darkness cannot have fellowship with GOD. For what fellowship has light with darkness? 2 Cor. VI, verse 16. If therefore he says he has it, he lies. He teaches therefore that this is required of those who have communion with GOD, that they should not walk in darkness, in the darkness of mind and intellect, as being ignorance of the true GOD and of JESUS Christ or errors against the saving doctrine: in the darkness of heart and will, or of sins and vices, in the darkness of unbelief and impenitence, which beget blindness, hardening, despair, and which are followed by the darkness of calamity and eternal death, of the deprivation of true light, and of the confinement of extreme infernal gloom. Cornelius a Lapide wishes the Gnostics, Ebionites, and others alien to the true faith to be noted, as well as those who lived in the darkness of sins, because sins are compared to darkness, because as darkness is the deprivation of light: So sins are the deprivation of grace: Just as one walking in darkness sees nothing and frequently stumbles: so those sinning in the way of salvation are blind and frequently stumble: Just as creatures of darkness hate the light, like owls: So also sinners hate the light of GOD and of men, John III, 20, and sins are the works of the prince of darkness, most things arise in darkness and from darkness, namely from practical error, and darken and blind the mind more, and drag it away to the eternal darkness of Gehenna, John X, v. 22. To walk in darkness, says Flacius, is to stick in the old Adam or corrupt nature, or not yet to be reborn, to be occupied in ignorance of GOD, in errors and corrupt religion, to be secure in that corrupt nature of one's own, and altogether to live according to the flesh without any true acknowledgment of GOD and of one's own injustice and of the wrath of GOD.

But by the light, in which one must walk, we can understand the light of truth and of faith, because, as Schlichting admits, darkness in the Holy Scriptures is accustomed to signify ignorance and errors, and thus light signifies truth by metaphor: because just as darkness blinds the eyes of the body, so errors and ignorance blind the eyes of the mind. But as light illuminates the eyes: so truth illuminates the minds. And in this sense also Christ is called the true light. Cornelius understands the light of reason, of faith, of the Gospel, of virtue, of grace, and explains that one must walk in it as a progress from virtue to virtue: which metaphorical sense of the word walking he embraces with St. Augustine, Sermon XV on the words of the Apostle & Bede in this place: Where indeed Estius warns that these things are not inferred by that word; since it is also said of Christ in chapter II, that he himself also walked, who yet did not progress in virtues by exercising virtues: But that by no means agrees with the testimony of St. Luke chapter II, v. 52. But he rightly observes: Not everyone in whom there is some darkness of sins, according to the Apostle, walks in darkness, or as he speaks in the following chapter v. 9, is in darkness, but those alone whom darkness dominates, that is, in whom sin reigns, Rom. VI, 12, & 14, and who are slaves of sin, in the same place verses 17 & 20. For even those who walk in the light, nay even who are light in the Lord, suffer and have some darkness. But those who are slaves to sins, and obey their own lusts, are said to walk in darkness, and they themselves are called darkness. For thus Paul says to the Ephesians, Chapter 5: But you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. But if, says St. John, we walk in the light of truth and faith, which is active through love, just as He Himself is light, that is, luminous, nay, the very substantial light, doing all things in the light of divine wisdom, prudence, truth, and holiness (where the particle 'as' denotes cause more than likeness, just as in 1 Peter 1:16 it is said: Be holy, because I am holy), we have fellowship with one another, that is, both mutually among ourselves and consequently also with God, as he had said in verse 3, that you also may have fellowship with us, and our fellowship may be with the Father and with His Son Jesus Christ. μετ̓ ἀλλήλων is among us, mutually us with you and vice versa. Compare Philippians 2:15. Proverbs 4:18. Just as by the proclamation of eternal life received through faith the pious have communion among themselves, as members of the same mystical body, and fellow citizens of the Church and spiritual brothers, so if they walk in that light of faith, and do not allow themselves to be snatched away from the path of saving doctrine, or to be enveloped by the darkness of errors and vices, that mutual communion will remain for them, and with God the Father and His Son Jesus Christ. He who adheres to the Lord through faith is one Spirit with Him, 1 Corinthians 6:17. Flacius therefore observes that here the medium or way to apprehend Christ the Savior is shown, namely, that conversion or faith is proposed. Briefly, he says at verse 6, he shows the way and reason, or the mode of apprehending that life-giving Word and communion with the Father and the Son, who are that very purest and holiest spiritual light. He affirms that to be the true conversion of man, namely, first the recognition of that very ineffable light, which is God Himself, and of His justice and will concerning every duty of man, justice and injustice, and then also of one's own most sad darkness and shadow of death, in which all men remain buried, the terror and grief for such horrible plagues, and the lot of our most sad state, which part is also called contrition and flight from evil. Therefore, he deals with this very part in this verse, forbidding ignorance of God and security, and dwelling in that horrible darkness, because God will by no means leave such children or worshipers or subjects unpunished. But regarding the seventh verse, Flacius has it thus: In the previous verse he warned about the first part of conversion, or about contrition; now he exhorts to the latter, or to faith: commanding that by embracing the true light of the Gospel and the Messiah, the illuminator and life-giver, we make ourselves participants of His members and of the heavenly Father, who is the source of all light and life, and make ourselves members of the household, or graft and implant ourselves into the body of Christ, as a life-giving vine or olive tree. Which, however, is to be understood passively, not actively, so that by embracing Christ through faith we may become members of God's household, and be grafted and implanted into the body of Christ by the grace of God and the power of the Holy Spirit.

And the blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanses us from all sin.] It is a metonymy. For he wishes to say, he shows who such a one is, that he is truly cleansed by the blood of Christ, that is, by that faith which the passion of Christ works in us. See Romans 3:25, 5:9, Ephesians 1:7, 2:3, Colossians 1:14, Hebrews 9:14, 10:19. And compare Acts 15:9. But it is often said to happen, what is made manifest.

We establish here a second requirement for the associates of God, which is cleansing from sins. Cleansing from sins follows our conversion and faith; which is done by the application of the expiation or purification made by the blood of Christ on the altar of the cross.

For there the blood of Christ cleansed the whole human race meritoriously, as that Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world, John 1:29, who was made a propitiation for sins not only ours, but of the whole world, 1 John 2:1, but here He cleanses us, who through faith apprehend Christ our propitiator and His propitiatory blood, and apply it to ourselves, as He whom God set forth for us as a propitiation through faith in His blood, to demonstrate His righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, Romans 3:25. Those who walk in the light of saving faith, apprehending Christ the true light through faith, the blood of Jesus Christ the Son of God cleanses them from all sin. Blessed Osiander says these things are added for consolation, lest anyone, because of sins committed, should think that he is not in the fellowship of the Father and the Son. Estius is almost similar, although he wishes to refer to sins committed before conversion, while this refers to sins into which the reborn fall: He shows, he says, that we do not walk in the light in such a way that we are entirely free from darkness: but that we have need of a continuous dissipation of darkness, that is, a purgation of sins, which is done through the blood of Jesus Christ the Son of God, that is, through the merit of His passion and death, in which He shed His blood for us. Nor does it seem improbable to him that John says this on account of the heretical Ebionites, who, while they walked in darkness, believed they were cleansed from their sins by frequent washings, not acknowledging the mystery of Christ's redemption, just as other Judaizers, against whom Paul deals in Colossians chapter 2 and elsewhere. But the former is to be preferred, or at least both explanations are to be joined; for because He cleanses from all sin, therefore both those which were committed before conversion, and if any are committed after conversion, all are cleansed only through the blood of Christ. St. Augustine connects these with the preceding ones thus: What then shall we do, my brothers? Fellowship with GOD must be had, there is no other hope of salvation. GOD is light, and there is no darkness in Him, but iniquities are darkness. We are pressed by iniquities, so that we cannot have fellowship with GOD. What hope then? GOD has given great security. We rightly celebrate Easter, where the blood of the Lord was shed, by which we are purged from every offense. Let us be secure. The devil held a bond of servitude against us, but it has been blotted out by the blood of Christ. The blood, he says, of the Son of God has purged us from every offense.

In this golden aphorism, however, let it be noted: I. The meritorious cause of purification is the blood of Jesus Christ, by which is expressed his entire obedience, both active and passive, which shone forth most greatly in the shedding of his blood, Phil. II, 8. The blood is designated primarily because reference is made to expiatory sacrifices, since the blood of beasts was given for the life of man, Levit. XVII, 11, and was poured out for the expiation and remission of sins, foreshadowing the blood of Christ as that immaculate Lamb, by which alone sins are truly expiated, and which had to be shed for the remission of sins. For not through the blood of bulls and goats, but through his own blood, Christ having entered, eternal redemption was found, Heb. IX, 12; and the blood of Christ, who offered himself through the eternal Spirit immaculate to God, cleanses our conscience from dead works, v. 14, which was shed for us for the remission of sins, Matth. XXVI, 28. Therefore we have in him τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τῆς αἵματος αὐτοῦ, τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων, Ephes. I, 7. τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν, Coloss. cap. I, v. 14.

Note II. The principle of cleansing, which is Christ Jesus, by which names the whole person is expressed, to whom this ἀποτέλεσμα (result/effect) belongs according to both natures, just as all the actions of his office do. Mention is made, however, particularly of the divine nature when the Son of God is designated, which is a concrete term for the divine nature, and not without cause: because the reason is thus expressed, namely why the blood of Christ cleanses us, or whence it has the power of cleansing from sin: because the blood is not of a mere man, but of the only-begotten, proper, and natural Son of God, who is of the same essence with the Father, true God, 1 John 5:20. For God with his own blood acquired the Church for himself, Acts 20:28. God himself laid down his soul for us, 1 John 3:15. God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us, Rom. 8:32. He understands, however, the Son manifested in the flesh, who was made a partaker of our flesh and blood, Heb. 2:14. The blood therefore poured out for our sins is the very blood of the Son of God himself, and thus it has from that source the divine power of cleansing us from sins. For because of the hypostatic union, the blood is as personally proper to the eternal Son of God as blood is essentially proper to Peter or Paul by nature. The blood of a mere man could never have provided that purification and expiation: for this is a work of divine and infinite power, and therefore it is necessary that divine and immense power be communicated to the blood of Christ, through which the appeasement of the wrath of God, the satisfaction of infinite divine justice, and the expiation for the whole human race could be accomplished. For the blood of no other man, says Osiander, could have cleansed us from sins and made satisfaction for the sins of the whole human race. But the blood of the Son of God could do this: and therefore Paul says: GOD redeemed the Church WITH HIS OWN BLOOD. Wherefore the ancients rightly said that a single drop of Christ's blood could have expiated the sins of the whole world. When, therefore, sins weigh upon us in our conscience, let us grasp this consolation, that it is not the blood of some mere man (such as Adam was before the fall), but the blood of the Son of God that has been poured out for us. The Jesuit Cornelius à Lapide himself proves what Clement VI in Extravag. Unigenitus, de pænitentia & remiss. asserts, that a single little drop of Christ's blood could have redeemed the entire world, because it was the blood of the Word through the hypostatic union. And what Gregor. Nazianzenus says: Nothing is to be compared with the miracle of my salvation, in which a few drops of blood restored the entire world: and Estius notes here in very few words that by the BLOOD OF THE SON OF GOD three heresies are destroyed: that of the Manichaeans, who took away the truth of human nature from Christ: that of the Ebionites, who denied that Christ was God: and that of the Nestorians, who divided the person in Christ, which we have taught elsewhere is also done by Papists and especially Jesuits, with the Calvinists, by the denied communication of idioms.

III. The act of purification: He cleanses us from all sin: In which these four things are to be noted (1.)

The act of cleansing is καθαρίζει (he cleanses), which is a sacrificial word in the Old Testament, and occurs frequently especially in Leviticus: It is used, however, for כִּפֶּר (kipper), he expiated, concerning the expiation of the altar, Ex. 29:25, Lev. 8:5; and for כִּבֶּר (kibber), likewise concerning the expiation of the altar, Ex. 39:37, 30:10; for טִהֵר (taher), he cleansed, concerning the cleansing of a leper, Lev. 6:2 ff., or of other unclean things, Num. 6:9, concerning the cleansing of the Levites and Priests, Num. 8:15, Neh. 12:30, of the sons of Levi, Mal. 3:3, and especially concerning purification from sins, Psalm 51:3, Jer. 33:8, Ezek. 36:25, 33; for קדש (qadesh), he sanctified, expiated, Job 1:5; for נקה (naqah), he absolved, Exod. 35:7, he cleansed, Psalm 19:13; סלח (salah), he forgave, Numbers 30:6. צדק (tsadaq), he justified, Dan. 8:14, and therefore τό καθαρίζειν (the cleansing) implies such an expiation, by which sins are so expiated before God that the forgiveness of the same and absolution from sins and justification are obtained for us: And since sins are uncleanness before God, we are purified from the filth and uncleanness of sins, which happens both by reason of merit, by which such purification was acquired for us through the blood of Christ poured out for us and the remission of sins was obtained, and by reason of efficacy and act, by which for those who apply to themselves by faith the καθαρισμόν (cleansing) acquired by the passion and blood of Christ, an actual purgation of sins occurs, not physically through washing, but morally through non-imputation, remission, and forgiveness, as Paul taught in Rom. 4 and elsewhere throughout, indeed the whole Scripture. Cornelius à Lapide warns that God does not scrape away sins, but cleanses them entirely, that is, purges and abolishes them, just as a stain is swept and cleansed from a face, mud from a garment, or filth from a house. But however much we may grant that sins are not scraped away through the blood of Christ, it is not to be admitted that they are abolished, for it is not a physical act, but a judicial one, since GOD justifies the ungodly not by wiping away or scraping away or abolishing impiety, or by removing it in any physical way, but by not imputing and by forgiving, and thus by absolving us from sins on account of the expiation of Christ made on the altar of the cross and by imputing the innocence of Christ to us in return, Acts 10:43, Chap. 13:38, Rom. 3:25, Chap. 9:5 ff. Furthermore, one must distinguish the purification in the article of redemption, which is the meritorious expiation of our sins, Isa. 53. & in the article of justification, which occurs by the apprehension of the meritorious expiation of Christ, and the remission of our sins, Ephes. I. v. 7. Coloss. I. v. 14. & in the article of sanctification; which occurs when by the renewing Holy Spirit the old man is put off and mortified, and the new is put on and created in us, and we are a new creature in Christ, and walk in newness of life, Ephes. IV, 24. Coloss. III, 10. 2. Corinth. V, 17. Gal. Chap. VI, 7. 15. Rom. VI, 4. Which are confounded by the Papists, but accurately distinguished in the Scriptures, since justification is one thing, sanctification another: The former precedes, the latter follows: The former is described by the remission of sin, which we obtain before the tribunal of God by the virtue of the blood and merit of Christ, and thus the blood of Christ cleanses us from sins, when on account of Christ's expiation apprehended by faith we are absolved from sins and received into favor. For sins are expiated, not so that they are not present, but so that they are not imputed. But this is, when those powers are given to us, that having abandoned sins we may strive for the holiness of life; where Estius acknowledges that we are not cleansed by the blood of CHRIST once and for all from every sin (because this cleansing must be attributed to the merit of the blood of Christ) so that anyone could say, I have no sin, or my heart is clean, I am pure from sin, Prov. Chap. XX. verse 6. But that we are cleansed day by day, yet so that we are never, while we live here, completely cleansed from every sin. Therefore that cleansing from every sin consists, as the Scholastics say, in the becoming, not in the being done, and is in an incomplete act, but not a complete one, except at the end, as Estius holds here. Concerning which purification 1. John III. verse 3. everyone who has this hope, ἁγνίζει

purifies himself, just as he himself is pure, and Apoc. Chap. XXII. verse 11. ὁ ἅγιος ἁγιασθήτω ἔτι, let him who is holy, be holy still. Cornelius a Lapide cites the Council of Trent, Sess. VI. chap. 7. that no one is just, except he to whom the merits of the passion of our Lord JESUS CHRIST are communicated, yet that this happens in the justification of the ungodly, while by the merit of the same most holy passion through the Holy Spirit the charity of GOD is poured forth in the hearts of those who are justified, and inheres in them. But if the ungodly is justified, then he who is justified is not endowed with charity toward GOD, by which he is justified. For good works, to which charity toward GOD pertains, follow the justified, they do not precede the one to be justified. For we are not justified by our own justice or obedience, or by charity, but by the obedience of one just man we are all made just, as many as are justified, Rom. Chap. V. verse 19. But that charity, of which verse 5 speaks, is not a quality inhering in us, but the grace of God and an affection of mercy in God toward us. And what need is there for the purification of the blood of Christ, and the communication of the merits of the Lord's passion, if we are justified by charity toward God or by our own obedience to the law. If justice is through the law, Christ died for nothing, Gal. Chap. II. verse 21. You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified by the law, Galat. Chap. V. verse 4. How the passion of Christ concurs to justification, Thomas explains thus, part III. q. 48. a. 6. To the third it must be said, that the passion of Christ, as it is compared to his divinity, acts by way of efficiency; but as it is compared to the will of the soul of Christ, it acts by way of merit. But as it is considered in the very flesh of Christ, it acts by way of satisfaction, in that through it we are freed from the debt of punishment. But by way of redemption, in that through it we are freed from the servitude of guilt: But by way of sacrifice, in that through it we are reconciled to GOD. Thus nothing is left to our charity toward God, if both merit and satisfaction and reconciliation of GOD, and the remission of sin or liberation from the debt of punishment, and liberation from the servitude of guilt are to be attributed to the blood and passion of Christ. The same q. 49. §. to the third. Christ by his passion freed us from sins causally, that is, by instituting the cause of our liberation, from which any sins whatsoever could be remitted at any time, whether past, or present, or future, just as if a Physician should make a medicine, from which any diseases could be healed even in the future. And art. III. I answer that by the passion of Christ we are freed from the debt of punishment in two ways, in one way directly, in that the passion of Christ was a sufficient and superabundant satisfaction for the sins of the whole human race; and with satisfaction exhibited, the debt of punishment is sufficiently taken away. In another way indirectly, in that the passion of Christ is the cause of the remission of sin, in which the debt of punishment is founded. And art. IV. I answer: The passion of CHRIST is the cause of our reconciliation to God in two ways: In one way, in that it removed the sin, through which men are made enemies of GOD according to Wisd. XIV. Similarly, the wicked and his impiety are hateful to GOD, and in Psalm V. You hate all who work iniquity: In another way in that it is a sacrifice most acceptable to God. For this is the effect of a proper sacrifice, that through it GOD is appeased, just as when a man remits an offense committed against him on account of some acceptable service, whence it is said 1 Kings XVI. If the Lord incites you against me, let the sacrifice be smelled; and similarly it was such a great good, that Christ voluntarily suffered, that on account of this good found in human nature God was appeased regarding every offense of the human race, as far as concerns those who are joined to Christ who suffered. Which opinion of Thomas, Cardinal Contarini follows and explains in de justif. oper. p. 542. Blessed Thomas says, when he speaks of the sacrament of baptism, that by it all sins are washed away, and all debt of guilt and punishment of whatever kind, and he gives the reason for it, that everyone is baptized into the death of Christ, and is buried with him, as the Apostle says. Therefore the baptized person is in such a state as if he himself, bearing the person of Christ, had died, suffered, and been buried with Christ, and had risen with Christ into a new life. Behold how clearly the most learned and at the same time most holy Man says that the death, passion, and merit of Christ are given to us, are imputed to us in baptism, which is the sacrament of faith, not because they inhere in us, who are already living, but because they are given and imputed to us. Nor do others among the Papists deny this entirely, who, as Vasquez admits in l. 2. disp. 204. c. 1., go over to this: That there is nothing in us, whether a habit or an operation, which by its own nature can justify the soul, and purge it from sins: But that for this we necessarily need the favor of GOD accepting that and pardoning or remitting the sin, by which favor, with inherent and intrinsic justice being added, our justification is completed. Such are those who in the same place 1. affirm that the quality of justice or inherent grace, by which we are justified, by its own nature does not fight with sin, nay rather can exist with it, and only by the constitution and will of God is it never with it. This is what Richard taught in 3. distinct. 31. a. 1. quest. 1. in the third way of opining, which he thinks is more probable, Soto in 4. distinct. 14. quest. 1. art. 2. after the fifth conclusion, Ockham in 4. quest. 3. letter E. And Johannes Medina in the code on penance quest. 12. follows as a corollary. For if that which inheres in us does not of itself fight with sin, but follows only from the constitution of GOD, it is clear that it does not of itself cleanse from sin, but that with the favor and pardon of GOD added, the sin is remitted, and thus our justification is completed by that favor. 2. Those who think that grace is expelled by sin, or conversely that sin is expelled by grace, only demeritoriously and not physically and by the nature of the thing. Which opinion Bonaventure indicated in 1, dist. 17, second part of the distinction, q. 3, and in 3, distinction 31, art. 1, q. 1, ad 2. Richard, however, openly followed it in the place alleged. Scotus in 2, dist. 37, q. 1, to the solution of those in the solution of a certain argument. Durandus in 1, dist. 17, q. 10, n. 4, and in 3, dist. 31, q. 1, num. 6. Paludanus in 3, dist. 28, q. 3, art. 3. Conrad above, q. 71, art. 4 (which two interpret the mind of St. Thomas in this sense). And Gabriel in 1, distinct. 17, q. 4, art. 3, dub. 3, conclus. 3, and in 3, distinct. 23, q. 2. Paludanus in 3, dist. art. 3, dub. 2, whom we alleged in disp. 91, art. 1. For those who assert that grace is expelled by sin only demeritoriously, and likewise must assert that sin is expelled by grace, they must also assert that grace and sin can by the nature of the thing exist together, and consequently that for the remission of sin the condonation of GOD remitting sins is necessary. 3.
