Those who philosophize in the same way about our inherent justice as they do about currency and its value, for they compare the habit and quality inherent in us to the metal from which currency is cast, and they compare the reason for grace or justice, on account of which we please GOD, to the value which a King imposes upon currency by his law and will, which some more recent writers they call something moral in currency, and without the valuation of the King, an ill-advised thing does not have the value of currency: so also that quality may be only a certain real entity, which by its own nature is not so pleasing and just, that it could not fail to please God as justice and grace, and render men dear and acceptable to God: but indeed, just as currency, upon the addition of the King's valuation, already has its value with no change of metal made in it itself: So also that quality inherent in us, upon the addition of the valuation and love and favor of GOD, already has the character of grace justifying and cleansing us from sin. This mode of philosophizing was that of the Nominalists, for Occam in 1. d. 17. q. 1. attacks the opinion of those who say that inherent justice is a quality which by its own nature could not fail to please GOD, and could not fail to render a man just, and to purge him from sin. Gregory also agrees in 1. d. 7. q. a. 2. in the proofs of the second conclusion, and in the solution of 3. §. against it. Gabriel q. 1. a. 1. notabil. 1. & a. 3. dub. 4. coroll. 1. to 1. & 2. and Petrus Alliacensis in 1. q. 9. a. 2. letter O. From the school of St. Thomas, Franciscus Victoria and Canus have agreed with these, as is commonly reported, and other more recent Thomists, whom I have often heard teaching thus in disputations. This Vasquez himself [says] l. c. Who furthermore disp. 222. c. 2. n. 14. has this to say about these matters: The Lutherans affirm that we are not justified by that renewal as a form, but that the very justice of GOD or of Christ, by which He Himself is holy, is imputed to us; they also assert that we are not truly just, but are only reputed to be, and that our sins are not blotted out and eradicated, but are covered and hidden by non-imputation and pardon, because they are not imputed to us for punishment. This very kind of imputation and application of the merits of CHRIST must be confessed by as many of the Catholics as assert that the justice inherent in us renders us pleasing to GOD, not by its own nature, but from the favor and acceptance of GOD, namely because GOD wills to love us, possessing such a form, whom He could choose not to love. It is necessary for them to confess this imputation and application for this purpose, that we may be rendered just. Similarly, those who judge that the quality inherent in us is indeed true holiness and justice, yet by its own nature does not purge us from sins, unless the new will and favor of GOD pardoning the sin is added, willy-nilly, are compelled to concede a new imputation of the merits of Christ after the infusion of habitual grace for the remitting and pardoning of sins. For where the favor of God, peculiar and distinct from others, comes to us, it proceeds to us from the merits of Christ, and therefore a peculiar application and imputation of the merits of Christ, distinct from others, must then take place.

2. Let the continuity of the act be noted. The Apostle does not use καθαρίζει without cause, but designates continuity, for he does not say, he has purified, since he is speaking not of the justification made on the altar of the cross, but of its application. For that has already been done, concerning which Heb. I, 3. ὅς δι᾽ ἑαυτῇ καθαρισμὸν ποιησάμενος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν, who after he HAD MADE purification of our sins by himself, sat down at the right hand of the Majesty. He did indeed cleanse us in baptism, 1 Cor. Ch. VI. v. 11. Acts XXII. v. 16. But he does not cease to cleanse; because we subsequently contract uncleanness by sinning, which must be cleansed by faith, and thus by the blood of Christ, which faith apprehends. As Jerome [says] l. II. contr. Pelag. That, he says, which is written, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin, is to be understood both in the confession of baptism and in the clemency of repentance.

3. The subject of purification: He cleanses us, says the Apostle, that is, the faithful, whom he includes along with himself, namely those who have communion with God, which is none without faith, Heb. ch. XI, 6. those who do not walk in darkness, but in the light, who apprehend the true light through faith, concerning which John: And the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not apprehend it ch. I, 5. But as many as have apprehended the Word of God Himself, that true light, to them he gave power to become children of God, who believe in His name, v. 12. Therefore faith is said to purify hearts, Acts XV, 9. through ῥαντισμὸν ἅιματος, the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, 1 Pet. II, 2.

4. The object, which is sins. He cleanses us from all sin. He speaks universally ἀπὸ πάσης ἁμαρτίας, FROM ALL SIN, so that it is not permitted to except any sin, whatsoever and howsoever great it may be, but that we are purified from it through the blood of Christ. He cleanses, therefore, not only from actual sin, but also from original, not only from venial sin, but also from mortal.

As for Grotius's gloss: The blood of Christ the Son of God cleanses us from all sin, who is such, that is, has communion with God, shows himself to be truly cleansed by the blood of Christ, that is, by that faith which the passion of Christ works in us; that is alien in more than one way. For there is no talk here of that by which communion with the Father or a sign of the same is shown: nor is cleansing from sin a sign of that communion. Furthermore, if the word cleansing is to be taken metonymically, the blood will be said to be cleansed, because it shows that we have been cleansed. But what kind of thing is this? But perhaps Grotius means this, that he who lives purely or according to the precepts of Christ, shows that he is truly cleansed by the blood of Christ. But how does this fit the present aphorism? Is not both the subject and the predicate changed in this way? For the subject is not he who lives purely, but the blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of GOD; the predicate is not 'shows himself to be a purifier,' but 'cleanses us from all sin.' And what kind of explanation is that, 'by the blood of Christ, that is, by that faith which the passion of Christ works in us'? Is the blood of Christ faith? Or is the subject here faith, and not rather the object of faith, which is directed toward the blood or passion of Christ? Nor indeed in those passages Rom. III. v. 25, chap. V. v. 9, Eph. I. v. 7, Col. I. v. 14, Heb. chap. IX. v. 14, chap. X. v. 19 is faith understood by the blood of Christ, nor is the passion of Christ even said to work faith, but in Rom. chap. III. v. 25 faith is distinguished from the blood of Christ, and is said to be directed toward the blood of Christ, as its proper object: ἡ πίστις ἐν τῷ ἀυτῦ αἵματι is faith, which is placed in the blood of Christ, and relies upon it; Coloss. I. v. 14 cf. Rom. IV. v. 24. 25. nor is it to be understood as faith, since in Eph. chap. I, v. 7 we are said to have τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τῦ ἅιματος ἀυτῦ. For there the blood is properly designated as the price of redemption, or that by which we have been redeemed, not is faith denoted by the blood; which if it were to be sought here, it should rather be sought in the words ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν. For we have the remission of sins through faith, or in him apprehended through faith, insofar as through faith we apprehend the redemption made through his blood. Nor indeed did Grotius himself in those passages understand faith by the blood of Christ, as in Roman. chap. III. v. 25 at the words διὰ τῆς πίσεως, he shows, he says, how each one could attain the effect of that goodness, that is, true righteousness, namely by having faith in the blood of Christ, Eph. I, 7. He explains διὰ τῦ ἅιματος through the life of Christ spent for us as a λύτρον, Ebr. IX, 14. τὸ ἅιμα Χρισῦ, even with Grotius himself as interpreter, denotes not faith, but, as the letter sounds, the blood of Christ: How much the blood of Christ the Son of God and the innocent one excels the blood of those lacking the faculty of reason, by so much must the purification be greater, Ebr. X, 19. He indeed invents a metonymical sense for the word ἅιματος; but there is no cause for a metonymical explanation. For in the blood, or through the blood of Christ as the meritorious cause, we have παῤῥησίαν for entry into the holy of holies. Nor is there in this place any necessity for a tropical locution, because we are purified by the blood of Christ as a meritorious cause, and thus the comparison with Acts XV, 9 is foreign: For there it is not a question of a meritorious cause, but an instrumental one, faith: But the meritorious cause, together with the principal one, namely grace, is included in verse 11, διὰ τῆς χάριτος Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ πισεύομεν σωθῆναι, where faith is openly distinguished from Christ and his merit, which it apprehends for salvation.

Furthermore, not only in the word of blood, but also in the word καθαρίσει, Grotius, together with Socinus, invents a metonymical sense without cause, which he himself had indeed solidly refuted in Defens. fid. Cathol. de Satisfact. cap. 7. pag. 237. Nor is it permitted to explain 1 John cap. I. vers. 7 as meaning that we are clean. For both the propriety of the words and the perpetual use of Scripture in this argument manifestly contradict it. Socinus admits that the name of uncleanness signifies guilt everywhere. Hence καθαρίζειν and ἁγιάζειν is to remove that guilt, or to effect remission, as the writer to the Hebrews himself explains the word καθαρίζειν c. IX. v. 22. Christ through himself made this καθαρισμὸν, Ebr. I, 3. Christ καθαρίζει the conscience from dead works, Ebr. cap. IX. v. 14. that is, with Socinus himself as interpreter, he frees the conscience from guilt and punishment and the fear of punishment. In the Old Testament also, Kipper has the same sense, Psalm LI. vers. 9. But what καθαρίζειν is in these places, this very thing is said by a similar reason ῥαντίζειν, X, 22. and λούειν to wash in the same verse, to which the prophecy of Zechariah cap. XIII, 1 also looks. Why one should depart from this sense, there is clearly no reason. Indeed, Grotius adds: It is entirely absurd to interpret καθαρίζειν as the declaration of cleansing, not as the cleansing itself, since shortly after ἀφιέναι and καθαρίζειν are joined in v. 9. The Apostle argues from things conjoined: If you walk in the light, you have cleansing, that is, remission through the blood of Christ: because sins are not imputed to anyone walking in the light. These things Grotius says there quite solidly, refuting his own annotations.

Even to Grotius in this place, the Socinian Schlichtingius is more sound, rendering this sense of the Aphorist; as if to say: And whatever we have ever sinned, this will not stand in our way to communion with God, provided we walk in the light: For the blood of Jesus Christ the Son of God cleanses us from all sin, none excepted, even if it were the greatest and most grievous. The blood of the Son of God is far more effective for purifying us than any sin is for contaminating and condemning us. There is an allusion here to the blood of victims, which were a type of Christ, and at the same time the blood of Christ is opposed to their blood. For the blood of victims did not have the power of purifying every sin, it purified only ignorances and infirmities, as is to be read in the law. (in which we have taught elsewhere that Schlichtingius is mistaken)

But the blood of the Son of God purifies every sin. For it was also shed for all the sins of all men by the will and command of God. And therefore it moves God, and binds him deeply, to forgive sins to all who believe in Christ and walk in the light, and to release them from their guilt and punishment: all the more so, because by this obedience of Christ, by which he gave himself as a victim for the sins of the world, and lowered himself to death, and that of the cross, he was most pleasing of all to GOD. Whence also Christ is said to have delivered himself for us as a victim and offering to GOD for a sweet-smelling savor, Eph. V. vers. 2. Thus, therefore, the blood of Christ not only cleanses our sins, but also shows them to be cleansed, as a most certain pledge of the remission of sins given to us by God.

But the things which Schlichtingius adds here, to support his heresy, are not easily explained away. It is to be noted, however, that the blood of JESUS CHRIST the Son of GOD cleanses us from all sin, not simply, but with the condition, if we walk in the light. From which condition it appears that the blood of Jesus the Son of GOD was not shed so that he might properly speaking pay our sins or debts to God, but so that God might forgive and remit them to us by the decree of his own will. For if the former were true, no condition could be required of us. For when a creditor receives his debt most fully, he has no further right to demand the debt from the debtor. Whence also the redemption, which was made in Christ JESUS, is called the remission of transgressions, Col. cap. I. vers. 14. Eph. I. vers. 7. These are the words of Schlichtingius.

To which we respond 1. That condition, if we walk in the light, coheres with our communion with God, but it does not make conditional the expiation of sins, which is done through the blood of Christ. 2. The particle καὶ can be taken in a causal sense. That they have communion with God who walk in the light. For the blood of GOD has cleansed them from all sin. 3. That condition is not legal, but Evangelical. For to walk in the light is to embrace the true light, which is Christ, or to receive the light of Evangelical truth through faith, and to remain in the same, just as in 2 John v. 4, to walk in the truth, with Schlichtingius as interpreter, is to be devoted to the truth. 4. It is not a question here of the expiation made on the altar of the cross, but of the remission of sins, which is purification in sins, and the application of that expiation, which is done through faith. 5. Purification from sins is not attributed here to our holiness, but to the blood of Christ; nor is our holiness a cause or a preceding condition, or a prerogative, so that the blood of Christ may cleanse us from sins. For the cleansing efficacy of the blood of Christ does not depend upon our holiness, but upon the intrinsic value of the satisfaction and expiation of sins made by Christ. 6. If, therefore, walking in the light were in the highest degree to be devoted to holiness, the pursuit of holiness could not be established as a cause or condition of the expiation of sins made on the altar of the cross; because δι᾽ ἑαυτῦ BY HIMSELF alone Christ made καθαρισμὸν, Heb. I, 3, or the actual purification of our conscience, which does not happen except by the power of the purification made through the blood of Christ, Heb. IX, 14. 15. 7. Wherefore this condition, which Schlichtingius makes, is not to be drawn to the καθαρισμὸν of the blood of Christ, which in no way depends upon the condition of our holiness. But rather, a sense of signification or indication by covenant would have to be admitted, in this way: If we are devoted to justice and holiness, that would be an indication and argument that we have communion with God, and the blood of the Son of God cleanses us from sin. If Grotius intended this metonymical sense, we would admit it thus far. 8. The description and requirement of the subject, which has communion with God, is exhibited here, namely that it is purified from sin by the blood of Christ, but that purification, or the cleansing thing, is not suspended upon walking in the light, much less upon the pursuit of holiness. 9. The Apostolic mode of speaking is to be observed, because John delights in such a manner of speech: If we say, if we walk, if we confess, which nevertheless do not bring in a condition properly of the coherence of the predicate with the subject, but rather a requirement and determination of the subject according to the mind of the Apostle: He who shall have said, he who shall have walked, he who shall have confessed: or they look to an argument a posteriori rather than to a condition a priori, just as the explanation of such things is had in chapter 2, verse 3. And by this we know that we have known him, if we keep his commandments. And verse 4, He that saith, etc. 10. Although we require faith for actual purification from sins, it is not so that the blood of Christ thence obtains any force to cleanse us, or that our faith cooperates toward the purification, which belongs entirely, not half-way, to the blood of Christ as the sole and solitary cause, not as a co-cause. But it is that our faith only apprehends and makes its own the purification and forgiveness of sins which was accomplished by Christ through his blood, which we have otherwise explained against the Arminians. It behaves itself rather passively by receiving than actively by cooperating. 11. Therefore, by such a required condition, the power of the blood of Christ is not evacuated, as if it were to be believed that it was not shed so that it might properly speaking pay our sins or debts to God, but rather satisfy for them; but that power of the blood of Christ is rather strengthened, because the satisfaction could not be applied to us and apprehended by us through faith, unless the same had been performed for us. 12. Vain also is the opposition of those ends of the shedding of the blood of Christ, that it might satisfy for us, or that a payment might be rendered to Divine justice for our sins, and that God might remit our sins to us by the decree of his will: for satisfaction does not take away remission: But it was performed for us by Christ, so that our debts might be remitted to us. 13. Therefore, what is said, if satisfaction has been performed for us by Christ, no condition can be required of us, we admit that regarding a legal condition. When a creditor receives his debt most fully, he has no right any longer to demand the debt from the debtor. Nor does God demand the debt from us, but graciously forgives it to us on account of the satisfaction performed for us. Through faith we do not pay anything to God, but we receive the ransom paid by Christ, and present it to God. 14. Redemption, therefore, which was made through the blood of Christ, is called the price of the remission of sins and transgressions, by which the same is had by us, or has become ours through faith, by which we receive the ransom offered to us in the Word of God; for to that extent the remission of sins reaches us, which Christ produced for us by the most precious ransom of his blood; we, however, have in Christ that redemption through faith, and by that reason we have the remission itself. For in redemption there is the acquisition of remission; in the reception or apprehension of redemption we have also the very forgiveness or remission of sins.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Ἐὰν δὲ ἐν τῷ φωτὶ περιπατῶμεν.] Si pure vivimus, id est, secundum Christi præcepta.

Ὡς αὐτός ἐστιν ἐν τῷ φωτὶ.] Semper versatur in actionibus purissimis.

Κοινωνίαν ἔχομεν μετ' ἀλλήλων.] Ea res nos inter nos ami- cos facit. Amicorum est eadem velle & nolle. Hæc in- ter bonos amicitia, inter malos factio est. Qui cum Deo colligantur, necessario etiam inter se colligantur. Vide Ephes. II. vers. 6. In Manuscripto pro μετ' ἀλλήλων videtur fuisse μετ' ἀυτῶ. Id indicat litura,plures literas non capiens."

In tenebris ambulare non est tantum impura opera facere; sed ambulant etiam ac imprimis in tenebris, qui luce vera non gaudent, quæ est Christus, & sine Christo, adeoque sine DEO sunt in hoc mundo, qui lux ἀυτοφυὴς & Pater lumi- num, Eph. II, 12. in ignorantia veræ lucis & errori- bus de vero DEO constituti : Nam qui non habet Filium non habet Patrem, 1. Joh. II. v. 23. qui sc- dere in tenebris, & umbra mortis dicuntur, Ef. IX, 1. C. XLII, 7. Luc. I, 79. imo tenebrae esse, Ephef. V. v. 8. & in loco parallelo, Job. I, 5. to Φω̃ς, LUX ILLA, de λόγω, lucebat in tenebris, & tenebrae non apprehenderunt ipsam. Declarat quorsum huc adduxerit mentionem lucis & tenebrarum, quasi dicat, si Deus lux est, nullas admittens te- nebras, ipseque homo in tenebris ambulans so- cietatem cum DEO habere non potest. Quae enim societas luci cum tenebris? 2. Cor. VI. vers. 16. Si ergo se dicat habere, mentitur. Docet itaque hoc requiri ab iis, qui communionem cum DEO habent, ut ne in tenebris ambulent, in tenebris mentis & intellectus, utpote ignorantiae veri DEI & JESU Christi vel errorum adversus doctrinam salvificam: in tenebris cordis & voluntatis, seu peccatorum & vitiorum', in tenebris incredulitatis & impoenitentiae, qua excaecationem, induratio- nem, desperationem pariunt, quamque sequuntur tenebrae calamitatis & mortis aeternae, privationis verae lucis, & constipationis extremae caliginis in- fernalis. Notari Gnosticos, Ebionitas, aliosque a vera fide alienos Cornelius a Lapide vult, necnon eos, qui in peccatorum tenebris vivebant, quia peccata tenebris comparantur, quod ut tenebrae privatio lucis: Ita peccata privatio gratiae sint: Sic- ut in tenebris ambulans nihil videt & crebro im- pingit: ita peccantes in via salutis caecutiant & cre- bro impingant: Sicut tenebriones lucem oderunt, instar noctuarum: Ita & peccatores oderint lucem DEI & hominum, Joh. III, 20. atque peccata ope- ra sint principis tenebrarum, in tenebris plera- que & ex tenebris errore nempe practici orian- tur, mentemque magis obtenebrent & excaecent, & ad tenebras gehennae aeternas abripiant, Joh. X. v. 22. Ambulare in tenebris, inquit Flacius, est ha- rere in veteri Adamo seu natura corrupta, aut non- dum renatum esse, versari in inscitia DEI, errori- bus & corrupta religione, esse securum in sua illa corrupta natura, & omnino secundum carnem sine omni vera agnitione DEI suaeq; injustitiae ac irae DEI versari.

Per lucem autem, in qua ambulandum, lucem veritatis intelligere possumus & fidei, quia fatente Schlichtingio, tenebrae in sacris literis solent signifi- care ignorantiam & errores, adeoque lux significat veritatem per Metaphoram: quia sicut tenebrae oc- caecant oculos corporis, sic errores & ignorantia oc- caecant oculos mentis. Ut autem lux illuminat oculos: Ita veritas mentes. Et hoc etiam sensu Christus vera lux appellatur. Lucem rationis, fidei, Evangelii, virtutis, gratiae intelligit Corne- lius, quodque in ea ambulandum, de profe- ctu de virtute in virtutem explicat: quem sensum Metaphoricum vocis ambulandi cum S. Augustino Serm. XV. de verb. Apost. & Beda in h. l. amplectitur: Ubi quidem Estius monet, per vocem istam haec non inferri; siquidem de Chri- sto cap. II. etiam dicatur, quod & ipse ambularit, qui vero non profecerit in virtutibus exercendo virtutes: Sed id haudquaquam convenit testimo- nio S. Lucae cap. II. v. 52. Recte autem observat: Non omnem eum, in quo sunt aliqua peccato- rum tenebrae, secundum Apostolum in tenebris am- bulare, aut ut sequenti capite v. 9. loquitur, in tene- bris esse, sed eos solos, quibus tenebrae dominan- tur, id est, in quibus peccatum regnat, Rom. VI, 12. & 14. quique servi sunt peccati, ibidem vers. 17. & 20. Nam tenebras aliquas patiuntur, & habent etiam illi, qui in luce ambulant, imo qui & lux sunt in Domino. Qui vero peccatis serviunt, & cupi- dicatibus suis obsequuntur, in tenebris ambulare di- cuntur, ipsique tenebrae vocantur. Sic enim Paulus Ephesios Cap. 5. Eratis autem, inquit, aliquando te- nebra, nunc autem lux estis in Domino. Si autem inquit S. Johannes in luce veritatis & fidei, quæ per charitatem operosa est, ambulamus, sicut ipse lux est, hoc est, lucidus, imo ipsa lux substantialis, omnia faciens in luce sapientiæ, prudentiæ, veri- tatis & sanctitatis divinæ (ubi particula sicut ma- gis causam quam similitudinem notat, quemad- modum 1. Petr. I, 16. dicitur: Sancti estote, quia ego sanctus sum) societatem habemus ad invicem, hoc est, tum inter nos mutuo, tum etiam conse- quenter cum Deo, ut v. 3. dixerat, ut & vos societa- tem habeatis nobiscum, & societas nostra sit cum Patre & cum Filio ejus Jesu Christo. μετ̓ ἀλλήλων est inter nos mutuum nos vobiscum & contra. Conf. Phil. II, 15. Prov. IV, 18. quemadmodum an- nunciatione vitæ æternæ per fidem accepta com- munionem habent pii inter se, ceu membra ejus- dem corporis mystici, & concives Ecclesiæ ac fra- tres spirituales, ita si in luce illa fidei ambulent, nec à doctrinæ salvificæ semita se abripi patiantur, aut tenebris errorum ac vitiorum involvi, manebit ipsis illa communio mutua, & cum Deo Patre ac Filio ejus Jesu Christo. Qui Domino adhæret per fidem, unus est Spiritus cum ipso, 1. Cor. VI. v. 17. Flacius itaque observat, hic monstrari me- dium aut viam ad Christum servatorem apprehen- dendum, proponi nempe conversionem aut fidem. Breviter, inquit ad v. 6. monstrat viam & ratio- nem, modumve apprehendendi istud vivificum Ver- bum & communionem cum Patre & Filio, qui sint illa ipsa purissima sanctissimaque lux spiritualis. Eam autem affirmat esse veram hominis conversio- nem, nempe primo agnitionem tum istius ipsius in- effabilis lucis, quæ est Deus ipse, ejusque justitiæ & voluntatis de omni hominis officio, justitia & inju- stitia, tum & suarum tristissimarum tenebrarum & umbræ mortis, in qua omnes homines sepulti hærent, perterrefactionem ac dolorem de tam horrendis pe- stibus, tristissimæque status nostri sorte, quæ pars voca- tur etiam contritio & fuga mali. De hac igitur ipsa parte hoc in versu agit, prohibens ignorantiam Dei & securitatem, & commorationem in istis hor- rendis tenebris, quia Deus tales filios aut cultores subditosve nequaquam inultos relinquet. Ad versum autem septimum ita habet Flacius: Præcedenti versu monuit de priori parte conversionis, seu de con- tritione, nunc hortatur ad posteriorem seu ad fidem: jubens ut fidem amplectendo veram lucem Evangelii & Meschiam illuminatorem ac vivificatorem nos par- ticipes membrorum ipsius & Patris cælestis, qui fons omnis lucis vitaque est, domesticos efficiamus, seu nos- met in corpus Christi, tanquam salutiferam vitem aut oleam inseramus implantemusque. Quæ tamen πα- θητικῶς intelligenda, non ἐνεργητικῶς, ut Christum per fidem amplectendo domestici Dei evadamus, & in corpus Christi gratia Dei ac virtute Spiritus S. inseramur ac implantemur.

Καὶ τὸ ἅιμα Ἰησῦ Χριστῦ τῦ ὑἷῦ ἀὐτῦ καθαρίζει ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ πάσης ἁμαρτίας.] Est Μετωνυμία. Vult enim dicere, osten- dit qui talis est, se vere repurgatum Christi sanguine, id est, fide ea, quam in nobis operatur Christi passio. Vide ad Ro- man. III, 25. c. V, 9. Eph. I, 7. c. II, 3. Col. I, 14. Ebr. IX, 14. c. X, 19. Et conf. Actor. XV, 9. Sæpe autem fieri dicitur, quod patescit.

Alterum hic constituimus requisitum socio- rum Dei, quod est mundatio à peccatis. Sequi- tur conversionem & fidem nostram mundatio à pec- catis; quæ fit applicatione expiationis vel purifi- cationis per sanguinem Christi in ara crucis factæ.

Ibi enim Christi sanguis mundavit totum genus humanum meritorie, ceu Agni illius Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi, Joh. I. vers. 29. qui pro- pitiatio factus pro peccatis non nostris tantum, sed totius mundi, 1. Joh. II, 1. hic vero mundat nos, qui per fidem Christum propitiatorem nostrum, & sanguinem ejus propitiatorium apprehendi- mus, nobisque applicamus, utpote quem Deus nobis proposuit ἱλαστήριον διὰ τῆς πίστεως ἐν τῷ αὐτοῦ αἵματι, εἰς ἔνδειξιν τῆς δικαιοσύνης αὑτοῦ διὰ τὴν πάρεσιν τῶν προγεγονότων ἁμαρτημάτων, Ro- man. III, 25. Qui ambulant in luce fidei salvificæ, Christum veram lucem apprehendentes, per fi- dem, eos mundat sanguis Jesu Christi Filii Dei ab omni peccato, B. Osiander addi hæc in consolatio- nem ait, ne quis propter peccata commissa cogi- taret, se non esse in societate Patris & Filii. Simi- liter fere Estius, quamvis ille peccata ante conver- sionem commissa respici velit, hic vero peccata, in quæ labuntur renati: Ostendit, inquit, non ita nos in luce ambulare, ut tenebris omnino careamus: sed opus nobis esse continua tenebrarum discussione, id est peccatorum purgatione, quæ fiat per sangui- nem Jesu Christi Filii Dei, hoc est, per meritum pas- sionis & mortis ejus, in qua sanguinem suum pro no- bis effudit. Nec improbabile eidem videtur, Jo- hannem hoc dicere propter Ebionitas hæreticos, qui cum in tenebris ambularent, crebris lotionibus se à peccatis suis emundari credebant, mysterium re- demptionis Christi non agnoscentes, quemadmodum & cæteri Judaizantes, adversus quos Paulus agit Col. c. II. & alibi. Præferenda autem prior, vel con- jungenda certe utraque explicatio; nam quia emundat ab omni peccato, ideo & ea, quæ ante conversionem commissa sunt, & si quæ post con- versionem committantur, omnia non nisi per san- guinem Christi emundantur. S. Augustinus ita hæc connectit cum superioribus: Quid ergo faciemus, fratres mei? Societas cum DEO habenda est, alia spes salutis nulla est. DEUS lux est, & tene- bræ in eo nullæ sunt, iniquitates autem tenebræ sunt. Iniquitatibus premimur, ne societatem cum DEO habere possimus. Quæ ergo spes? Magnam securitatem dedit DEUS. Merito Pascha celebra- mus, ubi fusus est sanguis Domini, quo purgamur ab omni delicto. Simus securi. Cautionem contra nos diabolus tenebat servitutis, sed sanguine Christi deleta est. Sanguis, inquit, Filii Dei purgavit nos ab omni delicto.

In hoc autem aureo aphorismo notetur I. E- mundationis causa meritoria, sanguis Jesu Christi, quo exprimitur tota ejus obedientia cum activa, tum passiva, quæ in effusione sanguinis maxime eluxit, Phil. II, 8. Designatur autem imprimis sanguis, quia respectus fit ad sacrificia expiato- ria, quum sanguis pecudum datus sit pro vita ho- minis, Levit. XVII, 11. effusus sit in expiationem & remissionem peccatorum, adumbrans sangui- nem Christi tanquam Agni illius immaculati, quo solo vere expiantur peccata, quique effundi de- buit in remissionem peccatorum. Non enim per sanguinem taurorum & hircorum, sed per pro- prium sanguinem ingresso Christo inventa est æterna redemptio, Ebr. IX, 12. & sanguis Christi, qui se per Spiritum æternum immaculatum obtulit Deo, mun- dat conscientiam nostram ab operibus mortuis, v. 15. qui pro nobis effusus est in remissionem peccatorum, Matth. XXVI, 28. Ideo habemus in ipso τὴν ἀπο- λύτρωσιν διὰ τῆς αἵματος αὐτοῦ, τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων, Ephes. I, 7. τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν, Coloss. cap. I, v. 14.

Notetur II. Emundationis principium, quod est Christus Jesus, quibus nominibus persona tota exprimitur, cui convenit hoc ἀποτέλεσμα se- cundum utramque naturam, quemadmodum omnes actiones officii. Fit autem peculiariter mentio divinæ naturæ, cum Filius Dei designatur, quod est concretum divinæ naturæ, nec sine causa: quia ratio ita exprimitur, cur nempe sanguis Christi nos emundet, aut unde vim emun- dandi à peccato habeat: quia sanguis est non puri hominis, sed unigeniti, proprie & naturalis Fi- lii Dei, qui ejusdem est cum Patre essentiæ ve- rus Deus, 1. Joh. V, 20. Nam Deus sanguine pro- prio acquisivit sibi Ecclesiam, Act. XX, 28. Deus ipse animam suam posuit pro nobis, 1. Joh. III. v. 15. Deus non pepercit Filio proprio, sed tradidit eum pro nobis, Rom. VIII, 32. Filium autem in carne manifestatum intelligit, qui carnis & sanguinis nostri particeps factus est, Ebr. II, 14. Sanguis ergo effusus pro peccatis nostris ipsiusmet Filii Dei proprius est, adeoque inde vim habet di- vinam mundandi nos à peccatis. Nam ob unio- nem hypostaticam tam proprius est æterno DEI Filio sanguis personaliter, quam proprius est Petro vel Paulo per naturam sanguis essentialiter. Sanguis puri hominis eam purificationem & ex- piationem præstare nunquam potuisset: Est enim hoc opus divinæ atque infinitæ virtutis, ideoque communicatam esse oportet sanguini Christi vir- tutem divinam & immensam, per quam iræ Dei placatio, infinitæ justitiæ divinæ satisfactio, & pro toto genere humano expiatio fieri potuerit. Non enim sanguis alterius alicujus hominis, in- quit Osiander, potuisset nos à peccatis mundare, & pro totius humani generis peccatis satisfacere. Sed sanguis Filii DEI hoc potuit: Ideoque Pau- lus dicit: DEUM SUO SANGUINE rede- misse Ecclesiam. Quare recte dixerunt veteres, una sanguinis Christi gutta potuisse totius mundi pec- cata expiari. Quando igitur nos peccata in con- scientia nostra gravant, hanc consolationem appre- hendamus, quod non alicujus puri hominis tantum, (qualis erat Adam ante lapsum) sanguis, sed Filii DEI sanguis pro nobis sit effusus. Jesuita Corne- lius à Lapide probat ipse, quod Clemens VI. Ex- travag. Unigenitus, de pænitentia & remiss. asserit, unam sanguinis Christi guttulam universum mun- dum redimere potuisse, quia erat sanguis Verbi per unionem hypostaticam. Et quod Gregor. Nazian- zenus ait: Nullum cum salutis meæ miraculo confe- rendum est, in quo exiguæ cruoris gutta universum orbem instaurarunt: notatque Estius hic pauci- simis verbis SANGUIS FILII DEI tres hæreses destrui: Manichæorum, qui veritatem hu- manæ naturæ Christo ademerunt: Ebionitarum, qui Christum Deum negarunt: Et Nestoriano- rum, qui personam in Christo diviserunt, quod etiam à Papistis & imprimis Jesuitis cum Calvi- nianis negata idiomatum communicatione fieri alibi docuimus.

III. Purificationis actus: Emundat nos ab omni peccato: In quo hæc quatuor notanda (1.)

Actus emundationis καθαρίζει, quod verbum sa- crificiale est in Veteri Testamento, & imprimis in Levitico frequenter occurrens: Usurpatur au- tem pro כִּפֶּר expiavit de expiatione altaris, Ex. XXIX, 25. Levit. VIII, 5. & pro כִּבֶּר itidem de ex- piatione altaris, Ex. XXXIX, 37. XXX, 10. pro טִהֵר mundavit de mundatione leprosi, Lev. VI, 2. seqq. aut aliorum immundorum, Num. VI. 9. de munda- tione Levitarum & Sacerdotum, Num. VIII. v. 15. Neh. XII, 30. filiorum Levi, Mal. III. v. 3. & im- primis de purificatione à peccatis, Psalm. LI. v. 3. Jer. XXXIII, 8. Ezech. XXXVI, 25. 33. pro קדש sanctificavit, expiavit, Job. I. v. 5. pro נקה absol- vit, Exod. XXXV. vers. 7. mundavit, Psalm. XIX. vers. 13. סלח condonavit, Numer. XXX. vers. 6. צדק justificavit, Dan. IIX. v. 14. ideoque τό καθα- ρίζειν infert talem expiationem, qua peccata co- ram Deo ita expiantur, ut eorundem condonatio & absolutio à peccatis ac justificatio nobis obtin- gat: Et quum peccata sint immunditia coram Deo, à peccatorum sordibus & immunditia purifica- mur, quod sit tum ratione meriti, qua nobis talis purificatio per sanguinem Christi pro nobis ef- fusum acquisita est & impetrata peccatorum re- missio, tum ratione efficaciæ & actus, qua illis, qui καθαρισμόν passione ac sanguine Christi acqui- situm fide sibi applicant, actualis peccatorum purgatio contingit, non physice per ablutionem, sed moraliter per non-imputationem, remissio- nem & condonationem, ut Paulus docuit Rom. IV. & alibi passim, imo Scriptura universa. Cor- nelius à Lapide monet, Deum non radere peccata, sed prorsus emundare, id est, expurgare & abolere, sicut macula è facie, lutum è veste, sordes è domo everruntur & emundantur. Sed utut donemus non radi peccata per Christi sanguinem, non ta- men admittendum, quod aboleantur, non enim actus physicus est, sed judicialis, cum DEUS justi- ficat impios non impietatem abstergendo vel ra- dendo, vel abolendo, aut quacunque ratione phy- sice tollendo, sed non imputando & condonando, ad- eoque à peccatis propter Christi expiationem in ara crucis factam nos absolvendo & contra inno- centiam Christi nobis imputando, Actor. X. vers. 43. Cap. XIII. v. 38. Rom. III. v. 25. Cap. IX. vers. 5. seqq. Porro distinguenda purificatio in articulo redemptionis, quæ est meritoria peccatorum no- strorum expiatio, Esa. LIII. & in articulo justifi- cationis, quæ fit apprehensione expiationis Christi meritoriæ, & remissione peccatorum nostrorum, Ephes. I. v. 7. Coloss. I. v. 14. & in articulo sanctifi- cationis; quæ fit cum à Spiritu Sancto renovan- te vetus homo exuitur & mortificatur, novusque induitur & creatur in nobis, nosque nova creatura in Christo sumus, & in novitate vitæ ambulamus, Ephes. IV, 24. Coloss. III, 10. 2. Corinth. V, 17. Gal. Cap. VI, 7. 15. Rom. VI, 4. Quæ confunduntur à Papistis, at accurate in Scripturis distinguuntur, quum aliud sit justificatio, aliud sanctificatio: Illa præcedat, hæc sequatur: Illa per remissionem pec- cati describatur, quam coram tribunali Dei virtu- te sanguinis & meriti Christi consequimur, ad- eoque ita sanguis Christi mundat nos à peccatis, cum propter Christi expiationem fide apprehen- sam à peccatis absolvimur & in gratiam recipimur. Peccata enim expiantur, non ut non insint, sed ut non imputentur. Hæc autem est, cum vires no- bis eæ donantur, ut relictis peccatis vitæ san- ctitati studeamus; ubi agnoscit Estius, nos non mundari per CHRISTI sanguinem simul & semel ab omni peccato (quia sanguinis Chri- sti merito hæc tribuenda est mundatio) ut di- cere quis possit, peccatum non habeo, vel mun- dum est cor meum, purus sum à peccato, Prov. Cap. XX. vers. 6. Sed mundari nos indies, ita ta- men, ut nunquam, dum hic vivimus, simus ab omni peccato prorsus emundati. Igitur ista mun- datio ab omni peccato consistit, ut Scholastici lo- quuntur, in fieri, non in facto esse, sitque actu incompleto, non autem completo, nisi in fine, ut hic habet Estius. De qua purificatione 1. Joh. III. vers. 3. omnis, qui spem istam habet, ἁγνίζει

ἑαυτὸν purificat seipsum, sicut ipse purus est, & Apoc. Cap. XXII. vers. 11. ὁ ἅγιος ἁγιασθήτω ἔτι, qui sanctus est, sanctificetur adhuc. Affert Cornelius a Lapide Concilium Triden- tinum Sess. VI. cap. 7. neminem esse justum, nisi cui merita passionis Domini nostri JESU CHRISTI communicantur, id tamen in impii justificatione fieri, dum ejusdem sanctissimae passionis merito per Spiritum Sanctum charitas DEI diffunditur in cordibus eorum, qui justificantur, atque ipsis inhaeret. Sed si justificatur impius, non ergo is, qui justificatur, praeditus est charitate erga DEUM, qua justificatur. Bona enim opera, ad quae charitas erga DEUM pertinet, se- quuntur justificatum, non antecedunt justifi- candum. Neque enim propria justitia vel obe- dientia, aut charitate justificamur, sed per u- nius justi obedientiam justi constituimur omnes quotquot justificamur, Rom. Cap. V. vers. 19. Illa vero charitas, de qua vers. 5. non est qualitas in nobis inhaerens, sed gratia Dei & affectus mi- sericordiae in Deo erga nos. Et quid opus san- guinis Christi purificatione, ac meritorum pas- sionis Domini communicatione, si charitate er- ga Deum vel obedientia legis propria justifica- mur. Si per legem justitia, Christus gratis mor- tuus est, Gal. Cap. II. vers. 21. Evacuati estis a Chri- sto, qui in lege justificamini, Galat. Cap. V. vers. 4. Quomodo concurrat ad justificationem passio Christi, sic explicat Thomas part. III. q. 48. a. 6. Ad tertium dicendum, quod passio Christi secundum quod comparatur ad divinitatem ejus agit per modum efficientiae; in quantum vero comparatur ad vo- luntatem animae Christi agit per modum meriti. Secundum vero quod consideratur in ipsa carne Christi agit per modum satisfactionis, in quantum per eam liberamur a reatu poenae. Per modum vero redemptionis, in quantum per eam libera- mur a servitute culpae: Per modum autem sacri- ficii, in quantum per eam reconciliamur DEO. Ita nihil relinquitur charitati nostrae erga Deum, si & meritum & satisfactio & reconciliatio DEI, & remissio peccati vel liberatio a reatu poenae, & liberatio a servitute culpae tribuenda sanguini & passioni Christi. Idem q. 49. §. ad tertium. Christus sua passione nos a peccatis liberavit cau- saliter, id est, instituens causam nostrae libera- tionis, ex qua possent quaecunque peccata quan- docunque remitti, vel praeterita, vel praesentia, vel futura, sicut si Medicus faciat medicinam, ex qua possint quicunque morbi sanari etiam in futurum. Et art. III. Respondeo per passionem Christi liberamur a reatu poenae dupliciter, uno modo directe, in quantum scilicet passio Christi fuit sufficiens, & superabundans satisfactio pro peccatis totius generis humani; exhibita autem satisfactione sufficienter tollitur reatus poenae. Alio modo indirecte, in quantum scilicet passio Christi est causa remissionis peccati, in quo fundatur reatus poenae. Et art. IV. Respondeo: Passio CHRISTI causa est reconciliationis nostrae ad Deum duplici- ter: Uno modo, in quantum removit peccatum, per quod homines constituuntur inimici DEI secun- dum Sap. XIV. Similiter odio sunt DEO iniquus & impietas ejus, & in Psalm. V. Odisti omnes, qui operantur iniquitatem: Alio modo in quantum est sacrificium Deo acceptissimum. Est enim hic pro- prii sacrificii effectus, ut per ipsum placetur DEUS, sicut cum homo offensam in se commissam remittit propter aliquod obsequium acceptum, unde dicitur 1. Reg. XVI. Si Dominus incitat te adversum me, odoretur sacrificium; & similiter tantum bonum fuit, quod Christus voluntarie passus est, quod pro- pter hoc bonum in natura humana inventum Deus placatus est super omni offensa generis humani, quantum ad eos, qui Christo passo conjunguntur. Quam Thomæ sententiam sequitur & explicat Cardinalis Contarenus de justif. oper. p. 542. Di- cit B. Thomas, cum loquitur de baptismi sacra- mento, quod eo abluuntur omnia peccata, & omnis reatus culpæ & pœnæ cujuscunque, & reddit ra- tionem eo, quod unusquisque baptizatur in mortem Christi, & cum eo sepelitur, ut inquit Apostolus. Id- circo se ita habet baptizatus ac si ipse gerens perso- nam Christi mortuus fuisset, passus & consepultus cum Christo, & cum Christo resurrexisset in novam vitam. Ecce quam præclare dicit doctissimus pa- riter ac sanctissimus Vir, mortem Christi passionem & meritum nobis donari, nobis imputari in ba- ptismate, quod est fidei sacramentum, non quod no- bis inhæreant, qui jam vivimus, sed quia nobis do- nantur & imputantur. Neque abnuunt omnino alii è Pontificiis, qui fatente Vasquezio in l. 2. disp. 204. c. 1. eo abeunt: Nihil nobis inesse sive habi- tum, sive operationem, quod suapte natura possit justificare animam, & à peccatis eam purgare: Sed ad hoc necessario nos indigere favore DEI ac- ceptantis illud ac condonantis aut remittentis pec- catum, quo quidem favore, accedente justitia inhærenti & intrinseca nobis nostra justificatio compleatur. Quales sunt, qui ibidem 1. affir- mant, qualitatem justitiæ seu gratiæ inhærentis, qua justificamur, suapte natura non pugnare cum peccato, imo cum eo esse posse, & solum ex Dei con- stitutione & voluntate nunquam esse simul cum eo. Id quod docuerunt Richardus in 3. distinct. 31. a. 1. quæst. 1. in tertio modo opinandi, quem putat esse probabiliorem, Sotus in 4. distinct. 14. quæst. 1. art. 2. post quintam conclusionem, Occam in 4. quæst. 3. litera E. Et Johannes Medina codice de pœnitentia quæst. 12. corollarie sequitur. Nam si il- lud, quod nobis inhæret, ex se non pugnat cum peccato, sed ex sola DEI constitutione consequi- tur aperte, illud ex se non emundare à peccato, sed accedente DEI favore & condonatione peccatum remitti, atque ita nostram justificationem favore illo compleri. 2. Qui censent gratiam expelli à peccato, vel contra expelli peccatum à gratia so- lum demeritorie non autem physice & ex natura rei. Quam opinionem indicavit Bonaventura in 1. dist. 17. secunda parte distinctionis, quæst. 3. & in 3. distinctionis 31. art. 1. quæst. 1. ad 2. Aperte tamen secutus est Richardus loco allegato. Sco- tus in 2. dist. 37. quæst. 1. Ad solutionem istorum in solutione cujusdam argumenti. Durandus in 1. dist. 17. q. 10. n. 4. & in 3. dist. 31. q. 1. num. 6. Palu- danus in 3. dist. 28. q. 3. art. 3. Conradus supr. quæst. 71. art. 4. (qui duo in hunc sensum interpretantur mentem S. Thomæ.) Et Gabriel in 1. distinct. 17. q. 4. art. 3. dub. 3. conclus. 3. & in 3. distinct. 23. q. 2. Paludanus in 3. dist. art. 3. dub. 2. quos allegavimus disp. 91. art. 1. Nam qui asserunt, gratiam ex- pelli à peccato solum demeritorie, & similiter peccatum à gratia asserere debent, gratiam & peccatum ex natura rei posse simul esse, ac pro- inde ad peccati remissionem necessariam esse DEI condonationem remittens peccata. 3. Qui eo- dem modo de justitia nostra inhærente, sicut de moneta & valore ejus philosophantur, compa- rant enim metallo, ex quo conflatur moneta, habitum & qualitatem nobis inhærentem, & rationem gratiæ seu justitiæ, ob quam DEO place- mus, comparant valori, quem Rex lege & volunta- te sua monetæ imponit, quod aliqui recentiores vocant quid morale in moneta, & inconsulera- tum sine Regis æstimatione non habet valorem mo- netæ: sic etiam qualitas illa sit solum entitas quæ- dam realis, quæ suapte natura non sit ita grata, & justitia, ut non possit Deo ut justitia & gratia non placere, & reddere homines Deo charos & ac- ceptos: at vero, quemadmodum moneta acce- dente æstimatione Regis habet jam suum valorem nulla in ipsa facta mutatione metalli: Sic etiam & qualitas illa nobis inhærens accedente æstima- tione & amore atque favore DEI habeat jam ra- tionem gratiæ justificantis & emundantis nos à pec- cato. Hic modus philosophandi fuit Nomina- lium, Occam enim in 1. d. 17. q. 1. impugnat sen- tentiam eorum, qui dicunt, inhærentem justitiam esse qualitatem, quæ suapte natura non possit DEO non placere, & non possit non reddere hominem ju- stum, & à peccato ipsum purgare. Consentiunt etiam Gregorius in 1. d. 7. q. a. 2. in probationibus secundæ conclusionis, & in solutione 3. §. contra il- lam. Gabriel q. 1. a. 1. notabil. 1. & a. 3. dub. 4. coroll. 1. ad 1. & 2. & Petrus Alliacensis in 1. q. 9. a. 2. litera O. Quibus ex schola B. Thomæ con- senserunt Franciscus Victoria & Canus, ut passim fertur, aliique recentiores Thomistæ, quos sæpius in disputationibus ita docentes audivi. Hæc Va- squezius ipse l. c. Qui porro disp. 222. c. 2. n. 14. ita de hisce habet: Lutherani affirmant non ju- stificari nos ea renovatione tanquam forma, sed ipsamet justitiam DEI aut Christi, qua ipse san- Etus est, esse nobis imputatam; asserunt etiam, nos non esse vere justos, sed tantum reputari, & peccata nostra non deleri & eradicari, sed per non-imputationem & condonationem tegi & radi, quia ad pœnam nobis non imputantur. Hoc ipsum genus imputationis & applicationis meritorum CHRISTI fateri debent, quotquot ex Catholicis asserunt, justitiam nobis inhærentem nos DEO reddere gratos, non suapte natura, sed ex DEI favore & acceptatione, nempe quia DEUS nos vult diligere, habentes talem formam, quos posset non diligere. Hanc autem imputationem & applicationem ipsos fateri necesse est ad hoc, ut nos justi reddamur. Similiter & illi, qui cen- sent, qualitatem nobis inhærentem esse quidem veram sanctitatem & justitiam, tamen suapte na- tura non purgare nos à peccatis, nisi accedente nova voluntate & favore DEI condonantis pecca- tum, velint nolint, coguntur concedere novam im- putationem meritorum Christi post infusionem gratiæ habitualis ad remittenda & condonanda peccata. Nam ubi favor Dei peculiaris ac distin- Etus à cæteris nobis accedit, è meritis Christi pro- venit nobis, ac proinde applicationem & imputatio- nem meritorum Christi peculiarem & distinctam à cæteris tunc fieri oportet.

2. Notetur actus continuitas. Non præter causam præsenti utitur Apostolus καθαρίζει, sed continuitatem designat, non enim ait, purifica- vit, quum non de justificatione in ara cru- cis facta, sed de ejusdem applicatione loquatur. Illa enim jam facta est, de qua Ebr. I, 3. ὅς δι᾽ ἑαυτῇ καθαρισμὸν ποιησάμενος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν, qui postquam per semetipsum purgationem FECIT peccatorum nostrorum, consedit ad dextram Majesta- tis. Mundavit quidem nos in baptismo, 1. Cor. Cap. VI. v. 11. Actor. XXII. v. 16. Sed non definit mundare; quia subinde immunditiam peccando contrahimus, quæ fide emundanda, adeoque san- guine Christi, quem apprehendit fides, purifican- da est. Quomodo Hieronymus l. II. contr. Pelag. Quod, inquit, scriptum est, & sanguis Jesu Filii ejus emundat nos ab omni peccato tam in confeffione ba- ptismatis, quam in clementia pœnitudinis accipien- dum est.

3. Purificationis subjectum: Emundat nos, in- quit Apostolus, hoc est, fideles, quos juxta se- cum comprehendit, eos nempe, qui communio- nem habent cum Deo, quæ nulla est sine fide, Ebr. cap. XI, 6. eos, qui non in tenebris ambulant, sed in luce, qui lucem veram per fidem apprehendunt, de qua Johannes: Et lux in tenebris lucet, & te- nebræ non apprehenderunt eam cap. I, 5. Quot- quot vero ipsum Verbum Dei, lucem illam veram apprehenderunt, illis dedit potestatem filios Dei fieri, qui credunt in nomen ipsius, v. 12. Ideo fides dicitur purificare corda, Actor. XV, 9. per ῥαντισμὸν ἅιματος, aspersionem sanguinis Chri- sti, 1. Petr. II, 2.

4. Objectum, quod sunt peccata. Purificat nos ab omni peccato. Universaliter loquitur ἀπὸ πάσης ἁμαρτίας, AB OMNI PECCATO, ut nullum peccatum qualecunque & quantum- cunque illud sit, excipere liceat, quin ab eo pu- rificemur per Christi sanguinem. Mundat er- go non tantum à peccato actuali, sed etiam ori- ginali, non tantum à peccato veniali, sed etiam à mortali.

Quod ad Grotii glossam: Sanguis Christi Filii Dei emundat nos ab omni peccato, qui talis est, hoc est, communionem habet cum Deo, ostendit se vere repurganum Christi sanguine, id est, fide ea, quam in nobis operatur Christi passio; aliena illa est non uno modo. Nam nec de eo, quo ostendatur communio cum Patre vel figno ejus- dem sermo est: neque emundatio à peccato est signum communionis istius. Adhæc si metony- mice accipiendum emundandi Verbum, sanguis emundari dicetur, quod ostendat, nos emundatos esse. Quid vero hoc rei est? Sed fortassis id vult Grotius, quod qui pure vivit vel secundum præcepta Christi, ostendat se vere repurganum esse Christi sanguine. Quomodo vero hoc convenit præsenti aphorismo? Annon ita & subjectum & prædicatum mutatur. Subjectum enim non est is, qui pure vivit, sed sanguis Jesu Christi, Filii DEI; prædicatum non est ostendit se esse repurganum, sed emundat nos ab omni peccato. Et quænam illa explicatio, sanguine Christi, id est, fide ea, quam in nobis operatur Christi passio? Num sanguis Christi est fides? Aut num hic de fide agitur, & non potius de objecto fidei, quæ fer- tur in sanguinem vel passionem Christi? Neque vero in istis locis Rom. III. vers. 25. cap. V. vers. 9. Eph. I. v. 7. Col. I. v. 14. Ebr. cap. IX. v. 14. cap. X. vers. 19. per sanguinem Christi fides intelligitur, vel etiam passio Christi fidem operari dicitur, sed Rom. cap. III. vers. 25. fides à sanguine Christi distinguitur, & in sanguinem Christi ferre dicitur, ceu in proprium objectum: ἡ πίστις ἐν τῷ ἀυτῦ αἵ- ματι est fides, quæ collocatur in Christi sangui- nem, eoque nititur; Coloss. I. v. 14. conf. Rom. IV. v. 24. 25. neque de fide intelligendum, cum Eph. cap. I, v. 7. habere dicimur τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τῦ ἅιματος ἀυτῦ. Nam ibi sanguis proprie de- signatur ceu pretium ἀπολυτρώσεως, vel per quod redempti sumus, non fides per sanguinem nota- tur; quæ si hic quærenda, potius in verbis ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν quærenda. Nam habemus remissionem peccatorum per fidem, vel in ipso per fidem ap- prehenso, quatenus per fidem apprehendimus redemptionem per sanguinem ejus factam. Nec vero Grotius ipse locis illis per sanguinem Chri- sti intellexit fidem, ut Roman. cap. III. vers. 25. ad verba διὰ τῆς πίσεως, ostendit, inquit, quomodo quis- que effectum illius bonitatis, id est, justitiam ve- ram posset assequi, nempe fidem habendo san- guini Christi, Eph. I, 7. διὰ τῦ ἅιματος explicat per vitam Christi impensam nobis ceu λύτρον, Ebr. IX, 14. τὸ ἅιμα Χρισῦ ipsomet etiam Grotio interprete non fidem, sed, quod litera sonat, sanguinem Christi notat: Quanto Christi Filii Dei & innocentis sanguis præstat sanguini ca- rentium ratione animantium, tanto purgatio de- bet esse major, Ebr. X, 19. Metonymicum quidem sensum fingit vocis ἅιματος; sed nulla explicatio- nis Metonymicæ causa est. Nam in sanguine, vel per sanguinem Christi ceu causam meritoriam ha- bemus παῤῥησίαν ad ingressum in sanctum sancto- rum. Neque hoc in loco ulla est necessitas tropicæ loquutionis, quia sanguine Christi purificamur ceu causa meritoria, adeoque collatio cum Act. XV, 9. aliena est: Nam ibi non de causa meritoria, sed instrumentali, fide, agitur: Meritoria vero una cum principali, gratia scilicet, comprehen- ditur vers. 11. διὰ τῆς χάριτος Ἰησῦ Χρισῦ πισεύο- μεν σωθῆναι, ubi fides aperte à Christo ejusque merito, quod apprehendit ad salutem, distin- guitur.

Porro non tantum in voce sanguinis; sed in voce καθαρίσει etiam sensum Metonymicum citra causam fingit cum Socino Grotius, quem vero ipse solide profligaverat defens. fid. Ca- thol. de Satisfact. cap. 7. pag. 237. Neque 1. Joh. cap. I. vers. 7. exponere licet, mundos nos esse. Re- pugnat enim manifeste & verborum proprietas, & perpetuus Scripturæ usus in hoc argumento. Im- munditiæ nomine significari passim reatum fatetur Socinus. Hinc καθαρίζειν & ἁγιάζειν est eum reatum tollere, sive efficere remissionem, ut ipse Scriptor ad Ebræos exponit vocem καθαρίζειν c. IX. v. 22. Christus per seipsum fecit hunc καθαρισμὸν, Ebr. I, 3. Christus καθαρίζει conscientiam ab operi- bus mortuis, Ebr. cap. IX. v. 14. hoc est, ipso Socino Interprete, à reatu & pœna pœnæque timore con- scientiam liberat. In Veteri quoque Testamento Kipper eundem habet sensum, Psalm. LI. vers. 9. Quod autem his in locis est καθαρίζειν, hoc ipsum simili ratione dicitur ῥαντίζειν, X, 22. & λούειν lavare v. eodem, quo respicit etiam vaticinium Zachar. cap. XIII, 1. Cur ab hoc sensu discedatur, ratio plane nulla est. Imo addit Grotius: Omnino absurdum est, καθαρίζειν de declaratione mundationis, non de ipsa mundatione interpretari, cum paulo post jun- gantur ἀφιέναι καὶ καθαρίζειν v. 9. Argumentatur Apostolus à conjunctis: Si in luce ambuletis, habe- tis mundationem, hoc est, remissionem per Christi sanguinem: quia nemini in luce ambulanti imputan- tur peccata. Hæc ibi Grotius satis solide, sua ipsius annotata refellens.

Etiam Grotio in hoc loco magis sanus est Schlichtingius Socinista, hunc reddens Aphoristi sensum; q. d. Et quicquid unquam peccavimus, hoc nobis non obstabit ad communionem cum Deo, dum- modo ambulemus in luce: Sanguis enim Jesu Christi Filii Dei emundat nos ab omni peccato, nullo excepto, etsi maximum & gravissimum fuerit. Sanguis Filii Dei longe efficacior est ad nos purificandos, quam ul- lum peccatum ad nos contaminandos & condemnan- dos. Alluditur hic ad sanguinem victimarum, quæ typus erant Christi, simulque earum sanguini Christi sanguis opponitur. Nam sanguis victimarum non habebat vim purgandi omne peccatum, solas tantum ignorantias & infirmitates purgabat, ut legere est in lege. (in quo falli Schlichtingium alias docuimus)

At Filii Dei sanguis omne peccatum purgat. Nam & pro omnibus omnium peccatis ex Dei voluntate & mandato fusus est. Ideoque Deum movet, & penitus obstringit, ut omnibus in Christum creden- tibus, & in luce ambulantibus peccata condonet, & eorum reatu ac pœna solvat: tanto magis, quod hac Christi obedientia, qua se victimam dedit pro mundi peccatis, & se demisit ad mortem, eamque crucis, DEO fuerit omnium gratissima. Unde etiam Christus dicitur se tradidisse pro nobis victimam & oblationem DEO in odorem suavitatis, Eph. V. vers. 2. Ita igitur Christi sanguis non tantum pecca- ta nostra emundat, sed etiam emundata esse ostendit, tanquam certissimum pignus remissionis peccatorum nobis a Deo datum.

Quæ vero attexit hic Schlichtingius, pro hæ- resi sua adstruenda haud ægre expediuntur. Notandum vero, quod sanguis JESU CHRISTI Filii DEI mundet nos ab omni peccato, non sim- pliciter, sed cum conditione, si in luce ambula- mus. Ex qua conditione apparet, sanguinem Je- su Filii DEI non esse fusum, ut peccata seu debita nostra proprie loquendo Deo exsolveret, sed ut ea Deus ex decreto voluntatis suæ condonaret nobis & remitteret. Nam si prius illud verum esset, nulla conditio a nobis posset requiri. Quando enim creditor debitum suum plenissime recipit, nullum amplius debiti a debitore exigendi jus ha- bet. Unde & redemptio, quæ facta est in Christo JESU, dicitur remissio transgressionum, Col. cap. I. vers. 14. Eph. I. vers. 7. Hæc Schlichtingius.

Ad quæ respondemus 1. Conditio illa, si in luce am- bulamus, cohæret cum communione nostri cum Deo, non vero conditionatam reddit expiatio- nem peccatorum, quæ fit per sanguinem Chri- sti. 2. Particula καὶ potest sensu causali acci- pi. Communionem illos habere cum Deo, qui in luce ambulant. Sanguis enim DEI emunda- vit ipsos ab omni peccato. 3. Conditio illa non est legalis, sed Evangelica. In luce enim am- bulare est, veram lucem, quæ Christus est, am- plecti, vel lucem veritatis Evangelicæ per fidem suscipere, & in eadem permanere, sicut 2. Joh. v. 4. ambulare in veritate, interprete Schlichtin- gio est veritati deditum esse. 4. Non agitur hic de expiatione in ara crucis facta, sed de remissione peccatorum, quæ est purificatio in peccatis, & applicatio expiationis istius, quæ fit per fidem. 5. Non tribuitur hic nostræ sanctitati purificatio a peccatis, sed sanguini Christi; neque sanctitas no- stra causa est vel conditio præstans, vel præro- gativa, ut sanguis Christi nos a peccatis mundet. Non enim dependet efficacia sanguinis Christi mundatoria a nostra sanctitate, sed ab intrinseco valore satisfactionis & expiationis peccatorum a Christo factæ. 6. Si ergo maxime in luce am- bulare esset sanctitati deditum esse, non posset sanctitatis studium causa vel conditio statui sive expiationis peccatorum in ara crucis factæ; quia δι᾽ ἑαυτῦ PER SEMETIPSUM unice fecit Christus καθαρισμὸν, Ebr. I, 3. sive purificationis actualis conscientiæ nostræ, quæ non fit, nisi vir- tute purificationis per sanguinem Christi factæ, Ebr. IX, 14. 15. 7. Quapropter hæc conditio, quam Schlichtingius facit, non trahenda ad καθα- ρισμὸν sanguinis Christi, qui a conditione no- stræ sanctitatis nulla ratione dependet. Sed admit- tendus potius foret ex pacto significationis vel in- dicii sensus, hoc modo: Si justitiæ & sanctitati simus dediti, indicio id fore atq; argumento, nos comunio- nem habere cum Deo, & sanguinem Filii Dei nos emundare a peccato. Quem sensum Metonymicum si Grotius intenderet, hactenus admitteremus. 8. Descriptio, & requisitum subjecti, quod communio- nem habet cum Deo, hic exhibetur, quod nempe illud purificatum sit a peccato per sanguinem Christi, non vero purificatio ista, aut res καθαριστι- κὴ suspenditur ab ambulatione in luce, nedum a stu- dio sanctitatis. 9. Observandus est modus loquen- di Apostolicus, quia delectatur Johannes tali λέ- ξει: Ἐὰν εἴπωμεν, ἐὰν περιπατῶμεν, ἐὰν ὁμολογῶ- μεν, quæ tamen non conditionem proprie cohæ- rentiæ prædicati cum subjecto, sed potius requisi- tum & determinationem subjecti inferunt ex men- te Apostoli: Qui dixerit, qui ambulavit, qui confes- sus fuerit: vel ad argumentum a posteriori potius, quam ad conditionem a priori spectant, quemad- modum explicatio talium habetur cap. 2. vers. 3. καὶ ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν, ὅτι ἐγνώκαμεν αὐτὸν, ἐὰν τὰς αὐτοῦ τηρῶμεν ἐντολάς. Et vers. 4. ὁ λέγων &c. 10. Quanquam vero fidem requiramus ad actua- lem purificationem a peccatis, non tamen ut san- guis Christi inde aliquam vim consequatur ad nos mundandos, aut fides nostra cooperetur ad purifi- cationem, quæ ex asse, non semissi sanguini Christi, ut causæ unicæ & solitariæ, non ut concausæ con- venit. Sed quod fides nostra apprehendat tantum, suamque faciat purificationem & condonationem peccatorum, quæ a Christo facta est per sanguinem ejus, quod alias contra Arminianos exposuimus. Habet sese potius παθητικῶς recipiendo, quam ἐνεργητικῶς cooperando. 11. Ejusmodi ergo condi- tione requisita non evacuatur vis sanguinis Chri- sti, quasi ideo credendus sit non effusus, ut peccata seu debita nostra proprie loquendo Deo exsolve- ret, sed pro iis satisfaceret; sed firmatur potius illa sanguinis Christi vis, quia per fidem nobis applica- ri & a nobis apprehendi non posset satisfactio, ni- si pro nobis eadem præstita foret. 12. Vana et- iam est oppositio finium istorum, effusionis sangui- nis Christi, ut pro nobis satisfaceret, vel solutio præ- staretur Divinæ justitiæ pro peccatis nostris, & ut Deus peccata nostra ex decreto voluntatis suæ nobis remitteret: nam satisfactio non tollit remissio- nem: Sed præstita est pro nobis a Christo, ut no- bis remitti possent debita nostra. 13. Quod er- go dicitur, si præstita est pro nobis a Christo satis- factio, nulla a nobis potest requiri conditio, id ad- mittimus de conditione legali. Quando creditor debitum suum plenissime recipit, nullum amplius debiti a debitore exigendi jus habet. Nec exigit Deus a nobis debitum, sed id nobis gratiose con- donat propter satisfactionem pro nobis præsti- tam. Per fidem non solvimus Deo quicquam, sed λύτρον a Christo solutum recipimus, Deoque sisti- mus. 14. Redemptio itaque, quæ facta est per sanguinem Christi pretium dicitur remissio pec- catorum & transgressionium, qua eadem habetur a nobis, vel nostra facta est per fidem, qua recipi- mus λύτρον in Verbo Dei nobis oblatum, eatenus enim obtingit nobis remissio peccatorum, quam peperit nobis Christus sanguinis sui λύτρῳ pretio- sissimo; nos vero ἔχομεν ἐν ἀυτῷ habemus in Chri- sto illam ἀπολύτρωσιν per fidem, eaque ratione habemus ipsam remissionem. Nam in ἀπολυτρώ- σει est remissionis acquisitio in receptione vel ap- prehensione ἀπολυτρώσεως habemus ipsam etiam ἄφεσιν vel remissionem peccatorum.

## 1:8
Vers. 8.

If we say that we have no sin) That is, as he soon explains, that we have not sinned. If we think that we had no need of Christ and his knowledge in order to be purged from sins. For otherwise, after the knowledge of the Gospel, some could have been without sin, so that the word sin is taken here, not to signify mere ignorances or sudden impulses, but those evil acts which have a drawing and do not forestall deliberation. To have sin is not now to be in sin, but to be able to be made guilty on account of sins, as appears in John 9:41, chapter 15:22, 24. In a similar sense in James 4:17, sin is to him. But understand 'to be able to be made guilty' here, if God had wished and were to wish to use his supreme right.

We deceive ourselves) We impose upon ourselves, to our greatest harm. That this is true appears in Rom. 5:6, 8. Philo in the book On the Giants: For if God should wish to judge the mortal without mercy, he will bring the condemning [sentence], since no man has run the life from birth until death blameless of himself. But [he has used] the one with voluntary, the other with involuntary [acts]...

And the truth is not in us) There is no pursuit of truth in us. In the Manuscript: Truth is not in us.

He teaches the necessity not only of cleansing, which we all need, because there is no one who does not have sin, but also of confession, lest anyone presume, or even boast, that he does not have sin, and as he previously comforted the humble, lest they despair in their sins; since the blood of the Son of God cleanses us from all sin; so now he rebukes the proud, who exalt themselves, as if they did not have sin, but were immune from all sin. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. Schlichtingius connects these to the preceding thus: On this occasion of our purification through Christ's blood, he refutes those who thought that they could be saved by their own works. Therefore, that they had no need of faith in Jesus Christ the Son of God; such were many of the Jews, against whom Paul also argues primarily in the epistle to the Romans and to the Galatians. The connection is not bad, provided the sense were good.

Moreover, Grotius's misinterpretation is evident: 1. from the arbitrary change of tenses: 'That we have no sin,' says John; Grotius perverts it to 'that we have sinned.' The text refers to sin of any kind; Grotius takes it as referring to more serious sin. The text speaks of the reborn and the faithful, for the Apostle professes this of himself and other believers: 'If we say'; Grotius speaks of the non-reborn, who had sin before the knowledge of the Gospel. The text sets before all the necessity of confessing, and therefore implies that even the reborn are not devoid of sin, and ought to confess their sins, and stand in need of their purification and remission. Grotius imagines that some can be without sin, which openly contradicts Holy Scripture, 1 Kings 8:46, 2 Chronicles 6:36, Job 9:3, Proverbs 20:9, Ecclesiastes 7:20, Romans 3:23, James 3:2. The words of St. John are clear regarding guilt and sin. Grotius, on the contrary, perverts these, noting not guilt but only liability to punishment: The literal sense of this saying implies actually having sin; the Gloss of Grotius interprets it not as the actual existence of sin, but as the possibility of being made liable for sin; and he wishes this to be understood even hypothetically, namely, if God had wished and were to wish to use his supreme right. He learned this subtlety from the Socinians, among whom Schlichtingius on this passage says: 'If we say,' that is, as some do, 'that we have no sin,' that is, 'we have not sinned,' as he speaks in verse 10, 'we are not held by the liability of any sin,' 'we deceive ourselves,' we imbue our mind with a false opinion, which will turn to our destruction. It is no wonder regarding the Socinians if they deny that we have sin after regeneration, because they do not believe in original sin, which the reborn never lay aside; but it is a wonder that Grotius denies it, unless perhaps in this he also pelagianizes with Socinus. And indeed, not only acts of mere ignorance or sudden impulse, but also sometimes evil acts, which involve deliberation and intent, do not fail to fall upon those who are reborn, as is shown by the example of Aaron, David, Peter, Thomas, and others in the Holy Scriptures: and therefore they can not only be made liable if God should wish to use his supreme right; but they are also actually guilty, according to the ordinary law of God, as long as they do not repent, they are men of death, 2 Sam. 12:7.

And therefore Estius rightly acknowledges that we have sin in various ways (1) on account of the affection of sin, insofar as no one is found in this age who is fully purged of every inordinate and vicious affection. Whence Augustine in his commentary on Psalm 118, conc. 10, says: We ought to understand, he says, however much anyone may progress in the justifications of the Lord, that he has the affection of mortal flesh regarding these earthly things, and in which human life is a temptation upon the earth. Thus also Leo the Great, sermon 7 on the Epiphany of the Lord: Who will be found so immune from guilt that justice does not have something in him to argue against? And sermon 6 for Lent: Such is the condition even of those who resist concupiscences, that they can never not find in their hearts what they disapprove of. And the sentence of Job 14 is general: No one is clean from filth.

2. On account of the guilt of sin, because during this life we are never free from all guilt. For there is always that for which we ought to say to God: Forgive us our debts. For if our affection is never fully purged in this life, therefore some guilt always remains even in a man recently baptized. Which, however, we do not admit in the Papistic sense, as if with the guilt remitted some guilt of punishment remains, but that that sin which is 'easily besetting' never rests; but always breaks forth in inordinate motions, which make us guilty and command even any saints to seek the remission of sins, and also to pray, 'Deliver me from hidden things, O Lord'; the Lord wished to show, says St. Augustine, book 21 of the City of God, ch. 27, however justly we may live in the darkness and infirmity of this life, that sins are not lacking to us, for the forgiveness of which we ought to pray. Leo, sermon 7 on the Epiphany. Lord, teaches that no one is immune from guilt, so that the mercy of God may have something in him to remit.

3. On account of the frequent and daily, and in a way continuous, act of sin. Which mode Jerome, Augustine, and other Fathers who wrote against Pelagius attended to. Whose doctrine it was that a just man could live without sin, and that there were many who had lived without sin.

4. On account of the sin in which we were born, or which we have since actually committed, on account of which we have need of Christ as propitiator and Advocate. According to which mode the sentence of John is referred to past sins, although remitted and blotted out, so that the sense is: If anyone should say that he has not sinned, nor ever been in sin, and therefore has no need of Christ as Patron, etc. In which mode, however, we desire this, that the sin in which we are born, or original sin, be distinguished from others, and that it be said ambiguously that it is blotted out. For it is indeed remitted and restrained, so that it does not dominate in the reborn, but it is never blotted out and extirpated unless when life itself is extinguished. Which sense, however, he confesses is not sufficient: Because the Apostle still demands the confession of sins, and proposes the hope of pardon from the promise of God, saying: If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to remit our sins. He speaks, therefore, of sins still to be remitted. And he certainly writes to the faithful, to whom original sin and grave actual sins had been forgiven by baptism. He wishes, therefore, that they still confess their daily offenses, just as also James the Apostle, who, when he had said in chapter 3, 'In many things we all offend,' afterwards in chapter 5 exhorts to the confession of offenses, saying: Confess your sins to one another.

Wherefore he observes that the third mode is especially to be regarded, and from the Council of Milevis, canon 6, 7.

VIII. Estius proves this, and to that end cites the confessions of the Saints, by which they humbly acknowledge this frequency of sinning in themselves: As Jerome to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem: We all sin daily, and in something we slip. Ambrose, book IV on the Sacraments, ch. 6: I who always sin, ought always to have medicine. And in the apology of David: How many things does each one of us commit every single hour. Augustine in his exposition of Psalm 128: If men truly beat their breasts, they are sinners. And who among us does not beat his breast? Gregory, book IV, epistle 31 to the Emperor Maurice: And because I sin incessantly every day against almighty God, I am struck by incessant blows every day. Bernard, epistle 24, at the end: I ask that you pray for me instantly, because I sin incessantly. John Gerson in his treatise on the statute of the Carthusians: We scarcely do anything where we cannot reasonably fear a venial sin. Add what Gennadius has in his book on Ecclesiastical Dogmas, canon 86: All truly assert themselves to be sinners, because in truth they have something to lament, if not by the reproach of conscience, certainly by the mobility and mutability of a treacherous nature. From which Estius teaches that the cavil of Pelagius is clearly refuted, by which he said that the saints confessed themselves to be sinners for the sake of humility, although in reality they had no sin. For John does not say: If we say that we have no sin, we exalt ourselves, and humility is not in us. Whence the Council of Milevis rightly condemns that sense of Pelagius with anathema, canon 6. Therefore also the Beghards and Beguines, and fanatics, who boasted that they could ascend to such perfection that they become impeccable, are rightly condemned. Cornelius a Lapide notes that Durandus in 2, d. 28, q. 3 does not depart far from these, who thinks that all deliberate venial sins can be avoided, but not all indeliberate ones, which happen by surprise.

Estius observes that the opinion of certain people is also refuted in this way, among whom is Clement of Alexandria, book VI of the Stromata, who think that the Apostles, after the resurrection of the Lord and having received the Holy Spirit, were so confirmed in the grace of God that they were henceforth subject to no sins and passions. It is refuted, I say, because it is the Apostle who says, if we say, etc., certainly including himself, just as in the preceding and following verses. So also James the Apostle: In many things we all offend. So Paul concerning Peter, the Prince of the Apostles, Galatians 2: That he was reprehensible. There exist open testimonies on this matter in Jerome, Augustine, Prosper, and other Fathers, which we omit for the sake of brevity. Which things are correct: And since he pronounces this universally concerning all whom the blood of Christ cleanses, not even Mary is to be excepted, whom Cornelius wishes to be excepted here. For she also needed Christ the Redeemer, and the purification of his blood. But what Estius adds: That these are very different, to have sin, and to sin in the present act, therefore it is by no means a consequence that if we always have sin, we always and in every work sin, which error the Council of Trent condemns, session 6, ch. 25, in this he perverts our opinion, whom the non-Catholic Papist iniquitously calls heretics, and wickedly approves the wicked anathema of the Papistic conventicle. For we do not say that a good work is formally in itself a sin, or that a just man, insofar as he works well, sins, which would be absurd and contradictory: But we assert that an imperfection adheres to a good work, which has the nature of sin, since all our righteousnesses are as a menstruous cloth, Isaiah 64. The calumny of Cornelius, encrusted with a historical commentary, is more serious: John, just as James, attacks the Simonians, Gnostics, and other heretics of that age, teaching that only infidelity is sin: for to the faithful all things are clean, even if he lives basely. Luther and the Libertines taught this same thing in this century. But where do histories teach that the Simonians, Gnostics, and others were considered heretics in that they taught only infidelity to be sin? taught that only infidelity condemns, along with Scripture. Where did B. Luther assert that to the faithful all things are clean, even if he lives basely? Let the Jesuits therefore swallow back those comments and calumnies. Finally, the ψευδερμηνεία (false interpretation) of Lyranus is also to be noted here, who takes the present passage concerning mortal sin, with Cornelius approving this sense: Although the just may lack it: Yet because no one knows for certain that he is just, and in the grace of God, hence likewise no one ought to presume, and assert for certain, that he is immune from mortal sin: just as John chapter 3, 14 refutes. We know that we have passed from death into life: And Paul Rom. 8, 1. There is no condemnation (ὀυδὲν κατάκριμα) for those who are in Christ Jesus: Indeed this aphorism: For those who have been purified from all sin, they can be certain of the grace of God.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Ἐὰν εἴπωμεν, ὅτι ἁμαρτίαν ὀυκ ἔχομεν) Id est, ut mox exponit, ὅτι ὀυχ ἡμαρτήκαμεν. Si putamus nobis Chri- sto & ejus cognitione opus non fuisse, ut a peccatis purgaremur. Nam alioqui post Evangelii notitiam potuere quidam esse sine peccato, ita ut peccati vox hic sumitur, non ut meras ignorantias, aut subitos motus significet, sed ut eos actus malos, qui tractum habent, & deliberationem non antevertunt. Habere peccatum non est nunc in peccato esse, sed ob peccata reum pos- se fieri, ut apparet Joh. 9, 41. cap. 15, 22, 24. Pari sensu apud Jacobum c. 4, 17. ἁμαρτία αὐτῷ ἐστι Reum autem posse fieri hic intellige, si Deus summo jure uti voluisset ac vellet.

Ἑαυτοὺς πλανῶμεν ) Imponimus nobismetipsis, no- stro maximo malo. Id verum esse apparet Rom. 5, 6. 8. Philo libro de Gigantibus: Εἰ γὰρ βουληθείη ὁ Θεὸς δι- κάσαι τῷ θνητῷ χωρὶς ἐλέους, τὴν καταδικάζουσαν οἴσει, μηδε- νὸς ἀνθρώπων τὸν ἀπὸ γενέσεως μέχρι τελευτῆς βίον ἄπταιστον ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ δραμόντος. Ἀλλὰ τῷ μὲν ἑκουσίοις τῷδε ἀκουσίοις χρησαμένου τοῖς ἐπ ποσὶν ὁμοθήμασιν

Καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν ἡμῖν) Non est in nobis studium veri. In Manuscripto: Ἀλήθεια ἐν ἡμῖν οὐκ ἔστιν.

Docet necessitatem non tantum καθαρισμοῦ, quo omnes indigemus, quia nemo est, qui non ha- beat peccatum, sed etiam confessionis, ne quis præ- sumat, vel etiam jactitet, se non habere peccatum, & ut prius consolatus est humiles, ne desperent in peccatis; siquidem ab omni peccato emundet nos sanguis Filii Dei; ita nunc corripit superbos, qui sese efferunt, quasi non haberent peccatum, sed im- munes essent ab omni peccato. Si dixerimus, quod peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus, & veritas non est in nobis. Schlichtingius ita hæc superioribus nectit: Ex hac occasione purificationis nostræ per Christi sanguinem redarguit eos, qui existi- marent, se operibus suis posse servari. Proinde sibi fide in Jesum Christum Dei Filium non esse opus, tales erant Judæorum multi, contra quos etiam disputat Paulus imprimis in epistola ad Romanos & ad Ga- latas. Nexus non malus, modo sensus bonus esset.

Grotii autem ψευδερμηνεία elucet 1. ex arbitra- ria temporum enallage: Quod peccatum non habe- mus, inquit Johannes, Grotius pervertit, quod pec- cavimus. Textus respicit peccatum quodcunque, Grotius de peccato graviori accipit. Textus de re- natis & fidelibus loquitur, nam de se & aliis fideli- bus profitetur id Apostolus: Si dixerimus: Gro- tius de non renatis, qui peccatum habuere ante no- titiam Evangelii. Textus omnibus opponit ne- cessitatem confitendi atq; ideo etiam renatos pec- cati expertes haud esse, ac peccata confiteri debe- re, eorumque purificatione ac remissione indigere innuit. Grotius fingit quosdam posse esse sine pec- cato, quod Scripturæ Sacræ palam repugnat, 2. Reg. 8,46. 2. Paral. 6,3. Job.9,3. Prov. 20.9. Eccles. 7, 21. Rom 3,23. Jac. 3,2. Verba S. Johannis luculenta sunt de culpa & peccato. Grotius ea ex adverso perver- tit non culpam sed reatum tantum notari: Τὸ ῥητὸν hujus dicti habere actu peccatum infert: Glossa Gro- tiana non de actuali existentia peccati, sed de τῷ posse reum fieri peccati interpretatur; idque ad- huc hypothetice intelligi vult, si nempe Deus sum- mo jure uti voluisset ac vellet. Didicit hanc σχε- θλότητα a Socinianis, e quibus Schlichtingius in h. l. Si dicamus, inquit, q. d. ut quidam faciunt, quod pec- catum non habemus, id est, non peccavimus, ut v. 10. loquitur, non tenemur peccati ullius reatu, nos ipsos decipimus, falsa opinione animum imbuimus, quæ nobis in perniciem vertet. Non mirum id de Soci- nianis, si negant, peccatum nos habere post rege- nerationem, quia non credunt illi peccatum origi- nis, quod nunquam deponunt renati, at Grotium, nisi forsan in eo etiam pelagianizat, cum Socino, id negare mirum. Nec vero tantum meræ ignoran- tiæ aut subiti motus, sed etiam quandoque actus mali, qui tractum habent & deliberationem, non antevertunt in eos, qui renati sunt, cadunt, ut ex- emplo sunt Aaron, David, Petrus, Thomas, alii in S. Literis: ideoque non rei tantum possunt fieri, si Deus summo jure uti velit ; sed etiam rei actu funt, secundum ordinarium Dei jus, quousq; non agunt poenitentiam, viri mortis sunt, 2.Sam.12,7.

Ideoque recte agnoscit Estius peccatum nos ha- bere variis modis (1) propter affectum peccati, qua- tenus nemo in hoc seculo reperitur, qui plene purgatus sit ab omni inordinato & vitioso affectu. Unde Augu- stinus in enarrat. Psal. CXVIII. conc. 10. Intelligere debemus inquit, quantumlibet quisq; proficiat in ju- stificationibus Domini, habere eum mortalis carnis affectum, circa ista terrena, & in quibus vita huma- na tentatio est super terram. Sic & Leo M. serm. VII. de Epiph. Domini : Quis invenietur ita im- munis a culpa, ut in eo non habeat justitia quod ar- guat ? Et serm.VI. Quadrag.
