Talis est conditio etiam eorum, qui concupiscentiis renituntur, ut nunquam possint in cordibus suis non invenire, quod reprobent. Et generalis est sententia Job. 14. Nemo mundus a sorde.

2. Propter reatum peccati, quia durante hac vi- ta nunquam sumus ab omni reatu liberi. Semper enim est, unde dicere Deo debeamus : Dimitte nobis debita nostra. Nam si nunquam plene sit expurga- tus in hac vita noster affectus, semper igitur remanet aliquis reatus etiam in homine recens baptizato. Quod vero non admittimus sensu Papistico, qua- si remissa culpa reatus aliquis poenae supersit, sed quod nunquam peccatum illud ευπερίστατον quie- scat; sed semper motibus inordinatis prorumpat, qui reos nos faciant & sanctos etiam quosvis re- missionem peccatorum petere jubeant, & orare quoque, ab occultis libera me Domine; ostendere vo- luit Dominus, inquit S. Augustinus l. XXI. de Civit. Dei cap. 27. quantumlibet juste in hujus vita caligi- ne atq; infirmitate vivamus, non nobis deesse peccata, pro quibus dimittendis debeamus orare. Leo serm. VII. de Eph. Dom. neminem immunem esse a culpa docet, ut in eo non habeat Dei misericordia, quod re- mittat.

3. Propter actum peccati frequentem & quoti- dianum, & quodammodo continuum. Quem mo- dum attenderunt Hieronymus, Augustinus, & alii Patres, qui contra Pelagium scripserunt. Cujus erat doctrina, justum hominem vivere posse sine peccato, ac multos fuisse qui sine peccato vixissent.

4. Propter peccatum, in quo nati sumus, vel quod aut qua deinde actu commisimus, propter quae opus sit nobis Christo propitiatore & Advocato. Juxta quem modum sententia Johannis refertur ad peccata praete- rita, quamvis remissa ac deleta, ut sit sensus : Si quis dixerit se non peccasse, nec in peccato unquam fuisse, ideoq; Christo Patrono opus non habere, &c. In quo modo tamen id desideramus, quod peccatum, in quo nascimur, vel originale cum aliis confundatur, illudque deletum ambigue dicatur. Nam remit- titur quidem id ac compescitur, ut non dominetur in renatis, nunquam autem deletur & extirpatur, nisi cum vita ipsa extinguitur. Quem vero sensum fatetur non sufficere : Quia Apostolus adhuc exigit confessionem peccatorum, ac proponit spem venia ex promissione Dei dicens : Si confiteamur peccata no- stra, fidelis est & justus, ut remittat nobis peccata no- stra. Loquitur ergo de peccatis adhuc remittendis. Et utiq; scribit ad fideles, quibus originale peccatum & gravia actualia baptismo fuerant dimissa. Vult igitur ut adhuc confiteantur offensas suas quotidia- nas, quemadmodum & Jacobus Apostolus, qui cum dixisset cap. III. In multis offendimus omnes, postea cap. 5. ad offensarum confessionem hortatur, dicens: Confitemini alterutri peccata vestra.

Quapropter potissimum tertium modum respici observat, & e Concilio Milevitano can. VI. VII.

VIII. probat Estius, eoque refert Sanctorum con- fessiones, quibus hanc peccandi frequentiam in seipsis humiliter agnoscunt: Ut Hieronymus ad Pamma- chium adversus errores Johannis Hierosolymitani: Quotidie peccamus omnes, & in aliquo labimur. Ambrosius l. IV. de Sacram. cap. 6. Qui semper pec- co, debeo semper habere medicinam. Et in apologia David: Unusquisq; nostrum per singulas horas quam multa delinquit. Augustinus in enarrat. Psal. 128. Si veraciter sibi tundunt homines pectora, peccores sunt. Et quis nostrum non tundit sibi pectus? Gre- gorius libr. IV. epist. 31. ad Mauritium Imperato- rem: Et quia omnipotenti Deo incessanter quotidie delinquo, incessanlibus quotidie plagis ferior. Bern- hardus epist. 24. in fine: Orari pro me instanter postu- lo, quia incessanter pecco. Johannes Gerson in tra- ctatu de statuto Carthusiensium: Vix facimus ali- quid, ubi non possimus rationabiliter formidare de peccato veniali. Adde quæ habet Gennadius l. de Eccl. dogm. can. 86. Omnes veraciter se asserere peccatores, quia in veritate habent, quod plangant, si non reprehensione conscientiæ, certe mobilitate & mu- tabilitate prævaricatricis naturæ. Ex quo manife- ste Pelagii cavillum refelli docet Estius, quo dice- bat, sanctos humilitatis causa confiteri se peccatores, quamvis revera peccatum non haberent. Non enim dicit Johannes: Si dixerimus, quia peccatum non ha- bemus, ipsi nos extollimus, & humilitas in nobis non est. Unde sensum illum Pelagii Milevitana Synodus merito damnat anathemate can. 6. Propterea etiam Beguardi, & Beguinæ, ac fanatici, qui ad eam per- fectionem se ascendere posse jactitarunt, ut fiant impeccabiles, merito damnantur. Nec longe ab his abire Durandum in 2. d. 28. q. 3. notat Cornelius a Lapide, qui putat omnia venialia deliberata posse vi- tari, non autem omnia indeliberata, quæ fiunt ex sub- reptione.

Refelli etiam ita opinionem quorundam, observat Estius, inter quos Clemens Alexandrinus l. VI. Stro- mat. qui putant, Apostolos post Domini resurrectio- nem accepto Spiritu sancto ita fuisse confirmatos in gratia Dei, ut deinceps nullis essent peccatis ac passioni- bus obnoxii. Refellitur, inquam, quia Apostolus est, qui dicit, si dixerimus &c. utiq; semetipsum comprehen- dens, quemadmodum & in præcedentibus ac sequenti- bus. Sic etiam Jacobus Apostolus: In multis offendi- mus omnes. Sic Paulus de Petro Apostolorum Principe Gal. 2. Quia reprehensibilis erat. Extant hac de re apud Hieronymum, Augustinum, Prosperum & alios Patres aperta testimonia, quæ brevitatis studio omit- timus. Quæ recte se habent: Et quum univer- saliter de omnibus ista pronunciet, quos expiat san- guis Christi, ne Maria quidem excipienda, quam hic exceptam vult Cornelius. Ea enim indiguit etiam Redemptore Christo, & purificatione san- guinis ejus. Quod autem addit Estius: Hæc mul- tum esse diversa, peccatum habere, & actu præsenti peccare, ideo nequaquam esse consequens, si sem- per habemus peccatum, semper & in omni opere nos peccare, quem errorem condemnet Synodus Tri- dentina sess. 6. c. 25. in eo nostram pervertit senten- tiam, quos hæreticos inique vocat Acatholicus Papista, & improbum anathema Papistici concilia- buli improbe approbat. Nam nos bonum opus formaliter in se peccatum esse, aut justum, qua be- ne operatur, peccare non dicimus, quod insulsum esset & contradictorium: Sed bono operi adhære- re imperfectionem, quæ peccati rationem habet, asserimus, quum omnes justitiæ nostræ sint instar panni menstruatæ, Es. 64. Gravior est Cornelii calu- mnia commento Historico incrustata: Perstringit Johannes æque ac Jacobus Simonianos, Gnosticos, aliosque illius ævi hæreticos, docentes solam infidelita- tem esse peccatum: fideli enim omnia esse munda, eti- amsi turpiter vivat. Idem hoc seculo docuit Luthe- rus & Libertini. Ubi vero docent historiæ, Simo- nianos, Gnosticos, aliosque in eo hæreticos habitos, quod solam infidelitatem peccatum esse docue- rint? Ubi tale quid docuit B. Lutherus? Etsi solam infidelitatem damnare cum Scriptura tradiderit. Ubi B. Lutherus fideli omnia esse munda, etsi tur- piter vivat, asseruit? Resorbeant ergo illa com- menta & calumnias Jesuitæ. Denique Lyrani etiam hic notanda ψευδερμηνεία, qui de peccato mortali præsentem locum accipit, sensum hunc approban- te Cornelio: Licet justi eo careant: Tamen quia nemo scit certo, se esse justum, & in gratia DEI, hinc pariter nemo præsumere debet, certeque asse- verare, se immunem esse a peccato mortali: quem- admodum refellit Johannes cap. 3, 14. Nos scimus, quia ex morte translati sumus in vitam: Et Paulus Rom. 8, 1. Nulla est condemnatio (ὀυδὲν κατάκριμα) illis, qui sunt in Christo Jesu: Imo hic aphorismus: Nam qui purificati sunt ab omni peccato, illi certi esse possunt de gratia Dei.

## 1:9
Vers. 9.

Ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν) If we confess that we lived in grave sins before the knowledge of the Gospel, and therefore had need of medicine, and that which follows, that we retain the Evangelical doctrine as necessary. For effects are wont to be understood from their causes.

This confession is again rashly restricted to sins committed before the knowledge of the Gospel, or rather before regeneration. For the discourse is about all sins which we commit, about all which are expiated by the blood of Christ, by whose blood indeed St. John teaches that we are purified from ALL sin, and therefore grace is promised to all who confess their sins. Concerning which St. Augustine says: Not only, he says, past sins, but also if we have perchance contracted any sins from this life: because a man cannot, as long as he carries flesh, not have even light sins. But do not despise those light ones which we speak of. If you despise them when you weigh them, shudder when you count them. Many light ones make one great one. Many drops fill a river, many grains make a mass. And what hope is there? Above all, confession, lest anyone call himself just. And afterwards: If I call myself just, who would bear it? Who would tolerate it? Let my justice be known before God. I, however, will call myself a sinner, not because I am, but lest I be found hateful through arrogance. Tell men what you are, tell God what you are. Because if you do not tell God what you are, God condemns what He will find in you. Do you not want Him to condemn? You condemn. Do you want Him to forgive? You acknowledge, so that you may be able to say to God, turn away your face from my sins. Say to Him also those words from the Psalm itself: for I acknowledge my iniquity. But if we have confessed our faults, He is faithful and just, that He may forgive us our faults, and cleanse us from all iniquity.

More rightly, therefore, Estius here again acknowledges that this is a general remedy, and that it extends to all sins. After he taught that no one is without sin, he now shows the general remedy for obtaining the remission of sins, whatever we have committed, whether great or small. Although indeed faith in Christ ought to be joined altogether with this confession, because we must be purified from sin through the blood of Christ, yet one should not, with Schlichting, include all the appendages of this confession, both the purpose and promise of not sinning anymore, and the execution of that purpose and promise: for such a purpose and promise is equally a consequence, as is the execution of confession or penance, and it pertains to the fruits of penance, which is absolved by contrition and faith. But the words themselves teach that the discourse here is not about retaining Evangelical doctrine, but about obtaining the forgiveness of sins. St. John, says Cornelius, suggests the remedy for sin, of which he said we all are, namely its true acknowledgment and humble confession and repentance; for through this the blood of Christ is applied to us, which cleanses us from it, as he said in v. 7.

Πιστός ἐστι καὶ δίκαιος, ἵνα ἀφῇ ἡμῖν τὰς ἁμαρτίας) He is so faithful and good that He will not be mindful of old crimes hereafter. He is faithful to stand by His promises 1 Cor. 1, 9. 2 Cor. 1, 18. 1 Thess. 5, 24. Heb. 10, 23. c. 11, 11. I interpret δίκαιος here as good, gentle. Thus δικαιοσύνη is the goodness of GOD, 1 Sam. 11, 7. See also Ps. 112, 8. and Matt. 6, 1. To remit is said here for not revoking the pardon, which is wont to be done against the ungrateful.

It is not a question of the oblivion of old crimes, but of the remission of any sins whatsoever: which the words of the Apostle clearly testify again. It is one thing to remit sins, another not to revoke pardon, which Grotius therefore confuses very badly, wickedly perverting the golden sentence of the Apostle. For we are taught here that as often as we confess our sins, that is, perform penance, we can obtain the remission of them; which God solemnly attested in Ezekiel 18:21 and chapter 33:14. Moreover, these things can be referred either to Christ, whose mention was made just before, or to the name a little further back, v. 7, pointed out by the pronoun αὐτοῦ, which is expressed in v. 5, ὁ Θεός. That double epithet suits both. However, almost all understand it of God, who is πιστὸς, faithful, because He keeps His promises; who warned us to pray for debts and sins, and promised fatherly mercy and that pardon would follow, as Cyprian says in his work on the Lord's Prayer. and δίκαιος, just, because He pardons the sins of those who are penitent and others who present to God the ἱλασμὸν καὶ καθαρισμὸν [propitiation and cleansing] through true faith in Christ, inasmuch as they are expiated through Christ, who satisfied for them, just as St. Paul speaks concerning the remission of sins and our justification, Rom. 3:26, εἰς τὸ εἶναι δίκαιον καὶ δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἐκ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ [that He might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus]. Nor does δικαιοσύνη occur in 1 Sam. 11:7 or Matt. 6:1, nor does that word denote goodness anywhere in Matthew. But in Psalm 112:8, it is not a question of the goodness of God, but of the mercy of men, as most explain, although justice can also be understood there, which, exercising itself in the faithful through works of mercy, remains forever. The explanation of the blessed Hunnius is easily agreeable to our opinion: God both can and wills to remit to those who confess. He can indeed, since He is just, and the fountain of all justice, who can communicate from His fullness to us and justify the ungodly, Rom. 4. He wills it, however, because He is faithful and a keeper of His promises, by which He promised in the Gospel that He wills to justify repentant sinners who have acknowledged their sins through His Son, namely by remitting sins on account of the blood of His Son. To this also tends the interpretation of Cajetan: that He is called just because Christ by His blood and death merited this pardon for us. Therefore, this remission of sins is just and owed by justice, but to Christ, not to us. Furthermore, Christ communicates, applies, and as it were appropriates His merits to the penitent, so that the penitent may offer them to God as if they were the proper ransom for his own sins. Wherefore God is just, who, receiving this ransom, remits sins; but because these merits are proper to Christ, and truly only appropriated to us by Him, that is, applied, hence the reason for justice in the remission of sins is properly with respect to Christ, not us, as Cornelius holds here, but not without ἑαυτομαχίᾳ [self-contradiction], since he later calls Him just: because the penitent satisfies God in some way when he humbly confesses the offense and seeks pardon with groaning, tears, and especially if he does it out of true and perfect contrition of soul. Who also explains just as equitable: Because it is equitable and congruent and worthy of God that He should remit sin to the penitent: both because He Himself promised it to the penitent, not as a reward of work, but as penance as a gift and a reward, John 20:23, Ezek. 18:32, and elsewhere. But a promise is a debt, which therefore it is just to pay: both because it is fitting and worthy of God and of Divine goodness and clemency that He should receive penitents into grace and reconcile them to Himself. And he adds a third reason for equity, but one which is hardly worth mentioning by the nature of the thing, the closest disposition to reconciliation and grace. Just as, therefore, it is naturally just that the form of fire should be induced into a hot piece of wood, as having the final disposition, so it is supernaturally equitable that, once repentance is placed as the final disposition, the form of grace should be induced, by which the sinner is reconciled to GOD. Thus Lyranus and Dionysius. That inept proposition, an apodosis contrary to Scripture, because the grace of God is not a form, but an affection in God; nor is it induced by our previous dispositions, but it embraces us freely without any merit of ours or the intervention of our works, Rom. 11:6. But the interpretation praised by Cornelius is futile: Suarez, 3rd part, vol. 3, disp. 11, sect. 1, concl. 3. God, he says, is faithful when He forgives mortal sins to penitents, just when He forgives venial sins to the just, because, forsooth, the just merit this forgiveness by works of repentance, charity, etc., as St. Augustine teaches in De corrept. & grat. c. 13. For Scripture acknowledges no merits of condignity here.

However, Cornelius a Lapide and Tirinus, along with Bellarmine and others, understand these things concerning the confession of sins before men or priests. But the interlinear gloss understands it of the confession which is made to God. God, who promised grace to men, is faithful in executing it and just, wherefore He justly forgives the one who truly confesses. Estius wishes confession to be designated in a general sense, which is described and commended throughout the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, that is, which proceeds from sorrow and shame over sins, and has the invocation of Divine mercy joined to it, whether that confession be made before God alone, or before a priest, the vicar of God.

And cleanse us from all sin) to cleanse is the same as to purify below, ch. 3:3, טהר. But here to cleanse is taken for that which is to keep pure, just as to make alive is often to preserve in life. And God does that mostly through His Spirit, strengthening and confirming us, Rom. 16:26, 1 Thess. 3:13, 1 Pet. 5:10. And in this, that God does it, He is said to be proved faithful, 2 Thess. 3:3. We shall be cleansed from offenses, as Tertullian speaks in De pudicitia, citing this book, walking in the light, in which there can be no offense. Thus he says we are cleansed not in that we offend, but in that we do not offend. For walking in the light, and not communicating with darkness, we shall act as cleansed, not by having put away the offense, but by not having admitted it. For this is the power of the Lord's blood, that those whom He has already cleansed from offense, and thereafter established in the light, He thereafter keeps clean, if they have persevered in walking in the light.

A new distortion again. The preceding context sufficiently teaches that this is not about preservation in purity, but about the remission of sin. It is added exegetically, so that it may be taught that God does not remit sins otherwise than by the cleansing which is done through the blood of Christ. And what are those circumlocutions? To cleanse is to purify, as 1 John 3:3, and this again is the same as to be kept in purity. Surely such things never entered anyone's mind, that to remit sins is not to revoke a remission already made, that to cleanse from all sin is to be kept in purity. What is clearer than that the remission of sin is promised to the confession of sin or repentance, which indeed is not done out of absolute grace, but through that cleansing which is done by the blood of Christ. Estius indeed wishes to introduce another sense, namely that the cleansing is done not by the mere non-imputation of sins, but by a true renewal of life: yet he is forced to acknowledge that that phrase, from all iniquity, is taken collectively in this sense, so that no iniquity remains, and that this cleansing is not perfected except in the future age, and therefore he prefers it to be taken distributively, so that the sense may be that there is no iniquity so great, either in number or magnitude, from which the blood of Christ does not cleanse us, if we have confessed it: and thus that this part agrees with that one above: The blood of Jesus Christ the Son of GOD cleanses us from all sin. Although Estius warns that Christ's blood does not cleanse us from sins only in this sense, that it removes the guilt of preceding sins; but also that it purges the will from the affection of sinning, providing a true conversion of the heart, and the operation of justice and virtues as a companion, since the merit of Christ is open to all these things, as Hesselius teaches, yet the words themselves confirm, and the comparison of the present verse teaches, that it is not about conversion or the renewal of the will in verse 7, but only about the cleansing of sins, because the remission of sins is here expressly stated, and the same is attributed to the blood of Christ, whereas the renewal of life, while it indeed belongs meritoriously to the passion of Christ, yet as regards its actual operation, it is attributed to the efficacy of the Holy Spirit in the justified: and the purification of sins through the blood of Christ is prior in nature to the renewal of our life itself. Schlichtingius does not deny our explanation in a certain sense regarding those words, and cleanses us from all iniquity, noting: By surely absolving us from the guilt of all iniquity and imputing justice to us. But the condition which he adds, if they have not already eluded God, and if they do it in time, he adds of his own, akin to the error of the Novatians, which we have expressly refuted in the Exeg. A. C. among the Socinians. God does not grant to us only once and again; but as often as we have turned, who also wishes that we should show mercy to our neighbor after His example, and forgive him even seventy times seven, Matt. 18:21, 35. By which, however, a license to sin is not made, but if we have sinned and have performed serious repentance, the forgiveness of sins is promised to us, as is clear from 1 John 2:1.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν) Si fateamur, nos in gravibus peccatis vixisse, ante notitiam Evangelii, ac propterea opus habuisse medicina, & quod consequens est, Evangelicam doctrinam, ut necessariam, retineamus. So- lent enim ex causis effecta intelligi.

Hæc confessio temere iterum restringitur ad pec- cata ante notitiam Evangelii, vel potius ante regene- rationem commissa. Nam de omnibus peccatis, quæ committimus, de omnibus quæ per sangui- nem Christi expiantur, per cujus vero sanguinem nos purificari ab OMNI peccato, docet S. Johan- nes, sermo est, ideoque omnibus confitentibus pec- cata gratią promittitur. Quo de S. Augustinus: Non tantum, inquit, præterita, sed & si qua forte con- traximus ex hac vita peccata: quia non potest homo quamdiu carnem portat non habere vel levia pecca- ta. Sed ista levia qua dicimus noli contemnere. Si contemnis quando appendis, expavesce quando nume- ras. Levia multa faciunt unum grande. Multa guttæ implent flumen, multa grana faciunt massam. Et quæ spes est? Ante omnia confessio, ne quisquam se dicat justum. Et postea: Si me justum dixero, quis ferat? Quis toleret? Apud Deum nota sit justitia mea. Ego tamen dicam me peccatorem, non quia sum, sed ne arrogantia odiosus inveniar. Dic hominibus quides, dic Deo, quid es. Quia si non dixeris Deo quod es, damnat Deus, quod in te inveniet. Non vis ut ille damnet? Tu damna. Vis ut ille ignoscat? tu agnosce, ut possis Deo dicere, averte faciem tuam a pec- catis meis. Dic illi etiam illa verba ex ipso Psalmo: quoniam iniquitatem meam ego cognosco. Quod si confessi fuerimus delicta nostra, fidelis est & justus, quod dimittat nobis delicta nostra, & purget nos ab omni iniquitate.

Rectius itaque hic iterum Estius agnoscit gene- rale esse hoc remedium, & ad omnia peccata se porrigere. Postquam docuit, neminem carere pecca- to, nunc commonstrat generale remedium obtinendæ remissionis peccatorum quacunque commiserimus seu magna seu parva. Quanquam vero cum hac con- fessione omnino conjuncta esse debeat fides in Christum, quia per sanguinem Christi purificari nos oportet a peccato, non tamen cum Schlichtin- gio omnia confessionis istius annexa, & propositum & promissum non amplius peccandi, & propositi ac pro- missi illius exequutio includenda: nam propositum & promissum tale consequens est æque & executio confessionis vel pœnitentiæ, & ad fructus pœniten- tiæ, quæ contritione & fide absolvitur, pertinet. Non autem hic de Evangelica doctrina retinenda, sed de peccatorum venia consequenda agi verba ipsa docent. Suggerit, inquit Cornelius, S. Johannes pec- cati, cujus omnes nos esse dixit, remedium, scilicet ve- ram ejus agnitionem & humilem confessionem ac pœ- nitentiam; per hanc enim applicatur nobis sanguis Christi, qui nos ab eo emundat, uti dixit v. 7.

Πιστός ἐστι καὶ δίκαιος, ἵνα ἀφῇ ἡμῖν τὰς ἁμαρτίας) Ita fidelis & bonus est, ut veterum criminum ultra memor non sit fu- turus. Fidelis est stare promissis 1. Cor. 1, 9. 2. Cor. 1, 18. 1. Thess. 5, 24. Ebr. 10, 23. c. 11, 11. Δίκαιος hic interpretor bo- num, lenem. Sic δικαιοσύνη est DEI bonitas, 1. Sam. 11, 7. Vide & Psal. 112, 8. & Matth. 6, 1. remittere hic dicitur pro non revocare veniam, quod solet fieri adversus ingratos.

Non de veterum criminum oblivione, sed de pec- catorum quorumvis remissione agitur: quod verba Apostoli luculenter iterum testantur. Aliud est re- mittere peccata, aliud non revocare veniam, quæ proinde pessime confundit Grotius, improbe per- vertens auream sententiam Apostoli. Docemur enim hic quotiescunque confitemur peccata, hoc est, pœnitentiam agimus, remissionem eorum nos consequi posse; quod Ezech. 18, 21. cap. 33, 14. Deus graviter contestatus est. Referri autem possunt hæc vel ad Christum, cujus proxime mentio facta est, vel ad paulo remotius nomen, v. 7. pronomine αὐτοῦ indigitatum, quod exprimitur v. 5. ὁ Θεός. Utrique convenit epitheton illud geminum. De Deo tamen plerique omnes id intelligunt, qui πι- στὸς fidelis est, quod promissa servet; qui orare nos pro debitis & peccatis monuit, paternam misericordiam promisit & veniam secuturam, dicente Cypriano de orat. Dom. & δίκαιος justus, quod pœnitentibus aliisque vera fide Christi ἱλασμὸν καὶ καθαρισμὸν Deo sistentibus peccata condonet, utpote per Christum expiata, qui pro illis satisfecit, quemad- modum de remissione peccatorum & justificatio- ne nostra S. Paulus loquitur, Rom. 3, 26. εἰς τὸ εἶναι δίκαιον καὶ δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἐκ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ. Neque 1. Sam. 11, 7. vel Matth. 6, 1. δικαιοσύνη occurrit, nec uspiam in Matthæo vox ea bonitatem notat. Psalmo vero 112, 8. non de bonitate Dei, sed miseri- cordia hominum agitur, ut plerique explicant, licet ibidem etiam justitia intelligi possit, quæ in fi- delibus per misericordiæ opera se exerens manet in æternum. Nostræ sententiæ facile consentanea est B. Hunnii explicatio: Deus & potest & vult con- fitentibus remittere. Potest quidem, cum justus sit, & omnis justitiæ fons, qui de plenitudine sua nobis communicare & impium justificare potest, Rom. 4. Vult autem, quia fidelis est & suarum promissionum servans, quibus in Evangelio promisit quod resipi- scentes peccatores agnitis peccatis per Filium justifica- re velit, remittendo scilicet peccata propter Filii sui sanguinem. Quo etiam abit Cajetani interpretatio: Justum dici, quia Christus suo sanguine & morte pre- meruit nobis hanc veniam. Justa ergo est hæc pec- catorum remissio & ex justitia debita, sed Christo, non nobis. Porro Christus sua merita pœnitenti communicat, applicat & quasi appropriat, ut ea pœ- nitens, quasi peccatorum suorum lytrum proprium Deo offerat. Quare justus est Deus, qui lytrum hoc accipiens peccata remittit; sed quia hæc merita sunt propria Christi, ab eo vero duntaxat nobis appropria- ta, id est, applicata, hinc ratio justitiæ in remissione peccatorum proprie est respectu Christi non nostri, ut hic habet Cornelius, sed non absque ἑαυτομαχίᾳ, quum postea justum dicat: quia pœnitens satisfacit aliqua ratione Deo, cum offensam humiliter confite- tur, veniamque petit cum gemitu, lacrymis, ac præ- sertim si id faciat ex vera & perfecta animi contritio- ne. Qui etiam justum explicat æquum: Quia æquum est & congruum Deoque dignum, ut pœniten- ti peccatum remittat: tum quia id ipse promisit pœ- nitentibus, non ut operis mercedem, sed ut pœnitentia donum & premium Joh. 20, 23. Ezech. 18, 32. & ali- bi. Promissum autem est debitum, quod proinde solve- re est justum: tum quia Deo ac Divinæ bonitati & clementiæ conveniens & dignum est, ut pœnitentes in gratiam recipiat, sibiq; reconciliet. Additq; tertiam æquitatis rationem, sed quæ vix digna est comme- moratu: Quia, inquit, pœnitentia quasi ex natura rei est proxima ad reconciliationem & gratiam dispo- sitio. Sicut ergo naturaliter justum est, ut in lignum calidum ut octo, quasi ultimam dispositionem habens, inducatur forma ignis: Sic supernaturaliter æquum est, ut posita pœnitentia quasi ultima dispositione indu- catur forma gratiæ, qua peccator reconcilietur DEO. Ita Lyranus & Dionysius. Inepta illa πρότασις, Scripturæ contraria ἀπόδοσις, quia gratia Dei non est forma, sed affectus in Deo; nec inducitur per prævias nostras dispositiones, sed nos complecti- tur δωρεὰν sine ullo nostro merito aut operum no- strorum interventu, Rom. 11, 6. Futilis vero est in- terpretatio laudata Cornelio: Suarez 3. p. tom. 3. disp. 11. sect. 1. concl. 3. Fidelis, inquit, Deus est cum condonat pœnitentibus mortalia peccata, justus cum condonat justis venialia, quia scilicet justi per opera pœnitentiæ, charitatis &c. merentur de condigno hanc condonationem, uti docet S. Augustinus de corrept. & grat. c. 13. Merita enim de condigno hic nulla agnoscit Scriptura.

Cæterum intelligunt hæc de confessione pecca- torum coram hominibus vel Sacerdotibus Corne- lius a Lapide & Tirinus cum Bellarmino aliisque. Sed de confessione, quæ fit Deo, intelligit glossa interlin. Deus qui promisit gratiam hominibus, fide- lis est exequendo & justus, quare vera confessioni juste dimittit. Estius confessionem in genere designari vult, quæ passim in Scripturis Veteris & Novi Te- stamenti describitur & commendatur, id est, quæ ex dolore & erubescentia super peccatis proficisci- tur, & invocationem Divinæ misericordiæ conjun- ctam habet, sive ea confessio coram solo Deo fiat, sive coram Sacerdote Dei vicario.

Καὶ καθαρίσῃ ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ πάσης ἁμαρτίας) καθαρίζειν idem quod infra ἁγνίζειν c. 3, 3. טהר. Sumitur autem hic καθαρίζειν pro eo, quod est purum servare, sicut ζωο- ποιεῖν sæpe est conservare in vita. Id autem Deus facit maxime per Spiritum suum, roborantem nos atque con- firmantem, Rom. 16, 26. 1. Thess. 3, 13. 1. Petr. 5, 10. Et in hoc quod facit Deus fidus probari dicitur, 2. Thess. 3, 3. Emandabimur a delictis, ut Tertullianus de pudici- tia loquitur, hunc librum citans, in lumine incedentes, in quo delictum esse non potest. Adeo sic emundari nos ait non qua delinquamus, sed qua non delinquamus. Incedentes enim in lu- mine, tenebris vero non communicantes emundati agemus, non deposito, sed non admisso delicto. Hæc est enim vis Dominici sanguinis, ut quos jam delicto mundarit, & exinde in lumine constituerit, mundos exinde præstet, si in lumine incedere perse- veraverint.

Nova iterum στρεβλότης. Non agi hic de conserva- tione in puritate, sed de remissione peccati, anteceden- tia satis docent. Ἐξηγητικῶς additur, ut doceatur, Deum non aliter remittere peccata, quam emun- datione, quæ fit per sanguinem Christi. Et quinam illi circuitus? καθαρίζειν est ἁγνίζειν, ut 1. Joh. 3, 3. & hoc iterum est idem, quod servari in puritate. Nemini profecto talia in mentem venere, remitte- re peccata esse non revocare factam remissionem, mundare ab omni peccato esse servare in puritate. Quid clarius, quam quod confessioni peccati vel pœnitentiæ promittatur remissio peccati, quæ ve- ro non ex absoluta gratia fiat, sed per eam emun- dationem, quæ fit sanguine Christi. Vult quidem Estius alium inferre sensum, quod nempe emunda- tio fiat non sola peccatorum non-imputatione, sed vera vitæ renovatione: Idem tamen agnoscere co- gitur, illud ab omni iniquitate, sic collective suma- tur hoc sensu, ut nihil restet iniquitatis, non per- fici eam mundationem nisi in seculo futuro, ideoq; distributive accipi malit, ut sensus sit, nullam esse iniquitatem tantam vel numero vel magnitudine, a qua sanguis Christi nos non emundet, si eam con- fessi fuerimus: adeoque convenire eam partem cum illa superiori: Sanguis Jesu Christi Filii DEI emundat nos ab omni peccato. Quanquam vero mo- neat Estius, Christi sanguinem non hoc solum sen- su nos emundare a peccatis, quod reatum tollat præ- cedentium peccatorum; verum etiam quod pur- get voluntatem ab affectu peccandi, præstans ve- ram cordis conversionem, & comitem justitiæ vir- tutumque operationem, siquidem ad hæc omnia patent meritum Christi, docente Hesselio, non ta- men v. 7. de conversione aut renovatione volunta- tis, sed de peccatorum emundatione solum agi tum verba ipsa confirmant, tum collatio versus præsentis docet, quia exprimitur hic diserte remis- sio peccatorum, eademq; sanguini Christi tribui- tur, quum renovatio vitæ meritorie quidem Chri- sti passioni conveniat, sed quoad ipsam ejus opera- tionem Spiritus sancti efficaciæ in justificatis tribua- tur: ac prior natura sit purificatio peccatorum per sanguinem Christi ipsa vitæ nostræ renovatione. Non abnuit nostræ explicationi certa ratione Schlichtingius ad verba illa, & mundet nos ab omni iniquitate, annotatis: Reatu nimirum omnis iniqui- tatis nos solvendo & justitiam nobis imputando. Con- ditionem autem quam addit, si non jam ante Deum eluserint, & in tempore id faciant, de suo addit, No- vatianorum errori affinem, quam in Exeg. A. C. in Socinistis ex professo confutavimus. Non se- mel atque iterum tantum nobis donat Deus; sed quotiescunque nos conversi fuerimus, qui etiam vult, ut ad exemplum ipsius misericordiam proxi- mo exhibeamus, eique vel septuagies septies con- donemus, Matth. 18, 21. 35. Quo vero non pec- candi licentia facta, sed si peccaverimus & seriam pœnitentiam egerimus, peccatorum venia nobis promissa est, ut e 1. Joh. 2, 1. patet.

## 1:10
Verse 10.

If we say that we have not sinned) He repeats in other words what he had said above in verse 8, so that we may the more beware of the crime of such an ungrateful spirit. And such repetitions are very customary for this Apostle.

We make him a liar). The same expression is found below in chapter 6, 10. To make a liar, הכזיב, Job 24:25, is to hold someone for a liar, or to speak of him as if he were a liar, just as they are said to crucify Christ, Heb. 6:6, who act in such a way as if he had been worthy of the cross. On the contrary, he is said to seal that God is true, John 3:33, who acts in such a way as it befits him to act who considers God to be true. Now in this place John refers to the prophecies especially looking toward the times of the Messiah, Isa. 1:18, ch. 27:9, ch. 40:2, ch. 43:25, Jer. 31:34, Mic. 7:19.

This sentiment can indeed be admitted as a repetition, but one which is made with an auxesis. For there it was said, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But here we make him a liar, which is much worse. If you say, says this St. Augustine, I have not sinned, you make him a liar, while you wish to make yourself truthful. Whence can it come to pass that God is a liar and man is truthful, when Scripture says the opposite: Every man is a liar and God alone is truthful. Thus, therefore, it will be the same thing, not to have sinned, and not to have sin, and therefore also the use of the past tense is more appropriate, since we have not sinned, than the present, since we do not sin: because although we may perhaps not be sinning in the present, we cannot nevertheless say that we do not have sin. For we have certainly sinned and we have sin, and it is necessary for us to say, forgive us our debts. But he who denies this makes Christ a liar, who prescribed this prayer to us as necessary for all. Moreover, another interpretation is asserted in this way: If any one of us, however, has gone to such a pitch of rashness that he not only says that he has no sin, but furthermore dares to say that he has not sinned, he is not only a liar, deceiving himself, but also makes God a liar, who condemns the whole human race of sin. The former, 'we have no sin,' cannot be said also for the reason that we were born in sin, which never ceases to cling to us, Rom. 7, 14. seqq. Heb. 12, 1. But the latter, 'we have not sinned,' retaining the proper meaning of the past tense, does not treat of original sin, although consequently Augustine proves that from it also, l. V. contra Jovin. cap. 15. For it comes from that, that we cannot be without actual sin, because we were born in sin, by which also the remission of concupiscence or the fuel remains, assiduously inciting us to sin.

And his word is not in us) The Word of God, namely, announced through the Prophets, is not in us, that is: it is not received by us. In like manner John 5, 37. 'You do not have his word remaining in you.' And 'it does not find room in you,' John 8, 37.

The Gloss understands this of the hypostatic Word: The Word of God, that is, Christ, through whom there is remission of sins, does not remain in us, as being incredulous and proud, because we overturn the merit of Christ's redemption, and we say that we, as being righteous, have not needed nor do need the Redeemer himself. But it is more correctly explained concerning the spoken word, just as he had said before: 'And the truth is not in us,' where truth, which is opposed to a lie, is understood. Cornelius a Lapide understands it of that word which Eccl. 3, 20. 'The greater you are, humble yourself in all things.' But that neither fits the confession of sin incumbent upon all, nor is it taken from a Canonical book. More correctly, therefore, Didymus, Cajetan, Dionysius, and Catharinus interpret it of the Word of GOD, which teaches that all are subject to sin, to which the whole Scripture tends, even Schlichting the Socinian: For God himself, he says, pronounces us all to be sinners and guilty of sin, see Rom. 3, 19. And while he offers remission to all through Christ, and delivered his Son to death for all, so that everyone who believes in him might not perish, but have eternal life, by that very fact he declares that all are held by the guilt of sins. Therefore John adds: And his word is not in us, namely through faith; we do not believe the word of God, to which, while we do not believe it, by that very fact we make God a liar. Estius has it thus: Some explain it thus: Christ, who is the Word of God the Father, is not in us, namely dwelling through grace. But the simpler sense here is: The Word or speech, which we sent by God announce to you concerning Christ the Redeemer, by whose blood we are all to be cleansed from sins, is not in you through faith, that is, you do not believe the Gospel of God announced by us, which is to make God a liar.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Ἐὰν εἴπωμεν, ὅτι οὐχ ἡμαρτήσαμεν) Repetit aliis verbis, quod supra dixerat v. 8. ut eo magis a tam ingrati animi crimine nobis caveamus. Et sunt tales repetitiones multum usitatæ huic Apostolo.

Ψεύστην ποιοῦμεν αὐτόν). Eadem loquutio infra c. 6, 10. Mendacem facere הכזיב Job. 24, 25. est aliquem habere pro mendaci, aut sic loqui de eo, quasi is mendax esset, sicut Christum crucifigere dicuntur, Ebr. 6, 6. qui ita agunt, quasi cruce ille dignus fuisset. Contra is signare dicitur Deum esse veracem, Joh. 3, 33. qui ita agit, sicut decet eum agere, qui Deum veracem putet. Respicit autem hoc loco Johannes va- ticinia ad tempora Messiæ præcipue spectantia, Esa. 1, 18. c. 27, 9. c. 40, 2. c. 43, 25. Jerem. 31, 34. Mich. 7. 19.

Admitti quidem potest hæc sententia ceu repe- titio, sed quæ cum auxesi fiat. Ibi enim dicebatur, ipsi nos seducimus, & veritas non est in nobis. Hic vero mendacem facimus eum, quod multo dete- rius. Si dixeris, inquit hic S. Augustinus, non pecca- vi, illum facis mendacem, cum te vis facere veracem. Unde fieri potest, ut Deus mendax sit, & homo verax, cum contra dicat Scriptura: Omnis homo mendax & Deus solus verax. Ita ergo idem erit, non pec- casse, & peccatum non habere, atq; ideo etiam conve- nientior usus præteriti, quoniam non peccavimus, quam præsentis, quoniam non peccamus: quia quamvis in præsenti forte non peccemus, dicere tamen non possumus, peccatum nos non habemus. Peccavimus enim utiq; & peccatum habemus, ac necessum est nobis dicere, dimitte nobis debita no- stra. Qui vero hoc negat, mendacem facit Chri- stum, qui hanc precationem nobis præscripsit tan- quam necessariam omnibus. Assertur autem & alia interpretatio hoc modo: Si quis vero nostrum co te- meritatis processerit, ut non modo dicat, se peccatum non habere, sed insuper audeat dicere, se non peccasse, is non solum mendax est, seducens seipsum, sed & De- um facit mendacem, qui totum genus humanum peccati condemnat. Prius peccatum non habemus dici non potest etiam ideo, quia in peccato nati su- mus, quod nunquam non adhæret nobis, Rom. 7, 14. seqq. Ebr. 12, 1. Hoc vero, non peccavimus, re- tenta propria significatione præteriti, non agit de peccato originali, quanquam per consequens id inde etiam probet Augustinus l. V. contra Jovin. cap, 15. Nam ex eo sit, ut sine peccato actuali esse non possimus, quia in peccato nati sumus, quo eti- am remissio concupiscentiæ seu fomes remanet, assidue nos ad peccatum incitans.

Καὶ ὁ λόγος αὐτῶ ὐκ ἔστιν ἐν ἡμῖν) Verbum Dei nempe per Prophetas enunciatum non est in nobis, id est; non reci- pitur a nobis. Pari modo Joh. 5,37. τὸν λόγον ἀυτῶ ὐκ ἔχετε μένοντα ἐν ὑμῖν. Et ὐ χωρεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν, Joh. 8, 37.

De Verbo hypostatıco intelligit Glossa: Verbum Dei, id est, Christus, per quem sit remissio peccatorum, non manet in nobis, utpote incredulis & superbis, quia evertimus redemptionis Christi meritum, di- cimusque nos utpote justos ipso Redemptore non eguisse nec egere. Sed rectius de verbo προφορικῷ explicatur, quemadmodum antea dixerat: Et ve- ritas in nobis non est, ubi veritas, quæ mendacio op- ponitur, intelligitur. Cornelius a Lapide de verbo illo quod Eccl. 3,20. Quanto major es, humilia te in omnibus, intelligit. Sed id nec convenit peccati confessioni omnibus incumbenti, nec e libro Ca- nonico depromptum est. Rectius ergo Didymus, Cajetanus, Dionysius & Catharinus de Verbo DEI, quod omnes obnoxios esse peccato docet, quo tota Scriptura tendit, interpretantur, etiam Schlichtin- gius Socinista: Deus enim ipse, inquit, nos omnes pec- catores & peccati reos esse pronunciat, Vide Rom. 3,19. Et dum omnibus per Christum remissionem offert, & pro omnibus Filium suum in mortem tradidit, ut omnis, qui credit in ipsum, non pereat, sed habeat vi- tam æternam, eo ipso omnes peccatorum reatu teneri declarat. Ideo addit Johannes: Et sermo ejus non est in nobis, nempe per fidem, non credimus Dei sermoni, cui dum non credimus, eo ipso Deum mendacem fa- cimus. Estius ita habet: Quidam sic exponunt: Christus qui est Verbum Dei Patris non est in nobis, scilicet habitans per gratiam. Verum simplicior hic sensus est; Verbum sive sermo, quem nos a Deo missi vobis annuntiamus de Christo Redemptore, cujus san- guine omnes a peccatis mundandi sumus, non est in vobis per fidem, id est, Evangelio Dei per nos annun- tiati non creditis, quod est Deum facere mendacem.

## 2:1 Argument
CHAPTER II.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

He dissuades from sin: If, however, we should sin, he sets forth Christ as Advocate and propitiation, and discourses on the true nature and signs of faith, and preaches the doctrine of Christ as most ancient, which is concerning the love of neighbor and the remission of sins through the name of Christ, which he commends to every age, with love, not the love of the world or of those things which are in the world, but the will of GOD, and predicting the Great Anti-Christ, he teaches that his forerunners, who have gone out from them, are to be avoided, and that the anointing is to be heard, with the principal character of the Anti-Christ assigned and the same dogma of Christ commended again, because it produces confidence and excites to the pursuit of righteousness. There are three parts: The first exhibits the scope of the doctrine delivered concerning Christ, to v. 6. The second contains the eulogy of the doctrine of Christ, to v. 17. The third institutes the antithesis of Anti-Christian seduction and the doctrine of Christ to v. 29.

PART I. Exhibiting the scope of the doctrine concerning Christ.

Ver. 1.

My little children) John was accustomed to address Christians by this name and to say: Little children, love one another. Being asked, however, why he repeated this so often, he replied: Because it is the commandment of the Lord, which if it alone is done, it suffices. Thus Jerome in his commentary on this epistle. It was fitting for both a Teacher and an Apostle to address them thus. See 1 Cor. 4, 13. 15, 17. 2 Cor. 6, 13. Gal. 4, 19. Eph. 5, 1. 1 Thess. 2, 7. 2 Thess. 5, 11. 1 Tim. 1, 2. 18. 2 Tim. 1, 2. cap. 2, 1. Philem. v. 10.

These things I write to you) both those which have preceded, and those which will follow.

This passage looks back specifically to those things which preceded, and delivers their scope. He writes that he has written concerning the incarnation and annunciation of the Word, not so that they might trust in the grace of God exhibited in Christ to serve sin, but rather that they might flee from sins as much as is in them: And if they have fallen in any way, that they might not despair in their sins. The scope, therefore, of this doctrine is both dissuasive from sin and consolatory, if by chance they have sinned, which he brings forward in v. 1 and 2, and he illustrates that former point more abundantly through the antitheses solemn to him in v. 3 and following. St. Augustine delivers the connection thus: Lest by chance he might seem to have given impunity to sins, because he said: He is faithful and just to cleanse us from all sin: And men might now say to themselves: Let us sin securely, let us do what we wish, Christ cleanses us, He is faithful and just, He cleanses us from all iniquity; he takes away from you evil security, and inserts useful fear. You wish wrongly to be secure, be solicitous: For He is faithful and just, to forgive us our sins, if you are always displeased with yourself, and are changed until you are perfected. Tirinus explains the same thing thus: These things which I said at the end of the preceding chapter, namely that all sin, I do not write so that you may neglect to avoid sins, but so that you may avoid them with greater zeal, and at least that you may not sin hereafter in graver sins, or altogether voluntarily.

Therefore, the Papists cannot prove the perfection of good works from this passage, unless they wish to say that a regenerate person does not sin in his whole life. Guilhelmus Estius delivers this coherence: Just as in the preceding chapter, saying: If we confess our sins, etc., he showed the remedy for obtaining the cleansing of sins, namely the confession of them: So now he shows an advocate or Patron, by whose intercession and merit that same cleansing may come to us.

Ἵνα μὴ ἁμάρτητε) He demands nothing impossible, as appears below in c. 3, 9. c. 5, 8. namely with the word of sinning taken not of habits alone, as some wish, but of acts, which were preceded by deliberation or time for deliberation, such acts as are not mere ignorance or mere sudden surprises.

The word of sinning is to be accepted neither of habits of sinning alone, nor of acts of sin deliberately committed, or which had time for deliberation, but in general of any sins whatsoever, which is evident from the preceding, because he had spoken of all that sin which we ought to confess, whose remission can be obtained, and which is expiated by the blood of Christ; indeed, he had expressly warned that he was speaking of every sin, of every iniquity; and also from the present text: because he says simply and in general μὴ ἁμάρτητε, and again ἐάν τις ἁμάρτῃ, which is likewise general: Finally from the consequences, because our Paraclete intercedes for the forgiveness of all sins, and has been made a propitiation for all our sins. However, it matters little here whether that which is required is possible: because exhortations against all sin are found everywhere in Scripture, even though it is certain that there is no one who abstains and is immune from every sin. For the consequence does not hold from a Divine command to our ability, from our owed duty to the performance of our duty. Therefore, only that is taught, toward which we ought to strive and contend with all zeal, but not what and how much we are able to perform in this life. We are warned not to sin, but we are not taught that we can live in such a way that we do not sin. For however much we may strive to live holily and abstain from sins, if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and we make God a liar. By such warnings, therefore, we are led only to acknowledge our ἀδυναμίαν [weakness], and we are compelled to seek out the grace of Christ.

And if anyone sins) If anyone, however, has sinned, add also that he has delivered himself to the Church to be governed and healed, infra c. 5, 16, such as those of whom Gal. 6, 1; 2 Cor. 2, 6; 1 Thess. 5, 14; 2 Thess. 3, 12 speak. But this happened more often to those who were still of tender faith, such as those Galatians and Peter before receiving the Holy Spirit. Clemens Strom. II. [Greek text omitted].

That 'add' is not from the Holy Spirit, but from Grotian audacity. For nothing is to be added to Scripture, just as nothing is to be taken away from it. Nowhere, if anyone has sinned, is he commanded to give himself to the Church to be governed and healed, if he wishes to obtain Divine grace. The Apostle did not require anything other than that we confess our sin to God and trust in the free remission and purification of sins through the blood of Christ. Indeed, everyone in the Church, not the Church itself, is warned to pray for a brother whom he sees sinning, with the promise of being heard and of Divine grace. But this condition, namely the intercession of a brother, is not designated as necessary for obtaining the remission of sins, since God does not disdain to hear the penitents themselves and grant them grace, Ezech. 18, 21; ch. 33, 14; so far is it from being required that one should deliver himself to the Church to be governed and healed: nor is any such thing prescribed in Gal. 6, 1; 1 Thess. 5, 14; 2 Thess. 3, 12. But as for 2 Cor. 2, 6, that is a special example concerning an excommunicated person. Grotius undoubtedly drew these things from the Papists, who demand sacramental confession and ecclesiastical satisfaction from penitents. Not only the Galatians and Peter, but also other believers were subject to various falls; nor did Peter fall only before receiving the Holy Spirit by his threefold denial of Christ; but he also fell when he did not walk uprightly, gave offense, and was openly rebuked by Paul, Gal. 2, 14. Nor does the Apostle speak here only of more serious sins; but his discourse is general; just as we have need of the remission of all sins; nor was the blood of Christ shed only to expiate certain sins, nor was he made an ἱλασμός [propitiation] only for more serious and deliberate sins: but all our sins were cast upon him, Is. 53, 6; he cleanses us from all sin, 1 John 1, 7. Which Estius acknowledges in this place. For since no sin, however small, can be washed away except by the blood of Christ the Mediator, he himself saying: If I do not wash you, you will have no part with me, John 13, there is no need to restrict this statement (as some do) to mortal sins, especially since also in what follows: And he himself is the propitiation for our sins, etc., sins are understood generally. Augustine in this place: But perhaps sin creeps in from human life. What then will happen? Will there now be despair? Hear: If anyone, he says, has sinned, we have an advocate.

We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous) He does not say 'he has an advocate,' but 'the Church has,' which prays for the fallen. But Christ, in the manner of an advocate, commends the prayers of the Church to God the Father, John 16, 26. And I interpret δίκαιον [righteous] here again as good and gentle, as above c. 1, 9. Christ pleads the cause of the Church before the Father, the Holy Spirit before men, as we said on John 14, 16, 26; c. 15, 26; c. 16, 7, where we also explained the word παρακλήτου [advocate]. Origen explains this passage beautifully in Homily VIII on Numbers.

The Apostle does not speak here of the Church, but of himself and other believers: nor does Christ intercede only for believers in general, but for individuals calling upon him, indeed for the whole human race. For he intercedes for those for whom he died: But intercession is of a different kind, namely, one is general, the other special. Scripture nowhere teaches that Christ is finally entreated to be our advocate for sins through the advocacy of the Church. For although the prayers of the Church assist us, our prayers are not nevertheless destitute of their efficacy, nor do they rely on the intervention of the Church. Nor does St. John say 'the Church has an advocate, which prays for the fallen,' but 'we have,' he says, 'an advocate': we who are taken from among the believers, he changes the pronoun so that he may make an application: if anyone has sinned, we have—I, you, he, whoever of us has fallen—an advocate: and since we all fall in many things, James 3, 2, we all have a παράκλητον [advocate]. Let us hear St. Augustine here: If sin has crept in from the infirmity of life, see it immediately, let it displease you immediately, condemn it immediately, and when you have condemned it, you will come to the judge secure. There you have an advocate, do not fear that you will lose the case of your confession. For if a man sometimes in this life commits himself to a learned tongue and does not perish, do you commit yourself to the Word and are you going to perish? Cry out: We have an advocate with God. And further: He did not say: you have, nor do you have me, he said, but he placed Christ, not himself, and he said 'we have,' not 'you have.' He preferred to place himself in the number of sinners, so that he might have Christ as an advocate, rather than to place himself as an advocate for Christ, and be found among the proud who are to be condemned.

Although indeed we could understand δίκαιον as good and gentle, and thus the sense of the word could also have a place in Job 1:9 without prejudice to the context: yet it does not appear why the more customary meaning should not be retained, because the foundation of our confidence and of the hearing of the intercession of our advocate is the justice of Christ, who is that just servant of God, who by the knowledge of himself or by faith placed in his merit justifies us, Is. 53:11. Moreover, he is just, because he fulfilled all the justice of God, Matt. 3:15, and perfectly performed the will of God, Ps. 40:8, by which performance of the Divine will he has sanctified us forever, Heb. 10:10. He himself is the Lord our justice, Jer. 23:15, made for us by God justice, 1 Cor. 1:30, the end and complement of the law for justice to every believer, Rom. 10:4. Therefore, by the virtue of this merit of his, because he fulfilled the law of God for us, he intercedes for us before the Father, whom he has reconciled to us most effectively by his blood.

Furthermore, by the word Paraclete here is not understood an exhorter or monitor, as Nazianzen explained in Orat. IV de Theol., nor a comforter, which is appropriate to the whole Trinity, but an advocate, to whose office three things pertain, as Johannes Hesselius teaches in this place. First, to allege before the judge those things by which justice may be satisfied without the condemnation of the defendant. Next, to present the humility and prayers of the defendant, who acknowledges his sin and asks for pardon. Finally, to intercede also with his own prayers before the Judge, so that he may deal with the defendant mercifully and compassionately, and not out of the rigor of justice. These three things most especially befit our Advocate Christ. For first, he offers his blood to the Father for a λύτρον or price of redemption paid for our sins.

Then he alleges the humble confession of the guilty party, concerning which [I spoke] before: If we confess our sins. Thirdly, he adds his own intercession for us, Rom. 8, Heb. 7. Which intercession is not to be defined merely by the presence of the body of Christ in heaven, as Theophylact wishes; for presence is one thing, intercession another; nor by love alone, as Chrysostom, nor by the power of Christ received from the Father, as the Socinians, nor is it merely interpretative, as Claudius Espencæus, Medina, and Vasquez among the Papists contend. For one must not depart from the literal meaning of a word to figures of speech, and from mere intercession a representation of the wounds of Christ is not to be invented; and therefore, the opinion of other Papists being rejected, Suarez asserts the proper intercession of Christ in heaven with St. Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, Bernard, and others. Cornelius a Lapide also agrees with this opinion: Christ, he says, is our advocate firstly by interpretative prayer, by exhibiting himself and his own wounds, and the scars of his wounds, and consequently by alleging his merits to the Divine sight, as all Doctors agree. For this reason, rising again, he retained these scars and brought them into heaven, so that he might continually represent them to God the Father as our High Priest and Mediator, and through them obtain for us pardon and grace. Secondly, many very probably judge that Christ is also our advocate by prayer properly so called, by which he prays and intercedes for us to the Father in heaven; by prayer, I say, not by which he might again merit or obtain (as was the case while he lived on earth and was a wayfarer), but by which he, now a comprehensor, asks and begs the Father by demanding the right merited in this life, and promised to himself, and therefore due, namely our grace and salvation. For Paul signifies this in the epistle to the Hebrews, where he teaches that Christ is our eternal High Priest in heaven, who entered once into the holy places through his own blood, having found eternal redemption, ch. 9, 12, and ch. 7, 25. Always living, he says, to intercede for us. And Christ, John 14, 16: I, he says, will ask the Father and he will give you another Paraclete, and Paul, Rom. 8, 34: Christ Jesus, etc., who is at the right hand of God and intercedes for us. If Paul signifies this, and Christ himself in the cited passages, then that opinion is not merely very probable, but altogether certain and indubitable, as being signified by the Holy Scriptures. Estius also agrees with Hesselius: But now, established in heaven, he prays not by prostrating himself before the Father in the manner of a suppliant, or by uttering miserable cries: But by speaking and expressing the desire for the salvation of his elect to God, both in mind and in words of such a kind as would not be unbecoming to the Son, glorious in his humanity and sitting at the right hand of God and reigning with him, just as we showed regarding that passage in Rom. 8: Who also intercedes for us: And further regarding the passage in Heb. 7: Always living to intercede for us. The intercession of Christ for us is certainly distinguished by St. John, according to which he is called an advocate and the propitiation made by his blood: and he not only presents his wounds to the Father in intercessory prayer (which, whether they are also represented in heaven, and were retained for that purpose, is not so expressly defined in the Scriptures, and therefore the proper intercession is without doubt more certain than the interpretative), but he also exhibits his justice and merits to the Father, and thus intercedes for us by the virtue of his merits, justice, and the satisfaction of his passion, blood, and death, by which name we said he is called here our just Advocate, whom St. John also calls the ἱλασμὸν for our sins. Concerning which Cornelius says: Just, he says, that is, innocent and holy, because by his holiness he is most pleasing to the Father and merits to be heard by him. Although he indeed adds: He is called just rather because he justly satisfied for our sins; and gave a just price and ransom for them, namely his blood and life: This, however, seems to be contained in the latter reason for intercession: as he adds: And he is the propitiation for our sins.

Latin:

CAPUT II.

ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Dehortatur a peccato: Si qua autem peccemus, Christum Advocatum & propitiationem si- stit, & de vera fidei indole ac signis disserit, ac doctrinam Christi ceu antiquissimam prædicat, quæ est de dilectione proximi & remissione peccatorum per nomen Christi, quam omni ætati, cum amore, non mundi aut eorum quæ in mundo sunt amorem sed voluntatis DEI commendat, ac Anti-Chri- stum Magnum prædicens, ejus prodromos, qui ex ipsis egressi, vitandos, unctionem audiendam esse docet, assignato præcipuo Anti-Christi charactere & commendato iterum iisdem Christi dogmate, quod id pa- reat fiduciam, & ad justitiæ studium ex- citet. Partes sunt tres: Prima scopum doctrinæ de Chri- sto traditæ exhibet, ad v. 6. Secunda elogium doctri- næ Christi continet, ad v. 17. Tertia Anti-Christiana seductionis & doctrinæ Christi antithesin instituit ad v. 29.

PARS I. Scopum doctrinæ de Christo exhibens.

Vers. 1.

Τεκνία μου) Solebat Johannes hoc nomine Christianos compellare ac dicere: Filioli, diligite alter alterum. Roga- tus autem cur toties hoc repeteret, respondebat: Quia præ- ceptum Domini est, quod si solum fiat, sufficit. Ita Hierony- mus commentario ad hanc epistolam. Conveniebat ita eos affari & Doctori & Apostolo. Vide 1. Cor. 4, 13. 15, 17. 2. Cor. 6, 13. Gal. 4, 19. Eph. 5, 1. 1. Thess. 2, 7. 2. Thess. 5, 11. 1. Tim. 1, 2. 18. 2. Tim. 1, 2. cap. 2, 1. Philem. v. 10.

Ταῦτα γράφω ὑμῖν) tum quæ præcessere, tum quæ se- quentur.

Respicit in specie hic ea, quæ præcessere, eorumq; scopum tradit. De Verbi incarnatione & annun- ciatione se scripsisse non ut peccato servirent gra- tia Dei in Christo exhibita confisi, sed potius ut peccata fugiant quantum in ipsis est: Et si qua la- psi fuerint, in peccatis haud desperent. Scopus er- go doctrinæ istius est tum dehortatorius a peccato, tum consolatorius, si forte peccarint, quem v. 1. & 2. affert, illumq; priorem uberius per antitheses si- bi solennes illustrat v. 3. seqq. Συνέχειαν ita tradit S. Augustinus: Ne forte impunitatem videretur de- disse peccatis, quia dixit: Fidelis est & justus qui mundet nos a peccato omni: Et dicerent jam sibi ho- mines: Peccemus securi, faciamus quod volumus, purgat nos Christus, fidelis est & justus, purgat nos ab omni iniquitate; tollit tibi malam securitatem, & in- serit utilem timorem. Male vis esse securus, solicitus esto: Fidelis enim est & justus, ut dimittat nobis deli- cta nostra, si semper tibi displiceas, & muteris donec perficiaris. Sic exponit eandem Tirinus: Hæc quæ dixi in fine capitis præcedentis, nempe omnes peccare, non ideo scribo, ut negligatis cavere peccata, sed ut majori studio illa evitetis, & saltem gravioribus pecca- tis, aut omnino voluntarie non peccetis imposterum.

Non ergo ex hoc loco perfectionem bonorum ope- rum probare possunt Pontificii, nisi velint dicere, renatum in tota vita non peccare. Guilhelmus Estius hanc tradit cohærentiam: Quemadmodum capite præcedenti dicens: Si confiteamur peccata nostra &c. remedium monstravit obtinendæ purgationis peccatorum, nempe confessionem eorum: Ita nunc advocatum seu Patronum ostendit, cujus inter- cessione & merito eadem purgatio nobis contingat.

Ἵνα μὴ ἁμάρτητε) Nihil exigit impossibile, ut apparet in- fra c. 3, 9. c. 5, 8. nempe verbo peccandi sumpto non de ha- bitibus solis, ut quidam volunt, sed de actibus, quos præces- sit deliberatio aut tempus ad deliberandum, quales actus non sunt meræ ignorantiæ aut meræ obreptiones.

Verbum peccandi neque de solis peccandi habiti- bus accipiendum, neq; de actibus solis peccati deli- ratis, vel qui tempus deliberandi habuere, sed in genere de quibus vis peccatis quod patet e præceden- tibus, quia de omni illo peccato, quod confiteri de- bemus, cujus remissio obtineri potest, & quod san- guine Christi expiatur, loquutus erat, imo de omni peccato, de omni iniquitate se loqui diserte monue- rat, nec non e textu præsenti: quia simpliciter & in genere ait μὴ ἁμάρτητε, atq; iterum ἐάν τις ἁμάρτῃ, quod itidem generale: Denique e consequentibus, quia Paracletus noster pro omnium peccatorum condonatione intercedit, & propitiatio factus est pro omnibus peccatis nostris. Parum autem huc facit, anne possibile sit, quod exigitur? Quia dehor- tationes ab omni peccato in Scriptura passim ob- viæ sunt, etiamfi neminem esse, qui abstineat & im- munis sit ab omni peccato, certum sit. Nam a Di- vino mandato ad nostrum posse, a debito nostro officio ad officii nostri præstationem non valet consequentia. Proinde id tantum docetur, quo anniti & conten- dere omni studio debeamus, non vero quid & quantum in hac vita præstare valeamus. Mone- mur ne peccemus, sed ita nos vivere posse, ut non peccemus, non docemur. Quantumcunque enim annitamur, ut sancte vivamus, & a peccatis abstine- amus, si dixerimus, nos peccatum non habere, nos se- ducemus, Deumque mendacem faciemus. Talibus er- go monitis solum ad ἀδυναμίαν nostram agnoscen- dam ducimur, & ad Christi gratiam exposcendam compellimur.

Καὶ ἐάν τις ἁμάρτῃ) Si quis tamen peccaverit, adde & se Ecclesiæ regendum sanandumque tradiderit, infra c. 5, 16. quales illi, de quibus Gal 6, 1. 2. Corinth. 2, 6. 1. Thess. 5, 14. 2. Thess. 3, 12. Sæpius autem id eveniebat iis, qui tenera ad- huc erant fide, quales illi Galatæ & Petrus ante acceptum Spiritum sanctum. Clemens Strom. II. Ἐ δυνατὸς ὧν ἅψηται ἐπὶ τοῖς, κὰι ἐν τῇ πίστει περιπίπτουσι τισι πλημμελήματι πολύυλος ὧν μετάνοια δευτέρα.

Illud adde non est a Spiritu sancto, sed a Groti- na audacia. Nihil enim addendum Scripturæ, ut nihil ei demendum. Nuspiam si quis peccavit jus- sus est se Ecclesiæ regendum & sanandum dare, si gratiam Divinam consequi velit. Non Apostolus aliud requisivit, quam ut Deo peccatum confitea- mur & de gratuita remissione ac purificatione in peccatis per sanguinem Christi confidamus. Mo- netur quidem non Ecclesiæ, sed quisque in Eccle- sia, ut pro fratre, quem peccantem viderit, oret cum promissione exauditionis & gratiæ Divinæ. Sed non hæc conditio ceu necessaria ad impetran- dam remissionem peccatorum designatur, inter- cessio nempe fratris, quum pœnitentes ipsos Deus exauditione ac gratia non dedignetur, Ezech. 18, 21. cap. 33, 14. tantum abest, ut hoc requiratur, ut quis se tradat Ecclesiæ regendum & sanandum: nec ta- le quicquam præscribitur Gal. 6, 1. 1. Thessal. 5, 14. 2. Thess. 3, 12. Quod vero ad 2. Cor. 2, 6. id speciale exemplum est concernens excommunicatum. Hausit hæc sine dubio Grotius a Papistis, confessio- nem sacramentalem & satisfactionem Ecclesiasticam a pœnitentibus postulantibus. Non Galatæ tan- tum & Petrus, sed & alii fideles variis lapsibus ob- noxii fuere; nec Petrus tantum ante acceptum Spiritum sanctum lapsus est trina Christi abnega- tione; sed lapsus est etiam, cum non recto pede in- cessit, scandala dedit, & a Paulo palam reprehensus est, Gal. 2,14. Nec vero de gravioribus tantum pec- catis hic loquitur Apostolus; sed generalis est ejus oratio; quemadmodum omnium peccatorum re- missione opus habemus; nec pro quibusdam tan- tum peccatis expiandis fusus est Christi sanguis, non ἱλασμός factus est pro peccatis tantum gravi- oribus & deliberatis: sed omnia peccata nostra in ipsum conjecta sunt Ef. 53, 6. ab omni peccato nos mundat, 1. Johan. 1, 7. Quod agnoscit Estius in h. l. Cum enim nullum peccatum, quamvis exiguum, ab- lui possit, nisi sanguine Christi Mediatoris, ipso dicen- te: Si non lavero te, non habebis partem mecum, Joh. 13. nihil opus est, hanc sententiam, (quod quidam fa- ciunt) ad mortalia peccata restringere, præsertim quum & in eo, quod sequitur: Et ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris &c. peccata generaliter intelligan- tur. Augustinus in h. l. Sed forte surrepit de vita hu- mana peccatum. Quid ergo fiet? Jam desperatio erit? Audi: Si quis, inquit, peccaverit, advocatum ha- bemus.

Παράκλητον ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν Πατέρα τὸν Ἰησῦν Χριστὸν δίκαιον) Non dicit habet ille advocatum, sed Ecclesia habet, quæ pro lapso precatur. Preces autem Ecclesiæ Christus more advocati Deo Patri commendat, Johan. 16, 26. Δίκαιον autem rursus hic interpretor bonum ac lenem, ut supra c. 1, 9. Christus causam Ecclesiæ agit apud Patrem, Spiritus sanctus apud homines, ut dixi- mus ad Johan. 14, 16. 26. c. 15, 26. c. 16, 7. ubi & vocem παρακλήτου exposuimus. Pulchre hunc locum explicat Origenes homilia VIII. ad Numeros.

Non Ecclesiæ hic loquitur, sed Apostolus de se, a- liisque fidelibus: nec tantum pro fidelibus in uni- versum intercedit Christus, sed pro singulis ipsum invocantibus, imo pro toto genere humano. Pro quibus enim mortuus est, pro iis etiam intercedit: Sed intercessio diversi est generis, alia nempe gene- ralis, alia specialis. Ecclesiæ advocaturâ demum Christum exorari, ut advocatus noster peccatorum sit, nuspiam docet Scriptura. Quanquam enim sub- veniant nobis Ecclesiæ preces, non tamen nostræ preces efficacia sua destituuntur, aut nituntur Ec- clesiæ interventione. Nec dicit S. Johannes Ec- clesia habet advocatum, quæ pro lapso precatur, sed habemus, inquit, advocatum: nos qui e fidelibus su- bimur, mutat pronomen, ut applicationem faciat: si quis peccaverit, habemus ego, tu, ille, quisquis e nobis lapsus fuerit, advocatum: & quum in multis labamur omnes; Jac. 3, 2. habemus omnes παρά- κλητον. Audiamus hic S. Augustinum: Si de infir- mitate vitæ surrepserit peccatum, continuo vide, con- tinuo displiceat, continuo damna, & cum damnave- ris, securus ad judicem venies. Ibi habes advocatum, noli timere, ne perdas causam confessionis tuæ. Si enim aliquando in hac vita committit se homo linguæ difer- tæ & non perit, committis te verbo & periturus es? Clama: Advocatum habemus apud Deum. Et por- ro: Non dixit: habetis, nec me habetis, dixit, sed & Christum posuit, non se, & habemus dixit, non habe- tis. Maluit se ponere in numero peccatorum, ut habe- ret advocatum Christum, quam ponere se pro Christo advocatum, & inveniri inter damnandos superbos.

Quanquam vero δίκαιον intelligere possemus bo- num ac lenem, adeoque vocis sensus Job. 1, 9. etiam locum habere possit salvo contextu: non apparet tamen, cur non potius retinenda sit usitatior signi- ficatio, quia fundamentum fiduciæ nostræ & exau- ditionis intercessionis advocati nostri est justitia Christi, qui est servus ille justus Dei, qui cognitione sui vel fide in meritum suum collocata nos justificat, Es. 53, 11. Justus autem est, quia omnem justitiam Dei implevit, Matth. 3, 15. & voluntatem Dei per- fecte præstitit, Psal. 40, 8. qua Divinæ voluntatis præstatione nos in æternum sanctificavit, Ebr. 10, 10. Ipse est Dominus justitia nostra, Jerem. 23, 15. fa- ctus nobis a Deo justitia, 1. Cor. 1. 30. finis & comple- mentum legis ad justitiam omni credenti, Rom. 10, 4. Hujus ergo meriti sui virtute, quia legem Dei pro nobis implevit, interpellat pro nobis apud Patrem, quem nobis sanguine suo reconciliavit quam effi- cacissime.

Cæterum Paracleti voce hic non intelligitur ex- hortator vel monitor, ut Nazianz.orat.IV.de Theol. exposuit, nec consolator, quod convenit toti Trini- tati, sed advocatus, ad cujus officium tria pertinent docente Joh. Hesselio in h.l. Primum ea allegare a- pud judicem, quibus citra rei condemnationem ju- stitiæ satisfiat. Deinde proferre humilitatem ac pre- ces rei, peccatum agnoscentis, veniamque postu- lantis. Tandem suis etiam precibus apud Judicem intercedere, ut clementer & misericorditer, non autem ex rigore justitiæ cum reo agat. Quæ tria maxime conveniunt Advocato nostro Christo. Pri- mo enim offert sanguinem suum Patri pro λύτρῳ seu pretio redemptionis pro peccatis nostris soluto.

Deinde allegat humilem rei confessionem, de qua antea : Si confiteamur peccata nostra. Tertio suam addit intercessionem pro nobis, Rom. 8. Ebr. 7. Quæ interpellatio non est tantum definienda per præsentiam corporis Christi in cælo, ut Theophylactus vult; aliud enim est præsentia, aliud intercessio; nec dilectione tantum, ut Chrysostomus, nec potestate Christi a Patre accepta, ut Sociniani, nec sit tantum interpretative, ut e Pontificiis Claudius Espensæus, Medina & Vasquez contendunt. Non enim a pro- prietate vocis ad figuras discedendum, & ex inter- cessione mera fingenda est vulnerum Christi re- præsentatio; ideoq; aliorum Pontificiorum senten- tia reprobata Suarezius propriam Christi in cælis intercessionem cum S. Cypriano, Ambrosio, Augu- stino, Bernardo & aliis adstruit. Cui sententiæ et- iam accedit Cornelius a Lapide: Christus, inquit, est advocatus noster primo oratione interpretativa, ex- hibendo se suasq; plagas, vulnerumq; cicatrices, ac consequenter sua merita allegando Divino conspectui, uti omnes Doctores consentiunt. Idcirco enim resur- gens has cicatrices retinuit, & in cælum intulit, ut eas jugiter Deo Patri quasi Pontifex & Mediator noster repræsentet, ac per eas veniam & gratiam nobis obti- neat. Secundo multi valde probabiliter censent, Chri- stum etiam esse advocatum nostrum oratione proprie dicta, qua pro nobis in cælis Patrem oret ac interpel- let; oratione, inquam, non qua denuo mereatur vel impetret, (qualis fuit dum viveret in terris, eratq; viator) sed qua jam comprehensor petit, rogatq; Pa- trem exigendo jus hac in vita promeritum, sibiq; pro- missum, ideoq; debitum, scilicet gratiam & salutem nostram. Hoc enim significat Paulus in epistola ad Ebræos, ubi docet Christum esse Pontificem nostrum æternum in cælis, qui per proprium sanguinem introi- vit semel in sancta, æterna redemptione inventa, cap. 9, 12. & cap. 7, 25. Semper vivens, inquit, ad inter- pellandum pro nobis. Et Christus Joh. 14, 16. Ego, ait, rogabo Patrem & alium Paracletum dabit vobis, & Paulus Rom. 8, 34. Christus Jesus &c. qui est ad dextram Dei & interpellat pro nobis. Si hoc signi- ficat Paulus, & Christus ipse locis citatis; non val- de probabilis tantum est ea sententia, sed omnino certa & indubitata, utpote S. Literis significata. Annuit & Estius cum Hesselio : Orat autem nunc in cælo constitutus non supplicium more sese prosternens ante Patrem, aut miserabiles edens voces: Sed deside- rium salutis electorum suorum eloquens atq; expro- mens Deo tum mente, tum verbis ejusmodi, quæ Fi- lium in humanitate gloriosum, & in dextra Dei se- dentem atq; cum eo regnantem non dedeceant, quem- admodum ostendimus ad illud Rom. 8. Qui etiam in- terpellat pro nobis: Et amplius ad locum Ebr. 7. Sem- per vivens ad interpellandum pro nobis. Distingui- tur certe a S. Johanne Christi pro nobis interces- sio, secundum quam advocatus dicitur & sangui- ne ejus facta propitiatio: nec solum vulnera sua Patri sistit in oratione intercessoria, quæ an repræ- sententur etiam in cælis, eoque fine retenta sint, in Scripturis adeo expresse definitum non est, ideoq; sine dubio certior est ipsa propria, quam interpreta- tiva intercessio; sed etiam justitiam & merita sua Patri exhibet, & ita virtute & meritorum justitiæ, & satisfactionis passionum sanguinis & mortis suæ pro nobis interpellat, quo nomine diximus ipsum hic justum dici Advocatum nostrum, quem eun- dem & ἱλασμὸν pro peccatis nostris, dicit S. Jo- hannes. Quo de Cornelius: Justum, inquit, id est innocentem & sanctum, quia sua sanctitate gra- tissimus Patri meretur ab eo exaudiri. Quanquam vero addat: Justum potius dici, qui juste pro peccatis nostris satisfecit; justumque pro eis dedit pretium & lytrum, scilicet sanguinem suum & vitam: Hoc ta- men posteriori ratione intercessionis contineri videtur: utpote subdat: Et ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris.

## 2:2
Ver. 2.

And he is the propitiation for our sins) ἱλασμὸς for ἱλαστὴς in the Hebrew manner, and ἱλάσκειν to cause sins to cease. For the sense is: he provides strength, so that we do not sin in the future. See Heb. 2, 17, and what is said there, and compare it with those things which will follow here. Moreover, there is a communion in the word ἡμῶν, such as are many in Paul.

Cornelius explains the particle καὶ causally as 'because': Since the office of an advocate is also to allege those things by which justice may be satisfied without the condemnation of the guilty party, just as Hesselius hints. More fully, says Estius, John explains the excellence of our advocate, namely that he is such that he does not offer another's satisfaction to the Father, but exhibits his own and proper one: through which he not only tries and strives (as advocates do before a human judge) to render God appeased to us: but most certainly renders God appeased and propitious to us. However these things may rightly stand, the more common sense of the particle καὶ, that is, copulative, can nevertheless be retained. For two duties of our Priest are joined, who made a cleansing of our sins by his blood: both the oblation, by which he was made a propitiation for our sins, and the intercession for us: which two things were incumbent upon the Priests of the Old Testament, both to sacrifice and to pray for the people: And both contribute to obtaining pardon for our sins, both Christ's propitiation, when he offered himself to God for us as an odor of sweetness, Eph. 5, 2, and his prayer, when he intercedes for us before the Father, which although it is done by the virtue and presentation of his satisfaction itself; yet these two duties remain distinct, and the ἱλασμὸς or propitiation was made on the altar of the cross, [while] the intercession, presenting the same and praying for pardon for us on account of the same, is in heaven, even if it was also made on earth in the days of Christ's flesh. St. John does not say ἱλαστὴς, propitiator, in the concrete, but what is more emphatic, ἱλασμὸς, propitiation, and propitiatory sacrifice.

CHRIST is indeed both Priest and propitiator, and the propitiatory sacrifice itself, because He offered Himself to God for us: But why should we depart from the letter, and not understand with Augustine himself the propitiatory sacrifice? Moreover, ἱλασμὸς, propitiation, or ἱλάσκειν, to propitiate, to appease, is not to cause sins to cease, but to cause anger on account of sins to cease; for it is the same as to reconcile, to make one who was angry, appeased, and that someone should return into favor with him whom he had offended; which native sense of the word no one is ignorant of, and therefore all interpreters have embraced it, if perhaps you except Socinus: and Grotius himself refuted that depravation in Socinus, defens. fid. Cath. de satisf. Christ. c. X. p. 135, that by this expression sacrifices are regarded. But that sense, that by generating faith through the sacrifice of CHRIST we are henceforth drawn away from sins, does not pertain to the sacrifice for sin. For sacrifices, he says, did not draw one away from sin, especially by producing faith in some thing: nor did they provide testimony to a remission already accomplished or certainly decreed, but as Socinus himself acknowledges, they were some antecedent requirement for remission, which those words show: He shall make atonement and it shall be forgiven. Therefore in this comparison is engaged, and it is clearly necessary that expiation signifies the same thing when applied to legal sacrifices and to Christ: because the writer to the Hebrews derives both from the same decree, namely that without the shedding of blood there is no remission, but expiation is made in blood, Heb. 9, 22. Grotius also observes this, that not only among the Hebrews, but also among the nations, sacrifices were believed to expiate sins, and therefore it is not to be doubted, since in this very argument of expiatory sacrifice the Greek word καθαρίζειν is used, but that it is used in that sense which the Greek language had received; just as also the word ἱλάσκεσθαι for victims.
