Homer and others very often applied [it], and the Greeks and others used lustral sacrifices or piacula to appease the Deity, and thus to obtain impunity for things previously committed, and from a comparison of authors it becomes manifest that these are equivalent: that God is appeased by some victim, that the wrath of the gods is expiated, or that the soul of someone is sufficient for the gods in place of the souls of others. And ch. VII. p. 92. It is very well known, he says, that to avert the wrath of someone is said in Greek ἱλάσκεσθαι, εἰρηνοποιεῖν, καταλάσσειν, ἀποκαταλλάσσειν, in Latin to appease, to pacify, to conciliate or reconcile, likewise to propitiate: both the act itself and that by which the act is properly performed are called ἱλασμὸς by the Greeks, and placamen by the Latins. In God, wrath, as we said above, is called anthropopathically, as if it were an affection of punishing: which the Apostle says is uncovered or revealed from heaven against all impiety and injustice of men, as those who detain the truth in injustice, that is, who resist the known commandments of God. No one, however, is excepted, since we are all by nature children of wrath, that is, subject to Divine wrath. This wrath remains upon some, John 3, 36. Upon whom it does not remain, it is averted from them. Christ obtains this aversion by his death, and therefore he is most rightly called a placamen. Thus the Apostle John calls him twice, when he said: If anyone has sinned, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the innocent one. And he himself is ἱλασμὸς for our sins, and indeed not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world, 1 epist. ch. 2. v. 1. 2. Likewise in this is his love, not that we loved God, but that he himself loved us, and sent his Son as ἱλασμὸν for our sins, ch. 4. v. 10. With which passage that Pauline one is to be compared: God commends his charity, that when we were still sinners, Christ died for us, Rom. 5, 8. For both Paul and John prove by the same argument that we did not love first, but were loved by God, and what Paul calls dying, this John calls being made a placamen. Furthermore, that passage of Paul is to be added: We are justified freely through the redemption in Christ Jesus, whom God proposed as ἱλαστήριον through faith in his blood, Rom. 3, 24. 25. Christ was therefore made ἱλασμὸς or ἱλαστήριον in his blood, which is what else than that very thing which Socinus denies, that God is appeased by Christ? For as to the fact that he interprets ἱλασμὸν in John as expiation, but by the word expiation understands the destruction of sin, he does this for no reason, fortified by no example. ἱλάσκειν among all Greek writers, poets, historians, and others, is to appease, and it is accustomed to be constructed with the Accusative designating the person whose wrath is averted. Nor is it used otherwise among the LXX Interpreters and Luke 18, 13. In one place only, which is Heb. 2, 17, Christ is said to be constituted high Priest εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ, where there is an enallage coming from Hebraism ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας, when it should usually have been said ἱλάσκεσθαι θεὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν. It signifies therefore there an expiation, but one which is made by appeasing. Otherwise this use of the word would have nothing in common with the nature of the word and its perpetual signification. Wherefore such an expiation as Socinus invents, that is, the destruction of sin, which is done without appeasement, this word ἱλάσκεσθαι and the ἱλασμὸς derived from it cannot denote. Thus Grotius. But even from the Socinians themselves, Schlichtingius here opposes the Grotius annotations on the present passage, so that Grotius seems to have turned out worse not only than himself, but also than the Socinians, the worst of heretics: By propitiation, he says, for our sins, he understands a propitiatory and expiatory victim, because namely he himself, God so willing and ordaining, shed his blood for the remission of our sins, and thus rendered God, to us sinners, if we do penance and amend our life, clearly propitious. And afterwards: A propitiatory victim is called a propitiation, because through it a propitiation is made, by a Metonymy of the effect for the cause, just as the Holy Spirit below ch. 2, 27 is called anointing, because it is that heavenly oil through which anointing is made. Schlichtingius adds: God is indeed propitiated not always so that he, being angry, may be appeased, but also when it is brought about that, having otherwise just causes for being angry, and containing his wrath with supreme clemency and mercy, he does not at length become angry and punish: which happens when he himself ordains a propitiatory victim, which if anyone neglects, then at last he will experience an angry God, but if he flees to it, a mild and propitious one, which was done most of all in Christ, whom not only God himself gave as a victim for the sins of the world, but also Christ himself celebrates the admirable charity of God toward the world in this, John 3, 16.

Which could have a sound sense: But Schlichtingius betrays his heresy when he adds: Which certainly (charity) does not in any way allow that God was then angry at the world. But unless the world flees to Christ as the unique expiation, and thus believes in CHRIST, it dies in its sins, and lives for God and justice henceforth, such great charity of God will turn into horrible wrath. And for this reason GOD gave CHRIST as a victim for the sins of the world and willed that he be made such, so that just as he bound himself to remit sins, so he might bind the world to abandon the same by such a victim. But in truth, it is in vain that the love of God demonstrated in giving the Only-Begotten Son to the human race is opposed to the wrath of God against the sin of the human race, just as they are not opposites, the conclusion of all under sin, and the commiseration of all, or Divine mercy and justice. Moreover, Scripture does not assign the end of the death of CHRIST on the part of GOD only to the fact that he willed to bind himself to remit sins, just as on the part of men it pleased him to bind the world to abandon the same by such a victim: Indeed, it makes the end of the death of CHRIST, who is a victim for our sins, the propitiation of God and the expiation of sins, so that they may be remitted to us, just as Grotius previously taught from the Levitical sacrifices: nor are we properly bound by the victim to abandon sins, because that is a confirmation of the doctrine handed down by CHRIST; but that benefit, that CHRIST gave himself as an expiatory sacrifice for us, binds us to this, that we should abandon sins, and give and consecrate ourselves to him who offered himself for us. Levitical victims did not bind one to abandon and flee sins henceforth, but properly served to expiate committed sins and to obtain their remission, which once obtained, it was the duty of the faithful to avoid sins and to serve God, but this is as a consequence of expiation and the remission of sins; thus it is not contained in the phrase ἱλασμᾶ περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν.

Cornelius a Lapide wishes for an allusion to be made by the word ἱλασμᾶ to the propitiatory overhanging the ark of the covenant, inasmuch as it represented Christ the propitiator, Rom. 3, 27. Exod. 25, 17. But although those things mutually explain each other, ἱλαςήριον & ἱλασμὸς; yet here it is not the cover of the ark that is being looked to, but rather propitiatory sacrifices, as the mention of blood & καθαρισμᾶ, which preceded, and the word paraclete or Advocate confirm.

Estius indeed discusses the propitiation itself, whether it is to be understood regarding sufficiency, or indeed regarding efficacy, or in both respects? He assumes the latter. For he thinks, he says, that John means Christ renders the Father propitious to us by the sacrifice of the cross not only sufficiently, as they say, but efficiently. For he does not say: And he was the propitiation, namely at that time when he was offered on the cross, but he is the propitiation for our sins in that he applies that sacrifice, sufficient for the salvation of all, continuously & up to the end of the age to whom he wills, for the remission of sins. And he alleges in that sense those things which Hesselius discussed here against Catharinus.

But sufficiency is spoken of ambiguously, either regarding the possible or the actual. That which the Calvinists are accustomed to posit, namely that if God had willed, it could have sufficed for all the sins of all, the ἱλὰσμὸς of Christ is to be entirely exploded here, and this, which is from the will of God the Father giving Christ to us εἰς ἱλασμὸν, 1 John 3, 10, and in Christ, who willed to be made ἱλασμὸς for our sins sufficient for all, satisfaction and propitiation was actually performed, and the remission of sins was acquired for all, is to be asserted.

Similarly, there is ambiguity in the word effectively. For it is understood either regarding the efficacy of acquisition; that the victim of Christ expiated the sins of all men, and God was rendered placable to the human race, nay even placated, so that he wills no one to perish, but all to be converted to repentance and saved, or regarding application and the effect of the remission of sins, that he applies to us the expiation of Christ, and by the act itself remits, which is not except for those who believe, and through faith in Christ. Although indeed the sufficiency of the ἱλασμᾶ of Christ is not to be posited as inefficacious; yet it is not to be believed that Christ was made propitiation for all so effectively or efficiently that all have obtained the remission of sins, which opinion of I know not what so-called Apostate in the Palatinate refutation of the golden chair, ch. IX, p. 36, is imputed to us by calumny: The sum according to their opinion is the same ratio for the damned (as the Helvetic Apostate of Derendingen hands down) as if an Emperor were to redeem some thousands of Christian captives from the Turks with a huge sum of money, and not only free them from the bonds and chains with which they were tied in the galleys, but also restore them to the empire, and lead them back from Turkey to their fatherland. In this way ALL would have been redeemed by the Emperor not only on account of the most fully paid λύτρον, but also by actual restoration to their former liberty. But because it is contrary to all the opinion of the Emperor, certain scoundrels take to flight, and rushing back into Turkey anew, maliciously seek again their former captivity, in which they must thereafter eternally remain and perish. But of these things elsewhere.

Now if we look to the force of the Apostolic aphorism, it does not treat of the application of the expiation of Christ, which is not universal by reason of act and event, even if it is universal by reason of affection and Divine intention, but of the propitiation itself made on the altar of the cross through the sacrifice of the body of Christ, and the shedding of his blood for the sins of the human race, by which actual remission of sins did not indeed reach all men, yet it was obtained and acquired for all, and God was placated for all, so that each one can appropriate it to himself, and thus obtain it, since the offering of the same was also provided for all, through this propitiation of Christ. In which sense Leo the Great, sermon XII on the passion: he says not only that the shedding of the blood of the just for the unjust was so powerful for a privilege, so rich for a price, that if the totality of captives believed in the Redeemer, no tyrannical chains would hold them, but he also adds that in Jesus our Lord all were crucified, all died, all were buried, and all were also raised.

(Not only for our own, but also for the whole world) He will provide this benefit to all men who wish to follow him. Περὶ ὅλου τοῦ κόσμου is said briefly for περὶ τὰ ὅλου τοῦ κόσμου, which the Latin interpreter rightly saw. A similar construction is in Heb. 11:4 and elsewhere. Moreover, it is rightly said, etc., ἱλάσκεσθαι or ἐξιλάσκεσθαι ἁμαρτίας and περὶ ἁμαρτίας, as can be seen in Exod. 32:29 and elsewhere.

The Apostolic aphorism does not sound concerning the will of God to provide the benefit of propitiation, nor is this propitiation suspended here on a condition, as if propitiation were made for all men if they wish to follow him, and the very expiation of sins made by Christ depended on the human will; but it concerns the same [expiation] viewed in itself, which Christ made before he sat at the right hand of the Majesty, as the Apostle testifies, Heb. 1:3. But these words, 'not for ours only, but for the sins of the whole world,' are not to be understood with Cyril, bk. XI on John ch. 19, as not for the sins of the Jews only, but also of all the Gentiles; nor with Oecumenius, as not only for our sins, that is, of those who now live, but also for the sins of those who are to be born as long as the world shall last; or with others, as not for ours only, that is, of those to whom I am writing, but truly for the sins of the whole Church, which is Bede's explanation; or as others interpret, for the sins not only of those who already believe, but also of all the elect whom he is yet to bring to the faith from all parts of the world: because nowhere in the Scriptures are the elect or the Church understood by 'the whole world.' But in this way, not only for our sins, i.e., of those of us who believe, but also for the sins of all men, as many as there are, have been, or shall be. For St. John speaks from the person of the believers, and indicates that Christ is the propitiation not only for them, but also for any men whatsoever; because by the name of τοῦ ὅλου τοῦ κόσμου all men are understood: to which sense Cyril's exposition easily returns, insofar as by the name of Jews and Gentiles not only the faithful from among the Jews and Gentiles are designated, but the men of the whole world, who are accustomed to be divided into Jews and Gentiles, John 11:51. And therefore to Estius, who explains it as concerning believers only along with the Calvinists, we here oppose Cornelius a Lapide: for he confesses that the explanation of Clement of Alexandria and others is better, i.e., not for our sins, who are believers only, but also for the sins of the unbelievers of the whole world. For these also Christ suffered, and for them he merited grace and glory, if they wish to believe in him and embrace his merits. Whence he also commanded this Gospel to be preached to all nations, and them to be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, Mark 16:15.

But to the Calvinist Maccovius, in his colleg. de prædestin. disp. XIII. p. 37, who contends that the opposition is instituted not between the elect taken universally and the world, or between the elect who were from the Jews and the elect who were from the Gentiles, John 12:52; likewise that the opposition is instituted between the elect who have believed, or are already faithful, and the world, that is, the elect who do not yet believe, John 17:10; and to others among the Calvinists, we oppose, besides the ancients who understood the human race by the whole world, Origen, hom. XXIV on Numbers, and Ambrose, bk. IX, ep. 71.

Prosper in Resp. ad Gall. capit: Johannes Huss in h. l., also from the Reformed themselves Rudolph Gualther in h. l., Job. Calvin in h. l., Bullinger serm. II. de nativit. Christ. p. 9, Wolfgang Musculus in explic. Matth. 26, Andreas Hyperius in explic. 1. Tim. 2. p. 68, Christopher Pezel in explic. 1. cap. Joh. p. 162, Zacharias Ursinus in explic. Catech. p. 70, Georg Sobnius disp. Marp. VI. th. 21, Barthol. Copen. disp. de satisf. Anno 1616. th. 25, Matth. Martin. disp. II. de univers. doctr. Christ. Relig. th. 18, Paul Stein in Evang. Ephes. fraternir. p. 1. c. II. p. 340, Johannes Crocius in exposit. epist. ad Tit. c. 2. II. doctr. II. & in beat. salut. scal. Germ. p. 161, Johannes Berg in explicat. dicti Joh. 3, 16. & in de convenient. & different. Evangel. p. 71. We oppose also the Palatine Theologians, refuting the golden and gilded ladder concerning the merit of Christ. Ann. 1592. p. 17. The Nassau Theologians, Johan. Heinrich Alsted and Georg Fabricius in their judgment on the second Remonstrant Article. The Theologians of Great Britain, George of Llandaff, John Davenant, Samuel Ward, Thomas Goad, Walter Balcanquhall, likewise in their judgment on the second article of the Remonstrants. Finally, we oppose the Bohemian Confession offered in the year 1551, article 6, which accepts this saying concerning all the sins of all men, and the brief German Heidelberg Confession published in the year 1562, p. 27: Christ's death is for the sins of the whole world, that is, not only for the sins of the elect, to whom he was writing, but also for all other men in the whole world who are to live until its end. What then? That Christ. Massonius in his Anatom. univers. part. I. c. 39. p. 333, judges that all the Fathers of the Synod of Dort understood this golden sentence of St. John in that way, Par. II. cap. 3, and that this interpretation is not easily contradicted by any of the (Reformed) Theologians, and that it is agreeable to the Gospel, because it shows a most sufficient propitiation in the most perfect merit of Christ for all men, and is no less congruent with the consolation which St. John proposes to sinners weak in faith, so that if anyone perhaps has been overtaken in his sins, he may not despair or seek remission anywhere else than in Christ, but may rely by faith and true confidence upon the one most perfect sacrifice of the Son of God, as being that which is rich, precious, and sufficiently efficacious for propitiation not only for their sins, but also for the sins of the whole world, etc.

Indeed, St. John not only employs the general name of the world, το̃ κόσμου, which, as Job. Crocius says, embraces within itself both believers and unbelievers, and, according to Bullinger, has greater emphasis and is far more efficacious than the word 'men,' which, as Rudolph Gualther admits in h. l., the Apostle wished to use so that we would not think anyone excluded from the merit of Christ: But the note of universality is also added, ὅλου του̃ κόσμου, so that we might not think it concerns only some from the world, but that we might believe all men in the world are equally propitiated through Christ. And not only that, but St. John also proceeds from the commemoration of the faithful to the whole human race with a very clear amplification, not for the sins of the whole world or of all men. Not content, says Gualther, with having called Christ our propitiation, he testifies that he was made a propitiation for our sins. And this does not suffice for him. For lest he should seem to speak only in his own person or that of the other Apostles, he adds, not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. Which amplification was indeed most necessary for the solid force of the Apostolic consolation, so that no sinner might despair and, swept away by the waves of doubt, presume himself excluded from the salutary fruit of this intercession of the Paraclete, the force of which reasoning Massonius acknowledges in the cited place. If by the word περὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων the elect are indicated, who were believing at that time, that word would certainly embrace not only the Jews but also the believing Gentiles, which is contrary to the prior explanation of Maccovius, which he nevertheless joins and defends both. If by the word 'for ours' those were designated who were believing at that time, but by the word 'of the whole world' those who were to believe at that time, what will become of those who had already believed before under the beginnings of the New Testament, who believed in the Old Testament, who believed from the beginning of the Church gathered after the fall? Yet, with that exposition placed in the first member, the force of universality remains intact in the latter in this way: not truly for ours only, who perhaps have believed, but for the whole world, that is, for the sins of the entire human race, for the sins of all men who ever were, are, or will be, so that all ought to have believed that Christ was made a propitiation for them, just as we also believe.

What Estius objects, that the Apostle declares Christ to be the propitiation for the sins of those whose Advocate he is, that is indeed true, but not in an exclusive sense; he is the ἱλασμός not only for them, but for the whole world entirely. For that indicates that as many as have fallen or sinned can flee with true confidence to Christ the Paraclete and Advocate, as one who has reconciled all men to God the Father, and intercedes before the Father for all who flee to him. But who could betake themselves with confidence to Christ the Paraclete, if the propitiation were for only some and those very few, and he wished to take upon himself the patronage and advocacy of these alone, with the rest entirely excluded or passed over, and that by an absolute decree? Add that He intercedes for all by the power of His merit, in that for a general intercession He even begs for a space of repentance and a delay for those who do not wish to repent, and prays for grace to be granted to them. See Luke 13:8, 9; ch. 23:34. Concerning which passage St. Augustine in this epistle, col. 582: What does He say? Forgive them, for they know not what they do. He was expelling eternal death from them by a most merciful prayer and most excellent power. Many of them believed and the blood of Christ shed was forgiven them. First they shed it when they raged, they drank it when they believed. Therefore, a distinction must be made between the special intercession, of which John 17:9 speaks: I pray not for the world, but for those whom Thou hast given Me: And the general one, according to which Isaiah ch. 53:12 taught that Christ also prays for the transgressors.

As for Estius comparing the passage of John 11:52 here, which was also done by Maccovius, where although a multitude of nations is signified, yet the discourse is restricted to the children of God, namely by predestination, that is, the elect: I reply: If the Jewish children of God are here opposed to the nations, as those to whom the adoption belonged, Christ died not only for the nations, but also for the Jews, and therefore for all; nor indeed are only the elect among the nations understood under the name of nations, nor only those by predestination under the name of children of God, but those to whom the adoption belonged in a peculiar way of old; among whom, however, most were not predestined. What of the fact that Estius acknowledges that some who are not elect sometimes become partakers of the propitiation of Christ: therefore for some who are not elect Christ was also made a propitiation. For those for whom He was not made a propitiation cannot by any means become partakers of the propitiation. Some understand by 'the nation' the Jewish nation, and by 'the children of God scattered throughout the world' the elect from the nations; because, given this interpretation, were all the Jews, for whom Christ is said to have died, elect? Did Christ also wish to gather from the nations only those who were predestined? Did He not rather intend to gather all, and to that end did He not take care that the Gospel be preached to every creature? Therefore, those things cannot be understood exclusively of the children of God alone, without prejudice to the analogy of faith; so far is it from being the case that, when Christ is said to have died so that the scattered children of God might be gathered, it is denied that propitiation was made for the sins of all men. These ends of Christ's death are subordinate, not opposed, namely, the propitiation of the human race and the gathering of the Church from the whole world.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Καὶ αὐτὸς ἱλασμός ἐστι περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν) ἱλασμὸς pro ἱλαστὴς more Ebræo, & ἱλάσκειν facere ut cessent peccata. Sensus enim est: vires præstat, ne peccemus imposte- rum. Vide Ebr. 2, 17. & ibi dicta, & confer cum iis, quæ hic sequentur. Est autem in voce ἡμῶν κοίνωσις, quales multæ apud Paulum.

Particulam καὶ causaliter explicat Cornelius pro quia: Siquidem advocati munus sit etiam allegare, quibus justitiæ citra rei condemnationem satisfiat, quemadmodum Hesselius innuit. Plenius, inquit Estius, explicat Johannes excellentiam advocati no- stri, nempe qui talis sit, ut non alienam offerat Patri satisfactionem, sed exhibeat suam ac propriam: per quam non solum conatur ac satagit (ut apud hominem judicem faciunt Advocati) Deum reddere nobis pla- catum: verum certissime Deum nobis placat ac pro- pitium reddit. Quæ utut recte se habeant, reti- neri tamen potest sensus usitatior particulæ καὶ, hoc est, copulativus. Nam conjunguntur duo Sa- cerdotis nostri, qui fecit peccatorum nostrorum καθαρισμὸν sanguine suo, munia: tum oblatio, qua factus est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, tum in- tercessio pro nobis: quæ duo incumbebant Sacer- dotibus Veteris Testamenti, & sacrificare, & orare pro populo: Et faciunt utraque ad veniam pro peccatis nostris impetrandam, tum Christi propi- tiatio, cum obtulit se Deo pro nobis in odorem suavitatis, Eph. 5, 2. tum oratio, cum pro nobis in- terpellat apud Patrem, quod etsi fiat virtute ac præsentatione satisfactionis ipsius; manent tamen hæc duo munia distincta, & ἱλασμὸς vel propitia- tio facta est in ara crucis, intercessio eandem si- stens, ac propter eandem nobis veniam exorans sit in cœlis, etiamsi quoque in terris in diebus carnis Christi facta sit. Non autem dicit S. Johannes in concreto ἱλαστὴς propitiator, sed quod ἐμφατικώ- τερον est, ἱλασμὸς propitiatio, & sacrificium propi- tiatorium.

Est quidem CHRISTUS & Sacerdos ac propi- tiator, & sacrificium ipsum propitiatorium, quia semetipsum obtulit Deo pro nobis: Sed cur disce- damus a litera, nec tum Augustino intelligamus ipsum sacrificium propitiatorium? Non autem ἱλα- σμὸς propitiatio vel ἱλάσκειν propitiare, placare, est facere, ut cessent peccata, sed ut cesset ira propter peccata; est enim idem quod reconciliare, facere ex irato, placatum, & ut aliquis in gratiam redeat pe- nes eum, quem offenderat; quem verbi sensum nativum esse nemo nescit, ideoque amplexi sunt omnes Interpretes, si forte Socinum excipias: & refutavit depravationem illam in Socino Grotius ipse defens. fid. Cath. de satisf. Christ. c. X. p. 135. quod hac loquutione sacrificia respiciantur. Sen- sus autem ille quod fidem ingenerando per sacrifi- cium CHRISTI abstrahamur imposterum a pecca- tis ad sacrificium pro peccato, non pertineat. Sacri- ficia enim, inquit, non abstrahebant a peccato, præ- sertim fidem alicujus rei faciendo: neq; etiam re- missioni peractæ aut certo decretæ testimonium præ- bebant, sed ut ipse Socinus agnoscit, erant aliquod an- tecedens requisitum, ad remissionem, quod oftendunt illa verba: Expiabit & remittetur. In hoc ergo versatur comparatio, planeque, necesse est idem signifi- care expiationem cum sacrificiis legalibus, & cum Christo applicatur: quia utramque, deducit Scriptor ad Ebræos ex eodem decreto, nempe ut sine sanguinis effusione remissio non fiat, sed fiat expiatio in sangui- ne, Ebr. 9, 22. Observat & hoc Grotius, quod non solum apud Ebræos, sed & apud gentes peccata expia- re credita sint sacrificia, neque adeo dubitandum sit, cum in hoc ipso sacrificii expiatorii argumento vox Græca καθαρίζειν adhibita sit, quin eo sensu usurpata sit, quem lingua Græca receperat; quem- admodum & vocem ἱλάσκεσθαι ad victimas. Home- rus aliique, sæpissime aptarint, & Græci aliiq́, sacra lu- stralia sive piamenta ad placandum Numen, & sic impetrandam impunitatem antecommissorum adhi- buerint, atq́, ex autorum collatione manifestum fiat, ista ἰσοδυναμεῖν, Deum placari aliqua victima, De- orum iram expiari, aut animam cujuspiam Diis sufficere pro aliorum animis. Et cap. VII. pag. 92. Notissimum est, inquit, iram alicujus avertere, id dici Græce ἱλάσκεσθαι, εἰρηνοποιεῖν, καταλάσσειν, ἀποκα- ταλλάσσειν, Latine placare, pacare, conciliare aut re- conciliare, item propitiare: tum actus ipse, tum id quo proprie actus peragitur, Græcis ἱλασμὸς, Latinis pla- camen dicitur. In Deo ira, ut supra diximus appel- latur ἀνθρωποπαθῶς puniendi quasi affectus: quam Apostolus ait retegi sive revelari cælitus in omnem impietatem atq́, injustitiam hominum, ut qui veri- tatem in injustitia detineant, hoc est, cognitis Dei man- datis reluctentur. Nemo autem excipitur cum omnes simus natura filii iræ, hoc est, iræ Divinæ obnoxii. Hæc ira super quosdam manet, Joh. 3, 36. Super quos non manet, ab iis avertitur. Hanc aversionem Chri- stus sua morte impetrat, ideoq́, placamen rectissime dicitur. Sic eum bis appellat Johannes Apostolus, cum dixit: Si quis peccarit, advocatum habemus apud Patrem, Jesum Christum illum innocentem. Et ipse est ἱλασμὸς pro peccatis nostris, neq́, vero pro no- stris tantum, sed & pro peccatis totius mundi, epist. 1. cap. 2. v. 1. 2. Item in eo sua est dilectio, non quod nos Deum dilexerimus, sed quod ipse dilexerit nos, & Fi- lium suum miserit ἱλασμὸν pro peccatis nostris cap. 4. v. 10. Cum quo loco conferendus est ille Paulinus: Commendat Deus suam charitatem, quod cum pecca- tores adhuc essemus, Christus pro nobis est mortuus, Rom. 5, 8. Uterque, enim tam Paulus quam Johannes eodem argumento probant, non priores nos dilexisse, sed dilectos a Deo, & quod Paulus dicit mortuum esse, hoc Johannes vocat placamen esse factum. Adden- dus præterea locus ille Pauli: Justificamur gratis per redemptionem in Christo Jesu, quem Deus proposuit ἱλαστήριον per fidem in sanguine ipsius, Rom. 3, 24. 25. Factus est ergo Christus ἱλασμὸς sive ἱλαστήριον in san- guine suo, quod quid est aliud, quam id ipsum, quod negat Socinus, placatum a Christo Deum? Nam quod ἱλασμὸν apud Johannem expiationem interpretatur, expiationis autem voce destructionem peccati intelli- git, id facit nulla de causa, nullo munitus exemplo. ἱλάσκειν apud Græcos Scriptores omnes, Poëtas, histo- ricos alios, est placare, soletq́, construi cum Accusativo designante personam, cujus ira avertitur. Nec aliter apud LXX. Interpretes & Luc. 18, 13. usurpatur. Uno duntaxat loco, qui est Ebr. 2, 17. dicitur Chri- stus summus Sacerdos constitutus εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας τοῦ λαοῦ, ubi est enallage ex Ebraismo veniens ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας, cum usitate dici debuerit, ἱλάσκεσθαι θεὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν. Signi- ficat ergo ibi expiationem, sed eam quæ fit placando. Alioqui hic vocis usus nihil haberet commune cum na- tura vocis ac perpetua ejusdem significatione. Quare talem expiationem, qualem Socinus comminiscitur id est peccati destructionem, qua fit sine placamento, ista quidem vox ἱλάσκεσθαι & inde derivata ἱλασμὸς denotare non potest. Hæc Grotius. Sed & e Socinia- nis ipsis Schlichtingius hic Grotianis in locum præ- sentem annotatis adversatur, ut non semetipso so- lum, sed Socinianis quoque hæreticorum pessimis deterior evasisse videatur Grotius: Per propitiatio- nem, inquit, pro peccatis nostris intelligit, victimam propitiatoriam & expiatoriam, quod scilicet ille ipse, Deo sic volente & constituente, sanguinem suum fu- derit in remissionem peccatorum nostrorum, & sic Deum reddiderit nobis peccatoribus, si pœnitentiam agamus & vitam emendemus, plane propitium. Et postea: Victima propitiatoria dicitur propitiatio, quod per eam fiat propitiatio, per Metonymiam effe- cti pro causa, sicut Spiritus sanctus infra cap. 2, 27. appellatur unctio, quod sit cæleste illud oleum, per quod fit unctio. Addit Schlichtingius: Propitiatur ve- ro Deus non semper ut iratus placetur, sed etiam quando efficitur, ne, justas alioquin irascendi causas habens, & iram summa clementia & misericordia continens, tandem irascatur ac puniat: quod fit cum ipse ordinat victimam propitiatoriam, quam si quis negligat, tum demum iratum experturus Deum, si vero ad eam confugiat, mitem ac propitium, quod ma- xime factum est in Christo, quem non solum Deus ipse dedit victimam pro peccatis mundi, sed etiam Chri- stus ipse admirabilem in hoc Dei erga mundum cha- ritatem celebrat Joh. 3, 16.

Quæ sanum sensum habere possent: Sed pro- dit hæresin suam Schlichtingius cum subjicit: Quæ certe (charitas) Deum mundo tum fuisse iratum, nullo modo patitur. At nisi mundus ad Christum tanquam unicam expiationem confugiat, & sic in CHRISTUM credat, peccatis moriatur, Deo ac ju- stitiæ imposterum vivat, tanta Dei charitas in iram vertet horribilem. Atque hanc ob causam DEUS CHRISTUM pro mundi peccatis victimam de- dit ac fieri voluit, ut sicut seipsum ad remittenda pec- cata, sic mundum ad eadem relinquenda tanta victi- ma obstringeret. Verum enimvero frustra oppo- nitur dilectio Dei in dando generi humano Filio Unigenito demonstrata, & ira Dei adversus pecca- tum generis humani, quemadmodum opposita non sunt, conclusio omnium sub peccatum, & commisera- tio omnium, vel misericordia & justitia Divina. Fi- nem autem mortis CHRISTI Scriptura ex parte DEI non adsignat tantum, quod seipsum ad remit- tenda peccata obstringere voluerit, sicut ex parte ho- minum mundum ad eadem relinquenda tanta vi- ctima obstringere placuerit: Imo vero finem mortis CHRISTI, quæ victima est pro peccatis nostris, facit placationem Dei & expiationem pecca- torum, ut nobis remittantur, quemadmodum Gro- tius e sacrificiis Leviticis ante docuit: neque per victimam proprie nos obstringimur ad relinquen- da peccata, quod illa sit confirmatio doctrinæ a CHRISTO traditæ; sed beneficium illud, quod CHRISTUS seipsum sacrificium expiatorium pro nobis dederit, obstringit nos ad id, ut peccata relinquamus, eique qui pro nobis sese obtulit, nos dedamus & consecremus. Victimæ Leviticæ non obstringebant ad peccata imposterum relinquenda & fugienda, sed proprie faciebant ad peccata com- missa expianda, eorumque remissionem obtinen- dam, qua obtenta officium erat fidelium evitare peccata, Deoque servire, sed hoc uti consequens est expiationis & remissionis peccatorum; ita in phrasi ἱλασμᾶ περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν non conti- netur.

Cornelius a Lapide voce ἱλασμᾶ vult allusionem fieri ad propitiatorium imminens arcæ fœderis, siquidem id repræsentarit Christum propitiatorem, Rom. 3, 27. Exod. 25, 17. Sed quanquam ista mutuo se explicent ἱλαςήριον & ἱλασμὸς; hic tamen respici non tegmen arcæ, sed potius sacrificia propitiatoria, sanguinis & καθαρισμᾶ mentio, quæ præcessit, & paracleti vel Advocati vox confirmant.

De ipsa vero propitiatione disputat Estius anne intelligenda sit quoad sufficientiam, an vero quoad efficaciam, vel utrasq; ratione? Quod posterius assumit. Sentit enim, inquit, Johannes Christum reddere nobis Patrem propitium hostia crucis non solum sufficienter, ut loquuntur, sed efficienter. Non enim ait: Et ipse fuit propitiatio, tunc scilicet, quando offerebatur in cruce, sed ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris in quantum videlicet hostiam illam pro omnium salute sufficientem continue & usq; ad finem seculi quibus vult, applicat, ad remissionem peccatorum. Allegatq; in eam sententiam illa, quæ adversus Catharinum disseruit hic Hesselius.

Sed ambigue dicitur sufficientia vel de possibili vel de actuali. Illa quam Calvinisni solent statuere, quod nempe si Deus voluisset, potuisset sufficere pro omnibus omnium peccatis, ἱλὰσμὸς Christi hic omnino explodenda, & hæc quod ex voluntate Dei Patris Christum nobis εἰς ἱλασμὸν donantis, 1. Joh. 3, 10. & Christo, qui fieri voluit ἱλασμὸς pro peccatis nostris sufficiens pro omnibus actu ipso præstita sit satisfactio, & propitiatio, omnibusque acquisita sit peccatorum remissio, asserenda est.

Similiter in voce efficaciter ambiguitas est. Nam vel intelligitur de acquisitionis efficacia; quod omnium hominum peccata expiarit victima Christi, Deusq; redditus sit generi humano placabilis, imo placatus, ut neminem velit perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam converti & salvari, vel de applicatione & remissionis peccatorum effectu, quod nobis applicet expiationem Christi, actuq; ipso remittat, quod non nisi credentibus sit, & per fidem in Christum. Quanquam vero non inefficax statuenda sit ἱλασμᾶ Christi sufficientia; non tamen credendum, quod ita efficaciter vel efficienter propitiatio pro omnibus factus sit Christus, ut omnes peccatorum remissionem consequuti sint, quæ sententia nescio cujus ita dicti Apostatæ in Palatinor. refut. sellæ aureæ c. IX. p. 36. nobis imputatur per calumniam: Summa juxta ipsorum opinionem eadem ratio damnatorum est (sicut Apostata Helveticus Derendigensis tradit) ac si Imperator a Turcis captivos Christianos aliquot millenos ingenti pecuniæ summa redimeret, nec tantum vinculis & catenis, quibus in triremibus alligati erant, liberaret, sed etiam imperio restitueret, & ex Turcia in patriam reduceret. Hac ratione OMNES per Imperatorem non tantum propter plenissime persolutum λύτρον, sed & actualem restitutionem in pristinam libertatem redempti essent. Quod autem sit præter omnem opinionem Imperatoris, quidam nebulones fugam capessunt, & in Turciam de novo se præripientes malitiose pristinam captivitatem repetunt, in qua deinceps ipsis æternum permanendum & pereundum est. Sed de his alias.

Jam si vim aphorismi Apostolici respiciamus, non de expiationis Christi applicatione agit, quæ universalis non est ratione actus, & eventus, etiamsi ratione affectus & intentionis Divinæ universalis sit, sed de ipsa propitiatione in ara crucis facta per sacrificium corporis Christi, & effusionem sanguinis ejus pro peccatis generis humani, qua non quidem obtigit omnibus hominibus actualis remissio peccatorum, omnibus tamen impetrata est & acquisita, ac placatus est Deus omnibus, ita ut quisque eam sibi appropriare, adeoque obtinere possit, quum oblatio ejusdem etiam omnibus parta sit, per hanc Christi propitiationem. Quo sensu Leo M. ferm. XII. de passione: non tantum ait, effusio pro in- justis sanguinis justi tam potens fuit ad privilegium, tam dives ad pretium, ut si universitas captivorum in Redemptorem crederet, nullum tyrannica vincula re- tinerent, sed addit quoq; in Jesu Domino nostro omnes crucifixi, omnes mortui, omnes sepulti, omnes etiam sunt suscitati.

Οὐ περὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων δὲ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ ὅλου τοῦ κόσμου) Omnibus hominibus, qui ipsum sequi volent, hoc benefi- cium præstabit. Περὶ ὅλου τοῦ κόσμου breviter dictum pro περὶ τὰ ὅλου τοῦ κόσμου, quod recte vidit Latinus Interpres. Par constructio Ebr. 11, 4. & alibi. Dicitur autem recte &c. ἱλάσκεσθαι aut ἐξιλάσκεσθαι ἁμαρτίας & περὶ ἁμαρτίας, ut vi- dere est Exod. 32, 29. & alibi.

Non de voluntate Dei præstandi beneficium ἱλασ- μοῦ, sed de ἱλασμῷ vel propitiatione sonat apho- rismus Apostolicus, nec suspenditur hic ἱλασμὸς a conditione, quasi omnibus hominibus factus sit propitiatio, si ipsum sequi volent, & a voluntate humana dependeat ipsa a Christo facta peccato- rum expiatio, sed de eadem in se spectata agitur, quam fecit Christus priusquam consideret ad de- xtram Majestatis teste Apostolo, Ebr. 1, 3. Verba au- tem ista non pro nostris tantum, sed pro totius mundi peccatis non cum Cyrillo l. XI. in Joh. cap. 19. intelli- genda, non pro peccatis Judæorum tantum, sed & gentium omnium; nec cum Oecumenio non tantum pro nostris peccatis, id est, eorum, qui nunc vivunt, sed etiam pro peccatis eorum, qui nascituri sunt, quamdiu mundus durabit, aut cum aliis non pro nostris tantum, id est, eorum, ad quos scribo, verum pro peccatis totius Ecclesiæ, quæ Bedæ est explicatio, aut prout alii interpretantur pro peccatis non tan- tum eorum, qui jam credunt, sed & omnium electo- rum, quos adhuc ex omnibus mundi partibus ad fidem adducturus est: quia nuspiam in Scripturis per totum mundum intelliguntur electi, vel Eccle- sia. Sed hoc modo non tantum pro peccatis no- stris, h. e. eorum, qui credimus, verum etiam pro pec- catis omnium hominum, quotquot sunt, fuerunt, aut futuri sunt. Loquitur enim S. Johannes ex perso- na credentium, neque tantum eorum, sed & quo- rumvis hominum Christum propitiationem esse indigitat; quia nomine τοῦ ὅλου τοῦ κόσμου intelligun- tur omnes homines: ad quem sensum facile redit Cyrilli expositio, quatenus Judæorum & gentium nomine non fideles tantum e Judæis & gentibus, sed totius orbis homines, qui consuevere in Ju- dæos & gentes distribui, designatur, Joh. 11, 51. Ideo- que Estio, qui de credentibus solis cum Calvinianis explicat, opponimus hic Cornelium a Lapide: is enim fatetur, melius habere explicationem Cle- mentis Alexandrini & aliorum, q. d. non pro peccatis nostris, qui sumus fideles tantum, sed & pro peccatis infidelium totius mundi. Pro his enim quoq; passus est Christus, eisq; meruit gratiam & gloriam, si in eum credere, ejusq; merita amplecti velint. Unde & jussit prædicari Evangelium hoc omnibus gentibus, easque baptizari in nomine Patris & Filii & Spiritus sancti, Marc. 16, 15.

Maccovio vero Calviniano colleg. de prædestin. disp. XIII. p. 37. qui contendit oppositionem insti- tui non inter electos universe sumptos, & mundum, seu inter electos, qui erant ex Judæis & electos, qui erant ex gentibus, Joh. 12, 52. Item oppositio- nem institui inter electos, qui crediderint sive jam fideles, & mundum, id est, electos, qui nondum credunt, Joh. 17. vers. 10. aliisque inter Calvinia- nos opponimus præter veteres per mundum uni- versum genus humanum intelligentes, Origenem hom. XXIV. super Numer. Ambrosium l. IX. ep. 71.

Prosperum in Resp. ad Gall. capit: Johannem Hus- sum in h. l. etiam ex ipsis Reformatis Rudolph. Gualtherum in h. l. Job. Calvinum in h. l. Bulinge- rum serm. II. de nativit. Christ. p. 9. Wolffgangum Musculum in explic. Matth. 26. Andream Hype- rium in explic. 1. Tim. 2. p. 68. Christophorum Pe- zelium in explic. 1. cap. Joh. p. 162. Zachariam Ursinum in explic. Catech. p. 70. Georgium Sob- nium disp. Marp. VI. th. 21. Barthol. Copen. disp. de satisf. Anno 1616. th. 25. Matth. Martin. disp. II. de univers. doctr. Christ. Relig. th. 18. Paulum Steinium in Evang. Ephes. fraternir. p. 1. c. II. p. 340. Johannem Crocium in exposit. epist. ad Tit. c. 2. II. doctr. II. & in beat. salut. scal. Germ. p. 161. Jo- hannem Bergium in explicat. dicti Joh. 3, 16. & in de convenient. & different. Evangel. p. 71. Oppo- nimus & Palatinos Theol. refut. scal. aureæ & au- reol. de merit. Christ. Ann. 1592. p. 17. Theologos Nassovicos, Johan. Henricum Alstedium & Georg. Fabricium in judicio de secundo Remonstrant. Articulo. Theologos M. Britanniæ, Georgium Landavensem, Johannem Davenantium, Samuelem Wardum, Thomam Goadum, Gualther. Blangval- lum itidem in judicio de secundo artic. Remonstr. Opponimus deniq; confessionem Bohemicam an- no 1551. oblatam artic. 6. quæ de omnibus omnium hominum peccatis hoc dictum accipit, & brevem confessionem Germanicam Heidelbergensem Anno 1562. editam p. 27. Christi mors est pro peccatis totius mundi, hoc est, non tantum pro peccatis e- lectorum, ad quos scribebat, sed etiam pro aliis o- mnibus hominibus in toto mundo usque ad finem ejus victuris. Quid ? quod Christ. Massonius A- natom. univers. part. I. c. 39. p. 333. universos Patres Synodi Dordrectenæ ea ratione intellexisse auream hanc S. Johannis sententiam Par. II. cap. 3. censeat, nec ab ullo Theologorum (Reformatorum) huic interpretationi contradici facile, eamque Evange- lio consentaneam esse, quod omnibus hominibus in perfectissimo Christi merito sufficientissimam propitiationem ostendat, nec minus congruere consolationi; quam S. Johannes in fide infirmis peccatoribus proponit, ne in peccatis suis, si quis forsan præoccupatus fuerit, desperet, vel alibi, quam in Christo remissionem quærat, sed fide & vera fiducia unico perfectissimo Filii Dei sacrificio innitatur, utpote quod dives, pretiosum, & efficax satis sit ad propitiationem non tantum pro illo- rum, sed etiam pro totius mundi peccatis &c.

Sane S. Johannes non tantum adhibet generale το̃ κόσμου mundi nomen, quod dicente Job. Crocio fideles & infideles complectitur in se, & majorem jux- ta Bullingerum, emphasin habet, longeque effica- cius est, quam vox hominum, qua fatente Radolpho Gualthero in h. l. uti voluit Apostolus, ne aliquem a Christi merito exclusum putaremus: Sed & addi- tur universalitatis nota ὅλου του̃ κόσμου, ne id aliquos solum e mundo concernere arbitremur, sed ut omnes ex æquo homines in mundo per Christum propi- tiatus crederemus. Nec id solum, sed procedit quoque D. Johannes a fidelium commemoratione ad universum genus humanum admodum luculen- ta ampliatione, non pro totius mundi vel omnium homi- num peccatis. Non contentus, inquit Gualtherus, Christum propitiationem nostram dixisse, eum pro peccatis nostris propitiationem factum esse testatur. Nec hoc illi sufficit. Ne enim vel in sua duntaxat, vel Apostolorum aliorum persona loqui videretur, addit, non pro nostris tantum, sed etiam pro totius mundi peccatis. Quæ quidem ampliatio ad solidam consolationis Apostolicæ vim pernecessaria erat ne quis- quam peccatorum desperet, & ab intercessionis Para- clesi hujus fructu salutari sese exclusum dubitatio- num fluctibus abreptus præsumat, cujus rationis vim agnoscit loco citato Massonius. Si voce περὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων indigitantur electi, qui tum temporis cre- debant, utique vox ea non solum Judæos, sed gen- tiles quoque credentes complectetur, quod con- trarium est priori Maccovii explicationi, quam tamen utramq; conjungit & tuetur. Si voce pro no- stris designati fuere, qui tum credebant actu, voce autem totius mundi, qui credituri erant actu, quid fiet de illis, qui jam antea crediderunt sub primor- dia Novi Testamenti, qui crediderunt in Veteri Testamento, qui crediderunt inde ab initio Eccle- siæ post lapsum collectæ? Posita tamen in priori membro ista expositione adhuc illibata manet in posteriori vis universalitatis hoc pacto, non vero pro nostris tantum, qui forte crediderimus, sed pro totius mundi, id est pro universi generis humani, pro omnium hominum peccatis, qui unquam fuerunt, sunt, erunt, adeo, ut omnes credere debuerint, pro se factum esse Christum propitiationem, prout nos etiam credimus.

Quod objicit Estius Apostolum declarare, Christum propitiationem esse pro illorum peccatis, quorum est Advocatus, id verum quidem est, sed non sensu exclusivo, non tantum illorum, sed pro toto omnino mundo est ἱλασμός. Id enim indicat, quotquot lapsi fuerint aut peccarint, confugere posse vera fiducia ad Christum Paracletum, & ad- vocatum, utpote qui omnes homines Deo Patri reconciliavit, & pro omnibus, qui ad ipsum confu- giunt, apud Patrem interpellat. Qui vero cum fi- ducia ad Christum Paracletum se recipere possent, si quorundam tantum eorumque paucissimorum propitiatio esset atque horum solum patrocinium & advocaturam in se vellet recipere, cæteris pror- sus exclusis vel præteritis, idque absoluto decreto? Adde quod pro omnibus intercedat vi meriti sui, quod ad intercessionem generalem etiam illis spa- tium pœnitendi & moram exoret, ac pro gratia ipssis concedenda precetur, qui nolunt pœnitere. Vid. Luc. 13, 8. 9. cap. 23, 34. De quo loco S. Au- gustinus in hanc epistol. col. 582. Quid ait? Ignosce illis, quia nesciunt quid faciunt. Mortem sempiter- nam ab eis expellebat prece misericordissima & po- tentia præstantissima. Multi ex eis crediderunt & dimissus est eis fusus sanguis Christi. Primo fuderunt cum sævirent, biberunt cum crederent. Distinguen- dum ergo inter specialem intercessionem, de qua Joh. 17, 9. Non pro mundo rogo, sed pro his, quos dedisti mihi: Et inter generalem, secundum quam etiam pro prævaricatoribus orare Christum Esaias cap. 54, 13. docuit.

Quod Estius locum Joh. 11, 52. hic confert, quod a Maccovio etiam factum, ubi licet multitudo gen- tium significetur, tamen restringatur sermo ad filios Dei, nimirum prædestinatione, hoc est, electos: Resp. Si gentibus hic opponantur Judæi filii DEI, utpote quorum erat adoptio, non tantum pro gen- tibus, sed etiam pro Judæis mortuus est Christus, adeoq; pro omnibus; nec vero ita vel sub gentis no- mine intelliguntur soli electi in gente, vel sub filio- rum Dei soli prædestinatione filii, sed quibus pecu- liari ratione conveniebat olim adoptio; inter quos tamen pleriq; erant non prædestinati. Quid quod quosdam non electos interdum propitiationis Christi participes fieri agnoscat Estius: pro quibusdam ergo non electis etiam Christus factus est propitiatio. Pro quibus enim non factus est propitiatio, illi neutiquam participes fieri possunt propitiationis. Nonnulli per gentem intelligunt Judaicam gentem, per filios Dei dispersos per orbem electos e gentibus, quia interpretatione posita, num Judæi, pro quibus mortuus dicitur Christus, electi erant omnes? Num colligere etiam voluit Christus e gentibus tantum eos, qui prædestinati fuere? Annon intendit po- tius omnes congregare, eoque fine omni creaturæ Evangelium prædicari curavit? Non ergo exclusi- ve de filiis Dei solis illa intelligi possunt salva fidei analogia, tantum abest, ut cum mortuus Christus dicitur, ut filii Dei dispersi colligantur, negetur propitiatio facta esse pro omnium hominum pec- catis. Subordinati sunt hi fines mortis Christi non oppositi, nimirum propitiatio generis humani, & collectio Ecclesiæ e toto terrarum orbe.

## 2:3
Vers. 3.

Καὶ ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν, ὅτι ἐγνώκαμεν ἀυτὸν, ἐὰν τὰς ἐν- τολὰς ἀυτοῦ τηρῶμεν) To perform the precepts of Christ is indeed the same thing as to cease from sins, of which I have already spoken. Thus we shall be certain that we have arrived at that knowledge of Christ which is useful, if we obey His precepts. There is a certain knowledge that is useless and damnable, Rom. 1:21. There is a certain useful knowledge, which is called knowledge κατ' ἐξοχὴν (by way of excellence) and often ἐπίγνωσις (full knowledge). Aristotle: 'To learn is said to be to understand, when one uses the knowledge.' What the Apostle handed down concerning the incarnate Word, and His benefits overflowing to us, communion with the Father, purification from sins and remission of sins or justification, concerning the advocacy of Christ for us before the Father, and concerning the propitiation made for our sins through Christ, he handed down for this reason: that they might receive Christ with true faith, and persevere in that faith, as being He from whom and in whom they have such great benefits. Now he explains the nature of that faith and the signs by which true faith is known, and warns us not to allow ourselves to be led away by the world and the Spirit of the Antichrist. The Apostle therefore commends to those to whom he writes the observation of the commandments of God, and especially concerning loving one's neighbor, and this on account of those who boasted of faith and the knowledge of the true God, while neglecting good works, which necessarily follow faith. And this is generally the interpretation of most. Flacius, however, prefers that it be taught here that Christ is rightly acknowledged and worshipped from the Gospel, not from the doctrines and commandments of men. Now furthermore, he says, he discourses on the doctrine through which we may be able to acknowledge and apprehend such a Savior, or the life-giving Word, and His benefits. He says, therefore, that the true acknowledgment and apprehension of Him comes to us from no other source than from His precepts, that is, from the most faithful acceptance, examination, and knowledge of His doctrine. For all wish to appear to be true worshippers of God, and to have known Him: but yet they do not wish to acknowledge and worship Him according to His Word, but according to their own dreams and the doctrines of men, by which they acknowledge and worship Him wrongly and in vain, just as Christ Himself testifies from the Prophet Isaiah. It is not a question here of the perfect obedience of the law of God; that someone might acknowledge himself to be a Christian from his own righteousness of works: but the observation of the commandments here signifies the true knowledge of His doctrine. Yet without neglecting the effort to conceive faith from it, and to lead a pious life. Thus also in John chapter fourteen CHRIST discourses copiously on the keeping of His sayings and commandments: this sentiment is not legal, but plainly Evangelical. See there especially in the twenty-third verse. 'Commandment' here simply signifies the doctrine of the Gospel, just as soon in verse 5 he uses the word 'saying' for this expression. Thus also in John 14 he uses these words interchangeably, as if they were equivalent. To which contributes what Flacius had observed in his Key at the word 'command,' that 'commandment' is worth the same as instruction, doctrine, and mandates, testimonies, judgments, statutes, Word, law, and the like. St. John had said that we have an advocate, Jesus Christ; now he prescribes the manner by which we may secure that advocate for ourselves, if we know Him, that is, embrace Him with true faith. He had said that He is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world; now he teaches how each one may enjoy this propitiation, namely through faith, the character of which he describes, and that those alone know Him who observe His precepts.

Καὶ ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν: And in this we know, which knowledge is not doubtful and conjectural, as the Papists wish, but certain and infallible, because a demonstration a posteriori, from a necessary consequence, leaves no doubt about the antecedent from which it necessarily flows, since it cannot arise from elsewhere: Whence Catharinus himself concludes that the just know certainly that they are just, and in the grace of God. For we conclude from the observation of the commandments of the Lord, which arises only from faith, the antecedent, faith itself, or that we know the Lord. Estius says that it is indeed certain that he who keeps the commandments of God knows God, but he denies that we are infallibly certain that we keep the commandments of God. Resp. If this is understood of the all-encompassing observation of the commandments of God, that we are most certain, there is no one who keeps the commandments of God, just as there is no man who does not sin, 1 Kings 8. But from a sincere effort to observe the commandments of the Lord, and from love that is unfeigned, we are indeed certain of faith: for this is working through love, Gal. 5:6; love is the fruit of faith. Can the consequent exist without the antecedent, the effect without the cause, the fruit without the tree?

By the word 'He' (αὐτὸς) some understand God, namely the Father, who was mentioned in v. 1; others understand Christ, who was designated immediately before by the same pronoun in v. 2. Which is more convenient, not only because He is immediately designated, but also because in the following verses He is understood by 'the same' (τὸν αὐτὸν), v. 3, where 'His commandments' (ἐντολαὶ ἀυτοῦ) are named, v. 5, where 'His word' (λόγος ἀυτοῦ) is expressed, and 'to be in Him' (ἐν ἀυτῷ εἶναι), v. 6, where 'to abide in Him' (ἐν ἀυτῷ μένειν), and to walk thus, 'just as He walked' (καθὼς ἐκεῖνος), we are commanded. And Christ, as our propitiation, is the proper object of faith.

ὅτι ἐγνώκαμεν αὐτὸν, because we have known him. Which knowledge, as the Papist interpreters Estius, Cornelius a Lapide, and others admit, is not merely speculative, but practical or affective, embracing an act of the intellect and of the will equally: yet it is not the knowledge of charity: for this would be to prove the same by the same; we acknowledge the Lord by the knowledge of charity, because we keep the commandments of the charity of God and of the neighbor. It is called practical, however, on account of the practice of faith, since we so acknowledge the Lord Jesus that we embrace him through faith, and adhere to him, so that we receive him through faith, John 1:12, put him on through faith, Galatians 3:27, and through faith are and remain in him, below verse 5, ἐὰν τὰς ἐντολὰς ἀυτῶ τηρῶμεν, if we keep his commandments. Which observation of the commandments of Christ is not to be understood as the perfect fulfillment of the law, but as a sincere obedience free from hypocrisy, and the charity of God and of the neighbor; which, if it be estimated with respect to the perfection of the Lord's commandments, consists more in affection and zeal and an unfeigned endeavor than in the effect and the work owed. For even if the affection breaks forth, and the zeal shows itself, yet more imperfection and impurity clings to it than that the observation of the law can be judged perfect in the eyes and judgment of God. For who is there who loves God with all his heart, with all his mind, with all his soul, and with all his strength? Who is there who loves his neighbor entirely, as himself? It is no wonder, therefore, that the Papists are uncertain about the grace of God, who place the grace of God in perfect charity. Cornelius argues thus against his Catharinus in this place: Be it so, let the righteous have grace and the love of God in their soul, yet they do not see it: Again, although they may observe the commandments of God outwardly, yet they do not know whether they observe them out of the love of God and with that love with which God commanded. Finally, suppose they feel that they love God, yet they do not know whether this love of the Deity is such as it ought to be, namely supernatural, purely for the sake of God, and that they love Him above all things. But the grace of God and the charity of God are first confused. The former is the affection of mercy or charity in God towards us: The latter is the affection of love in us towards God. Next, the state of the question is perverted; it is not asked whether we can be justified or obtain the grace of God from the love with which we embrace God. For we readily grant that no one is justified before God by the observation of the commandments of God or by the charity of God and neighbor, because by that sign, however, and τεκμηρίῳ, that we love God and neighbor not indeed perfectly, yet sincerely, we know, as the Apostle testifies, that we are endowed with true faith, which faith is the means of the remission of sins and of justification: and therefore from this τεκμηρίῳ we also know that we are in the grace of God. For who would not be in the grace of God, to whom God has forgiven sins? Furthermore, as we recognize charity proceeding outwardly: so also we are not ignorant that the same proceeds from the love of God, in which faith is active through charity. Who can know that this love of God is sincere, whose heart has been purified by faith, Acts 15:9. For although imperfections intervene, they do not, however, take away the sincerity of the affection: But they only show our weakness, and that renewal here is only begun, not consummated: since evil lies close to us when we wish to do good, about which Paul himself complained at length, Rom. 7:14 ff.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Καὶ ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν, ὅτι ἐγνώκαμεν ἀυτὸν, ἐὰν τὰς ἐν- τολὰς ἀυτοῦ τηρῶμεν) Facere præcepta Christi id vero idem est, quod cessare a peccatis, de quo jam dixi. Ita certi erimus, nos ad notitiam illam Christi, quæ utilis est, pervenisse, si præceptis ejus pareamus. Est cogni- tio quædam inutilis & damnosa Rom. 1, 21. Est quæ- dam utilis, quæ κατ' ἐξοχὴν cognitio & sæpe ἐπίγνωσις dicitur. Aristoteles: Τὸ μανθάνειν λέγεται συνιέναι, ὅταν χρῆται τῇ ἐπιστήμῃ. Quæ Apostolus tradidit de Verbo incarnato, e- jusque beneficiis in nos redundantibus, communione cum Patre, purificatione a peccatis & remissione peccatorum vel justificatione, de advocatura Christi pro nobis apud Patrem, & de propitiatio- ne pro peccatis nostris per Christum facta, ideo tradidit, ut vera fide susciperent Christum, & in ea fide perseverarent, utpote a quo & in quo tanta habeant beneficia. Jam naturam fidei istius & signa exponit, quibus fides vera cognoscitur, a qua ne per mundum, & AntiChristi Spiritum nos abduci patiamur, monet. Commendat ergo Apostolus iis, ad quos scribit, observationem mandatorum Dei, & præcipue de diligendo proximo, idque propter illos, qui de fide & notitia veri Dei gloriabantur, opera bona, quæ fidem necessario consequuntur, negli- gentes. Atque hæc fere plerorumque est inter- pretatio. Flacius tamen mavult hic doceri ex Ev- angelio recte Christum agnosci & coli, non ex do- ctrinis & mandatis hominum. Nunc porro, inquit, disserit de doctrina, per quam agnoscere & apprehen- dere tantum Servatorem, aut Verbum vivificum, ejusque beneficia queamus. Ait igitur veram ejus agnitionem & apprehensionem non aliunde nobis, quam ex ejus præceptis, id est, ex doctrina ipsius fide- lissima acceptione, scrutatione ac cognitione contigere. Omnes enim volunt videri esse veri cultores Dei, eumque novisse: Sed tamen nolunt eum agnoscere & colere secundum ejus Verbum, sed juxta sua propria somnia & doctrinas hominum, quibus eum male fru- straque agnoscunt & colunt, sicut & Christus ipse ex Propheta Esaia testatur. Non agitur hic de perfecta obedientia legis Dei; quod ex sua operum justitia ali- quis agnoscat se esse Christianum: Sed observatio mandatorum hic significat veram ejus doctrinæ co- gnitionem. Non tamen neglecto studio concipiendi inde fidem, & agendi piam vitam. Sic etiam Johan- nis decimo quarto CHRISTUS copiose disserit de sermonum & mandatorum suorum custodia: non est hæc sententia legalis, sed plane Evangelica. Vide ibi- dem præsertim versu vigesimo tertio. Mandatum hic simpliciter doctrinam Evangelii significat, ut mox vers. 5. pro hac dictione utitur voce sermonis. Sic quoque Johan. 14. promiscue istis vocibus utitur, tan- quam ipsis æquipollentibus. Quo facit quæ in Clave observarat Flacius ad vocem mando, quod manda- tum idem valeat, quod instructio, doctrina, & man- data, testimonia, judicia, statuta, Verbum, lex & si- milia. Dixerat S. Johannes advocatum nos ha- bere Jesum Christum; jam modum praescribit, quo advocatum illum nobis conciliemus, si eum cogno- scamus, hoc est, vera fide amplectamur. Dixerat propitiationem ipsum esse pro peccatis totius mundi; nunc quomodo quisque hac propitiatione frua- tur, docet, nimirum per fidem, cujus indolem de- scribit, ac quod ii demum cognoscant ipsum, qui praecepta ejus observant.

Kai ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν: Et in hoc cognoscimus, quae cognitio non est dubia & conjecturalis, quod Pontificii volunt, sed certa & infallibilis, quia de- monstratio a posteriori, a necessario consequente du- bium non relinquit de antecedente, e quo necessa- rio fluit, quum aliunde oriri non possit: Unde Ca- tharinus ipse colligit, justos certo scire, se esse justos, & in gratia Dei. Colligimus enim ex observatione mandatorum Domini, quae non nisi ex fide oritur, antecedens, ipsam fidem, vel quod Dominum co- gnoscamus. Estius certum quidem esse, ait, eum qui mandata Dei servat, nosse Deum, negat autem infal- libiliter certos nos esse, quod mandata Dei servemus. Resp. Si de omnimoda observatione mandatorum Dei id intelligatur, certissimos nos esse, tam nemi- nem esse, qui mandata Dei servet, quam non est homo, qui non peccet, 1. Reg. 8. Sed e sincero stu- dio mandata Domini observandi, & charitate ἀνυ- ποκρίτῳ certi sane sumus de fide: Haec enim ope- rosa est per charitatem, Gal. 5, 6. charitas fructus est fidei. Num consequens esse potest sine antece- dente, effectus sine causa, fructus sine arbore?

Voce αὐτὸς aliqui Deum intelligunt, Patrem ni- mirum, cujus v. 1. mentio facta, alii Christum proxi- me designatum eodem pronomine vers. 2. Quod convenientius, non tantum quod immediate is de- signatus sit, sed etiam quod in sequentibus per τὸν αὐτὸν intelligatur, v. 3. ubi ἐντολαὶ ἀυτῶ nominan- tur, v. 5. ubi λόγος ἀυτῶ exprimitur, & ἐν ἀυτῷ εἶναι, v. 6. ubi ἐν ἀυτῷ μένειν, & ita ambulare, καθὼς ἐκεῖ- νος sicut ille ambulavit, jubemur. Estque Christus tanquam propitiatio nostra objectum fidei proprium.

ὅτι ἐγνώκαμεν αὐτὸν, quoniam cognovimus ipsum. Quae cognitio fatentibus Pontificiis Interpretibus Estio, Cornelio a Lapide, aliis, non est tantum specu- lativa, sed practica, vel affectiva, complectens actum intellectus pariter & voluntatis: non tamen est cognitio charitatis: nam hoc foret idem per idem probare posse; agnoscimus Dominum noti- tia charitatis, quia servamus mandata charitatis Dei & proximi. Dicitur autem Practica ob praxin fidei, cum ita Dominum Jesum agnoscimus, ut per fidem eum amplectamur, eique adhaereamus, ut fi- fide eum recipiamus, Joh. 1, 12. per fidem eum indua- mus Gal. 3, 27. per fidem in ipso simus & maneamus infra vers. 5. ἐὰν τὰς ἐντολὰς ἀυτῶ τηρῶμεν, si man- data ejus servemus. Quae mandatorum Christi obser- vatio non de perfecta legis impletione intelligen- da, sed de sincera, & hypocriseos experte obedientia, & charitate Dei atque proximi; quae si respectu perfectionis mandatorum Domini aestimetur, magis in affectu & studio ac conatu minime fucato, quam in effectu & opere debito consistit. Nam etsi pro- rumpat affectus, & studium sese demonstret: plus tamen ei haeret imperfectionis, & impuritatis, quam ut perfecta censeri possit in oculis & judicio Dei legis observatio. Ecquis enim est, qui Deum ex toto corde, ex tota mente, ex tota anima & ex o- mnibus viribus diligat? Ecquis tantum est, qui pro- ximum ex asse diligat, sicut semetipsum? Non mi- rum ergo, incertos esse de gratia Dei Papistas, qui gratiam Dei in charitate perfecta constituunt. Cornelius adversus Catharinum suum ita disputat h. l. Esto, habeant justi in animo gratiam & charita- tem Dei, tamen eam non vident: Rursum licet man- data Dei exterius observent, tamen nesciunt an ea ob- servent ex amore Dei & eo amore, quo Deus jussit. Denique esto sentiant, se amare Deum, tamen ne- sciunt an hic amor Deitatis, qualis esse debet, puta supernaturalis pure propter Deum, utque eum ament super omnia. Sed confunditur primum gratia Dei, & charitas Dei. Illa est affectus misericordiæ vel charitatis in Deo erga nos: Hæc est affectus dile- ctionis in nobis erga Deum. Deinde pervertitur status, non id quæritur, anne possimus ex dilectio- ne, qua Deum complectimur, justificari, vel gra- tiam Dei consequi. Nam id ultro largimur ex ob- servatione mandatorum Dei vel charitate Dei & proximi neminem justificari coram Deo, quod il- lo tamen signo, & τεκμηρίῳ, quod non perfecte qui- dem, sincere tamen Deum & proximum diligimus, cognoscimus, Apostolo teste, nos nempe fide præ- ditos esse vera, quæ fides est medium remissionis peccatorum & justificationis: ideoque ex isto et- iam τεκμηρίῳ cognoscimus, nos esse in gratia Dei. Qui enim non in gratia Dei esset, cui remisit Deus peccata? Porro ut charitatem ad extra prodeuntem agnoscimus: ita etiam eandem ex amore Dei pro- ficisci non ignoramus, in quibus fides per charita- tem operosa est. Quem Dei amorem esse since- rum cognoscere potest, cujus cor purificatum est fide, Actor. 15, 9. Etsi enim imperfectiones inter- veniant, illæ tamen sinceritatem affectus non tol- lunt: Sed infirmitatem nostram modo ostendunt, & quod inchoata hic tantum sit renovatio, non consummata: quandoquidem nobis bonum ope- rari volentibus adjaceat malum, quo de Paulus ipse prolixe conquestus est, Rom. 7, 14. seqq.

## 2:4
Vers. 4.

Ὁ λέγων, ἔγνωκα αὐτὸν καὶ τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ μὴ τηρῶν ψεύστης ἐστί) He who says I know him, namely as is fitting. In the Manuscript ὁ λέγων ὅτι ἔγνωκα, which is a frequent expression among us.

Καὶ ἐν τούτῳ ἡ ἀλήθεια οὐκ ἔστιν) A repetition of the same thing or nearly the same, such as above c. 1:8.

If anyone says that he believes in Christ, and does not observe his commandments, he is a liar, and the truth is not in him. Show me your faith by your works, and I will show you my faith by my works, Jas. 2:18. Most rightly, therefore, it is gathered from that, that he who does not have charity lacks faith, the consequence of which Estius rashly denies. Do you want to know, O vain man, that faith without works or destitute of works, not having charity, is dead, says James again, ch. 2:20. Let not the mind be deceived, and consider itself to have known God, says Augustine, book on faith and works, ch. 12, if it confesses with dead faith, that is, without good works. Whoever does not love God, says Bede, truly shows that he does not know how lovable He is, and has not learned to taste and see how sweet and pleasant the Lord is, who does not strive to please His sight with continuous love. Cf. 1 John 3:7.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Ὁ λέγων, ἔγνωκα αὐτὸν καὶ τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ μὴ τηρῶν ψεύστης ἐστί) Qui dicit novi eum, nempe ut oportet. In Manuscripto ὁ λέγων ὅτι ἔγνωκα, quæ loquutio nostris frequens.

Καὶ ἐν τούτῳ ἡ ἀλήθεια οὐκ ἔστιν) Repetitio rei ejusdem aut prope ejusdem, qualis supra c. 1, 8.

Si quis dicat se in Christum credere, & non obser- vat mandata ejus, mendax est, & veritas non est in ipso. Ostende mihi fidem tuam ex operibus tuis, & ego ostendam tibi fidem meam ex operibus meis, Jac. 2, 18. Rectissime itaque inde colligitur. fide carere illum, qui charitatem non habet, cujus consequentia veritatem temere negat Estius. Visne scire, o homo vane, quod fides sine operibus vel o- peribus destituta charitatem non habens, mortua est, inquit iterum Jacobus cap. 2, 20. Nequaquam mens fallatur, & se æstimet Deum cognovisse, inquit Augustinus l. de fid. & operibus cap. 12. si cum fide mortua, hoc est sine bonis operibus confiteatur. Quis- quis Deum non amat, ait Beda, profecto ostendit, quia quam sit amabilis, non novit, & quam sit suavis Do- minus & dulcis, gustare & videre non didicit, qui ejus conspectibus placere continua dilectione non satagit. Conf. 1. Job. 3, 7.

## 2:5
Vers. 5.

ὃς δ' ἂν τηρῇ αὐτοῦ τὸν λόγον) By λόγον he understands that part of the Gospel which consists in precepts, as the following shows.

Ἀληθῶς ἐν τούτῳ ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ Θεοῦ τετελείωται) He does not only know God, but also loves Him perfectly. Love presupposes knowledge. And so there is an opposition here with an addition. The precepts of Christ express the will of God. But no one can show more strongly that he is held by the love of God than if he accommodates himself in all things to the will of God.

Now he explains the nature of faith as if a priori. But he who keeps his τὸν λόγον, Word or discourse; he is no longer speaking about a sign of faith or knowledge; but rather he explains in what properly faith in Christ is occupied, namely that it may keep His Word. Not without cause does he change the discourse: he does not say he who keeps His commandments, as he had spoken before about the commandments: although we have previously observed from Flacius that τὰς ἐντολὰς can also be explained as the Evangelical Word: But he who has kept His Word, and therefore the predicate is also different, namely ἀληθῶς ἐν τούτῳ ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ Θεοῦ τετελείωται, truly in him the charity of God is perfected. Without doubt he drew this phrase from the mouth of Christ, which Christ Himself also used in this way in John ch. 8:51. Ἐάν τις τὸν λόγον τὸν ἐμὸν τηρήσῃ θάνατον οὐ μὴ θεωρήσῃ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα: where it is certain that it deals with keeping the Evangelical Word, which is not kept except through faith. But in him who keeps the Word of the Gospel by faith, the love of God is truly perfected, and exerts itself perfectly; love, I say, not that with which we pursue God, but that with which God embraces us. For the love of God is poured out in the hearts of the faithful through the Holy Spirit, Rom. 5, 5. What is ἐκκέχυται there, this is τετελείωται in the present passage: there is a perfect diffusion, there is a perfect dilation of Divine love in our hearts, in both cases by reason of our sense, namely that we taste and feel the same abundantly in our hearts, and with the highest pleasure designated, and IN HIM here is the same as Paul's in their hearts, namely of the faithful. But if anyone prefers to understand the perfection of the love of God not as to sense but as to effect, it is not inconvenient likewise [to understand it as] the love of God towards us, and far more correctly of that, than of the love with which we pursue God; the latter is far from perfection. It is also to be observed that the love of God can be perfected, just as the power of God is perfected τελειῶται in our infirmity, 2 Cor. 12, 9, when it exerts itself more effectively; which happens entirely ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ in our infirmity, and so its efficacy is felt and acknowledged in us. We also discover this sense concerning the love of God towards us in similar Johannine passages, if we weigh the same more accurately. If we love one another, he says in chapter 4, 12, God abides in us and the love of God, which he explains as abiding in us, filling us with all his fullness Eph. 3, 19, τετελειωμένη ἐστιν ἐν ἡμῖν, is perfected in us, as to its perfect operation in us, and the tasting of the same, 1 Pet. 2, 3. For he speaks of Divine benefits towards us, namely the dwelling of God in us, and the full diffusion, exertion, and manifestation of grace, and of the love of God in our hearts, not of our duties, to which that ἐὰν ἀγαπῶμεν ἀλλήλους referred, because our mutual love is a sign and argument of the dwelling and habitation of God in us, and of the grace and Divine love extending itself in our hearts: which he then celebrates more fully in v. 16, in this we have known and believed the love which God has in us, and v. 17, ἐν τούτῳ τετελείωται ἡ ἀγάπη is perfected as to efficacy and sense, namely that ἀγάπη, ἣν ἔχει ὁ Θεὸς ἐν ἡμῖν, as he had designated it in v. 16, ἵνα παῤῥησίαν ἔχωμεν ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ κρίσεως, which boldness certainly not the perfection of our love towards God, but of God's love towards us generates in us, as is evident from the example of Paul, Rom. 8, 38, 39. Add also the words in St. John following in v. 18. Fear is not ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ in that Divine love, by which the same unfolds itself in us, and is felt in our hearts. But ἡ τελεία ἀγάπη that perfect and consummated Divine love known and perceived in the hearts of the faithful casts out all fear, because (servile) fear has punishment: for he who (thus) fears, οὐ τετελείωται ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ, is not perfected in Divine love. In him it is certain that Divine love does not unfold or exert itself, so that it may be felt and tasted how sweet the Lord is. For that taste does not consist with servile fear. Nor indeed does fear have a place in those, in whose hearts divine love has poured itself out, Rom. 5:5, and who through the Holy Spirit have been made strong to comprehend, καταβαλλέσθαι, what is the length, and breadth, and depth, and height of the divine love toward them, Eph. 3:18. The sense of the word ἐτελειώθη also occurs in James 2:22. Faith is perfected by works, because just as faith explains its efficacy through works, Gal. 5:6, so also it is recognized from works, and is thus perfected in relation to us, not in relation to itself. For it has all its perfection from its correlate, the merit of Christ, but the power and perfection of faith is recognized by us a posteriori from the works into which it pours itself.

If, however, anyone should think that the words ἡ ἀγάπη τῦ Θεῦ τελε- λείωται should be explained as referring to our love toward God, the perfection of our love or of our works will not therefore be elicited from this, as the Papists do: because we know from a comparison of Scripture that we do not attain true perfection in this life, but strive to obtain the same in the next life. We are indeed commanded to be perfect, Matt. 5:48, 1 Cor. 14:20, but we cannot therefore be perfect; indeed, those who think so, and judge themselves to be perfect, are easily confused with that Pharisaical youth, Matt. 19:21, and are warned by God not to make God a liar when they say they have no sin, 1 John 1:10. We do also aspire to some perfection here, 1 Cor. 2:6, Eph. 4:13, Phil. 3:15, Col. 4:12. Heb. 5:14, and this is to be attributed to the intercession of Christ, John 17:23, and for this the Holy Spirit labors through the word, that man may be presented perfect, Col. 1:28. But that perfection is relative, for that which is perfect, τὸ τέλειον, has not yet come; as we know in part, so also we love, 2 Cor. 13:10; but we shall be truly perfect only in the next life, Heb. 12:23, when we have finished our course here, 2 Tim. 4:7. For true perfection belongs not to travelers, but to those who have arrived, as the Scholastics say. This Estius acknowledges: Perfect, he says, according to the measure of perfection which we travelers can attain. Otherwise, that no man's love in this life is entirely perfect, that is, with all imperfection removed, St. John taught already before, when he testified that no one lives here without sins. And Paul also professes this of himself, saying in Phil. 3. Not that I have already attained or am perfect. And again: Brethren, I do not consider myself to have apprehended. This is the true righteousness of the perfect, says Leo in Sermon 2 on Lent, that they never presume that they are perfect, nor, ceasing from the action of a journey not yet finished, do they fall into the danger of failing where they have laid aside the desire of progressing. The perfection of this life denotes sincerity and love that is ἀνυπόκριτον (unfeigned), but not a consummated love: Whence Osiander: The word perfection in this place, he says, (as also in similar ones) is opposed to hypocrisy and simulation, nor does it signify such a perfection to which nothing is lacking, for that is reserved for the other age. But our former explanation is to be preferred, which I find now noted also by the most learned interpreter, Matt. Flacius, it is helpful to bring in his meditations that pertain to this: The love of God, he says, he understands here as His toward us, not ours toward Him. For he wishes to teach from where we can recognize God's favor toward us, or also by what instrument we can apprehend it, namely, he says, through the true knowledge of the Gospel of Christ. Wherefore he soon explains that favor of God toward us by the words being in Him, namely, to be and to be considered His son and heir. This very thing which he named the love of God, he called in the same sense in the previous chapter, verses six and

seven; to have communion with God, where it is certainly to be understood that He communicates His goods to us, not ours to Him, for since we make Him labor in our sins, as God explains in Isaiah, what good do we communicate to Him? The Papists here understand it to be about a certain most perfect love of ours toward God, which, however, no one at all performs in this life.

In this we know that we are in Him] He continues with other words what he had begun to say. For to be in someone or to remain (for in this whole epistle these are taken for the same) is to be joined to Him by the bond of love, as we said on John 6:56. He says, therefore, that he is about to say from where we can learn that we are such.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

ὃς δ' ἂν τηρῇ αὐτοῦ τὸν λόγον) Per λόγον intelligit partem eam Evangelii, quæ in præceptis consistit, ut ostendunt se- quentia.

Ἀληθῶς ἐν τούτῳ ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ Θεοῦ τετελείωται) Is non novit tantum Deum, sed & perfecte amat. Amor præsupponit cognitionem. Itaque oppositio hic sit cum accessione. Chri- sti præcepta Dei voluntatem exprimunt. Non potest autem quis validius Dei amore se teneri ostendere, quam si in omnibus ad Dei voluntatem se accommodet.

Jam explicat fidei indolem velut a priori. Qui ve- ro servat ipsius τὸν λόγον Verbum vel sermonem; non de signo fidei vel cognitionis jam loquitur; sed exponit potius, in quonam proprie occupetur fides in Christum, nempe ut servet Verbum ejus. Non absque causa mutat orationem: non dicit qui servat præcepta ejus, uti antea de præceptis loquutus erat: quanquam & τὰς ἐντολὰς de Verbo Evangelico explicari a Flacio antea observaveri- mus: Sed qui Verbum ejus servarit, ideoque præ- dicatum etiam aliud est nempe ἀληθῶς ἐν τούτῳ ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ Θεοῦ τετελείωται, vere in illo charitas Dei perficitur. Ex ore Christi sine dubio hanc phrasin hausit, qua etiam ita usus est ipse Christus apud Johannem cap. 8, 51.
