Ἐάν τις τὸν λόγον τὸν ἐμὸν τηρήσῃ θάνατον οὐ μὴ θεωρήσῃ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα: ubi de Verbo Evangelico servando, quod non nisi per fidem servatur, agi certum est. In illo autem, qui Verbum Evangelii fide custodit, charitas Dei vere perficitur, & perfecte sese exerit, charitas, in- quam, non qua Deum nos prosequimur, sed qua Deus nos complectitur. Diffundit enim sese in cordibus fidelium charitas Dei per Sp. sanctum, Rom. 5, 5. Quod ibi est ἐκκέχυται, hoc in præsenti loco est τετελείωται: ibi perfecta diffusio, ibi charitatis Divi- næ perfecta in cordibus nostris dilatatio, utrobiq; ra- tione sensus nostri, quod nempe eandem gustemus & sentiamus in cordib9 nostris abundanter, & cum summa jucunditate designata, estque hic IN IPSO idem, quod Paulo in cordibus ipsorum nempe fide- lium. Quod si quis malit perfectionem charitatis Dei non quoad sensum sed quoad effectum intelli- gere, non intõmode itidem dilectio Dei erga nos, & longe rectius de illa, quam de dilectione, qua nos Deum prosequimur; hæc a multum a perfectione abest. Observandum & hoc, quod perfici possit charitas Dei, quemadmodum potentia Dei perfi- citur τελειῶται in infirmitate nostra, 2. Corinth. 12, 9. quando sese efficacius exerit; quod omnino fit ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ in infirmitate nostra, adeoq; efficacia ejus in nobis sentitur & agnoscitur. Quem sensum de di- lectione Dei erga nos in similibus locis Johanneis etiam deprehendimus, si accuratius eadem expen- damus. Si diligamus nos invicem, inquit cap. 4, 12. Deus in nobis manet & dilectio Dei, quam explicat manens in nobis, implens nos omni plenitudine sua Eph. 3, 19. τετελειωμένη ἐστιν ἐν ἡμῖν, perfecta est in nobis, quoad perfectam in nobis operationem, e- jusdemq; γεῦσιν, 1. Petr. 2, 3. Nam loquitur de Divi- nis erga nos beneficiis, mansionis nempe Dei in no- bis, & plenæ diffusionis, exertionis ac manifesta- tionis gratiæ, & dilectionis Dei in cordibus nostris, non de officiis nostris, ad quæ spectabat illud ἐὰν ἀγαπῶμεν ἀλλήλους, quia mutua nostra dilectio si- gnum & argumentum est mansionis & habitatio- nis Dei in nobis, & gratiæ, ac charitatis Divinæ ex- pendentis sese in cordibus nostris: quam deinde uberius celebrat v. 16. in hoc cognovimus & cre- didimus charitatem, quam habet Deus in nobis, & v. 17. ἐν τούτῳ τετελείωται ἡ ἀγάπη perficitur quo- ad efficaciam & sensum, illa nempe ἀγάπη, ἣν ἔχει ὁ Θεὸς ἐν ἡμῖν, ut v. 16. eam designarat, ἵνα παῤῥη- σίαν ἔχωμεν ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ κρίσεως, quam παῤῥησίαν certe non perfectio charitatis nostræ erga Deum, sed charitatis Dei erga nos gignit in nobis, ut ab exemplo Pauli constat, Rom. 8, 38. 39. Adde & ver- ba apud S. Johannem sequentia v. 18. Timor non est ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ in illa charitate Divina, qua eadem in nobis sese explicat, atque sentitur in cordibus nostris. Sed ἡ τελεία ἀγάπη perfecta & con- summata illa charitas divina cognita & percepta in cordibus fidelium omnem timorem foris ex- pellit, quia timor (servilis) pœnam habet: qui enim (ita) timet, οὐ τετελείωται ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ, non perficitur in charitate Divina. In illo certum est, sese non explicare aut exerere Divinam charitatem, ut sentiatur & gustetur, quam suavis sit Domi- nus. Ille enim gustus cum timore servili non con- sistit. Neque enim timor locum habet in illis, in quorum cordibus sese diffudit charitas divina, Rom. V. v. 5. quique per Spiritum Sanctum fortes facti sunt ad comprehendendum, καταβαλλέσθαι, quænam sit longitudo, latitudo, & profunditas, & al- titudo divini amoris erga se, Eph. III. 18. Qui vocis ἐτελειώθη sensus etiam occurrit Jac. II. v. 22. Fides ex operibus perficitur, quia uti fides efficaciam suam explicat per opera, Gal. V. v. 6. ita etiam agno- scitur ex operibus, & ita perficitur ratione nostri, non ratione sui. Omnem enim perfectionem suam habet à correlato suo Christi merito, sed à nobis vis & perfectio fidei à posteriori agnoscitur ex operibus, in quæ sese diffundit.

Si tamen maxime verbis ἡ ἀγάπη τῦ Θεῦ τελε- λείωται explicanda quis censeat de charitate no- stra erga Deum, non tamen perfectio charitatis no- stræ aut operum nostrorum consummata hinc elicie- tur cum Papistis: quia novimus e collatione Scriptu ræ, nos in hac vita non consequi veram perfecti- onem, sed ad eandem obtinendam in altera vita contendere. Jubemur quidem esse perfecti, Matth. V. v. 48. 1. Cor. XIV. v. 20. sed non ideo perfecti esse possumus; imo qui ita censent, & se perfectos esse judicant, facile confunduntur cum illo juvene Pharisaico, Matth. XIX. v. 21. & commonentur à Deo, ne mendacem Deum faciant, cum dicunt se non habere peccatum, 1. Joh. I. v. 10. ad aliquam etiam perfectionem hic adspiramus, 1. Cor. II. v. 6. Eph. IV. v. 13. Phil. III. v. 15. Col. IV. 12. Ebr. V. 14. idque intercessioni Christi acceptum ferendum, Joh. XVII. v. 23. ac pro eo laborat Spiritus San- ctus per verbum, ut sistatur homo perfectus Col. I. vers. 28. Sed ea perfectio est secundum quid, non- dum enim venit τὸ τέλειον perfectum, ex parte ad- huc ut cognoscimus, ita & diligimus, 2. Cor. XIII. vers. 20. vere autem perfecti erimus demum in al- tera vita Ebr. XII. v. 23. cum hic perfecerimus cur- sum nostrum, 2. Tim. IV. 7. Perfectio enim vera non viatorum est, sed comprehensorum, ut Scho- lastici loquuntur. Quod agnoscit Estius: Perfecti, inquit, juxta modum perfectionis, quam viatores assequi possumus. Alioqui nullius hominis in hac vita charitatem omnino perfectam esse, remota scili- cet omni imperfectione jam ante docuit S. Johannes, quando testatus est, neminem hic vivere sine pecca- tis. Idque de se etiam profitetur Paulus, dicens Phil. III. Non quod jam acceperim aut perfectus sim. Et iterum: Fratres, Ego me non arbitror comprehendis- se. Hæc est perfectorum vera justitia, ait Leo serm. II. de Quadrag. ut nunquam præsumant, se esse perfe- ctos, nec ab itineris, nondum finiti, actione cessantes, ibi incidant deficiendi periculum, ubi proficiendi deposuerint appetitum. Perfectio hujus vitæ sin- ceritatem & charitatem ἀνυπόκριτον notat, non ve- ro consummatam charitatem: Unde Osiander: Perfectionis vocabulum hoc loco, inquit, (quemad- modum etiam in similibus) opponitur hypocrisi & simulationi, nec significat talem perfectionem, cui ni- hil desit, ea enim alteri seculo reservatur. Sed præ- ferenda est prior nostra explicatio, quam quia in- venio nunc animadversam etiam à Doctissimo In- terprete Matth. Flacio, ejus quoque meletemata huc facientia adducere juvat: Charitatem Dei, inquit, intelligit hic ipsius erga nos, non nostram er- ga ipsum. Vult enim docere, unde agnoscere possi- mus Dei erga nos favorem, seu etiam per quod instru- mentum illum apprehendere valeamus, nempe inquit per veram Evangelii Christi cognitionem. Quare mox illum Dei erga nos favorem exponit per verba in ipso esse, nempe esse ac censeri ejus filium & hæredem. Hoc ipsum quod nominavit dilectionem Dei, eadem se- re sententia inculcata superiori capite versu sexto &

septimo vocavit; Communionem cum Deo habere, ubi nimirum intelligendum est, quod ipse nobis sua bona communicet, non nostra ipsi, qui enim facimus laborare in peccatis nostris, ut in Esaia Deus exponit, quidnam boni ei communicemus? Papistæ hic intel- ligunt agi de quadam perfectissima nostra charitate erga Deum, quam tamen nemo omnino præstat in hac vita.

Ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν, ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐσμὲν] Aliis verbis pro- sequitur, quod dicere cœperat. Nam esse in aliquo aut ma- nere (in tota enim hac epistola ista pro eodem sumuntur) est amoris vinculo ei jungi, ut diximus ad Joh. VI. 56. Dicit ergo dicturum se, unde discere possimus nos esse tales.

## 2:6
Verse 6.

He who says he abides in Him, ought himself also to walk just as He walked] That οὕτως (thus) is superfluous, and is missing in the Manuscript, the Latin, and the Syriac. Those whom we love for their virtue, we ought to imitate in the same virtue. If the Pythagoreans imitate Pythagoras, the Stoics Zeno, the Academics Socrates, how much more should Christians imitate Christ? Περιπατεῖν (to walk) is הלךְ, to order one's life. See above 1:6, 7.

We admit that St. John is pursuing what he had begun to say. He had begun, however, to speak about the keeping of the Evangelical Word, which Grotius indeed rightly acknowledged, but he very badly perverted the doctrine of the Gospel, as if it consisted in precepts. He had also begun to speak about the love of God toward us, which is the chief part of Evangelical doctrine, not about the love of us, which is carried toward God. Nor are being in God and remaining in God exactly the same, but the latter implies the perseverance or continuation of the former. And not without reason does Cornelius à Lapide note: that St. John delights in the word of remaining, and uses it frequently, and through it signifies first an intimate conjunction, secondly a permanent stay and perseverance according to that of Christ in John 15:4, Abide in me and I in you. Thirdly, a continuous presence, friendly conversation, mutual familiarity, and all the true duties and offices of friendship. We are said to be in God, however, not so much because we are joined to Him by a bond of love, as because He deigns to come to us and dwell in us, John XIV. verse 23, communicating Himself to us out of love; and uniting us with Himself through faith, so that He may be in us, and we in Him, John XVII. Therefore, from the fact that we keep the Word of Christ through faith, it is not only that the divine charity is perfected in us, but we also know from this that we are in Him, in Christ, by a spiritual grafting into Christ and union with Christ, which is brought about only through faith. But what is added, that he who says he remains in Christ ought to walk just as He Himself walked, does not pertain to the means of remaining in Christ, but to the description of the subject who truly remains in Christ. Thus, when in Rom. VIII. v. 1, it is said that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, it is added, 'who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit': these things pertain to the description of those who are in Christ Jesus, to walk according to the Spirit, but they do not designate the means by which we are in Christ, or by virtue of which there is no condemnation in those who are in Christ.

Christ walked, however, in truth, in holiness, in justice, in charity, in humility, in patience, etc., and left us an example that we should follow in His footsteps, 1 Pet. II. 21, Matt. XI. 29, ch. XVI. 24, John XIII. v. 15, Eph. V. 2, Phil. II. 5, Col. III. v. 13. And therefore we also must walk in this way, whoever we are who desire to be true Christians. Flacius, as interpreter, therefore says that those who profess themselves to be members of Christ, and to remain in that vine, ought also, as living branches, to devote themselves to all piety and abstain from all injustice, just as He Himself did while acting here on earth.

For it is certainly most just that the nature and character of the members or branches should correspond to their remaining body and not disgrace its vine. What then, says Gregory of Nyssa to Olympius, is it fitting for him to do, who has been rendered worthy of the great surname of CHRIST, except to examine diligently all his thoughts, words, and deeds, and to judge whether each of them tends toward Christ or is alien to Him? It is not permitted to strike out the particle οὕτως, even if it is not expressed clearly in the Syriac and Latin. For they did not always render word for word for them. It makes for greater emphasis. But Grotius philosophizes too thinly concerning the imitators and the imitation of Christ, whom we ought not only to imitate because we love Him for His virtue, as the Pythagoreans did Pythagoras, etc., but because He bought us at a great price and claimed us for Himself, 1 Corinthians VI, verse 20; 2 Cor. V, v. 15; Tit. II, v. 14.

PART II. A eulogy of the doctrine of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Ὁ λέγων ἐν αὐτῷ μένειν, ὀφείλει καθὼς ἐκεῖνος περιεπάτησε καὶ αὐτὸς οὕτως περιπατεῖν] Illud οὕτως supervacuum est, & deeft in Manuscripto, Latino, & Syro. Quos amaus ob virtutem, eos imitari in eadem virtute debemus. Si Pytha- gorici Pythagoram, Stoici Zenonem, Academici Socratem imitantur, quanto magis Christum Christiani? Περιπατεῖν הלךְ est vitam instituere. Vide supra I. 6. 7.

Admittimus persequi sanctum Johannem, quod dicere cœperat. Cœperat autem dicere de custodia Verbi Evangelici, quod recte agnovit qui- dem Grotius sed pessime doctrinam Evangelii per- vertit, quasi in præceptis consistat. Cœperat etiam dicere de charitate Dei erga nos, quæ præcipua pars est doctrinæ Evangelicæ, non de amore nostri, qui in Deum fertur. Neque esse in Deo & manere in Deo idem prorsus sunt, sed hoc perseverantiam vel continuationem illius infert. Nec immerito notat Cornelius à Lapide: S. Johannem delectari verbo manendi, illudque crebro usurpare, ac per illud significare primo intimam conjunctionem, se- cundo moram permanentem & perseverantiam jux- ta illud Christi Joh. XV. v. 4. Manete in me & ego in vobis. Tertio continuam præsentiam, amicam conversationem, mutuam familiaritatem, omnia- que vera amicitiæ obsequia & officia. In Deo autem esse dicimur, non tam quod vinculo amoris ei jun- gimur, quam quod ipse ad nos venire, & in nobis habitare dignatur, Joh. XIV. vers. 23. se nobis ex amore communicans; nosque secum per fidem uniens, ut ipse in nobis, & nos in ipso simus, Joh. XVII. Ideo ex eo, quod Verbum Christi per fidem custodimus, non tantum est, quod charitas di- vina in nobis perficitur, sed cognoscimus etiam ex eo, quod in ipso in Christo simus spirituali in Christum insitione & unione cum Christo, quæ non nisi per fidem fit. Quod autem additur, qui dicit se in Christo manere, oportere, sicut ipse ambulavit, similiter etiam eum ambulare, non ad medium mansionis in Christo pertinet, sed ad descriptionem subjecti, quod vere in Christo ma- net. Ita cum Rom. VIII. v. 1. nulla condemnatio illis, qui sunt in Christo Jesu, esse dicitur, additur, non secundum carnem ambulantibus, sed secundum Spiritum: ad descriptionem eorum, qui in Christo Jesu sunt, hæc pertinent, ambulare secundum Spi- ritum, non vero medium designant, per quod in Christo sumus, aut vi cujus nulla in iis, qui in Christo sunt, condemnatio est.

Ambulavit autem Christus in veritate, in san- ctitate, in justitia, in charitate, in humilitate, pa- tientia, &c. nobisque exemplum reliquit, ut insi- stamus vestigiis ejus, 1. Petr. II. 21. Matth. XI. 29. cap. XVI. 24. Joh. XIII. v. 15. Eph. V. 2. Phil. II. 5. Col. III. v. 13. Ideoque nobis etiam ita ambulan- dum est, quicunque veri Christiani esse cupimus. Ait igitur interprete Flacio, eos, qui sese pro- fiteantur esse membra Christi, & permanere in ea vite, debere etiam tanquam vivos palmites ita omni pietati vacare, & ab omni injustitia abstinere, sicut ipse hic in terris agens fecerit.

Justissimum enim certe est, ut natura indolesque membrorum aut palmitum suo reliquo corpori cor- respondeat & non dedecoret suam vitem. Quid igi- tur, inquit Gregorius Nyss. ad Olympiad. opor- tet eum facere, qui magno CHRISTI cognomine dignus effectus est, nisi ut omnia sua cogitata, dicta, & facta diligenter exploret, & utrum eorum singula ad Christum tendant, an ab illo sint aliena, dijudicet. Particulam οὕτως expungere non licet, etsi in Syro & Latino non exprimatur diferte. Non enim semper illi verbum verbo reddidere. Facit ad majorem emphasin. Nimis autem exiliter philo- sophatur Grotius de imitatoribus & imitatione Christi, quem non tantum imitari debemus, quia amamus ob virtutem, uti Pythagorici Pythago- ram, &c. sed quia magno pretio nos mercatus est, & sibi adseruit, 1. Corinth. VI. vers. 20. 2. Cor. V. v. 15. Tit. II. v. 14.

PARS II. Elogium doctrinæ Christi.

## 2:7
Ver. 7.

Brethren, I write no new commandment to you, but an old commandment, which you had from the beginning] You Israelites have already long had this precept, Leviticus XIX. 18. This precept ought not to seem new to you, although it is extended more broadly and advanced more sublimely. For ἀδελφοὶ in the Manuscript there is ἀγαπητοὶ, and neither the Syriac nor the Latin read it otherwise. And ἀπ' ἀρχῆς is missing here in the Manuscript. But in the Syriac and Latin, this very thing is missing in the following member. The old commandment is the word which you heard from the beginning] You, that is, your ancestors, which kind of locution you have in Matthew XXIII, v. 35; Mark X, 3; John VI, 32; VII, 19, 22; Acts III, 22; VII, 38. To understand that ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, see Ezekiel XIX, 3, and what is said there. The word דבר is also said of the old law, but more often in the plural דברים because of the multitude of precepts, which John here gathers into a sum, and therefore uses the singular. Compare Romans XIII, verse 9; Galatians V, 19.

This is rashly restricted, along with the Papists and most others, to the precept concerning the love of one's neighbor, which is asserted—contrary to the truth of Scripture and based on a Jewish persuasion—to have been extended more broadly and advanced more sublimely by Christ. For Christ Himself taught, against Pharisaic tradition, that that precept of love in the Old Testament had extended just as widely (Luke X. 27 ff.; Matthew VII. 12), and was no less sublime when it was handed down by Moses than it was when repeated and inculcated by Christ, as He pronounced with a clear voice in Matthew XXII. 39, 40. Moreover, one must not walk only in the love of one's neighbor according to Christ's example, but also in other virtues, in which Christ set Himself as an example for us. Not only one's neighbor, but God above all is to be loved, from whose love the love of one's neighbor flows. But here the Apostle continues in his primary instruction, which he had begun concerning the λόγῳ or the Evangelical word of Christ. For by keeping that, He made them certain of the charity and divine grace to be most abundantly shown to them, v. 5. But this Word of Christ, this Evangelical doctrine, he teaches is not a new doctrine, but a most ancient one.

For ἐντολὴ, a commandment, is taken in the phrase of Scripture concerning doctrine, provided that the doctrine is handed down by God: so that it is demanded and commanded that it be embraced by us. And to command is sometimes to promise, as Flacius teaches in his Clavis under the word 'mando'. See Lev. XXV. 21; Deut. XXVIII. 8; Ps. XXXIII. 3; Ps. CV. 8, 11; Ps. CXI. 9; Heb. IX. 20. The Greek, says Flacius, ἐνετείλατο means 'he ordained', 'he promised', 'he proposed'. This meaning of the word צוה 'to command' is also to be noted because unskilled men take words speaking of Evangelical promises and the gratuitous mercy and grace of God in a legal sense, and transfer them to our good works. It also denotes sometimes the same as 'I signify' or 'I denounce', Gen. L, v. 15; Acts X, 36, as Flacius likewise observes: and 'commandment' or 'commandments', 'testimonies', 'judgments', 'statutes', 'word', etc., in Psalm CXIX and often elsewhere are synonyms. Thus ἐντολὴ occurs concerning doctrines handed down by Moses and the Prophets, not only concerning precepts, Matthew V. 19, ch. XV. 3, 6, which expression is especially solemn for John concerning the Evangelical doctrine which Christ received from the Father, and which is eternal life, John XII, verses 49, 50; concerning doctrines handed down by Christ, 1 John 2, v. 15, 21; ch. 15, v. 10. Add also 2 Peter 2, v. 21. And St. John did not only say ἐντολὴν in this chapter, but it is also taken concerning the doctrine of faith, ch. 3, v. 22, 23, 24, or at least it is included under that name of ἐντολῶν at the same time. See also ch. 5, v. 2, 3, and 2nd epistle, verses 4, 6; Apoc. 12, v. 17; ch. 14, v. 12; ch. 22, 14. Flacius rightly notes this sense of the word here, having commented thus in this place. He meets, he says, the tacit objection of those who, being either evil, might slander, or being weak, might fear: that the Apostle is bringing some new doctrine concerning the Word of life and His incarnation, and the remission of sins and eternal salvation to be received through Him. Therefore he says that he is by no means bringing any new doctrine, but that very one which they had had from the beginning or the time of the Prophets, namely, looking toward that part of those to whom he writes who had been converted from Judaism. For the same doctrine has always been proposed in the Church of God by the Prophets, Moses, and the Patriarchs, although somewhat more obscurely than in the time of Christ, concerning the coming blessed seed, who would take away our injustice and curse by His own justice and blessing. Thus also Paul in the first and third chapters of Romans testifies that the same doctrine of the Gospel concerning the propitiation of Christ was also formerly set forth in the Law and the Prophets, which he himself also urges and inculcates. Indeed, Christ himself also seriously acts to demonstrate that he preaches nothing which has not been previously foretold and delivered in the Scriptures. Nay, he even instructed the Apostles themselves, when sending them forth to convert the human race, by using this as a most abundant storehouse or even a horn of plenty, from which they might draw forth all saving dogmas for the world, namely, Scripture, and its true and saving understanding, and the ability to explain it usefully and copiously. Therefore, he who follows this doctrine of God, which is truly catholic for all times, he at last is a true Catholic and a member of the Church of Christ, even if he be among the Antipodes, ignorant of Rome and its mitred, and purple-clad, and masked Fathers.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Ἄδελφοὶ ὀυκ ἔν τολὴν καινὴν γράφω ὑμῖν, ἀλλ' ἐντολὴν πα- λαιὰν, ἣν εἴχετε ἀπ' ἀρχῆς] Vos Israelitæ jam olim habui- stis hoc præceptum Levit. XIX. 18. Non debet novum vobis videri hoc præceptum, quanquam protensum la- tius & provectum sublimius. Pro ἀδελφοὶ in Manuscripto est ἀγαπητοὶ, nec aliter legerunt aut Syrus aut Latinus. Et ἀπ' ἀρχῆς hic de est in Manuscripto. Apud Syrum autem & Latinum de est hoc ipsum in membro sequente. Ἡ ἐντολὴ παλαιά ἐστιν ὁ λόγος, ὃν ἠκούσατε ἀπ' ἀρχῆς] Vos, id est, vestri majores, qualem loquutionem habes Matth. XXIII. v. 35. Marc. X. 3. Johan. VI. 32. VII. 19. 22. Act. III. 22. VII. 38. Ad intelligendum illud ἀπ' ἀρχῆς vide Ezech. XIX. 3. & ibi dicta. דבר λόγος etiam de lege veteri dicitur, sed sæpius in plurali דברים λόγοι ob multitu- dinem præceptorum, quæ Johannes hic in summam colle- git, ideoque singulari utitur. Conf. Rom. XIII. vers. 9. Gal. V. 19.

Temere restringitur hoc cum Pontificiis & aliis plerisque ad præceptum de charitate proximi, quod latius protensum & sublimius provectum à Christo ex Judaica persuasione, & contra Scriptu- ræ veritatem asseritur. Nam æque late patuisse præ- ceptum illud dilectionis in Veteri Testamento Christus ipse contra Pharisæicam traditionem do- cuit Luc. X. 27. sqq. Matth. VII. 12. nec minus sublime fuisse, cum à Mose traditum est, quam quatenus à Christo repetitum & inculcatum, Matth. XXII. 39. 40. diserta voce pronunciavit. Non ambulandum autem tantum in charitate pro- ximi secundum Christi exemplum, sed etiam in aliis virtutibus, quibus Christus sese exemplum nobis præbuit. Non proximus tantum, sed im- primis Deus diligendus, ex cujus amore proximi amor fluit. Sed hic pergit Apostolus in informa- tione sua præcipua, quam cœperat de λόγῳ vel ver- bo Christi Evangelico. Id enim servantes certos reddidit de charitate ac gratia divina abundan- tissime ipsis exhibenda v. 5. Hoc autem Verbum Christi, hanc doctrinam Evangelicam docet esse non novam, sed antiquissimam doctrinam

Ἐντολὴ enim mandatum de doctrina Phrasi Scri- pturæ accipitur, siquidem doctrina à Deo tradatu: ita, ut nobis amplectenda demandetur ac præci piatur. Et mandare quandoque est promittere, u Flacius in Clave ad verbum mando docet. Vid Lev. XXV. 21. Deut. XXVIII. 8. Ps. XXXIII. 3. Ps CV. 8. 11. Ps. CXI. 9. Ebr. IX. 20. Græcum, inqui Flacius, ἐνετείλατο ordinavit est, promisit, proposui. Hæc significatio verbi צוה mandare etiam ideo es observanda: quia homines imperiti verba de pro missis Evangelicis & gratuita Dei misericordia a gratia loquentia legaliter accipiunt, & ad nostr bona opera transferunt. Notat etiam quandoque illud verbum idem quod fignifico, denuntio Gen. L. v 15. Act. X. 36. observante itidem Flacio: & man- datum aut mandata, testimonia, judicia, statuta, verbum &c. Psal. CXIX. & sæpe alias Synonyma sunt. Sic ἐντολὴ de doctrinis à Mose & Prophetis traditis, non de solis præceptis occurrunt, Matth. V. 19. cap. XV. 3. 6. quæ λέξις cumprimis Johanni solennis est de doctrina Evangelica, quam à Patre accepit Christus, quæque æterna vita est, Joh. XII. vers. 49. 50. de doctrinis à Christo traditis, 1. Joh. 14, v. 15. 21. cap. 15, v. 10. Adde & 2. Petr. 2, v. 21. Nec tantum hoc capite S. Johannes ita ἐντολὴν di- xit, sed etiam de doctrina fidei cap. 3, v. 22. 23. 24. ac- cipitur, vel certe illo nomine ἐντολῶν simul com- prehenditur. Vide & c. 5, v. 2. 3. & 2. epist. vers. 4. 6. Apoc. 12, v. 17. cap. 14, v. 12. cap. 22, 14. Hunc sensum vocis recte hic animadvertit Flacius, ita commentatus in h. l. Occurrit, inquit, tacitæ ob- jectioni eorum, qui vel mali existentes calumniari, vel etiam imbecilli vereri possent : Apostolum afferre novam quandam doctrinam de Verbo vitæ ejusque incarnatione, ac per eum accipienda remissione pec- catorum & salute æterna. Ideo dicit se nequaquam aliquam novam doctrinam afferre : sed eam ipsam, quam habuerint inde à principio seu tempore Pro- phetarum, nempe respiciens illam ipsorum, ad quos scribit, partem, quæ ex Judaismo fuerat conversa. Semper enim eadem doctrina, licet aliquanto ob- scurius, quam tempore Christi, à Prophetis, Mose, & Patriarchis in Ecclesia Dei proposita est, de ven- turo benedicto semine, nostram injustitiam maledi- ctionemque sua justitia ac benedictione ablaturo. Sic & Paulus Romanorum primo & tertio testatur, eandem doctrinam Evangelii de propitiatione Christi etiam olim in lege & Prophetis propositam esse, quam ipse quoque urgeat ac inculcet. Imo & ipsemet Chri- stus idipsum serio agit, ut demonstret, se nihil concio- nari, quod non antea in Scripturis prædictum sit tra- ditumque. Quin & ipsos Apostolos hoc ceu uberrimo penu aut etiam copiæ cornu, unde omnia salutaria dogmata mundo depromerent, ablegans eos ad con- vertendum genus humanum instruxit, nempe Scri- ptura, ejusque vero salutarique intellectu, & facul- tate utiliter copioseque explicandi. Hanc igitur vere omnium temporum catholicam Dei doctrinam qui sequitur, is demum vere Catholicus membrumque Ecclesiæ Christi est, etiamsi sit apud Antipodas, igno- rans Romam, & ejus mitratos, ac purpuratos lar- vatosque Patres.

## 2:8
vers. 8. Again a new commandment I write unto you] That 'again' is corrective. I said it is an old commandment, yet it is also a new one, in such a way that it was published to us by Christ, and therefore it is called new by Christ himself, John 13:33. You have 'again' used thus in Matthew 4:7 and elsewhere. Thus Donatus, regarding that phrase: 'Heus tu rogate rursum' [Hey you, ask again], interprets it as 'on the contrary'.

Which is true in him and in you] That which was true in him, that is, in Christ, that is, it appeared in reality, and it ought to be in you, namely. Or it should be read 'in you', as it is in the manuscript, so that it says that commandment is sincerely fulfilled both by Christ and by the Apostles. We ought not to wonder that after the word 'that' the pronoun 'which' follows, because it is not so much the commandment as the thing itself, which is contained in the commandment, that is regarded here. And we have already had a similar construction above at 1:23. Christ loved not a few men, but all, and in such a way that for the sake of their salvation he did not even hold his own life dear. Thus we also ought to do, below at 3:16, John 15:12, 13.

Because the darkness is passing away] He calls the time under the law of Moses 'darkness', namely, compared to the time of the new light of the Gospel: in which sense the law is also said to be 'growing old', Heb. 8:13. See Matthew 4:16, Luke 1:79, John 1:5, 3:19, 20, 21. 'To pass away' as in 1 Cor. 7:31, or 'to be passing away' here and below at verse 17, is to pass by. Moreover, here the present is used for the past. The Syriac 'abara' means passed by, went away. In the manuscript, instead of 'darkness' there is 'shadow', which is attributed to the law in Colossians 2:17, Hebrews 10:1.

And the true light now shineth] That great light. For that which stands out in any matter is usually called ἀληθινὸν (true), as we said at John 1:9. φαίνει וזרח (it shines), Ἐπανόρθωσις (correction) is entirely of the preceding sentence, which Flacius explains very well: That although this doctrine concerning Christ and his benefits is most ancient, yet it can truly be said to be new for a twofold reason: first, by reason of Christ himself, who now for the first time has truly fulfilled it, and at the same time has proclaimed it more clearly and fully: Then also by reason of men, who had either not heard it at all before, or certainly had never had it so clearly illustrated and fully perceived. Thus, therefore, it is true that this doctrine is new in Christ and to us. But he soon adds the reason or explanation of that novelty, which consists not so much in the essence of the doctrine as in the manner of its manifestation; because, he says, the light of the Gospel has now been so clearly, copiously, and widely propagated and divulged throughout the world, that it everywhere puts to flight and abolishes the darkness of Pharisaical opinions as well as of Gentile errors and previous ignorance. And therefore Paul explains both the antiquity and the novelty of the Gospel in the same way in several places, especially Eph. 3:5. This explanation is confirmed by that ἐπιφάνεια (manifestation) of the true light, which cannot be understood by reason of the commandments, since the commandments in the Old Testament were no less bright than in the New: those things which are attributed to Christ concerning the additions and perfection of the law, in the manner of the Pelagians and Socinians, do not at all agree with the office of Christ, who certainly ought not to have been a new νομοθέτης (lawgiver), John 1:17. There is no darkness in the law regarding divine precepts, nor in the Prophets, the interpreters of the law: Nor is τὸ Φῶς τὸ ἀληθινὸν ἤδη φαίνει (the true light now shines) said because precepts were handed down more clearly than in the law, but because the grace which in some way lay hidden under the wrappings of the law and the oracles of the Prophets, certainly did not appear in such an illustrious manner, much less shine to the whole world, now when the true light ἐπεφάνη (shone forth) in the appearance of the Son of God in the flesh, has been manifested by the light of the Gospel far more abundantly, more clearly, and more diffusely than in the Old Testament. Testament, and has put to flight the darkness of Gentilism no less than that of Judaism. Whence he gathers in the following verse that it is right that those who are in that light should love their brothers, for true faith is active through love, Gal. 5:6, nor does the light of the Gospel suffer the darkness of hatred of one's neighbor or other sins. Those who are light in the Lord must walk as children of light, and have no fellowship with the works of darkness, Eph. 5:8-9. The same sense shines forth more fully from the exposition of τῆς ἐντολῆς (the commandment), which he testified he was writing to the brothers in v. 7. & 8. but then, according to the distribution of ages, he applies it to all: for that ἐντολὴ (commandment), which he writes to the little children, according to v. 12, is the doctrine and promise concerning the remission of sins, namely, that their sins are forgiven them through the name of Christ; that which he writes to the Fathers is that instruction according to v. 13, that they themselves, from those things which the Apostles had handed down, had recognized him who is from eternity the λόγος τῆς ζωῆς (Word of life), that Word of life, of which ch. 1:1 sqq., in whose knowledge consists eternal life, John 17:3; that which he writes to the young men is that most joyful announcement that they have conquered that evil one, Satan: that which he writes to the little ones is that their Father is in the Only-Begotten Son, v. 13. Nothing here about the law or the precepts of the law, whence an invincible argument: That, without any doubt, is the ἐντολὴ (commandment) which the Apostle says he is writing to the brothers in v. 7. & 8. which he later explained distinctly, how he writes it and applies it particularly to the little children, the Fathers, the young men, and the boys. This, however, is not legal, but Evangelical doctrine concerning the remission of sins through the name of Christ, concerning faith in the incarnate Word, concerning the victory over Satan, concerning the grace of God the Father exhibited in Christ. Furthermore, that ἐντολὴ (commandment) is understood by St. John, which he again inculcates in v. 14 that he had written, not in another epistle, but in the preceding ones, namely at the beginning of the epistle: both to the fathers and to the young men, whence they could recognize him who is from the beginning, whom he had clearly described in ch. 1:1 sqq. & ch. 2:1-2, and whence they could have true strength, so that the Word of God might remain in them, and so that they themselves might be able to conquer the evil one, who strives with every effort to deprive them of the Word of salvation. Which doctrine and ἐπαγγε- λίαν (promise) he had handed down in ch. 1:5 sqq. Furthermore, that ἐντολὴ (commandment) is designated as doctrine, instruction, and announcement, from which he warns them not to allow themselves to be drawn away by the world and by the Anti-Christ, v. 15 sqq. But to which doctrine is the world more opposed than to the doctrine concerning Christ crucified, which to the Jews is a mere scandal, and to the Gentiles mere foolishness, 1 Cor. 1:23? To which does the Anti-Christ, with the whole crowd of heretics, oppose himself more than to this Evangelical doctrine? 2 Pet. 2:1. For Christ is that stone of stumbling and sign of contradiction, Is. 8:14, Luke 2:34. The blessed Hunnius himself explains the opposition of darkness and light in no other way than with respect to the Gospel: The Apostle illustrates the matter with a simile, and by a comparison of darkness and light compares both the time of the Old and New Testament with each other: in the same sense in which Paul writes to the Romans 13. The night is far spent, and the day is at hand, so that salvation is now nearer than when we believed. So in like manner John writes: The darkness has passed away, and the true light now shines. As if he were to say: In the Old Testament the knowledge of Christ was much more obscure, since he had not yet appeared, but was shadowed forth to the people under those obscure types of sacrifices. But now in the New Testament, those shadows having vanished, Christ himself has arisen, as the Sun of righteousness and the light of the whole world.

Latin:

vers. 8. Πάλιν ἐυτολὴν καινὴν γράφω ὑμῖν] Illud πάλιν est ἐπανορθωτικὸν. Dixi esse præceptum vetus, attamen & no- vum est, ita ut à Christo id nobis publicatum est, & ideo no- vum ab ipso Christo appellatur, Joh. XIII. 33. sic πάλιν habes Matth. IV. 7. & alibi. Sic Donatus ad illud : Heus tu rogate rursum, interpretatur, è contrario.

Ὅ ἐσιν ἀληθὲς ἐν ἀυτῷ καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν] Quod in ipso, id est, in Christo, verum fuit, id est reipsa apparuit, & in vobis sc. de- bet. Aut ἐν ὑμῖν legendum, ut est in Manuscripto, ut di- cat id præceptum sincere & à Christo, & ab Apostolis im- pletum. Mirari non debemus post vocem ὅτι ὅ,τι sequi pro- nomen ὅ, quia non tam præceptio quam res ipsa, quæ præ- ceptione continetur, hic respicitur. Et similem constructi- onem jam habuimus supra I. 23. Christus non paucos homi- nes, sed omnes dilexit, & ita ut præ ipsorum salute ne vitam quidem suam charam haberet. Sic & nos debemus facere in- fra III. 16. Joh. XV. 12, 13.

Ὅτι ἡ σκοτία παράγεται] σκοτίαν vocat tempus sub lege Mosis, nempe comparatum tempori novæ lucis Evangelicæ: quo sensu etiam lex dicitur ἐκνώμενη.. Ebr. VIII. 7. Vide Matth. IV. 16. Luc. L. 79. Joh. L. 5. III. 19. 20. 21. Παράγειν ut 1. Cor. VII. 31. aut παράγεσθαι hic & infra 17. est præterire. Tum vero est hic Præsens pro Præterito. Syrus עבר præteriit, abiit. In manuscripto pro σκοτία est σκιὰ, quod legi tribuitur Coloss. II. 17. Ebr. X. 1.

Καὶ τὸ φῶς τὸ ἀληθινὸν ἤδη φαίνει] Lux illa magna. Nam quod in re quaque eminet, solet ἀληθινὸν dici, ut diximus ad Joh. I. 9. φαίνει וזרח, Ἐπανόρθωσις omnino est præcedentis sententiæ, quam optime explicat Flacius : Quod licet ista do- ctrina de Christo ejusque beneficiis sit vetustissima, tamen duplici ratione vere dici possit esse nova : pri- mo ratione ipsius Christi, qui nunc primum eam ve- re impleverit, simul & clarius pleniusque evulgave- rit : Deinde etiam ratione hominum, qui eam prius aut prorsus non audiverant, aut certe ita clare illu- stratam pleneque perceptam nunquam habuerant. Sic igitur est verum, istam doctrinam esse novam in Christo & nobis. Addit vero mox rationem aut ex- plicationem istius novitatis, qua non tam in doctrinæ essentia, quam in patefactionis modo consistat ; quia, inquit, lux Evangelii jam ita clare, copiose, & la- tissime per orbem terrarum propagata divulgataque est, ut undique fuget ac aboleat tenebras Pharisaica- rum opinionum tum & errorum gentilium infci- tiæque prioris. Ideoque Paulus tum vetustatem tum novitatem Evangelii eodem modo pluribus in locis exponit, præsertim Eph. III. 5. Quam explica- tionẽ firmat illa lucis veræ ἐπιφάνεια, quæ ratione mandatorum intelligi non potest, siquidem man- data in V. Testam. non minus luculenta fuerint, quam in Novo : illa quæ de additamentis & per- fectione legis Christo affinguntur more Pelagia- norum & Socinianorum cum officio Christi, qui certe novus νομοθέτης esse non debuit, minime conveniunt, Joh. I. 17. nullæ in lege sunt tenebræ quoad præcepta divina, nullæ in Prophetis legis In- terpretibus : Nec τὸ Φῶς τὸ ἀληθινὸν ἤδη φαίνει di- citur, quod illustriora, quam in lege, tradita sint præcepta, sed quod gratia, quæ sub involucris legis & oraculis Prophetarum quodammodo latuit, cer- te tam illustri ratione non patuit, nedum toti orbi luxit, jam ubi vera lux ἐπεφάνη in apparitione Fi- lii Dei in carne, per lucem Evangelii manifestata sit uberius longe, luculentius, diffusius, quam in Vet. Testam. tenebrasque gentilismi non minus quam Judaismi profligarit. Unde æquum esse colligit vers. seq. ut, qui in luce illa sunt, fratres diligant, qui fides vera per charitatem operosa est, Gal. V. 6. neque lux Evangelii patitur tenebras odiorum proximi aut aliorum peccatorum. Qui lux sunt in Domino, ut filii lucis ambulare debent, nec com- mercium habere cum operibus tenebrarum, Eph. V. 8. 9. Idem sensus elucescit amplius ab expositio- ne τῆς ἐντολῆς, quam se scribere fratribus testatus est v. 7. & 8. deinceps vero secundum distributio- nem ætatum omnibus applicat : nam illa ἐντολὴ, quam filiolis scribit, secundum v. 12. doctrina & pro- missio est de remissione peccatorum, quod nempe cõ- donantur ipsis peccata per nomen Christi; quam scribit Patribus, est institutio illa secundum v. 13. quod ipsi ex iis, quæ tradiderant Apostoli, agnove- rint eum, qui ab æterno est λόγος τῆς ζωῆς, Ver- bum illud vitæ, de quo c. I, 1. sqq. in cujus cognitione consistit vita æterna, Joh. XVII. 3. quam scribit juve- nibus, est annunciatio illa lætissima, quod vicerint malignum illum Satanam : quam parvulis, quod ipsorum Pater sit in Filio Unigenito, v. 13. Nihil hic de lege vel præceptis legis, unde argumentum in- victum: Illa, sine omni dubio, ἐντολὴ est, quam τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς se scribere ait Apostolus v. 7. & 8. quam distincte exposuit postea, quomodo eam scribat ac peculiariter applicet filiolis, Patribus, juvenibus, & pueris. Hæc vero non est legalis, sed Evangelica doctrina de remissione peccatorum per nomen Christi, de fide in Verbum incarnatum, de victoria Satanæ, de Dei Patris in Christo exhibita gratia. Porro illa ἐντολὴ intelligitur à S. Johanne, quam iterum v. 14. inculcat se scripsisse non in alia episto- la, sed in superioribus, sub initium scilicet episto- læ: tum patribus, tum juvenibus, unde scilicet a- gnoscere potuerint eum, qui est ab initio, quem lu- culenter descripserat cap. I. 1. sqq. & c. II. 1. 2. & unde veram fortitudinem habere poterant, ut Verbum Dei in ipsis maneat, utque vincere ipsi possint malignum, qui eosdem Verbo salutis privare omni molimine contendit. Quam doctrinam & ἐπαγγε- λίαν tradiderat c. I. 5. sqq. Adhæc illa ἐντολὴ doctri- na, institutio & annunciatio designatur, à qua se per mundum ac per Anti-Christum abstrahi ne pa- tiantur, monet v. 15. sqq. Cui doctrinæ autem ma- gis adversus est mundus, quam doctrinæ de Chri- sto crucifixo, quæ Judæis merum scandalum, genti- bus mera stultitia est, 1. Corinth. I. vers. 23. Cui magis adversatur Anti-Christus cum turba hære- ticorum universa, quam huic doctrinæ Evangeli- cæ? 2. Petr. II. vers. 1. Christus enim est lapis ille offensionis & signum contradictionis, Es. VIII. 14. Luc. II. 34. Beat. Hunnius ipse tenebrarum & lu- cis oppositionem non aliter explicat, quam respe- ctu Evangelii: Similitudine rem illustrat Apostolus, & collatione tenebrarum & lucis comparat inter se utrumque tempus Veteris & Novi Testamenti: eo- dem sensu, quo Paulus ad Rom. 13. scribit. No- ctem esse progressam, & appropinquasse diem, ita ut salus nunc propior sit, quam tum cum crederemus. Sic pari modo scribit Johannes: Tenebræ præterie- runt, & verum lumen jam lucet. Quasi dicat: In Veteri Testamento multo fuit obscurior cognitio Chri- sti, cum is nondum apparuisset, sed sub obscuris illis sacrificiorum typis populo adumbraretur. Nunc autem in Testamento novo exortus est, evanescen- tibus umbris illis ipsemet Christus, tanquam Sol ju- stitiæ, & lux universi mundi.

## 2:9
Verse 9.

Ὁ λέγων ἐν τῷ φωτὶ εἶναι) That is, he who says that he follows the Gospel. Καὶ τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὑτοῦ μισῶν) whether a Jew or a foreigner. For all are called through Christ, and ought to be loved on account of Christ, Matt. V. 44 and following. Christ brought the matter back to its beginnings. We are all brothers in Adam. And thus the word 'neighbor' was used before the law, Gen. XI. 3, XXXI. v. 49, Exodus XI. 2. Ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ ἐστὶν ἕως ἄρτι) He even now, after such great light has appeared, remains in darkness, if not in those thicker ones of the pagans, certainly in Jewish ones. We shall have Ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ ἐστὶν and soon 11. Ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ μένειν, John XII. 35. You have ἕως ἄρτι in John V. 17, XVI. 24, 1 Cor. IV. 13, VIII. 7.

The Apostle teaches that hatred toward a brother cannot consist with the enjoyment of that true light, and that he who, while burning with hatred toward a brother, is persuaded that he is in the light, is not in the light, but is occupied in darkness both of mind and will, in order to show by what necessity charity is joined with faith and how faith cannot exist without charity. It is clearly absurd, (so the Hunnian paraphrase has it,) that he who hates his brother (by whose name any neighbor is understood) should boast of the light and true knowledge of God and Christ. For these are clearly opposites and inconsistent, which mutually tear each other down and cannot stand in one and the same subject, namely light and hatred of one's neighbor, which it is established is a work not of light but of darkness. But it is vain what Grotius says, that Christ brought the matter back to its beginnings: for that is not to be admitted except by reason of Pharisaical corruptions; as for the doctrine of Moses himself, which Grotius refers to, it is most false. Not only before the law, but in the law itself, the word 'neighbor' was taken universally according to the best interpreter of the divine law, Christ, Luke X.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Ὁ λέγων ἐν τῷ φωτὶ εἶναι) Id est qui dicit se Evangeli- um sectari. Καὶ τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὑτοῦ μισῶν) sive Judæum sive alienige- nam. Omnes enim per Christum vocantur, & ob Christum diligi debent, Matth. V. 44. & sequentibus. Retraxit rem Christus ad sua primordia. Fratres omnes in Adamo sumus. Et sic vox proximi sumpta ante legem, Gen. XI. 3. XXXI. v. 49. Exodi XI. 2. Ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ ἐστὶν ἕως ἄρτι) Is etiam nunc, postquam tanta lux apparuit, manet in tenebris, si non crassioribus illis pa- ganorum, certe Judaicis. Ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ ἐστὶν habebimus & mox 11. Ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ μένειν, Joh: XII. 35. ἕως ἄρτι habes Joh. V. 17. XVI. 24. 1. Cor. IV. 13. VIII. 7.

Non posse consistere odium erga fratrem cum fruitione lucis illius veræ, nec in luce esse, sed in tenebris cum mentis, tum voluntatis versari, qui, quum odio flagret erga fratrem, in luce se esse per- suasus est, docet Apostolus, ut qua necessitate cum fide copuletur charitas & quam non possit esse sine charitate fides, ostendat. Plane absurdum est, (ita habet paraphrasis Hunniana,) ut is, qui odia habet fratrem, (cujus nomine proximus quivis homo intelligitur) glorietur de luce & cognitione ve- ra Dei & Christi. Sunt enim hæc plane ἀντίθετα & ἀσύστατα, quæ se mutuo convellunt, & in uno eodem- que subjecto stare nequeunt, nempe lux & odium proximi, quod non lucis sed tenebrarum opus esse constat. Vanum autem est, quod dicit Grotius, re- traxisse rem Christum ad sua primordia: nam id non nisi ratione Pharisæicarum corruptelarum admittendum, quoad vero ipsius Mosis doctrinam, quam Grotius respicit, falsissimum est. Non tan- tum ante legem, sed in ipsa lege vox proximi uni- versaliter sumpta est secundum optimum legis di- vinæ Interpretem Christum, Luc. X.

## 2:10
v. 10. He who loves his brother, he finally follows the Evangelical light, he has passed from death into life, as is said below III. 13.

And there is no stumbling block in him. These are words from the Greek of Psalm CXIX. 65. It is, however, a metonymy, and the ἐν is redundant. For the sense is, he does not stumble. Why? Because he follows such a light. He who does not have such a light going before him does not know where he is going, John XII. 35. Therefore it is no wonder if he offends.

Latin:

v. 10. ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἁυτῶ ἐν τῷ φωτὶ μένει] Qui fratrem amat, is demum lucem Evangelicam sequitur, is tran- siit de morte in vitam, ut dicitur infra III. 13.

Καὶ σκάνδαλον ἐν ἀυτῷ ὐκ ἔστιν] Sunt verba ex Graeco Psalmi CXIX. 65. Est autem μετωνυμία, & ἐν abundat. Sensus enim est, ille non impingit. Quare? Quia ta- lem lucem sequitur. Qui talem lucem praeeuntem non habet, nescit quo vadat, Joh. XII. 35. Itaque non mirum est, si offendit.

## 2:11
v. 11. But he who hates his brother. With the word brother taken in the way we have already stated.

He is in darkness and walks in darkness. By the former member an affection is denoted, by the latter an act.

Neither metonymy nor pleonasm should be admitted here. The sense is not that he does not stumble, but that there is nothing in him by which another might be offended or stumble, as far as pertains to the precepts of the second table, by which true love of neighbor is contained, and indeed even of the first table, because sincere love of neighbor cannot have a place without love of God, and therefore love of neighbor is a sign and argument of the abiding in the light: because it is the nature of true faith to exert itself through charity. It is not possible, says Oecumenius, to be in the light of Christ, and to belong to Christ, if one hates him for whom Christ died. Yet the stumbling block can also be referred to both, as was done by Flacius: To remain in the light, he says, is here to persevere in the true knowledge, grace, and illumination of Christ. There is no stumbling block in him, it signifies, he does not impose upon himself, he does not deceive himself and others, by persuading himself that he is a Christian, and that he has God truly appeased, when it is by no means so. For by perverse persuasions men generate deception and a stumbling block for themselves, and seduce themselves, boasting in an empty persuasion of the favor of God and the expectation of eternal life, as do all hypocrites.

Therefore scandal, says Cornelius, that is, offense or stumbling block is not in him, whether active, as Saint Augustine says, or passive, as the Gloss says. For the diligent man offends or is offended by nothing, by no injury, by no customs, because charity is patient, is kind, etc., is not provoked, thinks no evil, etc., bears all things, believes all things, endures all things, 1 Corinthians XIII. verse 4. This is what the Wise Man says, Prov. XV. verse 19: The way of the just is without a stumbling block. And the Psalmist, Psalm CXIX. verse 165: Great peace have they who love your law, and there is no scandal for them.

And he does not know where he is going. Wherefore he also easily stumbles, as we have already said.

Because the darkness has blinded his eyes. It is a translation. For he wishes to say that he who is occupied in darkness sees no more than if he were blind: Blind, in Syriac, samia.

This can be understood either of the end of the way, or of the way itself, or of both. Estius brings forward those who understand it of the end: He does not know that he is going headlong into hell, he does not know that he is being dragged, ensnared in the traps of the Devil, into various temptations and stumbling blocks. But he calls the sense which we spoke of regarding the way more simple and genuine: Because of the darkness in which he walks, he does not see where he is going, what he is doing: he does not weigh and judge his actions by right reason, because the darkness in which he is placed has obscured the eyes of his mind. Flacius interprets it best regarding both, namely the intermediate and the ultimate end: He does not attend to the true end and scope of his actions, and the sad outcome of that feigned piety of his. He does not even consider where he is finally going to arrive, whether into the harbor of eternal salvation, or into the abyss of destruction. Darkness has blinded his eyes, by metaphor or similitude it signifies that the ignorance and blindness of the old Adam or his darkened mind, like the densest gloom of death, so occupies his internal eyes or intellect that he does not even once look at the way before his feet, and the goal of what he is doing or whither he is striving, and if he is going to arrive: Just as experience itself teaches, those secure and profane men do not even once judge themselves rightly and seriously, and consider and weigh whether their works, thoughts, and life are acceptable to God or not, and whether they are going to arrive at eternal life or destruction. Similarly, the blessed Hunnius: He does not know where they are rushing, because the Devil, the Prince of darkness, has blinded them with hatred, so that they stumble and strike against God and His holy law, and finally rush into the precipices of damnation. St. Cyprian on jealousy and envy: If you have begun to be a man of light, he says, which are truly of Christ, because Christ is light and day. Why do you rush into the darkness of jealousy? Likewise: For he goes unknowingly into hell, ignorant and blind he is cast headlong into punishment, receding, that is, from Christ the light, etc. Compare Prov. IV. 19. Psalm LIX. 10. Zeph. I. 17.

Latin:

v. 11. ὁ δὲ μισῶν τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἁυτῦ] Voce fratris ita sum- pta, uti jam diximus.

Ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ ἐστὶ κὶ ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ περιπατεῖ] Priori membro affectus, altero actus denotatur.

Neque Metonymia, neque Pleonasmus admitti hic debet. Sensus non est, quod ille non impingat, sed quod in ipso nihil sit, in quo alius offendatur vel impingat, quantum scilicet ad praecepta tabulae se- cundae, quibus continetur vera proximi dilectio, imo etiam tabulae primae, quia sincera proximi di- lectio sine dilectione Dei locum habere nequit, ideoque dilectio proximi signum est & argumen- tum τῆς μονῆς ἐν τῷ φωτί: quia fidei verae est exere- rese per charitatem. Non potest, inquit Oecume- nius, in lumine Christi esse, & ad Christum pertine- re, qui eum, pro quo Christus mortuus est, odit. Potest tamen etiam scandalum ad utrumque refer- ri, ut a Flacio factum: In luce manere, inquit, est hic in Christi vera notitia, gratia & illuminati- one perseverare. Offendiculum in eo non est, signi- ficat, non imponit sibimet, non facit sibi & aliis fu- cum, persuadendo sibi, quod sit Christianus, & Deum vere placatum habeat, cum nequaquam ita sit. Pravis enim persuasionibus homines sibimet fucum & offendiculum gignunt, seque ipsos sedu- cunt, sese lactantes inani persuasione favoris Dei & ex- spectationis vitae eternae, ut omnes hypocritae.

Scandalum ergo, inquit Cornelius, id est, offensio vel offendiculum in eo non est, sive activum, ut ait Sanct. Augustinus, sive passivum, ut ait Glossa. Diligens enim nulla re, nulla injuria, nullis mori- bus offendit vel offenditur, quia charitas patiens est, benigna est, &c. non irritatur, non cogitat malum, &c. omnia suffert, omnia credit, omnia sustinet, 1. Corinth. XIII. vers. 4. Hoc est quod ait Sapiens Prov. XV. vers. 19. Via justorum abs- que offendiculo. Et Psaltes Psal. CXIX. vers. 165. Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam, & non est illis scandalum.

Καὶ ὐκ οἶδε πῦ ὑπάγει] Quare & facile offendit, ut jam diximus.

ὅτι ἡ σκοτία ἐτύφλωσε τὺς ὀφθαλμὺς ἀυτῦ] Est translatio. Vult enim dicere, eum, qui in tenebris versatur, non plus vi- dere, quam si caecus esset: Τυφλῶν עור Syro סמי.

Id vel de fine viae accipi potest, vel de ipsa via, vel de utroque. De fine intelligentes adducit Estius: Nescit se praecipitem ire in gehennam, nescit se Dia- boli laqueis irretitum trahi in varias tentationes & offendicula. Simpliciorem autem ac germanio- rem dicit sensum, quem de via diximus: Praete- nebris, in quibus ambulat, non videt, quo eat, quid agat: actiones suas recta ratione non expendit & dijudicat, quia tenebra, in quibus est constitu- tus, mentis ejus oculos obscurarunt. Optime de utroque interpretatur Flacius de intermedio nem- pe & ultimo fine: Non attendit verum finem sco- pumque suarum actionum, & tristem exitum suae istius fucatae pietatis. Non considerat etiam, quo tandem sit perventurus, num in portum aeternae sa- lutis, aut in barathrum exitii. Tenebra oculos e- jus occaecarunt, per Metaphoram aut similitudinem significat, quod inscitia & caecitas veteris Adami seu obtenebrata ejus mentis tanquam densissima cali- go mortis, ejus oculos internos seu intellectum ita occupet, ut nec semel quidem prospiciat viam ante pedes, metamque quid agat aut quorsum contendat, sique perventurus: Sicut experientia ipsa docet, istos securos profanosque homines nec semel quidem recte serioque semet dijudicare, & considerare ac expendere, an sua opera, cogitationes vitaque sit Deo accepta, aut non, & an sint in æternam vitam aut exitium perventuri. Similiter B. Hunnius: Nescit quo ruant, eo quod Diabolus Princeps tenebrarum illos excæcavit odio, ut offendant & impingant in Deum & legem sanctam ipsius, & tandem in præci- pitia damnationis ruant. S. Cyprianus de zelo & livore: Si homo lucis, ait, esse cœpisti, quæ sunt Christi vere, quia lux & dies Christus est. Quid in zeli tenebras ruis? Item: It enim nescius in gehen- nam, ignarus & cæcus præcipitatur in pœnam, re- cedens scilicet à Christo lumine &c. Conf. Prov. IV. 19. Psal. LIX. 10. Soph. I. 17.

## 2:12
v. 12. I write to you, little children] In the Manuscript, I wrote to you, little children, is better, so that the ambiguity of the word little children, which he used generally before, may be avoided. He divides here and in the following verses Christians into three classes of children, young men, and old men, which distinctions ought to be understood not according to age, but according to the diverse degrees of that progress which is in Christ. See 1 Cor. III. 2. Heb. V. 13. Eph. IV. 13. That I wrote, however, refers to the preceding admonitions, which he now says were indeed written chiefly for the sake of the novices (see what was said above 1), yet not useless even to the others.

Because your sins are forgiven you for his name's sake] God has forgiven you the crimes of your former life for Christ's sake. You remember that this was said to you in baptism. His here signifies Christ, as his above 8. The good things which God confers upon Christians, he confers for Christ's sake, John XIV. 13, 14. XV. 16. XVI. 23, 24, 26. XX. 31. This also appeared in healings and the expulsions of demons, Acts III. 6, 16. IV. 10, 30. XVI. 18. But especially in the name of Christ, that is, for Christ's sake, sins are forgiven, which is said here, we also have in Acts X. 47. Sins, however, are forgiven so that hereafter one may live for Christ. And this is what he hints at here. See Luke I. 74. John V. 14.

Latin:

v. 12. Γράφω ὑμῖν τεκνία] In Manuscripto ἔγραψα ὑμῖν τεκ- νία, melius, ut vitetur ambiguum vocis τεκνία, quam ante ge- neratim usurpavit. Partitur hic & in sequentibus Christia- nos in classes tres puerorum, adolescentum & senum, quæ discrimina non secundum ætatem, sed secundum gradus di- versos ejus profectus, qui in Christo est, intelligi debent. Vide 1. Cor. III. 2. Ebr. V. 13. Eph. IV. 13. Illud autem ἔγραψα refert ad monita præcedentia, quæ jam dicit præcipua quidem scripta novitiorum causa (vide quæ dicta supra 1.) at- tamen non inutilia etiam cæteris.

Ὅτι ἀφέωνται ὑμῖν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι διὰ τὸ ὄνομα αὐτᾶ] Deus vobis vitæ prioris crimina propter Christum remisit. Me- ministis id vobis dictum in baptismo. Αὐτῶ Christum hic significat, ut αὐτῷ supra 8. Bona quæ Christianis confert Deus, ea confert propter Christum Joh. XIV. 13. 14. XV. 16. XVI, 23. 24. 26. XX. 31. Id etiam in sanationibus & ex- pulsionibus Dæmonum apparuit, Act. III. 6. 16. IV. 10. 30. XVI. 18. Præcipue vero in nomine Christi, id est ab Chri- stum remitti peccata, quod hic dicitur, habemus & Act. X. 47. Remissa autem sunt peccata, ut posthac Christo vivatur. Et hoc est, quod hic innuit. Vide Luc. I. 74. Joh. V. 14.

## 2:13
v. 13. I write to you, fathers] I desire these things to be written to you also, O old men. Old men are accustomed to be called Fathers, whence Fathers conscript, who were the Senators of Rome.

Because you have known him who is from the beginning] You have known God, who is the ancient of days, Dan. VII. 9, 32. He gives to each order what is suitable to it. From your first age you have known God, the maker of this world. But he is the one who sent Christ, and wished him to be heard for his own sake.

I write to you, young men] Having placed the extremes, he now places what is in the middle, בחורים, which is accustomed to be translated young men; those are called such who are of military age.

Because you have overcome the wicked one] He gives them what is suitable to military age; victory. You have conquered Satan, namely by a robust faith, through which the world also is conquered, below V. 4. Since you have prostrated the greatest enemy, the warfare hereafter under Christ the Leader will be easy for you.

I write to you, little children) Again in this Manuscript, I wrote. Chiefly, he says, I had written these things for your sake.

Because you have known the Father] It is sweet for little ones to know their father, that is, the Father's goodness. But those who know him well take care not to offend so good a parent, and change his goodness into wrath.

The ambiguity of the word is sufficiently removed from the distribution of the classes, which teaches that the word is not taken generally for any reborn persons whatsoever, but in opposition to young men and old men. For he passes from the thesis to the hypothesis, from the genus to the species, so that what he had written to all concerning the new commandment, he now applies specifically to the diverse degrees of either ages or progresses. Grotius prefers these, but the reason does not appear why we should not stop at the propriety of the words, so that the application may be the more clear, and any age may be able to transfer that to itself; although I do not deny that in the application such regard for age has been had, that it is hinted that according to its diversity, different degrees of progress are also required among Christians. But neither is it necessary that we should take little children in a different sense here than in the first sense, since it can be said that a general name is prefixed in the explanation of the commandment, which St. John writes to the faithful, designated in v. 7, 8, which indeed tends generally to this, that we all have remission of sins, in the name of Christ, whoever believes in him. Then, however, the application is made to the different ages of Fathers, young men, and children. Which explanation seems more convenient. Thus, to the Fathers is attributed the knowledge of the eternal Word, to the young men the victory over the Devil, to the little children the recognition of the true heavenly Father, not in a divided sense, but a composite one; whence Saint Augustine rightly says these three pertain to the same persons. In the sons, he says, is signified birth, in the Fathers antiquity, in the youths fortitude. That distinct assignment is made for the sake of elegance and κατ' ἀναλογίαν (by analogy), because the Fathers, being older in age, are referred to that most ancient one who is from eternity: who is indeed the Word and Son of God the eternal Father κατ' ἔσω (inwardly), but is the Father of all fathers κατ' ἔξω (outwardly), of whom Saint Augustine says: Christ is new in the flesh, but ancient in birth. He adds: remember that you are Fathers. If you forget him who is from the beginning, you have lost fatherhood; Christ is called the eternal Father, Isaiah ch. 9, verse 6. To the young men, however, is attributed victory, because there is usually greater strength in young men, and they are more vigorous and more apt for warfare than old men and children. If the evil one, says Augustine, is conquered by the youths, he fights with us. He fights, but he does not overcome. Why? Because we are strong? Or because he is strong in us, who was found weak between the hands of his persecutors? He made us strong, who did not resist those who persecuted him. For he was crucified out of weakness, but he lives by the power of God. Finally, to the little children is attributed the knowledge of the Father, because it is the custom of children to know and love their father, and little children are especially delighted by paternal love. Since I find Flacius to be of the same mind (ὁμόψηφον) in these matters, I add his gloss: He inculcates this sentiment in three whole verses, and that through a certain distribution: first indeed by addressing all in general, then by species of ages separately as if into individual classes, and by attributing to them something as if proper in this arduous warfare of Christ. In this verse, therefore, he first addresses everyone, saying that he writes these things to them about Christ and his benefits for this reason, that they may know that they have through him the remission of sins, which is the primary good, and from which all other things depend. But this remission of debts comes to us from the heavenly Father on account of the name of Christ, because he himself satisfied for us by obeying and suffering, and now also applies that merit of his to us by his intercession, as I said at the beginning of the chapter. The name of Christ here signifies Christ himself, except that it also embraces the knowledge and doctrine of him, for a name altogether brings some knowledge of its thing. And at verse 13: He now begins to address separately the individual classes or ages of the pious, applying those goods to them, and first he attributes to the elders the knowledge of God, who was from eternity: because wisdom and science befit the old above all. Then he attributes to the youths victory over Satan, partly by alluding to the custom of this earthly life, where, as Homer also says, strong works and battles are for the youths, since they excel in strength, and military and other laborious and dangerous works are demanded of them: and partly also because Satan tempts that fierce youth, agitated by various affections, even more than other ages: so that it behooves them all the more to battle strenuously against him by rejecting his temptations. Finally, he attributes to the little children the knowledge of the Father, alluding, of course, to common life, where little children ought to know and obey their parents. However, this distribution is not to be so precisely and strictly accommodated or restricted to those ages, since it pertains to all.

Whence it is not obscure that Saint John, as in other places, used the verb of the present tense γράφω (I write) rather than ἔγραψα (I wrote), as the Manuscript of Grotius has, so that the members might harmonize with each other in the distinction. Some here likewise understand Christ by the Father, among whom is Estius: Because you already know and love Christ as a Father, inasmuch as you are reborn from him through faith. For the preceding words, specifically that 'on account of his name,' persuade that it should be explained concerning Christ. But since these three, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, are one, little depends on that.

Latin:

v. 13. Γράφω ὑμῖν πατέρες] Etiam vobis, ô senes, hæc scri- pta cupio. Senes vocari solent Patres, unde Patres conscripti, qui Senatores Romæ.

Ὅτι ἐγνώκατε τὸν ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς] Novistis Deum, qui senex dierum, Dan. VII. 9. 32. Dat cuique ordini quæ ipsi conve- niunt. A prima ætate novistis Deum, mundi hujus opifi- cem. Is autem est, qui Christum misit, eumque pro se au- diri voluit.

Γράφω ὑμῖν νεανίσκοι] Positis extremis jam ponit, quod in medio est בחורים quod verti solet νεανίσκοι, dicuntur ii, qui militaris sunt ætatis.

Ὅτι νενικήκατε τὸν πονηρόν] Dat illis, quod militari ætati convenit; victoriam. Vicistis Satanam nempe robusta fide, per quam & mundus vincitur, infra V. 4. Cum maximum hostem prostraveritis, facilis vobis erit imposterum sub Chri- sto Duce militia.

Γράφω ὑμῖν παιδία) Rursus hic Manuscriptus ἔγραψα. Præcipue, inquit, vestri causa hæc scripseram.

Ὅτι ἐγνώκατε τὸν Πατέρα] Parvulis dulce, nosse patrem suum, id est Patris bonitatem. Qui autem eum bene norunt, cavent sibi, ne tam bonum parentem offendant, & bonitatem ejus in iram immutent.

Ambiguitas vocis satis tollitur è distributione classium, quæ docet non generatim vocem accipi pro quibusvis renatis, sed in oppositione ad ado- lescentes & senes. Transit enim à thesi ad hypo- thesin, à genere ad speciem, ut quod omnibus scripserat de nova ἐντολῇ, jam applicet speciatim ad diversos gradus sive ætatum sive profectuum. Hos mavult Grotius, sed non apparet ratio, cur non in proprietate vocum sistamus, ut eo luculen- tior sit applicatio, & qualibet ætas ista ad se trans- ferre possit; quamvis non diffitear, in applicatione ita ætatis respectum habitum esse, ut pro ejus di- versitate etiam requiri penes Christianos diversos profectuum gradus, innuatur. Sed nec id neces- sarium est, ut τεκνία alio sensu hic accipiamus, quam sensu primo, quum dici possit, præmitti generale nomen in explicatione ἐντολῆς, quam per- scribit ad fideles S. Johannes, designatæ v. 7. 8. quod nempe γενικῶς eo tendat, quod omnes habea- mus remissionem peccatorum, in nomine Christi, quicunque credunt in ipsum. Deinde vero appli- cationem fieri ad ætates diversas Patrum, adole- scentum & puerorum. Quæ explicatio convenien- tior videtur. Ita Patribus tribuitur cognitio æterni Verbi, adolescentibus victoria Diaboli, parvulis agnitio veri Patris cœlestis, non in sensu diviso, sed composito; unde recte Sanct. Augustinus hæc tria ad eosdem pertinere ait. In filiis significatur, in- quit, nativitas, in Patribus antiquitas, in juve- nibus fortitudo. Distincta vero illa assignatio ele- gantiæ causa fit & κατ' ἀναλογίαν, quia Patres ætate seniores remittuntur ad antiquissimum eum, qui ab æterno est: qui Verbum quidem & Filius est DEI Patris æterni κατ' ἔσω, sed omnium patrum Pater est κατ' ἔξω, de quo Sanct. Augustinus: Novus est Christus in carne, sed an- tiquus in nativitate. Addit: mementote vos Pa- tres esse. Si obliviscamini eum, qui a principio est, perdidistis paternitatem, Christus Es. IX. vers. 6. Pater æternus dicitur. Adolescentibus vero tri- buitur victoria, quia solet in adolescentibus ma- jus robur esse, ac vegetiores illi sunt, aptioresque ad militiam, quam senes & pueri. Si malignus, inquit Augustinus, a juvenibus vincitur, pugnat nobiscum. Pugnat, sed non expugnat. Quare? Quia nos sumus fortes? An quia ille est fortis in nobis, qui inter manus persequentium infirmus inventus est? Ille nos fortes fecit, qui persequen- tibus non restitit. Crucifixus est enim ex infirmita- te, sed vivit ex virtute Dei. Denique parvulis tribuitur notitia Patris, quia mos puerorum est, nosse & amare patrem suum, & parvuli maxime delectantur amore paterno. Quum in his Flacium inveniam ὁμόψηφον, addo ejus glossam: Inculcat hanc sententiam tribus integris versibus, idque per quandam distributionem: primum quidem in ge- nere omnes compellando, deinde per species æta- tum separatim singulas veluti classes, eisque aliquid quasi proprium in hac ardua militia Christi tri- buendo. In hoc igitur versu primum omnes alloqui- tur, dicens, se ideo iis hac de Christo scribere, ejus- que beneficiis, ut sciant, se per eum habere pecca- torum remissionem, quod est primarium bonum, & unde alia omnia dependcant. Remissio autem ista debitorum contingit nobis à Patre cœlesti propter nomen Christi, quia ipse pro nobis obediendo & pa- tiendo satisfecit, & nunc quoque nobis suum illud meritum sua intercessione applicat, ut initio cap. dixi. Nomen Christi hic ipsum Christum signifi- cat, nisi quod etiam notitiam ejus doctrinamque complectatur, nam nomen omnino aliquam sua rei notitiam affert. Et ad v. 13. Incipit jam separatim singulas classes aut ætates piorum alloqui, applicando ista bona ad eas, ac primum senioribus tribuit co- gnitionem DEI, qui fuit ab æterno: quia senes decet imprimis sapientia & scientia. Deinde ju- venibus tribuit victoriam de Satana, tum alluden- do ad istius terrenæ vitæ consuetudinem, ubi, ut etiam Homerus ait, fortia opera pugnæque sunt juvenum, quandoquidem ipsi robore excellunt, & militaria aliaque laboriosa & periculosa opera ipsis demandantur: tum etiam quia ferocem istam ju- ventutem variis affectibus agitatam Satan etiam magis tentat quam alias ætates: ut eos etiam tan- to magis contra eum strenue præliari rejiciendo ejus tentationes oporteat. Postremo tribuit puerulis Patris cognitionem, alludendo nimirum ad com- munem vitam, ubi pueruli debent suos parentes agnoscere & audire. Non autem hæc distributio est adeo præcise arctéque accommodanda aut restrin- genda ad illas ætates, cum ad omnes pertineat.

Unde haud obscurum est, Sanct. Johannem po- tius, ut in cæteris, adhibuisse verbum præsentis temporis γράφω quam ἔγραψα, ut Manuscri- ptus Grotii habet, ut membra sibi consonarent in distinctione. Nonnulli per Patrem hic itidem intelligunt Christum, è quibus Estius: Quia Christum jam novistis ac diligitis, ut Patrem, ut- pote per fidem ex eo renati. Nam ut de Christo ex- ponatur, suadent præcedentia, nominatim illud propter nomen ejus. Sed quum hi tres Pater, Verbum & Spiritus Sanctus unum sint, parum in eo situm est.

## 2:14
Verse 14.

I have written to you, Fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning.

Although these words are missing in certain Codices, they nevertheless occur in most, namely in the principal Greek ones, as also in the Syriac Codices, and Augustine, Bede, Thomas, and Oecumenius have the same. Nor does Cornelius obscurely prefer here those ancient Codices which have them, although the Vulgate was declared authentic by the Council of Trent, praising Franc. Lucas of Bruges. It seems, he says, that this little verse was omitted, both because it is very similar in words and matter to the one immediately preceding, and because it was read exactly the same a little before. For when the Apostle had added courage to every age, so that, increased by the benefits of the Savior, it might rejoice and glory in the Lord, desiring to penetrate minds with greater weight and to have it remain fixed, he did the same thing again. Estius observes that it is likewise read in some Latin Manuscripts, and it is equally probable to him that this little verse was omitted by scribes as if it were superfluous, because it was exactly the same as the former. But it varies, it is not the same. For above in the Present it was said γράφω, I write to you Fathers, now in the Preterite he says, ἔγραψα I have written, because Saint John does not only write about these things in this chapter, but also recalls to their memory that he had written above, and thus he wished to imprint more effectively that primary argument of his information upon those to whom he writes. Both Greek and Syriac Codices have the Preterite here and in the following verse, although in the Latin Vulgate the following verse is expressed in the Present: I write to you, young men, not without tautology, as Estius observes that other Latin copies also have, I have written to you, young men. Therefore, with this emphatic repetition, Saint John inculcates that he is both writing and has written these things. John; what else does he imply, than that this doctrine should never slip from memory, as being uniquely necessary, which he wishes to be handed down in the Church at all times for this reason, that it should not suffice that it has been handed down, but it must be handed down continuously, because JESUS Christ is yesterday, today, the same and forever, Heb. XIII. verse 8., and he signifies that it is useful and most necessary for every age, whether estimated according to age or according to progress, because eternal life is situated in it, Is. LIII. verse 11. John XVII. v. 3. 1. John V. 20.

Ἔγραψα ὑμῖν νεανίσκοι] Here γράφω is more correct. Think that the same things are being written to you also, you who are more robust.

Why the past tense should be retained here, we have already said.

Ὅτι ἰσχυροί ἐστε, καὶ ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν μένει, καὶ νενικήκατε τὸν πονηρόν.

That first καὶ has the value of 'because' here, the second καὶ is placed for 'on that account': such usages of the copulative particle are frequent among the Hebrews. You are already strong, but not by your own powers: but for that reason [because that Word of God which proceeded from Christ is in you (for the Writer here posits μένειν and to be in as the same thing) from there such strength has come to you, that also you might conquer the Prince of this world. You ought therefore to be thankful for so great a gift. It is your duty to be vigilant, and never to cast away the arms given to you. That which we have said about the word μένειν appears to be true above II. 6. 10. soon 24. 27. 28. III. 6. 7. 14. 15. 24. IV. 12. 13. 15. 16. See also what we have said on John III. verse 36. V. 38.

That in the repetition only two members are repeated, namely fathers and young men, it is not to be thought that little children are less in need of that doctrine, but rather that under the name νεανίσκων both young men and little children are comprehended, and that this is taken here more generally, so that with the fathers it exhausts every age, and thus it is also implied that all those predicates and eulogies, which are attributed to distinct orders, apply to all: because as to the young men, so also to the little children that spiritual strength and victory over that evil one is assigned, for which cause it is now inserted with these words, and the Word of God abides in you, where the particle καί can be taken illatively, you are strong, and therefore you have conquered the evil one, namely by strength supplied by God; just as the preceding ὅτι can be understood in a causal sense (nor does Grotius deny it) in this way: I write to you young men, because you are strong, if indeed the Word of God, which is sufficient strength for you, in the Lord, abides in you, that is, in the interpretation of Estius, you constantly retain the faith of the Gospel, from the comparison of 1 Pet. V. 9. whom resist strong in the faith, and therefore you have also conquered the evil one. Some understand the uncreated and incarnate Word: because when Christ abides in us through faith, we conquer in his virtue. The matter as regards the sense of this sentence comes to the same thing: because we do not conquer through the Word otherwise than as it exhibits and presents to us Christ the victor over Satan, so that we may apprehend the same through faith, from whom and in whom is all victory of faith, which that we may embrace by the efficacy of the Word, which is the power of God unto salvation, it is effected.

It appears, however, from this address to all the faithful, fathers, young men, little children, that holy Scripture is intended for all, is commended to all, and that all can derive fruit from it, obtain faith and remission of sins through it, know God the Father and Jesus Christ, attain spiritual strength, and conquer the evil one through Scripture, and therefore no one is to be debarred from the reading of holy Scripture, which is a letter of the omnipotent GOD, as Basil says, sent to all: a workshop of salvation and a spiritual panoply open to all.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Ἔγραψα ὑμῖν, Πατέρες, ὅτι ἐγνώκατε τὸν ἀπ' ἀρχῆς.

Etsi hæc verba in quibusdam Codicibus desi- derentur, in plerisque tamen occurrunt, in præci- puis nempe Græcis, ut & in Syris Codicibus, ha- bentque eadem Augustinus, Beda, Thomas, & Oecumenius. Nec obscure hic præfert Cornelius antiquos illos Codices, qui ea habent, Vulgatæ etsi authenticæ declaratæ à Concilio Tridentino, laudans Franc. Lucam Burgensem. Videtur, in- quit, hic versiculus omissus fuisse, tum quia proxi- me præcedenti verbis ac re simillimus est, tum quia paulo ante prorsus idem lectus est. Cum enim A- postolus omni animum addidisset ætati, ut Serva- toris aucta beneficiis in Domino gauderet gloriare- turque, cupiens majori id pondere mentes penetrare, fixumque inhærere, iterum idipsum egit. Estius in nonnullis Latinis Manuscriptis legi itidem observat, eique pariter probabile est, à libra- riis omissum hunc versiculum velut superfluum, quod prorsus idem esset cum priore. Sed variat, non idem est. Supra enim in Præsenti dictum erat γράφω, scribo vobis Patres, jam in Præterito inquit, ἔγραψα scripsi, quia non tan- tum in hoc capite scribit de his Sanct. Johannes, sed etiam supra se scripsisse in memoriam ipsis revocat, adeoque ita efficacius illud argumen- tum præcipuum suæ informationis imprimere iis voluit, ad quos scribit. Habent hic & in se- quenti commate Præteritum & Græci & Syriaci Codices, tametsi in Latinæ Vulgatæ sequens com- ma in Præsenti efferatur: Scribo vobis juvenes, non absque Tavtologia, ut Latina exemplaria alia observat Estius etiam habere, scripsi vobis adolescentes. Hæc ergo emphatica repetitione, cum & scribere & scripsisse se ista inculcat Sanct. Johannes; quid aliud innuit, quam ne unquam memoria hæc excidat doctrina, utpote unicè necessaria, quam omni tempore ideo tradi vult in Ecclesia, ut non sufficiat, eam traditam es- se, sed tradi debeat continua, quia JESUS Christus heri, hodie, idem & in secula, Ebr. XIII. vers. 8., omnique ætati tum secundum ætatem, tum secundum profectum æstimatæ utilem ma- ximéque necessariam significat, quia in ea vita æterna sita est, Es. LIII. vers. 11. Joh. XVII. v. 31. 1. Joh. V. 20.

Ἔγραψα ὑμῖν νεανίσκοι] Hic rectius γράφω. Eadem & vobis scribi putate, vos robustiores.

Cur hic Præteritum retinendum sit, jam dixi- mus.
