Ὅτι ἰσχυροί ἐστε, καὶ ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν μένει, καὶ νενικήκατε τὸν πονηρόν.

Illud prius καὶ valet hic quia, alterum καὶ positum est pro ob id: quales usurpationes particulæ copulativæ frequentes Ebræis. Fortes jam estis, sed non vestris vi- ribus: verum ideo [quia Verbum illud Dei profectum à Christo est in vobis (nam μένειν & inesse pro eodem hic ponit Scriptor) inde vobis robur tantum obtigit, ut & mundi hujus Principem vinceretis. Grati ergo esse debetis pro tanto munere. Vestrum est vigilare, nec unquam proji- cere arma vobis data. Quod diximus de voce μένειν verum esse apparet supra II. 6. 10. mox 24. 27. 28. III. 6. 7. 14. 15. 24. IV. 12. 13. 15. 16. Vide & quæ diximus ad Joh. III. vers. 36. V. 38.

Quod in repetitione duo tantum membra ite- rentur, de patribus nempe, & adolescentibus, non censendum, minus ea doctrina egere parvulos, sed sub nomine νεανίσκων potius & adolescentes & parvulos comprehendi, idque hic generalius acci- pi, ut cum patribus omnem ætatem exhauriat, adeoque innui etiam omnia illa prædicata & elo- gia, quæ distinctis ordinibus tributa sunt, conve- nire universis: quia ut juvenibus, ita & parvulis fortitudo illa spiritualis & victoria maligni illius assignatur, cujus causa nunc inseritur hisce ver- bis, & Verbum Dei manet in vobis, ubi potest particula καί illative accipi, fortes estis, & ideo vicistis malignum, nempe viribus à Deo suppedi- tatis; quemadmodum præcedens ὅτι sensu causali intelligi potest (neque abnuit Grotius) hoc mo- do: Scribo vobis juvenes, quoniam fortes estis, siquidem Verbum Dei, quod sufficit vobis robur, in Domino, manet in vobis, id est, interprete Estio, fidem Evangelii constanter retinetis, è collatione 1. Petr. V. 9. cui resistite fortes in fide, ideoque vi- cistis etiam malignum. Nonnulli Verbum increa- tum & incarnatum intelligunt: quia cum Christus in nobis manet per fidem, in virtute ejus vinci- mus. Res quod ad sensum istius sententiæ, eo- dem recidit: quia per Verbum non vincimus ali- ter, quam qua Christum victorem Satanæ nobis exhibet & sistit, ut eundem per fidem apprehen- damus, à quo & in quo est omnis fidei victoria, quem ut amplectamur Verbi efficacia, quod est potentia Dei ad salutem efficitur.

Apparet autem ex hac compellatione omnium fidelium, Patrum, juvenum, parvulorum, Scri- pturam sacram omnibus destinatam esse, omni- bus commendari, omnesque ex illa fructum ca- pere posse, fidem & remissionem peccatorum per eandem obtinere, cognoscere Deum Patrem & Jesum Christum, fortitudinem spiritualem con- sequi, & vincere malignum per Scripturam, ad- eoque neminem arcendum esse à Scripturæ sacræ lectione, quæ epistola est omnipotentis DEI, Basilio dicente, ad omnes missa: officina salutis & panoplia spiritualis omnibus aperta.

## 2:15
Ver. 15.

Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. He shows how it can best be done that we fulfill the precepts of Christ. Namely, if we do not enslave our affections to imitate the greater part of men, and to affect those things which the greater part of men value highly. By the name of the world John, both in the Gospel I. 10. c. 7, 7. c. 8, 23. c. 14, 19. c. 15, 18. 19. XVI. 8. H. 20. XVII. 14. and in this epistle, as can be seen below 16. 17. III. 1. 13. 17. IV. 5. V. 4. 5. often understands the human race, not entirely universal, as he sometimes takes that word, but κατὰ τὸ ἐπικράτουν, according to the greater part, which, as he says below, is set in wickedness, that is, is occupied in evil actions, and takes pleasure in them. He who loves some person willingly imitates him. He who loves some things, affects them. To be in the world is said here in an eminent way, those things which the world values highly: which are held before the eyes and mind of the world, which keep the affections of the world fixed.

As those who through faith have obtained remission of sins, and by abiding in the Word of God conquer that evil one, lest they be seduced by the world, which lies entirely in the evil one, 1 John V. 19, especially because the love of the world cannot consist with the love of God, and the world passes away, but he who does the will of God abides into eternity, the faithful are diligently warned not to love the world, and the things that are in the world. Flacius here begins the second principal part of the chapter; in which, after he has placed us in the possession of Christ and his benefits, he now also teaches us, so that we may be able to persevere all the more firmly in him, what contrary evils we ought to avoid: namely, first all the wicked attempts of the world, which tries to draw us away from CHRIST and true piety, either by its allurements or even by various assaults. Moreover, this warning about not loving the world can still be referred to the eulogy of the doctrine of Christ, which he commended as the Word, through which we conquer the Devil, provided we abide in the Word of CHRIST, and do not allow ourselves to be conquered by him through the desires of the world, since the love of God and the love of the world are incompatible, and only the Word of the Lord, and those who do the will of God, abide forever; but the world with its desires is about to pass away, so that through the doctrine of Christ we obtain remission of sins, the grace of God, and victory over the world through faith in the name of Christ; so it must be guarded against most carefully, lest, ensnared by the love of the world, we be drawn away from Christ, suffer shipwreck of faith, lose the grace of God, and be overcome by that evil one. Flee the world, says Augustine in this place, if you wish to be clean. If you are clean, the world no longer delights you; flee creatures, if you wish to have the Creator. Let every creature become vile, so that the Creator may become sweet in the heart. He does not teach here how the precepts of Christ are to be fulfilled, but what things deprive us of the salutary fruit of the evangelical doctrine of Christ.

By the world, however, is not understood the physical world, or the system of this world, as Cornelius à Lapide wishes, on the argument that those things which are in the world, or the lusts, are distinguished from the world; for the lusts are not in the world physically considered, but as it is corrupt, nor in all things in this world, but in man alone; nor is the worldly life itself or concupiscence in general understood, so that its three species are then added, which sense Cornelius also does not disapprove: For John distinguishes all those lusts from the world, and therefore the world must be something different, not the lusts themselves, which are said to be in the world, and from the world. What then? The same Cornelius admits that worldly men are designated by the word world, following the goods and allurements of the world, from a comparison of the passages John I. 10, chapter XVI. 18. and of others here and there in John; nor indeed is it to be thought, with Cornelius, that the world is taken here in all these three ways, and that Saint John looks now to one, now to another, and plays upon the word world. Estius is correct: He calls the world men given over to the things of this world. But the world thus accepted, that is, evil men, he forbids to be loved, insofar as they are such. For insofar as they are men, capable of the same blessedness as we, they are to be loved by us to this end, that, being rescued from the world, they may be saved. Our blessed Hunnius favors this sense: That general love which is owed to any men, whether impious or pious, is not forbidden: but that preposterous and overly special love, by which the impious are sometimes loved in such a way that their pursuits are at the same time approved and proposed for imitation. In which sense also 1 John V. 19 the whole world is said to lie in the wicked one. Nor does Grotius deny this explanation. And therefore by those things which are in the world are to be understood those which find the greatest place in the men of this world, those which the corrupt nature of men, which men occupied with worldly desires are accustomed to seek, as are pleasures, riches, honors.

If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. Naturally, because the Father wills one thing, the world wills another. And God and the world demand the whole man. Such two Masters cannot be served, nor can such two Masters be loved. See what we have said on this matter in Matt. VI. v. 24. The love of the Father here is that by which the Father is loved, as also above in verse 5. For πατρὸς in the Manuscript it is τοῦ Θεοῦ. The love of the Father can be understood either as the love by which the Father is loved, or by which the Father pursues us. I have taught above that the latter, not the former, is being dealt with in verse 5. Cornelius à Lapide, Estius, and others understand the former in this place. To which pertains that saying of Leo, Sermon V on the fast of the 7th month: There are two loves, from which all pleasures proceed, as diverse in their qualities as they are divided by their authors. For the rational mind, which cannot exist without love, is either a lover of God or of the world. In the love of God there is nothing excessive, but in the love of the world everything is harmful. And therefore one must inseparably adhere to eternal goods; but temporal things must be used transiently, so that as we are pilgrims and hastening to return to our homeland, whatever of the prosperities of this world we encounter may be a provision for the journey, not an enticement to stay. And what Augustine (or whoever the author is) has in the book on the 12 abuses, chapter 7: The love of the world and of God cannot equally inhabit the heart, just as the same eyes by no means look upon heaven and earth equally. But it is more fittingly understood as the love with which God embraces us. For he teaches that we cannot live in the grace of God, which we have obtained through faith in Christ, and rejoice in the remission of sins, which we have obtained in the name of Christ, if we love the world and the things that are in the world. To this can be referred what St. James says in chapter IV, verse 1, that the friendship of the world is enmity with God, and that he who wishes to be a friend of the world becomes an enemy of God; because it is opposed to the enmity of God, the grace of God in verse 6, and it is taught that he resists the lovers of the world as being proud, but does not bestow grace, which falls to the humble. But above all, what we observed regarding verse 5 serves this sense. Thus the Apostle persists in the same argument.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Μὴ ἀγαπᾶτε τὸν κόσμον, μηδὲ τὰ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ] Ostendit quomodo optime fieri possit, ut Christi præcepta implea- mus. Nempe si affectus nostros non mancipemus ad imi- tandam majorem hominum partem, & ad affectanda, quæ major pars hominum magni facit. Mundi nomine Johan- nes tum in Evangelio I. 10. c. 7, 7. c 8, 23. c. 14. 19. c. 15, 18. 19. XVI. 8. H. 20. XVII. 14. tum in hac epistola, ut videre est infra 16. 17. III. 1. 13. 17. IV. 5. V. 4. 5. Sæpe intelligit humanum genus, non plane universum, quomodo inter- dum sumit eam vocem, sed κατὰ τὸ ἐπικράτουν, secundum partem majorem, quæ, ut infra dicit, in malo posita est, id est, in malis actionibus versatur, inque iis sibi placet. Qui hominem aliquem diligit, libenter eum imitatur. Qui res aliquas diligit, eas affectatur. In mundo esse hic dicun- tur eximio modo, ea quæ mundus magni facit: quæ mun- do ob oculos animumque versantur, quæ mundi affectus defixos tenent.

Ut qui per fidem remissionem peccatorum con- sequuti sunt, & in Verbo Dei manendo τὸν πονη- ρὸν malignum illum vincunt, ne à mundo, qui totus in maligno jacet, 1. Joh. V. 19. seducantur, imprimis quia amor mundi cum amore Dei consistere non potest, ac mundus transit, qui vero Dei volunta- tem facit, in æternitatem permanet, sedulo mo- nentur fideles, ne mundum ament, & ea, quæ in mundo sunt. Flacius hic secundam partem capitis principalem inchoat; in qua postquam nos in Chri- sti ejusque beneficiorum possessione collocavit, jam etiam quo in eo tanto firmius perseverare queamus, docet nos, quænam contraria mala devitare debeamus: nempe primum omnes pravos conatus mundi, nos vel per illecebras suas, vel etiam per varias oppu- gnationes a CHRISTO veraque pietate abstrahere conantis. Referri autem hoc de non diligendo mundo monitum ad elogium doctrinæ Christi ad- huc potest, quam commendavit ceu Verbum, per quod vincimus Diabolum, modo in Verbo CHRISTI maneamus, nec per cupiditates mundi nos vinci ab eo patiamur, quum amor Dei & amor mundi ἀσύςατα sint, solumque Domini Verbum, & qui voluntatem Dei faciunt, in æter- num maneant; mundus autem cum desideriis ejus transiturus sit, ut per doctrinam Christi re- missionem peccatorum, gratiam Dei & victoriam mundi consequimur per fidem in nomen Christi; ita cavendum maximopere, ne amore mundi in- escati, a Christo abstrahamur, fidei naufragium patiamur, gratiam Dei deperdamus, & a maligno illo superemur. Fuge mundum, inquit Augustinus in hoc loco, si vis esse mundus. Si tu es mundus, jam non te delectat mundus; fuge creaturas, si vis habere Creatorem. Omnis creatura vilescat, ut Creator in corde dulcescat. Non hic docet, quo- modo Christi præcepta implenda sint, sed quæ do- ctrinæ Christi Evangelicæ fructu salutari nos privent.

Per mundum autem non intelligitur mundus physicus, vel systema hujus mundi, ut vult Cor- nelius à Lapide eo argumento, quod ea, quæ in mundo sunt, vel concupiscentiæ a mundo di- stinguantur; non enim concupiscentiæ sunt in mundo physice spectato, sed qua corruptus est, nec in rebus omnibus in hoc mundo, sed in ho- mine solo; neque etiam intelligitur ipsa mundana vita vel concupiscentia in genere, ut subjungantur deinde ejus tres species, quem sensum etiam non improbat Cornelius: Nam concupiscentias illas omnes Johannes distinguit a mundo, ideoque ali- quid diversi oportet esse mundum, non ipsas con- cupiscentias, quæ in mundo esse dicuntur, & ex mundo. Quid ergo? Homines mundanos voce mundi designari Cornelius idem fatetur, mundi bona & illecebras sectantes, e collatione locorum Joh. I. 10. cap. XVI. 18. & aliorum passim apud Jo- hannem; nec vero cum Cornelio censendum, omni- bus istis tribus modis mundum hic accipi, & Sanct. Johannem nunc ad unum, nunc ad alterum respi- cere, ac in voce mundi ludere. Recte Estius: Mundum vocat homines deditos rebus hujus mundi. Mundum autem sic acceptum, id est homines malos diligi vetat, quatenus tales. Nam quatenus homines sunt, ejusdem nobiscum beatitudinis capaces diligendi sunt a nobis ad hoc, ut eruti mundo salvi fiant. Cui sensui favet B. Hunnius noster: Non prohiberi generalem illam dilectionem, quæ debetur quibusvis hominibus seu impiis seu piis: sed præposteram nimisque specialem dilectionem, quæ ita nonnunquam diliguntur impii, ut simul studia illorum approbentur, & ad imitationem proponan- tur. Quo sensu etiam 1. Joh. V. 19. mundus totus in maligno positus dicitur. Nec abnuit huic ex- plicationi Grotius. Ideoque per ea, quæ in mundo sunt, intelligenda, quæ in hominibus hujus mun- di maxime locum inveniunt, illa, quæ corrupta hominum natura, quæ homines mundanis deside- riis occupati appetere solent, ut solent voluptates, divitiæ, honores.

Ἐάν τις ἀγαπᾷ τὸν κόσμον, οὐκ ἔστιν ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ Πατρὸς ἐν αὐτῷ) Nimirum quia alia vult Pater, alia vult mundus. Et Deus & mundus hominem totum postulant. Talibus Do- minis duobus serviri non potest, nec amari possunt tales Do- mini duo. Vide quæ ad hanc rem diximus Matth. VI. v. 24. Dilectio Patris hic est, qua Pater diligitur, ut & supra 5. Pro πατρὸς in Manuscripto est τοῦ Θεοῦ. Dilectio Patris intelligi potest vel de dilectione, qua Pater diligitur, vel qua Pater nos prosequi- tur. De hac, non de illa vers. 5. agi supra docui- mus. Illam hoc loco intelligunt Cornelius à Lapi- de, Estius, alii. Quo pertinet illud Leonis serm. V. de jejun. 7. mensis : Duo amores sunt, ex quibus prodeunt omnes voluptates, ita diversæ qualitatibus, sicut dividuntur autoribus. Rationabilis enim animus, qui sine dilectione esse non potest, aut Dei amator est, aut mundi. In dilectione Dei nulla ni- mia in dilectione autem mundi cuncta noxia. Et ideo æternis bonis inseparabiliter inhærendum; tem- poralibus vero transeunter utendum est, ut peregri- nantibus nobis, & ad patriam redire properantibus, quicquid de prosperitatibus mundi hujus occurre- rit, viaticum sit itineris, non illecebra mansionis. Et quod Augustinus, (vel quisquis est autor) libr. de 12. abusion. grad. 7. habet. Mundi amor & Dei pariter in corde cohabitare non possunt, quemad- modum iidem oculi cœlum pariter & terram ne- quaquam aspiciunt. Sed convenientius intelligitur amor, quo nos Deus complectitur. Docet enim non posse nos in gratia Dei, quam in Christo per fidem adepti sumus, conversari ac remissione peccato- rum, quam obtinuimus in nomine Christi, gaude- re, si mundum, & ea quæ in mundo sunt, ame- mus. Eo referri potest, quod S. Jacobus cap. IV. vers. 1. dicit, mundi amicitiam esse inimicitiam Dei, eum, qui vult mundi esse amicus, Dei inimi- cum fieri; quia opponitur inimicitiæ Dei gratia Dei vers. 6. & mundi amatoribus utpote superbis resistere, non vero gratiam largiri docetur, quæ obtingit humilibus. Sed imprimis huic sensui in- serviunt, quæ ad vers. 5. observavimus. Sic in eo- dem argumento persistit Apostolus.

## 2:16
Vers. 16.

For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. 'All that is in the world' is said in the same way as we say, 'this is his everything,' that is, he has great power with him. This sentiment, however, is taken from the ancient Hebrews, from whom Pythagoras received it, and from Pythagoras, Clinias: 'Whenever one must seek the causes of how it is that men are naturally inclined to do wrong. These happen to be three: love of pleasure in bodily enjoyments, greed in gaining, and love of honor in excelling one's equals or peers.' Philo to the Decalogue: 'For all the wars of the Greeks and barbarians, waged against themselves and against each other, flowed from one source of desire, either of money, or of glory, or of pleasure. For the human race withers around these things.' The desire of the flesh is concerning feasts, the belly, and anything similar. For that is satisfied through the flesh itself. The desire of the eyes is the desire for money, naturally because if you separate bodily pleasures from it, all money and possessions are nothing but fodder for the eyes. Menander: 'One must have a rich soul, but money is the appearance, a veil of life.' Thus in Ecclesiastes IV. 8: 'His eyes are not satisfied with riches.' And V. v. 10: 'Where there are many riches, there are many who eat them. And what does it profit the owner, except that he sees the riches with his eyes?' The pride of life is the love of honor, the desire for glory, under which the desire for vengeance is also included. Thus in Euripides' Iphigenia in Aulis, when Agamemnon had said: 'But those in honors are less envious,' the old man says: 'And yet, the beautiful is in the life there.' That is, in honors is the splendor of life. The general name for all these is 'desire,' which the Hebrews believe is mystically noted under Eve.

Who those ancient Hebrews are, the Polyhistor does not explain. We, however, assent to the interpretation which is to be preferred to that which Estius reports as sufficiently accepted: that by the name of the lust of the eyes is signified the whole genus of curiosity, that is, an inordinate desire for living, knowing, and experiencing; which extends very widely. As in learning vain and superstitious arts, in watching vain or lascivious spectacles, in exploring the vices of neighbors or other secrets not pertaining to oneself, in demanding signs and wonders without necessity. Estius himself acknowledges that the explanation of Thomas I. 2, question 77, article 5, and of Jansenius regarding avarice is sufficiently consistent with other places of Scripture in which the insatiable desire of the eyes is reproved, Eccl. IV, Sir. XIV. Prov. XXVII, and he prefers it, and gives the reason for this appellation: Because avarice is the desire for those things which everywhere strike the eyes, and whose desire is wont to be drawn in through the sense of the eyes, such as money, fields, houses, clothes, and beautiful and ample furniture. Whence also children (in whom this vice manifests itself) desire whatever beautiful thing they see, and it is wont to be said of them that they want to have whatever they see. For they do not cover or hide their desire, as men do. Wherefore those three things are indicated here, which are most desired by men who are corrupt by origin and not reborn: pleasure, riches, honors, but insofar as those are forbidden or are inordinately desired. To which the rest, which they wrongly desire, can easily be reduced. For St. John did not wish to explain so much the sins, as the worst roots of all sins. Concerning the concupiscence of the flesh, all agree that it is used in a special sense, inasmuch as it is distinguished from the concupiscence of the eyes and the pride of life: that by it is understood incontinence and intemperance, the species of which are, among others, gluttony and luxury. Concerning the pride of life, there is also no doubt. The Syriac has 'of the world,' Cyprian in De mortalitate, and Augustine in this place, 'ambition of the world,' because βίος signifies a kind of life, a manner, an institution, and a state, as they call it. Today they say 'reason of state.' Estius wishes to indicate that this is in Luke XII, verse 29: 'Do not be lifted up on high.' But there it is μετεωρίζεσθε, 'do not fluctuate, or be carried about by doubts like meteors.' Augustine refers the vanity of spectacles to the concupiscence of the eyes in an ambiguous sense in book III of De symbolo, chapter 1. To the concupiscence of the flesh, he says, belong the allurements of pleasures; to the concupiscence of the eyes, the vanity of spectacles; to the ambition of the world, the insanity of pride. Concerning avarice, however, Augustine declares elsewhere in book X of the Confessions, chapters 30 and following, with whom also Thomas, I-II, q. 75, art. 5, makes these three passions the three fountains of all temptations and sins, concerning which Baptista Mantuanus says:

Ambitious honor, and wealth, and foul pleasure, / These three the world holds as a threefold Deity. / Saint Hilary says: The world, he says, swells with pride, burns with avarice, foams with luxury.

It is not of the Father, but is of the world) The Syriac reads: 'This is.' And either it must be read thus, or some pronoun must be understood, namely ἃ or ταῦτα: such a substitution of pronouns we have had elsewhere. God has implanted in us the desires of nature, which require only a few and easily obtainable things. Other appetites are from bad upbringing and from bad examples. See Juvenal, Satire XIV.

But why is that necessary? Does not the discourse flow perfectly well and clearly, 'that all that is in the world (the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes, and the'

ἀλαζονεία τῦ βίε) is not of the Father, but is of the world. Grotius clearly wished to supply the preceding words, so that they might complete the full sense in this way: Πᾶν τὸ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, all that is in the world, has great power over him (the lover of the world). Therefore he also seeks a supplement for the rest. But those are entirely in vain. Furthermore, Saint John does not here understand the objects of the desires, as some wish, e.g., wine, or women, riches, honors, but the base and inordinate desires concerning such objects, because he says they are not from the Father, not desires implanted in nature by GOD, but perverse cravings: nor are these evil appetites only from a bad constitution and from bad examples, but primarily from a base origin, or congenital craving and concupiscence, which we call original sin. Which, against the Pelagians and Socinians, upon whom Grotius perhaps here pours cold water, is demonstrated elsewhere. The Apostle's argument, therefore, for not loving such things, which he said are in the unclean world and has comprised in three classes, is sought from the first origin, because they are not from the Father or from GOD, who made all things very good, Gen. I. last verse. He is the Father of lights, and ἀπείραστος τῶν κακῶν, James I. verses 12, 13, but from the perverse world, and consequently from the Devil, who seduced the first man to base concupiscence. Whoever, therefore, loves the world as it is perverse, and those things which are eminent evils in the world, follows the Devil and has him as his author, not GOD the Father. It is clear that he who is not from the Father, but from the world, is from the Devil, says Oecumenius here. Therefore the Devil is called the Prince of the world, John XII. 31, ch. XIV. v. 30, ch. XVI. v. 11.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Ὅτι πᾶν τὸ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἡ ἐπιθυμία τῆς σαρκός, καὶ ἡ ἐπιθυ- μία τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν, καὶ ἡ ἀλαζονεία τοῦ βίου] Πᾶν τὸ ἐν τῷ κόσ- μῳ sic dicitur, sicut dicimus, hic est illi τὰ πάντα, id est, plu- rimum apud illum potest. Sumpta autem hæc sententia ab Ebræis veteribus, unde accepit Pythagoras, à Pythagora Cli- nias: Ὁπόταν δὲ ἐκ τοῦ τὰς αἰτίας ἀναζητητέον ὡς εἶναι. ἀδι- κεῖν πέφυκεν ἀνθρώπους. αὗται δὲ τρεῖς τυγχάνουσι, Φιληδονία μὲν ἐν ταῖς ἀπολαύσεσι ταῖς διὰ σώματος, πλεονεξία δὲ ἐν τῷ κερδαίνειν, φιλοδοξία δὲ ἐν τῷ ὑπερέχειν τῶν ἴσων ἢ τῶν ὁμοίων. Philo ad Decalogum : Οἱ γὰρ Ἑλλήνων καὶ βαρβάρων πρός τε ἑαυτοὺς καὶ πρὸς ἀλλήλους πραγματευθέντες πόλεμοι πάντες ἀπὸ μι- ᾶς πηγῆς ἐῤῥύησαν ἐπιθυμίας, ἢ χρημάτων, ἢ δόξης, ἢ ἡδονῆς. Περὶ γὰρ ταῦτα κηραίνει τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένος. Cupido car- nis est circa epulas, ventrem & si quid simile. Ea enim per ipsam carnem expletur. Cupido oculorum est χρημάτων ἐπι- θυμία, nimirum quia si voluptates corporis ab ea separes, pe- cuniæ & possessiones omnes nihil sunt, nisi oculorum pabu- lum. Menander: Ψυχὴν ἔχειν δεῖ πλουσίαν, τὰ δὲ χρήματα Ταῦτ᾽ ἐστιν ὄψις παραπέτασμα τοῦ βίου. Sic Ecclesiastæ IV. 8. non satiantur oculi ejus divitiis. Et V. v. 10. Ubi multæ sunt opes, multi & qui comedunt eas. Et quid prodest possessori, nisi quod cernit divitias oculis suis? Ἀ- λαζονεία τοῦ βίου est φιλοδοξία, δόξης ἐπιθυμία, sub qua & ulti- onis cupiditas comprehenditur. Sic in Euripidis Iphigenia Aulidensi, cum dixisset Agamemnon: Τοῖς δὲ ἐν τιμαῖς ἧσσον ζηλῶ ait senex? Καὶ μὴν τὸ καλόν γ᾽ ἐνταῦθα βίου. Id est, in honoribus est splendor vitæ. Generale nomen ho- rum omnium est ἐπιθυμία, quam μυσικῶς sub Eva notari cen- sent Ebræi.

Quinam Ebræi illi veteres sint, non explicat Polybistor. Annuimus autem interpretationi, quæ præferenda illi, quam refert Estius ceu satis rece- ptam: Nomine concupiscentiæ oculorum significari totum genus curiositatis, id est, inordinatæ cupidi- tatis vivendi, sciendi, & experiendi; quod admo- dum late patet. Ut in addiscendis vanis & super- stitiosis artibus, in contuendis vanis aut lascivis spectaculis, in explorandis proximorum vitiis, aliis- ve secretis ad se non pertinentibus, in flagitandis sine necessitate signis & prodigiis. Agnoscit Estius ipse explicationem Thomæ I. 2. quæst. 77. art. 5. & Jansenii de avaritia satis consentaneam esse aliis Scripturæ locis, in quibus reprehenditur insati- abilis oculorum cupiditas, Eccl. IV. Sir. XIV. Prov. XXVII. eamque præfert, & rationem red- dit hujus appellationis: Quia avaritia cupiditas est earum rerum, quæ passim in oculos incurrunt, & quarum desiderium per sensum oculorum hau- riri solet, ut pecuniarum, agrorum, domorum, vestium, pulchræ & amplæ supellectilis. Unde & pueri (in quibus hoc vitium sese exerit) quicquid pulchri vident, concupiscunt, ac de iis dici solet, quod, quicquid vident, velint habere. Non enim tegunt aut dissimulant cupiditatem suam, sicut viri. Quapropter tria illa hic indicantur, quæ ab ho- minibus origine corruptis & non renatis maxime appetuntur, voluptas, divitiæ, honores, sed qua- tenus prohibita illa sunt, aut inordinate appe- tuntur. Ad quæ cætera facile reduci possunt, quæ male concupiscunt. Non enim tam peccata, quam peccatorum omnium pessimas radices explicare voluit Sanct. Johannes. De carnis concupiscentia omnes consentiunt, quia speciali sensu adhibetur, utpote quæ distinguitur à concupiscentia oculo- rum, & superbia vitæ: per eam intelligi inconti- nentiam, & intemperantiam, cujus species in- ter alia sint gula, & luxuria. De superbia vitæ etiam dubium nullum est. Syrus habet mundi, Cyprianus de mortal. & Augustinus in hoc loco ambitio seculi, quia βίος vitæ genus, rationem, institutum & statum, quem vocant, significat. Hodie rationem status dicunt. Quod Luc. XII. vers. 29. indicari vult Estius: Nolite in sublime tolli: Sed ibi μετεωρίζεσθε est, ne fluctuetis, vel dubitationibus circumferamini meteororum in- star. Ad oculorum concupiscentiam spectaculo- rum nugacitatem refert Augustinus ambiguo sen- su libr. III. de symbol. cap. 1. Ad concupiscentiam carnis, inquiens, pertinent illecebræ voluptatum, ad concupiscentiam oculorum nugacitas spectaculo- rum, ad ambitionem seculi insania superbia. De avaritia tamen alibi declarat Augustinus lib. X. Conf. cap. 30. seqq. cum quo etiam Thomas I. 2. q. 75. art. 5. hasce tres passiones facit fontes tres omnium tentationum & peccatorum, de quibus Baptista Mantuanus:

Ambitiosus honos, & opes, & fœda voluptas, Hæc tria pro trino Numine mundus habet. Sanct. Hilarius: Mundus, inquit, tumet super- bia, fervet avaritia, spumat luxuria.

Οὐκ ἔστι ἐκ τῦ Πατρὸς, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ τῦ κόσμυ ἐστί) Syrus le- git: Αὕτη ἐστιν. Et aut sic legendum, aut Pronomen aliquod subintelligendum, nempe ἃ aut ταῦτα: Qualem pronomi- num subfcentiam & alibi habuimus. Deus nobis indidit na- turæ desideria, quæ paucis tantum & parabilibus indigent. Cæteri appetitus à mala institutione sunt & à malis exemplis. Vide Juvenalem Sat. XIV.

Cur vero id necessarium? Nonne optime & plane fluit oratio, ὅτι πᾶν τὸ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ (ἡ ἐπι- θυμία τῆς σαρκὸς κὴ ἡ ἐπιθυμία τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν, κὴ ἡ

ἀλαζονεία τῦ βίε) ἐκ ἔσιν ἐκ τῦ Πατρὸς, ἀλλὰ ἐκ τῦ κόσμε ἐσὶ. Nimirum priora voluit supplere Gro- tius, ut plenum sensum absolvant hoc modo: Πᾶν τὸ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, omne quod est in mundo, plurimum apud illum (mundi amatorem) potest. Ideo etiam reliquis supplementum quærit. Sed ea frustra omnino sunt. Porro non objecta con- cupiscentiarum hic intelligit Sanct. Johannes, ut nonnulli volunt, verb. gr. vinum, vel mulie- res, opes, honores, sed desideria prava & inordinata circa talia objecta, quia dicit ea non esse à Patre, non desideria à DEO naturæ in- dita, sed perversas cupiditates: nec hi appeti- tus mali tantum à constitutione mala sunt, & à malis exemplis, sed imprimis à prava origine, vel congenita cupiditate & concupiscentia, quam peccatum originale vocamus. Quod adversus Pelagianos, & Socinistas, quibus forte frigidam hic suffundit Grotius, alias demonstratur. Ar- gumentum ergo Apostoli non amandi talia, quæ in mundo immundo esse dixit, & tribus classi- bus complexus est, ab origine prima petitum est, quia illa non à Patre vel à DEO, qui o- mnia fecit valde bona, Gen. I. ult. Pater lumi- num est, & ἀπείραστος τῶν κακῶν, Jac. I. vers. 12. 13. sed à mundo perverso, & consequenter à Diabolo, qui primum hominem ad pravam con- cupiscentiam seduxit. Qui ergo mundum amat qua perversus est, & illa, quæ in mundo emi- nent mala, Diabolum sectatur & autorem ha- bet, non DEUM Patrem. Eum qui ex Patre non est, sed ex mundo, ex Diabolo esse perspi- cuum est, ait hic Oecumenius. Ideo Diabolus mundi Princeps dicitur, Job. XI. 31. c. XIV. v. 30. cap. XVI. v. 11.

## 2:17
Vers. 17.

Καὶ ὁ κόσμος παράγεται] Petit, that is, it was made by such a law that it should one day perish. 2 Pet. II. verse 7. Psalm CII. verse 27. Καὶ ἡ ἐπιθυμία αὐτῦ] In the Manuscript, αὐτῦ is not present. With the world destroyed, the belly is also destroyed, 1 Cor. VI. verse 13. Then those desires of this life which are natural will also cease, Matt. XXII. verse 30, Mark XII. verse 25, Luke XX. 35.

The second argument, why the world is not to be loved, is that the world itself is about to perish. Here the word 'world' is now used in a different sense, insofar as it denotes the whole system of the world. Cf. Matt. XXIV. verse 35, 1 Cor. VII. verse 31, 2 Pet. III. verse 11. The nerve of the conclusion is that, since the whole world, in which those delectable objects, food and drink, riches and honors of the age are so greatly sought after by the sons of this age, is perishable and will eventually perish, eternity must be contemplated and we must be preserved by the will of GOD, and those who do this do not perish, but remain forever. But those things which are in the world are not to be loved with an inordinate love, which inordinate love the Apostle had already warned before could not consist with the grace of God. Saint Anselm on chapter XII to the Romans. Do not constantly love the world, since it itself, which you love, cannot remain; you fix your heart in vain as if it were remaining, while it flees, the very thing you love. ὁ δὲ ποιῶν τὸ θέλημα τῦ Θεῦ] He who fulfills that will of God which has been revealed to us through Christ. Μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα] The same expression in John VIII. verse 35, XII. verse 34, meaning the same as ζήσεται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα in John VI. v. 51, 58, that is, he will receive that life which is never to end. Under such a great hope, no labors should seem hard. We despise the perishable, we desire the eternal.

We easily admit that the will, which was more clearly revealed to us through Christ, but was known to the faithful in the Old Testament as much as was sufficient, is understood. But that is not the legal will, which is also inscribed in great part upon nature, but the Evangelical, which will Christ expressed, John VI. verse 40: This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son, and believes in him, may have eternal life. And Saint John 1 Epist. V. verse 20: And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son, verse 13: These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of GOD, that you may know that you have eternal life, and that you may believe in the name of the Son of God. Cf. John VI. verse 52. The lovers of the world and those who do the will of GOD are opposed, and since eternal life is promised to the latter in that opposition, what is more certainly to be feared by the former than death and eternal destruction. And Blessed Hunnius also extends the preceding to this: The world itself passes away; just as it has its beginning, so it will have its end; desire itself passes away; they too will pass away and perish who have followed earthly desires. If anyone, however, wishes to refer our sanctification to the will of GOD in this place, we do not deny it, since it is not proposed as a means of obtaining eternal life, but only the subject that obtains it is described: This will, says Hunnius, comprises first faith, John VI, then sanctification, 1 Cor. VI, 1 Thess. IV.

PART III. Establishing the antithesis of the Anti-Christian seduction and the doctrine of Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Καὶ ὁ κόσμος παράγεται] Petit, id est, ea lege factus est, ut aliquando pereat. 2. Petr. II. vers. 7. Psal. C II. vers. 27. Καὶ ἡ ἐπιθυμία αὐτῦ] In Manuscripto non est αὐτῦ. Mundo destructo destruitur & venter, 1. Corinth. VI. vers. 13. Cessabunt tunc etiam quæ naturalia sunt hujus vi- tæ desideria Matth. XXII. vers. 30. Marci XII. vers. 25. Luc. XX. 35.

Alterum argumentum, cur amandus non sit mundus, est, quod mundus ipse periturus. Hic jam diversa significatione adhibetur vox mundi, quatenus systema mundi totum notat. Conf. Matth. XXIV. vers. 35. 1. Corinth. VII. vers. 31. 2. Petr. III. vers. 11. Nervus concludendi est, quum totus mundus, in quo objecta illa dele- ctabilia, cibus & potus, opes & honores seculi tantopere expetuntur in filiis hujus seculi, cadu- cus, tandemque interiturus sit, æternitatem cogitandam esse & voluntate DEI conservari nos oportere, quam qui faciunt, non pereunt, sed in æternum permanent. Non vero amanda illa amore inordinato, quæ in mundo sunt, qua- lem inordinatum amorem cum gratia Dei con- sistere non posse jam antea monuerat Apostolus. Sanct. Anshelmus in cap. XII. ad Rom. Nolite constanter mundum diligere, quando ipse, quem diligitis, non potest constare, incassum cor quasi manen- ter figitis, dum fugit ipse, quem amatis. ὁ δὲ ποιῶν τὸ θέλημα τῦ Θεῦ] Qui implet eam Dei volun- tatem, quæ per Christum nobis patefacta est. Μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα] Eadem loquutio Joh. VIII. vers. 35. XII. vers. 34. idem valens, quod ζήσεται εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα Joh. VI. v. 51. 58. id est, vitam illam accipiet, quæ nunquam est defi- tura. Sub tam magna spe nulli labores duri videri debent. Spernimus caduca, appetimus æterna.

Voluntatem, quæ per Christum nobis lucu- lentius patefacta, fidelibus autem in Veteri Te- stamento, quantum satis erat, cognita fuit, fa- cile admittimus intelligi. Sed ea non legalis vo- luntas est, quæ magnam partem etiam naturæ in- sculpta, sed Evangelica, quam voluntatem ex- pressit Christus, Johan. VI. vers. 40. Hæc est voluntas ejus, qui misit me, ut omnis qui videt Filium, & credit in eum, vitam æternam habeat. Et Sanct. Johannes 1. epist. V. vers. 20. Et hoc est testimonium, quod vitam æternam nobis dedit Deus, & hæc vita in Filio ejus est, vers. 13. Hæc scripsi vobis credentibus in nomen Filii DEI, ut sciatis, quod habeatis vitam æternam, & ut credatis in no- men Filii Dei. Conf. Johan. VI. vers. 52. Oppo- nuntur amatores mundi & facientes voluntatem DEI, & cum his vita æterna in illa oppositione promittatur, quid illis certius timendum, quam mors & pernities æterna. Atque eo etiam extendit B. Hunnius antecedentia: Mundus ipse transit, sicuti suum habet initium, ita & finem habebit, transit una concupiscentia, transibunt & peribunt ii quoque, qui terrenas concupiscentias sectati sunt. Si quis autem ad voluntatem DEI etiam referre velit hoc in loco sanctificationem nostram, non abnuimus, quum non medium consequendi vitam æternam proponatur, sed subjectum tantum, quod eam consequitur, describatur: Hæc voluntas, in- quit Hunnius, complectitur primo fidem, Joh. VI. deinde sanctificationem, 1. Cor. VI. 1. Thess. IV.

PARS III. Anti-Christianæ seductionis & doctrinæ Christi antithesin instituens.

## 2:18
Vers. 18.

Παιδία, ἐσχάτη ὥρα ἐστί] Just as he instilled general warnings especially to the novices, so also the more special ones which follow: not that the same are not also useful to the more mature, but that he hoped these were better known to them, and that they were doing their duty sufficiently by themselves. Diligent instruction must be applied to tender years. On this place concerning the Anti-Christs, and another soon at the beginning of chapter IV, we have published a sufficiently rich commentary, and have appended it to our annotations on the Gospels: We shall now be briefer. These cohere well with the preceding. For those impostors, about whom he is going to speak, were merely worldly men; they pursued worldly things, they attracted men with worldly allurements. The last hour, that is, the last time, where the discourse is to the Jews, signifies the time near the destruction of the city and the temple and the commonwealth of the Jews. The time of the destruction itself is τέλος, Matt. XXIV. v. 6, כלה Dan. IX. verse 27. But those things are called extreme which approach the end. He rightly warns the children about this matter, however, because children always think that there will be enough time for them.

Παιδία are not novices, nor boys, as Schlichtingius maintains. St. John calls all believers 'little children' out of a feeling of love; just as parents are accustomed to address their older children, even those of advanced age, by the sweet name of little ones and children. Grotius himself admitted this in the notes to chapter II of this first epistle of John at verse 18 and following, annotated and attached to the Gospels, which it is helpful to append here as well. For he has it thus:

Vers. 18.

Παιδία little children] there is no reason why we should here distinctly take this name to signify a difference of age, as above, where he opposes 'little children' to both 'fathers' and 'young men.' For when this word is used absolutely, it is a term of endearment by which a teacher greets his disciples, as Christ himself does in the Gospel of this Apostle, XXI, v. 5.

Moreover, the coherence with what precedes is clear; even if those impostors are not viewed as worldly. For one had to beware of both, both from the perverse followers of the world and from false teachers. For by both, the little ones or the faithful could be seduced, namely by the example of the former and the word of the latter. But that the 'last hour' refers to the final stages of the Jewish Republic, both ecclesiastical and political times, is asserted without proof. By most, it is referred to the age of the world, which in truth is the last since the fullness of time. For three ages of the world are established by Chrysostom and Oecumenius. The first is up to the law; the second under the law; the third and last under Christ: Which Estius says is called the extreme time: because all things are to be completed in it in such a way that after it, until the end of the world and the coming of the Lord, no other state of affairs is to be expected, just as after the old age of a man, no other age is expected, but death. He had said the world was passing away, he now says it is the very last hour of the world, that is, the last time, because an hour is the most common measure of time. He also prefaces here that it is the last hour, lest the faithful wonder that so many new Masters are arising, teaching things diverse and contrary to those which had been handed down to them from the beginning. For Christ and the Apostles had predicted that many such would come in the last times. John therefore wishes the faithful to be attentive and cautious, lest they be deceived by them. Let us hear what Grotius says about these in the cited passage:

Ἐσχάτη ὥρα ἐςί it is the last hour.] The name of the extreme hour sometimes refers to the whole human race, sometimes to the Jewish people, from whom the Apostles and not a few of the Christians were. It is taken thus in Acts 2:17, where that terrible day which follows is the day of the destruction of Jerusalem, and at the same time of the Jewish nation, which is also sometimes signified by the name of the coming of Christ; it is also called the end, Matthew 24:14, where see what is noted by the learned; and do not take ὑσέροις καιροῖς (last times) 1 Tim. 4:1 and ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις (last days) 2 Tim. 3:1 in any other way.

We have spoken of the passages in Acts 2:17 and Matthew 24:14 in their proper place, as also of 1 Tim. 4:1 and 2 Tim. 3:1. There is no reason why we should explain these latter as being about times that are last only in a relative sense, namely with respect to the Jewish people. But this day of the Jewish destruction can in no way be understood here. For that hour or that time had already passed when the epistle was written, not before, but after the destruction of Jerusalem, as we said in the preface. Nor can that 1 Tim. 4:1 be drawn back to Simon Magus by Grotius's hypothesis, seeing that he had already been defeated by Peter long before, in the second year of Claudius, according to him. Nothing is more common for the Prophets than to call the time of the Messiah the last, because it is the last age of the world, and the last law, religion, and Church of Christ, to which no other will succeed, as Cornelius à Lapide has on 2 Tim. 3. Whence it is clear that the Papists are mistaken when they dream that the Anti-Christ will not come until the end of the century.

Καὶ καθὼς ἠκέσατε, ὅτι ὁ Ἀντίχριστος ἔρχεται (And as you have heard, that the Anti-Christ is coming)] ὅτι is absent in the Manuscript, not badly. The Anti-Christ will come, as you have heard; namely from the words of Christ, recited by John himself in verse 43.

Ἀντίχριστοι (Anti-Christs)] the same as ψευδόχριστοι (false Christs), that is, those who falsely say they are Christ, or claim his offices for themselves, concerning whom there is a prediction in Matthew 24:5 and 24, of which places the former pertains to the time before the destruction of the Temple, the latter to the time after that destruction. And so the Syrian here, where it is ἀντίχριστος, translates it משיחא דגלא, ψευδόχριστος, and no differently in what follows. Thus the Greeks call him ἀντιβασιλέα who falsely calls himself King. However, no age was more fertile in such ἀντίχριστοι or ψευδόχριστοι than that in which these things were being written, and which was around the same time: and this is because, not only through Judea but also through the whole East, the rumor had spread that in those times one would emerge from Judea who would rule over all nations, as we learn from Suetonius, Tacitus, and Josephus. Among them, however, one was to be more eminent than the rest, to whom that passage in John 5:43 properly pertains. But he was none other than Barchochebas, who in the times of Hadrian most openly called himself the Messiah, even to the Sanhedrin questioning him about that matter, and he drew the most learned men to his side: and he did not move only Judea, as others who had been before him, but Africa, Greece, Egypt, Cyprus,

and almost all places in which there were Jews, so that it is said that by his fraud there perished, by some accounts eight hundred thousand Jews, by others double the number of those who had gone out of Egypt. But only those Jews who were Christians in good faith did not allow themselves to be deceived by him, as Justin, Orosius, and others teach us. Ἔρχεται is present in sound, but is often used for the future. See Heb. 10:37. The passage 2 Thess. 2:3 is clearly not being referred to here. For that epistle was not yet in the hands of men when these things were written, especially of those who lived under the Parthians, and ἀντικείμενος is one thing, ἀντίχριστος is another. Ἀντικείμενος is he who professes himself an enemy to the supreme GOD. ἀντίχριστος is he who makes himself Christ.

In the earlier notes he has these things:

Καὶ καθὼς ἠκούσατε, & sicut audistis (and as you have heard)] Not from the Pauline epistles, which, when John was writing this, either had not been written or had not been published through the Churches, but from the Lord himself, Matthew 24:24, and from the Apostles, who had often inculcated the Lord's words to the Christians.

Ὅτι ὁ Ἀντίχριστος ἔρχεται (that the Anti-Christ is coming)] Christ had said that after the destruction of Jerusalem many would come falsely claiming the title of Christ for themselves, and therefore contrary to Christ, as can be seen in the cited passage of Matthew, where they are called ψευδοχρίστους (false Christs), who in this epistle are called ἀντίχριστοι (Anti-Christs), because no one is more opposed to Christ than he who falsely calls himself Christ, just as no one is more directly opposed to a King than those who impose the royal name upon themselves. Among them, however, the Spirit indicated to the Apostles that one would be exceptionally eminent. But who can that be other than he who led many thousands of Jews, and among them even the most learned men, into error and destruction, Barchochebas, concerning whom one can see the Rabbinical writers under the title of the Sanhedrin, chapter Helec; Justin Martyr in his Second Apology; Jacchiades on Daniel 11:34; Eusebius in his Ecclesiastical History, book 4, chapter 6. & in the chronicle around the year of Christ 136. Jerome calls him Chocibam in his Catalogue of Writers, where he speaks of Agrippa Castor. The same man calls him Barchochabam in his work against Rufinus, book III, chapter 7. Rabbi Johannes in Echa Rabathi says that eight hundred thousand men perished through his fault. But the Salmanticensian in the book Juchasin says that double the number of men who had gone out of Egypt perished in that war. Mention of that war is also in the book מאור עינים and the codex תענית, and in Beresith Rabba, section 65, and in the book Zemach David, by whose testimony that scoundrel stirred up Africa, Greece, Egypt, and Cyprus. This is the man whom Justin calls ὁ τ' Ἰουδαίων ἀποστάσεως ἀρχηγέτης, the leader of the Jewish rebellion, who dragged Christians to the most severe punishments unless they cursed the Lord Jesus. Orosius on the Emperor Aelius Hadrian: And he took vengeance on the Christians, whom they (the Jews), under the leadership of Chochaba, were torturing because they would not agree with them against the Romans. Among the ψευδοχρίστους, the false Christs, therefore, since no one was more distinguished in his following, more hostile to Christians, or more harmful to all in his end, this is the one to whom the name of Ἀντιχρίστου, Antichrist, with the demonstrative mark of excellence, is deservedly attributed.

There is no reason why the particle ὅτι should be omitted. Estius arranges the text thus: As you have heard that the Antichrist is coming, so hold fast. For he is certainly coming. But in the meantime, many Antichrists have already arisen. They had heard this not only from Christ but also from the Apostles; indeed, it had already been handed down by Daniel in chapter 11. The words of CHRIST in Matt. 24, verse 24, do not speak of the Antichrist, but of false Christs and false prophets. The words of John 5, verse 43, likewise have little to do with the Antichrist, of whom there is talk here; they deal in general with anyone coming in his own name, who was to be received by the Jews. Therefore, the seducers of the Jews foretell false Christs. Christ is speaking, says Maresius in 'The Antichrist Revealed,' in general terms: If another shall come in his own name, him you will receive. Why, therefore, this Barchochebas more than Theudas or Judas the Gaulonite, of whom Acts 5, verses 36 and 37 speak, or that Egyptian of whom Josephus also writes, or the false Moses of Crete, or Simon Magus? Why should this passage be understood more specifically of Barchochebas alone than the one parallel to it, Matt. 24:5, 'Many shall come under my name, saying: I am Christ, and will seduce many.' But why could they not have had this from the Pauline writings? For whence will it be proven that the Pauline epistles were not yet written at that time, or not circulated through the Churches? And how does Grotius agree with himself here? Above, he wanted Paul to have shown, in almost the first of all his epistles, that the time of the destruction of Jerusalem was not so near as some imagined; he wants John to speak here as if it has arrived, by saying, it is the last hour: And yet he thinks the Pauline epistles had not yet been written or circulated. One who invents such things ought to have better remembered his own statements: at the time of the impending destruction of the temple and the city, not only were Paul's epistles written and circulated, but he himself had been taken away by Nero. He had already received the crown of martyrdom: Let the Commentator himself be heard in another treatise, which he wrote on certain passages of Paul, James, and John concerning faith and works, at verse 21 of the second chapter of James: That, he says, many of the ancients, and among them Augustine in his book on faith and works, judge both this epistle and the first of John, and that which is called the second of Peter, to have been written against those who, interpreting the Pauline epistles perversely, said that faith without good morals was sufficient for salvation, is made probable both from the final words of that epistle which is ascribed to Peter, and because this James here uses the same example of Abraham, etc. One must lack either memory, or shame and conscience, who brings forth such contradictory things at the same time. Which Maresius reproaches him for in his dissertation on the Anti-Christ. Therefore, Maresius infers, the epistles of Paul were undoubtedly written and circulated through the Churches, specifically the second to the Thessalonians, when John applied his mind to writing, nor had this rumor about the coming Anti-Christ spread through the Churches from any other source. For what exists in Matthew 24:24 pertains rather to Pseudo-Christs and false Prophets in general than to the Anti-Christ specifically. But Grotius invented these things so that in place of the Roman Anti-Christ, whose advocate he acts, he might substitute a certain Jewish Pseudo-Christ, Barchocheba. But the Great Trifler is trifling.

Ὁ ἀντίχριςος is not properly one who makes himself Christ, but one who opposes himself to Christ, and attacks his person, office, dignity, and glory. But he who says or makes himself Christ, or Messiah, is called a Pseudo-Christ or Pseudo-Messiah. What the Greeks call ἀντιβασιλέα, he calls himself a King falsely, not by the force of the word, but by the consequence of the thing. For he who falsely calls himself a King, when there is another true King, opposes himself to the true King. Thus, consequently, a Pseudo-Christ also opposes himself to the true Christ, since he seizes for himself the honor of the true Christ, and consequently snatches away the honor due to Christ, since there is only one Christ, just as in one kingdom there is only one King. The propriety of words must be observed in the Holy Scriptures, and one must not depart from it. There existed, says Maresius, Antichr. Revel. page 174. Pseudo-Agrippas, Pseudo-Alexanders, Pseudo-Philips, Pseudo-Fredericks, who feigned and simulated their countenance, name, and authority: yet no sane person will judge that they can be called Anti-Agrippas, Anti-Alexanders, Anti-Philips, or Anti-Fredericks: In the disputes of the Anti-Popes, both being compared to each other could be called Anti-Popes, but are they therefore both Pseudo-Popes?

Furthermore, the Great Anti-Christ had to emerge not from the Jews, but from the Christians. For he is the head of those of whom St. John says in the following verse, 'they went out from us, but they were not of us.' But Barchocheba was a Jew and never professed Christianity, and therefore could not have gone out from true Christians. And although no one opposes a King more than he who imposes the royal name upon himself: yet he opposes the King more harmfully who, abusing his name, ruins his authority, tramples it by edict, and oppresses his subjects. Therefore, the Anti-Christ did not have to be an open enemy of Christ in order to be the most harmful adversary. Rather, he had to secretly promote the mystery of iniquity, and sit in the very temple, and assume to himself the horns of the Lamb, and carry out everything under the pretext of piety.

What of the fact that those deceivers of the Jews, of whom Matthew 24:5, 24 speaks, were not so concerned with overturning the Gospel of Christ, or recalling Christians from his profession, as with shaking off the yoke of the Romans and inciting the Jews against the empire? For they were not taking up arms against Christians, but were rebelling against the Romans, just as Judas the Gaulonite said it was not proper to impose another king on man besides God, nor to call anyone Lord, except the blessed God. Grotius trifles here with many such things according to his custom, especially in the Appendix, where he has attempted to assert these inventions of his, which we pass over dry-shod. Maresius discussed them diligently in the aforementioned work, from which we note only this: Through the empire of the Parthians, he says on page 202, part II of Anti-Christ. Revel. That the Apostle Peter disseminated the Gospel, with John as his companion, perhaps at the time when Peter was overcoming Simon Magus at Rome, or when he was writing his first epistle at Rome under the name of Babylon, or when John was already in exile from the times of Claudius on Patmos. That John the Evangelist was the perpetual companion of Peter's great journeys. That no Apostle announced the Gospel to the uncircumcised, unless delegated or substituted for that purpose by Paul. That those Christians whom John addresses were from the circumcision, and that John had insisted primarily on the conversion of the Jews: that he feared that the faithful living under the Parthians would pass over to Judaism and join the rebelling Barchocheba against the Roman empire. That the remnants of the ten tribes, which were ἐν τῇ διασπορᾷ beyond the Euphrates, were very anxious about the state of the Jews in Palestine, or could easily have joined the seditious in the Roman Empire by force, are great postulates of Grotius, conflicting partly with his own tenets, partly with truth and reason, which it will be easier for him to presuppose than to prove. These imitate the first principles of the sciences, which are indemonstrable. Just as he imagined the Jews exiles at Thessalonica, to whom Paul wrote the second [epistle], which is the first for him: So here he wishes the Parthians and those of the East, nay, the Christians of the whole world, to whom John wrote (for this epistle is indeed καθολικὴ καὶ ἐγκυκλικὴ, as Lorinus at least determines in his Prolegomena to it, chapter 5, written to the universality of the faithful, not to a distinct and certain province: for he does not assent to Baronius, who asserts it was sent specifically to the Parthians) to be Jews, because he wishes it, with no witness, with no indicator. But as for what will suffice for dispelling all those phantasms of ridiculous imaginations, let it be enough to have observed that these people, in truth, to whom John writes, wherever in the world they were, had been converted to Christ from gentilism and the worship of idols, at least for the greatest part of them, which is evidently clear from the clause of his last epistle: Little children, keep yourselves from idols, by which words he exhorts the faithful against that idolatry from which they had been liberated. Let Lorinus the Jesuit say this to the Great Man: Since Christ, he says, is the true God, this admonition is opportunely subjoined at the end, both against those denying Christ to be consubstantial with the Father, yet worshipping him as God, and lest those recently converted from idolatry should relapse into it. Thus Maresius.

But the fact that Grotius denies that the passage of Paul, 2 Thess. II, is referred to here, because there ἀντικείμενος is noted, and here Ἀντίχριςος, hardly deserves a response. For is not the Anti-Christ, or he who opposes himself to Christ, and is so named κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν (by way of eminence), in turn ἀντικείμενος? Is not he who opposes himself to Christ an enemy of the most high God?

And now many anti-Christs have arisen] Many indeed, of whom we treated in Matt. XXIV, verse 5, and in the preface to this epistle.

Whence we know that it is the last hour] For as soon as many such existed who snatched for themselves the roles of the Messiah, then the destruction of the Temple and the Republic ought to have been expected as imminent, according to the prediction of Christ, Matt. XXIV, 8, where there is that saying: 'But all these things are the beginning of sorrows.'

Previously he had written thus concerning these:

And now many anti-Christs have arisen] Christ himself had said, Matt. XXIV. 5, that even before the destruction of the city of Jerusalem some would come who would arrogate to themselves the name or power of Christ. Such, however, were all those Jews who professed themselves to be the defenders of liberty. For ὁ μέλλων λυτρῶσθαι τὸν Ἰσραὴλ, he who is about to redeem Israel, is a periphrasis or circumlocution for the Messiah. Among these were Theudas the πλάνος, impostor, and many καὶ ἀπατεῶνες, deceivers, as Josephus speaks, while Felix was procurator of Judea. The Egyptian impostor, named by the same Josephus and in the Acts of the Apostles, appeared under Festus, promising salvation and an end to evils. Simon Magus, who called himself the power of God, and Dositheus, who wanted to be called Christ, concerning whom see Origen, book II against Celsus and in Matt. tract. XXII.

Whence we know that it is the last hour.] By this sign we are certain that we are living in those times which do not much precede the destruction of the Jewish nation. For concerning that abundant crop of Pseudo-Christs, and related matters, Christ had spoken and added: 'These are the beginning of sorrows.'

But what do those Pseudo-Christs of Matt. XXIV. 5, who said 'I am Christ,' have to do with these Anti-Christs, whom John says have 'now' become such in his own time, when he was writing this? Those were before the destruction of Jerusalem: these are after the destruction. Those professed themselves to be Christ: of these Anti-Christs, indeed, the precursors of Christ among the Gentiles, it is not read that they sold themselves directly as the Messiah. By common calculation, therefore, heretics are understood here, who infested the truth of Christ, whether regarding his Deity or his Human Nature, or even impugned the office of Christ, which, as it was done by various heretics up to that Great Anti-Christ, so in him a certain collection of these flowed together. For what else is Papal Anti-Christianism than a sink of various heresies, notable for their impugning of Christ? Furthermore, although the Pseudo-Christs had preceded the destruction of the city, if the Anti-Christs of whom John speaks are those of whom Matt. 24:24 speaks, as the Grotian commentary wished above, how can they be dragged back to the times before the destruction, so that they are considered to be those of whom Matt. 24:5 speaks, unless we imagine them to be different people? Add that Grotius says the Anti-Christs are the impostors of the Jews. But how can the Egyptian mentioned by Josephus and in the Acts, Simon Magus, and Dositheus be called Jewish impostors? And how will it fit either Theudas or that Egyptian that they are called Anti-Christs who have gone out from the Christians, or such as Grotius explains, who had indeed given their name to Christ, but had soon departed from the Christian assembly? Moreover, it cannot be said that other impostors or heretics paved the way for Barchocheba, because they neither predicted that he would come, nor did their words or deeds serve to establish his authority. And why should we believe that those other impostors who preceded him paved the way for him, rather than that he paved the way for others who followed later? Without doubt, the interpretation of Johannes Ferus is correct here: Let us

return to the Pseudo-Prophets. For John also calls these Anti-Christs, that is, contrary or adverse to Christ. Now one can be adverse to Christ in two ways, namely, in doctrine and in life. This passage can be understood of both, since even while the Apostles were still living, there were found those who not only taught things contrary to Christ, like Ebion and Cerinthus, but also those who lived against the doctrine of Christ, like Simon Magus and that Nicolaus, one of the seven Deacons, from whom the Nicolaitans received their name; and finally those whom Paul lamented as enemies of the cross of Christ, and who made their belly their God. John, therefore, is not speaking of Jews and pagans who openly professed themselves enemies of Christ, but of those who profess the name of Christ, yet teach or do things contrary to Christ. Estius provides this paraphrase: i.e. One notable adversary of Christ is indeed to come, to whom therefore the name of Anti-Christ is due by antonomasia, but he has already begun to have many precursors, and they are Anti-Christs by participation in his name, because what he is going to do in general, to extinguish the name and glory of Christ, these do in part. Nor do the Jesuits deny this, to which society Grotius was very devoted: 'And now many anti-Christs have arisen': Anti-Christs, says Cornelius, that is, contrary to Christ, and true precursors of the Anti-Christ, because they equally with him impugn the faith, religion, Church, Sacraments, etc., of Christ, and indeed the very person and nature of Christ. For he notes the heretics of his own age, some of whom denied that Christ was God, others that he was true man. Such were Ebion, Cerinthus, Saturninus, Basilides, Menander, Simon the leader of heretics, and their followers, of whom Paul says: The mystery of iniquity already worketh, 2 Thess. 2. 7. The last hour of the world is now, says Tirinus, that is, the last time, at which time you have often heard that the Anti-Christ is to come. But many Anti-Christs, that is, seducers and impostors, opponents and enemies of Christ, forerunners of the great Anti-Christ, Ebion, Cerinthus, Basilides, Menander, and other followers of Simon Magus have already come forth into the light, which is a sign that the world has now grown old and is verging toward its end. For the final age of the world will teem with seducers and impostors, until at length, with the head and Prince of all seducers, the Anti-Christ properly so called, it receives its end. 2. Thess. II. 7. This hour or age of the world, therefore, although it is the last, which no other age will follow, nevertheless admits of great breadth like the preceding ages, concerning which more later. Because the early believers, such as St. Cyprian, Lactantius, Jerome, Gregory, and many other Fathers, did not sufficiently notice this, they thought the end of the world was imminent in their own age. But between the forerunners or heralds and the arrival of the King, whom they announce, there is often a great interval, as was evident in the penultimate and antepenultimate age of the world between the Prophets and Christ.

The confession of the martyrs concerning the Most Holy Trinity, which should be compared here, refutes expressly the accusation of Schlichting, who makes the defenders of the Catholic faith forerunners of the Anti-Christ because of their assertion of the Deity of Christ. John therefore understood the last hour not simply, insofar as it denotes that whole course from the advent of Christ until the end of the world, but insofar as that course of time was to be subject to various miseries and temptations according to the predictions of Christ, and the beginnings of which were already seen in that abundant crop of heretics in the age of John.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Παιδία, ἐσχάτη ὥρα ἐστί] Sicut generalia monita præci- pue novitiis adhuc instillaveat, ita & specialiora, quæ se- quentur: non quod non & adultioribus eadem sint utilia, sed quod sperabat eis hæc esse notiora, & eos per se satis offi- cium suum facere. Teneris annis diligens adhibenda est in- stitutio. In locum hunc de Anti-Christis & alterum mox initio cap. IV. commentationem satis uberem edidimus, & an- notatis nostris ad Evangelia subjunximus: Erimus nunc bre- viores. Bene cohærent hæc cum superioribus. Nam impo- stores illi, de quibus acturus est, erant homines mere munda- ni, mundana sectabantur, mundanis illecebris homines attra- hebant. Ultima hora, id est, ultimum tempus, ubi ad Judæ- os sermo est, significat tempus proximum excidio urbis ac templi & reipublicæ Judæorum. Ipfum tempus excidii est τέλος, Matth. XXIV. v. 6. כלה Dan. IX. vers. 27. Extrema au- tem dicuntur, quæ ad finem accedunt. Bene autem pueros hac de re monet: quia pueri semper existimant, satis sibi fo- re temporis.

Παιδία non sunt novitii, nec pueri, ut vult Schlichtingius. Parvulos ex affectu amoris dicit Sanct. Johannes quosvis credentes; quemadmo- dum parentes seniores filios suos etsi provectæ ætatis suavi parvulorum & filiorum solent com- pellare nomine. Fassus id est Grotius ipse in notis ad hujus cap. II. prioris epistolæ Johannis ad v. 18. & sqq. annotatis ad Evangelia adjunctis, quæ hic simul subjicere juvat. Ita enim habet:

Vers. 18.

Παιδία filioli] non est causa, cur hic distincte suma- mus hoc nomen ad significandum ætatis discrimen, ut supra, ubi παιδίοις filiolis opponit tum πατέρας pa- tres, tum νεανίσκους juvenes. Nam cum absolute ponitur hæc vox, blanda est appellatio, qua Doctor discipulos su- os salutat, ut Christus ipse in Evangelio hujus Apostoli XXI. v. 5.

Cæterum cohærentia cum superioribus in aprico est; etiamsi impostores illi non ut munda- ni spectentur. Nam ab utrisque cavendum erat, tum à perversis mundi sectatoribus, tum à falsis Doctoribus. Per utrosque enim parvuli vel fideles seduci poterant, illorum nempe exemplo, horum verbo. Ultimam autem horam ad extrema Rei- publicæ & Ecclesiasticæ & Politicæ Judaicæ tempora referri debere, precario asseritur. A plerisque ea ad mundi ætatem, quæ revera est ultima inde à plenitudine temporis, refertur. Tres enim ætates mundi constituuntur à Chry- sostomo & Oecumenio. Prima est usque ad legem; altera sub lege; tertia & ultima sub Christo: Quam extremum tempus vocari Estius ait: quia sic in eo complenda sunt omnia, ut post illud usque ad mun- di finem & Domini adventum non sit alius rerum status expectandus, quomodo post hominis senectu- tem non ætas alia, sed mors expectatur. Dixerat mundum transiturum, jam novissimam mundi horam esse ait, id est, tempus novissimum, quia hora est usitatissima temporis mensura. Præfatur etjam hic novissimam horam esse, ne mirentur fide- les, tot exurgere novos Magistros diversa & adver- sa docentes iis, quæ ab initio fuerant ipsis tradita, Multos enim tales venturos novissimis tempori- bus Christus & Apostoli prædixerant. Vult ergo Johannes, attentos esse fideles, & cautos, ne ab illis fallantur. Audiamus quæ de his Grotius loco citato:

Ἐσχάτη ὥρα ἐςί novissima hora est.] Nomen horæ extremæ modo totum genus humanum respicit, modo populum Judaicum, ex quo erant Apostoli, & non pauci Christianorum. Sic sumitur Act. II. 17. ubi dies ille terribilis, qui sequitur, est dies excidii Hierosolymo- rum, simulque Judaicæ gentis, qui & nomine adventus Christi interdum significatur; vocatur & finis, Matth. XXIV. 14. ubi ab eruditis notata vide; neque vero aliter sume ὑσέροις καιροῖς novissima tempora 1. Tim. IV. 1. & ἐσχάταις ἡμέραις 2. Tim. III. 1.

De locis Act. II. 17. Matth. XXIV. 14. in pro- pria sede diximus, ut & de 1. Tim. IV. 1. 2. Tim. III. 1. Quæ posteriora cur de temporibus secun- dum quid novissimis scilicet respectu populi Juda- ici explicemus, causa nulla est. Hic vero dies exci- dii Judaici intelligi nullo modo potest. Nam illa hora vel tempus istud jam transierat, quum scripta fuerit epistola non ante, sed post excidium Hiero- solymitanum, ut in proœmio diximus. Nec ad Si- monem Magum illa 1. Tim. IV. 1. per Grotii hypo- thesin retrahi possunt, utpote qui jam multo ante anno secundo Claudii secundum ipsum à Petro debellatus fuerat. Nihil usitatius Prophetis, quam Messiæ tempus vocare novissimum, quia est ul- tima mundi ætas, ultimaque lex, religio & Eccle- sia Christi, cui nulla alia succedet, ut habet Cor- nelius à Lapide ad 2. Tim. III. Unde liquet falli Pontificios, quando non nisi sub finem seculi An- ti-Christum venturum somniant.

Καὶ καθὼς ἠκέσατε, ὅτι ὁ Ἀντίχριστος ἔρχεται] ὅτι abest in Manuscripto, non male. Veniet Anti-Christus, sicut audistis; nempe ex Christi verbis, ab ipso Johanne recita- tis V. 43.

Ἀντίχριστοι] iidem qui ψευδόχριστοι, id est, qui falso di- cunt se esse Christum, aut ejus munia sibi vendicant, de qui- bus prædictio est Matth. XXIV. 5. & 24. quorum locorum il- le ad tempus ante excidium Templi, hic ad tempus post id excidium pertinet. Itaque Syrus hic ubi est ἀντίχριστος vertit משיחא דגלא, ψευδόχριστος, nec aliter in sequen- tibus. Sic ἀντιβασιλέα dicunt Græci eum, qui falso se Regem dicit. Nulla autem ætas talium ἀντιχρίστων sive ψευδοχρίστων feracior fuit ea, qua hæc scribebantur, & quæ fuit circa idem tempus: idque ideo, quia non per Judæam tantum, sed & per Orientem omnem fama pervaserat, illis tempori- bus proditurum ex Judæa, qui gentibus omnibus impe- raret, ut ex Suetonio, Tacito & Josepho discimus. In- ter eos autem unus futurus erat cæteris eminentior, ad quem proprie locus ille Joh. V. 43. pertinet. Is vero non alius fuit, quam Barchochebas, qui Adriani temporibus aper- tissime se Messiam dixit, etiam Synedrio de ea re interro- ganti, & eruditissimos homines traxit in suas partes: neque vero solam Judæam commovit, ut alii, qui ante eum fuerant, sed Africam, Græciam, Ægyptum, Cyprum,

& loca prope omnia, in quibus erant Judæi, ita ut frau- de ejus periisse dicantur, ab aliis octingenta Judæorum millia, ab aliis duplus numerus eorum, qui ex Ægypto exierant. Soli vero illi Judæi, qui bona fide erant Chri- stiani, ab eo se decipi passi non sunt, ut Justinus, Oro- sius & alii nos docent. Ἔρχεται est Præsens sono, sed pro futuro sæpe ponitur. Vide Ebr. X. vers. 37. Locus 2. Thess. II. vers. 3. plane hic non respicitur. Nam nondum ea epistola erat in manibus hominum, cum hæc scriberentur, præcipue eorum, qui sub Parthis vivebant, & longe aliud est ἀντικείμενος, aliud ἀντίχριστος. Ἀντικείμενος est is, qui DEO summo se hostem profitetur. ἀντίχριστος, qui se Christum facit.

In prioribus notis hæc habet:

Καὶ καθὼς ἠκούσατε, & sicut audistis] Non ex epi- stolis Paulinis, quæ, cum hæc scriberet Johannes, aut scriptæ non erant, aut non vulgatæ per Ecclesias, sed ab ipso Domino, Matth. XXIV. 24. & ab Apostolis, qui Do- mini verba sæpe Christianis inculcaverant.

Ὅτι ὁ Ἀντίχριστος ἔρχεται quia Anti-Christus ve- nit] Post excidium Hierosolymorum multos falso sibi Christi titulum vindicantes, ac proinde Christo contra- rios venturos esse, Christus dixerat, ut dicto Matthæi loco videre est, ubi ψευδοχρίστους vocantur, qui in hac epistola ἀντίχριστοι, quia nemo Christo magis adversa- tur, quam qui falso Christum se dicit, sicut Regi nulli directius adversantur, quam qui Regium sibi nomen im- ponunt. Inter eos autem unum futurum eximie emi- nentem Spiritus Apostolis indicavit. Quis autem ille po- test esse alius, quam is qui plurima Judæorum millia, & in iis etiam viros doctissimos in errorem exitiumque in- duxit, Barchochebas, de quo videri possunt Rabbinici Scriptores titulo de Synedrio, capite Helec; Justinus Mar- tyr Apologetico II. Jacchiades ad Daniel. XI. vers. 34. Eusebius historia Ecclesiastica libr. IV. cap. 6. & chro- nico circa annum Christi CXXXVI. Chocibam vocat Hieronymus Scriptorum catalogo, ubi de Agrippa Casto- re. Idem Barchochabam appellat adversus Rufinum lib. III. cap. 7. Rabbinus Johannes in Echa Rabathi ait ejus culpa periisse octingenta hominum millia. At Salman- ticensis in libro Juchasin duplum eo bello periisse ait ejus hominum numeri, qui Ægypto exierat. Mentio ejus belli & in libro מאור עינים & codice תענית, & in Beresith Rabba sectione LXV. & in libro Zemach Da- vid, quo teste commovit ille nebulo Africam, Græciam, Ægyptum & Cyprum. Hic Justino ὁ τ' Ἰουδαίων ἀποστά- σεως ἀρχηγέτης dux rebellionis Judaicæ, qui ad gravif- sima supplicia Christianos traxerit, nisi Domino Jesu ma- ledicerent. Orosius de Imperatore Ælio Adriano: Ul- tusque est Christianos, quos illi (Judæi) Chochaba duce, quod sibi adversus Romanos non assentarentur, excru- ciabant. Inter ψευδοχρίστους falsos Christos, igitur cum nemo fuerit comitatu insignior, Christianis insensior, exitu cunctis nocentior, hic est cui Ἀντιχρίστου, Anti- Christi nomen cum demonstratrice excellentiæ nota me- rito tribuitur.

Non est quod particula ὅτι omittatur. Textum ita ordinat Estius: Sicut audistis, quod venturus sit Anti-Christus: ita tenete. Nam omnino ven- turus est. Sed interim multi jam Anti-Christi facti sunt. Non autem à Christo tantum, sed etiam ab Apostolis audierant, imo à Daniele id jam traditum erat cap. XI. Verba CHRISTI Matth. XXIV. vers. 24. non de Anti-Christo, sed de Pseudo-Christis & Pseudo-Prophetis lo- quuntur. Verba Johannis V. vers. 43. pariter ad Anti-Christum, de quo hic sermo, parum fa- ciunt: in genere de quolibet in nomine proprio venturo, qui à Judæis suscipiendus erat, agunt. Pseudo-Christos ergo prænunciant Judæorum seductores. Loquitur Christus, inquit Mare- sius in Anti-Christo Revelato, in communi: Si alius venerit in nomine suo, eum recipietis. Cur ergo magis hic Barchochebas, quam Theudas vel Judas Gaulonites, de quibus Actor. V. vers. 36. 37. vel Ægyptius ille, de quo & Josephus, vel Pseudo-Moses Cretensis, vel Simon Magus? Cur magis specifice hic locus de solo Barchocheba intelli- geretur, quam ei parallelus, Matt.245. Multivenient sub nomine meo dicentes: Ego sum Christus, & plu- res seducent. Cur autem non habere id potuerint è scriptis Paulinis? Unde enim probabitur, epi- stolas Paulinas tum nondum scriptas, aut non vul- gatas per Ecclesias? Et quomodo hic secum con- sentit Grotius? Supra volebat Paulum omnium suarum epistolarum ferme prima ostendisse non tam prope esse tempus excidii Hierosolymitani, ac nonnulli imaginabantur, vult Johannem hic loqui, quasi ad- venerit, dicendo, novissima hora est: Et tamen putat epistolas Paulinas nondum scriptas fuisse aut vulga- tas. Talia fingentem melius dictorum suorum me- minisse decuit: instante excidio templi & urbis non solum scriptae erant & vulgatae Pauli epistolae, sed ipse per Neronem sublatus. Martyrii jam coronam retulerat: Audiatur ipse Commentator tractatu alio, quem scripsit in loca quaedam Pauli, Jacobi, & Johannis de fide & operibus ad V. 21. cap. secundi Jacobi: Quod, inquit, veterum multi ac inter eos Augustinus libro de fide & operibus censent & hanc epistolam & Johannis primam, & eam, quae Petri secunda dicitur, scriptas adversus eos, qui Paulinas epistolas prave interpretantes, fidem dicebant sine bonis moribus ad salutem sufficere probabile fit tum ex ultimis epistolae istius, quae Petro adscribitur, verbis, tum quod hic Jacobus ejusdem Abraha- mi exemplo utitur &c. Vel memoria, vel fronte ac conscientia carere oportet, qui eodem tempore tam pugnantia profert. Quae exprobrat ei Ma- resius in dissert. de Anti-Christo. Scripta ergo, in- fert Maresius, erant procul dubio & vulgatae per Ecclesias Pauli epistolae, nominatim secunda ad Thessalonicenses, cum Johannes animum ad scri- bendum appulit, nec aliunde certius hic rumor de Anti-Christo venturo pervaserat Ecclesias. Quae enim extant Matth. XXIV. 24. potius ad Pseudo- Christos & falsos Prophetas in genere, quam ad Anti- Christum speciatim pertinent. Commentus autem ista est Grotius, ut loco Anti-Christi Romani; cujus Advocatum agit, Judaicum quendam Pseu- do-Christum Barchochebam surroget. At nugas agit Nugo Magnus.

Ὁ ἀντίχριςος non est proprie, qui se Christum facit, sed qui se Christo opponit, ejus personam, officium, dignitatem, gloriamque impugnat. Qui vero Christum, vel Messiam se dicit aut facit, Pseu- do-Christus vel Pseudo-Messias dicitur. Quod ἀν- τιβασιλέα Graeci dicunt, falso se Regem dicit, non ex vi vocis, sed ex consequentia rei est. Qui enim se Regem falso dicit, cum verus Rex alius sit, oppo- nit se vero Regi. Sic per consequens etiam Chri- sto vero se opponit Pseudo-Christus, cum veri Christo honorem ad se rapit, consequenter vero Christi debitum honorem eripit, quum non nisi unus Christus sit, quemadmodum in uno regno non est nisi unus Rex. Proprietas autem vocum observanda est in S. literis, nec ab ea discedendum. Extiterunt, inquit Maresius Antichr. Revel. pag. 174. Pseudo-Agrippae, Pseudo-Alexandri, Pseudo-Philippi, Pseudo-Friderici, qui eorum vultum, nomen, autoritatem fingebant, simulabant: nemo tamen sanus eos censebit Anti-Agrippas, Anti-Alexandros, Anti-Philippos, Anti-Frideri- cos, vel dici posse: In Anti-Paparum dissidiis ambo sibi comparati Anti-Papae dici poterant, an ergo uter- que Pseudo-Papa.

Porro Anti-Christus Magnus non è Judaeis, sed Christianis prodire debuit. Caput enim est eorum, de quibus vers. sequ. S. Johannes ἐξ ἡμῶν ἐξῆλθον, ἀλλ᾽ ὐκ ἦσαν ἐξ ἡμῶν.
