Vers. 27. Καὶ ὑμεῖς τὸ χρίσμα, ὃ ἐλάβετε ἀπ᾽ ἀυτοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν μένει.] Καὶ hic est pro sed. Opponit enim Judæos credentes incredulis. Est constructio par ei, quæ supra 25. Res autem eadem quæ supra 20. Amoliri à se vult suspicionem, quasi minus bene de eis speraret. Ἀπ᾿ ἀυτοῦ à Christo, ἐν ὑμῖν μένει, est intra vos, idem quod supra ἔχετε.

Καὶ οὐ χρείαν ἔχετε, ἵνα τις διδάξῃ ὑμᾶς.] Nempe de eo, quod in singulis circumstantiis, ut dixi, faciendum est. Estis διδακτοὶ Θεοῦ, Jerem. 31, 34. Joh. 6, 45. Sunt enim differentiæ quædam, quas exigunt tempora, loca, personæ. Ideo admonitione sæpe opus ad inveniendam officiorum viam. Vide si vis Senecam epistola XCIV.

Ἀλλ’ ὡς τὸ αὐτὸ χρίσμα διδάσκει ὑμᾶς περὶ πάντων καὶ ἀληθές ἐστι, καὶ οὐ ψεῦδος, καὶ καθὼς ἐδίδαξεν ὑμᾶς μενεῖτε ἐν αὐτῷ.] Est bene sperantis atque ominantis. Ἀληθές ἐστι καὶ οὐ ψεῦδος primum est Metonymia Abstracti pro concreto. Nam ψεῦδος valet hic ψευδής : quomodo ἀλήθεια valet ἀληθής 2. Cor. IV, 14. Deinde idem bis dicitur, primum affirmando, deinde negando oppositum, quomodo supra I, 5. & hoc capite III, 8. Par locutio 1. Sam. I, 11. Ezech. 18, 21. c. 33, 15.

## 2:28
Vers. 28.

And now, little children, abide in him.] This is now the language of one admonishing. And 'and' signifies 'therefore'.

It is a repetition of the precept, says Estius, with a gentle address, by which he might declare his fatherly love toward them. For besides the most sweet name of 'little children,' that 'now' is also a particle of entreaty, corresponding to the Hebrew 'na,' which they use in their 'Hosiab-na.' Indeed, let common languages use that 'now' as an interjection of one coaxing or entreating. 'In him' refers either to Christ, in whom we abide through faith, or to that which they had been taught, in which they are commanded to abide. The former, however, from a comparison of v. 10 and 24, as also chapter III, 6, is more likely. Excellent is Augustine here: 'Faithful is He who promised, He does not deceive you; only do not fail, but wait for the Promiser. For the Truth does not know how to deceive. Do not you be a liar, so that you profess one thing and do another. You keep the faith, and He keeps the promise; but if you do not keep the faith, you have defrauded yourself, not Him who promised.' Oecumenius in loc. What could ever be more illustrious and more admirable than when we are about to be brought before Him to whom we have devoted our labors, we shall do so with confidence, and shall be suffused with no shame at His coming.

That when He shall be manifested.] Namely, the Son of God, which is repeated from long before. Thus Col. III, 4, 'When Christ shall be manifested.' Thus also Peter said, 'when the Chief Shepherd shall be manifested,' 1 ep. V, 4.

We may have confidence.] Let us appear with good confidence. Concerning this use of the word 'parrhesia,' see 2 Cor. III, 12. Eph. IV, 2. Heb. III, 6. IV, 16. X, 35. below here V, 14. The Syriac translates it 'revelation of the face'.

And may not be ashamed before Him at His coming.] Let us not be ashamed to be looked upon by Him. This is what is called 'standing before the Son of Man,' Luke XXI, 36.

The reward or fruit of perseverance is to have confidence in the promised life. According to Estius, this confidence can be taken in two ways. For either, he says, it is understood as the confidence which we now have in that time when Christ shall appear. For hope and confidence properly belong to this age. For in the other age, hope is converted into the thing itself. Or the sense is, that we may stand intrepidly and with great constancy of mind before Christ the Judge. Which sense agrees with the following member, and also with that which is said a little later, 'when He shall appear, we shall be like Him.' Likewise with that which the blessed Peter says in his 1st epistle, ch. V: 'When the Prince of Pastors shall appear, you shall receive the unfading crown of glory.' In whichever way it is explained, the Papists' doubt concerning the grace of God and eternal salvation is confounded. That he changes the person is not surprising, because he includes himself through 'communion,' as if to say: 'Abide, as we do, in that which you have learned, so that we may jointly have confidence'. There is no need, therefore, that we should seek here with Estius an accidental joy of the Teachers in the other life, when they have obedient hearers. For will they be suffused with blushing for that reason, when there are some such whom they are not going to have? But to be put to shame or confounded by Christ the Judge brings eternal ignominy, as Estius admits.

Latin:

Vers. 28.

Καὶ νῦν τεκνία μένετε ἐν αὐτῷ.] Hoc jam est monentis. Et καὶ valet igitur.

Repetitio est præcepti, inquit Estius, cum blanda appellatione, qua paternum erga eos amorem deolaret. Nam præter suavissimum nomen filiolorum etiam illud nunc obsecrandi particula est, respondens Ebræorum na, quo illi utuntur in suo Hosiab-na. Illo vero nunc utantur & linguæ vulgares tanquam interjectione blandientis aut obsecrantis. Ἐν αὐτῷ vel Christum respicit, in quo manemus per fidem, vel illud quod edocti erant, in quo manere jubentur. Prius tamen è collatione v. 10. & 24. ut & cap. III, 6. verisimilius est. Præclare hic Augustinus: Fidelis est, qui promisit, non te fallit, tantum noli deficere, sed expecta promissorem. Non enim novit fallere veritas. Tu noli esse mendax, ut aliud profitearis, aliud agas. Tu serva fidem, & servat ille pollicitationem, si autem non tu servaveris fidem, tu te fraudasti, non ille, qui promisit. Oecumenius in h. l. Quid illustrius & admirabilius esse unquam poterit, quam cum apud quem labores nostros relatari sumus, apud eum cum fiducia id faciemus, nulloque pudore in adventu ejus perfundemur.

Ἵνα ὅταν φανερωθῇ.] Nempe Filius Dei, quod ex longo repetitur. Sic Col. III, 4. ὅταν ὁ Χριστὸς φανερωθῇ. Sic & φανερωθέντος τοῦ ἀρχιποιμένος dixit Petrus 1. ep. V, 4.

Ἔχωμεν παῤῥησίαν.] Appareamus cum bona fiducia. De hoc usu vocis παῤῥησίας vide 2. Cor. III, 12. Eph. IV, 2. Ebr. III, 6. IV, 16. X, 35. infra hic V, 14. Syrus vertit revelationem faciei.

Καὶ μὴ αἰσχυνθῶμεν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ αὐτοῦ.] Ne pudeat nos ab illo conspici. Hoc est, quod stare ante filium hominis dicitur Luc. XXI, 36.

Præmium perseverantiæ vel fructus est habere fiduciam vitæ promissæ. Secundum Estium potest hæc fiducia dupliciter accipi. Nam vel intelligitur, inquit, fiducia, quam nunc habemus in illud tempus, quo Christus apparebit. Spes enim & fiducia proprie est hujus seculi. Nam in altero seculo spes in rem convertitur. Vel sensus est, ut intrepidi, magnaque cum animi constantia stemus coram Judice Christo. Qui sensus congruit cum membro sequenti, nec non cum eo, quod paulo post dicitur, cum apparuerit similes ei erimus. Item cum eo, quod dicit B. Petrus 1. epist. V. Cum apparuerit Princeps Pastorum, percipietis immarcessibilem gloriæ coronam. Utrovis modo exponatur, confunditur Papistarum dubitatio de gratia Dei & salute æterna. Quod autem mutet personam non mirum est, quia per κοινωνίαν se includit, q. d. manete, sicut nos, in eo, quod didicistis, ut conjunctim nos habeamus fiduciam. Non opus ergo, ut cum Estio hic quæramus amplius gaudium accidentale Doctorum in altera vita, cum auditores habeant obedientes. Num enim rubore ideo suffundentur, cum non habituri quosdam tales sunt? Atqui pudefieri vel confundi à Christo judice ignominiam æternam infert, fatente Estio.

## 2:29
Vers. 29.

Ἐὰν εἰδῆτε ὅτι δίκαιός ἐστι.] Namely God. He passes from Christ to God, although the name of God is not expressed here, as shortly after in 11, 15, & 16 from God to Christ. Nor is this surprising, since mention of both has preceded. A similar transition is below IV, 17 & 19. Γινώσκετε ὅτι πᾶς ὁ ποιῶν δικαιοσύνην.] To do righteousness, as here, is called ἐργάζεσθαι in Acts X, 35 & Heb. XI, 33, and κατεργάζεσθαι as in James I, 20, by one who does what is right and praiseworthy. The Latin correctly interprets that γινώσκετε as 'know ye'. Such is that expression, οἲ Θεὸν οἶσθα. Ἰσθ' ὅτι κἀι ῥῖξαι δαίμονι πᾶν δυνατόν. Thus also the manuscript here has: Ὅτι κἀι Ἐξ ἀυτῦ γεγέννηται.] That is, just as children draw their nature from the Father, so they do from God, 2 Pet. I, 4. For I think the true reading is γεγένηται, which appears in many books; and as the Latin reads. If Estius is to be heard here: After the admonition about fleeing from Anti-Christs, the Apostle passes on to describe the true children of God, and dwells on this in the whole of the following chapter. So that, just as Cajetan well observes, the beginning of the third chapter ought to be taken from this place. But there is no need to arrange the text otherwise. For he concludes what he had warned about both the fleeing of the world and Anti-Christian seduction; and about observing those things which the anointing teaches, whose function is not only to teach about the mysteries of the faith, but also to instruct in the pursuit of maintaining piety. Nor is there any reason why we should admit that a transition to the Father is made here. Estius renders the sense thus: If you know, that is, since you know (for it is an indubitable matter) that God or Christ (for he has spoken of Christ immediately before) is just and indeed most excellently just, who has also been made for us righteousness and sanctification, 1. Cor. I. Also know this, that everyone who works righteousness, that is, who lives justly, is his child, and born of him. For this is the second birth of man, which the scriptures call regeneration, by which he is reborn in Christ, and from Christ, as the second Adam, unto righteousness, who by the first birth had been born from the first Adam, unto iniquity, according to that saying: Behold I was conceived in iniquities, etc. By this sentence the Apostle signifies that every work of righteousness proceeds not from the virtues of nature, which we received from our first birth, but from Christ, the Author of our regeneration. Which explanation is to be praised in the Pontifical Doctor. Everyone who does righteousness is born of him, that is, is his child and heir. But a child is not confounded before his father, but appears with all security and confidence, even in his tribunal, so Didymus, Oecumenius, and others, as Tirinus says.

Latin:

Vers. 29.

Ἐὰν εἰδῆτε ὅτι δίκαιός ἐστι.] Nempe Deus. Transit de Christo ad Deum, quanquam nomine Dei hic non expresso, ut mox 11. 15. & 16. à Deo ad Christum. Nec id mirum, cum utriusque mentio præcesserit. Similis transitio infra IV, 17. & 19. Γινώσκετε ὅτι πᾶς ὁ ποιῶν δικαιοσύνην.] Δικαιοσύνην ποιεῖν, ut hic, ἐργάζεσθαι Act. X, 35. & Ebr. XI, 33. κατεργάζεσθαι ut Jac. I, 20. dicitur, qui recta atque laudanda agit. Illud γινώσκετε Latinus recte interpretatur, scitote. Tale est illud, οἲ Θεὸν οἶσθα. Ἰσθ' ὅτι κἀι ῥῖξαι δαίμονι πᾶν δυνατόν. Sic & hic Manuscriptus habet: Ὅτι κἀι Ἐξ ἀυτῦ γεγέννηται.] Id est, sicut filii de Patre naturam trahunt, ita illi de Deo, 2. Petr. I, 4. Puto enim veram lectio- nem esse γεγένηται, quæ in multis libris apparet; & quomo- do Latinus legit. Si hic audiendus Estius: Post admonitionem de Anti-Christis fugiendis transit Apostolus ad descri- bendos veros Dei filios, & in eo immoratur toto seq. cap. Ut proinde, quemadmodum bene Cajetanus ob- servat, ab hoc loco sumi deberet initium tertii capitis. Sed non opus est textum aliter disponere. Conclu- dit enim, quæ monuerat tum de fugiendo mundo, & seductione Anti-Christiana; tum de observandis illis, quæ docet unctio, cujus est non tantum docere de fi- dei mysteriis, sed etiam instruere de studio pietatis servando. Neque est quod hic transitum ad Patrem fieri admittamus. Sensum ita reddit Estius: Si scitis, hoc est, cum sciatis (est enim res indubitabilis) Deum seu Christum, (nam de Christo proxime loquutus est) esse justum & quidem excellentissime justum, qui & nobis factus est justitia & sanctificatio, 1. Cor. I. Illud etiam scitote, quod omnis, qui operatur justitiam, id est, qui juste vivit, sit ejus filius, atque ex ipso natus. Hæc enim est secunda nativitas hominis, quam scri- ptura regenerationem vocant, qua renascitur in Christo, atque ex Christo, tanquam secundo Adam, ad justitiam, qui prima nativitate fuerat natus ex primo Adam, ad iniquitatem, secundum illud: Ecce in iniquitatibus conceptus sum &c. Significat hæc sententia Apostolus, omne opus justitiæ proficisci non ex virtutibus naturæ, quas ex prima nativitate accepimus, sed ex Christo nostræ regenerationis Autore. Quæ explicatio in Doctore Pontificio laudanda. Omnis, qui facit justitiam, ex ipso natus est, id est, filius ejus & hæres est. Filius autem non confundi- tur coram patre, sed cum omni securitate & fiducia comparet, etiam in ejus tribunali, ita Didymus, Oe- cumenius, & alii, ut ait Tirinus.

## 3:1 Argument
CHAPTER III. ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

He continues concerning the sonship of God and its dignity which will one day appear, teaching that those who have that hope purify themselves: Inasmuch as Christ appeared that he might take away sin and destroy the works of the devil, and that this belongs to the children of God, not to sinners: but he who acts unjustly, and does not love his brother, is from the evil one, like Cain, and that it is proper to the world to hate the pious, and on the contrary, by that proof we know that we have passed into life, because we love the brethren, who are to be loved, just as Christ himself loved us in deed and in truth. Furthermore, from that it is also known that we are of the truth, and that our heart can be quieted, and obtain what we ask, and that in this the divine doctrine consists in summary, that one must believe in the name of the Son of God, and that we ought to love one another. The parts are two: The former concerning adoption, or the sonship of GOD and the children of GOD with an axiom and a property up to verse 12. The latter concerning the diverse pursuits of the world and of the children of GOD and the consequences, and the documents of our vivification, and of the tranquility of conscience and of divine grace to verse 24.

PART I. Concerning adoption, and the dignity and property of the children of GOD.

Verse 1.

Ἴδετε ποταπὴν ἀγάπην δέδωκεν ἡμῖν ὁ πατήρ.] This discourse coheres with the preceding, but by that ἴδετε a new attention is excited: And note the vocative ποταπὴ, as 2 Pet. III, 19. Interpret ἀγάπην here metonymically, as a sign of love.

Ἵνα τέκνα Θεῦ κληθῶμεν.] בנים לאלהי Thus to be called by Christ himself, who cannot be deceived, Matt. V, 9.45. The Manuscript has this added here, which the Latin also reads and the Syriac: Καὶ ἐσμεν, that is, and in truth we are such, by imitation of divine goodness. See in the Gospel of John I, 12.

This is the second fruit of the incarnation of the Word, spiritual regeneration, that we have been made children of God in Christ the Only-begotten Son of God. For Irenæus, book III, chapter 11, saying, The Son of God was made the Son of man to this end, that man also might become the Son of God, and as Augustine has it in book I, De Civ. Dei, ch. 15, The only Son of God by nature was made the Son of man for our sake by mercy, that we, children of man by nature, might become children of God by grace through him. St. John therefore celebrates this divine love and grace, that we are called children of God; for to be called is to be. It is not a title without the reality. But we are called children of God for this reason, because we are: Conf. Isa. I, ch. VII, 14. Luke I. What the Syriac and Latin therefore added for the sake of interpretation seems to respect the saying in Hos. II, 1, it shall be said to them, children of the living God. He had said that they were born of God, who work righteousness. Since to be born of God is not of our own powers or of our own will, he proclaims this grace of God, that he regenerates us and adopts us as his children. We are not children of God by imitation, but by adoption and generation from God, the consequence of which is the imitation of God, as is evident from v. 3. For we are born of GOD for this reason, that we may imitate God as our Father. Therefore, regeneration itself is not the imitation of God. But this is the cause of that.

But let us weigh these things a little more fully: ἴδετε, says St. John, of which Augustine says: Behold, as if admiring, he extols the divine charity. Ποδαπὴν, how great, or of what kind. In God, neither quality nor quantity has a place. But in our words and anthropopathically, the mercy of God is as great as God himself, Sir. II, last verse, and the length, breadth, height, and depth are ascribed to the charity of God, Eph. III, 18. Which immense charity of his is seen most especially in this, that he adopts us as his children: How great is the charity of a King or Monarch, when he adopts a vile and abject man as his son. How great, therefore, is that charity which the King of Kings and Lord of Lords has given us, that we should be named children of God? Charity here is not charity infused into us, as Cornelius à Lapide wishes, understanding charity as both active, that is, the act of God's love by which he loves us wonderfully, and passive, communicated and infused into us by God. But it is an affection in God, which he exhibited to us by the effect and the very work of adoption. He is said to have given charity to us, therefore, not because he infused a habit of charity into us, but because he exhibited his immense charity to us in that, just as Cornelius himself could not otherwise explain the mind of John than in this way: q. d. see what great charity, benevolence, and love he has given us, that is, has bestowed and exhibited, God, praising Vatablus's explanation: how much he loved us! But what he adds, when he gave and infused created grace and charity into us, by which we are named and are children of God, this he added of his own; it is not contained in John, nor anywhere else, that we are children of God in so much as GOD has infused a created habit of charity into us. But through faith he gave us the power to become children of GOD, who believes in the name of Christ, says St. John I, 12. You are all children of GOD through faith in Christ Jesus, says St. Paul, Gal. III, 26. Who gave or exhibited this charity to us? The Father, which name is taken essentially or commonly, because the Holy Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, claims it for itself equally: just as we expressly demonstrated this in the Rostock dissertation, when the matter of the paternity of God was treated externally. Works directed outward, such as regeneration and adoption, are common to the Holy Trinity and undivided; it is said of the Son of God in Isa. IX, 6, that he is the everlasting Father, and in the last verse of the preceding chapter we were said to be born of him. He cannot, therefore, be excluded from that paternity: he is said to give us the power to be children of God, John I, 12; it is likewise said of the Holy Spirit in John III, 6, that we are born of him, and for this reason we are baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that through this washing of regeneration we may be reborn by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We are therefore not only called children of God, but we are so in reality, because we are born of God, John 1:13, who of his own will begat us with the word of truth, James 1:18. Those who are called and are not, says Augustine, what does the name profit them where the thing itself is not? How many are called physicians who do not know how to cure? How many are called watchmen who sleep the whole night? Thus many are called Christians and are not found in reality, because they are not what they are called, that is, in life, in morals, in faith, in hope, in charity. But what have you heard here, brothers? Behold, what manner of love the Father has bestowed upon us, that we should be called and be the children of God. We are not, however, children of God by nature, which belongs to that one and only eternal Son of God, who is μονογενὴς παρὰ Πατρὸς, John 1:18. Psalm 2:7, it is fitting: But by grace: who, when we are by nature children of wrath, Eph. 2:3, deigns to regenerate us by carnal generation from water and the Spirit, and by the word of truth, so that we are no longer children of wrath, but children of God, cf. 1 Peter 1:3.

And indeed, because we are not only called but are children of God, Cornelius à Lapide rightly notes us, who think that we are not truly and intrinsically righteous on account of the concupiscence that is always inherent, but are only called so on account of the righteousness of Christ imputed to us. For these are not opposites in Apostolic Theology, inherent and imputed righteousness, but they consist together, nor do we deny that the faithful are intrinsically righteous, but we say that this righteousness is begun, by which we cannot stand before the tremendous judgment of God, so that we therefore have need of the righteousness of Christ, which is imputed to us through faith, by which alone we are constituted righteous before God, Rom. 5:19. But sonship or adoption is one thing, and justification, or the remission of sins, or the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, is another. Through the remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ we are justified before God; indeed, our very justification consists in this: But regeneration and adoption as children of God is a benefit distinct from justification. Regarding the former, we are said to be begotten of God, so that we may become children of God, just as those who are begotten by a parent are his children, which sonship of ours, because it is not natural, we are called children not by nature, but by gracious adoption: Regarding the latter, however, we are absolved from sins before the tribunal of divine judgment and are judged innocent, not because we are adopted as children of God, but because the innocence and righteousness of Christ is imputed to us, and that to this end, that as children of God we may become heirs of the kingdom of God and be saved eternally.

Διὰ τῦτο ὁ κόσμ®· ἐ γινώσκει ὑμᾶς.] That is, it does not acknowledge [us] as its own, but rather hates [us], John 15:18, and inflicts all evils upon [us], John 16:1, 2, 3. He meets a silent objection: You comfort us with a title, and the greatest part of men not only does not attribute it to us, but also treats us contumeliously, as if we were slaves.

Ὄτι ἐκ ἔγνω αὐτὸν.] The same sense in the cited places, John 15:21, 16:3. There is consolation in these words: See the reason why this happens to you. Those who treat you so are blind in the things of God.

Since it may be objected that the world pursues and persecutes us with hatred, and that therefore we obtain no privilege or dignity in the world through this title of children of God, St. John meets this by saying that it happens because the world judges perversely of the faithful, not understanding their dignity: therefore the world does not know us, how great that dignity is, that we are born of God, because it has not known God our Father; whence it cannot be estimated how great a thing it is to be a child of God. They do not know, says Chrysostomus hom. LXXVIII. in Joh., those who treat us with contumely, what kind of people we are, inasmuch as we are citizens of heaven and enrolled in the heavenly fatherland, and companions of the Cherubim. By not knowing we understand practically, that is, with affection, not to love, but to hate, so that it is also a μείωσις. Throughout the whole world, says Augustinus, are the impious, and throughout the whole world are the pious; those do not know us; how do we think? Because they do not know. They insult those who live well. It is no wonder, (so the Estian paraphrase holds,) if we are not children of God to the world, but on the contrary contemptible and hateful: for the world does not know or love us for this reason, because it neither knows nor loves God, whose children we are. Moreover, it ought not to be troublesome to us if we are not loved by them, because they do not love God either.

Latin:

CAPUT III. ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

De filiatione Dei, ejusque dignitate olim appa- ritura pergit, docens eos, qui spem illam ha- bent, se purificare: Siquidem Christus appa- ruerit, ut peccatum tolleret, & opera diabo- li destrueret, idque filiorum Dei esse, non pec- catorum: qui autem injuste agit, nec fra- trem diligit, à maligno esse, sicut Cainum, idque mundo proprium esse pios odisse, & ex adverso eo documento nos scire, quod in vi- tam transierimus, quia fratres diligimus, qui diligendi, sicut Christus ipse nos dilexit ope- re, & veritate. Porro inde etiam cognosci, quod ex veritate simus, nostrumque cor se- dari posse, & impetrare quod petimus, at- que in eo summatim consistere doctrinam divinam, quod credendum sit in nomen Fi- lii Dei, mutuoque nos diligere debeamus. Partes sunt duæ: Prior de adoptione, vel filiatione DEI & filiorum DEI cum axioma- te tum proprietate ad vers. 12. Posterior de diversis mundi & filiorum DEI studiis ac con- sequentibus, & documentis vivificationis nostræ, ac tranquillitatis conscientiæ & gratiæ divinæ ad vers. 24.

PARS I. De adoptione, & filiorum DEI dignitate ac proprietate.

Vers. 1.

Ἴδετε ποταπὴν ἀγάπην δέδωκεν ἡμῖν ὁ πατήρ.] Cohæret hic sermo cum superioribus, sed per illud ἴδετε רא nova excitatur attentio: Et nota provocabulum ποταπὴ, ut 2. Petr. III, 19. Ἀγάπην hic μετωνυμικῶς interpretare, signum dilectionis.

Ἵνα τέκνα Θεῦ κληθῶμεν.] בנים לאלהי Sic appel- lari ab ipso Christo, qui falli non potest, Matth. V, 9.45. Hic adscriptum habet Manuscriptus, quod & Latinus legit & Sy- rus: Καὶ ἐσμεν, id est, ac revera tales sumus, imitatione divi- næ bonitatis. Vide in Evangelio Joh. I, 12.

Alter hic est fructus incarnationis verbi regene- ratio spiritualis, quod facti simus filii Dei in Chri- sto Unigenito Dei Filio. Nam Irenæo l. III. cap. 11. dicente, Filius Dei factus est Filius hominis ad hoc, ut & homo fieret Dei Filius, & ut Augustinus ha- bet l. I. de Civ. Dei c. 15. Unicus naturæ Dei Filius propter nos misericordia factus est Filius hominis, ut nos natura filii hominis, filii Dei per illum gratia fie- remus. Hanc ergo divinam dilectionem, & gratiam celebrat S. Johannes, quod nos filii Dei vocemur; vocari enim est esse. Non est titulus sine re. Sed ideo vocamur filii Dei, quia sumus: Conf. Es. I. cap. VII. 14. Luc. I. Quod proinde Syrus & Latinus interpre- tationis causa addidere, videtur respicere dictum Hos. II, 1. dicetur eis, filii Dei viventis. Dixerat eos, ex Deo genitos esse, qui justitiam operantur. Quum ex Deo gigni non nostrarum sit virium, aut volun- tatis nostræ, deprædicat hanc Dei gratiam, quod nos regenerat, & adoptat in filios suos. Non imita- tione Dei filii sumus, sed adoptione & generatione ex Deo, cujus consequens est Dei imitatio, ut e v. 3. constat. Ideo enim gignimur ex DEO, ut Deum imitetur ceu Patrem nostrum. Non est ergo imitatio Dei ipsa regeneratio. Sed hæc il- lius causa est.

Sed expendamus hæc paulo uberius: ἴδετε in- quit S. Johannes, quo de Augustinus: Ecce quasi admirando divinam charitatem extollat. Ποδαπὴν quantam, vel qualem. In Deo nec qualitas nec quantitas locum habet. Verbis autem nostris & ἀν- θρωποπαθῶς misericordia Dei tanta est, quantus ipse Deus, Sir. II. v. ult. & charitati Dei longitudo, latitudo, altitudo, & profunditas adscribitur, Eph. III, 18. Quæ immensa ejus charitas vel maxime in eo conspicitur, quod nos in filios suos adoptet: Quanta est charitas Regis vel Monarchæ, cum in filium adoptat hominem vilem & abjectum. Quan- ta ergo illa charitas, quam Rex Regum & Domi- nus Dominantium nobis dedit, ut filii Dei nomi- nemur? Charitas non hic est infusa nobis charitas, ut Cornelius à Lapide vult charitatem tum activam pu- ta actum amoris Dei, quo nos mire amat, tum pas- sivam nobisque à Deo communicatam & infusam intelligens. Sed est affectus in Deo, quem exhibuit nobis effectu & opere ipso τῆς ὑιοθεσίας. Dedisse er- go charitatem dicitur nobis, non quod charitatis habitum nobis infuderit, sed quod charitatem su- am immensam nobis in eo exhibuerit, quemadmo- dum ipse Cornelius aliter explicare mentem Johan- nis haud potuit, quam hoc modo: q. d. videte, quantam charitatem, benevolentiam & amorem nobis dedit, id est, præstitit & exhibuit Deus, laudans Va- tabli explicationem: quantum dilexerit nos! Quod autem addit, cum gratiam & charitatem creatam nobis dedit & infudit, qua filii Dei nominamur & sumus, hoc de suo addidit, in Johanne id non habe- tur, nec uspiam alias, quod filii Dei sumus, in quan- tum nobis creatum charitatis habitum infudit DEUS. Sed per fidem dedit nobis ἐξουσίαν fieri filios DEI, qui credit in nomen Christi, inquit S. Joh. I, 12. Omnes filii DEI estis per fidem in Christum Jesum, inquit S. Paulus, Gal. III, 26. Quis dedit vel exhi- buit nobis hanc charitatem? Pater, quod nomen essentialiter vel κοινῶς sumitur, quia SS. Trinitas Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus ex æquo id sibi vendicat: quemadmodum in dissert. Rostoch. id ex professo demonstravimus, cum de paternitate Dei κατ᾽ ἔξω fuit actum. Opera ad extra qualis est re- generatio & ὑιοθεσία communia sunt S. Trinitati & indivisa; de Filio Dei dicitur Esa. IX, 6. quod sit Pater æternus, & v. ult. Cap. præced. dicebamur ex ipso nati. Non ergo potest ab ista paternitate exclu- di: dicitur nobis potestatem dare, ut simus filii Dei, Joh. I, 12. de Spiritu Sancto itidem dicitur Joh. III, 6. quod ex ipso nascamur, atque ideo baptizamur in nomine Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti, ut per hoc lavacrum regenerationis à Patre, Filio & Spiritu Sancto renascamur. Filii Dei ergo non tantum no- minamur, sed revera sumus, quia ex Deo nati Joh. II, 13. qui voluntarie nos genuit verbo veritatis, Jac. I, 17. Qui vocantur & non sunt, inquit Augustinus, quid illis prodest nomen, ubi res non est? Quam multi vocantur medici, qui curare non norunt? Quam multi vocantur vigiles, qui tota nocte dormi- unt? Sic multi vocantur Christiani, & in rebus non inveniuntur, quia hoc quod vocantur, non sunt, id est, in vita, in moribus, in fide, in spe, in charitate. Hic autem quid audistis fratres? Ecce, qualem dilectio- nem dedit nobis Pater, ut filii Dei vocemur & simus. Non autem sumus filii Dei per naturam, quod uni ac soli illi æterno Dei Filio, qui est μονογενὴς παρὰ Πατρὸς, Joh. I, 18. Psalm. II, 7. convenit: Sed per gratiam: qui nos quum τῇ φύσει simus filii iræ, Eph. II, 3. carnali generatione regenerare dignatur ex aqua & Spiritu, & per verbum veritatis, ut ne am- plius filii iræ, sed filii Dei simus, conf. 1. Petr. I, 3.

Nec vero ideo quia non nominamur tantum, sed sumus filii Dei, Cornelius à Lapide merito nos notat, qui censeamus, nos revera & intrinsece justos non esse ob inhærentem semper concupiscentiam, sed tantum nominari ita propter justitiam Christi nobis imputatam. Hæc enim in Theologia Apostolica opposita non sunt, inhærens & imputata justitia, sed simul consistunt, neque nos negamus intrinsece ju- stos esse fideles, sed eam justitiam inchoatam dici- mus, qua coram tremendo Dei judicio consistere non possimus, ut opus proinde nobis sit Christi ju- stitia, quæ imputatur nobis per fidem, qua una justi constituimur coram Deo, Rom. V, 19. Aliud autem est ὑότης vel ὑιοθεσία, aliud justificatio, seu remissio pec- catorum, vel imputatio justitiæ Christi. Per remissio- nem peccatorum, & imputationem justitiæ Christi ju- stificamur coram Deo, imo in eo consistit ipsa no- stra justificatio: Sed regeneratio & adoptio in filios Dei distinctum est beneficium à justificatione. Quoad illam ex Deo gigni dicimur, ut evadamus filii Dei, quemadmodum qui à parente generan- tur, ejusdem filii sunt, quæ ὑότης nostra quia non est naturalis, non natura, sed gratiosa adoptione filii dicimur: Quoad hanc vero coram tribunali judi- cii divini à peccatis absolvimur, & iñocentes judi- camur, non quia adoptati in filios Dei, sed quia im- putatur nobis innocentia & justitia Christi, idque eo fine, ut tanquam filii Dei regni Dei hæredes evadamus, & æternum salvemur.

Διὰ τῦτο ὁ κόσμ®· ἐ γινώσκει ὑμᾶς.] Id est, non agnoscit pro suis, imo odit, Joh. XV, 18. & malis omnibus afficit, Joh. XVI, 1. 2. 3. occurrit tacitae objectioni : Titulo nos solaris & eum maxima pars hominum nobis non modo non tribuit, sed & contumeliose nos tractat, velut mancipia.

Ὄτι ἐκ ἔγνω αὐτὸν.] Idem sensus dictis locis Joh. XV, 21. XVI, 3. Est in his verbis consolatio : Videte causam cur id vobis eveniat. Qui vos ita tractant, caeci sunt in rebus Dei.

Quum objici possit, quod mundus nos odio pro- sequatur & persequatur, adeoque in mundo nihil privilegii aut dignitatis per hunc filiorum Dei titu- lum consequamur, occurrit S. Johannes, ex eo id fieri, quod mundus perverse judicet de fidelibus, non intelligens eorum dignitatem: ideo mundus non novit nos, quanta illa dignitas sit, quod ex Deo nati simus, quia non cognovit Deum Patrem nostrum; unde aestimari non potest, quanti sit, esse filium Dei. Nesciunt, inquit Chrysostomus hom. LXXVIII. in Joh. qui nos contumelia afficiunt, quales simus, utpote qui caeli cives & supernae patriae adscripti, & Cheru- bim socii simus. Non cognoscere Practice intelligi- mus, id est, cum affectu, non amare, sed odisse, ut μείωσις etiam sit. Per totum mundum, inquit Augu- stinus, impii, & per totum mundum pii, illi nos non cognoscunt; quomodo putamus, quia non cognoscunt? Insultant bene viventibus. Non mirum, (ita habet paraphrasis Estiana,) si mundo non simus filii Dei, sed contra contemptibiles atque exosi: nam ideo mundus non novit nos nec diligit, quia Deum, cujus filii sumus, nec novit, nec diligit. Non debet autem molestum nobis esse, si non diligamur ab iis, quia nec Deum diligunt.

## 3:2
Vers. 2.

Ἀγαπητοὶ, νῦν τέκνα Θεῦ ἐσμέν.] We are now indeed children of God in the sense that has been stated.

Καὶ ὔπω ἐφανερώθη τί ἐσόμεθα.] And it does not yet appear what we shall be, that is, how we shall be children of GOD in that better age. And here 'and' is used for an adversative. 'What' is also accustomed to be referred to qualities.

Although, he says, we are despised, vile, and hated by the world, yet even now in this age, in that vile and oppressed state, we are in reality the sons of God. This dignity is proper and perpetual to us, whatever the world may determine concerning us: in which we glory even in the midst of tribulations. And behold, although this is the highest dignity and eminence, far surpassing and exceeding all worldly dignity and eminence, because we are not the sons of a Prince, not of a King, not of an Emperor, but of the highest God himself, the Lord of glory; yet it does not yet appear what we shall be, not only by reason of glory and happiness, but not even by reason of holiness, which here is very impure and imperfect in the state of wayfarers: nor by reason of wisdom and knowledge, because we know only in part, 1. Corinth. XIII, 9. It has not yet appeared how glorious you shall be in respect of the body, since the body τῆς ταπεινώσεως ἡμῶν shall be made conformable to the glorious body τῆς δόξης of Him, Phil. 3, 21. We walk here by faith, not by sight, 2. Cor. 5, 7. We are transformed into His image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord, the glory of the Lord κατοπτριζόμενοι, 2. Cor. 3, 18. But then we shall be fully glorious, seeing no longer di' ἐσόπτρου ἐν αἰνίγματι, but πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον, 1. Cor. XIII, 12. Your life is hid with Christ in God. When Christ, who is your life, shall appear, then shall you also appear with Him in glory, Col. III, 3.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Ἀγαπητοὶ, νῦν τέκνα Θεῦ ἐσμέν.] Sumus nunc quidem filii Dei eo, quo dictum est sensu.

Καὶ ὔπω ἐφανερώθη τί ἐσόμεθα.] Et nondum apparet, quid futuri simus, id est, quomodo futuri simus filii DEI in meliore illo seculo. Καὶ hic est pro adversativa. Τί solet et- iam ad qualitates referri.

Quamvis, inquit, mundo despecti, viles & infesti simus, tamen etiam nunc in hoc seculo, in vili isto & oppresso statu revera filii Dei sumus. Dignitas haec nobis propria est & perpetua, quicquid mundus de nobis statuat: qua gloriamur etiam in mediis tribu- lationibus. Et ecce quamvis summa haec dignitas & eminentia sit, omnem dignitatem & eminentiam mundanam longissime superans & excedens, quod non Principis, non Regis, non Imperatoris, sed quod ipsius summi Dei Domini gloriae filii simus; nondum tamen apparet, quid erimus, non modo ratione gloriae & felicitatis, sed nec ratione sanctita- tis, quae hic valde impura, & imperfecta est in statu viatorum: neque ratione sapientiae & cognitionis, quia ex parte tantum cognoscimus, 1. Corinth. XIII, 9. Nondum etiam apparuit, quam gloriosi futuri sitis ratione corporis, siquidem corpus τῆς ταπεινώσεως ἡμῶν σύμμορφον reddetur corpori τῆς δόξης glori- oso ipsius Phil. 3, 21. Per fidem hic ambulamus, non per speciem, 2. Cor. 5, 7. Transformamur in imagine ejus de gloria in gloriam, veluti a Domini Spiritu gloriam Domini κατοπτριζόμενοι, 2. Cor. 3, 18. tunc vero plene gloriosi erimus, visuri non amplius di' ἐσόπτρε ἐν αἰνίγματι, sed πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον, 1. Cor. XIII, 12. Vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo. Cum autem apparuerit Christus vita vestra, tunc & vos apparebitis cum ipso in gloria, Col. III, 3.

## 3:2
Ὅμοιοι αὐτῷ ἐσόμεθα,] Not only in holiness, but in eternity and blessedness, and thus much more His children than we are now.

There are no degrees of ὑότητος; we are children here just as in the other life. The sonship of God does not admit of more and less. However, we do not deny that there are degrees in conformity with God the Father and in likeness, which is not the very ὑότης itself. Nor indeed shall we be like God then only in sempiternity and blessedness, but also in holiness: because our inherent holiness will then be far greater and more perfect, as being not only begun, but consummated, not mutable, but immutable. Man will then become with God, as Bernard says to the brothers, from the mount of God, one Spirit, not only by the unity of willing the same thing, but by a more express unity of virtue, of not being able to will anything else.

Ὅτι ὀψόμεθα αὐτὸν, καθώς ἐστιν.] From the promise of Matt. V, 8. Since it was accepted among the Jews that God is not seen, that is, known as He is, except in the other life, from the passage of Exodus XXXIII, 20, he draws an argument from that as from a confessed fact. No thing can comprehend eternity except an eternal thing. Compare 1 Cor. XIII, 12.

The cause of such great likeness with God will be the intuitive vision of God; just as here in the state of wayfarers, when we, beholding the glory of God with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, 2 Cor. III, 18, so much more in the state of the blessed, when we shall see Him face to face, as He is, we shall be transformed into the same image, and we shall be like Him. If the cause of our μεταμορφώσεως is beholding And the enigmatic vision, by which we are transformed little by little and successively from glory to glory, will certainly bring about a perfect transformation in the other life, and the intuitive vision of God will initiate it, by which the glory of the Lord is about to irradiate and illuminate us at once and together for that glorious and eternal μεταμόρϕωσιν [transformation], so that we may be like Him forever, Apoc. XXII, 5. As the blessed Hunnius says, those who look into a mirror see the things that are placed behind them, but not as clearly and evidently as if someone were to turn away from the mirror and, turning his eyes to the things themselves placed behind him, were to look at them face to face; thus now in the mirror of the revealed Word we look at GOD as if from behind, but in the blessed life we shall look at Him face to face with as much perfection as can fall to a creature. Some refer the particle αὐτὸν to GOD, others to Christ: Estius embraces the latter: But the former is more suitable to the text, since in v. 1 and 2 God is named, but no mention is made of Christ: nor could Estius sufficiently explain how the glorification of the body has the vision of God as its cause: Since from the fact that we shall see Him bodily in glory, this effect does not follow, namely to be like Him in the glory of the body, since in His glorified humanity He is seen for a time even by the reprobate.

But as for what others say, that from the glory of the soul, which consists in the beatific vision of God, glory—that is, immortality and the remaining glorious gifts—redounds into the subject body, according to the opinion of Augustine in Epistle 56 to Dioscorus, we leave that in the middle: for it could rather be seen that the glorified gifts are given immediately by God to the bodies of the blessed through the glorious resurrection: Although that seems rather to favor the opinion which establishes that this blessed ὁμοίωσιν [likeness] is deduced by John from the immediate vision of God, by which we shall contemplate His Divine essence with our eyes not in any created likeness, but clearly and immediately, as it is in itself: rather than the one that judges it to be deduced from the vision of Christ according to both natures. Nor do we allow that vision to be restricted with Estius to the day of the most recent coming of Christ, for the reason that John speaks of us, that is, of men to be resurrected to life at the coming of Christ, not of souls. For he says that we shall see God, when it shall appear what it is to be a son of God, the inheritance of the sons of God having been obtained: which will appear as regards the soul when we depart in the Lord, but as regards the body on the day of our glorious resurrection. That we are named even when our souls are understood is not foreign to the phraseology of Scripture, which says that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob live, when it speaks of their souls, Luke XX, 38. That vision of God as He is brings about perfect knowledge of GOD, perfect love of the beloved, perfect enjoyment of the beloved, and in it perfect blessedness. Cornelius gives this reason for the consequence: We shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He is: We shall be perfectly holy, just, pure, loving God, because we shall be blessed, glorious, Divine. And just as God sees Himself, and enjoys and is blessed by that vision: So also our mind will see Him as He is, and all things that are formally in Him, and will enjoy and be blessed by this vision forever, and by it our sonship and adoption will be perfected: because as sons of God we shall obtain the glory, inheritance, and happiness of GOD. But you may more conveniently explain it thus: We shall be like God in respect of the mind by wisdom, in respect of the will by holiness and justice, in respect of the body by immortality, in respect of both by eternal glory and happiness, because we shall see God face to face: For from the intuitive vision of God will arise perfect knowledge and wisdom, perfect love and justice, as well as glorious immortality and blessedness. The intuition of the Divine mind will irradiate us with wisdom, of the will with love and justice, of the immortal and glorious nature with immortality and glorious blessedness. Psalm XVII, 11. Psalm XXXV, 10. 1 Cor. XIII, 12. Chap. XV, 45. Col. III, 3. Phil. III, 21.

Latin:

Ὅμοιοι αὐτῷ ἐσόμεθα,] Non sanctitate tantum, sed æter- nitate & beatitudine, ac sic multo magis filii ejus, quam nunc.

Non dantur gradus ὑότητος, filii æque sumus hic, ut in altero seculo. Filiatio Dei non recipit magis & minus. In conformitate autem cum Deo Patre & si- militudine, quæ vero ipsa ὑότης non est, gradus dari non abnuimus. Neque vero tantum sempiternitate & beatitudine tum similes Deo erimus, sed etiam sanctitate: quia longe major & perfectior erit tum nostra inhærens sanctitas, utpote non inchoata tan- tum, sed consummata, non mutabilis, sed immuta- bilis. Fiet homo tunc cum Deo, dicente Bernardo ad fratres, de monte Dei, unus Spiritus non tantum uni- tate volendi idem, sed expressiore quadam unitate virtutis aliud velle non valendi.

Ὅτι ὀψόμεθα αὐτὸν, καθώς ἐστιν.] Ex promisso Matth. V, 8. Cum receptum esset apud Judæos Deum non videri, id est, cognosci, qualis est, nisi in vita altera, ex loco Exodi XXXIII, 20. inde, ut ex confesso, argumentum ducit. Æter- nitatem nulla res nisi æterna potest comprehendere. Confer 1. Cor. XIII, 12.

Causa similitudinis tantæ cum Deo erit visio Dei intuitiva; uti hic in statu viatorum, cum nos reve- lata facie gloriam Dei speculantes in eandem ima- ginem transformamur à claritate in claritatem, 2. Cor. III, 18. ita multo magis in statu beatorum, cum videbimus ipsum à facie ad faciem, sicuti est, trans- formabimur in eandem imaginem, eiq; similes eri- mus. Si causa μεταμορφώσεως nostræ est specularis & enigmatica visio, qua transformamur paulatim & successive de claritate in claritatem, perfectam transformationem in altera vita afferet utique ac inchoabit intuitiva Dei visio, qua Domini gloria simul ac semel nos irradiatura & illustratura est ad gloriosam istam & æternam μεταμόρφωσιν, ut simi- les ei æternum simus, Apoc. XXII, 5. Ut qui specu- lum, inquit B. Hunnius, intuentur, vident ea, quæ à tergo sunt posita, non autem tam perspicue & eviden- ter, ac si quis à speculo se avertens, & ad res ipsas à tergo sitas oculos convertens illas coram intueatur, sic nunc in speculo Verbi revelati quasi à tergo DEUM aspicimus, at in vita beata à facie ad faciem intuebi- mur perfectione tanta, quanta in creaturam cadere potest. Particulam αὐτὸν nonnulli ad DEUM, alii ad Christum referunt: quod posterius ample- ctitur Estius: Sed prius textui magis convenit, quum v. 1. & 2. Deus nominatus sit, Christi au- tem nulla facta sit mentio: neque explicare satis potuit Estius, quomodo corporis glorificatio pro causa habeat visionem Dei: Siquidem ex eo, quod corporaliter eum videbimus in gloria non sequa- tur hic effectus, esse similem ei in gloria corporis, quum in humanitate glorificata ad tempus etiam à reprobis videatur.

Quod vero alii ajunt ex animæ gloria, quæ con- sistit in visione Dei beatifica, redundare gloriam, id est, immortalitatem, reliquasque dotes glorio- sas in corpus subjectum ex Augustini ep. LVI. ad Dioscor. sententia, id in medio relinquimus: nam videri potius id posset, dotes glorificatas immedia- te à Deo per resuscitationem gloriosam corpori- bus beatorum dari: Quanquam id potius illi sen- tentiæ favere videatur, quæ ὁμοίωσιν istam beatam è visione immediata Dei deduci à Johanne statuit, qua oculis nostris Divinam ejus essentiam non in aliqua creata similitudine, sed clare, & immediate, ut in seipsa est, contemplabimur: quam quæ è vi- sione Christi secundum utramque naturam eam deduci censet. Neque restringi patimur cum Estio illam visionem ad diem adventus Christi no- vissimi, eo quod de nobis loquatur Johannes, id est, hominibus in adventu Christi resuscitandis ad vitam, non de animabus. Nam visuros nos Deum dicit, cum apparebit, quid sit esse filium Dei, obtenta nempe filiorum Dei hæreditate: quod apparebit quoad animam, cum decedemus in Domino, quo- ad corpus vero in die resurrectionis nostræ gloriosæ. Nos autem nominari etiam cum animæ nostræ intel- liguntur, non alienum à phrasi Scripturæ, quæ Abrahamum, Isaacum & Jacobum vivere ait, cum de animabus eorum loquitur, Luc. XX, 38. Visio illa Dei sicut est, perfectam cognitionem DEI, perfectam cogniti dilectionem, perfectam dilecti frui- tionem, & in ea perfectam beatitudinem infert. Cor- nelius hanc rationem consequentiæ reddit: Simi- les erimus ei, quia videbimus eum, ficuti est: Erimus perfecte sancti, justi, puri, amantes Deum, quia eri- mus beati, gloriosi, Divini. Et sicut Deus se videt, eaque visione fruitur & beatur: Ita & mens nostra videbit eum sicuti est, & omnia, quæ in eo formaliter sunt, hacque visione fruetur & beabitur in æternum, eaque perficietur nostra filiatio & adoptio: quia ut filii Dei gloriam, hæreditatem & felicitatem DEI adipiscemur. Sed convenientius eam ita expo- nas: Similes Deo erimus ratione mentis sapientia, ratione voluntatis sanctitate, & justitia, ratione corporis immortalitate, ratione utriusque gloria & felicitate æterna, quia Deum à facie ad faciem vide- bimus: Nam ex intuitiva Dei visione orietur per- fecta cognitio & sapientia, perfectus amor & justi- tia, nec non gloriosa immortalitas & beatitudo. Intuitus mentis Divinæ nos irradiabit sapientia, voluntatis amore & justitia, naturæ immortalis & gloriosæ beatitudinis immortalitate & beatitudine gloriosa Psalm. XVII, 11. Psalm. XXXV, 10. 1. Cor. XIII, 12. Cap. XV, 45. Col. III, 3. Phil. III, 21.

## 3:3
Vers. 3. Οἴδαμεν δὲ ὄτι ἐὰν φανερωθῇ.] Namely that which we shall be. And here 'if' is used for 'when', just as the Manuscript had above at 2:7. And the same Apostle speaks thus here at 14:2. And the Hebrews use their 'im' in this way.

The appearing is not understood as that which we shall be, according to Estius, but as the appearing of Christ, from a comparison with Col. III, 3, because the appearing of that which we shall be is not the cause that we shall be like him, but the appearing of Christ will be the cause of our glorification. According to the sense of Grotius, it ought rather to have been said: We know that when we shall be like him, then that which we shall be will appear: but now he says, we know or are certain that when he shall appear, we shall be conformed to him in glory, which Estius understands of the glory of the body, Phil. III, 21. Moreover, because regarding the souls of those dying in the Lord, who are ἀπάρτι blessed, and thus enjoy the vision of God, Apoc. XIV, 13, the elect are like God, and it appears to them immediately what they shall be for eternity: Therefore the sense of that saying can be conveniently exhibited thus: We know certainly and undoubtedly, when that which is now hidden shall have appeared, namely that we shall be eternal then both in our blessed ἀναλύσει, and also in the glorification of our bodies, namely in the blessed and glorious resurrection, then we shall be like Him, there regarding the soul, here also regarding the glory of the body, not that the appearing of that which we shall be is the cause of that likeness, but that those things are joined, and that only then, when that is to appear, shall we truly have that likeness, whence B. Luther rendered it: Wenn es erscheinen wird. Most correctly does the paraphrase of B. Hunnius hold here: q. d. We are not called children of God by a bare and empty title, but we truly are, and the thing itself underlies the name: And indeed we are already in the present children of God, even in the midst of these calamities and the miseries of this world. But it has not yet appeared what we shall be, that is, we are already by faith children of God, which faith holds, and in the word of promise apprehends those things which do not yet appear. For although our ὑοθεσία, and the unfading inheritance which follows it, is not yet obvious to our eyes, but is as it were hidden in Christ: nevertheless, it is by no means to be doubted on that account, because it does not appear, because we know, he says, that when He shall have appeared, we shall be like Him. Where the Apostle expressed both his own and the πληροφορίαν of all true believers with the word (we know): as if he were saying: we doubt nothing at all, but we establish more certainly than certain that we are not being played with by empty titles or suckled by false hope, but that what we now believe by faith and expect by hope will one day appear, and when that shall have appeared, then we shall be like Him, that is, we shall be like Him in holiness, perfection, immortality, and blessedness, though not equal.

Latin:

Vers. 3. Οἴδαμεν δὲ ὄτι ἐὰν φανερωθῇ.] Nempe illud, quod erimus. Est & hic ἐὰν pro ὅταν, quomodo & Manuscriptus habebat supra II, 7. Et sic loquitur idem hic Apostolus XIV, 2. Et Ebraei suo אם sic utuntur.

Apparitio non intelligitur ejus, quod erimus jux- ta Estium, sed apparitio Christi, e collatione Col. III, 3. quia apparitio ejus quod erimus, non est causa quod similes ei futuri simus, sed apparitio Christi causa erit nostrae glorificationis. Juxta Grotii sen- sum dici potius debuisset: Scimus quoniam cum si- miles ei erimus, tunc appariturum, quod futuri su- mus: Jam vero dicit, scimus vel certi sumus cum ap- parebit, ipsi nos conformabimur ipsi in gloria, quod de corporis gloria Phil. III, 21. intelligit Estius. Cæterum quia quoad animas in Domino deceden- tium, quæ ἀπάρτι beatæ sunt, adeoque visione Dei fruuntur, Apoc. XIV, 13. similes Deo sunt electi, & apparet ipsis statim, quid in æternum sint: Idcirco sensus illius dicti commode ita exhiberi potest: Certo & indubitato scimus, quum apparuerit id, quod nunc latet, quod scilicet futuri æternum sumus tum in beata nostra ἀναλύσει, tum etiam in corporum nostrorum glorificatione, in beata nempe ac glo- riosa resurrectione, tunc similes ei nos futuros, ibi quoad animæ, hic etiam quoad corporis gloriam, non quod apparitio ejus, quod futuri sumus, causa sit illius similitudinis, sed quod conjuncta illa sint, quodque tum demum, cum id appariturum est, si- militudinem istam revera simus habituri, unde B. Lutherus reddidit: Wenn es erscheinen wird. Rectis- sime hic habet B. Hunnii paraphrasis: q. d. Nos non dicimur filii Dei nudo & inani titulo, sed vere sumus, & subest nomini res ipsa: Et quidem sumus in præsenti jam filii Dei, etiam in mediis calamitatibus hisce, & mundi hujus miseriis. Sed nondum apparuit id, quod futuri sumus, hoc est, nos fide jam sumus filii Dei, quæ fides tenet, & in verbo promissionis apprehendit ea, quæ nondum apparent. Quanquam enim ὑοθεσία nostra, & quæ illam consequitur immarcessibilis hæ- reditas oculis nostris haud dum obvia, sed in Christo velut abscondita est: nequaquam tamen ideo dubi- tandum de illa, quia non apparet, quia scimus, in- quit, quod quando apparuerit, similes erimus. Ubi Apostolus & suam & omnium vere credentium πλη- ροφορίαν verbo (scimus) expressit: quasi dicat: nihil penitus dubitamus, sed certo certius statuimus, nos non ludi inanibus titulis aut falsa spe lactari, sed ap- pariturum aliquando id, quod nunc fide credimus, & spe expectamus, & quando id apparuerit, tum si- miles ei erimus, hoc est, sanctitate, perfectione immor- talitate & beatitudine erimus ei similes, licet non æquales.

## 3:3
And everyone who has this hope in Him.] He who has the hope of such a great good in God, that is, in such a way as God wishes that hope to be conceived.

He purifies himself, that is, he makes and keeps himself pure from evil things. For both are included in this word, and it is in fact the same as walking in the light above, I, 7. The same effect is attributed now to God, now to Christ, now to us subordinately. But he who wishes to hope for eternal life does this: because he knows that it is not purchased for less.

As He is holy.] He refers to the passages Leviticus XI, 44 and XIX, 2, where for holy there is pure, as 1 Peter I, 16. Which are of such equal meaning that the Latin here has placed sanctifies for purifies, and holy for pure.

That a man purifies himself to obtain eternal life, because it is not purchased for less, is a dogma unwritten and counter-written, born in the workshops of the Pelagians, Socinians, and Papists. If we ourselves can purchase eternal salvation for ourselves, what need is there of Christ, and of the expenditure of such a price, by which He purchased us for Himself, and eternal life for us, when He gave Himself for the life of the world, John VI, 51. Acts XX, 28. 1 Cor. VI, last verse. Cornelius à Lapide thinks that the manner of attaining this, so that we may be like God and see Him as He is, is assigned here, because two things are required for it: 1. to place hope in God, 2. to strive for holiness. But hope is not brought forward in this place as a means, much less is the striving for holiness; it is only taught concerning those who have the hope of eternal life, how they conduct themselves and ought to conduct themselves; namely, that they strive to purify themselves by the help of the Holy Spirit; he purifies himself is to be understood of duty, and of the striving of those reborn of God and the faithful. But that it is meritorious is by no means asserted. And how will anyone attain the perfection of that duty, as He is holy? Who rises to that holiness in this imperfection, such as God's is: Which nevertheless God requires, Leviticus XIX, 2. Chapter XX, 7. 1 Peter I, 16. But a double argument for purification is had here, the one taken from the effect, because purification is the effect of the hope of eternal life. Whoever has conceived this hope in his heart, and holds it sealed by the earnest of the Holy Spirit, so that he is certain of the heavenly inheritance and the blessedness stored up and laid away for us in it, he purifies himself, that is, he guards himself against all the defilements of sins by the power of the Holy Spirit: as this B. Hunnius [says]. The other [reason] is sought from the example of God the Father, whose purity and holiness Christians ought to emulate, just as He Himself is pure, so that they may declare by the deed itself that they are truly the sons of God, and that they do not in the least degenerate from the nature and purity of their Father.

Latin:

Καὶ πᾶς ὁ ἔχων τὴν ἐλπίδα ταύτην ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ.] Qui spem tan- ti boni habet in Deo, id est, ita, sicut Deus eam spem vult concipi.

Ἁγνίζει ἑαυτόν.] Semet purificat מטהר, id est, purum se à rebus malis facit & servat. Nam utrumque hac voce com- prehenditur, estq; re ipsa idem, quod ἐν φωτὶ περιπατεῖν supra I, 7. Effectus idem modo Deo tribuitur, modo Christo, modo nobis subordinate. Hoc autem facit is, qui sperare vult vitam æternam: quia scit illam minoris non comparari.

Καθὼς ἐκεῖνος ἅγιός ἐστι.] Respicit loca Levit. XI, 44. & XIX, 2. ubi pro ἁγιός est ἅγνὸς, ut 1. Petr. I, 16. Quæ adeo paris sunt significatus, ut Latinus hic pro ἁγνίζει posuerit san- ctificat, & pro ἁγνὸς sanctus.

Ad comparandam vitam æternam hominem se- ipsum purificare, quod illa minoris non comparetur, dogma est ἄγραφον & ἀντίγραφον in officinis Pe- lagianorum, Socinistarum & Pontificiorum enatum. Si nos ipsi nobis comparare æternam salutem pos- sumus, quid opus est Christo, & pretii tanti impen- dio, quo nos sibi, & nobis vitam æternam compa- ravit, cum seipsum dedit pro mundi vita, Joh. VI, 51. Act. XX, 28. 1. Cor. VI. v. ult. Cornelius à Lapide hic modum id assequendi, ut similes Deo simus, & videamus eum, sicut est, assignari putat, quod ad eum requiratur 1. spem locare in Deo, 2. studere san- ctitati. Sed spes non adducitur hoc quidem loco, ut medium, nedum studium sanctitatis, solum doce- tur de iis, qui spem habent vitæ æternæ, quales se gerant, ac gerere debeant; quod nempe studeant seipsos ope Spiritus sancti purificare; ἁγνίζει ἑαυ- τὸν de debito intelligendum, ac de studio renatorum ex Deo & fidelium. Quod vero meritorium esse minime asseritur. Et quomodo assequetur quispi- am debiti illius perfectionem, καθὼς ἐκεῖνος ἁγνός ἐστι. Quis ad eam sanctitatem assurgit in hac imper- fectione, qualis Dei est: Quam tamen Deus requi- rit Levit. XIX, 2. Cap. XX. 7. 1. Petr. I, 16. Argu- mentum autem geminum hic habetur purificatio- nis, alterum ab effectu desumptum, quia purificatio effectus est spei vitæ æternæ. Quicunque hanc spem pectore suo concepit, eamque arrhabone Spiritus san- cti obsignatam habet, ut certus sit de hæreditate cœ- lesti, & beatitudine in illa nobis recondita repositaque, is purificat se, hoc est, ab omnibus inquinamentis pec- catorum virtute spiritus sancti sibi cavet: ut hic B. Hunnius. Alterum à Dei Patris exemplo petitum, cujus puritatem & sanctimoniam æmulari Christia- ni debent, sicut & ipse purus est, ut re ipsa declarent, se vere Dei filios esse, & à natura puritateque Patris sui minime degenerare.

## 3:4
Vers. 4.

Πᾶς ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν καὶ τὴν ἀνομίαν ποιεῖ.] That is, whoever sins (this verb being taken as we have said it is taken in this epistle) likewise offends God; he expressed this, however, by ἀνομίαν: because he who deliberately violates the law of any King, there is no reason why he should hope for a benefit from him. Ποιῶν ἀνομίαν is עשה עולה, Psalm 27, v. 1, Ezekiel 33, v. 13, 18, or פועל עולה, as Psalm 58, v. 3. And the Syrian here translates ἀνομίαν as פריח. But that word was taken one way in the time of the old law, and another way in the time of the new law, which is not a little purer than the old.

Καὶ ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἡ ἀνομία,] Here 'και' is 'for'. For a reason is given for the preceding statement. The sense is: For to us, however variously different philosophers may take and define the word ἁμαρτία, sin is any act whatsoever which you know and perceive to conflict with any law of God, that is, with any revelation of the Divine will, such as is primarily the Evangelical law. Such is חטאת and עון in Hosea 7:8.

The word ἁμαρτία is not taken restrictively concerning a more serious sin, but just as this proposition, and the definition subjoined teaches, generally concerning any sin whatsoever, because whatever is against the Divine law is sin; every illegality, I say, whether it be designated in excess or defect, in committing or omitting, in work or in heart, voluntarily or involuntarily by adding something to the law, or by committing something against the law. Augustine, Book XXII against Faustus, ch. 27, defines sin as a word, deed, or thought against the eternal law. Ambrose, Book on Paradise, ch. 8: What else is sin than a transgression of the Divine law and disobedience to the heavenly commandments. Estius acknowledges this sense and renders it thus: The clear sense is of this kind: And lest anyone flatter himself in certain sins, as if they were light, because they do not seem to be against the laws: I declare to you and affirm that every sin is iniquity, that is, a transgression of the Divine law, and that everyone who commits sin commits iniquity and transgresses the Divine law: and therefore he who remains in sins promises himself in vain a likeness of glory with the head, Christ. He speaks, however, chiefly of mortal sin, although venial sins also are certain iniquities, and are repugnant to some Divine law, and delay one from the entrance of the heavenly kingdom and from participating in the likeness of Christ, until they have been purged: Which does not happen except by the blood of Christ, 1 John 1:7. Chap. 2:1. That Ἀνομίαν is taken differently in the Old Testament and differently under the New Testament is a burdensome hearing: What was against the moral law in the Old Testament is also against the same in the New Testament, and sin is equally here as it is there. We have said more than once that the Gospel as such does not deliver the law, but exhibits him who is the fulfillment of the law, Rom. 10:4.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Πᾶς ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν καὶ τὴν ἀνομίαν ποιεῖ.] Id est, quis- quis peccat (verbo hoc sumpto, sicut in hac epistola sumi di- ximus) idem & Deum offendit, hoc autem expressit per μιλω- νομίαν: quia qui legem Regis alicujus consulto violat, non est, quod beneficium ab eo speret. Ποιῶν ἀνομίαν est עשה עולה, Psal, 27. v. 1. Ezech. 33. v. 13. 18. aut פועל עולה, ut Psalm. 58. v. 3. Et Syrus hic ἀνομίαν vertit פריח. Sed aliter ea vox sumebatur tempore legis veteris, aliter tempore legis novæ, quæ veteri non paulo est purior.

Καὶ ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἡ ἀνομία,] Και hic est nam. Ratio enim redditur præcedentis dicti. Sensus est: Nam nobis, utcunque varie Philosophi varii ἁμαρτίας vocem & fumant &definiant, peccatum est actus quivis, quem scias & sentias pugnare cum aliqua lege Dei, id est, cum aliqua patefactione Divinæ vo- luntatis, qualis imprimis est lex Evangelica. Tale חטאת & עון Os. VII, 8.

Vox ἁμαρτίας non accipitur restricte de peccato graviori, sed quemadmodum & hæc propositio, & definitio subjuncta docet, generaliter pro peccato quocunque, quia quicquid est contra legem Divi- nam, peccatum est; omnis, inquam, illegalitas, sive in excessu, sive defectu, sive committendo, sive omit- tendo, sive opere sive corde designetur, voluntarie an involuntarie legi aliquid addendo, seu contra le- gem aliquid committendo. Augustinus lib. XXII. contr. Faust. c. 27. peccatum definit dictum, factum vel cogitatum contra legem æternam. Ambrosius lib. de Parad. c. 8. Quid aliud est peccatum, quam legis Divinæ transgressio, ac cælestium inobedientia man- datorum. Quem sensum agnoscit atque ita red- dit Estius: Sensus perspicuus est hujusmodi: Ac ne quis sibi blandiatur in peccatis quibusdam, quasi levi- bus, eo quod non videantur esse contra leges: Declaro vobis & affirmo, omne peccatum esse iniquitatem, id est, legis Divinæ transgressionem, & omnem eum, qui peccatum committit, iniquitatem committere, legem- que Divinam transgredi: ideoque frustra eum, qui in peccatis hæret, sibi promittere similitudinem gloriæ cum capite Christo. Loquitur autem præcipue de peccato mortali, quanquam & venialia sunt iniquita- tes quædam, & legi Divinæ alicui repugnant, & ab ingressu regni cælestis ac similitudine Christi partici- panda remorantur, donec expurgata fuerint: Quod non fit, nisi sanguine Christi, 1. Joh. I, 7. Cap. II, 1. Ἀνομίαν aliter in Veteri, aliter sub Novo Testamento sumi, φορτικὸν ἄκουσμα est: Quod in Veteri Te- stamento contra legem moralem erat, etiam in No- vo Testamento contra eandem est, & peccatum pariter hic ut ibi est. Evangelium qua tale legem non tradere, sed eum, qui est complementum le- gis exhibere Rom. X, 4. plus vice simplici diximus.

## 3:5
Verse 5. And you know that he was manifested. We have already said that the name of Christ is to be understood here, although from afar, and although mention of GOD has intervened. He was manifested, that is, he appeared to the world, how that word is taken in John 1:31, 1 Peter 1:20. It is also said of the Gospel, 1 Timothy 3:16, and 2 Timothy 1:10, Titus 1:3, Hebrews 9:8, and above 1:2.

He in whom they ought to remain, Chap. 2:28, who is about to appear, and before whom, lest they be put to shame, one must take heed, that righteous one, v. 29, to whom manifestation is otherwise attributed, because he had to assume flesh and appear in the flesh, 1 Timothy 3:16, which has been sufficiently shown in its places above, chapter 1:2, that it is said there not of the Gospel, but of God the Word. He can also be taken antonomastically, he who is, as God calls himself, Exodus 3:18.

That he might take away our sins. In the Manuscript: that he might take away sins, that is, that he might make us sinners immune from sins. See what we have said at John 1:29, where the same expression is used. The sense is the same above 1:7 and 1 Peter 2:22, 23. Silently understand here: But if Christ's purpose in this matter lacks an outcome through your fault, certainly in that you vehemently offend Christ and likewise the Father, and therefore you ought not to hope for life and eternal glory. The passage Isaiah 53:11 is referred to.

He now draws an argument from the end of the incarnation of the Son of God, why we ought to abstain from sin: because, namely, he appeared in the flesh for this reason, that he might take away sin, that he might take upon himself and bear the guilt and punishment of sin in our place, and might free us from sin, not that we should serve sin, from which we have been freed, but that we should keep ourselves wholly for Christ the Redeemer, Titus 2:14. These ends are therefore subordinate, the bearing of our sins, or the satisfaction rendered for sins, and our regeneration as well as sanctification, because he satisfied for our sins for this reason, that by the virtue of his merit we, being regenerated as children of God, might truly strive to be sanctified, and might take heed for ourselves against sins. Since, therefore, the appearance of the Son of GOD himself in the flesh was required to take away our sins, nay, since our liberation from sins cost such a price, why should we involve ourselves in them again? 1 Corinthians 6:20. 1 Peter 1:17 ff. Certainly no place is left for us to sin (says Oecumenius here), for since Christ came to destroy sin, inasmuch as he was entirely immune from all sin, it is not permitted for you who are born of him, and confirmed by faith in him, to sin any longer. What is added, and sin is not in him, is both the reason why he could take away our sins, because he himself knew no sin, 2 Corinthians 5:21, just as the particle 'and' is not rarely taken causally, in whom there is no sin: He himself came to take away sin, says St. Augustine here. Compare Isaiah 53:9, Hebrews 7:26; and it sets forth an example, which we ought to imitate, that we may strive to become like him, and abstain from sins as much as is in us.

Latin:

Vers. 5. Καὶ οἴδατε, ὅτι ἐκεῖνος ἐφανερώθη.] Jam diximus subaudiri hic nomen Christi, quanquam ex longinquo, & quanquam DEI mentio intercessit. Ἐφανερώθη, id est, mun- do apparuit, quomodo ea vox sumitur Joh. I, 31. 1. Petr. I, 20. Dicitur & de Evangelio, 1. Tim. III, 16. & 2. Tim. I, 10. Tit. I, 3. Ebr. IX, 8. & supra I, 2.

Ille, in quo manere debebant Cap. II. v. 28. qui appariturus est, & coram quo, ne pudefiant, caven- dum, δίκαιος ille v. 29. cui Φανέρωσις alias tribui- tur, quia carnem assumere & in carne apparere debebat, 1. Tim. III, 16. quod ibi non de Evan- gelio, sed de Deo λόγῳ dici æque supra cap. I, 2. su- is locis satis ostensum est. Potest etiam ἐκεῖνος accipi ἀντονομαστικῶς, ille qui est, ut Deus se vo- cat, Exod. III, 18.

Ἵνα τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν ἄρῃ.] In Manuscripto: ἵνα ἁμαρ- τίας ἄρῃ, id est, ut peccatores nos immunes faceret a pecca- tis. Vide quæ diximus ad Joh. I, 29. ubi eadem est loquutio. Sensus idem supra I, 7. & 1. Petr. II, 22. 23. Tacite hic intelli- ge: Quod si Christi in hac re consilium per vestram culpam caret eventu, certe in eo Christum & pariter Patrem vehe- menter offenditis, ac proinde vitam gloriamque æternam spe- rare non debetis. Respicitur locus Esa. LIII, 11.

A fine incarnationis Filii Dei argumentum jam petit, cur à peccato abstinere debeamus: quia scili- cet ideo in carne apparuit, ut peccatum tolleret, culpam & pœnam peccati in se susciperet ac porta- ret nostri loco, nosque à peccato liberaret, non ut peccato serviremus, à quo liberati sumus, sed ut Christo Redemptori nos totos conservemus, Tit. II, 14. Subordinati ergo sunt hi fines, peccatorum nostrorum portatio, vel satisfactio pro peccatis præstita, & nostra regeneratio ut & sanctificatio, quia ideo satisfecit pro peccatis nostris, ut virtute meriti ipsius regeniti ceu Dei filii vere sanctificati studeamus, & à peccatis nobis caveamus. Quum itaque ad tollenda nostra peccata ipsius Filii DEI apparitio in carne requisita fuerit, imo satisfactio pro peccatis nostris, adeoque tanto pretio nostri à peccatis liberatio constiterit, cur his denuo nos involveremus? 1. Cor. VI. vers. 20. 1. Petr. I. vers. 17. seqq. Non sane peccandi nobis locus ullus re- linquitur (inquit hic Oecumenius) cum enim Chri- stus ad peccatum destruendum advenerit, quippe qui peccati omnis prorsus fuerit immunis, vobis qui ab ipso estis nati, & fide in ipsum confirmati, pecca- re amplius non licet. Quod additur, & peccatum non est in eo, tum causam quare tollere peccata no- stra potuerit, quia ipse peccatum non novit, 2. Cor. V, 21. uti non raro particula καὶ causaliter accipi- tur, in quo non est peccatum: Ipse venit auferre peccatum, inquit hic S. Augustinus. Conf. Esa. LIII. v. 9. Ebr. VII. v. 26. tum exemplum sistit, quod imitari debeamus, ut similes eidem fieri annitamur, & à peccatis, quantum in nobis est, abstineamus.

## 3:6
Verse 6.

And sin is not in him. Present for past, sin was not in him, namely when he was living a mortal life. So also Peter in the cited place: Who did no sin. Christ went before us not only in words but also by example, he leaves behind a pattern, as Peter says, Deuteronomy 32:4, there is no injustice in him, concerning God.

Everyone who remains in him does not sin. Some think that by 'to sin' here only a habit is designated. But the ancients believed that all such acts are designated as we have already described before, and we follow that under the leadership of Paul, 1 Corinthians 6:9, Galatians 5:14, Ephesians 5:5. He does not admit such a one who is truly joined to Christ by love, which is here called remaining in Christ: Just as a lover is said to be and dwell where he loves.

The Apostle silently warns again that we should remain in Christ through faith, just as he had warned in verses 10, 27, and 28, because by that means they can guard themselves from sins and abstain, not only from the custom of sinning and habitual sins, but also from any sins whatsoever that are committed against conscience, and insofar as they remain in Him, they do not sin. There is no discussion here of sins of daily incursion, which subsequent repentance immediately renders venial on account of faith in Christ, such as also creep upon the reborn against their will, indeed which even render them captives to the law of sin which is in their members, Rom. VII, 23, nor of the habit of original sin, which adheres to us until the last breath of life and is not laid aside except with life. For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us, 1 John I, 8. Everyone who remains in Him does not sin, in the composite sense, says Cornelius, that is to say, as long as he remains in Christ and in the grace of Christ, as long as he follows the guidance of grace. Therefore, it is not permitted to conclude from this, with Jovinian, Pelagius, and the Socinians, that the just live without sin: nor is it to be explained as if the truly faithful cannot fall into sins against conscience and cast off the grace of God, as the Calvinists wish, because the subject is not the faithful simply, but those who persevere in remaining in Christ; as the clear words have it: and who remain in Him: nor are the children of God and the children of the devil distinguished by this. For there are many children of God who do not persevere in justice, but fall into mortal sins and fall from grace: nor is it to be taken with Ambrose in his commentary on Isaiah, cited by Augustine in book IV against the two epistles of Pelagius, chapter 11, as referring to the future age, because he warns us in the present: These things I write to you, that you may not sin: In this the children of God and the children of the devil are manifest; nor is there any reason to interpret these things concerning the reborn, in that part in which they are reborn, with Augustine in book II on the Baptism of Infants, chapters 8, 9, 10, etc., and Bernard in his book on the nature and dignity of Divine love, chapter 6. For St. John speaks only of mortal sins that devastate the conscience, which in the reborn, as long as they are reborn and remain in Christ, do not fall, as Jerome in Book II against Jovinian, ch. 1, and Book I against Pelagius, ch. 3, and Augustine himself in Tractate V on this epistle interpret, where he explains the present passage concerning the sin by which fraternal charity is violated, under which, however, other similar sins are deservedly included, which are called works of the devil, verse 8. Whence 'to commit sin' is rightly explained by John Hessels as being to walk according to the flesh, to be under sin, to be a slave of sin.

Everyone who sins has not seen him, nor known him.] He who sins in the sense we have mentioned, when he sins, neither thinks of Christ as he ought, nor shows by his deed that he knows how much the will of Christ is to be valued. ראה, which corresponds to the word ὁρᾷν, is translated elsewhere by 'to look at,' elsewhere by 'to consider.' But γινώσκειν, like other similar words, often signifies not so much the thing itself as the testimony of the thing. Maimonides explains this at length in the Guide for the Perplexed XXIII, 24.

Thus also Estius, and not badly: John does not mean that he who sins has never truly believed; but the sense is that he who sins, at the time when he sins, is alienated from the affective knowledge of God. For past tenses are put for present, either according to the Hebrew custom, or as Cajetan wishes: to signify the causality of knowledge and vision with respect to the act of sinning or not sinning. And not dissimilarly Cornelius: 'He has not seen' is the same as 'he has not known,' for he who sins does not know Christ, namely practically, because practically he does not consider the immense love of Christ, the redemption, the benefits, and the rewards of eternal glory promised to the elect, and the punishments prepared by him for sinners in hell: for if he were to consider these attentively, he would certainly not sin, whence St. Basil in Moral Rules 80, at the end: 'What is the characteristic,' he says, 'of a Christian? To keep the Lord before his eyes always.' Didymus excellently: Everyone who sins, having become a stranger to Christ, has no participation in, nor knowledge of him, to which fact it is a consequence that he does not appear to have internal knowledge of him either.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Καὶ ἁμαρτία ἐν ἀυτῷ ἐκ ἔςι.] Præsens pro Præterito, pec- catum in eo non erat, nempe cum vitam mortalem viveret. Sic & Petrus dicto loco: Ὅς ἁμαρτίαν ἐκ ἐποίησε. Christus non verbis tantum sed & exemplo nobis præivit, ὑπολίμπα- νει ὑπογραμμὸν, ut ait Petrus, Deuteron. XXXII, 4. אין עול ἐκ ἔςιν ἀδικία ἐν ἀυτῷ de Deo.

Πᾶς ὁ ἐν ἀυτῷ μένων ἐχ ἁμαρτάνει.] Putant quidam per ἁμαρτάνειν hic designari solum habitum. At veteres credi- dere designari actus omnes tales, quales jam ante descripsi- mus, & id nos sequimur Duce Paulo 1. Cor. VI, 9. Gal. V, 14. Eph. V, 5. Talem non admittit, qui vero amore Christo con- jungitur, quod hic dicitur manere in Christo: Sicut amans dicitur esse & habitare ubi amat.

Tacite iterum monet Apostolus, ut in Christo per fidem maneamus, quemadmodum vers. 10. 27. 28. monuerat, quod ea ratione à peccatis sibi cavere, & abstinere possint, non solum à peccandi consuetu- dine, & peccatis habitualibus, sed etiam à peccatis quibusvis, quæ contra conscientiam committun- tur, & quatenus in eo permanent, non peccent. De peccatis quotidianæ incursionis, quæ subsequens statim pœnitentia ob fidem in Christum venialia reddit, qualia etiam renatis præter voluntatem ob- repunt, imo que captivos quoque ipsos reddunt le- gi peccati, quæ est in membris ipsorum, Rom. VII, 23. hic non est sermo, nec de habitu peccati origi- nalis, quod nobis ad extremum vitæ halitum ad- hæret, nec nisi cum vita deponitur. Nam si dicamus, quod peccatum non habemus, seducimus nos ipsos, & veritas non est in nobis, 1. Joh. I, 8. Omnis, qui in eo manet, non peccat, in sensu composito, ait Cor- nelius, quamdiu scilicet in Christo & Christi gratia manet, quamdiu ductum gratiæ sequitur. Non er- go cum Joviano, Pelagio & Socinianis hinc colli- gere licet, justos vivere sine peccato: nec eo illa ex- plicanda, ac si vere fideles non possint in peccata con- tra conscientiam labi, & gratiam Dei excutere, ut Calviniani volunt, quia agitur non de fidelibus sim- pliciter, sed qui in Christo perseveranter manent; ut verba diserta habent: & qui in illo manent: neque per hoc distinguuntur filii Dei, & filii diaboli. Multi enim sunt filii Dei, qui in justitia non per- severant, sed in peccata mortalia labuntur, gra- tiaque excidunt: nec cum Ambrosio in comment. supr. Esa. apud Augustinum lib. IV. contra duas epist. Pel. cap. 11. de futuro seculo hæc accipienda, quia monet nos in præsenti: Hæc scribo vobis, ut non peccetis: In hoc manifesti sunt filii DEI & filii diaboli; neque est, quod de renatis hæc ea parte, qua renati sunt, interpretemur cum Augustino lib. II. de Bapt. parv. cap. 8. 9. 10. &c. & Bernardo lib. de nat. & dignit. Div. amor. cap. 6. Loqui- tur enim S.
