Johannes tantum de peccatis mortali- bus conscientiam vastantibus, quæ in renatos, quamdiu renati sunt, & in Christo manent, non ca- dunt, ut Hieronymus lib. II. contr. Jovin. c. 1. & l. I. contr. Pelag. c. 3. & Augustinus ipse tract. V. in hanc epist. interpretantur, ubi de peccato, quo violatur fraterna charitas, locum præsentem exponit, sub quo tamen fraterno odio peccata alia similia meri- to comprehenduntur, quæ opera diaboli vocantur, vers. 8. Unde facere peccatum recte a Joh. Hesselio exponitur, quod sit ambulare secundum carnem, es- se sub peccato, servum esse peccati.

Πᾶς ὁ ἁμαρτάνων ὀυχ ἑώρακεν ἀυτὸν, ὀυδὲ ἔγνωκεν ἀυτὸν.] Qui peccat eo quod diximus sensu, cum peccat, neque de Christo sic cogitat, ut oportet, neque facto ostendit, se scire, quanti sit habenda Christi voluntas. ראה quod respondet voci ὁρᾷν, vertitur alibi per σκέπτων, alibi per κατανοεῖν. Γινώσκειν vero ut & alia verba similia sæpe non tam rem, quam rei testimo- nium significant. Late id explicat Maimonides Ductoris du- bitantium XXIII, 24.

Sic etiam Estius nec male: Non sentit Johannes, eum, qui peccat, nunquam vere credidisse: sed sensus est, eum, qui peccat, tunc quando peccat, ab affecti- va Dei notitia alienum esse. Ponuntur enim præ- terita pro Præsentibus, vel more Ebræo, vel ut vult Cajetanus: ad significandam causalitatem notitiæ & visionis respectu actus peccandi vel non peccandi. Nec absimiliter Cornelius: Idem est, non vidit, quod nec cognovit, qui enim peccat, non cognoscit Chri- stum, scilicet practice, quia practice non considerat im- mensum Christi amorem, redemptionem, beneficia ac præmia gloriæ æternæ electis promissa, & pœnas pec- cantibus ab eo præparatas in gehenna: Si hæc enim at- tente consideraret, utique non peccaret, unde S. Basi- lius in Moral. reg. 80. in fine: Quid proprium, ait, Christiani? Providere Dominum in conspectu suo sem- per. Præclare Didymus: Omnis, qui peccat, factus extraneus Christi non habet participium, nec scientiam ejus, cui rei consequens est, ut neque scientiam inter- nam ejus habere videatur.

## 3:7
Verse 7.

Little children, let no one deceive you.] And here the manuscripts have 'children,' not badly: namely, the Apostle hopes so well of those who are more advanced that he believes they do not need these warnings. See above II, 12 and the following. He does not say this in vain, however. For many both then flattered themselves, and now flatter themselves, wishing a certain desire for living well to suffice for salvation. You have similar openings to warnings in Luke XXI, 8; 1 Cor. VI, 9; and in this very argument, XV, 33; Gal. VI, 7; James I, 16; above I, 18. 'He who does righteousness is righteous.'] That is, he is finally held to be righteous before God, and is treated as righteous, and therefore the reward promised to the righteous belongs to him alone, who composes his actions according to the law of God, for that is what 'to do righteousness' is here, opposed to 'to sin' or 'to commit sin,' see above II, 29. 'As he is righteous.'] For so also Christ himself was righteous, or pleased God, by always acting rightly.

A precarious annotation. For 'little children' denotes sons, just as 'children' does, designated by a gentle form of address, out of the sweetest distinction of love. Therefore it is not opposed to those who are more advanced, as if they did not need these warnings. Nor is it established who even then maintained, or today maintains, that a certain desire for living well suffices for salvation; nor does the effort itself, joined to desire, contribute anything to salvation, which Christ alone, by his own merit, has both procured for us and bestows. Nor do traces of such a refutation or correction appear here, much less are Simon or the Gnostics refuted in it, who taught that a man is justified by faith alone, as Cornelius says, or even Balaam and the Nicolaitans, as Estius accuses; for this is the Apostolic doctrine, which he perversely misinterprets, because it follows from it that anyone could be righteous and at the same time indulge his own desires and live impurely: because although faith alone justifies, yet the justifying faith is never alone, or separated from charity; for if it exists alone, it is not alive, nor is it true faith, as St. James teaches. But that Estius directly opposes our faith to what follows, 'he who does righteousness is righteous,' with a secret accusation, is a false interpretation. The Apostle does not say that anyone is justified before God by the very fact that he does righteousness: for he would thus contradict Paul, who says that the ungodly is justified when God does not impute sins, when God imputes righteousness without works, Rom. IV, verses 6, 7. He only says that it is an argument that someone is righteous who does righteousness, just as Estius connects the final sentence: 'he who does righteousness is born of him': because the effort and operation of righteousness provide an argument for regeneration, but one is not reborn through these. For those are the effects, not the cause, of regeneration. Estius says that John understands righteousness not as habitual, but as good works, which are called works of righteousness, just as Augustine also declares in his Enarrations on Psalm 118, Discourse 16. From which it is a consequence that Christian righteousness consists in the operation of virtues, and not in the remission of sins alone: these things can be admitted, because besides the remission of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, there is a need, not indeed that we be justified before God, but that we demonstrate ourselves to be true Christians, that we do righteousness: and therefore Christian righteousness is both the righteousness which we have in Christ through imputation, and our incipient righteousness, which we have through justification. But Estius adds that it is not only signified that the works of righteousness are certain external signs which argue that a man is righteous before God: but that they are of such a kind that they have the nature of a formal cause, by which someone is righteous. For just as one is formally called walking from walking, so one is called just in act from the acts of justice which one exercises: and consequently just in habit from habitual justice: Just as, conversely, evil works formally constitute a man as sinning, and the stain contracted from them as a sinner. But in these he confuses the twofold denomination of the just. For one is called just either to whom the justice of God is imputed without works, or who devotes effort to the works of justice; we admit that a man is called just in both ways: But that former one pertains only to the article of justification: Nor does John inform us here about the formal cause of justification, at least he explains who is just, not by what a man is constituted just before the tribunal of God, which is done solely through the obedience of one Christ, Rom. V, 19. That one is just, whether in act or in habit, from the acts or habit of justice, contributes nothing to the forensic or judicial justification of man in the Divine judgment. St. John is now occupied with the article concerning sanctification, not justification. And therefore we do not deny that one is called just intrinsically who does justice: especially because it is added, just as He also is just. For those who are justified before God through faith, they also do justice, and are rightly called just because of their desire, intention, and zeal for justice, because they walk in justice, walk according to the Spirit and not according to the flesh, show themselves to be zealous for good works, and denying ungodliness and worldly desires, live temperately, justly, and godly in this present age Rom. VI, 13. Cap. VIII, 1. 12. Tit. II, 12. 14. That one is also formally called just from good works, after one has been justified through faith, does not contradict our opinion: As the blessed Höpfner, disp. X. de justific. We thus far, he says, agree with Estius, that actual justice is not only a sign and proof of habitual justice, as Bellarmine wishes, but also has the character of a formal cause, by which one is righteous through works. We also grant that John Chapter III, 7 speaks of actual righteousness not only as it is an effect and sign of habitual righteousness, but also because it makes one formally righteous, which is confirmed by the example of Christ proposed by John to the regenerate for imitation: finally, we concede that by the pursuit of good works, inherent righteousness can be increased and more perfected. But nevertheless, the most important question remains: whether we are justified before GOD by habitual righteousness, and whether we are more justified by actual righteousness, which Bellarminus and Estius and the entire Papacy assert, we utterly deny. For it does not follow: The regenerate are righteous also by inherent righteousness. Therefore, the regenerate are justified because of that righteousness, because this righteousness is an effect of justification. For the perfection of those righteous ones is not such as is required before the tribunal. And the particle 'as' in the cited passage from 1 John III, 7 denotes not equality but similarity, and that only of a certain kind, not however of every kind: just as also in Matthew V, 48. For as Augustine says in Book II, On the Merits and Remission of Sins, Chapter VII: 'Then we have already begun to be similar, having the first fruits of the Spirit, and yet we are still dissimilar through the remnants of the old nature.' Although that explanation of the blessed Hunnius can also have a place, that he who does righteousness declares himself to be justified: 'For he does not,' he says, 'reason here from cause to effect, as if exercising righteousness were the cause of our righteousness before God, as the Papists interpret: But that by exercising righteousness through just and good works they declare themselves righteous, and show the righteousness valid before GOD that has already preceded.' At the same time, however, he repeats and intersperses the argument drawn from the example of God: 'Just as He also is righteous.' For thus it is not a similarity of Christ's righteousness with ours that is insinuated—that we are righteous just as Christ is—but the reason is repeated why we ought to do righteousness, namely because Christ is righteous. Moreover, the blessed Hunnius joins both righteousnesses in the cited passages: 'Although,' he says, 'that righteousness by which we are righteous before the tribunal of God is acquired outside of us through Christ: yet as soon as it is apprehended by faith, this imputed righteousness immediately excites in the human soul a habit of begun righteousness and holiness, and impels the man to good and just works.' But here a great difference presents itself between the moral habit of righteousness, which is acquired by assiduous exercise and is obtained by the industry of men from preceding actions: and that theological habit of begun righteousness and holiness, which is not prepared by human industry, nor acquired from the preceding actions of man, but rather is given and infused by the Spirit of God in the conversion, regeneration, and justification of man, and thus is effective for producing holy actions pleasing to God. Thus, the works of righteousness do not precede their habit, but follow from the same divinely infused habit, just as the divine Augustine, discussing good works, says: 'Works follow the justified, they do not precede the one to be justified.'

Therefore, the argument of Estius falls into the sponge, who notes that from this passage the imputation of righteousness is destroyed, which is constituted in the remission of sins alone. For Christ, he says, who is most perfectly righteous, who was made for us by GOD righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor. I), is righteous by the rectitude of his mind alone, not also by the remission of sins, which he could have none of. For what else is gathered from this than that we, by the confession of Estius himself, are not righteous in such a way as Christ is righteous? For we are in need of the remission of sins, Christ is not in need: we must be justified as sinners, justification does not befit Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Τεκνία, μηδεὶς πλανάτω ὑμᾶς.] Et hic Manuscripti habent παιδία, non male: Nempe ita bene sperat Apostolus de pro- vectioribus, ut eos credat his monitis non egere. Vide supra II, 12. sequentibus. Non frustra autem hoc dicit. Multi enim & tunc sibi blandiebantur, & nunc blandiuntur, volentes de- siderium quoddam bene vivendi ad salutem sufficere. Simi- lia monitorum exordia habes Luc: XXI, 8. 1. Cor. VI, 9. & in hoc ipso argumento, XV, 33. Gal. VI, 7. Jac. I, 16. supra I, 18. Ὁ ποιῶν τὴν δικαιοσύνην, δίκαιός ἐστι.] Id est, is demum apud Deum justus habetur, & ut justus tractatur, ac proinde ei soli competit promissum justis præmium, qui actiones suas ad Dei legem componit, id enim hic est justitiam facere, oppositum τῷ ἁμαρτάνειν sive ἁμαρτίαν ποιεῖν, vide supr. II, 29. Καθὼς ἐκεῖνος δίκαιός ἐστι.] Nam sic & Christus ipse justus fuit, sive Deo placuit, recte semper agendo.

Precaria annotatio. Nam τεκνία filios notat, æque ut παιδία, blanda compellatione ita designa- tos, ex amoris suavissima διάστολῇ. Non ergo op- ponitur provectioribus, quasi his monitis non egentibus. Nec constat, quinam vel tunc ita statu- erint, vel hodie sic statuant, desiderium quoddam bene vivendi ad salutem sufficere; nec ipsum stu- dium desiderio junctum quicquam ad salutem fa- cit, quam solo suo merito Christus nobis & pepe- rit & donat. Neque talis elenchi aut epanortho- seos vestigia hic apparent, multo minus in eo refel- luntur Simon aut Gnostici, qui docuerint sola fi- de hominem justificari, ut Cornelius, vel etiam Ba- laam & Nicolaitæ, ut Estius criminatur; hæc enim Apostolica est doctrina, quam perverse traducit, quod ex ea sequatur, posse quemlibet esse justum, & simul indulgere suis cupiditatibus, ac impure vivere: quia etsi fides sola justificet, justificans ta- men fides nunquam sola est, vel separata a chari- tate; nam si sola existat, non viva est, nec vera fi- des, quemadmodum S. Jacobus docet. Nostram autem fidem directe ei quod sequitur, qui facit ju- stitiam justus est adversari secreta criminatione, Estiana est ψευδερμηνεία. Non ait Apostolus ju- stificari quempiam eo ipso coram Deo, quod faciat justitiam: Contradiceret enim ita Paulo, qui dicit justificari impium, cum DEUS peccata non im- putat, cum DEUS imputat justitiam sine operi- bus, Rom. IV. vers. 6. 7. Ait tantum id argumen- tum esse, quod quis justus sit, qui faciat justitiam, quemadmodum Estius consert finalem senten- tiam: qui facit justitiam, ex ipso natus est: quia ar- gumentum regenerationis præbet studium & ope- ratio justitiæ, non autem per hæc quis renascitur. Effectus enim illa, non causa sunt regenerationis. Justitiam, inquit Estius, Johannes intelligit, non ha- bitualem, sed opera bona, quæ vocantur opera justi- tiæ, quemadmodum & Augustinus declarat in enar- rat. Psalm. CXVIII. Conc. 16. Ex quo consequens est in operatione virtutum consistere justitiam Chri- stianam, non autem in sola peccatorum remissione: Hæc admitti possunt, quia præter peccatorum remissionem, & justitiæ Christi imputationem opus est, non quidem ut justificemur coram Deo, sed ut Christianos veros nos demonstremus, ut ju- stitiam faciamus: ideoque justitia Christiana est tum justitia, quam habemus in Christo per impu- tationem, tum inchoata nostra justitia, quam per justificationem habemus. Addit autem Estius, nec solum significari, quod opera justitiæ sint signa quædam exteriora, quæ arguant hominem esse justum coram Deo: sed esse ejusmodi, quæ rationem habe- ant causæ formalis, qua quis justus sit. Ut enim for- maliter ab ambulatione quis dicitur ambulans, ita ab actibus justitiæ quos exercet quis justus dicitur in actu: & consequenter à justitia habituali justus in habitu: Quemadmodum & è diverso mala opera formaliter hominem constituunt peccantem, & ma- cula ex eis contracta peccatorem. Sed in his con- fundit geminam justi denominationem. Nam ju- stus dicitur vel cui imputatur justitia Dei sine ope- ribus, vel qui operibus justitiæ operam navat, utroque modo hominem justum dici admittimus: Sed prior ille pertinet tantum ad articulum justifi- cationis: Neque hic de causa formali justificatio- nis nos informat Johannes, saltim quisnam justus sit, explicat, non per quod homo coram tribunali Dei justus constituatur, quod fit unicè per unius Christi obedientiam, Rom. V, 19. Quod justus quis sive actu sive habitu sit ab actibus vel habitu justitiæ, id ad hominis justificationem forensem vel judicialem in judicio Divino nihil facit. Oc- cupatur jam S. Johannes in articulo de sanctifica- tione, non de justificatione. Ideoque non abnui- mus justum intrinsece dici, qui facit justitiam: im- primis quia additur, sicut & ille justus est. Nam qui coram Deo justificati sunt per fidem, illi & ju- stitiam faciunt, & justi ob desiderium, intentionem & studium justitiæ recte dicuntur, quod in justitia incedant, secundum Spiritum ambulent non se- cundum carnem, zelotas bonorum operum se de- monstrent, & abnegantes impietatem, & mundi cu- piditates, temperanter & juste, ac pie vivant in hoc seculo Rom. VI, 13. Cap. VIII, 1. 12. Tit. II, 12. 14. A bonis operibus etiam formaliter justum dici, postquam quis per fidem justificatus est, nostræ sententiæ non repugnat: Quomodo B. Höpfnerus disp. X. de justific. Nos hactenus, inquit, Estio con- sentimus, quod justitia actualis sit non signum tan- tum, ac documentum habitualis justitiæ, ut vult Bel- larminus, sed etiam habeat rationem causæ formalis, qua quis per opera justus est. Largimur etiam Jo- hannem Cap. III, 7. loqui de actuali justitia non tan- tum, ut est effectus & signum habitualis justitiæ, sed etiam quia formaliter justum facit, quod confirmat exemplum Christi à Johanne ad imitationem renatis propositum: denique concedimus, studio bonorum operum augeri posse, & magis perfici inhærentem ju- stitiam. Sed nihilominus remanet potissima quæstio, an per habitualem justitiam coram DEO justice- mur, & an per actualem justitiam magis justificemur, quod Bellarminus & Estius ac Papatus universus afferit, nos pernegamus. Non enim sequitur: Renati sunt justi etiam inhærente justitia. Ergo renati pro- pter illam justitiam justificantur, quia justitia hæc est effectus justificationis. Neque enim justorum il- lorum perfectio est talis, qualis coram tribunali re- quiritur. Et particula sicut in allegato ex 1. Joh. III, 7. dicto non æqualitatem sed similitudinem notat, eamque tantum aliqualem, non autem omnimodam: quemadmodum & Matth. V, 48. Nam ut Augusti- nus libr. II. de peccat. meritis & remissione Cap. VII. inquit: Tunc similes esse jam cœpimus primitias ha- bentes Spiritus & adhuc dissimiles sumus per reliqui- as vetustatis. Quanquam etiam illa B. Hunnii ex- plicatio locum habere possit, quod qui justitiam fa- cit, se justificatum esse declaret: Neque enim, inquit, à causa hic ratiocinatur ad effectum, quasi exercere justitiam causa sit nostræ coram Deo justitiæ, ut Pon- tificii interpretantur: Sed quod exercendo justitiam per justa & bona opera se justos declarent, & justiti- am coram DEO valentem jam antegressam mon- strent. Simul autem repetit & interspergit argumen- tum à Dei exemplo ductum: Sicut & ille justus est. Ita enim non similitudo justitiæ Christi cum no- stra, quod ita justi simus, sicut Christus, insinuatur, sed ratio repetitur, cur justitiam facere debeamus, quia nempe Christus justus est. Conjungit autem B. Hunnius in LL. CC. utramque justitiam: Quam- vis, inquiens, ea justitia, qua coram tribunali Dei su- mus justi, per Christum extra nos acquisita est: tamen quamprimum apprehenditur fide, confestim impu- tata hæc justitia excitat in hominis animo inchoatæ justitiæ sanctitatisque habitum, & ad bona justaque opera hominem impellit. Verùm hic magna diver- sitas se offert inter justitiæ habitum moralem, qui as- sidua exercitatione acquiritur, & ex præcedentibus actionibus hominum industria comparatur: & inter Theologicum illum habitum inchoatæ justitiæ & san- ctitatis, qui non humanæ paratur industria, nec ex præeuntibus actionibus hominis acquiritur, sed poti- us in conversione, regeneratione & justificatione ho- minis donatur & infunditur à Dei Spiritu, atque sic ad sanctas DeoƧ placentes actiones producendas est efficax. Sic opera justitiæ non præcedunt suum ha- bitum, sed ex eodem cœlitus infuso consequuntur, quemadmodum Divus Augustinus de bonis operibus differens ait: Opera sequuntur justificatum, non præ- cedunt justificandum.

In spongiam ergo incumbit argumentum Estii, qui notat ex hoc loco destrui justitiæ imputationem, quæ constituitur in sola peccatorum remissione. Christus enim, inquit, qui perfectissime justus est, quis factus est nobis à DEO justitia & sanctificatio, & redemptio, 1. Cor. I. sola mentis rectitudine justus est, non etiam peccatorum remissione, quæ nulla habe- re potuit. Quid enim hinc aliud colligitur, quam quod nos ex confessione ipsius Estii tali modo ju- sti non simus, quemadmodum Christus justus est. Nos enim indigemus remissione peccatorum, Christus non indiget: nos ceu peccatores justificari oportet, Christo non convenit justificatio.

## 3:8
ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐκ τοῦ Διαβόλου ἐστὶ. i.e., he resembles the devil in character. See regarding this type of speaking what we said on John 8, 44 and 47. Thus also below 12, 'he was of the wicked one.' He means this: See how foul it is to imitate such a one.

To be of the devil is not only to resemble the devil in character, but to have and draw his wicked desires, actions, plans and works, morals, and habit of sinning from the devil's inspiration, direction, instinct, and impulse and cooperation, so that they can be considered his children and a brood of hellish vipers, Matthew III, 7. Regarding which Estius directly says: Christ is the Author to men of exercising righteousness, the devil is the author of sin, so that consequently some have Christ as their Prince, others the devil. Furthermore, Christ is the Author of righteousness to us, both because He merited righteousness for us before God the Father by His passion, and because He handed down to us both examples and precepts of righteousness: but the devil is the author of sin to men, since he both sinned first, and first suggested and persuaded man to sin, and never ceases to excite and impel miserable men to all kinds of sins. Therefore, everyone who does iniquity is of the devil, as from him who is the author and parent of sin. Whence the Lord to the Jews in John VIII says: 'You do the works of your Father.' And again: 'You are of your father the devil, and you want to fulfill the desires of your father.' Wherefore those who do sin are of the devil, not only by imitation (for it is for few to want to imitate the devil in that which they sin) but insofar as they sin and by the very fact that they sin, by consenting to his suggestions and temptations. For that is what the reason for the Lord's saying, indicated by the words, signifies: 'And you want to fulfill the desires of your Father.'

Although indeed we are incited to sins even by our own concupiscence, James 1:14, it remains, however, that the devil is the author of sin, from whom also that very depraved concupiscence itself is derived, brought in by the infernal serpent on account of the seduction of our first parents. By this antithesis, therefore, the children of God and the children of the devil, the reborn are warned not to indulge in sins against their conscience, and not to degenerate into children of the devil when they are children of God. The argument, says the blessed Hunnius, is taken from the efficient cause of sin. No one easily desires to have the devil as the author of their actions. But truly, he who commits sin is of the devil, and sins by his impulse. Therefore, one must be more on guard against sin, the more shameful its author is, and the more he is opposed and hostile to God. He who commits sin, says Cornelius, is of the devil, that is, of the devil's kingdom, family, and lineage, and follows and imitates him, as a son does a father: but not as if he were begotten from the transmission of the devil, as the Manichaeans dream. Cf. Ezekiel 16:3.

Ὅτι ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς ὁ Διάβολος ἁμαρτάνει.] That is, from the time he once sinned, he does not cease to sin. Such is that expression in John 15:27, ὅτι ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς μετ᾿ ἐμοῦ ἐστε. It is proper and perpetual to the devil to do evil.

This, therefore, is to be understood concerning the beginning not of the creation, but of the defection of the devil. For in the beginning of creation, God saw his works, and behold, they were very good, which, as it is said of corporeal creatures, Genesis 1:31, so it must also be believed concerning the devil. See Vol. IV of the System of Theology. As he was the first to sin, so he was the author of sinning for the others who sinned, and therefore all who sin are of the devil. The first origin of sin is from the devil, who from that very first beginning, not indeed of his creation (for he was created good) but of his defection, sins: not only because his entire nature is horribly contaminated, but also because he brings forth actual sins with indefatigable zeal: while not only does he himself sin against God and His will by a certain eternal purpose, but also drives to sins, incites and instigates men, as this blessed Hunnius holds. From the beginning the devil sins according to Bede, because from the time he began to sin in the beginning he never ceased, corrected neither by the enormity of present punishments, nor by the fear of future ones. Whence he is said to be of that law, who neglects to recall himself from sinning.

For this the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the Devil.] Take 'was manifested' again, as above v. 5. It is a new argument. It does not befit Christians to do those things which Christ came to destroy. But sin is the work of the devil, who not only sins, but also instigates others to sin. That Christ came, however, to take away the empire from the Devil, and consequently to destroy his works, is evident from his own words Matt. 12, 29. Luc. 10, 18. Joh. 12, 31. c. 16, 11. Λύειν to destroy, John 2, 19. 2 Pet. 3. verses 10. 11. 12.

We admit that a new argument of dehortation from sin is brought forward: namely, that we should not allow ourselves to be seduced, not so much by heretics, although we do not deny that their foul dogmas, which James c. 1 also noted, are noted here, as by our own desires and diabolical suggestions. But the Apostle pursues a more didactic genre here, showing the marks of the children of God by the antithesis of the children of the devil, so that he may execute that most eminent end of the incarnation of the Son of God, that he deigned to make us children of God, to which he wished to subordinate both the bearing of our sins above v. 5 and the destruction of the works of the devil. Cornelius says, he confirms that which he said, i.e., he who sins is so much from the devil, not from God, that Christ wished to assume flesh and appear in it to abolish sin as his enemy. The Son of God came, however, not only to destroy sin, which is the proper work of the devil, not as the creator, but as the destroyer of the Divine creature, not positive, such as the creatures of God are, but privative; but also to take away those things which followed sin, such as death and condemnation, diseases and miseries: finally corruption and corruptibility, the evils of body and soul, which are from sin. Λύειν properly is to dissolve. Then also to destroy: because destruction follows from dissolution. Here he designates total abolition, which is not indeed to be expected in this age, but in the other as to its effect at the appearance for judgment, where death the last enemy shall be destroyed, 1 Cor. XV, 26, which as to merit he obtained and procured in the appearance of the Son of God in the flesh by his passion and merit. To the word 'dissolve' Cornelius notes: Sins are like ropes, which the devil weaves, like a spider catching flies, so that he may entangle, perplex, and ensnare the sinner with them, so that he cannot extricate himself from them, which therefore Christ came to dissolve, so that he might extricate and rescue the sinner from them. This is what the Wise Man says Prov. V, 22. His own iniquities catch the wicked, and he is bound with the ropes of his sins, and Isaiah Chap. V, 18. Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as if with a cart rope. Hence Christ gave to Peter and the Apostles the power of loosing Matt. XVI, 19. and Joh. XX, 23.

Estius indeed objects that death is not the work of the devil, because it had a place in Christ, nor is it sin, but the punishment of sin, having God as its Author. But the death of Christ was voluntary, holy, deletory and destructive of sin and death: but the death of man introduced through sin, Rom. V, 12, is necessary, of itself neither holy, nor salutary, but by the virtue of the merit of Christ, since of itself it is only the destruction of nature, which in itself had nothing destructive, Wis. I, 14, and was introduced by the envy of the devil, Wis. II, 21. That, insofar as it is from the devil and is the ruin of man, had to be dissolved and destroyed by Christ, and for its sake the Son of God appeared, even if that effect does not follow in most people due to the fault of men. Strictly and properly speaking, however, sins are the works of the devil; those which have arisen from sin are called works of the devil only consequently and less properly. Among the works of the devil, says blessed Hunnius, sin certainly claims for itself not the last place, of which he himself is the Author and Father, which then draws with itself in a long series that infinite lerna of all evils: namely, innumerable temporal punishments, and finally perpetual damnation. Therefore, he who devotes effort to sins, as much as is in him, enervates and evacuates for himself the virtue of the incarnation of the Son of God. The Proto-Evangelium concerning the crushing of the serpent's head, Gen. III, 15, makes for this, concerning which see the commentary on Genesis.

Latin:

ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐκ τοῦ Διαβόλου ἐστὶ.] i. e. indole dia- bolum refert. Vid. de hoc loquendi genere, quæ diximus ad Joh. 8, 44. & 47. Sic & infra 12. ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ ἦν. Hoc vult: Videte, quam foedum sit, talem imitari.

Ex diabolo esse, non est tantum indole diabolum referre, sed pravas suas cupiditates, actiones, insti- tuta & opera, mores, & consuetudinem peccandi, à diaboli inspiratione, directione, instinctu, & im- pulsu ac cooperatione habere, ac trahere, ut filii ejus & semen viperarum infernalium censeri pos- sint, Matth. III, 7. Quo derecte Estius: Christus ho- minibus Autor est exercendæ justitiæ, diabolus autor peccati, ut proinde alii Christum Principem habeant, alii diabolum. Porro Christus justitiæ nobis Autor est, tum quia à Deo Patre nobis justiciam passione sua promeruit, tum quia nobis justitiæ exempla simul & præcepta tradidit: Diabolus vero peccati autor est hominibus, quoniam & primus peccavit, & pri- mus homini peccatum suggessit atque suasit, & ad omnia peccatorum genera miseros homines excitare atque impellere nunquam desistit. Igitur ex diabo- lo est omnis, qui facit iniquitatem, tanquam ex eo, qui peccati sit autor & parens. Unde Dominus ad Judæos Joh. VIII. Vos, inquit, facitis opera Patris vestri: Et iterum: Vos ex patre diabolo estis, & de- sideria patris vestri vultis perficere. Quocirca qui peccatum faciunt, ex diabolo sunt, non solum imita- tione (nam paucorum est, imitari velle diabolum in eo quod peccant) sed quatenus peccant & eo ipso quo peccant, suggestionibus illius & tentationibus consentiendo. Id enim significat ratio dicti Domini verbis indicata: Et desideria Patris vestri vultis per- ficere.

Quanquam vero ad peccata per propriam etiam concupiscentiam incitemur, Jac. I, 14. manet ta- men, diabolum peccati Autorem esse, à quo est et- iam ipsa prava concupiscentia propter seductio- nem primorum parentum, à serpente infernali in- vecta. Ista ergo ἀντιθέσει filiorum Dei, & filiorum diaboli commonefiunt renati, ne peccatis contra conscientiam indulgeant, & in filios diaboli, quum filii Dei sint, degenerent. Argumentum, inquit B. Hunnius, à causa efficiente peccati sumptum. Nemo cupit facile actionum suarum autorem habere dia- bolum. At vero qui committit peccatum, ex diabo- lo est, & ipsius impulsu peccat. Ergo à peccato magis cavendum fuerit, quo turpior ejus autor, & quo ma- gis is Deo adversus & inimicus est. Qui facit pecca- tum, inquit Cornelius, ex diabolo est, id est, ex diabo- li regno, familia & prosapia, eumque sequitur & imi- tatur, ceu filius patrem: non autem quasi ex traduce diaboli genitus sit, ut somniavunt Manichæi. Conf. Ezech. XVI, 3.

Ὅτι ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς ὁ Διάβολος ἁμαρτάνει.] Id est, ex quo semel peccavit, peccare non desinit. Talis loquutio illa Joh. XV, 27. ὅτι ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς μετ᾿ ἐμοῦ ἐστε. Est diabolo hoc proprium ut- que perpetuum male agere.

Hoc ergo de initio non creationis, sed defectionis diaboli intelligendum. In creationis enim initio vidit Deus opera sua, & ecce erant valde bona, quod uti de creaturis corporeis dicitur, Gen. I, 31. ita etiam de diabolo credendum est. Vid. Tom. IV. System. Theol. Ut ille primus peccavit: ita cæteris qui peccarunt, autor peccandi fuit, ideoq; omnes, qui peccant, ex diabolo sunt. Primum peccati exor- dium est à diabolo, qui jam inde à primo initio non quidem creationis suæ (conditus enim est bonus) sed defectionis peccat: non tantum quod universa na- tura ipsius horribiliter contaminata est, verum et- iam quod studio indefesso peccata profert actualia: dum non ipse solum contra Deum & ipsius volunta- tem æterno quodam proposito peccat, verum etiam ad peccata propellit, incitat & instigat homines, ut hic B. Hunnius habet. Ab initio diabolus peccat se- cundum Bedam, quia ex quo ab initio cœpit diabolus peccare nunquam desiit, nec præsentium scilicet pœ- narum enormitate, nec futurarum metu correctus. Unde ex illo jure esse dicitur, qui à peccando se revo- care negligit.

Eis τοῦτο ἐφανερώθη ὁ ἡὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἵνα λύσῃ τὰ ἔργα τοῦ Δια- βόλου.] Ἐφανερώθη rursum sume, ut supra 5. Novum est argu- mentum. Non decet Christianos ea facere, quæ Christus de- structum venit. At peccatum diaboli est opus, qui non peccat tantum, sed & alios ad peccandum instigat. Venisse autem Christum, ut Diabolo auferret imperium, ac proinde opera ejus destrueret, ex ipsius dictis constat Matth. 12, 29. Luc. 10, 18. Joh. 12, 31. c. 16, 11. Λύειν destruere, Johan. 2, 19. 2 Petr. 3. vers. 10. 11. 12.

Novum argumentum dehortationis à peccato adduci admittimus: ne scilicet nos seduci patia- mur, non tam ab hæreticis, etsi eorum fœda do- gmata, quæ Jacobus c. 1. etiam notavit, hic notari non diffiteamur, quam à propriis cupiditatibus & diabolicis suggestionibus. Sed magis didascalicum ge- nus hic prosequitur adhuc Apostolus, monstrans γνωρίσματα filiorum Dei ex ἀντιθέσει filiorum dia- boli, ut finem illum eminentissimum incarnationis Filii Dei exequatur, quod nos filios Dei facere di- gnatus est, cujus gratia & peccatorum nostrorum portationem supra v. 5. & operum diaboli destru- ctionem jam illi subordinare voluit. Confirmat, in- quit Cornelius, id, quod dixit, q. d. adeo qui peccat, est ex diabolo, non ex Deo, ut ad peccatum quasi ho- stem suum abolendum Christus carnem assumere, in eaque apparere voluerit. Venit autem Filius DEI non tantum ut peccatum, quod proprium est opus diaboli, destrueret, non ceu creatoris, sed destructo- ris creaturæ Divinæ, non positivum, quales sunt creaturæ Dei, sed privativum; sed etiam, ut ea, quæ consequuta sunt peccatum, utpote mortem & con- demnationem, morbos & miserias tolleret: corru- ptionem denique & corruptibilitatem, mala corporis & animæ, quæ sunt à peccato. Λύειν proprie est dif- solvere. Deinde etiam destruere: quia destructio se- quitur ex dissolutione. Hic totalem abolitionem, quæ non quidem in hoc seculo, in altero tamen ex- pectanda quantum ad effectum in apparitione ad judicium, ubi mors hostis novissimus destruetur, 1. Cor. XV, 26. designat, quam quoad meritum in ap- paritione Filii Dei in carne passione ac merito suo obtinuit & impetravit. Ad vocem dissolvit notat Cornelius: Peccata sunt quasi funes, quos plectit dia- bolus, instar aranei captantis muscas, ut iis implicet, intricet & irretiet peccatorem, ne iis se extricare pos- sit, quos proinde Christus venit dissolvere, ut iis pec- catorem extricet & eripiat. Hoc est, quod ait Sapiens Prov. V, 22. Iniquitates suæ capiunt impium, & fu- nibus peccatorum suorum constringitur, & Esaias Cap. V, 18. Væ qui trahitis iniquitatem in funiculis vanitatis, & quasi vinculum plaustri peccatum. Hinc Christus dedit Petro & Apostolis potestatem solvendi Matth. XVI, 19. & Joh. XX, 23.

Objicit quidem Estius, mortem non esse opus dia- boli, quia in Christo locum habuit, nec peccatum est, sed pœna peccati, Deum habens Autorem. Sed mors Christi voluntaria fuit, sancta, deletoria & destru- ctoria peccati & mortis: mors autem hominis inve- cta per peccatum, Rom. V, 12. necessaria est, per se neg; sancta, neg; salutaris, sed virtute meriti Christi, quum per se tantum sit destructio naturæ, quæ xa['] αὑτὸ nihil exitiosi in se habuit, Sap. I, 14. & invidia diaboli introducta Sap. II, 21. Ea, quatenus à dia- bolo est & pernicies hominis, dissolvenda fuit à Christo atque destruenda, ejusque causa Filius Dei apparuit, etsi effectus ille culpa hominum in ple- risque non sequatur. Κυριολέκτως tamen & proprie loquendo peccata sunt opera diaboli, quæ ex pec- cato enata sunt, consequenter tantum, & minus proprie diaboli opera dicuntur. Inter opera dia- boli, inquit B. Hunnius, non postremum certe locum sibi vendicat peccatum, cujus ipse Autor & Pater est, quod deinde secum longa serie trahit infinitam il- lam malorum omnium lernam: pœnas scilicet tem- porales innumeras, ac denique perpetuam damna- tionem. Proinde qui peccatis dat operam, is quan- tum in se est, enervat & evacuat sibi incarnationis Filii Dei virtutem. Facit huc Prot-Evangelium de contritione capitis serpentini, Gen. III, 15. de quo vid. comment. ad Genesin.

## 3:9
Vers. 9.

For everyone who has been born of God does not commit sin.] That is, he does not sin. For these are the same to this Apostle. That 'having been born' signifies here an act not passing, but permanent. For he who has once been a son of God can sin gravely. Tertullian in his book on modesty, having enumerated those kinds of sins of which we just spoke: He who has been born of God will not admit these, not being about to be a son of God if he should admit them. Therefore, this is that past tense for a verbal, as if he had said 'born' (יליד), Job 14, 1. c. 15, 4. or 'child' as below 10. He said before that we are called children of God because of a nature similar to the Divine. But such a one who will be, that is, while he will retain that nature, will not sin in the way in which it is posited here to sin. Augustine in sermon XXIX on the words of the Apostle, when he had said that he destroys homicides and adulteries with one blow, adds: Such a one does not do the good works of faith and Christian hope, but only those which are wiped away by the daily danger of prayer. The same to Psalm LI. Sin reigns if you have consented. Didymus on this place: It must be said that to commit sin is the same as to sin, when place is given to the devil. Jerome, the disciple of Didymus, in book 1 against Pelagius: He therefore who is born of God does not sin, as long as the seed of GOD remains in him, that is, vivid. And on Matth. VII. A good tree does not bear bad fruits, as long as it perseveres in the study of goodness.

For his seed abides in him.] The seed of God is the word of the Gospel, Matt. 13:19, Mark 4:14, 1 Pet. 1:23, Jas. 1:18. To abide here means to be present, as we said above. Thus in John 14:17 we have 'it abides and shall be in you,' where 'abides' designates the present tense, 'shall be' the future. Understand it to be present effectively, in such a way that it is neither dried up nor choked, but retains its nature and efficacy. Thus, for Aristotle, an eye that does not see is not an eye.

And he cannot sin, because he has been born of God.] That is, he is born, Augustine, On the Grace of Christ, Book I, ch. 21. According to that charity, the saying is better understood: 'He who is born of God does not sin,' and 'because he cannot,' because charity, according to which he is born of God, does not act perversely, does not think evil. Moreover, that 'cannot' is said here morally. For acts are accustomed to be similar to qualities. Ignatius: 'The carnal cannot do spiritual things.' Menander: 'No one who is good does a wicked thing.' Philo, On Nobility: 'It is not easy to exchange wicked characters for good ones.' Seneca, VI, On Benefits: 'A good man cannot but do what he does.'

Regarding this verse, toward the end of the annotations on the Gospels, Grotius has it thus:

Verse 9. Everyone who has been born of God.] Whoever puts on the character of the Divine nature, similar according to human measure. For those who are similar to someone are said by the Hebrews to be born of them or to be their children, John 8:39: 'If you were Abraham's children, you would do the works of Abraham'; ibid. v. 42: 'If God were your Father, you would love me'; v. 44: 'You are of your father the devil, and you want to do the desires of your father; he was a murderer from the beginning,' and what follows; 47: 'He who is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God.'

He does not commit sin.] Throughout this epistle, John uses 'to commit sin' and 'to sin' for the same thing, to which is opposed above in verse 7 'to do righteousness.' Some wrongly translate it as 'to devote effort to sin,' and from there infer that for one to be considered a child of God, the study and endeavor of living rightly is sufficient, even if those very things are not fulfilled in deeds, with the habit of sinning prevailing—a very pernicious notion. John is clearly dealing here with a twofold kind of life, the one consistent with the precepts of GOD, the other fighting against them. There are indeed some acts such that they exclude a man from the right to the heavenly kingdom, namely those which are committed neither through ignorance nor through surprise against the precepts of God. For the reason for rewards is one thing, the reason for punishment another. Rewards are not given except to those whom the whole tenor of life commends. For punishment, one crime is often sufficient, James 2:10-11. But here the Apostle wished to describe to us, as it were, two ways, which in the epistle of Barnabas are called the way of light and the way of darkness, namely that the distinction might appear more openly, he set opposites against each other. Which both Pythagoras and Prodicus of Ceos did.

Ὅτι σπέρμα αὐτῦ ἐν αὐτῷ μένει, because his seed abides in him.] Because the Word of God, which is as it were a seed, by which the Divine nature is begotten in us, exists alive in him. The Word of the Gospel is called seed everywhere. Mark 4:14, Matthew 13:19, 1 Peter 1:23. By this word we are begotten again, James 1:18. Μένειν here does not mean to endure, but to be present, John 14:17, παρ’ ὑμῖν μένει, καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν ἔσαι. The Spirit of truth is with you now, and will be hereafter, namely if you preserve him as is fitting; so above in chapter 2:5-6, εἶναι and μένειν in GOD are taken as signifying the same thing. Nor is this word used otherwise in the Gospel of John chapter 3:36 and this epistle chapter 3:14. In this sense, μένειν is used of the same Word of the Gospel in the Gospel of John chapter 15:7 and this epistle chapter 2:14 and 24. But such is the argument: It is impossible that he who is a Son of God should not have in him the Word, which is the Divine seed. But the power of that word is such that it keeps us from sins by commanding, forbidding, promising, and threatening; therefore we are said to be sanctified by the word, John's Gospel c. 17:17.

Καὶ ὐ δύναται ἁμαρτάνειν, and he cannot sin.] Οὐ δύναται here signifies that the matter in question is foreign to such a character. There is the same or a similar use of this expression in 2 Cor. 13:8, Acts 4:20, Jeremiah 13:23, Matthew 7:11, c. 12:34, c. 13:34, John 8:43-44, c. 14:17. Nor does Seneca speak otherwise when he says: A good man cannot but do what he does. Menander had said: Οὐδεὶς πονηρὸν πρᾶγμα χρηστὸς ὢν ποιεῖ: No one who is a good man will do an evil thing. Moreover, ἁμαρτάνειν, to sin, in this place signifies the same as ἁμαρτίαν ποιεῖν, to commit sin, above; it appears from the preceding verse, where it is said that ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, he who commits sin, is of the devil, because the devil ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἁμαρτάνει, sins from the beginning, that is, ἁμαρτίαν ποιεῖ, commits sin.

Ὅτι ἐκ Θεῦ γεγέννηται, because he is born of GOD.] The reason why the pursuit of sinning is foreign to the character of such a man is sought here from the name of the subject: as if he were saying: It is no wonder that he is averse to forbidden things, since he is, and remembers himself to be, a son of God, and therefore has GOD to imitate. From this, however, it does not follow that he cannot cease to be a Son of God. Tertullian, in his work on modesty, having enumerated the more serious crimes: He who has been born of GOD will not admit these at all, not being about to be a son of God if he should admit them. Thus a good tree cannot bring forth bad fruit, Matthew chapter 7:18, but it can become sterile, rotten, and finally vicious, and when it has become such, it can be cut down. It cannot bring forth bad fruit, says Jerome on that passage of Matthew, as long as it perseveres in the pursuit of goodness. And conversely, a bad tree can become good. Tertullian on the soul: A bad tree will not give good fruit if it is not grafted, and a good one will give bad fruit if it is not cultivated, and stones will become children of Abraham if they are formed into the faith of Abraham, and the offspring of vipers will do the fruit of repentance if they have spat out the poisons of wickedness. This will be the power of Divine grace, more potent than nature, having within us the power of choice subject to itself, which is called αὐτεξύσιον, which, since it is itself both natural and mutable, is turned in whatever direction nature is turned. Chrysostom on chapter 8 to the Romans: Ὥσπερ ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ φησιν, ὐ δύναται δένδρον σαπρὸν καρπὺς καλὺς ποιεῖν, not forbidding the change from vice to virtue, but the lingering in vice, saying that it cannot bear good fruit. Οὐ γὰρ εἶπεν ὐ δύναται δένδρον πονηρὸν καλὸν γένεσθαι, ἀλλ’ ὅτι φέρειν καρπὺς καλὺς ὐ δύναται μένον πο- νηρὸν, as it is said in the Gospel, a bad tree cannot bring forth good fruit, not impeding the change from vice to virtue, but denying that good fruits come forth from remaining in vice. For he did not say, a bad tree cannot become good, but he means this, that while it remains bad it cannot bring forth good fruit. M. Antonius the Emperor: Ὁ μὴ θέλων τὸν φαῦλον ἁμαρτάνειν, ὅμοιός τῷ μὴ θέλοντι συκῆν ὀπὸν ἐν τοῖς σύκοις φέρειν; he who wishes a bad man not to sin does the same as if he wished a fig tree not to have the juice of its kind in its figs.

PARAPHRASE.

You who have professed Christ wish to be called sons of God, and therefore heirs. But you must think again and again what kind of people those ought to be who are to be sons of God not in name only, but in reality. These certainly do not show obedience to the flesh, do not conform themselves to the examples of the world, are not carried outside the orbit of the Divine law wherever they please: for they keep in memory the word of the Gospel once heard and perceived in the heart, which not only commands obedience to the Divine commandments, but also elicits obedience by eternal promises, and deters from disobedience by the most grave threats: wherefore, mindful of that word, they restrain themselves from a wicked life, and indeed are averse in spirit from wickedness, and seriously hate it, as those who think that God is their Father, and therefore propose his goodness to themselves as a model, so that they may fulfill the measure of their name.

Some understand the seed of God as the Holy Spirit regenerating us, or the grace of the Holy Spirit: Others, with Oecumenius, as the Son of God; some explain it as the charity of God, most as the Word of God, along with Clement of Alexandria, Augustine, Bede, Hugh, the gloss, by which as an incorruptible seed we are reborn, Luke 8:11, 1 Peter 1:23, James 1:18. Not inconveniently, however, some interpret it as spiritual birth, which, insofar as it remains in the children of God, they do not sin, which Estius supports: But that explanation concerning the Word of God is simpler, since regeneration or birth from God, and the seed from which we are regenerated, are distinguished. These things do not treat of the perseverance of the saints, as the Calvinists wish, but of the efficacy of the Word, drawing us back from sin, if it is cherished with a faithful heart: nor is grace permanently inherent in the soul gathered from this, which Estius contends. For the seed of God is nowhere a certain habitual grace infused into us and permanently inherent: which is precariously assumed by Estius.

That 'he cannot sin' does not mean 'he ought not,' as Augustine in his book On Nature and Grace, ch. 14, and Orosius in his Apology; nor is it 'he does not wish to by habitual will,' as Oecumenius; nor, as others say, 'he cannot sin insofar as he is from God, or in the part in which he is reborn'—for thus he cannot even sin venially, which is not intended here; nor finally 'he cannot' because, being elected by God, he cannot fail on account of the absolute and inamissible grace of God, as the Calvinists contend; or 'he cannot sin in such a way that that seed by which he is regenerated does not always remain in him,' which they wish to be perpetually present, even if it is sometimes suppressed for a time so that it does not exert its power, like a live coal buried under ashes. Which sense was formerly condemned in Jovinian, and by the Augsburg Confession, whose associates the Calvinists also wish to be, article XII, in the Anabaptists; and in the Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession, it was refuted by most clear sayings and examples. What, then, is the genuine sense at last? Jerome explains it in book II against Jovinian. 'He cannot sin' as long as he remains a son, or as if the 'that' (ὅτι) were 'insofar as,' or 'as long as' he is born of God, or as before, 'that' (ὅτι) as 'insofar as' and 'as long as' the seed of God remains in him. For the Apostle indicates this very thing, that these two cannot stand together: to sin and to be a Son of God. For St. John is intent on explaining the distinction between the children of God and the devil. As the children of the devil, by the very fact that they are from the devil, sin: so the children of God, because they are from God, do not sin, and if they do sin, they cease to be children of God. Cornelius à Lapide, having brought forward six interpretations, says that those two seem most genuine: that he cannot sin gravely and mortally in a non-divided but composite sense, namely insofar as he is born of God, and as long as he preserves this birth and the seed of the grace of God by which he is reborn, and follows its guidance: He attributes this to Oecumenius, Thomas Anglicus, and Cajetan with Jerome. Then in the formal sense, as far as it pertains to the side of the Divine birth, if indeed you look at the power of birth and of Divine grace, for if this is allowed to act and work, and free will does not resist it, it is powerful and effective so as to exclude every sin, nor can sin consist with it. Thus St. Augustine on the grace of Christ, chapter XXI. John wishes to teach, says the blessed Hunnius, that rebirth and the purpose of sinning are so opposed that they necessarily remove and destroy each other and can by no means consist in the same man at the same time. Therefore, he who is born of God, insofar as he is reborn, and as long as he remains reborn, certainly does not commit sin: that is, sin against conscience, and proceeding from a deliberate purpose and counsel of the mind. Indeed, he cannot sin in the way already explained, so as to sin at the same time and nevertheless remain reborn. But rather, as soon as he sins knowingly and willingly by design, he immediately ceases to be reborn, that is, he loses that gift of rebirth, faith, and the grace of God, the seed of the word being suffocated and the Holy Spirit being shaken off. For it is evident from the XVIII chapter of Ezekiel, 1 Cor. IX, Rom. XI, and many other places that the reborn can fall away again from the grace of God through mortal or reigning sins. Nor is the seed said to remain in the reborn, which Perkins wishes in Tom. I. oper. de praedest. & grat. Dei p. 151, as if it always remains, nor is it an incorruptible seed by reason of the subject, which cannot vanish or be suffocated in him in whom it is; but as to its own nature it is ἄφθαρτον, indeed eternal, Luke XXI. 33, which cannot be corrupted in itself and by itself, whether it remains in him in whom it is, or does not remain: which by its own life-giving power, if not driven out by the man into whom it fell, is able to render the same man incorruptible and blessed, James I. 18.

They sin, however, against Calvinist logic when they form an absolute conclusion from a conditional antecedent in this way: The reborn, insofar as the seed of God remains in them, are born of God and do not sin. Therefore, they cannot lose faith, when they ought to conclude: Therefore, insofar as they are such, they cannot lose faith. Furthermore, that it is possible for many to cast away the Divine seed once received of their own accord, the parable teaches, Matt. XIII. 20, 21. How rashly also the fanatics deduce the ἀναμαρτησίαν of the reborn from this passage, the blessed Gerhard taught at length in disp. I. contr. fanat. th. 58. seqq., whose contrary arguments the blessed Walther reduced to a compendium in harm. adh. l. The Apostle wishes to show the distinction between the reborn and the not reborn, between the children of God and the children of the Devil, v. 10. Now, however, the children of God and of the Devil are not distinguished by this, that sin still dwells in the flesh, but that in the former sin is mortified, but in the latter it reigns and dominates. He who does righteousness is righteous, verse 7; he who does not do righteousness is not of God, v. 10. To do righteousness is to be diligent in holy works; not to do righteousness is to proceed securely in sins. That the righteousness which the reborn do is not in this life absolute in all respects, Scripture testifies everywhere. Finally, that it is not about just any sins, but about more serious ones, the subjoined species of homicide, v. 12, of hatred, v. 15, of lack of mercy, sufficiently teach, Conf. cap. V. v. 18. John designates the sin of those in verse 17 who do not have communion or fellowship with God, and teaches that he who is born of God cannot commit that. But those belong to this, who walk in darkness, John I. 8, maliciously transgress the commandments of God, cap. 4, have a stumbling block in themselves, and scandalize others, verse 10. Conf. B. Dn. D. König vindic. sacr. Loc. LXXVI.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Πᾶς γὰρ ὁ γεγεννημένος ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἁμαρτίαν ὀυ ποιεῖ.] Id est ὀυχ ἁμαρτάνει. Hæc enim huic Apostolo idem sunt. Illud autem γεγεννημένος significat hic actum non transeuntem, sed permanentem. Peccare enim graviter potest, qui ali- quando filius Dei fuerit. Tertullianus libro de pudicitia enumeratis illis, de quibus modo egimus, peccatorum gene- ribus: Hæc non admittet, qui natus e Deo fuerit, non futurus Dei filius si admiserit. Est ergo hic præteritum illud pro ver- bali, quasi dixisset γεννητὸς יליד, Job. 14, 1. c. 15, 4. aut τέ- κνον ut infra 10. Dixit ante dici nos Dei filios ob indolem Divinæ similem. Talis autem qui erit, id est, dum eam indo- lem retinebit, non peccabit eo modo, quo hic peccare poni- tur. Augustinus sermone XXIX. de verbis Apostoli, cum di- xiffet homicidia & adulteria uno ictu perimere, addit: Talis non facit bona fidei & spei Christianas, sed illa sola, quæ quo- tidiano orationis periculo tergunrur. Idem ad Psalmum LI. Regnat peccatum si consenseris. Didymus ad hunc locum: Dicendum est idem esse facere peccatum quod peccare, cum diabolo datur locus. Discipulus Didymi Hieronymus libro 1. adversus Pelagium: Qui ergo natus est ex Deo, non peccat, quamdiu semen DEI manet in eo, vividum scilicet. Et ad Matth. VII. Bona arbor non fert malos fructus, quamdiu in bonitatis studio perseverat.

Ὅτι σπέρμα ἀυτοῦ ἐν ἀυτῷ μένει.] Semen Dei est verbum Evangelii, Matth. 13, 19. Marc. IV, 14. 1. Petr. I, 23. Jac. I, 18. Μένειν hic est inesse, ut supra diximus. Itaque Joh. 14, 17. habemus μένει καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν ἔσται, ubi illud μένει præsens tempus designat, ἔσται futurum. Inesse autem intellige ἐνεργῶς, ita, ut nec arefactum sit, nec suffocatum, sed naturam effi- cientiamque retineat. Sic Aristoteli oculus, qui non videt, non est oculus.

Καὶ ὀυ δύναται ἁμαρτάνειν, ὅτι ἐκ Θεοῦ γεγέννηται.] Id est γεννητός ἐστιν, Augustinus de gratia Christi libro I. c. 21. Se- cundum istam charitatem melius intelligitur dictum, qui natus est ex Deo, non peccat, & quia non potest, quia charitas, secun- dum quam natus est ex Deo, non agit perperam, non cogitat ma- lum. Est autem illud δύναται hic dictum moraliter. Solent enim actus similes esse qualitatibus. Ignatius: Οἱ σαρκικοὶ τὰ πνευματικὰ πράττειν ὀυ δύνανται. Menander: Οὐδεὶς πονηρὸν πρᾶγμα χρηστὸς ὢν ποιεῖ. Philo de nobilitate: Ἤθη ὑπαλλάξαι πονηρὰ χρηστοῖς ὀυ ῥᾴδιον. Seneca VI. de benefi- ciis: Vir bonus non potest non facere, quod facit.

De hoc commate sub finem annot. in Evan- gelia ita habet Grotius:

Vers. 9. Πᾶς ὁ γεγεννημένος ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ, omnis, qui na- tus est ex Deo.] Quisquis indolem induit Divinæ na- turæ pro modo humano similem. Nam qui similes ali- cui sunt, ab Ebræis ab illis nati aut illorum filii dicuntur, Joh. VIII, 39. Si filii Abrahami essetis, opera Abrahamæ faceretis, ibid. v. 42. Si Deus Pater vester esset, amare- tis me, v. 44. vos ex patre diabolo estis, & cupiditates patris vestri facere vultis, ille homicida fuit ab initio, & quæ sequuntur: 47. qui ex DEO est, verba DEI audit, ideo vos non auditis, quia ex DEO non estis.

Ἁμαρτίαν ὀυ ποιεῖ, peccatum non facit.] Passim Jo- hannes in hac epistola pro eodem ponit ἁμαρτίαν ποι- εῖν peccatum facere, & ἁμαρτάνειν peccare, cui opposi- tum est supra comm. 7. δικαιοσύνην ποιεῖν facere justi- tiam male quidam vertunt dare operam peccato, atque inde inferunt, ut quis DEI filius censeatur, sufficere stu- dium & conatum recte vivendi, etiamsi ea ipsa factis non impleantur prævalente peccandi consuetudine, pernitiose admodum. Agit plane hic Johannes de duplici vitæ genere, altero præceptis DEI congruente, altero cum eis pugnante. Sunt quidem & actus non- nulli tales, ut hominem à regni cœlestis jure exclu- dant, nempe qui neque per ignorantiam, neque per fubreptionem contra Dei præcepta admittuntur. Alia enim est ratio honorum alia pœnæ. Honores non dan- tur, nisi his, quos totus vitæ tenor commendat. Ad pœnam sæpe unum crimen sufficit, Jac. II. vers. 10. 11. Sed hic duas veluti vias nobis describere Apostolus vo- luit, quæ in Barnabæ epistolæ vocantur via lucis & via tenebrarum, nempe ut apertius discrimen apparet, ex- tima opposuit. Quod & Pythagoras & Prodicus Ceus fecere.

Ὅτι σπέρμα αὐτῦ ἐν αὐτῷ μένει, quoniam semen ipsi- us in eo manet.] Quia Verbum Dei, quod quasi semen est, quo Divina natura in nobis gignitur, in ipso vege- tum existit. Verbum Evangelii semen dicitur passim. Marc. 4. v. 14. Matth. 13. v. 19. 1. Petr. 1. v. 23. Hoc ver- bo regignimur Jac. I. v. 18. Μένειν hic non est durare, sed inesse Joh. 14. v. 17. παρ’ ὑμῖν μένει, καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν ἔσαι. Spiritus veritatis in vobis & nunc est, & posthac erit, nempe si eum, ut par est, conservetis, ita supra cap. 2. v. 5. 6. in DEO εἶναι & μένειν sumuntur ut idem significan- tia. Neque aliter usurpatur hæc vox in Johannis Ev- angelio cap. 3. vers. 36. & hac epistola cap. 3. vers. 14. Hoc sensu de eodem Evangelii Verbo μένειν usurpatur Johannis Evangelio cap. 15. vers. 7. & hac epistola cap. 2. vers. 14. & 24. Est autem talis argumentatio: Fieri non potest, ut, qui Filius est Dei, in eo non sit Verbum, quod est semen Divinum. At verbi istius vis ea est, ut nos à peccaris arceat jubendo, vetando, pollicendo, com- minando, ideo per verbum sanctificari dicimur Johann. Evang. c. 17. v. 17.

Καὶ ὐ δύναται ἁμαρτάνειν, & non potest peccare.] Οὐ δύναται hic significat rem, de qua agitur, alienam esse ab ejusmodi ingenio. Idem aut similis usus est hujus lo- quutionis 2. Cor. 13. v. 8. Act. 4. v. 20. Jerem. 13. vers. 23. Matth. 7. v. 11. c. 12. v. 34. c. 13. v. 34. Joh. 8. v. 43. 44. c. 14. v. 17. Nec aliter Seneca loquitur, cum ait: Vir bo- nus non potest non facere, quod facit. Menander dixe- rat: Οὐδεὶς πονηρὸν πρᾶγμα χρηστὸς ὢν ποιεῖ: Nemo bo- nus qui vir sit rem faciet malam. Ἁμαρτάνειν peccare autem hoc loco idem significat, quod supra ἁμαρτίαν ποιεῖν peccatum facere, apparet commate præcedente, ubi dicitur ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, qui facit peccatum, esse ex diabolo, quia diabolus ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἁμαρτάνει ab initio peccat, id est, ἁμαρτίαν ποιεῖ peccatum facit.

Ὅτι ἐκ Θεῦ γεγέννηται, quoniam ex DEO natus est.] Ratio, cur peccandi studium alienum sit à talis homi- nis ingenio, hic petitur ex subjecti nomine: quasi di- cat: Non mirum est, eum aversum esse à rebus vetitis, quandoquidem est ac esse se meminit Dei filium, ac pro- inde DEUM sibi imitandum. Hinc vero non sequitur, eum non posse desinere Dei esse Filium. Tertullianus de pudicitia enumeratis criminibus gravioribus: Hæc non admittet omnino, qui natus è DEO fuerit, non fu- turus Dei filius si admiserit. Sic arbor bona non potest proferre fructus malos, Matth. cap. 7. vers. 18. at fieri sterilis, putris, vitiosa denique & ubi talis facta est, ex- scindi potest. Non potest proferre fructus malos, ait ad eum Matthæi locum Hieronymus, quamdiu in boni- tatis studio perseverat. Et contra arbor mala fieri bo- na potest. Tertullianus de anima: Non dabit arbor mala fructus bonos, si non inseratur, & bona malos da- bit, si non colatur, & lapides filii Abrahæ fient, si in fi- demAbrahæ formentur, & genimina viperarum fructum pœnitentiæ facient, si venena indignitatis exspuerint. Hæc erit vis Divinæ gratiæ potentior utique natura, ha- bens in nobis subjacentem sibi arbitrii potestatem, quod αὐτεξύσιον dicitur, quæ cum sit & ipsa naturalis & mu- tabilis, quoquo vertitur natura convertitur. Chry- sostomus in cap. 8. ad Romanos: Ὥσπερ ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγε- λίῳ φησιν, ὐ δύναται δένδρον σαπρὸν καρπὺς καλὺς ποιεῖν, ὐ τὴν ἀπὸ κακίας εἰς ἀρετὴν μεταβολὴν κωλύων, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἐν τῇ κακίᾳ διατριβὴν, λέγων, μὴ δύνασθαι φέρειν καρ- πὺς καλύς. Οὐ γὰρ εἶπεν ὐ δύναται δένδρον πονηρὸν καλὸν γένεσθαι, ἀλλ’ ὅτι φέρειν καρπὺς καλὺς ὐ δύναται μένον πο- νηρὸν, ut in Evangelio dicitur, non potest arbor mala bonos fructus facere, non impediens mutationem a vi- tio in virtutem, sed negans fructus prodire bonos ex per- mansione in vitio. Neque enim dixit, non potest ma- la arbor bona fieri, sed hoc vult, eam dum manet ma- la non posse proferre fructus bonos. M. Antonius Im- perator: Ὁ μὴ θέλων τὸν φαῦλον ἁμαρτάνειν, ὅμοιός τῷ μὴ θέλοντι συκῆν ὀπὸν ἐν τοῖς σύκοις φέρειν; qui hominem ma- lum vult non peccare, idem facit, ac si velit ficum arbo- rem in ficubus suis non habere sui generis succum.

PARAPHRASIS.

Vos Christum professi dici vultis Dei filii, ac proinde hæredes. Verum etiam atque etiam cogitare, quales esse oporteat eos, qui non nomine nudo, sed re ipsa Dei filii sint futuri. Hi certe non carni obsequium præ- stant, non ad mundi exempla se componunt, non extra legis Divinæ orbitam, qua lubet, feruntur: quippe qui memoria retineant auditum semel ac corde perceptum sermonem Evangelii, qui non tantum mandatorum Di- vinorum obedientiam præcipit, sed & æternis promissis elicit obedientiam, & minis gravissimis absterret ab in- obedientia: quare istius sermonis memores continent se à vita improba, quin & animo averso sunt ab improbi- tate, atque eam serio oderunt, ut qui cogitent Deum esse Patrem suum, ac proinde ejus bonitatem pro exemplari sibi proponunt, ut nominis sui mensuram impleant.

Semen Dei nonnulli intelligunt de Spiritu sancto nos regenerante, vel gratia Spiritus sancti: Alii cum Oecumenio de Filio DEI, quidam de charitate Dei, plerique de Verbo Dei explicant, cum Clemen- te Alexandrino, Augustino, Beda, Hugone, glossa, quo tanquam semine incorruptibili renascimur, Luc. IIX, 11. 1. Petr. I, 23. Jac. I, 18. non incommo- de tamen nonnulli de nativitate spirituali interpre- tantur, quæ quatenus manet in filiis Dei, non pec- cant, quibus suffragatur Estius: Sed simplicior est illa de Verbo Dei, explicatio, quum regeneratio vel nativitas ex Deo, & semen, ex quo regenera- mur, distinguantur. Non de sanctorum perseve- rantia, ut volunt Calviniani, sed de efficacia Ver- bi, retrahentis nos à peccato, si id corde fideli fo- veatur, hæc agunt: nec hinc gratia permanenter inhærens animæ colligitur, quod Estius contendit. Nam semen Dei nuspiam est gratia quædam habi- tualis nobis infusa & permanenter inhærens: quod precario assumitur ab Estio.

Illud non potest pec- care, non est, non debet, ut Augustinus l. de nat. & grat. c. 14. & Orosius in Apol. neque est, non vult habituali voluntate, ut Oecumenius, nec ut alii, non potest peccare, quatenus ex Deo est, vel qua parte re- natus est: sic enim ne venialiter quidem peccare potest, quod hic non intenditur: nec denique non potest, quia electus à Deo deficere non potest ob gra- tiam absolutam & inamissibilem Dei, quemadmo- dum Calviniani contendunt: vel non potest pecca- re ita, quin semper in eo maneat semen illud, quo re- generatus est, quod perpetuo inesse volunt, licet in- terdum ad tempus supprimatur, ut vim suam non exerat instar carbonis vivi sub cineribus sepulti. Qui sensus & in Joviano olim, & ab Augustana Confessione cujus socii etiam cupiunt esse Calvini- stæ, artic. XII. in Anabaptistis damnatus; & in Exeg. Aug. Confess. profligatus est, dictis & exem- plis luculentissimis. Quis ergo tandem sensus ge- nuinus est? Illum explicat Hieronymus lib. II. contr. Jovin. Non potest peccare, quamdiu manet filius, vel ut τὸ ὅτι sit quatenus, vel quousque natus est ex Deo, vel ut antea ὅτι quatenus & quousque semen Dei in eo manet. Id enim ipsum indicat Aposto- lus, stare simul hæc duo non posse peccare, & esse Filium Dei. Nam in eo est S. Johannes, ut discri- men filiorum Dei & diaboli exponat. Ut filii diaboli eo ipso, quo ex diabolo sunt, peccant: Ita filii Dei, quia ex Deo sunt, non peccant, & si pec- cent, desinunt ex filii Dei. Cornelius à Lapide ad- ductis sex interpretationibus, duas illas maxime genuinas videri ait, quod non possit peccare graviter & mortaliter in sensu non diviso, sed composito, quatenus scilicet ex Deo natus, & quamdiu nati- vitatem hanc & semen gratiæ Dei, qua renatus est, conservat, ejusque ductum sequitur: Eam tribuit Oecumenio, Thomæ Anglico, & Cajetano cum Hie- ronymo. Deinde in sensu formali, quantum scili- cet est ex parte nativitatis Divinæ, si videlicet vim nativitatis & gratiæ Divinæ spectes, hæc enim si sina- tur agere & operari, nec ei resistat liberum arbitri- um,potens est & efficax, ut excludat omne peccatum, necumeoposfit consistere. Ita S. Augustinus de gra- tia Christi cap. XXI. Docere vult Johannes, inquit B. Hunnius, renascentiam & peccandi propositum sic esse opposita, ut se mutuo ex necessitate tollant & destruant & consistere in eodem homine simul eo- demque tempore minime queant. Proinde qui ex Deo natus est, quatenus is est renatus, & quamdiu renatus permanet, peccatum certe non committit: peccatum scilicet contra conscientiam, & ex delibe- rato animi proposito consilioque profectum. Imo non potest peccare modo jam explicato, ut scilicet simul peccet, ac nihilominus renatus maneat. Quin potius quamprimum ex proposito sciens volensque peccat, confestim renatus esse desinit, hoc est, amittit donum illud renascentiæ, fidem & gratiam Dei, suffocato se- mine verbi, excussoque Spiritu sancto. Posse enim renatos gratia Dei rursus excidere per peccata mor- talia seu regnantia ex XVIII. cap. Ezechielis, 1. Cor. IX. Rom. XI. aliisq́; pluribus locis evidens est. Neq; vero semen dicitur manere in renato, quod Per- kinsus vult Tom. I. oper. de prædest. & grat. Dei p. 151. quasi semper maneat, neque incorruptibile se- men est ratione subjecti, quod evanescere nequeat, vel suffocari in eo, in quo est; sed quoad natu- ram suam ἄφθαρτον est, imo æternum Luc. XXI. 33. quod corrumpi non potest in se ac per se, sive maneat in eo, in quo est, seu non maneat: quod vi sua vivifica non exturbatum ab homine, in quem cecidit, incorruptibilem eundem ac beatum red- dere valeat, Jac. I. 18.

Peccant autem in Logicam Calviniam, quando ex antecedente conditionali formant conclusionem absolutam hoc modo: Renati quatenus semen Dei in illis manet, ex Deo nati sunt, & non peccant. Er- go fidem amittere non possunt, cum concludere de- berent: Ergo quatenus tales fidem amittere non pos- sunt. De cætero fieri posse, ut multi semen Divi- num semel susceptum de suo abjiciant, parabola docet Matth. XIII. 20. 21. Quam temere etiam fanatici ex hoc loco ἀναμαρτησίαν renatorum de- ducant, prolixe docuit B. Gerhardus disp. I. contr. fanat. th. 58. seqq. cujus argumenta contraria in compendium redegit B. Waltherus in harm. adh. l. Apostolus discrimen ostendere vult inter rena- tos & non renatos, inter filios Dei & filios Diabo- li v. 10. Jam vero filii Dei & Diaboli non distin- guuntur per hoc, quod peccatum adhuc in carne habitet, sed quod in illis peccatum sit mortifica- tum, in his vero regnet ac dominetur. Qui facit ju- stitiam, justus est, vers. 7. qui non facit justitiam, non est ex Deo, v. 10. Facere justitiam est sanctis operibus studere, non facere justitiam est in peccatis securo pergere. Justitiam autem illam, quam re- nati faciunt non esse in hac vita omnibus numeris absolutam passim testatur scriptura. Denique non de quibusvis peccatis, sed de gravioribus agi sub- junctæ species homicidii, v. 12. odii, v. 15. immise- ricordiæ satis docent, Conf. cap. V. v. 18. Eorum peccatum designat Johannes vers. 17. qui cum Deo communionem vel societatem non habent, illudque eum, qui ex Deo natus est, committere non posse docet. Pertinent autem illi, qui in te- nebris ambulant, Joh. I. 8. mandata Dei malitiose transgrediuntur, cap. 4. offendiculum in se ha- bent, aliosque scandalizant vers. 10. Conf. B. Dn- D. König vindic. sacr. Loc. LXXVI.

## 3:10
Ἐν τούτῳ φανερά ἐστι τὰ τέκνα τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ τὰ τέκνα τοῦ Διαβόλου. Πᾶς ὁ μὴ ποιῶν δικαιοσύνην οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ὁ μὴ ἀγαπῶν τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὑτοῦ) This means: There is no doubt that it is better to be children of God than of the Devil. So that you may always be the former, I will show you the distinction. They are of God who both do righteousness and love their neighbor, that is, whose works are both good and proceed from a good mind. For he who loves his neighbor for God's sake, he also loves God, as we said Rom. XIII. v. 9; but those who either do not do good works, or do not do them from such a mind, these are children of the Devil. You see also here that it is true what Aristotle said:

Ἐσθλοὶ μὲν γὰρ ἁπλῶς παντοδαπῶς δὲ κακοί. He calls him brother, as also above II. 9, τὸν πλησίον, any man according to the nature of the Evangelical law, although sometimes by the force of the subject matter that word is taken more strictly, so that it includes only Christians.

Latin:

Ἐν τούτῳ φανερά ἐστι τὰ τέκνα τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ τὰ τέκνα τοῦ Διαβόλου. Πᾶς ὁ μὴ ποιῶν δικαιοσύνην οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ, καὶ ὁ μὴ ἀγαπῶν τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὑτοῦ) Hoc vult: Non dubium est, quin malitis esse filii Dei quam Diaboli. Ut ergo illud sitis semper, ostendam vobis discrimen. Ex Deo sunt, qui & justitiam faciunt, & amant proximum, id est, quorum & opera sunt bona, & ex bono proficiscuntur animo. Nam qui proximum diligit Dei causa, is & Deum diligit, ut diximus Rom. XIII. v. 9. qui vero aut non faciunt bona, aut non ex tali animo, isti Diaboli sunt filii. Vides etiam hic verum esse, quod dixit Aristoteles:

Ἐσθλοὶ μὲν γὰρ ἁπλῶς παντοδαπῶς δὲ κακοί. Ἀδελφὸν vocat ut & supra II. 9. τὸν πλησίον hominem quemvis ex natura Evangelicæ legis, quanquam interdum ex vi materiæ vox illa sumitur strictius, ita ut solos comprehendat Christianos.

## 3:11
Vers. 11.

Ὅτι αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ ἀγγελία) See above 1, 5.

Ἣν ἠκούσατε ἀπ' ἀρχῆς) Even under the law, although now the word brother extends more widely, and the meaning of loving is more intense. But it is no wonder that imperfect things prelude perfections. You see, however, that love has always been of the highest value to God,

Ἵνα ἀγαπῶμεν ἀλλήλους) Israelites once loved Israelites, now anyone loves anyone, just as Abraham did even before the law.

The Apostle had taught that the children of God, who have the hope of the beatific vision of God, purify themselves, and that this grace has been given to us in the Son, that we might be children of God. On the other hand, he who commits sin commits injustice, for the sake of removing which the Son of God willed to appear. From this, therefore, he concludes that those who remain in the Son of God do not sin: which he confirmed against the seductions of heretics and of one's own depraved concupiscence, both from the nature of the children of God and the righteous: that they do not study to sin, but work righteousness, since He himself, in whom they are children of God, is righteous: then from the origin of the same, illustrated by the contrary, that those who commit sin are from the Devil, and thus are not children of God or born of God: then from the end of the coming of Christ, that the Son of God appeared that he might dissolve the works of the Devil, to whom those who are given to the proper works of the Devil, that is, to sins and iniquity, are repugnant: then from the seed, from which they have been regenerated, by the power of which they themselves cannot sin, regarding the proximate power of the Word, namely, which remains in them, even if by reason of remote power they are exposed to the falls of sin, namely of origin, and to sins; then from the sign and character by which the children of God and the children of the Devil are distinguished, that indeed those who do not study righteousness, but injustice, are not from God: All of which he illustrates, proceeding from the genus to certain species of sin: hatred toward a brother, homicide, unmercifulness, which are opposed to love toward one's neighbor, which is divinely commanded. That ἐν τούτῳ refers partly to the antecedents, in this are the children of God and the children of the Devil distinguished, namely in not sinning and in sinning, that the latter are given to sin, the former are not: partly to the consequents, that the latter do not do righteousness, do not love their neighbor. Whence it is clear that the children of God are understood according to their present state, not according to eternal predestination. Since the children of the Devil are also understood according to their present injustice. The Vulgate has: Everyone who is not righteous is not from God: The Greek, as also the Syriac text: Everyone not doing righteousness, etc. God is righteousness itself. Therefore, he who is from God devotes effort to righteousness. But they are said to do righteousness who, by working well, declare themselves to be righteous or justified. But they do not do righteousness who, by impious deeds and being alien to the norm of righteousness and holiness, betray the wickedness of their own mind, and declare by the thing itself that they are not yet righteous, whatever they may boast with their mouth about righteousness. Of these, therefore, not doing righteousness, he says that from be not of God. For although they are from Him by reason of creation, they are not so, however, in respect of the beneficial regeneration, by which alone the children of God are born from above.

Although good works ought indeed to proceed from a good mind, or rather from a heart purified by faith, yet since there is no mention here of the love of one's neighbor, that is not what is being looked at: But it descends to the kind, as we have said, of sins, of which the Apostle had spoken. What Grotius chatters about the cause of the Evangelical law, about the word 'brother' now extending more broadly than under the Gospel, and about the more intense love required in the New Testament, have already been discussed quite often. The Apostle, however, looks not so much to what they had heard under the law, as to what they had heard from the very mouth of Christ, John 13:34-35 and 15:12.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Ὅτι αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ ἀγγελία) Vide supra 1, 5.

Ἣν ἠκούσατε ἀπ' ἀρχῆς) Etiam sub lege, etsi nunc vox fratris latius pateat, & diligendi significatio sit intensior. Sed nihil mirum imperfecta præludere perfectionibus. Videtis tamen Deo in summo pretio semper fuisse dilectionem,

Ἵνα ἀγαπῶμεν ἀλλήλους) Israëlitæ Israëlitas olim, nunc quilibet quosvis, sicut & ante legem fecit Abrahamus.

Docuerat Apostolus filios Dei, qui spem habent visionis Dei beatificæ semetipsos purificare, eamq; gratiam in Filio nobis datam esse, ut simus filii Dei. Ex adverso vero qui peccatum facit, injustitiam committere, cujus tollendæ causa Filius Dei apparere voluerit. Inde ergo conficit, eos, qui in Filio Dei manent, non peccare: Quod confirmavit adversus seductiones hæreticorum propriæque concupiscentiæ pravæ tum ex indole filiorum Dei & justorum: quod non peccatis studeant, sed justitiam operentur, siquidem ipse, in quo sunt filii Dei, justus est: tum ex origine eorundem illustrata a contrario, quod qui peccatum faciunt ex Diabolo sint, adeoque non filii Dei vel ex Deo nati: tum ex fine adventus Christi, quod Filius Dei apparuerit, ut opera Diaboli dissolveret, cui repugnant, qui operibus Diaboli propriis dediti sunt, hoc est peccatis & iniquitati: tume seminis, e quo regeniti sunt, efficacia, vi cujus ipsi peccare non possunt, quoad potentiam proximam Verbi nimirum, quod in ipsis manet, etsi ratione potentiæ remotæ peccati nempe originis lapsibus & peccatis expositi sint; tum ex indicio & charactere, quo dignoscuntur filii Dei & filii Diaboli, quod nempe ex Deo non sint, qui non student justitiæ, sed injustitiæ: Quæ omnia illustrat a genere procedens ad certas species peccati odii erga fratrem, homicidii, immisericordiæ, quæ opponuntur amori erga proximum Divinitus præcepto. Illud ἐν τούτῳ refertur partim ad antecedentia, in hoc dignoscuntur filii Dei, & filii Diaboli, nimirum in non peccando & peccando, quod hi dediti sint peccato, illi non sint: partim ad consequentia, quod hi non faciant justitiam, non diligant proximum. Unde liquet filios Dei intelligi secundum statum præsentem non secundum æternam prædestinationem. Siquidem & filii Diaboli secundum præsentem injustitiam intelligantur. Vulgata habet: Omnis qui non est justus, non est ex Deo: Græcus ut & Syriacus textus: Omnis non faciens justitiam, &c. Deus ipsa justitia est. Proinde qui ex Deo est, justitiæ dat operam. Justitiam autem facere dicuntur, qui bene operando se justos vel justificatos esse declarent.
