Justitiam vero non faciunt, qui factis impiis, & a justitiæ sanctitatisque norma alieni animi sui improbitatem produnt, & re ipsa declarant, quod nondum justi sint, quicquid tandem ore de justitia jactitent. De his ergo non facientibus justitiam ait, quod ex Deo non sint. Licet enim ab illo sint ratione crea- tionis, non tamen benefica regenerationis respectu, qua sola filii Dei e supernis nascuntur.

Quanquam vero opera bona ex animo bono, imo e corde per fidem purificato proficisci debe- ant, non tamen cum dilectionis proximi hic men- tio sit, id spectatur: Sed ad speciem descendit, ut di- ximus peccatorum, de quibus loquutus erat Apo- stolus. Quae garrit Grotius de causa legis Evange- lica, de voce fratris latius nunc patente, quam sub Evangelio, de intensiori dilectione in Novo Testa- mento requisita, saepius jam discussa sunt. Respi- cit autem Apostolus non tam id, quod sub lege au- dierant, quam quod ex ipsius Christi ore Joh. XIII. 34. 35. & XV. 12.

## 3:12
Ver. 12.

Not as Cain was of the wicked one) The defect which is in this speech seems to me to be best supplied thus: we should not be of the wicked one as Cain was: that we may not be of a diabolical nature, as Cain was.

And he slew his brother) 'And' here is equivalent to 'who'. In the Glossary, 'σφάζω' means I slaughter, I kill, I strike, I slay, I murder. And the Greek Scholiasts interpret 'σφάζω' or 'σφάττω' as 'φονεύω' (I murder), 'κτείνω' (I kill). The Latin here says 'occidit' (killed). The Syrian uses 'קטל', which word the Hebrews also use for any kind of killing.

And for what reason did he slay him?) By this question he builds for himself an approach to the comparison between Abel and the Christians.

Because his works were wicked, but his brother's righteous) Most bitter hatreds arise from a diversity of morals. And that these two brothers were such appeared by the judgment of God, who was willing to accept the sacrifice of Abel, but not that of Cain. See what we have said regarding this history and the passage in Hebrews 11:4. 'The things of his brother', namely, his works, from the preceding.

Others repeat or understand the verb 'let us love', we do not love as Cain, who was of the wicked one, a son not of God but of the Devil. For the Devil, out of hatred for God, since he cannot harm Him, desires to harm His image, namely man, and to destroy him, just as a leopard, when it cannot harm a man, tears apart the image of a man, as Basil says in his homily on envy. The cause of Cain's hatred and fratricide is given as envy, because his works were wicked. His offering did not proceed from faith: But whatever is not of faith is sin, Rom. 14:last verse; but the works of his brother Abel were just, who offered sacrifice through faith: Since without faith it is impossible to please God, Heb. 11:5-6. Which example, as Estius warns, fits perfectly with the purpose of the blessed John, as he is dealing with that love of a brother by which one is loved so that he may live well and cleave to God, and likewise with that hatred which he suffers because he lives well and is dear to God. Which hatred is properly diabolical, and properly makes one a child of the Devil. For out of such hatred the Devil pursued and cast down man from the beginning, and killed him with the whole race by a double death. Every evil person, says St. Augustine in his commentary on Psalm 128, pursues the good because the good person does not consent to him in evil. From there, therefore, he prepares for himself an approach to the other part of the chapter, in which he discusses the different pursuits of the world and of the children of God and their consequences, and compares them with each other, primarily from the commandment of the love of one's neighbor.

PART II. On the different pursuits of the world and of the children of God and their consequences.

Vers. 12.

Οὐ καθὼς Καῒν ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ ἦν) Defectus, qui est in hoc ser- mone, ita mihi videtur optime posse suppleri : ἐκ ὦμεν ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ καθὼς Καῒν ἦν : ne diabolica simus indole, sicut Cain fuit.

Καὶ ἔσφαξε τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὑτοῦ) Καὶ hic valet qui. In Glos- sario σφάζω jugulo, interimo, caedo, occido, neco. Et Graeci Scholiastae σφάζω aut σφάττω interpretantur φονεύω, κτείνω. Latinus hic occidit. Syrus קטל qua voce & Ebraei utuntur de quavis interfectione.

Καὶ χάριν τίνος ἔσφαξεν αὐτὸν) Per hoc πύσμα aditum sibi struit ad comparationem inter Abelem & Christianos.

Ὅτι τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ πονηρὰ ἦν, τὰ δὲ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ αὐτοῦ δίκαια) Acerbissima odia ex diversitate morum. Tales autem fuisse duos istos fratres Dei judicio apparuit, qui Abelem litare voluit, Cainum non item. Vide quae ad istam historiam & ad locum Ebr. XI. vers. 4. a nobis dicta. Τὰ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ nempe ἔργα ex praecedenti.

Alii repetunt vel subintelligunt verbum ἀγα- πῶμεν, non diligimus sicut Cain, qui ex maligno erat filius non Dei sed Diaboli. Nam Diabolus ex odio Dei, quum ipsi nocere non possit, nocere cu- pit ejus imagini, nempe homini, ipsumque perdere, sicut pardalis, cum hominem laedere nequit, hominis imaginem discerpit, ut ait Basilius homil. de invi- dia. Causae odii & fratricidii Caini redditur invi- dia, quod opera ejus maligna fuerint. Oblatio ejus non profecta est ex fide: Quicquid autem non ex fide est, peccatum est, Rom. XIV. v. ult. fratris au- tem Abelis justa, qui per fidem obtulit sacrificium : Siquidem sine fide impossibile est Deo placere, Ebr. XI. 5. 6. Quod exemplum, Estio monente, optime convenit instituto B. Johannis, ut qui agat de ea fratris dilectione, qua diligitur, ut bene vivat & Deo inhaereat, itemque de eo odio quod patitur, quia bene vivit & Deo charus est. Quod odium proprie Diabolicum est, ac proprie Diaboli filios facit. Nam ex hujusmodi odio Diabolus hominem ab initio per- secutus dejecit, ac duplici morte cum toto genere oc- cidit. Omnis malus, inquit S. Augustinus enarr. Psal. CXXVIII. ideo persequitur bonum, quia non consentit illi bonus ad malum. Inde ergo aditum sibi parat ad alteram capitis partem, qua de diver- sis mundi & filiorum Dei studiis ac consequenti- bus differit, eademque inter se contendit e praece- pto imprimis dilectionis proximi.

PARS II. De diversis mundi & filiorum Dei studiis & consequentibus.

If the world hates you) Men indeed not unlike Cain. See what was said above at the beginning of this chapter and there.

## 3:13
Ver. 13.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

## 3:14
We know) We have learned from Christ what the world has not learned.

That we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren) That we have a right to eternal life, because we love our brothers, namely for God's sake, and in such a way that we testify to the same by our actions. For to such persons God promises through Christ that eternal life which is in question. You have passed from death unto life, in the same sense as we have here in this same writer of the Gospel, v. 24, where we said that it is signified by those words that they are transferred as it were from the city of death into the city of life. Moreover, a name of the thing itself is often given to a right to a thing.

The Apostle had said at the beginning of the chapter both about the axiom of the children of God, which came to us in Christ the only-begotten Son of God, and about the hatred of the world, which does not wish to acknowledge this, and therefore holds the faithful in hatred and persecutes them. Thence he has explained up to this point what he had said about the sonship of God. Now he also explains the hatred of the world and the diverse pursuits of it and of the children of God, and shows the consequences, that the world is opposed to the children of God, holds them in hatred and persecutes them, and that such persons remain in death, but do not have life remaining in them; whereas on the contrary the faithful love their neighbor, and thence know that they have been translated from death into life, that they are imitators of God, who laid down His soul for us, and that they can enjoy a tranquil conscience and have good confidence toward God. He had described the children of the Devil. Now he explains the character of the world, whose Prince is the Devil, whose nature it is to hate the faithful and to persecute them. He also deduces this sentiment as a consequence from the preceding antithesis of the children of God and of the Devil, as if to say: Just as Cain hates Abel, because Cain's works were evil, but Abel's were righteous; and so likewise the world, that is, the Gentiles and worldly men, hate Christians and true believers, because their own works are wicked, but those of the faithful are holy. He alludes to that saying of Christ in His Gospel, ch. XV. 18: If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you. What wonder if the children of the Devil hate the children of God, when their father the Devil extremely hates God and the children of God, as this Cornelius [says]. The example of Cain, says Blessed Hunnius, John transfers to a certain common place, and thus transfers the hypothesis to the thesis, warning namely that the faithful should not wonder if they experience the hatred of the world, since they understand from the proposed history of the first two brothers that this is not new, but that from the beginning of the world the pious have been exposed to the cross and the hatred of the impious. And page 148: The world is ruled by the nod and command of its Prince, who, as Christ attests, is the Devil. Just as therefore from the very first fall of men enmities have been placed between the seed of the woman and the ancient serpent, Gen. III. So also between the followers of both parties, that is, between the pious and the impious. And therefore let us not wonder, as this John says, if the world, addicted to the pursuits and desires of the Devil, persecutes us, who have given our name and faith to God and Christ, with hatred, and plots nothing but our destruction. Let this meanwhile be a consolation to us, that the hatred of the world is an indication of God's favor toward us and of our conjunction with Christ, just as the Savior taught His disciples, John XV: If the world hates you, you know that it hated me before you. If you were of the world, the world would love what is its own; but because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you. Therefore, from this it is gathered as by a certain sign that we have been segregated from the unhappy dregs of the world, if the children of this age together with their Prince the Devil hate us and have persecuted us in various ways and manners. Just as conversely it is easy for the world to agree with impious men who are hateful and hostile to God, which friendship of the world, however, ought to be rightly suspect to us, since the Holy Spirit in James IV asserts that this friendship of the world is enmity with God, so much so that whoever wishes to be a friend of the world is openly established as an enemy of God. It is therefore frivolous what Bellarmine, in Book I on Justification, chapter 10, infers, that the Apostle attributes life to charity because it is perfected by it. For the causal particle contains the cause here not of the thing but of the knowledge, as Lorinus acknowledges, when the Apostle says, 'we know that we have been translated'; he seems to show, as Salmeron says in disputation 23 on this passage, a sign by which we can know a posteriori that we are fulfilling the commandment of love. Which Stapleton explains at greater length in Promptuarium Morale, Sunday XII after Trinity, page 303: 'Just as the movement of the limbs is an argument for animal life, so the certain indication of spiritual life is love toward one's neighbor and works of charity toward him.' Hence St. John: 'We have been translated from death to life, because we love the brethren,' that is, by this argument it appears evidently that we live the life of grace. On the contrary, just as the numbness of the limbs and the cessation of movement is an argument for death or desperate illness, so a clear indication of extinguished grace is not to be affected toward one's neighbor and to cease from his love. Whence again St. John: 'He who has the substance of this world and sees his brother in need, and closes his bowels from him, how does the charity of God remain in him?'

‘Do not wonder, my brethren,’ he says; the Vulgate rendered it ‘do not wonder,’ omitting the address ‘my brethren,’ which both the Greek Codices consistently have and the Syriac reads. That this is not to be wondered at, as something new, is evident from the very ancient example of Cain. Cornelius lists here five causes why the world hates the saints and the faithful: The first is dissimilarity of morals: for worldly people have worldly morals, but the saints have heavenly ones. The former swell with ambition, avarice, gluttony, lust; the latter humble themselves with humility, poverty, sobriety, chastity. For just as similarity is the cause of love, so dissimilarity is the cause of hatred, says Aristotle. Cf. Wisdom 2:15. Leo the Great, Sermon IX on Lent: ‘In those, therefore, who are established in a good purpose, enmities from the dissimilar are not lacking, with the Devil instigating, and they easily break out into hatreds, whose wicked morals are more detestable by comparison with the upright.’ Iniquity has no peace with justice, drunkenness hates temperance, there is no concord for falsehood with truth. Pride does not love meekness, petulance does not love modesty, avarice does not love liberality, and that diversity has such persistent conflicts that even if it acquiesces outwardly, it nevertheless does not cease to disturb the very inner depths of pious hearts, so that it is true that those who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution, so that it is true that all this life is a temptation. The second cause of hatred is envy: because worldly people, entangled in their own concupiscences, cannot rise to the purity, virtues, and holiness of the saints, they grieve and envy them for it. The third is that worldly people see that the saints have separated themselves from their company and constantly flee it, whence they hate them as apostates from their assembly, Matt. 15:18, Wis. 2:16. The fourth is because the saints criticize and rebuke the depraved morals of the world; indeed, the very life of the saints is a silent reproach to worldly people, Wis. 2:12. The fifth is because worldly people are full of self-love, to which the saints are contrary, being full of the love of God; hence they acquire praise, dignity, and glory, which worldly people envy them, James 4:4. Rightly, therefore, Didymus on this passage: ‘It would be more,’ he says, ‘miraculous if depraved men loved those who live piously according to Christ.’

In this hatred of the world, however, there is this chief consolation, that we know we have been translated from death to life. That ‘We know’ implies not a conjecture, but certain knowledge, not only in general, that the faithful established in the bosom of the Church know this, as

Estius maintains that the discourse is general, and that the Apostle spoke in the person of the faithful, i.e., ‘We Christians know by certain faith that all good faithful people, of whose number we each trust ourselves to be, have been translated from death to life.’ But the Apostle speaks of himself and other believers, that indeed each one knows that he has been translated from death to life, namely, from the sincere love with which he loves the brethren, which arises from faith, Gal. 5:6, through which that translation happens, Gal. 2:10. Truly, therefore, Basil, Regulae Breviores, no. 116, and in Disputatio Regulae 296, citing and approving Cornelius a Lapide: ‘When can someone be CERTAINLY persuaded that God has forgiven his sins? Namely, if he has observed in himself an affection of the soul similar to that of him who said: “I have hated and abhorred iniquity.”’ And Gregory the Great, Book 1, Dialogues, chapter 1. The mind which is filled with the Divine Spirit has its MOST EVIDENT signs, namely, mighty works and humanity: which, if both come together perfectly in one mind, it is clear that they bear witness to the presence of the Holy Spirit. Estius rightly observes this, in that the Apostle says: We have been translated, namely, by God, so that the whole benefit of our salvation is to be ascribed not to our own strengths or merits, but to the grace of God. Cf. Col. I. 13. 14. Eph. II. 4. seqq. And further, regarding the words, 'because we love the brethren': He says, this does not signify a merit or at all the cause of the translation having been made, as if loving the brethren were prior, and being translated from death to life, that is, being justified, were posterior and the effect of that. For good works do not precede the one to be justified, but follow the one who has been justified, as St. Augustine aptly says in his book De fide et operibus, chapter 14. For through justification we are created in good works, which God has prepared, that we should walk in them, Eph. II. But this causality is to be referred to knowledge. For from brotherly love, as if from an effect and sign, we know that we have been translated from death to life: and as much as we are certain of the latter, so much are we also of the former. Let everyone return, says Augustine in this place, to his own heart; if he finds brotherly love there, let him be secure, because he has passed from death to life. These things are to be observed against other Papists, who judge that love is designated as the cause of the translation into life. Therefore, Estius is also sounder here than our Hugo, who says that we have a right to eternal life because we love our brethren. This is entirely against the mind of the Apostle, who renders not the cause of our translation into life, but of the knowledge of that translation. Nor is only a right to the thing designated: For we have truly been translated from the death of sin to the life of righteousness: from the kingdom of the Devil to the kingdom of the Son of God, nay, even from eternal death to eternal life, as far as concerns the spiritual communion and enjoyment of God, which is the beginning of heavenly happiness, Rom. XIV. 17. and a πρόγευσιν or foretaste of the powers of the world to come, Heb. VI. 5.

He that loveth not his brother abideth in death) He abideth in death, that is, he is in that condition which is subject to death. The ungodly, while they live, are dead, is a saying of the Hebrews. A similar figure to the preceding one. We have a right to life. Over them, death has a right. In the Manuscript: Τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς ὁ μὴ ἀγαπῶν.

Latin:

Ἡμεῖς οἴδαμεν) Nos ’ex Christo didicimus, quod mundus non didicit.

Ὅτι μεταβεβήκαμεν ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου εἰς τὴν ζωὴν, ὅτι ἀγα- πῶμεν τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς) Eo nos jus habere ad vitam æternam, quia fratres nostros diligimus propter Deum scilicet, & ita ut actibus idipsum testemur. Talibus enim Deus per Chri- stum vitam illam æternam, de qua agitur, promittit. Με- ταβήκατε ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου εἰς τὴν ζωὴν eodem sensu quo hic ha- bemus apud eundem hunc Scriptorem Evangelii V. 24. ubi diximus iis verbis significari, eos velut e civitate mortis in civitatem vitæ transscribi. Juri autem ad rem sæpe datur nomen rei ipsius.

Dixerat sub initium capitis Apostolus tum de axiomate filiorum Dei, quod in Christo unigenito Dei Filio nobis obtigit, tum de odio mundi, quod id agnoscere non vult, adeoq; odio habeat & per- sequatur fideles. Inde exposuit huc usque, quod de ὑότητι τοῦ θεοῦ dixerat. Jam exponit etiam odi- um mundi ejusque ac filiorum Dei diversa studia, & consequentia monstrat, quod mundus adverse- tur filiis Dei, eos odio habeat & persequatur, tales autem in morte maneant, non autem vitam habe- ant in se manentem; quum contra fideles proxi- mum diligant, & inde cognoscant, se ex morte in vitam translatos Dei, qui animam suam pro nobis posuit, imitatores esse, ac conscientia tranquilla frui posse, bonaq; erga Deum fiducia esse. Diaboli filios descripserat. Jam mundi, cujus Princeps est Diabolus, indolem exponit, cujus est, odisse fideles, ac persequi. Deducit etiam hanc sententiam tan- quam consequens ex antecedenti antithesi filio- rum Dei & Diaboli, q. d. Sicut Cain odit Abelem, quia Caini maligna, Abelis vero justa erant opera; & ita pariter mundus, id est gentiles & mundani homi- nes oderunt Christianos, verosque fideles, quia ipso- rum prava, fidelium vero sancta sunt opera. Alludit ad illud Christi in suo Evangelio cap. XV. 18. Si mun- dus vos odit, scitote, quia me priorem vobis odio habuit. Quid mirum si filii Diaboli oderint filios Dei, cum pater eorum Diabolus extreme oderit De- um Deique filios, ut hic Cornelius. Exemplum Cai- ni, inquit B. Hunnius, Johannes ad locum quen- dam communem, atq; sic hypothesin ad thesin trans- fert, admonens videlicet, ne mirentur fideles, si mun- di odium experiantur, cum intelligant ex proposita hiftoria primorum duorum fratrum, non novum hoc esse, sed ab initio mundi pios cruci & odio impio- rum fuisse expositos. Et pag. 148. Regitur mundus nutu imperioque sui Principis, qui Christo attestan- te est Diabolus. Quemadmodum ergo jam inde a primo lapsu hominum inimicitia posita sunt inter se- men mulieris & serpentem antiquum, Gen. III. Sic etiam inter utriusque partis asseclas, hoc est, inter pios & impios. Ideoque non miremur, ut ait hic Jo- hannes, si mundus studiis ac desideriis Diaboli addi- ctus, nos qui Deo & Christo nomen fidemque dedi- mus, odio persequatur, & nihil non in nostram perni- tiem moliatur. Sit hoc interim nobis solatio, quod mundi odium illud Dei erga nos favoris, & nostræ cum Christo conjunctionis indicium est, sicut disci- pulos suos docuit Salvator, Joh. XV. Si mundus vos odit, scitis quod me prius quam vos odio habuerit. Si de mundo fuissetis, mundus quod suum est, diligeret, quia vero de mundo non estis, sed ego selegi vos de mundo, propterea odit vos mundus. Ergo hinc velu- ti signo quodam colligitur, nos ex infelici mundi col- luvie segregatos esse, si filii hujus seculi una cum Principe suo Diabolo nos oderint, & variis modis ac rationibus persecuti fuerint. Quemadmodum e converso mundo facile convenit cum hominibus impiis Deo exosis & inimicis, quæ tamen mundi amicitia nobis merito suspecta esse debet, quandoqui- dem Spiritus sanctus Jacobi IV. hanc mundi amici- tiam cum Deo inimicitiam esse perhibet, adeo ut qui voluerit esse amicus mundi, is inimicus Dei palam constituatur. Frivolum ergo est, quod Bellarminus l. I. de justif. c. 10. infert, Apostolum vitam tribuere charitati, quoniam inde perficitur. Causalisenim particula causam hic continet non rei sed cognitionis, ut Lorinus agnoscit, cum Apostolus ait, scimus quoniam translati sumus; videtur ostendere, Salmerone disp. 23. in h. l. dicente, signum, quo præceptum dilectionis nosse possumus nos implere a posteriori. Quod pluribus explicat Stapleton. in promptuar. Moral. Dom. XII. post Trinit. pag. 303. Sicut vitæ animalis argumentum est motus membrorum: Sic vitæ spiritualis certum indicium est amor erga proximum, & opera charitatis in illum. Hinc D. Johannes: Translati sumus de morte ad vitam, quia diligimus fratres, id est, hoc argumento evidenter apparet, nos vitæ gratiæ vivere. Contra sicut mortis aut desperatæ valetudinis argumentum est stupor membrorum & cessatio motus: extinctæ gratiæ clarum indicium est, non affici erga proximum, & ab ejus dilectione cessare. Unde iterum D. Johannes: Qui habuerit substantiam hujus mundi & viderit fratrem suum necesse habere, & clauserit viscera sua ab eo, quomodo charitas Dei manet in eo.

Μὴ θαυμάζετε ἀδελφοί μꙋ, inquit, nolite mirari reddidit Vulgata, omissa compellatione fratres mei, quam & Græci Codices constanter habent, & Syrus legit. Non esse id mirandum, ceu aliquid novi e vetustissimo Caini exemplo constat. Quinqu; hic recenset Cornelius causas, cur mundus oderit sanctos & fideles: Prima est dissimilitudo morum: Mundani enim mundanos habent mores, sancti vero cœlestes. Illi tument ambitione, avaritia, gula, libidine, hi se deprimunt humilitate, paupertate, sobrietate, castitate. Nam sicut similitudo est causa amoris, sic dissimilitudo est causa odii, ait Aristoteles. Conf. Sap. II. v. 15. Leo Magnus serm. IX. de Quadrag. In bono, inquit, ergo proposito constitutis inimicitiæ dissimilium Diabolo instigante non desunt, & facile in odia prorumpunt, quorum improbi mores detestabiliores sunt comparatione rectorum. Iniquitas cum justitia non habet pacem, temperantiam odit ebrietas, falsitati nulla est cum veritate concordia. Non amat superbia mansuetudinem, petulantia verecundiam, avaritia largitatem, & tam pertinaces habet diversitas illa conflictus, ut etiamsi exterius acquiescat, ipsa tamen piorum cordium penetralia inquietare non desinat, ut verum sit, quod qui voluerint in Christo pie vivere, persecutionem patientur, ut verum sit, quod omnis hæc vita tentatio est. Secunda odii causa est invidia: quia enim mundani suis concupiscentiis irretiti non possunt assurgere ad puritatem, virtutes & sanctitatem sanctorum, dolent, eamque illis invident. Tertia est, quod mundani videant sanctos se separasse ab eorum consortio, illudque assidue fugere, unde eos quasi sui cœtus apostatas oderunt, Matth. XV. 18. Sap. II. 16. Quarta quia sancti carpunt & redarguunt pravos mores mundi, imo sola sanctorum vita est tacita mundanorum reprehensio Sap. II. 12. Quinta quia mundani pleni sunt amore sui, cui contrarii sunt sancti, utpote pleni amore Dei, hinc laudem, dignitatem, & gloriam acquirunt, quam eis mundani invident, Jac. IV. 4. Recte ergo Didymus in h. l. Magis, inquit, mirabile esset, si pravi homines diligerent eos, qui secundum Christum pie vivunt.

In quo vero mundi odio hæc præcipua est consolatio, quod sciamus nos esse translatos de morte ad vitam. Οἴδαμεν illud non conjecturam, sed certam scientiam infert non tantum in genere, quod fideles in Ecclesiæ gremio constituti hoc sciant, ut

Estius vult, sermonem generalem esse, & Apostolum in persona fidelium loquutum, q. d. Nos Christiani certa fide novimus omnes bonos fideles, quorum e numero nos esse singuli confidimus, translatos esse de morte ad vitam: Sed de se & aliis credentibus loquitur Apostolus, quod nempe quisque sciat, se translatum esse a morte ad vitam ex amore scil. sincero, quo fratres diligit, qui ex fide oritur, Gal. V. 6. per quam illa translatio fit, Gal. II. 10. Vere itaque Basilius Regul. Brevior. n. 116. & in disp. reg. 296. citante & approbante Cornelio a Lapide: Quando CERTO aliquis persuasus esse potest, Deum sibi pecata remisisse? Nempe si affectionem animi in se animadverterit similem illius, qui dixit: Iniquitatem odio habui & abominatus sum. Et Gregorius M. l. 1. Dial. c. 1. Mens quæ Divino Spiritu impletur, habet EVIDENTISSIMA signa sua virtutes scilicet & humanitatem: quæ si utraque perfecte in una mente conveniunt, liquet, quod de præsentia Spiritus sancti testimonium ferunt. Recte autem id observat Estius, quod dicat Apostolus: Translati sumus scil. a Deo, ut non nostris viribus aut meritis, sed Dei gratiæ totum salutis nostræ beneficium adscribendum sit. Conf. Col. I. 13. 14. Eph. II. 4. seqq. Et porro ad verba, quoniam diligimus fratres: Non hic, inquit, significatur meritum aut omnino causa factæ translationis, quasi prius sit diligere fratres, posterius autem & effectus illius, transferri de morte ad vitam, id est justificari. Neque enim opera bona præcedunt justificandum, sed sequuntur justificatum, ut concinne S. Augustinus dicit libr. de fide & operibus cap. 14. Nam per justificationem creamur in bonis operibus, quæ præparavit Deus, ut in illis ambulemus Eph. II. Sed causalitas hæc referenda est ad cognitionem. Nam ex dilectione fraterna velut effectu & signo cognoscimus nos de morte ad vitam translatos esse: & quantum de illa certi sumus, tantum & de isto. Redeat unusquisque inquit hoc loco Augustinus ad cor suum, si ibi invenerit charitatem fraternam, securus sit, quia transiit de morte ad vitam. Quæ contra alios Pontificios, dilectionem causam designari translationis in vitam censentes, observanda. Magis itaque sanus etiam hic Estius, quam Hugo noster, qui co nos, inquit, jus habere ad vitam æternam, quia fratres nostros diligimus. Prorsus contra mentem Apostoli, qui non causam translationis nostræ in vitam, sed cognitionis translationis istius reddit. Neque jus ad rem tantum designatur: Vere enim translati sumus de morte peccati ad vitam justitiæ: De regno Diaboli ad regnum Filii Dei, imo etiam de morte æterna ad vitam æternam, quantum ad communionem & fruitionem Dei spiritualem, quæ est initium cœlestis felicitatis, Rom. XIV. 17. & πρόγευσιν vel prægustum virtutum venturi seculi Ebr. VI. 5.

Ὁ μὴ ἀγαπῶν τὸν ἀδελφὸν μένει ἐν τῷ θανάτῳ) Manet in morte, id est, in ea est conditione, quæ morti est obnoxia. Impii dum vivunt sunt mortui, est dictum Ebræorum. Par figura cum præcedente. Nos jus habemus ad vitam. In illos mors jus habet. In Manuscripto: Τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς ὁ μὴ ἀγαπῶν.

## 3:15
Vers. 15.

Whosoever hateth his brother) Just as those worldly men not only do not love us, but even hate us.

He is a murderer) For if one desires that someone whom he fears should have perished, much more so one whom he hates. But by the law of Christ, which regards the inner man most of all, anyone is considered to have done what he willed. For what Christ said concerning adultery, Matt. V. 28, is to be applied with equal right to other crimes.

And ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him) Eternal life, that is, a right to eternal life in himself, that is, he does not have it with him. What he says is sufficiently clear. For if the law of Moses cannot bear such a man in an earthly society, how much less will Christ bear him in the heavenly city. It is easily understood that this concerns not the habit but the act of homicide, from the example of Cain.

The argument is clear. No murderer has eternal life remaining in him. Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, because he desires that the one whom he hates should have perished, as Jerome rightly says in Epistle LXII. Cf. Thomas 2. sec. Whoever hates his brother, says Cornelius, is a murderer, not in act and deed, but in affection and will, because as St. Jerome says in Epistle 26 to Castorina: Since homicide often arises from hatred, whoever hates, even if he has not yet struck with the sword, is a murderer in spirit. The Apostle, however, alternates the phrases, not to love and to hate one's brother. The judgment on both is the same: He who does not love remains in death, and he who hates does not have eternal life remaining in him, so that the sin of omission is designated as no less grave than the sin of commission, and to remain in death and not to have eternal life remaining in him are equivalent, whence it is not permitted to invent a middle state between death and eternal life. If, however, by spiritual death we understand the death of sin, so that he who does not love his brother is considered not to have passed from the death of sin to life, but to remain in that death, the explanation seems more elegant, although it comes to almost the same thing, because those who are dead in sins and destitute of spiritual life are destitute of faith, through which we live, Gal. II. 20. Again, those who are destitute of faith do not have charity, Gal. V. 6. But he who hates his brother remains in mortal sin, the wages of which being eternal death, he cannot have eternal life in himself. It is certain that one sins mortally not only by hating and persecuting a brother, but also by not loving and not showing the duties of charity. Cf. Matt. XXV. 42. seqq. There is, therefore, no reason why we should establish a meiosis here with Cornelius a Lapide, as if 'not to love' were taken for 'to hate,' when it can be understood properly, as Estius admits.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Πᾶς ὁ μισῶν τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὑτοῦ) Sicut isti mundani homines nos non modo non diligunt, sed & oderunt.

Ἀνθρωποκτόνος ἐστί) Nam si Quem quisque metuit, periisse expetit, Multo magis quem odit. Christi autem lege, quæ internum hominem potissimum respicit, fecisse quisquam censetur, quantum voluit. Quod enim de adulterio dixit Christus, Matth. V. 28. pari jure ad alia crimina aptandum est.

Καὶ οἴδατε ὅτι πᾶς ἀνθρωποκτόνος οὐκ ἔχει ζωὴν αἰώνιον ἐν αὑτῷ μένουσαν) Vitam æternam, id est jus ad vitam æternam in se, id est, apud se non habet. Quod dicit apertum satis est. Nam si Mosis lex in terrestri societate talem hominem ferre non potest, quanto minus eum Chri- stus feret in cœlesti civitate. Non de habitu sed de actu homicidii hic agi facile intelligitur ex Caini exemplo.

Argumentum luculentum est. Nullus homici- da vitam æternam habet in se manentem. Omnis qui odit fratrem suum est homicida, quia quem odit quis periisse cupit, ut recte Hieronymus epist. LXII. Conf. Thomas 2. sec. Qui odit fratrem suum, inquit Cornelius, homicida est, non actu & opere, sed affectu & voluntate, quia ut ait S. Hieronymus epist. 26. ad Castorin. Cum homicidium ex odio sæpe na- scatur, quicunque odit, etiamsi necdum gladio percuf- serit, animo homicida est. Commutat autem phra- ses Apostolus, non diligere & odisse fratrem suum. De utroque idem judicium: Ille qui non diligit, in morte manet, & qui odit, non habet vitam in se ma- nentem, ut peccatum omissionis non minus grave es- se designetur, quam peccatum commissionis, & in morte manere, ac vitam æternam in se manentem non habere ἰσοδυναμῶντα sunt, unde inter mortem & vitam æternam medium fingere non licet. Si ta- men per mortem spiritualem mortem peccati intel- ligamus, ut qui non diligit fratrem, non transiisse a morte peccati ad vitam, sed in morte illa manere censeatur, concinnior videtur explicatio, licet fere eodem recidat, quia qui in peccatis mortui vita spi- rituali destituuntur, fide destituti sunt, per quam vivimus, Gal. II. 20. Rursus qui fide destituuntur, charitatem non habent, Gal. V. 6. Qui autem odit fratrem suum, in peccato mortali hæret, cujus sti- pendium quum sit mors æterna, vitam æternam in se habere nequit. Id certum est non solum odiendo & persequendo fratrem, sed etiam non diligendo, & charitatis officia non exhibendo, peccari morta- liter. Conf. Matth. XXV. 42. seqq. Non ergo est, quod μείωσιν hic cum Cornelio a Lapide constitua- mus, quasi non diligere accipiatur pro odisse, quum proprie intelligi possit, fatente Estio.

## 3:16
Vers. 16.

In this we have known the love of God) Whence we learn how greatly God has loved us. That he laid down his soul for us) 'He' here is Christ, as above 5. It is to be understood here, however, that Christ did this with God so decreeing for our sake, which is expressed in Rom. IV. 8 and VIII. 32. See also below IV. 9 and in the Gospel III. 16. To lay down the soul, according to this writer of ours, is not properly to lay down life (although Christ did this too) but to expose it to dangers, as we said at John X. 11, 15, 17, chap. XIII. 38, 39, c. XV. 13.

Others more rightly refer the word 'he' to the preceding name of God, so that the second person of the Godhead, the Son of God, is designated, who laid down his soul for us, God, who acquired us with his own blood. We have, therefore, here an argument for the true Deity of Christ against the Socinians, whom Grotius wished to assist in this place. For he is called GOD who laid down his soul for us. But who is this other than Christ, Matt. XX. 28, Mark X. 45, John X. 15, etc.? That the one supreme God is to be understood, is taught both by the absolute use of the word 'God,' which is attributed to no one except the one God absolutely and simply, and by the addition of the article, which adversaries admit is an undoubted mark of the supreme God when the word 'God' occurs with the article; and by the very structure of the position, when the name of God is placed here so that it sustains the place of the subject: God laid down his soul for us. Since the adversaries profess that from such a position and subjective use of the word 'God' it is infallibly concluded that the discourse is about the supreme God.

Socinus objects against Wujeck, p. 356: (1) That the name of God itself is missing in the Greek, as also in the Syriac text. (2) If it were read at all, the pronoun 'he' should not be referred to it, as it can refer to and signify not only him who was named long before, but also him who was never openly named before. Resp. to 1: We admit that a diversity of readings occurs here. Meanwhile, because not only the Latin Vulgate exhibits the word 'God' here, to which Socinians are not infrequently accustomed to recur, and most Latin commentators read the same, but also in the Complutensian Greek edition, once adorned according to the faith of the most ancient copies, as Henry Stephens and Theodore Beza admit, the word 'of God' was found, we say that this argument is not to be held as worthless, especially since Socinus himself in his commentary on this place, p. 224, not a little favors the reading of the word 'of God,' and teaches from parallel passages that charity is entirely designated here, John III. 16. Rom. V, 8. To 2. Resp.: However much the pronoun 'he' may sometimes look to a more remote object, or even to one who has not been explicitly named, it cannot be denied that its ordinary use, like that of other relative and demonstrative pronouns, is to refer to and demonstrate someone; and that the adversaries reject this here is for no other reason than a preconceived opinion. But it is most rightly referred to the name 'of God,' as a parallel and similar passage teaches, Acts XX. v. 28, where God is likewise said to have acquired us with his own blood, just as here God is said to have laid down his soul for us. Furthermore, to return to Grotius, it is not said that 'he,' that is, Christ, laid down his soul with God decreeing it, but he is the same one who so loved us that he gave his very soul for us as the price of redemption, Matt. XX. 28, Mark X. 45, John X. 11, 15, 17. Nor indeed is Christ said only to have exposed his soul to dangers out of love, but in truth to have laid down his soul by laying down his life, both because the phrase itself properly imports that, and because this is a greater degree of charity. Moreover, Christ's charity is proclaimed as the greatest, John 15:13, both because Christ himself explains it so, John 10:17, 18. For he says he laid down his soul for all in the same way as he has ἐξυσίαν to lay down his soul, which he showed in death, and in turn to take it up again, which was done in the resurrection. Indeed, I, he says, lay down my soul, and I will take it up again. But he did not lay it down only by exposing himself to dangers, but by meeting death: nor did he take it up again by freeing himself from the dangers of death, but by rising from death itself. What? That he adds expressly: No one takes it from me, but I lay it down ἀπ' ἐμαυτοῦ. What could be said more clearly than that he lays down his soul for the sheep by undergoing death, either by dying voluntarily or by free power, which no one else could have forced upon him. These things will be explained only ineptly if they refer solely to the dangers of life.

(Καὶ ἡμεῖς ὀφείλομεν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀδελφῶν τὰς ψυχὰς τιθέναι) And here, therefore, it is lacking. The sense is: We therefore also ought to approach any dangers whatsoever, so that we may rescue other men, our brothers in original descent, from eternal destruction. Our life ought not to be dearer to us than his Son was to God. The Apostles and their helpers, and after them so many confessors and martyrs, fulfilled this commandment excellently.

We ought not only to approach the dangers of life for our brothers, but even to pour out life itself following the example of Christ, which indeed cannot be done by making satisfaction for sins: for a brother cannot redeem a brother, Psalm 49:8, 9, or as regards the kind of death, because Christ underwent even the infernal death itself for us, and Christ's death was vicarious, and meritorious, and also of most free power, such as falls to no mortal: It ought, however, to be done, by following Christ's example in a certain way, namely, that we should undergo temporal death if otherwise the brother were destined to perish in eternal death, because the order of charity demands that we love the soul of our neighbor more than our own body, and that we prefer the glory of God, which is situated in the salvation of the neighbor's soul, to our own life. However, a not insignificant doubt occurs here among the Casuists concerning an unjust aggressor, if he should be killed while about to perish eternally in that sin of his, since the order of charity demands that the spiritual life of the neighbor be preferred to our own bodily life: whether he ought to be killed, or rather should the one whom he attacked suffer his own destruction? This was the view of Gerson, Augustine of Ancona, Richard of St. Victor, Accursius, and according to some, even Augustine in Book 1 of De Libero Arbitrio, chapter 5. But the law of charity does not bind us to that. For the spiritual life of the neighbor is to be preferred to my bodily life when my own bodily life is necessary to the neighbor for his own spiritual life. But when the matter stands otherwise, and the neighbor himself can have and maintain his own spiritual and eternal life by himself without the loss of our temporal life, but out of his own wickedness he clings to sin, from which he could desist if he wished, then the law of charity does not bind us to the loss of our own life, lest we kill the unjust aggressor while defending ourselves with the moderation of blameless protection, who out of his own wickedness does not wish to desist from such great iniquity, lest he, by wickedly refusing, incur eternal destruction. Regarding Augustine, see Thomas, 2-2, question 64, article 7. Ordinarily, however, we are not bound to lay down our temporal life so that the neighbor may be preserved in temporal life, because this is to love the neighbor not as oneself, but more than oneself, which exceeds the rule of doctrine, as St. Augustine says in his book De Mendacio, chapter VI, and ordered charity begins with itself. Concerning extraordinary cases, when someone, out of obligation or covenant, must even pour out his own life, for example, a soldier and a servant for their master, let the Casuists and moral Theologians be consulted, as well as Cornelius on this passage. Moreover, that such great perfection of charity is not required of all Christians as is required of Pastors is a 'burdensome saying' of Estius. Nowhere does Scripture prescribe one law of charity toward the neighbor for Pastors and another for others. All are bound to love their neighbor as themselves, all to lay down their soul for their brothers.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Ἐν τούτῳ ἐγνώκαμεν τὴν ἀγάπην τοῦ Θεοῦ) Unde discimus, quantopere Deus nos dilexerit. Ὅτι ἐκεῖνος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ ἔθηκεν) Ἐκεῖνος hic est Christus ut supra 5. Subintelligendum autem hic est, hoc Christum fecisse Deo sic decernente nostri causa, quod expressum est Rom. IV. 8. & VIII. 32. Vide & infra IV. 9. & in Evangelio III. 16. Τιθέναι ψυχὴν apud hunc nostrum Scriptorem non est proprie vitam deponere (quanquam & hoc fecit Christus) sed objicere periculis, ut diximus ad Joh. X. 11. 15. 17. cap. XIII. 38. 39. c. XV. 13.

Vocem ἐκεῖνος ad nomen præcedens Dei recti- us alii referunt, ut designetur secunda Divinitatis persona Filius Dei, qui animam suam pro nobis po- suit, Deus, qui acquisivit nos sanguine suo. Habe- mus itaque hic argumentum veræ Deitatis Christi contra Socinianos, quibus succurrere hoc loco vo- luit Grotius. Etenim is dicitur DEUS, qui pro nobis animam suam posuit. Quis vero is alius, quam Christus Matth. XX. 28. Marc. X. 45. Joh. X. 15. &c. Quod autem unus ille summus Deus in- telligendus sit, docet tum absoluta vocis Dei usur- patio: Quæ nulli nisi uni Deo absolute & simplici- ter tribuitur, tum articuli adjectio, quem adversarii notam indubitatam esse summi Dei, cum vox Dei occurrit cum articulo; tum ipsa positus ratio, cum ita collocetur hic nomen Dei, ut subjecti locum su- stineat, Deus posuit animam suam pro nobis. Quan- doquidem ex ejusmodi positu & usurpatione sub- jectiva vocis Θεοῦ infallibiliter colligi de Deo sum- mo sermonem esse adversarii profiteantur.

Excipit Socinus contra Wujeck p. 356. In Græco nomen ipsum Dei de esse, ut & in Syro textu. (2.) S omnino legeretur, non tamen pronomen ἐκεĩνₑ ad illud referendum esset, ut quod non modo eum, qui multo ante, verum etiam eum, qui nunquam antea aperte nominatus fuerit, referre & signifi- care possit. Resp. ad 1. Fatemur lectionum diversitatem hic òccurrere. Interim quia non modo Latina vulga- ta vocem Dei hic exhibet; ad quam non raro so- lent recurrere Sociniani, leguntque eandem Lati- ni plerique commentatores, sed & in Complutensi editione Graeca, ad fidem antiquissimorum exem- plarium olim adornata, fatente Henr. Stephano, & Theodor. Beza, deprehensa fuit vox τῦ Θεῦ, non in- super habendum dicimus hoc argumentum, prae- sertim cum Socinus ipse non parum faveat in com. ad h. l. p. 224. lectioni vocis τῦ Θεῦ, doceatque ex locis parallelis omnino charitatem hic designari Joh. III, 16. Rom. V, 8. Ad 2. Resp. Utut pronomen ἐκεĩνₑ quandoque remotiorem, aut eum etiam, qui diserte nomina- tus non sit, respiciat, negari tamen nequit, ordina- rium ejus usum esse, ut aliorum pronominum rela- tivorum ac demonstrativorum, ut referant & de- monstrent, quem cum hic reprobent adversarii, nulla alia causa est, nisi praeconcepta opinio. Re- ctissime autem referri ad nomen τῦ Θεῦ, locus pa- rallelus & similis docet Act. XX. v. 28. ubi pariter Deus dicitur acqusivisse nos proprio sanguine, ut hic Deus animam suam posuisse dicitur pro nobis. Porro ut ad Grotium redeamus, non dicitur ἐκεĩνₑ, id est Christus, Deo decernente animam suam posuisse, sed idem est ille, qui nos ita dilexit, ut ipsam animam suam pro nobis in redemptionis pretium dederit, Matth. XX. 28. Marc. X. 45. Joh. X. 11. 15. 17. Nec vero Christus tantum dicitur ani- mam suam periculis objecisse ex dilectione, sed re- vera animam suam posuisse vitam deponendo, tum quia phrasis ipsa proprie id importat, tum quia hic major est charitatis gradus. Depraedicatur autem Christi charitas ceu maxima, Joh. XV. 13. tum quia sic explicat Christus ipse, Joh. X. 17. 18. Nam ita po- suisse animam suam pro omnibus dicit, quemad- modum ἐξυσίαν habet animam suam ponendi, quod in morte ostendit, & vicissim animam suam resumendi, quod in resurrectione factum. Imo ego, inquit, animam meam pono, & iterum sumam eam. Non autem posuit tantum se exponendo periculis, sed mortem oppetendo: nec resumsit se a periculis mortis expediendo, sed a morte ipsa resurgendo. Quid? quod addat diserte: Nemo tollit eam a me, sed ego pono eam ἀπ' ἐμαυτῦ. Quid luculentius dici poterat, quam quod animam suam ponat pro ovibus mortem subeundo, vel moriendo volunta- rie vel libera potestate, quam nemo alias ei inferre potuisset. Nonnisi inepte haec de periculis vitae so- lum explicabuntur.

(Καὶ ἡμεῖς ὀφείλομεν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀδελφῶν τὰς ψυχὰς τιθέναι) Et hic deest igitur. Sensus est: Debemus igitur & nos pe- ricula quaevis adire, ut alios homines fratres nostros in pri- ma origine exitio aeterno eripiamus. Non debet nobis cha- rior esse vita nostra, quam Deo Filius suus fuit. Hoc prae- ceptum egregie implevere Apostoli & eorum adjutores, & post eos tot confessores atque martyres.

Non tantum pericula vitae adire debemus pro fratribus, sed etiam vitam ipsam profundere ad exemplum Christi, quod quidem fieri non potest satisfaciendo pro peccatis: fratrem enim frater redimere non potest, Psal. XLIX. v. 8. 9. vel quoad mortis speciem, quia Christus mortem ipsam infer- nalem etiam subiit pro nobis, Christique mors vi- caria fuit, & meritoria, nec non liberrimae potesta- tis, qualis in nullum mortalium cadit: Fieri tamen debet, Christi exemplum certa ratione sequendo, ut nempe mortem temporalem subeamus, si cæteroqu in æterna morte pereundum foret fratri, quia ordo charitatis id postulat, ut plus animam proximi quam corpus nostrum diligamus, & gloriam Dei, quæ in salute animæ proximi sita est propriæ nostræ vitæ præferamus. Cæterum dubium hic non leve occurrit apud Casuistas de injusto aggressore, si interficiatur, æternum perituro in isto suo peccato, quum ordo charitatis postulet, ut vita spiritualis proximi vitæ nostræ corporali præponatur, anne interficiendus sit, vel potius is, quem aggressus est, decisionem sui pati debeat? Quod visum fuit Gersoni, Augustino de Ancona, Richardo de S. Victore, Accursio, & secundum quosdam etiam Augustino l. 1. de Lib. Arb. c. 5. Sed eo non obligat nos lex charitatis. Vita enim spiritualis proximi est anteponenda vitæ corporali meæ, quando vita propria corporalis proximo necessaria est ad suam spiritualem. Cum vero aliter se res habet, & proximus ipse per seipsum sine jactura vitæ nostræ temporalis suam spiritualem & æternam habere, ac tueri potest, sed ex sua nequitia inhæret peccato, a quo desistere posset si vellet, tum lex charitatis nos ad jacturam propriæ vitæ nostræ, ne nos cum moderamine inculpatæ tutelæ defendendo injustum aggressorem interficiamus, qui sua nequitia a tanta iniquitate non vult desistere, non obligat, ne ille nequiter nolendo æternum incurrat interitum. De Augustino vid. Thomas 2. sec. quæst. 64. art. 7. Ordinarie autem vitam nostram temporalem non tenemur ponere, ut in vita temporali servetur proximus, quia hoc est diligere proximum non sicut seipsum, sed plus, quam seipsum, quod doctrina regulam excedit, dicente S. Augustino l. de mendac. c. VI. & charitas ordinata incipit a seipsa. De extraordinariis casibus, cum quis ex obligatione vel pacto etiam vitam suam profundere debet, v. g. miles & servus pro Domino, conferantur Casuistæ & morales Theologi, ut & Cornelius in h. l. Cæterum non ab omnibus Christianis tantam perfectionem charitatis requiri, quanta a Pastoribus requiritur, Φορτικὸν ἄκουσμα est Estii. Nuspiam Scriptura aliam legem charitatis proximi Pastoribus præscribit, aliam aliis. Omnes tenentur proximum diligere, sicut semetipsos, omnes animam suam ponere pro fratribus.

## 3:17
Verse 17. 'But whoever has the goods of this world' (Ὃς δ' ἂν ἔχῃ τὸν βίον τοῦ κόσμου). He continues and shows by other things how far the obligation of loving a brother or neighbor extends. 'Bios' among the Greeks often signifies the things from which one lives, as in the proverb: 'He who needs life for life has no life.' And thus Luke uses it in 8:14, 15:12, 30, 21:4. But 'of this world' (τοῦ κόσμου) is added here so that we may understand that it deals with those things which pertain to life, not of another, but of this age. For it is sometimes expressed by the phrase 'of this age' (αἰῶνος τούτου), as in 1 Timothy 6:17, and sometimes by the word 'world' (κόσμου). The Rabbis say 'olam hazeh'. The Syriac here: 'd'alma qenyana'.

And sees his brother having need (Καὶ θεωρῇ τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὑτοῦ χρείαν ἔχοντα). Lacking necessities. See examples in Matthew 25:35, Luke 16:20, James 2:15, where he who is here 'having need' (χρείαν ἔχων) is called 'lacking daily food and the necessities for the body'.

And shuts his bowels from him (Καὶ κλείσῃ τὰ σπλάγχνα αὑτοῦ ἀπ' αὐτοῦ). Has shut his compassion from him, that is, has excluded him from the affection of mercy. Regarding the word 'splanchnon', see Luke 1:78, 2 Corinthians 6:12, 7:15, Philippians 1:8, Colossians 3:12, Philemon 7, 12, 20. To shut from someone is to exclude someone.

How does the love of God abide in him? (Πῶς ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ Θεοῦ μένει ἐν αὐτῷ;). How would the love which God demands be in him? We have already spoken several times about the word 'menein' (to abide).

Some understand this as the love of God which the first table of the law demands, and from which the love of the neighbor ought to overflow, which Grotius interprets as the love that is directed toward the neighbor; but it is most correctly understood as the love with which God pursues us: that such people who shut the bowels of mercy toward a needy brother do not have eternal life abiding in them; just so, neither can the grace or love of God abide in them, because 'judgment without mercy' awaits him who has not shown mercy, James 2:13. For St. John is about to treat in the next chapter the fact that active love of God cannot have a place in him who does not love his brother: hence he is occupied with the guilt, the liability, and the consequences of those who do not love their neighbor, that they do not enjoy the grace of God, do not have eternal life in themselves, but remain in death. And therefore true love of the neighbor is illustrated by the example of Christ and by the special case of one who shuts the bowels of mercy in the neighbor's need, and we are warned that we should love the neighbor not in word or tongue, but in deed and truth, lest on account of that lack of love we incur the guilt of homicide, the liability of death, and exclusion from the grace of God and eternal life: But through sincere love of the neighbor we may be made more certain of the truth of regeneration and the grace of God, and have a tranquil conscience, verse 19, and also confidence toward God and the gracious hearing of God in those things which we ask according to His will, as we keep the Divine doctrine, by which covenant we abide in Him, and we know that God and the love or grace of God ABIDES in us, namely from the Spirit which He has given us, verse 24. But the Apostle now seems to conclude in this way: If the charity of God binds us to even lay down our souls for our brothers, it will bind us much more to assist that needy person with alms. It is a great fault, says Ambrose in Book 1 of De Officiis, chapter 31, if a believer is in need while you know it, if you know he is without means, is laboring from hunger, is suffering distress, especially one who is ashamed to be in need. Bowels are a symbol of fatherly, or rather motherly, love, Philemon verse 7, where Jerome says: All children are the bowels of their parents.

Latin:

Vers. 17. Ὃς δ' ἂν ἔχῃ τὸν βίον τοῦ κόσμου) Pergit & aliis rebus ostendere, quousque se extendat fratrem sive proximum diligendi obligatio. Βίος apud Græcos sæpe significat ea, unde vivitur, ut in Proverbio: Βίου βίῳ δεόμενον οὐκ ἔστι βίον. Et sic Lucas usurpat VIII. 4. XV. 12. 30. XXI. 4. Additur vero hic τοῦ κόσμου, ut intelligamus de iis agi, quæ ad vitam pertinent, non alterius sed hujus seculi. Nam id modo αἰῶνος τούτου, ut 1. Tim. VI. 17. modo κόσμου voce significatur. Rabbini עולם הזה. Syrus hic: דעלמא קנינא.

Καὶ θεωρῇ τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὑτοῦ χρείαν ἔχοντα) Defici necessariis. Exempla vide Matth. XXV. 35. Luc. XVI. 20. Jac. II. 15. ubi qui hic est χρείαν ἔχων dicitur λειπόμενος τῆς ἐφημέρου τροφῆς καὶ τῶν ἐπιτηδείων τῷ σώματι.

Καὶ κλείσῃ τὰ σπλάγχνα αὑτοῦ ἀπ' αὐτοῦ) Clauserit miserationem suam ab eo, id est, excluserit eum ab affectu misericordiæ. De voce σπλάγχνων vide Luc. I. 78. 2. Cor. VI. 12. VII. 15. Phil. I. 8. Col. III, 12. Philem. 7, 12, 20. Claudere ab aliquo est aliquem excludere.

Πῶς ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ Θεοῦ μένει ἐν αὐτῷ;) Quomodo esset in eo dilectio, quam Deus exigit? De voce μένειν diximus jam aliquoties.

De dilectione Dei quam postulat prima legis tabula, & ex qua redundare debet dilectio proximi alii intelligunt, quod Grotius de dilectione, quæ in proximum fertur, interpretatur; Rectissime autem de dilectione, qua nos Deus prosequitur, accipitur: ut tales, qui viscera misericordiæ claudunt erga egenum fratrem, non habent in se manentem vitam æternam; ita nec gratia vel dilectio Dei in illis ma- nere potest, quia immisericors judicium potius il- lum manet, qui misericordiam non fecit, Jac. III. 13. Nam de eo, quod non possit dilectio Dei acti- va locum habere in eo, qui fratrem non diligit, proximo demum capite acturus est S. Johannes: hinc in culpa, reatu, & consequentibus eorum, qui proximum non diligunt, occupatur, quod gratia Dei non fruantur, vitam æternam in seipsis non ha- beant, sed in morte maneant. Atque ideo vera dile- ctio proximi exemplo Christi & casu speciali in in- digentia proximi claudentis viscera misericordiæ illustratur, monemurque, ut non verbo vel lingua, sed opere ipso & veritate proximum diligamus, ne ob non dilectionem illam culpam homicidii, rea- tum mortis & exclusionem a gratia Dei & vita æ- terna incurramus: Sed per sinceram proximi di- lectionem de veritate regenerationis & gratiæ Dei certiores reddamur, & conscientiam tranquillam habeamus v. 19. nec non fiduciam ad Deum & gra- tiosam Dei exauditionem in iis, quæ secundum voluntatem ejus expetimus, utpote servantes do- ctrinam Divinam, quo pacto in ipso manemus, & cognoscimus, quod Deus ac dilectio vel gratia Dei MANET in nobis, nimirum e Spiritu, quem dedit nobis v. 24. Concludere autem jam hoc modo vi- detur Apostolus: Si charitas Dei obligat nos, ut ponamus etiam animas pro fratribus, multo magis nos obligabit ut illi egenti succurramus eleemosy- na. Grandis culpa, inquit Ambrosius l. 1. offic. c. 31. si sciente te fidelis egeat, si scias eum sine sumptu esse, fame laborare, ærumnam perpeti, qui præsertim ege- re erubescat. Viscera sunt symbolum paterni; imo materni amoris, Philem. vers. 7. ubi Hieronymus: Omnes filii parentum sunt viscera.

## 3:18
Verse 18.

My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.) He loves in word who proclaims that he loves his neighbor, but does not truly love. Opposed to him is the one who loves in truth, that is, truly and sincerely; he loves in tongue who gives the needy good words: but in deed is he who also helps him. Those who love in word are spoken of in the same way as aretalogists, who speak of virtue but do not possess it. To comfort a miserable person with good words is not evil, but it would be empty if you have the abundance to help him and do not use it, as we said at James 2:15-16. We ought to love both in spirit and in deeds. Those who think that the desire to live well is sufficient for salvation are refuted here. In the Manuscript it is in deed and in truth.

The scope is not to require the exhibition and beneficence of charity toward a brother for the sake of obtaining salvation, or to teach that the desire to live well is not sufficient for salvation, which Grotius has indicated that some teach. It is without doubt a calumny, which silently attacks our faith concerning our justification and salvation, that it is obtained only through faith without the works of the law, which is the very doctrine of the Apostle. Perhaps more subtly than solidly, those terms 'to love in words' and 'to love in tongue' are distinguished by Grotius: which others like to distinguish thus, that he loves in word who loves affection while bestowing nothing; but he loves in tongue who indeed bestows, but looking toward his own advantage. But it is more correctly said that John used words of the same or similar meaning, by which he might inculcate the matter more diligently, as in Hosea 6:5 in a not dissimilar sentiment. He declares what kind of love there ought to be, namely not verbal but real, not idle but industrious, not talkative but truthful, that is, not adulatory, feigned, and hypocritical, but sincere, cordial, and true, because such was Christ's, as here Cornelius. Our love, says Gregory the Great, Morals, book 21, chapter 14, must always be exhibited, both by the veneration of speech and the ministry of bounty. Cf. Jas. II. 15. & Bernard, sermon 50 on the Song of Songs.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Τεκνία μου, μὴ ἀγαπῶμεν λόγῳ μηδὲ τῇ γλώσσῃ, ἀλλ' ἔργῳ καὶ ἀληθείᾳ.) Verbo amat, qui prædicat a se diligi pro- ximum, non autem vere diligit. Ei opponitur is, qui diligit ἀληθείᾳ, id est, vere ac sincere lingua diligit, qui egenti dat bona verba: facto autem qui eum etiam juvat. Οἱ λόγῳ ἀγαπῶντες sic dicuntur, quomodo aretalogi, qui de virtute loquuntur, nec eam habent. Bonis verbis solari miserum non est malum, sed inane sit, si copiam habeas eum ju- vandi, nec utaris, ut diximus ad Jac. II. 15. 16. Debemus diligere & animo & factis. Refelluntur hic, qui ad salutem sufficere putant bene vivendi desiderium. In Manuscripto est ἐν ἔργῳ καὶ ἀληθείᾳ.

Scopus non est requirere ad salutem consequen- dam charitatis erga fratrem exhibitionem & bene- ficentiam, aut docere ad salutem non sufficere bene vivendi desiderium, quod sufficere qui doceant ni- mirum indicavit Grotius. Calumnia sine dubio, est, quæ tacite petit fidem nostram de justificatione & salute nostra, quod obtineatur tantum per fidem si- ne operibus legis, quæ est ipsissima Apostoli do- ctrina. Subtilius forte quam solidius illa diligere verbis & diligere lingua distinguuntur a Grotio: quæ alii sic distinguere amant, eum verbo diligere, qui dilectionem amat nihil tribuens; eum vero lingua, qui tribuit quidem, sed ad proprium com- modum respiciens. Rectius vero dicitur, Johan- nem usum vocabulis ejusdem aut vicinæ significa- tionis, quo rem diligentius inculcaret, uti Os. VI. 5. in non absimili sententia. Declarat, qualis dilectio esse debeat, scilicet non verbalis sed realis, non otiosa sed operosa, non linguax sed verax, id est, non adula- toria, ficta & hypocritica, sed sincera cordialis & ve- ra, quia talis fuit Christi, ut hic Cornelius. Dilectio nostra, ait Gregorius M. l. XXI. mor. cap. 14. sem- per exhibenda est, & veneratione sermonis & mini- sterio largitatis. Conf. Jac. II. v. 15. & Bernhardus serm. L. in Cant.

## 3:19
Verse 19.

And by this we know that we are of the truth) That maxim "know thyself" is great; many flatter themselves and think they are Christians when they are not. Therefore, we ought to examine ourselves diligently 1 Cor. XI. 27. Whether each person has only a desire to do good, or indeed the purpose that is required, he will know by nothing better than a perpetual series of deeds. Just as to be from God is to have a Divine disposition, so to be from the truth, that is, from the Gospel, is to be in agreement with the Gospel. In the Manuscript: Ἐν τούτῳ γνωσόμεθα.

From the love of one's neighbor, inasmuch as it flows from true faith, we know a posteriori that we are of the truth; which is not to be in agreement with the Gospel, but to be regenerated from the word of truth, and thus materially the same as to be from God; not to mention that some understand God or Christ by the truth, so that to be from the truth is to be from God or Christ, since these are interchanged. John XIX. 37 it is said, "He who is of the truth hears my voice," and John VIII. 47, "He who is of God hears the words of God." To which also, as far as the matter is concerned, the explanation of those returns who understand by the truth the veracity of God in his promises, so that they are of the truth who are children of the promise, Rom. IX. 8. If to be of the truth is to be in agreement with the Gospel, which Grotius maintains, and the love of one's neighbor ought to be in agreement with the Gospel, what this saying might be, we know from the love of one's neighbor that is in agreement with the Gospel, that we are in agreement with the Gospel.

And before him we shall persuade our hearts) That is, we shall tranquilize our minds with confidence in God. Persuading is opposed to that which follows, condemning. Concerning this use of the word to persuade, we have spoken at Matt. XXVIII. 14. The Syrian: we shall render quiet. Philosophers dispute much about the tranquility of the mind. But there is nothing that more truly tranquilizes the mind than a just persuasion of such great love of God toward us, that he destines eternal life for us.

Some connect these to the preceding, namely, that we know we are of the truth by the fact that in the sight of God, that is, in our conscience, which God alone sees, we persuade our hearts; that is, we persuade ourselves that we help him out of love for our brother alone. But the knowledge that we are of the truth is more correctly referred to the fact that our love is an argument and sign of that matter, but here, by the particle "and," another fruit of true love is taught, namely, that our conscience is tranquilized, insofar as it flows from true faith. Concerning which, the blessed Hunnius says: If at any time in the examination of temptations we are cited as if to the tribunal of God, we shall be able to appear before him with a broad mind and a peaceful conscience, certain that we have not offended our neighbor with greater sins that are repugnant to Christian charity. For although it is faith properly that renders hearts tranquil and peaceful; yet this very thing is attributed to charity subsequently and consequently, while from the true zeal and exercise of love a man gathers that his faith is not an empty persuasion, and thus he knows more clearly that he has true faith, and through faith, a propitious God in Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Καὶ ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν ὅτι ἐκ τῆς ἀληθείας ἐσμὲν) Magnum est illud monitum γνῶθι σεαυτὸν; multi sibi blandiuntur, & Christianos se putant, cum non sint. Ideo diligenter nos- metipsos explorare debemus 1. Cor. XI. 27. de se quisque an desiderium tantum bene agendi habeat, an vero quale re- quiritur propositum, nulla re melius, quam perpetua facto- rum serie cognoscet. Sicut ex Deo esse est habere Divinam indolem, ita ex veritate esse, id est, ex Evangelio est con- gruere Evangelio. In Manuscripto: Ἐν τούτῳ γνωσόμεθα.

E dilectione proximi, utpote quæ e vera fide flu- it, cognoscimus a posteriori, nos esse ex veritate; quod non est congruere Evangelio, sed ex verbo veritatis regenitum esse, adeoque materialiter idem, quod ex Deo esse; ut taceam quod nonnulli per veritatem Deum vel Christum intelligant, ut ex veritate esse sit esse ex Deo vel Christo, quum hæc permutentur. Joh. XIX. 37. dicitur qui est ex veritate audit vocem meam & Joh. VIII. 47. qui est ex Deo, verba Dei audit. Quo etiam quantum ad rem eorum explicatio redit, qui per veritatem intelligunt Dei veracitatem in promissis, ut ex ve- ritate sint, qui filii sunt promissionis, Rom. IX. 8. Si e veritate esse est congruere Evangelio, quod vult Grotius, & proximi dilectio congruere debet Evan- gelio quid hoc dictum fuerit, ex dilectione proximi Evangelio congrua, cognoscimus, quod congruamus Evangelio.

Καὶ ἔμπροσθεν αὐτοῦ πείσομεν τὰς καρδίας ἡμῶν) Id est fi- ducia in Deum tranquillabimus animos nostros. Opponitur πείθειν ei quod sequitur καταγινώσκειν. De hoc usu vocis πείθειν diximus ad Matth. XXVIII. 14. Syrus מפסינן quietum reddemus. Multa disputant Philosophi de animi tranquillitate. Sed nulla est res, quæ verius tranquillet ani- mum, quam justa persuasio de tanto Dei ergo nos amore, ut nobis vitam æternam destinet.

Nonnulli hæc ad superiora trahunt, quod nem- pe nos ex veritate nos esse cognoscamus, per hoc, quod in conspectu Dei, id est, in conscientia nostra, quam solus Deus videt, persuademus cordibus no- stris; id est, nobis ipsis, ex sola nos fratris dilectio- ne ei succurrere. Sed cognitio, quod ex veritate simus, rectius eo refertur, quod nempe argumen- tum & signum ejus rei sit nostra dilectio, hic vero per particulam καὶ alius veræ dilectionis fructus do- cetur, quod conscientia nostra tranquiletur, qua- tenus illa ex fide vera fluit. Quo de B. Hunnius: Si quando in tentationum examine velut ad Dei tri- bunal citabimur, poterimus lato animo pacataque conscientia coram illo apparere, certi, quod proxi- mum grandioribus peccatis, quæ charitati Christia- næ repugnant, non offenderimus. Quanquam enim fides proprie est, quæ corda reddit tranquilla & pa- cata; tamen hoc ipsum charitati ἑπομένως & ex consequenti tribuitur, dum ex dilectionis vero studio & exercitio colligit homo, fidem suam non inanem esse persuasionem, atque sic se veram fidem, & per fi- dem propitium in Christo Deum habere, liquidius cognoscit.

## 3:20
Verse 20.

For if our heart condemns us) It is accustomed to be said: The guilty man condemns himself by the day on which he sins. Seneca, epistle XCVII. Conscience convicts them and shows them to themselves, and epistle CV. Let him suffer punishment, whoever expects it. These cohere with the preceding. Not in vain did I posit a great good in that tranquility of mind. It is clear from those who are otherwise. Let them feel torments now from fear, who will one day feel much greater ones.

For God is greater than our heart) That second "for" is absent in the Manuscript, and rightly so. Nor does the Latin read, God has much greater punishments in readiness.

And he will know all things) Juvenal concerning the Gods: A man is better known to them than to himself.

Thales, being asked whether anyone doing evil could be hidden from God, said, not even the one thinking it, which agrees with what we have in Rom. 11. 6. He who condemns himself, there is no doubt that he ought to expect condemnation from God. For he does things which he either knows or thinks are not right. See what was said at Rom. XIV. 23.

This sentence is taken by Thomas Anglicus and others as Evangelical. If our heart condemns us, let us know that God is greater, who for the sake of the Son absolves from sins, so that we may prefer the sacrosanct promises of God concerning the remission of sins proposed in the Gospel to the accusation of our heart. But we easily admit the legal sense, which the blessed Hunnius also approved: Others, he says, follow a legal rather than an Evangelical sense, explaining the γνώμην of the Apostle in this way: If a man's own heart and conscience, being ill-aware of his sins, condemns him, how much more does God condemn him. He, however, who does not love his brother, is condemned by his own heart, therefore much more by God. He judges this sentence to be more genuine and more suitable to the purpose of John. For he opposes that accusation of the heart with a certain antithesis to the confidence of the pious of which he had just spoken. And the reason which the Evangelist subjoins to his pronouncement by way of demonstration agrees more with this explanation, while it is added: that God knows all things. For this entirely indicates that not only is a man's own heart well aware of its own sins, but God himself also knows all things, and therefore those sins, that hypocrisy, and that simulation of charity, and the silent hatred of the heart against a brother cannot be unknown to God in the impious. This also appears from the following antithesis: If our heart does not condemn us, then we have confidence toward God, implying clearly that this confidence is badly hindered by the accusation of the heart or conscience: and therefore it differs from the preceding member concerning the impious who are ill-aware of themselves. Similarly Cornelius a Lapide, q. d. If you cannot hide your hypocrisy from your heart, much less will you hide it from God, who is greater and deeper than your heart, and sees it more intimately, and is more present to it than you yourself are. If your conscience reproves and condemns you, how much more will God reprove and condemn you, who is the President and Judge of the conscience. So also Estius, That hypocrisy does not escape our conscience, however small and knowing few things, but is refuted by it; how much more by GOD, who is incomparably greater than our heart, and therefore knows all things. GOD is said to be greater than our heart in regard to knowledge, by which he not only embraces whatever is in our heart and our narrow conscience, but also all other hidden things, since he is everywhere present and penetrating all things. And the Syriac version also tends to this: But if our heart reproves us, how much greater is God than our heart? And Oecumenius: If we cannot hide from our heart, which is small, how could we be able to hide from GOD, who is present everywhere? Also St. Augustine in h. l. You hide your heart from man, hide it from GOD, if you can. And further: Let your conscience bear witness to you that it is from GOD. If it is from GOD, do not wish to boast of it before men, because neither the praises of men lift you to heaven, nor do their reproaches cast you down from there: Let him see who crowns, let him be the witness, by whose judgment you are crowned. Add Diadochus on Spiritual Perfection c. 100, who says, the judgment of God is, he says, far greater than our conscience. But there is no reason why we should expunge the particle ὅτι. We know it often abounds according to the Hebrew style, and the speech can easily be supplied in this way. For if our heart reproves us we know or ought to know, that God is greater &c.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Ὅτι ἐὰν καταγινώσκῃ ἡμῶν ἡ καρδία) Solet dici: Illo nocens se damnat quo peccat die. Seneca epistola XCVII. Coarguit illos conscientia, & ipsos sibi ostendit, & epistola CV. Det pœnas, quisquis expectat. Cohæ- rent hæc cum superioribus. Non frustra in illa tranquillita- te animi magnum posui bonum. Liquet id ex iis, qui aliter se habent. Tormenta nunc ex metu sentiant, sensuri olim multo majora

Ὅτι μείζων ἐστὶν ὁ Θεὸς τῆς καρδίας ἡμῶν) Illud secundum ὅτι abest in Manuscripto & bene. Neque legit Latinus, Deus multo majores pœnas in promptu habet.

Kaì γνώσεται πάντα ) Juvenalis de Diis : ! Notior est illis homo quam sibi.

Thales interrogatus, an quis male agens Deo latere posset, dixit, ne cogitans quidem, quî cum convenit, quod habe- mus Rom. 11. 6. Qui se damnat, haud dubium est, quin a Deo damnationem expectare debeat. Agit enim, quæ aut scit aut putat esse non recta. Vide quæ dicta ad Rom. XIV. 23.

Sententia hæc a Thoma Anglico & ab aliis acci- pitur ut Evangelica. Si cor nostrum nos condemnat, sciamus majorem esse Deum, qui propter Filium a peccatis absolvit, ut præferamus accusationi cordis nostri sacrosanctas Dei promissiones de remissio- ne peccatorum in Evangelio propositas. Sed fa- cile admittimus sensum legalem, quem approbavit etiam B. Hunnius : Alii, inquit, legalem magis quam Evangelicum sensum sequuntur, hoc modo exponen- tes γνώμην Apostoli : Si proprium cor & conscientia hominem de peccatis male sibi conscium damnat, quanto magis Deus illum condemnat. Is autem qui non diligit fratrem, condemnatur a proprio suo corde, multo magis igitur a Deo. Quam sententiam ma- gis genuinam, propositoque Johannis convenien- tiorem judicat. Nam accusationem illam cordis antithesi quadam opponit fiducia piorum de qua mo- do dixerat. Et ratio quam pronuntiato suo demon- strando subjungit Evangelista magis congruit cum hac explicatione, dum scilicet additur : Deum nosse omnia. Omnino quippe hoc subindicat, non tan- tum proprium cor hominis esse de peccatis suis sibi probe conscium, sed Deum ipsum quoque nosse omnia, idcirco illa peccata, hypocrisin illam, & charitatis si- mulationem, tacitumque cordis adversus fratrem odium in impiis Deo ignota esse non posse. Apparet hoc etiam ex antithesi sequenti : Si cor nostrum non condemnat nos, tum fiduciam habemus erga Deum, innuens videlicet eam fiduciam accusatione cordis seu conscientia male impediri : ac proinde membro præcedenti de impiis male sibi consciis differit. Simi- liter Cornelius a Lapide, q. d. Si tuam hypocrisin non potes celare cor tuum, multo minus celabis eam Deum, qui corde tuo major & profundior est, ac intimius illud videt, magisque illi præsens est, quam tu ipse. Si tua conscientia te reprehendit & con- demnat, quanto magis reprehendet & condemna- bit te Deus, qui est Præses & Judex conscientiæ. Sic etiam Estius, Hypocrisis illa non latet conscien- tiam nostram, quamvis pusillam & pauca scien- tem, sed ab ea redarguitur; quanto magis a DEO, qui incomparabiliter major est corde nostro, adeo- que omnia novit. Dicitur DEUS major corde nostro quoad cognitionem, qua non tantum com- plectitur, quicquid est in corde nostro, & angu- sta conscientia nostra, verum etiam alia omnia abscondita, cum sit ubique præsens & omnia pe- netrans. Atque eo etiam abit Syriaca versio : Quod si cor nostrum reprehendit nos, quanto ma- jor est Deus corde nostro? Et Oecumenius : Si cor nostrum, quod exiguum est, latere nequimus, quo pa- cto DEUM, qui nusquam non adest, latere valea- mus ? Nec non S. Augustinus in h. l. Cor tuum abscondis ab homine, absconde a DEO, si potes. Et porro : Perhibeat tibi testimonium conscientia tua quia ex DEO est. Si ex DEO est, noli illam velle ante homines jactare, quia nec laudes hominum te levant in cœlum, nec vituperationes inde te depri- munt : Ille videat, qui coronat, ille sit testis, quo judice coronaris. Adde Diadochum de perfect Spir. c. 100. qui, longe, inquit, majus est judicium Dei con- scientia nostra. Non autem est, quod expunga- mus particulam ὅτι. Scimus eam sæpe juxta Ebrai- cum stylum redundare, & facile suppleri potest oratio hoc modo. Nam si reprehendat nos cor nostrum scimus aut scire debemus, quod major est Deus &c.

## 3:21
Vers. 21.

Beloved, if our heart condemn us not) If we are conscious of no evil deed or plan. For it is a metonymy of the effect for the cause. These words, however, are to be understood of that man who knows the precepts of Christ well, and examines himself by them as if by a mirror. That former 'ἡμῶν' is absent in the Manuscript.

We have confidence toward God) We have confidence placed in God. We trust that we are most dear to him.

Similarly, according to Estius, he explains here what had been said above, we shall persuade our hearts before him, as the Vulgate has it, as if he were saying: If our own conscience does not condemn us, but dictates to us that we pursue our brothers with true and sincere love, exhibiting it by deed where there is need, we have confidence toward God, that is, we conceive great hope that he will not condemn us in his judgment. Others understand this as the confidence of approaching God and asking something of him. But the antithesis concerning God more than our heart reproving us, when our own heart reproves us, and concerning the confidence of our heart not being reproved by God, when our own heart does not reprove us, is clearer according to the former sense, and follows from the hearing of prayers in the next verse, which confidence a good conscience produces entirely; but insofar as our heart has been purified by faith, Acts 15:9. & the conscience has been cleansed by the blood of Christ from dead works, Heb. 9:14, and therefore it is most correctly explained in general in this way: If our heart does not reprove us in anything: although the former explanation can also be recalled to this sense: If, with Estius, the custom of the Apostle is admitted here, by which he is accustomed to extol one part of righteousness, meanwhile implying this condition, if there is no defect elsewhere. Such is that in chapter 5: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God. Or certainly because sincere and Christian love of a brother is not without love of God, therefore he who sees that love of a brother in his heart, sees also the love of God, and consequently is not reproved by his heart. Add, however, what we have said, that this is not to be ascribed to the consummation of our love, but to faith in Christ, by which the heart has been purified, from which love flows, Gal. 5:6, by whose grace there is no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, Rom. 8:1, whence this confidence is altogether undoubted.

But in vain and not without contradiction is confidence without certainty feigned by the Papists. It is to be noted, says Estius, that John does not say we are certain, but we have confidence: since even if our heart does not reprove us, it may still lie hidden in it that God, who is greater than our heart, reproves us. But John says we have confidence toward God.
