Therefore we must be certain of the grace of God: and even if something were hidden in our heart, that God does not impute it to us for Christ's sake; nor can that of Estius be admitted, that this confidence ought to be understood as being as great as corresponds to the testimony of a good conscience, because it does not rely on the good deeds of the conscience, but on the divine promise, and the merit of Christ, which our faith apprehends, so that even hidden faults are not imputed, concerning which all who have the same Spirit of faith with David sigh along with him: Who understands his faults? Cleanse me from hidden ones, O Lord, Ps. 19:12. Nor does Paul say anything about the uncertainty of grace, 1 Cor. 4:4, but that we are not justified before the tribunal of God by the fact that we are conscious of nothing in ourselves, since we are justified solely not by our good works and the consciousness of them, but by the merits of Christ and faith in them, even if, lest we fall from the grace of God and faith, believers must diligently guard against sins that devastate the conscience, 1 Cor. 9:27.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Ἀγαπητοὶ, ἐὰν ἡ καρδία ἡμῶν μὴ καταγινώσκῃ ἡμῶν) Si nullius mali facti aut consilii nobis simus conscii. Est enim Μετωνυμία effecti pro causa. Intelligenda autem hæc verba de eo homine, qui præcepta Christi bene novit, & ad ea se tanquam ad speculum explorat. Illud prius ἡμῶν abest in Manuscripto.

Παῤῥησίαν ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν) Fiduciam habemus in Deo positam. Confidimus nos ei esse carissimos.

Similiter juxta Estium explicat hic quod supe- rius dictum erat, in conspectu ejus suadebimus corda nostra, ut Vulgata habet, quasi dicat: Si non condemnat nos propria conscientia, sed dictat no- bis, quod fratres vera & sincera dilectione prosequa- mur, opere eam exhibentes, ubi opus est, fiduciam habemus erga Deum, id est, spem magnam merito concipimus, quod suo judicio nos non condemnabit. Alii de fiducia accedendi ad Deum & aliquid pe- tendi ab eo intelligunt. Sed antithesis de Deo magis corda nostra reprehendente, cum ipsum cor nostrum nos reprehendit, & de fiducia non re- prehendendi cordis nostri a Deo, cum ipsum cor nostrum non reprehendit nos, juxta priorem sen- sum est luculentior, & de exauditione precum sequi- tur commate proximo, quam fiduciam omnino parit conscientia bona; sed quatenus cor nostrum purificatum est fide, Act. XV. 19. & conscientia mun- data est sanguine Christi ab operibus mortuis, Ebr. IX. 15. ideoque rectissime in genere exponitur hoc modo: Si cor nostrum in nulla re nos reprehendat: quanquam etiam prior explicatio ad hunc sensum revocari possit: Si cum Estio Apostoli consuetudo hic admittatur, qua sic unam aliquam justitiæ par- tem solet extollere, subintelligens interim conditio- nem hanc, si aliunde non sit defectus. Quale est illud cap. V. Omnis qui credit, quoniam Jesus est Christus, ex Deo natus est. Aut certe quia sincera & Christia- na fratris dilectio non est sine dilectione Dei, pro- pterea qui videt in corde suo illam fratris dilectio- nem, videt & dilectionem Dei, & consequenter a corde suo non reprehenditur. Adde tamen quod diximus, non adscribendum id esse dilectionis no- stræ consummationi, sed fidei in Christum, qua cor purificatum est, ex qua fluit dilectio Gal. V. 6. cujus gratia nullum est κατάκριμα iis, qui sunt in Chri- sto Jesu, Rom. VIII. 1. unde παῤῥησία hæc indubita- ta omnino est.

Frustra autem nec absque contradictione a Pontificiis fingitur παῤῥησία sine certitudine. No- tandum, inquit Estius, Johannem non dicere certi sumus, sed fiduciam habemus: quoniam etsi cor no- strum non reprehendat nos, potest tamen in eo latere, quod Deus reprehendat, qui major est corde nostro. At Johannes dicit fiduciam nos habere πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν apud Deum. Certi ergo sumus de gratia Dei oportet: ac etiamsi lateret in corde nostro aliquid, Deum id nobis propter Christum non imputare; neque admitti potest illud Estii, fiducia hæc tanta debet intelligi, quanta respondet testimonio bonæ con- scientiæ, quia non nititur benefactis conscientiæ, sed promissione divina, Christique merito, quod apprehendit fides nostra, ne imputentur etiam oc- culta delicta, de quibus cum Davide suspirant omnes, qui eundem fidei Spiritum cum ipso ha- bent: Delicta quis intelligit, ab occultis munda me Domine, Psal. XIX. 13. Neque de incertitudine gra- tiæ quicquam Paulus, 1. Corinth. IV. 4. sed quod non justificemur coram tribunali Dei per hoc, quod nihil nobis conscii sumus, siquidem non no- stris bonis operibus, eorumque conscientia, sed Christi meritis, eorumque fiducia unice justifice- mur, etsi ne gratia Dei, & fide excidamus, fidelibus a peccatis sedulo cavendum sit, conscientiam va- stantibus, 1. Cor. IX. 27.

## 3:22
Ver. 22.

Καὶ ὃ ἐὰν αἰτῶμεν) Namely, with those conditions of which we spoke at Matt. XVIII. 19 and James I. 5, IV. 3.

Λαμβάνομεν παρ᾽ ἀυτῦ) From the promise in Matt. VII. 7, XVIII. 19, XXI. 22, Luke IX. 9, John XIV. 15, XV. 7, 16, XVI. 23, 24, 26. Moreover, here the present tense is used for the future, λαμβάνομεν for λήψομεν. So also below in the same matter, V. 15, ἔχομεν for ἕξομεν.

If our heart, he says, does not condemn us, we have confidence before God not only of escaping damnation and preserving saving grace: but also of obtaining and receiving whatever we have asked of God. Spiritual things indeed unconditionally, if we have asked in faith; but bodily things, in so far as they are salutary for us.

Ὅτι τὰς ἐντολὰς ἀυτῦ τηρῦμεν, καὶ τὰ ἀρεστὰ ἐνώπιον ἀυτῦ ποιῦμεν) That latter καὶ is explanatory. It is no wonder that God grants our prayers, because we diligently keep His precepts, and thus do what is pleasing to Him, Heb. XIII. 16. Those who are good are accustomed to gratify those who do things pleasing to them, John VIII. 28. The sense is the same as it is in this place, John IX. 31, where see the remarks.

Τὰς ἐντολὰς ἀυτῦ τηρεῖν we can understand either as the keeping of the divine word through faith, as in John VIII. 51, Christ says, if anyone keeps or guards my word, he shall not see death; or as the observation of the commandments of God: although the matter seems to come to the same thing: For the commandments of the Decalogue or legal ones are not to be understood precisely, but rather the commandment concerning believing in the name of Jesus Christ the Son of God is regarded, or concerning faith, the consequence of which is mutual love, just as He gave us the commandment, that we should love the brethren after His example, as the appended explanation teaches. The reason, therefore, that we are heard and receive what we ask, is that we observe the precepts of God concerning faith in Christ and the love of neighbor connected with it, and thus do those things which are pleasing and acceptable before Him. For τὰ ἀρεστὰ, which please God and are pleasing to Him, are faith, without which it is impossible to please God, Heb. XI. 6, and the love which flows from faith. These things are also a proof to us that our prayers are not in vain. Therefore, the observation of the divine law is not established as the cause of the hearing of prayers, but those observing the commandment concerning faith in Christ and mutual love are made certain from it of the hearing of their prayers, because they believe in the name of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, in whose name prayers must be made, John XVI. 23, and they love the brethren according to the commandment of Christ. Rightly the blessed Hunnius: Even if we were to grant this much to the Papists, that by the little word ὅτι the cause of the Apostolic statement is designated: they still could not obtain what they want. For because the divine Apostle, among these precepts which he mentions here, counts in the first place that which is concerning faith in Christ: in this respect, surely, the cause of the hearing of our prayers would rightly be attributed to the observation of the precepts of God by synecdoche: in so far, namely, as by believing in Christ we obtain and receive by faith, as an instrumental cause, those things which we ask and strive for from God. And therefore, lest the Apostle should seem to understand by the observation of the precepts only that initial obedience which consists in doing good works, he soon declares his mind more explicitly, as to what kind of obedience he understands, and what that principal commandment is, to whose observance these things are attributed. This, he says, is his commandment, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ. Whence the argument of Estius, that the commandments of God can be fulfilled by us, taken from this passage, by which he thinks our dogma is most openly destroyed, is utterly deprived of its strength. For what does this, that we can have faith in Christ and strive for love of neighbor, contribute to the fact that we can render perfect obedience to the divine law and fulfill the same in all things?

Latin:

Vers. 22.

Καὶ ὃ ἐὰν αἰτῶμεν) Nempe cum illis conditionibus, de qui- bus diximus ad Matth. XVIII. 19. & Jacob. I. 5. IV. 3.

Λαμβάνομεν παρ᾽ ἀυτῦ) Ex promisso Matth. VII. 7. XVIII. 19. XXI. 22. Luc. IX. 9. Joh. XIV. 15. XV. 7. 16. XVI. 23. 24. 26. Est autem hic præsens pro futuro, λαμβάνομεν pro λήψομεν. Sic & infra in re eadem V. 15. ἔχομεν pro ἕξομεν

Si cor nostrum, inquit, nos non reprehendat, non solum habemus fiduciam apud Deum eva- dendæ damnationis & conservandæ gratiæ salutife- ræ: Sed etiam impetrandi & obtinendi, quicquid a Deo petierimus. Spiritualia quidem simpliciter, si ex fide petierimus; corporalia autem, in quantum ea nobis salutaria sunt.

Ὅτι τὰς ἐντολὰς ἀυτῦ τηρῦμεν, καὶ τὰ ἀρεστὰ ἐνώπιον ἀυτῦ ποιῦμεν) Illud posterius καὶ est ἐξηγητικόν. Non mirum est, Deum precibus nostris annuere, quia præcepta ipsius ser- vamus sedulo, & sic facimus, quod ipsi placet, Ebr. XIII. 16. Solent qui boni sunt gratificari iis, qui grata ipsis faciunt, Joh. VIII. 28. Idem sensus, qui hoc loco est, Joh. IX. 31. ubi dicta vide.

Τὰς ἐντολὰς ἀυτῦ τηρεῖν intelligere possumus vel de custodia verbi divini per fidem, ut Joh. VIII. 51. Christus, si quis verbum meum τηρήση servaverit vel custodierit, mortem non videbit; vel de obser- vatione mandatorum Dei: quamvis res eodem re- cidere videatur: Non enim intelligi mandata De- calogi vel legalia præcise, sed respici τὴν ἐντολὴν de credendo in nomen Jesu Christi Filii Dei, vel de fide, cujus consequens est dilectio mutua, quemad- modum dedit nobis præceptum, ut nempe ad exemplum ejus fratres diligamus, subjuncta docet explicatio. Causa ergo, quod exaudimur, & ac- cipimus quod petimus, est, quod præcepta Dei de fide in Christum ejusque connexa dilectione pro- ximi observamus, adeoque ea facimus, quæ coram ipso grata & accepta sunt. Τὰ ἀρεστὰ enim, quæ Deo placent, eique grata sunt, fides, sine qua im- possibile est placere Deo, Ebr. XI. 6. & quæ ex fide fluit dilectio. Hæc etiam documento nobis sunt, preces nostras non esse irritas. Non ergo legis di- vinæ observatio causa constituitur exauditionis precum, sed præceptum de fide in Christum & di- lectione mutua observantes certi ex eo redduntur de precum exauditione, quod in nomen Filii Dei Jesu Christi credant, in cujus nomine preces fieri debent, Joh. XVI. 23. & fratres secundum manda- tum Christi diligant. Recte B. Hunnius: Ut ma- xime Pontificiis hoc daremus, per voculam ὅτι cau- sam pronuntiati Apostolici designari: nondum ta- men quod vellent obtinere possent. Nam quia Di- vus Apostolus inter hæc præcepta, quorum hic me- minit, primo loco numerat id, quod de fide in Chri- stum est: hoc sane respectu observationi præcepto- rum Dei per Synecdochen causa exauditionis pre- cum nostrarum recte attribueretur: quatenus scili- cet credendo in Christum ea impetramus & accipi- mus fide, velut instrumentali causa, quæ a Deo pe- timus & contendimus. Ideoque ne videretur A- postolus per observationem præceptorum intelli- gere duntaxat illam inchoatam obedientiam, quæ in bene operando consistit, mox explicatius mentem suam declarat, quæ qualiaque obsequia intelligat, & quod sit illud principale præceptum, cujus observationi hæc tribuantur. Hoc inquit est ejus præceptum, ut credamus nomini Filii ejus Jesu Christi. Unde nervo penitus destituitur argumen- tum Estii, quod præcepta Dei a nobis impleri possint ex hoc loco petitum, quo apertissime dogma no- strum destrui putat. Quid enim hoc quod fidem habere in Christum, & charitati proximi studere possimus, ad id facit, quod perfectam legi divinæ obedientiam præstare, eandemque per omnia ad- implere possimus.

## 3:23
Καὶ ἅυτη ἐστὶν ἡ ἐντολὴ ἀυτοῦ, ἵνα πιστεύσωμεν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ Υἱοῦ ἀυτοῦ, καὶ ἀγαπῶμεν ἀλλήλους) Καὶ ἅυτη here means 'and this therefore'. He could have said ἐντολαὶ, but he preferred to use the singular number, because one flows from the other. And this is that excellent σύνοψις, which if it be in the mind and in deeds, nothing further is required for eternal salvation, as we said at the passage Jac. II. & Gal. V. 6. Therefore there is in these few words סוֹף דָּבָר τέλος λόγου which is said in Ecclesiastes XII. 13. Πιστεύειν τῷ ὀνόματι is the same as εἰς τὸ ὄνομα below V. 13. תְהֵימֵן בִּשְׁמָא as the Syriac has it here. That indeed is to believe because of Christ or with Christ as the Author, God. Thus ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι, Matth. 18, 5. Luc. 13, 35. & elsewhere.

Καθὼς ἔδωκεν ἐντολὴν ) Namely God through Christ. Joh. 12, 49. whence we understand that in that commandment of loving men, the commandment of loving God is tacitly included. For we do this because of Christ Joh. 13, 34. 35. 15, 12. and therefore also because of God.

The Evangelist comprehends two things here, as the blessed Hunnius says, which the Savior requires of us, and by which the whole of Christianity is completed: namely, faith in the Son of God, and then mutual love. The former of which, namely faith as just now explained, is the cause of the hearing of prayers, insofar as it apprehends him in whose merit and name a certain and infallible hearing is promised. The latter, however, namely love, is not the cause, but the sign, that we are heard: insofar as from charity one may determine concerning faith, and from this concerning the hearing of prayer. But Grotius less correctly explains 'to believe in the name of Christ' as 'to believe God because of Christ or with Christ as author': since 'to believe to the name of Christ', 'into the name of Christ', and 'into Christ' are said κατ’ ἰσοδυναμίαν in the scriptures, and it is implied that one places faith in the merit of Christ, or apprehends it with true confidence, Joh. I. 12. cap. III. 16. seqq. cap. XX. 21. To believe in the name of Christ is to believe in Christ, says Estius here. A believer by believing receives Christ, says Bellarmine l. I. de justif. cap. 15. To believe in Christ, says Claudius Guillaudus in cap. VI. Joh., is to determine certainly with oneself that righteousness and eternal life come through Christ, and to adhere to him with all one's heart, with all one's soul, with all one's strength. The Apostle adds mutual love, not because he wishes that besides the commandment of faith and the commandments of charity, there are things necessary for us to observe for salvation, as Estius thinks in this place, but because both faith and charity are required in a Christian, and each is necessary by reason of the divine mandate: for faith without charity is not, even though faith is required in the Gospel, but charity in the law, nor is salvation obtained through charity, but through faith alone. St. John does not here treat of the manner of obtaining salvation, for which he requires faith alone, Joh. III. 16. cap. XX. ult., equally as St. Paul. He has discoursed concerning love as a sign and argument of true and saving faith and of παῤῥησία toward God, of the hearing of prayers, as also of the translation from death into life: but now he embraces both, faith and love, as divinely commanded, and that he may exhibit them as a σύνοψις of the doctrine of Christ, as Grotius speaks.

Latin:

Καὶ ἅυτη ἐστὶν ἡ ἐντολὴ ἀυτοῦ, ἵνα πιστεύσωμεν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ Υἱοῦ ἀυτοῦ, καὶ ἀγαπῶμεν ἀλλήλους) Καὶ ἅυτη hic valet hæc er- go. Potuerat dicere ἐντολαὶ, sed maluit unitatis numero uti, quia altera ex altera fluit. Et hæc est egregia illa σύνοψις, quæ si in animo sit & in factis, nihil ultra ad salutem æternam requiritur, ut diximus ad locum Jac. II. & Gal. V. 6. Itaque est in his paucis verbis סוֹף דָּבָר τέλος λόγου quod dicitur Ecclesiastæ XII. 13. Πιστεύειν τῷ ὀνόματι idem quod εἰς τὸ ὄνο- μα infra V. 13. תְהֵימֵן בִּשְׁמָא ut hic habet Syrus. Id vero est propter Christum sive Christo Autore Deo credere. Sic ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι, Matth. 18, 5. Luc. 13, 35. & alibi.

Καθὼς ἔδωκεν ἐντολὴν ) Nempe Deus per Christum. Joh. 12, 49. unde intelligimus in præcepto illo diligendi ho- mines præceptum diligendi Dei tacite comprehendi. Faci- mus enim hoc propter Christum Joh. 13, 34. 35. 15, 12. ac pro- inde & propter Deum.

Duo hic comprehendit Evangelista, dicente B. Hunnio, quæ Salvator a nobis requirat, & quibus universus Christianismus absolvatur : nempe fidem in Filium Dei, & deinde dilectionem mutuam. Quorum prius, nimirum fides modo nunc exposita, est causa exauditionis precum, quatenus apprehen- dit eum, in cujus merito atque nomine certa & infal- libilis exauditio promissa est. Posterius autem nem- pe dilectio non causa est sed signum, quod exaudia- mur : quatenus ex charitate de fide, ex hac de exau- ditione statuere licet. Credere autem in nomine Christi minus recte Grotius explicat credere Deo propter Christum vel autore Christo: quum crede- re nomini Christi, in nomen Christi, & in Chri- stum κατ’ ἰσοδυναμίαν dicantur in scripturis, idque innuatur in meritum Christi fidem collocare, vel vera fiducia id apprehendere, Joh. I. 12. cap. III. 16. seqq. cap. XX. 21. Credere in nomine Christi, est cre- dere in Christum, inquit hic Estius. Credens creden- do recipit Christum, ait Bellarminus l. I. de justif. cap. 15. Credere in Christum, inquit Claudius Guil- laudus in cap. VI. Joh. est certo apud se statuere per Christum contingere justitiam & vitam æternam, eique toto corde, tota anima, totis viribus adhærere. Addit Apostolus dilectionem mutuam, non quod præter fidei præceptum, & charitatis præcepta ad salutem esse nobis observatu necessaria velit, ut Estius censet h. l. sed quod & fides, & charitas in Christiano requiratur, & utraque ratione mandati divini necessaria sit: nam fides sine charitate non est, tametsi fides in Evangelio, charitas vero in lege requiratur, nec per charitatem, sed per fidem solam salus obtineatur. Non hic agit S. Johan- nes de ratione consequendi salutem, ad quam so- lum fidem requirit, Joh. III. 16. cap. XX. ult. æque ut S. Paulus. De dilectione tanquam signo & ar- gumento veræ & salvificæ fidei & παῤῥησίας ad Deum, exauditionis precum, ut & translatio- nis e morte in vitam disseruit: nunc vero utrum- que & fidem & dilectionem complectitur, ceu divinitus mandata, & ut doctrinæ Christi σύνοψιν, quemadmodum Grotius loquitur, ex- hibeat.

## 3:24
Ver. 24.

Καὶ ὁ τηρῶν τὰς ἐντολὰς ἀυτοῦ) The commandments of God given through Christ.

Ἐν αὐτῷ μένει καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν αὐτῷ μένει) That is, God and he are most closely joined together in love. See above II. 6. 24. III. 6.

Καὶ ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν ὅτι μένει ἐν ἡμῖν, ἐκ τοῦ Πνεύματος οὗ ἔδωκεν ἡμῖν) This is a most certain argument that God is in us, that is, that we are loved by God, because he has given us of his Spirit. Than which certainly nothing greater could be given to us in this life. That 'his' is understood here, but it is expressed below IV. 13. The Syriac, however, adds דרוחו here also. He passes here from the third person singular to the first person plural, because the discourse is sweeter when he joins himself to other Christians.

He does not express the cause of the indwelling of God in us and of us in God. But he explains who those are in whom God dwells, and who dwell in God, namely those who keep the commandments of God: and he explains the sign whence we may recognize that mystical mutual περιχώρησις, namely that God has given us of his Spirit, which is to be understood not only of the Apostles finally ministering the Spirit, by which they confirmed their doctrine, to which sense Estius does not dissent, but of any believers whatsoever and of sanctifying gifts, through which spiritual communion with God shows itself and is recognized. For if you find that you have charity, says St. Augustine in this place, you have the Spirit of God, and you are inhabited by the whole Trinity. He proves, says Cornelius a Lapide, those who keep the commandments, and therefore diligently that God remains in God and God in them, as if to say From the Holy Spirit and his charity, which makes us love one another, and from his other mighty works and gifts, as if from effects, we know that the Holy Spirit himself and consequently the Father and the Son remain and dwell in us. And thus it is clearly shown, as the blessed Hunnius observes on page 158, that Christian men can be most certain of their perpetual salvation, not indeed from some opinion of theirs conceived in a human way, but from the Spirit given to us, who for this reason is called the Spirit of grace, the Spirit of adoption, the pledge of the promise, and the earnest of our inheritance, Zechariah XII, Romans VIII, 2 Corinthians I, Ephesians I. Because he seals the certainty of the eternal inheritance in our hearts and bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God. Since this Spirit is truth itself, we safely believe this internal testimony of his, and from this Spirit we are certain that God remains in us by his grace, whereas on the contrary those who contend that one must doubt the grace of God even when reborn, openly accuse this testimony of the Holy Spirit of being a lie. As it is written, he who does not believe God makes him a liar, because he does not believe in the testimony that God has testified concerning his Son.

Which things are to be opposed to Cornelius, who contends in this place that we do not know that we have faith and the grace of God by divine faith, as we assert, nor even by physical and absolute certainty, as Catharinus wishes, but only by moral and conjectural certainty, such as comes from signs and conjectures. For that certainty is had partly from the internal testimony, concerning which Bernard says in Epistle 190 to Innocent: 'How does anyone dare to call faith an estimation, unless he has not yet received that Spirit, or is ignorant of the Gospel, or thinks it a fable, etc. You prattle to me of ambiguity, than which nothing is more certain.' But Saint Augustine says: 'Faith,' he says, 'is not held in the heart by conjecturing or opining, in which it is from him whose it is, but by certain knowledge with the conscience crying out.' I confess that definition of his (the Apostle) pleases me: 'Faith is the substance of things to be hoped for.' By the name of substance something certain and fixed is set before us, for it is not an estimation of faith but a certainty. And Thomas, part 2, question 112, article 5, to the second point: Whoever has faith is certain that he has it, both from signs, and those likewise indubitable, inasmuch as they are as necessary consequences and effects bear witness concerning the antecedent and the cause of saving faith: And Cornelius a Lapide notes on Rom. VIII. 16. that Andreas Vega, Ruardus, and Pererius who followed them, think that some very holy men, without special revelation, from the signs and effects of the Holy Spirit, which they experience in themselves as very frequent, clear, and effective, have a certainty—not indeed infallible, such that they would dare to swear that they are in the grace of God—but such and so great that it excludes all fear and dread of the opposite, not only from effect and confidence, but also from the intellect and persuasion: so that such men know as certainly that they are in the grace of God as we know and believe that Constantinople or Alexandria exists, from the fact that everyone everywhere says that those cities are and exist. What? That Jansenius in his concord ch. 134. explains the words of Christ in John XIV. 20. 21. concerning the spiritual union of the faithful with Christ, and its knowledge, by the present testimony of John alleged for that purpose.

Latin:

Vers. 24.

Καὶ ὁ τηρῶν τὰς ἐντολὰς ἀυτοῦ) Dei præcepta per Chri- stum data.

Ἐν αὐτῷ μένει καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν αὐτῷ μένει) Id est, Deus & ipse inter se amore sunt conjunctissimi. Vide supra II. 6. 24. III. 6.

Καὶ ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν ὅτι μένει ἐν ἡμῖν, ἐκ τοῦ Πνεύματος οὗ ἔδωκεν ἡμῖν) Certissimum hoc argumentum est, Deum esse in nobis, id est, nos amari a Deo, quod nobis dedit de Spiritu suo. Quo certe nihil majus in hac vita nobis dari poterat. Illud, suo, hic intelligitur, exprimitur autem infra IV. 13. Syrus autem & hic addit דרוחו A tertia persona singulari hic transit in primam pluralem, quia suavior est sermo, cum & se aliis Christianis adjungat.

Non causam immansionis Dei in nobis & nostri in Deo exprimit. Sed quinam illi sint, in quibus Deus, & qui in Deo manent, nimirum qui servant mandata Dei: ac signum unde agnoscamus illam mutuam περιχώρησιν mysticam exponit, nimirum quod Deus nobis dederit de Spiritu suo, quod non de Apostolis tantum denique illis ministrantibus Spiritus, quibus doctrinam suam confirmabant, cui sensui non abnuit Estius, sed de fidelibus quibusvis & donis sanctificantibus intelligendum, per quæ communio spiritualis cum Deo sese demonstrat & agnoscitur. Si enim inveneris te habere charitatem, inquit, S. Augustinus h. l. habes Spiritum Dei, & inhabitaris a tota Trinitate. Probat, inquit Cornelius a Lapide, servantes mandata, ideoque diligenter Deum manere in Deo ac Deum in ipsis q. d. Ex Spiritu Sancto ejusque charitate, quæ facit nos alterutrum diligere, cæterisque ejus virtutibus & donis quasi ex effectibus cognoscimus, quod ipse Spiritus sanctus ac consequenter Pater & Filius maneant & habitent in nobis. Atque ita dilucide ostendit, B. Hunno pag. 158. observante, homines Christianos de perpetua sua salute certissimos esse posse, non quidem ex sua quadam opinione humanitus concepta, sed ex Spiritu nobis dato, qui hac de causa dicitur Spiritus gratiæ, Spiritus adoptionis, pignus promissionis, & arrha hæreditatis nostræ, Zachar. XII. Roman. VIII. 2. Corinth. I. Eph. I. Eo quod obsignet certitudinem æternæ hæreditatis in cordibus nostris & testimonium de Spiritu nostro, quod simus filii Dei. Qui Spiritus cum sit ipsa veritas tuto credimus huic ipsius testimonio interno, & ex hoc Spiritu certi sumus, quod Deus gratia sua in nobis maneat, cum econtra qui dubitandum de gratia Dei etiam renatis contendunt, hoc Spiritus sancti testimonium aperte mendacii arguant. Sicut scriptum est, qui non credit Deo, mendacem facit eum, quia non credit in testimonium, quod Deus testificatus est de Filio suo.

Quæ Cornelio opponenda contendenti hoc loco non fide divina, ut nos asserimus, nec etiam certitudine physica & absoluta, ut Catharinus vult, sed certitudine morali & conjecturali tantum nos cognoscere, nos habere fidem & gratiam Dei, qualis est ex signis & conjecturis. Nam certitudo illa partim a testimonio interno habetur, de quo Bernhardus epist. CXC. ad Innocent. Quomodo fidem audet quis dicere æstimationem, nisi qui Spiritum istum nondum acceperit, quive Evangelium aut ignoret, aut fabulam putet &c. Tu mihi ambiguum garris, quo nihil est certius. Sanctus Augustinus vero: Fides, ait, non conjectando vel opinando habetur in corde, in quo est ab eo cujus est, sed certa scientia acclamante conscientia. Placet mihi fateor illius (Apostoli) definitio: Fides est rerum sperandarum substantia. Substantia nomine aliquid certum fixumque præfigitur, non est enim fidei æstimatio sed certitudo. Et Thomas p. 2. q. 112. art. 5. ad 2. Quisquis habet fidem, certus est, se eam habere, tum ex signis, iisque itidem indubiis, utpote quæ tanquam consequentia necessaria & effe- ctus testantur de antecedenti & causa fide salvi- fica: Et notat Cornelius a Lapide ad Rom. VIII. 16. quod Andreas Vega, Ruardus & eos sequutus Pere- rius putent aliquos viros valde sanctos sine speciali revelatione ex signis & effectibus Spiritus Sancti, quos valde crebros, claros & efficaces in se experiun- tur, habere certitudinem non quidem infallibilem, ita ut ausint jurare, se esse in gratia Dei, sed talem & tantam, qua omnem metum & formidinem oppo- siti excludat, non solum ab effectu & fiducia, sed etiam ab intellectu & persuasione: ita ut tales tam certo sciant se esse in gratia Dei, quam certo scimus & credimus Constantinopolin vel Alexandriam esse, ex eo quod passim omnes dicunt, illas urbes esse & existere. Quid? quod Jansenius in concord. c. 134. verba Christi Joh. XIV. 20. 21. de spirituali unione fidelium cum Christo explicet, ejusque cognitio- ne, præsenti Johannis testimonio eam in rem al- legato.

## 4:1 Argument
CHAPTER IV. ARGUMENT AND PARTITION.

He warns about testing the Spirits by a given certain γνωρίσματι [mark] of the spirits, which are from God and which are not from God, and he prophesies concerning the Anti-Christ, and teaches likewise concerning pious and impious hearers, then he exhorts to mutual love by various arguments: from the origin of charity, from our regeneration, from the charity of God declared by the mission of the Son, from the indwelling of God in those who acknowledge Jesus the Son of God sent as the Savior of the world, to whom the infinite charity of God is manifested for confidence in the day of judgment, in whom also reciprocal charity toward God is bound together with love of neighbor, since God requires both.

There are two parts: The first contains the exhortation concerning the testing of spirits up to verse 6. The second deals with the love of the brethren up to verse 21.

PART I. Exhortation concerning the testing of spirits.

Ver. 1.

Ἀγαπητοὶ μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε [Beloved, do not believe every spirit]) He calls prophecy, whether truly or falsely so called, spirit, 1 Cor. XII. 10. below V. 6. Just as under the Old Testament there were true prophets, and there were also false ones, so also under the New, 2 Pet. I. 20. 21. II. 1.

Grotius had explained this part of the present chapter up to verse 5 in notes published separately and in annotations subsequently appended to the four Evangelists, which exegesis of five verses we shall here add and examine together. At the beginning of the chapter he has these things there thus:

Ver. 1.

Ἀγαπητοὶ μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε, [Beloved, do not believe every spirit]) By the name of spirit he understands prophecy, whether true or false, as in 1 Cor. XII. 10. and shortly V. 6.

The Apostle warns again concerning false spirits, about which he had provided information in chapter II. But there in a didactic manner, here in an exhortatory one: there specifically concerning the Anti-Christs and the great Anti-Christ, here generally concerning any spirits whatsoever, to which, however, a prophecy concerning the great Anti-Christ is also subjoined: Cf. 1 Corinth. XII. 10. 1 Thessal. V. 21. 1 Timoth. IV. 1. The reason for the repetition is found in the reason subjoined for the necessary caution and testing, because, namely, many Pseudo-Prophets had already gone out into the world, which imposes a necessity upon St. John to remind them studiously concerning the same. Therefore, by spirits are understood not prophecy but Prophet, whether true or false, with John himself as the interpreter, and not precisely those who prophesy about future things; but in general Teachers, whether they announce future things, or deliver dogmas, or interpret the scriptures. Maresius rightly [in his] dissert. On the Anti-Christ. p. 107. Just as those who hold the public office of teaching in the Church are sometimes called Prophets in the Scriptures, even if they are not extraordinarily inspired regarding future events: So also can those be called Pseudo-Prophets who bring forth depraved dogmas, as do all Heretics, and who peddle the public doctrine. Concerning which Grotius himself, on Matthew VII. 15, comparing 2 Peter II. 1, says: Among the Hebrews, Prophets were called not only those who predicted the future, but also others who came forward to teach the people, especially if they claimed to have received mandates from heaven. Such was Simon and Bar-Jesus, whom Luke calls a false prophet in Acts XIII. 6. Christ distinguishes these Pseudo-Prophets from the Pseudo-Christs below in chapter XXIV. 5, 11, 24, such as was Bar-Kochba. Moreover, Teachers are called Spirits because, as the blessed Hunnius holds, they deliver what they deliver by a motion more than human, being driven, that is, by one or the other Spirit, whether good or evil. From the good, indeed, come true Teachers for proposing sound doctrine. From the evil, however, come evil Teachers for bringing forth and defending perverse dogmas. Therefore, the proposition of this Apostolic admonition is not to be of too much credulity and ease toward any Teacher whose doctrine you have not yet examined by the canon of the revealed word. What then is to be done? But test the Spirits, whether they are from God. Test them, however, by the word of God, which is that Lydian stone, exactly proving whether all Teachers and the dogmas of those who teach are from God or otherwise.

Ἀλλὰ δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα) Pseudo-Prophets under the Old Testament were distinguished by two signs: first, if they led men away from the true God, Deut. XIII. 1, 2. And that matter was both open and easy, pertaining to the understanding of every Israelite, Deut. XIII. 8. In the New Testament, it must be added, or if he leads men away from Jesus Christ. And that knowledge also is easy and open to every Christian. Therefore, this testing belongs to individuals, as in Rom. XII. 2, Eph. V. 10, Phil. I. 10, 1 Thess. V. 21. The other investigation in the Old Testament was from the event, whether it corresponded exactly to the prediction. And because this knowledge was not so easy, therefore under the Old Testament it pertained to the Sanhedrin: but under the New, to the assemblies of Bishops, having called those who had the gift of the discernment of spirits, as we said on the aforementioned passage of the first to the Corinthians XII. 10 and XIV. 29. Here, however, it concerns that former judgment exposed to all, and the very same rule is given which is in 1 Corinthians XII. 3, where see the remarks.

In the former exegesis these things only are read:

Ἀλλὰ δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα, but test the Spirits) Examine them diligently.

Concerning the testing of prophecies, which are predictions of future events, by their fulfillment, whether in the Old Testament by the Sanhedrin or in the New by the assembly of Bishops, we read nothing divinely commanded. All the faithful there could explore and gather who were false Prophets, both from the prophecies and predictions of the true Prophets of God and from their fulfillment, and they are commanded to do so everywhere, even if the Sanhedrin with a fuller and judicial inquiry had the penalty reserved. In the New Testament, however, there is nothing at all about a meeting of such Bishops, whom Grotius, along with the Papists, makes distinct from Presbyters. But it is evident from this precept, prescribed to all the faithful, that the reading of Holy Scripture is to be prohibited to no one, since the testing of teachers and doctrines from Holy Scripture has been enjoined upon all, and therefore the Roman Pontiff acts contrary to this precept of the Holy Spirit when he prohibits the same to the Laity without a special indult. Cf. 2 Pet. 1:19, ch. 3:2, 1 John 2:12, 13, 14, 1 Thess. 5:21, 2 Thess. 2:2, Eph. 4:14. Ei ἐκ Θεῦ ἐσιν) Whether they are truly from God, as they say. For some of them prophesy either by the instinct of the Devil or by private audacity, Deut. 18:22, Ezek. 13:2, 22:28. He had handed down the same thing in the same way in the l. c. Ei ἐκ Θεῦ ἐσι, if they are from God) Whether they are from God, as they boast they are. Many run, not sent to this by God, but excited by ambition, avarice, or even the impulse of the Devil. See Deut. 18:22, Ezek. 13:2, 22:28.

But these things are not to be restricted to prophecies alone: indeed, in the opinion of Grotius himself, they pertain properly in this place to the dogmas of false Prophets, such as were exposed to the judgment of all according to the same author: of which kind was the dogma concerning Christ, who came in the flesh, v. 2. For this was not a prophecy or prediction here. Ὅτι πολλοὶ ψευδοπροφῆται ἐξεληλύθασιν εἰς τὸν κόσμον) That is, they have shown themselves publicly. Ἐξέρχεσθαι εἰς τὸν κόσμον is the same as ἔρχεσθαι εἰς τὸν κόσμον, concerning which locution we spoke at John 1:9 and elsewhere. In the prior exposition these things were handed down thus: Ὅτι πολλοὶ ψευδοπροφῆται ἐξεληλύθασιν εἰς τὸν κόσμον, because many Pseudo-Prophets have gone out into the world) This age, as the Lord foretold, is especially fertile in such impostors. To go out into the world is said of both good and bad Prophets, and signifies to appear to the people, John Evang. 6:14, 10:36, 17:18, 12:46, 18:37, Eph. 1:15.

But by the impostors, of whom that age was fertile, Grotius understands Pseudo-Christs, who sold themselves as Christ. But St. John speaks in general about false Teachers, of whom we warned before that there were not a few at that time. To go out into the world is not said in one way. For although it denotes coming out into public, or as Grotius says, appearing to the people when the discourse is about Spirits in general: yet where it concerns Christ, such as the passages adduced here (besides Eph. 1:15, which is entirely ἀλλότριός), it denotes the coming of the Son of God from heaven into this world, and infers pre-existence before the advent into the flesh: concerning which, against the Socinians, it was treated in the treatise on the προϋπάρξει of the Son of God, and the individual passages were weighed.

Latin:

CAPUT IV. ARGUMENTUM ET PARTITIO.

Monet de probandis Spiritibus dato certo γνω- ρίσματι Spirituum, qui ex Deo, & qui non ex Deo sunt, & vaticinatur de Anti-Christo, docetque itidem de piis & impiis auditori- bus, dehinc hortatur ad mutuum amorem argumentis variis, a charitatis origine, re- generatione nostra, a charitate Dei, missione Filii declarata, ab inhabitatione Dei in iis, qui Jesum Filium Dei missum Salvatorem mundi agnoscunt, quibus infinita Dei chari- tas ad fiduciam in die judicii manifestatur, in quibus etiam reciproca erga Deum chari- tas cum dilectione proximi devincta est, quum utramque Deus requirat.

Partes duæ sunt: Prima parænesin de probatione Spirituum continet ad v. 6. Secunda de dilectione fratrum agit ad v. 21.

PARS I. Parænesis de probatione Spirituum.

Vers. 1.

Ἀγαπητοὶ μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε) Spiritum vocat prophetiam sive vere sive falso ita dictam 1. Cor. XII. 10. in- fra V. 6. Sicut sub Veteri Testamento fuere Prophetæ veri, fuere & falsi, sic & sub Novo, 2. Petr. I. 20. 21. II. 1.

Hanc capitis præsentis partem Grotius usque ad v. 5. annotatis peculiariter editis & annotationibus ad quatuor Evangelistas postea subjunctis expo- fuerat, quam ἐξήγησιν quinque versuum hic simul addemus & expendemus. Ad initium capitis hæc ita illic habet:

Vers. 1.

Ἀγαπητοὶ μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε, charissimi no- lite omni Spiritui credere) Spiritus nomine intelligit prophetiam sive veram sive falsam, ut 1. Cor. XII. 10. & mox V. 6.

Monet iterum Apostolus de falsis Spiritibus, de quibus cap. II. informationem tradiderat. Sed ibi in genere Didascalico, hic in Parænetico: ibi in specie de Anti-Christis & Anti-Christo magno, hic in genere de quibusvis Spiritibus, quibus tamen sub- jicitur etiam vaticinium de Anti-Christo magno: Conf. 1. Corinth. XII. 10. 1.Thessal. V. 21. 1. Timoth. IV. 1. Causa repetitionis habetur e ratione subjun- cta necessariae cautionis & probationis, quia scili- cet multi Pseudo-Prophetae exierant jam in mun- dum, quae necessitatem imponit S. Johanni stu- diosus de iisdem commonefaciendi. Per Spiritus ergo non prophetia sed Propheta sive veri, sive falsi intelliguntur, interprete ipso Johanne, non autem praecise illi, qui de rebus futuris vaticinan- tur; sed in genere Doctores, seu praenuncient futu- ra, seu dogmata tradant, aut scripturas interpre- tentur. Recte Maresius dissert. de Anti-Christ. p. 107. Ut Propheta interdum dicuntur in scripturis, qui publicum munus docendi sustinent in Ecclesia, etsi extraordinarie de futuris non inspirentur: Ita Pseudo-Propheta etiam dici possunt, qui prava fe- runt dogmata, ut Haeretici omnes, & publicam do- ctrinam καπηλεύουσι. Quo de Grotius ipse ad Matth. VII. 15. conferens 2. Petr. II. 1. Ebraeis Pro- phetae dicebantur, non tantum praesagi futurorum, sed & alii, qui ad populum docendum procedebant, praesertim si mandata coelitus data prae se ferrent. Qualis erat Simon & Barjesus, quem ψευδοπρο- φήτην Lucas vocat Actor. XIII. 6. Hos Pseudo-Pro- phetas Christus distinguit a Pseudo-Christis infra cap. XXIV. 5. 11. 24. qualis erat Barchochebas. Di- cuntur autem Doctores Spiritus, quia, ut B. Hun- nius habet, motu quodam plusquam humano tra- dunt, quae tradunt, acti videlicet ab alterutro Spi- ritu vel bono vel malo. A bono quidem Doctores veri ad proponendam doctrinam sanam. A malo autem Doctores mali ad ferenda & defendenda perversa dogmata. Ergo propositio hujus Aposto- licae commonfactionis est, ne nimia credulitate ac facilitate cuivis Doctori, cujus doctrinam nondum ad revelati verbi canonem examinaftis. Quid ergo faciendum? Sed probate Spiritus, num ex Deo sint. Probate autem illos ex Dei verbo, quod est lydius ille lapis, Doctores omnes & docentium dogmata num ex Deo sint vel secus exacte com- probans.

Ἀλλὰ δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα) Pseudo-Prophetae sub Ve- teri Testamento duobus signis dignoscebantur, primum si abducerent homines a vero Deo, Deut. XIII. 1. 2. Eaque res & aperta & facilis ad cujusque Israelitae notionem per- tinebat, Deut. XIII. 8. In Novo Testamento addendum est, aut si homines abducat ab Jesu Christo. Et ea quoque cognitio facilis est, & cuivis Christiano patens. Itaque hoc δοκιμάζειν est singulorum, ut Rom. XII. 2. Eph. V. 10. Phil. I. 10. 1. Thess. V. 21. Altera disquisitio erat in Ve- teri Testamento ex eventu, an is praedictioni ad amussim conveniret. Et quia haec cognitio non erat adeo facilis, ideo sub Veteri Testamento pertinebat ad Synedrium: sub Novo vero ad conventus Episcoporum, advocatis iis, qui donum habebant διακρίσεως πνευμάτων, ut diximus ad di- ctum locum prioris ad Corinthios XII. 10. & XIV. 29. Hic vero de priori ista dijudicatione omnibus exposita agitur, daturque eadem plane regula, quae 1. Corinth. XII. 3. ubi dicta vide.

In priori ἐξηγήσει haec tantum leguntur:

Ἀλλὰ δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα, sed probate Spiritus) Explorate eos sedulo.

De prophetiarum qua praedictiones futurorum probatione e complemento sive in Veteri Testamento Synedrio, sive in Novo conventui Episcoporum propria divinitus praecepta nihil legimus. Poterant illic omnes fideles, cum e verorum Dei Propheta- rum vaticiniis & praedictionibus, tum e comple- mento explorare ac colligere falsos Prophetas id- que passim jubentur, etsi synedrio cum pleniori & judiciali cognitione pœna reservata fuerit. In Novo vero Testamento nihil omnino de conven- tu Episcoporum talium, quos a Presbyteris diver- sos facit Grotius cum Papistis. Patet autem ex hoc præcepto omnibus fidelibus præscripto, lectionem S. Scripturæ nemini prohibendam esse, quum omni- bus injuncta sit Doctorum & doctrinarum e S. Scriptura probatio, adeoque huic Spiritus Sancti præcepto contrariari Pontificem Romanum, cum eandem Laicis sine speciali indultu prohibet. Conf. 2.Petr.I.19.cap.III.2.1.Joh.II.12.13.14. 1.Thess.V.21. 2.Thess.II.2. Eph.IV.14. Ei ἐκ Θεῦ ἐσιν) An vere sint ex Deo, ut dicunt. Nam qui- dam eorum aut Diaboli instinctu, aut privata audacia vati- cinantur, Deuter.XVIII.22. Ezech.XIII.2. XXII.28. Eadem tradiderat eodem modo l. c. Ei ἐκ Θεῦ ἐσι, si ex Deo sint) Sint ne a Deo, ut esse ja- ctantur. Multi currunt, non a Deo in id missi, sed exci- tati ambitione, avaritia, aut etiam Diaboli impulsu. Vide Deut.XVIII.22. Ezech.XIII.2. XXII.28.

Quæ vero non restringenda ad vaticinia sola: imo ex sententia Grotii propria pertinent proprie hoc loco ad dogmata falsorum Prophetarum, qua- lia omnium dijudicationi juxta eundem exposita erant: cujusmodi dogma erat de Christo, qui in carne venerit v.2. Non enim hic prophetia vel va- ticinium erat. Ὅτι πολλοὶ ψευδοπροφῆται ἐξεληλύθασιν εἰς τὸν κόσμον) Id est, publice se ostenderunt. Ἐξέρχεσθαι εἰς τὸν κόσμον idem est, quod ἔρχεσθαι εἰς τὸν κόσμον, de qua loquutione diximus Joh.I.9. & alibi. In priori enarratione ita tradita hæc erant: Ὅτι πολλοὶ ψευδοπροφῆται ἐξεληλύθασιν εἰς τὸν κόσμον, quoniam multi Pseudo-Prophetæ exierunt in mundum) Hoc seculum ut Dominus prædixit, imprimis ferax est impostorum talium. Exire in mundum tam de bonis quam de malis Prophetis dicitur, & significat apparere populo, Joh.Evang.VI.14. X.36. XVII.18. XII.46. XVIII. 37. Eph.I.15.

Per impostores autem, quorum seculum illud fe- rax fuerit, Grotius intelligit Pseudo-Christos, qui se pro Christo venditarunt. At S. Johannes in genere de falsis Doctoribus loquitur, quorum isto tempore non paucos fuisse antea monuimus. Exire in mun- dum non uno modo dicitur. Nam etsi notet in publicum prodire, vel ut Grotius, apparere populo cum de Spiritibus in communi sermo est: tamen ubi de Christo agitur, qualia sunt loca hic adducta (præter Eph.I.15. qui prorsus ἀλλότριός est) notat Filii Dei de cælis in hunc mundum adventum, & præexistentiam ante adventum in carnem infert: quo de contra Socinianos in tractatu de προϋπάρ- ξει Filii Dei actum, & loca singula expensa sunt.

## 4:2
Ver. 2.

Ἐν τέτῳ γινώσκεται τὸ Πνεῦμα τῦ Θεῦ) He says he will give a mark by which a Pseudo-Prophet, even if he does some stupendous things from a prediction, or predicts other things unknown to men, will be able to be known. Πᾶν πνεῦμα ὃ ὁμολογεῖ Χρισὸν Ἰησῦν, ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα ἐκ τῦ Θεῦ ἐσι) Namely, if the outcome also corresponds to the predictions. He who acknowledges Jesus as Christ in the prophecy itself, and prophesying in the name of Christ, he also retains the true God, to whom Christ leads us. To acknowledge Jesus as Christ is to acknowledge that Jesus of Nazareth is that promised Messiah. See above 2:22 and below 5:1. That ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα, by a transposition not infrequent in John, ought to be referred to that Ἰησῦν. But the Apostle wished here to add to the name of Jesus this title, who came in the flesh, as if he were saying, I mean that Jesus who came not with royal pomp and armies, but in a humble, abject state, and subject to many evils and finally to the cross. For these things are accustomed to be signified by the name of flesh among the Hebrews, who say בשר or בשר ודם, where they wish a perishable and fragile lot to be understood: But also among our writers, as Heb. 2:14, 5:7, 1 Tim. 3:16, 2 Cor. 4:11, Gal. 4:13. To have come in the flesh is the same as to have come with flesh. Thus the particle ἐν is often taken among the Hebrews, and below v. 6, Rom. 15:32, 1 Cor. 4:21, and elsewhere. But the Apostle did not add this in vain, because many, lest they should hold Jesus for the promised Messiah, were perhaps led by the things exposed to his contempt, which Christ himself had also foretold, Matt. 11:6, 26:31. This is what both formerly kept the Jews from acknowledging Jesus as the Messiah, and still keeps them. For a like reason the Apostle Paul, when he had said that Christ was preached by him, added crucified, and added besides that it was a σκάνδαλον to the Jews. For many were enemies of the cross of Christ, Phil. 3:18, or of Christ because of the cross. It is of a great spirit not only not to be offended by that cross, but also to count it an honor to be called to its participation, Acts 5:41, Phil. 1:29.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Ἐν τέτῳ γινώσκεται τὸ Πνεῦμα τῦ Θεῦ) Dicit daturum se notam, qua Pseudo-Propheta, etiamsi stupenda quædam ex prædicto faciat, aut alia hominibus incognita prædicat, no- sci poterit. Πᾶν πνεῦμα ὃ ὁμολογεῖ Χρισὸν Ἰησῦν, ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα ἐκ τῦ Θεῦ ἐσι) Nempe si & eventus prædictis respondeat. Qui Jesum pro Christo agnoscit in ipsa prophetia, & Christi no- mine προφητεύων, is etiam Deum verum retinet, ad quem Christus nos ducit. Jesum agnoscere Christum, est agno- scere, Jesum Nazarenum esse illum promissum Messiam. Vide supra II. 22. & infra V. 1. Illud ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα per trajectionem Johanni non infrequentem ad illud Ἰησῦν re- ferri debet. Voluit autem Apostolus hic nomini Jesu ad- dere hunc titulum, qui venit in carne, quasi diceret, eum dico Jesum, qui non cum Regia pompa & exercitibus ve- nit, sed in statu humili, abjecto, multisque malis ac postre- mum cruci obnoxio. Nam hæc carnis nomine solent signi- ficari apud Ebræos, qui dicunt בשר vel בשר ודם, ubi sortem caducam & fragilem volunt intelligi: Sed & apud scriptores nostros, ut Ebr.II.14. V.7. 1.Timoth.III.16. 2. Corinth. IV. 11. Galat. IV. 13. In carne venisse idem quod venisse cum carne. Sic particula ἐν sumitur sæpe apud Ebræos, & infra V. 6. Rom. XV. 32. 1. Corinth. IV. 21. & alibi. Non frustra autem hoc addidit Apostolus, quia mul- ti ne Jesum haberent pro Messia promisso, adducebantur forte ejus contemptui exposita, quod & Christus ipse prædixerat Matth. XI. 6. XXVI. 31. Hoc est quod Judæos & olim retinuit, quo minus Jesum pro Messia agnoscerent, & adhuc retinet. Pari de causa Apostolus Paulus, cum di- xisset a se Christum prædicari addidit crucifixum, addi- ditque præterea Judæis σκάνδαλον. Nam multi erant ini- mici crucis Christi, Philip. III. 18. sive Christi ob crucem. Magni est animi non tantum ea cruce non offendi, sed & ho- -nori ducere vocari ad ejus participationem, Actor. V. 41. Philip. I. 29.

## 4:2
Vers. 2.

In this is the Spirit of God known) As if he were to say, I will give you a mark by which you may distinguish a God-breathed prophecy from a false one, given by the Lord Himself, Matt. XI. 6, XXVI. 31.

Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ) That prophecy which shows us no other Christ than Jesus of Nazareth, see above II. 22.

Having come in the flesh, is of God) Namely, him who came, that is, appeared, in the flesh, that is, with flesh, just as below V. 6 Jesus is said to have come in water and blood. Thus ἵνα ἐν χαρᾷ ἔλθω, that I may come to you in joy, Rom. XV. 32, that I may come with joy; ἐν ῥάβδῳ ἔλθω, I will come in a rod, 1 Cor. IV. 21, I will come with a rod. Flesh, however, in the Hebrew manner signifies a humble state, Heb. V. 7; thus בשר is accustomed to be taken by the Hebrews, nor is ἐν σαρκὶ (in the flesh) placed otherwise, 1 Tim. III. 16; ἐν τῇ θνητῇ σαρκὶ (in mortal flesh), 2 Cor. IV. 11; δι᾽ ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκὸς (through the weakness of the flesh), Gal. IV. 13. Thus also flesh and blood are placed, Heb. II. 14. The reason which many men were putting forward why

they did not hold Jesus for the Christ, both here and in the Epistle of John the Presbyter, who was a disciple and imitator of the Apostle v. 7. it is expressed here, namely because Jesus had not come with royal pomp and arms to compel the refractory. This is that Spirit which deceived the Jews, and now also deceives, because they want a Messiah with human power, not content with divine power, which shines forth most in patience and torments, and therefore they twist the head of Isa. LIII, where the humble state and torments of the Messiah are described, rather than acknowledge the true meaning. On the contrary, they bring forth a true and divine prophecy who preach him as Christ, who is crucified, 1 Cor. I. 2. 3. II. 2. who are not enemies of the cross of Christ Phil. III. 18. and so are not offended by that cross, that they even count it the highest honor to be made partakers of that cross, Act. V. 41. Phil. I. 28.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκεται τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ Θεοῦ, in hoc cogno- scitur Spiritus Dei) Quasi dicat, dabo tibi notam, quam prophetiam θεόπνευστον a falsa dignoscas, ab ipso Domino datam Matth. XI. 6. XXVI. 31.

Πᾶν πνεῦμα ὃ ὁμολογεῖ Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν, Spiritus qui con- fitetur Jesum Christum) Ea prophetia, quæ nobis non alium Christum monstrat, quam Jesum Nazarenum, vi- de supra II. 22.

Ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα, ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστι, qui in carne ve- nit, ex Deo est) Eum nimirum, qui venit, id est, appa- ruit, in carne, id est, cum carne, quomodo infra V. 6. Jesus dicitur venisse in aqua & sanguine. Sic ἵνα ἐν χαρᾷ ἔλθω, ut veniam ad vos in gaudio, Rom. XV. 32. ut cum gaudio veniam, ἐν ῥάβδῳ ἔλθω, in virga veniam 1. Cor. IV. 21. cum virga veniam. Caro autem more Ebræo significat statum humilem Ebr. V. 7. ita solet su- mi בשר ab Ebræis, nec aliter ponitur ἐν σαρκὶ in car- ne, 1. Tim. III. 16. ἐν τῇ θνητῇ σαρκὶ in carne nostra mor- tali, 2. Cor. IV. 11. δι᾽ ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκὸς per infirmita- tem carnis, Gal. IV. 13. Sic & caro & sanguis ponuntur, Ebr. II. 14. Causa quam multi homines obtendebant cur

Jesum pro Christo non haberent, tum hic tum in Epi- stola Johannis Presbyteri, qui Apostoli discipulus & imitator fuit v. 7. hic exprimitur, nempe quia Jesus non venerat cum pompa Regia & armis ad cogendos refractarios. Hic est Spiritus ille qui Judaeos decepit, & nunc etiam decipit, quod volunt Messiam cum vi humana, non contenti divina virtute, quae in patien- tia & cruciatibus maxime emicat, atque ideo caput Esa. LIII. ubi status humilis & cruciatus Messiae de- scribuntur quosvis potius detorquent, quam verum sensum agnoscant. Contra illi veram divinamq; affe- runt prophetiam, qui praedicant eum Christum, qui est crucifixus, 1. Cor. I. 2. 3. II. 2. qui inimici non sunt crucis Christi Phil. III. 18. adeoque ea cruce non offen- duntur, ut etiam summo honori ducant ejus crucis reddi participes, Act. V. 41. Phil. I. 28.

## 4:3
Ver. 3.

And every spirit that does not confess Jesus Christ having come in the flesh, is not of God, and this is that of the Antichrist) The prophecy of him who in the prophecy itself does not acknowledge Jesus as Christ, because he does not bring it in the name of Jesus, is not θεόπνευστος (God-breathed). Indeed, on the contrary, such a prophecy builds a way for that great and eminent Anti-Christ. In that ὃν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα (having come in the flesh) is the reason why those impostors deny that Jesus of Nazareth is the Christ. And the disciple of this Apostle, Polycarp, rightly expressed the sense of this passage in his epistle to the Philippians with these words: For everyone who does not confess Jesus Christ having come in the flesh, is an antichrist, and whoever does not confess the testimony of the cross, is of the Devil: Where flesh and cross are placed in an equal position, because the cross is the complement of the flesh, that is, the humble state of Christ. However, it seems that in that passage of Polycarp, by some error of the scribes or out of hatred for Marcion, ἐληλυθέναι was written instead of ἐληλυθότα, since it is evident that Polycarp had these words of John in his memory when he wrote it. Moreover, ἐληλυθότα is somewhat clearer than if you were to say ἐληλυθέναι, although the latter can be taken in that sense. For he who acknowledges Jesus as Christ, he acknowledges that the Messiah did not come with Royal pomp, but in the flesh. And thus, if we take Ἰησοῦν, it will have been added not necessarily, but ἐξηγητικῶς (explanatorily), so that it may be understood that the Christ who came in the flesh is not different from Jesus of Nazareth. For the same reason, it can be doubted whether Polycarp wrote ἀντιχρίστου ἐστὶ just as John did: This is that of the Antichrist. It is of the Anti-Christ, that is, he serves the Anti-Christ, he is of the Anti-Christ's Spirit, as Cyprian cites this passage of John. In the Manuscript only, it is: He who does not confess Jesus, is not of God. But what Socrates says in Ecclesiastical History VII. 32, that πᾶν πνεῦμα, ὃ λύει τὸν Ἰησοῦν (every spirit that dissolves Jesus) was written here from the beginning, but was removed by the Nestorians: Although I do not think that is true, I nevertheless acknowledge that this reading is ancient, not only from the Latin Interpreter, but also from Irenaeus III. 18. But I think it was not originally written so by John, but changed, so that it might agree with those of the Gnostics, who said that Jesus was one, Christ another, and the Monogenes another. See Irenaeus in the cited place, and our remarks in the preface to the Gospel of John. John, as here, so elsewhere is accustomed to oppose contraries to contraries, with almost the same words, as in the Gospel III. 36, V. 10, and here above IV. 2.

In the previous commentary, the same things had been proposed almost thus:

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Καὶ πᾶν πνεῦμα ὃ μὴ ὁμολογεῖ Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν σαρκὶ ἐλη- λυθότα, ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐκ ἔστι, καὶ τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ τοῦ Ἀντιχρίστου) Pro- phetia ejus qui in ipsa Prophetia Jesum pro Christo non agnoscit, quia eam non affert in nomine Jesu, non est θεό- πνευστος. Imo contra talis prophetia viam struit magno isti & eximio Anti - Christo. In illo ὃν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα causa est, cur illi impostores negent Jesum Nazarenum esse Christum. Et recte hujus loci sensum expressit hujus Apo- stoli discipulus Polycarpus in epistola ad Philippenses his verbis : Πᾶς γὰρ ὃς ἂν μὴ ὁμολογῇ Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα, ἀντίχριστός ἐστιν καὶ ὃς μὴ ὁμολογῇ τὸ μαρτύριον τοῦ σταυροῦ, ἐκ τοῦ Διαβόλου ἐστί: Ubi pari loco ponuntur caro & crux, quia crux est complementum carnis, id est sta- tus humilis Christi. Videtur autem in illo Polycarpi lo- co errore quodam exscribentium aut odio Marcionis scri- ptum ἐληλυθέναι pro ἐληλυθότα, cum apertum sit Polycar- pum hæc verba Johannis in memoria habuisse, cum id scri- beret. Est autem ἐληλυθότα aliquanto clarius quam si dicas ἐληλυθέναι, quanquam hoc in illum sensum accipi potest. Nam qui Jesum agnoscit pro Christo, is agnoscit Messiam non cum pompa Regia venisse, sed in carne. At- que ita si accipiamus Ἰησοῦν, erit non necessario, sed ἐξηγη- τικῶς additum, ut intelligatur eum Christum qui in carne venit, non alium esse ab Jesu Nazareno. Pari de causa du- bitari potest, annon scripserit Polycarpus ἀντιχρίστου ἐστὶ sicut Johannes : Τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ Ἀντιχρίστου. Est Anti-Christi, id est, Anti-Christo servit, est de Anti-Christi Spiritu, ut ci- tat hunc Johannis locum Cyprianus. In Manuscripto tan- tum, hic est : Ὁ μὴ ὁμολογεῖ τὸν Ἰησοῦν, ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐκ ἔστι. Quod autem Socrates dicit Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ VII. 32. ab initio hic scriptum fuisse πᾶν πνεῦμα, ὃ λύει τὸν Ἰησοῦν, sed a Nestorianis id sublatum: Id quanquam verum non arbitror, agnosco tamen istam lectionem esse veterem non ex Latino tantum Interprete, sed & ex Irenæo III. 18. Sed arbitror non ita primitus scriptum ab Johanne, sed muta- tum, ut congrueret in Gnosticorum illos, qui alium dice- bant esse Jesum, alium Christum, alium Μονογενῆ. Vide Irenæum dicto loco, & nostra in anteloquio ad Evange- lium Johannis. Johannes ut hic ita alibi solet contraria contrariis opponere, verbis prope iisdem, ut in Evange- lio III. 36. V. 10. hic supra IV. 2.

In priori commentatione eadem fere sic proposi- ta fuerant:

## 4:3
Vers. 3.

And every spirit that does not confess Jesus Christ) Every prophecy which denies that Jesus is the promised Messiah. Having come in the flesh) Relying on this argument, that Jesus came in a humble state, and one subject to the greatest evils. Is not of God) That prophecy is not divinely inspired, but false and fallacious. Polycarp, a disciple of this Apostle, in his epistle to the Smyrnaeans: For everyone who does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is an anti-Christ, and whoever does not confess the testimony of the cross is of the Devil, where you see that by those words 'to have come in the flesh' the cross is signified, as we have already said. And this is that of the Anti-Christ) This spirit, namely, here, namely, the Spirit. This Spirit or this prophecy will be in an eminent way proper to that eminent Anti-Christ, that is, Barchochebas, as we just said.

In which we find these things wanting: I. The passages Matt. XI. 6. chap. XXVI. 31. are falsely adduced, as if they provided a mark by which you might distinguish a divinely inspired prophecy from a false one. For in the former passage those are called blessed who are not scandalized in Christ, which is a meiosis, in this sense: those who believe in him without the scandal of the cross of Christ. In the latter, it concerns the disciples of Christ who were scandalized by his cross, not false Prophets.

II. The prophecy is not to be understood according to the Grotian use of the word, as if it were a prediction, when a different Christ is shown than Jesus of Nazareth, but it is a false dogma, and a denial of the true Christ.

III. It is not a question here of another Messiah or Pseudo-Christ, or a prophecy or prediction about another who is to come, who is the true Messiah, different from Jesus of Nazareth; but of such a false Teacher who does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, that is, that the Word or Son of God has been incarnated, or that the eternal life, which was with the Father, has appeared in assumed flesh, which is the antithesis to the Apostolic thesis proposed at the beginning of the Epistle, that is, who denies the incarnation of the Son of God, such as Cerinthus, Ebion, and other heretics were in the age of St. John.

IV. Therefore, those things which were joined together by John are badly torn apart by Grotius. There is no talk here of Pseudo-Christs or their preceding Pseudo-Prophets: Nor is it established that any Pseudo-Prophet in the time of St. John predicted that a Messiah was to come, who, upon arriving, claimed to be the Messiah, when in reality he was an impostor; so far is it from the case that many such false Prophets have gone out into the world: But false Teachers are noted, who did not confess, that is, denied, that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh. He exchanges Christ and the Son of God in a certain way, as is clear from the comparison of chap. II. 22. 23., because

it was certain that the Son of God would be the Messiah, to whom the ends of the earth were given as an inheritance from Psalm II. Therefore he notes those who denied the coming of the Son of God in the flesh, such as the Cerinthians and Ebionites.

V. By the word 'in the flesh' is not designated a humble state in the abstract, as Grotius wants with Socinus, but in the concrete, human nature, to which fragility and the form of a servant and a humble state happen, which, as has been shown in its proper place regarding other passages John I. 14, 1 Tim. III. 16, Heb. II. 14, so it holds here also because of the parallelism. He prefers, however, to say 'in the flesh' rather than 'into flesh', lest it be imagined that afterwards, when the Son of God had been incarnated, he no longer remained flesh, but departed into Deity, or that instead of true flesh there was some mere phantom, just as Marcion feigned the latter, and Eutyches and the fanatics the former. Nor indeed could the Son of God have appeared in the flesh as a being by nature bodiless and fleshless, unless he had come into the flesh, or had assumed flesh or human nature. Add that the particle 'in' is sometimes used for 'into', Mark I. 15, Luke I. 17, 1 Thess. IV. 3, 1 John IV. 9, Heb. IV. 17. Whence Drusius on this passage Thus we read ἐν οἴκῳ ἰέναι for εἰς οἶκον, to go home. Indeed, ἐν and εἰς alternate in the Attic dialect, just as the Hebrew ב is used for ל, and denotes motion to a place, Levit. XVI, 22. Nor do we deny that St. John used that phrase peculiarly, so that he might look at once to the office of Christ and the οἰκονομία of salvation, which was consummated in the days of his flesh: That Jesus Christ came in the flesh by being born, growing, teaching, obeying and serving, suffering, dying, rising again, etc. Heb. V. 7. chap. X. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. 19. Psalm XL. 8. 9. Although indeed by the name of flesh infirmities are sometimes connoted, as Gal. IV, 13, yet infirmities alone without the nature itself in the abstract are nowhere easily called so: concerning Christ certainly that is not found. But in the passage 1. Corinth. IV. 11, the added epithet θνητὴ denotes infirmity and mortality, not the word σαρκός itself. But that the word for flesh occurs everywhere for the nature itself simply, no sane person will deny, see Gen. VI. 12. 13. Isa. XL. 5. Joel II. 28. Rom. III. 20. As to the passage 1. John V. 6, it is evident from the preceding context that the particle ἐν is interchanged with διὰ, which sense also occurs in Luke I. 17, 1. Corinth. X. 2. But that is a particular case, and διὰ will not easily be found for μετὰ anywhere in the New Testament.

VI. The Apostle does not properly rebuke the Jews here, nor were they ignorant of, or did they deny, that Jesus had come in the flesh in the Grotian sense, that is, without pomp, external splendor, and arms, since for that reason they were unwilling to acknowledge him as the Messiah. But the Evangelist notes those heretics who were denying the truth of the person of Christ and of the cross.

VII. The passage of Polycarp, who was indeed Bishop of the Smyrneans, but left an epistle not to the Smyrneans but to the Philippians, as is evident from Jerome, Eusebius, and the published epistle (which error of memory Grotius nevertheless corrected in later annotations), does not teach that these are synonyms for him, to have come in the flesh and to have sustained the cross, but implies that two distinct heresies were noted by him, of which the one did not confess Jesus Christ, who came in the flesh, the other did not confess the testimony of the cross: Inasmuch as the Ebionites attacked the person of Christ, the Basilidians said that Jesus was not crucified by the Jews, but Simon of Cyrene in his place, which is also the delirium of Mahomet: but the Cerinthians then distinguished Jesus from Christ, as two persons, which heresy by a certain reasoning afterwards the Nestorians made their own, who dissolved the person; then they denied that Christ had suffered, because he flew away from Jesus, into whom he had descended at his baptism, and thus they did not admit that Christ had risen again, but only Jesus. There were also others who said that Christ did not undergo death in the reality of the thing, but only in the opinion of men as is evident from the Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans. What? That Marcion, who taught that Christ had appeared and suffered only in appearance, lived in the time of Polycarp, whom the holy martyr, when he met him, called the firstborn of the Devil. The things which are amended in Polycarp by Grotius are merely precarious, and rest upon no authority of the Codices.

But concerning that reading, 'who dissolves Jesus,' we easily agree that it is not genuine, although it expresses the thing itself, which pertains to that dissolution of the person of the Cerinthians, of which we have already spoken. Nor does Estius obscurely acknowledge the truth of the Greek reading: 'And every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not of God.' In place of this sentence, in the Greek and Syriac, the member opposite to the former is read: 'And every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not of God.' Except that the Syrian does not add 'Christ.' Cyprian supports the Greek reading, who in book II against the Jews, chapter 8, reads thus: 'But he who denies that he has come in the flesh (supply from the former member 'Jesus Christ') is not of God.' But indeed Irenaeus, who is older than Cyprian, expressly refers to the Latin reading, with the addition, however, of the word 'Christ,' in book III, chapter 18. Thus also the other Latins read, namely Leo the Pontiff, epistle X to Flavian, chapter 5. Prosper, book I on the calling of the Gentiles, chapter 23. Cassian, book V on the incarnation, chapter 10, and Bede in his commentary. To these I add Cyril the Greek in his book on the right faith to the Queens. Moreover, Augustine, treating this passage, explains both readings, so that it sufficiently appears that both had been read by him. Indeed, it is very likely, especially from Irenaeus, that the Greek Codices once had that which is in ours. And Socrates clearly testifies to this in book VII of his history, chapter XXXII. For he says that this was written in the ancient copies of this epistle, at any rate the Greek ones. But, he says, all who were striving to separate the Divinity from the humanity of Christ did not hesitate to delete and remove this sentence from the ancient copies. And he adds: Wherefore the ancient interpreters signified the same thing, namely that there were certain ones who had depraved that epistle, so that they might separate the man from God in Christ. These are his words. Estius indeed suspects that both were written, because Augustine explains both, and Tertullian asserts the Greek in his book on the flesh of Christ, chapter 24, and book III against Marcion, chapter 8; but the Latin in his book against the Psychics, chapter 2, and both that and this in book V against Marcion, chapter 16. But these do not yet suffice, unless they are supported by the authority of the Greek Codices, which cannot be produced here. But these things are paraphrased.

VIII. That limitation, if events also correspond to the predictions, is born in the brain of Grotius, and is not indicated by a single point in the text. But it is devised for that end, so that it may sustain the claim that a prophecy is hinted at here. St. John means this: that every spirit or teacher who confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God, provided he does not deny other things which have been handed down in Scripture concerning Jesus Christ, although those things are comprised in his advent in the flesh, connoted by that phrase in the economy of salvation. Similarly, the gloss about his prophet, who does not acknowledge Jesus as the Christ in prophecy, is a fabrication. For there is nothing here about prophecy or prediction, much less about such a prophecy by which the faith that Jesus is the Christ is taken away.

IX. Vain and futile, therefore, is the nonsense that Grotius trifles about a spirit or prophecy in an eminent way proper to the Anti-Christ. For St. John did not designate here any prophets of the Anti-Christ prophesying about him.

X. The most vain of all is the application of the Anti-Christ to Barchocheba, and of the spirit of the Anti-Christ to the prophecies about Barchocheba. For Barchocheba has nothing to do with this, as has already been said abundantly regarding chapter II, who was neither in power nor in act in the nature of things in the time of John, and emerged finally under Hadrian long after the departure of St. John, namely in the year of the Lord 130. Nor did Barchocheba make his progress among Christians, who had previously given their name to Christ in any way, but only among the Jews, the enemies of the Christian name, as history testifies. Nor is any prophecy about him looked to in this place, nor could one be produced from history that could have anything to do with this. Those glosses are mere trifles of a trifler, vainer than Sicilian nonsense.

We now subjoin the commentary of the blessed Hunnius, which is far more solid: The word 'Jesus Christ' signifies not a bare word but the incarnate one, and embraces his two natures together. Furthermore, 'to come' here does not signify that one who was previously absent locally now approaches from a distance. But Jesus Christ is said to come in the flesh when the Word, proceeding as it were from his secret seat, manifests himself on earth having assumed visible flesh. And because it is not without cause, but on account of the office of redemption, that he comes in that great way in the flesh: therefore the office also, for the sake of which the incarnation itself was done, is included here by consequence, so that the meaning of the Apostolic canon is this: Every spirit, that is, every teacher or preacher, who truly and from the heart confesses that Jesus Christ has come into this world, not by descending locally from the heavens, but by appearing visibly in assumed flesh, and indeed has come to this end, that he might deliver us men from eternal death: that spirit or teacher is truly of God, and teaches and professes these things from God. But the blessed Hunnius rightly adds: That the rule of John is to be accepted according to the subject matter. For he speaks especially of those articles which properly concern the acknowledgment of Christ. Therefore, this is what the Apostle's canon means: that whoever thinks and teaches concerning Christ Jesus, his person, and his office according to the prescribed rule, is to be heard in those principal chapters concerning the knowledge of Christ, and is to be held as sincere in them. Meanwhile, it does not deny that there may be other errors which do not touch upon the article concerning Christ's person and office, which also ought to be judged by other canons set forth in the scripture of the Prophets and Apostles.

Estius limits the Johannine rule thus: that every doctrine, and consequently every teacher, who confesses and teaches that the Son of God was truly made man, and that this is Jesus, the promised Messiah, is from God, namely in that part in which he teaches this. Which is to say nothing other than that such doctrine is from God: and also that he who so confesses and teaches is, in that part of his doctrine, from God. For certainly even heretics are not entirely lacking the supernatural gift of faith regarding the true articles of faith which they still retain, teach, and defend, although they do not have the integral and therefore Catholic faith. But this opinion, that heretics have the supernatural gift of faith and are from God, is by no means to be admitted. For heresy is a work of the flesh, Gal. V.

ὃ ἀκηκόατε ὅτι ἔρχεται.] Which Spirit Christ had predicted would one day come. For this is the spirit of those Pseudo-Prophets, of whom it is treated in Matt. 24, 11. 24. ἔρχεται is present in sound, future in sense, and refers to that time when Christ predicted this. So also above II, 18.

Καὶ νῦν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἐσὶν ἤδη.] In various places such Pseudo-Prophets already show themselves, who say that the Messiah is about to come with the power of this world.

In the other previously published commentary these things are thus: ὃ ἀκηκόατε, ὅτι ἔρχεται, of whom you have heard, that he comes.] Which most false and most harmful prophecy I have already predicted to you would come. See above ch. II. Καὶ νῦν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἐσὶν ἤδη, and now already he is in the world.] That fallacy already now through other lesser instruments, such as we named for the second chapter, tests its strength, about to arrive shortly at that highest pinnacle.

The most vain commentator finally understood concerning the Prophets predicting Barchochebam, what he had previously received concerning the lesser instruments of similar fallacy, both most falsely. For neither is anyone of the Pseudo-Prophets read to have published prophecies about him in the time of John; nor are they commemorated to have preluded to the Anti-Christ or rather the Pseudo-Christ of the lesser nations at that time. Concerning the passage of Matt. XXIV, it was spoken of before. Which S. John recalls to memory for our text, what Paul had predicted concerning the Great Anti-Christ, 2 Thess. II, and the Prophet Daniel ch. XI, XII, but he does not thus look back at his own prediction. Nor indeed had he predicted a prophecy or a Prophet concerning the Anti-Christ before, but the Anti-Christ himself. Ἔρχεται is taken for the future on account of certainty, as Cajetan observes, although Erasmus here and in ch. II, thinks it can be of future time. But in the world, he says, he is already, not according to person, but according to the likeness of the Spirit, with Cajetan as interpreter. For all the ancient heretics paved the way for the Anti-Christ, whose entire doctrine is nothing other than a patchwork of ancient heresies. Thus in the Nestorian distraction of the person of Christ the Papists had the Cerinthians as precursors; in the subversion of human nature through transubstantiation they were in a certain way preluded by the Marcionites; in the evacuation of the passion and cross of Christ they had various ancient heretics in many ways: concerning which matter this is not the place to speak. Rightly here B. Hunnius: For although the Anti-Christ could not yet break forth with his full effort in the time of the Apostles, nevertheless the Spirit, by whose impulse the Anti-Christ was to do all things, had then begun to lay the foundations of that structure, by attacking the person of Christ through Ebion and Cerinthus: and his office through the Pseudo-Apostles teaching the righteousness of the works of the law, and thus enervating the power and efficacy of the incarnation of the Son of God.

Estius has these things pertaining to the Greek reading: In Greek ὃ ἀκηκόατε in the neuter gender, which refers to Πνεῦμα, that is, the Spirit, so that it must be translated, whom you have heard, that is, of which Spirit you have heard, and the sense is of this kind: That Spirit dissolving Jesus is in a way the Spirit of the Anti-Christ himself, namely through consent of doctrine: of which Spirit of the Anti-Christ you have received it handed down, that he is to come. It must be known, however, that there exist Greek [texts] which have it thus: ὅτι ἀκηκόαμεν, ὅτι ἔρχεται, because (or since) we have heard that he is to come, namely the Anti-Christ. Estius has these things concerning the following words: And now already he is in the world, that is, already now the Spirit of the Anti-Christ, or the Anti-Christ himself, moves among men according to the varied reading of the upper part. For the Spirit of the Anti-Christ has existed in heretics already from the times of the Apostles, scattering certain seeds of the future kingdom of the Anti-Christ. The Anti-Christ himself also is already in the world and long ago began to be, according to his members and heretical precursors promoting his kingdom. Which two expositions fall back into the same sense.

Latin:

Vers. 3.

Καὶ πᾶν πνεῦμα, ὃ μὴ ὁμολογεῖ τὸν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν, & omnis Spiritus, qui non confitetur Jesum Christum) Omnis prophetia quae Jesum esse negat promissum Messiam. Ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα, qui in carne venit) Hoc argu- mento nixa, quod Jesus venerit in statu humili, malis- que maximis obnoxio. Ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐκ ἔστιν ex Deo non est) Non est illa di- vinitus inspirata prophetia, sed falsa & fallax. Poly- carpus discipulus hujus Apostoli in sua ad Smyrnen- ses epistola: Πᾶς γὰρ ὃς ἂν μὴ ὁμολογῇ Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθέναι, ἀντίχριστός ἐστι, καὶ ὃς μὴ ὁμολογήσῃ τὸ μαρτύριον τοῦ σταυροῦ ἐκ τοῦ Διαβόλου ἐστὶ, quisquis non con- fitetur Jesum Christum, qui in carne venit, Anti-Chri- stus est, & quisquis non confitetur testimonium cru- cis, ex Diabolo est. Ubi vides, vocibus illis venisse in carne significari crucem, ut jam diximus. Καὶ τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ τοῦ Ἀντιχρίστου, & hic est Anti-Christi) Τοῦτο nimirum πνεῦμα hic nimirum Spiritus. Hic Spi- ritus sive haec prophetia erit eminenti modo propria eminentis illius Anti-Christi, id est, Barchochebae, ut modo diximus.

In quibus haec desideramus: I. Falso adducun- tur loca Matth. XI. 6. cap. XXVI. 31. quasi tradant notam, quibus prophetiam θεόπνευστον a falsa di- gnoscas. In priori enim loco beati praedicantur, qui non scandalizantur in Christo, quae μείωσις est, hoc sensu, qui citra scandalum crucis Christi in ipsum credunt. In posteriori de discipulis Christi, qui cru- ce ejus scandalizabantur non de falsis Prophetis agitur.
