II. Prophetia non intelligenda est juxta Grotia- num vocis usum, quasi sit vaticinium, cum alius monstretur Christus, quam Jesus Nazarenus, sed est falsum dogma, & abnegatio veri Christi.

III. Non de alio Messia vel Pseudo Christo, aut Prophetia vel vaticinio de alio venturo, qui verus Messias sit, a Jesu Nazareno diversus hic agitur; sed de ejusmodi falso Doctore, qui non confitetur Jesum Christum in carne venisse, hoc est, Verbum vel Fi- lium Dei incarnatum esse, aut vitam aeternam, quae apud Patrem fuit, apparuisse in assumpta carne, quae ἀντίθεσις est Apostolicae θέσεως in principio Epistolae propositae, hoc est, qui negat incarnatio- nem Filii Dei, quales Cerinthus, Ebion & alii haere- tici fuere S. Johannis aetate.

IV. Male ergo discerpuntura Grotio, quae a Jo- hanne conjuncta sunt. Non de Pseudo-Christis vel eorum praeviis Pseudo-Prophetis sermo hic est: Nec enim constat, praedixisse quemquam Pseudo- Prophetam tempore S. Johannis, qui venturum Messiam vaticinatus sit, qui adveniens se Messiam dixerit, quum revera impostor esset; tantum ab- est, ut multi ejusmodi falsi Prophetae in mundum exierint: Sed falsi Doctores notantur, qui non con- fessi sunt, hoc est, negarunt, Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα. Christum & Filium Dei certa ratione commutat, ut e collatione cap. II. 22. 23. liquet, quia

Filium Dei Messiam futurum, cui dati sint fines or- bis terrarum in hereditatem e Pfalm. II. certum erat. Hos ergo notat, qui Filii Dei adventum in carne negabant, quales erant Cerinthiani & Ebionitæ.

V. Voce ἐν σαρκὶ non humilis status abstracte, ut cum Socino Grotius vult, sed in concreto natura humana, cui accidit fragilitas & forma servi, sta- tusque humilis designatur, quod uti de aliis locis Johan. I. 14. 1. Timoth. III. 16, Ebr. II. 14, in propria sede ostensum; ita hic etiam ob parallelifmum ob- tinet. Mavult autem dicere ἐν σαρκὶ, quam εἰς σάρκα, ne postmodum ubi ἐνσαρκωθεὶς fuit Filius Dei non amplius caro mansisse, sed in Deitatem abiisse, aut loco veræ carnis quoddam merum Φάντασμα fuisse fingatur, quemadmodum hoc Marcion, illud vero Eutyches & fanatici commen- ti sunt. Neque vero in carne Filius Dei natura ἀσώματ@ & ἄσαρκ@ apparere potuisset, nisi in carnem venisset, vel carnem seu naturam huma- nam assumsisset. Adde quod particula ἐν pro εἰς quandoque adhibeatur, Marc. I. 15. Luc. I. 17. 1. Thessal. IV. 3. 1. Johan. IV. 9. Ebr. IV. 17. Unde Drusius ad h. l. Sic legimus ἐν οἴκῳ ἰέναι pro εἰς οἶκον domum ire. Sane ἐν & εἰς Dialecto Attica alter- nant, sicut Ebræum ב pro ל usurpatur, & motum ad locum denotat Levit. XVI, 22. Neque abnui- mus ea phrasi peculiariter usum esse S. Johannem, ut officium Christi & οἰκονομίαν salutis simul respi- ceret, quæ in diebus carnis consummata est: Quod in carne venit Jesus Christus nascendo, crescendo, docendo, obediendo & serviendo, patiendo, mo- riendo, resurgendo &c. Ebr. V. 7. cap. X. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. 19. Pfalm. XL. 8. 9. Quanquam vero carnis no- mine quandoque infirmitates connotentur, ut Gal. IV, 13. solæ tamen infirmitates sine ipsa natura in abstracto nuspiam facile ita vocantur: de Christo certe id non invenitur. In loco vero 1. Corinth. IV. 11. epitheton additum θνητὴ infirmitatem & mortalitatem notat, non ipsa vox σαρκός. Pro ipsa autem natura simpliciter passim occurrere car- nis vocem nemo sanus inficiabitur, vid. Genes. VI. 12. 13. Esa. XL. 5. Joel. II. 28. Roman. III. 20. Quod ad locum 1. Joh. V. 6. voculam ἐν cum διὰ commuta- ri ex antecedentibus constat, qui sensus etiam oc- currit Luc. I. 17. 1. Corinth, X. 2. Sed id particulare est, neque facile uspiam διὰ pro μετὰ in Novo Testa- mento invenietur.

VI. Non carpit hic proprie Judæos Apostolus, neque illi ignorabant, aut negabant Jesum venisse in carne sensu Grotiano, hoc est, absque pompa, splendore externo & armis, quum ideo noluerint ipsum pro Messia agnoscere. Notat autem eos hæreticos Evangelista, qui persona Christi & crucis veritatem inficiabantur.

VII. Polycarpi, qui Smyrnensium quidem Epi- scopus fuit, non autem ad Smyrnenses, sed ad Philippenses epistolam reliquit, ut ex Hieronymo, Eusebio & epistola edita constat, (quod tamen ἁμάρτημα μνημονευτικὸν in posterioribus anno- tationibus emendavit Grotius) locus non docet, hæc Synonyma ipsi esse venisse in carne & cru- cem sustinuisse, sed duas distinctas ab ipso nota- tas esse hæreses innuit, quarum altera non con- fessa sit Jesum Christum, qui in carne venit, altera non confessa testimonium crucis: Siquidem Ebionitæ personam Christi impugnarint, Basili- diani Jesum non a Judæis fuisse crucifixum, sed ejus loco Simonem Cyreneum dixerint, quod etiam Mahometis est delirium: Cerinthiani ve- ro tum Jesum a Christo distinxerint, ceu duas personas, quam hæresin certa ratione suam postmodum fecere Nestoriani, qui personam solverunt; tum Christum passum esse negarint, quia a Jesu avolarit, in quem in baptismo descen- derit, adeoque nec Christum resurrexisse admise- rint, sed solum Jesum. Fuerunt & alii, qui Chri- stump mortem non in rei veritate, sed opinione tan- tum hominum subiisse dixere, quos forte notavit Polycarpus, ut ex Epistola Ignatii ad Smyrnenses constat. Quid? quod Marcion, qui Christum tantum Φαντασικῶς apparuisse, & passum docuit, Polycarpi tempore vixerit, quem S. Martyr pri- mogenitum Diaboli, quum ipsi occurreret, nomi- navit. Quae in Polycarpo emendantur a Grotio, mere precaria sunt, nullaque autoritate Codicum nituntur.

De lectione vero illa, qui Jesum solvit, facile annuimus, eam genuinam non esse, quanquam rem ipsam exprimat, quod ad λύσιν illam personae, Cerinthianorum, de qua jam diximus. Nec ob- scure agnoscit Estius Graecae lectionis veritatem: Et omnis Spiritus, qui Jesum solvit, ex Deo non est. Loco hujus sententiae in Graeco & Syriaco legitur membrum priori oppositum; Et omnis Spiritus, qui non confitetur, Jesum Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo non est. Nisi quod Syrus non addit Chri- stum. Graecae lectioni suffragatur Cyprianus, qui libr. II. adversus Judaeos cap. 8. sic legit: Qui autem negat in carne venisse (supple ex priori membro Jesum Christum) de Deo non est. At vero Latinam lectionem diserte refert Irenaeus Cypriano antiquior, addito tamen vocabulo Christum, libr. III. cap. 18. Sic & caeteri Latini legerunt, nominatim Leo Pon- tifex epist. X. ad Flavianum cap. 5. Prosper libr. I. de vocat. gent. cap. 23. Cassianus libr. V. de incar- nat. cap. 10. & Beda in comment. Quibus addo Cyrillum Graecum libro de recta fide ad Reginas. Caterum Augustinus hunc locum tractans utram- que lectionem exponit, ut satis appareat utrumque ei lectum fuisse. Sane valde verisimile est, maxi- me ex Irenaeo, Graecos Codices olim id habuisse, quod est in nostris. Idque perspicue testatur Socrates libr. VII. sua historiae cap. XXXII. Dicit enim hoc scriptum fuisse in vetustis hujus epistolae exemplari- bus utique Graecis. Sed, inquit, hanc sententiam omnes, qui Divinitatem ab humanitate Christi se- jungere studebant, ex vetustis exemplaribus delere tollereque non dubitarunt. Et addit: Quapropter veteres Interpretes idem ipsum significarunt, quos- dam videlicet esse, qui illam epistolam depravas- sent, quo in Christo hominem a Deo separarent. Haec ille. Suspicatur quidem Estius, quod utrum- que scriptum fuerit, quod utrumque exponat Augustinus, asseratque Tertullianus l. de carn. Christ. cap. 24. & l. III. contra Marc. cap. 8. Graecum: Latinum v. l. contra Psychicos cap. 2. & illum & istum l. V. c. Marc. cap. 16. Sed haec nondum suffi- ciunt; nisi autoritate Graecorum Codicum fulci- antur, quae hic proferri nequit. Verum ista παρα- φραδικῶς.

VIII. Limitatio ista si & eventa praedictionibus respondeant, in cerebro Grotii enata, in textu nullo apice indigitata. Est autem illa eo fine efficta, ut sustineat vaticinium hic innui. S. Johannes id vult, omnem Spiritum vel Doctorem, qui Jesum Christum in carne venisse confitetur, ex Deo esse, dummodo non neget alia, quae de Jesu Christo tradita in scriptura sunt, quamvis illa in ejus in carne adventu comprehensa sint in οἰκονομίᾳ salu- tis ea phrasi connotata. Similiter efficta glossa est de propheta ejus, qui in prophetia Jesum pro Christo non agnoscit. Nihil enim hic de prophetia vel vaticinio, nedum de ejusmodi prophetia, qua tollitur fides, quod Jesus sit Christus.

IX. Vanum itaque ac futile est, quod de Spiritu vel Prophetia eminenti modo propria Anti-Christo nugatur Grotius. Nullos enim hic Anti-Christi Prophetas de ipso vaticinantes designavit S. Johannes.

X. Vanissima omnium est applicatio Anti-Christi ad Barchochebam, & Spiritus Anti-Christi ad Prophetias de Barchocheba. Nam nihil huc facere Barchochebam, ad cap. II. jam abunde dictum, qui nec potentia nec actu in rerum natura tempore Johannis fuit, & emersit demum sub Adriano diu post excessum S. Johannis, anno videlicet Domini CXXX. Nec inter Christianos, qui Christo antea nomen suum ullo modo dederant, sed solum inter Judaeos Christiani nominis hostes Barchochebas progressus suos fecit, teste historia. Neque ullum de ipso vaticinium vel respicitur hoc loco vel produci potuit ex historia, quod huc facere queat. Glossae istae Nugonis nugae merae sunt, gerris Siculis vaniores.

Subjungimus jam B. Hunnii commentarium longe solidiorem: Vox Jesu Christi non λόγον nudum sed incarnatum significat, ejusque duas naturas junctim complectitur. Porro venire hic non significat localiter prius absentem nunc eminus accedere. Sed tum venire in carne dicitur Jesus Christus, quando λόγος ex sua velut arcana sede prodiens assumpta visibili carne se in terris manifestat. Et quia non sine causa, sed ob redemptionis officium magnum illud venit in carne: idcirco officium quoque, propter quod ipsa incarnatio facta est, hic per consequentiam includitur, ut sententia Apostolici canonis sit haec: Omnis Spiritus, hoc est, omnis Doctor seu Concionator, qui vere & ex animo confitetur, Jesum Christum venisse in hunc mundum, non localiter e caelis descendendo, sed visibiliter in assumpta carne apparendo, & quidem venisse hunc in finem, ut nos homines ab aeterna morte liberaret: is Spiritus seu Doctor vere ex Deo est, & ex Deo haec docet ac profitetur. Recte autem addit B. Hunnius: Regulam Johannis secundum subjectam materiam esse accipiendam. Loquitur enim potissimum de articulis iis, qui Christi agnitionem proprie concernunt. Proinde hoc vult canon Apostoli, quod quicunque de Christo Jesu, ejus persona & officio juxta praescriptam regulam sentit ac docet, is in principalibus illis de Christi notitia capitibus audiendus, & in eis pro sincero habendus sit. Non negat interim alios esse posse errores, qui articulum de Christi persona & officio non attingant, qui etiam ex aliis Canonibus in Prophetarum & Apostolorum scriptura propositis dijudicari debent.

Estius regulam Johanneam ita limitat: Omnem doctrinam, adeoque omnem Doctorem, qui confitetur ac docet Dei Filium vere hominem factum, & hunc esse Jesum, Messiam promissum, esse ex Deo, nimirum ea parte qua hoc docet. Quod non est aliud dicere, quam hujusmodi doctrinam esse ex Deo: nec non eum, qui ita confitetur & docet ea parte doctrina ex Deo esse. Nam certe nec haeretici circa veros fidei articulos, quos adhuc retinent ac docent atque defendunt: supernaturali dono fidei prorsus carent, quamvis integram & proinde Catholicam fidem non habeant. Sed haec sententia haereticos supernaturaie fidei donum habere, & ex Deo esse nullatenus admittenda. Haeresis enim est opus carnis, Gal. V.

ὃ ἀκηκόατε ὅτι ἔρχεται.] Quem Spiritum aliquando ven- turum Christus prædixerat. Hic enim est Spiritus illorum Pseudo-Prophetarum,de quibus agitur Matth. 24, 11. 24. ἔρ- χεται est sono præsens, sensu futurum, & refertur ad tempus illud, cum hoc prædixit Christus. Sic & supra II, 18.

Καὶ νῦν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἐσὶν ἤδη.] In variis locis jam ostendunt se tales Pseudo-Prophetæ,qui Messiam dicunt venturum cum potentia hujus mundi.

In altera prius edita commentatione hæc ita habent: ὃ ἀκηκόατε, ὅτι ἔρχεται, de quo audivistis, quoniam ve- nit.] Quam prophetiam summe falsam & summe noxiam venturam jam ego vobis prædixi. Vide supra c. II. Καὶ νῦν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἐσὶν ἤδη,& nunc jam in mundo est.] Illa fallacia jam nunc per alia minora instrumenta, qualia ad ca- put secundum nominavimus, vires suas prætentat, brevi ad summum illud fastigium perventura.

De Prophetis Barchochebam prænunciantibus postremo vanissimus commentator intellexit, quæ prius de fallaciæ similis minoribus instru- mentis acceperat, utrumque falsissime. Nam nec quisquam Pseudo-Prophetarum de ipso legitur vaticinia edidisse Johannis tempore; nec mino- rum gentium Anti-Christo vel potius Pseudo- Christo eidem tum prælusisse commemorantur. De loco Matth.XXIV.antea dictum.Quod ad tex- tum nostrum revocat S. Johannes in memoriam, quæ prædixerat Paulus de Anti-Christo Magno, 2. Thess. II, & Daniel Propheta c. XI, XII, non vero suam ipsius prædictionem sic respicit. Neque vero prophetiam vel Prophetam de Anti-Christo antea prædixerat, sed Anti-Christum ipsummet.Ἔρχεται pro futuro accipitur ob certitudinem, quemad- modum Cajetanus observat, quanquam Erasmus hic & cap. II, censeat posse id esse futuri temporis. In mundo autem, inquit, jam est, non secundum per- sonam, sed secundum similitudinem Spiritus inter- prete Cajetano. Omnes enim hæretici veteres stravére viam Anti-Christo, cujus universa do- ctrina nihil aliud est, quam cento veterum hære- sium. Ita in persona Christi distractione Nestoriana prævios habuere Papistæ Cerinthianos, in huma- næ naturæ eversione per transsubstantiationem cer- ta ratione ipsis prælusére Marcionitæ, in passionis & crucis Christi evacuatione multiplici varios an- tiquos hæreticos habuere: qua de re hic non di- cendi est locus. Recte hic B. Hunnius: Quanquam enim Anti-Christus tempore Apostolorum nondum pleno suo conatu poterat erumpere, tamen Spiritus, cujus impetu Anti-Christus omnia esset facturus, cœ- perat tunc fundamenta illius structuræ ponere, im- pugnando personam Christi per Ebionem & Cerin- thum: officium vero per Pseudo-Apostolos docentes justitiam operum legis, atque sic vim & efficaciam in- carnationis Filii Dei enervantes.

Ad Græcam lectionem pertinentia hæc habet Estius: Græce ὃ ἀκηκόατε Neutro genere, quod ad Πνεῦμα refertur, id est Spiritum, ut vertendum sit, quem audivistis, hoc est, de quo Spiritu audivistis, sitque sensus hujusmodi: Spiritus ille solvens Jesum quodammodo Spiritus est ipsius Anti-Christi, nem- pe per consensum doctrinæ: de quo Spiritu Anti- Christi traditum accepistis, quod sit venturus. Scien- dum tamen extare Græca, quæ sic habeant: ὅτι ἀκη- κόαμεν, ὅτι ἔρχεται, quoniam (seu quandoquidem) audivimus, quod venturus sit, scilicet Anti-Christus. Ad verba sequentia hæc habet Estius: Et nunc jam in mundo est, hoc est, jam nunc inter homines versatur vel Spiritus Anti-Christi, vel ipse Anti- Christus juxta variam lectionem partis superioris. Nam Spiritus Anti-Christi jam à temporibus Apo- stolorum in hæreticis exstitit, semina quædam spar- gens futuri regni Anti-Christi. Ipse etiam Anti- Christus jam in mundo est & olim esse cœpit, secun- dum membra sua & præcursores hæreticos regnum ipsius promoventes. Quæ duæ expositiones in eundem sensum recidunt.

## 4:4
Vers. 4.

Ὑμεῖς ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστε τεκνία.] He excites them to constancy with praises. You are from GOD, that is, you savor divine, not human things, and therefore the cross does not offend you. See above II, 16. III, 9. Καὶ νενικήκατε αὐτούς.] You have already despised many such Pseudo-Prophets. Thus above II, 14. Νενικήκατε τὸν πονηρὸν. That αὐτούς is not referred to any name, but to the thing signified by the name. Ὅτι μείζων ἐστὶν ὁ ἐν ὑμῖν, ἢ ὁ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ.] Christ, who dwells in you through the anointing, that is, His Spirit (above II, 10.) is more powerful than the devil, who rules in the world, Joh. XII, 31. XIV, 30. XVI, 11. 2. Corinth. IV, 4. Eph. VI, 22.

Latin:

Vers. 4.

Ὑμεῖς ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστε τεκνία.] Laudibus eos ad constantiam excitat. Vos ex DEO estis, id est, divina non humana sapi- tis, ideoque crux vos non offendit. Vide supra II, 16. III, 9. Καὶ νενικήκατε αὐτούς.] Multos jam tales Pseudo-Prophetas sprevisitis. Sic supra II, 14. Νενικήκατε τὸν πονηρὸν. Illud αὐ- τοὺς non ad nomen aliquod, sed ad rem nomine significatam refertur. Ὅτι μείζων ἐστὶν ὁ ἐν ὑμῖν, ἢ ὁ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ.] Christus, qui per unguentum, id est, Spiritum suum in vobis habitat (supra II, 10.) potentior est diabolo, qui in mundo dominatur, Joh. XII, 31. XIV, 30. XVI, 11. 2. Corinth. IV, 4. Eph. VI, 22.

## 4:5
Vers. 5.

Αὐτοὶ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου εἰσί.] They have affections such as the world has, that is, by far the greatest part of the human race. They love the splendor of this life, opulence, and pleasures, above II, 16. Ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου εἶναι signifies to be of the same disposition, as appears in the same place II, 16. Διὰ τοῦτο ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου λαλοῦσι.] That is, they teach and preach τὰ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου, things congruent with the affections of the world. Καὶ ὁ κόσμος αὐτῶν ἀκούει.] It follows them, it complies with them. It is customary for ἀκούειν to be said of disciples, as in Laertius several times.

In the previous commentary these two verses were explained thus: V. 4. Ὑμεῖς ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστε, τεκνία, you are from God, little children.] You savor divine things. Thus men of cruel malice are said to be from the devil, Joh. Evang. VIII, 44. Καὶ νενικήκατε αὐτούς, & you have conquered them.] You have conquered the temptations of those impostors who have been until now, whereas others allowed themselves to be drawn by their promises, you have not followed them. Ὅτι μείζων ἐστὶν ὁ ἐν ὑμῖν, ἢ ὁ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, because greater is he who is in you, than he who is in the world.] Christ, who dwells in us through His anointing, is greater and more powerful than every worldly force. Compare with those things which are above II, 20. & add Johann. Evang. XVII, 33. & below V, 4. 5. V. 5. Αὐτοὶ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου εἰσί, they themselves are of the world.] They savor worldly things, they pant after the pleasures, riches, and splendor of this life, and allow themselves to be led away by them, above II, 16. Διὰ τοῦτο ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου λαλοῦσι.] Therefore they speak of the world. Their dogmas are such as we have said their affections to be. Καὶ ὁ κόσμος αὐτῶν ἀκούει, & the world hears them.] They have many followers, because many are affected just as they are, enemies of the cross, whose god is their belly, and the goods of this age, Gal. V, 11. Phil. III, 18. 19.

St. John does not oppose true believers to the followers of the Prophets or to the Prophets of Bar-Kochba, but to Judaizing heretics, who taught legal matters in the Church, and undermined the truth of the incarnation of the Son of God, and the Deity of Jesus, and denied the passion and resurrection of Christ, who fled from the cross of Christ, and savored earthly things, seeking therefore Syncretism and union with the Jews. To which contribute those things which Grotius handed down regarding Matth. XXIV, 11: Just as Προφῆται were called by the Hebrews not only those who predicted future events, but also those who interpreted the law: so Christ calls false teachers by the known term ψευδοπροφήτας. There is no doubt that Satan, having excited the hatred of the world against Christians, when he saw that the power of the truth was so great that many who desired to deny it could scarcely do so with a mind struggling too much, added deceits to force, inventing certain pretexts which would make defection easier. Moreover, the constancy of Christians could be undermined either by the removal of the use of all religion, or by positing that any external worship is indifferent, or by sought-after reconciliations, which would mix the Christian religion with some religion, either publicly approved, such as that of the Gentiles, or at least tolerated, such as that of the Jews. And afterwards: They mixed the Christian religion with Judaism, not by tolerating Jewish rites (which we know the Apostles did in those first times) but by acknowledging Judaism as the only way of salvation, which had been announced both by other Prophets and also by Christ, Cerinthus and Ebion, whose chief study it was to escape those evils which particularly oppressed the Christians, in that manner which Paul clearly teaches in Phil. III, verse 18 and Galat. VI, verse 12. Against these same men, many things exist in the first epistle of John, but also in the Apocalypse. These, therefore, are all and such as these are they whom Christ calls false prophets, and Paul calls men speaking perverse things, Acts XX, v. 30, and false apostles, 2 Corinth. XI, 13, transforming themselves into Apostles of Christ, by whose dogmas the faith of many has been overturned, 2 Timoth. II, 18. Blessed Hunnius correctly expressed the sense of these words, saying: It is not difficult for you to prove and beware of the Spirit of Anti-Christ, because you are from God, and by the help and protection of God you overcome the Anti-Christs, being indeed instructed in the Word of GOD, and so founded in the truth that you do not allow yourselves, like a reed, to be moved from the truth once acknowledged, and to be carried off sideways to approve the perverse dogmas of heretics, but you remain constantly in the doctrine of Christ, following the lead of the Holy Spirit dwelling in you, who is greater and more powerful than that spirit which is in the world, that is, the devil, indeed surpassing him in strength and power by as great an interval as there is between the eternal Creator and a finite creature.

Estius says they are of the world because they belong to that much larger part of the human race which serves sin and concupiscences, Romans Chap. XVI. Such as these do not serve Christ the Lord, but their own belly. He explains why they speak of the world thus: Because they bring forth false doctrine, which is not from GOD, but from the world, and from the devil, the Prince of the world and father of lies, whether that doctrine approves of things which are pleasant to the senses, or which are contrary to the delight of the senses, such as were the heresies of certain ancients, like those forbidding to marry, or abstaining from foods which GOD created, 1 Tim. IV, and other similar ones. For doctrine of this kind is also from the world. Whence Paul in the same place calls them doctrines of demons. In the words, 'and the world hears them,' he warns that the rational particle is to be repeated, and therefore the world hears them: Namely, because they speak from the world. For there is a double inference: They are of the world, therefore they speak of the world. Likewise, they speak of the world, therefore the world hears them. The reason for the latter is because everyone willingly hears those things which belong to his own sect and school. However, all communicate in the school of the devil, although some are addicted to different desires or sects: Cf. John XV, v. 19. He says this last part is added so that the faithful might not be troubled on account of the multitude of those who adhere to heretics, saying: Although there are many who hear them, they are nevertheless of no value: because they are nothing but the world, that is, the dregs of the human race, namely that part which serves sin and the devil. But one man fearing the Lord is better than a thousand impious children, Eccl. XIV.

Latin:

Vers. 5.

Αὐτοὶ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου εἰσί.] Affectus habent, quales habet mundus, id est, pars longe maxima humani generis. Amant splendorem hujus vitæ, opulentiam, & voluptates, supra II, 16. Ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου εἶναι significat pari esse ingenio, ut apparet ibidem II, 16. Διὰ τοῦτο ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου λαλοῦσι.] Id est, τὰ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου do- cent & prædicunt mundi affectibus congruentia. Καὶ ὁ κόσμος αὐτῶν ἀκούει.] Eos sectatur, eis morem gerit. Solet ἀκούειν dici de discipulis, ut apud Laertium aliquoties.

In priori commentatione hi duo versus sic ex- positi erant: V. 4. Ὑμεῖς ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστε, τεκνία, vos ex Deo estis filioli.] Vos divina sapitis. Sic crudelis malitiæ homines ex diabolo esse dicuntur, Joh. Evang. IIX, 44. Καὶ νενικήκατε αὐτοὺς, & vicistis eos.] Vicistis illorum, qui hactenus fuere, impostorum tentamenta, cum alii illo- rum pollicitationibus trahi se paterentur, vos eos sectati non estis. Ὅτι μείζων ἐστὶν ὁ ἐν ὑμῖν, ἢ ὁ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, quoniam major est, qui in vobis est, quam in mundo.] Christus, qui per unguen- tum suum in nobis habitat, major, potentiorque est omni vi mundana. Confer cum iis, quæ supra II, 20. & adde Johann. Evang. XVII, 33. & infra V, 4. 5. V. 5. Αὐτοὶ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου εἰσί, ipsi de mundo sunt.] Mun- dana sapiunt, hujus vitæ voluptatibus, opibus, splendori in- hiant, eisque se abduci patiuntur, supra II, 16. Διὰ τοῦτο ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου λαλοῦσι.] Ideo de mundo loquun- tur. Dogmata illorum talia sunt, quales illorum affectus es- se diximus. Καὶ ὁ κόσμος αὐτῶν ἀκούει, & mundus eos audit.] Multos habent sectatores, quia multi pariter, ut ipsi affecti sunt, ini- mici crucis, quorum Deus venter, & hujus seculi bona, Gal. V, 11. Phil. III, 18. 19.

Non asseclis Prophetarum aut Prophetis Bar- chochebæ opponit S. Johannes veros fideles, sed hæreticis Judaizantibus, qui legalia docebant in Ecclesia, & incarnationis Filii Dei veritatem, ac Deitatem Jesu labefactabant, & passionem ac re- surrectionem Christi negabant, qui crucem Chri- sti fugiebant, & terrena sapiebant, Syncreti- smum & unionem cum Judæis ideo quærentes. Quo faciunt quæ ad Matth. XXIV, 11. Grotius tra- didit: Sicut Προφῆται dicebantur Ebræis non hi tantum, qui prædicebant futura, sed & qui legem interpretabantur: ita falsos magistros Christus no- to vocabulo ψευδοπροφήτας appellat. Dubium non est, quin Satan excitato mundi odio adversus Chri- stianos, cum videret tantam esse vim veritatis, ut eam abnegare multi qui cuperent vix possent nimi- um reluctante animo, ad vim dolos adjunxerit, prætextus aliquos comminiscens, qui defectionem redderent faciliorem. Poterat autem labefactari constantia Christianorum aut religionis omnis sub- lato usu, aut posito quemvis cultum externum esse ἀδιάφορον, aut quæsitis conciliaturis, quæ Chri- stianam religionem cum aliqua religione, aut pro- bata publice, qualis erat Ethnicorum, aut tolera- ta certe, qualis erat Judæorum permiscereut. Et postmodum: Cum Judaismo Christianam religio- nem miscuerunt, non tolerando ritus Judaicos, (quod Apostolos primis illis temporibus scimus fecisse) sed Judaismum agnoscendo unicam salutis viam, quæ tum ab aliis Prophetis, tum à Christo etiam essset annuntiata, Cerinthus & Ebion, quorum id præcipuum erat studium, ut mala illa, quæ Chri- stianos peculiariter premebant, ea ratione effuge- rent, ut clarè docet Paulus Phil. III. vers. 18. & Galat. VI. vers. 12. Adversus eosdem multa extant in prima Johannis epistola, sed & in Apocalypsi. Hi igitur omnes horumque similes sunt, quos Christus vocat ψευδοπροφήτας, Paulus ἄνδρας λαλοῦντας διεστραμμένα, Actorum XX, v. 30. ψευδαποστόλους, 2. Corinth. XI, 13. μετασχηματιζομένους εἰς Ἀποστό- λους Χριστοῦ, quorum dogmatibus multorum fides ever- sa est, 2. Timoth. II, 18. Sensum horum verborum rectè expressit B. Hunnius, q. d. Difficile vobis non est probare & cavere Anti-Christi Spiritum, quia vos ex Deo estis, & Dei ope præsidioque supera- stis Anti-Christos, instituti quippe in Verbo DEI, & in veritate sic fundati, ut non patiamini vos in- star arundinis ab agnita semel veritate dimoveri, & ad hæreticorum perversa dogmata approbanda transversos rapi, sed constanter in doctrina Chri- sti permanetis, sequentes ductum Spiritus Sancti habitantis in vobis, qui major & potentior est eo Spiritu, qui in mundo est, hoc est diabolo, nimi- rum robore potentiæque illum tanto intervallo su- perans, quantum inter æternum Creatorem & fini- tam creaturam interest.

Estius è mundo esse dicit, quia pertinent ad partem generis humani illam multo maximam, quæ servit peccato & concupiscentiis, Roman. Cap. XVI. Hujusmodi Christo Domino non serviunt, sed suo ventri. Illa vero, ideo de mundo loquuntur, sic explicat: Quod perferant falsam doctrinam, quæ non est ex DEO, sed ex mundo, & diabolo Principe mundi & patre mendacii, sive ea doctri- na probet, quæ sensibus sunt jucunda, sive quæ de- lectationi sensuum contraria sint, quales hæreses fuerunt quorundam antiquorum, ut prohiben- tium nubere, abstinentium à cibis, quos DEUS creavit, 1. Tim. IV. & aliorum similium. Nam & hujus generis doctrina è mundo sunt. Unde Paulus ibidem vocat eos doctrinas Dæmoniorum. In verbis, & mundus eos audit, monet, repetendam esse ra- tionalem particulam, & ideo mundus eos audit: Nempe quoniam illi ex mundo loquuntur. Est enim duplex illatio: De mundo sunt, ergo de mundo lo- quuntur. Item de mundo loquuntur, ergo mun- dus eos audit. Ratio posterioris est, quia quisque li- benter audit ea, quæ suæ sunt sectæ & scholæ. Com- municant autem omnes in schola diaboli, licet alii aliis cupiditatibus aut sectis addicti: Conf. Johan. XV. v. 19. Addi autem hoc postremum ait, ne fideles turbentur ob multitudinem eorum, qui hæreticis ad- hærent, q. d. Etsi multi sunt, qui eos audiunt, nul- lius tamen sunt pretii: quia non sunt nisi mundus, id est, humani generis colluvies, videlicet ea pars, quæ peccato servit & diabolo. Melior autem est unus ti- mens Dominum, quam mille filii impii, Eccl. XIV.

## 4:6
Vers. 6.

He who knows God, hears us.] He follows us, he gives himself to us to be taught. He who knows God, that is, he who, as is fitting, considers that God is eternal, and does not measure Him by the scope of the judgments of this age.

Certainly more things are required for the knowledge of God than these. For where are the other attributes of God? Where is the person of the divinity? Where is the knowledge of the divine will? Do they rightly know God who are ignorant of these things?

He who is not from God.] It comes back to the same thing to know God in the sense we have already stated and to be from God. Understanding and affection follow one another mutually: but by certain degrees.

He does not hear us.] Such a one as this seeks other Teachers and Prophets.

From this we know the spirit of truth and of error.] The Spirit of truth, that is, the truthful one; the Spirit of deception, that is, the deceiving Spirit. Deception, as in Ephes. IV, verse 14, 2 Thess. II, v. 11. For 'from this' in the Manuscript it is 'in this,' as above 2. We know, we distinguish, we discern, the simple for the compound, as above 12. But I refer that 'from this' to that affection concerning eternal things and concerning the world.

Although this sense can be admitted, the Hunnian explanation seems more convenient: But those who are not from God, these do not hear us, but follow those who forge dogmas contrary to Apostolic doctrine, and agreeable to blind human reason. And by this, he says, the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of error are known, or distinguished from one another: because the Spirit of truth precisely and tenaciously defends the doctrine of the Apostles, which was indeed handed down to them by Christ, and afterwards, according to the Savior's promise, was recalled to their memory by the Holy Spirit. The Spirit of error, however, neglecting the canon of Apostolic doctrine, indulges in its own opinions. Nor does Cornelius à Lapide deny this, saying: By this sign you will distinguish true Apostles from false and heretical ones, that the true ones love and teach true and divine things, the false ones love and teach false and carnal things. We therefore are from God, because, as Oecumenius says, we abhor worldly concupiscences, and being solicitous about the future life, we despise all fleeting and mortal goods. He alludes to that of Christ in the Gospel chap. X, 16, 'My sheep etc. hear my voice,' and chap. VI, 46, 'Everyone who has heard from the Father, and has learned, comes to me,' and chap. VIII, 47, 'He who is from God hears the words of God, therefore you do not hear, because you are not from God.' But Estius rightly warns concerning the latter words: That the Apostle speaks these in the person of the faithful. By this sign and argument, he says, we the faithful know and ought to know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error, that is, we discern between true and false doctrine, and consequently between true and false teachers. But from where will he prove that the former things were said not only in the person of the Apostles, but also of the Prelates, whom he calls the Church? As for his saying that the Apostles were all already dead by then, and only John survived, so be it: John could nevertheless say of himself and the other Apostles, 'He who knows God hears us,' because they could be heard while the Apostles were alive, and thereafter they could be heard also in their writings. No one could hear prelates such as those in Popery at that time. For such prelates did not exist in the nature of things.

PART II. On the love of one's neighbor.

Latin:

Vers. 6.

Ὁ γινώσκων τὸν Θεὸν, ἀκούει ἡμῶν.] Nos sectatur, nobis se dat docendum. Qui Deum novit, id est, qui sicut oportet, considerat Deum esse æternum, neque eum judicia sua hujus secuh ambitu metiri.

Plura utique ad Dei notitiam requiruntur, quam ista. Ubi enim cætera Dei attributa? Ubi persona divinitatis? Ubi cognitio voluntatis divi- næ? Num recte Deum cognoscunt, qui ista ignorant?

Ὃς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ.] Eodem recidit Deum nosse eo, quo jam diximus sensu & ex Deo esse. Intellectio & affectus mu- tuo se subsequuntur: sed per gradus quosdam.

Οὐκ ἀκούει ἡμῶν.] Talis qui est, alios quærit Doctores & Prophetas.

Ἐκ τούτου γινώσκομεν τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας κὴ τῆς πλάνης.] Spiritus veritatis, id est verax, Spiritus deceptionis, id est Spiritus deceptor. Πλάνη deceptio, ut Ephes. IV. vers. 14. 2. Thess. II. v. 11. Pro ἐκ τούτου in Manuscripto est ἐν τούτῳ, ut supra 2. Γινώσκομεν dignoscimus, internoscimus, simplex pro composito, ut supra 12. Illud autem ἐκ τούτου refero ad af- fectum illum circa æterna & circa mundum.

Quanquam hic sensus admitti possit, conve- nientior tamen videtur Hunniana explicatio: Qui autem ex Deo non sunt, hi non audiunt nos, sed sequuntur illos, qui dogmata cudunt Apostolica doctrina contraria, & humanæ cæcæ rationi con- sentanea. Et per hoc, inquit, cognosci, seu inter se dignosci Spiritum veritatis & Spiritum erroris: quoniam Spiritus veritatis præcise & mordicus do- ctrinam Apostolorum tuetur, quippe quæ à Christo cis tradita, & postmodum juxta Salvatoris pro- missum à Spiritu Sancto illis in memoriam revoca- ta est. Spiritus erroris vero, neglecto Apostolicæ do- ctrinæ canone propriis suis opinionibus indulget. Ne- que abnuit Cornelius à Lapide, q. d. Hoc signo di- gnosces veros Apostolos à falsis & hæreticis, quod veri ament & doceant vera & divina, falsi ament & doceant falsa & carnalia. Nos ergo ex Deo su- mus, quia, ut ait Oecumenius, à mundanis concu- piscentiis abhorremus, & de futura vita soliciti contemnimus omnia caduca & mortalia bona. Al- ludit ad illud Christi in Evangelio cap. X, 16. O- ves &c. vocem meam audiunt, & cap. VI, 46. O- mnis, qui audivit à Patre, & didicit, venit ad me, & cap. VIII, 47. Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit, propterea vos non auditis, quia ex Deo non estis. Recte autem monet Estius de verbis posteriori- bus: Loqui Apostolum ea ex persona fidelium. Hoc, inquit, signo & argumento nos fideles cognoscimus & cognoscere debemus Spiritum veritatis & spiri- tum erroris, id est, discernimus inter doctrinam ve- ram & falsam, & consequenter inter doctores veros & falsos. Priora autem non tantum in persona Apostolorum, sed etiam Prælatorum, quos vo- cat, Ecclesiæ dicta esse, unde probabit? Quod ait Apostolos vita jam tum defunctos omnes, & so- lum Johannem superstitem fuisse, esto: poterat tamen Johannes dicere de se & aliis Apostolis, qui novit Deum, audit nos, quia audiri poterant, cum viverent Apostoli, & dehinc poterant au- diri etiam in Scriptis suis. Prælatos, quales in Pa- pismo sunt, nemo tum audire poterat. Non erant enim tales Prælati in rerum natura.

PARS II. De proximi dilectione.

## 4:7
Ver. 7.

Ἀγαπητοὶ ἀγαπῶμεν ἀλλήλους.] Here he returns to that which he had already said before. I interpret ἀλλήλους here no less than above at III, 23, as referring to all, because of the argument which he is now about to bring forward concerning the manner of God toward men viewed universally.

Ὅτι ἡ ἀγάπη ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστι.] Reason itself dictates this, that it is from God, that is, that goodness is most pleasing to God. For by the name of God everyone understands the highest good. From this principle Cicero said in his dream that there is nothing for that Prince God, which is done on earth, more acceptable than the councils and assemblies of men associated by law.

St. John had required both faith in Christ and charity toward one's neighbor. For the sake of faith, he warned about testing the Spirits: now, therefore, he carries out the commandment concerning charity more fully: for the sake of which he first seeks an argument from the Efficient cause, because charity is from God, and therefore a divine thing. 'To be from God' does not mean to be pleasing to GOD, but to have its origin from GOD, even though those things which are from God are also pleasing to God, as if to say, according to Cornelius: The Spirit of truth is the Spirit of charity, that we may love one another, because just as truth, so also charity is from God, or rather, just as God is the primary and eternal truth, so He is more and rather the very highest and uncreated charity itself.

And everyone who loves has been born of God.] That is, he is a Son of God. For γεγέννηται here must be taken in the sense of remaining. Men beget a man once: God does so perpetually, unless man stands in his own way. See above chapter III. 9. In the Manuscript: Everyone who loves God. And knows God.] He shows that he knows God as he ought. In what way we have taken γινώσκειν, see also above III, 6.

Latin:

Vers. 7.

Ἀγαπητοὶ ἀγαπῶμεν ἀλλήλους.] Hic redit ad id, quod jam ante dixerat. Ἀλλήλους hic non minus quam supra III, 23. ad omnes traho, propter argumentum, quod jam afferet de more Dei erga homines universim spectatos.

Ὅτι ἡ ἀγάπη ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐστι.] Ipsa hoc dictat ratio, ex Deo esse, id est, Deo maxime placere bonitatem. Nam Dei no- mine quivis optimum quid intelligit. Ex hoc principio dixit Cicero in somnio, nihil esse illi Principi Deo, quod qui- dem in terris fiat acceptius, quam consilia cœtusque homi- num jure sociatos.

Requisiverat S. Johannes tum fidem in Chri- stum, tum charitatem erga proximum. Fidei causa monuit de probandis Spiritibus: Jam ergo præ- ceptum de charitate uberius exequitur: cujus gra- tia primum argumentum à causa Efficienti petit, quia charitas à Deo est, adeoque res divina. Ex τοῦ Θεοῦ εἶναι non est placere DEO, sedoriginem habere à DEO, etsi quæ à Deo sunt, Deo etiam placeant, q. d. secundum Cornelium: Spiritus veritatis est Spiritus charitatis, ut diligamus invi- cem, quia sicut veritas, ita & charitas est ex- Deo, imo Deus uti est prima & æterna veritas, ita magis & potius est ipsa summa & increata charitas.

Καὶ πᾶς ὁ ἀγαπῶν ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ γεγέννηται.] Id est, Dei est Filius. Γεγέννηται enim hic in sensu permansionis sumendum est. Homines semel gignunt hominem: Deus perpetuo, nisi homo sibimet obstet. Vide supra cap. III. 9. In Manuscripto: Πᾶς ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὸν Θεὸν. Καὶ γινώσκει τὸν Θεὸν.] Ostendit se Deum nosse sicut oportet. Quomodo γινώσκειν sumpsimus & supra III, 6.

## 4:8
Ver. 8.

He who does not love has not known God.] He does not show that he knows God in that way. For God is love.] That is, He is full of love. Such is that saying: You, however great you are, are nothing but wisdom.

Latin:

Vers. 8.

Ὁ μὴ ἀγαπῶν οὐκ ἔγνω τὸν Θεόν.] Non ostendit se Deum ita nosse. Ὅτι ὁ Θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστίν.] Id est, plenus est dilectione. Tale illud: Tu quantus quantus nil nisi sapientia es.

## 4:9
Ver. 9.

In this the love of God was manifested in us, that God sent His only-begotten Son into the world, that we might live through Him] Namely, all who obey Him. For the sentiment is the same as that in the Gospel of John III, 16. In us for to us, by a frequent manner of speaking. But when he names love here, he does not mean just any love, but that admirable love toward the ungrateful, who deserved nothing of the sort, who were thinking of nothing of the sort. And to what end? That we might live, namely, eternally. For this reason He sent the Son, and indeed the only-begotten, or most beloved to Himself (see concerning this word, which is at John I, 14) into a world so corrupt that from it nothing but the greatest evils could come to Him.

A second argument from the condition of the subject: Because he who loves or cherishes his neighbor is born of God: Charity is proper to the regenerate, because faith exists through regeneration, but charity arises from faith: Therefore he says that he who loves his neighbor knows God, which knowledge is not only speculative, but practical, bringing with it trust in God. Therefore he does not only show that he knows God, but he truly believes in God: Which St. John illustrates according to his custom by antithesis: He who does not love, does not acknowledge God. Especially regarding that which is, that God is entirely charity: Which, being known, is the cause why we love our neighbor also for God's sake, since charity is not only from God, but is God Himself: But if we do not love our neighbor, we testify that we do not even rightly know God, that He is charity itself. In which knowledge saving faith especially consists, insofar as God demonstrated His charity in the mission of His Only-begotten Son into this world, that through Him we might have life and eternal salvation through faith in Him: so that we who were addicted to eternal death on account of sin might, through Him as our Mediator and Redeemer, who took upon Himself and paid the entire debt by suffering and dying, be freed from death and live eternally; just as Christ Himself explained in John III, v. 16: in which lies a new argument for loving one's neighbor, already explained in 1 John III, v. 16. Cornelius à Lapide notes here: That God is formal charity in Himself, but in us He is causal, and that by every kind of cause, for instance material, because He Himself is the object of our charity: formal, because He Himself is the exemplar of it: Efficient, because He Himself produces it in us: Final, because He Himself is our end and the end of our love. But let the Socinian depravation of the word μονογενὴς in Grotius be observed, that it is 'most beloved,' when on the contrary that word denotes not charity or love, but the generation of the Son from the Father, and that a substantial one, by which the only- and sole-begotten Son of God was born from eternity from the substance of the Father, Psalm II, 7, Micah V, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 9.

Ἐν τούτῳ ἐφανερώθη ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν ἡμῖν, ὅτι τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ τὸν μονογενῆ ἀπέστειλεν ὁ Θεὸς εἰς τὸν κόσμον, ἵνα ζήσωμεν δι᾽ αὐτοῦ] Nempe omnes, qui ei obsequimur. Est enim sententia eadem, quæ in Evangelio Joh. III, 16. Ἐν ἡμῖν pro εἰς ἡμᾶς frequenti loquutione. Cum autem hic nominat dilectionem, non quamvis intelligit, sed illam admirabilem erga ingratos, nihil tale meritos, nihil tale cogitantes. Et quorsum? Ut vivamus, nempe in æternum. Hac de causa misit Filium, & quidem unigenam, sive sibi dilectissimum (vide de hac voce, quæ ad Joh. I, 14.) in mundum adeo corruptum, ut inde nonnisi maximam mala illi advenire possint.

Alterum argumentum à subjecti conditione: Quia qui amat vel diligit proximum, ex Deo generatur: Regenitorum propria est charitas, quia per regenerationem fides existit, charitas autem ex fide oritur: Ideo cognoscere ait Deum, qui diligit proximum, quæ cognitio non speculativa tantum est, sed practica, fiduciam in Deum importans. Non ergo tantum ostendit se nosse Deum, sed revera credit in Deum: Quod pro more per antithesin illustrat S. Johannes: Qui non amat, non agnoscit Deum. Quoad id imprimis, quod Deus totus charitas sit: Quod cognitum causa est, cur ob Deum etiam proximum diligamus, siquidem charitas non solum ex Deo sit, sed etiam sit ipse Deus: Si autem non amemus proximum, testamur, quod ne Deum quidem, quod sit ipsa charitas, recte cognoscamus. In qua cognitione maxime consistit fides salvifica, quatenus charitatem suam Deus demonstravit in Filii sui Unigeniti missione in hunc mundum, ut per ipsum vitam & salutem æternam habeamus per fidem in ipsum: ut qui æternæ morti addicti eramus propter peccatum per eum ceu Mediatorem & Redemptorem nostrum, qui debitum omne patiendo & moriendo in se suscepit & exsolvit, à morte liberati æternum viveremus; quemadmodum Johan. III. v. 16. Christus ipse exposuit: in quo novum diligendi proximi argumentum latet, 1. Joh. III. v. 16. jam expositum. Cornelius à Lapide notat hic: Quod Deus in se sit charitas formalis, in nobis autem causalis, idque omni genere causæ, puta materialis, quia ipse est objectum charitatis nostræ: formalis, quia ipse ejusdem est exemplar: Efficientis quia ipse eam in nobis producit: Finalis quia ipse est finis noster & amoris nostri. Observetur autem in Grotio Sociniana vocis μονογενὴς depravatio, quod sit dilectissimus, quum contra illa notetur non charitas, vel dilectio, sed generatio Filii a Patre, eaq; substantialis, qua uni- & soli-genitus Dei Filius ab æterno è substantia Patris natus est, Psalm. II, 7. Mich. V, 2.

## 4:10
Ver. 10.

In this is love.] What he had said more generally, he explains more specifically. In this, he says, it is, that is, that admirable love appears. Not that we loved God.] Not that, because not. There is indeed a certain love of God toward those who love God, and indeed greater than any other; but most admirable is the love toward those who are hostile. Paul teaches this very thing in Romans V, verses 6, 7, and Titus III, v. 4.

But that He Himself loved us] Freely and first: which is added below in verse 10. In the Manuscript, instead of 'He Himself' (αὐτὸς) it is 'that One' (ἐκεῖνος).

And he sent his Son as a propitiation for our sins] That he might extinguish sin in us. See above II, 2.

Not the extinction but the expiation of sin is denoted by the word ἱλασμοῦ. Compare 1 John II. 1; 1 John I. v. 29; Heb. I. v. 3; a propitiation, by which he appeased and reconciled us to GOD the Father, Rom. III. v. 25; chap. V, 10. Most explain it as an expiatory sacrifice. The Apostle, says Estius, signifies that God sent his Son, who was to be a sacrifice, which, being immolated on the altar of the cross, he himself might be reconciled to us, having been angry at our sins. Augustine, treating this passage in book XV de Trinit. chap. 17, reads 'litatorem' (sacrificer) instead of the word 'propitiationem'. Bede also mentions this reading. Moreover, Christ is a 'litator', that is, a sacrificer, because he sacrificed himself, that he might render the Father propitious to us. The Greek word ἱλασμὸς can be taken in either sense, but better in the former. Thus Estius. See what was said at 1 John II, 1.

Latin:

Vers. 10.

Ἐν τούτῳ ἐστὶν ἡ ἀγάπη.] Quod generalius dixerat, id specialius explicat. In hoc, inquit, est, id est, apparet admirabilis illa dilectio. Οὐχ ὅτι ἡμεῖς ἠγαπήσαμεν τὸν Θεόν.] Οὐχ ὅτι, ὅτι οὐχ. Est quidem & quidam amor Dei erga Dei amatores, & quidem major quam ullus ante; sed maxime admirabilis est amor erga infestos. Hoc ipsum docet Paulus Roman. V. vers. 6. 7. Tit. III. v. 4.

Ἀλλ' ὅτι αὐτὸς ἠγάπησεν ἡμᾶς] Ultro ac prior: quod ad- ditur infra 10. In Manuscripto pro αὐτὸς est ἐκεῖνος.

Καὶ ἀπέστειλε τὸν ὑἱὸν αὑτοῦ ἱλασμὸν περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν] Ut exstingueret in nobis peccatum. Vide supra II, 2.

Non exstinctio sed expiatio peccati voce ἱλασμοῦ notatur. Conf. 1. Joh. II. 1. Joh. I. v. 29. Ebr. I. v. 3. propitiatio, qua nos placavit & reconciliavit DEO Patri, Rom. III. v. 25. cap. V, 10. Plerique de sacrifi- cio expiatorio explicant. Significat, inquit, Estius, Apostolus, Deum misisse Filium suum, qui esset sa- crificium, quo in ara crucis immolato, ipse ob peccata nostra nobis iratus reconciliaretur. Augustinus hunc locum tractans lib. XV. de Trinit. cap. 17. loco vo- cabuli propitiationem legit litatorem. Cujus lectio- nis etiam Beda meminit. Est autem Christus lita- tor, id est, sacrificator, quia sacrificavit seipsum, ut Patrem nobis redderet propitium. Græca vox ἱλασμὸς utroque sensu potest accipi, sed melius priori. Hæc Estius. Vide quæ ad 1. Joh. II, 1. dicta.

## 4:11
Vers. 11.

Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.] Any men whatsoever, as above 7. 'So', that is, with no discrimination of men.

Now he urges the argument from the love of God. If God so loved us men, how much more ought man to love man. Compare Eph. V. v. 1. If God, says Oecumenius on this passage, so loved us, who have no communication with his nature, much more ought we also to love those who are related to us. 'So' does not look so much to the extensive magnitude of divine love as to the intensive, situated in the fact that he gave his own only-begotten Son as a propitiation for our sins.

Latin:

Vers. 11.

Ἀγαπητοὶ εἰ οὕτως ὁ Θεὸς ἠγάπησεν ἡμᾶς, καὶ ἡμεῖς ὀφείλο- μεν ἀλλήλους ἀγαπᾷν.] Homines quosvis, ut supra 7. Οὕτως id est, nullo hominum discrimine.

Jam argumentum à dilectione Dei urget. Si ho- mines nos Deus ita dilexit, quanto magis homo hominem diligere debet. Conf. Ephes. V. v. 1. Si Deus, inquit Oecumenius in h. l. ita nos amavit, qui nullam cum natura ejus communicationem ha- bemus, multo magis etiam nos amare eos, qui cognati sunt nobis, debemus. Οὕτως non tam divini amoris extensivam magnitudinem, quam intensivam re- spicit, in eo sitam, quod ipsummet Filium suum unigenitum propitiationem dederit pro peccatis nostris.

## 4:12
Vers. 12.

No one has ever seen God.] In this life, of course: as Augustine explains in epistles CXI and CXII. And the past tense is to be taken for any time, in the Hebrew manner. Compare John I. v. 18 and below 20. No one, therefore, can enjoy God in that way: but we can by loving God. For love is union. What is said here, that God is invisible, Empedocles says the same: 'It is not possible to approach with eyes, or to take with hands, those things which are attainable; nor does the path of Persuasion fall into the minds of men.'

This is also cited as if from the Sibyllines: 'For what flesh is able to see with eyes the heavenly and true immortal God who dwells in the sky? But not even are men, being mortal, able to stand opposite the rays of the sun.'

If we love one another, God abides in us.] He joins himself to the lover, as above III, 24.

And his love is perfected in us] He loves God perfectly, as above ch. II, 5; for he accommodates himself to the will of God, as we said there; add also that he imitates God. These two are the greatest things in love.

This either looks to the consequence of the preceding argument, such as he openly connects in v. 20, in which way Estius wishes to insinuate: God who is in himself from us; or it refers to the following words, as if to say: No one indeed has seen God or can see him in this life: yet God certainly dwells and remains in us, who sincerely love our neighbor, if that love flows from true faith and love toward God: and the love of God is explained and diffused in us. For although we do not see him, yet if we love our neighbor, he, though invisible, will be most present to us, and thus, remaining, will establish his seat and throne in our soul; nay, his love will be fully expressed and perfected in our soul, as Cornelius says from Oecumenius.

By ἀγάπην θεοῦ is understood the love with which God pursues us, not that with which we pursue God. For this is the divine grace of the τῆς μονῆς immanence or indwelling of God in us, whether it is considered as the cause, as it is viewed as an affection in GOD, or as the effect, by which He demonstrates Himself in us through various gifts. Estius offers this sense: His grace, he says, and his love is perfected (or consummated) in us. For it is the participle τετελειωμένη, and that in us ought to be referred to this participle. Some explain the copula 'And' causally, and understand the love of God, by which God loves us, so that the sense may be: If we love one another, God remains in us through his grace, because he loves us with a perfect love. Although he would prefer to understand that love by which we love God, which he calls perfect, that is, sincere, Christian, and conformable to the divine law, so that he may not have need to posit an imperfect love in God as well, yet this reasoning is nothing. For it does not follow: The love of God toward us is perfect in us. Therefore there is also a certain imperfect love in God. For this reason, Cornelius à Lapide is not averse to this interpretation of ours. These things can be understood, he says, not of our love, but of GOD'S. For this is what 'his' signifies, as if to say: God, although he is invisible, nevertheless remains in us through love, nay, he shows that he loves us with a perfect love, while remaining in us he effects, preserves, and increases the love by which we love not only him, but also our neighbor for his sake. The following verse and St. Augustine hint at this sense: Love, he says, him who has begun to dwell in you, so that by dwelling more perfectly he may make you perfect. From the context it is certainly clear that the discourse is continued concerning the grace and love of God toward us, from which he gives us of his Spirit, from which he also sent the Son as Savior of the world, to whom also it must be attributed that he deigns to remain and dwell in us. Of which he speaks most eloquently in v. 16. And we have known and believed the love that God has in us. He deals with our love toward God only subsequently in v. 19, and deduces it from God's love toward us. Hunnius does not reject the explanation: That from the study of love it can be gathered that the love of God is perfect in us. For although the love of GOD, by which he sent the Son into the world, is in itself always most perfect; yet unless it is apprehended by faith, it remains outside us, and thus is not yet perfect IN US, that is, with respect to us it is not yet apprehended. But when it is apprehended by faith, then that love of GOD is already perfect IN US also, because it is not only now acquired through the Son, but also truly and fully apprehended through faith and rendered our own, and furthermore made so alive that it now inflames our minds also toward love, and so by this means we, having a mutual and reciprocal love with God and at the same time with our neighbor, now complete as it were that circle of reciprocating love, and by the bond of perfection (which, as Paul testifies, is love, Coloss. III.), God and faithful men will be gathered toward each other into one as it were perfect body. The evidence of this love of GOD rendered perfect in us is our love toward our neighbor, as the Apostle says: If we love one another, the love of God is perfect in us, that is, it is known to be perfect in us. Flacius on this passage. His love is fulfilled in us, is said of his own gratuitous love toward us: Just as also before concerning his indwelling, not of our love toward our neighbor, which can never be celebrated as being truly full, which also is clear from the following, where he proclaims the benefits and love of God toward us, not the reverse of ours toward God.

Latin:

Vers. 12.

Θεὸν οὐδεὶς πώποτε τεθέαται.] In hac vita scilicet: quo- modo explicat Augustinus epist. CXI. & CXII. Et sumen- dum est Præteritum pro quovis tempore, more Ebræo. Con- fer Joh. I. v. 18. & infra 20. Nemo ergo eo modo Dei frui potest: sed possumus Deum amando. Amor enim ἕνωσις. Quod hic dicitur Deus inaspectabilis, idem dicit Empedocles: Οὐκ ἔστι πελάσασθαι ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἐφικτὰ Ἡμετέροις, ἢ χερσὶ λαβεῖν ὑπέρ τε μεγίστη Πειθοῦς ἀνθρώποισιν ἁμαξιτὸς εἰς φρένα πίπτει.

Citatur & hoc ut ex Sibyllinis: Τίς γὰρ σὰρξ δύναται τὸν ἐπουράνιον καὶ ἀληθῆ Ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἰδεῖν Θεὸν ἄμβροτον ὃς πόλον οἰκεῖ Ἀλλ' οὐδ' ἀκτίνων κατεναντίον ἠελίοιο Ἄνθρωποι στῆναι δυνατοὶ, θνητοὶ γεγαῶτες.

Ἐὰν ἀγαπῶμεν ἀλλήλους, Θεὸς ἐν ἡμῖν μένει.] Jungit se aman- ti supra III, 24.

Καὶ ἡ ἀγάπη αὐτοῦ τετελειωμένη ἐστὶν ἐν ἡμῖν ] Is perfecte Deum amat, ut supra c. II, 5. accommodat enim se Dei volun- tati, ut ibi diximus, adde & Deum imitatur. Quæ duo in amore maxima.

Id vel ad consequentiam præcedentis argumenti spectat, qualem nectit aperte v. 20. quo pacto E- stius insinuari vult: Deum qui in seipso à nobis; Vel ad sequentia verba se refert, q. d. Nemo qui- dem Deum vidit aut videre potest in hac vita: Deus tamen certo in nobis habitat & manet, qui proximum sincere diligimus, si dilectio illa ex ve- ra in Deum fide ac dilectione promanet: charitas- que Dei perfecta in nobis sese explicat & diffundit. Licet enim eum non videamus, tamen si proximum diligamus, ipse invisibilis erit nobis præsentissimus, adeoque sedem & thronum suum in anima nostra manens constituet, imo charitas ejus in anima no- stra plene exprimetur & perficietur, ut ex Oecumenio Cornelius.

Per ἀγάπην θεοῦ dilectio, qua Deus nos prose- quitur, intelligitur, non qua nos Deum. Est enim hæc gratia divina τῆς μονῆς immanentiæ vel manfi- onis Dei in nobis, sive causa, qua spectatur ceu affe- ctus in DEO, sive effectus, qua sese in nobis de- monstrat per varia charismata. Hunc sensum af- fert Estius: Grace, inquit, Et charitas ejus perfe- cta (seu consummata) est in nobis.. Est enim parti- cipium τετελειωμένη, & illud in nobis ad hoc parti- cipium referri debet. Copulam Et causaliter qui- dam exponunt, & charitatem Dei intelligunt, qua Deus nos diligit, ut sensus sit: Si nos invicem dili- gamus, Deus in nobis manet per gratiam suam, quia perfecta charitate nos diligit. Quanquam vero malit dilectionem illam intelligere, qua nos Deum diligimus, quam perfectam dicit, id est, sinceram, Christianam & legi divinae confor- mem, ne opus habeat, in Deo etiam imperfectam charitatem ponere, ratio tamen haec nulla est. Non enim sequitur: Dei charitas erga nos perfecta est in nobis. Ergo etiam in Deo est charitas quaedam imperfecta. Ideo Cornelius à Lapide non est alie- nus ab hac nostra interpretatione. Accipi hec possunt, inquit, de charitate non nostra, sed DEI. Hoc enim significat τὸ ejus, q. d. Deus licet sit invisi- bilis, per charitatem tamen manet in nobis, quin & charitate perfecta se nos diligere ostendit, dum in nobis manens efficit, conservat & auget charitatem, quae non tantum ipsum, sed & proximum propter ipsum diligamus. Hunc sensum innuit versus se- quens & S. Augustinus: Ama, inquit, eum, qui in te coepit habitare, ut perfectius inhabitando faciat te perfectum. E contextu certe patet, continuari sermonem de gratia & dilectione Dei erga nos, ex qua nobis dat de Spiritu suo, ex qua etiam misit Fi- lium Salvatorem mundi, cui etiam tribuendum, quod dignetur in nobis manere, & habitare. De qua disertissime loquitur v. 16. Et nos cognovimus & credidimus charitati, quam habet Deus in nobis. De charitate nostra erga Deum deinceps demum v. 19. agit, eandemque ex Dei erga nos dilectio- ne deducit. Non abnuit Hunnians explicatio: Quod ex studio charitatis possit colligi, quod charitas Dei in nobis sit perfecta. Etsi enim DEI charitas, qua mundo misit Filium, per se perfectissima sem- per est; tamen nisi fide apprehendatur, manet extra nos, & sic IN NOBIS nondum perfecta est, id est, respectu nostri nondum apprehensa est. Quando autem apprehenditur fide, tum jam IN NOBIS quoque perfecta est DEI charitas illa, quia non so- lum jam acquisita per Filium, verum etiam per fi- dem vere pleneque apprehensa & propria nobis red- dita, atque insuper sic viva effecta, ut jam nostros animos quoque ad charitatem inflammet, adeoque nos hac ratione mutuam habentes & reciprocam cum Deo simul & proximo dilectionem, jam quasi circulum illum reciprocantis charitatis absolvamus, perfectionisque vinculo, (quod, Paulo teste, dilectio est, Coloss. III.) Deus & homines fideles erga se in- vicem in unum veluti perfectum corpus colligentur. Cujus perfectae in nobis reddita DEI charitatis in- dicium est, & nota nostra in proximum amor, di- cente Apostolo: Si diligamus nos invicem, charitas Dei perfecta est in nobis, hoc est, cognoscitur perfe- cta esse in nobis. Flacius ad h. l. Charitas ejus expleta est in nobis, dicitur de ipsius gratuita dilectio- ne erga nos: Sicut & prius de ejusdem inhabitatio- ne, non de nostra dilectione erga proximum, quae nunquam celebrari potest, quod sit vere plena, quod etiam ex sequentibus liquet, ubi Dei erga nos bene- ficia charitatemque praedicat, non contra nostram erga Deum.

## 4:13
Vers. 13.

Ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ μένομεν, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν ἡμῖν, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος αὑτοῦ δέδωκεν ἡμῖν.] The sense is the same as above in chapter III, 24, except that here is added, ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ μένομεν, which is to be explained thus: from this we know, just as we are in God, so also God is in us. We are in

God through obedience, God in us through operation, God when he gives his Spirit to us can say: I could not give more, namely in this life.

The first ὅτι here is indicative, the latter is causal: In this we know, that we remain in him (that we remain in him) because he has given us of his Spirit, not as if the Spirit himself suffers division, but because the gifts of the Spirit are diverse and various, of which the Spirit distributes as he wills, 1 Corinth. XII. v. 11. Therefore Estius and others accept these things concerning the variety of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, not concerning love itself. But it can also be said that he has given us of his Spirit as a certification of that matter, that we remain in God; because the Spirit testifies as a pledge of salvation that we are children of GOD, just as the blessed Hunnius wishes the argument to be brought here to establish the certainty of the indwelling of God in us. Indeed, the reason brought forward concerning the dwelling of God in us through grace and the love of God, which implies our dwelling in God through faith, had to be confirmed, which therefore the Apostle wished to prove both from the donation of the Holy Spirit, who by his testimony in our heart makes us certain of the grace and gracious indwelling of God in us, and from faith and the confession of the Son of God, as being the faith through which we are in God, and conversely God in us, which he establishes from the end of the mission of the Son of God, since, as the Evangelical proclamation testifies, for this reason God sent his Son as the Savior of the world, that he who has received and confessed him by true faith might enjoy communion with GOD, v. 14. 15. and from the nature of GOD, that he is love itself, and so he who remains in love, remains in God, which he illustrates by his own example and that of the faithful, that they too, believing the love of God which God has toward us, embracing it by faith, enjoy this communion, and so feel and experience the grace of God that they have confidence in the day of judgment without any fear, v. 17. 18. Concerning the Spirit, says St. John, which Cornelius à Lapide acknowledges can be accepted in this way not only concerning the gifts, but also concerning the Spirit himself, he gave us of his Spirit, because the Hebrews construct verbs of partaking, such as 'he gave', with the preposition 'ex' or 'de' with the ablative, which sense Grotius also admits. The reason for the inference is manifest: Because he who has the Spirit, he can be entirely certain that he has communion with God, that God remains in him, and he is in God, since the Holy Spirit rejoices in internal testimony and the infallible pledge of divine grace, Rom. VIII. v. 16. 2. Cor. I. v. 21. 22. Eph. I. v. 14.

Latin:

Vers. 13.

Ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ μένομεν, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν ἡμῖν, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος αὑτοῦ δέδωκεν ἡμῖν.] Est idem sensus, qui supra cap. III, 24. nisi quod hic additur, ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ μένομεν, quod sic explicandum est: inde cognoscimus, quemadmo- dum nos in Deo sumus, ita & Deum in nobis esse. Nos in

Deo sumus per obedientiam, Deus in nobis per operationem, Deus cum Spiritum suum nobis dat dicere potest: Plus dare non potui, nempe in hac vita.

Prius ὅτι hic ὁριστικὸν, posterius αἰτιολογικὸν est: In hoc cognoscimus, quod nos maneamus in ipso (nos manere in ipso) quia de Spiritu suo dedit nobis, non quasi Spiritus ipse divisionem patiatur, sed quod Spiritus dona diversa & diversa sunt, de quibus prout vult distribuit Spiritus, 1. Corinth. XII. v. 11. Accipiunt ergo hæc Estius & alii de varietate donorum Spiritus S. non de charitate ipsa. Sed & de Spiritu suo dedisse nobis dici potest rei istius certificationem, quod in Deo maneamus; quia Spiritus testificatur tanquam arrha salutis, quod DEI filii simus, quemadmodum B. Hunnius argumentum hic adduci vult ad fanciendam certitudinem inhabitationis Dei in nobis. Nimirum confirmanda erat ratio adducta à μονῇ Dei in nobis per gratiam & amorem Dei, quæ nostri in Deo μονὴν per fidem importat, quam proinde Apostolus probare voluit tum à Spiritus S. donatione, qui testimonio suo in corde nostro certos reddit nos de gratia & gratiosa immansione Dei in nobis, tum à fide ac confessione Filii Dei, utpote per quam fidem nos in Deo sumus, & vicissim Deus in nobis, quod à fine missionis Filii Dei statuminat, quoniam, teste præconio Evangelico, ea de causa miserit Deus Filium suum mundi Salvatorem, ut qui vera fide eundem susceperit, ac confessus fuerit, communione cum DEO fruatur, vers. 14. 15. tum à DEI natura, quod ipsa charitas sit, adeoque qui in charitate manet, in Deo maneat, quam exemplo suo ac fidelium illustrat, quod & ipsi credentes charitatem Dei, quam Deus erga nos habet, fide amplectentes, hac communione fruantur, Deique gratiam ita sentiant & experiantur, ut fiduciam habeant in die judicii sine ullo timore, v. 17. 18. De Spiritu, inquit S. Johannes, quod agnoscit Cornelius à Lapide non tantum de donis, sed etiam de ipso Spiritu hoc modo accipi posse Spiritum suum dedit nobis, quia Ebræi verba contractus, quale est dedit, construunt cum præpositione ex vel de cum ablativo, quem sensum admittit quoque Grotius. Illationis ratio manifesta est: Quia qui habet Spiritum, ille certus omnino esse potest, se habere communionem cum Deo, Deum in sese manere, ac se in Deo esse, quum Spiritus S. interno testimonio & pignore divinæ gratiæ infallibili gaudeat, Rom. VIII. v. 16. 2. Cor. I. v. 21. 22. Eph. I. v. 14.

## 4:14
Vers. 14.

And we have seen and bear witness that the Father has sent the Son as the Savior of the world.] This means: That which I said, that the Son was sent by God to liberate men, no one ought to doubt. For we are many eyewitnesses of that fact. We saw Jesus dead, we saw him also resurrected. He had said, however, that he would die to redeem the human race, Matt. 20:28, 26:28. Nor would God have raised Jesus from the dead if that Jesus had wished to deceive the human race. Ἀπέσταλκε Σωτῆρα, that is, he sent, so that he might be the Savior. Thus ἐλήλυθας διδάσκαλος, John 3:2, that is, you have come so that you might be a Teacher. Thus just now ἀπέστειλεν ἱλασμὸν is equivalent to εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἱλασμὸν. Concerning the name Σωτῆρος see Luke 2:11, John 4:42, Acts 5:31, chapter 13:23. Great is the salvation of being snatched from destruction and led to eternal life. Mention of the world is made, however, because Christ excludes no one. See above chapter 2:2, John 3:16, chapter 4:42.

Grotius seems, along with the Socinians, to regard the death and resurrection of Christ only as a confirmation of the testimony and doctrine which he had proposed, not as a satisfaction for our sins and a merit for our sins; therefore he also made mention only of an example, verse 15. But St. John does indeed appeal to the vision not only of the death and resurrection of Christ, but also of the miracles by which he demonstrated himself as the promised Messiah, as the Son of God and true God with the Father, Matt. XI, v. 2, John V, 36, ch. X, 38, ch. I, v. 14, ch. II, 11, etc., who came into the world so that the world might be saved through him, John III, 17, not only to the vision, but to the proclamation or doctrine of Christ, for the sake of confirming which those miracles were performed, by which he professed himself the Savior of the world, not merely through information about obtaining salvation, but through the acquisition of salvation, not by the increase of the law, not by example, but by merit. Concerning which [I have written] most extensively in Socinismus profligatus. Previously, verse 9, he had called the Son of God the Only-begotten, sent into the world so that we might live through him, when he was dealing with our regeneration: Furthermore, verse 10, where he was urging the argument from the love of God, with which he pursued us, even though we were sinners, to the debt of our love toward our brothers, he said the Son of God was sent as a propitiation for our sins. Now, since he teaches that we enjoy communion with God through faith in Jesus the Son of God, he says the Son was sent as the Savior of the world, so that he who believes in him, and by true faith applies and appropriates to himself the salvation obtained through the merit of Christ, may become a participant in eternal salvation, which consists in the enjoyment of God in the kingdom of glory, v. 14, 15.

Latin:

Vers. 14.

Καὶ ἡμεῖς τεθεάμεθα καὶ μαρτυρῦμεν, ὅτι ὁ πατὴρ ἀπέσταλκε τὸν ὑιὸν Σωτῆρα τῦ κόσμε.] Hoc vult: Quod dixi missum à Deo Filium ad liberandos homines, de eo dubitare nemo debet. Sumus enim nos complures ejus rei testes oculati. Vidimus Jesum mortuum, vidimus & resuscitatum. Dixerat autem se moriturum ad redimendum genus humanum, Matth. XX. v. 28. c. XXVI. v. 28. Neque Jesum Deus à mortuis excitasset, si is Jesus decipere voluisset genus humanum. Ἀπέσταλκε Σωτῆρα, id est, misit, ut esset Servator. Sic ἐλήλυθας διδάσκαλος, Joh. III. v. 2. id est, venisti, ut Doctor esses. Sic modo ἀπέστειλεν ἱλασμὸν valet εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἱλασμὸν. De nomine Σωτῆρος vide Luc. II. v. 11. Joh. IV. v. 42. Actor. V. v. 31. cap. XIII. v. 23. Magna est salus eripi exitio & perduci ad vitam æternam. Mundi autem fit mentio, quia Christus neminem excludit. Vide supra c. II. v. 2. Joh. III. v. 16. c. IV, 42.

Videtur Grotius cum Socinianis Christi mortem & resurrectionem solum tanquam testimonii & doctrinæ, quam proposuerat, confirmationem, non tanquam satisfactionem pro peccatis nostris, & meritum pro peccatis nostris spectare, ideo & exempli mentionem solum fecit, v. 15. At provocat quidem S. Johannes ad visionem non autem tantum mortis & resurrectionis Christi, sed etiam miraculorum, quibus sese ceu promissum Mes- siam, ceu Filium Dei & verum cum Patre Deum demonstravit Matth. XI. v. 2. Johann. V, 36. cap. X, 38. cap. I. v. 14. cap. II, 11. &c. qui in mundum venerit, ut mundus salvaretur per ipsum Johann. III, 17. nec ad visionem solum, sed ad præconium vel doctrinam Christi, cujus confirmandæ gra- tia miracula illa patrabantur, qua sese Salvato- rem mundi professus est, non per informationem modo de salute consequenda, sed per salutis ac- quisitionem non legis augmento, non exemplo, sed merito. De quo fusissime in Socinismo profli- gato. Antea vers. 9. dixerat Filium DEI Unige- nitum, missum in mundum, ut viveremus per ipsum, quum de regeneratione nostra ageret: Porro vers. 10. ubi argumentum urgeret à Dei dilectione, qua nos prosecutus est, etsi peccatores, ad debitum dilectionis nostræ erga fratres, missum Filium Dei dixit ceu propitiationem pro peccatis nostris. Jam cum per fidem in Jesum DEI Filium nos communione cum Deo frui docet, Filium mis- sum ait ceu Salvatorem mundi, ut qui in eum cre- dit, & salutem per Christi meritum partam vera fide sibi applicat & appropriat, æternæ salutis, quæ in fruitione Dei in regno gloriæ consistit, parti- ceps fiat v. 14. 15.

## 4:15
Verse 15.

Whoever shall confess that Jesus is the Son of God.] Who will profess, not only in words but also in deeds, that Jesus is the Son of God, that is, proposed to us as an example. For whom should we imitate rather than the Son of God?

God abides in him, and he in God.] That is, just as he himself is united to God, so in turn God is to him, above [at] 12.

He urges confession, but one which proceeds from faith; unless he takes the same metonymically for faith, or synecdochically includes it together with faith, by the force of the parallel passage Romans X, 9, 10. He certainly describes the faithful as those who believe in Jesus the Son of God, so that there may be a more illustrious antithesis of the unfaithful and heretics, who do not believe, and therefore do not confess, that Jesus is the Son of God, verse 3. From the gift of the Holy Spirit he had concluded communion with God the Father, verse 12. Now, from the Son of God apprehended through faith, he proves the same in this 15th verse, and finally intends to confirm the same from the very nature of God, who is love, and deigns to communicate himself to us, so that he himself may be in us and we in him, verse 16, who through faith remain in love and divine grace, and trust in him alone. That confession regards Jesus by reason of merit, that he is the Son of God, the Savior of the world, and the propitiation for our sins, in whom through faith we alone have eternal life. Therefore, it is very poorly perverted by Grotius, as if it regarded Jesus proposed to us as an example, so that we might imitate him, and thus profess him by our deeds. For by the imitation of Christ in deeds and works, no one obtains eternal life and salvation, which we do not attain except through faith in Christ, as witnessed by St. John the Evangelist, ch. XX, 21, and the whole choir of Prophets and Apostles, Acts X, v. 43, ch. XV, verse 11.

Latin:

Vers. 15.

Ὅς ἂν ὁμολογήσῃ, ὅτι Ἰησῦς ἐσιν ὁ ὑὸς τῦ Θεῦ.] Qui non ver- bis tantum, sed & factis profitebitur Jesum esse Filium Dei, id est, nobis in exemplar propositum. Quem enim potius imitemur, quam Dei Filium?

ὁ Θεὸς ἐν ἀυτῷ μένει, καὶ ἀυτὸς ἐν τῷ Θεῷ.] Id est, sicut ipse Deo adunatur, ita vicissim Deus ipsi, supra 12.

Confessionem urget, sed quæ ex fide proficisci- tur; nisi Metonymicè eandem pro fide accipiat, vel Synecdochice una cum fide complectatur, vi loci paralleli Roman. X, 9. 10. Fideles certe ita describit, qui in Jesum credunt Dei Filium, ut illustrior antithesis sit infidelium & hæretico- rum, qui non credunt, adeoque nec confitentur, JESUM esse DEI Filium vers. 3. E Spiritus San- cti dono concluserat communionem cum DEO Patre vers. 12. Jam è Filio Dei per fidem appre- henso eandem probat hoc 15. commate, denique confirmaturus eandem ex ipsa Dei natura, qui charitas est, & communicare se nobis dignatur, ut ipse in nobis sit & nos in ipso, vers. 16. qui per fidem manemus in charitate & gratia divina, eidemque unice confidimus. Ὁμολογία illa Je- sum respicit ratione meriti, quod sit Filius Dei Sal- vator mundi, & propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, in quo per fidem unice habemus vitam æternam. Pessime ergo à Grotio pervertitur, quasi respiciat Jesum nobis in exemplum propositum, ut ipsum imitemur, adeoque factis eum profiteamur. Nam imitatione Christi factis & operibus nemo vitam & salutem æternam adipiscitur, quam non nisi per fidem in Christum consequimur, teste S. Johan- ne Evangelista cap. XX, 21. totoque Prophetarum & Apostolorum choro, Actorum X. v. 43. cap. XV. vers. 11.

## 4:16
Verse 16.

And we have known and believed the love that God has in us.] That which we teach others about the love of God toward us, that we ourselves have known, that is, have learned, namely from Christ, John III, 16, and we believe, which we show sufficiently by bearing so many evils for the sake of that faith. In the manuscript, for we have believed, it is we believe.

These things are not only brought forth in the person of the Apostles, as those things said in verse 14, but in the person of the faithful, who all acknowledge the love of God which he has toward us, and trust in it with true and firm confidence of heart.

These things are repeated now not only so that they may stick in the mind, or be received and kept with true faith, but for this reason, that the argument from the nature of God the Father, whose supreme love is proclaimed by Christ himself in John 3:16, may be urged for the sake of establishing the communion of the faithful with God.

Whence it is also clear that we are said to abide in love not because of the love with which we embrace God, but because of that with which God has embraced us, when we acknowledge that love which God has in us, or towards us, and place all our confidence in the same. For those who by faith receive that immense love exhibited especially in the mission of the Son and the gift of the Holy Spirit, and through faith abide in that love of God, and confidently and constantly rely upon it, so that they may be properly rooted in the love of God, they enjoy blessed communion with God, they abide in God, and God abides in them. Therefore, it is not created charity that is understood, but the immense love of God, not a habit of charity infused into us, or charity which is in us—which charity Lombard called uncreated, though the rest of the Papists argue against him that it is created, and say that his opinion was condemned in the Council of Trent: But the ineffable and incomprehensible affection of God's mercy towards us, which God, who is rich in mercy, demonstrates through his great love, with which he loves us, τὸν ὑπερβάλλοντα πλῦτον τῆς χάριτος αὑτῦ ἐν χρηστότητι ἐφ' ἡμᾶς ἐν χρισῷ Ἰησῦ, Ephesians 2:4, 7. Flacius teaches that divine love is referred to here, and observes that Thomas also understands the charity of God towards us, not our own, and that this 'who abides in charity' can be understood of the charity of God towards us, just as in Romans 11:22: 'If you continue in the kindness of God.' Grotius acknowledges that verse 17 deals certainly with the highest degree of God's love towards us. Why then should we not likewise understand the divine love towards us in verse 16?

God is therefore proclaimed by charity, and the fruit is described as overflowing from divine charity into us, who embrace the same by faith. And first, indeed, the briefest, yet sweetest definition of God is delivered: God is charity. He does not say with Moses in Deuteronomy 33:3, 'He loves the peoples,' nor with Paul, 'He is rich in mercy because of his great charity'; but in the abstract: God is charity; that is to say, an inexhaustible and infinite fountain of mercy and charity: Or as the great Luther most effectively says: Tom. VI. Jen. German. fol. 46. 'God is himself Love, and his essence is pure, sheer Love, so that if anyone wanted to paint and capture God, he would have to capture such an image that was sheer Love; as if the divine nature were nothing but a furnace and a fire of such love that fills heaven and earth.' And again, if one could paint and form love, one would have to make such an image that was not worldly, nor human, indeed not angelic, nor heavenly, but God himself. See, thus the Apostle can paint it here, that he makes one thing out of God and Love, so that through such a noble, precious, and lovely image he may the more entice and draw us to himself, to strive thereafter that we also have love among one another. Augustine, tract. IX. in 1 John. I do not know whether love could be commended to us more magnificently than by saying that God is love. A brief praise and a great praise, brief in speech, great in understanding.

As to the most noble fruit redundant in us from love: if we apprehend it by true faith: And he who remains in it, he says, (in love) remains in GOD, and God in him. How do we remain in God, insofar as he is love?
