By acknowledging God as love itself, by trustfully embracing him, and by relying solely upon the same, by wrapping ourselves in his love, and by hiding ourselves in the same as in a most safe and most sweet receptacle and bulwark, and by sustaining ourselves by the protection of the same against the gates of hell. Therefore, Blessed Luther says, l. c. fol. 49, that those who fail from faith in the time of temptation do not remain in love, and on fol. 50 he teaches that St. John urges this most strongly in this place, to remain in the doctrine of Christ, although he explains this passage concerning love toward one's neighbor. We do not deny that these things are discussed by St. John for the sake of commending this grace; but we maintain that those words refer immediately to the dwelling in the love of God through faith, through which God dwells in our hearts, Eph. 3:17. Which sense the context also confirms, concerning which Cornelius: The Syrian: For God is love, for he gives the reason why he said: And we believe in love, and why God has love in us, that is, toward us. For the reason is that God is love itself by essence, and therefore he cannot deceive the one who believes, hopes, and loves, but since he is pure and mere love, he communicates all his things and his whole self to him, and pours himself into him. And further: The reason, he says, why God is love by essence, is that he himself by essence is pure, mere, and supreme good, whose nature it is to be clearly and fully communicative and diffusive of himself, says St. Dionysius, which is the property of love. For God is a sea of honey, that is, an Ocean of goodness and love. GOD is as it were a fire always burning, igniting all things and transmuting them into himself. Therefore God is love, because love is as it were a spiritual flame inflaming all, and as it were a light shining everywhere, and illuminating all things. Hence St. Dionysius, On the Divine Names, ch. 14, p. 1, says that divine love is a motive force and one drawing upward into God, who alone is the beautiful and good in and of himself. Since, therefore, we remain in love, God, who is love itself, wishes to remain in us with all the treasures of immense grace, and to fill us with all his divine fullness, the breadth, and length, and depth, and height of which divine love we apprehend through faith, rooted and grounded in that love, Eph. 3:18. GOD demonstrated this love of his most powerfully in that work which St. John here so frequently and so magnificently proclaims, namely, the mission of his only-begotten Son; When it comes, says Blessed Luther fol. 47, to spiritual goods, he pours out, not sun and moon, nor heaven and earth, but his own heart, and his dearest Son, so that he even lets him shed his blood, and die the most shameful death for us shameful, wicked, ungrateful people. How can one say otherwise here, than that GOD is nothing but an abyss of eternal love, and again, that love is nothing else but pure GOD? Therefore, whoever has love must also have pure GOD, and be full of the same. But concerning that fruit of divine love apprehended by faith: He who remains (by faith) in love, remains in GOD, and GOD in him, Blessed Luther l. c. has it thus on fol. 52. John praises him who remains in love, not as a man, nor as a prince, king, or emperor, but as a God, and sets him above all creatures in GOD himself, so that he and GOD are undivided. What is now more precious and more glorious to wish for, than to be and remain one thing with GOD, where the high Majesty is? O holy union! O ineffable good! exclaims here Blessed Glassius. To be united with God is to be glued to him, and to be one Spirit with him, 1 Cor. 6:17, and thus to be made a partaker of the divine nature, 2 Pet. 1:4, and to be transferred into the communion of heavenly goods. God remains in us, as in his temple, which he fills with the fullness of his Majesty and grace. Conversely, we are in God, as in our sanctuary. For the Lord God Almighty is also our temple, Rev. 21:22, and they dwell in each other, says Augustine in this tract. VIII. he who contains and he who is contained. You dwell in God, but so that you may be contained; God dwells in you, but so that he may contain you, lest you fall, lest by chance you think yourself to become the house of God in the way that your house carries your flesh. If the house in which you are withdraws itself, you fall: if, however, you withdraw yourself, it will not fall. God is whole when you desert him, whole when you return to him. You are healed, you will not provide him anything: You are cleansed, you are restored, you are corrected. He is medicine to the sick, a rule to the crooked, light to the darkened, a dwelling to the deserted. Therefore all things are conferred upon you. And tract. IX. Let GOD be a house to you, be you a house of God: Remain in God, and let God remain in you. God remains in you, that he may contain you, remain in God that you may not fall. A happy union, says St. Bernard, sermon 71 on the Song of Songs; man and God cling to each other; but they cling on all sides by intimate and mutual love, being engrafted into one another, through which I would undoubtedly say that God is in man, and man is in GOD. But man is indeed from eternity in God, as if loved from eternity, if indeed he be of those who say: Since he loved and graced us in his beloved Son before the foundation of the world. But GOD is in man from the time he is loved by man. And in the book on conscience, col. m. 1096. Think therefore, when placed in the society of others, that you will not always be able to remain with them, and meanwhile choose a companion who, when all things have been taken away, keeps faith with his lovers, and does not withdraw in the time of distress. Gather together, therefore, all the distractions of your heart and the fluctuations of your mind, and fix your whole desire in God alone, so that your heart may be there, your desirable and much-lovable treasure. He frequently visits and willingly inhabits the tranquility of the heart and the leisure of a quiet mind, since he is peace, and his place is in peace. Therefore, prepare yourself in such a way that GOD may be present with you; let him be in your mouth, let him be in your heart, let him go with you, let him return with you, and let him not depart from you. Unless you are the first to dismiss him, he will never dismiss you; wherever you may be, you will never be able to be alone, but GOD will be with you. Cleanse, therefore, your conscience, and always be prepared, so that at whatever hour he may come and wish to dwell with you, he may find in you a dwelling prepared for himself, for he himself said: Make me a sanctuary, and I will dwell in the midst of you. Let us therefore strive to build the temple of God within us: first indeed so that the Lord may dwell in each of us, and so that he may dwell in all of us together, because he disdains neither individuals nor the whole. And afterwards: He who thus gathers the wanderings of the mind into one, and fixes all the motions of the heart in one desire for eternity, has truly already returned to his heart, already there willingly dwells, and is wonderfully delighted: and since he cannot conceive it for joy, he is led above himself, and by an excess of mind is elevated into the highest, and thus through himself by the thought of himself he ascends to the knowledge of GOD, so that he learns to think of him alone unceasingly, and to rest in him delightfully, when the love of Christ has absorbed the whole affection of the man, so that negligent and unmindful of himself he feels nothing but Jesus Christ alone, and the things that are of Jesus Christ; then at last, as I think, charity is perfect in him. He who is thus continually delighted in the love of God, frequently suffers excesses of mind, frequently being snatched from all present and earthly things is presented before GOD: And when he considers the beauty, and the magnitude of the beauty, he is astonished and suspended in admiration of it, he admires the glory of the King, the magnificence of the kingdom, the nobility of the heavenly city. And when he contemplates the happiness, the decorum of glory, the goodness of God, the sweetness of internal suavity, and the tranquility of eternal rest; he meditates on the power of the Father, the wisdom of the Son, the kindness of the Holy Spirit, and the blessedness of the Angelic creature. He is delighted from God in God, while he admires his piety, and contemplates his decorum. O how pleasant! if it were not so brief, he is snatched away rapidly, he contemplates only heavenly things, by contemplating he is made joyful. But when he tries to stay there longer, he suddenly slips, returning to himself he can intimate to no one what he saw, above himself, enticed by the agitation of sweetness, he tastes the suavity of sweetness, and admires that heavenly infusion of spiritual joy within himself. He also revolves in his heart with a silent mind the clarity of incorporeal light, the savor of intimate satiety, and another secret of internal rest, and a mystery of highest tranquility; in the love of this contemplation the sweet mind is delightfully affected, and wonderfully delighted. The same Bernard cited here by Thomas Anglicus: God is charity, says Bernard: What therefore is better than charity? And he who remains in charity, remains in GOD: What therefore is more secure than charity? And God is in him: What therefore is more pleasant than charity? Which things especially agree with divine charity. For than this there is nothing better, nothing more secure, nothing more pleasant. As in the other life GOD will be a temple to the elect; because there they will contemplate, adore, and praise GOD face to face, and in him, as in a divine and uncreated temple, they will obtain a divine and blessed mansion: So to the faithful God is a temple in this life, because in God they themselves see the glory of the Lord as with an unveiled face, 2 Cor. III. v. 17. and they adore and praise him remaining in this divine temple: which is a foretaste of the eternal most blessed mansion in God.

Latin:

Vers. 16.

Καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐγνώκαμεν κὰι πεπισεύκαμεν τὴν ἀγάπην ἣν ἔχει ὁ Θεὸς ἐν ἡμῖν.] Quod nos de Dei in nos amore docemus alios, id ipsi cognovimus, id est, didicimus, nempe à Christo Joh. III, 16. & credimus, quod ostendimus satis tot mala propter istam fidem ferendo. In Manuscripto pro πεπισεύκαμεν est πισεύομεν.

Non tantum hæc in persona Apostolorum, ut quæ vers. 14. dicta, sed in persona fidelium pro- feruntur, qui omnes agnoscunt amorem DEI, quem habet erga nos, eique confidunt vera & fir- ma cordis fiducia.

Non ideo tantum hæc, ut hæreant animo, vel ut vera fide suscipiantur, & custodiantur, sed ea de causa jam repetuntur, ut argumentum à natura Dei Patris, cujus amor summus Johann. III. v. 16. à Christo ipso deprædicatur, urgeatur, pro fidelium cum Deo communione stabilienda.

Unde etiam luculentum est, manere in amore nos dici non de amore, quo DEUM comple- ctimur, sed quo DEUS nos complexus est, cum amorem illum, quem DEUS habet in nobis, vel erga nos, agnoscimus, inque eundem no- stram fiduciam omnem collocamus. Qui enim fide amorem illum immensum in missione im- primis Filii & donatione Spiritus Sancti exhibi- tum suscipiunt, & per fidem in illo DEI amore manent, eodemque fiducialiter & constanter ni- tuntur, ut radicentur probe in amore Dei, illi beata Dei communione fruuntur, in DEO ma- nent, & Deus manet in ipsis. Non ergo crea- ta charitas, sed immensus DEI amor intelligitur, non habitus charitatis nobis infusus, aut chari- tas, quæ in nobis est, quam charitatem increa- tam Lombardus dixit, creatam vero esse adver- sus ipsum disputant reliqui Papistæ, ejusque sen- tentiam in Concilio Tridentino damnatam esse ajunt: Sed affectus Dei erga nos ineffabilis juxta & incomprehensibilis misericordiæ, qui DEUS dives misericordia per multam dilectionem suam, qua amat nos τὸν ὑπερβάλλοντα πλῦτον τῆς χάρι- τος αὑτῦ ἐν χρηστότητι ἐφ' ἡμᾶς ἐν χρισῷ Ἰησῦ demonstrat Ephes. II. v. 4. 7. Dilectionem di- vinam hic respici docet Flacius, & observat Thomam etiam intelligere DEI charitatem erga nos, non nostram, & hoc qui manet in chari- tate, intelligi posse de charitate DEI erga nos, sicut Roman. XI. v. 22. Si permanseritis in beni- gnitate Dei. De summo certe dilectionis Dei erga nos gradu vers. 17. agi, agnoscit Grotius. Cur ergo v. 16. non pariter dilectionem divinam erga nos intelligamus.

Deprædicatur ergo DEUS à charitate, & de- scribitur fructus à charitate divina in nos redun- dans, qui eandem fide amplectimur. Et primum quidem brevissima, at suavissima traditur Dei de- finitio, Deus est charitas. Non dicit cum Mose Deut. XXXIII. v. 3. diligit populos, non cum Pau- lo dives est in misericordia propter multam cha- ritatem suam; sed in abstracto: Deus est cha- ritas; q. d. fons inexhaustus & infinitus mise- ricordiæ & charitatis: Vel ut efficacissime Me- galander Lutherus: Tom. VI. Jen. German. fol. 46. GOtt ist selbst die Liebe, und sein Wesen ist eitel lauter Liebe, daß, wenn iemand wollte GOtt mahlen und treffen, so müste er ein solch Bild treffen, das eitel Liebe wäre; als sey die Gött- liche Natur nichts, denn ein Feuer-Ofen, und Brunst solcher Liebe, die Himmel und Erden füllet. Und wiederum, wenn man könnte die Liebe mahlen und bilden, müste man ein solch Bild machen, das nicht wercklich, noch mensch- lich, ja nicht englisch, noch himmlisch, sondern GOtt selbst wäre. Sihe, also kan es der Apo- stel hie mahlen, daß er aus GOtt und der Liebe ein Ding machet, auff daß er uns durch solch edel, köstlich und lieblich Bilde destomehr an sich locke und ziehe, darnach zu trachten, daß wir auch un- ter einander Liebe haben. Augustinus tract. IX. in 1. Joh. Nescio utrum magnificentius nobis chari- tas commendari possit, quam ut diceretur Deus cha- ritas. Brevis laus & magna laus, brevis in sermone, magna in intellectu.

Quod ad fructum nobilissimum in nos à cha- ritate redundantem : si vera fide eam apprehen- damus : Et qui manet in illa, inquit, (charita- te) in DEO manet, & Deus in illo. Quomodo in Deo, quatenus charitas est, manemus ? Deum ceu charitatem ipsam agnoscendo , fiducialiter amplectendo, inque eadem unice confidendo, nos charitati ejus involvendo, & in eadem ceu tutissimo, suavissimoque receptaculo & propu- gnaculo nos occultando, ejusdemque præsidio adversus inferorum portas nos sustentando. Ideo non manere in charitate dicit B. Lutherus l. c. fol. 49. qui tempore tentationis à fide deficiunt, & fol. 50. S. Johannem, docet, id maxime urgere h. l. in doctrina Christi manere , licet de charitate er- ga proximum hunc locum explicet. Cujus com- mendandæ gratiæ hæc à S. Johanne disseri non abnuimus ; sed ut verba illa immediate referant mansionem in dilectione Dei per fidem, per quam Deus habitat in cordibus nostris, Ephes. III. v. 17. Quem sensum etiam συνέχεια confirmat, qua de Cornelius : Syrus : Deus enim charitas est, dat enim causam, cur dixerit : Et nos credimus chari- tati, & cur Deus charitatem habeat in nobis, id est, erga nos. Causa enim est, quod Deus sit ipsis- sima per essentiam charitas, ac proinde credentem, sperantem & amantem se fallere non possit, sed cum sit purus merusque amor, sua omnia totumque se ei communicet, & in eum effundat. Et porro : Ratio, inquit, cur Deus per essentiam sit charitas, est, quod ipse per essentiam sit purum, merum & summum bonum, cujus natura est, esse sui plane ple- neque communicativum & diffusivum, ait S. Dion, quod proprium est charitatis. Deus enim est ma- re mellis, puta Oceanus bonitatis & charitatis. DEUS est quasi ignis semper ardens, omnia accen- dens & in se transmutans. Ergo Deus est chari- tas, quia charitas est quasi flamma spiritualis omnes inflammans, & quasi lumen ubique resplen- descens, & omnia illuminans. Hinc S. Dion de di- vin. nom. cap. 14. pag. 1. ait amorem divinum esse vim motricem & sursum trahentem in Deum, qui solus est ipsum per se pulchrum & bonum. Cum er- go in charitate maneamus, Deus, qui ipsa cha- ritas est, cum omnibus thesauris immensæ gratiæ in nobis manere vult, nosque omni sua divina plenitudine replere, cujus divinæ charitatis τὸ πλάτος, καὶ μῆκος, καὶ βάθος, καὶ ὕψος ap- prehendimus per fidem ἐν ἀγάπῃ ἐῥῥιζωμένοι, καὶ τεθεμελιωμένοι, in charitate illa divina probe ra- dicati & fundati Ephes. III, 18. Quam charitatem suam demonstravit in illo opere DEUS potissi- mum, quod hic tam frequenter, & tam magni- fice deprædicat S. Johannes, missione nempe Fi- lii sui unigeniti; Wenn es kömmt, inquit B. Lu- therus fol. 47. auff die geistlichen Güter, da schüttet er aus, nicht Sonn und Mond, noch Himmel und Erden, sondern sein eigen Hertz, und seinen liebsten Sohn, daß er ihn auch lässet sein Blut vergiessen, und des allerschändlichsten Todes sterben für uns schändliche, böse, un- danckbare Leute. Wie kan man hier anders sa- gen, denn daß der GOTT nichts sey, denn ein Ab- grund ewiger Liebe, und wiederum, die Liebe nichts anders, denn eitel GOTT? Darum wer die Liebe hat, der muß auch eitel GOtt haben, und Desselben voll seyn. De fructu vero illo apprehen- sæ per fidem charitatis divinæ: Qui manet (per fidem) in charitate, manet in DEO, & DEUS in ipso, B. Lutherus l. c. ita habet fol. 52. St. Johan- nes preiset den, der in der Liebe bleibet, nicht als einen Menschen, noch einen Fürsten, König oder Kayser, sondern als einen Gott, und setzet ihn über alle Crea- turen in GOtt selbst, daß er und GOtt ungeschieden seyn. Was ist nun köstlichers und herrlichers zu wünschen, denn mit GOtt ein Ding seyn und blei- ben, da die hohe Majestät ist? O sancta unio! O bonum ineffabile! exclamat hic B. Glassius. ' Uniri cum Deo est adglutinari illi, & unum cum eo Spi- ritum esse, 1. Corinth. VI. v. 17. & sic effici divinæ consortem naturæ, 2. Petr. I, 4. atque in commu- nionem cælestium bonorum transferri. Deus in nobis manet, tanquam in templo suo, quod Maje- statis & gratiæ suæ plenitudine replet. Vicissim nos in Deo sumus, tanquam sanctuario nostro. Nam & Dominus Deus omnipotens est templum nostrum Apoc. XXI. v. 12. & vicissim se habitant, in- quit Augustinus hic tract. VIII. qui continet & qui continetur. Habitas in Deo, sed ut continearis, ha- bitat in te Deus, sed ut te contineat, ne cadas, ne forte sic te putes domum Dei fieri, quomodo domus tua portat carnem tuam. Si subtrahit se domus, in qua es, cadis: si autem tu te subtrahas, non ca- det. Deus integer est, cum eum deseris, integer cum ad illum redieris. Tu sanaris, non illi aliquid præstabis: Tu mundaris, tu reficeris, tu corrigeris. Ille medicamentum est non sano, regula est pravo, lux tenebrato, habitatio deserto. Omnia ergo tibi conferuntur. Et tract. IX. Sit tibi domus DEUS, esto domus Dei: Mane in Deo, & maneat in te De- us. Manet in te Deus, ut te contineat, maneas in Deo ne cadas. Felix unio, inquit S. Bernhardus serm. LXXI. in Cant. inhærent sibi homo & Deus; inhærent autem undique intima mutuaque dilectio- ne, inviscerati alterutrum sibi, per hoc Deum in homine, & hominem in DEO esse haud dubie di- xerim. Sed homo quidem ab æterno in Deo, tan- quam ab æterno dilectus, si tamen ex illis sit, qui dicunt: Quoniam dilexit & gratificavit nos in di- lecto Filio suo ante mundi constitutionem. DEUS vero in homine ex quo dilectus ab homine est. Et in libr. de conscient. col. m. 1096. Cogita ergo in societate aliorum positus, quia non semper poteris manere cum illis, & interim elige socium, qui cum omnia subtracta fuerint, fidem servat dilectoribus suis, nec recedit in tempore angustiæ. Omnes igi- tur cordis distractiones & mentis fluctuationes in unum collige, & in solo Deo totum desiderium tuum fige, ut ibi cor tuum sit, thesaurus tuus desidera- bilis, multumque amabilis. Ipse frequenter visitat & libenter inhabitat tranquillitatem cordis & otium quietæ mentis, quoniam pax est, & in pace locus ejus. Propterea talem te præpara, ut tecum adsit DEUS, sit in ore, sit in corde, tecum eat, tecum redeat, nec à te recedat. Nisi tu prior illum di- miseris, nunquam ille te dimittet, ubicunque fue- ris, nunquam solus esse poteris, sed tecum DEUS erit. Munda igitur conscientiam, & semper esto paratus, ut quacunque hora venerit, & inhabitare tecum voluerit, paratam sibi in te inveniat mansio- nem, ipse namque dixit: Facite mihi sanctua- rium, & habitabo in medio vestri. Studeamus ergo templum Dei ædificare in nobis: primo quidem ut in singulis nobis Dominus, ut in omnibus nobis simul habitet, quia non singulos dedignatur, nec universos. Et postea: Qui sic evagationes mentis in unum colli- git, & omnes cordis motus in uno æternitatis desiderio figit, profecto jam ad cor suum rediit, jam ibi libenter immoratur, ac mirabiliter delectatur: ac cum ipsum prae gaudio concipere non possit, supra seipsum ducitur, & per excessum mentis elevatur in sum- ma, atque ita per semetipsum per cogitationem sui ascendit ad cognitionem DEI, ut discat eum so- lum indeficienter cogitare, & in eo delectabiliter requiescere, cum amor Christi totum absorbuit ho- minis affectum, ut negligens & immemor sui nisi solum Jesum Christum, & quae sunt Jesu Christi, sentiat; tunc demum ut arbitror perfecta in eo cha- ritas est. Qui sic in amore Dei jugiter delectatur, frequenter mentis excessus patitur, frequenter ab omnibus praesentibus & terrenis raptus coram DEO praesentatur: Et cum pulchritudinem considerat, & magnitudinem pulchritudinis attonitus in ejus ad- miratione suspenditur, miratur Regis gloriam, re- gni magnificentiam, supernae civitatis nobilitatem. Et cum felicitatem contemplatur, gloriae decorem, Dei bonitatem, internae suavitatis dulcedinem, & aeternae quietis tranquillitatem; meditatur Patris potentiam, Filii sapientiam, Spiritus Sancti beni- gnitatem, & Angelicae creaturae beatitudinem. Delectatur de Deo in Deum, dum ejus pietatem miratur, & decorem contemplatur. O quam ju- cundum! si non esset tam modicum, raptim rapitur, sola caelestia contemplatur, contemplando jucunda- tur. Sed cum ibi diutius stare conatur, subito la- bitur rediens ad se nulli potest intimare quod vidit, supra se agitatione suavitatis allectus gustat dulcedi- nis suavitatem, & illam caelestem infusionem lae- titiae spiritualis intra semetipsum miratur. Revol- vit etiam in corde tacita mente incorporeae lucis cla- ritatem, intimae satietatis saporem, & aliud inter- nae quietis secretum, & summae tranquillitatis ar- canum, in hujus amore contemplationis dulcis mens delectabiliter afficitur, & mirabiliter dele- ctatur. Idem Bernhardus citatus hic à Thoma Anglico: Deus charitas est, inquit Bernhardus: Quid ergo charitate melius? Et qui manet in cha- ritate, in DEO manet: Quid ergo charitate secu- rius? Et Deus in eo: Quid ergo charitate jucun- dius? Quae maxime charitati divinae conveniunt. Hac enim nihil melius, nihil securius, nihil ju- cundius. Ut in altera vita DEUS electis erit templum; quia ibi à facie ad faciem DEUM contemplabuntur, adorabunt & laudabunt, & in ipso, quasi in templo divino & increato divi- nam & beatam obtinebunt mansionem: Ita fide- libus Deus in hac vita templum est, quia in Deo ipsi vident gloriam Domini velut retecta facie, 2. Corinth. III. v. 17. ipsumque adorant & laudant in isto divino templo manentes: quae est πρόγευσις aeternae beatissimae mansionis in Deo.

## 4:17
Vers. 17.

Ἐν τούτῳ τετελείωται ἡ ἀγάπη μεθ' ἡμῶν.] That is, this is the highest degree of love towards us, if such as Christ was in this world, that is, exposed to the hatreds of the world and therefore to very many evils, such we also may be. For ἐν τούτῳ, as many have already warned, ought to be connected with that ὅτι καθὼς, etc., not with ἵνα. For we had a similar locution after ἐν τούτῳ above c. III. v. 24. here 9. 10. But what others understand concerning our love towards God, we prefer to understand concerning the love of God towards us: because the hatreds of the world and the subsequent torments are a testimony of the highest divine love towards us, as Peter teaches us in his former epistle c. II. v. 19. & c. IV. v. 16. See also Matth. V, 13. And this sense seems to be demanded by that μεθ' ἡμῶν. For it is a similar locution to 2. Cor. XIII. v. 13.

Ἵνα παῤῥησίαν ἔχωμεν ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῆς κρίσεως.] Therefore God disposes this in such a way, that we may appear with good confidence on the day of judgment, in which sense we had παῤῥησίαν also above c. II. v. 28. But these words ought to be accepted by an anticipated transposition, since they would have obtained their genuine place at the end of this period. For the constant enduring of evils after the example of Christ causes us to expect the best things from Christ, since we are like him. Great is the reward of that thing Matth. V. v. 12. 1. Petr. I. v. 7. Rom. VIII. v. 17. But this transposition was made, because those things which he wished to subjoin concerning the expulsion of fear, cohere better with those words which show that we are like Christ.

Not a few Interpreters indeed explain it concerning our love, but Grotius more correctly explains it concerning the love of God towards us. Concerning which we said it was treated in the preceding: to which also that μεθ' ἡμῶν agrees better, upon which solely rests the παῤῥησία, which we have on the day of judgment, which when it is felt in us, drives all fear from us. Nor does Flacius dissent in his gloss: If anyone, he says, wishes to understand this rather concerning the charity of GOD towards us (of which he spoke in the next verse), that the charity of God is highest in him and is seen to be so, because he not only bestowed his Son upon us, but also by his Spirit in our heart, crying Abba Father, kindles such confidence, that without any trepidation and indeed joyfully we dare to approach his judgment and tribunal, saying: If God is for us, who is against us? It is God who justifies, who is he who condemns? etc. Just as Paul copiously draws such confidence from that most ardent love of the heavenly Father towards us, Rom. VIII. I certainly would not dare to oppose this opinion as being both congruent to this place and analogous to faith. The sense therefore would be: From this the immense love of God is seen, when he excites the highest confidence by his Spirit in our heart, so that we do not shudder and tremble at his judgment.

Therefore ἡ ἀγάπη the love of God is perfected in us not by reason of itself, for thus it is absolutely perfect, immense, immutable, but by reason of us, not as to existence, but as to experience, or experimental knowledge, not as to essence, but as to operation, not as to affection, which in God admits no intension or remission; but as to sense, that we may more and more experience and feel the divine love. To which sense Blessed Höpfner does not dissent in disput. VIII. de justifc. pag. 606. In this τετελείωται is consummated (as to the knowledge of itself) the charity of God μεθ' ἡμῶν with us, (that is, it is demonstrated in us by a perfect sign and document) ἵνα παῤῥησίαν ἔχωμεν, even if he explains it concerning our charity.

Nor does Estius disapprove of this sense: If we read or supply, he says, the charity of GOD (the Vulgate reads it, and the Syriac put the pronoun 'his' in its place, although, as Estius admits, it is not read in the Greek, just as it is not in Augustine and Bede, nor in the text of the Glossa and Lyranus, and many other Latin codices, and those the more emended ones, both printed and manuscript, do not have it) by which, namely, God loves us, this will be the sense: This is the effect and fruit of that most perfect charity, by which God loves us as his children, that we do not fear the judgment of God very much, but with good confidence are prepared to meet him when he is about to judge, and to present ourselves at his tribunal. For he will not condemn those whom he loves as children, and for whom he has prepared the inheritance of the kingdom. Estius indeed prefers another explanation concerning fraternal charity, but that does not agree with the Vulgate canonized by the Council of Trent, nor is his reasoning of any moment, namely that τετελείωται is said participially as perfect, consummated, i.e., it has turned out perfect, which cannot be said of the love of God; for although by reason of itself the charity of God cannot be rendered more perfect, it is nevertheless rendered so by reason of our sense. And therefore ἵνα can be taken in its famous meaning: To this end, that the divine charity towards us may be felt or known by us as perfect, that we may have confidence. or even in this sign or document, that we may have παῤῥησίαν [boldness]: Which sense of the particle ἵνα pleases Bede and Hesselius, but not Estius: because the particle ἵνα is usually final and consecutive; but not conditional. But the blessed Höpffner shows that even this sense is not unusual, explaining the present passage concerning our charity: The particle ἵνα, he says, does not signify the end or effect of the charity of God, by which we love God, as if it were the cause of having confidence in the judgment of God, or that we love God because we have confidence, but a signification or document of love, which is increased and confirmed from it, or through it, when dying in the faith of Christ, we have confidence (of salvation) conceived from the gratuitous favor of God on account of Christ apprehended by present faith, just as the little word ἵνα is used in John 15:13. & ch. 16:2. especially ch. 15:8. where there is an illustrious example of this whole phrase, when John says: In this is my Father glorified, ἵνα καρπὸν πολὺν φέρητε [that you bear much fruit], that is, when you have borne much fruit. The same is the sense of the saying which Mayer alleges from 1 John 3:21. Briefly, the charity of God perfected in us, that is, sincere and serious, is not the cause of confidence in the judgment of GOD: For this arises from faith in Christ: but it is the cause of infallibly knowing the confidence. All of which Augustine beautifully teaches on 1 John 4:16, reasoning thus: Therefore brothers, take pains, act within yourselves, that you may desire the day of judgment: Otherwise charity is not proved perfect, unless that day has begun to be desired, etc.

Ὅτι καθὼς ἐκεῖνός ἐστι καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐσμεν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ τούτῳ [Because as he is, so are we in this world.] The same sense as John 15:18, 19. Ἐκεῖνος [He] here is again Christ, as in ch. 3:5.

Some refer the pronoun ἐκεῖνος [he] to God, others to Christ. Augustine, Bede, Hugo, Lyranus, Dionysius, and Estius refer it to God. Oecumenius, Gagnejus, and Cornelius à Lapide refer it to Christ, which is more convenient: Because it also befits Christ to have been in the world; and the pronoun ἐκεῖνος always refers to Christ in the present epistle, 1 John 2:6, ch. 3:3, 5, 7, 16, and we are likewise warned by John about imitating him, just as he walked, ch. 2:6, just as he is pure, ch. 3:3, just as he is just, v. 7, just as he laid down his soul for us, v. 16, and he had treated above of the Son sent into the world, v. 11, 14, whom he had proposed by reason of merit, he now sets forth as an example. But the Apostle does not act to celebrate the grace of God in that he deems us worthy of the cross, as it seemed to Grotius: But he teaches that by this sign and argument we are made more certain of it, that the grace of God is diffused in our hearts, and that it is felt to be perfect, which, whether the particle ὅτι is explained ὁριστικῶς [definitively] as 'inasmuch as', or αἰτιολογικῶς [causally] as 'because', as Christ is, so are we in this world, that we walk as he walked, and strive for purity and justice, as he was pure and holy, and thus love our neighbor as he loved, and finally patiently tolerate evils, as he tolerated them, leaving us an ὑπογραμμὸν [example], that we should follow in his footsteps, 1 Pet. 2:21, and shine in the world as lights, Phil. 2:15. Tirinus refers this sentiment to the confirmation of confidence and divine grace: that, being annexed and leaning upon God, we may shake off the useless terror and fear of evils not only in the present, but also in the future life, and specifically those hanging over us in the day of death and divine judgment, by a firm and constant confidence in the same God and in the merits of Christ: because just as that Christ is and always was a care and concern to God, as his beloved Son, in whom he was well pleased: So we too, the adopted sons of God, are a care and concern to him in this world, and will be throughout the whole course of life, and even in death and judgment itself, whence we have no cause for fear or anxiety. Thus generally St. Augustine, Oecumenius, Gagnejus. These are the words of Tirinus the Jesuit, which can not undeservedly be opposed to other Papists, who seek here a patronage for human merits. Charity, says Estius, makes us like to God. But he who recognizes in himself the likeness of God through the imitation of charity, rightly trusts that he will receive in his judgment the promised reward. Therefore this passage is valid for the confidence of good works done through the Spirit of God before God, against heretics who preach faith in mercy alone. Where, however, it must first and most certainly be established that our good works are from God to us, whose goodness is so great that he wills them to be our merits, which are his own gifts, to which argument both Estius himself, by the cited explanation of the passage concerning love and divine grace, and Tirinus, by the interpretation just adduced concerning confidence to be founded in the merits of Christ, cut the nerve. And however much the imitation of divine charity might be adduced, so that confidence might not be shaken by the fear of judgment, must the same therefore be established as meritorious of salvation? It can be in the likeness of a document and sign that we remain in the grace of God, because it is a consequence of faith, by which we please God, and thus make our election firm on our part, 2 Pet. 1. But it is not the cause of our election, or of our liberation on the day of judgment, or of the attainment of eternal life. Finally, does not Estius himself strike down merits, when he acknowledges that all confidence must be placed in the grace and mercy of God, and that the mercy of GOD is absolutely necessary so that daily faults may be remitted. For those who have need of the remission of sins on account of the merits of Christ, and therefore ought to place their confidence solely in the mercy of God, cannot and ought not to place their confidence in their own merits on the day of judgment.

Latin:

Vers. 17.

Ἐν τούτῳ τετελείωται ἡ ἀγάπη μεθ' ἡμῶν.] Id est, hic est summus gradus dilectionis erga nos, si qualis in hoc mundo Christus fuit, id est, mundi odiis & propterea malis plurimis expositus, tales & nos simus. Debet enim ἐν τούτῳ, ut plu- res jam monuere, connecti cum illo ὅτι καθὼς, &c. non cum ἵνα. Parem enim loquutionem habuimus post ἐν τούτῳ su- pra c. III. v. 24. hic 9. 10. Sed quod alii de amore nostro er- ga Deum intelligunt, nos intelligere malumus de amore Dei erga nos: quia odia mundi & cruciatus subsequentes testi- monium sunt summi in nos divini amoris, ut nos Petrus do- cet epistola priore cap. II. v. 19. & c. IV. v. 16. Vide & Matth. V, 13. Et videtur hunc sensum poscere illud μεθ' ἡμῶν. Est enim similis loquutio 2. Cor. XIII. v. 13.

Ἵνα παῤῥησίαν ἔχωμεν ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῆς κρίσεως.] Ideo Deus hoc sic disponit, ut cum bona fiducia appareamus in die judicii, quo sensu παῤῥησίαν habuimus & supra cap. II. v. 28. Debent autem haec verba accipi per trajectionem anticipa- ta, cum genuinum locum obtentura fuissent in fine hujus periodi. Nam constans perpessio malorum ad exemplum Christi efficit, ut à Christo optima expectemus, quippe cô- ipsi similes. Magna ejus rei merces Matth. V. v. 12. 1. Petr. I. v. 7. Rom. VIII. v. 17. Facta est autem hæc trajectio, quod ea, quæ de timoris expulsione subjicere voluit, melius cum verbis illis, quæ ostendunt nos Christo esse similes, cohæ- reant.

Exponunt quidem non pauci Interpretes de amore nostro, sed rectius Grotius de amore Dei erga nos explicat. De quo in antecedentibus actum diximus: cui convenit etiam melius illud μεθ' ἡμῶν, cui innititur unice παῤῥησία, quam habemus in die judicii, qui cum sentitur in nobis, omnem pellit timorem à nobis. Nec abnuit Flacius in glossa: Si quis, inquit, velit hoc potius de charitate DEI erga nos (de qua in proximo versu loquutus est) intelligere, quod charitas Dei in eo summa sit & esse cernatur, quod ille non solum Filium suum nobis est largitus, sed etiam Spiritu suo in corde nostro, Abba Pater clamante, tantam fiduciam accendat, ut sine omni trepidatione atque adeo læti ausimus ejus judicium & tribunal accedere, dicentes: Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Deus est qui justificat, quis est, qui condemnat? &c. Sicut talem fiduciam copiose Paulus ex ardentissimo Patris illius cælestis erga nos amore educit, Rom. VIII. huic sententiæ tanquam & loco huic congruenti, & fidei analogæ non ausim sane ego repugnare. Sensus igitur esset: Ex eo immensam Dei dilectionem conspici, quando ille suo Spiritu in corde nostro summam fiduciam excitat, ut non horreamus ac trepidemus ejus judicium.

Perficitur ergo ἡ ἀγάπη dilectio Dei in nobis non ratione sui, sic enim absolute perfecta, immensa, incommutabilis est, sed ratione nostri, non quoad existentiam, sed quoad experientiam, vel experimentalem notitiam, non quoad quidditatem, sed quoad operationem, non quoad affectum, qui in Deo nullam vel intensionem vel remissionem admittit; sed quoad sensum, quod nos divinam dilectionem magis magisque experiamur & sentiamus. Cui sensui non abnuit B. Höpfnerus disput. VIII. de justifc. pag. 606. In hoc τετελείωται consummata est (quoad notitiam sui) charitas Dei μεθ' ἡμῶν nobiscum, (hoc est in nobis perfecto signo & documento demonstratur) ἵνα παῤῥησίαν ἔχωμεν, etsi de charitate nostra explicet.

Neque improbat hunc sensum Estius: Si legamus aut suppleamus, inquit, charitatem DEI (legit autem Vulgata, & Syrus ejus loco posuit pronomen ejus, etsi fatente Estio non legatur in Græcis, ut nec apud Augustinum & Bedam, nec in textu Glossæ & Lyrani, multique præterea Latini codices iique emendatiores, tam impressi quam Manuscripti non habeant) qua scilicet Deus nos diligit, erit iste sensus: Hic effectus est & fructus illius perfectissimæ charitatis, qua nos ut filios suos diligit Deus, quod Dei judicium non admodum timeamus, sed cum bona fiducia parati simus ei judicaturo occurrere, & ad ejus tribunal nos sistere. Non enim condemnabit, quos ut filios diligit, & quibus hæreditatem regni præparavit. Præfert quidem Estius alteram explicationem de charitate fraterna, sed illa non convenit Vulgatæ à Concilio Tridentino canonizatæ, nec ratio ejus ullius momenti est, quod nempe τετελείωται participialiter dicatur perfecta, consummata, i. e. perfecta evasit, quod de dilectione Dei dici nequeat; nam etsi ratione sui non possit perfectior reddi charitas Dei, redditur tamen ratione sensus nostri. Ideoque ἵνα potest famoso significatu accipi: Ad hoc perfectam sentiri vel cognosci à nobis charitatem divinam erga nos, ut fiduciam habeamus. vel etiam in hoc signo vel documento, quod habea- mus παῤῥησίαν: Qui sensus particulæ ἵνα Bedæ placet & Hesselio non autem Estio: quod parti- cula ἵνα finalis, & consecutiva esse soleat; non autem conditionalis. Sed ostendit B. Höpffnerus etiam hunc sensum non esse insolentem, expli- cans locum præsentem de charitate nostra: Par- ticula ἵνα, inquit, non significat finem aut effe- ctum charitatis Dei, qua nos Deum diligimus, quasi sit ea causa fiduciæ in judicio Dei habendæ, aut ideo Deum diligamus, quod fiduciam habea- mus, sed significationem vel documentum dile- ctionis, quæ augetur & confirmatur ex eo, seu per illud, quando in fide Christi morientes, fiduciam (salutis) habemus conceptam ex gratuito favore Dei propter Christum fide præsente apprehensum, quemadmodum ita vocula ἵνα usurpatur Johann. XV. v. 13. & cap. XVI. v. 2. imprimis cap. XV. v. 8. ubi habetur totius hujus phraseos illustre exem- plum, cum ait Johannes: In hoc est glorificatus Pater meus, ἵνα καρπὸν πολὺν φέρητε, id est, cum multum fructum tuleritis. Idem sensus est dicti quod allegat Mayerus ex 1. Johann. III. v. 21. Bre- viter, charitas Dei in nobis perfecta, id est, sincera & seria non est causa fiduciæ in judicio DEI: Hæc enim oritur ex fide in Christum: sed est causa in- fallibiliter cognoscendi fiduciam. Quæ omnia pul- chre Augustinus docet ad 1. Joh. IV, 16. ita ratioci- nando: Ergo fratres date operam, intus agite vo- biscum, ut desideretis diem judicii: Aliter non pro- batur charitas perfecta, nisi cœperit dies ille deside- rari &c.

Ὅτι καθὼς ἐκεῖνός ἐστι καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐσμεν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ τούτῳ.] Sensus idem, qui Joh. XV, 18. 19. Ἐκεῖνος hic iterum est Chri- stus, ut c. III, 5.

Pronomen ἐκεῖνος alii ad Deum referunt, alii ad Christum. Ad Deum Augustinus, Beda, Hugo, Lyranus, Dionysius, Estius. Ad Christum Oecu- menius, Gagnejus, Cornelius à Lapide, quod con- venientius: Quia & Christo convenit fuisse in mundo; & pronomen ἐκεῖνος semper in epistola præsente Christum refert, 1. Joh. II. v. 6. cap. III. v. 3. 5. 7. 16. & de eo imitando pariter monemur à Johanne sicut ipse ambulavit, cap. II. vers. 6. sicut ipse purus est, cap. III. v. 3. sicut ipse justus est, v. 7. sicut ipse animam suam posuit pro nobis, v. 16. & de Filio in mundum misso supra egerat, v. 11. 14. quem ratione meriti proposuerat, jam instar ex- empli sistit. Non autem id agit Apostolus, ut gra- tiam Dei in eo, quod nos cruce dignetur, cele- bret, quemadmodum Grotio visum: Sed hoc signo & argumento nos de eo certiores reddi docet, quod gratia Dei diffundatur in cordibus nostris, eamque perfectam sentiri, quod sive ὁριστικῶς particula ὅτι per quatenus explicetur, sive αἰτιο- λογικῶς per quia, sicut Christus est, & nos sumus in hoc mundo, quod ambulamus, sicut ipse am- bulavit, & puritati ac justitiæ studemus, sicut ipse purus & sanctus fuit, proximumque ita amamus, quemadmodum ipse amavit, mala denique pa- tienter toleramus, sicut ipse toleravit, ὑπογραμ- μὸν nobis relinquens, ut insistamus vestigiis ejus- dem, 1. Petr. II. v. 21. & lucemus in mundo sicut lumina, Philip. II. v. 15. Tirinus hanc sententiam refert ad confirmationem fiduciæ & gratiæ divi- næ: quod annexi & innixi Deo inutilem terrorem & timorem malorum non modo in præsenti, sed & in futura vita, nominatimque in die mortis & judicii divini impendentium excutiamus firma constanti- que fiducia in eundem Deum & in merita Christi: quia sicut ille Christus est semperque fuit cura cor- dique Deo, utpote Filius ejus dilectus, in quo ipsi complacuit: Ita & nos filii Dei adoptivi illi curæ & cordi sumus in hoc mundo, erimusque toto vitæ de- cursu, atque etiam in ipsa morte & judicio, unde nullam habemus causam timoris vel anxietatis. Ita fere S. Augustinus, Oecumenius, Gagnejus. Hæc Tirinus Jesuita, quæ aliis Pontificiis non im- merito opponi possunt, meritis humanis hic pa- trocinium quærentibus. Charitas, inquit Estius, illa nos Deo similes facit. Qui autem in se Dei si- militudinem agnoscit per imitationem charitatis, merito confidit, se recepturum in ejus judicio mer- cedem promissam. Itaque valet hic locus pro fidu- cia bonorum & per Spiritum Dei factorum operum apud Deum, adversus hæreticos, qui solam fidem misericordiæ prædicant. Ubi tamen primo ac cer- tissime statuendum est, opera nostra bona nobis à Deo esse, cujus tanta est bonitas, ut nostra velit esse merita, quæ sunt ipsius dona, Cui argumento tum Estius ipse laudata explicatione loci de dilectione & gratia divina, tum Tirinus modo adducta in- terpretatione de fiducia in meritis Christi fundan- da nervum incidit. Et utut imitatio charitatis divinæ adduceretur, ut ne fiducia per timorem judicii labefactaretur, num ideo eadem meritoria salutis statuenda? Documenti & signi instar esse potest, nos in gratia Dei manere, quia fidei con- sequens est, qua Deo placemus, & ita electio- nem nostram firmam reddere ratione nostri, 2. Petr. I. Sed causa non est sive electionis nostræ, sive liberationis in die judicii, aut consecutionis vitæ æter- næ. Denique annon merita configit Estius ipse, cum agnoscit totam fiduciam collocandam esse in gratia & misericordia Dei, ac misericordiam DEI necessariam omnino esse, ut quotidiana delicta re- mittantur. Qui enim opus habent remissione peccatorum propter Christi merita, atque ideo in Dei misericordia unice fiduciam collocare de- bent, illi in propriis suis meritis in die judicii fi- duciam collocare nec possunt nec debent.

## 4:18
Verse 18.

There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear.] The Apostle, just as in this whole epistle he speaks alternately of the dwelling of God in us and of ours in God, so also he passes from the love which is in God to that which is in us, as here: and where love is perfect, there fear—namely, of dangers and evils—is expelled, or rather, is no longer there. This proverb is true even in common love, in which Alexis called it the boldness of a man, Sophocles, fearless force. Of the same, Aristarchus says: It makes the weak strong. Euripides calls the same the teacher of boldness and daring. But how great is the power of that love, by which we are kindled toward God and neighbor for God's sake, the fortitude of so many martyrs in despising the fear of poverty, death, and torments shows. Thus, as Tertullian understood this in Scorpiace: What perfect love does he affirm, if not the chaser-away of fear and the animator of confession?

There is no need for us to establish a transition here from the love of God to our own, since these things are likewise best understood concerning divine charity. In our charity there is not such perfection that it is devoid of all fear: nor is this said only of the fear of torments, which in martyrs is driven out through the love of God and Christ: which, however, is more to be attributed to confidence toward God and Christ, from which that love flowed: but primarily the discourse is about the expulsion of the fear of spiritual enemies, sin, the devil, death, and hell. For all fear is cast out through charity, according to John. Which properly pertains to divine charity, which, apprehended through faith, expels all servile fear. He who believes and feels that he is in the grace and love of God through the faith which he feels in his heart, is entirely certain and indubitable, that neither death, nor life, nor

Angels, nor powers, nor mighty works, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature can separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord, Romans VIII. vers. 38. 39. We have here the most learned Flacius as a fellow-thinker. By which he declares all the more the nature of the confidence of the pious, arising from the recognized love of GOD towards us, he says that love cannot consist together with fear, because the love of God truly recognized, just as he boasted that we have truly recognized it already in verse 6, casts out all servile fear and trembling. For the recognition of the love of God excites the highest tranquility and peace in our heart. Some understand this saying about our love towards God, that if we truly fear God, we do not tremble before him servilely. But it is certainly true that those two are not easily joined: for whom we fear servilely, we hate rather than love. But our love cannot so much cast fear out of the heart, as on the contrary, excessive fear casts out the love of him whom we tremble before. For whom men fear, they hate and wish that he had perished, as Cicero and experience itself testify. Indeed, a terrible object is not lovable. But the love of God and of any superior, when known to an inferior or subject, clearly frees him from that servile fear and trembling. Whence this whole passage is more correctly understood here concerning the love of GOD towards us known through faith, about which matter he discoursed much in the preceding.

Ὅτι ὁ φόβος κόλασιν ἔχει.] This word twisted the Interpreters. But I do not doubt that it was written κόλουσιν. They changed it, however, those to whom the word was less known. It signifies, however, mutilation. Glosses: κολόω, ἀτελῆ ποιῶ. Fear mutilates and breaks love, or prevents it from exerting itself.

The original text is changed in vain without the authority of any manuscript or at least versions, and against the consensus of all Interpreters. It is not mutilation, but punishment that is noted. For all servile fear exists on account of punishment, which is to be feared. Fear is not in love, says Augustine, epistle CXX to Honor. chap. 21, because perfect love casts out fear, but that servile one, by which when anyone abstains from an evil work, he is terrified by punishment, not delighted by justice. The fear of punishments, which an evil conscience has generated, torments the mind, and he who is conscious of evil and fears, he always turns over in his mind the punishment which he fears: But he who is certain of the grace of God is devoid of all fear that fears punishment.

Ὁ δὲ φοβούμενος οὐ τετελείωται ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ.] The little word δὲ, placed in the connection of two propositions to confirm that which has been said, demands that the word which preceded be repeated, as happens in the Arabic. For he reads correctly: ὁ δὲ κολουόμενος οὐ τετελείωται ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ. He who is mutilated or hindered in love, he is not perfect in it. For perfection is known from operation. There is here a syllogism placed not according to the rules of dialecticians, but from popular usage. In which first is placed that which is to be proved, which we call συμπέρασμα; then ἡ ἐλάττων πρότασις, then indeed ἡ μείζων, which is most frequent among Orators.

There is not here such an argumentation as Grotius assigns, so that there is a need to repeat the word κολουόμενος, which is fashioned from the word κόλουσις. Those interpretations are merely arbitrary: which neither the text serves, unless other words are substituted for others, nor the Apostolic scope. It is a sin to amend the Greek text from the Arabic. And what ineptitudes are those: He who is mutilated in love, is not perfect in it. Who is ignorant of this, so that the Apostle has need to inculcate it? Do such tautologies and identical propositions befit an Apostle? The antithesis therefore is rather subjoined according to the custom of the Apostle: He had said that perfect love casts out fear: now he subjoins antithetically: but he who fears is not perfect in love. Where the sense is that of divine love, and it exerts itself perfectly, and is perceived in our hearts, servile fear is altogether expelled. On the contrary, he who fears servilely is not perfect in the sense of divine love. Such perfection, however, is to be understood as that which has a place in this life, where there is only a foretaste of divine love: the full taste of which we expect in the other life, when we shall see God as He is, 1 John III, 2.

Latin:

Vers. 18.

Φόβος οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ, ἀλλ' ἡ τελεία ἀγάπη ἔξω βάλ- λει τὸν φόβον.] Apostolus sicut in omni hac epistola alternis loquitur de mansione Dei in nobis, & de nostra in Deo; ita etiam à dilectione, quæ in Deo est, transit ad eam, quæ est in nobis, ut hic: atque ubi perfectus est amor, ibi expelli, sive ibi ultra non esse metum periculorum scilicet & malorum.. Est hoc proverbium verum etiam in vulgari amore, in quo esse τόλμαν ἀνδρὸς dixit Alexis, ἄφοβον βίαν Sophocles. De eodem Aristarchus: Τὸν ἀσθενῆ σθένον τίθησιν. Euripides eundem τόλμης καὶ θράσους διδάσκαλον vocat. At quantæ ejus amoris vis sit, qua in Deum & proximum Dei causa ac- cendimur, ostendit tot martyrum fortitudo in spernendo me- tu paupertatis, mortis, tormentorum. Ita, ut nos hunc acce- pit Tertullianus Scorpiace: Quam dilectionem perfectam affirmat, nisi fugatricem timoris & animatricem confessionis?

Non opus est, ut transitum hic statuamus à dilectione DEI ad nostram, quum de charitate di- vina hæc itidem optime accipiantur. In charita- te nostra non est ea perfectio, ut ea omnis timoris expers sit: neque de metu tantum tormentorum, qui in martyribus per amorem Dei & Christi pul- sus id dicitur: quod tamen magis fiduciæ erga Deum & Christum tribuendum, ex quo amor ille fluxit: sed imprimis de expulsione metus hostium spiritualium peccati, diaboli, mortis & inferni sermo est. Omnis enim metus ejicitur per cha- ritatem, secundum Johannem. Quod proprie con- venit charitati divinæ, quæ apprehensa per fidem omnem servilem timorem expellit. Qui credit & sentit, se esse in gratia & amore Dei per fidem, quam in corde suo sentit, certus omnino atque indubius, neque mortem, neque vitam, neque

Angelos, neque potestates, neque virtutes, ne- que præsentia, neque futura, neque altitudinem, neque profunditatem, neque ullam aliam crea- turam se posse separare à dilectione Dei, quæ est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro, Roman. VIII. vers. 38. 39. Habemus hic doctissimum Flacium ὁμόψηφον. Quo tanto magis declaret naturam fiduciæ piorum, ex agnita charitate DEI erga nos orientis, dicit, non posse una consistere charitatem cum metu, quia charitas Dei vere agnita, sicut nos eam vere agnovisse jam vers. 6. gloriatus est, ejiciat omnem servilem timorem ac trepidationem foras. Agnitio enim dilectionis Dei summam tran- quillitatem pacemque in corde nostro excitat. Aliqui intelligunt hoc dictum de nostra dilectione erga Deum, quod si Deum vere timemus, eum servili- ter non trepidemus. Verum autem sane est, quod non facile ista duo conjungantur: quem enim ser- viliter timemus, potius odimus quam amamus. Sed non tam noster amor potest timorem è corde ejicere, quam contra timor nimius amorem ejus, quem trepidamus. Quem enim homines timent, oderunt ac periisse exoptant, teste Cicerone & ex- perientia ipsa. Sane objectum terribile non est amabile. Verum amor Dei & cujusvis superioris inferiori aut subdito cognitus, plane eum servili illo timore trepidationeque liberat. Unde rectius hic to- tus locus de amore DEI erga nos per fidem cognito intelligetur, de qua materia multum in præcedenti- bus disseruit.

Ὅτι ὁ φόβος κόλασιν ἔχει.] Torsit Interpretes hæc vox. Sed non dubito quin scriptum fuerit κόλουσιν. Mutaverint au- tem, quibus vox erat minus nota. Significat autem mutila- tionem. Glossæ: κολόω, ἀτελῆ ποιῶ. Metus amorem muti- lat atque infringit, aut prohibet ne se exferat.

Nequicquam mutatur textus originalis citra ullius codicis vel versionum saltem autoritatem, & contra omnium Interpretum consensum. Non mutilatio, sed pœna notatur. Nam omnis servi- lis timor ob pœnam, quæ metuenda, existit. Ti- mor non est in charitate, ait Augustinus epistol. CXX. ad Honor. cap. 21. quia perfecta charitas foras mittit timorem, sed illum servilem, quo cum quisque se ab opere malo abstinet, pœna terretur, non justitia delectatur. Timor suppliciorum, quem mala genuit conscientia, animum cruciat, & qui male sibi conscius timet, is pœnam animo sem- per versat, quam metuit: Qui vero de gratia Dei certus est, omnis timoris, qui pœnam metuit, ex- pers est.

Ὁ δὲ φοβούμενος οὐ τετελείωται ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ.] Poscit vo- cula δὲ, in connexione duarum propositionum ad confir- mandum id, quod dictum est, posita, ut vox, quæ præcessit, repetatur, sicut fit apud Arabem. Is enim recte legit: ὁ δὲ κολουόμενος οὐ τετελείωται ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ. Qui mutilatur aut impeditur in dilectione, is in ea perfectus non est. Perfe- ctio enim ex operatione noscitur. Est hic syllogismus non ex dialecticorum regulis, sed ex populari usu positus. In quo primum ponitur id, quod probandum est, quod συμπέρασμα dicimus; deinde ἡ ἐλάττων πρότασις, inde vero ἡ μείζων, quod apud Oratores frequentissimum.

Non est hic argumentatio talis, quam Grotius affignat, ut opus sit vocem κολουόμενος, quæ effin- gitur è voce κόλουσις, repetere. Sunt istæ inter- pretationes mere arbitrariæ: quibus nec textus, nisi verba alia pro aliis substituantur, inservit, nec scopus Apostolicus. Ex Arabico textum Græ- cum emendare nefas est. Et quæ ineptiæ illæ sunt: Qui mutilatur in dilectione, in ea perfectus non est. Ecquis hoc ignorat, ut Apostolus id inculcare opus habeat? Num decent Apostolum ejusmo- di ταυτολογίαι & identicæ propositiones? Anti- thesis ergo potius pro more Apostoli subjungitur: Dixerat perfectam charitatem timorem foras projicere: nunc ἀντιθετικῶς subjungit: qui vero timet, perfectus non est in charitate. Ubi sensus est charitatis divinæ, eaque perfecte sese exerit, ac percipitur in cordibus nostris, timor servilis omnino expellitur. Ex adverso qui serviliter ti- met, non perfectus est in charitatis divinæ sensu. Ta- lis autem perfectio intelligenda, qualis in hac vita locum habet, ubi prægustus tantum est amoris divini: cujus gustum plenum expectamus in al- tera vita, quando videbimus Deum, sicut est, 1. Joh. III, 2.

## 4:19
Vers. 19.

Ἡμεῖς ἀγαπῶμεν ἀυτὸν.] In the Manuscript ἡμεῖς οὖν, just as both the Syrian and the Latin have had in their codices. ἀγαπῶμεν can be of either the Indicative or Subjunctive mood, but since ἀγαπᾷ soon follows in the 21st in the Subjunctive, I think the Latin Interpreter has correctly translated it as 'let us love' (diligamus). This coheres well with the above. For he had already led us through love towards men to love God. Let us love, namely with the fear of the evils of this age expelled. And he correctly explains ἀυτὸν as God, as does the Syrian.

Ὅτι ἀυτὸς πρῶτος ἠγάπησεν ἡμᾶς.] He repeats what he had said above in 10, with πρῶτος added. In the Manuscript ὅτι ὁ Θεὸς, and below ἔχομεν ἀπὸ Θεῦ.

Latin:

Vers. 19.

Ἡμεῖς ἀγαπῶμεν ἀυτὸν.] In Manuscripto ἡμεῖς οὖν, quo- modo in suis codicibus habuerint & Syrus & Latinus. Potest ἀγαπῶμεν esse aut Indicativi aut Subjunctivi modi, sed cum ἀγαπᾷ mox 21. sequatur in Subjunctivo, puto Latinum Interpretem recte vertisse diligamus. Bene hoc co- hæret cum superioribus. Nam jam per dilectionem in ho- mines nos ad diligendum Deum perduxerat. Diligamus, nempe expulso timore malorum hujus seculi. Et ἀυτὸν recte explicat Deum, ut & Syrus.

Ὅτι ἀυτὸς πρῶτος ἠγάπησεν ἡμᾶς.] Repetit, quod dixerat supra 10. addito πρῶτος. In Manuscripto ὅτι ὁ Θεὸς, & infra ἔχομεν ἀπὸ Θεῦ.

## 4:20
Vers. 20.

Ἐάν τις εἴπῃ ὅτι ἀγαπῶ τὸν Θεὸν, καὶ τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἀυτοῦ μι- σῇ, ψέυστης ἐστίν.] Again he shows the connection of both loves. It is accustomed to be said, he who loves me, loves my dog. How much more is it to be said: He who loves God, loves also man, the most beautiful work of God.

For he who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, how can he love God, whom he has not seen? Philo on the Decalogue: It is impossible to be pious toward the invisible by being impious toward those who are visible and near. It is usually said: There is no desire for the unknown. But knowledge comes mostly through the eyes. The very sight excites one to love, and the poet marvels at him: Who never having seen, burned with love for a girl.

Latin:

Vers. 20.

Ἐάν τις εἴπῃ ὅτι ἀγαπῶ τὸν Θεὸν, καὶ τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἀυτοῦ μι- σῇ, ψέυστης ἐστίν.] Rursus ostendit connexionem dilectionis utriusque. Dici solet, qui diligit me, diligit canem meum. Quanto magis dicendum est: Qui diligit Deum, diligit & hominem, Dei opus pulcherrimum.

Ὁ γὰρ μὴ ἀγαπῶν ἀδελφὸν ἀυτοῦ, ὃν ἑώρακε, τὸν Θεὸν ὃν οὐχ ἑώρακε, πῶς δύναται ἀγαπᾷν;] Philo ad Decalogum: Ἀμή- χανον ἐυσεβεῖσθαι τὸν ἀόρατον διὰ τῶν εἰς τοὺς ἐμφανεῖς κὶ ἐγγὺς ἀσεβούντων. Solet dici: Ignoti nulla cupido. At notitia ma- xime per oculos. Ipse aspectus ad amandum excitat, & mira- tur illum Poëta: Qui nunquam vise flagravit amore puellæ.

## 4:21
Verse 21.

And this commandment we have from Him, that he who loves God, should love his brother also. A second argument why we ought to love our neighbor: because God commands it. It is the nature of one who loves to desire those things which are desired by the one who is loved. Everyone who loves GOD, that is, who wishes to be held by GOD as one who loves Him.

Now finally, from divine love and its benefits, he deduces the duties of our reciprocal love, especially that we should love God in return; since He Himself loved us first, Rom. 5:10, 1 John 4:9, 10. Behold, says Flacius at this place, he deduces all those movements of our soul to the love of God toward us, known through faith in Christ, from which it appears at the same time that all righteousness and salvation depend upon the mere and gratuitous benevolence of God. There is added also the sign of true love of God, the love of one's neighbor, which he confirms from the connection of both, both by reason of the thing, because the love of God and neighbor coheres, and he who does not love, but hates his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he does not see: and by reason of the commandment, because God commanded both, that indeed, he who loves God, should also love his brother. It is so ordered by nature that love and affection are carried toward sensible things, which we see. For eyes are the leaders in love. From these, says Gregory the Great, homily 11 on the Gospel, the mind rises from what it knows to the unknown, which it does not know, so that through that which it knows to love, it may learn also to love the unknown. Concerning the connection of the commandments of the love of God and neighbor, see Matt. 22:37-39, Luke 10:27, John 3:31, 1 John 3:23. Furthermore, if he is a brother, says Augustine, and you do not love him, how do you love God, whose commandment you despise?

PART II. OF THE EPISTLE, Concerning faith in Christ.

Latin:

Vers. 21.

Καὶ ταύτην ἐντολὴν ἔχομεν ἀπ᾿ ἀυτοῦ, ἵνα ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὸν Θεὸν, ἀγαπᾷ καὶ τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἀυτοῦ.] Alterum argumentum cur amare proximum debeamus: quia Deus id præcipit. Amantis est velle ea, quæ vult is, qui amatur. Omnis, qui DEUM amat, id est, qui a DEO pro amante ipsius haberi vult.

Jam demum è dilectione divina ejusque beneficiis reciproca dilectionis nostræ officia deducit, impri- mis ut κατ’ ἀμοιβὴν nos Deum diligamus; siqui- dem ipse prior nos dilexerit, Rom. V. v. 10. 1. Joh. IV. vers. 9. 10. En, inquit Flacius h. l. omnes istos animi nostri motus ad dilectionem Dei erga nos in Christo per fidem cognitam deducit, unde simul ap- paret, totam justitiam ac salutem ex mera gratui- taque Dei benevolentia pendere. Additur & signum veræ dilectionis Dei, proximi dilectio, quod à connexione utriusque confirmat, tum ratione rei, quia cohæret dilectio Dei & proximi, & qui non diligit, sed odit fratrem, quem vidit, Deum, quem non videt, diligere nequit: tum ratione præcepti, quia Deus utrumque præcepit, ut nempe, qui di- ligit Deum, etiam fratrem suum diligat. Natura ita comparatum est, ut amor & affectus rapiatur in sensibilia, quæ videmus. Oculi enim sunt in amore duces. Ex his, inquit Gregor. M. homil. XI. in Evang. quæ animus novit, surgit ad incogni- ta, quæ non novit, ut per hoc, quod scit notum dili- gere, discat & incognita amare. De nexu præce- ptorum dilectionis Dei & proximi vid. Matth. XXII. v. 1. 2. 3. Luc. X. v. 27. Johan. III. v. 31. 1. Joh. III. v. 23. Porro si frater est, inquit Augustinus, & eum non diligis, quomodo Deum diligis, cujus mandatum contemnis?

PARS II. EPISTOLÆ, De fide in Christum.

## 5:1 Argument
CHAPTER V.

ARGUMENT AND DIVISION.

He treats of the fruits of saving faith, the love of God and neighbor, and the victory of the world and its proofs, and of the testimony of the three witnesses, namely in heaven and the witnesses on earth, and the object, that he who believes in the Son of God, that He has given us eternal life through Him, may have the testimony in himself, and that we may have confidence through Him of the hearing of prayers poured out according to the will of GOD, which nevertheless He wills to be made for those who do not sin unto death. Finally, by a brief recapitulation and a summary of Theology delivered, he describes faith through the knowledge which the Son of GOD has given us, that we may be in God and in the Son of God, who is likewise the true God and eternal life, and warning against fleeing idols, he seals the epistle with the word Amen.

There are two parts: I. Concerning the fruits of faith, the testimonies confirming faith, and its proper object to v. 17. The Recapitulation, exhibiting the summary of the epistle and thus of all Theology to v. 20.

PART I.

A discourse concerning the fruits of faith, the testimonies, and the proper object.

Ver. 1.

Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ, is born of God.] He comes closer to that special love which Christians owe to Christians. Here also the minor premise is placed in the first position, the major in the second. The conclusion is suppressed, because from those things posited it is easily understood by anyone. He who believes Jesus to be the Christ, that is, shows himself to believe, by professing that, by hoping for the promised things from Him, and under that hope by following His precepts. The sense here is the same, but in other words, as above IV, 15. Is born of God, that is, is a Son of God, as we said above c. III, 9. c. IV, 7. This statement had less need of proof here, because we have already had the same sense and its proofs above, especially at the beginning of the epistle and c. IV, 14. seqq.

And everyone who loves Him who begat, loves also him who is begotten of Him.) This does not need proof, because it is evident to common sense. It is a saying of the Greeks: To a father, the child is most dear.

The Apostle indeed proceeds to teach the necessity of the coherence of the love of God and neighbor; but in such a way that he ascends to the origin, and derives both from our regeneration and faith. Therefore, he says that those who believe in Christ are born of God, because faith is not obtained by the powers of nature, but is a gift of grace, by which we are regenerated from God, whence he concludes: Everyone who loves Him who begat him, loves also him who is begotten of Him. He who loves the father, loves also those born of the same father as his own brothers. But everyone who believes in Christ, loves Him who begat him or his Father, that is God, because by that very fact, that he believes, he must be begotten of God. Therefore, everyone who believes in Christ, loves also others who are born of God, or his brothers. The discourse is about spiritual generation and fraternity. But the reasoning of the argument is general; whence just as natural birth from the same father binds us to the love of brothers, in that we are all procreated from one father from one blood, Acts XVII. v. 26. we ought to pursue all of us mutually with common love: so mystical birth from the same spiritual Father binds us to mutual brotherly love, which believers should owe specifically to believers. Our regeneration from God is the cause of the love of God the Father. That our neighbor is likewise regenerated from God is the cause that he himself is our spiritual brother, and therefore binds us to brotherly love toward him. However, there is no need for metonymy, so that he who believes Jesus is the Christ, is one who shows himself to believe. For why should we not understand believing properly? Is it not necessary for him who believes Jesus is the Christ to be born of God? The discourse here is especially about faith, which if anyone does not have in his heart, what will the profession of the mouth be, if not hypocrisy? Although profession is joined with true faith, as are the hope of the promised thing and the observance of God's commandments, yet these are not to be confused, nor is it the case that where there is profession, there is also faith. Regeneration, by which the powers of believing are given, and renewal, because the powers of acting well are restored, are connected; faith and the observance of God's commandments, or the pursuit of holiness, cohere. But are those therefore the same? If these are entirely the same, why does the Apostle deduce and prove the love of God from regeneration and faith, and the love of the neighbor from the love of God, which love of God and neighbor is certainly the observance of God's commandments? Not a few have indeed explained those things as referring to the Son of God, whose meaning Cornelius exhibits thus: i.e., Whoever loves God the Father, who begat, loves likewise God the Son begotten by the Father: but he who loves God the Son, loves also the other sons of God, as if they were his brothers and members: therefore, he who loves God the Father, loves also all the sons of God born of Him. These are the faithful, our neighbors; therefore they are to be loved with the same charity with which we love God, both Father and Son; so St. Augustine, Bede, the Glossa, Hugo, and others here, and Hilary, lib. VI. de Trinit. But the explanation of Didymus, Cajetan, Catharinus, and Estius concerning the spiritual sons of God is simpler. For those who love God, who begat the faithful, ought likewise to love those who were begotten by Him, both because the Father loves them, and because they are most closely joined to us, so that the argument is taken from the natural propensity which is perceived in men, which sentiment, however, Estius notes that theologians rightly use: To prove that in divine matters the Father can neither be loved nor seen without the Son, and thus neither the Son without the Father. Hence the Lord says: He who hates me, hates my Father also, John XV. and to Philip: He who sees me, sees my Father also, John XIV. For what is ordinary in human affairs is perpetual in divine affairs.

Latin:

CAPUT V.

ARGUMENTUM ET PAR- TITIO.

Differit de fidei salvifica fructibus, dilectione Dei & proximi, & victoria mundi ejus- demque documentis, & de testimonio trium testium nempe in cœlis & testium in terris, & objecto, quod qui credit in Filium Dei, quod vitam æternam nobis per ipsum de- derit, testimonium habeat in seipso, quod- que fiduciam per ipsum habeamus exaudi- tionis precum juxta voluntatem DEI fu- sarum, quas tamen fieri pro iis vult, qui non ad mortem peccant. Denique recapi- tulatione brevi, & summa Theologiæ tra- dita fidem per notitiam, quam Filius DEI nobis dedit, ut simus in Deo & in Filio Dei, qui verus itidem Deus est, & vita æterna, describit, & de fugiendis idolis monens voce Amen obsignat epistolam.

Partes duæ sunt: I. De fidei fructibus, testimo- niis fidem confirmantibus & proprio objecto ad v. 17. Ἀνακεφαλαίωσις, summam epistolæ adeoque totius Theologiæ exhibens ad v. 20.

PARS I.

Διήγησις de fidei fructibus, testimoniis, & objecto proprio.

Vers. 1.

Πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων, ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἐστιν Χριστὸς, ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ γεγέννηται.] Venit propius ad specialem illam dilectionem, quam Chri- stianis Christiani debent. Est hic quoque ἡ ἐλάττων πρότασις posita priore loco, ἡ μείζων posteriore. Illatio subticetur, quia ex illis positis facile à quovis intelligitur. Qui credit Jesum esse Christum, id est, credere se ostendit, id profiten- do sperando ab ipso res promissas, & sub ea spe præcepta ejus sequendo. Idem est hic sensus, sed verbis aliis, qui supra IV, 15. Ἐκ Θεοῦ γεγέννηται, id est, Dei Filius, ut diximus supra c. III, 9. c. IV, 7. Hoc dictum eo minus probare hic opus ha- buit, quia eundem sensum & ejus probationes jam supra ha- buimus, præcipue initio epistolæ & c. IV, 14. seqq.

Καὶ πᾶς ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὸν γεννήσαντα ἀγαπᾷ καὶ τὸν γεγεννημένον ἐξ αὐτοῦ.) Hoc probationis non indiget, quia sensu communi patet. Græcorum dictum est: Πατρὶ φίλτατον τέκνον

Prosequitur quidem Apostolus necessitatem cohærentiæ dilectionis Dei & proximi docere; sed ita ut ad originem adscendat, & utramque è regenera- tione nostra & fide deducat. Ideo qui credunt in Christum ex Dei genitos esse, ait, quia fides non na- turæ viribus obtinetur, sed gratiæ donum est, qua regeneramur ex Deo, unde concludit: Omnis, qui diligit eum, qui genuit illum, diligit etiam illum, qui genitus est ex ipso. Qui patrem diligit, diligit & natos ex eodem patre genitos ceu fratres suos. At omnis, qui credit in Christum, diligit eum, qui genuit ipsum vel Patrem suum, hoc est Deum, quia eo ipso, quod credit, genitum esse ipsum oportet ex Deo. Ergo omnis, qui in Christum credit, diligit etiam alios, qui ex Deo nati sunt, vel fratres suos. Sermo est de spirituali generatione, ac fraternitate. Sed argumenti ratio generalis est; unde quemad- modum nativitas ex eodem patre φυσικὴ ad amo- rem fratrum nos adstringit eo, quia omnes ex uno patre procreati sumus ex uno sanguine, Act. XVII. v. 26. communi amore omnes nos mutuo profe- qui debemus: ita nativitas μυσικὴ ex eodem Patre spirituali ad amorem mutuum fraternum alligat, quem specialiter fideles fidelibus debeant. Rege- neratio nostra ex Deo est causa dilectionis Dei Pa- tris. Quod autem proximus noster pariter ex Deo regenitus sit, causa est, quod ipse frater noster spiritualis sit, ideoque ad fraternam erga ipsum dilectionem nos obstringit. Non autem meto- nymia opus est, ut, qui credit Jesum esse Christum, sit, qui credere se ostendit. Cur enim non proprie intelligamus τὸ credere? Annon oportet ex Deo genitum esse, qui credit Jesum esse Christum? De fide præcipue hic sermo est, quam si quis non habeat in corde, quid professio oris erit, nisi hy- pocrisis? Licet autem cum vera fide professio con- juncta sit, ut & rei promissæ spes, & præceptorum Dei observatio, non tamen hæc confundenda sunt, neque reciproce, ubi professio est, ibi fides etiam est. Connexa sunt regeneratio, qua cre- dendi vires donantur, & renovatio, quia bene operandi vires instaurantur: cohærent fides, & observatio præceptorum Dei, vel studium sanctita- tis. Sed num illa idcirco idem sunt? Si hæc omnino idem, cur Apostolus ex regeneratione ac fide deducit, & probat dilectionem Dei, & ex di- lectione Dei dilectionem proximi, quæ dilectio Dei & proximi utique est observatio præcepto- rum Dei. Exposuere quidem illa non pauci de Filio Dei, quorum sensum ita exhibet Cornelius: q. d. Quicunque diligit Deum Patrem, qui genuit, diligit pariter Deum Filium à Patre genitum: at- qui qui diligit Deum Filium, diligit & cæteros Dei filios, quasi illius fratres & membra: ergo, qui di- ligit Deum Patrem, diligit quoque omnes Dei filios ex eo natos. Hi sunt fideles proximi nostri, ergo hi diligendi sunt eadem charitate, qua Deum tam Pa- trem quam Filium diligimus, ita S. Augustinus, Beda, Glossa, Hugo, & alii hic, ac Hilarius lib. VI. de Trinit. Sed simplicior est illa de filiis Dei spi- ritualibus explicatio Didymi, Cajetani, Catharini & Estii. Qui enim diligunt Deum, qui genuit fi- deles, debent pariter eos, qui ab eo geniti sunt, diligere, tum quia Pater eos diligit, tum quia no- biscum conjunctissimi sunt, ut argumentum sum- ptum sit à naturali propensione, quæ cernitur in hominibus, qua tamen sententia recte uti Theo- logos notat Estius: Ut probent in divinis nec dili- gi, nec videri posse Patrem sine Filio, adeoque nec Filium sine Patre. Hinc ait Dominus: Qui me odit, & Patrem meum odit, Joh. XV. & ad Philip- pum: Qui videt me, videt & Patrem meum, Joh. XIV. Quod enim ordinarium est in humanis, id per- petuum est in divinis.

## 5:2
Vers. 2.

By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and keep His commandments.) Interpreters labor much to connect these words with the preceding and following ones. The connection would be easy if a transposition were made, which I would gladly make if I had some ancient book as an author: By this we know that we love God, when we love His children, and keep His commandments. It is made clear that we are lovers of God if we love Christians supremely as sons of God, and do so because God commands it. Regarding the phrase ἐν τούτῳ see above IV. v. 6. Regarding the meaning see above c. III. vers. 10. 18. 24. cap. IV. v. 7. 8. Ἐντολὴ is sometimes said in the singular, as above c. II. v. 3. 4. c. III. v. 22. 24. and sometimes in the plural, as above c. II. 4. c. III, 2. 24. in the same sense: because the same commandment is repeated more often.

It does not appear that much labor is needed here, much less that a …transposition is necessary. And what kind of rashness is this, to invent a transposition in the consensus of all the codices? The Apostle teaches both that the love of the neighbor arises from the love of God and is rightly concluded, as far as our duty is concerned, or that by right we should love even the neighbor as a brother, because we ought to love God as our common spiritual Father: and also to know know that we sincerely love our neighbor in the very act, because we burn with the love of GOD, and out of the love of God we strive to keep his commandments. Although here also the conclusion of the Apostle may be understood, or a repetition or confirmation of the Apostolic inference, that indeed from this and for this reason we know and are certain that we love the children of God, when we love God, so that we observe his commandments out of sincere love for God; because he who loves God the begetter, loves also those born of God as children of God, and thus his brothers. As the Apostle previously taught how to discern true love of GOD from false, and affirmed that he does not love God who does not love his brother: so now he also discerns true love of neighbor from false, and shows that he does not love his brother who does not love God, and does not keep his commandments, but for the sake of a man dear to him does what conflicts with the word and command of God. Thus they do not love their neighbor who connive at false dogmas which are repugnant to the word of God. Nor do those love their brothers who allow crimes to go unpunished, which by reason of their vocation they ought to punish. Nor do those have love of neighbor who assist others in sinning, and comply with those soliciting them to impurity or injustice. This is not loving one's neighbor, but is loving wickedness. For true love of neighbor ought to be regulated and formed according to the norm of the commandments of God. And we ought to love God above all things, so that we do not violate his commandments for the sake of any man, as Osiander explains this.

Latin:

Vers. 2.

Ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν, ὅτι ἀγαπῶμεν τὰ τέκνα τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὅταν τὸν Θεὸν ἀγαπῶμεν καὶ τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ τηρῶμεν.) Multum la- borant Interpretes, ut hæc verba cum prioribus & sequenti- bus connectant. Facilis sit connexio si trajectio fiat, qua- lem ego libenter facerem, si librum aliquem veterem habe- rem Autorem: Ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν, ὅτι τὸν Θεὸν ἀγαπῶμεν, ὅταν ἀγαπῶμεν τὰ τέκνα αὐτοῦ, καὶ τὰς ἐντολὰς αὐτοῦ τηρῶμεν. Dei nos amantes esse patefit, si amemus summe Christia- nos ut Dei filios, & id faciamus, quia Deus id præ- cipit. De locutione ἐν τούτῳ vide supra IV. v. 6. De sensu vide supra c. III. vers. 10. 18. 24. cap. IV. v. 7. 8. Ἐντολὴ modo singulari dicitur, ut supra c. II. v. 3. 4. c. III. v. 22. 24. modo plurali, ut supra c. II. 4. c. III, 2. 24. sensu eodem: quia idem præceptum sæpius repetitum est.

Non apparet multo hic labore opus esse, ne- dum necessariam esse trajectionem. Et quæ hæc est temeritas in codicum omnium consensione tra- jectionem fingere? Utrumque docet Apostolus tum ex dilectione Dei oriri, & recte concludi di- lectionem proximi, quoad debitum nostrum, vel quod de jure diligamus etiam proximum ceu fra- trem, quia diligere debemus Deum ceu Patrem nostrum communem spiritualem: tum cogno- scere nos, quod actu ipso sincere nos diligamus proximum, quia amore DEI flagramus, & ex amore Dei præcepta ejus servare annitimur. Quanquam etiam hic conclusio Apostoli sigi possit, vel repetitio aut confirmatio illationis A- postolicæ, quod nempe inde & ideo cognosca- mus & certi simus, quod filios Dei diligamus, cum Deum diligimus, ut ex sincero Dei amore præcepta ejus observemus; quia qui diligit Deum genitorem, diligit etiam genitos ex Deo ceu fi- lios Dei, adeoque fratres suos.
